1 Introduction The Yellow River Basin (hereon in abbreviated to the YRB) is situated in northern China, linking provinces in the east and west, and serves as a significant economic hub bridging the transition from north to south (Feng et al., 2012 ) ( Fig. 1 ). The National Strategy for Ecological Protection and High-Quality Development of the YRB of China was initiated in 2019. The YRB supports 12 % of the population and contributes to 14 % of the GDP, but represents only 2 % of China's water resources (Chen et al., 2021 ). Despite being the second longest river in China, the Yellow River accounts for less than 7 % of the total water resources provided by the Yangtze River (the longest river) (Zhang et al., 2017 ). Additionally, although the per capita water resource occupancy of the YRB is only 27 % of the national average, its utilization rate reaches 80 %, significantly surpassing the recommended ecological alert level of 40 % (Tian et al., 2020 ). Consequently, conserving water resources has become a stringent requirement for ecological protection and the pursuit of high-quality development within the YRB. Within the framework of China's Dual Circulation Strategy (i.e., domestic and international circulation), economic agglomeration areas are anticipated to redistribute local water resources through virtual water transfer within domestic and international circulation, leading to secondary resource allocation. Therefore, the virtual water transfer at the city level within the YRB is crucial for actively integrating the YRB into China's Dual Circulation Strategy, potentially mitigating water shortages and facilitating the implementation of the YRB National Strategy. Scaling water resource transfers within trade flows of economic agglomeration areas is a crucial measure in securing water resources. Virtual water flow serves as a vital tool for balancing water distribution between water-rich and water-scarce areas (Qu et al., 2018 ; Zhi et al., 2018 ). Water resources transferred implicitly within trade flows are referred to as virtual water (Allan, 1993 ). The concept of virtual water has been extensively utilized to examine water transfers in specific trade flows at global, national and provincial levels. Two primary approaches are employed in studying virtual water transfers: top-down and bottom-up (Zhang et al., 2021 ). The former utilizes single-region input-output (SRIO) models or multi-region input-output (MRIO) models and their derivatives within a resource-environment domain to analyze the large-scale transfer characteristics of trade-induced flows, such as virtual water, embodied carbon and pollutants (Deng et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ). Conversely, the latter approach primarily employs a life-cycle methodology to analyze water consumption throughout the life-cycle of particular industries or commodities, such as agricultural products (An et al., 2021a, 2021b ). Nevertheless, this method is intricate due to extensive data collection and requirements, as well as high costs, making the analysis of virtual water across multiple sectors on a global or national scale challenging (Ding et al., 2020 ; Yin et al., 2021 ). Numerous studies have quantified virtual water transfers on global, national, provincial and even city scales, accompanied by inter-regional flows of goods (Hirwa et al., 2022 ; Nishad and Kumar, 2022 ). Global-scale studies suggest that virtual water imports and exports are increasing in both magnitude and heterogeneity, and that North America, South Asia and Australia are net exporters of virtual water, while North Africa, the Middle East, Mexico, Europe, Japan and South Korea are net importers (Deng et al., 2021 ; Fan et al., 2019 ; Novoa et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, agricultural products contribute to less than 35 % of the global demand for virtual water (Chen and Chen, 2013 ; Wierik et al., 2020 ). Studies at the national scale suggest that virtual water trading effectively mitigates local water scarcities in specific regions by facilitating the transfer of highly water-intensive products from external to the local regions (Zhao et al., 2018 ; Zhi et al., 2018 ). Increased virtual water imports notably reduce water pressure in China, with projections indicating a continued increase in imports from 2015 to 2030. While international trade still increases China’s environmental burden and tends to be unsustainable (Dalin et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). Provincial-level studies indicate a trend of water transfer from water-scarce regions in the north of China to water-abundant regions in the south and from west to east (Cheng et al., 2023; Song et al., 2020 ) and from less developed provinces to more developed regions (Chen et al., 2017 ), facilitated by trade in low-value, high-water intensive products (Liu et al., 2019 ). On the basis of MRIO model, these studies have aimed to expand the regional water cycle from the traditional “natural” pattern to a "natural-social-economic" pattern. At the scale of the YRB, virtual water transfer studies show that the YRB is exporting virtual water to the outside, exacerbating local water scarcity (Cheng et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2021 ). Upstream provinces of the YRB export virtual water primarily through agricultural product trade, exerting significant pressure on local water resources (Wei et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Virtual water transfer and allocation optimization were investigated across eight sectors with agriculture and manufacturing being the largest virtual water outflow sectors (Wang and Ma, 2024; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Previous studies either failed to consider specific contribution of virtual water tri-circulation of the YRB, such as international circulation, on a smaller statistical caliber, or failed to extend the assessment of virtual water transfer to the city level due to incomplete coverage of cities within the provinces along the Yellow River. Unaccounted factors mentioned above could potentially impact the precision of the YRB’s virtual water transfer. Limited information exists regarding the status of virtual water transfer of the YRB at the city level, particularly concerning the spatial heterogeneity of upstream provinces and downstream provinces in internal, external and international virtual water circulation within the YRB. This knowledge gap may hinder the integration of collaborative development within and outside the Yellow River basin under water resource constraints and ensure local water security. Therefore, based on a virtual water tri-circulation model, including internal, external and international virtual water circulation, this study aims to investigate the efficacy of trading mechanisms in mitigating regional water stress within the YRB at the city level. By analyzing the YRB’s virtual water trade internally, externally and internationally, it offers vital insights for optimizing water allocation strategies and fostering cooperative development between upstream and downstream regions amid water resource limitations. Furthermore, these insights lay the groundwork for advancing development of other economic agglomerations amidst the accelerated growth of domestic and international trade.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Methodology 2.1.1 The virtual water tri-circulation model The virtual water tri-circulation model employed here included the input-output relationships among industries within the YRB in terms of internal provinces, external provinces, and international regions as shown in  Table 1 . This analysis facilitated the determination of the corresponding transfer of water resources implied within these economic trade flows, commonly referred to as virtual water. Internal provinces within the YRB comprised nine regions: Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan and Shandong, while external provinces consisted of the remaining 22 regions. The model highlights the relationships between intermediate use, final use, exports and total output horizontally, as well as those between intermediate input, value added and total input vertically among regional industries at the city level. Consequently, it enabled an examination of the characteristics of inter-industry tri-circulation of water resources within the YRB in both directions. This study used value-based input-output tables. The total output of a specific sector is equal to the sum of intermediate use, final use and the export of products within that sector (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Final use comprises five components: rural consumption, urban consumption, government consumption, fixed capital formation and inventory increases. In an economic system considering r  regions and i  economic sectors, the inter-regional input–output table can be express as Eq. (5) :(6) w  i  r   = r  i  r    X  i  r          where r  i  r     denotes the water consumption of sector i  in region r , and the unit is m3 / CNY (Chinese Yuan). The complete water use coefficient (q i  r  s  ) represents the total amount of water resources (i.e., direct and indirect water use) required to increase the final demand per unit of product in each sector in region s  provided by sector i  in region r . Its value denotes the product of the direct water use coefficient and the complete demand coefficient matrix, which takes the matrix form Q = W ( I − A )  − 1     , where Q  and W  represent matrices with 1 row and m × n columns, respectively and the unit is m3 / CNY. The complete water use coefficient of import trade indicates the virtual water intensity of a product manufactured within the import country. Due to the numerous import countries and the small proportion of imports traded in each province within the YRB, this study adopted the "substitution effect" method to determine the virtual water consumption intensity. It assumes that the imported products in each province originate from that province, replacing the virtual water consumption intensity of imported products in each industry with the revised complete water demand coefficient of each province. In international trade, some imported products are re-exported as intermediate inputs, and therefore. Hence, when quantifying the virtual water imports of a product within an industry, it is essential to subtract the amount of water implied in that product. For import trade, the virtual water consumption intensity of each industry was therefore calculated by Q = W ( I − β A )  − 1     , where β  i  r     denotes the proportion of imported products utilized in domestic production and consumption in industry i  in region r . β  i  r   = 1 − e  i  r    i m  i  r   + X  i  r       , β  represents a diagonal matrix with m × n rows and m × n columns, wherein the elements along the main diagonal are represented by β i  . e  i  r     denotes the export volume of industry i  in region r , i m  i  r      indicates the import volume of industry i  in region r , and X  i  r     represents the total output of industry i  in region r . The virtual water tri-circulation model employed here accounts for the virtual water transfer of both intermediate input use and final use. It enables the determination of the virtual volume of water implied in interprovincial and international trade flows by multiplying the complete water use coefficients of each province and those of foreign countries in each industry with the corresponding trade flows (the unit is CNY). Furthermore, we also analyzed internal, external and international virtual water tri-circulation characteristics based on the aggregated virtual water transfer matrices of intermediate and final use across 17 industries within the 31 provinces at the city level. The export share of intermediate use by these 17 industries in 31 provinces, facilitated the subsequent determination of final use. The sum of virtual water transfer of intermediate and final use was then used to obtain the virtual water transfer matrix of the 17 industries in the cities within the YRB. Net virtual water outflow is then determined by subtracting the inflow from the outflow. A positive indicator indicates a net outflow, zero means that the outflow and inflow are equal, while a negative indicator indicates net inflow.  2.3 Data Sources The multi-regional input-output data (2017) at the city level used in this study were obtained from the Carbon Emission Accounts & Datasets (CEADs), covering key cities and their corresponding 42 sectors. This dataset, representing the latest available for China, comprises 1 agricultural sector, 27 industrial sectors, and 14 service sectors. For data analysis convenience, we aggregated the 42 sectors into 17 sectors, namely 1 agricultural, 14 industrial and 2 service sectors (see  Table 2  for detailed sector merging). Water usage data for the agricultural sector in each province was sourced from the China Statistical Yearbook (2018) and China Water Resources Bulletin (2018). Industrial sectors' water consumption was obtained based on the actual total industrial water use in 2017 relative to their total output. As for service sectors, water consumption was determined using the industrial allocation method (Zhang and Anadon, 2014). Given the incomplete nature of the current water use dataset for industrial sectors, the aforementioned indirect method is commonly used (Liu et al., 2019; Zhang and Anadon, 2014 ).   3 Results 3.1 Virtual water tri-circulation The overall results of the three circulations indicate a net outflow volume of 2547.59 Mt (depicted by the last blue bar in  Fig. 2 ). This means that provinces external to the YRB furnish goods for consumption within the YRB, mitigating water resource usage originating from the YRB production and easing the pressure on its water resources. Meanwhile, the net outflow under internal, external and international circulation amounted to 0, −5152.74 Mt (8.40 % of YRB’s virtual water consumption) and 2605.14 Mt (4.25 % of YRB’s virtual water consumption), respectively (depicted by the blue bar in Fig. 2 ). Virtual water transfer (the sum of outflow and inflow, i.e., the purple and green bar in Fig. 2 ) under internal, external and international circulation stood at 36378.01 (excluding self-supply and self-consumption), 80213.47 and 8570.22 Mt, respectively, accounting for 29.06 %, 64.09 % and 6.85 % of the total transfers. These findings indicate that the majority of virtual water within the YRB originates from external provinces of China via external circulation, i.e., domestic trade, partially mitigating the YRB’s water stress, while the export of virtual water to foreign countries through international circulation exacerbates pressure on the YRB’s water resources. Notes: The term "outflow" refers to the virtual water transferred from the cities of the YRB to external regions through trade; "inflow" indicates virtual water flowing into the cities of the YRB through trade; The "Net outflow" value equals the output minus the inflow. A positive net outflow signifies trade-induced virtual water intensifying local water resource pressure, while a negative value suggests the contrary.  3.2 Identification of key provinces and key circulation patterns The virtual water transfer pattern within the YRB shows that the upstream provinces export virtual water both to downstream provinces within the YRB and to developed provinces outside it. Conversely, downstream provinces receive virtual water primarily from the less developed provinces outside the YRB. The upstream regions transfer about 9580.18 Mt of virtual water resources to downstream regions.  Fig. 3 a represents the net outflow of virtual water through internal, external and international circulations of the YRB. The provinces with net virtual water outflows (triangular symbols above the zero mark in Fig. 3 a) include Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, acting as water resource suppliers. Conversely the provinces with net virtual water inflows (triangular symbols below the zero mark in Fig. 3 a) are Shanxi, Henan and Shandong, Sichuan, functioning as water resource receivers. Among the net outflow provinces within the YRB, Gansu, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (depicted on the left side of the bar chart, Fig. 3 a), with the net outflows of 5794.29 Mt, 2839.05 Mt, 1824.66 Mt, respectively, are dominated by internal circulation, with more than 50 % of their net virtual water outflow to the YRB downstream regions (Fig. 3 b, i.e. Shanxi, Henan and Shandong). Conversely, developed provinces such as Guangdong, Beijing, Zhejiang, Hebei serve as the primary export destinations for virtual water external circulation (Fig. 3 b). In contrast, Ningxia and Qinghai, with net outflows of 4549.01 Mt and 568.32 Mt respectively, are dominated by virtual water external circulation, exporting over 50 % of their net outflow to the provinces outside the YRB. This means that these upstream provinces within the YRB export substantial water resources both to the downstream region of the YRB and to external provinces through trade, thus mitigating local water stress in the downstream regions of the YRB. For the net incoming provinces in the YRB (Fig. 3 a), Shanxi, Henan, Shandong and Sichuan, exhibit net inflow of virtual water, with Shandong (6192.48 Mt), Henan (6007.75 Mt), Shanxi (5837.15 Mt), and Sichuan (85.54 Mt) ranking in descending order. Henan predominantly acquires virtual water from upstream regions of the YRB, such as Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, primarily through internal trade within the YRB (Fig. 3 c). Conversely, Shandong and Shanxi procure water resources from less developed provinces outside the YRB, including Xinjiang, Jilin, Anhui and Yunnan primarily through domestic trade (Fig. 3 c). These downstream provinces within the YRB obtain water resources from provinces within or outside the YRB through trade, mitigating local water consumption of the water-intensive commodity, and alleviating pressure on regional water resources. Unlike other upstream provinces with net virtual water outflows, Sichuan, as an upstream province, receives 85.54Mt water resources. Within the international circulation (Fig. 3 a), all provinces within the YRB show a net outflow of virtual water, signifying the exportation of virtual water resources from the YRB to developed economies such as EU27, US and Japan, UK and others, through the export of agricultural products. To some extent, the international circulation of virtual water in the YRB exacerbates water tensions in the YRB.  3.3 Identification of key sectors The main sectors of virtual water transfers differ between the YRB upstream and downstream regions. In the upstream regions, the tri-circulation exports about 14576.86 Mt of virtual water, with the descending order of magnitude: internal circulation > external circulation > international circulation (refer to blue rectangle in  Fig. 4 a). Among the 17 sectors, agriculture (st01) is the key net exporting sector, with a significantly higher export volume compared to other sectors (Fig. 4 a). All three circulations of agricultural virtual water in the YRB upstream region exhibit a net outflow totaling 20242.66 Mt, prioritized as follows: internal circulation (49.67 %) > external circulation (48.46 %) > international circulation (1.87 %) (refer to the red rectangle in Fig. 4 a). The water embedded in agricultural trade in the YRB upstream provinces is predominantly exported to the provinces within the YRB (refer to the red rectangle in Fig. 4 a), while other service industries(st17) and construction industry(st15) from the provinces outside the YRB are the main recipients of virtual water within the YRB upstream provinces. This trend may be attributed to the underdeveloped nature of the YRB upstream provinces, characterized by a high proportion of agriculture and placement at the lower end of the domestic industrial chain. The tri-circulation of the downstream provinces receives about 17939.56 Mt of virtual water, with the internal circulation as the largest recipient, followed by the external circulation, the international circulation exporting virtual water (refer to the blue rectangle in Fig. 4 b). The net inflow of virtual water trade in the YRB downstream provinces primarily involves food manufacturing and tobacco processing industry (st03), other service industries (st17), agriculture (st01), and others (refer to the red rectangle in Fig. 4 b) from the provinces outside the YRB, accounting for about 57.97 % of the net inflow of the YRB downstream provinces. it is noteworthy that agriculture (st03) and food processing industries (st01) from the YRB upstream provinces contribute to about 86.97 % of the net inflow in these sectors in the YRB downstream provinces. In summary, although the YRB alleviates the pressure on water resources by receiving virtual water from external provinces, the actual reduction in pressure occurs in the downstream provinces. These provinces receive agri-food products (e.g., st01, st03, etc.) from the upstream provinces and sectors at the back-end of the supply chain (e.g., st17, st15, etc.) from the provinces outside the YRB. However, it is the upstream provinces that exacerbate water stress, primarily through the export of water-intensive agricultural products to the downstream provinces, external provinces and foreign countries. Overall, international circulation of virtual water in the YBR exacerbates water stress in both upstream and downstream provinces through the export of water-intensive products.   4 Discussion 4.1 Impact of virtual water transfers on water allocation In our study, the Yellow River Basin receives virtual water at the city level, which is consistent with the net inflow of Wang and Ma (2024) , and the amount of net inflow of YRB virtual water was close to the value of Wang and Ma(2024) . In addition, Cheng et al.(2023)  also believe that the upper reaches export virtual water and the lower reaches import virtual water, which is consistent with our conclusions. However, differences in methodology, data, year and whether or not international circulation is included in the literature lead to inconsistent results (see  Table 3 ). Most YRB virtual water transfer studies are at the provincial level (Zhang et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2021 ), with few at the city level. We have taken the research to the city level, examined the YRB virtual water transfers in 17 sectors and considered virtual water tri-circulation including international trade. Therefore, this makes our YRB virtual water transfer results more accurate. The magnitude of virtual water transfers between the YRB upstream and downstream region is significant, and its impact on water resource allocation cannot be ignored (Wang and Ma, 2024 ). The upstream regions transfer about 9580.18 Mt of water resources to downstream regions, accounting for about 15.63 % of the YRB water consumption in 2017. To promote efficiency and equity in the YRB water resources, ecological compensation is essential for these provinces in many ways (Feng et al., 2021 ). Such compensations can be achieved by fund transfer between upstream and downstream regions, or by incorporating the adjustment of the Yellow River Water Diversion Project, considering virtual water transfers between the YRB upstream and downstream regions (An et al., 2021a, 2021b ). For example, an additional 15.63 % of the water resources should be allocated to the upstream regions that export substantial water resources for trade, to address the significant changes in water resources availability and the imbalance between supply and demand in the YRB. Similarly, when allocating water resources to the provinces within the YRB through inter-basin water transfers (e.g., the South-to-North Water Diversion Project), virtual water transfers between the YRB and the provinces along the Yangtze River must also be taken into account to foster equity and efficiency in regional water resource allocation. Agriculture, due to its large-scale trade and high-water consumption, emerges as a key sector for the virtual water transfers in the YRB (Wei et al., 2023 ). The annual net agricultural export from the YRB upstream regions (e.g., Qinghai, Sichuan, Ningxia, Gansu, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi) to the downstream regions (e.g., Shanxi, Henan and Shandong) was estimated at about 106419.07 million CNY, constituting approximately 49.79 % of the agricultural export from the upstream regions. Agriculture is notably water-intensive, consuming about six times more water per unit of output than the average for other sectors. When these water-intensive agricultural products are imported through trade from the upstream regions into the downstream regions to meet local food consumption, the downstream region also saves the water resources needed to produce these agricultural products. According to publicly available national statistics, the net transfer of water resources from the upstream regions to the downstream regions due to this trade in agricultural products could reach 26126.73 Mt, representing around 45.81 % of the water exported from the upstream regions in 2017. Hence, the significance of water resource transfer through trade in the YRB agricultural products cannot be ignored, making this sector a focal point for industrial and trade structure adjustments in the YRB amidst water resource constraint. Significant differences in water use efficiency exist between upstream and downstream regions within the YRB, with the upstream regions exhibiting inefficiency in water utilization and a net outflow of virtual water, thereby amplifying basin-wide water consumption. Water consumption per unit of output value in the upstream region surpasses that in the downstream region by 3.35 times, particularly evident in high water-consuming sectors like agriculture, where the disparity reaches 4.08 times. According to available public data, if the downstream region were to domestically produce agricultural products rather than importing them from the upstream region, the total basin consumption will would decrease by 71.35 % to 5684.58 Mt. This underscores how this trade exacerbates water resources usage. However, aligning the upstream area's water consumption per unit of output value with the downstream area’s average level could result in a saving of 83.75 Mt agricultural water consumption, constituting a 53.25 % reduction in actual water resource usage for the entire YRB. To prioritize efficiency and equity, water resource allocation in the Yellow River tends to favor the upstream region, but it's imperative for the upstream region to enhance its technological prowess to bolster water resource efficiency. The eastern part of China, marked by higher economic development and denser population, foresees a shift of primary industries to the central and western regions. The industrial transfer necessitates simultaneous transfer to avert declines in resource efficiency and consequent rises in resource and environmental pressures.  4.2 Limitations and future research Despite the findings, several limitations should be noted. Firstly, the data utilized were based on the MRIO in 2017. Currently, China's multi-regional input-output data are compiled every five years, with updates occurring in years ending in a 2 or 7. While the 2017 is the most recent available, analysis using a more current dataset is necessary. Additionally, employing extended input-output tables, compiled in years ending in a 0 or 5, could enhance the result. Secondly, given that urban agglomeration serves as hubs of production and exchange, they generate numerous virtual water flows. The development of the regional economies depends, to some extent, on a few key cities within it. Therefore, optimizing industrial structure within economic agglomerations, particularly under water constraints, is also closely tied to these key cities. Understanding the transfer process and mechanism of virtual water among key cities within the economic agglomeration is vital. Consequently, including these key cities in multi-regional input-output models is imperative for optimizing water allocation and facilitating targeted industrial restructuring. Thirdly, virtual water tri-circulation models should encompass both intermediate use and final demand components. In constructing the water transfer matrix of regional inter-industries, this paper determined the virtual water of final demands of sectors within each province based on the proportion of intermediate use in each sector. However, gaining a comprehensive understanding of total virtual water demands among sectors would be advantageous.  4.3 Policy implications (1) Increase water allocation to upstream areas to secure water for agriculture and ecology Given the YRB's limited water resources (Wei et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ), it's imperative to allocate them rationally (Wang and Ma, 2024 ). The YRB upstream regions serve as the principal source area for the river, yielding the highest surface runoff within the YRB. This region holds a crucial position in the basin’s water resources, food production and ecological balance. The upstream regions are characterized by sparse precipitation, heavily rely on the river as the primary water source for the majority of residents and agricultural land situated alongside. In the inter-provincial virtual water trade within the YRB, these upstream regions primarily export water resources to downstream region via extensive trade of agricultural products with high water intensity, exacerbating strain on local water resources. With agriculture accounting for over 70 % of the basin's water usage, opportunities for ecological water use are severely constrained. Furthermore, there exists a stark mismatch between water usage for production and ecological purposes. Hence, it is imperative to bolster water resources in upstream regions when distributing water resources across the provinces along the Yellow River. Consequently, in allocating water resources among the provinces along the Yellow River, prioritizing an increase in upstream water allocation is essential. Simultaneously, this effort must ensure adequate water usage for agriculture and ecology to sustainably develop agriculture and ecological infrastructure in the region. (2) Promoting a balance between the upstream and the downstream technology interaction and resource delivery Due to the YRB’s limited water resources, optimizing industrial and trade structures become imperative (Delpasand et al., 2023 ; Wang and Ma, 2024 ). This necessitates controlling the proportion of high-water-consuming industries and enhancing their technical level to reduce water intensity (Huang et al., 2023 ). Critical measures include adjusting the agricultural structure, fostering water-efficient agriculture, and improving the efficiency of agricultural water use. Despite a relatively high proportion of arable land in the upstream regions, agricultural water resources remain constrained, with suboptimal water utilization efficiency exacerbating the challenge of aligning arable areas with water provision. The YRB grapples with severe water scarcity, precipitating ecological and environmental concerns attributed to escalating regional irrigation water use. Urgent action is thus warranted to develop water-suitable, high-efficiency agriculture and advance core technology for efficient agricultural water resource utilization. Strengthening upstream-downstream technological collaboration is paramount (Si et al., 2019 ), necessitating robust adoption of water-saving agriculture and water-saving irrigation technologies, to rebalance supply between upstream and downstream regions, thereby alleviating the YRB's water shortage and fostering sustainable agricultural development. (3) Development of ecological compensation strategies The YRB implements planned water use and paid water use, adjusting water allocation schemes and water prices to enhance resource efficiency by integrating government control and market mechanisms (Feng et al., 2021 ), for example, Ningxia started in 2017, Henan and Shandong implemented in 2021. Market mechanism is explored for allocating the remaining water rights, and facilitating water transfer to agriculturally efficient areas. Utilizing water rights trading to replenish reserves, the study assesses agricultural water use options and conservation potentials, aiming to enhance water resource efficiency and conservation across the Yellow River basin (An et al., 2021a, 2021b ).   5 Conclusion The main objective of the evaluation of the YRB virtual water transfer in this study was to seek collaborative development strategies between upstream and downstream regions within the YRB under regional water resource constraints. Based on a virtual water tri-circulation, this study analyzed YRB’s virtual water transfer across internal, external and international circulation at the city level, investigating trade heterogeneity between upstream and downstream regions. It also highlighted the key circulation and sectors within the YRB in 2017. The principal conclusions drawn from this analysis are as follows.(1) Adjusting the volume of water resource transfer within the YRB's trade flow is a crucial measure to ensure local water resources security. This study found that virtual water tri-circulation mitigated the YRB’s water scarcity, resulting in a total net inflow equivalent to 8.40 % of its own virtual water consumption in 2017.  (2) The primary virtual water circulation within the YRB was external, characterized by the inflow of virtual water from underdeveloped, water-scarce regions (e.g., Xinjiang, Jilin, Anhui, Heilongjiang) mainly through agricultural trade. Conversely, it exported virtual water to developed regions (e.g., Guangdong, Zhejiang, Jiangsu) through trade in agri-food products and other service industries.  (3) Through virtual water trade, upstream regions have transferred 9580.18 Mt of virtual water to the downstream regions, constituting approximately 15.63 % of the YRB’s virtual water consumption. Notably, high water-intensive agriculture comprises 45.81 % of the water exported from the upstream regions, serving as the primary sector in virtual water trade.  (4) The measures advocated to harmonize the development of the YRB amidst water resource constraints could offer novel insights for policymakers, fostering the sustainable development of the YRB.  (5) The international circulation of virtual water in the Yellow River Basin shows a net outflow of virtual water, which to some extent exacerbates water tensions in the Yellow River Basin.    Overall, the findings of this study indicate that policy decisions should prioritize the key virtual water circulation, as well as key sectors within the economic agglomeration. Industrial restructuring in the context of regional water resource constraints should adopt a comprehensive approach to foster sustainable community development, particularly regarding the potential of virtual water transfers from urban agglomerations. Moreover, the study advances the regional water cycle from the traditional “natural” water cycle to a two-dimension (i.e., real water and virtual water) three-element ("natural-social-economic") water cycle paradigm.
1 Introduction In recent decades, droughts have become increasingly severe and have increased in duration in many regions of the world, which lead to water shortages for ecological, domestic, industrial, and agricultural purposes, and even threaten the quality of arable land, food security, and energy resources (Stagge et al., 2015 ). Based on the processes of their propagation, droughts can be classified into four types: meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic droughts (American Meteorological Society, 1997 ). A hydrological drought refers to the phenomenon whereby the water levels in rivers, lakes, and other water bodies fall below a critical threshold over a certain period (Anne and Van, 2015 ). Hydrological drought is more susceptible to anthropogenic influences than other types of droughts, and has a significant impact on socio-economic development (Wilhite, 2000 ). Researchers in the area have developed various indices to classify drought that are effective for hydrological monitoring and evaluation under stationary conditions. Examples include the standardized runoff index (SRI) (Shukla and Wood, 2008 ), Palmer's hydrological drought index (PHDI) (Palmer, 1965 ), surface water supply index (SWSI) (Shafer and Dezman, 1982 ), and streamflow drought index (Nalbantis and Tsakiris, 2009 ). Vasiliades et al. (2009)  evaluated the effectiveness of the PHDI in monitoring hydrological droughts based on river flow and soil moisture. The PHDI takes into account all components of the surface water balance and has a strong physical basis (Dai, 2011 ). However, the estimation is based on a two-layer bucket water balance model, which has been widely criticized for being too simple to accurately quantify the surface water balance (Sheffield et al., 2004 ). SWSI takes into account runoff, reservoir storage, and snow cover (Doesken et al., 2016 ), and Tareke et al. (2022)  used it for hydrological drought analysis in Ethiopia. However, the current SWSI has two conceptual weaknesses: one is the subjectivity of coefficient assignment, and the other is the statistical characteristics of the fuzzy index, which cannot well reflect the hydrological drought conditions in some areas (Garen, 1993 ). SDI is suitable for basins with significant water storage projects and performs well when dealing with insufficient data, but may have limited application (Nalbantis and Tsakiris, 2009 ). The SRI is widely used to assess hydrological droughts because it does not require a large amount of data, and it can quantify the intensity and duration of the drought (Zargar et al., 2011 ). Therefore, our study used SRI and constructed the non-stationary hydrological drought index based on SRI. These traditional drought indices are based on the assumption of stationarity of runoff data, that is, the statistical features of a data series, including the mean, variance, and covariance, remain constant over time (Villarini et al., 2009 ). For example, the SRI represents the severity of droughts based on the probability distribution of the long-term time series of the runoff, it is suitable for assessing runoff with stable fluctuations. However, traditional drought indices may confuse drought events with water scarcity if the regional hydrological conditions undergo an abrupt change that makes the water level non-stationary (Li et al., 2015 ). For instance, when the runoff exhibits a roughly decreasing (or increasing) trend, the normal level of water availability changes. Thus, drought events identified by the SRI may be concentrated in the later (or earlier) stages of the period of research, and thus likely fail to reflect drought occurring owing to an “abnormal level of water availability”. Nonetheless, the non-stationarity of hydrological conditions has become increasingly common in recent decades under the influence of climate change and human activities. The maximum, minimum, and average values of the runoff at 7250 global stations exhibited complex spatial trends from 1970 to 2010 (Gudmundsson et al., 2021 ), and the non-stationarity of the runoff or sequences of floods have been evident in basins worldwide (Villarini et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2022; Jehanzaib et al., 2020; Chiew et al., 2014 ). Non-stationary changes in hydrological conditions have made drought assessment more challenging (Das et al., 2020 ). Milly et al. (2015)  have argued that the assumption of stationarity is inapplicable to the assessment of water resources in a changing environment. Therefore, a method that can handle non-stationary data is needed for the accurate identification of hydrological droughts. The generalized additive model for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) is a useful tool for drought identification under non-stationary conditions, and some studies have attempted to incorporate the GAMLSS into traditional indices used to assess droughts (Russo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020 ). The GAMLSS allows the parameter of location (or scale and shape) of the fitted distribution to vary with time based on covariates. Russo et al. (2013)  used the GAMLSS to fit the non-stationary probability distribution of extreme precipitation in Europe, and found that it exhibited stronger capabilities than the stationary probability distribution in predicting precipitation. Li et al. (2018)  proposed a time-varying SRI (SRIt) that considered time, and used it to construct a time-varying gamma distribution by using the GAMLSS to fit the observed sequences of the runoff. They also proved that SRIt was more effective than the traditional SRI in identifying hydrological droughts in the Panjiakou Reservoir Basin in a changing environment. Wang et al. (2020)  developed a non-stationary model with covariates, including climate- and human-induced indices, and used it to assess the spatiotemporal patterns of hydrological drought in the Luan River Basin based on the non-stationary standardized streamflow index. Introducing such factors as the time as well as climate- and human-induced changes as covariates to construct non-stationary models can help identify drought in a changing environment. However, the above-mentioned studies did not consider the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of the covariates. In fact, the factors influencing the non-stationarity of the time series of the runoff may differ across regions and seasons. The Yellow River is predominantly located in arid and semi-arid regions of China, and is characterized by low precipitation and a high rate of evaporation. The region nonetheless has a densely concentrated population, large areas of irrigation, high levels of industrial development, and thus a significant demand for water use that has rendered it particularly sensitive to droughts. The Yellow River Basin (YRB) has undergone significant changes in its eco-hydrological processes, including increased vegetation coverage and decreased runoff, due to climate change and human activities, such as ecological restoration, that have increased water consumption in the area (Wang et al., 2016 ). This may enhance the non-stationarity of hydrological conditions in the basin (Zou et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2023 ), such that the assumption of stationarity is no longer applicable for assessing water resources in this changing environment (Milly et al., 2015 ). However, prevalent studies on hydrological droughts in the YRB often overlook the non-stationary characteristics of its runoff, and simply conclude that hydrological droughts have intensified in the region in recent decades (Wang et al., 2023 ). This raises questions about the exacerbation of droughts: does the use of suitable non-stationary methods explain the spatiotemporal patterns of droughts in the area? In light of the above, this study focused on hydrological droughts in the YRB under the effects of climate change and human activities. We first assessed the stationarity of the runoff, identified regions in which it exhibits non-stationary changes, and selected the factors driving the non-stationarity of the runoff, including the climate, vegetation, and water use. By using the selected factors as covariates, we then constructed non-stationary models for each sub-basin of the YRB and analyzed the spatiotemporal patterns of hydrological droughts in them based on non-stationary indices. Our analysis contributes to a better understanding of hydrological droughts in the YRB under non-stationary conditions, and provides a fresh perspective on drought assessment in changing environments.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Yellow River is 5464 km long, and is the second-largest river in China. The YRB spans from 96° E to 119° E longitude, and from 32° N to 42° N latitude, covering an area of approximately 795,000 km2  and accounting for 8 % of China's territory. Annual precipitation in the YRB ranges from 100 to 1000 mm, and decreases from southeast to northwest. There are significant inter- and intra-annual variations in precipitation, especially in regions with low annual precipitation. The average potential evapotranspiration of the YRB ranges from 700 to 1200 mm/yr, while the average natural streamflow in the entire basin is 58 billion m3 /yr.  Fig. 1  shows that it can be divided into seven secondary sub-basins (R1–R7) and one area of inflow (the blank region) based on its geological conditions and hydrological characteristics (http://www.geodata.cn ) (Huang et al., 2015 ). We focus here on its seven secondary sub-basins, and provide the details of each in  Table 1 .  2.2 Data sources and processing The data series used in this study spanned from 1986 to 2015, and can be categorized into four types: data on the runoff, meteorology, vegetation, and water use by humans. Data on the monthly runoff at seven hydrological stations along the Yellow River were collected from the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (http://www.yrcc.gov.cn ). The runoff of each sub-basin was calculated by the difference between the runoff at its outlet station and that at the corresponding inlet station. Data on the precipitation, temperature, specific humidity, and downward shortwave radiation used as covariates were obtained from the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD) (He et al., 2020 ). We then preprocessed these data and obtained the monthly average meteorological data for each sub-basin of the Yellow River Basin. The data, including daily records of precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures, wind speed, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sunshine duration, needed for the FAO Penman Monteith method to calculate potential evapotranspiration came from the China Meteorological Data Service Center (https://data.cma.cn ) (Wang et al., 2022 ). The status of the vegetation was represented by using the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), which was obtained from the ECOCAST website (https://ecocast.arc.nasa.gov/data/pub/gimms ) at a spatial resolution of 0.083° and a temporal resolution of 15 days. These data were acquired by the Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) on a satellite operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and were updated to the 3 g.v1 version by the Global Inventory Modeling and Mapping Studies (GIMMS) (Pinzon and Tucker, 2014 ). A dataset of the monthly NDVI was subsequently derived by using the mean synthesis method. Data on water use by humans (including agricultural, industrial, and domestic water use), and the storage capacities of large-and-medium-sized reservoirs in each sub-basin were obtained from the Yellow River Water Resources Bulletin (http://www.yrcc.gov.cn/ ) and past studies (Jiongxin, 2005; Kong et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2013; 2015; Ran et al., 2013 ).  2.3 Test of stationarity of runoff We used the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test to check the stationarity of the runoff. The ADF test is an augmented version of the Dickey–Fuller test that is designed to handle more complex sequential models, and has been widely used for testing the stationarity of time series (Dickey and Fuller, 1979 ). The null hypothesis (H  0    ) of the ADF test posits that the time series has a unit root, indicating non-stationarity, that is, the mean and variance of the runoff time series change over time. By contrast, the alternative hypothesis (H  1    ) suggests that the time series does not have a unit root, and is thus stationary. A model of regression of the unit root can be expressed as follows:(1) Δ y  t   = α + β t + γ y  t − 1   + σ  1   Δ y  t − 1   + σ  2   Δ y  t − 2   + … + σ  p − 1   Δ y  t – p – 1      + ϵ  t       where β   is the coefficient of the temporal trend and ϵ  t     is the error term. The statistical value of the ADF test can be represented as:(2) ADF = γ  S    SE γ  S             where γ  S     is the estimated value of γ   in the model of regression and SE is the standard error. We can test the stationarity of the time series by comparing the statistical value of the ADF test with a critical value: If the ADF test statistic is greater than the critical value, the hypothesis of the existence of a unit root cannot be rejected, indicating that the time series is non-stationary.  2.4 Construction of non-stationary model 2.4.1 Selection of covariates We first chose appropriate covariates for the non-stationary model of hydrological droughts. A covariate here represents the factors driving the non-stationarity of the runoff. These factors are of two types: 1) meteorological factors, such as the precipitation, radiation, temperature, and specific humidity; and 2) human activities, such as ecological restoration (normalized difference vegetation index), and the use and storage of water in reservoirs (Kong et al., 2016 ). We thus chose a total of six factors—the downward shortwave radiation, precipitation, temperature, specific humidity, vegetation, and water consumption by humans (the sum of the water used and changes in the water stored in reservoirs)—as alternatives of the factors driving the non-stationarity of the runoff. We used the Spearman rank correlation coefficient to examine the correlation between the runoff and the six covariates based on monthly data. Spearman's correlation coefficient is a non-parametric measure of rank correlation that assesses the strength of monotonic relationships between variables (Myers and Sirois, 2006 ):(3) ρ = 1 − 6 ∑ d  i  2     n ( n  2  − 1  )        where d  i     is the difference in ranks and n   is the sample size. According to the calculated correlation coefficients (Table S1), we added five of the above covariates that passed the test of significance (p < 0.01   ) to the non-stationary model: namely, the NDVI, specific humidity, precipitation, temperature, and water consumption by humans.  2.4.2 Standardized runoff index based on non-stationary model (SRI_cov) We established a non-stationary standardized runoff index based on the gamma distribution function containing the covariates (SRI_cov). The SRI, which was proposed by Shukla and Wood in 2008 (Shukla and Wood, 2008 ), is a standardized method used to assess hydrological droughts based on the runoff. It calculates the standard index of the runoff in a certain period by fitting the function of the optimal distribution of its sequence, and then converts the probability distribution of the function into a standard normal distribution. SRI_cov is consistent with the SRI, but uses covariates to construct parametric equations for the location (or scale and shape) of the distribution function. That is, the parameters of the distribution function are variable, and are dependent on the covariates. The specific steps are as follows: We first calculated the i  th accumulated runoff of the series of runoffs R  s   i       over the study period at a specific time scale s   by using the following formula:(4) R  s   i    = ∑ i = i + 1 − s  i   R i           Considering the capacity of the ecosystem to maintain stability, the scarcity of water needs to persist for a certain duration to cause a drought and have a substantial impact on eco-hydrological processes of the watershed. We set the time scale s   to a three-month accumulated runoff to capture the time lag between temporary water shortage and a hydrological drought (Shukla and Wood, 2008; Vicente-Serrano and López-Moreno, 2005 ). We then used a two-parameter gamma distribution to estimate the probability distribution function of the runoff series R  s      (Bhunya et al. 2007 ):(5) f x  |  α , β    = x  α − 1   β  α   e  − β x    Γ α           where x = R  s   i      , and α   and β   are the parameters of the shape and scale of the gamma distribution, respectively. The accumulative runoff is assumed to be in a state of R  s   p    ∼ Gamma α t    , β t          under non-stationary conditions. That is to say, the parameters of shape and scale change over time, and can be expressed as:(6) α t    = a  0   + ∑ i  n   a  i   c  i   t          (7) β t    = b  0   + ∑ i  n   b  i   c  i   t          where a  0     and b  0     represent constants, c  i     represents the i  th covariate, and t  represents time. We used the GAMLSS to fit the non-stationary gamma distribution. This model combines the generalized additive model with the generalized linear model to describe the linear or non-linear relationships between the response variables with arbitrary parameters and the explanatory variables (Stasinopoulos and Rigby, 2008 ; Rigby and Stasinopoulos, 2005 ; Fischler and Bolles, 1981 ). We subsequently transformed the cumulative probability distribution function (Eq. (8) ) into a standard normal distribution function to calculate SRI_cov (Eq. (9) ):(8) F R  s   i       = ∫ 0  x   f R  s   i       d x       (9) SRI_ cov = − ω + c  0   + c  1   ω + c  2   ω  2    1 + d  1   ω + d  2   ω  2   + d  2   ω  3     , ω = ln 1  F R  s   p       2          , 0 ≤ F R  s   i       ≤ 0.5   ω − c  0   + c  1   ω + c  2   ω  2    1 + d  1   ω + d  2   ω  2   + d  2   ω  3     , ω = ln 1  1 − F R  s   p          2          , 0.5 < F R  s   i       ≤ 1            where c  0   = 2.515517   , c  1   = 0.802853   , c  2   = 0.010328   , d  1   = 1.432788   , d  2   = 0.189269   , and d  3   = 0.001308    (Shukla and Wood, 2008 )。  2.4.3 Selection of optimal model We chose five factors—precipitation (P), specific humidity (H), temperature (T), NDVI (N), and water consumption by humans (M)—as covariates in the non-stationary model. We then identified the optimal combination of these covariates to determine the most suitable non-stationary model for simulating the runoff based on the gamma distribution. According to the number of covariates, we built six models (M0–M5) to simulate the runoff. M0 represents the inclusion of the zero covariate in the gamma distribution to form a stationary model with constant parameters. M1 to M5 are non-stationary models that include one, two, three, four, and five covariates, respectively. By considering all possible combinations of the five covariates, we generated a total of 32 models ( Fig. 2 ). We selected the optimal model based on the value of the Akaike information criterion (AIC). Proposed by the Japanese statistician Hirotsugu Akaike, the AIC is used to measure the goodness of fit of statistical models (Akaike, 1974 ). It is generally expressed as:(10) AIC = − 2 ln L  + 2 k     where k   represents the number of parameters in the statistical model and L   denotes the maximum likelihood of the likelihood function. A smaller value of the AIC indicates a better fit for the model. In addition, we also calculated NSE, R2 , and RMSE estimators to assist in the selection of optimal model (Fig. S1). The closer the NSE and R2 are to 1, the better the model performance is, and the smaller the RMSE is, the better the model performance is.   2.5 Drought identification based on non-stationary model We used the selected non-stationary models to calculate the SRI_cov for each basin to identify hydrological droughts.  Table 2  shows that when SRI_cov was greater than −0.5, the relevant area was considered to not have a drought; as the index decreased, the corresponding areas were identified as having mild, moderate, severe, and extreme droughts in sequence (Guttman, 1999 ). We then assessed the severity, intensity, and duration of each drought event based on run theory (Herbst et al., 1966 ). By using −0.5 as the baseline, instances in which SRI_cov was smaller than −0.5 were designated as negative runs, while those in which it was equal to or greater than −0.5 were classified as positive runs. Continuous negative runs were identified as drought events, with their severity, intensity, and duration represented by the area, extreme value, and length of the negative runs, respectively.   3 Results 3.1 Non-stationarity of runoff The series of runoff in the YRB exhibited non-stationary characteristics during 1986–2015. The results of the ADF test differed over regions and time scales ( Fig. 3 ). On annual scale, the null hypothesis of non-stationarity of the YRB (R) and all seven sub-basins could not be refuted. On seasonal scale, the significance level of all seasons in the seven sub-basins (R1-R7) and YRB (R) exceeded 0.05, except for the two seasons of R4. On monthly scale, the null hypothesis of non-stationarity of the YRB (R) could not be refuted in all months, and was at the level of significance of 0.05 in most months (89.3 %) in the seven sub-basins (R1–R7).  3.2 Performance of non-stationary model in runoff simulation It is evident from a comparison of values of the AIC of the 32 models presented in Fig. 2  that the non-stationary models (M1–M5) consistently outperformed the stationary model (M0) in terms of simulating the runoff in the YRB (Fig. S2). We identified the optimal non-stationary model by using various combinations of covariates for each region and each month, and using the minimum value of the AIC (Table S2). Similarly, we select covariates to construct non-stationary models on the seasonal scale (Table S3). The results showed that the AIC values of the non-stationary models in each basin and season were about 6 % lower than those of the stationary models.  Fig. 4 a shows that the most substantial improvement in the performance of the optimal non-stationary model was observed in the middle (R5) and lower (R7) reaches of the YRB, while the entire basin (R) underwent relatively minor changes. The effects of fitting of the results for sub-basins R1–R4 significantly improved compared with those of the baseline model from March to September, but this improvement was less pronounced in the winter. We also compared the quantiles and residuals of the optimal non-stationary model with those of the stationary model. Considering R7 as an example, our observations revealed that the quantiles in the non-stationary model had a superior fitting effect on the measured runoff series (Fig. 4 b–c). Moreover, the residuals of the non-stationary model were smaller and more evenly distributed within the confidence interval, especially in case of extreme values, thus demonstrating a more effective fit (Fig. 4 d–e). The calculation results showed that the optimal non-stationary model had better performance. We counted the proportion of covariates included in the optimal model by month and sub-basin ( Fig. 5 ). The main causes of hydrological drought were different in different months and regions, so the choice of covariates was different. For different months (Fig. 5 a), we found that the temperature covariate accounted for the highest proportion of the five covariates in January and February. The NDVI covariate accounted for the highest proportion from July to November. The water consumption by human covariate accounted for the highest proportion in December, January, and May. For different sub-basins (Fig. 5 b), we found that the differences in the proportions of the five covariates were relatively small in the R1-R3 sub-basins in the upper reaches of the Yellow River. However, the proportion of the NDVI covariate was significantly as high as 40 % in the R4 and R5 sub-basins in the middle reaches of the Yellow River. The proportion of water consumption by humans covariate was the highest among the five covariates in the R6 and R7 sub-basins.  3.3 Comparison of accuracy of drought prediction between stationary and non-stationary indices The characteristics of drought derived from SRI_cov differed from those based on the SRI (Fig. S3). To assess their accuracy, we compared their predictions for several drought events with the actual drought conditions recorded in the literature, which are based on government statistics and are a good representation of local conditions. For instance, the SRI of sub-basin R1 of the upper reaches of the YRB ( Fig. 6 a) indicated an extreme drought event spanning seven months from October 2002 to April 2003. However, the China Meteorological Yearbook 2004 indicates that although a drought occurred in the upper reaches of the YRB in the autumn of 2002 and the spring–summer of 2003, its intensity and duration were not adequate for it to qualify as an uninterrupted seven-month extreme drought. The actual drought conditions aligned more closely with the results obtained from SRI_cov. SRI_cov accurately identified the occurrence and severity of the spring drought in sub-basin R5 of the middle reaches of the Yellow River (Fig. 6 b) in April 1989, which has also been recorded in Chinese Agricultural Statistics, while the SRI failed to identify it. The SRI predicted a mild-to-moderate drought from May to November in 2004, but the China Meteorological Yearbook 2005 shows no evidence of such a drought during this time. SRI_cov accurately identified two drought events in sub-basin R7 of the lower reaches of the Yellow River (Fig. 6 c) in March 2013 and August 2014, as has been recorded by literature (Duan et al., 2014 ) and the Yellow River Yearbook (2015), respectively, while the SRI failed to reflection these events. A drought occurred in the entire YRB (Fig. 6 d) in 1986 (Qu, 1987 ). SRI_cov successfully identified three moderate and two mild drought events in this period, while the SRI failed to identify any of them. Moreover, a widespread drought occurred in the YRB from the winter of 2008 to the spring of 2009 (Wei and Ouyang, 2011 ), but the SRI failed to identify any drought event while SRI_cov once again accurately identified them. There were still many differences in the characteristics of droughts predicted by the SRI and SRI_cov. We have provided only a few examples here owing to limited available statistical data. However, our comparisons above clearly show that the proposed SRI_cov was more sensitive and accurate than the SRI. It not only accurately identified drought events that the SRI had failed to detect, but also accurately reflected the severity of the drought conditions.  3.4 Spatiotemporal patterns of hydrological droughts based on non-stationary model 3.4.1 Seasonal variations We used the optimal non-stationary models which were constructed at monthly scale to calculate the series of values of SRI_cov and identify the months and seasons in which drought occurred in the study area. Hydrological droughts predominantly occurred in the YRB in spring (26.6 %), followed by summer and autumn, and the lowest frequency of droughts was observed in winter. However, the variations among these seasons were minimal over the entire basin (R), with certain variations among the sub-basins ( Fig. 7 a). For example, drought primarily occurred in winter in sub-basin R2 (Fig. 7 a and Fig. S4). Fig. 7 b illustrates that mild drought mostly occurred in the summer, moderate drought in spring, severe drought in winter, and extreme drought primarily in autumn across the entire YRB. Nevertheless, the seasons in which different types of droughts predominantly occurred in different sub-basins differed (Fig. 7 c). Considering sub-basin R2 as an example, mild droughts in this sub-basin occurred more frequently in the spring, moderate droughts occurred primarily in the winter, and severe droughts were observed mainly in the summer. We also constructed non-stationary models at seasonal scale. The drought assessment results of the non-stationary model constructed based on the seasonal scale are shown in Fig. S4, which is similar to the monthly scale assessment results. For example, the frequency of extreme drought in the R1 and R basins was significantly lower than that in other sub-basins, while the extreme drought in the R3 sub-basin was the most severe. Moderate drought mostly occurred in spring, and extreme drought primarily in autumn across the entire YRB. However, there were some differences in the drought assessment results of the two-scale models. For example, the results at the monthly scale showed that mild drought in the entire Yellow River Basin mainly occurred in summer, and extreme drought mainly occurred in autumn (Fig. 7 ), while the seasonal-scale model showed that mild drought mainly occurred in autumn, and no extreme drought occurs (Fig. S4).  3.4.2 Interannual variations The number of months in which droughts occurred in the YRB from 1986 to 2002 exhibited a general trend of increase. After reaching its peak in 2002, the total number of droughts significantly decreased. However, extreme droughts began to occur in 2005 ( Fig. 8 h). The interannual variations in droughts in the sub-basins exhibited spatial heterogeneity. The number of months with droughts in sub-basins R1, R2, R5, and R6 peaked around 2000, while they continued to increase during 1986–2015 in sub-basins R3 and R4. After 2000, extreme droughts became more prominent. By contrast, the number of months in which droughts occurred showed a trend of decrease overall in sub-basin R7, while numerous extreme droughts occurred in this sub-basin in 1988 (six months) and 1989 (eight months). Sub-basin R4 had the lowest overall frequency of droughts, below 20 %; while sub-basin R1 had the highest frequency of 35.28 %.  3.4.3 Spatial pattern In terms of the number, duration, intensity, and severity of drought events, the middle reaches of the YRB underwent the most severe drought, followed by its upper reaches, with the lower reaches being the least affected. However, the spatial pattern of the duration of the droughts exhibited the opposite trend to that of their frequency, indicating that sub-basins with higher frequencies of droughts tended to have ones with shorter durations.  Fig. 9 a shows that from 1986 to 2015, sub-basin R5 was subjected to the highest number of drought events, 60, but the average duration of droughts was the shortest, with each lasting 2.6 months (Fig. 9 b). Conversely, sub-basin R7 had the lowest frequency of droughts, 42, but the longest average duration of droughts of 4.3 months. The spatial distributions of the average intensity and severity of droughts were similar. For instance, sub-basin R4 exhibited the most severe average intensity and severity of droughts, with values of −1.86 and 1.13, respectively. By contrast, sub-basin R7 had the mildest and least severe droughts, with values of only −1.39 and 0.5, respectively.    4 Discussion 4.1 Explanations for the spatiotemporal patterns variations of drought Hydrological droughts in the YRB showed a general increasing trend from 1986 and peaked around 2002. After that, the total number of droughts significantly decreased but the extreme droughts had become more prominent since 2005. These changes were consistent with the trend of meteorological drought. The YRB experienced the most severe meteorological drought around 2002 (Wang et al., 2022 ), and reduced precipitation in the YRB caused meteorological drought to transition into hydrological drought (Li et al., 2024 ), so the number of months with drought in the YRB from 1986 to 2002 showed an overall increasing trend, reaching a peak in 2002 (Fig. 8 ). We also compared the descriptions of the interannual trends of hydrological drought in the YRB in other researches during the same period. Based on our results, the total number of droughts significantly decreased after entering the 21st century, but the extreme droughts began to occur. But some research generally pointed out that drought were getting worse in the YRB (Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024 ), which ignored the details of hydrological drought to a certain extent. We provided a more complete picture from the perspectives of the number and the severity of droughts. Of course, there were also some researches pointed that the hydrological drought in the YRB had intensified since the 21st century, which was mainly due to the strengthening of water resources management and climate (Cong et al., 2009 ). Seasonally, hydrological drought was more frequently in spring. And among the seven sub-basins, drought was severer in the middle reaches of the Yellow River and was characterized by a high frequency, intensity, and severity. Spring is the season for planting wheat, and wheat requires a lot of water during its growing period. However, the YRB is mostly located in the monsoon climate zone, with distinct dry and wet seasons and little precipitation in spring (Wang et al., 2018 ), so hydrological droughts predominantly occurred in spring in the YRB (Fig. 7 ). Sub-basins with higher frequencies of droughts tended to have ones with shorter durations (Fig. 9 ). Here are some possible reasons. Firstly, once a long-lasting drought occurs, it is more difficult to recover than a short-lasting drought. Therefore, within a 30-year period, long-lasting droughts will not occur too many times. Secondly, the R5 sub-basin is located in the Loess Plateau. Loess is not conducive to water storage and is prone to water and soil loss, so the Loess Plateau is susceptible to drought (Li et al., 2024 ), and the intensity, and severity of drought events were the highest in the middle reaches of the Yellow River (Fig. 9 ). However, there are many heavy rains in summer (Liu et al., 2016 ), and a rain can solve the drought problem. Therefore, the drought in the R5 sub-basin is short. The R7 sub-basin is greatly affected by humans, and the water consumption for production and life is long-term, which is easy to cause some long-term droughts (Piao et al., 2010 ).  4.2 Impacts of climate change and human activities on the non-stationarity of runoff Climate change and human activities are the primary drivers of the non-stationarity of the series of runoffs in the Yellow River Basin, as has been substantiated by previous research (Kong et al., 2016 ). We used the precipitation, temperature, specific humidity, NDVI, and water consumption by humans as covariates of the non-stationary model in simulations of the runoff. Our results underscore the effectiveness of these covariates in ensuring the performance of the model (Fig. 4 ). Importantly, the impact of each covariate on the non-stationarity of the runoff varied across months and regions (Fig. 5 ). For example, the influence of the temperature on the runoff was significant in January and February. During these periods, runoff in the Yellow River occurred primarily due to the melting of glaciers and snow in the source region, and the volume of meltwater was predominantly influenced by the temperature (Li et al., 2021 ). Vegetation, as represented by the NDVI, had a significant impact during the summer and autumn, periods that align with the growing seasons when the demand for water is high (Mankin et al., 2019 ). Water consumption by humans, including for such activities as irrigation, reservoir regulation, and storage, invariably occurred in the spring, autumn, and winter (Haddeland et al., 2014 ). Consequently, they had a more substantial effect on the runoff during these seasons. Climate change had a comparable influence on the non-stationarity of the runoff in the sub-basins to that of the vegetation and water consumption by humans in the source region and upper reaches (R1–R3), as the frequencies of covariates (including precipitation, temperature, NDVI and water consumption by humans) in sub-basin R1-R3 are almost the same (20 %-25 %). However, in the middle and lower reaches of the YRB (R4–R7), the vegetation and water consumption had a more substantial impact than climatic factors. This discrepancy can be partly attributed to the fact that northwest China is an arid and semi-arid region (encompassing R1–R3), and is thus more sensitive to climate change than the other, relatively more humid, areas (Shi et al., 2007 ). Moreover, programs for ecological restoration, such as Grain for Green, the Three-North Shelter Forest, and the Protection of Natural Forest Resources, have been ongoing for decades in the Loess Plateau, which is primarily located in the middle reaches of the YRB (Feng et al., 2013 ). These programs have contributed to a significant improvement in the vegetation cover in the area, and most past studies suggest that this might have led to a reduction in the runoff of the YRB (Lv et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Ge et al., 2020 ). The lower reaches produce relatively little runoff, but consume a significant amount of water to cater to local needs (Tang et al., 2008 ); therefore, they are more influenced by human activities than climatic factors. In summary, hydrological research must consider the influence of human activities (Wada et al., 2013 ). Our results accurately capture the diverse roles of both human and climatic factors in the non-stationarity of the runoff across seasons and regions.  4.3 Implications and limitations of this study Eco-hydrological processes undergo complex transformations in the context of global climate change, and this poses new challenges to drought assessment in a changing environment. Our study focused on the non-stationarity of the hydrological conditions, and integrated it into the assessment of hydrological droughts in the YRB based on the standardized runoff index containing covariates (SRI_cov). Although previous studies attempted to calculate non-stationary drought indices in different regions, they generally only used time as a covariate (Li et al., 2018 ), or used the same covariate in the study area (Wang et al., 2020 ). Our study finds that the dominant covariates in different regions and seasons of the same basin may be inconsistent. In future studies of non-stationary drought, attention should be paid to the regionality and seasonality of covariate selection. All in all, our study proposed a non-stationary hydrological drought index in the YRB, which is highly original. When selecting covariates to construct a non-stationary model, we not only considered natural factors such as climate, but also the impact of human activities, which is novel. Moreover, our non-stationary hydrological drought index was more consistent with the actual drought situations and more accurate in identifying droughts. And our analyses provide a reliable approach to assessing droughts in regions undergoing non-stationary changes. This not only strengthens our understanding of droughts, but also serves as an informative foundation for strategic decision-making for local water resource management. Nevertheless, there are some limitations in this study. First, the factors driving the non-stationarity of the runoff are diverse, and often interact with one another. However, we analyzed a limited number of quantifiable and available variables. For example, the data on water consumption by humans were collected at the annual scale, which makes them less effective at capturing seasonal variations in it due to irrigation and industrial activities. Annual scale data may not be able to identify the impact of water consumption by humans on drought in each month of the year, but it may have little impact on the interannual variation trend of drought. We hope to collect monthly data in the future so that we can characterize the impact of human activities on drought in different months more accurately. Second, the duration of the study period (30 years) barely meets the minimum requirements for drought assessment based on the standardized drought index, suggesting that future studies should test the robustness of our model over longer time scales if more data become available. Third, drought can be identified or assessed at monthly, seasonal, or annual time scales. Although such characteristics of droughts as their intensity and duration may vary quantitatively at different time scales, their qualitative spatiotemporal patterns remain similar (Huang et al., 2015 ). We cannot decide the monthly scale model and the seasonal scale model which is better. The monthly scale model can describe short-term droughts in more detail, while the seasonal scale model can assess droughts from a long-term scale. Therefore, we can choose the appropriate scale to assess droughts according to the actual situation, or we can use the monthly scale and seasonal scale models at the same time, and their results can verify and complement each other.   5 Conclusion In response to the non-stationarity of hydrological conditions in the YRB, this study proposed a non-stationary model that integrates covariates to generate SRI_cov for drought assessment. Our research addressed the limitations in traditional indices of drought that are tailored to stationary conditions. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The AIC values of the non-stationary models in each basin and season were about 6 % lower than those of the stationary models, which meant that our non-stationary model outperformed the stationary model in simulating the runoff under the influence of climate change and human activities. (2) Based on SRI_cov, hydrological droughts in the entire YRB have most frequently occurred in spring. Mild and moderate droughts have most frequently occurred in the summer half-year, while severe and extreme droughts have most frequently occurred in the winter half-year. The number of months in which droughts occurred in the YRB exhibited a general trend of increase from 1986 and reached its peak in 2002, with extreme droughts becoming more prominent since 2005. Droughts in the middle reaches of the YRB were the most severe, and were characterized by a high frequency, intensity, and severity. (3) Our analysis provides a better understanding of hydrological simulations and drought assessment under non-stationary conditions, it can inform measures for managing water resources and adapting to the risk of droughts in a changing environment.
1 Introduction General circulation models (GCMs) are the most effective tools to quantify the impact of climate change due to increasing greenhouse gases (Wu et al., 2022 ). GCMs have shown continuous improvement in terms of spatial resolution and physical parameterization as the phases of the coupled model intercomparison project (CMIP) have progressed (Song et al., 2022b ). In addition, the recently released shared socioeconomic pathway (SSP) scenarios of CMIP6 can provide more reasonable projection of future climate change when coupled with the representative concentration pathways (RCP) scenarios of the previous CMIP5 (Su et al., 2021 ). Accordingly, several studies are quantifying the impact of future climate change using CMIP6 GCMs under SSP scenarios (Hamed et al., 2022; Dotse et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024 ). Also, many studies have been conducted to estimate the changes in future hydrological responses using physical hydrologic models (Chen et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023 ). However, many studies have emphasized the importance of considering the various uncertainties inherent in GCMs, despite the improved performance and widespread usability of CMIP6 GCMs (Wu et al., 2021; Senatore et al., 2022 ). Uncertainties inherent in the output of GCMs generally arise from an incomplete understanding of the physical climate simulation processes and limitations in implementation of the understanding (Yip et al., 2011 ). These uncertainties can be even larger due to the coarse spatial resolution and simplification of the natural heterogeneity of the climate system that exist at finer spatial scales, especially when simulating regional climates (Li et al., 2010; Virgilio et al., 2022 ), and can lead to biases between simulated and observed values.
