The raw GCMs have failed to reproduce regional climatic characteristics and have shown particularly poor performance in capturing precipitation characteristics in various studies (Song et al., 2022a; Tan et al., 2020 ). The bias between the observed and the simulated values due to GCM uncertainty can be critical to climate change and hydrological impact studies. Accordingly, many studies have adopted various bias correction (BC) methods to correct the bias in GCMs’ simulated values based on observed values when simulating regional climate (Miao et al., 2016; Cannon, 2018 ). However, some researchers have raised concerns about the impact of BC methods on the future projections. Ehret et al. (2012)  noted that BC methods can corrupt the benefits of GCMs by altering the relations among variables and violating the conservation principle. Cannon et al. (2015)  mentioned that the quantile mapping (QM) method, a commonly used BC method, may artificially corrupt the future projection trend of models. Despite these issues, efforts to improve the performance of BC methods have been ongoing, as the poor simulation performance of raw GCMs output at regional scales is a major obstacle to climate change projections and hydrological response studies (Yang et al., 2010; Cannon et al., 2015; Song et al., 2022b ). Evaluation of historical climate simulation performance of GCMs based on the BC has been consistently conducted in previous studies, demonstrating that it is possible to improve the output of raw GCMs (Hagemann et al., 2011; Song et al., 2022b; Brumatti et al., 2024 ). In addition, some studies have been conducted to quantify changes in future climate and hydrological impacts using various BC methods (Lafon et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2020; Mendez et al., 2020 ). Because future projection results by GCMs include various uncertainties, the uncertainty of future climate projections from bias corrected GCMs was quantified (Nguyen et al., 2017; Song et al., 2020 ). Additionally, the uncertainty in hydrological impact resulting from various GCMs’ climate projections was also analyzed (Zheng et al., 2018; Song et al., 2022b; Zheng et al., 2024 ). However, most studies have focused on the individual uncertainty of bias corrected climate variables and hydrological simulations. Currently, studies have quantified the contributions of various uncertainty sources (model, emission scenarios, BC method etc.) that affect the future climate and hydrologic projections using various GCMs (Iizumi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Paz and Willems, 2022; Wu et al., 2022; Mehboob and Kim, 2024 ). Many studies analyzing the uncertainty of future climate and hydrological response projections using GCMs' climate data have reported that GCMs significantly influence the uncertainty of the projection results (Gao et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021 ). However, these results can vary due to various reasons, such as the number of GCMs used, the diversity of different sources, or variations in the target area (Zheng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Paz and Willems, 2022; Ye et al., 2024 ). In particular, BC methods can influence not only the simulation performances of GCMs for historical periods but also the GCMs' projection results for future periods (Cannon et al., 2015 ). Therefore, if the projection results vary significantly due to BC methods, this variation may substantially affect the uncertainty of the projection results. In the ongoing research on climate change and hydrological responses using GCMs, the persistent use of BC methods emphasizes the importance of quantifying uncertainty when applying various BC methods. Despite the importance of BC methods, many studies have underestimated the impact of BC methods on the uncertainty of future climate and hydrological response projections. Previous studies exhibit several limitations, such as not using the latest GCM models (CMIP6 GCMs), considering a restricted number of future scenarios, using a limited number of BC methods, or focusing solely on the uncertainty contributions of climate conditions or hydrological responses. Therefore, the main objective of this study is to more intensively investigate the impact of BC methods on climate and hydrological runoff projections using CMIP6 GCMs under SSP scenarios. In order to accomplish the main objective, a relatively large number of BC methods were employed compared to previous studies, and the impacts of 20 GCMs, four SSPs, and seven BC methods on the uncertainty of projections for both climate (precipitation, maximum, and minimum temperature) and hydrological responses (hydrological runoff) were comprehensively quantified. The Mokgam River watershed, located in northwest of South Korea, was selected for the case study and the storm water management model (SWMM) was used for the long-term runoff simulation.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The Mokgam River watershed is located between longitudes 126°48´E ∼ 126°52´E and latitudes 37°23´N ∼ 37°29´N. The total area of the study area is about 57 km2 . The Mokgam River watershed has experienced ongoing flood damage as urbanization has progressed significantly in the downstream watershed. The Mokgam River watershed was divided into 27 sub-watersheds based on sewage and water system for hydrologic long-term runoff simulation. The climatic characteristics of the Mokgam River watershed are influenced by the climatic characteristics of the Seoul weather station using the Thiessen polygon approach. Most of the annual precipitation occurs in summer, while the least occurred in winter. The physical characteristics data of the 27 sub-watersheds were obtained from previous study (Chae et al., 2022 ), and the observed climate and runoff data were collected from the Korea meteorological administration (KMA) and the water management information system (WAMIS). It is important to note that this study addresses influenced hydrology rather than natural hydrology. The Mokgam River watershed has been divided into 27 sub-watersheds, and the SWMM parameters for each subbasin were calibrated using data from the Neobudae Bridge water level station. This station is one of the closest monitoring points to the outlet of the watershed and has the most extensive runoff data available, making it the best option for our study. Although having monitoring data directly at the outlet would have been ideal, it is often challenging to obtain such data in most studies. For this condition, the nearest hydrological observation can be utilized (Busico et al., 2020; Song et al., 2022c ). Therefore, the flow data from the closest monitoring station was used for model calibration. The 27 sub-watersheds of the study area and their land cover are shown in  Fig. 1 .  2.2 Data The daily observed climate variables (precipitation, maximum temperature (T  max    ), and minimum temperature (T  m in    )), streamflow, and potential evapotranspiration (PET) data were used for calibrating the hydrological model which is SWMM for long-term runoff simulations. The Seoul weather station data from 1985 to 2014 provided by KMA was used for climate data. The Neobudae Bridge water level station data from 2010 to 2020 provided by WAMIS was used for runoff data. The PET data from 2010 to 2020 was obtained from ERA5-land reanalysis dataset (Singer et al., 2021 ), which can be found at: https://data.bris.ac.uk/data/dataset/qb8ujazzda0s2aykkv0oq0ctp . For the consistency of data length, this study used climate data from 2010 to 2020 for model calibration and validation. The daily historical and future climate data were obtained from 20 CMIP6 GCMs according to four SSP-RCP scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5). The 20 CMIP6 GCMs used in this study have been commonly introduced to simulate the climate variables in East Asia (Kim et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, these GCMs provide complete daily precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures for the study area under four SSP-RCP scenarios within the same variant label (r1i1p1f1). The spatial resolution of the used GCMs varies from 0.7°∼2.5°, and specific information for each model is shown in  Table 1 . This study considered the outputs from the historical period (1985–2014) and two future periods which are near future (NF: 2021–2050) and distant future (DF: 2070–2099).  2.3 Bias correction methods The climate characteristics of the Mokgam River watershed are influenced by the Seoul weather station, based on the Thiessen polygon method. Since the GCMs provide climate data in grid format, spatial interpolation was conducted to simulate daily historical (1985–2014) climate variables at specific point locations using the GCMs’ grid-format data. The inverse distance weighting (IDW) method was used for spatial interpolation based on the coordinates of Seoul weather stations and the grid data of the four nearest GCMs. Even after performing spatial interpolation using the IDW method, biases still exist between the GCMs' and the observed climate data due to various sources of uncertainty. To adjust this bias, various BC methods have been adopted in climate change studies using GCMs. Among these methods, the QM method is the most commonly used (Enayati et al., 2021; Ahan et al., 2023; Brumatti et al., 2024 ). The QM method corrects the bias through the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the observed and simulated values, and can be expressed as shown in Eq. (1) . If the CDF and inverse CDF are estimated empirically from the data, QM interpolates between points in the quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot, which is the scatterplot between the empirical quantiles of observed and modeled data for the historical data (Cannon et al., 2015 ).(1) x  ˆ   m , p   t    = F  o , h    −   F  m , h   x  m , p   ( t )           where x  ˆ   m , p   t       is the bias-corrected climate data, x  m , p   ( t )    is the simulated value at time t   (for our case, day) in period p   (for our case, 1985–2014), F  m , h     is the CDF of GCMs’ simulated climate data, and F  o , h    −     is the inverse function of the CDF of observed climate data. The seven QM methods, which include two types of statistical transformations (non-parametric transformations (NPTF) and parametric transformations (PTF)), in the "qmap" package were used. The information of the seven BC methods used in this study is shown in  Table 2 . Considering that this study used GCMs' temperature data for the climate variable, distribution transformation methods were excluded as they do not account for negative values. 2.3.1 Nonparametric transformation method The NPTF method does not assume any specific distribution of the data and directly compares observed and model data to correct biases (Gudmundsson et al., 2012 ). This method considers the corresponding values of the quantiles of observed and modeled data in the Q-Q plot and interpolates model data at points closest to the observed data points using a regression line. Following the method described by Boé et al. (2007) , empirical CDFs are estimated using tables of empirical percentiles. The interpolation is then applied to estimate values between the percentiles. For both linear and monotonic tricubic spline interpolation (NPTF-L and NPTF-T), values between quantiles are estimated by fitting a local regression line to the nearest data points in the Q-Q plot. For smoothing splines (NPTF-S), a smoothing spline is fit to the Q-Q plot, which allows for a smooth adjustment of the distribution of the modeled data to match the observed data. NPTF methods do not require prior assumptions about data distribution, which can provide high flexibility. This flexibility can help reflect complex data patterns, potentially leading to more accurate corrections. However, due to the assumption that the highest quantile of future projections is adjusted to the highest quantile of the historical period, there might be limitations in simulating future extremes (Gudmundsson et al., 2012; Paz and Willems, 2022 ).  2.3.2 Parametric transformation methods The PTF method models the Q-Q relation between observed and modeled values using predefined mathematical functions (Gudmundsson et al., 2012 ). This method adjusts the distribution of the modeled data to match the distribution of the observations by applying these parametric transformation functions. Following Maraun et al. (2010)  and Piani et al. (2010) , the parametric transformation functions used in this study can be expressed as:(2) P  o   = a + b × P  m      × 1 − exp − P  m   − x  0       / τ            (3) P  o   = a + b × P  m       (4) P  o   = b × P  m   − x  0      c       (5) P  o   = b × P  m       where, P  o     and P  m     represented observed and modeled climate variables, a , b , c , x    and τ   are parameters that are subject to calibration. The Eqs. (2)-(5)  represent the PTF methods in sequence: exponential (PTF-E), linear (PTF-L), power (PTF-P), and simple scaling (PTF-S). PTF methods are easy to apply and efficient due to their mathematical simplicity. Additionally, by estimating the parameters of the distribution, the results can be more clearly and intuitively interpreted. Unlike NPTF methods, PTF methods do not require assumptions to adjust future extremes, making them relatively easier for estimating future extremes. However, because parametric methods assume a specific distribution, they can be less flexible compared to NPTF methods.   2.4 Storm water management model The SWMM, a free software developed under the auspices of the United States environmental protection agency (USEPA), was used for the hydrological modeling of the Mokgam River watershed. The SWMM is a dynamic rainfall-runoff model, which has advantages in hydrological modeling of urban watersheds because it can simulate pipe flow, but it can also simulate the flow of natural rivers. The SWMM was adopted as a hydrological model in this study because it is the most suitable model for comprehensively considering both surface runoff (river flow) and conduit flow (drainage system in a residential area). The basic elements such as 27 sub-watersheds, 22 conduits, and 22 junctions were established for the SWMM long-term runoff simulation at the study area. The daily precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature from the GCMs were considered as climate input to obtain runoff simulation results that considered the influence of evaporation in the long-term SWMM runoff simulation. For the historical period, observation data from 2010 to 2020, including climate data and runoff data from the Neobudae Bridge water level station, were used for model calibration. For the performance analysis of the SWMM long-term runoff simulation using bias-corrected GCMs climate data (precipitation, maximum and minimum temperature), the period from 2010 to 2014 was selected, because the historical data of GCMs is only available up to 2014, and our runoff observation data starts from 2010. However, since the observed runoff data for the historical period (up to 10 years) has limitations when compared to the simulated runoff values under future climate change scenarios (30 years: near future, NF: 2021–2050 and distant future, DF: 2070–2099), we considered the SWMM simulated values forced by observed climate data (1985–2014) as the historical runoff. A total of 140 SWMM simulations (20 GCMs and 7 BC methods) based on bias-corrected GCMs’ climate data, and 20 simulations (20 GCMs) based on raw GCMs’ climate data, were performed for the historical period. Additionally, a total of 560 simulations (20 GCMs, 4 SSPs, 7 BC methods) were performed for both future periods. The model calibration and validation are necessary for the reliability of SWMM runoff results when considering various uncertainties included in physical hydrologic models, such as incomplete topographical data and model parameters. Genetic algorithms have been used in many studies to calibrate the SWMM model due to their calibration performance and ease of application (Bahrami et al., 2019; Lopes and da Silva, 2021; Singh et al., 2023 ). Therefore, in this study, the model was calibrated using a genetic algorithm (GA) based on observed climate and flow data from 2010 to 2017, and validated from 2018 to 2020. The Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) was used as an objective function when calibrating SWMM with GA. The observed precipitation, PET (Singer et al., 2021 ), and runoff data for 2010–2020 were used as an input data for calibration. The ‘swmmr’ and ‘metaheuristicOpt’ packages in R programing language were used to calibrate the SWMM model.  2.5 Evaluation metrics This study evaluated the performance of climate and runoff simulations before and after bias corrected GCMs’ climate using four evaluation metrics based on observed runoff data from 1985 to 2014. The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NNSE), normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), KGE, and the modified index of agreement (MD) were used as evaluation metrics. The formulas, optimal values, and references of the four evaluation metrics used in this study are shown in  Table 3 . The O  i     and S  i     are observed values and GCMs simulated values, r   is the correlation coefficient between the observed and simulated values, α   is the relative variation in the observed and simulated values, and β   is the bias term. The climate simulation performance was evaluated by comparing GCMs' simulation values to daily observational data from 1985 to 2014. An evaluation of the runoff simulation performance was conducted using daily observed runoff data from the available period of 2010–2014, which considered the actual usable observational period.  2.6 Uncertainty quantification The Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) method was employed to quantitatively assess the relative contributions of GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods to the overall uncertainty in future climate and runoff projection results. This method has been consistently adopted to quantify the relative contributions of various sources to the uncertainty in GCMs' climate and hydrological response projection results, allowing not only for the derivation of the relative contributions of individual sources but also considering the impact of their interaction effects (Gao et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021; Senatore et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2022 ). The total sum of squares (SST) and the sum of squares (SS) of each source and their interactions were used to decompose the total variance into each source. The overall calculation was conducted using aov() function included in the stats package of the R programming language. Since three sources (GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods) contribute to the total uncertainty of future climate and runoff projection results, the three-way ANOVA method was adopted to analyze the relative and interactive contributions in all possible combinations, resulting in 560 subsets (20 GCMs, 4 SSPs, and 7 BC methods). The analysis is conducted based on the projected mean climate variables and runoff. Eq.
