The SWMM runoff performance during these periods is indicated by normalized NNSE and R² values. The performances of the seven BC methods used in this study were evaluated using four evaluation metrics. The NNSE and R2  values of simulated runoff from SWMM calibrated in this study were 0.76 and 0.7 in the calibration period, and 0.65 and 0.6 in the validation period, respectively. Considering the use of observed climate data, the NNSE and R2  values came out lower than expected. These results are attributed to the variation in flow due to domestic wastewater within the Mokgam River watershed. Furthermore, although the SWMM incorporates direct inflow functionality within junctions to account for base flow, this may not accurately reflect the actual base flow of the Mokgam River as the inflow values were derived from a daily time pattern based on winter flow data. Nevertheless, our calibration results consistently showed an NNSE value of 0.6 or higher during both the calibration and validation periods. These values fall within the satisfactory range (NSE > 0.5) (Moriasi et al., 2007; Martinez and Gupta, 2010 ). Such findings indicate the reliability of the SWMM used in this study.  3.2 Verification of bias correction methods The performances of the seven BC methods used in this study were evaluated through four evaluation metrics for the historical daily climate variables (1985–2014) and runoff (2010–2014). The box plots in   Figs. 3 and 4  depict the performances of daily precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature of 20 CMIP6 GCMs before (RAW in Figs. 3 and 4 ) and after the implementation of BC methods using four evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the runoff simulation performances based on climate data from 20 GCMs were also presented. Regarding climate simulation performances, the values of each evaluation metric were calculated by comparing observed climate data with GCMs' simulated climate data. For the runoff simulation performance, the evaluation metric values were calculated by comparing the observed runoff with the simulated runoff by SWMM using climate data from GCMs. The overall simulation performance of all CMIP6 GCMs were highly improved after implementing BC methods. The degree of improvement is particularly pronounced in precipitation rather than temperature, and this distinct enhancement is consistent in the runoff simulation performance. When averaging the improvement levels of GCMs' simulation performance for each BC method across evaluation metrics, precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures showed improvements generally exceeding 0.9 for NNSE, KGE, and MD values, and the improvement exceeded 0.7 for runoff. For NRMSE, it was consistently below 0.3 for the climate variables results, and below 0.62 for the runoff. While the runoff simulation performance was relatively poorer compared to climate simulation performance, this is attributed to the limitations of SWMM calibration mentioned in Section 3.1 . When comparing the improvements in simulated climate variables and runoff performances using four evaluation metrics, the NPTF BC methods consistently showed higher scores across all evaluation metrics compared to the PTF BC methods. Although other BC methods also showed meaningful improvement, the PTF_S method exhibited relatively modest improvements compared to other methods. Overall, all BC methods showed high performances in bias-corrected climate variables and runoff, but the degree of improvement varied depending on the BC method. Furthermore, even when using the same BC methods, the degree of improvement varied among different GCMs. These characteristics were particularly evident in temperature for the PTF_S and PTF_P methods, and for precipitation in the PTF_S method. In the case of runoff, all BC methods showed similar levels of improvement across different GCMs.  3.3 Changes in future precipitation and runoff The future climate was estimated by 20 GCMs under the four SSP scenarios and adjusted by seven BC methods. The adjusted climate variables were used as inputs for the SWMM for future runoff simulations. Changes in future climate variables and runoff compared to the historical period (1985–2014) are presented in     Figs. 5–8 , divided into NF (2021–2050) and DF (2070–2099). The NPTF BC methods estimated a decrease in precipitation and runoff in the NF for all SSP scenarios and an increase in the DF. However, for temperature, an increasing trend was observed in both NF and DF. For the PTF BC methods, there was a generally increasing trend in precipitation and runoff for all SSP scenarios during both future periods. The maximum and minimum temperatures showed generally similar trends, although the PTF_P method showed a predominantly decreasing trend in the NF. Both NPTF and PTF BC methods exhibited relatively higher rates of increase in climate and runoff during the DF compared to the NF, and these results were more pronounced in high emission scenarios (SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5) than in low emission scenarios (SSP1–2.6 and SSP2–4.5). The future climate and runoff changes varied among GCMs, and were generally more pronounced in PTF BC methods than in NPTF BC methods. This difference was particularly evident in precipitation and runoff results rather than temperature. For temperature, most BC methods, excluding the results of PTF_P and PTF_S, showed similar changes. However, there were notable variances in the estimation of precipitation and runoff between NPTF BC and PTF BC methods. Overall, there were substantial differences in the estimation of precipitation and runoff changes among GCMs and BC methods. For temperature, however, the differences were more influenced by GCMs and SSP scenarios than by BC methods, particularly evident in the DF based on SSP scenarios.  3.4 Variation of uncertainty sources The variation of the mean of future projection results was calculated using standard deviation (STDEV) during the NF and DF periods, and the results were presented sequentially for GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods in     Figs. 9–12 . The variation of GCMs’ projections was indicated by the STDEV values of the mean GCMs’ projection values during the NF and DF periods, differentiated by SSP scenarios and BC methods. The variation of SSPs and BCs was similarly determined. The variations of projection according to GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods were generally larger in DF than in NF, particularly evident in precipitation and runoff projections rather than in maximum and minimum temperature projections. Specifically, the variation in precipitation projections determined by GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods was notably more pronounced compared to the variation in other climate and runoff projections. In the future projections, the variation introduced by GCMs was most pronounced in precipitation (ranging from 3.47 to 25.75 for NF and 5.18–32.22 for DF), while it was notably lower in maximum and minimum temperatures (ranging from 0.39 to 1.86 for NF and 0.71–1.86 for DF). For runoff, the variation showed a larger range (ranging from 1.24 to 10.31 for NF and 1.4–12.45 for DF) compared to maximum and minimum temperatures but was relatively lower when compared to precipitation results. This trend was consistently observed in the variation results introduced by SSPs and BC methods. Overall, in the PR and RF projection results, the average variation introduced by BC methods was consistently the highest during both NF and DF periods, while the average variation introduced by SSPs was the lowest. During the NF period, the average variation introduced by GCMs was the highest for maximum and minimum temperature projection, while that introduced by SSPs was the lowest. In the DF period, for maximum and minimum temperature results, the average variation introduced by SSPs was the highest. The smallest average variation was consistently observed in both maximum and minimum temperature results introduced by BC methods.  3.5 Uncertainty contribution of sources The relative contributions of each source to the overall uncertainty in future climate and runoff projection results were derived using the ANOVA method, as shown in  Fig. 13 . The contribution of BC methods to the uncertainty in precipitation and runoff projection was consistently the highest during both NF and DF periods, followed by the interaction between GCMs and BC methods, and GCMs. The contributions of other sources were relatively minor, ranging from 0.5 % to 3.1 %. For the uncertainty in maximum and minimum temperature projection during the NF, the interaction between GCMs and BC methods contributed most significantly, followed by BC methods and GCMs for maximum temperature, and GCMs and BC methods for minimum temperature. During the DF, SSPs contributed most substantially, followed by GCMs and the interaction between GCMs and BC methods. The interaction between SSPs and BC methods consistently showed the lowest contribution to the uncertainty in maximum and minimum temperature projection during both NF and DF periods. When exploring the relative contribution to the uncertainty of each climate variable and runoff projection, the uncertainty contribution of RF was significantly similar to that of PR, with a low correlation observed with the results of maximum and minimum temperatures. Additionally, excluding the results of maximum and minimum temperature during the DF, BC methods, GCMs, and the interaction between GCMs and BC methods generally contributed significantly to the uncertainty of the projection. Assumptions of different BC methods for future climate projections might have caused varying climate predictions, thereby increasing the contribution of uncertainty in BC methods. Accordingly, the uncertainty contributions of three sources were re-quantified by considering only the five BC methods, excluding PTF-P and PTF-S, which showed significantly different projections from NPTF and other PTF methods in climate and runoff projection, as shown in  Fig. 14 . The contributions of each source to the uncertainty in precipitation and runoff projections, considering the five BC methods, showed no significant differences compared to when all seven BC methods were considered, except for a slight increase in the contribution of GCMs in the precipitation projection. However, the contributions of the sources to the uncertainty in the maximum and minimum temperature projection results showed significantly different outcomes between five and seven BC methods. The most significant difference was observed in the contribution of GCMs to uncertainty. The most important factors for seven BC methods were BC methods and GCMs in NF. Contrarily, in the use of five, GCMs showed a very high contribution in the NF period, while the contribution of BC methods significantly decreased. In the DF, SSP scenarios remained the largest source of uncertainty in both cases.   4 Discussion 4.1 Uncertainty associated with BC methods Although the output of GCMs has improved as the phases of CMIP progress, GCMs have shown poor performance in simulating regional scale climate due to various uncertainty factors (Senatore et al., 2022; Ahmad and Choi, 2023 ). This poor performance was recognized as a major obstacle in regional scale hydrologic response simulation studies using the climate data of GCMs. A variety of BC methods are being utilized to address this issue, resulting in enhanced performance of GCMs in simulating regional-scale climate patterns. Nevertheless, it prompted multiple discussions. One of the main concerns regarding BC methods is that they can artificially corrupt the raw projections of GCMs (Ehret et al., 2012; Maraun, 2013; Cannon et al., 2015 ). The statistical transformation BC methods (Gudmundsson et al., 2012 ) used in this study assume that the difference between model output and observations is stationary, i.e., the same corrections are applicable to future climates (Potter et al., 2020; Robertson et al., 2023 ). This assumption implies that future climate projections adjusted using statistical transformations may exhibit considerable variation based on the particular conditions associated with each method (e.g., correction method, parameters, etc.). Gudmundsson et al. (2012)  mentioned that most of the various statistical transformations can remove the bias in the precipitation output of climate models, but the performance of these methods varies, so the suitability of the data must be confirmed before applying the techniques. Paz and Willems (2022)  mentioned the distinct characteristics of ten different statistical transformation BC methods and showed the predictive differences of each method in future extreme precipitation projections. The difference in future climate projections according to BC methods was also observed in our research results (Figs. 5–7 ). The discrepancy between the NPTF and PTF projection results was clear, and in particular, the difference in projection among PTF methods was more distinct than among NPTF methods. This difference appears to be due to the assumption in the NPTF method that if the GCM simulation values in the empirical CDF are larger than the training values, they are replaced by the highest quantile values in the training period (Gudmundsson et al., 2012 ). The differences in future projections resulting from these BC methods can significantly impact the uncertainty in both future climate and hydrological response projections. Therefore, it is important to consider the influence of BC methods when conducting uncertainty analysis.  4.2 Impact of BC methods on future climate and runoff changes This study indicates that precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature in the study area will continuously increase over time in the future period compared to the historical period. These increases in climate for the future period according to the BC methods support the projection results of previous studies targeting the Asian region (Mishra et al., 2020; Moon and Ha, 2020; Song et al., 2021 ). Future runoff also showed a continuous increase during the future period, similar to the results for precipitation. These findings were consistent with previous studies projecting runoff in the Mokgam River watershed (Chae et al., 2022 ). The increase in climate variables using CMIP6 GCMs under SSP scenarios generally intensifies from NF to DF. This result is believed to stem from the assumption that the Tier 1 SSP scenarios used in this study reach approximately 2.6 W/m², 4.5 W/m², 7.0 W/m², and 8.5 W/m² of total radiative forcing by 2100 (O’Neill et al., 2016 ). The CO2  emission curves under SSP scenarios show that, except for SSP1–2.6 and SSP2–4.5, CO2  emissions consistently increase as it approaches 2100. This increase is more pronounced in high emission scenarios (SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5) than in low emissions (SSP1–2.6 and SSP2–4.5). The rise in CO2  emissions ultimately leads to an increase in global surface temperatures, which in turn can cause an increase in extreme precipitation and temperature events (IPCC, 2018 ). Figs. 5–7  illustrate the characteristics of precipitation and temperature increases according to the CO2  emission characteristics of these SSP scenarios. In the SSP1–2.6 and SSP2–4.5 scenarios, the increase between NF and DF is not significant, but in the SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios, there is a notable difference between NF and DF. It is reasonable to expect that the maximum and minimum temperatures in the study area will continuously rise in the future period compared to the historical period, following the assumptions of the SSP scenarios and previous studies in South Korea. In this study, most GCMs corrected by various BC methods showed an increase in maximum and minimum temperatures during the future period. However, a few GCMs corrected by PTF_P and PTF_S exhibited a decrease in maximum and minimum temperatures in the study area during the NF. These results imply the limitations of PTF BC methods as discussed in Sections 2.3.2 and 4.1 . PTF BC methods assume a specific distribution to correct model bias in the past period, making them relatively less flexible compared to NPTF BC methods. Additionally, the characteristic of the PTF BC method, which applies the specific distribution determined for the historical period directly to the future, may lead to the issue of using a distribution that doesn't accurately reflect the past climate characteristics. These results support the recommendation by Gudmundsson et al. (2012)  that it is advisable to verify the suitability of statistical BC methods for the model before application. This step ensures that the chosen BC method is reasonable for the specific model and its projections.  4.3 Contribution of various sources to projection uncertainties This study contradicts the results of previous studies (Wang et al., 2020; Senatore et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022 ), in which uncertainty contribution due to GCMs is generally the largest in the total uncertainty of precipitation and runoff projection. However, considering that different BC methods can affect the variation of future climate projections and runoff simulation results (Teng et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2020 ), further in-depth research on the contribution of uncertainties in GCMs and BC methods is needed. The contribution of uncertainties in GCMs can vary due to various reasons, and the significant impact of BC methods on the overall uncertainty of climate and hydrological response projections has been mentioned in previous studies. Paz and Willems (2022)  demonstrated that at the higher extremes of precipitation projections, the main source of uncertainty could be statistical downscaling method. They also confirmed that the contribution of uncertainty factors can vary by region. Lafferty and Sriver (2023)  mentioned that in precipitation predictions, extreme event forecasts, and considerations of complex terrain regions using GCMs, downscaling and BC methods could be major sources of uncertainty. Wang et al. (2020)  confirmed that the number of GCMs can influence the results of the uncertainty contributions. Therefore, this study included a large number of BC methods to more accurately assess the impact of uncertainties from BC methods, which have been underestimated in most previous studies. The finding of this study that GCMs do not make the largest contribution to uncertainties may be due to the assumptions of the BC methods used. The NPTF BC method, by replacing higher extreme values in future projections with historical extreme values if the value of future projection is higher than the value of historical, may provide relatively lower extreme values compared to PTF BC methods. Hence, significant uncertainty can be observed in the higher quartiles due to BC methods (Paz and Willems, 2022 ). In addition, this study examined the variation of projection results for each component, as shown in Figs. 9–12 , to support the findings of high contributions of BC methods in the projection results. Through the results of variation, it was observed that BC methods induced high uncertainty in precipitation and runoff projections. In the temperature projection, the main source of uncertainty during the NF period was primarily GCMs, while SSPs dominated during the DF period. These results have been observed in previous studies as well. Iizumi et al. (2017)  quantified the impact of CMIP5 GCMs, RCP scenarios, and BC methods on the uncertainty of future precipitation and temperature projections across 22 regions worldwide. The element that showed the greatest impact on the uncertainty of future temperature projections was GCMs for the near future and RCP scenarios for the distant future. Additionally, in the uncertainty of precipitation projection results, the impact of BC methods was dominant. Park et al. (2024)  confirmed that the uncertainty due to RCP scenarios increases over time in future temperature projections for East Asia and Korea, compared to the uncertainty from GCMs, based on RCMs and RCP scenarios. This study compared the contributions of various uncertainty sources when considering seven BC methods versus five BC methods, excluding PTF-P and PTF-S, because they showed significantly different climate projections compared to the others. Figs. 13 and 14  demonstrate that different climate projections of BC methods can increase the contribution of uncertainty in BC methods. Notably, when considering the five BC methods, the contributions to the total uncertainty in temperature projection changed. The contribution of GCMs increased while the contribution of BC methods significantly decreased. This appears to be due to the removal of the heterogeneous projection caused by PTF-P and PTF-S in future temperature change projections according to BC methods. Additionally, these results support our statement that different climate projections due to BC methods can increase the contribution of uncertainty. The BC methods significantly influence the variation of future climate and runoff projections, resulting in high variance and, consequently, high uncertainty contribution. However, when BC methods are combined with GCMs, their variances might offset each other or combine in a way that lowers the overall variation. This can lead to a lower contribution of the interaction between GCMs and BC methods to the total uncertainty than individual source. For example, BC methods, such as the NPTF BC method, replace future extreme values with historical ones, which can provide relatively lower extreme values. These characteristics can reduce the degree of variance resulting from the interaction between BCs and GCMs, leading to a lower contribution to uncertainty. Additionally, including a wide range of BC methods in the analysis, as this study, provides a comprehensive assessment and leads to BC methods showing a higher contribution to uncertainty compared to GCMs. The results of this study support some previous studies (Iizumi et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019; Meresa et al., 2021; Paz and Willems, 2022; Lafferty and Sriver, 2023 ) that have highlighted the significant impact of BC methods on the uncertainty of future climate and runoff projections. Especially, our findings emphasize that the contribution of uncertainty from BC methods, which has been underestimated in most previous studies, is substantial and cannot be ignored.  4.4 Limitations of the study While this study provides valuable insights into the uncertainty contribution of BC methods, there are several limitations that should be addressed in future research. First, during the SWMM modeling, this study did not consider hydrological facilities and elements like wastewater discharge, groundwater interactions, and other point sources affecting base flow. Second, because this study area is mixed landuse watershed as shown in Fig. 1 , it can be questioned whether SWMM is proper or not. Although SWMM accounted for conduit flow with a reasonable NNSE value above 0.5, other hydrological models can be considered. Third, GCMs' climate data have coarser resolutions than the study area, causing potential uncertainties. This study used the IDW method for spatial interpolation and seven statistical BC methods to correct biases, improving simulation accuracy (Fig. 3 ). However, other downscaling methods were not used, which may have contributed to high uncertainty from BC methods. Fourth, this study selected just Seoul weather station based on Thiessen polygons generated from 60 stations across South Korea. However, results may vary if more stations are considered, potentially affecting the study's findings and its robustness.   5 Conclusion This study analyzed the relative contributions of GCMs, SSP scenarios, and BC methods to the uncertainty of GCMs’ climate and hydrological runoff projection results. CMIP6 GCMs and SSPs scenarios were used for daily climate projections, and seven BC methods were used for adjusting the projection results. The long-term runoff simulations using SWMM according to GCMs’ climate variables were performed for the historical and future periods. The performances of GCMs’ climate and runoff simulations before and after the implementation of BC methods in the historical period were assessed by four evaluation metrics. The relative contribution of each source to the total uncertainty in climate and hydrological runoff projection in the future period was quantified using the ANOVA method. This study concluded the following. First, the bias corrected GCMs data showed better climate simulation performance than the raw GCMs data, and the runoff simulation results were consistent. The raw GCMs showed poor performance in simulating overall trends and extremes when compared to observed values, especially for precipitation. In other words, the BC method is inevitable in regional climate and runoff simulations in the historical period. Second, when projecting future climate and runoff using GCMs under SSP scenarios, the PTF BC methods increased the variation of GCMs' projection results more than the NPTF BC methods. These findings were particularly pronounced in precipitation and runoff projection results relative to temperature projections. Additionally, the NPTF and PTF BC methods exhibited relatively divergent outcomes in climate and runoff projections during both NF and DF periods across the four SSP scenarios. Third, when confirming the variation of future projection results driven by GCMs, SSPs, and BC methods, the variation in precipitation and runoff projections was consistently most pronounced due to BC methods in both future periods and least due to SSPs. In the case of maximum and minimum temperatures, the variation was similarly most influenced by GCMs for NF. However, during the DF, the variation was higher in the case of maximum temperature due to SSPs and in the case of minimum temperature due to GCMs. Fourth, BC methods can significantly contribute to the uncertainty of future precipitation and runoff projections, and the use of appropriate BC methods is recommended. In this study, when projecting future climate and runoff using CMIP6 GCMs under SSP scenarios, the impact of various BC methods was demonstrated. Additionally, the contributions of each source to the overall uncertainty of projection results were statistically quantified. The results of this study emphasize the importance of the influence not only of the traditionally emphasized GCMs but also of BC methods in the uncertainty of future climate and runoff projection results.
1 Introduction Arid regions, which are defined by their inability to compensate for surface evapotranspiration with regional precipitation, comprise over 40 % of the Earth’s terrestrial area (Feng and Fu, 2013 ). As integral parts of terrestrial areas, they are characterized by scarce water resources and pronounced susceptibility to global climate change (Dai and Zhao, 2017; Yao et al., 2021 ). Amidst global warming, significant shifts in global precipitation patterns have been observed, characterized by the expansion of arid regions (Cai et al., 2018 ). Concurrently, the escalation of both the frequency and intensity of drought-related disasters has garnered extensive attention. In arid regions, precipitation is the principal source of water, and its distribution and variability have significant implications for local ecosystems and the environment (Lioubimtseva et al., 2005 ). Therefore, enhancing the accuracy of precipitation forecasting in arid regions is crucial for the implementation of effective preparatory and response strategies to alleviate the adverse effects of drought. Current seasonal climate prediction models can be broadly classified as (1) physical, dynamic, or numerical; (2) empirical or statistical; and (3) physical-empirical (Hastenrath, 2015 ). Physical models that predict intricate processes occurring in the atmosphere, ocean, and land simulate rainfall using a series of complex physical equations. However, the limitations of predictability and the high computational costs associated with these models restrict their widespread application (Dash et al., 2018 ). Empirical models, which are presently the predominant approach to precipitation forecasting, establish statistical relationships grounded in the characteristics of historical precipitation time-series data to predict future values. Empirical methods are simple and easy to implement; however, they lack physical interpretation and feature a multitude of systematic errors (Xiaolong et al., 2013 ). Physical-empirical models take advantage of both physical and empirical methods by integrating the physical insights governing rainfall processes into statistical models. They markedly augment the predictability of precipitation, establishing them as an important tool for refining the accuracy of precipitation prediction (Gong et al., 2015; Li et al., 2023 ). In recent years, machine learning (ML) models have been found to be highly efficient in predicting precipitation (Baig et al., 2024; Dotse et al., 2024 ). ML algorithms can efficiently capture complex relationships between meteorological data and precipitation (Parmar et al., 2017 ). Moreover, they maintain their effectiveness in predicting precipitation even under conditions of incomplete input data or a limited understanding of certain physical mechanisms (Parmar et al., 2017 ). Many studies have demonstrated that ML algorithms such as artificial neural networks (ANN) (Pirone et al., 2023 ), boosted regression trees (Baig et al., 2024 ), and support vector machines (SVM) (Kumar et al., 2023 ), perform well at predicting precipitation and, in most cases, outperform traditional statistical methods in terms of prediction accuracy (Baig et al., 2024 ). Although ML models have demonstrated excellent capabilities in predicting precipitation, they are often perceived as ‘black boxes’ because of their interpretability challenges. These models do not sufficiently explain the process behind the generation of the predicted values, nor do they clarify the factors influencing these predictions. To overcome the aforementioned challenges, recent research has introduced explainable ML (XML) techniques, such as the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method (Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explainer (LIME) method (Ribeiro et al., 2016 ), and Anchors (Ribeiro et al., 2018). Studies have suggested that employing XML can significantly enhance model interpretability and aid in elucidating the relationship between prediction targets and features (Gibson et al., 2021; He et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2023; Pegion et al., 2022 ). So far, only a few studies have employed XML models for precipitation forecasting (He et al., 2024; Senocak et al., 2023 ). In addition, the utilization of these models to garner more profound insights has been scarce in research exploring climatic variables that influence precipitation. Xinjiang (XJ), China, is a typical arid and semi-arid region in Central Asia, far from the ocean, where precipitation is not directly influenced by the monsoon system (Xiao et al., 2015; Yang and Zhang, 2008b; Zhang et al., 2012 ). Surrounded by mountain ranges, Xinjiang has a complex landform that contributes to its extremely uneven distribution of precipitation. Annual precipitation in NXJ generally exceeds 200 mm, while in SXJ, it typically remains below 100 mm (Xie et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2021, 2022, 2024a, 2024b ). The annual precipitation in XJ is generally on an upward trend (Xie et al., 2018 ). The seasonal distribution of precipitation in Xinjiang shows a pattern with maximum precipitation in summer and minimum precipitation in winter. Summer precipitation accounts for 54.4 % of the annual total, and the intensity of summer precipitation largely determines the variation in both summer and annual precipitation. Precipitation in XJ is sudden and challenging to forecast (Yang et al., 2011; Yang and Zhang, 2008b ). Previous studies in Xinjiang (XJ), China, have focused on predicting precipitation by employing physical (Du et al., 2021; Xuetao et al., 2022 ) and empirical (Fu, 2019; Lu et al., 2023; Suqin, 2022 ) models. However, these predictions are constrained by several limitations, including complex interactions within the various components of the climate system and the scarcity of observational data. Furthermore, most studies tend to focus on a few key climate indices and fail to fully integrate multiple climate indicators (Yang and Zhang, 2008a, 2008b; Yao et al., 2022 ). Consequently, the combined effects of multi-scale factors on precipitation patterns are not effectively revealed. This study aims to contribute to accurate and reliable precipitation forecasting for arid regions, exemplified by the case of Xinjiang. Our research provides valuable insights into predicting summer precipitation in Xinjiang, enabling other researchers to utilize the key predictive variables identified in this study without the need for additional variable selection. Additionally, we investigated the physical mechanisms between these key predictors and precipitation, which has deepened our understanding of the processes governing summer precipitation in Xinjiang. The research questions include: (1) Can a machine learning-based model improve the accuracy of summer precipitation forecasting in Xinjiang? (2) What are the key climate variables affecting summer precipitation in Xinjiang, and how do these variables specifically influence summer precipitation? To answer the above-mentioned research questions, three machine learning methods, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were used to examine the potential of machine learning models for precipitation prediction in arid regions. The SHAP method was integrated with an extreme tree model to select predictors. By incorporating multi-scale factors, including atmospheric circulation indices, sea surface temperature indices, and land-surface indices, the model significantly improves the accuracy of precipitation prediction and reveals the combined effects of multi-scale factors on precipitation patterns. The structure of the paper is as follows: Section 2  introduces the data and machine learning methodology. Section 3  presents the main results, evaluating the performance of various machine learning models in predicting summer precipitation in Xinjiang. This section also identifies key predictive variables and clarifies their impact on summer precipitation. Section 4  discusses the physical mechanisms underlying these predictive variables and suggests improvements to enhance the accuracy of predicting precipitation anomalies. Finally, Section 5  summarizes the work and discusses prospective directions for model development, as well as identifying interactions between variables.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Study area XJ (73.66–96.38 °E, 34.42–49.17 °N) is located in the mid-latitude region of Eurasia in northwestern China, marking it as a significant arid region within Central Asia. XJ is predominantly characterized by vast deserts and arid lands, encircled by extensive mountain ranges. The region is geographically divided into Northern and Southern XJ by the Altai Mountains in the north, the Kunlun Mountains in the south, and the Tianshan Mountains running centrally. Located inland and distant from the sea, XJ has a temperate continental arid climate characterized by low average annual precipitation and a notable disparity in its spatial and temporal distribution. Precipitation in XJ predominantly occurs in the northern and central regions, where most areas receive an average annual precipitation of ∼200 mm. In contrast, Southern XJ generally experiences less than 100 mm of average annual precipitation (Yao et al., 2022 ). Precipitation in XJ is mainly concentrated in the summer, with summer rainfall accounting for ∼54.4 % of the yearly total (Yao et al., 2022 ).    2.2 Data description Monthly average precipitation data for XJ from 1961 to 2017 were obtained from the China Meteorological Administration (CMA, http://data.cma.cn/en ). Precipitation observation data from 95 meteorological stations in Xinjiang were used, excluding the data of 1969 from the Bachu and Meigaiti stations, which were missing. The missing data were substituted with long-term average values corresponding to the same dates in other years. Based on summer precipitation data, we constructed a time series for the precipitation anomaly percentage, spanning June to August from 1961 to 2017. Predictor data were derived from the National Climate Center of the China Meteorological Administration (https://cmdp.ncc-cma.net/cn ), with 88 atmospheric circulation indices, 26 sea surface temperature indices, and 16 land-surface indices. The indices of the preceding winter (December to February) and spring (March to May) periods were selected as the precursor signals. Predictor variables with missing values were excluded from the analysis, resulting in an initial screening of 98 predictors. Comprehensive details regarding the predictors are provided in the Supplementary Material  (Text S1 ).  2.3 Methods We followed a three-step methodology to predict summer precipitation in XJ from 2013 to 2017, using data available from the China Meteorological Administration. First, we introduced the Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) method to analyze normalized summer precipitation with the aim of discerning the primary spatial variability patterns in precipitation. Second, we applied the SHAP method to an Extreme Random Tree (ET) to identify the critical climate variables for precipitation forecasting. Finally, we tested three different ML methods: ANN, SVM, and XGBoost for their performance in XJ precipitation prediction. The specific process is shown in  Fig. 2 . 2.3.1 Feature selection methods The ET is an integrated learning algorithm based on decision trees. It extends the random forest to address supervised classification and regression problems more effectively (Geurts et al., 2006 ). The ET model was constructed using dimensionality-reduced predictor variables. Relying on Pearson’s correlation coefficient, we calculated the correlation coefficients between the precipitation and various features. Features exhibiting an absolute correlation coefficient value exceeding 0.3 were selected to establish the initial feature set, with the outcomes of this selection detailed in Text S2. The ET model provides a ranking of feature importance. In ET models, decision tree nodes are usually partitioned based on the Gini coefficient or entropy-based information gain, which quantifies the degree to which each feature enhances data purity during the tree construction process and serves as a crucial metric for evaluating feature significance. However, feature importance rankings obtained based on the contribution of features to the overall impurity of the data fall short of elucidating individual predictions (Meng et al., 2020 ). SHAP, proposed by Lundberg and Lee (2017) , is a game-theory-inspired methodology capable of quantifying the influence of each feature on a model’s predictions via both global and local analyses. Consequently, we introduced SHAP to interpret the contributions of individual features and conducted feature filtering. The SHAP package in Python was used to interpret the ET models.  2.3.2 Prediction methods The choice of machine learning methods is typically based on factors such as data types, volume, nonlinearity, efficiency, and accuracy (Adnan, 2019 ). In this work, a large number of multi-scale variables are input into the model, and the precipitation data exhibit a high degree of nonlinearity. Therefore, three machine learning (ML) methods namely, ANN, SVM, and XGBoost are considered for the prediction of summer precipitation in XJ. Here is a brief description of the ML methods. More details about the model setup are described in Table S1  to Table S3  of Supporting Information . An ANN is a flexible method for approximating non-linear functions, enabling the derivation of desired outputs from given inputs, where the relationships between variables are not explicitly known (Song et al., 2020 ). An ANN consists of an input layer, any number of hidden layers and an output layer. ANN, with its complex network structure, typically achieves high fitting accuracy of fitted models and demonstrates significant advantages in predicting precipitation time series (Tuba et al., 2021 ). However, to avoid the risk of overfitting associated with more complex network structures, we use only three hidden layers, with the maximum number of neurons approximating the number of predictors. ANNs typically have complex parameters. Parameters including the learning rate and training iterations significantly influence the accuracy, reliability, and operational efficiency of the ANN model (Dreyfus, 2005; Galushkin, 2007 ). Adjusting these parameters is time-consuming, making it difficult to find the optimal settings. To enhance model precision, this study employs a grid search to optimize the hyperparameters of the model. SVM demonstrate superior generalization and predictive capabilities in addressing problems associated with high dimensionality, and non-linearity (Collobert and Bengio, 2000 ). This is achieved by applying inner-product kernel functions to forge a linear relationship between the input and output data (Hearst et al., 1998 ). Due to its robustness in handling noisy data and its ability to avoid overfitting, SVM has become a popular method in hydrological forecasting (Gu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018 ). The performance of the SVM model is affected by the penalty factor C, along with hyperparameters such as the kernel function parameter gamma (Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ). In order to improve the model performances, the particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm was applied to optimize the parameters for SVM. The particle swarm optimization algorithm performs a global search to find the optimal SVM parameters, thereby avoiding local optima (Marini and Walczak, 2015 ). Furthermore, its high learning speed and low memory requirements make it suitable for various nonlinear applications in the hydrological field (Li et al., 2020; Pour et al., 2018 ). XGBoost is a ML algorithm that evolved from traditional gradient boosting techniques. It effectively mitigates the risk of overfitting by minimizing a regularized objective function and automatically managing missing values, thereby excelling in both classification and regression predictions (Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ). XGBoost is a powerful nonlinear relational modeling method that is widely used for precipitation prediction and provides state-of-the-art results (Dong et al., 2023; Monego et al., 2022 ). The XGBoost model has several critical hyperparameters that are amenable to tuning, including maximum depth, gamma, colsample by tree, subsample, and learning rate (Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ). These parameters are complex and time-consuming to adjust, so we optimize the configuration through a grid search.  2.3.3 Model validation To train the ML model, we used precipitation data from 1961 to 2012, whilst the forecast results from 2013 to 2017 were used for validation. Given the limited sample size, five-fold cross-validation was implemented to mitigate the risk of overfitting. The performance of the model was evaluated using two metrics: the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). The ML model demonstrating the best prediction performance was selected based on the aforementioned settings. Summer precipitation forecasts were validated for each station using the optimal model. To assess the accuracy of the precipitation forecasts, three quality assessment metrics for precipitation forecasting were utilized: Percentage Score (PS), Anomaly Correlation Coefficient (ACC), and Symmetric Consistency (SC). Detailed definitions of these three metrics are given in Eqs. 1–3 :(1) P s = a × N  0   + b × N  1   + c × N  2    ( N − N  0    )  + a × N  0   + b × N  1   + c × N  2   + M   × 100     where: N0  is the number of stations with correct climate trend prediction; N1  is the number of stations with correct first-order anomaly prediction; N2  is the number of stations with correct second-order anomaly prediction; N is the actual number of participating evaluation stations; M is the number of stations where there are no secondary anomalies and the precipitation anomaly percentage ≥100% or equal to −100 %; a is the weight coefficients of climate trend terms, b is the first-order abnormal terms and c is the second-order abnormal terms. Using this method, a = 1, b = 2, and c = 4.(2) A C C = ∑ i = 1  n  ( y  i   − y ¯   )  ( o  i   − o ¯   )   ∑ i = 1  n  ( y  i   − y ¯   )  2   ∑ i = 1  n  ( o  i   − o ¯   )  2           where: y  i   and o  i      represent the predicted and observed values, respectively; y  ̅  and o  ̅     represent the average values of the predicted and observed values, respectively; and n is the number of samples.(3) S C = N  0    N  × 100 %     where: N0  is the number of stations for which the climate trend prediction is correct; N   is the actual number of stations participating in the evaluation.    3 Results 3.1 Basic evolution of precipitation  Fig. 3  illustrates the interannual variability in summer precipitation in XJ. The results of the 5-year moving average indicated a general upward trend in summer precipitation in XJ, with a phase of low rainfall from the 1960s to the early 1980s, followed by an escalation in precipitation from the late 1980s to the 21st century, when it entered a period of high rainfall. There was a decline in summer precipitation in the mid-2000s, but it has increased significantly again since the 2010s, exhibiting clear phase changes. To supplement the characterization of precipitation, an Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis accounting for spatiotemporal patterns was introduced.  Fig. 4  illustrates the two predominant patterns and their corresponding Principal Components (PCs). The first and second eigenvectors account for 31.62 % and 13.55 % of the total variance, respectively, and are distinct from one another according to the criterion defined by North et al. (1982) . The principal components of the two eigenvectors (PC1 and PC2) are presented as bars in Fig. 4 b and d, respectively, with their trend lines shown as black dashed lines. The first and second principal component exhibited a positive trend, demonstrating a general upward trend in summer precipitation across XJ. The spatial distributions of the two eigenvectors are presented in Fig. 4 a and c, respectively. The spatial distribution of the first eigenvector exhibits a consistent sign pattern with the maximum loading located over the central Tianshan region of XJ (Fig. 4 a).This suggests that variations in summer precipitation in XJ over recent decades have been marked by a consistent pattern and that the Tianshan region has emerged as the central region most sensitive to precipitation change. The main feature of the second eigenvector is a north–south dipole structure characterized by an out-of-phase relationship between the regions north and south of the Tianshan Mountain (Fig. 4 c). A positive (negative) phase of the second eigenvector is featured by enhanced (suppressed) precipitation over the Northern XJ (NXJ) and suppressed (enhanced) precipitation over the Southern XJ (SXJ). Based on the results of the EOF analysis, we delineated Northern XJ (NXJ) and Southern XJ (SXJ) for further discussion.  3.2 Key variables contributing to precipitation predict from ET models Using the ET model, we computed the SHAP values of the model input variables, thereby identifying the key variables influencing precipitation in both Northern and Southern XJ.  Fig. 5  illustrates the mean absolute SHAP values for the 15 most significant features of the model. The Niño Region B Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (NINO B SSTA), Pacific Subtropical High Intensity (PSHI), Western Pacific Subtropical High Intensity (WPSHI), and Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI) were identified as the four most important predictor variables for summer precipitation in NXJ (Fig. 5 a). The SHAP values in  Fig. 6  show that the NINO B SSTA was the predominant climatic variable linked to the decrease in summer precipitation in NXJ. Additionally, a weakened PSHI or WPSHI reduced summer precipitation in NXJ. Positive SHAP values were predominantly associated with high MEI values, implying that El Niño potentially augmented summer precipitation in NXJ. The key predictors of summer precipitation in SXJ include the South China Sea Subtropical High Area (SASHA), South China Sea Subtropical High Intensity (SASHI), Western Pacific Warm Pool Strength (WPWPS), and Atlantic multidecadal oscillation (AMO) (Fig. 5 b). The SASHA, SASHI, and WPWPS were identified as the primary climatic variables contributing to the enhancement of summer precipitation in SXJ. Conversely, most AMO values exhibited negative SHAP values, indicating that this climate model exerted a negative influence on summer precipitation in SXJ. To better understand the correlations and dependencies among the predictors, we show the correlation matrix and SHAP dependency plots for the top four most influential variables. From Figure S1a , there is a strong positive correlation between WPSHI and PSHI with NINO B SSTA, suggesting that elevated sea surface temperatures (SST) in the Pacific are associated with the intensification of Pacific subtropical high, contributing significantly to the summer precipitation in NXJ ( Fig. 7 ). Specifically, when the MEI and NINO B SSTA indices are positive, an increase in Pacific SST intensifies the influence of El Niño on summer precipitation in NXJ. This suggests that El Niño events generally coincide with the intensification of Pacific subtropical high, consequently leading to an increase in summer precipitation in NXJ. This is consistent with the results reported by Chen et al. (2019)  and He et al. (2015) . Summer precipitation in SXJ is predominantly influenced by the South China Sea Subtropical High (SCSH), the WPWPS, and the AMO. Of these factors, WPWPS shows a strong positive correlation with AMO, as depicted in Figure S1b . Specifically, the majority of high WPWPS values are associated with higher AMO values, corresponding to high SHAP values. ( Fig. 8 ). This is consistent with the general belief that the AMO influences the SST of the western Pacific warm pool through various atmospheric coupling and oceanic teleconnection processes (Chen et al., 2019; He et al., 2015 ). When SST of the Atlantic and western Pacific warm pool are high, the warm oceanic waters supply moisture and heat to the atmosphere and release latent heat, consequently leading to an increase in summer precipitation in SXJ (Chen et al., 2004; Delcroix et al., 1996 ). Higher area and intensity of SCSH corresponds to high SHAP values, it suggests that the intensification of SCSH contributes to the increase in summer precipitation in SXJ. This is primarily due to the intensification of the SCSH, which enhances the component of the East Asian monsoon, enabling a greater influx of moisture from moisture pathways such as the Bay of Bengal, western Pacific, or South China Sea into Xinjiang (Rijin, 2008; Wang et al., 2007 ).  3.3 Precipitation prediction based on machine learning  Fig. 9  illustrates a comparative analysis of the observations and predictions of the three ML models during the training period. The predictions of the ANN model were almost in agreement with the observations, exhibiting a correlation coefficient exceeding 0.99 and achieving a significance level of 0.001. The XGBoost model demonstrated robust performance in NXJ yet exhibited suboptimal performance in SXJ. Compared with other ML models, the fitting accuracy of the SVM model was not satisfactory for either Northern or Southern XJ.  Fig. 10  illustrates the results of the quantitative evaluation of the predictive performance of the ML model during the forecast period. It can be observed that the ML models exhibited superior performance in NXJ compared to SXJ. For NXJ, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) values for the ANN, XGBoost, and SVM models were 15.34 (20.40), 22.58 (25.18), and 25.42 (29.51), respectively. In SXJ, the MAE and RMSE values for the ANN, XGBoost, and SVM models were 23.21 (30.01), 26.01 (35.46), and 42.97 (48.75), respectively. In summary, a comparative analysis involving the visual curve (Fig. 9 ) and mathematical statistical methods (Fig. 10 ) indicates that the ANN model exhibits superior predictability for summer precipitation in XJ. We further validated the prediction of summer precipitation variations at each meteorological station during the forecast period using the ANN model ( Fig. 11 ). The results showed that the ANN model performed well in both Northern and Southern XJ, with five-year average Ps, Acc, and Sc scores of 81.80, 0.06, and 0.60, respectively. In addition, the predicted results exhibited significant interannual differences. The Ps scores exceeded 80 for 2013, 2015, and 2016, and the corresponding Acc and Sc scores also demonstrated elevated levels in these years. Conversely, the Acc scores for NXJ in 2017 and SXJ in 2014 and 2017 were negative, suggesting that the model did not accurately capture the spatial distribution of precipitation during these years.  Fig. 12  shows box plots comparing the predicted and observed summer precipitation values for the forecast period in Northern and Southern XJ. The 2013 forecasts aligned closely with observations, particularly in NXJ, where the predicted and observed values were nearly identical. There were some differences between the predictions and observations in 2015 and 2016. The model underestimated summer precipitation for 2015 along SXJ, whereas it overestimated 2016 precipitation. In addition, the 2016 forecasts for NXJ exhibit increased fluctuations and uncertainty. The low levels of forecast observation concordance in 2014 and 2017 can be attributed to XJ experiencing extreme weather events, including floods and droughts, during these years (http://xj.cma.gov.cn/ ). These differences indicate the limitations of the ANN model in accurately predicting precipitation anomalies.  3.4 Importance of the anomalous precipitation variable For the results presented in Section 3.2 , the contributions of the predictor variables to precipitation were computed as yearly values. However, their contributions may vary across months. In this section, our investigation focuses on the importance of seasonal variables for years characterized by summer precipitation anomalies based on SHAP values. Table S4  presents the years characterized by summer precipitation anomalies in XJ.  Fig. 13 , predicated upon the ordering of precipitation anomaly percentages, illustrates the relative contributions of the top five variables from December of the previous year to May of the current year to precipitation in a typical summer precipitation anomaly year in NXJ. In 2016, the most important contributing variables were PSHI, WPSHI, NINO B SSTA, and Indian Ocean Basin-Wide Index (IOBWI), with WPSHI being the leading variable contributing ∼11–16 % to the precipitation along NXJ, followed by PSHI, which contributed 9–13 %. In 1993, the contributions of the main variables across each month were roughly the same (5–9 %), including the NINO 4 SSTA, MEI, and NINO C SSTA. Among these variables, the NINO 4 SSTA and MEI were the most important contributing variables, covering the entire period from winter to spring.  Fig. 14  illustrates the relative contributions of the top five variables from December of the previous year to May of the current year to the precipitation in a typical summer precipitation anomaly in SXJ. In 1984 and 1985, the major variables contributing to precipitation anomalies were similar for each month, including WPWPS, AMO, Oyashio Current SST (OC SST), Solar Flux Index (SFI), and South Indian Ocean Dipole (SIOD). In 1985, WPWPS and AMO contributed slightly more (7–9 %) than the other variables, whereas the contributions of the other variables were roughly the same (3–5 %). In 1984, the NINO W SSTA was the leading variable in predicting summer precipitation anomalies in SXJ (8–12 %). However, by 1985, this contribution had diminished to mere 1–2 %. This shift is potentially attributable to the diminishing influence of El Niño and the transition within the AMO, reflecting the interannual SST variability of sea surface temperatures within the NINO W region. Supplementary Figure S2  and Figure S3  provides information on the relative contributions of the major variables to precipitation in typical years with fewer precipitation anomalies in NXJ and typical years with excessive rainfall anomalies in SXJ.  Table 1 , based on the frequency with which variables feature among the top 5 ranked for each month, shows the common winter and spring variables for predicting summer precipitation anomalies in XJ. Specifically, NINO B SSTA, IOBWI, and NINO C SSTA are identified as the primary variables for forecasting summer precipitation anomalies in NXJ. These variables have considerable impact on both less precipitation anomalies and excessive precipitation anomalies and cover the entire winter to spring period. Other variables affecting summer precipitation anomalies in NXJ found in Table 1  are NINO A SSTA, NINO 4 SSTA, PSHI, and others. Although not as common as those mentioned above, they play an important role in precipitation prediction. In SXJ, the top five winter and spring variables affecting summer precipitation anomalies are nearly identical, with only a slight difference in rank order. AMO, NINO B SSTA, IOBWI, SCSHA, and SCSHI constitute the primary variables for predicting precipitation in the years of excessive precipitation anomalies, while SIOD, WPWPS, AMO, and SFI are identified as crucial for forecasting in years characterized by less precipitation anomalies. There are some differences in the variables that influence the anomalies of excessive and less precipitation: for instance, MEI is among the top five leading variables of the less precipitation anomalies in NXJ, yet it is absent from the top five variables of the excessive precipitation anomalies. Furthermore, the predominant variables influencing summer precipitation anomalies differed between Northern and Southern XJ. For example, precipitation anomalies in SXJ are intricately linked to variations in the South China Sea Subtropical High, whereas those in NXJ are largely unaffected. In addition, the precipitation anomalies exhibited distinct key variables across different seasons. For instance, the NINO 4 SSTA and WPSHI are among the top five leading variables of anomalous precipitation in NXJ in winter only, not in spring.   4 Discussion In this study, SHAP analysis was used to identify the relative importance of the predictor variables. Our results suggest that the key variables contributing to summer precipitation over the Northern XJ is different from those over the Southern XJ. The Niño Region B Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (NINO B SSTA), Pacific Subtropical High Intensity (PSHI), Western Pacific Subtropical High Intensity (WPSHI), and Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI) were identified as the four most important predictor variables for summer precipitation in NXJ. MEI and NINO B SSTA are important indicators used to reflect the impact of ENSO events on climate. Hu et al. (2021)  observed that during El Niño events, the sea surface temperature (SST) in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific increases, which subsequently strengthens the East Asian summer monsoon. This enhancement results in an increased transport of moist air to northern Xinjiang, thereby leading to increased precipitation. PSHI and WPSHI predominantly influence precipitation in Xinjiang by modulating monsoon airflow and moisture transport pathways (Hu et al., 2021 ). Specifically, when the WPSHI strengthens, the subtropical high-pressure system in the northwest Pacific extends northward, enhancing the monsoon airflow from the South China Sea and the western Pacific. This enhanced monsoon airflow transports moisture through Central Asia to northern Xinjiang, leading to increased precipitation (Hu et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2009 ); As the PSHI strengthens, the enhanced transport of westerly moisture fluxes facilitates the transport of moisture from the Pacific and Indian Oceans to northern Xinjiang, thereby increasing precipitation in this region (Ke et al., 2023 ). The key predictors of summer precipitation in SXJ include the South China Sea Subtropical High Area (SASHA), South China Sea Subtropical High Intensity (SASHI), Western Pacific Warm Pool Strength (WPWPS), and Atlantic multidecadal oscillation (AMO). Hu et al. (2021); Jin et al. (2023)  demonstrated that an increase in the area and intensity of the subtropical high over the South China Sea leads to a northward expansion of the control range of the South Asian high-pressure system. This expansion enhances the transport of moisture from the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea through the East Asian monsoon system and the westerlies, facilitating increased precipitation in Central Asia and southern Xinjiang. Ke et al. (2023)  demonstrated that the intensified WPWPS increases the evaporation over the Western Pacific, resulting in more water vapor being transported to southern Xinjiang through the East Asian monsoon system. Research by Shi et al. (2021); Zhao et al. (2022)  indicates that the positive phase of the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) enhances cross-regional atmospheric circulation patterns, such as Rossby wave trains and upper-level jet streams, facilitating the increased transport of moisture from the Atlantic Ocean to the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Subsequently, this moisture is conveyed to Northwest China and Central Asia via the South Asian and East Asian summer monsoon systems as well as the mid-latitude westerlies. Summer precipitation in XJ is influenced by a variety of climatic factors, such as SST and atmospheric circulation, including the North Atlantic Oscillation (Yang and Zhang, 2008a ), subtropical westerly jet (Yang and Zhang, 2008a ), Western Pacific Warm Pool SST (Chen and Jiang, 2022 ), South Asian High (Lu et al., 2019 ), and tropical Indian Ocean SST (Zhou et al., 2015 ). These climate indices are not isolated but interact and synergistically affect precipitation. In Section 3.2 , we briefly explained the correlation and dependency between variables and their statistical relationship with precipitation. However, the complex physical processes and their comprehensive impact on precipitation patterns exceed the scope of this study. To support our conclusions, we incorporate findings from previous research, which provide additional context. For instance, Chen et al. (2019); He et al. (2015)  demonstrated that the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) influences the sea surface temperature (SST) of the Western Pacific Warm Pool (WPWP) through various atmospheric coupling and oceanic teleconnection processes. Combining this with studies by Rijin (2008); Wang et al. (2007)  on the impact of increased SST in the Atlantic and WPWP on precipitation, we illustrate a potential mechanism by which WPWP and AMO may influence summer precipitation in southern Xinjiang; (Yang and Li, 2005 ) proposed that sea surface temperatures in the tropical Indian Ocean can influence the intensity and area of the South Asian High System through Walker and Hadley circulations, and (Shao and Zhang, 2012 ) suggested that when the Winter NAO is strong (weak), the East Asian subtropical westerly jet strengthens (weakens) in spring. In the future, studies are needed to further interpret the mechanisms of precipitation formation and evolution to help improve the accuracy of summer precipitation forecasts for XJ. Present study found the ANN model to perform better compared to PSO-SVM and XGBoost in prediction of summer precipitation in XJ. Predictions obtained from this study are compared with recent work conducted in arid areas. Zhang et al. (2023)  developed a multiple regression prediction model for summer precipitation in eastern Northwest China using a time-scale separation factor. The Percentage Score (PS) and the Symmetric Consistency (SC) score were 69 and 54, respectively, reflecting improvements of 6 % and 7 % over the model based on original sea surface temperature factors. Xie et al. (2023)  simulated precipitation changes in the arid regions of Central Asia using CMIP5 and CMIP6 models. The RMSE values for annual mean precipitation in the Xinjiang region ranged from 39.75 to 315.94 mm for the CMIP5 models and from 32.71 to 182.24 mm for the CMIP6 models. Therefore, despite the precipitation model representing a challenging task, the ANN model developed in this study has significantly improved performance, achieving RMSE values as low as 20.40 in northern Xinjiang and an average Ps score of 81.80. Although our ANN model performs well here, they could be improved further in anomalous precipitation prediction. Understanding the mechanisms behind precipitation anomalies is essential for enhancing the accuracy of anomalous precipitation prediction. In this study, we explore the variables for predicting summer precipitation anomalies in XJ. The South China Sea Subtropical High has a significant impact on excessive precipitation anomalies in SXJ. This finding was corroborated by Zhang (2021) , who suggested that moisture from the South China Sea provides moist air currents in XJ. Additionally, the SSIOD was associated with fewer precipitation anomalies in XJ. This is consistent with the results reported by Zhao et al. (2009)  and Zhang, 2021 . These studies suggest that variations in SSIOD can affect summer precipitation in XJ through alterations in the wind field and anomalies in water vapor transportation. The SFI is a key variable influencing lower precipitation anomalies in SXJ. Concurrently, some studies have found a pronounced response of the Pacific and Atlantic sea surface temperatures to solar activity, potentially explaining the mechanism by which solar activity indirectly affects precipitation in XJ through changes in sea surface temperatures (SST) (Zhou et al., 2021b ); In NXJ, MEI is identified as one of the top five variables contributing to less precipitation anomalies, suggesting El Niño and the Southern Oscillation exhibit a pronounced summer precipitation response in the region. This is consistent with the results reported by Chen et al. (2022); Lu et al. (2019) . Their results suggested that variations in ENSO offer predictability for summer precipitation anomalies in NXJ. Overall, the sea surface temperature anomalies across various regions, including the tropical Indian Ocean, Kuroshio Current, Western Pacific Warm Pool, tropical Mid-Eastern Pacific Ocean, and North Atlantic Ocean, are closely linked to summer precipitation anomalies in XJ. These findings are consistent with those of previous research (Yang et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2021a ), the employment of NINO B SSTA, IOBWI, WPWPS, and AMO as predictor variables was substantiated to increase the accuracy of forecasting summer precipitation anomalies in XJ. In addition, summer precipitation in XJ is influenced by various atmospheric circulation factors. This study suggests that the West Pacific Subtropical High and South China Sea Subtropical High are closely related to summer precipitation anomalies in XJ, which is consistent with findings from previous research on the circulatory characteristics of summer precipitation anomalies in XJ (He, 2005; Liu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020 ). Combining dynamical models with neural networks is a trend in future development. Currently, this combination is mostly reflected in Short-term precipitation forecasting and climate pattern recognition (Slater et al., 2023 ). The dynamic neural network model has demonstrated strong predictive capabilities for anomalous precipitation in short-term forecasts. Yao et al. (2024a), (2024b)  develop a dual-source attention dynamic neural network (DSADNet) for precipitation nowcasting. During a typical anomalous precipitation event, the DSADNet model accurately predicted the start and end times of precipitation several hours in advance, and capturing the fluctuations in precipitation intensity. Wang et al. (2024)  evaluated STPF-Net on radar data from southeastern China, training separate models for 6 and 12 h forecasts. The models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting the central location and primary intensity of heavy precipitation events. In the future, we can consider extending this approach to long-term precipitation forecasting to enhance the model's accuracy in predicting precipitation anomalies.  5 Conclusion Based on observational data from 95 meteorological stations in XJ and 130 climate indices, this study developed a ML-based model for summer precipitation prediction in XJ and explored the leading variables contributing to such predictions. The main conclusions are as follows:(1) The ANN model demonstrated robust performance during both training and prediction periods. For Northern and Southern XJ, MAE and RMSE values of the ANN model were 15.34 (20.40) and 23.21 (30.01), respectively, surpassing the predictive accuracy of other ML models. However, the ANN model demonstrated diminished predictive efficacy in years with precipitation anomalies (specifically, in 2014 and 2017), suggesting limitations in its ability to accurately forecast anomalous precipitation.  (2) NINO B SSTA, PSHI, WPSHI, and MEI were identified as the four most important predictor variables for summer precipitation in NXJ. The NINO B SSTA was the predominant climatic variable linked to a reduction in summer precipitation in NXJ. Additionally, a weakened PSHI or WPSHI reduced summer precipitation in NXJ. However, El Niño may have contributed to the increase in summer precipitation in NXJ. The key predictors of summer precipitation in SXJ include SCSHA, SCSHI, WPWPS, and AMO. The SASHA, SASHI, and WPWPS were identified as the primary climatic variables contributing to the enhancement of summer precipitation in SXJ. Conversely, the AMO exerted a negative influence on summer precipitation in SXJ.  (3) Sea surface temperatures across the tropical Indian Ocean and tropical Pacific Ocean were closely linked to summer precipitation anomalies in XJ. Furthermore, in SXJ, the South China Sea subtropical high, Solar Flux, and Sea Surface Temperatures of the North Atlantic and Western Pacific were significant factors influencing anomalous precipitation.    In future work, we plan to extend our approach by combining dynamical models with neural networks for long-term precipitation forecasting, as recommended in the discussion. We also note that the feature importance explained with SHAP mainly identifies the statistical co-incidence among the predictor variables and the precipitation. Given the co-linearity among the predictors, the effects of individual variables on precipitation prediction may become confounded, leading to potential ambiguity and reduced reliability in the results. Future work can consider Causal inference methods such as Do-Calculus, Structural Causal Models, and Granger Causality Analysis, to isolate direct causal effects even in the presence of confounding variables, thereby addressing challenges posed by co-linearity.
