1 Introduction Throughout human history, access to clean water has been a fundamental necessity. However, over time, the factors jeopardizing its availability have increased. In response to this growing challenge, industrialized countries have made remarkable strides in treating contaminated water supplies, thereby ensuring a plentiful and safe water supply for their populations (AbuKhadra et al., 2020; Abukhadra et al., 2022; Bellucci et al., 2022; Bin Jumah et al., 2021; Salam et al., 2021a ). Groundwater has a significant impact on human livelihoods, promoting agricultural output, economic growth, and ecological balance (Agbasi et al., 2023; Gad et al., 2023; Mthembu et al., 2020 ). However, the expansion of industrial and urban activity, particularly in developing countries, has raised concerns about groundwater pollution (Eid et al., 2023, 2024b; Gaagai et al., 2023; Hamdy Eid et al., 2022; Ibrahim et al., 2023; Salem et al., 2023 ). Both natural events and human-caused activities contribute to the degradation of groundwater quality in aquifers (Agbasi et al., 2023, 2024; Agbasi and Egbueri, 2022; Ayejoto et al., 2023, 2024; Eid et al., 2024c ). Consumption of contaminated groundwater endangers plants, humans, and animals alike (Danielopol et al., 2003; Madhav et al., 2020; Mthembu et al., 2020 ). Egypt's agricultural areas are under increasing pressure due to decreasing water sources and rapid urbanization. Egypt is currently dealing with a critical shortage of clean and fertile agricultural soil. Recent efforts have focused on growing Egypt's agricultural economy by reclaiming new lands and enforcing strict rules. The Egyptian Ministry of Agriculture has stated measures to restore about 1.5 million acres (607,028 ha) of marginal or desert land for agricultural use including Siwa Oasis (Elnazer et al., 2023; Ghoubachi, n.d. ). The composition of water has a strong effect on ecological components, soil, plant quality, and yield, ultimately affecting health of the individuals (Alengebawy et al., 2021; Eid et al., 2023, 2024c, 2024d ). Extensive contaminants have arisen as a major threat to the safety of groundwater, resulting in a lack of freshwater supplies (Islam and Mostafa, 2021 ). Groundwater's natural quality is defined by its inherent composition, which varies spatially across many scales and is governed by processes such as dissolution, rock weathering, and ion exchange leaching (Al-Mashreki et al., 2023; Eid et al., 2023, 2024b; Flores et al., 2023; Gaagai et al., 2023; Gad et al., 2023; Ibrahim et al., 2023; Salem et al., 2023 ). Beyond natural factors, human activities including intensive agriculture, unplanned urban expansion, and industrial and mining operations can all have an impact on groundwater quality (Ahamad et al., 2023; Saeed et al., 2023a, 2023b ). As a result, a thorough understanding of the mechanisms that determine groundwater quality, as well as robust assessment approaches, are critical for long-term groundwater resource management (Noori et al., 2023 ) A variety of strategies have been used to assess groundwater quality, including the fuzzy comprehensive evaluation method (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2022 ) and the matter-element extension method (Wang et al., 2019 ). The entropy-based weighted technique is used to calculate the weights of hydrochemical parameters in groundwater and then assess their quality with index called entropy-weighted water quality index (EWQI) (Agbasi and Egbueri, 2022 ). This method aids in minimizing the examination of excessive components, precisely defining water quality categories, and establishing if the assessed variables are consistent with decision-making criteria for certain functional areas (Ikram et al., 2024; Islam et al., 2017 ). The EWQI calculates groundwater quality precisely, allowing it to be ranked according to groundwater quality criteria (Amiri et al., 2014; Islam et al., 2017 ). Trace metal contamination in water is hazardous, especially during the early developmental stages of children and adults. Metals such as Fe, Mn, NO3 - , Pb, Cr, Cd, Ni, Cu, As, and Mo are classified as highly toxic by the United State Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA), presenting major concerns due to well-documented negative health impacts associated with excessive water consumption (Eid et al., 2024e, 2024a; Jat et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2021; Saeed et al., 2024 ). However, the current study investigates only Fe, Mn, and NO3 -  due to the presence of geogenic source and intensive agricultural activities that can increase their concentration in the groundwater and further investigation could fill this gap by analyzing more elements. Exceeding permitted amounts of iron, manganese, and nitrate can result in non-carcinogenic health hazards such as hyperkeratosis, hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, restrictive lung disease, and gangrene. Furthermore, chronic exposure to water contaminated with trace metals can cause cancer (Eid et al., 2024c; Ravindra and Mor, 2019 ). Heavy metal exposure, both acute and chronic, can cause several health risks in humans, including cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, dermal, hepatic, renal, respiratory, reproductive, neurological, immunological, developmental, hematological, and mutagenic outcomes (Eid et al., 2024c; Gad et al., 2023; Pandey et al., 2016; Saeed et al., 2023b ). Previous studies in different countries highlighted the most significant indices to evaluate the environmental and health risk developed from the accumulation PTEs in water which included heavy metal pollution index (HPI), ecological risk index, Hazard quotient (HQ), total hazard index (HI), and modified heavy metal index (MHMI) (Agbasi et al., 2023, 2024; Agbasi and Egbueri, 2022; Ayejoto et al., 2023, 2024; Eid et al., 2024c ). These indices could give a clear view of the vulnerability of individuals to non-carcinogenic risk regarding oral or dermal exposure to water contaminated with PTEs. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are increasingly being used to predict Water Quality Index (WQI) values based on key water quality indicators as alternative method of traditional WQI calculation which need complex sub index equations of several measured parameters (Khoi et al., 2022 ). ANNs provide an alternate method for understanding and managing groundwater quality, as well as aquatic water bodies (Nathan et al., 2017 ). They have demonstrated efficacy as a technique for computing and predicting water quality in a variety of aquatic situations. The prediction models using feed forward back propagation (FFBP-NN) can accurately forecast water quality indices and health risk indices using a subset of key parameters, saving time and resources (Jadhav et al., 2023 ). For instance, in Iran’s Karoon River, predictions of Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) were performed using nine input parameters (Emamgholizadeh et al., 2014 ). ANNs have also been utilized to forecast chloride, and alkalinity levels in streams by considering input attributes such as pH, temperature, and electrical conductivity (Wagh et al., 2018 ). There are many prediction models of WQIs were used in previous studies globally such as SVMR, RF, ANFIS, XGBoost regression, and Decision tree (Eid et al., 2023; Gaagai et al., 2023; Gad et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2019; Ibrahim et al., 2023; Mohd Zebaral Hoque et al., 2022; Salem et al., 2023 ) that were not tested in this study and could be covered in the future investigation. However, the ANN specifically (FFBP-NN) was reported to be the most common model was successful to predict water quality and risk indices with high accuracy and efficiency (Chalisa and Thitima, 2022; Kadam et al., 2019; Kulisz et al., 2021; Lee Yoot Khuan et al., 2002; Sakizadeh, 2016 ) and it was applied in the current study. The Siwa area in Egypt depends heavily on groundwater which is utilized in potable and irrigation. Because of the scarcity of freshwater streams, the Oasis is sustained by a combination of surface water (lakes and drains) and groundwater, which is vital to its survival(Aly, 2020 ; Hamdy Eid et al., 2022 ). Groundwater is sourced from hot springs and boreholes in aquifers such as deep aquifer (NSSA) and shallow aquifer (TCA). This underground water provides a variety of uses, including agriculture, drinking, and domestic use. Four salt lakes in the depressions of the Oasis region get their water from cultivated land drainage, hot springs, and boreholes that penetrate the aquifer systems (Abdulaziz and Faid, 2015; Eid et al., 2024b ). Groundwater demand in the study area (Siwa Oasis) has increased over time due to agricultural activities, tourist attractions, and the economy's expansion. Consequently, multiple wells have been constructed. However, the haphazard installation of these boreholes, along with an excessive amount of groundwater extraction, endangers water pressure and quality (Abdallah, 2007; Abdel-Mogheeth, 1996; Abou El-Magd and Faid, 2007; Aly, 2001; Aly et al., 2016; Aly and Benaabidate, 2010; El Hossary, 2013 ). Illegal groundwater drilling worsens these challenges, emphasizing the significance of researching for regular monitoring of the amount and purity of limited water resources. Studying hydrochemistry, stable isotopes, and heavy metals in groundwater is critical for sustainable water resource management, safe and reliable water supplies, and protecting human and environmental health, especially in Siwa Oasis. Metalloid and trace metal contamination caused by industrial operations, agricultural practices, and urban waste management is a major concern in western desert of Egypt. This problem is compounded by the country's rising industrialization and urbanization rates. Furthermore, agriculture occupies the bulk of Siwa land area. To increase grain productivity, agricultural techniques use a wide range of fertilizers and insecticides. Furthermore, manure from animal husbandry activities is used as an organic fertilizer in agriculture. As a result, these harmful elements mix with surface water and then permeate the groundwater aquifer directly or indirectly during precipitation recharge processes (Hamdy Eid et al., 2022 ). As a result, the objectives of this research were to: (1) determine the mechanisms that drive the enrichment of different elements and contaminants in groundwater using geochemical models and statistical methods; (2) Application of integrated wight water quality index (IWQI) method to detect suitability of different water resources for drinking; (3) Ecological, Environmental, and health risk assessment of water associated with nitrates and heavy metals; and (4) Development new model to predict the IWQI and health risk indices using FFBP-NN. This study is the first source-oriented health concern evaluation of all water resources in Siwa area, and it provides critical insights and reference information for the optimal mitigation and management of groundwater pollution.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Site description Siwa Oasis, a depression −18 m below sea level in Egypt's western desert (northern section), is located at 25°43' E and 29°12' N ( Fig. 1 ). It is located approximately 320 kilometers from the Mediterranean Sea and 560 kilometers from Cairo, covering an area of roughly 1100 square kilometers and housing an estimated 23,000 people (Aly et al., 2016 ). Agriculture, which includes palm tree cultivation, olive oil production, and various fruits and vegetable crops, is the primary economic activity, with industrial operations like mineral water bottling and olive oil extraction also playing important roles (Abdallah, 2007; Abdel-Mogheeth, 1996; Abou El-Magd and Faid, 2007; Aly, 2001; Aly et al., 2016; Aly and Benaabidate, 2010; El Hossary, 2013 ). Siwa Oasis experiences an arid climate characterized by a substantial evaporation rate (16.8 mm/d), which declines to approximately 5.4 mm/d in winter. Insufficient rainfall/precipitation, approximately 10 mm annually, exacerbates the parched conditions. This unique climatic environment, combined with the oasis's seclusion and limited water supply, presents obstacles for both residents and businesses (Abdulaziz and Faid, 2015; Eid et al., 2024b ).  2.2 Hydrogeology Siwa Oasis' geology consists of different hydrostratigraphic units ( Fig. 2 a), including deposits like dunes and salt flats (quaternary deposits) cover the ground surface and few meters depths, Miocene and Eocene units represent the Tertiary carbonate aquifer (TCA) comprised of limestone (LS) and dolomite intercalated with thin layers of shale and clay minerals. Layers from other geological ages, including the Palaeozoic (basement rocks), and Mesozoic (lower cretaceous Nubian sandstone and upper cretaceous shale), are also present (Abdallah, 2007 ; Elnaggar et al., 2016 ). Siwa's water resources are extracted mainly from two principal aquifers (deep NSSA and shallow TCA). The Miocene aquifer (Tertiary carbonate aquifer) serves agricultural and domestic requirements, whereas the Nubian sandstone aquifer (NSSA) is mainly used for drinking water and irrigation (Abdulaziz and Faid, 2015; Afifi, 2005; Aggour and Faid, 2007; El Hossary, 2013 ). Soil salinization and waterlogging around salt lakes such as Zeitoun (eastern Siwa lake), Aghormi, Siwa, (central Siwa lakes) and Maraqi lake (western lake) highlight the significance of efficient water resource management in ensuring the sustainability of oasis water sources while addressing environmental challenges (Abdallah, 2007; El Hossary, 2013; Misak et al., 1997 ). The groundwater flow direction based on the hydraulic head from 27 wells penetrating NSSA (Fig. 2 b) is South east- north west (SW-NE) and South west-north east. There is cone of depression in the central part of Siwa Oasis due to intensive agricultural activities require over extraction of groundwater for irrigation and drinking.  2.3 Sampling and analysis The sampling points were selected to cover all water resources in Siwa Oasis, in total, 120 samples were collected (February, 2022) including 103 water samples from deep and shallow aquifer (NSSA & TCA) that are used mainly for all kind of purposes. The rest of samples were collected from springs (6 samples), drains (6 samples) and surface lakes (5 samples). The physical parameters were conducted in the field (pH, temperature, and electric conductivity). three polyethylene bottles were used for each sample where one bottle for major ions and the second for heavy metals and the third for stable isotopes. The bottles of PTEs (Fe&Mn) were acidified with nitric acid to keep the elements dissolved in water. All samples were preserved in Ice box with temperature 4°C till it preserved in the laboratory for analysis. During the investigation, portable meters were calibrated to measure essential physico-chemical characteristics such as pH and EC (electrical conductivity). Flame photometry was used to quantify alkaline metal ions, specifically Na+  and K+ . The total hardness (TH) was measured using EDTA methods, while CO3 2−  and HCO3 −  were examined volumetrically. Ion chromatography was used to measure NO3 −  and SO4 2− enrichment. The Mg2+  concentration was determined using the TH and Ca2+  concentrations. Accurate chloride levels were determined using AgNO3  titration. The Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) method was used to investigate heavy metal concentrations. This analytical technique gives precise assessments of heavy metal content in water samples. The stable tracers’ measures were stated as (δ2 H) and (δ18 O) in per mil (‰) deviation of the 18  O/16 O and 2 H/1 H ratio in the standard formula termed as VSMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water), with δ18 O and δ2 H values of 0 ‰ (Gat and Gonfiantini, 1981 ). Los Gatos Research Liquid-Water Isotope Analyser-24d were used to conduct isotope analysis on water samples. The instrument utilizes off-axis integrated cavity ring-down spectroscopy to estimate the absolute levels of 2 H1 H16 O, 1 H1 H16 O, and 1 H1 H18 O by laser absorption. We used laboratory standards calibrated with international standard (δ2 H = −147.7 ‰; −74.9 ‰; and −9.0 ‰; δ18 O = −19.95 ‰; −10.41 ‰ and −0.53 ‰; for BWS1, BWS2, and BWS3) (Czuppon et al., 2018 ). Precisions were greater than 0.15 ‰ and 1.0 ‰ for d18 O and d2 H, respectively. 2.3.1 Quality assurance and control The water quality analysis followed the standard methodology specified by the American Public Health Association (APHA) in 2012. To ensure the accuracy of on-site testing equipment, we carefully standardized all instruments with deionized water and buffer solutions before starting sample analysis. Various quality assurance procedures were applied during the water sample examination. The analytical processes were validated by instrument calibration, accuracy, and predictability evaluations. Charging balance errors (CBE) were evaluated following field observations and then validated in the laboratory. The samples were examined in triplicate, and the average values were also given. Equation (1) was used to analyze anion-cation balance errors based on the principle of neutrality, which states that the sum of the number of cations equals the sum of the number of anions in meq/L. The CBE for all examined samples was within the permissible range of ± 5 %.(1) %CBE = (ΣCations-ΣAnions)/(ΣCations+ΣAnions) *100    Furthermore, the quality assurance of the analytical procedure was double-checked through a meticulous examination involving Certified Reference Material (CRM) and the blank technique analysis.   2.4 Hydrochemical evaluation The hydrochemical evaluation methods included Chadha, Gibbs, CAI-I, CAI-II, and Ionic ratios (Mg2+ /Na+  vs Ca2+ /Na+ , HCO3 - /Na+  vs Ca2+ /Na+ , NO3 - /Na+  vs Cl- /Na+ , NO3 - / Cl-  vs Cl- , and δ18 O vs Cl- ) plots to characterize the water type of different water samples and the mechanism controlling the water chemistry from the geogenic and anthropogenic origin. Digrammes software and Excel sheet were used for visualization of the graphs. The application of geochemical modeling to determine the mineral saturation state and the main minerals have the most contribution for enrichment of elements in water through the water-rock interaction. The model extracted from PHREEQC showed the output as saturation index (SI) for each mineral with positive value indicating super saturation state of specific mineral and negative value for under saturation state while zero value indicates equilibrium state where the water is not able to dissolve or precipitate certain minerals. The saturation index was calculated based on standard equation (Martinez et al., 2017; Parkhurst and Appelo, 1999 ) using log ion activity product divided by solubility product (SI = log (IAP/K).  2.5 Integrated weight water quality index (IWQI) The Integrated Weight Water Quality Index (IWQI) is a ranking system that indicates the overall impact of physicochemical characteristics on water quality, as determined by the Water Quality Index (WQI). In this work, IWQI was used to evaluate water quality (Al- Asad et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2020 ). IWQI computation consists of five steps: entropy weighting, CRITIC-based weighting, determining integrated weights, calculating the integrated-weight water quality index, and evaluating groundwater quality using WQI values. 2.5.1 Entropy weight calculation The entropy-weighted water quality index (EWQI) is an approach to estimate water quality that relies on certain hydrochemical variables to calculate an overall entropy value (Adimalla, 2021; Shannon, 1948 ). According to IWQI values, water can be categorized into five distinct classes (Al- Asad et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2020 ). When the IWQI value is below 100 (excellent to good category), the water is deemed suitable for oral consumption and other uses, between 100 and 150 indicates medium or intermediate quality, while the poor and extremely poor water quality fell between 150 to greater than 200.   2.6 Ecological risk index The prospective ecological risk index (RI) for metals is a powerful tool for assessing the ecological risk associated with the presence of PTEs in a certain ecosystem. This score takes into account characteristics such as heavy metal concentrations, kinds, sensitivity, toxicity, and background levels. While it can be applied to a variety of scientific domains, it was especially used in this study to assess the potential risk associated with PTEs in water resources. The formula is given as follows (Eq. (16) ):(16) RI = ∑ E  r  i   = T  r  i   × c  ⅈ    c i  bg             In the equation, E  r  i     reflects a substance's potential risk component; T  r  i     depicts the specified metal's toxic response variable (Table S1 ); c  ⅈ     designates a typical level of each metal in the water sample; and c i  bg      represents the background value of every metal (Table S1 ) which were used by previous study in the same study area (Mohamed et al., 2020 ). The RI represents the whole contamination's ecological impact. RI is classified into four categories of risk levels: low, moderate, significant, and very high with RI values <30, 30–60, 60–120, and >120, respectively (Saeed et al., 2023b; Yuan et al., 2015 ).  2.7 Heavy metal pollution index (HPI) The Heavy Metals Pollution Index (HPI) is a useful measure to estimate heavy metal pollution levels affecting water bodies (Al-Hejuje et al., 2017 ). The HPI is particularly useful in identifying the appropriateness of water for ingestion in the presence of PTEs. It is calculated using attribute ratings and weighted mean calculations. Each pollutant characteristic is weighted, and a grading system ranging from 0 to 1 is used to highlight the importance of each quality aspect or its relation to specified reference standards (Shankar, 2019 ). Eqs. Typically, three classifications is utilized to assess HPI. These classes are excellent (HPI below 15), good to intermediate quality (HPI between 15 and 30), poor quality (HPI greater than 30), extremely poor quality (HPI between 76 and 100), and significant pollution risk/unsuitable quality (HPI exceeds 100) (Edet and Offiong, 2002; Qu et al., 2018 ).  2.8 Health risk regarding PTEs and nitrates The human health hazards in this investigation are evaluated utilizing an approach approved by the USEPA (EPA, 2004 ). This risk analysis extensively explores how environmental pollutants (heavy metals) affect human health. The identified hazards are classed as carcinogenic (CR) or noncarcinogenic (NCR) (Habib et al., 2020 ). However, the current study focused on NCR risk of Iron and Manganese metals. Noncarcinogenic risks, focus on exposure issues such as genetic and teratogenic effects. In this study, heavy metals (HMs) identified in drinking and irrigation water sources are predominantly absorbed by the human body through food and skin contact (Gade et al., 2021 ). The mathematical calculation of the risk indices was performed using Equations 19 and 20. By considering different exposure pathways, the study provides a thorough knowledge of the possible health concerns linked to contaminants such as PTEs (Fe and Mn) in water supplies for drinking, providing significant insights for risk management and public health protection.(19) CDI  oral   = C × IR × EF  BW × AT    × ED     (20) CDI  dermal   = ( C × ET × EF × Kp × SA × CF )  ( BW × AT )    × ED      Here, C, IR, ED, BW, CF, SA, Kp, EF, ET, AT parameters or reference numbers represent element concentration in the water sample (mg/L), daily ingestion rate (L/day), exposure duration (year), body weight (kg), conversion factor (L/cm3), exposed skin area (cm²), skin permeability coefficient (cm/h), exposure frequency (day/year), contact duration (h/day), Average exposure time (day), The value of IR, ED, BW, CF, SA, Kp, EF, ET, AT are reported with references (Adimalla, 2020a; Alam et al., 2024; Giri and Singh, 2015; Liang et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2023; Phillips and Moya, 2013; Saleem et al., 2019; Stein, 1975; Wu et al., 2009 ) in Table S1 . The hazard quotient value (HQ) for each element and total health hazard for all metals combined together (non-carcinogenic risks) were determined using these equations (Equation 21,22 and 23):(21) HQ  dermal / oral   = CDI  dermal   / CDI  oral    RfD  dermal   / RfD  oral          (22) RfD  dermal   = RfD  oral   × ABS     (23) HI = ∑ HQ      The Reference Dose (RfD) is a crucial metric that represents the quantity of a chemical that an individual can be exposed to daily without significantly increasing the risk of undesirable health effects. ABS is used to calculate absorption efficiency in the digestive tract (Table S1 ). The US EPA developed this complete framework for analyzing human health concerns (EPA, 1997 ). The input parameters for the model were EC, TDS, pH, TH, Na+ , K+ , Cl- , HCO3 - , Fe, Mn, NO3 - and SO4 2−  for IWQI and two attributes were removed from the model (Ca2+  and Mg2+ ), while only three parameters (Fe, NO3 - , and Mn) were used to predict HI. The Ca2+  and Mg2+  were removed from the input attributes after testing several models which started by using all attributes first (14 parameters). Second, removing some parameters step by step and check the accuracy of the model till we achieved the minimum optimum parameters that could be used for the prediction of IWQI (Ca2+  and Mg2+ ). Models with fewer attributes were tested using stepwise regression method. The modeling process trained using the ANN Fitting APP and the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. The feed-forward network (FFBP-NN) with two layers, sigmoid hidden neurons, and linear output neurons was employed, featuring one hidden layer. The neurons number in the hidden layer (ranging from 2 to 14) and performance was experimentally determined based on mean square error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), relative squared error (RSE), root mean square error (EMSE) and regression value R. Using one hidden layer is recommended by some researchers for fitting few data sets while several hidden layers could give good fitting in more complex model (Thanh Nguyen et al., 2020 ). The training set comprised 70 % of the data for IWQI and 80 % for HI, while the test and validation set each accounted for 15 % for IWQI and 10 % for HI. Selecting the proportion of training, validation, and test was conducted after application of several models and the best performance was achieved when the test and validation was 15 % and 10 % and training was 70 % and 80 of the datasets for IWQI and HI, respectively. The pH values of sampling vary from 7.8 to 8.4, 7.9–8.6, 7.6–8.3, 6.9–8.7, 6.4–8.9, in the lakes, drains, springs, TCA, and NSSA, respectively showing that all water resources fell between neutral to slightly alkaline condition, with the suggested pH range (6.5–8.4) for irrigation and drinking purposes.The electrical conductivity (EC) values exhibit significant variation ranging from 23250 to 188800 μS.cm−1 , 8390–20490 μS.cm−1 , 1840–11790 μS.cm−1 , 672–62000 μS.cm−1 , and 268–642 μS.cm−1  in the lakes, drains, springs, TCA, and NSSA, respectively. There is large variation in the EC value between surface water and groundwater which indicate that the surface water fell between saline (drains) to hyper saline (lakes) water class. The majority of samples collected from TCA and springs have similar range of EC value and fell within brackish water category. The rest of samples collected from the deep aquifer (NSSA) showed fresh water quality based on EC value. The shallow aquifer (TCA) and deep aquifer (NSSA) are the main water resources used for irrigation, drinking, and domestic purposes. The current findings showed that the TCA water can have a negative effect on the soil and plants and the irrigation water from shallow aquifer could cause soil salinization. It is recommended to select salt tolerant plants or water treatment before irrigation process. The deep aquifer showed its suitability for drinking and irrigation based on WHO and FAO guidelines. The predominant ions in NSSA were arranged in descending order of abundance are Na+  > Ca2+  > Mg²⁺ > K+ , with average concentrations of 65, 24.7, 17.8, and 19 mg/L, respectively. HCO3 −  emerges as the most prevalent anion, followed by Cl- , SO4 2- , SiO2 , and NO3 - , with average concentrations of 135.8, 93.9, 48.4, 43, and 5.2 mg/L, respectively. These substantially elevated levels can be attributed to the dissolving of evaporite minerals as well as ion exchange process with shale and clay minerals intercalated with sandstone layers (Eid et al., 2024b; Ibrahim et al., 2023; Salam et al., 2021b ). Sodium concentrations range from 18 to 280 mg/L, all investigated samples fell below FAO and WHO standard irrigation and drinking limit. Potassium levels range from 13 to 23 mg/L, averaging at 19 mg/L, suggesting unsuitability for irrigation and drinking in all samples, possibly attributable to weathering of potash feldspars or the use of chemical fertilizers (Eid et al., 2023; Salam et al., 2021b ). Calcium concentrations vary between 9.8 and 64.7 mg/L. Notably, all samplings exhibit calcium levels lower than irrigation standard threshold, with these significant concentrations potentially stemming from dissolution of gypsum, calcite and the dolomite as a cement material between grains of sand and the confined layers of upper cretaceous shale that separate the different formation between sandy layers of NSSA and the dissolution and/or ion exchange is the main factor during the circulation of water between different sand layer through the fault planes. The concentrations of magnesium, ranging significantly from 2.3 to 56.5 mg/L, with all samples falling below the FAO and WHO guidelines (Ayers and Westcot, 1985 ). These low magnesium levels may be connected to the dissociation of ferromagnetic minerals and cation-exchange reactions (Al-Mashreki et al., 2023; Salem et al., 2023 ) Regarding bicarbonate concentrations, which varied from 89.7 to 185.3 mg/L, all samplings were confirmed to be under the acceptable level for drinking and irrigation. The chloride concentration of all samples varied between 40.6 and 174 mg/L, and all samples fell below the drinking and irrigation threshold. The geogenic source of the Cl ions in the NSSA aquifer could be due to the presence of some halite and sylvite minerals intercalated in the aquifer system or from the old trapped sea water where the aquifer is overlained by marine sediments (lime stone and dolomite). Sulphate contents varied from 1.6 to 353.3 mg/L, with all samples demonstrating sulphate contents below the FAO and WHO standard limit (Ayers and Westcot, 1985 ). The presence of sulphates can be attributed to the dissolution of gypsum. The predominant ions in TCA were arranged in descending order of abundance are Na+  > Mg²⁺ > Ca2+  > K+ , with average concentrations of 1052.65, 359.1, 257.4, and 42.09 mg/L, respectively. Cl-  emerges as the most prevalent anion, followed by, SO4 2- , HCO3 − , SiO2 , and NO3 - , with average concentrations of 2901.3, 310.01, 160.85, 39.7, and 6.06 mg/L, respectively. These substantially elevated levels of Mg over Ca can be attributed to the dissolving of dolomite and silicate weathering more than calcite. The same condition for increasing Cl over HCO3 -  is due to dissolution of evaporite minerals (e.g. halite and sylvite minerals) in the marine sediments of TCA more than carbonate weathering. Sodium concentrations range from 92 to 10,000 mg/L, only 19 % of samples fell below the WHO standard drinking limit and 67.8 % of samples fell below FAO standard irrigation limit. The concentration of Ca, Mg, K, SO4 , and Cl ions exceeded the limits of irrigation in 16.6 %, 97.6 %, 100 %, 2.3 %, 88 % of the water samples showing that extensive water treatment and management of the TCA is required before irrigation process to prevent deterioration of the soil and plants. The nitrate concentration ranges from 1.4 to 4.2 mg/l, 1.4–4.2 mg/l, 2.8–15.4 mg/l, 1.4–29.4 mg/l, 1.4–14.2 mg/l in the lakes, drains, springs, TCA, and NSSA, respectively. The nitrate was higher in the groundwater than surface water suggesting natural/geogenic and anthropogenic sources of NO3 -  in the groundwater. The concentration of the trace metals (Fe and Mn) in the majority of samples exceeded the permissible standard for drinking which could cause health risk for child and adults and the current investigation will detect the risk of PTEs and nitrates in the water resources in Siwa depression.  3.2 Mechanisms controlling water chemistry 3.2.1 Chemical evolution along flow path The Piper graphical plot (Piper, 1944 ) employed to identify the hydro-facies of the water samples from different resources ( Fig. 4 ). The analysis revealed four distinct water types. The first facies/type, Ca-Mg-SO4, constitutes 26.8 % of the samples and includes 35 from the TCA, three from drains, two from springs, and one from Zeituna lake. The second type, Na-Cl facies, encompasses 44 samples from the TCA, five from the NSSA, four from lakes, three from springs, and three from drains. The remaining samples from the NSSA and TCA fall into two mixed categories: Ca-Mg-Cl-SO4 and Na-Ca-HCO3 facies. Variations in facies within the NSSA are likely due to water-rock interactions during the upward flow through fault planes, which result in differing salinity and temperature at various depths. The water type was determined in the different water samples using piper plot including Lakes and drains as a surface water and springs, deep NSSA (Nubian aquifer), and shallow TCA (Tertiary aquifer). Fig. 4  showed that all surface water samples (Lakes and drains) and groundwater samples collected from shallow aquifer (TCA) and springs fell between three facies type (Ca-Mg-SO4 , mixed Ca-Mg-Cl/SO4 , and Na-Cl) while the deep NSSA indicated that the different trend of chemical evolution start with Na-Ca-HCO3 , mixed Ca-Mg-Cl/SO4 , and end with Na-Cl facies. Based on previous study, The NSSA contain paleo-water and dose not receive any recharge due to lack of rain fall in the current arid study area and it is the only source recharge the shallow aquifer through upward flow under high pressure along the fault planes (Eid et al., 2024b ). The current findings demonstrate that the geochemical evolution of water chemistry (water type) in Siwa Oasis start by Na-Ca-HCO3  type as a first stage due to the paleo precipitation and interaction of water with NSSA (sandstone intercalated with clay minerals) and the precipitation of marine sediments of TCA (limestone and dolomite intercalated with traces of shale and clay) created a confined condition for the deep NSSA. The over pressure in the NSSA and presence of several fault planes facilitate the upward flow of fresh water to the TCA where the condition change of water-rock interaction due to the presence of limestone and dolomite with shale and clay minerals which increase the salinity (brackish water) change the water type from Ca-Mg-SO4  and then Na-Cl. The similarity in the water type of TCA, springs, and surface water could indicate that most of the springs in the study area originated from TCA through the fracture system and the main aquifer used for irrigation is the TCA that’s why the drains and lakes have similar facies. Several ionic ratios and indices were used to detect the ion sources and the mechanisms controlling water chemistry are Mg2+ /Na+  vs Ca2+ /Na+ , HCO3 - /Na+  vs Ca2+ /Na+  (Tlili-Zrelli et al., 2013 ), Na+ /(Na+ +Ca2+ ) vs TDS, TDS vs Cl- /(Cl+HCO3 - ) (Gibbs, 1970 ), Chloro alkaline index (CAI-I &CAI-II). These methods were used recently by several researchers (Mahmoudi et al., 2017; Schoeller, 1977 ).  Fig. 5 a, b shows three probable mechanisms could affect the water chemistry evolution based on the ionic ratio of Ca2+ /Na+  vs Mg2+ /Na+  and Ca2+ /Na+  vs HCO3 - /Na+  (Evaporation dissolution, Silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering). The water samples in the study area fell between two mechanisms, Evaporation dissolution and Silicate weathering. The water samples of the deep NSSA showed the dominance of silicate weathering factor influence the water chemistry while the rest of samples (TCA, springs, and surface water) fell between silicate weathering and evaporation dissolution mechanism. The sandstone, shale, and clay in the geological composition of the deep aquifer facilitate the water chemistry to be influenced with silicate weathering. On the other hand, the shallow aquifer consists of dolomite and limestone with some traces of clay minerals/shale could have strong effect on the water chemistry of through dissolution and ion exchange/silicate weathering. The ratio of Na+ /(Na+ +Ca2+ ) vs TDS and Cl- /(Cl+HCO3 - ) vs TDS (Fig. 5 c, d) can also give indication about different possible mechanisms affect the water chemistry in Siwa Oasis through three main zones in Gibbs Plot (Precipitation, Rock weathering/water rock interaction, and Evaporation crystallization). The current study showed that there is a sharp difference between the mechanisms controlling water chemistry in deep aquifer and shallow aquifer, springs and surface water. The groundwater chemistry in the deep aquifer system is affected only with interaction of water with sandstone and silicate minerals (rock weathering), while the TCA and springs samples are affected with crystallization/mineralization as well as the surface water were located in the top right of Gibbs scatter plot referring to evaporation factor. To detect the type of ion exchange (direct or reverse ion exchange), two chloro alkaline indices (Fig. 5 e) were implemented (CAI-I & CA-II). The positive and negative values result from the calculated index refers to reverse (Equation 34) and direct (Equation 35) ion exchange respectively.(34) 1/2Ca2+ -X + Na+ →1/2Ca2+  + Na+ -X (reverse ion exchange)   (35) Na+ -X + 1/2Ca2+ →Na+  + 1/2Ca2+ -X (ion exchange)    The results revealed that the two type of ion exchange exist in the aquifer systems. All samples collected from shallow aquifer, springs, surface water (Lakes & drains), and 50 % of deep NSSA are influenced by reverse ion exchange Ca2+  and Mg2+  in the rock (limestone and dolomite) were replaced with Na+  and K+  in water. The other 50 % of deep NSSA samples have negative values of CAI-I and CAI-II indicating direct ion exchange where Ca2+  and Mg2+  in the water were replaced with Na+  and K+  in the rock (Sandstone, shale and clay).   3.3 Nitrate, major ions, and PTEs source detection 3.3.1 Anthropogenic activities Anthropogenic activities have significantly impacted the water quality in the study area, primarily due to the discharge of domestic waste water, and agricultural activities. increasing the concentrations of SO4 2- , Cl− , and NO3 − . The elevated levels of SO4 ²−  and Cl−  in water samples are primarily due to evaporite dissolution and agricultural activities, while NO3 −  mainly originates from domestic sewage and agricultural activities. The ratios of Cl− / Na+  vs NO3 − /Na+  (Kou and Hua, 2019 ) ratios were used to characterize the influence of anthropogenic natural activities on water quality. As shown in  Fig. 6 , the deep aquifer (NSSA), shallow aquifer (TCA), springs, and drains water samples were affected by agricultural activities, while evaporite activities had significant impact on the lake samples.  3.3.2 Mineral saturation state and geogenic source of ions The application of PHREEQC models to calculate the saturation index or mineral phases in the surface water and groundwater is a significant tool to detect the main source or contribution of major ions in the water quality and mechanisms affecting water chemistry. The positive, negative, and zero values are the three pillars detect the precipitation, dissolution, and equilibrium state of minerals in water respectively. In the current study the physico-chemical parameters measured in water samples were used as an input parameter for the PHREEQC model and the output represented by +Ve, -Ve, or zero values of saturation indices (SIs) of Calcite, Dolomite, Gypsum, and Halite minerals. The relationship between SI value of the four minerals and the major ions could give a clear view about the effect of water rock interaction on the water chemistry and the source of major ions in water samples. The relationship between Ca2+  vs SI (calcite), Ca2+  vs SI (dolomite), and Ca2+  vs SI (gypsum) ( Fig. 7 a, b, c) demonstrated that Calcite and dolomite minerals are supersaturated while gypsum mineral is undersaturated in the majority of water samples collected indicating the capability of surface water, springs and groundwater in all aquifer system to precipitate calcite and dolomite. On the other hand, there is possibility for gypsum mineral to be dissolved in all water resources. At the same time the fitting curve and R2  values between Ca2+  vs SI (calcite), Ca2+  vs SI (dolomite), and Ca2+  vs SI (gypsum) (Fig. 7 a, b, c) showed that the source of Ca2+  in water samples originate from the three minerals in descending order gypsum > calcite> dolomite with R2  values 0.91, 0.66, and 0.60 respectively. The source of Mg2+  could be from Silicate weathering or dolomite dissolution. Fig. 7 d showed that the fitting curve between Mg2+  and SI (dolomite) has intermediate correlation with R2  value 0.61 which means there is a significant contribution from silicate minerals weathering beside dolomite dissolution as a source of Mg2+  in the surface water (drains &lakes) and groundwater. The source of Na+  and Cl-  could be determined by the relationship of Na+  vs SI (halite) and Cl-  vs SI (halite). Fig. 7 e, f revealed that all water resources in Siwa Oasis are undersaturated regarding halite and has the capability to dissolve more of this mineral. At the same time there is strong correlation of Na+  vs SI (halite) and Cl-  vs SI (halite) with R2  value equal 0.99 of the fitting curve which confirm the significant contribution of evaporite minerals such as halite as a main source of Na+  and Cl- . Fig. 7 g was utilized to confirm the paleo recharge source of the aquifer system based on the relationship between δ18 O and Cl-  and the range value of the δ18 O and δ 2 H (Table 2 ). The results revealed that there is depletion of the δ18 O (-8.57 to −10.29) and δ 2 H ( −66.3 to −78.5) in the groundwater samples (Table 2  and Fig. 7 g) confirming the ancient or paleo water in the shallow and deep aquifer and lack of recent recharge due to very hot and dry weather in the study area. All NSSA samples and significant number of TCA samples showed horizontal trend between Cl-  concentration and δ18 O and constant range of δ18 O values (between −11 and −12) with increasing concentration of Cl-  which represent ancient recharge source and water rock interaction only influence the water chemistry. On the other hand, few samples of TCA, springs, lakes, and drains showed enrichment of δ18 O with increasing the Cl-  concentration which indicate that evaporation, mixing of different water resource are two significant factors influence the water chemistry of these samples due to the contact with atmospheric temperature and mixing of different water, agricultural drainage and sewage water. Although the NSSA represent the main recharge source of shallow water in TCA, the chemistry of shallow water could be affected by water-rock interaction due to the carbonate minerals in TCA (limestone and dolomite), residence time, evaporation, and ion exchange causing salinity increase from fresh in NSSA to brackish in TCA which was clearly stated in Figure and Fig. 5 a, b, c, d, e (Ionic ratio, Gibbs plot, and CAI)  3.3.3 Source of Fe and Mn in water resources Most water samples collected showed high contamination of iron (Fe > 0.3) and manganese (Mn > 0.1), with mean value over the drinking or consumption limits based on WHO standards. This elevated concentration needs further treatment to avoid health risk of individuals in Siwa Oasis. Previous studies proved that the lower Miocene Moghra formation (north Siwa Oasis) mainly composed of limestone, clay, shale, and dolomite while the facies change in the east direction to sandstone with carbonate cement material rich in glauconite and bands of iron oxides. The iron oxides are mainly in the form of hematite minerals. Eid (Eid et al., 2024b ), applied geochemical modeling of 120 water samples and confirmed the super saturation of water with hematite minerals. Another study reported 0.6 % of MnO and 36.1 % of Fe2O3 were found in the geological composition of the Moghra formation MnO (Tawfik et al., 2018 ). The integration between our results and previous studies could prove the geogenic source of Fe and Mn and their concentration increased due to water rock interaction. The minerals hematite and rhodochrosite play a role in introducing iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) into groundwater due to their ability to dissolve in specific conditions within geological formations. Factors like pH levels, redox potential, temperature and the existence of matter can impact how quickly these minerals dissolve, thus affecting the levels of Fe and Mn present, in groundwater. Regions that have amounts of hematite and rhodochrosite may naturally contain high levels of iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) in their groundwater supply (Hu et al., 2022 ). This can impact the quality of water and its treatment processes. The results of PHREEQC model ( Fig. 8 a) demonstrated that the all samples collected from different resources were supersaturated with hematite indicating possibility of precipitation of this mineral in the soil or the floor of the salt lakes. The fitting curve between SI (Hematite) and Fe revealed that the aquifer system (TCA and NSSA) contains hematite (Fe2 O3 ) as a main source of Fe with R2 =0.97. Similarly, the fitting curve between SI of Rhodochrosite (MnCO3 ) and Mn metal showed high R2  value equal 0.82 (Fig. 8 b) which indicate the main source of Mn in water of Siwa Oasis is Rhodochrosite in the geological composition of the aquifer system. Fig. 8 a, b showed that the NSSA is more saturated in hematite and Rhodochrosite because it above basement rocks that contain geothermal water could feed NSSA with this mineral. Based on the isotope analysis and depletion of 18 O and 2 H in the current study and hydrodynamic condition from previous study (Eid et al., 2024d ), it is concluded that there is upward flow of water from NSSA to TCA as the only recharge source of shallow aquifer. The minerals saturation of Rhodochrosite and hematite change or decrease in TCA based on the several factors including geological composition, fracture system, flow path, redox environment, pH, residence time and groundwater extraction from TCA that discharge finally to the surface water (lakes and drains) through agricultural drainage.   3.4 water quality assessment based on IWQI The water quality index for drinking purposes based on IWQI can be classifies into four main quality type (extremely poor, poor, medium or intermediate good, and excellent quality) according to the calculated values. The range of this classification is >200, 150–200, 100–150, 50–100, and 0–50 for extremely poor, poor, medium or intermediate good, and excellent quality respectively.  Fig. 9 a classifies water based on IWQI values, indicating that 49.16 % of water samples fell into the extremely poor category (IWQI >200) including all surface water samples, five samples of springs (S104, S105, S106, S107, and S108), three samples of NSSA (S16, S18, and S19), and 32 samples of the TCA%. The results showed that 20.83 % of samples had IWQI values between 150 and 200 which fell within poor quality range represented by 25 samples collected from TCA. The IWQI value in 25 % of samples raged from 100 to 150 including 11 samples of NSSA, 1 spring sample and 18 samples of TCA which indicates medium quality category. The rest of samples (6 % of samples) fell within good to excellent quality represented mainly by NSSA samples and 1 sample of TCA. The current findings demonstrated that the deep Nubian Sandstone aquifer contain fresh water suitable for drinking except some locations in the western Siwa area between El-Maraqi Lake and Siwa lake. The drinking water quality of the NSSA based on IWQI increases from west to east direction. On the other hand, the groundwater of TCA is suitable for drinking purposes only in the south eastern part of Siwa Oasis while the central and western part is more deteriorated and not suitable for human consumption. The study area, primarily agricultural, involves extensive crop cultivation with fertilizer application and significant animal husbandry activities. The main reason for the quality deterioration of the TCA is increasing the salinity due to water rock interaction and over extraction of water for irrigation purposes as well as return back of agricultural drainage through the fracture system. Previous study reported that there is small contribution from the salt lakes to the TCA through downward leakage causing salinity increase. The NSSA is in covered by thick layer of upper cretaceous shale creating a confined condition and prevent contamination or increasing the salinity while in the western Siwa there are faults and shale layer is thin and cone of depression in the water level which facilitate downward leakage from the shallow aquifer.  3.5 Ecological risk and heavy metal pollution indices The ecological risk factor is a broadly recognized tool for estimating the degree of contamination with heavy metals/PTEs (Fe and Mn) and its anticipated impact on water and sedimentary habitats (Saeed et al., 2023b ). This indicator takes into account heavy metal levels ecological and toxicological impacts, and broader environmental consequences, resulting in a comprehensive assessment of the ecological risks associated with heavy metal contamination in sediment and water systems. In this work, the possible ecological risk indicator (RI) for potential harmful components was investigated, as shown in  Fig. 10 a. The RI values for the NSSA, TCA, springs, drains, and lake samples ranged from 8.3E-05–0.002, 2.6E-06–0.006, 6.2E-06–1E-04, 1.3E-05–1.2E-04, and 6.8E-05–0.003, respectively. These data suggest that the heavy metals examined in the water supplies of Siwa Oasis, Egypt, pose no serious ecological danger, with RI values less than 30. Fig. 10 a depicts possible ecological risk in relation to the sampling sites within the research area, indicating the relationship between pollution level and related ecological risk. The research area is characterized by extensive agricultural activity as well as residential zones. These zones contribute to the accumulation of larger quantities of heavy metals in sediment, which can then seep downward into groundwater or wash off into surface water. The relatively low RI values suggest limited immediate ecological risk; however, the presence of heavy metals still warrants concern due to their potential to accumulate and exert long-term effects on aquatic ecosystems. It is crucial to conduct continuous monitoring and comprehensive risk assessments to detect any changes in pollution levels and associated risks promptly.  3.6 The heavy metal pollution index (HPI) The heavy metal pollution indicator (HPI) is crucial tool for evaluating the overall contamination level in water resources, specifically assessing the PTEs impact on water quality and potential health risks associated with exposure to this metals (Rahman et al., 2022). In this study, the HPI values for heavy metals in water samples fell within the three main range zone of HPI classification (HPI < 15, 15 ≤ HPI ≤ 30, and HPI > 30) indicating low, medium, and high pollution regarding potential toxic element (Fe & Mn). The HPI value for NSSA, TCA, Springs, drains, and lakes, ranges from 5 to 114.9, 0.158–321.7, 0.35–4.9, 0.74–7.08 while for lakes it was between 3.3 and 153.8. According to the classification by (Edet and Offiong, 2002 ), nearly 84.6 % of samples including the majority of springs, drains, lakes, NSSA, and TCA water samples had HPI value below 15 indicating low level of pollution regarding iron and manganese for human consumption. It was noted that 6.6 % of water samples including three NSSA samples and five TCA samples had HPI value between 15 and 30 indicating medium pollution with respect Fe and Mn metals. The rest of samples (10 %) including two samples of NSSA, one lake sample, and nine samples from TCA fell within high pollution category regarding to heavy metals with HPI value greater than 30. This indicates that while the majority of groundwater and surface water samples are mostly free from severe heavy metal contamination, the levels of iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) are notably higher, contributing to elevated HPI values in western Siwa area (Fig. 10 b). The presence of Fe and Mn at significant levels poses potential health risks, as these metals can accumulate in the human body over time, leading to adverse health effects such as neurological and developmental disorders. Therefore, it is essential to take proactive measures to mitigate these risks. Previous research has shown that the tertiary carbonate rocks in Egypt's northern desert contain glauconite and Fe oxide detrital grains. Specifically, the Moghra Formation in the research area has been found to contain about 1.6–36.1 mg/l of Fe2 O3 , and 0.6 mg/l of MnO. This composition suggests that the geogenic sources significantly contribute to the elevated Fe and Mn in the water samples. Establish continuous and comprehensive monitoring programs to track PTEs concentrations in surface water and groundwater, particularly focusing on Fe and Mn levels. This will help in early detection and timely intervention. Upgrade water treatment facilities to incorporate advanced technologies capable of efficiently removing heavy metals, including Fe and Mn, from ground water before it reaches consumers especially in the western Siwa depression. By adopting these recommendations, the potential risks linked to Fe and Mn contamination in the Oasis area can be effectively managed, ensuring the safety and well-being of the local population and preserving the water quality for future generations.  3.7 Non-carcinogenic risk of potential toxic elements The non-carcinogenic hazard indices (HI) were assessed by calculating ingestion and dermal absorption pathways' hazard quotients (HQ). The outcomes reveal the combined potential health risks for humans from exposure to Fe, NO3 -  and Mn metals for both children and adults. The toxic elements iron (Fe), nitrate (NO3 - ) and manganese (Mn) were measured to estimate the NCR risk in different age groups (child & adult). The hazard quotient values (HQ) for oral contact in adults oscillated as follows: Fe: 0.0001–1.56, Mn: 0.0003–4.24 ( Table 3 ). For children, the HQ ingestion values were: Fe: 0.0005–5.96, Mn: 0.001–16.17 (Table 3 ). According to the HQ ingestion scores, the health concerns linked to iron and manganese consumption are often greater for younger children than older individuals. In most water samples, the HQ oral levels of Fe and Mn for both child and adult fell within the permitted range (HQ < 1). These values indicate significant health risks from these metals, particularly for children. At the same time some locations showed significant health risk regarding iron and manganese in the two groups through oral expossure. The results showed that 2.5 %, 8.3 %, 9.16 %, and 10.3 % of water samples had HQ ingesion value greater than one regarding HQFe (adult), HQMn (adult), HQFe (child), HQMn (child), respectively indicating high and significant health risk in these sampling locations. The HQ values for dermal exposure in adults were: Fe: 3E-06–3.7E-02, Mn: 3.0E-05–5.0E-01 (Table 3 ).For children, the HQ dermal values were: Fe: 8.7E-06–1.1E-01, Mn: 8.8E-05–1.5 (Table 3 ). The HQ (dermal & adult) values in all samples fell within the permissible level (HQ < 1) for all heavy metals (Fe & Mn), indicating low risk from these metals through skin contact. In case of Child, The HQ (dermal) value was acceptable (HQ < 1) for iron, indicating low risk from Fe metal through skin contact, while the HQ dermal values for Mn was above one (HQ > 1) in 3.33 % of samples, demonstrating significant or increasing health risk from Mn metal through skin contact (Table 3 ). These findings highlight the necessity for stringent actions to mitigate Fe and Mn contamination in the water resources of Siwa area to protect human health, particularly for vulnerable populations such as children. In this investigation, a health risk assessment for adults and children regarding nitrate exposure was performed in accordance with the guidelines established by the EPA (EPA, 1997 ). Table 3  summarizes the results of this assessment. The results of HQDermal  were consistently lower than zero for all three age groups, whereas HQOral  ranged from 0.03 to 0.71 with an average of 0.14 for adult, and 0.06–1.23 with an average of 0.24 for children (Table 3 ). This data demonstrates that nitrate consumption resulting from groundwater intake directly via oral/ingestion contact poses an elevated or severe health risk (HQ > 1) for children in only 1.66 % of water samples, but no danger exists for the adult population in the analyzed location. In other words, the hierarchy of HQ under oral and cutaneous exposure was clearly obvious, with HQOral  > HQDermal  (Table 3 ). Based on the risk assessment guidelines established by the EPA (EPA, 1997 ), a non-carcinogenic risk is deemed acceptable if the total Hazard quotient (HQ) is less than one (HQ <1). When the HQ surpasses one, it indicates a heightened probability of adverse health effects resulting from exposure. Notably, among the 120 water samples analyzed, the levels of nitrate exposure in drinking water exceeded the acceptable limit (HQ oral >1) in two samples located in the central and western part of the investigated area for children while the HQ oral for adults does not have threats or health risk regarding exposure to nitrates in water (HQ <1). Specifically, the results highlight that children in the study area face a heightened risk of non-carcinogenic effects due to the consumption of drinking water with elevated nitrate concentrations. The central and western part of Siwa oasis is affected by high concentration of nitrates compared to eastern part due to the intensive agricultural activities and decline of the water table (cone of depression) because of over extraction of groundwater for irrigation purposes which increase the possibility of irrigation water return back to the aquifer contaminated with nitrates from the soil. This observation aligns with previous research by Adimalla (2020c, 2019) , which has consistently emphasized the increased susceptibility of children to chronic non-carcinogenic risks owing to their smaller body weight and distinct behavioral characteristics compared to adults. The geographic distribution of the HQ strongly suggests that adults, and children in the west and center parts of the Siwa area are at an elevated health risk than the eastern region. Groundwater samples taken from TCA (S77 and S94) are particularly inappropriate for direct consumption due to inadequate non-carcinogenic values. Excessive nitrate intake can cause a variety of negative biological effects, including hypertension, severe cyanosis, blue baby syndrome/methemoglobinemia, infant mortality, stomach cancer, goiter, thyroid gland abnormalities, migraines, rashes, cytogenetic defects, and congenital deformities. (Adimalla, 2020c, 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ). The non-carcinogenic risk of nitrate in drinking water is particularly critical in many regions worldwide where populations rely solely on groundwater without prior quality inspection (Adimalla, 2020c, 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ). An integrated study by Ravindra (Ravindra and Mor, 2019 ) in northern India evaluated the potential health risk of nitrate, revealing that 29 out of 80 groundwater samples posed higher non-carcinogenic health impacts on children due to high nitrate concentrations. Similarly, (He and Wu, 2019 ) investigated the health implications of nitrate in the northern Shandong Peninsula of China and found that 87.6 % of groundwater samples were unsuitable for drinking based on nitrate levels. Their study also indicated that health risks due to nitrate intake through oral and dermal exposure pathways were most injurious to infants and children. Ravindra (Ravindra and Mor, 2019 ) conducted a comprehensive investigation in the north of India to assess the feasible health hazards of nitrate, and found that 29 of 80 sampled groundwater had increased non-carcinogenic adverse health effects on children due to elevated nitrate levels. In a similar way He, (He and Wu, 2019 ) investigated the health effects of nitrate in the north Shandong Peninsula of China and discovered that 87.6 % of sampled groundwater were unsafe to drink due to nitrate content. Their research also found that the health concerns associated with nitrate intake via oral and cutaneous exposure pathways were especially harmful to babies and children. The outcomes of this study emphasize the growing health concerns connected with consuming contaminated drinking water. The findings of this research study highlight the escalating health hazards linked to ingesting impure drinking water. Therefore, it is crucial for local governments to initiate immediate measures and monitoring to reduce nitrate contamination in groundwater and ensure the supply of safe water in the affected locations of Siwa region The hazard index (HI) is a useful measure to gauge the overall likelihood of health risk caused by toxic metals in ground and surface water. It takes into account all potential ways of exposure, particularly oral and skin routes. The HQs related to every specific metal and contact route are added together to compute the HI. This holistic method provides a fuller understanding of the cumulative health risks linked to metal contamination in Siwa Oasis' water resources, as well as an appraisal of the region's overall health effect and water source safety. The HI oral values ranged from 0.06to 5.77 with mean value 0.56 for adults and 0.13–20.99 with average value 1.86 for children (Table 3 ). The HI dermal levels ranged between 0.0004 and 0.51 with mean value 0.04 for adults and 0.001–1.51 with mean value 0.12 for children (Table 3 ). Although the majority of surface water and groundwater samples had low risk for child and adult regarding Hazard index value (HI<1) through ingestion and skin contact, there are some locations showed very high risk. The current findings showed that there is no health risk through dermal contact for adult in all samples. On the other hand, 10 %, 10.83 %, 2.5 % of water samples had high health risk through oral and dermal exposure with hazard index value greater than one in the following orders HI oral (adult), HI oral (child), and HI dermal (child) (Table 3 ,  Fig. 11 ). This clearly shows that children have become more susceptible to oral and cutaneous exposure with Fe and Mn than adults. Given these findings, it is critical to regularly track the content of these elements in the various water bodies of Siwa Oasis and examine their possible health impacts. The groundwater in the research area is non-rechargeable and serves as the principal source of water for a variety of purposes, making the circumstances even more severe. The HI values distribution maps for people of all ages, obtained by both cutaneous and ingestion, revealed that the center and western regions of Siwa Oasis are the most susceptible to NCR risk. These findings highlight the urgent need to implement efficient control and mitigation techniques to reduce the accumulation of PTEs and protect public health, particularly among children, who are more vulnerable to the negative health impacts of these contaminants.  3.8 Prediction model using FFBP-NN The prediction model using FFBP-NN was used to predict the water quality and health risk indices (IWQI and HI). In the case of the integrated weight water quality index (IWQI), the input parameters were selected after several models were run with 1000 epochs, and the accuracy was checked based on maximizing R2  and minimizing mean square error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), relative square error (RSE), and root mean square error (RMSE). The optimum features or parameters that were successful to predict the IWQI are EC, TDS, pH, TH, Na+ , K+ , Cl-, HCO3 - , Fe, Mn, NO3 - and SO4 2− . The current model showed that the best structure of FFBP-NN to predict the IWQI based on physicochemical parameters and PTEs was using one hidden layer with five neurons and the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. The optimum prediction was obtained at epoch 86 from 1000 iterations used, where performance showed a successive decrease in the MSE and an increase of R2  for the training, validation, and testing with the training period.  Table 4  presents the results of network training (MSE, MAE, RSE, RMSE, and Regression R-value), categorized into training, validation, and testing subsets. The regression value (R) for the training, validation, and test data were 0.999, 0.998, and 0.963, respectively. In each case, R > 0.95, which is indicative of a good fit for the network. The overall regression coefficient was 0.99, confirming a high overlap between the measurement points and the fit line with the ideal Y = T prediction line. This strong correlation suggests that the FFBP-NN model effectively captured the relationship between the input variables and the IWQI, providing reliable predictions across the training, validation, and testing datasets after testing different models by removing different features (one at a time) from the input data. It was found that the model with the best performance resulted after 12 features from 14 features were utilized where Ca2+  and Mg2+  were removed and achieved MSE, MAE, RSE, and RMSE of 0.57, 0.59, 1.0E-05, and 0.75 for training, and 0.45, 0.47, 2.9E-05, and 7.9E-05 for validation, and 0.66, 0.63, 2.5E-05, and 0.81 for test, respectively. The slight difference of MSE, MAE, RSE, and RMSE between the training, validation, and test showed the accuracy of the model and there is no overfitting which indicate the prediction model was successful to predict IWQI of the unseen data. This model’s performance was similar to a more complex model that used all the original features. According to  Fig. 12 , there was a strong relationship between the true IWQI (calculated data) and the predicted IWQI made by the FFBP-NN model using the best set of input features with R2 = 0.963. The model was used to predict the IWQI in the aquifer system of Siwa Oasis including shallow and deep aquifers. The model was performed for the two aquifers together where the NSSA recharge the TCA and both aquifers have similar chemical characteristics except the salinity of water that increased in the shallow aquifer due to water-rock interaction and mixing with old trapped sea water in the fracture system in some locations. The potential toxic elements (Fe, NO3 -  and Mn) only were used as input parameters to predict the health risk indices (HIoral and HIdermal) for children and adults through oral and dermal exposure to iron, nitrates and manganese. The structure of the neural network included three inputs and the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. The model showed the best performance with one hidden layer and five neurons. The model was performed to stop after six times of errors and 1000 iterations with a learning rate of 0.01. The MSE, MAE, RSE, and RMSE were calculated with R2  value to avoid overfitting in the prediction model. The model was tested with two to seven neurons in the hidden layer, and the optimum case was five neurons in one hidden layer; the model showed high performance after seven epochs. Fig. 12  and Table 4  illustrated that the relationship between actual and predicted HI was strong with R2  values 0.998, 0.999, 0.998, and 0.998 and MSE values 0.009, 4.6E-05, 5.4E-05, and 3.08E-05, and MAE values 0.085, 0.005, 0.005, and 0.003, and RSE values 0.030, 0.001, 006, and 008, and RMSE values 0.095, 0.007, 0.007, and 0.006 for HI (oral, child), HI (oral, adult), HI (dermal, child), and HI (dermal, adult), respectively. The current model using FFBP-NN was successful in predicting the health risk indices regarding oral and dermal exposure to PTEs in children and adults without overfitting which was confirmed by the slight difference of MSE, RMSE, MAE, and RSE between training, validation, and test (Table 4 ). In summary, the current research study proved that the FFBP-NN models are strong tools to predict the water quality and health risk indices with high accuracy. The prediction model could be very useful tool for the decision makers for water management implications in the study area saving time and cost of analysis which was clearly obvious in case of IWQI that we could predict the IWQI without need for Ca2+  and Mg2+  measurements.  3.9 Limitation of the current study and recommendation for future research Although, the current study offers a comprehensive approach through integration of hydrochemistry, geochemical modeling, water quality and the environmental and health risks developed from PTEs in all water resources of Siwa Oasis, there is still gap could be covered in the future work. This gap includes collecting more water samples from the deep aquifer could give more and general details regarding water quality in all Siwa Oasis. The PTEs in this study included only Fe, NO3 -  and Mn for the risk evaluation, while the future work could include several PTEs such as Cd, Cr, Pb, Ni, As, Zn, Co, Mo, V, etc to interpret the carcinogenic risk and source of more toxic metals that threaten the population health in Siwa region. Several advanced prediction models could be applied in future study such as Multiple linear regression, random forest, support vector machine, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to detect the most accurate model that could be generalized in the study area to predict WQI, HI, and carcinogenic risk (CR). More advanced statistical methods could be useful to determine the mechanism controlling water chemistry in the aquifer system such as self-organizing map, principal component or factor analysis, and mixing model using isotopic tracers with physicochemical parameters.   4 Conclusion The current research was performed by selecting 120 sampling sites to cover all water bodies in Siwa region, Egypt. The main aim of the study focused on using advanced methods such as integrated weight water quality index (IWQI), ecological risk and heavy metals pollution indices (RI and HPI), Health risk indices (HQ and HI) regarding oral and dermal exposure to potentially toxic elements (Fe and Mn) and Nitrates (NO3 - ). The FFBP-NN tool was applied to predict the water quality and risk indices based on physicochemical parameters and heavy metals. Hydrochemical evaluation integrated with ionic ratio and geochemical model was applied to detect the nitrate and primary ion sources. The key findings of this research showed the dominance of NSSA by mixed Ca-Mg-Cl/SO4  fresh water facies and mainly influenced by silicate weathering. In contrast, the shallow aquifer (TCA) is mainly affected by evaporation- dissolution processes, silicate weathering and reverse ion exchange, increasing its salinity to be dominated by brackish water with Ca-Mg-SO4  and Na-Cl facies/water type. The primary sources of Ca2+  were found to be in descending order gypsum > calcite> dolomite with R2  values 0.91, 0.66, and 0.60 (Ca2+  vs. saturation index), while The Mg2+  originated from dolomite and silicate weathering. Halite mineral was the main contributor of Na+  and Cl-  in the samples of water. In contrast, the nitrates sources fell between atmospheric inputs in the case of NSSA, soil nitrogen in TCA, springs, and drains, while sewage water has a strong effect on the lakes. The current findings demonstrated that the NSSA water is suitable for drinking except in some locations in the western Siwa area between El-Maraqi Lake and Siwa Lake. At the same time, TCA is suitable for drinking purposes only in the southeastern part of Siwa Oasis based on the IWQI values. The ranges of RI values for NSSA, TCA, springs, drains, and lakes samples were from 8.3E-05–0.002, 2.6E-06–0.006, 6.2E-06–1E-04, 1.3E-05–1.2E-04, and 6.8E-05–0.003, respectively. These findings indicate that the heavy metals investigated in the water resources of Siwa Oasis, Egypt, pose a relatively low ecological risk with RI values below 30. The HPI value for NSSA, TCA, Springs, drains, and lakes ranges from 5 to 114.9, 0.158–321.7, 0.35–4.9, 0.74–7.08, while for lakes, it was between 3.3 and 153.8. This indicates that while most groundwater and surface water samples are primarily free from severe heavy metal contamination, the iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) levels are notably higher, contributing to elevated HPI values in the western part of the study area. The current findings showed that there is no health risk through dermal contact for adults in 100 % of samples. On the other hand, 10 %, 10.83 %, and 2.5 % of water samples had high health risk through oral and dermal exposure with hazard index values greater than one in the following orders: HI oral (adult), HI oral (child), and HI dermal (child). The results highlight that children in the study area face a heightened risk of non-carcinogenic effects due to drinking water with elevated nitrate concentrations. The western and central Siwa depression is affected by high concentrations of nitrates compared to the eastern part due to the intensive agricultural activities and decline of the water table (cone of depression) because of over-extraction of groundwater for agricultural purposes, which increase the possibility of irrigation water return to the aquifer contaminated with nitrates from the soil. The FFBP-NN model was a powerful and successful tool for predicting IWQI and HIwhere the relationship between the actual and predicted value had R2  greater than 0.95 and mean square error (MSE) range from 5.4E-05–0.66, root mean square error (RMSE) between 0.006 and 0.81, and relative square error (RSE) between 0.001 and 2.4 E-05. The current study represents a solid-based material that integrates hydrochemistry, water quality, and health risks regarding heavy metals and nitrates contamination supported with a machine learning model that highlights the main points required for future water management and the type of treatment that the decision could consider.
