Lai 22 algorithm interpolates daily data between predefined points, namely Control Points (CPs), where CPs located at the months’ midpoints and edges are called mid-CPs and wall-CPs, respectively. A few steps should be followed to disaggregate the monthly data to daily ones for a month of interest (e.g., July 2000) at station y . First, 1) a 3-month data window centred on this month should be determined (i.e., June, July, and August 2000). Then, 2) this 3-month data is compared to the data for the same three months of each year records at station x  (e.g., June, July, and August for 1990–2010) using the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Accordingly, 3) the year in station x  that achieves the minimum RMSE is selected. Finally, 4) the month of interest in the selected year (e.g., July 1995) at station x  is used to disaggregate the target month (i.e., July 2000) at the target station y  using proportionality by employing Eq. 10 , adapted from (Acharya and Ryu, 2014 ). The steps from 1 to 4 should be repeated for all the target station y  months.(10) Disaggregated Daily Flow  ( y )  = Daily Flow  ( x )  Monthly Flow  ( x )    x Monthly Flow  ( y )      Acharya 14 method’s performance is sensitive to the similarity between the source and target stations’ datasets. Therefore, for good performance, these stations should be located at outlets of subbasins having similar characteristics (Acharya and Ryu, 2014 ). Since this is not the case in the NRB, which consists of large subbasins with significantly different characteristics (Sutcliffe and Parks, 1999 ), this method is not expected to perform well here. However, to confirm this expectation, Acharya 14 is tested for one example where Dabus and Tamaniat were used as target station and source one, respectively. The results were then compared to the interpolation methods.  2.2.3 Performance Indices The disaggregation methods’ performances were evaluated using three indices, i.e., Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Absolute Error (MAE). The NSE index (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) described by Eq. 11  (Ferreira et al., 2020; Wöhling et al., 2013 ) was used to quantify the method’s performance in mimicking the observed daily values. It is one of the most widely used metrics to evaluate hydrologic models’ performances in simulating observed streamflow (Ferreira et al., 2020; Wöhling et al., 2013; Westerberg et al., 2011; Gupta et al., 2009 ). It was also used for testing streamflow disaggregation methods by many studies (e.g., Al-Zakar & Sarlak, 2017; Acharya and Ryu, 2014 ). The methods’ performances are classified according to NSE into unsatisfactory (NSE ≤ 0.5), satisfactory (0.50 < NSE ≤ 0.65), good (0.65 < NSE ≤ 0.75), and very good (0.75 < NSE ≤ 1), as recommended by Moriasi et al. (2007) .(11) NSE =  1 −  ∑ i = 1  n   ( Q  c  i       − Q  o  i      )  2      ∑ i = 1  n   ( Q  o  i       −  Q  ¯   o  i      )  2           Where Q o (i)   and Q c (i)   are the observed and calculated daily streamflow at day i ,  Q  ¯   o i        is the observed mean streamflow, and n is the number of days. Contrarily, MAE and RMAE quantify the method’s performance in preserving mass balance by calculating the monthly volumetric errors. MAE is the average of the monthly absolute errors time series, where the errors represent the differences between observed and interpolated monthly streamflow volumes, as described in Eq. 12 , adopted from Ferreira et al. (2020) . It was recommended by Ferreira et al. (2020)  over many other competitive metrics for calculating the streamflow volumetric errors independently of the river type (e.g., perennial or intermittent). The RMAE indicates the MAE relative to the streamflow mean monthly volume, as described in Eq. 13 , adopted from Ferreira et al. (2020) . RMAE is vital to compare performances at stations with high and low streamflow means. The NSE index was applied only to the tested RSs and VSs since it was calculated using observed and interpolated daily data. However, the MAE and RMAE indices were applied at TSs in addition to RSs and VSs since they were calculated using observed and interpolated monthly data.(12) MAE =  1  N   ∑ i = 1  N   V  c  i       − V  o  i               (13) RMAE =  MAE  V  ̅  o       Where V o (i)   and V c (i)   are the observed and calculated monthly streamflow volumes at month i ,  V  ¯   o i        is the observed mean streamflow volume, and N is the number of months.  2.2.4 Data pre-processing and post-processing In terms of data pre-processing, the monthly streamflow time series datasets used to be disaggregated were checked to be continuous (without gaps) since codes for some tested methods (i.e., Lai 22, Ruiz 22, Acharya 14, and MaM 2nd-order spline) do not work if gaps exist. Also, for RSs and VSs with daily streamflow data, monthly means were calculated to be disaggregated using different methods. Regarding data post-processing, when the monthly streamflow datasets include months with a mean value of zero, all resulting daily values were replaced with zero (i.e., there should not be negative values). Also, negative daily values resulting from interpolation methods (e.g., MaM) at some stations (e.g., Gilgel Abay, Gumara and Ribb) were replaced with zero.    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Disaggregation methods’ performances at the RSs and selection of the best-performing one The resulting interpolated versus observed daily flow hydrographs and Flow Duration Curves (FDCs) at the RSs are presented in  Figs. 2 a-2 f and  Fig. 3 , respectively. The interpolation methods captured the low and moderate flows well at all RSs except for minor mismatches at a local zone at Gumara (Fig. 3 ). The interpolated peak flow values are close to the observed ones at RSs. However, at some RSs, local mismatches can be noticed at flows with low probabilities of exceedance (Fig. 3 ), i.e., less than 4 % (at Didessa and Gilgel Abay) and 15 % (at Gumara and Ribb). However, these mismatches do not significantly impact the overall performance of the interpolation methods. The peak flows are best captured by Lai 22 (Figs. 2 a-2 f and Fig. 3 ) and at high-flow rivers (i.e., Tamaniat and Dabus). Based on the NSE, all interpolation methods performed well at the RSs ( Fig. 4 ). However, performances at the small flow river stations, i.e., Ribb, Gumara, and Gilgel Abay, (NSE varies between 0.84 and 0.9) are lower than other RSs, i.e., Tamaniat, Dabus, and Gilgel Abay (NSE varies between 0.92 and 0.99). These relatively low performances could be due to the limitation of the interpolation methods in capturing the high fluctuations observed in the daily streamflow data (Figs. 2 d-2 f). This interpretation is also supported by Lai and Kaplan (2022) , who reported the interpolation methods’ limited capability in capturing the local maxima and minima. The high fluctuations in daily streamflow data may be natural or due to data measurement errors. Examples of natural reasons are 1) the existence of these stations downstream of small catchments, which have quick responses to rainfall events, and 2) the absence of upstream lakes or reservoirs, which could have reduced the daily fluctuations by attenuating the flow. However, one possible reason for the measurement errors is the indirect daily streamflow datasets estimated by Haile et al. (2023)  at Ribb, Gumara, and Gilgel Abay. Another possible reason for the measurement errors is the location of the stations at the headwaters of the Blue Nile, where rivers are usually highly heterogeneous with exposed bedrock, woody debris, cascades, and step-pools (Santos et al., 2021; Montgomery and Dietrich, 1989 ). The performances of the interpolation methods vary at different stations but are comparable at the same stations. Fig. 4  indicates that the differences between the interpolation methods’ highest and lowest NSE values at the same stations range from 0.01 to 0.02, which is insignificant. Therefore, the NSE index should not be the dominant aspect while comparing the interpolation methods. In contrast, the proportionality method (i.e., Acharya 14) performance at Dabus ( Fig. 5 , NSE is 0.87) is significantly lower than all the interpolation methods (NSE varies between 0.95 and 0.99). It also produced unexpected high and low daily values compared to the observed daily ones (Fig. 5 ). Therefore, in addition to the reasons mentioned in Section 2.2.2 , the Acharya 14 method has not been applied to other stations, and it is deemed unsuitable for this case study. Thus, one of the interpolation methods is selected to be further tested at the VSs and applied at the TSs. The MAE and RMAE test values resulting from the interpolation methods at the RSs are shown in simi-log charts,   Figs. 6 and 7 , respectively. The results reveal excellent performances achieved by Lai 22 (RMAE ranges between 0.016 and 3×10−5 ) and Ruiz 22 (RMAE ranges between 0.015 and 3.7×10−3 ), better than other interpolation methods (RMAE ranges between 0.1 and 0.028). This significant variation in the MAE and RMAE indices indicates their importance for evaluating the disaggregation methods when the volumetric balance is critical. Figs. 6 and 7  also reveal that Lai 22 performance is better than Ruiz 22 at most RSs and in addition to Tamaniat, which is located at an NRB major subbasin outlet (similar to the VSs and TSs). The same finding can be observed from Figs. 2 a-2 f as well. Since Lai 22 was the best-performing method in preserving the volumetric balance and capturing the low, moderate, and peak flows at the RSs, it was selected to be further tested at the VSs and TSs.  3.2 Selected disaggregation method’s performances at the VSs and TSs Lai 22 is tested at the VSs to check its validity to be applied at the NRB major subbasins outlets. The resulting interpolated versus observed daily streamflow data are presented in  Figs. 8 a-8 c. Lai 22 performed very well at all VSs with NSE values of 0.97, 0.87, and 0.82 at Gambella, Abbay near Kessie, and Tekeze, respectively. The relatively lower NSE value at Tekeze can be interpreted by the high daily fluctuations (Fig. 8 c). As resonated earlier for Gilgel Abay, Gumara, and Ribb (Section 3.1), these fluctuations could be caused by potential measurement errors due to the station’s location on the headwaters (Fig. 1 ) or the absence of lakes or dams, which could have reduced the fluctuations. However, since the TSs are either at the outlet of or downstream lakes or reservoirs (Fig. 1 ) that reduce daily fluctuations, the Lai 22 method’s very good performances revealed at the RSs and VSs are expected to be achieved at the TS. Lai 22 captured well the low, moderate, and peak flows at Gambella and Abbay near Kessie, except for mismatches for peak flows exceeding 3000 CMS at Abay near Kessie (Fig. 8 a & 8b). However, Lai 22 showed lower performance in capturing the moderate and peak flows at Tekeze (Fig. 8 c). In addition, Lai 22 performed very well at all the VSs and TSs with minor MAE and RMAE values, as depicted from the simi-log charts in   Figs. 9 and 10 , respectively. It performed better at stations closer to dams or lake outlets (e.g., Jebel Aulia Dam, Aswan Dam) and best at Jebel El-Aulia Dam (RMAE = 5.65×10−6 ).  3.3 Applicability and limitations of the disaggregation methods and recommendations for future studies This study showed that the interpolation methods can perform very well in disaggregating monthly streamflow to daily. When evaluating the disaggregation method, indices are important to measure performances in mimicking the daily values (e.g., NSE) and preserving the monthly means (e.g., MAE) since each provides different insights. Also, FDCs should be used to investigate a method’s capability to capture low, moderate, and high flows. The daily streamflow data fluctuations impact the interpolation methods’ performances. Hence, these methods are more recommended for use at stations where fewer fluctuations are expected, such as downstream of lakes or dams. However, future work is recommended to improve the capabilities of interpolation methods to capture local maxima and minima so that they work better with highly fluctuating data. It is also recommended to investigate disaggregation methods that generate daily streamflow data based on observed daily rainfall data (e.g., Slaughter et al., 2015 ) and other meteorologic and hydrologic parameters (e.g., Terzi et al., 2023 ). However, the spatial variations of these parameters within the NRB and the existence of regulated structures (e.g., dams) should be particularly considered. Besides, the current work revealed that mean-preserving interpolation methods (i.e., Lai 22 and Ruiz 22) used for disaggregating climatic variables can perform very well and are recommended for further investigation in disaggregating monthly streamflow in other climatic regions. In addition, the stations studied here are located on relatively high-flow rivers. Therefore, testing the disaggregation methods at smaller and ephemeral rivers in Africa is recommended. Also, there should be carefulness when applying the proportionality method for streamflow disaggregation, as it should be applied at stations located at outlets of catchments with very similar characteristics. Otherwise, less performance with unexpected high and low streamflow may result. Specifically, in the current case study, the interpolation methods performed much better than the proportionality ones due to the variety of the NRB catchments’ characteristics. Although all the interpolation methods achieved good and close performances in mimicking the observed daily values, their performances significantly varied in preserving the mass balance. Lai 22 is recommended for use in this case study since it performed the best at all RSs, VSs, and TSs. However, it should be tested and compared with other methods before being applied to other case studies in different hydroclimatic regions. Regarding challenges related to applying the tested methods, the MaM methods were straightforward. However, applying Acharya 14 using Excel was time-consuming, while running the codes for both Lai 22 and Ruiz 22 required minor modifications (e.g., Fig. S1) unrelated to the interpolation algorithm.   4 Conclusions This study encompasses an assessment of eight monthly to daily streamflow disaggregation methods at 21 critical stations (i.e., RSs, VSs, and TSs) in the NRB. These methods include five MaM (i.e., linear, 2nd-order spline, 3rd-order spline, Pchip, and MAkima) and two mean preserving (i.e., Lai 22 and Ruiz 22) interpolation methods in addition to one proportionality method (i.e., Acharya 14). They were evaluated using three indices, i.e., NSE, MAE, and RMAE, and visual investigations through hydrographs and FDCs. All interpolation methods performed well in streamflow disaggregation, better than the proportionality method, which is limited to be applied at catchments with similar characteristics. However, high daily streamflow fluctuations affect the performance of interpolation methods. However, this limitation should not be significant at the TSs located downstream of natural lakes or dams, which smoothen the daily streamflow. However, future studies should investigate methods to overcome this limitation. The performances of all interpolation methods in mimicking the observed daily streamflow data at the same station are close. However, they significantly vary in preserving the mass balance, where Lai 22 and Ruiz 22 performed better than other methods, and overall, Lai 22 performed the best. In addition, the FDCs showed that all the interpolation methods captured the low and moderate flows well. However, the peak flows were better captured at large rivers (e.g., Tamaniat) than others and best captured by Lai 22, amongst other disaggregation methods. Therefore, Lai 22 was selected and tested at the VSs and TSs, where it performed well, achieving high NSE and minor MAE and RMAE values. However, this selection is limited to the characteristics of the studied stations, e.g., their locations at relatively high-flow rivers and downstream dams or lakes. Therefore, future studies may need to evaluate the selected disaggregation methods when applying them at other regions. The daily streamflow datasets generated through this study can help enhance the hydrologic response estimation, water management practices, and hydrologic model development in the NRB.
1 Introduction A water deficit due to an imbalance between supply and demand is often known as a drought (Abdiaziz et al., 2023; Afroz et al., 2023 ). Because of massive climatic shifts, which in turn produce changes in Relative Humidity (RH), air temperature, Wind Speed (WS), and solar radiation, this has occurred (Hamed et al., 2023a ). Water availability depends on the hydrological cycle, which in turn is affected by climate conditions; hence, predicting evapotranspiration aids in guiding and evaluating the effects of climate change on agriculture and food security (Bouabdelli et al., 2022 ; Houmsi et al., 2019 ; Pour et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ). Creating appropriate methodologies or approaches to forecast climate change-related variables that impact water availability, such as evapotranspiration (ET) (Hendy et al., 2023 ; Lotfirad et al., 2021 ; Muhammad et al., 2021 ; Sobh et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ), has recently emerged as the primary obstacle in water shortage research. Evapotranspiration plays a critical role in the hydrological cycle and has significant implications for agricultural practices, climatological change, water balance, and irrigation management (Hamed et al., 2023a ; Singh et al., 2021). The stability of a region's ecology and its environmental conditions are determined by ET. ET is the cumulative effect of transpiration and evaporation in the transmission of water from the soil-plant system to the atmosphere. The subjective measurement of ET in situ entails to uncertainty and is highly costly and time-consuming. FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation is the most extensively recognized standard procedure for estimating reference evapotranspiration (ETo) (Sobh et al., 2022 ). However, the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation requires a lot of meteorological data, which is limited in some areas, particularly in developing countries (Fan et al., 2018 ). Consequently, for water resource management and irrigation scheduling, a straightforward alternative model is necessary to estimate ETo with good stability and reasonable accuracy using fewer meteorological data (Bellido-Jiménez et al., 2021 ). Daily ETo forecasts are notoriously difficult due to the extreme non-linearity and non-stationarity that characterize ETo (Hern et al., 2011 ). However, Machine Learning (ML) models have exceeded various empirical models in estimating ETo using incomplete meteorological data (Xing et al., 2022 ). Several studies indicated the ability of ML for the ETo calculation, demonstrating its high precision results, such as artificial neural network (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), multilayer perceptron (MLP), gene expression programming (GEP), long short term memory (LSTM), random forest (RF), extreme learning machine (ELM), support vector machine (SVM), multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS) and generalized regression neural network (GRNN) (Bellido-Jiménez et al., 2021; Chia et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2017a; Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020; Gocic et al., 2016 ; Hendy et al., 2023 ; Shen, 2018 ; Sobh et al., 2022 ; Yin et al., 2020 ). Mehdizadeh et al. (2017)  found that the MARS model performed best among different ML methods and empirical equations. Adnan et al. (2021)  proved the superiority of group method of data handling neural network (GMDH-NN) in Turkey. However, Sobh et al. (2022)  found that RF was the best ML method in Egypt to simulate the ETo. Climate change is one of the most pressing issues facing our world today (Hamed et al., 2023b ; Salehie et al., 2022 ; Salehie et al., 2023 ). Throughout the globe, people are starting to feel the effects of climate change. In some regions, temperatures have risen to record highs; extreme weather events such as floods and droughts have become more frequent in other areas (Rajsekhar and Gorelick, 2023; Tripathy et al., 2023 ). These changes have devastated ecosystems and human communities alike (Luo et al., 2023; Tripathy et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Global Climate Models (GCMs) mimic Earth's climate system (Eyring et al., 2016 ). They are used to project future climate change and understand the effects of human activities on the environment (Ullah et al., 2023; Ullah et al., 2020 ). GCMs are essential for understanding the global climate and informing policy decisions (Hendy et al., 2023 ); (Lin et al., 2021 ). The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, now in its sixth phase (CMIP6), has just issued a fresh batch of GCM projections (Eyring et al., 2016 ). In order to address a broader range of scientific questions, CMIP6 incorporates and utilizes more extensive models and experiments than its predecessor. CMIP6 is distinct from its predecessors in accurately representing the Earth's physical processes (Hamed et al., 2022b; 2022d; Herman et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2023; Rickard et al., 2023 ). Shared Socioeconomic Paths (SSPs) are unique scenarios that CMIP6 projects (Hamed et al., 2022c; Schlund et al., 2020 ). Because they intend to lessen the uncertainties in climate change estimates, the newly published CMIP GCMs are crucial for SSP-based climate projections. When projecting the future of the climate, these alternative scenarios consider societal and economic shifts, technological developments, changes in land use, and other environmental factors. Therefore, mitigation measures must be based on these CMIP scenarios (Saleem et al., 2021; Scaff et al., 2021 ). Selecting GCMs for accurate climate predictions is a significant difficulty in the climatological study. Considering the importance of accurate ETo data, this study assesses the potential of the hybrid machine learning model (RF-GX boost) and traditional machine learning models (RF and XG boost) in Egypt to forecast daily ETo with limited climate data after assessing the best machine learning model and assess the impact of climate change on ETo under different future climate change scenarios. Therefore, this study aims to 1) develop and evaluate a hybrid machine learning model that enhances the accuracy of estimating historical ETo and identifies geographical regions of ETo, 2) identify the contributions of climatic factors to changes in ETo under different climate change scenarios across Egypt's climate zones; (3) deploy the best model in order to forecast ETo up to 2099 using CIMP6 for SSP1–26, SSP2–45 and SSP5–85.  2 Study area and datasets 2.1 Study area Egypt is a country located in northeastern Africa (Yang, 2012 ) ( Fig. 1 ). The country's climate has changed significantly, with the historical climate being much wetter than it is today (Nashwan et al., 2019 ). Egypt has a hot desert climate with high temperatures and minimal annual precipitation (Nashwan et al., 2019 ). Egypt has a wide range of altitudes, from below sea level to over 2000 m to Mount Catherine (the highest point in Egypt) in the Sinai Peninsula. Egypt has a hot, dry summer and a moderate, wet winter. July and August are the warmest months, with average highs of 50°C. Temperatures can dip to around 10°C in the winter months of December and January. The annual average rainfall in Egypt is about 25 mm, with the heaviest rainfall in the winter. The weather in Egypt is a significant barrier to progress. The lack of rainfall makes it difficult to grow crops, and the hot weather can burden the population (Sobh et al., 2022 ). Many studies tried to classify Egypt's climate into different zones (Nashwan and Shahid, 2022 ) (Hamed et al., 2022a; Hbrc, 2006; Ibrahim et al., 1994; Ouda and Norledin, 2017; Peel et al., 2007; Sayed et al., 2013 ), they suggest a new climatic zone categorization for Egypt, dividing the country into seven distinct regions as shown in Fig. 1 . Adapting the image-classification algorithm spherical evolution, they demonstrated a novel clustering approach to climate-zone delineation. This classification was made to fill in the blanks that  earlier ones had left. The climatic zone map of Egypt is a helpful resource for studying the effects of global warming.  2.2 Datasets 2.2.1 Historical reanalysis of gridded dataset ECMWF Reanalysis v5 ([47]ERA5 Reanalysis, 19 (2022). ) is the fifth generation of reanalysis developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (Hersbach et al., 2019 ); (Hersbach et al., 2020 ) and is a worldwide reanalysis of the atmosphere, ocean, and land surface. A more comprehensive and accurate picture of the global climate system, it is the successor of the ERA-Interim reanalysis. Several factors include altitude, pressure, temperature, humidity, wind speed, and precipitation. Researchers in climate science, meteorology, numerical weather prediction, air quality modeling and environmental impact assessment can all benefit from ERA5 data (Al-Sakkaf et al., 2024 ; Houmsi et al., 2023 ; Kamruzzaman et al., 2022 ; Kong and Huber, 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022; Liu and Yang, 2022 ; Ullah et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ). The ECMWF makes the ERA5 dataset available to the public at no cost. This dataset spans the entire planet, from the North Pole to the South. At 0.25 degrees, its spatial resolution is significant enough to capture fine details in Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and landscapes. With a temporal precision of 1 hour, it can detect and record even the most fleeting climatic shifts. Since it is based on a cutting-edge atmospheric model, it reliably represents the underlying physical processes that control the climate. High-quality global climate data is essential for various uses, and ERA5 provides just that. The ERA5 database contains daily updates beginning in 1940. The study employed daily data from 1975 to 2014 as its foundation, a time frame comparable to that of GCMs, following the suggestion from WMO for using at least 40 years to capture the region's climate (WMO, 2017 ). The parameters include maximum (Tmax) and minimum (Tmin) temperatures, WS and RH. PET estimations were made daily from 1975 to 2014, following a method similar to that of Singer et al. (2021) .  2.2.2 Historical and future GCMs GCMs are computer simulations of the Earth's climate system used in CMIP6. The models run on supercomputers are meant to consider various climate-altering events, such as greenhouse gas emissions and land-use changes. The CMIP6 GCMs represent the pinnacle of climate simulation technology. Scientists worldwide rely on them to learn about climate change's history, predict its future, and create plans to combat it. Understanding climate change and creating solutions to lessen its consequences is impossible without the CMIP6 GCMs. They provide crucial information for researchers, lawmakers, and the general public. Clouds, aerosols, and ocean circulation are only some processes improved in CMIP6 models. More effort is spent running the CMIP6 models from pre-industrial to the late 21st century. When compared to their predecessors, the CMIP5 GCMs and the CMIP6 GCMs represent a considerable step forward, and they will continue to shed light on Earth's climate system for many years to come (Hamed et al., 2022b; 2022d; 2022e ). Selecting the starting variation (r1i1p1f1) is crucial so that any preconceived notions about the climate system do not skew the evaluation. If all models are initialized and parametrized the same way, then any discrepancies in the outcomes must be attributable to the underlying models themselves. To better comprehend the possible implications of climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has established a new set of scenarios called Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The five possible scenarios to create SSPs reflect varying degrees of economic growth, technical advancement, and environmental sustainability. The most optimistic SSP is SSP1, SSP2 represents the medium ground, and SSP5 represents the most pessimistic. The ambition shown toward climate change mitigation is a crucial differentiator between SSP1, SSP2 and SSP5. In SSP1, the world is assumed to take robust measures to cut emissions of greenhouse gases, whereas in SSP5, the world is assumed to do nothing to combat climate change. SSP2 is somewhere in between, assuming that the world will take some action to mitigate climate change but not enough to prevent significant warming. The different levels of ambition in these two storylines will significantly impact the future of climate change. The daily GCMs (18 GCM) were used in this study for the historical and future projection simulation from 1975 to 2014 for historical and 2015–2099 for future projection for the same variables used in the historical reference dataset (Tmax, Tmin, WS and RH). SSP1–2.6, 2–4.5 and 5–8.5 were selected to represent the different levels of ambition for climate change mitigation.    3 Methods The general methodology of the present study is shown in  Fig. 2 . The figure illustrates the methodology for forecasting ETo (evapotranspiration) in Egypt, divided into seven climate zones, by emphasizing the iterative process of data evaluation, model training, and validation across different climate zones. The study used multi-data sources, including remote sensing and climate data, as input variables to single and hybrid algorithms and assessed the performance of several input scenarios with each algorithm to define the best approach to predict ETo across Egypt. The downloaded GCMs data for different scenarios (Historical, SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP5–8.5) and evaluate GCMs against ERA5 using KGE metric, finally select the top 4 GCMs and apply Quantile Mapping for bias correction. The selected model is used to forecast future ETo based on different scenarios. 3.1 Calculation of ETo The reference evapotranspiration (ETo) was based on the Penman-Monteith equation (Allen, 2000 ); (Mokhtar et al., 2020a; 2020b ), which is recommended by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) (Abdo et al., 2022; Allen, 2000; Mokhtar et al., 2020c ) and has been successfully used by Abdel-Hameed et al. (2022); Sumner and Jacobs (2005) . The ETo values calculated by the standard FAO56-PM model were applied as benchmarks for calibrating and assessing the applied methods (Allen et al., 1998 ). The necessary meteorological inputs of the applied mass transfer-based models are Tmax, Tmin, RH and WS. Hence, a subject matter expertise was used, and the proposed RF models were constructed based on the following input combinations Tmax, Tmin, RH, WS.(1) ET  o   = 0.408 ∆ R  n   − G    + γ 900  237 + T  mean     WS ( e  s   − e  a   )  ∆ + γ ( 1 + 0.34 WS )       where (△) is the Saturated vapour pressure and temperature curve slope, kPa ℃−1 ; (Rn ) represents the net radiation, W.m−2 ; (G) represents the soil heat flux density, MJ.m−2 ; (γ) represents the wet and dry table constant, kPa.℃−1 ; Tmean  represents average air temperature, ◦C; (WS) represents wind speed at 2 m height, m.s−1 ; (es ) represents the saturated water vapour pressure, kPa; (ea ) represents the actual water vapour pressure, kPa.  3.2 Spatial and temporal analysis Nonparametric Sen's slope test (Sen, 1968 ) presented a nonparametric method for the analysis of time series by developing and expanding a series of statistical studies conducted by Thiel (1950) . This method has more priority than the Man-Kendall method in analysing the trend of time series in which the frequency of repeated data is high and provides more acceptable results. This nonparametric method calculates a median slope for a time series of data using difference analysis between observations of a time series. Sen's slope test has widely been used to identify the significance of hydrologic and climatic trends thus in this study, trend analyses of the climate variables and ETo were examined by Sen's slope test to statistically assess if there is a monotonic upward or downward trend of the variable of interest over time. Using the Sen method, a slope is calculated for each pair of consecutive data. The calculated slopes form a time series, and the series's median shows the trend line's slope (Solaimani and Bararkhanpour, 2022 ). In contrast, this study used spatial analysis through interpolation algorithms to estimate spatial changes in climate variables and ETo. The inverse distance weighting method (IDW) had the lowest mean error among the standard interpolation methods. It was applied with highly variable data analysis to get the lowest mean error in comparison with the standard interpolation methods, which were developed by the U.S. National Weather Service in 1972 and are classified as a deterministic method (Feng et al., 2017b; Moeletsi et al., 2016 ; Mokhtar et al., 2020a; 2020b ).  3.3 GCM selection and bias correction The historical GCMs were evaluated against ERA5 using the KGE metric to rank them and select the best replicate GCM to the historical period. The selection was made for the GCM, which was ranked at the top of all metrological variables. The quantile mapping employing parametric transformations (QM) was utilized to rectify the bias in GCM simulations for past and future simulations (Gampe et al., 2019; Homsi et al., 2020; Kirdemir et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2020 ). QM is a statistical technique that can adjust climate models for consistently inflated or depressed precipitation and temperature estimates. It does this by mapping the quantiles of one probability distribution to the quantiles of another distribution. In contrast to parametric approaches, QM offers flexibility and dependability for a wide range of data since it does not assume anything about the data's underlying distribution.  3.4 Machine learning models In this study, three input scenarios are considered to emphasize predicting ETo using limited meteorological variables (maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed and relative humidity) to investigate their effects on rice production and evaluate the contribution of each variable ( Table 1 ). This may help improve water resources analysis for data scarcity regions. The data were divided into two subsets: 70 % for training and 30 % for testing. The decision to use RF and XGB for this study was based on their proven effectiveness in ETo prediction, ability to handle large datasets with complex interactions, and robustness to overfitting. So, the advantages of RF and XGB in feature importance analysis and computational efficiency further supported their selection over other advanced machine learning techniques (Mokhtar et al., 2024 ). 3.4.1 Random Forest (RF) Random Forest, a tree-based method developed by (Breiman, 2001 ). As the number of trees increases, extra randomness is introduced. Rather than searching for the best feature to split a node, it searches for the best feature among a randomly selected subset of features, thus creating greater tree diversity (Feng et al., 2017a ). Random forest is designed to form an ensemble of weak unbiased classifiers which combine their results during the final classification of each object. Individual classifiers are built as classification trees. Each tree is constructed using a different bootstrap sample of the training set. Each bootstrap sample results from drawing with the replacement of the same number of objects as in the original training set. As a result, roughly 1/ 3 of objects are not used for building a tree but instead for performing an out-of-bag (OOB) error estimate and for importance measurement. A different subset of attributes is randomly selected at each step of the tree construction. The RF classification algorithm is relatively quick, can usually be run without tuning parameters, and gives a numerical estimate of the feature's importance. It is an ensemble method in which classification is performed by voting of multiple unbiased weak classifiers decision trees. These trees are independently developed on different bagging samples of the training set. We applied the RF model by using the grid search method for the n estimators (number of trees) (100, 200, 300, 400 and 500) and max depth (1, 2, 5 and 10) and the default values of the other hyperparameters. The best n estimator for the scenarios was 200, on the other hand, the best max depth was 2.  3.4.2 Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) Recently, XGB proposed by Chen and Guestrin (2016) , XGB has gained significant attention in machine learning competitions (Adam-Bourdarios et al., 2015 ). Based on decision trees, this algorithm differs from RF in how the tree ensemble is constructed. XGB utilizes previous ideas from gradient boosting to create each tree based on information from previously created trees. Additionally, XGB can estimate the importance of input variables and exhibits higher computational efficiency and better ability to handle overfitting (Fan et al., 2018 ). The XGB algorithm is a novel improvement of the Gradient Boosting Machine based on regression trees. The algorithm is based on the idea of "boosting", which combines all the predictions of a set of "weak" learners to develop a "strong" learner through additive training strategies. It is a machine learning algorithm realized by gradient lifting technology; it is an enhanced GBDT algorithm. Its base classifier is the Classification and Regression Tree (CART). XGB is a tree integration model that combines multiple CART (Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ). The XGB model is built by adding trees iteratively. During hyperparameter tuning, the number of trees was adjusted (n_estimators), and the maximum tree depth was adjusted (max_depth). To get the best score, an XG boost model was trained using the grid search method for the n estimators (number of trees) (100, 200, 300, 400 and 500) and max depth (1, 2, 5, and 10) and the default values of the other hyperparameters.  3.4.3 Hybrid model (RF-XGB) A hybrid machine learning model was used, combining RF and XGB in an RF XGB model. The hybridization between the RF and XGB aimed to improve the performance of single models. Every single model was described in the previous sections. The hybrid model of RF-XGB is described in  Fig. 3 ; RF and XGB reported high accuracy in different fields related to agricultural activities (Mokhtar et al., 2021a; 2021b ). All random forest and extreme gradient boost models improve the accuracy of determining irrigation timing for agriculture using real-time data. The XGB and RF models achieved 87.73 % and 84.74 % of accuracy, better than Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), support vector machines (SVM), and decision trees (Cardoso et al., 2020; Mokhtar et al., 2024 ). For predicting the growth environment in agriculture, RF and XGB perform better than Ridge regression and Lasso regression, where the study targeted the control of the saturation value in the adequate range in tomato cultivation (Fujita et al., 2021). In the water quality field, the random forest recorded the best accuracy (R² = 0.9853) among eight machine learning models in predicting the water quality index (WQI) based on the minimum set of inputs (Kouadri et al., 2021). A similar paper deals with the modeling of irrigation suitability indices, the random forest found to be suitable for predicting total dissolved salts (TDS), potential salinity (PS), sodium adsorption ratio (SAR), and exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP), with a performance based on Pearson coefficient (r) equal to 0.87, 0.92, 0.83 and 0.65 for RDS, PS, SAR, and ESP respectively (Trabelsi and Bel hadj ali 2022).   3.5 Performance comparison criteria The models were evaluated for each zone using root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R²), Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE), Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), and the mean absolute error (MAE). In contrast, an NSE value of 1 indicates a perfect fit, greater than 0.75 is a very good fit, between 0.64 and 0.74 is a good fit, between 0.5 and 0.64 is a satisfactory fit and less than 0.5 is an unsatisfactory fit (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). The mean of maximum air temperature was in the range of 23.25 – 28.15 °C, and those of the minimum air temperature were in the range of 13.1 –17.6 °C; concerning the wind speed the mean range was 2.3 – 3.25 m/s, and the mean of the relative humidity was in the range of 50.11– 69.84 %. The Sen's slope test is a statistical method used in this study to determine the significance of trends in various climatic variables for the seven zones of the study area (reference evapotranspiration, temperature, wind speed, and relative humidity). The Sen's slope showed an increasing trend for all seven zones, the Tmax  and Tmin ; otherwise, the trend for WS did not act the same for all seven zones. For zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, the trend slightly decreases, but for zone 7, the trend showed slight increases, as shown in Fig. (3) . For RH, the trend showed a slight increase for all seven zones, as shown in Fig. 3 (e). These climatic factors are reflected in the change of the ETo, which showed an increase in the ETo for zones 3,4 and 7 and a slight increase in the ETo for zones 1, 2, 5 and 6, as shown in Fig. 3 (a), that agreed with previous studies with the same weather (Mokhtar et al., 2020a; Tang et al., 2021 ). The spatiotemporal distribution from 1975 to 2014 reveals interesting patterns and trends.  Fig. (4)  illustrates Egypt's spatial annual trend for reference evapotranspiration, temperature, wind speed, and relative humidity. Over this period, the spatial annual trend of ETo ranged from −26.2 to +40.27 mm/decade. It showed an increasing trend for the study area, especially in upper Egypt (+ 40.27 mm/decade), except a part of the middle showed a decreasing trend in Fig. (4 a). The spatial annual trend of Tmax  ranged from −0.19 to +0.69 ᴼC/ decade, which showed an increasing trend for Egypt except for a tiny part in the southeast of Egypt, which showed a decreasing trend in Fig. (4 b). The spatial annual trend of Tmin  ranged from +0.18 to +0.78 ᴼC/decade, showing an increasing trend for Egypt Fig. (4 c). The spatial annual trend for WS ranged from −0.06 to +0.05 m/s/decade. It showed a decreasing trend in the North of Egypt and an increasing trend in the South of Egypt Fig. (4 d). For RH, the spatial annual trend ranged from −0.68 to +0.92 %/decade, and it showed a decreasing trend for most of Egypt and an increasing trend in the middle of Egypt. The results unveiled notable trends in climatic variables (Tmax , Tmin , RH, WS) and reference evapotranspiration (ETo) throughout the seven zones.  4.2 Performance evaluation of the applied models The results obtained from the RF, XGB and RF-XGB models using different input datasets are presented in  Table 3  and   Figs. 5 and 6 . The input datasets were Sc1(Tmin , Tmax ), Sc2(Tmin , Tmax,  WS) and Sc3(Tmin , Tmax,  RH, WS) for the seven zones. The input datasets were randomly divided into training and testing groups before entering into the models. The models were then implemented, and their estimations were assessed using the R2 , MAE, RMSE, KGE, NSE and SI criteria. For all zones, the evaluation criteria values are higher for the hybrid model (RF-XGB) and the Sc3 scenario, which shows that the model performs well in ETo estimation which is consistent with several studies (Mokhtar et al., 2023 ; Valipour et al., 2023 ; Xing et al., 2022 ) that the hybrid machine learning models are more accurate. Among these datasets, using all seven zones, the R2  results were 0.857942–0.989698 for RF, 0.857366–0.98948 for XGB and 0.945707–0.995879 for hybrid model (RF-XGB) as shown in Fig. (5) , Compared RF to RF-GX boost, the R2  values were improved by 9.28 %, 4.44 %, 2.36 %, 1.30 %,0.62, 0.88, and 3.16 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. The MAE is considered a metric to assess a model's performance quality. In machine learning, absolute error refers to the difference between an observation's prediction and actual value. The best results were for the RF-XGB model, with values ranging from 0.074 to 0.200. On the other hand, the RF and the XGB models were closed, and less accuracy values ranged from 0.131 to 0.373, as shown in Fig. (5) . Compared RF to RF-XGB, the MAE values were improved by 13.71 %, 16.45 %, 20.36 %, 19.68 %,23.27 %, 18.86 %, and 16.85 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. Moreover, compared XGB to RF-XGB, the RMSE values were improved by 7.20 %, 7.98 %, 16.21 %, 8.96 %,15.31 %, 13.56 %, and 11.75 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. On the other hand, compared XGB to RF-XGB, the RMSE values were improved by 9.34 %, 4.71 %, 2.35 %, 1.40 %,0.64 %, 0.88 %, and 3.16 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. The models' performance is considered better when the RMSE values approach zero. The hybrid model (RF-XGB) presented the best estimation of the models, followed by RF-XGB across all zones, as shown in Fig. (6) . The RF and the XGB results are so similar and had the weakest accuracy with RMSE = 0.178654–0.491017 mm d−1 , for the RF model and RMSE = 0.18053–0.492055 mm.d−1 , for the XGB model. On the other hand, the hybrid (RF-XGB) model resulted in a more accurate estimation with RMSE = 0.11385–0.304826 mm d−1 . Compared RF to RF-XGB, the RMSE values were improved by 38.91 %, 42.29 %, 39.96 %, 37.73 %,43.07 %, 39.11 %, and 38.21 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. Furthermore, compared XGB to RF-XGB, the RMSE values were improved by 38.57 %, 39.34 %, 40.21 %, 33.80 %,41.43 %, 38.91 %, and 38.22 % on average for zones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. These results suggest that combining Random Forest and XGBoost models can improve accuracy in predicting values compared to using either model individually. The SI values obtained for the models for all seven zones were analyzed to evaluate their performance. Based on the SI criteria, the models were categorized into different levels. In this study, none of the models achieved an SI value less than 0.15, which would classify them as "excellent". However, most models performed well and achieved satisfactory results in the hybrid model, as shown in Fig. (6) . The models performed satisfactorily in all the study zones in the RF model with SI values between 0.04144 and 0.143804, and the XGB model with SI values between 0.041389 and 0.143571. On the other hand, good performance was observed for the RF-XGB model in all the study zones with SI values between 0.025913 and 0.089394. The NSE is the main performance metric utilized in hydrology. It can be described as a standardized version of mean squared error (MSE). KGE gives an alternative to metrics that rely on the sum of squared error, such as the two preceding ones. It achieves this by assigning equal importance to mean bias, variability, and correlation measurements, combining them into a single metric. Compared RF and XGB to RF-XGB, the NSE values were improved using a hybrid model for all 7 climatic zones; in addition, the best performance was for the Sc3 as shown in Table 3 . These results indicate that the highest performances of all models are observed in the middle and southern parts of Egypt, which exhibit the strongest correlation between temperature and ETo. The accuracy decreases in the northern part of Egypt with the weakest correlation between temperature and ETo, this finding consists with (Valipour et al., 2023 ). From previous studies (Feng et al., 2017a; Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020 ; Hendy et al., 2023 ; Xing et al., 2022 ) using multimale climate data such as Tmax , Tmin , RH, and WS as climatic input data give the lowest error in accuracy and better estimation of ETo, at this study the RF, XGB, and hybrid RF-XGB models were evaluated for their ability to estimate ETo with incomplete weather data, this study found the RF-XGB achieved the best performance for estimating daily ETo using incomplete data, therefore, the RF-XGB model proposed in this study, as a transformative deep learning model, to assess the impact of climate change on ETo forecasting under different future climate change scenarios for 7 different zones in Egypt, this finding was consistent with several prior simulation studies (Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020; Mokhtar et al., 2023; Xing et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020 ).  4.3 Future climate scenarios The best-selected ML model was combined with the climate model projections to investigate ETo under three different scenarios for the seven zones of the study area, according to Hamed et al. (2022a) . SSP1–2.6, 2–4.5 and 5–8.5 were selected to represent the different levels of ambition for climate change mitigation. The daily GCMs were used in this study for the historical and future projection simulation from 1975 to 2014 for historical and 2015–2099 for future projection for the same variables used in the historical reference dataset (maximum temperature, minimum temperature, wind speed, and relative humidity) for estimating the ETo as shown in  Fig. 7 . The results showed that the ETo in each climate change scenario acts differently for each zone; for the SSP5–8.5 scenario, the ETo increased over the years for all zones. The ETo increase from 3.74, 3.87, 4.2, 4.76, 5.31, 5.92 and 3.85 mm/day at year 2015–3.91, 3.93,4.39, 4.87, 5.49, 6.01 and 4.06 mm/day (4.38 %, 3.71 %, 4.27 %, −2.16 %, 3.26 %, 1.35 %, 5.22 %) at year 2099, for zone 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 respectively, as shown in  Fig. (8) . However, the SSP2–4.5 scenario showed a slight increase in the ETo from 2020 to 2060 and then a slight decrease to 2099, as shown in Fig. (8) . For all seven zones, the ETo showed a slight increase from 3.61, 3.68, 4.00, 4.24, 4.60, 5.27 and 3.61 mm/day at 2015–3.64, 3.69, 3.99, 4.23, 4.64, 5.29 and 3.64 mm/day (0.86 %, 0.22 %, 0.13 %, 0.11 %, 0.69 %, 0.32 %, 0.57 %) for the year 2060 and then a slight decrease to 3.48, 3.56, 4.89, 4.10, 4.49, 5.18 and 3.47 mm/day (-3.41 %, −3.33 %, −2.97 %,- 3.45 %, −2.43 %, −1.74 %, −4.21 %) at the year 2099, for zone 1, 2,3,4,5,6 and 7 respectively. The same trend for the SSP1–2.6 scenario showed a slight ETo increase from 2020 to 2060 and then a slight decrease to 2099, as shown in Fig. (8)  for all seven zones. The ETo showed a slight increase from 3.42, 3.46, 3.79, 4.13, 4.65, 5.36 and 3.57 mm/day at the year 2020–3.48, 3.55, 3.86, 4.21, 4.68, 5.29 and 3.58 mm/day(1.78 %, 2.54 %, 1.95 %, 1.81 %, 0.57 %, 1.49 %, 0.35 %) for the year 2060 and then a slight decrease to 3.33, 3.40, 3.73, 4.08, 4.67, 5.33 and 3.46 mm/day (-2.80 %, −1.59 %, −1.16 %, −0.41 %, −0.52 %, −3.32 %) at the year 2099, for zone 1, 2,3,4,5,6 and 7 respectively. The results indicated varying impacts of climate change on ETo across zones. Under SSP5–8.5, ETo showed consistent increases across all zones; this is the result of the increase of Tmax , which is consistent with findings of previous research (Gui et al., 2021 ), while under SSP2–4.5 and SSP1–2.6, slight increases followed by decreases were observed in some zones; also our study aligns with the findings of Jia et al. (2023)  who investigated the evolution of ETo in various future scenarios these findings underscore the importance of considering different emission scenarios when assessing future ETo.  4.4 Contributions of driving variables to changes in ETo Based on the results obtained from the single RF and XGB models, it is the superiority of the XGB model compared to the RF model; thus, the XGB model was applied to analyze the joint contributions of subsets of features while maintaining a fast convergence during iterations. The predictor variables in the XGB model were used to investigate the importance of these predictor variables. As a result of the varying impacts of climate change on ETo across zones, it was important to study the contributions of climatic variables (Tmax, Tmin, RH, and WS) in predicting ETo. The Tmin , Tmax , RH and WS are the most critical factors that affect the ETo.  Fig. (9)  presents the relative importance ranking of the features in ETo prediction for the seven zones for historical data and each climate change scenario (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP2–8.5). This figure indicates that for the historical period, the RH and WS have an average effect on ETo for all zones, Tmax  has a large effect on the ETo for all zones except zones 5 and 6, Tmin  has a large effect on the ETo for zone 5 and 6 only as shown in Fig. (9 a). For the SSP1–2.6 climate change scenario, RH showed a low effect on the ETo for all zones, Tmax  showed a large effect on the ETo for all zones except zones 6 and 7, WS showed a minimum effect on the ETo for all zones except zone 4 and 7, Tmin  showed a large effect on the ETo for zone 6 only as shown in Fig. (9 b). SSP2–4.5 climate change scenario RH showed a low effect on the ETo for all zones, Tmax  showed a large effect on the ETo for zones 1,2 and 3 only, WS showed a minimum effect on the ETo for zones 1,2,3 and 5 and a large effect on zones 4,6 and 7, Tmin  showed a large effect on the ETo for zone 5 only as shown in Fig. (9 c). SSP2–8.5 climate change scenario RH showed a low effect on the ETo for all zones, Tmax  showed a large effect on the ETo for zones 1,2,5 and 6 only, WS showed a minimum effect on the ETo for zones 1,2,5 and 6 and large effect on zones 3,4 and 7, Tmin  showed a no effect on the ETo for all zones except a low effect on the ETo for zone 6 as shown in Fig. (9 d). These results indicate that Tmax  plays a more crucial role in influencing ETo than other meteorological factors (Patle and Singh, 2015 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ). This different relative importance ranking of the features in ETo prediction makes the different effects for each climate change scenario in each zone.   5 Conclusion Reference evapotranspiration has significant implications for agricultural practices, climatological change, water balance, and irrigation management, so this study concludes that using the Mann-Kendall test indicated increasing trends in maximum and minimum air temperatures and relative humidity. In contrast, wind speed trends varied among zones. These climatic changes were reflected in the reference evapotranspiration (ETo), with varying trends observed across the zones. Furthermore, the performance evaluation of machine learning models demonstrated the effectiveness of the hybrid model (RF-XGB) in ETo estimation. The hybrid model consistently outperformed RF and XGB individually regarding R2 , MAE, and RMSE across all zones, indicating its superior predictive capabilities. Moreover, assessing climate change scenarios using the selected machine learning model revealed varying impacts on ETo across the seven zones. Under different scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP5–8.5), ETo exhibited distinct trends, with some zones experiencing increases while others showed slight decreases over time. The relative importance of climatic variables in ETo prediction varied across scenarios and zones, highlighting the complex interactions driving changes in ETo under different climate change scenarios. This study highlights valuable insights into understanding climate change impacts on ETo estimation, essential for sustainable water resource management. Additionally, the performance evaluation of machine learning models demonstrates the potential for improving ETo prediction accuracy. Therefore, further research focusing on refining climate models and assessing the impacts of climate change on water resources is essential for enhancing resilience and sustainability in agricultural and water management practices.
