Stations that clustered at the lower end of the line of best fit represent the seawater endmember, suggesting that mixing of terrestrial groundwater sources with seawater occurs in most of the reef lagoon. Concentrations of NOx -  ranged between 0.1 and 488 (in µM; σ = 168, μ = 74). There were no significant differences in NOx - , as ln(NOx - ), between categories, but the trends were still examined (Fig. 6 b ). The highest NOx -  concentrations were observed at lagoon station sites (488 µM), while the lowest was at Limones and Bonanza reefs. The best predictor of NOx -  was 223 Ra, explaining 22 % of NOx -  variability (Fig. 7 b ), suggesting that NOx -  production occurs within short time frames. Among springs, Gorgos and Ojo de Aqua had the lowest NOx -  but the highest 223 Ra activities. NTSpring had high levels of both NOx -  (488 µM) and 223 Ra (31 dpm·m−3 ). Elevated NOx -  concentrations were found at proximal shore stations within the LL. Hydrogen phosphate concentrations, ranging from 0.2 to 1.8 µM, did not differ significantly between categories when transformed (p > 0.1; Fig. 6 c).  The cenotes, along with other springs and stations, exhibited overlapping concentrations of HPO4 2- , with the Coastal only slightly more elevated (0.7 µM). Additionally, the Gorgos spring (1.1 µM), the Inlet (1.7 µM), and the front of Limones reef (1.8 µM) displayed the highest concentrations of HPO4 2- . The best models derived from the multiple linear regression analyses accounted for less than 1 % of the variability in HPO4 2-  concentrations indicating unlikely correlations between HPO4 2-  presence in the lagoon or groundwater and the radiogenic tracers or the stable isotopes or salinity. Contrary to HPO4 2- , HSiO3 -  followed a similar trend to NH4 +  in that natural logged concentrations were significantly higher in cenotes and in springs than in stations (p < 0.05 and p < 0.01, respectively), but the springs and cenotes were similar (Fig. 6 d ). The springs, with HSiO3 -  (in µM) ranging from 4 to 45 (with only Gorgos exceeding 19, at 45), and cenotes with HSiO3 -  varying from 14 to 42, had higher average HSiO3 -  and 223 Ra than stations (Figs. 4 b and 6 d ). Stations NTLagoon and L24 are exceptions, with HSiO3 -  nearing springs and cenotes. The best predictors of HSiO3 -  were salinity ( Fig. 8 a ) and 223 Ra (Fig. 8 b ), which together explained 44 % of the observed variability. In this study, concentrations of urea (in µM) ranged between 0.3 and 2.9 (σ = 0.8, μ = 1.1) with no significant differences between sampling categories (Fig. 6 e ). 223 Ra alone explained 17 % of the variation in urea concentrations, achieving the best model score among all tested models, with an AICc value of 18.5 ( Fig. 9 ). Urea exhibited a positive linear relationship with 223 Ra, a relationship mainly explained by the XcaHa and Private 2 groundwater samples. In contrast, the other two shallow groundwater samples fell at the lower end of the range for both parameters, while the Inlet sample exhibited higher urea concentrations and 223 Ra activities at the high end for all stations. XcaHa, Inlet, and Private 2 samples, which exhibited high urea concentrations and among the highest 223 Ra activities (except for the springs), were identified as the source endmembers in the regression model. These findings establish 223 Ra as a key groundwater tracer for urea inputs to the lagoon, with XcaHa, Inlet, and Private 2 being the primary sources.  3.3 Nutrient Fluxes The nutrient flux rates were determined as the product of the SGD rates (advective and volumetric) from each specific Ra isotope tracer and solute endmember concentrations identified in the regression model for each type of nutrient. The NH4 +  fluxes were estimated as the product of the 226 Ra-derived SGD rates and the combined average of XcaHa, Private 2, Ojo de Aqua (H.T. and L.T.), and Gorgos concentration (µ = 55.7 µM). Accordingly, the NH4 +  flux to the UL per square meter (in mmol·d−1 ·m−2 ) ranging from 4.7 to 57 (μ = 18.6) was approximately three times lower than the lower region’s (ranging from 13.6 to 167.4 (μ = 53.9;  Fig. 10 a ). The SGD rates from the 223 Ra mass balance were used for all other nutrient fluxes, while the solute endmembers varied depending on the regression model results, as indicated in Section 3.2 . In the case of NOx - , using the solute endmember from the combined average concentration of XcaHa, NTSpring, and Private 2 (µ = 169.7 µM). The average fluxes of NOx -  per square meter (mM·d−1 ·m−2 ) were found to be 45 times higher in the LL (ranging from 17.7 to 1027, µ = 357.5) than the UL (ranging from 0.1 to 22.6, µ = 7.9), like the rest of the nutrients except NH4 + . For HSiO3 - , the combined average of Gorgos, Private 2, and Ojo de Aqua (H.T. and L.T.) concentrations (µ = 30.7 µM) resulted in fluxes ranging from 34.2 to 95.7 (μ = 64.4) in the LL and from 0.8 to 2.1 (μ = 1.4) in the upper area. The HPO4 2-  and urea fluxes were lower in magnitude than the other nutrients. The HPO4 2-  flux (in mmol·d−1 ·m−2 ) ranged from 0.05 to 0.08 (μ = 0.07) in the UL and from 2.4 to 3.6 (μ = 3) in the lower part. Similarly, urea flux rates (in mmol·d−1 ·m−2 ) in the upper area ranged from 0.113 to 0.132 (μ = 0.124) and from 5.1 to 6.0 (μ = 5.6) in the LL. The relatively lower variability in the solute flux rates within each lagoon region can be primarily attributed to the generally lower concentrations in the groundwater endmembers. This results in a narrower range between the minimum and maximum flux rates. Additionally, the significant differences in solute flux rates between the UL and LL (Fig. 3 ) are due to substantially larger SGD rates in the latter. As previously stated, the nutrient fluxes per unit area of the lagoon daily were significantly higher in the LL than the UL area (as illustrated in Fig. 10 a ). This observation is consistent with the varying rates of SGD, which were higher in the LL. Variations in the magnitudes of solute flux between the two areas of the lagoon can also be attributed to differences in the magnitudes of concentrations of individual nutrients in the groundwater endmembers.   4 Discussion 4.1 Radon and Radium Activities and SGD Rates The variability in 222 Rn activities highlights the diversity of groundwater inputs into the lagoon. High radon activities at sites like XcaHa and Ojo de Aqua indicate robust groundwater inputs. In contrast, lower activities at sites like UNAM and NTReef suggest dilution or more distant groundwater sources. The higher LL inventories than the UL suggest more substantial and possibly more frequent groundwater inputs in the LL. This is expected, given the observed presence of underwater springs in this part of the lagoon. The reliance on 222 Rn for estimating SGD underscores the importance of understanding radon dynamics in different environmental conditions. While the mass balance approach accounts for degassing, the observed variability still suggests complexities in groundwater contributions that may need to be fully captured. High-resolution spatial measurements provide a comprehensive view of groundwater inputs' spatial distribution. Yet, the potential for underestimating SGD rates remains due to factors like degassing and diverse groundwater sources with varying radon activities (Savatier and Rocha, 2021 ). The differences in volumetric and advective 222 Rn-derived SGD rates between the UL and LL, which align with the observed radon activities, reinforce the significance of groundwater inputs in the LL. However, this disparity in SGD magnitudes between the two areas of the lagoon also underscores the need for further investigations into the factors influencing groundwater flow and radon distribution. These factors include aquifer characteristics and environmental conditions. The comparison of 222 Rn-derived SGD rates with those from 224 Ra and 223 Ra underscores the varying contributions of fresh and recirculated groundwater. The lower 224 Ra and 223 Ra-derived SGD rates in the UL, coupled with higher 226 Ra-derived rates, suggest that older groundwater contributions are likely more significant in this region. This suggestion is supported by the larger 222 Rn inventories observed in the LL, indicating a more complex interaction of groundwater sources and flow dynamics. This is consistent with the findings of Savatier and Rocha (2021) , who noted that radon-based SGD estimates must account for the spatial heterogeneity of water ages to avoid significant underestimation of SGD rates. This study's findings align with previous work by Burnett et al. (2001b) , who emphasized the significance of direct groundwater discharge into the coastal zone and highlighted the challenges in estimating such contributions due to spatial and temporal variability (Savatier and Rocha, 2021 ). Similarly, Sadat-Noori et al. (2015)  demonstrated the importance of considering spatially distributed radon time series to assess groundwater discharge rates in estuarine environments accurately. The observed differences in volumetric and advective 222 Rn-derived SGD rates between the UL and LL further underscore the need for more refined methods to account for these variabilities, as highlighted by Rocha et al. (2015)  in their study on nitrogen retention and fate in coastal bays. Distinct patterns in the 224:223 and 224:226 activity ratios across different sites and water types highlight the varying sources and processes affecting radium distribution. Groundwater and springs had the lowest ratios, while NTLagoon, Bonanza, and Limones reef stations had the highest 224:223 ratios, and Bonanza, NTReef, and Limones reef had the highest 224:226 ratios. Ratios were generally higher near reef locations than cenotes and springs, with 224:223 ratios > 10 and most 224:226 ratios > 0.5. Additionally, both ratios were the lowest in the LL. Ratios ˂ 1 suggest a deficiency in 224 Ra, potentially caused by fresher groundwater inputs, which increases Ra sorption to aquifer/sediment materials or decay. On the other hand, in saline-water-flushed sediments/rocks, as observed herein, short-lived isotopes like 224 Ra and 223 Ra desorb and regenerate quickly (Rodellas et al., 2015 ), compared to long-lived 226 Ra (Moore, 2006 ), leading to higher 224:226 and 224:223 ratios. Warmer temperatures and increased primary production are also culprit conditions for increased Ra desorption (Kadko et al., 1987 ). Furthermore, under increasingly higher salinity conditions, microorganisms promote anoxic conditions in sediments, reducing metal oxides and releasing Ra into pore water (Tamborski et al., 2017 ). This, combined with Ra’s interaction with biogenic minerals (Bishop, 1988; Krest et al., 1999 ), produces short-lived Ra isotopes in porewater and increases their surface water fluxes (Garcia-Orellana et al., 2021; Lopez et al., 2020 ). Additionally, environmental factors and the geochemical behavior of these isotopes influence their activities, with 224 Ra often being more responsive to sediment-water interactions, leading to its higher abundance in certain aquatic systems. The high observed 224:223 activity ratios can also be explained by the unique properties of coastal karst aquifers. Seawater intrusion and recirculation in these systems cause changes in pH, redox potential, and higher ionic strength, leading to increased solubility and mobility of Ra in the water (Faraj et al., 2020 ). The interaction of seawater with the Ra-bearing minerals in the aquifer leads to the rapid dissolution and release of 224 Ra from thorium-rich carbonate minerals, resulting in higher abundances compared to 223 Ra. On the other hand, the pervasive occurrence of 224:226 activity ratios ˂ 1 is likely explained by the greater abundance of 226 Ra, possibly a result of its long half-life, the richness of its parent isotope uranium-238 (238 U) in the Earth's crust, and higher chemical stability. Thus, 226 Ra remains in the water for extended periods, leading to higher activity than shorter-lived isotopes. While this study did not assess dissolved oxygen, oxidation-reduction potential, or collect porewaters, detecting NH4 +  in groundwater and springs indicates reducing conditions in the aquifers and subterranean estuary. These conditions favor the desorption of short-lived isotopes near discharge points. Because Ra input from sediments is largely dependent on the production time relative to the releasing mechanism of each Ra isotope, it is expected that a near-continuous availability of 224 Ra followed by 223 Ra with respect to 226 Ra will occur (Garcia-Orellana et al., 2021 ). The higher presence of 224 Ra than 223 Ra is mostly due to its shorter half-life and rapid regeneration from thorium-228 (228 Th), which is more abundant in sediments than uranium-235 (235 U), the parent isotope of 223 Ra (Weinstein et al., 2021 ). This study provides valuable insights into the variability and complexity of SGD rates and radium activities in coastal karst environments and shows important spatial variability of the groundwater radiogenic tracers and SGD within a reef lagoon, ultimately enhancing our understanding of nutrient dynamics and their impacts on coastal ecosystems.  4.2 Nutrient Dynamics and the Importance of Groundwater Tracer Selection The spatial distribution and source predictive analyses of various nutrients reveal significant insights into the nutrient dynamics within the lagoon. Concentrations of NH4 +  are best explained by 226 Ra, accounting for approximately 53 % of the variability. This strong association suggests that NH4 +  inputs are primarily from groundwater sources, such as XcaHa, Private 2, Ojo de Aqua, and Gorgos. Stations clustering at the lower end of the NH4 +  and 226 Ra relationship indicate the mixing of terrestrial groundwater with seawater in most parts of the reef lagoon. High NH4 +  and 226 Ra levels near discharge points suggest that SGD significantly enriches these areas with nutrients, particularly during high-velocity discharges, which reduce the oxidation time of NH4 +  to NOx- within the water column. This is especially important in spring-dominated areas (Zehr and Capone, 2021 ). Although elevated 226 Ra levels in groundwater and springs are expected to correlate with higher 222 Rn levels, potential atmospheric evasion due to turbulent flow and dilution with seawater at discharge points can reduce 222 Rn activities. In addition, high-velocity flow may reduce the time required for water to reach equilibrium with respect to 222 Rn when the rate of 222 Rn production from 226 Ra decay balances with the rate of 222 Rn decay. Likewise, the nitrification of NH4 +  to NO3 -  is limited near these types of discharge points. While 222 Rn was not an explanatory variable in the NH4 +  model, comprehensive hydrogeological and geochemical analyses would aid in understanding these dynamics better. Concentrations of NOx -  exhibit considerable variability across station sites, with the highest and lowest levels found in the lagoon. The lowest concentrations were observed at Limones and Bonanza reefs, possibly due to the coral holobiont's nitrogen uptake primarily in the form of NH4 +  and NO3 -  (Rädecker et al., 2015 ) or due to a limited terrestrial supply. The best NOx -  predictor is 223 Ra, explaining 22 % of its variability. Given the half-life of 223 Ra, transit times may vary from mere seconds to tens of days, with the latter at the higher salinity end indicating that NOx -  production occurs within short time frames, primarily near discharge locations (Garcia-Orellana et al., 2021 ). In the springs, the lowest NOx -  but highest 223 Ra activities were observed at Gorgos and Ojo de Aqua, while NTSpring had higher levels of both NOx -  and 223 Ra. This pattern underscores the importance of using 223 Ra-derived SGD rates to calculate NOx -  fluxes, as they reflect recent groundwater inputs and highlight nearshore oxic groundwater pathways for NOx -  entering the lagoon. For HPO4 2- , the regression models accounted for less than 1 % of the variability, indicating unlikely correlations with radiogenic tracers, stable isotopes, or salinity. The primary origin of HPO4 2-  in the lagoon might not be terrestrial groundwater but rather in situ processes or other factors influencing its distribution. Phosphate is a limiting factor for primary productivity in coastal biogeochemical cycles (Silbiger et al., 2020 ) and can become enriched in groundwater due to anthropogenic contaminants such as sewage or fertilizers. Yet, with the limited number of samples available, this study captured only relatively low concentrations of HPO4 2-  in groundwater. While more research is needed on the topic, it has been shown that the behavior of HPO4 2-  is nonconservative in carbonate aquifers, particularly in coastal areas where terrestrial freshwater mixes with seawater (Elliott, 1999 ). Phosphate may adsorb to carbonate mineral surfaces and subsequently precipitate as calcium phosphate (Santos et al., 2021 ). The HPO4 2-  mobility in groundwater poses a challenge in predicting its behavior. Further research incorporating additional variables like major cations, redox potential, dissolved oxygen, and pH is needed to understand HPO4 2-  dynamics better. Given the intricate nature of these processes and the potential for HPO4 2-  to leach into the groundwater from the breakdown of minerals in nearby underground estuaries (for example, through springs such as Gorgos) with active recirculation or through the mangroves (in this case at the location of the Inlet) (Hernández-Terrones et al., 2011 ), 223 Ra is employed as a proxy to track any terrestrial groundwater inflows to the lagoon as it accurately mirrors the timing of these processes. Concentrations of HSiO3 -  were best predicted by salinity and 223 Ra, explaining 44 % of the observed variability. It is expected that HSiO3 -  is mostly derived from land-based minerals (Khan et al., 2015 ), and its concentration in aquifers increases directly proportional with groundwater residence time (Marchand et al., 2002 ), particularly where silicate minerals like quartz, feldspar, and mica, among others, are abundant. Assuming stable and favorable conditions for desorption, 226 Ra activity will also increase with longer residence times (Szabo et al., 2012 ). Thus, a positive correlation between HSiO3 -  and 226 Ra is anticipated. For instance, weathering processes are a likely source of HSiO3 -  in aquifers, Sprinkle (1989)  found that the mineral weathering processes may affect silicates in carbonate formations in the Floridan aquifer. Thus, groundwater concentrations of HSiO3 -  are expected to increase with groundwater residence time, with a positive correlation with 226 Ra possibly emerging. XcaHa is the highest in 226 Ra, yet it is among the lowest in groundwater HSiO3 - , which alters the correlation. When excluding XcaHa, a positive HSiO3 -  - 226 Ra correlation suggests that 226 Ra could explain 45 % of the variability in the regression model. This correlation is primarily driven by the Gorgos spring, which is the only sample confirming the suggestion above, and this could be why 226 Ra did not represent an indicator of HSiO3 -  in the regression model. The larger HSiO3 -  in the springs compared to stations, and the more elevated 223 Ra reflect a terrestrial input within time scales of days, indicating that the greatest addition to SGD occurs in the nearby coastal aquifers. Although our dataset is limited, Null et al. (2014)  also reported elevated levels of silica in groundwater samples compared to surface waters. Notably, higher concentrations were found in fresh groundwater compared to stations, and other studies found saline beach groundwater to be lower in HSiO3 -  than fresh groundwater (Hernández Terrones et al., 2011). Null et al. (2014)  hypothesized that higher dissolved silica in fresh groundwater is related to either the leaching of silicates from the shallow soil layer or dissolution under reducing conditions in the subterranean estuary, a phenomenon also observed in other carbonate-dominated karst settings (Fourqurean et al., 1993; Asano et al., 2003 ). Based on our dataset's findings regarding the correlation with 223 Ra and past research indicating elevated silica levels in fresh groundwater, we propose that HSiO3 -  may be seeping from the sandy beach aquifer and the unconfined calcareous sandstone, which is known to reach depths of around 10 m below the surface (González-Herrera et al., 2022 ). This finding is exemplified by the samples from Private 1, Private 2, and Mojarras. Based on the regression model outcomes and the presumed primary origin of HSiO3 - , the solute flux evaluations rely on the SGD rates derived from 223 Ra. In contrast, salinity does not yield pertinent insights for an SGD mass balance due to the considerable disparities between the shallow groundwater resources and the lagoon waters, including springs that were marginally more saline than the stations. However, the added variable plots of 223 Ra and salinity versus HSiO3 -  resulting from the regression model groups the Gorgos spring with the Private 1, Private 2, and Mojarras cenotes as the endmember sources (Fig. 8 ). Urea, commonly found in groundwater, originates from various sources such as agricultural activities, animal manure, and industrial waste, or to a lesser extent, naturally from the decomposition of organic matter (Beig et al., 2020 ). Its high solubility and low adsorption to soil particles make urea highly mobile in groundwater systems. The persistence of urea in groundwater depends on factors such as soil type, temperature, pH, and the presence of specific microorganisms. For instance, higher temperatures enhance the enzymatic hydrolysis of urea, leading to increased ammonia production (Dadrasnia et al., 2021 ). This hydrolysis yields NH4 +  (King et al., 2017 ), which can further undergo nitrification, especially in the presence of oxygen, to form NO2 -  and NO3 - . This transformation increases nitrogen compounds in the water, enriching surface water bodies and potentially stimulating harmful phytoplankton blooms, as observed in Sarasota Bay, Florida (Ivey et al., 2020 ). The role of urea in promoting coastal harmful algae blooms (HABs) is supported by studies in estuarine (Glibert and Terlizzi, 1999 ) and lagoonal (Collos et al., 2014 ) environments, where blooms often follow substantial urea inputs (Fan et al., 2003 ). Kudela et al. (2008)  found that many HAB species on California’s coast prefer urea as a nitrogen source, even at low concentrations (≤0.9 µM). This is particularly relevant to our findings that high urea concentrations are associated with more elevated 223 Ra activities (in springs and cenotes), indicating substantial groundwater contributions in the Puerto Morelos to Cancun reef lagoon. The regression model identified two distinct trends regarding urea distribution. Urea entering the LL through springs (e.g., XcaHa) is likely sourced from high-velocity conduit flows, allowing less time for hydrolysis reactions due to short residence times within the aquifer. Conversely, Private 2 and the lagoon inlet samples cluster with other stations and shallow groundwater samples, suggesting a more diffuse flow through the beach sand aquifer or the unconfined calcareous sandstone formation into the UL. This diffuse flow allows for more extended hydrolysis and transformation processes, explaining the observed variability in urea concentrations. Identifying 223 Ra as a key groundwater tracer for urea inputs highlights the importance of using specific tracers to accurately determine the sources and dynamics of SGD. This finding aligns with previous research indicating that radium isotopes effectively trace groundwater inputs and nutrient dynamics in coastal environments (Bejannin et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021 ). By employing robust tracer-based methods with nutrient measurements and statistical modeling, this study highlights the critical role of environmental conditions and spatial groundwater discharge dynamics in influencing isotope distributions and nutrient inputs in coastal karst lagoons. Future research should focus on incorporating additional environmental variables to account for spatial and temporal heterogeneity in groundwater endmember’s chemistry and variability in coastal waters.  4.3 Nutrient Fluxes and Regional Relevance The primary inorganic nutrients entering the sampled lagoon were NOx - , NH4 + , and HSiO3 - . Similar to Null et al. (2014) , who reported greater NO3 -  concentrations in beach groundwater compared to springs, lagoons, and offshore waters, this study found higher concentrations of NOx -  near the coast (e.g., Coastal) and reef areas closer to the shore (e.g., Backreef, and NTReef). The excessive accumulation of sargassum seaweed on Caribbean beaches in recent years was found to be one of the causes of eutrophication in the coral reefs of the Mexican Caribbean (Velázquez-Ochoa and Enríquez, 2023 ). According to a study by Rutten et al. (2021) , 2018 saw a significant increase in pelagic sargassum. The natural biodegradation of sargassum on beaches may introduce substantial amounts of NH4 +  into the beach aquifer, which can oxidize to form NO3 -  upon discharge into oxic waters. Therefore, there is a need to evaluate multiple groundwater sources when studying nutrient fluxes. This is especially pertinent to the analysis of NOx -  fluxes fluctuations, which are heavily influenced by the solute origin, the flow velocity (Almillátegui Martínez, 2023 ), and other biogeochemical conditions within the stratified karst aquifers and the subterranean estuary (Brankovits et al., 2022 ). The nearshore spring inputs (e.g., NTSpring) led to the largest NOx -  inputs, contrasting with the NH4 +  fluxes driven predominantly by distant groundwater inputs (XcaHa). This suggests that different groundwater sources have distinct nutrient profiles, influencing the overall nutrient dynamics in the lagoon. Additionally, the higher NO2 -  concentrations in beach groundwater, as reported by Null et al. (2014) , complement our hypothesis regarding the conversion of NH4 +  to NOx -  upon contact with oxic seawater, also observed in numerous other studies (Weissman et al., 2021; Wilson et al., 2024 ). This conversion is expected to be responsible for most of the measured NOx - , yet additional sources are likely, as evidenced by the high NOx -  and low NH4 +  concentrations in the coastal spring and other nearshore locations, as mentioned above. Furthermore, the HSiO3 -  statistical model finds salinity as a key predictor, suggesting that recirculation intensifies water-rock interactions, potentially increasing HSiO3 -  through mineral dissolution (Mora et al., 2020 ). Elevated HSiO3 -  levels in shallow groundwater and springs (e.g., Private 2 and Gorgos) corroborate this. The urea and HPO4 2-  fluxes were the lowest nutrient fluxes, with no significant concentration variability among sample categories (Fig. 6 c, e ). The regression model does not identify the source endmember for HPO4 2- , which calls for caution when considering groundwater-derived fluxes. As discussed in Section 3.2 , HPO4 2-  exhibits a nonconservative behavior (Elliott, 1999; Santos et al., 2021 ), with the endmember concentrations fluctuating with the salinity and oxidation-reduction potential of water entering the aquifer, which cannot be accounted for with the current study design. Additionally, HPO4 2-  may originate from in situ organic matter degradation and bird excrement. Thus, additional sources may further obscure the sea solute mass balance. Despite these complexities, the SGD daily fluxes of HPO4 2-  and urea using this study’s groundwater endmembers hint at groundwater as inputs that should not be neglected. This study’s nutrient fluxes are within the range of other fluxes reported in the literature that represent coastal karst worldwide. For instance, Hernández-Terrones et al. (2011)  reported that Puerto Morelos Lagoon receives 3.57×107  mmol·d−1  (or 200 kg N monthly) from a flow of 1.38 ×103  m3 ·d−1  through SGD. Compared to this study's daily average flux of 2.29×109  mmol N (including urea) for the UL and 1.41×1010  for the LL, these previous estimates are marginal due to larger SGD rates measured in this study (3–5 orders of magnitude higher). Notably, both studies were sampled in a single season (e.g., October), specifically targeting the highest water table levels, when the groundwater flow and its mixing with underlying saline water are near their annual highest. These findings also align with other studies showing that SGD may contribute ∼70 times more N and ∼194 times more P of anthropogenic origin than the decomposition of the pelagic macroalgae Sargassum spp  (Camacho-Cruz et al., 2022 ). On the other hand, a study by Liu et al. (2019)  reported a DIN flux of (50.4–328) × 106  for the KRE Surface Layer (Adriatic Sea, Croatia), aligning more closely with our study's UL values but still lower than the global average and the LL in this study. Additionally, NO3 -  fluxes from the Côte Bleue, French Mediterranean karstic coastline were at least 3 orders of magnitude lower 4.0 (±2.0) ×106  (Bejannin et al., 2020 ). Similarly, NO3 -  fluxes from the tropical karstic region of Gunung Kidul (southern Java Indonesia) ranged from 5×106  to 139×106  (Oehler et al., 2017 ). In Zaton Bay (Mediterranean Sea), DIN fluxes from SGD (1.4–3.3×107 ) were found (Chen et al., 2020 ) to be in the same order of magnitude as the UL. In comparison, the global ocean nutrient fluxes (Cho et al., 2018 ), were between 2 and 3 orders of magnitude higher (e.g., 6.3 (± 1.6) ×1012 ) than those reported in this study and much larger than other coastal karst areas. Fluxes of phosphate (or DIP) ranged between 5.67×106  in the UL to 1.01×108  P mmol·d−1  in the LL, which are more in line with the global ocean estimates of 1.6 (±0.5) ×1011  (Cho et al., 2018 ) compared to other coastal karst areas. For instance, Hernández-Terrones et al. (2011)  reported DIP fluxes were much lower, ranging from 0.02 to 0.06×106 , even though endmember concentrations were one order of magnitude higher than those measured in the current study. Liu et al. (2019)  reported rates between 0.16–0.91×106,  nearing the rates found herein for the UL. The median DIP flux for the Mediterranean Sea (0.5–1.7×105 ) was also orders of magnitude lower (Chen et al., 2020 ). Santos et al. (2021)  state that the DIP fluxes reaching the Mediterranean Sea are about three times lower than those reaching the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. This is because the Mediterranean coastline has many karstified aquifers that retain phosphate, as also mentioned in the study. Silicate (or DSi) was found to enter the UL and the LL areas at rates of 1.22×108  and 2.19×109 , respectively, which are nearing the global ocean DSi fluxes of 10.4 (±2.7) ×1012  reported by Cho et al. (2018) . Additionally, DSi fluxes from the Gunung Kidul coast of Indonesia ranged from 50 to 310×106  (Oehler et al., 2017 ), with those for the Adriatic Sea (Liu et al., 2019 ) from 47.0–270×106 . Contrary to karst aquifers' carbonate-reach lithologic and mineral composition with a generally lower abundance of silicate minerals, some areas may contribute to the global ocean silicate budget. Our flux analyses strongly suggest karst areas as substantial contributors to the aforementioned budget, particularly where the lithology includes other sedimentary facies like the unconfined calcareous sandstone. These findings highlight the importance of using groundwater tracers to determine the correct SGD rates and emphasize the need for further research to fully understand the dynamics of nutrient fluxes and their ecological impacts in coastal karst environments.  4.4 Ecological Impacts of Groundwater Nutrient Inputs to Coral Reefs Coral reefs rely on nutrient inputs to survive in otherwise nutrient-depleted waters. Recycled nutrients, or those originating from within the reef system, are present in organic and inorganic forms taken up by benthic organisms and primary producers (Pawlik et al., 2016 ). “New” nutrients, or those resulting from bottom upwelling, riverine inputs, and atmospheric deposition, may increase DIN concentrations in reef waters, potentially overwhelming nutrient cycling processes and leading to nutrient overaccumulation (Pawlik et al., 2016 ). The absence of new nutrients from riverine inputs in the study area means that terrestrial nitrogen supply to corals depends heavily on SGD. The variability in nutrient forms and magnitudes supplied via SGD can benefit or harm coral health and symbiosis, depending on environmental conditions and timing. Eutrophication is a well-established localized threat that may harm coral health by resulting in the proliferation of algae and algal mats. Multiple disturbances, including coral bleaching, loss of herbivores, and overfishing, can reduce coral resilience and increase substrate availability for algae proliferation. Hughes (1994)  and Hughes et al. (2011)  documented the large-scale degradation of Caribbean coral reefs, showing that the loss of herbivores, particularly due to disease affecting the sea urchin Diadema antillarum , led to a phase shift towards macroalgal dominance. The decline in herbivory was the culprit for the macroalga outcompeting corals, significantly changing reef community structure. In this study’s one-time assessment, the reef lagoon of Puerto Morelos, nutrient inputs from the lower and upper lagoon exhibit distinct characteristics hypothesized to influence coral symbiosis and ecosystem health differently. As seen in  Fig. 11 , in the Si-rich zone, groundwater endmember sites such as OdeA2 (L.T.), Private2, Private1, and Mojarras and the seawater NTLagoon location exhibit high DIN ratios and relatively balanced DIN ratios close to the Redfield ratio of 16:1 for N. These conditions suggest a favorable environment for diatom growth, supporting a stable base for the food web and promoting coral health. The high silica concentrations at NTLagoon indicate significant SGD inputs, likely from the shallow aquifer, as described in Sections 3.3 and 4.2 . These areas need to be monitored for their long-term impact on nutrient dynamics and coral health. Conversely, sites like NTReef and Backreef in the N-rich zone show similarities to the submarine groundwater springs in the LL area, XcaHa, and OdeA1 (H.T). Nutrient concentrations such as DIN above 1.0 µmol·L−1  can facilitate macroalgal proliferation, especially without effective herbivory, leading to macroalgal dominance over corals (Lapointe, 1997, 1999 ). Elevated DIN relative to DIP can result in an overabundance of symbiotic algae (Symbiodiniaceae ) within corals (Wiedenmann et al., 2013; Cunning and Baker, 2013 ). This imbalance may increase the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) under thermal and light stress, causing oxidative stress and coral bleaching. Thus, these N-rich sites in the LL area are particularly vulnerable. In the P-rich zone, sites like Limones, UNAM, FR2, FR3 Inlet, and Bonanza show higher DIP levels relative to DIN and DSi and do not show signatures like the sampled groundwater endmembers. It is important to note that elevated phosphorus can also contribute to localized eutrophication and shifts in coral reef dynamics if not balanced with nitrogen (Rädecker et al., 2021 ). Concentrations of DIN and DIP above 1.0 µmol ·L−1  can lead to phase shifts from coral to macroalgae-dominated reefs (Lapointe, 1997; Hughes, 1994; Hughes et al., 2011 ). Several sites exceed these thresholds (Fig. 11 ), highlighting the risk of such phase shifts in the study area, particularly those in the UL where SGD inputs of new nutrients are limited, and most N species, in particular, are believed to be of recycled nature. While it has been shown that increased nutrient levels can change coral reef communities, the long-term ENCORE experiment on the Great Barrier Reef demonstrated that nutrient addition did not significantly increase macroalgal growth unless nutrients were limiting. In addition, herbivory played a crucial role in controlling macroalgal biomass even under elevated nutrient conditions (Koop et al., 2001; Szmant, 2002; McCook, 1999; Bell et al., 2007 ). In our study, the higher nutrient inputs from SGD in the lower lagoon (LL) require effective herbivory to prevent macroalgal overgrowth and maintain coral health. On the other hand, reefs in the UL may lack effective herbivore communities, potentially impacted by the imbalance in DIP to DIN ratio. Studies should focus on evaluating the abundance of these regulators to ensure that SGD-derived nutrient inputs, or lack of them, will not negatively impact the health of reefs. While our study provides significant insights into the impact of SGD-derived nutrients on coral health, it is essential to consider its limitations. The absence of data on organic nutrients, such as dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and dissolved organic nitrogen (DON), limits our understanding of their role in coral reef ecosystems. Organic nutrients account for most of the total nitrogen in coral reef environments and can significantly influence nutrient cycling and availability, impacting coral health and resilience (Lin et al., 2024 ). For instance, high coral diversity and coverage are often associated with low organic matter concentrations and high C/N ratios, while macroalgae-dominating sites had elevated organic matter levels. Focusing on the balance between new and recycled nutrients is crucial to better understanding the health status discrepancy among the coral reefs and maintaining coral health and ecosystem stability. Future research should focus on the following areas to better understand the potential ecological impacts of nutrient dynamics on coral reefs and identify and evaluate potential sites for coral restoration: (1) Incorporate measurements of DOC and DON to provide a more comprehensive understanding of nutrient dynamics; (2) Conduct time-series sampling to capture seasonal and diurnal variations in nutrient concentrations and their impacts on coral health; (3) Investigate the role of microbial communities in nutrient cycling and their interactions with organic matter in coral reef environments; (4) Establish long-term monitoring programs to assess the impacts of global warming, ocean acidification, and anthropogenic influences on nutrient dynamics and coral reef health.   5 Conclusion This study underscores the critical role of SGD in influencing nutrient dynamics within coastal karst environments. Our investigation reveals that different nutrient forms, specifically NH4 + , NOx - , HSiO3 - , HPO4 2- , and urea, exhibit distribution and source contributions variability. Statistical regression and process-based analysis allowed us to elucidate the complex interactions between SGD and nutrient dynamics. The study effectively quantifies relationships between multiple groundwater tracers as predictors of different nutrient types and their presence in the lagoon by identifying radium isotopes as key predictors. Radium-226 was a significant predictor for long-term nutrient inputs associated with terrestrial groundwater discharge, while 223 Ra provided insights into short-term nutrient variability linked to recent groundwater discharge. This dual approach highlights the importance of integrating statistical and process-based methods to capture nutrient fluxes' temporal and spatial variability in the reef lagoon.  Limitations and Future Research Despite the valuable insights gained, this study has limitations that warrant further investigation. The focus on specific nutrients may overlook other significant compounds that impact coral health and ecosystem dynamics. Future research should expand the range of studied nutrients and consider factors such as dissolved organic matter and trace metals. Additionally, the temporal scale interaction between long-term and short-term nutrient processes needed to be deeply explored. Future studies should integrate multiple temporal assessments to capture the dynamics of SGD inputs more accurately. This could involve using advanced modeling techniques to understand better the interplay between different nutrient sources and their impact on coral reefs. Moreover, additional predictors like dissolved oxygen, pH, and the stoichiometry of ambient nutrients and coral symbiosis should be evaluated to better understand the interplay between groundwater and surface water interactions and their impact on coral health.  Broader impacts The results from this study, while focused on the Puerto Morelos to Cancun reef lagoon, have wider implications and relevance to other coastal karst regions. The observed nutrient dynamics and groundwater inputs are not unique to this area but represent processes occurring in similar environments worldwide. For example, the variability in nutrient fluxes and the influence of SGD observed here align with Mediterranean and Adriatic Sea findings. Similar patterns of radium isotopes and nutrient distributions have been documented in these regions, indicating that the mechanisms driving nutrient fluxes in the Caribbean sea’s reef lagoon apply to other coastal karst systems. Moreover, the spatial patterns observed in this study, divided into upper and lower lagoon regions, provide a detailed understanding of how groundwater inputs vary within small transects. This level of detail is crucial for comprehensively understanding nutrient dynamics on a regional scale. As indicated by radium isotopes, the differentiation between fresh and recirculated groundwater and the impact on nutrient concentrations significantly contribute to the broader knowledge of SGD processes. The findings from this study can inform regional environmental management strategies by illustrating the importance of accounting for the diverse sources and pathways of nutrient inputs. For instance, the high nutrient fluxes in the lower lagoon area, driven by both long-term and short-term groundwater inputs, highlight the potential for eutrophication and its ecological impacts. Such insights are vital for developing targeted conservation efforts in similar coastal karst environments facing similar challenges. Furthermore, the study underscores the need for integrated, multidisciplinary approaches combining geological and ecological perspectives to manage and conserve coastal ecosystems effectively. Advanced modeling techniques to differentiate between sources of SGD and nutrient inputs provide a framework that can be applied to other regions to enhance the understanding of nutrient dynamics and their ecological implications. This study significantly contributes to understanding nutrient fluxes into a reef lagoon. It specifically focuses on a nearshore karstic environment with varying land-to-water subsurface hydrologic connections and types of SGD. The study offers valuable insights that apply to coastal karst environments globally. By emphasizing the importance of localized studies and groundwater tracers capturing long- and short-term inputs, the research contributes to a broader understanding of regional and global nutrient cycles, essential for managing and conserving coastal ecosystems in the face of ongoing environmental changes.
1 Introduction Baseflow typically refers to the groundwater originating from antecedent precipitation and the gradual replenishment of other water resources, which plays a critical role in contributing to streamflow, particularly serving as the predominant source of streamflow during dry seasons (Zhang et al., 2013; Apurv and Cai, 2020 ). Global assessments reveal a median baseflow index (the ratio of baseflow to total streamflow) varying between 0.49 and 0.77 across major climatic zones, underscoring the substantial contribution of groundwater to streamflow (Lee and Hoori, 2023 ). Furthermore, the detailed study of baseflow is essential in various aspects of water resource research. This includes its significance in industrial and agricultural water supply, water security, assessment of non-point source pollution, water resource evaluation and exploration, as well as in the modeling and simulation of rainfall-runoff dynamics (Beck et al., 2013; Hellwig and Stahl, 2018 ). However, the magnitude of baseflow is closely associated with a range of environmental factors such as topography, climate, soil composition, vegetation cover, basin size, and other characteristics of the underlying surface (Hellwig et al.,2021 ). Due to this complex interplay, accurately determining baseflow cannot be reliably achieved through direct observation alone. It necessitates the use of indirect estimation methodologies (McMahon and Nathan, 2021; Partington et al., 2012 ). Consequently, the process of baseflow separation stands as a critical and challenging aspect in the field of hydrology, attracting considerable focus and research efforts (Chen et al., 2006; Koskelo et al., 2012 ). Various methodologies for baseflow separation have been developed and proposed by scholars worldwide. Up to date, there are more than ten methods for baseflow separation, including direct separation method (e.g. liner separation method and curve method (Chen et al., 2006 ), water balance method (e.g. hydrological simulation method), isotope method (Frisbee et al., 2022 ), and time series analysis method (e.g. baseflow index method, digital filtering method (Arnold and Allen, 1999 ) and smooth minimum value method (Aksoy et al.,2009 )). However, there is significant controversy and lack of universality in various theories and methods of baseflow separation (Qian et al., 2011; McMahon and Nathan, 2021 ). For example, the linear separation method is relatively simple to implement, but it tends to provide coarse outcomes. The analytical method, while detailed, involves numerous parameters and poses difficulties in identifying sources of error (Partington et al., 2012 ). The isotope tracer method, though precise, is less commonly used in practical applications due to its high costs (Kissel and Schmalz., 2020 ). In contrast, the digital filtering method, despite lacking a foundational hydrological basis, effectively addresses these limitations. This method treats the runoff sequence as a composition of high-frequency (surface runoff) and low-frequency (baseflow) signals (Hu et al., 2017 ). By employing computer automation, it separates and isolates the baseflow component from these signals. This technique mitigates the subjectivity and randomness associated with manual separation methods, offering ease of operation, high efficiency, and practicality. Through continuous improvement by subsequent researchers, the digital filtering method has become the most widely used baseflow separation method internationally (Zhang et al., 2017 ). Due to the important role of baseflow in maintaining the ecological function of rivers and providing water for industrial and agricultural production, numerous researches have been undertaken concerning the evolution of baseflow. These include time series characteristics of baseflow, reasons for baseflow changes, regional applicability of baseflow separation methods, regression analysis of baseflow index, and so on (Yu et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2018 ; Xia et al., 2021 ). For example, Xia et al. (2021)  utilized nine numerical simulation techniques to separate baseflow from the total streamflow of at specific hydrological stations in the Yanwachuan River basin, and conducted trend analyses and abrupt change tests on the basin's baseflow. Li et al. (2018) selected five pivotal hydrological stations in the Poyang Lake basin for baseflow separation analysis, and examined the temporal variations of baseflow and the baseflow index. Some studies have analyzed the changes in baseflow and major causes at both global and regional scales. For example, Tan et al. (2020)  analyzed the changes in baseflow and baseflow index (BFI) at 2374 hydrological stations worldwide from 1970 to 2016, and pointed out that there are significant spatial differences in changes in base flow and BFI due to the influence of regional climate and surface vegetation. Murray et al. (2023)  highlighted that warmer temperatures and increased snow cover across much of Canada have contributed to increased baseflow likely from shifts in snow melt timing and volumes. However, the research about the spatiotemporal characteristics of geographical elements is an eternal theme in geography. Characteristics of surface processes should not only be reflected in the changes in time series, but also demonstrate their spatial distribution patterns. At present, most baseflow studies are limited to temporal analysis of selected hydrological stations, lacking insufficient visualization of the spatial distribution of baseflow across the entire basin. This research gap is attributable to the fact that hydrological stations are mostly installed along major river courses and significant tributaries. As a result, fewer stations are present in smaller and medium-sized basins, leading to a scarcity of comprehensive streamflow data across the basin (Sun et al., 2023 ). The SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) model, a well-known distributed watershed hydrological model based on GIS, excels in simulating various hydrological processes, effectively partitioning complex basins into multiple sub-basins. Due to its operational efficiency, temporal continuity, and easy access to various data sources, the SWAT model stands out among various hydrological models, providing a solution for the lack of measured streamflow data in smaller and medium-sized basins (An and Fang, 2021; Yamini and Manjula, 2021 ). The feature of distributed hydrological simulation of the model have also opened up new avenues for the spatialization and quantitative analysis of baseflow within river basins, and provides possibilities for the evaluation of baseflow changes under climate or land-use change scenarios. Based on the simulation of the baseflow of each divided sub-basin in the SWAT model and the application of GIS spatial interpolation, the spatial distribution of the baseflow across the basin can be characterized (Hu et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2023 ). Building on this theoretical groundwork, the current study has successfully amalgamated the digital filtering method with the SWAT model. Initially, the digital filtering technique was employed for a comprehensive analysis of traditional baseflow temporal characteristics in Ganjiang River Basin, a subtropical mountainous river basin in the southern China. Based on this foundational analysis, the spatial distribution of baseflow in the Ganjiang River Basin was then meticulously mapped by utilizing the methods of SWAT model parameter calibration, GIS spatial interpolation and global trend analysis. The primary objective of this study is to present a detailed and comprehensive overview of the spatiotemporal distribution patterns of baseflow within the basin. Furthermore, the study incorporates an extreme land-use scenario analysis, facilitating a quantitative evaluation of the influence exerted by major land use types on baseflow dynamics in the river basin. Outcomes of this study are anticipated to be instrumental in guiding the sustainable management and conservation of groundwater resources in the basin and in informing the development of efficacious river ecological water demand policies.  2 Study area and data acquisition The Ganjiang River is one of the main tributaries of the Yangtze River and the largest river in Jiangxi Province, China ( Fig. 1 ). The river basin (113°35′E ∼ 118°29′E and 24°29′N ∼ 30°05′N) has a total drainage area of 81,244 km², accounting for 51 % of the territory of Jiangxi Province in central China (Liu et al., 2023 ). The Ganjiang River originates in the Shi Liaodong region of the Wuyi Mountain and flows 823 km northward before entering the Poyang Lake. The basin is located in a subtropical climate zone marked by plentiful rainfall. Annual average precipitation of the basin is about 1400 ∼ 1800 mm (Lu et al., 2021 ). The terrain of the basin is mainly composed of hill and mountain landscapes with an elevation decreasing from south to north (Zhang et al., 2020 ). Due to significant climatic variability and irregular precipitation patterns, the Ganjiang River Basin has suffered from frequent meteorological floods and droughts in recent decades. The rapid economic growth and urbanization in the basin have led to expansion in construction land and changes in underlying surface conditions (Li et al., 2022 ). These have brought great crisis to the local water resources, and have aroused wide concerns to the shrinkage of Poyang Lake and the deterioration of wetland ecosystem. In recent decades, in order to regulate the uneven seasonal distribution of river runoff, many reservoirs have been built in the Ganjiang River Basin, including the Wan'an Reservoir (was built in 1994), the Shihutang Navigation-Power Junction (was built in 2013) and the Xiajiang Water Conservancy Junction (was built in 2015). Land use change and construction of water conservancy projects, to some extent, may affect the spatiotemporal variations of surface and subsurface runoff processes (Li and Zhang, 2018; Duan et al., 2023 ). However, the exact mechanism by which land use/land cover changes affect baseflow alterations is yet to be fully understood. In our research, we have obtained complete natural geographic data of the Ganjiang River Basin, including digital elevation model (DEM), soil type data, land use data, station meteorological data, and observed daily streamflow data from local gauging stations ( Table 1 ). Among which, the three hydrological stations, namely Xiashan, Xiajiang, and Waizhou, are the key control gauging stations to the upper, middle and lower reaches of the Ganjiang River Basin, respectively.  3 Methodology This study examined the spatiotemporal distribution of the baseflow in the Ganjiang River Basin by combining the SWAT model and digital filtering method (illustrated in  Fig. 2 ). Firstly, the digital filtering method was used for baseflow separation of major hydrological stations in the basin, and temporal variation of the calculated baseflow was then analyzed. Secondly, the SWAT model for the Ganjiang River Basin was constructed, and the model was calibrated and validated by using the observed runoff and calculated baseflow from major hydrological stations. Thereafter, the baseflow characteristic values of each sub-basin in the Ganjiang River Basin were simulated and obtained, which were further interpolated to characterize the spatial distribution of baseflow in the whole basin based on GIS spatial analysis. Finally, three hypothetical extreme land use change scenarios were constructed to simulate and analyze the response of baseflow to land use change in the basin. 3.1 Digital filtering method The digital filtering method operates by segregating high-frequency signals from low-frequency ones, thus facilitating the isolation of baseflow (Arnold and Allen, 1999 ). Research conducted by Li and Fan. (2023)  has demonstrated that this method is particularly effective in the Yangtze River Basin context because it can reduce variance and smooth extremes in baseflow separation results. The equation used for digital filtering in this study is as follows:(1) q  t   = α q  t − 1   + 1 + α  2   Q  t   − Q  t − 1          (2) b  t   = Q  t   − q  t       where Q t  and q t   are the measured streamflow and surface runoff at time t , respectively, and satisfy Q t   ≥ q t   (m3 /s); Q t-1   and q t-1   are the measured streamflow and surface runoff at time t- 1, respectively, and satisfy Q t-1   ≥ q t-1   (m3 /s); b t   is the baseflow at time t  (m3 /s); α is the filtering parameter. Previous studies have shown that when the filtering times are set to 3 and α is set to 0.925, better separation results can be achieved (Li and Fan, 2023 ). Moreover, in our study, the baseflow modulus (BFM) and baseflow index (BFI) are utilized as key characteristic values to quantify the distributional attributes of baseflow within the study area. The BFM is defined as the ratio of baseflow to the catchment area, serving as an indicator of the intensity of groundwater recharge to the river channel (Lin et al., 2009 ). The BFI, on the other hand, represents the ratio of baseflow to the total streamflow, signifying the proportion of baseflow in the overall streamflow dynamics (Quan et al., 2023 ). The BFM and BFI can provide important information for the hydrological behavior of river basin.  3.2 SWAT model The SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) model, collaboratively developed by the US Department of Agriculture and the Agricultural Research Service, is a comprehensive basin-scale model anchored in solid physical principles (Olivera et al., 2006 ). It anchored in the principle of water balance and integrated with the ArcGIS platform, offers robust spatial representation capabilities for geographical elements (Gassman et al., 2007 ). This flexibility allows researchers to engage in secondary development, facilitating the creation of a comprehensive visualization system for hydrological information pertinent to river basins. SWAT model adeptly simulates the main components of hydrological processes, including precipitation, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, percolation, lateral subsurface flow, and interactions between shallow aquifers and sediment, striving for high-fidelity representation of natural processes (Lai et al., 2012 ). According to principle of the SWAT model, the SCS-CN (Soil Conservation Service Curve Number) method is used to calculate surface runoff (Lee et al., 2019 ). The model incorporates two types of aquifers: shallow and deep. The shallow aquifer, in particular, is a critical source of baseflow in the river channel. The water balance for the shallow aquifer is given as:(3) aq  sh , i   = aq  sh , i − 1   + W  rchrg , sh   − Q  gw   − W  revap   − W  pump , sh       where aq  sh , i     and aq  sh , i − 1     respectively represent the water storage in the shallow aquifer on the i  and i -1 day (mm); W  rchrg , sh     is the recharge of shallow aquifer on the i  day (mm); W  revap     is the flowing back water to the root zone from the shallow aquifer on the i  day (mm); W  pump , sh     is the output water from the shallow aquifer on the i  day (mm); Q  gw     is the baseflow into the river on the i  day (mm), and expressed by the following formula:(4) Q  gw , i   = Q  gw , i − 1   × exp − α  gw   × ∆ t    + W  rchrg , sh       (5) 1 − exp − α  gw   × ∆ t       , aq  sh   > aq  shthr , q      (6) Q  gw , i   = 0 ,  aq  sh   ≤ aq  shthr , q       where Q  gw , i     and Q  gw , i − 1     are the baseflows into the river on the i  and i-1 day respectively (mm); α  gw     is the regression constant or proportional constant of the baseflow; ∆ t    is the time step; aq  shthr , q     is the water level threshold of shallow aquifer (mm). The SWAT-CUP methodology was applied to perform calibration and uncertainty analysis of the model. Specifically, the SUFI-2 algorithm within the SWAT-CUP was chosen for its robust ability to integrate uncertainties related to monitoring data, model structure, and parameters comprehensively (Ozdemir and Leloglu, 2019 ). The performance of the SWAT model was evaluated by three widely recognized indicators: the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), the coefficient of determination (R²) and the Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE). Detailed methodologies for computing these three indicators can refer to relevant literature (e.g. Wang et al., 2022 ; Moriasi et al., 2015 ). The NSE, ranging from (-∞, 1), is a crucial tool for assessing the overall accuracy and effectiveness of hydrological models. A value approaching 1 indicates a higher reliability and accuracy of the model. The R² quantifies the degree of linear correlation between the simulated and observed data, with its values spanning [0,1]. The NRMSE, ranging from [0,1]. In this study, model simulations are considered to be credible and reliable when R² exceeds 0.6, NSE exceeds 0.5 and NRMSE is below 0.5, aligning with established academic benchmarks (Moriasi et al., 2015 ). These criteria ensure a rigorous and robust assessment of the model's performance.  3.3 Land use scenario setting The influence of land use changes on baseflow arises from the cumulative impacts of various land use categories, making the quantitative analysis of individual land use type on baseflow a complex task. In the Ganjiang River Basin, the predominant land use types are cultivation land, forest, and grassland, which collectively account for 95 % of the basin's total area. To effectively dissect the impact of these principal land use types on the spatiotemporal variations of baseflow in the basin, this study adopts the land use pattern of 2020 as the baseline scenario (S0) and constructed three additional hypothetical extreme scenarios (S1, S2, S3), as delineated in  Table 2 . These scenarios are designed to facilitate simulations under extreme land use conditions, providing a more comprehensive understanding of land use impacts on baseflow dynamics. Specifically, the scenarios include: Forest Scenario (S1), which preserves the current urban and rural construction land, unused land, and water bodies, while converting all grassland and cultivated land areas into forest; Grassland Scenario (S2), under this scenario, urban and rural construction land, unused land, and water bodies are retained in their existing state, with all forested and cultivated land areas being transformed into grasslands; Cultivated Scenario (S3), this involves maintaining the existing urban and rural construction land, unused land, and water areas, while reclassifying all forest and grassland regions as cultivated land.   4 Results 4.1 Variations of calculated baseflow using the Digital Filtering Method 4.1.1 Intra-annual variation  Fig. 3  delineates the monthly variations in observed streamflow and calculated baseflow and BFI at the three hydrological stations along the Ganjiang River. The data reveals a pronounced 'single-peak' pattern in both streamflow and baseflow at these stations, manifested as an initial surge followed by a gradual diminution over the year. Notably, the peak streamflow of these stations was recorded in June, while the lowest point occurs in December. However, the monthly baseflow exhibits varied patterns; the highest average baseflow was observed in June at Xiashan station (385.00 m³/s) and in May at Xiajiang (1688.77 m³/s) and Waizhou stations (650.63 m³/s), while the lowest was in December at Xiashan Station and in January at the other two stations. This evidences a significant disparity in the monthly variations of streamflow and baseflow across the basin. The BFIs of the three stations are generally opposite to the variations of streamflow, with the lowest in June and the highest in December.  4.1.2 Inter-annual variation  Fig. 4  graphically presents the inter-annual variations of streamflow, baseflow and precipitation at the three stations since 1960. The figure elucidates a steady linear relationship between the annual baseflow and streamflow at these stations, and manifests a significant positive correlation with regional precipitation. This pattern underscores that variations in both streamflow and baseflow are substantially influenced by precipitation. In contrast to streamflow, the baseflow demonstrates a more stable inter-annual fluctuation pattern, with the annual baseflow in the upper, middle, and lower reaches varying from 53.40 m³/s to 354.12 m³/s, 259.15 m³/s to 1104.77 m³/s, and 370.39 m³/s to 1432.40 m³/s, respectively. This observation highlights the critical and consistent role of baseflow in augmenting streamflow within the basin.  Fig. 5  eloquently illustrates that at the three representative hydrological stations, the BFI showed a large fluctuation but insignificant increasing trend. In the Ganjiang River Basin, the BFI values at these stations fluctuated between 0.30 and 0.59, 0.23–0.59, and 0.28–0.67, correspondingly, with multi-year average values of 0.45, 0.46, and 0.47. It is noteworthy that the long-term change trend of BFI was generally consistent with the increasing trend of local annual precipitation, while negative correlations were found between the two at the three stations. In addition, the proportions of baseflow within the streamflow displayed marginal variations across different sub-basins. An observable trend was the gradual widening of this fluctuation range from the upstream to the downstream segments of the basin. This pattern underscores the notion that the baseflow proportion in streamflow is influenced not merely by precipitation levels but also exhibits increased variability concomitant with the augmentation of basin area and streamflow.   4.2 Model calibration and performance 4.2.1 Parameter optimization The SWAT model optimization was conducted according to the observed streamflow and calculated baseflow at the three stations in the Ganjiang River Basin. 13 key parameters were finally selected for calibration based on the results of sensitivity analysis, including the runoff curve number (CN2) and the baseflow alpha factor (ALPHA_BF). In this study, the two years from 1960 to 1961 was set to the model warming-up period. The calibration of the SWAT model was designated to a 21 years period from 1962 to 1982, while the validation encompassed another similar 21 years period from 1983 to 2003. The calibration process involved 2000 iterations to ultimately determine the final parameter values and their optimal configuration.  Table 3  provides a systematic and detailed explanation of these parameter values and their optimal configuration.  4.2.2 Model performance  Fig. 6  shows the comparison of simulated and observed streamflow during model calibration and validation periods. From visual inspection, the model producing an overall good fit, with the simulated streamflow fluctuations at the three hydrological stations are highly consistent with the observed results on a monthly time scale. The performance of the SWAT model were further rigorously evaluated by the indicators of NSE, NRMSE and R². As shown in  Table 4  that during both calibration and validation periods, the R² of all hydrological stations consistently exceeded 0.6, the NSE remained above 0.5 and the NRMSE below 0.5. This performance benchmark indicates that the optimized SWAT model can proficiently replicate the runoff dynamics within the Ganjiang River Basin, demonstrating its robust capability in simulating the region's hydrological processes. The simulated monthly baseflow at the three stations along the Ganjiang River were also compared with the calculated results of digital filtering method. As shown in  Fig. 7 , R2  of the three typical hydrological stations are all greater than 0.6, indicating that the results obtained by the two methods have a good degree of fitting. The simulated baseflow exhibits a spatial variation characteristic that gradually increase from upstream to downstream. Detailed process indicates that the separation results of digital filtering method were higher than those of SWAT model simulation method. The relative error of simulation results at the three hydrological stations was between 8 % and 12 %. The model simulation results were higher than those of the digital filtering method in months with higher baseflow, while the model simulation results were lower than that of the digital filtering method in months with lower baseflow.   4.3 Spatial distribution characteristics of baseflow To visually elucidate the spatial distribution of baseflow within the Ganjiang River Basin, this study examined the multi-year annual average baseflow and the BFM at a sub-basin scale from 1960 to 2003. Utilizing the established SWAT model, the Ganjiang River Basin was delineated into 33 distinct sub-basins. These include 8 sub-basins in the upper basin, 15 in the middle basin, and 10 in the lower basin. The multi-year average baseflow values and BFM for each sub-basin were accurately extracted to their central points from the simulation data. The Geographic Information System (GIS) spatial analysis methodologies, notably the Kriging interpolation and global trend analysis within geostatistical tools, were then applied to discern the spatial distributions of the annual average baseflow and BFM across these sub-basins. As depicted in  Fig. 8 , the spatial distribution of the annual average baseflow and BFM within the Ganjiang River Basin exhibits significant variability. Specifically, baseflow in the upper Ganjiang River Basin varies between 31 and 1509 m³/s, the middle basin varies between 103 and 3371 m³/s, and the lower basin varies between 191 and 4860 m³/s (Fig. 8 a). Predominantly, the annual average baseflow is observed to be greater in the lower Ganjiang River Basin, showing a discernible decreasing trend from the northern to the southern parts of the basin. This is complemented by a spatial pattern of higher values in the central regions and lower values towards the peripheral areas, as illustrated in Fig. 8 a. Concurrently, the GIS global trend analysis highlights an increasing northward gradient in the annual average baseflow, accompanied by a spatial variation that initially rises and then falls from west to east (Fig. 8 c). The BFM was calculated by dividing the baseflow at the terminal section of each sub-basin by its corresponding controlled watershed area. The BFM acts as a pivotal indicator, reflecting the intensity of average regional groundwater recharge into surface water runoff. Fig. 8 b illustrates the spatial distribution of the annual average BFM across the Ganjiang River Basin, with BFM varies between 26×103  m³/s/km2  and 110×103  m³/s/km2 . An observable trend of increasing BFM from the upstream areas to the downstream areas can be obtained, as evidenced in the spatial distribution map and corroborated by GIS global trend analysis (Fig. 8 d). Notably, in the northwestern region of the Ganjiang River Basin, BFM values ranging from 90×103  m³/s/km2  to 110 ×103  m³/s/km2 , which signify an area of very strong recharge.  4.4 Response of baseflow to land use change The optimized SWAT model was further applied to conduct a quantitative analysis of land use change impact on local baseflow. This facilitated the simulation of the baseflow spatiotemporal distribution under three distinct land use scenarios (S1, S2, and S3), while maintaining constant climatic and soil variables within the model framework. By using the simulated baseflow under the 2020 baseline land use scenario (S0) as a reference, we conducted an analysis of the baseflow changes under three alternative land use scenarios. The spatial distribution patterns of the multi-year annual average baseflow under the three scenarios (S1, S2, and S3) largely mirrored those in the baseline scenario in terms of spatial variability ( Fig. 9 ). However, noticeable differences were observed in the magnitude of baseflow. The ranking in terms of baseflow magnitude is as follows: S1 (1155.5 m³/s) > S2 (1036.3 m³/s) > S0 (1006.7 m³/s) > S3 (866.7 m³/s). Under the fully cultivated land use scenario, the baseflow may experience a decrease of 13.9 % in comparison to the basic scenario. Conversely, under the fully forested and fully grassland scenarios, the baseflow may witness an increase of 14.7 % and 2.9 %, respectively, relative to the basic scenario.   5 Discussions The Ganjiang River Basin is characterized by a subtropical climate, marked by distinct seasonal fluctuations in precipitation and temperature. These climatic variances play a crucial role in modulating the streamflow and baseflow dynamics within the basin (Lu et al., 2021 ). Seasonal variation of baseflow positively correlate with concurrent precipitation, indicating that precipitation is the main recharge source for baseflow. However, seasonal BFI shows opposite pattern to that of baseflow. In addition, this study also identified a negative correlation between the annual BFI and precipitation. Xu et al. (2013)  previously utilized the elastic coefficient method to assess the quantitative impact of precipitation and potential evapotranspiration on baseflow, noting a negative precipitation elasticity coefficient for baseflow without providing an explanation. This study hypothesizes that the negative correlation may result from basin precipitation typically occurring during the flood season, where concentrated seasonal precipitation boosts the surface runoff component in streamflow, thereby reducing the relative contribution of baseflow and in turn leads to a decrease in the BFI. However, there are currently over a dozen baseflow separation methods used, and the estimation results of each method vary greatly. The digital filtering method used in this study may not necessarily be the best method for baseflow separation. Due to limited space, this study didn’t compare and differentiate this method with other methods. Compared to the limitations of digital filtering method, the SWAT model has advantages in evaluating the spatial distribution of basin baseflow and local groundwater resources. Previously, Hu et al. (2017)  revealed that the spatial pattern of baseflow is largely influenced by the topography of the basin and the flow direction of rivers. In this study, the annual average baseflow exhibits an increasing trend from south to north, which is closely related to the overall terrain characteristics and river systems of the Ganjiang River Basin. The interaction between topography and runoff distribution is very complex. The basin exhibits a clear terrain gradient, gradually decreasing from higher altitude in the south to the lower altitude in the north. The central and northern regions of the basin are primarily characterized by low hills, ridges, and plains. In these areas, the convergence of surface runoff predominantly occurs in the low-lying regions, and baseflow positively correlated with runoff. This relationship makes the elevation proportional to baseflow magnitude. Obviously, sub-basins with high baseflow (exceeding 1500 m³/s), specifically sub-basins 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15, 22, and 23, are all located in confluence zone and the downstream plain of the basin. In addition, it is worth noting that the northwest region of the Ganjiang River Basin has very strong groundwater supply with higher BFM. The northwest section of the Ganjiang River Basin is characterized by extensive carbonate rock formations. Compared with other sub-basins, this geological feature helps to enhance the intensity of baseflow recharge. Previously, many studies examined the impact of vegetation change on runoff, but few focused on baseflow responses, and the qualitative conclusions were also different. Some scholars argue that afforestation or vegetation restoration enhances soil infiltration, thus increasing river baseflow, while others believe that this will increases transpiration and interception evaporation, thereby reducing baseflow (Wu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019 ). These inconsistencies may stem from the complexity of factors affecting baseflow, making it challenging to isolate the impact of vegetation changes from other factors. Cultivated lands typically exhibit lower permeability, which impedes the effective infiltration of surface water. This leads to the generation of direct runoff, with a constrained infiltration capacity, thus reducing baseflow. In contrast, the interception of precipitation by forest and grassland vegetation assists in converting a part of surface runoff into groundwater. Furthermore, the root systems of forest and grassland vegetation enhance the soil infiltration capacity. This process increases the quantity of precipitation that can infiltrate and subsequently contribute to the replenishment of baseflow, resulting in an overall increase in baseflow under these scenarios. This paper applied the extreme land use scenarios in the SWAT model to ensure that only land use changes occur during simulation process, reducing the influence of other factors on baseflow. The simulation results suggest that an increase in vegetation coverage will increase the supply of baseflow. Sun and Huang (2019)  also pointed out in their study of the Yangtze River Basin that the increase in forest land can lead to a maximum increase of 15 % in baseflow. The spatial distribution of baseflow to a certain extent reflects the richness of groundwater in a basin. Although changes in baseflow and BFI are attributable to the combined effects of climate and human activities across the basin, baseflow variations are expected to be more sensitive to climate than human activities (Li and Zhang, 2018 ). Human activities in the Poyang Lake Basin are not sufficient to alter the basic distribution pattern of surface and subsurface water resources (Duan et al., 2023 ). Fig. 8  visually illustrates the spatial pattern of the baseflow in the Ganjiang River Basin, which is highly correlated to the topography and river system of the basin. However, the inherent relationship between this distribution and the local climate, vegetation, and soil of the basin, as well as the impact of the distribution and changes of these factors on water production and convergence in the basin is still unclear. These issues should be the focus in future research. The digital filtering method can achieve daily flow separation of baseflow, and calculate the BFI, which provides a scientific reference for the parameter optimization of the SWAT model, and effectively improves the simulation efficiency of the SWAT model.  6 Conclusion The combined method of SWAT model and digital filtering method was used to effectively simulate the spatiotemporal dynamics of baseflow and land use change impact in the Ganjiang River Basin. Major results indicate that seasonal variation of baseflow in the Ganjiang River Basin exhibits a single peak pattern, with highest in June and lowest in December. The variation of baseflow index is generally opposite to that of streamflow. A positive correlation has been noted between the annual baseflow and streamflow in the Ganjiang River Basin, while a negative correlation was found between BFI and precipitation. The spatial patterns of the annual average baseflow and baseflow modulus within the Ganjiang River Basin exhibit significant variability. Both show an increasing trend from south to north, which is determined by to the overall terrain characteristics and river systems of the Ganjiang River Basin. In comparison to the basic scenario, the fully cultivated land use scenario exhibits a decrease in baseflow by 13.9 %. Conversely, the full forest and full grassland scenarios demonstrate an increase in baseflow by 14.7 % and 2.9 %, respectively. The main purpose of this study is to explore the spatiotemporal characteristics of the baseflow in the Ganjiang River Basin. In this study, we only used one baseflow separation method as the basis for model calibration and didn’t consider the comparison of different baseflow separation methods. In addition, knowledge the impact of climate and human activities on baseflow changes is meaningful for understanding the hydrological cycle and groundwater resources in river basins. An in-depth analysis and discussion of this issue is left for future research.
