Baseflow is an important component of river runoff, which is of great significance for the understanding of hydrological cycle and calculation of groundwater resources in river basins. In this study, the digital filtering method provided a scientific reference for the parameter optimization of the SWAT model, especially in areas lacking groundwater observation data. The combination of the two methods can effectively analyze and evaluate the temporal and spatial variations of the baseflow across the basin. The conclusions obtained in this study can provide theoretical support for the development and utilization of water resources and ecological environment protection in the Ganjiang River Basin. In addition, this paper applied the extreme land use scenarios in the SWAT model, which has a positive effect on quantitatively understanding the baseflow response under the changing environment.
1 Introduction The hydrological situation of global rivers has changed significantly in recent decades (Wu et al., 2023b ), and the impacts of climate change (CC) and human activities (HA) on them will become more and more significant (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023 ). As one of the world's most water-scarce countries, the runoff of most rivers in China has been declining in recent years (Bai and Zhao, 2023 ), especially in the middle reaches of the Yellow River Basin (Ni et al., 2022b ). The Loess Plateau (LP), through which the middle reaches of the Yellow River pass, is one of the most serious areas of soil and water loss in the world (Fu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015 ). The ecological environment of this region is fragile and prone to degradation, and the restoration process is challenging and slow (Fu et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2008 ). However, following the ecological management of the Chinese government in recent decades, coupled with regional CC (Chen et al., 2023 ), significant vegetation greening on the LP (Kou et al., 2021 ) has intensified the non-stationarity of the runoff sequence in the region (Milly et al., 2008 ), resulting in significant changes in runoff characteristics. The region's ability to prevent soil erosion and maintain ecological security is seriously threatened by notable changes in river runoff in the LP. Many researchers have studied the runoff variability in the region and its influencing factors. Sun et al. (2019)  analyzed the water-sediment relationship and its response to soil and water conservation in a basin on the LP from 1960 to 2010. The results showed that soil and water conservation measures changed the basin's water–sediment relationship; however, extreme sediment transport events may still occur, requiring increased prevention. Zhang et al. (2020)  used partial least-squares regression (PLSR) to explore the influence of different climatic factors on runoff in the LP's Loess hilly and gully regions. The findings demonstrated that adopting ecological restoration techniques was the primary cause of the decline in runoff, with the contribution rate increasing from 59 % during 1980–1999–82 % during 2000–2015. Gao et al. (2020)  analyzed the impacts of various HA and CC on runoff in the Jinghe River Basin in the LP. The results showed that HA's contribution to runoff reduction increased sharply from 14.3 % to 57.6 % from 1961 to 2015, and the direct factor (water intake) in HA accounted for the fastest growth. Deng et al. (2020)  took the Weihe River Basin in the LP as an example and quantified the contribution of driving factors to the runoff variation of the main and tributary rivers based on the Budyko hypothesis. The results showed that the underlying surface was the dominant factor in the runoff changes. Zheng et al. (2021)  selected 16 typical basins in the LP, used monthly observation sequences of runoff and precipitation (1961–2015), and used the elastic coefficient method based on the Budyko framework to eliminate the impact of precipitation changes on runoff, and analyzed the characteristics of changes in runoff capacity brought about by variations in land use in various basins. Overall, the Grain for Green Project (GGP) weakened the surface runoff capacity. However, existing studies have either analyzed the runoff changes of one or more primary tributaries of China's main water system as a whole (Dai et al., 2023; Hou et al., 2022; Huang and Qiu, 2022 ), analyzed the runoff changes at different spatial scales within the same basin on an annual time scale (He et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023a ), or only analyzed the runoff changes at different time scales within the same basin (Li et al., 2020; Xin et al., 2019 ). While large-scale studies are important and can provide a quick overview of temporal and spatial trends (Wang et al., 2024), when it comes to the actual management of water resources in a basin, a more localized analysis of runoff attribution may provide an effective reference for decision-making in local basin management. Especially in the LP, the topography, ecological management measures, etc. of the upper, middle and lower reaches of the same basin are quite different, and the distribution of precipitation in time is also extremely uneven, which leads to the development of the local agriculture and soon, mostly in accordance with the solar terms summarized from the local climate from the ancient times to the present day. Therefore, there is an urgent need to study runoff changes at multiple scales in the LP for accurate evaluation and management of river runoff, flood risk prevention, and fine scientific management of soil and water loss. The largest basin in the LP is the Wuding River, and the Dali River Basin (DRB) is a key primary tributary. The DRB has a fragile ecology and severe soil erosion. Since 1949, numerous soil and water conservation measures have been implemented in the DRB, and there are differences in the underlying surface changes during different periods of soil erosion control. Therefore, this study takes the DRB as a typical basin in the LP, explores its runoff changes from multiple temporal and spatial scales, quantitatively analyzes the driving factors of runoff changes, and further analyzes the potential influencing factors from underlying surfaces in the basin. This study enhances the scientific relevance of ecological management on the LP. This addresses the lack of multiscale runoff change analyses in specific basins of the LP. The research mainly addresses the following: (1) clarifying the variation characteristics of hydrological factors at multiple spatial and temporal scales; (2) clarifying the contribution rate of the driving factors of runoff change and its spatial and temporal differences; (3) exploring the temporal and spatial variation of potential influencing factors from underlying surface in the basin. This provides a scientific basis for the implementation of specific measures in the basin management of the LP.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The DRB ( Fig. 1 ) is situated in the middle of the LP, stretching 170 km, with a basin area of 3906 km2  (Yang et al., 2023 ). According to the geographical function division of the LP, the basin is located in the first sub-region of the Loess hilly and gully regions, with geomorphological features characterized by dense gullies and fragmentation (Hu et al., 2020 ). Four hydrological stations, Qingyangcha, Lijiahe, Caoping, and Suide, were arranged from upstream to downstream in the basin, corresponding to the Upper Dali River (UDR), Xiaoli River Basin (XRB), Chabagou Basin (CB), and DRB. The catchment areas of each hydrological station were 662 km2 , 807 km2 , 187 km2 ,  and 3893 km2 , respectively, accounting for 16.9 %, 20.7 %, 4.8 %, and 99.7 %, respectively. The region above Qingyangcha is the river source gully region (Fig. 1 a), and the region below Qingyangcha can be divided into a hilly ridge region of loess hills and a valley plain region. The hilly ridge region of the Loess Hills (Fig. 1 b) is mainly composed of ridges with more ridges, fewer hills, and developed gullies. The ratio of intergully land to gully is 1:1. The valley plain region (Fig. 1 c) is commonly known as ' Miliangchuan ( In Chinese, it refers to the flat and low-lying areas where river terraces between local hills can produce grain) is characterized by the development of river terraces, open rivers, flat land, and relatively low altitudes. The terrace of the DRB was 500–800 m wide, and the valley altitude was 863–1003 m. The XRB terrace is 200–500 m wide, and the elevation of the river valley is 926–1022 m. The terraces of the CB are 50–400 m wide. In this study, UDR, XRB, and CB represent the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the DRB, respectively. The XRB and CB are both primary tributaries on the right bank of the basin.  2.2 Data requirement and preprocessing Hydrological data (1960–2020 at Suide Station in the DRB, 1960–2020 at Qingyangcha Station in the UDR, 1960–2020 at Lijiahe Station in the XRB, 1970–2020 at Caoping Station in the CB) were sourced from the Hydrological Handbook of Yulin  and Hydrological Data of Yellow River Basin . Meteorological data were derived from the China Meteorological Data Service Center (http://data.cma.cn/ ), and evapotranspiration (PET) was obtained using the Brutsaert model (B2015 model) (Brutsaert, 2015 ). Basin surface precipitation was calculated using the Thiessen polygon method.  2.3 Data analysis 2.3.1 The 24 solar terms The 24 solar terms originating in the middle and lower reaches of the YRB accurately reflect natural rhythm changes and guide the time system of agricultural production. To date, 24 solar terms have been used in the DRB for agricultural production and folk customs. Therefore, based on field investigations in the DRB, this study divided the year into four seasons: spring (February-April), summer (May-July), autumn (August-October), and winter (November-January).  2.3.2 Trend analysis 2.3.2.1 Mann-Kendall test The Mann-Kendall method is widely used in hydrological research to test for trends in series values of hydrological elements at a given level of significance (Zhang and Yao, 2023 ). The series values of hydrological elements x (x1, x2, …, xn) are assumed to be distributed independently and randomly. When n  ≥ 8, S  approximately obeys the normal distribution, and the mean value is 0. If | Z |  ≥ 1.96  , the trend is significant at p ≤ 0.05   .  2.3.2.2 Linear trend regression analysis Linear regression is a parameter estimation method that assumes that a hydrological series is composed of deterministic and random factors:(5) x  t   = P  t   + ε  t       (6) P  t   = a + b  1   i + b  2   i  2  + ⋯ + b  n   i  n      (7) b ˆ  = ∑  t = 1  n   ( t − t ¯   )  ( x  t   − x ¯   )    ∑  t = 1  n   ( t − t ¯   )  2         (8) a ˆ  = x ¯  − b ˆ  t ¯      (9) ∂  2  = ( ∑  t = 1  n   ( x  t   − x ¯   )  − b ˆ   2  ∑ t = 1  n  ( t − t ¯   )  2    )  / ( n − 2  )   ∑ t = 1  n  ( t − t ¯   )  2         where a  and b n   are coefficients. Let R t   – t  = d t;   then, the rank correlation coefficient r of R t   is tested by T the t-test method to construct the test statistic T as follows:(10) r = 1 − 6 ∑ t = 1  n  d  t  2     n  3  − n       (11) T = r ( n − 4  1 − r  2     )  1 / 2       where n  denotes the length of the hydrological series. Assuming that the series has no trend, given a significance level of 0.05, when | T |  > t  α / 2     occurs, the original hypothesis is rejected, and the sequence trend is considered significant; otherwise, the sequence has no significant trend.  2.3.2.4 Double mass curve (DMC) The DMC is a statistical analysis method commonly used in hydrology to evaluate the relationship between precipitation and runoff (Gao et al., 2017 ). Using the DMC of precipitation-runoff, it can be found that the hydrological series data points show a roughly distributed straight line on the figure, and the slope is the proportional constant between precipitation and runoff. The change in the slope indicates that the original relationship between runoff and precipitation has changed.  2.3.2.5 Lee-Heghinian test The Bayesian-based method is suitable for testing mean variation (Tian et al., 2019 ). The location of the mutation point is assumed for the hydrological series (x1, x2, …, xn). The population is assumed to follow a normal distribution, and the prior distribution of the location of the mutation point τ   obeys the uniform distribution. The posterior conditional probability density function of the location of the mutation point τ   is:(12) f ( τ / x  )  = k [ τ τ ( n − τ  )     ]  1 / 2   [ R ( τ )   ]  − ( τ − 2 )  2    , ( 1 ≤ τ ≤ n  )      (13) R ( τ )  = [ ∑ t = 1  τ  ( x  i   − x ¯   τ    )  2   + ∑ i = τ + 1  n  ( x  i   − x ¯   η    )  2    ]  ∑ i = 1  n  ( x  i   − x ¯   n    )   2         The k in the formula is a proportional constant, generally takes 1. x ¯   τ    and x ¯   η    are the sequence mean values before and after the mutation point, respectively. The study period (1960–2020) is much shorter than the continuous loess-paleosol sequence of the Quaternary Period in the LP (Guo et al., 2024 ). It is believed that the climate was relatively stable during the study period, and its impact on the underlying surface of the basin was also relatively stable. That is, under this premise, the change of basin runoff is more affected by the disturbance of the underlying surface by HA in the basin. In this way, the basin runoff change can be attributed to two major driving factors, CC and HA, which do not affect each other. 2.3.3.1 Annual attribution analysis of runoff variations Budyko-type equations based on the Budyko framework were used to attribute changes in runoff, which have also been widely applied in the LP (Jiang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Luan et al., 2021 ). This study employed five different equations: Budyko (Mianabadi et al., 2020 ), Truc-Pike (Wu et al., 2024 ), Fu (Cheng et al., 2023 ), Zhang (Zhang et al., 2001 ) and Wang (Wang and Tang, 2014 ). The main methods include the vertical decomposition and elasticity coefficient methods. The effect of CC on the runoff change was first analyzed, and the influence of HA was then determined by deducting the impact of CC from the overall runoff change using the elastic coefficient approach. The vertical decomposition method can be used to directly calculate the specific impacts of CC and HA on changes in runoff (Wang and Hejazi, 2011 ).(14) E P  = P E T  P   tanh ( P P E T    )  [ 1 − exp ( − P E T  P   )   ]        (15) E P  = 1 + P E T  P  − [ 1 + ( P E T  P   )  n   ]  1 / n       (16) E P  = [ 1 + ( P E T  P   )  − n    ]  − 1  / n       (17) E P  = 1 + ω P E T  P   1 + ω P E T  P  + ( P E T  P   )  − 1         (18) E P  = 1 + P E T  P  − ( 1 + P E T  P   )  2  − 4 ε ( 2 − ε  )  P E T  P     2 ε ( 2 − ε  )        where P , E,  and PET  are precipitation, actual evapotranspiration, and potential evapotranspiration, respectively. n , ω,  and ε  are all parameters that characterize other actual impacts on basin runoff, primarily associated with underlying surface conditions such as soil characteristics, vegetation, topography, and human activities such as water intake.  2.3.3.2 Attribution analysis of runoff variation on a seasonal scale 2.3.3.2.1 ABCD model The ABCD model is a climate hydrological model that Thomas proposed with four parameters (Jehanzaib et al., 2020 ). With precipitation and PET as inputs, it can simultaneously simulate changes in evapotranspiration, runoff, soil water, and groundwater and is suitable for hydrological simulation of basins with time scales of months or years. The model generalizes the water storage space of the basin into soil water and groundwater layers and divides the runoff into direct runoff and base flow. Direct runoff comes from precipitation and soil water transformation, whereas base flow stems from soil water and groundwater leakage. Because actual evapotranspiration E  is a function of P  and soil water storage S , Thomas et al. defined two state variables (effective water volume W  and possible evapotranspiration Y ) and assumed the two obey a non-linear function relationship. The main calculation process for the model is as follows:(19) Y  i   ( W  i    )  = W  i   + b  2 a   − [ ( W  i   + b  2 a    )  2  − W  i   b  a   ]  1 / 2       (20) W  i   = P  i   + S  i − 1   ; Y  i   = E  i   + S  i       (21) D  i   = ( 1 − c  )  ( W  i   − Y  i    )  ; Q  i   = c ( W  i   − Y  i    )      (22) F  i   = d G  i   ; R  i   = D  i   + F  i       (23) Δ R = R  o b s 2   − R  o b s 1   = Δ R  h   + Δ R  c       (24) Δ R h = R  o b s 2   − R  s i m       i  and i –1 in the formulas represent the start and finish of the period, respectively. S  is soil water storage. D  is the direct runoff. Q  is the groundwater recharge. F  is the base flow. G  is the groundwater reserve. R  is the total runoff. The a  indicates the likelihood of runoff occurring before soil saturation, with a value range of (0,1). When a  = 1, precipitation was used for evapotranspiration, and changes were made in soil water storage without generating surface runoff. b  is the maximum value of products E  and S . The distribution coefficient of direct runoff and groundwater recharge is denoted by c . groundwater retention time reciprocal is represented by d . Runoff's total variation is denoted byΔ R   . Δ R  c      and Δ R  h      are the runoff changes caused by CC and HA, respectively. The meanings of the other variables were the same as above.  2.3.3.2.2 Vertical decomposition method on a seasonal scale Chen et al. Temperature differed significantly across time scales in the following order: summer > autumn > spring > winter. The order of PET on different time scales is: year > summer > spring ≈ autumn > winter. Precipitation and runoff were mainly concentrated in summer and autumn. Temperature, PET, precipitation, runoff trends, and other factors were examined using the Mann-Kendall trend test, linear regression trend analysis, and Spearman rank correlation test. The Lee-Heghinian test and DMC were used to determine the mutation points of the runoff series. The BP and CP of the four basins were divided and combined with the actual basin conditions. Annually, the Temperature, precipitation, and PET of the four basins exhibited notable increasing trends ( Table 1 ). Runoff in the other three basins demonstrated a major declining tendency, except for the UDR, which exhibited a considerably increasing trend. Regarding the seasonal scale, the Temperature and PET in the DRB showed an upward trend, in which the temperature grew noticeably outside autumn, and the PET rose dramatically in winter. Precipitation showed a significant upward trend in the summer. Runoff decreased significantly in all seasons except in winter, when it did not increase significantly. Precipitation in the other three basins (UDR, XRB, and CB) did not change significantly, except for significant increases in summer and autumn in the UDR and summer in the XRB. The runoff of these three basins decreased significantly, except that the UDR increased significantly in all four seasons, most prominently in spring and winter. The mutation years of the annual and seasonal scales of the four basins were the same; in particular, the summer runoff series mutated in sync with the annual runoff series. In addition, it can be found that among the four basins, the mutation years of runoff series in DRB and XRB are almost the same on the annual and seasonal scales, while the mutation years of runoff series in UDR and CB located in the lower reaches of DRB are relatively delayed in time. The BP of DRB, UDR, XRB, and CB are 1960–1971, 1961–2010, 1961–1970, and 1970–1996, respectively. The CP of DRB, UDR, XRB, and CB are 1972–2020, 2011–2020, 1971–2020, and 1997–2020, respectively.  3.2 Analysis of runoff change attribution 3.2.1 Attribution analysis under different spatial scales at annual scale The attribution analysis findings of the runoff variations in the four basins are displayed in   Figs. 3 and 4  using the vertical decomposition and elastic coefficient methods. The curves fitted based on the four Budyko-type equations were slightly different; however, the overall difference was not significant (Fig. 3 ). The data representing CP (marked by orange hollow triangles) are mostly located above the curves, which indicates that the combined influence of CC and HA is the cause of the runoff change during CP. The vertical decomposition method results showed that HA contributed an average of 65.12 % to runoff change in the DRB (Fig. 4 a). Specifically, CC dominated in the UDR, whereas HA dominated in the XRB and CB. The closer the basin was to the downstream, the more significant the contribution of HA to runoff changes. The CC and HA contribution rates to runoff change showed no significant differences among the four equations. Both CC and underlying surface condition changes influenced runoff changes over time, as seen by the interannual fluctuation of the elastic coefficient. From Fig. 3 e, f, and g, it was found that the elastic coefficient of precipitation varies (1.9, 3.3), promoting basin runoff, while the elastic coefficients of PET and underlying surface were between (–2.3, –0.9) and (–4.8, –0.8) respectively, hindering basin runoff. Except for the UDR, in which the absolute value of the underlying surface elastic coefficient was significantly smaller, the other three basins exhibited significantly larger absolute elastic coefficients. In particular, the underlying surface elastic coefficient of the XRB fluctuates significantly. The attribution analysis results (Fig. 4 b) showed that HA primarily drove changes in runoff, with closer downstream basins having higher HA contribution rates. In DRB, the CC (precipitation, PET) contribution rates were 46.28 % and 146.28 %, respectively. Precipitation, PET, and HA contributed at 123.62 %, 1.9 %, and –25.53 %, respectively, to runoff fluctuations in UDR. The XRB were 6.87 %, 9.57 %, and 83.56 %, respectively. The CB were –142.77 %, 30.09 %, and 211.68 %, respectively.  3.2.2 Attribution analysis under different spatial scales at seasonal scale Runoff was simulated using the ABCD model.  Table 2  presents the parameter calibration and evaluation indices of the simulation results. The results showed that the Nash efficiency coefficient (NSE) for seasonal runoff in the BP was > 0.70, and the coefficient of determination (CD) was > 0.68; NSE and CD in the CP were > 0.67 and > 0.62, respectively. This shows that the simulation results matched expectations, and the ABCD model proved reliable and applicable in the DRB. The ABCD model was used to calculate actual evapotranspiration, soil water content change, and groundwater storage change, which were incorporated into the seasonal Budyko model. The contributions of each factor to runoff change were quantitatively analyzed using the vertical decomposition method after parameters ω  and φ  were calibrated using the least squares method using data for BP (Table 2 ). The results ( Fig. 5 ) indicate that the results obtained by the two methods in the four basins were the same, with differences arising from the different principles of runoff simulation. During runoff simulations, the model must also simulate changes in evapotranspiration, soil water content, and groundwater storage. Compared with the BP, except for the UDR, CC dominated the runoff change during the CP, whereas HA dominated the other three basins. CC dominated in spring and winter seasonally, whereas HA dominated in summer and autumn. In spring, the runoff variation in DRB, UDR, XRB, and CB was –2.5 mm, 4.6 mm, –3.1 mm, and –3.8 mm, respectively. As calculated by the two methods, the average runoff changes caused by CC were –3.8 mm, 7.7 mm, 3.4 mm, and –3.7 mm, respectively. The average runoff changes caused by HA were 1.4 mm, –3.1 mm, –6.5 mm, and –0.1 mm, respectively. In summer, the runoff changes in DRB, UDR, XRB and CB were –5.3 mm, 9.4 mm, –4.1 mm, and –4.2 mm, respectively. As calculated by the two methods, the average runoff changes caused by CC were 3.2 mm, 7.8 mm, 2.9 mm, and –1.4 mm, respectively. The average runoff changes caused by HA were –8.4 mm, 1.6 mm, –7.0 mm, and –2.8 mm, respectively. In autumn, runoff changes in DRB and UDR were –7.4 mm and 13.4 mm, respectively. Average runoff changes from CC calculated by both methods were 5.9 mm and 12.6 mm, respectively. Average runoff changes from HA were –13.3 mm and 0.8 mm, respectively. In winter, runoff changes in UDR, XRB, and CB were 4.8 mm, –1.0 mm, and –2.4 mm, respectively. The average changes in runoff from CC were 5.8 mm, 2.7 mm, and 4.2 mm, respectively. Average runoff changes from HA were –0.9 mm, –3.7 mm, and –6.5 mm, respectively.   3.3 Analysis of potential influencing factors in HA Numerous studies have investigated the effects of various HA, including land use changes (Zhao et al., 2022; Zuo et al., 2016 ), vegetation changes (Ni et al., 2022a; Tian et al., 2022b; Wen et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024 ), terraces (Zhang et al., 2021 ), Yudiba dams (Guo et al., 2022; Sun and Wu, 2022 ), coal mining (Song et al., 2021 ), water intake (Gao et al., 2020 ), According to field investigations, the terraced fields in the Dali River Basin account for approximately 5 % of the total area. There is only one urban area of Zizhou County, a county-level administrative district, about 35 km away from the basin outlet. The daily water supply in this urban area is about 2500 m3, and the water intake accounts for about 1 % of the runoff. The water conservation measures that have a significant impact on runoff changes in the underlying surface of the basin mainly include engineering measures (Yudiba dams) and forest and grassland measures (returning farmland to forests and grasslands). Therefore, an analysis is conducted on the land use, vegetation cover, and Yudiba dams within the basin. 3.3.1 Land use change The primary land uses in DRB are cultivated land, grassland, and forest land, comprising 99.7 % of the basin area ( Fig. 6 ). Land use was relatively stable before 2000, with transfers occurring chiefly after 2000. Before 2000, cultivated land, grassland, and forest land accounted for approximately 53 %, 40 %, and 6 %, respectively. After 2000, the proportion of cultivated land declined to less than 50 %, whereas grassland and forest land increased to 42 % and 8 %, respectively. The proportions of cultivated land, grassland, and forestland in the UDR, XRB, and CB varied slightly. Before 2000, cultivated land accounted for 50 %, 56 %, and 57 % of the area, respectively; grassland for 44 %, 41 %, and 39 %, respectively, and forest land for 5 %, 2 %, and 3 %, respectively. After 2000, cultivated land accounted for 45 %, 54 %, and 56 % of the area, respectively, grassland for 47 %, 42 %, and 40 %, and forest land for 8 %, 4 %, and 4 %, respectively. A gradual decrease in cultivated land and increased forest and grassland areas occurred upstream to downstream.  3.3.2 NDVI change The interannual variations in the mean and maximum NDVI in the four basins from 1981 to 2020 showed an overall growth trend ( Fig. 7 ). The order of the average NDVI in the four basins was consistent for each decade: CB > XRB > DRB > URB. Compared to the 1980s, the average NDVI of the four basins increased by approximately 10 %, 30 %, and 60 % in the 1990s, 2000s, and 2010s, respectively. The average NDVI of the DRB, UDR, XRB, and CB in the 1980s was 0.33,0.30,0.34, and 0.36, respectively, whereas the average in the 2010s reached 0.53,0.49,0.53, and 0.58, respectively. As shown in Fig. 7 b, the maximum NDVI of the four basins exhibited an overall increasing trend; however, the growth rates were significantly different. Specifically, compared with the 1980s, the maximum NDVI of DRB increased by 12 %, 32 %, and 73 % in the 1990s, 2000s, and 2010s. The UDR was 16 %, 49 %, and 94 %, the XRB was 6 %, 24 %, and 60 %, and the CB was 8 %, 31 %, and 75 %. The maximum NDVI values of the DRB, UDR, XRB, and CB in the 1980s were 0.43,0.35,0.42, and 0.38, respectively, while the mean values in the 2010s reached 0.74,0.68,0.67, and 0.67, respectively.  3.3.3 Construction and operation of Yudiba dams The Yudiba Dam is a unique and effective gully control measure for mitigating soil and water losses in the LP. Flood detention and sediment retention are crucial in reducing runoff and sediment transport (Li et al., 2019; Xin et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022 ).  Fig. 8  shows the number and storage capacity of large and medium-sized Yudiba dams in the DRB. Regarding Yudiba Dam numbers, peak construction occurred mainly in the 1960s and the 1970s. Among these, 283 and 727 medium-sized Yudiba dams were built in the 1960s and the 1970s, respectively, and their corresponding storage capacities increased by 70 million m3  and 180 million m3 , respectively. During this period, 53 and 161 large Yudiba dams were built, and the corresponding storage capacities increased by 55 million m3  and 203 million m3 , respectively. The spatial distribution of large Yudiba dams in the basin (Fig. 8 a) shows that those built in the 1960s were mainly in the UDR and XRB. During the 1970s, dam construction was focused on the middle and lower reaches of the DRB. Since 2000, most of the Yudiba Dam construction has been concentrated within the CB. Regarding the spatial distribution of medium-sized Yudiba dams (Fig. 8 a), it is evident that Yudiba Dam construction in the 1950s was mainly concentrated in the mid-region of the DRB, including the XRB. In the 1960s, the Yudiba Dam was densified and expanded to the middle and lower reaches of the DRB, which had been built in the previous period. In the 1970s, the spatial distribution density of the Yudiba Dams further increased and expanded to the UDR based on the previous two periods. In the 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s, the construction of the Yudiba Dam decreased significantly, which manifested as leak filling in the XRB and CB. According to deposition information for large Yudiba dams (Fig. 8 b), those with a sediment deposition ratio of over 0.8 in the DRB were mainly distributed in the middle and lower mainstream reaches and the XRB. The sediment deposition ratio for large Yudiba dams in UDR and CB was mainly 0.6–0.8. Those with ratios of 0.2–0.4 were mainly on the DRB's right bank. Their construction period was possibly also the peak of small- and medium-sized Yudiba Dam buildings (1970s). Small and medium-sized Yudiba dams retained most sediment, limiting large Yudiba dam traps. Possibly, this area had a low sediment yield and less obvious siltation. Relatively detailed information on sediment deposition in the large Yudiba dams in the UDR, XRB, and CB reflects their key role in reducing river runoff and sediment.    4 Discussion In recent decades, runoff and sediment into the YRB in the LP have sharply decreased because of the combined effects of CC and HA. Scholars have researched changes in water and sediment in the YRB tributaries but not the variation characteristics and attribution analysis of runoff changes across different spatial and temporal scales within the same basin. Therefore, this study selected the DRB in the LP as a case study and analyzed the spatial and temporal variations in runoff and the impact of driving factors. Furthermore, the potential factors influencing runoff change were explored to inform refined ecological management development in the LP. The results showed that hydrological factors differed significantly at different time scales. Precipitation and runoff primarily occur in summer (May-July) and autumn (August-October), with Temperature and PET peaking during these seasons. Precipitation and runoff in the UDR showed an increasing trend. As the distance from the basin outlet decreased, the precipitation in the XRB and CB decreased at each seasonal scale, whereas runoff increased. The abrupt change years for the four basins were relatively consistent on yearly and summer scales; however, on the spatial scale, the abrupt change years of the XRB closely matched those of the DRB (around 1970), whereas the CB occurred in the 1990s. However, the years of abrupt change in the UDR significantly differed from those in the other three basins, which occurred after 2000. This is consistent with previous studies on runoff variation in the LP (Shi et al., 2013 ). On an annual scale, the attribution analysis of runoff change indicated that CC dominated the UDR, while HA increasingly contributed and became dominant in the lower reaches. CC dominated in spring and winter seasonally, whereas HA dominated in summer and autumn. These findings generally agree with other attribution analyses of LP-runoff changes (Liang et al., 2015 ). Analysis of the potential factors influencing runoff change showed that the main land uses were cultivated, forest, and grassland. After 2000, the cultivated land proportion dropped below 50 %, whereas grassland and forest land increased to 42 % and 8 %, respectively. The reduced cultivated land area and increased forest and grassland areas in the UDR, XRB, and CB gradually decreased. Regarding vegetation coverage, the average and maximum NDVI of the four basins showed an overall growth trend, with differences in the specific values and growth rates of NDVI. The turning point of the NDVI growth coincided with the GGP in the LP in 1999 (Wang and Sun, 2021 ). The DRB has a continental monsoon climate with springtime drought, hot summers with heavy rain, average rain, a rapidly cooling autumn, and a cold, dry winter. Large-scale ecological management has been conducted; however, the focus of management measures differs across different periods. In the early years (1949–1978), ecological management mainly focused on developing productivity, with afforestation and the Yudiba dam construction for resource provision. However, ecological management during this period did not achieve remarkable results, as cultivated land expanded and vegetation decreased with severe soil erosion and frequent natural disasters. After the reform and opening up (1978–2012), local income and ecological awareness significantly improved, especially with major strategic measures such as returning farmland to forests and grasslands, closing hillsides for greening, individual contracting, and food for relief in 1999. This has promoted ecological development in the basin, increased vegetation coverage (Zhao et al., 2017 ), and alleviated soil erosion. Since 2012, with the Chinese government's heightened focus on ecological protection (green development was written in the national document for the first time) (Liu et al., 2022 ), projects such as the GGP have been further implemented and improved. Soil and water loss management has become more scientific and reasonable, and vegetation coverage has significantly increased (Fu, 2022 ). These results suggest scientific and reasonable ecological management of the basin based on spatial and temporal distributions. Cultivated land reclamation and overgrazing should be avoided in the upper basin, and the Yudiba dam system should be constructed to reduce flood disasters. Intense HA in the middle and lower basins requires the maintenance of existing water and soil conservation measures, construction of drainage-side canals (Wang et al., 2022 ), and prevention of fires during dry seasons. The LP has great internal differences (Yang et al., 2019 ), such as uneven spatial and temporal distribution of precipitation, where the northern part of LP receives less precipitation, is mostly a sandy area of agricultural and pastoralism, and is rich in mineral resources, with relatively large surface runoff disturbances from mining, while the southern part receives more precipitation, is mostly a loess area, and is relatively densely populated, with terraces, Yudiba dams, croplands, and forested areas occurring frequently. The DRB selected for this study only represents the largest loess hill and gully area within the LP. In addition, although Budyko's hypothesis and ABCD model were used in this study, it is currently more of a quantitative distinction between the effects of CC and HA on runoff changes at different spatial and temporal scales in the basin, and more methods need to be introduced to further refine the specific contribution of each potential influencing factor within the driver, and to comparatively analyze the differences between the results and verify the reasonableness of the results. Subsequent studies should integrate local topography and geomorphology (Guo et al., 2021 ), farming activities, economic development (Wang et al., 2023a ), and regional policies (Li et al., 2021 ) to better understand the contribution of each factor to changes in runoff from the HA (Wang et al., 2023b ). In addition, personal experience of the '7–26' extreme rainstorm in the DRB in 2017 highlighted the need to address extreme precipitation events. Analyzing the specific effects of factors on runoff changes in different years is crucial for evaluating the ecological management benefits in the basin and beyond. Large-scale vegetation restoration may reduce the regional water supply, hinder vegetation growth, and affect ecosystem function (Feng et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Reduced grassland mowing is recommended to offset these issues (He et al., 2024 ). It is also essential to quantify the impact of iterative governance measures aimed at identifying new problems regarding runoff changes in the ecological governance of the LP.  5 Conclusions This study analyzed runoff changes in the DRB, a typical basin in the LP, from annual and seasonal perspectives, as well as in the upper and lower reaches and different sub-basins. The Budyko and ABCD models were used to analyze the attributes of runoff changes and the main human activities in the basin were explored. More targeted control measures can be formulated and implemented by understanding the temporal and spatial variations in runoff in a typical basin in the LP and its attribution analysis. The research results provide a reference for more scientific and targeted ecological management of the Loess Plateau. Findings showed:(1) Runoff and its variations mainly occurred in summer (May-July) and autumn (August-October). In space, runoff changes from upstream to downstream show apparent differences, and the closer it is to the downstream, the more pronounced the runoff changes. On an annual scale, runoff increased in the UDR but significantly decreased in the XRB and CB in the lower reaches of the DRB. The mutation years in the three basins were 2010,1970, and 1996.  (2) The CC and HA contribution rates to the runoff change shifted from upstream to downstream, with HA being dominant closer to the downstream. HA had a more significant impact on the runoff in summer and autumn, whereas CC had a more significant impact in winter and spring.  (3) Differences in the spatial and temporal distribution of human activities represented by the return of farmland to forest and grassland, NDVI growth, and Yudiba Dam construction may be the main reasons for runoff changes at different spatial and temporal scales.

1 Introduction In recent decades, climate variability and Land Use (LU) change combined with various Other Human Activities (OHA) greatly influenced the hydrological processes in watersheds (Dai et al., 2020; dos Santos et al., 2021 ). With the continued global warming, climate variation has changed the hydrological processes all over the world to different degrees and directions (Thackeray et al., 2022 ; Dou et al., 2022 ). In addition, extensive OHA has further altered hydrological processes by various routes such as soil erosion control services (Liu et al., 2022 ), dam construction (Djan’na Koubodana et al., 2023 ), reservoir regulation (Zhang et al., 2022 ), agricultural irrigation (Han et al., 2023 ), et al. LU change would also affect the hydrological processes by changing plant evapotranspiration (Ma et al., 2022 ), interception (Gardon et al. 2020 ), streamflow concentration process (Aneseyee et al., 2022 ), soil erosion process (Wei et al., 2023b ), et al. Many scholars have investigated the effects of climate variability and Human Activities (HA) on various hydrological processes. From an indirect perspective, HA could change the LU which further affects the runoff and sediment processes (Zhang et al., 2021 ); from a direct perspective, HA could affect the various hydrological processes through dam construction, reservoir regulation, agricultural irrigation et al. (Djan’na Koubodana et al., 2023 ). In the previous studies, various methods were proposed to separate the effects of climate variability and HA on the hydrological processes. The most used methods in such investigations contain hydrological modeling, scenario combination, Budyko Framework, paired catchment, and empirical statistics (Zeng et al., 2020 ). These methods separate the whole period into two sub-periods and assume that the hydrological process during the previous sub-period was natural while that during the lateral sub-period was affected by climate variability or HA, the hydrological processes during different sub-periods were compared to quantify the effects of climate variability and HA. Zhang et al. (2017)  evaluated the contributions of precipitation and HA to runoff within the Yi River Basin from 1964 to 2010, results indicate that the attribution of HA and precipitation variations was 46.34 ∼ 41.74 % and 53.66 ∼ 58.25 %, respectively. Shi et al. (2023)  separated the contributions of HA and climate change to the streamflow and baseflow within the Bahe River Basin from 1959 to 2016, with results showing that the contributions of HA and climate change to streamflow were 37 ∼ 75 % and 25 ∼ 63 %, respectively, and was different from that to baseflow. The investigation conducted by Jehanzaib et al. (2020)  indicates that climate variability mainly affects hydrological drought at a longer (6- and 12-month) time scale and HA attributes 20 ∼ 25.6 % for the hydrological drought changes within various watersheds. In general, the contributions of HA and climate change to the various hydrological processes were different in different regions and periods. As mentioned before, HA could affect the hydrological processes directly (such as dam construction, reservoir regulation, and agricultural irrigation) and indirectly (accelerating the land use/cover change process). Whereas, the contributions of LU change and OHA to various hydrological processes have been seldom discussed and are still unclear. During the past decades in China, OHA such as dam construction, implementation of soil and water conservation measures, catchment disturbance, and agricultural practices have greatly affected the Sediment Yields Loads (SYL) within the major Chinese rivers (Liu et al., 2021 ). However, most of the existing studies have considered the effects of climate variability and HA on runoff and SYL but ignored the Suspended Sediment Concentration (SSC). SSC is an indicator that represents the relationship between runoff and sediment which indicates the ability of streamflow to carry the suspended sediment and source of sediment (Downs and Soar, 2021 ). In most regions, the variations in runoff and SYL were inconsistent. For example, the runoff was detected as an insignificant reduction trend (Yang et al., 2022 ) while the SYL has been found a significant declining trend (Liu et al., 2021 ) in the Yellow River Basin. In addition, it was found in Shao et al. (2021)  that climate variability has led to a great reduction in runoff with a proportion of 82.2 % but only attributed ∼4.55 % to the variations of SYL in the Jialing River Basin. These phenomenons indicate that the effect of climate variability and HA on SSC was complicated due to their different impacts on runoff and SYL. Hence, it is essential to investigate the effect of climate variability, LU change, and OHA on the SSC under the background of a changing environment. Huaihe River Basin (HRB) is an important agricultural base in China, which has suffered severe soil erosion. It has been found that the annual average runoff and SYL have decreased from 1950 to 2005 (Liu et al., 2008 ). Understanding the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to runoff and SYL would benefit the designing of the soil and water conservation measures within the HRB. Previous study indicates that climate change and HA change attribute 87.2 % and 12.8 %, respectively, to the variations of runoff in the middle reaches of the HRB (Gao and Ruan, 2018 ). However, it has not separated the contributions of LU change and OHA, which would not be able to quantify the role of various OHA in runoff. In addition, the previous work also has not considered the contributions of various influence factors to SYL and SSC. The Upper Huaihe River Basin, which is controlled by the Wangjiaba Hydrological Station (abbreviation as WJB), has been reported that have contributed a huge proportion of the total SYL within the HRB (Cai et al., 2012 ). It is significant to evaluate the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the runoff-sediment processes for local soil erosion prevention. The Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model is a widely used physical-based distributed hydrological model, which could reflect the influence of climate variability (precipitation input) and LU change on the hydrological processes in the simulation of hydrological processes. In our study, an attributing framework was proposed by combining the Double Mass Curve (DMC) method and the SWAT model based on the Control Variable Theory to quantify the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the runoff-sediment processes (contains runoff, SYL, and SSC). The main objectives of this study were to: (1) establish the SWAT model to simulate the hydrological processes within the WJB during different sub-periods of 1981 ∼ 2019; (2) analyze the climate variability and LU change during 1981 ∼ 2019 within the WJB; (3) evaluate the spatial-temporal variations of runoff, SYL, and SSC within the WJB during 1981 ∼ 2019; and (4) quantify the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the runoff, SYL, and SSC within the different sub-regions of the WJB using the newly proposed attributing framework.  2 Materials and methodologies 2.1 Study area The HRB is situated in mid-eastern China and occupies an area of 2.7×105  km2  between 111°55′∼121°20′ E to 30°55′∼36°20′ N ( Fig. 1 ), generated from the Tongbai and Dabie Mountains and flows into the Yellow Sea. Agricultural land occupies ∼70 % of the total area of HRB, which makes it an important agricultural base of China. In addition, the HRB was suffering severe soil erosion owing to its intensive agricultural activity, especially for the WJB (Wei et al., 2022b ), The drainage area of the WJB is ∼3.01×104  km2 , but contributing ∼68.4 % of the total sediment yields of the whole HRB (Cai et al., 2012 ). The WJB is mainly dominated by the hilly terrain in the western and southern areas (the highest elevation was 1110 m a.s.l.) while dominated by the plain terrain in the central and eastern regions (the lowest elevation was 21 m a.s.l.). In addition, the annual average temperature ranged between 5.5 ∼ 15.9 ℃, which was higher in the southern WJB; the annual average precipitation ranged from ∼800 to ∼1400 mm, and more than 60 % of the precipitation occurs during the flood season (June ∼ September); the annual average rainfall erosivity value was 5061 MJ mm hm−2  h−1  (Wei et al., 2022b ). In recent decades, as many soil erosion control projects were conducted in the WJB (Chu et al., 2009 ), the runoff, SYL, and their relationships have been changed. It is significant to evaluate the change trends of these hydrological characteristics and the reasons for these variations within the WJB for better soil erosion prevention.  2.2 Data preparation The data used in this study includes the digital elevation model (DEM), LU maps, soil map, meteorological data, and hydrological data ( Table 1 ). In addition, the LU maps were obtained in 1980, 2000, and 2015, and the overall LU types were divided into 7 categories: paddy land, dry cropland, forest land, shrub land, grass land, water area, and urban land ( Figs. 2 a-2 c). The accuracy of these LU maps was checked by the researchers in the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Science before being published. The soil map shown in Fig. 2 d, the WJB contains 18 categories of various soil types. The number of Climate Forecast System Reanalysis (CFSR) stations is 30, which were used to calculate the parameters of the meteorological database for the SWAT model to represent the meteorological characteristics within the study region. The measured daily precipitation in 65 stations and the monthly streamflow and SYL in 3 stations were collected from the Hydrologic Bureau of Huaihe River Commission (1980 ∼ 2013) and the Hydrological Yearbook of Huaihe River Basin (2014 ∼ 2019).  2.3 Methodologies 2.3.1 Overall study approach The main purpose of this study is to investigate the spatiotemporal variations of runoff-sediment processes, and their responses to climate variability, LU change, and OHA. Firstly, the data of the study region used to run a SWAT model were collected; secondly, the measured annual water yields and SYL were separated by the DMC to obtain the breakpoints and separated the whole period into several sub-periods; thirdly, the SWAT model was run for each sub-periods and simulated the runoff-sediment processes; finally, the cross simulations based on various LU maps and precipitation input for different sub-periods to quantify the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the variations of runoff-sediment processes. The overall technical routing of the study is shown in  Fig. 3 .  2.3.2 Indicator selection To investigate the characteristics of runoff-sediment processes within the WJB, four indicators were used in this study. Runoff was selected to represent the amount of Water Yields (WY), which has excluded the effect of the watershed area compared to WY. SYL was selected to represent the total amount of soil losses, which measured the total sediment yields that were transported by the channel river. The SSC was selected to represent the characteristic of the relationship between runoff and sediment in the channel, which indicates the sediment-carrying capacity of runoff. In addition, when evaluating the spatial variations of SYL, the Soil Erosion Module (SEM, t km−2 ) was used to represent the average SYL per unit within each sub-watershed.  2.3.3 Double mass curve The DMC method is a widely used method to identify the breakpoints in the hydrological variables (Xu et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2017 ). For DMC, it assumed that the characteristic of a variable would remain constant if there was no factor influencing it. In this study, we supposed that the relationships between precipitation and runoff (or SYL) would be constant without the effects of climate variability, LU change, and OHA. For each stage, the values of the two continuous accumulation variables could be expressed as a straight line, and the change point for the slope of the straight line could be identified as the breakpoint. In this way, we separated the whole study period into several sub-periods for different hydrological characteristics, further investigating the effects of different driving forces on the hydrological process changes.  2.3.4 SWAT model The SWAT model is one of the most used semi-distributed ecohydrological models, which was developed by researchers from the Agricultural Research Center of the United States Department of Agriculture (Arnold et al., 1998 ). The SWAT model separates the watershed into several sub-watersheds and further divides each sub-watershed into several Hydrological Response Units (HRUs) based on the unique combination of LU type, soil type, and slope belt. Benefiting from its physical mechanism, it was widely used in relevant studies, such as hydrology, watershed management, ecology, etc (Aloui et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2022 ). The water balance equation (refer to (Wei et al., 2023a )) is the basis of the water circulation simulation in the SWAT. The runoff simulation comprised two processes named runoff generation and flow routing. The SCS curve number and characteristic river-length method were used in this study to calculate these two processes. The soil erosion simulation in the SWAT model is divided into sediment generation and channel transport processes. In this study, the MUSLE equation and the simplified Bagnold model were adopted to simulate the sediment generation and channel transport process, respectively (S.L.Neitsch, 2012 ). The SWAT2012, which was integrated into the ArcGIS 10.2 was used in this study (Neitsch et al. 2011 ). The WJB was divided into 74 sub-watersheds and further separated into 2004 HRUs. Three SWAT models were established for different periods with model settings kept constant except for LU and precipitation inputs. In this way, different SWAT models with different parameter sets could represent the hydrological conditions for different periods. A number of 27 parameters relevant to the runoff process and 12 parameters relevant to the soil erosion process were selected to conduct the sensitivity analysis using the global sensitivity method with the indicator of the p-value (Abbaspour, 2013 ). The p-value ranges from 0 (more sensitive) to 1 (less sensitive), and the parameters with a p-value lower than 0.1 were regarded as sensitive parameters that need to be calibrated (dos Santos et al., 2021 ). The definitions of these parameters are shown in Table S1  and Table S2 . The SUFI-2 (Sequential Uncertainty Fitting Version 2) was adopted to calibrate the sensitive parameters, and three evaluating indicators (R2  (Coefficient of Determination), NSE (Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency), and PBIAS (Percent Bias), more details were shown in Table S3 ) were chosen to evaluate the performance of each parameter set. For each sub-period and sub-region, the parameter sensitivity analysis and calibration were conducted separately.  2.3.5 Contributions attributing framework Many factors could affect runoff, sediment yields, and their relationship. The most acceptable influence factors are climate variability, LU change, and OHA (Li et al., 2020a; Mikaeili and Shourian, 2023; Yang et al., 2020 ). In this study, we have proposed an attributing framework to separate the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA on the variations of runoff-sediment processes. The assumptions of this method were (1) the factors that influence the runoff-sediment processes contain climate variability, LU change, and OHA; and (2) the simulated runoff-sediment processes by the calibrated SWAT model were reasonable and could represent the hydrological processes in the corresponding sub-period. Under these assumptions, the procedures of this attributing framework are as follows:(1) Detect the abrupt change year of runoff-sediment processes using the DMC method, to separate the whole period into several sub-periods (P  1   ,   P  2   ,   … ,   P  n        ). For different sub-periods, there exist some factors that affect the runoff-sediment processes.  (2) For different sub-periods, a proper LU map (L U  1   ,   L U  2   ,   … ,   L U  n        ) needs to be selected to represent its LU condition; the precipitation records (C L  1   ,   C L  2   ,   … ,   C L  n        ) during these sub-periods need to be collected to represent its climate condition; the measured hydrological data should be collected to represent the real hydrological condition for different sub-periods.  (3) For each sub-period, a SWAT model (M  1   ,   M  2   ,   … ,   M  n        ) was established to simulate the hydrological processes under the current condition and used to simulate the hydrological processes under different LU change and climate variability scenarios.  (4) Simulate the hydrological processes using different SWAT models for various periods. For example, the runoff simulated by different SWAT models with different LU and precipitation inputs could be expressed as (a) R  M  1   , L U  1   , C L  1      : simulated annual average runoff under the condition during P  1     with L U  1      and C L  1      as input; (b) R  M  1   , L U  2   , C L  1      : simulated annual average runoff under the condition during P  1     with L U  2      and C L  1      as input; and (c) R  M  1   , L U  1   , C L  2      : simulated annual average runoff under the condition during P  1     with L U  1      and C L  2      as input.  (5) Y  t o t a l    , Y  C L    , Y  L U    , and Y  O H A     represent the changes in the variables caused by all factors, climate variability, LU change, and OHA, respectively. Based on the Single Variable Controlled Theory, the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA on the variations of runoff-sediment processes could be calculated by the following equations:   (1.1) { Y  t o t a l   = R  m e a s u r e _ P  2     − R  m e a s u r e _ P  1        Y  C L   = R  M  1   , L U  1   , C L  2     − R  M  1   , L U  1   , C L  1        Y  L U   = R  M  1   , L U  2   , C L  1     − R  M  1   , L U  1   , C L  1        Y  H A   = Y  t o t a l   − Y  C L   − Y  L U            Where R  m e a s u r e _ P  1       and R  m e a s u r e _ P  2       represent the measured annual average runoff for the P  1     and P  2     period, respectively. In the mentioned equations, the change between the annual average runoff during different periods was regarded as the Y  t o t a l    ; the change between annual average runoff simulated by the SWAT with different land use or precipitation input is regarded as the Y  L U     or Y  C L    ; and the Y  H A     could be calculated by subtracting Y  L U     and Y  C L     from Y  t o t a l    . The contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA on the variations of runoff-sediment processes within the WJB were calculated based on the proposed attributing framework.  2.3.6 Analysis methods In this study, the LU maps of 1980, 2000, and 2015 were used to analyze the LU change during 1980–2015. The LU change amount and rate during 1980–2000, 2000–2015, and 1980–2015 were analyzed, and the conversions between different LU types during this period also been analyzed. The variations of hydrological processes were analyzed by linear regression method, which could reveal the changing trend of each variable. In addition, the significance of the trend was detected by t-test, the change trend is regarded as significant if it passes the 95 % confidence test.    3 Results 3.1 Periods separations The breakpoints of WY and SYL for the DPL, XX, and WJB were detected by the DMC method ( Fig. 4 ), and the relationships between precipitation and WY (and SYL) changed in 1992 and 2009. In general, the total period (1981 ∼ 2019) could be separated into three sub-periods: P  1    : 1981 ∼ 1991, P  2    : 1992 ∼ 2009, and P  3    : 2010 ∼ 2019. For WY, the rates of different sub-periods were changed slightly for all stations; while the rates of different sub-periods for SYL were changed more obviously. During P  1    , P  2    , and P  3    , the rate between accumulative annual precipitation and WY for DPL (XX and WJB) was 2.50 (1.65 and 3.39), 2.52 (1.59 and 3.59), and 1.89 (1.15 and 2.94), respectively; the rate between accumulative annual precipitation and SYL for DPL (XX and WJB) was 3.59 (1.81 and 2.68), 3.39 (1.31 and 1.34), and 1.09 (0.64 and 1.06), respectively. In this study, the total period was separated into three sub-periods (P  1    , P  2    , and P  3    ), and the SWAT model was established for each sub-period.  3.2 Performances of the established SWAT model The parameter sensitivity analysis results for each sub-period and sub-region are shown in Figure S1 , the sensitivity of parameters was changed during different sub-periods and sub-regions. For P  1    , P  2    , and P  3    , the number of sensitive streamflow parameters was 8, 12, and 9, respectively; the number of sensitive sediment yields parameters was 9, 7, and 7, respectively. A number of 14 streamflow parameters and 9 sediment yields parameters need to be calibrated for the hydrological simulation within WJB. After calibrating the sensitive parameters, the SWAT model could simulate the streamflow and sediment yields properly for each sub-period and sub-region ( Table 2  and  Fig. 5 ), the fittest parameter sets are shown in Tables S4 and S5 . For the streamflow simulation during different sub-periods, the values of R2 , NSE, and PBIAS ranged between 0.77 and 0.93, 0.71–0.93, and −16.4 %∼20.89 %, respectively. For the SYL simulation during different sub-periods, the values of R2 , NSE, and PBIAS ranged between 0.66 and 0.94, 0.57–0.97, and −62.57 %∼29.11 %, respectively. Generally, the performance of the SWAT model in simulating the streamflow was better for WJB compared to DPL and XX, while the performance of the SWAT model in simulating SYL was better for DPL compared to XX and WJB. The performance of the SWAT model was better during P2  compared to other sub-periods. The simulated streamflow processes fitted well with those measured, while the simulated sediment yields were underestimated for some peak values during 1990 ∼ 2003 (Fig. 5 ). For the streamflow simulation at DPL and XX, several peak values were underestimated during 1996 ∼ 2010. Combining the results of evaluating indicators and directly comparing simulated and measured processes, the established SWAT model could simulate the streamflows and sediment yields process properly from 1981 to 2019 for all sub-regions with the WJB.  3.3 LU change analysis The LU changed differentially in various sub-regions ( Table 3 ). In general, the main LU change characteristics of the WJB were an increase in paddy land, forest land, water area, and urban land, and a decrease in the dry cropland, shrub land, and grass land. The LU in DPL changed dramatically from 2000 to 2015 with an obvious increase in paddy land (26257 ha) and urban land (1982 ha) and a decrease in dry cropland (28473 ha). On the contrary, the paddy land decreased obviously (59450 ha) while the dry cropland increased (43950 ha) within the regions between DPL and XX. For the regions between XX and WJB, an increase was detected for paddy land (15260 ha) and urban land (13663 ha) while a decrease was detected for dry cropland (13733 ha) and grass land (17833 ha) from 1980 to 2000. The LU conversion characteristics from 1980 to 2015 were analyzed in  Fig. 6 . For the DPL, the main loss in paddy land was converted into dry cropland and urban land while the main gain in paddy land was converted from dry cropland; the main increase in urban land was converted from dry cropland. For the XX, there is a large amount of mutual conversion between paddy land and dry croplands; besides, the increase in urban land mainly converted from dry cropland and paddy land. For the WJB, a large amount of dry cropland was converted into paddy land, urban land, and forest land; dry cropland was supplied by the conversions from paddy land, urban land, and grass land. In addition, the mutual conversion between paddy land and dry cropland over the WJB was different in different sub-regions. These discrepancies were mainly caused by the spatial differences in terrain and water resources within different sub-regions. The economic income benefit from the paddy land and dry cropland also varied due to the differences in crop types (Wei et al., 2022a ), which could affect the willingness of the farmers to choose the tillage method, further causing the mutual conversion between paddy land and dry cropland in different periods. The difference in increasing urban land within different sub-regions may result from the ability and sustainability of urbanization in different sub-regions (Rashed, 2023 ). Overall, these different changes in land use within the various sub-regions of the WJB show the intensifying effect of HA.  3.4 Climate variability analysis The main indicator of climate variability is precipitation and temperature, and the changes in precipitation could affect the hydrological process directly (Mirani et al., 2022 ). The typical precipitation characteristics for DPL, XX, and WJB during different periods were analyzed in  Table 4 . For all sub-regions of the WJB, the annual average precipitation has suffered a decrease trend from P  1     to P  3    , as well as the flood season average precipitation. The annual average precipitation for DPL (XX and WJB) during P  1    , P  2    , and P  3     was 1038.48 (1069.43 and 999.29) mm, 978.49 (979.49 and 916.81) mm, and 911.27 (898.70 and 834.81) mm, respectively. In addition, the highest and lowest annual precipitation during P  1     was higher than other sub-periods for all sub-regions, and the interannual variation of precipitation within DPL was higher than in other regions. In general, the precipitation within the WJB decreased from 1981 to 2019, and the decrease mainly occurred during the flood season period.  3.5 Variations of hydrological processes during the past 40a within WJB 3.5.1 Variations of runoff The variation of runoff during 1981 ∼ 2019 was analyzed on the annual and monthly scale ( Fig. 7 ). On the annual scale, the runoff showed a decreasing trend with a slope of 2.16 mm a−1 , 5.27 mm a−1 , and 1.3 mm a−1  for the DPL, XX, and WJB, respectively. The runoff shows an obvious gradient decrease from P  1     to P  3     for XX compared to that for DPL and WJB. On the monthly scale, a decreasing trend was detected for most months from P  1     to P  3    . For DPL and WJB, the average runoff during P  1     in July was higher than that during P  2    , and the average runoff during P  3     in September and October was higher than that during P  2    . The annual runoff shows a decreasing trend from the southwestern to the northeastern WJB, and it was highest (502 mm) and lowest (102 mm) in the southwestern and mid-northern, respectively ( Fig. 8 a). The annual runoff shows an increasing trend in the eastern WJB, while shows a decreasing trend in the middle WJB (Fig. 8 d). The highest changing rate for the increasing and decreasing trend for the regions within the WJB was 4.34 mm a−1  and −7.41 mm a−1 , respectively. In addition, the trend for most regions was insignificant, only several sub-watersheds located in middle and western WJB show a significant decreasing trend (P < 0.05) (Fig. 8 g).  3.5.2 Variations of SYL and SEM On the annual scale, the SYL showed a decreasing trend with a slope of 1.02×104  t a−1 , 5.23×104  t a−1 , and 8.49×104  t a−1  for the DPL, XX, and WJB, respectively ( Fig. 9 ). The SYL shows a dramatical decrease from P  2     to P  3     within DPL, while shows a dramatical decrease from P  1     to P  2     within XX and WJB. On the monthly scale, the average SYL during different sub-periods varied obviously during the flood season. For DPL, the average SYL during P  3     in most months was lower than other sub-periods, and the highest sediment generation month was August and July during P  1     and P  2    , respectively. For the XX and WJB, the average SYL in most months (except for September and October) was highest during P  1    , followed by P  2     and P  3    . The SEM shows an increasing trend from the northeastern to the southwestern WJB, the value of SEM in the northeastern was much lower than that in the southwestern (Fig. 8 b). The highest and lowest values of SEM within WJB were 1886.55 and 1.37 t km−2 , respectively. The annual SEM decreased in the middle and southwestern WJB while increasing in the western, eastern, and southeastern WJB (Fig. 8 e). The highest changing rate of SEM for the increasing and decreasing trend for the regions within the WJB was 63.84 t km−2  a−1  and −10.24 t km−2  a−1 , respectively. In addition, most sub-watersheds located in the southeastern and northern WJB show a significantly increasing trend (P < 0.05) in SEM, several sub-watersheds located in the mid-southern and western WJB show a significantly decreasing trend (P < 0.05) in SEM (Fig. 8 h).  3.5.3 Variations of SSC The annual SSC shows a similar changing trend to that of the annual SYL, and the change in SSC was more obvious than that in SYL ( Fig. 10 ). On the annual scale, The changing trend of SSC for DPL, XX, and WJB was −0.02, −0.01, and −0.01 kg m−3  a−1 , respectively. The SSC decreased dramatically from P  1     to P  2     at the XX and WJB station, while decreased dramatically from P  2     to P  3     at the DPL station. This indicates that the SSC varied inconsistently in different channels within the WJB. On the monthly scale, the overall rank of the SSC was P  1     > P  2     > P  3     for all months at the WJB station. The SSC during P  1     was higher than that during P  2     and followed by P  3     in most months (except for July and September) at the XX station. The SSC changes were irregular at the DPL station, the SSC in May, June, July, and August during P  1     and P  2     were much higher than that during P  3    . The annual average SSC in the channels within the WJB has an obvious difference, the annual average SSC decreased from the southwestern to the northeastern WJB (Fig. 8 c). The highest and lowest annual average SSC was 3.21 and 0.02 kg m−3 , respectively. Compared to SEM, the SSC changed significantly in most sub-watersheds (Fig. 8 i). The highest increase and decrease rates of the SSC were 103.96 and −19.72 g m−3  a−1 , respectively. In addition, some channels near the main channel suffered a significant increase (P < 0.01) in SSC, and some channels located in the southern and western WJB suffered a significant decrease (P < 0.01) in SSC.   3.6 Contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the runoff-sediment processes The contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the variations of runoff for different regions within the WJB have been analyzed in  Table 5 . Overall, the total runoff variation from P  1     to P  2     and P  2     to P  3     within DPL (XX and WJB) was −51.99 (−74.01 and 74.84) mm and −90.21 (−105.89 and −150.99) mm, respectively. This indicates that the runoff decreased within the upper XX from P  1     to P  3    , while increased during the regions between XX and WJB from P  1     to P  2    . In general, the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the runoff variation were −29.79 ∼ 71.09, −97.33 ∼ 1.16, and −22.86 ∼ 192.74 mm, respectively, occupied −27 % ∼ −75 %, −108 % ∼ 1 %, and −44 % ∼ 160 %, respectively. Climate variability and LU change have a negative effect on the runoff variation, while OHA has a positive effect. The contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the SYL variations for different regions within the WJB have been analyzed in  Table 6 . The total SYL variations from P  1     to P  2     and P  2     to P  3     within DPL (XX and WJB) were −7.53 (−89.42 and −173.96)×104  t and −17.89 (−50.06 and −28.90)×104  t, respectively. The SYL only increased in the regions between XX and WJB from P  2     to P  3    . In general, the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the SYL variations were −66.11 ∼ −6.97, −58.40 ∼ 4.05, and −111.90 ∼ 76.25×104  t, respectively, occupied −162 % ∼ −22 %, −202 % ∼ 4 %, and −79 % ∼ 264 %, respectively. Climate variability has a negative effect on the SYL variations from P  1     to P  3    ; LU change has a slight positive effect on the SYL variations from P  1     to P  2     while has a negative effect on the SYL variations from P  2     to P  3    ; OHA has a negative effect on the SYL variations from P  1     to P  2     while has a positive effect on the SYL variations from P  2     to P  3    . The contributions of climate variability, LU, and OHA to the SSC variations in different river sections within the WJB have been analyzed in  Table 7 . The total SSC variation from P  1     to P  2     and P  2     to P  3     for the river section of DPL (XX and WJB) was −0.0473 (−0.1553 and −0.7248) kg m−3  and −0.2437 (−0.0683 and 0.0974) kg m−3 , respectively. The SSC kept decreasing trend from P  1     to P  3     for the river section of DPL and XX. For the river section of WJB, the SSC decreased obviously from P  1     to P  2     while increased slightly from P  2     to P  3    . In general, the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the SSC variations were −0.0761 ∼ 0.0730, −0.0911 ∼ 0.0296, and –0.7127 ∼ 0.2195 kg m−3 , respectively, occupied −161 % ∼ 30 %, −94 % ∼ 12 %, and −142 % ∼ 225 %, respectively. Climate variability has a negative effect on the SSC in most cases. LU change has a positive effect on the SSC for the river section of DPL from P  2     to P  3    , and has a negative effect on the SSC for the river section of XX and WJB from P  2     to P  3    . OHA has a positive effect on the SSC for the river section of DPL from P  1     to P  2    , while has a negative effect on the SSC for the river section of DPL from P  2     to P  3    . In addition, OHA has a negative effect on the SSC for the river section of XX and WJB from P  1     to P  2    , while has a positive effect on the SSC for the river section of XX and WJB from P  2     to P  3    .   4 Discussion 4.1 Uncertainties in the hydrological simulations The attributing framework proposed in this study to quantify the contributions of climate variability, LU change, and OHA to the hydrological processes was based on the DMC method and calibrated SWAT model. Hence, a proper SWAT model with a fit parameter set is guarantees for the accuracy of this attributing framework. The SWAT model has been widely used in a hydrological simulation for many kinds of studies as it simulates the hydrological processes based on various parameters that represent different hydrological physical processes (Aloui et al., 2023 ). Our study separates 1981 ∼ 2019 into three sub-periods based on the DMC method; then, three SWAT models were run with different LU and precipitation as input, and they have been conducted parameter sensitivity analysis and calibration separately. As shown in Figure S1  and Tables S4 and S5 , the parameters’ sensitivity and fittest value were changed during different sub-periods. This indicates that the sensitivity of the same parameter in SWAT within a region would change when the data input changed. Similar results have been found in other studies which reveal that the changes in precipitation inputs for the SWAT model would affect the parameter sensitivity analysis results (Wei et al., 2023a ). Besides, the LU input for P  1     (1981 ∼ 1991), P  2     (1992 ∼ 2009), and P  3     (2010 ∼ 2019) was LU map obtained in 1980, 2000, and 2015, respectively. The LU variations during the simulation periods have not been considered in this study, which would affect the results of the contribution of LU change to the hydrological processes (Sharma et al., 2022 ). Particularly, the changes in values of parameter sets and LU input would change the simulated hydrological process in different components (such as the ratio of surface runoff and underground runoff, the amount of soil water et.al) (Wei et al., 2022a ). However, according to the evaluation criteria proposed by Moriasi et al. (2007) , the performances of the established SWAT models on streamflow simulation were excellent for most periods and sub-regions, and the performances on sediment yields were acceptable for almost all periods and sub-regions. In addition, the baseflow ratio of the WJB simulated by the calibrated SWAT was 0.25, 0.34, and 0.30 for the sub-period of P  1    , P  2    , and P  3    , respectively, which is close to the value (0.3069) in the existing study (Wei et al., 2023c ). Hence, though there exist some uncertainties in the hydrological simulations, the acceptable performance and reasonable baseflow ratio of the simulation results indicate that the established SWAT model could be used in this study and it is convincing.  4.2 Impacts of climate variability, LU change, and OHA on the runoff-sediment processes In our study, climate variability has decreased runoff, SYL, and SSC within WJB from P  1     to P  3     (Tables 5,6 ). This indicates that under the background of global climate change, WY within the WJB has been reduced, as well as soil erosion and sediment transportation. HRB is an important crop product base within China, which frequently suffers drought disasters (Zhang et al., 2013 ), the reduction in the precipitation (Table 4 ) not only resulted in the reduction of runoff, SYL, and SSC, but also increased the risk of suffering a drought disaster (Dixit and Jayakumar, 2021 ). In previous studies, the decrease in precipitation was also detected within the HRB (Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2023a ), which was one of the direct causes of the streamflow reduction (Sun et al., 2018 ). In our study, the contribution of climate variability to the variations of runoff was 27.6 % (Calculated by (61/(61+160), Table 5 ), which is similar to the results obtained by Liu et al. (2017) . However, in the study conducted by Zhu et al. (2015) , the runoff changes within the whole HRB were mainly attributed to climate variability. This indicates that the contribution of climate variability on the runoff varied in different regions within the HRB, which also was a result of our study (Tables 5,6 ). Hence, it is important to adjust the water resource management within the study regions. As shown in Table 4 , the annual average precipitation within the WJB exhibited a decreasing trend, and the annual average precipitation within the WJB was ranked as “DPL > XX > WJB”. It could be inferred that the amount of precipitation within the regions ranges between XX and WJB would be lower where were highly covered by paddy land and dry cropland (Fig. 2 ). More irrigated reservoirs should be built in these regions to better manage the water resources under the background of precipitation reduction, further enhancing local food security and sustainability. LU changes from P  2     to P  3     have decreased runoff and SYL within the whole WJB, while increasing the SSC at the river section of DPL and decreasing the SSC at the river section of XX and WJB (Tables 5,6 ). The LU changes from P  1     to P  2     have a slight effect on the hydrological processes, but the effect of the LU changes from P  2     to P  3     on the hydrological processes were apparent. For the DPL, the main LU changes were a decrease in dry cropland and an increase in paddy land and urban land (Table 3 ). Correspondingly, the runoff, SYL, and SSC were changed by −108 %, −73 %, and 12 %, respectively. The increased paddy land would derive much more water resources during its growth stage, and mitigate soil erosion (Ouyang et al., 2018 ). However, the decrease in runoff was much higher than that of SYL, which increased SSC. For the WJB, the main LU changes were a decrease in dry cropland and an increase in forest and urban land (Table 3 ). Correspondingly, the runoff, SYL, and SSC were decreased by 46 %, 202 %, and 94 %, respectively. Overall, the increase in forest land and the decrease in dry cropland were the main causes of the hydrological variations.
