To better understand the seasonal effects such as rain on snow, it would also be interesting to look at winter and melt seasons as well.  4.3 Soil moisture behaviour in response to afforestation Soil moisture content varied significantly between locations with different stages of afforestation and grassland in response to precipitation. Our observations indicate that soils covered by forest have a higher soil moisture content on average than grassland and soils that lack vegetation. Remarkable were the findings that in the deeper soil layers covered with forest, soil moisture dynamics remained strongly visible. This could indicate that water transport still occurs in these layers and processes such as percolation and subsurface flow may take place. It was previously also found that macro- and micro-topographic properties affect soil moisture and runoff behaviour, where forests can enhance the infiltration capacity. That forests play an important role in enhancing infiltration to deeper soil layers was also shown in other forested headwater catchments and seems to be consistent with our observations (Vichta et al., 2024 ). Fig. 9   gives a conceptualization of soil moisture behaviour in response to afforestation based on the measurements, where an average of the different forest covers (young and old-growth) has been taken. In Fig. 9 a the dashed line represents the end of the left whisker (dry conditions) and the solid line is the right whisker (wet conditions) based on the results (Fig. 4 ) for the summer season. This difference between dry and wet conditions is larger for the forest, indicating more soil water storage than unvegetated soils (bare soils) during the summer season. Fig. 9 b provides a conceptual representation of the varying behaviour of the infiltration processes between land covers, based on the rainfall events presented in Fig. 5 . The results indicate that bare soils represent a shallow soil water storage and that grassland and forest land cover types can infiltrate more water and also deeper during a rainfall event. Fig. 9 c illustrates that forest cover and grassland minimize soil evaporation, which contributes to a delayed decrease in soil moisture compared to bare soils during a dry spell. From our measurements we learn that forest soils act like a sponge, buffering soil water during rainfall events and slowly releasing it during dry spells. The higher soil moisture content and more gradual changes observed in the forest could be reflected by higher infiltration rates and more retention, leading to a smaller loss of rainwater as downslope surface runoff (Mongil-Manso et al., 2022 ). This can be explained by the macroporosity, macropore connectivity and presence of roots in the forest that are important for determining infiltration rates (Archer et al., 2016; Beven, 2004; Weiler & Naef, 2003 ). Vegetation composition and plant species richness have a clear relationship with rooting parameters and infiltration capacity (Tasser et al., 2021 ). Another effect that can explain the higher soil moisture content in the forest, is the higher water storage capacity of the soil and ground cover by vegetation that reduces evaporation from the ground. Other influencing factors that may have contributed to wetter soils in the forest are local root systems, shade by the canopy, mosses and litter cover that retains soil moisture longer (Tiebel et al., 2023; Williams et al., 1993 ). Important mechanisms that continue to change with forest growth are water demand, rooting depth and canopy cover. Our results differ in some respect with a study on juvenile forest and mature forest that indicated soil moisture is higher in younger forest due to a lower physiological water demand (Rabbai et al., 2023 ). However, during high rainfall events, mature forest showed a greater adaptability to uptake soil moisture that is consistent with our results. However, during high rainfall events, mature forest showed a greater adaptability to uptake soil moisture that is consistent with our results. More similar results of high soil moisture values were found in another region, where a field study indicated that soil moisture tends to decrease first and then increase again as the afforestation years increase (Yao et al., 2023 ). It is generally known that a forest has a higher evapotranspiration than grassland or other land cover types without vegetation (Zhang et al., 2001 ). The hydrological effects of greenings with NBS, which leads to more percolation and evapotranspiration, can result in a reduced fraction of surface runoff and potentially also a lower soil moisture content (Ilstedt et al., 2016 ). This reducing effect on soil moisture seems to be less decisive in our catchment, because we measured a relatively higher soil moisture content in the forest than for grassland. This finding differs in that respect from other research in a Mediterranean area that indicated soil moisture content was lower on hillslopes under forest cover than in downslope areas covered by grasses (Llorens et al., 2018 ). In addition, there are also other important influencing factors that can increase soil moisture and should be considered such as a higher organic matter content and the effect of morning dew (Penna et al., 2009; 2013 ). Also notable were the results that during the cold spells, soil moisture content decreased significantly at the zero-state and grassland locations while this was less the case at the forest sites. This behaviour could be due to lower temperatures and soil freezing at the open exposed sites that can lead to freeze–thaw processes as well. Such freeze–thaw processes are known to be stronger in bare soils and grasslands than in forests (Xu et al., 2021 ). In Fig. 10   we visualised our soil moisture monitoring locations and possible influencing factors on soil moisture variability in an Alpine catchment that we based on our field observations and the literature mentioned in this paper. In this study we focussed on monitoring the soil water dynamics in response to afforestation. However, forests can also increase water storage through the litter layer and interception by the canopy in addition to soil water buffering. This means that the total water retention may be greater than our estimated soil water storage for the selected precipitation events. In addition to soil water storage also surface roughness may change with forest growth that can contribute to runoff reduction.  4.4 Capturing soil moisture behaviour during convective precipitation events The results show the importance of continuous measurements and the added value of a high sample frequency. The spatial variability of soil moisture for the five depths at the plots varied throughout the selected monitoring period of June-August 2022, especially during convective precipitation events. During convective precipitation events, rapid changes in soil moisture were measured that strongly depended on the rainfall amount and intensity, but also on the initial conditions (wet or dry state). Significant changes in soil moisture can occur within a few minutes where even rapid changes in soil moisture can be observed for individual sensors at a depth of 80 cm, while others remain constant. The short soil moisture peaks for individual sensors in the deeper layers may indicate that water can infiltrate more rapidly to deeper soil layers. In Fig. 11   we highlighted the soil moisture responses of two events with different initial conditions and rainfall characteristics. These two events had a similar cumulative rainfall amount, but different intensity and duration as mentioned in Table 2 . We assume that the observed rapid local soil moisture responses at greater depths were caused by preferential flow paths during convective precipitation favoured by dry initial conditions (Fig. 11 a). Rainfall intensity and antecedent soil moisture conditions are often discussed as variables associated with faster soil wetting processes, originated by preferential flow (Kang et al., 2023; Lozano-Parra et al., 2015 ). Our observations are consistent with studies that concluded that relatively dry initial soil moisture conditions provide more suitable conditions for preferential flow (Demand et al., 2019; Hardie et al., 2011; 2013; Wiekenkamp et al., 2016 ) On the other hand, a rainfall event with a longer duration can also lead to a soil moisture response in the deeper soil layers, but at a slower rate and only visible after several days instead of minutes or hours (Fig. 11 b). These slower soil wetting processes are often more related to flow velocity, soils or vegetation (Lozano-Parra et al., 2015 ). Although the infiltration rate was lower at the start of the event with dry initial conditions, dry soils seemed to be able to store more water eventually. This observation is consistent with other studies that stated that dry pre-conditions can lead to more infiltration in total and a slight reduction of surface runoff (Meißl et al., 2021 ). We used a higher measurement frequency than other high temporal resolution monitoring studies (Lozano-Parra et al., 2015 ). However, the infiltration processes appear to be even faster in some cases and show that significant local increases in soil moisture can take place within minutes. Subsequently, this high temporal resolution provides insight into percolation and interflow processes as well. Our observational data indicates that smaller time steps are mainly of interest during convective precipitation events and for artificial rainfall simulations. A high sample frequency is less of interest during dry conditions when changes in soil moisture take place at a slower rate compared to the wetting-up phase. Although our monitoring equipment allows to increase the sample frequency, in remote locations, such as the forest, it is important to find the right balance between the data quantities and measurement intervals. Smaller time steps provide more insight, but can go at the cost of battery resources and transmission speeds. Especially during dark, cold and snowy winter months, the battery capacity of the datalogger in the forest sometimes decreased. Moreover, it is important to have precipitation measurements available with a comparable measurement interval. At the rainfall test site, the datalogger requires some computational time to get through all measurement points, saving and uploading them. This procedure is a limiting factor for smaller measurement intervals.   5 Conclusions In summary, the findings from the continuous monitoring data provide a significant addition to quantitative evidence of soil moisture behaviour on different spatial–temporal scales in an afforested Alpine catchment. We obtained a soil moisture record of more than three years in the forested part of the catchment covering different stages of forest growth and established a high-density soil moisture network in four experimental plots that provided insight into the small-scale soil moisture variability including the deeper soil layers. Our observations contribute to an improved process understanding of the effects of afforestation on soil moisture dynamics and are relevant to many practical questions related to land-use management, ecosystem restoration and water management throughout the Alpine Region. The measurements show that the soil moisture dynamics differ between different stages of afforestation and grassland throughout the year. Higher and more stable soil moisture values are found in soils that are covered with young and old-growth forest than in soils with a lack of vegetation. The greatest temporal differences in soil moisture occur in the topsoil (5 cm), where soil moisture for every season is on average more than twice as high in the forest soils than in the bare soil. Grassland has on average a lower soil moisture content at all depths than the forest locations. During larger precipitation events, the vegetated locations have a higher soil water storage change than unvegetated locations and show that rainwater can infiltrate deeper. The young forest showed a stronger improvement in infiltration rates than old-growth forest. Furthermore, forest soils can retain soil moisture longer than grassland and bare soils during dry spells. Initial conditions of soil moisture, precipitation amount, peak intensity and duration are important factors in determining how much water can infiltrate and be retained in the soil. When the initial conditions are dry, soils are able to retain more water in total during a convective precipitation event, however the infiltration rate is lower at the start. During wet initial conditions, forest soils still seem to be able to absorb water, while the percentage of soil water storage change of the precipitation decreases for grassland. In the deeper soil layers, soil moisture content stays in general more constant, but during heavy precipitation events rapid changes can be observed even at 80 cm of depth within minutes. These short local soil moisture peaks at greater depths, caused by preferential flow, occur especially with convective precipitation after dry spells, while changes take place at a slower rate (order of days) at these depths with longer duration rainfall events and wetter pre-conditions. We demonstrated that our high-resolution soil moisture monitoring strategy provides more insight into the soil moisture variability, especially during convective precipitation when processes take place within minutes. A strong heterogeneity of this alpine soil was observed for each soil depth layer, where the mean soil moisture content can horizontally differ up to 11%–26% within 1.5-meter distance depending on the depth. In the upper soil layers at 5 and 10 cm depth, the spatial differences are smaller than in the deeper soil layers at 40 and 80 cm. Interpolated maps of soil moisture indicated that spatial variability of soil moisture increases with depth by a factor of three (CV 0.15 at 5 cm; CV 0.46 at 80 cm) on average at plot scale for the analysed summer period. Our findings confirm “the sponge effect” of alpine forest soils and indicate that afforestation has a positive impact on soil water buffering, which can be beneficial for runoff reduction. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that many processes play a role on different scales and that our rainfall test site offers opportunities for more experiments to gather evidence-based data on soil moisture conditions related to surface runoff generation. Future work could involve hydrological modelling where our field data can be used as input to determine hydrological states and for validation. As a next step, more field experiments are needed to determine runoff coefficients and to define thresholds of runoff generation that can be used as validation and to determine the upscaling potential of NBS.
1 Introduction The unsaturated zone, which links the soil surface to the groundwater phreatic surface, includes the root zone, the intermediate zone, and the capillary fringe (CF) (Dingman, 2014 ). The CF is not only characterized by the sharp spatial transition between water saturation and sub-saturation, but also by temporal variations in water saturation (Dingman, 2014 ). The sharp saturation gradient of the CF typically parallels a steep redox gradient that, in turn, modulates the reactants, products, rates and pathways of many biogeochemical processes, therefore, the CF is a biogeochemical hotspot (Borch et al., 2010; Rezanezhad et al., 2014; Rühle et al., 2015 ). The dynamic hydrology of the CF further drives temporal variations in local redox status, yielding events of elevated biogeochemical turnover, also referred to as: “hot moments” (Dorau et al., 2016 ). The redox state is crucial in controlling the spatial and temporal distributions of microbial community structure and activity in soils (Crawford et al., 2000; Song et al., 2008; Störiko et al., 2022 ). Oxygen (O2 ) is a common and powerful electron acceptor in soil systems (Pett-Ridge and Firestone, 2005 ). In the absence of direct porewater O2  measurements, the redox potential (Eh ) can be used to delineate O2 -rich (>300 mV) and O2 -depleted (<300 mV) zones in soils (Fiedler et al., 2007 ), both with marked differences in microbial communities and microhabitats (Song et al., 2008 ). Under varying redox conditions in one system, different facets of the resident microbial community can activate various metabolic pathways (Seybold et al., 2002 ) that display strikingly different microbial community structures (DeAngelis et al., 2010 ). For example, under oxic conditions (high Eh ), obligate aerobes rely on oxidative respiration and phosphorylation, while the activity of obligate anaerobes (e.g., methanogens, iron and sulfate reducers) is suppressed because of O2  toxicity due to a lack of catalase and superoxide dismutase enzymes (Pett-Ridge and Firestone, 2005 ). By contrast, under anoxic conditions (low Eh ), obligate anaerobes are active and obligate aerobes are inactivated (Pett-Ridge and Firestone, 2005 ). In anoxic soil habitats, fermentation is widespread and diverse inorganic and organic compounds other than O2  can be utilized as terminal electron acceptors by microorganisms (Pett-Ridge et al., 2006; Klüpfel et al., 2014 ). In environments where O2  availability fluctuates, facultative microbes that utilize multiple electron acceptors/donors may become more abundant than specialists like obligate aerobes and anaerobes (Pett-Ridge et al., 2006 ). Dynamic hydrologic regimes cause changes in water content and porewater geochemistry (e.g., aqueous O2  availability, N speciation) that, in turn, drive shifts in microbial activity (Cruz-Martínez et al., 2012; Rühle et al., 2015 ). Water table fluctuations and infiltrations can recharge and redistribute O2 , nutrients and other bioactive compounds (Peralta et al., 2014 ). Then, labile N and C substrates are released into the porewater from the solid phase through various biogeochemical pathways (Cruz-Martínez et al., 2012 ). Hence, the microbial community can be expected to differ between stable and fluctuating water table conditions (Peralta et al., 2014; Rühle et al., 2015 ). For example, Rühle et al. (2015)  conducted experiments in a 50 cm height column with sandy soil, constant infiltration (0.19 cm· h- 1 ) and the water level oscillating between 13 and 37 cm depth at a rate of 1 cm· h- 1  over 2 d intervals by adjusting the outflow for 273 d duration. By comparing to the reference column with a stable water table in the middle of the column after the same constant infiltration, they found that the bacterial community composition (based on T-RFLP analysis) in the fluctuating zone was unique and with added abundance. Rezanezhad et al. (2014)  carried out a soil column experiment, incubated under either a stable (static water table) versus a fluctuating water table (with water inflow and withdrawal from below) for 4 cycles (75 d). They showed that the redox oscillations accompanying the fluctuations in water table elevation enhanced heterotrophic activity and, consequently, resulted in faster degradation of soil organic matter and greater emission of CO2  to the atmosphere. They also identified the start of differentiation of the bacterial communities in the lower (reducing) and upper (oxidizing) soil regions, but with no systematic difference in the microbial community structure depth profiles between the stable and fluctuating water table columns. Hence, they concluded that variations in microbial activity rather than microbial community composition explained the differences between the stable and fluctuating water table columns. Using a similar soil column system for 5 cycles (329 d), Pronk et al. (2020)  also showed that enhanced carbon turnover in the fluctuating water table zone was driven by a more active microbial community, but that the same taxa dominated as in the same depth interval of the stable water table column. Resident microbes possess physiological tolerance mechanisms that allow them to adapt to fluctuating redox potential conditions (Pett-Ridge and Firestone, 2005; Pett-Ridge et al., 2006; DeAngelis et al., 2010 ). Nunes et al. (2015)  analyzed soil microbial community responses to continuously saturated, continuously unsaturated, and 6 and 18-d cycles of drying-wetting regimes. They found few differences in the soil microbial communities under different treatments. This was attributed to high bacterial abundances, bacterial attachment to the peat matrix, and a large percentage of isolated pores in peat that sustained stable soil microbial communities. These authors further suggested that frequent and more prolonged time scales (months) of water level fluctuation may lead to a more significant differentiation of the soil microbial community than observed in the shorter time scales (days to weeks). While soil microbial communities under different hydrologic regimes have been previously analyzed, relatively few studies have considered the adaptation and stratification of microbial community structure and function in the CF under dynamic water table conditions (Rezanezhad et al. 2014; Pronk et al. 2020; Zhang and Furman, 2021b; Shen et al., 2022 ). The main goal of the present study is to relate the microbial community composition dynamics to the predicted corresponding microbial functions and the biogeochemical cycles of N and C within the CF under variable hydrologic regimes. Our experiments were inspired by the hydrological conditions in the Shafdan soil aquifer treatment site, Israel (with a 30–40 m depth of the water table) (Goren et al., 2011; Sopilniak et al., 2017 ), thus, soil–plant systems (e.g., agricultural systems) are outside the scope of this work. In two previous papers (Zhang and Furman, 2021a; 2023 ), we presented detailed descriptions of the zonation of geochemical (e.g., based on NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    concentration profiles) and redox (e.g., based on the Eh  distribution) properties that developed in sand column experiments under diverse hydrologic regimes. Here, we focus on the depth-time distributions of microbial community composition, determined via 16S rDNA sequencing, the associated predicted microbial interactions and metabolic pathways at three time points (start, middle and end of the experiment) in the aforementioned experiment. The following five hydrologic regimes were imposed on a sandy soil column: (1) a constant water table position separating the unsaturated and saturated zones (static regime, 32 d), (2) periodic pulse infiltration events with a constant water table position (infiltration regime, 27 d), and (3) water table fluctuations under three drainage-imbibition cycles of 6, 12 and 18 d (fluctuating regime, 123 d). Based on the results in Zhang and Furman (2021a; 2023) , we hypothesize that a metabolically versatile microbial community will be established under the fluctuating hydrologic regime in the alternating oxic/anoxic mid-column zone. By contrast, a sharper separation in microbial community function would characterize the unsaturated (oxic) and saturated (anoxic) zones. Our analyses highlight the linkages between microbial community composition and water table dynamics, which help to unravel the relative roles of microbial community structure and function in explaining the different biogeochemical responses under variable hydrologic regimes.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Soil column experiment The experimental setup is detailed in Zhang and Furman (2021a) . Briefly, the air-dried soil was collected from the Shafdan soil aquifer treatment site, Yavne 2, Israel (Goren et al., 2011; Sopilniak et al., 2017 ), then sieved through a 4 mm sieve and any grassroots, stones, plastics, and other unrelated materials were separated manually. The soil was composed of 98.47 % sand, 0.66 % clay and 0.87 % silt (Hydrometer Method; Gee and Or, 2002 ), and contained 1.10 % organic matter (Loss-On-Ignition Method; Nelson and Sommers, 1996 ). The particle size distribution of the soil (Hydrometer Method) is provided in Table S1  (Supplementary Information , SI). The soil was homogenized and packed into a rectangular Perspex column (inner size: 19.3 × 9.9 × 100.0 cm) to a depth of 91 cm with a porosity of ∼42 % (calculated from the water content in the saturated state). The soil column setup is depicted in Fig. 1  a. Note that all depths are expressed relative to the top (0 cm) of the column and the bottom is 100 cm. Self-made three-probe time-domain reflectometry (TDR) (Length: 15 cm, Interval: 1.5 cm) was used for measuring volumetric soil water content at eight depths (20, 30, …, 90 cm). The Eh  electrodes (#461, ecoTech®) were set at ten depths (10, 20, …, 90, 95 cm), with a reference electrode (#4622, ecoTech®) set at 25 cm. Measurements with the datalogger for water content and Eh  were conducted every 15 min. The water table was read from a PVC tube connected to the bottom of the column every ∼12 h. To simulate infiltration from the soil surface, the system was fitted with a custom Perspex sprinkler (inner size: 19.3 × 9.9 × 6.0 cm) designed to yield uniformly (spatially) distributed water infiltration from the top. The sprinkler head had a matrix of 23 × 12 hole arrays for needle emplacement. Flow, via sprinkler infiltration or the bottom inlet, was controlled using a peristaltic pump (Model 7524-55, MASTERFLEX®, L/S®, Cole-Parmer®). A photo of the soil column in the laboratory is provided in Fig. S1  (SI). Following packing, the column was subjected to a series of five sequential hydrologic regimes (Fig. 1 d). Firstly, the column was incubated under a static (S) hydrologic regime , during which the water table was kept constant at a depth of 55 cm for ∼33 d. Porewater samples were collected every 3 d. To counterbalance the small water loss from the sampling, the water level was stabilized via bottom-up inflow following each sampling event. Secondly, an infiltration (I) hydrologic regime  was imposed and lasted for ∼28 d. Infiltration was initiated by activating the sprinkler after porewater sampling (every 3 or 4 d). The sprinkler released influent at 4.5 mL/min for ∼5 h, resulting in a total volume equivalent to 15 % of the porewater volume in the column. During and after each infiltration event, the water table was kept constant at 55 cm depth by draining surplus water out of the column through a tube at the bottom and into a plastic bottle (free drainage condition). Thirdly, the soil column was incubated under a fluctuating (F) hydrologic regime , with, in succession, low, medium and high frequency (LF, MF and HF)  water table oscillations characterized by 18, 12 and 6-d cycles (denoted as Regimes LFF, MFF and HFF ). The water table was moved up by 20, 30 and 60 cm, respectively, every 3 or 4 d from its lower limit of 85 cm. The water table was then moved down by 20, 30 and 60 cm, respectively, every 3 or 4 d from its upper limit of 25 cm. The duration of these three hydrologic subregimes was ∼43, ∼46 and ∼36 d, respectively. Porewater samples were collected before the water table adjustment. The compositions for the infiltration and groundwater recharge influents based on the Shafdan water are given in Table S2  (SI).  2.2 Sampling and analytical procedures of soil and water The soil was sampled three times during the experiment: at the start, middle and end. The original air-dried and homogenized soil represented the initial background condition (Sample Start). After the infiltration regime (∼63 d after the start of incubation), three depth intervals were selected to extract soil samples (∼20 g each): the near-surface (9–20 cm), water table transition (45–55 cm) and water-saturated zone (85–90 cm) (denoted as Samples Mid15, Mid50 and Mid88 in Fig. 1 b, respectively). For each depth interval, soil samples were retrieved from three ports (2–7 cm depth) within the depth interval using a mini-auger (see Fig. 1 ). The three samples were then combined and mixed manually. Any soil removed from the column was replaced by the same amount of fresh air-dried soil after sampling. Once a port was sampled and refilled, it was not used again. At the end of the experiment (∼253 d), the soil was collected at 10, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90 cm depths. At each depth, the samples from three ports were combined and manually mixed (Samples End10, End30, End40, End50, End60, End70, End80 and End90; the depth of 20 cm was not sampled; Fig. 1 b). After filtering through a 0.22 µm filter unit (PVDF membrane, Millex®GV), porewater and the effluent from the bottom tank were analyzed for nitrate (NO 3 -   ; American Public Health Association et al., 2017 ) and ammonium (NH 4 +   ; Ministry of Ecology and Environment of People’s Republic of China, 2009 ) by the spectrophotometer (GENESYS 10S UV–Vis, Thermo Fisher Scientific®), and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) by the TOC-V (Shimadzu®).  2.3 Soil DNA extraction The microbial diversity in different soil samples was estimated via 16S rDNA sequencing. To this end, DNA was extracted from 0.5 g of mixed soil samples (in triplicate for each sampled depth or depth interval) with the FastDNA® Spin Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals®). The extracts were then stored at -20 °C. After examining the extracted DNA’s purity and concentration using a NanoVue® Plus spectrophotometer, extracted DNA samples were delivered to Shanghai Majorbio Bio-pharm Technology Co., Ltd., China, for 16S rDNA sequencing (V3-V4 region). This region was amplified with primer pairs 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). The retrieved sequences have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database under the accession number SRP286981.  2.4 Data processing 2.4.1 Spatial moment analysis We performed a spatial moment analysis to characterize the time-dependent vertical distribution of porewater chemical species concentrations (NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC). Spatial moments are widely applied to describe the spatio-temporal variability of water content and solutes, and provide statistical parameters that summarize their distribution in space and time (e.g., Ye et al., 2005; Lazarovitch et al., 2007 ). The one-dimensional spatial moment for a given porewater solute, Mi  , is given by the following general expression (Ye et al., 2005 ),(1) M i  ( t )  = ∫ - ∞  + ∞   c ( z , t ) θ ( z , t )  z i  d z     where c (z ,t ) is the solute concentration at time t  and depth z , θ (z ,t ) is the volumetric water content, and i  is the order of the moment (i  = 0, 1, 2). The zeroth moment (i  = 0), M 0 , corresponds to the total mass of the solute in the specified domain. The first moment (i  = 1), M 1 , is related to the location of the center of the solute mass. The second moment (i  = 2), M 2 , is a measure of its vertical spread. The center of mass (zc  ) and the spatial variance (σ ) of the porewater solute as a function of its center of mass are given by Equations (2) and (3) ,(2) z c  = M 1  M 0       (3) σ 2  = M 2  M 0   - z c 2       Here, the spatial domain for the moment analysis was between 100 cm (lower domain boundary and the physical bottom of the soil column) and 40, 50 and 20 cm (upper domain boundary that is determined by the ranges of N and C species concentrations measurements) for the static, infiltration and fluctuating regime, respectively. At depths beyond the upper domain boundary, volumetric water content was too low to extract water for chemical analysis, and thus we excluded shallower depths from our moment analysis. We performed a spatial and temporal interpolation of our measured concentrations, using the “Kriging correlation” method in OriginPro® 9.0 (OriginLab Corporation, 2012 ), to generate a smoothed dataset for the spatial moment analysis. The final resolution for the porewater geochemistry dataset was increased two times on both spatial (10 cm) and temporal scales (3–4 d), respectively. We further performed statistical analysis on our spatial moments results. The correlations between zc   and σ  for NO 3 -   , NH 4 +   , DOC, the location of the water table, and the water content were assessed using the “Spearman” correlation method. Significant differences of zc   and σ  for NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC between regimes were analyzed with the “Mann-Whitney U” method. These statistical analyses were conducted in SPSS® 19.0.0 (IBM Corporation, 2010 ).  2.4.2 Sequencing data analysis Sequencing data processing, unless otherwise specified, was performed on the Majorbio Cloud Platform (Shanghai Majorbio Bio-pharm Technology Co., Ltd., 2020 ). The effective sequence reads were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs), sharing 97% identity within each OTU. The OTUs were classified against the SILVA 138 database to acquire the taxonomy based on the RDP Classifier algorithm at a confidence threshold of 70%. The alpha-diversity, including Shannon’s Diversity Index, Simpson’s Index of Diversity (Gini-Simpson Index), Chao1 richness index, ACE and Good’s coverage, was used to measure the diversity inside a group. Cluster dendrogram analysis was conducted in the “pvclust” package using R (Version 3.6.2) (R Core Team, 2019 ) for OTU-based grouping. The analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was used to test the differences between groups from the cluster dendrogram analysis to distinguish the diversities. The linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) method was used to detect OTUs yielding significant differences between groups (Segata et al., 2011 ). The hierarchically clustered heatmap was generated based on the “pheatmap” package in R and the Mantel test was performed using the “vegan” package in R. The statistical differences between every two groups of the predicted metabolic pathways were determined via a Welch’s t -test by Statistical Analysis of Metagenomic Profiles (STAMP) (Parks et al., 2014 ). The microbial diversity and a prediction of the biogeochemical processes can be carried out by the microbial community via 16S rDNA sequencing (Heenan et al., 2017 ). The bioinformatics software Functional Annotation of Prokaryotic Taxa (FAPROTAX) 1.2.1 (Louca et al., 2016 ) was used to extract microbial functional profiles based on the 16S rDNA sequences. FAPROTAX recognizes biogeochemical pathways based on the currently available literature on lab-cultured strains. It utilizes the strength of amplicon-based and metagenome sequencing approaches by comparing taxonomic results from the 16S rDNA sequences to the existing databases of assembled genomes to predict microbial function (Wood et al., 2016 ). That is, the predicted relative abundances of possible metabolic pathways are mapped based on the relative abundances of OTUs in each sample. Co-occurrence network analysis was used to assess possible microbial interactions under different environmental conditions. Only OTUs representing more than 0.1 % of the total relative abundance occurring in at least one sample were selected as nodes (541 OTUs in total). The connection (edge) between nodes reflects a significant (p  < 0.05) and strong (0.6 < |r| < 1) Spearman’s correlation. The networks were visualized and the topological parameters were calculated by Gephi 0.9.2 (Bastian et al., 2009 ). To evaluate the nonrandom pattern of the studied networks, these networks were compared with random networks with equal numbers of nodes and edges generated by the Network Randomizer plugin (Tosadori et al., 2016 ) in Cytoscape 3.8.0 (Shannon et al., 2003 ). Module analysis was used to reveal the relationships between the topological nodes and functional roles in the complex network (Cumbo et al., 2014 ). The GIANT plugin achieved this analysis in Cytoscape (Cumbo et al., 2014 ). Modularity is the appearance of densely connected groups of vertices with only sparser connections between groups (Newman, 2006 ), calculated from Gephi. Each node in the network can be characterized by two parameters: within-module connectivity (z-score) and among-module connectivity (c-score) (Fan et al., 2018a; Fan et al., 2018b; Qi et al., 2019 ). The z-score defines the degree to which a node is linked to the other nodes within its module, and the c-score defines the degree to which a node is linked to different modules (Qi et al., 2019 ). Based on the threshold values of these two parameters, the nodes fall into four quadrants: network hubs (z-score > 2.5, c-score > 0.6), connectors (z-score < 2.5, c-score > 0.6), peripherals (z-score < 2.5, c-score < 0.6) and module hubs (z-score > 2.5, c-score < 0.6) (Fan et al., 2018a; Fan et al., 2018b ). The network hubs are highly connected within and between modules. The module hubs are highly connected within modules, the connectors are highly connected between modules, and the peripherals have few links to other OTUs (Poudel et al., 2016 ). Generally, network hubs, module hubs, and connectors are considered keystone taxa, contributing significantly to maintaining microbial communities’ resistance and stability (Fan et al., 2018a ).    3 Results and discussions 3.1 Spatio-temporal distribution of Eh , nitrogen and carbon The Eh  (Fig. S2 , SI), nitrogen (N) and carbon (C) dynamics, and the description of the biogeochemical behavior of the experimental system in response to the various flow regimes were discussed in an accompanying paper (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ). Here, we focus on the geochemical zonation of the system and not on the magnitude of concentrations. We propose a conceptual model of the reaction pathways in the soil column in Fig. 2  , based on the combined results of Zhang and Furman (2021a)  and the molecular biological results (will be introduced in Section 3.3 ) obtained here. The conceptual model highlights the dependence of O2  diffusion on water content and the resulting zonation of nitrification and aerobic respiration in the upper sections of the column and denitrification below the water table. The NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC zones (Fig. 1 ) correspond to the distribution of Eh , where higher (400.0 ± 87.4 mV) were measured in the upper sections (10–50 cm) of the column and lower values (-366.0 ± 129.3 mV) at depth (80–100 cm). The distribution and N species concentrations (NO 3 -    and NH 4 +   ) allow a division of the soil column into four zones in the fluctuating regime (Fig. 1 c). The lower boundary of the NO 3 -   -dominant zone was sensitive to the water table, highlighting the water saturation-dependent O2  supply. The upper boundary of the zone of high NH 4 +    was constant, and NO 3 -    was hardly detected below this boundary, indicating that denitrification reached its maximum capacity in the strongly reducing zone (70–100 cm, i.e., all NO 3 -    was reduced). Low NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    concentrations were detected in the middle of the column (50–60 cm) due to simultaneous nitrification and denitrification. DOC was consumed mainly through aerobic respiration or denitrification in the soil column. Increasing the frequency of groundwater fluctuations decreased the magnitude of DOC concentrations (average DOC concentrations are 32.6, 22.0 and 18.7 mg/L for Cases 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, respectively), most likely due to an increased O2  supply driving more oxidation of DOC as well as nitrification and the production of a subsequent electron acceptor, NO 3 -   , fueling further DOC oxidation. With N being the main nutrient in the soil column experiments under dynamic redox states, nitrification and denitrification were the major redox processes in the oxic and anoxic conditions, respectively.  3.2 Spatial moment analysis for nitrogen and carbon distribution Based on the spatial moment analysis, the center of mass (zc  ) and the spatial variance (σ ) for NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC as a function of time for five hydrologic regimes are displayed in Fig. 3  . Both zc   and σ  of NO 3 -    and DOC, in the fluctuating regimes, correlated strongly with the location of the water table and the center of mass of water content (zc  (θ )) (Figs. 3 c, 3d and 3f; p  < 0.05, Table S3 , SI). This was consistent with the fact that the lower boundary of the NO 3 -   -dominant zone was sensitive to the location of the water table (Figs. 7 - 9 in Zhang and Furman (2021a) ). However, zc   and σ  of NH 4 +    were insensitive to the location of the water table and zc  (θ ) with almost no significant difference in the fluctuating regimes (Figs. 3 c, 3d and 3f; p  > 0.05, Table S3 ), which was consistent with the constant upper boundary of the high NH 4 +    zone. These phenomena were also supported by visual observations of the distributions of NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC (Figs. 7 - 9 in Zhang and Furman (2021a) ). Furthermore, the hydrologic regime can also be reflected by the distribution of water content. zc   and σ  for water content as a function of time for five hydrologic regimes are displayed in Fig. S3  (SI). Strong correlations were observed for zc   and σ  of water content and the water table in the static and fluctuating regimes (p  < 0.05, Table S4 , SI). Additionally, the correlation coefficients between zc  (θ ) and zc  , and zc  (θ ) and σ  for NO 3 -    and DOC increased from Regime LFF to Regime HFF, indicating the increasing influence with a larger spatial range of the water table fluctuation. The averages and standard deviations of zc   and σ  for NO 3 -   , NH 4 +    and DOC in each regime are listed in Table 1  . Considering the comparison between the static regime and the infiltration regime, zc  (NO 3 -   ) increased a little depths (2.8 cm), while zc  (NH 4 +   ) and zc  (DOC) decreased (6.4 cm and 14.8 cm) in the infiltration regime. Under the influence of infiltration in the infiltration regime, zc  (NO 3 -   ) was still stable in a deep depth (>60 cm) as in the static regime. NO 3 -    from the initial soil in the upper depths moved to lower depths with the water flow. After four cycles in the infiltration regime, the residual NO 3 -    in the upper regions was washed and the soil column reached a steady condition, indicated by the new N distribution. With water flow, O2  could be transported easily to the lower depths (<70 cm); thus, O2  availability could stimulate ammonification and aerobic respiration of DOC at most depths (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ). Then, zc  (NH 4 +   ) and zc  (DOC) could shrink to lower depths. Due to the initial condition, NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    had the most significant spatial variance in the static regime than in other regimes, and σ (DOC) in the static regime was larger than that in the infiltration regime. Considering the comparison between the static and fluctuating regimes, zc  (NO 3 -   ) increased by 31.1 cm in the fluctuating regimes. Water table fluctuations could lead to NO 3 -    accumulation in the shallower depths (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ), contributing to the increase of zc  (NO 3 -   ). From the view of the single N species, which kept strict stratification and reached a steady state in each subregime of the fluctuating regimes, σ (NO 3 -   ) and σ (NH 4 +   ) decreased (6.3 cm and 4.3 cm) in the fluctuating regimes. However, σ (DOC) increased a lot (6.8 cm) in the fluctuating regimes, due to the excess of DOC and limited DOC consumption at all the depths (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ). Regarding comparing the subregimes in the fluctuating regimes, zc  (NO 3 -   ) increased, while zc  (NH 4 +   ) decreased from Regime LFF to Regime HFF. With the increasing frequency of the water table fluctuation, the rising trend of zc  (NO 3 -   ) implied that more O2  could efficiently resupply into the soil column; a little decrease of zc  (NH 4 +   ) indicated the expanded depths to be anoxic, which was consistent with the behavior of Eh  at 70 cm (Figs. 3c, 3d, 3e in Zhang and Furman (2021a) ). With the expanded depths of anoxic condition, zc  (DOC) in Regimes MFF and HFF were lower than that in Regime LFF, because the consumption by denitrification was stronger than aerobic respiration for the excess DOC. All the σ  of NO 3 -    and DOC increased gradually from Regime LFF to Regime HFF, which indicated that water table fluctuations could contribute to the expansion of their spatial variance. With the relatively stable upper boundary of the NH 4 +   -dominant zone, σ (NH 4 +   ) displayed little difference in the subregimes of the fluctuating regime. Additionally, the patterns of zc   and σ  for NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    could indicate the depth stratification of 10–50 cm, 50–70 cm and 70–100 cm.  3.3 Microbial diversity and community composition In total, 3,401,803 quality sequences were obtained from the 36 soil samples, and 8,340 OTUs were observed across all samples, ranging between 4,384 and 5,150 OTUs in each soil sample. The number of OTUs classified according to phylum, class, order, family and genus of each sample are listed in Table S5  (SI). Table S5  also includes indexes of alpha diversity (Shannon’s Diversity Index, Simpson’s Index of Diversity, Chao1 richness index, ACE and Good’s coverage). The Good’s coverage values of all soil samples were over 0.98, and the rarefaction curves of Shannon indexes were saturated (Fig. S4 , SI), suggesting that the sequencing depth was adequate to cover most of the microbes and even included some rare species (Zhou et al., 2019 ). The microbial community composition at the phylum level in the twelve soil samples is shown in Fig. 4  a. Proteobacteria , the most abundant phylum (28.9–41.1%), contain facultative or obligate anaerobic and heterotrophic species (Ding and Xu, 2023 ). Organic carbon and nitrogen can substantially affect the abundance of facultative anaerobic bacteria (Ding and Xu, 2023 ). The microbial community composition at the family level is shown in Fig. 4 b. The most abundant family was Nitrososphaeraceae , which accounted for 6.2–17.8% and is an ammonia-oxidizing archaeon (Louca et al., 2016 ). Sixteen of the top 23 OTUs at the family level were 1–3%. Defluviicoccus  (the only genera in the second most abundant family, Defluviicoccaceae , 2.7–6.9%) is suitable for alternating aerobic-anaerobic conditions (Burow et al., 2007; Oehmen et al., 2010 ). Pure cultures of Defluviicoccus  use acetate as a carbon source (Burow et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2018 ) and can only reduce NO 3 -    (Oehmen et al., 2010 ), that is, they are known denitrifiers. The deduced primary functions of the other major families presented in our samples are reported in Table S6  (SI). “Others” in Fig. 4 b occupied a large percentage (36.4–47.6 %) of the family level. A conceptual model was proposed (Fig. 2 ) for the main microbial roles at the family level (>1%) in both the unsaturated and saturated zones. Only the microbes at the family level (based on Table S6 ) involved in the main biogeochemical processes in the soil column were selected to build this conceptual model. It supported that N and C cycling processes were the main redox processes in this soil column. Based on the OTUs, the dendrogram revealed five distinct groups for the twelve soil samples related to the different regimes (Fig. 5  ). The first group (G1) separates the initial soil from the rest, indicating significant changes due to the regimes. The second group (G2) distinguishes the near-surface in the infiltration regime. The CF and saturated zone in the infiltration regime are grouped as a third group (G3). The fourth group (G4) represents the unsaturated zone in the fluctuating regime. The fifth group (G5) implies a saturated zone in the fluctuating regime. The analysis of similarities (ANOSIM, r = 0.33, p  < 0.001) supported the significant differences between the groups.  3.4 Co-occurrence network pattern The co-occurrence network analysis explored the complexity of the interactions of soil microbial taxa during the soil column’s operation. As more than one sample is needed for each group to perform the calculation for the co-occurrence network analysis here, we re-grouped the microbial samples presented in Fig. 5  to achieve the largest number of groups to analyze the depth profiles in high resolution. Then, the soil samples were redivided into five groups: (N1) Samples Start and Mid15; (N2) Samples Mid50 and Mid88; (N3) Samples End10, End30 and End40; (N4) Samples End50 and End60; (N5) Samples End70, End80 and End90. OTU-based visualized network plots are shown in Fig. S5  (SI), and the topological properties are displayed in Table 2  . The order of the network edges is N3 > N5 > N1 ≈ N2 > N4. The orders of the positive and negative edges, average degrees and average clustering coefficients in the networks are the same, but the order of the average path lengths is reversed. In these five groups, the module analysis revealed that all the nodes belong to the connectors and the peripherals (Fig. 6  ). Generally, the five groups have similar compositions of a high percentage of connectors and a low percentage of peripherals. The order of the connectors’ percentages is N3 ≈ N5 > N1 > N2 > N4. Higher average path lengths, modularity values and average clustering coefficients in the studied networks relative to the random networks (Table S7 , SI) indicate that microbes assembled nonrandomly and adjusted to the environment (i.e., hydrologic regime here) (Chen et al., 2018 ). The modularity values were higher than 0.4, which suggested a modular structure of these five groups (Chen et al., 2018 ). From the number of edges (Upton et al., 2020 ), our results confirmed that stronger connections among OTUs (i.e., stronger connected community) were shaped in the prevailing oxic and anoxic zone (N3 and N5) in the fluctuating regime, while the weaker connections (i.e., weaker connected community) were observed in the alternating oxic/anoxic zone (N4) in the fluctuating regime. Specifically, from the number of positive edges (indicating cooperation) and the number of negative edges (indicating competition) (Lin et al., 2019 ), the strength in these two kinds of connections kept the same order as the general connections. This meant that the cooperation and competition relationships changed in coordination with the general relationships in these five groups. Generally, the higher network connectivity values (i.e., average degree and the number of edges) and average clustering coefficient indicated that the OTUs tended to use the resource more effectively and displayed a strong metabolic hand-off (Zhao et al., 2019 ). Liu et al. (2020)  highlighted that a highly connected network allows for functional redundancy and greater community stability, which consequently favors stronger resistance to disturbances (biotic and abiotic). Combining modular analysis with indexes of network connectivity and average clustering coefficients, we suggested that the network stabilities of the five groups are in the following order: N3 ≈ N5 > N1 ≈ N2 > N4. In these non-hub-based networks (nodes belong to connectors or peripherals), the connectors played essential roles in maintaining the networks’ stability (Fig. 6 ). The high percentages of connectors in the five groups suggested stability and resistance of the microbial communities in general (Fan et al., 2018a ). In the fluctuating regime, constant stable Eh  was observed for oxic and anoxic depths all the time (except 60 and 70 cm; Fig. S2 ). The Eh  at 60 cm fluctuated in cycles with the water table fluctuation. The Eh  at 70 cm decreased slowly from oxic to anoxic conditions. Upon water table changes, the distribution of NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    concentrations reached stable conditions within three days. As the redox patterns were maintained at each depth, the microbial communities at each depth were supposed to be accustomed to their environments, respectively. The alternating oxic/anoxic zone (N4) in the fluctuating regime was likely more flexible in response to water table fluctuations. Here, the easier accessibility to NO 3 -    from the upper oxic zone and NH 4 +    from the lower anoxic zone allowed for the co-occurrence of aerobic and anaerobic reactions as well as low NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    concentrations (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ), possibly resulting in fewer dependencies between individual microbes, thereby reducing diversity (Nunes et al., 2015; Upton et al., 2020 ). After rapid (less than 3 d) nitrification and denitrification in the prevailing oxic zone (N3) and prevailing anoxic zone (N5), respectively, in the fluctuating regime, these depths became resource-limited (Zhang and Furman, 2021a ). Most likely, the microbial community built tighter relationships relative to the alternating oxic/anoxic zone to face such an unbeneficial situation.  3.5 Microbial functional profile The microbial functional contributions in the soil samples were predicted according to OTUs using FAPROTAX. A small proportion (15.0 %, 1,250 out of 8,340) of the OTUs was classified into specific functional categories based on the FAPROTAX analysis. The functional category of the rest of the OTUs could not be identified. The results revealed a total of 67 metabolic pathways of 90 currently presented in the database. The predicted metabolic pathways from the FAPROTAX analysis of the microbial community correlated significantly with the taxonomic composition (Mantel r = 0.67, p  < 0.001), indicating a reasonable functional prediction for all the samples (Li et al., 2019 ). Fig. 7   is the heatmap of the predicted relative abundance of metabolic pathways. The group of microbial diversity (Fig. 5 ) was adopted to analyze microbial function, which was helpful for the explanation. Based on Fig. 2  and Fig. 7 , organic carbon could be both decomposed in the unsaturated and saturated zones by respiration and denitrification, respectively. Fig. 7  showed that the initial soil (G1) exhibited higher relative abundances of nitrification and ammonia oxidation pathways and lower relative abundances of denitrification, ureolysis and aerobic chemoheterotrophy pathways. The initial soil was incubated under an “air-dried” condition, likely representing the historical microbial community structure in the Shafdan field site. Samples from the infiltration regime highlighted an initial shift in the functional potential of the microbial community, most likely related to the presence of residual organic carbon in the soil and pulsed O2  supply. In the near-surface (9–20 cm, Sample Mid15, G2), aerobic chemoheterotrophy became the most prevalent functionality, along with ureolysis. The chemoheterotrophic and aerobic chemoheterotrophic bacteria could participate in the soil carbon cycle (Ding and Xu, 2023 ). The appearance of ureolysis as a relevant function of the microbial community likely related to the taxa that activate in response to the infiltration regime and not the actual breakdown of urea, which may not be present in the infiltrating water nor the original soil matrix. In Samples Mid50 and Mid88 (G3, including depths of 45–55 and 85–90 cm), the functional potential of the microbial community to denitrify started to increase in relative abundance. A more pronounced predicted functional zonation became apparent via the more highly spatially resolved sampling at the end of the HFF treatment. Most notably, and in line with our conceptual understanding of the system, at the minimum depth of the water table (ca. 85 cm), the OTUs of denitrification and ammonification dominated (Sample End80), with denitrification-related OTUs prevailing over nitrification ones in the sample above (Sample End70). While ammonification-related OTUs were more prevalent than denitrification-related OTUs in Sample End80, both were the most abundant functionality in the microbial community. This co-occurrence of nitrification and denitrification functional potential was hypothesized by Zhang and Furman (2021a)  to occur due to the presence of anoxic microsites, a phenomenon previously observed in a soil column by Subramaniam et al. (2016)  and Friedman et al. (2018) . In the fluctuating regime, almost no NH 4 +    was observed at shallow depths (10–30 cm) and no NO 3 -    at deep depths (80–100 cm), because after each water table shift, fast nitrification and denitrification consumed NH 4 +    at shallow depths and NO 3 -    at deep depths in the column in three to four days, respectively. However, contrasting active functionalities could still be maintained in one microbial community under such pulse stimuli (Pronk et al., 2020 ). As the anammox process was almost undetected at the end of the experiment, denitrification was the dominant metabolic pathway for N removal from this system. Below the minimum depth of the water table (Sample End90), the OTUs of alternative terminal electron-accepting pathways, other than denitrification, including methanogenesis, sulfate reduction, and to a lesser extent manganese oxidation, increased in their relative abundances. The distribution of sulfur and the inferred generation of FeS supported the expanded range of anaerobic conditions from Fig. 11 in Zhang and Furman (2021a) . This shift in functional potential suggested an adaptation to the strong and constant reducing conditions below the denitrification zone. Based on the comparison of the relative abundances of the metabolic pathways predicted by the FAPROTAX between every two groups, significant differences (p  < 0.05) between G5 and other groups were found (Table S8 , SI), which supported G5 was prevailing in reducing conditions. The FAPROTAX-derived microbial functional contribution provided a functional link between the potential pathways carried out by the microbial community and centers of mass and spatial variances of the nitrate and ammonium concentration zones in the soil column. The depth classification based on microbial function was internally consistent with the classification based on the Eh  and N species distributions, spatial moment analysis of NO 3 -    and NH 4 +    concentrations, and microbial community composition. Most notably, it not only supported our previous conceptual model of the biogeochemical reaction pathways that governed the geochemical evolution of the system throughout the different water table regimes in the incubation (Fig. 12 in Zhang and Furman (2021a) ), but also supported our current conceptual model (Fig. 2 ) of the roles of functional microbes for the biogeochemical reaction pathways in the soil column. As evidenced by the microbial community compositions and functions from the FAPROTAX, diverse metabolic pathways (aerobic or anaerobic pathways for C, N, S, Fe and Mn) in the soil column responded to water table changes. The microbial depth stratification was related to the dynamic hydrologic regimes (frequent pulse recharge in the infiltration regime and frequent groundwater fluctuation in the fluctuating regime). The metabolic pathways exhibited clear differences between five depth-related groups (Fig. 7 ). In contrast, the dominant microbial families did not change (Fig. 4 ) and little statistical difference (through LEfSe) was observed in the taxonomy. This aligned with findings by Pronk et al. (2020)  and suggested that different facets of the community became more active in response to water table fluctuations but that the general composition of the microbial community remained unchanged. Moreover, the experiments mimicked the conditions in the Shafdan field site, therefore, the initial soil microbial community was well adapted to variable redox conditions.   4 Conclusions Our results highlighted the importance of hydrologic forcing on the changes in biogeochemical processes and microbial community structure in soils and sediments. We propose that a metabolically more active, rather than a more compositionally diverse or abundant soil microbial community, drives the activation and deactivation of biogeochemical pathways under fluctuating moisture content conditions. Our DNA-based analysis provided additional evidence that sheds light on the specific reaction pathways that drove the spatially and temporally variant turnover of oxygen, nitrogen species and carbon in the experimental system. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed the strength of the microbial interactions under specific soil moisture conditions. Moreover, the predicted functionalities provided key insights into the functional potential of the microbial community and further highlighted that microbial communities could adapt their functional potential, that is, the genes they expressed did not significantly shift their taxonomical composition. However, DNA-based approaches only capture the potential pathways that a microbial community can catalyze. Additionally, DNA-based methods also capture the signals of dead cells, extracellular DNA and the DNA of dormant microbes (Lennon and Jones, 2011; Herzog et al., 2015 ). Therefore, they do not reflect the actual current functional potential, but rather a time-integrated reaction potential which retains a biogeochemical memory based on the conditions experienced by the microbial community at time scales comparable to the lifetime of DNA in soils. In addition to a DNA-based characterization, future work in fluctuating water table regimes should focus on direct measurement of the pathways that are activated, by focusing on RNA-based methods, capturing the abundances of gene transcripts (Herzog et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Antunes et al., 2016 ). The latter will help to constrain the duration of periods of activation of specific reaction pathways and link the metabolic potential with the actual metabolic activity.
1 Introduction The most feasible technology option to contain greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2 ) from various industrial sources is carbon capture and storage (CCS). The CCS technology captures the carbon dioxide emitted as a byproduct from industries (e.g., steel plants, cement plants, and thermal power plants) and stores it in deep geological formations through large gas injections executed for several hundred days (IEA GHG, 2009 ). However, suitable deep geological formations need the required porosity for significant storage capacity and higher permeability to transport CO2  gas easily (Bachu, 2015 ; Pavan and Govindarajan, 2023 ). Therefore, sedimentary formations are recommended for storing vast amounts of CO2  (Bachu, 2003 ; Benson and Cole, 2008 ; Li et al., 2009 ; Ershadnia et al., 2021 ). These deep geological aquifers are covered by impermeable formations known as caprock (i.e., aquitard) on either end (i.e., top and bottom) and are essential to trap the injected CO2  gas in the geological formation (Shukla et al., 2010 ; Castelletto et al., 2013 ; Song and Jong, 2013 ; War et al., 2022 ). The leakage paths in caprock constitute a significant concern for the possible leak of CO2  from the storage aquifers (Deremble et al., 2011 ; Korre et al., 2011 ; Celia et al., 2011 ; Sun et al., 2013 ). The leakage of CO2  has a substantial influence on the surficial and underground freshwater bodies and leads to the contamination of water resources (Fig. 1  , left). Such potential leakage paths comprise abandoned wells, faults, and fractures (Nordbotten et al., 2005 ; Humez et al., 2011 ; Celia et al., 2015 ). Moreover, a proper site selection approach can eliminate the densely packed faults and fractured geological formations. But, abandoned wells cannot be ignored as they are most common in many subsurface deep geological aquifers due to miscellaneous drilling activities in the past, such as oil and gas wells, geothermal wells, mineral and groundwater exploration wells, monitoring wells, and research-based wells (Gasda et al., 2004 ; Vrålstad et al., 2019 ). The leakage paths from the abandoned wells are formed due to the well's damaged structural integrity or degraded cement plugs inside the well (Fig. 1 , left). These abandoned wells were drilled through the caprock in the past and must be sealed to increase the overall storage capacity of deep geological aquifers (Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). Abandoned wells are predominant in many parts of the world, especially along the coastal regions (Nicot, 2009 ). These abandoned wells penetrate through the caprock, compromise the caprock integrity, and minimise the storage capacity of the deep geological aquifers by forming potential leakage paths for CO2  gas escape. Therefore, it is essential to plug these leakage pathways formed from abandoned wells to achieve required storage capacity for trapping CO2 . Traditional cement plugging methods to seal abandoned wells can become inefficient due to poor cementation, cement degradation and casing failure (Pawar et al., 2009 ; Watson and Bachu, 2009 ). Therefore, sustainable and efficient treatment methods are needed to overcome the current challenges of plugging the leaky abandoned wells. In the past decade, sustainable biomediated methods such as the microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) process have proved effective in reducing the porosity of geomaterials by precipitating cementitious calcium carbonate within the pore network (Dejong et al., 2006 ; Montoya and Dejong, 2015 ; Jain and Arnepalli, 2019 ; Bhukya et al., 2023a ,b ; Sun et al., 2024 ). The application of MICP in the subsurface formations eventually minimises the permeability of the target area. However, the MICP is a microbially mediated process that advances with the release of the urease enzyme by hydrolysing the urea (Eq. (1) ). The hydrolysed urea in a calcium-abundant environment precipitates calcium carbonate (CaCO3 ) and releases ammonium ions (NH4 + ). The most common bacterial species used for MICP treatment is Sporosarcina pasteurii . The calcite precipitation through MICP treatment has a potential application for closing the openings in the caprock (Fig. 1 , right). Besides, the MICP was proven to be a sealing technology that plugs fractures in the rock masses (Cuthbert et al., 2013 ; Phillips et al., 2016 ; Cunningham et al., 2019 ). The MICP technology injects the bacteria, which is less viscous and has lower-sized biomass constituents that can penetrate the pore spaces easily compared to the traditional cement grouting technique for leakage path plugging (Cunningham et al., 2011 ).(1) CO ( N  H  2  )  2  +  2 H  2  O   +  C  a   2 +    → urease   2 NH 4  +  +  CaC O  3          The Sporosarcina pasteurii  is a halophilic bacteria and can survive in a saline environment (Dikshit et al., 2022 ). The higher pore gas pressures and supercritical conditions (7.5 MPa - 10 MPa, 32 °C) at laboratory scale were observed to have relatively less effect on bacterial growth (Mitchell et al., 2013 ). Also, the Sporosarcina pasteurii  can survive even at extreme temperatures (i.e., 10 °C - 50 °C), as per Kim et al. (2018) . Besides, once the bacteria is accumulated at the desired concentration, the urease hydrolysis rate of Sporosarcina pasteurii  becomes the most prominent parameter for the reaction and is the function of urea concentration, attached bacteria concentration, pH, temperature, calcium ion concentration, encapsulation, and salt content (van Paassen, 2009 ; Peng et al., 2022 ; Bhukya et al., 2023b ). The temperature of the geological media above and below an optimum temperature (typically 35 °C) reduces the urea hydrolysis rate of bacteria (Xiao et al., 2021 ). Similarly, the pH lower and higher than the optimum value (pH = 9) reduces the urease activity (Lauchnor et al., 2015 ). But, acidic conditions significantly alter the urease activity compared to alkaline conditions (van Paassen, 2009 ). In addition, the rise in salinity value was observed to affect the urease activity of bacteria, but beyond a particular salt concentration (e.g., ∼ 0.5 mol/l), the effect becomes constant (Peng et al., 2022 ). The study by Dikshit et al. (2022)  suggests that Sporosarcina pasteurii  can retain its considerable proportion of urease activity (i.e., the ability to hydrolyse the urea) up to a NaCl concentration of 5% w/w in water. Likewise, there is another significant process reducing the urease activity i.e., encapsulation, by which calcium carbonate precipitated during biocementation covers the attached biomass and makes the attached bacteria inactive (Cuthbert et al., 2013 ; Bhukya et al., 2023b ). Among all, temperature, salinity, and encapsulation are the predominant factors influencing the urease activity of bacteria (Wang et al., 2024 ; Dikshit et al., 2022 ; Bhukya et al., 2023b ). Besides, the factors mentioned above that influence urease activity indicate the complex multi-physical relations between various physical domains, which must be understood thoroughly through experimental, field, and numerical studies. In the context of plugging CO2  leaks, the modelling study performed by Ebigbo et al. (2010)  plugged the leaks near the injection well using the biofilm volume fraction. The simulation results of Ebigbo et al. (2010)  indicated a reduction in the permeability of the leakage zone due to significant biofilm formation in the pores spaces of caprock by the end of 400 days. Actually, the biofilm formation alone was employed near the zone of interest to seal the leakage paths (Ebigbo et al., 2010 ). Later, Ebigbo et al. (2012)  extended the biofilm-based technique of Ebigbo et al. (2010)  to MICP treatment, which precipitated calcite in the pores in addition to the biofilm formation, significantly reducing the permeability. Ebigbo et al. (2012)  modelled the MICP treatment with the injection of chemicals (i.e., urea and calcium source) after injecting bacterial species, but with an additional oxygen (O2 ) supplement for biomass growth. Thereby, the reduction in porosity became quite significant as the porosity of the zone of interest was reduced due to the volume fractions of biofilm and calcite. However, the calcite fraction contribution towards porosity reduction was higher than the biofilm volume fraction (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ). Cunningham et al. (2011)  extended the earlier work of MICP in a reactor of Cunningham et al. (2009)  and performed MICP treatment on sand columns with the prime motive of mitigating leaks from the leakage paths of caprock through biofilm and calcite plugging. Therefore, the experimental study by Cunningham et al. (2011)  encouraged applying MICP treatment as a CO2  leak mitigation technology in leaky carbon geosequestrated aquifers. Moreover, to plug the leakage from complex fractures, Cuthbert et al. (2013)  treated the domain of fracture inclined at a dip angle of 25° at a depth of 25 m below the ground level using MICP treatment. The fracture aperture was initially ∼ 0.67 × 10−3  m, reduced by the end of the biocementation process to ∼ 99 % near the injection well. Besides, the modelling study on the fracture domain also revealed reduced transmittance near the injection well due to MICP treatment (Cuthbert et al., 2013 ). In a similar attempt, Phillips et al. (2013)  cored a 0.762 m diameter sandstone, created a fracture using the hydraulic fracturing technique and sealed the fracture by reducing the permeability from 2.4 × 10−12  m2  to 1 × 10−16  m2 . This is a significant change in permeability, indicating the potential of MICP treatment to reduce leakage of fluids (e.g., CO2 ) from sandstone/shale formations. Hommel et al. (2013)  conducted a numerical modelling study on a small sandstone core experiment under higher effluent pressure to represent the reservoir conditions and reasonably predicted the sandstone's permeability reduction (∼ 1 order change). In continuation of the effort to seal the leakage paths, Phillips et al. (2016)  sealed a fractured sandstone located at a depth of 340.8 m using MICP treatment. After the treatment, the annulus pressure test on the well revealed a reduction in pressure decay to 7% from an earlier decay rate of 30%, indicating the sealing of fractures. The field observations reported by Phillips et al. (2016)  further improved the confidence in MICP as a potential treatment method for mitigating leaks from a CO2 -sequestrated aquifer. In an attempt to simulate the experimental study by Phillips et al. (2016) , Cunningham et al. (2019)  adopted a re-calibrated numerical model developed by Hommel et al. (2015)  to study the MICP treatment in a large domain of 8 m (radius) × 50 m (depth) with a preexisting highly permeable fracture of 0.05 m thick placed at the vertical centre. The simulations of Cunningham et al. (2019)  indicated calcite precipitation in the fracture aperture, thereby reducing the permeability along the fracture aperture. The above-mentioned experimental, field and modelling studies improved the understanding of using MICP as a sealing technology for plugging the leakage paths. Recently, Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  simulated CO2  injection into a leaky aquifer in various geometrical settings of leakage paths. Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  evaluated the leakage rate from the abandoned wells before and after MICP treatment. The bacteria were injected into the leaky aquifer for enzyme secretion, oxygen for microbes growth and urea for reaction. Also, the water was injected after each biochemical species injection to transport the suspended components (i.e., microbes, oxygen, urea, CaCl2 ) to target distances. Besides, Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  performed multiple chemical injection cycles of urea and calcium chloride for the reaction to initiate and seal the leakage path completely. Nevertheless, significantly higher flow rates (7.2 × 10−4  to 5 × 10−3  m3 ·s−1 ) and chemical injection concentration (5 kmol·m−3 ) were utilised for the large-scale modelling studies. Therefore, the leakage rate became insignificant by the end of the third chemical injection cycle. The injections in the modelling study by Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  were mainly focused on plugging the leakage paths located at a 100 m distance from the injection well. However, the injection durations of biochemicals in the modelling study were adjusted manually to precipitate calcium carbonate near the target region. Therefore, the higher injection velocity has resulted in lower injection durations for bacteria and chemical injections. A similar study was carried out by Bhukya et al. (2023a) , employing biocementation for plugging the leakage path at 100 m from the injection source. Although there are numerous numerical models for MICP treatment, only a few numerical studies are available in the state-of-the-art for large-scale applications such as mitigating CO2  leaks from abandoned wells through biomediated treatments (Ebigbo et al., 2010 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ; Bhukya et al., 2023a ). Besides, employing MICP treatment requires a generalised methodology to seal the leakage paths at variable distances from the injection source. While the study by Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  sealed the leak at a distance of 100 m, a design methodology for fixing the biochemical and water injection durations for a given injection velocity was not proposed. The commonly used injection velocity was in the order of 1 × 10−5  m·s−1  in the experimentation of MICP as well as in the field to avoid particle misarrangement and over pressurisation at the injection source (Martinez et al., 2013 ; Faeli et al., 2023 a ,b ; Cuthbert et al., 2013 ; Ebigbo et al., 2010 ). Therefore, an optimisation methodology is crucial to adjust the injection durations for specific injection velocity and achieve maximised precipitation. However, the leakage path distance from the injection source could vary based on past drilling operations at the site, forming near-field or far-field leaks. Consequently, it is necessary to specify the injection approaches for biocementation treatment to seal near-field and far-field leakage paths at respective distances from the injection source. Besides, the MICP application for any field problem needs such methodology for convenient calculations in deciding the biochemical injection durations. Therefore, the generalisation for defining the injection duration of biochemicals is yet to be understood by extending the past modelling studies. As a result, optimisation approach for the biochemical injections is demanding to accommodate the MICP treatment for large-scale applications. Also, optimisation could reduce the excess injections of biochemicals, thereby reducing the cost of MICP application for a specific injection velocity. Therefore, the present study extends our past modelling work conducted in Bhukya et al. (2023a)  and develops an optimisation procedure for determining the optimal durations of injections and retentions for the MICP treatment to achieve the desired target permeability. Accordingly, the current study proposes an optimisation methodology to seal the leakage paths near-filed and far-field distances from the injection source. To do so, the study developed a two-phase BCH mathematical framework to simulate MICP and CO2  injections in leaky deep geological aquifers connected by the leakage path of an abandoned well passing through the caprock. The primary emphasis of the study is to provide optimised durations of injection and retention of MICP treatment for the adopted injection velocity and demonstrate the applicability of optimisation methodology for sealing the leakage paths situated in the caprock at both near-field and far-field distances and making CO2  leakage rates insignificant. In addition, a cost analysis was performed to understand the cost-effectiveness of the MICP treatment compared to the traditional cement plugging method for sealing abandoned wells. Overall, the study attempts to indicate the field applicability of MICP treatment for sealing leaks, the procedure to optimise the treatment process and cost scenarios for variable target distances.  2 Two-phase MICP model concept The biochemical species’ flow and transport decide the MICP treatment's efficacy in precipitating the desired calcite. Besides, when the CO2  gas is injected into the water-saturated aquifer, the two-phase fluid flow occurs in the deep geological aquifer. Therefore, the current section discusses the coupled processes involved during the two-phase fluid flow and the MICP treatment, coupling the domains of biology (B), chemistry (C) and hydraulics (H). In addition, the assumptions considered in the current modelling study for simplifying the mathematical framework are explained in detail. 2.1 Coupled processes The MICP process undergoes an enzyme-driven biochemical reaction (Eq. (1) ) to precipitate calcium carbonate within the pore network of geomaterial. During the MICP treatment, the reaction is initiated upon injection of a chemical species into the system (C↔H) following the bacterial and growth media (i.e., oxygen) injection (B↔H). The advective-dispersive transport (H) dominates the movement of biochemical species inside the geomaterial pores compared to diffusion (Bhukya et al., 2023b ). The progressive urea hydrolysis and subsequent precipitation (B↔H) alter the pore space, thereby modifying the porosity and permeability of the system (Fauriel and Laloui, 2012 ) and affecting the advective flow velocity (H). Besides, the bacterial concentration after biological injection phase is governed by attachment, detachment, decay, and growth processes. Biomass attachment on the solid surface of the geological media is a significant phenomenon that accumulates attached bacterial concentration, thereby the urea hydrolysis rate (Faeli et al., 2023b ; Bhukya and Arnepalli, 2024 ). At the same time, bacterial detachment can occur at the injection source (B↔H) due to predominant shear stresses generated by the fluid pressure gradient (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ).
