Further, biomass decay initiates due to unfavourable conditions in the system, which is a prolonged process but still considerable for large timescales (Wang and Nackenhorst, 2020 ). Similarly, the growth of bacteria is vital for improving the bacterial concentration through supplemental growth media such as oxygen (Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). The oxygen is injected into the system for such cases where there is a requirement for an excess biomass concentration compared to the prevailing concentration (B). However, multiple bacterial injection cycles also intensifies attached bacterial concentration due to excess biomass presence (Martinez et al., 2013 ). On the other hand, the urea hydrolysis rate depends on urea and attached biomass concentration (Lauchnor et al., 2015 ), driving the reaction towards the precipitation of calcium carbonate (C). As well, the injected oxygen concentration decays due to suspended and attached bacterial growth in the media (Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). In contrast, during the injection of CO2 , a two-phase fluid flow (H) occurs with the development of capillary pressures between the fluids (Ebigbo et al., 2007 ). The capillary pressures are developed inside the pore spaces upon injection of CO2  into the fully saturated geological media. Also, the buoyancy forces accommodate the CO2  plume movement towards the top surface, as the injected fluid is lighter than water (Celia et al., 2015 ). Therefore, gas migration occurs due to the combined influence of the interactions between capillary pressure and buoyancy forces (Fig. 2  ). Overall, bio-chemo-hydraulics (BCH) governs the MICP treatment process and two-phase flow hydraulics (H) govern the CO2 -water interfacial flow.  2.2 Assumptions The present study assumes two-phase fluid flow occurs within the geological media when the CO2  is injected into the aquifer (Ebigbo et al., 2007 ). However, all the MICP injections were performed in the water saturated media (i.e., deep saline aquifer). Accordingly, the biochemicals (i.e., bacteria and chemicals) were suspended in the solvent (i.e., brine) by matching the salinity of the deep saline aquifer and injected into the domain to avoid disturbing the aquifer's natural chemistry and maintain ecological balance. Also, halophilic and the most widely used Sporosarcina pastuerri  was adopted as the bacterial strain can survive in a saline environment (Dikshit et al., 2022 ). The urease activity remains unaffected as the present study considers the brine concentration to be 3.9 % w/w (< 5% w/w as per Dikshit et al., 2022 ). In addition, the bacteria are assumed to survive with the total capacity of urea hydrolysis under the aquifer's pH (Lauchnor et al., 2015 ), pressure (Mitchell et al., 2013 ; Verba et al., 2016 ), encapsulation (Bhukya et al., 2023b ) and temperature conditions (Xiao et al., 2021 ) for computational simplification and rigorous optimisation. In contrast, the CO2  is only injected after the MICP treatment (Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). As the CO2  gas phase is abscent during MICP injections, hence it is assumed not to influence the biomass or the biochemical reaction. The density and viscosity of the fluids were unaltered during all the injection stages (during MICP and CO2  injections). The present work does not consider the solid deformation due to geostatic stresses and their influence on the pore water pressure. All the solid constituents during transport (i.e., solid grains, CaCO3 , and attached bacteria) were assumed incompressible, and their diffusion and dispersion were negligible (Fauriel and Laloui, 2012 ). The mass of precipitated calcium carbonate gets accumulated on the soil solid media; therefore, the calcite will not be present in the fluid (Wang and Nackenhorst, 2020 ). The storage of CO2  inside the aquifer is primarily governed by hydrodynamic and capillary trapping (Celia et al., 2015 ), whereas dissolution and mineral trapping were assumed to be insignificant in the considered time frame. Also, the dissolution of precipitated calcite due to acidic conditions of CO2  injection was assumed to not occur in the time frame considered for the study (Renard et al., 2005 ). Isothermal conditions were considered in the aquifer during all the fluid injections. It is assumed that the caprock has a discontinuity (i.e., an abandoned well), which serves as a leakage path and is assumed to have a higher permeability than the storage aquifer (Pavan et al., 2024 ). Moreover, for the determination of relative permeabilities and capillary pressures, the Brooks-Corey model was adopted (Brooks and Corey, 1966 ). First-order urea hydrolysis rate (Michaelis-Menten kinetics), attachment rate (Constant rate), decay rate (Constant rate), and growth rate (Monod kinetics) were considered for the reaction kinetics (Bhukya et al., 2023b ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). The detachment rate was assumed to follow a nonlinear power law with the water pressure gradient (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ). The attachment of chemicals was considered to be insignificant compared to the reaction rate (Wang et al., 2024 ). Usually, in a calcium-rich environment, the precipitation rate of calcium carbonate is the same as that of the urea hydrolysis rate (van Paassen, 2009 ; Qin et al., 2016 ; Hommel et al., 2016 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). Past researchers have considered a similar assumption with identical ureolysis and precipitation rates and obtained reasonable calcite profiles in their validations of modelling works (Mehrabi and Atefi-Monfared, 2022 ; Ramos and Kwon, 2023 ; Bhukya et al., 2023b ; Wang et al., 2024 ). Therefore, the precipitation rate was assumed to be the same as the urea hydrolysis rate (Bhukya et al., 2023b ). The study considers whole-cell kinetics instead of biofilm kinetics; therefore, the attached microbes were represented as attached bacteria instead of biofilm (Wang and Nackenhorst, 2020 ). Besides, as the contribution of porosity reduction from biofilm formation is very small compared to the calcite volume fractions (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ), the study's assumption of attached biomass instead of biofilm provides computational viability. The nonlinear power law governs the reduction in the permeability due to biocementation (Thullner et al. 2002 ). Darcy's law governs advective flow, as the fluid flow is assumed laminar (i.e., Reynold's number, Re  < 1), and Fick's law controls the diffusion.   3 Numerical model development The present study modified the mathematical framework adopted in Bhukya et al. (2023b)  to simulate other vital processes for field-scale studies, such as growth, detachment and velocity-dependent attachment. The governing and constitutive equations were formulated to simulate MICP treatment to seal the leaky aquifer's near- and far-field leakage paths (Bhukya et al., 2023b ; Mehrabi and Atefi-Monfared, 2022 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). To explore the performance of deep saline aquifer for storing CO2  after treating the aquifer with MICP, the present study developed a coupled BCH model and employed the finite element method for solution. The processes described in the coupled processes section were represented using the governing balance equations and supplemented with constitutive equations. The aquifer is a sedimentary porous media holding saline water and CO2  in the pores; however, based on the injection type (i.e., CO2  or constituents of MICP), the number of fluid phases in the system was altered. Biochemical component mass balance equations were formulated in the current section to evaluate the concentration of biochemical species using the advective-diffusive-dispersive-reactive transport equations. Mass conservation equations of the two-phase fluids were adopted to understand the two-phase fluid flow characteristics in the aquifer domain. A detailed description of the mass balance and constitutive relations is given below. 3.1 Balance equations The governing partial differential equations for two-phase fluid flow through the porous domain are obtained from the mass conservation of immiscible fluid phases, α (i.e., for water: α = w and gas: α = g). The governing equations are formulated as the advection phenomenon as the dominant flow process (Eq. (2) ).(2) − ∂ ( ϕ ρ α  s α  )   ∂ t   = ∇ ( ρ α  u α  )         where ϕ  is the porosity of the geomaterial (-), ρ α  is the density of fluid phase α (kg·m−3 ), s α  is the fluid saturation of phase α (-), u α  is Darcy's flux of fluid phase α (m·s−1 ). However, considering the water-saturated domain, the MICP treatment was performed under single fluid phase conditions (i.e., water, α = w ). The spatiotemporal distribution of the suspended species in the water, i.e., urea, ammonium, oxygen, and suspended bacteria, is described using the mass balance of respective aqueous components. The flow and transport processes considered for the mass balance of these suspended components include advection, diffusion, dispersion and reaction. Therefore, the changes in concentration of aqueous chemical components such as urea (u), calcium (Ca2+ ) and ammonium ions (NH4 + ) are governed by the mentioned processes (Eqs. (3)  and (4) ). The coefficients to the reaction terms are accommodated from the chemical stoichiometric coefficients provided in Eq. (1) . However, the stochiometric coefficient of calcium ion concentration resembles urea; therefore, calcium ion concentration was not explicitly evaluated as C Ca2+   will be equal to C u . Also, as a part of the reaction in the MICP process, the urea concentration (C u ) was altered due to the utilisation of urea during the hydrolysis via enzymes and was accommodated using biochemical reaction rate (-K react ) in Eq. (3) . Similarly, hydrolysis of urea releases ammonium during the reaction, increasing concentration of ammonium (C NH4 +  ), captured using (+2K react ) in Eq. (4) . Regardless, the spatial-temporal distribution of the growth component (i.e., oxygen) was assessed following an additional growth process in addition to conventional transport mechanisms. The oxygen concentration (C o ) reduces as the suspended microbes and attached microbes consume the available oxygen for growth (Eq. (5) ). Furthermore, the concentration of suspended microbial concentration (B f ) is formulated mainly by considering the above-mentioned conventional transport processes but also with several mechanisms of bacterial kinetics included in the reaction term (Eq. (6) ). As a part of reactive source terms, the suspended microbial concentration increases as the microbes consume oxygen (+K growth ). Further, the detachment of attached microbes from a solid surface into the water due to interface shear force is represented using (+K detach ) term. The concentration of suspended bacteria is reduced as the microbes decay (K decay ). Also, due to the attachment of bacteria from the suspended state onto the solid surface, the concentration of suspended bacteria reduces (–K attach ). All the bacterial reaction terms are represented as source/sink terms in Eq. (6) . Typically, the general form of mass balance equation of suspended species in the fluid-saturated geomaterial possesses the structure of Eq. A1 . It can be observed that, the porosity terms have to be inside the time and spatial derivatives for all the transport equations. However, the rate of change of porosity with time (∂ϕ /∂t ) can be evaluated from the fluid phase mass balance equation under complete saturation (Eq. (A2) ), and the component transport equation could be further simplified. After substituting the porosity change terms in the component balance equation and rearranging, the final equations were obtained. The porosity of geological media reduces with a progression in calcium carbonate precipitation (Eq. (9) ). Although the biofilms form for more extended injection periods of microbes during the biocementation process, the present study disregarded the biofilm formation for porosity/ permeability alteration. This is because biofilm fractions are very small compared to calcite volume fractions, as evident from past modelling works (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ), where biofilm volume fractions are in the order of 1 × 10−4  to 1 × 10−2 , whereas the calcite volume fractions are 0.01 to 0.1.(9) ∂ ϕ  ∂ t   = − ∂ ϕ c   ∂ t       where ϕ c  is the fraction of calcite in total void volume (= S c ·(1- ϕ )/ϕ ) and S c  is the calcite volume fraction over total solid volume (= m c ·C c / ρ c ).  3.2 Constitutive relations Additional supplemental relationships are necessary to solve the fluid flow and transport equations. Accordingly, the hydraulic constitutive equations and biochemical reaction rates make the balance equations solvable. The current section discusses the relevant supplementary relations for solving the bio-chemo-hydraulic problem. 3.2.1 Hydraulic constitutive equations Darcy's law accompanies the advective flow in the porous domain. Accordingly, the current study adopted a velocity-dependent attachment rate (K attach ) for assessing bacterial attachment by correcting the constant attachment rate (k att ) of biomass (Eq. (19) ). The velocity-dependent factor (V att ) is evaluated based on lower (v l ) and upper (v u ) limits of velocities (Minto et al., 2019 ). If the magnitude of seepage velocity (|vf  |) is lower than the lower velocity limit, complete attachment of bacteria occurs (i.e., V att  = 1), and if greater than the upper-velocity limit, zero attachment occurs (V att  = 0). The velocity dependence factor is interpolated if the velocity is between lower and upper limits (Mehrabi and Atefi-Monfared, 2022 ). The velocity dependence is an essential mechanism that simulates the zero attachment near the injection source due to the higher flow velocity, representing reality.(19) K attach  = V att  k att       Similarly, microbes can be detached from the solid surface and put into the water due to shear forces exerted on the surface of the solid during fluid flow. The present study considers the detachment rate (K detach ) as a proportional function to the pressure gradient of fluid flow with a power law (Ebigbo et al., 2012 ; Landa-Marban et al., 2021 ). The urea hydrolysis rate is the most essential component of biochemical reaction kinetics (K react ). The utilisation rate of urea in the MICP process is evaluated using the Michaelis-Menten equation (Eq. (23) ). Besides, the present study assumes the urea utilisation rate to be the same as the precipitation rate. Because in a calcium-rich environment, the precipitation rate of calcium carbonate is identical to the urea hydrolysis rate (van Paassen, 2009 ; Qin et al., 2016 ; Hommel et al., 2016 ; Landa-Marbán et al., 2021 ). (2007)  with the Brooks-Corey capillary pressure relationship. The geometry and boundary conditions containing the aquifers and leakage path were acquired for model verification. However, simplifications were performed to the three-dimensional geometry of Ebigbo et al. (2007)  by considering a two-dimensional cross-section to reduce the computations for the considered case. Accordingly, to reflect the reduced dimensionality, the injection flow rate of Ebigbo et al. (2007)  was adjusted to maintain mass balance and represent the flow process realistically. The leakage path in the caprock stands 100 m in height and 0.3 m in diameter, representing an abandoned well. Two deep saline aquifers of 30 m thickness and 1000 m long are separated by an aquitard (i.e., caprock) with a preexisting leakage path (i.e., abandoned well). The CO2  was injected into the bottommost saline aquifer for 1200 days to observe the leakage rates along the abandoned well. Additional details about model parameters can be found in Ebigbo et al. (2007) . A non-dimensionalised leakage rate, q * (i.e., the ratio of leakage rate to injection rate, q leak /qg  ), was evaluated to verify the leakage from the abandoned well during CO2  injection. The obtained observations from the present study have shown good agreement with the normalised leakage rates of the numerical solution obtained by Ebigbo et al. (2007) , as depicted in Fig. 3  a. However, the minor differences in the comparison between present study and Ebigbo et al. (2007)  is attributed to the differences in the governing equations (black oil model vs. compositional model), utilised numerical method for solution (finite element vs. finite volume) and simplification of geometry (three dimensions to two). But, overall, the developed model reasonably captured the non-dimensionalised leakage rates. Therefore, the present modelling framework with a two-phase flow module in two dimensions was further employed to predict the CO2  migration in the aquifer and leakage through the abandoned wells before and after MICP treatment.  3.3.2 MICP treatment validation The present numerical model was validated before its employment to simulate MICP treatment in the leaky aquifer with the experimental observations of calcium carbonate reported by Whiffin et al. (2007) . However, as discussed in the previous section, the current modelling framework has been modified after the Bhukya et al. (2023b)  framework by accommodating two-phase fluid flow and bacterial growth due to oxygen. Therefore, the developed model was validated for the limit case of single-phase flow (i.e., water saturated flow) and the absence of oxygen (i.e., no biomass growth) in the soil column. Besides, assuming the single-phase flow and no biomass growth is appropriate as they represent the laboratory conditions (Wang and Nackenhorst, 2020 ). A two-dimensional long soil column of 5 m (Height) × 0.06 m (Diameter) was considered for the simulation to validate the model. The geometry and boundary conditions were adopted from our past study (Bhukya et al., 2023b ). The numerical observations agreed reasonably well with the experimental calcite profile reported by Whiffin et al. (2007) , as shown in Fig. 3 b. Therefore, the developed model was further employed to biocement the abandoned well using MICP injections through a series of cases for optimisation of the treatment process to seal the leakage path.    4 Optimisation methodology As discussed in Section 2 , the bacteria accumulated on the solid grains significantly impact the urea hydrolysis rate, affecting calcite precipitation. The bacterial population must be enhanced via attachment or growth to achieve the required concentration of attached bacteria at the zone of interest. Accordingly, there are two ways to accumulate the desired biomass after initial biomass injection (1. Oxygen injection and 2. Multiple bacterial injection). Among them, the oxygen injection (OI) initiates the growth of bacteria, whereas the multiple bacterial injection (BI) additionally attaches the incoming bacteria at the target region. In addition to the bacterial and oxygen injections, the water must be injected (WI) to transport the front to the target distance (d ), where the retention of bacteria is initiated for attachment (BR) and growth (OR). Similarly, after the bacterial accumulation phase, the chemicals are injected (CI) for the reaction phase, followed by water injection (WI) for transport and chemical retention (CR) for the reaction. The water injection is a crucial step; otherwise, injecting biochemicals without water injection has severe implications, such as injection point clogging and a rise in application costs. Accordingly, the present study proposes optimisation methodology for the injections (i.e., bacteria injection-BI, oxygen injection-OI, chemical injection-CI, water injection-WI) and retention (bacterial retention-BR, oxygen retention-OR, chemical retention-CR) durations based on the target distance (d ) for MICP treatment. The larger-scale biocementation treatment can be broadly categorised based on the treatment's target distance (d ). The target distance less than the critical distance (d crit ) is termed the near-field domain, and the target distance greater than d crit  is the far-field domain. The necessary distance is evaluated based on the critical time (t crit ) and injection seepage velocity (v s ). However, it is essential to note that the oxygen injection is recommended for near-field injection scenarios (i.e., d  < d crit ). In contrast, multiple bacterial injection cycles are recommended for MICP treatment at far-field distances (i.e., d  > d crit ). The reasoning behind the mentioned conditions is discussed in the upcoming section (Section 6.3.1 ). Accordingly, as a part of the bacterial accumulation phase, for near-field cases, the sequence of injections and retention follows BI, WI:1, BR, OI, WI:2, OR, for a single cycle. In contrast, for far-field MICP treatment, the sequence is followed as BI, WI:1, and BR for multiple cycles of N. After biomass accumulation, if the average leakage path attached biomass concentration (B s ) reaches the B s-target , the optimisation of the reaction phase is initiated; otherwise, the injection concentrations must be revised. Consequently, upon reaching the target attached biomass concentration, chemicals (CI) and water (WI) are injected to reach the target region. Following the water injection, the retention phase (CR) is initiated for the biochemical reaction to precipitate calcium carbonate at the target region. Thus, the reaction phase for near-field injections follows the sequence of CI, WI:3, and CR, whereas the far-field injections follow CI, WI:2, and CR for multiple M and P injection cycles, respectively. Once the leakage path permeability (k leak ) becomes lower than or equal to the target permeability (k target ), the reaction phase is ended at that particular chemical injection cycle (Fig. 4  ). Nevertheless, there is an optimisation step for both the bacterial accumulation phase and reaction phase to decide the optimised duration of injections and retentions. Initially, the optimisation for injection and retention durations is performed to get the desired attached bacterial concentration (B s-target ) for the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) and target leakage path permeability (k leak ) for the reaction phase (Phase II). Optimisation of injection durations was initiated by calculating the injection seepage velocity (v s  = q bc /ϕ ) with biochemical injection velocity (q bc ) and porosity (ϕ ), thereby evaluating the critical distance (d crit  = v s ·t crit ) and average transport time (t a  = d /v s ). The study assumed a critical injection time (t crit ) of 250 h (∼ 10 d). The injection duration of a biochemical species beyond t crit  is assumed to be far-field injections relative to the injection velocity (q bc ). Consequently, the biochemical injection velocity is an important parameter that decides such a classification and must be considered carefully by also avoiding particle misarrangement and overpressurisation at the injection source (Martinez et al., 2013 ; Faeli et al., 2023 a ,b ; Cuthbert et al., 2013 ). If the condition is near-field (d  < d crit ), the minimum and maximum bacterial injection duration is evaluated as per the workflow proposed in Fig. 5  . It has to be noted that if the average transport time (t a ) is less than 150 h and greater than 60 h, the minimum BI time (t BImin ) must be reduced by a duration of 50 h to avoid zero or negative injection times that could be inefficient for optimisation. If not (i.e., t a  > 150 h), a reduction of 100 h could be employed so that the minimum bacterial injection duration (t BImin ) cannot cross 50 h. Similarly, the maximum injection duration (t BImax ) is specified with an additional 100 h to the average transport time (t a ). Likewise, the oxygen (OI) and chemical injections (CI) are followed with the same maximum (t OImax , t CImax ) and minimum (t OImin , t CImin ) values as their limits, as only the component inside the water has changed while the flow characteristics remain the same. Meanwhile, water injections are performed at half of the maximum and minimum bacterial injection duration limits, which restricts the dilution effects to 50 % so that biochemicals are not excessively diluted and injection point accumulation can be avoided (i.e., t WI- 1 min  = t WI- 2 min  = t WI- 3 min  = t BImin /2 and t WI-1max  = t WI-2max  = t WI-3max  = t BImax /2). Furthermore, the minimum retention duration is considered the maximum bacterial injection time (i.e., t BRmin  = t OImin  = t CImin  = t BImax ), and the maximum retention duration is limited to t Rmax  (i.e., t BRmax  = t OImax  = t CImax  = t Rmax ). This is because the retention phase has always had a positive influence on attachment (BR), growth (OR) and reaction (CR). Therefore, its minimum value should at least be equivalent to the maximum injection duration (t BImax /t OImax /t CImax ). However, the maximum value should not exceed the maximum retention time (t Rmax ), which can be fixed based on the possible cost-effective idle time without injections. Similar limits apply to far-field injections, except that an oxygen injection cycle is absent, and multiple bacterial injections are recommended to avoid injection point clogging during the reaction phase (Fig. 5 ). In order to understand the relative scaling of all durations of injection and retention, a relative scale is indicated for near and far-field scenarios which vary from 0 to t Rmax  in Fig. 5 . After evaluating the minimum and maximum limits for the respective cases (near-field and far-field), the design of experiments (DOE) approach with response surface optimisation procedure is followed. The response optimisation method (RSM) is a second-order regression model that provides the quadratic dependence of continuous factors on the response variable (Kakelar et al., 2016 ). In the case of the near-field bacterial accumulation phase, six continuous factors (t 1 , t 2 , t 3 , t 4 , t 5 , t 6 ) need to be considered with a single injection cycle optimisation (Fig. 8 ). In contrast, four continuous factors (t 1 , t 2 , t 3 , N) must be considered with the optimisation of multiple injection cycles (N) for the far-field scenario (Fig. 8 ). A central composite design (CCD) method with a two-level full factorial through added centre points is adopted to generate the response surface design for both scenarios in MINITAB software. The CCD design matrix generates 53 sets of continuous parameters for the near-field and 31 sets of continuous parameters for far-field scenarios. In the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I), the attached biomass concentration (B s ) in the leakage path is the response variable that must be evaluated for each set of parameters before optimising the durations of injection and retention. Later, the response optimisation is used to determine the continuous factors that provide a target biomass concentration (B s-target ) in the bacterial accumulation phase and is consequently used for the reaction phase (Phase II). If the target biomass concentration (B s-target ) is not achieved even after optimisation, one must revise the injection concentrations accordingly (Fig. 4 ). Once the target biomass concentration (B s-target ) is achieved, the chemical injections are optimised with four continuous factors (Near-field: t 7 , t 8 , t 9 , C 0 ; Far-field: t 4 , t 5 , t 6 , C 0 ) through response surface optimisation for one chemical injection cycle (Fig. 8 ). One injection cycle alone is sufficient for optimisation as it is intuitive that a single injection could provide information about the need for multiple injections. Accordingly, the central composite method is adopted to generate the response surface design matrix with 31 sets of continuous variables for near and far-field scenarios. The leakage path permeability is considered a response variable and evaluated for each set of continuous factors. After optimisation, the response optimiser is utilised to assess the injection and retention durations that could provide the leak permeability (k leak ) of the minimum value possible within the maximum and minimum time limits provided. If the optimised permeability exceeds the target value (k target ), one must go for multiple chemical injection cycles of M,  P for near-field and far-field scenarios, respectively. Otherwise, if the target permeability is achieved within one injection cycle, the optimisation is achieved, and the algorithm can be stopped (Fig. 4 ).  5 Numerical strategy The numerical simulations of the present study were performed in finite element-based software COMSOL multiphysics by selecting the inbuilt modules of multi-phase flow in porous media and transport of diluted species in porous media. However, the fluid type for injections (single-phase or two-phase) was chosen based on the treatment category (i.e., MICP or CO2  injections). Later, a two-dimensional geometry of two deep saline aquifers connected by the leakage path (Fig. 7 ) was discretised with four noded quadrilateral (Q4 ) elements in an unstructured manner to ensure adaptability to the geometry. The mesh was chosen with a finer average element size, observed to have a mesh size of 2 m in the aquifer region and a minimum element size of 0.15 m near the connecting portion of the leakage path with the aquifer. Besides, the bio-chemo-hydraulic model parameters were accommodated to understand the coupled processes using numerical modelling. The framed BCH system was solved in a monolithic approach with the Petrov-Galerkin finite element method's streamline and crosswind diffusion variants (Hauke and Hughes, 1998 ; Codina, 1998 ). These variants are essential to avoid numerical instabilities due to the high advective-reactive nature of biochemical transport (i.e., high Péclet and Damköhler numbers) in the considered problem. Furthermore, the primary variables solved during MICP treatment are pore pressure (p w ), biochemical concentrations (B s , B f , C u , C NH4 +  , C o , C c ) and porosity (ϕ ). The primary variables were evaluated at the current timestep (k) to reach the convergence criteria in the backward differentiation formula (BDF) implicit solver. Also, an adaptive time stepping was considered to maintain the accuracy of the primary variables. Upon convergence, the secondary variables of permeability and biochemical reaction parameters (k, K attach , K growth , K detach , K react ) were updated with the solutions of primary variables from the previous time step (k-1), as shown in Fig. 6  . Once the simulation reached the last time step (end), the pore pressure, porosity and permeability were updated for the two-phase flow module to solve the primary variables of pore pressures (p α ) and saturations (s α ) of each fluid phase α (i.e., water and CO2 ). If the non-dimensional CO2  gas leakage rate (q *) is zero, the results are analysed; otherwise, the optimisation is repeated to achieve enhanced target-attached bacterial concentration (B s-target ) and desired k leak  by adjusting injection velocity (q bc ) and the number of injection cycles (N,  M,  P) to seal the leakage path (Figs. 4 , and 6 ).  6 Biochemical injection strategies for minimising CO2  gas leakage The biochemical injections must be framed to yield maximum calcite precipitation inside the leakage path. Accordingly, the current study utilises the optimisation algorithm proposed in the earlier section (Section 4 ) to evaluate the best possible solution for injection and retention periods that can achieve the target requirements (B s-target , k leak ). The MICP process has numerous variables (i.e., injection and retention duration, biochemical injection concentrations, flow rate) that must be optimised to achieve targeted permeability change at the desired location. However, keeping the injection flow velocity constant (i.e., for a particular injection velocity), the duration of injection, retention and biochemical injection concentration must be optimised in case there is a need to seal the target region some distance from the injection source. Accordingly, with the injection velocity (q bc ), the cases considered (20 m: near-field and 100 m: far-field) are set up based on alterations in injection and retention duration to achieve the desired attached bacterial concentration in the target region (B s-target ); thereby, the reduction in porosity near the leakage path follows. However, based on the outcomes of the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) in these cases, the optimised duration of bacteria, water, oxygen, and retentions are fixed in the upcoming chemical injection phase (Phase II) optimisation. The model domain, boundary conditions and results of the present study are discussed in detail in the current section. The model domain consists of two deep saline aquifers of 30 m thickness and 500 m long, situated approximately 1800 m below the groundwater table. The saline aquifers are connected by an abandoned well of 0.3 m diameter and 100 m height, which functions as a leakage path (Fig. 7  ). Although the geometry is two-dimensional, the study has assumed a unit thickness in the out-of-plane direction (i.e., 1 m) and the height of the aquifer (30 m) to modify the injection flow rates to mass flow rates appropriately (q bc  and q g ). The abandoned well is situated in an aquitard (i.e., caprock) and originates nearly at a d  distance from the left boundary (i.e., injection boundary). The entire domain length of the aquitard, except the leakage path and left portion of the top saline aquifer, is not considered to simplify the geometry of the problem and the subsequent computations (Fig. 7 ). The study is conducted in two stages covering biochemical injections (Stage 1) and subsequent CO2  injection (Stage 2). Initially, the developed MICP model under single-phase simplification was employed to evaluate the optimised injection duration using response surface optimisation in Stage 1. Later, the CO2  leakage rates from the sealed abandoned wells in the aquifer were assessed using the two-phase flow module in Stage 2. However, the model geometry for all the stages conducted remains the same as the CO2  gas and biochemicals (i.e., bacteria, oxygen, urea and calcium) are injected into the same domain. However, the sequence of biochemical injections is based on the injection strategy attained from the proposed optimisation methodology for the respective cases (Near-field vs Far-field), as discussed in Section 4 . 6.1 Injection strategy The present study fixed the flow rate based on the commonly used value in the experimentation of MICP as well as in the field to avoid particle misarrangement and over-pressurisation at the injection source (Martinez et al., 2013 ; Faeli et al., 2023 a ,b ; Cuthbert et al., 2013 ; Ebigbo et al., 2010 ). Therefore, the study considered a flow velocity of 1 × 10−5  m·s-1  (flow rate ∼ 3 × 10−4  m3 ·s-1 ). Besides, if the injection velocity is higher, the critical distance (d crit ) increases. However, the over-pressurisation of the aquifer is also possible. On the other hand, if the injection velocity is very low, the injection duration drastically increases, making it a far-field scenario and uneconomical. Therefore, such scenarios must be handled before the injection velocity is decided. Although the procedure was developed for the CO2  geosequestration application, this kind of division also applies to other field MICP applications. Based on the flow velocity, the classification of both cases was based on the d crit  value of ∼ 50 m obtained using a critical injection time of 250 h (∼ 10 d). Accordingly, two different leakage path distances (i.e., d  = 20 m: Near-field; d  = 100 m: Far-field) were considered for the current problem. Thus, the average transport time (t a ) of near-field and far-field domains are obtained as 110 h and 550 h for the respective cases. Also, the present study considers a value of 1000 h of maximum retention time (i.e., ∼ 42 d). Following this, the response surface design (Tables S1, and S3 ) is generated as per the methodology proposed in Section 4  using minimum and maximum duration values generated in Table 1  . The response surface optimisation of the near-field scenario generated 53 trials (6 time variables - t 1  (BI), t 2  (WI:1), t 3  (BR), t 4  (OI), t 5  (WI:2), t 6  (OR)) for the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) as shown in Table S1  and the optimised solution from those trials were utilised for the subsequent 31 trials (3 - time variables - t 7  (CI), t 8  (WI:3), t 9  (CR) and one injection concentration variable - C 0 ) for the reaction phase in Phase II as shown in Table S2  and Fig. 8  a. The superscript of t 7  (CI), t 8  (WI:3), t 9  (CR) with I, II, III represent chemical injection cycles until a maximum of M cycles. Similarly, for the far-field case, the response optimisation generated 31 trials (3 - time variables - t 1  (BI), t 2  (WI:1), t 3  (BR) and one injection cycles variable - N) for bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) as shown in Table S3 . The subsequent optimised variables from the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) were utilised for 31 trials (3 time variables - t 4  (CI), t 5  (WI:3), t 6  (CR) and one injection concentration variable- C 0 ) of the reaction phase in Phase II as shown in Table S4  and Fig. 8 b. The superscript of t 1  (BI), t 2  (WI:1), t 3  (BR), t 4 (CI), t 5  (WI:3), t 6  (CR) with I, II, III represent number of bacterial and chemical injection cycles until a maximum of N and P cycles, respectively. The present study considers a B s-target  of 2 OD and k leak  of 1 × 10−16  m2  as a criterion for the optimisation. The target biomass concentration was fixed as per the maximum concentration available in the literature (Fauriel and Laloui, 2012 ; Whiffin et al., 2007 ). The target permeability was fixed as per the preliminary investigation conducted in the present study to achieve zero CO2  leakage for a particular leak permeability.  6.2 Boundary conditions Two aquifers connected with the leakage path were considered to have 18 MPa of initial pore water pressure (p 0 ) and zero initial biochemical concentrations (B f  = 0, C NH4 +   = 0, C u  = 0 and C o  = 0). Also, the right boundaries of saline aquifers (Γright ) were always maintained at initial water pressure (p  = p 0 ) and natural mass flux of the suspended biochemical component i  (i.e., Di   (ϕ ∇C i   )·n  = 0) during CO2  gas and biochemical injections. All the remaining boundaries were maintained at no fluid flux (q w ·n  = 0 and q g ·n  = 0) and natural mass flux (Di   (ϕ ∇C i   )·n  = 0). Moreover, entire injections (CO2  gas, water and biochemicals) were performed from the injection source (Γleft ) located on the bottom left boundary of aquifer 1, represented as a line injection source with aquifer thickness (Fig. 7 , Table 2  ). In Stage 1, the bacteria were injected at a concentration of B 0 , oxygen was injected at the concentration of O 0 , chemicals are injected at the concentration of C 0,  and water was injected at zero concentration of biochemicals (B 0  = 0, O 0  = 0 and C 0  = 0) for both the cases (near-field and far-field). All the biochemicals (B f , C o , C u , C NH4 +  ) and water injections were performed with q bc  injection velocity. The sequence and durations of injections for optimisation are discussed in the earlier section (Section 6.1 ). In Stage 2, the CO2  gas was injected from the left boundary from the line source at a flow rate of q c . The injection of CO2  was performed for 1200 days to compare plume lengths and leakage rates for near-field and far-field cases. As the MICP treatment alters the aquifer's hydraulic parameters, the porosity, permeability and pore pressures obtained at the end of Stage 1 for the concerned cases were given as initial values before starting the simulations of Stage 2 (Fig. 6 ). Besides, the plume length of CO2  was not able to cross the length of the aquifers (i.e., 500 m) within 1200 d of injection. Hence, the injection duration of 1200 d was a reasonable choice for comparison. However, as biochemicals were absent for the entire duration of the CO2  injection, simulating only the two-phase fluid flow conditions in the aquifer without any biochemical transport is a reasonable choice to reduce the computational cost. The boundary conditions of Stages 1 and 2 are clearly described in Table 2 . All the input model parameters and injection boundary conditions considered for the simulated studies are reported in Table 3  . However, chemical injection concentration (C 0 ) was evaluated as a part of the optimisation of the reaction phase (Phase II); therefore, the optimised value of C 0  (kmol·m−3 ) was reported in the results and discussion section (Section 6.3 , Table 5 ).  6.3 Results and discussion 6.3.1 Scenario analysis for optimising leakage path attached biomass (stage 1: phase I) The scenario analysis using the DOE with response surface optimisation in Phase I indicated that the BI duration (t 1 ) substantially affects the leakage path attached biomass concentration for near and far-field scenarios. Following that, for the near-field scenario, OI duration (t 4 ) has a reasonable influence on the attached biomass concentration. However, along with BI duration (t 1 ), the number of bacterial injection cycles (N) substantially influenced the attached biomass concentration for far-field injections. After analysing the response surface (Tables S1, S3 ), to achieve the attached biomass concentration of 2 OD, the following optimised durations of the bacterial accumulation phase obtained in Table 4   must be employed. It was observed that to attain approximately 2 OD of attached biomass concentration within the leakage path, a single injection cycle of bacteria and oxygen was sufficient for the near-field scenario. Meanwhile, the far-field distance case needed three bacterial injection cycles (N = 3) as per the response optimisation. To understand the dynamics of the attached biomass distribution under near-field and far-field leak distances, the biomass profile was plotted along the length of the bottom aquifer (i.e., horizontal 200 m profile from injection source) and the leakage path height (i.e., 100 m). In the near-field scenario, the oxygen injection contributes towards the growth of the bacteria, enhancing the attached bacterial concentration in the domain of interest. The injection of oxygen accommodated the rise in attached biomass at the target zone reasonably along the horizontal profile. However, for the same near-field leak distance, the attached bacteria concentration peak in the bottom aquifer was higher for the multiple bacterial injections (2 cycles) case. Therefore, the bacterial accumulation became predominant in bottom aquifer compared to the case of utilisation of oxygen injection cycle (Fig. 9  a). Nevertheless, when observed within the leakage path, the attached bacterial concentration was higher for the case of oxygen injection after bacterial injection, indicating the efficacy of oxygen injection in the case of near-field scenario (Fig. 9 b). This is because of the transport characteristics of oxygen, where the oxygen was rapidly transported to the leakage path, leading to an excessive growth within the leak compared to the bottom aquifer region. Also, the fluid flow velocity will rise inside the leakage path as it is nearer to the injection source. Additionally, due to its reduced cross-sectional area, the attachment rate of bacteria gets lowered because of velocity dependency. Therefore, the biomass growth rate is predominant inside the near-field leak path compared to the attachment of biomass. However, oxygen injection was observed to be inefficient for far-field scenarios compared to near-field ones. Because when compared to multiple bacterial injections (2 cycles), the oxygen injection followed by bacterial injection has shown bi-modal peak formation in the horizontal profile (Fig. 9 a). The primary peak was formed near the injection point, and the secondary peak was at the target region. This indicates that when oxygen is injected, the bacteria near the injection source grow at a faster rate near the injection source and lowering the oxygen concentration at the target region (Fig. 9 a). This has a severe implication in the field application during chemical injection as the primary attached biomass peak near the injection source will lead to the formation of injection point clogging and chemicals could not be transported farther to seal far-field region. Nevertheless, multiple bacterial injection cycles (N = 2 cycles) indicated a reasonable distribution of attached biomass, providing the peak near the target region at the far-field. A similar observation was found within the leakage path that, compared to oxygen injection, multiple bacterial injection is effective in improving the attached bacteria inside the leakage path (Fig. 9 b). Here, the oxygen concentrations within the leakage path are much lower and so is the fluid velocity, therefore, the attachment rate of biomass is a dominant process at far-field locations. Thus, multiple injections of bacteria are preferred for far-field scenarios, as the attachment process accumulates the required biomass compared to growth. Overall, it is evident from the observations that bacterial injection followed by oxygen injection is preferred for near-field scenarios, and multiple bacterial injections are preferred for far-field scenarios. However, as per the optimised injections and retentions reported in Table 4 , one bacterial and oxygen injection cycle for the near-field scenario and three bacterial injection cycles (N = 3) were recommended for the far-field scenario from the response surface optimisation. The attached bacterial concentration profiles of optimised cases indicate that the higher biomass concentration along the horizontal profile was observed for far-field distance case where three continuous bacterial injection cycles were employed (Fig. 9 a). Similarly, the attached biomass concentration along the leakage path height was higher for far-field scenario compared near-field distance case. In the case of near-field distance, the bacteria accumulated higher at the bottom of the leakage path where the bottom aquifer was connected, and along the leakage path, the attached biomass concentration proportionally reduced, reaching approximately 1 OD at the top. However, for the far-field leak distance, as the flow velocity gets uniform at such greater distances, the biomass distribution within the leakage path was uniformly distributed (Fig. 9 b). Besides, the suspended bacteria for the near-field scenario were observed to drop after the oxygen injection cycle as biomass growth is predominant for attached biomass but not for suspended biomass. At the same time, the decay and attachment effects are higher for suspended bacteria, reducing their concentration. However, for the far-field scenario, the suspended bacterial concentration rises after each bacterial injection cycle due to the accumulation of excess bacteria in each injection cycle through transport (Fig. 10  ).  6.3.2 Scenario analysis for leakage path permeability (stage 1: phase II) After optimising the bacterial accumulation phase (Phase I) to achieve the desired attached bacterial concentration, the reaction phase with chemical injection duration and its concentration (C 0 ) were optimised using the response surface methodology in Phase II. It has been observed that, for near-field cases, chemical injection concentration (C 0 ) and water injection (WI) duration played a predominant role in altering the permeability within the leakage path. However, the duration of chemical injection (CI) and retention (CR) significantly influenced the precipitation amount for far-field scenarios. This indicates that the influential factors are different for both near and far-field cases that significantly affect the biochemical reaction, precipitating calcium carbonate and subsequent permeability reduction. Therefore, a unique approach for both scenarios will not work for efficiently employing the MICP for leak mitigation. The optimised chemical injection cycle durations and concentration from the response surface optimisation to achieve the leakage path's target permeability (i.e., k target  ∼ 1 × 10−16  m2 ) were evaluated and reported in Table 5  . Besides, a single injection cycle of chemicals (M = 1) with the optimised injection cycle durations (t 7 -t 9 ) and concentration (C 0 ) of 3.8 kmol·m−3  was observed to be sufficient for near-field cases to achieve the required target permeability of the leakage path. Hence, further injections of chemicals were not performed multiple times. But, in the far-field scenario, the optimised durations could not achieve the required permeability change in a single injection cycle. Consequently, multiple injections of chemicals were performed with optimised injection, retention durations (t 4 -t 6 ) and at an injection concentration (C 0 ) of 1.5 kmol·m−3 . Following that, the target permeability of the leak was achieved at five chemical injection cycles (P = 5). Within the chemical injection cycle, the calcium carbonate profiles along the horizontal profile of the aquifer indicated a sharp peak near the respective target distances of near-field and far-field cases (Fig. 11  a). The horizontal calcium carbonate profiles were relatively proportional to the attached biomass profiles obtained as a part of optimisation in the previous section (Fig. 9 a). This indicates that attached biomass profile eventually decided the calcite concentration and hence adopting the optimised injection strategies through the proposed methodology was successful in gaining these observations. Similar observations of calcium carbonate profiles were obtained within the leakage path proportionally following the attached bacterial profiles (Fig. 9 b). Inside the leakage path, the higher calcium carbonate concentration was obtained at the start of the leakage path where the bottom aquifer is connected and the calcite concentration gradually reduced towards the top where the top aquifer is connected. However, the leakage path calcite profile was uniformly reduced towards the top of the leakage path for the near-field case. In contrast, the far-field case has a sudden dipping trend of calcite and becomes zero after 20 m height (Fig. 11 b). This is because the transport rates of biochemicals far from the injection zone were lower and uniform. This leads to a uniform accumulation of bacteria and chemicals inside the aquifer (Fig. 11 a) and a minimal upward movement near the leakage path entry in the far-field scenario. Therefore, the calcite attained a peak distribution near the entry of the leakage path (Figs. 9 b, and 11 b). Although the attached biomass concentration inside the leakage path is significantly higher and uniform, as the reaction is dominant compared to advection velocity, the overall rate of attached biomass consumption due to the reaction was minimal. Hence, only 20% of the leakage path is biocemented within the five chemical injection cycles (Fig. 9 b). In addition to calcium carbonate concentration, the calcite saturation (S c ) was depicted in Fig. 11 , which followed a similar trend of calcite. Nevertheless, calcite saturation values specifically become helpful in modelling the mechanical behaviour of biocemented geomaterials. As biocementation progresses, the porosity and permeability of the aquifer and the leakage path reduce. The reduction in the porosity is proportional to the precipitation of the calcium carbonate. These alterations in the porosity cause a decrease in the permeability at a proportional rate with a cubic power law (Eq. (16) ). The altered leakage path properties (i.e., reduction in porosity and permeability) along the leakage path height were depicted below (Fig. 12  ). The maximum porosity reduction was observed almost equal along the horizontal profile for both near-field and far-field scenarios (Fig. 12 ), this is attributed due to similar range of calcium carbonate production (Fig. 11 a). However, the porosity did not cross the critical porosity in the bottom aquifer, thereby minimum permeability (k min ) was not acquired for both near-field and far-field scenarios. This is a sensible scenario to avoid clogging the aquifer; in a later stage, CO2  can be transported within the aquifer for greater distances. However, within the leakage path, the porosity reached a critical value (i.e., 0.1) for both cases for certain portions of leakage path height, leading to the development of minimum permeability of the leakage path (i.e., 1 × 10−20  m2 ), thereby completely sealing the leakage path and tackling the objective of the study. Nevertheless, to understand the spatial variation of porosity, the two-dimensional contours of altered porosity were depicted in Fig. 13  . The porosity change was observable till an extensive distance in the case of far-field scenario as the biochemicals were transported farther from the injection source to reach the target region (Fig. 13b) . However, the extent of reduced porosity region lowers as the target region decreases (i.e., near-field), as shown in Fig. 13 a. Also, for both near-field and far-field leak distance, the porosity reduction is not visible clearly in the top aquifer due to the number of injection cycles adopted for the transport of biochemicals could not transport them towards the end of the leakage path. Nevertheless, the present study is only focused on sealing the leakage path; therefore, transporting biochemicals to the top aquifer is not the scope of the present study. Moreover, it was observed that the injection point clogging was minimal in both near and far-field scenarios as the attached biomass is not accumulated at the injection source due to the detachment effects because of higher injection velocity near the injection zone (Fig. 13 ). Nevertheless, a heterogeneous distribution of porosity was observed near the regions connecting top aquifer and bottom aquifer. This is because MICP treatment led to a heterogeneous distribution of biochemicals forming a non-uniform biocement in the pore spaces of the aquifer and the leakage path (Fig. 13 ).  6.3.3 CO2 plume migration dynamics (Stage 2)  In Stage 2, the current study performed CO2  injection into the biocemented domain with the initial porosity, permeability and pore pressures updated from the previous stage (i.e., after biocementation). Besides, for comparison, the CO2  leakage through the leakage path was observed before and after the MICP treatment with two-dimensional contours of CO2  saturation plumes and estimated leakage rates from the leakage path. The saturation plumes of CO2  gas under near and far-field leakage scenarios are depicted in Fig. 14  . The plumes of CO2  gas for the untreated case transported to the top aquifer due to the leakage from the leakage path (Fig. 14 a.i, b.i). The plumes arrived at their respective leakage paths due to the buoyancy effects. The bottom aquifer's plume length was higher for the far-field scenario than the near-field leak distance. However, the length of the plume in the top aquifer (l 2 -d ) was higher for the near-field leak distance than the far-field leak distance. This indicates that the higher the leak distance from the injection source, the lower the leakage of CO2  to the top aquifer. However, for the MICP-treated domain, the leakage of CO2  to the top aquifer was diminished, proving the treatment's effectiveness for plugging the leakage paths for both near-field and far-field cases (Fig. 14 a.ii, b.ii). Regardless, the plumes of treated domains are locally heterogeneous near the leakage path due to the formation heterogeneity achieved during MICP treatment through the development of local heterogeneity in the porosity during MICP treatment (Fig. 13 ). This led to slowing down the plume but with a uniform front formation until the leakage path, after which buoyancy dominated the CO2  front movement. However, the plume length in the bottom aquifer was higher for the far-field scenario compared to the near-field scenario due to these heterogeneities in the system. It is observable from the saturation plumes that the near-field scenario has provided a greater resistance towards the flow compared to the far-field scenario, which is also evident from the permeability alteration depicted in Fig. 12 . All the details about the lengths of plumes and arrival times were reported in Table. 6  . Although a qualitative description was indicated above, quantitatively, the leakage rate from the paths was evaluated using a non-dimensionalised leakage rate (q *). The non-dimensionalised leakage rate is the ratio of leakage flux through the abandoned well (q leak ) to the CO2  gas injection flux rate (q g ). The non-dimensionalised leakage rates of various leak distances are depicted in Fig. 15  . Besides, the amount of CO2  that has been migrated to the top aquifer can be indirectly inference from the area under the curves indicated in Fig. 15 . As the distance of the leakage paths were different (d  = 20 and 100 m), the duration at which the leakage initiates (i.e., arrival times) are different for each leak distance (80 and 250 d). However, the peak non-dimensionalised leakage rate was observed to be higher for the near-field leak distance, which is also evident from the CO2  saturation plumes depicted in Fig. 14 . The observations signify that higher escape of CO2  to the top aquifer occurs in the near-field scenario and reduces with increase in leak distance. In addition, the leak rate observations signify that the biochemical injections to seal the leak at a higher distance require a significant duration of injections, water flushing and retention phases. This analogy was already more apparent in the previous sections where the biochemicals are injected into the domain. In addition, the leakage rates were evaluated after MICP treatment, and the leakage path permeability played a predominant role in improving the storage of the bottom deep saline aquifer. Besides, as discussed earlier, there was no leakage from both the leak distances of the geometry, and the non-dimensionalised leakage rate was negligible for both cases. Although the leakage path was only biocemented till the first 20 m in the far-field scenario, that was observed to be sufficient to leakproof the leakage path (Fig. 11 b). Also, compared to the cases without MICP treatment, the leakage rates of considered cases were insignificant. This shows that MICP treatment effectively sealed the leakage paths in near- and far-field scenarios.  6.3.4 Model limitations and future research directions The numerical model developed in the present study reliably simulated the coupled reactive transport for MICP treatment and two-phase fluid flow for CO2  migration. However, some simplifications were made in the constitutive relations of reactive transport in the current study. The urea hydrolysis rate was assumed to depend only on urea and attached biomass concentration. However, several factors (i.e., encapsulation, calcium ion concentration, temperature) influence the urea hydrolysis rate, thereby the precipitated calcium carbonate content. The calcium carbonate precipitated during biocementation could cover the attached biomass through encapsulation, thereby reducing the reaction rate (Cuthbert et al., 2013 ; Bhukya et al., 2023b ). Besides, it was observed in past studies that the concentration of calcium source injected along with urea has an inhibitory effect on the urease activity (Yi et al., 2021 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ). Also, temperature is another critical parameter that alters the urease activity if it is below or above an optimum temperature of 35 °C (Wang et al., 2024 ). Although these factors influence the reaction rate, the present study assumed simple ureolytic whole-cell kinetics proposed by Lauchnor et al. (2015)  for computational simplification due to the numerous simulations pertaining to the optimisation of MICP treatment. However, further studies can be performed to include the influence of the parameters mentioned above on the biocement content, thereby, the leakage rates. An empirical relation to include the effect of such influential parameters on urease activity was proposed by van Paassen (2009)  and can be incorporated to represent urease activity decay better. Also, the bacterial accumulation rate is influenced by the bacterial straining process (i.e., accumulation of bacteria in narrow pore throats) in addition to attachment. Therefore, the attachment rate model in the present study can be improved by including some sophisticated models, as specified in Bhukya et al. (2024) . Besides, the biocement precipitation during this reaction phase could be an essential addition to the mechanical performance of the aquifer in the target region (Bhukya et al., 2023b ), and it can tackle seismic events in light of induced seismicity. Therefore, improving the current model by incorporating a mechanics module can realistically represent the strength and stiffness alterations in the aquifer and leakage path. Although the prime goal of the present work is not to improve the strength, this becomes an obvious and relevant application. In the context of CO2  migration, the present model disregarded the dissolution process for the sake of computational simplification using black oil model-based governing equations. Biocement precipitated could be prone to dissolution due to the acidic conditions in the aquifer after CO2  injection (Xie et al., 2023 ). However, it has to be noted that the target distance for MICP treatment matters for the dissolution to occur. Because, for the case of a near-field scenario, the CO2  concentration would be significant near the injection source, resulting in the greater dissolution of biocement. Nevertheless, the dissolution characteristics for the far-field scenario will be minor compared to the near-field biocementation (Fig. 14 ). Besides, before the biocement inside the leakage path starts dissolving, the biocement in the aquifer must dissolve for active dissolution at the target. Therefore, the dissolution is a long-term process in MICP-treated leaky aquifers and needs to be understood thoroughly in future modelling studies. Further, the interaction of CO2  with the precipitated calcite enables the carbonation of the biocement, which in turn transforms the amorphous phases of biocement into more crystalline phases. Hence, CO2  injection results in both dissolution and recrystallisation of precipitated calcite simultaneously (Padmaraj and Arnepalli, 2021 ; Padmaraj et al., 2024 ). Moreover, compositional models with source terms capturing mass transfer between the fluids and dissolution kinetics can be employed to understand this dissolution process in the long term (Ebigbo et al., 2007 ). Also, modelling studies can be extended to employ MICP treatment under two-phase conditions for the scenarios with the leakage path detected far ahead of the injection. In addition, the present modelling study can be extended to understand the effectiveness of the MICP process for higher leak distances and to decide the treatment efficacy past 100 m leak distances.    7 Cost analysis The cost analysis was performed using an approximate cost evaluation method based on the duration of biochemical injections and the flow rate of injections. The cost of the raw materials required for the operation of MICP treatment and CO2  injections was considered for the analysis. However, only the material cost was considered during the estimation procedure, utilising the unit cost of materials (in USD) for one cubic meter of the volume injected. Accordingly, the cost estimation of the components of nutrient broth with urea (NB + U), urea, calcium chloride and oxygen for biochemical injections was considered. The cost of nutrient broth with urea was included because the accumulation of desired bacterial concentration is essential before injection (3 g/L of NB and 20 g/L of urea ∼ 445 USD/m3,  as per Kariminia et al., 2023 ). Besides, as oxygen was injected as a growth component for near-field scenarios, it was included in the cost assessment (∼ 0.12 USD/m3 ). However, the remaining components, urea (0.5 kmol·m−3  ∼ 6 USD/m3  as per Rahman et al., 2020 ) and calcium chloride (0.5 kmol·m−3  ∼ 11.1 USD/m3  as per Rahman et al., 2020 ) are essential for the reaction phase, therefore contained within the analysis. Besides, the CO2  fluid cost was considered part of the comparison for 1200 d of injection into the leaky aquifer (∼ 50 USD/tonne as per Holt et al., 2009). The cost of sealing a 20 m leak distance (i.e., near-field) was observed to be lower (∼ 0.12 M USD) compared to sealing a 100 m leak distance (i.e., far-field) from the injection source (∼ 0.95 M USD). This is apparent because the injection durations were much higher for the case of the far-field scenario obtained from the optimisation methodology. However, few data points were considered from the literature for comparison from Zeng et al. (2021)  and Ramos and Kwon (2023) . As the zone of influence was very minimal (∼ 1 m) in the modelling study of Ramos and Kwon (2023) , the cost estimated for MICP treatment was negligible. However, the field implementation of MICP for sealing a 2.5 m radius of influence by Zeng et al. (2021)  was estimated to have cost 0.12 M USD, equal to the treatment cost for a 20 m leak distance in the present study. Besides, the cost of acquiring CO2  for injecting 1200 d meant for near-field and far-field scenarios for the present study is approximately 0.04 M USD. Nevertheless, the cost analysis of the Landa-Marbán et al. (2021)  modelling study indicated a huge cost (∼ 246 M USD) pertaining to its very high urea concentration (5 kmol·m−3 ) and higher injection flow rate (5 × 10−3  m3 ·s−1 ) hence the data point was not included in Fig. 16 .  Comparatively, the optimised duration of injections obtained in the present study for sealing same 100 m leakage path was observed to be cheaper. Besides, the CO2  gas leaked to the top aquifer through the leakage path without MICP treatment for near and far-field scenarios, resulting in losses of approximately 8700 USD and 7300 USD, respectively. The evaluation was approximate and assessed from the area of CO2  migration fronts in the top aquifer depicted in Fig. 14  (a.i, a.ii). This was not intended because leakage has several environmental consequences besides the loss of resources mentioned above (i.e., contamination of freshwater resources, human health risk, and global warming if large quantities of CO2  are escaped). Therefore, sealing the leakage paths is an essential step, and MICP treatment could be a better and sustainable option to ensure this. From the optimisation and cost analysis of the present study, it is evident that it can be an economical and efficient option if it is implemented at larger scales compared to a traditional cementing method, which is unsustainable in terms of carbon footprint and has integrity issues with time (Bai et al., 2016 ). Although the initial cost of MICP treatment reasonably increases with target distance, the biocement has a greater advantage over plugging efficiency and long-term stability unless the aquifer becomes highly acidic. Also, the application cost of MICP is reasonable compared to the detrimental effects on the environment caused by CO2  leakage into the atmosphere and freshwater bodies. Besides, the cost of conventional cement plugging by Riami et al. (2021)  indicated that plugging an abandoned well located at 1800 m consumes a minimum of 1440 USD and a maximum of 2.2 M USD. Therefore, the biocementation treatment is comparatively cost-effective (∼ 0.95 M USD for 100 m of leak distance from the injection source) and must be considered a suitable technology for abandoned well plugging.  8 Summary and conclusions The present study conducted a large-scale modelling study on MICP treatment in a leaky deep aquifer to seal the preexisting leakage path of an abandoned well for CO2  storage application. Accordingly, a two-phase MICP model was developed to simulate the two-phase fluid flow and multicomponent biochemical reactive transport. The MICP treatment was optimised following the methodology proposed for near and far-field leak distances (Stage 1). From the optimisation methodology, it was observed that bacterial injection duration played a dominant role in altering the desired concentration of attached bacteria near the leakage zone. However, chemical concentration and injection-retention duration significantly influenced the target leak permeability for near- and far-field scenarios, respectively. The CO2  gas migration rates were significant through the leakage path (i.e., abandoned well) before MICP treatment. However, after the optimised MICP treatment near the leakage path, the leakage rates became insignificant due to the lowering of the leak permeability. A cost analysis was also carried out to understand the cost dynamics of the leak distances. The cost of MICP treatment was observed to be reasonable within the considered leak distance limit of 100 m compared to the conventional cement grouting method. Further, the model limitations and future direction of the research were highlighted in the present study. Overall, the study indicated the importance of sealing abandoned wells through the sustainable technology of MICP treatment. The study depicts the potential of MICP technology to plug the leakage paths through an abandoned well situated in a CO2  sequestrated aquifer. For the desired bacterial accumulation, oxygen injection is recommended for the near-field scenario, whereas multiple bacterial injections are recommended for the far-field scenario. However, chemical concentration and injection-retention time are crucial in augmenting the biochemical reaction for the reaction phase. The MICP process efficiently avoids the environmental impacts of CO2  gas leakage from aquifers into the atmosphere, thereby avoiding human health risks. Also, for near-field scenarios, the biocementation treatment is cost-effective. However, for the far-field scenarios, the cost of the MICP treatment increases. But, it is essential to note that MICP treatment is more efficient than conventional cement plugging methods, where cement might degrade over time. Besides, the MICP treatment leakproofs the target region in and around the leakage path. Also, future modelling studies can be conducted to employ MICP treatment under complex geological conditions with leakage paths such as faults and fractures. Above and beyond, incorporating mechanics in extension to the present model to simulate the geostatic stresses can realistically represent the coupling between flow, deformation and transport characteristics.
1 Introduction Coreflooding experiments are used regularly for reservoir and aquifer characterization in various applications, such as, CO 2     geosequestration, groundwater remediation, oil and gas production, enhanced oil recovery and gas storage. Furthermore, these experiments have been instrumental in fundamental multiphase flow studies (Hadia et al., 2007; Suekane et al., 2009; Akbarabadi and Piri, 2013 ) and in developing new technologies (Agbalaka et al., 2009; Sohrabi et al., 2012; Baldygin et al., 2014 ). In recent years, investigations are being conducted using detailed models of coreflooding, which include varying sub-core properties distributed in the core interior. The main process for constructing these models is the estimation of permeability distribution and the ensuing capillary pressure spatial behavior. This work is dedicated to establishing and promoting methods of sub-core permeability estimation, presenting new and improved methods, and evaluating their accuracy using a numerical approach. Investigation of sub-core phenomenon has been a topic of wide interest for over three decades. It was established long ago that computed tomography (CT) imaging is a useful tool for analysis of the porosity and fluid distribution inside the core sample (Wellington and Vinegar, 1987; Withjack, 1988 ). Since then, numerous publications have utilized coreflooding with CT imaging to investigate the physical mechanisms pertaining to multiphase flow (e.g., Peters and Hardham, 1990; Perrin and Benson, 2010; Tang et al., 2019 ), in particular capillary trapping (Huang et al., 1995; Pentland et al., 2011; Krevor et al., 2011 ). It allowed to characterize sub-core properties, i.e., the relative permeability and capillary pressure (Pini and Benson, 2013; Reynolds and Krevor, 2015; Krause and Benson, 2015 ), and to understand phenomenon such as rate dependence of these properties (Ataie-Ashtiani et al., 2002; Rabinovich et al., 2015; Moreno et al., 2021 ). Permeability, is likely the most fundamental property in flow through porous media and thus should be thoroughly investigated on the sub-core level. We note that while CT is the most common technology for imaging coreflooding experiments, there have been other alternative techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Chen et al., 1994; Maru et al., 2021; Tromp and Cerioni, 2021 ), gamma-ray positron emission tomography (PET) (Zahasky and Benson, 2017 ) and synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (Voltolini et al., 2017 ). Many of the studies mentioned in the above focus on CO 2    -brine coreflooding, in the context of CO 2     geosequestration aimed at reducing anthropogenic CO 2     emissions. Considering this application, small scale processes are particularly influential to the CO 2     distribution in the cores and resolving them is important for reservoir scale modeling, where there have been some recent observations of anomalous CO 2     migration believed to be related to small-scale heterogeneity (Jackson and Krevor, 2020 ). One of the main motivations for this work is to contribute to methods of CO 2    -brine coreflooding analysis. Identifying sub-core permeability (k  ) distribution of a core sample is beneficial for a number of reasons. First it provides information on the heterogeneity of the rock, allowing to characterize various k   structures, e.g., lamination, low permeability zones and stochastic parameters of the distribution (Rabinovich, 2017 ). Second, it allows to construct numerical models of the core, which can then be used for coreflooding simulations, characterizing the core under different conditions (flow rates, boundary conditions, etc.) to supplement the experimental data. The sub-core model can also be used for various investigations of the flow physics. Finally, the sub-core k   allows to relate between the fine-scale and core-scale properties, which also provides insight on upscaling from the core scale to the larger scales. A number of methods for k   estimation from coreflooding experiments were implemented in the past. Wlthjack et al. (1991)  used a bundle of tubes model to estimate permeability variation using porosity and solvent concentrations obtained from CT imaging. Others developed methods in which the porosity (ϕ  ) maps obtained from CT imaging were used to estimate permeability (e.g., Huang et al., 1996; Mavko and Nur, 1997; Izgec et al., 2008 ), assuming a known relationship between k   and ϕ  , e.g., the Kozneny–Carman equation (Carman, 1937 ) or fractal geometry based relationships (Pape et al., 1999, 2000 ). However, these relationships are often inaccurate (Nelson, 1994; Honarpour et al., 1995; Huang et al., 1996 ). An iterative method of k   estimation which does not require any permeability-porosity empirical relationships was developed by Krause et al. (2011, 2013)  and Anto-Darkwah et al. (2021) . The method is based on inverting the capillary pressure function, assuming it scales by ϕ / k     as the Leverett scaling relationship prescribes (Leverett et al., 1942 ). This method has been applied to various drainage coreflooding experiments (Anto-Darkwah et al., 2023 ) and extended to imbibition modeling as well (Anto-Darkwah and Rabinovich, 2022 ). One of the major limitations of this method is that in regions where there is trapped water (i.e., fully water saturated, see Moreno and Rabinovich, 2021b ), the method does not provide accurate estimates of k  . A recent paper by the authors of this work (Wei and Rabinovich, 2023 ) studied the general inverse problem of k   estimation, which is related to the coreflooding application that is the focus of this work. It was found that the inversion method presented therein, which is similar to that of Krause et al. (2013) , is accurate for a wide range of problem parameters. By analyzing synthetic cases, we were able to delineate the range of parameters where the method accuracy is low and explain the mechanisms responsible for the accuracy reduction. An interesting finding was that taking the initial permeability estimation in the method based on the capillary limit assumption, as suggested by the procedure in Krause et al. (2013) , was not associated with higher accuracy compared to other choices for initial k  . While it was previously thought to be an important step in the procedure, our results showed that adopting a homogeneous effective k   as an initial guess is robust and the iterations are the significant part of the method. It was further shown in Wei and Rabinovich (2023)  that errors of the inverse method are large for cases in which the flow was capillary dominated as a result of the locations where water was trapped (capillary trapping). Errors also increased towards a viscous dominated flow regime and for high heterogeneity, characterized by a large variance of k  . These findings lead to the conclusion that further improvements are required to enhance k   estimation accuracy. Additionally, it was found that the approach of using synthetic data generated by numerical simulations is promising, since it allows to evaluate the performance of different inversion methods, whereas the conventional approach of applying inverse methods directly on experiments does not provide much information about the accuracy. This work presents new methods for k   estimation of core samples, improving those of Krause et al. (2013)  and Wei and Rabinovich (2023) , and evaluates their accuracy. The main contribution is a method combining multiple coreflooding experiments with different fluid-flow rates, which is shown to significantly increase the accuracy of k   estimations in comparison to the case of using data from only a single coreflooding experiment. A second method presented here, includes treatment of the water trapped zones, increasing the k   estimation accuracy when capillary trapping is present. Finally, a method which estimates k   based on simplified equations, representing single-phase flow, is presented and discussed. It is developed in order to increase computationally efficiency of the k   estimation procedure, however, results show limited use due to issues with accuracy. The importance and novelty of this work is not only in the development of new methods, but also in the systematic analysis of estimation errors in a large number of test cases. While sub-core estimation methods are rapidly increasing in the literature, almost all of them are applied only to a few experiments and therefore cannot be validated or evaluated (e.g., Krause et al., 2013; Anto-Darkwah and Rabinovich, 2022; Anto-Darkwah et al., 2023 ). This work allows to systematically evaluate our new methods and therefore address the specific limitations of existing methods.
