The approach taken in this work provides a framework for developing the robust procedures presented here, as well as those that will be developed in the future. The plan of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 , we detail the problem of identifying k   using data obtained from coreflooding experiments and present the coreflooding model, which is solved using a numerical simulator. In Section 3 , the methods used for k   estimation are presented. Section 4  presents the results of applying the methods to various test cases and the accuracy evaluation of each case. Finally, a summary and discussion of the main conclusions is presented in Section 5 .  2 Problem statement The general problem we are interested in solving is how to obtain the permeability distribution in a core sample using results of steady state drainage coreflooding experiments. Coreflooding experiments are typically conducted by placing a cylindrical rock sample in an apparatus which allows to apply the reservoir pressure and temperature. Then, two fluids are injected though the sample at different fluid fractions, f  , until steady state is reached and the pressure drop Δ p = p  i n   − p  o u t      is measured (p  i n     and p  o u t     are the measured pressures at the inlet and outlet, respectively). During the steady state flow, CT scans of the core are taken and used to construct three-dimensional (3D) maps representing the porosity, ϕ  e x p    , and saturation, S  w  e x p    , in the core interior. These maps can be considered spatially varying functions, i.e., ϕ  e x p   ( x , y , z )     and S  w  e x p   ( x , y , z )     (where x  , y   and z   form a Cartesian coordinate system) or, in a more accurate discrete description, a 3D tensor with size determined by the resolution of the data. These experiments are usually repeated for different f   values of the two fluids, while maintaining the same total flow rate of injection Q  t   = Q  w   + Q  n w     , where Q  w     and Q  n w     are the wetting phase and nonwetting phase injection flow rates, respectively. The flow fraction (or fluid fraction) is defined as (1) f = Q  n w    Q  t     .      Next, values of relative permeability (k  r    ) are calculated for each experiment by substituting the measured steady state pressure drop Δ p    in Darcy’s law and, when coupled with the average core saturation of the experiment, this provides a point on the k  r   ( S  w   )     curves. The process is repeated for all the experiments (with varying f  ) to obtain a number of points on the k  r     curves. Then, these data points are fitted with a function to represent the relative permeability. In this work we will consider the common form of the curves (Brooks and Corey, 1966 ), given by: (2a) k  r w   = S  ˜    w  n  w     ,    (2b) k  r n w   = k  r n w  m a x   ( 1 − S  ˜    w   )   n  n w     ,       for the wetting phase (subscript w  ) and nonwetting phase (subscript n w   ) relative permeability, respectively. The coefficients k  r n w  m a x    , n  w     and n  n w     are fitting parameters allowing to match the data points. The normalized wetting phase saturation is given by (3) S  ˜    w   = S  w   − S  w , i r    1 − S  w , i r     ,     and S  w , i r     is the irreducible wetting phase saturation. The latter is often determined to be the smallest wetting phase saturation value in the steady state experimental results S  w  e x p     for injection at f = 1   . The k  r     functions are assumed to be uniform in the porous medium, a simplifying assumption which allows to avoid considering varying sub-core relative permeability. Nevertheless, the k  r     curves which are obtained experimentally, as described above, are effective properties that represent the entire core, and generally depend on injection rate. Therefore the curves calculated by the procedure detailed above can be different than the uniform sub-core k  r     curves, often coined the “characteristic” or “intrinsic” curves. In this work, we assume that the procedure for obtaining the k  r     curves was conducted on coreflooding experiments with high flow rate, representing viscous dominated conditions, in which experimentally measured k  r     are equal to the intrinsic curves. The capillary pressure as a function of saturation P  c   ( S  w   )     should also be estimated experimentally. This can be done in a number of ways (e.g., Brown, 1951; Borazjani et al., 2021 ), and we assume here that the common approach is adopted, in which mercury intrusion experiments are conducted on a separate core sample representing the core plug. Thus, data points of capillary pressure are available and can be fitted with a function P  c   ( S  w   )    , taken here to be of the (Brooks and Corey, 1966 ) form: (4) P  c   ( S  w   )  = α ( S  ˜    w   )   − 1 / λ   ,     where α   is the capillary entry pressure parameter and λ   is the pore size distribution index. Both parameters are obtained by fitting the data. In addition to these experiments, single-phase flow coreflooding is carried out and pressure drop is measured providing estimated effective permeability, k  e f    . Summarizing the problem, we seek the 3D permeability map, k ( x , y , z )    , given all the data from experiments with different f   and Q  t    : saturation maps, S  w  e x p    , porosity map, ϕ  e x p    , effective permeability, k  e f    , irreducible wetting phase saturation, S  w , i r    , viscosity of the fluids, density of the fluids, intrinsic relative permeability given by Eqs. (2) , and capillary pressure curve given by Eq. (4) . 2.1 The forward problem: Simulating coreflooding In this work, we modeled coreflooding experiments via the mathematical problem described below (the forward problem) and solved it using numerical simulation. This is an important step of the k   estimation method (i.e., the inverse problem) and naturally also serves the overall goal of constructing accurate coreflooding models. We consider two-phase flow in which the nonwetting and wetting phases are injected from one side (inlet) of the domain and flow out from the other side (outlet). The governing equations for two-phase immiscible flow and incompressible rock and fluid is given as (5) ϕ ∂ S  j    ∂ t   − ∇ ⋅ k  r j   ( S  j   )   μ  j     k ⋅ ∇ p  j   + ρ  j   g z     = 0 ,     where subscript j   represents different phases (j = w    or j = n w   ), Sj   is the saturation of phase j , krj   is the relative permeability to phase j , μ  j     is the viscosity of phase j , pj   is the pressure of phase j , ρ  j     is the density of phase j , k   is the permeability tensor, g  is the gravitational acceleration and z  is the vertical coordinate. The relationship between the non-wetting phase pressure and wetting phase pressure is governed by (6) p  n w   − p  w   = P  c   ( S  w   )  ,     where P  c   ( S  w   )     is assumed to be of the form given by Eq. (4) . For heterogeneous core samples, such as the ones considered in this work, the capillary pressure curves are typically multiplied by a scaling factor which varies spatially according to porosity and permeability. Therefore, the curves can be represented by a function P  c   ( ϕ , k , S  w   )    . This will be further discussed in Section 3  and Eqs. (7) –(9) . The boundary conditions for the forward problem are no-flow conditions for all the surfaces perpendicular to the injection direction, since a sleeve is usually used in the experiments to confine the porous rock in those directions. For the flow injection direction (taken to be along the x  -axis), we assume a given flow rate at the inlet (x = 0   ) and given phase pressures at the outlet (x = L   , where L   is the length of the core). In addition, the capillary pressure is assigned a zero value at the outlet (P  c   = 0    at x = L   ) and therefore the outlet phase pressures are equal (p  w   = p  n w   = p  o u t      at x = L   ). We further simplify the problem by assuming that the k   tensor in Eq. (5)  is in fact a scalar function k ( x , y , z )     representing an isotropic permeability field. The isotropy assumption is justified considering the small dimensions of the sub-core domains assigned with k   (typically cuboids of 1–3 mm lengths) and that the permeability in the directions perpendicular to the applied flow direction is less influential (Dagan, 2012 ). The forward problem is solved numerically using the reservoir simulator by Computer Modeling Group (CMG) Ltd. with the IMEX package (IMEX, 2000 ). It is a fully implicit finite volume solver and the two-phase oil–water module is used to account for immiscibility between the phases. The geometric model contains 52 × 25 × 25 grid blocks with 52 blocks in x   direction, 25 blocks in y   direction, 25 blocks in z   direction, and each cubic grid-block is 2.5 mm×   2.5 mm ×   2.5 mm in size. The physical size and resolution taken here are in agreement with a typical core sample size and CT image resolution (after post processing). The porous domain is initially fully water saturated (S  w , i   = 1    for all grid blocks i  ). The boundary conditions in the simulator must be implemented using wells. Therefore, the first and last vertical planes or slices (the inlet and the outlet) at x = 0    and x = L    are in fact artificial slices of grid blocks which enforce the boundary conditions. The inlet grid blocks are populated with injection wells, injecting both fluids, with constant rates of Q  w     and Q  n w    , according to the fluid fraction f   and the total injection rate Q  t    . The outlet blocks are populated with production wells of a constant producing pressure p  o u t    . We note that in some coreflooding models boundary conditions are applied only to part of the inlet and outlet faces (Gao et al., 2024 ), but in this work we consider the case in which fluids are uniformly distributed on the entire end surfaces (inlet and outlet) of the core samples. A homogeneous permeability is assigned to the inlet and outlet grid blocks, i.e., k  i   = k  e f      at the x = 0    and x = L    blocks, in order to ensure a uniform distribution of fluxes (Anto-Darkwah et al., 2021 ), and P  c , i   = 0    is assigned to the outlet blocks, as required by the outlet boundary conditions.   3 Methods The method of estimating k  , i.e., solving the problem described in Section 2 , is detailed in Wei and Rabinovich (2023)  and extended here to include multiple experiments. A main component in the method is an empirical relationship between capillary pressure and heterogeneity i.e., P  c     is a function of k   and ϕ   as well as S  w    . In this work we will consider the well-known Leverett J  -function relationship (Leverett et al., 1942 ) given by: (7) P  c   ( S  w   , k , ϕ )  = σ cos θ ϕ  k     J ( S  w   )  ,     where σ   is the interfacial tension, θ   is contact angle between non-wetting phase and wetting phase and J ( S  w   )     is the J  -function. Eq. (7)  represents the distribution of the capillary pressure in the core interior according to the heterogeneity and the saturation of each grid block. The P  c   ( S  w   )     function is obtained experimentally on a separate sample cut from the extracted rock, near the core plug used for the coreflooding experiments. It is reasonable to assume that this sample has a permeability approximately equal to the core permeability, i.e., k  e f    , and a porosity of ϕ    , where the triangular brackets indicate averaging over the entire core. To increase the likelihood of this assumption, P  c     curve measurements can be repeated on a number of samples around the core plug and results averaged to obtain a final P  c   ( S  w   )     curve. An expression for P  c     can be obtained by substituting k  e f     and ϕ     in Eq. (7) , replacing k   and ϕ  . On the other hand, P  c     is also given by Eq. (4) ; therefore, the J  -function can be derived by equating Eqs. (4) and (7)  to arrive at the following expression: (8) J ( S  w   )  = α  σ cos θ   k  e f    ϕ       ( S  ˜    w   )   − 1 / λ   .     Then, the capillary pressure variation inside the core sample can be expressed by (9) P  c   ( S  w   , x , y , z )  = α k  e f   ⋅ ϕ ( x , y , z )   ϕ   ⋅ k ( x , y , z )      ( S  ˜    w   )   − 1 / λ   .       From Eq. (9) , an expression of permeability can be derived which will be used to estimate k ( x , y , z )    . By inversion we obtain: (10) k  i   = κ ϕ  i    P  c , i  2     k  e f    ϕ     [ α ( S  ˜    w , i   )   − 1 / λ   ]   2   ,     where subscript i   indicates the grid-block number representing a specific voxel in the core interior, and κ   is a scaling factor that has been added in the formulation to ensure permeability is in agreement with the experimentally measured k  e f    . Thus, the permeability in block i   (k  i    ) depends on the porosity (ϕ  i    ), capillary pressure (P  c , i    ) and saturation (S  ˜    w , i    ) of that block. The saturation and porosity can be obtained from experiments, where they are measured by CT scans and have been denoted S  w  e x p     and ϕ  e x p    . Other parameters in the equation: k  e f    , α   and λ   can also be obtained through experiments, as described in Section 2 . Porosity ϕ     is obtained simply by averaging ϕ  e x p    . We now detail the procedure in which k  i     and P  c , i     are calculated simultaneously using numerical simulations. It is emphasized that for each new k   estimation, the effective permeability will be calculated and factor κ   will be chosen to make sure the estimated permeability has the same k  e f     as the value obtained in the single-phase coreflooding experiment. Fig. 1  presents the new procedure for k   estimation using data from multiple coreflooding experiments. The first step (Step I) entails constructing coreflooding models corresponding to the experiments that were conducted, as detailed in Section 2 , and using an initial guess of permeability, taken to be simply the constant value of k  e f    . In Step II, simulations are carried out for all the different experiments (each with a unique f   and Q  t    ) until steady state is reached. The saturation error is calculated for each experiment separately by the following expression: (11) E  S  w     = 1  N   ∑  i = 1  N   | S  w , i  o u t p u t   − S  w , i  e x p   |  ,     where S  w , i  e x p     is the grid block saturation from the experiments and S  w , i  o u t p u t     is the grid block saturation output from the simulations, i.e., the estimated saturation. If the saturation error E  S  w       is smaller than the predetermined threshold value E  S  w    c r i t e r i a     for all the experiments, then we have found an accurate model and therefore the procedure is terminated with the estimated k  i     having been found (Step IV). If however, one or more of the experiments has an error E  S  w     > E  S  w    c r i t e r i a     , then we continue to Step III, in which we update the permeability. Step III entails using Eq. (10)  with the grid-block values of P  c , i     taken from the simulation output and S  ˜    w , i  e x p     taken from the experiments. This leads to a new permeability distribution for each of the experiments and the final permeability distribution is obtained by simply averaging them (arithmetic average was found to be most accurate). Then, Step II is repeated with the final average permeability distribution used in all the simulations for all of the experiments. Steps II and III are repeated iteratively until the error is sufficiently small, i.e., E  S  w     < E  S  w    c r i t e r i a      for all the experiments. We note that we also calculate the overall saturation error by averaging the E  S  w       for all the estimated saturations that represent different experiments and denote this error E  S  w    o v e r a l l    . If at any point during the procedure the overall error is consistently increasing with iterations, we stop the procedure and take the final permeability distribution to be the one obtained at the iteration with the lowest E  S  w    o v e r a l l    . 3.1 Estimating k   for fluid trapped regions A major limitation of the method described above is that grid blocks in which S  ˜    w , i  e x p   = 1    do not provide sufficient information to estimate k   (Krause and Benson, 2015; Wei and Rabinovich, 2023 ). These are regions in which the wetting phase is trapped due to the high capillary entry pressure and therefore the nonwetting phase does not invade. The capillary pressure in a block with S  ˜    w , i  e x p   = 1    is ill defined and only an upper limit on k   can be obtained for that block, determined by the constraint that capillary entry pressure does not drop below the capillary pressure of the adjacent blocks, in which case the nonwetting phase will migrate into the S  ˜    w , i  e x p   = 1    block. In order to improve the accuracy of permeability estimation for those trapped blocks, we develop a method to treat those regions as follows.  Fig. 2  presents a flowchart of the procedure. The first step (Step I) is to run the previously described iterative method, as presented in Fig. 1 . Then, in Step II, all blocks in which the experiment showed wetting phase trapping, i.e., S  ˜    w , i  e x p   = 1    are identified. If the estimated saturation (output of the final simulation in the iterative method) for those blocks showed that S  ˜    w , i  o u t p u t   < 1   , then these blocks (denoted with index l  ) will be treated by modifying their initial permeability. This is Step III of the procedure in Fig. 2 , in which blocks with S  ˜    w , i  e x p   = 1    and S  ˜    w , i  o u t p u t   < 1    are assigned an initial permeability of k  i  i n i t i a l   = 0 . 9 k  e f     , while all other blocks are assigned k  i  i n i t i a l   = k  e f     . The iterative procedure is carried out again for the new initial k  . We note that here, we consider the iterative procedure for only a single experiment, therefore k   is estimated only for one specific experiment rather than the combination of multiple experiments. The sequence of updating k  i  i n i t i a l     and then running the iterative procedure is repeated, each time taking a smaller k  i  i n i t i a l     for the l   blocks. With each iteration of the procedure there are less l   blocks, until finally there are no such blocks and the procedure is terminated. At the end of this supplemental procedure for treating the trapped blocks, both the saturation error and permeability estimation error will decrease in comparison to the original iterative method of Fig. 1 , as will be discussed in Section 4 .  3.2 Single-phase method The methods for k   estimation described above entail solving the multiphase flow forward problem (Section 2.1 ) many times using numerical simulations. This can be rather computationally expensive. In efforts of reducing the computational cost, we present a modified method based on solving only single-phase flow equations. The general idea has been previously implemented for estimating intrinsic relative permeability (Rabinovich et al., 2019; Anto-Darkwah et al., 2021 ), however has not been applied to k   estimation. We note that the problems solved using the single-phase method are the same as discussed previously in Sections 2 and 3 , i.e., we still consider two-phase flow coreflooding experiments with all the relevant experimental data. The reason we coin the new method “single-phase method” is due to the calculations which are reduced to solving only single-phase flow equations, as explained in the following. The governing equations for coreflooding at steady state are obtained by reducing Eqs. (5)  to (12a) ∇ ⋅ [ k  r w   ( S  w   )  k ( x , y , z )   μ  w     ∇ ( p  w   + ρ  w   g z )  ]  = 0 ,    (12b) ∇ ⋅ [ k  r n w   ( S  w   )  k ( x , y , z )   μ  n w     ]  ∇ ( p  n w   + ρ  n w   g z )  = 0 ,       for steady state conditions. The governing equations can be further reduced to two independent single-phase flow equations if we substitute the experimental saturation data S  w  e x p     in the relative permeability in Eqs (12) . (13a) ∇ ⋅ K  w   ( x , y , z )   μ  w     ∇ p  w   + ρ  w   g z     = 0 ,    (13b) ∇ ⋅ K  n w   ( x , y , z )   μ  n w     ∇ p  n w   + ρ  n w   g z     = 0 ,       where phase permeability (K  j    ) is given by (14) K  j   ( x , y , z )  = k ( x , y , z )  ⋅ k  r j   S  w  e x p   ( x , y , z )    .      The relative permeability in Eq. (14)  is no longer a function of saturation, but rather a known spatial distribution of values.  The above formulation allows to solve for the pressure distribution in a two-phase coreflooding model, given the saturation distribution from the experiments. Eqs. (13a)  and (14) , together with the boundary conditions of given Q  w     at the inlet and p  w , o u t     at the outlet can be solved for the pressure distribution in the core p  w   ( x , y , z )    . Similarly, Eqs. (13b)  and (14)  with Q  n w     and p  n w , o u t     can be solved to obtain p  n w   ( x , y , z )    . Then, the capillary pressure distribution P  c   ( x , y , z )     can be calculated using Eq. (6) . To summarize the single-phase approach, the saturation is known and plugged into the governing equations. Therefore, it is no longer calculated in our simulations. However, the capillary pressure is not known and calculated using Eqs. (13a) ,(13b) , (14)  and (6) . The procedure for estimating k   based on the single-phase flow equations is detailed in Fig. 3  and is similar to the original procedure (Fig. 1 ), but includes using the simplified equations for the forward model. The first step (Step I) is to set the initial permeability to k  i  i n i t i a l   = k  e f     . In Step II, we calculate phase permeability K  w     and K  n w     (see Eq. (14) ) using k  i  i n i t i a l   = k  e f      and substitute these in the single-phase flow equations (see Eq. (13) ). After solving the single-phase flow equations (here we use CMG IMEX software), the phase pressures are obtained and capillary pressure at each grid block (P  c , i    ) is calculated according to Eq. (6) . Step III entails using P  c , i     in Eq. (10)  to calculate a new permeability distribution. In Step IV we test the convergence of the method. This cannot be done by a saturation error via Eq. (11)  as in the previous method, because we are only solving for pressure in the single-phase equations. Therefore, we compare the permeability maps between the previous iteration (k  i  o l d    ) and the current iteration (k  i  n e w    ) using a measure of convergence given by (15) E  k  i t e r   = 1  N   ∑  i = 1  N   | k  i  o l d   − k  i  n e w   |  / k  i  n e w   .     If this measure is smaller than a predetermined E  k  c r i t e r i a     value, then the procedure is terminated and k  i  n e w     is the final permeability. Otherwise, the procedure is repeated starting with Step II and using the updated k  i  n e w    .   4 Results In this section we will present many examples of implementing the methods introduced in Section 3  on synthetic data and analyze the accuracy of the methods. We consider mainly a cuboid domain of 52 × 25 × 25 grid blocks representing the core sample (a more realistic cylindrical domain is also considered to show compatibility). A Permeability for each grid block is generated by the Stanford Geostatistical Modeling Software (SGeMS), an open-source software for generating spatial realizations of variables (Remy et al., 2009 ), using the Sequential Gaussian Simulation (Deutsch et al., 1992 ) package. The permeability is taken to be lognormally distributed with arithmetic mean of about 100 mD and dimensionless correlation length of l = 0 . 1    (normalized by the domain length and an exponential variogram was used). An example of a permeability realization with a log-variance of σ  Y  2   = 1    (Y = ln k   ) is plotted in Fig. 4 a. Next, synthetic coreflooding data is generated by solving the forward problem via numerical simulations with permeability realizations as discussed above. The input parameters for the simulations are detailed in Table 1 . We note that some input parameter values are not rounded. This is a result of unit conversions, since the rounded values used as input in the numerical simulator are often in different units than those presented here. Both oil–water and supercritical CO 2    -water are considered as the injected fluid pairs. Furthermore, ϕ  i   = ϕ   = 0 . 2    is taken for all voxels to simplify the calculations and this is considered throughout this work (porosity typically varies much less then permeability and has less impact on P  c     and on the steady state solutions). A coefficient value of k  r n w  m a x   = 1    in Eq. (2) b is taken. Now, using synthetic data generated by the simulations to represent experimental results, we implement the k  -estimation method discussed in Fig. 1 .    First, we apply the procedure to estimate k   considering a single experiment, i.e., synthetic data from a single simulation. Most of these results, and a detailed analysis, have been presented in Wei and Rabinovich (2023)  and we provide a summary of the cases considered and the accuracy of the method in Table 2 , mainly for the purpose of comparison. It can be seen in the table that many cases pertaining to different flow rates and fluid fractions were tested. The results are presented by the saturation error of the model E  S  w       (see Eq. (11) ) and by a quantitative measure of the estimated k   accuracy E  k    , which is expressed as (16) E  k   = 1  N   ∑  i = 1  N   ( | k  i  e s t   − k  i  r e a l   |  / k  i  r e a l   )  ,     where N   is the number of grid blocks (N = 31  250    in the cuboid domain, after removing the inlet and outlet blocks), k  i  e s t     is the estimated permeability in block i  , and k  i  r e a l     is the real permeability in block i  . Results in Table 2  are divided into two systems pertaining to the fluids considered: oil–water or CO 2    -water. The two cases differ from each other in our simulations by the input values of the fluid density and viscosity (see Table 1 ). The domain representing the core is cuboid in all these cases (and all following cases as well). However, to test the impact of the domain shape, we consider a cylindrical core, which is a more accurate representation for real coreflooding. The case of oil–water injection with f = 50 %   , Q  t   = 13 . 9    ml/min and σ  Y  2   = 1    (Case 3 in Table 2 ) is considered. The input permeability for this case, which we refer to as the real permeability, is presented in Figs. 4 a,b. It can be seen that the cylindrical domain is “cut out” of the cuboid central part so that the permeability of the two is the same in that region. The results of the k   estimation are presented in Figs. 4 c,d. It can be seen that the estimated and real permeability are visually similar for both the cuboid and cylindrical domains. The estimation errors are E  k   = 6 . 3 %    and E  k   = 11 . 0 %    for the cuboid and cylindrical domains, respectively. The slightly larger error of the cylindrical domain is most likely a result of the lower resolution (less grid blocks) and perhaps also related to the inaccuracy of representing a curved boundary with cubic grid blocks. Nevertheless, the relatively similar errors show that, for the sake of evaluating the estimation methods, using the simple cubic domain representing a core sample, instead of a more realistic cylindrical one, is a valid approach.  Fig. 5  presents the saturation comparison for the same case discussed in Fig. 4  (Case 3 in Table 2 ). The real saturation, i.e., the synthetic data representing the experimental data, is plotted in Fig. 5 a. The estimated saturation is plotted in Fig. 5 b, i.e., the simulation saturation output with the estimated k   from Fig. 4 d used as input. The two appear to be the same showing that the model is accurate. The error of the estimated saturation is E  S  w     = 0 . 0049   , similar to the cubic domain error of E  S  w     = 0 . 0046    (see Table 2 ). We note that a stopping criteria for the estimation methods in this work was taken to be E  S  w    c r i t e r i a   = 0 . 005    for all cases, including the multiple experiment cases. It can be seen in the fourth column of Table 2  that some cases reach the criteria while others do not and the method is terminated due to an increase of E  S  w       with iterations. The total number of iterations is provided in the last column of Table 2 . 4.1 Improved estimation for fluid trapped regions We now implement the method discussed in Section 3.1  to improve the estimation of k   in regions where there is trapped water, i.e., S  w  e x p   = 1   . We consider three cases, presented in Table 3 , in which there is significant water trapping. The number of blocks with trapped water are 8102, 11 872, and 6217 for Cases 1–3, respectively. Out of these, the number of blocks in which the estimated saturation is less than one (S  w  o u t p u t   < 1   ) are 7362, 11 682 and 5928, respectively. These blocks were found to significantly contribute to the k   estimation error. The phenomenon occurs at capillary dominated regimes characterized by low flow rates and large capillary pressures, as seen by the values of Q  t     and α   taken in the three test cases.   Table 3  shows the final error of k   estimation for the three cases after implementing the treatment for trapped blocks. It can be seen that all E  k     values have been reduced (for Cases 1 and 2 by around 50%) and the final errors can be considered small (below 20% for two cases and slightly over 20% for the third). It can also be seen that saturation error remains below the convergence criteria of E  S  w    c r i t e r i a   = 0 . 005   , similar to the errors before applying the additional treatment. The detailed permeability estimation accuracy, before and after applying the procedure, can be seen in Fig. 6  for all three cases. The permeability results before applying the procedure (green circles) are seen to overestimate the real permeability for the lower k   values. This occurs because at blocks with small k  , the entry pressure is large, leading to water trapping and subsequently to unknown capillary pressure values, which can be smaller than the actual entry pressure of the block. This underestimation of block P  c     leads to larger estimated permeability than the real one. However, applying the new procedure for trapped block treatment entails gradually reducing the initial k   for those blocks, which leads to smaller k   estimations. This is seen in Fig. 6  where the estimated permeability is significantly improved for most of the trapped blocks as seen by the blue circles overlaying the “perfect match” line. The inset plots in Fig. 6  present histograms of the error E  k , i     for the improved method. It can be seen that the vast majority of blocks have small error of 0 − 10 %   . Only at the very smallest estimated permeability there is still a significant error, seen by the vertical column of blue circles. However, these are much smaller in number compared to the overall number of trapped blocks, and thus the general k   estimation error is reduced.  4.2 Estimation with multiple experiments   This section presents and discusses results for k   estimation using the new method incorporating data from multiple experiments. The experiment results are represented by synthetic data generated from simulations with different injection flow rates and fluid fractions. A large number of cases were tested and results are summarized in Table 4  for oil–water flow and in Table 5  for CO 2    -water flow. Overall, 22 different cases consisting of different combinations of experiments with varying Q  t    , f  , σ  y  2    , λ   and n  w   = n  n w      were evaluated. The permeability errors can be seen in the second column from the right side in Tables 4 and 5 , calculated via Eq. (16) . The errors are considered small (below 20%) for almost all of the cases tested. Only the large k   variance cases, i.e., Cases 11 and 12 (σ  y  2   = 4    for oil–water injection), and Case 22 (σ  y  2   = 2    for CO 2    -water injection), are seen to have errors significantly larger than 20% (Case 19 has an error only slightly larger than 20%). Even these cases have an error which can be considered reasonable of 47%–82%. Comparing Tables 4 and 5  to Table 2  it is apparent that the errors have been significantly reduced when considering multiple experiments rather than a single one; the latter is seen to have 34 out of 45 cases with errors larger than 20%, while the former has only 4 cases out of 22. Even in cases where only two experiments were used for k   estimation (Cases 3, 4, 15, 16 and 17) a significantly higher accuracy is observed compared to the single experiment results. In fact, for cases 3, 15, 16 and 17, the overall E  k     is smaller than both of the single cases considered separately (see Cases 1, 3, 26, 28, 30 and 31 in Table 2 ). Another example is given by Case 5 (f =    90%) in Table 2 , which has an error of E  k   = 82 . 8 %   , however when combined with Case 3 (f =    50%) the error reduces to 15.5% (see Case 4 in Table 4 ).  Fig. 7  presents convergence plots for two example cases of the multi-experiment method. Convergence can be evaluated by observing the saturation error (E  S  w       given by Eq. (11) ) as it changes with iterations, for each case separately and also by observing the overall error (E  S  w    o v e r a l l    ) obtained by averaging E  S  w       values. Fig. 7 a shows the convergence of Case 1, consisting of multiple flow rates (see details in Table 4 ). It can be seen that in this case all of the saturation errors are monotonically decreasing until convergence of the method is achieved, when all E  S  w       are smaller than E  S  w    c r i t e r i a    . The E  S  w       at the final iteration are presented in the fourth column in Table 4 , where it can be seen that for Case 1 the values are all below E  S  w    c r i t e r i a   = 0 . 005   . The overall error in Fig. 7 a is also seen to decrease monotonically until convergence is achieved, with a final value of 0.0024 (see fifth column in Table 4 ). Fig. 7 b presents convergence for Case 2 with multiple fluid fractions (see details in Table 4 ). It can be seen that in this case some of the saturation errors start to increase with iterations and do not fall below E  S  w    c r i t e r i a     (see fourth column in Table 4 ). Similar behavior is seen for E  S  w    o v e r a l l     and therefore the procedure is terminated and the final result is taken at iteration 12, when E  S  w    o v e r a l l     has its smallest value. While the procedure may be terminated in two ways, as discussed above: with convergence (Fig. 7 a) and without (Fig. 7 b), both are seen to result in relatively accurate k   estimations (< 20 %   ). Nevertheless, there is a clear trend of better estimations when convergence is achieved and an overall smaller E  k     with smaller E  S  w    o v e r a l l    . To observe this behavior we plot E  k     as a function of E  S  w    o v e r a l l     in Fig. 8  for all 22 cases. It is apparent that the points representing converged cases are clustered at the bottom left corner of the plot indicating a low estimation error. Furthermore, a general trend of increasing E  k     with larger E  S  w    o v e r a l l     is seen, though there are slight deviations from this general behavior.    Fig. 9  presents results for Cases 1 and 2 from Table 4  for the oil–water systems. In Fig. 9 a, multiple experiments with different flow rates are used and the k   estimation is seen to be excellent, with the blue data circles closely packed around the “perfect match” line. For comparison, results are also presented for a single-experiment case of Q  t   = 0 . 14    (Case 6 in Table 2 ). A large scatter is seen for this case, shown with green circles, and an overestimation of k   for many of the lower permeability grid blocks is apparent. This overestimation is associated with water trapped blocks, as discussed previously in Sections 3.1 and 4.1 . It occurs at capillary dominated regimes such as that prevailing for the low injection rate of Case 6. Fig. 9 b presents results for multiple experiments with different flow fractions and the comparison case (green circles) is of a single experiment with f = 90 %    (Case 5 in Table 2 ). It can be seen that the comparison case has a very large scatter indicating a significant error in the estimated k  . This occurs at high flow fractions such as in Case 5, because of the low water saturation prevailing in the core, which leads to more sensitivity in the inverse procedure as the viscosity effects of the oil become more dominating (see discussion in Wei and Rabinovich (2023) ). The plot illustrates clearly how adding additional experiments with lower fluid fractions improves the k   estimation drastically. The inset plots presenting E  k , i     histograms show that the vast majority of blocks have small error between 0 – 10 %    for Case 1 and 0 – 25 %    for Case 2. Fig. 10  presents results for Cases 13 (Fig. 10 a) and 14 (Fig. 10 b) from Table 5  for the CO 2    -water systems. Results are compared to single-experiment cases: Case 31 (Fig. 10 a) and Case 28 (Fig. 10 b). It can be clearly seen that the multi-experiment cases result in much more accurate k   estimations. The low flow rate comparison case presented in Fig. 10 a suffers from errors due to trapped blocks, as was discussed previously regarding Fig. 9 a, and this is significantly improved when additional higher rate experiments are added to the analysis. The single fluid-fraction case presented in Fig. 10 b for f = 50 %    shows low accuracy of k   estimation, similarly to what was observed for the f = 90 %    case in Fig. 9 b. The reason for the lower accuracy in the CO 2    -water case of lower fluid fractions is the increase in viscosity effects (as water saturation increases and replaces low viscosity CO 2    ) which reduces the significance of the capillary pressure and thus k   estimation via Eq. (10)  becomes less accurate. Significant improvement can be seen when additional higher fluid-fraction experiments are added to the analysis. Particularly, high accuracy can be observed in the inset plots of Fig. 10 , which show that the improved method has errors of only 0 − 10 %    in almost all of the grid blocks. The results of the multi-experiment k   estimation method presented in this section show that this method is a significant improvement in comparison to the single-experiment method. Furthermore, the sensitivity of estimation errors to the experimental Q  t     and f  , which was thoroughly discussed in Wei and Rabinovich (2023) , is drastically reduced here. The main parameter impacting the estimation accuracy is therefore the degree of heterogeneity, expressed by σ  Y  2    . This parameter also had an impact on the simulation times and convergence, as large σ  Y  2     cases in CO 2    -water flow were slow to converge and when combined with low flow-rate cases, convergence often failed (i.e., simulations crashed). This is the reason CO 2    -water cases were only tested up to σ  Y  2   = 2    (see Table 5 ). Other important, yet less influential factors that were found to impact estimation accuracy are the fluid viscosity ratio (μ  C O  2     / μ  w      vs μ  o   / μ  w     ) and the entry pressure (α  ). The computational cost for carrying out the multi-experiment method varies widely depending on the cases considered and the problem parameters. In general, the method is approximately the same in computational time as the single-experiment method because the number of iterations is similar and simulations are conducted in parallel. Comparing the last columns of Tables 4 and 5  to that of Table 2 , it can be seen that for the multi-experiment cases the number of iterations is 7–28 for oil–water flow and 7–70 for CO 2    -water flow, while for the single-experiment cases it is 9–85 for oil–water flow and 4–67 for CO 2    -water flow. Furthermore, the simulations at each iteration are conducted in parallel, so that there is no significant added time associated with the multi-experiment method (although there is additional computational cost). However, simulations with low flow rate and high heterogeneity are much slower and therefore the main factor impacting the computational time is whether such simulations are included. For example, the longest computational time for a single iteration is for Case 22 (σ  Y  2   = 2    and Q  t   = 6 . 9    ml/min), which takes 3.9 h of simulation. Considering a lower ln k    variance, as in Case 18 (σ  Y  2   = 1    and Q  t   = 6 . 9    ml/min) the simulation time of a single iteration drops to around 2.5 h. For comparison, the typical computational time for a single iteration of the oil–water cases with σ  Y  2   = 1    is only a few minutes.  4.3 Single-phase method We now present results for the single-phase method, discussed previously in Section 3.2 . The method was tested on a 1D discretized domain of 4000 cells with randomly assigned k   from a lognormal distribution with σ  y  2   = 1   , implemented as described in Section 4 . Synthetic data is generated, mimicking coreflooding experimental data, as described in Section 4 , i.e., two fluids (oil and water or CO 2     and water) are injected into the 1D porous domain until steady state is reached and saturation maps are obtained. Other parameters are used in this section are f = 50 %   , α = 200  kPa   , n  w   = n  n w   = 2    and λ = 2    for the oil–water cases, and f = 99 %   , α = 5  kPa   , n  w   = n  n w   = 2    and λ = 2    for the CO 2    -water cases. Additional parameters are given in Table 1 . Varying injection rates were tested as detailed in Table 6 , where it is shown that altogether 8 cases were considered.    Fig. 11  presents the oil pressure as a function of the length of the 1D domain, expressed in terms of the block number (block 1 is the inlet and 4000 is the outlet) for Case 2 in Table 6 . We note that, similar to the 3D cases, block 1 and 4000 are artificial blocks, taken to enforce the boundary conditions, and are therefore not considered part of the domain Moreno and Rabinovich (2021a), Wei and Rabinovich (2023) . When comparing the oil pressure from the two-phase flow simulation with that of the corresponding single-phase flow simulation (solving Eq. (13b)  and (14) ), we find that there is a mismatch. Closer examination reveals that the mismatch occurs due to a jump in the pressure of the single-phase simulation near the outlet, between blocks 3999 and 3998 (see red line in Fig. 11 ). We believe this occurs due to a difference in the boundary conditions of the two-phase system vs the single-phase system, where the former also has a P  c   = 0    assigned at the outlet, in addition to the prescribed pressure. However, the oil-pressure is seen to have the same structure as the two-phase curve, the two appearing to be separated by a constant value. We apply a correction by removing the pressure jump of the single-phase simulation at the outlet, as follows: (17) p  n e w  e n d   = p  o l d  e n d    ,    p  n e w  e n d − 1   = p  n e w  e n d   + ( p  o l d  e n d − 2   − p  o l d  e n d − 1   )   ,        p  n e w  e n d − 2   = p  n e w  e n d − 1   + ( p  o l d  e n d − 3   − p  o l d  e n d − 2   )   ,      . . .   ,  p  n e w  2   = p  n e w  3   + ( p  o l d  1   − p  o l d  2   )   ,    p  n e w  1   = p  n e w  2   + ( p  o l d  1   − p  o l d  2   )  ,      where p   is the pressure of the nonwetting phase (oil or CO 2    ) and the postscript denotes the block number, with “end” indicating the last block in the domain (end=3999); “new” indicates the values after correction and “old” indicates the values before correction. From the calculation of p  n e w  3998    , it can be seen that we used the pressure drop between blocks 3997 and 3998 rather than that between the blocks of 3998 and 3999. Fig. 11  shows that after applying the correction, the pressure profiles are visually matching (compare blue solid curve and black dashed curve). We note that information from the two-phase simulation is not required in order to apply this correction. Furthermore, the water saturation does not require a correction as the single-phase and two-phase water pressure profiles are in close agreement. We now implement the single-phase method of k   estimation as described in Section 3.2  and Fig. 3 , adding the correction described above when calculating P  c     in Step III of the procedure. Fig. 12  presents results for the convergence of the procedure for Cases 1 and 8 in Table 6 , expressed by the change in permeability between each iteration, E  k  i t e r    , calculated via Eq. (15) . It can be seen that for Case 1 (Fig. 12 a), E  k  i t e r     is monotonically and rapidly decreasing with the first few iterations, dropping to small values below 0.005 and then levels off. This indicates that the method is converging. However, the E  k  i t e r     curve fluctuates around a small value and therefore we adopt the approach of stopping iterations at the smallest E  k  i t e r     value. This value was found to be 0.1× 1 0  − 3      for Case 1, presented in the 5’th column of Table 6  and denoted by E  k  c o n v    . Similar results were observed for convergence of Cases 1–3 and 5–7, with the values of E  k  c o n v     provided in Table 6 . Results of E  k  i t e r     for Case 8 are presented in Fig. 12 b, where convergence is clearly not achieved and k   estimations vary widely with each iteration. Similar results were seen for Case 4 in Table 6  and the reason for this behavior is related to errors in P  c     calculation at each iteration, which will be discussed in more detail below.  Fig. 13  presents the results of the k   estimation for all 8 cases evaluated, showing k   as a function of the 1D domain normalized length x  ˜   = x / L   . It can be seen that for both oil–water and CO 2    -water cases there is an excellent agreement between the estimated and real k   for Cases 1–3 and 5–7. Only a minor mismatch is seen at the inlet of the domain (x  ˜   < 0 . 05   ) for the lowest injection rates (Cases 1 and 5). Similarly, the good estimations can be observed in Table 6 , where the overall estimation error E  k     is provided, showing values between 2.5% and 11.7% for these 6 cases. However, a very large mismatch is seen in Fig. 13  for cases 4 and 8, also observed in Table 6 , where E  K   = 1 . 6 × 1 0  8      % and 518% for cases 4 and 8, respectively. The last column in Table 6  shows values of the ratio between the pressure drop and the overall average capillary pressure. It can be seen that the estimation errors E  k     generally increase with increase of this ratio, and the largest errors occur when the ratio is significant, i.e., 41.9 and 27.8 for Cases 4 and 8, respectively. The reason for the errors in k   estimation is that P  c     is calculated via Eq. (6)  as the difference between p  n w     and p  w    , and when the two are large in comparison to P  c    , the latter is sensitive to error. For example, if p  n w   = 1050    psi and p  w   = 1000    psi, and these values have an error of only 5% in comparison to the two-phase pressures, then P  c   = p  n w   − p  w      could have a large error of up to around 250%. A large pressure drop indicates large phase pressures and therefore the ratio Δ p / P  c        corresponds to large estimation errors. Overall, the single-phase flow method was found to be applicable to cases in which Δ p / P  c        is approximately smaller than 20. This is only a subset of the many possible scenarios expected in coreflooding experiments and therefore it is a very limiting requirement. Furthermore, when testing the method on 2D and 3D cases, we found errors due to inaccuracies associated with the nonwetting-phase pressure correction, rendering the method inapplicable to these cases. The computational time of the single-phase method is significantly reduced using the simplified set of equations (Eqs. (13) –(14) ). The typical simulation time for a single iteration in Case 1, is around 2 min however the corresponding single-phase flow method iteration time would take only around 32 s.   5 Summary and conclusions This work advanced methods for estimating the sub-core, mm-scale permeability distribution in core samples from coreflooding experiments. First, we presented results of previous k   estimations, using synthetic coreflooding data from numerical experiments, that were conducted using only a single experiment. The method was extended here to include multiple experiments with different injected fluid fractions and flow rates. This new method was shown to improve k   estimations significantly and consistently, leading to high accuracy in 18 of the 22 cases we tested. Many of the limitations that were found in our previous work, such as decreasing accuracy with viscous and capillary dominated regimes, were dramatically reduced when using the multi-experiment method. Therefore, when planning coreflooding experiments, it is beneficial to conduct at least two flow rates and/or two flow fractions, and generally, including more experiments is beneficial. This work also presented a new method for dealing with regions in the core in which water is trapped. These regions are known to have limited information regarding capillary pressure, and therefore are challenging for estimating k   accurately. The new method was able to increase the overall k   estimation accuracy by up to 50% and significantly improve the accuracy of those grid blocks with trapped water. An additional method that relies on single-phase simulations for estimating k was examined. It is based on reducing the model equations by substituting the saturation experimental data in the equations. This method can potentially reduce the computational cost of the k   estimation method dramatically. However, our tests showed that while accurate estimations were achieved for 1D cases, major issues were encountered for cases in which the pressure drop is significantly larger than the average capillary pressure. In particular, the method was not feasible for 2D and 3D cases. We believe that detailed sub-core property estimations and accurate coreflooding models can significantly contribute to coreflooding analyses for characterizing reservoir rocks. These could become standard procedures in the future, both for academic research and industry, in particular in the context of CO 2     storage projects. This work presents methods which could be useful for practitioners and also provides insight on the expected accuracy of k   estimations and numerical models of coreflooding. We note that the current work is limited to drainage coreflooding, however, should be extendable to imbibition processes as well.
1 Introduction Accurate, high-resolution, and timely precipitation data are critical for a wide range of research and decision-making activities, from climate-, weather-, and water-related studies to monitoring agricultural yields and natural hazards such as floods, droughts and landslides. While conventional precipitation data are mainly collected using rain gauges, the spatial representativeness of gauge measurements is limited due to the point-scale sampling nature and uneven distribution (Kidd et al., 2017 ). Weather radars can provide three-dimensional high-resolution observations of precipitation over a large domain; however, they have only been deployed and routinely operated in a small number of developed countries (Saltikoff et al., 2019 ). Compared to those ground-based measurements, satellite-based precipitation products (SPPs) offer great advantages by extending our ability to map precipitation around the entire globe, especially over oceans, rural and remote regions, and complex terrain areas. Satellite-based precipitation measurements are typically based on infrared (IR) radiometers, passive microwave (PMW) imagers/sounders, and active microwave (AMW) sensors. Compared to IR, PMW and AMW provide more direct observations of precipitation but are currently limited to Low-Earth-orbiting (LEO) satellites only (Kidd et al., 2021b ). This leads to substantial sampling gaps between infrequent microwave overpasses, which must be filled through interpolation techniques to produce SPPs onto a consistent spatial and temporal grid (see Levizzani et al., 2020  for more details). One such interpolation algorithm is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center (CPC) MORPHing technique (CMORPH; Joyce et al., 2004 ), which was initially developed as a key component of the first-generation CMORPH (hereinafter referred to as “CMORPH1”) product. It was later enhanced with a Kalman filter to include PMW-calibrated IR precipitation (Joyce and Xie, 2011 ), and then further integrated to produce other SPPs such as the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission (IMERG; Huffman et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019 ). Thanks to the high-resolution (typically 4–10 km, 30-min), decades-long precipitation information from such SPPs, studies and simulations of the water cycle at continental and global scales have been significantly advanced in the past decade (Wu et al., 2014; Kirschbaum and Stanley, 2018; Peters-Lidard et al., 2018 ). Despite their widespread success, SPPs inevitably contain considerable estimation errors that may be attributed to three major uncertainty sources (Maggioni et al., 2022 ), stemming from sensors (Behrangi et al., 2012; Kidd et al., 2021a ), retrieval and interpolation algorithms (Tan et al., 2020 ), and sampling and scale mismatches (Steiner et al., 2003; Tang et al., 2018 ). In operation, there are continuing efforts to reduce these uncertainties and improve the accuracy of SPPs, with updates in input sensors, processing algorithms and output resolution. For example, the CPC has recently upgraded its operational SPP to the experimental second-generation CMORPH (hereinafter referred to as “CMORPH2”) by incorporating PMW observations from the new Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) sensors and forecasts from NOAA’s global forecast system (GFS). This new version is developed to provide real-time (with only 1-h latency) global precipitation estimates with improved quality especially for the cold season and over mid- and high-latitudes (Xie et al., 2019 ). In addition to improving the products themselves, the usefulness of SPPs can also be enhanced by developing reliable uncertainty estimates for them. Many works have been dedicated to this goal, with various error models developed over the years. Examples include the 2-Dimensional Satellite Rainfall Error Model (SREM2D; Hossain and Anagnostou, 2006 ), the Precipitation Uncertainties for Satellite Hydrology framework (PUSH; Maggioni et al., 2014 ), the Censored, Shifted Gamma Distribution (CSGD) based error modeling framework (Scheuerer and Hamill, 2015; Wright et al., 2017 ), the Probabilistic QPE using InfraRed Satellite Observations methodology (PIRSO; Kirstetter et al., 2018 ), and other semiparametric and nonparametric modeling techniques (Yan and Gebremichael, 2009; Gebremichael et al., 2011 ). Generally, such statistical models are trained to estimate “true” precipitation p   given any SPP retrieval S  , i.e., the conditional distribution f ( p ∣ S )    . This probabilistic characterization is particularly useful as it readily translates deterministic SPPs into ensemble input forcings, which can be straightforwardly used to drive hydrological and environmental models to account for input uncertainty (Hossain and Lettenmaier, 2006; Hartke et al., 2022 ). Owing to the challenging observing environment, the uncertainty of SPPs is particularly pronounced in complex terrain areas such as the western United States (Derin et al., 2016; Bytheway et al., 2020; Adhikari and Behrangi, 2022 ). Previous studies have shown that all precipitation-capable sensors–IR, PMW and AMW–struggle to detect and estimate orographic precipitation reliably due to its shallow nature (Arulraj and Barros, 2021; Adhikari and Behrangi, 2022 ). In addition, mountainous areas typically exhibit substantial environmental heterogeneity (e.g., in terms of topography, temperature, wind, and precipitation intensity and phases), which likely increases the uncertainty associated with SPPs. As an alternative approach to estimate precipitation over mountains, high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) models have demonstrated complementary or even better performance compared to SPPs (Zhang et al., 2018; Lundquist et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Amjad et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, these NWP models provide additional benefits by simulating other environmental variables, which can be used as additional predictors to further constrain the uncertainty estimates for SPPs (Wright et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023 ), particularly those linked to orographic precipitation (Zhang et al., 2013, 2018; Derin and Kirstetter, 2022 ). While CMORPH1 has been widely used and validated, the performance of the newly developed CMORPH2 has yet to be thoroughly examined (with only a few studies, e.g., Xie et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023 ). In this study, we focus on Northern California, where the complex terrain is known to be challenging for most SPPs including CMORPH1 (Bytheway et al., 2020 ). With a pilot reprocessing of CMORPH2 for two years (2018–2019), we employ the CSGD error modeling framework to quantify the uncertainty of both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2, using NOAA’s Stage IV product as the ground reference for error model training and verification. The CSGD-derived grid-scale uncertainty estimates for the two CMORPH products are then evaluated and compared across the study region and during heavy precipitation events. As far as we are aware, this is the first study to assess the relative performance of CMORPH2 over its predecessor, CMORPH1, in complex terrain. It should be noted that this is highly relevant to future developments of CMORPH2, as improving representation of orographic precipitation is one of the primary goals for developing CMORPH2 (Xie et al., 2019 ), though it has not yet been implemented. This study thus serves as a prototype investigation into this direction. Unlike a prior study from our team that utilized static terrain information to correct daily CMORPH1 errors (Chen et al., 2022 ), this study advances by exploring the feasibility of incorporating dynamic NWP model simulations to improve uncertainty estimates for both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 at sub-daily scales. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2  describes the study domain and datasets. In Section 3 , we detail the preprocessing method for the datasets, the CSGD error modeling framework, and introduce the strategies for error model training and verification. Section 4  presents the results of error characterization, error model validation, and error modeling with covariates, followed by a discussion in Section 5 . Finally, Section 6  addresses the conclusions and future directions of study.    2 Study area and datasets 2.1 Study area The study domain is centered around the San Francisco Bay Area in Northern California, covering 35°–40°N latitude and 120°–125°W longitude (Fig. 1 a). This 5° ×   5°region is characterized with large physiographic gradients that span from west to east, including the California Coast Ranges (which consist of the Northern and Southern Coast Ranges), the Central Valley, and the Sierra Nevada mountains. In this work, we only focus on the land region, and precipitation over the ocean is not considered. Northern California is dominated by a Mediterranean climate, in which most of the precipitation falls in a short wet season between November and March. Atmospheric rivers (ARs) accompanying Pacific storm systems contribute to the majority of annual precipitation in this region, transporting an extremely high volume of water vapor within a narrow, elongated corridor towards the West Coast of the United States (Smith et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2020a ). When the AR-induced southwesterly water influxes reach the windward slopes of the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada mountains, orographic uplift results in heavy rainfall and snowfall at higher elevations in these mountains (Dettinger et al., 2011 ). This orographic precipitation significantly impacts both California’s water resources and floods; therefore, accurate quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) is critical for decision-makers to balance the needs between water supply and flood mitigation. As previously noted, all SPPs including CMORPH1 struggle to resolve orographic precipitation and perform poorly in this region (Bytheway et al., 2020 ), making it an ideal place for implementing the error modeling framework described below.  2.2 Datasets 2.2.1 CMORPH products This study evaluates two versions of CMORPH, both developed at NOAA CPC. The first-generation CMORPH (CMORPH1) provides 30-min, 8-km gridded precipitation estimates with quasi-global coverage (60°S–60°N). This version has been reprocessed for a 25-year period from 1998 to the present to construct a Climate Data Record (CDR; Xie et al., 2018 ). Like other multi-sensor SPPs, CMORPH1 integrates PMW and IR measurements from various LEO and geostationary (GEO) satellites (Joyce et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2017 ). It primarily uses the instantaneous PMW precipitation retrievals from the LEO satellites. To fill the sampling gaps between infrequent PMW overpasses, CMORPH1 performs a time-weighted interpolation of the PMW retrievals based on motion vectors, which are computed from consecutive GEO IR images. This involves propagation in both forward and backward directions, and the satellite-only CMORPH1 precipitation estimates are calculated as the weighted mean of the propagated PMW retrievals from both directions. This “morphing” technique was first developed as part of CMORPH1, and it also functions as a key component of the IMERG algorithm (Tan et al., 2019 ). At the final stage, a bias correction is applied through PDF matching against the CPC daily gauge analysis over land and the pentad Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) gauge-satellite merged precipitation analysis over ocean (Joyce and Xie, 2011; Xie et al., 2018 ). We use the bias-corrected CMORPH1 in this study. The second-generation CMORPH (CMORPH2) has been extended to cover the entire globe (90°S–90°N). CMORPH2 is built upon the Kalman filter based merging algorithm (Joyce and Xie, 2011 ), and differs from CMORPH1 mainly in five aspects: (1) inter-calibration of PMW precipitation retrievals through PDF calibration against the Goddard Profiling Algorithm estimates (GPROF; Kummerow et al., 2015 ); (2) integration of PMW-calibrated IR precipitation estimates via the Kalman filter when PMW retrievals are not available; (3) globally-available motion vectors, which are derived using both IR images and the forecast precipitation fields from NOAA’s GFS; (4) inclusion of the latest JPSS PMW data and the JPSS-supported PMW snowfall (solid precipitation) retrievals (Meng et al., 2017 ); (5) computation of the fraction of solid precipitation, which is based on the bias-corrected GFS surface air temperature using the Sims and Liu (2015)  scheme. Because of these updates, CMORPH2 is able to produce global 30-min precipitation fields on a refined 0.05°(∼  5 km) grid with improved quality, especially for cold season precipitation (Xie et al., 2019 ). Currently CMORPH2 includes only satellite-based estimates (without gauge correction).  2.2.2 Ground reference: Stage IV We use NOAA’s Stage IV QPE product as the ground reference for training, validating and verifying the error models for the two CMORPH products. This product combines weather radars and rain gauges to provide hourly precipitation estimates (2002–present) with approximately 4-km resolution over the contiguous United States (CONUS) (Lin, 2011 ). The Stage IV dataset is subject to gauge correction and quality controls (QC) performed at 12 CONUS River Forecast Centers (RFCs). In particular, the western CONUS RFCs including the California–Nevada RFC do not include radar QPE in their production of Stage IV. Instead, they use Mountain Mapper, a gauge-only algorithm, to better reproduce the climatological variations of orographic precipitation (Nelson et al., 2016 ). Due to its high quality, Stage IV has been extensively used as the reference to validate SPPs and NWP simulations over the CONUS (Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022 ). It should be emphasized that the gauges used in Stage IV are independent of those employed in the CPC gauge analysis, which is incorporated in CMORPH1 for bias correction.  2.2.3 High-resolution regional climate simulations High-resolution (6-km) regional climate simulations (1981–2019) are obtained from a Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) modeling system for the western United States (between 29°–54°N and 132°–93°W) (Gao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018 ). The system adopts the Advanced Research WRF model version 3.8 (Skamarock et al., 2008 ), and simulations are performed at 35 sigma levels (up to 100 hPa). Its parameterization schemes include: the Morrison double-moment cloud microphysics scheme (Morrison et al., 2009 ), the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model for global climate model parameterization (RRTMG) for longwave and shortwave radiation (Iacono et al., 2008 ), the Mellor-Yamada-Janjić turbulence closure scheme (Janjić, 1994 ), and the Noah land surface model (Chen and Dudhia, 2001 ). Initial and boundary conditions (e.g., winds, temperature, pressure, and surface variables) are obtained from the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR; Mesinger et al., 2006 ). More details of the WRF model’s configuration can be found in Gao et al. (2017) . This set of regional climate simulations has successfully been used to study ARs and their hydrologic impacts over the western United States (Chen et al., 2018, 2019; Chen and Leung, 2020 ). In this study, we explore the potential to incorporate these simulations as covariates to improve the uncertainty estimates for CMORPH products. The variables considered include the WRF simulated precipitation (WRFP; mm), vertically integrated water vapor (IWV; kg m−2 ), integrated water vapor transport (IVT; kg m−1  s−1 ), and convective available potential energy (CAPE; J kg−1 ). While WRFP is archived at an hourly resolution, the latter three are only available at 6-hourly intervals. The selection of the three non-precipitation variables (IWV, IVT, and CAPE) is informed by previous studies on error modeling for SPPs over the contiguous United States (Wright et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023 ), and on the ARs-induced precipitation in California (Dettinger et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020b ). It is important to note that the aim of this study was not to search for the most effective predictors for orographic precipitation, but rather to explore the potential for improving uncertainty estimates with such predictors.    3 Methodology 3.1 Preprocessing of datasets The study period spans from 2018 to 2019, which is mainly limited by the availability of the experimental reprocessed CMORPH2 data. Since CMORPH1, CMORPH2, Stage IV and WRF simulations differ in spatial coverage, as well as in spatial and temporal resolutions, they must be reprocessed to ensure matching in space and time over the study domain (see Fig. 1 b). First, CMORPH1, Stage IV, and WRF simulations (WRFP, IWV, IVT and CAPE) are spatially resampled to CMORPH2’s 0.05° ×   0.05°grid within this region using nearest neighbor interpolation. Then, the precipitation fields from CMORPH1, CMORPH2, Stage IV, and WRFP are temporally aggregated into 6-hourly intervals for training and evaluating the CSGD error models over each grid box. This temporal scale was selected because IWV, IVT, and CAPE are only available at 6-h intervals; however, the CSGD model can readily be fitted to SPP’s native resolution if the reference data (and covariates) also match this resolution (Li et al., 2023 ).  3.2 CSGD-based error modeling framework The Censored, Shifted Gamma Distribution (CSGD) technique was first developed in Scheuerer and Hamill (2015)  to post-process ensemble precipitation forecasts, and was adapted in Wright et al. (2017)  to quantify the uncertainty of a daily, 0.25°SPP. The two-parameter gamma distribution Γ  μ , σ     has been extensively used in modeling the PDF of precipitation intensities, as reviewed in Martinez-Villalobos and Neelin (2019) . The CSGD adds a “shift” parameter δ   (δ < 0   ) into the gamma distribution, to allow for simultaneous description of precipitation occurrence and magnitude. The CSGD’s cumulative distribution function (CDF) is as follows: (1) Γ  μ , σ , δ   ( x )  = Γ  μ , σ   ( x − δ )  ,   if x ≥ 0 .   0 ,   otherwise .          where x   represents the grid-scale, 6-hourly precipitation amount (mm). We fit Eq. (1)  to the training reference data (i.e., Stage IV) to estimate the “climatological CSGD” parameters μ  , σ  , δ  . The CSGD’s CDF is “left-censored” at zero and all negative values are replaced by zero. Consequently, the vertical intercept Γ  μ , σ , δ   ( x = 0 )     describes the probability of zero precipitation (PZP), while the CDF to the right of zero, Γ  μ , σ , δ   ( x > 0 )    , is for the distribution for nonzero precipitation. In the next stage, we fit a regression system, as detailed in Eqs. (2c) (a)–(c), to obtain “conditional CSGD” parameters μ ( t )    , σ ( t )    , δ ( t )     based on the fitted climatological (i.e., unconditional) CSGD: (2a) μ ( t )  = μ α  2   + α  3   S ( t )   S  ̄          (2b) σ ( t )  = α  4   σ μ ( t )   μ        (2c) δ ( t )  = δ       where S  ̄     denotes the mean of the training SPP 6-hourly data series. All the CSGD parameters and regression coefficients α  2    –α  4     are estimated by training a past record of paired SPP and reference data. It assumes the conditional CSGD mean μ ( t )     linearly increases with SPP estimate S ( t )     at time t  , and the conditional standard deviation σ ( t )     increases proportionally with the square root of μ ( t )    . Hereafter, this regression system (Eq. (2c) a-c) is referred to as the “linear CSGD model”. To account for a nonlinear regression, Eq. (2c) (a) can be replaced with: (3) μ ( t )  = μ  α  1     log 1 p e x p m 1 ( α  1   )  α  2   + α  3   S ( t )   S  ̄             where log1p(∗) = log ( 1 + ∗ )    , and e x p m 1 ( ∗ )  = e x p ( ∗ )  − 1   . This Eq. (3)  in conjunction with Eq. (2c) (b)–(c) is hereafter referred to as the “nonlinear CSGD model”. This regression system can be extended to include additional predictors C ( t )     to improve the modeling of μ ( t )    . In this case, Eq. (3)  can be rewritten as follows (similar adjustments can be made to Eq. (2c) a for the linear version): (4) μ ( t )  = μ  α  1     log 1 p e x p m 1 ( α  1   )  α  2   + α  3   S ( t )   S  ̄     + α  5   C ( t )   C  ̄              The regression coefficients α  1    –α  5     as well as the climatological CSGD parameters [μ  , σ  , δ  ] are estimated by minimizing the mean continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) between empirical and theoretical CDFs, as detailed in Scheuerer and Hamill (2015) . Once trained, the conditional CSGD model with parameters μ ( t )    , σ ( t )    , δ ( t )     can be used to estimate the conditional distribution of possible “true” precipitation f ( p ∣ S ( t )  )    , given new SPP estimate S ( t )     (and optional predictors C ( t )    ) at time t  .  3.3 Error model training, validation and verification The CSGD error models are separately constructed for CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 for every 0.05°grid within the study area. For each grid box, the preprocessed, coincident 6-hourly data (CMORPH1, CMORPH2, Stage IV, and WRF simulations) are randomly divided into training (80%) and validation (20%) datasets to train and validate the error models, respectively. To ensure a sufficiently large sample size, the error models are trained by pooling data samples from the eight adjacent grid boxes. Before the training/validation split, two heavy precipitation events, namely, April 6–7, 2018 and February 13–15, 2019, are excluded and reserved for independent verification of the trained error models. Detailed descriptions of the events are documented by NOAA National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) in the yearly storm summaries ( https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/storm_summaries/storm_summaries.shtml ). We investigate different error model configurations, including linear and nonlinear CSGD models, both with and without covariates. In this study, WRFP, IWV, IVT, and CAPE are each considered as individual covariates, although the CSGD modeling framework allows for multiple covariates (not shown in Eq. (4) ; see Scheuerer and Hamill, 2015  for further details). For each 0.05°grid box, CSGD-estimated statistics can be computed from the fitted conditional distributions f ( p ∣ S ( t )  )     (as detailed in Section 3.2 ) given CMORPH estimates and optional covariates. These statistics include the CSGD-estimated mean, quantiles (e.g., 25% quantile, median, and 75% quantile), and confidence intervals (CI; e.g., the 50% CI represents the spread between the 25% and 75% quantiles). The probability of precipitation (POP; POP=1-PZP) can also be computed using Eq. (1) . For any given CMORPH 6-hourly precipitation amount S  ′   ( t )     (e.g., 0.5, 1, 2, …, 32 mm), the CSGD mean μ   (S  ′   ( t )    ) conditioned to this amount can be derived from Eqs. (2c) a and (3) . The conditional relative bias is then calculated by comparing the CSGD mean to S  ′   ( t )    : (5) R B = ( S  ′   ( t )  − μ ( S  ′   ( t )  )  )  / μ ( S  ′   ( t )  )  × 100 %      The CSGD-estimated quantiles and CIs are compared with Stage IV to assess whether the CSGD error models appropriately characterize the random errors of CMORPH. We compute the mean absolute error (MAE) by comparing the CSGD-derived median against Stage IV, to determine whether the trained error models can appropriately remove the systematic error in CMORPH estimates: (6) M A E = 1  n   ∑  i = 1  n   | q  c s g d , i   − o b s  i   |      where q  c s g d , i     is the CSGD-estimated median, and o b s  i      is the Stage IV reference observation. n   is the total number of data samples included in the calculation. To fully evaluate the predicted conditional CSGD distributions, we employ the CRPS, a probabilistic measure of goodness of fit that is mathematically identical to the deterministic MAE: (7) C R P S = ∫  − ∞  ∞   [ Γ  μ ( i )  , σ ( i )  , δ ( i )    ( x )  − I ( x ≥ o b s  i   )  ]   2   d x     where Γ  μ ( i )  , σ ( i )  , δ ( i )      denotes the CDF of the trained conditional CSGD with parameters μ ( t )    , σ ( t )    , δ ( t )    , and I ( ⋅ )     is a step function that takes the value of 1 if x ≥ o b s  i      and 0 otherwise. Low CRPS indicates the CSGD’s density is sharp and concentrated around the Stage IV reference, while high CRPS implies the fitted distribution is either too wide or heavily biased. The skill score based on CRPS – the continuous ranked probability skill score (CRPSS) – is also employed to measure the relative performance of trained CSGD error models over the climatological CSGD: (8) C R P S S = 1 − C R P S  C R P S  c l i m         Positive values of CRPSS indicate higher predictive skills over the climatological CSGD, with the perfect value being 1. If CRPSS is close to zero, it suggests that the fitted conditional CSGD has limited predictive skills and performs similarly to the climatological CSGD, which relies solely on the reference data.   4 Results 4.1 Error model training and uncertainty characterization Fig. 2  compares the trained linear and nonlinear CSGD error models for the selected grid boxes (GB2 and GB3; see Fig. 1 a) in the Central Valley and Sierra Nevada, respectively. To better visualize small values, which constitute the majority of precipitation data, the trained CSGD models are plotted against the 2D density of the training data samples on a logarithmic scale. The CMORPH uncertainty is characterized using a CSGD mean and a 95% confidence interval (CI; between the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles) in Fig. 2 . The former represents the conditional bias associated with CMORPH, while the latter indicates the degree of random errors.  The results suggest that the nonlinear CSGD models outperform the linear ones. The blue solid lines consistently pass through the densest areas of the scatterplots, indicating that the estimated nonlinear CSGD mean better captures the conditional bias in CMORPH. Moreover, approximately 95% of points in the scatterplots fall between the upper and lower blue dashed lines. This demonstrates a good agreement between the estimated 95% CI and the empirical spread of the reference data (when conditioned on CMORPH estimates). The CRPS scores in Fig. 2  further confirm the superior performance of the nonlinear models over their linear counterparts. Regional evaluation shows that CRPS scores for nonlinear models are generally lower than those for linear models across all grid boxes within the study area (see Figure S1 in Supplementary Material); thus, subsequent analyses focus only on nonlinear CSGD models. Intercomparison of the CSGD means (solid blue and red lines in Fig. 2 ) highlights the differences in bias patterns between the two products. Both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 6-hourly data tend to overestimate precipitation when it exceeds 10 mm. However, the bias is more pronounced in CMORPH1, as evident in the more noticeable deviation of its CSGD mean from the 1:1 line. In contrast, while CMORPH2 also exhibits overestimation, its CSGD mean either aligns more closely with or rises above the 1:1 line when the estimates are below 10 mm. In addition, the uncertainty of CMORPH products, particularly in terms of random errors, appears to be influenced by terrain. As shown in the upper versus lower panels in Fig. 2 , the CSGD-estimated 95% CI is broader for GB3 than for GB2, and the CRPS scores for GB3 are correspondingly higher. This indicates that random errors increase when moving from the Central Valley to the Sierra Nevada. For CMORPH2, the CSGD-estimated mean also clearly indicates a potential location-dependent underestimation bias, which is further discussed below.  Fig. 3  compares the estimation biases of CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 for different satellite-observed precipitation amounts. The relative bias is calculated (see Eq. (5) ) by comparing the CSGD mean – estimated from the trained gridded (0.05°) CSGD database – with the given CMORPH precipitation amount. To account for light, medium, and heavy precipitation scenarios, 6-hourly CMORPH precipitation amounts of 2 mm, 8 mm, and 16 mm are respectively applied in Fig. 3 . Generally, CMORPH1 tends to overestimate medium-to-heavy precipitation across the entire region, while CMORPH2 features a “mixed” and less biased pattern overall. For light precipitation, both products are characterized by an overall underestimation bias, but CMORPH1 indicates some highly localized anomalies with significant overestimation. These anomalies coincide with large water bodies within the study domain, such as San Francisco Bay, Lake Tahoe, Clear Lake, Lake Berryessa, and Folsom Lake (see Fig. 3 a).
