This is known as a false-alarm issue of PMW precipitation retrievals over inland water bodies, which could introduce elevated, unrealistic rainfall events (Tian and Peters-Lidard, 2007 ). The new product, CMORPH2, appears to have successfully mitigated most of these detection errors. Region-dependent bias becomes evident in Fig. 3 : both products generally overestimate precipitation in the Central Valley, particularly in its southern half. For mountainous regions such as the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada, CMORPH2 consistently underestimates precipitation, while CMORPH1 is more likely to overestimate it under the heavy precipitation scenario. Fig. 4  further examines the uncertainty of CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 in terms of other CSGD-derived statistics, including the POP and 25% quantile (Q1). Compared to CMORPH2, CMORPH1 consistently displays higher POP values across the study area (Figs. 4 a–b). The POP, which indicates the likelihood of actual non-zero precipitation when the satellite observes none, implies that CMORPH1 has missed more precipitation events. The elevated POP values for CMORPH1 are particularly notable in the Sierra Nevada. While CMORPH2 demonstrates substantial improvements, it still records relatively higher POP values in the Northern Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada, highlighting the challenges faced by spaceborne sensors in effectively detecting orographic precipitation in these areas. For the medium CMORPH precipitation amount (8 mm), the CSGD-estimated Q1 (Figs. 4 c–d) – and even Q3 (the 75% quantile; see Figure S2 in Supplementary Material) – for CMORPH1 remains low and is biased towards zero in certain locations such as the San Francisco Bay, lakes and the inner Sierra Nevada mountains. For those water bodies, it is clear that this bias is caused by the false alarms of PMW retrievals as discussed above. In the case of the Sierra Nevada mountains, this is likely attributed to certain precipitation events being masked out over snow/ice-covered areas due to the snow/ice screening procedure in the CMORPH1 algorithm (Joyce et al., 2004 ). The upgraded CMORPH2 algorithm has addressed most of these errors, shifting the density of conditional CSGD upward towards the 1:1 line. Consequently, the estimated Q1 for CMORPH2 increases and well captures the orographic gradients of precipitation in the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada. Despite this enhancement, the interquartile range (between Q1 and Q3) suggests that the random errors in CMORPH2 remain large over the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada (see Supplemental Figure S2d).    4.2 Error model validation Fig. 5  provides a direct evaluation of the CSGD uncertainty estimates based on the validation dataset at the selected locations (see Fig. 1 a). Regardless of the specific bias type – whether it is overestimation in CMORPH1 (Fig. 5 b) or underestimation in CMORPH2 (Figs. 5 a,c) – the varied systematic errors in both products can be effectively corrected using the CSGD-estimated median at different locations (similar results for the CSGD mean are not shown). The majority of Stage IV observations are well bracketed by the CSGD-estimated 50% CI. For those unbracketed outliers, a wider estimated CI (e.g., 95% CI) can be applied to account for larger random errors. Additionally, the estimated uncertainty bounds can be further improved with the inclusion of additional predictors (detailed in Section 4.3 ). Similar to the findings in Fig. 2 , the width of the 50% CI for both CMORPH products is wider over the grid boxes GB1 and GB3 than GB2, suggesting increased random errors in complex terrain areas. Evaluation metrics corresponding to Fig. 5 , which account for the entire validation dataset, are detailed in Supplemental Table S1. These statistics further confirm the validity of the trained CSGD error models.  Fig. 6  extends the validation across the entire study domain and compares the CSGD estimated median against Stage-IV grid by grid. Results show that the trained CSGD error models can reduce bias in both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 (Figs. 6 a,d), lowering MAE by 28.4% and 12.8% on average (Figs. 6 c,f), respectively. After applying the CSGD-estimated median, CMORPH1 achieves an MAE level (Fig. 6 b) similar to that of the original CMORPH2 (Fig. 6 d). This relative strength of the satellite-only CMORPH2 over the gauge-corrected CMORPH1 proves the success in improving CMORPH2 precipitation retrievals. Interestingly, areas with the highest MAE – such as the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada – still exhibit relatively high MAE values after accounting for the nonlinear bias. Similar to the results in Figs. 6 b,e, the CRPS maps for the trained CSGD models (not shown) also indicate lower overall CRPS scores for CMORPH2 while its largest CRPS values are primarily found in the mountainous areas. Both deterministic and probabilistic measures reflect the fact that the uncertainty of CMORPH2 in estimating orographic precipitation is largely attributed to random errors, which require additional predictors to explain.   Fig. 7  examines the predictive skills of the trained CSGD models in comparison to their climatological counterparts, as measured by CRPSS. The error models trained for CMORPH2 yield more skillful predictions than the climatological CSGDs. The CRPSS for CMORPH1 generally features lower values, and even falls between 0.0–0.05 in the northeast corner of the study domain (Fig. 7 a). This indicates that, in the high-altitude area of Sierra Nevada, the trained conditional CSGDs for CMORPH1 are close to the climatology (i.e., the unconditional CSGD distributions solely fitted by the reference). In this region, CMORPH1’s performance is hindered by several factors, including false alarms, missed precipitation, and reduced data samples due to the snow/ice surface screening procedure as previously noted. These complicating factors lead to inefficient fitting of the parametric error models, relegating the model’s performance to a climatological standard. It is worth noting that the CRPSS values in Fig. 7 b also decrease in this region, suggesting that even the error models for CMORPH2 experience some degradation there.  4.3 Error modeling with WRF-simulated covariates Fig. 8  presents the relative improvements obtained by including different WRF-simulated predictors into the error models for CMORPH2 (refer to Figure S3 in Supplementary Material for a similar analysis for CMORPH1). It is not surprising that the WRFP stands out as the most informative predictor, with a CRPS reduction of up to 35% (Fig. 8 a). The spatial map in Fig. 8 b further reveals that WRFP can introduce widespread and substantial increases in model performance across the entire study region, especially in the Northern Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada. Following WRFP, CAPE and IVT offer modest improvements with CRPS decreases typically below 6%, mainly observed along the coast. This coastal feature of IVT- and CAPE-induced enhancements may result from the interaction between incoming oceanic moisture (indicated by IVT) and terrain barrier, which could introduce forced vertical motion in the Coasts Ranges (Huang et al., 2020b ). Although CAPE itself does not cause vertical motion, its high values suggest a potential for strong vertical motion, which is a key indicator of orographic precipitation (Derin and Kirstetter, 2022 ). Incorporating IWV results in only minimal improvements (less than 1%), so only WRFP, CAPE, and IVT are further discussed below. As the error models trained for CMORPH1 demonstrate less skillful performance, they generally achieve larger and more extensive improvements when incorporating these WRF-simulated covariates (comparing Fig. 8  with Fig.S3).  Fig. 9  compares the CSGD-estimated median and 50% CI from the error models with and without WRF-simulated covariates at three selected locations. These locations correspond to the yellow grid boxes highlighted in Figs. 8 b–d, each representing a grid where the WRF-simulated covariates – WRFP, CAPE, and IVT – have notably reduced the training CRPS, respectively. This comparison clearly demonstrates the relative improvements of the covariate-incorporated error models. WRFP helps in capturing the Stage-IV observations more accurately while narrowing the estimated CIs, leading to improved CSGD estimates in most cases (Fig. 9 a). The benefits offered by WRFP imply the promising performance of NWP models relative to SPPs in resolving orographic precipitation. IVT only offers benefits in specific situations, mainly enhancing the estimated CIs to better bracket the reference observations, especially for CMORPH1 (Fig. 9 c). CAPE also improves the CSGD uncertainty estimates in a few cases (Fig. 9 b), with results that seem to correlate better with Stage IV observations. Evaluation metrics based on the entire validation dataset for the three grid boxes are summarized in Supplemental Table S2. These statistics further substantiate the improvements offered by incorporating the covariates into the error models: the covariate-constrained CSGD median typically reduces the MAE and increases the correlation with the reference Stage IV, while the estimated CIs are more likely to capture the Stage IV observations.  Fig. 10  compares the mean CRPSS maps of the CSGD error models that incorporate the covariate of WRFP, CAPE or IVT, respectively. Compared to Fig. 7 , the incorporation of WRFP elevates the CRPSS to 0.4–0.6 across most of the study domain. The CRPSS maps for both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 after incorporating WRFP are similar (Figs. 10 a,d), eliminating the difference between the two products as shown in Fig. 7 . This suggests that the uncertainty, which is not well characterized by the non-covariate error model for CMORPH1, can be addressed by incorporating WRFP. The shortcomings of CMORPH1 in resolving orographic precipitation can be effectively compensated by WRF-simulated precipitation. The increases in CRPSS provided by IVT and CAPE are localized. Relative to Fig. 7 , IVT only adds some predictive skills at certain coastal areas and around inner Sierra Nevada, while CAPE is most effective along the coast. Similar results are obtained through the evaluation using the deterministic MAE (see Figure S4 in Supplementary Material).    4.4 Performance in heavy precipitation events The performance of different error models is further assessed during the two independent heavy precipitation events. Fig. 11  compares the precipitation amounts for the April 6–7, 2018 event, including the Stage-IV estimates, original CMORPH2 estimates and CSGD-estimated median and 75% quantile from both the non-covariate and WRFP-incorporated error models.  Comparing the original CMORPH2 (Fig. 11 d) with Stage IV (Fig. 11 a), CMORPH2 noticeably underestimates the total precipitation across most of the region, failing to reproduce the spatial gradients and capture the orographic enhancement of precipitation in the Northern Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada. The application of the non-covariate error models enhances the representation of both the spatial pattern and storm centers (Fig. 11 b), though the magnitude remains below Stage-IV estimates. This discrepancy is due to the substantial random errors of both CMORPH products in mountainous regions, which cannot be adequately addressed by the CSGD median, as previously discussed. To account for this residual uncertainty, the CSGD-estimated 75% quantile provides a better approximation of storm total accumulations (Fig. 11 c). Incorporating WRFP into the error models leads to further enhancements (Figs. 11 e,f). With WRF-simulated precipitation, the 75% quantile estimates more accurately reproduce the storm patterns as observed by Stage-IV. Fig. 12  examines the performance of the trained error models for CMORPH1 during the same event. Unlike CMORPH2, CMORPH1 generally captures the heavy precipitation band in the north of the study area, but the storm center is shifted to the west of the Sierra Nevada (Fig. 12 d). Because of the snow/ice surface screening procedure, there is also substantial “missed” precipitation in the northeastern high-altitude mountains. In this case, even using the 75% quantile estimates, the precipitation totals in the Sierra Nevada cannot be resolved by the non-covariate error models (Figs. 12 b,c). In contrast, the storm center in the Sierra Nevada is well recovered when WRFP is incorporated as the covariate. Similar evaluation results for the February 12–15, 2019 event also demonstrate the promising performance of the trained error models, especially the WRFP-incorporated models (refer to Figures S5–S6 in Supplementary Material for details). As the WRF model simulates orographic precipitation more accurately in this instance (not shown), the performance of the trained error models for CMORPH2 is even more superior compared to the 2019 event (Fig. 11  vs. Supplemental Fig. S5). Nonetheless, the results for CMORPH1 do not display a comparable relative enhancement. Because too many CMORPH1 retrievals were masked out (mainly over the Northern Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada) during this winter precipitation event, it becomes challenging to recover those missing precipitation, even with the more accurately simulated WRFP covariate. Supplemental Table S3 provides the evaluation metrics for the two heavy precipitation events, demonstrating substantial improvements in MAE and correlation coefficients when the CMORPH estimates are corrected by various CSGD models.     5 Discussion Over the study area, CMORPH2 shows notable improvements over its predecessor, particularly in resolving the orographic precipitation gradients over the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada (Figs. 3 , 4 , and 6 ). This may be due to the improved estimates of cold season precipitation in CMORPH2 (Xie et al., 2019 ), as most of California’s precipitation occurs during the winter months. Future studies will further evaluate CMORPH2’s performance in estimating orographic precipitation in complex terrain areas with diverse climates. The study also demonstrates the promise of the CSGD-based error modeling framework, which offers a simple yet flexible way to quantify the uncertainty of CMORPH, even in complex terrain. The trained CSGD database can be employed to derive a variety of statistics to diagnose the errors in historical CMORPH records (Figs. 3 , 4 ), and to predict the uncertainty associated with new CMORPH estimates (Figs. 5 , 9 ). This echoes the call for a “paradigm shift” of error analysis of SPPs, moving from metrics-based evaluation to error modeling, as an error model encapsulates the full error information distilled into its parameters (Tian et al., 2016 ). Using these parameters, advanced statistics can be created to meet various application requirements. For instance, the fitted pixel-scale CSGD database can be combined with a space–time correlation model to generate ensemble precipitation fields for hydrological modeling (Hartke et al., 2022, 2023 ). Despite its great potential, the trained error models face the most challenges in the high-altitude Sierra Nevada (Fig. 7 ). To improve the uncertainty estimates there, inclusion of additional predictors such as WRF-simulated precipitation seems a promising solution. In this way, the CSGD modeling framework serves as a parametric scheme to merge data- and physics-driven precipitation estimates for better mapping of orographic precipitation (Li et al., 2020; Amjad et al., 2020 ). While other WRF-simulated covariates – IVT, CAPE and IWV – are also explored, it is not surprising that they are less informative relative to WRFP in enhancing the error model’s performance. To maximize the value of these simulations, the method of their incorporation needs to be meticulously designed. For example, the explanatory power of IVT may be underestimated as this study only considers grid-scale IVT estimates. Prior studies indicate that IVT’s effectiveness in predicting precipitation amounts requires its integration over space and time and along its transport path (Chen et al., 2018 ). In addition, atmospheric variables directly linked to orographic precipitation may better constrain the uncertainty estimates. Previous studies have recommended a number of diagnostic variables that account for moisture availability and orography-induced air motion (i.e., orographic lifting) (Shige et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2017; Derin and Kirstetter, 2022 ), which are worth exploring in future work. Because the mountainous environment is highly variable, physiographic predictors like IVT, CAPE, and IWV often exhibit complex, nonlinear, and time-varying relations and interactions in determining orographic precipitation. This poses challenges to parametric models like the CSGD method due to their subjective way of selecting predictors and their inflexible prescribed model structure (e.g., Eq. (4) ) for ingesting predictors (Ghazvinian et al., 2021 ). In contrast, recent advances in machine learning (ML) have demonstrated the superior performance of ML models in discovering skillful predictors (Zhang et al., 2022 ), explaining their space–time interactions and patterns, and modeling the complex relations between them and SPP errors (Chen et al., 2022 ). This is another direction for future investigations. It should be also noted that CMORPH and the reference Stage-IV differ in spatiotemporal scales: CMORPH data actually represent instantaneous precipitation retrieved from a PMW overpass in a 30-min time window, while Stage IV precipitation is aggregated on an hourly scale. This scale mismatch could introduce additional uncertainty, but the 6-hourly aggregation we applied might have mitigated this issue to a certain degree. The Stage IV reference data also contains errors, especially over the complex terrain areas such as the western United States (Nelson et al., 2016 ). However, it remains arguably one of the best reference datasets currently available for this region.  6 Conclusions Satellite-based precipitation products (SPPs) have expanded our ability to access precipitation information globally, particularly in ungauged areas such as complex terrain regions. However, space-borne sensors face challenges in detecting and estimating orographic precipitation, which greatly increases the uncertainty of SPPs in such places. As part of continuing efforts to improve the accuracy of SPPs, NOAA CPC has recently upgraded its operational SPP to CMORPH2, the second-generation CMORPH (Xie et al., 2019 ). In addition, the reliability of SPPs can be further enhanced by developing robust uncertainty estimates (Li et al., 2023 ). This study aims to demonstrate the potential of integrating advancements in both these areas to improve the performance of SPPs in complex terrain areas. With a pilot reprocessing of CMORPH2 for two years (2018–2019), we employ the CSGD error modeling framework to build error models for the new product CMORPH2 and its predecessor, CMORPH1, at a 6-hourly scale over Northern California. The relative improvements of CMORPH2 over CMORPH1 are quantified in terms of error reduction using a set of CSGD-derived statistics. Their uncertainty estimates, derived from the trained CSGD error models, are evaluated against the ground reference Stage IV in both the validation phase and independent heavy precipitation events. With high-resolution regional climate simulations, this study also investigates the possibility of enhancing uncertainty estimates of orographic precipitation retrievals by incorporating additional physics-based covariates. The major conclusions are summarized as follows: (1) The CSGD-based uncertainty characterization results highlight the superior performance of CMORPH2 over CMORPH1. While CMORPH1 tends to overestimate medium-to-heavy precipitation across the study region, the overall estimation bias in CMORPH2 has been generally reduced. Additionally, CMORPH2 has successfully reduced the detection errors contained in CMORPH1, including the false-alarm errors (over the inland water bodies) and the missed precipitation events (mainly in the Sierra Nevada). Consequently, CMORPH2 is generally better able to capture the orographic precipitation gradients over the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada. (2) Validation results show that the trained CSGD error models for both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 provide reliable uncertainty estimates over most of the study region. These models reduce bias in both products, lowering MAE by an average of 28.4% for CMORPH1 and 12.8% for CMORPH2. Despite this correction, the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada still exhibit high residual random errors that require additional predictors to reduce. The most challenging area remains the high-altitude Sierra Nevada. Over this area, the predictive skill of the model for CMORPH2 is greatly reduced (with CRPSS of 0.2–0.3), while the model for CMORPH1 shows almost no skill (with CRPSS close to 0). (3) Incorporating WRFP as a covariate can lead to substantial, region-wide enhancement of the error models, resulting in a CRPS reduction of up to 35%. The WRFP-incorporated error models for CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 boost their CRPSS values to 0.35–0.5 over the challenging high-altitude Sierra Nevada, demonstrating improved uncertainty estimates for orographic precipitation. Both CAPE and IVT only offer modest improvements locally, with CRPS decreases generally below 6%. IVT adds some predictive skills in certain coastal areas and the inner Sierra Nevada, while CAPE is most effective along the coast. (4) Independent verification further underscores the solid performance of the trained error models for both CMORPH1 and CMORPH2 during two heavy precipitation events (April 6–7, 2018, and February 12–15, 2019). Due to relatively large random errors in such extremes, the CSGD-estimated 75% quantile provides a better approximation of storm total accumulations. The inclusion of WRFP further improves the uncertainty estimates for orographic precipitation in the Sierra Nevada, which is particularly critical for CMORPH1 in estimating storms over this region. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the parametric CSGD framework in characterizing the uncertainty of CMORPH products over Northern California, while also point to the critical role of physically-simulated atmospheric variables in enhancing the uncertainty estimates of their orographic precipitation retrievals. However, as discussed in Section 5 , the selection of environmental predictors and the way they are incorporated may not be optimal in this study. Future studies will focus on deepening our understanding of the relationship between environmental predictors and CMORPH2 errors across various complex terrain regions. With the newly released continental “convection-permitting” (4-km) hydroclimate reanalysis dataset (Rasmussen et al., 2023 ), we are working to develop ML tools to automatically identify the most informative environmental predictors and to model their interactions with orographic precipitation. Advances in this direction could ultimately contribute to enhance the uncertainty estimates for CMORPH2 in representing orographic precipitation on a broader scale.
1 Introduction In recent years, biochar is widely applied in environmental remediation, soil improvement, and greenhouse gas emission reduction due to high specific area, high adsorption, and rich functional groups (Cao et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2023 ). It has been extensively reported that biochar has great potential for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing organic carbon sequestration (Woolf et al., 2010; Xia et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2021 ). Biochar is also used to fertilize farmland, improve soil structure, remediate heavy metal contamination, and improve soil water retention (Choudhury and Lansing, 2020; Feng et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2023 ). When biochar enters the soil environment, the large particles of biochar will be cracked and aged to produce much more micro-scale and nano-scale biochar particles (Spokas et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019 ). Then, they are transported through runoff, infiltration into deeper soil zones, and even groundwater (Chen et al., 2022; Guggenberger et al., 2008 ). In particular, the sub-micron biochar (0.45–2 μm) is considered to be the main source of BCs dispersed in the soil (Fang et al., 2020 ). Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is quite an active component and can influence the transport of many materials in soil or groundwater. Because the biogeochemical properties of DOM are primarily influenced by its structure (e.g., molecular weight, composition, and functional groups), it has complex chemical diversities (Kellerman et al., 2014 ). Previous studies have found that the presence of DOM can significantly play an essential role in influencing the transport and retention of microplastics, heavy metal, and other micro- and nanoparticles and colloids (Chen et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2021; Wu and Cheng, 2016; Yan et al., 2019 ). However, the effect of DOM on the transport of micrometer and nanoparticles is either potentially facilitative or inhibitory under different conditions. It has been reported that DOM can cause aggregation of micro- and nanoparticles by electrostatic adsorption and complexation, then deposit them in porous media (Zhang et al., 2024 ). Ren et al. found that DOM makes the particles susceptible to collision, aggregation, and even precipitation via electrostatically adsorbing on the surface of nano-TiO2  (Ren et al., 2017 ). On the contrary, Le et al. found that DOM can increase the apparent solubility of hydrophobic organic compounds and decrease the adsorption of hydrophobic organic compounds to sediments (Le and Hwang, 2023 ). It has been found that BCs affect the release of soil organic matter as they transport vertically through the soil (Zhao and Shang, 2024 ). However, it is not clear how soil organic matter affects BCs transport. A number of laboratory studies have been reported that biochar can adsorb humic/fulvic acid from soil through hydrogen bonding and π-π bonding (Hao et al., 2024; Yang and Xing, 2010 ). In addition, It has been reported that the presence of fulvic acid significantly promoted their transport in porous media (Yang et al., 2019 ). However, natural soil is a real and complex resource, whether DOM extracted from soil facilitates or inhibits the transport of BCs in porous media deserves more in-depth studies. Furthermore, the effects of multidimensional conditions and different layered structures have not been considered, which may not be a good representation of complex natural soil and groundwater systems. Compared with the one-dimensional experiments (column experiments), the two-dimensional (2-D) experiments are closer to the natural hydrodynamic conditions (Dong et al., 2019 ). This method breaks through the limitations of the “black box” method and visualizes the actual transport process of BCs in porous media. The 2-D visualization system is mainly based on the theory of light transmission and uses a CCD camera to record the transport behavior of experimental samples in a 2-D sand tank in real-time. Due to the linear relationship between fluid saturation and light intensity (Alazaiza et al., 2019 ), real-time high-resolution images of BCs can be transformed into concentration distributions by this technique. Based on light transmission visualization (LTV) technique, Li et al. investigated the distribution and transport pattern of LNAPL in inclined soil layers, and continuously and dynamically observed its changes throughout the transport process (Li et al., 2023 ). LTV has also been used to reflect the transport behavior of micro- and nanoparticles with colloidal contaminants(e.g., graphene oxide, DNAPL, and NZVI) in 2-D porous media in real-time and without intrusion (Dong et al., 2019; Kashuk et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2022 ). Based on previous 2-D experiments, Zhao et al. successfully analyzed the migration pattern of biochar colloids in porous media using LTV (Zhao et al., 2023 ). Through this method, the spatial distribution of BCs under different conditions can be provided almost instantaneously, enabling non-invasive concentration measurements. In this study, the overarching purpose is to reveal the transport mechanisms of BCs in the presence of DOM derived from natural soil in porous media. using a real-time, non-invasive 2-D visualization system. The transport behavior and main mechanisms of BCs under different combinations of layer structure, pH, IS, and DOM were investigated by LTV and 2-D sand tanks. The specific objectives are as follows: (1) to determine the effects and mechanism analysis of different DOM concentrations on the transport of BCs; (2) to study the effects and mechanism of the transport of BCs by changing the layer structure, pH, and IS in the presence of DOM; (3) to simulate the transport of BCs under the combined conditions. These results will provide a perspective to help assess the transport behavior of BCs in the presence of DOM and whether its interaction will introduce new environmental hazards.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 DOM and biochar colloids preparation This study collected a 0–20 cm surface layer of uncontaminated black soil in Xiangfang District (116.31° N, 40.45° E), Harbin City, with few artificial disturbances at the sampling sites. Soil bulk density was 1.4 g/cm3 , pH=6.9 and soil organic matter content was 2.1 %. 10 g of soil was mixed with 20 mL of deionized water and shaken at room temperature and 200 rpm for 24 h, centrifuged at 10000g for 20 min and filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane. Finally, they are freeze-dried for further use and storage at 4℃. Wheat straw was pulverized and heated to 500 °C at 10 °C/min for 2 h under high temperatures and anaerobic conditions (Xu et al., 2016 ). In preparing BCs, 6 g of biochar was sonicated with deionized water, 0.45–2 μm biochar particles were obtained according to Stokes' law (Zhao et al., 2023 ). Detailed preparation process is described in the Supplementary Information S1  .  2.2 Characteristics of biochar and DOM The morphological characteristics of BCs of DOM were characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, HT7820, Japan). Measure the static contact angle of biochar based on the sessile droplet method using a contact angle meter (Kino Industry Co., Ltd, USA). Functional groups of biochar and DOM were analyzed using FTIR (Nicolet IS10) using the KBr pressing method. ζ-potential and the hydrodynamic diameter (HDD) of BCs were determined using a Zetasizer (Malvern) under different solution chemistry conditions with different DOM concentrations. The three-dimensional excitation-emission matrix (3D-EEM) fluorescence spectra of soil DOM samples were obtained by a fluorescence spectrophotometer (RF-6000).  2.3 Porous media preparation 20/40, 40/80, and 80/120 mesh translucent quartz sand were used. The quartz sand should be soaked in 0.25 M HNO3  and 0.25 M NaOH solution for 24 h before use and finally rinsed with deionized water until pH is neutral and dried at 70℃ (Michael R.Niemet, 2001 ).  2.4 2-D visualization system The 2-D visualization system includes a 2-D sand tank, light source, dark room, and CCD camera, and the schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 1  a. The sand tank is 50 cm long, 30 cm high, and 3 cm wide. Three channels are evenly distributed on both sides of the sand tank. The entire experiment was done in a dark room (Fig. 1 b).  2.5 2-D sand tank experiments The flow field in the 2-D sand tank consists of a background flow field and an injection flow field. The porous medium was constructed by filling the sand tank with treated quartz sand. For different porous media, two types of heterogeneous sand tanks were constructed (Fig. 1 c and d). Type 1: The upper layer is medium sand, and the lower layer is fine sand. Type 2: The upper layer is medium sand, and the lower layer is coarse sand. In both types of filling, the proportion of layers is 50 %. Throughout the experiments, the flow rate of the background flow field was controlled at 2 mL/min. The injection port was set 5 cm from the left side and 10 cm from the bottom of the sand tank. The flow rate of the injection flow field was 0.5 mL/min, and the injection duration was 200 min. The total duration of the experiment was 600 min. The detailed experimental conditions are shown in Table 1  . Gray level images (Fig. S2, S3, S4 and S5 ) in the sand tank were captured by CCD camera with an interval of 1 min. After subtracting the background from the gray-level images, a MATLAB program is developed to process and analyze the image and convert gray-level images to color figures based on the Beer-Lambert law.  2.6 Numerical simulations and DLVO theory Several numerical models are useful for simulating micro/nanoparticle transport in porous media. This study uses a simplified Double-Monod model to fit the BTC for BCs transport with the presence of DOM in the 2-D porous medium. The model has been shown to successfully simulate the fate and transport of hydrocarbons in multidimensional saturated porous media (Dong et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2023 ). In which the transport of BCs in porous media was analyzed mainly by comparing the first-order sorption coefficient in the model. By simulating the transport behavior of BCs in the presence of DOM conditions, the understanding of the transport behavior of BCs in porous media can be further advanced. Specific details of the model are detailed in Supplementary Information S2  .  The interactions between BCs and quartz sand under different experimental conditions were explained using the DLVO theory, and the specific calculations will be described in detail in Supplementary Information S3  .   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Properties of DOM and biochar Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images (Fig. 2  a, b, and c) showed that the BCs were irregular lumps or flakes with an average particle size of about 590 nm. The contact angle of biochar under water was measured to be 121.14°, indicating that the BCs used in this study were hydrophobic. 3D-EEM spectra of DOM derived from soil in this study showed the presence of humic acid-like substances (Fig. 2 d). Two different peaks were detected in region V, indicating that the DOM used in this experiment was mainly humic acid-like organic matter. In addition, the DOM EEM spectra were calculated to have a fluorescence index (FI) of 1.75, a biotic index (BI) of 0.729, and a humic index (HI) of 13.05. The UV–vis spectra of the BCs and DOM were presented in Fig. 2 e The UV250 /UV365  value for DOM was 6.68 (>3.5) (Velten et al., 2011 ), indicating that the organic matter extracted from the soil in this study was dominated by fulvic acid. According to the results of elemental analysis (Element Analyzer，Thermo Scientific Flash Smart), the elemental composition of DOM is C (14.02 %), N (0.66 %), H (2.14 %), and S (0.71 %). In addition, by Zetasizer (Malvern), the value of ζ-potentials of DOM is negative, indicating that the surface distribution of DOM consists of negative charges (Fig. S1 ). In this study, we chose the wavelength at 672 nm to evaluate the concentration of BCs in the effluent, and the corresponding calibration curve is shown in Fig. 2 f The FT-IR results of BCs clearly confirmed the presence of –OH (3640 cm−1 ), C-H (3046 cm−1 ), C=O (1601 cm−1 ), C=C (1436 cm−1 ), and C-O (1108 cm−1 ) functional groups on the surface of BCs (Fig. 2 g). Additionally, the FT-IR of DOM shows that it is rich in oxygen-containing functional groups, including mainly –OH (3434 cm−1 ), C-H (2927 cm−1 ), C=C (1409 cm−1 ), C-O-C (1108 cm−1 ), and C-O (1024 cm−1 ). The ζ-potentials and hydrodynamic diameter of the BCs were presented in Fig. 2 h and Fig. 2 i, respectively. Under different chemical conditions and in the presence of DOM, BCs show a large number of negative charges. In addition, the negative charge density on the surface of BCs tended to increase with increasing DOM concentration, decreasing IS, and increasing pH. In contrast, the hydrodynamic diameter of BC in the presence of DOM tended to decrease with increasing DOM and decreasing IS with increasing pH.  3.2 Visualization of BCs in the presence of DOM transport and retention in 2-D porous media 3.2.1 Effects of DOM concentration The visualization images of the transport of BCs observed at different time intervals under the influence of DOM are shown in Fig. 3  a. The plume of BCs in the presence of DOM during transport was clearly visible as it dispersed upwards in the 2-D sand tank. As in previous studies, gravity had little effect on BCs transport in the experiment (Cai et al., 2015 ). In addition, by comparing the images of BCs transport at the same time, we found that the plume area of BCs in the sand tank was larger with increasing DOM concentration. Especially after 300 min, the plume of BCs under 20 mg/L DOM and 50 mg/L DOM conditions was able to flow well out of the whole sand tank compared with 10 mg/L DOM. It can be seen from Fig. 3 a that BCs are more accessible to flow out of the sand tank when the DOM concentration is 50 mg/L. Fig. 3 c shows the observed and simulated BTCs for the transport of BCs. The (C/C0 )max  values of BCs increase from 0.09 to 0.14 as the DOM concentration increases from 10 mg/L to 50 mg/L. Correspondingly, the total mass recovery (TMR) of BCs also increases dramatically from 36.94 % to 64.27 % (Table.1 ). The k values of the BCs transport decreased from 0.0057 min−1  to 0.0028 min−1  as the concentration of DOM increased from 10 mg/L to 50 mg/L. These results suggested that the mobility and stability of BCs increased as DOM concentration increased. Due to the loose and porous structure of BCs (Fig. S1 ) and the presence of functional groups such as –OH, C=C, etc. (Fig. 2 g), a small amount of DOM was adsorbed or physically filled on the surface of the biochar through hydrogen bonding interactions/ π-π bonding interactions (Fig. 3  b) (Engel and Chefetz, 2019; Pan et al., 2008; Yang and Xing, 2010 ),. In addition, through the TEM images of BCs we found that the stability of BCs was higher and the dispersion was better with the increase of DOM concentration. The ζ-potential of BCs in the presence of DOM and quartz sand was negative in all experiment conditions (Fig. 2 h and Table S2 ). The average ζ-potential of BCs decreased from –32.8 mV to −41.5 mV with the increase of DOM concentration from 10 mg/L to 50 mg/L. As a result, the surface negative charge density of BCs becomes larger, which further enhances the electrostatic repulsion between BCs and the quartz sand surface. Similar results have been observed in the HDD of BCs. The BCs under high DOM conditions had better dispersion and stability, and their HDD was smaller. Based on DLVO theory (Fig. 3 d), the repulsive electrostatic force between BCs and quartz sand is less than the attractive Van der Wales force under different concentrations of DOM. The total interaction energy increased with the increase in DOM concentration. Furthermore, based on previous studies (Bradford et al., 2006 ), collector and colloid dimensions, the ratio of colloid diameter to collector diameter is considered to be an important factor affecting pore clogging, especially more significant when the value of dp (colloid diameter)/dc (collector diameter) is greater than a critical value dp/dc = (min (0.0017), max (0.18)). The maximum ratio of BCs mean diameter to quartz sand was 0.0034, 0.0032, and 0.0024 (>0.0017) at 10 mg/L, 20 mg/L, and 50 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 3 e). It suggests that although the presence of DOM increases the repulsion between BCs, it also induces a clogging effect for large-size BCs in small-size quartz sand media. Hence, the enhanced transport of BCs in the presence of DOM could be explained by decreased aggregation and clogging effect and increased electrostatic repulsion.  3.2.2 Effects of porous media Due to the change of layer structure, the transport behavior of BCs in the presence of DOM in the sand tank was also changed (Fig. 4  a). The direction of diffusion of the BCs plume changed significantly after 30 min of BCs injection. The presence of coarse sand layer in Type 2 resulted in preferential channel (Allaire et al., 2009 ), most of the BCs entered into the coarse sand layer, and only a few in the medium sand layer. It is inferred here that there may be a capillary barrier at the interface junction of the layer structure (Cho et al., 2009 ), which altered the transport path of BCs. In addition, changes in flow velocities in different sand layers due to changes in sand grain size, which in turn can also have an impact on the transport of BCs (Dong et al., 2022 ). The coarse sand layer (0.124 cm/min) in Type 2 has a greater flow velocity compared to the fine sand layer (0.054 cm/min) in Type 1. The decrease in flow velocity caused BCs to slow down significantly in the fine sand layer, which prolonged the interaction time between BCs and quartz sand and caused more BCs to be retained in the sand tank. In addition, the reduction in flow velocity led to a decrease in hydrodynamic shear stress, which inhibits the transportation of BCs in the porous medium. In significant contrast to Type 2, all of the BCs in Type 1 entered the middle sand layer. It is hypothesized here that it may be due to the fact that the capillary barrier between the sand layers in Type 1 is larger than the dispersion threshold of BCs in the fine sand layer, which leads to all of the BCs entered into the upper layer. Compared to coarse sand, the addition of fine sand provided more adsorption sites for BCs, which inhibited BCs transport in the fine sand tanks. Furthermore, based on previous research (Kamrani et al., 2018 ), fine quartz sand is more prone to the presence of dead ports in 2-D sand tanks, causing BCs to be trapped in the fine sand in large quantities. Consistent with the trend of BCs transport in the visualized images, the (C/C0 )max  values of BCs increased from 0.07 to 0.14 with the increase of sand particle size (Fig. 4 b). Correspondingly, the TMR of BCs also increased from 26.12 % to 63.97 %. In particular, most of the BCs were transported out when coarse sand was added to the porous medium in the sand tank. It was further confirmed by modeling that BCs mainly enter into small-size media from large-size media through vertical dispersion. When the underlying medium is fine sand, the k value of the medium sand layer is 0.0127 min−1 , and when the underlying medium is coarse sand, the k value of the medium sand layer decreases to 0.0053 min−1 . As quartz sand size increased from fine sand to coarse sand, the ζ-potential of quartz sand decreased from −48.99 mV to −53.63 mV (Fig. 2 h), which indicates that coarse sand has more negative charges. However, according to the DLVO theory (Fig. 4 c), the total interaction energy with different grain sizes was also not significant. The results suggest that the effect of electrostatic repulsion due to changes in particle size on the transport of BCs in the quartz sand tank was not significant. Moreover, compared to coarse sand media, fine sand has smaller pores and is less permeable. In particular, the HDD to quartz sand ratio of BCs ((dBC /dS )Min  = 0.0034, (dBC /dS )Max  = 0.0051) in the presence of DOM exceeded 0.0017 in the fine sand layer, which largely inhibited the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM in the sand tank (Fig. 4 d). Consequently, although DOM acted as a mediator to facilitate the transport of BCs in the porous medium, physical clogging caused by variations in quartz sand particle size and changes in inlet flux weakened the facilitating effect of DOM on BCs.  3.2.3 Effects of IS Fig. 5  a illustrated the visualized transport of BCs under DOM presence conditions. A significant distinction of the visualization images was observed in the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM. By comparing the plume images of BCs at each time, it was found that the effect of IS became more serious especially after 180 min had passed. With the increase of IS, the transport of BCs in the sand tank was inhibited. Especially most obvious at IS=50 mM, almost all of the BCs were retained in the sand tank. Correspondingly, the BTCs of BCs showed that the (C/C0 )max  values of BCs decreased with the increase of IS (Fig. 5 b). The TMR of BCs at IS=50 mM (6.57 %) is much smaller than TMR at IS=1 mM (36.94 %). Additionally, the Double-Monod model (R2  > 0.94) could well describe BCs transport well. The k values of the BCs in the presence of DOM transport increased from 0.0057 min−1  to 0.0107 min−1  as IS increased from 1 mM to 50 mM. Note that the ζ-potential of BCs increased from –32.80 mV to −24.04 mV (Fig. 2 h), and the negative potential density on the surface of the quartz sand has also decreased (Table S2 ). Therefore, due to the shielding of negative charges by high IS, which in turn leads to reduced repulsion between BC-BC and between BC-quartz sand. In addition, increased IS compresses the double electric layer on the BC surface, which also reduced the repulsive forces between BCs and BCs. It was further shown by DLVO interaction energy calculations that with increasing IS, the repulsion between BCs and the quartz sand surface decreases, and BCs are more likely to be retained in the sand tank (Fig. 5 c). Accordingly, the HDD of the BCs increased significantly has also been attributed to the decreased repulsion force and charge shielding. As IS increased from 1 mM to 50 mM, the agglomeration of BCs became more and more obvious, and the HDD increased from 612.96 nm to 2529 nm. Moreover, primary minimal deposition or large aggregates can also cause BCs to be more challenging to transport out of the quartz sand medium under high IS. In particular, the minimum value of the ratio of the average diameter of BCs to quartz sand exceeds 0.0017 at both IS=10 mM and IS=50 mM (Fig. 5 d).The results show that IS greatly alters the transport behavior of BCs, and the effect of DOM is much smaller than that of IS. Although the presence of DOM brings a large amount of negative charges to the surface of BCs, these negative charges are shielded as IS increases. The presence of DOM increased the mobility of BCs in 2-D porous media under low IS conditions compared to previous single transport studies on biochar colloids (Zhao et al., 2023 ). However, the enhancement of stability and dispersion of BCs by DOM was weakened under high IS, and the agglomeration rate of BCs increased. Therefore, the increase of IS decreased the electrostatic repulsion between BCs in the presence of DOM. As a result, the aggregation of BCs was enhanced and the transportation of BCs was inhibited.  3.2.4 Effects of pH Fig. 6  a illustrates the transport pattern of BCs in the presence of DOM under various pH. By comparing the images of BCs plumes at various times, it was found that the effect of pH on the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM became apparent after the BCs plume reached the right exit (180 min). Especially at 300 min, a large number of BCs flowed out of the sand tank as can be seen from the images. Clearly, BCs had higher mobility at pH=9 compared with pH=5. In addition, the (C/C0 )max  values of BCs increased from 0.08 to 0.14 from pH=5 to pH=9 (Fig. 6 b). Interestingly, when pH>7, the (C/C0 )max  values of BCs significantly increased with the increased pH. The results suggested that alkaline conditions had a more significant effect on the mobility of BCs. Compared to pH=9, only 30.12 % of BCs were detected in the effluent at pH=5. With the increased pH, the TMR of BCs rose from 30.12 % to 62.53 %. Similarly, the k values of the BCs transport increased from 0.0059 min−1  to 0.0041 min−1  as pH increased from 5 to 9. With pH increased from 5 to 9, the ζ-potential of BCs decreased from − 27.82 mV to − 43.52 mV(Fig. 2 h). According to the FT-IR results (Fig. 2 g), both BCs and DOM are rich in oxygenated functional groups. pH increase induces the dissociation of oxygenated functional groups, which leads to a significant increase in the negative charge, and increases the repulsion between BC particles and BC-quartz sand. Fig. 6 c showed the total interaction energy between the BCs and the quartz sand surface, which showed a decrease in the total interaction energy as the pH increased. Fig. 2 i gives the average size of BCs as pH varies. In general, BCs agglomerates possessing larger sizes are more susceptible to sedimentation and clogging. As the pH increased from 5 to 9, the maximum ratio of the mean diameter of BCs to quartz sand rose from 0.0025 to 0.0051 (>0.0017), and the possibility of strain of BCs increased (Fig. 6 d). Especially under acidic conditions, the minimum ratio also exceeded 0.0017, which largely inhibited the transport of BCs in the sand tank. With the increase of pH, more hydroxide ions were introduced into the background solution, and the negative charge density on the BCs surface was greatly increased. Moreover, the presence of DOM brings more negative charges to the BCs, which even further increases the promotion. Therefore, in the presence of DOM, the high pH greatly improved the mobility and stability of BCs in the sand tank.    4 Conclusion In this paper, the transport and retention of BCs in the presence of DOM in porous media is investigated. A visualization system was used to visualize the real-time transport behavior of BCs in the presence of DOM. The results showed that the mobility of BCs in porous media was promoted with increasing DOM concentration. The DLVO theory and clogging mechanisms driving the enhanced BCs transport induced by the addition of DOM were discussed. It was found that because of hydrogen bonding, π-π bonding, and physical adsorption, DOM improves the stability and mobility of BCs. Changes in the BCs property resulting from the negative increase in the ζ-potentials of BCs are found to contribute to the enhanced transport of BCs. In addition, this study also tested the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM in porous media by different porous media particle sizes, IS, and pH. We found that increasing IS and decreasing pH led to a decrease in the ζ-potential of BCs, which reduced the repulsion between BC-BC and BC-quartz sand. Moreover, BCs are more prone to agglomeration and clogging in porous media under high IS and low pH. Therefore, compared with the coarse sand layer, the fine sand layer is more likely to cause the clogging of BCs. Furthermore, the Double-Monod model well described the transport of the BCs in the presence of DOM in 2-D porous media. This study highlights several environmental implications for the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM. Based on the above results, the DOM can act as a mediator that enhances the transport of BCs in the porous medium. However, changes in environmental factors can also have a significant impact on the transport of BCs in the presence of DOM. Especially in areas of loose, alkaline, and low IS porous media, the long-term transport risk posed by the high number of BCs still needs to be considered.
1 Introduction The microbial food webs are key components of the river ecosystem, consisting of complex interactions between abiotic and biotic species that control the flow of organic matter (Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Detritus (i.e., dead organic matter) is a basal resource exploited by primary consumers in river ecosystems and a critical base for nutrient interactions, food webs, and even global biogeochemical cycles (Bovill et al., 2023, Robbins et al., 2023a ). The human-induced alterations in material fluxes between nutrients and living organisms had global consequences on aquatic biodiversity and water environmental quality, leading to the decomposition of detritus a key process in the river ecosystems (Moore et al., 2004 ). It has been reported that detritus increased the standing stock of each trophic level of the food web by supporting detritivores and providing energy to predators (Manzoni et al., 2010, Mooshammer et al., 2014 ), which in turn altered river ecosystem function. Therefore, revealing the detritus dynamics is crucial for protecting river ecosystem health. Microbial decomposition dominated the detritus decomposition and constituted the main nutrient and energy input to the food webs in rivers (Hieber and Gessner, 2002 ). An increasing number of studies have shown that the relationship between detritus and microorganisms was reciprocal. On the one hand, the microorganism in the food webs affected detritus mass and density through nutrient uptake and excretion (Moore et al., 2003 ). Recent researches has revealed that the remineralisation of detritus was carried out by heterotrophic bacteria (Anderson et al., 2023, Robbins et al., 2023b ), which facilitated the entry of detritus into the organism and promoted detritus circulation through the food web (Arnosti 2011, Karnan et al., 2021 ). More importantly, the detritus entering the microbial food web laid the ecological basis for the evolution and maintenance of microorganisms (Moore et al., 2004 ). Detritus has been demonstrated to be the limiting resource for many microbial taxa and proved to have significant impacts on the higher trophic species in the microbial food web through bottom-up trophic cascades (Halvorson et al., 2016 ). The increased availability of detritus would provide energy for predators and in turn maintain high growth rates of low trophic species through top-down control. It has been reported that the detritus availability for heterotrophic bacteria affected the richness of protozoan and metazoan through bottom-up trophic cascade (Halvorson et al., 2016 ). However, how detritus availability affects the behaviors of multi-trophic microbiota and the predation efficiency of microbial food webs through bottom-up trophic cascades is still not clear. Detritus transformation processes (i.e. detritus availability) would alter the energy flux of the microbial food web and further affected the ecological function of the microbial food web. However, the dynamics of detritus in river ecosytems was determined by both flow-induced transport and transformation processes (Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Studies showed that spatial heterogeneity of detritus distribution is related to local inputs (biological, especially microorganism-induced transformation) and allochthonous inputs (abiological, especially flow-induced transport) (Moore et al., 2003, Moore et al., 2004, Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Changes in hydrodynamic conditions affected the transport processes of detritus and further influenced the detritus bioavailability by altered the generation and retention (Power et al., 2013, Arroita et al., 2015, Wang et al., 2023 ). Thus, declaring the detritus bioavailability under the influence of complex hydrodynamic in rivers is crucial for protecting the functions of river ecosystems (Moore et al., 2004 ). However, the effect of transport and transformation processes to detritus is less considered separately in river ecosystems since transport and transformation processes existed interdependently in nature rivers, although it is important for understanding nutrient uptake mechanism of microbial food web in rivers. River confluence are essential structures of river ecosystems. The convergence of two channles will lead to intense flow exchange and promote material exchange between two channels. Recent studies had shown that the effects of biogeochemical cycles processes occurring at river confluence were sustained and significantly affected ecosystem function in downstream (Hui et al., 2022, Hui et al., 2023 ). Therefore, revealing patterns of detritus food webs in river confluence is significant for preserving the river ecosystem functions. Previous studies had identified that hydrological variations in river confluence played an important role in shaping distribution of inorganic matter (Li et al., 2020 ), as well as the composition distribution of bacteria, protozoans and metazoans (Li et al., 2023 ). However, how detritus availability responds to complex hydrodynamic conditions in river confluence and how detritus availability affects microbial food web patterns through bottom-up trophic cascade are still unclear. Therefore, this study aims to decouple the detritus transport and transformation processes under the influence of complex hydrodynamic conditions in a river confluence, and further identify the influence of detritus availability on the diversity and assembly of multi-trophic microbiota as well as the trophic transfer efficiency of microbial food webs. Analysis was conducted to (1) identify how transport and transformation (i.e. the detritus availability) processes influence detritus distribution (2) investigate the effects of detritus availability on the diversity and community assembly of multi-trophic microbiota; (3) illuminate the impacts of detritus availability on microbial food web patterns and quantify the influence of detritus availability to the trophic transfer efficiency of microbial food web. Results of this study can be beneficial to declare the effect of detritus availability on the benthic microbial ecosystems under the impacts of complex hydraulic conditions and provide support to the river ecological protection.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Sample sites and measurement of physicochemical parameters Thirty sampling points were set at the channel confluence in the Qinhuai River in Nanjing, China (located latitude 32° 00 N and longitude 118° 49 E) (Fig. S1 a). There were no pollution sources within the sample sites, avoiding the interference caused by human activities to a certain extent. Considering the hydrodynamic characteristics of the river confluence area (Yuan et al., 2022 ), ten sampling sections were set up at research area. The adjacent sections were 15–20 m (m) apart. Thirty sediment samples were collected at 0–5 cm depth. To maintain the activity of biomacromolecules, all samples were stored in an ice box at −80 °C. Total organic carbon (TOC), which was used to represent the detritus according to the method of previous study (Yang et al., 2022 ). To remove the inorganic carbon in the sample, 0.05 g sediment sample were calcined in a porcelain crucible at 950℃, and 50 % pure hydrochloric acid was slowly added until no bubbles emerged from the samples. Samples were further analyzed for TOC using the TOC analyzer (Model 1030, OIAnaltica, USA). An Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP, RIV-600, TRDI Ltd., Thousand Oaks, California, USA) was used to measure mean 3-D velocity profiles in the sample sites. The ADCP probe was 0.5 m below surface water on measurement, avoiding air-bubble entrainment effects. The 3-D velocities, including vertical velocity (Vv), eastern velocity (Ve) and northern velocity (Vn), of study eara were recorded. Vector addition was used to integrat Ve and Vn to caculated plane 2-D velocity (Ve-n). Datas that beyond the 10 % quantile and values below 90 % quantile were considered as the valid datas and were retained for futher analysis. The flow field were visualize using Ve-n by Tecplot 360 (Fig. S1 b).  2.2 DNA extraction and bioinformatics For sediment samples, following the specification, DNA extraction was conducted using the FastDNA spin kit (Q-BIOgene, Carlsbad, CA). The universal bacterial primer set 341F(5′-CCTAYGGGRBGCASCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACNNGGGTATCTAAT-3′) were used to amplify the V3-V4 regions of the 16S rRNA, and TARTAReuk454FWD1 (5′-CCAGCASCYGCGGTAATTCC-3′) and TAReukREV3 (5′-ACTTTCGTTCTTGATYRA-3′) were used to amplify the V4 region of the 18S rRNA genes. Illumina MiSeq sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification were both completed at Shanghai BIOZERON Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The specific method was provied in our previous study (Li et al., 2020, Li et al., 2023 ). The raw FASTQ files were quality-filtered in QIIME2 v2021.2 and UCLUST was used to obtain Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The GreenGenes database and the NCBI Genbank reference database were used for bacteria and eukaryotes, seperately. Row data of bacteria and eukaryotes were available on the Sequence Read Archive (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/  ), project reference PRJNA541057 and PRJNA904109.  2.3 Structure of the modelling system Transport processes of detritus in sediment can further be decoupled into the mixture of sediment with detritus from different sources, and the adsorption and desorption processes between sediment and overlying water. Considering the detritus was granular, attached to the sediment and not easily adsorbed or desorbed by sediment (Hellweger, 2013 ), the adsorption–desorption equilibrium of detritus could be accessed easily in natural river ecosystems. Therefore, it was rational to assume that the detritus transport processes in sediment were determined by the mixture of sediment from different sources (Moore et al., 2004 ). MIKE 21 model was used to simulated the transport processes of sediment. The governing equations of transport processes simulation can be expressed as follows (Song et al., 2022 ): Continuity:(1) ∂ h  ∂ t   + ∂ h u  ¯    ∂ x   + ∂ h ν  ¯    ∂ y   = 0          Momentum:∂ h u  ¯    ∂ t   + ∂ h u  ¯    2   ∂ x   + ∂ h uv  ¯    ∂ y   = f ν  ¯   h - g h ∂ η  ∂ x   - h ∂ p a   ρ 0  ∂ x   - g h  2  ∂ ρ  2 ρ 0  ∂ x   + τ sx   ρ 0   - τ bx   ρ 0       (2) - 1 ρ 0   ∂ s  xx   ∂ x   - ys  xy   ∂ y     + ∂ h T xx      ∂ x   + ∂ h T xy      ∂ y           ∂ h v  ¯    ∂ t   + ∂ h v  ¯    2   ∂ y   + ∂ h uv  ¯    ∂ x   = f ν  ¯   h - g h ∂ η  ∂ y   - h ∂ p a   ρ 0  ∂ y   - g h  2  ∂ ρ  2 ρ 0  ∂ y   + τ sy   ρ 0   - τ by   ρ 0       (3) - 1 ρ 0   ∂ s  yx   ∂ x   - ys  yy   ∂ y     + ∂ h T yy      ∂ y   + ∂ h T xy      ∂ x           where t  represents time; x  and y  are Cartesian co-ordinates; η  represents surface elevation; h = η + d  represents total water depth, where d  is still water depth; u  and v  are velocity components in x  and y  direction; u  ¯     and v  ¯     are the depth-averaged velocities; f  represents the Coriolis parameter; g  represents the gravitational acceleration; ρ  represents the density of water; sij   represents the components of radiation stress tensor; pa   represents the atmospheric pressure; ρ0   represents the reference density of water; Tij   represents the lateral stresses, including viscous frication, turbulent friction and differential advection. Two inlet boundaries were set at upstream of main branch and tributary, and one outlet was set at downstream of main branch (Figure S1 ). The sediment was composed of two fractions: the sediment from the main branch was designated as Fraction M  (FM  ), and the sediment from the tributary was designated as Fraction T  (FT  ). Since detritus in sediment was determined by the mixture of sediment in the main branch and the tributary when two rivers mixed and null of other detritus source existed in the study area, the concentrations of detritus in the simulated area can be finally calculated by:(5) C N  = F M  ∗ C NM   + F T  ∗ C NT           where CN   represents the concentration of detritus in a specifit point at simulated area; FM   represents the sediment from main branch; FT   represents the sediment from tributary; CNM   represents the concentrations of the detritus in main branch; CNT   represents the concentrations of the detritus in tuibutary. The modelling area consisted of two inlet boundaries, one outlet and the river bed (Figure S1 ). The morphology of river bed, based on the river depth, was measured using ADCP, and the river bed was defined as the wall boundary, with no-slip conditions. The inlet boundaries were set as velocity inlet boundary condition. Detailed information of inlet boundary conditions was listed in Table S1 . The outlet boundary was set as pressure outlet boundary condition. The flow velocity was measured using the ADCP.  2.4 Analysis of microbial food web To identify the microbial food web patterns, common trophically-linked species were extracted from the pool of both bacterial and eukaryotic OTUs, referring to the method of previous researches (Parry, 2004, Weitere et al., 2018, Yang et al., 2020 ). Heterotrophic bacteria (HB) are the dominant roles in benthic heterotrophic food web (Hillebrand et al., 2002 ). Hetrotrophic flagellates (HF) are the major predator that feed on bacteria in aquatic systems. Amoeba, protozan group, are the major attached bacteria predators. Ciliates are another bacteria-feeding protozoan, which can also prey on protozoan (such as flagellates) smaller than themself. Meiofauna, such as nematoda and rotifera, are the prevailing predators of both bacteria and protozoan in river benthic systems. The trophic transfer efficiency between different trophic levels was represented by predator–prey biomass ratio. Since the copies number of each species was effacted by species size and biomass, thus the number of reads was used to represent fractional biomass (Singh et al., 2019, Yang et al., 2021 ). According to the predation characteristics of microorganisms of different trophic levels, trophic transfer efficiency between bacteria and protozoan was represented as HF:HB, Amoeba:HB and Ciliates:HB, and transfer efficiency between protozoans was represented as Ciliates:HF. Trophic transfer efficiency between bacteria and meiofauna was caculated as Meiofauna:HB. Trophic transfer efficiency between protozoan and meiofauna was represented as Meiofauna:Protozoan (Yang et al., 2020, Yang et al., 2022, Li et al., 2023 ). To identify the relationship between nutrient availability (i.e detritus availability) and the transfer efficency among multi-trophic levels, a structural equation model (SEM) was further constructed. The SEM was performed using Amos v.23 (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) (Yang et al., 2020 ).  2.5 Diversity estimates and statistical analysis The diversity estimates and statistical analysis were all conducted in R software (v. 4.3.1). To identify species abundance, diversity, and evenness, the indices of microbial α-diversity, including Richness, Shannon, Simpson, Pielou, invsimpson, Chao1 and ACE, were calculated using “Vegan” package (Shu and Huang, 2022 ). For β-diversity, both the partition of β-diversity and the β-diversity of each trophic level were considered and conducted in R package “betapart” (Shen et al., 2020 ). The Sørensen-based multiple-site dissimilarity (βSOR ) was used to estimated the overall β-diversity. The Simpson-based multiple-site dissimilarity (βSIM ) as well as nestedness-resultant multiple-site dissimilarity (βNES ) were used to estimated the turnover and nestedness components of β-diversity, respectively. The mantel test (based on Euclidean distance matrices) was estimated to identify the interactions of flow velocity with detritus transformation processes, as well as the influence of detritus transformation processes on α-diversity indices of multi-trophic levels. To identify the factors that affected phylogenetic assembly of multi-trophic microbiota, the βNTI value, based on the phylogenetic null model, was estimated, referring to the methoes of previou studies (Stegen et al., 2013, Stegen et al., 2016 ).   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Contributions of transport and transformation processes to detritus distribution The detritus was considered non-living and its ontogeny was dependent in part on the actions of other species (Moore et al., 2004 ). The distribution of detritus was controlled by abiotic and biotic processes (Manning et al., 2016 ), which could be attributed to flow-induced transport and microorganism-induced transformation processes (Moore et al., 2004, Li et al., 2020, Robbins et al., 2023a ). Transport and transformation processes of detritus existed interdependently in river ecosystems and was uneasy to depart or distinguish. However, since detritus was non-living and neither reproduced nor disappeared suddenly, the transport process of detritus was controlled by hydrodynamic conditions (Moore et al., 2004 ). Therefore, the transport processes could be simulated using hydraulic models (Weitere et al., 2018 ). The contribution of transformation process could further be estimated by subtracting the contribution of transport processes from the measured value. Therefore, the distribution of detritus only caused by transport processes was estimated using MIKE 21. Sediment compositions of all sampling points stabilized after about 12 h of model operation. The flow velocity, as the most variable and extensively used index in hydrodynamic simulation, was considered as the proxy to evaluate the accuracy and usability of the hydraulic model. The model showed that the measured and simulated velocities showed no significant difference (p  = 0.16), and the mean relative error between them was 28 % (Figure S2 ). Thus, the hydraulic model was stable and accurate enough for simulation (Briggs et al., 2015 ). The distribution of detritus caused by transformation processes (i.e., the portion that was utilized or generated by microorganisms) were represented by the deviations between measured value and simulated value (measured results minus simulated results). Positive deviations illustrated that transformation processes decreased the detritus concentration, which indicated the detritus was available for microorganisms as well as consumed by microorganisms, representing the detritus availability. Negative deviations illustrated that transformation processes increased the detritus concentration, which mean the detritus was produced by microbial death or excretion. Results showed that there existed significant difference between the simulated and measured results of detritus (p <  0.05), indicating the transformation processes had a great influence on the distribution of detritus. As shown in Fig. 1  , positive or negative detritus transformation deviations were observed at different sampling points, due to the fact that the detritus could be used as the reactant or the product in different biological reactions. Besides, the contribution of transport and transformation processes to detritus concentrations at different sampling points were different. The detritus in the upstream of the tributary was mainly transformed by microorganisms, while detritus in the upstream of main branch was produced by microorganisms. However, the contribution of transformation processes showed complex spatial heterogeneity when the junction of main branch and tributary occurred. Since transport processes might contribute to a homogeneous distribution while transformation processes might contribute to a heterogeneous distribution (Jacob et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2020 ), the complex spatial heterogeneity of detritus transformation processes existed in river confluence. The spatial heterogeneity of detritus transformation processes might be affected by the macro and micro detritus consumers as well as the hydrodynamic environment (Williams et al., 2017 ). Thus, to identify external factors that affected the distribution of detritus, with considering the complex hydrodynamic conditions in the study area, mantel test was conducted to investigate the relationship between detritus distribution and flow velocity. Results showed that there existed the significantly negative correlation between detritus transformation concentration and flow velocity (p  < 0.01, R=-0.19), indicating that flow velocity was an important factor affecting the detritus transformation processes. These results demonstrated that flow velocity was the main driver that caused the inconsistent detritus transformation processes in river confluence. The high flow velocity might intensify the collision and metabolic capacity of microorganisms, which in turn promoted the production of detritus (Peng et al., 2023, Shen et al., 2024 ). However, there existed more intense detritus transformation processes with flow velocity decreased, indicating that detritus availability increased in the region with low flow velocity. This result could be ascribed to the decrease of flow rate would increase the residence time of microorganisms, which further effect the microbial activity (Yang et al., 2021 ). Previous study had found that the turbulence in the flow velocity region increase contact rates of predator and prey (Arnott et al, 2021 ). In aquatic systems, detritus transformation processes might alter the composition, distribution and diversity of predators (Moore et al., 2004, Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Evidences suggested that hydrodynamic condition changed in detritus could propagate to higher trophic levels through bottom-up cascades and ultimately affected the stability and resilience of microecosystem (Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Therefore, the above results suggested that there were differences of detritus transformation processes in different region under the influence of flow velocity at the river confluence, which might lead to the differences of multi-trophic microbiota composition and diversity.  3.2 Detritus availability shapes the microbial food web composition through bottom-up trophic cascades Since the detritus transformation processes were significantly related to microorganisms, the relationship between detritus transformation and multi-trophic microbiota was further explored. After bioinformatic analysis, Proteobacteria (42.1 %), Chloroflexi (17.5 %) and Acidobacteria (10.8 %) were found dominated the bacteria communities (Figure S3 ). About 65 % of the eukaryotes OTUs were protozoans and metazoans (Fig. 2  ). The protozoan community was formed by SAR (72.51 %, including Stramenopiles, Alveolates and Rhizaria), followed by Amoebozoa (16.59 %). Bilateria (97.59 %), including Nematoda, Arthropoda, Chordata and Rotifera, was the abundant metazoan community. The abundant communities, such as Amoebozoa, Nematoda, Rotifera, were demonstrated to be the significant components of microbial food webs. Detritus was proved to sustain the richness of detritivores, including Bilateria (Ince et al., 2007, Schlacher et al., 2017 ), which further supported for predatory, such as arthropods (Dugan et al., 2003 ). The α-diversity indexes of bacteria, protozoan and metazoan were shown in Table S2 , Table S3 , and Table S4 , separately. The Simpson, Shannon, and Richness of bacteria were significantly higher than those of both protozoan and metazoan (p  < 0.05 for all). These results reiterated that the pivotal role of heterotrophic bacteria in microbial ecosystem (Wu et al., 2013, Chen et al., 2018, Yang et al., 2021 ). As a major driver of biogeochemical cycles, nutrient cycling, and organotrophic transfer (Falkowski et al., 2008 ), bacterial diversity was critical for detritus uptake and predation efficiency for higher trophic levels (Saleem et al., 2013 ). In order to further explore the impact of detritus transformation processes on α-diversity, mantel tests were conducted (Fig. 3  ). Results found that the detritus transformation concentration was significantly positively correlated with α-diversity index (including Chao1, ACE, Shannon, Simpson, Pielou) of bacteria, protozoan and metazoan (p  < 0.5 and R > 0 for all) (Fig. 3 ), indicating that detritus availability promoted the diversity of multi-trophic levels. The higher diversity of multi-trophic microbiota could contribute to the larger community niche space, which would result in a more adaptable microbial ecosystem (Kaymak et al., 2018, Guzman et al., 2022 ). Moreover, these results showed that detritus transformation concentrations had a greater impact on bacterial diversity (p  < 0.05, r = 0.20) than protozoan (p  < 0.05, r = 0.17) and metazoan diversity (p  < 0.05, r = 0.17), indicating that detritus availability had a greater effect on low trophic levels than higher trophic levels in microbial food web. There were growing evidences illustrated that detritus availability had a strong bottom-up effect on food webs in river ecosystem, especially for primary consumers (Scherber et al., 2010, Yan et al., 2021 ). The above results indicated that detritus availability shaped the microbial food web composition through bottom-up trophic cascades, promoting the α-diversity of all trophic microbiota (including bacteria, protozoan and metazoan), and especially having a greater effect on low trophic levels (bacteria) than higher trophic levels (protozoan and metazoan) (Yang et al., 2022 ). These results were consistent with previous study (Wang et al., 2023 ), indicating that the inconsistency between bacteria with protozoan and metazoan might due to the basis position of bacteria in the ecosystem and bacteria would rapidly change in their dynamics in response to the changes of nutriment availability. The results in this study reiterated the importance of nutriment availability in shaping the composition of microbial food webs.  3.3 Detritus availability determines the community assembly of multi-trophic microbiota Considering the characteristics of detritus distribution and the multi-trophic microbiota community composition, it was acceptable to hypothesize that the community assembly of multi-trophic microbiota were related to shifts in detritus transformation processes. Therefore, whether the detritus transformation processes affected the assembly of multi-trophic microbiota was further identified, based on the theory of microbial community assembly (Jacob et al., 2018 ). The results showed that the detritus transformation concentration was significantly correlated with community assembly values (βNTI) of bacteria (p < 0.05, r = 0.021), but showed no significant correlation with βNTI of higher trophic levels (including protozoan and metazoan) (p = 0.08, r = 0.20) (Fig. 4  ). Results indicated that detritus transformation processes had an effect on the community assembly of lower trophic microbiota community assembly, but had little effect on the higher trophic levels community assembly. These results indicated that detritus availability affected the community assembly of multi-trophic microbiota through bottom-up cascading effects and further verified the more significant promotion of detritus availability on the α-diversity of lower trophic. It has been widely shown that heterotrophic bacteria were the important participants in detritus transformation processes, which could promote detritus availability by mineralizing and decomposing detritus (Anderson et al., 2023, Robbins et al., 2023a, Halvorson et al., 2016 ). The results of this study reemphasized that detritus availability could also in turn influence the species characteristics of detritus predators. Characteristics of species, including composition, structure and assembly mechanisms, had different properties of dispersion or resistance to environmental disturbance, which were related to both local diversity and species substitution or loss (Baselga 2010, Legendre 2014 ). Therefore, β-diversity of multi-trophic microbiota was further calculated for investigating the responses of multi-trophic microbiota survival characteristics to detritus transformation concentration (Table S5 ). Results showed that there was a high dissimilarity existed in species between different sample points at river confluence, with the total multi-trophic β-diversity (βSOR ) was estimated as 0.87. The replacement component of total multi-trophic β-diversity (βSIM  = 0.65) was slightly larger than nestedness component (βNES  = 0.22). These results indicated that, at river confluence, species replacement, rather than species loss, was the mainly ecological processes that determined β-diversity of multi-trophic levels. The β-diversity of each trophic level of microbial food web were further estimated (Fig. 4 , Table S6 ).
