The values are averaged when there are two valid records from the two orbits on the same day.  2.4.3 SMOS SM The SMOS SM is derived from brightness temperature observations using the L-band microwave emission of the biosphere (L-MEB) model, in which the SM and vegetation optical depths can be retrieved simultaneously from multi-angular observations based on generalized least-squares iterative algorithm (Wigneron et al., 2007 ). The SMOS L2 SM product released by the European Space Agency (ESA) is selected to synchronize with COSMOS ground observations (i.e. , from September 2, 2021 to September 1, 2023), whereas the SMOS SM data delivered by Centre Aval de Traitement des Données SMOS (CATDS) has not been updated since 2021. Two criteria are used to filter the qualified data: 1) the SM with Data Quality Index (Soil_Moisture_DQX) should be below 0.1, and 2) the probability of radio frequency interference (RFI_Prob) cannot exceed 0.2 (Ma et al. 2019 ). The values are averaged when there are two valid records from the two orbits on the same day.  2.4.4 SMAP SM The NASA SMAP mission was launched in January 2015, operating at a fixed incidence angle of 40° and utilizing microwave L-band frequencies centered at 1.41 GHz (Entekhabi et al., 2010a). In this study, we utilize version 8 of SMAP L3 data. The new baseline algorithm has been updated to the Dual Channel Algorithm (DCA), employing both H-polarized and V-polarized brightness temperature observations to retrieve SM and vegetation optical depth simultaneously, which presents a departure from the Single Channel Algorithm-Vertical Polarization (SCA-V) used in prior versions (O’Neill et al., 2021 ). Those SM observations with ‘soil_moisture_error’ greater than 5 % is excluded as ‘poor quality’. Similar to ASCAT, the values are averaged when there are two valid records from the two orbits on the same day.  2.4.5 CYGNSS SM The CYGNSS SM product, released by the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), represents a novel application of CYGNSS data in land surface monitoring. The CYGNSS SM value is developed using effective soil reflectivity obtained by the received GPS transmit power correction and its correlation with SMAP SM (Chew and Small, 2020; Kim et al., 2021 ). Due to several strict data quality control steps in the process of generating SM, we directly utilize the CYGNSS SM with valid records in this study.   2.5 Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 data Meanwhile, to further analyze the impact of soil salinity on satellite-based SM products' accuracy, the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) multi-spectral remote sensing product is used to derive continuous soil salinity information in the study area. The HLS project aims to establish a Virtual Constellation (VC) by integrating surface reflectance (SR) data from both the Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 remote sensing satellites, and the users can directly acquire the SR of any pixel at any time as though it comes from a single sensor (Claverie et al. 2018 ). To ensure the quality of spectral data, only the HLS data with cloud coverage of less than 10 % are selected. The HLS data is resampled to a 20 pixels × 20 pixels window (i.e. , 400 m × 400 m) centered at the COSMOS site. The Salinity Index (SI) calculated by dividing the Short-Wave Infrared 1 (SWIR1) by the near-infrared (NIR) band (i.e. , SI=SWIR1/NIR) is chosen as the index of soil salinity (Nicolas and Walter, 2006; Wang et al., 2022b ).   3 Methodology Fig. 2   presents the flowchart of this study. The study comprises three main sections: (1) Data preprocessing: collecting COSMOS data, SM sensor data, and various satellite SM products, and conducting preprocessing operations; (2) COSMOS SM estimation: converting the raw neutron counting rate into SM with high accuracy by considering the effect of atmospheric pressure, atmospheric water vapor, and solar activity; (3) Quantification of soil salinity effect: evaluating the effect of soil salinity of three different types of SM sensors and five satellite-based SM products, respectively, treated the COSMOS SM as a benchmark. The detailed descriptions for each part of the flowchart are elaborated below. 3.1 Data preprocessing The dataset collected from COSMOS, i.e. , raw neutron counts and supporting data, are aggregated into hourly time steps. To ensure the quality of data, the mean value (μ) and the standard deviation (σ) of all the raw neutron counting rates during the time period are calculated; then, the 3σ principle is applied to eliminate data outliers, and data deviating from the mean value (μ) by more than 3σ are considered an outlier for measurements. Since SM has always remained at a relatively high level in the study area for a long time, the effective depth of COSMOS is limited to the topsoil (see Fig. 4  in Section 4.1  for more details). Therefore, the COSMOS SM can be used as the surface SM, and is suitable for the validation of SM sensors installed at topsoil (i.e. , 10 cm depth) and satellite-based SM products. Meanwhile, all the SM data are processed on a daily scale, and the SM sensors and SM products are matched to COSMOS SM according to the date.  3.2 SM estimation from COSMOS Generally, the scattered neutron intensity exhibits a negative correlation with SM. The quantitative relationship between the SM and neutron counting rate is expressed by the following equation (Desilets et al., 2010 ):(2) θ = a 0  N / N 0     - a 1    - a 2      · ρ b      where θ  is the SM; N  is the neutron counting rate normalized to a reference atmospheric pressure and solar activity level (Kuwabara et al., 2006 ); N0   is the neutron counting rate over ideal dry soil under the same condition; ρb   (g cm−3 ) is the soil bulk density; a 0 , a 1 , and a 2  are fitting coefficients, for the case of θ  > 0.02 kg kg−1 , the SM dependence of near-surface neutron intensity on a per mass basis in the fast to epithermal energy range is given by a0   = 0.0808, a1   = 0.372, and a2   = 0.115, respectively (Desilets et al., 2010 ; Zreda, M., et al., 2012; Mujumdar et al., 2021 ). In most practical scenarios, the neutron activity is affected by atmospheric pressure. High atmospheric pressure increases collisions between high-energy cosmic ray particles and atmospheric particles, primarily due to dense air particles. Consequently, the intensity of high-energy particles reaching the ground weakens, resulting in fewer fast neutrons recorded by COSMOS. Therefore, it is imperative to calibrate for the effect of air pressure (Zreda et al., 2012; Schrön, 2016 ):(3) f P  = exp ( P - P 0   L  )      where fP   is the atmospheric pressure correction factor; P0   is the reference atmospheric pressure; P  is the site-measured atmospheric pressure; L  is the mass attenuation length of high-energy neutrons. Moreover, atmospheric water vapor is a crucial input of hydrogen atoms and significantly affects the counting rate of high-energy particles. In coastal areas, atmospheric water vapor is notably high and non-negligible, underscoring the importance of correcting for atmospheric water vapor variation. The neutron counting rate is corrected using the atmospheric water vapor correction factor fh   (Franz et al., 2012b; Rosolem et al., 2013; Zreda et al., 2012 ), as follows:(4) f h  = 1 + 0.0054 h - h 0          where h  is the site absolute humidity (g m−3 ); h0   is the average absolute humidity under reference conditions. The absolute humidity value can be calculated using the site temperature and relative humidity measured by auxiliary sensors attached to the COSMOS instrument (see Appendix A ). In addition to the environmental factors, the flux of neutrons is also affected by solar activity, resulting in variations in the intensity of incoming primary cosmic-ray particles (Hawdon et al., 2014; Schrön, 2016 ). To normalize the source intensity, the intensity correction factor fi   is proposed (Zreda et al., 2012; Schrön, 2016 ):(5) f i  = I 0  / I     where I  is the real-time counting rate for the Jungfraujoch monitoring station neutron monitoring; I0   is the reference counting rate monitored at the Jungfraujoch monitoring station neutron on May 1, 2011. The data is available from the neutron monitoring database (https://www.nmdb.eu/ , accessed on December 10, 2023). In summary, the corrected counting rate of fast neutrons (Ncorr  ) can be expressed as:(6) N corr   = N raw   · f P  · f h  · f i      Note that the value of N0   in Eq. (2)  is contingent on specific measurement conditions and needs to be calibrated using the field-scale in-situ SM. In this context, we set the COSMOS Nraw   and N0   values ranging from 1000 to 2000 into Eq. (2)  to compute COSMOS SM. The N0   corresponding to the computed COSMOS SM that best aligns with the field-scale in-situ SM has been selected. All those mentioned parameters used for computing the COSMOS SM, along with their values or ranges are summarized and listed in Table 3  . Additionally, the effective depth of COSMOS SM measurement is estimated using the semi-empirical equation proposed by Franz et al., (2012a) , as follows:(7) z = 5.8  ρ b  τ + θ + 0.0829       where z  is the effective depth z (cm); ρb   is the soil bulk density; τ  is the weight fraction of lattice water of soil mineral grains (g g−1 ); θ is the SM.  3.3 Evaluation metrics To comprehensively and quantitatively evaluate the effect of soil salinity on point-scale SM derived by SM sensors and satellite-based SM products, five classical statistical metrics are employed: correlation coefficient (R), root mean square error (RMSE, m3  m−3 ), standard deviation (STD, m3  m−3 ), Bias (m3  m−3 ), and unbiased RMSE (ubRMSE, m3  m−3 ). The equations for these metrics are detailed in Table 4  .   4 Result 4.1 Performance of the COSMOS SM Fig. 3    (a) – (d) illustrates the variations of the correction factors, including the pressure factor, water vapor factor, intensity factor, and the combined factor (calculated as a multiplier of the three aforementioned factors). As depicted in Fig. 3  (a), the overall magnitude of the pressure factor is substantial throughout the entire period, with frequent sharp variations occurring within short intervals (e.g. , from December 2021 to January 2022). Conversely, the temporal patterns of the water vapor and intensity factors are relatively stable, albeit with notable seasonal variations, as shown in Fig. 3  (b). Notably, the intensity factor experienced a sharp peak in November 2021, possibly attributed to short-term solar activity (Fig. 3  (c)). The bottom panel in Fig. 3  (d) depicts the variations of the combined factor. Visually, atmospheric pressure emerges as the most influential factor in the counting rate of fast neutrons, followed by atmospheric water vapor and source intensity. Moreover, as mentioned in section 3.2 , we set the N0   ranging from 1000 to 2000 to compute COSMOS SM values corresponding to dates of the field-scale sampling based on Eq. (2)  and Eq. (6) , and compare the computed COSMOS SM to the field-scale in-situ SM. The accuracy variations between the five field-scale in-situ SM measurements and the computed COSMOS SM with respect to different N0   values are depicted in Fig. 3  (e). As depicted, the accuracy of COSMOS SM is significantly enhanced to a higher level after correction. The minimum value of RMSE decreases from 0.0391 m3  m−3  to 0.0278 m3  m−3 , and the corresponding R increases from 0.807 to 0.985. The RMSE undergoes significant changes with N0   for both Nraw   and Ncorr   inputs. The result indicates that the three factors, i.e. , pressure factor, water vapor factor, and intensity factor, significantly influence COSMOS SM measurements. Consequently, we select the N0   as the optimal value when RMSE is at its minimum. In this context, we set the N0   value to 1625, with the minimum RMSE value 0.0278 m3  m−3 . Fig. 4  (a) presents the daily variations of COSMOS SM from September 2, 2021 to September 1, 2023, and the precipitation data obtained from the synchronous ground measurement is also provided for comparison. The precipitation data are obtained from the TR-525 M Tipping Bucket Rain Gauge installed about 5 m away from the SM sensors, and the raw hourly-collected precipitation data are all accumulated on a daily scale. The COSMOS SM exhibits a strong correlation with the five field-scale in-situ data (R=0.985, RMSE=0.0278 m3  m−3 ), demonstrating sensitivity to changes in SM in response to precipitation. Overall, the COSMOS SM remains relatively high (SM>0.18 m3  m−3 ) over the entire period, possibly due to the relatively close distance to the sea and the high underground water level. The COSMOS SM increases significantly after each precipitation event, particularly during the rainy season, e.g. , from early-July to mid-July. Simultaneously, owing to the intense evapotranspiration induced by high temperature, the COSMOS SM experiences a notable decline in summer (e.g. , from mid-July to August). In summary, COSMOS has been proven to be capable of providing accurate SM over a long time series. It possesses the capability to validate other SM products for the subsequent work in this study. The effective depth calculated based on Eq. (7)  is depicted in Fig. 4  (b). As the effective depth depends on the wetness of SM and the SM always maintains at a relatively high level, the effective depth typically fluctuates in the topsoil (around 10 cm), indicating that only the surface SM are measured by COSMOS and it makes COSMOS SM suitable for the validation of SM sensors and SM products.  4.2 Influence of soil salinity on point-scale SM measurements As depicted in Fig. 5  , the HydraProbe overestimates the SM from July to September each year. This phenomenon occurs during rainy seasons, and it is highly plausible that the rapid increase in SM distorts of the HydraProbe measurements. Concurrently, the Hydraprobe SM experiences a substantial increase, reaching its peak in mid-July, which is attributable to the heavy precipitation. Conversely, the CS655 shows a significant bias during this period, with the measured SM decreasing instead of rising in July 2022. There are mainly two reasons that may cause this phenomenon: first, the in-situ SM value of CS655 is beyond the sensor range; second, the sensor malfunctions due to soaking in the soil ponding. As for 5TE, it underestimates the SM during its relatively short observation time. However, it should be noted that the operational period of 5TE is shorter (since November 23, 2022) than the other two SM sensors, with only 284 valid records; this limitation may introduce statistical errors. The comparison of the point-scale SM derived from SM sensors and COSMOS SM is presented in Fig. 6  . Overall, all three SM sensors are affected by soil salinity and deviated from the COSMOS data. The result indicates that HydraProbe (R=0.647, and ubRMSE=0.055 m3  m−3 ) significantly outperforms both CS655 (R=0.570, and ubRMSE=0.059 m3  m−3 ) and 5TE (R=0.416, and ubRMSE=0.058 m3  m−3 ). In particular, the error and uncertainty of 5TE SM measurements are relatively large, indicating that 5TE is not suitable for SM measuring in the study area. To further assess the effect of soil salinity on SM, Fig. 7   compares COSMOS SM with the SM retrieved by CS655 and HydraProbe varying with in-situ soil salinity content, respectively. Here, in-situ soil salinity content (S , unit: ‰) is classified into four levels, i.e. , S <5‰, 5 ‰ < S <15 ‰, 15 ‰ < S <30 ‰, and S >30 ‰. The RMSE values of the two sensors in Fig. 7  are 0.066 m3  m−3  and 0.091 m3  m−3  for the HydraProbe and CS655 sensors, respectively. It can be seen that the HydraProbe SM is relatively closer to the COMSOS SM and less affected by soil salinity, while the CS655 SM decreases obviously when the soil salinity content is relatively high (Fig. 7 ). When soil salinity content exceeds 15 ‰, the RMSE values of CS655 is obviously larger than HydraProbe, with RMSE=0.060 m3  m−3  vs. 0.037 m3  m−3 . It is due to the physical basis of the HydraProbe and CS655 for SM measurements based on real and apparent dielectric permittivity, respectively; real dielectric permittivity is less responsive to soil salinity, while soil salinity content significantly affects imagery dielectric permittivity according to previous studies (Seyfried and Murdock, 2004; Szypłowska et al., 2018 ). As soil apparent dielectric permittivity is a composition of both soil real and imagery dielectric permittivity, it is influenced by soil salinity content in addition to SM (Logsdon, 2005 ). It should be noted that even when soil salinity content is relatively low, inconsistency in SM between COSMOS and SM sensors is observed. This inconsistency primarily arises from low soil salinity content often associated with increased precipitation, leading to distortions in HydraProbe and malfunctions in CS655, which aligns with our prior evaluation of these two sensors.  4.3 Influence of soil salinity on satellite-based SM products The accuracy of satellite-based SM products and COSMOS SM is listed in Fig. 8  , and Table 5   summarizes the corresponding accuracy indicators. The five products are categorized into two groups based on their working bands (i.e. , C/X-band and L-band). It is noteworthy that most SM products lack spatiotemporal integrity. In particular, the CYGNSS SM product displays significant data gaps, with only 141 valid points. Overall, the satellites working in C-band outperform the L-band in retrieving SM in the coastal saline area, with mean R=0.409 and mean ubRMSE=0.068 m3  m−3  vs. R=0.200 and ubRMSE=0.102 m3  m−3 . Regarding the L-band satellite-based SM products, the accuracy of SMOS SM is much lower than that of SMAP SM and CYGNSS SM. Time-series variation reveals that the dispersion degree of SMOS SM is considerably higher than the SMAP and CYGNSS retrievals (STD=0.140 m3  m−3  vs. 0.077 m3  m−3  and 0.064 m3  m−3 ), indicating that SMOS exhibits greater volatility and noise. As the ASCAT SM is obtained indirectly by multiplying relative wetness (%) by point saturated SM, the bias of ASCAT is relatively more minor than other SM products, resulting in a value for ASCAT SM that is closer to COSMOS SM than other products. Time-series SM variations of SM products compared to COSMOS SM are illustrated in Fig. 9  , the AMSR2 SM products overestimate the SM throughout most of the observation period, with bias values ranging from 0.134 m3  m−3  to 0.186 m3  m−3  (Table 5 ). Among the three products of AMSR2, the AMSR2 C1-band performs best, boasting the highest R-value of 0.422. The ASCAT correlates well with the COMSOS SM; the correlation of ASCAT SM behaves similarly to AMSR-2 X-band SM, but the ubRMSE value is lower. Meanwhile, it can be clearly seen from Fig. 9  that the fluctuation and uncertainty of L-band SM products are much higher than that of C-band, which can support the accuracy of comparison between the two types of SM products. To evaluate the uncertainty of the above SM products at different periods, the annual SM data are categorized into four seasons, i.e. , winter (from December of last year to February), spring (from March to May), summer (from June to August), and autumn (from September to November). Two evaluation metrics (i.e. , R and ubRMSE) for SM products are calculated in each season. Fig. 10   illustrates the variations of seasonal SM accuracy, while Fig. 11   displays the boxplots depicting distinct seasonal patterns for R and ubRMSE. Seasonal AMSR2 SM exhibits greater stability compared to seasonal ASCAT SM (Fig. 10  (a)), manifesting smaller fluctuations in both the values of R and ubRMSE (Fig. 11  (a)). Conversely, the R-value of SM products based on the L-band microwave remote sensing is relatively low (Fig. 10  (b)), whereas the seasonal accuracy of SMAP SM is comparatively higher compared to SMOS SM and CYGNSS SM (Fig. 10 (b) and Fig. 11 (b)). Furthermore, the long-term SI derived from the HLS data is also provided to evaluate the correlation between COSMOS SM and satellite-based SM under different soil salinity levels. The SI derived from the HLS data strongly correlates with the point-scale in-situ soil salinity (R=0.646, P-value < 0.01). As illustrated in Fig. 12  , R and ubRMSE values ranging with SI levels are depicted. The effect of soil salinity on satellite-based SM products varies with the working bands, potentially introducing errors in SM measuring. Regarding SM products derived from the C-band (i.e.,  AMSR2 and ASCAT), the R and ubRMSE values are relatively stable across different saline levels. In contrast, the accuracy undergoes significant changes with varying SI levels for SM products derived from the L-band. Particularly for SMAP SM, the R-values, and ubRMSE decrease and increase monotonously from a low saline level to a high saline level, respectively. Overall, the accuracy of L-band SM products is lower than that of C-band when SI is relatively high, suggesting that L-band is more susceptible to saline interference in SM retrieval than C-band. This is consistent with previous research on soil dielectric experiments, where the L-band is more responsive to soil salinity than the C-band (Logsdon, 2005, Szypłowska et al., 2018 ), causing the L-band SM products to be more prone to disturbance from soil salinity than the C-band SM products.   5 Discussion 5.1 The impact of spatial mismatch effects Owning to the different spatial resolutions of the data used in this study, the effect of spatial mismatch inevitably occurs, and may potentially influence the conclusions to some extent. Therefore, it is necessary to discuss the scale effect further. Here, two salinity-independent different spatial scales, i.e. , point-scale in-situ SM, and coarse-scale reanalysis SM products, are compared with COSMOS SM. The point-scale in-situ SM data can be obtained from the collected soil samples dried in an oven at 105 ℃ for 24 h; and the high-precision SM data with coarse spatial resolution is obtained from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) (Kędzior and Zawadzki, 2016 ), with a spatial resolution of 0.25°×0.25°, similar to the spatial resolution of satellite SM products. The comparisons of COSMOS SM with point-scale in-situ SM and GLDAS SM are depicted in Fig. 10 . The COSMOS SM demonstrates good agreement with point-scale in-situ SM, with R=0.815, and ubRMSE=0.032 m3  m−3 . Simultaneously, COSMOS SM and GLDAS SM also have goodness of fit, with R=0.845, and ubRMSE=0.031 m3  m−3 , which indicates that the resolution difference between SM products in tens of kilometers has a negligible impact on the conclusion. Although the spatial mismatch between COSMOS and SM sensors and SM products would inevitably impact the results, the spatial effect has little influence on the conclusions. The spatial mismatch effects' negligible impact may also be due to the plain and relatively homogeneous land surface. We can thus infer that COSMOS has the potential for SM evaluation to bridge the knowledge gap of multi-scale dielectric-based SM from point scale to coarse scale.  5.2 SM sensors calibration based on COSMOS SM As the COSMOS SM is very close to the point-scale in-situ SM in this study (Fig. 13   (a)). This section uses the long period of continuous COSOMS SM data as a benchmark for SM sensors calibration. The 70 % COSMOS SM is used for calibration, while the rest is used for validation. The SM sensors are calibrated using different fitting methods, including linear fit (y  = ax  + b ), quadratic fit (y  = ax 2  + bx + c ), and exponential fitting (y  = aebx  ). The accuracy of calibration, and validation are listed in Table 6  , and the accuracy of validation is used for calibration evaluation. Due to the small amount of data records and low precision of the 5TE sensor, only HydraProbe and CS655 sensors are calibrated to ensure the reliability of the statistical results. The linear fit is the commonly used method for SM sensors calibration by correcting the deviation between the SM sensors and the COSMOS data, and after linear fit calibration, the validation RMSE values of HydraProbe, and CS655 decreased by 27.6 %, and 3.9 %, respectively. Moreover, the accuracy of SM sensors can be significantly improved with a proper calibration method, e.g. , exponential fit for HydraProbe and Quadratic fit for CS655: with R increasing 3.4 % and 10.9 %, and RMSE decreasing 25.3 % and 21.6 %, respectively. It can be inferred that COSMOS has the potential for SM sensors calibration, especially under suitable fitting methods.  5.3 Advantages and potential drawbacks In this study, we quantify the effect of salinity on dielectric-based SM measurements, spanning from point to coarse scales, treating COSMOS SM as a benchmark. The findings reveal that the effect of soil salinity on dielectric-based SM measurements is non-negligible. Furthermore, the results indicate that the effect of soil salinity should be considered in the core algorithm of existing SM data products to improve SM measurement accuracy. These findings can support the improvement of the SM sensors' quality in the saline area, and serve as a reference for researchers to choose suitable SM data products in coastal saline areas. Additionally, this study can offer a novel approach to address the knowledge gap in soil salinity quantification on multi-scale dielectric-based SM. Nevertheless, there are some limitations. First, due to the absence of continuous soil salinity values over an extended period, future research should focus on quantitatively analyzing the interactions between soil salinity and SM. Additionally, the quantified results need to be verified on a COSMOS observation network in the typical saline regions instead of only one site. Subsequent research will also consider the impact of the mismatch between microwave penetration depth and COSMOS effective depth. In addition to soil salinity, there are several factors that can also affect the accuracy of satellite-based SM products, e.g. , irrigation amounts, vegetation mass, and soil organic matter (SOM) (Kim et al., 2023 ). In particular, despite the poor performance of the L-band based SM products (i.e. , SMAP and SMOS) due to the effect of soil salinity, they have been proven to be advantageous in SM estimation in tropical areas of medium vegetation coverage (Ma et al., 2023). Meanwhile, relevant research teams also keep constantly updating these SM data products, and have made specific improvements in accuracy (Colliander et al., 2023 ).   6 Conclusion Motivated by exploring the uncertainties associated with soil salinity on dielectric-based SM measurements, this paper quantifies the effect of soil salinity on three SM sensors (i.e. , HydraProbe, CS655, and 5TE) and five types of mainstream ongoing satellite-based SM products (i.e. , AMSR-2, ACSAT, SMOS, SMAP, and CYGNSS) utilizing the salinity-independent COSMOS records. The COSMOS SM, obtained with high accuracy, is retrieved by considering the effects of atmospheric pressure, atmospheric water vapor, and solar activity on COSMOS’ raw neutron counting rate. Subsequently, the soil salinity influences on the point-scale and coarse-scale SM measurements are evaluated and characterized, with COSMOS SM serving as a benchmark. The key findings can be summarized as follows:1) This study reveals that COSMOS has the potential to bridge the knowledge gap in multi-scale dielectric-based SM from point scale to coarse scale. The COSMOS SM, considering the effects of atmospheric pressure, atmospheric water vapor, and solar activity, has shown a high agreement with in-situ SM (R=0.815, and ubRMSE=0.032 m3  m−3  and GLDAS SM (R=0.845, and ubRMSE=0.031 m3  m−3 ), respectively.  2) All three SM sensors are affected by soil salinity and deviated from the COSMOS data. The result indicates that HydraProbe (R=0.647, and ubRMSE=0.055 m3  m−3 ) performs notably better than CS655 (R=0.57, and ubRMSE=0.059 m3  m−3 ) and 5TE (R=0.416, and ubRMSE=0.058 m3  m−3 ). Moreover, SM accuracy can be improved to some extent by using appropriate SM sensor calibration methods.  3) The influence of soil salinity on satellites-based SM measurements is non-negligible; L-band SM products are more susceptible to disturbance from soil salinity than C-bands, with mean R=0.409 and mean ubRMSE=0.677 m3  m−3  for the C-band compared to mean R=0.200 and mean ubRMSE=0.102 m3  m−3  for the L-band, respectively.
1 Introduction Extreme precipitation events pose significant social, economic, and environmental risks to a range of human and natural systems. Extreme precipitation events have caused significant economic loss in China in recent years. (Chen and Zhai, 2013; Gu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021b ). For instance, heavy rainfall events caused severe flooding over the Yangtze River basin from 12th June to 23rd August in 1998, leading to over 3000 deaths and $40 billion in direct economic losses (Liu et al., 2008 ). A persistent heavy rainfall event occurred from mid-June to mid-July 2018 in parts of Sichuan, Gansu, and Shanxi provinces in central western China, and the direct economic loss was over $1.3 billion (Zhang et al., 2020 ). Moreover, the intensity and frequency of extreme precipitation are also found to be significantly increased in recent years in many parts of China (Jiang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021a; Sun et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023b ). Skillful and reliable extreme precipitation prediction is crucial for disaster prevention and mitigation (White et al., 2022 ). However, it remains challenging as extreme precipitation events occur at multiple spatiotemporal scales (Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023a ). Most previous studies focused on predicting seasonal statistics of extreme precipitation events using large-scale circulation anomalies as predictors. Zeng et al. (2011)  predicted seasonal maximum 5-day accumulated precipitation over Canada using sea surface temperature and 500 hPa geopotential height anomalies as potential predictors. Wei et al. (2020)  introduced a decision-tree approach to predict extreme precipitation in the rainy season. Han et al. (2019)  established a seasonal prediction model to predict extreme precipitation days over northeast China during midsummer. Much fewer studies focus on sub-seasonal extreme precipitation forecasts as the sources of predictability are much fewer compared to seasonal forecasts (Vitart and Robertson, 2018 ). One of the most common approaches for sub-seasonal extreme precipitation forecasts is to run general circulation models (GCMs) (Pegion et al., 2019; Vitart et al., 2017 ). However, the prediction skill of sub-seasonal extreme precipitation derived from GCMs is always low as the GCMs are of low capability in capturing dynamic sources, misrepresentation of atmosphere–ocean interactions and atmosphere–ocean interactions in GCMs, and many other aspects (Wu et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2024 ). The boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation (BSISO), which is the predominant variability of the Asian summer monsoon, is considered one of the major sources of predictability for extreme weather events at sub-seasonal time scales. The BSISO has been proven to have significant impacts on extreme precipitation events in China (Chen and Zhai, 2017; Hsu et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2018 ). Recently, several studies have investigated the possibility of predicting extreme precipitation with BSISO indices as potential predictors. Lee et al. (2017)  predicted the occurrence of extreme precipitation at different BSISO phases over Asia using empirical probability distributions. Zhu et al. (2023b)  developed a hybrid dynamical-statistical model to predict sub-seasonal precipitation anomalies using novel indices. Deep learning models were also proposed to predict sub-seasonal extreme rainfall events with the GCM predicted large-scale circulation patterns as predictors (Xie et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, the definition of “extreme” is not unique (Gimeno et al., 2022 ). There are various statistical techniques to define extreme precipitation. Most previous studies predicted the occurrence of sub-seasonal extreme precipitation events defined by fitting extreme value distributions. However, it is not sufficient to estimate the chance of predicting sub-seasonal extreme precipitation. In addition, the relationship between BSISO and extreme precipitation is of high uncertainty. It is still unknown to what extent can the BSISO indices help to improve the prediction skill of extreme precipitation events. To address the above challenges, we introduce a hybrid statistical-dynamical framework to predict monthly maximum one-day precipitation (Rx1D) and monthly maximum five-day precipitation (Rx5D) over China. To have a more comprehensive assessment, we also evaluate the prediction skill of the occurrence of extreme precipitation events with exceedance probabilities of 50 %, 20 %, and 5 % for both Rx1D and Rx5D. In the following section, the data and methodology are briefly introduced. The prediction skill and reliability of extreme precipitation events are presented in Sect. 3, while the results are discussed in Sect. 4. Key findings are summarized in Sect. 5.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Data 2.1.1 Precipitation dataset In this study, China is divided into 17 hydroclimatic regions based on both watershed division and climate classifications (Fig. 1   and Table 1  ). We also use the latest Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation version 2.8 (MSWEP V2.8) dataset to derive the area-weighted precipitation of each hydroclimatic region over China. Studies have indicated that the MSWEP precipitation dataset outperforms other datasets in estimating extreme precipitation in different regions (Li et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022b ).  2.1.2 Reanalysis dataset and OLR dataset The daily mean zonal wind at 850 hPa (U850) is derived from the ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020 ) reanalysis dataset at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ . The daily mean outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) data is provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL), Boulder, Colorado, USA, from their website at https://psl.noaa.gov . All daily mean data including U850 and OLR are bilinear interpolated onto a horizontal resolution of 2.5° × 2.5°.  2.1.3 Hindcast dataset The ECMWF hindcast data of precipitation, U850, and OLR are retrieved from the S2S database at https://apps.ecmwf.int/datasets/data/s2s/ . Compared to other GCMs, the ECMWF model shows the highest forecast skill in various aspects (Jie et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2021 ). In this study, we choose hindcasts when the ECMWF model version dates are in the year 2021 from May to October. Thus, the hindcasts cover the period of 2001–2020. The gridded precipitation hindcasts are area-weighted averages through 17 hydroclimatic regions as the observational data. All atmospheric hindcast fields including U850 and OLR are bilinear interpolated onto a horizontal resolution of 2.5° ×   2.5° as the reanalysis dataset.   2.2 Methodology 2.2.1 Extreme precipitation indices Numerous extreme indices have been proposed and used to quantify different aspects of climate phenomena. The Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI; https://www.wcrp-climate.org/etccdi ) defined 27 indices to characterize different aspects of moderate temperature and precipitation extremes. These indices have been largely adopted in various studies, especially in Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reports (Seneviratne et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2011 ). However, we should note that different climate indices are calculated at different temporal scales. In this study, we select the monthly maximum one-day precipitation (Rx1D) and maximum five-day precipitation (Rx5D) as predictands (Table 2  ). As we mentioned above, the Rx1D and Rx5D characterize moderate precipitation extremes. To have a more comprehensive assessment, we also evaluate the performance of forecasts in terms of events with exceedance probabilities of 50 %, 20 %, and 5 % for both Rx1D and Rx5D. These precipitation thresholds approximately correspond to annual exceedance probabilities (AEP) of 1:2 AEP, 1:5 AEP, and 1:20 AEP (Table 2 ). Fig. 2   presents the spatial distribution of climatological monthly maximum 1-day precipitation (Rx1D) and maximum 5-day precipitation (Rx5D) over the 17 hydroclimatic regions in China. The spatial patterns of Rx1D and Rx5D are consistent with the onset process of East Asia Summer Monsoon (EASM).  2.2.2 BSISO indices We follow the same approaches as Lee et al. (2013)  and Lee et al. (2015)  to obtain both observed and hindcast BSISO indices. The U850 and OLR anomalies are firstly obtained by removing the mean and first three harmonics of climatological annual variation, and the running mean of the last 120 days as in Wheeler and Hendon (2004) . The climatology and normalization factors are derived for the period from May 1st to October 31st from 1981 to 2010 using reanalysis data. A multivariate empirical orthogonal function (MV-EOF) is then applied on the normalized U850 and OLR anomalies. The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) of the MV-EOF analysis are defined as observed BSISO1 index to represent the canonical northward propagation with quasi-oscillating periods of 30–60 days. The PC1 and PC2 are referred to as BSISO1_1 and BSISO1_2 for brevity. The third and fourth PCs (PC3 and PC4) are defined as observed BSISO2 index to represent the northward/northwestward propagation with periods of 10–30 days, and the PC3 and PC4 are referred to as BSISO2_1 and BSISO2_2 in the following sections. Fig. 3   presents the phase space composite curves of BSISO1 and BSISO2. When the convection associated with BSISO1 first appears in Phase 1 (equatorial Indian Ocean), it propagates eastward to Phases 3–4 (Maritime continent) in the following days. When the convection associated with BSISO2 is first located in Phase 1 (Indian Ocean) and Phase 2 (the Philippine Sea), it propagates northwestward to Phase 3 (Indian and South China Sea) and Phase 4 (Bay of Bengal). For hindcast BSISO indices, the model climatology of U850 and OLR is first removed as a function of the initial date and lead time. The interannual variability is further removed by subtracting the running mean of the last 120 days. Here, the observed anomalies of U850 and OLR are used before the initial date of hindcasts to make enough data for the running mean. Finally, the hindcast BSISO1 and BSISO2 indices are obtained by projecting the normalized hindcast anomalies of U850 and OLR onto the observed BSISO EOF modes.  2.2.3 The hybrid statistical-dynamical framework We introduce a hybrid statistical-dynamical framework proposed by Schepen et al. (2012)  to generate probabilistic prediction of Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation for each month and each hydroclimatic region over China. This approach consists of three parts, including calibration, bridging, and merging. A Bayesian joint probability (BJP) approach is first applied to calibrate raw precipitation forecasts derived from GCMs. This is referred to as the calibration model. The BJP approach is also used to generate probabilistic forecasts using large-scale circulation patterns as predictors. This is referred to as the bridging model. The calibrated forecasts and bridged forecasts were then merged through the Bayesian model averaging (BMA) method (Wang et al., 2012a ). Thus, the hybrid statistical-dynamical framework is also known as the Calibration, Bridging, and Merging (CBaM) method. It has been proven to be able to generate skillful and reliable seasonal precipitation and temperature forecasts over different regions (Peng et al., 2014; Schepen et al., 2016; Schepen et al., 2014; Strazzo et al., 2019 ). However, much less work has been done on sub-seasonal time scales. In this study, the predictor X   is the ensemble mean of ECMWF forecasted monthly Rx1D or Rx5D for the calibration model. For bridging model, the predictor X   is the ensemble mean of ECMWF forecasted monthly mean value of each BSISO index. Therefore, there is one calibration model and four bridging models for each month and each hydroclimatic region. A leave-one-year-out cross-validation strategy is used to evaluate the prediction skill and reliability of sub-seasonal extreme precipitation. The BACs for the forecasted BSISO indices are mostly over 0.5 for all months, while the BMSEs are below 2   . This suggests that the ECMWF model can provide skilful predictions for both the BSISO1 and BSISO2 index for all months compared to climatological forecasts.  3.2 Prediction skill and reliability of monthly Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation Fig. 5   presents the CRPS skill score of the calibration model (Calibration), bridging models (BSISO1_1, BSISO1_2, BSISO2_1, BSISO2_2), and merged forecasts (BMA) for monthly maximum one-day precipitation (Rx1D) over China. The calibration model, which uses the ensemble mean of precipitation forecasts of ECMWF model as predictors, shows little skill in predicting Rx1D precipitation in May. The CRPS skill scores are mostly negative for the calibration model. In comparison, the bridging models show higher skill in predicting monthly Rx1D precipitation in May. Positive CRPS skill scores are found over Region 4 (Yellow River), Region 8 (Liao River), Region 10 (Huai River), and Region 14 (Middle Yangtze River) when the BSISO1_1 is used as the predictor. The merged forecasts (BMA) are generally more skillful compared to both calibration model and bridging models. Similar results are also found in other months in June, July, August, and September. The calibration model shows higher prediction skill compared to bridging models in October, suggesting that the ensemble mean of precipitation forecasts of ECMWF model can provide more useful information than BSISO indices. This may be explained by the occurrence of Rx1D precipitation during October. The CRPS skill score of monthly maximum five-day precipitation (Rx5D) over China is shown in Fig. 6  . In general, the prediction skill of Rx5D is higher than that of the Rx1D. This suggests that the Rx5D is of higher predictability compared to Rx1D. The BSISO indices can provide useful information for predicting Rx5D precipitation when the precipitation forecasts of ECMWF model are of low accuracy. The CRPS skill score is negative over Region 13 (Yangtze River) for the calibration model in May. In comparison, positive CRPS skill scores are found when the BSISO1_1 is used as the predictor. In addition, the merged forecasts are more skillful than both the calibration model and bridging models, especially in May and August. However, we should also note the prediction skill in July is relatively lower than in other months. Positive skill scores are only found in Region 7 (Songhua River), Region 12 (Southwest rivers in Yunnan), Region 15 (Lower Yangtze River), and Region 16 (Pearl River). To have a better illustration of the advantages of merged forecasts, we analyze the number of regions where CRPS skill scores are greater than 0 % and 5 % for Rx1D and Rx5D in each month (Fig. 7   and Fig. 8  ). In general, the number of regions with positive skill scores increases when the calibrated forecasts and bridging forecasts are merged through the BMA approach. The improvement is more pronounced for Rx5D than Rx1D, especially in August. There are only six hydroclimatic regions where the CRPS skill scores are greater than 5 % for Rx5D in August for calibrated forecasts. In comparison, there are ten hydroclimatic regions for merged forecasts. However, we also note that the number of hydroclimatic regions slightly decreases after merging in July and October. This indicates that the calibrated forecasts show better performance compared to the merged forecasts. The reliability of merged forecasts for Rx1D and Rx5D is presented in Fig. 9  . The α-index of merged forecasts is mostly over 0.9 for almost all regions and all months, indicating that the merged forecasts are of high reliability.  3.3 Prediction skill of the occurrence of extreme precipitation events Fig. 10   presents the Brier skill score (BSS) of merged forecasts for Rx1D, 5Rx1D, and 20Rx1D precipitation over 17 hydroclimatic regions in China. The spatiotemporal patterns of BSS are similar to the CRPSS shown in Fig. 4 . Although the prediction skill decreases for 5Rx1D, positive Brier skill scores still can be found over certain regions and months. The merged forecasts show lowest prediction skill for 20Rx1D, and the Brier skill scores are mostly negative for almost all months and all hydroclimatic regions. The Brier skill score (BSS) of merged forecasts for Rx5D, 5Rx5D, and 20Rx5D is shown in Fig. 11  . The prediction skill of Rx5D, 5Rx5D, and 20Rx5D is higher than that of Rx1D, 5Rx5D, and 20Rx5D, respectively. Positive Brier skill scores are observed for Rx5D for most months and regions except July. Although the prediction skill of 5Rx5D is lower compared to that of Rx5D, the Brier skill scores are mostly positive in May, August, September, and October. The merged forecasts show limited skill in prediction 20Rx5D, where the Brier skill scores are mostly negative. Positive skill scores are only observed in several regions in September and October.   4 Discussion In this study, we introduce a hybrid statistical-dynamical framework to predict sub-seasonal extreme precipitation for each month from May to October over 17 hydroclimatic regions in China. The results suggest that the hybrid approach can provide skillful and reliable probabilistic sub-seasonal extreme precipitation prediction over China. However, the prediction skill is of high spatial and temporal variability. Fig. 12   presents the date of occurrence of Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation for each month from May to October. Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation mostly occur in the second and third pentads in May, June, and July. Whereas, the sub-seasonal precipitation forecasts derived from GCMs are of low accuracy especially when the lead time is beyond 10–14 days (de Andrade et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021b ). This may explain the low prediction skill of the calibration model for Rx1D and Rx5D in these months. In comparison, the forecasted BSISO indices are of high accuracy as shown in Fig. 4 . This provides great opportunities for improving Rx1D and Rx5D predictions. Fig. 13   shows the model weights of the calibration model and bridging models for Rx1D prediction in May. The model weights of bridging models are higher than the calibration model over most hydroclimatic regions, except Region 5 (Upper Yellow River), Region 6 (Hai River), and Region 13 (Yangtze River). This suggests that the BSISO indices help to improve Rx1D and Rx5D prediction skill in May. We also note that the distributions of BSISO indices vary over different hydroclimatic regions. The weights of BSISO1 indices are higher than BSISO2 indices over Region 3 (Inland rivers in Inner Mongolia), Region 6 (Hai River), Region 7 (Songhua River), Region 8 (Liao River), Region 9 (Upper Yangtze River), Region 12 (Southwest rivers in Yunnan), Region 14 (Middle Yangtze River), and Region 17 (Southeast rivers). This indicates that the BSISO1 indices can provide more information compared to BSISO2 indices. Similar results are found in other months in June, July, August, and September. In October, Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation generally occurs in the first pentad. The precipitation forecasts of ECMWF model therefore can provide useful information for predicting Rx1D and Rx5D, and the calibration model shows much higher model weight compared to bridging models (Fig. 14  ). We should also note that the prediction skill in July is much lower than in other months. Both the calibration model and bridging models show negative skill scores over most hydroclimatic regions. This may relate to both the occurrence of extreme precipitation events and weak relationship between BSISO and precipitation anomalies. Liu and Lu (2022)  suggested that the BSISO was significantly related to precipitation anomalies over South China during many phases in May and June, but related to very weak anomalies during all the phases in July and August. In addition, the prediction skill of 20Rx1D and 20Rx5D is still too low, which suggests that there is much room for improvement. The influences of extratropical anomalies on extreme precipitation should be investigated. Recently, Zhu et al. (2023b)  proposed two sets of novel indices based on the compound zonal displacements of the South Asia high (SAH) and the western Pacific subtropical high (WPH) to monitor and predict the intraseasonal variation of Meiyu. These climate indices will be introduced in the future to improve the forecast skill.  5 Conclusions Skillful and reliable sub-seasonal extreme precipitation forecasts are crucial for disaster prevention and mitigation. In this study, we introduce a hybrid statistical-dynamical framework to predict sub-seasonal extreme precipitation (monthly Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation) by combining the strengths of both dynamical models and statistical models. The ECMWF forecasts of precipitation and boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation (BSISO) indices are used as predictors to establish calibration model and bridging models, separately. The calibration model and bridging models are then merged through the Bayesian Modeling Averaging (BMA) method. The accuracy and reliability of sub-seasonal extreme precipitation are evaluated through a leave-one-year-out cross-validation strategy. To have a more comprehensive assessment, we also evaluate the prediction skill of the occurrence of extreme precipitation events with exceedance probabilities of 50 %, 20 %, 5 % for both Rx1D and Rx5D. Our results suggest that the forecast skill of the calibration model is higher compared to bridging models in August, September, and October, while the bridging models show better performance in predicting Rx1D and Rx5D in May, June, and July. The BMA merged forecasts take advantage of both calibration model and bridging models, and can provide skilful and reliable forecasts for both Rx1D and Rx5D precipitation. The Brier skill score of merged forecasts suggests that the hybrid statistical-dynamical framework can also provide skilful forecasts for 5Rx1D and 5Rx5D precipitation in comparison to long-term climatology. The results of α-index suggest that BMA merged forecasts are of high reliability. However, we also note that the prediction skill is of high spatial and temporal variability. The prediction skill in July is much lower than other months owing to both the occurrence of extreme precipitation event and weak relationship between BSISO and precipitation anomalies. In addition, the prediction skill of 20Rx1D and 20Rx5D is still too low, which suggests that there is much room for improvement for such rare events. We show that the prospects for the sub-seasonal prediction of extreme precipitation are promising. In the future, the influences of extratropical anomalies on the extreme precipitation should be investigated. The lagged relationships between atmospheric intraseasonal oscillations and precipitation anomalies will also be considered to further improve sub-seasonal extreme precipitation forecast skill.
1 Introduction Traditional (non-interacting) particle-tracking methods are often used for advection-dominated groundwater systems because of their numerical stability and because they simulate advection without incurring spurious numerical diffusion that impacts dispersion, dilution, and mixing (Labolle et al., 1996; Pérez-Illanes and Fernàndez-Garcia, 2024 ). This is especially important when simulating chemically-reactive transport because the typically nonlinear reactions are highly sensitive to concentration fluctuations and/or errors (Tartakovsky et al., 2012; Paster et al., 2014 ). In order to simulate chemical reactions, the particles must either exchange mass, or have their masses mapped to concentrations through spatial averaging (Tompson and Dougherty, 1992; Benson and Bolster, 2016; Sole-Mari and Fernàndez-Garcia, 2018; Sole-Mari et al., 2020; Perez et al., 2019a ). The mass-transfer particle tracking (MTPT) techniques move mass between all particles according to their proximity, and any geochemical reactions may be completed on the particles. The MTPT algorithm is uniquely useful for simulating transport and chemical reaction because it does not necessarily solve an upscaled, volume-averaged advection–dispersion-reaction equation. First, MTPT is able to realistically simulate mixing at a rate slower than spreading because the two processes are simulated separately (Benson et al., 2019 ). As a result, a single diffusion coefficient is not forced to represent the two processes in one equation. Second, the MTPT methods simulate a stochastically-perturbed equation and may faithfully preserve the sub-grid fluctuations of velocity, dispersion, and/or chemical concentrations (Schmidt et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2017; Benson et al., 2017, 2019; Sole-Mari et al., 2017; Sole-Mari and Fernàndez-Garcia, 2018 ). In the case of highly nonlinear chemical reactions, these perturbations may dominate the overall behavior of the systems. The capability of MTPT to simulate systems undergoing chemical reaction in a purely Lagrangian manner was unlocked by allowing each particle to carry an unlimited number of chemical species (Bolster et al., 2016; Benson and Bolster, 2016 ). The particles (which may be fluid or solid, Schmidt et al. (2019, 2020) ) undergo reactions occurring at the particle level. This means that mass must move between  numerical particles in a physically realistic way. This mass-transfer may, therefore, be formulated as a true, local, mixing process (Benson et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2021 ), which is straightforward to implement when a good approximation of the probability distribution (i.e., the Green’s function) of local diffusion or transverse dispersion is known (Benson et al., 2019; Perez et al., 2019b ). A physically-based model for the amount of mass transfer between any two particles originally was given by the probability of particle “interaction” based on their separation vector (Benson and Meerschaert, 2008 ). For example, a locally isotropic and Fickian diffusion process dictates that the mass transfer between any two particles labeled i   and j   is proportional to the density function of their co-location (Benson and Meerschaert, 2008; Schmidt et al., 2018 ) and given by (1) p  i , j   = 1  ( 2 π ( D  i   + D  j   )  Δ t )   d / 2     exp − | x  i   − x  j   |   2    2 ( D  i   + D  j   )  Δ t     ,     where p  i , j     is the probability that the two particles will interact over a time-step of length Δ t   , D  i     and D  j     are each particle’s local diffusion coefficient, d   is the number of dimensions, and x  i     and x  j     are the particle position vectors (Benson and Meerschaert, 2008; Schmidt et al., 2018 ). This is easily generalized when the local dispersion is anisotropic and each D   is a d × d    matrix (Appendix). These probability density values dictate the proportion of the mass of each species that is transferred between particles or the amount that stays “at home” when i = j   . We denote this specific approach as Mass-Transfer Particle-Tracking or MTPT. Clearly the mass transfer decreases rapidly with particle separation distance (which can be exploited algorithmically), but theoretically, each particle can interact with all others, even if the amounts are minuscule. This latter feature becomes a complication and a bottleneck when compared to traditional PT methods, in which each particle is completely independent of all others. The trade-off for these new capabilities of MTPT is increased computational complexity. A naive application of Eq. (1)  among a total of N  P     particles in a domain would build an N  P   × N  P      matrix of all particle interaction probabilities (Appendix). For more than a few tens of thousands of particles, the full interaction matrix approach would exceed the memory capacity of most desktop computers. This approach would also be inefficient because many of the particle interactions are negligible due to large separation distances. As a result, the full-matrix approach required improvement to make it computationally feasible. One of the traditional ways of reducing the size of large matrices is called domain decomposition, which can be visualized as a geometric process in which the physical domain is subdivided into a set of adjacent tiles (Fig. 1 ). Computations can be performed on these subsets of the domain, as long as potential interactions between adjacent tiles are properly treated. These geometric-based decompositions include very simple “checkerboard” tilings (Schauer et al., 2023 ) or more advanced tree-based subdivisions, including quad-tree (2-d  ), oct-tree (3-d  ), and kd-tree (Bentley, 1975; Kennel, 2004 ), wherein each tile is created to possess approximately equal numbers of particles. In this paper we also develop a novel non-geometric, or list-based, decomposition that simplifies computations significantly. The common thread is that any decomposition seeks to reduce the overall computational load and has the added benefit that parallel processing threads may handle the subdivisions simultaneously.  The foundations for parallelizing MTPT were explored by Engdahl et al. (2019)  who found that simply subdividing the spatial domain resulted in a reduction of the total number of calculations, or floating-point operations (flops) for a full-matrix formulation. Even when implemented serially on a single-processor machine, the algorithm showed remarkably linear speedup with the number of subdivisions. The basis of the speedup derives from the fact that a forward full-matrix calculation requires a number of flops proportional to n  2    , where n   is the number of rows and/or columns. Using Eq. (1)  on all N  P     particles in a simulation requires roughly k N  P  2      flops, where k   is an arbitrary constant related to the difficulty of certain operations (e.g., calculating particle separations versus actual mass transfer). In a perfect world, subdividing the particles into S   roughly equally load-balanced sub-domains means that each sub-domain requires k ( N  P   / S )   2      flops for a total of S × k ( N  P   / S )   2   = k N  P  2   / S    flops. However, the approach still built a “full” interaction matrix for all particles within each subdomain, leaving significant room for improvement. Despite the notable speedup, the performance of the simple domain decomposition algorithm can be rapidly outpaced by that of tree-based search algorithms. These searches can efficiently find particles within a defined radius, so that more distant particles can be ignored and the matrices become much more sparse, which serves the dual purpose of reducing the number of flops and significantly decreasing memory requirements. Depending on the tree construction and data clustering, each search among N  P     particles in a single tree may scale somewhere between O ( ln N  P   )     and O ( N  P  2   )    , with O ( N  P   )     being typical (Finkel and Bentley, 1974 ). The gains afforded by search trees means domain decomposition might not be necessary in many cases, but the key advantage of the decomposition is that it allows the set of particles to be distributed among a collection of processors when each has its own memory (Schauer et al., 2023 ). However, the question of speedup on a shared memory system is not as clear. For example, subdividing the domain reduces computations within each subdivision, but if these computations are performed in parallel, the demands on shared memory increase substantially. In short, performance and efficiency under a shared memory architecture are under-explored facets of the MTPT acceleration schemes, and the question becomes: How fast can the MTPT methods be made without sacrificing accuracy? In this paper, we examine the effects of problem physics, user decisions, and algorithm design on the efficiency of the MTPT method. Here, we focus exclusively on shared-memory multi-core and multi-threading CPUs because of the ease of implementation using OpenMP directives. This allows us to concentrate on speed and memory requirements of the algorithms themselves. We investigate geometric domain decomposition using the full-matrix scheme of Engdahl et al. (2019)  and a sparse-matrix version thereof. Even though it is known to be a non-optimized scheme, the full matrix version provides a standard benchmark against which several improvements may be judged. To this end we also develop and test a non-geometric, list-based decomposition that should allow for optimal parallelization. Before embarking on the analyses, we emphasize that the term “core” refers to a separate processing unit on a multiprocessor chip. Each core makes calculations independent of each other. Any core will have some idle time when making calculations and moving data to and from memory, so compilers may take advantage and run other sets of instructions on a core during idle time in a process called multi-threading. The term “thread” refers to a set of calculations performed on a core, and (for example) the parallel compiler commands in OpenMP allow two threads to be run simultaneously per core. A single thread on a core runs at full speed, but a second thread, looking for idle time, will run somewhat slower than the “first”. Most users looking for parallel performance will use all available threads when they get a chance, so we will show performance for all thread numbers, up to twice the number of physical cores, so scaling behaviors will change when more threads are requested than physical cores. Our estimates of speedup below are based on each core running at full speed.  2 Parallelization memory requirements and speed Before exploring the various means of parallelization, it is instructive to examine the basic operation of the mass transfer algorithm. A vector of the masses on all particles at any time t   is advanced over some finite timestep via a forward matrix multiplication P × m ( t )  = m ( t + Δ t )     (see, e.g., Schmidt et al. (2018), Engdahl et al. (2019) ). The matrix P   encodes the degree to which each particle pair will exchange mass, based on their separation distance and direction. To conserve mass, the matrix is doubly-stochastic, being square, symmetric, with all row- and column-sums equal to unity (Appendix). Either during the creation of the initial condition, or during disordered transport, the particle masses in the vector m ( t )     may become irregularly positioned in the domain. As a result, the matrix P   in the operation of mass transfer will be non-structured (Fig. 4 ). Furthermore, many of the entries in P   will be negligible in magnitude and may be omitted, as in Fig. 4 , leading to a sparse matrix. When the matrix is first constructed by applying Eq. (1)  for each particle pair i , j   , it is symmetric, inasmuch as the Gaussian probability density associated with any two particles is the same, irrespective of the order. However, because of the particles’ discrete nature of approximating the continuous Gaussian, the rows will not exactly sum to unity (as required for mass conservation — see Appendix). One method (Herrera et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2018 ) normalizes each value in the matrix by the average of its row-sum and column-sum. For the red-highlighted entry in Fig. 4 , this is represented by the red highlighting of row 20 and column 71. Because of matrix symmetry, the symmetric “partner” probability (the blue entry at the end of the arrow) has a column-sum equal to the row-sum of the partner and vice-versa (denoted by the blue row and column). Therefore, normalization using an arithmetic average of the row- and column-sums maintains matrix symmetry. However, because each value in a row gets a unique renormalization factor, the row sums (hence column sums) are not guaranteed to sum to unity. The renormalization can be repeated (this is called the Sinkhorn–Knopp algortihm (Knight, 2008; Young, 2024 )) until a suitable closure is reached. A new matrix normalization algorithm (Appendix), eliminates the column sums by estimating the particle spacing a priori . Then the row-sum alone is used to estimate probabilities and any discrepancy between the row-sum from unity is adjusted at the main diagonal term alone. This algorithm maintains whole matrix symmetry, and also provides a new form of parallelism, because without the column-sums, a single row may be created, and the mass transfer calculated, independently of all others. The rows may be calculated in the order they are listed in memory, on different cores or threads, without any regard for the actual particles’ spatial locations. We call this algorithm “list-based decomposition”, because any subset of rows corresponding to a list of particles may be sent to a processor. This method relies on normalization using the row-sums alone so that any row of the matrix is independent of all others. Because this method is completely new, we provide an analysis of the accuracy immediately. 2.1 List-based algorithm accuracy When β = 1   , the solution progresses via convolution of the probability matrix with the current masses (Appendix). Therefore, the probabilities in matrix P   are discrete approximations of the Green’s function of the local mixing — without loss of generality a Gaussian is used here. In the new algorithm, the “peak” value is adjusted, based on the sum (discrete integral) of the probability values in a row. Of course, for multiple time steps, the continued convolution of this near-Gaussian with itself will converge to a Gaussian, but for a smaller number of timesteps, and a smaller number of particles, how error-prone is the method? First, we simulate two similar scenarios as for the speed tests that follow: a 2-d   domain Ω = [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]    , D = 1 0  − 3     , total time = 100, with Δ t = 10    and 1. A single particle at the center of the domain is given a mass of Ω / N  P     , where N  P     is the total number of particles. A range of particle numbers were used, giving a range of particle spacings Δ x = ( Ω / N  P   )   1 / 2     . Here we use uniform, non-random spacing and no random walks to isolate the performance of the algorithm in its pure form. The performance is judged by the RMSE between particle masses domain-wide and the analytical 2-d   Gaussian Green’s function. Clearly, as the number of particles is increased (and the inter-particle spacing, Δ x    is decreased), the discrete integral of the Gaussian approaches unity and the adjustment at the center particle (i.e., P  i , i    ) tends to zero. The transition from poor fits to essentially perfect fits occurs fairly rapidly, at around Δ x ≈ D Δ t      (Fig. 2 ). For smaller spacings, the error drops to the level of machine precision (∼ 1 0  − 16     ).  Constructing a discrete version of the Green’s function is best done with regularly-spaced (and stationary) particles, as in the last example. But when particles move due to differential advection and/or random walks, the particle spacings, hence number of particles in each matrix row, may change drastically. There is no explicit analytic solution for this problem, so we compare the new algorithm to the row- and column-normalized method that has been tested extensively elsewhere (Sole-Mari et al., 2019a ). We generated a divergence-free, two-dimensional velocity field v ( x )     and placed 20,000 initially mass-free particles randomly in a circle with radius = 10 surrounding a single particle with mass representing a Dirac delta function (Fig. 3 a). The velocity field was generated using a finite-difference solution of the equation ∇ ⋅ ( K ∇ h )  = 0   , with Dirichlet conditions for hydraulic head h = 1    and h = 0    on the left and right and ∂ h / ∂ y = 0    on the top and bottom boundaries (Fig. 3 a), and a grid spacing of Δ x = Δ y = 1   . The underlying random correlated hydraulic conductivity (K  ) field is log-Normal with an isotropic correlation length of l n ( K )     of 10 length units, E ( l n ( K )  )  = 0    and σ ( l n ( K )  )  = 0 . 5   . Once h   was solved, the velocity is given at each grid-cell interface by v ( x )  = K ∇ h   . Velocity vectors at each particle were then calculated by linear interpolation of interface velocities, preserving the divergence-free velocity (Labolle et al., 1996 ). The number of particles was chosen so that the inter-particle spacing Δ x = ( π 1 0  2   / 20000 )   1 / 2   = 0 . 125   , giving each finite-difference cell on the order of 64 particles for good resolution of the sub-grid velocity. The same random seed was used for initial particle positions for both mass transfer algorithms, so the particles would be advected to the same positions at any time. We chose an isotropic mass-transfer dispersion coefficient D = D  m o l   + α  T   | v |    , with D  m o l   = 1 0  − 8     , α  T   = 5 × 1 0  − 3     , and the mean velocity was on the order of 0.05. It is important to note that the optimal time steps for advection and mass transfer are very different. From Fig. 2  we see that the algorithm requires the condition Δ x = ( V / N  p   )   1 / d   < D Δ t     , or Δ t > ( V / N  p   )   2 / d   / D   . Using the largest D   in the field, this gave a value of Δ t > 35   . On the other hand, the particles were advected using simple forward Euler methods and limited to traversing 1/2 of each underlying velocity grid with block of size 1 on each side, giving Δ t < 5   . As a result, during the operator splitting, a number of advective steps were performed before each mass transfer step. The plume is split and strongly elongated in the mean travel direction (Fig. 3 a). The plume, shown in red, is also elongated and slightly multi-modal (Fig. 3 b). Even with very different normalization algorithms, the two methods agree quite well, even at extremely low concentrations (Fig. 3 b,c).    2.2 Memory-usage comparison It is clear that the row-sum normalization will be faster than the row-and-column-sum normalization for the same problem, simply because the column-sum calculations are eliminated. Also, the calculations that determine which particles are in a geometric subdomain are eliminated. But another major concern is the memory requirement. Referring to Fig. 1 , we can estimate bounds on how much more computer memory the domain decomposition with row- and column-normalization will consume. 2.2.1 Full-matrix, domain decomposition For a full-matrix computation, the number of particles within a subdomain, plus the neighboring “ghost particles” that may influence particles inside that subdomain (Fig. 1 ), define the number of rows in one subdomain’s matrix (full or sparse) (Fig. 4 ). For a domain with fairly uniform particle density and cubic subdivisions, the total number of rows in a subdomain is somewhere between N  P   / S    and N  P   / S + ( N  P   / S )  ( 2 × d × 3 4 D Δ t   ( Ω / S )   ( d − 1 )  / d   )    , where N  P     is the total number of particles in the entire domain and S   is the number of (evenly distributed) subdivisions (Schauer et al., 2023 ). The second term counts ghost particles in all directions in d  -dimensions. Subdomains along the full domain edge have fewer ghost particles, and the distribution of particles in the domain can also create irregularities, so this is an approximate upper bound. If the number of ghosts is considered small compared to the subdomain size, then a fair approximation for the number of rows is just N  P   / S   , and if C   cores are used simultaneously (each given a separate subdomain so that C ≤ S   ), then the number of matrix entries required for the parallel, full-matrix domain-decomposition method (denoted M  F M    ), has a lower bound of (2) M  F M   > C N  P    S      2   .       2.2.2 Sparse-matrix, domain decomposition A sparse matrix row stores only the entries for particles within the region of influence (defined by the user), of the i  th particle, as some multiple of the local diffusion distance. This is the average particle density times the volume of that region of influence N  P    Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t   )   d     . The constant κ   is a function of the dimensionality of the system: κ = [ 2 / π , 1 , 4 / 3 ]     for d = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]    . Therefore, a sparse matrix has on the order of N  P  2    S Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2      entries as a lower bound. Given a certain number of cores, C  , on which to make the calculation in parallel, the total number of entries held in memory in the separate P   matrices is on the order of (3) M  S M   ≈ C N  P  2    S Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2   .     The ratio of total full- to sparse-matrix entries for any given simulation (M  F M   / M  S M     ) is therefore on the order of Ω / S  π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2      . The numerator is the volume of real particles in a subdomain and the denominator is a measure of the ghost particle volume. When the latter is as large as the former, then the sparse matrices are full again, as every particle in the subdomain has an influence on all others. In other words, the sparse matrices only “help” when the user-controlled ratio Ω / S  π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2       is large.    2.2.3 List-based decomposition Particle attributes are typically held in some sort of array, and as the particles move around the domain under the influence of heterogeneous velocity and random walks representing macrodispersion, there is no guarantee that neighbors in the array are also neighbors in the spatial domain. This leads to an unstructured matrix and the need to consider all rows when employing previous row- and column-normalization. The large matrices then necessitate the creation of geometric subdomains. In the methods previously discussed, a normalization of the probability values in a matrix row must also be transferred to all of the other rows that represent nearby particles. In other words, a row i   contains information about nearby particles with values of j   that may be anything between 1   and N  P    . Any changes to these values (the P  i , j   s )    must then be reflected in each of the many j   rows to maintain a symmetric P   (Appendix). A possible solution to this bottleneck in performance is to modify the previous algorithms so that only row or  column normalization is required. We propose a new list-based decomposition that adjusts only the diagonal value in each row to ensure each row-sum is equal to unity (Appendix). Doing so, all values of P  i , j     remain unchanged for i ≠ j    during the renormalization process and symmetry is always maintained. Any single row (any single particle’s new mass) may now be calculated independently of all others, and the calculations can proceed down the “list” of particles, irrespective of their spatial positions. Arbitrary portions of the list can be sent to different processors in chunk sizes that are best suited for the problem at hand and the computational architecture. The caveat to this is that updated masses m ( t + Δ t )     must be written to a temporary array until the list is completed, but this is simply a vector of length N  P     for each compound, rather than a square matrix. In practice, the j   particles surrounding particle i   are generally never exactly spaced Δ x    away from each other because of random or non-uniform particle motion. The non-uniform spacing gives a non-unit total probability, and the difference is absorbed by the i   particle. This also means that widely spaced particles (i.e. fewer than average particles) will more likely integrate to less than unity, and the probability of mass staying “home” at the i   node is increased. Overall this reflects less mixing when local particle densities are lower than average. This can be the result of divergence-free fluid deformation (Engdahl et al., 2014 ), which may increase or decrease mixing depending on the relationship of concentration gradients to particle position changes. In the list-based decomposition, a single particle (i.e. matrix row) may be computed independently of all other rows. Each matrix row has the number of entries in the surrounding volume already shown to be N  P    Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     . Using C   cores simultaneous means a list-based memory consumption (M  L    ) of (4) M  L   ≈ C N  P    Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2   .     Therefore, the ratio of the sparse row-column normalization to the list-based row-normalization (M  S M   / M  L     ) is simply N  P   / S   . Under normal conditions, the number of particles far outnumbers the number of subdivisions — this ratio is typically in the hundreds to millions range. To give an idea of the scaling, imagine a typical 2-d   simulation with 100,000 particles, D = 1 0  − 3     , Δ t = 10   , and S = 100    subdivisions run on C =    10 cores. Then the three methods require storing, for the MT matrices, > 1 0  7     , 1 . 9 × 1 0  7     , and 1 . 9 × 1 0  4      entries, respectively. In this case, the full-matrix and the sparse-matrix methods are comparable because the subdomains are small enough (relative to the ghost-particle distance) that the sparse matrices are essentially full, and the list-based algorithm requires 1000 times less memory.   2.3 Computation time and parallel speedup Intuitively, one would like to use as many threads as are within reach for any given simulation. But this can be a problem with diminishing or even decreasing returns due to the physics of the problem and/or the structure of the processors and memory. For the sake of analysis, we will assume here that the problem domain Ω   is relatively uniformly filled with N  P     particles. We may define the domain as rectilinear with volume Ω  x   × Ω  y   × Ω  z     . For the geometric domain decomposition, the domain is subdivided by integers S  x   , S  y   , S  z     , so that the total number of sub-domains is S = S  x   S  y   S  z     . Also for simplicity of overall analysis we assume that D   is a constant. Here we are only looking at performance as a function of domain partitioning, so a simple “checkerboard” decomposition is very close to optimally load-balanced. The particle influence probability density Eq. (1)  implies that particles within about three standard deviations of a sub-domain should be included as ghost particles (e.g., Fig. 1 ). For each of the following examples that have accompanying simulations, Fortran codes were compiled with the GNU gfortran (gcc) compiler version 13.1 using -O3 optimization and OpenMP directives. The fortran codes may be found in the Github repository https://github.com/dbenson5225/parallel_particle_mass_transfer . Unless otherwise noted, the simulations use a 2-d   domain of size [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]    , with N  P   = 100 , 000    particles, D = 1 0  − 3     , Δ t = 10   , and total time = 100   . 2.3.1 Tree-based particle searches One of the keys to either geometric or list-based decomposition is using an efficient algorithm for nearest-neighbor searches, because a naive brute-force search through N  P     particles requires O ( N  P  2   )     calculations. Tree-based algorithms, including quad-tree, kd-tree, and recursive-coordinate-bisection, subdivide the domain (in various ways) into smaller and smaller chunks, keeping track of which chunks are nearest to each other (Finkel and Bentley, 1974; Bentley, 1975; Berger and Bokhari, 1987 ).
