When a request is made to find particles near one another, the algorithm only needs to look at particles in nearby chunks, eliminating extra calculations. In previous work (Paster et al., 2014; Benson et al., 2017 ), we have used a publicly-available Fortran code KDTREE2 (Kennel, 2004 ), but the code is not easily made safe in a shared-memory parallel environment. Instead, we coded a Fortran version of a Python quad-tree code (https://scipython.com/blog/quadtrees-2-implementation-in-python/ ) and provide a brief analysis of its performance here. A quad-tree mesh is based on subdividing a rectangular domain with successive identical quadrants (Finkel and Bentley, 1974 ). When the number of particles in any quadrant exceeds some user-defined threshold value, that quadrant is subsequently subdivided in equal quadrants. This happens recursively until the final quadrants all have less than the threshold “bucket” number of particles. A large bucket enables faster tree generation because of fewer subdivisions. It is thought that a large bucket also makes for slower searches — especially when looking for a fixed number of nearest neighbors (a kNN search). However, we require all particles within a certain radius, so it is unclear how big the bucket size should be. To illustrate, a bucket size of four particles was initially chosen (Fig. 5 a). In keeping with simulations to come later in this paper, the domain is set to [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]     with total number of particles ranging from 100,000 to 5,000,000. After the trees were generated (typically taking less than a few seconds), a loop was set up to vary a search radius from 0.25 to 5 (half the domain size. The total search time versus the number of particles found shows a clear scaling trend: the search times for a given radius are approximately linear with the total number of particles N  P    . However, for large particle numbers there is an obvious performance degradation for the smaller searches. This led us to increase the bucket size systematically over a range of search radii for a single large N  P   = 5 × 1 0  6      (Fig. 5 b). In this case, a bucket size of approximately 500 (10−4  times the total number of particles) minimizes the search times. We also compared the performance of the (Kennel, 2004 ) KDTREE2 code (circles, Fig. 5 b). That kd-tree code is less susceptible to performance degradation due to bucket size, and is also about 2 times faster than the quad-tree code when both are optimized. As mentioned before, we choose the quad-tree because of ease of parallelization. Interestingly, the kd-tree also performs best with a bucket size of 500 with 5 × 1 0  6      total particles.  One might think that the creation of the tree is time-consuming compared to the search for particles. However, the previous results were for finding a number of particles near a single particle in the center of the domain. In the MTPT case, each particle must find its neighbors, which for the worst case is an N  p   × N  p      problem. Here we gauge the relative time requirements for searching for nearest neighbors for every particle in a square domain, and compare that to the tree creation time. We choose two search radii to assess the effect on search times and bucket sizes: r = 0 . 5    and r = 5    in a [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]     domain with either N  p   = 1 0  5      or 1 0  6      particles. Simulations were run on a Macbook air with M2 chip and ample memory. For all values of N  p     and r  , a bucket size of approximately N  p   / 1000    performs best, and searching most of the domain (i.e., r = 5   ) for all 1 0  6      particles is costly in terms of CPU time (Fig. 6 ). Also, the time to create the trees is vastly shorter than the searches themselves.    2.3.2 Geometric decomposition with full matrices One advantage of using a full matrix (i.e., using Eq. (1)  for all particles in every subdomain) is the algorithmic simplicity. There is no need to determine which subsets of particles should be included in the MT matrix before making costly calculations such as distance and total probability. For sub-domains away from the domain edges, the ghost-particle zones will be on all sides of the sub-domain, so the number of rows in the mass-transfer matrix calculation is N  P    S  x   S  y   S  z     = N  P    S     . Each row has a number of entries (counting ghost particles in both directions) on the order of (5) N = N  P   ( Ω  x   / S  x   + 6 4 D Δ t   )  ( Ω  y   / S  y   + 6 4 D Δ t   )  ( Ω  z   / S  z   + 6 4 D Δ t   )   Ω  x   Ω  y   Ω  z       .     If the number of flops for a full matrix is proportional to the product of rows and columns, then the flops for a sub-domain is (6) flops  S   = k N  P  2    S Ω   ( Ω  x   / S  x   + 6 4 D Δ t   )  ( Ω  y   / S  y   + 6 4 D Δ t   )  ( Ω  z   / S  z   + 6 4 D Δ t   )    .     So as D Δ t → 0   , the approximation used by Engdahl et al. (2019) , N  S   = N  P   / S   , is valid and the total number of flops for the S   sub-domains is S k ( N  P   / S )   2   = k N  P  2   / S   . In this case, the ratio of flops for the subdivided domain to the undivided one is approximately 1 / S   . This naive calculation would encourage a user to use as many sub-domains as possible, even with one processing thread, because the total number of flops decreases with the number of sub-domains S  . Furthermore, another naive assumption, that each sub-domain could be sent simultaneously to a different core (where there are a number C   of available processing cores), decreases the relative computation time T  R     like T  R   = 1 / C S = 1 / C  2     . In a perfect world, the speedup by parallelization of the mass transfer algorithm scales like C  2     — dramatically faster than the “optimal” linear speedup of most algorithms with number of processors. However, one simple factor limits the speedup of the algorithm. When the 12 D Δ t      ghost-particle term becomes large relative to the sub-domain size (as must happen when S   gets very large), the constant penalty in (6)  becomes large. It is worth examining Eq. (6)  for some simple examples to see overall behavior. First, let the domain be cubic with cubic sub-domains, so Ω  x   = Ω  y   = Ω  z      and S  x   = S  y   = S  z     . Furthermore, assume that the contribution of over-counted ghosts from the sub-domains on the edges is reasonably small compared to the interior. Then in d  -dimensions (and neglecting a few smaller terms), for each sub-domain the number of entries in P   is the square of the particle density times the volume of the cube: (7) flops  S   ≈ k N  P    Ω   Ω  x    S  x     + 6 4 D Δ t      d      2   = k N  P  2   1  S  x     + 6 4 D Δ t    Ω  x        2 d   .     Now multiplying by the total number of subdomains S = S  x  d     , and assuming that there is enough memory to store and calculate subdomains on C   cores simultaneously (with C ≤ S   ), we may calculate the approximate amount of clock time spent in calculations relative to an undivided domain on a single core (k N  P  2     ) via (8) T  R   ≈ k N  P  2   S  C   1  S  x     + 6 4 D Δ t    Ω  x        2 d    k N  P  2        (9) = 1  C   1  S  x  1 / 2     + S  x  1 / 2   6 4 D Δ t    Ω  x        2 d   .       This simplified equation shows several features that are common to all geometric domain decomposition. First, for a small number of subdomains, the first number of the brackets dominates, and substantial speed gains are had with increasing subdivisions. At some point, however, the first term is smaller than the second and further subdivisions only provide more speed when there are additional cores to reduce the factor 1 / C    in front of the brackets. Second, there is both a blessing and a curse of dimensionality: while more dimensions require many, many more particles for a given density, the leading term in the brackets S  x  − d     means a much greater increase in speed when the domain is subdivided. This is true even when computed in serial on one thread on one core, i.e., when C = 1    (Fig. 7 , top). The speedup is substantially amplified if each sub-domain’s computation can be made simultaneously (with no memory transfer cost); then C = S  x  d      and the theoretical relative speedup is greater than linear when the first term in (8)  dominates (Fig. 7 , bottom). Note also that for this example shown in Fig. 1  (D = 1 0  − 3     , Ω  x   = 10   , Δ t = 10   ), in which the typical diffusion distance per time-step 2 D Δ t     is about 1.4% (1/70th) of the domain length of Ω  x   = 10   , the optimal total number of sub-domains for serial execution, using Eq. (8)  and C = 1   , is about 8 in each dimension (i.e., 64 total in 2-d  , 512 in 3-d  ). Actual simulations in 1-, 2-, and 3-d   (filled symbols in the top plot of Fig. 7 ) show good agreement in 1-d  , and fewer optimal subdivisions in 2- and 3-d  . We conjecture that the main culprit for the mismatch is the assumption that each subdivision resembles an interior region with no edges: this assumption is worse as the domain surface area to volume ratio increases with dimension. However, using the simple Eq. (8)  will get the user close enough that some minor experimentation will easily find the optimal vale of S  x    . On the other hand, if sub-domains can be computed simultaneously, there is no absolute maximum number of sub-domains indicated, and the theoretical speedups are substantial in 3-d   (Fig. 7  bottom). In 1-d  , on the other hand, the speedup levels off after a few tens of sub-domains, even for perfectly parallel computations. The reason for this difference is that the ratio of subdomain volume to ghost-particle volume decreases much more rapidly in 1-d   as the domain is subdivided. For these full-matrix computations in 2-d   and 3-d  , a fairly large number of subdomains is required for the optimal conditions, which realistically can only be achieved on distributed-memory, multi-processor machines, and then the transfer of data becomes a major consideration on relative speedup (e.g., Schauer et al., 2023 ).    2.3.3 Geometric decomposition with sparse matrices In addition to saving memory relative to the full matrices, the sparse matrices also reduce the number of calculations and therefore speed up overall simulations. A question remains regarding the relative speedup. The number of entries in the mass-transfer matrix for a single subdomain is the number of rows N  P   / ( S  x   S  y   S  z   )  = N  P   / S   , multiplied by the number of entries for each row N  P    Ω   π κ ( D Δ t )   d / 2     . The number of flops in a subdomain is therefore (10) flops  S   ≈ k N  P  2    S Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     .     To estimate the parallel computation time, we merely multiply by the number of subdomains S   and divide by the number of cores C  , with the constraint that C ≤ S   . Then the computation time follows (11) T ≈ k N  P  2    C Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     .     The term in the brackets may be considered a constant, so that the relative computation time for the entire domain among C   cores is independent of S   and scales like (12) T  R   = T ( C = 1 )   T ( C )    = 1  C   .     Importantly, this estimate of speed suggests that there is little to no penalty for using more subdivisions. Previously, the total memory requirement was found to be proportional to N  P  2   / S    ((3) ), so that even simulations with a large number of particles should be able to run if S   is made large enough. We verified this somewhat counter-intuitive result — that the overall speed is independent of S  , by specifying one thread and varying S  x   = 1 , 2 , … , 10   , i.e., S   varies from 1 to 100 in a square domain Ω = [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]    , with D = 1 0  − 3   , Δ t = 10   , over 10 timesteps using N  P   = 100 , 000    particles. The clock times actually increase, although not drastically, as S   increases (Fig. 8 a). This slowdown can be attributed to moving each subdomain’s data in and out of the CPU’s cache memory. More subdomains mean more duplicate ghost particle information being swapped in and out. We then picked the simulation with S = 16    to verify that speedup is fairly linear with the number of computational threads (Eq. (12) ) by varying the thread numbers from one to eight while holding all else constant (Fig. 8 b). The simulations were run on a MacBook Air with an M2 processor containing 4 performance and 4 efficiency cores. The speedup relative to using a single core T  R   ( C = 1 )  / T  R   ( C )     is close to the theoretical linear model up to 4 threads, with a dropoff in speed from 5 to 8.    2.3.4 List-based (non-geometric) decomposition The number of rows in the matrix to be computed remains N  P    , and the number of entries in each row is the particle density times the volume of the d  -dimensional sphere around a typical point, N  P    Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     , so the total flops is (13) flops ≈ k N  P  2    Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     .     with the caveat that the computation constant k   will be smaller because, all things equal, the list-based method only calculates the row-normalization. For C   cores in parallel, the computation time follows (14) T ≈ k N  P  2    C Ω   π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2     .     which is identical to the time for sparse matrices Eq. (11)  except for the smaller value of k  . This also shows that the algorithm should have linear speedup with the number of cores using Eq. (12) . We ran the new, list-based method for identical simulations, first using the same parameters as the previous simulations for the matrix-based solutions, namely a domain Ω = [ 0 , 10 ]  × [ 0 , 10 ]    , D = 1 0  − 3     , Δ t = 10   , and N  P   = 100   ,000 particles that are uniformly randomly distributed in space. The simulations were parallelized using OpenMP on the loop that traversed the i   index of the matrix shown in Fig. 4 . Special care must be taken to make sure that overly large arrays are not packed into the CPU cache, so the value of m  i   ( t + Δ t )     was passed to/from subroutines as a private scalar, not as a member of a larger public array (e.g., Chabbi et al., 2018 ). Scaling appears reasonably linear with the number of threads up to the 4 performance cores on a MacBook Air (Fig. 8 b). These simulations verify that scaling of the sparse-matrix and list-based methods are similar, with the list-based algorithm performing about 2 ×    faster across all parallelization levels. The total times of less than 10 s may mean that a significant amount of work was just overhead like input/output, so we re-ran the simulations using 500,000 particles (5 times the original simulations) on five different machines: (1) a two-Xeon, 20-core (40-thread) Ubuntu desktop; (2) a single Xeon, 18-core (36-thread) Mac-Pro running MacOS; (3) an 8-core (16-thread) Xeon iMac running MacOS, (4) a Macbook Air with M2 processor with 4 performance and 4 efficiency cores, and (5) a MacStudio with an M2 Ultra chipset of 16 performance and 8 efficiency cores.  The expected linear speedup is seen across a range of different processors, up to the number of cores available (Fig. 9 a). As expected, when running multiple threads (up to a maximum of two) per core, the speedup drops somewhat. Furthermore, the newer M2 chips contain performance and efficiency cores (denoted by (performance + efficiency) in the figure legends), and the linear speedup only applies to the number of performance cores. Adding more cores or multiple threads per core does not slow down a simulation (as it might with distributed work that must synchronize), but speedup is less than linear with the number of threads. In terms of raw speed, the Macbook Air with the M2 chip executed the serial runs fastest, but was eventually overtaken when the number of performance cores (four) was surpassed (Fig. 9 b).    3 Conclusions Extending the mass-transfer particle-tracking technique to 2-d   and 3-d   is not a trivial matter when the computational details are considered. More dimensions require many more particles to resolve the concentration field and this can easily overwhelm a typical machine’s RAM without efficient computational schemes. The literature revealed that the extent of these burdens was, at best, qualitatively understood, so we investigated various numerical techniques here in a more quantitative manner. The main driver of speed and memory use is the number of entries in a mass-transfer matrix P  , and reducing this will lead to increased speed. Previous methods (Engdahl et al., 2019 ) used full matrices to track all particle interactions, so we began with those and expanded our consideration to sparse arrays, despite the naive nature of using full versions of sparse matrices in terms of memory requirements. Both methods conserve mass by normalizing array elements using an average of row- and column-sums, but differ only in the number of elements stored and used. We also developed and tested a novel list-based decomposition that only uses the row-sum normalization. The full matrices require on the order of Ω / S  π κ ( 36 D Δ t )   d / 2       times more memory than sparse matrices, which require another N  P    S     times more memory than the list-based decomposition. Each of these factors are user-controlled by specifying the number of particles and subdivisions, but for most problems the memory savings for the list-based method will be orders-of-magnitude. For practical reasons, we only checked the parallel speedup of the sparse-matrix, row-and-column normalization scheme and the list-based (row-only normalization) decomposition scheme. Both showed linear speedup with increased numbers of (performance) cores, with a drop-off of speedup when either threads were run on slower cores or when multiple threads were run on some cores. Overall, given the same number of single threads per core, the new list-based decomposition runs about 2 ×    faster than the geometric, sparse-matrix decomposition. The latter of these also showed speed degradation as the number of spatial subdomains is increased, which was required on the Macbook Air because of memory constraints when moving from 100,000 to 500,000 particles in 16 Gb of RAM. We further performed a limited investigation of the accuracy of the list-based decomposition and showed that evenly-spaced, stationary particles yield machine-precision levels of accuracy when the constraint on inter-particle spacing Δ x < D Δ t      is maintained. As such, the assessment of the proposed algorithm is that it is faster, consumes far less memory, and is just as accurate as the other schemes. Within a deforming plume in a spatially heterogeneous velocity field, the newer algorithm gave very similar results to prior methods that have been extensively benchmarked. However, a more detailed error analysis could be performed using highly heterogeneous variable-velocity fields, to assess whether the new algorithm is similarly robust when local particle spacings may change drastically over time.
1 Introduction It has become a consensus to reduce fossil energy consumption (Ji et al., 2017 ) and promote the utilization of clean energy such as nuclear energy under the dual carbon strategy (Ramirez-Corredores et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ). Natural uranium is an indispensable fuel for nuclear power plants, but the supply of uranium resources in China is far below the demand, thus, accelerating the development of uranium resources has become an urgent task (Bersano et al., 2020 ). Sandstone-type uranium deposits (STUD) are the largest type of uranium resource in China, which is usually mined by in-situ leaching (ISL) method (Robin et al., 2020; Shayakhmetov et al., 2023 ). ISL is the process of injecting a specific leaching solution into the target uranium deposit using injection wells, leaching metallic uranium through a series of physical–chemical reactions, and lifting the leaching solution out of the surface through production wells to achieve uranium extraction in a surface factory (Kurmanseiit et al., 2022 ) (Fig. 1  ), possessing characteristics of low cost, good efficiency, high resource utilization rate, environmental protection (Sheng et al. 2023; Fatahi Nafchi, et al., 2021 ). However, over 70 % of STUD in China exhibit low permeability characteristics (permeability coefficient < 0.1 m/d), causing the leaching solution to be unable to migrate within the deposits, thereby limiting the large-scale application of ISL (Dushyantha et al., 2024 ). Sulfuric acid is a commonly used leaching agent in ISL and can also be used for the acidizing reservoir stimulation. But chemical stimulation methods are highly dependent on the mineral composition of deposits. Combining the chemical stimulation with physical stimulation (such as fracturing and blasting) is expected to significantly improve the permeability of low-permeability sandstone-type uranium deposits (LPSTUD) (Gharehdash et al., 2021 ). To investigate the feasibility of chemical-physical composite stimulation for LPSTUD, it is necessary to conduct an in-depth study on the microstructure, hydraulic and mechanical behaviors of uranium-bearing sandstone after acidization (Huang et al., 2023; Niu et al., 2021a; Patel et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023 ). The investigation on microscopic characteristic response of rocks is the key to understand the function mechanism of acidification reaction (Akono et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2020 ). For example, Zhu et al. (2022)  found that the minerals and elements content in the sandstone are decreased, and the aqueous elemental Ca, Na, K and Mg concentrations in the reacted solution are improved after acidification. Tao et al. (2022)  and Liang et al. (2023)  focused on the changes in pores of rock, and revealed that sulfuric acid erosion destroyed the bonding between minerals in rocks, resulting in increased porosity. However, the pore evolution of rock during the acidification process is not constant, and its understanding has been continuously deepened with the application of testing methods such as computer tomography (CT), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and mercury injection porosimetry (MIP) (Niu et al., 2018 ). Huo et al. (2018)  quantified the microscopic damage of sandstone after acid-rock reactions using CT, the CT number of samples increase at first then decrease with the increasing reaction period due to the alternating change of sandstone absorbing acid speed and the acid penetration speed. Zeng et al. (2021)  divided the rock pores during acid ISL into three stages, the first and second stages are mainly chemical plugging caused by surface reactions, and the third stage is physical plugging caused by diffusion of fine particles inside the rock. Tan et al. (2020)  found that the salt dissolution could make the clay swelling and fine migration in saline-lacustrine carbonate reservoir after water–rock reaction, inhibiting the increment in porosity and permeability. Especially for sandstone with a wide variety of minerals, whether the acid-rock reaction promotes or inhibits its porosity, and how the porosity evolves under the influence of acid concentration and reaction time, these issues need further investigation. The changes in the internal structure of rocks induced by complex geochemical reactions (dissolution, precipitation, oxidation, and reduction, etc.) are crucial for exploring the permeability and mechanical evolution laws of the ore bed (Niu et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021; Ostad-Ali-Askari, 2022 ) under in situ geological conditions (Niu et al., 2021b; Niu et al., 2017; Niu et al., 2023b; Tian et al., 2023 ). Overall, most studies suggested that acidification has a significant effect on improving permeability depends on the acid type and reaction time, etc. (Alameedy et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2024; Izadpanahi et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2022 ). According to reports, hydrochloric acid pre washing can increase sandstone permeability by 80 %−90 % (Gussenov, 2023 ), while the increased permeability amplitude can reach more than one order of magnitude for andesite and coal (Chen et al., 2021; Farquharson et al., 2019 ). The permeability improvement effect is significant in a short period of time (8–24 h), and then gradually stabilizes (Li et al., 2023 ). However, acidification can also have a negative impact on permeability because the pore throats are plugged by the clay mineral expansion and non-swelling mineral dispersion or migration (Ahmad et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2023 ). After the acid-rock reaction, the mechanical properties of the rock deteriorate, showing an increase in the duration of compaction stage and a decrease in the duration of elastic stage on the stress–strain curve. And the mechanical parameters (compressive strength, tensile strength, and elastic modulus) exhibit a decrease trend (Li et al., 2021 ), depending on the pH and acidification time. Currently, most studies believe that as the pH decreases and the acidification time increases, the reduction in rock mechanical parameters becomes greater (Afolagboye et al., 2023; Alameedy et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024 ). But there is no monotonic relationship between them, which is influenced by acidification time and lithology, etc. For example, the peak strength of sandstone shows a three-stage change with acid treatment time, which is respectively affected by surface dissolution, internal dissolution, and large-scale dissolution (Geng et al., 2023 ); The mechanical properties of highly cemented rocks deteriorate more severely, and the reduction in mechanical parameters of dolomite after acidification is significantly lower than that of limestone (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The degradation of mechanical properties of rocks after acidification is closely related to their pore structure. The porosity shows a negative exponential relationship with the uniaxial compressive strength (Eremin, 2020; Parandeh et al., 2023 ), especially with large pores (diameter >1 μm) having a more significant impact on the mechanical parameters of rocks after acidification (Chen et al., 2023 ). The predecessors mainly explored the variation degree in permeability and mechanical parameters after acidification reactions, but their understanding of the controlling mechanisms was not in-depth. Besides, research on the energy and permeability evolution characteristics during the loading-deformation-failure process of rocks after acidification reactions was also insufficient, which limits the understanding of mechanisms and effects of chemical-physical composite stimulation of LPSTUD. Therefore, to study the influence of acidification on the mineral composition, pore structure, permeability-mechanical properties, a series of experiments (acid-rock reaction experiment, X-ray diffraction (XRD), thin section identification, high-pressure mercury intrusion porosimetry (HPMIP), and stress-seepage coupling experiment) are conducted. Based on this, the impact mechanism and law of acidification on the permeability-mechanical coupling behaviors are analyzed, and the suggestions for on-site acidification enhanced permeability are proposed. This study will provide a theoretical basis for enhanced mining of LPSTUD.  2 Experimental work 2.1 Sample collection and preparation Samples used in this work were collected from Jurassic sandstone in Ordos Basin. After collecting the rock blocks, they were packed with several plastic wraps, transported to the laboratory, and stored in a constant temperature and humidity box. According to the suggestion by International Society for Rock Mechanics (ISRM) (Alejano et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2019 ), the rock blocks were drilled, cut, and polished to obtain the flat and smooth cylindrical standard samples (with a diameter of 50 mm and a length of 100 mm). Then, to obtain the homogeneous and comparable samples, each sample was subjected to a wave velocity test, samples with a longitudinal wave velocity difference of < 5 % were used as the test samples in this work.  2.2 Experimental design To study the influence of acidification reactions on the mineral composition, pore structure, permeability-mechanical properties of rocks, the prepared core, particle and powder samples were first conducted the acid-rock reaction experiment to simulate the acid ISL process, then the mineral composition, pore structure, and permeability-mechanical properties of samples were respectively obtained by the X-ray diffraction (XRD), thin section identification, high-pressure mercury intrusion porosimetry (HPMIP), and stress-seepage coupling experiment (Fig. 2  ).  2.3 Experimental process and method 2.3.1 Acid-rock reaction experiment Based on field or indoor experiments from Zhang et al. (2017)  and Wen et al. (2019) , the concentration of sulfuric acid leaching agent is within 10 g/L. Thus, the sulfuric acid concentrations selected for this work are respectively 2 g/L, 4 g/L, 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L (Table 1  ). Huang et al. (2021)  considered that significant changes occur in the mechanical properties and mesoscopic structure of sandstone within 40 days of acid-rock reaction, the reaction time selected for this work is thus 15 d, 30 d, 45 d, 60 d, and 75 d, respectively (Table 1 ). The experimental procedure of acid-rock reaction experiment is as follows: (1) dehydrate the prepared sample in a constant temperature oven and place it in a reaction kettle; (2) prepare the sulfuric acid solution with given concentration; (3) pour the prepared sulfuric acid solution into the reactor and ensure that the sample is completely submerged; (4) seal the reaction kettle, discharge the air by a vacuum pump, and conduct the acid-rock reaction experiment until the designed reaction time is reached.  2.3.2 Mineral composition test The mineral composition of samples in this work was measured by the X-ray diffractometer produced by Bruker Company in Germany (D8 ADVANCE). Firstly, the rock samples were crushed into powder samples with a size of < 200 mesh with the aid of a grinder, which was then adhered to a metal slide for mineral composition analysis. Typical radiation conditions were 40 kV, 30 mA, and Cu Kα radiation (1.5405 Å) with the 2θ scan ranging from 10° to 90° at a speed of 2°/min. After the measurement was completed, according to the standard powder diffraction data provided by the International Data Center of the Powder Diffraction Federation, the collected information was converted into the type and content of elements through comparative analysis based on the diffraction judgment standards that match the crystal plane spacing and the diffraction intensity.  2.3.3 Pore structure test The pore structure of samples in this work was measured by a high-pressure mercury intrusion porosimetry (HPMIP) experiment using a Micromeritics Autopore IV 9620 Instrument (Micrometrics, USA). Firstly, the sample was broken into particle samples with a particle diameter of 2–5 mm, which were then placed in a drying oven and dried for 24 h at a temperature of 60 ℃ to remove moisture. 3 g of dried particle samples were put into the sample chamber of the mercury porosimeter. The mercury pressure was increased gradually from 0 psi to 60,000 psi, detecting the structure of pores with sizes from 0.003 μm to 950 μm. During the testing process, the instrument automatically recorded the mercury pressure and the injected mercury amount to calculate the pore structure parameters in the sample. Mercury has a poor wettability for porous material (i.e., the contact angle is greater than 90°), the pore diameter can be obtained by using the (Washburn) equation by assuming that the pore is cylindrical:(1) D = - 4 γ cos  θ / P     where D  is the pore diameter; θ  is the contact angle of mercury to solids; γ  is the surface tension of mercury (480 Nm−1 ).  2.3.4 Stress-seepage coupling experiment (1) Experimental device. The rock triaxial multi-field coupling testing system consists of the liquid injection system, the pressure control system, the temperature control system, the monitoring system, the data acquisition and processing system. The maximum liquid injection pressure is 60 MPa, and the pressure control system can apply confining pressure in the sample chamber, with the maximum value of 60 MPa, the maximum axial force applied can reach 1000 kN. The temperature control system can maintain a constant temperature in the sample chamber, with a maximum temperature of 150 ℃. Measurement accuracies of pressure and temperature are 0.01 MPa and 0.01 °C. The circumferential extensometer and LVDT are used to test the axial and radial strains, the measurement accuracy is lower than 1 % FS. The mass flowmeter is adopted to monitor the outlet flow, with an accuracy of 0.01 mL/min. All monitored data is transmitted to a computer and calculated using built-in software to obtain test results. (2) Permeability calculation method. The steady-state method is adopted to calculate the permeability. The flow rate at the outlet of the sample is recorded in real time by applying a differential osmotic pressure to the two ends of the sample.(2) k = μ L V  A Δ P Δ t      where k  is the permeability of the sample, L  is the height of the sample, μ  is the fluid viscosity, Δ P    is the osmotic pressure difference between the upper and lower ends of the sample, A  is the cross-section area of the sample, V  is the fluid outflow volume at time interval (Δt ). (3) Testing process. According to the research results by Meng et al. (2013)  regarding the relationship between the ground stress, and reservoir pressure with buried depth in Ordos Basin. The initial confining pressure and initial axial pressure for this experiment are 10 MPa and 20 MPa. To analyze the effect of the acid-rock reaction on the permeability of the sample during the progressive loading-deformation-failure process, the permeability of the sample was tested for each increase in axial pressure of 5 MPa until it was destroyed. The experimental procedure for testing mechanical properties and permeability during loading-deformation-failure process is as follows: (1) Place the prepared sample in distilled water and soak for 12 h to make the sample fully saturated with water; (2) Place the saturated sample into a heat shrinkable tube, and install a circumferential extensometer and LVDT on the sample, avoiding hydraulic oil from the pressure chamber entering the interior of rock sample; (3) Fill the pressure chamber with oil, and gradually increase the confining pressure and axial pressure to 10 MPa and 20 MPa, respectively; (4) after the confining pressure and axial pressure are stabilized, apply pore pressure and maintain the osmotic pressure difference of 5.3 MPa, then measure the outlet flow; (5) apply an axial pressure of 5 MPa one by one, and measure the outlet flow of sample under each level of stress until the sample is damaged (Fig. 3  ); (6) after the test, remove the sample and save the stress–strain data and flow data, and calculate the permeability according to Eq. (1)  .    3 Results and Discussion 3.1 Influence of acid-rock reaction on mineral composition The main chemical reactions during the acid ISL process of sandstone-type uranium deposits are shown in Table 2  . The calcium carbonate, dolomite and potassium feldspar can be dissolved by the sulfuric acid, forming sulfate precipitations and quartz. The uranyl ions (UO2 2+ ) are converted from the oxide of tetravalent uranium (UO2 ) by the oxidizing agents (Fe3+ , O2 ), which are then reacted with sulfuric acid to generate uranyl sulfate (UO2 SO4 ) and uranyl sulfate complex (UO2 (SO4 )2 2−  and UO2 (SO4)3 4− ) and form uranium containing leaching solution. Besides, the accompanying clay minerals (kaolinite, etc.) and mineral debris transported by solution within the pore system. The complex physical and chemical behaviors are thus appeared in the acid ISL process. Fig. 4   represents the thin section images of samples with different acid-rock reaction concentrations. The essential minerals of the original sample are composed of quartz, kaolinite, plagioclase, dolomite, and calcite, the interstitial materials between minerals are clay matrix, dolomite cement, calcium cement, and siliceous cement, conforming to the basic petrological characteristics of sandstone. The calcareous cements (e.g., calcite) produce intense chemical reactions during the acidification reaction process. The boundaries of calcite in samples that reacted with 4 g/L, 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L sulfuric acids became more irregular, while that reacted with 2 g/L sulfuric acid disappeared. It indicates that the chemical reaction degree depends on the concentration of sulfuric acid, the sulfuric acid with low concentration can achieve the better dissolution effect. Moreover, numerous pores are developed in potassium feldspar and kaolinite after the acid-rock reaction, changing the surface of these minerals from smooth to coarse. This means that the local dissolution of weakly soluble minerals can induce internal chemical damage. Fig. 5   represents the thin section images of samples with different acid-rock reaction times. When the acid-rock reaction time increases from 0 d, 15 d, 30 d, 45 d, 60 d to 75 d, the calcite cement shrinks gradually and stacks between mineral particles in smaller sizes. The potassium feldspar on the surface of samples becomes smooth and only a small amount of kaolinite can be seen in some intergranular pores and fractures. The interstitial materials are still visible in samples as the reaction time increases because the concentration of H+  inside the solution continuously decreases and causes the weakening of dissolution reaction. The changes in mineral composition of samples after acid-rock reactions are shown in Fig. 6  . The calcite, feldspar, and kaolinite contents all decrease after the acid-rock reaction, independent of sulfuric acid concentration, while the quartz exhibits an increasing trend. The change law of mineral content is non-linearly correlated with the sulfuric acid concentration, the soluble minerals are easily reacted with sulfuric acid concentrations of 2 g/L and 8 g/L. The calcite, feldspar, kaolinite, and quartz contents show monotonically increasing or decreasing relationships with the prolonging of reaction time, the calcite, feldspar, and kaolinite contents decrease respectively from 28 %, 10 %, and 26 % to 18 %, 3 %, and 10 %, while the quartz content increases from 35 % to 69 %. It can be inferred that the choice of sulfuric acid concentration depends on mineralogy characteristics, and extending the reaction time will promote the reaction level and exacerbate the changing trends of mineral content.  3.2 Influence of acid-rock reaction on pore structure The mercury injection/ejection curves of samples during the acid-rock reaction process are shown in Fig. 7  . The cumulative mercury volume shows the nonlinear variation law with the mercury pressure, and the mercury injection/ejection curves can be divided into three stages: stage A, stage B and stage C, corresponding to the gently inclined stage, steep inclined stage and stationary stage. The acid-rock reaction significantly influences the stage B. During the acid-rock reaction with different concentrations, samples soaked by 2 g/L sulfuric acid solution have the most inclined stage B, followed by those soaked with 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L sulfuric acid solution, and those soaked with 0 g/L and 4 g/L sulfuric acid solution possess the most gradual stage B. However, the inclination degree is gradually improved with the increasing acid-rock reaction time, which indicates that the influence mechanisms of sulfuric acid concentration and reaction time on pore structure are distinctive. According to the pore classification method by Li et al. (2022)  and the curve characteristic of pore size distribution, the pore is divided into five categories: ultra-macropore (>10000 nm), macropore (1000 ∼ 10000 nm), mesopore (100 ∼ 1000 nm), transition pore (10 ∼ 100 nm), and micropore (0 ∼ 10 nm). The pore size distribution curves of samples during the acid-rock reaction process are shown in Fig. 8  . The shape of pore size distribution curve has not changed significantly, indicating the acid-rock reaction can hardly change the distribution characteristics of different-sized pores. The pores with a diameter between 20–5000 nm dominate the pore volume, whose volume accounts for 70 % − 85 % of the total pore volume. The variation trend of pore size distribution of samples after acid-rock reaction is different. No matter what the acid concentration or the reaction time is, the volume of micropores and transition pores in the sample decreases, while the volume of mesopores, macropores, and macropores increases after the acid-rock reaction, indicating that acidification has a pore expanding effect on samples. This is because the narrow throat of small pores is more easily blocked by precipitates, while dissolution promotes the development of larger pores. Liu's research also mentioned this issue, but due to its research on coal containing a large amount of organic matter, the mesopores are more prone to blockage during the acidification process (Liu et al., 2021; Kutchko et al., 2020 ), which is inconsistent with the research in this work. Influence of acid-rock reaction on pore volume of samples at different sizes is shown in Fig. 9  . The total pore volumes of samples after soaked by sulfuric acid with concentrations of 0 g/L, 2 g/L, 4 g/L, 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L are 0.039 ml/g, 0.061 ml/g, 0.040 ml/g, 0.041 ml/g, 0.051 ml/g, and 0.050 ml/g, respectively. When the acid-rock reaction time increases from 0 d, 15 d, 30 d, 45 d, 60 d to 75 d, the total pore volumes of samples increase from 0.039 ml/g, 0.041 ml/g, 0.048 ml/g, 0.050 ml/g, 0.062 ml/g, and 0.071 ml/g, respectively. Although pores with different pore sizes exhibit various change trends after acid-rock reaction, it can be found that adopting a concentration of 2 g/L and the longest possible time is beneficial for stimulating the pore structure of uranium deposits.  3.3 Influence of acid-rock reaction on mechanical properties and permeability The above discussions have clarified the direct response of pore structure characteristics of samples by acid-rock reaction at the micro-scale, which subsequently causes the changes in mechanical properties and permeability at the macro scale. However, the chemical reactions induced by sulfuric acid immersion have not altered the brittleness characteristics of samples because all the stress–strain curves can still be divided into five stages (Fig. 10   and Fig. 11  ): (1) compression stage, (2) linear elastic deformation stage, (3) stable crack propagation stage, (4) unstable crack propagation stage, and (5) post-peak stage. During the compression stage, the primary pores and cracks are closed under external stress. The increase in strain corresponds to the closure of pore-crack structure in samples after acid-rock reaction because their pores and cracks are more developed. Additionally, almost no seepage water is detected at the outlet because the permeability is extremely low. At the end of the linear elastic deformation stage, the phenomenon of pore-crack compression has reached its maximum, the permeability then decreases to the lowest value. For the stable and unstable crack propagation stages, the damaged cracks gradually develop until they are uncontrollable. and the permeability increases exponentially accompanied by the loading of external stress. Then, the stress–strain curves reach the maximum, just like the permeability, and the post-peak stage initiates. The peak strength, elastic modulus, shear modulus, and Poisson's ratio are used to characterize the mechanical properties, as shown in Fig. 12   and Fig. 13  . After the acid-rock reaction, the peak strength, elastic modulus, and shear modulus of samples are decreased, while the Poisson's ratio is increased. When the acid concentrations are 0 g/L, 2 g/L, 4 g/L, 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L, the peak strengths of samples are 98.05 MPa, 72.67 MPa, 77.06 MPa, 75.32 MPa, 62.28 MPa and 60.61 MPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 38.18 %; the elastic moduli are 9.93 GPa, 6.71 GPa, 8.16 GPa, 8.13 GPa, 5.49 GPa and 5.27 GPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 46.92 %; the shear moduli are 4.43 GPa, 2.77 GPa, 3.51 GPa, 3.47 GPa, 2.21 GPa and 2.02 GPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 54.41 %; the Poisson's ratios are 0.12, 0.21, 0.16, 0.17, 0.28 and 0.30, with a maximum increase percentage of 150.00 %. When the acid-rock reaction times are 0 d, 15 d, 30 d, 45 d, 60 d, and 75 d, the peak strengths are 98.05 MPa, 75.32 MPa, 70.04 MPa, 56.27 MPa, 50.44 MPa and 48.51 MPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 50.52 %; the elastic moduli are 9.93 GPa, 8.13 GPa, 6.50 GPa, 5.44 GPa, 4.37 GPa and 3.77 GPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 62.03 %; the shear moduli are 4.43 GPa, 3.47 GPa, 2.70 GPa 2.07 GPa, 1.60 GPa and 1.34 GPa, with a maximum decrease percentage of 69.75 %; the Poisson's ratios are 0.12, 0.17, 0.20, 0.31, 0.36 and 0.40, with a maximum increase percentage of 233.33 %. Overall, the increase in acid concentration gradually has a nonlinear impact on the mechanics properties of samples (Fig. 12 a , Fig. 13 a ). This is inconsistent with previous research because the chemical reactions are more complex (Abdulraheem, 2022 ). For example, at moderate sulfuric acid concentrations (4 g/L-6 g/L), more precipitation or acidic products (CaSO4 , etc.) are produced, which blocks pore channels, inhibits acid-rock reactions, and leads to a relatively small decrease in mechanics properties of samples within this concentration range. When the reaction time increases from 0 d to 75 d, the strength and elastic parameters of samples decrease rapidly in the first 45 d, with a maximum decrease of 43.33 %. However, after 45 d acid-rock reaction, the blockage of the channels for the acid solution and the decrease in H+  concentration weaken the chemical reactions and reduce the rock damage, resulting in a maximum decrease of only 15.21 %. The evolution of peak strength, shear modulus, elastic modulus, and Poisson's ratio of rock samples under different reaction times can be fitted by exponential functions with R2  greater than 0.96 (Fig. 12 b , Fig. 13 b ), which can be used to accurately describe the evolution law of mechanical parameters during the acid-rock reaction process. Overall, the evolution of mechanics parameters reflects the weakening effect of acid-rock reaction on rock mechanics performance, manifested in the increase of porosity, the increase in matrix compressibility, and the alteration in the brittle-plastic characteristics of samples. Especially after 45 d acid-rock reaction, the stress–strain curve gradually becomes nonlinear in the elastic stage. As shown in Fig. 10  and Fig. 11 , with the increase of external load, the permeability of rock samples shows a trend of initially decreasing and then increasing, which is closely related to the changes in the internal pore-fracture structure of samples during the compaction stage, the elastic deformation stage, the stable fracture expansion stage, and the unstable fracture expansion stage. Obviously, the acid-rock reaction does not change the permeability evolution trend of samples during the loading-deformation-failure process, while it changes the span and value of permeability in different loading-deformation-failure stages (Fig. 14  ). For example, with the increase of acid-rock reaction time, the samples are more likely to enter the unstable fracture expansion stage under the same applied load, resulting in a sharp increase in permeability. The permeability of rock samples is closely related to the original pore structure, mineral composition, and damaged crack structure. The mechanism is complex and can be reflected through Fig. 15  . Before the acidification reaction, the flow channels in the samples were narrow and few resulting in low permeability, as shown in Fig. 15 a . After acidification, the mineral composition and internal structure of samples show significant changes (Fig. 15 b ) and controlled by the concentration of sulfuric acid. The influencing mechanism can be divided into three cases. Firstly, after reacting with 2 g/L sulfuric acid, the soluble filling materials in the pore of the sample are dissolved, and fewer precipitates are produced, resulting in enlarged pores and enhanced connectivity, leading to a significant increase in permeability (Fig. 15 g ). Secondly, after reacting with 6 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L sulfuric acid, the soluble filling materials are dissolved (Calcite, feldspar, kaolinite, etc.), and precipitates are also produced (sulfate minerals), which have a certain inhibitory effect on the permeability enhancement (Fig. 15 e ). Therefore, it has a moderate effect on permeability improvement. Thirdly, after reacting with 4 g/L sulfuric acid, the production of precipitates is stronger than the dissolution of soluble substances (Fig. 15 f ), leading to the blockage of pore throats in the sample, resulting in a decrease in permeability after acidification. With the increase in acid-rock reaction time, the change of mineral composition affects the internal matrix skeleton structure of the sample. When the reaction time increases from 45 d to 75 d, the permeability of the sample decreases significantly before reaching the maximum compaction point. This indicates that acidification leads to a decrease in the strength of the pore skeleton and an increase in pore volume, increasing the permeability stress sensitivity of the sample. At the same time, the stable expansion stage of the cracks is significantly shortened, allowing the sample to enter the yield stage faster, resulting in a significant increase in permeability. However, the efficiency of permeability enhancement does not continue to increase with the increase of reaction time. For example, after 60 d acid-rock reaction, the increase in permeability due to acidification slows down (only increases by 5 %), which is related to the partial blockage of pore throats by precipitates in the sample.  3.4 Influence of acid-rock reaction on energy evolution The loading-deformation-failure process of samp is always accompanied by the input, conversion, and dissipation of energy. In the absence of heat exchange, the total strain energy input to the rock sample by external forces is denoted as U . Under triaxial test conditions, the formula for calculating the strain energy density is as follows:(3) U = U d  + U e  = U 1  + U 3  = ∫ σ 1  d ε 1  + 2 ∫ σ 3  d ε 3      (4) U e  = 1 2 E   [ σ 1  2  + 2 σ 3  2  - 2 v ( 2 σ 1  σ 3  + σ 3  )  ]     where U 1    represents the positive work done by the axial stress, which is converted into the strain energy density of the rock sample; U 3  represents the strain energy density released by negative work; U d  represents the dissipated energy density; U e  represents the elastic strain energy density. According to the stress–strain curves of rock during the loading-deformation-failure process, the U 1   , U 3   , U e   , and U d    were determined by Eq. 3  and Eq. 4 . The energy evolution law of the sample during the loading-deformation-failure process can be obtained (Fig. 16   and Fig. 17  ). The dissipation ratio (U d /U ) is the ratio of the dissipated energy density (U d ) to the total input energy density (U ) during the loading-deformation-failure process of the rock sample. The dissipation ratio of samples after acid-rock reaction at different concentration and time are shown in Fig. 18  . The dissipation ratio initially increases with the axial strain, then decreases, and finally increases again. When the dissipation ratio is equal to 0.5, the elastic energy and dissipative energy are equivalent. When the dissipation ratio is less than 0.5, the elastic energy dominates during the loading-deformation-failure process, while when it is greater than 0.5, the dissipated energy dominates. Both this study and previous research (Zhang et al., 2020 ) found that the dissipation ratio of unreacted rock samples is less than 0.5, while the dissipation ratio of reacted rock samples increases significantly, exceeding 0.5 during the compaction stage. This can be attributed to the acid-rock reaction effect, the acid-rock reaction promotes the development of a secondary pore-fracture structure. During the loading process, the input energy is mainly used to induce the compression and closure of pores and fractures in the rock sample, rather than being stored within the sample. During the stable fracture expansion stage and the unstable fracture expansion stage, the dissipation ratios of samples reacted by sulfuric acid concentrations of 8 g/L and 10 g/L are all larger than 0.5, this is because the samples are intensely chemically damaged and the fractures are more easily formed, accompanied by a large amount of energy being dissipated in this loading failure process. Whether the sample is involved in an acid-rock reaction or not, during the post-peak stage, the dissipation ratios of samples all exceed 0.5, indicating that the energy storage capacity rapidly decreases once the sample is completely damaged. And in this process, the influence of chemical reactions on energy evolution is thus inappreciable. The influence of acid-rock reaction time on energy evolution is significant and regular. As shown in Fig. 18 b , the dissipation ratios of samples monotonically increase with the increase of reaction time. When the reaction time reaches between 30 d and 75 d, the dissipation ratios are all larger than 0.5, this is because prolonging acid rock reactions not only significantly reduces the mechanical properties of the samples but also promotes the transition of the sample's behavior from ductile to brittle, i.e., the plastic characteristics of samples gradually emerge with the increase of reaction time. The process of a rock sample transitioning from a stable state to an unstable state is the process of internal damage accumulation leading to unstable failure. The relative stability of the loaded rock sample can be reflected by the energy consumption ratio (Guo et al., 2022; Saadatmand Hashemi and Katsabanis, 2020 ), which is the ratio of the dissipated energy density (U d ) to the elastic strain energy (U e ) of the loaded rock sample. After the acid rock reaction, the energy consumption ratio at the peak point of the rock sample is greater than 1 (Fig. 19  ), and it is in an unstable state.  3.5 Enlightenments on enhancing in-situ leaching mining of low-permeability sandstone-type uranium deposit For low-permeability sandstone-type uranium deposits, acidification enhanced permeability is a potential way to improve the development effectiveness (Schulz et al., 2022 ). However, the choice of acid concentration and reaction time is crucial in engineering applications. The original unacidified uranium reservoir has a permeability ranging from 0.41 mD to 0.71 mD, which is considered low-permeability and severely limits the ISL of uranium resources. Acidification reactions have different effects on the permeability-mechanical properties, expecting to create favorable reservoir conditions for ISL mining. Under low-concentration acid-rock reaction conditions (2 g/L), soluble minerals in the reservoir can be extensively dissolved, resulting in a significant increase in permeability to 5.08 mD−7.76 mD. This acid concentration is suitable for reservoirs with abundant soluble minerals for acidification enhancement permeability. Under high-concentration acid-rock reaction conditions (8 g/L to 10 g/L), the mechanical properties of the reservoir are significantly weakened, but the increase in permeability is limited. In this case, combining physical reservoir stimulation methods can induce the formation of damaged cracks, thereby promoting the permeability enhancement effect. Under medium-concentration acid-rock reaction conditions (4 g/L to 6 g/L), the weakening of the reservoir's mechanical properties is not significant. Simultaneously, the reaction precipitates can block pores, affecting the pore expansion effect. Therefore, it is not recommended to use sulfuric acid in this concentration range for the permeability enhancement. Increasing the reaction time can improve permeability and weaken the mechanical properties of the reservoir. Obviously, a longer reaction time leads to better in-situ leaching effectiveness. However, when the acid-rock reaction time exceeds 45d, the permeability enhanced efficiency and the weakening of mechanical properties decreases compared to the first 45 d. Considering economic and timely factors, the acid-rock reaction time of a 45 d is generally sufficient to meet the requirements of permeability enhancement. However, for ultra-low permeability uranium deposits or when the permeability needs to be increased to a desired threshold, it may be necessary to extend the acid rock reaction time appropriately. This understanding can be applied to uranium deposits similar to the study area, and its applicability to uranium deposits under other geological conditions needs further research.   4 Conclusions (1) Affected by the complex dissolution and precipitation reactions, the contents of calcite, feldspar and kaolinite show a decreasing trend, while the quartz content increases of samples after acidification. With low-concentration (2 g/L) acidification reaction, the pore volume and permeability are increased by 56 % and 993 %, with a superior enhanced permeability effect; with the moderate-concentration (4 g/L-6 g/L) acidification reaction, the pore volume is only increased by 2.5 %-5.1 %, with a weak enhanced permeability effect; with high-concentration (8 g/L-10 g/L) acidification reaction, the permeability is promoted by 543 %-769 % and the enhanced permeability effect is acceptable because the chemical damage is stronger than precipitation blockage. The effect of reaction time on permeability is monotonically increased, the pore volume and permeability of samples after 75 days of acid-rock reaction are improved by 82 % and 4334 %, respectively. (2) The acid-rock reaction alters the mechanical properties of samples, manifested in the fact that the peak strength, elastic modulus, and shear modulus reduce, while the Poisson's ratio increases. The impact of acid concentration on the mechanics properties is nonlinear, the decrease in mechanics properties of samples is small at moderate-concentration (4 g/L-6 g/L) acidification reaction. The relationships between the peak strength, elastic modulus, shear modulus, and Poisson's ratio with reaction time obey exponential function expression. After the acid-rock reaction, the energy storage performance of samples during the loading-deformation-failure process decreases, indicating the gradual plasticization of samples. (3) For reservoirs containing adequate soluble minerals, it is better to use a low-concentration (2 g/L) sulfuric acid to enhance the pore connectivity and achieve an efficient enhanced permeability effect. For reservoirs with high mechanical strength and few soluble minerals, the high-concentration (8 g/L-10 g/L) sulfuric acid is suggested to reduce the stress threshold of crack propagation for the physical reservoir stimulation. Considering economic and timely factors, the recommended time for on-site acidification enhanced permeability is 45 d. However, the reaction time can be appropriately extended to improve the reservoir stimulation effect for uranium deposits with higher mechanical properties.
1 Introduction Precipitation has an important impact on all aspects of human production and life, and the monitoring of precipitation information has long been a hot topic of research (Bruins et al., 1986; Roxy, 2017; Sarojini et al., 2016 ). Microwave links have been proven to be an effective means of monitoring high spatio-temporal resolution precipitation information (Chwala and Kunstmann, 2019 ). Compared to rain gauges (Strangeways, 2010 ), it is relatively low cost to organize and maintain network operation (especially for commercial microwave links (CMLs) as the network exists), and has a wider spatial representation; compared to weather radar (Marzano et al., 2008 ) and rain measuring satellites (Prigent, 2010 ), it is less subject to interference by ground clutter or the complex upper atmosphere due to its deployment often being tens of meters above the ground. Hence, precipitation observation experiments based on microwave links have been widely carried out in countries around the world. Precipitation observation experiments using microwave links first began at the turn of the century (Messer et al., 2006 ). A simulation experiment on the reconstruction of precipitation fields based on a non-linear laminar imaging model was carried out in Israel with a network of 249 microwave links in the coastal plain (Zinevich et al., 2008 ). The results demonstrate a high mean spatial correlation between simulated and reconstructed rainfall fields. The Netherlands has developed a rainfall retrieval algorithm that can be applied in real-time based on a network of approximately 2400 microwave links with a temporal resolution of 15 min across the country, confirming the effectiveness of microwave links for real-time rainfall monitoring over large areas by comparison with weather radar data (Overeem et al., 2013 ). Based on 4000 commercial microwave links (1 min temporal resolution, frequencies 10–40 GHz, lengths 0–30 km) across the whole territory, quantitative precipitation assessment at different landscapes and time scales was carried out in Germany (Graf et al., 2020 ). The results display a good agreement between the rainfall accumulations in the hours, months and seasons and the rainfall accumulations obtained from gauge-adjusted radar data, except in winter. Australia utilizes 144 microwave links above 10 GHz (length of 0.2 km to 25 km) to invert precipitation with two sampling strategies (average and minimum/maximum) based on the freely available RAINLINK package (but with revised parameters), and the gauge-adjusted S-band weather radar data of about two years is used as a reference value (Pudashine et al., 2021 ). In addition to the experiments carried out in the above-mentioned developed countries, it is actually particularly interesting to use microwave link-based rainfall inversion tools in the areas where dedicated terrestrial rainfall sensor networks are often practically unavailable. Also, based on the RAINLINK package, 145 microwave links are located in São Paulo North, Brazil for rain rate and cumulative rainfall assessment (in less than 3 months) (Rios Gaona et al., 2017 ). Comparison with the results of the dense automatic rain gauge network demonstrates its ability to capture the dynamics of average urban rainfall. In the Ouagadougou region of Burkina Faso, West Africa, microwave links were numerically modelled based on high-resolution rain maps from meteorological radar, and the effects of quantification level, link location and orientation, length and frequency of operation on rainfall and simulated flow estimates were analyzed to determine the ability of the microwave link network to quantify rainfall in urban watersheds and capture spatial and temporal variations in rainfall (Turko et al., 2021 ). Sri Lanka inverted rain maps based on 1140 microwave link data covering most of the area for 3.5 months (Overeem et al., 2021 ). These data were compared locally with hourly and daily rain gauge data and with rain maps from the Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar on the Global Precipitation Measurement Core Observing Satellite. The potential of CML for real-time tropical rainfall monitoring was illustrated. China, the world's largest developing country, also has an urgent need for access to precipitation and hydrological information in its precipitation-rich eastern and southern regions. At present, precipitation observation experiments based on microwave links are still relatively rare except for a few regions in China (Song et al., 2021 ). This study presents a one and half year long precipitation observation experiment with microwave links in eastern China. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2  presents information on the study area, equipment, data pre-processing, and the inversion method of the rainfall based on microwave links. The overall inversion errors of rain rate and cumulative rainfall as well as precipitation inversion processes are analyzed in Section 3 . Next, quantitative winter precipitation inversion performance is evaluated, and the sources of microwave link precipitation inversion errors are discussed in depth in the discussion section. Finally, this study is summarised.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study area and equipment Located in the North subtropical humid monsoon climate zone (annual precipitation of 1100 mm), Suzhou (Jiangsu Province, in eastern China) borders Shanghai to the east and embraces Taihu Lake (the third largest freshwater lake in China) to the west, as shown in Fig. 1  . The topography of the city is low and the area around the lake and river is densely populated. A large amount of water drains from Taihu Lake from west to east into the Taipu River, which then flows into the Huangpu River (in Shanghai) and eventually into the Yangtze River and the East China Sea. Two dedicated microwave links (operating at 26 GHz, vertically polarized), both across the river (named Link1 and Link2 respectively), have been laid out at the entrance from Taihu Lake to the Tapu River to launch a precipitation monitoring experiments, where precipitation monitoring is particularly essential to emergency departments, as high cumulative rainfall in a short period of time can cause natural disasters such as urban waterlogging. The coordinates at the ends of Link1 (Link 2) are (120.5246°, 31.0209°) and (120.5058°, 31.0027°) ((120.4939°, 31.0069°) and (120.5047°, 31.0142°)). The lengths of Link1 and Link2 are 2.70 and 1.31 km, respectively, and the distance between the midpoints of the two links is about 1.5 km. The quantization resolution of the receiver terminal level is 0.1 dBm and the transmitter terminal level is a constant. The Received Signal Level (RSL) (in dBm) values are sampled at second resolution at the receiver terminal and then averaged at intervals of 1 min, which are stored locally in real time by the specialist software. In addition, an OTT PARSIVEL disdrometer (Löffler-Mang and Blahak, 2001 ) is located at the northeast end of Link2 as a reference instrument, which is about 1.25 km vertical distance from Link1. The disdrometer outputs a file every 1-min recording the number of precipitation particles sensed at 32 size bins (from 0 to 26 mm) and 32 velocity bins (from 0 to 22.4 m s−1 ).  2.2 Data and preprocessing The experimental period is from October 2020 to March 2022. Not all data were available during the experiment, and some failed to record valid data due to device malfunction. The data availability status of the two microwave links and the disdrometer during the experiment is depicted in Fig. 2  . The effective operation time of disdrometer, Link1 and Link2 accounted for about 84.3 %, 97.6 % and 96.0 % of the whole period, respectively. In order to ensure that the object of the study is pure liquid precipitation, only the data from March 1 to November 31 are firstly selected for quantitative rainfall inversion here. For RSL data directly measured by Link1 and Link2, missing values were determined by the linear interpolation processing. According to disdrometer data, raindrop size distribution (RSD) can be calculated as follows:(1) n ( D i  )  = ∑ j = 1  32  n i , j   v j  · Δ t · s · D i    , i = 1 , 2 , . . . , 32     where ni  , j   is the count value of both the i th  size bin and the j th  velocity bin in Δt  (1-min), s  (mm2 ) is the horizontal sampling area of the disdrometer, vj   is the representative value of the jth velocity bin and Di   (mm) is the representative value of the i th  size bin. In this study, a rainfall event is defined as a time period that simultaneously conforms to the following these criteria: 1) no rainfall occurs for 3 h before or after the time period, 2) the maximum adjacent rainfall interval within the time period does not exceed 30 min, 3) the cumulative rainfall time within the time period exceeds 30 min, and 4) the cumulative rainfall exceeds 1 mm. According to the above criteria, a total of 56 effective rainfall events were obtained from March to November 2021 (there are few rainfall events that meet the above during other non-winter times), and the specific time period and cumulative rainfall are described in Table 1   and Table A1 .  2.3 Identification of rainy and dry periods Two typical algorithms for rainy and dry period identification are the standard deviation method (Schleiss and Berne, 2010 ) and the correlation coefficient method (Rahimi et al., 2003 ). Standard deviation method refers to judging the current moment as rainy or dry period according to the standard deviation of RSL in the past time window:(7) σ = 1 W s   ∑ t = - ( W s  - 1 )  0  RSL ( t )  - 1 W s   ∑ t = - ( W s  - 1 )  0  RSL ( t )      2        where Ws   (min) is the time window length, RSL (t ) (dBm) is the RSL value at the t th  minute in the past. Ws   is set to 25 min as in Ref. The σq   value is determined based on the historical RSL data over a period of time. Considering robustness, the data from March to July 2021 are used to determine the σq   value, while the data from August to November 2021 (specifically, the 16 rainfall events shown in Table 1 ) are used to evaluate the identification effect of dry and rainy periods. This correlation coefficient method is based on the Pearson correlation coefficient of RSL of two microwave links ρ :(9) ρ = ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 1 ( t )  - 1 W ρ   ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 1 ( t )     R S L 2 ( t )  - 1 W ρ   ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 2 ( t )        ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 1 ( t )  - 1 W ρ   ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 1 ( t )      2    ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 2 ( t )  - 1 W ρ   ∑ t = 1  W ρ   R S L 2 ( t )      2          where Wρ   (min) is the time window length, RSL 1(t ) and RSL 2(t ) are the RSL value at the t th  minute during the time window for Link1 and Link2, respectively. For the standard deviation method, the rainy period is the minute corresponding to rain rate greater than 0.1 mm h−1  calculated from the disdrometer data, while for the correlation coefficient method, the rainy period is the 15-min period in which the number of minutes of rain rate greater than 0.1 mm h−1  calculated from the disdrometer data exceeds two. In addition, the True Positive Rate (TPR), False Negative Rate (FNR), False Positive Rate (FPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR) are respectively defined as follows:(11) TPR = RR  RR + R D       (12) FNR = RD  RR + R D       (13) FPR = DR  DD + D R       (14) TNR = DD  DD + D R       where RR  and RD  refer to the number of rainy samples identified as rainy samples and dry samples, DR  and DD  refer to the number of dry samples identified as rainy samples and dry samples, respectively.  2.4 Quantitative rainfall inversion The transmitted signal of a line-of-sight microwave link is subject to atmospheric component (precipitation, gases and others) attenuation and path loss on the one hand, and to the gain of the antenna at both ends of the path on the other. Therefore, the RSL of microwave link with line-of-sight propagation can be expressed as (Han et al., 2020 ):(15) RSL = T S L + G T  - A preci   - A gas   - A other   - A path   + G R      where TSL  (dBm) refers to the transmitted signal level, GT   (dB) and GR   (dB) refer to the transmit and receive antenna gain, Apreci   (dB) is the attenuation associated with precipitation, Agas   (dB) is the attenuation induced by gas (mainly oxygen and nitrogen), Aother   (dB) is the attenuation caused by other factors (such as aerosols), Apath   (dB) is the propagation path attenuation. When TSL , GR   and GT   are set as fixed values, and the attenuation caused by gas and other non-precipitation factors changes slowly along the microwave propagation path in a period of time, Apreci   can be approximated by the following ways:(16) A preci   = B L - R S L     where BL  (dB) is the attenuation baseline, which is a slowly changing value for a stable operating microwave link. In this experiment, the determination of BL  is based on the hourly base unit. Firstly, the average value of the RSL for the i th  hour (RSLi  ) is calculated. Then, the baseline value for the i th  hour can be set to the median of hourly average values during a one-week time window as follows (Fencl et al., 2020; Pu et al., 2020a ):(17) B L i  = m e d i a n { R S L i - 84   , . . . , R S L i - 1   , R S L i  , R S L i + 1   , . . . , R S L i + 84   }      However, the method does not yield a real-time baseline, which may be essential for precipitation monitoring and early warning. Therefore, the tail of the level sequence is taken instead of the centre of the level sequence to take the sliding median:(18) B L i  = m e d i a n { R S L i - 168   , R S L i - 167   , . . . , R S L i - 2   , R S L i - 1   }      Fig. 4   (a) and (b) present the baseline values obtained by taking the sliding median at the centre and tail of the level sequence respectively. It can be seen that taking the sliding median at the tail of the level sequence still gives a good baseline for an overall smooth baseline. However, when there is a step in the baseline (artificial operation or equipment drift), this method generates a lag period during which the pre-step baseline level is still maintained (marked by the purple dashed line in Fig. 4 (b)). If rainfall occurs during this period, serious errors may arise. Here, we add a new limiting constraint to alleviate the situation: when RSLi  -1 -RSLi  -2  > c  or RSLi  -2 -RSLi  -1  > c , the baseline at i th  hour is no longer determined by Equation (18) , but is calculated as the p -quantile of RSL in that hour, (i  + h )th  (h  = 1, …, H ) hour baseline is also calculated from the p -quantile of RSL in i th  to (i  + h -1)th  hours. From (i  + H )th  hour onwards, the baseline is redetermined by Equation (18) . For both link characteristics here, we set c  to 10 dB, p  to the 90th  quantile and H  to 96 h (4 days). Fig. 4 (c) exhibits the baseline established by the modified method. It can be observed that the modified method also addressed the step problem described above on the basis of providing a baseline in real time. From this, the value of Apreci   per minute can be obtained. For liquid precipitation, Apreci   is mainly composed of two parts:(19) A preci   = A rain   + A wa       where Arain   (dB) refers to the rain-induced attenuation along the propagation path, and Awa   (dB) is the attenuation caused by the water film attached to the antenna surface. Some early studies ignored the Awa   value and directly regarded the Apreci   value as Arain   to invert the rain rate (Rahimi et al., 2003 ). However, Awa   tends not to be very small relative to Arain   in many cases (Leijnse et al., 2007 ), especially when the link length is short, which causes a large rain rate inversion error. Preset constants (Overeem et al., 2011 ) or an exponential model (Kharadly and Ross, 2001 ) are commonly used Awa   correction methods, but are not refined for real-time rain rate inversion. Here, a dynamic model of Awa   based on the LSTM neural network (Pu et al., 2020a ) is applied in this experiment, because it can accurately and dynamically capture Awa   changes. According to the results calculated by RSD in Equation (3) , the rainy and dry labels of each minute in each rainfall event can be defined as:(20) label = rainy ,  i f  R ≥ 0.1  mm h   - 1     dry ,  i f  R < 0.1  mm h   - 1            It is assumed that the current moment Awa   is determined by a combination of the previous moment Awa   and the current signal characteristics. The model can be represented by a memory cell, as in Fig. 5  , which takes the previous cell state St  -1  and wet antenna attenuation Awa  , t  -1 , and the current moment features (labelt  -1  and Apreci  , t  -1 ) as input and outputs the wet antenna attenuation value for the current moment Awa  , t  . With the Awa   value obtained, the rain rate can be calculated as follows:(21) R inverse  = A preci  - A wa   0.10 L     1 1.10   ,  i f  A preci  - A wa  > 0   0 ,  i f  A preci  - A wa  ≤ 0          where L  (km) is the length of the microwave link. The dynamic model of Awa   based on the LSTM neural network needs to be trained according to the data set to determine the specific parameters (as depicted in the enlarged subfigure in Fig. 5 ), see Pu et al. (2020a)  for details. The model parameter optimization is based on this adaptive moment estimation method. The 56 rainfall events are used as the data set, among which the 1st to 40st  rainfall events are the train set, and the 41st  to 56th  rainfall events are the test set (the ratio of the train set to test set sample size is approximately 7:3). In addition, the hyperparameters of the model (e.g. hidden units, fully connected layers and dropout probabilities) were determined based on a 5-fold validation process, where the 40 rainfall events of train sets are equally divided into 5 groups and one of them was selected as the validation set without duplication. The average prediction error of the validation set for different combinations of hyperparameters is presented in Figure A1 , with the first hyperparameter combination being applied in this study. During the training process, the Awa   as the truth value is computed as follows:(22) A wa  = A preci  - 0.10 L R 1.10  ,  i f  A preci  - 0.10 L R 1.10  > 0   0 ,  i f  A preci  - 0.10 L R 1.10  ≤ 0             3 Result 3.1 Performance for rainy/dry period recognition Fig. 6   depicts the identification results of the standard deviation method for the dry and rainy periods of 16 rainfall events from August to November 2021. As can be seen from the figure, when q  decreases, overall TPR  and FPR  are increasing, while TNR  and FNR  are the opposite. This is easy to understand, as the standard deviation method is actually based on the assumption that RSL fluctuates significantly during rainy periods, while RSL changes are relatively flat during dry periods. When q  is relatively large, the criterion is too harsh for identifying the rainy period and only a small number of strong rainfall samples are correctly identified, while at the same time the criterion is too loose for identifying the dry period and almost all dry samples are correctly identified. As q  becomes smaller, more and more rainfall samples are correctly identified, but more and more dry periods are misclassified as rainy periods. When q  is equal to 85 or 80, both dry and rainy periods can be correctly identified at the same time with a rate greater than 0.8 (median value, the middle line of the box plot), which may be a good compromise for both links. However, this compromise choice may not be appropriate in practical applications, as the effect of the rainy period being identified as the dry period and the dry period being identified as the rainy period may not have an equal effect on the rainfall inversion. When q  is taken to be relatively small, although some of the dry periods may be misidentified as rainy periods, the extracted rain-induced attenuation value may be negative or a small value and the inversion may have little effect on the accumulation.
