But when q  is relatively large, a certain proportion of the dry periods may be identified as dry periods and the extracted rain-induced attenuation values may be directly assigned to 0 in the process, which results in an underestimation of the accumulation. Fig. 7   illustrates the results of identification of rainy and dry periods based on the correlation coefficient method. The underlying assumption of the correlation coefficient method is that, during rainy periods, the RSLs of the two links fluctuate in tandem affected by rainfall and therefore the correlation is significantly higher. Similar to the standard deviation method, the TPR  and FPR  become progressively larger as the correlation coefficient increases, while the opposite is true for the TNR  and FNR . As can be seen from the figure, the ρ 0  equal to 0.4 can make the correct identification rate for both the rainy and dry periods higher than 0.8.  3.2 Error for quantitative rainfall inversion The quantitative rainfall inversion procedure in Section 2  is based on an explicit rainy and dry label from the disdrometer deployed in the experiment. In fact, there are much existing literatures that determine the rainy and dry label only based on the link data itself, but the effect is not always ideal (also exhibited in the previous section). As far as we know, almost no method can effectively identify both dry and rainy periods with an accuracy of more than 90 %, even if self-determining parameters are applied per link. In fact, a variant strategy is to deploy a rain sensor near the link. Unlike specialist meteorological instruments such as rain gauges or disdrometers, rain sensors can be made very inexpensive, perhaps even costing only a few tens of RMB (or about US$10) in China. Of course, this study only explores the feasibility of the experimental approach and does not address operational requirements. Based on the inversion method as described in Section 2 , the rain rate inversion results of the whole test set are compared with the reference rain rate (calculated from the OTT PARSIVEL disdrometer data), as shown in Fig. 8  . Here, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE, in mm h−1 ), Mean Error (ME, in mm h−1 ), and Correlation Coefficient (CC) are also annotated in the figure. It can be seen that the rain rate inverted by Link1 and Link2 shows an obvious positive correlation with the reference rain rate, and there is a certain negative bias phenomenon on the whole. Compared with Link1, Link2 is with a lower RMSE (2.93 mm h−1  vs. 2.07 mm h−1 ) and a higher correlation coefficient (0.84 vs. 0.92) for the inversion of rain rate. It can also be seen from the figure that the two-dimensional scatter of Link2 is more concentrated around the red line (y = x line). The possible reason is that the disdrometer, as the reference instrument, is closer to Link2, so the rain rate values of the rainfall area observed by the two are more consistent. In addition to the 1-min rain rate samples, the inversion results for the 5-min, 10-min and 15-min mean rain rates are also compared to the reference values as displayed in Fig. 9  . As the temporal resolution is reduced, lower RMSE and higher CC are showcased. In addition, the accumulation of 16 rainfall events in the test set is also compared with the accumulation calculated based on the disdrometer data, as described in Table 1 . Accumulation is calculated based on the cumulative sum of rain rate in each minute of a rainfall event divided by 60. For most rainfall events, the inverted accumulation correlated well with the true accumulation, with a correlation coefficient of 0.79 and 0.87 for Link1 and Link2 respectively, as shown in Fig. 10  . However, for several strong rainfall events, with accumulation between 10 and 20 mm, a more significant underestimation occurs, which also corresponds to the negative bias of the inverted rain rate in Fig. 8 . Fig. 11   illustrates the quantitative rainfall inversion process under a typical continuous rainfall event. Starting at about 2:00 on September 13, the intermittent drizzle held then it suddenly increased in intensity at noon on September 13 (maximum rain rate about 27 mm h−1 ), then gradually weakened until the rainfall ended. As can be seen in Fig. 11 (a), (c) and (e) ((b), (d) and (f)), the fluctuations in RSL are well synchronized with the changes in rain rate and wet antenna attenuation. In addition, as in Fig. 11 (e) and (f), the rain rate inversion based on Apreci   appears to be significantly overestimated compared to the reference rain rate, especially in the case of heavy rainfall, which also reflects the need for wet antenna attenuation correction. After the wet antenna attenuation correction, the inversion of the rain rate shows a very significant improvement. Fig. 11 (g) and (h) also indicated that the accumulation based on the wet antenna attenuation correction is significantly closer to the reference accumulation than the uncorrected one. In addition, the quantitative inversion process for the 50th  and 51st  rainfall events, which are not pointed out in Fig. 10 , is presented in Figs. A2 and A3. Not only is there a large difference in accumulation, but the inverted rain rate variation does not match the reference rain rate. It can be seen that the fluctuations in RSL do not appear to be consistent with the rain rate variation, unlike the case for the above rainfall event. Furthermore, the range of level fluctuations for both links is only about 0.5 dB throughout the rainy period. It is speculated that this may have been due to a malfunction in the instrumentation or recording software during that period.   4 Discussion 4.1 Error source Quantitative inversion errors in rainfall based on microwave links are multi-sourced. In terms of the experimental design itself, only one disdrometer has been placed at one end of a link, given the cost considerations. Due to the spatial variability of natural rainfall, using the rain rate measured by one disdrometer as a reference value introduces a degree of error. In addition, there are differences between the concepts of point and path-averaged rain rate measured by microwave links, which are only fully consistent when the rain rate is uniformly distributed along the path. Moreover, the accuracy of the algorithms for rain rate inversion is also subject to further validation in the future. For example, the wet antenna attenuation correction algorithm, which is applied in this study based on an LSTM neural network, although can obtain a corrected value of wet antenna attenuation in real time, its applicability under different rainfall conditions is also to be evaluated with respect to more rainfall samples. Fig. 12   illustrates the error distribution of the predicted wet antenna attenuation corresponding to different rain rate intervals with respect to Link1 and Link2. It can be seen that the median error of Awa   is around 0 dB when the rain rate is small (0.1 to 1 and 1 to 5 mm h−1 ), but for large rain rates, Awa   shows a significant positive bias. This means that the wet antenna attenuation is over-revised for the heavy rainfall case, which in turn makes the overall rain-induced attenuation and rain rate underestimated, as demonstrated in Section 3.2 . Furthermore, the stability of the link level itself has an impact on the inversion results. The baseline determination method proposed in this study enables a fast response to level drift (as displayed in Fig. 4 ), but short-time random fluctuations in level are difficult to suppress effectively, and more relevant pre-processing methods may also be significant in future operational use.  4.2 Winter precipitation The previous analysis was entirely based on observations from March to November 2021 to ensure that the subject was liquid precipitation. However, the beginning and end of this experiment also actually observed the precipitation data of two winters in 2020 spanning 2021 and 2021 spanning 2022. Quantitative assessment of winter precipitation is extremely difficult at present due to the complex extinction properties of non-liquid precipitation particles. At present, only a few studies have attempted to identify precipitation types based on microwave links (Holt et al., 2008; Pu et al., 2020c ). In this section, winter precipitation was tried to be assessed quantitatively based on the model developed in this study, and the signal level changes involving non-liquid precipitation days are analyzed to clarify the level characteristics affected by non-liquid precipitation. Table 2   lists all historical weather information that may involve non-liquid precipitation during the experimental period, of which only 8 days between January and February 2022 have valid data. On these precipitation days, the minimum surface temperature was 1 or 2 degrees Celsius, indicating that the precipitation during this period may have been a mixture of liquid and non-liquid precipitation. Therefore, there is a need to further distinguish between different types of precipitation. The precipitation type identification method used here comes from Pu et al. (2020b) , who use disdrometer data to determine the precipitation particles in a certain minute according to the empirical V  − D  relationship of different types of precipitation particles and divide them into three categories (rain, graupel and snow). In total, 25 precipitation events are associated with winter during the experiment (December of one year to February of the next) according to the precipitation event identification criteria in Section 2.2 . Four of these precipitation events involve non-liquid precipitation samples, as summarized in Table 3  . These four non-liquid precipitation events largely match the historical weather forecasts in Table 2 , and can therefore indicate that the precipitation type classification method being applied from Pu et al. (2020b)  is reliable. The accumulation for the 25 winter precipitation events, still calculated by the previous process of inversion of liquid precipitation, is depicted in Fig. 13  . It can be seen that, with the exception of the four winter precipitation events containing non-liquid precipitation, the accumulative rainfall for the other winter precipitation events is small (almost all below 10 mm). The inverted accumulation for the purely liquid winter precipitation events maintains a good positive correlation with the reference accumulation of 0.86 and 0.88 for Link1 and Link2, respectively. In addition, the difference is that the Link1 inversions slightly overestimate the cumulative rainfall, unlike the non-winter precipitation, which underestimates it. However, once the four non-liquid precipitation events are included, the performance of the cumulative rainfall inversion becomes poor, mainly due to the first and third clearly discrete non-liquid precipitation events. As recorded in Table 3 , there are a large number of non-liquid precipitation minutes (402 and 479 min, respectively) in these two precipitation events. Fig. 14   (a) shows the precipitation rate and type from January 28 to 29, 2022. Here the precipitation rate is calculated by assuming liquid precipitation. There is a period of heavy non-liquid precipitation in the hours before and after the early morning of January 29. The theoretical rain-induced attenuation (calculated with the dielectric properties and shape of liquid raindrops) of both links during this period is presented in Fig. 14 (c) and (e) to be much greater overall than the extracted Apreci  , which is quite unreasonable. The possible reason for this is the presence of large diameter solid precipitation particles, who would be misidentified by the OTT disdrometer as oversized raindrops, but the extinction degree for microwave is not up to the corresponding level (possible dry snow scenario). Fig. 15   shows the same meaning as Fig. 14  except in January 31 to February 2, 2022. During this period, there is only a small amount of non-liquid precipitation and its intensity is very weak, so RSL does not show obvious characteristics. Figs. 16 and 17    present the same content from February 6 to 7 and February 17, 2022, both of which exist theoretical rain-induced attenuation values greater than Apreci   during non-liquid precipitation. However, this is not always the case and sometimes the opposite occurs. This may be the effect of the wet antenna attenuation component, or it may be that the solid precipitation particle shells are melting, resulting in precipitation particles that may have both large scale and strong extinction capabilities, further reducing the RSL  more significantly. In addition, another special phenomenon is that the consistency between RSL  and precipitation rate during solid precipitation is far less obvious than that during liquid precipitation. The possible reason for this is that the relationship between size and shape and extinction characteristics of solid precipitation particles may be difficult to be approximated monotonically. Furthermore, the precipitation type classification method here is not fine enough, because the empirical V  − D  relationship used to match precipitation types is only a statistical average condition, and there may be misclassification for specific samples, especially in the presence of turbulence. Moreover, for a certain minute precipitation sample, it may be composed of several precipitation particles of different types, and its influence on RSL  is also difficult to estimate. A more advanced precipitation microphysical characteristics measurement instrument, such as the Multi-Angle Snowflake Camera (Minda et al., 2017 ), may be beneficial to study RSL variation characteristics in the case of solid precipitation in the future work.   5 Conclusion In this study, a microwave link precipitation observation experiment for the period October 2020 to March 2022 is presented. Two microwave links (at 26 GHz, vertically polarised) and an OTT PARSIVEL disdrometer are deployed on a river in eastern China throughout the experiment period. First, two rainy and dry period identification methods (standard deviation method and correlation coefficient method) are evaluated separately based on this experimental link data. the two methods can achieve a correct identification of both dry and rainy periods in excess of 80 % when suitable parameters are selected. In addition, to ensure that the quantitative inversion targets liquid precipitation, 56 rainfall events with cumulative rainfall greater than 1 mm from March to November 2021 comprise the dataset. Based on this, a LSTM neural network-based dynamic model of wet antenna attenuation is applied to the inversion of rainfall per minute. Considering the robustness of the evaluation, the first 70 % of the rainfall events are used as the train set and the last 30 % as the test set. The results indicate that the minute rain rates in the inversion of both links have a high positive correlation with the rain rate calculated from the disdrometer data, and that the inversion results for Link2 were better than those for Link1 due to the closer geographical proximity. Moreover, the accumulation for the test set of rainfall events maintained good agreement with the reference accumulation. Furthermore, inversion process analysis of rainfall event reveals that the wet antenna attenuation correction could significantly reduce the cumulative rainfall error, although the model may not perform well in thunderstorm weather conditions. Finally, quantitative inversion of winter precipitation is performed using two microwave links. The results demonstrate that winter liquid precipitation can still be well estimated quantitatively, but that large biases may arise when non-liquid precipitation is involved, which may be associated with the particular extinction properties of non-liquid precipitation particles. There are shortcomings in this study. In particular, this study is still in the experiment stage and is still a long way from the operational operation. More scenarios of rainfall events are also needed to further verify the validity of the model. In addition, experiments such as precipitation classification and precipitation field reconstruction based on more microwave links can also be further investigated in the future.  6 Samples, and data This research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 42222505 and 41975030), and the Excellent Youth Scholars of Natural Science Foundation of Hunan Province of China (Grant No. 2021JJ20046). The authors thank the Jiangsu M&R Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd, China for maintaining the microwave links and collecting the data used in this study.
1 Introduction Mountain glaciers are key freshwater resources and vital components of the hydrological cycle. Water resources are directly influenced by the dynamics of snow and glaciers melt runoff. The impact of climate change on the melting of snow and glaciers has been attracting the attention of researchers in the last decades due to pronounced glaciers’ retreat observed in various regions of the world. Fang and Pomeroy (2023)  and Xiang et al. (2024)  are recent examples of such research outcomes for the Canadian Rockies and Himalaya. Blöschl et al. (2019)  identified snow and glacier melt under changing climate as one of twenty-three unsolved problems in hydrology that demand stronger cooperation between communities. It is worthwhile to consider the significance of glacial runoff dynamics for millions of people living downstream around the world. These questions are especially challenging for the Indus Basin which is considered as a climatic hotspot region (Immerzeel et al., 2015 ). The Upper Indus Basin (UIB), carrying an area of 163528 km2  gauged at Besham Qila, is enriched with world largest natural reserves, except Greenland and Antarctica ice sheets, of snow and ice that retain freshwater balance in this region and surrounding valleys (Immerzeel and Bierkens, 2010 ). Trends in ablation of snow and glaciers retreat depend upon initial ice reserves, climatic conditions and geographical features which vary across sub-basins in High Mountain Asia (HMA). The economy of Pakistan is largely dependent upon the Indus River system which is providing indispensable water supply for irrigation, hydropower generation, municipal and industrial use (Kult et al., 2012 ). Indus River from UIB receives its major share of water, around 90 % of overall flow, and about 60 % comes from snow and glacial melt (Biemans et al., 2019 ). This makes UIB glaciers a crucial source of fresh water for millions of downstream residents. Thus, any change in UIB flow would have a significant impact on the water-food and energy nexuses of the country. Several studies examined and found a number of uncertainties in previous hydrological studies in this region. These uncertainties are primarily associated with lack of reliable input data, diverse modelling tools and complex hydrology of the area. Some studies found rising rate of glaciers retreat in the Himalaya and Hindu Kush region (Benn et al., 2012; Muhammad et al., 2019 ) while others exhibited advancing in central Karakoram (Bolch et al., 2017; Berthier and Brun, 2019; Muhammad et al., 2019 ). Hewitt (2005)  coined the term 'Karakoram Anomaly', indicating the stability or abnormal growth of glaciers in the central Karakoram, as opposed to glaciers retreating in nearby mountain ranges such as the Himalayan range and other mountain ranges worldwide. Farinotti et al. (2020)  conducted a review of the 'Karakoram Anomaly', analysing its diverse manifestations, potential causes, and broader implications. The authors emphasized the need for continued research into glacier dynamics in the Karakoram mountain range in order to interpret the underlying mechanisms and project future changes. Although it remains unclear whether the anomaly appears throughout the central part of the Karakoram, as in the Hunza basin and will continue to exist in the near future, the authors argued that its continued existence seems unlikely given the substantial warming expected in the far future scenarios, as projected by current climate projections. Zemp et al. (2019)  using an extrapolation of glaciological and geodetic observations showed that glaciers distinct from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets contributed 27 ± 22 mm to global mean sea-level rise from 1961 to 2016 and that Asia South West (ASW) is the only region in the world in which glaciers slightly gained mass from 1961 to 2016. Their study highlighted how regional specific-mass-change rates for 2006–2016 range globally from − 0.1 m to − 1.2 m of water equivalent per year (m w.e yr-1) and that the ASW region exhibits the smallest retreat at a rate of − 0.03 ± 0.12 m w.e yr−1 . Bishop et al. (2014) analysing remote sensing images pointed out that in Pakistan many glacier termini are variably stationary, advancing, or retreating. These evidences of the peculiar dynamics of glaciers in Pakistan justify the need of an investigation about the meteorological factors and the hydro-glaciological processes that may result in different dynamics in this ‘anomalous’ region, being the outcomes of worldwide and not only local interest. Javed et al. (2022)  found ∼10 % increase in precipitation and higher percentage of snow fall (65 %) from western disturbance (WDs) relative to total seasonal snowfall behind the emergence and continual presence of Karakoram anomaly in recent years. Hence, it is also essential to incorporate reliable tools and methods for modelling snow-glacier melt and runoff dynamics to handle the expected climate change impacts. Over the past years, several hydrological and temperature index models have been used to evaluate glacio-hydrological regimes in Himalaya and Karakoram including HBV (Bergström, 1976; Fowler and Archer, 2006; Akhtar et al., 2008 ; Ali et al., 2018 ), the snowmelt runoff model (Tahir et al., 2011; Adnan et al., 2017 ; Hayat et al., 2019 ), SWAT (Garee et al., 2017 ; Shah et al., 2020 ) and the J2000 model (Xiang et al., 2024 ). Hasson et al. (2019)  used a semi-distributed energy balance hydrological model from the University of British Columbia (UBC). But considering climate change, temperature-index-based hydrological models are disputable when applied to snow-fed and glaciated basins, as they often oversimplify the melt process leading to inadequate representation of actual hydrological processes (Sicart et al., 2008; Farinotti et al., 2010; Miles et al., 2018; Dahri et al., 2021 ). Additionally, some researchers used simple conceptual models and adopt a lumped approach as compared to a physically based, spatially distributed one due to less data demand, smaller computational time and easier calibration in UIB in order examine melt and hydrological dynamics in current and future climatic scenarios (Immerzeel et al., 2009;Pellicciotti et al.,2012; Naeem et al., 2016;Tahir et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2020; Ayub et al., 2020 ). Although fully distributed models have been also used in UIB (Shrestha et al., 2015; Lutz et al., 2016; Shrestha and Nepal, 2019 ), they demand extensive amount of data, time and efforts to correctly extrapolate snow glacier melt rate in high altitude terrains where surface atmosphere and meteorological process are widely varied and their application is still in a pioneering stage in this area, with a resolution of 500 m to 1 km that is still coarse to simulate in detail glaciers’ energy and mass balance. In this study, high altitude automatic weather station hourly data were used to assess the melt rate using a fully distributed energy balance model with a resolution of 90 m in the Naltar catchment. The present research employed the energy balance model Physically based Distributed Snow Land and Ice Model (PDSLIM) developed and tested in Alps (Ranzi and Rosso, 1991; Ranzi et al., 2010; Grossi et al., 2013 ) and for the first time in the Karakoram region, for the Naltar catchment (Pakistan) located in the Hunza river basin. Hunza river basin is the second largest glacierized basin in UIB. Earlier studies on snow glacier melt runoff using energy balance modelling in Karakoram region were carried out using reanalysis, gridded with combination of observed data (Mihalcea et al., 2008; Shrestha et al., 2015; Shakoor and Ejaz, 2019; Liu et al., 2023 ). Although reanalysis and satellite data are good sources in hydrological modelling studies, both datasets present some deficiencies compared to observations, particularly precipitation is overestimated especially in the mountainous region and needs bias correction before its use in hydrological modelling studies (Liaqat et al., 2022 ; Ansari et al., 2022)  . Recently, Aftab et al. (2023) conducted a study on the elevation-distributed hydro-climatic regime of the Hunza Basin using Distance Distribution Dynamics (DDD) model. Their research revealed that the model they used exhibited reliable performance when it came to simulating runoff processes, and that glacier melt made a significant contribution to net streamflow. However, they also found that gridded data sets (ERA5 and JRA) did not reproduce the sharp flow peaks of the monsoon season well in the snow-covered and glacierized Hunza Basin. Further, few studies were found where hydrological simulations were carried out at hourly scale using detailed observed data. For instance, Shakoor and Ejaz (2019)  examined the feasibility of Snowpack and its distributed version Alpine 3D for the first time using detailed observed data to simulate hydrological regimes in Passu catchment located in the Hunza river basin. However, the findings of this study are limited to one hydrological year without inclusion of high flood events in this region and detail explanation of snow and glacier melt dynamics both at spatial and temporal scale. The current study augments the previous studies in the data-scarce Naltar catchment, Hunza Basin with the following objectives: (1) to describe in a comprehensive and complete way the energy-balance distributed PDSLIM model and its streamflow routing component and apply using detailed observed data at hourly scale, and verifying it with streamflow observations and 250 satellite images of snow cover extent in the Karakoram, (2) to quantify the contribution of rainfall, snow and glacier melt to net river runoff and explore the ability of the model to simulate rapid and slow flow components of the streamflow hydrograph, (3) estimate the mass balance of glaciers in the Naltar catchment thus assessing whether the Karakoram anomaly applies also in the central part of this region. The study would provide a path to create a sound modelling framework for prospective energy and mass balance studies in this region under climate change scenarios and uncertainty assessment (Liaqat et al., 2024 ). The novelty of this work and of its development in perspective appears to rely on the fact that such a detailed high resolution modelling of the mass balance and the hydrological regime in the melt season of this region with in-situ hydro-meteorological observations in both the current and future climate is absent to the authors knowledge and sheds light on the ‘Karakoram anomaly’ which is of general interest being this region the only one where glaciers advanced in the recent decades (Zemp et al., 2019; Farinotti et al., 2020 ).  2 Material and methods 2.1 Description of the study area The Naltar catchment is geographically located 36° 10′ -36° 37′  N and 74° 01′ -74° 25′ , in a climatically temperate region of Hunza river basin. Hunza basin is the second largest glacierized basin of the UIB (Liaqat et al., 2021). The catchment is characterised by small lakes, pine forests, glaciers,and hosts one famous spot for winter skiing for national and international visitors (Gardezi et al., 2022 ). The elevation of Naltar catchment varies from 2270 m to 5886 m with mean elevation 3980 m. It is situated in Hunza basin about 42 km away from Gilgit city and 208 km from K2 (the second largest mountain peak in the world) in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan. The total area of Naltar catchment is 242.62 km2  with glacierized area covering 17.31 % of its surface. The largest glacier within the Naltar catchment is Shani glacier with an area of 19 km2 . The proportion of debris cover glaciers is 9.13 % in the Naltar catchment. Debris cover was detected from satellite images and incorporated in the energy balance model that considers the effect of debris cover as well. The average annual precipitation and temperature recorded at Naltar station (2898 m asl) is 685 mm yr-1 and 6.5 °C (Liaqat et al., 2022 ). The streamflow was measured at Naltar Bala stations with mean flow of 11 m3 /s over the 2006–2016 observation period. The water further flows through the Naltar stream into the Hunza river which is one of the main tributaries of the Indus River. Fig. 1   shows the location of Naltar catchment and the location of five meteorological and streamflow gauge stations used in this study.  2.2 Meteorological data The PDSLIM model requires six meteorological parameters to effectively simulate snow depletion and runoff regimes. In High Mountain Asia, it is quite challenging to access substantial and reliable quality of meteorological data (temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, wind speed and relative humidity) to run energy balance mode at hourly scale such as PDSLIM for year-to-year simulations. All parameters except pressure were operated by Water and Power development Authority (WAPDA), located in Gilgit and Hunza basin. The detailed description of these stations is given in Table.S1  as well as shown in Fig. 1 . The stations are selected due to their location. A consistency check revealed that this dataset had some missing values for some variables at different dates and times. Initially, we selected 8 out of 11 years for which missing values amounted to less than 20 %. The final set of years was 2006, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2014 and 2016. The missing values were estimated through multiple linear regression with surrounding stations as used by (Prabnakorn et al.,2019 ). Reconstructed hourly pressure values were obtained from (Bair et al., 2020 ). The hydrological response in the Naltar catchment during winter is silent without melt or runoff changes, apart the recession of subsurface flow, and because of the less reliability of solid precipitation measurements we preferred to initialise the hydrological model on the 15th of March and then simulate with our model until 30th September in each year independently. The initialisation was done with SWE estimated from Bair et al. (2019)  by the end of accumulation period and initial observed runoff. Model parameters were set at the values obtained from the calibration period. Then we added a warm-up period lasting from 15th to 30th of March as the warm-up period in each simulated year.  2.3 Hydrological data The hydrometric station was installed at Naltar Bala since 2006. This streamflow measurement equipment was installed by WAPDA. Currently, Naltar-IV hydro-power plant is operational in Naltar. It has a small reservoir which holds enough water to produce electricity at full capacity of 18 MW. To a limited extent, the plant can shape hourly water releases during the day such that production is higher during peak load hours. The mean Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) curve (2006–2016) for Naltar streamflow is shown in Fig. 2  .  2.4 Satellite data In order to make an effective spatial distribution of the variables and to estimate energy balance, the digital elevation model of the study area, albedo, land use/ land cover, the leaf area index and the terrain view factor were used in this study. The STRM DEM with 90 m resolution data was used to define catchment boundary and topography. Further details about sources, descriptions and type of data used in this study can be found in Table S2 . The mean monthly temperature data and lapse rate, estimated from ground observations in the Naltar, Gilgit and Hunza basins and changing with clear sky and cloud covered conditions, were also used to compute the freezing line altitude (FLA) i.e. the 0 °C isotherm as shown in Fig. 3  . The temperature lapse rate was computed at 100 m elevation using Naltar and Yasin station by applying linear gradient. The sensitivity of model performance was tested for the change in temperature lapse rate, TLR 0.0065–0.0085 °C m−1  for clear sky and 0.0051–0.0045 °C m−1  for cloud cover conditions. . The land use land cover (LULC) based on ENVISAT’s MERIS Level 1B with spatial resolution of 300 m were obtained from GlobCover land cover product developed by the European Space Agency (ESA)-GlobCover. Further, the data was clipped according to the shape file of Naltar catchment in order to obtain the desired map of LULC. Based on LULC, Naltar catchment has 15 classes. The dominant LULC classes in the Naltar catchment are snow/glacier, grassland, rocks, and mixed forest. The glaciers layer derived from the Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) Version (V) 6.0 released on July 2017 and is overlaid on land cover data. The LULC and albedo map of Naltar catchment are shown in Fig. 4  .. MODIS 8DAY composite LAI product MYD15A2H.006 was acquired from Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Centre (LPDAAC) (https://lpdaacsvc.cr.usgs.gov/appeears/task/area  ) from the start of the peak melt period (June- July) for each simulated year depending upon cloud cover. Naltar catchment has a wide spatial variability of ice, snow and seasonal snow cover. MODIS daily satellite images are a common source to monitor spatial and temporal variability of snow cover areas with resolution of 500 m. Because a significant proportion of cloud cover in images especially in winter and monsoon season may cause underestimation of snow and ice cover extent, the present study used 216 improved MODIS snow cover product (M*D10A1GL06) images developed by Muhammad and Thapa (2021)  derived from original MOD10A1 (Terra) and MYD10A1 (Aqua) to reduce snow cover estimation caused by cloud cover and by swath and lower spatial resolution. The initial value of Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) used in PDLSIM was derived from high resolution reconstructed SWE products using MODSCAG and SPIRES approaches developed by (Bair et al., 2019 ). MODSCAG uses surface reflectance visible and infrared images derived from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and different algorithms to estimate SWE while, SPIRES based SWE based on passive microwave data such as AMSR2, machine learning applications and meteorological data. In this study, we used both products (MODSCAG and SPIRES) to assess uncertainty of simulated results. The values of both products differ from one another. In general, MODSCAG-based SWE values are low while SPIRES-based SWE values are high. As a result, we used the terms low and high along with MODSCAG and SPIRES in the following sections. The SWE was reconstructed from to the date of maximum SWE at the beginning of the melting season using satellite-based retrievals of MODIS fractional snow cover area in combination with energy balance equations and land surface meteorological variables (Bair et al., 2016; Rittger et al., 2016 ). Further validation of reconstructed SWE product in High Mountain Asia (HMA) was carried out by employing a full distributed energy balance model (SNOWPACK and ALPINE 3D) and in-situ values of snow depth collected and maintained by the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat (AKAH) (Bair et al., 2020 ). Further information about these products and its developing mechanism can be found in Bair et al. (2018, 2019)  and in (Rittger et al., 2016 ).  2.5 Mass balance 2.5.1 Snow water equivalent at the beginning of the melt season For a given period, the annual mass balance is equal to the sum of winter and summer mass balances. It is usually expressed in terms of equivalent water volume B  [L3 ] or specific equivalent for unit area expressed in millimetres. It is assumed that winter starts on 1st of October indicated as tow  of the previous year and ends on the 15th of March, denoted as tfw  of the current year. The ablation season is assumed to start on the 16th of March tos  of the given year also considering a warm up period, and ends on the 30th of September tfs  of the balance year. The snow water equivalent at the beginning of the melt season can be considered the result of the winter glacier’s mass balance, being computed as the sum of the snow mass balance and the firn and ice mass balance. The ice and firn mass balance Bw,ice  is equivalent to the total volume of the snow water equivalent Sweq(tow) left at the beginning of the balance year, for us on the 1st of October, which starts its metamorphosis into firn and, later, ice. Ice melt is assumed to be negligible in winter. The snow winter balance, from the beginning of the accumulation year to the start of the melt season, Bw , is given by the difference Sweq  (tfw )- Sweq (t0w ), between the snow water equivalent observed at the end Sweq  (tfw ) and at beginning, Sweq (t0w), of the winter season. Hence, the glacier’s winter mass balance is:(1) B w   =  B w , i c e   + B w , s n o w   = S weq   t 0 w      + S weq   t fw      - S weq   t 0 w      = S weq   tfw         In this study snow water equivalent at the beginning of the melt season in each simulated year, Sweq(tfw), was derived from a combination of ground snow data and satellite data (Bair et al., 2016, 2020 )  2.5.2 Summer mass balance The summer mass balance of the glacier is computed as the areal sum of the point mass balance over each pixel of the study domain, measuring an area dA=90 m x 90 m. Summer mass balance Bs  over the glacier area, Ag (t) = Ag , assumed constant in one balance year, is computed as the sum of Bs,snow  , the mass balance of snow-covered areas Asnow (t) and Bs, ice, the mass balance over the snow-free areas, Aice(t), both areas changing dynamically over time. For clarity, the mass balance is splitted into that of the solid phase of water, accumulating as snowfall and melt and sublimation and the liquid one, through rain on snow and evaporation of the liquid phase:(2) B s , s n o w   = S weq   t fs      - S weq   t 0 s      = ∫ t 0 s    t fs    ∫ A snow   t      r A t    , t     + s A t    , t     - m snow   A t    , t     - e snow   A t    , t         d A d t     Here, s shows snowfall, msnow  (comprising drainage of the snow liquid water content), r depicts the rainfall rate on snow and esnow  characterise the net snow sublimation and evaporation losses. All above mentioned terms have dimensions [LT−1  ]. The rainfall over firn and ice areas is assumed to flow as runoff on the surface and on subsurface channels of the glacier. Therefore, summer balance Bs,ice   of this part of glacier with area Aice (t)  is always negative being the sum of the sublimation rate eice   and melt rate mice   calculated as:(3) B s , i c e   ∫ t 0 s    t fs    ∫ A ice   ( t )    [ - m ice  ( A ( t )  ,t )  - e ice  ( A ( t )  ,t )  ]  dAdt      The summer mass balance of ice and snow over the glacier’s area Ag (t) which can be considered constant and in one year is(4) B s , s n o w   = ∫ t 0 s    t fs    ∫ A g ( t )    [ p snow  ( A ( t )  ,t )  -m ( A ( t )  ,t )  -e ( A ( t )  ,t )  ]  dAdt     Here psnow   shows total precipitation rate over snow, either snow, s , or rain, r, m = msnow  + mice   represents the total melt from ice or snow as well as drainage from the snowpack, and e = eice  + esnow   evaporation and sublimation from snow and ice, with negative sign representing condensation of air water vapour. All these terms have dimension [LT−1  ]. Total precipitation over the glacier is the sum of the total precipitation on snow psnow , rain on ice, rice  that does not contribute to the glacier mass balance because it runs off the glacier’s surface. The annual mass balance is represented by the sum of the winter and summer mass balance:(5) B s ,  s n o w   = S weq ( t f w )    +   ∫ t 0 s    t fs    ∫ A g  ( t )    [ p snow  ( A ( t )  ,t )  -m ( A ( t )  ,t )  -e ( A ( t )  ,t )  ]  dAdt      The annual specific mass balance over a unit surface of the glacier, with dimension [L], can be obtained as:(6) b = B A g   = B snow   + B ice    A g       It is noted that areal changes of Ag (t) are neglected in the annual mass balance computation as their estimation would require a continuous monitoring or modelling of the glacier’s areal extent.  2.5.3 Energy balance of snow and ice In this section, the energy balance model, known as PDSLIM (Physically based Distributed Snow Land and Ice Model) is described. The PDSLIM model is the evolution of the PDSM model, applied at catchment scale to simulate snowmelt and snowpack dynamics in the Cordevole river first by Ranzi and Rosso, (1991) , tested and verified with snowpack measurements and passive microwave measurements by Cagnati et al. (2004) , and then applied to the Belvedere glacier (Ranzi et al., 2004 ). PDSLIM includes a soil-vegetation atmosphere exchange component using a Penman Monteith scheme similar to that described by Wigmosta et al., (1994) . It was initially developed for the Toce catchment by Grossi and Falappi (2003)  and then applied to the Adamello glacier by Ranzi et al., (2010)  and Grossi et al., (2013) . The model also accounts for the heat and mass fluxes of glaciers partially covered by debris. The debris cover extent (9.13 % of the glacier’s area in the Naltar basin) was estimated from satellite images as described in section 2.1 . The description of modelling debris cover glaciers in PDSLIM using the Fourier law of conductive heat flux assuming 0 °C temperature at the debris-ice interface can be found in Ranzi et al. (2004)  with its verification in the Belvedere debris-covered glacier in Italy. For a unit area, melt rate for finite depth of layer ice or snow superimposed over ice is computed using the energy balance equation:(7) H m  + H c   = S sn   + L ln   + H l  + H s  + H p  + H g      Here units of all terms are W/m2 . Hm : energy available for melt, Hc : internal energy of the snow or ice layer, Ssn : net shortwave radiation, Lln : net longwave radiation, Hl : latent heat, Hs : sensible heat, Hp : advective heat from precipitation, Hg : conductive heat at the bottom side of the snow or ice layer. The detailed description of the energy balance model in its snowpack, ice melt, radiative and turbulent fluxes components, can be found in the above mentioned papers as well as in the supplementary material .  2.5.4 Calibration with MODIS and LANDSAT snow cover area The PDSLIM derived snow cover area was compared with the MODIS snow cover product (M*D10A1GL06) for 216 satellite images and with 36 LANDSAT images, and the comparison was used to calibrate the snow and glacier related parameters and verify the model’s performances. The snow and ice melt progression was carried from April 1st to September 30th at daily scale for each of eight simulation years. Both the statistical evaluation and visual inspection were employed to develop comparison between model and MODIS/LANDSAT based snow cover extent.   2.6 Hydrological simulations In this study, the output of PDSLIM model, including snow melt on ice, runoff from ice melt, rainfall and evaporation on ice, melt from snow in ice free areas, net rainfall over terrain i.e., snow and ice-free areas, is used to compute glacier runoff, subsurface runoff, surface runoff. The total runoff in this study is the sum of flow resulting from routing glacier runoff, subsurface runoff, and surface runoff. The snow and ice-melt on the glacier is treated as a specific component separate from the off-glacier melt because the hydraulics of a glacier’s body (Röthlisberger H, Lang H., 1987) is very different from that of a surface runoff and subsurface flow in a soil interacting with vegetation, organic matter and the atmosphere. The main objective of this description was to conclude that the time response of glaciers is faster than that of ice-free areas and that it had to be treated as a separate component of the hydrological response. Surface runoff on a glacier runs fast in supraglacial channel and is trapped by moulins and crevasses, thus feeding subglacial channels with a flow that obeys more to Chezy-type laws (Röthlisberger and Lang, 1987; Walder, 1986 ) and is faster than a slower Darcian-type flow in soils. Water is stored in glaciers in large water pockets, sometimes generating sudden glacial outbursts, and in subglacial deposits with a faster time response. Evaporation from snow and ice is different from transpiration from soil and vegetation controlled by soil moisture and stomatal resistance. The time response of the two systems is different and therefore the model of the hydrological response of the glacier assumes a linear reservoir with its time constant, the simplest conceptual model using one parameter and considering storage, as it occurs in glaciers, as a key component. The off-glacier component, where the source of water is the sum of snowmelt and net rain, after subtracting evaporation, is partitioned, through a runoff coefficient into a surface rapid flow, with a linear reservoir time constant, and a subsurface slow flow, with the third linear reservoir response time scale. This linear method integrates the behaviour of the basin into three separate reservoirs and is similar to that of (Baker, 1982 ). The baseflow is the low flow regime from October to March of next year. The resulting Linear Reservoirs Model called LRM, based on the theory of linear reservoir system as shown in Fig. S1  is used to route the net precipitation and melt to simulate streamflow. For simplification, the linear reservoir equation is further divided into sub-components of streamflow discharge: glacier, surface and subsurface runoff. For glacier runoff discharge:(8) q g  t    =  q ice    t - Δ t      e - Δ t  k ice      +  p g  t     1 - e - Δ t  k ice              For surface runoff::(9) q s  t    =  q s   t - Δ t      e - Δ t  k s     +  p s  t     φ s  1 - e - Δ t  k s             For the subsurface runoff(10) q sub   t    =  q sub    t - Δ t      e - Δ t  k sub      +  p s  t     1 - φ s      1 - e - Δ t  k sub              Here: p g  t       is composed of snow melt on ice, runoff from ice melt, rainfall – evaporation on ice. The input to the off-glacier runoff component, p s  t    ,    is composed of melt from ice free areas and net rainfall over terrain or snow on ice-free areas. Glacier, surface and subsurface runoff, q(t)g , q(t)s , q(t)sub  , respectively, are computed at time t, with q t - Δ t        being he flow rate recorded at the previous time step; kice , ksurface , ksub  :  (h) are the time constant of reservoirs; φs ,  is the runoff coefficient, partitioning the melt and net rain into surface and subsurface runoff. The calibration parameters for the PDSLIM and LRM models are listed in Table.S6 . These parameters are optimised using statistical indices to compare simulated and observed runoff. The performance of simulated runoff was evaluated using a combination of several efficiency criteria, including Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), Percent bias (PBIAS), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Coefficient of Determination (R2 ), and Kling Gupta efficiency (KGE) since single criteria are not adequate to examine model performance. The runoff data for the years 2006, 2008, 2010 and 2016, marked as low, medium and high flows were used for calibration, while the remaining years 2009, 2011, 2012 and 2014 were used for validation. Model performance was evaluated using both efficiency criteria and visual inspection in relation to systematic (overestimation or underestimation) and dynamic (rising/falling limbs, timing) as well as baseflow behaviour.  2.7 Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis Data availability and quality are critical factors that determine the performance of any model. The sensitivity of model performance was tested for the change in temperature lapse rate, TLR 0.0065–0.0085 °C m−1  for clear sky and 0.0051–0.0045 °C m−1  for cloud cover conditions. The values depict a range of temperature lapse rate during clear sky and cloud conditions that we incorporated into the model to examine its impact on melt rate. In addition, observed weather stations are unable to estimate SWE, which is used in PDSLIM as a substitute for snow depth. To estimate the uncertainty of simulation results, we used both products in this study. Multiple statistical indicators were used for sensitivity analysis of model parameters in order to assess snow and ice dynamics and catchment runoff.  2.8 Visualizing water balance change in Non-Dimensional Space The use of dimensionless parameters can be useful in the study of water balance, particularly in complex catchments with limited data. One of the most prominent theories is that proposed by Turc (Turc, 1955 ) and (Budyko et al., 1974 ). The Turc-Budyko plot was used in this study as an effective way for analysing the observed precipitation data in order to reproduce an appropriate water-energy balance. In this method, the realistic closure of water-energy balance was examined using observed precipitation data. The seasonal runoff coefficient or water yield (Q/P ) was plotted as a function of seasonal long term aridity index (P/ETp  ) (Coron et al., 2015 ).(11) Q / P    =  f P / ET  p         Here, ETp , Q  and P  depict potential evapotranspiration, specific runoff and precipitation in the Naltar watershed, respectively. If a relationship for a specific year lies above the water limit i.e. (Q>P) limit, it is referred to as glacier dominating catchment/ “Gaining zone” (Andréassian and Perrin, 2012 ). The Gaining zone (Q>P) indicates that there are additional water resources that contribute to net streamflow for glacierized catchments. Glacier melt contributes to this additional water supply. Alternatively, a catchment is considered as rainfall dominating catchment when a relationship for a simulated year is located below the water limit and accumulated runoff is less than available energy, which means either precipitation is overestimated or some of the net runoff is not properly accounted for in the water balance. Water balance equation in a glacierized catchment can be written as follows:(12) Δ S  Δ t    = P -  〈 Q +  ET  a   〉  - M B       Here MB and ETa  depict snow and ice mass balance and evapotranspiration in the catchment. Δ S  Δ t      is change in water storage including glacier's mass balance. If Δ S = 0   , the catchment is marked as “True” catchment. Normally, it is observed that “Gaining”/glacier dominating catchment mostly have negative change in storage (ΔS<0) while “Leaky” rainfall dominant catchment has generally positive change in storage (ΔS>0).   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Snow cover simulation The ability of PDSLIM model to simulate snow cover dynamics was first assessed with an ‘internal verification’ of the model, based not just on the runoff output but, as in Blöschl et al. (1991) , also by comparing simulated Snow Cover Areas (SCA) with LANDSAT and MODIS (M*D10A1GL06) snow and ice cover maps from 1st April to 30th September for each simulated year. The spatial and temporal distribution of modelled SCA based on MODSCAG and SPRIES approaches is shown in Fig. 5  , FigS3 , Table. 1  . The PDSLIM-modelled snow cover areas results in good agreement with satellite products, with R2  = 0.96, NSE=0.95, and a negative average bias of just −1.8 % using SPIRES and R2  = 0.96, NSE=0.94, and positive average bias + 6.12 % using MODSACG. According to this analysis, both approaches are capable of reproducing snow and ice melt progression quite well. Furthermore, it was found that combined snow and ice cover dynamics exhibited a slight underestimation using MODSCAG and a slight overestimation using SPIRES, at the end of the melting season. Such underestimation/overestimation is possibly related to misclassification or the coarse resolution of MODIS pixels and low or high values of SWE products which ultimately are incorporated for the initialisation of the model. Hasson et al., (2014) reported that estimates of SCA in the Hunza Basin with 83 % ± 4 % during the winter/spring season and 17 % ± 6 % during the summer season in the Hunza Basin from 2001 to 2012. Shrestha and Nepal (2019)  presented estimates for SCA in the Hunza Basin, with a range of 30 % in summer and 87 % in winter from 2000 to 2010. Recently, Aftab et al., (2023) observed estimates for SCA in the Hunza Basin, with a range of 90 % ±5% during the accumulation period and 15 % ± 5 % by the end of the melting season from 2006 to 2010. The results of our study align with the previous findings. The slight variations in the results can be attributed to differences in model structures, the use of observed/gridded datasets (spatial and temporal resolution) and the scale of analysis, ranging from catchment to basin level. The mean maximum simulated snow cover area using MODSCAG and SPIRES was recorded as 92.4 % and 94.2 % of the basin area respectively which were closer to MODIS based snow cover 94.5 %. Similarly, the results of the minimum simulated snow cover areas at the end of the melting season using the two methods (MODSCAG and SPIRES) were determined to be 18.4 % and 23.2 % respectively, confirming that these results also corresponded to the minimal MODIS snow cover area of 19.8 % (48 km2 ). The snow melt generally reached its peak by the end of July except in high elevation zones where snow persists throughout the ablation period as shown in Fig. 6  . Afterwards, glacier melt begins, except in some high elevation zones where the temperature is low. Additionally, it has been observed that both simulated and MODIS-derived snow cover areas experienced a very abrupt snow accumulation in 2009 and 2010. Such changes are possibly due to the occurrence of precipitation as a snowfall event at high elevation zones where temperature is already below 0 °C as shown in Fig.S3 . It is also important to mention that we used a fixed number of classes from improved MODIS snow cover product (M*D10A1GL06) against model derived snow and ice cover areas developed by Muhammad and Thapa (2021)  since they cover a combination of snow-covered and ice-covered areas. Nevertheless, pixels within these classes showed significant changes in snow and ice cover simulations during the years of 2006, 2009 and 2011. It is likely that such a rise or drop in snow and ice cover area is caused by coarse resolution or misclassification of original MODIS SCA data. Additionally, the simulated results of SCA were also cross checked with those from high resolution LANDSAT SCA to ensure the model's reliability at a higher spatial and temporal scale. A 20 % cloud cover threshold was applied when selecting LANDSAT tiles for specific areas of interest. As shown in the supplementary material , the model represents satisfactory results for snow and ice melt dynamics at high spatial resolution throughout the entire melting season, except for a moderate underestimation for the 2016 year. This underestimation may be attributed to the presence of cloud covers in the Naltar catchment, which are clearly visible in the NIR bands as shown in Fig. S2 .  3.2 Hydrological simulations The primary source of flow in the Naltar catchment comes from snow and glacier melt, as the is located in a region influenced by westerlies. Simulated runoff computed by the LRM conceptual hydrological model was compared with observed runoff on a daily basis during the melt season. The autumn and winter period (October to March) was not simulated because of the low reliability of solid precipitation measurements in the cold season. From March to September, instead, the role of snow- and ice-melt and of the rainfall precipitation can be better simulated or monitored. Fig. 7   and Fig.S4  show the observed and simulated daily runoff relationship for both calibration and validation periods, along with a bar graph showing the amount of net precipitation. As it can be seen in Table.2  , the graphical and statistical comparison revealed that LRM model reasonably develop hydrological simulations with a mean R2  value of 0.92 and NSE of 0.90 for calibration and mean R2  value of 0.93 and NSE of 0.89 for the validation period based on outputs of PDSLIM as shown in Table.2 . It was concluded that simulated runoff is in agreement with observed runoff in both the calibration and validation periods based on the NSE, KGE, and R2  thresholds as suggested by Moriasi et al. (2007)  to ensure a reliable functioning of any hydrological model. In the calibration phase, the maximum flow during the ablation period was recorded as 18.0 mm d-1  observed vs. 14.6 mm d-1  simulated for a heavy rainfall event. Similarly, the mean maximum runoff in validation (10.13 mm d-1  simulated) was in good agreement with the observed 11.35 mm d-1 . Generally, simulated runoff exhibits two peak periods in a year; the first occurs in the spring due to snow melting and the second occurs in the summer due to glacier melt and monsoon rains. While rainfall contributes a smaller portion to net runoff, significant high flow peaks have been observed in some years (2010, 2014, 2016). The model is also able to capture reasonably well peak flow timing and intensity especially during the flood of 2010 in this region. In mid-April, the runoff curve began to rise and reached its apex in mid-July to early August while in mid-August until late September, runoff began to decline. A hydrological response of the Naltar catchment is primarily due to the runoff from snow-glacier melt followed by rainfall during the monsoon season. Baseflow was fairly simulated during both the calibration and validation phases. The simulated runoff limbs were generally in agreement with observed runoff with slight overestimations and underestimations. According to Tahir et al. (2011) , the peak flows for the Hunza basin were underestimated, and this was attributed to their precipitation input. Similarly, Dahri et al. (2021)  also found that it was difficult to accurately assess hydrologic processes in the high-altitude Indus Basin due to the scarcity of reliable input data. ERA5-land meteorological reanalysis data present biases compared to observations, particularly overestimation of wet days and precipitation amount in the HMA and needs bias adjustment before its usage in hydrological modeling studies (Ansari et al., 2022; Liaqat et al., 2022 ). Recently, Nazeer et al. (2023) found that the sharp flow peaks of monsoon season are not reproduced well using gridded data sets in the snow covered and glacierized Hunza Basin in the upper Indus while our results exhibited reliable performance to reproduce peak flows during summer season using observed data. A further example of the model's capability is evident in Fig. S4 , which illustrates the detection of the extreme flood event in August 2010. Similarly, the observed runoff could be affected by both random and systematic measurement errors. As an example, abnormal rises/drops in runoff limbs were observed in 2006 and 2011. Such abnormal behaviour in observed runoff series is probably due to water level measurement and its conversion using discharge rating curve. Although the calibration and validation period flow data are assumed to be accurate, given the measurement techniques and data quality employed by WAPDA, it is important to note that the flow data may still have uncertainties resulting from measurement errors. A study conducted by Nespak-Aht-Deltares (2015)  evaluated the river and canal flow measurement protocols of the Indus River System and observed overall uncertainties of 3–8 % at five canal headworks. Fig.S5  also illustrates the scatter plot relationship between daily simulated and observed runoff values, with a satisfactory performance. The total runoff in this study is the sum of glacier runoff, subsurface runoff, and surface runoff. Surface runoff is composed of rainfall on land, glacier runoff is composed of snowmelt, runoff and ice melt on ice, and sub-surface runoff is composed of the infiltration of snowmelt and net rainfall over ice free areas. The baseflow is the low flow regime from October to March of next year. As it is already mentioned the current study did not simulate winter flow as we considered that in winter meteorological data are not very reliable and the hydrology of the river basin is almost 'silent’. The values of baseflow were derived by taking observed runoff at the beginning of the melt period and its estimated recession coefficient to account for runoff rate and volumes resulting from previous rain and melt. Baseflow mainly derives from lakes within the study area, groundwater and snowmelt from lower elevation zones in the study region when temperatures rise and melt threshold. The results in Fig. 7  revealed that glacier and snow melt are in consistent agreement with the maximum flow peak of the runoff except for some abnormal underestimations noted for 2014 and 2016 as shown in Fig.S4 . There can be two possibilities for such abnormal behaviour: (1) precipitation occurs as snow during the summer season at high elevation zones or (2) uncertainties in observed datasets especially in temperature, rainfall and wind speed which have significant impact on melting from snow and ice. Another possible limitation for abnormal behaviour could be associated with using a fixed temperature lapse rate in this study. It would be better to use a varied temperature lapse rate in different elevation zones of a watershed which could further improve the model accuracy. The flow composition analysis shows that the largest contribution came from subsurface flow (42 %), followed by glacier runoff (40 %) and surface runoff (18 %). A comparison between year-to-year variations in the runoff components and their climatic variables (temperature and precipitation) are shown in Fig. 8  . A greater contribution of subsurface water can be attributed to the dominance of snowmelt in groundwater storage which is returned to surface flow via baseflow. The results of the current study about mixed snow-glacier melt composition are also in agreement with Lutz et al. (2016)  who also found similar mixed melt composition for Hunza basin in western Karakorum. The results of (Shrestha et al. 2015 ) are also consistent with the findings of the current study, which found that snow melt and glacier melt contribute significantly to the total Hunza river runoff (50 % and 33 %), followed by summer rainfall (17 %). Recently, Haq et al. (2023)  also found that glacier-snow melt derived runoff (85.46 %) and runoff due to rainfall was 14.4 % during 1995 to 2010 in the Hunza River Basin. Xiang et al. (2024)  showed that adopting different modelling approaches in four Himalayan catchments the estimated glacial runoff may vary a lot in the 3 % to 29 % range. And snowmelt runoff in the 5 % to 17 % range. The findings from all the studies, including our own, suggest that the individual impact of snow and glacier melt may vary, but there is a general consensus on their combined effect. Specifically, snow and glacier melt collectively account for 82–86 % of the net runoff, while rainfall accounts for 14–18 %. Fig. 9   (a) and (b) illustrate the average monthly observed and simulated runoff values and a scatter plot of the daily observed and simulated runoff values. In light of the graphical and statistical evaluation, it can be concluded that the PDSLIM model reproduces fairly adequately the hydrological dynamics. In summary, snow-glacier melt and glacier melt dominate the seasonal summer hydrological cycle of the Naltar catchment, with a small contribution from monsoon rainfall. According to Table 3  , individual runoff components contributed in a different way to net runoff on a monthly basis. The subsurface contribution to all simulated years was higher until mid-July and the snow-glacier contribution was higher from mid-July to the end of September. It was also observed that the time response of the catchment is quite slow, as the values of the time parameters in Table S6  are high, for a midsize catchment as the Naltar, with the subsurface flow being more than twice slower than the glacier’s response. The lack of long-term, consistent hydro-meteorological observed data remains a challenge in providing an accurate explanation of the evidence of hydrological response in the region. Other uncertainties rise for the discrimination of surface, subsurface and glacier runoff. The parameters representing the average response time of the respective storages indicate a long residence time. The use of isotope tracers (Kendall and McDonnell 1998 ) to discriminate between surface and subsurface streamflow components, as in Penna et al. (2016) , in snowmelt-fed catchments could provide experimental evidence for a more physically based calibration and process understanding. The results in Table S8  indicate that the net simulated runoff volume computed by PDSLIM was in reasonable agreement with observations, being only 1 % higher than the mean observed runoff volume with NSE, R2 , MAPE of 0.66, 0.72, 4.95 %, respectively. In their study Jain and Sharma (2014) , suggested that the performance of a model is considered “satisfactory” when the percentage error falls within 15–23 %. Hence, these results motivate the future usage of PDSLIM in the Hindukush, Karakoram and Himalayas (HKH) mountain ranges and recommend that additional good results can be achieved if it is executed with better quality input data.  3.3 Water balance Water balance in a glacierized catchment can be represented by the contributions to streamflow, Q, from various sources such as precipitation (P), baseflow from deep aquifers, snowmelt and glacier melt (GM). The base flow refers to the low flow period that generally comes from October/November to March of the following year. This flow is mainly derived from local lakes, ground water, and snowmelt at lower elevations during winter, when temperatures rise above the melting point. At the same time, the amount of water available for streamflow is reduced by losses due to evapotranspiration (ET), depletion in the snowpack (SWE), glacier ice (WGlacier ), surface (Wsurf ), and subsurface (Wsubsurf ) reservoirs.(13) Q   =  P   -  ET   +  GM   + SWE o  -  SWE  end      + W surf . 0   -  W  surf . end       + W subsurf . 0   -  W  subsurf . end       + W Glacier . 0   -  W  Glacier . end       +  Baseflow      Where, P is precipitation, GM is contribution from glacier’s melt, ET is evapotranspiration, (Wsurf.0 - Wsurf.end ) represent change in surface storage change, (Wsubsurf.0  – Wsub-surf.end ) shows change in subsurface storage and (WGlacier.o  – WGlacier.end ) depicts glacier storage change. Table.4   presents a quantification of each component of water balance during the summer season over eight years in Naltar catchment. The results indicated that snow precipitation plays a more significant role in the Naltar catchment compared to rainfall. Our simulations also show mean seasonal summer evapotranspiration of 611 mm.  3.4 Water balance analysis using Truc-Budyko The water balance analysis in each simulated melt season (AMJJAS) was tested and plotted on the Truc-Budyko plot as shown in Fig. 10  . The runoff coefficient (Q/P) and aridity index (P/ETp) were computed and plotted on the y-axis and x-axis, respectively. It is shown that almost all points were above the water limit (Q/P=1). These points marked the Naltar as a “gaining” catchment. In gaining catchments, precipitation is not sufficient to complete the water balance cycle additional water is required to close the water balance. This additional water is fed by snow and glacier melting. Such phenomena result in negative glacier storage change (ΔS<0), as shown in Table.5  . The results indicate that all simulated years had negative glacier storage, indicating that glacier melt was a significant contributor to net runoff. The storage change varies from 314 mm w.e. a-1  to −1354 mm w.e. a-1  for all simulated years with mean value −811 mm w.e. a-1 .  3.5 Net glacier mass balance simulations There are four primary components of net glacier mass balance (NGMB): precipitation, SWE, ice melt, and evaporation. It is difficult to simulate the glacier mass balance, particularly for large river basins. It is therefore convenient and informative to examine the NGMB and physical aspects of the cryosphere at a smaller scale. In Table.5 , results of the average mass balance of all glaciers residing within the Naltar catchment over the eight simulated years are presented. For each simulated year the NGMB was computed from 1st April to 30th September and was estimated in the range −334 mm w.e. a-1  to −1354 mm w.e. a-1  and −600 mm w.e. a-1  to −837 mm w.e. a-1  during the calibration and validation phase. Overall, the Naltar catchment exhibited a negative mass balance of −811  mm w.e. a-1 . The findings show that the ‘Karakoram anomaly’ has less impact in Central Karakoram. This study confirms the findings of some previous works based on remote sensing and geodetic mass balance that indicate glacier mass balance in the Karakoram region being relatively stable or slightly decreasing (Kääb et al., 2012; Berthier and Brun, 2019; Muhammad et al., 2019 ). Similarly, Shrestha et al. (2015)  investigated the mass balance in different glaciers in the Hunza basin. They also found that glaciers near the Naltar catchment such as Mianpin, Batura, and Pasu also experienced negative or slightly positive mass balance. The study provides a foundation for evaluating the influence of climate change on the hydrology and glaciology of the Naltar catchment and the central Karakoram in the future.  3.6 Sensitivity analysis to the lapse rate and initial SWE The PDSLIM model appears to be well calibrated and validated, as described in the previous sections; however, there is a need to investigate the potential uncertainty associated with the input (SWE) and some parameters such as the temperature lapse rate. It was observed that both low (MODSCAG) and high (SPIRES) derived SWE values have a substantial impact on snow and ice melt and consequently on the mass balance, as shown in Fig. 5  and FigS3 , Table.1  (a, b) and Table S7 (a, b). In the first scenario, with the standard temperature lapse rate (−0.0065 °C m−1 ) marked as TLR and the use of low MODSCAG-based SWE values, early melt of snow leads to early exposure of glaciers. Consequently, glacier melt increased causing average net mass balance loss (−2114 mm yr−1 , NSE 0.94, MaxE=14.03 km2 , RMSE=13.60 km2 ) while SPIRES-based SWE with TLR (−0.0065 °C m−1 ), ultimately reduced the negative mass balance (−811 mm yr−1 , NSE=0.95, MaxE=14.31 km2 , RMSE=12.8 km2 ). In the second scenario, by decreasing temperature lapse rate (−0.0085 °C m−1 ) marked as TLR1 using MODSCAG, and SPIRES shows the opposite situation as expected with less NMB (−1792 mm yr−1  and −443 mm yr−1 ). Although NMB decreases when lapse rate is changed, it also decreases model efficiency and underestimates runoff, particularly for SPIRES TLR1. As a result of these analyses, both SWE and TLR changes have a significant impact on the net mass balance simulations and snowmelt. Table.S9  provides the overall picture of net mass balance by incorporating two scenarios. Based on sensitivity analysis, it is evident that improving one efficiency criterion may negatively impact the performance of the other criterion, as was observed by SPIRES TLR1 where only NMB loss has been observed (−443 mm yr -1 ) however, model efficiency may be compromised when it comes to snow and ice melt. Therefore, it is recommended to use the SPIRES_TLR combination followed by MODSCAG_TLR1 for simulating future glacio-hydrological and mass balance studies in this region.   4 Conclusion and recommendations In this study, the distributed energy balance PDSLIM model was applied to assess the hydro-glaciological behaviour of the Naltar catchment located in the Hunza basin (Pakistan), where snow and glacier melt runoff contributes to runoff in significant amounts. Based on the results of this study, the following conclusions can be drawn. The snow and ice cover simulation indicates that the model simulates the spatial and temporal distribution of snow cover areas against MODIS and LANDSAT SCA with mean negative bias –1.8 %, NSE=0.95, RMSE=12.8 km2  and R2  = 0.96. Some overestimation and underestimation were observed during the spatial and temporal analysis of SCA in the comparison with satellite data. The bias may be the result of misclassification or the coarse resolution of MODIS pixels or uncertainty in the observed data. Based on the streamflow dynamics, the LRM hydrological model, which is used to convert melt and net precipitation into runoff, is capable of developing a reliable relationship between model and observed runoff, with KGE, NSE, and RMSE equal to 0.89, 0.90, 0.78 mm/day, respectively. Both low and high simulated flow limbs were reasonably in agreement with observed runoff. Based on the findings, subsurface runoff contributed 42 %, glacier melt runoff contributed 40 %, and rainfall-induced surface runoff contributed 18 % to net runoff. In the Naltar catchment, the net glacier mass balance displayed a negative balance of –0.810 ± 0.31 m w.e. a-1 . In a similar manner, Truc-Budkyo theory identifies the Naltar catchment as a “gaining” catchment, indicating additional water from glacier melt is required to close the water balance in the April to September period. In summary, results of this study suggest that the PDSLIM model can be applied to study the glacio-hydrological process in high altitude Hindukush, Karakoram and Himalayas (HKH) to compute snow and ice melt dynamics, streamflow, water balance, and glacier mass balance. Moreover, it is important to note that the performance of this energy balance can be improved if higher quality observed data at higher altitude are included for optimization and simulations. A careful selection of weather stations which depict accurate trends of weather in the study area plays a crucial role in model accuracy. Based on the existence of uncertainties, gaps, and outliers, the study strongly indicates the need of performing quality control checks on observed hourly data obtained from meteorological stations. In particular the existing stations are unable to monitor snow water equivalent properly. In addition, the study recommends setting up new or modifying existing hydrometeorological stations that are equipped with snow depth sensors and solid precipitation gauges to better monitor accumulation zones in glacierized catchments. The study also encourages monitoring the expansion and contraction of ice volumes and the extent of permafrost. Although high resolution satellite data become available on a daily basis, the need for ground-based values cannot be substituted. The so-called “Karakoram anomaly” could exist in some areas of the region but, based on our findings, we raise some doubts it holds also for the Naltar glacierized catchment in the central Karakoram. However, because of the modelling and monitoring uncertainties still remaining, long term monitoring, especially at higher altitudes, should develop to ensure that hydrologists and other stakeholder agencies have adequate information to implement existing or new water management plans with a sound scientific basis.  5 Author's contribution L, M.U., R.R., formal analysis, methodology, investigations, and validation.
