1 Introduction Network models are commonly used to evaluate and analyze quasi-static (Blunt, 2001 ) and dynamic (Joekar-Niasar and Hassanizadeh, 2012 ), single and multiphase flow through porous media. These models are used to predict the flow and transport through the media or to upscale pore-scale features to the Darcy scale hydraulic properties, such as retention and permeability. Conceptualization of the media as a pore network (rather than a bundle of capillaries) goes back to the work of Fatt (1956) , where at its simplest form, it conceptualizes the media as a lattice of conductors, disregarding the pore shape. Another conceptualization involves an interconnected pore network with assumed circular pores (Koplik, 1982 ). A more complex (and realistic) modeled pore network is comprised of both bonds (relating to the pore throats) that represent most of the resistance and sites (relating to the pore bodies) that represent most of the capacitance (Blunt, 2017 ). In this context, many pore network models use a dual probability density function for the pore bodies’ and throats’ size distributions (Dullien, 1975 ). More detailed pore network models, accounting better for pores shapes and connections, such as equilateral triangles, squares, or stars (Hoogland et al., 2016; Mason and Morrow, 1991 ), do not capture the full complexity of the actual pores but represent a compromise between the over-simplicity of a cylindrical capillary tube network and the directly-imaged pore shape models (Ben-Noah et al., 2023a ). In this study, we aim to evaluate the trade-off between model simplicity in terms of the required detailed information about the pore space and the accuracy of the models’ evaluations of different flow statistics. Reduction in the water saturation decreases the volume fraction in which the flow can take place and the mean and size distribution of water-filled pores. The pore system connectivity is also reduced, which increases the structural tortuosity of the medium. In turn, the reduction of the saturation degree reduces the media’s permeability (sometimes referred to as the effective permeability) and affects the flow velocity distribution. The velocity distribution broadens because of the formation of dead-end regions with slow velocities. These broad velocity distributions give rise to dispersive and non-Fickian solute transport (Van Genuchten and Cleary, 1979; Ben-Noah et al., 2023b; Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2017 ). The pore structure also affects the velocity distribution (de Anna et al., 2017; Koplik, 1982 ). The impact stems from the effect of the pore system geometry with wide pore bodies (low velocity) and narrow throats (high velocity) and the Newtonian fluid’s viscosity with lower velocities near the grains surfaces and higher velocities in the pore throats centers. In this context, the capability of pore-networks conceptualization to evaluate the complex velocity fields needs to be investigated. Moreover, the importance of the different phenomena for different saturation degrees is unknown. Here, we use different network models based on different levels of information about the pore space and assumptions about the pore geometry to evaluate the importance of the different physical phenomena. We first describe the experimental results of steady flow through variably-saturated milifluidic devices, the image analysis method used for pore segmentation and pore space characterization, and the numerical simulation of the flow on the exact pore space geometry. Second, we describe the different network models evaluated in this work (i.e., regular lattice, diluted lattice, random lattice, and detailed network representation of the pore system) and the different pore geometries under consideration (i.e., strip and parabolic). Lastly, we present the ability of the different models to evaluate the media’s permeability, the spatial distribution of pressures and flow rates, the hydraulic tortuosity of the media, and the complex velocity distribution. The flow characteristics are compared to the values obtained by the numerical simulations.  2 Porous media and pore-scale flow In this section, we describe the porous media and pore-scale flow characteristics used in this work and to test the performance of the different network models given in Section 3 . 2.1 Pore space characterization Porous media geometry is obtained from the binary images, i.e., the representation of the pores and the matrix as zeros and ones, of a milifluidic device at different saturation degrees (Fig. 1 ) from the experimental work of Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2017) . The experiments established a steady flow of a water and glycerol mixture in variably saturated (i.e., containing also a stagnant air phase) hydrophilic millifluidic device. The air buddies in the device are trapped, and their pressure is not necessarily atmospheric. Four effective saturation degrees of S  e   = 1 . 00   , 0.80, 0.73, and 0.65 (Fig. 1 a,b,c, and d in accordance) are considered, where S  e     is defined as the fraction of the porosity (ϕ  ) filled with the continuous and percolated liquid phase. Flow was controlled so that the phase distributions were not altered during the flow experiments, that is, steady-state imbibing conditions were attained. The flow rates, corresponding to a capillary number of about 3 ⋅ 1 0  − 5     , are considered capillary-dominated.   2.1.1 Image analysis and pore space partitioning Using images of a two-dimensional flow device allows us to evaluate the topological features of the media that are usually unattainable, especially in partially saturated media. The image analysis used in this work follows the methodology presented in Ben-Noah et al. (2024a) . In a nutshell, a “λ  -based” medial axis method is used to segment the pore space into distinct pores. This method uses the binary images of the pore space (Fig. 1 ) to form the distance map, i.e., the Euclidean distance of each point from the closest phases’ interface (Fig. 2 a). In the distance map, positive and negative values are assigned for the pore space and stagnant phase in accordance. Then, the distance map curvatures and the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix of the distance map are calculated at each point (Fig. 2 b). A new binary image is then derived from the small eigenvalue (λ  1    ) map, which hold information about the “valleys”, in which negative values are assigned with 1 (i.e., the blue colored areas in Fig. 2 b) and the rest with 0. The union of the lines formed by the skeletonization of the new binary image and the pore space in the original binary image (i.e., excluding the solid phase) gives a binary image of the throats (Fig. 2 c). Thus, the difference between the original binary image and the throats image gives a new binary image of the segmented pores (Fig. 2 d). The pore bodies’ sizes, in terms of the maximal disk that can fit within the pore, are given by the maximal value of the original distance map in each pore (blue circles in Fig. 2 d), i.e., not accounting for the throats for the confinement of the sphere. Similarly, the throats’ sizes are the maximal values of the distance map on each distinct throat line, i.e., disregarding the tortuosity of the throat line. The eigenvalue (λ  1    ) map is processed using a Gaussian filter as discussed in the appendix of Ben-Noah et al. (2024a) . For the saturated case, a single-layer filter with a standard deviation (σ = 5   ) is used. Conversely, a Gaussian pyramid filter is used for the partially saturated cases with a base level standard deviation (σ  0   = 0 . 25   ), standard deviation increments of (Δ σ = 0 . 005   ), and a scale space factor of (γ = 0 . 75   ).  2.1.2 Saturation degree and pore space topology The effect of the saturation degree on the flowing-phase-filled pore size distributions and connectivity was discussed in Ben-Noah et al. (2024a) , and the effect of S  e     on the velocity distribution in Ben-Noah et al. (2023b) , for reader’s convenience, we summarize it here. The reduction in S  e     reduces the mean water-filled pore size distribution because capillary forces preferentially drive air to invade large pores. Moreover, air, being the non-wetting phase, invades water-filled pores through their center. Thus breaking up large pores into small water films surrounding the grains. The latter mechanism forms a dual pore-size distribution (Fig. 3 a,b). The throats’ size distributions (Fig. 3 b) of this granular media are of the same order of magnitude as the pore bodies, slightly decreasing with the reduction in S  e    . The coordination number (Z, Fig. 3 c) is the number of interconnected pores. The reduction in the saturation degree increases the number of dead-end pores (Z =   1) and of pores connected in series (Z = 2   ). In turn, the mean coordination number (〈 Z 〉   ) reduces with the reduction in S  e    , with a maximal value of 3.14 and minimal 2.97 for the saturated (S  e   = 1   ) and S  e   = 0 . 65    cases in accordance.      2.2 Direct numerical simulations of pore-scale flow The flow field is characterized in terms of its velocity distribution, stagnant region volume, permeability, and hydraulic tortuosity. The two-dimensional water flow field for each analyzed image is determined by solving the steady-state Stokes equation assuming an incompressible single phase laminar flow (1) μ ∇  2   u − 12 μ u / b  2   = ∇ p     ∇ ⋅ u = 0 ,     where u   [L/T] is the flow velocity, μ   [ML−1 T−1 ] the fluid’s dynamic viscosity and b   [L] the device height. The term − 12 μ u / b  2      in (1)  accounts for the viscous forces induced by the millifluidic device’s top and bottom plates (Homsy, 1987 ). 2.2.1 Numerical setup We use the COMSOL (COMSOL®, 2018 ) multiphysics platform for the numerical simulation. A unit pressure gradient was imposed between the left (inlet) and right (outlet) boundaries, i.e., p ( 0 , y , t )  = ρ g  c   L    and p ( L , y , t )  = 0   , with ρ   [ML−3 ] the fluid density, g  c     [LT−2 ] the gravitational constant, and L [L] the device length. The linearity of the flow Eq. (1)  implies that both pressure and velocity (normalized by their mean values) are independent of the fluid properties (i.e., density and viscosity). A no-slip boundary condition was set at the phases’ interfaces. Using the no-slip assumption on the liquid-gas interface during the liquid (wetting), phase flow was evaluated and justified in Ben-Noah et al. (2023b) .  2.2.2 Flow statistics Permeability. The media permeability, hydraulic tortuosity, and velocity distribution of the different saturation degrees of the numerical simulation are considered the “ground truth” and the basis for estimating the applicability of the different network models.     3 Pore network models We present here pore network models of different complexities to represent the porous media discussed in the previous section. We first summarize the basic methodology for solving flow on networks. Then, we discuss two representations of the pore geometry and the corresponding pore-scale flow distribution and target flow statistics. With these preparations, we define the network models used to represent the flow properties in the model porous media presented in the previous section. Pore network models represent a porous medium as a network of sites and bonds, which connect them. Sites are typically located at the centers of pore bodies, the bonds align with the pore throats. Both are identified during the pore-space partitioning process. These basic network features can be supplemented with information on the pore shape, diameter, and other relevant geometric and hydraulic characteristics. In the following, we use the terminology “sites” and “bonds” when we refer to the network model and “body” and “throat” when we refer to the actual porous medium. 3.1 Flow on networks The flow rate Q  i j     along the bond connecting the sites i   and j   is given by Hagen–Poiseuille law (Poiseuille, 1839 ) (5) Q  i j   = − g  i j   ( P  j   − P  i   )  ,     where P  i     and P  j     are the pressures at sites i   and j  . The bond conductance is g  i j   = κ  i j   / ℓ  i j      [M−1 L 4    T] with ℓ  i j     [L] the bond length and κ  i j     [M−1 L 3    T] the bond conductivity. The bond conductivity (κ  ) depends on the pore geometry as discussed in detail in Section 3.2 . Note that Q  i j   = − Q  j i     . If Q  i j   > 0   , flow is directed from node i   to j   and vice versa. Volume conservation requires that the sum of the flow rates in the bonds meeting at a site j   is zero, (6) ∑  [ j i ]    Q  i j   = 0 ,     where the notation ∑  [ j i ]      denotes summation over the sites j   that are connected to site i  . The coordination number of site i  , that is, the number of sites j   connected to site i   is Z  i   = ∑  [ j i ]      . The flow rate Q  i     at an internal site i   of the network is evaluated from the sum of the flow rates Q  i j     through the bonds that are connected to the site i   as (7) Q  i   = 1  2   ∑  [ j i ]    | Q  i j   |  .     In words, Q  i     equals half the sum of the absolute values in the rows of the flow rate matrix Q  . Combining Eqs. (5) and (6)  gives the following system of equations at all internal sites of the network, (8) L ⋅ P = 0 ,     where P   is the vector of pressures at all sites of the network, L = D − G    is the weighted Laplacian matrix. It is given by the difference of the degree matrix D   and the conductance matrix G  . The degree matrix is a diagonal matrix that contains the degrees of each node, that is D  i k   = δ  i k   ∑  [ j i ]    g  i j     . The weight matrix contains the conductances between connected sites G  i j   = g  i j      and 0   else. The pressure boundary conditions used here are implemented by defining L  ′     such that L  i j  ′   = L  i j      for all sites i   that are not, and L  i j  ′   = δ  i j      for all sites i   that are in the inlet or outlet boundaries such that (9) L  ′   ⋅ P = b ,     where the vector b   on the right side of Eq. (9)  contains the boundary conditions. We assign the pressure b  j   = p  0   = ρ g  c   L    at the sites j   at the inlet boundary and b  j   = 0    else.  3.2 Pore geometries and conductivities Pore network models can also include representations of the geometry of the phase-filled pore space (Koplik, 1982; Gostick et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2024 ), in which the bodies represent most of the phase capacitance and throats most of the resistance to the flow (Blunt, 2017 ). 3.2.1 Rectangular pore shape The rectangular (“strip-work”) pore shape is characterized by the pore channel height b   and width w  . Recall that from the pore-space partitioning, we know the sizes of the pore bodies and pore throats and their distributions (see Fig. 3 ). Since most of the resistance to the flow is in the throats, we set w = 2 r  t      (black line in Fig. 4 b). For a rectangular channel, the conductivity is given by Boussinesq (1868) (10) κ = b  3   w  12 μ   − 16 b  4    μ   ∑  n = 1  ∞   cosh ( 2 β  n   w  b   )  − 1  β  n  5   sinh ( 2 β  n   w  b   )    ,  β  n   = ( 2 n − 1 )  π ,     The distribution of bond conductivities is then given by (11) p  κ   ( k )  = ∫  0  ∞   d r f  t   ( r )  δ [ k − κ ( r )  ]  .      Note that the pore throat, in principle, has zero length as it marks the boundary between two pores. Thus, assigning a finite length to the bond underestimates the conductance of the pore. The velocity profile in a rectangular pore is approximated by the Hagen–Poiseuille equation (12) u ( y )  = 3 Q  2 b w   1 − y  2    w  2       ,     where the pore flow rate is Q = κ | Δ P |  / ℓ   , where Δ P    is the pressure drop along the length ℓ   of the pore.  3.2.2 Parabolic pore shape The second geometry under consideration assumes a parabolic shape of the pore (red line in Fig. 4 b). This parametrization of the aperture is agile enough to give a good approximation to the actual aperture, for example, given by the minimal distance from the pore-media interface of the medial axis (blue line in Fig. 4 a and b). where the aperture (w  ) of a pore changes from approximately the pore throat diameter (2 r  t     ) at one end (x = 0   ) to the pore body diameter (2 r  b     ) at its other end (x = l   ), where x   is the axis of the main flow direction taken to be perpendicular to the pore throat facing away from the pore center. Moreover, the parabola has a minimal value at the pore throat, which means that the derivative of w ( x )     at the throat location x = l    is zero. Then, the pore aperture is given by (13) w ( x )  = 2 r  t   + 2 ( r  b   − r  t   )  x  2    l  2           For laminar flow, the effective pore conductance κ  e     is evaluated by the harmonic sum of the local conductivities along the pore channel with variable width w ( x )     by using Eq. (10)  for κ ( x )    (14) 1  κ  e     = 1  ℓ   ∫  0  ℓ   d x  κ ( x )    .     Note that κ  e   = κ  e   ( r  b   , r  t   )     is a function of the body and throat radii because κ ( x )     depends on w ( x )    . Assuming that r  t     and r  b     are independent variables, that is, disregarding the correlation between the bodies and the throats and also disregarding the correlation between r  b     and the coordination number (Z  ), the distribution of conductivity can be determined as (15) p  κ   ( k )  = ∫  0  ∞   d r ∫  0  r   d r  ′   f  b   ( r )  f  t   ( r  ′   )  δ [ k − κ  e   ( r , r  ′   )  ]  .     Note that we use the condition that r  t   < r  b     . This condition causes a bias towards smaller throats and larger bodies. The magnitude of this bias depends on the overlap of the pore body and throat size distributions (Fig. 3 ). For a small overlap, the bias is small. On the other hand, a significant overlap means that the pore bodies and throats are of the same size. In this case, the pore geometry is essentially rectangular. In the model media, the rectangular pore geometry (Fig. 4 c) has many more small conductors for the unsaturated cases than the parabolic geometry (Fig. 4 d). The saturated cases (blue lines) are very similar in both magnitude and distribution because the differences between f ( r  b   )     and f ( r  t   )     are not very large (Fig. 3 ). For a more detailed representation, the pore space is reconstructed by joining semi-parabolas at the pore throat such that they have the same r  t    , but in general, different r  b    , see Fig. 5 . The pore geometry also affects the intra-pore velocity distribution with higher velocity in the narrow section of the pore throat due to volume conservation. That is, the mean cross-sectional velocity is inversely proportional to the w ( x )    . The no-slip condition at the pore-grain boundary gives a parabolic velocity profile for laminar flow conditions. Here, for simplicity, we approximate the velocity profile across the pore by the Hagen–Poiseuille equation (16) u ( x , y )  = 3 Q  2 b w ( x )    1 − y  2    w ( x )   2       ,     where Q = κ  e   | Δ p |  / ℓ    is the pore flow rate. Note that we set the average cross-sectional velocity to u  x    ¯  = Q  b   / b w ( x )    . The maximum flow velocity is u  m   = 3 u  x    ¯  / 2    at the center of the conduit. The resulting velocity distribution is illustrated in Fig. 5 .     3.3 Flow statistics Permeability. The permeability k   of the network is determined from the flow rates at the inlet sites, which are given by Q  j   = ∑  [ j i ]    Q  j i     , where j   is a site at the inlet boundary. The flux q  m     is then given by q  m   = ∑  j   Q  j   / ( W b )    . From q  m     we obtain the network permeability according to the expression in Eq. (2) .  Distribution of flow speeds. The distribution of flow speeds in a single bond is denoted by p  i j   ( u )    . For the parabolic profile (12)  it is given by (17) p  i j   ( u )  = b w  i j    3 Q  i j   1 − 2 u b w  i j   / Q  i j           for 0 < u < 3 Q  i j   / 2 b w   . For the velocity profile (16)  it is accordingly given by (18) p  i j   ( u )  = 1  ℓ  i j     ∫  0  ℓ  i j     d x b w  i j   ( x )   3 Q  i j   1 − 2 u b w  i j   ( x )  / 3 Q  i j       .     The speed distribution across the network is then obtained by the weighted sum of the p  i j    , that is, (19) f  u   ( u )  = ∑  i > j   p  i j   ( u )  A  i j    ∑  i > j   A  i j     .       Distribution of flow rates. The distribution of flow rates Q  i j     is determined in analogy to the distribution of flow speeds as (20) f  Q   ( Q  k   )  = ∑  i > j   I ( Q  i j   , Q  k   )   Δ Q  k     .       Hydraulic tortuosity. We suggest to estimate the hydraulic tortuosity of the network as the ratio between the average flow rate magnitude and the average flow rate in the network, that is, (21) τ = ∑  i > j   | Q  i j   |   ∑  i > j   Q  i j   cos ( α  i j   )    ,     where α  i j     is the bond angle with the x  -axis. We can define an average bond velocity as (22) v  i j   = Q  i j    A  i j     ,     where A  i j     is the average surface area of the bond cross-section. If we assume that the bond lengths are not very variable and can be replaced by the network average, ℓ  i j   = 〈 ℓ 〉    , definition (21)  becomes (23) τ = ∑  i > j   | v  i j   |  V  i j    ∑  i > j   v  i j   cos ( α  i j   )  V  i j     = 〈 v 〉   〈 v  x   〉    = χ ,     where we set the bond volume V  i j   = A  i j   〈 ℓ 〉    .   3.4 Network models 3.4.1 Regular networks  A regular network (Fig. 6 ) refers to a lattice with a constant coordination number (Z  ). Regular networks are the most basic networks under consideration in this study. They require only a pore size distribution as input parameters and an estimate of the mean coordination number to decide the lattice geometry. The coordination number is considered the single most important topological feature of the medium (Hunt and Sahimi, 2017 ). It has been shown that regular networks and topologically disordered networks variable Z   have similar transport properties if they share the same mean coordination number 〈 Z 〉    (Sahimi et al., 1990 ). The mean coordination number of the study media presented in Section 2.1  is close to 〈 Z 〉  = 3    for all cases, see Fig. 3 c. Therefore, a regular hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice with Z = 3    and a constant bond length ℓ   is used. Moreover, for each saturation degree, the number of sites of the corresponding honeycomb network model is equal to the number of pores obtained from the pore space segmentation in Section 2.1.1 , while the physical dimensions of the network are kept constant. This implies that the bond lengths of the different network models are slightly different. The longest diagonal of the network is aligned with the main flow direction. The bond conductances are assigned randomly from the distribution f ( g )     (Fig. 4 ). As discussed in Section 3.2 , we consider both rectangular and parabolic pore geometries. This process disregards any spatial correlation in the pore size distribution, which is in line with the pore structure of the porous media considered in this study. For correlated networks, we refer readers to Sahimi (1998) .  3.4.2 Diluted regular networks  The diluted regular networks comprise a more detailed variation of the regular networks (Fig. 7 ). In these networks, a regular lattice with Z  l a t t i c e   > 〈 Z 〉     is imposed. Then bonds are eliminated until the mean coordination number of the diluted network is equal to the mean coordination number of the porous medium, 〈 Z  d i l u t e d   〉  = 〈 Z 〉    . That is, the coordination number is variable but does not necessarily follow the distribution of coordination numbers in the porous medium. As for the regular networks, the bond conductances are assigned randomly from the distribution f ( g )     (Fig. 4 ) for both rectangular and parabolic pore geometries. For each medium, the mean coordination number can be evaluated from the number of bonds (N  b    ) and sites (N  s    ) through the relation 〈 Z 〉  = 2 N  b   / N  s     . The regular and diluted models (square and hexagonal) has the same number of bonds (N  b    ) equal to the number of pore throats taken from the image analysis. Since we keep the original device dimension, this means that the bond lengths are slightly different (l  s q   > l  h e x     ). For the diluted regular networks, we use a regular square lattice (Z  g r i d   = 4   ) for all cases (S  e    ) and a hexagonal lattice (Z  g r i d   = 3   ) only for the lowest saturation degree (S  e   = 0 . 65    for which the mean coordination number is 〈 Z  m e d i a   〉  = 2 . 97   ). Comparing this case with different lattices allows us to separately evaluate the role of the lattice dimensionality and dilution. We start with a fully saturated grid, i.e., with a number of bonds equal to the number of throats obtained from the pore segmentation using the image analysis. Then, the conductors are randomly assigned from the distribution f ( g )    . As in the regular network model, we compare the strip and parabolic pore geometries (described in Section 3.2 ) by accounting for the different conductances support (g  ) and distribution (f ( g )    ). Then, the grid is diluted to obtain the 〈 Z 〉    of each case (of different S  e    ), and in consequence, N  s     equals the number of pores in the device. The dilution method applied here follows a simplification to the protocol described by Raoof and Hassanizadeh (2010) . Each bond is randomly assigned with a dilution (or elimination) number. Then, an elimination threshold value is used so that all bonds with an elimination number larger than the threshold are assigned zero conductivity. The elimination threshold is related to the mean coordination number through (24) f  e t   = 〈 Z  media   〉  / Z  grid   ,     where Z  grid     is the coordination number of the regular lattice before dilution. The conductance distribution is adjusted to account for the dilution, i.e., adding g = 0    with a dilution probability of p ( g = 0 )  = 1 − N  b   / N  s     . The random elimination of bonds by assigning zero conductance can create singular points or regions, that is, subregions of the network that are not connected to the inlet and outlet. Such regions are artifacts of the network generation procedure and do not reflect the real medium structure. From a numerical point of view, disconnected regions may cause numerical problems since they lead to a singular or ill-conditioned Laplacian matrix. The challenge of addressing this singularity issue was raised in several diluted network models (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2010 ). Usually, this issue is solved by preconditioning the matrix or by using a search algorithm to find and remove all ill-connected sites and clusters. In this contribution, we use the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) method as an efficient way to eliminate the singular points of the matrix (Ben-Noah et al., 2024b ). Regarding the flow behavior, diluted regular networks may display more stagnant regions than regular networks, that is, sites of very low or zero velocity due to the occurrence, for example, of dead-end pores. For regular and diluted networks, k   can be evaluated using the Effective Medium Approximation (EMA).   3.5 Effective medium approximation (EMA) The effective medium approximation (EMA) states that the network of variable conductors can be represented by a regular uniform network with an effective conductance g  e    . The EMA automatically obeys the smooth field approximation (Burganos and Sotirchos, 1987 ), i.e., the macroscopic pressure field is a smooth function of position in the porous medium (Sahimi et al., 1990 ), or in other words, the pressure gradient at each pore is the projection of the macroscopic pressure gradient in the direction of the pore axis (Friedman et al., 1995 ). The effective conductivity g  e     is calculated from the conductance distribution f  g   ( g )     by requiring that the average of the flow perturbation caused by the EMA is zeroed (Kirkpatrick, 1973 ) (25) ∫ g − g  e    g + ( Z  2   − 1 )  g  e     f ( g )  d g = 0     Then the EMA permeability of the media (k  E M A     [m 2    ]) can be evaluated from g  e    (26) k  E M A   = μ N  W    b W   g  e       where N  W     is the number of junctions on the lattice cross-section perpendicular to the main flow direction. For a square grid N  W   = W  l  s q        while for the hexagonal case, where the hexagons are oriented with the long diagonal in the direction of the flow, N  W   = W  3   l  h e x       . For the diluted network, we describe the conductance distribution in a binary form as a summation of two terms (Kirkpatrick, 1973 ), a fraction p   of diluted bonds with zero conductance and the fraction of the surviving bonds (1 − p   ) so that f  1   ( g )  = p δ ( g )  + ( 1 − p )  f ( g )    , where δ ( g )     is the Dirac delta function and f ( g )     is the conductance probability density function (Fig. 4 ). 3.5.1 Random network  In this section, we describe the generation of a random network (Fig. 8 ) that has the same coordination number distribution as the porous medium (not just the same mean). We start from a regular square lattice of sites that are also connected along the diagonals, i.e., with a constant coordination number of Z  l a t t i c e   = 8   . This value is equal to the largest observed coordination number (Z = 8   , Fig. 3 c). Unlike for the previous networks, in this case, the length is not constant because the diagonals are longer than the horizontal and vertical bonds by a factor of 2    . As for the previous networks (Sections 3.4.1 and 3.4.2 ), conductance values are assigned randomly to all the bonds from the distribution f ( g )    . Adjusting the distribution of coordination numbers of the lattice to a prescribed distribution is done iteratively through diluting and concentrating schemes as described in the following. The algorithm is initialized by assigning a target coordination number Z  j   ≤ Z  l a t t i c e      to each site j   drawn randomly from the distribution f ( Z )     (Fig. 3 c), and by assigning a random elimination number to each bond of a site from a uniform distribution between 0   and 1  . All site coordination numbers at initialization are Z  j  ( 0 )    ≥ Z  l a t t i c e     . At the next step (dilution step), if a site coordination number is larger than the target value (Z  j  ( 0 )    > Z  j     ), the bond with the smallest elimination number is removed by assigning zero conductance. After the dilution step, all coordination numbers are updated. The dilution step is followed by a concentration step. If the grid coordination number at the site is smaller than the target value (Z  j  ( 1 )    < Z  j     ), then a random bond is added (to one of the available locations, keeping the initial conductance value) and a new random elimination number is assigned to the bond. After the concentration step, all coordination numbers are updated, and a dilution step follows. These steps are repeated until the distribution of coordination numbers in the random network has converged to the target distribution. As a convergence criterion, we use a threshold value for the difference between the target and lattice mean coordination number. That is, the algorithm has converged after the k  th iteration if | 〈 Z 〉  − 〈 Z  ( k )    〉  |  < 1 0  − 4     . For the media under consideration, the coordination number distribution converges to the prescribed distribution after less than 30 iteration steps.  3.5.2 Detailed network representation of the pore system  The detailed representation of the pore system accounts for the spatial location of the pores, their coordination number, and the sizes of the pore bodies and throats (Fig. 9 ). In order to generate the detailed network, the segmented pore label image (attained from the image analysis), in which each pore is assigned a different index (label), is used to form a graph. The graph holds information about the connectivity of each pore and its neighbors (on an 8-connectivity directions basis). The site location is set equal to the location of the maximal distance map value in the pore, i.e., to the center of the maximal disk (Fig. 2 d). The bond length between each connected pores couple is set as the distance between pore centers. The pore geometry in the detailed network representation is parabolic, see Section 3.2.2 .    4 Results and discussion In this section, we study the estimates of the different network models for permeability, hydraulic tortuosity, and the distributions of pressure and flow rate and compare them to the results of the direct number simulations, which represent the ground truth. These are the key quantities for the understanding of pore-scale flow and solute dispersion in saturated and partially saturated porous media (Dentz et al., 2018; Puyguiraud et al., 2021; Ben-Noah et al., 2023b ). 4.1 Permeability The ability to estimate the permeability (k  ) of a representative elementary volume (REV) is a basic prerequisite for using network models to upscale pore-scale flow phenomena to the Darcy and field scales. In general, pore networks are valuable for evaluating the permeability of two and three-dimensional media, even for partially saturated scenarios (Sahimi, 2011; Zahasky et al., 2020; Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2012 ). Fig. 10  shows the k   estimated from the different network models and k   based on the effective medium approximations (EMA) versus the permeabilities obtained from the direct numerical simulations (DNS). The estimates from the pore network models are based on averages of 25 network realizations for each pore geometry. The regular and diluted networks give a relatively narrow span of permeabilities for different realizations, suggesting that the domain is large enough to be considered a REV. As expected, for all network models, the permeability monotonically increases with the saturation degree S  e    . Even if the permeabilities from the network models and direct simulation do not coincide, the network models may give a good estimate for the relative permeability k  r   = k / k  s     , where k  s     is the saturated (intrinsic) permeability. The effect of S  e     on k  r     for the different networks is presented in Fig. 11 . Regular networks.   The regular networks (and also the diluted and random) estimate better the relative permeability (k  r    , Fig. 11 ) than the absolute one (k  , Fig. 10 ). This is in accordance with the literature (Hunt and Sahimi, 2017 ). Here, the regular networks slightly underestimate the effect (slope) of S  e     on the relative permeability k  r   = k / k  s      (Fig. 11 a). The increase in the standard deviations of the permeabilities (seen in the box plots in Fig. 10 a,b) with the reduction of the saturation S  e   = 1    in the hexagonal grid is due to the changes in the pore size distribution with a broader distribution and many more small pores accounting for the narrow water films. The k   evaluated by the EMA for the rectangular pore geometry (red rectangular markers in Fig. 10 a) and parabolic (blue circle markers) pore geometries are very close. This is because of their relatively similar conductance probability density functions (Fig. 4 ). As expected, the k   evaluated by the EMA is very close to the mean k   evaluated by the regular network models (box plots, Fig. 10 a). Interestingly, the strip pore geometry (red) gives better agreement between the EMA and the network. Maybe because of the smaller variability in the bond conductances.  Diluted networks. The diluted networks (Fig. 10 b) provide a better estimate for k  r     as a function of S  e     than the regular networks (Fig. 11 b), but give worse estimates for k  , mostly underestimating the data from the direct numerical simulations. This effect is more notable in the strip pore geometry because using r  t     as bond aperture underestimates the bond conductances. The strip pore geometry in the diluted network (red boxes in Fig. 10 b) presents higher variability between realizations (wider box plots) compared to the parabolic geometry. This is because of the combined effect of the larger fraction of low conductances (Fig. 4 a) and the network’s dilution, which may form singular and dead-end sites. Interestingly, the k   values obtained from the diluted EMA are lower than the ones evaluated by the network models. The permeability estimated by the EMA increases linearly with the fraction of conducting bonds. At the same time, for a square lattice, the percolation threshold (p = 0 . 5   , for any conductance distribution) and the conductivity at saturation evaluated by the EMA are accurate. This means that the EMA is expected to overestimate the dependence of the conductance of a square lattice (Sahimi et al., 1983 ) on the fraction of conducting bonds, which is expected to be convex near percolation and linear away from percolation. On the other hand, the EMA assumes symmetry (Kirkpatrick, 1973 ), i.e., the conducting and nonconducting regions are treated on an equal footing (Bruggeman, 1935 ). Meanwhile, the actual media and diluted networks are characterized by a conducting “background” surrounding the nonconducting “inclusions”. Therefore, the EMA does not account for the preferential, highly conducting paths of heterogeneous media, which may result in an underestimation of permeability (David et al., 1990 ). In other words, the diluted network model allows for flow in preferential paths of conductors while the EMA forces the whole flow to pass through a lattice fully occupied with the effective (EMA-evaluated) conductor.  Random networks. The estimates by the random networks (Fig. 10 c) for k   and k r     are similar to those of the regular and diluted networks. This suggests that the added information held in the distribution of Z   as opposed to the mean coordination number does not improve the estimation of k  .  Detailed networks. The permeability estimates of the detailed network model (Fig. 10 d) are in excellent agreement with the direct numerical simulations. This confirms the ability of the detailed network model to represent the mean flow behavior through porous media. However, this model relies on detailed pore space information that may often not be available.   4.2 Tortuosity Fig. 12  shows the hydraulic tortuosity estimates from the network models versus the tortuosity obtained from the direct numerical flow simulations using the digitized images of the porous media. Recall that the definition of tortuosity used for the network models in Eq. (21)  is different from the definition in Eq. (4)  for the direct numerical simulations. The two definitions coincide only if the bond lengths are constant, which is the case for regular networks. We observe for the networks and direct numerical simulations that tortuosity increases monotonically as the saturation degree decreases, which is due to the increasing complexity of the fluid phase configuration. Generally, the network models overestimate the values obtained from the direct flow simulations. A possible cause is the geometry of the lattice underlying the network models and its angle with respect to the pressure gradient. Another reason the network models overestimate tortuosity is that they define the bond length by the distance between the pores’ body centers. However, this is the maximal flow path, where most flow is done in shorter routes. This means that the overestimation of the tortuosity by network models depends on the bond’s aspect ratio (Friedman and Seaton, 1995 ). We define the relative tortuosity τ  r   = τ / τ  s     , where τ  s     is the tortuosity of the fully saturated case S  e   = 1   . The effect of S  e     on the tortuosity can be evaluated from the slope of the markers or centers of the boxes compared to the dashed line in Fig. 12 . It can be seen that all the models, except the regular networks, give a reasonable estimation of τ  r    . This suggests that the changes in the conductance distribution alone cannot explain the increase of tortuosity with the reduction of S  e    . Regular networks.  In the regular lattice models, tortuosity (τ  ) originates from the geometry of the grid and from the distribution of the conductances. The conductances in this model are randomly assigned and not correlated. Thus, these models may underestimate preferential pathways and, therefore, slightly overestimate the actual hydraulic tortuosity χ  , see Fig. 12 a.  Diluted networks. As outlined above, diluted regular networks may be characterized by singular regions, that is, disconnected subnetworks, and may also display stagnation points, such as dead-end pores. These features increase the hydraulic tortuosity so that the τ   for the diluted networks (Fig. 12 b) are generally higher than for the regular networks (Fig. 12 a).  Random networks. The random networks (Fig. 12 c) have the largest tortuosity, which suggests that the number of diluted bonds has a more significant effect on the tortuosity than the formation of stagnation and singular points.  Detailed networks. The tortuosity estimated from the detailed network model gives the best approximation for χ  . This can be traced back to the effect of the dead-end regions on the preferential flow.   4.3 Velocity and flow rate distribution The velocity and flow rate distributions play a key role in the understanding and prediction of solute transport from the pore and continuum scales. Variations in the micro-scale flow velocities give rise to the phenomenon of hydrodynamic dispersion (Bear, 1988 ). The distribution of pore-scale velocities determines the evolution of solute dispersion and the tailing behavior of solute breakthrough curves (Dentz et al., 2018; Gouze et al., 2021; Ben-Noah et al., 2023b ). The velocity distribution is a key property for the prediction of large-scale solute transport. It is not clear a priori that network models capture the velocity distribution observed in porous media because (1) networks do not account for the intra-pore velocity distribution, (2) networks do not reproduce the exact topological features of the pore space, and (3) the networks may display more stagnation sites, that is dead-end pores than one finds in the real medium. The effect of the saturation degree on the spatial pressure and flow distribution is depicted in Fig. 13  for the saturated case and the partially saturated medium with S  e   = 0 . 65   . The saturated case has a relatively uniform flow velocity at the device scale and local low flow velocity regions between grains that are aligned in the main flow direction. For the partially saturated case in contrast, the local pressure gradients diverge from the main flow direction, causing a more tortuous flow. It is also visible that the unsaturated case has significant regions of low flow velocities and small pressure gradients. Fig. 14 a shows the probability density functions of the flow velocity from the direct numerical flow simulations with flow velocities that range over almost ten orders of magnitude. The distributions are characterized by significant tails toward low velocities. As the complexity of the fluid-filled medium portion increases, the probability of low velocities increases, which is due to the low-velocity regions depicted in Fig. 13 . The low-velocity end of the velocity distribution determines the long-time tails of solute breakthrough and the evolution of dispersion.    4.3.1 Regular, diluted and random networks Fig. 15  shows the spatial pressure and flow rate distributions for the medium with saturation S  e   = 0 . 65    obtained from the (top panels) regular and (center panels) diluted and (bottom panels) random networks. The three network models have the same conductance distribution and mean coordination numbers of 〈 Z 〉  ≈ 3   . The random network matches the distribution of coordination numbers of the porous medium. Stagnation points, that is, sites of zero flow rate, are relatively frequent in the square lattice (diluted network, Fig. 15 d) but not very common in the hexagonal lattice (regular network, Fig. 15 b). This suggests that the orientation of the pore throats and not just the connectivity of the pore space is important for pressure and flow rate distributions. For the saturated case (Figure SF1 in the supplementary material), both network models give spatial pressure and flow rate distributions that look qualitatively similar to those from the direct numerical simulations. Also, the velocity and flow rate PDFs estimated from the networks compare well to those obtained from the direct flow simulations (see Fig. 14 c and d). However, for unsaturated media, the three network models cannot describe either the pressure and flow rate maps or their PDFs. While none of the network models can reproduce the increase of low velocities with decreasing saturation, the random network picks up the wide range of flow velocities observed in the direct flow simulations. These observations indicate that the preferential flow patterns observed in the unsaturated medium in Fig. 13  cannot be explained by the variability in conductance or coordination number alone. For the diluted networks, the grid dilution to achieve the desired mean coordination number of 〈 Z 〉  = 3    increases the number of stagnation and dead-end points compared to the regular square grid. These points give rise to the white regions in the Q   map (Fig. 15 d), and blue regions in the pressure map (Fig. 15 c). However, dilution also gives rise to a more pronounced preferential flow as compared to the regular network. The pressure distributions of the square diluted lattice (Fig. 15 c) are more disordered than the regular hexagonal pressure distribution (Fig. 15 a), for the same mean coordination number. This is because of the larger amount of dead-ends (white regions in Fig. 15 b and d) caused by the higher absolute dilution (starting from a higher saturated Z  ). This illustrates the limitation of a grid’s mean coordination number to generally represent the medium’s connectivity. The random network (Fig. 15 e and f) shows a smaller number of singular points and dead-end pores than the diluted network (Fig. 15 c and d), despite the larger degree of dilution (from Z  g r i d   = 8    for the base lattice to 〈 Z  m o d e l   〉  ≈ 3   ). This suggests that a wide distribution of the coordination number increases the pore-space connectivity. For illustration, consider the situation of ten pores, nine of which have a coordination number of 1   and one of them a coordination number of 9  . Then, they are all connected. In general, the size and spatial configuration of the stagnation areas are not well described by the lattice networks. This is to be expected because these network models (regular, diluted, and random) do not account for the spatial correlation of the porous space, only mean properties such as the mean coordination number and the one-point distributions of conductance and coordination number (only random network). Moreover, these network (lattice) models do not account for the actual porosity and saturation degree of the media. In other words, the volume fraction of each site is not accounted for. Note that the singular regions in the diluted networks are merely artifacts of the network generation process and do not contribute to the estimation of saturation of porosity. Moreover, the air phase is typically spatially correlated, as shown in Fig. 13 , which is not accounted for in these network models. Nevertheless, the random network models can reproduce some of the features obtained from the direct numerical simulations, such as the preferential flow paths (Fig. 15 f) and the broad spectrum of flow in flow rates (Fig. 14 ).    4.3.2 Detailed networks Fig. 16  shows the pressure and flow rate maps for S  e   = 1    and 0.65 obtained from the detailed network representations of the media. The detailed networks show similar pressure and flow rate distributions as the numerical simulations (Fig. 13 ) for the two saturation degrees. Also, the PDFs of flow rates closely match the ones obtained from the direct flow simulations, as shown in Fig. 14 b. The detailed network model accounts only for the percolated connected fluid phase. Thus, it does not generate singular points or regions. In this model, the number of stagnation sites with zero velocity is small and comparable to the number of sites with Z = 1   . This is in accordance with the numerical simulations in which zero velocity prevails only at the solid-fluid interface and does not exist at any finite volume (mesh element). As seen in the map of flow rates both from the direct flow simulations (Fig. 13 ), the air phase encloses extensive connected dead-end regions (of many pores) in which the flow is very slow. These regions do not participate in the conductance of fluids, which reduces permeability and increases preferential flow. Moreover, these regions give rise to non-Fickian solute transport due to diffusion-based solute entrapment and release (Liu and Kitanidis, 2012; Gjetvaj et al., 2015; Ben-Noah et al., 2023b ). All of these features are present in the detailed network models shown in Fig. 16 . This observation shows the importance of accounting for the morphology of the connected fluid phase and pore space and demonstrates the viability of using network models to quantify not only the mean flow but also the flow distribution in porous media. The detailed model is able to reproduce all features of the PDF of flow rates for the different media (Fig. 14 b). It accounts correctly for the increase of low flow rates with decreasing saturation and captures the full range of flow rates. The flow rate PDFs are very similar in magnitude and shape to the volumetric flow rate PDFs, indicating that there is no large variability in the pore cross-sections. For the saturated case, however, the range of flow rates is much larger than the range of volumetric flow rates, indicating that the distribution of intrapore velocities is important. However, with increasing heterogeneity of the pore space, i.e., with decreasing saturation, this difference vanishes and both flow rates and volumetric flow rates show a similar range and shape. Thus, the intrapore velocity distribution reproduction is less important for these cases.      5 Conclusion The conceptualization of a porous medium as a network of conductors is valuable and effective for quantifying flow and transport phenomena and evaluating the media’s hydraulic properties. However, accurately describing this conceptualization hinges on detailed information about the pore space, which may not be attainable in real-world scenarios. The amount of detailed information required for pore-space characterization depends on the complexity of the flow phenomenon and the flow and transport processes of interest. In this study, we demonstrated how different levels of information about the phase configuration in the pore space can be used to evaluate different properties of single-phase flow in variably saturated media. The media permeability, even for the partially saturated cases, is well quantified even by relatively simple regular network models. For the saturated medium under consideration, the regular network model gives a good approximation of the hydraulic tortuosity and velocity distribution, albeit not for the velocity range. However, the network models overestimate the hydraulic tortuosity, which is a major limitation in evaluating complex transport phenomena. Moreover, the velocity distribution is governed by the spatial configuration of the fluid phase. Thus, the accurate evaluation of this factor relies on a relatively detailed description of the pore space, its spatial distribution, and its connectivity. This information may be available for the pore space in saturated porous media but not necessarily for the more complex fluid distribution and fluid-filled pore space in a partially saturated medium. Addressing this issue requires the quantification of the spatial configuration of the fluid phase and identifying its relevant quantifiers.
1 Introduction An estuary is a typical place where fresh water meets saline water and characterized by the intricate interplay between river discharge and tide, which is significantly relevant to hydrodynamic regimes. River-tide dynamics, one of the most important dynamics in estuarine environments, is vital for sustainable water resources management, including flood control, salt intrusion prevention, sedimentary regime maintenance, and ecosystem stability (Hoitink and Jay, 2016; Hoitink et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023 ). Previous studies have highlighted that tide is considerably distorted and attenuated as it propagates from the ocean to an estuary, mainly attributed to the nonlinear modulation of river discharge and channel geometry (Godin, 1985; Savenije, 1992; Horrevoets et al., 2004; Ji and Zhang, 2019; Cai et al., 2023a ), especially in river-dominated estuaries, where the quantification of the relationship between the riverine and tidal forcing is difficult to be completely understood. It was shown that the increasing river discharge may lead to an increase in water level gradient (Cai et al., 2014a,b ) and affect the sedimentary regime (Liu et al., 2023 ), which is closely related to the effective friction along the channel thereby resulting in the enhancement in the tidal damping effect (Cai et al., 2018, 2019a ). In recent decades, large-scale human activities have been the primary driver of estuarine evolutions (Vörösmarty et al., 2003; Syvitski et al., 2005; Dai et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Talke and Jay, 2020 ), such as those occurred in Mekong River (Fu et al., 2008 ), the Yangtze River Estuary (Dai and Liu, 2013; Wang et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2019a, 2022 ), the Lingdingyang Bay (Wu et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021a,b ) and the Modaomen Estuary (Liu et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020 ), impacting morphological evolution, sedimentary patterns, and river-tide dynamics, which have irreversible influences on the dynamical equilibrium in estuaries compared to the natural stage when human interventions have minimum impacts. The major anthropogenic activities in estuaries include dam constructions, sand excavations, channel dredging, embankment connections by constructing sluices, and land reclamations etc. These activities significantly affected the river-tide dynamics in terms of water level and tidal range by changing the sedimentary patterns, estuarine geometry and morphology. For instance, dam construction traps sediment in the upstream reservoir, reducing the downstream sediment flux (Syvitski et al., 2005 ) and accelerating the erosion and sinking in deltas (Syvitski, 2008; Liu et al., 2014 ). Sluice constructions, on the one hand, usually lead to an increasing water level in the central part and a decreasing water level gradient in the upper part. In addition, these activities reduce the delivery capacity of sediment in the channel or lake wetlands and result in deposition, thereby consequently decreasing the water connectivity and exchange capacity (Huang et al., 2023; Kim and Woo, 2023; Yang et al., 2024 ). Large-scale sand excavations in the channel lead to an increase in the suspended sediment concentration, and a considerable increase in channel depth (Luo et al., 2007 ), affecting the sedimentary transport processes and the estuarine maximum turbidity, with important relevance to the river-tide dynamics (Winterwerp et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2019; Chu et al., 2020 ). Land reclamations directly reshape coastlines near the estuary mouth and artificially move deltas towards seaward, thereby significantly reducing the water surface area. These changes in the morphology eventually caused variations in the water level and tidal range (Gao et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2018, 2019b ) in conjunction with global warming. In response to these morphological alterations, land subsidence has occurred in coastal areas with dense populations (Edmonds et al., 2020 ), increasing the risk of coastal flooding due to the rising relative sea level (Fang et al., 2022 ). This is challenging for reducing flood probabilities and the associated property losses (Hallegatte et al., 2013 ). For instance, due to the increasing flood risk, it is estimated that the inundated urban land areas in the future are projected to be 4 to 19 times that at present in seven urban agglomerations that are home to over 750 million people in China (Jiang et al., 2023 ). In addition, statistics indicate that 82 % of these coastal flooding events are tide-dominated due to sea level rise (Rueda et al., 2017 ). However, current global efforts appear insufficient to slow the rise in global temperatures (Matthews and Wynes, 2022 ), which is the primary cause of coastal disasters. Therefore, due to the combined effects of the complicated hydrodynamics and intensive human interventions in estuaries, it is necessary to clarify the spatial distribution of river-tide dynamics and its response to anthropogenically-induced modifications. With respect to the descriptions of the spatial distribution of river-tide dynamics, the most direct method is to reproduce the time-dependent water level and tidal range series. However, due to the multiple external controlling factors of water level and tidal range, there are relatively few approaches capable of achieving this aim. Many previous studies focused on the reproductions of water level in estuaries, while one of the most widely used methods is tidal harmonic analysis, this has some limitations. For instance, the classical tidal harmonic analysis (such as T_TIDE) is applicable only in tide-dominated regions due to its assumption of stationary signals (Pawlowicz et al., 2002 ). In fluvial rivers, methods such as Nonstationary Harmonic Analysis (NS_TIDE, Matte et al., 2013, 2014 ), Enhanced Harmonic Analysis (Jin et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018 ), and River Discharge Driven Harmonic Analysis (R_TIDE, Cai et al., 2023a ) have been adopted to reproduce water levels and tidal range, showing good agreement with observations. However, these methods involve complex calculations, and the physical meaning of model coefficients is not fully understood. Moreover, river discharge data at the upstream station and tidal range data at the downstream station are required for some of them (e.g., NS_TIDE and R_TIDE), limiting their applicability to specific regions and conditions (e.g., river-dominated estuaries or estuaries with available river discharge records). In river-dominated estuaries where river discharge significantly influences water level distributions, the successful application of the Triple Linear Regression (TLR) model in reconstructing water levels in the Yangtze River (Cai et al., 2022 ) suggested that water level variations were closely related to changes in upstream river discharge and downstream water levels. This provided a new insight that the river-tide dynamics could be estimated using several simple parameters. However, these approaches could only reproduce water level and tidal range at specific positions (e.g., gauging stations) rather than arbitrary positions in an estuary. To overcome this disadvantage, the analytical models could be used to reproduce the water level and tidal range anywhere within an estuary and explore the underlying mechanism of river-tide interplay (Jay, 1991; Kukulka and Jay, 2003 ). However, most of them only focus on a single predominant tidal constituent (e.g., M2 ) and neglect the mutual interactions of different constituents, which lets down the performance of these models (Horrevoets et al., 2004; Schuttelaars et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014a, 2016, 2018, 2019a; Wang et al., 2021 ). In addition, assuming that cross-sectional area, estuarine width, and water depth converge exponentially might lead to inaccuracies if geometry characteristics are heterogeneous (Cai et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2021b ). Moreover, most of them do not take potential impacts of external forcing over short timescales, such as local winds, storm surges and heavy precipitations (Wang et al., 2020 ). Additionally, although some empirical equations (e.g., Manning’s Equation and Chezy’s Equation) can indirectly reproduce the hydrodynamics with some appropriate adaptations (Bjerklie et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2023 ), they are not very straightforward and involve complex coefficients. On the other hand, numerical experiments can be used to simulate water levels under some specific conditions, such as the changing estuarine geometry (Chu et al., 2022 ), sea level rise (Khojasteh et al., 2021 ) and typhoon events (Liang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a,b ), yet the underlying mechanism and the descriptions of river-tide dynamics need further study. Therefore, developing a simple yet feasible method to describe the spatial distributions of water level and tidal range is of essential significance for quantifying the river-dynamics characteristics in an estuary and their response to intensive human interventions. Recently, Guo (2022a–c)  proposed a general unit hydrograph (GUH) theory applicable to predicting flood hydrograph from a known storm in a watershed, and baseflow separation from rainfall and streamflow. These studies established three hypotheses on instantaneous unit hydrograph (UH) based on observations, leading to a general and analytical framework describing discharge resulting from continuous excess rainfall occurring at a uniform rate for an indefinite period. This framework, termed the S-hydrograph, represents excess rainfall volume and could generate a UH for any storm duration. For the extensions of this theory, Guo et al. (2022)  analyzed the probability distribution of marathon race completion times due to its analogy to the rainfall-runoff process in watersheds. They noted similarities between the S-hydrograph and the cumulative number of runners finishing the marathon race within a specific timeframe, as well as between the instantaneous UH and corresponding histograms. Additionally, they identified two inflection points in the instantaneous UH corresponding to maximum and minimum slopes in the rising and recessing limbs, respectively, and classified types of runners accordingly. Inspired by them, Cai et al. (2023b)  proposed a general and analytical expression for the salinity distribution and salinity gradient by making four hypotheses based on observations, demonstrating its effectiveness in real estuarine applications. The objective of this study is to propose a general and analytical description of the spatial distribution of water level and tidal range in an estuary, building upon these previous studies (Guo, 2022a–c; Guo et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2023b ). It is worth noting that the shape of the S-hydrograph appears like the water level and tidal range distributions along estuaries, while the instantaneous UH curve resembles the water level and tidal range gradient. This alignment suggested the potential applicability of the GUH method for expressing the spatial variations in river-tide dynamics within estuaries. Similar to the approach proposed by Cai et al. (2023b) , we also formulated four hypotheses in our model based on observations and proposed a novel model for water level and tidal range distributions, thereby deriving the corresponding gradient curves. To validate the application of this theory in a real estuary, we applied it to the Modaomen Estuary in the Pearl River Delta, China, and detected the stepwise and seasonal differences in the river-tide dynamics. Furthermore, we categorized the four types of water level and tidal range distributions and explored the underlying mechanism of the regime shifts in river-tide dynamics by linking the boundary conditions to the model coefficients. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , the overview of the study area (the Modaomen Estuary) and the datasets adopted in this study are introduced in detail. The model is developed in Section 3 , accompanied by the sensitivity analyses of the model coefficients. The model performance, the stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the spatial distribution of river-tide dynamics, the relationship between the critical hydrodynamics, as well as the classification of the spatial distribution of river-tide dynamics are displayed in Section 4 . Based on the results derived from the newly proposed approach, the discussions concentrate on the underlying mechanism of the regime shift in river-tide dynamics (Section 5 ). Finally, some conclusions are drawn in Section 6 .  2 Study area and datasets 2.1 Overview of the Modaomen Estuary The Pearl River Delta ranks as the third largest river delta in China and is regarded as one of the most complex deltas in the world, comprising three major tributaries (West, North, and East Rivers) and debouching into the South China Sea through eight estuarine outlets, including Yamen, Hutiaomen, Jitimen, Modaomen, Hengmen, Hongqili, Jiaomen and Humen, located from west to east (Fig. 1  ). The Modaomen Estuary, the primary outlet of the West River, directly connects and delivers the largest portion of freshwater and suspended sediment to the South China Sea (Cai et al., 2012 ). The Modaomen Estuary represents a typical river-dominated estuary, characterized by a complicated hydrodynamic pattern along the channel. The river discharge varies between wet (from April to September) and dry season (from October to December and from January to March), with the value of approximately 10,800 m3 /s and 3440 m3 /s, respectively. The tidal regime exhibits irregular semi-diurnal characteristics, with average amplitudes of the four predominated tidal constituents of M2 , K1 , O1  and S2  being 0.43, 0.42, 0.37 and 0.18 m, respectively, at the Sanzao tidal gauging station (near the estuary mouth), alongside a corresponding tidal form number of 1.30 (Gong and Shen, 2011 ). Notably, the mean annual tidal range at the Sanzao tidal gauging station stands at 1.11 m but decreases to approximately 0.86 m at the Denglongshan tidal gauging station, situated about 21 km upstream from Sanzao, indicating the significant influence of river discharge on tidal attenuations. Previous studies have highlighted the significant impacts of intensive human interventions on the estuarine dynamical equilibrium, showing that large-scale and high-intensity anthropogenic disturbances may trigger considerable shifts in the river-tide dynamics (Zhang et al., 2015; Talke and Jay, 2020 ). In recent decades, the Modaomen Estuary has been subject to intensive human activities, primarily including reservoir constructions in the drainage basins, sand excavations in the channel, and land reclamations near the estuary mouth. The total capacity of the major reservoirs in the West River Basin reached approximately 5.38 × 1010  m3  by 2006, accounting for approximately 24.7 % of the water discharge (Liu et al., 2018 ). Reservoir constructions resulted in sediment retention in dams, significantly reducing downstream sediment supply and accelerating channel erosion (Wang et al., 2011 ). Sand excavations, which initially occurred in the 1970s and intensified in the early 1990s to meet the demands of rapid urbanization, slowed down after the prohibition by the government in the 2000s. Large-scale sand excavations led to an increase in water depths (together with channel volume), ranging from 0.59 m to 1.73 m along the Modaomen Estuary (Luo et al., 2007 ). Land reclamations near the estuary mouth began in the mid-1980s and altered the estuarine geometry intensely, with 16.5 km2  of the shoals reclaimed by 1997 (Tan et al., 2019 ). Besides, a reduction of the width of the Modaomen outlet (from 6.2 km to about 2.4 km) was observed, which resulted in the alterations in water and sediment load and hydrodynamics of tidal channels (He et al., 2019 ).  2.2 Datasets To clearly identify the water level and tidal range distributions along the Modaomen Estuary, the monthly averaged data spanning from 1965 to 2017 were collected from five tidal gauging stations, including Sanzao (SZ), Denglongshan (DLS), Zhuyin (ZY), Jiangmen (JM) and Ganzhu (GZ), as well as from the hydrological station at the apex of the channel, namely Makou (MK). Fig. 1  illustrates the relative distances of each station from the Sanzao tidal gauging station nearest to the estuary mouth. To quantify the influence of river discharge on the hydrodynamics regime, the monthly averaged river discharge for the corresponding period was also adopted. These datasets were provided by the Guangdong Hydrology Bureau of the People's Republic of China. The water levels were corrected using the reference local mean sea level (i.e., Pearl River datum). Following Eqs. (A.1) and (A.2)  (see Appendix A ), the whole datasets were normalized to range from 0 to 1, as shown in Fig. S1  in the Supporting information .   3 Methodology 3.1 Descriptions of hydrodynamics To illustrate the hydrodynamics pattern in the Modaomen Estuary, the water level gradient and tidal range gradient are adopted to describe the river-tide dynamic regime and its spatial–temporal evolution. Based on the observed water level (Z) and tidal range (H ), the water level gradient (δZ  ) and tidal range gradient (δH  ) over a reach of length Δx  could be calculated by the following equations:(1) δ Z  = Z 2  - Z 1   Δ x       (2) δ H  = H 2  - H 1   Δ x       where Z 1  and H 1  are the water level and tidal range at the seaward station, respectively, and Z 2  and H 2  are the corresponding values at a distance of Δx  upstream, respectively.  3.2 Accumulated anomaly curve The Accumulated anomaly curve is a simple but effective and direct method to detect the inflection points of the time series. For a given time series xi  , the accumulated anomaly value at the moment t  can be calculated by the following equation:(3) S t  = ∑ i = 1  t  x i  - 1 n  ∑ i = 1  N  x i     ,  t = i , i + 1 , . . . , N - 1 , N .      In Eq. (3) , the temporal variation of St   at N  moments can be used to identify the inflection points where the gradient with respect to the time is zero (Zhang et al., 2021a ). Notably, the number of inflection points depends on the trend of data facts.  3.3 General unit hydrograph (GUH) theory 3.3.1 The GUH theory for water level and tidal range distributions In this study, we propose a GUH model to describe the water level and tidal range distributions. The GUH model source code is available at https://github.com/Huayangcai/General-Unit-Hydrograph-Model-for-River-tide-Dynamics-V1.0-Matlab-Toolbox.git . According to the review of the GUH theory introduced in previous studies, such as the applications of predictions of flood hydrograph from a known storm in a watershed (Guo, 2022a–c ), probability distributions (Guo et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2023c ) and salinity distribution (Cai et al., 2023b ), after some algebraic manipulations (readers can refer to Appendix A  for more details of the derivation), one can derive the dimensionless water level (Z *) and tidal range (H *) distributions along the relative distance x  from the estuary mouth, which are expressed as:(4) Z ∗  x   = 1 - 1 + m exp μ x x p   - 1          - 1 m        (5) H ∗  x   = 1 + m exp μ x x p   - 1          - 1 m        where μ  and m  are the model coefficients. The position x  = xp   represents the position where the maximum dZ */dx  and the minimum dH */dx  (maximum absolute value of tidal range gradient) are reached. Therefore, the gradient curves for water level and tidal range are written as:(6) d Z ∗  x    dx   = μ x p   exp μ x x p   - 1       1 + m exp μ x x p   - 1          - 1 + 1 m           (7) d H ∗  x    dx   = - μ x p   exp μ x x p   - 1       1 + m exp μ x x p   - 1          - 1 + 1 m            To give a direct insight into the conceptual diagram of the water level and tidal range distribution fitted by the newly proposed GUH model, we make a transform namely x *=x /xp  , letting x  dimensionless scaled the xp   (the position of the inflection point).
