Fig. S2  (see the Supporting Information ) illustrates the analytical solutions of the dimensionless water level (Z *) and tidal range (H *) along with their gradients as a function of μ  and m . It can be clearly observed that the coefficient μ  determined the range of the water level and tidal range along the channel by controlling the changing rate of both the rising and recessing limbs. Specifically, a larger coefficient μ  corresponds to a larger gradient. As for the coefficient m , it exerts a similar influence on the water level and tidal range distribution before the inflection point (x * < 1), beyond which it has the opposite effect. Fig. S3  (see the Supporting Information ) demonstrates that the coefficient m  had a greater impact on the water level and tidal range distribution after the inflection point (x * > 1), as reflected in the three shapes of the instantaneous UH (i.e., the gradient curve): a symmetric gradient about x * = x /xp   = 1, if m  = 1; a negatively skewed gradient, if 0 < m  < 1; and positively skewed gradient, if m  > 1. Eqs. (11)–(14) reveal that the inflection lengths x 1,2  and their separation σx   to xp   are determined by the model coefficients, particularly µ and m , owing to their physical significance. For the first inflection length x 1 , the physical significance lies in its positivity and negativity, only the value of x 1  is positive, and its physical significance can be confirmed, which can be noted that it is mainly determined by the m  in the logarithmic functions in the numerator, but also influenced by the μ  in the denominator, i.e., if the values of μ and m are too small and large, respectively, the value of x 1  might smaller than zero. Similarly, the value of the second infection length x 2  should not exceed the distance from the estuary mouth to the apex of the channel, which also requires a combination of relatively large μ  and relatively small m . With regard to the separation of x 1, 2  to xp   (σx  ), its significance is determined by the range of validity of x 1, 2 , only if they are meaningful, the discussions on σx   are practical. Fig. S4  (see the Supporting information ) illustrates the analytical solutions of x 1,2  and σx   as functions of µ  and m  for a given xp   = 1, where the red dashed lines represent the critical value where the parameters become meaningful (i.e., x 1  = 0, x 2  = 2 and σx   = 1, respectively, the values to the right of these red dashed lines are meaningful). With regard to the interpretation of the model parameters, x 1  increases with μ  in the denominator and decreases with m  in the logarithmic functions in the numerator. On the other hand, both x 2  and σx   decrease with μ  and increase with m . This indicates that while the observed and analytically computed water levels and tidal ranges might exhibit good correspondence in some cases, they could still vary in terms of different distribution characteristics, which could be classified based on the values of the inflection points and their separation.    4 Results 4.1 Model performance Based on the observed monthly averaged water levels and tidal ranges for the six stations, the three model coefficients xp  , μ  and m  can be determined by fitting Eqs. (4) and (5) , which could be easily conducted with methods of a nonlinear curve-fitting method in the least-squares sense (such as using the MATLAB “lsqcurvefit.m” function). Fig. 3   illustrates the comparison between the observed and computed water levels and tidal ranges at the six stations, suggesting a good agreement between them. The average RMSE and R2  for water levels and tidal ranges at the six stations were calculated by Eqs. (15) and (16) . Additionally, to highlight the good performance of the GUH model, a comparison between the proposed model and the conventional Logistic Model in terms of water level and tidal range along the Modaomen Estuary was carried out. The comparison of the computed coefficients for water levels and tidal ranges derived from the two models at each station is listed in Table 1  . Specifically, for the GUH model, the maximum RMSE values are 0.05 m for the water level and 0.03 m for the tidal range, while minimum R2  are 0.95 and 0.91 for the corresponding parameters, respectively, which show better satisfactory correspondence between the observations and computations than the conventional Logistic Model. Additionally, we compared the water level and tidal range spatial distributions fitted by the two models in cases of average state, wet season and dry season (see Section S3 in the Supporting Information ), which confirmed that the proposed GUH model was more applicable for illustrating the water level and tidal range spatial distributions. Consequently, the proposed GUH model showed promise for further studies of the water level and tidal range distributions.  4.2 Stepwise alterations in the river-tide dynamics regime It is worth noting from Fig. 3  that the fluctuations in water levels and tidal ranges are considerable during the studying period. For instance, at MK station, the water level ranged from −0.01 m to 7.65 m, and the tidal range spanned from 0.02 m to 0.72 m. These variations could be mainly attributed to the seasonal fluctuations in river discharge and intensive human interventions (see also Section 2.1  and Fig. S5  in the Supporting information ). Therefore, it is crucial to delineate the long-term evolution of the hydrodynamic regime and identify the stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the water levels and tidal ranges, along with their spatial distributions and changing rates (i.e., the gradient). Here, we adopted the accumulated anomaly curve to detect the inflection points of the water level gradient (δZ  ) and the absolute value of the tidal range gradient (|δH  |, reflecting the tidal damping effect). All data were normalized using Eqs. (A1) and (A2)  (see Appendix A ), and the accumulated anomaly values were calculated by Eq. (3) . Fig. 4   illustrates the accumulated anomaly values of the yearly averaged δZ   and |δH  | along the Modaoemen Estuary (i.e., the reach from MK to SZ), where a shift of the δZ   and |δH  | was observed in 1988 and 1998, respectively. The accumulated anomaly values increased before 1988 and decreased after 1998, indicating relatively large and small values during the corresponding periods, respectively. With reference to the influence of human activities, the sub-periods corresponding to the accumulated anomaly curve can be determined, including the Pre-human Period (1965–1988), characterized by relatively weak human interventions and mainly influenced by natural processes, the Transitional Period (1989–1998), subject to substantial modification of hydrodynamics regime by human activities, and the Post-human Period (1999–2017), featured by the self-adoptive adjustment after the intensive anthropogenic interventions. To identify the stepwise evolution of the hydrodynamics regime, the multiyear averaged δZ   and |δH  | along the Modaomen Estuary for the three distinct periods are summarized in Table 2  . Both the δZ   and |δH  | decreased with the studying period (by approximately 50 % and 35 % from the Pre-human Period to the Post-human Period, respectively), suggesting a slower water surface slope and weaker tidal damping effect, thereby altering the whole hydrodynamics regime in terms of the water level dynamics and tidal attenuations along the Modaomen Estuary. To further understand the impacts of the intensive human interventions on the hydrodynamics regime, the data during Pre-human Period and Post-human Period (instead of the three sub-periods) were used to identify the stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the water level and tidal range distributions in the following analysis.  4.3 Stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the water level and tidal range distributions Fig. 5   illustrates the stepwise alterations (a, b) and seasonal differences (c–j) in the water level and tidal range distributions fitted by the proposed GUH along with their gradients along the Modaomen Estuary, where the solid and dashed lines represent the Pre-human Period and the Post-human Period, respectively. Regarding the fundamental distribution characteristics, the water levels (Z ) increased along the estuary, while the tidal range (H ) decreased. Notably, the stepwise alterations in water levels and tidal ranges displayed considerable spatial–temporal differences (see Figs. S6, S7  and Table S1  in the Supporting information ). For instance, the water levels at the SZ tidal gauging station generally increased from the Pre-human Period to the Post-human Period by approximately 0.12 m on average. For DLS and ZY tidal gauging stations, water levels slightly increased in winter (by approximately 0.06 m and 0.04 m, respectively), yet decreased in other seasons, especially in summer when the most considerable alterations occurred (by approximately 0.03 m and 0.21 m, respectively). For other stations (i.e., JM, GZ and MK), water level generally decreased with a relatively small value in winter and a large value in summer. They decreased by approximately 0.03 m, 0.05 m and 0.19 m, while by 0.64 m, 0.98 m and 1.82 m in summer, displaying significant seasonal differences. With regard to the tidal ranges, they generally increased except for the SZ tidal gauging station (decreased by approximately 0.05 m). Specifically, the stepwise alterations increased along the estuary, with the values being 0.11 m, 0.18 m, 0.21 m, 0.22 m and 0.26 m at the DLS, ZY, JM, GZ and MK stations, respectively. For the seasonal difference, the maximum difference generally occurred in autumn corresponding to the largest relative mean sea level, while the minimum value occurred in winter (except for MK station) due to the reservoir regulations. The instantaneous UHs also demonstrated considerable variations similar to water level and tidal range. It should be noted from the spatial distributions of the tidal range gradient that the tidal damping effect (the absolute value of dH /dx ) tended to decrease in the upper part (part of GZ-MK reach) from the Pre-human Period to the Post-human Period, due to the relatively more intense tidal energy. To quantify the stepwise and seasonal changes in water level and tidal range distributions due to human interventions, the regression coefficients in the GUH model for the Pre-human Period and Post-human Period were subsequently summarised in Table 3  . For the water level, we generally observed a clear decrease in the coefficient μ , and an increase in the m  from the Pre-human Period to the Post-human Period, except for the m  in winter, which showed a decreasing tendency. The changes in the xp   varied by seasons, indicating an increase in winter, but a decrease in other seasons. Consequently, there was a considerable decline in the average value of xp   in the average value (by approximately 27.25 km), showing that the position of maximum dZ /dx  moved seaward. According to the characteristics and sensitivity analysis of the coefficient μ  and m  from Fig. S2  (see the Supporting information ), the decreasing μ  and increasing m  reflected a tendency for the water surface to become more linear, while the gradient displayed a slower changing rate, consistent with the observations depicted in Fig. 5 . As for the tidal range, the three regression coefficients in the GUH model generally decreased due to human interventions (except for the xp   in spring and the m  in autumn). Although the decreasing m  suggested a greater decline in tidal range and its gradient, the decreasing μ  had a more pronounced effect due to its relatively smaller value compared to the m . This eventually led to an increase in tidal range in the central and upper parts and weaker tidal damping along the Modaomen Estuary. The inflection point xp   was relatively small (less than 7 km) compared to those in water level distributions (larger than 51 km), indicating that the maximum tidal damping effect generally occurred near the estuary mouth due to the estuarine geometry. The differences in the regression coefficients for the water level and tidal range distributions were closely related to the boundary conditions (i.e., upstream river discharge, tidal range near the estuary mouth, and relative mean sea level). According to Eqs. (4) and (5) , the inflection point xp   corresponds to the position where the maximum dZ /dx  and the minimum dH /dx  occur. Since the hydrodynamics regime in terms of water levels and tidal ranges and their gradients experienced an abrupt shift along the Modaomen Estuary, these extreme values changed with the entire river-tide dynamic pattern. To be more specific, the maximum dZ /dx  and the minimum dH /dx  from the instantaneous UHs were extracted to illustrate the stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the characteristics of water level and tidal range distributions, which are also summarized in Table 3 . A similar response to the stepwise alterations and seasonal differences in the water level and tidal range distributions can be seen, displaying a significant decline in the maximum dZ /dx  and the absolute value of minimum dH /dx , with the decline ratio being approximately 56 % and 54 % on average, respectively. For both the Pre-human Period and Post-human Period, these extreme values showed considerable seasonal differences. For instance, for both the maximum dZ /dx  and the minimum dH /dx , their maximum and minimum stepwise alterations occurred in summer and winter, respectively, closely related to the seasonal changes in river discharge. The water level gradient is considered a crucial descriptor of the hydrodynamics regime, as its spatial–temporal evolution directly reflects the influence of changes in geometry on tidal wave propagations. The analytical expression for water level gradient can be derived from the one-dimensional momentum equation (Savenije et al., 2005 ):(17) ∂ U  ∂ t   + U ∂ U  ∂ x   + g ∂ Z  ∂ x   + g h 2 ρ 0    ∂ ρ  ∂ x   + g U U    K 2  h 4 / 3     = 0     where Z  is the surface elevation (i.e., water level); t  is the time; g  is the gravity acceleration; ρ  is the water density; K  is the Manning-Strickler frictional coefficient; h  is the water depth; U  is the average velocity in the cross-sectional consisting of the river flow velocity U r  and tidal wave velocity U t :(18) U = U t   - U r   = υ sin ( ω t )  - Q / A r      where υ  is the velocity amplitude; ω  is the frequency; Q  is the river discharge. In a tidal cycle, the baroclinic gradient term and inertia acceleration are negligible. The analytical solution of the water level gradient is obtained by integrating Eq. (17)  in a tidal cycle:(19) ∂ Z   ¯   ∂ x   = - U U     ¯   K 2  h  ¯   4 / 3         where the overline in Eq. (19)  represents tidal-averaged. Eq. (19)  elucidates that the water level gradient approximately equals the effective friction term resulting from the modulation of river discharge and the river bed (Buschman et al., 2009; Sassi and Hoitink, 2013; Cai et al., 2014a ), implying that the larger the water level gradient corresponds to more considerable effective friction. The maximum dZ /dx  reflected the most intense effective friction. Moreover, it could be inferred that river discharge attenuated tidal wave propagation by increasing the quadratic velocity in the numerator of the friction term and reducing the residual frictional effect by increasing the residual water level, thereby increasing the water depth in the denominator (Cai et al., 2014a,b, 2016, 2019a,b ). Hence, it is worth exploring the mutual interactions between the two hydrodynamic characteristics by linking the influence of river discharge on river-tide dynamics. From a steady state perspective, the seasonal changes in the tidal range gradient performed as a function of river discharge and exhibited considerable threshold phenomenon (Yang et al., 2020 ). Here, we observed a similar phenomenon between the minimum dH /dx  and river discharge (Fig. 6  a–d). Different from the conclusions drawn by Yang et al. (2020) , the minimum dH /dx  decreased with the increasing river discharge, but slowed down under the conditions of large river discharge (e.g., values exceeding 20,000 m3 /s), with the threshold phenomenon only occurring in summer during Pre-human Period (the critical river discharge was approximately 26,600 m3 /s). As for the relationship between the maximum dZ /dx  and the minimum dH /dx  (Fig. 6 e and f), it displayed a similar tendency to the river discharge since the water level gradient was almost linearly proportional to the river discharge, so was the maximum dZ /dx  (see Fig. S8  in the Supporting information ). The minimum dH /dx  decreased with the maximum dZ /dx , and similarly, the threshold relationship only occurred in summer during the Pre-human Period (the critical minimum dZ /dx  is approximately 7.42 × 10−5 ), yet disappeared in the Post-human Period. Such a phenomenon can be primarily attributed to the regime shift in river-tide dynamics in terms of water level gradient caused by the significant deepening of the riverbed (thus enlarging the channel storage), and the reduction in river discharge regulated by the reservoirs in the drainage basin.  4.4 Extension of the GUH for the different types of water level and tidal range distribution curves Table 4   details the numbers of valid inflection lengths in the water level and tidal range distribution curves for the two distinct periods. The results show that the valid x 1  and x 2  values for water levels often occurred in summer during the Pre-human Period, however, their occurrence decreased during the Post-human Period. This suggests that the water level changed along the channel with an almost linear tendency due to intensive human interventions instead of an exponential tendency. As for the tidal range, the valid x 1  occurrence was rare, likely due to the linear damping effect on the tidal energy near the estuary mouth with the negligible impacts of river discharge. The valid x 2  occurred almost in all fitted curves, mainly attributed to the mutual and nonlinear interaction between river discharge and tide in the upper part of the channel. According to the occurrence of the valid inflection lengths, the water level and tidal range distribution curves could be classified into the following four types: Type 1: this type occurs when there are strong dynamics at the boundary (large river discharge or tidal range input), featured by the synchronous occurrence of the two valid inflection lengths; Type 2 and Type 3: they occur when there is considerable mutual interaction between the two distinct external forces (i.e., upstream river discharge and downstream tidal range). Type 2 is characterized by the occurrence of only x 1 , while Type 3 is characterized by the occurrence of only x 2 . Type 4: this type occurs when the river discharge is relatively small, featured by the absence of the two valid inflection lengths. Fig. 7   illustrates several examples of the four types of characteristics of water level and tidal range distributions. In the case of water levels, the shape featured by Type 1 manifested in the wet season, characterized by significant riverine forcing leading to increased cross-section area in the upper part and reduced water level gradient. The shape featured by Type 2 and 3 commonly occurs in spring and autumn when the river discharge is moderate and the tidal range at the estuary mouth is relatively large, resulting in minimal nonlinear alterations in water level gradient due to mutual river-tide dynamic interactions. The shape featured by Type 4 predominated in winter due to the small river discharge and minimal tidal damping effect, resulting in a water level gradient almost linearly proportional to river discharge. Notably, for the tidal range, there were no distributions featured solely by Type 2, suggesting that the valid x 1  always accompanied the valid x 2 , typically observed in the shape featured by Type 1. In general, the tidal range generally decreased in a nearly linear fashion at the mouth of the estuary, primarily due to linear friction rather than the minimal effect of river discharge. Unlike water level, for the tidal range, the valid x 2  occurred 631 times in the whole 636 months in the study period, indicating significant tidal attenuations due to the nonlinear modulation caused by river discharge throughout all the seasons. Specifically, the shape featured by Type 4 occurred only in a few months in winter, similarly, mainly attributed to the relatively weak riverine forcing, resulting in minimal changes in the dH /dx  along the channel (with variance approximately 1.94 × 10−14 ). It is worth noting that the separation σx   of x 1,2  to xp   is meaningful only in Type 1 distributions. Considering the results obtained by Table 4 , the σx   for different periods were calculated. The results showed that the σx   for water level always occurred in the wet season, but its frequency of occurrence decreased considerably in the Post-human Period, and the values were 51.32 and 57.18 km for the Pre-human and Post-human Period on average, respectively. This indicated that even during the wet season, the water level increased almost linearly from seaward to landward, reflecting the impact of reservoir regulations on the river discharge, thereby reducing the influence of upstream river discharge on the river-tide interactions. Conversely, for the tidal range, the σx   were rare, observed only in March 2010 during the Post-human Period, whereas occasional occurrences were noted in August and September during the Pre-human Period, particularly when the relative mean sea level was high. The average σx   values for the Pre-human and the Post-human Periods were 17.75 km and 31.92 km, respectively, indicating a regime shift in river-tide dynamics characterized by significant changes in the position of the minimum tidal range gradient.   5 Discussions 5.1 Underlying mechanism for the alterations in the water level and tidal range distributions To more clearly clarify the underlying mechanism behind the alterations in the water level and tidal range distributions, a comparison of monthly averaged river discharge, tidal range at the estuary mouth, and relative mean sea level for the two distinct periods was conducted (Fig. 8  ). The monthly averaged river discharge at MK hydrological station (Fig. 8 a) increased in January, June and December, while decreased in other months, mainly owing to the freshwater regulations by upstream reservoirs. The largest and smallest monthly averaged river discharge occurred in summer and winter, respectively, resulting in larger and smaller water levels and their gradients in the central and upper parts. Meanwhile, the tidal ranges and their gradients were the smallest and largest in corresponding seasons, responding to the seasonal differences in river discharge. At the downstream boundary, the tidal range at SZ station displayed a minor decline tendency of approximately 0.04 m (representing only 4 % of the average value), with negligible influence of the tidal input. Although the relative mean sea level (indicated by the monthly averaged water level at SZ station) exhibited an apparent increase due to global warming, this rise was relatively small compared to changes in channel bathymetry caused by sand excavations, implying a relatively minor impact on the hydrodynamics regime (approximately 4.29 mm/year). In addition to the dynamical boundary conditions, the morphological evolution caused by large-scale sand excavations along the channel and land reclamations near the estuary mouth also significantly contributed to the regime shift in river-tide dynamics. The thalweg elevation between DLS and MK decreased by approximately 5.16 m from 1962 to 2014 (equating to approximately 9.73 cm/year, exceeding the yearly average increase in relative mean sea level by more than 26 times), causing the surface water level profile to gradually decline in response to the new riverbed elevation. This led to a consistent decline in water levels in the central and upper parts of the Modaomen Estuary (Yang et al., 2020 ). Meanwhile, the uneven deepening of the riverbed led to the amplification of the tidal forcing in terms of the faster tidal wave celerity and weaker tidal damping effect (Cai et al., 2012 ). Conversely, land reclamations near the estuary mouth artificially extended the channel seaward (approximately 16.5 km from 1978 to 2014) and reduced the area covered by water (Tan et al., 2019 ), leading to a slight decline in tidal range due to the reduction of the tidal prism. These combined changes ultimately reduced the ranges of water level and tidal range from seaward to landward (referring to Table S1  in the Supporting information ), thereby causing the regime shift in hydrodynamics by both the decreasing water level gradient (dZ /dx ) and the absolute value of tidal range gradient (dH /dx ). Since both the hydrodynamics regime and the boundary conditions demonstrated clear stepwise alterations and seasonal differences, further studies are necessary to explore the relationship between marginal input and the model coefficients (xp  , μ  and m ). Here, we compared the impacts of upstream river discharge, tidal range near the estuary mouth, and relative mean sea level on the three model coefficients for water level and tidal range, respectively (Fig. 9  ). For water levels, critical river discharge thresholds for xp   and μ  (approximately 5000 m3 /s and 7500 m3 /s for both the Pre-human and the Post-human periods) were identified, corresponding to minimum values for water level distributions, while the m  exhibited an almost exponential decrease with river discharge. Similar trends were observed in the relationship between relative mean sea level and μ  and m  (Fig. 9 n and o). However, the correlations between the tidal range at the estuary mouth and the model coefficients were relatively weak. For tidal ranges, river discharge attenuated tidal energy by reducing the coefficient μ  and m , tending to shift the maximum tidal damping effect seaward. The characteristics of tidal range distributions were closely correlated with the tidal range near the estuary mouth (Fig. 9 k and l), indicating that more intense tidal energy input led to more pronounced tidal attenuations. In conclusion, the river discharge and relative mean sea level affected considerably the changes in the regression coefficients, especially the μ  and m , thereby contributing to variations in water level distributions. For the tidal range distributions, the primary controlling factors were the tidal input, followed by river discharge and relative mean sea level. This suggested that the model coefficients were related to the dynamical boundary conditions, providing scientific guidelines for exploring the underlying linkages among them in the future and a possible line of inquiry for future research.  5.2 Underlying mechanism for the formation of different types of distribution curves for water level and tidal range Since the spatial distributions of water level were closely related to river discharge and reflected by the alterations in the coefficient m , it is essential to explore the water fluctuations and elevations induced by river discharge and the riverbed elevations in cross sections. Previous studies have shown abrupt morphological evolutions along the Modaomen Estuary, characterized by a narrowing and deepening tendency (Liu et al., 2019 ). Here, we adopted a conceptual diagram (Fig. 10  ) depicting different cross-sections to illustrate and simulate the morphological evolutions in the Modaomen Estuary. It was notable that the influence of river discharge was relatively minor, with the changing ratio being 9 % in both wet and dry seasons. Therefore, the self-adaptive adjustment of water levels caused by the variations in the channel bathymetry and volume was the major controlling factor of the regime shift in river-tide dynamics in terms of the difference in types of water level and tidal range distribution curves. As shown in Fig. 10 , the water level might decrease due to the channel deepening. Seasonal differences and varying river discharge conditions slightly altered the range of water levels, primarily due to relatively minor alterations in river discharge, while fluctuations (i.e., tidal range) also increased due to the geometry convergence (Zhang et al., 2021a,b ). This phenomenon indicated that the alterations in water levels and tidal ranges were primarily driven by the seasonal variations in the storage area. In the case of the dry season with a low river discharge and relatively small water level, the response of channel bathymetry to the different river discharge values was considerably faster than that due to the cross-sectional area primarily because of the smaller lateral storage area (Yang et al., 2020 ), which resulted in a faster changing rate in water level along the channel. Conversely, the increasing rate of the channel bathymetry slowed down with increasing river discharge (corresponding to the wet season) due to the substantial enhancement in the lateral storage area (i.e., water surface area), thereby slowing down spatial variations in water level. Similarly, with respect to the stepwise alterations in the morphology and its influence on the river-tide dynamics, the more sensitive response of the water level variations to the lateral storage area in the Post-human Period compared to the Pre-human Period was attributed to the increasing channel depth and volume along the Modaomen Estuary. Consequently, this eventually led to a shift in water level and tidal range distribution curves. To more precisely assess the significant influence of morphological changes on the river-tide dynamic regime, we investigated the boundary conditions (upstream river discharge, tidal range, and water level at the estuary mouth) under which the four types of distribution curves were formed, alongside differences across two distinct periods. Notably, the spatial distribution curves for tidal range, characterized as Type 2 in both periods and Type 4 in the Pre-human Period, were absent, indicating rapid damping near the estuary mouth and a generally linear damping trend in certain situations, like in winter when tidal forces were stronger. Section 4.4  reveals that the pattern associated with Type 1 occurred only once, making detailed discussions about stepwise changes for these instances unrepresentative. We noted a decrease in average river discharge from about 12,700 m3 /s to 7,300 m3 /s when shifting from Type 1 to Type 3 in the Pre-human Period, and from roughly 6,800 m3 /s to 3,000 m3 /s from Type 3 to Type 4 in the Post-human Period, coinciding with a decrease in tidal range at the estuary mouth. For water level distribution curves, we consider four types across both periods. The average river discharge decreased with the transition from Type 1 to Type 4 during both periods, aligning with findings from Section 4.4 . Notably, river discharge increased for all types, largely due to the effects of varying river discharges and corresponding storage areas on water levels. Type 1 configurations required higher river discharges (approximately 13,500 m3 /s and 17,700 m3 /s in the Pre-human and Post-human periods, respectively) to accommodate the increasing cross-sectional area. In contrast, Type 4 configurations often emerged with lower river discharges and smaller lateral storage areas, with increases in river discharge (by approximately 1,000 m3 /s) likely due to redistribution effects from reservoir regulations. Further analysis included the water level near the estuary mouth (at the SZ tidal gauging station) and river discharge. Generally, river discharges associated with Type 2 were significantly higher than those for Type 3 in both periods, with different patterns observed for the relative mean sea level. In the Pre-human Period, nonlinear changes in water levels near the estuary mouth for Type 2 could be due to the high relative mean sea level, whereas for Type 3, with its relatively low mean sea level, water levels increased along the channel with moderate river discharge. An interesting slowing in the rate of increase at the channel's apex was noted, possibly due to a sudden expansion in the water surface area. Significant changes in estuarine geometry and the submerged delta near the estuary mouth impacted the hydrodynamic regime along the channel. In the Post-human Period, differences in channel bathymetry and the reduction of shoals near the estuary mouth made the lower morphology more channel-like, facilitating clearer identification of the formation mechanisms for Types 2 and 3. The water level distributions in the Post-human Period showed a closer correlation with relative mean sea levels, approximately −0.18 m and −0.12 m for Types 2 and 3, respectively. The pattern for Type 2, resulting from high river discharge and low sea level, suggested that the river discharge's increasing effect on water level could not fully counteract the diminishing effect of an expanding storage area, leading to a nearly linear increase in the upper part. Conversely, for Type 3, a relatively moderate river discharge could support the nonlinearity of water level variations in the upper part due to the high relative mean sea level. In summary, the formation of the four types of distribution curves for water level and tidal range, along with their stepwise alterations, were closely linked to the morphological evolution, variations in river discharge and relative mean sea level. Moreover, the combinations, mutual interactions and relative strength (especially some opposing effects on the river-tide dynamics) among these variables under different conditions were also the major factors contributing to varying characteristics for river-tide dynamics spatial distribution curves. Further studies on the influence of such alterations caused by intensive human interventions (e.g., reservoir constructions, sand excavations, channel dredging, and land reclamations) on the spatial–temporal evolution of river-tide dynamics are needed to further explore the underlying mechanisms.  5.3 Implications for the water resources management The results derived from this study have indicated that the intensive human interventions, mainly including reservoir regulations, sand excavations, channel dredging, and land reclamations, had substantially changed the hydrodynamics regime along the Modaomen Estuary because of the changes in dynamical boundary conditions and morphology on both seasonal and interannual scales. Specifically, in response to these changes, reservoir regulations result in a redistribution of water discharge and sediment load, reflected by a slight decline in river discharge and water levels, yet an increase in tidal range due to less tidal damping effect (Liu et al., 2014, 2019 ). Sand excavations reduce the effective friction on tidal propagations (Cai et al., 2018 ), thereby reducing the water level and increasing the tidal range, similar to the impacts of channel dredging (Jia et al., 2013 ). Land reclamations lead to a slight decrease in tidal prism (Shen et al., 2022 ), hence the tidal range at the estuary mouth. On the other hand, the water levels increase due to the decline in the area covered by water, combined with global climate changes (Cai et al., 2019c ). Additionally, due to these human interventions, the probability of extreme water levels during wet seasons considerably decreased (She et al., 2023 ). Particularly, the results derived from the GUH model suggest a trend towards decreasing water level and its gradient, alongside increasing tidal range and its gradient, ultimately leading to enhanced tidal dynamics, especially in the central and upper parts of the Modaomen Estuary. Such considerable human-induced alterations have vital implications for sustainable water resources management in the estuarine environments (Hoitink and Jay, 2016; Passalacqua et al., 2021 ), closely linked with sediment transportation (Talke et al., 2009; de Jonge et al., 2014; Jalón-Rojas et al., 2016 ), water quality (Zhu et al., 2015 ), and ecosystem stability (Tao et al., 2020; Niu et al., 2020 ). For example, alterations in the relationship between river discharge and minimum dH /dx  suggest a reduced tidal damping effect under identical river discharge conditions, which assists in preventing salinity intrusions and enhancing water quality security. This indicates that appropriate flood discharge can be carried out to increase the tidal attenuations during severe salinity intrusion events. However, flood discharge may increase the water level and its gradient, which must be considered for embankment safety. Additionally, the alterations in the relationship between model coefficients and dynamical boundaries (e.g., river discharge, tidal range at the estuary mouth and relative mean sea level) can identify the regime shifts influenced by these external forces. This can simulate the river-tide dynamics in estuaries under some specific conditions (e.g., sea level rise, flood events and large tidal energy input), assisting in the development of scientific strategies for sustainable water resources management while planning policies such as bridge construction, regular channel dredging, land reclamation, and other water resource allocation projects, considering the development needs of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and the effects of human interventions. Numerous previous studies have confirmed the substantial influence of human interventions on river-tide dynamics in estuaries worldwide, with stepwise alterations closely linked to sediment patterns (e.g., suspended sediment concentration and mouth bar formation) (Liu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022 ), energy transport (Zhang et al., 2024a,b ), morphodynamic equilibrium (Guo et al., 2015 ) and water security concerns (e.g., flood, salt intrusion and storm surge prevention) (Zhang et al., 2021c; Gong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024 ). Over the last half-century, the Modaomen Estuary was subject to large-scale and high-intensity anthropogenic interventions resulting in uneven increases in bathymetry that weaken tidal damping effects and effective friction. Moreover, some potential future human interventions, such as bridge constructions (e.g., Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link and Huangmaohai Sea-crossing Passage), regular channel dredging, regular land reclamations (e.g., artificial islands of the sea-crossing bridges), some water resource allocation projects (e.g., the Pearl River Delta Water Resources Allocation Project), and other measures that satisfy the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, may further affect the river-tide dynamics in the Modaomen Estuary or the whole Pearl River Delta. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the impacts of these highly modified boundary conditions on the dynamic equilibrium in the channel, as they played a significant role in the sustainable water resources management in the Modaomen Estuary, even the whole Pearl River Delta. The successful application of the proposed GUH model to the Modaomen Estuary to reconstruct the river-tide dynamics demonstrated that this new approach could be a simple yet useful tool for identifying the influence of natural forcing (e.g., natural process and global changes) and human activities (e.g., reservoir constructions, sand excavations and land reclamations) on the hydrodynamic regime in the highly human-modified estuaries worldwide. For specific applications, readers can make some appropriate adaptations, such as the relative distances, water level and tidal range series based on the data facts, to make use of the GUH model in other estuaries worldwide. For more details, readers can refer to https://github.com/Huayangcai/General-Unit-Hydrograph-Model-for-River-tide-Dynamics-V1.0-Matlab-Toolbox.git  for another example of the Yangtze River Estuary. Additionally, with the perspective of the simulations of water level and tidal range distributions, the proposed GUH model can well reproduce water levels and tidal ranges both within and outside the estuary compared to several interpolation methods (e.g., Spline, Piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (Pchip) and Modified Akima piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (Makima)). The results display that the performance of the GUH model, especially for the tidal range, is much better than other interpolation methods, with the limitation of the extrapolation (see Fig. S9  in the Supporting Information ). This improvement can be validly used for the prediction of the river-tide dynamics, thus providing scientific guidelines for sustainable water management (such as flood control and salt intrusion) and contributing to the modelling of water level and tidal range distributions in the future.   6 Conclusions In this study, we proposed a new GUH model to describe the spatial distributions of water level and tidal range to systematically investigate the regime shift in the river-tide dynamics in the Modaomen Estuary. The evolution of hydrodynamic pattern in terms of both water level gradient and tidal range gradient, in principle, was delineated into three distinct periods by the accumulated anomaly curve, including the Pre-human Period (1965–1988), the Transitional Period (1989–1998), and the Post-human Period (1999–2017). Observations revealed a significant alteration in the river-tide dynamics along the Modaomen Estuary, marked by a decline in water level and an increase in tidal range. These changes were mainly attributed to the impact of intensive human interventions on the seasonal variations in river discharge and stepwise alterations in the morphology. To quantify the regime shift in the river-tide dynamics, the new GUH model was applied to reconstruct the water level and tidal range along the channel, with good correspondence between the observed and computed data. The good performance of the proposed GUH model in the Modaomen Estuary is mainly due to the fact that Eqs. (4) and (5)  are monotonic functions whose first derivatives (i.e., Eqs. (6) and (7) , respectively) do not change signs and have only one maximum and minimum value, respectively, which correctly corresponds to the characteristics of spatial distributions of water level and tidal range along the Modaomen Estuary, together with their gradients. Such an application to the Modaomen Estuary requires the monotonicity of data inputs (see Fig. 5 ), suggesting that the nonmonotonicity of data facts may lead to inaccuracy of the GUH model, which restricts the applicability while applying it to other estuaries where the hydrodynamic regime is complicated. The results derived from the model showed that the model coefficients (xp  , μ  and m ) for reproducing water level and tidal range have experienced stepwise alterations and seasonal differences, generally with a decrease in μ  yet an increase in m  for water level distributions, and a decrease in both μ  and m for tidal range distributions, thereby reducing the maximum dZ /dx  and the absolute value of dH /dx . Additionally, the relationship between river discharge and them altered considerably, revealing the regime shifts in river-tide dynamics due to morphological evolutions. Sensitivity analyses elucidated the impact of boundary conditions on spatial distributions of water level and tidal range through their influence on model coefficients, especially the μ  and m , in varying manners. Based on this, we categorized the distribution types of water level and tidal range according to the number of the inflection points in the instantaneous UH, elucidating their characteristics and the underlying mechanism. The good performance of this model suggests that it can be used as a useful tool for providing scientific guidelines for sustainable water resources management in the Modaomen Estuary and other estuaries subject to intensive human interventions.
1 Introduction Accurate depiction of the subsurface rock's pore structure and physical properties is crucial for various applications, including hydrogeology, geotechnical engineering, petroleum engineering, natural gas hydrate recovery, underground gas storage, and geological sequestration of carbon dioxide (Yang et al., 2021 ; Cai et al., 2022 ). Digital rock technology, recognized for its efficiency and intuitiveness, has become a widely used tool in quantitative analyzing rock structures and studying multi-physical field response characteristics (Dong et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2020 ; Al Balushi et al., 2022 ; Mitchell et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Digital rock physical simulations minimize both the duration and expense associated with traditional experiments, simulate conditions that are challenging to achieve in a laboratory setting, have better repeatability, and clarify the internal physical processes (Karimpouli et al., 2016 ; Ettemeyer et al., 2020 ; Lissa et al., 2021 ). Accurate reconstruction of the pore structure is fundamental to rock physics simulations, and conventional techniques encompass both numerical reconstruction and physical experimental approaches. Numerical methods involve the 3D reconstruction of pore structures from 2D images or derived parameters such as porosity, particle size, and the distribution of pores and throats obtained from experimental test data. They include techniques like Gaussian field method (Torquato and Lu, 1993 ), process-based method (Coelho, 1997 ), simulated annealing (Hazlett, 1997 ), sequential indicator simulation (Keehm et al., 2004 ), multiple point statistics (Okabe and Blunt, 2004 ), and Markov chain Monte Carlo method (Wu et al., 2006 ). Physical experimental methods, such as Computed Tomography (CT) scanning (Xiao and Zhou, 2023 ), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) (Golsanami et al., 2022 ), and Focused Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM) (Liu et al., 2023 ), are used to visualize and capture realistic representations of pore structures. Given the distinct advantages and limitations of each method, they are often combined in practical applications to obtain a more comprehensive pore structure (Sok et al., 2010 ; Wang et al., 2022 ). Numerical reconstruction methods alone often fall short in accurately reconstructing 3D pore structures, leading to a growing preference for physical experimental methods in rock physics research in recent years. However, there is a contradiction between the field of view and resolution precision in a single testing method: higher resolution yields data that represent a smaller physical scale. For example, high-precision FIB-SEM typically represents an extremely small physical size. While CT scanning provides 3D imaging, its pore identification accuracy at equivalent resolutions is significantly lower than that of SEM due to differences in the imaging mechanisms of the equipment (Chi et al., 2024 ). The primary challenge in digital rock analysis is the precise reconstruction of pore structures from test data. This typically requires a combination of physical and numerical methods, such as the superposition of data from various sources and scales to create a multiscale digital rock model that integrates information across different resolutions (Tahmasebi et al., 2015 ). This approach is highly efficient for merging data sets with a small difference in resolution, but may encounter issues with structural overlap during the superposition process. Template matching is a method to compare whether two scales of information match, specifically using fine-scale information to find the area with the highest correlation on coarse-scale data, achieving refinement of coarse-scale data (Lin et al., 2019 ). This technique uses the 3D morphological attributes of the data, factoring in the correlation between data at varying resolutions. The simultaneous use of physical imaging and numerical reconstruction enhances modeling precision. Furthermore, while multiscale pore network modeling offers an efficient means for studying pore transport properties, its inability to accurately display real pore morphologies and to investigate rock mechanical properties, therefore it is not discussed in the present paper (Sun et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2024 ). In recent years, deep learning techniques, particularly generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models, have been increasingly applied to the modeling of digital rocks (Wang et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2024 ). Diffusion models offer more stable training but demand greater computational resources, presenting a significant challenge in processing 3D rock images (Luo et al., 2024 ). In contrast, GANs are more efficient in data generation, providing a distinct advantage in 3D image reconstruction. Early multiscale rock data fusion methods primarily used super-resolution techniques, such as variants of Super-Resolution Convolutional Neural Network (SRCNN) combined with architectures including GANs, U-Nets, Transformers, and diffusion models (Wang et al., 2020 ; Roslin et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Esmaeili et al., 2024 ; Xing et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2024 ). Initially proposed in computer vision, these methods have been adapted by researchers to enhance rock image quality. Each method has unique characteristics: GANs generate detailed images but may have unstable training; U-Nets preserve multiscale features for precise rock structure reconstruction but demand high computational resources; Transformers capture long-range correlations in rock images at the cost of significant computational resources; diffusion models produce high-quality images but involve complex training and slower inference speeds. From existing research, the super-resolution generative adversarial network (SRGAN) series of methods, which are more computationally efficient, have seen broader application in 3D digital rock reconstruction tasks (Wang et al., 2021 ). However, super-resolution technology, fundamentally an image enhancement technique, can only refine image details without adding missing structural information (Yan et al., 2023 ). This limitation is particularly evident when there is a substantial difference between high and low-resolution data. Moreover, super-resolution of rock images usually requires paired training data, which is difficult to obtain in practical applications. To address the challenge of obtaining paired training data, researchers have integrated SRCNN with cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) for inter-domain transformation between high and low-resolution images (Chen et al., 2020 ; Liu and Mukerji, 2022 ; Yan et al., 2023 ). This approach enables the mutual transformation of high and low-resolution rock images, avoiding the requirement for paired training data. By leveraging the gray-level distribution of both datasets, it can infer ambiguous, low-resolution information into a clear, high-resolution structure. This effectively integrates the visual fields and resolutions of high and low-resolution data, achieving a seamless fusion. However, constrained by computational limitations, current research mostly focuses on the transformation of 2D data, enhanced by longitudinal interpolation for 3D reconstruction. This includes the transformation of 2D data between CT images, and between CT and SEM images, followed by stacking to form a 3D representation. Moreover, even with adequate computational resources, existing data fusion methods are restricted to direct transformations within the same dimensions, either 2D to 2D or 3D to 3D, and are incapable of directly integrating 2D and 3D images. Consequently, there is a need for a method capable of directly incorporating high-precision 2D information of porous rocks into a 3D model. In light of the previously mentioned considerations, this paper introduces a GAN-based framework for the fusion of 2D and 3D rock images. The approach uses a hybrid super-resolution network that integrates both 2D and 3D structural components. The generative network employs a 3D structure to process low-resolution 3D images, yielding their high-resolution counterparts. Concurrently, the discriminative network, which is structured in 2D, refines the output of the generative network to align with the attributes of high-resolution 2D images. We conducted experiments using two distinct datasets of sandstone: the sample S1 derived from CT scans at varying resolutions and the sample S2 obtained through a combination of CT and SEM testing for tight sandstone. A comparative analysis of the pore structure characteristics and transport properties between the reconstructed and actual datasets was performed to ascertain the efficacy of our fusion method. The results from S1 confirm the high degree of correspondence between the synthesized high-resolution samples and their real-world counterparts. Furthermore, the outcomes of S2 demonstrate the capability of our approach to integrate pore structures from both SEM and CT data.  2 Methodology 2.1 Generative adversarial network for 2D and 3D data fusion Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a type of deep learning framework composed of a generator and a discriminator, used for generating high-quality images. The generator's objective is to transform random noise vectors into the data space, creating synthetic data samples that are similar to the distribution of real data. Conversely, the discriminator's role is to identify between these synthetic samples and real ones. During the training process, the Generator receives random noise as input and gradually learns how to generate more realistic samples. The task of the discriminator is to identify these generated samples in order to improve its ability to identify between real and fake samples. As training progresses, the generator and discriminator compete with each other in an adversarial environment, driving the performance of both to improve. The advantage of GANs lies in their ability to learn complex data distributions without presupposing the distribution of the training data. This feature has positioned GANs at the forefront of image generation research. Adversarial training enables the generator to ultimately generate indistinguishable synthetic samples, making them visually identical to real samples. This process causes continuous evolution of both the generator and discriminator, enhancing the performance of the model. Compared to other generative models, GANs provide a combination of high efficiency and generation quality, rendering them highly suitable for digital rock reconstruction. A GAN comprises a generator, which maps the latent space to the data space, and a discriminator, which differentiates between generated and actual data. Building upon this foundation, the SRGAN model was developed, with the generator and discriminator tasked to convert low-resolution (LR) data into high-resolution (HR) data and to distinguish between generated HR data and actual HR data, respectively. The existing approaches are categorized into two categories: in cases of a simple neural network architecture, operations are conducted directly on 3D LR and HR data; in contrast, with complex neural network structures, the computational demands on 3D data are more substantial, necessitating a shift to 2D data for processing. There is still a shortage of research on directly enhancing the quality of 3D data using 2D data. Employing the concept of super-resolution, we have developed a lightweight network framework that integrates 3D LR with 2D HR data (Dahari et al., 2023 ). Fig. 1   shows the network architecture for the entire workflow, featuring a 3D generator and a 2D discriminator. The generator is designed to impart the characteristics of 2D HR data to 3D LR data. After ample training iterations, the generator ultimately learns the underlying data distribution of actual samples, enabling the transformation of LR data into corresponding HR data, to the extent that the discriminator cannot discern whether the input is genuine. Considering the balance between the complexity of pore structure in 3D reconstruction tasks and the computational load of neural networks, the generator adopts only a residual structure, with upsampling performed at a later stage. Each 3D convolutional layer has a kernel size of 3, with padding and stride both set to 1, followed by batch normalization and activation functions. This design ensures that data dimensions only alter during upsampling, increasing to double the original size at each step. As illustrated, employing two upsampling layers results in output dimensions that are quadruple the input size. Additionally, we found that transposed convolution upsampling was less effective in this task, hence we adopted the method of convolution after interpolation. The discriminator is composed of a sequence of 2D convolutional layers with activation functions, processing both real 2D HR images and reconstructed HR slices, and providing discrimination outcomes. Each 2D convolutional layer uses a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 2. The training process begins with the input of a 3D LR data into the generator, yielding a 3D HR sample that is subsequently sliced along the x, y , and z  axes. These slices, along with the real 2D HR data, are separately input into the discriminator for training. Ultimately, the output of the generator is shaped by the input 3D LR pore structure while capturing the characteristics of 2D HR data. To avoid the risks of vanishing or exploding gradients and to enhance the stability of the training process, the model was trained using Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) (Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Chi et al., 2023 ). WGAN-GP uses the continuous Wasserstein distance to provide more stable gradient information and employs gradient penalty to ensure the discriminator meets Lipschitz continuity, preventing issues of exploding and vanishing gradients. A key distinction from traditional GANs is that WGAN-GP necessitates several discriminator updates for each generator update. The loss function consists of two components: the WGAN-GP loss and the reconstruction loss. Both the generator and the discriminator use the WGAN-GP loss, with an additional reconstruction loss added to the generator. This reconstruction loss, measured by the mean squared error (MSE), assesses the fidelity of the generated HR data G (ILR  ) relative to the original LR data ILR  . The reconstruction loss is formulated as follows:(1) L M S E   = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( I L R  i  − G ( I L R  i  )  ↓ )   2       At this point, the loss of generator can be expressed as:(2) L G  = − E I L R   ∼ p L R     [ D ( G ( I L R   )  )  ]  + β L M S E        The of discriminator loss is represented as:(3) L D  = − E I H R   ∼ p H R     [ D ( I H R   )  ]      + E I L R   ∼ p L R     [ D ( G ( I L R   )  )  ]      + λ E I L R   ∼ p L R     [ ( ∥ ∇ D ( α I H R   + ( 1 − α )  G ( I L R   )  )  | | 2  − 1 )  2  ]          Where LMSE , LG  , and LD   represent the mean squared error loss, generator loss, and discriminator loss, respectively.
