Given its sensitivity to parameters, meticulous calibration is essential to adapt the function to different contexts (Qin et al., 2024a ). The Flood Value is calculated based on four key factors: Inundation Factor (IF ), Population Factor (PF ), and Financial Loss Factors for Residential (LFr  ) and Non-Residential (LFnr  ) buildings:(4) V  i    = w 1  ∙ I F ( i )  + w 2  ∙ P F ( i )  + w 3  ∙ LF  r  ( i )  + w 4  ∙ LF  nr   ( i )      where w1  , w2  , w3  , and w4   represent the weights allocated to the four factors and may be adjusted to emphasise the significance of individual factors according to various objectives of the flood mitigation tasks; IF  has a value of 1 when the water depth is above a threshold, otherwise 0; PF , based on population density, indicates higher risk in more densely populated areas and is normalised for uniform assessment; LFr   and LFnr   quantify the flood-induced financial loss respectively to residential and non-residential buildings, both averaged and normalised across adjacent cells. The water depth impacting a building is determined by the maximum water depth in the cells defining the building edges. Financial loss per building (LFr   or LFnr  ) is derived from a function fitted to depth-damage data from the Multi-Coloured-Manual (MCM) handbook (Penning-Rowsell et al., 2014 ), where the flood loss changes linearly with the natural logarithm of maximum water depth (hmax  ) affected the building:(5) F i n a n c i a l  L o s s = m ln h  max   + n        Herein, the parameters m  and n  are adjustable to account for the sensitivity to flood depth and are influenced by various factors, such as construction materials, flood resistance, values of building contents, local development, and market price. In this work, different m  and n  values are used for residential and non-residential buildings to reflect different financial impacts. By integrating these different factors, the Flood Value offers a detailed measure of flood risk, encompassing both the human impact and property damages.  2.4 Reinforcement learning 2.4.1 Coupling with the subsystems The RL module directly interacts with the human and natural subsystems in the CHANS modelling framework. As depicted in Fig. 1 , state spaces are constructed for RL agents by integrating the predicted water depth with the stored social data to underpin the agents’ actions, i.e. guiding the decision-making processes of the governmental commander and pump executor agents within the human subsystem. The decisions in turn affect the natural subsystem dynamics, thus impacting flood risk. Rewards are generated based on the impact on flood risk, providing crucial feedback to support the learning and adaptation of RL agents.  2.4.2 Hierarchical decision-making structure The decision-making process for pump deployment is complex, given the vast array of potential at-risk zones, placements, and routes. As illustrated in Fig. 3  , this study employs a hierarchical RL strategy that divides decision-making into two levels. The computational domain is first evenly divided into a small number of Higher-level Zones (HZs), each of which is then further subdivided into Lower-level Zones (LZs). The higher-level RL agent is responsible for selecting the most critical HZ. After that, the lower-level agent will step in to refine pump placement to a specific LZ within the selected HZ. The final pump placement will be at the lowest point within the selected LZ.  2.4.3 Sequential training and integration The training and integration of RL agents within the hierarchical decision-making framework are conducted sequentially (Botvinick, 2012 ), as illustrated in Fig. 4  . Initially, the lower-level agent undergoes extensive training across different HZs until it achieves satisfactory performance, focusing on making decisions on precise pump placement in a LZ within any of the HZs under different flooding conditions. After achieving optimal performance, the lower-level agent is transitioned to an ‘offline’ mode, freezing its policy for consistent application without further updates. Subsequently, training commences for the higher-level agent, which is tasked to identify the most critical deployment zones in broad-scale flooding across the whole domain. The pre-trained lower-level agent is incorporated as a fixed-policy subroutine within this phase, informing the higher-level agent to decide the specific pump placement once an HZ is selected.  2.4.4 Configuration of the RL agents Fig. 4  shows the integration of the three core components – state, action, and reward – of RL agents at time step t  in each iterative episode (i.e., a flood event) during the training process. The detailed configuration of these components is described below.• State of RL agents    The state of an RL agent incorporates the observation information available at the time step to support its decision-making process. For a lower-level agent, the state is assessed based on observation data from all LZs within the selected HZ. The data involved includes water depth (h ) in flooded cells, population density (D ), and the count of flooded cells surrounding buildings (C ). A loss adjustment coefficient (lc ) is applied to non-residential buildings, reflecting their potential for higher flood losses. In an arbitrary LZ, these quantities are calculated and normalised at time step t  as follows:(6) h t  = ∑ h i     h max        (7) D t  = ∑ D i     D max        (8) C t  = ∑ ( C r  ( i )  + l c ∙ C nr   ( i )  )  C max        where i  is the index of a flooded cell in the LZ under consideration, subscript ‘max ’ denotes the maximum values of a specific quantity, and ‘r ’ and ‘nr ’ respectively represent residential and non-residential buildings. For an HZ divided into q  LZs, the state (slt  ) for the lower-level agent at time t  becomes a 3  × q -dimensional vector containing all the normalised state values in these LZs:(9) s lt   = h t 0   , h t 1   , ⋯ h  tq   , D t 0   , D t 1   , ⋯ D tq   , C t 0   , C t 1   , ⋯ C tq           Similarly, the higher-level agent processes similar state information for all p  HZs to provide an overview of the entire region.• Action of RL agents    The higher-level agent generates an action indexed by an integer ranging from 0 to p -1, where each number corresponds to one of the p  HZs. Similarly, the lower-level agent generates an action for each of the q  LZs within the selected HZ. The pump is placed at the lowest position in the LZ selected by the lower-level agent at time t . If the RL agents select the same zones at time t  as they did at the previous time interval, the pump remains in its current position for the next time interval.• Reward of RL agents    The rewards (rt  ) for both the higher- and lower-level agents are designed by quantifying the extent of reduction in the overall flood risk within a time interval. The higher-level agent evaluates the flood risk reduction across the entire region, while the lower-level agent focuses on a specific HZ. The overall flood risk at time t  (FRt  ) is determined using the approach outlined in Section 2.3 . To evaluate the effectiveness of pump deployment in changing flood risk, baseline scenarios without human interventions are simulated to produce a series of reference results from t  = 0 ∼ T (FRb0   ∼ FRbT  ) for each of the time intervals. The change in flood risk due to pumping (dFR ) is calculated by subtracting the baseline risk (FRbt  ) from the current risk (FRt  ):(10) dFR  t  = FR  t  - FR  bt        Negative dFR  indicates effective pumping operation leading to lower flood risk. To ensure the calculated risk reduction is solely attributed to pump action within a specific time interval (denoted as dFR't  ), it is necessary to exclude the reduction of risk that represents the cumulative reward (CRt  ) achieved before the current time interval:(11) dF R  ′   t  = dFR  t  - - CR  t         (12) CR  t  = ∑ 0  t - 1   r t       Finally, the negative dFR ′t   provides the reward to the RL agents after the current time interval:(13) r t  = - dF R  ′   t  = dFR  t - 1   - dFR  t      • Algorithm to enable RL agents    Both RL agents employ the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm to enable their learning, which is known for stable and efficient policy learning (Schulman et al., 2017 ). This gives agents the ability to recognise the most advantageous course of action in response to sequential observations of environmental states. PPO’s key features, such as truncated importance sampling and a surrogate objective function, enable effective strategy learning through controlled policy updates (Wang et al., 2020 ). These features help prevent destabilising performance variations, a crucial advantage in the variable and dynamic urban flooding context. The algorithm’s balance between substantial learning and stability makes it well-suited for managing the complexity of flood risk reduction strategies.   2.5 Sensitivity analysis The lower-level agent is trained using specific rainfall data across different HZs. Varying rainfall inputs may lead to different flood conditions in each HZ. This study examines two key types of sensitivity: (a) the overall flood risk across HZs under diverse rainfall scenarios, and (b) the effectiveness of lower-level agent’s actions in reducing flood risk across HZs under these scenarios. To support sensitivity analysis, two metrics are employed:• Overall Flood Risk Ratio (OFRR ) that compares the maximum flood risk resulting from different rainfall inputs against the risk produced by the rainfall datasets used for training in each HZ:   (14) OFRR = R max   ( j )   R max   ( j ′ )        • Flood Risk Reduction Ratio (FRRR ) that measures the effectiveness of lower-level agent’s actions in risk reduction under different rainfall scenarios vs the training conditions in each HZ:   (15) FRRR = Re ( j )  Re ( j ′ )       where j  and j'  are respectively used to index the scenario and training rainfall datasets, Rmax   represents the maximum flood risk in each HZ, and Re  denotes the flood risk reduction in each HZ.   3 Case study 3.1 Ninh Kieu District in the City of Can Tho The proposed CHANS framework is applied to explore the optimal mobile pump deployment strategies in the Ninh Kieu (NK) District, Can Tho City, Vietnam. As the largest city in the Mekong Delta, Can Tho faces significant urban flooding challenges (Huong and Pathirana, 2013 ). Known as the most flood-prone urban district within Can Tho, NK District is characterised by its low-lying terrain, riverside location, and high population and building densities. Specifically, as illustrated in Fig. 5  , the northeastern part of NK District, with dense population, high coverage of buildings and public facilities, is particularly vulnerable to pluvial flooding induced by heavy rainfall, making it the most high-risk region. The region is embraced by rivers on three sides and contains a lake at the centre, rendering it an ideal case study site for the current research. Herein, mobile pumps are envisioned to alleviate flooding by transferring stormwater to the nearby river channel, assuming that such action will not lead to river overflow.  3.2 Design pluvial flood events In this study, the RL agents are trained using the pluvial flood induced by a 1-in-20-year design rainfall event. The training is performed in two periods/scenarios: (a) concurrent pluvial flooding (CPF) lasting 90 min, and (b) post-rainfall pluvial flooding (PPF) extending for 120 min. To enhance training efficiency and reduce computational time, the RL agents are initially trained through CPF, followed by fine-tuning through PPF. The detailed training methodology will be elaborated in Section 3.5.4 . To evaluate the sensitivity and adaptability of RL agents to various flood scenarios induced by different rainfall, 50 and 100-year design rainfall for the present time (year 2020) and 10-year rainfall projected for the future (2050) are utilised for testing, as listed in Table 1  .  3.3 Data collection and processing For hydrodynamic modelling, the simulation domain is represented using a 3 m Digital Terrain Model (DTM), resampled from a 5 m DTM provided by Can Tho University. Building shapefiles are extracted from Microsoft Bing Maps’ open-source global building footprints, obtained from satellite imagery. All cells occupied by buildings are raised by 5 m to create the final 3 m Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Land-use and land-cover (LULC) data, with a resolution of 10 m, are obtained from the 2020 high-resolution products released by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) Earth Observation Research Center (EORC). Finally, the hydrodynamic simulations are driven by the uniform design rainfall data provided by Can Tho University, as specified in Table 1 . For ABM, the population density in the NK District is derived from the High Resolution Population Density Maps + Demographic Estimates by the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), resampled to a 3 m resolution using gradient interpolation, as depicted in Fig. 6  (a). Within each 100 m resolution grid, residential buildings are randomly identified based on population and building area ratios. The population is distributed among the buildings according to their size, as depicted in Fig. 6 (b). Except for residential buildings, the rest are flagged as non-residential buildings, as shown in Fig. 6 (c). Information on the cells defining building edges is processed using ArcGIS to extend the building polygons by 3 m and then rasterise them into 3 m raster data aligned with the DEM.  3.4 The baseline and control simulation scenarios 3.4.1 Baseline scenario The baseline scenario simulates the natural pluvial flooding process, excluding human interventions. The computational domain is segmented into 25 square zones, each 13.7 s wide, based on geographical coordinates. The 15 zones covering the high-risk area, sequentially numbered from 0 to 14 (Fig. 7  ), are selected as the potential HZs for pump deployment. To train the lower-level RL agent, as detailed in Section 2.4.4 , the baseline simulation tracks the time-varying flood risk in each HZ to provide the necessary data for calculating rewards.  3.4.2 Control scenario As illustrated in Fig. 8  , each HZ is subdivided into 16 square LZs for the pump executor to select the location for pump placement. In each LZ, the placement location will be the lowest point on any accessible road. An LZ lacking accessible roads will be labelled as Null  by the pump executor and excluded from selection. A set of control simulation scenarios are designed by adopting a traditional risk reduction strategy thatfocuses on the lowest locations prone to water logging, to serve as the benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of pump deployment guided by RL agents. Across the whole domain, the LZ-5 in HZ-10, the lowest location across the entire domain, is chosen for pump deployment to create the overall control scenario. In each of the HZ, the LZ with the lowest loication is selected for pump placement to form a localised control scenaior. The selections made in the different control scenarios are detailed in Table 2  , listing the LZ selected for each HZ and the entire region, respectively.   3.5 Model setup Application of the proposed CHANS framework involves configuring the natural and human subsystems and the RL agents, which will be introduced in the following sub-sections. 3.5.1 Hydrodynamic modelling For hydrodynamic modelling using HiPIMS, the computational domain is discretised using a 3 m DEM, involving about 350,000 grid cells. Uniform rainfall inputs as summarised in Table 1  are used to drive the simulations. The domain is assumed to be initially dry for all CPF simulations, whilst all PPF simulations start from the flooding conditions predicted for the corresponding 90-minute rainfall events. Manning coefficients are assigned according to different land use types as listed in Table 3  . In the absence of urban drainage data, a calibrated constant infiltration rate of 57 mm/h is applied to urban roads. The infiltration rate of 3 mm/h for other urban areas is derived from soil characteristics via the SPAW model (Jiang, 2022 ).  3.5.2 Human subsystem modelling In the current study, the pump vehicle is equipped with a parallel group of pumps and has an overall efficiency of 0.3 m3 /s. To prevent running dry, the minimum operating water depth is set at 0.15 m. When the local water depth falls below this threshold, the pump ceases operation until the next command from the RL agents arrives. As 20 min are required for pump dispatch and deployment, no pump operation is assumed during the first 20 min of a flood event. The subsequent pump deployment decisions are made every 10 min. Residential and non-residential buildings are defined as heterogeneous agents, each storing their type tags and edge cell indexes. The parameters for financial loss calculation are derived from local field surveys (Chinh et al., 2016a,b ), with m  = 800 and n  = 1.6 assigned for residential buildings, and m  = 2000 and n  = 1.2 for non-residential buildings to reflect higher average loss. Accordingly, the coefficient lc  = 2 is used in calculating the RL state, indicating the relative loss between building types.  3.5.3 Flood risk assessment The overall flood risk is determined by aggregating the risk values calculated in individual grid cells (Eq. (2) ), as previously introduced in Section 2.3 . The parameters k  = 15 and d  = 0.25 are used for the calculation of flood probability (Eq. (3) ), chosen based on local surveys. It assumes the flood probability is negligible at a water depth of 0.1 m or lower, but escalates sharply beyond 0.25 m of depth (Chinh et al., 2016a ). To calculate IF , the threshold is also set at 0.1 m to indicate the presence of flooding. Given the high density of population and buildings in the study domain, PF , LFr  , and LFnr   are prioritised in the calculation of Flood Value (Eq. (4) ). Acknowledging the greater financial impact on non-residential buildings due to business disruptions, LFnr   is assigned with a weight doubling that of LFr   (Chinh et al., 2016a ). Consequently, the weights, w1   (IF ), w2   (PF ), w3   (LFr  ), and w4   (LFnr  ), are set at 0.1, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.4, respectively, to balance the various factors contributing to flood risk.  3.5.4 RL training For RL training, each rainfall event constitutes a training episode. At the onset of each episode, the RL environment resets the simulation arrays generated by HiPIMS predictions and reinitialises water depth and velocity data for new calculations. To diversify training contexts and avoid overfitting, the lower-level agent is presented with a randomly selected HZ at the start of each episode. The first two time intervals of every episode are allocated for the pump executor to travel to the initial destination, during which the pumps remain inactive. A curriculum learning strategy is employed to support RL training, which is segmented into initial training and fine-tuning phases. In the initial phase, agents are trained on CPF events, characterised by their immediate and intense nature. The initial learning rate (α) is set at 0.001 to balance stability and aggressiveness to ensure progressive and effective policy development. The discount factor (γ) is set at 0.99, reflecting a focus on long-term outcomes by accounting for both immediate and cumulative effects of pumping actions over time. Upon convergence of the cumulative reward in the initial training phase, the training transitions to a fine-tuning phase adapted to PPF events. In this phase, three key hyperparameters are adjusted: the learning rate (α), clip range (ε), and entropy coefficient. The learning rate, which controls the step size for policy updates (Schulman et al., 2017 ), is slightly reduced to refine the policy without causing instability. The clip range, which limits the magnitude of policy updates (Zhang et al., 2019 ), is adjusted to prevent large, destabilising changes during further training. The entropy coefficient adds an entropy term to the reward function to encourage exploration and it is raised to promote exploration and prevent the agents from adhering to potentially suboptimal strategies in the more complex PPF scenarios (Schulman et al., 2017 ).    4 Results 4.1 Flood conditions in the baseline simulation In the CPF baseline simulation, the score of flood risk for each of the HZs progressively increases from 0 to its peak (Fig. 9  ), consistent with gradual increase of urban runoff and water accumulation induced by the uniform design rainfall. Fig. 10   depicts the spatial distribution of flood risk in these HZs at different output times. HZ-6 records the highest overall flood risk at the end of the rainfall. During the PPF baseline simulation, the flood risk in each HZ gradually declines after rainfall stops, attributed to urban drainage and surface infiltration. Fig. 11   illustrates the temporal change of the risk scores across the 15 HZs, highlighting the dynamic nature of the flooding process and risk in the aftermath of rainfall.  4.2 The effectiveness of traditional deployment strategy In the control simulations implemented with the traditional deployment strategy, the mobile pump is positioned at the lowest location across the whole domain or in an HZ, as specified in Table 2 . During the CPF event, Fig. 12  (a) illustrates the change in flood risk scores and the scale of risk reduction due to pump deployment across the 15 HZs. As the first 20 min of the event are needed for pump dispatch and setup, noticeable risk reduction commences only after that. The traditional deployment strategy is observed to reduce flood risk in all 15 HZs, with notable reductions in HZ-1, 3, 9, and 11 by approximately 60 points. Similarly, for the PPF event, Fig. 12 (b) shows the change of flood risk scores and risk reduction levels. Overall, the traditional pump deployment strategy is shown to significantly reduce flood risk in about half of the HZs, especially in HZ-3 where the risk reduction is calculated to exceed 100 points. However, it is found to be less effective in the remaining HZs. Over the entire domain, the mobile pump is stationed at LZ-5 of HZ-10, i.e. the lowest location in the domain. Fig. 13   shows the change of risk score and risk mitigation level for both CPF and PPF events. The trend of risk reduction appears to be similar to that of HZ-10 as shown in Fig. 12 , indicating that traditional strategy only creates noticeable outcomes in the HZ where the pump is located.  4.3 Performance of RL-based pump deployment After applying the RL-based pump deployment strategy, Table 4   entails the lower-level agent’s pump deployment schedule across all HZs, encompassing 9 actions for the CPF events and 12 for the PPF events. Herein, identical LZ numbers in sequence indicate the pump continues to operate in the same location, whereas differing consecutive numbers suggest the pump’s relocation to a new LZ, with a temporary stop of its operation to accommodate the movement. The first 10-minute slot is used to discuss and form the first decision, and marked with ‘x’ to indicate no pumping activity. Fig. 14  (a) shows the temporal changes in flood risk scores across all HZs during the CPF event, highlighting the reduction of flood risk achieved through the RL-based deployment strategy, which outperforms the traditional deployment approach in almost all HZs. In over half of the HZs, the RL-based approach scores better than the traditional strategy’s maximum reduction of 60 points. Particularly, the difference in risk reduction scores exceeds 50 points in HZ-0 and HZ-6. Exceptions are noticed for HZ-1, HZ-5, and HZ-12, where both strategies select the same location for pump placement, leading to similar risk reduction scores. Overall, the results demonstrate the enhanced effectiveness of the RL-based deployment approach in mitigating flood risk across various urban zones. For the PPF event as illustrated in Fig. 14 (b), the RL-based deployment produces a final risk reduction score surpassing that achieved by the traditional approach by more than 50 points in most of the HZs. Notably, the resulting risk reduction scores reach almost 200 in HZ-3, and approximately 150 in HZ-0, 1, and 6. In HZ-0, 2, 4, 6, 13, and 14, the risk reduction scores produced by the RL-based approach are 3 to 10 times higher than those achieved by the traditional deployment method. Over the entire domain, Table 5   entails the combined decisions made by the higher- and lower-level agents for pump deployment over both HZs and LZs during the CPF and PPF events. For the 90-minute CPF event, the RL-guided strategy starts with operating the pump in LZ-6 of HZ-6 for 40 min, followed by 20 min in LZ-3 of HZ-3, with a 10-minute transition time between the two locations. In the 120-minute PPF event, the RL-guided strategy involves shifting the mobile pump across three different HZs, starting from HZ-0, moving through three successive locations in HZ-3, and ending up in HZ-6. Fig. 15   illustrates the dynamic change of flood risk in the entire region to demonstrate the effectiveness of RL-guided deployment strategy respectively for CPF and PPF events. In the CPF event, there shows a noticeable dip in risk reduction when the mobile pump is being relocated and not in operation. Conversely, during the PPF event, the risk reduction score maintains a generally increasing trend even during the pump is being repositioned, although the increasing rate is flat for a few periods of time. The orange dotted line highlights the advantage of the RL-guided strategy in comparison to the traditional approach. The RL-guided strategy is shown to achieve twice higher in final risk reduction score for the CPF event, and nearly four times higher for the PPF event, compared with that obtained through the traditional approach.  4.4 The training episodes and time The training and testing of the RL agents are conducted on a server configuring an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Silver 4210R CPU @ 2.40 GHz, 128 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA A100-PCIe GPU with 40 GB of memory. The convergence of the PPO algorithm is determined by monitoring the cumulative reward and loss function over the training episodes. Table 6   records the number of training episodes (n ) and the corresponding training durations. The lower-level agent demonstrates optimal performance after around 3000 episodes, with its cumulative reward and loss function becoming stabilised; thus n  = 3000 is taken as the optimal count for the initial training episodes. Coming to the fine-tuning phase, the cumulative reward and loss function become stabilised after approximately 1200 episodes; thus n  = 1200 is adopted as the optimal number of episodes for fine-tuning. Subsequently, the higher-level agent, integrated with the pre-trained lower-level agent, undergoes training across the entire study domain. For the samples drawn from the CPF and PPF events, the higher-level agent shows commendable performance based on the same convergence criteria after respectively 900 and 600 training episodes.  4.5 Sensitivity analysis 4.5.1 Flood risk induced by different rainfall inputs Utilising the approach described in Section 2.5 , the Overall Flood Risk Ratios (OFRRs ) are calculated for the flood events driven by three different rainfall inputs across the 15 HZs and displayed in Table 7  . The Confidence Intervals (CIs) at a 95 % confidence level are further quantified for the OFRR  results. A narrow range of CIs signifies that the OFRRs  are tightly distributed around their mean values. This demonstrates the stability and consistency of the flood risk assessment results produced by the CHANS framework, confirming its reliability in flood risk assessment under various rainfall conditions. Fig. 16   presents the scatter plots to further demonstrate the relationships between the three sets of OFRR  results, with each subplot comparing two sets of results. The plots clearly indicate that the results are uniformly stable across all HZs. All calculations return similar increases in flood risk although the training datasets for the RL agents are associated with different flood risk assessment scores, with higher rainfall intensities leading to increased risk. The observation aligns with the conclusions from the CI analysis, underscoring a stable relationship between varied rainfall inputs and flood risk assessment across the HZs.  4.5.2 Effectiveness of RL agent in flood risk reduction For the CPF and PPF events, the Flood Risk Reduction Ratio (FRRR ) in each HZ is calculated against the flood scenarios induced by three different rainfall inputs, as shown in Table 8  . A more diverse distribution of CIs is observed in the FRRR  results as rainfall intensity increases, suggesting a decline in the robustness of the lower-level agent for both flood events. However, the more consistent CIs for the FRRRs  calculated for rainfall P50 and P100 indicate that the lower-level RL agent maintains stable performance in flood risk reduction under these rainfall conditions. The scatter plots presented in Fig. 17   depict the relationships between the three sets of FRRR  results, respectively for the CPF and PPF events, revealing that with increasing rainfall intensity, the effectiveness of the lower-level RL agent’s decision-making in reducing flood risk becomes increasingly variable, aligning with the CI analysis results. The strongest correlations are observed in the left panels of both Fig. 17 (a) and (b), which compare the FRRR  results for the P50 and P100 rainfall inputs, indicating stable performance. In all plots, the scatter points predominantly locate below the diagonal line, suggesting that the effectiveness of the lower-level RL agent in flood risk reduction decreases as the rainfall intensity increases.    5 Discussion 5.1 About the traditional strategy The traditional pump deployment strategy targets the lowest geographical points in a domain, based on the assumption that these locations are vulnerable to waterlogging and inherently subject to the highest flood risk. The results from Fig. 12  show that this approach indeed lowers water level at these critical points and helps reduce flood risk. However, the effectiveness of this strategy cannot be evidenced in over half of the HZs, primarily due to two factors:• The low-lying areas, whilst having more potential to accumulate flood water, may not be always associated with high flood risk, especially when taking the densities of population, buildings and economic development into account.  • To effectively reduce flood risk, the flood depth across a broader area around the lowest geographical point needs to be lowered to or below a specific threshold (As indicated in Eqs. (1) and (3) ). Given the limited pumping duration and potentially more flood water accumulating around these lower points, the pumping operation may only achieve limited effect in reducing the water level, and consequently flood risk.    This highlights the need for a more nuanced strategy that considers not just geographical features but also the socio-economic components and flooding process for more effective flood risk mitigation.  5.2 Performance of the pump deployment strategies in the two types of flooding processes During a CPF event with flood risk increasing from zero due to intensifying surface runoff and waterlogging, the RL agents tend to station the mobile pump at a single location throughout the event in most HZs. Such optimised strategy is formed in relation to the flooding process because surface runoff created by ongoing rainfall will quickly refill the areas cleared off by the pump when it is relocated to elsewhere, thus erasing the prior risk mitigation efforts. In comparison to the traditional pump deployment strategy, the RL-guided strategy, which does not always align with the lowest geographic locations of the domain, can achieve more than double the risk reduction scores in many zones. This demonstrates that a stationary pump, when it is strategically placed, may lead to a much better outcome in reducing flood risk than just deploying it in the lowest locations, highlighting the advantage of the RL-based approach in automatically incorporating flood dynamics and risk distribution to form an optimised flood mitigation strategy. During a PPF event, characterised by ceased rainfall and diminishing flood conditions, the RL-based strategy significantly outperforms the traditional approach, achieving over four times better in flood risk reduction in many HZs. From Table 4 , it appears that the RL agents often opt to operate the mobile pump in one location for a while before relocating to another, creating a relatively stable risk level during the transitions as shown in Fig. 14 (b). The success of such strategy is attributed to the absence of rainfall, preventing the recreation of flooding conditions by surface runoff. Conversely, in four specific HZs (HZ-5, 7, 8, 9) characterised by low-lying ground susceptible to continuous runoff replenishment, the RL agents adopt a stationary pump strategy, mirroring their approach for the CPF event. The results demonstrate that the RL agents are able to adapt to varying flood conditions and risk factors to develop an optimised pump deployment strategy to enhance flood mitigation effectiveness. As a whole, the RL agents are able to optimise performance for maximum rewards by making balanced decisions across zones to prioritise areas to achieve efficient risk reduction, rather than focusing solely on the areas with the highest water level or risk. As a result, the pump deployment strategy informed by the RL agents yields significantly better outcomes than the traditional approach, successfully improving the performance of the mobile pump in reducing the overall flood risk by 2× during the CPF event and 4× during the PPF event.  5.3 Robustness of the flood risk assessment and RL approaches The analysis of OFRR  results suggests a stable assessment of flood risk across different HZs under different rainfall conditions, showing the robustness of the flood risk assessment module within the CHANS framework. The stable results contribute to the efficient training of RL agents. Additionally, for the flood events driven by the P50 and P100 rainfall intensities, the variation in the FRRR s calculated for different HZs remains within an acceptable range, showing the adaptive ability of the RL agents in handling flood conditions induced by varying rainfall. This is particularly important given the unpredictable nature of rainfall and resulting flooding in urban settings. The ability of the RL agents diminishes in the events induced by F10 rainfall, where the high-intensity precipitation significantly amplifies both the extent and depth of flooding. Under such conditions, pumping the same volume of floodwater yields limited return in lowering the water level, flood extent and risk. In such scenarios, additional mobile pumps with higher capacity may be needed to produce acceptable flood mitigation outcomes.  5.4 Factors affecting the RL agents’ policy The following factors may affect the policy established by the RL agents for mobile pump deployment:• Pumping capacity − The capacity and efficiency of the mobile pump directly influence the reward function, and subsequently, the policy established by the RL agents. Higher pumping efficiency allows for quicker water level reduction, offering the RL agents greater flexibility in handling those zones with significant water accumulation.  • Number of mobile pumps – The current study considers a single mobile pump to simplify the action space for the RL agents, but it constrains the scope of flood mitigation efforts. Incorporating multiple pumps will complicate decision-making but enhance the capability of flood response by enabling simultaneous actions across multiple locations.  • Scale of LZs − The size of LZs, about 10,000 m2  in this study, affects both the complexity of RL training and the effectiveness of flood mitigation. Finer LZ division allows for more targeted pump placement, but increases the RL state space and extends training durations. Finding an optimal scale for dividing LZs is essential, which should consider the layouts of urban roads and other features to ensure efficient pump deployment without excessive training times.  • Weights and parameters in the risk function – Rewards for RL agents are based on flood risk reduction, with weights assigned to four risk factors (inundation, population, financial loss of residential, and non-residential buildings). Adjusting the weights and parameters to shift the emphasis on different risk factors may significantly alter the RL agents’ optimal solutions. Therefore, they should be selected following meticulous calibration based on local field surveys and data.  • Additional rewards – Introducing additional rewards may motivate the RL agents to prioritise the protection of important or severely affected facilities, like hospitals and schools, further enhancing the socio-economic impact of the resulting flood risk mitigation strategy.      6 Conclusions This study introduces an innovative CHANS modelling framework that leverages hierarchical reinforcement learning to guide the scheduling and placement of mobile pumps for pluvial flood risk mitigation. Integrating a hydrodynamic model with a distributed agent-based model in a high-performance GPU computing environment, the proposed framework facilitates high-resolution data processing and storage. It generates real-time predictions of flood inundation, incorporating human factors such as population density and building losses into a comprehensive flood risk assessment system to enhance RL training with detailed simulation and feedback data. Applied to a focus area of the NK district in Can Tho, Vietnam, the CHANS framework forms RL-informed optimal mobile pump deployment strategies for flood risk reduction in both CPF and PPF events. The performance of the RL-guided strategy is compared with the traditional approach that focuses on deploying pumps at the lowest geographical locations. Findings indicate that the RL-guided strategy outperforms the traditional approach and enhances the level of flood risk reduction by 2× in the CPF event and 4× in the PPF event. Moreover, the RL agents present the capability of adapting decision-making to local flooding dynamics and risk conditions, offering a promising approach to tailor pump scheduling and placement to meet specific needs. Sensitivity analysis underscores the robustness of the CHANS framework in handling varying rainfall and flooding conditions. However, the performance of the RL-guided strategy declines in the flood scenarios induced by rainfall with very high intensities, suggesting that risk mitigation for such extreme events would require a pump with much higher capacity or multiple pumps. Overall, this exploratory study successfully develops and demonstrates a new tool for developing mobile pump deployment plans to support emergency flood management.
1 Introduction Minimizing water-driven soil loss is critical for maintaining the productivity of rangeland ecosystems (Havstad et al., 2009 ). Rangeland degradation through soil loss can adversely affect the ability of rangelands to support healthy ecosystems and decrease their ability to sustainably produce goods and services. Such degradation is potentially more likely in the future as the climate warms, leading to an enhanced hydrologic cycle and potentially more extreme storms (Nearing et al., 2004; Walthall et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012 ). As such, land managers need reliable models to predict runoff and soil loss (Flanagan et al., 2001 ). One such model, the Rangeland Hydrology and Erosion Model (RHEM), is capable of simulating overland flow runoff, soil erosion, and sediment delivery at the hillslope scale for disturbed and undisturbed rangelands (Al-Hamdan et al., 2017; Nearing et al., 2011 ). RHEM has been widely used to characterize the hydrologic vulnerability of hillslopes to soil loss associated with vegetation degradation (Hernandez et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2022 ), and it is a web accessible tool to help resource managers understand potential runoff and erosion rates under various land management scenarios (Hernandez et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2016 ). Despite its wide adoption, one of the major limitations of RHEM is that it is designed to predict overland flow runoff and erosion due to rainfall events and does not consider mixed-phase precipitation. RHEM treats all precipitation events as rainfall, regardless of whether the temperature is cold, and the event should be regarded as snowfall. For many rangelands, consideration of precipitation events as rainfall is not a wrong assumption if intense precipitation occurs primarily as rainfall during the summer months (e.g. during summertime thunderstorms). However, some rangelands experience substantial snowfall during the winter season, especially at higher latitudes and/or elevations. In these areas, misclassifying snowfall as rainfall and not considering the impact of snow on the ground during rain-on-snow (ROS) events can substantially impact resulting runoff and erosion estimates (Marks et al., 2001; Nayak et al., 2010; Seyfried and Wilcox, 1995 ). In general, snow changes the timing of hydrological inputs, storing precipitation from winter storms and later releasing the water as snowmelt. Commonly, snowmelt occurs relatively slowly, resulting in little hillslope erosion in most cases, though this is not always true, especially when the soil is frozen or partially frozen (Wu et al., 2018 ). Conversely, some wintertime precipitation events can cause substantial hillslope erosion if they have high enough intensity or are of long duration (Wade and Kirkbride, 1998 ). For example, atmospheric rivers (ARs) can bring large amounts of rain and snow to the western US, with some areas receiving more than half of wintertime precipitation from just a few events (Demaria et al., 2017; Dettinger et al., 2011 ). Incorrectly classifying these events at higher elevations (where snow occurs) as rainfall could lead to overestimates of the amount of runoff and erosion because the water would instead accumulate as snow and may melt more slowly at a later date. The impact of this misclassification, though, has not been quantified for hillslope erosion on rangelands. Rain-on-snow can have various impacts on runoff and erosion, depending on atmospheric conditions, snowpack mass and energy content, and soil moisture/frozen ground. In some cases (e.g. if snowpack is cold and/or deep), the snowpack can absorb some of the rainfall, thus reducing the immediate hydrological impact of the precipitation event. However, other snowpacks cannot (e.g. if they are shallow or close to isothermal). Instead, rainfall on these snowpacks either percolates through the snowpack, or if it does freeze, the latent heat release associated with freezing causes a substantial amount of snowmelt (Wever et al., 2014 ). In addition, these events can be accompanied by an increase in longwave radiation (Mazurkiewicz et al., 2008 ), and there can be an efficient transfer of energy between the atmosphere and snowpack during ROS events, especially in open areas (Marks et al., 1998; Marks et al., 2001 ). In addition to ROS events, there are a variety of underlying processes that can result in complex runoff generation and erosion in cold environments, but these processes are challenging to incorporate into a mathematical model. For example, freeze–thaw cycles can enhance erosion by loosening soil aggregates and causing higher runoff when the soil is frozen or partially frozen (Blackburn et al., 1990; Seyfried and Flerchinger, 1994; Wei et al., 2019 ). Other processes such as snow gliding (i.e., the slow movement of snowpack down a slope) can also be significant drivers of erosion (Meusburger et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2019 ). These processes deserve additional research and a modeling framework in which they may be incorporated. An important first step, though, is having a snow model that reasonably predicts water inputs from snowmelt using the information available to existing erosion models. In this study, we developed a snow module for RHEM that enables us to simulate snow accumulation and melt. The snow module keeps track of the evolution of snowpack through the winter as well as the rainfall and snowmelt inputs to drive the event-oriented runoff and sediment transport model in RHEM. It also satisfies the fundamental computational and logistical constraints of coupling to the RHEM model (i.e. being forced with hundreds of years of stochastically generated daily weather data in a user-driven environment where model execution must be fast). The objectives of this paper are to 1) describe the snow module and its integration with RHEM, 2) evaluate its performance against observed hydrological data, and 3) assess the impact that it has on liquid water inputs (LWI), locally generated overland flow runoff (Q), and erosion (E) estimates from RHEM.  2 Methods 2.1 Model description The snow module in RHEM-Snow is a computationally efficient hybrid between an energy balance and degree-day snowmelt model. It has separate layers representing the snowpack and soil, and a thin surface layer to compute radiative and turbulent exchanges with the atmosphere. The model codes developed in this study (in Python and Fortran) can run multiple hundred-year fully coupled simulations for a single site in a few minutes using a single processor. This computational efficiency means that the model can run in an on-demand fashion, so that it could be included in a decision support tool like the RHEM web tool (https://dss.tucson.ars.ag.gov/rhem/ ). Like a mass and energy balance snowmelt model, the snow module in RHEM-Snow keeps track of the continuous mass and energy balance of the snowpack:(1) dSWE  dt   = P s  + P r  - E - M     (2) dcc  dt   = Q n  + Q h  + Q e  + Q g  + Q p  + Q m      where dSWE  dt     is the change in snow water equivalent per day, dcc  dt     is the change of cold content per day, P s    is snowfall, P r    is rainfall, E   is sublimation, M   is liquid water leaving the snowpack, and Q n   , Q h   , Q e   , Q g   , Q p   , and Q m    are, net radiation, sensible heat flux, latent heat flux (i.e. sublimation to/from the snowpack), ground heat flux, heat flux from precipitation (which considers sensible heat transfer from falling precipitation as well as latent heat transfer if liquid precipitation freezes to the snowpack), and heat due to phase change during melt/freezing. Note that all terms on the right sides of Eqs. (1) and (2)  are mm/day and J/(m2 -day), respectively. In addition, the snow module accounts for attenuation/enhancement of solar radiation due to topography, temporally variable albedo and snow density, and sublimation of intercepted snow. Snow albedo is parameterized as a simple exponential decay since the time of last snowfall (Broxton et al., 2015 ), and snow density is modeled using an equation that densifies snow based on age of snowpack, overburden, and liquid water in the snowpack (Goodrich et al., 2023 ). Interception, canopy snow storage, sublimation of intercepted snow, snow unloading, and melt-drip from the canopy is modeled using the methodology in Liston and Elder (2006) . RHEM-Snow, along with its documentation can be downloaded at https://github.com/ARS-SWRC/RHEM-Snow . Model equations can be found in Goodrich et al. (2023) . Equations for most terms in Eqs. (1) and (2)  are fairly standard, but a couple of model formulations (Eqs. (3) and (4) ) that make RHEM-Snow unique are described in detail below. Given its computational constraints, there is a simplification regarding snow surface temperature to facilitate faster model performance than a more detailed energy balance snow model might have. Namely, instead of solving for snow surface temperature iteratively, it is estimated as a function of air temperature, radiation, and relative humidity, which we determined empirically at a field site in Arizona (referred to below as Site S5):(3) T s  = T a  + 0.0258 × Q sn   + Q li     + 0.0648 × R H - 14.5601     where T s    (°C) is the snow surface temperature, T a    (°C) is the air temperature, Q sn     (W/m2 ) is net (incoming-outgoing) solar radiation, Q li     (W/m2 ) is incoming longwave radiation, and RH    (%) is the relative humidity. This model estimates the snow surface temperature well both at the Arizona site where it was developed, as well as other areas with independent measurements. For the Arizona site, it predicts surface temperature of snow with an R2  of 0.95 and an RMSE of 0.9 °C, and for 5 flux tower sites located in the Reynolds Creek Experimental Watershed in Idaho, it predicts snowpack temperatures with R2 s ranging from 0.85 to 0.93 and RMSEs ranging from 1.1 to 2.0 °C (Fig. S1 ). Like RHEM, RHEM-Snow is forced with 300 years of daily CLImate GENeration [CLIGEN; Nicks et al. (1995) ] weather generator data. CLIGEN produces daily estimates of precipitation, temperature, dewpoint, wind, and solar radiation for individual geographic points. CLIGEN input parameters are derived from over 2600 high-quality, long-term (>30 years), meteorological stations in the United States and recently with near global coverage at a 0.25° spatial resolution (Fullhart et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2019 ). However, we have also included the capability to force RHEM-Snow with user-generated forcing datasets representing real observations. This allows for offline testing of the snow module with observed weather data (see Section 2.2 ). LWI (rainfall and snowmelt) from the snow module is used to drive the hydrologic model that simulates overland flow in RHEM. RHEM is an event-oriented model that simulates infiltration, Q, and E resulting from precipitation events at high temporal frequency (Hernandez et al., 2017 ). RHEM (without the snow module) is forced with disaggregated CLIGEN daily precipitation, including time to peak intensity, peak intensity, and storm duration at a specific location. With this information, a sub-daily storm hyetograph can be derived using a double exponential function (Wei et al., 2007 ). The double exponential function was selected after extensive testing (Lane and Nearing, 1989; Zhang and Garbrecht, 2003 ), as it was found to produce good runoff predictions in natural watersheds. For example, for the cases tested by Lane and Nearing (1989) , the overall goodness of fit of the computed runoff volume and peak runoff rate using the disaggregated rainfall intensity was good when compared to runoff computed with the observed rainfall intensity: using the disaggregated rainfall as input to a calibrated infiltration-runoff model explained some 90 % of the variance in runoff computed using the observed rainfall. Note also that watersheds in rangeland areas tend to have small rainfall-runoff ratios [for example, the four range sites within the Long Term Agroecosystem Research network have runoff-rainfall ratios ranging from 0 to 0.11 (Baffaut et al., 2020 )], and under these conditions, it is generally less important to closely reproduce the observed hyetograph from the disaggregated daily CLIGEN outputs because of the substantial attenuation of rainfall storm depth and temporal variability in the transformation of rainfall to runoff. RHEM-Snow uses the same method (double exponential function) to disaggregate rainfall inputs, but it uses a different method to disaggregate snowmelt inputs, which have very different diurnal intensity patterns, with peaks occurring during the afternoon. Snowmelt inputs are disaggregated using a beta function (Webb et al., 2017 ):(4) FDM ( t )  = t  α - 1   1 - t    β - 1   Γ α + β    Γ α   Γ β         where FDM    is the fraction of daily melt Γ   is the gamma function, t is the time of day (as a decimal between 0:00 and 23:00, and α   and β   are fitting parameters. This function was shown by Webb et al. (2017) , using snow pillow data, and contextualized with soil moisture data, to be able to fit the diurnal cycle of fractional daily melt measurements. This function creates a single snowmelt peak during the daytime, and similar to Webb et al. (2017) , we use fitting parameters such that the peak occurs in the late-afternoon, near the time of peak heating. To simplify the combination of inputs, all LWI inputs are disaggregated to a 5-min timestep in RHEM-Snow. When there is both snowmelt and rainfall (e.g. which occurs on days with ROS), snowmelt is added to the rainfall input that percolates through the snowpack. The amount of water that percolates through the snowpack during the ROS event depends on the thermodynamic properties of the snowpack (i.e. the cold content), the rainfall amount, and the energy exchange that occurs during the event. To match how events are simulated in RHEM, each day’s net water input is regarded as a single “event”, and initial conditions (e.g., prescribed initial soil moisture) are the same as in RHEM.  2.2 Evaluation of the snow module RHEM-Snow’s snow module is evaluated using two tests: first, in order to determine the effectiveness of the snow module to reproduce in-situ snowpack measurements when forced with observed weather data, we evaluate the model deterministically, where the model is forced with observed weather station data at five field sites (3 in Idaho and 2 in Arizona) and evaluated against in situ snowpack measurements at these sites. Second, to demonstrate that the snow model still performs well in the context that the RHEM-Snow is run (i.e. forced with CLIGEN weather generator data), we also evaluated the model stochastically, where the model is forced with 300 years of CLIGEN data at the 1199 sites in the western US (Srivastava et al., 2019 ) and evaluated with the climatological distribution of snowpack properties from the University of Arizona Snowpack Data (Broxton et al., 2019a ), which includes daily SWE maps covering the entire conterminous US at 4 km resolution since 1981. For the deterministic simulations, we implemented the model at two field sites in central Arizona’s highlands, as well as three sites in the USDA Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) Reynolds Creek Experimental Watershed (RCEW) in Idaho (Sites S1–S5 in Fig. 1  ). The sites at RCEW include both sheltered (which has deeper snow; Site S1) and exposed (which has less deep snow; Site S2) snow measurement locations at a high elevation site with a seasonal snowpack (called Reynolds Mountain East), as well as another lower elevation site with an ephemeral snowpack (called Lower Sheep Creek; Site S3) (Marks et al., 1998; Reba et al., 2011; Seyfried et al., 2018; Seyfried and Wilcox, 1995 ). The sites in Arizona also have contrasting seasonal vs. ephemeral snowpacks (Broxton et al., 2019b; Dwivedi et al., 2023 ), though temperatures at these sites are generally warmer than those at RCEW. The seasonal snowpack site in Arizona (Site S4) is at the Maverick Fork SNOTEL (Site #617), in the White Mountains of Eastern Arizona, and the ephemeral snowpack site (Site S5) is at the Baker Butte SNOTEL (Site #308), which is located along the Mogollon Rim in central Arizona. These sites were chosen because they have contrasting ephemeral and seasonal snowpacks and represent diverse environments that can occur in rangeland areas in the western United States. For each site, the model forcing and validation data include measurements of precipitation, wind speed, air temperature, humidity, solar radiation, snow depth, and SWE (at Sites S1, S4, and S5). At RCEW, these datasets are based on in-situ measurements made by the USDA-ARS in Boise, Idaho. For Sites S1 and S2, these data include a 25-year dataset (from 1984 to 2008) assembled by Reba et al. (2011) , and for Site S3, the data (we use data from 2009 to 2019 due to a more limited snow depth observational period at this site) were assembled using data provided through a web portal maintained by the USDA-ARS (https://www.ars.usda.gov/pacific-west-area/boise-id/northwest-watershed-research-center/docs/reynolds-creek-experimental-watershed-data/ ). At the Arizona sites (Sites S4 and S5), long term snowpack, precipitation, and temperature data are from the Baker Butte and Maverick Fork SNOTELs, and other forcing variables (e.g. relative humidity, solar radiation, wind speed, and pressure) are from the National Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) (Xia et al., 2012 ). All data are aggregated to a daily resolution to match the snow module’s timestep. The stochastic simulations at the 1199 western US CLIGEN sites are driven with 300 years of CLIGEN forcing data (Nicks et al., 1995 ). Validation data for these tests come from the daily University of Arizona (UA) snowpack dataset (Zeng et al., 2018 ), which is extracted for the grid cells containing each site. Because of the stochastic nature of the CLIGEN-produced weather data, climatological values (e.g. seasonal snowfall, peak SWE, number of snow-covered days, and first and last day of snow cover) predicted by CLIGEN-forced RHEM-Snow simulations are compared with those from the UA snowpack data (which has 40 years of data). Note that to ensure a match between the snowfall computed from the UA snowpack data (which is taken as the positive daily increments of SWE for each grid cell), we implement a spatially variable rain-snow partitioning method in RHEM-Snow:(5) f s  = m a x 0 , m i n 1 , 1  - dh  dx   T a  - T min     - dh  2 π   sin 2 π  dx   T a  - T min               where T a    is the air temperature, T range    , the range over which the rain-snow transition occurs, T max   = T mid   + T range   / 2    (where T mid     is the temperature at which half of the daily precipitation falls as snow), T min   = T mid   - T range   / 2   , dh = 1   , and dx = T a , m a x   - T a , m i n      (where all terms have units of (°C). This function smoothly transitions from 1 (representing all snowfall) at colder temperatures to zero (representing all rainfall) at warmer temperatures, and it captures the widely observed impact of decreasing snowfall fraction as temperature increases (Dai, 2008; Kienzle, 2008; Marks and Winstral, 2007 ), including at a site used in this study where precipitation phase is well quantified (Site S1; Fig. S2 ). Here, the value of T a    is spatially variable and is chosen to ensure that on average, the annual fraction of precipitation that falls as snowfall is the same in RHEM-Snow as is predicted by the UA snowpack dataset. In general, T a    is higher in the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains and lower along the west coast (Fig. S3 ). Note that all other parameters for the snow module in RHEM-Snow are spatially and temporally constant.  2.3 Comparing runoff and erosion estimates between RHEM and RHEM-Snow To understand the impact of including the snow module on Q and E, we ran RHEM-Snow in two configurations at each site. In the first configuration (called the Rain-Only, or RO   configuration, which is the same as RHEM), all precipitation events were treated as rainfall and snowpacks never developed, regardless of the air temperature, and in the second configuration (called the Rain-Snow, or RS   configuration, which is the same as RHEM-Snow), some precipitation was considered as snowfall (based on Eq. (5)  and the spatially variable T a    shown in Fig. S3 ), and seasonal snowpacks were allowed to develop. The parameters needed to run the hydrology simulations in RHEM (related to soil texture, slope, and vegetation cover and life form) are derived from USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service’s National Resources Inventory (NRI) points that are located close to each CLIGEN site (Nusser and Goebel, 1997; Weltz et al., 2014 ). Note that RHEM-Snow’s snow module also uses these parameters, along with topographic aspect, to model things like the attenuation/enhancement of solar radiation and interception. There are multiple NRI points associated with each CLIGEN site, but we choose parameters from only one NRI point for each CLIGEN site to demonstrate the impact of including the snow module in different regions. When analyzing the simulation differences, we divided the results based on event type (where each day with rainfall and/or snowmelt was considered as an event):• All : All events  • R → R : Events that are categorized as rainfall in both the RO  and RS  configurations when the RS  configuration does not have a snowpack  • R → S:  Events that are categorized as rainfall in the RO  configuration but where at least some snowfall occurs in the RS  configuration  • 0 → M:  Events that only occur in the RS  configuration because they are caused by snowmelt on days without precipitation  • R → ROS:  ROS events, where precipitation is considered as rainfall in the RS  configurations when there is snow on the ground    For all categories, we assessed the impact of including the snow module by looking at total changes to runoff and erosion, and the average annual contribution of each event type to total precipitation. For ROS events, we also analyzed changes in runoff and erosion on a per-event basis (by comparing the event-scale changes to event characteristics, e.g. total net water input, changes in peak intensity, pre-existing snowpack). This is because ROS events are unique because they can either enhance or suppress runoff (and also subsequent hillslope erosion) depending on factors such as snowpack thickness and whether the snowpack has enough cold content to freeze rain that falls on it (Marks et al., 1998; Marks et al., 2001 ). At six sites, labeled C1-C6 in Fig. 1 , we performed a detailed analysis of the overall contributions of each event type and the generated LWI, Q, and E from those events. However, at the remaining sites, we also perform the same coupled simulations, and key metrics (such as LWI, Q, and E differences between RO  and RS  simulations in the different event categories) are mapped across the western US to get an idea of where the inclusion of the snow module makes the largest difference for LWI, Q, and E. Changes in LWI, Q, and E between the Ro and Rs simulations are presented both as a fraction of LWI, Q, and E for each site (as we are particularly interested in how large changes in wintertime LWI, Q, and E changes are relative to total annual values of LWI, Q, and E), as well as absolute differences of LWI, Q, and E.   3 Results 3.1 Snow module validation Fig. 2   shows that RHEM-Snow’s snow module is able to reproduce the snowpack dynamics at the two Arizona and three Idaho validation sites. Unsurprisingly, model performance was better at the sites with more substantial and continuous winter snowpacks. For example, at the seasonal snowpack site in Arizona, the R2  and RMSE between modeled and observed SWE were 0.89 and 42 mm (site S5), while at the ephemeral snowpack site in Arizona, they were 0.73 and 79 mm (site S4). At the Idaho sites, SWE is only measured at the sheltered seasonal snowpack site (site S1), while the exposed seasonal snowpack site and the ephemeral snowpack site (sites S2 and S3) only had snow depth measurements (so only snow depth validation is performed at the latter sites). Compared to the Arizona sites, the sheltered seasonal snowpack site in Idaho also showed favorable model performance (R2  = 0.91; RMSE=73 mm). The performance of the model for snow depth was generally lower than for SWE (note the lower R2 s for snow depth comparisons in Fig. S4  than for SWE comparisons in Fig. 2  for Sites S1, S4, and S5). However, like the SWE comparison, the agreement was generally better at the sites with deeper snow (compare Fig. 2 a with b and c). Note that the annual cycles of SWE and snow depth (e.g. peak SWE, the accumulation period, and the ablation period) are represented well at all sites. The snow module, when fully integrated into RHEM-Snow and forced with CLIGEN data, is also successful when characterizing the climatological properties of snowpack across the Western US. Fig. 3   shows that compared to UA snowpack data, a variety of characteristics related to the annual cycle of snowpack are represented well. Fig. 3  shows that there is an extremely close correspondence between snowfall, peak SWE, snow cover duration, first snow-covered day, last snow-covered day, and date of peak SWE predicted by RHEM-Snow vs. those from the UA snowpack data (R2  in all cases is >0.88). There is a slight bias for the first snow-covered day, last snow-covered day, and date of peak SWE (RHEM-Snow, on average, predicts these dates 7–10 days too early), though generally, these differences are small.  3.2 The impact of snow on RHEM’s runoff and erosion estimates Generally, the impact of the snow module on Q and E is limited by how much Q and E occurs in the Ro simulation on days that are either categorized as R →  S, 0 → M, or R →  ROS, as these days are the ones where the inclusion of the snow module can affect sediment yield and runoff differences. For most sites, Q and E are dominated by summertime events where rainfall events are not reclassified (and hence there is no change between RHEM and RHEM-Snow). For example, for four of the six sites shown in Table 1   (all except for sites C3 and C4), 51–82 % of precipitation falls during R →  R events and 72–91 % of Q and 81–93 % of E occur during these events (which is likely due to the higher intensity of summertime precipitation events). For some sites, this leaves little room for change due to the inclusion of snowfall. However, at sites where a higher percentage of Q and E were generated during events that either should have been classified as snowfall or ROS (e.g. Sites 3 and 4, which have most precipitation, Q, and E being produced during the winter), the resulting Q and E could be significantly lower in the Rs simulation, mainly because these quantities were close to zero on R →  S days. Note that at these sites, Q and E was relatively small on 0 → M days. The impact of ROS on Q and E is mixed in the Rs simulation. Note in Table 1  that some sites had more Q and E in the Rs simulation while others had more in the Ro simulation. In addition, the effect of ROS was also mixed for individual ROS events. Fig. 4   shows that on ROS days, Q and E changes are dependent both on whether individual ROS events increased or decreased LWI and whether they changed its intensity. Note that for ROS events which occur over isothermal snowpacks, LWI tends to increase because there is no cold content to freeze the rain to the snowpack, and the warm and potentially windy conditions tend to add additional snowmelt. However, on days when the snowpack is below freezing (i.e., has cold content), it can absorb more energy during the ROS event, including that released by rain freezing to the snowpack, resulting in lower LWI on those days. Note that while total LWI differences between the Ro and Rs simulations are especially highly correlated with Q and E differences between the two simulations, peak intensity differences are also fairly highly correlated with Q and E differences (Fig. 4 ), underscoring the importance of precipitation (or LWI) intensity for producing Q and E.  3.3 Mapping snow impacts on runoff and erosion across the ConUS Fig. 5   shows for each event type, the relative differences between LWI from the Ro and Rs simulations across the western continental US (ConUS), relative to total LWI from the Ro simulation. Generally, these relative LWI differences (%ΔLWIs) were larger in the Inner Mountain West and Upper Great Plains (note that these areas have substantial snowpack accumulations in Fig. 3 ). The differences can amount to more than 20 % of the total LWI (Fig. 5 a), and can be attributed to the sublimation of snow, which is most pronounced in areas where snow persists for a long time (e.g. in the Rocky Mountains), or in areas that have dry, windy climates (e.g. in the Great Basin and Upper Great Plains). When looking at individual event types, reductions of LWI are most dramatic in the Rs simulations for R →  S events (up to 40 % of total LWI in some areas), but these reductions are partially made up for during snowmelt (0 → M) events, which, by definition, did not have any water inputs in the Ro simulation. R →  ROS events can have either higher or lower LWI in the Rs simulation because ROS is sometimes partly absorbed by the snowpack, and sometimes it melts the snowpack (see Section 3.2 ). At any rate, the %ΔLWIs are generally smaller than those that occur during R →  S, and 0 → M events. Note that to complement Fig. 5 , Fig. S5  shows the absolute values of LWI for the Ro simulation, and the absolute values of ΔLWI (which are not scaled by total LWI from the Ro simulation). Fig. 6   shows the same things as Fig. 5 , except for Q instead of LWI. While there are some similarities between the %ΔLWIs in Fig. 5  and the relative Q differences (%ΔQs) in Fig. 6 , there are also substantial differences. First, %ΔQs are generally smaller than the %ΔLWIs. In fact, for R →  S and R →  ROS events, %ΔQs are less than half of %ΔLWIs at most sites (compare Figs. 5 b-c and 6 b-c). Also, snowmelt does not produce much Q (Fig. 6 d) in this implementation of RHEM-Snow except for a few sites. As with %ΔLWIs, %ΔQs during R →  ROS events are much smaller than %ΔQs for R →  S events, so in general, overall reductions of Q are generally attributable to reductions of Q that occurred during R →  S events. Note that Q nearly drops to zero during R →  S events in the Rs simulation (which can also be seen for the six sites in Table 1 ). This is because snowfall itself does not cause runoff, but there can still be a little bit of runoff because some rainfall and/or melt can also occur during R →  S events (which are defined as having at least some snowfall − see Section 2.2 ). Similar to Fig. S5 , Fig. S6  shows the absolute values of Q for the Ro simulation, and the absolute values of ΔQ between the Ro and Rs simulations. Note, that at many sites ΔQ is relatively small because there is not a lot of Q produced in the first place, even during the summer (Fig. S6 ). In fact, the amount of Q produced is highly dependent on land cover characteristics (e.g., soils, vegetation cover). Overall, the spatial maps of relative E differences (%ΔEs), which are shown in Fig. S7 , look almost identical to those of the %ΔQs, with the main difference being that the magnitude of %ΔEs are typically a little smaller than %ΔQs (compare Figs. S5 g–i and S6g–i). Also, like Q, the absolute values of E are much less spatially consistent than LWI (compare the top panels in Figs. S4–S6 ), as both Q and E depend heavily on the land cover characteristics of a given site, which are spatially heterogeneous. To get a sense of the overall reduction of LWI, Q, and E as a function of precipitation amounts for the two event categories where significant changes occur (R →  S and R →  ROS events), Fig. 7   summarizes %ΔLWI, %ΔQ, and %ΔE for all locations with significant sediment production (>100 kg/ha-yr) as a function of precipitation that falls during R →  S and R →  ROS events. Unsurprisingly, as snowfall increases, LWI, Q, and E all generally decrease. For example, for sites that receive close to 100 mm of liquid equivalent snowfall per year, annual LWI decreases by ∼ 15–40 %, annual Q decreases by 10–30 %, and E decreases by 5–20 % (though keep in mind that absolute Q and E differences depend on how much total annual Q and E are produced in the first place). %ΔLWI, %ΔQ, and %ΔE for R →  ROS events are smaller and more variable, but tend to slightly decrease for sites that do not receive much ROS (e.g. those average less than 25 mm of ROS per year) and increase for sites that receive more ROS (e.g., those average less than 100 mm of ROS per year).   4 Discussion In this study, we have addressed a shortcoming of the RHEM model: that all precipitation, regardless of temperature, is treated as rainfall. This can be a problem for areas that receive snowfall because snowmelt has lower intensity than even moderately intense precipitation events and, therefore, produces less Q and E than would occur if the precipitation fell as rain. At the same time though, this impact can be modified by things like frozen or saturated soils. The snow module that we developed is continuous (keeping track of snowpack development and ablation through the winter), yet computationally efficient enough so that it could be implemented as an on-demand model that can be run by rangeland managers to understand vulnerability to erosion. While it is relatively simple (with intermediate complexity between a temperature index snow model and a full energy balance snow model) − it is able to accurately predict snowpack dynamics at test sites (Fig. 2 ), as well as to reproduce the observed climatological characteristics of snowpack across the ConUS when forced with the same weather simulator data that is used in RHEM (Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, it does not require additional forcing information than RHEM, making it relatively straight forward to run in an existing decision support framework. 4.1 The impact of treating winter precipitation as snowfall As expected, including the snow module decreases overland flow runoff and erosion estimates in areas with substantial snowfall. This is primarily due to the reclassification of precipitation events from rainfall to snowfall. While most high-intensity precipitation events occur during the summer when it is warmer, there are regions (such as the Central Rockies) where the large volume of precipitation that occurs as snowfall makes the wintertime precipitation inputs relatively more important for erosion. In these areas, annual Q and E can decrease more than 20 % when considering wintertime precipitation as snowfall (Fig. 7 ). While the absolute amounts of this decrease are small at many sites due to the fact that not a lot of overland flow runoff and erosion is produced in the first place (Figs. S5 and S6 ), this reduction can still amount to 10–50 mm/year for overland flow runoff or >100 kg/ha-yr for erosion (Table 1 ). Not only does some of the snow sublimate to the atmosphere, especially if snowpacks persist for a long time or occur in high energy or arid environments (Fig. 5 a), but the subsequent melting of snowpack is less intense than most precipitation. In fact, in our simulations, snow melting by itself rarely caused enough overland flow to cause erosion. This does not mean, though, that real snowmelt events cannot cause erosion. In fact, in some areas, most streamflow is generated during times of spring snowmelt, and such times can also be associated with large amounts of erosion (Wade and Kirkbride, 1998; Wu et al., 2018 ). However, during the cool season, lateral subsurface flow (which is not modelled by RHEM) is particularly important (Kelleners et al., 2010; McNamara et al., 2005; Wilcox et al., 1997 ), leading to channel erosion, which is different than the overland flow-caused erosion that is modeled by RHEM. In addition, the impact of frozen and saturated soils is very important in the winter (which, as noted below, we will address in a future study) (Seyfried and Flerchinger, 1994 ). In particular, infiltrability can be reduced by repeated cycling between frozen and unfrozen soils (Fouli et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018 ), and frozen soil, itself, might be largely impermeable. Infiltrability also decreases for wetter soils (Kane and Stein, 1983 ), which can be common during the winter due to low evapotranspiration rates, especially in environments where snowpacks are ephemeral (Dwivedi et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, the snow module in RHEM-Snow provides enough complexity to accurately simulate snowmelt under a variety of conditions. It accounts for the impacts of topography (slope and aspect) and vegetation cover on snow accumulation and ablation, and includes representation of many processes that are important for representing snowpack under a variety of conditions (e.g. enhancement/attenuation of solar radiation due to topography, interception, snowpack sublimation). Also, the snow module does a good job representing SWE, both at individual sites when driven with observed forcing data as well as when driven with the stochastic weather generator data that is used in RHEM (Figs. 2 and 3 ). While the snow module in RHEM-Snow does not explicitly separate SWE into ice water and liquid water, which is typically a few percent or less of SWE, but can be much higher when ice layers are present (Avanzi et al., 2015; Singh et al., 1999 ), snowmelt leaving the snowpack is still mediated by the accumulation and loss of cold content in the snowpack, resulting in realistic magnitudes of SWE loss (and hence meltout). Furthermore, sub-daily variations in snowmelt are modeled using a beta function that can accurately simulate the daily timing and duration of snowmelt (Webb et al., 2017 ).  4.2 The impact of rain on snow ROS events are unique in our simulations, as ROS events can involve enough precipitation with sufficient intensity to generate large amounts of overland flow runoff and sediment production on the hillslopes. In general, though, the presence of snowpack does not necessarily enhance or mute the impact of ROS events (Li et al., 2019; Wever et al., 2014; Würzer et al., 2016 ). Rather, it depends on precipitation and snowpack characteristics, as shallow, isothermal snowpacks are more likely to melt during ROS events, thereby adding to the LWI. Conversely, deep, cold snowpacks might be able to absorb a substantial amount of precipitation without melting. As a result of this contradictory behavior for individual events, the overall impact of ROS events is somewhat muted in our simulations, and hence the reductions of Q and E that occur due to the reclassification of precipitation from rainfall to snowfall are, overall, more important (Figs. 5–7 ). However, similar to snowmelt runoff generation noted above, runoff generation during ROS may be underestimated here because in reality, it is substantially related to the priming of the soil profile for initiating lateral subsurface flow and streamflow in channels (Garvelmann et al., 2015 ), and the impact of saturated and frozen soils (which is not addressed in the current work) is important for driving runoff and erosion during such events.  4.3 Future work To address these limitations, future work will focus on updating the subsurface parameterization that is used in RHEM (which currently initialize all events with the same soil saturation and does not allow for frozen soils). Updating this parameterization could potentially have large impacts on overland flow runoff generated during snowmelt, and especially during ROS events, as the current implementation precludes one of the major mechanisms through which ROS causes large amounts of runoff (runoff over frozen soils). Furthermore, runoff efficiencies from ROS events, as well as other events, are heavily linked to catchment wetness and how permeable the soils are. Furthermore, freezing and thawing and excessive wetness can make winter soils more susceptible to erosion (Bajracharya et al., 1998; Wade and Kirkbride, 1998 ). The impact of variable saturation is likely to extend to the warm season as well, making it a potentially critical issue for erosion modelling given that, in many areas, most Q and E occurs during the warm season.
