ET in MOD16, FLUXCOM, and some reanalysis products (e.g., JRA55 and MERRA2) are expressed as latent heat flux in units of W/m2  or MJ ∙    m−2 ∙    d-1 , which are converted to the equivalent water depth (mm/month) using a constant latent heat of vaporization of 28.35 W/m2  or 2.45 MJ/kg (FAO, https://www.fao.org/3/x0490e/x0490e07.htm ).  2.4 Estimation of DET The DET is the difference between ET-WB and modeled ET (MET). The MET is obtained from a total of 18 models, including 10 land surface models from the GLDAS generation (four GLDAS1.0 models, three GLDAS2.0 models, and three GLDAS2.1 models), WGHM, and seven global reanalyzes (Table S2 ). Most of them follow the same data sources as P to make the error distribution consistent. All of the 18 models neither consider human activities such as reservoir regulation and groundwater extraction nor are directly calibrated by ET observations (Table S4 ). We note that R and Δ    S from the WGHM are from the “standard run” and account for the human effects, while the MET is simulated under the “naturalized mode” that accounts only for the natural climate variabilities to be consistent with the other 17 models. We estimate monthly DET as the residual between each subset of MET and ET-WB for global river basins. Overall, we obtained 4,669 (ET-WB) × 18 (MET) = 84,042 combinations of DET globally, helping us fully reveal and assess the spread range of different datasets.  2.5 Comparison of DET with individual estimates To evaluate the contribution of human influences to DET, we compare it with independent ET losses induced by reservoir impoundment, land cover and land use changes (LULC), and human water use from 2003 to 2016. These factors are considered the major human factors causing the variations of ET and follow our definitions for DET (Castle et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017 ). The monthly global reservoir ET losses are obtained from Tian et al. (2022) , which are generated using the methodology proposed by Zhao and Gao (2019)  based on the two newest datasets, i.e., the Global Reservoir Surface Area Dataset (GRSAD) and the Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD). The global land cover-induced ET every five years (2002–2006, 2007–2011, 2012–2016) is provided by Wang et al. (2021) , who use a Budyko-type method and observed land cover maps to generate global LULC-induced ET. Although human activities such as food and fuel production, social development, and city expansion are the significant contributors to global LULC changes during the study period (Song et al., 2016), climatic variabilities such as precipitation increase and restoration after bushfires may also lead to changes in LULC over specific regions (e.g., Sahara Desert). We calculate the LULC-induced ET changes by subtracting the ET during the baseline 1982–1986 from our study period (i.e., 2003–2016). The baseline period is assumed as a naturalized period without significant human interventions. The ET loss from human water use is simulated by the global water use model as incorporated in WGHM, which refers to the part of abstracted water (from both surface and groundwater) that evaporates during water use, including irrigation, livestock, domestic, and manufacturing (Müller Schmied et al., 2021 ).  2.6 Uncertainty analysis Based on a large ensemble of ET-WB (4,669), MET (18), and DET (84,042) estimations, we derive the continuous confidence quantiles ranging from 0 % to 100 % with the median time series as a benchmarking product. Further, we employ the four-way multifactorial ANOVA algorithm for decomposing the variance in multi-year mean DET into four main sources comprising P, R, ΔS, and MET, as well as their interactions (Vetter et al., 2015 ). The ANOVA method defines the total variance (called Total Sum of Square, TSS) in DET estimates as the sum of the square of the difference between DET results of every single combination (DET  p , s , r , m e t     ) and the arithmetic mean (DET  ¯     ):(2) TSS = ∑ p = 1  N P   ∑ s = 1  N S   ∑ r = 1  N R   ∑ met = 1  N MET    DET  p , s , r , m e t   - DET  ¯      2      where NP  , NS  , NR  , and NMET   are the number of subsets in P, ΔS, R, and MET dimensions, respectively. The total variance can further be decomposed into 15 items consisting of different combinations of variables as:(3) TSS = SS  P  + SS  S  + SS  R  + SS  MET   + SS  P ∙ R   + SS  P ∙ S      + SS  P ∙ M E T   + SS  R ∙ S   + SS  R ∙ M E T   + SS  S ∙ M E T   + SS  P ∙ S ∙ R      + SS  P ∙ S ∙ M E T   + SS  S ∙ R ∙ M E T   + SS  P ∙ R ∙ M E T   + SS  P ∙ S ∙ R ∙ M E T           where SSP  , SSS  , SSR  , and SSMET   represent the variances caused by P, ΔS, R, and MET datasets, respectively. Similarly, the two-order interaction items (e.g., SSP  ∙   S  ) indicate the variances derived from the interactions between two variables (e.g., P and ΔS). The total 11 interaction items include six two-order interactions, four three-order interactions, and one four-order interaction. Therefore, we can estimate the relative contribution (RC ) of each component variance as the ratio of the particular variance item in the ANOVA method (SSi  ) versus the total variance:(4) RC  i  = S S  i  TSS        The variable and/or interactions with the highest RC  can be identified as the dominating factor in DET. The detailed calculation procedures and interpretations of each variance item can be found in previous studies (Hattermann et al., 2018 ). To avoid the “survivor bias” derived from the different number of datasets in P (23), ΔS (7), R (29), and MET (18), we randomly selected seven subsets from P, R, and MET datasets to be consistent with ΔS data. 100 repeated experiments in our analysis imply that different combinations of datasets for ANOVA analysis only alter the qualitative results constrainedly with the standard deviation in the contribution of P, ΔS, R, MET, and their interactions of 18 %, 0 %, 4 %, 16 %, and 0 % for the global land, respectively.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Evaluation of water balance ET The total ET estimates from the ET-WB ensemble show clear seasonality, with a peak in July and a trough in January (Fig. 2   a and 2b). The global median value varies from 20 to 70 mm/month (mm/m), with higher deviation during the low ET periods. Several non-monotonic changes in ET-WB are also observed, primarily driven by various physical mechanisms of moisture supply and climate variability, which are consistent with previous global studies (Jung et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2022 ). We report a median level of the multi-year mean ET-WB of ∼ 500 mm per annum (mm/a) worldwide, with humid (highest of 1,565 mm/a with a 5 % spread range of 1525–1604 mm/a for Kapuas River basin) and arid (lowest of 127 mm/a with a 5 % spread range of 122–133 mm/a for Tarim basin) basins having relatively higher and lower ET, respectively (Fig. 2 c). Multi-year global mean ET-WB generally ranges from 500 to 600 mm/a, with an ensemble median of 549 mm/a (5 % spread range: 543–554 mm/a). It is comparable to previous studies such as 519–778 mm/a during 2000–2013 by Jung et al. (2019) , 482 mm/a during 2000–2010 by Rodell et al. (Rodell et al., 2015 ), and 415 to 586 mm/a during 1985–1999 by Haddeland et al. (2011) . The bounds of the ensemble ET provide an observational constraint on the ET limits and rigorously account for the implicit uncertainties, thus providing confidence in our findings. The long-term mean ET-WB over global river basins is compared against four different global ET products, with a statistically linear relationship fitted with the slope of 1.02 (R2  = 0.91) (Fig. 2 a). Considerable variations between different ET products are found, especially for those regions with higher ET. On a global scale, the multi-year mean ET reaches 560 mm/a with a standard deviation of 50 mm/a, close to our ET-WB estimates. The seasonality of ET-WB is additionally examined, with ∼ 80 % of global river basins having a shifted seasonal phase less than two months than global ET products in terms of the peak timing (Fig. 2 b). These assessments show ET-WB can reasonably well capture the long-term mean and seasonality of regional and global ET. However, the bias in the multi-year mean estimates and seasonality of total ET may lead to the shifted capture of DET upon comparison with model results.  3.2 Global distributions of DET By combining 4,669 subsets of ET-WB with 18 different MET simulations, we generate a total of 84,042 combinations of DET. Long-term mean DET is compared with the cumulative results from reservoir-induced ET loss, LULC change-driven ET, and consumptive human water use from surface water and groundwater sources (Fig. 4  a and 4b). We observe the positive DET primarily distributed in South Asia, Australia, Central Asia, North and South Africa, and Southwest United States. On the contrary, the negative DET is identified in the Siberian Plain, Europe, Central Africa, Southern South America, and East North America. This suggests a spatial heterogeneity due to diversified degrees of human disturbance and variance of different models and datasets. Despite this, five main regions with significant human interventions (positive DET values) are identified, which are either in agreement with independent ET estimates or reported in previous local investigations (e.g., Castle et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022 ). These consist of South Asia (including South and North China, India, and the Lancang-Mekong region), Central Asia and East Europe (including Northwest China and Arab region), South and North Africa, the scattered areas of North America (including West United State and some high-latitude basins, e.g., Yukon, La Grande, and Churchill River basins), and Northern and Eastern parts of South America. In addition, a few basins with negative DET values are also evidenced by the independent results, such as the Congo River basin, the majority of South America, and some small basins in Northeastern of the North America continent. The regions are impacted by a variety of human activities, of which the most significant is the consumptive water use, especially over India, North China, and Western United States (Fig. 5  ). The reservoir ET loss is also detected in the northwestern parts of North America, while the decreased ET in South America and Central Africa is mainly caused by LULC dynamics. However, mixed results are found in regions located in Australia, Southern South America, Central North America, East Europe, and Russian basins. These regions have relatively less positive DET values (<10 mm/a) from independent ET products but negative values from water balance estimates. Such negative DET values may partly result from the inadequate representation of surface characteristics in the modeled ET and partly from the water balance closure residuals. This may also be caused by complex and underrepresented hydrological processes, such as condensation, seawater intrusion, and snow hydrology (Rodell et al., 2011 ). Consistent with previous regional investigations (Castle et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017 ), the uncertainty may outweigh the DET estimation itself in a few regions with minimal human impacts. Globally, a positive median DET of 7 mm/a (–2 to 16 mm/a for the 5 % spread range) is estimated, comparable to the results from individual sources (13 mm/a; 3, 1, and 10 mm/a for reservoirs, LULC, and human water use, respectively). The differences can be the consequence of an inaccurate representation of human activities in these ET datasets and uncertainties in DET estimates. Overall, we discovered 72 (17) river basins with positive (negative) DET estimates confirmed by the independent ET sources. We further quantify the long-term average ratio of DET versus ET-WB in these basins to evaluate the intensity of human influences on regional ET alteration (Fig. 3 c). We report significant human influences with DET/ET-WB higher than 10 % in South and East Asia, Western United States, and Northern Africa. Specifically, we compare our ensemble results with previous estimates for the regional cases, such as Haihe (6 % in this study vs. 12 % by Pan et al. (2017)  vs. 8 % by Liu et al. (2022) ), Colorado (6 % in this study vs. 12 % by Castle et al. (2016) ), and Liaohe, Huaihe, Yangtze, and Pearl (6 %, 11 %, 9 %, and 17 %, respectively, in this study vs. 11 %, 7 %, 8 %, and 13 %, correspondingly, by Liu et al. (2022)  River basins. The differences show that the human influences have become detectable but to different extents due to diversified bias depending on data sources. Despite the evenly matched distribution of the positive and negative results, we calculated a percentage of 1.29 % (–0.29 to 2.87 % for the 5 % spread range) of DET/ET-WB for the global land. These findings highlight the potentially growing influence of human activities on the terrestrial water cycle and the need to integrate multi-type and multi-source products. We additionally evaluate the seasonality of DET over global river basins (Fig. 6  a). We discover the maximum DET in JJA over most river basins in humid climate zones such as the Mississippi and Yangtze River basins. It can be related to the stronger atmosphere demand during the boreal summer due to higher air temperature, particularly in areas with dense human-made reservoirs. Conversely, DJF dominates the intra-annual DET in Southeast Asia and Australia, which may result from the extensive agricultural irrigation during the local growing season (e.g., the pre-monsoon season in the Mekong River basin and summer in the Murray River basin). MAM controls the seasonal DET peaks in several tropical regions around the equator, while SON is the season with maximum DET over the most high-latitude basins where the multi-year mean is always negative. Given the dominating role of agricultural irrigation in global water consumption, we select five river basins with the highest irrigation rates to further demonstrate DET behavior qualitatively and its consistency with seasonal water availability and human activities (Fig. 6 b-6e). The Ganges, for example, witness a maximum negative DET in the monsoon season, i.e., JJAS, when the basin receives ∼ 80 % of the annual precipitation. The water extraction from groundwater might have a few anomalous peaks in the monsoon season concurrent with the Karif crops during the below-normal precipitation years or late onset of monsoon. This is reflected in July, where the confidence range varies from positive to negative, while in August, when water extraction is minimal, it is well below zero. It implies the inadequate model representation of MET. For example, the surface characteristics change very rapidly from dry and bare soil in May to flooded fields with minimal vegetation in June and finally to flooded fields with significant vegetation in July and August. MET ignores flooding and uses vegetation growth indicators like NDVI and LAI for ET estimation. It further leads to negative DET in such months. During another major cropping season, namely, Rabi (Nov-Feb), the precipitation is minimal, but some extent of water extraction is there to meet the crop water requirements. This has ultimately led to the increasing DET trends (Fig. 6 d). We also identify the DET peaks possibly corresponding to summer maize irrigation in the Haihe and Huaihe River basins of North China, with signals of winter wheat irrigation in April. A similar behavior can be seen in the increasing tendency of DET from April to October over the San Joaquin and Po River basins, which roughly coincide with the irrigation season of the Western United States and Italy. We observe the negative values in seasonal DET due to the shifted phase in MET and the large deviation of ET-WB, especially during dry months (Figure S2 ). Overall, our examinations for the seasonality of DET provide insights into the intra-annual variability of human activities and highlight the need for local evidence for a more detailed investigation.  3.3 Variance contribution to DET estimations The magnitude of DET is determined in part by the uncertainties in the constituent datasets of P, ΔS, R, and MET. We calculate the normalized variance of the global multi-year mean DET estimate as the ANOVA approach to reveal the regional inter-ensemble reliability. Relatively higher inter-ensemble variances of DET are observed over humid regions, including South America, South Africa, and East and South Asia. On the contrary, relatively lower variances are found in arid regions such as Australia, North and South Africa, and Central Asia (Fig. 7  a). We also find relatively obvious variances in some small regions where human influences are generally considered significant, like some European river basins. Such variances may be responsible for the negative value of the multi-year mean DET. To investigate further the contribution of different variables to DET, we perform the ANOVA analysis on the large ensemble of multi-year mean DET for the global land and the studied 168 basins (Fig. 7 b). We discover that P and MET are the predominant variables over most basins. However, ΔS and R have relatively less influence on the DET estimations and govern the total variance in DET in a few regions like the Gauge River basin. It is worth noting that the global pattern of ANOVA results can slightly differ with the randomly selected input datasets, particularly for the variables P and MET. Globally, the contribution of P to the uncertainty in DET is as high as 23 % and reaches 8 % and 69 % for R and MET, respectively. ΔS and interactions of all variables contribute < 1 % to these uncertainties. Specifically, we provide the relative contribution of P, ΔS, R, and MET over global basins to quantify the contribution of various factors to DET (Figure S3 ). The contribution of MET over most basins ranges from 30 % to 60 %, with the other three main variables accounting for the remaining parts (mainly from P), where the relative contribution of ΔS and interactions is negligible. These uncertainties suggest we consider different data sources of the variables and thereby better account for the possible uncertainty range. These probabilistic estimates are expected to converge to a stable level if the number of subsets is sufficient (Hausfather et al., 2022 ).  3.4 Constraining the multi-source uncertainties In addition to the ANOVA-based uncertainty attribution analysis, we broadly classify the multisource uncertainty into three categories: (a) the inherent bias of individual products (e.g., P and MET) given the simplified model physics and quality of meteorological inputs, (b) post-processing procedures implicit to the water balance model (e.g., aggregation over scales and periods), and (c) propagated errors of various water cycle fluxes (Beck et al., 2017; Ghiggi et al., 2021; Fekete et al., 2004 ). In general, the uncertainty in the input hydrological fluxes themselves governs the uncertainty in DET estimations. This is because P, one of the largest and most important input variables in the water cycle, is the main contributor to the uncertainty in the water balance and climate impact estimations. While numerous P datasets have been developed in the last decades, a marked deviation of up to 90 mm/a has been observed among them when applied to the global land (Beck et al., 2017 ). This variability and uncertainty in different P datasets affect DET estimates and the derived metrics. For example, the performance of the G-RUN ENSEMBLE dataset, which is a multi-forcing global runoff reanalysis, is largely determined by the uncertainty stemming from atmospheric forcing (i.e., P) (Ghiggi et al., 2021 ). Similar issues have also been recognized for other R datasets, such as GloFAS, although these products have been corrected/calibrated by in-situ discharge measurements. Similarly, the performance of MET simulations may be inherently determined by P values. According to the ANOVA analysis, the propagated uncertainty of P in MET simulations can be implied by the higher contribution of MET to the total variance of DET compared to R and ΔS. On the other hand, post-processing of data, such as spatial resampling and temporal averaging, is usually required to integrate the difference in spatial (from 0.1° to 1.875°) and time scales (from 1 day to 1 month), which can affect the DET estimates on the regional scales. For instance, the SSA method that is used to statistically interpolate the GRACE data during the missing months would introduce probable bias in the derived ΔS time series. Overall, apart from the individual contribution, the uncertainties can spread and propagate between each other and beyond, which finally affects the DET estimations. As discussed above, it is challenging to attribute various uncertainty sources explicitly. To tackle such a challenge, several approaches were applied to reduce the impacts of the complex multisource uncertainties in our DET estimations. First, a plethora of datasets from different (and independent) sources are used to improve the accuracy of the quantification that helped understand the potential uncertainty in the specific variable. For example, we derive a total of 84,042 DET combinations from 23P, 7 ΔS, 29 R, and 18 MET products from remote sensing, hydrological modeling, global reanalysis, and in-situ observations. A large number of data combinations favorably demonstrate and help in constraining the uncertainty in DET globally. Second, applying methods/models with improved schemes potentially reduced the impacts of uncertainty on trend calculation. For instance, the ensemble median and the probabilistic method avoid outliers and auto-correlation in time series. Third, the systematic analysis of different uncertainty sources (e.g., ANOVA) helps to reveal the respective contribution of various variables to the final results statistically.  3.5 Implications It has been growingly recognized that global models and water balance methods have been increasingly applied in assessing ET changes, especially under the intensifying anthropogenic disturbances on global water and energy cycles (Douville et al., 2013 ). However, their comparisons have not been performed, and the ET changes induced by human activities have not been analyzed on a global scale. Moreover, a few regional studies dealing with this issue have utilized limited datasets and/or covered relatively short periods and do not necessarily provide uncertainty assessment and attribution analysis. To fill this knowledge gap, we used an unprecedented number of datasets to investigate the global patterns of DET, including its spatiotemporal variability, influential factors, and uncertainty over the past two decades based on the water balance method and multiple models. We portend the significant influence of human activities on the water cycle and reveal the uncertainty involved in various water cycle components (e.g., P, ΔS, and R) at the global scale for research communities. We also provide water resources managers with the ensemble estimates of changes in DET for their understanding of hydrological and climatic alterations. Our uncertainty-constrained DET results can facilitate the selection of appropriate datasets for water balance research and identify components that need to be improved in the regional modeling tailored for management purposes. Apart from putting forward the bulk quantification of the terrestrial DET, our results also highlight the divergent regional hotspots with implications for both global and regional water, energy, and carbon cycles. The detailed diagnosis of terrestrial DET and the compounding mechanisms affirms the premise of water cycle intensification. It, therefore, provides useful evidence of significant human activities and is critical for predicting surface climate change, evaluating impacts on water resources and ecosystems, and designing adaptation policies. Future studies may consider examining whether or not and how the effect of human activities on ET are contained in climatic variables to reveal the detailed hydrological mechanism of the coupled human-water systems and how global DET affects and is affected by the moisture demand or supply. Moreover, the thermodynamic driving mechanisms of precipitation variability and subsequent effects on the observed changes in the water cycle can be examined along with past and future socio-economic exposure assessments (Yin et al., 2022, 2023 ).   4 Conclusions ET estimates from the water balance framework and global models have been widely used in evaluating hydrological regimes, benchmarking ET products, and projecting future changes. However, systematic comparisons between them remain unexplored, which are critical for the understanding of human disturbance in water cycles. Here, we use the unprecedented combinations of water balance ET (ET-WB) and multiple models (MET) to analyze the spatiotemporal characteristics of their differences (DET) on a global scale. Individual ET loss from different sources is collected to explain the human contributions to DET. Uncertainty assessment has been performed to attribute the variance contributors to DET. Our results show that (a) ET-WB presents reasonably good accuracy in capturing long-term average and seasonality over global river basins by comparing with multi-source ET products. The multi-year mean ET reaches 560 mm/a with a standard deviation of 50 mm/a, close to our ET-WB estimates (549 mm/a with a 5 % spread range of 543–554 mm/a); (b) 72 (17) out of 168 selected river basins show positive (negative) average DET confirmed by the independent ET estimates, which are mainly located in South Asia, Central Asia and East Europe, South and North Africa, the scattered areas of North America, and Northern and Eastern parts of South America. The positive DET may be related to heavy water consumption, and the negative values may be caused by human deforestation (e.g., Amazon). Regional cases in river basins with significant irrigation demonstrate the DET seasonality related to agricultural practice; (c) apart from human interventions, uncertainty derived from different variables in deriving DET also leads to discrepancies between ET-WB and MET. They are mainly contributed by variance in precipitation, which can further propagate into MET simulations. Our results suggest that human activities can induce discrepancies in long-term mean and seasonality between ET-WB and global models, combined with the uncertainty of different inputs like precipitation. Our analysis highlights the urgent need to explicitly consider human activities in global models and the potential risk in deriving actual ET based on the water balance approach. This study can provide useful insights for large-scale modelers and regional water managers.  5 Code availability The code can be requested from the corresponding authors.
1 Introduction Underground Hydrogen Storage (UHS) in porous formations is a promising technology for large-scale (TWh) energy storage. To ensure the efficiency of the storage operation, multiscale modeling and simulation strategies are essential, in which the micro-scale physics are studied to derive input parameters for the continuum-scale dynamic models. In addition to pore-network modeling (Hashemi et al., 2021a ), recent studies have employed direct numerical simulations and CFD modeling to analyze hydrogen–water flow dynamics. They highlighted the significance of these approaches in understanding the intricate flow behaviors (Wang et al., 2023; Bagheri et al., 2023 ). Therefore this study aims to extend the initial study of this complex process using quasi-static pore-network modeling (Hashemi et al., 2021a ) and properly characterize the dynamics of the system. The present study uses a dynamic pore-network modeling (D-PNM) approach (Koch et al., 2021 ) to simulate the immiscible two-phase flow of hydrogen and water through a pore network model of a porous structure. The model input parameters are based on the experimentally obtained fluid–gas properties as presented in literature (Hashemi et al., 2021a ). As for the rock, statistical pore network models are generated to mimic the digital network information which is based on 3D X-ray images of porous samples. To preserve the simulation stability, the D-PNM solves the transient multi-phase Stokes equations fully implicitly, for pressure and phase volume concentrations. Through several test cases, we analyze the transport characteristics of the hydrogen/water interface, especially the fingering and spreading physics. These results shed new light on how a representative continuum-scale model should be created to study the process at the field scale. Pore network modeling  Large-scale numerical simulation of multi-phase flow in porous media is crucial for predicting various phenomena in hydrology, environmental engineering, and petroleum engineering. Accurate descriptions of macroscopic properties such as capillary pressures and relative permeabilities are necessary for numerical reservoir simulations of multi-phase flow (Bo et al., 2023 ). These properties can be measured by time-consuming and costly laboratory experiments, or alternatively, physically-based models can be developed to predict multi-phase flow at the pore scale and estimate these macroscopic properties at the macro-scale (Ryazanov et al., 2012 ). To simulate multi-phase flow in porous media, an accurate pore space structure is required. This can be obtained from CT imaging (Blunt et al., 2013 ) or 3D reconstructions (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2010 ). Pore network modeling provides an effective tool for estimating macroscopic transport properties with arbitrary wetting conditions, making it an attractive option for numerical simulations of multi-phase flow. However, PNM has limitations in dealing with gas compressibility and fingering effects, which are crucial for accurately predicting hydrogen behavior during storage and recovery processes. For more detailed information about pore-network modeling and the effect of compressibility, readers are referred to the literature (Blunt, 2017; Bagheri et al., 2023 ), respectively. In pore network modeling, the pore space refers to the empty space within a porous material where fluids can flow or be stored. It is the network of interconnected voids or pores that characterize the porous structure of a material, such as a rock, soil, or membrane. The description of the pore space in pore network modeling involves characterizing the geometry, topology, and connectivity of the pores within the material. This can be done using various techniques, such as imaging (Blunt et al., 2013 ), and statistical modeling (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2010 ). The resulting data can then be used to construct an equivalent model of the pore network, which can be used to simulate fluid flow and transport processes within the material. The pore space can be characterized by several parameters, such as the pore size distribution, the tortuosity of the pores, and the connectivity of the network. These parameters can have a significant impact on the fluid flow behavior and transport properties of the material, such as absolute and relative permeability, and capillarity. The detailed information can be found in literature (Dong and Blunt, 2009; Joekar-Niasar et al., 2010a ) An accurate and detailed description of the pore space is crucial for understanding the transport and storage behavior of porous materials and for optimizing their performance in various applications, such as oil and gas recovery, water filtration, and energy storage. The appropriate pore-scale model can be used by considering the existing flow regimes (Lenormand et al., 1988 ). Two main types of network modeling tools are defined by the flow regime: capillary-dominated and viscous-dominated. In the case of a low capillary number (Shams, 2018; Boujelben and McDougall, 2017; Piri and Blunt, 2005 ), N  c    , which is defined as, N  c   = μ u  σ   ≤ 1 0  − 5      where μ   is viscosity, u is fluid velocity and σ   is interfacial tension, the viscous forces are insignificant and the flow is governed by capillary forces. In this case, quasi-static network modeling can be applied. Otherwise, dynamic network modeling should be used where both viscous and capillary forces are accounted for. Given how important Nc is for determining the suitability of the quasi-static approach, it is essential to evaluate how well this model performs as conditions get close to this threshold. This evaluation is especially important since real-world situations might have Nc values close to 10−5 , which could impact the accuracy and usefulness of the model’s predictions. For conditions where Nc exceeds this threshold, indicating a significant influence of viscous forces, dynamic network modeling should be employed. This study considers both quasi-static and dynamic PNM, providing a more comprehensive analysis of fluid dynamics across different flow regimes. Despite the limitations of the quasi-static model, it provides valuable insights into the pore-scale dynamics under capillary-dominated conditions. However, realistic subsurface conditions can often present scenarios where the capillary number approaches or exceeds this critical threshold. Therefore, it becomes important to assess the quasi-static model’s validity and performance under varying conditions closer to this boundary. Dynamic pore network models  Dynamic pore network models have become a powerful tool for understanding fluid behavior in porous media, allowing for the capture of changing fluid properties and pore structure over time (Koplik and Lasseter, 1985; Al-Gharbi and Blunt, 2005; Aghaei and Piri, 2015 ). While previous dynamic pore network models have used explicit or semi-implicit approaches, these had limitations in accurately capturing the complex behavior of the fluid flow. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed new modeling approaches, such as fully implicit dynamic pore network models, which improve accuracy and provide greater insight into two-phase flow and phase change in porous media (Chen et al., 2020; Weishaupt and Helmig, 2021 ). The behavior of residual fluids in porous media is an important topic of study with a range of applications, including oil recovery, groundwater management, carbon sequestration, and energy storage. Dynamic pore network modeling has been used in several studies to investigate residual fluid behavior in porous media (An et al., 2020; Gong et al., 2023; Li et al., 2017 ). For instance, Li et al. (2017)  used dynamic pore network models to investigate the effect of heterogeneity on residual fluid configurations during the imbibition process. They found that heterogeneity significantly affects residual fluid configurations, and the spatial distribution of residual fluids is highly dependent on the degree of heterogeneity in the porous medium. Specifically, the study demonstrated that in more heterogeneous media, the residual fluid configurations tend to be more dispersed and less connected, which can lead to higher residual saturation levels. Conversely, in more homogeneous media, the residual fluids are more likely to form larger, continuous clusters, which can be more easily mobilized and displaced. Fluid configurations refer to the spatial arrangement and connectivity of the wetting and non-wetting phases within the pore space. It includes how the fluids occupy the pores and throats, the formation of ganglia or clusters of trapped fluid, and the overall distribution of these clusters throughout the porous medium. These configurations are crucial because they influence the efficiency of fluid displacement processes and the overall recovery of the injected or displaced phase. Chen et al. (2020)  presented a study that investigated various numerical modeling approaches and quantified their level of accuracy in dynamic pore-network modeling of two-phase flow and phase change in porous media. The study demonstrated the limitations of explicit and semi-implicit approaches and presented fully implicit approaches for dynamic pore network modeling. Similarly, Weishaupt and Helmig (2021)  presented a dynamic pore network model that used a fully implicit approach to simulate two-phase flow in porous media. The authors validated their model using a synthetic porous media structure and demonstrated its ability to accurately simulate complex fluid flow behavior. Overall, these new modeling approaches offer promising ways to more accurately simulate the behavior of two-phase flow in porous media and provide greater insight into the underlying physics of fluid flow. They have potential applications in a range of fields, including the oil and gas industry, environmental science, and materials science. For more information on the dynamic pore network models, please refer to the Appendix , which includes Table A.1 . The structure of the paper is as follows. First, the methodology and simulation approach will be described. Then the numerical modeling results of the dynamic simulation for hydrogen-brine system are reported in comparison with the quasi-static modeling and air–water systems. In the following section, the results of cyclic modeling by using experimentally measured contact angles for the hydrogen-brine system are shown. Finally, concluding remarks are presented.  2 Materials and methods The following section aims to provide a summary of the methodology that has been used in DuMux which is an open-source simulator for flow and transport in porous media (Weishaupt and Helmig, 2021 ). The readers for more detailed information are referred to this Weishaupt (2020) . 2.1 Displacements and transport properties In addition to characterizing the pore space, it is also important to understand the displacement and transport properties of fluids in porous media. Displacement refers to the movement of one fluid by another fluid in the pore space, and transport properties refer to the ability of fluids to move through the porous material. Threshold capillary pressure  Threshold capillary pressure is an important parameter that affects displacement behavior in porous media. The threshold capillary pressures associated with each mechanism are explained below and illustrated in Fig. 1 .  It is the minimum pressure required to initiate fluid displacement in a pore network. When fluid flows through a porous medium, the narrowest parts of the medium, known as pore throats, limit the rate of drainage. To pass through the throat, a minimum pressure, known as the entry capillary pressure, must be exceeded. This pressure is determined by the radius of curvature and the contact angle of the phases. This pressure is calculated using the radius of the inscribed pore throat (r  i j    ) and the contact angle of the receding meniscus (θ  r    ). If the throat cross-section is circular, p  c , e     can be easily calculated using a simple formula. However, for non-circular throats, the calculation of p  c , e     is more complex and depends on the presence of wetting layers in the corners of the throat. The entry capillary pressure for circular throat cross-sections is given by (1) p  c , e   = 2 γ cos ( θ  r   )   r  i j     ,     where γ   is the surface tension, θ  r     is the receding contact angle, and r  i j     is the inscribed radius of the pore throat connecting pore bodies i   and j  . For angular throat cross sections, wetting layers may be present in the corners of the throat only if a certain condition is met, i.e., (2) β + θ  r   < π  2   ,     where β   is the corner half angle. For a rectangular throat with β = π  4     , for instance, this means that the wetting phase can only be present in the corner if θ  r   ≤ π  4      in order to keep a positive capillary pressure, i.e., a concave arc meniscus. The capillary pressure within that layer reads (3) p  c   = γ  r  a m     ,     where r  a m     is the radius of the arc meniscus. For the irregular throat cross-sections, the entry capillary pressure can be derived analytically using the Mayer–Stowe–Princen (MSP) method (Patzek, 2001 ). The MSP method considers an energy balance for displacing the wetting phase and equates the curvature of the arc meniscus with that of the invading fluid’s terminal meniscus. Blunt (Blunt, 2017 ) generalized this approach for arbitrary cross-sectional shapes, i.e., (4) p  c , e   = γ ( 1 + 2 π G   )  cos ( θ  r   )  F  d   ( θ  r   , G )   r  i j     ,     where G   is the shape factor (the ratio of area to the square of the perimeter) of the cross-section and (5) F  d   ( θ  r   , G )  = 1 + 1 + 4 G E / cos  2   ( θ  r   )     1 + 2 π G     ,     with (6) E = π − 2  3   θ  r   + 3 sin ( θ  r   )  cos ( θ  r   )  − cos  2   ( θ  r   )   4 G   .      The snap-off capillary pressure, also known as the snap-off threshold, refers to the pressure required to cause the sudden disconnection or snap-off of a fluid phase in a porous medium (Patzek, 2001 ). It is particularly relevant in the context of layer swelling, where the behavior of fluid phases in the porous medium is of interest. The snap-off capillary pressure can be calculated based on the geometry of the throats, which are narrow constrictions within the porous medium. Importantly, unlike other capillary pressure calculations, determining the snap-off capillary pressure does not require an energy balance analysis. This characteristic makes it a convenient parameter to study and analyze the behavior of fluids in porous media. If the advancing contact angle is less than the maximum value given in Eq. Local capillary-pressure saturation relationship  To accurately model pressure and saturation in pore-network models, a local capillary-pressure saturation relationship per pore body must be formulated. This relationship is often derived based on geometrical assumptions, as in the case of the cubic pore body i   described by Joekar-Niasar et al. (2010a) . They proposed a simplified relationship for this cubic pore body where the local saturation S  w , i     is related to the capillary pressure p  c , i     via Eq. (2.35), i.e., (9) p  c , i   ( S  w , i   )  = 2 γ  r  i   ( 1 − e x p ( − 6 . 83 S  w , i   )  )    .      Meanwhile, a similar relationship for truncated octahedron can be found in the work of Joekar-Niasar and Hassanizadeh (2012) . Transport properties  Transport properties such as permeability and diffusivity are also critical in predicting fluid flow and transport in porous media. Permeability is a measure of how easily fluids can flow through a porous material, and diffusivity is a measure of how quickly a fluid can diffuse through the material. These properties can be influenced by the pore size distribution, connectivity, and tortuosity of the pore network (Blunt, 2017; Weishaupt, 2020 ). Estimation of the macroscopic fluid transport properties, including absolute permeability, relative permeabilities of each phase, and capillary pressure; can be done through the entire pore network. Absolute permeability is determined by simulation of single-phase flow on the fully saturated network and solving Darcy’s law, i.e., (10) K = μ  p   Q  t o t a l , s p   L  A ( Φ  i n l e t   − Φ  o u t l e t   )    ,      where μ  p     is the viscosity of a single-phase p  , and L   and A   are the length and cross-sectional area of the network, respectively. Imposing a potential drop (Φ  i n l e t   − Φ  o u t l e t     ) at two parallel surfaces of the network creates Q  t o t a l , s p    ; total flow rate. Therefore, the relative permeability of each phase can be calculated as (11) K  r p   = Q  t m p    Q  t s p     ,      where Q  t m p     is the flow rate of phase p   in a multiphase flow and Q  t s p     is the total flow rate . To find the total flow rate, we use mass conservation at each pore body i  , i.e., (12) Σ  j   q  p , i j   = 0 ,      where j   is used to refer to all pore throats connected to pore i   and q  p , i j    , is the flow rate from pore i   through throat j  . The basic assumptions are considering incompressible fluid and ignoring viscous pressure drops compared to the capillary pressure. The volumetric flow rate between two pore bodies i   and j   is calculated by the Hagen–Poiseuille equation, (13) q  p , i j   = g  p , i j    L  i j     ( Φ  p , i   − Φ  p , j   )  ,      where L   is the distance between the centers of the two connected pore bodies i   and j  . g  p , i j     is the flow conductance between the two pore bodies. For the detailed calculation of hydraulic conductance, readers are referred to these references of Blunt (2017)  and Patzek and Silin (2001) . By solving a set of mass conservation nonlinear equations, pore body pressures and saturation of phases can be calculated.  2.2 Two-phase flow modeling The two-phase flow in porous media can be modeled by a set of governing equations. Dynamic PNM  Dynamic pore-network models take into account time-dependent phase displacement processes and are able to model non-equilibrium capillary pressure states while considering the fluid phases’ viscosities. These models solve for pressure fields and phase fluxes based on mass or volume conservation, similar to conventional Darcy-type models. However, due to their highly non-linear behavior, dynamic models are computationally more complex and resource-intensive compared to quasi-static models (Blunt, 2017 ). The D-PNM solves the non-equilibrium state of two-phase flow in porous media. This means that transient behavior is involved. The pressure difference across the domain is not constant but varies over time due to fluid injection or withdrawal. Therefore, global pressure is not necessarily equal to local pressure at each time step. Joekar-Niasar and Hassanizadeh (2012)  extensively reviewed the different solution strategies for dynamic two-phase pore-network models. They classified dynamic models into two general types: 1. The first type assigns a single pressure to each pore body, assuming either the exclusive presence of a single phase or the concept of an equivalent pressure that accounts for both phases (Koplik and Lasseter, 1985; Mogensen and Stenby, 1998; Al-Gharbi and Blunt, 2005 ). While this approach reduces the computational complexity of the problem, Al-Gharbi and Blunt (2005)  found inconsistencies with respect to equivalent quasi-static simulation results for networks with angular cross-sections.  2. The second type of algorithm used in this study is based on the two-pressure model, initially introduced by Thompson (Thompson, 2002 ). This model aims to solve for an individual pressure field for each phase and adopts a sequential solution strategy that decouples the pressure and saturation variables to accelerate the solution of the linearized problems. It bears a resemblance to the IMPES (implicit pressure, explicit saturation) method commonly employed in reservoir models. In the two-pressure model, the algorithm first solves the pressures for each phase. This decoupling enables a faster solution but necessitates the use of small time steps to maintain numerical stability during the explicit saturation update. Although the two-pressure model demonstrated limitations in accurately capturing quasi-static results and was found to be unsuitable for very low capillary numbers (Ca) (Thompson, 2002 ), it provided valuable insights into the dynamics of multiphase flow in porous media. To enhance the accuracy of the two-pressure model and address the highly non-linear nature of the processes, Joekar-Niasar et al. (2010b)  proposed an improvement by introducing a semi-implicit saturation update. This enhancement allows for a better representation of complex multiphase flow behavior. Since then, this improved two-pressure model has been successfully applied in various studies (Qin et al., 2016; Khayrat and Jenny, 2016 ). Governing Equations  In the two-pressure model, the following equations govern the flow unknowns: (a) Conservation of mass for phase 1 (wetting phase) (14) ∇ ⋅ ( ρ  1   v  1   )  = ∂  ∂ t   ( ϕ s  1   ρ  1   )  + ∇ ⋅ ( ϕ s  1   ρ  1   v  1   )         (b) Conservation of mass for phase 2 (non-wetting phase) (15) ∇ ⋅ ( ρ  2   v  2   )  = ∂  ∂ t   ( ϕ s  2   ρ  2   )  + ∇ ⋅ ( ϕ s  2   ρ  2   v  2   )         (c) Darcy’s law for phase 1 (wetting phase) (16) v  1   = − k  r 1    μ  1     ∇ p  1   − ρ  1    g ∇ z          (d) Darcy’s law for phase 2 (non-wetting phase) (17) v  2   = − k  r 2    μ  2     ∇ p  2   − ρ  2    g ∇ z          (e) Capillary pressure-saturation relationship (18) p  c   = p  1   − p  2        These equations capture the pressure and saturation evolution and provide a foundation for simulating flow behavior in porous media using the two-pressure model.       Considering incompressible phases, mass conservation equations for the wetting and non-wetting phases read (Weishaupt, 2020 ): (19) V  i   ∂ S  i  w    ∂ t   + ∑  j = 1  N  i  j     Q  i j  w   = Q  i  w   ,     (20) V  i   ∂ S  i  n    ∂ t   + ∑  j = 1  N  i  j     Q  i j  n   = Q  i  n   ,     where S  i  w     and S  i  n     represent the wetting and non-wetting phase saturations in pore i  . V  i     denotes the volume of pore i  , while N  i  j     represents the number of throats connected to pore i  . Q  i j  w     and Q  i j  n     denote the flow rates of the wetting and non-wetting phases between pore i   and throat j  , respectively. Furthermore, Q  i  w     and Q  i  n     represent the total flow rates of the wetting and non-wetting phases in pore i  , respectively. The main difference between quasi-static and dynamic PNM is the inclusion of a time-related term in Eqs. (14) and (15) . In the quasi-static approach, only mass conservation is considered by summing the flow rates into a pore body and there is no saturation change to the time. The relationship between the wetting and non-wetting phase saturations reads: (21) S  i  w   + S  i  n   = 1 .      The capillary pressure, Pc , can be defined as the pressure difference between the wetting and non-wetting phases, i.e., (22) P  i  c   = P  i  n   − P  i  w   .      This system is well-posed with four equations for the four unknowns (S  i  n   , S  i  w   , P  i  w   , P  i  n     ), incorporating local rules to calculate capillary pressure, entry pressure, snap-off mechanism, and conductance. DuMux, an open-source simulator for flow and transport in porous media, provides a platform for simulating and studying these phenomena. By utilizing a pore network model, DuMux enables the simulation of fluid flow and transport in porous media, allowing for the exploration of various parameter impacts on fluid behavior within the pore space. For further details on the simulation methodology, we refer to the Weishaupt and Helmig (2021)  and Weishaupt (2020) . Simulation approach:  The simulation approach for dynamic PNM is a fully implicit method, which is used when pressure and saturation are strongly coupled, such as in low capillary number flows or unfavorable displacements (M < 1   ). The sequential coupling employed by IMPES and IMP-SIMS can pose numerical challenges in such cases. A fully implicit method ensures numerical stability by treating the pressure and saturation equations simultaneously. To solve the system of equations using a fully implicit method, numerical schemes such as Newton–Raphson are used. The fully implicit method enables the simultaneous solution of the pressure and saturation equations, enhancing numerical stability and capturing the strong coupling between pressure and saturation in low capillary number flows or unfavorable displacements. In the next section, the results of the transport of hydrogen through a network with box-shaped pores and square cylinder throats using dynamic pore-network modeling are reported. The used network statistics, fluid and gas properties are summarized in Tables 1 and 2 , respectively.    The average saturation of water in the network, denoted as 〈 S  w   〉   , and the average capillary pressure, denoted as 〈 p  c   〉   , were calculated using, (23) 〈 S  w   〉  = ∑  i   ( S  w   V )   i    ∑  i   V  i         (24) 〈 p  c   〉  = ∑  i   ( S  n   p  n   V )   i    ∑  i   ( S  n   V )   i     − ∑  i   ( S  w   p  w   V )   i    ∑  i   ( S  w   V )   i     .     where S  w     denotes the wetting phase saturation and V   is the pore volume and p   is the pressure of each phase. In the model, pore throats are assumed to be volumeless, serving only to control flow resistance, while the pore bodies are assumed to store the phases.   3 Results and discussion The simulation results were compared with quasi-static pore- network modeling to assess the accuracy and reliability of the dynamic approach.1  1 To replicate the results of this paper the source code can be accessed via this link https://git.iws.uni-stuttgart.de/dumux-pub/weishaupt2020a  using the network information in Table 1  and the fluid and gas properties reported in Table 2 . The simulation results showed a good agreement between the dynamic and quasi-static modeling approaches. When the dynamic simulation (yellow line) reaches a steady-state – defined here as the point where the saturation of hydrogen–water remains constant over time – the results of the dynamic (green circle marker) and the quasi-static (red dash-line) simulations match. This steady-state condition is characterized by no further changes in the saturation levels of the two phases. Before reaching steady state, the models show some differences due to transient effects (yellow line in Fig. 3 ), but these differences diminish as the system stabilizes. The match between these two methods indicates that the quasi-static simulation can be used as a reliable and efficient method for studying hydrogen transport in similar networks.  • The capillary pressure function of hydrogen–water against air–water was also analyzed, and the results are presented in Fig. 4 .  • The behavior of hydrogen–water in the network was analyzed by calculating the Nc and M values for drainage and imbibition processes.
