In tidal systems, the infiltration of saltwater creates a saltwater circulation cell that overtops the freshwater discharging via a so-called freshwater tube that itself resides on top of a saltwater wedge. Hence, distinctly different water compartments with variable salinity are encountered in the STE (Michael et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2007 ). Groundwater flow and transport patterns in this zone are dynamic and complex, depending on many factors such as, for example, density, aquifer characteristics, (seasonal) fresh groundwater flux, tidal amplitudes, wave heights and storm floods (e.g., Michael et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2007; Evans and Wilson, 2016 ). Following passage through the STE where it is chemically modified, saline and fresh groundwater and with it dissolved matter discharge into coastal waters, affecting coastal elemental cycles and budgets, surface water quality and ecosystems (e.g. Santos et al., 2008; Morrow et al., 2010 ). To understand groundwater flow and transport in STEs and as a prerequisite for biogeochemical studies, profound knowledge on the salinity distribution is needed. Spatial and temporal variabilities of near surface salinities in coastal aquifers were found to be large, especially under high-energy conditions (Waska et al., 2019 ). High-energy conditions are defined as areas with a high mean tidal range as well as high significant wave height (Hayes, 1979 ). Large spatio-temporal variability of salinity was also suspected at greater depths for high-energy conditions based on numerical modelling (Greskowiak and Massmann, 2021 ). Therefore, methods are needed that are able to accurately capture the porewater salinity distribution throughout the STE. Conventional groundwater monitoring wells can provide salinity time-series in STEs, however only for a very limited number of points in space due to the limitations in the number of positions and screening depths. Additionally, direct methods like porewater lancets or borehole-based sampling tools are commonly used to extract porewater from the subsurface (e.g. Grünenbaum et al., 2023 ). Typically, the salinity of the porewater is estimated trough measuring the electrical conductivity of the water sample, i.e. the fluid, directly in the field (in the following referred to as EC f    ); however chemical analyses in the lab are the only way to derive the ion composition and the total dissolved solid (TDS) concentration of a water sample. In contrast, indirect methods often use the (bulk) electrical conductivity (in the following referred to as EC b    ) as a proxy parameter for salinity as there is a strong correlation once the porosity and general lithology is known. Besides methods that measure EC f     directly, there is a large number of geophysical methods that are able to retrieve the EC b     from very small scales (quasi-point measurements) to large areas of investigations. Those methods can be subdivided into direct-current (DC) and electromagnetic induction (EMI) techniques. The latter excite an alternating primary field (typically 1 kHz to 100 kHz) into a transmitter loop and thus induce currents in conductors that in turn generate a secondary field, which is measured by a receiver coil. DC techniques use a quasi-zero frequency current injection into two electrodes and measure a potential difference between two potential electrodes. These methods can be applied on the Earth’s surface, in boreholes or fixed installations, but also mounted to ground-penetrating tools that are also known under the term Direct Push (DP) (Dietrich and Leven, 2006 ). Originally designed for discriminating different geological units (e.g. clay and sand) by mechanical parameters (core pressure and mantle friction), they can also bear tools for measuring EC b     (e.g., Vienken et al., 2017 ) or hydraulic pressure (Butler et al., 2007 ). In saturated sediments, boreholes often need to be cased for stability reasons which limits tools to EMI. Hermans et al. (2012) , for example, used an frequency-domain EM tool using audio-frequency currents to discriminate sand from clay in a coastal aquifer system. From the surface, EC b     can be mapped by coil-coil (EMI) systems or with four-electrode (DC) arrays (Paepen et al., 2020 ). Both provide an apparent conductivity (or resistivity, its inverse) that is a weighted mean of a part of the subsurface. The respective extent and depth of penetration depends on the sensor distance and the used frequencies. So-called multi-electrode systems make use of a large number (typically 30-100) of pre-installed electrodes that can be used as current or potential electrodes in an automated scheme, so that a two-dimensional conductivity image is generated through an inverse modelling procedure (e.g., Dahlin and Zhou, 2004  comparing different arrays). This method, also known as Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT), has gained great popularity in hydrology and has been applied to coastal aquifer imaging (e.g., Comte et al., 2010; Hermans et al., 2012; Beaujean et al., 2014; Buquet et al., 2016; Kazakis et al., 2016; Ayari et al., 2023 ). The ERT method is particularly interesting in coastal environments because it can be repeatedly applied by so-called time-lapse ERT. By doing so, processes like seawater intrusion can be monitored (e.g., de Franco et al., 2009; Morrow et al., 2010; Palacios et al., 2020 ). For long-term monitoring, permanent installation of electrodes can be done as for the well-established ALERT system that has been developed to monitor seawater intrusion in coastal aquifers (Ogilvy et al., 2009 ). Grinat et al. (2018)  developed a saltwater monitoring system (SAMOS) using a vertical electrode chain that monitors the saltwater–freshwater interface at two positions on Borkum island (Germany) in a fully autonomous mode. Similar system were subsequently installed at a salinized German mainland site and in the vicinity of groundwater production wells on the island of Spiekeroog (Germany). Ronczka et al. (2020)  demonstrated how data can be processed in a way that near-surface anomalies can be distinguished from the undisturbed subsurface. All of the abovementioned methods targeting either EC b    , EC f    , or porewater salinity exhibit specific spatial and temporal coverage and resolution. In this paper, we aim to compare methods to assess EC b     used at the DynaDeep coastal aquifer observatory on the North Sea island Spiekeroog in Germany (Massmann et al., 2023 ). The site is presently subject to extensive investigations to understand the functioning of high-energy STEs. Methods applied to assess EC to understand coastal groundwater flow and transport and as baseline information for biogeochemical investigations include ERT, DP, SAMOS, as well as porewater EC measurements. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first site where such a broad range of methods is applied, allowing for an intercomparison of the different methods. This allows to assess the potential, but also challenges and pitfalls, of the individual methods that should, ideally, all deliver similar values. Furthermore, it provides the basis for their combination in order to further optimize coastal aquifer imaging and monitoring. This work serves as a reference for salinity imaging of coastal aquifers in general and at the specific high-energy beach site on Spiekeroog.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The work is done within a large interdisciplinary cooperative project called DynaDeep (The dynamic deep subsurface of high-energy beaches), that studies the biogeochemical functioning of STEs using hydrological, geomorphological, geophysical, geochemical and microbial methods. The overall study area and project infrastructure is described in detail in Massmann et al. (2023) . Here, we focus explicitly on EC methods and their contribution to salinity imaging.  The study area is located at a high-energy beach at the northern shore of Spiekeroog, a barrier islands at the North Sea coast in Germany (Fig. 1 ). We chose the island due to the access to a high energy beach, low anthropogenic influence, and a general dense knowledge of the island due to research projects such as installing a coastal observatory (Zielinski et al., 2022 ), investigations of the freshwater lens formation (Röper et al., 2013a ), and its hydrochemical evolution (Seibert et al., 2018 ). A general overview of the geology, geomorphology as well as hydrology of the island is given by Röper et al. (2013a) . At the site, the beach has a variable width of roughly 300 m from the dune base to the low-water line. The intertidal zone is about half as wide, with strong tides having a mean tidal range of around 2.7 m with mean significant wave heights of 1.4 m (Herrling and Winter, 2015 ). Storm tides during the winter season can reach to the base of the dune area and greatly influence topography and bathymetry (Waska et al., 2019; Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ) and can shift the beach line by tens of metres. Three major facies form the upper beach aquifer: The upper approx. five metres consist of young beach sands that are underlain by approx. 15 m of tidal flat sediments deposited during the Holocene. Below, Saalian glacial sands (Massmann et al., 2023 ) were encountered that are underlain by a continuous clay aquitard in about 40 m below sealevel (Röper et al., 2012 ).  2.2 Monitoring concept In the study area, several methods for investigating the electrical conductivity are regularly used: ERT, SAMOS, DP, EC f     measurements in water samples using probes, as well as data logging with automatic loggers for EC f     and temperature placed in observation wells, whereby the herein used ML2 is located near the high water line (Fig. 1 ). The overall aim of the geophysical work within DynaDeep is to repeatedly calculate the cross-shore salinity distribution along a 2D transect to assess its development over time. Two-dimensional ERT profiles are measured approximately every 6 weeks starting in 2021, whereby only the January and March campaigns are used for this intercomparison study. EC b     images from ERT data are rather smooth as long as no additional data (EC f     or structural information) are used in the inversion process. The DP is regularly used to further log EC b     at specific points using a probe (for more details refer to Massmann et al., 2023 ). This in turn can be used in the inversion process of the ERT. A SAMOS system (Grinat et al., 2018 ) was installed near the high water line (Fig. 1 ) and is measuring a vertical ERT profile every 48 h to monitor salinity changes over time. All three methods (ERT, DP probing and SAMOS) measure EC b     as a function of the porespace fluid and matrix. In order to gain salinities, the EC f     needs to be computed first. This is by multiplying the EC b     with the formation factor. Porewater samples for direct measurement of in-situ EC f     are obtained regularly within the project from the DP locations every three depth metre. In addition, multilevel observation wells ( 6, 12, 18 and 24 metre depth) are both sampled as well as used for EC f     and temperature logging (reference logger). The EC f     measurements are subsequently compared to the SAMOS bulk data and used to calculate the formation factors over depth. Fig. 1  shows the fixed locations of SAMOS and multi-level groundwater wells ML1 and ML2 on the beach, as well as DP probing sites in January (DP2, DP2.5, DP3 and March (CP).  Fig. 2  shows an overview of the location and depth range of the used methods illustrated by their different sensitivities to highlight limitations and advantages. For the intercomparison of different methods to assess porewater salinities within this paper, we focus on two campaigns in early January and early March, 2023 and the time in-between (SAMOS, logger). Whereas in January several DP soundings were measured, fluid samples along with a representative DP sounding were retrieved in March between the SAMOS and ML2 wells, all at the same position (comparison point (CP), see Fig. 1 ).  2.3 Porewater conductivity In porewater samples obtained from DP and well sampling, EC f     and temperature were measured using a MultiLine® Multi 3630 IDS portable metre with the TetraCon® 925 conductivity probe. In the permanently installed wells EC f     and temperature are recorded in five minute intervals using data loggers (μ  S-Log3040 from Drisen + Kern) in each filter screen of ML2 at 6 m, 12 m, 18 m, and 24 m (These loggers are pre-calibrated by the company). Temperature dependence Most EC devices used in water samples including the ones we used measure EC f     and temperature simultaneously, but display and save the conductivity value valid for a temperature of 25 °C. In contrast, all of the methods applied to measure EC b     are related to the in situ temperature. Temperature measurements and corrections are thus important for all methods. For the sake of comparison, we show both EC f     and EC b     only for in situ temperature, i.e. we are correcting the EC f     back to in situ temperature T   using the following equation (Hayashi, 2004 ): (1) E C  T   = E C  25   ∗ ( 1 + ( T − 25 )  ∗ α )      with an α   value of 0.02, i.e. a two percent increase of conductivity per degree. For converting spatially variable EC, temperature needs to be measured or modelled.    The formation factor: Bulk vs fluid EC In fully-saturated aquifers, the porewater porosity (ϕ  ) is the main contributor to E C  b     , along with surface conductivity E C  s      representing two resistors in parallel as described by the modified Archies law (Waxman and Smits, 1968 ) (2) E C  b   = E C  f   / F + E C  s   = E C  f   ϕ  m   + E C  s   .      The surface conductivity EC s     results from cation exchange at the electrical double layer at the grain surface of fine/clay sediments. The formation factor F = E C  f   / E C  b      depends on the pore size distribution and is typically around 4 for coarse, well-sorted sands, and increases with decreasing grain size and degree of sorting (Schön, 2015 ). At our site, the clay content is very small and furthermore the fluid conductivity EC f     dominates due to the high salinity, which is why we can neglect EC s     throughout this investigation. At the study site, Grünenbaum et al. (2023)  compared EC f     from porewater sampled with porewater lances with ERT results and obtained a formation factor of about F = 4 . 5    at the surface. They also observed an increase to values of about F = 7    at greater depths. These values correspond to porosities between 34% and 22% assuming a so-called cementation exponent of m = 1 . 3    typical for porous sandy sediments. Note that without surface conductivity, the two formulas (1) and (2)  are just factors and can be combined so that EC b     can directly be converted to 25 °C which simplifies the interpretation of temporal changes to salinity changes only.   2.4 Direct push We used a Geoprobe® 7822DT, with a hydraulically operated Geoprobe® GH60 Series (GH64R) impact hammer for rods up to 3.25 inches in diameter. For EC b     measurements soil conductivity probes of type SC520 from Geoprobe® are used. The measurements are realized as Wenner array, with two current and two potential electrodes installed on each side of the probe. The electrodes each have a diameter of 7.5 mm and are arranged vertically with a distance of 23 mm between electrode midpoints. To reach the desired depth, single rods with a length of 4 ft and a diameter of 1.75 inches are used, which can be mounted on each other until the desired depth is reached. The EC probe is connected to the control unit by a cable inside the hollow rods. The control unit Geoprobe® FI6003 field device is used to supply the probe with power and to record the measurement voltage. The Geoprobe® DI acquisition software is used to record the measurements. Parameters measured are depth, speed of advance, and apparent EC b    , with a single measurement point representing an integrated value over a certain depth range. Before each measurement, the probe is checked for proper functioning using the supplied software. This is done by transferring a test voltage to the electrodes using a supplied connector. Then three tests are carried out to check whether the incoming voltage and the outgoing voltage are measured within the basic conditions and whether the required line resistances are given. This test is also performed after the measurement to verify that the probe has remained functional throughout the measurement. Only measurements that are within the acceptable test parameters before the measurement and after the measurement are retained for further processing. The four DP-EC probes were further tested (and calibrated) in the lab with three different bucket sizes (10 L, 20 L, and 50 L) and water with variable salt concentrations ranging from tap water (∼  0 mg L−1 ) to saltwater with 30 mg L−1  sodium chloride. The electrodes were sandpapered to remove eroded material that can interfere with the measurement (under field conditions, the subsurface material takes care of this) as recommended by Geoprobe. Smaller gaps around the electrodes were filled with super-glue. A calibrated handheld WTW multiprobe device is used for comparison purpose. Results of this test are shown in Fig. 3 . The upper sub Fig. 3 a shows a direct comparison of the measured EC value of the four probes (y-axis) over the expected value from the WTW reference probe on the x  -axis. The DP EC probes number 1 (blue), 3 (green) and 4 (red) where used for most of the measurements within the project. Probe number 2 (yellow) has never been used so far and is for reference only. The DP EC probe values (in the absence of porous medium = EC f    ) deviate from the reference line with increasing salinity/EC f     of the water. The factors to correct the respective offsets are shown in the lower sub Fig. 3 b, leading to a mean correction factor for the range of interest (expected in-situ E C  b      values) of 1.6 (i.e., +60%).  2.5 SAMOS The saltwater monitoring system (SAMOS) at the site is a permanent electrode that was installed into an open borehole. It is equipped with a ERT measuring device automatically doing the measurements in predefined time intervals. It consists of a chain with 80 electrodes every 25 cm and was accomplished in July, 2022. At the time of installation, the first electrode was installed at 0.9 m depth so that the whole chain reached down to a depth of 20.65 m below ground. As the topography is changing, data is plotted in absolute coordinates, i.e. metres below sea level (m bsl). The system can measure whole pseudosections with varying electrode arrays and distances, just like a standard ERT profile. The measured data, i.e. current and voltage, are transferred into apparent resistivity, which is representing an integral value over a certain volume whose size depends on the distribution of the electrodes used. In order to retrieve a true subsurface resistivity distribution, an inversion process is carried out that takes the correct geometry of the chain and the electrodes into account. This procedure is described in detail by Ronczka et al. (2020)  who focused on distinguishing installation effects close to the borehole from the undisturbed subsurface. As a result, it provides a two-dimensional resistivity/conductivity image along depth and distance to the electrode chain, assuming cylindrical symmetry (1D conditions) around the system. Assuming 1D conditions, we subsequently only use the values of a fixed distance to the SAMOS chain, when comparing different results over time. The cells of the chosen layer represent the values between 28 cm and 72 cm distance to the chain, which is far enough to avoid effects related to the chain itself yet still an area with high resolution. A total of ten temperature sensors are evenly distributed along the SAMOS chain. The temperature data allows to account for any temperature-related seasonal drifts of the SAMOS EC b     results as well as for comparison to the other EC f     data.  2.6 ERT ERT data is collected using the 12-channel ABEM Terrameter LS2 instrument. With an additional switch-box ES-64C we are able to use up to 128 electrodes at the same time. A separation of 2.5 m is achieved by shifted cables with 5 m takeout distance, thus leading to a maximum profile length of 317.5 m. The ERT transect is measured in one go from the dune base up to the low water line (some electrodes are placed into the water as well). As the topography and the length of the accessible beach are changing with time, mostly between 80 and 100 electrodes are used. We use the multiple-gradient array (Dahlin and Zhou, 2004 ) as it can very efficiently use multiple-channels with a good data quality. Measurement speed is of utmost importance given the short accessibility of the intertidal zone as we measure during low tide. The specific designed multiple-gradient array for half-overlapping cables is minimizing the number of current injections needed compared to classical arrays like Wenner or Dipole-Dipole. The inversion as well as the data processing is done using the open-source pyGIMLi package (Rücker et al., 2017 ) in Python. Specific tasks and modifications are made with self-written extensions in Python which are added to the pyGIMLi source code as soon as they are tested and published. We use a geostatistical regularization method (Hermans et al., 2012; Jordi et al., 2018 ) to specify horizontal and vertical correlation lengths, the vertical are used by investigating the DP data. This procedure is similar to the one used in preliminary measurements of Grünenbaum et al. (2023)  in 2019 and 2021.  2.7 Temperature and salinity We base our interpolated temperature model on the data logger in ML2 and in the SAMOS chain as well as independently derived values for the surface water. We linearly interpolate these values into a continuous 1D model over depth and time, which is used to convert EC values from SAMOS and the other methods close to the comparison point to 25 °C. The seawater temperature from the Spiekeroog coastal observatory (Zielinski et al., 2022 ) is used as upper boundary condition. For computing salinity from EC f    , the concentration of the total dissolved solids (TDS) is needed. Assuming the relative ion contents are constant, a conductivity conversion factor for Spiekeroog island was determined by Holt et al. (2017)  with a value 0.6768 g cm L−1  mS−1  that we will use throughout this study, based on a temperature-corrected E C  f      at 25 °C.   3 Results 3.1 ERT  Fig. 4  shows the two ERT images for the two campaigns in early January and early March, 2023. Additional locations where data was obtained are indicated by grey dots (samples and logger), dotted black lines (SAMOS) and solid black lines (DP). Both ERT images in Fig. 4  show low E C  b      at shallow depths close to the dunes and high conductivity in the shallow intertidal zone from x=90 m to 220 m. At greater depth a lower conductivity is observed that is attributed to the freshwater discharge tube. A prominent feature is a thin conductive layer between x=50 m to 80 m that is more pronounced in the March result as compared to the January result.  3.2 SAMOS  Fig. 5  shows the inversion results at the SAMOS chain for the two dates when ERT and DP data were acquired (January and March, 2023), in terms of EC b     (grey lines indicate area used for stacking over time). They show in principle a similar behaviour as the ERT profiles, i.e., decreasing EC b     from January to March in the upper 5 m. At the top, a less conductive layer resulting from partial saturation is visible. Similar EC b     values than the ERT profiles can be observed at depths greater than 15 m, which we interpret as the freshwater discharge tube (FDT) that was already imaged by Grünenbaum et al. (2023) . At this depth, we also expect the change from tidal-flat to glaciofluvial sediments according to Massmann et al. (2023) . At about 13 m a thin conductive layer can be seen with increasing EC b     over time. Stacking the single time steps together results in Fig. 6  which gives a more continuous picture of the temporal development of EC b     at SAMOS. Fig. 6  a shows the inverted EC b     values after the geophysical inversion at in situ temperatures. Generally, the overall structure and the depth layering remain largely constant indicating rather slow processes. A decrease of EC b     over time can be seen in the upper metres and an increase at a depth at about 12 m to 15 m. Fig. 6  b shows the temperature distribution over time based on the 10 temperature sensors along the SAMOS chain. It clearly shows how the temperature decreased over time during the 2 months shown. Sub Fig. 6  c finally shows EC b     over time referenced to 25 °C. Hence, changes visible in Fig. 6  c are solely due to changes in salinity and not caused by temperature changes in the subsurface.    3.3 Formation factors We calculate the formation factor over time as ratio of EC f     measured in well ML2 and EC b     from SAMOS (Fig. 7 ). Gaps in later January for 6 m and in early January for 12 m and 18 m result from malfunctioning of the data logger. The values are not randomly distributed but follow some temporal trends, however in a rather limited range. The mean values for the 6 m and 12 m loggers are 3.9 and 4.6, respectively. Both agree well within their standard deviations.  The lowest logger at 18 m is located in the glacio-fluvial sediments (Massmann et al., 2023 ). Its mean value F   = 5.58 is significantly larger than above and corresponds to porosities between 27% and 33%, which are lower than those expected for the sediments above, as the glacio-fluvial sands have a wider grain size distributions. Assuming cementation exponents between 1.3 and 1.5 from literature values (e.g. Schön, 2015 ) for Archies law, these correspond to porosities between 36% and 41%. We therefore consider a value of 4.25 representative for the sandy tidal-flat sediments and the significantly higher value of 5.58 for glaciofluvial sediments. Grünenbaum et al. (2023, Fig. 4)  likewise described an increasing formation factor with depth, from 4.5 for shallow depths to 7 for depths larger than 20 m. However, the need to correct DP values was unknown at the time, and correction would lower values by Grünenbaum et al. (2023)  to a similar range. Moreover, the layered geology was not known at the time. Hence, formation factors based on lithology appear more justified than the linear increase chosen by Grünenbaum et al. (2023) .  3.4 Temporal dynamics With the formation factors at hand, we can compare the temporal behaviour of the EC f     from ML2 loggers at 6, 12 and 18 m depth with SAMOS (EC b    ) data. Fig. 8  plots the time series of both data sets along with the EC b     measured in porewater for the three different depths.  As the filter screens of ML 2 have a width of 1 m, we compare the values with SAMOS values of the mean filter depth ±  0.5 m (Fig. 8 , orange lines). In general, the curves align reasonably well with each other, particularly for 6 m and 12 m depth. The shallowest logger clearly shows a tidal signal which is also noticeable for the largest depth but not for the logger at twelve metre. The SAMOS is not reflecting the tidal signal, however this is expected as the resolution is lower. This can be explained by the SAMOS signal origin, as it has a larger footprint due to the sensitivity associated with the measurement technique (Fig. 2 ) and processing steps involved. Whereas at 6 m the conductivity decreases over time, it stays more or less constant at 12 m and increases at 18 m, for which the values are generally lower as seen before.  3.5 Spatial variability Whereas the loggers and samples average over the screen length, both DP and SAMOS exhibit an increased spatial resolution. Fig. 9  shows EC b     depth profiles from DP and SAMOS along with ERT results for the two campaign in January and March, 2023. The curves illustrate the spatial resolution of the different methods, that is a few cm for DP (blue), a few dm for SAMOS and in the m range for ERT showing a smoothed curve, particularly with increasing depth. Local maxima or minima are partly similar between DP and SAMOS but cannot be imaged by ERT due to the lower resolution. Note that even though the spatial dynamics of the DP values align, the absolute DP values shown were multiplied by a factor 1.6 as found by our bucket calibration measurements (see Fig. 3 ). Generally, all curves match well, except the DP data are higher between -2 m bsl and 3 m bsl in January. The DP reaches values well above the shown 12 mS cm−1  which are not shown here. As values above 9 mS cm−1  (given the known temperature and formation factor) correspond to saltwater, we believe the DP calibration is insufficient for this part of the profile.  Fig. 10  shows the spatio-temporal dynamics of the salinity distribution around the SAMOS chain based on the calculated formation factor and temperature models: Unlike for the EC b     in Fig. 5 , changes due to temperature changes (temporally) or due to a change of the formation factors (spatially) are removed. This results in a smooth transition over the boundary separating the two geological layers. Overall, the salinity is rather high, as the location is in the infiltration zone and close to the sea. There is little change over time and values are almost constant in some depths. In the upper 5 m, the salinity is slightly decreasing, whereas it increases at depths below 12 m. There are a few layers with lower salinity visible that are constant over time, that are likely linked to lithological features. The preliminary lithological investigation of the ML2 cores are supporting this statement (Massmann et al., 2023 ), even though the drilling is roughly 14 m away. Unfortunately no core was drilled during the installation of the SAMOS system.     4 Discussion The methods to measure either EC f     or EC b     applied in this study come along with limitations in spatial and temporal resolution as well as accuracy. Direct push EC measurements The presented DP measurements are seemingly only comparable after suitable calibration. The DP method provides high resolution 1D data, yet care must be taken when comparing it with other measurements on a quantitative level, at least for higher conductivity, as in this study. According to our tests, the calibration factor appears to vary with the tools used and with time. This is supported by findings of Demuth et al. (2015) , especially for the used point electrode DP tool. Therefore, careful calibration in a controlled environment before and after each campaign is necessary for the DP data to become a reliable addition to the other methods presented. Once calibrated, DP is a useful tool to retrieve information about EC b     and EC f     and to get access to 1D formation factor models at other positions along the transect with the aim to retrieve a 2D salinity distribution in the end.  Formation factor The formation factor may be depth-dependent, which affects the transformation of EC b     to EC f    , as apparent in the present study. Additional information (geological or geophysical) is required to delineate a general lithological model before a suitable parametrization can be derived. In our case, a two layer case best reflects the plausible porosities considering Archies law. The formation factor model based on the SAMOS and fluid samples at the comparison point consists of a simple two layer model that is in general agreement with previous investigations Grünenbaum et al. (2023)  as well as the local lithology. The values of the first metres also agree well with the value of F  =3.83 retrieved by Günther and Müller-Petke (2012)  for Borkum island for comparable subsurface conditions. However, limitations of the models are clearly seen in Fig. 10  in terms of vertical variations in the salinity model. We consider those variations not to reflect salinity changes, but instead attribute them to local lithological changes (laterally and/or vertically) of the tidal flat sediments, as also observed in the DP data. Variations in compaction and/or grain size distribution of the beach sand could, for example, produce formation factor changes in the range of the observed salinity deviations. This can be observed when comparing the EC b     from Fig. 6  c to the salinity in Fig. 10 . The strong EC b     gradient at the depth of 13 m to 14 m disappears when taking the formation factors into account, i.e., the salinity changes smoothly across the lithological boundary. This is the expected behaviour, as the salinity changes are likely not as abrupt. Nevertheless, some uncertainty due to inherent measurement errors will always remain and has to be taken into account when using ERT and SAMOS results for subsequent interpretations. Note that we assumed surface conductivity to be negligible as a precondition before applying the presented algorithms for the conversion between EC b     and EC f    . This assumption may not always hold, especially for aquitards with clay or silt contents. Under such conditions, the temperature conversion and EC f     calculation would produce artifacts, and hence the salinity model would become unreliable. Information on the silt and clay contents is needed to identify respective subsurface areas and limit the salinity models accordingly. Surface nuclear magnetic resonance measurements for example can help to discriminate clay from saltwater aquifers and provide direct information on the subsurface porosity and therefore information about the formation factors, also in 2D (Skibbe et al., 2021 ).  Temperature Temperature logging and appropriate correction is crucial when deriving salinity. The temperature data from the SAMOS chain provided a 1D model through linear interpolation that also involves surface water temperature. Generally, groundwater temperatures are rather constant and reflect average surface water temperatures in the respective region (Röper et al., 2013b ). However, the temperature distribution in the subsurface can be complex and temperatures may strongly vary. Seasonal effects lead to infiltration of surface water into the aquifer as described for river bank filtration sites (Henzler et al., 2016 ). The 1D temperature model needs to be taken with caution as the 1D conditions at the SAMOS location do not necessarily reflect the 1D conditions at other positions along the transect. The data loggers in the groundwater monitoring wells that also record temperature could be used in future to further extend the 1D model into 2D as needed by ERT. Additional long-term monitoring in addition to groundwater flow and transport modelling is mandatory to deliver a more reliable temperature model in 2D and over time.  Temporal dynamics In the presented time interval of two months in winter, only minor temporal changes in the EC and temperatures were observed. The fact that the dynamics were low in the chosen time interval in combination with high data density provided the opportunity to focus on the comparison of the different methods with little disruptive factors. However, as the target area is a high-energy beach, more dynamic changes in EC f     over time are expected as shown in a generic numerical groundwater flow and transport model accounting for hydro- and morphodynamics at the site (Greskowiak and Massmann, 2021 ).    Salinity model Several aspects described in 1D need further consideration before attempting to use these results for subsequent, particularly multi-dimensional and dynamic, studies. Even when the data showed in Fig. 9  fit together, we do not believe that the ERT is capable of resolving the envisaged salinity distribution as standalone method. This has also be shown by Paepen et al. (2022) , showing that a quantitative analysis of the data (in their case ERT with the aim towards salinity) is strongly depending on the resolution of the methods. We, however, believe the broader coverage of the ERT is a good way to interpolate in between points of higher resolution from ERT, monitoring and/or fluid samples. Using the described 1D temperature and formation factor models, Fig. 11  summarizes the data from all methods (SAMOS, DP, loggers) in a 2D salinity image and points out the challenges. The two subfigures again represent the January and March campaigns, respectively. Both models resemble the upper-saline plume already visible in the EC b     image from Fig. 4 , but show a prominent gradient at the formation factor step incorporated into the model. As discussed above, the change in salinity results from insufficient knowledge of the formation factor distribution in space, except at the SAMOS location. A parameter jump like in Fig. 11  is expected for the EC b     and not for the EC f     which is the basis of the salinity image. The classical ERT inversion inverts EC b    , i.e., the bulk values will be smoothly distributed due to the inherent mathematical algorithm stabilizing the inversion process. For many real world scenarios, however, this is not the truth. Instead, in many cases EC f     is smoothly distributed, whereas the EC b     may change at formation boundaries. The problem becomes apparent when using a smooth bulk distribution with a formation factor model to calculate salinity as done in Fig. 11 . The resulting salinity distribution shows a sudden increase in salinity at the formation factor change, that should not be present. We propose for future applications that aim at salinity, one should invert directly to EC f     instead of EC b     and include the formation factor distribution (and temperature conversion) prior to the inversion. This however needs a modification to existing inversion algorithms. Similar to the current approach, the formation factor model as well as temperature model need to be known. However, even with insufficient information, the inversion will search for a smoothly distributed EC f     (salinity) model (instead of EC b    ), which is an overall more realistic assumption for many cases. Moreover, the resolution of the ERT could be improved in general by inserting DP and SAMOS models directly into the inversion process. This has been attempted already by Grünenbaum et al. (2023) , however they did not correct the DP data sufficiently. The general agreement of the different used methods in this work is better seen in Fig. 9  for the 1D model that served as a basis to calculate the formation factors.  2D distribution Temperature and formation factors are not 1D horizontally layered as shown by Massmann et al. (2023) . In reality, the lithology is 3-dimensional, as will be the resulting distribution of the formation factor. Depending on groundwater flow the temperature and salinity distributions are likewise 3-dimensional and transient, and cannot be expected to be layered horizontally, given the fact that different water bodies mix in the subsurface and enter the STE more or less horizontally (freshwater flux from inland) or vertically (saltwater infiltration from upper saline plume). However, with the calibration for the DP measurements we think it is possible to retrieve multiple vertical 1D temperature/formation factor models along the horizontal profile to ultimately calculate the salinity distribution in 2D. In summary, the selection of the appropriate technique depends on the target. For 1D models a combination of DP or SAMOS and a suitably dense spatial distribution of EC f     and temperature measurements should be utilized to calculate a salinity model for the site at a given point in time. A combination of DP with ERT helps to interpolate between the distinct 1D vertical profiles. In order to retrieve time-lapsed inversion models, monitoring of EC is recommended at least at one position to be able to extrapolate the temporal changes to other locations. However, as we do not show a sophisticated time-scale model here, this is more a hypothetical recommendation and needs further work for validation. Each of the methods applied also comes with their own uncertainty defined by the method itself (integration, resolution, scaling effects) and the used device (shifts and time drifts, calibration etc.).   5 Conclusions In this study, we compared different methods to determine porewater salinity through the proxy parameter electrical conductivity. Fluid samples provide direct values but are laborious to retrieve via wells or DP techniques in high resolution. Multi-level loggers provide good temporal, but limited (filter screen) spatial resolution. DP soundings shows high vertical resolution but needs to be calibrated repeatedly in the field if EC accuracy is required. ERT provides a good overview on the spatial salinity distribution, but with limited (particularly vertical) resolution and possible artifacts. SAMOS, as a special variant of vertical ERT monitoring, provides high vertical and temporal resolution, however only at one position with significant installation effort. When comparing logger or sample data with geophysical results, temperature needs to be measured and taken into account. To derive EC f     from EC b     (e.g. using DP, ERT, SAMOS), the (depth-depending) formation factor has to be computed using high vertical resolution bulk data (SAMOS, DP) and fluid data (samples, logger). Depending on subsurface conditions (2D), several 1D measurements for EC f     and EC b     might be necessary. Overall, the distribution of temperature (over space and time) and formation factors (over space) is required when the electrical conductivity is analysed. For 2D monitoring of salinities in STEs, we recommend a combination of ERT with DP and multi-level wells. To investigate the salinity dynamics, SAMOS has proven to be a suitable tool. Integration of all measurements should be done to achieve the most reliable and comprehensive salinity images, e.g. by integrating DP or logger data into ERT imaging. DP measurements can, with suitable calibration, be an effective tool to access the formation factor distribution and therefore lead the way to 2D salinity imaging. The combination of methods is critical to lower the overall uncertainty. Again, a combined inversion of the data, where individual data errors can be accounted for, is the next logical step.
1 Introduction Elevated suspended sediment (SS) concentrations pose several risks to the healthy functioning of aquatic ecosystems (Bilotta and Brazier, 2008; Cooper et al., 2015 ). Excessive SS loads can reduce the capacity of reservoirs and cause channel and harbour siltation (Owens et al., 2010 ), which can increase flood risks (Nones, 2019 ). Having reliable information on the origin of SS, and a robust understanding of the processes leading to SS mobilization, is therefore very important to be able to mitigate excessive SS inputs to rivers and streams (Cooper et al., 2015; Owens et al., 2005; Vercruysse et al., 2017a ). Sediment fingerprinting is a widely adopted approach for providing such information (see reviews by e.g., Collins et al., 2020, 2017; Haddadchi et al., 2013; Owens et al., 2016; Walling, 2005 ). The approach is based on the comparison of source material and target SS properties (i.e., fingerprints). Current methods to sample source material and target SS (e.g., manually or using time-integrated SS traps), together with the need to measure conventional fingerprint properties (e.g., geochemistry or radionuclides), are often onerous in terms of workloads and costs (Cooper et al., 2015; Horowitz, 2013; Martínez-Carreras et al., 2016; Poulenard et al., 2012 ). This poses limitations for SS sampling and inhibits SS source fingerprinting at high temporal frequencies (Collins et al., 2020; Legout et al., 2013 ) and over long time-frames (Martínez-Carreras et al., 2016 ). This is despite many studies having reported substantial intra- and inter-event variations in SS sources (e.g., Cooper et al., 2015; Legout et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023; Navratil et al., 2012; Vale et al., 2020; Vercruysse and Grabowski, 2019 ), with sampling at low frequency or short duration thus failing to record important facets of SS source dynamics. Low sampling frequencies can lead to misleading sediment fingerprinting results by failing to collect samples during the activation and deactivation of different dominant sources (e.g., Legout et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023 ). Successfully capturing high-frequency dynamics in SS source contributions requires high temporal frequency and/or long duration observations (Abbas et al., 2023; Poulenard et al., 2012 ). Current state-of-the-art, conventional sediment fingerprinting procedures, based on low resolution sampling, might therefore not provide sufficiently detailed information to underpin robust solutions to combat excessive sediment inputs to rivers (Vale et al., 2020; Vercruysse et al., 2017b ). To overcome associated issues of high workloads and costs, an array of novel sediment fingerprinting methods has been reported (Brosinsky et al., 2014; Cooper et al., 2015, 2014; Evrard et al., 2019; Krein et al., 2003; Martínez-Carreras et al., 2010b, 2010a; Poulenard et al., 2012; Pulley and Collins, 2021; Pulley and Rowntree, 2016 ). These so-called ‘low-cost tracers’ are often associated with reduced workloads and/or costs per sample, ultimately facilitating the collection and analysis of more samples for providing more detailed information on the spatial and temporal variations of SS sources (Evrard et al., 2019 ). Low-cost tracers include colour coefficients, which can be calculated from diffuse reflectance spectrometry measurements in the visible range (Evrard et al., 2019; Martínez-Carreras et al., 2010b ) or using an ordinary office scanner together with colour imaging software (García-Comendador et al., 2020; Krein et al., 2003; Pulley and Collins, 2021; Pulley and Rowntree, 2016 ). Other examples include geochemical properties predicted directly from filter papers using diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectrometry (Cooper et al., 2015, 2014; Poulenard et al., 2012 ), or predicted from UV–Vis reflectance (Brosinsky et al., 2014; Martínez-Carreras et al., 2010a ). However, although these techniques significantly reduce workloads, they nonetheless require the analysis of physical samples in the laboratory for calibration, and limitations regarding the sampling of potential SS sources and target SS thus remain. Recently, several authors have reported the opportunity to use field-deployable submersible spectrophotometer sensors, measuring in-stream absorbance spectra in the UV–Vis range, to estimate SS properties at high temporal frequency (Bass et al., 2011; Jeong et al., 2012; Martínez-Carreras et al., 2016; Sehgal et al., 2022a ). The absorption of light in the visible (Vis) region is largely influenced by SS concentration (Thomas et al., 2017 ) and SS particle sizes (Berho et al., 2004 ). Furthermore, specific regions of the absorbance spectrum are affected by dissolved components (e.g., dissolved organic carbon and nitrates), allowing the application of spectrophotometer sensors in water quality monitoring (e.g., D’Acunha and Johnson, 2019; González-Morales et al., 2020; Haas et al., 2023; Prairie et al., 2020 ). For such applications, spectrophotometric measurements on physical samples are used to calibrate relationships between SS properties/dissolved components and absorbance; the wavelength or (range of) wavelengths that best correlate with the specific properties in question can thereby be determined. For instance, Bass et al. (2011)  and Jeong et al. (2012)  predicted total organic carbon and dissolved organic carbon from absorbance at high temporal resolution. Martínez-Carreras et al. (2016)  estimated SS loss-on-ignition (LOI) using the specific absorbance wavelengths that best correlated to SS LOI values. Similarly, Sehgal et al. (2022a)  inferred sediment carbon content and mean particle size from previously identified wavelengths of the absorbance spectra. Lake et al. (2022a)  recently reported the potential use of submersible spectrophotometers for SS source fingerprinting. The authors successfully un-mixed artificial mixtures into their respective soil sample contributions in the laboratory. Experiments were performed in a large tank set-up, wherein the spectrophotometer measured the absorbance of the artificially created mixtures and the soil samples in suspension. The MixSIAR Bayesian un-mixing model (Stock et al., 2018; Stock and Semmens, 2016 ) was then used to estimate the relative proportion of each soil sample to the artificial mixtures. Following this proof-of-concept, Lake et al. (2023)  reported on the successful use of absorbance data to quantify the relative contributions of spatial SS sources in a confluence-based approach. Here, grab samples were collected at a series of confluences within a catchment (44 km2 ) in Luxembourg. Absorbance was measured on these grab water samples using a spectrophotometer in a laboratory set-up. Again, the MixSIAR Bayesian un-mixing model was used to estimate the relative proportion of SS coming from each confluence to the downstream target SS sampling location. Against the above context, the new work presented herein reports further investigation of a high temporal frequency sediment fingerprinting procedure. More specifically, absorbance measurements collected by submerged spectrophotometer probes were directly used to fingerprint SS spatial sources at high temporal frequency (5-minute intervals) for a 5-month duration. A confluence-based monitoring strategy was adopted to investigate spatial SS source contributions and their dynamics over time. The estimated spatial source contributions were compared with a SS mass-balance (i.e., sediment budget) to quantify accuracy.  2 Materials and methods The study was undertaken in the Attert River basin (Luxembourg). Submersible spectrophotometers, measuring in-stream (in situ ) absorbance at 5-minute intervals, were installed at the confluence of two tributaries draining sub-catchments with distinct underlying geology (see section 2.1 ). This was hypothesized to allow for the un-mixing of downstream target SS based on absorbance differences found in the spatial sources (i.e., the Tributary and Upstream sites). A total of 7 periods were monitored, consisting of storm runoff events of different magnitude and a low flow period. Note that the field set-up follows the approach used by Lake et al. (2022b)  to fingerprint spatial SS sources using particle size distribution data. 2.1 Study area The Attert River basin (247 km2  at Useldange) is located in the eastern part of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg (Fig. 1  d). The catchment is underlain, from north to south, by schists, slates and phyllites bedrock, marls, and Luxembourg sandstone. The tributary (Roudbach) drains a sub-catchment (44 km2 ) of the Attert River basin that is mainly underlain by red sandstone (“Buntsandstein”), with schists, slates and phyllites bedrock in the northern higher sloping areas. Land use in the Attert River Basin consists of forests (mainly in the higher sloping areas), grasslands and croplands (Fig. 1 e). Altitudes range from 238 m to 553 m above sea level. The climate is semi-oceanic, with maximum mean monthly temperatures between 0 and 18 °C and a long-term average annual rainfall of ca. 845 mm (1954–1996; Pfister et al., 2005 ). Three sites were instrumented (Fig. 1 e, f): two sites were located in the Attert River, before and after the Roudbach tributary confluence, and the third site was located at the outlet of the Roudbach tributary. At all three sites, a submersible spectrophotometer probe equipped with an automatic cleaning brush (S::can spectro::lyserTM; Scan Messtechnik GmbH, Vienna, Austria) measured absorbance (UV–Vis; 200–730 nm) at 5-minute intervals from March to July 2021. Simultaneously, these sensors measured turbidity by using the manufacturer calibration. The spectrophotometers were mounted horizontally onto a stepladder that was immersed near the river bank (see Fig. 1 a–c for details). Furthermore, all three sites were equipped with automatic water samplers (ISCO 6712 FS; Teledyne ISCO, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA), collecting discrete samples during the 7 selected sampling periods (Period A-G; see Table 1   and Lake et al., 2022b  for more details on these periods). At the Tributary site, the spectrophotometer did not record data during a 3-hour time span due to very high SS concentrations (04/06/2021 18:00 – 04/06/2021 21:00; Period F). The periods were selected to include different hydrological conditions to support robust comparison of sensor performance. Period A and C cover relatively large storm runoff events (Table 1 ). Period G covers the flood event which occurred in central Europe in July 2021, with a return period for the Attert River basin of >20 years. Period D and E cover small storm runoff events, while period B covers a low flow discharge recession (Table 1 ). Discharge was measured at the Upstream site by the Luxembourg Water Agency (Administration de la Gestion de l’Eau) (Reichlange station; https://www.inondations.lu ), and at the Tributary site by the ‘Observatory for Climate, Environment & Biodiversity’ of the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology. Precipitation was obtained from the weather station in Useldange (Fig. 1 ), managed by the ‘Administration des Services Techniques de l'Agriculture’ (ASTA; https://www.agrimeteo.lu ).  2.2 Sediment budget Suspended sediment concentrations (SSCs) were determined by filtering a known volume of each sample through 1.2 μm pore size Whatman GF/C glass fibre filters. SSC measurements were used to establish a calibration curve with the turbidity measured in situ  (r2  = 0.84, 0.86 and 0.88, and n = 126, 121 and 129 for the Upstream, Tributary and Downstream sites, respectively; Lake et al., 2022b ). Samples were collected over the course of the hydrograph, including samples at low, mid and high flow (see Fig. 3 ). The calibration curves were used to predict SSC from optically-measured turbidity at 5-minute intervals at the Upstream and Tributary sites (Fig. 1 ). A new relationship, based on the sum of the measurements made in the Upstream and Tributary sites, was used for the Downstream site. This decision was made because it became clear from the measured SSCs Downstream, as well as from the resulting sediment calibration curve (estimated SSCs), that SSCs measured at the Downstream site were constantly lower when compared with the sum of the SSCs measured at the Upstream and Tributary sites. We hypothesized that this was due to the installation settings in the Downstream site, where the location of the water sampler inlet did not allow for the collection of samples fully representative of the SSC in the river cross-section. Therefore, the use of the SSCs measured on these samples would have caused an underestimation of the SS load. Although sediment dynamics and backwater-driven deposition of tributary sediment fluxes can complicate the construction of sediment budgets using turbidity data, this was not considered to be an issue in the study catchment. To overcome this problem with underestimation, it was hypothesised that the total sediment Downstream was the sum of the sediment from the Upstream and Tributary sites and a new calibration curve was created. This solution was deemed viable given the rather low intermediate inputs of sediment and the absence of important sediment deposits on the river bed observed between the Upstream and Downstream sites during the monitored periods (Lake et al., 2023 ). Similarly, as discharge measurements were not available at the Downstream site, values were calculated as the sum of discharges from the Upstream and Tributary sites with half an hour delay, which was estimated to be the average travel time of the water between the Upstream and Downstream sites (as used in Lake et al., 2022b ).  2.3 Fingerprint selection Spectrophotometers measured absorbance in the 200–730 nm range, at 2.5 nm intervals. In this study, we used measurements in the 390–730 nm. This range of wavelengths is known to be influenced to a larger extent by SS particles (Rieger et al., 2004 ), and less by dissolved components (Byrne et al., 2011 ). Absorbance data was compensated for SSC to eliminate the effect of concentration, to thus retain the absorbance influenced by SSC specific properties (Lake et al., 2022a ). This was done by dividing absorbance values by predicted SSCs from the established calibration curves (see section 2.2 ). Data was not compensated for the absorbance of dissolved components because: (i) it was not possible to sample, filter and measure the absorbance of the filtered water when measuring at 5-minute intervals, and; (ii) based on tests in Lake et al. (2023) . These tests in Lake et al. (2023)  obtained comparable modelled source contributions (mostly the same dominant source with differences in relative contributions largely within 10–15%) when using absorbance in the 200–730 nm range (n=213 values) compensated for the absorbance of both dissolved compounds and SSC, to when using absorbance in the 390–730 nm range (n=137 values) but only compensated for SSC. Additionally, in the present study, the number of wavelengths were reduced by increasing the intervals between wavelengths to 10 nm (i.e., reducing the resolution; n=35 values) to allow faster model calculations and to facilitate high-frequency un-mixing. Lake et al. (2023)  showed that when reducing the resolution of the data from 2.5 nm to 10 nm intervals, model calculation times were up to 40 times faster (when using the settings and facilities described in section 2.5 ) and results showed only a 1.6% deviation. Absorbance values measured in the 390–730 nm range at 10 nm intervals were considered as individual fingerprints.  2.4 Range test A range test was performed for each time step to check if the absorbance measured at the Downstream target site fit within the range of the absorbance values measured for the upstream spatial sources. This was done for the absorbance measurements (5-minute intervals) during the 7 selected periods. For the Upstream and Tributary sites (i.e., spatial sources), at a given time t, absorbance data measured at that time (t), plus the absorbance data measured one time step (5-minutes) before and one time step (5-minutes) after (t-1, t+1) were used as spatial source data (n=3). This approach was used to reduce possible uncertainties associated with relying on just one measurement. At the Downstream site (i.e., mixtures), data were delayed by half an hour (section 2.2 ) compared with the upstream spatial source data (i.e., Upstream and Tributary) to account for the transport of SS from the upstream sources to the downstream target SS monitoring site. Downstream target SS absorbance data were created by the same principle; i.e., using the absorbance measurements at t, t−1 and t+1. For each time step, it was determined if the value from at least one of the three measurements at the Downstream target site (t-1, t, t+1) was within the limits (minimum and maximum value) of the two spatial sources (using for both sources t-1, t, t+1), for each wavelength (n=35 at each time step). A wavelength was therefore considered out of range if any of the following conditions (Equation (1) ) was met:(1) m i n S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ      ⩽ D t - 1 , λ    ⩽ m a x S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ        m i n S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ      ⩽ D t , λ    ⩽ m a x ( S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ    )    m i n S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ      ⩽ D t + 1 , λ    ⩽ m a x S t - 1 , λ    ,  S t , λ    ,  S t + 1 , λ            where S represents the absorbance value, calculated at each wavelength λ, for the upstream spatial sources (i.e., Upstream and Tributary sites), and D represents the absorbance value, calculated at each wavelength λ, for the Downstream target SS site. The range test was not used to discard data for specific wavelengths, but the results were explored to evaluate the proposed method. There were three reasons for this approach. First, tracers (i.e., absorbance at different wavelengths) were expected to behave conservatively. Both spatial source and target SS samples had the same nature (i.e., all samples were SS) and the travel distance (ca. 3 km) between them was relatively short (Fig. 1 ). Contrarily, in classical sediment fingerprinting studies, source samples often have a different nature to the target sediment samples (e.g., topsoil samples and SS samples) and travel distances are longer. Secondly, the objective of this study was to develop and test a simple and fully automated approach. It has been recently suggested that watershed managers and regulators would utilise the sediment fingerprinting approach more if they could input the required data and obtain outputs without themselves having to perform complicated statistics and modelling (Owens, 2022 ). Thirdly, the model used to un-mix the absorbance data (section 2.5 ) was able to cope with wavelengths that did not pass the range test (equation (1) . Thereby, in situations where not all 35 wavelengths are out-of-range, the data represented by the non-out-of-range wavelengths could still be useful for source apportionment. Data, and thus also the wavelengths which are out-of-range could be (slightly) biased due to e.g., uncertainties introduced during SSC compensation, resulting in Downstream absorbance being only just outside the bounds of the spatial source data. Therefore, additional out-of-range analysis was performed. This was to investigate whether the absorbance data could still hold valuable information for un-mixing out-of-range cases. This was done in the form of adding a small uncertainty to the spatial sources absorbance data (i.e., adding a 5% and 10% uncertainty to the spatial source fingerprint values by increasing maximum source values and decreasing minimum source values by 5% and 10%, respectively).  2.5 MixSIAR model The MixSIAR Bayesian un-mixing model (Stock et al., 2018; Stock and Semmens, 2016 ) open source R-package (Stock et al., 2018 ) was used for un-mixing the absorbance sediment fingerprint data. Absorbance data compensated for SSC from the Upstream and Tributary sites were used as spatial source input data. Absorbance data compensated for SSC from the Downstream location was used as target mixture input data. For both spatial source and target SS sites, a mean value with a variance was computed (Blake et al., 2018 ). Herein, this was computed for each wavelength (n=35), using measurements at time t, t+1 and t−1. The MixSIAR model calculates the relative average contributions from each source with a standard deviation. For all model runs, the Markov Chain Monte Carlo parameters were used according to the predefined ‘long’ settings (chain length = 300000, burn = 200000, thin = 100, chains = 3). Model convergence was evaluated using the Gelman-Rubin diagnostics (variables <1.1). All models were run using the High Performance Computing (HPC) facility at the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology. For this, the model code was edited to permit running MixSIAR in a loop. Model outcomes were compared with the estimated sediment budget to validate the predicted source apportionment. No modelling was possible during time steps with excessively high turbidity values (see section 2.1 ) and clear visual outliers, associated with unrealistic turbidity values, were manually removed (5 % of total measurements). Corresponding absorbance data was excluded from the modelling exercise and further analyses. A flow diagram of the data processing procedure is shown in Fig. 2  .   3 Results 3.1 Range test Fig. 3   shows an overview of the number of wavelengths that were out-of-range at each time step (i.e., failing the conditions as described in equation (1) , section 2.4 ), for each period. A rather large number of wavelengths were out-of-range at low flow conditions (Period B and D), where there were roughly 15–25 wavelengths (out of 35) failing the range test. For Period E, the number of out-of-range wavelengths generally ranged from 0 to 15. Period F exhibited a wide range of wavelengths being out-of-range (0–15). In this case, the number of out-of-range wavelengths (30–35) increased during the rising limb. During high flow conditions, the number of out-of-range wavelengths was lower (Period A and C) and almost absent during the discharge peaks. In general, the number of out-of-range wavelengths decreased before the discharge peak and increased again during the discharge recession. Period G, which was a flood event, in general showed a lower number of out-of-range wavelengths. Here, the number of out-of-range wavelengths increased at the start of the rising limb but decreased halfway through the rising limb. Again, the lowest number of out-of-range wavelengths coincided with the peak discharge. Fig. 3  furthermore shows the outcomes of the out-of-range analysis, introducing a 5% and 10% uncertainty to the source fingerprint values. The results, looking at the 5% uncertainty, exhibited instances of target SS absorbance being out-of-range during the low flow periods (Period B and D), but for a lower number of wavelengths (Fig. 3 ). The number of wavelengths that were out-of-range decreased further when source values were modified by assuming 10% uncertainty. For Periods A and C, it was observed that out-of-range behaviour was still visible both before and after the peak discharge, with again, less out-of-range observations. During the higher discharges, out-of-range behaviour was mostly absent. For Periods E, F and G, this absence of out-of-range observations was true for the whole measurement periods, both for the 5 and 10% uncertainty (though with occasional exceptions visible).  3.2 Sediment budget and modelled spatial sediment source contributions The sediment budget (Table 1  and Fig. 4  ) suggested that the Upstream site is the most dominant SS spatial source. This was true for the total SS load per period, as well as for the relative SS contributions during most of the time steps in each period (Fig. 4 ). Only for a couple of time-steps, was the relative contribution of the Tributary spatial sediment source higher (Periods D and F). Modelled source contributions are shown in Fig. 4 . The Tributary relative contribution was always lower than the contribution from the Upstream source. But, the relative contribution of the Tributary spatial sediment source increased during the rising limbs of the hydrographs, with a sudden decrease before the discharge peaks (Period A, C and F; Fig. 4 ). Standard deviations of the predicted source contributions were higher during the discharge recession (Period B) than during other sampling periods (Fig. 4 ). During period D, despite discarding a relatively high number of absorbance values (section 2.5 ) because they were associated with turbidity outliers (9% of total measurements), the predicted spatial sediment source contributions still exhibited high temporal variability and unstable patterns (Fig. 4 ). Modelled spatial source contributions were close to, and mostly followed the patterns of the SS source contributions calculated from the independent sediment budget (Fig. 4 ). For Periods C, E and G, the mean absolute errors between the modelled spatial sediment source contributions and the sediment budget estimates were the lowest (8.2, 7.3 and 5.3%, respectively; Table 1 ). Periods A and B showed slightly higher average differences (11.8 and 10.4%, respectively) than the aforementioned periods. During the first half of Period A, the modelled spatial source results showed an overestimation compared with the sediment budget data, whereas an underestimation was observed during the second half. Period B, covering a low flow period, exhibited constant modelled spatial source apportionments throughout the period and, as a result, the lowest standard deviation in the absolute errors (2.7%; Table 1 ). Similarly, the sediment budget for this period exhibited relatively constant spatial source contributions which deviate, on average, 10.6% from the MixSIAR modelling results. The highest mean absolute error was observed for period D (12.3%). This period was characterised by relatively low discharges and the MixSIAR modelling results showed a high degree of relatively short-term variation associated with the turbidity readings. The highest standard deviation was observed in period F (10.6%). At the start of this period, the spatial sediment source contributions based on the budgeting were highly variable, whereas the modelled contributions during that time were stable. Differences between the MixSIAR source apportionment results and sediment budget were smaller for the rest of the period, resulting in a low mean and standard deviation of the mean absolute error (6.9 ± 5.3). Uncertainty therein can be associated to the data gap between 03/06/2021 13:00 and 03/06/2021 19:30) (see section 2.1 ) due to very high SSCs. Deviations during this time frame were therefore not accounted for. Data at the start of the discharge peak do, however, show that the modelled spatial source contributions followed the pattern of the sediment budget contributions.   4 Discussion 4.1 Experimental approach: Validity and uncertainties The work presented in this paper is a logical extension to the work reported previously by Lake et al. (2023 ), Lake et al. (2022a) . The results presented herein showed a relatively good performance (9.4 ± 6.0 % mean absolute error when combining the 7 studied periods) when compared with these previous proof-of-concept studies, using high resolution approaches for sediment source fingerprinting. Lake et al. (2022a)  un-mixed artificially created mixtures in a controlled laboratory experiment using the absorbance at 200–730 nm (at 2.5 nm increments) as fingerprints. The modelling results using MixSIAR were evaluated against the known source contributions to the artificially created mixtures. This comparison showed an overall mean absolute error of 14.5 ± 13 %. Lake et al. (2022a)  thereby indicated that these outcomes were in the same order of magnitude compared with other sediment fingerprinting studies evaluating their mixing model accuracy using artificial mixtures (e.g., Gaspar et al., 2019; Haddadchi et al., 2014 ). Lake et al. (2023)  collected SS samples using a confluence-based approach. The grab water samples were then analysed using a spectrophotometer in a laboratory set-up. Comparison of MixSIAR modelling results against an independent sediment budget (i.e., similar to the approach reported herein) showed a mean absolute error of 18 ± 15 %. Although the new work herein returned a lower absolute error compared with our earlier work, the results must be considered carefully because the number of measurements is much larger (n=7,282) compared with both Lake et al. (2022a)  (n=249) and Lake et al. (2023)  (n=31). Therefore, the influence of large absolute errors (e.g., as found in period F) is mitigated. Lake et al. (2022b)  did, however, report a slightly lower average absolute error of 7 ± 4% when using particle size distributions as sediment source fingerprints, at the same measurement sites and during the same monitoring periods as the new work herein, despite a lower number of measurements (n=101). From the results it is has become clear that the period with the lowest mean absolute error (Period G) was the period with the highest discharges. Lake et al. (2022b) , comparing un-mixing outcomes to the same sediment budget, also observed the lowest mean absolute errors for the same period. It was therein hypothesised that the reason for this could be the strong control of discharge. During the rising limb of a hydrograph, sediment transported can be originating from many different locations (Walling et al., 2000 ), such as the resuspension of sediments stored on the channel bed (Lee et al., 2019 ). When stored on the channel bed, sediment properties might have undergone physical or chemical changes (e.g., Collins et al., 1997; García-Comendador et al., 2023; Koiter et al., 2013 ), challenging the conservative behaviour of the SS properties between source sites and the target SS measurement site. However, these initial sources might become exhausted and other sources might become more important during significant and lengthy events (Walling et al., 2000 ), adding to the earlier argument that fingerprint property conservatism is expected to be more evident with shorter distances between sampled sources and target SS sites. Higher water velocities and SS mixing in the water column might also limit flocculation and favour the breakdown of loosely-bound flocs (Krein et al., 2003 ). This can thereby limit the influence of particle size changes on absorbance (Berho et al., 2004; Lake et al., 2022a; Sehgal et al., 2022a ). During low flows, sudden and extreme outliers in predicted source contributions can be linked to sudden changes in absorbance readings. These sudden changes can be linked to, for example, air bubbles (e.g., Salgado Brito et al., 2014 ) or (partial) obstruction of the measuring window (e.g., large flocs, leaves, debris). Since the spectrophotometers used in this study also reported turbidity values, absorbance outliers could be easily excluded from the dataset by identifying time steps which exhibited extreme turbidity outliers. This was especially observed during Period D, where, on this basis, multiple outliers were removed. Period D showed that besides these multiple extreme outliers, turbidity values were generally much more variable compared with the other periods. This resulted in much more variable source contributions over time, causing potential uncertainties in the results. The reason why there are many more outliers and extreme outliers in Period D, compared to all other periods, and in particular the other periods with similar discharge patterns, is unknown. A possible explanation could be found in one of the aforementioned reasons. Besides, also drifts in measurements can occur due to fouling (Martínez-Carreras et al., 2016 ). To avoid these drifts, the spectrophotometers were equipped with automatic cleaning brushes (S::can GmbH, Vienna, Austria) that wiped the window before each measurement (see also Sehgal et al., 2022b ). In this study, only visual outliers were removed, but other methods (e.g., statistically-based approaches) have yet to be tested and implemented, and those could eventually lead to more standardized protocols for using absorbance measurements to source fingerprint SS. Alongside the larger uncertainties in SSCs and absorbance readings, a higher number of out-of-range wavelengths were observed at low flows. It is likely that the measurement uncertainty for SSCs in the laboratory, and their subsequent effects in the absorbance data when compensating for SSC (section 2.3 ), played an important role here. Special attention should therefore be paid to quantifying SSC accurately in order to reduce uncertainties when compensating absorbance data. This is especially important at low flows, wherein deviations in SSC can cause a relatively large uncertainty in the resulting compensated absorbance data. This influence is likely from the observations in Fig. 3 , where the larger number of out-of-range wavelengths are observed during low flows. From Fig. 3 , it can be seen that upon introducing some small uncertainties to the source values, the number of out-of-range observations drastically decreased. This indicating that the original out-of-range situations are only failing the range test by small margins, potentially influenced by the uncertainties mentioned above. These observations strengthen the hypothesis that, despite certain wavelengths being out-of-range, the data can still retain useful information for source fingerprinting and the corresponding time steps do not need to be discarded. Furthermore, we hypothesized that there were no substantial inputs of SS (i.e., other active sources) in between our measurements sites (i.e., between the sediment source sites and Downstream target site). In addition, it was deemed sensible to limit the distance between the monitoring sites for the upstream spatial source sampling sites and the Downstream target SS (acknowledging too short a distance would not allow sufficient SS mixing at the confluence) to reduce the likelihood that: (i) SS properties changed during transport (Koiter et al., 2013, 2015 ), and; (ii) sediment settled on the channel bed, meaning that the same sediments are not seen by both upstream and downstream sensors during the same rainfall-runoff event. Storage on the river bed can also favour SS biogeochemical and physical changes (e.g., Collins et al., 1997; García-Comendador et al., 2023; Legout et al., 2013 ). These, upon resuspension, would potentially no longer represent any of the upstream spatial SS sources. A longer distance between the upstream spatial source sampling sites and the Downstream target SS site could also favour distinct flocculation dynamics in different sections of the river, leading to changes in floc composition (Droppo, 2001 ) and differences in SS particle sizes (Berho et al., 2004; Lake et al., 2022a; Sehgal et al., 2022b ), influencing the absorbance readings.  4.2 Outlook Our study herein is a first attempt to trace SS spatial sources at high-frequency using absorbance readings collected in situ . The chosen sampling strategy (i.e., confluence-based approach) has, in reality, limited scope for guiding sediment management. This because SSC data is needed to correct the absorbance data, which, in itself, already provides a basis for the quantification of the relative contribution of each spatial source when discharge data is available. Likewise, it is important to consider the number of sources that can be unmixed, as earlier laboratory work showed that the accuracy of the results when using four sources was significantly lower than when using two and three sources (Lake et al., 2022a ). We are, however, hoping that the work presented herein will underpin and inspire new research to move towards high-frequency sediment source tracing, overcoming some of the limitations that we faced. High-frequency sediment fingerprinting requires solving an un-mixing model for each sensor measurement. Time intervals should be selected as a function of the specific needs and purpose, and should be considered with due regard to, for instance, catchment hydrological state (e.g., high flow vs. low flow, initial conditions), catchment characteristics (e.g., sources) and catchment size (Haddadchi & Hicks, 2020; Vale et al., 2020 ). A high temporal resolution might not be needed during low flow periods when source contributions might be stable (e.g., Period B; Table 1 ). Continuous datasets provide the opportunity to select only discrete subsets of the time series, e.g., extreme rainfall-runoff events that transport most of the SS load (as highlighted in e.g., Gonzalez-Hidalgo et al., 2010; Lake et al., 2022b; Navratil et al., 2012 ). High-frequency sediment source fingerprinting is most likely of greater benefit in smaller, highly dynamic catchments, where SS sources might change rapidly and regularly (Collins et al., 2020 ).
