At larger spatial scales, processes are often averaged out and thereby result in less pronounced changes in source contributions over time (Vale et al., 2020 ). Observations at high temporal resolutions may therefore in those situations not necessarily further improve our understanding of sediment dynamics compared with conventional time-integrated sampling. Reducing the amount of model input data (i.e., increasing intervals from 2.5 nm to 10 nm) decreased modelling times (∼40 times faster). However, each model run still took around 30–45 minutes. In this study the model was run 7,722 times (n=7,282 after eliminating outliers). The HPC facility at the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology was used to run this large amount of model simulations in parallel. We are, however, aware that such facilities might not be available to everyone. To this end, future research should explore if the number of wavelengths can be further reduced. Some authors have argued that a higher number of tracers can reduce prediction uncertainties (Martínez-Carreras et al., 2008; Sherriff et al., 2015 ), but absorbance data show a high degree of collinearity and a reduced number of wavelengths could also maximise source discrimination and avoid the use of redundant data (Small et al., 2004 ). Further work is also needed to better understand the link between absorbance at specific wavelengths and SS properties (e.g., as in Martínez-Carreras et al. (2016) , who correlated a range of wavelengths to SS loss-on-ignition, and Sehgal et al. (2022a) , who identified a specific wavelength to infer SS particle size and carbon content). However, specific SS properties affecting absorbance change (i.e., turbidity, particle size, carbon content) generally increase simultaneously with increasing discharge, making it difficult to isolate their individual influence. Suspended sediment concentration measurements are needed to establish calibration curves and compensate absorbance data. Establishing calibration curves is demanding, especially for relatively short-term deployments, and a calibration curve might not be reliable if only limited data is available (Navratil et al., 2011 ). In this respect, the development of a generic relationship between turbidity and SSC (e.g., Sehgal et al. 2022a ) could allow the direct use of turbidity to compensate absorbance spectrophotometer measurements. This could reduce sampling requirements and allow easier implementation of measurements campaigns. Here, however, it needs to be kept in mind that the compensation of absorbance data by SSC can possibly introduce un-mixing errors. The amount of uncertainty remains to be quantified. The spatial sediment source estimates generated in the work herein were validated against the SS budget. Validation of sediment fingerprinting model predictions is an important step (Gaspar et al., 2019 ), and the use of a sediment budget for this purpose has been demonstrated before (e.g., Collins et al., 1998; Dabrin et al., 2021; Lake et al., 2022b; Tiecher et al., 2022 ). Discharge time series are therefore needed to calculate the SS budget, and the availability of any type of data for validation must also be considered carefully when selecting measurement sites for high resolution source tracing (Batista et al., 2022 ). Other means of validation of predicted source contributions can also be considered in future studies, including the use of artificial or virtual mixtures (e.g., Batista et al., 2022; Gaspar et al., 2019; Haddadchi et al., 2014 ), or grab sampling to cross-check the high-frequency data (e.g., Martínez-Carreras et al., 2016 ).   5 Conclusions This study presents an application of a sediment fingerprinting approach that uses absorbance data measured in situ  and at high temporal frequency. The approach was applied in a confluence-based setting, aiming to discriminate between the SS contributions of the main river and a large tributary. Un-mixing results for 7 periods, with different hydrological conditions ranging from a low flow discharge recession to a flood event with a return period >20 years for the selected catchment, showed an average deviation of 9.4 ± 6.0 % compared with the source contributions calculated by the sediment budget. The best results (5.3 ± 4.3 %) were observed for Period G, which was the period covering the flood event. However, some issues remain to be elucidated in future research. These include minimising outliers in the datasets, e.g., by installing the measurement equipment in a representative location in the river cross-section. It is also important to identify at each new site the number of sources to be un-mixed, and to determine if they can be discriminated using absorbance data; for instance, by determining if sources exhibit sufficient differences in colour and/or geochemistry (as highlighted in Lake et al., 2022a ). Limitations related to computing times should also be addressed, and it must be considered if high-frequency data will provide additional insights in certain catchments (e.g., related to catchment size) compared with more conventional sediment fingerprinting methods. Despite uncertainties associated with the reported method remain to be evaluated (e.g., the impact of SSC absorbance correction), our results for source apportionment exhibit similar mean absolute errors to those reported in other sediment fingerprinting studies. The direct use of in situ  and at high temporal frequency absorbance data (i.e., without target SS sampling and/or without need for laboratory analyses) can lead to an improved understanding of catchment sediment dynamics. We anticipate that long-term measurement campaigns will provide information on the activation of SS sources and mobilization thresholds at different sites, during different/contrasting storm runoff events and seasons.
1 Introduction El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has a significant impact on the terrestrial water cycle across the world (Zhang et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2023 ), especially manifested on time scales ranging from 2 to 7 years (McPhaden et al., 2006; Rehbein and Ambrizzi, 2022 ). ENSO event, El Niño (La Niña), is respectively caused by wind stress exerted by easterly (westerly) trade winds on the sea level anomaly (SLA) in the equatorial sea region resulting in a 120 m-depth thermocline tilting east (west), and consequently, the changes in sea surface temperature anomaly (SSTa) (Clarke et al., 2000; Wang, 2018 ). Hence, SLA should provide an earlier response to ENSO than SSTa for forecasting the changes in terrestrial hydroclimatic conditions (THCs). In fact, the interannual SLA obtained by satellite altimetry was shown to be highly correlated with ENSO both globally and regionally (Nerem et al., 1999; Cheng et al., 2016 ). Rather than a single physical quantity for ENSO monitoring, SLA (i.e., sea surface height minus the mean sea surface) is an integrated quantity inferring oceanic transport over larger scales that comprehensively considers changes in ocean temperature, salinity, and pressure at various ocean depths, as well as mass transport driven by geostrophy and wind (Cazenave and Nerem, 2004; Shi et al., 2020; Legeais et al., 2021 ). Compared to SSTa, SLA is less noisy and more spatially coherent (Mohamed et al., 2019 ). This indicates the potential of SLA to supplement existing ENSO indices. Fundamentally, the SLA is the sum of steric and non-steric sea level. The steric SLA (SSL) is associated with seawater temperature, pressure, and salinity at all depths (Cheng and Qi, 2010; Xi et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023 ). Non-steric SLA (also called oceanic mass SLA, NSSL) is the ocean bottom pressure adjusted by the inverted barometer effect, which is generated from oceanic water mass redistribution due to tides, circulation, and mass flux (Cazenave and Nerem, 2004; Cheng et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023 ). The ocean bottom pressure can be monitored by satellite gravimetry (e.g., Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE)) since 2002 (Chambers, 2006 ). SSL significantly alters SLA over deep water (Dangendorf et al., 2021 ), while NSSL substantially impacts coastal SLA within South China Sea (Cheng and Qi, 2010 ). SSL changes can be driven locally and remotely by winds and surface buoyancy fluxes (Piecuch and Ponte, 2011; Chen et al., 2020a ), while the dominant component of SSL change is temperature-related (i.e., thermosteric component) (MacIntosh et al., 2017 ). Ocean bottom pressure (i.e., NSSL plus inverted barometer effect) can be influenced by wind-driven Rossby waves (Piecuch et al., 2015 ) and wind-induced Ekman transport (Liu et al., 2023 ), where an analytical relationship is derived between wind and ocean bottom pressure under barotropic assumption (Boening et al., 2011 ). From the above, wind, which serves as ENSO’s intermediary, alters SSL, NSSL, and SLA. Consequently, in-depth analyses of SLA, SSL, and NSSL variations compared against sea surface temperature (SST) in Niño 3.4 (central equatorial Pacific) region likely add a new dimension to ENSO characteristics in spatial association with THCs. Besides the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), SSTa index in Niño 3.4 region is conventionally served as the ENSO index to assess the potential impact on THCs, such as temperature (Villafuerte and Matsumoto, 2015; Yin and Zhou, 2020; Fu et al., 2022 ), precipitation (Mera et al., 2018; Loaiza Cerón et al., 2020 ), potential evapotranspiration (Tamaddun et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2021 ), and runoff (Le et al., 2021; You et al., 2021 ). Being a medium between the atmosphere and land for hydrometeorology, terrestrial water storage (TWS) and its variation were found to be highly correlated with ENSO in previous studies (Phillips et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2018; Han et al., 2019 ). In particular, 80 % of TWS spatiotemporal variation in China was attributed to ENSO variability (Huang et al., 2019 ). It is known that ENSO variations affect THCs with a lag of 7–8 months over the Yangtze River (Zhang et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2022 ), and 6 months over the Mekong River (Fok et al., 2018 ). These time lag represents the total time required for ENSO remote connection to THCs in China and Indochina. In essence, the total time duration of the remote connection between ENSO and THCs represents the time taken for ENSO to affect THCs, through the coupled physical mechanisms of ocean-atmospheric circulation. For example, during the development stage of El Niño, a decrease in SSTa in the western tropical Pacific weakens convective activity around the South China Sea and the Philippines (Zhang et al., 2015 ). This result in a southward shift of the subtropical high, favoring flood (drought) events in the Yangtze River and Huaihe River basins (Yellow River basin, South China, and the Indo-China peninsula), because the Asian summer monsoon rainfall belt tends to establish and persist (Huang and Wu, 1989; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Conversely, the opposite phenomenon was observed in China and Indochina during the El Niño decay stage (Huang and Wu, 1989; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021 ). The above processes rely on the Walker circulation (e.g., Bjerknes, 1969; Williams and Funk, 2011; Tokinaga et al., 2012; Sandeep et al., 2014 ) serving as a direct conduit for propagating ENSO impact from the eastern Pacific Ocean, and eventually, to China. Therefore, it was justifiable to count the total time duration of THCs in different regions in response to ENSO, setting a time constraint for the qualitative explanation of each atmospheric circulation process. Meanwhile, it is currently unclear how ENSO-related SLA and SSL/NSSL variation can affect THCs in China, which may have added-value for forecasting THC anomalies earlier. This study, therefore, aims to comprehensively assess the similarities and differences of SLA/SSL/NSSL and SSTa indices over Niño 3.4 region, before examining the lagged-relationship between these ENSO-related indicators and THCs in China. To do so, we use multi-channel singular spectral analysis, wavelet coherence, and cross-correlation to analyze from temporal and spatial perspectives, respectively. The manuscript is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we present an overview of the datasets utilized in the study. Section 3  details four methods employed to address the above research goals. Section 4  discusses and understands the similarities and differences between SST and SLA/SSL/NSSL and corresponding indices (i.e., SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI and NSSLI) over Niño 3.4 region from temporal perspectives, and the lagged-relationship between these indices and THCs from spatial perspectives, respectively. Finally, in Section 5 , we summarize the key outcomes and discuss their implications.  2 Data Various THCs, including surface pressure, temperature, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and terrestrial water storage (TWS), were acquired from satellite data products and reanalysis data (cf. Section 2.1 ). Sea surface temperature (SST) based on Extended Reconstructed SST V5 (ERSSTv5) for the Niño 3.4 region was obtained from the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA; cf. Section 2.2 ). The dataset information was presented in Table 1  . To ensure consistency and comparability, we resampled all satellite products and reanalysis data to match the spatial resolution of the GRACE/GRACE-FO mascon TWS (i.e., 0.25° × 0.25°), as depicted in Fig. 1  . Since THCs differ in their units and magnitudes, the data standardization method with a normal distribution assumption was employed to make them comparable (Fok et al., 2020 ). 2.1 Regional hydroclimatic data Our study utilized monthly surface pressure and temperature data between 2003.01 and 2023.05, which were obtained from the high-resolution ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset (i.e., 0.1° × 0.1°). ERA5-Land was generated by improving the land component of the ERA5 climate reanalysis products (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2022 ). ERA5 is a fifth-generation reanalysis product developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), accessible through the Copernicus Climate Change Service (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu ). It integrates various observations, ranging from in-situ  weather stations to remote sensing satellites, for monitoring atmospheric and surface conditions. Precipitation and evapotranspiration are two critical components in understanding the regional water balance (Zhang et al., 2019 ) and the broader variability of climate conditions (Ma et al., 2016 ). In this study, we utilized the 0.1° × 0.1° integrated multi-satellite retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Version 07 precipitation data from 2003.01 to 2023.05. This dataset is provided by the NASA Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center at https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov  (Huffman et al., 2015 ). For evapotranspiration data, we used the 1 km × 1 km MODIS MOD16 A2 dataset from 2003.01 to 2023.05, which employs the improved retrieval algorithm from Mu et al. (2011) . This dataset can be accessed through the United States Geological Survey Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center website at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mod16a2v061/ . GRACE observations capture time-varying mass transport in the Earth system (Tapley et al., 2019 ). In this study, monthly TWS was derived from the Center for Space Research (CSR) GRACE/GRACE-FO RL06.2 Mascon Solutions (RL0602) to represent terrestrial mass variation. This data product has replaced the imprecise low-degree coefficients with SLR data (Loomis et al., 2019 ), and corrected glacial isostatic adjustment based on the model ICE6G-D (Peltier et al., 2018 ), in which glacial isostatic adjustment model uncertainty is still present (Huang et al., 2013 ). Note that many data were missed, especially during the transition period between GRACE and GRACE Follow-On satellites. To maintain the continuity of the data time series, the singular spectrum analysis method was used to fill the data gaps within the data product (c.f. Yi and Sneeuw, (2021)  for detailed procedures). Finally, the complete TWS time series from 2003.01 to 2023.05 was used in this study.  2.2 Ocean data In this study, monthly SLA data were derived from the gridded sea level anomaly data combining multiple satellite observations, including T/P and ERS-1/2, Jason-1/2, and Envisat, provided by the Archiving, Validation, and Interpretation of Satellite Oceanographic (AVISO) data center. The spatial resolution of the product is 0.25° × 0.25°, and the relevant data can be obtained from https://www.aviso.altimetry.fr/en/data/products/ . Altimetric SLA comprises steric SLA, SSL, and non-steric SLA, NSSL (i.e., SLA  = SSL  + NSSL ), where NSSL is the ocean bottom pressure adjusted by the inverted barometer effect (i.e., NSSL  = ocean bottom pressure -inverted barometer ). SSL was obtained by subtracting NSSL from SLA in this study. Notably, ocean bottom pressure was also derived from the CSR GRACE/GRACE-FO RL06.2 Mascon data to represent oceanic mass variation. In contrast to TWS, ocean bottom pressure includes the oceanic component and atmospheric pressure effects acting on the sea surface without accounting for upper-air density anomalies (Uebbing et al., 2019 ). The same processing steps as TWS were also used for ocean bottom pressure. The monthly ocean bottom pressure time series were computed by averaging their values over the Niño 3.4 region (5°N–5°S, 120°W–170°W) and its mean value was subtracted before usage. The monthly mean SST based on ERSSTv5 for the Niño 3.4 region was derived from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Climate Prediction Center (NOAA CPC), which is available at https://psl.noaa.gov/data/correlation/nino34.data .   3 Methods To explore the ability of altimetric SLA and its two major components (i.e., SSL and NSSL) to observe ENSO-related signals on spatiotemporal scales, we divided the data analysis procedures into four steps: i) calculating the average time series of SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL over Niño 3.4 regions and identifying common signals between SST and SLA/SSL/NSSL via wavelet coherence; ii) assessing the long-term variability signal association between SST and SLA/SSL/NSSL with multi-channel singular spectral analysis method; iii) deriving the Niño 3.4 index based on SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL and analyzing their time series and wavelet coherence; iv) examining the spatial association between the Niño 3.4 index and THCs. Notably, the calculation of the Niño 3.4 index (referred to as SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI, respectively) based on SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL involves three steps: (a) removing trend and monthly climatology (i.e., 2003.01–2023.05) from SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL time series to obtain anomalies; (b) smoothing the anomalies with a 5-month running mean; (c) standardizing the smoothed values by their respective standard deviation and mean values. The same processes were also used for THCs to highlight ENSO-related signals. 3.1 Wavelet coherence In time–frequency space, wavelet coherence is a measure of the intensity of the covariance of the two series and identifies common signals (Jevrejeva et al., 2003 ). In this study, wavelet coherence was first applied to analyze the common signals between the mean SST and SLA/SSL/NSSL time series over Niño 3.4 regions, respectively. Then, wavelet coherence was used to calculate coherence and phase between SSTaI and SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI in the Niño 3.4 regions, respectively. Following Torrence and Webster (1999) , the wavelet coherence of two time series x n     and y n     is formulated as:(1) R n 2  = S s - 1   W n xy   s            2  S s - 1   W n x  s        2      · S s - 1   W n y  s        2            where S  is a smoothing operator; W n xy   s       represents the result of cross-wavelet transform; W n x  s       and W n y  s       are the continuous wavelet transforms of time series x n     and y n    , respectively. More details can be found in Grinsted et al. (2004) .  3.2 Multi-channel singular spectral analysis Multi-channel singular spectral analysis is a data-adaptive method for time series analysis, effectively separating trends, fluctuating components, and noise (Ghil et al., 2002; Walwer et al., 2016 ). Its primary advantage lies in systematically identifying oscillatory patterns in spatial and temporal behavior across a wide range of time scales. Multi-channel singular spectral analysis captures both propagating and standing oscillatory patterns (Sezginer Unal and Ghil, 1995 ). Here, we employed multi-channel singular spectral analysis to extract long-term variability from SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL, assessing whether they exhibit similar long-term variability. The calculation process can be divided into three steps. First, we calculate the grand covariance matrix. Given a time series X l  t      , t = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , N ; l = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , L     , which consists of N  time epochs with L  data points, the trajectory matrix of each channel can be calculated as:(2) X ∼  l  = X l  ( 1 )    X l  ( 2 )    ⋯  X l  ( M )     X l  ( 2 )    X l  ( 3 )    ⋯  X l  ( M + 1 )     ⋮   ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   X l  ( R )    X l  ( R + 1 )    ⋯  X l  ( N )               In Eq. (2) , M  is an integer window length, and R = N - M + 1    is the number of overlapping views of time series for each point in a channel. To represent the trajectory matrix in multi-channel form, D ∼  = X ∼  1   X ∼  2   ⋯  X ∼  L         T     is defined. Hence, the lag-covariance matrix of the multi-channel trajectory matrix D ∼    , C ∼  D     can be calculated as:(3) C ∼  D  = 1 R  D ∼   T  D ∼  = C 1 , 1    C 1 , 2    ⋯  C 1 , L     C 2 , 1     C 2 , 2    ⋯  C 2 , L     ⋮   ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   C L , 1     C L , 2    ⋯  C L , L              where each element is computed by C l , l  ′    = ( 1 / R )  X ∼  l  T  X ∼  l  ′     . Second, we perform a singular value decomposition. The eigenvalues λ k     and eigenvectors E k     of matrix C ∼  D     are obtained according to Λ = E T  · C · E   . The λ k     and E k     are sorted in descending order and their corresponding eigenvectors to calculate the k -th principal components (PCs) of single-channel time series. The k -th PCs are given as:(4) A k  ( t )  = ∑ j = 1  M  ∑ l = 1  L  X l  t + j - 1     E l k  j          where Λ    is a diagonal matrix with eigenvalues λ k    , E  is a matrix with eigenvectors E k    , A k     is called the k- th PCs , and E l k  j       is the j -th element of E k    . Third, we reconstruct the timeseries. The partial signal R C l k     can be then reconstructed with E k     and A k     as:(5) R C l k  ( t )  = 1 t  ∑ j = 1  t  A k  ( t - j + 1 )  E l k  ( j )   ,   1 ≤ t ≤ M - 1    1 M  ∑ j = 1  M  A k  ( t - j + 1 )  E l k  ( j )   ,    M ≤ t ≤ N - M + 1    1 N - t + 1   ∑ j = t - N + M  M  A k  ( t - j + 1 )  E l k  ( j )   ,    N - M + 2 ≤ t ≤ N              However, in this study, we focused solely on long-term variability, retaining only RC1 and not displaying the other RCs.  3.3 Cross-correlation analysis We performed correlation analyses to investigate the relationship between THCs within China, X , and Niño 3.4 SSTaI (or SLAI/SSLI/NSSLI), Y , respectively. The cross-correlation coefficient, R , which is a Pearson correlation coefficient accounting for the time-lagged effect, was employed as in Van Viet (2021) :(6) R = ∑ i = 1  n  X i + Δ t   - X  ¯      Y i  - Y  ¯         ∑ i = 1  n  X i + Δ t   - X  ¯       2  · ∑ i = 1  n  Y i  - Y  ¯       2          where X  ¯      and Y  ¯      are the mean values of X  and Y , respectively. i  and n  are the number of months counted continuously from the beginning and total length of the X  or Y , respectively;Δ t   (months) is the lagged time between X  and Y , ranging from 0 to 12 in this study.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Temporal association between SST/SLA/SSL/NSSL and ENSO Regional NSSL (SST) represents the oceanic mass (energy) variation, whereas SLA is the sum of SSL and NSSL. To investigate the temporal association between SLA/SSL/NSSL and SST for observing ENSO events, we initially computed and compared the average time series of SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL over Niño 3.4 region (Fig. 2  a). We found that the time series changes in SLA/SSL and SST exhibited similarities, with a pronounced linear upward trend in SST/SLA/SSL during 2011–2016. This indicated that sea surface temperature and sea level in the equatorial Pacific rose rapidly after 2011, consistent with the accelerated trend of global mean sea level since 2011 (Yi et al., 2015, 2017 ). In contrast to SLA and SSL, NSSL time series displayed significant disparities compared to SST. To further check the similarities and differences between the time series of SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL in the time–frequency domain, wavelet coherence spectra were computed (Fig. 2 b–d). The wavelet coherence spectra revealed that SST, SLA, and SSL exhibited significant common variance at timescales between 2- and 4-year, while SST and NSSL displayed common variance on annual timescales (1-year). It potentially indicated that the common signals in SST and NSSL were only apparent on annual scale, whereas SST, SLA, SSL exhibited common signals on interannual timescales (>2 year). We also found that the statistical relationships among SST, SLA, and SSL were in-phase on a 2–4 year timescale. Therefore, considering the power and phase changes in common signals among SLA, SSL, and SST in long-term variability, it is suggested that SLA and SSL likely capture ENSO-related signals. However, almost no common variance between NSSL and SST was found in long-term variability, indicating that ENSO-related signals might not be observed by NSSL. To verify SST connection to SLA, SSL, NSSL on interannual timescales, multi-channel singular spectral analysis was utilized to extract interannual variability in SST, SLA, SSL and NSSL (Fig. 3  ). We found that variations in SST, SLA, and SSL across Niño 3.4 region were consistent, while NSSL exhibited a difference and showed clear increasing long-term trend, especially from 2003 to 2016. This may indicate that SLA and SSL possess similar capabilities to SST in capturing long-term ocean anomaly signals related to ENSO, but not NSSL. However, it should be noted that NSSL exhibited a robust long-term linear trend, necessitating further analysis to determine whether ENSO-related signals were obscured. Therefore, we calculated the SSTa/SLA/SSL/NSSL indices (i.e., SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI) over Niño 3.4 regions by removing their long-term trends and monthly climatology. Detailed calculation steps were outlined in Section 3 . Fig. 4   illustrates the time series of SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI during 2003.01–2023.05, along with the wavelet coherence between SSTaI and SLAI/SSLI/NSSLI, respectively. Like in Figs. 2 and 3 , the SSTaI (see Fig. 4 a) was found to be highly correlated with SLAI and SSLI (correlations of 0.91 and 0.88, respectively). In contrast, NSSLI presented substantial differences and a lower correlation (0.40) with SSTaI, indicating that NSSLI might either lack ENSO-related signals or encompass ENSO-related signals not present in SSTaI. Furthermore, the wavelet coherence between SSTaI and SLAI (Fig. 4 b), SSLI (Fig. 4 c), and NSSLI (Fig. 4 d) also demonstrated that, like SSTaI, SLAI and SSLI could capture ENSO-related signals, while NSSLI did not. We found that SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI showed strong coherence with statistical significance higher than 95 %, while SSTaI showed little coherence with NSSLI across timescales. Notably, despite the removal of monthly climatology and long-term trends from SST, SLA, SSL, and NSSL prior to calculating SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI, along with a 5-month running mean procedure to eliminate seasonal and annual variations, SSTaI and SLAI/SSLI still exhibited high coherences on timescales less than 2 years, particularly during ENSO events (e.g., 2007–2011). We speculated that may be due to limitations in the wavelet coherence method or intrinsic factors determining seasonal variabilities. This could potentially generate ENSO signals. As for the former, wavelet coherence was considered for finding significant coherence even though the common power of two time series was low (Grinsted et al., 2004 ). As for the latter, the Kelvin and Rossby wave activities during the intra- and inter-seasonal period were considered partly responsible for generating time-varying periodicities across 2–7 years (i.e., ENSO periodicities). For instance, Li and Clarke (1994)  along with Clarke et al. (2000)  proposed an analytical ENSO model. This suggests that the equatorial Kelvin wave takes approximately one month to reach the eastern boundary, while the Rossby wave requires three months to reach the western boundary. Consequently, the entire process took approximately four months to complete, thereby establishing it as an intrinsic mechanism for ENSO generation (Li and Clarke, 1994; Clarke et al., 2000 ). Additionally, Sprintall et al. (2020)  also mentioned that intra-seasonal Kelvin wave activity can initiate the development of El Niño. Nevertheless, due to a complex and diverse ENSO generation mechanism, further exploration is required in the future, in order to determine whether the phenomenon revealed by the wavelet coherence in Fig. 4  is related to the ENSO generation induced by the Kelvin and Rossby wave activities during the intra- and inter-seasonal period. In summary, within the recognized ENSO periodicities (i.e., 2–7 years), SLAI/SSLI exhibited strong coherence and phase consistency with SSTaI, indicating that SLAI and SSLI might observe ENSO-related signals. Therefore, we conducted a cross-correlation analysis between SLAI/SSLI/NSSLI and THCs in China when, comparing these results with those of SSTaI, as discussed in Section 4.2 .  4.2 Spatial association and time lag between SST/SLA/SSL/NSSL and THCs The response of hydroclimatic variables to ENSO-related signals is an intuitive expression that effectively reflects the influence of ENSO events. Previous studies have extensively explored the impact of ENSO on THCs in China (e.g., Zhang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2022 ). Given the coherence among the time series of SLAI, SSLI, NSSLI and SSTaI, we further tested the applicability of using SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI as a complement for SSTaI in studying the ENSO-related impact on THCs at interannual scales in China, and compared with the conclusions of previous studies. Fig. 5   displays the spatial distribution of the maximum cross-correlation between five standardized THCs (i.e., surface pressure, temperature, evapotranspiration, TWS, and precipitation) at the interannual time scale and SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI, and NSSLI over Niño 3.4 region. The spatial pattern of the maximum cross-correlation between SLAI/SSLI and THCs was similar to SSTaI, while NSSLI exhibited differences from SSTaI. The maximum cross-correlation spatial pattern between TWS and SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI was similar to precipitation. Compared to TWS and precipitation, surface pressure, temperature, and evapotranspiration exhibited different characteristics. The maximum cross-correlation spatial pattern between surface pressure and SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI showed an almost uniform positive correlation, while the distribution of temperature and evapotranspiration was more divergent, especially for evapotranspiration. The spatial correlation pattern of TWS associated with SLAI and SSLI was similar to that obtained for SSTaI, while the effect of NSSL on TWS was different. SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI were remarkably correlated to TWS over China with significant regional variations across China. The regions with positive correlation were mainly in northern and southern China, while the major negative correlation areas were found mainly in western China (i.e., southern part of CORB) and central eastern China. The positive (negative) correlations between TWS and SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI indicated that the TWS changes largely follow (oppose) the variation of SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI, respectively. Note that the spatial pattern of the maximum cross-correlation between TWS and SLAI/SSLI were consistent with the spatial patterns of the maximum cross-correlation between TWS and SSTaI, consistently with Huang et al. (2019) . Compared to four other THC indicators, the spatial pattern of maximum cross-correlation between precipitation and NSSLI was similar to SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI, except for northeast China (i.e., SLRB). The positive correlations were mainly concentrated in northwest (i.e., northwest part of CORB) and southern (i.e., YARB, PERB, SERB, and southern part of SWRB) China. It is also worth noting that these regions were all regions with abundant precipitation (Chen et al., 2023 ) and located in the tropical and subtropical monsoon zone (c.f., Lv et al. (2019)  and Fig. 1 ), except for northwest China. Previous studies had extensively demonstrated that ENSO had a significant impact on precipitation in the tropical and subtropical monsoon zone of China (e.g., Zhou et al., 2012; Lv et al., 2019; Zhi et al., 2023 ). For northwest China, the positive cross-correlation between precipitation and SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI indicates that ENSO also significantly impacts on precipitation in this region, despite being located inland and far from the ocean. This finding agrees with the results presented by Lu et al. (2019) . Fig. 6   also yielded the spatial patterns of time lag corresponding to the maximum cross-correlation. We found that the time lag pattern between SLAI, SSLI and THCs was also consistent with SSTaI, while NSSL was significantly different from them, aligning with the maximum cross-correlation patterns. This further demonstrated that SLAI and SSLI almost synchronized with SSTaI's response, before affecting THCs. It might also suggest that SLAI and SSLI may be indices equivalent to SSTaI in revealing the time lag of ENSO-related signals on THCs in China. However, the spatial patterns of time lag between SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI and THCs were scattered, making it difficult to compare whether the time lag of SLAI and SSLI correlated with THCs were consistent with the results of SSTaI in the specified regions. Therefore, the average time lag of each of the nine river basins in China (c.f., Fig. 1 ) was calculated (Fig. 7  ). Based on Fig. 7 , we observed that the resulting time lag in the relationship between SLAI, SSLI and THCs was basically consistent with SSTaI in various basins and differed by about ±1 months from the results of SSTaI in most basins (c.f., Fig. S1 a–b in the supplemental files). However, the time lag between NSSLI and THCs significantly differed from SSTaI, surpassing the threshold of ±1 months in most basins (Fig. S1 c in the supplemental files). This further indicated that NSSLI cannot be utilized for observing ENSO-related signals. Therefore, we presented only its results without further discussion. Our results, regarding the time lag in the relationship between THCs and SSTaI, are consistent with those obtained by Huang et al. (2019)  and Chen et al. (2020b) . For instance, we found a time lag of ∼8 month between TWS and SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI in YARB, as in Zhang et al. (2015)  and Cui et al. (2022) . Although the time lag between SLAI, SSLI and TWS in YARB was slightly larger than that of SSTaI, their differences were both below the threshold of 1 month (i.e., they differed 0.59 and 0.55 months, respectively). Therefore, comparing their common impact features can provide an in-depth understanding of ENSO’s impact on TWS in YARB. Similar results were also revealed in other river basins, but substantial differences were also exhibited in different river basins. For example, the time lag between SLAI (or SSLI) and TWS was smaller than that of SSTaI in some river basins (e.g., CORB, SWRB, SLRB). The difference in time lag among different regions and variables may be attributed to the physical linkage between ENSO and THCs from a temporal perspective, which is detailed in Section 4.3 . Furthermore, we speculate that the difference in time lag of different regions and variables may also be attributed to the complex terrain (c.f., Fig. 1 ), especially differences in land cover types (c.f., Fig. S2  in the supplemental files). Focusing on the basins in interior China, due to its spatial span across eastern, central, and western regions of China, characterized by a wide regional scope, significant geographical diversity, and variable climate, THCs within YARB response to ENSO often exhibit noticeable regional variations (Zhang et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2022 ). Another reason likely attributed to different land cover types (e.g., grassland, cropland, forest, and water) in YARB across eastern, central, and western (c.f., Fig. S2  in the supplemental files). In terms of other river basins, the southern region of CORB is situated in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, while the northern region is located in the Tarim Basin and Junggar Basin, resulting in a significant elevation difference between the north and south. Furthermore, CORB also reveals a significant land cover type difference between northern (i.e., barren) and southern (i.e., grassland). The northeastern part of SWRB and the western part of YERB are also situated in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, leading to substantial topographic differences among different regions within the basins, with YERB additionally encompassing the Loess Plateau. Compared to terrain, land cover type did not exhibit significant differences in YERB, indicating that land cover type did not impact on time lag differences between THCs and SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI in this region. Similarly, a comparable situation for SLRB is exhibited, with the northwest characterized by the Greater Khingan Mountains, the southeast by the Changbai Mountains, and the central region comprising the Northeast China Plain, displaying a high elevation contrast between the two sides and the middle. Interestingly, the distribution features of land cover type are similar to terrain in SLRB, with the forest characterized in the mountain regions (i.e., northwest and southeast), and the cropland characterized in the central region. Therefore, the time lag in the SLRB may be influenced by both in terrain and land cover types. Compared to basins in interior China, the time lag in the basins near the coasts (i.e., PERB, SERB, HARB, and HURB) was less affected by differences in terrain and land cover types. However, the time lag is likely affected by abundant rainfall, monsoon, and climate anomalies in adjacent oceans and/or in basins near the coasts (Chen et al., 2020b ). Therefore, we speculate that the fundamental reason for the dispersed time lag in the response of THCs to ENSO in inland (coast) basins may be attributed to the diverse topography with notable geographical features and land cover types (rainfall/monsoon), respectively. Overall, despite substantial differences in time lag between SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI and THCs, all resulting time lag at a basin scale between SLAI/SSLI and SSTaI was similar. This further implied that SLAI/SSLI and SSTaI have comparable abilities in revealing ENSO-related signals affecting THCs. We speculate that the combined analyses of the time lag determined between SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI and THCs can eventually complement the analysis based solely on the SSTaI, which in turn, provides a more comprehensive understanding of ENSO's influence on THCs in China.  4.3 The potential physical linkage and time lag mechanism between ENSO and THCs Based on Section 4.2 , it can be concluded that the differences in the time lag between ENSO and THCs in different regions. Taking the Yangtze River Basin as an example, previous studies have found that the impact of ENSO on TWS in the Yangtze River Basin (YARB) has a time lag of about 7–8 months (e.g., Zhang et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2022 ), which is basically consistent with this study. In essence, the time lag is considered to be related to the physical linkage of ENSO’s influence on THCs in China through atmospheric circulation (Lv et al., 2022 ). As the most prominent mode of climate variability on earth, ENSO can alter Walker circulation by changing tropical ocean thermal conditions, thereby triggering climate anomalies in related areas (Wei et al., 2020 ). For example, during El Niño (La Niña) events, a cooling (warming) in SST in the western tropical Pacific, coupled with a weakening (strengthening) of convective activity around the South China Sea and the Philippines, results in a southward (northward) shift of the subtropical high (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021 ). These changes will influence the local wind field and induce extreme climate anomalies in China, such as floods (droughts) in the Yangtze River basin during El Niño (La Niña). Furthermore, the locally and remotely generated wind field was also a factor impacting steric changes (i.e., SSL) and seawater transport across the sea surface and hence affecting total sea level variations (Han and Huang, 2008; Piecuch and Ponte, 2011 ). Therefore, the role of various factors in the entire propagation path likely led to time lag differences for different variables across different regions. To quantify the above physical explanation, the optimal spatiotemporal transport path and time lag of (1) the moisture flux via oceanic evaporation, and (2) its transport from the Niño 3.4 region to YARB in the China at the 300 hPa pressure level were simulated via Dijkstra method (see Ma and Fok, 2023  for details) (Fig. 8  ). Regarding to the first process, ∼4.90 months are required for the moisture flux generated by oceanic evaporation transported to the 300 hPa pressure level over the Niño 3.4 region. For the second process, ∼3.70 months are required for the moisture flux from the Niño 3.4 region transported to YARB in the China at the 300 hPa pressure level. These two dynamic processes require a total duration of 8.60 months, which is basically consistent with the time lags of 8.07 (or 8.03) months calculated via cross-correlation between SLAI (or SSLI) and TWS in the YARB in this study. In contrast, the time lag between SSTaI and TWS in the YARB is a month shorter (7.48 months) (Fig. 7 ). From the above simulation result, this indicates that SLAI/SSLI variability appears to be more accurate than that of SSTaI, presented, suggesting SLAI/SSLI variability can be served as a complement to existing ENSO indices. Notably, the moisture flux was calculated using wind and specific humidity data from daily NCEP-NCAR reanalysis, which had a high temporal resolution (i.e., daily) but a low spatial resolution of 2.5° × 2.5°. Consequently, uncertainties exist in calculating the time required for the two propagation paths shown in Fig. 8 . In addition, the Dijkstra algorithm yields the most optimal propagation path, but in reality, the propagation of moisture flux is consistent with the wind field and is influenced by various factors, making it difficult to accurately simulate the propagation paths. These represent the limitations of this study.   5 Conclusions The initiation of ENSO results from the thermocline tilts east and west due to wind stress exerted by a trade wind on the sea level anomaly in the equatorial sea region. Consequently, SLA emerges as a potential new indicator for identifying ENSO-related signals. In this study, we initially examined the relations between sea surface temperature and SLA, as well as its two major components (i.e., steric SLA and non-steric SLA) in Niño 3.4 region from temporal perspectives. Subsequently, we explored their spatial association with THCs in China. In our analyses, we found a robust alignment between the long-term variability signal from SLA/SSL and SST over the Niño 3.4 regions. Notably strong correlations between SSTaI and SLAI/SSLI were also found. In contrast to SLAI and SSLI, NSSLI displayed significant differences in time series changes and a lower correlation with SSTaI. Furthermore, the in-phase (orthogonal) relationships and larger (minimal) coherence between SSTaI and SLAI/SSLI (NSSLI) were revealed via wavelet coherence analysis. Notably, SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI not only showed significant coherence in long-term variability signals (i.e., 2–4 years) but also exhibited higher coherence in periods less than 2-years, especially during alternating ENSO events (e.g., 2007–2011). Overall, across temporal scales, SSTaI and SLAI/SSLI displayed notable consistency, indicating that SLAI and SSLI may be the equivalent indices to SSTaI in observing ENSO-related signals. Apart from temporal analysis, notable similarities were observed in the capabilities of SLAI and SSLI to SSTaI when examining the ENSO-related impact on THCs at spatial scales, while NSSLI exhibited marked distinctions. The maximum cross-correlation spatial pattern between surface pressure and SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI showed an almost uniform positive correlation, while the distribution of temperature and evapotranspiration was more divergent, especially for evapotranspiration. SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI were remarkably correlated to TWS over China with significant regional variations across China, while NSSLI exhibited significant differences compared to SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI. In comparison to the other four THCs, the spatial pattern of maximum cross-correlation between precipitation and NSSLI resembled that of SSTaI, SLAI, and SSLI, except for Northeast China (SLRB). Furthermore, the generally similar pattern for the time lag corresponding to maximum cross-correlation in the relationship among SSTaI, SLAI, SSLI and THCs was also revealed. However, the spatial pattern exhibited dispersion. The resulting time lag at a basin scale between SLAI/SSLI and THCs was comparable to SSTaI, implying that the combined analyses of the time lag determined between SSTaI/SLAI/SSLI and THCs can eventually complement the analysis based solely on SSTaI. These findings demonstrated a potential advancement in the usage of satellite altimetric data over Niño 3.4 regions for enhancing our knowledge of ENSO dynamics and its influence on regional hydroclimatic patterns in China.
1 Introduction Evapotranspiration (ET) serves as a crucial nexus within the water, energy, and carbon cycles (Mianabadi et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2014; Yang et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2016 ). ET can typically be partitioned into vegetation transpiration (Et), soil evaporation (Es), canopy interception loss (Ec), snow sublimation (Esn), and evaporation from open water. Excepting open water evaporation, these components are strongly influenced by vegetation dynamics (Good et al. 2017; Liu et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2023 ). Against the backdrop of global greening (Chen et al. 2019; Piao et al. 2020 ), changes in vegetation introduce substantial uncertainties into the accurate partitioning of ET (Cao et al. 2022; Li et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2023 ). Accurate ET components are essential for agricultural water management and assessing ecological project benefits. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms of ET components is crucial in regions facing high water stress, ensuring food security, and maintaining ecological and environmental conditions (Mu et al. 2007; Song et al. 2018 ). Previous studies have employed various technologies to estimate ET and its components, including remote sensing-based models, field experiments, and process-based land surface models. Regarding remote sensing-based models, while they cannot directly extract ET from satellite images, they can integrate satellite data (e.g., vegetation parameters and energy balance products) with physical or empirical formulas to estimate ET and its components (Mu et al. 2007; Tian et al. 2013; Zhang et al. 2019 ). Over the past several decades, such remote sensing-based models have been the primary approach for regional and global ET estimation because of the availability of various remote sensing products (Bastiaanssen et al. 1998a; Bastiaanssen et al. 1998b; Zhang et al. 2008 ). However, partitioning ET using remote sensing-based models remains challenging, partly because these models oversimplify physical processes, such as neglecting the contribution of water constraints during the evaporation process. (Lian et al., 2018; Miralles et al., 2016; Talsma et al., 2018b ). Alternatively, in field experiments to estimate ET, models based on field-measured data have been proposed to estimate Et and other components (Duursma et al. 2013; Fisher et al. 2008; Jiao et al. 2018; Jiao et al. 2015; Jung et al. 2019; Sus et al. 2014 ). However, owing to the constraints imposed by various local conditions, field experiments often focus more on an individual ET component than on all components or the full water balance at a point scale (Schlesinger and Jasechko 2014; Zhang et al. 2023 ). For example, after using a global field experiment dataset to estimate Et, Gao et al. (2022) highlighted the importance to consider both biotic and abiotic factors when estimating other ET components. This undoubtedly poses greater challenges for experimental instruments and field conditions during monitoring. Process-based land surface models, including the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model (Liang et al. 1994 ), Noah Multi-parameterization (Noah-MP) model (Chen et al. 1996 ), and Community Land Model (CLM) (Oleson et al. 2004 ), offer several advantages in estimating ET and its components (Ge et al. 2011; Yeh et al. 2011; Zhang et al. 2017 ). By coupling water and energy balances with biogeophysical processes to capture large-scale ET, these process-based models enable a deeper comprehension and explication of ET (Haddeland et al. 2006 ). Consequently, they have extensive applications at the regional and global scales (Jiang et al. 2022; Lawrence et al. 2007; Luo et al. 2016 ). Nevertheless, ET component estimation remains controversial owing to the inadequate consideration of vegetation dynamics during ET partitioning. Process-based land surface models generally apply land cover information within a region to partition ET into biotic (e.g., Et and Ec) and abiotic (i.e., Es) components (Haddeland et al. 2006 ). The subsequent estimation of Et and Ec depends on vegetation structure dynamics, such as the leaf area index (LAI) (Liang et al. 1994; Yang et al. 2021 ). Process-based models are typically subject to the representation of vegetation conditions and generally adopt two approaches to address vegetation dynamics. The first approach couples a dynamic vegetation module to the CLM or Noah-MP (Hosseini et al. 2022; Jasechko et al. 2013; Lawrence et al. 2019; Sato et al. 2014 ), utilizing vegetation physiology and biophysical formulations to derive vegetation dynamics (Dickinson et al. 1998 ). The second approach integrates satellite vegetation parameters into a physical model, such as the VIC model, to capture the dynamic state of vegetation (Bohn and Vivoni 2016; Jiang et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2020; Xie et al. 2015 ). However, dynamic vegetation modeling remains characterized by substantial uncertainty because of the complexity of biophysical processes (Anav et al. 2013; Cadule et al. 2010; Shu et al. 2022; Sitch et al. 2015 ), whereas satellite products are reliable means for obtaining regional and global vegetation dynamics. Nevertheless, the extent to which satellite dynamic vegetation parameters can enhance ET partitioning in land surface models remains unclear. To elucidate the role of satellite vegetation parameters in estimating the ET components in land surface models, in this study we applied a representative VIC model as an example. Selecting the Loess Plateau (LP) region in China as the study area where vegetation recovery occurred. By integrating remote sensing vegetation parameters, we first investigated the influence of these parameters on the performance of ET partitions at a point scale. Our study then identified the sensitivity of the ET components to the dynamics of the LAI and fraction of vegetation coverage (FVC) under different climatic conditions. Finally, we explored the responses of ET components to vegetation greening at a regional scale in the Loess Plateau. This study enhances ET components estimation accuracy by integrating satellite vegetation parameters. Such integration provides a reference for accurately assessing water consumption in ecological projects and studying water use efficiency in agriculture.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study area The LP is situated in the upper and middle reaches of the Yellow River in China and covers a total area of 632,520 km2  (Fig. 1  a). The region experiences a continental monsoon climate characterized by hot and rainy summers and cold and dry winters. The precipitation distribution is spatially uneven, with an annual precipitation of approximately 200 mm in the northwest and 750 mm in the southeast (Liu et al. 2023 ). In terms of precipitation conditions, the LP region can be divided into humid (HU), subhumid (SH), arid (AR), and semi-arid (SA) zones. The annual ET in the region is around 390 mm, increasing at a rate of 5.73 mm yr−1  (Jiang et al. 2022 ). Around 2000, the Chinese government initiated the Grain for Green Project to restore the ecological environment in the LP (Jiang et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2022 ), leading to significant vegetation greening (Fig. 1 b, c). The predominant vegetation types in the area include grasslands, forests, and shrubs, with vegetation improving gradually from the northwest to the southeast (Fig. 1 a). The extensive range of climatic conditions and pronounced vegetation variation renders the LP favorable for detecting the role of satellite vegetation products in partitioning ET with generalizable findings.  2.2 Data availability The basic inputs for the VIC model include meteorological data, soil parameters, vegetation parameters, land cover types, and topographic data. Meteorological data on precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures, and relative humidity were obtained from the China Meteorological Administration (https://data.cma.cn/ ). In this study, 571 sites in and around the LP for which these data were available were selected for spatial interpolation (Jiang et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2017; Xie et al. 2015 ). The temporal scale of the data is daily, from 2000 to 2020. For subsequent experiments, meteorological data were interpolated at resolutions of 0.01° and 0.0625°. The 0.01° data were used to drive the model for evaluation and point-scale experiments, whereas the 0.0625° data were employed to simulate the ET components across the entire LP. The soil and vegetation parameters were obtained from widely used datasets provided via the VIC website (https://vic.readthedocs.io/en/master/Datasets/Datasets/ ). Nijssen et al. (2001)  compiled and released this dataset, which has been widely utilized. Land cover types were derived from Landsat TM images to generate a multi-year 1 km resolution raster dataset of land cover in China, available at the National Earth System Science Data Center (https://www.geodata.cn/ ). During the study period from 2000 to 2020, there was minimal change in land cover types in the study area; thus, we used data from 2010 as the basis. Topographic data were acquired using a digital elevation model provided by the United States Geological Survey (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/ ) and employed for accurate elevation during site validation and point experiments. The satellite vegetation parameters within the study area were represented by the LAI and FVC, both of which were obtained from the Global LAnd Surface Satellite (GLASS, https://www.geodata.cn ) (Liang et al. 2021 ). The GLASS LAI product derived from MODIS surface reflectance data using a bidirectional long short-term memory model (Ma and Liang 2022; Xiao et al. 2014; Xiao et al. 2016 ). This model effectively utilizes global LAI datasets, along with temporal and spectral information from MODIS surface reflectance. The GLASS FVC product was developed using a multivariate adaptive regression spline approach based on MODIS data (Yang et al. 2016 ). The FVC product has been intensively evaluated using high-resolution satellite and ground measurement data with favorable performance (Jia et al. 2016; Jia et al. 2018 ). To evaluate the ET and its components estimated using the VIC model, in this study we leveraged multiple covariance flux towers and field experimental sites. The observational data for ET were obtained from covariance flux towers, whereas the ET components (e.g., Et, Es, Ec) were derived from diverse field experiments. Detailed information and references are presented in Table 1 and 2   . Et was predominantly observed using the sap flow method, Es using a micro-lysimeter, and Ec using a pluviometer. Additionally, owing to the challenges in acquiring experimental data on a daily scale, the evaluation of ET components was conducted on a monthly scale. Considering the spatial representativeness of the field experimental sites, we conducted model validation at a spatial resolution of 0.01° (approximately 1 km2  for a grid cell). Pearson correlation coefficient (R), root mean square error (RMSE), and bias metrics were used to evaluate model accuracy.  2.3 Land surface model for ET partitioning The VIC model (version 4.2. d) was used to partition ET (Liang et al. 1994 ). VIC is widely recognized as a land surface hydrological model with extensive applications in Earth system science and hydrology-related engineering (Jiang et al. 2022; Leng et al. 2015; Long et al. 2014 ). It utilizes regular grid cells to simulate surface energy and water balance. Within each grid cell, the model considers multiple sub-grid cells representing various vegetation types and bare land. The model calculates water and energy balances for each land cover type at a sub-grid scale, then aggregates these according to the proportions of each land cover type within the grid. The VIC model is capable of estimating four ET components: Es, Et, Ec, and Esn. The Penman–Monteith equation was first used to model the potential ET before calculating the actual Es based on the soil moisture function. VIC then delineated ET based on internal vegetation cover calculations within each grid (Fig. 2  a), which can be expressed by the following formula:(1) ET =  ∑ n = 1  N  C n  ∙ Ec  n  + Et  n    + C N + 1   ∙ E s + E s n ,     where C n    represents the FVC of the n th vegetation type, C N + 1     is the bare land fraction.
