For model calibration and validation, the parameter values, except for LAI and FVC, were obtained from Jiang et al. (2022) , in which the water balance, including the total ET and water discharge, was well evaluated, and acceptable performance was achieved.  2.4 Dynamic vegetation parameters in ET partitioning The VIC model considers both the water constraints within the grid cells and the energy balance process, endowing it with the advantage of reflecting clear physical processes and reliable performance. Previous studies predominantly used the VIC model's default/static assumption, where LAI was prescribed with 12-month climatological values, and FVC was defined as the proportion of vegetated sub-grid cells within each grid cell. Under this assumption, VIC only considers the seasonal variation of LAI and a fixed FVC (i.e., FVC=1). Thus it disregards inter-annual variations in LAI and both inter- and intra-annual variations in FVC. According to the computation of W im     in Eq. (9)  and r c    in Eq. (10) , variations in LAI strongly influence the estimation of Ec and Et. As illustrated in Eq. (1) , the FVC within a grid cell is also important in ET partitioning. While a fixed FVC may introduce minor errors in densely vegetated areas (Fig. 2 b), substantial uncertainties will arise in sparsely vegetated regions (Fig. 2 c). Therefore, the static assumption of vegetation conditions introduces considerable uncertainty into ET estimation in the VIC model. In this study, we examine a dynamic vegetation framework within VIC to address the limitations of the default assumption. In this framework, daily-scale dynamic LAI and FVC data are integrated into the forcing dataset, replacing the default/static vegetation information. When employing dynamic vegetation parameters to partition ET, the GLASS LAI are used to compute Ec and Et for the computation of W im     in Eq. (9)  and r c    in Eq. (10) , and the GLASS FVC are used to partition ET components according to Eq. (1) . We prepared a daily scale satellite vegetation parameter-driven model to explore the effect of dynamic vegetation parameters on ET partitioning. We designed two simulation scenarios at point scales: one using the default vegetation conditions (static LAI and FVC), and the other incorporating satellite vegetation parameters (dynamic LAI and FVC). We calculated the differences in the ET components between the two scenarios at three temporal scales: annual averages, inter- and intra-annual variations. The configuration of the experimental sites is elaborated in detail in Section 2.5 . To investigate the sensitivity of ET and its components to dynamic vegetation conditions, we further designed a series of scenarios with various scale factors for the LAI and FVC at point scales. Based on the mean LAI in the study area (LAIs = 1.23 m2  m−2 ), we prescribed scale factors varying from zero to 1.5; thus, 15 scenarios were evaluated with mean LAI values ranging from zero to 1.85 m2  m−2 . Given the mean FVC in the study area (FVC=0.4), the scale factors were prescribed from 0.1 to 1.1, resulting in 11 scenarios with FVC values ranging from 0.04 to 0.41. It should be noted that the default FVC in the VIC was 1.0, as explained in Subsection 2.3. The upper limit of the FVC was 1.0; therefore, we considered the maximum scale factor value only up to 1.1 times the original FVC to prevent regions with high FVC from exceeding this limit. To explore the effect of temporal variations in LAI and FVC on the VIC model simulation of ET and its components, we proposed the following sensitivity coefficient (Sankarasubramanian et al. 2001 ):(14) S x  = dE / E  dx / x   = dE  dx   ∙ x E   ,     where E  represents the ET and its components, x  represents the dynamic vegetation parameters, and Sx   is the sensitivity coefficient. Sx   can be understood as the percentage change in the ET and its components resulting from a certain percentage change in the dynamic vegetation parameters over time. A larger absolute value of the sensitivity coefficient indicates a stronger effect of the factor on the ET and its components.  2.5 Experimental design The effects of dynamic vegetation on ET partitioning may vary with climatic conditions. We examined this effect at a point scale and selected study sites from four different climatic conditions according to long-term average annual precipitation: AR (annual precipitation < 200 mm), SA (annual precipitation between 200 and 400 mm), SH (annual precipitation between 400 and 800 mm), and HU (annual precipitation > 800 mm) regions. The experimental sites were selected according to three criteria: (1) vegetation parameters (LAI or FVC) at the study site varied significantly (P<0.05) among years during the study period, assessed with the Mann-Kendall trend test; (2) vegetation type at the sites primarily specified as forest; and (3) relatively uniform spatial distribution of the vegetation across the entire study area, with each site covering at least six grid cells (approximately 6 km2 ) to eliminate potential uncertainties from variability in individual grid cells. Based on these criteria, we defined 15 sites for the four climatic conditions, as shown in Table 3  . The distribution of the 15 sites is shown in Fig. 1 a along with the vegetation types and stratum boundaries.   3 Results 3.1 Model evaluation First, we evaluated the VIC model with and without dynamic satellite vegetation parameters. As shown in Fig. 3  , the VIC model was capable of simulating the temporal variations in ET. Under default conditions, the average R value was 0.46, with a lower accuracy observed at specific stations (Fig. 3 c). Following the incorporation of the satellite vegetation parameters, the VIC model demonstrated improved ET simulation accuracy, with an average R value of 0.75 and an average RMSE of 1.25 mm day−1 . For ET partitioning, the VIC model with default vegetation tended to overestimate Et and Ec (Figs. 4 and 5   ) and significantly underestimate Es (Fig. 6  ). Upon the inclusion of satellite vegetation parameters, the model demonstrated marked improvements: a substantial increase in R for Et by 0.89 (1620 %), with a mean decrease in RMSE of 12.68 mm mon−1  (65.77 %), and an average reduction in bias of 124.83 % (86.52 %). Similarly, it raised the average R for Ec by 0.48 (141.18 %), leading to an average decrease in RMSE by 17.50 mm mon−1  (80.52 %) and an average reduction in bias by 676.28 % (94.87 %). In the simulation of Es, the inclusion of satellite vegetation parameters yielded an average R of 0.73, an average RMSE of 5.03 mm mon-1 , and an average bias of 40.02 %.  3.2 Influence of dynamic LAI on ET partitioning We first evaluated the influence of dynamic LAI on ET partitioning under the four climatic conditions. After incorporating dynamic LAI into the VIC model (Fig. 7  ), the overall mean of ET decreased slightly, with an average reduction of 6.98 mm yr−1  (2.25 %). Among the different ET components, dynamic LAI resulted in increased Es and Et and decreased Ec and Esn, except under AR conditions. Under different climatic conditions, the differences induced by dynamic LAI gradually diminished with increasing precipitation. In HU regions (Fig. 7 d), the disparities in the ET components narrowed to within 2 %. Incorporation of dynamic LAI markedly reshaped the components of ET regarding interannual variations (Fig. 8  ), primarily resulting in an increase in Es and Et and a decrease in Ec and Esn. Notably, the interannual trends of Ec and Et were also altered, with accelerated interannual variation in Et in AR and SA regions albeit delayed change in Ec (Fig. 8 a, b). Conversely, the Ec trend was accelerated in the SH and HU regions (Fig. 8 c, d). In comparison, dynamic LAI incorporation predominantly affected the Et and Ec components related to intra-annual variations (Fig. 9  ). In particular, the peak value of Et occurred earlier throughout the year (Fig. 9 b, c, d), resulting in a deceleration of the intra-annual variation in Ec (Fig. 9 a, b). ET increased with higher LAI coefficients, exhibiting a pattern of rapid growth followed by a slower increase (Fig. 10  ). In particular, the proportion of Es decreased as LAI increased, showing a pattern of rapid decline followed by a gradual decrease. Alternatively, the proportion of Et initially increased and then decreased; this pattern became more pronounced with increasing precipitation in the respective regions. In turn, the proportion of Ec increased linearly, whereas that of Esn did not markedly change. Moreover, the influence of the LAI on ET and its components gradually diminished from AR to HU regions (Table 4  ). Among the ET components, Et and Ec exhibited the highest sensitivity to LAI changes, whereas the sensitivities of Es and Esn were relatively low.  3.3 Influence of dynamic FVC on ET partitioning After incorporating dynamic FVC into the VIC model (Fig. 11  ), the overall mean of ET slightly increased, with an average rise of 17.15 mm yr−1  (5.35 %). Among the different ET components, Et, Ec, and Esn were decreased, with Et experiencing the most notable decline, whereas Es was improved. Similar to the results obtained for dynamic LAI, the differences induced by dynamic FVC gradually diminished with increased humidity. Notably, in the absence of dynamic FVC, over 70 % of the Es was allocated to other ET components in AR and SA regions (Fig. 11 a, b), introducing substantial biases in the simulation of other ET components. The effect of dynamic FVC was relatively small for interannual variations; however, it enhanced the ET growth rate in the AR region (Fig. 12  ). Alternatively, dynamic FVC had minimal influence on the overall magnitude and trend of ET with regard to intra-annual variations, although it delayed the peak value of ET throughout the year. The effects of dynamic FVC on ET components were mainly manifested in Es and Et, with Es exhibiting a transition from negligible to notable intra-annual dynamics, and Et showing a substantial reduction (Fig. 13  ). Increasing humidity also gradually diminished the influence of dynamic FVC on these components. ET gradually increased with increasing FVC coefficients in the AR and SA regions (Fig. 14  a, b), whereas in the SH and HU regions, it initially increased and then decreased with increasing FVC coefficients (Fig. 14 c, d). In particular, the proportion of Es decreased linearly with increasing FVC, that of Et showed a fluctuating upward pattern, whereas that of Ec exhibited logarithmic growth. Moreover, the influence of FVC on ET and its components gradually decreased from the AR to HU regions (Table 5  ). Among the ET components, Et exhibited the highest sensitivity to changes in FVC, followed by Ec, Es, and Esn. Notably, ET and its components were more sensitive to changes in FVC than to changes in LAI.  3.4 Spatial variation of ET components on the LP Given the favorable performance of VIC incorporating dynamic vegetation, we simulated the ET and its components on the LP using the VIC model under two scenarios: with the inclusion of satellite vegetation parameters or in a static or default state. Subsequently, the spatial differences between the two scenarios were compared (Fig. 15  ). Across both scenarios, ET and its components exhibited an increasing trend from the northwest to southeast of the LP. Notably, with the incorporation of the satellite parameters, we observed a substantial increase in Es across the LP, particularly in the central forested regions (Fig. 15 d, e, f). However, the inclusion of satellite dynamic vegetation parameters led to an overall decrease in both Et and Ec in the LP. Specifically, Et exhibited substantial reductions in the central and eastern regions (Fig. 15 i), whereas Ec showed prominent decreases in the central region (Fig. 15 l), with reductions of 139.63 and 41.88 mm yr−1 , respectively.   4 Discussion 4.1 Mechanism of ET partitioning in land surface hydrological modeling The inclusion of dynamic LAI had a more pronounced influence than the static LAI on the interannual variability of Ec and ET as determined through VIC modeling. The dynamic LAI increased the interannual variability of Et (Fig. 8 ) relative to that using the VIC model with its default LAI (Liang et al., 1994 ). Under this default or static application, the LAI exhibited only intra-annual variability without interannual changes, resulting in a smoother Et variation profile (Fig. 16  a). The inclusion of the dynamic LAI allowed the model to capture the interannual variability in vegetation growth. An increase in LAI directly augments the leaf stomatal conductance, leading to a reduction in transpiration resistance and an increase in transpiration (Meinzer and Evolution, 1993 ). This change was more evident in regions with limited water availability (i.e., AR and SA regions) (Fig. 8 a, b). However, the VIC is sophisticated when considering soil moisture constraints on Et (Liang et al., 1994 ). Excessive transpiration induces soil moisture stress, thereby restricting the increase in Et (Fig. 16 b). This explains the observed trend of an initial increase, followed by a decrease in the response of Et to the LAI coefficient (Fig. 10 ). In turn, the increase in the LAI directly enhanced the maximum interception capacity of vegetation, resulting in a linear increase in the proportion of Ec with the increase in the LAI coefficient (Fig. 10 ). The most notable effect of dynamic FVC inclusion in the model was observed with regard to altering the pattern of ET partitioning, allowing for the simulation of forest gaps (Fig. 16 b). This stems from the default setting of the VIC model, wherein during the computation of the vegetated tile, it is assumed that the tile is entirely veiled by vegetation (i.e., FVC=1.0) (Liang et al., 1994 ). Consequently, the model failed to account for the Es within these designated subgrids (Fig. 16 a). With the incorporation of dynamic FVC, the model divides the grid cells based on the actual FVC at the current time for each subgrid, enabling the simulation of Es from forest gaps (Fig. 16 b). Under water-limited conditions, that is, in AR and SA regions, the presence of forest gaps becomes more apparent. This explains why the ratio of Es to ET increased by over 70 % in AR and SA regions after introducing dynamic FVC (Fig. 11 a, b). Our findings indicate that, under conditions of static vegetation cover, interstitial Es is misallocated to Et during ET partitioning, leading to an overestimation of Et. This overestimation was evident in our model validation using the field experiment results. For example, at the TQG and YJG2 sites (sites encompassing all ET components) (Fig. 4 a, b; Fig. 5 a, c), the VIC model under default conditions consistently overestimated both Et and Ec. Such discrepancies can engender considerable uncertainty in eco-hydrological vegetation research. After incorporating dynamic LAI and FVC, Es increases while Et and Ec decrease across the entire LP, with the greatest changes observed in the central forested regions. This adjustment reveals gaps in previous Es simulations erroneously allocated to Et and Ec. Spatially, regions with sparse vegetation in the northwest show smaller changes compared to densely forested areas in the central region, highlighting the critical need to integrate dynamic vegetation parameters for ET partitioning in forested regions.  4.2 Importance of considering vegetation dynamics for estimating ET components Dynamic vegetation parameters in land surface modeling are effective in reducing the uncertainty in ET partitions. Among the currently available ET component products, significant variations exist in the proportions of different components across various datasets (Talsma et al., 2018a, Talsma et al., 2018b, Bowen et al., 2019, Miralles et al. 2016, Lian et al. 2018 ). For example, across different datasets, the T/ET ratio ranged from < 45 % to > 80 % (Bowen et al. 2019 ). This variability stems from the diverse assumptions made during the allocation of ET components in different datasets, with particular uncertainty in Es estimation (Talsma et al. 2018a ). Moreover, Et is generally overestimated in existing products (Good et al. 2015 ). Our findings indicate that incorporating dynamic vegetation parameters considerably enhances the accuracy of ET partitioning in the VIC model compared to static vegetation conditions. This approach reduces uncertainty in Es (Fig. 6 ) and mitigates overestimations of Et and Ec (Figs. 4 and 5 ). Therefore, considering dynamic vegetation is crucial for reducing uncertainty in ET allocation. A few studies have shown that incorporating dynamic vegetation parameters enhances the reliability of ET simulations (Cao et al. 2022; Jiang et al. 2022; Paschalis et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2014; Wei et al. 2017; Yang et al. 2023 ). However, these studies generally focused on a single vegetation parameter. For example, Yang et al. (2022)  considered FVC but overlooked LAI, while Bai et al. (2018)  concentrated solely on dynamic changes in LAI and disregard changes in FVC. Our study illustrates that FVC and LAI exert distinct yet equally significant impacts on the simulation of ET components. Specifically, FVC changes the allocation pattern of ET components in forested areas, while LAI affects intra- and inter-annual trends in ET components. Therefore, accurately simulating ET components in land surface hydrological models requires comprehensive consideration of dynamic FVC and LAI. Vegetation dynamics from satellite retrieval offer advantages relative to vegetation growth modules in land surface models (Shu et al. 2022, Anav et al. 2013, Cadule et al. 2010 ). In land surface models, such as the CLM and Noah-MP, the vegetation growth module, based on vegetation physiology, incorporates the relationships between environmental variables and vegetation growth to simulate vegetation dynamics (Hosseini et al. 2022, Lawrence et al. 2019, Jasechko et al. 2013, Sato et al. 2014 ). However, owing to the assumptions in biophysical formulations, uncertainties in model parameters, and input data, the accuracy of these models remains problematic (Shu et al. 2022 ). Numerous studies have relied on satellite vegetation data to validate the performance of vegetation dynamics simulated by land surface models (Dickinson et al. 1998, Shu et al. 2022 ), supporting satellite vegetation data as the most dependable option for assessing genuine vegetation conditions in a given region. The vegetation dynamics module is particularly applicable for evaluating vegetation predictions and carbon cycling (Dickinson et al. 1998, Sato et al. 2014 ). In the land surface models, when partitioning ET, the sensitivity to FVC was higher than that to LAI. This is because FVC directly influences the partitioning of ET component proportions. Specifically, Et showed the highest sensitivity to FVC (Table 5 ), primarily because in land surface models, Et is calculated only in areas with vegetation cover. Alternatively, Es in vegetated areas was suppressed. Therefore, accurately considering the dynamic changes in FVC is crucial for accurately simulating Et and Es. The FVC and LAI also have significant effects on Ec, as FVC and LAI respectively determine the spatial extent and overall magnitude of the Ec calculations. Notably, ET components exhibit heightened sensitivity to vegetation changes in AR and SA regions, where vegetation conditions are poorer, resulting in more pronounced disturbances to ET components. In particular, we focused solely on the LP region, which encompasses multiple climatic zones; however, the vegetation status within individual climatic zones may exhibit relatively uniform characteristics. Hence, we experimented with multiple vegetation parameter magnitudes to account for this variability. Similarly, to obtain the aforementioned findings, we incorporated the closely related variables LAI and FVC separately into the model and analyzed their distinct mechanisms for partitioning ET components.   5 Conclusion This study investigated the role of satellite vegetation products in allocating ET components (i.e., Es, Et, Ec, and Esn) within land surface models. We employed the VIC model, which integrates water and energy balances but lacks a dynamic vegetation module. The results indicate that although the inclusion of dynamic vegetation parameters marginally improves the ET estimation, it enhances the correlation coefficient R of the ET components by 0.70 and reduces the RMSE by 11.74 mm mon−1 . Among the various dynamic vegetation parameters, the inclusion of dynamic LAI alters the inter- and intra-annual variations in Et and Ec, whereas dynamic FVC reshapes the distribution pattern of ET components, enabling the model to simulate canopy gaps in Es, thereby mitigating ET overestimation. Among different climatic zones, the effect of dynamic vegetation parameters is particularly pronounced in arid and semi-arid regions because of sparser vegetation compared with that in subhumid and humid regions. Increased vegetation led to a linear decrease in Es, a rapid initial increase in ET, followed by a gradual decrease and a linear increase in Ec, highlighting the sensitivity of ET components to vegetation dynamics. Temporally, Et exhibited the highest sensitivity to vegetation dynamics, followed by Ec and Es. Across the entire LP region, the incorporation of satellite vegetation parameters resulted in a 192.25 mm yr−1  increase in Es, which was primarily concentrated in the central forested areas, whereas Et decreased by 139.63 mm yr−1  and Ec decreased by 41.88 mm yr−1 . Our findings underscore the notable effect of satellite vegetation parameters on the allocation of ET within land surface models, particularly highlighting how dynamic FVC alters the distribution patterns of ET components. These results provide a theoretical groundwork for more precisely evaluating the hydrological effects of ecological restoration projects and the influence of vegetation greening on the water cycle.
1 Introduction Water distribution systems (WDSs) are a collection of hydraulic elements such as pumps, pipes, tanks, and valves, designed to convey water from sources to consumers. The behavior of the system is determined by physical laws of mass and energy conservation; water demands; and its layout. The optimal design problem of WDS is the task of sizing certain elements in the system such that would satisfy its constraints, such as the supply of nodal demand, minimal pressure, and water quality standards, and result in an optimal objective value, traditionally set as minimal total construction and operation cost (Perelman and Ostfeld 2007 ). Designing an optimal water distribution network presents a multifaceted challenge that requires careful consideration of hydraulic performance, cost efficiency, and sustainability. Engineers must balance the complex interactions between pipe diameters, network topology, and operational constraints to ensure reliable water supply and efficient system operation. Factors such as pressure requirements, flow rates, water quality standards, and resilience to external disruptions further complicate the design process. Optimization involves minimizing both capital and operational costs while maximizing system reliability and resilience to future demands and uncertainties. The variables that are considered in such optimal design problems are traditionally pipe diameters, tank volumes and pumping station capacities. Due to the non-linear and non-convex relationship between flow and head in WDS, and the use of discrete diameter sizes, the problem is regarded as highly complex (Bragalli et al., 2011 ) and found to be NP-Hard (Yates et al., 1984 ). Linear programming techniques can be utilized (Alperovits and Shamir 1977 ) to minimize costs while satisfying constraints on pipe diameters, flow rates, and pressure requirements. During the 1980′s and 1990′s several non-linear solution methods have been developed such as enumerations (Gessler 1985 ) and decomposition (Fujiwara and Khang 1990, Eiger et al. 1994 ). Over the past three decades, a significant amount of research has concentrated on the development and application of heuristic methods to solve the optimal design problem. Those methods can allow the efficient exploration of large solution spaces, which are tackled as part of the optimal design problem. Among those methods are genetic algorithms (Savić and Walters, 1997 ), simulated annealing (Zoppou and Reed 2001 ), shuffled from leap algorithm (Eusuff and Lansey 2003 ), differential evolution algorithm (Suribabu 2009 ), particle swarm optimization (Montalvo et al. 2008 ), ant colony optimization (Ostfeld and Tubaltzev 2008 ) and whale optimization algorithm (Ezzeldin and Djebedjian 2020 ). Several examples also exist for the combination of analytical methods with heuristic ones (Zheng et al. 2014, Reca et al. 2017 ). Power grids (PGs) are networks of transmission lines, substations, transformers, and distribution points designed to deliver electricity from power plants to consumers. Designing an optimal power grid is a complex challenge that requires balancing numerous factors to ensure efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. Engineers must consider geographical factors such as terrain and population distribution, as well as economic variables like cost-effectiveness and scalability. The grid must be robust enough to handle peak demands while also integrating renewable energy sources effectively to reduce environmental impact. Furthermore, technological advancements in energy storage and transmission play a crucial role in enhancing grid resilience and stability. Achieving an optimal design involves navigating these multifaceted considerations to create a system that meets current and future energy needs efficiently and sustainably. Traditionally, decision variables for the power grid optimal design problem are generator capacities, sizes of energy storage facilities (Yang et al. 2020 ), transmission line sizes (Khalil and Ismail 2006 ), and the integration of renewable energy sources (Garni et al. 2018; Majidi et al. 2022 ). A similar problem which is often tackled in research is the problem of power grid expansion, dealing with the planning of an additional section of the grid (Kim and Hur 2021, You et al. 2016 ). These problems are deemed mathematically complex, due to the non-linear and non-convex nature of the power flow equations (Lavaei and Low 2010 ). Common methods used to overcome the computational challenges are linear and quadratic programming (Fortenbacher and Demiray 2019 ), second-order cone programming (Baradar et al. 2013 ), semidefinite programming (Molzahn et al. 2013 ), along with many other relaxation and approximation methods (Molzahn and Hiskens 2019 ). The link between the systems has been studied from various perspectives (Hamiche et al. 2016 ), with most work linking WDSs and PGs concerned with their joint operation (Oikonomou and Parvania 2019; Takahashi et al. 2017; Sun et al. 2018 ). Hari et al. (2023)  have considered a joint expansion problem, designing storage and generation facilities for the conjunctive system. In their work, they define the objective as maximizing the demand that is supplied by the system, rather than the traditional minimal cost objective. However, the network considered there is quite simplistic and does not consider loops, multiple water consumers, or multiple storage and pumping facilities, which can significantly complexify the problem. Yao et al. (2023)  proposed an optimal design problem of WDS under uncertainty, combining the uncertainty in water demand with uncertainty of solar power availability. A behind-the-meter (BTM) component was also designed as part of the work to support the supply of power to the WDS. The PG itself and its constraints were not considered. They found that while robustness of the solution is improved, the design of a solar component did not affect the sizing of components inside the WDS. Yao et al. (2021)  suggested to optimally design water tanks in the system to enhance the flexibility of the power system and to improve water quality. In their work they do consider the PG’s structure and constraints, but the problem focuses on tanks rather than the design of the entire system, and without any decision variables on the PG side. This paper proposes a conjunctive optimal design problem, combining the design of a WDS and a PG to explore ways in which the sizing of components in one system affects the other and the operational policies of both systems. On the WDS side, capacities of storage and pumping facilities are determined, and on the PG side – the capacity of a solar field is determined. This paper is aimed to provide two main contributions to existing literature. The first is the very presentation and mathematical formulation of the conjunctive design problem, which represents a relatively novel and more holistic approach to water resources management, taking into consideration the explicit modelling of adjacent and interconnected systems (in this case, a power system), as opposed to the traditional approach which usually considers merely the WDS standpoint. Hopefully, this will spark a discussion about the joint examination of those two interconnected infrastructure systems. The second contribution lies in the analysis of the results, which clearly shows how those two systems depend on and even constrain one another. The joint analysis provides unique and often counterintuitive insights into the link between different components in those systems and proposes ways to design them together in a way that takes advantage of those links. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: section 2  includes a mathematical formulation of the conjunctive design problem; section 3  details the solution of two example applications, including sensitivity analyses; and section 4  includes the conclusions of the work. The work has the potential to help design better infrastructure in the future, which in turn will increase the systems’ efficiency, reduce operational costs, and environmental impact.  2 Problem formulation The formulation of the conjunctive design problem is brought here, comprising all constraints and decision variables that form each of the two problems of WDS optimal design and PG optimal design. 2.1 Decision variables Since a system’s operation is highly dependent on its design, the operational costs must be considered as part of the problem’s objective (as will be discussed further in the Objective function sub-section). Hence, the decision variables include also operational decisions and could be divided into two categories – design variables, and operational variables. The design decision variables for the conjunctive design problem are: P max    [kW] − pumping capacities of all pumping stations in the WDS; V s   [m3 ] − storage capacities of all tanks in the WDS; SF   [MW] − solar field capacities of all solar fields to be constructed and connected to the PG. The operational decision variables are: Q  [m3 /hr] − flows in all links in the WDS; H  [m] − heads in all nodes in the WDS; n  [rpm] – pump rotation speeds in all pumps in the WDS; p in    [p.u], q in    [p.u] − active and reactive power generation quantities at all generators in the PG; p  [p.u], q  [p.u] − active and reactive power at all buses in the PG, respectively; v  [p.u] − voltages at all buses of the PG. As opposed to the design decision variables, the operational decision variables are to be determined for each timestep of the optimization horizon. Fig. 1   shows the water and power demand patterns that were used, along with a solar generation curve that limits the amount of power that could be generated at any given hour of the day (Jahid et al. 2018 ).  2.2 Constraints The optimal design problem includes the following constraints on the WDS side, which constitute node mass conservation (1), tank continuity (2), tank closure (3), pump curve (4), link energy conservation (5), node head bounds (6), pump rotation speed bounds (7), and non-negative pump flow (8), and head (9):(1) A  T  ∙ Q  t  = d  t    ∀ t ∈ T     (2) H tank , s  t  = H tank , s  t - 1   + Q tank , s  t  ∙ Δ t  α tank , s      ∀ t ∈ T ∀ s ∈ S     (3) H tank , s  24  ≥ 0.95 ∙ H tank , s  0  ∀ s ∈ S     (4) H p , l  t  = a pumps , l   ∙ n p , l  t  n max       2  - b pumps , l   ∙ Q p , l  t     2    ∀ l ∈ L  ∀ t ∈ T     (5) A ∙ H  t  = - R Q  t  Q  t     0.852   - A 0  ∙ H 0  + A pumps   ∙ H p  t    ∀ t ∈ T     (6) H min  t  ≤ H  t  ≤ H max  t    ∀ t ∈ T     (7) n min  t  ≤ n p , l  t  ≤ n max  t    ∀ t ∈ T ∀ l ∈ L     (8) Q p , l  t  ≥ 0   ∀ t ∈ T ∀ l ∈ L     (9) H p , l  t  ≥ 0   ∀ t ∈ T ∀ l ∈ L     where: A  T    is the network's incidence matrix; n p , l  t    is the pump speed of pump l  ; n max     is the maximum pump speed [rpm]; H min     and H max     are vectors of the upper and lower head bounds at the nodes [m]; and n min     and n max     are the minimum and maximum pump rotation speeds, respectively. This formulation is novel in the sense that it allows formulating the problem as a non-linear program (NLP), instead of the well-known mixed-integer non-linear program (MINLP) formulation, as it is usually modelled in other studies found in the literature. The optimal operation problem of WDS is categorized as an MINLP, as it required the use of integer variables to correctly model the operation of pumps. When a pump is off, the result is a disconnection of a source from the network. In that case, (5) will require the inclusion of integer variables. When using variable speed pumps, modelling such a disconnection could be achieved without the use of integer variables. A pump will be considered off when pump flow is equal to zero. The pump rotation speed variable will then act as a free variable to adjust the head at the pump’s downstream node, virtually allowing the pump to function as a valve and regulate a virtual head gain along the pump. The inclusion of variable speed pumps allows formulating the problem as a continuous non-linear problem and helps avoid the employment of binary variables, although the inclusion of regular pumps (i.e., single speed pumps) would significantly reduce the solution space on one hand, while limiting the flexibility of the WDS design and operation on the other hand, which is essential for presenting the ability to adjust the WDS operation to the operation of the PG in this particular work. In this paper, the results of two different problems will be presented and compared: the first being an optimal design problem of an independent WDS, with its results imposed on the power grid as a given load; and the second being the conjunctive optimal design problem, when both systems are designed simultaneously. Here, both the objective function of the independent WDS design problem and the objective function of the conjunctive design problem will be presented. When formulating the independent design problem, energy tariffs were not considered for the operation of pumps. Those tariffs are usually the result of an optimization done by the PG operators. It was the authors’ goal to present a reasonable comparison between the solutions to the two design problems, and therefore the decision was made not to consider energy tariffs. This matter is addressed in more detail in the conclusion section. The objective function of the independent problem comprises of the cost of constructing all pumping stations and tanks in the system. In both examples, the same water and power demand patterns presented in Fig. 1 a, along with the solar generation profile in Fig. 1 b, were used. Tanks were assumed to have a constant cross-section area, and therefore the volume decision variable was replaced with the tank’s maximal level. An initial condition was set for the tanks to be full at the beginning of the system’s simulation. The model was coded using YALMIP optimization package through MATLAB, which is a MATLAB package that allows the straightforward formulation of optimization problems (YALMIP, 2023 ). Although the problem is quite complex, the examples presented below did not require any intervention in the solution process of the development of a solution strategy, and they were simply solved using IPOPT local solver, with a 64-bit Intel i7 4-core CPU at 2.00 GHz and 8-GB RAM. The optimization horizon was set to equal 24 h. However, since the problem is highly complex, timestep length was set to 3 h, resulting in a solution for 8 timesteps. 3.1 Illustrative example I Example I comprise of a four-node WDS, with one tank located at node 4 and one pump, which is supplied with power by a three-bus power grid that contains one conventional generator that is located at bus 1. The system layout is presented in Fig. 2  . The WDS and power grid attributes are given below in Table 2  . 3.1.1 Results The results of the base run are reported in Table 3  , and they are compared to the results of the optimal design of the independent WDS. Combining the two systems under one optimization model has an impact. The results show a difference in tank volume, with a slight difference in pumping capacity between the independent optimal design and the conjunctive optimal design. A drop in total cost is observed in the conjunctive approach compared to the independent one, with the most prominent reduced cost component being power generation cost. Evidently, allowing the construction of a solar generation field leads to a reduction in conventional generation, which translates directly into a reduction in generation cost, but is transformed into an investment in solar field construction. Nonetheless, the sum of solar field construction and conventional generation costs is still less than power generation costs in the independent design. The sustainable energy source encourages higher pumping capacity, which in result leads to a smaller tank size. This can be interpreted as a direct link between the type of power source to the optimal capacities of the different facilities inside the water system. Fig. 3   presents the WDS optimal operation policy derived from the obtained optimal design, including pump power demand (Fig. 3 a) and tank level (Fig. 3 b). The operational policies obtained in each of the considered problems seem quite similar (Fig. 3 a and 3b). The larger tank size obtained in the independent problem helps to slightly reduce pump power demand during the morning and noon, when both power and water demands peak. The tank volume is not fully utilized as a result of both the nodal head constraint, which is binding at 17:00 in node 2, and the closure constraint in Equation (3) , which forces the pump to operate in higher capacity to fill it and makes it less attractive to empty the tank. Fig. 4   compares the PG operation policies obtained by the independent and conjunctive optimal design problems. Depicted are the power generation quantities (Fig. 4 a and 4c) and voltage amplitudes at all buses of the PG (Fig. 4 b and 4d). It can be observed in Fig. 4 c that although the solar capacity is chosen to be 3.3 MW, the actual solar generation does not exceed 2 MW. As mentioned, the solar capacity variable is multiplied by the solar generation curve presented in Fig. 1 b to create the solar generation limit. Therefore, constructing a 3.3 MW capacity solar field will allow the system to generate enough solar power required during off-peak hours, such as morning and evening. As can be observed in Fig. 4 b the independent optimal design produces an infeasible solution from the standpoint of the power grid, as minimal voltage bound constraints cannot be satisfied. This result highlights the importance of the conjunctive approach and advocates for the consideration of intertwined systems when designing a water distribution system.  3.1.2 Sensitivity analysis To test the model and its validity, a sensitivity analysis comprising of 7 scenarios was conducted. This analysis was applied only to the conjunctive problem. In each of the scenarios, a slight modification was made to one of the parameters in the base run, as presented in Table 4  . The scenarios were designed to highlight different aspects of the problem and they way that they would influence it. The magnitudes of the modifications were set randomly. The results of the sensitivity analysis are presented in Fig. 5  , and include the tank volume (5a), pumping capacity (5b), solar capacity (5c) and objective value (5d). Widening the pipe diameters in scenario 1, demonstrating the effect of including pipe diameters in the optimization, is expected to lead to reduced power demand in the WDS, as the energy dissipation in pipes is reduced. We can observe that pumping capacity in fact reduces, along with tank volume, shrinking to 3,940, which is less than half the value obtained in the base run, and the smallest value out of all examined scenarios. Due to the system being of a small scale, the tank operates in tight coordination with the pump, and as pump head gain is reduced, so does tank level – being the two components that govern the distribution of energy in the system. As the conjunctive design problem is already quite complex, pipe diameters were omitted as decision variables, and it was the authors’ decision to concentrate on energy facilities in the WDS and PG. However, it should be mentioned here that the result of scenario 1 demonstrate the importance of including diameters in the design problem. Modifying water base demand, demonstrating a scenario of increased water demand by a factor of 1.2 due to population growth, results in the highest tank volume and pumping capacity out of all scenarios. To deal with the increase in water demand, a higher capacity pumping station must be constructed, along with a larger tank, to balance energy costs. No change is observed in solar capacity, leading to the conclusion that it is more expensive to increase the solar capacity than to conventionally generate the difference in power. This result means that a population growth that would lead to increased water demand is likely to not be translated in larger renewable energy capacity in the PG. Reducing base power demand in scenario 3 results in a slight reduction of tank volume and a slight rise in pump capacity. The most prominent effect of this modification is a reduction of approximately 700 kW in solar capacity and a drop in objective value. A similar trend is observed after reducing line impedance to 0.05j, to demonstrate the effect of including transmission line material in the optimization (equivalent to WDS pipe diameters), although in this case the drop in solar capacity is less prominent. Reducing the line impedance results in less power being lost along transmission lines, and in turn allows to generate less power to satisfy the demand. Reducing the strain on the power grid allows for larger quantities of power to flow to the pump, and a reduction in tank volume is observed as a result. This result emphasizes that an improved PG could significantly benefit the operation of the WDS and save costs in design. In scenario 5, a fourth water consumer is connected to the WDS by closing the loop 1–3-4, to demonstrate an expansion of the WDS. The total water consumption is kept as is, but is now equally split between the four consumers. A reduction in both tank size and pumping capacity is observed, with no change in solar capacity. A likely explanation for this result is that due to the additional pipes in the system, the distribution of flow leads to reduced longitudinal head loss, in a similar logic to the result of scenario 1. This result further advocates for the inclusion of pipe diameters as part of the optimization problem. Lowering service pressure to 20 m, to demonstrate a relaxation of pressure constraints, as done in scenario 6, seems to lead to the same trend – a reduction in tank size and pumping capacity, with no significant change in solar capacity. This result demonstrates the dominant influence that pressure constraints impose on the design and shows that results could significantly change based on the system’s scale and designation. The three scenarios addressing energy parameters in the WDS – scenarios 1, 5 and 6, all result in the lowest values of tank size and pumping power, with the same value of solar capacity as obtained in the base run. In scenario 7, reducing the cost of solar field construction to 0.004 MU per W to demonstrate the availability of a more efficient renewable energy source results in a steep rise in solar capacity, and a rise in pumping capacity as a result. We now obtain much higher tank size and pumping capacity compared to scenario 1, in which the objective value is the same. This result indicates how beneficial the development of cheaper and more efficient power sources can be, and their potential to improve WDS design.   3.2 Illustrative example II Example II is slightly more complex compared to Example I. It comprises of a nine-node WDS with 11 pipes, two tanks located in nodes 8 and 9, and two pumps placed on links 1 and 2. A 14-bus PG supplies the pumps with power, along with 6 other demand buses along the PG. Similar to example I, the PG includes one conventional generator located at bus 1, and a solar generation field to be constructed and connected to bus 2. The system layout is presented in Fig. 6  . The existence of multiple pumping stations and multiple tanks allows higher flexibility in the design and operation, which significantly enlarges the solution space and complexifies the problem. Furthermore, this would allow the examination of trade-offs between different zones inside the WDS, and will enable to observe how each of them is affected by the power grid. On the PG side, more power consumers and transmission lines result in a more complex optimal power flow problem, which would also influence the complexity of the conjunctive problem and help gain meaningful insights into the design of the joint system. The attributes of the WDS and the PG are given in Table 5  . In this example, the 24-hour optimization was divided into 3-hour long timesteps (meaning – a total of 8 timesteps), due to the complexity and difficulty of achieving a solution for a 24-timestep long optimization. Since the focus of this study is the optimal design of the two systems, the operational decisions can be grossly estimated with longer time steps that relax the computational challenge. 3.2.1 Results The solution of the conjunctive optimal design problem is brought in Table 6  , alongside a comparison to the solution of the independent optimal design problem. The two tanks and two pumps in the WDS seem to respond differently to the connection of the PG to the optimization problem. Compared to the results of the independent design problem, the size of tank 8 is reduced, while the size of tank 9 is slightly increased; the capacity of pump 1 is reduced, and the capacity of pump 2 is increased. This result reflects the effect of the system’s structure – as water demand is larger in the top area of the WDS, it would be more beneficial to invest in the construction of pump 2 and tank 9, which are located more adjacent to the center of demand. Another factor is the power grid itself – pump 1 is connected to bus 9, which lies further away from the generators in the power grid. Therefore, the voltage drop between the generators and bus 9 is more significant, which makes it less attractive to supply power to pump 1, and encourages the system to rely on pump 2, which is more adjacent to power generation components. This analysis is supported by Figs. 7 and 8   , which respectively show the WDS and PG operational policies obtained by the design, and compare the operation suggested by the independent solution and the conjunctive solution. The conjunctive solution seems to allow a more efficient operation of tank 9, emptying it completely twice a day (Fig. 7 d). Although we can observe that pump 2 is more dominant in the operation and operates at a higher capacity (Fig. 7 b), pump 2 is turned off during the night hours and pump 1 is responsible for filling the tanks to meet their closure constraint at the end of their operational cycle (Fig. 7 a). The same phenomenon that was presented in example I occurs here – the optimal design obtained for the WDS is not feasible from the PG standpoint, and a solar generator must be constructed to satisfy voltage magnitude constraints (Fig. 8 b and 8d). In this case, the conjunctive solution produces a more expensive solution compared to the solution of the independent problem. This result stems from the combination of the dominance of solar power generation inside the power grid and the voltage boundaries. In this case study, solar generation constitutes a smaller percentage out of the total power demand in the PG, and while it does reduce power generation costs quite dramatically, it is not able to reduce them to the point where the total cost is reduced below the independent solution total cost. Although not constructing a solar field at all is deemed a cheaper solution, voltage constraints cannot be satisfied this way, which forces its construction and creates a more expensive solution, which satisfies all constraints. In the independent solution, no generator is connected to bus 2 and therefore there is no power generation there (Fig. 8 a). As opposed to the results of example I, now we can observe that the solar capacity is exploited to its fullest, reaching the maximal value of 2.09 MW at 12:00 (Fig. 8 c).  3.2.2 Sensitivity analysis A more limited sensitivity analysis was performed to gain a slightly deeper insight into the interaction between the different components in this system. The examined scenarios are detailed in Table 7  . The results of the sensitivity analysis are shown in Fig. 9  . *BR – base run. Scenarios 1 and 2 examined the solution’s sensitivity to solar field construction cost. When solar field construction cost is reduced, we do not observe a significant change in results. When the cost increases, however, we see a reduction in the size of tank 8; an increase in size of tank 9; a reduction in pumping capacity of pump 1; and an increase in capacity of pump 2. This result validates the analysis that was previously presented, about the effects the different components have on the operation, and their relationship with the availability of sustainable power. We can also notice a 70-kW reduction in solar capacity, as a result of increased construction cost. The third scenario examines a different configuration of the system, where pump 2 is connected directly to bus 2, where the solar field is located. We obtained the same results as we did in scenario 2 but are now able to operate with a much smaller solar field. This result demonstrates the magnitude of the influence that both the voltage constraints and the loss of power along transmission lines have on the optimal solution.    4 Conclusion This paper presents the novel concept of conjunctively optimizing the design of a water distribution system and a power grid. The optimization problem is formulated such that the decision variables are storage and pumping capacities on the WDS side, and solar generation capacity on the power grid side. The conjunctive problem comprises of all constraints forming each of the two independent design problems, and the two systems are linked through the WDS’s pump power demand. The concept is applied to two illustrative examples. The results of the conjunctive optimal design problems are compared to the results of the optimal design of the independent WDS, and the impact of the connection of the power grid to the WDS optimal design problem is noticeable. The inclusion of voltage constraints in the problem reveals the inability of the power grid to operate under the independent WDS optimal design requirements and forces the connection of the grid to a sustainable power source. The availability of a sustainable power source in the system influences the design of storage and pumping components in the WDS, favoring the upgrading of pumping stations at the expense of storage volume – a somewhat counterintuitive result that advocates for the importance of the conjunctive approach. The examination of two illustrative examples casts light on the complexity of the problem and the inner mechanisms that are at play. Analyzing the results of example I could be considered a simple task, since the system includes only one tank and one pump, but as the system is of a slightly larger scale the relationship between components can become quite complex, even when looking at a relatively small system such as the one brought as example II. The different components respond differently to the connection of a sustainable source to the system, based on their adjacency to demand nodes and their connections to the power grid. The PG configuration favors the employment pumps located in the proximity of generation epicenters. Storage facility volumes inside the WDS are in turn affected by this based on their proximity to pumps, as they must operate in coordination with pump head gains. Regarding the cost, no clear trend was observed, as the conjunctive approach is able to reduce cost for example I but is not able to do the same for example II. As power generation is the most dominant component in the objective, it is evident that the dominance of the renewable energy source inside the power grid is responsible for the ability to reduce the total cost. Approximating the dominance of a renewable energy source in the PG is therefore a step that should be taken before the application of this conjunctive model, in order to assess whether total cost could be reduced. A sensitivity analysis that was performed helped establish and validate the obtained results, and to also gain novel insights into the optimality of the obtained solution. It was observed that pipe diameters, along with transmission lines, could be very significant decision variables in this problem, and their inclusion could provide more deep and interesting insight. An issue that required the authors’ attention is the basis for comparison between the independent design and the conjunctive design. Usually, the operation of WDS takes into consideration energy tariffs for pumps. Those tariffs are imposed on the WDS by the PG operators. Since the design and operation of the PG are also being solved as part of the conjunctive approach, the incorporation of those energy tariffs in the conjunctive problem would defeat the purpose of this work – here, the model is intended to be solved all at once, simultaneously, rather than in stages (optimizing the design and operation of the PG, obtaining energy tariffs for the WDS, and then optimizing the operation of the WDS with respect to the obtained tariffs), in order to utilize the interdependency between the systems.. In this work, we resolved this matter by assuming that a single operator oversees the operation of both the WDS and the PG. This assumption allows to neglect pump energy tariffs and only consider power generation costs from the standpoint of the PG. Although it is rarely the case in reality, it does allow us to present a relatively beneficial comparison in this work. Another option could be performing a calculation of energy tariffs in a dynamic way, during the optimization. This option is much more complex. It requires a focus on the methods that are used for the determination of energy tariffs by PG operators and regarded by the authors as out of the scope of this paper. That said, the incorporation of energy tariffs does require more attention and poses a significant challenge that could be the focus for future work. The optimization problem presented here is solved by IPOPT, an off-the-shelf non-linear solver. As the networks get more complex, the process of obtaining a solution this way would get more difficult, and at some point, perhaps impractical. Nonetheless, applying this conjunctive approach to case studies of a larger scale will help better understand the magnitude of their interdependency on optimal design of such systems, and is imperative for advancing the field of infrastructure operation and management. An additional work that’s currently being carried out is the development of a tailored solution method, that would allow the application of the conjunctive approach to larger case studies, and will shed light on new insights with respect to the scale of the problem. As mentioned throughout this manuscript, the work presented here constitutes a first step in the direction of a more holistic approach for water distribution systems analysis, specifically with a focus on their relationship with the power grid. There are several suggestions that could be of use for future work that would expand the idea that was brought here. Widening the range of decision variables, to include pipe diameters, transmission line materials and even batteries for power storage in the power grid side would significantly complexify the problem, and is likely to generate rich insight into the interdependencies between the systems. The addition of decision variables is also likely to require more sophisticated and computationally complex solution approach, such as branch and bound, decomposition techniques like outer approximation (OA), heuristics or sequential quadratic programming (SQP).Testing the model on a much larger scale systems is an interesting direction as well, which will require a closer look at the problem formulation in order to develop new and tailored solution methods. The development of such methods could be another research direction in and of itself, to allow for a more suitable optimization approach and provide robustness to the optimization process. In pursuing any of these directions, different objectives could be considered such as robustness, resilience or even water quality standards. A multi-objective problem could be tackled, and the competition between those different objective functions could be presented as a pareto front, to demonstrate the limitations of the conjunctive approach. Different aspects of uncertainty could also be examined, using different methods to solve the operation part of the problem in a more realistic way, such as robust optimization, folding horizon and predictive control models. 1 Introduction In the application of practical engineering problems across numerous fields, challenges related to multi-objective dynamic optimization and complex constraints are prevalent (Liu et al., 2023 ). Traditional static multi-objective optimization methods fall short in meeting the comprehensive needs of such issues (Liu and Luo, 2019; Yu et al., 2023 ). Taking the reservoir operation issue as an example, it generally involves a combination of conflicting objectives such as comprehensive consideration of disaster prevention needs as flood control, drought relief, and maximizing the utilization of beneficial resources like power generation and water supply, all while operating within complex constraints related to reservoir capacity, outflow, and ecological considerations (Zhang et al., 2020; Dash et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024 ). Additionally, the multi-objective couplings in reservoir operation models and the complex operational conditions associated with environmental attributes and decision preferences dynamically change with the operational period and environmental variations (Dalcin et al., 2023 ). The operation approach effective at one moment may not meet the demands of the current operational state. Reservoir operation plans need to adapt based on the latest environmental information to achieve optimal allocation of water resources across multiple objectives (Li et al., 2021 ). Consequently, dynamic multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (DMOEAs) have emerged in response to the characteristics of dynamic multi-objective optimization problems (DMOPs) that are closely linked to the changes of time and environment (Yang et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023 ). The dynamic response strategies of DMOEAs can quickly monitor and identify changes in direction and magnitude when environmental changes occur, guiding populations to evolve in new directions by adjusting optimization strategies in real-time (Bai et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023a ). Static optimization strategies, in contrast, can quickly track the optimal solution set corresponding to the current environmental conditions when no changes occur, thus continuously and efficiently finding the best solutions that meet the operational conditions under dynamically changing environments (Guo et al., 2023 ). DMOEAs also adapt to dynamic changes in objective sets and constraints, forming relatively stable trends in Pareto Front (PF) and Pareto Set (PS) as the environment changes (Zheng et al., 2023b ). The strategies for handling dynamic changes in DMOEAs can primarily be categorized as follows (Wang et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2023 ): memory methods archive historical solutions to better respond to cyclical environmental changes, diversity methods preserve population diversity to more accurately reflect the true nature of MOPs, predictive methods use prediction mechanisms to make timely strategy adjustments to environmental changes, and the combined use of various mechanisms effectively balances population diversity and convergence, deeply exploring and promptly responding to cyclical environmental changes (Coello et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2022; Gee et al., 2017 ). However, DMOPs vary in characteristics and decision preferences across different research fields, thus the optimization models based on DMOEA require further in-depth discussion tailored to specific domain applications (Wu et al., 2022 ). Taking the operation control strategies of reservoirs during the flood season as an example, reservoir operation control methods of flood season have evolved through three developmental stages: single fixed water level control, staged fixed water level control, and dynamic operation water level control (Zhu et al., 2022 ). Single fixed water level control methods define the highest water levels during the flood season based on flood control limits or flood restriction levels (Jain et al., 2023 ). However, influenced by extreme climate changes and human activities, actual inflow conditions can significantly differ from the design conditions (Wang et al., 2019 ). For instance, in dry years, if the reservoir operates under single fixed water level control without encountering floods, it could lead to substantial wastage of flood resources, adversely affecting power generation benefits and increasing the difficulty of subsequent water storage and safe operation of the reservoir. With advances in hydrological forecasting and operation technology, reservoir management has adopted staged fixed water level control considering the sequence of floods to enhance resource utilization (Shao and Jin, 2021 ). However, this method does not utilize flood forecasting information, leading to difficulties in flood discharge and water storage during the flood season, severely impairing water resource allocation benefits. On the other hand, aiming to ensure flood control safety, dynamic water level control is to scientifically adjust control indicators like operating water level, risk prevention, flood control and water storage based on forecast information and decision-making results. This method can flexibly respond to actual water conditions, effectively utilize water resources, improve power generation efficiency, and simplify the water storage process to meet social, economic and ecological needs (Pan et al., 2022 ). Current research on dynamic water level control of flood season mainly focuses on constructing multi-objective operation models by considering different key factors such as channel storage capacity, forecast deviation, capacity compensation, and predicted hydrological variables, and solving the problems with static multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and research theories like aggregation-decomposition methods, credibility theories and forecasting techniques (Reddy and Kumar, 2006; Jiang et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2022 ). Although numerous dynamic control methods for reservoir multi-objective operation water levels of flood season based on diverse optimization strategies have been proposed, research predominantly focuses on static multi-objective algorithms and operation optimization models (Sharifi et al., 2022; Mu et al., 2022 ). Relying solely on input training data for decision-making, these approaches overlook the dynamic variability of decision variables and external environments, potentially leading to significant deviations between optimization results and actual conditions. Therefore, effectively improving forecast accuracy, accurately identifying environmental changes, promptly matching decision preferences, significantly reducing operational risks, and appropriately determining operation models to achieve decisions suitable for dynamically changing scenarios are urgent issues in research on dynamic control water levels of flood season. To address these issues, this paper targets power generation, flood control and water supply benefits, bases its strategies on risk prevention, and uses a risk rate calculation method based on dynamic anticipation period and multiple models forecasting to analyze the interrelationships in reservoir flood season water level control. It establishes a dynamic control operation model for reservoir water levels of flood season and proposes a dynamic multi-objective multi-strategy co-evolution (DMMC) algorithm which can quickly adapt to environmental changes through strategies such as memory individual optimal adaptation strategy, diverse individuals dynamic updating strategy and forecast individual collaborative updating strategy, providing technical support for dynamic control of flood season water levels. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2  elucidates the basic concepts of DMOP and constructs a dynamic multi-objective optimization operation model, including operation objectives, related constraints, and model construction. Section 3  details the strategies of DMMC algorithm. Section 4  evaluates the performance of the DMMC algorithm through benchmark functions, proving its effectiveness. Section 5  applies DMMC to solve real-world reservoir operation optimization problems established. Finally, Section 6  presents the conclusions and suggestions for future research.  2 Dynamic multi-objective operation optimization model This section introduces the definition and classification of DMOPs, matches the befitting classification of dynamic control problem about reservoir water level during flood season. Consequently, a multi-objective operation optimization model for dynamically controlling reservoir water levels in evolving flood season environments. 2.1 Dynamic multi-objective optimization problems (DMOPs) Dynamic multi-objective optimization problems (DMOPs) refer to multi-objective optimization issues where components such as objective functions, constraints, and decision variables undergo dynamic uncertainties due to changes over scheduling phase or environmental conditions (Yang et al., 2023 ). DMOPs are characterized by uncertainties in the problems, conflicts among multiple objective and variability in the decision-making process, all of these characteristics significantly increase the difficulty of optimizing solutions (Liu and Luo, 2019 ). To illustrate, consider a problem aiming to minimize a dynamic multi-objective optimization issue, which can be mathematically described as follows:(1) min  y = F ( x , t )  = f 1  ( x , t )  , f 2  ( x , t )  , ⋯ , f M  ( x , t )          s  .t .      g j  ( x , t )  ⩽ 0 , j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , J       h k  ( x , t )  = 0 , k = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , K            Where, x  denotes the decision variables; f  is the objective function of x  at time t ; g  and ℎ respectively represent sets of inequality and equality constraints; t  denotes the time or environment variable; M  represents the number of objectives in the problem. Moreover, multi-objective optimization problems involve four fundamental concepts: Dynamic Pareto dominance, dynamic Pareto optimal solution, dynamic Pareto optimal front, and dynamic Pareto optimal set. (1) Dynamic Pareto Dominance : Let p  and q  be any two individuals in the population. p  is said to dominate q  if and only if it satisfies Eq. (5) .(5) PS ( t )  ∗  = x i ∗  | ¬ ∃ f  x j  , t     ≺ f x i ∗  , t     , f x j  , t     ∈ F M           Farina et al. categorized dynamic multi-objective optimization problems based on the changes over time of the optimal Pareto Front (PF) and the optimal Pareto Set (PS) into the following four types (Farina et al., 2004 ): Type I: The optimal P S ∗     changes over time, while the optimal P F ∗     remains unchanged; Type II: Both the optimal P S ∗     and P F ∗     change over time; Type III: The optimal P S ∗     remains unchanged, while the optimal P F ∗     changes over time; Type IV: Neither the optimal P S ∗     nor the optimal P F ∗     changes over time, but the objective functions or constraints change over time. Considering the fluctuation and uncertainty of runoff forecast and storage changes caused by environmental changes like the alternation of rainy and dry seasons, torrential rains and floods, high temperatures and droughts, as well as the prominent needs for decision-making preferences in water supply, power generation, and ecology, the objective functions and constraints of the dynamic multi-objective optimization problem for reservoir water level control of flood season change with time and environmental conditions. Based on the hydrological conditions and social demands at different periods, the dynamic strategy for seeking optimal solutions for reservoir water level control of flood season most closely aligns with Type II (as shown in Fig. 1  ), meaning both the optimal P F ∗     and P S ∗     change with time and external environmental changes.  2.2 Objective functions Dynamic control of reservoir water levels during the flood season is an important method aimed at the integrated utilization of floodwater resources, without compromising existing flood control standards (Li et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2014 ). From the perspective of flood control, within the runoff forecast period (t 0  ≤ t  ≤ Ty  ), when facing various operational scenarios, the goal is to minimize the maximum flow at the downstream flood control sections under the condition of ensuring safe release volumes and reservoir safety, which minimizes the impact of peak flood flows. From the perspective of maximizing the utilization of flood resources, the principle of maximum power generation and water supply in the reservoir during the safe operation of floods is followed to meet the needs of social development for energy and water resources. (1) Objective 1: Maximize the power generation To achieve the goal of maximizing the benefits from water resource-based power generation, enhance hydroelectric power output, and fully meet the power supply demands and sustainably use energy resources, this objective is expressed as follows:(6) max  E t    =  ∑ t = 1  t + T y    P t  · Δ t  ,    P t  = A · Q t  · H t      E    is the total power generation. t    represents the period of environmental change, which is consistent with the actual scheduling period. T y     is forecast lead time. P t    , Q t     and H t     are the power output, generation flow and hydraulic head of t -th period. A    is the power coefficient of reservoir. (2) Objective 2: Minimum peak flow To reduce the operational pressure of flood regulation during the flood season, the aim within the flood forecast period is to minimize the maximum flow at the downstream flood control sections as much as possible, thereby smoothing the flood peak process and reducing the impact of peak flows on downstream areas. (3) Objective 3: Maximizing water supply To achieve the maximum possible water supply from the reservoir, it is necessary to dynamically control the reservoir’s water supply capability and storage capacity during the operation period, thus maximizing the utilization of water resources to meet water supply needs. The model processing mechanism mainly includes runoff forecast series acquisition, dynamic risk assessment, and decision scheme dynamic response, as illustrated in Fig. 2  . 2.4.1 Runoff forecast series acquisition based on multivariate forecast models and random simulation with feature configuration Deep learning forecasting models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with Attention Mechanism are used to obtain multiple models' runoff forecast data P  based on precipitation forecast data. The first step involves processing the runoff forecast data P  from multiple models using a weighted average to obtain the future inflow data I P t     for the optimization operation model. Subsequently, the runoff forecast data P  from multiple models are integrated and ordered to determine the forecasted inflow runoff interval. Lastly, a feature configuration random simulation method is employed within the forecast interval to generate a large number of random forecasted runoff sequences R . The results of the risk assessments are then used as risk constraints. Based on the current water levels of the reservoir, dynamic risk thresholds are set. If these thresholds are exceeded, the operation plan is discarded; if not, the plan is deemed feasible. The specific process is as follows:Risk within the forecast lead time: If there are NR  sets of random simulated forecast results R , and in the n -th operation plan (N  being the set of operation plans), if NR1n   sets of data exceed the upper and lower threshold limits of reservoir water levels allowed by the operation model constraints, it is considered that these NR1n   sets of data pose a risk within the forecast lead time Ty  . The risk rate for the operation plan within the forecast lead time is denoted as R1n  . Machine learning is used to match the results of random runoff forecasts obtained from previous forecast models with those in the forecast database. The matched forecast results are used to extract historical forecast data for twice the length of the forecast period. For the NR  sets of randomly simulated data, if NR2n   sets exceed the permissible upper and lower limits of reservoir water levels in the n -th operation plan, it is determined that these NR2n   sets pose a risk within twice the forecast lead time, 2Ty  .
