Environmental DNA (eDNA) provides comprehensive opportunities for biodiversity assessments (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023a ). Numerous studies indicate that 18S rDNA sequencing technology surpasses alternative primers and traditional microscopy in capturing the composition and diversity of plankton in aquatic ecosystems (Zhang et al., 2023b ). Our study examined the mainstream and 16 first-order tributaries of the upper Hanjiang River, as well as the mainstream and six first-order tributaries of the Danjiang River. We collected 187 samples across 22 tributaries and two mainstreams. This study addresses the following questions: (1) How do spatiotemporal variation patterns in plankton communities evolve within large-scale mountain river ecosystems, and how do environmental factors and geographical characteristics influence these patterns? (2) What are the assembly mechanisms underlying plankton community dynamics from upstream to downstream? (3) How does community stability vary across the river continuum? Here, we hypothesized that hydro-morphology could significantly influence the spatial variation patterns of plankton from upstream to downstream.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study region and sample sites This study was conducted in the Danjiang River and the upper Hanjiang River (Fig. 1  ). This region covers an area of 3 × 105  km2 , spanning from 33◦ 42′N,106◦ 18′E to 37◦ 20′N,110◦ 37′E, including Shaanxi, Gansu, Henan, Sichuan, Chongqing, and Hubei provinces (Chen et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2017 ). It represents a typical subtropical monsoon climate zone. This area was chosen due to its unique environmental pressures and spatially varying hydro-morphological gradients. For instance, the upstream reaches exhibit lower land use intensity and superior ecological conditions compared to the midstream and downstream reaches (Liu et al., 2024b ). Moreover, notable hydro-morphological differences exist between upstream and downstream reaches (Liu et al., 2024b ). In the present study, the watershed of the upper Hanjiang River spans 68,739 km2 , significantly larger than the 17,300 km2  watershed of the Danjiang River. The upper Hanjiang River basin also receives higher precipitation, has a more complex river network, and boasts more tributaries with substantial water resources. To ensure representative results, we selected twice as many tributaries in the upper Hanjiang River compared to the Danjiang River. Our study examined the mainstream and 16 primary tributaries of the upper Hanjiang River and the mainstream and six primary tributaries of the Danjiang River. A total of 187 samples were collected from 22 tributaries and two mainstreams. One representative site was selected for sample collection in each tributary's upper, middle, and lower reaches, while 25 sites were deployed in the mainstream (Fig. 1 a-d). The sampling sites were strategically arranged to capture the hierarchical structure of the dendritic river system. The field samples were collected in March and August 2023.  2.2 Water quality and hydro-morphology Water samples were collected at each river site, with three 1-liter samples stored in sterile bottles in a car refrigerator at 4°C. Within 12 h, one liter of water from each site was filtered through a 0.22 μm polycarbonate membrane filter (47 mm diameter, Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) using an oil-free portable diaphragm vacuum pump. The filtered membranes were then collected in sterile centrifuge tubes and frozen at −80°C until DNA extraction. Water quality properties, including pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), water temperature (WT), salinity (PSU), and oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), were measured using a multiparameter water quality analyzer (Hydrolab HL7, HACH, USA). The samples were collected and analyzed in triplicate at all monitoring sites. Afterward, they were stored in a car refrigerator at 4°C and protected from light during transportation to the laboratory for further analysis. Total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), nitrate nitrogen (NO3 – -N), nitrite nitrogen (NO2 – -N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4 + -N) were analyzed following Han et al. (2024) . DOC was measured using a total organic carbon analyzer (Shimadzu, TOC-L, Japan), and humification index (HIX) was analyzed by a fluorescence spectrometer (RF-6000; Shimadzu). River width was measured with a laser range finder (TruPulse 200; Laser Tech Inc., CO, USA) and flow velocity was determined using a portable flow meter (MGG/KL-DCB). Climatic data for all sampling sites were obtained from the WorldClim database (https://www.worldclim.org). Land use parameters for each site were calculated using a 30-meter resolution land use raster map derived from Landsat 8 remote sensing imagery, within a buffer zone extending up to a 5-kilometer radius upstream. Five types of land use were identified: forest, grassland, agricultural land, shrubland, and urbanization. The 5-km buffer radius was chosen because human activities within this range significantly impact aquatic communities (Li et al., 2023b ). Radius buffers were selected instead of equidistant stream corridors because streams within river systems are naturally connected. This connectivity means multiple ecological disturbances can have significant cumulative impacts. Therefore, the stream networks of the upstream sub-basins were considered to assess the localized effect of land use on plankton communities. Basic water quality and hydro-morphological data from upstream to downstream can be found in Tables S3-S4.  2.3 DNA extraction, PCR, and high throughput sequencing DNA of each water sample was isolated using a Qiagen Power Water DNA isolation kit, following the manufacturer's protocol. Agarose gel electrophoresis was performed at a 1% concentration to verify DNA extraction. DNA quality was assessed using a NanoDrop ND-1000 Spectrophotometer. To amplify the 18S rRNA V9 region, primers 1380F (TCCCTGCCHTTTGTACACAC) and 1510R (CCTTCYGCAGGTTCACCTAC) were utilized (Amaral-Zettler et al., 2009 ). PCR amplification and sequencing procedures were followed previously established methods (Zhao et al., 2022 ). Reads with an average Phred score below 20, ambiguous nucleotides, homopolymers exceeding six units, or primer mismatches were excluded (Bokulich et al., 2013 ). Subsequently, the remaining high-quality reads were linked to their respective samples through unique barcodes on the reverse primers. These sequences were then classified into amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) using the Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm 2 (DADA2) within the QIIME2 framework (Bokulich et al., 2018 ). ASVs appearing only once (singletons) were discarded to enhance data analysis efficiency. Taxonomic classification of the ASVs was conducted using the QIIME2 software, utilizing the SILVA 138 database for reference (Yilmaz et al., 2014 ). ASVs identified as plankton were categorized separately with a custom R script, and their taxonomic classification at the phylum level was reassigned. Finally abundance tables for phytoplankton and zooplankton ASVs were standardized across samples by normalizing to the minimum observed read count (11,078 for phytoplankton and 5,102 for zooplankton).  2.4 Statistical analyses The “vegan” package was used to calculate plankton community richness and assess compositional differences using Bray-Curtis distance-based principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) and the Adonis test. Alpha diversity indices and community distances between upstream and downstream samples were analyzed using the Student's t -test (t.test function). Seasonal variations in the relative abundances of plankton taxa were analyzed using the Wilcox rank-sum test (wilcox.test function). An aggregated boosted tree (ABT) analysis was conducted to measure the impact of hydro-morphology and water quality on the richness and community composition of plankton, utilizing the “gbmplus” package with 500 trees for the boosting process (De'Ath, 2007 ). The envfit function in the “vegan” package was used to examine the relationships between environmental factors and plankton community structures, and then canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was performed. The Euclidean distances for environmental variables and geographic distances were determined between pairs of sampling sites. Subsequently, a linear regression analysis was conducted to assess the distance-decay relationships in the plankton community similarities. Additionally, to quantify the relative importance of environmental and geographic factors in shaping plankton structure, variation partitioning analysis (VPA) was performed using the “rdacca.hp” package. Furthermore, the potential significance of stochastic processes in community assembly was investigated using a neutral community model (NCM), where the m value estimates inter-community dispersal, and the R-squared value quantifies the contribution of stochastic processes (Sloan et al., 2006 ). Niche breadth and dispersal ability are crucial factors influencing the impact of environmental selection and passive dispersal mechanisms on community dynamics (De Bie et al., 2012 ). The niche breadth of plankton communities was quantified using Levins' niche breadth index via the “spaa” package. The average B-values for all taxa within a community (Bcom) were used to measure habitat niche breadth at the community level, suggesting that a broader niche breadth indicates greater metabolic flexibility (Pandit et al., 2009 ). To assess the dispersal ability of each taxon, which is influenced by water movements, the pairwise shared proportion of sequence numbers was calculated. The average shared proportion was used to represent dispersal effectiveness. A higher shared proportion of sequences indicates more efficient passive transport through currents (Yeh et al., 2015 ). A Student's t -test was applied to compare the niche breadth and dispersal abilities of plankton communities. Samples collected in the same season were aggregated to form a co-occurrence network for seasonal comparison. Subsequently, samples collected from the same reaches in the same season were aggregated to form eight co-occurrence networks. The number of samples used to construct these networks was highly similar across different reaches. In April, the sample counts were: upstream 23, midstream 23, downstream 24, and mainstem 24. In August, the counts were: upstream 23, midstream 24, downstream 23, and mainstem 23. Networks were constructed using robust correlations with Spearman's correlation coefficients (ρ) > 0.6 or <  − 0.6 and p-values < 0.001, which was a standard threshold significant in both mathematical and biological contexts (Jiao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022b ). Network topological properties were analyzed using the “igraph” package (Jiao et al., 2022 ). The robustness and vulnerability were calculated to evaluate plankton network stability under different hydrological conditions. The robustness was simulated when 50% of the nodes were randomly removed. The vulnerability represents the maximum decrease in network efficiency caused by removing a single node (Yuan et al., 2021 ). In addition, the absolute value of negative:positive cohesion was calculated according to Hernandez et al. (2021) . Structural equation modeling (SEM) was utilized to examine the direct and indirect influences of prominent environmental variables on plankton communities and network stability. Before modeling, data underwent normality testing and a logarithmic transformation of all environmental factors. SEM analyses were conducted using AMOS 20.0 (AMOS IBM, USA). Furthermore, standardized effect sizes were calculated to assist in interpreting the SEM results.   3 Results 3.1 Spatiotemporal variation and environmental drivers of plankton communities 3.1.1 Plankton community composition The sequencing of 18S ribosomal RNA amplicons from 187 water samples yielded 15,807,739 reads, which were clustered into 340,932 high-quality Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs). The rarefaction curves for the 187 samples across two seasons showed saturation, indicating sufficient sequencing data (Fig. S1 ). All ASVs from phytoplankton and zooplankton were successfully annotated at the phylum and lineage levels, respectively (Fig. S2 ). A total of nine phyla of phytoplankton were identified, including Chlorophyta, Bacillariophyta, Cryptophyta, Glaucophyta, Chrysophyta, Pyrrophyta, Xanthophyta, Euglenophyta, and Rhodophyta (Fig. S3 , Fig. 2  a). Zooplankton composition analysis revealed twenty-five lineages, mainly comprising Ciliophora, Copepoda, Amoebozoa, Rhizopoda, and Apicomplexa (Fig. S4 , Fig. 2 b). Our results revealed significant seasonal differences in relative abundance (Fig. 2 c-d, Fig. S11 ): Bacillariophyta, Chrysophyta, and Xanthophyta were more abundant in March, while Chlorophyta, Glaucophyta, and Euglenophyta showed higher levels in August. Copepoda showed significantly higher abundance in March for both plankton communities; however, lineages such as Ciliophora, Apicomplexa, and Chonaoflagellida were more abundant in August. From upstream to downstream, Bacillariophyta significantly decreased from 37.12% to 33.07% in March (p < 0.05) and from 27.68% to 25.36% in August (p < 0.05). Euglenophyta significantly decreased from 1.04% to 0.53% in March (p < 0.01) and 10.48% to 2.16% in August (p < 0.001). Cryptophyta significantly increased from 17.43% to 25.78% in March (p < 0.001) and 9.18% to 17.95% in August (p < 0.001). Pyrrophyta significantly decreased from 5.83% to 3.44% in March (p < 0.01) and increased from 4.63% to 14.62% in August (p < 0.01). Chlorophyta and Chrysophyta remained relatively stable throughout the gradient, particularly in August. Ciliophora significantly increased from 67.17% to 85.04% in August (p < 0.001). Copepoda significantly increased from 13.43% to 20.24% in March (p < 0.001) and 5.76% to 7.18% in August (p < 0.05). Amoebozoa significantly decreased from 12.18% to 8.26% in March (p < 0.05) and 14.53% to 4.70% in August (p < 0.01). These results indicated significant differences in plankton community compositions at different geographical locations of the river.  3.1.2 The α-diversity of plankton in response to environmental factors Fig. 3  a showed that a consistent pattern between the diversity of phytoplankton and zooplankton, suggesting that increased richness in phytoplankton corresponded to higher richness in zooplankton. The ABT results showed that HIX, water temperature, pH, NO3 – -N, NH4 + -N, and DO were the primary drivers explaining variation in phytoplankton richness (Fig. 3 b). Conversely, for zooplankton, HIX, water temperature, NH4 + -N, pH, river width, and ORP emerged as the main factors elucidating variability in zooplankton richness.  3.1.3 The β-diversity of plankton in response to environmental factors Our findings revealed that both zooplankton and phytoplankton exhibited smaller within-group differences in August compared to March, indicating higher taxonomic diversity across different river reaches during the March (Fig. 4  a). Additionally, significant disparities between plankton were observed in both March and August (Fig. S5 , Fig. S6 ). Water temperature, HIX, elevation, and ORP were the primary drivers of phytoplankton composition variation (Fig. 4 b-c, Table S1 , Table S2 ). Similarly, the variation in zooplankton community composition could be explained mainly by water temperature, HIX, pH, river width, and ORP. The main environmental drivers of zooplankton and phytoplankton community composition were similar, playing a crucial role in explaining plankton richness. Fig. 4 c showed that the sample clusters of upstream, midstream, and downstream plankton communities were disassembled by spatial location of rivers. This phenomenon implied that plankton communities are shaped by distinct river reaches through hydro-morphological variations and nutrient dynamics.   3.2 Plankton community assembly processes 3.2.1 Distance decay relationships The DDRs results (Fig. 5  a) revealed that neither phytoplankton nor zooplankton showed significant environment-based distance-decay patterns during March. However, such a pattern was observed in August, with a more substantial effect on zooplankton than on phytoplankton. There was a significant relationship between phytoplankton and zooplankton in both seasons regarding the geographic-based distance-decay pattern. Still, the decay with increasing distance was significantly more pronounced in August than in March. Importantly, our results demonstrated that the explanatory rate and correlation of the environmental distance-based decay model were higher than those of the geographic distance-based model for both zooplankton and phytoplankton.  3.2.2 Relative contribution of deterministic and stochastic processes Furthermore, the hierarchical partitioning results revealed that geographic factors accounted for 63.68% of the variation in March phytoplankton, 63.03% in August phytoplankton, 63.34% in March zooplankton, and 62.79% in August zooplankton (Fig. 5 b). Geographic factors were significant determinants of variations in community of both plankton groups in both seasons. However, the influence of environmental factors became more pronounced in August. Therefore, the relationship between plankton based on an environmental distance-decay pattern was not significant in March, but it became significant in August. In March, NCM accounted for 63.0% and 47.4% of the variation in zooplankton and phytoplankton communities, respectively. In August, it explained 66.11% and 49.5% of the variations in these communities, respectively (Fig. 5 c). Notably, the explanatory rate of NCM was lower for zooplankton than for phytoplankton in both March and August. A similar trend was also observed through m-values. Passive dispersal rates showed that phytoplankton had significantly higher dispersal ability than zooplankton in both seasons (Fig. 5 d). Moreover, phytoplankton had a greater ecological niche width than zooplankton, indicating stronger adaptability to environmental conditions (Fig. 5 d). Furthermore, the niche breadth was higher in March compared to August for both plankton communities, suggesting higher ecological pressure in August than March. The explanatory rate of phytoplankton NCM (Table 1  ) varied across upstream (35.4%), midstream (47.7%), downstream (44.6%), and mainstream (50.9%) in March, while it ranged from 47.7% to 56.5% in August. The explanatory rates of the zooplankton community in March were 19.6%, 17.6%, 23.6%, and 27% for the upstream, midstream, downstream, and mainstream reaches, respectively. In August, these rates were 19.8%, 30.6%, 20.2%, and 32.8%, respectively. Our findings suggested that, except downstream of the zooplankton, the explanatory rate of the NCM model was generally higher in August compared to March. Consequently, both plankton groups exhibited stronger stochastic processes in August across these river reaches. The comparison of m-values further revealed a significant increase in August compared to March across different river reaches, indicating higher plankton dispersal ability in August. The explanatory rate of zooplankton NCM was significantly lower than that of phytoplankton across various river reaches, and the m-values consistently supported this finding.   3.3 Stability of plankton communities and their major environmental drivers 3.3.1 Co-occurrence networks of plankton Notable differences in node degree and distribution patterns among taxa were found in the networks between March and August (Fig. 6  a). Specifically, Cryptophyta had higher connectivity than other taxa in the March network, forming a relatively extensive aggregation with Ciliophora (Fig. 6 a-b). Although Bacillariophyta were not central or highly connected in the network, they were evenly dispersed across different regions, highlighting their crucial role in maintaining stability. Conversely, in August, Chlorophyta and Ciliophora occupied intermediate positions within the network, exhibiting significantly higher connectivity compared to other taxa (Fig. 6 a-b). The mutualistic interaction between Chlorophyta and Ciliophora was crucial for maintaining stability in phytoplankton-zooplankton networks during August. Additionally, the even dispersion of Ciliophora throughout the August co-occurrence network implied that its potential to regulate other phytoplankton through top-down control mechanisms, thus preserving overall ecological stability. As a result, Ciliophora was crucial for both plankton communities. Furthermore, the degree values were higher in August than March (Fig. 6 b). However, the heterogeneity in degree values among different river reaches was more pronounced in March. In August, the degree value in the mainstream significantly surpassed those in other reaches. Betweenness centrality also exhibited a general increase in August compared to March. Finally, closeness centrality showed higher values in March than in August. The cohesion of the plankton co-occurrence network was significantly higher in March than in August (Fig. 6 c), while robustness showed a slight increase in March compared to August. Additionally, the vulnerability was significantly lower in March than in August. These findings highlight the impact of hydrology on the stability of plankton networks. The stability of plankton networks was significantly higher in the midstream and upstream reaches compared to the downstream and mainstream reaches in March. In August, the stability of these networks in the midstream and upstream reaches was also significantly higher than in the downstream reaches, but this pattern reversed for the mainstream. The stability of the mainstream in August was higher compared to other river reaches. Further comparison of network stability differences between seasons in the same river reach revealed no significant difference in cohesion in the upstream reach. However, cohesion was significantly higher in March than in August in the midstream reaches, while in the downstream and mainstream reaches, it was significantly higher in August than in March. Vulnerability followed a similar pattern.  3.3.2 Effects of hydro-morphology and water quality on plankton stability Hydro-morphological and nutrient factors explained 57% of the variation in Bacillariophyta, 81% in Chlorophyta, 22% in Cryptophyta, 77% in Chrysophyta, 70% in Pyrrophyta, and 58% in Euglenophyta (Fig. 7  a, Fig. S9 , a priori model). These factors implied significant impacts on the community compositions of diverse plankton phyla or lineages (Fig. S7 , Fig. S8 ). Water temperature and nutrients positively influenced plankton communities across phyla, whereas hydro-morphological factors such as river width and agricultural activity had negative effects on these communities. Additionally, hydro-morphological factors, nutrients, and phytoplankton accounted for 42% of the variation in the zooplankton community. Hydro-morphological factors positively influenced the zooplankton community, including water temperature, forest cover, TP, HIX, and the phytoplankton community. The water temperature had a greater positive effect, whereas other hydro-morphological factors, NH4 + -N, and NO3 – -N primarily exerted negative effects. The Bacillariophyta community had the most positive effect on zooplankton, followed by Cryptophyta, while Chrysophyta had the least positive effect on zooplankton. The model successfully explained 42% of the variation in the co-occurrence network of plankton (Fig. 7 b, Fig. S10 , a priori model). Quantifying the total, direct, and indirect effects of various factors on network stability revealed significant negative impacts from hydro-geomorphic factors such as water temperature, flow velocity, and river width, as well as nutrient parameters including TP, NH4 + -N, and NO3 – -N. These results indicated that, despite occasional deviations, the combined influence of hydro-morphological and nutrient factors predominantly negatively impacted the stability of plankton networks.    4 Discussion 4.1 Community variation and driving factors The hierarchical partitioning results (Fig. 5 b) showed that geographical factors contributed more than 60% of the variation in plankton community composition in the study area. This result implied a significant spatial variation in these communities from upstream to downstream. Similarly, Ding et al. (2021)  identified spatial factors as the primary influence on phytoplankton community variations in the Yellow River mainstream. In the present study, plankton community composition and diversity showed distinct spatial patterns at different geographic locations of the river. Disparities in flow velocities between upstream and downstream reaches are crucial in shaping the spatial distribution of plankton. The average ratio of upstream velocity to downstream velocity is 1.39, with a maximum ratio reaching 6.49. Take one of the tributaries, the Xushuihe River, as an example. The upstream river slope exceeds 15%, while the downstream slope is only 3%. This geomorphological variation results in turbulent flow in the upstream reaches and slower flow in the downstream reaches. Flow velocity significantly influences the growth and physiology of plankton (Woodward et al., 2019 ). Generally, as flow velocity increases, phytoplankton growth is initially promoted but subsequently inhibited (Zhang et al., 2015 ). Reynolds (1984)  identified 0.15 m/s as the optimal flow velocity for the proliferation of Microcystis aeruginosa . Abu Hajar et al. (2017)  conducted indoor experiments and determined 0.3 m/s as the optimal flow velocity for the growth of Scenedesmus dimorphus . Likewise, zooplankton growth is also influenced by variations in flow velocity (Peters and Marrasé, 2000 ). The variation in flow velocity caused by slope differences from upstream to downstream may impact the spatial distribution of zooplankton (Czerniawski and Kowalska-Góralska, 2018 ). It was reported that obvious slope differences from upstream to downstream in the Weihe River basin resulted in disparities in both zooplankton abundance and biomass across different river reaches (Song and Liang, 2023 ). In addition, the reliance of zooplankton on phytoplankton for sustenance is also important. Sommer et al. (2001)  found that Cladocera biomass and density strongly correlated with phytoplankton biomass (Chl-a concentration), implying that changes in phytoplankton structure elicited the variation in zooplankton community. The duration of plankton growth is directly influenced by the flow velocity at each site and the channel distance from the sampling site to the river source (Ball et al., 2018 ). In the present study, the travel time for plankton from the river source to an upstream site was estimated to be about five hours, excluding potential effects from hydraulic engineering. The travel time to a downstream site was approximately 75 h. Plankton growth from the river source to an upstream site is limited to five hours. However, some benthic diatoms can still grow continuously and spread into the water column, contributing to the phytoplankton community in the upstream reaches (Hamilton et al., 2011 ). Read et al. (2015)  reported that the influence of water retention time on bacterioplankton community composition was considerable. Han et al. (2024)  analyzed the phytoplankton and benthic algae communities at 44 sampling sites along the Yellow River mainstream. They found that the similarity between phytoplankton communities and benthic algae communities in the upstream reaches was significantly higher than in the lower reaches. Similarly, the similarity between planktonic and benthic diatom communities in the upstream reaches was about twice as high as the value in the downstream reaches of the Yangtze River (Wang et al., 2019 ). The above phenomena indicated that benthic algae contributed more to the upstream phytoplankton community than that of the downstream community. The rivers in the study area exhibited an average elevation drop of 873 m, resulting in a substantial increase in August water temperature from 17.8°C upstream to 27.9°C downstream. Water temperature could significantly influence the growth of plankton (Haberman and Haldna, 2017 ). Our results found that plankton diversity increased with increasing water temperature when the value was less than 20°C but decreased when the value was higher (Fig. S12 ). These findings indicated that as water temperature increased upstream to downstream, plankton diversity initially increased, then decreased. Consequently, temperature variations also affected the community composition of plankton. The present study demonstrated a gradual increase in nutrient concentrations from upstream to downstream. Despite the potential impacts of pollutants on plankton, the study area experiences minimal chemical and industrial pollution, resulting in negligible toxic stress. As the river flow through various land use areas, particularly in the downstream reaches, increased human activities and agricultural practices significantly elevate nutrient levels in the river water (Wang et al., 2023a ). These nutrient levels reflect human influence and potentially imply hydro-morphological impacts (Han et al., 2021 ). The increased nutrient levels in the Weihe River significantly impacted zooplankton communities, changing their composition downstream (Song and Liang, 2023 ). Cryptophyta and Pyrrophyta, which require higher nutrient levels (Xiao et al., 2018 ), thrived in the nutrient-rich downstream environments. Similarly, Zeng et al. (2024)  noted a higher abundance of Cryptophyta in the heavily polluted downstream reaches of the Dongjiang River. Gao et al. (2019)  reported an increase in Pyrrophyta operational taxonomic units (OTUs) from the source to the mouth of the Songhuajiang River, suggesting a preference for nutrient-rich environments. Thus, the increase in nutrients from upstream to downstream significantly determines the spatial pattern of plankton communities. Interestingly, the present study revealed that the HIX value robustly predicted both the richness and community composition of zooplankton and phytoplankton. HIX indicates the humification level of dissolved organic matter in rivers, which can be used to reflect land use in basins and assess the contribution of non-point source pollution (He et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the HIX indices are a valuable tool for predicting plankton communities, allowing rapid assessment of river ecological status. In summary, plankton communities in river ecosystems exhibit distinct spatial patterns influenced by hydro-morphology, water temperature, and water quality both upstream and downstream. Our study also found a decrease in Bacillariophyta and Pyrrophyta from downstream tributaries to the mainstream in March, with an increase in Cryptophyta. In August, Pyrrophyta increased while Chrysophyta decreased. Additionally, Ciliophora and Copepoda increased in August. The richness of both plankton groups was also reduced in downstream tributaries. The mainstream represents the downstream continuation of multiple converging tributaries. During water confluence, the merging of communities from tributaries and the mainstream alters the mainstream community composition due to variations in tributary plankton assemblages (Mansour et al., 2018 ). The environmental differences between a tributary and the mainstream lead to heterogeneous selection, reducing diversity in the mainstream (Rocca et al., 2020 ). These environmental differences may explain the further decrease in richness for both plankton groups in the mainstream.  4.2 Community assembly mechanisms The present study found that deterministic processes predominantly influence the assembly of zooplankton and phytoplankton communities in most tributaries, with a stronger impact upstream than downstream. However, the effects of deterministic processes were weaker in the mainstream compared to tributaries. Interestingly, stochastic processes played a significant role in shaping phytoplankton communities in the mainstream, this phenomenon was also reported by Chen et al. (2019) . The fast upstream flow velocity, low water temperature, and nutrient scarcity contribute to short growth periods and restricted phytoplankton growth rates (Tian et al., 2021 ). The phytoplankton community primarily relies on benthic algae, whose dispersal into the water column is influenced by currents (Li et al., 2023c ). Upstream, the composition of the benthic algae community is primarily determined by the river’s water environment (Wu et al., 2010 ). However, hydrodynamic forces and physiological traits influence their dispersal into the water (Nikora, 2010 ). These factors collectively governed the deterministic processes (Benedetti-Cecchi et al., 2015 ). Therefore, the dominance of deterministic processes in shaping the upper river’s phytoplankton community is attributable to the deterministic assembly of benthic algae (Yang et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the deterministic assembly of the zooplankton community is likely due to selective predation on phytoplankton as a food source (Masuda et al., 2017 ). In the present study, the contribution of stochastic processes of plankton communities in the downstream and mainstream reaches was higher than in the upstream reaches, primarily due to dispersal and drift. Increased dispersal in these communities is attributed to the introduction of diverse exogenous algae, protists, and micro-fauna from varied land use types within the basin (Ding et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024 ). Additionally, the influx of tributaries introduces more species sources, intensifying plankton dispersal, and thus augmenting stochastic processes (Benda et al., 2004 ; Chang et al., 2024 ). Drift primarily results from reduced downstream water velocity and elevated nutrient concentrations, which promote the proliferation and reproduction of plankton, thereby amplifying drift effects (Istvánovics et al., 2014 ). Our study demonstrated that deterministic processes dominated zooplankton community assembly more than phytoplankton in both March and August. This discrepancy can be attributed to variations in their passive dispersal abilities. It is well recognized that phytoplankton have a higher passive dispersal ability than zooplankton (Du et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2023 ). Phytoplankton exhibited a wider niche width than zooplankton, indicating greater adaptability within the community (Fig. 5 d). Consequently, environmental selective pressures on phytoplankton are diminished. Moreover, phytoplankton can survive in soil and enter rivers via surface runoff (Ding et al., 2022 ). Additionally, it is notable that phytoplankton generally have smaller body sizes than zooplankton. In microbial ecology, body size is widely accepted as crucial in determining the dispersal ability and community assembly of microorganisms (Luan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023b ). Larger organisms are more susceptible to environmental selection, while smaller ones are more influenced by stochastic dispersal events (Wang et al., 2023b ). Consequently, phytoplankton exhibit greater passive dispersal ability than zooplankton. As a result, deterministic processes have a consistently greater impact on zooplankton community assembly than on phytoplankton in both March and August.  4.3 Network complexity and stability The present study revealed a decline in the stability and complexity of plankton networks along the river, associated with increased river width, expanded agricultural land, and higher nutrient levels. Studies of rivers in the same subtropical climate zone consistently showed that increased water nutrient concentrations lead to significant decreases in aquatic community stability and network complexity (Li et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2024a ). The present study also found significant negative impacts of expanding agricultural land on the stability of plankton communities. This is primarily due to the increased use of fertilizers and livestock manure, leading to higher nutrient discharges into the water bodies (Rashmi et al., 2020 ). Additionally, pesticides used on agricultural land can enter downstream water bodies via surface runoff, further disrupting the structure and stability of plankton communities (Rumschlag et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the present study also revealed that flow velocity did not significantly influence the stability of the plankton network. In contrast, increases in river width and discharge had a significant negative impact on stability. Similarly, Zeng et al. (2024)  found that water flow and river width significantly disrupted the stability of invertebrate communities in the Yangtze River mainstream. Areas with large discharges and extensive river widths are typically located downstream or in the mainstream regions of a basin, where human activities are more intense than in other areas (Ren et al., 2002 ). Consequently, these factors lead to a decline in the stability of plankton networks. Therefore, changes in hydro-morphological factors often indirectly destabilize plankton communities by affecting water quality. Our study revealed that increased stability in the phytoplankton community led to enhanced stability in the zooplankton community, particularly influenced by diatoms and Chlorophyta. Phytoplankton are the primary food source for zooplankton, and increases in Chlorophyta, Bacillariophyta, and Cyanobacteria significantly stimulate specific zooplankton growth (Tillmanns et al., 2008 ). Field studies indicated that Bacillariophyta primarily facilitate rotifer proliferation (Gabaldon et al., 2013 ). Simultaneously, Chlorophyta, Cyanobacteria, euglenoids, and Dinophyceae support the development of microcrustaceans (e.g., Copepoda and Cladocera), ciliates, and Lamellibranchia larvae (Florescu et al., 2022 ). Zhang et al. (2022a)  observed that phytoplankton in China's coastal ecosystems formed complex and stable co-occurrence networks with smaller zooplankton. Specifically, Bacillariophyta tended to interact with small zooplankton, while dinoflagellates preferred interactions with larger zooplankton. These findings emphasize the crucial role of diverse phytoplankton taxa in maintaining zooplankton diversity and the overall stability of the phytoplankton-zooplankton network. In the present study, the overall stability of the co-occurrence network between plankton was higher in March than in August (Fig. 6 c). Huang et al. (2023)  found that seasonal hydrological events like floods reduced the average clustering coefficient and network complexity of eukaryotic algae, thereby weakening network stability. The transition from dry to wet periods increases connectivity among habitats, facilitating microbial exchange (Schönbrunner et al., 2012 ). Increased microbial exchange enhances microbial migration frequency, disrupting ecological interactions and reducing the complexity and stability of ecological networks (Herren and McMahon, 2018; Widder et al., 2014 ). Our results showed that the disparity in stability among different river reaches within the same season was greater than the disparity between different seasons in the same reach (Fig. 6 c). This suggests that geographical location influences the stability of plankton networks more significantly than seasonal factors. These geographic variations may reflect the cumulative impacts of diverse hydro-morphological factors such as land use, flow velocity, and river width. To enhance the understanding of riverine plankton community dynamics, future research should focus on two key areas. Firstly, long-term monitoring studies are essential to observe how plankton communities respond to different hydro-morphological conditions over extended periods. These studies will provide valuable insights into the long-term trends and stability of these communities under varying environmental pressures. Secondly, experimental studies should be designed to establish the causal effects of specific hydro-morphological factors on plankton communities. By systematically manipulating variables such as water flow, sediment load, and nutrient availability, researchers can uncover the mechanisms driving changes in plankton community structure and function. The results of these studies will significantly contribute to our knowledge of aquatic ecosystems and the development of effective management strategies.   5 Conclusion This study showed that geographic and environmental factors contributed to plankton community distribution, with geographical factors accounting for over 60% of the variation. The assembly of plankton communities was mainly determined by deterministic processes. Phytoplankton communities were primarily shaped by stochastic processes in the mainstream. Additionally, the passive dispersal ability of phytoplankton was greater than that of zooplankton, resulting in a stronger influence of deterministic processes on the assembly of zooplankton communities in both March and August. There was a general decline in both network stability and complexity of plankton from the upstream to downstream reaches. This decline could be attributed to increased variation of hydro-morphology (river width, flow velocity, and agricultural land) and nutrient concentrations. Maintaining diverse phytoplankton taxa was crucial for sustaining zooplankton diversity and ensuring stability within the phytoplankton-zooplankton network. Furthermore, geographical location had a greater impact on the stability of these networks than seasonal factors, due to the combined effects of hydro-morphology like land use, flow velocity, and river width. Our findings have important implications for watershed management and ecological conservation, suggesting that protecting and restoring natural hydro-morphological features are important for maintaining healthy and stable plankton communities. This study provides new insights into understanding plankton community distribution patterns and environmental responses in mountain river ecosystems.
1 Introduction China has led global afforestation efforts, launching several ecological initiatives such as transforming cropland into forest and grassland in the Loess Plateau, the Three-North Shelterbelt Project, and protecting natural forests (Cao et al., 2011 ). These land use changes can affect ecohydrological processes, altering groundwater quantity and quality in arid and semi-arid areas (Li et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Research has expanded to explore the interactions among surface water, groundwater, and vegetation, highlighting the dynamic relationship between vegetation growth and water cycling (Li et al., 2021 ). While early ecohydrology studies mainly focused on surface water processes and minimally on vegetation's role in groundwater dynamics (Porporato et al., 2002 ), recent research increasingly recognizes the importance of integrating surface and groundwater processes amidst vegetation changes (Li et al., 2022 ). Climate change (such as reductions in precipitation and increases in potential evapotranspiration) and land use change (such as agricultural expansion) are two primary factors driving changes in hydrological processes. These changes directly influence the formation and distribution of runoff, exerting profound impacts on the availability of water resources within ecosystems (Shahid et al., 2018 ). Plant roots play a pivotal role in the soil–plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC), not only connecting the aboveground portions of plants with the soil but also responsible for absorbing water to meet the evaporation demands of the canopy (Feddes et al., 2001; Mencuccini et al., 2019 ). Nevertheless, water scarcity, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions reliant on rainfall, frequently poses a severe threat to ecosystem functions (Ng et al., 2020 ). Remarkably, tree roots exhibit robust adaptability and resilience, capable of adjusting their structures and functions in response to drought, ensuring survival over extended periods (Ivanov et al., 2012 ). Tree roots play a central role in regulating water absorption, a process intimately tied to soil moisture. Specifically, root depth exhibits a high sensitivity to soil water content (SWC), a characteristic significantly influenced by precipitation infiltration and groundwater level fluctuations (Fan et al., 2017; Schenk & Jackson, 2002 ). Notably, native and artificial forests exhibit distinct rooting patterns, reflecting their respective adaptive strategies for seeking water amidst environmental changes (Brunner et al., 2015; Sivandran & Bras, 2013 ). Further research has revealed that tree roots can penetrate soil to an average depth of 7.0 ± 1.2 m, with certain tropical species reaching depths of 20–50 m (Fan et al., 2017 ). This deep-rooting capability not only enhances trees' drought tolerance but also improves their water use efficiency. Hence, a profound understanding of the interplay between roots and soil moisture is paramount for developing accurate ecohydrological models, particularly in arid regions where trees' water uptake capacity is crucial for ecosystem survival and development (Smithwick et al., 2014 ). This insight not only aids in better grasping the dynamic balance between forest and water resources but also provides a solid theoretical foundation for refining ecohydrological models. Incorporating dynamic root systems into ecological models is essential for accurately predicting vegetation responses to drought, highlighting the importance of understanding root depth strategies for survival (Molina et al., 2019 ). Dynamic root modeling captures root system growth in response to changing environmental conditions like soil moisture in hydrological or terrestrial biosphere models, including root water uptake processes. Current models consider root depth or density changes but often fail to fully account for dynamic root adaptation to environmental changes. The interaction between rooting depth (Christina et al., 2017; Gayler et al., 2014; Hashemian et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020 ), root density, SWC, and soil moisture distribution is crucial for accurately modeling root water uptake (Drewniak, 2019; Niu et al., 2020 ). Under varying environmental conditions, the growth and adaptability of root systems directly impact our understanding of phenomena such as drought, groundwater depletion, and agricultural production (Warren et al., 2015 ). Accurately modeling how roots respond to environmental changes, particularly alterations in water availability, is crucial for predicting and mitigating the impacts of these environmental stresses on agricultural productivity and water resource management. Current earth system models are critiqued for overlooking factors like resource investment, timing, and physical constraints affecting deep root growth in competitive settings (Sakschewski et al., 2021 ). To address this issue, researchers integrated variable rooting strategies and dynamic root growth into the LPJmL4.0 model, which can enhance its ability to simulate root adaptation to diverse environmental conditions by considering a broader array of influences. However, their model, which calculates maximum rooting depth and fine root distribution through growth and shape functions, did not explore how plant roots interact with soil moisture. In a subsequent study, Li et al. (2022)  studied the dynamics between plant root development and soil moisture, which employed an optimal benefit function to link root growth with soil moisture, specifically examined Robinia pseudoacacia in the Loess Plateau. Their work, however, omitted the impact of age-related biomass accumulation and the varying interactions between root growth and soil moisture under different vegetation types. This work therefore aims to understand how vegetation interacts with soil in artificial forests by developing a model to simulate the dynamic relationship between vegetation roots and soil moisture. Using apple orchards and wheat fields in the Loess Plateau as case studies, the objectives of this work are as follows: (1) Improving the CLM by developing root parameterization to simulate the dynamic growth of vegetation roots; (2) Analyzing how these root growth dynamics affect soil moisture on a daily basis, incorporating a cost-benefit function for accurate root growth predictions, associated with the dormant period and plant mature processes; and (3) Comparing root-soil water interactions under static and dynamic root system simulation methods, and across different species to understand their impact on soil moisture.  2 Methods and Materials 2.1 Model development 2.1.1 General description of the ecohydrological coupling models Eco-hydrological model is valuable for integrating hydrological and ecological processes into a single modeling framework. This method allows for the modeling of hydrological flows, water quality, and the response of ecosystems, specifically vegetation growth, to various environmental scenarios. Various eco-hydrological models were evaluated, among which the RHESSys (Regional Hydro-Ecological Simulation System) stands out due to its incorporation of relatively complex biophysical processes. This feature necessitates the handling of extensive data and parameters during model construction and operation. Additionally, the RHESSys model can be computationally expensive, requiring substantial computational resources and time (Tague & Band, 2004; Lin et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2023 ). These factors limit its application in simulating large-scale regions or long time series. In contrast, the VIC (Variable Infiltration Capacity) model (Liang et al., 1994; Hamman et al., 2018 ), a large-scale distributed hydrological model, does not perform well at the point scale or small watershed scale during model development. The SWAT model is a semi-distributed hydrological model developed by the Agricultural Research Service of the United States Department of Agriculture (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The model, grounded in physical concepts, utilizes 3S technologies including Remote Sensing (RS), Global Positioning System (GPS), and Geographic Information System (GIS) to simulate and analyze various aspects of watersheds, such as the hydrological cycle, soil erosion, transport of pesticides and nutrients, and water quality. The CLM is the land surface process model component within the Community Earth System Model (CESM) (Lawrence et al., 2011 ). It is a comprehensive land surface model that was developed by incorporating the strengths of various land surface models such as Biosphere-Atmosphere Transfer Scheme (BATS), Land Surface Model (LSM), and Institute of Atmospheric Physics Land Surface Model version 1994 (IAP94), and further enhanced by the inclusion of hydrological processes. Currently, CLM is one of the most well-developed and widely used land surface models internationally. Since the SWAT model can only briefly describe groundwater hydrology and root water absorption processes, while the CLM4.5 model lacks surface hydrology processes, the description in this method is not detailed enough. Therefore, we choose the advantage modules of the two models for coupling. In this work, the model is developed using different modules of the SWAT (Arnold et al., 2012; Neitsch et al., 2011 ) and the CLM4.5 (Oleson et al., 2013 ) (Fig. 1  ). To ensure an effective integration, it is essential to adjust the selected modules for optimal coupling. In our research, adjustments were made to the root growth and root suction modules, along with a cost-benefit function designed to enhance the dynamic interaction between root system development and soil moisture. Additionally, this work utilized the SWAT model's representation of leaf area index and biomass accumulation changes over time due to tree aging to accurately model vegetation growth dynamics associated with tree age (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The SWAT model's surface process module simulates surface water related processes, including evaporation, transpiration, canopy interactions, and runoff (Neitsch et al., 2011 ), while the SWAT model is relatively simple in simulating groundwater and vegetation root growth processes, and adopts more idealized parameters. Soil water movement is modeled using the one-dimensional Richards' equation, solving by a finite difference approach using the CLM4.5 (Oleson et al., 2013 ). For aspects concerning aboveground biological processes such as plant phenology, development of Leaf Area Index (LAI), and biomass growth, the study integrates methodologies from both SWAT and CLM4.5. Regarding the belowground modules (i.e., root growth simulation), CLM4.5 follows the process-based approach directly implemented in the Biome-BGC (Biogeochemical Cycles) model (Thornton et al., 2002 ). Within this framework, roots are categorized into coarse and fine types. A fixed value represents root depth, and the distribution pattern of fine roots within the soil is determined by a predefined shape function that specifies root density throughout the soil profile. This model analyzes how root systems interact with water, incorporating root depth and the distribution of fine roots as key inputs and serving as items in the Richards equation. It also evaluates the impact of soil moisture on root development and optimizes the trade-offs between investing in coarse and fine root biomass and their water uptake capabilities using a cost-benefit analysis. Our modified model employs three different approaches to simulate growth, which will be detailed in subsequent sections: (1) the static root distribution approach from CLM4.5, which maintains constant rooting depths for coarse roots and a fixed distribution for fine roots by Oleson et al. (2013) ; (2) a strategy that allows for a variable distribution of fine roots while keeping the rooting depth of coarse roots unchanged by Drewniak. (2019) ; and (3) a novel approach that permits both the distribution of fine roots and the rooting depth of coarse roots to adjust dynamically.   2.2 Improvement of root simulation methods 2.2.1 Static distributions of coarse and fine roots The first method is to follow the static exponential function in CLM4.5 to represent the fine root fraction of the different soil layers (Zeng, 2001 ):(1) f r i  = 0.5 exp ( - r a  z h , i - 1   - 1 )  + e x p ( - r b  z h , i - 1   - 1 )                                  - e x p ( - r a  z h , i   - 1 )  - e x p ( - r b  z h , i - 1   - 1 )                        1 ≤ i ≤ n   0.5 exp ( - r a  z h , i - 1   )  + e x p ( - r b  z h , i - 1   )                                   i = n          where fri   is a fractional root, zh,i   is the depth between the soil surface and the current soil layer bottom, n    is the total number of subdivided soil layers occupied by root depth, ra   and rb   are two distribution parameters depending on the PFT root distribution parameter (Oleson et al., 2013 ), and the shape parameter can be obtained by fitting observation results of different plant types, the fine root samples of apple trees in this study were set at 4.8 and 0.8, and the fine root samples of wheat were set at 6.0 and 3.0, respectively (Oleson et al., 2013 ). The method employs an exponential distribution, aligning closely with global observational data. However, it only accounts for changes in root distribution with soil depth, neglecting the impact of variables such as soil moisture and nutrients on root development. Furthermore, within this method, the depth of coarse roots can only be determined by selecting vegetation types, which is a static value. Additionally, it does not accurately represent root growth in ecosystems within arid or semi-arid regions.  2.2.2 Dynamic distribution of fine roots The approach to dynamically distribute fine roots is based on the premise that the newly assimilated biomass is allocated in a fixed ratio to fine and coarse roots. Typically, a direct linear correlation exists between carbon mass and total biomass. Henceforth, in the text, the term “carbon” will be used to denote the biomass of various plant parts. With the rooting depth remaining unchanged, the spatial arrangement of fine roots across different soil depths is influenced by the moisture levels in the soil. It employs intricate equations to model the root growth dynamics, utilizing cost-benefit analyses. Furthermore, it determines the most efficient distribution of biomass or carbon to the underground portion, allocating it between coarse and fine roots. Soil profiles can be plotted into adjacent soil layers and correspond to numerical solutions of the Richards equation. The following equation can describe simulated root growth in discrete soil layers.(1) Carbon allocation between the coarse and fine roots    The cost-benefit function is described as quantifying costs through the carbon allocated to develop coarse and fine roots. This framework draws upon the pipeline model theory (PMT, Shinozaki et al., 1964 ) to elaborate on the formation of the root growth mechanism (Fig. 2  a). Lehnebach et al. (2018)  encapsulated the core principle of PMT as the provision of a consistent pipeline thickness or cross-sectional area per unit of leaf, offering dual functions of vascular transport and structural support across the various layers from leaf to stem. This theory allows for a quantitative linkage between leaf and stem, a methodology also applicable to understanding the underground aspects of plant anatomy (Chen et al., 2019 ). The theoretical model for roots has been formulated, tested through simulations, and corroborated by various databases (Carlson & Harrington, 1987; Richardson & Dohna, 2003 ). The carbon content of the divided coarse roots (d  > 2 mm) and fine roots (d  ≤ 2 mm) maintains a certain ratio according to specific parameters:(6) CR 0 i   = ρ · Z i  · k A  · FR i         where CR  0 i      is the equivalent carbon for coarse roots in the zone between the ground surface and bottom of soil layer i   , FRi   is the carbon for fine roots within soil layer i   , ρ  is the mass density of coarse roots (g cm−3 ), Zi   is the depth from the surface to the bottom of soil layer i    (cm), and k A     is a constant that can be determined from field observations. The sum of carbon added by coarse and fine roots is equal to the carbon Δ   TR  allocated to the underground part. The ratios of Δ C R    and Δ F R    to the total newly added carbon in the root system (ΔTR ) are defined as K FR      and K CR     , respectively.(2) Spatial distribution of new coarse and fine roots    Typically, fine roots are more prevalent in moist soils, aiming to secure sufficient water and minimize water stress. The availability of carbon enables the expansion of both thick and fine roots into deeper layers of soil, offering the advantage of accessing more water from these lower strata. Regarding water uptake by roots, regardless of their thickness, the distribution strategy they follow represents an advanced and optimal root system arrangement, designed to maximize water acquisition (Fig. 2 b). In our updated model, the start and end of the dormant period are defined by the day length threshold, which is calculated as follows:(13) T DL , t h r   = T DL , m n   + t dorm           where TDL,thr   represents the day length threshold at the beginning of the dormancy period, h; TDL,mn   represents the shortest day length of the watershed in a year, h; tdorm   represents the dormancy threshold, h. In autumn, when the day length is less than TDL,thr  , except for the warm-season annual plants, other plants in the watershed will enter the dormancy period. The dormancy threshold t dorm      varies with latitude:(14) t dorm  = 1.0                                  φ  > 40  °  N  o r  S   φ - 20  20       20  °  N  o r  S ≤ φ ≤ 40 °  N  o r  S   0.0                                  φ  < 20  °  N  o r  S          where t dorm      represents the dormancy threshold, which compares the actual day length and the minimum day length, φ    represents the latitude in positive values. At the beginning of the dormancy period, part of the biomass was converted into residues, and the leaf area index of the tree species was set to the allowable minimum value (the biomass fraction of residues and the minimum LAI were defined in the plant growth database). For perennial plants, 10 % of their biomass was converted to residues at the beginning of the dormancy period, and their leaf area index was also set to the allowable minimum. For cool-season annuals, biomass was not converted to residues.  2.3.2 Adjustment of tree biomass calculation 2.3.2.1 Biomass accumulation and distribution During the simulation, the model can calculate the potential growth of the plant per day, which is the amount of plant growth under ideal growing conditions. Ideal growing conditions include adequate water, nutrient supply and a suitable climate. Plant growth is simulated by simulating leaf growth, light interception, and conversion of light energy to biomass at specific plant species radiative use efficiencies. The daily solar radiation intercepted by plant leaves can be calculated by Beer's law (Monsi, 1953 ). Radiation use efficiency refers to the dry biomass generated by a unit of intercepted solar radiation, defined in the plant growth database, and assumed to be independent of the plant growth stage. The equation for estimating the maximum increase in biomass from intercepted photosynthetically active radiation on a given day is as follows (Neitsch et al., 2011 ):(15) IPAR = 0.5 · H day  · 1 - exp k n  L A I              (16) RUE = RUE max  · REG d         (17) Δ b i o = I P A R · R U E        where IPAR    is the solar radiation intercepted by plant leaves (MJ m−2 ); RUE    is the radiation use efficiency of plants (kg MJ−1 ); RUE  max      represents the radiation use efficiency of plants (kg MJ−1 ); REG  d     is the stress factor combined with water and temperature on day d discussed in more details below; where k n     represents the extinction coefficient; H day      is the total incident solar radiation (MJ/m−2 ); Δ b i o    represents the photosynthetic compound that increases the total plant biomass (kg m−2 ).  2.3.2.2 Biomass allocation The annual plants and perennial plants can fully mature within a calendar year. However, trees take several years from seedling to sapling, and then to a large tree. To simulate the less accumulated biomass during the seedling/sapling stage, trees' annual growth is limited by the fixed growth determined by their age. The plant growth database defines the age of trees and their biomass at maturity. In our undated model, the cumulative annual biomass at maturity for trees is:(18) bi o annual  = 1000 y r cur   y r fulldev      · b i o fulldev         where bi o annual     represents the annual biomass accumulation of a tree, in kg hm−2 ; y r cur     denotes the current age of the tree, a; y r fulldev     signifies the full development age of the tree species, a; bi o fulldev     indicates the biomass at maturity for a certain tree species, in t hm−2 ; and 1000 represents the conversion factor. Once the total increment of annual biomass, bio, reaches the threshold value of bi o fulldev    . The plant will no longer grow for that year and will be recalculated starting from the following year. After ceasing growth for that year, the daily increment of plant biomass, Δ   bio   , is set to 0. In the Biome-BGC model, the distribution ratio is assumed to be constant. According to the relevant work of Biome-BGC simulation of Robinia locust on the Loess Plateau (Zhang et al., 2015 ), the ratio of coarse root pool to fine root pool and new leaf biomass is 0.5 and 1.0, respectively. Therefore, the initial fractional value assigned to the total assimilated substances for fine roots is 0.2. Wheat root biomass varies significantly during different growth stages. Taking into consideration the growth process, we assume that the ratio of wheat root biomass to total biomass is set at 0.4. Subsequently, in the dynamic process of fine root distribution and the root depth method, the newly assimilated biomass allocated to fine roots (FR) and coarse roots (CR) is updated at each step.    2.4 Surface hydrological processes 2.4.1 Evapotranspiration The concept of potential evapotranspiration (PET, potential evapotranspiration) was first introduced by Thornthwaite (1948)  as part of the climate classification scheme. He defined potential evapotranspiration as follows: the maximum evapotranspiration over a large area under uniform vegetation cover, adequate soil water supply and no convective or heat storage effects. Because the evapotranspiration rate is strongly affected by the surface characteristics of many vegetation, Penman (1956)  redefined PET as “the amount of water emitted by low grass crops that completely cover the ground, are of the same height, and are never short of water.” Potential evapotranspiration (PET, mm d-1 ) was partitioned between canopy (TP, mm d-1 ) and soil (EP, mm d-1 ). There are many methods for estimating PET, and SWAT uses three methods: Penman-Monteith method (Allen, 1986; Allen et al., 1989; Monteith, 1965 ), Priestley-Taylor method (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 )and Hargreaves method (Hargreaves and Samani, 1985 ). In this study, the Penman-Monteith method calculates the potential evapotranspiration. Based on meteorological data, the potential evapotranspiration on day i    was calculated. The calculation equation of the canopy potential evapotranspiration (T p    , mm d-1 ) is as follows:(19) T p  = ET p  · 1 - exp - K n  · L A I              where K n     represents the extinction coefficient. In this work, due to the influence of extreme temperature, water and nutrient deficiency, the growth conditions of plants in the actual growth process are different from those in the ideal state. Two factors, temperature and moisture, are considered to stress plant growth. Actual transpiration (T R a    , mm d-1)  was calculated as follows:(20) REG d  = 1 - WS trs     · 1 - TS trs            (21) TR a  = T p  · REG d         where W S trs      is expressed as water stress coefficient, and T S trs      is expressed as temperature stress coefficient. Temperature stress is a function of the average daily air temperature and the optimum temperature for plant growth. Near the optimum temperature, plants are not subject to temperature stress. As the daily average temperature deviates from the optimum temperature, plants suffer from temperature stress. The calculation method of temperature stress is based on SWAT (Neitsch et al., 2011 ), and the calculation is as follows:(22) TS trs  = 1              T avg  ≤ T base  , T avg  ≥ T opt         (23) TS trs  = 1 - exp - 0.1054 · T opt  - T avg     2   T opt  - T base  - a b s T avg  - T opt                           T base  < T opt          In the equation, T avg      represents the daily average temperature, °C; T opt      represents the optimum temperature for plant growth, °C; T base      (Christina et al., 2017 ) represents the minimum temperature for plant growth, °C. Under ideal water conditions, water stress is 0. When the soil moisture gradually departed from the ideal moisture condition, the water stress value gradually approached 1.0. Water stress is expressed as a smooth sigmoid function (Sun et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012 ):(24) WS  trs   = 1 1 + R E W / h REW      - k REW                Where h REW      is the SWC at which transpiration is halved. when REW    is the value of h REW     , W S trs      = 0.5. k REW      is the shape coefficient, and the larger k REW      value indicates a more rapid decline feature. Finally, the actual soil evaporation index is calculated considering the availability of soil moisture in the soil profile. In this study, soil evaporation was assumed to occur in the uppermost layer (Neitsch et al., 2011 ).  2.4.2 Growth cycle (thermal unit index) The SWAT model mainly adopts the thermal unit theory to control the growth cycle of plants. Different types of plants need to grow within a certain temperature range, including the lowest temperature at the beginning of growth, the highest temperature of tolerance and the optimal temperature at the highest growth rate. The heat unit theory assumes that the heat demand of plants is quantified and related to the maturity time. It assumes that the plant needs a quantitative total amount of heat units throughout the growth cycle, and heat is accumulated every day from the beginning of growth to maturity. The upper boundary condition was set as evapotranspiration and precipitation after canopy interception. Previous studies have shown that soil moisture content in deep soil (20–100 m) remains relatively constant around field capacity (Qiao et al., 2018 ), thus setting the constant soil moisture content under field capacity as the lower limit. During model calibration and validation, measured values of SWC from apple orchards and wheat fields with different tree ages were used as the initial soil moisture profile. For long-term simulations of the model, the initial soil profile moisture content was set as field capacity.  2.6.2 Numerical simulations The saturated water conductivity Ks  and constant B  in the soil moisture characteristic curve were determined using the measured contents of sand, clay, and organic matter in the soil (Cosby et al., 1984 ). Adjustments to these parameters were then made to improve the accuracy of soil moisture content simulations in the Loess Plateau. Parameters for vegetation growth were sourced from Zhang et al. (2015) , who applied the Biome-BGC model to simulate the growth of Robinia pseudoacacia in the Loess Plateau. Additional vegetation parameters were derived from the SWAT model, as documented by Neitsch et al. (2011)  and Sun et al. (2011) .  2.6.3 Model development environment Both SWAT and CLM4.5 models are open-source and written in FORTRAN90 language. Visual Studio 2019 Community Edition software was used as the development environment where two extra toolkits developed by Intel should be installed which are Intel oneAPI HPC Toolkit and oneAPI Base Toolkit (https://www.intel.com ). During the model development process, the source code of relevant modules in the CLM used was incorporated into the SWAT model code for coupling.  2.6.4 Model warm-up In this work, weather data from the years 1992 and 1993 were utilized for the initial processing of the model, targeting the challenge of unrecognizable soil moisture levels prior to planting apple trees. For the simulation of soil moisture, the model's initial value was defined as the soil's field capacity.  2.6.5 Parameters sensitivity analysis The Latin Hypercube sampling (LHS) and Sobol methods were used to analyze the parameter sensitivity of soil moisture which is an efficient statistical method used to generate near-random samples of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution. The LHS method divides the cumulative distribution function of each parameter into 'n' non-overlapping intervals of equal probability. One value from each interval is randomly selected concerning each parameter to form a sample, ensuring that the entire range of each parameter is explored. The Sobol method is a global sensitivity analysis technique that quantifies the impact of input variables on output variance. In this evaluation, the first-order (S1) sensitivity index and the global (ST) sensitivity index are selected as the evaluation indicators. Among them, S1 measures the contribution of a single input parameter to output variation, without considering the interaction with other parameters. ST measures the total contribution of a single input parameter and its interaction with other parameters to output variation. Based on the Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) method with 1000 generated samples, the impact of five parameters were evaluated which are soil layer thickness (dz), precipitation (Prep), evaporation (Evap), soil water diffusivity (D), and saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks)—on the model results, and obtained the sensitivity analysis results in Fig. 3  . From the results (Table 1  ), it can be seen that in terms of first-order sensitivity indices (S1), precipitation has the greatest impact on soil hydraulic conductivity, reaching 0.527. This indicates that changes in precipitation have the most significant individual effect on soil hydraulic conductivity. Saturated hydraulic conductivity follows with a first-order sensitivity index of 0.197, demonstrating its substantial influence on soil hydraulic conductivity as well. In contrast, evaporation has a relatively smaller first-order sensitivity index of 0.004, indicating a lower direct impact. In terms of total sensitivity indices (ST), precipitation exhibits the highest total sensitivity index at 0.669. This suggests that precipitation not only directly impacts the model output significantly but also likely interacts strongly with other parameters, collectively influencing the overall variability of the model output. Soil water diffusivity and saturated hydraulic conductivity have total sensitivity indices of 0.261 and 0.246, respectively, indicating their importance in the total variability of the model output as well, especially considering their potential interactions with other parameters. Soil layer thickness and evaporation have relatively smaller total sensitivity indices of 0.047 and 0.006, respectively, reflecting their lower impact on the overall model variability. In summary, precipitation stands out as the most influential parameter both in terms of direct impact (S1) and total variability (ST). Saturated hydraulic conductivity and soil water diffusivity also play significant roles, while soil layer thickness and evaporation have comparatively minor effects.  2.6.6 Model calibration and validation The adjustment of model parameters mainly included the maximum leaf area index (LAImax  ), saturated water conductivity (Ks  ), and index (B ) of soil–water characteristic curve. The above parameters were calibrated and validated. Initial values of Ks   and B  are calculated based on laboratory measurements of samples collected from the field. Soil hydraulic parameters of different soil layers vary according to soil texture and organic matter content. Calibration is performed manually using the observed soil moisture content as the target. The performance of the adjusted simulation was evaluated using the indicators mentioned in section 2.6.7 . The calibrated values are listed in Table 2  .  2.6.7 Evaluation indices The statistical indicators used to evaluate model performance include determination coefficient (R2 ), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE). Their specific values are as follows:(39) R 2  = ∑ i = 1  n  S i  - S ¯     O i  - O ¯      ∑ i = 1  n  S i  - S ¯     ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - O ¯               (40) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - S i     2   ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - O ¯     2           where S i     and S    are the simulated values and the mean of the simulated values at time step i   , O i     and O  are the observed values and the mean of the observed values at time step i   , n is the number of time steps. R2  and NSE are dimensionless. The Coefficient of Determination (R2 ) assesses regression model fit, with values near 1 signifying strong explanatory power and values near 0 indicating poor performance. The Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) quantifies model accuracy by comparing the squared residuals with total variance, where higher values denote better prediction capability.  2.6.8 Water balance equation The preceding studies have indicated that afforestation significantly reduces soil moisture content and deep drainage, consequently exerting a further impact on the hydrological components of the soil (Ge et al., 2020 ). In this study, we employ the following equations (Kool et al., 2014 ) to analyze the soil water balance.(41) P = E + T + Δ S + D + R         where P    is precipitation, mm yr−1 ; E    is evaporation, mm yr−1 ; T    is transpiration, mm yr−1 ; Δ S    is the change of soil water storage, mm yr−1 ; D    is deep drainage, mm yr−1 ; R    is surface runoff, which is ignored in this study because the sampling sites are flat with negligible runoff, mm yr−1 .   2.7 Data collection and analysis 2.7.1 Site description The data of this study were collected in LPC (Fig. 4  ), spanning 35°12′∼35°16′N and 107°40′∼107°42′E, covering 6.3 km2  within a warm, semi-humid continental monsoon climate. Historical climate data (1957–2015) show an average annual temperature of 9.4 °C, evapotranspiration of 893 ± 69 mm, and annual rainfall of 578 ± 125 mm, with 55 % occurring from July to September. The terrain features loess plateaus, ridges, and gullies, at 946 to 1226 m elevations. The soil is mainly silt, accounting for more than 70 %, and the water table is between 60 and 100 m. The loess is yellowish, sandy, and permeable, while older soils are reddish, slightly cohesive, yet still loose. Land use is predominantly rain-fed agriculture with crops like wheat and maize on uplands, apple orchards in gardens, grasslands on slopes, and trees like apricot and black locusts across the area.  2.7.2 Meterology Meteorological data spanning from 1992 to 2016 were acquired from the National Meteorological Station in Changwu County, Shaanxi Province, China, via the China Meteorological Data Service Center. This data, including daily records of precipitation, temperature, humidity, wind speed, and sunshine hours, supported extensive climate simulations. Analysis of the 25-year dataset revealed significant yearly climate variations, especially in dry and wet conditions, with an average annual precipitation of 570 mm and a standard deviation of 126 mm (Fig. 5  ).  2.7.3 Soil water and root profile observations To assess long-term soil moisture consumption by forests, two main approaches are used: long-term fixed monitoring, which is direct but time-consuming, and a “spatial trade-off for time” method, which involves comparing water profiles from different forest ages and locations simultaneously to infer long-term changes. In this study, soil and root samples were taken from five apple orchards aged 8, 11, 15, 18, and 22 years in July 2016. A total of 18 soil samples were collected, including 3 agricultural soil samples. Sampling depths were conducted on a soil profile ranging from 0 to 25 m. SWC measurements were taken at intervals of 20 cm and 40 cm respectively, above and below the 2 m depth of the soil profile. These orchards, relying solely on rain for water, were previously farmlands. Sampling was conducted in flat plateau areas with uniform soil from aeolian deposits, as indicated by consistent SWC profiles (Li et al., 2019a ; Li et al., 2019b ). Despite minor age differences among the orchards and consistent regional precipitation patterns over decades, soil, climate, and management practices were considered stable enough to support the spatiotemporal substitution approach for studying soil moisture dynamics. Soil samples were taken from deep-rooted and shallow-rooted areas using a hollow stem auger drill at 0.20 m to 13–25 m to analyze soil cores from deep layers (Fig. 6  ). Sampling sites were strategically chosen near each tree to reduce spatial variability, drawing on methods from prior studies on root distribution around apple trees (Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2019a ). Samples were mixed, dried at 105 ℃ for moisture content analysis, and averaged a bulk density of 1.42 g cm−3 .
