The executable of the software code (IMOD-WQ) is available at https://oss.deltares.nl/web/imod for Windows machines. Input data for LHM fresh-salt is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7419219. Complementarily, the NHI data portal (https://data.nhi.nu) gathers several inputs as the 3D groundwater salinity distribution of The Netherlands.
1 Introduction Snow in high-elevation mountainous regions plays a significant role in the hydrological cycle (Powell et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2018 ), which can be regarded as a natural water tower (Viviroli et al., 2007 ), providing a water source for surface and subsurface runoff. The accumulation and ablation of seasonal snow-pack influence the seasonal flow variations of many major rivers worldwide (Tobin, 2020; Viviroli and Weingartner, 2004 ). The runoff generated from snowmelt during the melting period serves as a water source for downstream cities, agricultural irrigation, and hydropower generation, benefiting over a billion people globally (Beniston et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, the spring floods resulting from snow melt can increase the risk of localized flooding, posing threats to the lives and properties of downstream residents (Rott et al., 2010 ). Hydrological models are crucial tools for reproducing streamflow in high-elevation mountainous areas (Kavetski and Fenicia, 2011 ), while identifying snow distribution is a prerequisite for accurately capturing changes in runoff. Nevertheless, the lack of ground-based observation of snow data for validation makes it challenging to decipher snow distribution in hydrological models. Getting rid of this dilemma and enhancing models’ performance of snow and runoff simulation in these areas are currently hot topics in hydrology, glaciology, and related scientific fields. Reliable observational data is one of the prerequisites for reasonable hydrological modeling in the cryosphere (Moradkhani et al., 2005 ). Therefore, acquiring the spatio-temporal distribution characteristics of snow is essential for improving the accuracy of runoff simulations, particularly in the context of snowmelt runoff. High-elevation regions present challenges for establishing ground observation stations due to their complex and hazardous terrain (Han et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2017 ). Fortunately, advancements in space-based observation technologies have greatly improved the ability to obtain surface hydrological data in these areas. Currently, the widely available and timely satellite observation data have been extensively used to enhance the precision of surface hydrological process modeling, yielding significantly superior results compared to those simulations without incorporating such imagery. (Bormann et al., 2018 ). Optical sensors, such as MODIS, provide high-quality temporal and spatial snow data and have been widely validated for snow identification (Clark et al., 2006; Kuter et al., 2018; Barton et al., 2000; Thaler et al., 2023 ). Several studies have confirmed their usability and accuracy in snow identification through cloud masking algorithms (Klein et al., 2003; Hall and Riggs, 2007 ). On the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the spatio-temporal distribution of snow has been quantified using multiple optical images, and verified by field observations (Li et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2018 ). Additionally, passive microwave remote sensing allows for snow cover observation under various weather conditions, which links microwave brightness temperature to snow parameters like depth (Chang et al., 1987 ). Thus, remote sensing methods provide a solid foundation for understanding snow processes in high-elevation mountainous regions. Apparently, quantitatively estimating hydrological processes of snow and runoff through suited hydrological models is a prominent approach in high-elevation mountainous areas (Siderius et al., 2013 ). Distributed hydrological models that incorporate considerations of snow structure can calculate snow distribution and the resulting runoff for each grid cell. These models’ structural characteristics hold the abilities to simulate the representation of physical processes, as evidenced in various studies conducted in high-elevation mountainous regions, thus demonstrating the adaptability of distributed hydrological models combined with energy balance computation methods (Shrestha et al., 2015; Umair et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2013 ). Moreover, addressing the imperfections in capturing snow and snowmelt runoff due to uncertainties in model’s performance, existing studies have made attempts and improvements by introducing remote sensing data to enhance the performance of these models (Cherkauer et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2014 ). Snow Cover Area (SCA) is one of the key variables for assessing snow distribution, while Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) is one of the most important variables for quantifying conversion of snow to runoff (Salomonson and Appel, 2004 ). For the identification of snowmelt runoff in high-elevation mountainous areas, SCA and SWE are crucial tools and foundations, which are dominant state variables influencing the snowmelt runoff mechanisms in cold regions, profoundly affecting the runoff variations during the ablation period (Dong, 2018 ). By redefining the spatial distribution characteristics of snow through SCA or SWE, corresponding changes in runoff processes were noticed (Bowling et al., 2004; Thirel et al., 2013 ). These endeavors have enhanced our understanding of runoff processes in high-elevation regions. Basically, the integration of remote sensing imagery with distributed hydrological models is an effective solution to enhance the performance of snow simulation. Current methods have sought to improve the effectiveness of snow simulations through various approaches, including data assimilation using statistical schemes (Andreadis and Lettenmaier, 2006 ), integrating remote sensing data with modelling snow data (Tang and Lettenmaier 2010 ), retrieving model parameters via imagery (Wanders et al., 2014 ), and incorporating imagery as calibration references (Chen et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019 ). Among these, the method of adding remote-sensed calibration references retains the hydrological models' inherent ability to capture surface hydrological processes. Generally, the calibration of hydrological modelling following a single data reference method produces “acceptable” outputs but falls short of providing a deeper understanding of hydrological processes. (Hay et al., 2006; Rajib et al., 2016 ). And insufficient attention to tracking snow hydrological processes limits the advantages of distributed hydrological models. Therefore, the characteristics of seasonal snow strongly necessitate considering different hydrological effects of snow accumulation and ablation to reduce simulation errors. At present, some studies started to consider the extraction of spatial information of snow cover throughout the hydrological process, relying on both ground observations and satellite information to improve the accuracy of hydrological modelling (Chen et al., 2017; Duethmann et al., 2014; Han et al., 2019; Parajka and Blöschl, 2008 ). Nevertheless, the choice of calibration references lacks diversity, often relying on single datasets or failing to track snow variables in hydrological processes. Particularly, further research is needed to identify and extract the contributions of snowmelt runoff by analyzing snow signals and understanding the physical processes involved in snowmelt runoff generation. Based on the current research progress, this study emphasized snow parameters and snowmelt runoff signals by introducing optical and microwave snow products. The overall objective of this study is to establish a two-step enhancement strategy incorporating satellite-based snow products with the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model, and favorably refine the model’s runoff simulation capability in high-elevation regions. The two-step enhancement strategy involves: (1) introducing SCA and SWE imagery data as additional calibration references, and (2) quantifying the contribution of snowmelt to total runoff. To accomplish the predetermined targets, satellite imagery products in the Dadu River Basin from 2012 to 2022 were collected, and the calibration of snow-related parameters and simulation of snowmelt runoff were conducted. This strategy facilitates the identification and quantification of snow parameters and hydrological processes on runoff simulation in high-elevation basins. The research outcomes hold significant importance for enhancing the comprehensive modeling capabilities, improving understanding of hydrological and physical mechanisms and providing references for water resource management in this basin and potentially similar regions globally.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area In this study, the upstream basin of the Dadu River basin above Dajin gauging station is selected as the study area (Fig. 1  ). The Dadu River originates from the southern foothills of the Animaqin Mountains in Qinghai Province, China, and is situated in the eastern part of the Tibet Plateau. It is the main source or largest tributary of the Min River, a tributary of the Yangtze River (Yang et al., 2018 ). The basin covers an area of approximately 41,000 km2  (roughly ranging from 99°33′ ∼ 102°46′ E and 31°12′ ∼ °42′ N), accounting for about 2.5 % of the Yangtze River basin. The elevation ranges from 2,136 to 5,374 m, with an average elevation of approximately 4,000 m. Fig. 1  provides an overview of the study area, including its geographical location, basin boundaries, digital elevation model (DEM) (Fig. 1 a), land use (Fig. 1 b), and spatial distribution of annual average precipitation (Fig. 1 c). The DEM data is sourced from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) 30 m dataset (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/sensors/srtm ), the land use data is from the MODIS 500 m dataset (https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/ ), and the precipitation data (includes rainfall and snowfall) is obtained from MSWEP (https://www.gloh2o.org/mswep ). The primary land use types in the basin are grassland and forest. However, due to the high elevation and low temperature in winter season, snow cover is widespread. Fig. 1 b displays the MODIS image classification results from February 10, 2012 (peak snow cover day), showing seasonal snow cover extending over more than 86 % of the basin area, while the snow cover lasts for 4 to 5 months. The areas covered by perennial snow and glaciers constitute less than 0.05 % of the total area, which has minimal impact on the runoff. The upper reaches of the basin experience a typical plateau mountain climate. Influenced by the southwest monsoon, the basin is clearly divided into distinct wet and dry seasons. During 2012 ∼ 2022, the annual average precipitation in the area ranges from 500 to 850 mm (Fig. 1 c) with less than 2 % precipitation falls in winter. Because of the monsoon, over 75 % of the rainfall occurs during the summer season. Consequently, during the flood season (from May to October), runoff accounts for nearly 70 % of the total annual runoff. The basin’s runoff is mainly supplied by rainfall and snowmelt. The topography and climatic characteristics of this basin make the region highly susceptible to significant threats such as floods and other disasters during ablation period. Therefore, as a typical high-elevation basin, precise simulation of runoff is essential and has the potential for generalization in analogous basins globally.  2.2 Data and pre-processing 2.2.1 Generation of daily SCA and SWE datasets The SCA dataset used in this study was sourced from the MODIS Daily Cloud-free Fractional Snow Cover Dataset of the Asian Water Tower Region, which has a spatial resolution of 0.005° and is referenced to the WGS84 datum with an equal latitude and longitude projection (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn ) (Jiang et al., 2022 ). The raw data for generating this SCA dataset was obtained from the MODIS global surface reflectance product MO/YD09GA. Following evaluation using Landsat-8 imagery and ground meteorological station data, the accuracy metric (R2 ) exceeded 0.80, demonstrating merit applicability in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. As for SWE dataset, there are significant uncertainties in current SWE products in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region (Yang et al., 2015 ). Theoretically, some research of field experiments has demonstrated that SWE, as a variable representing the amount of solid water in snow, can be inferred from the ratio of snow pressure to liquid water density, where snow pressure is proportional to the power of snow depth (USACE, 1956 ). Simplistically, the determination of SWE relies on snow depth (Dai et al., 2012 ), obtaining snow depth data is a prerequisite for calculating SWE. Therefore, effectively establishing a relationship mapping between snow depth and SWE can maximize the use of applications in the study area, thus reducing the uncertainty caused by error. Snow depth product was derived from National Tibetan Plateau Data Center with a spatial resolution of 0.25° (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn ) (Che et al., 2015 ). The raw data for generating the snow depth dataset was retrieved from passive microwave brightness temperatures (Che et al., 2008; Dai et al., 2017; 2015 ). Before calculating SWE, we collected ground-based data from in-situ snow observations as a criterion for assessing the accuracy of the snow depth and SWE products. Detailed information about the those observed records can be found in the Section 1  of the Supplementary Information . The recorded data from snow depth stations distributed both inside and around the study area validated the relatively high accuracy of the remote-sensed snow depth product, with an R-squared value close to 0.86 (Fig. 2  a). Concurrently, an examination was conducted on the snow pressure and snow depth data gathered from these snow measurement stations, culminating in the establishment of a functional relationship between the two variables (Equation (1) . The outcomes revealed a fitted R-squared value of approximately 0.88 (Fig. 2 b). Subsequently, following the determination of the relationship between snow pressure and snow depth, the formulation for SWE computed from snow depth was derived (Equation (1) . Precision comparison ensued between the SWE computed from remote-sensed snow depth product and the observed SWE, yielding an R-squared value surpassing 0.86 (Fig. 2 c), thereby indicating high precision and affirming the suitability of SWE computed from snow depth within the study area. Considering the inconsistency in spatial resolution between the SCA data and subsequent model settings, the daily SCA dataset for the study area from 2012 to 2022 was generated with a spatial resolution of 5 km. Admittedly, SWE represents the amount of water stored in solid form within the snowpack, despite the relatively coarse resolution of SWE might potentially lead to deviations. In comparison to SCA, SWE provides further insights into the volume of water present. Furthermore, the SWE data derived from 2012 to 2022 were standardized to a spatial resolution of 5 km to maintain consistency with SCA data. These two datasets were employed as a reference for subsequent the hydrological model calibration (see Section 3 ).(1) SWE = S P / ρ water      S P = 0.181 × S D 1.072             where SWE  means snow water equivalent, SP  represents snow pressure, ρ water     denotes the density of liquid water and SD  snow depth.  2.2.2 Ancillary datasets The topological information was from DEM data, processed using Google Earth Engine from SRTM 30 m data (https://earthengine.google.com ). Vegetation information was obtained from MODIS land use data product (https://earthengine.google.com ), classified using the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) classification scheme, resulting in 17 land use types, with corresponding vegetation parameter information associated with each land use type. Soil type data for each grid cell were derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) (https://gaez.fao.org/pages/hwsd ) at a 30-arc-second resolution, which includes information on over 20 soil types and their physical properties such as particle size and roughness. Meteorological data include daily precipitation, maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and wind speed. Precipitation data was sourced from MSWEP (https://www.gloh2o.org/mswep ) with a spatial resolution of 0.1 degree (Beck et al., 2017; 2019b ), which integrating with ground-based observations and multi-source data by enhancing through bias correction of precipitation frequency. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated in high-elevation mountainous regions (Liu et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2024; Thackeray et al., 2022 ). Minimax temperature and wind speed data were obtained from ERA5 reanalysis data (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu ) with a spatial resolution of 0.25 degree. Several evaluation studies have confirmed the broad applicability of this dataset (Beck et al., 2019a; McNicholl et al., 2021; Urraca et al., 2018 ). In addition, the accuracy of EAR5 in reproducing the spatio-temporal characteristics of temperature and wind speed data was also demonstrated in this study through comparing with observations, which can be found in Figure S2  of the Supplementary Information . Daily discharge data (2012–2022) used for runoff simulation at the Dajin gauging station was collected from the Water Resources Monitoring and Forecasting Center, Ministry of Water Resources, China.    3 Methodology 3.1 Two-step enhancement strategy Broadly, the snowmelt runoff, as a variable directly influencing factor of the runoff characteristics in the hydrological process, needs to be emphasized. Inaccurate simulation of runoff in high-elevation regions often arises when temperatures rise in spring (Zhang et al., 2013 ). It’s evident that a crucial reason for the disparity between simulation and observation lies in the neglect of capturing snowmelt runoff (Barnett et al., 2005 ). Distributed hydrological models possess the capacity to decompose runoff components, yet the uncertainties arising from the absence of corroborating observed streamflow component data and issues related to parameter equifinality have impeded hydrologists' assessments. Utilizing remote sensing imagery as a surrogate for lacking in-situ measurements presents an alternative viewpoint. Despite the intrinsic uncertainties in remote sensing products that may propagate and impact the confidence of the result, the consistency assessment of snowmelt runoff captured from both model decomposition and remote sensing imagery, i.e., hydrological consistency, endeavors to mitigate constraints posed by errors. Significantly, it offers explanatory solutions from the standpoint of snow hydrological processes. In this study, we propose a two-step enhancement strategy to assess the snow-related parameters and improve the modeling capability of snowmelt runoff. Firstly, we conduct sensitivity analysis to identify sensitive parameters related to snow in the model. These parameters are then calibrated using satellite-derived SCA and SWE data as references, followed by using observed discharge as a reference for traditional soil parameters. Secondly, focusing on snow hydrological processes, we prioritize the reconstruction of snowmelt runoff. Following the principle of hydrological consistency, we separate snowmelt runoff from two data sources: satellite-derived SWE products and model structure. The framework of the two-step enhancement strategy established in this study is shown in Fig. 3  . 3.1.1 Parameters calibration Before implementing the enhancement strategy, based on the VIC model used in Fig. 3 , we evaluated the types of calibration parameters and their corresponding optimal values (Table 1  ). A sensitivity analysis of adjustable snow parameters was conducted, following a Latin Hypercube sampling method utilized in previous studies (Sun et al., 2019 ). The image-based SCA and SWE products were used as references to output sensitivity analysis results, determining the sensitive snow parameters. 10,000 parameter sets were sampled within the numerical ranges of those snow parameters, comparing them with remote-sensed SCA and SWE, using the uniform sampling distribution strategy adopted by Kottegoda & Rosso (1997) . Detailed information regarding all adjustable parameters and references can be found in Section 3  of the Supplementary Information .  3.1.2 Snowmelt quantification The direct measurement of snowmelt runoff poses significant challenges. Fortunately, hydrological models and image data provide opportunities for indirect quantification (Li et al., 2021 ). The original structure of distributed hydrological models allows each grid to be traceable for hydrological processes, including snow accumulation and melt. Therefore, tracking snowmelt from its generation can be calculated through hydrological fluxes and other state variables representing water magnitude in the model (Li et al., 2017 ).(2) f Q , s n o w   = ∑ Q snow   / ∑ Q      where Qsnow   represents the runoff component originating from snowmelt, and Q  is the total runoff. Regarding glacier meltwater, on the one hand, the glacier account for only 0.05 % of the total area, making its meltwater contribution negligible. The widespread seasonal snow in the study area predominantly is the predominant driver that causes increase of streamflow during the melt season. On the other hand, tracking glacier meltwater on a daily scale is challenging due to the difficulty of obtaining reference imagery to validate the model’s effectiveness. Therefore, this study primarily focuses on quantifying meltwater from seasonal snow.   3.2 Distributed hydrological model settings and performance metrics 3.2.1 VIC model construction In this study, the proposed two-step enhancement strategy was performed based on the VIC model (Liang et al., 1994 ) with a version of 4.2.d, which employs a two-layer energy balance approach to represent snow accumulation and melting at the land surface, considering heat fluxes (such as longwave and shortwave radiation, latent heat, etc.) and energy exchanges within the snowpack (Andreadis et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2019 ). The study area was divided into 1694 grid cells with a spatial resolution of 5 km, and the model was run at daily time steps to match the generated SCA and SWE datasets. The model was pre-warmed for two years, specifically 2010 and 2011, and then simulations of SCA, SWE, and runoff were conducted from 2012 to 2022 with a daily time step. The calibration period for the model was from 2012 to 2016, while the validation period was from 2017 to 2022. A Fortran-based routing model was coupled with the VIC model.  3.2.2 Metrics for model performance This study introduces different criteria to assess the simulation performance of snow and runoff simulation. The simulation efficiency of the VIC model for snow variables is evaluated using Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) (McCuen et al., 2006 ) and relative error (RE) (Walker and Willgoose, 1999 ) as evaluation metrics. The specific objective functions established are as follows:(5) Ob j snow   = α O b j SCA   + ( 1 - α )  O b j SWE      O b j SCA / S W E   = NSE + 1 - RE     2            where Objsnow   means the comprehensive objective of snow parameter calibration, ObjSCA   and ObjSWE   represent the objective of simulated SCA and SWE compared with remote-sensed SCA and SWE products respectively. In this study, the weight α   for ObjSCA   and ObjSWE   was set to 0.5, indicating that the loss function evenly weights the loss from both SCA and SWE. When using the Shuffled Complex Evolution-University of Arizona (SCE-UA) optimization algorithm (Duan et al., 1994 ) for calibrating parameters related to SCA and SWE, the Objsnow   in the calibration results should approach 1, indicating a better modeling outcome. Streamflow often exhibits significant differences in peak and low-flow processes. Therefore, this study evaluates the performance of streamflow using NSEQ   and NSE(  log Q)  , where the former is sensitive to peak flows and the latter is better at capturing low-flow processes (Chen et al., 2017 ). A weighting factor α   is included in the calculations. In this study, the weights of NSEQ   and NSE(  log Q)   were equally assigned a value of 0.5. The objective Objrunoff   is formulated as follows:(6) ob j runoff   = α N S E Q  + ( 1 - α )  N S E ( log Q )           4 Results 4.1 Simulation of SWE and SCA 4.1.1 Time series simulated SCA and SWE The simulation results of the VIC model for daily SCA and SWE series are visualized (Fig. 4  ). The model, before the selected calibration period and validation period, used 2010 and 2011 as warm-up years. Table 2   reveals the specific evaluation metrics for the simulation of two snow state variables. For SCA simulation, a highest NSE  of 0.79 and RE  of −17.5 % were showed during the calibration period, with an ObjSCA   of 0.81. The validation period exhibited an ObjSCA   of 0.78, accompanied by NSE  of 0.72 and RE  of −15.3 %. An NSE  of 0.76 and RE  of −14.7 % were appeared during the entire period, with an ObjSCA   value of 0.81. Additionally, from the daily SCA results in Fig. 4 , multiple peaks can be observed each year. This phenomenon was evident in both the VIC model and the remote sensing imagery results, indicating rapid changes in snow accumulation throughout the year. The model captured the simulation of multiple peaks, suggesting the model’s ability to represent the fast-changing nature of snow accumulation within a year (Han et al., 2019 ). In terms of lower values, when summer temperatures rise, there was a significant change in SCA, and the VIC model noticed this trend consistently with the imagery data, indicating its ability to decipher SCA variations during periods of temperature increase. For SWE simulation, an NSE  of 0.81 and RE  of −9.2 % were showed during the calibration period, displaying an ObjSWE   of 0.86. A middle-of-the-road performance showed during the validation period, with an NSE  of 0.67, RE  of −13.5 % and Obj SWE  of 0.76. Over the entire study period, the NSE  and RE  were 0.71 and −11.5 %, respectively. Overall, the model was capable of accurately simulating the start and end of SWE and accurately rep-resenting the transitions between zero and non-zero values of SWE. This feature aligned well with the imagery data. Nevertheless, for peak values, especially during the early stages of the snow season, the model tended to underestimate the peak magnitude of SWE. As a result, there was some discrepancy between the model and imagery data during the snow season. It is worth noting that previous studies have shown that imagery-based SWE results tend to overestimate SWE, particularly in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (Dai et al., 2018 ). In general, the simulated SCA exhibited superior performance compared to the simulated SWE, except for a lower NSE during the calibration period (0.79 for SCA compared to 0.81 for SWE). However, the RE results indicate that the simulated SWE outperformed the simulated SCA overall, meaning that the total volume was closer to the imagery results. The NSE values for simulated SCA during the validation period and the entire period were 0.72 and 0.76, respectively, both surpassing those of simulated SWE (0.67 for the validation period and 0.71 for the entire duration). MODIS data has been widely utilized to mitigate the interference from clouds and topographical features in basin valleys, although the performance of optical sensors is limited in shadowed areas (Kuter et al., 2018 ). Nonetheless, simulated SCA still exhibits a high level of accuracy, consistent with the findings in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Han et al., 2019 ). Additionally, while data suffers from the drawback of low spatial resolution, its microwave imaging mechanism can circumvent cloud interference (Chang et al., 1987 ). Consequently, it remains a stable reference for simulating SWE processes.  4.1.2 Spatial distribution of simulated SCA and SWE The spatial distribution results of simulated SCA and SWE from 2012 to 2022 were compared with the multi-year mean values derived from remote sensing imagery. Fig. 5   shows the RE  values between the simulated snow state variables and the corresponding image values. As for SCA, from 2012 to 2022, the absolute values of the RE  between the simulated values and image values were predominantly within 5 %, except for significant biases in 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2018. Considering the terrain characteristics, areas with high bias in SCA simulation often occur in valley regions, consistent with traditional experience and related studies (Nagler et al., 2008; Thirel et al., 2013 ). Vegetation such as trees and shrubs in valley areas can affect optical sensors' detection of the ground surface, leading to errors in distinguishing snow-covered and snow-free pixels (Dong, 2018; Kuter et al., 2018; Schmugge et al., 2002 ). Regarding SWE, the results align with the daily SWE results, with over 50 % of the region showing absolute values of the RE  between simulated and remote-sensed SWE values controlled within 5 % except 2017, 2018, 2021, and 2022. The average multi-year average SCA, and SWE derived from remotely sensed images were compared with the simulated results by the VIC model from 2012 to 2022 (Fig. 6  ). In terms of SCA, the imagery results indicated fewer high-value regions compared to the simulated SCA. The high-value areas (SCA > 0.35) in the imagery accounted for approximately 6.9 % of the total area, while the simulated high-value areas represented around 33.8 %. For SWE, the imagery and simulated results were similar, with the high-value areas (SWE > 5 mm) accounting for approximately 10.2 % in the imagery results and around 4.7 % in the simulated results. Overall, the synchronicity between snow cover and high-elevation areas is also manifested spatially.   4.2 Quantification of streamflow and snowmelt 4.2.1 Streamflow simulations The application of hydrological models for runoff simulation is a fundamental task in hydrology (Beven, 2011 ). Therefore, the effectiveness of runoff simulation by the VIC model under the enhanced strategy was analyzed. Considering the peak flow and low-flow processes in the model performance metrics, accuracy assessment was conducted according to objective function Objrunoff  . Fig. 7   and Table 3   describe the performance of the model in runoff simulation at daily and monthly scales. From the daily runoff simulation results, the Objrunoff   value was highest during the calibration period, reaching 0.87. The NSE(logQ)   evaluation for low-flow simulation also indicated the merit performance during the calibration period (0.88), while the lowest metric value was observed for NSEQ   during the validation period, with a value of 0.82. The overall Objrunoff   for the entire period reached 0.85, indicating a relatively high level of simulation performance. On a monthly scale, except for the validation period where the NSE(logQ)   value was 0.89, all other periods and metrics exceeded 0.9. During the calibration period, the Objrunoff  , NSEQ  , and NSE(logQ)   all reached their highest values (0.93), demonstrating the model’s outstanding performance. The evaluation of the effectiveness of peak flow and baseflow will be compared with the performance of the original VIC model in the discussion section. Overall, the VIC model with the enhanced strategy consistently achieves an Objrunoff   exceeding 0.84 at the daily scale, and monthly scale exceeding 0.9 throughout the calibration, validation, and entire study periods. The runoff processes depicted in Fig. 7 , encompassing baseflow simulation during cold winters, spring floods induced by snowmelt, and peak flow simulation during summer monsoons, are all adequately captured by the model. In terms of performance, when compared to certain runoff simulation studies conducted in high-altitude mountainous regions, this demonstrates a considerable performance advantage (Musselman et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2022 ), particularly in capturing low-flow and spring runoff processes. This suggests the model’s capability to capture the flow dynamics of sparse precipitation and snowmelt runoff during the snowmelt season, underscoring the significance of snow as a primary contributor to runoff (Guan et al., 2013 ).  4.2.2 Calculation of snowmelt by snow tracing and remotely sensed datasets The magnitude of snowmelt runoff was statistically analyzed through snow tracing in the VIC model and the snowmelt loss rate of remotely sensed SWE (Fig. 8  ). From the perspective of model decomposition, the first peak of snowmelt runoff transpired in spring season, with notably concentrated snowmelt runoff. This observation underscored the substantial influence of snowmelt on spring discharge, seamlessly aligning with our hydrological understanding. A second peak of snowmelt runoff appeared in autumn, but its proportion of the total runoff averages around 10 %, significantly lower than the spring peak. Although there was still snowfall in autumn, the higher temperatures leaded to rapid snowmelt, unlike in spring when snow accumulates. This resulted in a lower proportion of snowmelt runoff in autumn compared to spring. Regarding the computed results from remote sensing SWE products, similar features were obtained in snowmelt runoff calculation, with two peaks occurring in spring and autumn. It is noteworthy that the snowmelt runoff calculated from SWE images was higher than the modeled values for the years 2014 ∼ 2017. A comparison of the SWE daily series in Fig. 4  revealed that the SWE values from remote sensing images for 2014 ∼ 2017 were higher than the modeled SWE values, explaining the differences between the two sources. Furthermore, the peak snowmelt volume interpreted from images was higher than the model results, which may stem from differences in their calculations (Equation (3) & (4) ). Studies focused on precipitation in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau have found an overall increase in both rainfall and snowfall in the past two decades (Li et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Global warming contributes to increased precipitation, especially evident in the form of increased snowfall in high-elevation regions (Musselman et al., 2017 ). In the years where SWE values from remote sensing images exceeded the simulated values by the VIC model, the impact of increased moisture transport from the Indian Ocean and enhanced summer monsoons was more pronounced (Li et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019 ). In summary, the statistical characteristics of snowmelt runoff from both sources were similar, indicating the occurrence of two peaks in snowmelt runoff during spring and autumn, significantly influencing the overall runoff and the appearance of the two annual peaks in the flow.  4.2.3 Comparison of snowmelt contribution in temporal and spatial scales Based on the snowmelt calculation in the VIC model and remotely sensed SWE of this study, an attempt was made to separate the portion of runoff generated from snowmelt in the total runoff. The quantitative results of statistical analysis on the contribution percentage of snowmelt runoff indicated that there was little difference between the annual average snowmelt runoff contributions calculated by the model and those based on image-derived SWE, demonstrating a strong hydrological consistency (Fig. 9  ). The percentages of snowmelt runoff calculated by both methods fluctuated between 2012 and 2022. The simulation results showed that the lowest contribution occurred in 2020 at 23.8 %, while the image-derived results revealed the lowest contribution in 2016 at 28.0 %. The maximum contributions were observed in 2013 for the simulation results at 40.1 % and in 2014 for the image-derived results at 39.1 %. The multi-year average contribution rates for the simulation and image-derived results were 31.8 % and 33.4 %, respectively, showing relatively consistent outcomes. For baseflow quantification, the proportion of baseflow contributed by snowmelt to the total runoff fluctuated between 5.0 % and 11.5 %, peaking at 11.5 % in 2017. Meanwhile, the proportion of baseflow from rainfall to the total runoff ranged between 9.9 % and 18.6 %. Overall, the quantified results of snowmelt runoff contribution were slightly higher than the 23 % value reported by Zhang et al. (2013)  for the upper reaches of the Yangtze River Basin. This discrepancy may be attributed to the presence of glaciers in their study area, whereas glaciers are relatively scarce in our study area. Both the model and remote sensing SWE calculations exhibited synchronous hydrological consistency, providing a solution for quantifying basin snowmelt runoff contributions in the absence of direct snowmelt runoff measurements. Fig. 10   denoted the spatial variation of snowmelt runoff contributions by the two approaches. The snowmelt runoff contribution based on the VIC model and remotely sensed SWE calculations exhibit a highly spatial similarity. Regions with significant snowmelt runoff contributions (>0.3) are observed upstream of rivers (northwest region) and sporadically distributed in high-elevation areas. These areas are characterized by higher elevations and are prone to snow accumulation, leading to a higher contribution of snowmelt runoff during the snowmelt period.    5 Discussion 5.1 Evaluation of the enhanced strategy on the runoff modeling capability Typically, research focusing on incorporating image references as calibration datasets tends to lean towards adjusting parameter distributions (Rajib et al., 2016; Yeste et al., 2023 ), lacking reconstruction of key hydrological variables and physical processes, especially snow distribution and snowmelt runoff in high-elevation basins. Thus, the primary motivation behind introducing remote-sensed snow products in this study was to utilize the distribution of snow captured in imagery to calibrate the snow component simulated by the model. This approach, which was implemented through an enhanced strategy framework for snow parameter calibration of the VIC model, aimed to enhance the model’s capability to simulate snow, thereby improving the accuracy of runoff simulations. To better elucidate the impact of the proposed enhanced strategy framework on runoff simulation, we conducted a compared test with three schemes: the solely observed streamflow calibrated reference strategy with traditional soil parameters (S1), integration of soil parameters with snow-related parameters calibrated solely based on observed discharge (S2) and the two-step enhancement strategy incorporating additional remote-sensed snow products and streamflow records (S3). From the runoff simulation results, it was evident that the performance of S1 was significantly inferior to that of S2 and S3 during both the calibration period (2012–2016) and the validation period (2017–2022). This highlighted the crucial role of snow parameters in enhancing the precision of runoff simulation, a trend corroborated by similar research findings (Houle et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019 ). Additionally, all three schemes adequately accounted for autumn snowmelt events, as snowfall persists in high-elevation regions during autumn, albeit to a lesser extent compared to spring and summer monsoon seasons. The distinction between S2 and S3 lies in the evaluation of their respective schemes using a snow calibration reference. During calibration, S2 demonstrated an NSE of 0.84, marginally lower than the 0.85 achieved by S3. However, in the validation phase, S2 exhibited a higher Objrunoff   of 0.88 compared to S3’s 0.87, predominantly due to S2’s superior performance in the low-flow evaluation metric NSE(logQ)   (0.91). Notably, during validation, Objrunoff   results suggested comparable performance between S2 and S3, with no significant disparity observed over the entire period. This aligned with the findings of certain studies indicating that more intricate parameter calibration schemes do not necessarily yield substantial enhancements in runoff simulation capabilities (Chen et al., 2017; Rajib et al., 2016 ). Nonetheless, S3 displayed satisfactory performance, slightly surpassing S2 in NSE across all periods. Furthermore, a comparison of the maximum daily snowmelt error between two strategies (S2 and S3) and imagery results indicated noteworthy discrepancies (Fig. 11  d). Particularly, the disparities between S2 and imagery in maximum daily snowmelt error were more pronounced than those between S3 and imagery. Additionally, S2 tended to underestimate snowmelt runoff peaks, which further validates the advantage of S3 in calculating snowmelt runoff. Thus, the superior results from S3 suggested that heightened snowmelt during the monsoon period serves as a significant water source, thereby enhancing hydrological consistency with imagery while advancing our understanding of snow hydrological processes in high-elevation basins. The separation of snowmelt from total runoff serves as evidence supporting our proposition: validating snow parameters in the VIC model by referencing remote-sensed data can potentially clarify snow hydrological processes in high-elevation basins. The results also demonstrate the enhancement of our hypothesis and the enhanced strategy in improving runoff modeling capabilities (Fig. 11  and Table 4  ). Despite the snowmelt runoff volumes computed by S2 and S3 have not been verified against observed snowmelt, their ability to explain the division of snowmelt runoff provides evidence of the role of snowmelt replenishment during the initial stages of the flood season (when temperatures rise but the rainy season in the basin has not yet begun) and throughout the entire flood season (Chen et al., 2017 ). Thus, the snowmelt runoff proofs the enhanced strategy proposed in our study in terms of its ability to simulate runoff and trace snow hydrological processes.  5.2 Reconstruction error of snow accumulation and ablation Snow accumulation and ablation significantly impact the hydrological cycle process (Singh, 2001 ), where accumulation reduces surface runoff due to freezing effects, while ablation increases streamflow. Consequently, accurately deciphering the dates of snow accumulation and ablation can directly reflect the role of hydrological models in reconstructing physical processes, thereby reflecting the relevant state of snow at the basin scale. In our study, when introducing two remote-sensed snow products (SCA and SWE) as references for calibrating the snow parameters of the VIC model, we integrated the multi-objective function Objsnow   as the output condition for the optimal parameter set. Existing arguments suggest that the uncertainty brought by multiple imaging data does not significantly improve the overall performance of hydrological models, possibly due to the increased model complexity gradient caused by the uncertainty of multiple data (Tang and Lettenmaier, 2010; Wrzesien et al., 2019 ). To clarify the uncertainty associated with the combined use of SCA and SWE products, we evaluated snow reconstruction separately for parameter combinations of Objsnow  , ObjSCA  , and ObjSWE  , including the time error between the simulated snow accumulation start date and the date of snow appearance in the SCA product, as well as the time difference between the simulated snow ablation date and the date of nearly complete disappearance of solid water in the SWE product. From different combinations of snow parameters, distinct characteristics were emerged during snow accumulation and ablation periods. During the accumulation period, the simulation results of snow parameters calibrated with ObjSCA   as the objective function demonstrated superior performance, showing smaller temporal error values (Fig. 12  b) and also relatively smaller median and average. As for the ablation period, the simulation results of snow parameters calibrated with Objsnow   as the objective function exhibits a favorable distribution of temporal error values, reflecting merit results in terms of the date range and spatial distribution of temporal errors. Basically, the differences among the three approaches are not significant, while simulated dates of snow accumulation and ablation appeared an average deviation of approximately one week compared to the imagery results. The ablation analysis results calibrated with ObjSWE   as the objective function showed a lower median, although the average was not higher than that of Objsnow   results. The superior results of ObjSCA   during the accumulation period were related to the higher spatial resolution of the SCA imagery, which advantageously captured the spatial distribution of snow. On the other hand, the SWE product during the ablation period is sensitive to notice the solid water state, and despite the uncertainty caused by its lower spatial resolution (Dong et al., 2005 ), its ability to capture snowmelt remains preferable for current hydrological simulations (Han et al., 2019 ). Moreover, integrating the strengths of SCA and SWE obviously provides valuable support for snow reconstruction in high-elevation basins.   6 Conclusion In this study, we constructed a two-step enhancement strategy incorporating remotely sensed snow products with VIC model, which ameliorated the snow and runoff simulation in a high-elevation basin. In Step 1, the results showed an NSE  of 0.76 for SCA and 0.71 for SWE in daily scale throughout 2012 ∼ 2022. Additionally, the NSE  reached 0.84 for daily runoff simulation, and an NSE  of 0.92 for monthly simulated runoff indicating a significant improvement compared to the strategy reliant on soil parameters with single calibrated reference (NSE  of 0.66 for daily), and exhibited comparability to the strategy incorporating snow parameters but calibrated solely based on discharge data (NSE  of 0.83 for daily). In Step 2, snowmelt runoff was calculated using both the VIC model and remotely sensed SWE data, demonstrating high consistency between the two data sources. The multi-year average snowmelt runoff contributions from the model and images calculations were 31.8 % and 33.4 % respectively. Additionally, simulated dates of snow accumulation and ablation appeared an average deviation of approximately one week compared to the imagery results. In a nutshell, the two-step enhancement strategy proposed in this study have significantly refine the runoff simulations within the VIC model. Moreover, a universal enhancement significance is applicable in distributed hydrological models with similar structure. Prioritizing snow parameters and snow hydrological process variables can enhance the hydrological understanding of high-elevation basins where direct measurements of snowmelt runoff are lacking. The method proposed in this study can improve the accuracy of runoff simulation in a high-elevation basin and can be applied to similar basins, thereby enabling better water resource management in those basins globally.
1 Introduction Integrated hydrological models have gained popularity owing to their improved mechanistic representation of the watershed dynamics (Kollet and Maxwell, 2006; Coon et al., 2019; Wang and Kumar, 2022 ). However, the corresponding improvement in spatio-temporal resolution is not without its computational challenges. Even with the growing availability of high-performance computing resources, executing these models remains expensive, often making only a few hundred runs affordable for a few simulation years (Clark et al., 2017 ). This significant computational overhead impedes the efforts of parameter estimation using ensemble simulations. It is, therefore, imperative for hydrologists to exercise careful discretion when selecting the streamflow observation data for parameter learning (or inverse modeling). Early studies focused on assessing the impact of observation lengths on inverse modeling for hydrological models (Sorooshian and Gupta, 1983; Yapo et al., 1996; Anctil et al., 2004; Boughton, 2007; Li et al., 2010 ). Sorooshian and Gupta (1983)  investigated the impact of observed streamflow lengths on calibrating the lumped version of the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model (SAC-SMA) (Burnash and Ferral, 1973 ) and found that at least one water year of observations should be used. Later, Yapo et al. (1996)  studied the influence of observation length on the same model using 40 years of observations and concluded that approximately eight years of data are needed to achieve robust parameter estimates. Li et al. (2010)  furthered the analysis on fifty-five watersheds across Australia using a simple hydrology model and achieved the same conclusion of using eight years of observations to obtain reliable estimates of model parameters. Similar research has also been performed on other models, either process-based (Boughton, 2007 ) or data-driven (Anctil et al., 2004 ), concluding that multiple years of continuous observations are necessary for robust inverse modeling. In the last two decades, attention has been shifted to studying how many informative observations are needed in watershed model parameter learning. Perrin et al. (2007)  conducted a study on two conceptual rainfall–runoff (RR) models and found that about 350 daily observations from a multi-year observation dataset are sufficient for robust parameter estimation. Subsequently, a suite of research (Juston et al., 2009; Seibert and Beven, 2009; Abebe et al., 2010; Singh and Bárdossy, 2012; Viviroli and Seibert, 2015; Pool et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018 ) has focused on the conceptual HBV hydrology model to investigate the sensitivity of the model parameter to streamflow observations, as well as the number of observations needed in parameterizing the model (Bergström, 1995 ). Singh and Bárdossy (2012)  showed that hydrological models can be well calibrated using observations from a small number of so-called unusual time periods that share limited information with each other. Zheng et al. (2018)  analyzed the influence of splitting calibration and evaluation data through a data-driven RR model using artificial neural networks. Nevertheless, the existing studies have been only performed on computationally efficient hydrological models, either a fast data-driven model (e.g., artificial neural network) or a conceptual process-based model (e.g., the HBV and SAC-SMA models). As a result, these prior research findings might not apply to an integrated hydrological model with much higher model complexity, often employed at finer spatio-temporal resolutions, and consequently, more computationally expensive. Recently, Jiang et al. (2023)  developed a knowledge-informed deep learning inverse method that identifies informative observations to estimate model parameters through deep learning models. The proposed method has shown promise in using just a few hundred model runs to calibrate the Advanced Terrestrial Simulator (ATS; Coon et al., 2019, 2020 ), a computationally demanding hydrological model that solves the coupled two-dimensional diffusive wave equation for overland flow and the three-dimensional Richards equation for subsurface flow. Such knowledge-informed calibration is consistent with inverse modeling approaches maximizing information retrieval from observations in parameter learning (Vrugt et al., 2002 ) but is more flexible as a postprocessing procedure without the necessity to be integrated with the model as traditional data assimilation techniques do (Jiang et al., 2021 ). As a study quantifying the amount of information stored in or communicated among variables (Cover and Thomas, 2006 ), information theory has been widely applied in hydrology in the past several decades. Singh (2013)  provides a comprehensive review of the early applications of entropy in hydrology and water resources engineering, such as derivation of distributions, design of hydrological networks, reliability assessment of water distribution systems, etc. Since then, the theory has been used beyond engineering-oriented applications to scientific discoveries. To name a few, Nearing and Gupta (2015)  proposed using information theory to quantify the information provided by a hydrological model; Thiesen et al. (2019)  developed a data-driven approach using information theory to identify rainfall–runoff events; Jiang and Kumar (2019)  developed an information flow-based causal analysis framework to investigate how the fractal signature of a stream chemistry system is sustained by interdependencies among the system components; Azmi et al. (2021)  evaluated the performance and complexity of hydrological models using a novel “bit by bit” methods. All these applications benefit from the powerful capability of information theory to quantify uncertainty and capture multivariate nonlinear relationships, thus necessitating the theory’s role as a diagnostic tool in uncovering the information encoded in observations used for learning model parameters. Therefore, the objective of this study is to assess the roles of observation length, observation information content, and gage locations in facilitating parameter learning and calibration of an integrated hydrological model. Particularly, we addressed the following two questions: (1) How to select the calibration period for parameter estimation given multi-year streamflow observations using a fully integrated hydrological model?  and (2) To what extent can the observations of a sub-catchment gage be used in calibrating the watershed outlet streamflow?  To this end, we performed inverse modeling on an integrated hydrological model at the Upper Neversink River watershed within the Delaware River Basin. The watershed is largely forested and has a humid climate and a warm summer, supporting primarily perennial streams. Eleven gages are available and provide streamflow observations with varying record lengths (see Fig. 1 ). We targeted calibrating ATS, a state-of-the-art distributed hydrological model recently applied in various applications, such as watershed hydrology (Coon et al., 2020 ), artic hydrology (Painter et al., 2016 ), reactive transport modeling (Molins et al., 2022 ), agriculture studies (Rathore et al., 2024 ), etc. We first did an exploratory data analysis on the observations to uncover the information characteristics of streamflow. The obtained insights further facilitated the generation of our hypotheses that guided the design of different scenarios of parameter learning using the knowledge-informed deep learning method (Jiang et al., 2023 ).    2 Exploratory data analysis on the Upper Neversink Watershed 2.1 Study watershed The Upper Neversink Watershed is located in the northeastern part of the Delaware River Basin on the east coast of the United States (Fig. 1 (a)). The majority of the discharge flows through the west and east branches of the Neversink Rivers from the northeast to the southwest, which converges at the outlet of the watershed. Based on the Köppen classification system (Köppen and Geiger, 1930 ), this watershed is classified as warm summer and humid continental climate (Dfb) with a mean annual temperature of 6.25 °C. The long-term Daymet forcing dataset (Thornton et al., 2021 ) shows that the watershed receives ∼  1310 mm of precipitation annually, among which 20.7% is contributed by snowfall. Snowmelt usually occurs from late April to early June. The elevation of the watershed ranges from 450 m at the valley bottom to 1280 m at the mountain top, where more than 80% of land cover is composed of deciduous forest. Streamflow observations are available through 11 USGS gages that are located at the outlet (Gage 01435000) and each sub-catchment of the watershed (Fig. 1 (b)), from 01-October-1990 through 30-September-2003. These gages record daily discharge with varying record lengths (Fig. 1 (c)), with overlapping periods from 1992 to 1993. In this study, we divide the observations into the spin-up period (from 01-October-1990 through 30-September-1991), the calibration period (from 01-October-1991 through 30-September-1999), and the evaluation period (from 01-October-1999 through 30-September-2003).  2.2 Exploratory data analysis We employ the following information-theoretic metrics to characterize the information contents of streamflow observations (Cover and Thomas, 2006 ): Shannon’s entropy H  , the spectral entropy S H   , and the mutual information I  , as below: (1) H ( X )  = − ∑  X = x   p ( x )  log p ( x )     (2) S H ( X )  = − ∑  X = x   p ( s  x   )  log p ( s  x   )     (3) I ( X ; Y )  = ∑  X = x   ∑  Y = y   p ( x , y )  log ( p ( x , y )   p ( x )  p ( y )     )  ,       where p   is the discretized probability function; x   and y   are specific values of variables X   and Y  ; and s  x     is the power spectrum of x   through the discrete Fourier transform. We use natural log, and the units of H   and I   are nats. H   and S H    play complementary roles in delineating the variability of X   in time and frequency domains. H   quantifies the amount of uncertainty or information associated with the variable X  . S H   , on the other hand, is a measure of uncertainty of the spectral power distribution of X   and has been widely used to distinguish signal patterns in various applications (Inouye et al., 1991; Pan et al., 2009 ). I   takes one step further and uncovers the shared dependencies between two variables X   and Y  . For each of the three metrics, the higher the value is, the larger the variability or dependency is. We calculate each metric on 10 evenly divided bins on each dimension, leading to 10 and 100 bins in the one-dimensional space p ( x )     and the two-dimensional space p ( x , y )    , respectively, consistent with Jiang et al. (2022) . In the exploratory data analysis, X   and Y   refer to the logarithmic daily streamflow to reduce the adverse impact of strong streamflow skewness on probability calculations in Eqs. (1) –(3)  (note that there is no zero streamflow in the observations).  Streamflow variability over years.  We calculated H   and S H    on one and multiple consecutive years of the streamflows at each gage during the calibration period (from 01-October-1991 through 30-September-1999). Figs. 2 (a) and (b) show the changes of H   and S H    over the number of consecutive observation years, with purple and gray dots representing Gage 01435000 (the outlet) and the other gages, respectively. For instance, the only purple dot using eight observation years was calculated using the outlet observations from 01-October-1991 through 30-September-1999 based on Eqs. (1) and (2) . The three purple dots using six years were calculated using three sets of successive six years, i.e., 01-October-1991 through 30-September-1997, 01-October-1992 through 30-September-1998, and 01-October-1993 through 30-September-1999. When using fewer than five years of observations, H   and S H    vary greatly as a result of dynamic streamflow conditions across wet and dry periods. However, when more observation years are involved, the variations reduce, and the two metrics slightly fluctuate around 1.9 nats (H  ) and 0.6 (S H   ) over >   four observation years. The convergence of the information contents suggests that >   four years of streamflow observations largely encode the streamflow variability in this 8-year time frame. In other words, the additional information that using the entire 8-year observations brings is marginal. Therefore, we hypothesize that streamflow prediction in this watershed outlet is mostly improved when using at least four or five years of observations for learning sensitive model parameters.  Relation between streamflow variability and magnitude.  When plotting S H    against H   (Fig. 2 (c)), we observe a ‘tradeoff’ between the two metrics, implying that a larger variability in the time-space (H  ) comes with a reduced variability in the frequency-space (S H   ) in this watershed. This tradeoff, in fact, results from the dependency of the two metrics on streamflow magnitude at a given period. As depicted in Fig. 2 (d), the mean of the logarithmic streamflow is negatively correlated with H   using the observations from Gage ‘01435000’ (also see the plot of H   versus the logarithmic streamflow at other gages in Fig. A.1 ). This inverse trend suggests that while dry years reduce the stochasticity of the streamflow fluctuations and lead to smaller S H   , the few floods can be more ‘surprising’ and thus result in larger H   . Let us take the water year 1991 (WY1991; labeled as A), WY1995 (labeled as B), and WY1992 (labeled as C) for illustration, corresponding to the first two highest and the lowest S H   , respectively (see the corresponding streamflow observations of the three scenarios in Fig. 2 (e)). C’s streamflow encodes the greatest H   mostly due to a big runoff event in the early spring of 1993. The river subsequently dried up in the summertime of 1993, leading to a series of flattened streamflows and correspondingly the lowest S H   . Conversely, we observe much more streamflow fluctuations with similar magnitudes in A   and B   than C  , attributed to the largest S H   . However, these fluctuations with similar magnitudes reduce the overall year-around variability, causing the lowest H   in the three scenarios. The varying characteristics of streamflow observations consequently give rise to our second hypothesis that the information content of streamflow observations tells the potential that a model can improve its representation . Note that although to what extent the model can effectively assimilate the observations is contingent on the model complexity, quantifying the complexity information is extremely hard if not impossible without running the model (Weijs and Ruddell, 2020; Azmi et al., 2021 ). Here, we target identifying the maximum observation information a model can leverage to learn the parameters. Dependency among sub-catchments streamflows. Fig. 2 (f) shows the heatmap of I   calculated between streamflows of each pair of gages at WY1992 when all the gages have observation records. In both axes, the gages are ranked according to their distance to the outlet. The figure shows that I   increases when the pair of gages gets close to the outlet (i.e., at the lower right of the plot). It complies with the aggregation of streamflows across the watershed such that downstream dynamics encode information from upstream. This information aggregation results in our third hypothesis that observations at an informative gage can be used to constrain the model to predict the streamflows at a nearby gage .     3 ATS ensemble runs and parameter learning 3.1 ATS model setup and ensemble runs ATS is an open-source code that solves integrated, distributed terrestrial hydrological processes across surface, subsurface, canopy, and snowpack (Coon et al., 2019, 2020 ). The backbone of the model is the coupled surface-subsurface flow solver. Surface flow is represented by a two-dimensional diffusion wave approximation of the Saint-Venant equation and coupled to the three-dimensional Richards equation for flow in variably saturated soil in the subsurface. The water and energy balances of snow and canopy are solved at each surface grid cell using a simple land surface model (Bhanja et al., 2023 ). Multiple fluxes are calculated and then incorporated as source or sink terms in the coupled surface-subsurface equation, such as the throughfall, drainage, sublimation, and melt of the snow, the interception, evaporation, and transpiration of the canopy, and the evaporation of the bare ground. The Priestley-Taylor equation calculates the potential evapotranspiration of canopy evaporation, canopy transpiration, snow sublimation, and bare ground evaporation. For more details of the land model employed by ATS, see the appendix of Bhanja et al. (2023) . Model setup.  We used the Watershed Workflow Python package (Coon and Shuai, 2022 ) to generate the mesh and obtain the surface and subsurface characteristics of the watershed from public databases, shown in Figs. 3 (a)–(c). A total of 389,655 cells are generated. The surface mesh consists of 18,555 two-dimensional triangle cells with sizes varying from ∼  100 m near the stream network to ∼  320 m away from the river (Fig. 3 (a)). The surface land cover types are delineated using the National Land Cover Database. The subsurface is divided into 21 terrain-following layers with a total depth of 45 m. The vertical resolution gradually increased from 0.05 m at the surface to 0.5 m at 2 m depth, further increased to 4 m at 11 m depth, and remained constant at 4 m grid size until the bottom. The top soil layers encompass 2 m of the vertical domain. The depth to bedrock is determined from the measurements by USGS. The fractured bedrock layers are sandwiched by the top soil layers and the bottom bedrock. As shown in Fig. 3 (c), the depth to bedrock ranges from near zero inland, where bedrock could be exposed to the surface, to a maximum of 45 m at some river reaches. This implies that the permeability of the fractured bedrock layers around the river corridor can be critical to transporting subsurface flows to the stream. The soil characteristics are obtained by querying the National Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) soils database through the Watershed Workflow. We used the k  -means algorithm (Likas et al., 2003 ) to generate five clusters of soil properties based on the saturated hydraulic permeability or intrinsic permeability values retrieved from SSURGO (Fig. 3 (b)), consistent with a prior study (Jiang et al., 2023 ). The five clustered soil types, named S1, S2, S3, S4, and S5, have the averaged intrinsic permeability as −12.669, −13.183, −13.598, −14.559, and −12.193 log m  2     , respectively. The clustering result exhibits the landscape characteristics of the watershed. For example, the soil type S1 is mostly close to the river reach and has higher intrinsic permeability values, while most soil type S2 represents inland areas away from the river corridor. Model spinup.  Before ensemble runs, we performed two model spin-ups sequentially to ensure the physically appropriate initial model state before the full transient simulations. The first spinup ran for 1000 years with constant rainfall to reach a steady state. Initialized by the first spinup, the second spinup was driven by cyclic yearly-averaged Daymet forcing and repeatedly ran for 10 years of transient simulation. Finally, the model state from the end of the second spinup was used to initialize the transient simulations performed from 1 October 1990 through 30 September 1999.  Parameters to be estimated and ensemble runs.  We select a total of 13 parameters to be estimated, capturing the processes of snowmelt, evapotranspiration (ET), and surface and subsurface flow. Snowmelt is controlled by the snow melting rate (sm-rate) and the temperature determining the snow melting (sm-diff). The ET parameters are four coefficients used by the Priestley-Taylor equation in calculating canopy evaporation (PT-canopy), ground evaporation (PT-ground), snow evaporation (PT-snow), and transpiration (PT-trans). Surface runoff is governed by a 2D diffusive wave equation through the parameterization of Manning’s coefficient (i.e., manning_n). Subsurface hydrological properties are described by the fractured bedrock intrinsic permeability (perm-bedrock) as well as the five clustered soil intrinsic permeability (perm-S1, perm-S2, perm-S3, perm-S4, and perm-S5). Using the Sobol sequence (Sobol, 1967 ), we generated 600 parameter sets to perform the ensemble runs from 1 October 1990 through 30 September 1999, with 596 runs completed, shown in Fig. 3 (b). To further account for any numerical instability induced by varying parameter values of each run, we discard the first year of the simulation from 1 October 1990 through 30 September 1991 as an additional spin-up. We used the remaining simulation from 1 October 1991 through 30 September 1999 for model calibration. Table A.1  describes the description and sampling ranges of the parameters.  3.2 Parameter learning of ATS Learning scenarios.  Corresponding to the exploratory data analysis in Section 2.2 , different portions of the multi-year multi-gage discharge observations are used for learning the parameters. These scenarios can be grouped into two categories: (1) using only one year or consecutive multiple years of outlet discharges at Gage 01435000, from WY1991 - WY1998; and (2) using one shared year of discharge at each of the sub-catchment gages in WY1992. The first category contains an overall of 36 scenarios (i.e., ( 8 + 1 )  × 8  2    ), aimed at assessing the impact of the observation period and quantity on inverse modeling. The second category has 10 learning scenarios each of which confronts the model against one sub-catchment gage streamflow. This setup leads to a total of 46 scenarios listed in Table A.2  of Appendix . Knowledge-guided deep learning inverse mapping.  For each scenario in Table A.2 , we estimated the model parameters by using a recently developed knowledge-guided deep learning method (Jiang et al., 2023 ). The method leverages a mutual information-based global sensitivity analysis to facilitate the development of the inverse mappings from discharges to parameters and demonstrates its robustness in parameter estimation using a few hundred realizations. The general procedures are as follows (Fig. 4 ). Based on the ensemble runs, mutual information is calculated between each parameter and discharge at each time step of a given scenario (e.g., WY1991). The sensitivity analysis is then used to identify the streamflows that are sensitive to the associated parameter. For each parameter, a separate inverse mapping taking the sensitive streamflows as inputs is constructed by using a fully connected deep neural network. The resulting inverse mapping finally estimates the parameter given the observed streamflows. We followed the same approach of mutual information calculation and inverse mapping development as Jiang et al. (2023) . I   is calculated between each pair of parameter and streamflow on their joint probability density function which is discretized and estimated using 10 evenly divided bins along each dimension. The nonsignificant I   is then filtered out through a statistical significance test with a significance level of 95% based on 100 bootstrap samples. For a given calibration scenario, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) model is trained to estimate each parameter from sensitive streamflows within the calibration period of a scenario. The overall completed 596 runs are sequentially split into 496, 50, and 50 runs for training, validation, and test datasets, respectively, according to the Sobol sequence. The training set is used in the Adam optimization algorithm to train the MLP on the mean square error loss function over 1000 epochs with a batch size of 32. The validation set is used to tune the MLP architecture through hyperparameter tuning (Jiang et al., 2023 ). Once trained, the performance of MLP is evaluated on the test data on the modified Kling–Gupta efficiency (mKGE; Kling et al., 2012 ), which is a scale-independent and generalized metric that accounts for correlation, bias, and variability.  3.3 Evaluation of calibrated ATS runs For each scenario, ATS was rerun on the estimated parameters till WY2002. We confronted the calibrated streamflow simulations with observations based on mKGE, the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE; Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), and the logarithmic NSE (logNSE; Oudin et al., 2006 ): (4) m K G E = 1 − ( r − 1 )   2   + ( β − 1 )   2   + ( γ − 1 )   2        (5) N S E = 1 − ∑  i = 1  N   ( q  o , i   − q  e , i   )   2    ∑  i = 1  N   ( q  o , i   − μ  q  o     )   2        (6) l o g N S E = 1 − ∑  i = 1  N   ( log q  o , i   − log q  e , i   )   2    ∑  i = 1  N   ( log q  o , i   − μ  log q  o     )   2     ,       where r   is the correlation coefficient between the observed and simulated streamflow; β   is a dimensionless bias ratio; γ   is a dimensional variability ratio; q  o     and q  e     are the observed and estimated streamflows, respectively; i   is the time index; μ   is the mean operator; and N   is the total number of time steps in a scenario. β   and γ   are calculated as: (7) β = μ  q  e      μ  q  o          (8) γ = σ  q  e     / μ  q  e      σ  q  o     / μ  q  o       ,       where σ   is the standard deviation operator. Each metric considers various facets of simulation performance. mKGE combines correlation, bias, and variability to assess the performance in the most balanced way. NSE focuses on the capability of capturing the variability of the observations. logNSE, calculated on the logarithmic transformation, is less sensitive to extreme values or outliers and emphasizes more on low values than NSE. Note that different from deep learning inverse mapping development, we used not only mKGE but also NSE and logNSE to assess the performance of the calibrated runs in capturing the high and low flow variabilities.   4 Results     4.1 Mutual information-based sensitivity analysis Fig. 5  plots the mutual information between the parameters and the streamflow at the watershed outlet (Gage: 01435000) estimated by the 596 realizations. We rank the parameters based on their temporally averaged I   shown on the right. Streamflow is mostly sensitive to the intrinsic permeability of fractured bedrock (perm-bedrock), illustrating the importance of subsurface flow contributing to surface runoff in this watershed. The sensitivity is then followed by the four PT coefficients, the soil intrinsic permeability S1, the Manning’s coefficient, and the two snow melting parameters, affecting the streamflow in different seasons. During the low-flow regime (from summer to winter), evapotranspiration and subsurface intrinsic permeability have great control over streamflow. Meanwhile, the impact of the snow melting process starts to kick in during spring and contributes to the high flow in this wet season, with the sensitivity of PT coefficients diminished. At other sub-catchment gages, we observe similar sensitivity rankings of streamflow as shown in Fig. A.3  of the appendix.  4.2 Learning model parameters through inverse mapping Fig. 6  shows the boxplots of mKGE of the developed inverse mappings evaluated at the 50 test runs for each parameter. Each boxplot displays a data set’s 25th-75th percentiles as the box, the median value plotted as the horizontal line, the minimum and maximum values (except the outliers) as the Whisker, and the outlier points. The varying performances of these mappings are highly associated with the averaged sensitivity of the parameters to streamflow, which are shown in the bottom using the outlet gage 01435000 for illustration. The most sensitive parameter, perm-bedrock, has the best-trained inverse mappings with averaged mKGE close to 1 and the highest among all parameters. This is followed by PT-trans, sm-rate, sm-diff, and manning_n which are the second group of sensitive parameters that generate reasonably well inverse mappings with averaged mKGE above 0.6. For parameters with limited sensitivities (e.g., perm-S2, perm-S3, perm-S4, and perm-S5), streamflows are not informative to estimate these parameters whose corresponding mKGE are mostly negative. This analysis demonstrates the interpretability and robustness of the knowledge-informed inverse mappings. Impact of observation length on parameter learning. Fig. 7  shows the violin plots of the mKGE and the NSE on the test data of the inverse mapping trained on 1-yr, 2-yr, 3-yr, 4-yr, and more than 4-yr of observations. For most parameters, using only one year of observations yields mKGE of the inverse mappings with the lowest median and the largest variation. When longer periods of observations are used in learning, mKGE increases with reduced variation. Particularly, for sensitive parameters, such as PT-trans, sm-diff, and manning_n, 4 years of data proves sufficient to robustly learn the parameters from observations.    4.3 Calibrated ATS runs on estimated parameters We reran ATS for each scenario using the parameters estimated from streamflow observations by using the trained inverse mappings (see Table A.1 ). Fig. 8  shows both the calibrated ATS runs at the watershed outlet (Gage: 01435000; red lines) and the ensemble before parameter estimation (light blue lines). Compared with the 596 ensemble runs, the calibrated simulations converge to the observations plotted in the black line, in both calibration and evaluation periods. The convergence suggests reasonably good parameter estimations using deep learning-based inverse mappings.  4.4 Impact of observation length on calibrated ATS runs Fig. 9  plots the number of observation years used in parameter learning against the three performance metrics calculated for the outlet streamflow in both calibration and evaluation periods. The metrics converge when using at least four years of observations, consistent with the convergences of the corresponding H   and S H    shown in Figs. 2 (a) and (b). It illustrates that the model calibration performance largely depends on the associated information contents encoded in the observations. Additionally, the convergence of the calibration performance corresponds to the convergence of the parameter learning performance shown in Fig. 7 . When using four years of observations, the improved estimation of parameters such as PT-trans and sm-rate facilitates better-calibrated runs over using two or three years of observations. On the other hand, parameter estimation is marginally improved when more observations are used (≥   5), leading to limited improvement on the calibrated model runs. This convergence over observation years has also been observed using other metrics, such as Kullback–Leibler divergence, in a separate analysis (results not shown here for brevity). Thus, in this specific watershed, this result verifies the hypothesis that using at least four years of streamflow observations can produce model calibration as good as using the entire 8 years.  The convergence of the modeling performance, or information “saturation”, is further evidenced by the reduced uncertainty of estimated parameters over observation years. Fig. A.2  shows the boxplots of the estimation on each parameter using 1-yr, 2-yr, 3-yr, 4-yr, and more than 4-yr observations. Using multiple observation years facilitates the estimations of the parameters that are sensitive to streamflow (e.g., perm-bedrock, perm-S1, PT-trans, etc.). Indeed, for these parameters, we observe the decreased estimation range when at least four years of streamflow observations are used in the inverse mapping. On the other hand, more observations do not necessarily reduce the estimation uncertainty for other parameters that are less sensitive to streamflow (e.g., perm-S2) and have limited influence on streamflow prediction.    4.5 Impact of observation information on calibrated ATS runs We further use the scatter plots to visualize the relation between observation information content and the resulting ATS calibration performance in the evaluation period in Fig. 10 . Each scatter point is colored by the corresponding observation years used in parameter estimation.
