The total arsenic contents in sediment varied from 3.21 to 9.12 mg/kg, averaging 5.19 mg/kg, similar to the reported average level of 5–10 mg/kg for global modern unconsolidated sediment (Gan et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2014 ). Fig. 3  a–c demonstrates the total arsenic distribution in three sediment profiles. In PM01, the total arsenic contents varied between 3.21 and 9.12 mg/kg (Table S6 ), with an average value of 5.78 mg/kg. Except for the area above the water level, the arsenic-rich area in the sediment of PM01 was distributed 0–300 m from the river bank and 2–4 m deep below the water level. The total arsenic contents in PM02 and PM03 were relatively lower, and the distribution was more uniform. The total arsenic contents were 3.37 to 8.35 mg/kg (average 4.67 mg/kg) for PM02 and 4.41 to 6.75 mg/kg (average 5.16 mg/kg) for PM03 (Table S6 ).  3.2.2 Arsenic species distribution in the riparian sediment To further investigate the distribution of arsenic species in the sediment, the Tessier sequence extraction method (Tessier et al., 1979 ) was used to extract different species of arsenic, including Ex-As, Carb-As, Ox-As, Om-As, and Res-As, were extracted from the sediment samples and their distributions were investigated. The former four arsenic species exhibit mobility and bioavailability, which are considered to be hazardous since they can be released into pore water upon environmental changes, while Res-As is relatively stable and least hazardous (Ge et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020 ). Fig. 4   and Table S6  show the arsenic speciation results in three profiles. Overall, the average contents of various arsenic species in the sediment of the study area followed the sequence: Ex-As (0.015 mg/kg) < Carb-As (0.070 mg/kg) < Ox-As (0.176 mg/kg) < Om-As (0.304 mg/kg) < Res-As (4.625 mg/kg). The most stable form, Res-As, occupied the highest proportions and displayed a similar distribution pattern with the total arsenic. In PM01, Ex-As, Carb-As, and Ox-As were enriched in an area beneath the water level and 50–150 m from the river bank, where the river water and groundwater interaction was intense. Om-As and Res-As were more uniformly distributed in PM01, tending to accumulate in the same area as above. All the arsenic species in PM02 were more evenly distributed, except that Carb-As was enriched at the bottom of the profile. Only Carb-As was enriched at the bottom of points 3–3 in PM03, close to the edge of the intense river water and groundwater interaction zone. Other arsenic species, except Res-As, were more uniformly distributed, tending to accumulate in the same area as Carb-As in PM03.  3.2.3 Correlations of arsenic with other parameters in the riparian sediment The distribution of TOC in the sediment was highly consistent with the total arsenic (Fig. 3 d–f). The correlation analysis result in Table S7  indicated that the total arsenic positively correlated with TOC and Fe. It has been reported that arsenic in sediment is prone to be adsorbed by Fe minerals (Xie et al., 2009 ). Organic matter can form an As-organic or As-Fe-organic complex through ligand exchanges with arsenic or adsorbed-As (Sun et al., 2022 ). Besides, The total arsenic showed significant correlations with Al, K and Mg. The correlation with K, Mg and Al indicated that clay minerals, such as kaolinite, montmorillonite, sepiolite, illite, and rectorite may serve as important arsenic deposition matrix in the sediment, which also explained why the total arsenic in PM01 (mainly clay sedimentary) was higher than that of PM02 and PM03 (primarily sandy sedimentary). This finding was consistent with previous reports stating that arsenic distribution in sediment is generally dependent on the lithology, with the higher arsenic concentration presenting in fine particle sediment, such as clay, silty clay and silty sand layers (Fig. S5 ) (Duan et al., 2017 ). K is the composition element of clay minerals, and TOC is enriched in clay sediments (Ma et al., 2020 ). The Ex-As was negatively correlated with TOC and K (Table S7 ), implying that the clay minerals deposition generated by river water recharge is not conducive to the release of Ex-As because of the higher adsorption capacity of clay minerals (Lu et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2023 ). The Carb-As was negatively correlated with TOC and positively correlated with Fe, Mn, Ca, and Mg, the constituent elements of carbonate minerals (e.g. siderite, rhombite, calcite and dolomite). The results indicated that the organic matter input from river water was degraded and generated bicarbonate (Yu et al., 2015 ), which was converted into carbonate minerals and combined with arsenic. The Ox-As was enriched in the riparian zone, which is affected by river water and showed significant correlations with Fe, Al, and Mn. It has been reported that a Fe-oxide curtain is formed in the hyporheic zone due to the oxygen carried by river water (Jung et al., 2015 ), which could trap and immobilize arsenic. The Om-As positively correlated with TOC due to forming the As-organic or As-Fe-organic complex through ligand exchanges (Sun et al., 2022 ).   3.3 Co-transformation of arsenic and iron from pore water to solid phase 3.3.1 Co-transformation of arsenic and iron under different bicarbonate concentrations and river water ratios According to the above results, Carb-As and Ox-As were concentrated in the riparian zone affected by river water charge, which were closely related to organic matter and DO inputs from river water. In a sedimental environment, the formation of carbonate minerals is highly dependent on transforming input organic carbon into inorganic carbon. During the interaction between river water and groundwater in the riparian zone, the organic matter carried by river water can be converted into HCO3 –  (Corson-Rikert et al., 2016; Fudyma et al., 2021; Wong and Williams, 2010; Yang et al., 2023 ), which can further form a series of carbonate minerals. The substitution of CO3 /OH groups with As-O groups and forming complexes on the carbonate minerals' surface are the dominant mechanisms of As(V) adsorption (Gong et al., 2022 ). The abundant Fe(II) and HCO3 –  in the pore water of the riparian zone may form siderite, which could affect the transformation of As(III) (Guo et al., 2010 ), resulting in the formation of a Carb-As curtain below the water level and near the river bank. However, under the dual effects of DO changes caused by river-groundwater interaction and different concentrations of HCO3 – , the co-transformation of Fe(II) and As(III) from pore water to solid phase needs further investigation. Therefore, batch experiments were designed to simulate the mixing of river water and groundwater, and the co-transformation of Fe(II) and As(III) from the aqueous phase to the solid phase was detected. The coupling effects of DO gradient (reflected by river-water proportion) and HCO3 –  concentration were further studied. As shown in Fig. 5  a, the final residual concentration of aqueous arsenic decreased with the river-water proportion increasing. The presence of HCO3 –  generally promoted the solidification of aqueous As(III), especially when the river water proportion was lower than 30 %. A decreased aqueous Fe(II) concentration was simultaneously found with the river-water proportion and HCO3 –  increasing (Fig. 5 b).  3.3.2 Mineralogy characterization of the solids transformed from aqueous arsenic and iron With the decline of Fe(II) and As(III) in the aqueous phase, reddish-brown mineral precipitates were produced in batch experiments (Fig. S6 ). The XRD patterns showed that the formed solid was amorphous, except that the signals of lepidocrocite started to appear as the river-water proportion reached 90 % (Fig. S7 a). XPS analysis was further used to characterize arsenic and Fe species on the surface of the formed solid. Fig. 6   shows the splitting results of arsenic. Two peaks appeared at 44.2 eV and 45.4 eV, corresponding to the signals of As(III) and As(V), respectively (Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The formation of As(V) indicated that the mechanism of the aqueous As(III) transformation into solid arsenic is not only the adsorption and coprecipitation with the formed Fe oxides or siderite but also oxidation to As(V) before being adsorbed. With the HCO3 –  concentration increasing from 0 to 10 and 20 mM, the percentage of As(V) decreased from 66.29 % to 46.09 % and 41.72 % (Fig. 6 a–c). Meanwhile, when the proportions of river water increased from 10 % to 30 % and 90 %, the percentage of As(V) increased from 33.36 % to 46.09 % and 50.30 % (Fig. 6 d–f), indicating that the oxidation of As(III) was facilitated by DO from river water but inhibited by HCO3 –  in the pore water. XPS was further used to characterize the species of Fe, and the details of peak-differentiating and fitting are shown in Text S5. With the HCO3 –  concentrations increasing from 0 to 10 and 20 mM, the proportions of FeCO3  generated rose from 0 % to 28.65 % and 31.00 %. This result suggested that HCO3 –  reacts with Fe(II) to form siderite. Siderite could be subsequently partly transformed into Fe(III)OOH (Guo et al., 2013 ). Meanwhile, the total proportions of Fe(III) (including Fe-OOH1 and Fe-OOH2) dropped from 71.86 % to 50.30 % and 47.81 % (Fig. 7  a–c), indicating that higher HCO3 –  concentrations inhibited the oxidation of aqueous Fe(II) and siderite into Fe(III)OOH. When the proportions of river water increased from 10 % to 30 % and 90 %, the percentage of FeCO3  generated decreased from 31.55 % to 28.65 % and 22.63 %, while Fe(III) increased from 41.00 % to 50.30 % and 57.22 %, respectively (Fig. 7 d–f). Therefore, the increase of river water proportions facilitated the oxidation of Fe(II), while the rise of HCO3 –  concentration hindered the Fe(II) oxidation. XAS was adopted as an additional analysis of arsenic species in the Fe mineral generated in the presence and absence of 10 mM bicarbonate while mixing river water and groundwater (Fig. 8  , Table S8 ). With the addition of HCO3 – , the percentage of As(V) declined from 74.5 % to 59.6 %, confirming the inhibitory effects of HCO3 –  on As(III) oxidation, which was consistent with the results of XPS. This inhibitory effect is likely be ascribed to the ROS scavenging capacity of HCO3 –  (Augusto et al., 2002; Wang and Wang, 2021 ). EXAFS spectra of arsenic in the formed solids were modelled with R-factors of 0.029 (Table S8 ). The bonds of As-O and As-Fe were present in all samples. The As-O was modelled at the distance of 1.69 Å, which was consistent with ∼ 1.70 Å in AsO4  tetrahedra and provided further evidence of the oxidation of As(III) to As(V). The As-Fe bond was modelled at the distance of 3.31–3.32 Å, suggesting that an AsO4  tetrahedron with two FeO6  octahedra via double corner linkage (2C configuration), which was similar to reported studies (Maillot et al., 2013; Van Genuchten et al., 2012 ). The HCO3 –  supply influenced the number of atoms of the As-O and Fe-As, whereas the complexation geometry for arsenic to Fe mineral did not change (Fig. 8 , Table S8 ).   3.4 Summarized mechanism for the formation of arsenic-rich areas in the riparian sediment According to the results of the batch experiments, the mechanism for forming arsenic-rich areas in the riparian sediment is illustrated in Fig. 9  . The Fe(II) and As(III) flow with groundwater into the riparian zone. River water brings DO and DOC into the riparian zone. DO promotes the Fe(II) oxidation to form Fe(III)(hydr)oxides and the production of hydroxy radical (•OH). Although As(III) can hardly be oxidized into As(V) by the DO in river water, it can be oxidized by •OH generated during the oxidation of Fe(II) by oxygen (Ding et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The oxidized As(V) is then adsorbed together with As(III) onto the surface of the formed Fe(III)(hydr)oxides and siderite. The increase in river water proportions can promote the oxidation and transformation of As(III) by accelerating the Fe(II) oxidation and precipitation process. DOC can be degraded to form HCO3 – . The presence of HCO3 –  inhibits the oxidation of Fe(II) and As(III) but promotes the precipitation of Fe(II) by forming siderite. Therefore, its overall influence on As(III) solidification is compromised.   4 Conclusion The two-dimensional distribution of arsenic in the pore water and sediment was investigated, and the co-transformation mechanism of arsenic and Fe from aqueous to solid phase was discussed. The results showed that: (1) The distribution of arsenic in the pore water was related to the redox environment, and the enrichment of arsenic in the pore water tended to occur in the areas of the riparian zone with higher TOC, Fe(II), HCO3 –  and low Eh; (2) Even though the Om-As and Res-As were more abundant in the sediment, Ex-As, Carb-As, and Ox-As were more obviously aggregated in an area of the riparian zone where the interaction of river water and groundwater was intense. (3) The forming of the arsenic-rich area in the riparian sediment was derived from the oxidation of Fe(II) and As(III) from groundwater, controlled by the DO from river water and HCO3 –  from organics degradation. These results shed light on the biogeochemical process of arsenic in the riparian zone and give us a better understanding of the role of the riparian zone in arsenic restraint.
1 Introduction Dam-break flows are characterized by strong flow depth and velocity changes and by the presence of wetting and drying fronts, thus representing a typical example of highly unsteady flows. Owing to their characteristics, dam-break waves may mobilize large amounts of sediment even, comparable to the one of the flowing water (Capart, 2000 ). Moreover, the erosion, the transport, and the deposition of the sediment may directly cause damages to properties and infrastructures which may be even larger than those resulting from the water flood. Numerous laboratory experiments of dam-break flows over non-erodible bed, are reported in the literature. Dam-break flows of Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids have been object of several experimental analyses in straight (typically rectangular) channels, and through geometric singularities (such as channel constrictions and bottom sills). Moreover, the wave impact against isolated obstacles (such as walls or vertical columns of various shapes) or multiple obstacles (such as idealized urban areas) has been deeply experimentally investigated. An extensive review of the experimental researches on these topics has been recently provided by Aureli et al. (2023) . In such a review, a comprehensive overview of the considered test conditions, of the used measuring techniques along with the collected data is provided. On the other hand, owing to the increased complexity of the involved phenomena, the dynamics of dam-break waves over erodible bottom has not been so deeply experimentally investigated. The sudden erosional flow initiated by the release of a dam-break wave over a loose sediment bed was theoretically and experimentally studied by Fraccarollo and Capart (2002) . The experiments were carried out in horizontal prismatic flumes of rectangular cross-section and the bed material consisted of cylindrical PVC pellets. The validity of the theoretical results, based on the Riemann wave description of erosional dam-break flow, was shown comparing with the measured interface profiles and velocity fields. Leal et al. (2006)  performed experiments in straight rectangular flumes in which a sluice gate is rapidly removed, simulating an instantaneous and complete dam failure. Five types of bed material were used. The role that friction and inertia play on the magnitude of dam-break wave-front was put in evidence. A series of small-scale laboratory experiments of dam-break waves propagating over loose granular beds was provided by Spinewine and Zech (2007) . Two bed materials, i.e. sand and Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC), were used. Imaging techniques were employed to identify the characteristic flow regions and to derive full velocity fields. A dam-break flow in a channel where both the bed and the banks are made of uniform erodible material was experimentally studied by Soares-Frazão et al. (2007) . The initial channel cross section was of trapezoidal shape and the sand was used for both bed and bank. A non-intrusive laser sheet technique was used to measure the shape of the cross sections. Goutiere et al. (2011)  carried out experiments of dam-break flow on mobile bed in an abruptly expanding horizontal channel. The bed material consisted of a coarse uniform sand. Measurements of the flow evolution and the final bed topography were obtained using ultrasonic sensors and digital imaging techniques. Experiments of two-dimensional dam-break flows over a mobile bed made of coarse sand were presented by Soares-Frazao et al. (2012)  and used as benchmark for blind test simulations used to evaluate the modeling capabilities of different numerical models within the framework of the NSF–PIRE project, entitled “Modelling of Flood Hazards and Geomorphic Impacts of Levee Breach and Dam Failure”. The water level evolution at eight gauging points was measured as well as the final bed topography. Spinewine and Capart (2013)  performed experiments in a horizontal rectangular flume and sediment bed was composed by either PVC or sand grains. Measurements were realized combining particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) with a novel method of concentration measurement based on recording the penetration depth of a laser light sheet. Wave profiles, velocity maps and detailed measurements of evolving concentration profiles at selected cross-sections were acquired. Dam-break flows over sediment bed under dry and wet downstream conditions were experimentally investigated by Biswal et al. (2018) . The experiments were conducted in a straight horizontal rectangular flume and the bed material was sand. Downstream the gate, flow velocity was measured by using Ultrasonic Velocity Profilers and the bed elevation was also acquired at the end of the experiment. For a dam-break flow over a non-cohesive sand bed, Fent et al. (2019)  realized detailed velocity measurements both in the clear water layer and in the moving sediment layer. The channel had a rectangular cross section with glass walls to allow optical access to the bed. Finally, Liu et al. (2022)  discussed the evolution of bed morphology under 2D dam-break flow by performing a set of laboratory experiments. The tests were carried out in a glass flume with non-uniform fly ash as bed material. The water levels were measured by pressure sensors which were buried under the sediment layer. Furthermore, the bed morphology was acquired using an ultrasonic ranging system. From the above literature review it follows that although the modifications of the dam-break wave dynamics induced by the presence of erodible bed have been experimentally documented, none of the above contribution has ever addressed the wave interaction with a single or multiple obstacles for mobile bed conditions. The numerical modeling of dam-break flows over erodible riverbeds has been the focus of several studies, employing various models. The performance of the models has been assessed by comparing the numerical results with the available experimental data. The most widely used model, which is also the simplest one, is the equilibrium model, i.e., the Saint-Venant–Exner model (Graf and Altinakar, 1998 ). For this kind of model, two types of numerical strategies can be used, i.e., weakly coupled and fully coupled. In the former, the equations are solved using a two-step method (Juez et al., 2014 ), while in the latter all the equations are simultaneously solved (Soares-Frazão and Zech, 2011 ). More complex models have been proposed and adopted to simulate dam-break waves in presence of erodible bed. Indeed, single-layer (e.g., Wang et al., 2000 ), multi-layer (e.g., Swartenbroekx et al., 2013 ) or multi-phase (e.g., Di Cristo et al., 2016 ) models have been used to reproduce the features of the dam break-wave detected experimentally. However, all of the above numerical studies did not simulate any interaction of the wave with obstacles. As far as we are aware, only few numerical studies have investigated the dynamics of a dam-break wave, propagating over an erodible bed, in presence of obstacles. Inspired by a fixed-bed study for which extensive experimental and numerical data are available (Aureli et al., 2015 ), the effects of the obstacle on the changes in the bottom topography were put in evidence by Di Cristo et al. (2020) . The numerical study was carried out using a morphodynamic model belonging to the multi-phase class. With reference to the same test-case of Di Cristo et al. (2020) , the effects of sediment inertia were investigated by Di Cristo et al. (2021) . The study compared the numerical results of fully coupled equilibrium model with those of a multi-phase one. Independently of the sediment inertia, it has been shown that the presence of an erodible bed may alter the force acting on the obstacle, while the presence of the obstacle may strongly modify the morphodynamics of the erodible bed. More recently, Xu et al. (2023)  used a two-phase mesh-free method to simulate the impact of dam break wave against a rigid wall in presence of erodible bed. It has been found that the backward-moving wave caused by the wave impact against the wall can scour the sediment close to the wall itself. It is worth of note that these last three studies could not provide any comparison against experimental data, since the measurements that would have been required to this aim are not available in the literature. Therefore, the above studies do not allow to conclusively assess the reliability of the numerical models in describing the impact dynamics and to predict the force against the obstacles. The present paper combines experimental and numerical analyses with the aim of contributing to fill the two aforementioned gaps: first, provide a reliable dataset of dam-break wave impacting against obstacles in mobile bed condition; secondly, assess the reliability of the simplest morphodynamical model in predicting the impact dynamics and force. The considered laboratory setting, already used in Del Gaudio et al. (2024)  for experiments with the fixed-bed configuration, is a rectangular channel closed downstream by a vertical wall, which constitutes the obstacle hit by the dam-break wave. The bottom is covered with uniformly graded non-cohesive sand. Measurements of flow depth and of the impact force against the wall are presented and compared with the corresponding ones in identical conditions over fixed bed. The presented dataset and discussion is further widened by independently changing the water depth upstream the dam and length of the reservoir in the streamwise direction. From the numerical standpoint, the performance of a fully-coupled equilibrium model in reproducing the main features of the flow dynamics and the impact force against the wall is investigated by direct comparison with the available experiments. The manuscript is structured as it follows: the laboratory set-up and the numerical methods are described in Section 2 , whereas Section 3  discusses the results from both the experimental and the numerical points of view. Finally, conclusion are drawn in Section 4 .  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental set-up We carried out an original set of laboratory experiments at the Hydraulics Lab of the University of Naples “Federico II”. The experimental setting consisted of a rectangular Perspex channel, 2 . 92 m    long, 0 . 4 m    wide, and 0 . 5 m    high (Fig. 1 a). As indicated in Fig. 1 , the reference system has the x  ̃     axis as the streamwise coordinate, the z  ̃     axis is vertical, while the y  ̃     axis is oriented along the spanwise direction.  The channel is divided into two regions by a movable sluice gate: the reservoir on the left-hand side and the floodplain area on the right side, where a L  5   = 1 . 36    m sand bed embankment, whose thickness is s = 0 . 04    m, is placed at L  4   = 0 . 015 m    from the gate. The sand bed embankment presents a short ramp (θ = 45 °   ), followed by a p = 0 . 025    m high flat bottom. We used the same sand of the experiments carried out by Di Cristo et al. (2018) , with the following characteristics: median diameter d  50   = 1 . 60 mm   , bulk density in air ρ  s   = 2560 kg m  − 3     , porosity ϕ = 0 . 47    and internal friction angle between 37 °    and 41 °   . The sediment grain size was carefully selected in order to adopt the smallest non-cohesive sediment that could be mobilized by the flow resulting from the dam break. As shown in the following Sections, the sand layer is weakly eroded and shaped by the flow except that close to the original position of the dam. We clarify that this is not a limitation of present study, since the comparison of different test case is made considering the same availability of granular material. Before each experiments, the embankment was saturated with water. A full-width rigid wall is placed at the end of the channel. The reservoir was filled with water, and the final water level h  0     was measured using a hydrometric rod. Three different initial conditions, i.e.: h  0   = 0 . 16    m, 0.2 m and 0.24 m have been considered. We investigated three different reservoir lengths, by changing the distance of the upstream wall to the lift gate: L  1   = 1 . 50    m, L  2   = 0 . 75    m and L  3   = 0 . 50    m. For the experiments with L  1    , we used both the sand embankment and a rigid one, in order to investigate the influence of a movable bed on the dynamic of the dam-break wave and on the extent force on the endwall. The dam-break wave develops as a pneumatic system suddenly lifts the gate. The lifting velocity of about 1 . 35 m s  − 1     , allows the removal of the dam in a time, t  R    , which has been compared with the characteristic scale t  C     (Lauber and Hager, 1998 ), defined as: (1) t  C   = 2 h  0    g     ,     where g   is the gravity. For all the runs t  R   < t  C     , such that the gate removal may be considered as instantaneous (Lauber and Hager, 1998 ). Each experiment was recorded by two high-speed CCD cameras (Iron 250 Kaya Instruments) with a resolution of 5 MegaPixels. The cameras were horizontally aligned and placed perpendicularly to the channel in front of the gate and the downstream vertical end wall. A digital video recording software (Norpix StreamPix) was used to control and synchronize the CCD cameras. The post-processing of the two synchronous frames (performed by MATLAB Toolbox (Zh, 2000 ) and MATLAB stereo camera calibrator (Heikkila and Silvén, 1997 )) allowed to obtain, for each time step, a unique, referenced image devoid of focal distortion. Using image analysis, the instantaneous free surface profiles were obtained. The vertical wall at the downstream end of the channel was equipped with 9 Gefran TSA pressure transducers (P  i    ) (Fig. 1 b). As indicated in Fig. 1 , five transducers, P  0     to P  4    , are vertically spaced with a 0.02 m interval along the channel centerline, with P  0     at 0.01 m above the bottom. The transducers P  5     to P  8     are vertically distributed with the same 0.02 m spacing on the right of the centerline. Each transducer can sample pressures with a maximum frequency of 2000 Hz and an accuracy of 0.5% on the full-scale output (0.1 bar). A data acquisition system (Labjack T7) reads and converts the resulting samples into digital values that are analyzed with MATLAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2022 ). Each transducer was calibrated under hydrostatic conditions. Cameras and transducers were synchronized with the computer timeline and their acquisition frequency was set at 100 Hz. The instantaneous impact force on the end-wall induced by the dam-break wave was evaluated by integrating on the vertical axis the pressures measured by the centerline transducers, assigning to each one the corresponding influence area of a B ×   2 cm stripe. The experimental repeatability has been verified for tests with L  1   = 1 . 50 m    by performing 5 times the experiment for the same experimental condition. The RMS (Root mean square) of the pressure and force measurements cases are about 4% and 3.7%, respectively for fix bed cases and 6% and 5.6% for mobile bed ones. The relative predicted accuracy of the peak force values were 5.0%, 5.1%, 5.2% for the fixed bed for h  0   = 0 . 16    m, 0.20 m and 0.24 m, respectively; whereas for the mobile bed the corresponding values were 6.9%, 7.0%, 4.0% for h  0   = 0 . 16    m, 0.20 m and 0.24 m, respectively.  2.2 Numerical model The Saint-Venant–Exner model (SVE) is derived under the shallow-water assumption by depth-averaging the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations The integration assumes pressure distribution as hydrostatic, and unitary value of the momentum correction coefficient. The Saint-Venant–Exner equations read (Graf and Altinakar, 1998 ): (2) ∂ h  ̃    ∂ t  ̃     + ∂ q  ̃    ∂ x  ̃     = 0     (3) ∂ q  ̃    ∂ t  ̃     + ∂  ∂ x  ̃     q  ̃    2    h  ̃     + g h  ̃    2    2     + ∂ z  ̃    b    ∂ x  ̃     = − τ  b    ̃    ρ       (4) 1 − ϕ   ∂ z  ̃    b    ∂ t  ̃     + ∂ q  s    ̃    ∂ x  ̃     = 0     where t  ̃     denotes the time and x  ̃     the horizontal coordinate, h  ̃     the flow depth, z  ̃    b     the bottom elevation, respectively. In (3) , g   represents the gravity acceleration, ρ   is the liquid density and q  ̃     (resp. q  s    ̃    ) is the liquid (resp. solid) flow rate (per unit width). In what follows, the Chezy formula is used to express the bed shear stress (τ  ̃    b    ) as: (5) τ  ̃    b   = ρ q  ̃    2    C  h  2   h  ̃    2     ,     where C  h     is the dimensionless Chezy coefficient. Under the customary equilibrium hypothesis, the solid flow rate in Eq. (4)  immediately adapts to the transport capacity of the uniform flow under the shear stress τ  ̃    b    , which is evaluated through the Meyer–Peter and Müller formula (Meyer-Peter and Müller, 1948 ): (6) q  s    ̃    d g d r     = K  M P M   τ  ̃    b   − τ  c    ̃    ρ g d r      3  2     ,     where r = ( ρ  s   − ρ )  / ρ   , d   the sediment particle diameter and τ  c    ̃     the threshold shear stress for particle motion. The Meyer–Peter and Müller coefficient (K  M P M    ) was originally estimated as K  M P M   = 8   . Cordier et al. (2011)  have shown that the PDEs system (2) –(4) , whenever a formula such as the Meyer–Peter and Müller equation (Eq. (6) ) is used for the bed-load discharge, has a hyperbolic nature. The corresponding eigenvalues are the solutions of the following equation (Carraro et al., 2018 ): (7) λ  ̃    c  ̃        3   − 2 F λ  ̃    c  ̃        2   − 1 − F  2   + 1  1 − ϕ   ∂ q  s    ̃    ∂ q  ̃       λ  ̃    c  ̃       − 1  1 − ϕ   ∂ q  s    ̃    ∂ h  ̃     1  c  ̃     = 0 ,     where c = g h  ̃        and F= q  ̃    h  ̃   c  ̃        denotes the Froude number. The roots of Eq. (7)  easily follow from the Cardano’s formula, and they read: (8) λ  1    ̃    c  ̃     = 2  3   F − k  ′     cos ψ − π  3           (9) λ  2    ̃    c  ̃     = 2  3   F − k  ′     cos ψ + π  3           (10) λ  3    ̃    c  ̃     = 2  3   F + k  ′     cos ψ  3           where: (11) ψ = arccos k  ′ ′    4 k  ′             (12) k  ′   = 3 1 + 1  1 − ϕ   ∂ q  s    ̃    ∂ q  ̃       + F  2       (13) k  ′ ′   = − 2 F  3   + 18 F 1 + 1  1 − ϕ   ∂ q  s    ∂ q     + 27  c  ̃     1  1 − ϕ   ∂ q  s    ̃    ∂ h  ̃     .     In what follows, Eqs. (2) –(4)  have been numerically solved with the method described by Di Cristo et al. (2018) , as a degenerated case of the general 2D unstructured quadrilateral meshes therein considered. A mixed cell-centered (CCFV) and node-centered (NCFV) finite-volume discretization is considered, with the former adopted for the hydrodynamic variables h  ̃     and q  ̃    , defined at the grid cell centers, whereas the latter applies to the bed elevation z  ̃    b    . The corresponding control volumes are constructed around the mesh nodes by the median-dual partition (Barth and Jespersen, 1989; Nikolos and Delis, 2009 ). The first-order Harten–Lax–Van Leer (HLL) scheme (Amiram Harten and Leer, 1983 ), with second-order reconstruction of the free-surface elevation for subcritical flow (Di Cristo et al., 2018 ) is employed to compute the numerical fluxes in the CCFV discretization. The eigenvalues of the problem are given by Eqs. (8) –(13) . Owing to the hyperbolic character of the problem, the numerical stability of the solution is ensured provided that the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition is satisfied for the largest eigenvalue. Finally, the slope source term in (3)  is treated as proposed by Greco et al. (2008)  to ensure the satisfaction of the C-property. Numerical integration has been performed with a timestep Δ t  ̃   = 1 / 2048 s    and a spatial step Δ x  ̃   = 5 ⋅ 1 0  − 3   m   . Two values of the dimensionless Chezy coefficient have been considered, one for the smoother non-erodible bottom (C  h   = 22   ) and one for the coarser sediment-covered bottom (C  h   = 12   ). These values have been chosen by fitting the simulated wave tip celerities to the corresponding experimental values. An a-posteriori analysis confirmed that the considered C  h     values are consistent with those predicted by widely used resistance laws for moderate depth-to-grain size ratio i.e., below 100 (e.g., see Fig. 4 in Yadav et al., 2022 ). The simulations have been carried out by setting the physical properties of the sediment equal to the corresponding measured values and assuming d = d  50      and τ  c    ̃   = 0 . 047  ρ g d r   .   3 Results All the experimental tests both in fixed and mobile bed conditions have been numerically reproduced. The force acting at the centerline of the wall (F  ̃    ) is estimated by integrating the instantaneous pressure (P  ̃    ) distribution derived numerically, in order to compare it with the measured value. In presenting the results, the following dimensionless variables are introduced: (14) t = t  ̃    t  c     ,  z = z  ̃    h  0     ,  x = x  ̃    h  0     ,  v = v  ̃    ( g h  0   )   0 . 5     ,  P = P  ̃    P  c     ,  F = F  ̃    F  c     ,     where t  c     is defined by Eq. (1) , P  c   = γ h  0      with γ = 9810 Nm  − − 3      the specific weight of water, F  c   = 0 . 5 γ h  0  2     , and v  ̃     denotes the front celerity. 3.1 Mobile and fixed bed tests: experiments and simulations    This paragraph discusses the effect of the mobile embankment on the dam-break wave propagation and on its interaction with the vertical end wall, along with the ability of the SVE model to reproduce the phenomenon. Fig. 2  shows the measured and computed free-surface profile along the channel at times ranging between t = 4 . 8   , when water surge is propagating in the channel, and t = 18 . 8    when the dam-break wave is almost completely reflected, for both fixed bed (LabExp–FB) and mobile bed experiments (LabExp–MB). Moreover, for all performed tests Fig. 3  depicts the time evolution of the measured pressure at the transducers P  0     and P  1    , while Fig. 4  shows the time evolution of the measured force, and the comparison with the corresponding numerical predictions. Let us first discuss the process dynamics as it appears from the experiments. In the case of fixed bed, after the gate removal the wave propagates with a front celerity of about v = 1 . 78    until it reaches the end wall at t = 5    (Fig. 3 b). For the mobile bed configuration, the shape of the embankment is suddenly altered in consequence of the surge transit. After this phase, the surge propagates on the embankment at an almost constant front celerity of about v = 1 . 07    and it reaches the end wall at t = 6 . 43   , about t = 1 . 43    later than the LabExp–FB. After colliding with the obstacle, the wave forms a vertical jet that runs-up the wall. For LabExp–FB, the jet forms a 90 °    angle with the incoming water until it reaches the maximum run-up height at t = 7 . 1    (Fig. 2 c). At the wave arrival, the transducer closest to the bottom (i.e., P  0    ) measures a single impulsive pressure increase (Fig. 3 b), corresponding to a sudden growth of the force (Fig. 4 b). Later on, a counter clock-wise vortex forms due to the falling jet, causing the entertainment of a large quantity of air (Fig. 2 e,g) which produces oscillations and irregular pulsations of the pressure (Fig. 3 b). Successively, due to the further income of water, the force increases (Fig. 4 b) until it reaches the maximum value when the water level on the wall is maximum and the front of the backward propagating bore is in the middle of the floodable area (Fig. 2 g). It is worth of remark that this phase is characterized by a nearly hydrostatic distribution of the pressures acting over the wall and by the release of downstream-propagating Favre waves (Del Gaudio et al., 2024 ). In mobile bed conditions, sediment entrained by the wave front deposits close to the end wall forming a more gradual pathway for the jet impact (Fig. 2 f). The maximum run-up height is reached at t = 10   , then, the counter clock-wise vortex develops (Fig. 2 h). Since some flow momentum is likely to be transferred to sustain the bed-load transport, the flow impact on the wall is less impulsive, as indicated by the pressure signal of the P  0     transducer, which does not show the aforementioned peak (Fig. 3 b) and presents less oscillations than LabExp–FB. This corresponds to monotone and less steep increment of the force (Fig. 4 b). In terms of bed evolution, in the first part of the embankment 2-D bed forms are present (Fig. 2 d, f, h, l), while an irregular pattern is formed on the bottom close to the wall, due to the presence of the vortex during the early stage of the impact. The bed modification influences the free surface, that shows a more undulated profile than the LabExp–FB. After the impact phase (t > 10   ) the differences between the fixed and mobile bed cases are smaller (Fig. 3 b, Fig. 4 b). For the LabExp–MB, the force time series shows slightly higher values (Fig. 4 b). It could be hypothesized that this relatively small increase of the force in the nearly hydrostatic phase is due to a reduction of the overall bottom resistance resulting from the previous morphodynamical changes in the embankment shape. The other two cases behave similarly to the h  0   = 0 . 2 m    one, under both fixed and mobile bed conditions. Results show that the differences between LabExp–FB and LabExp–MB tests, in terms of wave arrival time to the end wall and maximum force values, decrease with the initial water depth (Figs. 3 and 4 ). In particular, the shift in the arrival time are t = 3 , 1 . 5 , 0 . 9    and percentage differences of peak force values are 9.3%, 6.5%, 5.0% for h  0     = 0.16 m, 0.20 m and 0.24 m, respectively. This behavior may be attributed to the reduction of the mobile bed embankment influence as the p / h  0      ratio decreases. Let us now focus on the reproduction of the process dynamics by the SVE model. It is expected that since the SVE model assumes negligible vertical accelerations, several flow features of the wave–structure interaction which were observed experimentally could not be captured. For instance, the SVE simulations cannot capture the formation of vortexes in the vertical plane nor air entertainment from the free-surface. This notwithstanding, there is still room for understanding to what extent the SVE model, despite its limitations, may reproduce some relevant aspects of this complex process, such as the time development of the impact force, its peak value and the embankment morphodymanics. In what follows, results from the fixed and mobile bed simulations are denoted as SVE–FB and SVE–MB, respectively. Fig. 4  reports the comparison of the time evolution of the measure dimensionless impacts forces with the prediction of the SVE–FB and SVE–MB simulations. The model qualitatively reproduces the shift in the arrival time of the surge at the endwall between the fixed and mobile conditions. However, there is a systematic underestimation of the temporal shift, larger for lower h  0     values. In fact, when the ratio among the embankment height and the initial water depth increases, the vertical accelerations become more prominent when the surge impacts against the embankment, with a consequent worse agreement of the SVE simulated results. The SVE simulations predict a monotonic increase of the force until the maximum value is reached, without reproducing the oscillatory behavior observed in the experiments. The maximum force value is reached slightly later than in the experiments and the same values are predicted by the fixed and mobile bed cases. The error on the prediction of the measured maximum impact force is less than 10% respect both mobile and fixed bed cases.  3.2 Effect of the reservoir length Additional experiments with mobile bed were carried out by varying the length of the reservoir aiming to assess the influence of this parameter on the impact force on the vertical wall, to extend the experimental dataset and to perform wider benchmark conditions for the SVE models. Specifically, for each initial water level h  0    , we considered the three different reservoir lengths reported in the setup description (i.e., L  i    , with i = 1 , 2 , 3    in Fig. 1 ). Consistently with the previous analysis, the measured time evolution of dimensionless impact forces are compared with those obtained from the SVE–MB model in Fig. 5 .  Changing the reservoir length at constant h  0     does not affect the wave propagation phase after the gate removal. The waves reach the vertical wall approximately at the same dimensionless time (e.g., at t ≃ 8    for h  0   = 0 . 20 m   , in Fig. 5 b). The wave propagation speed, indeed, mostly depends on the initial water depth, i.e., on the potential energy of the released fluid. As described in the previous section, the inertial forces still dominate when the dam-break wave impacts against the wall and a vertical jet forms running up on the end wall. During this phase there is no appreciable effect of the reservoir length and the measured time histories of the forces nearly superpose, for all the considered h  0     values. However, the duration of this phase, in which the impact force progressively grows, increases with the reservoir length. Correspondingly, for each h  0    , the force reached at the end of this phase also increases with the reservoir length (Fig. 5 ). For cases LabExp–MB–L3 and LabExp–MB–L2 the force values reached at the end of the inertial phase also represent the absolute maxima during the entire experiment. After the inertial phase, a quasi–hydrostatic stage follows, during which a nearly hydrostatic distribution of the pressure occurs at the end wall (Del Gaudio et al., 2024 ). During this quasi–hydrostatic phase, cases LabExp–MB–L1 reach the absolute maxima (see black lines in Fig. 5 ). The numerical simulations reasonably reproduce the general trend of the experiments. Specifically, the SVE–MB model is able to capture the two interrelated effects of the increasing reservoir length: the increase of the force peak and the time shift. In particular, the peak force is better reproduced for cases LabExp–MB–L1, where it occurs during the quasi–hydrostatic phase. As expected, the SVE–MB model under-performs when the peak force is attained during the inertial phase, characterized by non-hydrostatic pressure distribution at the end-wall. In fact, for the lower reservoir length values, L  2     and L  3    , the simulations show a progressive shift in the time of the peak force occurrence respect to the experimental value. This shift increases as the initial water depth decreases, maybe due to an increase of the influence of the embankment height for the combined effect of a lower h  0     and a smaller volume. Indeed, along with the increase of p  h  0      , the faster decay of the flow depths consequent to the smaller reservoir length further contributes to a more pronounced deviation from the assumption of a nearly-horizontal shallow flow. Despite this intrinsic limitation, the comparison of the measured and simulated peak impact forces shows that the SVE–MB model is still characterized by an accuracy of less than 10%. It is therefore to be concluded that under the investigated conditions both experiments and numerical simulations suggest that the reservoir length considerably affects the interaction of the dam-break waves with the end wall, primarily in terms of peak values and temporal evolution of the impact force. The key mechanism can be summarized as follows: the peak force is attained during the quasi-hydrostatic phase, unless the emptying of the reservoir does not significantly reduces the momentum of the incoming wave at the impact. Conversely, the peak force is associated to the inertial phase in which the incident wave runs up the end wall.   4 Conclusions A novel series of laboratory experiments have been designed and performed to examine the impact of dam-break waves on a vertical wall under both mobile and fixed bed conditions. To the authors’ knowledge, this experimental analysis of the impact force evolution under both conditions is unprecedented in the literature. The same experiments have been also reproduced through the Saint Venant–Exner model in order to evaluate its effectiveness in predicting impact force dynamics. Additional experiments explored the effect of reservoir length in mobile bed conditions. In the presence of a mobile bed, as expected, the wave dissipates more energy during propagation compared to the fixed bed configuration, resulting in a longer propagation time. Sediment transport develops unevenly along the embankment, generating both depositional and erosional regions. The sediments accumulated close to the vertical wall forms a curved ramp which leads the impinging wave to induce less pronounced oscillations in the impact force, compared to the fixed bed configuration. Our results show a slightly higher peak of the impact force occurring under mobile bed conditions. This counterintuitive finding is related to the induced mobilitation of sand particles during wave propagation, which modify the bed shape. The length of the reservoir crucially affects the impact force dynamics. For sufficiently long reservoir, the peak impact force is reached during the quasi-hydrostatic phase. Conversely, for shorter reservoirs, it occurs during the inertial phase. The Saint Venant–Exner (SVE) numerical model reasonably predicts the overall behavior of the dam-break phenomenon during both propagation over the mobile bed and the impact phases, with an error in peak impact force estimation below 10%, regardless of reservoir length. However, the numerical simulations better align with the experimental results when the peak of the impact force occurs during the quasi-hydrostatic phase. These findings suggest several new avenues for investigating the interaction of dam-break waves with physical obstacles in the presence of an erodible bed, which can alter the impact process and potentially lead to more severe damage.
1 Introduction The spatio-temporal evolution and propagation of flood and drought events are important for predicting their occurrences (Gemmer et al., 2008; He and Sheffield, 2020; Ren et al., 2023 ). Global warming and frequent human activities have intensified the global hydrological cycle, and runoff, as a key component of the hydrological cycle, is closely related to the occurrence of flood and drought events (Alfieri et al., 2017; Arnell and Gosling, 2016; Hu et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022; Zhai and Tao, 2017 ). Drought is one of the most severe natural disasters, severely affecting drinking water safety, food security, and socio-economic development (He et al., 2019; Kuriqi et al., 2021; Markonis et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2020 ). Droughts are generally classified into meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic droughts based on different types of deficiencies in the hydrological cycle (He and Sheffield, 2020; Van Loon and Laaha, 2015; Wei et al., 2024 ). Reduction in surface runoff or groundwater leads to hydrological drought (Wada et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018 ). Due to its flexible time scale, relatively simple calculation, and limited data requirements, the Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) is widely used for the assessment of hydrological drought (Muhammad et al., 2020; Salimi et al., 2021; Shukla and Wood, 2008; Zhu et al., 2016 ). Current focus on hydrological drought mainly entails the analysis of trends and driving forces of regional SRI changes (Jiao and Yuan, 2019; Omer et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020 ), as well as the propagation characteristics and driving force analysis from meteorological drought to hydrological drought (Shi et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022b ). Drought propagation is mostly analyzed using statistical methods (Apurv and Cai, 2020; Konapala and Mishra, 2020; Veettil et al., 2018 ) and hydrological modeling (Longobardi and Van Loon, 2018; Van Lanen et al., 2013 ). Statistical analysis methods, such as correlation analysis and machine learning, are used to identify climate and basin characteristics that control drought propagation. Most of the studies have only considered the changes of drought t the temporal scale and have not delved into the changes at the spatial scale, which rendered the dynamic changes and driving mechanisms of drought spatial propagation unclear. Compared to other hydroclimatic extreme events, droughts occur over larger spatial scales and longer time scales (Apurv and Cai, 2020; Herrera-Estrada et al., 2017 ). The spatiotemporal propagation of droughts may translate into a three-dimensional (latitude, longitude, and time) structure, typically spanning hundreds to thousands of kilometers and lasting for several months to several years (Konapala et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2024 ). Investigating the spatial propagation of droughts can help understand the mechanisms of drought formation. Based on spatial topological relationships and considering lag effects, hydrological droughts exhibit characteristics of spatial propagation along river channels from upstream to downstream, and from tributaries to main streams. Due to the characteristics of hydrological droughts changing along river channels, their spatial propagation is important for the rational use of water resources and for the prevention and control of water-related disasters in river basins. The concept of complex networks has been introduced to investigate the spatial propagation characteristics of droughts (Boers et al., 2013; Konapala et al., 2022; Mondal and Mishra, 2021 ). For example, Konapala et al. (Konapala and Mishra, 2017 ) constructed a complex network of droughts using the method of event synchronization, and used strength indicators of complex networks to reveal the spatial and temporal propagation characteristics of mild and severe drought events in the United States. However, this method can only qualitatively analyze the direction, distance, and intensity of drought propagation, and the propagation of droughts of different levels may be different. Like correlation analysis, it cannot quantitatively analyze the PP and duration of droughts of different levels. This study constructed a probability assessment model to evaluate the propagation of droughts of different levels, based on copula functions and conditional probability, and estimate the spatial PP and time of hydrological droughts (Li et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021 ). In the context of ever-changing environment, frequent human activities have caused hydrological processes to deviate from their natural patterns, adding complexity to the propagation of droughts (Zhang et al., 2022a ). The impacts of irrigation, water extraction, changes in land use, urbanization, and reservoir storage can either exacerbate or mitigate the variations in droughts, altering their process of propagation (Mao et al., 2024 ). Factors driving drought propagation are key to understanding the mechanisms of propagation. Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2021a ) proposed a basin comparison method, based on observed natural and anthropogenic influences, to assess the impact of climate change and human activities on the transition from meteorological drought to hydrological drought. In order to quantify the role of human activities, Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2023 ), compared the results of drought indices and PT using simulated natural and observed streamflow. Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2024 ) simulated hydrological processes under natural and anthropogenic scenarios using the PCR-GLOBWB v2.0 hydrological model, assessing how human activities affect hydrological drought and its propagation in China. To further explore the factors driving hydrological drought propagation, this study calculated the spatial PP and time of hydrological drought using natural runoff after removing human activities and observed runoff, and determined the relative contribution of direct human activities to the variability in the PT of hydrological drought. The Yellow River is the second-largest river in China. Over the past few decades, water resources in the YRB have been excessively exploited, leading to a significant decrease in surface runoff in some parts of the basin (Huang et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017 ). Under the dual influence of climate change and human activities, the YRB has experienced frequent extreme droughts, and the conflict between water supply and demand has become increasingly prominent. Analyzing the spatial propagation characteristics and driving factors of hydrological drought in the YRB is of great significance for disaster mitigation and early warning of hydrological drought in the basin. Therefore, considering the YRB as the study area, this paper explored the spatial propagation characteristics of different levels of hydrological drought in the Yellow River basin, using copula functions and conditional probability. It was assumed that the natural runoff sequence was affected by only climate change, while the observed runoff sequence was influenced by both climate change and direct human activities. Taking the variation point of the observed runoff sequence as the dividing point, this study quantified the driving factors affecting the spatial propagation of hydrological drought by comparing the propagation characteristics of hydrological drought under observed and natural runoff conditions.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The Yellow River is the second-largest river in China, located between 95°53′ and 119°05′ East longitudes, and between 32°10′ and 41°50′ North latitudes. The river flows from west to east, with a total length of 5,464 km and a basin area of 795,000 square kilometers. The YRB is situated in the mid-latitude region, belonging to the subtropical, temperate, and plateau climate zones, which are significantly influenced by the complex atmospheric circulation and monsoons. There are marked climatic differences across various regions within the basin. The multi-year average precipitation in the YRB is about 480 mm, showing a trend of decreasing from the southeast to the northwest. Precipitation is mainly concentrated in the summer and autumn seasons, accounting for 70 % of the annual precipitation in the basin. The average annual evaporation rate in the basin is up to 1100 mm, with frequent drought events, prominent conflicts between water supply and demand, and constraints on the sustainable economic development of the region. The high-intensity areas of meteorological drought in the YRB are mainly concentrated in the middle and lower reaches, and the intensity of meteorological drought on a short time scale shows an increasing trend (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Meteorological drought in the basin has a clear spatial propagation characteristic (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Human activities have increased the intensity of hydrological drought in the basin on a short time scale (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Hydrological drought shows an increasing trend on all time scales, and the trend of intensification of hydrological drought becomes more apparent with the increase of time scale (Wang et al., 2020 ). With the continuous increase in the frequency and severity of droughts, an in-depth exploration of the spatial propagation characteristics of hydrological drought and its driving factors is of great significance for the comprehensive utilization of water resources in the basin and for drought early warning.  2.2 Data The hydrological data for the YRB originates from the Yellow River Conservancy Commission. Based on the runoff data provided by them, we collected monthly observed runoff and the restored natural runoff data from 1956 to 2016 for twelve main river hydrological stations in the YRB, namely Tangnaihai (TNH), Guide (GD), Xunhua (XH), Lanzhou (LZ), Xiaheyuan (XHY), Shizuishan (SZS), Toudouguai (TDG), Longmen (LM), Tongguan (TG), Huayuankou (HYK), Gaocun (Gin C), and Lijin (LJ). Natural runoff can be understood as the volume and process of runoff within a basin that has not been influenced by human activities such as water conservancy measures and hydroelectric projects. The distribution of hydrological stations the basin is shown in Fig. 1  .   3 Methods 3.1 Mann-Kendall trend test and Rescaled range analysis The Mann-Kendall trend test was a non-parametric test recommended by the World Meteorological Organization and was widely used by many scholars to analyze trends in precipitation, runoff, water quality, temperature, and other meteorological variables (Burn and Hag Elnur, 2002; Wang et al., 2021b ). The advantage of this method was that it did not require the sample to follow a specific distribution, and the results were not affected by a few outliers. A positive value of the statistical variable Z indicated an increasing trend in the time series, while a negative value indicated a decreasing trend. When the absolute value of Z was greater than or equal to 1.96 and 2.58, it passed the significance test at the 95 % and 99 % confidence levels, respectively. The specific calculation methods could be referred to the study by Wang et al. (2021b ). The R/S analysis method, also known as Rescaled Range Analysis, was commonly used to analyze the fractal characteristics and long-term memory processes of time series (Barunik and Kristoufek, 2010; Zhang et al., 2017 ). The R/S analysis method used the Hurst index (H) to determine the fractal structure and the persistence of the state of the time series. When H was equal to 0.5, the time series was close to a random walk with no directional movement; when 0 ≤ H  < 0.5, the overall future trend was contrary to the past, indicating a sustainability of adverse states (negative correlation), and as H approached 0, the sustainability of adverse states gradually strengthened; when 0.5 < H  ≤ 1, it indicated that the overall future trend was consistent with the past, indicating a sustainability of states (positive correlation), and as H approached 1, the state became more persistent. The specific calculation methods could be referred to the study by Zhang et al.(Zhang et al., 2017 ). These two methods could reveal the trends of time series from different perspectives. In this study, the M-K test and the R/S analysis had been combined. The M-K test was used to determine whether the trend characteristics were increasing or decreasing, while the R/S method was used to analyze the persistence or anti-persistence of the seasonal scale SRI sequence trends.  3.2 Standardized runoff index (SRI) The Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) was a measure proposed by Shukla and Wood (2008 ) to describe the state of hydrological drought. The principle of its calculation was based on runoff as the foundational data, where cumulative runoff at different scales was calculated. Distribution parameters were then fitted under an assumed distribution, and finally, the cumulative probability was standardized to compute the SRI. The specific calculation method can be referred to the principles of SRI (Li et al., 2020; McKee et al., 1993; Wang et al., 2022b ). This study used the SRI at a three-month scale for May, August, November, and February to characterize hydrological droughts for spring, summer, autumn, and winter, respectively. The classification of drought grades or levels corresponding to SRI is shown in Table 1  .  3.3 Estimation of spatial PP and PT of hydrological drought 3.3.1 Copula functions Copula functions, first proposed by Sklar in 1959 (Sklar, 1959 ), can flexibly construct joint distributions with marginal distributions of any type, and have been widely applied in hydrological frequency analysis (Jehanzaib et al., 2021; Seyedabadi et al., 2020; Won et al., 2020 ). To explore the spatial propagation of hydrological drought, this study used a two-dimensional copula function to establish the joint distribution of the SRIU  sequence of upstream hydrological stations and the SRID  sequence of downstream hydrological stations.F SR I 3 U  , S R I i D    u , d     = P SR I 3 U  < u , S R I i D  < d     = C F SR I 3 U    u    , F SR I i D    d             The upstream station was represented by the three-month scale SRIU , where i  indicates the time scale (3–24 months) of the downstream station SRID ; u  and d  correspond to different drought grades for the SR I 3 U     and SR I i D     sequences, respectively. F SR I 3 U  , S R I i D       denotes the joint distribution, while F SR I 3 U       and F SR I i D       are the marginal distributions for the SR I 3 U     and SR I i D     series, respectively. C  represents a specific copula function. Since SRI is a standardized normalized variable, the normal distribution was chosen as the marginal distribution for both the SRIU  and SRID  sequences. Five copula functions commonly used in the field of hydrology and meteorology (Gaussian, Gumbel, Frank, Clayton, t) were selected as candidate functions (Fang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021 ), and the optimal copula function was selected for each grid by the least Squared Euclidean Distance (SED) and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). The SED served as a measure of the discrepancy between vectors, representing the square of the distance between two vectors. The AIC was employed as a standard for evaluating the goodness of fit of statistical models. To identify the optimal Copula function, an empirical Copula function for the joint distribution was initially defined based on the marginal distribution functions. Following this, the SED between the candidate functions and the empirical function was assessed, and the AIC values were computed. The candidate function that exhibited the least SED and the lowest AIC value was deemed to be the best Copula function.  3.3.2 Identification of PT of different drought at levels To calculate the hydrological drought PT from upstream to downstream, we first calculated the probability of downstream hydrological drought occurrence given an upstream hydrological drought at different levels using conditional probability. Then, the accumulated time length corresponding to the maximum probability was taken as the PT from upstream to downstream. If the probability value was less than 0.6, it was considered that the propagation was obstructed. Considering that the PP of mild drought was relatively low, this study mainly focused on the spatial propagation of hydrological drought under moderate, severe, and extreme scenarios, as shown in Table 2  . The drought PP and PT for different levels were calculated accordingly. Taking the occurrence of moderate or above hydrological drought in the upstream area as an example (Scenario M-m):P m - n   = P SR I i D  ≤ - 1 - 1.5 < S R I 3 U  ≤ - 1         = P - 1.5 < S R I 3 U  ≤ - 1 , S R I i D  ≤ - 1      P - 1.5 < S R I 3 U  ≤ - 1          = C F SR I 3 U    ( - 1 )  , F SR I i D    ( - 1 )      - C F SR I 3 U    ( - 1.5 )  , F SR I i D    ( - 1 )       F SR I 3 U    ( - 1 )  - F SR I 3 U    ( - 1.5 )            where i  = 3, 4, 5, …, 24, we found the maximum value of Pm-n   and its corresponding i * value. n  is the accumulated time length corresponding to Pmax  , where n  = i *-3. If n  = 0, it indicates that the PT of hydrological drought from upstream to downstream was less than one month. Therefore, Pmax   and n  represent the PP and PT, respectively, for hydrological drought from upstream to downstream. Utilizing the copula theory and the framework of conditional probability, the proposed method for calculating the drought PT not only analyzed the propagation of hydrological drought of different levels but also separated the non-drought information within the sequence of drought indices (Li et al., 2022 ).   3.4 Heuristic segmentation algorithm The heuristic segmentation algorithm is a method for detecting mean variation in non-stationary sequences, proposed by Bernaola-Galvan in the study of human heart rate data (Bernaola-Galvan et al., 2001 ), and later extended to fields, such as meteorology and hydrology (Jehanzaib et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). The heuristic segmentation algorithm divides a non-stationary time series into several stationary time series with different mean values based on the t -test, overcoming the drawbacks of previous detection methods for non-stationary time series. During the segmentation process, it uses a method of repeatedly iterating a bisection approach, which greatly reduces the computational load and is highly practical. The impact of white noise and spike noise on the heuristic segmentation algorithm is relatively small, making it a very effective method for dealing with nonlinear and non-stationary time series. The heuristic segmentation algorithm requires that the minimum segmentation scale of the sequence l 0  should be greater than or equal to 25. The length of the observed runoff series in the YRB is 61, which is suitable for analyzing the variation of observed runoff using this method. The detailed calculation process can be referenced from the literature (Wang et al., 2023 ).   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Temporal trend changes of hydrological drought To analyze the temporal trend characteristics of hydrological drought, this study combined the M-K trend test and the R/S analysis. The M-K trend test was used to analyze whether the trend characteristics were increasing or decreasing, while the R/S method was used to analyze the persistence or anti-persistence of the seasonal scale SRI sequence trends. Based on the monthly observed runoff series from 1956 to 2016, the SRI for 12 hydrological stations along the main stream of the YRB was calculated. The SRI for May, August, November, and February, on a three-month scale, was used to represent the hydrological drought of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, respectively. The statistical Z-value was calculated according to the M-K trend test, and the Hurst index was calculated according to the R/S analysis. The main results can be seen in Table 3  . The SRI had the characteristic that the smaller the value, the more severe the drought. In spring, except for TNH and XH, there was some alleviation of hydrological drought in the upstream area of the basin (above TDG); in the middle and lower reaches (below TDG), the SRI showed a significant downward trend, indicating an exacerbation of hydrological drought with the potential for continued worsening. In the summer and autumn, there was a significant downward trend in the SRI across the entire basin, with an increased risk of hydrological drought and the potential for continued worsening. In winter, except for the alleviation of hydrological drought at TNH, the trend changes were similar to those in spring. The Hurst index was less than 0.5 only at TNH and XH during the summer and autumn, and greater than 0.5 for the rest, with all Hurst indices being around 0.5, suggesting that the persistence of trend changes may not have been very enduring. According to the temporal trend changes of hydrological drought shown in Table 3 , it could be observed that hydrological drought in the summer and autumn may have been more likely to propagate spatially to downstream stations than in the spring and winter.  4.2 Spatial propagation characteristics of hydrological drought According to the trend characteristics of hydrological drought, further explore the spatial propagation process of hydrological drought. Based on monthly observed runoff sequences from 1956 to 2016, the SRI for the 12 main river hydrological stations in the YRB was calculated on a time scale of 3 to 24 months. The SRI on a three-month scale for May, August, November, and February was used to represent the hydrological droughts of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, respectively. Considering the spatial topological relationships between hydrological stations and accounting for the lag in transmission, the propagation sequence of hydrological drought was determined to be from upstream to downstream and from tributaries to the main river. Starting from the river source control station TNH, we identified the PP and PT of hydrological drought occurring at each downstream station in sequence when a hydrological drought occurred at TNH (see Table 4  ). Based on the method of estimation of the spatial PP and PT of hydrological drought, the computational results are shown in Fig. 2  . In order to facilitate the observation of spatial variation of drought characteristics, the spatial distribution map for Scenario E-m, having the longest propagation distance and a more complete propagation process, was created (Fig. 3  ). Overall, the propagation of hydrological drought in the YRB tended to decrease in probability as the distance increased, and the PT tended to increase, presenting a gradually attenuating propagation characteristics along the river channel. Moreover, as the drought level increased, the propagation distance became shorter, and the PP decreased. Hydrological drought propagates from upstream to downstream along the river channel, and the propagation process is similar to the domino effect. In spring, the main scenario of hydrological drought was E-m, which means that when the TNH station experienced extreme hydrological drought, the downstream areas mainly suffered from moderate hydrological drought. In summer, the propagation efficiency of hydrological drought was higher; when the TNH station experienced extreme hydrological drought, the downstream areas experienced moderate, severe, or even extreme hydrological drought, with the PT mainly ranging from 0 to 4 months. In autumn, the propagation distance of hydrological drought was the longest, mainly characterized by scenarios E-m and S-m, with shorter PT. In winter, the propagation distance of hydrological drought was the shortest, but the PT was longer. Cuo et al. (2013 ) found in their analysis that the presence of the Longyangxia and Liujiaxia Reservoirs significantly altered the seasonal runoff distribution in the upper reaches of the Yellow River. At both dams, the outflow during spring and winter was greater than the inflow, while the outflow during summer and autumn was less than the inflow. Thus, the negative runoff trend in summer and autumn and the positive trend in spring and winter can also be partially attributed to the operation of the reservoirs. This finding corroborates our research results. The outflow exceeded the inflow during spring and winter, with the reservoirs releasing water, which is more likely to cause drought upstream. Consequently, the propagation of upstream drought to downstream is hindered, leading to longer PT and shorter distances. This was consistent with the findings of Li et al. (2021 ), who believed that these direct human activities might to some extent alleviate severe hydrological droughts, thereby prolonging the drought propagation time. In contrast, during the summer and autumn seasons, the outflow was less than the inflow, with the reservoirs storing water, which is more likely to lead to downstream drought. Therefore, the time for the propagation of upstream drought to downstream is shortened, and the distance is extended. In summary, the propagation distance of hydrological drought in the summer and autumn seasons was longer than in the winter and spring, and the PT was shorter, indicating that the propagation efficiency of hydrological drought in the summer and autumn was higher. Based on the fluctuating changes in PT, it was speculated that the downstream hydrological drought was not only influenced by the upstream station but may also be related to its own previous state and the state of the adjacent upstream stations. To further explore the spatial propagation characteristics of hydrological drought, starting points of LZ, TDG, TG, and HYK were used to identify the PP and PT of downstream stations experiencing hydrological drought in sequence when each control station experienced drought. The computational results can be found in the appendix (Figs. 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, 1-4 ). Comparative analysis revealed that the main propagation characteristics of each control station were similar to those of TNH, but when starting from LZ, TDG, and HYK, the PT of hydrological drought was shorter, mainly ranging from 0 to 1 month. The propagation efficiency of hydrological drought in LZ was high in all seasons, with a longer propagation distance in summer and autumn. In winter, the propagation distance of hydrological drought from TDG was the shortest, only reaching its adjacent station, LM, and was obstructed when propagating to TG and downstream stations. The PT of hydrological drought from HYK was less than one month, except in winter. However, when starting from TG, the PT of hydrological drought was longer, especially in winter, reaching 14–15 months. That is to say, the upstream hydrological drought was obstructed in its propagation towards TG, and the PT of the prior hydrological drought at TG itself was prolonged. This was an intriguing anomaly. Upon reviewing the literature, we found that the TG hydrological station is the control station for floods of the Yellow River, the Weihe River, and the Beiluo River, and it is also the intake station for the Sanmenxia Reservoir (Zhang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Consequently, it is highly probable that this phenomenon was induced by human activities. For example, measures such as reservoir water release could alleviate hydrological drought during the dry season. This was in line with the results reported by Li et al. (2021 ), who believed that these direct human interventions might mitigate severe hydrological droughts to a certain extent, thereby extending the propagation time of drought. As a result, in winter, the hydrological drought at TNH could only propagate as far as LM and found it difficult to spread to TG and the downstream areas. Delving into the spatial propagation characteristics of hydrological drought, the PP and PT of hydrological drought between adjacent stations were calculated, as shown in Fig. 4  . The PT of hydrological drought between adjacent stations was mainly within 0–1 month. The PT of hydrological drought during the summer and autumn seasons was relatively short, with the PT from TNH to GD, GD to XH, LM to TG, and TG to HYK being 2–3 months during the summer. In spring, the propagation of hydrological drought from TNH to GD was obstructed, and the PT from LM to TG (scenario E-s) was 17 months. In winter, the PT from TNH to GD was 6 months, the propagation of drought from GD to XH was obstructed, the PT from XH to LZ was 7 months, the PT from LM to TG was 20 months, and the PT from TG to HYK (scenario E-s) was 15 months. In summary, it can be observed that the propagation of hydrological drought from TNH along the river channel was affected to varying degrees at control stations, such as GD, XH, TG, and HYK, leading to fluctuating changes in PT. In addition to climate change, these effects may be related to water extraction and construction of water conservancy hubs.  4.3 Comparative analysis of the spatial propagation of hydrological drought under observed and natural runoff conditions To explore the influencing factors of the spatial propagation of hydrological drought, it was assumed that the natural runoff sequence was only affected by climate change, while the observed runoff sequence was influenced by both climate change and direct human activities. The hydrological drought index was calculated separately for natural and observed runoff sequences. Taking the river source control station TNH as the starting point, the PP and PT of downstream stations experiencing hydrological drought in sequence when TNH experienced drought were identified. According to the estimation method of the spatial PP and PT of hydrological drought, the computational results are shown in Figs. 2 and 5  , and the spatial distribution for Scenario E-m is depicted in Fig. 6  . Compared with the observed sequence, the propagation efficiency of hydrological drought was higher under natural runoff conditions. Figs. 5 and 6  showed that under natural runoff conditions, when TNH experienced hydrological drought, the PP gradually decreased and the PT gradually increased with the increase of propagation distance, presenting a gradually attenuating transmission process along the river channel between upstream and downstream. The propagation distance was longer in summer and autumn, with the PT mainly being 0–1 month in summer except for TDG. The propagation distance was the longest in autumn, and the PT was less than 1 month. The propagation distance was shorter in winter and spring, with the PT mainly being 0–2 months in spring and 0–12 months in winter. When analyzing the spatial propagation of hydrological drought under observed and natural runoff conditions, focusing on scenario E-m due to its longest propagation distance and more complete propagation, the results are shown in Figs. 7, 8, 9, and 10     . When the TNH station experienced an extreme hydrological drought, the probability of downstream areas experiencing moderate or higher levels of hydrological drought generally showed a decreasing trend along the river channel, with the PP of the observed sequence being slightly lower than that of the natural sequence. In spring, compared to the natural runoff sequence, the observed sequence TNH-GD was obstructed, and the PT of the observed sequence was longer than that of the natural sequence, with the longest PT observed for TNH-LM. In summer, the observed sequence had a shorter propagation distance than the natural runoff sequence, and except for TNH-XH and TNH-TDG, the PT of the observed sequence was longer. In autumn, the PT of the observed sequence was longer than that of the natural sequence, with the longest PT for TNH-LM. In winter, the propagation distance of hydrological drought was shorter, and except for TNH-TDG and TNH-LM, the PT of the observed sequence was longer than that of the natural sequence. Compared to the natural sequence, under observed runoff conditions, the fluctuations in the propagation of hydrological drought were more pronounced, and anomalies occurred during the propagation at TNH-GD, TNH-XH, TNH-TDG, and TNH-LM. The causes of these anomalies were inseparable from the impact of human activities.
