Human intervention, such as irrigation, water extraction, and reservoir operation, has altered the frequency, intensity, and spatial distribution of hydrological droughts (Wada et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2017 ). Due to the scarcity of water resources in the YRB, reservoirs are primarily used for water supply during the dry season, which coincides with the growing season of irrigated crops that require substantial amounts of water, thus reducing the flow during the dry season (Liu et al., 2018 ). This indicates that human irrigation practices have exacerbated hydrological droughts in the region (Yang et al., 2020 ). Using winter to represent the dry season, it was observed that there were significant differences in the propagation of hydrological drought in winter compared to other seasons. The PT of the natural runoff sequence was noticeably extended, while the fluctuation in PT of the observed sequence was more pronounced. Under measured runoff conditions, the PT of TNH-GD in winter significantly increased, and the PT of TNH-TDG was noticeably shorter than the natural sequence. This may be related to the regulation of the Longyangxia Reservoir between TNH and GD, as well as the irrigation water use in the Hetao Irrigation District before TDG.  4.4 Impact of direct human activities and climate change on drought propagation To further quantify the roles of climate change and human activities in the spatial propagation of hydrological drought, the study period was divided into two sub-sequences. The sub-sequence before the change point was more stable and less affected by human activities. The change point in the observed runoff sequence was analyzed using a heuristic segmentation method, with the results shown in Table 3 . No change point was found for TNH, the change point for XH was 1990, for LJ it was 1985, and for the rest, it was 1986. For the convenience of calculation and analysis, 1986 was uniformly adopted as the dividing point, dividing the study period into two parts: 1956–1986 and 1986–2016. Starting from TNH, the PT of hydrological drought for each sub-sequence under both natural and observed runoff conditions was calculated. The results are shown in Figs. 11, 12, 13, and 14     , where the sequence after the change point showed significant fluctuations in variation. In spring, before 1986, the PT of TNH's hydrological drought was relatively stable, with the observed sequence's PT being slightly longer than that of the natural sequence. After 1986, the PT increased, and the drought propagation was obstructed for the observed sequences TNH-GD, TNH-LZ, and TNH-TDG. In summer, the PT was relatively short. Before 1986, the PT of the observed sequences TNH-LM and TNH-TG was less than that of the natural sequence, while after 1986, the PT of these observed sequences exceeded that of the natural sequences. In autumn, the PT of hydrological drought was short and stable for both observed and natural sequences before 1986, but after 1986, the drought propagation was obstructed for the observed sequences TNH-GD, TNH-LZ, TNH-TDG, and TNH-LM, with an increase in PT. Compared to spring, summer, and autumn, the variation in PT during winter was more pronounced. Compared to before 1986, the PT of hydrological drought after 1986 was shorter. The changes in PT for TNH-LZ, TNH-TDG, TNH-LM, TNH-TG, TNH-HYK, and TNH-GC showed opposite trends before and after 1986. Assuming that the natural runoff sequence was solely influenced by climate change, while the observed runoff sequence was affected by both climate change and direct human activities, the relative contributions of direct human activities and climate change to the propagation were determined by comparing the differences before and after the change point in 1986: ( 1 - Δ P T nat   / Δ P T obs   ) × 100 %   . The computed results are depicted in Fig. 15  , where negative values indicated an inhibitory effect on the propagation. On average, the relative contributions of direct human activities to the changes in the PT of drought during spring, summer, autumn, and winter seasons were 39.7 %, 62.9 %, 55.3 %, and −67.2 %, respectively. Winter showed a completely opposite contribution rate compared to the other three seasons. According to Figs. 14 and 15 , we could find that the negative contribution in winter was mainly related to the significant reduction in propagation time in the middle and lower reaches of the YRB (below TDG) after 1986. This was similar to the results reported by Zhang et al. (2023 ). The land types in the middle and lower reaches are primarily arable land, with a dense population, and therefore the highest water resource consumption. Once a drought occurs in winter, human activities can lead to more severe drought in the middle and lower reaches. Direct human activities, such as artificial water extraction, may have a greater impact on rivers in winter than during the growing season, thus shortening the PT of drought (Wan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In most cases, the PT of hydrological drought was subject to the combined impact of direct human activities and climate change. In spring, the PT of hydrological drought for the sequences TNH-GD, TNH-LZ, and TNH-XHY was predominantly affected by direct human activities, while the PT for TNH-GD was mainly influenced by climate change. In summer, the PT for the sequences TNH-GD, TNH-XH, TNH-HYK, TNH-GC, and TNH-LJ was primarily influenced by direct human activities. In autumn, the PT for the sequences TNH-LZ, TNH-XHY, TNH-TDG, TNH-HYK, and TNH-LJ was mainly affected by direct human activities, whereas the PT for TNH-XH and TNH-TG was primarily affected by climate change. In winter, the PT for the sequences TNH-TDG, TNH-GC, and TNH-LJ was predominantly influenced by direct human activities, while the PT for TNH-GD and TNH-XH was mainly affected by climate change. Existing studies have shown that human activities are the main factors affecting the changes in runoff in the YRB (Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2012 ). The construction of reservoirs has reduced the connectivity of rivers, disrupted natural hydrological processes, and has thus affected the propagation of hydrological drought (Xing et al., 2021 ). The Longyangxia Reservoir, located 133 km downstream of the TNH hydrological station, between the TNH and GD hydrological stations, began impounding water in October 1986, leading to a sudden change in runoff of the entire basin before and after 1986 (Guo et al., 2020 ), which affected the propagation of hydrological drought. In summer, direct human activities led to an increase in the PT of hydrological drought from TNH-GD after 1986, which was closely related to the construction of the Longyangxia Reservoir. In winter, the PT of TNH-GD was mainly influenced by climate change. Similarly, the construction of water conservancy hubs, such as the Lijiaxia, Liujiaxia, and Sanmenxia, has varying degrees of impact on the propagation of hydrological drought in the main stream of the YRB. The Hetao Irrigation District is one of the three major irrigation areas in China and the largest gravity irrigation area in Asia, with an irrigation area of 5.74 × 105 ha (Liu et al., 2015 ). Due to the insufficient precipitation in the area (about 150 mm/year), the entire growing season of crops requires irrigation (Xu and Song, 2022 ). In summer, the relative contribution of direct human activities to the change in the PT of drought from TNH-TDG was 66.7 %, and under the combined influence of human activities and climate change, the PT of hydrological drought became shorter. In winter, the PT of TNH-TDG was only affected by direct human activities, which was related to the operation of upstream reservoirs and the irrigation water use in the Hetao Irrigation District during the dry season. Similarly, the irrigation water used in the Yellow River Diversion Irrigation Area between XHY and SZS also affects the propagation of hydrological drought. The construction of water conservancy hubs along the way, human water extraction, and irrigation, and other direct human activities, led to changes in the PT of hydrological drought, with reservoirs playing a significant regulatory role in the propagation of drought.  4.5 Potential impact of land cover change on drought propagation Land use and land cover changes reflected, to a certain extent, the impact of human activities on the Earth's surface (Cao et al., 2015; Chi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2001 ). We discussed in Section 4.4  the construction of reservoirs and other water conservancy hubs, as well as human activities such as water diversion for irrigation, and their more direct and intense impact on the spread of hydrological drought compared to land cover changes. Land cover change was an important indicator of the impact of human activities on natural ecosystems (Liu et al., 2014 ). It could affect hydrological processes such as surface runoff, evapotranspiration, and soil moisture, thereby influencing the spread of drought (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Research by Zhao et al. (Zhao et al., 2022 ) showed that from 1990 to 2020, grasslands, forests, and cultivated land were the main types of land cover in the YRB. Since 1990, there had been a continuous trend of reduction in cultivated land and grasslands in the YRB, while the area of urban land use, forest land, and water areas generally showed an increasing trend, and the area of deserts or other land generally showed a declining trend. The main factors causing land cover change were population density, followed by altitude and temperature. In Section 4.4 , we used a heuristic segmentation algorithm to analyze the change points in the observed runoff sequence. The results indicated that no change points were found in TNH, the change point for XH was in 1990, for LJ it was in 1985, and for the rest, it was in 1986. That is, after approximately 1986, except for the upstream source station TNH, the runoff of the entire basin underwent a sudden change. Apart from the construction and operation of water conservancy hubs such as Longyangxia and the impact of irrigation water use in the Yellow River irrigation areas, land cover change could be one of the reasons for the sudden change in runoff. For example, since 1984, a series of soil and water conservation measures had been implemented, especially the “Yellow River Middle Reaches Soil and Water Conservation Key Gully Control Project Construction Plan” compiled by the Yellow River Middle Reaches Management Bureau in 1985. The main cause of the runoff mutation in 1990 was the surge in water use and the change in the underlying surface in the YRB during the 1980s and 1990s. Research results by Cuo et al. (2013 ) indicated that in the upper reaches of the YRB, the impact of land cover/use change above TNH was relatively small. This might have been related to the difference in population density: the density above TNH was low, and the density below TNH was much higher. High population density indicated intensive water use activities related to agriculture, industry, and urban areas. Therefore, the change in the PT of hydrological drought in the upper reaches of the YRB around 1986 was relatively stable. Research by Bao et al. (2019 ) found that in the middle reaches of the YRB, cultivated land was the main type of land use, followed by grasslands. Around 1980, cultivated land decreased, and forests increased. Land use/cover change was the main reason for the reduction of runoff in the middle reaches of the YRB, especially after 2000. Due to intensive water use activities related to agriculture, industry, and urban areas, the change in the PT of hydrological drought in the middle and lower reaches of the YRB was more intense. The sudden change in runoff led to changes in hydrological drought along the river channel, which in turn caused the PT of drought to become shorter or longer. For example, in the summer, direct human activities led to an increase in the PT of hydrological drought from TNH to GD after 1986, while the PT of hydrological drought from TNH to TDG became shorter. In summary, in areas with relatively dense human activities, the impact of land cover change/use on the hydrological cycle, including agriculture, industry, urbanization, and reservoir operation, became important.   5 Conclusions This study took the Yellow River Basin (YRB) as the research area and used the Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) at a three-month scale in May, August, November, and February to characterize hydrological drought in spring, summer, autumn, and winter, respectively. Based on the copula function and conditional probability, it identified the propagation probability (PP) and propagation time (PT) of hydrological drought of different levels in space. Assuming that the natural runoff sequence was only affected by climate change, and the observed runoff sequence was influenced by both climate change and direct human activities, the study used the change point of the observed runoff sequence as the dividing point. By analyzing the propagation of hydrological drought under observed and natural runoff conditions, it quantified the impact of direct human activities and climate change on the propagation. The main conclusions of the study are as follows:(1) The propagation distance of hydrological drought in summer and autumn was longer than in winter and spring, while the PT was shorter. In other words, the propagation efficiency of hydrological drought in summer and autumn was higher. Overall, as the distance increased, the PP of hydrological drought in the YRB generally showed a decreasing trend, and the PT showed an increasing trend, presenting a gradually attenuating propagation along the river channel. Moreover, as the drought level increased, the propagation distance became shorter, and the PP decreased. The spatial propagation process of hydrological drought is similar to the domino effect.  (2) Under scenario E-m, when the TNH station experienced extreme hydrological drought, the probability of downstream areas experiencing moderate or higher levels of hydrological drought generally showed a decreasing trend along the river channel, with the PP of the observed sequence being slightly less than that of the natural sequence. Compared with the natural sequence, under observed runoff conditions, the fluctuation of the hydrological drought propagation was more pronounced, mainly occurring at TNH-GD, TNH-XH, TNH-TDG, and TNH-LM.  (3) Taking 1986 as the dividing point, the study quantified the driving factors of the spatial propagation of hydrological drought. In spring, summer, autumn, and winter, the average relative contribution rates of direct human activities to the change in drought PT were 39.7 %, 62.9 %, 55.3 %, and −67.2 %, respectively. In most cases, the PT of hydrological drought was affected by the combined impact of direct human activities and climate change. The construction of water conservancy hubs along the way, human water extraction, and irrigation, and other direct human activities, led to changes in the PT of hydrological drought, with reservoirs playing a significant regulatory role in the propagation of drought.
1 Introduction The functions of water conservation projects include providing drinking and irrigation water, flood control, power generation, and shipping, and these functions play important roles in human social life (Maavara et al., 2020a; Wang et al., 2023 ). Many new dams are being constructed in South America and Asia to meet the need to expand energy production in growing economies (Grill et al., 2019; Moran et al., 2018 ). It is undeniable that the water environment problems caused by the operation of water conservation projects, such as sediment and nutrient retention, water quality deterioration and eutrophication, cannot be ignored (Lee et al., 2023; Tanvir et al., 2021 ). The backwater area extends to tributaries after the construction of dammed river reservoirs, resulting in an increased water depth and reduced flow velocity, thus forming water areas similar to lakes referred to as tributary bays (Li et al., 2021a ). The backwater area represents the connection between the different habitats of the mainstream and tributaries and is an important region for physical, chemical and biological exchange processes between adjacent habitats (Holbach et al., 2015; Ran et al., 2019 ). The Three Gorges Dam (TGD), built in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, is one of 45,000 large dams worldwide (Maavara et al., 2020b; Zhao et al., 2016 ). The eutrophication of secondary rivers in the Three Gorges Reservoir Region (TGRR) has remained one of the most severe environmental issues in China since its impoundment (Ma et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2022 ). Dramatic changes in both nutrient concentrations and hydrodynamic conditions have been observed in mainstream–tributary interactions (such as in backwater areas); these changes include extended water retention times, increasingly severe eutrophication and multiple occurrences of algal blooms in backwater areas (Hwang et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2015 ). Researchers have analysed the main driving factors of eutrophication through on-site sampling and monitoring of typical tributaries in the TGRR (Sha et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012 ). In addition, the sources and seasonal variation characteristics of nutrients in tributaries in the TGRR have been analysed via a coupling mechanism model and monitoring data, and measures for reducing nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) have been proposed to fundamentally control eutrophication (Chen et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2016 ). In addition, the hydrodynamic variation characteristics of the backwater area have been studied via hydrodynamic and water quality model simulations to explore the influences of reservoir water level operation on the water age and water quality (Gao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020 ). These studies have provided insight into the mechanism of eutrophication and algal blooms in the tributary backwater area within the TGRR. However, we should analyse the spatial and temporal variation characteristics and driving factors of the nutritional status in the backwater area of tributaries in the TGRR to formulate effective eutrophication prevention and control measures. To explore eutrophication in backwater areas, field monitoring and numerical modelling are the most commonly used methods. However, understanding the process of annual eutrophication in backwater areas is restricted to confined regions and monitoring periods due to the lack of large-scale refined monitoring data (Nong et al., 2020 ). Thus, numerical methods could be useful alternatives for assessing hydrodynamics and water quality on a fine scale and could be employed to explore the nutritional status and variation when combined with evaluation methods (Vinçon-Leite and Casenave, 2019 ). The Environmental Fluid Dynamics Code (EFDC) model can simulate three-dimensional hydrodynamic, sediment transport and water quality variations and provides detailed data support for analysing the nutritional status to overcome the high cost of large- and fine-scale monitoring (Zheng et al., 2021 ). The use of stable D-H2 O and 18 O-H2 O isotopes has been demonstrated to be effective in clarifying the complex interactions among different sources and could be adopted to explore the hydrological processes and water cycle accompanying the supply of nutrients (Wu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2016 ). Thus, in this study, the EFDC model was combined with stable isotope technology to analyse the variation characteristics and driving factors of eutrophication in the backwater area of the TGRR. The primary objectives of this study were as follows: (1) to explore hydrodynamic and water quality variation characteristics in the backwater area of a typical tributary and study the retention characteristics of N and P from the mainstream and tributary; (2) identify the spatial and temporal characteristics of the nutritional status in the backwater area and analyse the main driving factors; and (3) evaluate eutrophication prevention and control strategies for the backwater area by changing N and P inputs from the mainstream and tributary regions to provide theoretical and technical support for solving reservoir eutrophication.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Daning River is a typical first-order tributary on the northern bank of the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, spanning from 108°44′E, 31°04′N to 110°11′E, 31°44′N. The river has a total length of 250 km and covers an area of 3720 km2 . After the completion of the Three Gorges Reservoir, the Daning River became a tributary bay of the TGRR. In this paper, the 55-km long reach of the Daning River affected by backwater jacking and intrusion from the TGRR was selected as the study area (Fig. 1  ). Due to the influence of backflow in the mainstream, the N and P concentrations in the tributary backwater area significantly increase. On this basis, when the water velocity is low and the retention time increases, suitable environmental conditions create stable external conditions for algae growth, which promotes large-scale proliferation of algae and significantly increases the risk of algal blooms in the study area. Since 2003, spring blooms have been reported every year in the study area (Wang et al., 2012 ).  2.2 Isotope sampling and analysis The full operation cycle of the TGRR from 2019 to 2021 was selected for sampling and analysis. A total of 10 sampling sections were set up upstream of the backwater area, the backwater region and the main stream of the Yangtze River (Fig. 1 ), including 1 point upstream of the backwater area (S1), 7 points in the backwater region (S2-S8) and 2 points in the main stream (S9-S10). The sampling times were July 22, 2019 (low-water-level operation period), September 23, 2020 (impoundment period), December 5, 2020 (high-water-level operation period), and April 7, 2021 (discharge period). There was no stratified sampling in the shallow upper reaches of the Daning River backwater area. The backwater area was divided into left, middle and right sections, and water samples were collected at 10-m depth intervals until the bottom of the river. In the main stream of the Yangtze River, water samples were collected only from the surface layer and at a depth of 10 m because of the uniform water mixing. We obtained 69, 40, 43 and 35 samples in impoundment period, high-water-level operation period, discharge period and low-water-level operation period, respectively. The water samples were analysed for dissolved oxygen (DO), total N (TN), NO3 − -N, ammonia N (NH4 + -N), total P (TP), total dissolved P (TDP), and δD-H2 O and δ18 O-H2 O. The samples for isotope analysis were filtered through a 0.45‐μm polycarbonate membrane (Whatman) and then stockpiled in 100‐mL polyethylene bottles during sampling. All the samples were stored in a refrigerator at −20 °C until pretreatment in the laboratory. A segmented continuous flow analyser (Futura, France) was used to measure the TN, NO3 − , and NH4 +  concentrations. A digital transceiver (DLT‐100, Williams Sound, LGR, USA) was used to measure the O- and H-isotopic compositions. Each sample was injected six times, and the average of the last three measurements was used for isotope ratio calculation. The results were calibrated against international Vienna standard mean ocean water (VSMOW), and the analytical precisions for δ2 D and δ18 O were ±2 ‰ and ±0.3 ‰, respectively. The TDP concentration was determined by a UV spectrophotometer using the molybdenum blue method, as adopted by Wu et al. (2018) . The TP concentration was obtained using persulfate digestion and ion chromatography following the methods of De Borba et al. (2014) .  2.3 Mechanism model simulation 2.3.1 Environmental Fluid Dynamics Code The EFDC model developed by John Hamrick et al. (1992)of the Virginia Institute of Marine Science at William Mary University can simulate three-dimensional hydrodynamics, sediment transport, nutrient processes and toxic contaminant transport in long and narrow water bodies (Hamrick, 1992 ). This model has been widely used in the study of rivers, lakes, reservoirs, wetland systems, estuaries and oceans across countries (Bai et al., 2022; Shin et al., 2019 ). Details on the simulation processes and governing mass balance equation for each of the water quality state variables can be found in Tetra Tech, Inc. (2007) . The hydrodynamic and water quality simulation area of the EFDC model in this study ranged from the tributary bay of the Daning River to the end of the upstream backwater, and the mainstream extended from Fengjie County to Badong, which is 40 km from the intersection of mainstream and tributary, as shown in Fig. 1 . The 180-m contour line was extracted as the boundary of EFDC model meshing and terrain construction because the water level in the reservoir area ranged from 145-175 m. The EFDC model in this study used curvilinear orthogonal grids along the horizontal direction as the curved grid boundary and orthogonal grid intersection, which is especially suitable for simulating narrow or complex regional boundaries. The simulation area was divided into 4345 grids on the plane and 3 layers along the vertical direction (Fig. A.1 ). Considering the numerical stability and running time of the EFDC model, the calculation time step was set to 0.2 s. Notably, 24 and 52 h were needed to complete the one-year hydrodynamic and water quality simulations, respectively. In the EFDC model, the average error (AE), relative error (RE), and root mean square error (RMSE) are employed to evaluate the model for statistically representing the goodness of fit between the simulated and monitoring data. The AE, RE and RMSE are defined as follows (Shin et al., 2019 ):AE = ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - X i      N      RE = ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - X i      ∑ i = 1  N  O i    × 100 %     RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - X i     2   N        where O  is the observed value, X  is the simulated value of the model corresponding to the observed value in space and time, and n  is the number of observed values. The RMSE is the square root of the sum of squares of the difference between the observed and simulated values and is widely used in model performance evaluation. The RMSE should be equal to 0 under ideal conditions. The RE is defined as the percentage of the average AE to the average observed value and expresses the degree to which the average predicted value is consistent with the average observed value.  2.3.2 Data source for the EFDC model The boundary conditions required for successful operation of the EFDC model include flow boundaries, water level boundaries, water quality boundaries and meteorological data. The flow and water quality boundaries of the upper reaches of the Yangtze River were based on data of the Wanxian Station, and the water level boundary of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River was based on data of the Badong Station. Flow and water quality data (DO, TN, NO3 – , NH4 + , TP, and TDP) were collected from the Hydrology Bureau of the Yangtze River Water Resources Commission. The flow boundaries of the upper reaches of the Daning River and its secondary tributaries were based on data obtained by Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model simulations (Chen et al., 2022 ). Meteorological data of the atmospheric pressure, air temperature, wind speed and direction, rainfall, evaporation, relative humidity and solar radiation in the study area were downloaded from the National Meteorological Science Data Center (https://dict.cnki.net/index# ) (Figs. A.2-A.5 ). Water quality boundary data for the Daning River and its secondary tributaries were obtained mainly from the Wushan Environmental Monitoring Station. Details of the model boundary conditions can be found in the Supplementary Material .  2.3.3 Data treatment The flow, water level and meteorological boundaries data collected in this study are daily scale, which are directly input into the EFDC while constructing the model. The water quality data obtained in this study are monthly-scale, the EFDC model obtains daily-scale water quality boundary data based on the built-in interpolation method and the input monthly-scale water quality data.   2.4 Simulation of the nutritional status It is generally accepted that excess nutrients (N and P), a low flow velocity, and suitable temperature and light conditions are the most crucial factors for phytoplankton growth (Abbas et al., 2023; Barathan et al., 2023 ). Many studies have shown that TN, TP, flow rate and water temperature exert key impacts on the occurrence of eutrophication in the backwater area of tributaries in the TGRR (Xiang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Therefore, in this study, the EFDC model, used to simulate TN, TP, flow rate and water temperature in the study area, was combined with the scoring method to evaluate the nutritional status of the water body to obtain the nutritional status-sensitive area and period of the backwater area. This method was further subdivided on the basis of oligotrophic, mesotrophic and eutrophic types, and appropriate indicators were selected as evaluation factors, which were assigned values ranging from 0 to 100 points; moreover, the linear difference method was used to obtain the scores between the various grades and the comprehensive score to reflect the nutritional status of the target water body (Shu, 1993 ). Since the tributaries of the Daning River are above the mesotrophic level and eutrophication occurs mainly in spring and summer under suitable temperature conditions, the water temperature was obtained via the piecewise value method (Table 1  ). A temperature within the suitable growth temperature range (18℃<T<25℃) for phytoplankton was assigned a value of 60 points. When the temperature occurred outside the optimum growth temperature range (T<18℃ or T>25℃), a value of 40 points was assigned corresponding to the mesotrophic state of the tributaries. When the temperature was not suitable for algae growth, a value of 30 points was assigned corresponding to the oligo-mesotrophic state. This method can be expressed as follows:M = ∑ i = 1  n  M i  n      where M , n  and Mi   are the score value of the target water nutritional status, the number of selected indicators and the score value of the evaluating indicator, respectively. The study area can be classified into different nutritional statuses based on M  values: if M <30, then it is oligotrophic; if 30 ≤ M <50, then it is mesotrophic; if 50 ≤ M , then it is eutrophic; if 50 < M≤60 , then it is slightly eutrophic; if 60 < M≤70 , then it is moderately eutrophic; if 70 ≤ M , then it is severely eutrophic (Table 1 ).   3 Results 3.1 Isotopic resolution of the intersection characteristics of the mainstream and tributary water masses 3.1.1 δD and δ18 O characteristics of the mainstream and tributary Fig. 2   shows the δD and δ18 O abundance values of the water masses during the different operation periods. The isotope values of the water masses in the upstream tributary of the backwater area (δD: −74.779 ‰ ∼ −57.544 ‰; δ18 O: −11.106 ‰ ∼ −9.611 ‰) are significantly greater than those in the mainstream (δD: −84.079 ‰ ∼ −71.326 ‰; δ18 O: −12.293 ‰ ∼ −11.100 ‰) (P<0.01). This occurs because the water depth of the upstream tributaries of the Daning River in the backwater area is shallower. High evaporation leads to the fractionation of hydrogen and oxygen isotopes, and heavy isotopes are retained in the water mass (Chen et al., 2018 ). The δD and δ18 O values of the water masses in the backwater area (δD: −85.965 ‰ ∼ −60.204 ‰; δ18 O: −12.347 ‰ ∼ −9.282 ‰) occur between those of the mainstream and upstream tributaries in the backwater area during the different operation periods and show a trend towards a gradual decrease from the end of the backwater area to the tributary bay. The δD and δ18 O values of the water masses during the low-water-level operation period are greater than those during the other periods (Fig. 2 c), primarily because the higher temperature during the low-water-level operation period aggravates isotope fractionation of the water body. In addition, rainfall and the exchange of water masses cause changes in the isotope values of the water masses. However, there are differences in the intersection characteristics of the mainstream and tributary water masses during the different operation periods. Fig. 2  shows that the δD and δ18 O values of the mainstream water masses during the high-water-level operation period, water storage period and discharge period approach those near the tributary bay, which indicates that the water masses of the mainstream and tributary bay were basically evenly mixed during these three operation periods.  3.1.2 Mixing characteristics of the mainstream and tributary In this study, the average δ18 O values of the mainstream and upstream tributaries in the backwater area were used to analyse the contribution rates of these two types of water bodies to the backwater area. The vertical distributions of the mixing ratios in the backwater area were obtained via interpolation and are shown in Fig. 3  . The mixing ratio in the backwater area ranged from 18 % to 100 %, with an average value of 53.5 % during the sampling period. Furthermore, the approximate path through which the mainstream water mass entered the backwater zone could be detected by the vertical variation in the contribution ratio. The results indicated that the invasion characteristics of the mainstream water masses were heterogeneous during the different operation periods. During the high- and low-water-level operation periods (Fig. 3 a and c, respectively), the mainstream water mass intruded into the backwater area mainly through the surface and middle layers, while the upstream tributary of the backwater area water mass mainly entered the backwater area through the bottom layer; these results are consistent with the mainstream invasion characteristics of other tributaries in the TGRR (Liu et al., 2012; Li et al., 2020 ). During the discharge and impoundment periods (Fig. 3 b and d, respectively), the mainstream water mass mainly entered the backwater area through the bottom layer, descended into the middle layer and then ascended into the middle layer. The average contribution rates of the mainstream water mass were 41 %, 38 %, 61 % and 74 % during the high-water-level, water discharge, low-water-level and impoundment operation periods, respectively.   3.2 Hydrodynamic and water quality simulations 3.2.1 Calibration and validation The EFDC model of the study area was calibrated on a daily scale considering multiple variables (WL, WT, DO, NO3 – , TN and DTP). The results indicated that the model exhibited acceptable performance in reproducing hydrodynamic and water quality variations. The statistical results of model calibration at the different sites are provided in Tables A1-A2 , and comparisons of the time series of the simulated and observed values are shown in Figs. A.8-A.16 . The hydrodynamic module showed favourable agreement between the observed and simulated WT values (AE: 0.51; RE: 3.07 %; RMSE: 0.52) (Table A1 ) and WL values (DC station: AE: 0.21, RE: 0.238 %, RMSE: 0.569; WS station: AE: 0.105, RE: 0.066 %, RMSE: 0.145) (Fig. A.6 ). This indicated that the module suitably reproduced the water balance related to inflow/outflow, precipitation and evaporation, and the model produced a reasonable thermal dynamic process, which provides a basis for verifying the dynamic process of the water quality. Consistent with the water level and water temperature, the model could also reproduce the water quality status in the study area well (Tables A1-A2 and Figs. A.8-A.16 ). Overall, the EFDC model could be used for further analyses.  3.2.2 Distributions of N and P in the backwater area In this study, the characteristics of N and P variations in the backwater area of the Daning River were simulated and analysed by extracting the TDP, NO3 –  and TN concentrations along the longitudinal section of the river (Fig. 4  ). The average concentration of nutrients in each grid during the different operation periods was calculated. The inflection point of the variation in the N and P concentrations along the backwater area could be considered the farthest point of invasion of the mainstream. The NO3 –  and TN concentrations in the backwater area showed a decreasing trend from the intersection of mainstream and tributary to the end of the study area during the different operation periods. After reaching the inflection point, the NO3 –  and TN concentrations fluctuated within a narrow range: 1.2 mg L-1  during the high-water-level operation and impoundment periods and 0.9 mg L-1  during the discharge and low-water-level operation periods. The variation in TDP in the backwater area slightly differed from that in N, which was mainly reflected during the low-water-level operation and discharge periods, in which the TDP concentration near the tributary bay and at the end was higher than that in the central region of the backwater area. This might occur because the P input from the upstream tributaries is diluted with increasing water volume, resulting in a decrease in the P concentration in the central backwater area. In addition, biogeochemical transformation of nitrogen in water could explain this difference. Overall, the influence range of mainstream intrusion into the tributaries differed among the four operation periods. The variations in nutrient concentrations during the high-water-level, low-water-level and discharge operation periods occurred at 4.5, 12 and 6 km, respectively, in the backwater area (Fig. 4 a-c). The small difference in the NO3 –  and TN concentrations in the backwater area during the impoundment period indicates that the mainstream imposed a far-reaching influence of approximately 30 km (Fig. 4 d). These results are consistent with the isotope analysis results, indicating that the intrusion of water masses and contaminants from the mainstream is an important reason for the deterioration in the water quality and eutrophication in the backwater area of the Daning River.  3.2.3 Intersection fluxes of N and P in the backwater area The water mass exchange capacity in the backwater area exhibited seasonal variation characteristics (Fig. 5  ). It was lower in spring and summer and higher in autumn and winter, which is related to the anti-seasonal operation process in the TGRR. Water mass migration is also accompanied by the convergence cycle of N and P. Fig. 6   shows the N and P fluxes in the Daning River tributary bay. The N and P fluxes in the tributary bay were mainly input from the mainstream to the tributary and were only balanced during the high-water-level operation and impoundment periods. The average annual TN, NO3 –  and TP retention levels were 217.47 ± 98.57 t, 346.91 ± 85.36 t and 124.79 ± 16.18 t, respectively, which are 0.94 %, 1.77 % and 12.03 %, respectively, of the total inputs to the mainstream and tributaries (Table 2  ). The NH4 +  output was −209.48 ± 56.85 t, approximately 12.86 % of the total input from the mainstream and tributaries (Table 2 ). The possible reason was that the denitrification of nutrients in the tranquil flow state within the backwater area resulted in a higher NH4 +  output than the input, and P is easily deposited in the low flow state, inducing higher P retention.   3.3 Identification of eutrophication risk areas in tributary backwater areas Figs. 7–9     show the temporal and spatial variation characteristics of the nutritional status index in the backwater area of the Daning River tributary in 2018, 2019 and 2020. As shown in the diagrams, the tributary backwater area is in a mesotrophic status overall, and eutrophication is mainly observed from May-October, namely, at the end of the discharge period, during the low-water-level operation period and during the impoundment period of the TGRR. The areas prone to eutrophication in the backwater area can be divided into three main parts: the end of the backwater area, the open area of the backwater area and the tributary bay. The water body at the end of the backwater area is in a state of eutrophication from May to June and from September to October, with mesotrophic conditions during the remainder of the time. These findings are consistent with the actual situation in the backwater area, where severe algal blooms occur in May and October every year. The water body in the open area of the backwater area is eutrophic from May to July and from September to November, while in other months of the year, it is mesotrophic. After the impoundment and operation of the TGD, the middle and lower reaches of the tributaries were greatly affected by the backwater area of the mainstream Yangtze River, resulting in a lower flow velocity and notable widening of the water surface, which created ideal environmental conditions for algae growth (Li et al., 2020 ). The water body in the tributary bay is in a eutrophic state from April to October, and the nutritional index is greater than 60. From November to March of the next year, the nutritional index is less than 60 (mesotrophic state). The tributary bay is the most intensive area for merging the mainstream and tributary regions of the TGRR and features complex hydrodynamic and water quality conditions.   4 Discussion 4.1 Rationality analysis of the results The D and 18 O stable isotopes of H2 O can provide useful information for tracing water sources in rivers based on the unique isotopic signatures of different water sources (Holloway-Phillips et al., 2023 ). The water mass from the mainstream was predominantly partitioned into the Daning River during the different operation periods, which is consistent with the findings of previous studies for the same tributary but is lower than that in the tributaries near the TGD (Yang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2016 ). The different sampling times during the same operation period and the distance from the tributary to the dam could explain the diverse results. Water discharge in the mainstream is controlled mainly by anthropogenic reservoir regulation and consequently controls the mixing process in the backwater area (Li et al., 2020 ). The variation in the contribution rate of the mainstream water mass also reflected the difference in incidence during reservoir operation. The mainstream water mass carries abundant nutrients into the backwater area of tributaries, which exacerbates severe environmental issues associated with secondary rivers in reservoirs (Fu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2008 ). The spatial and temporal distribution characteristics of the nutrient status in backwater areas not only help us to better understand the occurrence of eutrophication but also provide insight into the underlying factors and facilitate the formulation of targeted prevention and control measures (Andreoni et al., 2022 ). The monitoring data of eutrophication in the TGRR indicated that these tributaries were generally above the mesotrophic status, and algal blooms were mainly concentrated from April to October (Chen et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2018 ). Studies of reservoir tributary backwater areas have indicated that the trophic state index has significant spatial heterogeneity and that tributary estuaries are sensitive to eutrophication (Li et al., 2020; Suresh et al., 2023 ). A comparison with related studies proved that the nutritional status evaluation results of this study are reasonable and can represent the actual situation in the study area.  4.2 Factors inducing nutritional status variation In addition to the intensification of human activities, including wastewater discharge, agricultural fertilizer use and energy consumption, the construction of large dams has led to notable accumulation of sediments and nutrients, resulting in excess nutrients in many aquatic systems or changes in nutritional chemistry (Chen et al., 2022; Glibert, 2017; Suresh et al., 2023 ). Periodic eutrophication and cyanobacterial blooms also occurred in the backwater area after impoundment of the TGD (Hu et al., 2020; Zuo et al., 2024 ). The nutrient status in the backwater area exhibited significant spatial and temporal variation characteristics (Figs. 7-9 ), which is the comprehensive result of various factors, such as nutrients, hydrodynamic conditions and water temperature (Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021 ). The water level of the reservoir slowly decreases during the discharge period, while at the end of the tributary backwater area, the water level remains relatively static due to the influence of the inflow tributary. In addition, chemical and biomass fertilizers are used to maintain soil fertility and increase crop production at the spring cultivation stage, and gradually increasing precipitation causes higher nonpoint source N and P emissions (Chen et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2021 ). However, it is undeniable that excessive nutrients and basically static hydrodynamic conditions are not factors inducing eutrophication in these regions. The reason is that the N and P concentrations in the tributary exceed the limit concentration for eutrophication (Fig. 4 ), and the hydrodynamic characteristics here do not change significantly throughout winter or spring. Therefore, a gradually increasing water temperature (Fig. S4 ) should be the factor inducing eutrophication and algae blooms. Studies have shown that temperature is an important factor in eutrophication, and temperatures above 20 °C promote the growth and reproduction of algae (Li et al., 2020; Romarheim et al., 2015 ). From September-October, relatively static hydrodynamic conditions (flow velocity) should be the factor inducing water eutrophication, as the mainstream intrudes into this area during the impoundment period, decreasing the water velocity (Xu et al., 2022 ). The tributary bay has always been the intense confluence region of mainstream and tributary in the backwater area, and it is a region with frequent eutrophication and algal blooms in the TGRR (Wang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Blooms in the tributary bay of the reservoir were mainly concentrated from April-May and September-October, while the chlorophyll-a content in the tributary bay was higher from June-September (the low-water-level operation period) (Yang et al., 2019 ). Studies have proven that stratified flow caused by temperature differences significantly affects water exchange and algae transport between the reservoir mainstream and tributaries (Liu et al., 2012 ). The algal bloom coverage rate in tributary estuaries could reach 82 %, while the mainstream could invade through the middle or bottom layer, and the tributary could enter through the surface layer (Li et al., 2021a ). The seasonal development and disappearance of temperature stratification in the reservoir result in seasonal deepening of the mixing depth and promote the seasonal onset and succession of phytoplankton blooms (Longo et al., 2021 ). Hydrogen and oxygen isotope analysis of the water masses (Fig. 3 c) and the EFDC model simulation results indicated that the mainstream water masses invaded the tributary bay region in the form of intermediate-density flow. In addition, the retention of excess P in the estuarine region provided the limiting nutrients required for algae growth (Fig. 6 ). After the impoundment period, uplift of the water level caused a large water mass of the mainstream to invade the tributaries, and vertical water mixing near the tributary bay was severe, which was not conducive to algae growth (Buta et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2017 ).  4.3 Suggestions for management Scholars have reached a consensus on the treatment of eutrophic water bodies, and it is necessary to control the pollution source first and then implement ecological restoration accordingly (Ogura et al., 2022; Schindler et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2023 ). According to the US National Rivers and Stream Assessment, 46 % of rivers and streams were in poor biological conditions by miles, and P and N were the most prevalent chemical stress factors assessed (National Rivers and Streams Assessment 2008–2009 ). Many countries and regions in the world have formulated relevant laws and regulations on pollutant control and management (Rycewicz-Borecki et al., 2017; Calomeni et al., 2017 ), the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System authorized by the Clean Water Act is the main means for the protection and restoration of surface water bodies such as rivers and lakes in the United States. Due to the implementation of the system, the pollution of water bodies in the United States has been well controlled and the water quality has been significantly restored (Rycewicz-Borecki et al., 2017 ). Previous studies have shown that the TN and TP concentrations in the mainstream and tributaries of the TGRR far exceed the surface water III standard, which is required for water function zoning (Li et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the input boundary of the EFDC model of the upstream tributaries and mainstream of the Yangtze River during the nutritional status-sensitive period was set to the surface water III standard (TN: 1.0 mg L-1 , TP: 0.05 mg L-1 ) to study the effect of N and P inputs on the nutritional status in the backwater area, and the results are shown in Figs. 10 and 11   , respectively. Fig. 10  indicates that the nutritional status at the end of the backwater area changed significantly after the upstream tributaries reached the III water quality standard. The nutritional status index during the nutritional status-sensitive period decreased from 60 to 70 (eutrophic state) under the actual water quality conditions to 50–60 (mesotrophic state) and even below 50 (mesotrophic state). High- and extreme-risk areas of agricultural pollution are often distributed along rivers, so the farmland adjacent to important river systems must be regulated, and riparian protection is indispensable for sustaining aquatic ecosystems (Chen et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2021 ). The improvement in the water quality of the upstream tributary helps to improve the nutritional status at the end of the backwater area and mitigate the outbreak of algal blooms, but it exerts a limited effect on estuaries and reservoir bays far from the upstream tributary boundary, which reflects that simple water quality standards are not enough to eliminate the eutrophication risk in the backwater area (Abbas et al., 2023 ) and that the tributary bay is notably affected by intrusion of the mainstream (Li et al., 2021b ). Fig. 11  indicates that the nutritional status of the tributary bay and the reservoir bay area in the backwater area improved relative to the actual input water quality conditions after the mainstream and tributary reached the level III water quality standard. The nutritional state index decreased from 65 to 70 (eutrophic state) to 55–60 (mesotrophic state), and the eutrophic state area significantly decreased. The results proved that improving the water quality in the mainstream is helpful for improving the nutritional status in the tributary bay and reservoir bay areas within the backwater area, but it cannot completely reduce the nutritional status index to mesotrophic state status. The backwater area of a reservoir tributary contains artificial static water, and its hydrodynamic characteristics vary with periodic reservoir operation (Wang et al., 2021 ); additionally, eutrophication in this region is the result of various influencing factors (Suresh et al., 2023 ). Nonpoint source pollution in watersheds at different scales should be reduced through fertilization management and BMP optimization to satisfy water quality standards (Liu et al., 2022 ). The United States Clean Water Act and Water Quality Act make clear requirements for the control of agricultural non-point source pollution to prevent, prevent and mitigate the occurrence of pollution, and put forward prevention and control measures (Diamond, 2018 ). It is also necessary to study reservoir operation strategies under regular objectives (flood control and power generation) to alter the hydrodynamic conditions in the confluence area to prevent and control the proliferation of algal blooms (Song, 2023; Vigouroux et al., 2020 ).   5 Conclusion and future work In this study, we employed multiple-isotope analysis, the EFDC model and a scoring method to investigate the hydrodynamic, water quality and nutritional status characteristics of the backwater area of a typical tributary in the TGRR. Our analysis revealed that the water mass and N and P in the backwater area mainly originated from the mainstream region of the Yangtze River, and the period of nutritional status sensitivity in the backwater area mainly ranged from May to October every year. The water temperature and intermediate-density flow were the factors inducing deterioration in the nutritional status at the end of the backwater area and the tributary bay, respectively. The risk of algal blooms in backwater areas should be reduced by strictly controlling the water quality of upstream tributaries and the mainstream to meet water quality standards. Moreover, a more systematic and reasonable operation scheme for reservoirs should be explored on the basis of nutrient reduction. The suitable conditions for algae growth in the backwater area of reservoir tributaries can be eliminated by adjusting the hydrodynamic characteristics of the tributary bay region through optimal reservoir operation strategies. This paper only studied the spatial and temporal characteristics of water nutrient status and identified the potential eutrophication risk area by coupling hydrodynamic water quality model and scoring method. The method used in this study was helpful for the macroscopic grasp and understand the nutritional state of the water body. Due to the variability and complexity of the mechanism by which eutrophication is driven, the method used in this study cannot profoundly elucidate the drivers of eutrophication and its influence. In the future, more finely simulation should be implemented based on the results of this paper and water chlorophyll sampling data to explore the driving mechanism of eutrophication in the backwater area. Future work should explore the nonlinear relationship between reservoir water level variations and key hydrodynamic parameters according to the interaction between the tributary backwater area and the mainstream of reservoir, and optimize the reservoir operation scheme in combination with the influence threshold of hydrodynamic parameters on eutrophication, so as to achieve the goal of eutrophication prevention and control in the tributary backwater area.
1 Introduction Climate change has led to increased frequency of extreme precipitation events, causing large-scale floods in various regions, where arid or semi-arid regions have been heavily impacted. In 2022, the Pakistan peak flood, occurred on August 25th, claimed more than 200 lives in a week (ABC News, 2022 ). In July 2023, flash floods killed thousands of people in northeastern Lybia (CNN News, 2023 ). In semi-arid regions, when precipitation intensities exceed usual levels, the volume of water would surpass the soil’s infiltration capacity, leading to the formation of flash floods that rapidly propagate downstream (Maidment, 1993 ). In the past decades, hydrologists have utilized regional rainfall-runoff (RR) models to predict severe flood events and propose effective prevention measures based on scenario analysis. RR models can generally be classified into two categories: process-based models (PBMs), which are based on physical laws, and data-driven models (DDMs), which automatically extract features and approximate functions from data. PBMs use physical equations to characterize runoff generation and concentration processes. The model parameters have physical significance and the prediction results are interpretable (Beven, 2012 ). Various PBMs have been constructed for streamflow forecasting, including lumped models like the Xinanjiang (XAJ) model (Zhao, 1992 ) and the GR4J model (Perrin et al., 2003 ), and distributed models like the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) (Arnold et al., 1998 ) and the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model (Liang et al., 1994 ). These models have performed well in streamflow forecasting and scenario analysis under different conditions (Brocca et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2018 ). However, in some regions, the presence of spatial-temporally heterogeneous hydrological relationships (e.g., in semi-arid regions) or insufficient observational data (e.g., in ungauged watersheds) can result in inadequate understanding and unreliable prediction of hydrological processes (Bahat et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2022; Kratzert et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2023 ). Without requiring prior physical knowledge and complex modeling procedures in PBMs, RR processes can also be conveniently simulated using DDMs. DDMs work by extracting information from hydrological data and can generally produce more accurate prediction results and easier utilizations than PBMs (Remesan & Mathew, 2015 ). The use of DDMs can be traced back about 170 years when linear regression analysis was used to extrapolate flood processes (Mulvaney, 1851 ). Later, researchers applied autoregressive models and similar methods in streamflow forecasting (Box et al., 1970 ; Hsu et al., 1995; Karlsson & Yakowitz, 1987 ). However, the linearity assumption of these methods limits their effectiveness in simulating complex RR processes. Since the 1990 s, machine learning (ML) methods such as support vector machines (SVMs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs) have been used in RR modeling (Bray & Han, 2004; Hsu et al., 1995 ). Although ANNs have universal approximation capabilities, their practical effectiveness is limited by computational resource and network architecture. Subsequently, with continued improvements in network design and computational power, deep learning (DL) has brought about a revolution in various domains like image recognition and time series analysis, and holds great potential for use in RR studies. Several researchers have shown that DL outperforms PBMs in simulating RR with extreme events and in ungauged watersheds (Kratzert et al., 2018, 2019; Yin et al., 2021, 2022 ). Additionally, transfer learning techniques such as pre-training-fine-tuning provide new approaches for RR modeling (Kratzert et al., 2019 ). The application of DL in streamflow forecasting is growing rapidly. Initially, due to their ability to process sequential data, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks received a lot of attention from hydrologists (Gao et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 1997; Kratzert et al., 2018 ). Later, large-scale networks with an encoder-decoder structure, such as Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al., 2014 ) and transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017 ), have also been explored for their potential use in RR studies (Xiang et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2021, 2022 ). Compared with simple RNNs, Seq2Seq that is powered by multi-head attention mechanism can process inputs with varying lengths and excels at multi-step predictions (Yin et al., 2021 ). Nevertheless, without a sufficient number of valid training samples, these large-scale networks with extensive parameterization are prone to overfitting (Domhan, 2018 ). To address this issue, researchers are seeking to enhance the learning capabilities of simpler networks (Chen et al., 2021a ; Zhou et al., 2021 ). One such network is the temporal convolutional network (TCN), proposed by Lea et al. (2016, 2017) . TCN applies causal dilated convolution layers to fit temporal correlations and uses residual connections to enhance the learning capability. Bai et al. (2018)  showed that TCN exhibits a superior performance compared to RNNs through studies on time-series data. As a result, TCN is receiving increasing attention for their potential applications in water science, including streamflow forecasting (Lin et al., 2020; Van et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2023 ). Although both PBMs and DDMs have been widely used in streamflow forecasting, their successful application in semi-arid regions presents challenges. The infrequency of hydrological events and lack of high-quality observations hinder both the construction of reliable DDMs and the design of adequate PBMs (Pilgrim et al., 1988 ). Variability in sequences is an inherent expression of temporal heterogeneity in hydrological features (Esling & Agon, 2012 ). Semi-arid regions, shaped by their distinct climatic conditions, exhibit a unique set of hydrological characteristics. Unlike humid or semi-humid regions where moisture is abundant, semi-arid regions are predominantly characterized by high evaporation rates, leading to extended periods of water deprivation in the soil. In contrast to arid regions, semi-arid regions experience infrequent but heavy or sustained rainfall during their wet periods. This rainfall saturates the soil, altering the runoff generation mechanisms. These distinct climatic conditions contribute to the temporal heterogeneity of hydrological features, a characteristic uniquely observed in semi-arid areas. The mixed and stochastic runoff generation regimes, combined with the high temporal heterogeneity of hydrological patterns, can result in a transition from infiltration-exceed to saturation-exceed mode within a single rainfall event, posing a significant challenge to the temporal processing capabilities of existing models. To address the issue of temporal heterogeneity in the semi-arid basins, research on PBMs primarily focuses on flexible modeling (Liu et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2023 ) and time-varying parameters (Jeong & Kim, 2023 ), while studies on DDMs concentrate on data segmentation (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) and model enhancement (Kapoor et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023 ). Among these, one can identify and segment time periods during which the physical process remains consistent, and simulate RR in these periods separately to reduce the complexity of modeling. Segmentation methods based on clustering with alignment distance (Chu et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2020 ; J. Wu et al., 2023 ) or similarity indicators (Fang et al., 2022; Mishra et al., 2013; Ouyang et al., 2010 ) of sequence samples have been used in streamflow forecasting to reduce the modeling challenge and improve process understanding. However, determining the optimal number of clusters and ensuring an adequate number of valid samples within each cluster is difficult, particularly in semi-arid regions where infrequent hydrological events further complicate the situation. As a semi-arid watershed located in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, the Wei River basin displays a pronounced temporal heterogeneity in precipitation conditions (Chen et al., 2021b ). In this basin influenced by the East Asian monsoon, high temperatures and low rainfall are common, but summer storms can scour the previously desiccated soil and carry sediment downstream, leading to the coexistence of flash floods and water scarcity (Li et al., 2013 ). Effective regional streamflow forecasting are necessary to understand these problems. Jin et al. (2022)  utilized one PBM (i.e., XAJ) and three DDMs (i.e., SVM, LSTM and CNN-LSTM) to simulate RR processes from 2000 to 2020 in 54 major sub-watersheds of the Yellow River, including the Wei River basin. Their results suggest that on average, DDMs outperform PBM by approximately 0.15 in terms of Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), which is significant given that the mean NSE of DDMs is only 0.60. Chang et al. (2015)  used the VIC model to simulate daily RR processes in the Wei River basin. Despite selecting a study period (from 1956 to 1970) with low levels of human interference on the RR process, the simulated NSE remained at a modest level of 0.74 in the study area. These experiments suggest that to overcome predictive challenges in semi-arid basins, both PBMs and DDMs must be flexible enough to match the temporal heterogeneity of hydrological features and runoff generation regimes. Additionally, the model used must be robust enough to effectively extract relationships from infrequent hydrological events. In this study, we propose an effective modeling framework for streamflow forecasting in semi-arid basins that combines a novel data segmentation method with DL. This approach introduces the attention mechanism to TCN to enhance its ability to handle heterogeneous sequences. Given the limited and heterogeneous hydrological data, the segmentation method (BPX) enhances the performance of TCN by integrating the Bai-Perron breakpoint detection (Bai & Perron, 1998 ) with the XGBoost algorithm (Chen & Guestrin, 2016 ). The BPX method autonomously divides the original sequence into wet and dry subsequences from hydro-meteorological predictors, allowing for separate modeling of each subsequence to increase reliability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using nearly 20 years of hydro-meteorological data from the Wei River basin of China. Our proposed approach can provide new tools that may address the above issues.  2 Data and methods In this section, we will demonstrate the theories and implementation details of the proposed methods. Performance of our approach will be demonstrated with nearly 20 years of hydro-meteorological data from the semi-arid Wei River basin of China (Fig. 1  ). 2.1 Data sources and pre-processing The Wei River basin is characterized by a continental monsoon climate. The annual precipitation in this area ranges from 400 to 800 mm, while the annual potential evapotranspiration spans from 1100 to 1500 mm. Over 65 % of the precipitation takes place from July to September. In this study, daily measurements of runoff data at Huaxian (6209 days, from 2001 to 2017) and Linjiacun hydrometric stations (8035 days, from 1995 to 2016), and meteorological feature sequences are utilized for streamflow forecasting. The meteorological data include daily precipitation (Prec), evapotranspiration (Evp), mean temperature (Tem), mean air pressure (Prs), mean ground surface temperature (GST) and relative humidity (Rhu). When forecasting runoff values with DDMs, pre-processing of raw data is required to facilitate a proper training of model. Here, interval normalization is applied to the meteorological data to standardize each feature sequence within the range of [0, 1], and the Box-Cox transformation is implemented on the runoff data to make them compliance with normal distribution:(1) R ∼  λ    = R  λ  - 1  λ  , λ ≠ 0 ,    ln R , λ = 0 ,                where  R = ( r 1  , r 2  , ⋯ , r n  )    is the original runoff sequences, R ∼  ( λ )     is the transformed data, λ   is the parameter estimated by maximum likelihood estimation to ensure that R ∼  ( λ )    N w X , σ  2      . To objectively represent the overall variance and minimize the risk of random errors, this study utilizes cross-validation for time-series, where the entire sequence data are split into a + 1    equal segments for a   times cross-validation. For the t   th cross-validation set, the preceding t   segments are treated as the training set, while the ( t + 1 )    th segment serves as the validation set.  2.2 Rainfall-Runoff modeling based on data segmentation and deep learning Water allocation conflicts and drought/flood disasters in the semi-arid basins emphasize the need for an effective RR modeling method. However, the temporal heterogeneity in hydrological patterns poses a significant challenge to traditional modeling approaches. To address this challenge, here we propose a novel framework for effective streamflow forecasting in the semi-arid basins (Fig. 2  ). Based on the pre-processed data, we adopt Bai-Perron analysis to segment historical runoff sequences and identify the breakpoints between the dry and wet periods. These segmented samples are then used to train an XGBoost model for classification with hydro-meteorological variables as predictors. This model can be used to identify future data as in the dry or wet period. After that, we utilize the entire time-series data to train a basic DDM (e.g., TCN with attention). Using dry and wet data, this model is fine-tuned to obtain two sub-models for the wet and dry periods, respectively. Theories and implementation details of the proposed approach are presented below. 2.2.1 The data segmentation method (a) Bai-Perron Analysis. Bai-Perron analysis (Bai & Perron, 1998 ) is a widely used method for detecting changing points caused by significant external events in economic time series (Furuoka, 2017; Weideman et al., 2017 ). In this study, we employ this method to partition annual runoff sequences into three segments by identifying the two most significant changing points between the dry and wet periods within each year. For more details, one can refer to (Bai & Perron, 1998 ). (b) The XGBoost Algorithm. However, Bai-Perron analysis cannot account for changes in runoff and meteorological sequences simultaneously and lacks the ability of future prediction. To address this issue, XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016 , see its Figs. 1-6      for a better understanding) is adopted to enhance Bai-Perron analysis. XGBoost is an improved implementation of the Gradient Boosting Decision Tree method (Friedman, 2001 ). It works by continuously splitting the features and reducing the residuals with gradient descent:(4) c ^  i  t  = ∑ k = 1  t  f k  X i    = c ^  i  t - 1   + f t  X i    , f k  ∊ F ,     where c ^  i  t    is the predicted value (wet or dry) of the i   th sample in the t   th iteration, X i    is the value matrix of the i   th sample, f k  X i       is the fitting function of the k   th tree model, F   is the spatial ensemble of the trees. In this study, XGBoost is implemented using the scikit-learn package (Pedregosa et al., 2011 ).  2.2.2 Streamflow forecasting with attention-based TCN In several experiments conducted by Bai et al. (2018) , TCN outperformed RNNs in time-series analysis. In this study, TCN is employed as the suitable DDM for streamflow forecasting, with the addition of a self-attention mechanism to further enhance its performance. The architecture of the TCN-attention model is depicted in Fig. 3 . In contrast to the commonly used same or valid padding convolution in image recognition, TCN employs causal dilated Conv1D for extracting information from time-series data (Tompson et al., 2015 ). As shown in Fig. 3 , the dilated causal Conv1D applies the filter over an area larger than its length by skipping input values at fixed intervals, allowing the network to achieve large receptive fields with just a few layers. The residual connection links intermediate inputs to the output of a group of convolution blocks, facilitating smoother gradient flow and ensuring that important features are carried through to the final layers without adding computational load to the network. To prevent overfitting, layer normalization and spatial dropout are employed. The self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017 ) has had a significant impact in the field of natural language processing. When added as a layer after the input layer, it can extract relationships between items from the global sequence. In this study, the TCN model is enhanced with a self-attention layer to leverage both the local perception capability of TCN and the global weighting property of self-attention. The self-attention layer operates as follows:(5) O = { H  1  , H 2  , ⋯ , H n  } W ,      (6) H i  = f A W i  Q  , A W i  K  , A W i  V    ,     (7) f Q , K , V   = s o f t m a x QK  T  d k      V ,     where O   is the output of the attention layer, H i     is the hidden state at position i   of the attention layer, W = { W  Q    ,  W  K    , W  V  }     is the weight matrix, A = { a 1  , a 2  , ⋯ , a m  }    is the input with m   elements, Q = A W  Q     is the query (Q) vector used for matching values, K = A W  K     is the key (K) vector to be matched with Q  , V = A W  V     is the value (V) vector to be extracted by paired Q - K   , s o f t m a x x   = e  x i   ∑ e  x i        is an activation function that normalizes its input values, d k    is the dimension of K  , respectively. To balance numerical deviation and trend error in streamflow forecasting with DL, a combined loss function is developed by combining L1  and L2  terms:(8) L = δ ∗  ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r i  p r e d      2   ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r  ¯    o b s      2    + 1 - δ   n  ∗  ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r i  p r e d     r i  o b s    ,     where δ   is a coefficient that is either artificially assigned or determined through calibration, r i  o b s     is the observed value of flow at moment i  , r i  p r e d     is the predicted value of flow at moment i  , r  ¯    o b s     is the mean value of observations, and n   is the number of samples, respectively.   2.3 Benchmark comparison settings This study focuses on comparing RNNs, including classical RNN, LSTM, and GRU, with TCN for use in streamflow forecasting. To evaluate the effectiveness of the BPX method for data segmentation, standard DDMs will be compared with their BPX-enhanced counterparts. The structures and hyper-parameters for the DDMs are provided in Table S1  (Huaxian station) and Table S2  (Linjiacun station). Default values/settings are adopted for unlisted hyper-parameters. The XAJ and GR4J models represent the PBMs for comparison. We use a particle swarm algorithm to optimize these models’ parameters based on parameter ranges and subsurface characteristics in semi-arid regions (Zhao, 1992; Perrin et al., 2003 ), as shown in Table S3  and Table S4 . We also incorporate a comparison with autoregressive models, represented by Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average Model (ARIMA), to mitigate the potential inadequacy of “online model” comparisons. All tests are run with Python 3.8 (Ubuntu 18.04), TensorFlow 2.5.0 (Abadi et al., 2016 ), and CUDA 11.2 with Nvidia RTX 3090 (24 GB GPU). To fully evaluate our models’ performance in semi-arid streamflow forecasting, we use the same training and validation datasets for our approach and other models. The predictive performance is evaluated using four metrics: mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), Nash efficiency coefficient (NSE; Nash & Sutcliffe, 1970 ), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE; Gupta et al., 2009 ):(9) M A E = ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r i  p r e d      n  ,     (10) R M S E = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r i  p r e d      2    ,     (11) N S E = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r i  p r e d      2   ∑ i = 1  n  r i  o b s   - r  ¯    o b s      2    ,     (12) K G E = 1 - c o  - 1    2  + μ p r e d   μ o b s    - 1    2  + σ p r e d   σ o b s    - 1    2    ,     where c o    is the Pearson correlation coefficient between observed and predicted runoff sequences; μ   and σ   are the mean value and standard deviation of runoff sequences.   3 Results and discussion Based on the data and methods described above, we conducted comprehensive analysis of various methods for simulating RR process in semi-arid regions. After pre-processing the data, we used the BPX method to segment wet/dry periods and evaluated the results. We then simulated the RR process at the Wei River basin using different models. These methods were tested under different time periods, including the entire prediction period, dry/wet periods, and period for multi-step predictions. By comparing the performance of different prediction models, we identified the most promising one for handling hydrological heterogeneity in semi-arid regions. We also proposed a strategy to enhance multi-step predictions. 3.1 Segmentation of dry and wet periods We used the Bai-Perron method to divide the intra-annual runoff sequences into dry-wet-dry periods. This method requires a complete dataset of intra-annual runoff and relies on univariate characteristics for segmentation. Then we used historical samples with the segmentation results from Bai-Perron analysis to train an XGBoost model. In this model, the meteorological-hydrological variables, including daily precipitation, evapotranspiration, mean temperature, mean air pressure, mean ground surface temperature and relative humidity, are employed as predictors to enable the identification of future dry/wet periods across multiple years and variables. The outcomes obtained by both the Bai-Perron and BPX methods are illustrated in Fig. 4 . The Bai-Perron method identifies the mutation point within each year as the moment with the maximum mutation rate based on univariate variation. This excludes certain pre-flood events from wet periods (e.g., years 2004, 2010, 2017 in Fig. 4 ). In contrast, the BPX method may include or exclude some pre-flood events in wet periods due to the influence of extra meteorological/hydrological predictors. Thus, the BPX method is more general and might be able to provide more informative segmentation results.  3.2 Performances of different modeling approaches 3.2.1 Model performances within the entire prediction period For the entire prediction period, we calculated metrics for both PBMs and DDMs by combining all four validation sets in time-series cross-validation (Huaxian station: 2004.08.22–2017.12.31, Linjiacun station: 1999.06.01–2016.12.30). We trained/calibrated each DDM (except ARIMA) separately in each cross-validation and derived the results in Fig. 5  from 20 repetitions. Among all the evaluated models, the PBMs exhibit an overall weakness in the streamflow forecasting of the study area, with the lumped PBMs showing inferior performance compared to the distributed PBM. Specifically, the lumped XAJ model displays the poorest performance across various metrics, including MAE=80.12 m3 /s, RMSE=213.36 m3 /s, NSE=0.437, and KGE=0.415 in the upstream basin of Huaxian station. In contrast, the lumped GR4J model produced MAE=87.34 m3 /s, RMSE=271.03 m3 /s, NSE=0.548, and KGE=0.427. As for the distributed PBM, VIC, it achieved an NSE of 0.72 during the period from 1956 to 1970 (Chang et al., 2015 ) in the upstream basin of Huaxian station. Besides, after the calibration, we employed the ARIMA (5, 0, 5) model, where the order of the autoregressive term is 5, the degree of differencing is 0, and the order of the moving average term is 5. The ARIMA model achieved MAE=48.44 m3 /s, RMSE=130.95 m3 /s, NSE=0.766, and KGE=0.827. For the basic DL models without using the data segmentation or attention mechanism, we observed varying performances that TCN>LSTM>GRU≈RNN, as demonstrated in Fig. 5 . If the attention mechanism is added to LSTM or TCN, further improvements in model performance can be obtained, especially for LSTM. If we fine-tune the basic DL models (classical RNN, GRU, LSTM and TCN) with dry/wet period-specific data respectively, significant improvements can be observed. For the LSTM/TCN model, it appears that incorporating the attention mechanism yields less improvement compared to the enhancement achieved through the inclusion of the BPX method. BPX-TCN obtained the best overall performance and thus it was suggested as an adequate model for streamflow forecasting in the semi-arid regions. We also implemented streamflow forecasting with various DDMs for the upstream basin of the Linjiacun station for the entire prediction period.
