The structural designs and hyper-parameters of these models are provided in Table S2 . As shown in Table 1  , the performance outcomes are similar to those at the Huaxian station. However, at the Linjiacun station, extremely low runoff (<10 m3 /s) frequently occurred during dry seasons, in contrast to high runoff during flood seasons. This distinct process poses challenges in developing a universally applicable RR model for the entire periods, impeding the efficacy of DL models with or without adopting the attention mechanism. In contrast, the BPX method demonstrated its great potential in improving the performance of DDMs in simulating this heterogeneous process.  3.2.2 Model performances within the dry or wet period As illustrated in Fig. S1 , the autocorrelation analysis for runoff and correlation analysis between runoff and meteorological features reveal distinct meteorological and hydrological characteristics between the dry and wet periods. These findings provide further evidence of the temporal heterogeneity in hydrological patterns in the semi-arid Weihe River basin. To delve deeper into the heterogeneity and evaluate the ability of our proposed approach, we conducted a comparative analysis focusing on streamflow forecasting in specific dry or wet period for the upstream basin of the Huaxian station. In this subsection, the TCN and TCN-Attention models were first trained using the entire sequence, based on which the BPX-TCN and BPX-TCN-Attention models underwent fine-tuning by using subsequences corresponding to the dry or wet period. We then investigated the performances of the above four models in specific periods of dry or wet condition. The comparison presented in Fig. 6  reveals that, the wet periods characterized by higher runoff variation and larger water volume present a notable challenge in prediction, with higher errors, particularly in metrics such as MAE and RMSE. Based on the TCN model, the inclusion of different additional modules brings distinct effects. Specifically, the incorporation of the BPX method alone reduces prediction uncertainty, whereas the addition of the attention mechanism alone increases the uncertainty of the model. Therefore, while the attention mechanism may enhance specific models, caution must be exercised when incorporating it alone or in combination with the BPX method. Consistent with previous findings, the BPX-TCN model exhibits superior performance compared to other tested models in both the dry and wet periods. To validate the effectiveness of the attention mechanism and additional meteorological inputs, we compared two input configurations using both a classical time series model (LSTM) and its enhanced version (LSTM-attention) across different rainfall conditions. The input data types examined were: (1) past runoff data alone, and (2) a combination of past runoff and meteorological data. The findings, illustrated in Fig. S3 , demonstrate that integrating the attention mechanism improves model performance, particularly during wet periods. This enhancement allows the model to capture more intricate meteorological-runoff relationships, thereby yielding more precise and consistent runoff prediction outcomes. To better understand the model’s performance during the crucial wet period, which is a primary source of error in streamflow forecasting, this study further analyzed and compared three distinctive flood events, as shown in Fig. 7  . The metric values in Fig. 7 (a-c) show improvement in the order of TCN, BPX-TCN, TCN-Attention, and BPX-TCN-Attention. Specifically, BPX-TCN-Attention performs similarly to TCN-Attention, while BPX-TCN is comparable to TCN. This suggests that the attention mechanism may contribute more improvement to TCN’s performance than the BPX method during the wet periods. The attention mechanism’s global view is helpful for model fitting and bias correction in flood prediction. Nevertheless, as shown in Fig. 7 (b), adding the attention mechanism to TCN may still underestimate the extreme runoff due to a lack of referable historical samples for training, which can be possibly addressed through improving the quantity and diversity of the training data.  3.2.3 Performances of TCN-Based models in Multi-Step predictions The weak correlation between different features and the high variability in runoff sequences observed in Fig. S1  already present a significant challenge for single-step prediction. When considering multi-step predictions, the autocorrelation coefficient of runoff drops below 0.5 after a lag of 4 days. Moreover, the correlation coefficients between meteorological factors and runoff are even lower, which fail to provide effective guidance for the model predictions. For multi-step predictions, the same cross-validation datasets used for the upstream basin of the Huaxian station were employed. Here, the input data include hydro-meteorological features over a seven-day period, while the output data consist of the corresponding runoff values in the next seven days. The wet/dry period of the seven days corresponding to the outputs is identified by the BPX method. As shown in Fig. 8  , the performance of multi-step predictions is not as satisfactory as in the previous subsections, with a trend of BPX-TCN≈BPX-TCN-Attention > TCN>TCN-Attention across all four metrics. The comparison between TCN and TCN-Attention is consistent with previous results, where the addition of attention brings a substantial predictive improvement to TCN. However, both BPX-TCN and BPX-TCN-Attention outperform the standard TCN model. Notably, BPX-TCN no longer maintains a clear advantage and even underperforms BPX-TCN-Attention after Day 5. These findings are consistent with the flood hydrograph results presented in Fig. 7 , suggesting that including attention can improve results in more challenging tasks. Specifically, BPX-TCN-Attention demonstrates enhanced performance in multi-step predictions.  3.2.4 Basin response time and model choices Generally, there is a strong correlation between the physical characteristics of the basin and the selection of hydrological models. In our case, we observed that the performance of a certain model is significantly affected by the duration of input data. Before model calibration, we conducted an analysis of feature correlation and the related lag time for the upstream basin of both Huaxian and Linjiacun stations, as shown in Fig. 9  . The upstream basin of Huaxian station covers an area of 106,798 km2 , which is more than three times the area of the upstream basin of Linjiacun station, which spans 31,066 km2 . The upstream basin of Huaxian station also has a more complex distribution of underlying surface characteristics, as illustrated in Fig. S2 . According to the feature correlation and lag time analyses presented in Fig. 9 , the outlet runoff at Huaxian station exhibits a longer response time to internal precipitation events or other meteorological features, with a peak correlation with about a four-day lag. In contrast, the peak correlation for Linjiacun station occurs at a lag of approximately two days. Furthermore, urban development within the upstream basin of Linjiacun station is relatively limited, resulting in a smaller impervious surface area. However, in the region between Linjiacun station and Huaxian station, larger cities have led to a concentrated distribution of impervious surface. The urban heat island effect has significantly influenced the meteorological-runoff relationship in the upstream basin of Huaxian station, notably enhancing the correlation between runoff and both evapotranspiration and relative humidity. Consequently, the rainfall-runoff relationship in the upstream basin of Huaxian station should consider longer meteorological characteristics. When analyzing the effect of input duration on the performance of BPX-TCN-attention model at both the Huaxian and Linjiacun stations, we observed phenomena that support the aforementioned viewpoints, as shown in Fig. 10  . Regarding input duration, excessively short or long prior input durations led to suboptimal outcomes. It is crucial to ensure sufficient prior information without being diluted by overly lengthy irrelevant inputs. The appropriate input duration for the upstream basin of Huaxian station is five to seven days, while it is around two days for the upstream basin of the Linjiacun station. This aligns with the previous meteorological-runoff correlation analysis shown in Fig. 9 , reflecting the difference in response times of outlet runoff volumes to precipitation events in the two nested basins. Therefore, when training DDMs, the input duration significantly impacts model performance. Similarly, this lag time is also reflected in the calibration of XAJ model. Multiple analyses collectively validate the consistency of real-world physical patterns in the performance and selection of the model in use.  3.2.5 The capacity of proposed models to capture meteorological-runoff relationships Acknowledging the challenges of multi-step forecasting, we undertook a thorough examination on the effect of model inputs. In the upstream basin of Huaxian station, we investigate whether the BPX-TCN-attention model could extract the meteorological-runoff relationship and whether the input of meteorological features had a positive effect on the forecasting. This was achieved by comparing the results of inputting individual meteorological features (as shown in the first six boxes in Fig. 11  ) with those of inputting all six meteorological features simultaneously (as shown in the last blue box in Fig. 11 ). Our results indicate that, separately inputting meteorological features brought limited performance to the model, with precipitation yielding the most promising results among them. However, simultaneous input of all six meteorological features led to a notably improved simulation performance, even outperforming the XAJ model in certain metrics. Further, to investigate the importance of input features on the model prediction, we conducted an analysis of the Shapley values of different TCN models. This investigation maintains its focus on runoff prediction at the Huaxian station with different input durations, as depicted in Fig. 12  . The findings reveal that the standard TCN predominantly prioritizes runoff, precipitation, and temperature as key features for prediction, with a particular emphasis on information within the past three days. The incorporation of the attention mechanism resulted in the model elevating the importance of air temperature and ground surface temperature of the previous day. Additionally, it strengthened the importance of evapotranspiration and relative humidity, thereby amplifying the influence of water consumption factors on the final runoff prediction. However, it diminished the importance of precipitation, consequently impacting the prediction stability of TCN-attention. In further model refinement, BPX-TCN-attention adjusted the importance of other features and shifted its focus towards precipitation. Moreover, it implemented distinct strategies for wet and dry periods. In general, both TCN-attention and BPX-TCN-attention models, to varying degrees, deviate from TCN’s focus on runoff, offering deeper insights into the relationship between meteorological features and runoff. This nuanced approach aligns more closely with empirical and physical understandings. With respect to the input duration, both the TCN-attention and BPX-TCN-attention models focused more on the features of the past four to seven days. This pattern partially aligns with the findings of the correlation analysis and implicitly reflects the basin lag time of the upstream basin of Huaxian station. Both enhancement models allocated importance to inputs at further past time steps compared to TCN, aiming to extract effective relationships from a longer-term perspective.    4 Conclusions and remarks Several studies (Chen et al., 2021b ; Wu et al., 2022 ) and our own analysis have demonstrated the complex relationships between hydro-meteorological features and high runoff variation in the semi-arid basins. This work proposes and tests a new framework for streamflow forecasting to address the challenges originated from temporal heterogeneity of hydrological patterns and infrequency of extreme events that are commonly encountered in semi-arid basins. Our approach involves the integration of a novel data segmentation method, BPX, with an attention-based DL model. In BPX, we first use Bai-Perron analysis to identify the changing point between the wet and dry periods within each year. To enable predictive ability, we further train an XGBoost model with hydro-meteorological variables as predictors. In the BPX method, the function of Bai-Perron analysis is to capture the runoff variation, and the XGBoost classifier aims to achieve future prediction ability and incorporate meteorological features. In a “runoff-oriented and meteorological-supported” manner, the segmentation of dry/wet periods by the BPX method can be more informative than the Bai-Perron analysis alone. The TCN model that balances model performance and structural complexity is suggested as the basic DDM. The attention mechanism is used to further improve the performance of TCN. For comparison, the XAJ model, the GR4J model, the ARIMA and three other DDMs (classical RNN, GRU and LSTM) with or without the attention mechanism that have been extensively used were also tested. For the DDMs, a pre-training-fine-tuning strategy was employed to convert the basic DL model (pre-trained by full sequences) into period-specific models (e.g., BPX-TCN) fine-tuned with dry/wet period sub-sequences, facilitating customized prediction for distinct periods with relatively consistent hydrological processes. The proposed BPX-TCN and BPX-TCN-Attention models demonstrate promising performance in runoff prediction in the Wei River basin. After systematic benchmarking, it is found that: (1) Compared to DDMs like LSTM and PBMs like XAJ that have been widely used in hydrological research, TCN offers a more effective solution for RR modeling in semi-arid regions. (2) Both the BPX segmentation and the attention module enhance the performance of streamflow forecasting and facilitate a more profound exploration of objective physical laws. (3) Among the various modeling approaches, BPX-TCN demonstrated superior performance throughout the entire prediction period, achieving a Kling-Gupta efficiency of 0.91, compared to 0.45–0.88 for the other models, while BPX-TCN-attention provides more accurate predictions of floods and multi-step predictions. Although DDMs show promising performance, their physical interpretability remains an active area of research. To address this, several strategies can be employed. (1) Model-Agnostic Methods: Techniques like SHAP (Shapley additive explanations), as used in this study, can be utilized to interpret feature importance and explain predictions. Our findings reveal a specific input–output relationship: the prediction of future runoff is strongly correlated with a basin’s physical characteristics and historical meteorological sequences. (2) Incorporating Physical Laws: To enhance the robustness of DL model predictions, it is feasible to encode known physical laws into the training process of DDMs. This ensures that the predictions are more consistent with existing scientific knowledge. (3) Quantifying Uncertainty: Assessing the uncertainty of model predictions is crucial. In this study, we evaluated uncertainty by running repetitions of the same modeling method. For practical applications, model training and inference can be implemented within a Bayesian framework, or an ensemble of multiple PDMs and DDMs can be used to enhance prediction reliability. (4) As a state variable in the RR process, the initial soil moisture condition can significantly affect streamflow simulations, particularly during extreme events like droughts and floods (Li et al., 2023; Sazib et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024 ). Therefore, it is crucial to consider the spatiotemporal relationships among soil moisture, precipitation, and streamflow. Integrating soil moisture data, such as reanalysis records, as an input can enhance the accuracy of RR models, whether using PBMs or DDMs, especially in poorly gauged basins. These strategies merit further exploration to improve the reliability and interpretability of streamflow forecasting models.
1 Introduction As one of the widespread global environmental problems, eutrophication and accompanying algal blooms (ABs) of water bodies pose a serious threat to worldwide public health and aquatic ecosystems (Hamilton et al., 2018 ). Eutrophication is closely related to the scope and intensity of human activities, along with excessive inputs of nutrients into natural waters, while nutrients and appropriate environmental factors are beneficial for the growth of harmful algae (Huo et al., 2022; Schindler et al., 2016 ). Recently, the frequency and intensity of ABs have been continuously increasing, followed by environmental disasters such as habitat shrinking for wildlife and clean water loss for humans (Dai et al., 2023; Hou et al., 2022; Wurtsbaugh et al., 2019 ). For a long time, pollution has been considered the main cause of ABs, but recent case studies have shown that some lakes with rare human activities still suffer ABs risk under warming climate such as the sub-arctic region and Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Lin et al., 2017; Sivarajah et al., 2021 ). With the continuous promotion of environmental protection measures, pollutant discharge is being reduced in many regions, and ABs under climate change are receiving unprecedented attention (Kakouei et al., 2021; Kalcic et al., 2019; Woolway et al., 2020 ). Climate change promotes ABs by altering the external environment of phytoplankton growth, the increased precipitation carries more pollutants into water bodies, and more directly, the warming climate can accelerate the development process of algae (Kosten et al., 2012; Sinha et al., 2017 ). The adverse impacts of climate change on lakes have been reported in both historical assessments and future projection studies, more severe heatwaves and other extreme weather conditions further increase the risks for humans and ecosystems, and climate will continue to have adverse effects on lakes before the end of 21st century under current emission scenarios (Tong et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023c ). Specifically, more frequent and widespread ABs events are one of the important negative effects of climate change, warming is considered one of the key causes in widely reported cases of lake ABs (Irani Rahaghi et al., 2024; Woolway et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023b ). Additionally, the water bodies in plateau areas are facing even more serious threats from climate change, and multiple studies have proved that high-altitude regions are warming faster and ABs events in alpine lakes occur more frequently under warming conditions (Clark et al., 2021; Marta et al., 2023; Pi et al., 2021 ). Since the release of the IPCC's sixth assessment report (AR6), the uncertainty of global warming predictions has been further reduced. However, further exploration is needed to quantify the ABs risk in alpine lakes under future warming scenarios. Lake Dianchi is a typical low-latitude plateau eutrophic lake with a long history of eutrophication, and is also one of the earliest lakes in China to implement environmental management, billions of dollars have been invested in its pollution control (Yan et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2023 ). Lake Dianchi is one of the important plateau lakes, playing a positive role in regional water resource supply, socio-economic development, and ecological barrier support (Luan et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021 ). Since 2018, Lake Dianchi has maintained Class IV water quality for six consecutive years according to the standard of China, compared to Class V or worse water quality in previous decades (Zhang et al., 2024 ). However, as a climate-sensitive area (Chen et al., 2021 ), there are still large-scale ABs in Lake Dianchi under the strong heatwave. Given the record-breaking meteorological observation in the Lake basin in 2023 (Dong et al., 2023 ), a warming climate is suspected to be an important cause of ABs events. Therefore, Lake Dianchi is an ideal area for studying the response and future risks of lake ABs under global warming. This work tries to quantify the impact of global warming on lake surface water temperature (LSWT) and algal blooms in plateau lakes, to explore the feedback mechanism of alpine lakes under future warming scenarios. Lake Dianchi is selected as the study area, three years of lake surface observation and long-term remote sensing images are adopted to train an ensemble learning model to establish the relationship between climate and water temperature. A Bayesian model averaging method is applied to assemble multiple global climate models (GCMs) to reduce uncertainty in future climate projections. A novel risk assessment method based on the regression between water temperature and algal density has been applied to predict the ABs risk dynamics under future scenarios. This study aims to establish a systematic LSWT-based ABs risk projection scheme, aiming to reduce the uncertainty in predicting the adverse effects of climate change and provide a reference for basin planning and water resource management.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Lake Dianchi (DC) is located at a longitude range from 102°35′49″E to 102°47′07″E, and a latitude range from 24°40′09″N to 25°01′27″N. It is a typical low-latitude shallow eutrophic lake with an average water surface elevation of 1887.4 m    and an average water depth of 5.3 m   . DC Lake has a water area of approximately 330 km  2     and is the sixth-largest freshwater lake in China. As one of the important sub-catchments of the upper Yangtze River, the DC Lake watershed has nurtured a large-scale city with a population of over eight million. The study area belongs to a subtropical monsoon climate, with an average annual temperature of about 15.3 ° C    and an average annual precipitation of around 880 mm   . Except for the underpopulated mountainous areas in the west, most areas of DC Lake are surrounded by cropland and impervious surfaces (Fig. 1  ). The full names and basic information of the weather station and water quality station can be found in Supplementary  (Table S2 ).  2.2 Data 2.2.1 Grid data The data involved in this study include MODIS LSWT, GCM datasets, on-site observations of surface water temperature, algal density, and meteorological observations. The LSWT is extracted from the daytime temperature layer of MODIS product MOD11A2 (Wan et al., 2021 ) using the lake boundary, and every pixel near the boundary is removed to distinguish the lake from the land surface. The temporal resolution of LSWT is eight days, the spatial resolution is 1 km, and the data is obtained from March 2000 to November 2023. The data is sourced from the USGS (United States Geological Survey, data available at https://ladsweb.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/archive/allData/61/MOD11A2 ). The GCM dataset comes from models from 24 institutions in 15 countries. The future climate variables used in this work include average temperature (TEM), maximum temperature (TMX), and minimum temperature (TMN). There are 40 models for TEM (31 models for TMX and TMN), and the data is obtained from January 1990 to December 2060 (both historical and future scenarios) on a monthly scale. The future data comes from four scenarios including SSP (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways)1 2.6, SSP2 4.5, SSP3 7.0, and SSP5 8.5. Detailed data information can be found in Supplementary Table S1 , and all GCM data is retrieved and downloaded from the website of LLNL (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, data available at https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/ ).  2.2.2 Observed data The water temperature and algal density data are obtained from fixed water quality stations settled by CNEMC (China National Environment Monitoring Center). Excluding stations with abnormal data and stations that cannot be covered by MODIS images, data from a total of 10 stations are collected (detailed information is shown in Supplementary Table S2 ). The water temperature is detected by the electrode method (accurate to ±0.2 °C), and algae density is observed by the fluorescence method (accurate to ± 10 %   ). The data collection process strictly follows the technical rules (HJ 915-2017) for the automatic monitoring of surface water in China. The data are sampled every 4 h (local time at 12 am, 4 am, 8 am, 12 pm, 4 pm, and 8 pm) from December 2020 to November 2023. Among them, the average values of water temperature monitoring data at 8 am and 12 pm are used to correct LSWT to correspond to the transit time of the MODIS satellite (10:30 am). The observed climate data comes from the observation of the China National Meteorological Station, eight parameters are obtained at a daily scale including average temperature (TEM), maximum temperature (TMX), minimum temperature (TMN), precipitation (PRE), sunshine duration (SSD), average wind speed (WIN), relative humidity (RHU), and evaporation (EVP). The temperature data (including TEM, TMX, and TMN) since 1990 have been averaged into monthly data to validate and correct GCMs, while data since 2000 have been averaged into an 8-day scale dataset to establish a regression between climate and LSWT. The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) index data comes from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration of the United States (NOAA, data available at https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/nao/ ), the data is obtained on a monthly scale from 2000 to 2023. It is worth noting that the historical period referred to 2000–2023 in this study, which is the start and end date of available observed data, while the base period for climate change is set from 2001 to 2020 to compare relative changes in future periods.   2.3 MODIS LSWT correction The accuracy of MODIS products is fair enough in detecting surface water temperature, but errors still exist compared to observational data. Among the existing 10 stations, the average R  2     between the raw MODIS data and station observations is 0.85, the average RMSE is 1.80, and the overall performance of raw MODIS data is relatively uniform, with stations in the northern area performing slightly better (with an average R  2     of 0.87 and an average RMSE of 1.65 for four stations in the north). Therefore, it is necessary to conduct an error correction procedure to further enhance its reliability. In this study, a density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) method is used to identify and remove outliers, and the Geographic Ratio Analysis (GRA) and Geographic Difference Analysis (GDA) are used for error correction, these methods are widely used in processing and correcting spatiotemporal data (Jing et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020 ).  2.4 GCMs data downscaling GCMs have a relatively rough grid (from 50 km to 500 km), which leads to uncertainty in regional research. In this study, inverse distance weighted (IDW) interpolation and Bayesian model averaging (BMA) are used to downscale GCM data (Duan et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2023 ). The downscaling process includes interpolating the GCM grid to corresponding meteorological stations and using climate observation data to select reliable GCMs and synthesize them. The IDW is a deterministic algorithm for multivariate interpolation with known discrete data points. In this study, four adjacent GCM data points were used for IDW interpolation, to downscale the grid GCM data to the location of each meteorological station, the equation is expressed as:(1) Z x , y    = ∑ i = 1  n  d i   - 2   ∑ j = 1  n  d j   - 2     ∙  Z x i  , y i          the Z x , y       and Z x i  , y i        illustrate the data value (temperature) of climate station points and GCM data points; the d    represents the distance between them; and n    stands for the number of sampled GCM data points, which is four in this study. The interpolated data is further screened into the top ten datasets with the highest accuracy. Then the BMA is used to fuse those ten datasets to obtain a highly accurate data sequence for the analysis of this study. It is worth noting that due to the unverifiability of future climate data, well-performing historical data for each GCM means that its future sections are also reliable. The BMA is based on Bayes' theorem, which determines the weight of each model by considering its posterior probability (calculated by comparing simulated values with observed values). In this study, multiple different GCM data sequences are weighted and averaged to obtain one data sequence. The probability prediction of BMA can be represented as:(2) p y    = ∑ k = 1  K  p y |  f k     ∙ p f k  |  y  T         where the p f k  |  y  T        illustrate the posterior probability of the k    th model (f k    ) given the observed data y  T    ; the p y |  f k        represent the conditional probability of the climate variable (y   ) under k    th model (f k    ); the K    is the number of GCM models, which is 10 in this study. The top 10 GCM values with the best correlation with surface observations are used for the BMA ensemble to obtain future warming trends. The future warming is divided into two time periods, the 2030s (average value from 2021 to 2040) and 2050s (average value from 2041 to 2060).  2.5 Climate-LSWT regression model Ensemble learning is a machine learning method that uses a series of base models for learning and integrates the results of each model to achieve better learning outcomes than a single model. Bagging, boosting, and stacking are the three most popular techniques of ensemble learning. In this study, a classic Bagging model, the Random Forest (RF) model (Biau, 2012 ), is used to establish the relationship between climate factors and LSWT. The random forest model randomly samples from the original dataset to form n    different sample datasets, and then builds n    different decision tree models based on these datasets. For a model established for regression, these decision tree models will be averaged to obtain the result. Taking this study as an example, the decision tree of the climate-LSWT regression model is shown in Figure S4 . RF was applied in three aspects of this work: 1. calculating the feature importance of eight climate variables; 2. establishing a regression model between the selected climate variables and LSWT; 3. using the regression model to predict LSWT under climate change. Eight climate variables are used for RF feature selection, a part of the data is used for training, while the rest is used to calculate the importance level. In each decision tree of the RF model, a coefficient of each feature is calculated first, then the coefficients of the corresponding features in each tree are averaged, and the coefficients of all features are normalized to obtain feature importance. Finally, the importance level ranking of the climate variables is presented in Fig. 2  . The importance of three temperature variables (TMN, TEM, and TMX) all exceed 0.12, while the importance of other variables is all below 0.10 (Fig. 2 a). Thus the three temperature variables are used to simulate the LSWT. Based on the monthly data from March 2000 to February 2023 (276 months), 75 % of the data is used for training and 25 % is used to test its performance, and the results are shown in Fig. 2 b and Fig. 2 c. It can be seen from the figure that the randomly selected validation data (Fig. 2 b, red point) performed well, with NSE and MAPE reaching 0.89 and 3.95 %, respectively (Fig. 2 c), which can be used for predicting the future LSWT.  2.6 ABs risk classification and accuracy evaluation index The AGNES (Agglomerative Nesting) algorithm is a bottom-up hierarchical clustering algorithm (Kaufman and Rousseeuw, 1990 ), which has been widely used in the classification of the relationship between climatic and ecological factors (Cranko Page et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2023 ). The algorithm initializes each sample in the dataset as a cluster first, then merges the two closest clusters. The whole process is repeated until the preset number of clusters is reached. The AGNES is used to implement the classification of ABs risk levels through the regression between LSWT and algae density. In the classification, a total of six levels of ABs risk are classified. The LSWT ranges corresponding to the six risk levels, from low to high, are < 13.4 ° C   , 13.4–15.5 ° C   , 15.5–19.3 ° C   , 19.3–20.9 ° C   , 20.9–21.5  ° C   , and > 21.5 ° C   , respectively (Fig. 3  b and Table 1  ). These risk level thresholds are further applied to the historical ABs risk changes and future ABs level predictions. The evaluation indicators include the Coefficient of determination (R  2    ), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). R  2     and RMSE are used to evaluate the fitting degree between GCM model data and observed meteorological data, while NSE and MAPE are used to evaluate the simulation accuracy of the RF model for LSWT, in which the optimal value is 1 for NSE and R  2     and 0 for RMSE and MAPE. These four indicators have been widely applied in the fields of meteorology, hydrology, and environment (Peng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021b ).   3 Results 3.1 Historical dynamics of LSWT 3.1.1 Spatial distribution of LSWT The corrected daytime MODIS product is used to average the monthly scale and annual distribution of LSWT, with a data period range from March 2000 to February 2023 included, and the results are shown in Fig. 4   (The months in Fig. 4  and later are abbreviated, such as January being Jan, etc.). In general, MODIS LSWT is lower in the center of the lake and higher on the shores and the northern narrow water areas (Fig. 4  Annual). In the corrected-MODIS dataset and ground observations, the lowest temperature appeared in the lake center, which is 16.8 ° C    for MODIS (average since 2000) and 17.6 ° C    for observation (average since 2020). The highest temperature of both appeared on the east bank, which is 18.3 ° C    for MODIS (average since 2000) and 18.7 ° C    for observation (average since 2020), further proving the reliability of the data. It is worth noting that although the hottest season in Lake Dianchi is summer, which is also the season with the highest ABs frequency, the LSWT on the lake shore is also high in late spring and early autumn. For example, the average LSWT on the lake shore (within one pixel) from September to October is 19.2 ° C   , and it reached 20.0 ° C    from April to March, which implies possible expansion of ABs under future warming.  3.1.2 Historical warming trend of LSWT The warming/cooling rate of DC Lake over the past 23 years (from 2000 to 2023) is shown in Fig. 5   together with the weather station. On an annual scale, over 73 % (116 of 157) of pixels are significantly warming (over 95 % of pixels warming) with an average warming rate of 0.21 ° C / 10 a   , and the LSWT change rate of the entire lake is evenly distributed (Fig. 5  Annual). On a monthly scale, the warming in November is prominent, with over 90 % (142 of 157) of pixels showing significant warming, with an average warming rate of 0.64 ° C / 10 a   , ranging from 0.40 to 0.99 ° C / 10 a    (Fig. 5  Nov). Besides, the warming rate of LSWT is generally lower than that of TEM. Especially in months with a large TEM increase rate, which indicates that the lake can slow down climate change, and the increased evapotranspiration under warming protects the water body from excessive warming rate. It is worth mentioning that April is the only month when all three weather stations are cooling in TEM, and the cooling rate of the KM station in the north reaches 0.50 ° C / 10 a    (Fig. 5  Apr), which is an anomaly that needs further analysis.  3.1.3 Historical trends of critical threshold of LSWT The corrected original LSWT (with 8-day resolution) is presented in Fig. 6  a. Firstly, the LSWT data (average value of whole lake) exhibits periodic fluctuations, with the lowest value typically occurring in December or January and the highest value occurring from June to August (Fig. 6 a). However, more detailed information (e.g. the duration of LSWT range suitable for the algae growth) is difficult to directly analyze from Fig. 6 a. The duration, occurrence, and end of different levels of risk are included in the further analysis (Fig. 6 b to 6e). The duration of high and above risk shows a slightly upward trend but is not significant, with an average linear increase rate of 6.1 (0.76 scenes) days / 10 a    (Fig. 6 b). The duration of the noteworthy and above risk shows a significant upward trend (p-value < 0.01), with an increase rate reaching 15.6 days / 10 a    (Fig. 6 c). Furthermore, the start time of noteworthy and above risk is being advanced (Fig. 6 d), and the end time is being postponed (Fig. 6 e). Particularly, referring to the average trend, the noteworthy and above risk of ABs in DC lake has advanced by 11.1 days and delayed by 8.6 days in the past 23 years. It is worth mentioning that the LSWT has been removed outliers and corrected in the above section (Fig. S1 ), demonstrating higher reliability.   3.2 The ABs risk assessment under future scenarios 3.2.1 Future climate change assessment under different scenarios The fitting results of integrating parameters and measured data demonstrate high accuracy (Fig. S2  and Fig. S3 ), thereby reducing the uncertainty of climate change results in this section. In the 2030s (Fig. 7  a), the warming differences between scenarios are small, with a warming range from 0.56 ° C    to 0.76 ° C    Compared to the base period (2001–2020). Specifically, the months with large warming rates in the base period (Air in Fig. 3  Mar, Fig. 3  May, and Fig. 3  Nov) still maintain a stable warming trend in the 2030s compared to other months (Mar in Fig. 7  a1, a2, a3, a4; May in Fig. 7  a1, a3, a4; Nov in Fig. 7  a2, a4). The month with the largest cooling rate in the base period, April, began to warm up in the 2030s, but its warming rate is still lower than its adjacent months (March and May), especially under the ssp370 (Apr in Fig. 7  a3, 0.50 ° C   ) and ssp585 (Apr in Fig. 7  a4, 0.60 ° C   ) scenarios. Overall, the warming trend in the 2030s is a continuation of the base period. In the 2050s (Fig. 7 b), the gap between different scenarios widened, and the influence of high-emission scenarios (ssp585) emerged. Compared to the base period, the average temperature increased by 1.55 ° C    under ssp585, with the highest value in January (Jan in Fig. 7 b4). Spring is still the season with the strongest warming trend, and the increase in April is comparable to the other two months (Mar, Apr, and May in Fig. 7 b). What's different is that the warming trend in winter is more prominent, with the average increment for all scenarios reached 1.29 ° C    (compare with 1.31 ° C    in spring, 1.20 ° C    in summer, and 1.22 ° C    in autumn). In addition, the warming trend at the annual scale of both periods is shown in Fig. 7 c, with the highest warming rate of 0.38 ° C / 10 a    under ssp585, and the lowest warming rate of 0.26 ° C / 10 a    under ssp245 (Fig. 7 c).  3.2.2 The ABs risk assessment in the 2030s and 2050s The risk assessment for the future period is based on the results of climate change projection, LSWT simulation, and risk classification. In the 2030s, the months with prominent changes in ABs risk are March, May, June, August, and November. The risk escalation in March and May mainly occurs in the lake center. A large area of low risk in the base period in March transformed into moderate, with only a small portion of low risk remaining under ssp370 (Fig. 8   MAR), while many of the moderate areas in the lake center transformed into noteworthy in May except ssp585 (Fig. 8  MAY). The risk changes in June mainly occur on the lakeshore, with a large number of noteworthy turning into high and high turning into extreme under all scenarios (Fig. 8  JUN). As for August and November, their changes in four scenarios are similar, both of which are risk escalation in the lake center: high to extreme in August and low to moderate in November (Fig. 8  AUG and NOV). In addition, the risk of the three winter months has been almost unchanged (Fig. 8  DEC, JAN, and FEB). In the 2050s, more months get involved in the ABs risk levels change, such as December and February in winter, with more insignificant pixels transitioning to low, and it is worth noting that the insignificant pixels disappear and several moderate pixels appear in February under ssp585 (Fig. 9   DEC and FEB). In March and May of spring, the trend of risk increasing in the central area continues (Fig. 9  MAR and MAY), and the low risk in March and the moderate risk in May disappear under any scenario (Fig. 8  and Fig. 9 ). April remains the month with the least change in spring (Fig. 9  APR). As for summer, high risk replaced the majority of noteworthy risk in June, while July and August are dominated by extreme risk (Fig. 9  JUN, JUL, and AUG), and August is almost completely occupied (only 4 pixels left under ssp126 and ssp245). In autumn, the significant change only happens in September and is limited to ssp585, a large number of noteworthy pixels have become high risk, and some even turn to the extreme (Fig. 9  SEP ssp585).    4 Discussion 4.1 Driving factor of the spatiotemporal pattern of LSWT The DC Lake is characterized by typical lakes LSWT distribution: lower in deep water and higher in the shoreline (Fig. 4 ), which is common in many shallow lakes (such as Lake Kasumigaura and Lake Balaton) or shallow areas of deep lakes (such as lakes in the Great Lakes region) (Fichot et al., 2019; Hatvani et al., 2020; Sugita et al., 2020 ). Moreover, compared to deep water, shallow water areas or shallow lakes have lower resilience (Thayne et al., 2022 ), making them more susceptible to external environmental variation including climate change and pollutant emissions. However, the heterogeneity of LSWT within lakes is often overlooked and replaced by a homogeneous single value in many research (Shatwell et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020 ). More importantly, the higher temperature on the shore not only accelerates the photosynthesis of algae, but also accelerates the release rate of nutrients in the water, making the shallow lakeshore or coastal shoals high-risk areas for ABs (Gobler, 2020; Xiao et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Additionally, the human activity-intensive side (east side) of Lake Dianchi has higher temperatures and a greater warming rate from 2000 to 2023, under the heat island effect, the lake acts as a sink for the exported urban heat, and the lake-city interaction mainly characterized by lake breeze and heat island effect is being widely reported, the wind-induced ABs drift is one of the important reasons affecting their spatial patterns (Cosgrove and Berkelhammer, 2018; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023a ). The LSWT of DC Lake has shown a warming trend over the past 23 years, but its warming rate is weaker than that of air temperature (Fig. 4  Annual), especially in months with larger air temperature warming rates, where the difference between LSWT and air temperature is prominent (Fig. 4  Mar, May, Jun, and Nov). Specifically, data analysis from another weather station (Anning, 15 km away from the west coast of DC Lake, with a mountain in between) shows that the warming rate has reached 0.44 ° C / 10 a    during the same period (Fig. S5 ), higher than any other three stations around DC Lake (with a mean value of 0.30, Fig. 4  Annual). The above facts prove that lakes are not only affected by global warming but also partly offset it at the regional scale (Shi et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2019 ). In addition, global scale studies showed that lakes are widely warm slower than air temperature (Tong et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023 ), which is consistent with the results of this work. Although lakes can partly resist the adverse effects of climate change, other downsides of warming cannot be offset, such as drought and accompanying water quality deterioration, which have already occurred in the adjacent basins of Lake Dianchi (Chen et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2024b ).  4.2 Climate warming: The past and the future The negative effects of climate change on inland water involve irregular hydrological regimes (shrink, outburst, etc.), physical variables disorder (warming, melting, etc.), and deterioration of water quality (eutrophication, hypoxia, salinization, etc.) (van Vliet et al., 2023; Woolway et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021 ), while in this work, it is mainly reflected in the extension of the warm period. In historical periods, there is a significant warming rate in both the early (Fig. 5  May, 0.89 ° C / 10 a   ) and late months (Fig. 5  Nov, 0.85 ° C / 10 a   ) of the ABs period. This trend will continue in the future period (Fig. 7 a and 7b) and is likely to advance to April in the 2050s (Fig. 7 a Apr). The extension of the warm period is a chief factor that triggers the expansion of the noteworthy or high ABs risk duration in DC Lake (Fig. 6 ). The relatively high ABs risk of Dianchi Lake in summer and autumn has been confirmed by multiple studies, and the results of this study indicate that the early growth season in spring cannot be ignored, additionally, extensive research has shown that the algal phenology is being affected under global warming (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b; Woolway, 2023 ). Notably, there is an abnormal decrease in air temperature in April during the historical period, with a cooling rate of 0.32 ° C / 10 a   , clearly different from the other two months of spring (Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, the abnormal April will continue in the future, and its warming rate will be lower compared to March and May (Fig. 7 a). A few studies have reported on the impact of NAO on the Tibetan Plateau and its downstream (northwest of this research site), and evidence suggests that spring climate anomalies are related to a NAO-related winter cooling signal originating from North Africa (Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Li et al., 2005 ). Even though the Tibetan Plateau is adjacent to the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, further confirmation is still necessary. Therefore, a teleconnection analysis is conducted between the monthly air temperature of the DC lake basin and the NAO index (Fig. S6 ). The results indicate a significant negative correlation (R = −0.31, p-value < 0.05) between the winter NAO index and April air temperature, while insignificant figures are found in March (−0.02) and May (−0.04), which indicate the time when the cold air reaches the Lake Dianchi, which is also one of the important reasons for the early spring cooling in the southwest region of China. In addition, warming will have a negative impact on the ABs risk on both annual and seasonal scales. According to publicly available data from an annual scale algal bloom occurrence study (Wang et al., 2023d ), there is a significant positive correlation between annual algal bloom occurrence and average temperature in Lake Dianchi (p-value < 0.05). In this work, LSWT showed a promoting effect on algal density in all four seasons (Figure S5 ). For spring and autumn, the ABs risk types are mainly moderate and noteworthy currently (Figure S7 ), as the heatwave continues to expand towards these two seasons (Shan et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023 ), there will be a large amount of water area entering high or even extreme risks in the future.  4.3 Uncertainty and variation of ABs risk under future scenarios The growth of algae is influenced by various anthropogenic and natural factors, for example, some global studies indicate that the global trend of harmful ABs caused by anthropogenic pollution and climate change is continuously increasing, but there is also research suggesting that there is no direct evidence for the increasing global trends, and a case-by-case basis should be considered in future work. (Hallegraeff et al., 2021; Trainer et al., 2020 ). Therefore, only LSWT is taken into consideration in this work, for the reason that the water quality of this region has remained stable for several years, while the temperature has repeatedly broken historical records. Given predictive assessment in future scenarios is involved in this study, single-factor assessment can minimize uncertainty as much as possible. Due to the complexity of urban water networks and human activities being more uncontrollable compared to climate projections, the nutrient background for ABs risk classification is determined as the level of the past three years, thereby reducing the errors introduced when considering nutrient concentrations (concerning predictions of population, land use, government behavior, etc.) (Xia et al., 2024 ). Subject to the above conditions, this work strives to curtail the uncertainty in the prediction of ABs risk, including correction of remote sensing products (which most studies do not do), screening of climate factors, and integration of GCMs. In addition to the aforementioned issues, insufficient consideration of the phytoplankton structure is another reason for uncertainty. Although the algae species in Lake Dianchi are relatively stable, the reliability of the research will be further enhanced if community survey data can be integrated. In the forthcoming future (2030s), the climate will maintain its trend and feature in historical periods (Fig. 7 a), which indirectly proves the reliability of the results. Meanwhile, there is no obvious variation in ABs risk during the algae prevailing season (summer), and the area transit to higher risk is limited in the early and late stages of the growing season. Although there is little research on the prediction of ABs, some air temperature projection cases confirm the fact that the forthcoming future warming is similar to historical periods and has a small variability across scenarios (Kong et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2021a ). Research on LSWT prediction has confirmed that differences under multiple emission scenarios began to emerge in the mid-21st century (Wang et al., 2023c; Wu et al., 2024 ). In this study, there will be considerable changes in the pattern of ABs risk in the 2050s, especially under high emission scenarios, where there will be a large area of risk escalation in most months, and the lake system will face unprecedented ecological threats. As the ABs risk continue to expand in scale and magnitude, a low greenhouse gas emission scenario is a decisive mitigation measure that should be followed.   5 Conclusion The lake's eutrophication and following algal blooms greatly threaten the ecosystem's integrity and socioeconomic development and intensify under the promotion of global warming. Through this study, the interrelationship between climate and eutrophication, as well as the predictability of eutrophication risk under warming, have been demonstrated at the regional scale. Climate, water temperature, and lake biological indicators are denoted through observation data and satellite products, and are interconnected through machine learning and clustering methods. Although there are still limitations in this paper, such as insufficient consideration of biological indicator components and projection of future human activities, the entire process and results of this work are presented for further research reference. The main conclusions of this study are as follows:(1) The Lake ABs risk under warming exhibits spatiotemporal heterogeneity, the early and late stages of the algae growth season are more sensitive to climate change, while the shallow and narrow areas in the water body are more susceptible to the effects of warming.  (2) Global warming is undoubtedly harmful to lake ecosystems, and the level increase of ABs risk under high emission scenarios will emerge within a decade. By the mid-21st century, even in the most conservative scenarios, large-scale risk escalation will take appearance.  (3) For the following research, accurate prediction of human interference, such as pollutant emissions and water utilization, is the key to reducing the uncertainty of such studies. Additionally, distinguishing the algae type will further increase the reliability of the results.
1 Introduction Global circulation models predict an intensification of the hydrological cycle as the climate warms, leading to increased precipitation variability and higher frequency of extreme rainfall events (Easterling et al., 2000; Allen and Ingram, 2002; USGCRP, 2018; Jones, 2019; IPCC, 2021 ). Warming and shifts in precipitation patterns have been recorded in recent decades in many parts of the world (Garbrecht et al., 2004; Dore, 2005; Rahmani et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2020 ), and these trends are expected to continue to change global carbon, nutrient, and hydrological cycles (IPCC, 2021 ). In the Great Plains ecoregion of the central United States, projected impacts of climate change on precipitation regimes include (1) no change or slight increases in total annual precipitation, (2) increased precipitation variability, resulting in longer dry periods punctuated by fewer, but larger, rain events, and (3) shifts toward greater winter and / or spring precipitation (USGCRP, 2018; IPCC, 2021 ). These shifts have the potential to alter local and regional water cycles, as precipitation timing and event sizes can substantially influence runoff and groundwater recharge (Small et al., 2006; Meixner et al., 2016; Pumo et al., 2016 ), water infiltration dynamics (Loague et al., 2010; Price, 2011 ), plant available water (Fay et al. 2002, 2003; Heisler-White et al., 2009 ), and water chemistry and quality (Li et al., 2022; van Vliet et al, 2023; Li et al. 2024 ). In addition to changes in climate, the encroachment of woody vegetation (shrubs and trees) into historically grass-dominated ecosystems is also occurring in the Great Plains ecoregion (Briggs et al., 2005; Archer et al., 2017 ), as well as in grasslands and savannas around the world (Knapp et al., 2008; Eldridge et al., 2011; Stevens et al., 2017 ). Woody encroachment can alter water cycling dynamics independent of changes in climate (Huxman et al., 2005; Viglizzo et al., 2015; Acharya et al., 2018; Zou et al., 2018 ). Woody shrubs and trees are typically more deeply rooted (Canadell et al., 1996; Schenk and Jackson, 2002 ) and transpire at greater rates than the grasses they replace (Scott et al., 2006; O’Keefe et al., 2020 ). In mesic grasslands where precipitation generally exceeds evapotranspiration (ET), excess water is stored in deeper soil layers that are recharged each year (Huxman et al., 2005 ). As woody cover increases in these systems, shrubs and trees can access water stored deeper (>30 cm) in the soil profile, allowing ET to outpace precipitation, particularly during drier years (Logan and Brunsell, 2015; Wilcox et al., 2022 ). Over time, this can lead to drying of deeper soil layers in infrequently burned watersheds with high woody cover (Craine and Nippert, 2014 ), decrease the amount of water flow reaching stream and groundwater systems (Acharya et al., 2018; Keen et al., 2022; Dodds et al., 2023a ), and possibly shift the relative proportion of shallow and deep groundwater flow paths contributing to streamflow generation (Macpherson and Sullivan, 2019; Sadayappan et al., 2023 ). While increasing tree and shrub cover typically increases ET in mesic grasslands (Huxman et al., 2005; Wilcox et al., 2022 ), shifts in rooting architecture and root depth distributions with woody encroachment can also alter belowground water fluxes, as the rooting systems of woody vegetation impact soil structure differently than the shallow, fibrous rooting systems of grasses (Lu et al., 2020 ). Shallow rooting zones dominated by fibrous grass roots are expected to facilitate more lateral subsurface flow (Alaoui et al., 2011; Sullivan et al., 2018 ), while deeper, coarser rooting systems of shrubs and trees tend to facilitate more vertical recharge of water via creation of macropores (Beven and Germann, 1982; Jarvis, 2007; Alaoui et al., 2011; Bargués Tobella et al., 2014 ). These conflicting impacts of woody encroachment – increased water loss from soils via transpiration, but potentially increased infiltration of water to greater depths in the soil profile – make it difficult to predict the net hydrological effects of woody encroachment and the consequences for grassland water yield, particularly if precipitation dynamics are changing at the same time. Previous assessments of the ecosystem state transition from grassland to shrubland or woodland – which often exhibits hysteresis (Beisner et al., 2003; Collins et al., 2021 ) – have focused primarily on shifts in vegetation cover and species composition through time (Ratajczak et al., 2014b; Collins et al. 2021 ). Yet, the impact of ecosystem state transitions on belowground structure and, thus, the hydrologic cycle, has received far less attention. In one example, Robinson et al. (2018)  reviewed potential environmental changes or disturbances (e.g., severe drought or changes in plant cover) that can lead to shifts in soil structure, chemical properties, and ultimately soil moisture dynamics that may be irreversible or very slow to recover to the original state. Recent work has shown that shifts in soil structure as a result of climate and land-cover change are occurring at decadal scales and can have substantial effects on critical zone function (Sullivan et al., 2022 ). Knowing that shifts in plant functional type dominance with woody encroachment (i.e., grasses to shrubs) have the potential to impact ET (Zhang et al., 2001; Huxman et al., 2005; Scott et al., 2006; Logan and Brunsell, 2015 ), long-term soil moisture dynamics (Craine and Nippert, 2014 ), and groundwater recharge (Acharya et al., 2018 ), it is possible that ecosystem state transitions could be observable in the hydrological cycle and subsurface structure as well as in vegetation communities in mesic grasslands. To examine how changes in climate and land-cover have altered the hydrological cycle over time, we leveraged a mesic grassland site that has experienced woody encroachment over the last three decades (Briggs et al., 2005; Ratajczak et al., 2014a ). At this site (Konza Prairie Biological Station; KPBS; northeastern, KS, USA), long-term data shows that stream flow has declined, and the number of no-flow days have increased, despite an increase in annual precipitation over the last 30–40 years (Dodds et al., 2012; Keen et al., 2022; Sadayappan et al., 2023 ). Extensive temporal hydrological records (precipitation, stream flow, groundwater) and vegetation cover at KPBS allowed us to assess the impacts of changes in climate (inter- and intra-annual precipitation dynamics) and land-cover on grassland ecohydrology. Specifically, we analyzed the long-term precipitation record from the nearby city of Manhattan, KS (1898–2022) as well as a shorter-term precipitation record from KPBS (1984–2022) to ask whether precipitation total amounts, variability, seasonality, or event sizes have changed over the last 40–120 years. We then examined the relationship between precipitation and stream flow to understand the degree to which coherence among these two variables may have changed over the last four decades. Finally, we used a 10 + year record of water stable isotopes (δ18 O and δ2 H) of precipitation, stream flow, and groundwater at KPBS to assess whether connectivity between these water pools has changed.  2 Methods 2.1 Site description This study occurs in northeastern Kansas, which is located on the western edge of the tallgrass prairie portion of the Great Plains (Samson et al., 2004 ). Tallgrass prairie ecosystems are dominated by warm-season C4  grasses (primarily Andropogon gerardii , Panicum virgatum , Sorghastrum nutans , and Schizachyrium scoparium ), but also contain a high diversity of subdominant grasses (C3  and C4 ), forbs, and shrub / sub-shrub species (Collins and Calabrese, 2012 ). The climate in northeastern Kansas is mid-continental, with warm, wet summers and cold, dry winters. This region receives ∼ 830 mm of precipitation each year, with ∼ 75 % of precipitation occurring during the growing season (April − September; Hayden, 1998; Goodin and Fay, 2003 ). Growing season precipitation is primarily derived from warm air masses moving north out of the Gulf of Mexico, while dormant season precipitation is primarily derived from cold air masses moving south out of Canada (Sullivan et al., 2019 ). Konza Prairie Biological Station (KPBS; 39.1°N, 96.9°W), a 3,487-hectare tallgrass prairie south of Manhattan, KS, is intensively monitored and has multi-decadal records of precipitation and stream flow, in addition to long-term water stable isotope records (precipitation, stream water, groundwater). KPBS is located within the Flint Hills, a ∼ 2.5 million hectare region in the western-portion of the tallgrass prairie characterized by rolling hills underlain by alternating limestone and shale bedrock layers (Vero et al., 2018 ). This site is co-owned by Kansas State University and The Nature Conservancy and is a Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) site that was established in 1980. KPBS is divided into replicated, experimental watersheds that have varying grazing (ungrazed, grazed by cattle (Bos taurus ), or grazed by bison (Bison bison )) and fire (1-, 2-, 4-, and 20-year burn frequency) treatments. These treatments provide a range of severity of woody encroachment, with a greater degree of woody cover in watersheds that are burned less frequently (Briggs et al., 2005 ). In this study, we leveraged data from four bison-grazed watersheds: N1B (1-year burn frequency, 120.9 ha), N2B (2-year burn frequency, 78.2 ha), N4D (4-year burn frequency, 120.4 ha), and N20B (20-year burn frequency, 84.4 ha). These watersheds were chosen because they all have long-term stream discharge records, and three of them (N1B, N4D, and N20B) have long-term records of plant cover. Non-riparian woody cover ranges from ∼ 20 % (N1B) to > 50 % (N20B) on these watersheds as a result of the range in burn frequencies (Hartnett et al., 2023 ). The primary encroaching woody species at this site are clonal shrubs – Cornus drummondii  (rough leaf dogwood) in particular has rapidly spread in cover over the last 3–4 decades, but other encroaching clonal shrubs include Rhus glabra  and Prunus americana  among others (Briggs et al. 2005; Ratajczak et al. 2014a ). Eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana ) is also encroaching at this site, but primarily in ungrazed, infrequently burned watersheds (Ratajczak et al. 2014a ). Eastern redcedar is almost entirely absent from bison-grazed watersheds because bison frequently kill seedlings and prevent establishment of mature redcedars (Hoch 2000 ). In all four watersheds included in this study, upland soils are shallow and rocky and are classified as cherty silty clay loams (Benfield-Florence and Clime-Sogn complexes), while lowland soils can reach depths of > 2 m and are classified as silty clay loams (Ivan silt loams; Ransom et al., 1998; Ratajczak, 2023 ). Stream flow at KPBS is intermittent, largely due to high rates of evapotranspiration during the spring and summer months that can outpace precipitation inputs (Sullivan et al. 2019 ). Declining stream discharge and an increase in the number of no-flow days have been observed at KPBS since the 1980′s (Dodds et al., 2012 ). Stream discharge at this site is primarily driven by groundwater supply – past studies have determined that well-developed connections exist between the groundwater and stream systems, evidenced by rapid water-table responses following rainfall events (Brookfield et al., 2017 ) and isotopic signatures of stream and groundwater (Keen et al., 2022; Hatley et al., 2023 ).  2.2 Long-term hydrological records A long-term record of daily precipitation (1898 to 2022) for Manhattan, KS was obtained through the National Climate Data Center’s Global Historical Climatology Network (station ID: USC00144972; https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/datasets/ ). Daily precipitation and stream discharge records (1983 to 2022) for KPBS were obtained through the Konza Prairie LTER database. Stream discharge measurements were taken every five minutes at a triangular-throated flume on watersheds N1B, N2B, N4D, and N20B (Dodds, 2023b -e; datasets: ASD02, ASD04, ASD05, ASD06), and precipitation amounts were measured at KPBS headquarters using a Belfort weighing rain gauge from January 1983 to April 2010, and an Ott Pluvio2 rain gauge from March 2010 to December 2022 (Nippert, 2023 ; datasets: APT01). Co-located wet deposition collectors, deployed as part of the National Atmospheric Deposition Program (NADP), collected precipitation samples used to assess precipitation water chemistry. Precipitation was collected from the wet deposition collectors every Tuesday morning (when water was available), following the NADP protocol. These subsamples were then used for water isotope analysis (δ18 O and δ2 H) – each sample collected for isotope analysis therefore integrates the signatures of events from the previous seven days. The wet deposition collectors were sealed in the closed position except during active precipitation events, eliminating the potential for evaporative isotopic enrichment of the precipitation samples (more detail on the wet deposition sensor can be found in the metadata of Blair, 2019 ). Groundwater samples were collected weekly from the Edler Spring well at KPBS, and stream water samples were collected weekly from the weirs at each watershed (N1B, N2B, N4D, and N20B) when water was present. After collection, all water samples were stored in sealed vials in a −20 °C freezer and archived at Kansas State University. Archived precipitation (2001 to 2022), stream water (2007 to 2021), and groundwater (2010 to 2022) samples were subsampled and analyzed for δ18 O and δ2 H to develop long-term water stable isotope records. Water samples were analyzed for δ18 O and δ2 H using a Picarro WS-CRDS isotopic water analyzer at Kansas State University. Isotopic ratios were expressed in per mil (‰) relative to the international standard V-SMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water). The long-term precision of water isotope analyses was assessed using three in-house standards to calculate a calibration curve, along with a laboratory working standard (n = 16 per run) used for within-run drift correction. More information on our water isotope methodology can be found in Appendix 2 of Keen et al. (2024). Assessed as standard deviation, the precision across and within runs was < 0.3 ‰ for δ2 H and < 0.15 ‰ for δ18 O.  2.3 Changes in precipitation dynamics through time 2.3.1 Precipitation amounts and variability Changes in mean annual precipitation and precipitation variability through time were assessed using running mean, standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation (CV). The long-term Manhattan, KS precipitation record (122 years; hereafter referred to as the ‘MHK record’) and the shorter-term KPBS precipitation record (37 years; hereafter referred to as the ‘KPBS record’) were analyzed separately. For both records, a 10-year moving window was used to remove substantial inter-annual variability in precipitation and observe long-term precipitation trends. Trends in running mean, standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation (CV) were assessed using modified Mann Kendall trends tests with trend-free pre-whitening (Kendall, 1948; Mann, 1945; Von Storch, 1999 ) using the tfpwmk function in the modifiedmk package (Patakamuri et al., 2020 ) in R (version 4.3.0).  2.3.2 Seasonality of precipitation In all seasonal analyses in this study, the growing season includes April – September and the dormant season includes October – March. Changes in the amount of growing and dormant season precipitation, as well as the proportion of annual precipitation occurring in the growing vs. dormant seasons, were assessed for both precipitation records using 10-year moving windows. These trends were also assessed using modified Mann Kendall trends tests with trend-free pre-whitening.  2.3.3 Sizes and number of precipitation events Changes in the number of precipitation events – both annual number of events and number of events during the growing vs. dormant seasons – were assessed using 10-year moving windows and analyzed using modified Mann Kendall trends tests with trend-free pre-whitening. We defined a precipitation event as an individual day with precipitation > 5 mm, since both records contained daily precipitation amounts. This 5 mm cutoff was established to isolate ‘ecologically significant’ precipitation events that would not be completely intercepted and / or evaporated before reaching the soil surface. These smallest events (<5 mm) have historically been ignored in ecological studies (Coupland, 1950; Sala and Lauenroth, 1982; Hao et al., 2012 ). In addition, measurement accuracy of the smallest precipitation events has likely improved over the last century, so removing the smallest event sizes is also expected to reduce measurement error associated with older precipitation records, particularly for the longer MHK dataset. Changes in mean event size – both annually and in the growing and dormant seasons – were also assessed using 10-year moving windows for both records. Again, precipitation events were defined as individual days with precipitation > 5 mm.   2.4 Shifts in precipitation-discharge relationship 2.4.1 Precipitation–discharge relationship through time To determine how precipitation and stream discharge dynamics have shifted over time, annual and monthly relationships between discharge (Q) and precipitation (P) were assessed. Annual Q/P ratios were calculated using stream discharge from four watersheds at KPBS (N1B=120.9, N2B=79.2, N4D=120.4, N20B=84.4 ha). To account for differences in watershed size, annual mean specific discharge was calculated by dividing daily discharge values (m3 /day) by watershed size (m2 ) before summing across each year (m year-1 ). A 10-year moving window was used to remove substantial inter-annual variability and assess long-term trends in annual Q/P. Changes in annual Q/P ratios, as well as 10-year moving window mean annual Q/P ratios, were assessed using modified Mann Kendall trends tests with trend-free pre-whitening. Monthly mean specific discharge was also calculated by dividing daily discharge values (m3 /day) by watershed size (m2 ) before summing across each month (m month−1 ). We assessed the relationship between monthly mean specific discharge and monthly precipitation amounts using a moving-window correlation analysis to assess changes in correlation strength through time. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated for monthly mean specific discharge and monthly precipitation using a 10-year moving window for the years 1987–2020. Results from additional moving-window lengths (5-, 7-, and 9-years) can be found in Fig. S1 .  2.4.2 Shrub cover and grassland-to-shrubland transitions To compare trends in woody encroachment to shifts in the precipitation–discharge relationship, we also updated and modified a figure from Ratajczak et al. (2014b)  showing changes in woody cover over time. We obtained long-term shrub cover data for KPBS for watersheds N1B (1-year burn frequency), N4D (4-year burn frequency), and N20B (20-year burn frequency; Hartnett et al., 2023 ). These watersheds were selected because they contain permanent species cover plots that have been maintained since 1983 (Hartnett et al., 2023 ; dataset: PVC02) as well as long-term records of stream discharge (Dodds, 2023b–e ). Four 50-m transects for species cover were established in each watershed, with five 10 m2 plots established along each transect. At each plot, species cover was measured annually using a modified Daubenmire scale based on percent cover (0–1 %, 4–5 %, 5–25 %, 25–50 %, 50–75 %, 75–90 %, and 95–100 %) for each species, and the midpoint of each range was used to calculate cover (as in Ratajczak et al., 2011; Collins and Calabrese, 2012 ). For this study, we included shrub and tree species that can grow higher than the grass canopy and that are actively encroaching outside of the riparian corridor; short-statured sub-shrub species were excluded (e.g., Amorpha canescens ). Table S1  contains a list of woody species included in this analysis. Changes in cover for each watershed were calculated separately. In addition, an average weighted by watershed size (N1B=120.9, N4D=120.4, N20B=84.4 ha) was calculated to determine the overall trend across fire frequencies.   2.5 Stable isotope trends in precipitation, stream water, and groundwater 2.5.1 Long-term water isotope trends The precipitation isotope record spanned from 1/30/2001 to 11/29/2022. Amount-weighted least squares regressions were used to assess changes in precipitation δ18 O over this time period. Note that, since each isotope sample represents an integrated signature from the previous seven days (see Section 2.2 ), total weekly precipitation amounts were used as weights in the regressions. Precipitation δ18 O was also split into growing (March – September) and dormant seasons (October – February) to assess whether temporal trends occurred within either season. Amount-weighted least squares regressions were performed for each season separately over the same time period. The stream water isotope record spanned from 2/19/2007 to 8/10/2020, and the groundwater isotope record spanned from 1/13/2010 to 12/28/2022. Trends in stream water and groundwater δ18 O were assessed using linear regression analyses.    3 Results 3.1 Mean and variability of precipitation In the MHK record, results from the modified Mann-Kendall trends tests showed that annual precipitation increased from 1898 to 2021. This trend was not significant for raw annual precipitation values (p = 0.112, τ = 0.097), but the 10-year running mean value increased significantly (p < 0.001, τ = 0.517; Fig. 1  a). Variability in annual precipitation increased from 1898 until the 1960′s, and then declined through 2022 (Fig. 1 b,c). Over the entire time period, there was a significant increase in 10-year running SD (p < 0.001, τ = 0.281; Fig. 1 b) and 10-year running CV (p = 0.045, τ = 0.127; Fig. 1 c; Table S2 ). In the KPBS record, precipitation also increased over the last ∼ 40 years. This trend was not significant for raw annual precipitation values (p = 0.961, τ = 0.007), but there was a marginally significant increase in the 10-year running mean (p = 0.074, τ = 0.232). Variability (both 10-year running SD and CV) decreased significantly during the same period (SD: p < 0.001, τ = -0.674; CV: p < 0.001, τ = -0.697; Fig. 1 b,c; Table S3 ).  3.2 Seasonality of precipitation In this region, a greater proportion of precipitation occurs in the growing season compared to the dormant season, and this trend was apparent in both the MHK and KPBS records (Fig. S2 ). In the MHK record, there have been significant increases in 10-year running mean growing season (p < 0.001, τ = 0.414) and dormant season (p < 0.001, τ = 0.478) precipitation. In the KPBS record, there has been a significant increase in 10-year running mean dormant season precipitation (p = 0.011, τ = 0.239), but not growing season precipitation (p = 0.412, τ = 0.108; Fig. S2 a; Tables S2, S3 ). In both records, there has been a significant increase in the 10-yr running mean proportion of annual precipitation occurring during the dormant season (MHK: p < 0.001, τ = 0.229; KPBS: p = 0.019, τ = 0.306; Fig. S2 c, Table S2 , Table S3 ).  3.3 Number and size of precipitation events Both records show a significant increase in 10-year running mean event size (MHK: p < 0.001, τ = 0.571; KPBS: p = 0.005, τ = 0.366; Fig. 2  b, Table S2 , Table S3 ). In the MHK record, there have been significant increases in 10-year running mean event size in both the growing season (p < 0.001, τ = 0.465) and dormant season (p < 0.001, τ = 0.562; Table S2 ). In the KPBS record, there has been a marginally significant increase in 10-year running mean event size in the growing season (p = 0.054, τ = 0.251) but not the dormant season (p = 0.116, τ = 0.205; Table S3 ). There has been an increase in the number of precipitation events annually in the KPBS record (p = 0.002, τ = 0.398; Table S3 ) – this trend is driven by an increasing number of events in both the dormant (p = 0.014, τ = 0.32) and growing seasons (marginally significant; p = 0.064, τ = 0.241). In the MHK record, there was no significant trend in annual number of events (p = 0.108, τ = -0.101; Table S2 ), but there was a significant decrease in the number of growing season events per year (p = 0.005, τ = -0.178).  3.4 Shifts in precipitation-discharge relationship Modified Mann-Kendall tests showed that there was no trend in raw specific Q values over time (p = 0.722, τ = -0.045) when values were averaged across all four watersheds, but 10-year running mean specific Q declined significantly (p < 0.001, τ = -0.754; Fig. S4 ). The 10-year running mean specific Q also declined significantly in each watershed separately (Fig. S5 , Table S4 ). Similarly, raw Q/P values did not change significantly through time when values were averaged across all four watersheds (p = 0.676, τ = -0.053), but 10-year running mean Q/P did decline significantly (p < 0.001, τ = -0.812; Fig. 3  c). The 10-year running mean Q/P also declined significantly in N1B (p < 0.001, τ = -0.804), N2B (p < 0.001, τ = -0.558), and N4D (p < 0.001, τ = -0.768), and the decline was marginally significant in N20B (p = 0.097, τ = -0.246). Across the entire time period (1987 – 2020), the Pearson’s correlation between precipitation and discharge was 0.63 (Fig. S6 ). The 10-year moving window Pearson’s correlations were calculated over the same period. Correlations were highest in the late 1990′s and early 2000′s, but declined after ∼ 2003, reaching a minimum value of 0.47 (Fig. 3 b). Changes in woody cover through time were also calculated for watersheds with long-term vegetation monitoring (N1B, N4D, and N20B). Mean woody cover was calculated and weighted by watershed size to determine overall changes in woody cover from 1983 to 2021 (Fig. 3 a). Woody cover was highest and increased most rapidly in the watershed with a 20-year burn frequency, while the watershed with a 4-year burn frequency had an intermediate rate of increase, and the annually burned watershed had the lowest overall woody cover and slowest rate of increase through time (Fig. 3 a). In all three watersheds, the rate of change in woody cover increased sharply around the year 2000.  3.5 Stable isotope trends in precipitation, stream water, and groundwater Precipitation stable isotopes (δ18 O and δ2 H) were more variable than either stream water or groundwater δ18 O and δ2 H (Fig. 4  ; Fig. S7 ). Precipitation and stream / groundwater stable isotopes showed consistent and diverging trends through time at KPBS. Linear regression results showed that stream and groundwater δ18 O and δ2 H have both declined significantly through time (p < 0.001 in all cases; Fig. 4 b,c; Fig. S8 ; Table S5 ).
