In contrast, there has been no change in amount-weighted precipitation δ18 O overall (p = 0.213), or during the growing season (p = 0.412). However, dormant season precipitation δ18 O had a marginally significant increasing trend (p = 0.06; Table S4 ). There has been no change in amount-weighted precipitation of δ2 H overall (p = 0.201) or in either season (growing season: p = 0.095; dormant season: p = 0.753; Table S5 ).   4 Discussion The physical and biogeochemical changes associated with ecosystem state transitions co-evolve to control the trajectory of water cycling and partitioning across landscapes (e.g., Harman & Troch, 2014; Troch et al., 2015 ). However, such linkages and feedbacks have rarely been explored and quantified (Troch et al., 2013; 2015; Wagener et al., 2007; Wagener et al. 2010 ). Exploring changes in the water cycle following ecosystem state transitions has great potential to propel new theories and frameworks in hydrological science and further identify linkages in critical zone processes (e.g., Wilcox et al., 2022 ). Here, we used long-term records of precipitation, stream discharge, and water stable isotopes in a woody encroached mesic grassland system to explore why significant increases in annual precipitation over the last century have not been mirrored by an increase in stream discharge (Dodds et al., 2012; Keen et al., 2022, Dodds et al., 2023a ) and explore why modeling results suggest that groundwater is playing an increasing role in streamflow generation (Sadayappan et al., 2023 ). Our results show diverging trends in the isotopic composition of precipitation compared to streamflow and groundwater through time at KPBS (Fig. 4 ), as well as a rapid decrease in correlation between monthly precipitation and stream discharge (Fig. 3 b) and declining annual Q/P ratios (Fig. 3 c). Together, these results suggest that either changes in intra-annual delivery of precipitation or shifts in the physical landscape following a replacement of grasses by woody plants are altering patterns of connectivity between incoming precipitation and stream discharge. Below, we discuss these two possible mechanisms in detail. 4.1 Changes in precipitation patterns do not explain changes in streamflow generation, but may contribute to changes in stream and groundwater isotopic signatures In recent decades, increasing precipitation has been documented for multiple sites in the central Great Plains (Garbrecht et al., 2004; Dore, 2005; Rahmani et al., 2015 ). However, greater annual precipitation is typically associated with sizable increases in streamflow, and these responses are often non-linear. For example, Garbrecht et al. (2004)  reported that an increase in precipitation of just 10 % typically leads to an increase of ∼ 60 % in streamflow and a more modest increase in ET (∼5%) across sites in Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma, yet this is not what has been observed at KPBS. According to climate projections, northeastern Kansas is expected to experience increased precipitation variability in the future, leading to fewer, but larger rainfall events (Easterling et al., 2000; USGCRP, 2018; Jones, 2019; IPCC, 2021 ) – this would likely result in decreased surface soil moisture as time between rainfall events increases (Fay et al., 2002, 2003; Heisler-White et al., 2009 ), and could alter patterns of runoff and groundwater recharge (Huxman et al., 2005; Acharya et al., 2018 ). However, this trend is not yet apparent in the MHK and KPBS precipitation records. Although we have seen a shift toward larger rain events in the MHK record (Fig. 2 b; Table S2 ), there has been no accompanying reduction in the total number of rainfall events over the past century (Fig. 2 a; Fig. S3 ), leading to an overall increase in annual precipitation (Fig. 1 a). The observed patterns in the stable isotope records of stream water and groundwater could be partially attributed to an increasing proportion of precipitation falling in the dormant season, resulting in lower stream and groundwater δ18 O and δ2 H signatures over time (Fig. 4 ; Table S5 ). Dormant season precipitation is typically depleted in 18 O compared to growing season precipitation in temperate systems (as seen in Fig. 5   and Fig. S9 ), leading to clear seasonal patterns in precipitation δ18 O and δ2 H (McGuire and McDonnell, 2007; Sprenger et al., 2016; Bowen et al., 2019 ). An increase in dormant season precipitation (lower δ18 O), therefore, could contribute to a decline in stream and groundwater δ18 O over time. Both the longer-term MHK record and shorter-term KPBS record show a small but significant increase in the proportion of precipitation occurring during the dormant season (Fig. S2 c). However, over the last two decades, δ18 O of amount-weighted dormant season precipitation has increased slightly, becoming more similar to the signature of growing season precipitation (Fig. S9 ). We suggest that, in addition to these small shifts in precipitation seasonality, the contribution of dormant season precipitation to groundwater recharge has increased due to physical changes to the system.  4.2 Grassland-to-shrubland state transition further drives an increase in dormant season contribution to groundwater recharge Vegetation cover is one of the primary determinants of groundwater recharge dynamics in many terrestrial systems (Kim and Jackson, 2012; Jasechko et al., 2014 ), and changes in land-cover can substantially impact groundwater recharge dynamics. In Great Plains grasslands, woody encroachment has been proposed as a likely mechanism for observed declines in groundwater recharge (Huxman et al., 2005; Acharya et al., 2017; Acharya et al., 2018 ), particularly in more mesic systems (Wilcox et al., 2022 ). Higher woody cover has the potential to increase ET substantially in mesic grasslands (Huxman et al., 2005 ), and ET has been shown to outpace precipitation in encroached portions of tallgrass prairie during dry years (Logan and Brunsell, 2015 ). Woody shrubs and trees typically have higher canopy transpiration rates compared to grasses (O’Keefe et al., 2020 ), or the ability to continue gas exchange into the dormant season in the case of evergreen Juniperus species (the primary encroacher in the southern Great Plains; Awada et al., 2013; Caterina et al., 2014 ). Increased cover of woody species at the expense of grasses, therefore, leads to an increase in vegetation water-use at the watershed- or landscape-scale during the growing season in mesic grasslands (Huxman et al., 2005; Keen et al., 2022 ). Over the last four decades, there has also been an increase in 10-year running mean vapor pressure deficit (VPD; p < 0.001, τ = 0.596; Table S6 ). It is possible that increasing VPD could contribute to reductions in water yield since higher VPD increases atmospheric demand for water, which can increase evaporation and transpiration rates. However, it is likely that these trends in VPD also exacerbate the effects of woody encroachment on ET – previous work has shown that canopy transpiration of woody shrubs increases more rapidly with increasing VPD compared to grasses and forbs in tallgrass prairie (O’Keefe et al., 2020 ). In short, increased water-use by woody vegetation during the growing season (particularly under higher VPD conditions) could decrease the amount of growing season precipitation available to contribute to groundwater recharge (Fig. 5 a), leading to a proportional increase in the contribution of dormant season precipitation. Due to the seasonal differences in precipitation δ18 O, a decline in the contribution of growing season precipitation to groundwater recharge over time could drive reductions in stream and groundwater δ18 O. Woody encroachment could also potentially increase the contribution of dormant season precipitation to groundwater recharge by altering soil water infiltration pathways (Fig. 5 b). Coarse rooting systems of shrubs and trees can modify soil water infiltration pathways by creating macropores and increasing preferential flow of water to greater depths (Beven and Germann, 1982; Jarvis, 2007; Alaoui et al., 2011 ). Greater preferential flow may increase deep infiltration of dormant season precipitation, as most plants are not actively taking up water during the dormant season. Both of these scenarios – decreased contribution of growing season precipitation to groundwater recharge as a result of greater ET (Fig. 5 a) and / or increased contribution of dormant season precipitation to groundwater recharge as a result of altered soil water infiltration pathways (Fig. 5 b) – are physical consequences of woody encroachment that have the potential to drive, or contribute to, the observed declines in stream and groundwater δ18 O over time.  4.3 Implications of ecosystem state transitions on water cycling in tallgrass prairie While aboveground evidence for ecosystem state transitions and hysteresis in mesic grasslands has been building over the last decade (Ratajczak et al., 2014b; Collins et al., 2021 ), we do not have a solid understanding of how these transitions impact the hydrological systems to which they are intricately linked. We do know that hydrological systems can exhibit threshold behaviors – for example, recent work in tallgrass prairie groundwater systems has found that stream discharge occurs only when thresholds of groundwater storage have been reached (Hatley et al., 2023 ). This threshold behavior indicates that decreasing groundwater recharge due to woody encroachment may have non-linear effects on stream discharge, and that restoration of stream flow by removal of woody vegetation may have substantial lag-effects depending on the degree to which groundwater has decreased (Dodds et al., 2023a ). As such, these results have implications for management strategies aimed at restoring streamflow or groundwater levels by mechanically removing woody vegetation. The timing of the observed ‘breakdown’ in connectivity between precipitation and stream discharge at KPBS corresponds temporally with the rapid increase in woody cover that occurred in ∼ 2000 (Fig. 3 a,b; Ratajczak et al., 2014b ; also documented in Macpherson et al., 2019 ). This linkage is not evidence of direct causation, but it does illustrate that declining stream discharge is more closely linked with changes in woody cover than with changes in precipitation dynamics over the last ∼ 40 years (Sadayappan et al., 2023 ). In addition, our results show that stream discharge has declined in all of the watersheds observed in this study, not just the infrequently burned watersheds (Fig. S5 ) – we do not currently know the extent to which stream discharge and groundwater recharge in one watershed are impacted by encroachment across the broader landscape (i.e., upstream or in neighboring watersheds). Groundwater dye tracer studies at this site have demonstrated that groundwater can enter and leave a watershed without ever showing up in the stream (Barry, 2018 ) and geophysical data suggest a high degree of connectivity across this merokarst system (Sullivan et al. 2019 ). Therefore, it is presumable that groundwater flow does not strictly follow watershed boundaries, and extensive woody encroachment in one watershed could have implications for water yield beyond the boundaries of that specific watershed. While the consequences of woody encroachment on hydrological fluxes in tallgrass prairie are becoming evident (e.g., increasing ET, declining streamflow), identifying mechanisms responsible for alterations to the whole hydrological system requires decadal-scale observations. Changes in hydrological functioning, or potentially a shift to an alternative hydrological state, as a result of woody encroachment could take decades or centuries to reverse. Understanding the hydrological impacts of land-cover change, particularly within the context of changing climate conditions, is vital to predicting how these ecosystems will change and transform in the future.
1 Introduction Contaminated groundwater is particularly hazardous to human health (Li et al., 2021a ; Rashid et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2024; Süme et al., 2024 ). Cut-off walls are extensively utilized to control pollution spread in the contaminated site due to its low cost and limited permeability (Xu et al., 2019; He et al., 2020; Koda et al., 2019; Malusis and Barlow, 2020; Feng et al., 2023; Sample-Lord et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022 ). Soil-bentonite, cement-bentonite and high-density polyethylene geomembrane have been developed and applied to extend the service life of cut-off walls, like adsorption, chemical compatibility (Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024 ). However, the hydrogeology and contaminant properties may influence the cut-off wall performance, leading to an expended polluted area (Fu et al., 2021; Akbarpour and Mahdikhani, 2023; Norouzi et al., 2023 ). The accurate estimation of cut-off wall performance and prediction of contaminant transport under varying site condition is critical to cut-off wall design (Xie et al., 2023b; Yang et al., 2022 ). The numerical method is an efficient way to investigate the service life of a cut-off wall in complex scenario (Ding et al., 2020 ). Hassanzadeh et al (2020)  applied an upwind finite-volume method to predict the contaminant transport behavior in two scenarios, with and without cut-off wall. Shu et al (2022)  evaluated the cut-off wall service life using finite element method. They found that increasing cut-off wall thickness is a more effective way to isolate contaminant from transporting. Mostafa et al (2020)  shows that the utilization of double cut-off walls can significantly restrict contaminant transport, especially when the upstream cut-off wall is larger. Wu et al (2015)  numerically assessed the leakage behavior of cut-off walls. Ke et al (2021), Gao et al (2022), Sun et al (2019)  and Shen et al (2020)  assessed the performance of cut-off wall in controlling seawater or nitrate contaminants in costal aquifer by numerical model. Unfortunately, the possibility of instability and long calculation time restricts the numerical model in some problems (Xie et al., 2023b ). The analytical model offers distinct advantages, including convenient calculations, independence from specific software requirement, and the ease of conducting sensitive analysis. Furthermore, analytical methods can offer a deeper insight into the physical mechanisms of contaminant transport compared to numerical models (Peng et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2023a; Ding et al., 2021 ). Many analytical models have been developed for prediction of solute transport in cut-off wall in recent years (Chen et al.,2023; Ding et al., 2020; Ding and Feng, 2022a; Yan et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2023b; Lin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024 ). For example, Yan et al (2021)  and Ding et al (2020)  developed 2-D dual domain analytical model to investigate the pollution migration in the cut-off wall and aquifer. Ding and Feng (2022a)  further studied the transport behavior of solute with time-dependent point sources. However, the effects of lower layer of aquitard on pollution transport in cut-off wall system are rarely addressed. It is generally assumed that hydraulic conductivity of aquitard is closed to the cut-off wall (Batlle-Aguilar et al., 2016 ). Recent studies reported that flow in aquitard significantly affected contaminant migration in groundwater (Halloran and Hunkeler, 2020; Filippini et al., 2020; Pauloo et al., 2021 ). The contaminant leakage in the cut-off wall can be detected through seepage in the low-permeability clay (Gao et al., 2022; Roushangar et al., 2023 ). Li et al (2021b)  carried out a laboratory experiment to examine the solute transport in a two-layered heterogeneous system. They reported that the advection in aquitard was not negligible. The average darcy velocity in aquitard is about 1 × 10-7  m/s, leading to the contaminant reaching the maximum concentration in 600 h. Additionally, molecular diffusion is a key mechanism in influencing pollution migration in the cut-off wall with low-permeability (e.g., <10-9  m/s) (Fu et al., 2021; Sample-Lord et al., 2021 ). Consequently, the contaminant may release from the contaminated cut-off wall to the lower aquitard through vertical diffusion. Besides, the contaminants deposited in aquitards may serve as the secondary pollution source to groundwater. The risk that contaminants slowly released into the aquifer or underground environment has been a concern, so-called back-diffusion (Ding and Feng, 2023; Ding and Feng, 2022b ). Overall, the aquitard cannot only serve as the potential paths for contaminant transport, but it also plays a key role as the potential pollution source when the main source is maintained. Thus, further study of the cut-off wall and aquitard system is of essence to cut-off wall design. The purpose of this study is to develop a 2-D analytical model for the contaminant transport in the cut-off wall and aquitard system (CAS). The accuracy of the present solution is verified by the numerical method. The key influence of the retardation factor, hydraulic conductivity, aquitard height, and system thickness on contaminant migration in the CAS are assessed.  2 Mathematical model 2.1 Basic assumptions The cut-off wall is constructed in the contaminated site, embedded into the aquitard, to prevent the spread of pollutions. Fig. 1   presents a conceptual model illustrating contaminant transport within a CAS. The two-dimensional model for the diffusion, dispersion, advection, and adsorption of contaminants in CAS is proposed (see Fig. 1 b). The cut-off wall has a height of B1  , and the aquitard has height of B2  . The inlet concentration is assumed to be constant. Some basic assumptions are given as follow: (i) pollution diffusion obeys Fick’s second law; (ii) the porous medium is saturated, isotropic and homogeneous; (iii) adsorption is a linear and equilibrium process (Yan et al., 2020). The toluene (TOL) is considered to represent the typical organic pollutant in the contaminated site. Dispersion and advection are regarded as the main migration mechanism. The inlet concentration of the contaminant is 10 g/ml (Bonaparte et al., 2002 ). The allowable value of TOL in groundwater is 1 mg/L (USEPA, 2009 ). The relevant parameters are listed in Table 1  . First, we verify a case of contaminant migration in the CAS without considering the adsorption processes by setting Rd,1   = 1. Fig. 2  a presents the breakthrough curves (BTCs) in the aquitard (z  = 2.5 m), cut-off wall (z  = 7.5 m), and at the interface (z  = 5.0 m) using the numerical results (symbols) and our current solutions (lines). Fig. 2 b shows the relative concentration profiles across the CAS along the depth at three locations (z  = 2.5 m, 5.0 m, 7.5 m) at t  = 5 years. Secondly, we investigated a case of contaminant transport by setting Rd,1   = 4. Fig. 2 c and 2d show that the breakthrough curves are similar to those presented in Fig. 2 a and 2b. The primary difference is that there is a delay phenomenon observed due to the adsorption of contaminant in the cut-off wall. All figures demonstrate that our present solution agrees very well with the numerical solution.  4 Results and discussion 4.1 Comparison with analytical solution based on 1-D approximations In recent years, many 1-D analytical solutions are developed to model the migration of contaminants in a cut-off wall system (Liu et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2023b; Peng et al., 2021 ). In this section, we compare the 2-D results obtained from the current solution with the 1-D model developed by Chen et al. (2023) . The simplified 1-D cut-off wall model (see Fig. 3  ) exhibited an overestimation of the contaminant breakthrough time compared to the 2-D model. Increasing the aquitard hydraulic conductivity k2   from 1 × 10-9  m/s to 5 × 10-9  m/s results in an overestimation of breakthrough time by a factor of 0.2 and 5 compared to 1-D model, respectively. Overall, the cut-off wall shows the capacity to control the contaminant transport. However, the breakthrough time can be overestimated if the aquitard is not considered. Fig. 4   illustrates effects of aquitard hydraulic conductivity (k2  ) on contaminant concentration (see Fig. 4 a) and cumulative mass outflow (CMF) (see Fig. 4 b). The difference is quantified by ε  = V2-D -V1-D . V2-D  and V1-D  are the contaminant concentration or CMF predicted by the 2-D model and 1-D model, respectively. Cumulative contaminant mass outflow from the cut-off wall and aquitard system is given by (Neville and Andrews, 2006; Qiu et al., 2021 ):(50) M = ∫ 0  T  ∫ 0  B 1  + B 2    n × v × c - n × D x  ∗   × ∂ c  ∂ x     d z d t     where, T  is the service time of wall. The service time is assumed to be 30 years in this study. The allowable value of cumulative mass outflow is 5 mg/year (Yan et al., 2021 ). To comprehensively investigate the performance CAS, the contaminant concentration is all sampled from the point (1 m, 5 m), which is located at the interface between the aquitard and cut-off wall. Additionally, the ratio of the Peclet number between cut-off wall and aquitard (Pe1  /Pe2  ) is introduced to assess the difference between 2-D and 1-D models with different value of k2  . Aquitard can serve as a preferential pathway for contaminant transport when Pe1  /Pe2   < 1 (k2   > 5 × 10-10  m/s), resulting in a positive concentration difference (see Fig. 4 a). For example, the concentration may reach 0.35 at t  = 20 a for k2   = 5 × 10-9  m/s, causing an earlier breakthrough to 2-D system. On the contrary, cut-off wall may have a short breakthrough time when Pe1  /Pe2   > 1 (e.g., k2   < 5 × 10-10  m/s). For example, the barrier system can be broken through at 7a, but the aquitard will not be broken through until 25 a. In the comparison of cumulative mass outflow, the existence of aquitard, as a preferred pathway to contaminant, causes a severe release of contaminant when k2   > 7 × 10-10  m/s (Pe1  /Pe2   < 1). The CMF difference for k2   = 1 × 10-8  m/s and B2   = 5 m reaches 487 mg, which is 3 times higher than the allowable. Additionally, it can also be observed that the iso -difference is almost parallel to the curve of constant transmissivity (k2   × B2  ) when 5 × 10-9  m/s < k2   < 1.1 × 10-8  m/s as the advection is the main mechanism governing the transport of contaminants.  4.2 Effects of aquitard hydraulic conductivity and cut-off wall thickness Fig. 5   presents the coupled effects of aquitard hydraulic conductivity (k2  ) and cut-off wall thickness (W ) on contaminant cumulative mass outflow. Increasing k2   contributes to a larger Darcy velocity in aquitard (Xie et al., 2023b ). As a result, a larger mass outflow can be captured at the outlet of aquitard. For example, increasing k2   from 1 × 10-10  m/s to 5 × 10-10  m/s leads to a rise of CMF by a factor of 1.5 for the case with W =1.1 m. CMF reduces with the cut-off wall thickness increasing (Qiu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023 ). CMF at W =0.6 m can be 2 times larger than that at W =1.2 m with k2   = 1 × 10-10  m/s. The main reason for the phenomena is that the contaminant transport path is increased for the case with thicker cut-off wall. The coupled effects of aquitard hydraulic conductivity (k2  ) and the cut-off wall thickness (W ) on the contaminant transport are complicated. CMF for the case with k2   = 1 × 10-9  m/s and k2   = 1 × 10-10  m/s can be 50.7 % and 3.3 % higher than that for the case with k2   = 1 × 10-11  m/s when W =0.8 m. However, CMF for the case with k2   = 1 × 10-9  m/s and k2   = 1 × 10-10  m/s can be 64.3 % and 2.3 % higher than that for the case with k2   = 1 × 10-11  m/s when W =1.2 m. Overall, the increase in cut-off wall thickness weakens the effect of aquitard hydraulic conductivity when k2   is relatively low (e.g., 1 × 10-10  m/s), while its impacts are enhanced when k2   is relatively high (e.g., 1 × 10-9  m/s). Reducing the cut-off wall thickness allows the contaminant to reach the outlet earlier. The CMF for the cases with relatively high k2   (e.g., k2   = 1 × 10-10  m/s) are more sensitive to the variation of W  due to its broader distribution of contaminant. This phenomenon can be observed in Fig. 5 . The iso -concentration line tends to be vertical to the x -axis when k2   < 1 × 10-9  m/s. The 150 mg allowable cumulative mass outflow line is added in Fig. 5  to assess the performance of cut-off walls. This curve may contribute to the design of the CAS as it can be easily used to assess whether the CMF requirement is met. It can be observed that the thicker cut-off wall is required to ensure the CMF will not exceed the allowable value when k2   is in a higher value (e.g., 1 × 10-9  m/s). For example, W =0.8 m is sufficient for k2   = 1 × 10-10  m/s, but W =1.1 m is required when k2   = 1 × 10-9  m/s. CMF are always higher than the allowable value when the thickness of cut-off wall is lower than 0.6 m. This phenomenon is mainly because that the contaminant mass outflow from the cut-off wall becomes the main source. Fig. s1  presents the effects of k2   on contaminant mass outflow released from cut-off wall and aquitard. CMF from the aquitard rapidly decreases to 0 with the decrease of k2  , but CMF from the cut-off wall keeps at 108 mg. An approximate fitting formula expression for the determination of the thickness of the wall from the allowable CMF curve is presented (R2  > 0.9):(51) W = 0.73457 + 3.6911 × 10 8  × k 2       This equation can be used to calculate the required thickness of cut-off wall based on the aquitard hydraulic conductivity to ensure that the CMF is allowable. For example, the thickness is required to be larger than 1.11 m when k2   = 1 × 10-9  m/s, according to Eq. (51) . The variation of aquitard hydraulic conductivity may influence the result of parameters analysis. Furthermore, the same standards should be adopted to conduct the parameters analysis. Thus, in the following section, Eq. (51)  is used. The change of k2   will be transformed to the variation of W . The cumulative mass outflow of cut-off wall and aquitard system will meet the allowable CMF at any value of k2  . Thus, the influence of parameters can be quantified by observing its ability in reducing CMF.  4.3 Effects of the cut-off wall adsorption The influences of the cut-off wall adsorption (Rd,1  ) on the contaminant breakthrough behavior are shown in Fig. 6  . The retardation factor of aquitard (Rd,2  ) is set as a constant (e.g., Rd,2   = 3.33). Eq. (51)  is applied to ensure that CMF is compliant under different thickness of cut-off wall. It should be noted that the increase of W  may lead to the increase of k2  . The curve of allowable CMF is almost parallel to the x -axis. This proves the effectiveness of Eq. (51) . An increase of Rd,1   may result in a reduction in CMF. For example, the CMF for Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 5 is 32 % and 26 % less than that for Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 2 when W =1.2 m and W =0.8 m. An increase of Rd,1   leads to an increase in the ability about delaying contaminant transport through adsorption (Liu et al., 2023 ). As a result, the less contaminant is accumulated at the outlet of the cut-off wall for a limited time (e.g., 30 a). Additionally, the impact of cut-off wall thickness on the breakthrough of contaminant is sensitive to the variation of Rd,1  . Increasing W  from 0.8 to 1.2 m leads to 10 mg decrease of CMF for the case with Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 5. However, an increase in CMF can also be observed for W  increasing when Rd,1 /Rd,2   < 2. For example, CMFs for the case with W =1.2 m can be 7 mg larger than that for the case of W =0.8 m when Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 1.5. The primary reason is the disproportionate increase and decrease in the CMF from the CAS. CMF from the cut-off wall and aquitard exhibits distinct response to changes in W  resulting from the application of Eq. (51) . Fig. s2  shows the effects of cut-off wall thickness on CMF from the cut-off wall and aquitard for the case with Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 1.5 (Fig. s2 a) and Rd,1 /Rd,2   = 4 (Fig. s2 b). Increasing W  from 0.8 m to 1.2 m leads to a 58 mg increase of CMF from the aquitard for all cases. However, the CMF from the cut-off wall is decreased by 50 mg and 68 mg for the case with Rd,1  /Rd,2   = 1.5 and Rd,1  /Rd,2   = 4, respectively. The response of CMF from the cut-off wall to the change of W  is influenced by value of Rd,1  . A high value Rd,1  /Rd,2   (e.g., Rd,1  /Rd,2   = 4) can lead to a lay of contaminant transport. This leads to a significant decrease of CMF from the cut-off wall.  4.4 Combined effects of aquitard height and cut-off wall thickness The combined influences of the aquitard height (B2  ) and the cut-off wall thickness (W ) on CMF are shown in Fig. 7  . The total height of the cut-off wall and aquitard system is assumed to be constant (e.g., B1   + B2   = 15 m). The curve of allowable CMF is given in Fig. 7 . Increasing W  or decreasing B2   can effectively reduce the value of CMF. For example, the CMF is about 150 mg for the case with W =1 m and B2   = 5 m. However, the CMF for the case with W =1.2 m and B2   = 2 m and the case with W =0.8 m and B2   = 6 m, are 135 mg and 137 mg, respectively. This can be attributed to the fact that k2   changes with W  due to Eq. (51) . As discussed in Sec. 4.1, the ratio of Peclet number can be used to estimate the performance of aquitard with different value of W  (k2  ). The aquitard is served as the preferential pathway for contaminant transport when W =1.2 (k2   = 1.24 × 10-9  m/s and Pe1 /Pe2   < 1). As shown in Fig. s3 a, increasing B2   from 1 m to 6 m leads to a 41.4 mg reduction of CMF from the cut-off wall while a 67.9 mg increase of CMF from the aquitard for the case with W =1.2 m (Pe1 /Pe2   < 1). Thus, the insert depth of cut-off wall should be increased (increasing B1  ). Aquitard shows the capacity to prevent the spread of contaminant when W =0.8 m (Pe1 /Pe2   > 1). Increasing B2   from 1 m to 6 m leads to a 1.36-fold reduction of CMF from the cut-off wall and a 6-fold increase of CMF from the aquitard. Thus, the intrinsic advantage of aquitard should be used effectively to reduce construction cost through increasing B2  .  4.5 Discussion The aquitard is assumed to be the impermeable layers to eliminate its influence and simplify the transport model (Ding et al., 2020; Ding and Feng, 2022a; Peng et al., 2021 ). This assumption facilitates the development of a 1-D solution for the predition of contaminant behavior in the cut-off wall. However, we showed that the earlier breakthrough behavior of contaminant can be predicted by the 1-D model due to the neglection of aquitard (see Sec. 4.1 and Fig. 3 ). For example, the breakthrough time predicted by 1-D model developed by Chen et al., (2023)  can be 1.4 times longer than that of the present solution (see Fig. 3 ). In consequence, the long-term performance prediction of the cut-off wall using a 1-D model may be unreliable. The hydraulic conductivity of the aquitard is a key factor influencing the service life of the cut-off wall system (Filippini et al., 2020; Pauloo et al., 2021 ). We quantified the effect of aquitard on the breakthrough behavior of contaminant using Peclet number ratio (Pe1  /Pe2  ) between the cut-off wall and aquitard. Aquitard can serve as a preferential pathway for contaminant transport when Pe1  /Pe2   < 1. The 1-D model presented by Chen et al. (2023)  is sufficient to simulate and predict the contaminant transport in the cut-off wall when Pe1  /Pe2   ≥ 1. However, the 1-D cut-off wall model may ignore the fact that the aquitard can serve as a preferential pathway, resulting in an underestimation to contaminant concentration when Pe1  /Pe2   < 1. There are generally three ways to enhance the performance of a cut-off wall: reducing the hydraulic conductivity (Xie et al., 2023b ), increasing the width/height (Ding et al., 2020 ), and improving the adsorption capacity (Liu et al., 2023 ). The experimental results show that increasing the cut-off wall height is an effective method to improve the long-term performance of a cut-off wall (Shen et al., 2020 ). However, we showed that this method is less effective when accounting for the influence of the underlayer aquitard in cases where Pe1  /Pe2   > 1. Increasing the height of the cut-off wall may reduce the amounts of contaminants in the aquitard when Pe1  /Pe2   > 1, but it will also result in a higher cumulative mass outflow from the cut-off wall (see Fig. 7  and Fig. s3 ). Under the circumstances, enhancing the adsorption capacity and decreasing hydraulic conductivity of cut-off walls can be effective methods to maintain its long-term performance for contaminant isolation. It is noted that the analytical model presented in this study is based on the assumptions outlined in Section 2.1  of the model development. One limitation is that the cut-off wall is saturated, homogeneous, and isotropic. It does not account for the unsaturated region resulting from transpiration and groundwater fluctuation. The contaminant transport in the CAS is limited to a steady-state groundwater flow. However, this assumption may achieve a more conservative result (Ding et al., 2020 ). In addition, it does not consider the degradation of contaminants within the source and barrier system, making it unsuitable for predicting the transport of organic contaminants with unstable degradation products in the wall (Xie et al., 2023b; Ding et al., 2020 ). The inlet and outlet boundary conditions are assumed to be of constant concentration and semi-infinite. Due to uncertainties in accurately determining transport properties and boundary conditions, simplified initial and boundary conditions may be preferable, particularly for preliminary cut-off wall design (Xie et al., 2023b ). Despite these limitations, the proposed analytical model remains valuable for evaluating the performance of a cut-off wall, considering the effects of underlayer aquitard.   5 Conclusion This paper presents a two-dimensional analytical model to study contaminant transport in the cut-off wall and aquitard system, considering advection, dispersion and adsorption processes. These processes were coupled by the continuity of contaminant mass fluxes and concentration the interface between the cut-off wall and aquitard. The present solution is verified with a series of numerical result. The present solution was compared to the one-dimensional analytical model. We showed that the simplified 1-D cut-off wall model exhibited an overestimation of the contaminant breakthrough time compared to the 2-D model. The breakthrough time predicted by 1-D model can be 1.4 times longer than that of the present solution. Therefore, the prediction of the service life of the cut-off wall using a 1-D model that does not account for the effects of the underlying aquitard may be compromised. The ratio of Peclet number between the cut-off wall and aquitard can demonstrate the case when the aquitard should be considered. The aquitard shows the equivalent or stronger capacity to prevent the spread of contaminant when Pe1  /Pe2   ≥ 1. However, the aquitard can serve as the preferential pathway for contaminant transport when Pe1  /Pe2   < 1. The hydraulic conductivity of aquitard plays a key role in affecting cumulative mass outflow from the cut-off wall and aquitard system. For example, increasing the aquitard hydraulic conductivity from 1 × 10-10  m/s to 1 × 10-8  m/s results in a rise of cumulative mass outflow by a factor of 1.5. In addition, we claimed that enhancing the adsorption capacity of the cut-off wall can effectively improve its long-term performance when accounting for the influence of the underlayer aquitard in cases where Pe1  /Pe2   > 1.
1 Introduction Deep neural networks (DNNs) have experienced significant development and have seen widespread use over the past decade in nearly every scientific field, such as healthcare and economics (Esteva et al., 2019 ; Tahmasebi et al. 2020 ; Chai et al., 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Vu and Jardani; 2023 ; Virupaksha et al., 2024 ). The exceptional ability of DNNs to identify patterns and intricate relationships in various types of data, such as text, images, and audio, is mainly due to their sophisticated training algorithms, numerous adjustable parameters, and multi-layered nonlinear architectures. Deep learning has been propelled by sophisticated algorithms and significant advancements in computational hardware, especially the evolution of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) that enable the training of expansive DNNs within a reasonable timeframe. To be robust and reliable, DNNs require proper training, which typically necessitates a substantial amount of training data. Generally, the performance of a DNN improves with the quantity and quality of data used in the training (Alzubaidi et al., 2021 ; Whang et al., 2023 ). However, this data requirement can create a bottleneck in scientific applications where obtaining such datasets is prohibitively expensive or impractical. Training on such limited data would yield DNNs with questionable performance and poor reliability. Nonetheless, the fundamental physical laws governing the processes are well-known and understood in many scientific applications. Given the constraints of limited data availability in scientific domains, it is crucial to incorporate these established physical laws to inform and constrain the learning process of neural networks (NNs). Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) present an effective solution to the challenge of data scarcity in scientific machine learning that have been explored by Lagaris et al. (1998)  and revisited in detail by Berg and Nyström (2018)  and Raissi et al. (2019) . PINNs ensure that the network's predictions adhere to the relevant physical principles by incorporating the governing physical laws as regularization terms within the loss function. This integration of a priori knowledge maintains consistency with physical laws and improves the model's generalization capabilities, accuracy, and convergence in situations with limited datasets (Raissi et al., 2019 ). PINNs can be readily applied for high-dimensional problems and naturally incorporate noisy data, an invaluable requirement for tackling real-world applications. They are particularly suited for solving inverse problems, requiring only minor modifications to the algorithm to switch from forward to inverse tasks (Karniadakis et al., 2021 ). Another technical advantage is PINNs’ use of automatic differentiation to compute the derivatives necessary for the governing partial differential equations (PDEs), which is straightforward and permits evaluations at machine precision (Baydin et al., 2018 ; Raissi et al., 2019 ). The strengths of PINNs, including their ability to operate without local time-stepping, gridding, or linearizing problems, coupled with their proficiency in high-dimensional spaces, position them as a promising alternative to both conventional solvers and data-driven DNNs. PINNs have been receiving increased attention for various applications related to porous media. For instance, Fuks and Tchelepi (2020)  investigated the standard Buckley-Leverett problem representing two-phase flow in porous media. Shan et al. (2023)  extended the work on this problem by adopting a novel physics-informed long short-term memory (LSTM) network with an attention mechanism. Amini et al. (2022)  explored the use of PINNs to simulate thermo-hydro-mechanical processes in porous media, relying on a sequential training strategy. Amini et al. (2023)  extended this application to parameter identification. Du et al. (2023)  utilized PINNs to investigate CO2  sequestration in saline aquifers that involve density-driven convection processes in porous media. Pour and Voskov (2023)  used PINNs to simulate two-phase immiscible and miscible compositional transport in porous media for CO2  storage in subsurface reservoirs. Bandai and Ghezzehei (2022)  applied PINNs with domain decomposition for forward and inverse modeling of water flow in heterogeneous soil. Chen et al. (2023)  modeled water flow in unsaturated soils while utilizing different variants of PINNs with loss balancing. In the same context, Bandai and Ghezzehei (2021)  used PINNs for parameter estimation and Wang et al. (2023)  extended this application to coupled flow and heat processes. Faroughi et al. (2023)  investigated the use of PINNs to solve the 2D solute transport problem in heterogeneous porous media governed by the advection-dispersion equation. Chew et al. (2024)  modeled clogging dynamics in groundwater systems to predict effluent discharge concentrations from closed and saturated porous media systems. Aliakbari et al. (2023)  proposed a framework to improve inverse transport modeling in heterogeneous domains using an ensemble of NNs. PINNs were also used to simulate heat conduction in porous media utilizing a physics-informed convolutional encoder-decoder neural network (Xu et al., 2023 ). When dealing with modeling flow, transfer, or mechanical processes in porous media, a commonly faced challenge is the heterogeneity of the porous domains. Heterogeneity is key in controlling these processes (Kolditz et al., 2018 ). In several cases, such as in fractured domains or block heterogeneity, the parameters of the porous media can exhibit sharp discontinuities (Bear, 2018 ). In such cases, PINNs often fail to produce accurate results or face convergence issues (Haghighat et al., 2021 ; Lehmann et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2022 , 2023a ). This lack of accuracy and robustness is attributable to the use of automatic differentiation, which is required for evaluating the partial derivatives. Automatic differentiation can produce questionable results when handling problems that feature discontinuities (Hückelheim et al., 2023 ). Several solutions have been proposed to address this shortcoming related to heterogeneity. Tartakovsky et al. (2020)  and Wang et al. (2020)  incorporated an analytical expression to represent the heterogeneous hydraulic conductivity field. Although achieving such analytical expressivity for hydraulic conductivity is improbable in real-world scenarios, this method allows for the calculation of the derivatives of hydraulic conductivity either analytically or through automatic differentiation. He et al. (2020)  employed a DNN to estimate the heterogeneous hydraulic conductivity field, allowing for automatic differentiation to find the spatial derivatives. Lehmann et al. (2023)  showed that the performance of this approach is questionable when the conductivity field is highly discontinuous. Zhang et al. (2023b)  applied finite volume discretization to the governing equations of two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media and incorporated the outputs from PINN into these discretized equations, thus eliminating the need for automatic differentiation. Alhubail et al. (2022)  and Bandai and Ghezzehei (2022)  utilized a domain decomposition technique that divides the domain into homogeneous subdomains and connects them using interface rules, thereby avoiding automatic differentiation at discontinuous interfaces. One approach that has recently garnered increased attention for dealing with heterogeneous domains is the use of the mixed formulation of the governing equations. This formulation proceeds by using both pressure head and velocity as primary variables, in contrast to the standard formulation, which typically only uses the pressure head (Lehmann et al., 2023 ; Aliakbari et al., 2023 ; Hoteit and Firoozabadi, 2008 ). The use of the mixed formulation allows for avoiding the spatial derivatives of the hydraulic conductivity field. Lehmann et al. (2023)  investigated several test cases of flow in heterogeneous domains where standard PINNs fail to converge due to heterogeneity. They also showed that PINNs with the mixed formulation overcame convergence issues and achieved accurate solutions in highly heterogeneous domains. The use of the mixed formulation is not limited to porous media. In the work of Haghighat et al. (2021) , the mixed formulation was employed to solve both the forward and inverse problems in solid mechanics. It was found that using an independent NN for each variable of interest, such as displacement and stress, resulted in greater accuracy than finding the remaining quantities of interest through differentiation, such as finding stress from displacement. Rezaei et al. (2022)  showed that the mixed formulation can extend to various engineering problems involving heterogeneity, such as linear elasticity and steady-state diffusion problems. Harandi et al. 2023  extended the use of the mixed formulation to coupled thermo-mechanical processes and showed its high performance. More generally, the mixed formulation of PINNs is similar to first-order PINNs in its approach to solving PDEs. Unlike standard PINNs that solve the PDE directly, first-order PINNs target a reduced complexity by incorporating the PDE's first-order formulation into the loss function (Gladstone et al., 2023 ). This integration is accomplished by designing the NN to output the primary variables and their first-order derivatives. Although a single NN could be used to output all the primary variables and their first-order derivatives, some previous experiments indicate that employing a separate NN for primary variables and first-order derivatives results in better performance (Lehmann et al., 2023 ). Reducing the order of the PDE can improve the accuracy of PINNs, as demonstrated in the case of flow through heterogeneous porous media, as well as reduce the training time by avoiding the need to evaluate high-order derivatives through automatic differentiation. This approach avoids additional backpropagation, which is memory-intensive and time-consuming (Rezaei et al., 2022 ; Gladstone et al., 2023 ). Although the mixed formulation, developed by Lehmann et al. (2023) , allows for accurate simulation of fluid flow in heterogeneous porous media, this formulation necessitates the inclusion of additional equations to be solved. Applying the mixed formulation for flow in porous media requires solving the mass continuity and Darcy's equations separately. This results in more terms in the loss function that PINNs must satisfy. Thus, a multi-term loss function is required, for which weighting the different terms is a challenging issue that could impact the accuracy and convergence of the training algorithm. Appropriate weighting of the loss terms is crucial; otherwise, PINNs might not converge to the desired solution (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ). A simplistic approach might involve assigning equal weight to each term, but this could lead to convergence issues or solutions with reduced accuracy (Maddu et al., 2022 ). A similar problem is encountered when addressing multi-physics problems with PINNs. When modeling multiple coupled physical processes that act simultaneously, each process is represented by a loss term within the overall loss function. This creates a complex loss function landscape, which can lead to unstable optimization during training. This instability often results in trivial solutions that do not capture the nuances of the modeled coupled processes (Haghighat et al., 2022 ; Amini et al., 2022 ; Harandi et al., 2023 ). Thus, with the mixed formulation, it is imperative to balance the weights appropriately to ensure optimal training. To the best of our knowledge, weighting the loss function of the mixed formulation for flow in heterogeneous domains has not been discussed previously. The main goal of this work is to address this gap by exploring the performance of different weighting strategies developed in the literature. Thus, the main objective of this paper is to advance a new implementation of the mixed formulation developed by Lehmann et al. (2023)  to improve the convergence, efficiency, and accuracy of the previous implementations. As a first step, we conduct a survey of existing weighting strategies with PINNs. This survey helps identify potential strategies that could be useful for modeling flow in heterogeneous domains using the mixed formulation. These strategies include Max-Average weighting (Wang et al., 2021 ), inverse Dirichlet weighting (Maddu et al., 2022 ), dynamically normalized weighting (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ), neural tangent kernel (NTK)-based weighting (Wang et al., 2022 ), self-adaptive weighting (McClenny and Braga-Neto, 2023 ), residual-based weighting (Anagnostopoulos et al., 2024 ), and differentiable adversarial self-adaptive weighting (Zhang et al., 2023a ). A series of test cases with increasing complexity are defined and simulated based on these weighting techniques. These test cases are used to investigate the performance of the weighting techniques in terms of accuracy and convergence.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Governing equations The equations that govern single-phase fluid flow within heterogeneous porous media are Darcy's law and the continuity equation. Under steady-state conditions, Darcy's law can be expressed as:(1) u = − K ∇ h     where u   is Darcy velocity [L.T −1 ], K  is the heterogeneous hydraulic conductivity field [L.T −1 ], and h  is the pressure head of the fluid [L ]. The continuity equation, assuming there is no source term, is given by:(2) ∇ · u = 0      Though these two equations are commonly coupled and solved simultaneously, with the mixed formulation approach, they are kept decoupled. This allows us to avoid computing the spatial derivatives of hydraulic conductivity. Associated with these equations, there may be Dirichlet boundary conditions for the imposed pressure head and Neumann boundary conditions for the imposed velocity.  2.2 Physics-Informed neural networks PINNs, as introduced by Raissi et al. (2019) , are algorithms for solving both forward and inverse problems related to PDEs. For the forward problem, as is the focus of this work, PINNs act as a surrogate model that estimates the state variables of the PDEs. They use NNs which take the independent spatial and temporal variables as input and produce the state variables as output. Typically, a fully connected NN is utilized, which can be evaluated recursively, as follows:(3a) a  l  = W  l  z  l − 1   + b  l  ,  for   l = 1 … L     (3b) z  l  = σ ( a  l  )      (3c) f N N   = W  L + 1   z  L  + b  L + 1        Eqs. (3a)  and (3b ) allow for evaluating the outputs of a layer l  (z l  ) using the outputs of the previous layer (z  l  − 1 ), the weight matrix of layer (W l  ), the bias vector of layer l  (b l  ), and the activation function (σ). In Eq. (3a) , z  0  represents the input to the NN. Eq. (3c)  allows for evaluating the output of the NN (fNN  ) based on the weight matrix of the last layer (W  L  + 1 ) and its bias vector (b  L  + 1 ), where L  is the total number of hidden layers. The NNs must satisfy the governing equations and their constraints (i.e., boundary and initial conditions) to yield an accurate solution to the problem. This is achieved via an iterative training process in which the loss function is optimized by adjusting the NNs’ trainable parameters (all weight matrices and bias vectors) until reaching a user-specified threshold. The loss function typically includes terms reflecting the PDEs, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and any available labeled data. The PDE loss term is computed by evaluating the residuals of the governing equations at collocation points, which are distributed within the problem's overall temporal and spatial domain. To find the PDE residuals, it is necessary to compute the derivatives of NNs’ outputs with respect to the inputs. Automatic differentiation is employed, which efficiently calculates these derivatives using the chain rule. Similar to the PDE loss, the loss terms for initial and boundary conditions are evaluated at selected points along the boundaries of the domain. The training procedure ideally leads to a simultaneous minimization of all loss terms. In our application, we allocate a distinct NN to the pressure head (h ) and to each component of Darcy's velocity (u  and v ) (Fig. 1  ). It is possible to use one NN with multiple outputs (h ,  u , and v ), or one NN for h  and another for u  and v . However, as discussed by Lehmann et al. (2023) , the implementation with three different NNs had the best accuracy and convergence. A single, unified multi-term loss function is utilized to train all three NNs simultaneously, as can be seen in Fig. 1 . Each loss term can have an associated weight to adjust the relative importance of the different terms and facilitate the training process. The total loss function can be expressed as follows:(4) L = L P D E   + L B C       where L   is the total loss representing the sum of the PDE loss (L P D E    ) and the boundary conditions loss (L B C    ). These two terms explicitly are:(5a) L P D E   =  λ D x   L D x   + λ D y   L D y   + λ C E   L C E       (5b) L B C   =  λ B C D   L B C D   + λ B C N   L B C N        Where L D x     and L D y     are the loss terms for x - and y -components of Darcy's law, respectively, L C E     is the continuity equation loss term, and L B C D     and L B C N     are the loss terms for the Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, respectively. λDx  , λDy  , λCE  , λBCD  , and λBCN   are weights associated with each corresponding loss term, each sharing the same subscript notation as its respective loss term. We employ the Mean-Squared Error (MSE ) metric to compute the individual loss terms. The terms can be written as follows:(6a) L Dx   =  MSE ( u + K ∂ h  ∂ x   )   =  1 N PDE   ∑ i = 1  N PDE   ( u + K ∂ h  ∂ x   )   2  |  ( x i  , y i  )          (6b) L Dy   =  MSE ( v + K ∂ h  ∂ y   )   =  1 N PDE   ∑ i = 1  N PDE   ( v + K ∂ h  ∂ y   )   2  |  ( x i  , y i  )          (6c) L C E    =  M S E ( ∂ u  ∂ x   + ∂ v  ∂ y    )   =  1 N P D E    ∑ i = 1  N P D E    ( ∂ u  ∂ x   + ∂ v  ∂ y    )   2  |  ( x i  , y i   )       (6d) L B C D   =  M S E ( h − h B C    )  =  1 N B C D    ∑ i = 1  N B C D    ( h − h b c    )   2  |  ( x i  , y i   )       (6e) L BCN   =  MSE ( u − u BC  )  + MSE ( v − v BC  )      =  1 N BCNu   ∑ i = 1  N BCNu   ( u − u bc  )   2  |  ( x i  , y i  )         +  1 N BCNv   ∑ i = 1  N BCNv   ( v − v bc  )   2  |  ( x i  , y i  )          where NPDE   represents the total number of collocation points used for enforcing the PDE within the domain, NBCD   denotes the number of points for the Dirichlet boundary condition, and NBCNu   and NBCNv   indicate the number of points for the Neumann boundary conditions of the x  and y  components of velocity, respectively. hbc   represents the value of the pressure head for the Dirichlet boundary conditions, while ubc   and vbc   represent the values of the x  and y  components of velocity for the Neumann boundary conditions, respectively. The coordinates (xi ,yi  ) represent the points at which each respective loss is evaluated. Therefore, these coordinates are confined to the boundaries for L B C D    , but they can be located anywhere within the domain for L C E    .  2.3 Weighting methods As previously discussed in the introduction, the mixed formulation necessitates a multi-term loss function, which can be highly non-convex due to the interactions among several competing terms. Training NNs with such a loss function may not guarantee optimal convergence. In this context, it is crucial to appropriately weigh the different loss terms to improve the training algorithm's convergence. This section aims to discuss weighting techniques that could prove useful for applying PINNs to model flow in heterogeneous porous media. Following the classification suggested by Anagnostopoulos et al. (2024) , the weights can be categorized as either global or local. A global weight is a scalar that multiplies the associated loss term, whereas a local weight is a vector that applies to the individual points contained within that loss term. Global weights could be considered a special case of local weights that apply uniformly to all points. The literature contains numerous global and local weighting strategies. We focus the discussions on a select few, chosen for their demonstrated rate of improvement across various applications, computational costs, prevalence in the literature, and suitability for flow in heterogeneous domains. 2.3.1 Global weights Many studies used the baseline implementation of PINNs, which assign unity weights to all loss terms (Raissi et al., 2019 ). In some studies, the weights of the loss terms are manually tuned through a trial-and-error process (Mao et al., 2020 ; Jagtap et al., 2020 ; Rasht‐Behesht et al., 2022 ; Cheng Wong et al., 2024 ). Other studies use weights that are optimized during network training (Li and Feng, 2022 ). Significant improvements in the performance and accuracy of PINNs have been achieved through techniques that dynamically update the loss term weights during training based on the gradients of the loss terms with respect to NN parameters. Four such techniques are discussed below.- Max-Average Weighting Technique (MA-PINN)     This technique is developed by Wang et al. (2021) . The weights are updated during training based on the back-propagated gradients of the individual loss terms with respect to NN parameters. It proposes to use the statistics of these gradients to find weights that ensure similar gradient magnitudes for the different loss terms. Here, the loss function is reformulated as follows:(7) L = L 1  + ∑ k  λ k  L k      where L 1    is a designated loss that is used as a reference and L k    represents the remaining loss terms. At an iteration n  of the training algorithm, the weights of the loss terms ( λ k n  )    are updated using the weights of the previous iteration ( λ k n − 1   ) ,    as follows:(8a) λ ^  k n  = max { | ∇ θ  L 1   |  }  λ k n − 1   | ∇ θ  L k   |   ‾        (8b) λ k n  = α λ k n − 1   + ( 1 − α  )  λ ^  k n      where λ ^  k n    is a preliminary estimation of the new weight, ∇θ  represents the gradient with respect to all NN parameters, m a x { |  ∇ θ  L 1   |   }    is the maximum absolute gradient value of the designated loss term L 1   , |  ∇ θ  L k   |   ¯    is the mean absolute gradient value for loss term L k   , and α is a smoothing or decay factor. As seen in Eq. (8a) , the weights are updated based on the ratio of the maximum absolute gradient value of the designated loss term to the mean absolute gradient value of each loss term. This ratio establishes the relative significance of each term compared to the designated loss L 1   , which is assigned a weight of one. Typically, the designated loss L 1    is the PDE loss term. In cases involving multiple equations, it is the loss term for the equation containing the highest order derivatives, since its gradient tends to dominate the gradients of the other terms (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ). The algorithm then applies a moving average to the weight values to mitigate the noisy behavior that is a byproduct of training with gradient descent methods (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ). This smoothing is controlled by the factor α.- Inverse-Dirichlet Weighting Technique (ID-PINN)     Maddu et al. (2022)  proposed another statistics-based weighting method where the purpose of the weights is to equalize the gradient variances across all loss terms. The weight for each loss term is determined by the ratio of the standard deviation of the gradient of a designated loss, s t d ( ∇ θ  L 1  )   , to the standard deviation of the gradient for each respective loss term, s t d ( ∇ θ  L k  )   . The weight of the designated loss term is set to one, and a moving average is applied to the weights.(9a) λ ^  k n  = s t d ( ∇ θ  L 1   )   s t d ( ∇ θ  L k   )        (9b) λ k n  = α λ k n − 1   + ( 1 − α  )  λ ^  k n      - Dynamically Normalized Weighting Technique (DN-PINN)     Instead of gradient statistics, Deguchi and Asai (2023)  find weights based on the quadratic norm of the gradients. The weight of each loss term is the ratio of the norm of the gradient of a designated loss, |  |  ∇ θ  L 1   |   |   2   , to the norm of the gradient for each respective loss term, |  |  ∇ θ  L k   |   |   2   . Similarly to the previous techniques, the weight of the designated loss term is one, and a moving average is applied to the weights.(10a) λ ^  k n  = | | ∇ θ  L 1   |  |  2  | | ∇ θ  L k   |  |  2       (10b) λ k n  = α λ k n − 1   + ( 1 − α  )  λ ^  k n      - Neural Tangent Kernel Weighting Technique (NTK-PINN)     This technique, as proposed by Wang et al. (2022) , aims to find optimal weights based on the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. Unlike the prior empirical methods that focus on balancing back-propagated gradients, this approach is grounded in theory, using NTK to analyze the training dynamics of fully connected NNs. The assigned weights balance the convergence rate of the different loss terms. For a loss function L = ∑ k  λ k  L k    , where L k  = MSE ( r k  )    , the weights are determined using the following equations:(11a) K k  = J k   J k T      (11b) λ k  = ∑ i  T r ( K i  )   T r ( K k  )         Here, Jk   (and its transpose J k T  )     represents the Jacobian matrix of the residuals rk   in the L k    term with respect to NN parameters θ. Kk   represents the NTK for the k th  loss term, and Tr  denotes the trace of a matrix. The convergence rate of each term is influenced by the eigenvalues of its corresponding NTK, and the trace of the NTK is equal to the sum of the eigenvalues. For detailed proofs and the derivation of these equations, we refer the reader to the original paper (Wang et al. 2022 ). Generally, global weighting techniques require longer training times than standard PINNs for the same number of iterations. This increased duration stems from the need for additional backpropagations, which are used to determine weights based on gradient values. It is worth noting that these computations can be highly expensive, especially when using deep and wide NNs (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ). As a result, it is common practice not to update the weights at every training iteration. Instead, the frequency of updates is user-defined; for instance, weights might be updated every five iterations (Deguchi and Asai, 2023 ). In the case of the NTK method, the updates may only happen every 100 iterations because it is more computationally intensive than other global methods.  2.3.2 Local weights Unlike global weights, which influence the entire loss term, local weights are applied to the individual points within each loss term. Some studies showed that this approach could enable more effective training of PINNs, particularly in problems where certain regions of the solution demand additional focus. Such scenarios include multi-scale problems, highly nonlinear problems, problems with discontinuous solutions, or problems with steep solutions with sharp changes (Zhang et al., 2023a ; McClenny and Braga-Neto, 2023 ; Anagnostopoulos et al., 2024 ). Three local weighting techniques are discussed here. To illustrate these techniques, we express the loss function as follows:(12) L = ∑ k  L k  = ∑ k   M S E ( w k  R k   )       Where L k    represents the loss terms, and R  k    and w  k    are the corresponding residual and weight vectors defined over all the collocation points, respectively.- Self-Adaptive Weighting Technique (SA-PINN)     This technique has been introduced by McClenny and Braga-Neto (2023) . It involves assigning a trainable weight to each individual point within each loss term. These weights are trained simultaneously with the network's trainable parameters. The core principle is that points with higher residuals contribute more significantly to their respective loss term. By assigning greater weight to these points, the network is encouraged to pay more attention to them. To facilitate this, a minimax adversarial training strategy is adopted where weights are updated by gradient ascent, and network parameters are updated by gradient descent. The local weights are updated dynamically during the training process using gradient ascent such that:(13) w k  n + 1   = w k  n  + η w  ∇ w k   L k      where n  represents the iteration, ηw   is the learning rate for the weights, and ∇ w k   L k     is the gradient of L k    with respect to the local weights. This process is applied consistently across all loss terms. Concurrently, the network parameters undergo standard training, potentially with a different learning rate, while utilizing the weighted loss.- Residual-Based Attention Weighting Technique (RBA-PINN)     This technique has been proposed by Anagnostopoulos et al. (2024) . It is a local weighting method that does not require additional networks, extra trainable parameters, or the computation of gradients. This method calculates weights based on the values of the normalized residuals of the loss terms, as expressed in Eq. (14) .(14) w k  n + 1   = γ w k  n  + η  *  ∥  R k  ∥ ∞    | R k  |       In Eq. (14) , the first term, containing the RBA decay parameter γ, gradually decreases the contribution of prior weights, and the second term, with the RBA learning rate η* incorporates current residual information into the weights. The term |R  k   | denotes the absolute value of the residual vector corresponding to the loss term L k   , while ||R  k   ||∞  is the maximum absolute value of the vector. Initially, the weights are set to zero and the RBA learning rate to one. In subsequent iterations, the user specifies the learning rate. This approach ensures that the weights remain bounded, with bounds for the local weights defined as w i  n  ∈ (  0 ,  η  *  1 − γ    ]      as k  → ∞. This condition holds, provided that |  R k  |   ∥  R k  ∥ ∞    ∈ [ 0 , 1  ]     and w i  0  ≠ 0   .- Differentiable Adversarial Self-Adaptive Weighting Technique (DASA-PINN)     DASA has been proposed by Zhang et al. (2023a) . This approach utilizes sub-networks to find the weights for each individual point within each loss term. The weights λ k   for loss term k  are found using the following equations:(15a) o k  =  o N N ,  k   ( x )      (15b) α  k  = o k  − o k ,  m i n    o k , m a x   − o k , m i n         (15c) w k  = N k  ∑ i  N k   α k , i     α  k      where o NN , k   is a sub-network that gives a first estimation of the weights of the loss term L k    as a function of the coordinates of the collocation points. Scaled values of weights o  k    are used in the evaluation of the loss function. The weights o  k    undergoes two scaling operations: a min-max normalization (Eq. (15b) ) followed by a second normalization (Eq. (15c) ) that produces weights such that mean (w k  ) = 1. Nk   is the number of points used to evaluate the loss term L k   . Similarly to SA-PINN, the goal of these weights is to highlight the points with larger residuals, thus the sub-network is trained to maximize the loss. DASA-PINN training involves a four-step process: training the main network only, training the weight sub-networks only, adversarial training on both the main network and the sub-networks simultaneously, and finally only training on the main network to finetune the results. The sub-network is typically smaller than the main network and is used to find the weights at every training iteration. DASA technique can be applied to all loss terms, but it can also be applied only to the PDE loss term (Zhang et al., 2023a ). It should be noted that both SA-PINN and RBA-PINN require static collocation points since the weights are updated at those specific coordinates. This is not the case for DASA-PINN, as the weights are derived from NNs. Similar to global weighting techniques, local weighting techniques involve additional calculations that not only increase memory needs but also slow down the training process, with the degree of slowdown varying based on the specific technique employed. In contrast to global weighting methods, local technique weights are updated at every iteration.    3 Results and discussions for the homogenous domain (Test case 1) Numerical codes have been implemented for the different weighting techniques presented above. A simple test case is designed to verify the correctness of these numerical codes and to assess the impact of tuning parameters specific to the different weighting techniques. Thus, we simulated Darcy flow within a homogeneous square of size 10 m, with left-to-right flow. The domain and boundary conditions are inspired by a large experimental site SCERES (Controlled Experimental Site for Water and Soil Remediation Research, Dridi et al., 2009 ). A schematic of this test case is represented in Fig. 2  a. The solution of this homogenous case is independent of the value of hydraulic conductivity, but a value of 10–5  m/s can be used for numerical simulation. A pressure head of 10 m is imposed on the left side, while the pressure head on the right side is assumed to be 0 m. The lateral walls are assumed to be impermeable. Domain and boundary conditions are shown in Fig. 2 b. This test case is simulated using the baseline PINN and the seven weighting techniques discussed in the previous section. All the simulations used the non-dimensional form of the governing equations. These equations and the dimensional analysis are summarized in Appendix A . The size of the domain is used as the characteristic length, while the hydraulic conductivity is used as the characteristic velocity. For consistent comparisons, the initial parameters of the NNs are kept the same across all simulations. The architecture of the PINN for flow in porous media with the mixed pressure head-velocity formulation consisted of three NNs: one for the pressure head and two for the x- and y-components of the Darcy velocity. Each NN featured four hidden layers, each with 50 nodes, utilizing hyperbolic tangent activation functions. The weights of the hidden layers are initialized using the Xavier initialization method, while the biases were set to zeros, as is commonly used in the literature (Bandai and Ghezzehei, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). To evaluate the PDE and the boundary condition loss terms, we used a static grid of points. This approach allowed us to compare different weighting techniques fairly and conveniently, including those like SA-PINN, which require the use of static points. Specifically, the residuals of the three PDE loss terms were calculated across a grid of 101  ×  101 uniformly spaced points. The boundary condition loss terms were evaluated using 101 uniformly spaced points along each boundary. The optimization process utilized an Adam optimizer to update the parameters of the three NNs, starting with an initial learning rate of 1  × 10−3 . We adopted a learning rate scheduling approach as recommended by Wang et al. (2021) , reducing the learning rate by a factor of 0.9 every 5 % of the total training iterations. The training was capped at 1000 iterations, which proved sufficient to obtain an accurate solution with the baseline PINN. The PINN-generated solutions are compared to the analytical solution. For this sample test case, the analytical solution is given by a linear variation of the pressure head between the left and right walls. We assessed the global accuracy of the various weighting techniques using the relative L2-error metric across the 101  ×  101 grid of points. It should be noted that each of the various weighting techniques requires specific parameters. The selection of these parameters typically involves a trial-and-error process to identify the optimal values that can help achieve the best convergence. For most techniques, we closely adhered to the parameter recommendations provided by the original authors. However, we also explored alternative parameters and made modifications to the algorithms where necessary. For the global weighting techniques, the evaluation of the weights requires calculating gradients of a given loss term with respect to parameters of all NNs contributing to this loss term. For instance, the loss term for the continuity equation involves the derivatives of u  and v . Consequently, the weight of this loss term requires us to calculate the gradients with respect to the parameters of the NNs that represent u  and v . These gradients are then concatenated and processed using operators such as the norm, maximum, average, or standard deviation, depending on the chosen global weighting technique. This approach is applied consistently across all loss terms. It should be noted that this added complexity arises from incorporating weighting techniques into the mixed formulation of PINNs, where multiple NNs contribute partially to the loss terms. As explained previously, the global techniques MA-PINN, ID-PINN and DN-PINN require a smoothing or decay factor, represented by the factor α in Eqs. (8b) –(10b ). For both MA-PINN and ID-PINN, we set this factor to 0.5, whereas for DN-PINN, it is set to 0.99, to accommodate their different stabilization needs, as suggested by the original authors. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we update the weights every five iterations for these three techniques. Additionally, in MA-PINN, ID-PINN, and DN-PINN, a specific loss term L 1    must be defined as a reference to determine the remaining weights relative to this term. In the case of MA-PINN, the best results have been obtained when the continuity equation loss term is statically defined as L 1   , rather than dynamically assigning L 1    to the loss term with the greatest absolute gradient value. Conversely, for both ID-PINN and DN-PINN, a dynamic approach to defining L 1    has yielded better results. In this dynamic approach, L 1     is selected in each iteration based on the loss term with the highest gradient standard deviation for ID-PINN and the highest gradient norm for DN-PINN. Fig. 3   illustrates the relative L2-error across all grid points for the MA-PINN, ID-PINN, and DN-PINN weighting techniques, using both static and dynamic approaches for selecting L 1   . This, along with all subsequent figures featuring 'epoch' on the x-axis, represents the number of training iterations performed using the Adam optimizer. The figure indicates that the dynamic approach greatly increases the accuracy of ID-PINN, marginally enhances the accuracy of DN-PINN, and leads to poorer results for MA-PINN. For NTK-PINN, the only adjustable parameter is the frequency of weight updates. Given the slow rate of change of the NTK-based weights during training and the high computational cost of Jacobian calculations, we set the update frequency at 100 iterations. For SA-PINN, we initialize the weights for all points associated with each loss term to one. These weights are then updated at every iteration using gradient ascent utilizing an Adam optimizer with a learning rate (ηλ   ) of 5  × 10−2 . In the case of DASA-PINN, we introduce four sub-NNs to generate the weights for the three PDE and the boundary condition loss terms. We train these sub-NNs using an Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 5  × 10−4 . Similarly to the optimizer of the main NNs, we employ a scheduler that reduces the learning rate by a factor of 0.9 every 10 % of the total DASA iterations. The number of iterations of the first, second, and third training stages are 100, 300, and 600, respectively, while omitting the final fine-tuning stage. For RBA-PINN, we initially set all weights to one. We use RBA decay parameter γ of 0.999 and RBA learning rate η* of 0.01. These settings allow the RBA weights to vary within the range of (0,  10]. To gain a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of the different weighting techniques, we conducted ten runs for each technique. For each run, we generated new NN weights using a unique seed. These NN weights are shared across the different weighting techniques to ensure a fair comparison. We assessed the accuracy of the runs by analyzing both the best and the mean relative L2-error across these runs. All experiments were performed on an RTX 4090 graphics card, utilizing 64-bit precision. In this and subsequent test cases, all pressure and velocity results are provided in their dimensionless form, with plots displayed across the dimensionless spatial domain. Fig. 4   presents the dimensionless pressure head map obtained with the analytical solution, alongside the error maps for the baseline PINN and the seven weighting techniques, all plotted over the dimensionless spatial domain. The results are given for the first seed. It is clear from Fig. 4  that all techniques converged to the correct solution but with varying levels of accuracy. This is corroborated by Table 1  , which summarizes the accuracy of the different implementations across the ten runs. It is important to note that these results were obtained under a fixed condition of 1000 iterations to ensure consistency in comparing different PINN implementations. Under this assumption, Table 1  shows that the best results, considering both best and mean relative L2-error, are obtained with MA-PINN. The results of the homogenous test case indicate that the different implementations achieve nearly equivalent accuracy on average. This gives more confidence about the correctness of the codes developed for the different weighting techniques. It is also relevant to mention that maximum errors are acceptable for the different weighting techniques, as shown in Fig. 4 . Yet, MA-PINN, SA-PINN, and ID-PINN provide the best results in terms of maximum error.  4 Results and discussions for the heterogeneous test cases In this section, we investigate the performance of the different weighting techniques in two test cases that involve heterogeneous domains. Test case 2 focuses on a stochastic hydraulic conductivity field, which is commonly used in real-world applications. Test case 3, on the other hand, presents a conductivity field with block heterogeneity, which poses numerical challenges due to its highly discontinuous nature, resulting in sharply distributed pressure and velocity fields. These test cases not only allow for investigating the performance of the weighting techniques but also test the capability of the mixed formulation in dealing with realistic and complex conductivity fields. Unless otherwise stated, all hyperparameters and parameters for the weighting techniques remain consistent with those used in the homogeneous test case. 4.1 Test case 2: stochastic hydraulic conductivity field For this test case, we construct a hydraulic conductivity field (lnK ) following the methodology implemented by Guo et al. (2023) . The process involves first generating a Gaussian spatial covariance function. This function is then analyzed through principal component analysis (PCA) where we retain only the top 50 principal components. These components form a projection matrix that captures the essential features of the covariance distribution. These variables are then projected to form a new random field of hydraulic conductivity. Finally, we extract hydraulic conductivity values at the 101 × 101 collocation points from this generated field to use in the training. As the simulations are performed using the non-dimensional form of the governing equations, the hydraulic conductivity field is generated over a domain size of 1  ×  1 and a spatial resolution of 101  ×  101, with a grid spacing of 0.01 for both the x  and y  directions. We standardize the conductivity field to have a mean of 0 and a variance of 1. The correlation lengths are set to 0.15 for both x  and y  directions. This produces a stochastic dimensionless conductivity field with values ranging between 0.07 and 17.
