Fig. 5   shows the dimensionless hydraulic conductivity field used in this test case, plotted over the dimensionless spatial domain. In this test case, we used 150,000 training iterations as this has proven sufficient for the baseline PINN to converge and stabilize. The parameters for the different weighting techniques were consistent with test case 1, except for DASA-PINN where the number of iterations varied across the four training stages. We tested various iteration counts for each stage to evaluate the effectiveness of this weighting technique under different combinations, and the results can be seen in Table 2   for the same seed. Based on the results of this Table, we decided to continue to use combination 4 for the remaining runs. It is important to note that DASA-PINN has the most adjustable parameters among the weighting techniques we examined. A more exhaustive analysis would be necessary to fully understand the limitations of DASA-PINN. Similarly to the prior test case, ten runs are performed for each weighting technique. The PINN solutions are compared to a reference solution obtained with the finite element method, using COMSOL Multiphysics. The COMSOL model is developed using the Darcy module under steady-state conditions. The hydraulic conductivity field is supplied to COMSOL based on the same grid used for PINN (101  ×  101 points). These grid values are used to generate a function evaluating the conductivity as a function of the space coordinates, using the linear interpolation tool available with COMSOL. A mesh sensitivity analysis is performed to ensure a mesh-independent solution. The finite element reference solution for the dimensionless pressure head, as well as PINN error maps of the baseline and the seven weighting techniques, plotted over the dimensionless spatial domain, can be seen in Fig. 6  . Again, the results are given for the first seed. Contrary to test case 1, it can be seen that not all techniques converged to the correct solution. This is also confirmed by the relative L2-error values in Table 3  . The largest relative L2-error occurred for ID- and DN-PINNs as they were unable to obey the Dirichlet boundary conditions at the left and right sides, as seen in Fig. 6 . On average, the highest accuracy was produced by SA-PINN, followed by MA-PINN. This is consistent with the results of test case 1. The results of test cases 1 and 2 show as first insight that MA-PINN is the most accurate global weighting technique for simulating flow in porous media, while SA-PINN is the most accurate local weighting technique. Fig. 6  also shows that the MA-PINN and SA-PINN provide the best results in terms of reduced error. Fig. 7   illustrates the progression of weights for the global weighting techniques for the first seed. These techniques produce distinct weight patterns, which can vary significantly in magnitude. In MA-PINN, the continuity equation is used statically as the reference loss, explaining why its weight remains constant at one throughout the training. Techniques that generated relatively higher weights to the boundary condition loss term, such as MA-PINN and NTK-PINN, yielded better results. The spatial distribution of the local weights generated by the three local weighting techniques is plotted in Fig. 8   across the dimensionless spatial domain. This figure shows the weight maps at the end of the training for the first seed. Contrasting SA-PINN with the other local techniques, we observe that the weight values for SA-PINN are unbounded and can produce weights that are orders of magnitude larger than the other local techniques. For SA-PINN, the weight distributions associated with the loss terms of the x - and y -components of Darcy's law (wDx   and wDy  , respectively) appear to correlate with the hydraulic conductivity field; lower weight values are obtained where hydraulic conductivity is high, and vice versa. This trend is less evident for RBA-PINN and not observed in DASA-PINN. For RBA-PINN, wDx , wDy   and wBC   span the entire possible range of values of (0,  10]. The weights produced in DASA-PINN change smoothly across the domain, a natural outcome of them being generated by shallow NNs. Across the three methods, wBC   tends to be highest on the left side, likely to satisfy the nonzero pressure head boundary condition. It is important to remember that these weight maps are at the end of the training process. The training process is dynamic, and different areas of the domain might have been emphasized differently at various stages of training. We investigated the effect of the weighting techniques on the convergence of the training algorithm, focusing on MA-PINN and SA-PINN. Fig. 9   illustrates how the relative L2-error evolves for the baseline PINN and the two techniques over the course of training. The discussion is limited to MA-PINN and SA-PINN as they were the best-performing global and local techniques, respectively. The figure reveals that SA-PINN consistently achieves lower relative L2-error than baseline PINN throughout the training process. In contrast, the comparison between baseline PINN and MA-PINN is less straightforward. During the first 25,000 iterations, baseline PINN produced a lower relative L2-error on average. Beyond this point, MA-PINN consistently exhibited lower relative L2-error than baseline PINN. If we consider a required relative L2-error level of accuracy of 1  × 10−3 , SA-PINN and MA-PINN reached this threshold within approximately 55,000 and 80,000 iterations, respectively. In contrast, baseline PINN did not reach this level of accuracy even after 150,000 iterations, on average. This result highlights that an appropriate weighting strategy can improve both the accuracy of PINNs as well as the convergence of the training algorithm. It is important to note, however, that both weighting techniques necessitate additional memory due to the extra calculations required to generate the weights. For a more quantitative comparison, we analyze in Fig. 10  a the capacity of PINN in capturing the dimensionless pressure head contours. Again, we limit the analysis to SA-PINN and MA-PINN. However, as the results of both techniques are similar, only results of SA-PINN are shown for the sake of brevity and simplicity. Fig. 10 a depicts the pressure head contours obtained with the finite element and the SA-PINN solutions. It shows that the contours are irregular due to the stochastic heterogeneity. Fig. 10 b shows the velocity field as arrows over the hydraulic conductivity field. This figure shows a complex 2D velocity field with preferential flow paths in zones of high permeability. Despite this complexity, Fig. 10 a demonstrates perfect agreement between PINN and finite element solutions. We should mention that in most previous studies on the application of PINNs for porous media, the accuracy of PINN is usually evaluated using error maps. The analysis with the pressure head contours, as presented in Fig. 10 a, allows for a more reliable assessment and demonstrates the ability of PINNs to capture physics with high fidelity. The mixed formulation with PINNs, as suggested by Lehmann et al. (2023) , has never been applied to stochastic conductivity fields. The results confirm that the mixed formulation can be intrinsically extended to stochastic simulations without any special treatment while still achieving high accuracy. Fig. 10 c and d investigate the accuracy of the resulting dimensionless velocity field. In fact, the assessment of the pressure field is not enough with the mixed formulation because the velocity components are considered as output of the neural networks, and they are not evaluated with a posttreatment of the pressure field using the gradient operator. Furthermore, the accuracy of the velocity field is a crucial factor, especially when flow is used for simulating mass or heat transfer processes. With PINNs, it is known that obtaining an accurate velocity field is more complex than obtaining an accurate pressure field. Fig. 10 c and d depict the distribution and the contours for the x- and y-components of the dimensionless velocity field, obtained with SA-PINN and finite element solutions. These figures confirm the occurrence of preferential flow in the highly permeable zones. They show perfect agreement between PINN and the finite element solutions. These results confirm the capacity of the mixed formulation in generating, not only an accurate pressure head, but also a highly accurate velocity field.  4.2 Test case 3: block heterogeneity The main goal of this test case is to evaluate the performance of the different weighting techniques under a more challenging configuration of heterogeneity. For this reason, we consider a domain with block heterogeneity. This test case is inspired by Marceau's laboratory experiment (Hoteit et al., 2002 ). It deals with 16 square blocks of different hydraulic conductivities, as shown in Fig. 11  . The same configuration of heterogeneity has been treated in Lehmann et al. (2023) . The geometry and boundary conditions are kept the same as for test cases 1 and 2. The dimensionless hydraulic conductivity values are between 0.01 and 0.9, as shown in Fig. 11 . At some interfaces separating two adjacent blocks, the hydraulic conductivity can jump almost two orders of magnitude. The highly discontinuous conductivity field results in complex and sharply varying distributions of pressure head and velocity. This is evident in Fig. 11 , where the velocity vectors, obtained from the finite element solution, change significantly between neighboring blocks. Therefore, this configuration poses significant challenges for PINNs. For this test case, we trained the different PINN implementations for 200,000 iterations, 50,000 iterations more than the stochastic test case. The hyperparameters for PINN and the parameters for the different weighting techniques are kept the same as the previous test cases. For DASA-PINN, we use the same proportions for the training stages as those in combination 4 of test case 2. Thus, the first, second, and third training stages account for 10 % (20,000 iterations), 30 % (60,000 iterations), and 60 % (120,000 iterations) of the total training iterations, respectively, while the fourth training stage is skipped. Ten runs were conducted for each weighting technique in a similar fashion to test case 2. The runs are compared to the reference solution from COMSOL Multiphysics. For PINN, the hydraulic conductivity field is given at the 101  ×  101 collocation points. Fig. 12   displays the dimensionless pressure head solution from the finite element method along with PINN error maps for the baseline and the seven weighting techniques, plotted over the dimensionless spatial domain. The results are presented for the first seed among the ten runs. It is evident from the figure that, except for MA-PINN, both the baseline and all other weighting techniques failed to converge to a satisfactory solution. This occurs despite all techniques resulting in relatively small loss values. While these methods satisfied the boundary conditions, they did not accurately capture the correct pressure head distribution within the domain. This is also confirmed by the relative L2-errors in Table 4  . This result shows that capturing the physics of flow in the case of sharp pressure field is a challenging task for PINNs. It indicates that the use of an appropriate weighting technique becomes crucial for ensuring the convergence of PINNs. Furthermore, the error maps in Fig. 12  confirm the ability of MA-PINN to produce accurate results in terms of maximum error. Most techniques converged to unphysical solutions characterized by almost locally constant dimensionless pressure head with some jumps between the local values. These jumps typically coincide with locations where there are significant discontinuities in hydraulic conductivity, as can be seen in Fig. 13  , which shows the dimensionless pressure head solution from finite element and the different PINN implementations. These unphysical solutions satisfy the boundary conditions, and they show a constant velocity field with small values across the entire domain. Such a constant velocity field ensures a minimal continuity equation loss because the spatial derivatives of the velocity components will be zero. Furthermore, the locally constant pressure field, along with the constant and minimal velocity fields, result in small residual values for the Darcy equation, except at locations where sharp jumps in the pressure head occur as they lead to large pressure head gradients and thus, larger residuals. Although the final solution of these techniques converged to an unphysical solution, baseline PINN, NTK-PINN, SA-PINN, and DASA-PINN were initially converging to the solution of interest, as can be interpreted from Fig. 14  . In Fig. 15  , we show the best results for these four PINN variations before they start diverging from the solution of interest. Note that these results still do not reach the accuracy of MA-PINN. Fig. 16   depicts the progression of global weights during the training of the first seed. The weight trend for MA-PINN resembles that of test case 2, where the weight for the continuity equation loss term (λCE  ) remains constant at one, while the other weights are comparable in value. For ID-PINN and DN-PINN, λCE   is many orders of magnitude larger than the other weights. These algorithms significantly increase the value of λCE   to ensure that the contribution of the continuity equation is balanced with other terms. This behavior is aligned with the constant velocity field observed in the unphysical solution. Except for λCE  , NTK-PINN produced weights that have the same profile but of different magnitudes. In addition, unlike in test case 2, λCE   is consistently low in this test case. Overall, Fig. 16  shows that better solutions are obtained when more emphasis is placed on the Darcy's law component of the loss function compared to the continuity equation, which can be expected because Darcy's law is very sensitive to the discontinuity of hydraulic conductivity. The spatial distribution of the local technique weights at the end of the training is given in Fig. 17  . Results are shown for the first seed. Similarly to test case 2, SA-PINN produced weights that are orders of magnitude larger than the other local techniques. SA-PINN weights show a trend for wDx   and wDy  , where the weight values are usually largest at the interfaces separating the different blocks. Again, this trend is less evident for RBA-PINN and not observed in DASA-PINN. For RBA-PINN, only wBC   span the entire possible range of values of (0,  10], with wBC   being largest at the left boundary. The weights produced by DASA-PINN are smooth and they do not show a clear trend. The weight maps are dynamic and change during training, and here, we only show the end-of-training weight maps. Fig. 18  a demonstrates the dimensionless pressure head solution from MA-PINN and compares the pressure head contours with the finite element solution. Despite the complex and discontinuous nature of the hydraulic conductivity field in this test case, the pressure head contours from MA-PINN successfully captured the irregular profile, which contains sharp corners due to blocky heterogeneity. Fig. 18 b shows the velocity field obtained from MA-PINN as arrows superimposed on the hydraulic conductivity field. A preferential flow path can be observed through the connected highly permeable zones. Accuracy of the dimensionless velocity components obtained with MA-PINN is investigated in Fig. 18 c and d, by comparing it to the finite element solution. The comparison shows a good agreement between the two solutions. This analysis demonstrates that MA-PINN can accurately produce both pressure head and velocity fields. For the same block heterogeneity configuration, Lehmann et al. (2023)  achieved a similar level of accuracy to MA-PINN despite using baseline PINN, albeit with different boundary conditions. In that work, however, significantly larger NNs were utilized, where each NN featured four hidden layers with 256 nodes each, resulting in a total of 595,203 learnable parameters. In contrast, this study uses only 50 nodes per hidden layer, leading to a total of 23,553 learnable parameters. Furthermore, Lehmann et al. (2023)  employed 262,144 collocation points and 1024 boundary condition points, whereas this study utilizes substantially fewer points, with only 10,201 collocation points and 404 boundary condition points. Moreover, Lehmann et al. (2023)  implemented a two-step optimization strategy for training PINN, initially using the Adam optimizer for the first 15,000 iterations, followed by the l -BFGS optimizer for the subsequent 200,000 iterations. MA-PINN was able to converge with satisfactory accuracy without the need for a significant scale-up in NN architecture, an increase in the number of training points, or the use of multiple optimizers. This demonstrates that properly balancing the loss function can achieve the most effective results with minimal resources.   5 Conclusion The application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for flow in heterogeneous porous media faces significant challenges. The mixed formulation of PINNs has been shown to effectively overcome the limitations encountered with standard PINNs. It has been increasingly used in several applications due to its robustness. This formulation proceeds by decoupling the continuity equation and Darcy's law and by considering the pressure head and the velocity components as primary variables. This leads to a loss function with multiple terms. Balancing the contribution of these terms is an important factor that controls the convergence of the training algorithm. Lehmann et al. (2023)  implemented the mixed formulation for the simulation of fluid flow in heterogeneous porous media. This study presents an adaptation of the previous implementation by suggesting an appropriate weighting technique for the mixed formulation of PINNs. We implemented and tested four global and three local weighting techniques, and we intercompared the performance of these implementations. We also compared the performance of these implementations to the baseline PINN, where unity weights are attributed to all terms. Three test cases dealing with homogenous, stochastically heterogeneous, and block heterogeneous domains are used to perform these comparisons. All implementations are compared under similar and coherent conditions. In all test cases, the accuracy of the solutions is assessed based on both pressure head and velocity fields. In addition, for all test cases, ten runs are performed for each weighting technique to ensure that the initial randomness of neural network parameters does not affect comparisons between the different weighting techniques. The results from the homogeneous test case confirmed the correctness of the developed codes, as all implementations converged to the analytical solution. In the case of the stochastic hydraulic conductivity field, the results of the PINN implementations were compared to a finite element solution obtained using COMSOL. This comparison highlighted the superior performance of one global (max-average: MA-PINN) and one local (self-adaptive: SA-PINN) weighting technique. MA-PINN updates weights during training based on the gradients of the individual loss terms with respect to the network parameters. The maximum and average values of these gradients are used to balance the weights. With SA-PINN the weights are applied to each training point individually. These weights are treated as trainable parameters, and they are updated based on the residual of the individual points. In this test case, baseline PINN achieved a similar level of accuracy as MA-PINN and SA-PINN, but the latter techniques accelerated the convergence of the training algorithm. The third test case, dealing with highly discontinuous block heterogeneity, proved challenging because all techniques except MA-PINN failed to converge. The results of this test case confirm that MA-PINN is the most suitable technique for flow in heterogeneous porous media. Baseline PINN also failed to converge in this test case, indicating that the use of an appropriate weighting technique becomes imperative for simulating flow in highly heterogeneous domains using PINNs. The results of this test case also show that using an appropriate weighting technique allows for the optimal use of the neural network parameters, thereby avoiding the need for larger and deeper networks. Overall, the findings of this study suggest that MA-PINN is the most suitable weighting technique for simulating flow in heterogeneous porous media with the mixed formulation. This technique allows for accelerating and ensuring the convergence of the training algorithm, even in highly heterogeneous domains. This work also highlights the importance of proper weighting in optimizing computational resources. This insight underlines the importance of refining PINNs, as it can broaden their applicability in the simulation of various problems. While the simulations in this study were limited to steady-state conditions, exploring the performance of these weighting techniques in transient simulations could be a valuable area of future investigation. This study points out the capacity of the mixed formulation of PINNs in dealing with stochastic flow simulations. The new implementation, based on the MA-PINN weighting technique, is generic and can be extended to multiphase flow and transient simulations. In multiphase flow, the spatial distribution of the conductivity field could present sharp fronts or discontinuity. Furthermore, the transient simulations require including the storage term in the governing equations. Thus, there is a significant potential in extending the newly developed PINNs implementation to multiphase flow in heterogenous domains under transient conditions. This topic requires further investigation. Extending the study to fractured domains is a relevant prospect, as it would allow for covering more types of heterogeneity.
