1 Introduction As a vital freshwater resource globally, groundwater plays a significant role in the global carbon cycle (McDonough et al., 2022 ). The enrichment of dissolved CO2  in groundwater, despite its weakly soluble properties (MacMinn et al., 2011 ), is an indisputable fact. It typically exceeds atmospheric CO2  levels by 1–2 orders of magnitude (Macpherson, 2009 ), and in some cases, even surpasses 4 orders of magnitude (Choi, 2019 ). Dissolved CO2  in groundwater mainly originates from a variety of anthropogenic and natural processes, including CO2  leaching from soil (Savoy et al., 2011 ), biological processes (Nikolenko et al., 2019 ), water–rock interactions, thermal metamorphism of carbonate rocks (Choi, 2019 ), and leakage of CO2  from geological carbon sequestration (GCS) (Qafoku et al., 2017 ). Groundwater is commonly associated with the decomposition and transformation of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), thereby becoming one of the potential sources of CO2  (Deirmendjian et al., 2018; Nikolenko et al., 2019 ). DOC, the carbon structure of dissolved organic matter (DOM), plays a significant role in groundwater microbial metabolism (Shen et al., 2015 ). However, the relationship between the optical properties of DOM and CO2  in groundwater is unclear, potentially leading to a gap in the understanding of organic matter transformations and carbon cycling in groundwater. Indeed, DOM is widely distributed in aquatic environments (Hudson et al., 2007 ), and its structure, composition, and abundance affect global biogeochemical processes and the carbon cycle (McDonough et al., 2022 ). There is an evolving comprehension of the traits, origins, and biogeochemical interactions of DOM in aquatic environments, facilitated by the use of three-dimensional fluorescence parallel factor techniques (Hudson et al., 2007; Fellman et al., 2010; Jaffé et al., 2014 ). Clarifying the sources and sinks of carbon in aquatic environments is crucial due to the severity of climate change. DOM is a key provider of available organic carbon in these ecosystems and plays an active role in microbial carbon and nitrogen transformations (Battin et al., 2009; Fellman et al., 2010 ). Several recent studies of greenhouse gases (CO2 , CH4 , and N2 O) from aquatic environments have demonstrated that DOM is an important factor influencing the distribution of these gases within such systems (Sierra et al., 2020; Amaral et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023 ). The inherent instability of DOM in aquatic environments, leading to significant loss during its transport through riverine networks due to photodegradation and biodegradation (Hansen et al., 2016 ), may result in the release of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere (Moody and Worrall, 2017 ). Worrall et al. (2016)  found that the loss of DOM in UK rivers contributed 2.65 Tg C yr−1  to the atmosphere. Greenhouse gas concentrations in the three major rivers of the Ganges, Mekong and Yellow Rivers in Asia have been confirmed to be significantly affected by DOM concentrations and optical properties (Begum et al., 2021 ). Natural water DOM predominantly consists of humic-like and protein-like substances, with varying characteristics and fluorescence presenting different environmental effects (Amaral et al., 2021 ). Humic-like substances typically generate CO2  via photodegradation and mineralization processes (Amaral et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2023 ). A study in the salt-marsh tidal creeks of eastern China has indicated that the degradation of humic-like substances accounts for up to 80 % of the riverine CO2  emissions (Liang et al., 2023 ). In contrast, protein-like substances are more prone to contribute to the production of CH4  and N2 O (Amaral et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023 ). These findings offer new evidence for understanding carbon turnover and addressing greenhouse gas source-sink issues in aquatic environments (Zhang et al., 2022 ). Globally, groundwater exhibits lower average DOC concentration of 3.8 mg C L-1  compared to surface waters (Regan et al., 2017; McDonough et al., 2020 ). Previous studies indicated that decomposition and mineralization of DOC may contribute to the saturation of CO2  in groundwater (Nikolenko et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021 ). In fact, groundwater DOM, acting as a carrier of the DOC, primarily originates from the leaching of organic matter and plant wastes in the vadose zone (Inamdar et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2015 ), as well as releases from aquifer sediments (McArthur et al., 2004 ). The diverse DOM molecules, shielded from photodegradation in the subterranean environment, act as the main carbon source and energy supplier for heterotrophic metabolism in groundwater (Shen et al., 2015 ), exerting a wide influence on the groundwater carbon cycle (McDonough et al., 2022 ). Previous studies have investigated the sources, characteristics (Longnecker and Kujawinski, 2011; Huang et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2023 ), and anthropogenic impacts of groundwater DOM (Zhang et al., 2021 ), as well as its relationship to contaminants (Kulkarni et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2022 ). These studies found that optical characteristics of groundwater DOM exhibited significant seasonal variations (Yang et al., 2020 ) and vertical dimension differences (Inamdar et al., 2012 ). Generally, shallow aquifers have a higher humification index (Inamdar et al., 2012 ), while deeper aquifers are considered to have higher microbial activity (Kulkarni et al., 2019 ). However, DOM is a possible contributor to groundwater CO2 , the relationships between the fluorescence characteristics of DOM and CO2  concentrations in groundwater are poorly understood. Therefore, this study hypothesized that the characteristics of DOM play a significant role in the generation of CO2  in groundwater systems. In order to verify this hypothesis, the study was conducted during one year in the west-central Guanzhong Basin, China. We measured the dissolved CO2  concentration and physicochemical parameters and analyzed the component of DOM aiming to (1) understand the spatial and temporal characteristics of dissolved CO2  and DOM in groundwater, (2) reveal the coupling relationship between DOM and CO2  in groundwater, and (3) elucidate the potential sources and emissions of CO2  in local groundwater. This study clarifies the seasonal and vertical variations of CO2  and DOM in groundwater, as well as their coupling relationships, which are crucial for a deeper understanding of the carbon cycle in groundwater.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study is conducted in the central and western agricultural region of Guanzhong Basin, China (Fig. 1  ). It has distinct seasons with a mean annual temperature of 12.9 ℃ and an annual rainfall of about 650.6 mm, of which nearly two-thirds occurs in summer and autumn (Wang and Xia, 2014 ). The aquifer primarily consists of a phreatic aquifer, as well as both shallow and deep confined aquifers, while the vadose zone exhibits high permeability, facilitating robust exchange with the subjacent saturated layers (Gao et al., 2021 ). In this study, wells at or exceeding a depth of 50 m are classified as deep wells, while those below this threshold are classified as shallow wells, based on the burial depth of the phreatic aquifer (Huo et al., 2022 ). The primary recharge sources of groundwater include irrigation, lateral seepage, and precipitation, while discharge occurs predominantly through anthropogenic usage and replenishment of rivers (Wang and Xia, 2014 ). A detailed description of the aquifer has been provided in a previous study (Huo et al., 2022 ). Additionally, there is a typical agricultural area with no records of GCS projects or volcanic eruptions. Therefore, the aquifer's CO2  is highly unlikely to originate from geothermal sources or leaks from GCS.  2.2 Sample collection and measurement Groundwater samples were collected at three-monthly intervals from September 2021 to June 2022, representing autumn, winter, spring, and summer, respectively. Prior to the collection of samples, the submersible pump was operated for a duration exceeding five minutes to purge the pipes of stagnant water. A 500 mL polyethylene bottle was used to collect groundwater for the determination of DOC and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), while a 60 mL syringe was used to collect groundwater for the determination of dissolved CO2 . To further confirm the supersaturated state of groundwater CO2 , a 100 cm pipe connected to a 30 mL syringe was utilized to extract air from the wellhead. Three replicate samples were collected at each sampling site. Gas samples were stored at ambient room temperature, while water samples were preserved in darkness at a controlled temperature ranging from 0 to 4 °C throughout transportation. All samples were analyzed within 48 h following collection. Throughout the sampling period, 86 valid samples were obtained from 23 groundwater wells, with the sampling process being limited by the availability of some farmers to provide power for accessing the groundwater. The depth of the groundwater wells was determined through inquiries with local farmers. A Hydrolab DS5X water quality multiprobe (HACH Environmental, Loveland, CO, USA) was employed for in situ measurements of groundwater pH, temperature (T), and electrical conductivity (EC). DIC concentrations were obtained using a TOC-L total organic carbon analyzer (Shimadzu Corp., Kyoto, Japan) after filtration of water samples through a 0.22 μm water filtration membrane (PES). DOC concentrations were measured using the same filtration method prior to acidifying the samples to pH<2 (Hinshaw and Dahlgren, 2013 ). Groundwater dissolved CO2  gas was equilibrated with a headspace containing 30 mL of groundwater and 30 mL of high-purity nitrogen (Huo et al., 2022 ). Subsequently, a 10 mL sample of headspace gas was injected into a gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) to obtain the integrated area. The integrated area and the concentration of the standard gas were then used to calculate the concentration of dissolved CO2  in the groundwater, ppm. More details on sample collection and measurement can be found in a previous study (Huo et al., 2022 ).  2.3 DOM optical analysis Groundwater samples were filtered using a 0.22 μm water-based filter membrane (PES). The excitation-emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence was then obtained using a spectrophotometre (Hitachi F-7000), with the excitation wavelength (Ex) set at 200–500 nm at 5 nm intervals and the emission wavelength (Em) set at 250–550 nm at 2 nm intervals (Dong et al., 2022 ). Excitation and emission slit widths were set to 5 nm and 10 nm, respectively. The scanning speed was 2400 nm min−1 . A blank sample of Milli-Q water was measured to eliminate Raman scattering. To minimize inner filter effects, approximately 8 % of the samples with UV254  values exceeding 0.3 were diluted prior to analysis (Ohno et al., 2002 ). When exporting data from the Hitachi-7000 Fluorescence Spectrophotometer, Rayleigh scattering is effectively mitigated through the implementation of code within the DOM-Fluor Toolbox. In addition, the samples were scanned at 1 nm intervals between 200–800 nm in the UV spectrophotometer (UV-1780, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) after calibrating the baseline offset and scattering with Milli-Q water. The absorption coefficient is recommended to apply a baseline correction by subtracting the average absorbance between 600 and 800 nm to the measured absorption spectrum (Green and Blough, 1994 ). We used a254  to represent the content of DOM in groundwater and was calculated as follows (Coble, 2007; Zheng et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021 ):(1) a 254  = 2 . 3 0 3 × A 254  / L     where a254  is the absorption coefficient at 254 nm, A254  is the absorbance at 254 nm, and L is the optical path length (m).  2.4 Calculation of CO2  emission potential To quantify the emissions of dissolved CO2  from groundwater, this study determined the potentially atmospherically-releasable concentration of CO2  by subtracting the atmospheric CO2  concentration from that of the dissolved CO2  in groundwater (Wood and Hyndman, 2017 ). This difference is then multiplied by the volume of groundwater extraction to estimate the total amount of CO2  that could be released during the extraction process. The calculation formula is as follows:(2) F   = C g  - C a     × V     where F is the emissions of dissolved CO2  from groundwater extraction (t), Cg  is the mean concentration of dissolved CO2  in groundwater (11,300 ppm), Ca  is the atmospheric CO2  concentration locally (490.6 ppm), V is the volume of the extracted groundwater (2.57 billion m3 ) (Wang et al., 2018 ).  2.5 Data handling Three-dimensional fluorescence parallel factor is an effective technique for characterizing the source, composition of DOM in the aquatic environment (Stedmon and Bro, 2008 ). In this study, the DOM-Fluor toolbox in MATLAB 2018 was utilized to construct PARAFAC model. It was sequentially subjected to anomaly testing, residual analysis, split-half analysis and random initialization to determine the components of DOM and obtain the EEM matrix (Murphy et al., 2013 ). Fluorescence indices, including the humification index (HIX), fluorescence index (FI), autochthonous contribution (BIX), and freshness index (β:α), were calculated from the EEM matrices to assess the degree of humification, source, and microbial activity of groundwater DOM (Parlanti et al., 2000; Mcknight et al., 2001; Huguet et al., 2009 ). Details on the calculation of the fluorescence indices are provided in Text S1  . Component types were identified by matching load data with Tucker congruence coefficients that exceed 0.95 in the OpenFlour database (Murphy et al., 2014 ). The peak fluorescence intensity of each component was normalized to Raman units (Lawaetz and Stedmon, 2009 ). Principal component analysis (PCA) was employed to explore the relationship between dissolved CO2  concentrations and DOM optical parameters in groundwater, utilizing data dimensionality reduction. Pearson's correlation was used to test the correlation between the concentration of dissolved CO2  and other indicators. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied to assess significant differences between data sets. For non-normally distributed datasets, a natural logarithm transformation was applied during correlation and ANOVA analyses. All data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise stated. The study area was mapped using Arcgis 10.8. Other visualizations were created in Origin 2023.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Variation and distribution of physico-chemical indicators in groundwater The physicochemical indicators of groundwater across seasons and at different depths are presented in Table 1  . The annual average pH value was near neutral, at 7.11 ± 0.31, with a peak in winter at an average of 7.31 ± 0.36. Deep wells exhibited slightly higher pH values compared to shallow wells throughout all seasons. The average electrical conductivity (EC) of groundwater for the entire year was 1090.5 ± 408.8 μS cm−1 , indicative of a higher salinity level (Tutmez et al., 2006 ). The EC values remained relatively stable across seasons, but were significantly higher in shallow wells compared to deep wells in terms of vertical dimension (p  < 0.05). The average concentration of DIC in all groundwater samples was 49.03 ± 29.84 mg C L−1 , which aligns with the findings of Dong et al. (2022)  in the groundwater of the Guanzhong Basin. The average concentration of DIC was higher in shallow wells compared to deep wells, with the highest average concentration observed in summer at 85.28 ± 37.99 mg C L−1 , more than double the levels of other seasons. In contrast, the average concentration of DOC was significantly higher in spring than in other seasons (p  < 0.05). Groundwater DOC accounts for approximately 7 % of the total dissolved carbon (TDC) with a median value of 1.95 mg C L−1 , marginally higher than the global median of 1.2 mg C L−1  (McDonough et al., 2020 ). The a254  values exhibited a significantly positive correlation with DOC (r = 20.7 %, n = 84, Fig. S1  ) and were higher in shallow wells compared to deep wells (p  < 0.05) (Kulkarni et al., 2019 ).  3.2 Variation and distribution of dissolved and wellhead CO2  concentrations The seasonal and vertical distribution of dissolved CO2  in groundwater is depicted in Fig. 2  a . The average concentration of dissolved CO2  in groundwater was consistently supersaturated, at 11,300 ± 5,788 ppm, which is about 27 times higher than the global atmospheric average of 413 ppm in 2020 (WMO, 2021 ). Seasonally, average concentrations of dissolved CO2  in groundwater were approximately 1.5 times higher in summer (13,131 ± 6,093 ppm) compared to winter (8,966 ± 5,490 ppm), likely due to increased rainfall and irrigation facilitating the transport of vadose zone CO2  into shallow aquifers, as suggested by some studies that have shown CO2  concentrations in the vadose zone to rise with increasing depth (Carmi et al., 2013; Li and Li, 2018 ). Additionally, average groundwater temperatures were more than 4 °C higher in summer than in winter (Table 1 ), which promotes the decomposition and mineralization of DOC, leading to increased CO2  production (O'Donnell et al., 2016 ). In terms of vertical distribution, the concentration of dissolved CO2  in groundwater was higher in shallow wells compared to deep wells, which aligns with findings from existing studies (Nikolenko et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021 ). Specifically, the concentration of dissolved CO2  in shallow wells averaged 13,508 ± 5,617 ppm, nearly 1.7 times higher than that in deep wells. This vertical variation is partly attributed to the difficulty of CO2  penetration from the vadose zone to the deeper aquifer due to the obstruction of the aquiclude. Additionally, the higher conductivity and lower pH values in shallow wells (Table 1 ) indicate a higher chemical weathering (Jurado et al., 2018 ), which further implies CO2  generation through strong water–rock interaction in calcareous rocks (Zhang et al., 2019 ). The degassing of supersaturated CO2  in groundwater led to high CO2  concentrations accumulating at the wellheads (Fig. 2 b ), exhibiting variability characteristics similar to those of dissolved CO2 . Throughout the year, the average wellhead CO2  concentration was 35,579 ± 8,4385 ppm. Specifically, the average CO2  concentration at the wellhead in summer reached 117,318 ± 14,0498 ppm, significantly higher than in other seasons (p  < 0.001). The high concentration of CO2  during summer can be partly attributed to the elevated levels of dissolved CO2  in the groundwater (Fig. 2 a ), and partly to higher groundwater temperatures which reduce CO2  solubility, causing low-density CO2  to rise and accumulate at the wellhead (Iglauer, 2017 ). Additionally, the heightened CO2  concentrations in the vadose zone during the warmer periods act as a driving force for the gas migration towards the wellhead (Carmi et al., 2013 ), thereby amplifying the CO2  levels detected there in the summer. Clarifying the seasonal and vertical distribution characteristics of dissolved CO2  is crucial supplement to the understanding of groundwater carbon dynamics. The accumulation of CO2  at wellheads strongly signifies the supersaturation of CO2  in groundwater. This study estimates CO2  emissions from groundwater pumping in the Guanzhong Basin to be 40,092 t CO2  yr−1 , as calculated using Equation (2)  . However, this estimate may be impacted by the end-use of the extracted groundwater. For instance, approximately half of the groundwater pumped in the Guanzhong Basin is used for irrigation. Previous studies demonstrated that irrigation methods significantly influence the degassing potential of dissolved CO2  in groundwater, resulting in partial outgassing and subsequent CO2  infiltration into the soil (Huo et al., 2022; Huo and Gao, 2024 ). This finding suggests a potential overestimation of our calculated emissions. Nevertheless, it is crucial to emphasize that the direct release of CO2  due to groundwater pumping should not be overlooked in the global carbon budget.  3.3 Variation and distribution of DOM optical characteristics Five components of DOM were identified in groundwater (Fig. 3  ; Table 2  ), including four humic-like substances (C1, C2, C3, and C4) and one tryptophan-like protein (C5), based on a comparison with the online OpenFluor database (Murphy et al., 2014 ). Components C2, C3, and C5 had previously been detected in a study focusing on the groundwater DOM of the Guanzhong Basin (Dong et al., 2022 ). Specifically, components C1 and C2 are generally regarded as originating from terrestrial sources related to agriculture (Stedmon and Markager, 2005; Amaral et al., 2021 ), with C1 associated with peak A and C2 with peak C, respectively (Coble et al., 1998; Stedmon et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2010 ). Component C3 might be a microbial humic-like substance of marine endmember (Stedmon and Markager, 2005 ), potentially associated with planktonic productivity (Coble et al., 1998; Stedmon et al., 2003 ). Component C4, derived from freshly produced biologically unstable materials (Singh et al., 2010 ), displays the properties of microbial humic-like substances (Kulkarni et al., 2017 ). Component C5 is identified as a tryptophan-like protein (Kim et al., 2020 ), which is an autochthonous and biologically labile component (Yamashita et al., 2008 ). The variation in fluorescence intensity and relative abundance of DOM in groundwater are shown in Fig. 4  . The average fluorescence intensity of groundwater DOM peaks in summer at 0.04 RU and reaches its lowest in winter at 0.02 RU. In comparison to deep wells, shallow wells exhibit a higher humic-like fluorescence intensity. Specifically, humic-like substances (C1, C2 C3, and C4) in shallow wells account for an average of 75.9 % of the total in spring and winter. However, the abundance of tryptophan-like proteins is higher in summer and autumn (Fig. 4 b ), with an average of 41.0 %, which exceeds by 1.7 times the average of 24.1 % observed in spring and winter. In fact, higher pH values are known to inhibit the formation of protein-like substances in groundwater (Fig. S2  ) (Hu et al., 2023 ). In this study, the average pH of groundwater was lowest in autumn, at only 6.93 (Table 1 ), which may explain the larger proportion of protein-like components. In addition, fluorescence indices (BIX, FI, HIX, β:α) are widely used to indicate the source, microbial activity, and the degree of humification of DOM. The sampling wells were located in the west-central area of the Guanzhong Basin, where a previous study have considered the HIX of groundwater DOM to be low, with a mean value of 1.41 (Dong et al., 2022 ). In this study, the average HIX in shallow groundwater was 0.74 ± 0.43 (Fig. 5  b ), which is 1.5 times higher than that in deep wells, indicating a greater degree of humification in shallow wells (Inamdar et al., 2012; Kulkarni et al., 2019 ). Generally, DOM of terrestrial origin is characterized by higher HIX values, whereas autochthonous DOM typically exhibits lower HIX values and is more readily utilized by biological organisms (Hu et al., 2023 ). Although several shallow wells displayed lower BIX and FI values, the average BIX and FI values for all samples were 1.87 ± 0.66 and 2.20 ± 0.45, respectively (Fig. 5 a, c ), both exceed the respective thresholds of 1 and 1.9, suggesting that the DOM in groundwater predominantly originates from microbial sources (Ma et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2022 ). Particularly in deep wells, where FI values are usually higher than in shallow wells (Fig. 5 a ), this implies more active microbial activity in deeper aquifers (Inamdar et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2020 ). Moreover, the significant negative correlation between DOC and FI implies active microbial utilization of DOC (Fig. S2  ), indirectly confirming the strong microbial activity of DOM in groundwater (Yamashita et al., 2008 ). Concurrently, the lower β:α ratio in shallow wells indicates a stronger contribution of newly formed microbes in deeper groundwater (Fig. 5 d ) (Kulkarni et al., 2019 ). In summary, the components and optical parameters of DOM in groundwater exhibit distinct variations in both seasonally and vertically. Groundwater DOM may primarily originate from terrestrial sources, predominantly due to the migration of deep soil organic matter, and from microbial sources driven by microbial metabolism (Lipczynska-Kochany, 2018 ), which presents similar characteristics with groundwater DOM sources in arid-semiarid regions of northern China (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Existing studies indicated a close linkage between the vadose zone and shallow aquifers in Guanzhong Basin (Gao et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2022 ). Soil water containing pesticides and organic residues infiltrates shallow aquifers via irrigation and rainfall, thereby contributing to a terrestrial source signature of DOM (Hu et al., 2023 ). In contrast, this infiltration pathway is unlikely to extend to the deeper aquifers. For instance, in the two deepest wells of this study (G14 and G18), which have depths of 180 and 200 m respectively, the mean FI and BIX values were 2.76 ± 0.23 and 0.32 ± 0.04 (Table S1  ), respectively. These values highlight a strong microbial source of DOM in deep groundwater. The significant negative correlation of fluorescence intensity of components C1, C2, and C3 with well depth as well as the positive correlation of %C5 and well depth may assist this conclusion (Fig. S2  ).  3.4 Linkage between DOM optical indices and dissolved CO2  DOM serving as a crucial carbon source for metabolic processes in groundwater (Shen et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020 ) and actively influencing the global carbon cycles (McDonough et al., 2022 ). Principal component analysis revealed that the 95 % confidence intervals for DOM optical indices and CO2  concentrations overlap across different seasons (Fig. 6  ), suggesting that the seasonal variability of DOM is not significant. However, the first two axes (PC1 and PC2) together accounted for 74.7 % of the total variance. PC1 accounted for 56.4 % of the total variance, demonstrating a significant positive correlation with a254, CO2 , C3, HIX, C1, and C2, and a significant negative correlation with %C5, β:α, BIX, and FI. The PC2 accounted for 18.3 % of the total variance, exhibiting a significant positive correlation with C5, C4, and %C4. Therefore, humic-like substances, which are a major carbon reservoir in the biosphere, facilitate the production of CO2  in inland water bodies and soils (Lipczynska-Kochany, 2018; Amaral et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023 ), with groundwater being no exception. However, in contrast to surface water environments, the decomposition of humic-like substances might not be the main source of CO2  in groundwater, particularly in shallow aquifers. Conducting separate Pearson correlation analyses for shallow and deep wells as distinct groups could potentially elucidate this issue. A weak positive correlation between dissolved CO2  concentrations and HIX, C1, C2, and C3 in shallow wells (Fig. S3  a ) (p  < 0.05) indicates that the decomposition of humic-like substances has a limited impact on the CO2  levels. In fact, the high concentrations of CO2  stored in deep soils lead to the hypothesis that CO2  in shallow aquifers primarily originates from the leaching effect in vadose zone soils due to rainfall (Baldini et al., 2018 ), a theory supported by the highest dissolved CO2  levels observed in summer and the lowest in winter (Fig. 2 ). Additionally, the local groundwater is typically characterized by a chemical composition of HCO3 -Ca and HCO3 -Na (Zhang et al., 2019 ). The higher EC values in shallow wells indicate that water–rock interactions between groundwater and carbonate rocks lead to changes in bicarbonate equilibrium, thereby promoting the production of dissolved CO2 . Conversely, due to the barrier created by aquicludes, the migration of leached CO2  from the vadose zone into deeper aquifers, especially into confined aquifers, is unlikely. However, some deep confined aquifers still exhibit dissolved CO2  concentrations that are supersaturated relative to the atmosphere. For instance, the average CO2  concentration in the two deepest wells reached 5,613 ± 723 ppm (Table S1  ), which is more than 13 times the atmospheric level. The average EC values of these wells are at a moderate to low level (Tutmez et al., 2006 ), indicating a weaker contribution from water-rock interactions to CO2  production. However, the mean FI in deep wells exceeds those in shallow wells (Fig. 5 a ), suggesting that the DOM in these aquifers has a significant microbial contribution. Pearson correlation analysis for all deep wells revealed a significant positive relationship between dissolved CO2  concentration and components C1, C2, C3, C4, and HIX (p  < 0.05) (Fig. S3  b ), indicating that CO2  saturation in deep groundwater is more influenced by humic-like substances and their degree of humification compared to shallow wells. The positive correlation between EC and HIX suggests that an increase in groundwater residence time leads to a rise in autochthonous humic-like substances (Fig. S2  ), resulting in higher CO2  production (Huang et al., 2015 ). Therefore, we postulate that the primary source of CO2  in deep wells may be the biological metabolism, coupled with relatively weaker water–rock interactions. Groundwater plays an active role in the global carbon cycle. This study suggests that the decomposition of humic-like substances contributes to the saturation levels of CO2  in groundwater. Future research should focus on quantitatively exploring the contribution of DOM to CO2  levels and clarifying the microbial pathways of humic-like substance decomposition, as well as its fate in groundwater. Understanding these aspects is crucial for comprehending the mechanism and dynamics of the groundwater carbon cycle, especially in the context of regional geological structures.   4 Conclusions This study investigated dissolved CO2  concentrations and DOM characteristics in groundwater in the agricultural area of the Guanzhong Basin in China. The results indicate that the concentration of dissolved CO2  in groundwater is higher in summer than in winter, and is greater in shallow wells compared to deep wells. The DOM in groundwater originates from a mixed source of terrestrial and microbial origins. Principal component analysis (PCA) and Pearson correlation analysis suggest that the decomposition of humic-like substances might one of the contributing factors to the supersaturation of CO2  in groundwater. It is noteworthy that the CO2  in shallow wells may primarily originate from the leaching of deep soil CO2 , due to the close connectivity between the vadose zone and the shallow aquifer. The saturation of CO2  in deep groundwater is primarily influenced by the decomposition of microbial source humification and water–rock interactions. Groundwater plumping in the Guanzhong Basin results in an annual degassing of CO2  amounting to 40,092 t. Future carbon budgets should emphasize the emissions of CO2  and the dynamics of carbon in groundwater.
1 Introduction Grasslands cover approximately 40 % of the terrestrial ecosystem, serve as crucial carbon (C) reservoirs, and harbor significant global biodiversity (Borer et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2022 ). Despite their importance, up to 49 % of grasslands worldwide are experiencing degradation, and the rate of degradation is accelerating (Bardgett et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2023 ). Grassland degradation, characterized by declining soil organic matter, soil salinization, soil compaction, loss of biodiversity, and decreased vegetation productivity, severely compromises the ecological services of grasslands and the sustainable development of pastoral economies (Coban et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2019 ). Soil amendments, which are effective materials for restoring grassland ecosystem structure and function, have been widely applied to improve soil structure and enhance fertility (Gebhardt et al., 2017; Ohsowski et al., 2012; Shikha et al., 2023 ). The hydrological characteristics of the soil play a vital role in determining soil water movement, retention, and nutrient transfer, potentially exerting a significant influence on soil amendment responses (Dong et al., 2022 ). The application of soil amendments can alter plant-water interactions, soil structure, and soil properties, thereby affecting soil hydrology and erosion processes (Glab et al., 2016 ). Therefore, understanding the soil hydrological characteristics and their driving factors in the context of soil amendment applications is crucial for assessing soil water dynamics in grassland ecosystems. Soil hydrological processes involve the movement and redistribution of water within the soil and play a critical role in material exchange and energy flow within plant and soil ecosystems (Lv et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2014 ). Key hydrological indicators include soil water storage (SWS), saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks), field capacity (FC), and saturated water-holding capacity (SWHC) (Bormann and Klaassen, 2008; Jacka et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2024 ). These parameters are indispensable for simulating the soil water retention capacity, runoff processes, and sediment transport capabilities (Dai et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023 ). Soil amendments can improve soil structure, enhance soil fertility, and increase soil water retention capacity, thereby significantly influencing the soil hydrological characteristics (Glab et al., 2016; Meena et al., 2020 ). Different types of soil amendments exhibit variation in their modulation pathways and functional intensities (Ojeda et al., 2015; Wesseling et al., 2009 ). For instance, the application of aluminum ferric sulfate to alkaline soils can hydrolyze colloidal particles, thereby improving soil permeability and alleviating soil compaction (Luo et al., 2015 ). Biochar, as a nutrient-based amendment, can increase the organic matter content of degraded soil and soil aeration and enhance soil water flow (Qian et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2023 ). However, the specific effects of soil amendments on the hydrological characteristics of degraded grassland soils remain unclear. The effects of soil amendments on soil hydrological characteristics may arise from alterations in vegetation characteristics, soil organic matter, soil structure, and soil biology (Fischer et al., 2019; Ibrahimi and Alghamdi, 2022; Zhou et al., 2019a ). Changes in surface litter and fine root biomass induced by soil amendments can influence soil SWS and Ks by improving infiltration pathways and promoting the formation of water-stable aggregates (Dong et al., 2022; Luna et al., 2018 ). Additionally, root growth and increased vegetation biomass can enhance soil organic matter accumulation and biological metabolic activity, thereby changing soil hydrological characteristics (Wu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, recent studies have indicated significant correlations among soil texture, pH, and Ks in the background of soil amendment applications (Glab et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2023 ). Plant and soil properties may affect the hydrological properties of the soil in different ways, which may affect the application of soil amendments (Duarte et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023 ). However, a consensus on the relative contributions of these factors to changes in soil hydrological characteristics under soil amendment has not yet been reached. Grassland ecosystems on the northern Loess Plateau provide crucial support for biodiversity, pastoral development, and soil and water conservation (Jia et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In recent decades, severe soil degradation and significant declines in vegetation productivity have occurred in this region, leading to notable changes in the soil hydrology and erosion processes (Yao et al., 2023 ). Ecological and hydrological changes in grasslands on the northern Loess Plateau have important implications for the utilization of Yellow River water resources and vegetation growth (Huang and Zhang, 2004 ). An increasing number of studies have attempted to restore the structure and function of grassland ecosystems by applying different types of soil amendments (Ohsowski et al., 2012 ). It is imperative to study changes in grassland soil hydrological characteristics and their driving factors in the context of soil amendment applications in the northern Loess Plateau. Moreover, many studies have focused primarily on surface soil, neglecting the response of deep soil layers (Meena et al., 2020; Zema et al., 2019 ). Therefore, it is necessary to elucidate the pathways and key driving factors through which soil amendments affect hydrological characteristics at different soil depths. Consequently, we conducted a five-year soil amendment experiment to investigate the influence of soil amendments on the soil hydrological dynamics of grasslands in the northern Loess Plateau. We also measured the vegetation characteristics and soil physicochemical properties to elucidate the responses of soil hydrological characteristics to soil amendments. The objectives of this study were: (1) to investigate the response characteristics of soil hydrological indicators in Loess Plateau grasslands to different types of soil amendments and (2) to determine the key driving factors of soil amendments on soil saturated hydraulic conductivity and soil water retention capacity.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Site Description and experimental design This study was conducted at the ecological research stations in Shenmu (38°51′N, 110°30′E), Mizhi (37°45′N, 110°11′E), and Youyu (39°59′N, 112°28′E) located in the agricultural and pastoral areas of the Loess Plateau, China (Fig. S1 ). These areas have been considered major disaster areas for soil erosion and water loss. These regions exhibit a warm-temperate semiarid climate, with an average annual temperature of 7.9 °C and an average annual precipitation of 435 mm. According to the soil classification of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the predominant soil type in this area is loess. The primary vegetation includes Potentilla acaulis , Leymus chinensis , Artemisia gmelinii  and Lespedeza floribunda . In October 2017, a soil amendment experiment was initiated in semiarid grasslands using a randomized block design. Three types of soil amendments were selected as the experimental treatments. Four treatment methods, including a control with no amendment (CK), aluminum sulfate (AS), biochar (BC), and a combination of aluminum sulfate and biochar (AB), were established at each grassland experimental site at the research stations. Each treatment consisted of three replicate plots and the size of each test plot was 3 × 3 m2 . Detailed information for each site is provided in Table S1 . The biochar used in this study was produced from straw via slow pyrolysis at 600 °C. The combined amendment was applied at a 1:1 ratio of AS to BC. The application rate of the soil amendments was 1.5 t hm−2 , which is equivalent to 0.8 % of the soil quality. The soil amendments were spread evenly over the soil surface in each plot and mixed with the soil using a shovel.  2.2 Sampling and analysis Three representative sampling points were randomly selected from each plot in July 2022. Plant litter collected from the grassland was dried to constant weight at 60 °C and used to estimate litter biomass (LB). At each sampling point, soil samples were collected using a shovel to excavate an 80 cm soil profile, and samples were obtained at three depths (0–20 cm, 20–40 cm, and 40–80 cm) using a cutting ring (diameter 5 cm) and sealed in self-sealing plastic bags. Additionally, soil samples were collected at depths of 0–20 cm, 20–40 cm, and 40–80 cm were collected using a soil auger (diameter, 5 cm). After removing the soil debris and fine roots, a portion of the soil samples was used to determine the soil hydrological characteristics. The remaining soil samples were sieved through a 2 mm mesh screen and used for the analysis of soil physicochemical properties. Soil cores were collected at three depths from three representative sampling points in each plot. Fine roots (diameter < 2 mm) collected from the soil samples were dried to constant weight at 60 °C to estimate fine root biomass (FRB). The weights of all the cutting rings and empty aluminum boxes were recorded (W1  and W0 , g). Soil moisture content was determined by drying the soil samples in a 105 °C oven to constant weight. Subsequently, the preweighed soil samples were immersed in distilled water in plastic trays. During the saturation process, the water level was maintained at the soil surface level. To prevent erosion, a filter paper was placed at the bottom of each cutting ring. After soaking for 24 h, the saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks, mm min−1 ) was measured using the constant head method (Fodor et al., 2011 ). The soil cores (W2 , g) were transferred to trays to collect the water drained under gravity after 2 h and 48 h (W3  and W4 , g) (Aimrun et al., 2004; Blanco-Canqui et al., 2017 ). The dry weight of the drained soil (Wds ; g) was also determined. Subsequently, soil moisture content ( %), soil bulk density (SBD, g cm−3 ), total porosity (TP,  %), capillary porosity (CP,  %), and non-capillary porosity (NCP,  %) were calculated as follows:(1) M o i s t u r e = W w e t   - W d r y    W d r y   - W 0    × 100  %     (2) S B D = W d s   - W 1   V      (3) T P = 1 - S B D  d s     × 100  %     (4) C H C = W 3  - W d s    W d s   - W 1    × 100  %     (5) C P = S B D × C H C     (6) N C P = T P - C P     where Wwet  (g) and Wdry  (g) are the weights of the wet and dry soils in the aluminum box, respectively. V is the volume of the cutting ring (100 cm3 ). where CHC is the capillary-holding capacity ( %). The ds is the soil particle density (generally being 2.65 g cm−3 ). Soil water storage (SWS), field capacity (FC,  %), and saturated water-holding capacity (SWHC,  %) were calculated as follows:(7) S W S = D e p t h × S B D × M o i s t u r e × 10  - 1       (8) S W H C = W 2  - W d s    W d s   - W 0    × 100  %     (9) F C = W 4  - W d s    W d s   - W 0    × 100  %      Soil organic matter (SOM) content was determined using the K2 Cr2 O7  oxidation method. Soil texture, including clay, silt, and sand content, was measured using a laser particle size analyzer (Mastersizer 2000, Malvern Instruments Ltd., UK). Soil pH was measured using a pH meter after stirring the soil–water (1:5 w/v) suspension for 30 min.  2.3 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using the IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows (version 22.0; IBM Corp.). Before conducting statistical analyses, normality and homogeneity of variance of the data were tested using the Shapiro-Wilk  test and Levene  statistic, respectively. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to test the effects of the soil amendment treatments and soil depth on FRB and soil properties. Additionally, the least significant difference (LSD) method was used to assess the differences in the mean values of the soil properties under different types of amendment treatments. The response characteristics of the variables to the different experimental treatments were evaluated and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. All data are reported as mean ± standard error (SE). Redundancy analysis (RDA) was used to assess the relationships between different plant and soil variables at different soil depths and soil hydrological characteristics using the vegan  and ggplot2  packages. The effects of plant and soil physicochemical variables on soil hydrological characteristics were analyzed using the ggplot  and corrplot  packages in R software version 4.1.3. The key driving factors of soil hydrological characteristics were determined using random forest models implemented in the randomForest  package.   3 Results 3.1 Plant characteristics and soil variables Soil amendments significantly increased the LB of grasslands, with the LB under the BC and AB treatments increasing by 58.68 g m−2  and 89.06 g m−2 , respectively (p < 0.05) (Fig. 1  ). Amendment addition and soil depth significantly influenced FRB (p < 0.01), with the AS treatment showing no significant effect on FRB (Fig. 2  ). The FRB decreased significantly with increasing soil depth (p < 0.01). FRB in the 0–20 layer increased by 6.04 % and 16.55 % under the BC and AB treatments, respectively. The BC and AB treatments increased the FRB in the 20–40 cm layer by 11.16 % and 25.91 %, respectively. Soil amendments had no significant effect on FRB in the 40–80 cm layer. SOM, pH, SBD, and moisture showed significant responses to soil amendment and depth (p < 0.05) (Fig. 2 ). The BC treatment led to an increase in SOM of 21.02 % and 18.88 % in the 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers, respectively. Under the AB treatment, SOM increased by 24.82 % and 23.53 % in the 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers, respectively. Soil amendment significantly decreased pH and SBD in the 0–20 and 20–40 cm layers (p < 0.05). The AS, BC, and AB treatments increased soil moisture by 20.98 %, 36.82 %, and 51.07 %, respectively, in the 0–20 cm layer. Soil moisture increased by 17.57 % and 22.55 % in the 20–40 cm layer in the BC and AB treatments, respectively. Soil amendments significantly increased the clay content in the 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers but decreased the sand content. However, the differences in silt content among treatments were not statistically significant. TP and CP showed significant responses to soil amendments and soil depth (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3  ). NCP did not show significant differences among the treatments. Specifically, TP and CP significantly decreased with increasing soil depth (p < 0.05). The AS, BC, and AS treatments led to increases of 16.02 %, 13.11 %, and 13.81 %, respectively, in TP in the 0–40 cm layer. Similarly, CP increased by 17.70 %, 14.04 %, and 17.26 % in the 0–40 cm layer in the AS, BC, and AB treatments, respectively.  3.2 Soil hydrological properties Under soil amendment treatments, SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks significantly increased in the 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers (Fig. 4  ). Specifically, SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks increased by 19.04 %, 27.39 %, 1.57 %, and 19.03 %, respectively, in the 0–40 cm depth range under the AS treatment. The BC treatment led to increases of 20.09 %, 17.56 %, 12.94 %, and 16.66 % in SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks, respectively, at 0–40 cm. The combination of AS and BC treatments resulted in increases of 25.74 %, 35.45 %, 18.47 %, and 25.80 % in SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks in the 0–0 cm layer. In the 40–80 cm layer, soil amendments had no significant effect on soil hydrological properties.  3.3 Relationships between plant characteristics, soil variables, and soil hydrological properties In the 0–20 cm layer, the first and second axes of RDA accounted for 26.73 % and 37.26 %, respectively, of the variation in the relationship between soil hydraulic properties and plant-soil variables (Fig. 5  a). The direction of change induced by soil amendments in Ks significantly matched with FRB, moisture, and clay but was opposite to sand and SBD. FC and SWHC were positively correlated with LB, NCP, SOM, moisture, and clay, but negatively correlated with pH. In the relationship between soil hydrological properties and plant-soil variables in the 20–40 cm layer, the first and second RDA axes accounted for 24.36 % and 35.40 %, respectively (Fig. 5 b). The direction of change in the SWHC, which was regulated by soil amendments, was similar to that of clay and SOM. Ks and FC were significantly positively correlated with FRB, LB, and moisture, but significantly negatively correlated with sand and pH. The variation coefficients of RDA in the 40–80 cm layer were not statistically significant. There were close relationships between soil hydrological properties and plant-soil variables (Fig. 6  ). Specifically, FRB, SOM, moisture, clay, TP, and CP showed significant positive correlations but negative correlations with pH, SBD, and sand (p < 0.05). SWHC, FC, and Ks were significantly positively correlated with FRB, SOM, moisture, clay, TP, and CP but significantly negatively correlated with pH and SBD (Table S2 ). The results of the random forest model emphasized that SOM, FRB, moisture, TP, Clay, and SBD primarily regulated the changes in soil hydrological properties under soil amendment (Fig. 6 b).   4 Discussion 4.1 Impact of soil amendments on plant characteristics and soil variables The application of AS did not significantly affect plant biomass or SOM but had a profound impact on other physicochemical properties in the upper soil (0–40 cm). Halim et al. (2018)  found that Al3+  was toxic to plant roots under acidic conditions. However, in our study, AS treatment did not significantly affect FRB, which is consistent with Zhou et al. (2019b) , who reported that the inhibitory effect induced by prolonged exposure of plant roots to aluminum counteracted the promoting effect. He et al. (2019)  indicated that aluminum toxicity mainly inhibits root elongation and division; however, this effect is not universal across all soil and plant conditions. AS increases soil acidity which suppresses microbial activity, thereby influencing SOM decomposition and accumulation (Kunito et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2015 ). Additionally, Al3+  forms stable complexes with organic matter, thereby inhibiting the decomposition of plant residues (Makarov and Kiseleva, 1995 ). These factors likely contributed to the relative stability of SOM under the AS treatment (Xiao et al., 2022a; Zhao et al., 2019 ). Our results showed that the application of AS reduced SBD and sand content by promoting soil particle aggregation and improving the soil structure. Some studies have suggested that Al3+  forms stable bonds with soil particles, facilitating their aggregation and increasing clay content (Zhou et al., 2019b ). This aggregation effect transforms larger sand particles into smaller clay particles, increasing the soil clay content and reducing SBD (He et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2015 ). The increase in TP might be due to Al3+  enhancing soil microaggregate formation, thereby improving the soil structure (Xiao et al., 2022a ). Although AS did not significantly affect FRB, its improvements in soil physical properties may indirectly enhance plant water and nutrient uptake (Gill et al., 2008; Qasim et al., 2018 ). The BC treatment significantly increased grassland litter biomass, upper soil FRB, SOM, and soil moisture. Lehmann et al. (2011)  showed that biochar promotes root growth and litter accumulation by providing additional C sources and improving soil structure, which is consistent with our results. This consistency across different ecosystems demonstrates the high water retention and nutrient supply capacities (Carvalho et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020 ). Jeffery et al. (2011)  also found that BC significantly enhanced the SOM content and water retention, supporting our findings. BC increases SOM by providing rich organic C and improves the physical structure of the soil; its porous nature enhances water retention (Obour et al., 2020; Zanutel et al., 2024 ). These improvements significantly boost plant growth, particularly root expansion and litter accumulation (Hol et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2023 ). BC also enhances soil moisture retention and aeration, creating a more favorable environment for plant growth, thereby increasing grassland ecosystem productivity (Gebhardt et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2020 ). Our research indicated that the combined application of BC and AS was more effective than either treatment alone. Graber et al. (2010)  noted that BC combined with other soil amendments significantly boosted the nutrient supply and plant root growth, which is consistent with our findings. Abel et al. (2013)  found that combining BC with mineral amendments optimized soil pH and nutrient dynamics, further promoting plant growth. The significant effects of the combined treatment likely stem from BC providing rich organic C and improving soil structure, whereas AS regulates soil pH and enhances nutrient release and absorption (Xiao et al., 2022a; Zhou et al., 2019b ). Their synergistic effects optimize soil conditions, enabling more efficient water and nutrient use by plants, and thus significantly improving grassland ecosystem productivity and health (Hardie et al., 2014; Ibraheem et al., 2024 ). The combined treatment improved both soil chemical and physical properties, providing a more balanced growth environment (Oldfield et al., 2018; Rashad et al., 2021 ). Soil amendments did not significantly affect the physicochemical properties of the deep soil layer (40–80 cm). Goyal et al. (1999)  noted that deep soils have lower nutrient and organic matter contents with limited microbial activity, leading to minimal impacts from soil amendments. Ma et al. (2020)  also noted that surface soils are the primary beneficiaries of soil amendments because they do not effectively penetrate deep soils. The relative stability and low microbial activity of deep soils limits the transmission of amendment effects (Lundquist et al., 1999; Mi et al., 2016 ). Deep soils typically have lower vegetation biomass and organic matter content, which restricts the impact of amendments (Gaudel et al., 2022 ).  4.2 Response of soil hydrological properties to soil amendments and key drivers The AS treatment significantly improved the saturated SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks in the upper soil layer. AS application primarily focuses on acidifying soils (Halim et al., 2018 ), whereas this study was conducted on alkaline soils. Our results aligned with those of Zhou et al. (2019b) , who showed that AS enhanced soil particle aggregation, improved soil structure, and increased water retention and conductivity. AS lowers soil pH, increases acidity, alters microbial communities, and affects SOM decomposition and accumulation (Dong et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2022b ). Al3+  in acidic conditions promotes soil particle aggregation, increases porosity, and improves soil structure, collectively enhancing the SWHC and FC (Xiao et al., 2022a ). An improved soil structure also boosts conductivity and enhances soil water retention and transport capacity (Dai et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023 ). The BC treatment significantly increased SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks in the upper soil layer. Carvalho et al. (2020)  demonstrated that the porous structure and high surface area of biochar significantly improved the soil water retention and conductivity, which is consistent with our findings. Zhou et al. (2019a)  also found that BC significantly enhanced soil hydrological properties, supporting our results. BC increases SWHC and FC owing to its porous structure and high surface area. Organic matter in BC stabilizes soil aggregates and increases soil porosity, thereby improving the hydrological properties (Glab et al., 2016 ). BC also supplies rich organic C, enhances SOM, and improves the physical and chemical properties of soil, further promoting water retention and conductivity (Omondi et al., 2016 ). The combined treatment with BC and AS had more pronounced effects on SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks in the upper soil layer than the single amendments. Key drivers such as SOM, FRB, TP, clay, and SBD significantly regulate hydrological property changes. Graber et al. (2010)  found that combining BC with other amendments significantly enhances water retention and conductivity, which is consistent with our findings. BC with mineral amendments optimizes the soil pH and nutrient dynamics, further promoting plant growth (Smebye et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2022 ). Owing to their complementary physical and chemical properties, the synergistic use of BC and AS significantly improved SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks. BC has a porous structure and is rich in organic C, which improves soil aeration and fertility (Giannetta et al., 2024; Hairani et al., 2016 ), whereas AS adjusts soil pH and facilitates nutrient release and absorption (Islam et al., 2004 ). This synergy optimizes soil conditions, allowing for more efficient water and nutrient use by plants, and significantly improving productivity (Dass et al., 2011; Shyam et al., 2023 ). However, deep soil hydrological properties, including SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks, showed no significant responses to soil amendments. This could be due to lower microbial activity in deep soils, which limits amendment effects (Mi et al., 2016 ). In addition, the stable physical structure of deep soils results in minimal changes in particle aggregation and porosity, making amendments less effective (Tuyishimire et al., 2022; Velykis and Satkus, 2018 ). Lower organic matter and nutrient content and fewer plant roots in deep soils weaken the impact of amendments on soil hydrological functions (Mi et al., 2016; Sandén et al., 2019 ). Overall, amendments mainly affected upper soils, while deep soil hydrological properties remained stable owing to their physical and chemical environment, indicating a limited response to amendments. Future studies should focus on the penetration and long-term mechanisms of amendments within soil profiles to comprehensively understand their effects on different layers.  4.3 Implications for grassland management Our study provides key insights into the effects of soil amendments on the hydrological properties of grassland soil, thereby revealing the differential effects of various amendments on improving grassland ecosystems. Recent studies have shown that Al3+  forms stable complexes with organic matter, inhibiting decomposition, whereas microbial community adaptation and continuous plant residue input maintain the SOM balance (Dong et al., 2022; He et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2022b ). BC significantly boosts vegetation productivity and soil moisture retention by increasing SOM and improving the soil physical structure (Glab et al., 2016; Omondi et al., 2016 ). Its porous structure and high surface area enhance SWHC and FC while providing rich organic C that stabilizes soil aggregates, increases TP and CP, and improves hydrological properties (Dong et al., 2022; Ran et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the combination treatment significantly improved the soil hydrological functions, demonstrating its effectiveness in regulating soil hydrodynamics and fertility. These findings are crucial for grassland management and suggest that the strategic selection and combination of soil amendments can comprehensively improve grassland ecosystems and enhance productivity and environmental stability (Dong et al., 2022; Ibrahimi and Alghamdi, 2022; Omondi et al., 2016 ). The relative stability and lower microbial activity of deep soils limit the amendment effects, which have an insignificant impact on deep soil hydrological properties (Mi et al., 2016; Tuyishimire et al., 2022 ). Overall, our findings promote the application of soil amendments in grassland management, providing an important reference for enhancing the soil water storage capacity and saturated hydraulic conductivity of grassland ecosystems.   5 Conclusions To assess the effects of soil amendments on the hydrological properties of grassland soils, we conducted a five-year soil amendment experiment in a semi-arid grassland on the Loess Plateau. Our findings indicated that both AS and BC significantly influenced vegetation and soil properties. AS application reduced soil pH, enhanced soil particle aggregation, and improved soil structure and hydrological properties, such as soil SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks. BC increased SOM and moisture content and improved soil structure, leading to enhanced SWHC, FC, SWS, and Ks. Notably, the combination of AS and BC resulted in the most significant improvements, markedly enhancing vegetation biomass, root biomass, and all measured soil hydrological properties. The primary drivers of these changes were the alterations in SOM, FRB, TP, and SBD. Overall, the combined use of AS and BC was particularly effective at improving soil fertility and hydrological properties. This combination offers valuable insights for the sustainable management of semi-arid grasslands, demonstrating the potential of soil amendments to increase the soil water storage capacity and saturated hydraulic conductivity.
1 Introduction The contaminated sites caused by landfill leakage, relocation of polluting factories, illegal discharge of industrial sewage and mineral exploitation have frequently occurred worldwide, leading to serious damage to the surrounding soil and groundwater (Ding et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021 ). The vertical cutoff wall is one of the most commonly used pollution control measures and can be an excellent choice for the contaminated sites not requiring immediate remediation, thereby reserving time for more cost-effective and efficient remediation measures (Neville and Andrews, 2006; Sharma and Reddy, 2004 ). The geosynthetic clay liner (GCL)-soil composite cutoff wall is a new type of composite antifouling barrier that can effectively restrict contaminant transport, and it is constructed using a bentonite slurry-supported trench into which a GCL is subsequently installed and then backfilled with low-permeability materials (e.g., soil-bentonite, cement-bentonite, soil–cement-bentonite) (Rowe and Jefferis, 2022; Xie et al., 2023a ). The GCL composite cutoff wall has a lower permeability, higher adsorption capacity and better durability, which is able to overcome various issues faced by other types of cutoff walls, including frequent leakage of construction joints, difficulty in installing geomembrane and poor anti-seepage performance of walls due to poor contact between geomembrane and adjacent soil (Liu et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023a ). However, contaminants can readily break through the cutoff wall via diffusion, dispersion and other mechanisms, posing a pollution risk to the surrounding environment. Therefore, investigating the contaminant transport behavior in the GCL composite cutoff wall is crucial for the design and evaluation of cutoff walls. Numerous researchers have extensively studied the contaminant transport behaviors in cutoff walls. Initially, several steady-state analytical solutions were proposed for contaminant transport in cutoff walls (Devlin and Parker, 1996; Britton et al., 2004; Neville and Andrews, 2006 ), but these solutions cannot describe the temporal evolution of contaminant transport. Later, many transient analytical solutions emerged to overcome this limitation and emphasized the importance of accounting for the downstream aquifer in the contaminant transport process in vertical cutoff walls (Xie et al., 2018a; Ding et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020, 2021; Ding and Feng, 2022 ). However, analytical solutions are difficult to use in large and complex scenarios, so the numerical methods (e.g., finite difference method and finite element method) are widely used for contaminant transport analysis in cutoff walls as well (Harte et al., 2006; Koda and Osinski, 2017; Jiang et al., 2023 ). The aforementioned studies have accounted for the effects of advection, molecular diffusion, mechanical dispersion, degradation and adsorption, but all have ignored the semipermeable membrane effect. For bentonite-based cutoff walls (such as the GCL composite cutoff wall in this study), the semipermeable membrane effect has a significant impact on the contaminant transport process, and it is crucial to consider this semipermeable membrane effect in the design and analysis of bentonite-based cutoff walls (Shackelford, 2014; Shackelford and Scalia, 2016 ). It has been extensively observed in experimental studies that the low-permeability engineered clay barriers (e.g., soil-bentonite backfill, bentonite-amended compacted clay, GCL) exhibit semipermeable membrane effect (Shackelford, 2011; Shackelford and Scalia, 2016 ). This effect means that the barriers can restrict chemical solute transport while relatively not impede solvent transport (Malusis and Shackelford, 2002a ). The semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient, ω , was used to quantify the restricting capacity of the semipermeable membrane, ranging from 0 to 1. The case of ω  = 0 indicates no semipermeable membrane effect, i.e., the solute transport is unrestricted, whereas ω  = 1 represents an ideal semipermeable membrane, i.e., the solute transport is impeded completely (Malusis et al., 2003 ). Yeo et al. (2005)  evaluated the semipermeable membrane effect of two soil-bentonite (SB) backfills, and found that the SB backfills exhibited larger ω  than natural clay backfills, providing the first quantitative evidence for the existence of the semipermeable membrane effect in SB vertical cutoff walls. Henning et al. (2006)  examined two SB backfills from field-constructed SB cutoff walls and found that the membrane effect can be significant, with ω  ranging from 0.0019 to 0.0172, depending on the void ratio and clay content of backfill. Kang and Shackelford (2010)  and Tang et al. (2014, 2015)  investigated the semipermeable membrane effect of compacted clay liner, pointing out that the unamended clay is unlikely to behave as semipermeable membrane unless amended with bentonite or composed of high swelling clay minerals. Malusis and Daniyarov (2016)  and Shackelford et al. (2016)  reported that the ω  of GCL ranged from 0.15 to 0.73 and was higher than that of SB and modified clay. Bohnhoff and Shackelford (2013)  and Fu et al. (2021a, 2021b)  performed semipermeable membrane tests on novel modified bentonite-based materials (i.e., bentonite polymer nanocomposite, sand/SHMP-amended bentonite backfill and magnesium-activated slag-bentonite–sand), finding that modified materials have improved semipermeable membrane effect, with ω  generally increasing by 109% to 433%. Based on numerous studies, Kang and Shackelford (2011), Shackelford (2012)  and Sample-Lord and Shackelford (2018)  concluded that the semipermeable membrane effect in engineered clay barriers tends to increase with increasing bentonite content and effective confining stress and with decreasing void ratio, solute concentration and degree of saturation. In order to quantitatively study the effect of semipermeable membrane effect on solute transport, Manassero and Dominijanni (2003)  established a solute transport model that incorporates this effect based on fundamental thermodynamic principles. Similarly, Malusis and Shackelford (2002b, 2004a, 2004b)  developed coupled solute transport equations that consider the constant semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient. Tong and Sample-Lord (2022)  conducted experimental and computational studies on polymer-enhanced bentonite GCL and found that the steady-state mass flux through GCL decreased by 5.8% to 61% when considering the semipermeable membrane effect. Ni et al. (2022)  studied the soil-bentonite backfill consisted of sand and Xanthan gum-amended bentonite, finding a 15.26% decrease in steady-state mass flux through the cutoff wall when considering the semipermeable membrane effect. However, these aforementioned studies only focused on the steady-state contaminant transport or constant semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient. It is necessary to propose a computational method for the transient (i.e., time-varying) contaminant transport in the composite cutoff wall-aquifer system considering the semipermeable membrane effect, as well as the concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient. This study presents a numerical model for contaminant transport through the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, with the feature of considering semipermeable membrane effect. The proposed model is first solved using the finite difference method, and then the solution is validated against the semipermeable membrane tests of Tong and Sample-Lord (2022) , the analytical solution of Liu et al. (2023)  and numerical simulations of a commercial finite element software. Using the proposed numerical solution, parametric studies are conducted to analyze the effects of semipermeable membrane effect, concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient, thickness of the bentonite-based cutoff wall, distribution coefficient of the bentonite-based wall and hydraulic conductivity on the transport law of lead in the composite GCL cutoff wall-aquifer system.  2 Mathematical model 2.1 Schematic diagram and basic assumptions Fig. 1   presents the configuration of the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system consisting of three individual components: a bentonite-based soil wall, a geosynthetic clay liner and an aquifer, with a contaminant source at the inflow boundary and a river or stream at the outflow boundary. The thicknesses of the bentonite-based wall, GCL and aquifer are L bw , L g  and L a , respectively, and the total thickness of the composite cutoff wall is L cw  = L bw  + L g . The horizontal coordinate x  is defined as positive rightward, with its origin located at the interface between the bentonite-based wall and the contaminated site. The contaminant transport in the cutoff wall-aquifer system is transient. Advection, diffusion, mechanical dispersion and degradation occur throughout the system, while the semipermeable membrane effect is considered only in the wall and not in the aquifer due to its high hydraulic conductivity and low content of high swelling smectite minerals (Shackelford, 2012 ). Based on existing experimental and theoretical studies, the proposed model adopts the following assumptions: (1) the composite cutoff wall-aquifer system is assumed to be homogeneous, rigid, isotropic and fully saturated; (2) the contaminant concentration in the contaminated site is sufficiently dilute and does not change the properties of the system (Ruhl and Daniel, 1997 ); (3) the contaminant transport is assumed to be one-dimensional process along the x -axis for conservative consideration (Peng et al., 2021 ); (4) the sorption/desorption is assumed to be linear, equilibrium, isothermal and instantaneous (Xie et al., 2018a ); (5) the degradation follows first-order kinetic model (Williams and Tomasko, 2008 ); (6) the flow of pore water in the cutoff wall-aquifer system is in steady state that obeys Darcy’s law.  2.2 Governing equations Based on the aforementioned assumptions, the governing equations for contaminant transport in the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system are as follows (Manassero and Dominijanni, 2003; During the tests, KCl solutions and de-ionized water (DIW) were circulated across the upper and lower boundaries of the specimen to maintain a fixed concentration gradient across the specimen. The proposed solution is used to analyze the contaminant transport behaviors considering the semipermeable membrane effects of the specimen in the aforementioned experiment. The specimen had a thickness of 18 mm and porosity of 0.9. Three tests with various KCl source concentrations (i.e., 5, 10 and 50 mmol/L) are chosen. Table 1   gives the other related parameters for the semipermeable membrane effect tests of Tong and Sample-Lord (2022) . The comparisons of cumulative KCl outflow mass for different KCl source concentrations are presented in Fig. 2  . The results obtained by numerical solution are in good agreement with the experimental results of Tong and Sample-Lord (2022) . The slight discrepancy arises because the concentration at the bottom of the sample is assumed to be 0 in the numerical calculation process, whereas in reality it exceeds 0.  3.2 Comparison with analytical solution (triple-layer soil ignoring semipermeable membrane effect) Liu et al. (2023)  presented an analytical solution for one-dimensional contaminant transport through a SB-GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, considering advection, hydrodynamic dispersion, sorption and degradation. Compared with the proposed solution in this paper, the analytical solution of Liu et al. (2023)  neglected the effects of semipermeable membrane effect and effective porosity. To verify the proposed solution, it is assumed that ω  = 0.0001 (approaching zero) and the effective porosity equals to the total porosity. The Darcy velocity v d  is set to 1 × 10-9  m/s. The concentration at the inflow boundary is fixed at 1 mg/L, while the outflow boundary maintains a zero concentration, with an initial condition of zero concentration for all three layers. Table 2   gives the other related parameters in SB-GCL cutoff wall system of Liu et al. (2023) . The results in Fig. 3   indicate that the relative concentration profiles obtained by the proposed solution are consistent with those of Liu et al. (2023) , suggesting that the proposed numerical solution can accurately analyze the contaminant transport process in the triplelayered cutoff wall-aquifer system.  3.3 Comparison with COMSOL simulation (triple-layer soil considering semipermeable membrane effect) The COMSOL Multiphysics software, a finite element calculation software typically used to study the contaminant transport behaviors (Jiang et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023b ), is adopted to further verify the proposed numerical solution. In this section, we consider a hypothetical composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, consisting of a 0.59-m bentonite-based wall, a 0.01-m GCL and a 10-m aquifer. Lead is selected as the contaminant, as it is a toxic heavy metal pollutant commonly found in contaminated sites. The source concentration of lead is assumed constant (=0.1 mg/L), following Xie et al. (2018a) . The ω  of the bentonite-based wall, GCL and aquifer are 0.28, 0.56 and 0 (Tang et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2021a ). The bentonite-based wall has effective and total porosities of 0.42 and 0.52, respectively. The GCL has effective and total porosities of 0.6 and 0.7, respectively. The aquifer has effective and total porosities of 0.47 and 0.52, respectively. The hydraulic gradient h g  is set to 1. Table 3   gives the contaminant transport properties of the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system. Fig. 4   shows the contaminant transport results obtained by the proposed solution and COMSOL software, including relative contaminant concentration profiles, contaminant mass flux and cumulative contaminant outflow mass over time. Excellent agreement between the two methods is observed, which further validates the proposed numerical solution for contaminant transport in the composite cutoff wall-aquifer system.   4 Parametric analyses Based on the example in section 3.3 , the proposed numerical solution is used to investigate the effects of semipermeable membrane effect, concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient, thickness of bentonite-based wall, distribution coefficient of bentonite-based wall and hydraulic conductivity on the contaminant transport behaviors in the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system. For each series of analyses, only the variable of interest is changed, while other variables remain constant and equal to those given in section 3.3 . 4.1 Effect of semipermeable membrane effect Significant semipermeable membrane effect has been observed in both laboratory and field tests, with significant variations in the semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient ω  for different materials. For example, for 3.9 mmol/L KCl solutions, Yeo et al. (2005)  found that ω  of natural clay backfill ranged from 0.018 to 0.024, while ω  of soil-bentonite backfill ranged from 0.118 to 0.166. Kang and Shackelford (2011)  reported that ω  of GCL was much higher (between 0.427 and 0.680). To illustrate the importance of considering ω  in the analysis of lead transport through the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, Fig. 5   presents the relative lead concentration C w /C 0  and lead mass flux J  at the exit of the composite cutoff wall for different ω bw  (=0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4) and ω g  (=0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8), where ω bw  = ω g  = 0 means no semipermeable membrane effect. The breakthrough time t b , commonly used to evaluate the service performance of cutoff wall, is defined as the time when C w  reaches a specific concentration (i.e., breakthrough concentration) (Xie et al., 2023c ). According to the World Health Organization drinking water quality standard (WHO, 2011 ), the breakthrough concentration of lead is 0.01 mg/L. As the lead source concentration C 0  is 0.1 mg/L, the breakthrough point is the time when C w /C 0  = 0.1 (shown in Fig. 5 ) . Fig. 5  shows that ignoring the semipermeable membrane effect will significantly underestimate breakthrough time, overestimate contaminant mass flux and thus underestimate the anti-fouling performance of cutoff wall. Furthermore, as ω  increases, t b  gradually increases and J  decreases. This is because the semipermeable membrane effect retards the contaminant transport process through the mechanisms of hyperfiltration, chemico-osmosis and restricted solute diffusion. These mechanisms manifest as follows: (1) the traditional advective flux is reduced by a factor of (1-ω ) due to the filtering of semipermeable membrane; (2) chemico-osmosis causes liquid to flow from the lower solute concentration side to the higher solute concentration side (opposite to the direction of advection and diffusion), thereby reducing the total solute mass flux; (3) anion exclusion leads to a lower effective diffusion coefficient, reducing the diffusion flux. To better understand the differences between considering ω  and neglecting ω , the t b  and the steady-state mass flux J ss  for different ω bw  and ω g  are listed in Table 4  . Table 4  also includes the increase in t b  and decrease in J ss  relative to ω bw  = ω g  = 0 (no semipermeable membrane). In Table 4 , ω g  has much smaller influence on the increase of t b  and decrease of J ss  relative to ω bw . Namely, the effect of semipermeable membrane effect of bentonite-based wall on the contaminant transport is stronger than of the GCL, because the GCL is much thinner than the bentonite-based wall (10 mm vs. 590 mm). For example, as ω bw  increases from 0.05 to 0.4, t b  increases from 60 to 100 years (increased by 66.7%) and J ss  decreases from 0.2266 to 0.1419 mg/m2 /yr (decreased by 37.4%). By contrast, as ω g  increases from 0.1 to 0.8, t b  increases from 80 to 83 years (increased by only 3.8%) and J ss  decreases from 0.1715 to 0.1708 mg/m2 /yr (decreased by only 0.4%). In summary, Table 4  suggests that ignoring the semipermeable membrane effect can underestimate the breakthrough time by 7.1%∼78.6% and overestimate the outflow mass flux by 5.3%∼40.7%.  4.2 Effect of concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient Although the semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient ω  is typically regarded as a constant in the majority of existing studies (e.g., Malusis and Shackelford, 2004b; Malusis et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2021 ), experimental results have shown that ω  changes significantly with various factors including solute concentration (Malusis and Shackelford, 2002a; Henning et al., 2006; Kang and Shackelford, 2011 ). For example, Fu et al. (2021a)  measured the ω  of a cutoff wall backfill composed of reactive magnesium-activated slag, bentonite and sand (referred to as MSBS backfill) using Pb(NO3 )2  solutions at different concentrations (0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 10, 50 mg/L) and the obtained corresponding ω  = 0.558, 0.446, 0.362, 0.321, 0.195 and 0.108, respectively.
