A semi-logarithmic linear function can well fit the data of Fu et al. (2021a)  to describe the variation of ω  with concentration (see Fig. 6   and Eq. (29) ). Here, Eq. (29)  is used to calculate the variable ω bw , while ω g  is considered constant as we have concluded in Section 4.1  that ω g  has very limited impact on the solute transport due to its small thickness. Note that the ω  is between 0 and 1 and therefore if ω bw  calculated by Eq. (29)  is > 1 (or < 0), ω bw  is set to 1 (or 0). Furthermore, it should be pointed out that Eq. (29)  does not have universal applicability and is only specific to the transport behavior of lead in MSBS backfill. For other contaminants and backfill materials, corresponding semipermeable membrane tests are needed to establish the corresponding relationship.(29) ω = 0.37984 - 0.17008 log ( C )      To investigate the effect of concentration-dependent ω , simulations are performed with different C 0  (=0.1, 1 and 10 mg/L), different k bw  (=1 × 10-8 , 1 × 10-9 , and 1 × 10-10  m/s) and different h g  (=0.5, 0 and −0.5). Three cases are considered: constant ω bw , variable ω bw  (i.e., concentration-dependent ω bw ), and ignoring semipermeable membrane effect (i.e., ω bw  = 0). Fig. 7  (a), 7(b) and 7(c), respectively, presents the relative concentration C w /C 0  for different C 0 , that for different h g  and the mass flux J  for different k bw . The results indicate that the concentration-dependent ω bw  has a more pronounced retardation effect on contaminant transport compared with the constant ω bw . As shown in Fig. 6 , ω  decreases from 0.558 to 0.108 as solute concentration increases from 0.1 to 50 mg/L. In the initial stage of transport, contaminant concentration in the bentonite-based wall is low and thus ω bw  is higher, resulting in stronger retardation effect. Fig. 7 (a) also indicates that at low source concentrations, the concentration-dependent ω bw  has a more significant effect on retarding the contaminant transport. For example, as C 0  decreases from 10 to 0.1 mg/L, the difference in C w /C 0  at t  = 200 years between the variable ω bw  and the constant ω bw  increases from 16.5% to 80.9%. Furthermore, when ignoring ω bw  (=0), C 0  has no effect on C w /C 0  and the C w /C 0  curves completely overlap. By contrast, when considering ω bw , C 0  significantly affects the C w /C 0  curves, with the higher the source concentration producing the faster contaminant transport. Fig. 7 (b) illustrates that lower hydraulic gradient enhances the retardation effect of concentration-dependent ω bw . For example, as h g  decreases from 0.5 to −0.5, the difference in C w /C 0  at t  = 200 years between the variable ω bw  and the constant ω bw  increases from 26.1% to 63.9%. This is because h g  directly affects both the flow direction and seepage velocity, i.e., lower h g  produces slower contaminant transport and, thus, the concentration-dependent ω bw  is higher and so is the associated retardation effect. Moreover, Fig. 7 (b) indicates that lowering the water table inside the cutoff wall (e.g., via pumping method) can effectively improve the wall’s anti-fouling performance especially when the water table inside the wall is lower the outside (i.e., h g  < 0). When considering the concentration-dependent ω bw , as h g  decreases from 0.5 to 0, C w /C 0  at t  = 200 yr decreases from 0.295 to 0.128 (decreased by 56.6%); on the other hand, as h g  decreases from 0 to −0.5, C w /C 0  at t  = 200 yr decreases from 0.128 to 0.0245 (a larger decrease of 80.9%). This is because negative hydraulic gradient causes advective flux towards the contaminated site (opposite to the direction of diffusion), reducing the diffusive flux and thus decreasing the contaminant transport rate. Fig. 7 (c) shows that the retardation effect of the concentration-dependent ω bw  is stronger at lower hydraulic conductivity. For example, as k bw  decreases from 1 × 10-8  to 1 × 10-10  m/s, the difference in J  at t  = 200 years between the variable ω bw  and the constant ω bw  increases from 8.7% to 59.0%. This is because lower k bw  produces slower contaminant transport and the contaminant concentration remains at lower level for longer duration and, thus, the concentration-dependent ω bw  is higher (Fig. 6 ). In summary, Fig. 7  indicates that it’s more necessary to consider the concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane effect for lower source concentration, lower hydraulic conductivity and lower hydraulic gradient.  4.3 Effects of thickness and distribution coefficient of bentonite-based wall The thickness and distribution coefficient of the composite cutoff wall both have significant effects on the breakthrough time, t b . Typically, GCL is factory prefabricated, so its thickness L g  (=0.01 m) and distribution coefficient K d,g  does not vary much and thus are assumed constant. The thickness of bentonite-based wall L bw  varies from 0.6 to 1.2 m, consistent with the typical values in the design specification (e.g., HG/T 20715-2020 ). Fig. 8  (a) and 8(b) shows the variations of t b  with L bw  and K d,bw  considering and ignoring semipermeable membrane effect, respectively. It’s observed that t b  increases as L bw  and K d,bw  increase. Comparing Fig. 8 (a) and 8(b), the contour lines of t b  considering semipermeable membrane effect are denser and have higher values than those ignoring this effect. When considering semipermeable membrane effect, for constant K d,bw  (=2.0 mL/g for example), t b  increases from 48 to 118 years (145.8% increase) as L bw  increases from 0.6 to 1.2 m, because thicker cutoff wall means longer contaminant transport path and lower seepage velocity (see Eqs. (5) to (7) ); for constant L bw  (=0.6 m for example), t b  increases from 29 to 84 years (189.7% increase) as K d,bw  increases from 1.0 to 4.0 mL/g, because higher K d,bw  means greater retardation effect. Moreover, the contour lines of t b  become denser with increasing L bw  and K d,bw , because higher K d,bw  results in stronger retardation effect per unit thickness of the cutoff wall.  4.4 Effect of hydraulic conductivities of bentonite-based wall and GCL Hydraulic conductivity is a crucial factor for the antifouling performance of composite cutoff wall. To achieve good anti-seepage performance, the cutoff wall is required to have a low hydraulic conductivity (typically no greater than 10-9  m/s). Nevertheless, external environmental factors (e.g., high salinity/strong acid-base leachate, wet-dry cycles, and freeze–thaw cycles) can easily result in significant increase in hydraulic conductivity during the service life of cutoff wall (Lin and Benson, 2000; Foose and Thomson, Jr., 2002; Scalia et al., 2014 ). To evaluate the effects of bentonite-based wall’s hydraulic conductivity k bw  and GCL’s hydraulic conductivity k g , simulations are performed with k bw  ranging from 1 × 10-7  to 1 × 10-10  m/s and k g  ranging from 5 × 10-8  to 5 × 10-12  m/s. These k bw  and k g  values are selected according to the measurements reported in the literature (e.g., Joshi et al., 2010; Shackelford et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2022 ). Fig. 9   shows the breakthrough time t b  for varying k bw  and k g . Fig. 9  indicates that t b  decreases with the increase of either k bw  or k g  and that the t b  considering the semipermeable membrane effect is always longer than that ignoring this effect. Table 5   presents the difference in t b  between considering and ignoring the semipermeable membrane effect (denoted as Δtb ). Overall, the Δtb  (absolute value) is larger when k bw  and k g  values are lower. For example, Δtb  is as high as 41.05 yr for low k bw  of 1 × 10-10  m/s and k g  of 5 × 10-12  m/s, whereas Δtb  is as low as only 0.46 yr for high k bw  of 1 × 10-8  m/s and k g  of 5 × 10-8  m/s. Interestingly, in terms of relative difference, the corresponding values (= (t b,consider_ω  – t b,ignore_ω ) / t b,ignore_ω ) remain in a narrow range between 40% and 45% for all the values of k bw  and k g  considered. When considering ω , for k g  = 5 × 10-11  m/s, the t b  decreases from 133 to 37 years (a 72.2% decrease) as k bw  decreases from 1 × 10-10  to 1 × 10-7  m/s. The t b  significantly decreases because hydraulic conductivity directly affects the seepage velocity of pore liquid and the advective flux of contaminant. Additionally, when either k bw  or k g  is low, the change in t b  is very small; on the contrary, when either k bw  or k g  is high, the change in t b  is significant. When k bw  increases from 1 × 10-10  to 1 × 10-7  m/s, t b  decreases from 136 to 111 years (a 18.4% decrease) for a low k g  of 5 × 10-12  m/s, while t b  decreases from 133 to only 2 years (as high as 98.5% decrease) for a high k g  of 5 × 10-8  m/s. Similarly, when k g  increases from 5 × 10-12  to 5 × 10-8  m/s, t b  decreases from 136 to 133 years (only 2.2% decrease) for a low k bw  of 1 × 10-10  m/s, while t b  decreases from 111 to only 2 years (as high as 98.2% decrease) for a high k bw  of 1 × 10-7  m/s. When either the bentonite-based wall meets the regulatory requirement (i.e., k bw  = 1 × 10-9  m/s, by HG/T 20715-2020 ) or the GCL meets the regulatory requirement (i.e., k g  = 5 × 10-11  m/s, by GI 2016 ), the composite wall would perform well, with t b  always > 40 years. Therefore, it is crucial to avoid simultaneous deterioration of both the bentonite-based wall and the GCL.   5 Summary and conclusions A numerical solution is presented for 1D contaminant transport through a GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, with the addition of considering the effect of semipermeable membrane effect. The solute transport algorithm of the model accounts for advection, hydrodynamic dispersion, sorption, degradation and semipermeable membrane effect. The numerical solution is validated by comparison with the semipermeable membrane test results of Tong and Sample-Lord (2022) , the analytical solution of Liu et al. (2023) , and the numerical simulation of a commercial finite element software. Using the verified solution, a series of simulations are conducted to investigate the effects of semipermeable membrane effect, concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient, thickness of the bentonite-based wall, distribution coefficient of bentonite-based wall and hydraulic conductivity, on the transport of heavy metal lead through the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system. The following conclusions are drawn: (1) The semipermeable membrane effect can greatly retard contaminant transport through the GCL composite cutoff wall-aquifer system, and ignoring this effect will underestimate the contaminant breakthrough time, t b , and overestimate the contaminant mass flux, J . For the conditions examined in this paper, considering semipermeable membrane effect results in a 7.1%∼78.6% increase in t b  and a 5.3%∼40.7% decrease in J ; and the semipermeable membrane effect in the bentonite-based wall, relative to that in the GCL, has greater impact on the contaminant transport results as GCL is much thinner. (2) The concentration-dependent semipermeable membrane efficiency coefficient ω  retards the contaminant transport more significantly than a constant ω  does, particularly under the conditions of low hydraulic conductivity, low source concentration and low hydraulic gradient. For the conditions examined in this paper, the difference in C w /C 0  or J  between ignoring ω  and considering concentration-dependent ω  ranges from 39.2% to 95.3%. (3) Simultaneous deterioration of both the bentonite-based wall and the GCL should be avoided in practice, such that the breakthrough time doesn’t decrease significantly. Nonetheless, when either the bentonite-based wall meets its regulatory requirement (i.e., k bw  = 1 × 10-9  m/s) or the GCL meets its regulatory requirement (i.e., k g  = 5 × 10-11  m/s), the composite wall would perform well, with t b  > 40 years.
1 Introduction Aquatic vegetation, as an integral component of aquatic ecosystems, plays a crucial role in stabilizing the health of hydroecological systems. Aquatic plants contribute to ecosystem health not only through biological and chemical processes but also by modifying the hydrodynamic processes within aquatic environments (Afzal et al., 2019; Costanza et al., 1997; Xu et al., 2022, 2024 ). Through their stems and leaves, aquatic plants generate resistance against water flow, reducing flow velocity, thereby helping to minimize riverbed erosion and sediment transport and maintaining the stability of river courses (Curran and Hession, 2013 ). Additionally, the canopy enhances sediment deposition in the water, anchoring organic matter and plant seeds in the riverbed, which promotes the evolution of vegetation (Liu et al., 2024; Shan et al., 2023; Yamasaki et al., 2019 ). The complex geometric forms of plant canopies interact with the flow to produce multi-scale turbulence, which directly affects the transport processes of nutrients and the growth of algae, meeting the flow preferences of various aquatic organisms such as fish (Oliveira et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2023 ). This enhances the water’s self-purification capabilities and maintains biodiversity. Thus, submerged canopy is often employed in environmental and ecological restoration projects for rivers and lakes. The ecological functionality of aquatic vegetation also depends on local hydrodynamic conditions; for instance, the efficiency of pollutant absorption by stems and leaves is related to the flow dynamics around the leaf boundaries (Nepf, 2012 ). Therefore, the study of how aquatic vegetation influences the hydrodynamic characteristics of water flow has garnered widespread attention due to its significance in protecting river hydrology and aquatic environments, and achieving sustainable river development. Submerged canopy, due to its significant effectiveness in the restoration of river and lake aquatic environments, has been extensively studied through experimental and numerical investigations of its over-flow dynamics (Follett and Nepf, 2018; Ghisalberti, 2009; Huai et al., 2019; Koken and Constantinescu, 2023; Przyborowski and Loboda, 2021; Yan et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020 ). The ratio of flow depth H  to canopy height h  defined as the submergence ratio, categorizes submerged canopy flow into shallow submergence (1 < H /h  < 5) and deep submergence (H /h  > 10), with shallow submergence being typical in rivers and shallow lakes (Nepf, 2012 ). Due to the vertical discontinuity in canopy resistance, the flow through submerged canopy is divided into a lower-velocity vegetated layer and a higher-velocity upper free stream layer (Huai et al., 2021 ). The transition of flow velocities at the interface between the vegetated layer and the free stream layer creates an inflection point in the vertical velocity distribution, similar to a free mixing layer (Stoesser et al., 2009 ). This leads to shear layer instabilities that induce the formation and development of shear-scale Kelvin-Helmholtz (K-H) vortices, which are a significant dynamic feature of submerged canopy flows (Ghisalberti, 2009 ). However, shear-scale vortices occur only when canopy blockage is high, Cd ah  ≥ 0.1, where Cd   is the drag coefficient of vegetation stems, and a  is the frontal area of the vegetation stems facing the flow (a  = nd , with n  being the number of vegetation stems per unit bed area and d  the diameter of the stems) (Huai et al., 2021; Nepf, 2012; Nepf and Vivoni, 2000 ). Unlike the free mixing layer where K-H vortices continuously grow downstream, the confined mixing layer above the canopy top does not exhibit such growth. However, Wang et al. (2024)  innovatively discovered that at certain canopy densities, the canopy mixing layer displays asymptotic behavior for the variation of bed friction and water shallowness, consistent with classic shallow mixing layers. Ghisalberti and Nepf (2004)  conducted flume experiments and found that the growth of K-H vortices ceases when the shear-scale turbulent energy production at the interface is balanced by the turbulent energy dissipation within the canopy layer, followed by the vortices penetrating downward into the canopy layer, with the depth of penetration dependent on canopy resistance, ∼ (Cd a )-1 . The penetration of the vortex has proven closely linked the flow structure through canopy. Yan and Wang (2024) , based on the characterization of canopy-scale vortex, reconstructed the turbulent length scale incorporated into the Spalart-Allmaras model, effectively refining the modeling dissipation of the velocity profile in the canopy layer from other traditional turbulence models. Beyond this point, the vertical distribution of flow velocity and turbulence intensity does not significantly change along the flow, reaching a so-called fully developed state (Okamoto and Nezu, 2013 ). The distance required to reach this state, X *, is negatively correlated with canopy density and submergence (Chen et al., 2013 ). The development of shear-scale vortices in submerged canopy does not commence immediately at the canopy leading edge but follows an initial adjustment segment characterized by significant vertical flow deflection (Chen et al., 2013; Okamoto and Nezu, 2013 ). The fluid dynamics insights concerning submerged canopy flows have primarily been derived from studies assuming continuous canopy distribution. However, in natural fields, the reality of discontinuous canopy distribution is widespread. Such discontinuous distributions form longitudinal gap zones, which, while providing habitats for aquatic life, inevitably impact the local flow field (Colomer et al., 2017; Maltese et al., 2007; Poëtte et al., 2017 ). This impact alters the previously established energy balance modes in upstream canopy flows and affects the ecological functionality of the canopy. Ranjan et al. (2022)  utilized high-resolution Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and flume experiments to study the adjustments in flow within the gaps between two sufficiently long emergent canopy patches, with their interest particularly focused on the differences in turbulence statistics within the gap compared to those in the upstream canopy patches. Compared to gaps in emergent canopy, the flow adjustments in submerged canopy gaps are more complex. When upstream canopy patches provide sufficient flow resistance, submerged canopy gaps will exhibit the classic dynamics of cavity flow (Folkard, 2011; Fontan et al., 2013; Hamed et al., 2020 ). For cavity flow, the mean flow pattern within the cavity depends on the aspect ratio L /h , where L  is the length of the cavity along the flow direction (Mignot et al., 2019 ). When L /h  crosses a certain threshold (≈ 1.5), the flow pattern shifts from the skimming flow regime to the wake interference regime. The primary difference between submerged canopy gaps and cavity flow is that the former exhibits bleeding flow exiting the upstream canopy patch and entering the gap (Fontan et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2022 ). Folkard (2011)  identified flow regimes within gap zones of flexible canopy patches through laboratory flume experiments, categorizing them into five types: skimming flow, recirculation flow, boundary layer recovery, canopy through-flow, and isolated roughness flow, and concluded that the flow regime depends on the Reynolds number and the aspect ratio L /h . It has been noted that submerged canopy flows require initial adjustment lengths and shear layer development lengths to reach a fully developed state (Chen et al., 2013; Ghisalberti and Nepf, 2004 ). As Hamed et al. (2020)  pointed out, Folkard's (2011)  experiments did not consider this, which has a significant impact on the parameter thresholds (i.e., Reynolds number and L /h ) that cause flow regime transitions. Fontan et al. (2013)  compared the mean and turbulent momentum transfer within and near the gap regions with solid and porous boundaries at L /h  = 3 through flume experiments, observing deeper turbulence penetration into the gap in the latter scenario. This phenomenon was also confirmed by Hamed et al. (2020) . They used Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) to measure the time-averaged flow field in the gap region located at the fully developed submerged canopy flow area, revealing the influence of L /h . Despite the presence of recirculation vortices in all gap regions due to the considerable canopy density upstream, different mixing layer penetration patterns were observed at L /h  ≤ 1 and L /h  ≥ 2. The former was characterized by interface shear layers that did not undergo significant growth and high longitudinal momentum and turbulent energy that did not significantly penetrate the gap, indicative of the skimming flow regime. The latter featured significant growth of the interface mixing layer and deeper penetration into the gap, termed the shear layer growth regime (Hamed et al., 2020 ). However, as they themselves noted, the anticipated transition in flow regimes is sensitive to canopy density, which is precisely what their studies lacked. Moreover, the vertical momentum and mass exchange driven by the mixing layer between the gap and the upper free stream, crucial for the transport of nutrients and plant seeds, was not discussed. This study employs high-resolution LES to explore the flow dynamics within the gap regions of fully developed submerged canopy flows. Two canopy density values and four gap aspect ratios are considered to investigate their effects on the time-averaged recirculation patterns within the gap and the penetration of the mixing layer from the interface with the free stream into the gap. The subsequent vertical momentum and mass transfer across the interface are also investigated, which has been previously lacking in research. The organization of this work is as follows: the numerical model and computational setup are described in Sec. 2; Section 3  presents model validation along with an analysis and discussion of the simulation results. The main conclusions are summarized in Sec. 4.  2 Method 2.1 Numerical models LES is utilized for high-resolution resolution of the flow field. Within the LES framework, large-scale fluid motions (larger than the filter scale) are directly resolved, while the smaller scales (smaller than the filter scale) are modeled using a subgrid-scale model to reflect their impact on the larger scales. In this study, the LES solves the spatially filtered continuity and momentum equations for an incompressible viscous fluid,(1) ∂ u ∼  i   ∂ x i    = 0     (2) ∂ u ∼  i   ∂ t   + u ∼  j  ∂ u ∼  i   ∂ x j    = - 1 ρ  ∂ p ∼   ∂ x i    + ν ∂ 2  u ∼  i   ∂ x j  ∂ x j    - ∂ τ ij    ∂ x j    - f i      where the “∼” represents spatial filtering; ui   = (u , v , w ) are the velocity components in the directions xi   = (x , y , z ); t  denotes time; ρ  is the density of water; p  is the pressure; ν  is the kinematic viscosity of water; τij   is the subgrid-scale stress tensor, representing the impact of the filtered small-scale turbulence on the directly resolved large-scale fluctuations. In the simulations of this study, the Wall-Adapting Local Eddy-viscosity model developed by Nicoud and Ducros (1999)  is employed to compute the subgrid-scale stress tensor. Because it can correctly predict the wall asymptotic behavior [i.e., νt   = O (z 3 )] for the wall-bounded flows and return a zero value of eddy viscosity for the laminar shear flows, without employing wall-damping functions (Nicoud and Ducros, 1999; Rodi et al., 2013 ). fi   represents the drag imposed by vegetation stems on the flow, implying that in this study, aquatic vegetation is modeled using a drag source term rather than explicitly resolving the stem-scale flow. Compared to directly resolving stem-scale turbulence, using a drag source term to model canopy does not significantly affect the resolution of large-scale shear flows, and also reduces the number of computational grids, thereby enhancing computational efficiency (Qu and Yu, 2021; Sonnenwald et al., 2019; Stoesser et al., 2003; Yan et al., 2017 ). The canopy drag is calculated using the quadratic drag formula for rigid stems.(3) f i  = 1 2  C d  a  1 - ϕ   u ∼  i  u ∼  j  u ∼  j        where Cd   represents the drag coefficient of the stems, calculated using the drag predictor developed by Liu et al. (2020) . The effectiveness of this model has been validated by Liu et al. (2022) . The canopy density, ϕ,  is defined as the proportion of bed area occupied by vegetation stems, and can be calculated as ϕ  = πnd 2 /4 = πad /4. The term (1-ϕ ) considers the volume of water excluded by the canopy stems (King et al., 2012; Sonnenwald et al., 2019 ). The flow field is solved using a three-dimensional LES code (ANSYS Fluent) based on the finite volume method. The pressure–velocity coupling is addressed using the SIMPLEC algorithm. The convection and diffusion terms in the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations are discretized spatially using a second-order accurate central differencing scheme. Temporal advancement is handled using a second-order accurate fully implicit scheme.  2.2 Simulation setup In this study, a canopy gap zone is formed between two long submerged canopy patches upstream and downstream, as illustrated in Fig. 1  . Four gap lengths L =0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4  m are considered to explore the impact of canopy gap length on the fluid dynamic characteristics, corresponding to gap aspect ratios L /h  = 1, 2, 3, and 4. For each gap aspect ratio, two canopy densities, ϕ  = 0.08 and 0.15, are considered, which are lower than the 0.2 employed by Hamed et al. (2020) . These densities correspond to dense canopy (ah  ≫ 0.1), where the fluid dynamics are characterized by K-H vortices at the interface between the canopy layer and the overlying free flow layer, with the K-H vortices penetrating toward the bed within the vegetated area but not reaching the bed (Huai et al., 2021; Nepf, 2012; Nepf and Vivoni, 2000 ). In the presence of a gap area, canopy drag is free across the entire stem height, and the high turbulence caused by K-H vortices at the interface will penetrate the gap area, leading to significant adjustments in the flow field that had reached equilibrium upstream, thereby altering the material transport processes. In contrast, sparse vegetation (ah  ≪ 0.1) behaves as bed roughness, and the presence of gaps would only result in localized changes in bed roughness, not expected to significantly impact the dominant turbulence scales. Therefore, sparse vegetation is not the focus of the current study. The primary parameters of the eight simulation cases are summarized in Table 1  . The computational domain width B  and height (i.e., water depth) H  are kept constant across all runs at 0.2  m and 0.4  m, respectively. As described in Eq. (3) , the reduction factor accounting for stem height variation is not included, indicating that stem deformation is not considered, the patch height remains constant at h  = 0.1  m and does not vary with the flow, corresponding to a submergence ratio H /h  = 4, classified as shallow submergence (H /h  < 5) (Nepf, 2012 ). The length of the canopy patch upstream of the gap, Lu  , is 6  m, and downstream, Ld  , is 3  m. The length of the computational domain varies between 9.6 and 10.0  m depending on the gap length. In rigid submerged canopy flow flume experiments by Chen et al. (2013)  under the same submergence ratio (H /h  = 4), the distance X * required for the mixing layer to reach a fully developed state was 1.6  m for ϕ  = 0.026 and 1.1  m for ϕ  = 0.098. They also noted that the development distance X * is inversely proportional to a  and H /h , suggesting that in this study, the interface mixing layer in the upstream canopy patch can reach a fully developed state before arriving at the gap zone. The origin of the Cartesian coordinate system is located at the bed level at the rear edge of the upstream canopy patch, with the x -axis pointing in the flow direction, the y -axis in the width direction, and the z -axis towards the water surface. At the inlet of the computational domain, a turbulent velocity distribution obtained from previous LES studies of unbounded open channel flow is specified. The cross-sectional average velocity is U 0  = 0.11  m/s. The channel Reynolds number, ReH  =U 0 H /ν  = 44,000, and the Froude number, Fr  = U 0 /(gH )0.5  = 0.056, are controlled to remain constant across all cases. A pressure outlet boundary condition is designated at the exit of the computational domain. The lateral sides of the domain are assigned periodic boundary conditions, signifying an infinitely wide channel unaffected by side walls. The bed surface is defined as a no-slip smooth solid wall, and no wall model is utilized. Given the relatively high submergence of the canopy, surface waves and deformations are neglected in the calculations; the water surface is generalized as a free-slip rigid lid and set as a symmetry boundary, which is a reasonable simplification when Fr  < 0.5(de Oliveira et al., 2024; Koken and Constantinescu, 2023; Liu et al., 2021 ). The entire computational domain is discretized with a fully hexahedral structured mesh. The grid resolution can be described by the dimensionless grid size Δn +  = Δnu */ν , where Δn  is the grid size in the x  ,y , and z  directions, and u * is the friction velocity (Stoesser et al., 2010 ). In the upper free stream layer, the maximum grid size is approximately Δz +  = 19, gradually decreasing towards the top of the vegetated layer. At the interface, the grid height is Δz +  = 1.1 to 1.8. In the middle height of the canopy layer, the grid height is Δz +  = 10 to 18, with transitioning denser from z /h  = 0.5 vertically towards the interface and the bed. Near the bed, the first layer grid height is Δz +  = 0.55 to 1, ensuring that the flow within the viscous sublayer is directly resolved and avoiding the need for a wall model. Laterally, the grid nodes are uniformly distributed, corresponding to Δy +  = 24 to 35. In the x -direction, the grid size in the upstream and downstream canopy patches is Δx +  = 25 to 40, and it is densified within and near the gap region to ensure accurate resolution of flow transitions and recirculation within the gap. The grid size within the gap is Δx +  = 5 to 16. In terms of time discretization, the time step in numerical calculations is fixed at 0.001H /U 0 , resulting in a relatively low Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) number. Before the LES simulation, a steady-state RANS simulation using the SST k-ω model was conducted to obtain initial velocity and pressure fields, significantly shortening the time required for the flow to reach a statistically steady state during LES, a technique widely adopted in large-scale LES simulations(Liu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021 ). After an initial LES simulation lasting 22H /U 0 , flow variables are collected and time-averaged and turbulent statistics calculated. The collection duration of flow variables continues for 100H /U 0 , sufficient to obtain converged statistics.   3 Results and discussions 3.1 Model validation To validate the current LES model's effectiveness in simulating the hydrodynamics of submerged canopy mixing layers, an additional validation case was calculated using the experimental setup of Ghisalberti and Nepf (2006)  for submerged canopy flow. Their rigid canopy run R8 was selected for comparison. The validation case had a canopy density ϕ  = 0.04, canopy height h  = 0.138  m, and flow depth H =0.467  m, corresponding to a submergence ratio of H /h  = 3.38, close to H /h  = 4 in this study. Fig. 2   displays a comparison of the Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter (ADV) measurements from Ghisalberti and Nepf (2006)  with the current LES simulation results, including the time-averaged longitudinal flow velocity ū , Reynolds stress u ′  w ′    ¯     , and turbulent kinetic energy k , all non-dimensionalized by the cross-sectional average velocity U 0 . LES simulation results from Yan et al. (2017)  are also included for comparison. Overall, the vertical distribution of the longitudinal flow velocity in the LES simulations aligns well with the ADV measurements, including the noticeable reduction in the lower canopy layer induced by the additional drag of vegetation stems and the increase in the upper free flow layer. Particularly, the local decrease in velocity near the water surface related to the secondary flow at the cross-section was also accurately simulated. Near the interface at the top of the canopy, the flow velocity exhibits a hyperbolic tangent distribution along the vertical, with a clear inflection point. This induces K-H instability and the development of the mixing layer, leading to a significant increase in turbulence levels, as shown in Fig. 2  (b) and (c). This feature has been accurately captured by the current LES calculations. The good agreement between the experimental measurements and LES simulation results demonstrates that the current LES model can accurately simulate the dynamic characteristics of submerged canopy flows. Furthermore, the capability of the current numerical model to precisely simulate cavity flow has been proven in a previous study (Liu et al., 2022 ). Therefore, there is confidence that this LES model can accurately reproduce the cavity flow characteristics expected in the canopy gap regions investigated in this study.  3.2 Time-averaged flow patterns within the gap area As previously mentioned, periodic boundary conditions are employed laterally in the simulations of this study, which suggests that the time-averaged flow field is uniform across the lateral direction. Therefore, the following discussion will focus only on the fluid dynamics characteristics within the vertical plane. Fig. 3   illustrates the impact of the canopy gap aspect ratio and canopy density on the distribution of time-averaged longitudinal flow velocities within the vertical plane. Due to the discontinuity in resistance provided by submerged canopy along the depth, the flow exhibits distinct stratification. These include a lower-velocity layer in the canopy zone, a high-velocity layer in the upper free stream area, and a transitional layer between them, namely the shear mixing zone. In Fig. 3 , contours of ū /U 0  = 0, 0.2, and 1.1 are superimposed, where ū /U 0  = 0.2 and 1.1 lines help to visually represent the changes in the width of the mixing layer along the streamwise direction. In both canopy densities, within the upstream canopy patches, the ū /U 0  = 0.2 and 1.1 lines remain horizontal and parallel, indicating that the velocity distribution no longer changes significantly along the stream, which is a key indicator of the flow reaching a fully developed state. At L /h  = 1 and 2, the ū /U 0  = 1.1 line remains horizontal above the canopy gap area, showing no vertical growth, irrespective of the density. However, at larger canopy gap aspect ratios, L /h  = 3 and 4, the ū /U 0  = 1.1 line shows a slight upward shift, but this growth is trivial compared to what was observed in the flume experiments of Hamed et al. (2020) . This is expected. The growth of shear-scale vortices in a submerged canopy mixing layer does not continue downstream. Typically, the upper boundary of the mixing layer does not reach the water surface (as observed in the upstream canopy patch by Hamed et al. (2020) ), and the lower boundary does not reach the bed. Yan et al. (2017)  computed submerged canopy flow with a submergence ratio of 3.38 using both lateral solid wall and periodic boundary conditions in LES, finding that when lateral periodic boundary conditions are used, the absence of secondary flow within the cross-section leads to a continuous growth of the mixing layer's upper boundary up to the water surface (see Fig. 2  in Yan et al. (2017) ). In this study, to eliminate the influence of lateral boundaries on the flow, periodic boundary conditions are used on the lateral sides of the computational domain, hence the mixing layer's upper boundary continuously evolves towards the water surface, with the highest velocity located at the water surface, and the upper area of the mixing layer lacks a uniform velocity segment (typically represented by U 2 ). Therefore, before reaching the canopy gap area, the upper boundary of the mixing layer has already reached its limit, so any upward shift of the ū /U 0  = 1.1 line will be very slight. In contrast, in the experiments of Hamed et al. (2020) , where the flume width was only 0.2  m, approximately 1.8H , this channel aspect ratio generates considerable secondary flows, then constraining the upper boundary of the mixing layer to a height below the water surface, which allows the mixing layer to expand vertically above the gap area. In the upstream canopy patch, as typically observed in submerged canopy flows, the mixing layer penetrates downward into the canopy layer, with its penetration depth decreasing as canopy density increases. When defining the penetration depth as the vertical position where Reynolds stress decreases to 10 % of its maximum value at the interface, the penetration depths for ϕ  = 0.08 and ϕ  = 0.15 are respectively 0.55 h  and 0.34 h . Upon reaching the canopy gap area, the high velocity continues to penetrate towards the bed, as indicated by the expansion of the ū /U 0  = 0.2 lines towards the bed. To facilitate a more intuitive comparison of the mixing layer’s penetration into the gap area under different conditions, Fig. 4   extracts the vertical distance δ = h - z |  u  ¯   = 0.2 U 0       between the ū /U 0  = 0.2 lines and the top of the canopy, showing the variation along the length of the gap. It is observed that for ϕ  = 0.08, the ū /U 0  = 0.2 lines expand almost linearly across the entire length of the gap, with only slight deviations from linearity in L /h  = 3 and 4 cases at x   > 2 h . In contrast, for ϕ  = 0.15, regardless of the gap aspect ratio, the initial stages show a highly linear expansion of the ū /U 0  = 0.2 lines, approximately between 0 ≤ x  ≤ 0.62 h , and this range does not vary with L /h . Compared to ϕ  = 0.08, the rate of linear expansion of the mixing layer is faster for ϕ  = 0.15, as can be seen from the slope changes of the dashed lines in Fig. 4 . Beyond x   > 0.62 h , the expansion trend of the ū /U 0  = 0.2 lines significantly deviates from linearity, which is associated with recirculation vortices generated within the gap area, to be discussed later. Notably, the depth of mixing layer penetration into the gap area does not continuously increase longitudinally but reaches its maximum at a certain distance before the leading edge of the downstream canopy patch (indicated by arrows in Fig. 4 ). Beyond this point, due to the flow beginning to sense the resistance of the downstream canopy patch, δ  gradually decreases, which is absent at ϕ  = 0.08. The longitudinal position where δ  reaches its maximum value is 0.1 h  for L /h  = 1, and 0.28 h  for L /h  = 2, 3, and 4. The maximum increase in the penetration depth of the mixing layer into the gap area, Δδmax   (defined in Fig. 4 (b)), increases with increasing L /h , as larger L /h  values imply a longer distance for mixing layer expansion. When L /h  is fixed, increased canopy density also leads to deeper mixing layer penetration, but the effect of canopy densification diminishes with increasing L /h , as shown in Fig. 5  . As depicted in Fig. 2 , the high-velocity fluid penetrating the canopy gap area transports longitudinal momentum into the downstream canopy patch, thereby elevating flow velocities over a considerable longitudinal distance within the downstream patch. Then, under the sustained influence of canopy resistance, the flow velocity gradually diminishes, reverting towards the flow velocity profile seen in the upstream canopy patch. This means that the shear-scale turbulent energy production will again reach equilibrium with the turbulent energy dissipation caused by canopy resistance. This study focuses on the adjustments within the gap area, whereas the recovery process of the flow within the downstream canopy patch is not in the interest of this research. However, it can be anticipated that the distance required for the flow to fully recover to its undisturbed state will vary with canopy density and the gap aspect ratio. Higher canopy densities are expected to require shorter distances due to the greater drag. For a given canopy density, a larger gap aspect ratio implies a longer distance over which the mixing layer penetrates the gap, introducing more high-momentum fluid into the downstream canopy patch and thus leading to a longer recovery distance. Time-averaged flow patterns visualized by streamlines are shown in Fig. 6  . At ϕ  = 0.15, a clockwise recirculation vortex is generated within the canopy gap, similar to what is observed in classical cavity flows with solid boundary (Mignot et al., 2019 ). For cavity flows, at L /h  > 1.5, two recirculation vortices appear within the cavity area, including a primary recirculation vortex occupying most of the area and a secondary recirculation vortex, corresponding to typical features of the wake interference regime. Unlike this, the current LES simulations always exhibit only a single primary recirculation vortex in the gap, consistent with observations in ϕ  = 0.2 submerged canopy gaps by Hamed et al. (2020) . This is due to the longitudinal momentum brought into the gap by the bleeding flow from the upstream canopy patch, as explained in Liu et al. (2022) . Differently, in all cases at ϕ  = 0.08, no recirculation vortex is observed within the canopy gap, with only some streamlines slightly lifting near the bed surface, corresponding to the canopy through-flow regime (Folkard, 2011 ). In Liu et al. (2022) , weak recirculation vortices were generated in two cases at ϕ  = 0.06 with L /h  = 2 and 3. However, the larger canopy density case ϕ  = 0.08 in the current study shows almost no tendency for vortex formation, likely due to different flow structures at the interface caused by different geometries of canopy patches in Liu et al. (2022) . The canopy gap array of Liu et al. (2022)  consists of finite-sized square canopy patches with periodic presence and release of canopy resistance, whereas the current study's single gap area lies within a fully developed zone of submerged canopy flow. For cases exhibiting a recirculation vortex at ϕ  = 0.15, flow separation occurs at x   = 0.54 h  for L /h  = 1. For other cases, the flow separation points are near x   = 0.75 h  and do not vary with L /h . Correspondingly, for L /h  = 1, the recirculation vortex starts at x   = 0.38 h , very close to the 0.35 h  observed by Hamed et al. (2020) . For L /h  > 1, the recirculation s generally start around x   = 0.5 h  and are independent of L /h . Hamed et al. (2020)  also found the upstream end of the recirculation vortex remains unchanged for L /h  ≥ 2, although their position was around x   = h , delayed compared to this study. This might be attributed to the PIV measurement plane of Hamed et al. (2020)  being between two rows of vegetation stems, where larger longitudinal flow velocities were present. While the starting positions of the recirculation vortices do not significantly change with L /h , the morphology of the vortex changes with L /h . When L /h  > 1, due to the significant penetration of the mixing layer into the gap, the recirculation bubbles become larger and flatter along the gap area, but their vertical dimension does not significantly change. Except for the L /h  = 4 case, recirculation vortices in other cases extend into the downstream canopy patch, and the distance they penetrate decreases with increasing L /h . Noticeable vertical flows are only presented near the upstream and downstream ends of the canopy gap at ϕ  = 0.15. The bleeding flow into the gap is entrained by the recirculation vortex, generating an upward flow deflection, with a maximum vertical velocity of around 0.038U 0 , very close to the 0.04U 0  reported by Hamed et al. (2020) . Since the flow reattachment zone (corresponding to the downstream end of the recirculation vortex) is located within the downstream canopy patch, there is no significant upward flow deflection observed in the upper corner area of the downstream canopy patch leading edge. Due to the high momentum carried by the mixing layer penetration, the longitudinal velocity in the upper corner area of the downstream canopy patch is significantly elevated, as shown in Fig. 3 . In the submerged canopy gap area, the mean recirculation and the penetration of the mixing layer significantly affect the bed shear stress. This impact is crucial for the resuspension of bed sediments, migration of plant seeds, and organic matter, potentially influencing the evolution trends of canopy patches (Calvani et al., 2022; Yamasaki et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015; Yang and Nepf, 2018 ). LES simulations facilitate easy acquisition of distributions of bed shear stress, offering a significant advantage over flume experiments. Fig. 7   displays the longitudinal distribution of the bed shear stress component τx  , including areas within both upstream and downstream canopy patches. Τ 0  represents the x -direction bed shear stress component within the fully developed area of the upstream canopy patch, undisturbed by the gap area. Overall, the downstream change in τx   is divided into five stages, with an example from the ϕ  = 0.15 L /h  = 2 case illustrated in Fig. 7 (b). In Stage I, τx   begins decreasing from τ 0 , starting inside the upstream canopy patch and continuing within the gap until flow separation occurs, where τx   = 0. This stage starts earlier in the ϕ  = 0.08 case. Additionally, the height consistency of τx   = 0 positions across L /h  = 2, 3, and 4 cases reconfirms that the flow separation point is independent of L /h . Beyond the flow separation, Stage II begins where the near-bed flow reverses, causing τx   to start increasing towards negative values and reaching its maximum negative value near the downstream end of the gap area. Stage III then starts as τx   begins to decrease again until it reaches 0 a second time, which corresponds to the flow reattachment point. After this, τx   turns positive and gradually increases, reaching a peak after a certain distance, which corresponds to Stage IV. Notably, all of Stage IV occurs within the downstream canopy patch. Moving further downstream, Stage V begins where τx   decreases for the third time and gradually returns to τ 0 , covering a considerable longitudinal distance. Interestingly, even though no obvious recirculation was observed in the ϕ  = 0.08 case in Fig. 6 , near-bed flow separation and reattachment still occur (see Fig. 7 (a)). Throughout the longitudinal variation of bed shear stress, the most notable aspects are the extremes of τx   and their locations. These extremes are the maximum negative and positive shear stress values, which occur near the end of the gap area and within the downstream canopy patch, respectively. The location of the maximum positive shear stress slightly decreases with increasing L /h , averaging about 0.9 h  for the ϕ  = 0.15 case. When the canopy density is fixed, the maximum negative shear stress value shows a non-monotonic change with increasing L /h . The turning point occurs at L /h  = 3 for ϕ  = 0.08 and at L /h  = 2 for ϕ  = 0.15, with corresponding extreme values of −0.5τ 0  and −3.3τ 0 , respectively. The maximum positive shear stress value consistently increases with L /h . For the ϕ  = 0.08 case, only the positive shear stress within the downstream canopy patch exceeds τ 0 , reaching up to about 2.2τ 0  at L /h  = 4. However, for the ϕ  = 0.15 case, both the maximum negative shear stress in the gap area and the maximum positive shear stress within the downstream canopy patch significantly exceed τ 0 , with the highest value reaching 3.7τ 0 . Even in the ϕ  = 0.15, L /h  = 1 case, the shear stress extremes can reach as high as −2.3τ 0  and 1.7τ 0 . High shear stress areas covering the downstream part of the gap area and the initial segment of the downstream canopy patch could be detrimental to the stability of the plants at the forefront of the downstream canopy patch. Combined with the local high longitudinal velocities at the upper corner shown in Fig. 3 , the forefront plants may face the risk of being uprooted.  3.3 Penetration of turbulence into the gap area In the upstream fully developed submerged canopy flow, there are two dominant turbulence scales: the K-H vortices at the interface mixing layer scale and the stem-scale wake vortices. The stem-scale wake vortices can be advected with the bleeding flow from the upstream canopy patches into the gap area, thus influencing the turbulence characteristics within the gap. Since the current calculations use a drag source term to generalize the effect of the canopy, the stem-scale wake vortices are not directly resolved. However, considering that the canopy density in this study is relatively high, the stem-scale turbulence does not dominate over the interface mixing layer-scale vortices (Ghisalberti and Nepf, 2004; Sonnenwald et al., 2019; Stoesser et al., 2009 ). Therefore, the biases introduced by using the drag source term approach are acceptable (expected to slightly underestimate the turbulence within the gap). The results of this study still meaningfully reveal the qualitative turbulence statistical characteristics of the gap area. The contour plots of turbulent kinetic energy k  within vertical planes for all simulated cases are depicted in Fig. 8  , overlaid with time-averaged streamlines. The turbulent intensity at the top region of the canopy layer is significantly enhanced due to shear instability and the development of K-H vortices induced by velocity gradients between the canopy layer and the upper free-flow layer, penetrating into the canopy layer. As previously mentioned, for the ϕ  = 0.08 and 0.15 cases in this study, the penetration depths are 0.55 h  and 0.34 h , respectively. In the canopy gap area, accompanying the penetration of the mixing layer, the high turbulent kinetic energy zone gradually expands from near z  = h  towards the interior of the gap. In the initial section, the penetration of high turbulent kinetic energy towards the gap is approximately linear. However, due to the constraints imposed by recirculation bubbles within the gap, the turbulent kinetic energy penetration does not persist throughout the entire length, especially for L /h  > 1 cases, consistent with the variations trend of the 0.2U 0  lines in Fig. 3 . Overall, the penetration intensity is related to L /h . Larger L /h  values indicate longer development distances of the mixing layer, thus deeper high turbulent kinetic energy penetration, consistent with observations in the canopy gap array by Liu et al. (2022) . In the streamwise direction, high turbulent kinetic energy also penetrates into the downstream canopy patches, especially in the upper corner regions of its leading edge. To better visualize the variation of k  along the gap area, Fig. 9   plots the vertical distribution of k  at three longitudinal positions within the gap: the upstream end at x   = 0, the mid-point at x   = 0.5L , and the downstream end at x   = L . At x   = 0, the vertical distribution of k  is consistent, showing a peak above the canopy interface towards the free-flow layer side due to the vertical displacement of the K-H vortex centers (Ghisalberti and Nepf, 2004 ). Above the canopy gap, from 0 < x  < L , although the canopy drag is released, the position of the maximum turbulent kinetic energy is preserved. In the region z  > h , the turbulent kinetic energy at the three longitudinal positions collapses, consistent with Hamed et al. (2020) . This characteristic appears to be independent of canopy density and the gap aspect ratio. However, below z  < h , the vertical distribution of k  varies along the streamwise direction and is related to both ϕ  and L /h . At x   = 0.5L , k  increases significantly compared to x   = 0 across all cases. In the L /h  = 1 case, regardless of canopy density, a notable enhancement of turbulence is observed at x   = 0.5L  and L , with the latter showing an increase greater than 100 %. However, in the ϕ  = 0.2 L /h  = 1 case of Hamed et al. (2020) , no significant increase in turbulence intensity was detected at x   = 0.5L  and L . This discrepancy may be attributed to the smaller canopy density in the current study. Because lower canopy density leads to a deeper initial high turbulence penetration (i.e., stronger penetration at x   = 0), considering that the depth of penetration is inversely related to canopy density (Huai et al., 2021 ). When the gap aspect ratio exceeds 1, unlike the distinct increase in k  from x   = 0 to 0.5L , the variation trend from x   = 0.5L  to L  is less clear. Only in ϕ  = 0.08 L /h  = 2 and 3 cases, there is a slight increase in k  at the downstream end compared to the midpoint. In ϕ  = 0.15 L /h  = 3 and 4 cases, a reduction in k  is even observed. This is partly because the recirculation vortices within the gap, as shown in Fig. 8 , restrict the continued penetration of high-intensity turbulence. Additionally, it can be attributed to the reduced k  at the interface, considering that increases in turbulence within the gap are fed by strong shear at the interface. Fig. 10   displays the longitudinal distribution of k  along the mouth of the gap. It is evident that for all cases, k  initially increases in the early section of the gap, then begins to decrease at a certain distance from the downstream canopy patch. This decrease continues within the downstream canopy patch, expected to cease only when the shear-scale turbulent energy production and canopy dissipation rebalance. In the initial area of the gap, the high interfacial turbulence, created by the large vertical velocity gradients and strong K-H vortices in the upstream canopy patch, maintains and continuously supplies the gap. In the downstream section of the gap, due to the penetration of the mixing layer causing a significant recovery in velocity, the vertical velocity gradient decreases, subsequently weakening the turbulence production. This phenomenon of turbulence initially increasing and then decreasing longitudinally has also been observed in Hamed et al. (2020)  and Liu et al. (2022) . As previously mentioned, high bed shear stress covers a portion of the gap area near the downstream canopy patch. The connection between high bed shear stress and the sediment incipient motion has long been established(Huai et al., 2021 ). Near-bed turbulent kinetic energy can also be a useful indicator for predicting sediment incipient motions and bedload transport, as discussed by Yang et al. (2016)  and Yang and Nepf, (2019) , respectively. Recent studies have also linked sediment resuspension with local high turbulent kinetic energy in near-bed regions (Tinoco and Coco, 2016; Tseng and Tinoco, 2021 ). Therefore, considering the high shear stress and turbulent kinetic energy on the bed surface of the gap area, there is an enhanced risk of bed erosion due to increased sediment resuspension, with the ϕ  = 0.15 case expected to be more severe than the ϕ  = 0.08 case. Hamed et al. (2020)  classified the flow in submerged canopy gaps into two regimes: the skimming flow regime and the shear layer growth regime. The former is characterized by the interface mixing layer not significantly growing along the streamwise direction or deeply penetrating the gap area, maintaining lower velocities and turbulence within the gap. The latter, however, is characterized by significant penetration of the mixing layer and the resultant substantial recovery in flow velocity and increase in turbulence levels within the gap. In their study, L /h  = 0.5 and 1 were categorized as skimming flow regimes, while L /h  = 2, 3, and 4 were considered as shear layer growth regimes. However, the numerical results of this study indicate that within the range of parameters covered, significant high momentum penetration and turbulence enhancement are observed in the gap area, even at L /h  = 1 (as shown in Fig. 9 (e)), suggesting that all cases fall within the shear layer growth regime. This reflects the impact of changes in canopy density, which is manifested in one aspect by the deeper vertical penetration of the mixing layer established in the upstream canopy patch, and on the other hand, by changes in the intensity of the bleeding flow exiting the upstream canopy patch.  3.4 Vertical momentum and mass exchange across the interface One of the primary characteristics of cavity flow is the intense momentum and mass exchange between the flow inside the cavity and the free flow outside. The sustenance of recirculation vortices within the cavity mainly relies on the momentum exchange at the interface, which continuously entrain high-momentum into the cavity(Juez et al., 2018; Ouro et al., 2020 ). The mass exchange at the interface, meanwhile, relates to the removal of materials such as pollutants and sediments from the cavity. The intensity of the interfacial momentum and mass exchange highly depends on the geometry of the cavity, such as the aspect ratio, as the cavity flow pattern changes accordingly (Mignot et al., 2017; Ouro et al., 2020 ). For the canopy gap formed by the discontinuities in the submerged canopy patches in this study, given the typical cavity flow characteristics displayed, such as mean recirculation and momentum penetration, an interfacial momentum and mass exchange is also expected to occur at the mouth of the canopy gap. The dependence of the vertical momentum and mass exchange across the interface between the canopy gap and the free flow area on canopy density and the gap aspect ratio will be analyzed next. The vertical flux of longitudinal momentum, uw   ¯     , can be decomposed into the mean transport flux, u ¯    w ¯     , and the turbulent transport flux, u ′  w ′    ¯      (Cintolesi et al., 2021 ). Their distribution along the gap mouth is depicted in Fig. 11  , where solid and dashed lines respectively represent u  ¯    w  ¯      and u ′  w ′    ¯     . It is observed that along the entire interface length, the momentum transport flux is consistently negative. This indicates that longitudinal momentum is always entrained downward from the upper free-flow layer into the gap area to sustain the main recirculation vortex within the gap. Turbulent exchange consistently dominates the vertical momentum exchange. Streamwisely, the mean transport gradually strengthens, while turbulent transport gradually weakens, a trend more pronounced for the ϕ  = 0.15 case. This can be explained as follows. On one hand, the downward flow driven by the downstream part of the recirculation vortex within the gap area increasingly manifests itself. On the other hand, as the mixing layer penetration, the flow velocity within the gap is significantly increased, reducing the vertical velocity gradient at the interface, thereby weakening turbulent transport. It is anticipated that upon entering the downstream canopy patch, the vertical turbulent exchange at the canopy top interface will be increased again, as the reintroduced canopy resistance will increase the vertical velocity gradient. Although significant upward vertical velocities are present at the beginning of the gap area in the ϕ  = 0.15 case (as shown in Fig. 6 ), this does not significantly contribute to the flush out of momentum at the interface. To further explore the dependence of momentum exchange intensity across the interface on canopy density and the gap aspect ratio, the mean momentum exchange coefficient β  ¯     , turbulent momentum exchange coefficient β' , and total momentum exchange coefficient β  were calculated for all cases and depicted in Fig. 12  . The momentum exchange coefficient can be calculated as β = 1 U 0 2  L B   ∫ 0 L  ∫ 0 B  uw   ¯    d y d x   , β ¯   = 1  U  0  2   L B   ∫  0  L   ∫  0  B   u ¯    w ¯   d y d x   , and β ′  = 1 U 0 2  L B   ∫ 0 L  ∫ 0 B  u ′  w ′    ¯    d y d x    (Tanaka and Ohmoto, 2013 ). Consistent with the findings presented in Fig. 11 , the momentum exchange coefficients are always negative, indicating that the net momentum flux is characterized by the entrainment of high momentum into the gap area across the entire interface. The turbulent exchange coefficient is significantly larger than the mean exchange coefficient. As ϕ  increases from 0.08 to 0.15, the turbulent exchange intensity increases to varying degrees, while the change in mean exchange intensity is quite subtle. When ϕ  is fixed and L /h  increases, both mean and turbulent exchanges show a slight increase and decrease, respectively. Due to the enhanced mean exchange compensating for the weakened turbulent exchange, the total momentum exchange coefficient remains approximately independent of L /h  but slightly increases with canopy density. For ϕ  = 0.08 and 0.15, the total momentum exchange coefficients β  are around 0.02 and 0.024, respectively. Notably, both values are lower than the exchange coefficients (0.035 and 0.03) for the canopy gap arrays in Liu et al., (2022) . Additionally, in their study, the turbulent exchange coefficient shows a negative correlation with canopy density, whereas, in the current study, denser canopy leads to stronger turbulent exchange. These differences imply that the interfacial exchange is also highly dependent on the geometry of the canopy forming the gap area. At the interface, shear-scale coherent structures not only entrain high longitudinal momentum from the free flow layer into the gap area but also drive vertical mass exchange. Following the cavity flow(de Oliveira et al., 2024; Ouro et al., 2020 ), the dimensionless vertical mass exchange coefficient for the gap area is defined as the ratio of the interfacial exchange velocity E  to the bulk velocity U 0 , K =E /U 0 . The exchange velocity E  is calculated as (It is assumed that the flux entering the gap area equals the flux reintegrating with the free flow layer, leading to the integral being divided by 2 (Juez et al., 2018; Mignot et al., 2016 ))(4) E = 1 2 L B   ∫ 0 L  ∫ 0 B  w  ¯       d y d x      Fig. 13   reports the dependence of the dimensionless vertical mass exchange coefficient K  on canopy density ϕ  and the gap aspect ratio L /h . When ϕ  is fixed, K  increases with increasing L /h , and this trend remains consistent regardless of ϕ  value. However, the impact of ϕ  on K  is not uniform across fixed L /h  values. Specifically, at L /h  = 1 and 2, higher canopy density shows weaker vertical mass exchange. At L /h  = 3 and 4, the situation reverses. It suggests that the strength of vertical mass exchange exhibits a coupled relationship with both canopy density and the gap aspect ratio.   4 Conclusion The current study employs high-resolution Large Eddy Simulation (LES) to investigate the time-averaged and turbulent patterns within the gap areas of submerged canopies, as well as the vertical momentum and mass exchanges across the interface between the gap area and the upper free-flow layer. The gap area is situated within a fully developed region of submerged canopy flow. The simulations maintain a constant channel Reynolds number ReH  =44000 and canopy height h , considering four different gap lengths, corresponding to aspect ratios L /h  ranging from 1 to 4. For each L /h  value, two canopy densities, ϕ  = 0.08 and 0.15, were considered to reveal the effects of changes in canopy density. At ϕ  = 0.08, the bleeding flow exiting the upstream canopy patch directly enters the downstream canopy patch without presenting recirculation flow within the gap area, corresponding to the canopy through-flow regime described by Folkard (2011) . Recirculation vortices within the gap only appear at ϕ  = 0.15. Except for the L /h  = 4 case, the recirculation flow significantly penetrates the downstream canopy patch, and the penetration distance decreases with increasing L /h . However, the starting position of the recirculation vortices appears to become independent of L /h  at L /h  ≥ 2, consistently located near x   = 0.5 h . Influenced by wall flow separation and reattachment associated with the recirculation vortices, the bed shear stress changes sign twice longitudinally, achieving negative and positive maximum values near the end of the gap area and within the downstream canopy patch, respectively. This is disadvantageous for the stability of plants at the forefront of the downstream canopy patch. Different from cavity flows, interfacial turbulence starts to develop within the upstream canopy patches. Within the parameter range covered in this study, the penetration of the mixing layer vertically into the gap area always occurs, consistently falling within the shear layer growth regime defined by Hamed et al. (2020) . Even in the L /h  = 1 case, a notable increase in turbulence is observed within the gap area, contrasting with the skimming flow regime described by Hamed et al. (2020) , which highlights the impact of canopy density changes. When the gap area is longer (L /h  ≥ 2), the growth of the mixing layer towards the gap area initially maintains an approximately linear trend before the expansion rate significantly slows due to constraints imposed by the main recirculation vortex. The final penetration depth is inversely related to L /h . Affected by high momentum entrainment, the longitudinal velocity and turbulence intensity in the upper corner regions of the downstream canopy patch's leading edge are enhanced, but similar to Hamed et al. (2020) , no significant upward flow deflection is observed. Turbulent transport consistently dominates the vertical momentum exchange across the interface between the submerged canopy gap and the upper free flow layer, and its intensity decreases downstream along the gap area. Although turbulent and mean exchanges show different trends with L /h , the total momentum exchange remains approximately independent of L /h , with larger canopy densities resulting in stronger momentum transport. Overall, mass exchange increases with L /h  and is more efficient in ϕ  = 0.15 L /h  = 3 and 4 cases. The current study focuses on dense canopy (ah  ≫ 1), and the conclusions drawn are not applicable to sparse canopy (ah  ≪ 1). It is important to note that, since the current simulations do not explicitly resolve stem-scale flows and use periodic boundaries laterally, this inevitably homogenizes the flow field laterally, at least at the stem scale. Therefore, the results presented in this study tend towards laterally-averaged fields and not effectively capture lateral variations in the flow field. The precise simulation of transient turbulent structures is an inherent advantage of LES, whereas this study has focused on the turbulence statistical properties to analyze flow adjustments within submerged canopy gaps. More detailed analyses of transient fields, including vortex scale evolution, will be conducted in future research. Additionally, as Folkard (2011)  has pointed out, the channel Reynolds number also influences the classification of flow regimes in the gap area. Besides canopy density, the dynamics of submerged canopy flows also depend significantly on submergence, stem rigidity, and the complex geometry of real vegetation. Shallow submergence can limit the scale and intensity of mixing layer vortices, while flexible canopy and complex geometries are associated with “monami” phenomena and drag instability. These factors can potentially affect the intensity of interface exchange and the recirculation patterns within the gap area, and should also be the focus of future research.
1 Introduction The increasing frequency of extreme weather and climate events is an undeniable reality (Guo et al., 2024 ). Current global climate fluctuations are reshaping the frequency, intensity, duration, and spatial extent of these extremes, thereby amplifying the complexity and variability of their spatiotemporal characteristics (Zhou et al., 2023 ). Utilizing extreme precipitation as a case in point, recent years have borne witness to the onset of floods and droughts, stemming from such occurrences, which have posed significant hazards and impediments to both human existence and socioeconomic advancement (Sun et al., 2021; Gründemann et al., 2023 ). In recent years, China frequently experiences extreme precipitation, leading to urban flooding and a series of related disasters, causing significant economic losses (Tang et al., 2021; Deng et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the examination of the spatial and temporal dynamics and evolutionary trends of extreme precipitation events in China, along with their sensitivity to climate change, is increasingly garnering attention (Yuan et al., 2017 ). Furthermore, investigating the disparities in the spatial and temporal distribution of extreme precipitation in China, and elucidating the factors underlying these variations, constitutes pivotal groundwork for addressing the imminent challenges posed by climate change (Wu et al., 2021 ). Numerous studies have investigated extreme precipitation events in China (Yuan et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2022 ). Overall, in recent years, extreme precipitation events have been occurring more frequently across many river basins in China (Li et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021 ). The conclusion drawn from the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (IPCC AR5) was that “since around 1950, regions experiencing an increase in the frequency of heavy precipitation events may have outnumbered those experiencing a decrease” (Alexander, 2016 ). Sun et al. (2021)  estimated that for every 1 K increase in global mean surface temperature (GMST), the observed increase range of maximum 1-day precipitation (i.e., Rx1day) worldwide is 5.1 % to 8.2 % K−1 , and the increase range of maximum 5-day precipitation (i.e., Rx5day) is 5.0 % to 8.0 % K−1 , both of which are close to the expected strength (7.0 % K−1 ) of the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship (O’Gorman, 2015; Zhang and Zhao, 2019 ). In China, spatial disparities in extreme precipitation are influenced by multiple factors such as topography, moisture sources, and atmospheric circulation (Xu et al., 2022a ). Human activities have exacerbated climate warming, thereby increasing the uncertainty surrounding these disparities (Madakumbura et al., 2021 ). Therefore, analyzing the impact of natural and human factors on extreme precipitation in China has gradually become a key focus in the field of extreme climate research (Li et al., 2021 ). However, despite numerous studies that have analyzed the variations of extreme precipitation in China due to climate warming, there is still a need to strengthen comparative explorations across multiple river basin scales (Zhu et al., 2021 ). This is particularly pertinent for extensive comparisons between regions with abundant and limited precipitation (Han et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, due to the influence of multiple factors, extreme precipitation in China exhibits even greater complexity in its spatial distribution (Xu et al., 2022a ). While some research has investigated the impacts of factors such as atmospheric circulation on extreme precipitation in various river basins in China, further research is required to delve into the interactions among multiple factors affecting extreme precipitation (Shi et al., 2017 ). Strengthening efforts in these areas not only contributes to improving understanding of the evolving trends of extreme precipitation under climate change but also provides theoretical support for short-term prediction and long-term estimation of extreme precipitation (Wasko et al., 2021 ). Therefore, building upon preceding research endeavors, the aim of this study is twofold: 1) to explore the sensitivity of extreme precipitation to climate warming across nine distinct river basins in China, and 2) to quantify the extent to which the interaction of multiple natural and societal factors accounts for spatially stratified heterogeneity in extreme precipitation across multiple river basins in China. Such insights are imperative for the formulation of climate change adaptation strategies and facilitate comprehensive assessments of the probability of extreme event occurrences (Wu et al., 2021 ). Moreover, they contribute to the provision of scientific counsel for mitigating disaster challenges.  2 Methodology and data collection 2.1 Study area In recent years, there has been an increase in the occurrence of extreme climate events in China, particularly with multiple instances of extreme precipitation events at the river basin scale (Wu et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, variations exist among different river basins regarding the frequency, intensity, and spatial extent of these extreme precipitation events (Tang et al., 2021 ). For the purpose of comparative analysis, this study selected nine major river basins in China: Song-Liao River Basin, Haihe River Basin, Yellow River Basin, Huaihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, Southeast River Basin, Pearl River Basin, Southwest River Basin, and Continental River Basin, as depicted in Fig. 1  . The delineation of these river basins is based on previous research (Liu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020 ).  2.2 Precipitation, temperature, and extreme indices The ERA5 dataset, sourced from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), is utilized in this study. It represents the fifth generation of reanalysis data for past global climate and weather. The ERA5 dataset combines model data with observational results from around the world using physical laws to ensure completeness and consistency on a global scale (Tarek et al., 2020; Lavers et al., 2022 ). Currently, this dataset is widely applied across various fields (Cantoni et al., 2022; Rolle et al., 2022 ). In this study, hourly temperature and precipitation data from 1961 to 2022 are used, with a spatial resolution of 0.25°× 0.25°. Before calculating extreme precipitation indices, hourly-scale data is converted into daily-scale data. In this study, four indices, namely R95p, Rx5day, R10mm, and SDII, are selected to characterize the changes in extreme precipitation (Table S1 ). These indices, developed by the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI), are widely used to assess the spatiotemporal variations of extreme events (Donat et al., 2023; Kurniadi et al., 2023 ). The use of these indices can comprehensively reflect changes in extreme precipitation from multiple perspectives, such as intensity and frequency.  2.3 Natural and societal factors To investigate and quantify the explanatory power of multiple factors for the spatial stratified heterogeneity in extreme precipitation, various natural and societal factors are selected in this study. Natural factors such as vegetation, climate, elevation, and soil, as well as societal factors including population and GDP. The reasons for choosing these factors are based on their importance in influencing the spatial distribution of precipitation (Huang et al., 2021 ). These factors encompass various aspects of natural environment and human activities, aiding in a comprehensive understanding of the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of precipitation. Elevation affects temperature and precipitation distribution, while different climate zones exhibit varying precipitation patterns and frequencies (Huang et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023 ). Additionally, vegetation types vary in their sensitivity to precipitation (Bai et al., 2023 ). Soil types and their moisture content respond differently to precipitation, impacting runoff and consequently affecting the spatial distribution of precipitation (Taylor et al., 2013 ). Moreover, population and GDP reflect the intensity of human activities, influencing urbanization processes, land use, and water resource management, thereby indirectly affecting precipitation distribution (Pham et al., 2024 ). The spatial resolution of vegetation distribution and soil type data is 1°×1°. The climate zone data (1976–2000) are in shapefile format and can be detailed using ArcGIS software. The names and meanings of the categories are available on the data download page. Elevation data have a spatial resolution of 60 arc-seconds. Population and GDP data span from 1980 to 2100 (in 10-year intervals) with a spatial resolution of 0.5°×0.5°. This study only uses data up to 2020. Since the geo-detector requires categorical data, further processing of the raw data is necessary. First, bilinear interpolation is applied to all data, except the climate zone data, to standardize them to 0.25°×0.25°. As vegetation, soil, and climate zone data are already categorical and lack temporal divisions, it is only necessary to identify the category of each 0.25° grid point within the study area. Elevation data (in meters) also lack temporal divisions and are classified into seven categories (0–500, 500–1000, 1000–2000, 2000–3000, 3000–4000, 4000–5000, >5000) based on previous study (Ding et al., 2014 ). For population data (in millions), the mean values across all years are taken, and the data are categorized into five classes (0–5, 5–10, 10–15, 15–20, >20). GDP data (in PPP, Billion US$2005/yr) are processed similarly to population data and categorized into five classes (0–100, 100–200, 200–300, 300–400, >400). Finally, the categories for elevation, population, and GDP for each 0.25° grid point within the study area are identified.  2.4 The geo-detector method The geo-detector is a statistical method used to detect spatial stratified heterogeneity and reveal the underlying driving forces (Wang et al., 2016 ). Its core idea is based on the assumption that if an independent variable has a significant impact on a dependent variable, then the spatial distributions of the independent and dependent variables should be similar (Wang and Hu, 2012 ). The geo-detector determines whether there is interaction between two factors, as well as the strength, direction, linearity, or non-linearity of the interaction, by separately calculating and comparing the q  values of each single factor and the q  value after the combination of the two factors (Ji et al., 2022 ). It has effectively identified and quantified the spatial heterogeneity and multi-factor driving mechanisms of extreme precipitation, which significantly differs from traditional statistical methods such as regression analysis. Its factor detection and interaction detection functions reveal the interactions between driving factors, offering a unique advantage in analyzing complex geographical phenomena (Guo et al., 2022 ).(1) q = 1 - ∑ h= 1  L  N h  σ h  2   N σ  2    = 1 - SSW SST       In the equation, q  is the explanatory power, h  represents the classification of factor F ; Nh   and N  denote the number of units in class h  and in the entire set, respectively; σh  2  and σ 2  are the variances of the Y  values within class h  and for the entire set, respectively. SSW  and SST  are the Within Sum of Squares and the Total Sum of Squares, respectively. The range of q  is [0, 1]. In this study, the geo-detector is used to assess the extent to which natural and societal factors explain the spatial stratified heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. The description and types of interactions are shown in Table 1  .  2.5 Mann-Kendall temporal trends The Mann-Kendall trend analysis is a statistical technique often utilized to evaluate the presence of a significant persistent change over time within a long-term dataset (Mallick et al., 2021 ).
