The null hypothesis (H 0 ) suggests the absence of any consistent trend in the dataset over the long term, while the alternative hypothesis (H 1 ) indicates the presence of a trend that is either steadily increasing or decreasing. Rejecting the null hypothesis, signifying statistical significance at the predetermined α  confidence level, indicates a clear upward or downward trend in the dataset. This method has become popular in examining variations in temperature, precipitation, and runoff due to its advantages (Shawul and Chakma, 2020; Khand and Senay, 2021 ). In particular, the Mann-Kendall approach does not necessitate adherence to a specific data distribution and is less influenced by anomalies, rendering it a reliable tool for identifying trends in climatic variables across extended durations. Due to its widespread application, this method is not further elaborated in this study. Detailed information can be referred to in previous research (Meshram et al., 2020; Jain et al., 2022 ).  2.6 Sensitivity of extreme precipitation to temperature The sensitivity of extreme precipitation to temperature is represented by the ratio of extreme precipitation to the change in mean temperature (Liang et al., 2023 ). Based on the overall study period (i.e., 1961–2022), the first 31 years (i.e., 1961–1991) are selected as the reference period. Initially, the mean of extreme precipitation during the reference period is calculated. Subsequently, the mean of extreme precipitation for the subsequent 31 years (i.e., 1992–2022) is computed, and the difference in extreme precipitation between the two consecutive 31-year periods is obtained. Similarly, the mean temperature during the reference period is calculated, and the difference in mean temperature between the two time periods is determined. Finally, the ratio (unit: %/K) of the difference in extreme precipitation (ΔP , unit: %) to the difference in mean temperature (ΔT , unit: K) is calculated. Overall, this study involves a significant amount of data and methodologies. To facilitate understanding of the research content and overall logic, a flowchart is necessary (Fig. 2  ).   3 Results 3.1 Variations of extreme precipitation This study firstly examines the variations in the multi-year mean of extreme precipitation (Fig. 3  ). Overall, extreme precipitation is found to occur more frequently in the southeastern part of China, exhibiting a spatial pattern of more in the southeast and less in the northwest. At the basin scale, extreme precipitation is more prevalent in the Southeastern River Basin, the Pearl River Basin, the Yangtze River Basin, and the Huaihe River Basin, while occurring least frequently in the Continental River Basin. The spatial distribution of extreme precipitation indicated by the four indices aligns with the spatial distribution of multi-year average precipitation (Fig. S1 ). This is because the eastern and southeastern coastal regions of China often receive ample moisture input, resulting in relatively abundant precipitation and a higher likelihood of extreme precipitation events (Nie and Sun, 2022 ). For R95p, the mean value for all nine river basins is 138.3 mm. Among them, the maximum occurs in the southeastern basin (445.0 mm), followed by the Pearl River basin (427.6 mm). Meanwhile, the Yangtze River Basin (266.3 mm) and the Huaihe River basin (235.7 mm) are relatively similar. Additionally, there are slight differences among the Song-Liao River Basin, the Haihe River Basin, the Yellow River Basin, and the Southwestern River Basin. The Continental River Basin has the smallest value, only 28.3 mm. The other three extreme precipitation indices (i.e., Rx5day, R10mm, and SDII) show similar results, with high values appearing in the Southeast River Basin, Pearl River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Huaihe River Basin, while low values appear in the Continental River Basin. In summary, the four different attribute indices elucidate the spatial distribution of extreme precipitation in the nine river basins of China over the past six decades. Moreover, the research findings clearly indicate that there are differences in extreme precipitation conditions among different basins, particularly obvious disparities between the basins in the southeastern and the northwestern regions. The findings in this section are largely consistent with previous research (Xu et al., 2022b ).  3.2 Trend in extreme precipitation Fig. 4   displays the spatial distribution of the long-term trends in four extreme precipitation indices. Fig. 5   presents the percentage of grid points in each of the nine river basins exhibiting different trend patterns in extreme precipitation. Overall, the majority of river basins show a positive or significantly positive trend in extreme precipitation, while fewer river basins exhibit a negative or significantly negative trend. For R95p (Figs. 4 A and 5 A), more than half of the grid points in the Song-Liao River Basin, Yellow River Basin, Huaihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, Southeast River Basin, and Pearl River Basin exhibit a positive trend, with percentages of 62.6 %, 64.6 %, 76.7 %, 69.6 %, 58.2 %, and 65.3 %, respectively. Meanwhile, nearly half of the grid points in the Haihe River Basin and Southwest River Basin show a negative trend, with percentages of 48.9 % and 45.8 %, respectively. Additionally, the Southeast River Basin and Continental River Basin have 39.1 % and 22.4 % of grid points, respectively, showing a significant positive trend, while the percentage range for other river basins showing a significant positive trend is only from 1.9 % to 17.3 %. It is worth noting that the percentage of grid points exhibiting a significant negative trend in all river basins is relatively small, with the maximum value being only 3.8 % (Haihe River Basin). Due to the lower precipitation in the Continental River Basin, there are areas where the precipitation does not exceed the precipitation threshold (i.e., the 95th percentile) when calculating R95p, resulting in a larger proportion of grid points (47.1 %) showing no trend. For Rx5day (Figs. 4 B and 5 B), over half of the grid points in the Song-Liao River Basin (61.2 %), Yellow River Basin (59.2 %), Huaihe River Basin (72.4 %), Yangtze River Basin (62.2 %), Southeast River Basin (70.2 %), Pearl River Basin (53.4 %), and Continental River Basin (65.6 %) exhibit a positive trend. Similarly, the Haihe River Basin (61.8 %) and Southwest River Basin (47.9 %) also have a larger proportion of grid points showing a negative trend. Additionally, in Southeast River Basin (11.0 %) and Continental River Basin (20.2 %), several grid points also exhibit a significant positive trend. Moreover, grid points demonstrating significant negative or no trend represent only a small proportion in all nine river basins. For R10mm (Figs. 4 C and 5 C), there is evidently a considerable proportion of grid points showing no trend. Similar to R95p, this is because the number of days with precipitation exceeding 10 mm has been zero over the years, thus no trend can be detected. Only the Southeast River Basin (73.9 %) and Pearl River Basin (50.1 %) have more than half of the grid points exhibiting a positive trend. While in the Southwest River Basin (25.7 %) and the western part of the Pearl River Basin (22.6 %), there is a larger proportion of grid points showing a negative trend. Grid points demonstrating a significant positive trend are mainly distributed in the Continental River Basin (14.4 %) and the Song-Liao River Basin (18.2 %), but the proportion is relatively small. Grid points indicating a significant negative trend are sporadically distributed in the Southwest River Basin (7.6 %), with a small proportion as well. For SDII (Figs. 4 D and 5 D), in almost all basins, more than 50 % of grid points exhibit a positive trend. Grid points indicating a negative trend are predominantly found in the Southwest River Basin (47.7 %) and the Continental River Basin (23.2 %). Grid points showing a significant positive trend are mainly distributed in the Southeast River Basin (47.8 %) and the northern part of the Continental River Basin (21.0 %), while the proportion of grid points demonstrating a significant negative trend or no trend is very small and can be disregarded. In summary, the four indices consistently indicate a positive trend (including significant positive trend) in extreme precipitation in most regions. Particularly in the Southeast River Basin, Pearl River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Huaihe River Basin, the proportion of positive trends exceeds 50 %. Negative trend (including significant negative trend) is mainly concentrated in the Southwest River Basin, accounting for around 40 %. Previous studies have investigated the historical trends of extreme precipitation in China. The findings in this section, especially the spatial distribution of extreme indices showing positive or negative trends, are also similar to previous conclusions, even though these studies used a limited number of meteorological stations or data with lower spatial resolution (Ren et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021 ). The mean precipitation also exhibits a spatial distribution pattern similar to that of extreme precipitation (Fig. S2 ). However, it is noteworthy that the trend of significant positive (i.e., indicated by the cyan regions) in mean precipitation is particularly evident in the Continental River Basin. This conclusion further corroborates the trend of wetting in the northwest China (Wang et al., 2020 ).  3.3 Asymmetrical sensitivity across dry and wet river basins In this study, there are differences in the extreme precipitation attributes reflected by the four indices. Relative to the other three indices, Rx5day can indicate prolonged periods of extreme moisture conditions and may be related to widespread regional flooding and landslides (Sun et al., 2021 ). Therefore, this extreme index is employed in this study to reflect the sensitivity of extreme precipitation to temperature changes. To ascertain the response level of precipitation to climate warming, two consecutive 31-year periods (i.e., 1961–1991 and 1992–2022) of extreme precipitation and mean precipitation differences (ΔP , unit: %) are calculated in this study. Subsequently, by dividing this difference by the variation in mean temperature change (ΔT , unit: K), the sensitivity of extreme precipitation and mean precipitation to climate warming is estimated. Fig. 6   depicts similar spatial distribution patterns between extreme precipitation and mean precipitation. However, overall, extreme precipitation exhibits greater sensitivity compared to mean precipitation. The sensitivity of extreme precipitation (Fig. 6 A) shows a strong increase (>30 %/K) in the western and northern regions of the Continental River Basin, as well as in the western regions of the Southwest River Basin. Additionally, there are increases (5 ∼ 10 %/K) in the Southeast River Basin, eastern regions of the Pearl River Basin, eastern regions of the Yangtze River Basin, northern regions of the Yellow River Basin, northern regions of the Song-Liao River Basin, the Haihe River Basin, and the Huaihe River Basin. Conversely, strong decreases in extreme precipitation sensitivity are mainly concentrated in small areas in the central part of the Continental River Basin. Moreover, there are also decreases (around 5 %/K) in the western regions of the Pearl River Basin, southern regions of the Southwest River Basin, central regions of the Yangtze River Basin, central regions of the Yellow River Basin, and southern regions of the Song-Liao River Basin. The sensitivity of mean precipitation to temperature is similar to that of extreme precipitation, which will not be further elaborated (Fig. 6 B). These results indicate that the larger sensitivity of extreme and mean precipitation to temperature may increase the variability of regional precipitation. As the process of climate change intensifies, the evolution of sensitivity in the near and potentially longer future is expected to have an impact on the sustainable development of regional ecosystems (Liang et al., 2023 ). Further exploration into the frequency distribution of different sensitivities (all river basins average) reveals that the sensitivity of extreme precipitation to temperature (9.6 %/K) is 1.1 times that of mean precipitation (8.8 %/K), with the latter being closer to the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship (∼7%/K). Fig. 6 C and D depict those regions experiencing increases (i.e., >0) and decreases (i.e., <0) in sensitivity to extreme precipitation account for 72 % and 28 %, respectively, while for mean precipitation, these proportions are 80 % and 20 %, respectively. The increase and decrease proportions of extreme and mean precipitation sensitivity for individual river basins are not analyzed in detail here and can be found in Figs. S3–S4 . The changes in sensitivity between relatively dry and relatively wet river basins are also investigated in this study. Based on the annual mean precipitation and extreme precipitation (Fig. S1  and Fig. 3 ), the Continental River Basin is categorized as relatively dry region, while the other river basins are considered relatively wet region (Student’s t -test: p  < 0.05). For dry regions, the sensitivity of extreme precipitation is 19.7 %/K, while for mean precipitation is 18.2 %/K. For wet regions, the sensitivities (multiple river basins average) of extreme and mean precipitation are 3.8 %/K and 3.3 %/K, respectively. This result indicates that the sensitivities of precipitation in relatively dry region are higher than those in wet region. The sensitivity of extreme precipitation in relatively dry region is approximately five times that of wet region. For mean precipitation, this value is also about five-fold. In summary, these conclusions are consistent with previous research. For example, Liang et al. (2023)  analyzed the sensitivity of extreme and mean precipitation to temperature using the global climate models. Their findings indicated that the sensitivity of extreme precipitation is approximately three times that of mean precipitation. Generally, with the rise in temperature, there is an observed increase in extreme precipitation events (Tian et al., 2023 ). However, this correlation is not a simple linear relationship but is influenced by multiple factors, including topography, atmospheric circulation, and other complex elements (Zeder and Fischer, 2020 ). Therefore, further exploration of the specific mechanisms underlying the relationship between temperature and extreme precipitation in different regions and seasons is essential.  3.4 Spatial stratified heterogeneity of extreme precipitation The preceding results of this study indicate obvious spatial heterogeneity in precipitation concerning its spatial distribution, trend variations, and sensitivity to temperature. Multiple factors such as surface vegetation, climatic zones, and elevation explain this spatial heterogeneity through their singular or interactive effects. The q  values of the geo-detector have clear physical meanings, indicating that each independent variable explains 100 × q % of the spatial heterogeneity of the dependent variable. When q  is 1, it means that the independent variable X  completely explains the spatial heterogeneity of the dependent variable Y . Conversely, when q  is 0, it indicates that there is no relationship between X  and Y . Fig. 7   presents the calculation results of the q  values for all explanatory variable factors. The categorical variable X  consists of six natural and societal factors. The dependent variable Y  represents the multi-year average of extreme precipitation (1961–2022). The results indicate that the explanatory power of natural factors is generally higher than that of societal factors. For the four extreme precipitation indices, factor F 1  (i.e., vegetation) has the highest q  value. The q  values for the four extreme indices are 0.70, 0.63, 0.72, and 0.61, respectively, indicating that vegetation is the primary factor determining the spatial pattern of extreme precipitation among all six variables. Additionally, factors F 2  and F 3  also have relatively high values. For the four extreme indices, the q  values for factors F 2  (F 3 ) are 0.65 (0.55), 0.57 (0.54), 0.68 (0.56), and 0.58 (0.62), respectively, highlighting the significant role of climate type and elevation in explaining the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. Factor F 4  exhibits weaker explanatory power compared to the first three factors, and the explanatory power of the two societal factors (i.e., F 5  and F 6 ) is also relatively small. It needs to be noted that the physical meaning of interaction (i.e., q (F 1  ∩ F 2 )) is to assess whether the combined effect of two factors increases or decreases the explanatory power of spatial heterogeneity of the dependent variable. The interactions are categorized into five types. This is based on initially calculating the q -value of each factor individually (i.e., q (F 1 ) and q (F 2 )) when explaining the spatial heterogeneity of Y . Further calculation involves determining the q -value of the interaction between the two factors, and comparing q (F 1 ), q (F 2 ), and q (F 1  ∩ F 2 ). The details about interaction can be found in Table 1 . Fig. 8   displays the explanatory power of the interaction effects between factors on the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. The colors represent the q  values of interactions between pairs of factors, while triangles denote different types of interactions. The results indicate that most q  values between pairs of factors exceed the maximum q -value of individual factors. This phenomenon is particularly evident among pairs of natural factors. The findings reveal a bivariate enhancement pattern of interaction between factors, meaning that the combined action of two factors increases the explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. For R95p, the interaction between factors F 1  and F 3  has the highest explanatory power, with a q  value of 0.81, exceeding the individual q  values of the two factors. This indicates that the interaction between vegetation and elevation has a greater explanatory power for the spatial variability of extreme precipitation than individual factors alone (i.e., q (F 1 ) = 0.70 and q (F 3 ) = 0.55). This conclusion applies equally to the other three extreme precipitation indices, with their interaction q  values being 0.74 (Rx5day, q (F 1 ) = 0.63 and q (F 3 ) = 0.54), 0.82 (R10mm, q (F 1 ) = 0.72 and q (F 3 ) = 0.56), and 0.76 (SDII, q (F 1 ) = 0.62 and q (F 3 ) = 0.61), respectively. Additionally, the interaction between natural and societal factors also exhibits relatively stronger explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. In contrast, the interaction among societal factors shows relatively less explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation, with q  values of 0.26 (R95p), 0.23 (Rx5day), 0.27 (R10mm), and 0.32 (SDII), respectively. In general, the geo-detector elucidates the degree to which various natural and societal factors, individually and interactively, explain the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. Regarding individual factors, vegetation exhibits the greatest explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation, with q  values ranging from 0.61 to 0.72 (for four indices). Furthermore, the explanatory power of natural factors surpasses that of societal factors. Additionally, compared to individual factors, interactions between factors enhance the explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. Among them, the interaction between vegetation and elevation demonstrates the highest explanatory power (q  values: 0.74–0.82 for four indices), with interaction among natural factors exhibiting higher explanatory power than that among societal factors.   4 Discussion 4.1 The reliability of extreme precipitation characterization The first part of this study explores the trends of extreme precipitation at the river basin scale. Its findings, especially the spatial distribution of trends in extreme precipitation increase or decrease, are largely consistent with previous studies (Dong et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021 ). However, it is worth noting that this study uses ERA5 reanalysis data to calculate extreme precipitation indices and further analyze their trend changes. Previous research has evaluated the ability of multiple datasets, including ERA5, to characterize extreme precipitation in China using statistical tools, distribution functions, and extreme indices (Jiang et al., 2023 ). The assessment results also indicate that various datasets exhibit spatial variability and statistical errors to varying degrees when characterizing extreme precipitation. To be frank, due to serious shortages in meteorological stations in some regions and issues such as missing data in existing stations, the spatial uniformity of observed data, including precipitation, is being challenged (Sun et al., 2021 ). This study uses ERA5 data to assess changes in extreme precipitation in China. It is important to note that ERA5 data combines observations and model data, which inevitably introduces some biases, especially in capturing and simulating extreme events (Jiang et al., 2021 ). Acknowledging these limitations, it is recognized that this study faces some uncertainty in evaluating changes in extreme precipitation in China. Overall, reanalysis data has become an indispensable tool to address the issues with station data to some extent (Hu and Franzke, 2020 ). Future research should further explore how to fully enhance the quality of reanalysis data and focus on leveraging the advantages of coupling multiple reanalysis data sources to reduce the biases associated with individual data products (Ur Rahman et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2021 ).  4.2 The uncertainty of the spatial stratified heterogeneity Beyond the reliability of observational data, the selection of natural and societal factors, as well as methodological limitations, collectively contribute to the uncertainties in the results of this study on the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. There are six factors are selected in this study to explore their explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation, with a particular focus on analyzing the impact of interaction among factors. However, it must be acknowledged that the spatial heterogeneity of precipitation is influenced by a variety of factors such as topography, geographical location, and large-scale climate teleconnections, and its complexity has not been fully understood (Zhang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024 ). Additionally, various social factors such as the urban heat island effect resulting from human activities also influence the spatial heterogeneity of precipitation (Steensen et al., 2022 ). However, due to constraints in data availability, the current research cannot encompass all influencing factors, which may lead to uncertainties in the final conclusions. Nevertheless, the quantitative analysis of spatial stratified heterogeneity of extreme precipitation in this study is an effective exploration for a profound understanding of the mechanism of extreme event occurrence. Although the selected natural and social factors are limited in number, their significant impact on the spatial distribution of precipitation has been widely validated (Huang et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2023; Pham et al., 2024 ). It is worth mentioning that the geo-detector used in this study has significant advantages when analyzing the interaction between two factors (Wang et al., 2016 ). However, it cannot be directly applied to the analysis of more complex interactions involving multiple factors (e.g., three or more) and may need to be combined with other methods (Wang and Hu, 2012 ). Exploring the interactions among multiple factors is undoubtedly a very important research direction (Gilman and Wu, 2023 ). Therefore, it is necessary to conduct further research through improved methods and other means.   5 Conclusion This study analyzes the variation trends of extreme precipitation in different basins of China from 1961 to 2022, subsequently quantifies the sensitivity of extreme precipitation to temperature, and further explores the explanatory power of natural and societal factors for the spatial stratified heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. The results of this study indicate that over the past 60 years, extreme precipitation has been more frequently in southeastern China, showing a spatial pattern of more in the southeast and less in the northwest. At the river basin scale, extreme precipitation is more prevalent in the Southeast River Basin, Pearl River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Huaihe River Basin. The analysis of precipitation sensitivity to temperature reveals an asymmetric spatial pattern, with extreme precipitation and mean precipitation sensitivity being larger in the northwest Continental River Basin than in other river basins. The precipitation and extreme precipitation sensitivity in relatively dry region is about five times that in relatively wet area. Furthermore, vegetation exhibits the strongest explanatory power for the spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation, with q  values ranging from 0.61 to 0.72 across the four indices, and the explanatory power of natural factors exceeds that of societal factors. Additionally, compared to individual factors, interactions between factors enhance the explanatory power for spatial heterogeneity of extreme precipitation. Among them, the interaction between vegetation and elevation exhibits the highest explanatory power (q  values ranging from 0.74 to 0.82 for the four indices), and the explanatory power of interactions between natural factors is higher than that of interactions between societal factors.
1 Introduction Droughts, characterized by limited water availability and exacerbated by climate change, pose significant threats to ecosystems and human well-being due to their increasing intensity, duration, and frequency (Anderegg et al., 2013, 2020; Dai & Zhao, 2017; Tripathy & Mishra, 2023; Xu et al., 2024 ). So far, several main drought types are divided, e.g., meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural droughts according to drought evolution and impacts (Bachmair et al., 2016 ). Meteorological droughts, as the firstly-occurred ones over these types, are characterized by deficient precipitation over an extended period (Quiring, 2009 ). Under this circumstance, it is urgent to gain knowledge of vegetation sensitivity to precipitation for climate-change adaptation and forest management (Chen et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2023 ). Southern China is in the only humid zone at the same latitudes of Northern Hemisphere (Fensholt et al., 2015 ), and it also has the most extensive distribution of fragile karst landscapes with soluble bedrocks and high water permeability (Wang et al., 2019 ). After extensive reforestation projects and hundreds of billions investment over the past two decades, the region has experienced a remarkable greening trend (Tong et al., 2020 ). However, the remarkable achievement is likely to be undermined by the severe drying trends in the region, particularly in its western part (Deng et al., 2020 ). Specifically, observational evidences suggest decreasing annual precipitation trends in southern China, implying the region is more prone to meteorological droughts, posing a threat to the great greening achievement (Dai & Zhao, 2017 ). It should be noted that regional distinctions in precipitation are significant there with spatially-different drought risks. Western part of southern China is assumed to be more sensitive to meteorological droughts than its eastern part, as it receives less precipitation and thus less sufficient water source (Fig. 1  B). Not surprisingly, many studies have focused on the effects of extreme drought events on vegetation in the southwest region (e.g., Li et al., 2019; Song et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023 ). Besides, geological settings including bedrock types also impact sensitivity of vegetation to droughts (Jiang et al., 2020; Callahan et al., 2022 ). Previous studies revealed that the fragile karst environment in southern China affects vegetation restoration (Liu et al., 2019 ), and vegetation in karst areas is more impacted by droughts compared to non-karst areas (Jiang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023 ). While remotely sensed observations have shown the sensitivity of vegetation to precipitation that include or partially include southern China, these studies have not adequately addressed the impact of warming on vegetation (e.g., Piao et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2009 ) or demonstrated how the sensitivity varies in different geological settings (Chen et al., 2020 ). To this end, we here investigate the sensitivity of vegetation growth to meteorological drought index (i.e. precipitation) between karst and non-karst areas across eight provinces in southern China, covering an area of approximately 1.8 million square kilometers. Our research questions are: (1) whether vegetation in the region is temperature-dominated or precipitation-dominated? and (2) how vegetation’s sensitivity to precipitation varies between karst and non-karst areas? Firstly, we attempt to compare the relative importance of precipitation and temperature to vegetation growth between karst and non-karst areas. Furthermore, we detect vegetation’s sensitivity to precipitation under the two geological settings while controlling temperature effects, and specific mean annual precipitation (MAP) thresholds are identified for drought-sensitive regions. This geological setting comparison and MAP threshold establishment is a crucial step towards sustainable development and resilience against climate variability and change for the greening region.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study region The study region encompasses the primary karst distribution area in southern China, with karst landscapes comprising 27 % of the total area (Fig. 1 A). There is a general west-to-east increasing gradient of temperature and precipitation in the study region. Mean annual temperature in the study area ranges from −5.14 ℃ to 24.59 ℃ and annual total precipitation varies from 339.80 mm to 2247.8 mm (Fig. 1 B, C). However, there are no notable differences in monthly temperature and precipitation between karst and non-karst areas (Fig. S1 ). This indicates that vegetation in karst and non-karst areas grows under similar climatic conditions, ensuring the effectiveness of subsequent comparisons between these two areas.  2.2 Climate and geology setting data Monthly precipitation and temperature data were derived from Climatic Research Unit Time Series (CRU TS) 4.05 dataset. CRU TS is a high-resolution (0.5°×   0.5°) dataset of monthly climate observations spanning a long historical period. It is periodically updated and refined, and the 4.05 version was released March 2021, covering the period of 1901–2020 (Harris et al., 2020 ) (Table 1  ). In addition, daily evapotranspiration (ET) data were derived from a harmonized global land evaporation dataset (Lu et al., 2021 ). This dataset combines three model-based products to reduce uncertainties, covering a period of 1980–2017 at a spatial resolution of 0.25° (Table 1 ). A 1:100,000 geological map was provided by the Institute of Karst Geology of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences. According to the map, karst (areas with carbonate rocks) and non-karst (areas with non-carbonate rocks) areas were converted into 500-meter resolution raster data (Wang, 2024 ).  2.3 Vegetation data Two key remotely sensed indicators, Leaf Area Index (LAI) and kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (kNDVI), were chosen to reveal vegetation growth. LAI, defined as the total leaf area per unit ground surface area, can well reflect the amount of foliage, photosynthetic capacity and thus plant productivity. NDVI is a simple graphical indicator calculated from the near-infrared and visible lights reflected by vegetation. More healthy vegetation will reflect more near-infrared lights and have a higher NDVI value. Because NDVI fails to account for higher-order relations between the spectral channels, kNDVI was proposed to address the issue (Camps-Valls et al., 2021 ). A simplified calculation of the kNDVI is demonstrated in eq. (1)  below (Wang et al., 2023 ):(1) k N D V I  =  t a n h NDVI  2         Currently, various datasets of the two indicators are available, presenting a trade-off between spatial resolution and the duration of coverage − in essence, offering higher spatial detail but over more limited time periods. In the study, we gave extensive temporal coverage the priority and put aside the spatial resolution to estimate vegetations’ sensitivity to precipitation over a timescale as long as possible. Therefore, two datasets of LAI and NDVI based on Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), one of the longest-running sensor launched in 1978, were obtained. The LAI data was derived from Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS) dataset, covering a period of 1981–2017 at a spatial resolution of 0.05° and temporal resolution of 8 days (Liang et al., 2021 ). This LAI product was produced with a combination of integrated satellite-derived LAI time series data and surface reflectance data from AVHRR satellites employing General Regression Neural Networks (Liang et al., 2021 ). NDVI data was derived from NOAA Climate Data Record (CDR) dataset, which is structured on a 0.05° global grid and spans from 1981 to the present (Vermote, 2019 ). The kNDVI was then calculated using the eq. (1)  above.  2.4 Data analysis Data preprocessing mainly includes the unification of spatiotemporal resolution and vegetation type identification. We unified the spatial resolution of climate and vegetation data to a 0.1 ×   0.1° resolution through bilinear interpolation. For the geological setting data, areas were classified as karst or non-karst if more than 50 % of their area within a 0.1°×0.1° grid was composed of that type. Regarding the different temporal resolutions, we summed the daily-resolution data into monthly resolution ones. The common period, 408 months over 1982–2015, was selected for the main analysis. The main data analysis contains three steps. Firstly, Random Forest (RF) models were used to explore the relative importance of climate factors on kNDVI and LAI. RF algorithm has a high prediction accuracy and is highly tolerant to outliers and noise (Breiman, 2001 ). It effectively analyzes non-linear data with collinearity and interactions, and can provide variable importance measures while analyzing the data. The analysis collect data in every pixel of karst (4626 pixels) and non-karst (12447 pixels) areas over 1982–2015, and it considers four climatic factors: mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), and the seasonal variations in temperature and precipitation. Seasonal variation in precipitation (Pre_season ) is calculated as the ratio of the difference between the maximum (Pre_max ) and minimum (Pre_min ) precipitation over three months to MAP in a year (eq. (2) . Similarly, seasonal variation of temperature (Temp_season ) is defined as the ratio of the difference between the highest (Temp_max ) and lowest (Temp_min ) three months of temperature to MAT in a year (eq.
