R2  values range from 0.635 to 0.791, and the performance metrics in detail are summarized in Table S1 . We here focus on the relative importance of the four chosen factors to vegetation growth between karst and non-karst areas. As Fig. 2   illustrates, the impacts of the two precipitation factors, particularly Pre_season, on LAI and kNDVI are greater in karst areas compared to non-karst areas. Pre_season has a relative importance of 24.02 % to LAI and 25.27 % to kNDVI in karst areas, but only 13.46 % to LAI and 11.63 % to kNDVI in non-karst areas. Temp_season has the greatest impact on vegetation growth in non-karst areas, with a relative importance of 39.96 % for LAI and 40.23 % for kNDVI.  3.2 Sensitivity of vegetation growth to precipitation at pixel scale Fig. 3   displays the partial correlation coefficients between monthly LAI or kNDVI and precipitation in karst and non-karst areas of southern China over 408 months from 1982 to 2015, with temperature fluctuations factored out at pixel scale. Notably, the r  values tend to be higher and more positive in the western region with less precipitation compared to the eastern region (Fig. 3 ). We conducted a further examination to determine if specific MAP thresholds exist for regions sensitive to meteorological droughts. This involved using point density plots to analyze the relationship between MAP and r  values for each grid cell, considering different vegetation types. Our analysis reveals consistent, significant negative linear relationships for karst and non-karst areas (p  < 0.01) (Fig. 4  ). This suggests that vegetation is less sensitive to precipitation with higher precipitation levels in both karst and non-karst areas. The identified MAP thresholds vary from 1337 mm to 1438 mm. Specifically, karst areas exhibited slightly higher precipitation thresholds, with 1347 mm identified from LAI data and 1438 mm from kNDVI data. In contrast, non-karst areas had the lower thresholds of 1337 mm from LAI data and 1427 mm from kNDVI data. As mapped in the Fig. 3 , these thresholds can roughly distinguish the high precipitation-sensitivity regions from regions exhibiting negative vegetation-precipitation correlations.   4 Discussion 4.1 Precipitation factors dominate vegetation growth in karst areas Vegetation growth in the subtropical/tropical study region is generally considered to be temperature or energy-controlled (Qu et al., 2018, 2020 ), a conception that suits the non-karst areas in the region where temperature factors exhibit greater importance on LAI and kNDVI (Fig. 2 ). However, we highlight the greater influence of precipitation factors, especially precipitation seasonality, than temperature impacts on vegetation in karst areas (Fig. 2 ). Due to the soluble carbonate bedrock, karst regions typically experience slow soil formation, shallow soil profiles, inadequate mineral nutrients, and rapid precipitation infiltration, which leaves vegetation highly susceptible to water scarcity (Zhang & Wang, 2009; Yue et al., 2023 ). It has been noted that even when rainfall is sufficient to exceed the soil’s field capacity, the available water typically only satisfies the transpiration needs of vegetation for about 7 to 14 days (Zhou & Pan, 2001 ). Moreover, karst vegetations suffer more during dry seasons or periods (Liu, 2009; Hu et al., 2024 ). Several studies have also suggested that during same-level drought conditions, growth and activity of vegetation in these karst areas decline more significantly compared to non-karst areas (Jiang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023 ), well supporting our findings. These results underscore the importance of considering the unique hydrogeological characteristics of karst regions when assessing the impact of droughts on vegetation.  4.2 Spatial differences in vegetation-precipitation sensitivity and MAP thresholds Vegetation in western part of southern China shows higher sensitivity to precipitation than that in eastern part (Fig. 3 ), possibly because of the prolonged dry seasons and less MAP in south Asian monsoon region than east Asian monsoon region (Wu & Chen, 2021 ). As Fig. 4  shows, there are consistently decreasing vegetation-precipitation correlation coefficients along with MAP gradient, in line with prior research (Wu et al., 2009 ). The MAP thresholds for karst and non-karst areas, ranging from 1337 to 1438 mm, were further established (Fig. 3 ). These thresholds in karst areas are slightly higher than those in non-karst areas, consistent with the slightly higher importance of MAP to LAI and kNDVI (Fig. 2 ). Ground measurements indicate that plant transpiration reaches a maximum of around 800 mm in the subtropical or tropical regions of southern China (Zhang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2023 ), which is lower than our proposed thresholds. Additionally, with evaporation considered, the modeled annual evapotranspiration (ET) values are at a maximum of 1250 mm for non-karst areas and 1064 mm for karst areas (Fig. 5  ) (Lu et al., 2021 ), close to our proposed thresholds. When MAP falls below these thresholds, water sources from precipitation fail to meet the transpiration needs of vegetation in addition to photosynthesis and surface water evaporation, making the vegetation sensitive to precipitation. Conversely, as MAP surpasses these thresholds, vegetation's response to precipitation becomes negligible or even negative (Fig. 3 , Fig. 4 ), as excessive precipitation might reduce plant photosynthesis due to diminished solar radiation (Piao et al., 2003 ). In the tropical humid Amazon forest, a broader critical MAP range that encompasses our MAP thresholds have been identified (Nian et al., 2024 ), reinforcing the validity of our thresholds.  4.3 Implication and limitation Our findings imply that vegetation growth in karst areas of southern China is more sensitive to precipitation changes and thereby faces higher risks from ongoing drying trends than non-karst areas in southern China from two aspects. Firstly, karst vegetations respond more to precipitation factors, especially seasonal precipitation variations, than non-karst ones (Fig. 2 ). Secondly, the proportion of grids with annual total precipitation below the proposed MAP thresholds in karst areas is higher than that in non-karst areas almost every year (Fig. 6  ), indicating that a greater precipitation-sensitive percentage of karst vegetation. In certain dry years, such as 2003 and 2011, vegetation in almost the entire karst region grids were precipitation-sensitive (Fig. 6 ). This situation potentially threatens the regional carbon sink stability and undermines the success of ecological restoration efforts in this global “greening” hotspot (Yue et al., 2023 ). Similar example has happened in tropical Amazon rainforest, where reduction in rainfall since 2000 has diminished vegetation greenness, accounting for 55 % of NDVI declining (Hilker et al., 2014 ) and slowing down vegetation recovery (Van Passel et al., 2024 ). To ensure the long-term sustainability of vegetation restoration projects in southern China karst areas, adaptive strategies that account for the increasing aridity and variability in precipitation is required. Over the next 100 years, large-scale reforestation efforts should shift towards spatial optimization of ecological construction to effectively address these challenges (Yue et al., 2024 ). We acknowledge certain limitations in our study and recommend further research in these areas. Our focus was primarily on the long-term sensitivity of vegetation to precipitation, thereby overlooking the impacts of extreme drought (e.g., megadrought in 2022) on vegetation growth. Additionally, we did not consider the delayed effects of precipitation on vegetation, as our aim was to investigate the immediate responses between precipitation and vegetation, aligning more closely with the concept of “sensitivity”. Furthermore, vegetation on different carbonate bedrocks in karst areas (mainly limestone and dolomite) exhibits varying responses to droughts (Feng et al., 2021 ), necessitating further investigation into their precipitation sensitivity.   5 Conclusion Two key findings are highlighted in this research. Firstly, we demonstrate that precipitation factors, particularly variations in precipitation seasonality, are more significant for vegetation growth in the karst areas of southern China than temperature factors. This challenges the traditional perception of the tropical/subtropical region as temperature- or energy-dominated. Secondly, we establish MAP thresholds of 1337 to 1438 mm to identify regions at risk in drought assessments, with slightly higher thresholds for karst areas. These findings indicate a higher vulnerability of southern China's karst landscapes to ongoing drying trends compared to non-karst areas. Our research provides a crucial foundation for informed decision-making in climate-change adaptation and sustainable forest management in the region.
1 Introduction Hydrothermal activity occurs frequently in the shale oil reservoirs, and hydrothermal fluid upwells along faults, triggering strong fluid–rock interactions, thus affecting the reservoir development (Harlov and Austrheim, 2013; Oliver and Bons, 2001; Yu et al., 2018; Zhi et al., 2021 ). However, the mechanism of fluid–rock interaction and controlling factors under integrated hydrothermal fluid and fault remain unclear, hindering the evaluation, exploration, and development of shale oil resources (Xu et al., 2022a; Jin et al., 2021 ). China has abundant reserves of unconventional oil and gas resources, including shale oil (Loucks and Ruppel, 2007 ; Dong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2018; Yang and Zou, 2019; Shen et al., 2019 ). The Mahu Sag is situated in the northwestern Junggar Basin, China, as shown in Fig. 1  . The potential resources of shale reservoir in Mahu Sag are huge, showing the coexistence of several types of reservoirs, multi-layer oil-bearing system and multiple reservoirs. The Fengcheng Formation is the main source rock (Xiao et al., 2021 ). The shale reservoir of Fengcheng Formation is an alkali lake in a closed or semi-closed environment, which is the oldest alkali lake deposit reported at present (Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018 ). The mud shale reservoirs in the Fengcheng Formation are highly developed with inorganic pores (Kuang et al., 2012 ). Mineral transformation induced by fluid–rock interaction plays a crucial role in the development of reservoir (Gasparrini et al., 2013; Teboul et al., 2019 ). In the Fengcheng Formation, it is generally believed that the fluid–rock interaction triggered by hydrothermal activity along the fault upwelling has a significant influence on reservoir development (Lu et al., 2015b; Tian et al., 2015; Xin et al., 2022 ). Hydrothermal dolomite and alkaline minerals are common in Fengcheng Formation reservoir, which are the product of fluid-rock interaction under the comprehensive control of hydrothermal fluid and fault (Wilson et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2022 ). However, most of the existing studies are based on thin section observation, carbon and oxygen isotope measurement and other petrological testing methods. Although some qualitative understanding has been obtained, the degree of fracture-hydrothermal transformation to the reservoir cannot be clearly answered. The numerical simulation technology can effectively simulate the evolution process of the reservoir on the time scale of millions of years, and quantitatively calculate the real-time change of mineral content and porosity. In this study, the shale reservoir of Fengcheng Formation in Mahu Sag was selected. Based on previous petrological tests, a multi-component, multi-phase flow and reactive solute transport program was used to simulate hydrothermal migration along the fault, and calculate the real-time change of mineral content and porosity. The purpose of this study is to reveal the fluid-rock interaction and mineral transformation mechanism controlled by hydrothermal fluid and fault, and identify the controlling factors.  2 Geological background As shown in Fig. 2  , the Mahu Sag is comprised of four formations from bottom to top, i.e., the Jiamuhe Formation, Fengcheng Formation, Xiazijie Formation, and Wuerhe Formation (Cao et al., 2005; Li et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2023 ). The Fengcheng Formation reservoir is composed of complex and diverse fine-grained sedimentary rock with variable tectonic sedimentary and solid heterogeneity, making it a challenging reservoir to explore (Zhi et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021, Jiang et al., 2023 ). The Fengcheng Formation is characterized by a sediment thickness range of 800 ∼ 1800 m (Qin et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhi et al., 2019; Zhi et al., 2021 ). Under volcanic activity and tectonic movement, the Fengcheng Formation experienced two stages of hydrothermal activity (Zhang et al., 2018; Bai et al., 2023 ). The first occurred in the early stage of sedimentation, which increased the salinity of the lake basin (Chen et al., 2023 ). It induced the formation of dolomite crystals and other salt minerals precipitated under evaporation (Song, 2018 ). The second occurred in the middle and late stages of deposition when the salinity was higher and alkaline minerals precipitated, such as reedmergnerite. (Zhang et al., 2018 ). In the Mahu Sag, the dolomitic rock of the Fengcheng Formation is crucial for shale reservoirs (Zhang et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021 ). Two types of dolomite exist in this formation. The first type is lamellar micritic micritic dolomite (called as dolomite(I) in this work), which is deposited directly by hydrothermal fluid at the bottom of the lake (Wen et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023 ). The second type is fine-grained dolomite (called as dolomite (II) in this work) precipitated after hydrothermal activity, formed by deep hydrothermal action (Xue et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2023 ). The fine-grained dolomite is mainly distributed in faults, cracks, interlamellar cracks, and their surroundings (Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021; Plumlee et al., 1994; Kuang et al., 2012 ). The Fengcheng Formation reservoir is highly densified, the average porosity of the reservoir is relatively low, and the rock permeability is highly variable (Yu et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2020 ). Based on analysis of the existing S1 Well reservoir rock samples, the porosity ranges from 0.11 % to 10.1 %, with an average of 3.61 %. The permeability ranges from 0.01 to 2.57 mD, with an average of 1.263 mD (Huang et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Zhi et al., 2021; Kuang et al., 2012 ). During the sedimentary period of the Fengcheng Formation, the tectonic movement was strong, and the fault zone was associated with a large number of fractures, which significantly improved the physical properties of the reservoir (Tao et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020 ;). The fractures are a favorable space type for shale reservoirs and are conducive to transportation and storage of oil and gas (Tang et al., 2022 ). Some samples with low porosity show relatively high permeability. It is speculated that the fractures in the reservoir may improve its physical properties (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhi et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022 ). The second and third members of the Fengcheng Formation have relatively good physical properties. The pores and fractures in this area are more developed, conducive to oil and gas storage, and have “sweet spot” reservoir characteristics (Huang et al., 2022; Lyu et al., 2023; Kuang et al., 2012 ).  3 Numerical simulation 3.1 Model tool TOUGHREACT is used for calculation in this study. It could simulate multiphase flow and heat transport, solute transport, convection, diffusion, and chemical reactions in gas and liquid phases at different scales (Xu et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2023a; Yang et al., 2023b ). This program is very good at building one-dimensional, two-dimensional and three-dimensional geological heterogeneity models (Yang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023c ). According to a series of parameters such as buried depth, temperature, pressure, porosity, permeability, mineral content and ion concentration, a model consistent with the actual geological conditions is established. It is also possible to set the fault in the model according to the morphology of the actual fault. Simulate a series of fluid-rock reactions that occur during the upwelling of hydrothermal fluid along the fault. Chemical reactions such as cation exchange, complexation, and redox reactions are considered. The spatiotemporal evolution of mineral content and porosity throughout the process is calculated.  3.2 Geological model To investigate the mechanism and controlling factors of dolomite formation via hydrothermal processes, a one-dimensional model is established incorporating three variables: temperature, Mg2+  concentration, and flow rate. Considering the buried depth, fluid and hydrodynamic conditions of Fengcheng Formation, three indexes are set for each variable to cover the actual geological conditions. According to the actual geological conditions, and the test results show that dolomite in Fengcheng formation is mainly formed in three temperature intervals of 60 ∼ 90 °C, 90 ∼ 120 °C and 120 ∼ 150 °C (Chang et al., 2016; Pan, 2013; Tang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, 100 °C, 120 °C and 140 °C are selected as representative temperatures and set in single-factor models. The Mg2+ /Ca2+  ratios in the fluid used in the models were 1×, 3×, and 6 × . The hydrothermal flow rates were 250, 500, and 750 mm3 /s. The fluid-rock interaction caused by hydrothermal fluid upwelling from the bottom into the reservoir is simulated, and the influence of hydrothermal activity on mineral transformation under different conditions is investigated. In addition, a section with a buried depth of 4,640 ∼ 4,740 m was selected to study the fluid–rock interaction and its influence on reservoir development following the hydrothermal fluid upwelling into the shale reservoir along the fault. During the sedimentary evolution of the Fengcheng Formation, a large number of dolomitic rocks formed in the early diagenesis stage. At the same time, the biological processes in the lake basin produced a large amount of organic matter, which was overlaid on the dolomitic rocks and developed interbedded layers. As the selected section consists primarily of mud shale and mud dolomite, the model features varying vertical interbedding of mud shale and mud dolomite.  3.3 Conceptual model There were two types of models. The first was a one-dimensional model containing sub-models varying in temperature, Mg2+ /Ca2+  ratio, and hydrothermal filling rate (Fig. 3  ). The total length in the Z direction was 100 m, and the model was uniformly divided into 100 grids of 1 m. The width is 1 m in the X direction, and the thickness is 1 m in the Y direction. The grid in the X and Y directions is not divided, so the model is one-dimensional in the Z direction. The bottom (Z=-100 m) is the injection grid, that is, where the hydrothermal fluid enters the reservoir and then migrates upward. At the top (Z=0 m) is the boundary grid of fixed flow, which corresponds to the infinite boundary of the actual formation. The simulation duration was 10,000 years. The second was a two-dimensional (XZ) model (Fig. 3 ). The total length in the Z direction was also 100 m (0 and  -100 m) divided into 100 grids of 1 m. The total length in the X direction was 40,000 m with 15,000 grids. A fault with an angle of 32.53° was set in the model. The hydrothermal fluid enters the reservoir from the bottom of the fault and migrates upward.  3.4 Initial conditions 3.4.1 Geological conditions of the reservoir In the two-dimensional model, according to the actual reservoir temperature, the temperature was set to 80 °C. The average pressure coefficient in the vertical direction was 1.21. The top pressure was 61.8 MPa and the pressure at -100 m was 62.76 MPa. The distributions of temperature and pressure are shown in Fig. 4  . The setting of porosity and permeability should be noted. The numerical simulation of diagenesis is a recovery process of an event that has already occurred. Therefore, the initial parameters of the model are based on the existing measured parameters, combined with diagenetic time and events. In the early stage of the Fengcheng Formation, the reservoir mainly developed dolomitic rocks and organic-rich shale, and the compaction was not strong. Compared with current conditions, the porosity and permeability at this stage were relatively large. In the process of backguessing the parameters, we keep doing the inversion and forward modeling to ensure that the parameters are reasonable. Therefore, we made a guess based on current measured data. the initial porosity and permeability of the mud shale were 20 % and 0.2 mD, of the mud dolomite were 25 % and 2 mD, and at the fault were 50 % and 2,000 mD, respectively (Fig. 5  ).  3.4.2 Water chemistry conditions As mentioned above, it can be seen from Fig. 5  that there are two different lithologies in the model, namely mud shale and mud dolomite. The water chemistry conditions corresponding to each lithology are different. According to the mineral composition of different lithofacies, the corresponding ion concentrations are calculated separately. In addition to the two fluids corresponding to the two lithologies, there is also hydrothermal injection in the model. Therefore, the model contains three fluids, as shown in Table 1  .  3.4.3 Mineral composition and content The mineral composition and relative content in the model were determined based on the measured data, as shown in Table 2  . For mud shale, it mainly contains silicates, such as clay minerals, while carbonate minerals are relatively less abundant. For mud dolomite, the mineral composition is mainly dolomite and calcite, and there may be hydrothermal processes producing silicification and quartz.   3.5 Boundary conditions In all models, the volume of the boundary grid is infinite to stabilize the pressure system and guarantee that the factors, such as pressure and ion concentration, do not change with time. The boundary infinity grid also achieves the condition of infinite geological scale.  3.6 Mineral kinetic parameters Ten kinds of minerals are included in the model. Among them, the reaction speed of calcite and gypsum is very fast, so it is controlled by equilibrium. Other minerals are kinetically controlled, as shown in Table 3  . The kinetic data were taken from the TOUGHREACT database (Xu et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2011 ).   4 Results 4.1 Single-factor model Fig. 6   shows change in relative contents of the typical minerals in one-dimensional model under the influence of a single factor. The content of albite decreased, while the dolomite content increased, under different conditions, but the processes underlying these decreases/increases varied. The content of albite continued to decline, indicating its dissolution during the reaction (Fig. 6 a). The dissolution rate was slow in the first 1,000 years and suddenly became more significant between 1,000 and 5,000 years. Albite was depleted at 5,000 years. Meanwhile, the weight relative content of dolomite gradually increased under all three temperature conditions (100 °C, 120 °C and 140 °C), and at 10,000 years reached 20.77 %, 21.04 %, and 21.68 %, respectively. The growth rates under different temperature conditions differed significantly after 2,000 years. The average growth rates under the conditions of 100 °C, 120 °C, and 140 °C were 0.31 %, 0.24 %, and 0.20 % in one thousand years, respectively. The dolomite growth rate decreased with increasing temperature. Fig. 6 b shows the change of albite content in the 3 × and 6 × Mg2+ /Ca2+  fluids, indicating that the dissolution of albite was consistent, with both showing depletion by 2,000 years. In contrast, the dissolution rate of albite was relatively low in the 1 × Mg2+ /Ca2+  fluid. The curves of dolomite content under three different Mg2+  concentrations shown in Fig. 6 b indicated that dolomite content increased faster with increasing Mg2+  concentration. In the 3 × and 6 × Mg2+ /Ca2+  fluids, the dolomite content peaked at 8,000 and 3,000 years, respectively. Both the albite and dolomite content changed more rapidly with increasing flow rate, indicating that flow rate speeds up the reaction (Fig. 6 c). With the three different flow conditions of 250, 500, and 750 mm3 /s, albite was depleted at 5,000, 2,000, and 2,000 years, respectively. In 10,000 years, the dolomite content increased by 2.93 %, 25.09 %, and 44.28 % under flow rates of 250, 500, and 750 mm3 /s, respectively. Compared with the minimum (250 mm3 /s) and maximum (750 mm3 /s) hydrodynamic conditions, the increase of dolomite content increased by more than 15 times when the flow rate increased by 3 times.  4.2 Two-dimensional model The changes in mineral content and porosity triggered by hydrothermal fluid upwelling along the fault are shown in Fig. 7  . During hydrothermal fluid activity, the range of fluid–rock interaction did not cover the entire two-dimensional model. To express the simulation results clearly, we selected the part where the fluid–rock interaction was strong, i.e., the area of − 100 to 0 m in the Z direction and 0 ∼ 2,000 m in the X direction, as an area for results presentation and data analysis. After the hydrothermal upwelling, a series of changes in temperature, porosity, and various minerals within the reservoir occurred. The temperature changes because hydrothermal fluids were continuously injected during the period from 0 to 250,000 years. First along the fault, which is “dominant channel”, and then enter the reservoirs. Due to the high temperature of the hydrothermal fluid, the temperature at the bottom of the fault increased first. Then, with the flow of hydrothermal fluid, significant temperature increases occurred inside the fault, and the heat diffused resulting in an increase in reservoir temperature near the fault. As shown in Fig. 7 , minerals dissolution and precipitation occurred in the lower half of the fault. Calcite, quartz, albite, and clay minerals dissolved, while dolomite and K-feldspar precipitated. This was due to the rapid increase in temperature at the bottom of the fault, up to 86.23 °C, and the high concentrations of various ions here, which prompted the reaction. The fluid spread around, increasing the Mg2+ /Ca2+  and temperature, intensifying the calcite dissolution in the reservoir near the fault and precipitating dolomite that would fill the fault. The filling of dolomite, quartz, and K-feldspar occurred within the fault. The overall precipitation at the fault was greater than the dissolution, and the porosity decreased. The maximum porosity reduction is 30 %. The fluids within the fault diffused into the reservoir in all directions. Calcite, K-feldspar, and montmorillonite dissolved in the mud dolomite, while dolomite, albite, and illite precipitated. Montmorillonite and illite were interconverted. The precipitation of large amounts of dolomite by dolomitization can cause a decrease in reservoir porosity. However, K-feldspar was mainly dissolved in the mud shale reservoir. The total dissolution of silicate minerals was slightly larger than the total precipitation, which increased the porosity and facilitated of the reservoir development. The increase in porosity is up to 25 %.   5 Discussion 5.1 Fluid–rock interaction mechanism Based on the results of this study, combined with the genesis types and mechanisms of different dolomites, the dolomites of the Fengcheng Formation are concluded as two genetic types (Fig. 8  ) (Feng et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019 ). For the first type(I), in the early stage of sedimentary evolution of the lake basin, the hydrothermal fluid at the bottom of the fault entered the lake bottom and formed chemical precipitates, as shown in Equation (1). The main form is mud-size microcrystalline dolomite(I), mainly produced as a laminated structure and interbedded with shale. The second dolomite (II) was formed by hydrothermal fluid–rock interactions occurring near the fault, as shown in Equation (2). The main form is fine-grained dolomite(II), which is different from the dolomitization of Mg2+  replacing Ca2+  that commonly occurs. This is a type of dolomite with hydrothermal genesis. Mg2+ +Ca2+ +2CO3 2– ⇌   CaMg (CO3 )2  (1) Hydrothermal fluid+ (Na2 O·Al2 O3 ·6SiO2 ; K2 O·Al2 O3 ·6SiO2 ; CaCO3 ) → CaMg (CO3 )2  (dolomite) + SiO3 2-  (2) The dolomites distributed in the form of agglomerates and fault filling in the Fengcheng Formation all have a coarse powder-fine crystal morphology (Lu et al., 2015a; Lu et al., 2015b ). For S1 Well, both carbon and oxygen isotope data and cathodoluminescence tests indicate the presence of multi-stage cementation of carbonate minerals, including early chemical precipitation and late metasomatism (Zhao et al., 2023 ). In the late sedimentary period, the concentrations of Na+ , Mg2+  and Ca2+  increased, which led to the increase of salinity in the Fengcheng Formation (Zhang et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019 ). After the upwelling into the reservoir, the hydrothermal fluid reacts with various minerals to varying degrees. Typical minerals and porosity maps (Fig. 9  ) show that the dissolved minerals are dominated by calcite, albite and potassium feldspar, while the precipitated minerals are dominated by dolomite and quartz. Comparing the dissolution rate of different minerals, the dissolution rate of albite is significantly higher than that of potassium feldspar and calcite. In addition, dolomite content gradually increases, and its precipitation rate is much greater than the dissolved amount of calcite. Hydrothermal dolomite is formed after the hydrothermal fluid entering the mud dolomite reservoir. During the dissolution of albite and K-feldspar, SiO3 2−  is released and forms H4 SiO4 , which eventually hydrolyzes to SiO2  precipitates, as shown in Equation (3). This siliceous precipitation represents evidence of hydrothermal activity. Moreover, the calcite dissolution is partly due to the entry of Mg2+  into the calcite lattice, which undergoes dolomitization and eventually converts into dolomite. The hydrothermal fluid lowers the pH value. As shown in Equation (4), the increase in H+  content and the decrease in Ca2+  content will lead to calcite dissolution. H4 SiO4  (aq) → SiO2  (s) + 2H2 O (3) CaCO3  + H+  → Ca2+  + HCO3 –  (4) In this study, when albite and K-feldspar were completely dissolved, the dissolution of calcite reached a maximum rate.. At this time, calcite mainly underwent dolomitization, which caused the maximum precipitation rate for dolomite. Large amounts of Ca2+  and Mg2+  concentrated in the contact area between fluid and calcite, and a small amount of dolomite would still precipitate quickly. In the final stage, dolomite precipitated at the slowest rate observed in the models. The analysis suggested that clay minerals in the reservoir will be transformed and montmorillonite will gradually transform into illite after hydrothermal fluid upwelling. Small amounts of Ca2+  and Mg2+  will be released in the process of their mutual transformation. With increasing temperature, the kinetic barrier for dolomite generation will be broken, thus precipitating dolomite (Whitaker Fiona et al., 2004; Pan et al., 2022 ).  5.2 Factors controlling fluid–rock interaction 5.2.1 Temperature In the early stage of fluid–rock interaction, albite dissolves and dolomite gradually precipitate (Fig. 6 a). With increasing temperature, the rates of albite dissolution and dolomite precipitation decrease. From the results of kinetic analysis, the dissolution of albite first requires energy absorption to break the bond energy between ions, which causes dispersal of the ions into the solution (Hellmann et al., 1990; Zhang and Lüttge, 2007 ). This process involves heat absorption, so the increasing temperature should accelerate the albite dissolution. However, the opposite trend was observed in this study. This is because there are other minerals present in the reservoir. In addition to albite dissolution, other minerals also reacted. The transformation between montmorillonite and illite affects albite dissolution. Montmorillonite dissolution will also release SiO3 2− . The higher the temperature, the faster the montmorillonite dissolves, and more SiO3 2−  is released into the fluid, which decreases albite dissolution rates. In a deep burial environment, the reservoir is at a relatively constant temperature. However, heat diffusion from hydrothermal upwelling will lead to an increase of temperature within the reservoir and can aggravate fluid–rock interactions. The change in temperature affects most of the fluid–rock interactions, and is also an important factor in breaking through the kinetic barriers of dolomite dissolution (Cui et al., 2018; Ishikawa et al., 2008 ). For the hydrothermal upwelling process in the shale reservoir of the Fengcheng Formation in the Mahu Sag, numerous fluid–rock interactions are influenced by temperature. The increase in temperature increases the intensity of fluid–rock interaction in the reservoir, promoting the dissolution, precipitation, and transformation of minerals, which can impact the reservoir development.  5.2.2 Fluids As shown in Fig. 6 b, when Mg2+  concentration increased, the dissolution rate of albite accelerates, and the precipitation rate of dolomite increased. By increasing the Mg2+  concentration in the hydrothermal fluid, the effective collision numbers between Mg2+  and minerals will be increased, thus promoting the reaction. However, the dissolution rate of albite in hydrothermal fluid with 3 × Mg2+  concentration was almost the same as that in hydrothermal fluid with 6 × Mg2+  concentration. Coupled with the relatively low albite content in the reservoir, the acceptable activated Mg2+  content on the rock surface reached the maximum when 3 × Mg2+  concentration. Therefore, the effects on albite dissolution rate of increasing the Mg2+  concentration of hydrothermal fluid to 6 × and 3 × were almost the same. The excessively high Mg2+  concentration will inhibit albite dissolution (Bagheri, et al., 2022 ). As shown in the Fig. 6 b, during the period from 2,000 to 5,000 years, albite dissolution had already occurred, and the “competitiveness” of Mg2+  in the system decreased, while the content of dolomite increased significantly. This is because the substantial increase in Mg2+  concentration in the hydrothermal fluid will not only promote the albite dissolution but also increase the Mg2+ /Ca2+  ratio, thus enhancing the dolomitization. In the case of high calcite content, the dolomitization is strongly dependent on Mg2+  (Xu et al., 2013; Hosseini et al., 2015 ). Higher Mg2+  concentration not only increases the salinity of hydrothermal fluid but also the Mg2+ /Ca2+  ratio. The fluid–rock interaction induced by hydrothermal fluid mainly involves ion exchange, and both Mg2+  and Ca2+  separated from the fluid are hydrated. Mg2+  has a 40 % smaller ionic radius than Ca2+  and a greater binding force with water molecules, and Mg2+  is more likely to combine with H2 O in the fluid to form complexes (Dian et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2019; Lippmann, 2012 ). The hydrothermal fluid will dissolve the carbonate and silicate within the fault during upwelling to form a high-salinity fluid and diffuse into the surrounding reservoir. A portion of Mg2+  in the hydrothermal fluid will be solvated to form Mg2+ –H2 O by hydration, with the remaining portion being free in the fluid to participate in different fluid–rock interactions. The extent to which the Mg2+  concentration in hydrothermal fluid affects fluid–rock interaction is related to the content of minerals dissolving.. When the content is sufficient, the higher the concentration of Mg2+  in the hydrothermal fluid, and the faster the fluid–rock interaction rate. The ratio of the mass of dissolved substance to the mass of the fluid determines the salinity, where higher contents are generally seen for ions such as Na+ , Mg2+ , and Cl− . High salinity is one of the essential factors for breaking through the kinetic barrier for dolomite generation (Hanshaw and Back, 1979; Morrow, 1982 ).  5.2.3 Flow rate As shown in in Fig. 6 c, albite was completely dissolved at all three flow rates during the period from 0 to 5,000 years. The higher the flow rate, the faster the albite dissolves, and the greater the dolomite precipitation rate, indicating that dolomite was mainly dominated by hydrothermal processes during this period. After the albite has dissolved completely, the dolomite content shows a significant increase, and the higher the flow rate, the larger the increment. The dissolution of albite and the generation of dolomite occurred on the contact surface between fluid and rock (McHargue and Price, 1982 ) When albite dissolves, the generated ions first accumulate on the contact surface. They then diffuse to the center of the fluid with a lower concentration. The flow of hydrothermal fluid will accelerate the diffusion process, thus accelerating the dissolution of albite. The generated dolomite crystal nuclei first appear on the contact surface and then grow to form complete dolomite. The flowing hydrothermal fluid will take away the newly generated dolomite nuclei and promote the reaction to further generate dolomite, i.e., the amount of dolomite generation increases with increasing hydrothermal fluid flow rate. As shown in Fig. 6 c, the dissolution rate of albite increases significantly when the hydrothermal fluid flow rate is increased. The effects of hydrothermal fluid flow rate on the reaction is greater than that of increasing the Mg2+  concentration and temperature. The temperature of the reservoir and the hydrothermal fluid are considered to have reached those suitable for reaction during the deep burial period, and the hydrothermal fluid further increased the reservoir temperature during the diffusion process, thus reducing the effect of increasing temperature on the reaction. The deep hydrothermal fluid containing more anions and cations will dissolve carbonates and silicates along the fault upwelling process, and the generated Ca2+ , Mg2+ , K+ , Na+ , and other substances will enter the fluid. With the mixing of the hydrothermal fluid and formation water, the mixed water itself contains large amounts of Mg2+ . During the sedimentary evolution of the lake basin, deep hydrothermal fluids were transported upward along the faults due to volcanic activity and tectonic movement, which facilitated the fluid–rock interaction (Fournier, 2007; He et al., 2016 ).  5.2.4 Influence of hydrothermal fluid and fault In the two-dimensional model, at the base of the fault, calcite, quartz, and albite dissolution occurred, while dolomite precipitated. The amount of dolomite precipitation was greater than the amount of calcite that dissolved, resulting in a reduction of reservoir porosity. This is unfavorable for reservoir development. As hydrothermal fluids are continuously injected, they will first follow the “dominant channel” and then fault to enter the reservoir (Xu et al., 2022b ). The heat will diffuse, resulting in an increase in reservoir temperature near the fracture (Fu et al., 2016 ). The fault has much greater porosity and permeability than the reservoir, and the fluid is in full contact with the reservoir rocks, resulting in a vigorous fluid–rock interaction. The entire fault is accompanied by fluid–rock interaction during the upwelling of hydrothermal fluid (Stober et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022 ). The bottom of the fault reacts most strongly due to the rapid increase in ion concentration, making it easy to reach saturation. The hydrothermal fluid is then transported along the fault to the top, which is covered by a mud shale reservoir with low porosity and permeability. This largely obstructs fluid movement, causing the fluid to aggregate at the top and intensifying the reaction between the fluid and rock. The fluid carries large amounts of metal ions, including Ca2+  and Mg2+ , which disrupt the fluid–rock equilibrium in the reservoir and facilitate fluid–rock interaction (Rendel et al., 2022; Xu and Pruess, 2001 ). The fluid near the fault spread and entered different lithofacies reservoirs vertically, resulting in mineral dissolution and precipitation. Because overall dissolution was less than precipitation, the porosity of mud dolomite reservoirs decreased. Moreover, in the mud shale reservoir, the total dissolution of silicate minerals slightly exceeded the total precipitation, leading to an increase in porosity, which is favorable for reservoir development. Therefore, the fluid–rock interaction under the integrated hydrothermal fluid and fault had a dual effect on the reservoir, which could be constructive in some reservoirs and destructive in others.    6 Conclusions Temperature, salinity, and hydrodynamic conditions (flow rate) are critical factors in breaking through the kinetic barriers of dolomite precipitation. Within a specific range, increasing temperature and Mg2+  concentration promoted hydrothermal processes. The hydrothermal flow rate influenced the ions accumulation on the fluid–rock contact surface, thus controlling mineral dissolution rates. In a certain range, when the flow rate is increased by 3 times, the growth rate of dolomite content is increased by more than 15 times. Hydrothermal fluid flowing near the fault underwent chemical action more readily than in other areas. The fluid near the fault spread and entered different lithofacies reservoirs vertically, resulting in mineral dissolution and precipitation. The influence of hydrothermal fluid and fault on reservoir development was both constructive and destructive. The porosity of mud dolomite reservoirs decreased by 30 % while increased by 25 % in the mud shale reservoir.
1 Introduction Watershed data are increasingly available due to expanding sensor networks. This sudden surge of measurements has created new challenges in water management as quality controlling, processing, and integrating these data requires a great deal of highly skilled labor (Devia et al., 2015 ). Many process-based models were created in the context of time series data scarcity and are therefore not readily amenable to data ingestion or data assimilation (Castelletti et al., 2012; Francipane et al., 2012; Sorooshian et al., 2008; Silberstein, 2006 ). Machine learning approaches can automate data ingestion, Sarafanov et al. (2021)  and Olson and Moore (2016)  but their opacity may limit insight and stakeholder trust (Jajarmizadeh et al., 2012; Babovic and Abbott, 1997a ). Both approaches require large amounts of computational power and data (Kumar et al., 2013; Wagena et al., 2020 ). In light of these challenges, a parsimonious middle ground has been sought between pure process-based and data-driven modeling, posing the question: in the age of ever increasing new data, how can the interpretability and comprehensibility of process-based models be preserved, while taking advantage of the scalability of data-driven methods ? This paper introduces a new method to discover rainfall-runoff equations strictly from raw sensor data. The contribution of this work is an automated and scalable methodology, which discovers differential equations and estimates latent states within hydrologic systems using only rainfall and runoff measurements. These latent states represent transient storage in the catchment such as increased soil moisture, overland flow, and elevated groundwater levels. The novelty of the approach lies in its ability to discover fundamental equations governing hydrologic systems solely from data, while preserving the automaticity of data-driven methods.  2 Background Prior efforts have pursued a combination of automaticity and interpretability through modification of existing process-based models, theoretical derivation, and explainable AI (XAI) (Devia et al., 2015; Angelov et al., 2021; Jajarmizadeh et al., 2012; Babovic and Abbott, 1997b ). Process-based hydrologic models are often derived from first principles and thus support interpretability, but their calibration and construction is highly manual. While XAI has made gains in the interpretability of machine learning methods, the resulting model parameters may still not be straightforwardly mapped to readily understood hydrologic concepts. This may make it difficult to understand or tune model behavior using domain knowledge (Angelov et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2022 ). Methodological and computational advances have led to significant progress in hydrologic modeling, with the ability to represent more granular process and complexities. Once a model is developed and calibrated, it can be used to study scenarios by changing its many parameters and inputs. Reformulating an existing computational model can speed simulation, enable the use of tools not compatible with the original form, or support the interpretation of model features for domain understanding (Welch et al., 1995; Hespanha, 2018; Bartos and Kerkez, 2021; Alex et al., 2020 ). If the original model was already calibrated, these approaches need little additional data (Troutman et al., 2017 ) or computational power (Santos et al., 2018 ). Even with these barriers eliminated, a reliance on manual processes presents a bottleneck (Wong and Kerkez, 2018 ) given the large data sets and systems involved. A tractable system of differential equations can also be used to represent catchment dynamics, and can be constructed by derivation from first principles with appropriate simplifying assumptions (Kirchner, 2009 ). The interpretability and tunability of differential equation-based models is good as these models are rooted in physics and established domain principles. Modeling hydrologic systems using differential equations is also computationally efficient, particularly if the derived algebraic relations have a closed-form solution (Jakeman and Hornberger, 1993 ). However, implementation may be difficult due to data requirements, time granularity, and limited automaticity. These approaches are typically demonstrated on unusually long and clean records provided from experimental catchments (Kirchner, 2009 ). They also tend to focus on daily data, Song et al. (2019)  which may not be granular enough to support many important applications. Lastly, appropriate simplifying assumptions may differ by catchment, which makes data processing manual. A principal advantage of machine learning-based methods is automaticity, but a core critique has focused on the “black box” nature of the resulting models. In the field of XAI, techniques such as dynamic mode decomposition (Schmid, 2022 ), Koopman operator construction (Mauroy et al., 2020 ), and others (Juang and Pappa, 1985; Ho and Kalman, 1966 ) offer structures ripe for mathematical interpretation (Tian et al., 2022 ). However, this mathematical interpretability may not relate tractably to physical characteristics of the system or well understood hydrological concepts. Genetic programming has also been a prominent approach within XAI (Babovic and Abbott, 1997a,b ). This approach seeks to develop governing equations directly from data using an evolutionary approach (Babovic and Keijzer, 2002 ). More recent work has explored embedding expert knowledge to improve the accuracy and interpretability of the generated models (Babovic, 2009 ). The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks used for rainfall-runoff modeling in Kratzert et al. 2018 and 2019 provide some interpretability through examination of the evolution of the cell states throughout time (Kratzert et al., 2019, 2018 ). Work in Jiang et al. (2022)  extended the interpretation of LSTMs to explicitly attribute flow peaks to snowmelt or rainfall events and examine characteristic differences between catchments. However, the models in Kratzert et al. (2019, 2018)  have over 10,000 parameters which obscures the relation to catchment characteristics. Hybrid modeling combines process-based modeling with data- driven approaches and often results in better, more consistent results (Kapoor et al., 2023; Fathian et al., 2019 ). One common approach within this vein is training ML models on the errors or residuals remaining between observations and process-based outputs (Schneider et al., 2022 ). To the extent that the process-based model predicts the observations, the results can be traced back to the model structure. That is, when the residuals the ML component is correcting for are small, interpretability is still similar to purely process-based models. Another approach is using domain knowledge to decompose a large problem into smaller subproblems which are easier to train data-driven models on. For example, predicting effluent contaminant concentrations from a resource recovery facility directly from the characteristics of the input may be more difficult than building a network of smaller models approximating intermediate processes within the facility. With this approach it may also be clearer which processes are poorly modeled and thereby causing error in the final prediction. To illustrate the challenge of model selection via example, we consider a measured storm in a mid-size city in the Midwestern United States in the Summer of 2022 (Fig. 1 ). The hydrograph is generated across 30 km  2      of urbanized landscape and responds to rainfall events with a large initial peak, smaller delayed peak, and nonlinear recession. In pursuit of the “middle ground” we referred to in the introduction, we would like to have an automatically generated model with sufficient fidelity to represent these unusual dynamics, but which is still amenable to inspection and tuning. “Out of the box” solutions could include a machine-learning approach, which would need many more storm observations and a high parameter space to capture these dynamics. A process-based hydrologic model could capture these dynamics, but would need to be calibrated across many physiographic inputs and process parameters (infiltration, runoff, routing, etc.). Alternatively, a model could be derived from first principles and manually increased in complexity until the dynamics are adequately captured. To that end, two approaches which may supply the automaticity and interpretability we seek are unit hydrographs – well established, but limited in their ability to capture complex dynamics – and differential equation discovery.  The unit hydrograph approach reduces streamflow prediction to a transformation of the rainfall time series by assuming watersheds are linear and time invariant (LTI) dynamical systems (Bedient et al., 2008 ). This is computationally efficient, handles delay well, and can acceptably approximate watershed response in many cases. However, this approach is generally unable to represent complex responses such the example in Fig. 1 . A unit hydrograph based on a gamma distribution (Ghorbani et al., 2017 ) can fit either the initial peak (Fig. 1 , first row, dot-dash red) or recession (Fig. 1 , first row, dotted cyan), but not both. Alternatively, representing catchment response as a system of differential equations would be computationally efficient and present a model structure prevalent in the hydrology community. Model discovery automatically generates differential equations from data, and has been demonstrated for systems ostensibly more complex than watersheds (de Silva et al., 2020; Brunton et al., 2016 ). However, due to their instantaneous nature, differential equations cannot represent delayed causation (Fig. 1 , second row). Given these challenges, in the following section we introduce a new methodology (Fig. 1 , third row) to recover the delay and dynamic complexity of watersheds solely from data, while providing the ability to evaluate the resulting model structure and parameters in the context of hydrologic domain knowledge.  3 Methods In this study, we introduce Model Discovery in Partially Observable Dynamical Systems (Dantzer, 2023b ), which we also implement as an open-source software tool. We present the single input, single output hydrologic analogy of the method here for conciseness. The delay between rainfall (P  ) and runoff (Q  ) is typically thought of in terms of time, but can also be conceptualized as a gap in observability. Though we perceive delayed causation, the processes between rainfall and runoff (e.g., soil saturation, flow routing) are actually instantaneous. It is our inability to fully observe the catchment that gives the appearance  of delay. Instead of finding the time-shift between precipitation and discharge, we represent this delayed and diffused causation by optimally estimating the unit hydrographs of the effective subcatchments (unobserved states) within the watershed. We then learn a differential equation relating these subcatchment unit hydrographs to the measured hydrograph. Young’s data-based mechanistic modeling approach has similar aims and results, but addresses partial observability by including pure delay terms in the differential equations used to model the system (Young, 2012, 2006 ). Genetic programming approaches also tend to represent delay as “pure” or “advective” (Babovic and Abbott, 1997b ). Modeling the delay and dispersion between rainfall and runoff as intervening unobservable states has origins at least as old as Nash’s suggestion (Nash, 1959 ) of a cascade of linear reservoirs to approximate a unit hydrograph. Sugawara’s Tank model (Lee et al., 2020; Chadalawada et al., 2020; Herath et al., 2021b,a ) has a different topology, but evinces the same notion. The approach presented here is similar, but more dynamically flexible and amenable to real-time data ingestion. The catchment is thought of as being composed of effective subcatchments (Fig. 2 ) that represent not geographic areas, but constituent processes such as surface runoff, tributary contribution, or interflow. In our formulation, the only sources of data to estimate the parameters of these subcatchments are rainfall and streamflow. We achieve this by transforming the rainfall forward to estimate the unit hydrographs and then using those unit hydrographs to learn the differential equation that governs the discharge. 3.1 Watersheds as dynamical systems of subcatchments We approximate the subcatchment unit hydrographs using a gamma probability density function (Eq. (1) ). This function has been used for approximating unit hydrographs in prior studies (Ghorbani et al., 2017; Nadarajah, 2007; Haktanir and Sezen, 1990 ): (1) g ( t + d , α , β )  = β  α   t  α − 1   e  − β t    ( α − 1 )  !       where β   is the rate or inverse scale, α   is the shape, and d   is the location. These parameters have interpretable meanings in the context of hydrologic dynamics. Decreasing the β   parameter delays and broadens the peak of the unit hydrograph. The α   parameter controls asymmetry about the peak (skewness). The delay parameter (d  ) shifts the transformation in time without affecting shape. The time to peak is T  p   = α − 1  β   + d   . Note that α ≥ 1    in this study. The similar expression T  50   = α  β   + d    is the time at which half the total contribution has been made. T  50     can be thought of as the mean or center of gravity of the transformations shown in dotted red and dotted yellow in Fig. 2 . The approximations of the subcatchment unit hydrographs are evaluated by how strongly they connect observed precipitation (p  o    ) with observed runoff (q  o    ) through the following differential equation: (2) d q  o    d t   = f ( q  o   , p  o   , T  i   ( p  o   )  )      where d q  o    d t     is the instantaneous rate of change of water level or discharge, T  i   ( p  o   )     are the subcatchment unit hydrographs generated by transforming the input rainfall p  o    , and f   is some nonlinear function of compatible dimension. f   is then constrained as follows: (1)  constant bias terms are omitted because d q  o    d t     is not a function of time, (2)  interaction terms are omitted because the instantaneous interaction between rain and stage has no physically meaningful interpretation, and (3)  only polynomial terms are included because they are sufficient to capture the dynamics at the resolution we desire (Taylor’s Theorem). This yields: (3) d q  o    d t   = P  q   ( q  o   )  + P  p   ( p  o   , T  i   ( p  o   )  )      where P  q     and P  p     are polynomials excluding the zero order term. P  q     describes the shape of the recession curve as it is the autocorrelation on stage or discharge. P  p     describes the contributions of the instantaneous precipitation p  o     and subcatchment unit hydrographs T  i   ( p  o   )    . The most complex models trained in this study will have polynomial order three and two effective subcatchment unit hydrographs. They have the form: (4) d q  o    d t   = a  1   q  o   + a  2   q  o  2   + a  3   q  o  3   + b  01   p  o   + b  02   p  o  2   + b  03   p  o  3      + b  11   T  1   ( p  o   )  + b  12   T  1   ( p  o   )   2   + b  13   T  1   ( p  o   )   3   + b  21   T  2   ( p  o   )  + b  22   T  2   ( p  o   )   2   + b  23   T  2   ( p  o   )   3         All results presented in this study will be produced by models which are no more than this ordinary differential equation and six unit hydrograph parameters that describe the shapes of T  1     and T  2    . This model configuration has 18 parameters. The differential equations are integrated using the Explicit Runge–Kutta method of order 5 provided by Scipy’s solve ivp function (Virtanen et al., 2020 ).    3.2 Approximating the subcatchment unit hydrographs using data The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) (de Silva et al., 2020 ) algorithm is used to predict the derivative of the output using Eq. (3) . We denote x  i  ′     as the measured derivative and y  i  ′     as our estimate. The established SINDy implementation chooses the coefficients of the differential equation (P  q     and P  p    ) to maximize the coefficient of determination (R  2    ) between the observed and predicted derivative. (5) max  P  q   , P  p     1 − ∑ ( x  i  ′   − y  i  ′   )   2    ∑ ( x  i  ′   − x  ′    ̄   )   2            Finding optimal differential equation coefficients (a  i   , b  j     ) is the inner loop. The outer loop is the optimization of the subcatchment unit hydrographs (T  i    ) shown in Algorithm 1. As there is no analytical derivative this optimization is performed via compass search. The steps proceed as follows: (1) : The algorithm starts with one subcatchment and evaluates increasing numbers of subcatchments until the maximum number is reached or the last one added less than 0.5% to the R  2     score. If the returns of the last one added are marginal, it is removed and the model with one less subcatchment is returned as the final model. That is, if the j  th subcatchment produces marginal returns, the model with j   rainfall transformations is the last to be evaluated and a model with j − 1    transformations is returned. If m = m  m a x      delivers non-marginal returns on accuracy, the model with m  m a x     subcatchments is returned. Note that for this study we build models of one and two effective subcatchments and evaluate both. (2) : An initial guess is chosen for the subcatchment unit hydrograph. For records with more than one event (Fig. 3  and beyond) the first transformation is Eq. (1)  with parameters ( α , β , d )  = ( 1 , 1 , 0 )     and additional transformations are broader peaks centered at timesteps 24, 48, and so on. For records of only one event (Figs. 1 and 2 ), the starting shapes are based on timesteps of maximum derivative in the output. By identifying timesteps with large derivatives we are attempting to identify distinct events or times of arrival in the delayed causation between input and output. As identifying these times of arrival is less clear when multiple driving events occur, a simpler heuristic is used in that case. (3) : Larger s   corresponds to a larger perturbation. So the optimization begins looking at large perturbations and converges to small steps. (4) : Candidate unit hydrographs are generated by perturbing the shape of the last iteration’s best performing transformation. The perturbations are scaled by s  . In this paper we evaluate eight perturbations, but that number is not specific to this application. Rather, it is because we define the optimization space to have four axes: one for each of the three parameter values (α , β , d   ) and a fourth which changes α   and β   at the same time. This fourth direction changing α   and β   at the same time makes the distribution wider or narrower without affecting its center of mass. (5) : The 9 input transformations (8 perturbations and the best from last time) are scored by how well the differential equation identification procedure performs as measured by R  2    . (6) : The best performing input transformation is saved. (7) : If the best performing input transformation is the same as last iteration, none of the perturbations were helpful. s   is reduced by the factor α  . If s   is now less than one, the algorithm will exit the loop at (3) . If the best performing input transformation is not the same as the last iteration, a step was taken that did improve performance. In that case, we return to (4) .    Algorithm 1.
