1 Introduction The distribution and impact of marine microplastics (MPs) is a growing concern in the field of environmental science and marine biology (Clark et al., 2016 ). In fact, according to recent estimations, the oceans may currently contain a staggering amount of plastic debris with an upper limit of roughly 3 . 57 ⋅ 1 0  14      pieces and weighing approximately 4 . 86 ⋅ 1 0  6      tons (Eriksen et al., 2023 ). Even if the term “microplastic” refers to small plastic particles (or residuals) with a broad size spectrum, the upper limit is conventionally established at 5 millimeters (Eriksen et al., 2014 ). However, this criterion appears too simplistic to properly describe the vast variety of synthetic debris present in marine systems. As a result, recent studies (Hartmann et al., 2019; Frias and Nash, 2019 ) have emphasized the need for a more refined approach to categorize MPs. The key suggestion is to incorporate additional factors into the definition, such as composition (type of polymer), physical state (solid and insoluble at ambient temperature), and potentially shape (Hartmann et al., 2019 ). The main sources of MPs in marine systems include discarded plastic products, fibers from clothing and textiles, and microbeads from personal care products (Bashir et al., 2021 ). Once they reach the seas and oceans, they can interact with the flora and fauna by, for example, entering the food chain through ingestion by marine organisms, including zooplankton, invertebrates & fish (Derraik, 2002 ), and eventually reach humans. In this regard, ongoing research efforts aim to better understand the sources (Coyle et al., 2020 ), motion & distribution (Kooi et al., 2017; Rahmani et al., 2022 ), and effects (Bhuyan, 2022 ) of MPs in marine ecosystems, with the ultimate goal of finding ways to mitigate their consequences on both marine life and human health (Eerkes-Medrano et al., 2015; Sutherland et al., 2023 ). One of the main challenges is the so-called “missing plastic” problem: viz. out of the 8   metric tons of plastic entering the ocean every year, on average, only 1  % has been found floating at the surface (van Sebille et al., 2015 ). The prevailing hypothesis suggests that the primary reason is the sinking of lighter-than-water plastic debris to deeper layers of the oceans (Woodall et al., 2014 ). As recently suggested and analyzed (Kooi et al., 2017; Rahmani et al., 2022; Michels et al., 2018 ), this phenomenon may be connected to the presence of biogenic material within marine environments, which contribute to the formation of (i) biofilm on plastic debris, and (ii) aggregates composed of MPs and biogenic particles (BPs). Specifically, biogenic particles include living and dead zooplankton, phytoplankton and bacteria with sizes ranging 1 μ  m to 1 cm and densities varying between 1050 to 2700 kg/m  3     (Rahmani et al., 2022 ), and consequently their amassment with MPs may result in aggregates heavier than seawater. Additionally, the formation of biofilms is characterized by complex communities of microorganisms, which have significant impact on the physical and chemical properties of MPs (Kooi et al., 2017 ) by changing their buoyancy, toxicity, stickiness and persistence in marine environments. This process is termed “biofouling” and has a particularly pronounced effect on smaller particles, primarily because they have a larger relative surface area. Consequently, smaller particles tend to lose their buoyancy more rapidly compared to larger ones (Fazey and Ryan, 2016 ). In this regard, the scientific community is actively addressing the challenge of understanding biofilm formation and growth on microplastics (Kooi et al., 2017 ) by analyzing factors like water chemistry, microbial community composition, and plastic properties (Flemming, 2010 ). However, there is no consensus on the impact of flow conditions (e.g., turbulence intensity) on biofilm dynamics (Tsagkari et al., 2019; Teodósio et al., 2011 ). The issue stems from the conflicting effects of turbulent shear stresses, which simultaneously enhance nutrient diffusion and erode the biofilm through mechanical stresses. The formation of biofilm on MPs in oceanic environments and its interaction with BPs leads to the formation of aggregates of different sizes and composition. The aggregation process comprises two distinct stages (Burd and Jackson, 2009 ): (i) the collision phase, primarily influenced by the flow properties of the medium; and (ii) the adhesion phase, which is contingent upon physico-chemical factors, such as nutrient concentration in the medium, the biogenic species involved, and various environmental conditions (Kiørboe and Andersen, 1990 ). Cohesive interactions between particles can arise from various forces, such as electrostatic, van der Waals, liquid bridging, and magnetic forces (Balakin et al., 2012 ). These effects can be studied and quantified for a small number of particles (Zhang et al., 2022 ), but limitations arise when the systems become larger in number of particles and/or more complex. Indeed, examining the aggregation processes of particles occurring in ocean turbulence is a daunting challenge due to the intricate nature of the problem, which involves a vast number of particles, a turbulent flow carrier phase, and various biophysical properties associated with biofilms and BPs. In order to shift from a microscopic analysis to a global quantification in which large numbers of particles interact, the coagulation efficiency or stickiness parameter has been introduced (Kiørboe and Andersen, 1990; Burd and Jackson, 2009; Jackson, 1995 ). The stickiness is essentially the proportion of actual coalescence events to the overall number of collisions. Therefore, it can span values between 0   (no adhesion) and 1   (perfect adhesion). In this context, numerous studies and analyses have been conducted to assess how the type of biogenic particles, salinity, and environmental factors (Chen et al., 2021 ), such as nutrient conditions (Kiørboe and Andersen, 1990 ) and concentration (Balakin et al., 2012 ), impact the stickiness coefficient α  , revealing that this parameter is highly responsive to each of these factors, as they can alter the electro-chemical conditions, and ultimately render models quite intricate to calibrate. Interestingly, variations in stickiness coefficient values have been also related to flow conditions (Thomas and H.J.L.S, 1993 ), showing a general trend to decrease with increasing turbulence intensity. The primary objective of this study, therefore, is to examine the impact of the stickiness parameter α  , which quantifies the adhesive nature of biofouled MPs and BPs on the behavior of particles and aggregation phenomena. More precisely, a sensitivity analysis is conducted by considering three values of stickiness (α = 1 / 3 , 2 / 3 , 3 / 3   ) for three different cases of microparticles combination. The analysis of the effects of the stickiness parameter on the distribution and aggregation of particles provides the essential information for how MPs interact with biogenic material and how this interaction changes their tendency to sink/float. With these objectives in mind, the paper is structured in the following manner. Section 2  presents the physical models and mathematical framework utilized to describe the fluid flow and the discrete phase (microparticles), together with the discussion of the dimensionless numbers characterizing the problem. The second part of Section 2  is dedicated to the presentation of the coagulation theory and, specifically, the modeling approach for the stickiness parameter. This is followed by Section 2.3  describing the problem setup and data generated. Next, Section 3  presents the results and their discussion. Finally, the paper concludes by summarizing the key contributions and their implications in Section 4 .  2 Material and methods 2.1 Physical models The problem of marine MPs can be studied from the perspective of particle-laden turbulence (Rahmani et al., 2022 ); viz. turbulent flow (carrier phase) interacting with particles (dispersed phase). In this regard, from a mathematical point of view, the present work makes use of the point-particle (PP) Lagrangian-Eulerian (LE) direct numerical simulation (DNS) approach as its properties are advantageous for the application of interest, e.g., applicability to a wide range of mass loading fractions and Stokes numbers, and ability to represent particle–particle collisions (Burd and Jackson, 2009 ). The representation of particles as Lagrangian points is motivated by the fact that their size is considerably smaller than the smallest relevant (Kolmogorov) flow scales. Therefore, the N  p     particles can be approximated as infinitesimally small Lagrangian points. The masses of particles are defined as m  p   = ( π / 6 )  ρ  p   d  p  3      with ρ  p     and d  p     being their densities and diameters, respectively, and their time-dependent positions and velocities are denoted by x  p     and v  p    . 2.1.1 Eulerian description of turbulent flow Under the assumptions of isothermal, incompressible flow conditions, and by choosing the fluid density ρ  f    , dynamic viscosity μ  f    , Taylor microscale λ  , and root-mean-square velocity fluctuations U  r m s     as scaling parameters (Jofre et al., 2020b ), the dimensionless continuity and Navier–Stokes equations read (Jofre et al., 2017, 2020a ) (1) ∇ ⋅ u  f   = 0 ,    (2) ∂ u  f    ∂ t   + ∇ ⋅ u  f   ⊗ u  f     = − ∇ p + 1  R e  λ     Δ u  f   + f  TWC   ,       where u  f     and p   are, respectively, the dimensionless fluid velocity and pressure, and R e  λ   = U  r m s   λ / ν  f      is the Taylor Reynolds number with ν  f   = μ  f   / ρ  f      being the kinematic viscosity of the fluid. The term f  TWC     corresponds to the two-way coupling term representing the effect of particle forces on the fluid, which is defined as (3) f  TWC   = ∑  k = 1  N  s     Φ  m  k      S t  λ  k     N  p  k       ∑  p = 1  N  p  k       v  p   − u  p     δ x − x  p     ,     with u  p     being the dimensionless fluid velocity at particle locations, N  s     the number of particle classes, and δ x − x  p        the Dirac delta function concentrated at the particle positions. Defining the flow and particles relaxation times as τ  λ   = λ / U  r m s      and τ  p   = ρ  p   d  p  2   / ( 18 μ  f   )    , respectively, the Stokes number S t  λ   = τ  p   / τ  λ      based on the Taylor microscale is obtained. Finally, Φ  m   = ρ  p   Φ  v   / ρ  f      is the mass fraction of particles in the fluid, with Φ  v   = N  p   m  p   / ( ρ  p   / L  3   )     being the corresponding volume fraction.  2.1.2 Lagrangian representation of particles Consistent with typical conditions encountered in marine environments, particles and aggregates in their early stages of formation are significantly smaller than the Kolmogorov flow scale η = λ / 1 5  1 / 4   R e  λ  1 / 2      [assuming homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT)], i.e., d  p   / η ≪ 1   . Furthermore, the influence of settling/rising velocity is neglected due to its relatively large time scale τ  s     when compared to τ  λ     (see Table 2 ). Moreover, following the values described in the literature (Rahmani et al., 2022 ), the density ratios between particles and fluid are fixed to ρ  p   / ρ  f   = 0 . 97    for MPs and ρ  p   / ρ  f   = 1 . 46    for BPs. As a result, the description of particles in terms of dimensionless positions and velocities is given by (4) d x  p    d t   = v  p   ,    (5) d v  p    d t   = u  p   − v  p    S t  λ  k       .       Particularly, in this work, it is assumed that the particles forming an aggregate are assembled into a spherical, packed configuration (equivalent to assuming a fractal dimension of d  f   = 3   ), and the resultant aggregate follows the Lagrangian PP equations of motion and collision given by (4) –(5) . The density of the aggregate is computed as ρ  agg   = ∑  p   m  p   / ∑  p   V  p      and its diameter is calculated as d  agg   = ( ∑  p   d  p  3   )   1 / 3     , where the sums are over all the particles composing the aggregate. Finally, in the context of PP approximations, interactions between particles are usually characterized using collision models that rely on the conservation of the total momentum and energy (Rahmani et al., 2022 ).     2.2 Coagulation theory & stickiness parameter Multiple approaches are available in the literature to model the adhesion between two or more particles (Kiørboe and Andersen, 1990; Balakin et al., 2012; Burd and Jackson, 2009 ). The simplest approach assumes that particles (or aggregates) coalesce at impact (Rahmani et al., 2022 ). In this work, however, a more realistic strategy that relies on coagulation theory (Burd and Jackson, 2009 ) through the utilization of the stickiness parameter (coagulation efficiency) α   is considered. This strategy is based on modeling the time-evolution of particle size spectrum n  , which is function of mass m   and time t  , through the coagulation equation (Smoluchowski, 1916 ) (6) d n m , t    d t   = α  2   ∫  0  m   β m  j   , m − m  j     n m − m  j   , t   n m  j   , t   d m  j   −  α n m , t   ∫  0  ∞   β m , m  j     n m  j   , t   d m  j   − n m , t   U  s   m    Z   + I m , t   ,      where Z   represents the water depth, U  s     is the settling velocity, and I   is the input rate of particles. The first term on the right-hand side accounts for collisions that add elements within the spectrum range m , m + d m    , while the second term describes the collisions that remove elements from the same range. The third and fourth terms, respectively, indicate the loss rate due to settling and the input rate of new particles. Finally, β   corresponds to the coagulation kernel, describing the collision rate between particles of masses m  i     and m  j    . In this work, the main focus will be on studying the effects of α  , whose dependence on microscopic forces has been observed (Han et al., 1997; Vanni and Baldi, 2002; Thomas et al., 1999 ), and can be generalized as (Balakin et al., 2012 ) (7) α = α F l , S t  λ   , D  c   / d  p   , E / μ  f   γ     ,     where F l = 6 π μ  f   γ d  p  3     / 8 A      is the flow number quantifying the interplay between van der Waals attraction and repulsion forces induced by the flow, A   is the Hamaker constant, and γ   is the mean flow shear rate. The last two parameters correspond, respectively, to the agglomeration efficiency related to the minimum distance between particles D  c    , and the ratio of particle stiffness E   (Young’s modulus) to flow stiffness μ  f   γ   . Table 1  shows the range of the stickiness parameter of biogenic debris reported in the literature as well as the expressions proposed. However, in the present study, since the biophysical timescales that control the stickiness of particles [O ( 1 0  4   )   s   ] are significantly larger than the flow timescales [O ( 1 0  0   )   s   , see Table 2 ], implementing a time-dependent stickiness parameter will not have any influence on the aggregation process. Therefore, constant values of 1/2, 2/3, and 3/3 are considered for α  . These values represent typical conditions found in laboratory experiments for algae species and diatom bloom (Jackson, 1995; Engel, 2000 ); see Table 1 . A unitary stickiness value has been measured, e.g., in the initial conditions of the diatom bloom, attributed to a high concentration of transparent exopolymer particle (TEP) and chlorophyll (Dam and Drapeau, 1995 ). Conversely, smaller values are indicative of species such as Emiliana huxleyi in a more developed stage (Chen et al., 2021 ).  2.3 Numerical experiments As represented in Fig. 1 , the process of the aggregation of microparticles in seawater systems encompasses several complex phenomena. In detail, Fig. 1 (a) illustrates the problematic of MPs in marine environments, which may become even more prevalent in the coming decades if policy measures are not implemented as estimated in Fig. 1 (b). In this regard, to comprehend the mechanisms of particles aggregation, computational tools are necessary. For instance, DNS approaches, schematically shown in Fig. 1 (c), prove particularly useful as they enable a comprehensive analysis and access to detailed information of the physics involved. In addition, as shown in Fig. 1 (d), the present model incorporates two classes of particles dispersed in a turbulent marine upper layer [Fig. 1 (e)], and influenced by chaotic flow motion [Fig. 1 (f)]. The subsections below will provide a detailed description of the problem setup, computational approach and simulation parameters.   The setup of the problem considers a periodic cubic domain of size L = 0 . 5  m    containing a mixture of HIT and particles as depicted in Fig. 1 (c). In the upper ocean, the wind-driven turbulence mixes the water column (Burchard et al., 2008 ) similar to HIT. The fluid density and dynamic viscosity are assumed to be ρ  f   = 1027  kg/m  3      and μ  f   = 1 . 41 ⋅ 1 0  − 3    Pa  s   , respectively, which are representative of seawater at 10   ∘   C   . The fluid phase is volumetrically driven by means of a turbulence forcing scheme (Bassenne et al., 2016 ) targeted to produce an average turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) k = ( 3 / 2 )  U  r m s  2      such that the ratio between domain size and Kolmogorov length scale is L / η ∼ O ( 1 0  2   )    , and therefore the small-scale features of the flow are not affected by the triply periodic boundaries. The root-mean-square velocity fluctuations U  r m s   = 4 . 3 ⋅ 1 0  − 3    m/s    and Taylor microscale λ = 1 . 95 ⋅ 1 0  − 2    m    of the flow are selected to represent wind-induced turbulence with R e  λ   ≈ 60    as characterized by a wind speed of 4  m/s    (Thorpe et al., 2003 ). The principal time scales of the problem for the particle sizes considered are summarized in Table 2 . In this table the settling/rising velocity of particles, taking into account the added mass effects, is U  s   = [ 1 − 3 ρ  f   / ( 2 ρ  p   + ρ  f   )  ]  g τ  p      with g   being the gravitational force. As the settling/rising time scales of the particles are relatively large compared to other time scales, including particle settling/rising has been deferred to future work, and therefore in the simulations the settling/rising velocity of particles is set to U  s   = 0   . The Kolmogorov time scale is estimated based on the kinematic viscosity ν  f     of the fluid and TKE dissipation rate ɛ   as τ  η   = ( ν  f   / ɛ )   1 / 2     . The dispersed phase is initialized after the flow reaches turbulent steady-state conditions with N  p  1       and N  p  2       randomly distributed particles representative of microplastics and biogenic particles, respectively. Following the ranges provided by Nowald et al. (2006), Eerkes-Medrano et al. (2015)  and Monroy et al. (2017) , the density of microplastics is set to ρ  p  1     = 1000  kg/m  3      and the density of biogenic particles is prescribed to ρ  p  2     = 1500  kg/m  3     , while the diameters and number densities of particles are chosen to vary for the 3 different cases studied as described in Table 3 . As a result, the Stokes numbers of the particles for the different cases remain inherently small. Regarding the number density of microplastics in seawater systems, there is a large disparity of values between published works. For example, in cold ocean regions, values of roughly 100  prts/m  3      have been measured (Frias et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Tekman et al., 2020 ), whereas a wide range of values have been observed in other aquatic systems, like in the Mediterranean Sea (Adamopoulou et al., 2021 ). In this work, thus, number density values of order 1 0  7      have been selected to propitiate the study of collision and aggregation between MPs and BPs. Table 3  also provides the values of mixture volume fraction, which are calculated as Φ  v   = N  p  1     Φ  v  1     + N  p  2     Φ  v  2       / N  p  1     + N  p  2         .   2.3.1 Computational approach The equations of fluid motion (1) –(2)  are discretized by means of second-order central finite differences implemented in an in-house flow solver (Esmaily et al., 2015, 2018 ) with support for non-uniform Cartesian meshes. A fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme is used for integrating the equations in time, together with a fractional-step method for imposing conservation of mass (Jofre et al., 2014 ). The linear system resulting from the Poisson equation utilized to impose mass conservation is solved via a fast Fourier transform (FFT) solver. Integration in time of the Lagrangian position, velocity and collision of particles (4) –(5)  is fully coupled with the advancement of the flow equations to ensure fourth-order accuracy. The collision and aggregation of particles is controlled by a specific kernel carefully designed to detect particle interactions and generate aggregates as described in Section 2.1.2  (Rahmani et al., 2022 ). This multiphysics computational flow solver has been extensively developed, verified, and validated in a plethora of different particle-laden turbulent flow problems (Fairbanks et al., 2020; Dunton et al., 2017, 2020; Esmaily et al., 2020; Jofre et al., 2020b,a ). The conservation equations are solved on a computational domain discretized by 196 × 196 × 196 uniform grid points with resolution η / Δ ∼ O ( 1 )     to capture the Kolmogorov scale, and integrated in time together with the particles motion and collision by prescribing a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) condition (Courant et al., 1928 ) of CFL = 0 . 3   . For cases A and C, simulations are advanced in time for 5   Taylor time scales τ  λ    , while 1   flow relaxation time is considered for case B due to its significantly large number of particles, which results in significantly high computational costs.    3 Results & discussion The subsections below present and discuss the results of the computational experiments listed in Table 3 . Case A exhibits a lower particle size and number density, whereas Case B and C showcase higher number density and particle size, respectively. Additionally, each case involves three different levels of stickiness. The focus is first placed on analyzing the spatio-temporal distribution of particles. Next, the study delves into the rates of collision and coalescence, along with characterizing the underlying mechanisms. Finally, the analysis turns to the composition of the resulting aggregates. Throughout the analyses, careful consideration will be given to distinguish between MPs, BPs and their combined effects. 3.1 Particle collision & coalescence rates The normalized collision and coalescence rates of particles are shown in Fig. 2 . As it can be observed, the influence of number density and particle sizes on the evolution of these two quantities is significant; viz. larger particles exhibit a greater propensity for collision and subsequent coalescence. This observation holds true for higher volume fractions of particles as well. Furthermore, while the collisions seem to be affected by the stickiness of particles α  , the coalescence curves do not show marked differences. For cases A and C with α = 1   , the asymptotic levels do not show clear oscillations, suggesting that the highest probability of attachment leads to a faster establishment of a steady-state particle dynamics, primarily because collisions are not continuously sustained. Because both the collision and coalescence curves do not present substantial changes in the final times, i.e., 1 ≤ t / τ  λ   ≤ 5    (and partly for case B), a time-averaged estimation of the steady-state values has been performed with the results plotted in the collision (g) and coalescence (h) regime diagrams of Fig. 2 . The contrasting tendencies between collision and coalescence rates are evident in the distinct locations of their peak values. For collisions, the maximum occurs at higher volume fractions, corresponding to case C with low stickiness. In contrast, for coalescence, the peaks are observed at α = 1   . The substantial increase of both parameters is primarily dependent on the volume fraction Φ  v     rather than α  , suggesting that particle properties, rather than the physico-chemical features, play a crucial role in these scenarios.    3.2 Particle distribution & preferential concentration As particle distribution reaches a steady-state at larger times, the analysis will be conducted using the final time for each simulated case. To examine the spatial disposition of particles and their tendency to gather in specific flow regions, leading to eventual collision-coalescence-aggregation events, the radial distribution function (RDF) is employed. The RDF enables to quantify the probability of finding MPs or BPs at a specific distance from a reference particle, normalized by the expected probability in a homogeneous random distribution (Ray and Collins, 2011 ). Mathematically, RDFs can be computed for a set of M   particles by binning them according to their separation distance and calculating (8) g r   = N  r    V  r     V  N   ,     where N  r     is the number of particle pairs in a spherical element of volume V  r     with radius r   from a test particle location, N = M ( M − 1 )  / 2    is the total number of particle pairs in the volume, and V   is the total volume. In this regard, Fig. 3  displays RDFs as a function of the average particle radii 〈 r  p   〉  = r  p  1     N  p  1     + r  p  2     N  p  2       / N  p  1     + N  p  2         . Although MPs and BPs exhibit a tendency to attain an homogeneous spatial distribution [g r   = 1    in plots (a), (b), and (c)] as they mostly act as flow tracers due to the small S t  λ      values, their behavior changes when considered collectively. In other words, when considering a reference particle, it is more likely to find a different class of particle around it rather than the same type. This is clearly shown in plots (g), (h) and (i) of Fig. 3 , where the MPs-BPs combination g r   ≥ 1    for a distance covering at least 15 particle radius. This effect is illustrated, for clarity, in plot (j). In this particular instance, approximately 12000 particles (evenly distributed between MPs and BPs) are present. Nonetheless, as depicted in the zoomed-in plots, BPs and MPs tend to approach each other spatially. The underlying mechanism, graphically illustrated in the bottom schematic, explaining this behavior corresponds to: MPs, being particles lighter than the fluid, tend to migrate towards vorticity-dominated flow regions, while BPs, being heavier than the fluid, concentrate in high-strain zones away from vortices (Balachandar and Eaton, 2010 ). Notably, the impact of stickiness is discernible in case A (left column), as the distinct curves display varying values. In contrast, the distinctive characteristic of case B is the higher values reached by the BPs-BPs combination, attributable to the substantial presence of biogenic particles (see Table 3 ).    3.3 Temporal evolution of aggregates The temporal evolution of the characteristics of aggregates encompasses factors such as number of particles, size, density ratio with respect to the fluid and composition. Additionally, key parameters, such as Stokes number and volume fraction, are quantified for aggregates showing that properties are closely linked to the behavior of the initial particles. In particular, Fig. 4  shows the time-evolution of the number of aggregates (normalized by the total number of individual particles) together with the cubic domain to qualitatively illustrate the distribution of aggregates. In general, after a steep transition, between 0 ≤ t / τ  λ   ≤ 0 . 2    where the initially randomly distributed particles start to coalesce and generate the first aggregates, the curves exhibit a linear trend, and the influence of stickiness merely shifts the values for each given case. Notably, there is no clear pattern with respect to α  . For case A, overlaps are observed across three distinct stickiness levels. Conversely, case B, characterized by a significantly higher particle count, presents the highest number of aggregates for the smallest α  . This result may seem counter-intuitive, as lower stickiness values should theoretically lead to a reduced probability of coalescence. However, due to a negative feedback loop, higher stickiness hinders optimal particle collision, consequently impeding the likelihood of coalescence. Generally, the number of aggregates is orders of magnitude lower than the initial particle count. For such dilute systems, therefore, the formation of aggregates relative to the turbulent flow scales is quite infrequent.  Following the analysis of Fig. 4 , in the corresponding cubic domains on the right, specifically for α = 1    (owing to its similarity with other stickiness values), several phenomena can be observed: (i) there is a notable variation in spatial distribution among the different cases, accompanied by differing diameter distributions; (ii) case C exhibits a high concentration of aggregates, primarily distributed within a range characterized by (relatively) medium-small diameters (depicted in white/yellow colors), with only a few sparse aggregates approximately twice the original particle mixture diameter; (iii) in contrast, case A generates aggregates predominantly of relatively large size (depicted in dark colors); and (iv) intriguingly, case B produces the smallest aggregates, rarely exceeding the average diameter of the original mixture. Observation (iv), as will be elaborated in Section 3.4 , can be attributed to the 2 ×    number of initial biogenic particles, each half the diameter of MPs, contributing more significantly to the aggregation phenomena.  With the aim of determining whether aggregates tend to sink or float — a crucial consideration in environmental scenarios (Michels et al., 2018; Kooi et al., 2017 ) —, the subsequent analysis is devoted to estimating the ratio between aggregate and fluid densities. To that end, Fig. 5  illustrates the percentage of aggregates with density lower than that of the surrounding fluid for cases A, B and C, which remarkably exhibit varying percentages of “light” aggregates. In case A, there is a notable difference among the three stickiness values, with α = 1    showing the highest values. However, as time progresses, the curves for the three stickiness values converge. Conversely, case B displays a much lower percentage of light aggregates. The discrepancy between case B and the other two is attributed to the abundance of heavier biogenic material. As a result, the aggregates tend to be, on average, heavier than those in other cases. On the other hand, case C exhibits more consistent and uniform behavior, and the values remain nearly constant between 50 % < ρ  a g g   / ρ  f   < 52 %   , with intermediate stickiness yielding the denser aggregates. Once again, it is noteworthy to highlight that the stickiness parameter α   does not monotonically influence the final tendency to form heavy aggregates, due to the subtle interplay with particle dynamics. The last plot in Fig. 5 (d) illustrates the positioning of aggregates with respect to the contour field representing the Q-criterion Q = 1 / 2 ‖ Ω ‖  2   − ‖ S ‖  2       . In the region where Q > 0    the flow field is vortex-dominated, while the regions with Q < 0    are strain-dominated (Rahmani et al., 2022 ). Aggregates with a lower density (depicted as yellow points) than the surrounding fluid exhibit a tendency to disperse within the vortex regions (as indicated by the yellow arrow highlighting this behavior), conversely, aggregates denser than the fluid (depicted as red points) tend to concentrate in areas characterized by higher strain. This observation aligns with classical particle motion theory (Balachandar and Eaton, 2010 ).  3.4 Characterization of aggregates To finalize the analysis, the investigation is extended to the composition of the aggregates at the final simulation time, as the aggregates are more developed. As shown in Fig. 6 , the quantitative characterization of different types of aggregates is presented in the left plots. Generally, aggregates can be classified into two categories: (i) heterogeneous aggregations involving two different species of initial particles, and (ii) homogeneous aggregations where the same type of particles coalesce (Wayman and Niemann, 2021 ). In the present scenario, the heterogeneous entities are substantially simple, consisting of only one microplastic and one biogenic particle. These species represent approximately 40% of the total number of aggregates for cases A and C, and about 50% for case B, owing to the higher concentration of biogenic particles. The significant presence of heterogeneous aggregation can be elucidated by referring to the RDFs analyzed in Fig. 3 , which reveal a preferential concentration of MPs relative to BPs. This category of aggregates has been identified as the preferred pathway for sinking (Michels et al., 2018; Fazey and Ryan, 2016 ). Conversely, homogeneous aggregates are also prevalent, constituting approximately half of the total, and are predominantly composed of MPs. The substantial contribution of MPs, which have double the diameter of BPs, to the coalescence phenomenon results in aggregates that are larger compared to a scenario dominated solely by hetero-aggregation. This result explains why in Fig. 4  cases A and C present large ratios of d  a g g   / 〈 d  p   〉    .  Notably, MPs are significantly more prevalent in the aggregates – a phenomenon also experimentally observed (Michels et al., 2018 ) – even when they are less abundant in the initial mixture. This is proved by case B, where there are more occurrences of the (2,0) combination than (0,2). This underscores that particle sizes is the most influential parameter in initiating the aggregation process. Instead, case A (upper plot) exhibits relatively simple aggregates involving no more than three original particles, whereas case B and, particularly, case C showcase more diverse and rich compositions. Consequently, the number and, notably, the initial size of particles, rather than stickiness, determine the morphology of the aggregates. However the coagulation efficiency α   also has an influence, as it predominantly impacts the formation of more complex aggregates [i.e., combinations with (MPs, BPs) > ( 1 , 1 )    ], which, due to their very low probability, may be categorized as “rare events”. Interestingly, within this category, microplastics are more abundant. This aligns with the observation that MPs tend to aggregate more with older aggregates (Michels et al., 2018 ). To summarize the analysis and categorize the nature of the aggregates, Table 4  presents the averaged values for two key governing parameters, namely the Stokes number and the volume fraction. These values provide valuable insights into the category of particle-flow relationships. The very small values of Φ  a g g  v     indicate that the formed aggregates represent a highly dilute mixture within the flow. Additionally, the small S t  a g g      values suggests that they lack sufficient inertial force to form large aggregates (e.g., marine snow) in time scales comparable to the ones of turbulence.     4 Conclusions This research investigated the distribution and aggregation of microplastics in upper-ocean turbulence through computational experiments. For the first time, a model that combines the physics of particle-laden turbulence with biophysical effects, expressed through the coagulation efficiency, was employed to assess particle motion in ocean turbulence and analyze the formation of microplastic aggregates. The key findings can be summarized as follows. (i) The dynamics and distribution of particle classes, as well as aggregate formation, are primarily governed by the size and number density of microplastics and biogenic particles. Larger initial particles undergo more collisions and tend to form approximately an order of magnitude more aggregates. (ii) The influence of the particles coagulation efficiency α   is complex. Unexpectedly, the largest number of aggregates is not observed for the most sticky particles. This counter-intuitive result arises from the proportional inverse relationship between stickiness and collision rate. (iii) The formation of aggregates is a relatively “rare event” in comparison to the time scales of turbulent flow. In general, the number of aggregates increases linearly with time, exhibiting a relatively small number of particles. Instead, the composition of complex aggregates are highly dependant on stickiness. Given that larger particles contribute the most to the aggregates, it can be concluded that, larger microplastics present in the oceans have a greater effect on the formation of aggregates than smaller biogenic material. Finally, based on the assumptions made for the size/density of BPs/MPs and the negligible settling velocity, (iv) the analyses performed indicate that 50% to 70% of aggregates are lighter than seawater and, therefore, tend to float, while the other 30%–50% present a tendency to sink. These results align with estimates provided in the existing literature. The coagulation efficiency proves to be a crucial parameter in all the studied behaviors, underscoring the significance of not underestimating the complex interactions between biological phenomena and the physics of particle-laden flow in subsequent marine microplastic studies.
1 Introduction This paper is the second part (Part II) of a series of two papers (see van de Craats et al. (2024)  for Part I), in which we consider shallow (fresh) water lenses forming when upward seepage of groundwater and downward infiltration of recharge water occur simultaneously for at least part of the year. Such lenses are typically thin, i.e. at most a few meters, as opposed to the classical situation of lenses forming under coastal dunes, having thicknesses of tens of meters (Badon-Ghijben, 1888 ; Herzberg, 1901 ). Thin water lenses may form in areas with a homogeneous total density such as fen meadows or brook valleys, where they are typically of relevance to nature areas. They may also form in environments with saline groundwater (referred to as freshwater lenses), such as small oceanic islands (e.g. Werner et al., 2013 ), in riparian aquifers (e.g. America et al., 2020 ) and coastal zones (e.g. Cozzolino et al., 2017 ; de Louw et al., 2011 ; Siemon et al., 2019 ; Stofberg et al., 2017 ; Vandenbohede et al., 2014 ). In all cases, these water lenses are of importance as the waters can be of different origin and have experienced different residence times and environments within the soil. This results in distinctly different properties of the two waters in terms of e.g. nutrient status and carbonate content, providing essential gradients for sustaining a high biodiversity (e.g. Antonellini and Mollema, 2010 ; Bedford and Godwin, 2003 ; Cirkel et al., 2014 ) or density and salinity, providing a viable source of fresh water for natural vegetation, crops or even drinking water supply (e.g. America et al., 2020 , Maas, 2007 ; Stofberg et al., 2017 ; Werner et al., 2013 ). Depending on the local conditions and land use, thick (source of fresh water) or thin (gradients in abiotic conditions) lenses may be preferred. In this series of two papers, we are particularly concerned with the mathematical description of flow in a 2D cross section between two outflow faces, which may be e.g. ditches or drains, in areas under the influence of upward seepage. In Part I (van de Craats et al., 2024 ), a general introduction to water lenses is given, including the formulation of equations and boundary conditions describing the fluid flow and solute transport valid for both homogeneous and heterogeneous fluid density. Also in Part I, we considered in detail the steady state and transient behavior of water lenses in a setting with a homogeneous fluid density, including a steady state description of the mixing zone. In this Part II, we focus on both the steady state and transient behavior of water lenses in a setting with a heterogeneous density, considering fresh, infiltrating recharge water floating on top of saline, upward seeping groundwater. The higher density of salt water compared to fresh water results in a buoyant force, which causes freshwater lenses to be thinner compared to a situation with a homogeneous total density (e.g. Eeman et al., (2011) ). In conditions with saline groundwater, also surface waters tend to be highly affected by salts (Delsman et al., 2014 ), rendering this water source unsuited for irrigation. This further amplifies the importance of freshwater residing in these lenses. Understanding the key drivers of freshwater lenses is crucial in order to find potential measures to improve the freshwater availability, and to assess the effects of changing environmental conditions, such as changing weather patterns, land use and sea level rise. In Part I already the general behavior in homogeneous density situations was examined, and in this Part II we extend this analysis to the effects of a heterogeneous density. We build upon the theory outlined in Part I (van de Craats et al., 2024 ). In particular, the problem setting (Section 2 of Part I) and the simplified mathematical model setting (Section 3 of Part I) apply to both the situations with a homogeneous and a heterogeneous total density, and is therefore discussed only briefly in Section 2  of this Part II. In Section 3 , we present a mathematical model description of steady state flow for a heterogeneous total density and analyze example results using the same parameter combinations as used in Part I, except for the density of upward seeping groundwater, which is increased compared to Part I. In Section 4 , we present an example of a transient solution, where we focus on the effect of a heterogeneous fluid density on the change in interface position under oscillatory boundary conditions. These examples are modelled with the mathematical models presented, as well as with the numerical model SUTRA (Voss and Provost, 2002 ).  2 Problem setting In this Part II, we consider a situation which is similar to the situation in Part I (van de Craats et al., 2024 ), where we outlined a mathematical description of the flow in a cross-sectional domain between two drains in a homogeneous and isotropic soil. Rather than assuming a homogeneous density throughout the domain, we now consider a situation with a heterogeneous density, where the density of upward seeping water exceeds the density of downward infiltrating water. The basic theory and underlying equations are identical for both the homogeneous and heterogeneous cases. This section provides a brief summary of Sections 2 and 3  in Part I showing the key equations and assumptions required for this Part II. For details, we refer to Part I (van de Craats et al., 2024 ). We describe the domain D ⊂ R  2     in x  and y , with x  denoting the horizontal coordinate perpendicular to the drain and y  denoting the vertical coordinate, defined positive in the upward direction. The drain is situated at {x  = L, y  = 0}, with L  [dimension: L] being half of the distance between two parallel drains. The drains themselves are situated at depth D  [L] below the soil surface. Due to symmetry of the flow problem, it suffices to describe only half of this cross section. We model this domain with a simplified mathematical model further detailed in this paper, as well as with the numerical finite element model SUTRA version 2.2 (Voss and Provost, 2002 ). The domain as used in SUTRA is given as D n u m   = { ( x , y  ) : 0 < x < L ,  − H < y < D  }     (Fig. 1 A). This domain is chosen to include both the water saturated and unsaturated zones, and therefore the effect of a head buildup midway between the drains. SUTRA considers both the fluid and solute mass balances, where fluid discharge q →  = ( q x  , q y   )     [LT-1 ] is described using Darcy's equation. For flow in the unsaturated zone, the Mualem-van Genuchten expressions are used to describe the water retention and permeability characteristics. The solute mass balance is described using the convection-diffusion equation, where dispersion and diffusion of solutes are represented by Fick's first law. Density effects are accounted for by means of a linear dependence of the fluid density on the solute mass fraction. A simplified mathematical model allowing analytical analyses was presented in Part I, which holds for situations with both homogeneous and heterogeneous fluid density. This simplified model employs three simplifying assumptions compared to the complete numerical model:1. The vertical domain changes to (Fig. 1 B)D = { ( x , y  )  : 0 < x < L ,  − ∞ < y < 0  }  ,        such that the drain is situated in the corner point {x  = L, y  = 0}.2. The soil is fully saturated.  3. The Boussinesq approximation holds, meaning that we impose a constant fluid density, except in the gravity term of the Darcy equation.    Combining these assumptions with the fluid mass balance and Darcy's equation results in (Eq. Similar to Part I, we separate our domain into two parts, which we refer to as the recharge part D N    and the seepage part D K   . They are indicated in Fig. 1 B in blue and red, respectively. In D N    resides recharge water which entered the domain at the top (y  = 0). In D K    resides seepage water which entered the domain at the bottom (y  = −∞). The interface between the two types of water is the major focus of our analyses, as this determines the maximum depth of the freshwater lens and thus also the lens volume. In the simplified mathematical model, the interface is assumed to be sharp since solute convection and dispersion are disregarded. This is in contrast to the SUTRA model, where diffusion and dispersion of solutes result in a diffuse interface, referred to as mixing zone, between the recharge and seepage water. With SUTRA, we obtain an estimate of the interface position as function of x  by taking the first moment of the concentration gradient in the vertical direction. In steady state, the interface I  [L], being a continuous increasing function of x , is given as the streamline where ψ = 0, as imposed by the boundary conditions (5) :(6) ψ ( x , y  )  = 0 ⇔ y = I ( x )   for   0 < x ≤ L .      The boundary conditions in terms of ψ (5)  and the definition of the interface (6)  imply that ψ ≤ 0 across the boundary of D N    and ψ ≥ 0 across the boundary of D K   . Using the strong maximum principle (Alt and van Duijn, 1990 ), we therefore conclude that(7) ψ 〈 0  in   D N   and   ψ  〉  0  in   D K  . The problem is that (23)  depends on the interface shape along the entire transect. This makes (numerical) iterative procedures highly non-trivial. In the next section we propose an approximate procedure. Note that the interface should satisfy the following constraints:(i). Near the drain, the interface has an inclination which does not depend on the density difference, but solely on the flux ratio K /N . At x  = L , the interface intersects the drain, such that(24c) I ( L )  = 0 .          3.1.2 Approximation of the interface position midway between the drains In search of an approximation of the interface position, we limit ourselves to finding the interface location midway between the drains (x, y ) = (0, I (0)), a position which was also of special interest in Part I, see Eq. (33) in van de Craats et al. (2024) ), i.e.(39) I h o m   ( x )  = L π  ln ( sin ( K N + K    π x  2 L    )   sin ( 2 N + K  N + K    π x  2 L    )    )  ,     in the right hand side of (36) . Setting(40) f ( I h o m   ( 0 )   )  = − 1 π  ∫ 0 L  R e { w −  }  d d ζ   ( d I h o m    d ζ   1 + ( d I h o m    d ζ   )   2    )  d ζ + 1 π  ∫ 0 L  I m { w +  }  d d ζ   ( 1 1 + ( d I h o m    d ζ   )   2    )  d ζ ,     we obtain from (28)  the approximation(41) I f  ( 0 )  = L π  ln ( K + γ f ( I h o m   ( 0 )   )   2 N + K − γ f ( I h o m   ( 0 )   )    )  .      Obviously, the accurateness of Ihom  (x ) with respect to the actual interface position I (x ) depends on the choice of parameters, and in particular the fluid density difference between infiltrating recharge water and upward seeping groundwater. As a heterogeneous fluid density situation results in thinner water lenses, one expects that f ( I h o m   ( 0 )   )  > ∂ v  ∂ x   ( 0 , I ( 0 )  )    , such that an underestimation of the actual freshwater lens thickness is to be expected when using (39)  as initial interface estimate. This is also reflected in the example results (Section 3.2 ), demonstrating a (physically impossible) situation where the estimate of If  (0) rises above drain level for certain parameter combinations. In an attempt to find an alternative expression for the initial interface that is closer to the actual interface for heterogeneous fluid density cases, we searched for an expression which (i) adheres to the constraints in (24 ), (ii) reduces to Ihom  (x ) for homogeneous fluid density distributions (γ = 0) and (iii) is a function of γ. One such expression is given by(42) I h e t   ( x )  = L π  tan ( N ( N + K  )   π 2   )  tan ( K N + K + a γ   π 2   )  ln ( sin ⁡ ( K N + K + a γ    π x  2 L    )   sin ⁡ ( 2 N + K + 2 a γ  N + K + a γ    π x  2 L    )    )  ,     in which a  [-] (a  ≥ 0) is a factor providing flexibility to adjust the initial interface position depth. Defining g (Ihet  (0)) in a similar way as (40) , we obtain(43) I g  ( 0 )  = L π  ln ( K + γ g ( I h e t   ( 0 )   )   2 N + K − γ g ( I h e t   ( 0 )   )    )  .      For convenience, an overview and potential simplification of the terms in f  and g  is given in Appendix B . The introduction of a  in (42)  allows Ig  (0) to vary between y  = Ihom  (0) and y  = 0. This enables us to find an initial interface position which is close to the actual interface position by simple iterative calculations. Do note that the shape as dictated by (42) , regardless of the value of a , remains an approximation. Therefore, this iterative procedure does not yield the exact interface depth midway between the drains. For that, an (iterative) evaluation of (23)  throughout the domain remains required.   3.2 Example results In this section we discuss example solutions of the mathematical model presented, using a reference set of parameters identical to those used in Part I (Table 1 in van de Craats et al. (2024) ), except for the salt expansion coefficient. This coefficient is set to 0.7686. Using a seepage mass flux ratio, wk  , of 0.03507, this results in seepage water having a density of 1024.9 kg m-3 . This is in the range of seawater, and may be considered on the extreme side for most natural situations. The corresponding value of the density difference induced fluid flux, γ, is 0.002 m d-1 , such that for the reference simulation we obtain a ‘density flux ratio’, defined as γ/N , of 4.0. The stream function for the reference case as calculated with (15)  is shown in  Fig. 2  B. Function v (x, y ), necessary for obtaining the stream function, was acquired using I (x ) = Ihet  (x ) with a  = 0.46. The interface position, given as the position where the stream function is zero, can readily be seen in Fig. 2 . The calculated interface matches the interface obtained with SUTRA (long-dashed line) rather well. Comparing the interface position in case of heterogeneous fluid density with the homogeneous fluid density situation (short-dashed line) shows a decrease in depth of approximately 25% for the reference case. The shape of the interface is also affected by a heterogeneous density distribution: the relative loss in thickness as function of x  is largest midway between the drains, and decreases towards the drains. Therefore, the overall decrease in water lens volume is less than 25%. Comparing the reference situation with the situations with higher (Fig. 2 A) and lower (Fig. 2 C) seepage rates, the change in thickness due to a heterogeneous fluid density distribution decreases with increasing upward seepage rates, both in absolute and relative sense. The contribution of v  to the stream function (grey dashed lines in Fig. 2 ) is larger for thicker water lenses. This also follows directly from the fact that v (x, y ) is a function of ∂I /∂x ; the larger this gradient, the larger the ‘source’ of v  (see e.g. (17)  or (23) ). The influence of the upward seepage rate on the effect of fluid density differences on the interface depth is clearly shown when plotting the interface depth midway between the drains as function of the seepage flux ratio K /N  and the density flux ratio γ/N  (Fig. 3  ). The effect of a heterogeneous fluid density is much more pronounced in situations with a low seepage rate compared to those with a high seepage rate, owing to the thicker lenses forming under conditions with relatively low seepage rates. In other words, if the lens is already shallow due to high seepage fluxes, a heterogeneous density has limited effect on the lens thickness, whereas with relatively thick lenses a heterogeneous density could result in a substantial decrease in lens thickness. For situations where K γ  ≥ 1    (i.e. the upper left triangle in Fig. 3 B), the relative decrease in lens volume due to a heterogeneous fluid density is less than 10%, but lens thickness decreases rapidly when this ratio falls below 1. The approximate interface positions If  (0) and Ig  (0), the latter derived using a  = 1, are given in Fig. 4  A and B, respectively. The relative difference between If  (0) and the actual interface depth I (0) (Fig. 4 D) is small when also the initial interface depth Ihom  (0) is close to the actual interface depth. This is the case for when K γ  ≥ 1    (Fig. 3 ). However, for situations where K γ  ≪ 1   , the interface position If  (0) is too shallow and may even become positive: the interface supposedly rises above the drain level. Obviously, as recharge water infiltrating at y  = 0 must be discharged through the domain D  , a negative thickness is impossible in view of the mathematical model description. It appears that indeed the contribution of f (Ihom  (0)) to the stream function is too large. Obtaining Ig  (0) with a  = 1, we find that again the interface is well approximated for K γ  ≥ 1   . However, rather than underestimating the actual lens thickness I (0) in case K γ  < 1   , actual lens thickness is now overestimated. In fact, for K γ  ≪ 1   , the estimated lens thickness increases with increasing density differences at some point. Clearly, these are unrealistic results as well. Ihet  (0) (Fig. 4 C and F) underestimates lens thickness for K γ  ≪ 1   , which, in analogy of the results of If  (0), provides the explanation for the fact that Ig  (0) exceeds the actual lens thickness: the contribution of g (Ihet  (0)) to the stream function is too small. Interestingly, the initial estimate Ihet  (0) (Fig. 4 C) provides a better estimate of the interface position compared to both If  (0) and Ig  (0), even when using a default value a  = 1. We determined the value of parameter a  for which the interface position Ig  (0) was situated at the position where the steam function midway between the drains equals zero, supposed that the shape of the interface was given by Ihet  (x ) (Fig. 5  A). The stream function value was determined by combining (18)  with (23) . For increasing density flux ratios, parameter a  becomes substantially smaller than 1. This corresponds with the results in Fig. 4 F, showing a too shallow estimated interface position for Ihet  (0). For practical purposes, to easily obtain an estimate of the interface position in case of heterogeneous fluid density situations, we may fit an empirical expression for a  as function of density flux ratio or seepage flux ratio. Clearly, both γ/N  and K /N  affect the optimal value of a  (Fig. 5 A), but as the fluid density flux ratio increases, the influence of the seepage flux ratio diminishes. As seen from Figs. 3 and 4 , the interface position is mainly predicted erroneously in the higher ranges of γ/N , where the influence of the seepage flux ratio is limited. Therefore, we let a  be a function of only γ/N . Using a non-linear regression model, we find a  to be well-approximated (in the parameter range considered) by(44) a  ∼  0.016 γ / N − 0.169 γ / N   + 0.74     for K /N  = 1. This relation is given in Fig. 5 B. Obtaining Ihet  (x ) with a  given by (44) , we can once again estimate Ig  (0). The relative difference between Ig  (0) and the actual interface I (0) as given in Fig. 3  is shown in Fig. 5 C, indicating a maximum overestimation of lens thickness of 15% in the parameter range considered. Therefore, solving Ig  (0) with Ihet  (0) as initial estimate and using an estimate of a  given by (44) , provides a reasonable and practical approximation of the actual interface depth obtained with the mathematical model presented.   4 Transient flow 4.1 Mathematical model description In this section we present some basic results on transient flow, based on the findings in Part I. The interface motion equation, describing the change of the interface position over time as function of the stream function, is given as (see also Chan Hong et al. (1989)  and van de Craats et al. (2024) , their Eqs. (44) and (47)):(45) η ∂ I ( x , t  )   ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ x   { ψ ( x , I ( x , t  )  , t  )   }   or  ∂ I ^   ∂ t ^    = ε  ∂ ∂ x ^    { ψ ^  ( x ^  , I ^  , t ^   )   }  ,     where the second equation shows the interface motion equation in its dimensionless form. Note that all scaled parameters are indicated by the notation ^, as e.g. I ^  = I x R     , with the reference values xR   = L , ψR   = N 0 L  and TR   = T . Here, ε  = N 0  T  η L     , with N 0  denoting the characteristic recharge rate (e.g. the average recharge rate) and T  denoting the characteristic time scale, e.g. an oscillation period in case of sinusoidal boundary fluxes. Parameter ε therefore describes the ratio of the oscillation period over the transport time; the larger this term, the more important oscillations are. The scaled stream function is given as (compare with (14) )(46) ψ ^  ( x ^  , I ^  ( x ^  , t  )  , t ^   )  = K ^  ( t ^  )  x ^  − ( N ^  ( t ^  )  + K ^  ( t ^  )   )   u ( x ^  , I ^  ( x ^  , t ^   )  , t ^   )  + γ  v ( x ^  , I ^  ( x ^  , t ^   )  , t ^   )  ,     from which we can distinctly separate the effects of changing boundary conditions (terms 1 and 2 on the right-hand side) and the effects of a heterogeneous fluid density (term 3 on the right-hand side). Terms 1 and 2 respond instantaneously to changing boundary conditions (as demonstrated in Part I), whereas the change in term 3 is expected to be decidedly slower as it is a function of the interface position itself, which displaces only gradually (Part I). Let us consider the same situation as in Part I, where the boundary conditions in terms of N ^  ( t ^  )     and K ^  ( t ^  )     are given by(47) N ^  ( t ^  )  = 1 + A ^  sin ( 2 π t ^   )     K ^  ( t ^  )  = K ^  + A ^  sin ( 2 π t ^   )      .      Rather than attempting to find an analytical approximation to (45)  (as in Part I), we only solve the interface motion equation numerically using the fourth order Runge-Kutta method in time and central differences in space. The contribution of v  to the stream function (46)  is obtained only at the start of each time step and is not updated on each intermediate step in the Runge-Kutta method, to save calculation time.  4.2 Example results This section gives a few example solutions to the interface motion equation for situations with fluid density differences. In all situations, we use N 0  = A  = 0.5 mm d-1 , and T  = 364 days, similar as in Part I. We distinguish three cases which deviate only in their initial conditions (corresponding to the initial conditions as used in Fig. 2 ), and one case where ε is doubled with respect to the reference situation. All other parameters are identical to the reference case. Movement of the interface (Fig. 6  A) described by the numerically resolved interface motion Eq. (45)  agrees well with the interface position as obtained with SUTRA. A slight offset in initial position is noticeable between the two representations for the situations with initial conditions K /N  = 0.5 and K /N  = 2 (see also Fig. 2 ). This offset slowly diminishes as the front moves towards its final position where K ^  = N ^    . A minor phase shift can be observed as well, similar as observed for the situation with a homogeneous fluid density (Part I). Subtracting the interface position midway between the drains for the heterogeneous fluid density solution from the corresponding solution for a homogeneous fluid density reveals the influence of the heterogeneous fluid density on the transient solution (Fig. 6 B). Clearly, as the interface position is shallower in the heterogeneous fluid density case, the difference between the two is positive, and more so for deeper water lenses for reasons discussed before. For the situations with initial conditions K /N  = 0.5 and K /N  = 2 using ε = 0.081 (red and blue lines in Fig. 6 ), the difference between the heterogeneous and homogeneous solution is quite constant for the first two periods, and only then starts to change substantially towards the final difference (green line). This behavior is modelled similarly by both the interface motion equation and SUTRA results. In these cases, the initial rate of change of the interface position after a sudden change in boundary conditions is hardly dependent on fluid density differences. However, as the absolute difference in initial and final interface position is smaller for the heterogeneous density case compared to the homogeneous one, the interface position reaches its final equilibrium position more rapidly in case of a heterogeneous fluid density. As such, the rate of change of the interface position must reduce compared to the homogeneous situation; as a result, the difference between the two cases changes. This behavior is less well visible for the situation with a higher value of the ratio (ε) of the characteristic travel time (T ) over the characteristic travel time (η L  N 0    ), due to the fact that the final position is reached much more rapidly (Fig. 6 A). The amplitude of the oscillations seems hardly affected by a heterogeneous fluid density for the situations considered. Only for the simulation with the higher value for ε, the influence of oscillations is clearly visible in Fig. 6 B by the slight oscillations in the purple line, but the amplitude of these oscillations is at least two orders of magnitude smaller than those in the actual front (Fig. 6 A). Based on these observations, it may be expected that only in case of very shallow lenses combined with a relatively large contribution of ε to the interface movement, differences in oscillation amplitude between the heterogeneous and homogeneous case may become relevant to the general front behavior.   5 Conclusions In this Part II of a series of two papers on flow in shallow water lenses subject to upward seepage of groundwater and downward infiltration of recharge water, we expanded the results of Part I to a situation with a heterogeneous density distribution, where seepage water has a higher density compared to recharge water. Using the same sharp interface approach as in Part I, we obtained the interface position in case of a heterogeneous fluid density. This requires an iterative procedure as the interface position at any point is a function of the integral of the interface. We therefore also presented a method to approximate the steady state interface position midway between the drains for the heterogeneous case in a simple way. Steady state positions in an environment with a heterogeneous fluid density were found to be shallower than the corresponding homogeneous cases. This effect is small (less than 10%) as long as the seepage flux exceeds the density flux (i.e. K  > γ), but increases rapidly as the ratio between the seepage and density flux decreases below 1. This behavior relates to the thickness of the water lens: the thicker the water lenses in the homogeneous fluid density case, the larger the effect, both relative and absolute, of a heterogeneous fluid density on lens thickness. Using the interface motion equation, we demonstrated that the initial rate of change of the interface following a change in boundary conditions is comparable between corresponding homogeneous and heterogeneous situations. Consequently, as lenses for the heterogeneous case are shallower, a new equilibrium is reached more rapidly in this case. For the cases considered, a heterogeneous density distribution hardly imposes significant effects on the amplitude of seasonal oscillations of the front position. We have shown that in all cases the results of the mathematical analyses presented in this paper agree well with numerical finite element model results of the model SUTRA. The latter solves the convection, dispersion and diffusion, accounting for fluid density differences, in the two dimensions considered, and as such does not employ the sharp interface approach but rather a representation of the actual solute concentration and corresponding fluid density distribution. The good agreement of the two models provides confidence in the simplifications presented in this paper, allowing the use of the mathematical models and approximations for determining the interface position between recharge water and seepage water in heterogeneous fluid density cases, without the need for general numerical models.
1 Introduction Drought is a natural disaster characterized by long duration, wide-ranging influence, and high frequency (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). The occurrence of droughts affects local water resource supply, agricultural production, ecological environment, and socio-economic development (Li et al., 2021 ). Global warming has led to a greater rise in land temperatures compared to the oceans, a disparity that alters atmospheric circulation patterns. These shifts in atmospheric circulation result in decreased relative humidity near the Earth's surface, thereby increasing both the intensity and probability of drought events (Intergovernmental Panel On Climate Change, 2023 ). Drought concerns many scholars and countries around the world (Aryal and Zhu, 2020; Sam et al., 2019 ). Drought indices have been extensively used and are generally classified as standardized, non-standardized, and comprehensive types to identify drought events and assess the severity of drought quantitatively. The standardized drought indices offer comparability at various time scales and is applied to most climatic areas. The early-proposed standardized drought indices, based on the stationary hypothesis and considering uni/bivariates, such as the standardized precipitation index (SPI; McKee et al., 1993 ), standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ), standardized runoff index (SRI; Shukla and Wood, 2008 ), and standardized soil moisture index (SSMI; Hao et al., 2014 ), were computed based on the probability distribution function (PDF). Standardized drought indices have been extensively applied in drought characterization (Zalokar et al., 2021 ), drought monitoring (Lotfirad et al., 2022; Salimi et al., 2021 ), drought risk assessment (Bian et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020 ), and similar drought measurements. However, the validity of the stationary hypothesis had been questioned due to the strong influence of global warming and human activities (Jehanzaib et al., 2020; Shao et al., 2022 ). Milly et al. (2008)  long had asserted that “stationarity is dead”, necessitating the identification of nonstationary characteristics in drought events. Recent research investigations emphasize the nonstationary characteristics of drought (Liu et al., 2019; Omer et al., 2020 ). The Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS), proposed by Rigby and Stasinopoulos (2005) , were widely used in the development of nonstationary drought indices. The GAMLSS model, a frequently used parametric/semiparametric regression model, characterizes non-stationarity by constructing linear or nonlinear functional relationships between parameters and explanatory variables. Previous studies on nonstationary drought indices established by the GAMLSS model mainly focused on location parameters (μ), dividing temporal-variate types into linear and nonlinear cases. Wang et al. (2015)  proposed a temporal-variate standardized precipitation index by fitting the nonlinear temporal-variate parameter μ of Gamma distribution in the Luanhe River Basin of China. Similarly, Bazrafshan and Hejabi (2018)  proposed the nonstationary reconnaissance drought index by fitting the linear temporal-variate parameter μ of the Log-normal distribution. Later studies on nonstationary drought indices using the GAMLSS model considered both parameter μ and scale parameter (σ), introducing climate indices and human-activity factors as covariates. Rashid and Beecham (2018) proposed a nonstationary standardized precipitation index (NSPI), where the covariate of Gamma distribution parameters were climate indices. Additionally, considering the influence of not only climate change but also human activities, Shao et al. (2022)  introduced the nonstationary standardized runoff index (NSRI), with climate indices and water consumption being the covariates in the GAMLSS model. These studies demonstrate the flexibility of the GAMLSS model in specifying the variation of the response variable and establish the superior performance of nonstationary drought indices compared to their stationary counterparts. In the GAMLSS model, previous research applied low-order polynomials to construct nonstationary drought indices, but such modifications proved insufficient. Especially under the conditions of abrupt climate change and intense human activities, many abrupt changes have been detected in the data series. In this case, it is necessary to capture more complex nonstationary features (Liu et al. 2023 ). In addition, climate indices and human factors were taken as covariables, which improved the performance of drought indices (Shao et al., 2022 ). However, the selection of appropriate climate indices and human factors was challenging, and the performance was not compared with the temporal-variate GAMLSS model. Thus, constructing the optimal functional relationship between location and scale parameters (μ and σ) based on the GAMLSS model remains essential for developing more accurate nonstationary drought indices. Previous research primarily applied simple GAMLSS models, which may not have fully captured the inner nonstationary characteristics in the studied variables, such as precipitation (P) in NSPI, water deficit (D) in NSPEI, soil moisture (SM) in NSSMI, and runoff (R) in NSRI. Moreover, the influence of the probability distribution function (PDF), smoothing function (SF) and degrees of freedom (DF) on the model fitting effect were not comprehensively considered. To improve the recognition performance of drought index, our study aims to develop nonstationary drought indices (NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI) based on the GAMLSS model, focusing on accurately identifying and characterizing different types of droughts in the YRB. Our specific objectives are: (1) to modify nonstationary drought indices. We not only considered three cases (stationary (S), linear (L) and nonlinear (N)) of temporal-variate position and scale parameters, but also compared the effects of three elements (PDF, smoothing function and degrees of freedom) on the GAMLSS model; (2) to prevent overfitting in the GAMLSS model by introducing the Mann-Kendall mutation test to constrain the model's degrees of freedom; (3) to evaluate the applicability and reliability of the developed nonstationary drought indices by comparing them with historical typical drought events.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study area and data collection Yellow River, the second-longest river in China and the sixth-longest in the world, stretches 5464 km in length and covers an area of 752,443 km2  (Xie et al., 2019 ). The river originates from the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, flowing through the Loess Plateau and the eastern alluvial plain, before finally winding into the Bohai sea. It is the main water source of the Yellow River Basin (YRB; 95°53′E − 119°5′E, 32°10′N − 41°50′N) in North China, supporting 9 % of China’s population and 17 % of its agricultural land. The YRB encompasses arid, semi-arid and semi-humid regions, distributed in the upper, middle and lower reaches respectively (Liu et al., 2024 ). The daily meteorological data at the selected 85 stations in the YRB from 1961 to 2022 were obtained from the National Meteorological Information Center at the China Meteorological Administration (https://data.cma.cn/). This data includes maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, wind speed at 2 m height, atmospheric pressure, average relative humidity, and sunshine duration. Daily soil moisture data at 0–10 cm and 10–40 cm depths in the YRB from 1961 to 2022 were obtained from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) datasets downloaded from the Google Earth Engine cloud platform (https://earthengine.google.com/). The GLDAS data, which is grid-based, was extracted into site-scale soil moisture data based on the same resolution (0.5°× 0.5°), ensuring that soil moisture stations were consistent with meteorological stations. The global land surface data products from GLDAS have been widely used in soil moisture research and have verified the reliability of GLDAS datasets (Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018 ). The monthly runoff data at 28 hydrological stations over 1956–2016 were collected from the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (YRCC; https://www.yrcc.gov.cn/), covering 13 mainstream stations and 15 tributary stations of the YRB. The homogeneity and reliability of the runoff data were rigorously checked and evaluated by the YRCC. The locations of the selected 80 meteorological stations and 28 hydrological stations were mapped in Fig. 1  . Historical drought event records from 1961 to 2000 were collected from the Encyclopedia of Meteorological Disasters in China , and records after 2000 were obtained from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China  (https://www.mwr.gov.cn/sj/). The specific data were primarily sourced from the bulletins of local statistics bureaus.  2.2 Mann-Kendall mutation test The Mann-Kendall mutation test is a nonparametric method, which has the advantages of not requiring samples to obey a certain distribution and not being disturbed by a few outliers (Zhuang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023 ). It can effectively identify whether the hydro-meteorological sequence has mutation, including the number and time of mutation. The number of mutations we used to detect time series was used to determine the degree of freedom of GAMLSS model. First, for a hydrometeorological sequence X (x 1 , x 2 ,⋯, x n ) of length n , we constructed an order sequence:(1) S k  = ∑ i = 1  k  r i    ;  r i  = 1  ,   x i  > x j         0  ,   x i  ⩽ x j                    ;  ( k = 2 ,   3 ,   ⋯ ,   n )    ( j = 1 ,   2 ,   ⋯ ,   n )                  where Sk   is the cumulative value at time k , xi , xj  is the value of X  at times i  and j . The statistic U F k     is calculated as follows:(2) U F k  = S k  - E ( S k  )     Var ( S k  )    ,  ( k = 1 ,   2 ,   ⋯ ,   n )     E ( S k  )  = n ( n + 1 )  4                                       Var ( S k  )  = n ( n - 1 ) ( 2 n + 5 )  72                               where E ( S k  )    and Var ( S k  )    are the mean and variance of order sequence, respectively. Construct reverse time series, defining the statistic as UB  k    and satisfying UB  k  = - UF  k    . When UF  k  > 0   , the time series is upward trending; when UF  k  < 0   , the time series is downward trending; when UB  k    and UF  k    have an intersection point and are located between the critical lines, the time node is the beginning of the mutation (Li et al., 2022 ). The number of all intersections is the number of mutation points.  2.3 Computation of nonstationary drought indices 2.3.1 Principle of the GAMLSS model Generally, the computation of nonstationary drought indices (e.g., NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI) followed similar procedures, so we gave the details of the NSPEI computation process as an example. The GAMLSS model was used to fit the time series X i  m    and the goodness of fit. The fitting value of the parameter in the optimal PDF was used for calculating the cumulative probability F (x). The GAMLSS model can develop a relationship between distributional parameters and explanatory variables through an additive model, written as:(3) g k  ( θ k  )  = η k  = X k  β k  + ∑ j = 1  J k   h jk   ( x jk   )       where the subscript k  in θk   with k = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4    represents the distribution parameter vectors µ, σ, ν and τ, respectively, gk  (.) is a monotonic link function, βk   is a parameter vector of length Jk  , Xk   is a known design matrix, and where xjk   for j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , J k     are also vectors of length n . The function hjk   is an unknown function of the explanatory variable Xjk   and X jk   = h jk   ( x jk   )     is the vector which evaluates the function hjk   at xjk  . If J k  = 0    for all k = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4   , Eq.(3) can be reduced to a fully parametric model of g k  ( θ k  )  = η k  = X k  β k    . Usually, the former two population parameters θ1   and θ2   are characterized as location and scale parameters, denoted here by μ and σ, which are key parameters in the GAMLSS model. Because this study mainly discusses the influence of time-varying parameters, the interference of random terms is not considered. The GAMLSS model established in this study is as follows:(4) g 1  ( μ )  = η 1  = X 1  β 1     g 2  ( σ )  = η 2  = X 2  β 2              To ensure the fitting performance of the GAMLSS model, we selected hydro-meteorological sequences of over 60 years for fitting. The performance of the GAMLSS model was assessed by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Schwarz Bayesian Criterion (SBC). AIC appraised prediction accuracy, while SBC appraised the goodness of fit (Sober, 2002 ). The smaller the AIC and SBC values, the better the goodness of fit of GAMLSS model. After the optimal GAMLSS models were determined, the Q-Q plots and worm plots were used for qualitative evaluation, and the residual analysis was used for quantitative evaluation (Shao et al., 2022 ).  2.3.2 Detailed process of the GAMLSS model modification The GAMLSS model assumed that the vector of explanatory variables has a PDF family. The PDF was the core to determining the GAMLSS model. Based on the described model in Eq. (3) , the key parameters of PDF were μ and σ (Rashid and Beecham, 2019 ). Parameters (μ and σ) were used to construct the nine temporal-variate GAMLSS models with different combinations of parameters (μ and σ) and temporal-variate types (stationary (S), linear (L) and nonlinear (N)), namely stationary model (μSσS), linear models (μLσS, μSσL and μLσL) and nonlinear models (μNσS, μNσL, μSσN, μLσN and μNσN) in Table 1  .(1) Step 1:  We selected 24 PDFs from the distribution function family (Table S1 ). According to the parameter range of PDF, model convergence and AIC criterion, 10 PDFs (covering all sites) were preliminarily screened out.
