Based on AIC and SBC criteria, the recommended PDF (covering 90 % of the sites) was selected for nine time-varying GAMLSS models (assuming that the smoothing function was cubic spline and the degree of freedom was 3).  (2) Step 2:  We had obtained the recommended PDFs and assumed that the degree of freedom (DF) was 3. Based on the applicability of the smoothing functions, we selected six types of smoothing functions (Fig. S2 ). These were constrained splines (cs); penalized B-splines (pb); B-splines (bs); fractional polynomial splines (fp); penalized splines (ps); and orthogonal polynomials (poly). Five temporal-variate GAMLSS models (μSσN, μLσN, μNσS, μNσL and μNσN) were constructed for different time scales and smoothing functions, and we recommend appropriate smoothing functions (covering more than 90 % of the sites) by SBC criterion.  (3) Step 3:  We had determined the recommended PDF and SF. This step determined the DF recommended by GAMLSS model. The number of mutation points (MP) in time series (P, D, SM and R) was obtained by Mann-Kendall mutation test, and the range of DF (MP-3 ≤ DF≤MP+3) was preliminarily determined. To prevent over-fitting, the lower limit of DF was 2 and the upper limit was 9. Therefore, the recommended DFs in time series of different time scales were all obtained.  (4) Step 4:  After determining the recommended PDFs, SFs and DFs, we constructed all temporal-variate GAMLSS models. Based on AIC and SBC criterion, the optimal model was selected from nine GAMLSS models. Due to the influence of many factors, the results of SBC criterion might be biased. Therefore, the residual analysis of the optimal GAMLSS model was carried out, and the results of residual analysis (mean, variance, skewness coefficient, kurtosis coefficient and Filliben coefficient) were taken as an important basis to judge the performance of GAMLSS model. The schematic diagram of constructing the optimal GAMLSS model was shown in Fig. 2  . The cumulative probability value F(x) of time series (such as D in NSPEI) was calculated based on the optimal GAMLSS model. Nonstationary drought indices (NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI) were calculated by standardized F(x) (refer to Eq.(8) and (9)).     2.3.3 Calculation of NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI The computation of NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI were generally similar, so the computation procedures of SPEI were taken as an example as follows. NSPEI was calculated based on the difference between P  and ET 0 . First, the monthly ET 0  was calculated using the Penman-Monteith formula (Allen et al. 1998 ). Second, the water deficit of the i th month (D i  = P i  - E T 0 , i     ) and the cumulative values at the m th time scale were calculated:(5) X i m  = ∑ i - m + 1  i  D i    ,  i ⩾      m      Then the optimal PDF parameters were obtained by using the optimal GAMLSS model. The distribution parameters were substituted into PDF to calculate the probability value F(x) of the time series. Taking the gamma distribution as an example, its calculation formula is as follows:(6) f ( x | μ , σ )  = x ( 1 / σ 2   - 1 )   e [ - x  / ( σ 2    μ ) ]    ( σ 2  μ )  1 / σ 2    Γ ( 1 / σ 2   )        (7) F ( x )  = ∫ 0 x  f ( x | μ , σ )   d x      Finally, The NSPEI at the m -month scale was calculated:(8) w = - 2 ln P x        (9) NSPEI = w - c 0  + c 1  w + c 2  w 2   1 + d 1  w + d 2  w 2  + d 3  w 3      ,  P x  ⩽ 0.5        c 0  + c 1  w + c 2  w 2   1 + d 1  w + d 2  w 2  + d 3  w 3    - w   ,  P x  > 0.5                 where Px  is the cumulative probability, when Px   ≤ 0.5, Px   = 1- F(x) ; when Px   > 0.5, then Px   is replaced by F (x ). The parameters used were c0  = 2.515517, c1  = 0.802853, c2  = 0.010328, d1  = 1.432788, d2  = 0.189269 and d3  = 0.001308. Generally, the computation procedures of NSPI, NSSMI and NSRI were similar to NSPEI except that the D i  in NSPEI was replaced by P i  in NSPI, SM i  in NSSMI and R i  in NSRI. The drought category was given in Table 2  .   2.4 Time series analysis in optimal GAMLSS model construction Although PDF, SF and DF are indeed fundamental components in constructing the optimal GAMLSS models, the time series itself may directly impact the construction of GAMLSS models. Therefore, we selected hydro-meteorological sequences (D, SM and R) across four-time scales (1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales) and four intervals (1961–1990, 1961–2000, 1961–2010 and 1961–2020) to construct the optimal GAMLSS models. We explored the impact of the time series itself through the spatial distribution and quantity statistics of the optimal GAMLSS models.  2.5 Run theory Run theory is used to extract the characteristics of drought events, such as drought duration, drought severity and drought intensity, to identify and quantify drought events more accurately (Jiang et al., 2021 ). Ru , Rm  and Rl  are defined as the upper, middle and lower thresholds for drought event detection, respectively. T0 , T1  and T2  are the drought duration in drought events. S0 , S1  and S2  are the cumulative values of indices in corresponding drought events (Fig. 3  ). The definition and identification of drought events was classified into three types: (1) When the index value was below Rl  (Rl  = -2), it indicated extreme drought in that month. The drought duration (DD) was recorded as T0 , the drought severity as S0 , and the drought intensity (DI) was calculated using the formula DI=S0 /T0  . (2) If a drought event extended beyond one month and the corresponding index value was below Rm , this condition signified a drought period. In such cases, the drought duration was noted as T1 , the drought severity as S1 , and the intensity was computed using DI=S1 /T1  . (3) When the time interval between two adjacent drought events was less than m -months (where m  was the time scale of drought index), and the index value during this period was below Ru , these events could be merged into a drought event. In this case, the drought duration as T2 , the drought severity as S2 , and the drought intensity was calculated using DI=S2 /T2  . If these criteria were not met, they were considered as two separate drought events. The threshold values and specific identification process were given in Fig. 3 .   3 Results 3.1 Construction of the optimal GAMLSS model We used AIC and SBC criteria to evaluate the performance of the GAMLSS model. The most important factor determining the fitting effect of the GAMLSS model was the PDF, followed by the SF and DF. Therefore, the optimal PDF, SF and DF were selected for the time series (P, D, SM and R) to construct the optimal GAMLSS model. 3.1.1 Selection of the optimal PDF As described in step 1 of section 2.2.3, we identified recommended PDFs as shown in Fig. S2  and Table S3 . The spatial distribution and quantity statistics of PDFs for constructing the optimal GAMLSS model for P, D, SM and R at 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales were illustrated in Fig. 4  . There were significant differences in the distribution of optimal PDFs for different time series across various time scales. For P, the optimal PDFs at the 1-month scale were JSU and SHASH, at the 3-month scale included BCPE, SEP2, SHASH, ST2 and JSU, at the 6-month scale mainly BCPE and SEP4, and at the 12-month scale BCPE, GA, IG and SEP4 (Fig. 4 a-d). The optimal PDFs for P showed regionally distinct distributions at 1-, 3- and 6-month scales. For D, SEP2, SEP4, SHASH and ST4 were optimal across multiple time scales, but their spatial distribution was more dispersed and the quantity statistics varied greatly (Fig. 4 e-h). Particularly at the 12-month scale, the optimal PDF for D was more dispersed. At 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales, the best PDFs for SM varied significantly (Fig. 4 i-l). BCPE, GG, IG and NO appeared more frequently at these scales, but the distribution of PDFs changed. In Fig. 4 m-p, the main optimal PDFs for R were BCPE and SHASH, with BCPE primarily distributed at mainstream sites, but the optimal PDFs at tributary sites varied noticeably with the time scale. Therefore, selecting the optimal PDF for constructing the GAMLSS model according to the time series was very important.  3.1.2 Selection of the optimal SF As described in step 2 of section 2.2.3, we identified recommended smoothing functions (SFs). Combined with Fig. S2 , it was observed that four smoothing functions (bs, cs, pb and poly) showed prominent fitting effects. However, the results of cs/pb and bs/poly tended to be consistent with each other, hence cs and poly were recommended as the smoothing functions for constructing the optimal GAMLSS model. The statistics of the optimal SFs across different sites were shown in Fig. 5  a-d. There were significant differences in the optimal SFs for P, D and R at 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales. At the 1- and 3-month scales for P and D, the number of sites with stationary models (μSσS) and linear models (μSσL, μLσS and μLσL) was more, while those with nonstationary models (μSσN, μLσN, μNσS, μNσL and μNσN) were fewer. However, as the time scale increased, the number of sites with nonstationary models became dominant. At the 12-month scale for P and D, the primary smoothing function for the optimal GAMLSS model was cs (82 and 85, respectively). At 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales for R, nonstationary models dominated in terms of site numbers. The number of sites with cs increased with the time scale (68, 77, 82 and 82, respectively). At the 3-, 6- and 12-month scales for R, nonstationary models dominated, and the trend of cs and poly changed similarly with the time scale. Therefore, it was found that with the increase of time scale, the number of sites with nonstationary model increased significantly (the number of sites applying cs tended to increase, but the number of sites applying poly tended to decrease). This aspect showed that cs was suitable for higher-scale time series, while poly is more suitable for lower-scale time series.  3.1.3 Selection of the optimal DF As described in step 3 of section 2.2.3, we were able to determine the number of mutation points for P, D, SM and R, which in turn defined the range of Degrees of Freedom (DF). The greater the number of mutation points in a time series was, the more pronounced the nonlinear changes were, leading to a higher DF. To prevent overfitting, we constrained the DF within the range of [2, 9]. Taking the Minhe station as an example, the number of mutation points at the 6-month scale for P, D, SM and R were 1, 0, 1 and 1, respectively. Therefore, the DF range for P, D, SM and R at the 6-month scale was set to [2, 4], [2, 3], [2, 4] and [2, 4], as shown in Fig. 5 e-h. At this stage, we could construct nonstationary models with different DFs (μSσN, μLσN, μNσS, μNσL and μNσN). The optimal DF was then determined by selecting the best GAMLSS model based on the SBC criterion. In Fig. 5 e-h, it was evident that the optimal GAMLSS models constructed at the 6-month scale for P, D, SM and R were μNσS, μNσN, μNσL and μNσL, respectively, with corresponding degrees of freedom of 2, 3, 4 and 4. Following the same steps, we were able to determine the optimal DFs for all the stations in the Yellow River Basin, as illustrated in Fig. 5 i-l. Taking the 6-month scale as an example for P, D, SM and R, in P, the number of sites with stationary and nonstationary models for parameter μ were similar, with DFs mainly being 2 and 3, and parameter σ primarily fitted with stationary and linear models. In D, the DFs for parameter μ were mainly 3 and 4, with parameter σ predominantly having a DF of 2. In SM, the DF for parameter μ was mainly 4. In R, the DFs for parameter μ were mainly 3 and 4, with parameter σ primarily fitted with stationary and linear models.  3.1.4 Distribution of the optimal GAMLSS model As described in step 4 of section 2.2.3, we had obtained the recommended PDFs, SFs and DFs. Based on these recommendations, GAMLSS models for P, D, SM and R were constructed and the optimal models were selected. The number of sites for P, D, SM and R were 80, 80, 80 and 28, respectively. The spatial distribution of the optimal GAMLSS models for P, D, SM and R was shown in Fig. 6  . As the time scale increased, the number of stationary models significantly decreased while the number of nonstationary models increased. The μSσS model was applicable to most sites of P and D at 1- and 3-month scales (Fig. 6 a, b, e and f), with the number of sites being 72/59 and 65/44, respectively. At the 6- and 12-month scales, nonstationary models were suitable for most sites of P, D, SM and R. Four GAMLSS models (μSσL, μSσN, μLσL and μLσN) were distributed at a very few sites (less than 5 sites). In contrast, μNσS, μNσL and μNσN models were suitable for most sites of SM and R at the 6- and 12-month scales. The μNσS and μNσL models were more applicable to the central part of YRB in SM at 1- and 3-month scales (Fig. 6 i-j), as well as the sites of R at 3- and 6-month scales (Fig. 6 n-o). At the 12-month scale, the μNσN model was suitable for most sites of P, D, SM and R, with 54, 65, 57 and 24 sites, respectively (Fig. 6 d, h, l and p). Overall, the μSσS model was applicable to hydro-meteorological series at lower time scales, while nonstationary GAMLSS models were most suitable for higher time scales.   3.2 Performance of the optimal GAMLSS model 3.2.1 Performance of GAMLSS model Taking Minhe station as an example, the AIC and SBC values of the nine temporal-variate GAMLSS models of hydro-meteorological series (P, D, SM and R) were illustrated in Fig. 7   (6-month scale) and Fig. S1  (1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales). The variations of AIC were the same as SBC for the GAMLSS models of P, D, SM and R (Fig. 7 a-d). For P and R, the parameters μ and σ affected the goodness of fit of the GAMLSS models. However, the goodness of fit of the GAMLSS models for D and SM was determined more by parameter μ than by parameter σ, but it was also affected by the time scale. When the parameter σ was fixed, there was a small difference between the stationary (S) and linear (L) models of the parameter μ (Fig. 7 a-d). Similar results were shown for denoting the temporal-variate GAMLSS model at 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month scales. The difference between AIC and SBC decreased with the increasing time scales, and the optimal GAMLSS models selected based on AIC and SBC always pointed to the nonlinear type (Fig. S1 ). Comparing AIC and SBC values of nine temporal-variate GAMLSS models, the optimal GAMLSS models for P, D, SM and R at 6-month scale were μLσS, μNσN, μNσN and μNσN models, respectively (Fig. 7 a-d). As shown in the Q-Q plots in Fig. 7 e-h, the actual residual distance distribution was basically consistent with the theoretical residual reference line, and the goodness of fit of the selected GAMLSS model fitted well. According to the worm plots in Fig. 7 i-l, the residual values were distributed within the 95 % confidence interval. There was no obvious excess, so the fitting effect of the optimal GAMLSS model met the requirements. In addition to evaluating the GAMLSS model by AIC and SBC, the goodness of fit of the GAMLSS model was quantitatively evaluated by residual analysis (Table S4 ). At Minhe Station, the residual analysis results of the optimal GAMLSS model met the standard: mean is close to 0, variance is close to 1, skewness coefficient is close to 0, kurtosis coefficient is close to 3, and Filliben coefficient is greater than 0.970. Thus, the optimal GAMLSS model was selected through the quantitative and qualitative analysis of the GAMLSS model. Compared with the stationary GAMLSS model, the performance of the optimal GAMLSS model was greatly improved. Through quantitative evaluation of the AIC and SBC criterion and residual analysis, the optimal GAMLSS model was determined for all the studied sites in the YRB.  3.2.2 Parameter variations of the optimal GAMLSS models Take the Minhe station as an example. The variation curves of the parameters μ and σ (represented by the red and orange lines) for the optimal GAMLSS model were depicted in Fig. 8  . From the graph, it can be observed that the location parameter μ of the optimal GAMLSS model effectively captured the central tendency of the data (Fig. 8 e-h), while the scale parameter σ captured the variability of the data (Fig. 8 m-p). As the time scale increases, the dispersion of data points decreased, while the trend in data changes became more pronounced, leading to nonlinear variations in the parameters μ and σ. The GAMLSS model could adapt to the level of data dispersion by adjusting the scale parameter σ and potentially shape parameters, thereby improving the goodness of fit. A decrease in the scale parameter σ implied that the data became more concentrated, resulting in reduced variability. This indicated that the GAMLSS model allowed for more refined and flexible data analysis compared to traditional linear regression or generalized linear models. However, at higher time scales (6- and 12-month scales), increasing the degrees of freedom of the smoothing function makes the model more flexible, enabling it to capture more complex data patterns, but it might also lead to overfitting. Therefore, the variation in parameters of the optimal GAMLSS model was directly related to the model's degree of freedom. It was essential to determine a reasonable range for the degree of freedom based on the Mann-Kendall mutation test. Based on the distribution of parameter sequences and data in Fig. 8 , selecting a longer time series was crucial for fitting the GAMLSS model to the parameter sequences. A time series of appropriate length allowed for obtaining more reasonable parameter sequences through fitting with the GAMLSS model.  3.2.3 Impact of time series length on constructing GAMLSS models By constructing optimal models for time series in four intervals (1961–1990, 1961–2000, 1961–2010 and 1961–2020), we found that the length of the time series significantly affects the GAMLSS model (Fig. 9  ). The optimal GAMLSS model for hydro-meteorological sequences varied across different intervals, resulting in different fitted parameter sequences, which in turn influenced the nonstationary drought index (Fig. 9 a). The optimal GAMLSS models built on 6-month scale for D were more dispersed across different intervals without clear regional characteristics (Fig. 9 b-e). The optimal GAMLSS models for SM on 6-month scale predominantly consisted of μNσS, μNσL and μNσN. Moreover, as the length of the time series increased, μNσS gradually dominated most sites (Fig. 9 f-i). For R on 6-month scale, the optimal GAMLSS models shifted with increasing time series length, showing a decrease in stationary and linear models and an increase in nonstationary models (μNσS, μNσL and μNσS) (Fig. 9 j-m). Additionally, we compared the impact of time series length on the optimal model solution across different time scales. The optimal GAMLSS models built for D were less affected by the time series length and more by the time scale (with an increase in time scale, μSσS models significantly decreased, and nonstationary models significantly increased) (Fig. 9 n-q). The optimal GAMLSS models for SM were influenced by both time series length and time scale. With the increase in both time scale and time series length, μNσN models mainly showed an increasing trend (Fig. 9 r-u). The optimal GAMLSS models for R were also affected by both time series length and time scale. With the growth in time scale and time series length, μSσS models significantly decreased, and nonstationary models (μNσS, μNσL and μNσN) significantly increased (Fig. 9 v-y). These results indicate that constructing the GAMLSS model is influenced not only by internal factors such as PDF, SF and DF but also by external factors such as the length and scale of the time series.   3.3 Applicability of nonstationary drought indices 3.3.1 Identification of historical drought events in typical stations In the comparative study of drought indices at the Minhe station, it was observed that the drought indices on a 6-month scale aligned most closely with historical drought events (Fig. 10  ). Specifically, SPI and NSPI exhibited similar patterns of variation, effectively identifying historical drought events, albeit with occasional overestimations (Fig. 10 a). Notably, NSPEI demonstrated a more accurate identification of historical drought events compared to SPEI, particularly during the periods 1980–2004 and 2013–2022 (Fig. 10 b). In terms of SSMI and NSSMI, while their applicability in drought event detection was similar, disparities were evident in the assessment of drought intensity. Prior to 2000, both indices exhibited limited effectiveness in recognizing mild and moderate drought events, yet accurately identified severe and extreme drought occurrences. Beyond 2021, NSSMI outperformed SSMI in drought event detection (Fig. 10 c). Overall, NSRI surpassed SRI in identifying historical drought events, especially in the intervals 1956–1968 and 2001–2020 (Fig. 10 d). Additionally, comparing multi-site identification results with historical drought events revealed that stationary and nonstationary drought indices generally produce consistent results. However, some sites indicated that nonstationary drought indices align better with actual conditions (Table S5 ). Comparing nonstationary drought indices (NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI) with stationary drought indices (SPEI, SSMI and SRI) showed that both perform well in detecting drought events and accurately identifying historical drought events. However, Nonstationary drought indices had a wider value range, clearly reflecting extreme wet and dry conditions.  3.3.2 Drought duration and intensity identification in typical years To validate the performance of nonstationary and stationary drought indices in drought event identification, our study, beyond analyzing typical sites, also compared the drought intensity and duration identified by NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI in the typical year (2000) with those determined by SPI, SPEI, SSMI and SRI. Although both sets of drought indices exhibited similar spatial distribution in terms of drought intensity and duration, differences were observed at individual sites (refer to Fig. S4 and S5 ). Table 3   showed the drought intensity and duration at 14 sites, including historical records and identifications by the drought indices. The results indicated that NSPEI outperformed SPEI in identifying the intensity and duration of droughts, although the duration identified by NSPEI was generally shorter than the historical drought duration (notably at Xiji, Xixian and Xining station). NSPI showed better applicability compared to SPI, but the difference was marginal. The agricultural drought intensity identified by SSMI and NSSMI was generally weaker than meteorological drought. This finding suggested a higher consistency of historical drought event records with meteorological drought. In 2000, the drought situation in the main tributaries of the YRB was extremely severe, with instances of dry-up in tributaries like Wenjiachuan and Wuzhi. The drought events determined by SRI and NSRI were highly consistent with historical records (Fig. S4 ). Moreover, the hydrological drought identified by NSRI aligned more closely with the meteorological drought events in the corresponding basins. Overall, NSPEI performed excellently in drought identification. While NSPI and NSSMI performed better than SPI and SSMI, they still needed improvement. NSRI was better at identifying extreme drought conditions.    4 Discussion 4.1 Modeling elements of the GAMLSS model The GAMLSS model was mainly divided into two types: full parametric model (Eq.4) and semi-parametric model (Eq.3). The full-parameter model was used to establish the relationship between distribution parameters (μ and σ) and covariate (time), which were constructed to three forms, namely: stationary, linear and nonlinear. Among them, the first two forms were simple to construct, and we found that they were more suitable for hydro-meteorological series with lower-scales (1- and 3-month scales). Conversely, the nonlinear model was more suitable for hydrological series (R) and meteorological series (P and D) with higher-scales (6- and 12-month scales), which was consistent with our findings. The optimal PDF was the core of constructing an optimal GAMLSS model, and it was also the premise of calculating standardized drought index. Gamm and GEV were often considered as the optimal PDFs for SPI and SPEI respectively (Marcos-Garcia et al. 2017 ), while Pearson 5 and Weibull were reported as the optimal PDF of SPI and CZI in Urmia Lake Basin, respectively (Jahangir et al. 2023 ). However, the optimal PDF was often unique in time and space to simplify the calculation process in most studies. To improve the goodness of fit of the GAMLSS model as much as possible, we selected the optimal PDF for the hydro-meteorological series (P, D, SM and R) of each site in the YRB. According to Fig. 7  and Table 3 , the optimal GAMLSS model had excellent performance. However, the modeling process was complicated for calculating the nonstationary drought index. To get the optimal GAMLSS model, the influence of the smoothing function (SF) and degree of freedom (DF) was also considered, which was particularly important in the construction of the nonlinear GAMLSS model. SF and DF had a significant influence on the fitting effect of the GAMLSS model. cs and poly showed a good fitting effect, while DF showed significant differences on different time scales (Fig. 5 ), which was closely related to the degree of dispersion of the time series itself (Fig. 8 ). Considering the calculation principle, this modeling method reduced the influence of periodicity of the time series itself and further reflected the non-stationarity of the hydro-meteorological series. Although the complexity was increased, the accuracy was greatly improved. This approach would describe the non-stationarity of hydro-meteorological series accurately and further improved the ability of drought monitoring and evaluation.  4.2 Influence of time series length on the GAMLSS model In the process of fitting time series data using the GAMLSS model, we identified a significant impact of the time series length on the model's fitting effectiveness. This influence was particularly prominent in four key aspects (Fig. 9 ). (1) The length of the time series is a critical factor in determining the sufficiency of data. Longer time series provide more data points, enabling the model to capture long-term trends in the data more effectively, a point that has been widely supported in existing literature. In contrast, shorter time series may fail to adequately reveal these important trend characteristics, thus limiting the model's explanatory power and predictive accuracy. (2) The length of the time series also directly impacts the accuracy of parameter estimation (Zhang et al., 2020 ). We found that in longer time series, the increased number of data points available for parameter estimation enhanced the accuracy and stability of these estimates. However, in shorter time series, parameter estimation may be affected by marginal data and outliers, leading to potential instability or bias. This was particularly evident during the period 1995–2000, where significant changes in the NSPEI index were primarily caused by parameter changes induced by marginal data fluctuations (as shown in Fig. 9 a). (3) Additionally, we observed a significant impact of time series length on the complexity of the GAMLSS model. Longer time series typically require the construction of more complex models to accommodate the nonstationary nature of the data. For instance, in the optimal GAMLSS models constructed by 6- month time series of D, SM and R, as the length of the time series increased, the number of sites suitable for nonstationary models increased, while those fitting stationary and linear models decreased (Fig. 9 b-m). This trend was also evident for D, SM and R indicators on 1-, 3- and 12-month scales (Fig. 9 n-y). (4) The length of the time series was particularly important when dealing with time series that exhibit distinct seasonality or cyclicality (Van Der Spek and Bakker, 2017 ). We found that longer time series were more conducive to accurately identifying and modeling these cyclical patterns. (5) While longer time series required more complex models in regions with highly variable climates and intense human activity (e.g., the Yellow River Basin), this was not true for all areas. Model selection was based on the specific data and characteristics of the target region. In regions with more stable climates, simpler models were sufficient, whereas in other areas, more complex models were needed to handle data nonstationarity. In summary, to ensure the accuracy of parameter estimation and the effectiveness of the model, we recommend using hydro-meteorological sequences of at least 60 years when constructing GAMLSS models. Such a length of time series not only helps to capture long-term trends and cyclical patterns but also enhances the model's applicability and accuracy at different sites. Additionally, the choice of long time series was crucial for datasets with significant seasonal or cyclical characteristics. Future research should explore the impact of different time scales and data characteristics on GAMLSS model performance and how to optimize models for varying time series lengths. To ensure model applicability in different regions, it is advisable to first conduct a data characteristic analysis, understand the climatic and hydrological features of the target area, and then select the appropriate model complexity based on the specific conditions.  4.3 Performance analysis of nonstationary drought index The GAMLSS model had been widely applied in hydro-meteorological series, especially in the areas of precipitation, evapotranspiration, soil moisture and runoff (Villarini et al., 2010 ). Based on the GAMLSS model, temporal-variate nonstationary drought indices, including NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI, had been developed. NSPI, NSSMI and NSRI considered the non-stationarity of single factors. In contrast, NSPEI integrated both precipitation and evapotranspiration, encompassing a broader range of meteorological factors. NSPEI not only broke the traditional assumption of stationarity but also incorporated the impacts of a wider range of meteorological elements. These indices share the advantages of a standardized drought index, including a clear calculation process, flexibility in time scale, and temporal and spatial comparability. In the aspect of drought monitoring and identification, our comparison of nonstationary drought indices revealed that NSPEI was superior to NSPI in identifying the intensity and duration of meteorological drought. This finding was closely related to the semi-arid climate characteristics of the upper and middle reaches of the YRB, and the high evapotranspiration in the region (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Agricultural drought identified by NSSMI gradually weakened from northwest to southeast, exhibiting lower intensity but longer duration (Fig. S4 ). Additionally, there was a noticeable decreasing trend in the runoff in the YRB. Hydrological drought in the tributaries of the YRB was heavier than that in the mainstream of the YRB. The main reason for this phenomenon may be the regulation of the Yellow River Water Conservancy Project, which is dominated by human factors. Although we had evaluated the performance of nonstationary drought indices at typical sites and years, the limited historical drought event records precluded a comprehensive verification of their effectiveness at all sites in the YRB. However, this at least provided a scientific basis for constructing the optimal GAMLSS model and computing nonstationary drought indices. Future drought research should focus on constructing a nonstationary drought index that integrates multiple variables, such as precipitation and runoff, evapotranspiration and soil moisture, precipitation and soil moisture, among others. Beyond incorporating time as a covariate, climate indices or human factors should also be included to monitor and evaluate drought conditions more accurately amid the intensifying effects of climate change and human activities.   5 Conclusions We meticulously constructed optimal GAMLSS models to develop nonstationary drought indices (NSPI, NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI), providing a nuanced assessment of various drought types in the YRB. The selection of the probability distribution function (PDF), smoothing function (SF) and degrees of freedom (DF) were pivotal in this process. We found that the fitting effectiveness of the GAMLSS model largely depended on the PDF, with SF and DF also playing significant roles. The selection of the optimal PDF revealed spatial variations across different time scales, with distinct distributions of parameters like precipitation (P), water deficit (D), soil moisture (SM) and runoff (R). The SFs and DFs were chosen based on their ability to prevent overfitting and accurately reflect the data dispersion and trend changes at different time scales. In terms of model performance, our study demonstrated that nonstationary drought indices provided a more precise and reliable assessment of drought events compared to stationary indices. This was particularly evident when evaluating the historical drought events at specific sites like Minhe station. The nonstationary indices, such as NSPEI, NSSMI and NSRI, showed superior capabilities in detecting drought events and intensity, closely aligning with historical records. They effectively identified variations in drought duration and intensity, offering a more comprehensive understanding of drought dynamics. The integration of the GAMLSS model with these nonstationary indices significantly enhanced the robustness and applicability of drought assessment. By accommodating the inherent non-stationarity in hydro-meteorological time series, these indices provided a more accurate representation of extreme wet and dry conditions across the YRB. Our study underscores the importance of considering nonstationary aspects in drought analysis, paving the way for more informed water resource management and mitigation strategies in response to the complexities of climate variability and change.
1 Introduction Human activities in watersheds, including agricultural practices and urbanization, release elevated nutrient loads into surface and subsurface water, subsequently deteriorating the water quality of aquatic systems (Wurtsbaugh et al., 2019 ). The increased nutrient loads are linked to eutrophication, harmful algal blooms, and hypoxia (Smith et al., 1999; Kelly et al., 2019 ). Total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorous (TP) are major nutrients that exhibit remarkable concentrations in stream water affected by anthropogenic sources. Both compounds are frequently used to evaluate water quality. The precise identification of TN and TP sources to manage water quality more efficiently is imperative, considering the effects of seasonal variations and surface runoff accompanied by rainfall events (Kelly et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, the identification of TN and TP sources and their contributions to the water quality in small streams is a prerequisite for evaluating the nutrient loads in reservoirs such as lakes, streams, and rivers in watersheds (Black, 1997; Richards et al., 2021 ). In addition to the TN and TP, nitrate-nitrogen (NO3 - -N), which constitutes a large fraction of TN in the aquatic environment, is derived from various natural (e.g., soil and rainfall) and anthropogenic sources (e.g., manure, chemical fertilizer, and sewage) within the watershed (Ryu et al., 2021 ). The representative sources supplying nitrate to the aquatic system have distinct nitrogen and oxygen isotope compositions (Kaushal et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2015 ). Therefore, nitrate has been efficiently used to trace natural and anthropogenic sources in surface and subsurface water (Lee et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2023 ). However, few studies have comprehensively evaluated stream water quality according to seasonal variations and rainfall events using TN, TP, and nitrate isotopes in small streams. Nutrients in streams primarily originate from natural sources such as mineral erosion and atmospheric deposition, whereas excessive nutrients are derived from various anthropogenic sources (e.g., fertilizers, manure, and sewage) (Böhlke et al., 1997; Cao et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2019; Vega et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019 ). Consequently, nutrient concentrations are closely related to land-use patterns in watersheds. In agricultural regions, excess fertilizer and livestock manure applied to fields are transported to streams through surface and subsurface water pathways, resulting in elevated TN and TP concentrations in stream water (Chen et al., 2016 ). Similar to streams in rural areas, TN and TP concentrations in streams passing through urban areas downstream were significantly higher than those in forested areas upstream (Manning et al., 2020 ). Seasonal variations in nutrient concentrations were more pronounced in streams running through agricultural areas than those in other regions. According to Peñuelas and Sardans (2022) , many solutions have been globally implemented to address this issue as follows: preventing fertilizer misuse, enhancing plants' access to phosphorus (P) sources, stimulating and subsidizing P recycling through legislative regulations at national or regional levels, and reducing livestock production. Nevertheless, the contribution of anthropogenic sources associated with land-use patterns to nutrient concentrations in streams is still facilitated during rainfall events. For example, soil profiles in agricultural areas contain high nutrient loads derived from fertilizers and manure. Widespread impervious surfaces (e.g., roads and residential areas) in urban areas can prevent the absorption of nutrients into the soil, resulting in increased nutrient concentrations in the stream. Previous studies have suggested that elevated N deposition resulting from fertilizer application in agricultural settings may lead to a greater increase in N than in P (Arbuckle and Downing, 2001; Manning et al., 2020 ). In contrast, nutrient sources such as sewage runoff within urban watersheds are more prone to elevating P relative to N (Downing and McCauley, 1992; Manning et al., 2020 ). Unlike TN and TP, the nitrate anion consists of nitrogen and three oxygen atoms. Thus, both nitrogen and oxygen isotope compositions are typically used to identify sources contributing to water quality in aquatic systems because these sources can be distinguished on a plot of nitrogen and oxygen isotope compositions. According to many previous studies, stream water affected by manure and sewage typically exhibits the highest nitrogen isotope compositions, ranging from 2 to 20 ‰ (Jung et al., 2021; Xuan et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024 ). Nitrate contributions from natural sources such as soil and rainfall result in relatively low nitrogen isotope compositions, ranging from 0 to 12 ‰ (Lohse et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2020 ). This discrimination also reflects isotope fractionation occurring from various transformation processes by which nitrate is formed (e.g., mineralization and nitrification) or removed (e.g., denitrification). In particular, oxygen isotope composition in streams is in general lowered to ∼10 ‰ by microbial nitrification (Kendall and Aravena, 2000; Zhang et al., 2015 ), whereas both nitrogen and oxygen isotope compositions are greatly elevated by denitrification as nitrate concentration decreases. Therefore, spatiotemporal variations of TN and TP concentrations in streams, combined with nitrate isotopes as identifiers, can help trace natural and anthropogenic sources related to land-use patterns within a watershed. This combination of TN, TP and nitrate isotopes provides valuable insights for efficient water management by assessing the impact of anthropogenic sources within the watershed. This study aimed to discern the sources influencing stream water quality and assess the impact of land-use patterns on water quality. To achieve this, stream water from small watersheds with distinct land-use patterns was subdivided into main channels and tributaries. Water samples were collected during storm and non-storm periods to evaluate the variations in TN, TP, and nitrate-nitrogen (NO3 - -N) concentrations under various environmental conditions, including seasonality. In addition, the dual isotope compositions of nitrate (NO3 - ) were used to identify the sources affecting the water quality in streams underlying different land-use patterns. Statistical analyses were performed to verify the contributions of natural and anthropogenic sources to aquatic ecosystems.  2 Site and methodology 2.1 Description of the study area The Seohwa stream is one of the major tributaries of Daecheong Lake and supplies water to residents in central Korea. The Seohwa watershed has a discharge area of 191 km2  and a length of 42 km. In the middle and lower reaches of the Seohwa stream, tributaries (Sanggok and Geumgu streams) are introduced into the main stream ( Fig. 1 ). The Sanggok and Geumgu watersheds have discharge areas of 42 km2  and 34 km2 , respectively. The Seohwa drainage basin mostly consists of forests (66 %), agricultural areas (18 %), and residential areas (9 %). Agricultural areas are extensively distributed in the upper reaches, and the proportion of forests progressively increases with the flow toward the lower reaches (Fig. 1 ). The Seohwa basin consists mainly of well-drained (approximately 80 %) and poorly drained soil. The soil profiles corresponding to 73 % and 21 % of the basin are developed at depths of 20–50 cm and > 100 cm, respectively (http://soil.rda.go.kr/ ). In the basin, the number of populations is approximately 40,000 according to the Water Emission Management System in Korea. Approximately > 50 % of livestock, such as cows and pigs were farmed in the Geumgu watershed, but approximately 70 % of poultry was farmed in the upper reaches of the Seohwa watershed (Ministry of Environment, 2018 ). The Sanggok watershed is mostly forested with a small agricultural area. In contrast, the Geumgu watershed includes an agricultural area (29 %) and a residential area (21 %) with a relatively low forest area (42 %). In the upper to middle reaches, the agricultural area spreads extensively, and the proportion of residential areas increases toward the lower reaches. Most residents live in the Geumgu basin, where the largest amount of livestock is fed. The study area has four distinct seasons with a normal annual temperature and precipitation of 12.2 °C and 1260 mm/yr, respectively. Approximately 70 % of the precipitation was concentrated in the rainy season (June–September) (https://data.kma.go.kr ).  2.2 Sampling and analysis Sampling was conducted between October 2017 and October 2018. Stream water samples were collected one or two times per month during non-rainy periods at four sites in the main channel (MS-1, MS-2, MS-3, and MS-4) and six sites in the tributaries (TS-1, TS-2, TS-3, ST-1, ST-2, and ST-3). To evaluate the effect of runoff related to rain events on stream water chemistry, water samples were collected when the rain fell from early spring to late summer. During the rain events, samples were collected according to a method modified from that of Stenstrom and Kayhanian (2005) . After rainfall event, water sampling started at the time when the stream water level increased in ∼10 % from initial level. All sampling procedures were performed using an ISCO 6712 autosampler containing 24 1-L bottles. The water samples were collected in 30 min intervals for 4 h (8 1-L bottles), and sampling was then continuously conducted in 1 h intervals for 8 h (8 1-L bottles), 2 h intervals for 12 h (6 1-L bottles), 4 h intervals for 24 h (6 1-L bottles) until the stream water level was reached at the level when the first water sampling was initiated. The sampler was programmed to fill a bottle with stream water for a specified time (Teledyne ISCO 2015 ). The first two bottles were mixed when withdrawing them from the field; the other samples were collected in parallel; at least 2-L of water samples were necessary to analyze the contents of TN, TP, and NO3 - -N in this study and various parameters (e.g., BOD, COD, TOC, and SS) conducted in the companion study. During sample collection, the water levels at all sites were measured every 5 min using an ISCO 730 bubbler flow module interfaced with an autosampler (Teledyne Isco, USA). For TN and TP contents, the samples were analyzed using a Skalar SAN++ continuous flow analyzer (Skalar Analytical, The Netherlands). Nitrate concentrations were analyzed using a Metrohm 850 Professional IC (Metrohm Inc., Switzerland). All the samples were analyzed at the Geum River Environment Research Center. In addition to the sampling campaigns, we collected stream water samples one time in early November 2021 to determine the dual isotope composition of nitrate (δ15 N and δ18 O). The δ15 N and δ18 O values were reported in the delta (δ) notation relative to Air and VSMOW, respectively, where δ (‰) = (Rsample /Rstandard  − 1) × 1000, and R represents 15 N/14 N and 18 O/16 O, respectively. The analyzed isotopic values were normalized using international standards: USGS-34 (−1.8 ‰ for δ15 N and −27.9 ‰ for δ18 O), IAEA-NO3 -  (4.7 ‰ for δ15 N and 25.6 ‰ for δ18 O) and USGS-35 (2.7 ‰ for δ15 N and 57.5 ‰ for δ18 O).  2.3 Event mean concentration (EMC) and hydrological modeling Typically, TN, TP, and NO3 - -N concentrations of stream water vary during the runoff event. To estimate representative concentrations, the event mean concentration (EMC) was calculated using a flow-weighted average as shown in previous studies (Bertrand-Krajewski et al., 1998 ; Kim et al., 2007a ):EMC =  ∫ 0  t   C t    ∙ Q t    dt   ∫ 0  t   Q  t    dt        where C(t ) and Q(t ) represent the pollutant concentration and discharge rate at a given time t  during a storm event, respectively. The discharge rates were simulated hourly using the Hydrological Simulation Program-Fortran (HSPF) model, with input data such as geographic information system (GIS) data (digital elevation model (DEM), land use, and river network) and meteorological data (air temperature, precipitation, dew point temperature, wind movement, solar radiation, cloud cover, and potential evapotranspiration) (Donigian et al., 2018 ). To evaluate whether the application of the HSPF model to the field was appropriate, the simulated discharge rates were compared with those measured in the field from January 2017 to December 2018. As performed in previous studies (Kim et al., 2007b; Lee et al., 2020 ), the calibration was carried out for 10 hydrological parameters using HSPEXP software (Table S1 ). The accuracy of the model was guaranteed by a coefficient of determination (R2  = 0.801), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE = 0.793), percentage bias (PBIAS = −  0.380 %), and root mean square error (RMSE = 1.531 m3 /s), which were successfully simulated according to the criteria suggested by Moriasi et al. (2007) .  2.4 Statistical analysis Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to identify the major factors affecting stream water quality (or chemistry) associated with land-use patterns. Varimax rotation was employed to assess the extent to which each principal component explained various variable domains (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016 ). This rotation method allows for comparison because it elucidates the different interpretations of each principal component. PCA was performed using the XLSTAT Pro software (Addinsoft, New York, NY, USA).   3 Results The TP, TN, and NO3 - -N concentrations in samples collected from the main stream (MS-1, MS-2, MS-3, and MS-4) in 2017 and 2018 are listed in Table S2 . The same datasets were provided for samples collected from one of the main tributaries (TS-1, TS-2, and TS-3) and from small streams introducing TS (ST-1, ST-2, and ST-3). The main stream samples contained TN concentrations ranging from 0.65 to 6.42 mg/L ( Fig. 2 b and Table S2 ). The TN concentrations showed seasonal variation, which was highest in winter (November 2017 to February 2018) and lowest in summer (August to September 2018), regardless of the sampling location (Fig. 2 b). In spring, TN concentrations progressively decreased between winter and summer. With the temporal variation, the samples showed the spatial variation that had higher TN concentrations in the upper reaches than those in the lower reaches during the non-storm periods; on average, 3.82 ± 1.91 mg/L in MS-1, 4.09 ± 1.18 mg/L in MS-2, 2.84 ± 1.44 mg/L in MS-3, and 2.94 ± 1.17 mg/L in MS-4 (Fig. 2 b and Table S2 ). The spatiotemporal variations in TN concentrations in the main stream were attributed to dilution by precipitation and land-use patterns. TP concentrations in the stream water samples collected during storm events were higher than those collected during non-storm periods (Fig. 2 e, f, g and Table S2 ). Seasonal variation was not clearly observed in TP concentrations, but spatial variation was observed. The TP concentrations were overall higher in the upper reaches than in the lower reaches (Fig. 2 e and Table S2 ), decreasing from 0.16 ± 0.05 mg/L in MS‐1 to 0.04 ± 0.02 mg/L in MS-3 during the storm events and from 0.07 ± 0.04 mg/L in MS‐1 to 0.02 ± 0.02 mg/L in MS-3 during the non-storm periods. The concentrations in MS-4 (average 0.05 ± 0.05 mg/L) were relatively high compared to those in MS-3, which was attributed to the inflow of TS with higher TP concentrations (average 0.11 ± 0.07 mg/L) (Fig. 2 e, f). Such TP variations, related to storm events and downstream distances, were observed in the TS and ST samples (Fig. 2  f, g).  4 Discussion 4.1 Spatial and temporal variation of TP and TN 4.1.1 Total nitrogen (TN) TN in streams is elevated by the introduction of nutrient loads derived from anthropogenic sources within the watershed (Pieterse et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2016 ). TN can be diluted and vary spatiotemporally when the contribution of natural sources (e.g., precipitation and forest) to TN in the stream increases with distance downstream. In this study, the spatiotemporal variations in TN concentrations in the main stream were attributed to dilution by precipitation and land-use patterns. This suggest that the ratio of the proportion of agricultural areas (or residential areas) to the proportion of forest (A/F or R/F) can be employed to evaluate the relationship between TN and areas affected by anthropogenic sources at individual sampling sites. In this study, the A/F ratio decreased from 41 % in MS‐1 to 36% in MS-2 and 22 % in MS-3 ( Table 1 ). The higher A/F ratio in MS-4 (29 %) than that in MS-3 would be closely related to the land-use pattern in the TS watershed. Likewise, the observation was explained by the inflow of tributary sample with the higher TN (i.e., 3.62 ± 1.07 mg/L in TS-3). Such spatial variations were observed in samples from the tributaries. The A/F ratios of TS-1 and TS-2 were estimated at 63 % and 69 %, respectively (Table 1 ). The lower TN content in TS-3 compared to TS-2 was due to dilution by ST-1 and ST-3 (3.55 mg/L and 2.25 mg/L, respectively). However, temporal variations in the TS samples were not clear considering that TN frequently fluctuated between 1.15 and 6.56 mg/L (e.g., TS-2 and TS-3) and between 2.20 and 10.1 mg/L (e.g., TS-1) during the study periods (Fig. 2 c). Similarly, TN for ST samples was fluctuated between 1.42 and 7.25 mg/L (e.g., ST-1 and ST-2) and between 1.02 and 4.78 mg/L (e.g., ST-3) (Fig. 2 d). The A/F ratios in the MS, TS, and ST samples showed a slight positive correlation with TN concentrations (R2  = 0.41) ( Fig. 3 a). These results indicate that the agricultural practices prevalent in watersheds regulate water chemistry in the upper reaches, and TN contribution from forests progressively increases with downstream distance. The approach to the correlation between TN and the A/F ratio more clearly showed that land-use patterns contributed to TN concentration in a small stream. Based on data from Fox et al. (2021) , TN and the proportion of agricultural area were positively correlated with a linear regression line of R2  = 0.54, and TN and A/F ratio also showed strongly positive correlation with R2  = 0.77. The proportion of urban areas is a crucial factor affecting water chemistry. The proportion of residential areas compared to forest areas (R/F) was much higher in TS-3 (49 %) than in the others (TS-1 and TS-2) (Table 1 ).  4.1.2 Total phosphorus (TP) Soil phosphorus is classified into organic and inorganic forms, and organic phosphorus is mineralized by microbial activity (Bünemann, 2015 ). With the natural sources of phosphorus in the soil, pollutants such as manure, chemical fertilizers, and sewage are major phosphorus (and phosphate) sources in soil and surface water within watersheds. Numerous studies have reported elevated TP concentrations in the surface waters of watersheds where agricultural and residential areas have developed (Withers and Jarvie, 2008; Duan et al., 2012; Janke et al., 2014; Bowes et al., 2015; Manning et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2021 ). In addition, TP in the soil can be transported to surface water as runoff from rainfall. According to a simulation conducted by Shigaki et al. (2007) , the behavior of TP in soil amended with P sources is significantly correlated with rainfall intensity. The spatial variation in TP could be closely related to land-use patterns, as mentioned for TN. Thus, considering the representative sources of TP, the ratio of the proportion of agricultural and residential areas to the proportion of forest (AR/F) was estimated to judge whether TP was controlled by land-use patterns. The AR/F ratio decreased from 54 % in MS‐1 to 31% in MS-3 and the ratio in MS-4 (44 %) increased because of the existence of the TS watershed with an AR/F ratio of 117 % (Table 1 ). The AR/F ratios corresponding to the TS and ST sampling sites ranged from 95 % to 117 % and from 94 % to 173 %, respectively. The ST samples showed relatively high TP concentrations (average 0.17 mg/L) compared to those in MS and TS samples. All AR/F ratios were positively correlated with TP concentrations (R2  = 0.90) regardless of the sampling period (Fig. 3 b). These results indicated that the TP in the stream water was derived from agricultural and residential areas and that runoff accompanied by rainfall elevated TP concentrations. Meanwhile, as performed in the relationship between TN and A/F ratio, TP was related to AR/F ratio based on data from previous study (MacKenzie et al., 2022 ), which showed a positive correlation with R2  = 0.46. TP related to the proportion of agricultural and residential areas also showed a similar R-squared value (R2  = 0.45). Despite this similarity, we suggest that the AR/F ratio is reasonable to account for TP derived from anthropogenic sources because TP contribution from natural sources is excluded when normalized by forest.   4.2 Relationships of TN and NO3 - -N Of the TN components in the stream water, NO3 - -N is predominant, typically. According to results reported in previous studies, NO3 - -N concentration generally accounts for approximately 80 % (up to ∼100 %) of TN (Chen et al., 2016; Weller and Jordan, 2020; Lin et al., 2021a ). Thus, the relationship between TN and NO3 - -N has been used to estimate nitrate and organic N sources in streams and to elucidate instream processes. Chen et al. (2016)  found that NO3 - -N and TN in streams showed a significant linear correlation and that the proportion of NO3 - -N increased with the TN concentration in the surface runoff. This resulted from an increase in the amount of fertilizer used in the watershed. In contrast, the NO3 - -N/TN ratio can be reduced due to the organic N increase associated with the biological utilization of instream sources, such as inorganic and organic nitrogen (Edwards et al., 2000 ). This process is prevalent in summer when algal growth is favored and surface runoff (e.g., soil solution) is lowered (Edwards et al., 2000 ). In this study, the NO3 - -N/TN ratio ranged from 0.29 to 0.99, displaying higher ratios in dry seasons compared to wet seasons (Table S2  and  Fig. 4 ). In addition, the relationship between NO3 - -N and TN showed a positive correlation overall with some exceptions (Fig. 4 ). Considering that variations in NO3 - -N related to TN are associated with surface runoff (Chen et al., 2016 ), these results indicated that many samples in this study were mainly explained by surface runoff occurring in the watershed, and the N formed in the watershed was mainly transported to the stream in the form of NO3 - -N. To constrain sources contributing to N loads in stream water, NO3 - -N and TN were correlated only for samples collected in winter, which was expressed by the following equation: NO3 - -N = 1.05 * TN – 0.63 (Fig. 4 a), where the slope is similar to that (0.98) reported by Chen et al. (2016) . The estimated line can be regarded as the representative N load of groundwater in the watershed. Regardless of seasonal changes, the MS samples were on and near the line, indicating that N loads in groundwater were derived from the same sources as surface runoff and introduced into the stream. In contrast, many TS and ST samples were far from the line, plotted on the right side of the line, and had relatively low NO3 - -N/TN ratios (at least 0.29) (Table S2  and Fig. 4 b). As mentioned earlier, these observations can result from increased organic N due to the active growth of microorganisms and algae through the utilization of instream sources. Simulation of nitrogen export in restored reach showed that approximately 40 % of nitrogen uptake by algae instream was mineralized into ammonium and then taken up by algae again after nitrification (Lin et al., 2021b ). Subsequently, approximately 60 % of nitrogen uptake by algae was store as organic N. According to the model's prediction, nitrogen corresponding to ∼55 % of the nitrogen taken up by algae was removed by instream denitrification as well. In the present study, the effect of the denitrification process on nitrate removal was ignored. Dissolved oxygen concentration (DO) higher than >5 mg/L (Table S2 ) represented that the studied streams were under an aerobic environment, not an anoxic environment that can occur due to algae bloom. In addition, the denitrification process was not observed in the relation between nitrogen and oxygen isotope compositions (Table 3 ). For example, both isotope compositions slightly increased or did not vary while running from TS-1 to TS-3, with decreasing nitrate concentrations.  4.3 Relationships of TN and TP As previously described, TN and TP in stream water originated from forests, agricultural areas, and residential areas in watersheds. Various anthropogenic sources (e.g., manure and domestic wastewater) supplying TN and TP to stream water are typically derived from agricultural and residential areas. TP variation in stream water was mainly affected by rainfall intensity-related surface runoff, but not TN. In addition, additional anthropogenic inputs (domestic sewage and industrial wastewater) derived from urban areas increase TP in stream water. TP has high soluble P concentrations, which are loosely adsorbed onto sediments in urbanized streams and subsequently released into streams via desorption or dissolution processes (Edwards and Withers, 2007; Wu et al., 2018 ). Based on the relationship between TN and TP for a large number of samples, stream water characterized by agriculture-dominant areas had a higher TN/TP ratio than that of residential areas (Manning et al., 2020 ). Likewise, the TN/TP ratio in stream water, especially small-scale streams, can be characterized by land-use patterns considering the representative sources of TN and TP and the flow pathways of rainfall (e.g., urban, forest, and agricultural areas). In a non-storm period, the TN/TP ratio showed a wide range from 7 to 1472 in MS (average 161 ±   217, n = 72), from 10 to 366 in TS (average 94 ±   94, n = 52), and from 5 to 128 (average 31 ±   24, n = 48) in ST ( Fig. 5 a). By comparison, the TN/TP ratio in storm events had a relatively narrow range from 11 to 131 in MS (average 45 ±   33, n = 31), from 3 to 44 in TS (average 16 ±   11, n = 17), and from 3 to 31 in ST (average 11 ±   8, n = 27) (Fig. 5 a). In the plots of TN/TP ratio and TP, the TN/TP ratios for water samples during non-storm periods were clearly discriminated from those during storm events. Regardless of the existence of storm events, the overall TN/TP decreased in the order of MS > TS > ST, whereas TP concentration increased. Considering the factors of TP variation in streams, as described in Section 4.1.2 , these resulted from natural and anthropogenic inputs derived from the dominant land use proportion in the MS, TS, and ST watersheds. To verify whether the TN/TP ratio was dependent on the land-use pattern, the average TN/TP ratio in every sample was correlated with the proportion of forest, residential, and agricultural areas (Fig. 5 b, c). The TN/TP ratios related to forests showed a positive correlation with TN/TP ratios, whereas residential and agricultural areas were negatively correlated with TN/TP ratios. In addition, the TN/TP ratio during storm events progressively decreased as the proportion of residential and agricultural areas increased, whereas the proportion of forests decreased. During storm events, the relationship between TN/TP ratios and the proportion of residential areas showed a strong negative correlation with R2  = 0.92, with the exception of two samples (MS-2 and MS-3) in which the contribution of the forest was remarkably elevated. In previous studies, urbanized streams had elevated P concentrations with rainfall-runoff, but no clear pattern for N variation (Duan et al., 2012; McDowell et al., 2019 ). In addition, impervious surfaces (i.e., residential areas) consisting of man-made structures, such as pavements covered with waterproof materials, have no or very limited infiltration capacity (Withers and Jarvie, 2008 ). The development of impervious surfaces prevents natural processes, such as P infiltration and soil adsorption, from occurring in the watershed, subsequently leading to the transport of more P into the stream (Hobbie et al., 2017 ). In this study, the ST watershed was characterized by a higher proportion of residential areas (20 %–25 %) than those in the MS (6 %–12 %) and TS (13 %–21 %) watersheds (Table 1 ). These land-use patterns contributed to higher P concentrations in the runoff. Therefore, this study demonstrated that the TN/TP ratio was mainly determined by solutes derived from residential areas rather than from other areas (McDowell et al., 2019; Manning et al., 2020 ).  4.4 Statistical findings The three major factors (F1, F2, and F3) were selected using PCA accounting for 80.9 % of total variance. The F1, F2, and F3 accounted for 35.7 %, 25.6 %, and 19.6 %, respectively ( Fig. 6 ). The proportions of agricultural and residential areas and TP concentrations were positively correlated with F1 ( Table 2 ). In contrast, the proportion of forests showed a strong negative correlation with F1. These indicated that water quality in streams was regulated by natural and anthropogenic sources related to the representative land-use pattern and that the TP was supplied to streams by anthropogenic sources rather than natural sources. F2 was strongly and positively correlated with TN and NO3 - -N concentrations, whereas F3 was positively correlated with precipitation, flow rate, and TP (Table 2 ). These results imply that water quality in the stream was affected by the difference between the relative contributions of precipitation and groundwater. Groundwater with a high NO3 - -N concentration would be introduced into stream water, especially during the dry season. Surface runoff would play a crucial role in supplying TP to the stream. On the plots of F1, F2, and F3, TS and ST samples and MS samples were clearly discriminated by F1, confirming that water quality in TS and ST was mainly determined by anthropogenic sources, whereas MS was by natural sources.  4.5 Identify sources using isotope For water samples additionally collected in winter (December 2021), δ15 N-NO3 -  and δ18 O-NO3 -  values ranged from 8.0 ‰ to 10.6 ‰ and from 2.0 ‰ to 4.8 ‰ and the values were within the typical cluster of manure and sewage ( Fig. 7  and  Table 3 ). These implied that the stream water chemistry was primarily affected by agricultural practices and domestic wastewater was derived from watersheds. The δ15 N-NO3 -  value was correlated with Cl-  concentration to identify natural and anthropogenic sources in more detail (Fig. 7 ). Evaporites have not been previously reported in South Korea (Chough et al., 2000 ). Chloride is not involved in physicochemical or biological transformations (Ding et al., 2015 ). Thus, the high Cl-  concentration in stream water originates from anthropogenic sources such as manure and sewage (Shin et al., 2023 ). Compared to those in the other samples, Cl-  concentration and δ15 N-NO3 -  value in MS samples varied within a narrow range of ∼30 mg/L and 8.0–8.5 ‰, respectively (Fig. 7 ). While flowing from MS-1 & −2 to MS-3 & −4, the stream water exhibited a lower NO3 - /Cl-  ratio. These could be related to the contribution of natural and anthropogenic inputs associated with land-use patterns. The proportion of agricultural area decreases with an increase in the proportion of forest flowing from the upper to the lower reaches. By comparison, ST samples showed clear spatial variation for the Cl-  and δ15 N-NO3 -  values, and their NO3 - /Cl-  ratios gradually decreased from 0.73 to 0.12. Similarly, TS samples characterized by δ15 N-NO3 -  values of >10 ‰ showed Cl-  increased from the upper-middle reaches to lower reaches, with a decreased NO3 - /Cl-  ratio. Contaminant sources released from urban areas would cause spatial variations in isotope and chemical compositions, considering that the proportion of urban areas was relatively high in ST-3 and TS-3. These results verified that the water quality in the studied stream was mainly affected by anthropogenic sources related to land-use patterns.   5 Conclusions Total nitrogen, TP, and NO3 - -N concentrations in the studied streams showed notable spatial and temporal variations, indicating complex interactions between natural and anthropogenic sources. TN concentrations in the streams exhibited distinct seasonal patterns, peaking during winter and declining in summer. This variability results from the continuous input of TN from agricultural practices and domestic wastewater, and TN concentrations were diluted by rainfall during wet seasons. During non-storm periods, TN concentrations were higher in the upper reaches (3.82 and 4.09 mg/L) compared to the lower reaches (2.84 and 2.94 mg/L), which can be explained by the increase of relative contribution of TN derived from agricultural area. The ratio of agricultural area to forested area tended to increase with increase of TN concentrations. Similarly, the ratio of agricultural and residential area to forested area was strongly positively correlated with TP concentrations during storm (R2  = 0.84) and non-storm periods (R2  = 0.90). The TP concentrations during the storm periods (0.04–0.16 mg/L) were higher than those during the non-storm periods (0.02–0.07 mg/L). These results indicate that TP concentrations in streams were determined by a significant impact of agricultural and residential runoff, especially during storm events. The spatiotemporal variations of TN and TP were more clearly shown in the relationship between TN/TP and TP with the proportion of forest, agricultural area and residential area. On the plot of TN/TP and TP, streams characterized by forest-dominant areas had the highest TN/TP ratios with the lowest TP, but the ratio progressively decreased with increasing contributions from agricultural area and furthermore residential area. These observations were facilitated due to increase of rainfall intensity. These findings were supported by statistical analyses and a plot of the dual isotopic compositions of nitrate and Cl-  with variations in NO3 - /Cl-  ratios. Effective watershed management strategies are crucial to mitigate nutrient pollution and safeguard water quality, especially in urbanizing landscapes where anthropogenic pressures continue to intensify. Future studies integrating advanced modeling and isotopic analyses could further clarify the specific sources and pathways of nitrogen and phosphorus inputs, facilitating targeted interventions for sustainable water resource management.
1 Introduction As an important component of the water cycle (Liu et al., 2021 ), river runoff connects the land and marine ecosystem through the transport of water, energy, and matter (Battin et al., 2023 ), and supports biodiversity, biogeochemical cycles, and human society (Messager et al., 2021 ). Changes in runoff have a strong association with global warming. Approximately 50 % of the world’s regional hydrological cycles are experiencing substantial changes, with conspicuous shifts in runoff patterns across several regions in response to ongoing global warming (Hobeichi et al., 2022 ). Global warming increases rainfall and enhances atmospheric evapotranspiration, leading to increases and decreases in runoff, respectively (Berghuijs et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2018 ). Warming and precipitation changes cause changes in vegetation cover and soil moisture (Zhu et al., 2016; Berg et al., 2017 ), which can subsequently alter the distribution of precipitation to runoff and evapotranspiration on the land surface, thus, affecting runoff volumes (Mankin et al., 2019 ). It has been reported that runoff increases in winter but decreases in summer in many river basins around the world (Koeplin et al., 2012 ; Safeeq et al., 2013 ), however, such seasonality of runoff has also changed with global warming (Barnett et al., 2005; Jenicek et al., 2021; Muelchi et al., 2021 ). The temporal distribution of runoff has also changed, resulting in difficulties in water resources management. The frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as extreme heat, drought, and heat waves, have increased in recent decades with global warming (Seneviratne et al., 2014; Van Loon et al., 2016 ), presenting a threat to the natural environment and the sustainable development of human society (AghaKouchak et al., 2020 ). The frequency and severity of flood disasters caused by high temperatures and rainstorms are gradually increasing in many regions, such as the Tarim River Basin, Qilian Mountains, and Colorado River Basin (Cheng et al., 2021; Merz and Blöschl, 2003 ). Warm temperatures accelerate the melting of snow and glaciers, causing flood events. This is followed by inevitable streamflow declines with greater inter/intra-seasonal variabilities after the tipping point is reached (Milly and Dunne, 2020; Yang, et al., 2022 ). When extreme weather events occur, the increased precipitation increases the surface and subsurface runoff (Sungmin and Park, 2023 ), while rising temperatures decreases snowfall and enhances snowmelt, which results in an early thaw and decreasing summer runoff (Yang et al., 2024; Kraaijenbrink et al., 2017 ). The temporal distribution of water resources is influenced by the uncertainty of extreme climate change and the increasing intensity and frequency of extreme weather events (Milly and Dunne, 2020; Intergovernment Panel on Climate Change, 2022 ). To better manage and regulate water resources, most studies focus on the simulation of river runoff and the analysis of flood characteristics (Blöschl et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2021 ; Jiang et al., 2022 ). Climate change and human disturbance are altering the hydrological cycle (Milly and Dunne, 2016, 2017 ), especially in cold-arid regions covered by permanent or seasonal ice/snow (Yang et al., 2024 ). However, there has been a limited analysis of how extreme weather events affect the changes in the annual distribution of runoff and the extent to which human activity affects runoff. Similarly to the temporal distribution of precipitation changes (Rajah et al., 2014 ), investigating changes in the concentration of runoff could improve the management and utilization of water resources. This is particularly the case in river basins where runoff is the main water resource for ecosystems (Ling et al., 2019 ). Arid regions are vulnerable to climate change and extreme weather (Cheng et al., 2021 ), with surface runoff maintaining the development of agriculture, ecology, and the social economy (Yao et al., 2022 ). Vegetation growth in arid basins mainly depends on water flow during the high flow period (Ling et al., 2019 ). Therefore, understanding changes in the concentration of runoff is crucial for water resources management, water, regulation, and flood control in arid regions. However, how runoff change and whether these changes are affected by extreme weather due to climate change remails unknown under the background of extreme climate change. Considering the sensitivity of arid regions to climatic and hydrological changes (Yao et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019 ), this study investigated the typical arid region of the Tarim River Basin as a case study to determine the effect of an extreme climate on runoff. There has been significant climate change in the study region, with the warm indices of extreme temperature and extreme precipitation increasing significantly, while the cold indices of extreme temperature have decreased significantly (Yao et al., 2022 ). There have also been significant changes in the hydrological processes within the basin (Yao et al., 2022 ). The Gini coefficient is an important tool for the quantitative evaluation of wealth gaps in economics and can also be used to analyze the heterogeneity of hydrology and meteorology (Masaki et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020 ). It can therefore be further used to reflect the variations in the temporal distribution of runoff. Therefore, the characteristics of the changes in the concentration of runoff were analyzed using the Gini-runoff coefficient, and the relationship between extreme weather and the Gini-runoff coefficient were explored. This enabled the impact of human interference on runoff to be determined. In predicting future hydrological changes, previous studies simulated runoff changes based on mathematical physics or conceptual models (Wu et al., 2015; Meresa et al., 2023 ), with most studies mainly adopting distributed hydrological models (Xu and Di Vittorio, 2021; Maina et al., 2022 ). The extensive data requirements for calculating hydrological model parameters, coupled with the large spatiotemporal variations in these parameters and the strong uncertainty, have increasingly limited the performance of hydrological models. As a consequence, the future changes in the time of runoff concentration have been predicted using machine learning methods, which have performed well in predicting river runoff (Fan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020; Yoosefdoost et al., 2022 ), flooding and flood mechanisms (Kao et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2022 ), and the determination of the effects of climate change on runoff (Wang et al., 2018 ). Additionally, changes in atmospheric circulation patterns have been used to analyze the causes of changes in key climate extremes, and the atmospheric processes affecting the concentration of runoff have finally been identified. The results presented here will provide scientific guidance for water resources management, and disaster prevention and control, as well as providing a reference for the allocation of water resources in arid regions.  2 Study area The Tarim River is the longest inland river in China (Wang et al., 2021 ). It is located in the south of Xinjiang, far from the ocean and is surrounded by mountains. It has a marked continental climate characterized by large changes in temperature, an abundance of sunshine, and low precipitation, all of which are typical for arid and semi-arid inland areas (Yang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020 ). It lies in the subtropical westerlies, with water vapor from the Atlantic, Arctic, Black, and Caspian seas entering Xinjiang by westerly transport (Zhou et al., 2019 ). This promotes the formation of warm and wet climate conditions in the basin. However, there are ongoing conflicts between the supply and demand of water resources in this region, and the regulation and management of water resources remains a critical issue. The runoff in the Tarim River Basin is mainly derived from the Aksu, Yarkant, and Hotan rivers, which account for 42 %, 34 %, and 24 % of total runoff, respectively (Gao et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011 ). The three headwaters originate from the Tianshan, Karakoram, and Kunlun mountains (Chen et al., 2019 ), and are seasonal glacier/snowmelt rivers. The sensitivity of the regional climate to global warming (Shi et al., 2007 ), and the type and seasonal characteristics of runoff make the Tarim River Basin a useful research area to achieve the goal of this study. In the Hotan River, the Wuluwati station (Hotan_w) began to artificially regulate the discharge in 2001, creating favorable conditions for analyzing the impact of human interference. An overview of the study region is presented in  Fig. 1 .  3 Materials and methods The Gini-runoff coefficient was calculated based on the monthly runoff for each river. Their interannual and periodic variations revealed the characteristics of runoff changes in the headwaters of the Tarim River Basin. To identify the features of extreme climate change in the study area, the 26 core extreme climate indices (extreme temperature and precipitation indices) introduced by the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI, http://etccdi.pacificclimate.org ), and the precipitation amounts were used. The characteristic changes of these indices revealed the tendency and periodicity of extreme climate change in the study region. The reasons for changes in the Gini-runoff coefficient were explored by considering the relationships between extreme climate indices and the Gini-runoff coefficient, runoff in the warm and cold seasons, and average days of snow cover. The effect of reservoir regulation on the time of runoff concentration recorded at Hotan_w was quantified using the periodic superimposed trend model. There were three steps in the prediction of future Gini-runoff coefficient change. First, a correlational analysis was conducted between extreme climate indices and the Gini-runoff coefficient to evaluate the impact of extreme climate change on the concentration of runoff, and to identify the key extreme climate indices. Second, four general machine learning methods were applied to construct a prediction model of the Gini-runoff coefficient using these key indices. Finally, the optimal model for each river was determined using the root mean square error (RMSE), the coefficient of determination (R 2  ), and F test (p < 0.01).
