The final step was the calculation of the key climate extreme indices for each river over three scenarios using the data provided by four global climate models (during 2024−2050), which were input into the corresponding optimal model to generate predictions for the Gini-runoff coefficient in 2024−2050. The specific technology roadmap was as follows ( Fig. 2 ). 3.1 Data ① Hydrometeorological data. The monthly runoff for five hydrological stations during 1961−2020 (Aksu River: Xiehela, Shaliguilk; Yarkant River: Kaqun; Hotan River: Wuluwati, Tongzilocke) in the Tarim River headstreams were provided by the Xinjiang Tarim River Basin Authority. The daily maximum and minimum precipitation data (Tmax and Tmin, respectively) of five meteorological stations (Aksu River: Akqi, Aksu; Yarkant River: Taxkorgan, Shache; Hotan River: Hotan) in the Tarim River headstreams were downloaded from The China Meteorological Data Service Center (https://data.cma.cn ). ② Meteorological grid data. The daily precipitation data were obtained from a new daily gridded precipitation dataset for the Chinese mainland based on gauge observations with a resolution of 0.25 × 0.25° (Gao et al., 2023 ), provided by the National Tibetan Plateau/Third Pole Environment Data Center (https://cstr.cn/18406.11.Atmos.tpdc.300523 ). The 16 extreme temperature indices for 1961−2020 were derived from a grid dataset of extreme temperature indices in China at 0.25 × 0.25°, which was downloaded from the Digital Journal of Global Change Data Repository ( https://doi.org/10.3974/geodb.2024.05.06.V1 ). The values were calculated using the daily dataset of basic meteorological elements from China's national ground meteorological station (V3.0) (Chen et al., 2024 ). ③ Climate model data. The daily Tmax , Tmin  and precipitation data for 1957−2060 were derived from NASA Global Daily Downscaled Projections, Phase 6 of the Climate Model Intercomparison Project (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6) (Thrasher et al., 2022 ). The model data was largely selected with reference to the results of previous extreme climate simulations and assessments in arid regions (Zhu et al., 2022 ). Four CMIP6 models were selected for use in this study, with each model included in three future scenarios (see Supplementary 2.1). ④ Snow cover days. Data were obtained from the China AVHRR Daily Cloudless 5 km Snow Area Product Dataset, provided by National Cryosphere Desert Data Center (http://www.ncdc.ac.cn ), at a scale of 5 km. ⑤ Atmospheric circulation data. Total cloud cover (TCC), snowmelt, and geopotential height at 200, 500, and 1000 hPa were obtained from the ERA5 dataset in the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu ), at a scale of 0.25 × 0.25°.  3.2 Methods 3.2.1 Data processing Data processing involved the calculation of the Gini-runoff and Gini-pre coefficients, extreme climate indices, the extraction of snow cover days, and climate model data, with the data averaged from four climate models. The calculation of the Gini-runoff coefficient was based on the calculation of the Gini coefficient in economics, while data averaging from the four climate models used the reliability ensemble averaging method. All data processing was conducted using code within the R software environment. The software version was R4.3.1 and the language was English. The details of the method were as follows. ① The extreme climate indices The 26 core indices introduced by the ETCCDI were applied, with the definition of all extreme indices used in the study given in Supplementary 2.2. The extreme temperature indices were extracted from the datasets referred to in Section 3.1 . We calculated the extreme precipitation indices based on gridded daily precipitation data. For the code used in the data quality control and indices calculation, refer to the RClimDex software (http://cccma.seos.uvic.ca/ETCCDI/software.shtml ), which was developed and maintained at the Climate Research Branch of the Meteorological Service of Canada (Zhang and Yang, 2004). The final time series was the average of the overall basin, and all calculations were performed in R 4.3.1. ② Gini-runoff coefficient and Gini-precipitation (Gini-pre) coefficient To calculate the two coefficients, the monthly runoff and precipitation were reordered in ascending order and then cumulatively converted into a fraction of the total runoff and precipitation to obtain the Lorentz curve. The coefficients were derived by doubling the area within the Lorenz curve and the 45°  diagonal line, representing a uniform distribution of runoff or precipitation. This can be expressed as follows (Rajah et al., 2014 ):(1) Gini = 1  n   ( n + 1 − 2 ( ∑  i = 1  n   n + 1 − i    yi   ∑ i = 1  n   yi    )         where Gini represents the Gini-runoff coefficient or Gini-pre coefficient, and y i   denotes the runoff or precipitation in every month in a year. A Gini value equal to zero means that the runoff or precipitation distribution is perfectly uniform throughout the year. ③ Reliability ensemble averaging Although the CMIP6 model is a substantial improvement over the CMIP5 model for extreme climate simulation (Chen et al., 2020 ), there are still large uncertainties in climate change prediction using only a simple arithmetic mean set scheme. Therefore, we used the upgraded reliability ensemble averaging method (UREA) to calculate the climate indices needed for future climate extremes (Zhu et al., 2022 ). Based on the REA framework, UREA proposes an improved REA scheme that considers the simulation performance of different aspects of the model simulation observation of climate state and time variability. The reliability coefficient calculation R i   can be calculated as follows:(2) R  i   = f  1   T  bias         m 1   × f  2   T  abs , war         m 2   × f  3   T  var         m 3        (3) f  1   T  bias      = ε  T    abs ( T  mod   − T  obs   )       (4) f  2   T  abs , var      = ε  STD    abs ( STD  mod   − STD  obs   )        (5) f  3   T  rel , var      = 1.0  1.0 + ( STD  mod    STD  obs     − STD  obs    STD  mod     )  2          where f 1   represents the ability of models to reproduce observed climate states; f 2   and f 3   represent the ability of the model to simulate the absolute and relative deviations of the observed interannual variability, respectively; T bias   is the deviation term of the climate state in simulated observations; T abs,var   is the absolute deviation term of the interannual variability of the simulated observation; T rel,var   is the relative deviation term of the interannual variability of the simulated observation; ε T   and ε STD   are measures of exponential natural variability; T mod   and T obs   are the simulated and observed climate states; STD mod   and STD obs   are the interannual variabilities of the simulation and observation; and abs represents the absolute value. The values of f 1  , f 2  , and f 3   range from 0 to 1. The parameters m1, m2, and m3 are used to adjust the relative contributions of each item on the right side of the equal sign, all of which were set to 1 in this study. The reliability coefficient R i   of each model was calculated by formula 2 and then used to identify the weight of each pattern.(6) W  i   = R  i    ∑ i = 1  N   R  i          where N  is the number of models; R i   is the reliability coefficient of the i-th model; W i   indicates the weight of the i-th model; and W i   is the normalized value of R i  .  3.2.2 Analysis of the variation characteristics and influencing factors A nonparametric test was used to analyze the characteristics of all indices. This was superior to other tests, which can detect trends (Mann–Kendall trend test) or abrupt changes (Mann-Whitney abrupt-change test) without establishing the statistical distribution (Wang et al., 2002 ). Wavelet analysis (WA) was developed by the French engineer Morlet, who proposed its use in 1980 when analyzing seismic data. It can characterize the nonstationary process in a hydrologic time series analysis (Wang et al., 2002 ), and was used here to analyze the periodic changes of all indices. A Spearman rank correlation was used to analyze the relationships among indices due to its robustness against assumptions regarding the distribution and sample size of variables (Myers and Sirois, 2004 ). The main methods adopted were as follows. ① Mann-Kendall trend test The Mann-Kendall statistical test method is a nonparametric test method that involves sequentially comparing time sequence X1 , X2 , X3 , …, Xn.  The results were expressed as sgn (θ  ):(7) sgn ( θ )  = { 1 , . θ > 0   0 , . θ = 0   − 1 , θ < 0          The Mann-Kendall statistical calculation results were determined as:(8) s = ∑ i = 1  n  ∑ k = i + 1  n  sgn ( x  k    − x  i   )     where xk  and xi  are random variables, and n is the length of the selected data sequence. The test statistic Zc  was determined as:(9) Z  c   = { s − 1  var ( s )      , s > 0   0 , ………… s = 0   s + 1  var ( s )      , s < 0          In the formula, when |Zc | ≥1.96, the sample sequence has a significant trend change at the 0.05 level. When |Zc | >2.58, the trend of the sample sequence changes significantly at the 0.01 level (Kendall, 1975 ). When Zc  is positive there is an upward trend. When Zc  is negative there is a downward trend. ② Mann-Whitney abrupt-change test The abrupt point should be determined before an abrupt-change test. The point was determined according to the trend change of a cumulative anomaly value. The basic principles of the Mann-Whitney test are as follows: Let the time sequence be (1,2, …, n) and its subsequences Y = (X1 , X2 , …, Xn ) and Z = (Xn1 + 1 , Xn1 + 2 , …, Xn1 + n2 ). The mutation test is then expressed as:(10) Z  c   = ∑ t = 1  n  1     r ( x   t   ) − n  1   ( n  1   + n  2   + 1 ) / 2  n  1   n  2   ( n  1   + n  2   + 1 ) / 12         where r (xt) is the rank of the observed value; n1  is the number of time series before the abrupt change; and n2  is the number of time series after the abrupt change, n1 +n2 =n. If Z1-a/2 ≤ Zc ≤ Z1-a/2 , the null hypothesis is accepted. Given the testing level of a, Z1-a / 2  is the quantile of the 1-a / 2 standard normal distribution. ③ Wavelet change analysis For the time sequence function f (t), the wavelet change is defined as:(11) W  f   ( a , b ) = 1 a    ∫ − ∞  ∞  f ( t )  ψ  *   ( t − b  a  )  d t     where Wf  (a, b) is the wavelet coefficient, a is the scaling factor, which determines the wavelet width; b is a translation factor, which is a parameter reflecting the movement of the wavelet position; and ψ is the conjugate function of ψ*.(12) ψ ( x )  = C e  − x  2   2     cos ( 5 x )      The wavelet variance is:(13) W  p   ( a )  = W  f   ( a , b )  2       Wavelet variance indicates the strength (energy) of the periodic fluctuations of the time sequence in this scale. The scale at the corresponding peak is the main period of the sequence (Gao and Li, 1993 ).  3.2.3 Predicting changes in the Gini-runoff coefficient under future climate scenarios The fundamental concept of machine learning is to enable computers to mimic the learning behavior of humans. Through repeated training and learning using large data, the useful information in the data can be mined to obtain new knowledge (Reichstein et al., 2019 ). To improve the accuracy of predicting results, four machine learning methods were applied in this study: ridge regression (Ridge), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and back propagation artificial neural network (BP-ANN). These machine learning models were implemented in R4.3.1 (see Supplementary 1 for the details of each method). The four models all used extreme climate factors as inputs and the Gini-runoff coefficient as the output. The data were partitioned as 75 % for learning and the other 25 % for a test calibration, with the data from 1962 to 2001 used for training, and the data from 2002 to 2020 used for validation. The R 2   values of the models and the RMSE between the actual and predicted values for the calibration and validation processes were used to evaluate the prediction ability of different models. The model with the lowest RMSE, highest R 2 , and F-test (p < 0.05) values was considered the optimal model, and was therefore selected as the prediction model for each river to predict the Gini-runoff coefficient. The formula for calculating the RMSE was as follows (Zhou et al., 2020 ):(14) RMSE = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   Y  i , a   − Y  i , p      2          where Y i,a , Y i,p , and n are the actual Gini-runoff coefficient values in a certain year, the predicted value, and the number of years, respectively.  3.2.4 Periodic superimposed trend model If the long-term dynamics of time-series data are influenced by upward or downward trends at a steady rate and by the seasonal cycle, and the time sequence fluctuations caused by the seasonal period are the same for each period, the time sequence can be predicted using a seasonal periodic superposition trend model (Ling et al., 2013). This method is used in the data processing system (DPS) software. The model used in this study first predicted the changes in runoff without human influence, and then quantified the impact of human activities by comparing it with actual values.    4 Results 4.1 The characteristics of changes in runoff For the three headwaters of the Tarim River Basin, the trend changes and cumulative anomaly of annual runoff, and the corresponding Gini-runoff coefficient in 1962−2020 are shown in  Fig. 3 . There was a significant increasing trend in runoff, but the corresponding Gini-runoff coefficient displayed a significant decreasing trend (Fig. 3 a−d,  Table 1 ). The runoff of Aksu River, Yarkant River, and Tongzilocke (Hotan_t) and at Hotan_w in Hotan River Basin abruptly increased in 1993, 1993, 2001, and 2002 ( Fig. 4 a−d, Table 1 ), respectively, and the mean runoff increased by 15.2 %, 15.7 %, 18.6 %, and 16.8 %, respectively, after the abrupt change. The concentration of runoff in Aksu River Basin, Yarkant River Basin, and Hotan_t decreased abruptly in 2002, while at Hotan_w there was an abrupt decrease in 2001. The corresponding Gini-runoff coefficient decreased significantly in 2002, 2002, 2001, and 2002, respectively, and the average values decreased by 7.3 %, 6.3 %, 5.0 %, and 16.8 %, respectively, after the abrupt change. The changes in wavelet period and wavelet coefficient of the Gini-runoff coefficients are given in   Figs. 5 and 6 . The Gini-runoff coefficient of Aksu River had 9, 14, and 21-year periods. In both the 9 and 14-year periods, the Gini-runoff coefficient fluctuated more significantly after 1993 (Figs. 5 a and 6 a). The Gini-runoff coefficient in the Yarkant river has 9, 15, and 21-year periods. In the 9-year period, the wavelet coefficients changed significantly between 1990 and 2005, although periodicity was not observed. In the 15-year period, the wavelet coefficients changed significantly after 1990 (Figs. 5 b and 6 b). The Gini-runoff coefficient at Hotan_t had 6, 21, and 25-year main periods. There were 10, 17, and 21-year main periods at Hotan_w, with the period changes exhibiting a consistent fluctuation pattern. (Figs. 5 c and 6 c).  4.2 Effects of extreme climate on runoff and characteristics of change 4.2.1 The correlation between extreme climate indices and the Gini-runoff coefficient The correlation coefficients for the relationships between the Gini-runoff coefficient and extreme climate indices are shown in  Fig. 7 (a−d). The Gini-runoff coefficient was negatively correlated with the extreme precipitation index and the warm index of extreme temperature, but positively correlated with the cold index of extreme temperature. There were 9, 7, and eleven key extreme climate indices selected in Aksu River, Yarkant River, and Hotan River, respectively, which was based on the significance of the correlation (p <0.05). The ranking of the importance of key climate extremes affecting the Gini-runoff coefficient is shown in  Fig. 8 (a−d). The order of importance was TN90, CWD, WSDI, R20, R95, R25, R10, CDD, DTR for Aksu River, and TXx, DTR, CDD, TN90, Rx1, Rx5, CWD for Yarkant River. Four extreme climate indices affected the concentration of runoff at Hotan_t, SU, TN90, TN10, and DTR. There were six main extreme climate indices that affected the runoff volume at Hotan_w, including CDD, CWD, TNx, TNn, TXn, and TXx. Extreme temperature indices, including DTR, TN90, TR, and TXx, were the main factors impacting the Gini-runoff coefficient in the three headwaters. Among the extreme precipitation indices, CWD had the greatest effect on the Gini-runoff coefficient in Aksu River, CDD had the greatest effect in Yarkant River, and CDD and CWD had the greatest effect in Hotan River.  4.2.2 The characteristics of the changes in key extreme climate indices The characteristics of the changes in selected key extreme climate indices were analyzed ( Fig. 9 , Supplementary 2.3−2.5). The warm indices of extreme temperature and extreme precipitation increased, while the cold indices of extreme temperature decreased. There was an abrupt change in the extreme indices around the late 1990s and early 2000s. In the Aksu River Basin, the extreme precipitation indices displayed an increasing trend, while DTR and CDD displayed a decreasing trend and the tendencies of all indices to change were significant except for R10 and DTR (Fig. 6 , Supplementary 2.3). The key extreme climate indices TN90 and CWD displayed a significantly increasing trend (p < 0.01) with abrupt changes occurring in 1995 and 2001, respectively, and the main wavelet periods were 8, 17, and 21 years. The other indices, including WSDI, R20, R95, R25, R10, CDD and DTR, had abrupt changes in 2002, 1996, 2000, 1995, 1997, 2002, and 1997, respectively. The main wavelet periods were 8−9, 21, and 25 years (Supplementary 2.4 to Supplementary 2.5). As shown in  Fig. 10  and Supplementary 2.3−2.5, the effects of TXx, Rx1, and Rx5 on the Gini-runoff coefficient in the Yarkant River Basin displayed an insignificant increasing trend (p > 0.05), while for CWD, there was a significant increasing trend (p < 0.05). For TN90 there was a very significant increasing trend (p < 0.001), while for DTR and CDD, there was a very significant decreasing trend (p < 0.001). For DTR and CDD, there were abrupt decreases in 2001 and 1986, respectively, while for TXx, TN90, CWD, Rx1, and Rx5, there were abrupt increases in 2004, 1998, 1989, and 2001, respectively. The main wavelet periods of the main four extreme climate indices (TXx, DTR, CDD, and TN90) were 8−11, 17, and 21 years. As shown in  Fig. 11 , DTR, TN10, and CDD affected the Gini-runoff coefficient, with an extremely significant decreasing trend in the Hotan River Basin (p < 0.001). For TN90, SU, TNx, and TNn there was an extremely significant increasing trend (p < 0.001). For CWD, TXn, and TXx there was an insignificant increasing trend (p > 0.05). For CDD, CWD, TXn, and TNn there were abrupt decreases during 1986−1989, while the ranges of the other indices changed abruptly between 1996 and 1999. The main wavelet periods of the five most important extreme climate indices (TN90, DTR, TR, FD, and WSDI) were 9−12, 17, and 21years.   4.3 Projected changes in the Gini-runoff coefficient under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) The RMSE and R 2   values for the simulated Gini-runoff coefficient during the calibration and validation processes across the three headwaters are presented in  Table 2 . Across all three rivers, the RMSE was minimal and exhibited no significant variance among the four models. However, the R 2   values were notably higher than those of other models when the RF was employed during both the calibration and validation phases. The R 2   values for both predicted and simulated values in each of the three headwaters exceeded 0.80 during calibration, while they surpassed 0.60 during validation. These results suggest that predictions derived from the RF were closely aligned with observed data. Consequently, the Gini-runoff coefficients under three prospective emission scenarios were determined by incorporating key future extreme climate indices into the RF model. As shown in  Fig. 12 , the Gini-runoff coefficients of runoff in the Aksu River Basin and Hotan_t continued to decrease significantly under the three emission scenarios (i.e., SSPs) (p < 0.001), indicating that the concentration of runoff will decrease. The Gini-runoff coefficient of Yarkant River Basin and Hotan_w changed insignificantly under the same three emission scenarios (p > 0.05). The average value of the future Gini-runoff coefficient under the same three scenarios decreased by 3.3 % and 2.6 % in the Aksu and Hotan river basins, respectively. In Aksu River Basin, the decrease in the concentration of runoff was ranked as low, high, and medium forcing in the three SSPs, while in the Yarkant and Hotan river basins, the order was high, medium, and low forcing, respectively.   5 Discussion 5.1 The reasons for the changes in the concentration of runoff Discharge in the Tarim River Basin is primarily influenced by glacier and snow cover. There has been a discernible increasing trend in discharge in the three headwaters over the past 60 years (Fig. 3 a−d). The runoff in Aksu River Basin displayed a decreasing trend after 2000. There were several reasons for this. As the major headwater of Aksu River, the Kumalak River Basin has a large number of glaciers and an extensive frozen area. The rate of glacier retreat has slowed significantly from 1990 to 2000, and was still decreasing after 2000 due to the reduced summer temperatures following the increasing trend in precipitation (Zhang et al., 2020 ). In the Toxkan River region, reductions in precipitation and glacier area, coupled with early spring snowmelt, have led to a reduction in the snow meltwater supply in summer, which in turn contributed to the decrease in runoff. Moreover, the glacier mass balance also slowed from 2002 onward (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The concentration of runoff in the three headwaters remained relatively stable as the overall runoff in the basin increased (Fig. 3 a-d), indicating that the differences in the annual distribution of runoff have gradually decreased in recent years. A further analysis revealed that the decrease in the concentration of runoff was related to the significant increase in runoff in the cold season. The monthly runoff in each river basin displayed an increasing trend ( Fig. 13 a), with the trend in May to September being much smaller than in other months, and the trend was insignificant during June to August. The increasing runoff rate in the cold season was much stronger than in the warm season (Fig. 13 ), and the timings of the abrupt changes in the concentration of runoff in the three river basins were consistent with the runoff in the cold season (Aksu:1999, Yarkant: 2001, Hotan_t: 2001, Hotan_w:2001) in this study (Fig. 3  and Supplementary 2.6). At the same time, the periodicity of runoff in the cold season changed significantly after 2000 in the main periods (Supplementary 3.1). Therefore, the increasing runoff in the cold season reduced the concentration of runoff and the changes in its periodicity on multiple time scales, which improved the uncertainty of extreme hydrological events. With the prolonging of the warm season, the rising temperature led to precipitation occurring by rain rather than snow in early and late winter, and the early snowmelt (Barnett et al., 2005; Stewart et al., 2004 ) resulted in runoff increasing in the cold season. Based on the relationships between runoff in both the cold and warm seasons and the extreme climate indices, the key extreme climate factors influencing the concentration of runoff in the three headwaters were identified. The runoff in the three river basins in the warm season was influenced by the extreme high temperature indices (TR, TXx, TN90, and TXn), while the extreme precipitation indices (R10, R20, R25, R95, CDD, CWD), the extreme low temperature indices (FD, TN10, and TNn), and DTR significantly impacted the runoff in the cold season ( Fig. 14 ). The decreasing CDD and DTR had a significant negative effect on the cold season runoff in each river basin, TN90 had a significant positive effect on runoff in each river basin, while the extreme low temperature indicator TNn had a significant negative effect on the cold season runoff at Hotan_w (Fig. 14 a1−d1). In particular, the increase in the extreme precipitation indices (R10, R10, R25, R95, CWD) had significant positive effects on the cold season runoff in the Aksu River Basin. Both continuous and extreme precipitation increased the amount of snow cover and promoted the release of snow and glacier melt water after warming (Winsemius et al., 2016; Hirabayashi et al., 2021 ), while the decrease in extreme low temperatures could also affect runoff through an increase in rain−snow weather in the cold season (Merz and Blöschl, 2003 ). In the warm season, TN90 had a positive effect on runoff in the Aksu River Basin, Yarkant River Basin, and Hotan_t, with the latter also extremely significantly affected by TXx (Fig. 14 a−d). The warm season runoff was significantly affected by TNx and CWD at Hotan_w because snowmelt peaked in the warm season, and extreme high temperatures further promoted snow melt and increases in runoff. In the Aksu River Basin, runoff in the warm and cold seasons increased more slowly than in the other two river basins (Fig. 13 b), and the runoff in the warm season was only affected by TN90 (Fig. 14 a). The extent of snow cover and glacier area have decreased in recent years in the Aksu River Basin (Zhang et al., 2019), and runoff sources have decreased. The cold season runoff in the Yarkant and Hotan River Basins is influenced by snow cover, as evidenced by the correlation between snow cover days and runoff during the cold and warm seasons. A significant decline in cold runoff was observed following the significant decreasing trend of snow cover days ( Fig. 15 a, b). The influence of runoff in the warm season in Aksu River Basin was stronger than in the cold season, mainly because the ice and snow retreat rate in the basin has slowed and is significantly affected by precipitation. The positive effects of extreme precipitation have been offset by increased evaporation due to the extreme temperatures (Milly and Dunne, 2016, 2017 ). Furthermore, it has been reported that runoff has increased in winter but has decreased in summer in many river basins around the world (Koeplin et al., 2012 ; Safeeq et al., 2013 ). The base flow in winter increases in the headwaters of the Yellow River in China, and the recession process slow down (Wu et al., 2020 ). Seasonal variations of runoff in glacier- and snowmelt-dependent basins are predominantly influenced by several factors, including warmer winters, increased rain and snow, and earlier snowmelt (Chen et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Tarasova et al., 2020a ). In arid regions, mountain reservoirs and hydro-junctions are mainly used for flood storage, regulation of irrigation water, and hydropower (Sen et al., 2021 ), all of which affect the concentration of runoff. The Gini-runoff coefficient exhibited a minor decrease prior to human regulation, but the reduction was not significant. However, following the construction of the Wuluwati Hydro-junction in 2001 there was a large decline in extreme events (p <0.001). Through the periodic superimposed trend model, the human regulation of water volume at Hotan_w was found to promote a 12.1 % decrease in the concentration of runoff from 2001 to 2020( Fig. 16 ). Changes in time of concentration of runoff present major challenges for water resources management in many rivers (Barnett et al., 2005 ). The results reported here explain the annual distribution of runoff for Tarim River Basin and are applicable to similar arid inland river basins. They will help to improve the efficiency of water resources regulation. The occurrence of extreme weather events can be explained effectively by analyzing the long-term changes in atmospheric circulation patterns (Ye and Qian, 2021 ). The driving mechanism of the main factors influencing changes in DTR and extreme high temperature indices was further investigated. The significant decrease in DTR was consistent with the global trend, while the significant decrease in DTR could be attributed to the increase in TCC and the increase in precipitation ( Fig. 17 ). An increase in TCC reduces DTR due to a decrease in daytime surface insolation and an increase in night-time downwards longwave radiation (Li et al., 2022 ) Extreme high temperatures are directly related to changes in atmospheric circulation. For example, the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) has a significant positive driving effect on high temperatures in autumn and winter (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The enhanced center of the South Asian High in recent years has also contributed to the extreme high temperature events that have occurred in northwest China (Wu et al., 2017 ). Additionally, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation also has a significant positive effect on the occurrence of extreme high temperatures and a significant negative effect on the occurrence of extreme low temperatures in Xinjiang (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The heightened frequency of extreme precipitation events in Xinjiang could be linked to the unusual warming trend observed in the Indian Ocean, which has facilitated the increased evaporation of water from the ocean. Furthermore, abnormal cyclonic activity in the Central Asia region has played a role in directing this moisture-laden air from the Indian Ocean to Xinjiang via the Iranian Plateau and Central Asia (Yao et al., 2022 ), resulting in extreme precipitation in Xinjiang. Based on the changes in geopotential height (Supplementary 3.2 ), changes in TCC and precipitation were associated with a wave-like pattern in the geopotential height trend. This extended from the north Atlantic, mid-latitude Europe, central Asia, to northwestern China, and there were below-normal anomalies over central Asia and northwestern China (Fig. 13 ). Therefore, atmospheric circulation changes alter the concentration of runoff by influencing extreme climate change. The extreme climate change in the Tarim River Basin may also be affected by other climate factors, such as arctic oscillation/NAO (Fan et al., 2021 ). Further study is therefore required to determine the key atmospheric circulation factors affecting the concentration of runoff.  5.2 The future variation of the concentration of runoff and its uncertainty Future warming will coexist with extreme high temperatures by reducing the future extent of glaciers and snow cover at high altitudes (Harrell et al., 2022 ), thus reducing runoff from snowmelt and increasing the concentration of runoff. This will lead to a pronounced decline in runoff volume. In the future (2024−2050), the concentration of runoff in the Aksu and Hotan river basins will decrease significantly under the three SSP emission scenarios (Fig. 9 ), indicating that the temporal distribution of the two rivers in the future will tend to be dispersed. When glacier cover decreases by 15−73 % in the future, the runoff in Aksu River Basin will first increase and then decrease, while runoff in the Hotan and Yarkant river basins will increase by 15−60 %. Relative to the mean area in 1971−2000, glaciers will retreat by 35 % in the near term, 2−64 % in the mid-term, and 8−89 % in the long term under the RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5 climate scenarios (Wortmann et al., 2022 ). The retreat of the Karakoram glaciers (the headstream of the Yarkant River) is expected to peak in the coming decades, presenting a risk of glacial lake outburst flooding (Nie et al., 2021 ). Glaciers are retreating rapidly, and heterogeneous glacier retreat will likely change river patterns (Nie et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, the advance of the snowmelt date and the acceleration of melting speed will result in the rapid reduction of snow and ice resources. When a certain threshold value is reached, rainfall and snowmelt will dominate the formation of runoff (Immerzeel et al., 2012; Lutz et al., 2016; Wijngaard et al., 2017 ). With the depletion of snow and ice resources, the concentration of runoff will continue to decrease, and the watershed will face the risk of hydrological drought. Additionally, water shortages are a further problem affecting the social economy and natural environment in arid and semi-arid areas. With the gradual increase in temperature, the risk of water shortages increases (Yang et al., 2022). Researchers and local government departments have attempted to determine the optimal water resource allocation scheme and water utilization technologies in arid areas to reduce this risk, including the establishment of a water resource allocation model (Nassery et al., 2017 ; Kizhisseri et al., 2021 ; Banadkooki et al., 2022 ), and the establishment of a framework for water resources management (Mirdashtvan et al., 2021; Ghimire et al., 2023; Hesamfar et al., 2023 ). However, the applicability of available water resource allocation schemes decreases with the decline in the concentration of runoff, leading to a weakened regional resistance to drought (especially flash drought). There is also an increased risk of vegetation degradation, which is primarily caused by the stress of reduced carbon uptake during vegetation growth in the early stage of drought (Sungmin and and Park., 2023 ). Some regions, such as the Mediterranean Basin (Mostafa et al., 2021a,b; Rolim et al., 2017 ), Heihe River Basin in China (Wang et al., 2018 ), Tarim River Basin in China (Wang et al., 2019 ), and Iran (Nazari et al., 2018 ) have experienced increased agricultural water demand with rising temperatures, increasing the risk of seasonal water shortages. Increases in climate aridity, therefore decrease the availability of water resources (Rocha et al., 2020 ). Simultaneously, the availability of water resources has reached a critical level with the increase in agricultural water demand in several regions of the world (Mancosu et al., 2015 ). The decline in the concentration of runoff has further reduced the availability of water resources in areas with water shortages, exacerbating the risk of water security in arid areas (Xia et al., 2017 ). To reduce these risks and continuously optimize water resource allocation, strategies such as water banking have been implemented in the western United States (Carney et al., 2021 ). However, the legacy of past preferential allocation systems, poses a significant threat to water security under these new systems. The results of this study provide a theoretical basis for the implementation of water storage policies to reduce hydrological drought risks and enhance resistance to meteorological drought. In the Tarim River Basin and regions with a similar climate worldwide, water resources management departments should increase the storage of water during the cold season to alleviate the pressure on water use in the basin during the warm season; therefore, increasing the basin's drought resistance. The selection of climate datasets, correction of climate bias, establishment of a climate hydrological model, and other processes will generate uncertainty in the prediction results (Meresa et al., 2023 ). In this study, machine learning was used to simulate the relationship between key extreme climate indices and the Gini-runoff coefficient to reduce the influence of uncertainty in the hydrological parameters in hydrological models. Second, the climate data used for modeling underwent a quality control process to ensure the accuracy and reliability of weather stations. Data from four general circulation models (GCMs) were used to analyze extreme climate change in the future. These datasets played a pivotal role in the forecasting process. The four GCMs were evaluated to determine which was optimal for climate simulation in this region (Xiang et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022; Lai, 2023 ), and all models were corrected. Future extreme climate indices (2024−2050) were calculated by a reliability ensemble averaging method to reduce the uncertainty caused by the differences in climate models, which acquires weights based on the reliability coefficient for each pattern. Based on four machine learning simulation results, the optimal method was selected to predict the Gini-runoff coefficient using the RMSE and R 2   values, which further improved the accuracy of prediction. However, the understanding of trends in the concentration of runoff remains uncertain due to the assumption conditions, the data used, and the explainability of the models. In this study, it was assumed that the concentration of runoff was affected by extreme climate change, focusing solely on this aspect without incorporating additional factors into the models. Factors such as mean climate conditions, fluctuations in evaporation, soil moisture levels, groundwater dynamics, and changes in ice and glacier melt were not considered in the modeling process (Zhang et al., 2016 ). Additionally, the uniqueness of GCMs and the challenges associated with interpreting these models, where confidence levels are below 80 %, also increases the uncertainty in predicting results. Furthermore, runoff has spatiotemporal variability and high levels of uncertainty due to the anthropogenic forcing of the land and atmospheric processes (Milly and Dunne, 2016; Xie et al., 2022 )including the regulation of reservoirs and water use. In arid regions, reservoirs play a crucial role in water resource regulation. Mountain reservoirs, which are mainly used for flood storage and the regulation of irrigation water and hydropower (Beca et al., 2023; Sen, 2021 ; ), have a decisive effect on the concentration of runoff. Climate change has highlighted the problem of water shortage in reservoirs (Tramblay et al., 2020 ), and the concentration of runoff will be directly affected. The management of multi-purpose reservoirs is a complex process, and the competition between water users and other stakeholders needs to be considered (Beca et al., 2023 ). In the present study, the specific processes regulating the hydro-junction were unclear, which increased the uncertainty of the prediction results. Despite these uncertainties, our findings provide significant insights into the drivers of extreme climate on the concentration of runoff. The results will enable informed and rational decision-making regarding future water resource utilization. Similarly to the results of this study, winter runoff increases and summer runoff decreases have been reported in the eastern United States and Godavaris River Basin in India (Kuriqi et al., 2020 ). In arid areas, despite runoff being mainly distributed from June to August, even minor runoff can trigger major flood events that are difficult to capture in flood samples (Tarasova et al., 2020 ). Future studies should attempt to predict runoff changes and extreme hydrological events in the cold season, which would improve the prediction accuracy of future hydrological events.   6 Conclusion Surface runoff is an important factor in water resource utilization and management. In the past 60 years, the annual runoff has increased significantly in the Tarim River Basin, while the concentration of runoff has decreased significantly. After an abrupt change occurred, the average increase in runoff volume was 14.3 %, and the average decrease in the concentration of runoff was 8.3 %. The abrupt change and periodic change in the concentration of runoff were consistent with the corresponding changes in the cold season. Based on the results of an attribution analysis, the concentration of runoff was negatively correlated with the warm indices of extreme temperature and extreme precipitation indices, and positively correlated with the cold indices of extreme temperature. By affecting the runoff in the cold season, the extreme temperature index DTR decreased the concentration of runoff in the Yarkant and Hotan river basins, while the TN90 and CWD extreme precipitation index simultaneously led to a decline in the time of concentration in Aksu River Basin. The hydro-junction led to a decrease in the concentration of runoff of 12.11 % from 2001 to 2020 at Hotan_w. The significant decrease in DTR was due to below-normal anomalies of the geopotential height (200 hPa), which promoted an increase in TCC and precipitation, while the extreme high temperature indices (TN90, TXx, and TR) were mainly related to the NAO, El Niño-Southern Oscillation, and the northward shift of the South Asian center. The future Gini-runoff coefficient in the three headwaters will continue to decline under the three emission scenarios, and the rate of decline was determined for each of the low, medium, and high emission scenarios. This was related to the continuous increase in extreme weather events in the future and the continuous retreat of glaciers in the original area. There was forecast uncertainty due to the decreasing trend in the concentration of runoff in the future. The driving mechanism of the time of concentration runoff change should be further analyzed and combined with snow cover dynamics and atmospheric patterns to understand the factors controlling future changes in the concentration of runoff.
1 Introduction A desert oasis ecotone (DOE) is a key natural barrier between desert and oasis ecosystems, and these areas are some of the areas that are most seriously affected by climate change and human activities (Zhao and Chang, 2014 ). Due to excessive livestock grazing, overcultivation and intensive farming, the DOE exhibits two opposite evolutionary processes: a positive succession that leads to the creation of oases and a negative succession that leads to desertification (Li et al., 2016 ). To prevent and control desertification, the large-scale planting of shrubs has become a common practice for vegetation restoration in desert oasis ecotones (Li et al., 2006; Bryan et al., 2018 ) and plays an important role in maintaining the ecological and environmental security of oases (Zhou et al., 2016a ). However, the large-scale planting of shrubs in arid regions could cause salt accumulation in the soil surface layer, especially in high groundwater table areas (Wang and Zhao, 2015 ). This soil salinization process leads to significant environmental and ecological problems that seriously threaten the stability of oases. Therefore, it is very important to study the formation process of soil salinization to maintain the ecological security of the oasis in arid areas. Globally, more than 1000 M ha of land is affected by salinization (Ondrasek and Rengel, 2020 ), and the area of salinized land is expanding with global climate change and intensive human activities (Jesus et al., 2015 ). Exploring the formation process of soil salinization is the basis and key to salinization treatment, and the synergetic variations in soil water, temperature and salt control the formation and treatment of salinization to a certain extent and determine the success or failure and efficiency of salinization treatment. In recent years, local and foreign scholars have carried out a series of studies on the synergistic changes in soil water, heat and salt in different regions and environments during freezing and thawing (Mohammed et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2011 ). Studies have shown that soil water phase transitions can significantly alter soil hydrothermal properties and soil water potential (Hansson et al., 2004; Stuurop et al., 2021 ), affect soil water and salt transport and possibly lead to soil salinization (Wu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021 ). Due to the soil initial water content and soil texture, soil with a high water content is more likely to freeze under similar temperature conditions (Nagare et al., 2011 ). In China, research on the soil water, temperature, and salt has focused mostly on the mountainous areas of Northeast China, Inner Mongolia, the Loess Plateau and the Qinghai Tibet Plateau (Liu et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2018; Bo et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ), and the most relevant research has been carried out on forests, grasslands, farmlands and other ecosystems. Studies have shown that during freezing, soil water and salt tend to move up to the frozen layer from the unfrozen layer. Then, during thawing, the accumulation of soil water and salt in the frozen layer gradually decreases due to evaporation and infiltration (Wu et al., 2018 ). Wang et al. (2022)  studied the soil water, temperature, and salt dynamics of permafrost-affected meadows in the northeastern Qinghai Tibet Plateau and reported that when thawing occurred from depths of 10–80 cm, the soil water and bulk electrical conductivity at a depth of 10 cm exhibited synchronous high-frequency fluctuations, and both increased linearly. In the farmland area of the middle reaches of the Heihe River (Cui et al., 2014 ), the soil temperature changed dramatically with the air temperature during the freeze thaw period, and the amplitude of variation decreased with increasing soil depth. However, these studies were limited to a single season, and soil water, temperature, and salt evaluations in different landscapes were conducted on short time scales; research on regional salt accumulation, medium- and long-term changes and the relationships between them and the factors that influence them is still insufficient. The Hexi Corridor is in the arid and semiarid region of Northwest China, which is characterized by low precipitation, high evapotranspiration, severe wind erosion and sensitivity to climate change. The region is predicted to have a high risk of drought and water scarcity in the next twenty years (Xia et al., 2017 ). In arid regions, water is the main ecological factor governing plant growth (Zhang et al., 2022a,b ), and hydrological processes determine the evolutionary direction and ecological functions of the soil-vegetation system, which plays an important role not only in regulating the use of soil water by plants but also in the water cycling process of ecosystems; furthermore, water has an important impact on carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and nutrient balances of subsurface soil ecosystems (Borga et al., 2014 ). Water also has an important impact on key processes, such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and nutrient balance in subsurface soil ecosystems (Liu et al., 2020 ). Numerous studies have shown that evapotranspiration is an important driver of water, solute and heat flow between the near-surface soil layer and the atmosphere (Liu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ). The effect of evapotranspiration on salt accumulation is more complex because it is influenced not only by water saturation but also by salt concentration in the soil, as well as precipitation (Nachshon et al., 2011 ). Moreover, in desert ecosystems, vegetation plays an important role in regulating hydrological fluxes, with significant effects on shallow desert soils and deeper air-packed zones (Zhao et al., 2017 ). In addition, changes in atmospheric precipitation and groundwater fluctuations affect the processes of salt accumulation, dilution and desalination (Zuecco et al., 2018; Van der Kamp et al., 2003; Johnson et al., 2004 ). The above studies on soil water, temperature, and salt in the Hexi Corridor focused mainly on the spatial variability of soil water and salt. However, there is a lack of research on the coupled relationships among the soil water, temperature, and salt content of areas with H. ammodendron  in forests with different ages in this area. H. ammodendron  is one of the dominant shrub species that is planted in the largest area in the desert areas of China and is mainly located in the Xinjiang Autonomous Region, the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Qinghai Province and Gansu Province (Liu et al., 2011 ). Due to its remarkable drought resistance and ability to survive in arid areas, H. ammodendron  is widely used as a pioneer species to prevent desertification in the Hexi Corridor region (Zhou et al., 2016b ). As H. ammodendron  grows, the root system gradually penetrates deeper into the soil profile, it transitions from using water from the shallow soil layer to the deeper soil layer to groundwater (Zhu and Jia, 2011; Wang and Zhao, 2015; Zhou et al., 2016a ), and a large amount of salt ions dissolve (Wang et al., 2009 ). In addition, as a salt-tolerant halophyte, H. ammodendron  contains high levels of Na ions to maintain a low root water potential and mitigate the effects of drought on plant growth through osmotic compensation (Kang et al., 2013 ). Previous research focusing on seasonal or interannual factors (Wang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016b; Yu and Wang, 2018 ), although helpful in understanding the trend of soil salinity, cannot describe soil water–salt dynamics in detail, and there are few observational studies on the spatial and temporal changes in soil water, temperature, and salt in the root zone of H. ammodendron  in forests of different ages in consecutive years. In this research, the soil water, temperature, and salt content in the 0–200 cm soil layer in 20-, 30-, and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forests were continuously monitored for more than three years (11 August 2018–11 June 2022). We hypothesized that planting shrubs could change the soil water, temperature, and salt content. Specifically, we (1) systematically analysed the dynamic changes in the soil water, temperature, and salt in H. ammodendron  forests with ages of 20, 30 and 50 years. (2) we explored the coupling relationships and key processes of soil water, temperature, and salt in H. ammodendron  forests of different ages in a typical DOE.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site This study was carried out near the Linze Inland River Basin Research Station of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in the central part of the Hexi Corridor in Gansu (38°57′−39°42′ N, 99°51′−100°30′ E) at an altitude of 1420 m; this region is located in a typical desert oasis ecotone at the southern edge of the Badain Jaran Desert ( Fig. 1 a). The region has a temperate continental desert climate. The annual evaporation, as found via evaporative dish, is 2388 mm, while the average annual precipitation is only 117 mm (1965−2012), and the average annual temperature is 7.6 ℃, with high temperature and precipitation mainly concentrated in July−September (Yi et al., 2015 ). The groundwater depth in this study area is shallow (3−5 m), and the groundwater has a high salinity (Table S1 ); furthermore, the soil is sand or sandy loam and has a low organic matter content (Su et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020 ). H. ammodendron  seedlings have been gradually planted on mobile sand dunes to promote ecosystem restoration since the 1970s; large areas of H. ammodendron  plantations have been established and subsequently expanded along mobile dunes. After 50 years, the wind-blown sand activity gradually weakened, the vegetation in the oasis edge zone was restored, and the mobile dunes gradually transformed into fixed dunes.  2.2 Sampling In mid-July 2018, in an H. ammodendron  plantation near the Linze Inland River Basin Research Station of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), H. ammodendron  forests with planting ages of 20, 30, and 50 years were selected for locational sample plots, and 5TE soil water, temperature, and electrical conductivity sensors (Decagon, Decagon Devices, Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) were installed within the 0−200 cm soil profile for long-term observations (Fig. 1 b). The soil temperature, water content and electrical conductivity were observed in five soil horizons, namely, 0−40 cm, 40−80 cm, 80−120 cm, 120−160 cm, and 160−200 cm, in the root zone of the H. ammodendron  forest, and the data were collected every half hour (CR1000, Campbell Scientific, Inc., Logan, UT, USA). The collected data were then processed and analysed. In addition, soil samples were collected from five soil horizons (three stand ages × five depth gradients) in 20-, 30-, and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forests for physico-chemical analyses of H. ammodendron  plantation soils, and the physico-chemical properties of the soils at the experimental sites are shown in Table S2 . Meteorological data (e.g., temperature, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and net solar radiation) were obtained from the Linze Inland River Basin Research Station, Northwest Institute of Eco-Environment and Resources, Chinese Academy of Sciences (http://lzd . cern.ac.cn/meta/metadata) (Figs. S1,S2 ).  2.3 Research methods Through comprehensive analyses of the dynamic changes in the soil temperature, water and electrical conductivity in H. ammodendron  forests of different ages, the freeze thaw period was further divided into a freeze thaw period and a thawing period based on three time points, namely, persistent temperature below 0 °C, maximum freezing depth and complete thawing; additionally, the depth of the 0 °C isotherm was calculated by linear interpolation of soil temperatures in a depth interval of 0−120 cm, which was used as the depth interval of freezing and thawing (Frauenfeld et al., 2004 ). Trees in this study area usually germinate in late April and start shedding their leaves in late September, and the vegetation growing season in the desert is from April to October. Therefore, we divided the data collected in this study into three periods: the freezing period (late November to late January), the thawing period (late January to early March) and the growing period (April−October). In this study, a "spatial" rather than a "temporal" approach was used to investigate the dynamic processes of water, heat and salinity and their coupling relationships in H. ammodendron  soils of different ages at the edge of a desert oasis. The "spatial" rather than the "temporal" approach is generally considered a reliable method for monitoring and studying long-term changes (Su et al., 2007 ). This approach was adopted because a series of artificial H. ammodendron  forests established over 20, 30, and 50 years provided time-series revegetation at sites with similar soils, climatic conditions, and land use histories. In addition, soil electrical conductivity is significantly correlated with salinity, and soil electrical conductivity can directly characterize soil salinity (Rhoades et al., 1989 ).  2.4 Statistical analysis Significant differences (alpha = 0.05) between the soil water, temperature, and salt content in H. ammodendron  forests of different planting ages were investigated by one-way analyses of variance (ANOVAs) using SPSS 26.0 (IBM Corp., Chicago, IL, USA) software. Origin 2022 was used for mapping (OriginLab Corp., Northampton, MA, USA).   3 Results 3.1 Soil temperature, water and salt variations in H. ammodendron forests of different ages With increasing H. ammodendron  forest age, the maximum freezing depth decreased gradually, and the mean values of the 20-, 30- and 50-year plots were 106.04 cm, 90.74 cm, and 86.57 cm, respectively ( Fig. 2 a-c). With increasing soil depth, the change in the soil temperature gradually lagged behind the change in the air temperature (Table S3 ). The soil water content at 0−80 cm gradually decreased with increasing age of H. ammodendron  forests (Fig. 2 d-f), with soil water contents of 6.167 ± 0.478 %, 5.070 ± 0.419 % and 4.186 ± 0.281 % for the 20-, 30-, and 50-year plots, respectively, while the salinity increased and then decreased, with EC values of 0.047 ± 0.006 dS m−1 , 0.055 ± 0.010 dS m−1  and 0.050 ± 0.018 dS m−1 , respectively. However, soil water increased significantly in the deeper 160−200 cm layer, with soil water values of 4.883 ± 0.278 %, 8.348 ± 1.099 % and 12.610 ± 0.234 % in the 20-, 30-, and 50-year plots, respectively. Similarly, the salinity at 160−200 cm first increased and then decreased, with EC values of 0.006 ± 0.006 dS m−1 , 0.246 ± 0.156 dS m−1  and 0.057 ± 0.009 dS m−1 , respectively (Fig. 2 g-i). During the freeze thaw period (late November to early March), the solidification of liquid water in the soil into ice resulted in significantly less soil water and salt than that during the growing period (April−October). The monthly mean soil temperatures in 20-, 30-, and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forests generally reached their lowest values in January-February (with mean values ranging from −7.97 to 6.19 °C, −7.16 to 5.30 °C and −7.03 to 6.48 °C, respectively). The highest values were between July and August (with mean values ranging from 19.28 to 30.95 °C, 19.01–28.51 °C and 17.72–26.88 °C, respectively). The amplitude of the soil temperature in each layer decreased with increasing age and soil depth of H. ammodendron  but was not significantly different ( Fig. 3 a-c). The soil water and electrical conductivity fluctuated distinctively in the 0–80 cm layer and were significantly different from those in the 160−200 cm layer in the 50-year-old H. ammodendron  plantation (P  < 0.05) (Fig. 3 d-i). In addition, the soil water and salt in the 0−200 cm layer of H. ammodendron  forests generally showed an increasing trend (P < 0.05) from year to year (Fig. S3 ), and soil water increased significantly in the deeper 160−200 cm layer with increasing H. ammodendron  planting age (P  < 0.05) (Fig. S4 ).  3.2 Dynamics of soil temperature, water and salt during the different seasons (freezing, thawing and growing seasons) 3.2.1 Freezing season From late November to late January of the following year, the freezing depths of the seasonal permafrost layer from the ground surface downwards ranged from 0−120 cm, and the freezing rate of the soil was fast and then slow, showing fluctuating changes. The soil water and electrical conductivity of the unfrozen soil in the frozen layer fluctuated and decreased with increasing permafrost thickness, which indicated "desalination", and the liquid water changed to solid water ( Fig. 4 a1–4 , c1–4 , e1–4 ). The most significant changes in soil water and electrical conductivity were observed in the 0−40 cm layer during this period (P  < 0.01), and the rates of decrease in soil water in H. ammodendron  forests aged 20, 30, and 50 years were 0.005−0.042 % day−1 , 0.005−0.013 % day−1  and 0.001−0.054 % day−1  (P  < 0.01), respectively; similarly, the EC reduction rates in the 0−40 cm depth interval were 0.021−0.076 mS m−1  day−1 , 0.007−0.012 mS m−1  day−1  and 0.025−0.348 mS m−1  day−1  (P  < 0.01) (Fig. 4b1–4 , d1, 3, 4,  f1–4 ). The soil water content and electrical conductivity stabilized at lower values during the late freezing period, with soil water and electrical conductivity remaining largely constant at approximately 4 % and 0.01 dS m−1 , respectively, from 0−40 cm within the freezing layer of the 20- and 30-year-old H. ammodendron  forest plots, but the values were approximately 2 % and 0.03 dS m−1 , respectively, at the 40 cm level of the 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forest plot.  3.2.2 Thawing season Starting in late January, the temperature gradually increased, and the permafrost slowly melted from the unfrozen layer to the surface under the influence of heat flow from the subterranean thawing layer; then, it rapidly melted from the surface downwards and from the subterranean upwards, after the average daily temperature in the second half of February was > 0 °C. The 20-year-old H. ammodendron  soil showed a seemingly double freezing layer during this period, which lasted from 3 to 9 days; in contrast, the 30-year-old and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forests did not have a seemingly double freezing layer when they were rapidly thawing, which might be related to the temperature and initial content of the different ages of H. ammodendron  stands. In addition, the 2020 thaw was characterized by large temperature variations, leading to large fluctuations in freezing and thawing during the thawing period. The soil water and electrical conductivity in the 0−80 cm layer of the seasonal permafrost layer fluctuated and increased simultaneously with the thawing of the permafrost, revealing the process of salt accumulation ( Fig. 5 a1–4 , c1–4 , e1–4 ). Additionally, the soil water and electrical conductivity of the 0−40 cm layer showed synchronous high-frequency fluctuations, there was a significant positive correlation between the two (R  > 0.90, P  < 0.01), and the overall trend of soil water and electrical conductivity increased significantly (P  < 0.01). The rates of increase in soil water in H. ammodendron  with plot ages of 20, 30, and 50 years were 0.027−0.152 % day−1 , 0.005−0.039 % day−1  and 0.006−0.086 % day−1 , respectively (P  < 0.01); similarly, the rates of increase in the EC at a depth of 40 cm were 0.07−0.311 mS m−1  day−1 , 0.028−0.088 mS m−1  day−1 , and 0.106−0.376 mS m−1  day−1 , respectively (P  < 0.01) (Fig. 5 b1–4 , d1,3, 4 , f1–4 ). In addition, the freezing depths in 2019−2020 were shallow (74.11−98.08 cm), and the rate of salt accumulation during thawing was low, but the 30-year-old H. ammodendron  showed a significant decrease in soil electrical conductivity (−0.030 mS m−1  day−1 ) (P  < 0.01) (Fig. 5 d2 ). The rates of change in soil water and salinity were generally greater during the thawing period than during the freezing period, suggesting that the rate of salt accumulation was greater than the rate of desalination. In addition, this study revealed that the seasonal permafrost region (0−120 cm) and the nonpermafrost region (120–200 cm) exhibited different changes in the soil water, temperature, and salt content during the freeze thaw period. The seasonal permafrost regions exhibited a decrease in the soil water and salt content with decreasing temperature during the freezing period and an increase in the soil water and salt content with increasing temperature during the thawing period. Nonfrozen areas showed a continuous decrease in soil temperature during the freeze thaw period due to the lag in temperature. The 20- and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  soil water decreased significantly with decreasing temperature, and the soil temperature showed a linear relationship with water (P  < 0.01); however, the change in salinity was not significant ( Fig. 6 ). Moreover, the 30-year-old H. ammodendron  soil water and salinity increased and then decreased with decreasing temperature, and the soil temperature, soil water and salinity exhibited a quadratic pattern (0.98 < R 2   ≤ 0.99, T and VWC; 0.61 < R 2   < 099, T and EC) ( Fig. 7 ).  3.2.3 Growing season Soil water and salinity showed different patterns in the shallow (0−80 cm) and deep (80−200 cm) layers during the growing period (April−October). The soil water and salinity in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) were more volatile during the growing season ( Fig. 8 ). With increasing forest age, the shallow (0−80 cm) soil water gradually decreased, which might be related to the combined effects of air temperature, precipitation and transpiration during the growing period. In July−August, shallow (0−80 cm) soil water and EC generally decreased or were at their lowest values (2.5−5 %, VWC; < 0.03 dS m−1 , EC), but after a large precipitation event (> 10 mm) in September, the shallow soil salinity increased sharply with water within 1−2 days and then decreased rapidly. The changes in the 40−80 cm layer in the soil water salinity content fluctuated gradually with increasing stand age. During the growing period, the soil water in the deep layer (80−200 cm) generally maintained a steady increasing trend and slightly decreased in October. With increasing forest age, the soil water in the deep layer (160−200 cm) increased significantly (Fig. 8 a1–3 , c1–3 , e1–3 ); the process of salt concentration mainly occurred in the deep layer (80−200 cm), with different patterns of change for different ages of H. ammodendron . During the growing period, 20-year-old H. ammodendron  had the lowest soil salinity content in the deep layer (Fig. 8 b1–3 ), and the deep layer electrical conductivity increased by 0.004−0.008 dS m−1 ; 30-year-old H. ammodendron  had an increase in the deep layer electrical conductivity of 0.022−0.214 dS m−1  and had the highest salinity content (Fig. 8 d1–3 ); and for the 50-year-old H. ammodendron , the deep soil electrical conductivity increased steadily during the growing period (Fig. 8 f1–3 ), with an increase of 0.01−0.012 dS m−1 . In addition, in July−August, the soil electrical conductivity in the deeper (80−200 cm) soil layers of 30-year-old H. ammodendron  significantly increased, which significantly differed from that in the shallower (0−80 cm) layers, with rapid increases of 0.063 dS m−1  and 0.1 dS m−1  in the 80−120 and 160−200 cm soil layers, respectively (Fig. 8 d1–3 ), representing the most significant changes in the salt content. Soil salinity changes were more stable in the deeper (80−200 cm) layers of 20- and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  soil layers than in the 30-year-old H. ammodendron  soil layers (Fig. 8 b1–3 , f1–3 ).    4 Discussion 4.1 Changes in the soil water content and salt distribution in H. ammodendron soils of different forest ages In this study, we found that the soil water content gradually decreased in the 0−80 cm layer with increasing H. ammodendron  planting age, but the soil water content significantly increased in the deeper 160−200 cm layer (P  < 0.05) (Fig. 2 a-c, Fig. S4 ). This result was mainly due to the gradual increase in soil water consumption with increasing H. ammodendron  forest age (Wang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016b ), the distribution of H. ammodendron -absorbent root systems in the shallow 0−80 cm layer, and the transition of the water use of H. ammodendron  from the shallow soil layer to the deeper soil layer and then to groundwater (Zhu and Jia, 2011; Wang and Zhao, 2015; Zhou et al., 2016b ). The shift in water resources causes dissolved salt ions from groundwater to be lifted into the deeper soil layer (Wang et al., 2009 ), and the salt content of the soil at shallow depths increases (Su and Liu, 2020 ). This study also revealed that the salinity at depths of 160−200 cm first increased and then decreased with increasing H. ammodendron  forest age (Fig. 2 d-i). In particular, in the 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forest, a clay layer was present at a depth interval of 160−200 cm (Table S2 ), where the soil bulk weight decreased, the porosity increased, and the soil water content was the highest, while the water content and salinity were lower in the 120−160 cm layer. Sun et al. (2018)  also found the presence of a clay layer at the same study site, and Gong et al. (2005)  reported that alluvial or loess-like matrices were the main soil-forming matrices in the region. The clay layer has good water retention and salt isolation capacity, and the presence of the clay layer increases the heterogeneity of soil water and salinity by altering the soil water status and water and process of salt transport in the profile (Feng et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018 ). The soil water–salt distribution is mainly related to the soil texture and root distribution (Zhou et al., 2016a; Sun et al., 2018 ). In this study, we found that there was no significant change in precipitation over the past fifty years; thus, the changes in the soil water, heat, and salt were mainly attributed to long-term shrub plantation (Fig. S5 ).  4.2 Soil water and salt transport mechanisms in H. ammodendron stands of different ages during the freezing process In this study, the soil water and electrical conductivity of the 0−80 cm soil within the seasonal permafrost layer fluctuated and decreased with increasing permafrost thickness (Fig. 4 a, c, e). With decreasing air temperature, the water (salt) in the surface layer gradually froze in the permafrost, and the ice content in the freezing layer increased, which resulted in the formation of freezing fronts below 0 °C (Zhang et al., 2023 ). As the soil water potential in the frozen layer decreased, a free energy gradient was created, and the soil water contained in the unfrozen layer below the freezing front was continuously transported to the frozen layer (Zhao et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2022 ). This process also resulted in salts in soil continuously accumulating with water and moving upwards along channels in the soil (Xue et al., 2017 ). During soil freezing, the soil temperature and water potential gradient were the main factors driving vertical soil water–salt transport (Wang et al., 2019 ). This study also revealed that during the freezing process (late November to early February), the transport of unfrozen water and salt was mainly controlled by the soil temperature gradient. As the soil temperature in the freezing layer decreased, the soil water and electrical conductivity decreased nonlinearly with the absolute value of the soil temperature (|T |), with the water and electrical conductivity obeying power and logarithmic functions, respectively (  Figs. 9–10 ). This is because the water content in the unfrozen soil and the salt mobility in water in unfrozen soil are greater than those of frozen soil within the contact surface at the peak of freezing, and soil freezing leads to the movement of water in soil from the unfrozen region to the freezing front (Zhang et al., 2023 ). The significant increase in the salt content of water in frozen soils reflects the temperature gradient that controls the direction of salt transport in water and its distribution pattern in saline soils (Wang et al., 2019 ). In addition, the migration of water and salt was greater in the early stage of freezing, and the migration rates of both unfrozen water and salt in the permafrost layer decreased with a further decrease in soil temperature. With increasing stand age, the shallow (0−80 cm) soil water gradually decreased (Fig. 2 a-c), and the initial water content of the soil before freezing had an important influence on the freezing process (Wang et al., 2019 ). Sun et al. (2021)  measured the soil water content and soil temperature at different depths (0−2 m) under freezing and thawing conditions in the semiarid agricultural and pastoral areas of northern China. After monitoring and investigation, it was concluded that the initial water content in the soil sample was the main factor affecting the freeze thaw process. Our study confirmed that the freeze thaw process in H. ammodendron  soils of different stand ages varies significantly due to differences in the initial soil water characteristics.  4.3 Soil water and salt transport mechanisms in H. ammodendron stands of different ages during the thawing process In this study, the soil water in the thawing layer increased slowly and then rapidly during the melting process. As the temperature increased, the meltwater from snow and permafrost seeped downwards (Zhao et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2010 , pp. 130−170), resulting in a redistribution of soil water (Shi et al., 2020 ). During the thawing process from late January to early March, soil water and salt at the 0−40 and 40−80 cm depths in the 20-, 30-, and 50-year-old seasonal permafrost layers showed significant positive correlations, with correlation coefficients (R ) of 0.964 and 0.922, 0.934 and 0.884, and 0.803 and 0.791, respectively. There was a significant linear relationship (P  < 0.01) with the redistribution of thawing soil water as it melted, and there was a linear trend of increasing salinity with increasing soil water during thawing ( Fig. 11 ). During the thawing process, the infiltration of free water in the thawing layer is usually dominant, while the downwards migration of unfrozen water driven by the temperature gradient in the frozen layer (Zhao et al., 2000 ) results in the simultaneous downwards transport of coupled heat fluxes, which ultimately leads to the overall downwards migration of salts in soil water and salt accumulation and deposition. In this study, we also found that once the average daily air temperature was > 0 °C in late February, soil melting was bidirectional, starting from the soil surface and the lower end of the freezing zone and melting in both directions until complete ablation. Compared with upwards thawing of the soil caused by a single subsurface heat flow, the thawing rate of the soil was much faster at temperatures > 0 °C. Differences in the soil thermal conductivity during freezing and thawing lead to faster soil thawing than freezing (Wang et al., 2022 ). As the age of the H. ammodendron  forest increased, the soil temperature tended to increase, the permafrost layer became shallower, and at the same air temperature, the 30- and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  melted faster, and the bisimilar freezing layer appeared for a shorter time or was almost absent. In addition, shallow (0−80 cm) soil water gradually decreased with increasing stand age (Fig. 2 a-c), and Sun et al. (2021)  reported that the higher the initial water content was, the lower the rate of thawing. In addition, the soil water and electrical conductivity in the nonpermafrost region (120−200 cm) were less affected by seasonal freeze thaw cycles. The soil temperature maintained an overall decreasing trend during the freeze thaw period, and the soil temperature was strongly correlated with the water temperature (R  > 0.96, 20-; R  > 0.76, 30-; R  > 0.98, 50-year-old). The soil temperature is the main driver affecting soil water and salt movement during soil freeze thaw cycles (Wang et al., 2019 ). By comparing the soil electrical conductivity before and after freeze thaw cycling, this study revealed that seasonal freeze thaw cycling can cause soil salinization. However, it was not the main cause of soil salinization in the region. The electrical conductivity of 20-year-old shallow H. ammodendron  plots (0−80 cm) did not change significantly before and after freeze thaw cycling, and the electrical conductivity increased by 0.001−0.003 dS m−1  at deeper depths (80–200 cm). Moreover, the electrical conductivity of the 30-year-old shallow H. ammodendron  layer increased on average by 0.001−0.002 dS m−1 , and the electrical conductivity decreased by 0.004−0.079 dS m−1 . Finally, the electrical conductivity of the 50-year-old H. ammodendron  shallow soil did not change significantly before and after freezing and thawing, and the deeper electrical conductivity increased by 0.01−0.012 dS m−1 .  4.4 Soil water and salt transport mechanisms in H. ammodendron stands of different ages during the growing period In this study, we found that the water and salinity in the shallow 0−80 cm layer were unstable (Fig. 8 ) during the growing period (April−October). Changes in soil water were mainly affected by rainfall, evaporation and transpiration (Zhao et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ), and soil salt accumulated on the soil surface under strong evaporation and limited rainfall (Liu et al., 2019 ). For example, rainfall infiltration after a large rainfall event (>10 mm) not only increased the soil water content but also leached soil salt from shallow depths (Liu et al., 2019 ). Shallow soils experienced a dramatic increase in soil water within 1−2 days, and water infiltration also increased salinity at greater depths (Lai et al., 2016 ). With increasing stand age, a physical salt crust gradually forms on the surface layer of the soil in H. ammodendron  forests, and the thickness of the salt crust increases with stand age (Su and Liu, 2020 ). Precipitation events can leach salts from the salt crust into the underlying soil and form new soil water with the existing soil water (salt) (Schwinning and Sala, 2004 ). Small precipitation events (< 5 mm) are the most common type of precipitation in desert regions, with large precipitation events occurring less frequently (Sala and Lauenroth, 1982; Loik et al., 2004 ). In general, pulsed small precipitation events cause only small fluctuations in soil water salinity in the surface layer, whereas large precipitation events can recharge soil water in the deeper layers, and pulsed precipitation, together with strong evaporation, results in numerous periods of high or low pulsed soil water salinity in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) (Sala and Lauenroth, 1982; Schwinning and Sala, 2004 ). In this study, we also found that temperature, evaporation, and net solar radiation showed a single peak curve over time, with evaporation being the most vigorous and little precipitation occurring in July−August, when net solar radiation and temperature were the highest (Figs. S1,S2 ), and soil water and electrical conductivity generally decreased or reached their lowest values in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) (Fig. S6 ), whereas the soil water in the deeper layer (80−200 cm) generally maintained a steady increasing trend; furthermore, with increasing forest age, the soil water in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) gradually decreased, and the soil water in the deep layer within 160−200 cm increased significantly. Zhu et al. (2017)  also found that the deep soil water content of mature H. ammodendron  was greater than that of intermediate-aged H. ammodendron  and bare ground by investigating the temporal and spatial changes in soil water in the root zone of different age classes of H. ammodendron . In the artificial H. ammodendron  woodland, with increasing age, the proportion of the deep root system of H. ammodendron  increased, and the main water source of H. ammodendron  gradually changed from precipitation to groundwater (Zhu and Jia, 2011; Zhou et al., 2016b ). Moreover, the root system of H. ammodendron  is located in both the surface layer and the deep soil layer, and when there is less precipitation, H. ammodendron  can utilize groundwater for its survival. When there is an increase in precipitation, H. ammodendron  can use a large amount of precipitation, i.e., it has the typical characteristics of a dimorphic root system (Zhou et al., 2016a ). After twenty years, the water source for H. ammodendron  changed from sparse and highly variable precipitation to stable and abundant groundwater (Zhou et al., 2016b ). This transition process changed the source of water for H. ammodendron  from sparse and highly variable precipitation to stable and abundant groundwater, and the development of artificial sand-fixing vegetation reached a stable water balance in the vegetation–soil system after 50 years (Zhou et al., 2016b ). As the age of the forest increased, the water consumption of H. ammodendron  increased, the amount of soil water in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) gradually decreased, and the contributions of deep soil water and groundwater increased, significantly increasing the amount of soil water within the deep layer (160−200 cm), thus ensuring the sustainable development of the artificial H. ammodendron  forest. Dai et al. (2015)  reported that more than 90 % of the water used by H. ammodendron  in the dry season comes from deep soil water or groundwater acquired by the deep root system. The water resources of H. ammodendron  shift from soil water to shallow groundwater after 30 years (Zhou et al., 2016b ), and a large amount of salt in groundwater accumulated in the deep soil due to absorption by the H. ammodendron  root system (Su and Liu, 2020; Wang et al., 2009 ). Moreover, the soil salt content at greater depths increased with increasing salt content in the groundwater (Fig. S7 ). Therefore, salt ions were continuously transported to deep roots with soil water, and the amount of water and salt in deep soil gradually increased as the age of the forest increased (Yu and Wang, 2018; Su and Liu, 2020 ).
