The soil water and salinity in the 20-year-old H. ammodendron  were concentrated in the shallow (0−80 cm) range, and both the water and salinity contents in the deeper layers were low. With increasing forest age, the 30- and 50-year-old stands had concentrated salt mainly in the deeper 80−200 cm layer. In the 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forest, the water-insulating (saline) effect of the presence of a clay layer at 160−200 cm altered the water and salt transport in the soil profile (Sun et al., 2018 ), resulting in lower soil salinity than that in the 30-year-old H. ammodendron . In the soil–vegetation system, the rhizosphere–soil interface is considered a functional region in the terrestrial surface soil ecosystem with the most frequent exchanges of matter and energy and the most active biological, physical, and chemical regulatory actions and processes (Li, 2011 ). As the age of H. ammodendron  increased, the proportion of shallow root biomass gradually decreased, while the proportion of deeper roots continued to increase (Zhou et al., 2016a ). The H. ammodendron  root system tended to increase and then decrease vertically, and the peak H. ammodendron  root biomass gradually shifted from approximately 0.5 m to approximately 1.0 m with age (Zhou et al., 2016a ). The results of this study showed that in areas with high root biomass (80−120 cm), the soil water–salt content of both 30- and 50-year-old H. ammodendron  stands was greater. Moreover, H. ammodendron  is a salt-diluting halophyte that absorbs a large amount of Na+  during growth and development to maintain low root water potential and mitigate the effects of drought on plant growth through osmotic compensation, leading to significant accumulation of deep soil salts (Kang et al., 2013 ). Compared with soil salinity accumulation caused by freeze thaw cycles, deep soil salinity accumulation in the deep layer (80−200 cm) caused by water pumping and salt absorption by the deep root system of S. H. ammodendron  during the growing period was more significant, and it was the main cause of soil salinity caused by planting areas located in arid zones. By analysing the correlations between soil water, heat and salt in different soil layers of different forest ages, it was concluded that the correlation between air temperature and soil temperature was highly significant, the correlation between different layers was also highly significant (R  > 0.9, P  < 0.001), and the correlation between the air temperature and soil temperature gradually weakened with increasing forest age and soil depth ( Fig. 12 a, d, g). The correlation between soil water in different layers in the shallow layer (0−80 cm) was highly significant and gradually weakened with increasing forest age and soil depth; the correlation between water in different layers in the deep 80−160 cm layer increased with increasing forest age (P  < 0.001), and the changes in salinity were similar to those in water, which was manifested in the correlation of salinity in the deeper soil layer increasing with increasing forest age (P  < 0.001). Moreover, the correlation of water and salt between different layers within the 120−200 cm layer of 30-year-old H. ammodendron  forest was greater than that of 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forest. The above analyses revealed that the hydraulic enhancement of the H. ammodendron  root system led to a diffuse increase in the water and salt contents in the soil profile, and it was also proven that the clay layer in the deeper 160−200 cm layer of 50-year-old H. ammodendron  forest had an obstructive effect on the transport of water and salt. Temperature, water potential and salt gradient are important driving factors for soil water, temperature, and salt transport. Water drives salt transport, salt concentration alters hydraulic properties, salt can alter heat transfer properties, temperature causes salt to undergo a phase change, and temperature gradients provide a driving force for water, which in turn can alter temperature transfer properties (Zhang et al., 2023 ) (Fig. S8 ). The complexity of soil–vegetation–atmosphere transport processes is determined by the combined nature of precipitation, soil heterogeneity and differences in vegetation types in arid regions (Li, 2011 ).   5 Conclusions In this study, we assessed the changes in soil water, temperature, and salt dynamics and their coupling relationships in H. ammodendron  of different stand ages (20, 30, and 50 years). With increasing planting age, the soil water in the shallow 0−80 cm layer gradually decreased, while the soil water in the deeper 160−200 cm layer gradually increased. Soil salt first increased in the 30-year plot and then decreased in the 50-year plot. The salt content in the 0–80 cm freezing layer decreased during the freezing season, but in the thawing season, salt accumulation occurred; moreover, the salt accumulation rate during the thawing season was much greater than the desalting rate during the freezing season. With increasing forest age, the freezing depth of the soil gradually became shallower, and the lag in soil temperature gradually increased. The soil water and salinity in the shallow 0−80 cm layer were highly volatile under the influence of temperature and precipitation events. Temperature is an important driving factor affecting soil water and salt transport, and there is a significant linear relationship between soil water and salt. During the freezing process, as the soil temperature decreased, the soil water and electrical conductivity decreased nonlinearly with the absolute value of the soil temperature (|T |), following a power function and logarithmic function, respectively. This research can provide a scientific basis for the study of soil salinization caused by long-term shrub or tree plantations.
1 Introduction In the 1900s, water resources were typically regarded as public property and managed by the government in most countries (Bjornlund and McKay, 2002 ; Santos Coelho et al., 2022 ). However, the global demand for water has surged due to rapid economic growth and population expansion (Yuan et al., 2023 ). In response to this challenge, one prominent global trend in water resources management is the implementation of economic mechanisms for resource distribution (Yang et al., 2021 ). The water rights trading (WRT) exemplifies this trend by optimizing water resource allocation and promoting sustainability through market mechanisms, with successful implementations worldwide (Bhave et al., 2018 ). Several countries such as the USA, Australia, and Chile are considered to be early representatives of WRT market construction (Bjornlund and McKay, 2002; Connell, 2015; Hearne, 1997; Settre and Wheeler, 2016 ).Following their lead, other nations such as Peru (Ulloa et al., 2022 ), Mexico (Radonic, 2017 ), and Spain (Arriaza et al., 2002; Gómez-Limón et al., 2021 ) have also started to adopted market mechanisms to manage and regulate water resources. In South Asia, such as India (Singh al., 2020 ), and Pakistan (Meinzen-Dick, 1998 ) see informal WRT thrivesing in the agricultural irrigation sector. China initiated a shift from engineering-based water construction to sustainable water development in the early 21st century (Sun, 2009 ), marking its foray into water markets with the 2000 WRT event in Dongyang and Yiwu, Zhejiang Province (Zhang et al., 2021 ). The majority of the existing studies focus on the allocation of initial water rights (Kapetas et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2022 ), and the associated water use efficiency (WUE) (Anwandter and Ozuna, 2002; Cheng et al., 2023 ). Based on the results of a Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) model (DEA model), Razzaq et al. (2019)  found that farmers in Pakistan can improve WUE by participating in WRT. To alleviate slacks in inputs and outputs, Deng et al. (2016)  extended the existing DEA model and used the Slack-Based Measure (SBM)-DEA model to calculate the WUE of each province in China (Deng et al., 2016 ). Apart from investigating the WUE from an input-output perspective, some scholars have analyzed the environmental and economic benefits of WRT from a property rights perspective (Hu et al., 2022; Mu et al., 2022; Sun, 2009 ). Mu et al. (2022)  constructed a difference-in-difference model (DID) and found that the establishment of WRT pilots in China alleviated regional water poverty (Mu et al., 2022 ). Du et al. (2022)  considered economic and geographic linkages between regions but found that trading in national pilots occurred more often within provinces and that spatial spillover effects were not significant (Du et al., 2022 ). However, the study only considered national pilots, which would underestimate the true impact of WRT. Therefore, Zhang et al. (2021)  further distinguished the impact of national and provincial pilots of WRT (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Since the starting time of WRT in different regions is not uniform, the inclusion of all provincial and national pilots in the treatment group would cause measurement errors. Therefore, endogeneity issues are not properly addressed. In addition, the implementation effects of WRT are often underestimated due to the existence of local government competition effects as well as pilot demonstration effects. Existing studies have helped us understand the policy effects of the WRT, but there are still three aspects that deserve further exploration: (1) Existing studies on WRT and WUE have predominantly remained in the theoretical exploration phase. While a few empirical studies exist using econometric models, most of them establish DID models with uniform time settings, neglecting temporal variations in WRT implementation across different provinces and failing to adequately address endogeneity issues. (2) The majority of previous studies have generally concentrated on the effectiveness of the initial allocation of water rights. The studies on WRT have focused on the results of the environmental benefits it brings and often neglect in-depth exploration of its impact mechanisms and specific causal pathways. Additionally, greater attention should be paid to the differentiated effects of WRT on improving WUE in both inter-regional and inter-industry transactions. (3) WRT often exhibits a demonstration effect, influencing water consumption in the neighboring or even upstream and downstream regions. However, existing studies typically focus only on national WRT pilots in China. This would ignore the real demonstration effect brought by WRT and underestimate the policy effect. To help fill these significant knowledge gaps, this study aims to comprehensively evaluate the impact of WRT on WUE. Specifically, we use long-term provincial panel data in China (1999–2021) to construct a multi-period DID model that accounts for different provincial WRT start times, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional DID models and addressing endogeneity issues. Furthermore, we build a theoretical framework and employ econometric models to uncover the pathways through which WRT enhances water efficiency, providing a detailed exploration of the mechanisms and causal pathways involved. It can effectively open the "black box" and deeply explore the connection between the WRT and WUE. Finally, using a spatial DID model, we investigate the spatial spillovers and time lags of WRT to accurately reveal its demonstration effect and enhance the policy assessment. This empirical understanding aids policymakers in optimizing water resource management, enhancing water use efficiency, and promoting sustainable development. This paper offers a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the WRT. Theoretically, it contributes to the evaluation of policy effects within existing WRT markets, providing a solid foundation for addressing the imbalance between water supply and demand. Practically, it furnishes valuable insights and evidence for reform in provinces that have not yet implemented WRT pilots, supporting the advancement of a water-conserving society in China. Additionally, it delivers empirical evidence that can aid in the further optimization of the global WRT market.  2 Literature review and theoretical hypothesis 2.1 WRT and WUE Before the establishment of the WRT market in China, water resources were primarily allocated through administrative channels, which often limited the efficiency and effectiveness of water utilization (Sun, 2009 ). Administrative allocation lacked timeliness, with long adjustment cycles for water distribution plans, hindering the ability to promptly address evolving demands. In contrast, market mechanisms for allocation facilitated the transfer of water rights from less efficient to more efficient water users (Rosegrant and Binswanger, 1994 ). The shift was driven by the understanding that water resources hold varying marginal net benefits across different sectors. Consequently, water rights were allocated more effectively and efficiently to the highest bidder, promoting optimal utilization (Chen et al., 2022 ). The management of water resources through WRT generally involves two key phases: allocation and trading. A well-defined and rational allocation serves as a fundamental prerequisite for WRT (Hatamkhani et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2022 ). While many studies highlight the positive impact of WRT on WUE during the trading phase, some research indicates limited effectiveness due to the restricted scope and scale of trading (Du et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Transaction costs are a significant factor potentially discouraging WRT. Coase's theorem emphasizes that market mechanisms effectively address externalities when property rights are clear and transaction costs are negligible (Friesen et al., 2020; Friesen et al., 2023 ). The establishment of the WRT market aims to mitigate transaction costs, fostering inter-regional or inter-sectoral WRT. Additionally, by enhancing the perceived value of water resources, WRT prompts water users to consider the opportunity cost of wasteful water practices more diligently, leading to reduced water use and subsequently improved WUE (Gohar and Ward, 2010 ). Therefore, Hypothesis 1  was proposed：Hypothesis 1 The WRT effectively improves the WUE.    2.2 How WRT can improve the WUE 2.2.1 Technological innovations (TEIN) The implementation of the strictest water-resources management system and sustainable water-saving policy in China provides inspiration for global water-resources management (Jia et al., 2022 ). Combining the water quota system with WRT, water-use indicators create mandatory constraints, encouraging more efficient technologies to avoid penalties for exceeding limits (Di et al., 2020; Du et al., 2022 ). The Porter hypothesis suggests that appropriate environmental regulation can boost TEIN, offsetting the compliance costs while enhancing the environmental and economic performance (Porter and van der Linde, 1995 ). A notable feature of Chinese agriculture is its high water consumption but relatively low WUE (An wt al., 2022 ). The establishment of the WRT market assigns market value to water resources, instilling the recognition that 'water has a price' among agricultural water users. This shift prompts inefficient water users to reconsider prevalent irrigation practices, like heavy watering, by factoring in the opportunity cost of water usage. Fang et al. found that WRT has a positive moderating effect that motivates farmers to improve irrigation technologies to save agricultural water use (Fang and Zhang, 2020 ). Furthermore, the adoption of water-saving technologies in agriculture results in surplus water resources (Wang et al., 2023 ). Consequently, water users gain access to additional water resources. This access, coupled with the benefits derived from participating in the WRT market, acts as an incentive for further innovation in water conservation technologies. This sets in motion a 'cumulative effect,' fostering a continuous cycle of improvement in agricultural WUE. The characteristics of the industrial sector often include high water demand and serious effluent discharge (Chen et al., 2019 ). Under the water resources constraint, it is difficult for the industrial sector to keep using water resources without any limitation according to its original production method. Meanwhile, when the cost of TEIN is less than the cost of purchasing water resources in the WRT market, some water-scarce subjects may focus more on development and application of water-saving technologies. Conversely, when the marginal benefits of TEIN are less than those of purchasing rights, firms participate more actively in the WRT market (Liu et al., 2022 ). The aim is to break through existing production constraints. Therefore, Hypothesis 2  was proposed：Hypothesis 2 TEIN is a mediation variable for WRT to improve the WUE.    2.2.2 Factor mobility (FM) Considering the small marginal benefits of water-saving devices for the agricultural sector, its willingness to use water-saving engineering techniques to save water may not be high. In this case, industries tend to contribute to improve agricultural canals issues such as leakage and seepage in order to obtain tradable water (Ringler et al., 2010 ). This can lead to a conversion of water resources agricultural and industrial sectors by saving water in agriculture, ultimately improving WUE (Wang, 2012 ). This type of WRT is widespread in areas with imbalances between agricultural and industrial sectors. For instance, in the Yellow Coast region of Inner Mongolia, the agricultural sector's water value is significantly lower than that of the industrial sector. To prevent excessive water transfer, Inner Mongolia's WRT management stipulates that only water saved through conservation can be traded (Chen et al., 2023 ). This approach achieves Pareto improvement, enhancing resource allocation efficiency. It is worth noting that this kind of WRT is mostly government-led. The disadvantage of government-led is that the micro-elasticity of government-led is small. Also, a government-led WRT platform can easily lead to "rent-seeking", among other issues. However, since this kind of WRT introduces a partial market mechanism and thus avoid the need to establish additional market discipline rules, transaction costs are lower. Therefore, Hypotheses 3, 3a, and 3b  were proposed：Hypothesis 3 WRT enhances WUE through water resources factor transfer. In other words, the transfer of water resources factors is the mediation variable for WRT to optimize regional WUE.  Hypothesis 3a :  Inter-regional water FM is the mediation variable in the WRT to improve the WUE in each sector and region.  Hypothesis 3b :  Inter-sectoral water FM is the mediation variable in the WRT to improve the WUE in each sector and region.     2.3 Spatial spillover of WRT With the increasing marketization across regions, the delineation of the market boundaries is progressively blurring. Formerly small-scale transactions of water rights have evolved into extensive inter-industry and inter-regional exchanges. This transformation of factors often transcends geographical constraints, thereby significantly enhancing spatial connectivity between regions and generating discernible spatial spillover effects. Notably, regional WRT in China exemplifies this trend. In addition, due to the special conditions of China, there is often government competition between regions. The WRT market is precisely a government-led "quasi-market", strategically fostering interactions. When the local government are incentivized by the WRT market, advancements in water-saving technologies are achieved, resulting in dual enhancements in WUE and economic performance. Other local governments in close geographical proximity will be the first to feel the effects of this improvement. With a competitive bonus in local government fiscal spending, other regions within short geographic distances can learn and imitate the established measures with fewer transportation costs. Consequently, WRT pilots have been instrumental in catalyzing shifts in production models and elevating WUE standards. With the radiation effect of geographic distance, other geographically distant areas will gradually improve the WUE through imitation and learning. In particular, the development of digital technology has greatly shortened the impact of geographic location in practice in the context of increased facilitated access to information. The advancement in digital technology effectively increases the ease of imitation and learning between regions. This dynamic reinforces the robust demonstration and imitation effects, further amplifying the spatial spillover impacts of the WRT market. Therefore, Hypothesis 4  was proposed:Hypothesis 4 WRT optimizes regional WUE and generates significant spatial spillover.    Fig. 1 . illustrates the framework of the theoretical hypothesis.   3 Methodology and data 3.1 WRT Pilot The Ministry of Water Resources of the People’s Republic of China selected seven WRT pilots in 2014. Most of the existing studies have chosen 2014 as the year of policy application (Du et al., 2022 ). It is worth noting that some regions, such as Yiwu and Dongyang in Zhejiang, had already experienced WRT cases as early as 2000. Although the number of such cases is small and the volume of transactions is not large, we believe that these cases have optimized the WUE to some extent. These cases provide ideas for the subsequent development of a WRT market in China (Fig. 2 ). Apart from the seven national-level pilots in China that have carried out the practice of WRT, many trades have also occurred in some of the non-national pilot provinces after the construction of the China Water Rights Exchange in 2016. Consequently, it would be unreasonable to select the seven national pilots in 2014 as the treatment group. The effect of the policy of starting WRT in other provinces that were not selected as national-level pilots is ignored. Considering the differences in the timing of the occurrence of WRT in each province. We take reference from Fang and Zhang and set the time of WRT in some provinces before 2016 (Fang and Zhang, 2020 ). Based on this, the timing of WRT in some provinces after 2016 was added by reviewing relevant information for modification ( Table 1 ). A multi-period DID model was set up using panel data from 1999 to 2021. Fang and Zhang (2020)  utilizes data only up to 2016, but some provinces with WRT starting in 2016 are present in the model (Fang and Zhang, 2020 ). Parallel trend assumptions are difficult to meet and the setting of the econometric model remains problematic. Accordingly, we update the data to 2021. It not only compensates for the deficiencies of the existing econometric model setting to a certain extent but also can effectively observe the dynamic effects of WRT. The setting time of WRT in each province is shown in Table 1 . The spatial distribution of WRT pilots is shown in  Fig. 2 .  3.2 Variables Selection 3.2.1 Explained variables Referring to existing studies (Fang and Zhang, 2020; Gómez-Limón et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2022 ), the following three indicators were selected for measuring WUE in this study. Agricultural water efficiency (awe ): awe  was measured by average irrigation water consumption per hm2 . This indicator reflects not only the water savings in the agricultural sector but also the WUE in the agricultural sector. Industrial water efficiency (iwe) : Water consumption of 10,000 CNY of industrial added value was used to measure the iwe . It is obtained by calculating the industrial water consumption (m3 ) ratio to industrial value added (10,000 CNY) in province i  in year t . Total water efficiency (twe ): Water consumption of 10,000 CNY of GDP was chosen to observe the twe . It is measured as the ratio of total water consumption (m3 ) to regional GDP (10,000 CNY) in province i  in year t .  3.2.2 Other relevant variables The following control variables were chosen to reduce potential endogeneity issues of omitted variable bias by integrating pertinent ideas and studies. The control variables are divided into three dimensions, including human capital factors, physical capital factors, and market factors. Human capital factors include population density (pop ), degree of urbanization (cit ), and education level (edu ). Physical capital factors include per capita water supply (psw ), industrial structure (is ), and average annual rainfall (rai ). Market factors include agriculture, forestry, and water expenditure in finance (afwc ) per capita GDP (pgdp ), degree of marketization (mar ). According to the previous mechanism analysis, TEIN and FM are the mediation factors. The variable selection showed in  Table 2 .   3.3 Econometric models As shown in Fig. 3 , in this study, we first explore the effect of WRT on WUE using a multi-period DID model. Second, we validate the parallel trends assumption and analyze the dynamic effects of WRT through dynamic DID modeling based on event analysis. To explore the spatial characteristics of WRT, we investigate its spatial spillover effects using the Generalized Spatial Two-Stage Least Squares (GS2SLS) and Han-Phillips Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) models, employing the Moran index to measure spatial correlation of key variables. Finally, we assess the intrinsic mechanisms of WRT's impact on WUE by verifying the mediating effects of technological innovations (TEIN) and factor mobility (FM) through a three-step mediation analysis.  3.3.1 Benchmark model The multi-period DID model is not inherently different from the traditional DID model but does not explicitly set a control group. Specifically, the exogenous shocks that occur in the region at different times are put in the same model (Lin and Huang, 2022 ). Each region is the control group before WRT occurs and becomes the treatment group after WRT occurs. When estimating the effect of WRT on WUE, common trends in time can be removed by using other regions where WRT has not yet occurred as a comparison. The model is constructed as follows:(1) we  it   = β  0   + β  1   wrt  it   + ∑ i = 1  j   β  i   control  it   + γ  t   + μ  i   + ε  it        Where, we  it     is the WUE of province i  in year t , wrt  it      is the dummy variable. When province i  starts WRT in year t , wrt  it   = 1   ; otherwise, wrt  it   = 0   . To relieve the endogeneity problem arising from omitted variables, a series of observable and measurable control variables control  it     are included in the model. β  j     is the coefficient of control variable j . μ  i     is a province-fixed effect to eliminate the effect of unobservable heterogeneity that does not vary over time. γ  t     is a time-fixed effect, which can somewhat alleviate the endogeneity problem caused by non-random grouping.  3.3.2 Dynamic effect model (Dynamic DID model) An important prerequisite assumption for the DID model is that the 'parallel trend assumption' must be true. A dynamic DID model is constructed to extend Eq. (1)  through event study. Not only does it further reveal the persistence of the impact of the WRT on WUE, but it also verifies the parallel trend hypothesis. The model is set up as follows:(2) we  it   = β  0   + ∑ k = 1  k   F  k   wrt  i , t − k    + ∑ j = 1  j   L  j   wrt  i , t + j    + ∑ i = 1  j   ω  i   control  it   + γ  t   + μ  i   + ε  it         In the Eq. (2) , wrt  it     is the dummy variable, indicates that province i  in year t  started WRT. wrt  i , t − k    represents the leading term of period k . The wrt  it     is set to test whether there is the same trend between the treatment and control group before the WRT. If the F  k     are all not significant, it means that there was no significant systematic difference between the treatment amd control group before the construction of the WRT. Then the assumption of parallel trend is established. wrt  i , t + j     indicates the lagged term of period j . The purpose of setting the wrt  i , t + j     is to identify the sustained impact of the WRT on WUE. Other variables are set consistent with Eq. (1) .  3.3.3 Mechanism analysis model The mediation effect is tested using stepwise regression. The model is constructed as follows:(3) mediation  it   = θ  0   + θ  med   wrt  it   + ∑ i = 1  j   ω  i   control  it   + γ  t   + μ  i   + ε  it        (4) we  it   = φ  0   + φ  CR   wrt  it   + φ  med   mediation  it   + ∑ i = 1  j   ω  i   control  it   + γ  t   + μ  i   + ε  it        where, mediation  it     are the mediating variables. The stepwise regression is mainly three steps. Step 1: Verify that WRT does affect WUE. Provided that the β  1     of model  (1) are significant, the θ  med     in Eq. (3)  and the φ  med     in Eq. (4)  are tested sequentially. If both coefficients are significant, it implies that the mediating effect exists and proceeds to step 3. If at least one of the coefficients is not significant, proceed to step 2. Step 2: Bootstrap method is used to test the original hypothesis: θ  med   × φ  med   = 0   . If the original hypothesis is rejected, the mediation effect is established and proceed to step 3, otherwise stop the analysis. Step 3: If the φ  CR     in Eq. (4)  is not significant, then indicating that the model has mediation effects only. If the φ  CR     is significant, then further comparing the sign of θ  med   × φ  med     and φ  CR    .If the sign is consistent, it implies the presence of partial mediation effects. On the contrary, it implies the existence of masking effect.   3.4 Data description To investigate the impact of WRT on WUE comprehensively, a 23-year panel data is constructed for 31 provinces across China. Specifically, we set the time span of the panel from 1999 to 2021 and exclude Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan regions with missing data in order to obtain a larger control group sample to improve the unbiasedness and validity of the estimation results. The long-term panel data used in the study can effectively identify the long-term dynamic effects brought by the WRT. awe , iwe , twe , psw , rai , i-rwfm , and i-iwfm  are mainly from the China Statistics Yearbook on Environmental . is , pow , afwc , pgdp , and tech  were obtained by calculating the data from the China Statistical Yearbook . pop  was obtained from the China Urban-Rural Construction Statistical Yearbook . mar  was from the Marketization Index of China’ Province: Neri Report . The relevant variables and the descriptions are shown in Table 2 .   4 Results 4.1 Benchmark regression results The results in columns (1), (3), and (5) of  Table 3  show that wrt  has a significant negative effect on awe , iwe , and twe  at the 1 % level when controlling variables are not included. The regression coefficients are −472.115, −398.156, and −208.196, respectively.To mitigate the endogeneity problem due to omitted variables, columns (2), (4), and (6) of Table 3  further include a set of control variables. The results find that WRT continues to have a significant negative effect on awe , iwe , and twe  at the 1 % level. The regression coefficients are −574.724, −366.136, and −210.770, respectively. The absolute values of the regression coefficients of WRT become smaller. Regardless of the addition of control variables, WRT is effective in enhancing WUE in the agricultural and industrial sectors, as well as at the regional level.  4.2 Dynamic effects of WRT and parallel trend test The dynamic effects of WRT and the results of the parallel trend tests are shown in  Fig. 4 . The results found that the effects of WRT on awe , iwe , and twe  were not statistically significant before the application of the WRT. It indicates that the parallel trend assumption is consequently validated. After the application of the WRT, awe , iwe , and twe  showed significant differences between the control and treatment group. The coefficients of all three variables show an overall decreasing trend, with only some detailed differences. This result indicates that WRT effectively improves the overall WUE of the region, and this effect has some continuity and shows an increasing effect annually. Moreover, it can be seen that the impact of WRT in the industrial sector is relatively weak compared to the agricultural sector. Note: ① vertical line indicates 90 % confidence interval; ② C0 indicates the year when WRT started, L1 indicates the year after the implementation of wrt , F1 indicates the year before WRT, can deduce the rest from this.  4.3 Robust test 4.3.1 Goodman-Bacon decomposition The bias of multi-period DID model with two-way fixed effects (TWFE) has been discussed (Baker et al., 2022 ). TWFE regressions are often heterogeneous across treatment groups or treatment times. It may lead to the problem of "bad treatment groups" or even negative weights. Accordingly, we refers to the Goodman-Bacon (2021)  decomposition of the DID estimator to examine the degree of bias in multi-period DID with TWFE (Goodman-Bacon, 2021 ). It was found that the inappropriate treatment effect Later Treatment vs. Early Control of awe , iwe  and twe  had an estimate of −197.4559 with 9.64 %, −21.7571 with 14.11 %, and −3.4724 with 14.11 %,respectively. While the appropriate treatment effect had a weight of 90.36 %, 85.89 %, and 85.89 %,respectively. Meanwhile, the core findings can be considered more robust due to the negative DID estimates for both categories and the smaller weight of the unsuitable treatment effect.  4.3.2 Mitigate selection effects Even though the previous section in the parallel trend test has preliminarily verified that WUE of the treatment and reference groups have the same trend before the establishment of the WRT. The empirical results still need to be interpreted with caution. Because it is reasonable to suspect that systematic differences existed between regions prior to the implementation of the WRT. For example, the abundance of water resources and the regional economic development level can have different effects over time trends. For this, the interaction term of the control variables with the time trend is added to model (1). This method can further control for differences in inherent characteristics between regions that may affect WUE from a linear perspective. The results showed that wrt  has a significant negative effect on awe  at the 10 % level, and on iwe , and twe  both at the 1 % level (columns (1)-(3) of  Table 4 ). These results are further to confirme the robustness of the benchmark results.  4.3.3 Excluding the effects of other policies Although the aforementioned tests offer additional confirmation of the validity of the empirical findings, it is inevitable that the application of any policy will be influenced by other policies. Considering that China has enacted other water management policies to promote WUE at the same time. Thus, the dummy variables set in the model (1) to measure WRT may contain shocks from other water management policies and water conservation policies. It might be overestimating the effects of the WRT. China’s Water Resource Tax Reform (CWRTR), which aims to encourage the sensible development and exploitation of water resources, started to be implemented in Hebei in 2016. As a result, in order to exclude the impact of the CWRTR on the WUE. We take 2017 as the time point and set the dummy variable for CWRTR (tax ), which is added to the model (1). The results show that after controlling for the CWRTR, WRT still negatively affects awe , iwe , and twe  at the 1 % level (columns (4)-(6) of Table 4 ). It shows that the benchmark regression results are still robust after further excluding the effect of CWRTR.  4.3.4 Placebo tests It is worthwhile to consider whether the effect is confounded by other unobservable factors. Regarding this, we further construct a series of Placebo Tests. If the same improvement in WUE is observed under the influence of the constructed spurious policies, then it suggests that the creation of the WUE improvement effect possibly comes from other unobservable factors rather than the introduction of the WRT. (1) Construct time dummy variables pre5  and pre7  to incorporate the implementation of WRT in each province 5 and 7 years in advance into the model (1). The results( Table 5 ) show that neither pre5,  nor pre7 , has a statistically significant effect on awe , iwe  and twe . This meant that there was no optimization effect of WUE in the fake WRT by advancing the time, except for the true year. (2) The provinces were randomly assigned into treatment and control groups using the Bootstrap and the regression was repeated 1000 times according to model (1). The results confirmed that the t-values of the fictitious wrt  on awe , iwe , and twe  are approximately normally distributed. It indicates that the percentage of both significantly positive and significantly negative regression coefficients of constructed fictitious wrt  on awe , iwe , and twe  are small in randomized 1000 experiments, which are small probability events ( Fig. 5 ).   4.4 Spatial spillover analysis Before the estimation of the spatial econometric model, the inverse distance matrix was first determined as the spatial weights. Subsequently, Moran's index (Moran's I ) was used to determine the significance of the spatial spillover effects of the key variables. Fig. 6  shows that the global Moran's I  are all greater than 0, and the original hypothesis of the absence of spatial correlation is strongly rejected at the 1 % level. It indicates that the influence of WRT on WUE has a spatial effect in the inverse distance matrix.  Based on the evidence of spatial spillovers for all the main variables in the model, a spatial panel model is considered for further robustness testing. The Generalized Spatial Two-stage Least Squares (GS2SLS) was used, which is more advantageous in dealing with model endogeneity and heteroskedasticity problems (Arraiz et al., 2009; Shao et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2023 ).In addition, to overcome the weak-variance problem of the traditional instrumental variables method and differential generalized method of moments (GMM) estimation, the Han-Phillips GMM estimation is chosen to further validate the dynamic spatial effect of the impact of the WRT on the WUE. The GSPA2SLS results showed that the spatial lag terms of awe, iwe,  and twe  were all significantly positive at 1 % level (columns (1)-(3) of  Table 6 ). It showed that there is an obvious strategy competition effect on WUE among provinces and regions. The dynamic spatial results showed that the spatial lag terms of the WRT were negatively significant at the 5 %, 1 %, and 1 % levels, respectively (columns (4)-(6) of Table 6 ). It indicates that the WRT exhibits obvious spatial spillover effects.Hypothesis 4 is confirmed.    4.5 Mediation analysis 4.5.1 TEIN The results of the step 1 test indicate that wrt  has a positive effect on tech  at the 1 % level (columns (1) of  Table 7 ). However, the coefficients of tech  on awe , iwe  and twe  are insignificant. The results of the Sobel Test at step 2 found that the z-values for direct and indirect impacts for awe  were 1.93 and −4.12 respectively; for iwe  is 2.29 and −4.81 respectively; for twe  is 2.65 and −4.16 respectively. The existence of the mediation effect of tein  can be proved. The result of step 3 showed that there is a significant negative effect of wrt  on both awe , twe  at 1 % level. And the sign is consistent with that of θ  med   × φ  med    , indicating the existence of a partial mediating effect. While the wrt  is negatively significant to iwe  at 1 % level, the sign is inconsistent with θ  med   × φ  med    , indicating the existence of a masking effect. Therefore, the mediation effect of tech  is 6.74 %, 1.32 % and 1.46 % respectively.  4.5.2 FM The results of the step 1 indicate that wrt  has a positive effect on i-rwfm  at the 5 % level (columns (1) of  Table 8 ). Meanwhile, the i-rwfm  has a positive effect on awe , iwe , and twe  at the 1 %, 1 %, and 5 % levels, respectively. This indicates the existence of the mediating effect of interregional water FM. The results of step 3 show that the WRT has a significant positive effect on the awe , iwe , and twe  at the 1 %, 10 % and 5 % levels, respectively. However, the sign is not consistent with θ  med   × φ  med    , which implies that i-rwfm  have a masking effect. As a result, the mediating effects of i-rwfm  are 20.48 %, 11.57 % and 8.23 %, respectively. The i-iwfm  has a positive effect on awe , iwe , and twe  at 1 % level. It confirms that WRT can indeed reduce awe , iwe , and twe  by increasing inter-industry FM. Since both θ  med     and φ  m e d     are significant in step 1, step 3 is followed directly. The results show (Table 8 , columns (6)-(8)) that the wrt  has a positive effect on awe , iwe  and twe  at the 1 % level. The sign is consistent withθ  med   × φ  med    , which implies the existence of partial mediation effect of i-iwfm . Accordingly, the mediation effects of i-iwfm  are 12.17 %, 26.66 % and 10.45 %, respectively.    5 Discussion 5.1 Improvement effect of WRT on WUE According to the previous results, WRT enhances regional WUE, aligning with the conclusion of Mu et al. (2022) , who found a close relationship between WUE and water poverty. The operation of WRT increases the trading value of water resources, effectively incentivizing water users to adopt water conservation measures and optimize the allocation of water resources. In the Ningxia,China, for example, after the implementation of the WRT, wolfberry cultivation was converted from diffuse irrigation or border irrigation to drip irrigation cultivation. The net field irrigation quota can be reduced by 2686.56 m3 /ha. After the conversion of drip irrigation for water conservation in Zhouta Township in Ningxia, China, the water-saving potential per ha of wolfberry cultivation was 10,739.94 m3 . This finding highlights the practical implications of WRT in promoting efficient water use practices and the potential for significant water savings in agriculture. The mediation analysis results indicate that WRT improves regional TEIN capacity, consistent with Mu et al. (2022) . Clear macro-policy directions in China for water conservation and emission reduction reduce uncertainty and provide economic incentives for water users to innovate. When WRT benefits outweigh TEIN costs, water users are further motivated to adopt water-saving innovations, creating a virtuous cycle of cumulative effects. However, WRT negatively affects inter-industry water FM. This may be due to the application of water-saving irrigation techniques, which have led to the agricultural sector saving more water than the industrial sector. The Zhouta Township in Ningxia, China, has been transformed into an agricultural water-saving facility with up to 7,160,000 m3  of tradable water, fully meeting the demand of the Ningxia Jingneng Power Plant. Contrary to Du et al. (2022) , we find that the spatial spillover of WRT is significant and that the impact of WRT on inter-regional WRT is also significant. Du et al. (2022)  based their analysis on national-level WRT pilots, while our study includes spontaneous provincial-level promotions of WRT, offering a more comprehensive view. However, in addition to the national-level pilots, there are also some provinces in China that spontaneously promote the WRT. Measurement of the WRT market should not be limited to the pilots alone but should be based on the actual volume of transactions as well as the number of transactions. Although some areas are national-level pilots, the actual volume of transactions in these areas may not be as much as in provincial-level pilots. Rather than the 7 pilots, using the WRT starting time of provinces as the policy treatment variable better identifies the policy effect of WRT. However, the small coefficient indicates that the impact of WRT in promoting inter-regional water factor mobility is relatively minor, possibly due to the preliminary construction stage of WRT market in China. Even if inter-regional WRT exists, it is usually a water flow between different industries.  5.2 Spatial-temporal effects Both static and dynamic spatial results confirmed the spatial spillover and time lag of WRT. This positive spatial spillover effect can be attributed to several factors: (1) Extensive geographic and economic links between provinces create strong correlations in economic activities and water management. The government-dominated operation of WRT in China is influenced by the "promotion tournament" among officials, where water resource management has become a key performance indicator (Kahn et al., 2015 ). In order to obtain more political benefits and promotion opportunities, local government officials tend to adopt a more aggressive attitude in promoting WRT in their regions. Specifically, for regional WRT, there is an obvious strategic interaction effect among local governments (Hong et al., 2020 ). Such an effect can help local governments form a healthy competitive relationship in the process of improving the WUE. (2) Successful WRT implementation increases WUE, and this improvement is often imitated and learned by spatially or economically connected regions. Inter-regional information exchange, official mobility, and technology spillover facilitate this demonstration effect, encouraging other regions to establish WRT and making the market more active. Theoretically, this study enhances the understanding of the policy impacts of WRT markets by providing a foundational framework to address water supply and demand conflicts. Practically, it delivers crucial insights and evidence for reforms in non-WRT pilot provinces, aiding the development of a water-efficient society in China. Additionally, the study provides empirical evidence for further optimizing the global WRT market. By recommending enhanced transparency and platform integration, promoting institutional and legal frameworks, strengthening inter-regional and cross-border linkages, adoption of water-saving technologies, and addressing negative externalities, this research offers a comprehensive framework for improving the efficiency and sustainability of WRT on a global scale.   6 Conclusions The aims of this study are to accurately assess the policy effects of revealed water rights trading (WRT) in China using a multi-period difference (DID) model. This prompts the independent variable for measuring WRT to break through the traditional seven national pilot provinces. Moreover, the internal transduction pathways of WRT to optimize water use efficiency (WUE) are investigated from the perspectives of technological innovation (TEIN) and water factor mobility (FM). Finally, the static and dynamic spatial effects of WRT are revealed, recognizing and validating the impact of the demonstration effect of WRT on WUE. The main conclusions drawn are as follows: (1) The multi-period DID results show that the WRT significantly improves the WUE. WRT reduced agricultural water efficiency (AWE), industrial water efficiency (IWE) and total water efficiency (TWE) by 574.724, 366.136, and 210.770 units respectively. The results remain robust after a series of robust tests. (2) There are significant spatial spillovers and time lags in the WRT. This indicates that inter-regional imitation and learning exist, whereby the implementation of WRT in one region drives the development of WRT in neighboring regions. (3) TEIN and water FM act as mediators in the relationship between WRT and the optimization of WUE. Firstly, TEIN exhibits a partial mediating effect on AWE and TWE, while it has a masking effect on IWE Second, both inter-industry and inter-regional water FM demonstrate partial mediating effects. In light of the main findings of this study, the following policy recommendations are proposed. First, in the process of promoting WRT at the national level, not only should information such as the total water consumption index be clarified, but it is also necessary to integrate the existing WRT platforms. This will alleviate the problems of information asymmetry and agency in WRT, effectively reduce the cost of WRT, and increase the probability that farmers, enterprises, and other water users will engage in WRT through water-saving behaviors. These strategies provide valuable insights for improving WRT markets globally, suggesting that enhanced transparency and platform integration can lead to more efficient and inclusive water trading systems worldwide. Second, inter-regional linkages should be strengthened to break through the existing market trading boundaries. This promotes increased activity in the WRT market and offers a model for other regions to emulate, fostering global cooperation and knowledge sharing in water rights trading. By facilitating cross-border water trading and cooperation, regions can benefit from shared experiences and best practices, enhancing the global water trading framework. Finally, promoting advanced water-saving technologies and ensuring the flexible allocation of water resources across sectors and regions will not only bolster national WRT efforts but also provide a blueprint for international practices, contributing to the optimization of the global water rights trading market. Although this study explores the impact path of WRT on WUE from the perspective of TEIN and FM, there are still some limitations that cannot be ignored. We used macro-level statistics, which are at the provincial level. To more accurately assess the policy effects of WRT, it is more effective to use micro-level transaction data. Currently, the WRT market in China is still in the exploratory stage, and it is difficult to collect transaction data at the micro level. However, as the WRT market in China continues to expand, the establishment of a trading platform will make it easier to collect transaction data in the future.
1 Introduction Approximately 70 % of South Korea's territory is mountainous. The water from mountain streams in these areas responds immediately to rainfall, flowing quickly. Therefore, when a drought occurs, the flow rates in the streams significantly decreases, making it difficult to supply water. For example, in Mullori Valley area, Chuncheon City, Gangwon Province, residents use small-scale storage facilities to store water from mountain valleys, but often leading to water shortages during prolonged droughts. Additionally, during winter, the streams can freeze as temperatures drop. This led to an incident in the winter of 2016 when the government had to provide bottled water to residents (Chung et al., 2022 ). The freezing of mountain streams is a major cause of water supply disruption in winter, making it essential to implement measures to prevent freezing or to secure alternative water resources. To overcome this issue, Chuncheon City considers the following strategies: securing alternative water resources through groundwater development, artificial recharge of stream water, and constructing new storage facilities such as sand dams or underground dams to ensure stable water supply during droughts and winter. Among them, sand dams are considered to be suitable for the valleys in mountainous areas. A sand dam is a water-management structure consisting of a horizontal barrier (cutoff wall) installed across riverbeds filled with natural or artificial sand (Aerts et al., 2007; Castelli et al., 2022; Maddrell and Neal, 2012 ; Jadhav et al., 2012 ). Unlike underground dams, which are usually referred to as groundwater dams, sand dams primarily store surface or interflow water. Compared with open-water dams, sand dams offer distinct advantages, such as reduced evaporation losses and reduced water pollution (Villani et al., 2018; Yifru et al., 2021 ). Additionally, sand dams are recognized as a structure for artificial recharge, contributing to an increase in groundwater levels (Yifru et al., 2018 ). Sand dams can effectively function as recharge facilities in areas with strong river–aquifer connections (Quinn et al., 2019 ). Aquifer recharge through seepage flow from streambeds sustains increasing groundwater levels throughout the year (Eisma and Merwade, 2020; 2022 ). The induced recharge, as well as the stored water in sand dams, offers resilience against droughts, making sand dams a valuable technology for solving water shortage problems caused by long-term climate change (Lasage and Verburg, 2015 ; Aerts et al., 2007 ; Ryan et al., 2022 ; Eisma and Merwade, 2021 ; Ngugi et al., 2020 ). Sand dams are well-known cost-effective water-storage facilities in arid and semiarid regions. They have been successfully used in Africa and the Middle East (Rao and Rasmussen, 1987; Ertsen and Hut, 2009; Villani et al., 2018; Kamel and Almawla, 2016 ). Despite the focus on arid and semi-arid regions, a sand dam was constructed in the Mulori Valley area of Chuncheon-si, Gangwon-do, Korea, which has a large difference in water quantity between the flood and dry seasons as it experiences a monsoon climate (Chung and Lee, 2021 ). This area is highly vulnerable to water supply disruptions owing to winter valley water freezing during extreme droughts. To resolve this problem, a sand dam was built to enhance water supply. Its specifications include a 120-m2  area, 1.9-m height to the top of the weir, and 2.4-m height to the top of the wall. The sandfill material consists of three layers (Chung and Lee, 2021 ). Construction is expected to enable a stable water supply of 200 m3 /day during normal periods and 10 m3 /day during droughts (Chung et al., 2022 ). However, sand dams may reach their limits in meeting the water demand during extreme droughts. Therefore, in this study, a small-scale groundwater dam was constructed downstream of a sand dam. The purpose of adding a groundwater dam is to increase the reservoir capacity by sending water collected from the underground dam to the sand dam when the reservoir capacity of the sand dam reaches its limit during extreme droughts. The sand dam was designed to match the storage capacity of a 20-year-frequency drought. For even more severe droughts, underground dams serve as an additional safety measure for the water supply. The hybrid structure operates primarily by supplying water through the sand dam under normal conditions, but combines the two water sources to cope with severe droughts. In this study, we evaluated the effectiveness of the combined operation of a sand dam and a small-scale groundwater dam using hydrological routing simulations.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Description of the study area South Korea belongs to the monsoon climate zone, so seasonal differences in temperature and precipitation are very severe. The study area of the Mulori Valley, in Chuncheon City, South Korea, is surrounded by mountainous terrain. The residents rely on a small-scale water storage tank that utilize water from mountain valleys, which leads to water shortages during droughts. The freezing of valley water as temperatures drop in winter further complicates water supply. For example, water tank trucks had to supply water to the villages in February 2016 because the valley water had frozen and the water sources had dried up. To mitigate water shortages during emergencies and to ensue stable water supply, a sand dam was constructed in the region ( Fig. 1 ). The catchment area is approximately 1.6 km2  with diverse topography ranging from 298 to 950-m above sea level. The combined impact of this topography and low population density has resulted in an area lacking a distributed water-supply network. During the 2016 drought, residents relied solely on trucks to meet their drinking water needs. The local water supply capacity is 30 m³/day. The primary source is the interflow in the mountains, which provides a steady flow of underground water. In addition, a small water intake facility exists on the valley side. A sand dam was built downstream of the intake facility to create a bypass water design. The sand dam installed in the study area has a distinct advantage: it is a gravity-drained, non-powered water supply facility, eliminating the need for electricity ( Fig. 2 (a)). However, even with its 120-m2  surface area, during severe droughts, insufficient inflow might lead to unmet water demand. Therefore, to enhance the system’s resilience to extreme droughts and secure more stable water resources, a supplementary solution was implemented. As shown in Fig. 2 (b), a small groundwater dam, bounded by a horizontal barrier about 4 m wide and 3 m deep, was installed downstream of the existing sand dam to provide additional water resources. Unlike the sand dam, the bottom of the groundwater dam is open for groundwater inflow As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the horizontal retaining wall impedes flow through the underlying groundwater table beneath the sand dam. This causes an increase in groundwater levels and storage. The stored groundwater is reintroduced into the sand dam via pumping ( Fig. 3 ). While directly conveying groundwater to a village water tank may seem appealing, the cost of constructing connecting pipelines is a significant obstacle. Additionally, the difference in elevation between the two is insufficient for natural gravity drainage. Therefore, an effective solution involves the use of a submersible pump to temporarily return stored groundwater to the sand dam. This establishes a cyclic water-supply system through strategically placed water-level sensors within the sand dam. When the water level falls below a predetermined threshold at the bottom of the sand dam, a submersible pump can automatically draw water from the groundwater dam and inject it back into the sand dam structure. This creates a closed-loop water-supply system that prioritizes passive water supply through the sand dam. If a sand dam alone proves insufficient, a hybrid system is activated by utilizing the downstream groundwater dam for an active water supply.  2.2 Construction of sand dam hydrological outflow routing model In general, the hydrological outflow routing of a reservoir involves calculating the water level and outflow hydrograph using a continuity equation (mass-balance equation). As mentioned by Fenton (1992) , the governing equation represented in terms of the water level has a special advantage in implementing controlled reservoir outflow by valves or spillway gates. In this study, to calibrate the weir coefficient C  w    , the drainage valve was closed so that only weir flow occurred, which could be easily modeled by setting C  d   = 0    in Eq. (7) . When the sand dam water level dropped below a user-defined threshold level, the system automatically activated and pumped approximately 50 m3 /d of groundwater from the adjacent dam and reinjected it into the sand dam. In this study, the pumping rate was treated as the controlled inflow I  c      in this study.  2.3 Analysis procedure The impacts of the hybrid operation of the sand dam and groundwater barrier on the water supply at the study site were investigated using the reservoir routing model described in Section 2.2 . First, the main parameters of the routing model, drainage coefficient, and weir coefficient were calibrated for the period from May 1, 2022, to July 7, 2022, when both the sand dam inflow and the water level within the sand dam were measured. Reservoir routing was then performed for the previous period, March 16, 2020, to July 6, 2022, in which only the outflow through the existing water intake pond located upstream of the sand dam used as the sand dam inflow was measured.  Fig. 4  shows the analytical procedures employed in this study. The weir coefficient (Cw ) was calibrated by matching the simulated and measured water level data from May 1 to May 29, 2022, when the valve between the drainpipes and main pipe supplying water to the village was closed. The drain coefficient (Cd ) was also calibrated using water-level data measured from May 30 to July 7, 2022, allowing outflow through the drainpipes by opening the drain valve. The outflows were simulated using the calibrated reservoir routing model under the condition that the sand and groundwater dams were assumed to be constructed for the period of March 16, 2020, to July 6, 2022. The behavior of the drainage rates for different threshold water levels, below which water pumped from the groundwater dam was transferred to the sand dam, was analyzed. The minimum drainage rate resulting from the combined operation of the sand and groundwater dams was compared with the result of operating the sand dam alone. The sand dam water levels were simulated for historical hypothetical inflow rates, and the spillway capacity was evaluated by comparing the maximum water level at the top of the weir.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Estimation of drainage coefficient and weir coefficient In the model, the drainage coefficient (Cd ) and weir coefficient (Cw ) are critical parameters that determine the water level of the sand dam, drainage rate through perforated pipes and discharge volume through the weir, respectively. From May to early July 2022, these coefficients were iteratively adjusted until the model-calculated water level closely matched the observed value measured at the sand dam weir, approximately 2 m below the sand layer. Initially, the drainage pipes were disconnected from the village’s water tank supply line and control valves were installed between them. This allowed discharge only through the upper weir, enabling the weir coefficient to be determined. Subsequently, the valve was opened in the latter part of the observation period to permit drainage through the pipes and facilitate calculation of the drainage coefficient.  Fig. 5  demonstrates a good agreement between the observed and simulated water levels, when using the calibrated values of Cd  = 7.0 and Cw  = 0.5, indicating that the model successfully captured the overall pattern of the observed water levels. Fig. 5  shows the time-series of the simulated drainage rate through the drainage pipe during the observation period. The drainage rate followed fluctuations in the sand dam water level. Notably, during the early part of the observation period, when the water level began to increase, the simulated drainage rate closely resembled the measured value of 200 m³/d. This coincided with the sand dam reaching an inundation high water level of 1.9 m, indicating the onset of weir flow.   3.2 Effects of installing sand dam and groundwater dam on improving water supply An existing small intake structure, previously used for water supply, is located upstream of the sand dam and is bounded by a retaining wall. Excess water exceeding the capacity of the intake structure overflowed from the weir and flowed into the sand dam. On March 14, 2020, before the construction of the sand dam until May 14, 2022, water-level data measured at this intake were used to calculate the inflow to the sand dam. This involved applying a water level–flow relationship derived from concurrent measurements of the weir flow depth and discharge during this period to the intake water level data.  Fig. 7  shows that the average daily inflow over the 2-year and 2-month periods, even including months with zero inflow from the existing water source, was approximately 1800 m³. Storing this substantial inflow represents significant potential for an additional water supply.  Fig. 8  presents an analysis of the simulated potential additional water supply achieved through the sand dam, modeled as a reservoir routing system. The figure shows the simulated maximum drainage rate through the drainpipes of 232.6 m3 /day and an average of 126.4 m3 /day. On average, 13 % of the inflow was discharged through drainpipes, and the remainder was discharged through weirs. The observed inflow time series shown in Fig. 6  reveals that zero inflow occurred on 253 d, corresponding to approximately 30 % of the observation period. Notably, the storage effect of the sand dam decreased the number of days with zero drainage rate to 107 d, accounting for 12.7 % of the total period. It is expected that the non-water supply period can be shortened by increasing the delay effect by filling the inside of the dam with sand material with a smaller specific gravity and size, or by decreasing the opening ratio of the perforated drain pipe. However, the sand dam in the study area was filled with coarse sand to decrease sand loss during floods and to prevent the blockage of perforated pipes.  Fig. 9  presents the simulated results of operating a pump to reinject 50 m3 /day of water from the groundwater dam into the sand dam whenever the water level falls below a specified threshold. Figs. 9 (a) to 9 (d) depict the calculated drainage rates when the sand dam water levels reach 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, and 0.5 m from the bottom, respectively.  Table 1  summarizes and compares the results. The analysis revealed that, compared with operating the sand dam alone, the integrated operation of a sand dam with the groundwater dam increased the minimum drainage rate by 50.0, 46.5, 35.0, and 24.6 m3 /day, respectively, depending on the threshold. Setting the pump activation threshold at 0.8 m resulted in a similar increase in drainage rate as the pumping rate itself (50.0 m3 /day). However, as the threshold decreased to 0.5 m, the increase in the drainage rate diminished, reaching approximately 50 % of the initial injection rate. Nevertheless, all four threshold levels satisfied the community’s minimum daily water demand of 15 m3 /day for the community. Additionally, lowering the threshold decreases pump operating periods and consequently decreases power consumption. However, considering the potential decrease in groundwater pumping rates and capacity due to decreased groundwater levels during droughts, along with the increasing water demand in the area, a flexible setting of the pump activation threshold will be necessary. It would be more accessible to pump water directly into storage tanks instead of pumping it back into the sand dam. However, if the groundwater from the dam is directly pumped into the storage tank, its limited capacity is quickly exhausted, decreasing its storage effectiveness. Additionally, because the retention time is longer in the sand dam, this setup demonstrates that the sand dam can be more useful during drought periods. Furthermore, if the inflow from upstream is very small, a stagnant flow may occur within the sand dam, which may have a negative impact on water quality. However, reinjection has the advantage of enabling the continuous circulation of water within the sand dam.  3.3 Evaluation of the spillway capacity of the sand dam weir When the water level in the sand dam surpasses 1.9 m (height of the weir crest), excess water is discharged through the weir located in the upper part of the downstream retaining wall. This weir had a height and bottom width of 0.5 and 2.0 m, respectively.  Fig. 10  depicts the simulated daily water levels within the sand dam considering the re-injection of groundwater dam inflow and the inflow conditions from Fig. 7  using a reservoir outflow routing model. The water level fluctuates between a minimum of 0.68 m and maximum of 2.19 m, with an average of 1.44 m. As the maximum water level within the sand dam remains below the total height of the sand dam structure (1.9 m for the weir crest + 0.5 m for the weir height), our simulation indicates that the entire excess water quantity can be discharged through the weir.  Fig. 11 (a) and (b) show the simulated water level fluctuations for scenarios where the inflow rates were doubled and tripled, respectively, compared with Fig. 10 . In the doubled-inflow-rate scenario, the highest simulated water level reached 2.36 m, still below the overall height of the sand dam structure at 2.4 m. This indicates sufficient weir capacity to discharge excess water. However, the tripled inflow rate scenario experienced water levels exceeding the structural height from July 21–25, 2021, with a maximum of 2.50 m, indicating insufficient spillway capacity. Chung et al. (2022)  combined long-term runoff simulations using the SWAT model with hydraulic runoff routing simulations of a sand dam using the MODFLOW model to generate inflow data for an 11-year period from 2011 to 2020. Their results predicted that the maximum inflow could reach approximately 3.3 times the 2021 inflow. While the current sand dam weir, with a maximum spillway capacity of 0.6 m3 /sec at a weir flow depth of 0.5 m, can handle inflow rates up to 2.5 times that in 2021, it may not be sufficient for the extreme scenarios predicted by Chung et al. (2022) . Therefore, the installation of additional weirs for emergency preparedness or expansion of the current weir width is recommended.   4 Conclusions This study investigated the combined operation of sand and downstream groundwater dams to assess their effectiveness in improving water supply. Hydrological reservoir routing was employed to analyze both systems and their interactions. In addition, the discharge capacity of a weir installed to manage excess water exceeding the storage capacity of a sand dam was evaluated. A cyclic reinjection system was established within the sand dam using a sensor. When the water level fell below a preset threshold, the system automatically pumped groundwater from the downstream dam and reinjected it back into the sand dam, maintaining continuous internal circulation. This system significantly improved the minimum discharge rates compared with the operation of the sand dam alone. The simulations showed increases of 50.0, 46.5, 35.0, and 24.6 m³/day for critical water level thresholds of 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, and 0.5 m for initiating reinjection, respectively. Setting the activation threshold at 0.8 m can supply water at a rate similar to the pumping rate of 50.0 m³/day. However, decreasing the threshold to 0.5 m decreased the increase in discharge to approximately 50 % of the pumping rate, indicating a diminishing effect with lower thresholds. Daily simulations using a reservoir routing model showed sand dam water level fluctuations ranging from 0.68 to 2.19 m, with an average of approximately 1.44 m. Importantly, the highest water level remained below the total sand dam structure height (weir crest at 1.9 m + weir height of 0.5 m), ensuring sufficient discharge capacity through the weir during the study period. This study is the first case of constructing and evaluating the performance of a water supply facility connecting a sand dam and a groundwater dam. It has value in contributing to solving the water shortage problem in areas with weak water supply, such as mountainous areas vulnerable to drought and freezes.
