1 Introduction Lakes are important water resource systems of the water cycle, contributing significantly to the regulation of an area’s hydro-climatic conditions and providing a wide range of ecosystem services for local biodiversity (Hassan and Jin, 2014; Jenny et al., 2020 ). Across the globe however, there is evidence of water resource system degradation arising from various environmental stressors largely classified as anthropogenic, encompassing climatic and, to an extent, geological factors (Liu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022; Zadereev et al., 2020 ). Human-induced causes, primarily from various intensive and unregulated human interventions, are known to directly or indirectly affect the qualities and ecology of water systems concerned, with short to long term effects (Kast et al., 2021; Shams Ghahfarokhi and Moradian, 2023; Spears et al., 2022 ). In some regions, shifts in regional hydro-climatic patterns contribute to lake water level fluctuations, leading to short-term decreases or increases in volumes over the climatic periods (Hassan et al., 2023; Herrnegger et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2018 ). Today, sufficient evidence from paleo-studies of many lakes across the globe indicates that water bodies have either changed course, geometry or otherwise completely desiccated over geological time-scales. A review of the lacustrine deposits of some of the lakes that exhibit a changed status relative to their pre-Anthropocene status is available through lake sediment archives (Jenny et al., 2020 ). In the East African Great Rift Valley (Gregory, 1896; Suess, 1891; von Höhnel et al., 1891 ), several lakes have witnessed substantial water level increases since ∼2010 (Avery, 2020; Herrnegger et al., 2021; Onywere et al., 2013 ). In Kenya, a majority of the Rift Valley lakes are biodiverse eco-zones, classified as RAMSAR wetlands of international importance (Ramsar Convention, 2022 ) and designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites (UNESCO World Heritage Convention, 2023 ). The water level increases of the Kenyan lakes not only affect the biodiversity, but have also inundated the basis of rural livelihoods and existing social amenities such as schools, hospitals, national parks and agricultural land. Consequently, up to eighty thousand households with ∼400,000 people have been affected by the inundations (Government of Kenya and UNDP, 2021; Obando et al., 2016; Tower and Plano, 2023 ). Herrnegger et al. (2021)  presented evidence that changes in rainfall and evapotranspiration characteristics – the major hydro-climatic drivers defining the water balance of the lakes – have with high probability resulted in the lake water level increases. The study shows that in the period 2010–2020 mean annual rainfall increased by up to 30 % for the different lake catchments. After 2018, annual catchment rainfall increased by even more than 50 %. Regional climate in Eastern Africa has shown exceptional variability in the past, fluctuating between long-lasting periods of severe drought and wetter periods as we are currently observing (e.g. Bessems et al., 2008 ; Flohn, 1987 ; Nicholson, 2001, 2019 ; Nicholson et al., 2022 ; Nicholson and Yin, 2001 ; Sutcliffe and Parks, 1999 ; Verschuren et al., 2000 ; Whittaker, 2019 ). The existing scientific literature on the historic and paleo-climatic water levels, extending back 30,000 years, indicate comprehensively that climate variability over the same region has led not only to the complete desiccation of some lakes, but also to high water levels in the distant past (e.g. Bessems et al., 2008 ; Dommain et al., 2022 ; Flohn, 1987 ; Garcin et al., 2009 ; Nicholson, 1998 ; Nicholson and Yin, 2001 ; Okech et al., 2019 ; Olaka et al., 2010 ; Owen and Renaut, 1986 ; Pavitt, 2008 ; Petek, 2018 ; Robakiewicz et al., 2023 ; Stager et al., 2005 ; Tiercelin and et al., 1987 ; Trauth and Strecker, 2019 ; Verschuren, 2019, 2001 ; Verschuren et al., 2000 ; Whittaker, 2019 ; Whittaker and Johnson, 2019 ; Wuytack et al., 2017 ). Lake Naivasha in Kenya, for instance, was dramatically reduced to a puddle around 1850, which was a period of widespread and extreme aridity throughout most of Africa and seen in other East African lakes. Also, particularly low levels persisted throughout the 1940s and 1950s. (Nicholson, 1998; Richardson, 1966; Trauth and Strecker, 2019 ). Pavitt (2008)  quoted that “Three years of drought in the mid-1890s followed a decade of below-average rainfall and caused Lake Naivasha to virtually dry up. […]. The Maasai could drive their cattle straight across the ‘lake’. By 1900 exceptionally heavy rain began to restore the level of the lake. […]. ” (see Figure A1 ). This evidence is somewhat supported by reconstructions of Naivasha lake levels in the scientific literature (Verschuren, 2001 ). In 2020, high water levels of Lake Naivasha, which is today a popular destination for leisure seekers from the capital city of Nairobi, led to the flooding of built-up areas, farms, lodges, camp sites and protected areas. Studies have documented historically extreme high water levels in Kenya’s Rift Valley lakes in the period between 8000–12,000 years ago, when the area exhibited a completely different hydrological and river network pattern as compared to today. Lake Turkana (Avery and Tebbs, 2018; Ojwang et al., 2016 ), now one of the largest desert lakes in the world, drained towards the Nile. Lake Turkana (formerly Lake Rudolf), now receiving most of its water from Ethiopia via the Omo River, was part of a river system having its headwaters in today’s Lake Elementaita area. The catchment boundaries were very different, not only for Lake Turkana (Dommain et al., 2022; Garcin et al., 2009 ). For Lake Baringo, after Lake Turkana the second largest lake in the Kenyan Eastern Rift, Okech et al. (2019)  provide information on water level dynamics from 1790 to 2014 based on sediment core samples and the abundance of planktonic and benthic diatom taxa and the planktonic/benthic ratio as a proxy. Information provided by Bessems et al. (2008)  also indicate that the most recent complete desiccation episode of Lake Baringo occurred in the late 18th and early 19th century – the complete opposite of what is being observed today. Late Pleistocene-Holocene reconstructions of water levels in Lakes Baringo and Bogoria show that the two lakes were connected around 8000 years ago (Ashley et al., 2004; de Cort et al., 2018; Dommain et al., 2022; Garcin et al., 2009; Tiercelin and et al., 1987; Wuytack et al., 2017 ). Today, the increases in water levels of Lake Bogoria may lead to a repetition of the paleohydrological conditions. There is fear of an ecological catastrophe should the current water levels of alkaline Lake Bogoria continue to rise. The result would be an overflow towards and mixing with freshwater Lake Baringo, the basis of the local community, supporting agriculture, tourism and fisheries as well as drinking water (Avery, 2020; Muita, 2021; The EastAfrican, 2014; Wambui et al., 2021 ). Using data from the year 2020 (Facebook Connectivity Lab and Center for International Earth Science Information Network - CIESIN - Columbia University, 2016; Tiecke et al., 2017 ), our estimates suggest that 6000–25,000 people would be affected. The large range reflects the uncertainties of estimation and depends on the specific areas affected. Although the current lake level rises in Kenya have received some attention in the scientific literature (see references in Herrnegger et al., 2021  or Kiage and Douglas, 2020 ; Kimaru et al., 2019 ; Muita, 2021 ; Onywere et al., 2013 ; Walumona et al., 2022 ), no one has considered the potential overflow of Lake Bogoria into and cross-mixing with Lake Baringo. There is currently a lack of analysis regarding the topographical and landscape conditions on the Loboi plain situated between the two lakes, as well as the potential flow paths that might emerge in the event of an overflow. The risk and extent of water level increases required for Lake Bogoria to reach its spill point remains uncertain. Also unclear are the rainfall conditions which are necessary to lead to sustained flows from Lake Bogoria towards Lake Baringo. Taking these constraints consideration, this study seeks to assess:(i) the rainfall conditions in the proximity of the lakes,  (ii) the overflow or spill point location and potential flow paths towards Lake Baringo,  (iii) the required lake water level and volume changes until the spill point is reached and  (iv) the mean rainfall conditions which would be necessary to provide the required volume and a sustained flow towards Lake Baringo.     2 Materials and methods 2.1 General characteristics of the study area Lake Bogoria and Baringo are located in the Central Rift Valley of Kenya, which is part of the East African Rift System, ranging from the Gulf of Aden at the Horn of Africa to the south of Lake Malawi between Malawi and Mozambique ( Fig. 1 ). In total, the study area and lake basins cover an area of 7615 km². Lake characteristics are summarized in  Table 1 . Both lakes lie in closed basins, where the lake is a sink and where no obvious surface outlets are present. Lake Bogoria and Baringo are located in the Rift floor, encircled by high mountain ranges and escarpments. The lowest lake in terms of lake level and with a mean catchment elevation of 1722 m, is Baringo, which is a freshwater system. Despite high potential evapotranspiration rates, Lake Baringo has not become saline, indicating that there is substantial underground loss of water through seepage, which hinders the accumulation of dissolved solids through flushing (Becht et al., 2006; Darling et al., 1996, 1990; Derakhshan, 2017; Yihdego and Becht, 2013 ). A potential emergence site of Lake Baringo seepage waters could be the hot springs in Kapedo (1°10'47.52"N, 36°6′41.31"E), which lie about 50 km to the north. Lake Bogoria, in contrast, is highly saline, which does not therefore mean that no underground seepage is present: The magnitude of underground seepage is simply low compared to the freshwater lake (McCall, 2010 ). Lake Baringo (Kiage and Douglas, 2020; Obando et al., 2016; Odada et al., 2006; Onywere et al., 2013 ) is internationally recognized for its biodiversity, and is also important to the communities in its basin as a source of water for domestic and agricultural use and for watering livestock. Other important uses are income generation through tourism, biodiversity conservation and fishing. Three indigenous human communities live in the basin, namely the Ilchamus, Pokots and Tugens. Seasonal rivers that drain into Lake Baringo include Ol Arabel, Makutan, Tangulbei, Endao and Chemeron. Perkerra and Molo are perennial, but show strong seasonality with significantly lower discharges during the dry season. Lake Baringo experiences very high annual evaporation rates (1650–2300 mm) relative to an annual rainfall of 450–900 mm and therefore lake levels depend heavily on inflows from rivers originating from the humid parts of the drainage basin, where the annual rainfall varies between 1100 mm and 2700 mm (Herrnegger et al., 2021; Onywere et al., 2013 ). Conductivity is reported to be around 1760 μS/cm (De Bock et al., 2009 ), 894.4 μS/cm (Obando et al., 2016 ) or 450–500 μS/cm (this study). The orographic catchment size of Lake Baringo is around 6610 km², having a north-south extent of around 150 km and 70 km from west to east. The area around Lake Baringo is presently inundated, with several hotels and rural infrastructure, including homes, agricultural fields and grazing areas, dispensaries, health centres and schools affected. Lake Bogoria (see e.g. Agembe et al., 2016 ; McCall, 2010 ; Renaut et al., 2017 ; Tiercelin and et al., 1987 ) is located in a deep depression with comparatively steeper slopes than Lake Baringo. Although the lake level increases when measured in absolute numbers are high, the steeper topography of the surrounding area limits the spread of flood waters mostly to the north of the lake. The lake is located within a National Reserve, where the main road, main gate and administration building have been flooded. Geothermal springs associated with the lake region (Renaut et al., 2017 ) are a prominent tourist attraction but are now submerged. The lake is highly alkaline, with a reported conductivity of 31 046 μS/cm (Obando et al., 2016 ) and 33 800 μS/cm (this study). The catchment area is ∼1060 km², receiving mean annual rainfall of 1035 mm for the period 1981–2020. No systematic mapping or quantitative information regarding the groundwater conditions around Lake Bogoria is available (Olago et al., 2009). The many fresh hot- and cool-springs, however, show the presence of groundwater and have been discussed in the literature (Ashley et al., 2004 , 2002; Renaut et al., 2017 ; Renaut and Owen, 2023 ; Scott et al., 2008 ). Rainfall patterns in the Kenyan Rift Valley are complex due to different moisture sources and large-scale ocean-atmosphere dynamics. The Indian Ocean is the primary moisture source, with warm sea surface temperatures (SSTs) driving evaporation and easterly winds transporting moisture. Moisture influx from the Congo Basin plays a role, especially during the long rains (March-May). Short rain (October-December) variability is largely tied to the Indian Ocean and an equatorial Walker circulation pattern (Hastenrath et al., 2011). The Rift Valley's topography further influences localized rainfall patterns (Nicholson, 2017; Palmer et al., 2023 ). The classical explanation for the seasonal cycle is the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). However, the ITCZ does not penetrate into the region (Nicholson, 2017). The shifting tropical rainbelt, a zone of high moisture and instability, dictates the seasonal rainfall cycle (Yang et al., 2015). Its northward movement brings the long rains, while its southward shift leads to the short rains. Key factors like El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) can alter this circulation. El Niño events generally bring heavier rainfall to the Rift Valley, while La Niña often leads to drier conditions (Nicholson, 2015). A positive IOD weakens prevailing easterlies, lessening subsidence and increasing rainfall. Conversely, a negative IOD strengthens the easterlies and creates a drier climate (Nicholson, 2015; Palmer et al., 2023). While ENSO and IOD often work together, they can also influence rainfall independently. For example, the exceptionally wet years of 1961 and 2019 were largely linked to a positive IOD with minimal ENSO influence (Nicholson et al., 2022 ; Wainwright et al., 2021 ).  2.2 Data basis The analysis builds on data with information on (a) elevation and topography, (b) lake levels, lake areas and lake volume variations, (c) electrical conductivity and temperature conditions, current extents of swamps, river courses and vegetation cover and (d) rainfall, runoff and water balance.  Fig. 2  provides an overview of all these data sets. 2.2.1 Elevation and topography Different elevation models including TanDEM-x (with a spatial resolution of 12 m, Wessel, 2018 ), EDTM30 (30 m, Ho et al., 2023 ), SRTM (90 m, Jarvis et al., 2008 ), MERIT Hydro DEM (90 m, Yamazaki et al., 2019 ), as well as a drone or Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS)-based elevation model with a 5 cm resolution, are all used for delineating watershed boundaries, extracting profiles, modelling shorelines and analyzing the spill point and potential flow paths. The TanDEM-x dataset also constitutes the basis for estimating lake shores and water volumes and for visualizing the region. To take care of geoid undulations, corrections of some of the elevation data were performed to compensate for differences in the vertical datum of the raster data. The horizontal and vertical datum of the TanDEM-x digital elevation model (DEM) is the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84) in G1150 realization (Rexer and Hirt, 2016 ). The same ellipsoidal vertical datum is present in the UAS DSM (Unmanned Aircraft System Digital Surface Model). In contrast, EDTM, SRTM and MERIT use the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84) as horizontal datum and the Earth Gravitational Model (EGM96) geoid as vertical datum. Elevations based on the Earth Gravitational Model used in EDTM30/SRTM/Merit are also used in this study. The difference between absolute elevation values due to the different vertical datums of TanDEM- x/UAS DSM and EDTM30/SRTM/Merit lies from around 14.4 m in the south of Lake Bogoria to around 15.1 m in the south of Lake Baringo, with values of around 15 m on the Loboi Plane. The geoid is thereby higher relative to the TanDEM- x/UAS DSM. Figure A2  in the Appendix shows the spatial distribution of the geoid undulations used for the additive correction for the study area, which is an interpolated field based on 5000 randomly sampled points, for which the geoid undulation was calculated using UNAVCO (2021) . The UAS-based DSM covers 392 ha near the location of the Bogoria spill point and was acquired on 26 May 2022. It was the second attempt to capture the elevation data after the first drone crashed into the lake southeast of the former, now flooded, Loboi Health Clinic. All flights were performed following best practice guidelines (e.g. Strelnikova et al., 2022 ), using a stationary Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS) station for spatial reference improvements. Processing of the RGB images and deriving the DSM was performed using AgiSoft (AgiSoft, 2016 ).  2.2.2 Lake levels, areas and volume variation Lake levels, areas, and volume variation data for Lakes Baringo and Bogoria from the “Database for Hydrological Time Series over Inland Waters” (DAHITI, Schwatke et al. (2020), (2019), (2015)  are used and are partially based on the data and results processed in Herrnegger et al. (2021) , covering the years 1984–2020. Additional DAHITI water level data extending until June 2023 was provided for the study. Furthermore, maximum water extents from the Global Surface Water product (GSW 1.1; (Pekel et al., 2016 )) are used as an additional reference for water surfaces.  2.2.3 Information and mapping of river courses, swamps, and vegetation cover A field campaign in October 2022 provided information on the electrical conductivity and temperature characteristics of 49 locations (Table A1 ), starting in the headwaters of the Molo and covering the different tributaries to Lake Bogoria and Baringo, but also the streams, swamps and other water bodies in the area between the lakes (Loboi Plain). A WTW cond315i conductivity meter was used to do the measurements, with accuracies of ±0.5 % for electrical conductivity and ±0.1°C for water temperature. Kenya topographic maps with a scale of 1:50,000 (Lake Baringo, sheet number - quarter 91–3, published 1982; Ngelesha, 105–1, 1973; and Solai, 105–3, 1973) of the Survey of Kenya proved to be valuable for orientation and mapping, and for assurance as to the current situation in the Loboi Plain. The swamps and river courses are based on OpenStreetMap (OpenStreetMap contributors, 2023 ) and were downloaded using the QuickOSM plugin in QGIS (QGIS Development Team, 2023 ). Additionally, river courses and water areas and extents were manually checked for plausibility via satellite imagery using Copernicus Sentinel-2 data and Google Earth Pro. Information on vegetation cover and spatio-temporal change (see Fig. 1 ) based on the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) was derived using the MODIS MOD13Q1 product (Didan, 2015 ), using R (R Core Team, 2023 ) and different packages therein for processing, e.g. Busetto and Ranghetti (2016) .  2.2.4 Rainfall, runoff and water balance Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS (Funk et al., 2015 )) and in-situ rainfall information from station data measured at Marigat (STN102) in the proximity of the lakes were used as rainfall input. Although some discharge data are available to us, the frequent data gaps and partially questionable data integrity hinder the use of these data for analyzing the water balance. The Integrated Catchment Response (ICR [mm]) from Herrnegger et al. (2021)  provides information on the fluxes of the lakes. The ICR is the integral runoff depth of all  flows resulting in a change of water volume. It is based solely on changes in lake volumes and therefore integrates and includes all fluxes to and from the lakes, also including runoff to the lake, rainfall and evapotranspiration from the lake surface or potential groundwater flows. The ICR reflects a mean watershed or catchment value of the runoff coefficient, thereby averaging out spatial variability of hydrological processes e.g., of rainfall of evapotranspiration. We use the long time series of the ICR, which is calculated using lake volume variation data from 1984–2020, for estimating the hydrological conditions influencing the lake levels. No quantitative information is available on groundwater flows towards the lakes.   2.3 Estimation of spill point location and potential flow path The derivation of the spill point location is based on terrain analysis using QGIS (QGIS Development Team, 2023 ) utilizing the different DEMs available for the area of interest. For finding the location of the spill point, a catchment delineation is performed for the locality. The lowest point in the catchment divide between Lake Bogoria and Lake Baringo can then be defined as the spill point. Field work in February and October 2022 was essential for plausibility checks of the results. The derivation of the potential flow path of the Bogoria-Baringo stream is based on a stream network delineation as a first guess, followed by the analysis of water courses depicted in the 1:50,000 scale topographical maps of the study area and GIS data on swamps and water courses from OpenStreetMap (Kray, 2023 ). Satellite imagery, as well as field work and electrical conductivity measurements used as a proxy for understanding the current flow conditions, are used to check plausibility of the delineated water course. Finally, after deriving the spill point and the potential water course, an elevation profile was generated by sampling mean elevation values from different elevation models (TanDEM-x, EDTM30, SRTM, UAS DSM) along the potential water course.  2.4 Lake level and volume changes until spill point is reached The estimation of the necessary water level and volume changes of Lake Bogoria until the spill point is reached is based on the elevation of the Bogoria spill point and the maximum water level present in the DAHITI database. The differences in the water levels of these two states (maximum observed water level and spill point water level) yield the necessary lake level increase until the spill point is reached. For additional evaluation, the water levels at the time of writing in the first half of 2023 are also used as a reference. The elevation contour line of the spill point elevation is used to model the water surface of Lake Bogoria which would occur if the water level reached the spill point. For the area of the spill point, the DEM derived from the UAS-data was integrated into the TanDEM- x since we have higher confidence in these elevation values. Subtracting the two water surfaces of the maximum water level (and the water level of February 2023) from the spill point water surface yields the water depth for every grid cell. This information has a spatial resolution of 12 m since we used the TanDEM-x as a basis. Considering the grid cell size and water depth, a volume can be calculated for every grid cell. These volumes can then be integrated to receive the total volume change. A reconstruction of the water surface at the maximum water level of DAHITI was also necessary since plausibility checks showed that the water areas included in DAHITI substantially underestimated the real water areas. This is the case for Lake Bogoria and Lake Baringo. This underestimation is also present when comparing DAHITI water areas with delineations available in Government of Kenya and UNDP (2021)  and Onywere et al. (2013) , and is also discussed and shown in Herrnegger et al. (2021) ; see e.g. Fig. A6 and Fig. A7  therein). To assess the risk of an overflow of Lake Bogoria, we use historical lake level data as a proxy. These lake level fluctuation data are used to calculate the empirical probability of water levels to reach the spill point. We estimate the likelihood that the spill point is reached assuming that the temporal sequence of observed lake level rises and also declines exhibit patterns reflected in 39 years of water level data.  2.5 Mean rainfall conditions to provide a sustained flow towards Lake Baringo Understanding the underlying mechanisms leading to the lake level fluctuations necessitates an analysis of the temporal characteristics of the water balance and inflows to the lakes. The following longer-term water balance equation for a lake watershed  can be defined as (all units in [mm])(2) V = R + Q  gw   − A ET − Q  out   + ∆ S ,      where V refers to storage or volume in the lake (i.e. increase/decrease in lake water volume from one year to the next), R is catchment rainfall, Qgw  is additional potential underground flow from neighbouring watersheds, AET is the actual catchment evapotranspiration (including evaporation from the lake surface), Qout  is runoff from the lake (i.e. outflow through a surface water body or the seepage into the underground) and, finally, ΔS is for changes in storage in the catchment (e.g. change in soil moisture, groundwater or water stored in biomass). The lake volume variation data from DAHITI can be interpreted as the right-hand side of Eq. (2)  since V integrates potential changes occurring in the catchment. It allows the quantification of the magnitude of changes to be expected on the right-hand side of the water balance equation. The year-to-year lake volume variation data is, in combination with the orographic catchment area, used to derive a magnitude for every year t, which we refer to as “Integrated Catchment Response” (ICR, mm):(3) ICR  t   = S  t   [ km  3   ] − S  t − 1   [ km  3   ]    * 10  12    Area [ km  ²   ] * 10  6     [ mm ]      In Eq. (3) , the difference in lake volume variation S from one year to the next is calculated and converted from [km³] to [dm³] and is then normalized by the orographic catchment area (Area), which is converted from [km²] to [m²].
