To assess the catchment rainfall values necessary for a sustained flow, we establish a relationship between the observed Integrated Catchment Response (ICR) and catchment rainfall to provide a function to simulate necessary rainfall conditions for different sustained flow scenarios. For the evaluation, different flow scenarios ranging from 10 L/s to 1500 L/s are considered.   3 Results 3.1 Water-related characteristics of the Loboi Plain  Fig. 3  provides a general overview of the Loboi plain and situation between Lake Bogoria in the south and Lake Baringo in the north. The map depicts the minimum and maximum lake water surfaces between 1984 and 2020. Anticipating the results, the map also shows the contour lines of the elevation of the spill points of Lake Bogoria and Baringo and the potential flow path of the water course between the two lakes. To the south-east of Baringo, the courses of the perennial Perkerra and Molo rivers, the main water sources of Baringo, are visible. Both are extensively used for irrigation in the Loboi plain and are essential lifelines in the semi-arid area. The Molo flows into the Ng’arua Swamp and the Perkerra ends in the Oloimatashu swamp, which is currently mostly submerged and part of Lake Baringo. Just west of Lake Bogoria, the Loboi River is visible. It is to our knowledge perennial, having its permanent source in Maji Moto hot springs, around 10 km south of the northern end of Lake Bogoria. The catchment of the Loboi River, however, extends much farther to the south. The Loboi River flows into the Loboi Swamp and is also used for irrigation. The diversions made for irrigation purposes divert water towards the Kiborkoch Swamp (see panel (b) in Fig. 3 ). East of Lake Bogoria, the Waseges or Sandai River runs through a 70–80 m deep canyon in the village of Sandai. Although the flows are seasonal, water from the river is diverted for an extensive irrigation scheme. Fig. 3  also shows a spatial overview of the electrical conductivity (EC) of the surface water bodies. The tabulated values, including water temperature values, are available in the Appendix. In the southwest, where the water sources are the Perkerra and Molo, lower EC values mostly in the range of 130–200 μS/cm are observed. In contrast, the EC values in the southeast around Lake Bogoria lie within the range of 550–1500 μS/cm. The Loboi river, for example, showed an EC value of 1042 μS/cm. The highest EC value of 33,800 μS/cm was measured at Lake Bogoria (Number 17 in Fig. 3 ). EC measurements at the Loboi stream between the Loboi and Ng’arua swamps showed surprisingly high values of ∼1600 μS/cm (number 40, 48 and 49 in Fig. 3 ). The very small stream had a flow of only a few litres per second and was very turbid. The high EC values do not fit into the larger picture since the Loboi flowing towards the Loboi Swamp from the south showed lower EC values of around 1000 μS/cm and waters from the hot springs at the Lake Bogoria Spa Resort also feeding the swamp showed values of approximately 650 μS/cm. The reason for the high EC values remains at this time speculative and may be a result of accumulation of salts due to strong evaporation in the Loboi Swamp, contributing to (subsurface) flows from Lake Bogoria or resuspension of sediments due to cattle watering.  3.2 Rainfall conditions since the 2010 lake level rises Marigat, to the west of the Loboi plain, is the main town and trading center in the region. Marigat received 463 mm of mean annual rainfall in 1986–2009. Although this value increased to 978 mm for the period 2010–2018 (corresponding to +111 %), the number of days with rainfall has decreased by 19 % ( Table 2 ;  Fig. 4 (a)). Also consistent with local accounts (Petek-Sargeant, 2023 ) is the fact that the days with intense rainfall have increased by nearly 320 % in the last decade (Table 2 ; Fig. 4 (b)). The division of the time series is based on the finding from Herrnegger et al. (2021) , who show that 2009 was a breakpoint year, where the means and structure of the catchment rainfall time series changed. The tabulated values of annual rainfall are documented in Table A2  in the Appendix. The seasonality of rainfall measured in terms of the mean monthly rainfall shows an increase in rainfall in all months, except February (Fig. 4 (c)). The largest increases in the means, at least in relative terms, are found for the months July, August and September, with increases of 517 %, 208 % and 291 % when comparing mean monthly rainfall 1986–2009 and 2010–2018. People in the area report that the seasonality in rainfall - essential for planning agricultural decisions, e.g., when to plow or for defining sowing dates - has become erratic and difficult to predict. This is also supported by the analysis of the Marigat rainfall data. Fig. 4 (d) shows the monthly rainfall variability measured by the standard deviation for 1986–2009 and 2010–2018 and compared to the long-term values of 1986–2018. The standard deviation is thereby calculated for every single month. From the plot it is evident that the monthly rainfall variability has increased substantially. Like the mean monthly rainfall, the highest increases in variability are found for July, August and September, with increases of 455 %, 236 % and 246 %. On average and for all months, the variability has increased by 200 %, consistent with reports from the local population.  3.3 Spill point location and potential water course The spill point of Lake Bogoria is located ∼150–250 m north of Lake Bogoria and the new Loboi-Sandai road, which was constructed after the old road passing further south was flooded ( Fig. 5 ). The lake shore reached the dam of the new road during the observed maximum water level. Based on DAHITI, the lake level reached 999.5 m in November 2020. This maximum water extent shown in Fig. 5  was reconstructed based on the DAHITI water level corrected for geoid undulations. The DAHITI water extent data for that time is biased due to misclassification of shallow water and poor image quality, hence it was not used. The spill point based on the UAS-based Digital Surface Model (UAS DSM) is close to the TanDEM-x (12 m resolution) and EDTM30 (30 m) estimates. This is the case, although the high-resolution UAS-data has 57,600 (360,000) more information points - per raster or pixel - compared to the 12 m (30 m) satellite-borne data sets. Trees and vegetation clearly influence the local topographical situation. This is also evident in the high resolution 5 cm UAS-based Digital Surface Model (UAS DSM) and partially explains the proximity of the three estimates. When filtering and removing trees and vegetation from the Digital Surface Model and deriving a DEM (UAS DEM) applying RemoveOffTerrainObjects  from the WhiteBox Tools (Lindsay, 2023 ), the estimated spill point moves around 90 m to the east to the foot of Baryat Hill, which is around 100 m high relative to the surrounding terrain. The estimated location of the UAS DEM is the most realistic estimate and corresponds to our observations in the field.  Fig. 6  shows the elevation profile for the potential water course between Lake Bogoria and Baringo. The water course is also depicted in the map of the study area in Fig. 3 . The elevation profile also shows the minimum and maximum water level in Lake Bogoria and Baringo based on DAHITI for 1984–2020, as well as approximate locations of the different swamps in the area through which the water course would probably flow. The Kiborkoch swamp is located at the foot of Baryat Hill north of Lake Bogoria and stretches towards the north. The swamp is also mentioned in Wambui et al. (2021) , however with a name which could not be verified by the local people. This swamp generally exhibits a very minor gradient towards Lake Baringo and can be seen as a spill point swamp and the origin of a bifurcating stream. Figure A3  in the Appendix provides a visual impression of swamp in the proximity of the spill point. Due to the slight gradients, water will also flow towards the south and Lake Bogoria if water levels in the swamp are high enough. This was the case during our field visit in October 2022, when a minor flow moved southwards. The origin of the water in the Kiborkoch swamp was irrigation water diverted from the Loboi river. Similar electrical conductivity values of the two bodies of water of around 1000 μS/cm, but also flow paths visible in the drone images support this hypothesis (see also spatial distribution of EC values in Fig. 3 ). The potential water course would transvers the Kiborkoch Swamp, followed by the Loboi Swamp, which has a much higher gradient, also compared to the Ng’arua and the mostly submerged Oloimatashu Swamp. In the Loboi Swamp, the potential water course would join and follow the channels already present leading to Lake Baringo (Fig. 3 ). The length of the potential water course, using the maximum water extents of Lake Bogoria and Baringo in 2020 as reference, is around 17.5 km. When the two lakes showed minimum water levels, the length of the potential water course would have been nearly double that value, namely 33.2 km. The general picture of the elevation profile and gradients shown in Fig. 6  is similar for all evaluated elevation models. Very prominent, however, are larger deviations and spikes of the SRTM compared to the other DEMs, likely due to the coarser resolution of the SRTM of 90 m. This leads to a biased elevation around the spill point area since the 100 m high Baryat Hill next to the Kiborkoch swamp is somewhat reflected in the average grid cell values. Further downstream, between km 10 and km 20, the larger deviations of around 5 m in elevation can be explained by trees and vegetation, which surround the Molo River and which the potential water course would follow.  3.4 Lake water levels and volume changes until spill point is reached The previously shown elevation profile illustrates that the maximum water levels in Lake Bogoria in November 2020 were very close to the spill point elevation. Compared to the maximum water level of 999.5 m observed by satellite altimetry, only 70 cm additional water level or 0.033 km³ additional lake volume would have been necessary for the lake to reach the spill point.  Table 3  shows the spill point elevation for the different elevation models and the necessary water level and lake volume increases until the spill point is reached. As described in the previous section, the numbers found from the UAS DEM provide the most realistic estimate. For a visual impression of the situation, the reader is referred to Fig. 5 , which also illustrates the water extents for a lake level of 999.5 m and the spill point elevation.  Fig. 7 (a) shows the lake water levels for Bogoria from January 2009 to February 2023, including the annual averages and the spill point elevation of 1000.2 m. A plot on the lake volume variation data can be found in Figure A4  of the Appendix. The numerical values of annual lake levels and lake volume variation are documented in Table A3 . From 1984–2009 the DAHITI data show a very low variability in lake water levels, ranging from 993.1 m to 994 m, with an average of 993.5 m and a range of only 0.7 m. From January 2009 to November 2020, lake levels rose from 993.8 m to 999.5 m, an increase of 5.7 m. It is also observed that the margin to the spill point elevation (dashed line in Fig. 7 (a)) was only 0.7 m. Fig. 7 (a) also shows that the lake level has fallen since the high stand and lay at 998 m in February 2023. At the time of writing, the last reported value from DAHITI for Bogoria was from 27 June 2023 with a water level of 997.9 m. Compared to the value of 998 m, the elevation difference to the spill point is now 2.2 m. Fig. 7 (b) (numerical values in Table A4 ) shows the year-to-year change in average annual water level, highlighting the low interannual variability before 2009. After 2009–2010, although year to year values of decreases exist between 2014 and 2016 and 2021–2022, lake levels mostly increased. Annual water level increases of around +1 m were frequent, with a maximum of +1.7 m from 2019 and 2020. The observed year to year changes in water level are used to derive the empirical probabilities of Lake Bogoria reaching the spill point elevation, evaluated for the maximum observed water level in November 2020 (999.5 m) and water levels from February 2023 (998 m). Additionally, since the characteristics of lake level fluctuations differ before and after 2009, the empirical probability is also evaluated for the two climate conditions, namely the long-term climate 1984–2022 and the wetter one 2009–2022. The evaluation of the empirical probabilities relies solely on lake level fluctuations and does not include any other data. The empirical probabilities are assessed by computing the relative occurrence of the observed year to year water level changes before reaching the spill point from both initial values (2.2 m - 2023, 0.7 m - 2020). The probabilities of reaching the spill point within 2–5 years are also assessed by computing the relative occurrence within the respective time periods, but instead of using the single year to year water level changes, the cumulative water level changes for 2, 3, 4, and 5 years are calculated (see Table A5  and Table A6  in the Appendix). These results are shown in Fig. 7 (c) and summarized in  Table 4 . The risk or empirical probability of lake levels reaching the spill point elevation depends on three factors: (i) climate conditions, (ii) the initial lake level and (iii) years anticipated for the lake to overflow. For the wetter climate assumption and the maximum observed lake level, the risk for the overflow lay between 38 % and 77 %, depending on the number of years considered. When assuming the long-term and overall drier climate, the risk for the overflow was lower, even for the maximum water level case. Here, again depending on the number of years considered, the risk lay between 13 % and 29 %. The lake levels have fallen by 1.5 m and currently lie at around 998 m. The risk of overflow has fallen accordingly. Assuming wetter climate conditions (long-term climate), the risk now lies between 0 % and 31 % (0 % – 12 %), depending on the anticipated number of years.  3.5 Rainfall conditions for a sustained flow Specific rainfall and climate conditions in the Lake Bogoria watershed (1060 km²) lead to lake level fluctuations and to observed changes in lake level and lake volume. Based on the DAHITI lake volume variation data (Figure A4  and Table A3 in the Appendix ), year-to-year changes can be calculated. These year-to-year changes in lake volume variation are then used to calculate the Integrated Catchment Response (ICR, mm) depicted in Fig. 7 (d) (Table A4 ). Note that volume variation data is only available until the end of 2020 and was not recalculated for this study, as was the case for the water levels. The ICR is a magnitude that integrates all potential processes of the water balance of the lake and thus includes rainfall less evapotranspiration fluxes, year-to-year storage changes, but also potential sub-surface flows towards and from the lake. For example, in Fig. 7 (d), the high ICR of ∼50 mm in 2019–2020 led to a lake level rise of 1.7 m, as shown in Fig. 7 (b). In contrast, negative ICR-values lead to a decline in water level, e.g., between 2004–2005 or 2014–2015. This pattern is true for all years, except for 2015–2016, where the data show a decline in water level of around 0.5 m, but a slight increase in ICR (see Figure A5  for a systematic comparison of ICR and water level). Lake volume variation data is a function of data on water level and lake extent (Schwatke et al., 2020 ). The reason for the inconsistency between lake level and lake volume variation in these single years may lie in different data bases and inconsistencies therein. After 2016, lake levels are available from altimetry data, which is more trustworthy compared to the water levels before 2016, which are derived from hypsometry. Hypsometry defines a relationship between surface area and water level. It is used to extend water level data to periods where satellite altimetry was not available and is associated with higher uncertainties, also resulting from potential biases in estimates of lake area. For the current assessment we removed single water level and lake variation data points from the time series which showed an unrealistically strong increase or decrease in a single observation inconsistent with the overall trend. This, however, did not resolve the inconsistency between lake level and ICR for 2015–2016. The relationship between rainfall and the partitioning of actual evapotranspiration and rainfall for the Bogoria catchment is illustrated in  Fig. 8 . This relationship is calculated for 2-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year moving averages, with the aim of smoothing out effects of catchment storage from one year to the next as well as potential errors in single year observations. Independent of the number of years used for calculating the moving average, the results show that a very high percentage – on average 99.7 % – of catchment rainfall is lost to actual evapotranspiration. Thus, only around 0.3 % of rainfall feeds the lake on average. The data of 2-year averages (Fig. 8 (a)) shows that wetter years with higher rainfall show a slightly lower AET to R ratio of ∼97 %. On the other hand, dryer conditions with lower rainfall led to ratios above unity. In these years, catchment AET was higher compared to rainfall and the lake levels decreased. This pattern is also evident for the longer-term moving averages. To derive the rainfall conditions necessary for a sustained flow from Lake Bogoria towards Lake Baringo, we use the relationship or transfer function between the ICR and the CHIRPS-based catchment rainfall shown in  Fig. 9 . Positive ICR-values and corresponding rainfall refer to periods where lake levels increased. As with AET/R, smoothing of the data using longer-term moving averages leads to a loss of variability, but an increase in the coefficient of determination R². Given the case that lake levels are at spill point elevation, additional discharge into the lake would lead to an overtopping and flow towards Lake Baringo. The quantity of flow would depend on the quantity of water feeding Lake Bogoria. This is the sum of different sources, including flows from the seasonal Waseges or Sandai River, the thermal springs or rainfall on the lake, and are reflected in Fig. 9 . For this analysis, we assume different sustained flow scenarios, which refer to mean annual discharge values. The flow would probably experience temporal variability. This we ignore here and estimate a mean annual flow. The mean annual flow can be related to an annual volume, which would be needed to sustain a flow over one year. The mean flow values (in L/s or dm3 /s) are multiplied by the number of seconds in a year and then divided by the catchment area in [m²]. This results in a mean runoff depth of the catchment required in order to obtain a water volume such that the condition of sustained flow is satisfied. Here, we provide several scenarios ranging from 10 L/s to 1500 L/s or 1.5 m³/s ( Table 5 ).  Fig. 10  shows the mean annual rainfall conditions which – given the case that Lake Bogoria water levels are at spill point elevation – would be necessary to provide a sustained flow of different magnitudes as shown on the x-axis. Mean annual flows of 500–1000 L/s would have been sustained with the mean annual rainfall value for 2010–2020. In contrast, it is also evident that on average no sustained flow would have been possible under rainfall conditions before 2010. Finally,  Fig. 11  shows the simulated rainfall values based on the 5-year moving average model and their corresponding sustained flow scenarios in relation to the observed catchment rainfall values in the past 37 years. It is evident that after 2010, mean annual rainfall of ∼1230 mm/a was high enough to – on average – generate a flow of 500–1000 L/s. In the period 1984–2009, with a mean rainfall of around 950 mm/a, on average no flow would have been sustained.   4 Discussion 4.1 Spill point and risk of overflow A mere 70 cm lake level increase would have been necessary for Lake Bogoria to reach the spill point elevation of 1000.2 m, compared to the maximum observed lake levels of 999.5 m. The likelihood or empirical probability of Lake Bogoria's water levels reaching the spill point elevation is dependent on the assumptions made about (i) climate conditions, (ii) the initial lake level, and (iii) the number of years anticipated for the lake to overflow, all of which significantly influence the risk assessment. For scenarios assuming wetter climate conditions than we have observed in the last decade together with the maximum observed lake level, the risk of overflow was found to range between 38 % and 77 %, depending on the projected time frame. However, when considering long-term climate conditions, the risk of overflow decreased, even for the case of the maximum water level, varying between 13 % and 29 %. Recently, the lake levels have declined by 1.5 m, and the current level is approximately 998 m. Consequently, the risk of overflow has decreased accordingly. Assuming wetter climate conditions (or the long-term climate), the risk now lies between 0 % and 31 % (or 0–12 %), depending on the projected time frame. The findings suggests that the risk of Lake Bogoria reaching the spill point is generally higher when using the wetter period 2009–2022 as a reference for climate conditions. This period exhibited increased precipitation and resulted in significantly higher lake level fluctuations compared to historical data. Additionally, the risk is amplified when considering not only one year but multiple years (up to 5 years) of observed lake level fluctuations for the empirical risk calculation. The initial lake level assumption plays a crucial role in determining the risk. A lower initial lake level, such as the 998 m level recorded in February 2023 (2.2 m below the spill point), leads to a reduced risk since the water levels would need to increase more substantially to reach the overflow point. Conversely, a higher initial water level assumption, like the maximum observed water level of 999.5 m (where the spill point was only 70 cm away), results in a higher risk of overflow. In using the empirical probability data to evaluate the risk of overtopping, we assume that future climatic conditions are comparable to the past. In using the observed lake levels for the evaluation of risk, general changes in rainfall and the catchment water balance are implicitly taken into consideration. The relationship between lake level and lake volume change are also inherently captured since the lake level-volume-relationship is already considered in the year-to-year changes in the lake levels used as a data basis. In these changes, the potential non-linearity between lake level and volume change, which is relevant in terms of the quantity of inflows, on-lake rainfall as well as evaporation, is taken into account.  4.2 Trends in rainfall By examining data collected from the Marigat station, located approximately 30 km northwest of Lake Bogoria, we have found substantial shifts in the rainfall quantity and temporal distribution since 2010. Mean annual rainfall has more than doubled and the variability has also substantially increased, making planning based on the well-known rainfall seasons more difficult. These extraordinary changes, which have not been previously examined, particularly in relation to the ongoing elevation of lake levels, underscore the unique nature of this hydrometeorological phenomenon in the Rift Valley. The rainfall increase suggested by the Marigat data is exceptional. There are numerous cases in eastern Africa of individual years reaching extremely anomalous values. However, a step function increase in sustained rainfall of the magnitude seen at Marigat is very unusual. Nevertheless, several observations suggest that the trends at Marigat are realistic. It is relevant that the greatest variability in monthly totals is for the three months of the boreal summer, July through September, which is the driest season in most of eastern Africa. The increase is particularly strong in July. Ideally, one would make a comparison with nearby stations, but the available data are limited. However, at nearby Nakuru average July rainfall for the period 2010–2013 was 142 mm, one standard deviation above the long-term July mean of 96 mm. As in the Marigat record, the wettest July was 2013. Rainfall was 174 mm in that year, nearly two standard deviations above the mean of 96 mm. The excellent agreement between year-to-year changes in the level of Lake Bogoria and rainfall at Marigat helps to confirm the Marigat record (Nicholson and Yin, 2001 ). The trends in the levels of Lake Bogoria are also matched by those at lakes Baringo, Elementaita, Nakuru, Naivasha, and Solai (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). The changes seen in the area of these lakes are not representative of East Africa as a whole. There, annual rainfall has been stable in recent years, while October-November rainfall has increased and March-April-May rainfall has decreased (Nicholson et al., 2018 ). However, the tremendous increase in the level of Lake Bogoria of 2019/20 does correspond to a major wet episode throughout the region (Nicholson et al., 2022 ). The meteorological factors affecting Lake Bogoria are complex. An important one is that it lies in a region subject to the transition to boreal summer rainfall to the west. In fact, its variations are more closely linked to that region than to those elsewhere in eastern Africa (Nicholson, 2019 ). A case in point is the similar trends in western Uganda, as seen at the station Arua. There the mean for 2010–2016 was 214 mm, considerably greater than the long-term mean of 149 mm. A small eastward shift in the boreal summer rainfall regime can account for the large July-to-September increases seen at Lake Bogoria. A second factor is that Lake Bogoria and the other lakes mentioned lie upon a ridge of the Rift Valley. Orographic factors can markedly enhance variations in rainfall. The findings are in line with the results presented in Herrnegger et al. (2021) , although (i) magnitudes differ and (ii) different time periods and (iii) footprints (i.e. point data here vs. catchment averages in previous work) are compared in this study. Compared to the catchment averages, the point data show a much more pronounced change signal, e.g. in rainfall increases. For example, catchment averages for the Baringo catchment, covering an area of around 6 800 km², increased by around 30 % compared to 111 % for the point measurement at Marigat. This is not surprising and can be explained by the phenomenon that averages for a larger area will always be smoother since extremes at single locations tend to average each other out. The local-scale changes are notably more pronounced when compared to the average changes observed in the entire catchment area. This increase in rainfall has consequently led to rises in lake levels as well as expansion of vegetation.  4.3 Vegetation increases As illustrated in Fig. 1  of the current study, there has been a noticeable expansion in vegetation cover as measured by the NDVI, with many regions experiencing growth rates exceeding 10 % between 2001–2009 and 2010–2020. This transformation in vegetation serves as an additional indicator of heightened rainfall and challenges the assertions made by other experts that attribute the lake level increases to alternative causes. It has been speculated that the tectonic activities occurring in the geologically active Rift Valley have diminished underground seepage, which serves as the sole outflow for the endorheic lakes, thus contributing to the elevation of lake levels. Recent geological studies in the region, however, do not support this hypothesis (Conti et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2023; Ng’aari, 2022 ). Moreover, anthropogenic land degradation has been proposed as a factor, resulting in increased erosion and sedimentation rates, potentially obstructing and impeding the underground water pathways while augmenting surface runoff. Our findings firmly support the notion that changes in rainfall alone are sufficient to account for the observed rises in lake levels.  4.4 Use of catchment averages for the assessment The assessment of the hydrometeorological conditions contributing to the elevation of lake levels, as well as the examination of sustained overflow, is conducted based on the average rainfall observed within the catchment area. The watershed or catchment of Lake Bogoria encompasses a large region of approximately 1060 km², spanning a maximum width of 30 km from west to east and extending around 60 km to the south from the spill point. It is important to consider that spatial and temporal variations in rainfall exist within this area, as demonstrated through our analysis of the Marigat station data. The headwater regions of the Waseges River receive an annual rainfall of approximately 1200–1500 mm, while the southern vicinity of Lake Bogoria and the western parts of the catchment experience notably drier conditions (refer to Fig. 7  in Herrnegger et al. 2021 ). Station data from the northern area of Lake Bogoria indicate an average annual rainfall of around 700 mm between 1976 and 2001 (Ashley et al., 2004 ). To estimate the water balance of Lake Bogoria, we rely on catchment average rainfall and lake volume variations. This approach assumes that (i) catchment boundaries are correct and (ii) the properties of lake levels can be adequately modeled using the average rainfall across the catchment area, disregarding the spatial and temporal variability of rainfall. However, our results demonstrate that employing longer-term aggregated rainfall data establishes a strong relationship with changes in lake levels and volume. As a result, we have confidence in the validity of this approach for assessing the water balance and fluctuations in water levels of the lake.  4.5 AET/R ratio Our findings reveal that, in relation to the entire catchment of Lake Bogoria, only a small fraction of rainfall contributes to the lake inflows. The ratio of actual evapotranspiration to rainfall (AET/R) indicates that, during wetter years, approximately 3 % of rainfall reaches the lake, while on average only 0.3 % of rainfall directly replenishes the lake. Lake Bogoria receives an exceptionally small percentage of rainfall from its catchment area. This conclusion is drawn from changes in the lake's volume and the Integrated Catchment Response (ICR, Fig. 7 (d)), which averaged only 16.9 mm/year between 2010 and 2020. During this time, the catchment received an average rainfall of 1215 mm/year. After accounting for actual evapotranspiration (AET) of 1198.5 mm (Eq. 4 ), this indicates a remarkably low annual catchment runoff coefficient of only 1.4 %. Such a low coefficient is highly unusual and not reflected in existing research (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Potential evapotranspiration in the region is approximately 2600 mm/year, more than double the annual rainfall, implying the environment has ample capacity for evaporation. Unfortunately, discharge data, which could confirm these findings, is unavailable. It is crucial to emphasize that these percentages are based on catchment averages. Local variability is not considered in our analysis, hence the results should be interpreted as a representation of the catchment water balance. The partitioning of AET/R in the headwaters of the Waseges River will exhibit different dynamics. Furthermore, the calculated AET/R ratio includes anthropogenic influences and water abstractions affecting the water balance since, e.g., the Waseges River is also used for irrigation and food production in the headwaters.  4.6 Uncertainties The assessment is subject to various uncertainties stemming from both the input data utilized and the adoption of simplified methods and assumptions, as previously mentioned. The assessment of the spill point location and elevation is based on different digital elevation models. They differ regarding spatial resolution as well as methods used to derive the elevation values. Moreover, different vertical datums are present in the elevation data sets so that corrections had to be applied. These transformations always include uncertainties. To assess the spill point elevation and to reduce the uncertainties, a geometric terrestrial survey is required. Our analysis of the water balance and hydrological changes in Lake Bogoria heavily relies on satellite-based data, primarily the CHIRPS rainfall data. While this data source offers the advantage of providing insights into the spatial distribution and variability of rainfall, it is important to acknowledge that uncertainties exist regarding the accuracy of the quantities, despite efforts to enhance it with station data. Despite such qualifications, CHIRPS data generally shows good performance in the study region (Omonge et al., 2022 ). Additionally, the DAHITI data also introduces uncertainties into our analysis. Specifically, the water extent data exhibits partial biases and necessitates critical review. Consequently, the water level data derived from hypsometry, reliant on the water extent information, also gives rise to uncertainties that need to be acknowledged. For assessing the risk of Lake Bogoria reaching the spill point, we use the concept of empirical probability. It relies solely on the measured lake level data, which we assume describes the natural variability in a sufficient manner. The notion of empirical probability does not imply any assumptions regarding specific statistical models or probability distribution. The application is transparent; no additional parameters need to be estimated. A disadvantage, however, may lie in the comparatively short time series used. Although 40 years of lake level data ranging from 1984 to 2023 are used, it is uncertain to what extent this time series covers the natural variability. The estimation of the AET/R ratio, as well as the rainfall conditions necessary for a sustained flow, uses the ICR as input. In applying the ICR we assume that underground seepage and outflows from Lake Bogoria are either (i) very small and thus negligible or (ii) stationary in time. Lying in an endorheic basin, Lake Bogoria does not have surface runoff. For the case that substantial underground losses to Lake Baringo do exist, the estimation of AET would be too high and the ratio between AET/R would be lower values relative to our results. For the case that the outflows show substantial changes over time, the use of lake volume variation data and the ICR would probably not be appropriate since boundary conditions would change from year to year, making it difficult to distinguish between changes in the hydrological regime of the catchment and underground outflow. However, based on the information available to us, there is no evidence to suggest substantial underground losses in Lake Bogoria. The lake's high alkalinity supports this hypothesis as it indicates that no salts are being flushed out through underground pathways. Unlike Lake Baringo, where hot springs in Kapedo might serve as an outflow location for seepage waters, no similar springs in Lake Bogoria have been reported.  4.7 Potential impacts If Lake Bogoria were to overflow, several effects would ensue, both in the short and long term. In the short term, there would be a potential cross-contamination of the alkaline waters from Bogoria, impacting the now freshwater Kiborkoch, Loboi, and the Ng'arua Swamps, as well as the watercourse of the potential stream. These also include the lower stretch of the current Molo River and ultimately Lake Baringo itself. The specific nature of these cross-mixing and dilution effects is currently uncertain and requires further investigation. The Loboi plain experiences exceptionally high potential evapotranspiration rates, resulting in substantial water losses that may strongly reduce the water reaching Lake Baringo. Hence, additional research is necessary to assess and comprehend potential dilution effects. On a longer timescale, assuming a sustained and significant overflow of Lake Bogoria coupled with above-average runoff reaching Lake Baringo, the lake levels of Lake Baringo would continue to rise. However, Lake Baringo would not rise until it reaches an equilibrium with the spill point elevation of Lake Bogoria. Prior to that, the spill point of Lake Baringo (Lobat Gap), which sits approximately 9.7 m lower than the spill point of Lake Bogoria at 990.5 m, would be exceeded, leading to the outflow of water towards the Suguta Basin in the north, a situation reminiscent of conditions approximately eight to ten thousand years ago (see contours of spill point elevations in Fig. 3  and potential water extents in Figure A6 ). Nevertheless, it is crucial to acknowledge that such changes would be dramatic and significantly impact the lives and livelihoods of tens of thousands of people in the area.  4.8 Mitigation measures The rise in lake levels is primarily influenced by changes in rainfall, and our ability to control these causes is limited. Water retention measures can be taken in the lake watersheds, with the aim of retaining water in the catchments (Stecher et al., 2023 ). Afforestation, implementation of soil water conservation measures, enforcing infiltration of rainfall and surface runoff by technical and natural means are beneficial (Mwanake et al., 2023; Nyirahabimana et al., 2021; Turinawe, 2019 ). They are no-regret measures and tend to increase infiltration to groundwater as well as reduce flood peaks. At Lake Bogoria, options also exist with respect to implementing technical measures. The topographic conditions in the area of the Lake Bogoria spill point would provide a good setting for constructing a dam to artificially increase the spill point elevation. Careful investigations would, however, be essential before such measures are taken in order to understand the potential effects of such an undertaking, including an assessment of the effects on the local community as well as the environmental effects on flora and fauna and the ecosystem in general. Given the low level of availability and accessibility of measured hydroclimatic data on the ground, it is challenging to evaluate and provide clearer understanding of the on-going phenomenon described herein. Expanding the rainfall and discharge measurement network to an extent already existent in the past, along with careful data quality control, would provide a stronger foundation for planning and understanding lake level rises at Lake Bogoria, including the risk of overtopping. Beyond the immediately local advantages to be gained by taking such steps, such information and data would be valuable for water resources planning, allocation and management more generally (Omonge et al., 2020 ). Preparedness is a category in flood risk management which can significantly reduce human and economic losses. Anticipatory flood risk maps showing riparian areas together with relevant or critical infrastructure such as roads, hospitals or schools, which may be flooded if lake levels continue to rise, would make dealing with such unexpected consequences of natural phenomenon more plannable and approachable. Taking historic high stands of water levels into account in such efforts would further help local and external actors put what may be a worst-case scenario into perspective.   5 Summary and Conclusions Starting around 2010, several of Kenya’s Rift Valley lakes experienced significant rises in water levels. Nearly eighty thousand households with 400,000 people are affected. There is fear of an ecological catastrophe should the current water levels of the alkaline Lake Bogoria continue to rise. The result would be an overflow into and mixing with the freshwater Lake Baringo. This research therefore examines the risk of Lake Bogoria reaching its spill point, leading to an overflow towards Lake Baringo, a situation that occurred around 8 000–10 000 years ago. The data reveal significant meteorological and hydrological changes in the region over the past decade. For Marigat, located at the edge of the Loboi plain, average annual rainfall has more than doubled (+111 %), accompanied by a substantial increase in rainfall variability, with an average over all months of +200 %. Although the number of days with rainfall has decreased in the last decade (-19 %), the number of days experiencing intense rainfall has increased by +318 %. Overall, these changes have made planning based on the well-known rainfall seasons more difficult. Results show that a mere 70 cm increase in lake level would have been necessary for Lake Bogoria to reach the spill point of 1000.2 m from its maximum observed level in November 2020. The risk of overflow is influenced by climate conditions, and assuming wetter climate conditions observed in the last decade, the risk ranges from 38 % to 77 %, depending on the number of years of lake level fluctuations anticipated in the assessment. However, with long-term climate conditions of 1984–2022 taken into account, the risk decreases to 16–29 %. Recently, the lake level has declined by 1.5 m to approximately 998 m, resulting in a decreased risk of overflow. On the assumption that the wetter climate conditions from the last decade persist (or long-term climate), the risk is between 0 % and 23 % (or 0–9 %). Given that the water levels of Lake Bogoria are at spill point elevation, we provide several scenarios for a sustained flow towards Baringo. Here, results indicate that the mean annual catchment rainfall of around 1230 mm/a observed after 2010 was high enough to provide an average annual flow of 500–1000 L/s, while during the period 1984–2009, with a mean rainfall of around 950 mm/a, no sustained flow would have been possible on average. The results regarding the analysis of the catchment water balance and the partitioning of actual evapotranspiration and rainfall indicate that on average around 99.7 % of catchment rainfall is lost to AET, leaving only about 0.3 % to feed the lake. Wetter years with higher rainfall show a slightly lower AET to rainfall ratio (around 97 %), while drier years with lower rainfall have ratios above unity, resulting in decreased lake levels. If Lake Bogoria were to overflow today, it would have both short-term and long-term effects. In the short term, there could be potential cross-contamination of the alkaline waters from Lake Bogoria, impacting the watercourse of the potential stream and freshwater ecosystems such as Kiborkoch, Loboi, the Ng'arua Swamps and, finally, Lake Baringo. The Loboi plain experiences high evapotranspiration rates, leading to significant water losses that could, however, reduce the amount of water reaching Lake Baringo. The specific effects of this mixing and dilution are not yet understood and require further investigation. On a longer timescale, assuming a sustained and significant overflow of Lake Bogoria with above-average runoff reaching Lake Baringo, the lake levels of Lake Baringo would continue to rise. However, before reaching equilibrium with the spill point elevation of Lake Bogoria, Lake Baringo's water levels would rise past its spill point elevation at the Lobat Gap, which is about 9.7 m lower than that of Lake Bogoria (at 990.5 m). This would lead to the outflow of water towards the Suguta Basin in the north, a situation reminiscent of conditions thousands of years ago. Such changes would be drastic and have a significant impact on the lives and livelihoods of thousands of people in the area. The rise in lake levels is mainly driven by changes in rainfall, and while we have limited control over these causes, we can focus on mitigating the symptoms and adaptation. At Lake Bogoria, technical measures like constructing a dam to artificially increase the spill point elevation are possible, but careful investigations are necessary to understand the potential effects on the community and environment.  Author Statement MH, GS and PK designed the study and established the methodological framework. MH, GS, NC, LO and DO participated in the field work for the study. MH, PK and GS performed all analyses. MH prepared the maps and figures. MH drafted and compiled the manuscript with contributions, checks and revisions by all other co-authors.
1 Introduction Understanding past and current rainfall patterns provides valuable insights into historical climate variations and helps supporting predictions of future climate scenarios (Pappenberger et al., 2009; Fantini al., 2016; Bandhauer et al., 2022 ). This knowledge is crucial for assessing the potential impacts of climate change on water availability, agriculture, and ecosystems, as well as for developing effective strategies for sustainable and climate-resilient growths. Moreover, reliable rainfall data support informed decision-making in sectors such as water infrastructure planning and design and preparedness for water-related extreme events, such as floods, droughts, and landslides. Large-scale gridded datasets, such as those derived from satellite observations or the assimilation of multi-parameter and multi-platform observations and forecasts in a numerical weather prediction system (denoted as reanalysis), or created by interpolating weather station observations onto a regularly spaced grid, provide long-term continuous estimates of climate variables on a grid covering either the globe or a region (Hu and Franzke, 2020 ). These gridded data products have found widespread application in atmospheric and climate sciences, as well as hydrological studies. For instance, they have been used as benchmark datasets to investigate climate variability and change, evaluate climate model simulations, and investigate extreme weather and climate events (e.g., King et al., 2013 ; Alfieri et al., 2022 ). Albeit designed for large-scale applications (from continental to global scale), these datasets have also been frequently used in regional studies (e.g., Santos et al., 2023 ; Varlas et al., 2022 ). A relevant temporal scale for such applications is the monthly scale, as demonstrated by several water balance and drought studies (e.g., Di Giovanni et al., 2023 ; Rossi et al., 2023 ; Salvati et al., 2008 ). Among the gridded datasets available at the Pan-European level, the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Data Store (CDS) includes two of the most widely used, namely the E-OBS daily gridded observational dataset (Cornes et al., 2018 ), and the ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020 ) reanalysis dataset. Another commonly used dataset derived from ERA5 is the ERA5-Land (Munoz-Sabater et al., 2021) product. Due to the strong connection between ERA5 and ERA5-Land in the meteorological variables (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ), only the former is considered in this study, as it is the original data source (without downscaling) with a spatial resolution consistent with E-OBS. Other gridded precipitation datasets covering the region, such as CRU (Harris et al., 2020 ) and GPCC (Schneider et al., 2017 ) are characterized by lower spatial resolution (0.5 degrees) in their near-real time product, hence were not considered in this study. Despite the increasing availability and applicability of these products in hydroclimatic studies, they are still subject to considerable uncertainties at the local scale. For instance, E-OBS accuracy is proven to strongly depend on data density (Bandhauer et al., 2022 ), hence, its reliability may suffer from sparse spatial coverage in some regions, particularly over mountainous or remote areas. Time series of the stations used as inputs for interpolation in E-OBS are usually not corrected for inhomogeneities (except for E-OBSv19.0eHOM), and station density is not constant either through time or space. Accuracy of ERA5 precipitation has been proven to be generally better in the extratropical regions compared to the tropic, but estimates may still exhibit biases locally due to model uncertainties or deficiencies in representing certain physical processes (Lavers et al., 2022 ). Spatio-temporal inhomogeneity in underlying data is also a drawback for ERA5 and ERA5-Land products during the assimilation process. It follows that analyses based on the E-OBS and ERA5 datasets should be treated with caution when conclusions at the local scale are drawn, and a careful evaluation, although challenging, is essential for studying climate dynamics and informing decision-making processes, especially when the data are used at regional or higher spatial scale. One crucial aspect of evaluating these datasets is their skill to accurately represent the target region's climate variability and trends. In fact, one of the main limitations of large-scale gridded datasets is the relatively coarse spatial resolution (never less than 10 km) and the corresponding spatial smoothing effect, which hinders applications at relevant hydrological scales. In this regard, the Mediterranean region, due to its complex topography and sea-land interactions, is particularly challenging, but at the same time very interesting given the relevance of this region as a hot-spot of climate change (Cos et al., 2022 ). Within the Mediterranean region, southern Italy is a highly populated region where most of the typical Mediterranean conditions can be found, making this area an interesting test bed for gridded precipitation products. Evaluation of rainfall gridded products usually involves comparing the datasets with high-resolution observed records from meteorological stations across the region of interest, considering the dataset's spatial and temporal resolution, biases, and uncertainties. Comparisons by using statistical metrics (e.g., bias, root mean square error, correlation coefficient, Kling-Gupta efficiency, among others) have been carried out in various regions worldwide, such as Ethiopia (Reda et al., 2021 ), Iran (Saemian et al., 2021 ), Southwest United States (Ehsani et al., 2022 ) and high-latitude Asia (Lan et al., 2023 ). With reference to the Mediterranean region, a poor capability of the E-OBS gridded dataset to satisfactorily reproduce precipitation data has been found both at large (Kostopoulou et al., 2012 ), and small spatial scale (Turco et al., 2013; Dumitrescu and Birsan, 2015; Curci et al., 2021 ). A recent study by My et al. (2022)  revealed that the E-OBS and CRU gridded datasets allow for only general indications of the spatial and temporal behavior of climatic variables over a southern Italy region (Apulia) in the period 1956–2019, especially in regard to precipitation data. On the other hand, the E-OBS dataset at 0.10° resolution was utilized as ground truth in a study aimed at improving the prediction of extreme rainfall events using ERA5 reanalysis in another southern Italy region (Calabria), given the noticeable input received from the local rain gauges network (Mastrantonas et al., 2022 ). In the present study, we perform a comprehensive trend analysis of seasonal and annual precipitation from 1979 onwards in Southern Italy. The study period is selected as the most recent climatological baseline (WMO, 2017 ), often used as a reference to characterize current climate conditions. The study area is of particular interest as it exhibits a complex climate influenced by various factors such as Mediterranean Sea dynamics, topography (ranging from coastal areas to mountainous regions), and proximity to North African weather systems. Specifically, the study area encompasses five administrative regions (Campania, Basilicata, Apulia, Calabria and Sicily), each covered by a dedicated monitoring network, requiring the merging and homogenizing of the observed data. This dataset can be used as a valid benchmark due to the data completeness, consistency and high spatial density. The study focuses on the quantities characterizing the climatology, including average values and inter-annual fluctuations (via the coefficient of variation), which are analyzed through a combination of some consolidated techniques, such as the nonparametric Mann–Kendall test (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1975 ) to identify the presence of significant trends in the long-term mean of the time series, and the Theil–Sen approach (Sen, 1968 ) to quantify the trend magnitude, the modified Mann-Kendall (Yue and Wang, 2004 ) to detect trends in the presence of serial correlation, and the Pettitt test (Pettitt, 1979 ) to detect jumps or discontinuities in the series. After a description of the case study area and the data in Section 2 , we introduce the methodology in Section 3 . The results are presented and discussed in Sections 4 and 5 . Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 6 .  2 Study area and rainfall datasets 2.1 Description of the study area The precipitation pattern in Italy is complex due to the intricate topography, geographical positioning, and elongated shape of the peninsula, covering an approximate span of 10 degrees of latitude (between 36°N and 46°N). Additionally, the peninsula exhibits a pronounced west-to-east inclination as it extends into the Mediterranean Sea. The study domain ( Fig. 1 ) covers a significant portion (28 %) of the Italian territory, including the regions of Apulia (with a surface of 19,500 km2 ), Basilicata (10,000 km2 ), Calabria (15,000 km2 ), Campania (13,500 km2 ), and Sicily (26,000 km2 ), with a population of about 17.3 million inhabitants (about 30 % of the whole Italian population). Located within the Mediterranean basin, the continental area is encircled by the Adriatic Sea to the east, the Ionian Sea to the southeast and the south, and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west. This geographic location and the proximity to the sea result in distinctive precipitation gradients, leading to high spatial variability with notable local effects. As other areas in the Western Mediterranean, the Mediterranean Sea is the main moisture source for the region, with an average input to precipitation of almost 35 %. The North Atlantic is the second most important source, with an average percentage of 25 % (Insua-Costa et al., 2022 ). Spatial differences are further enhanced by a complex orography due to the north-to-south Apennine chain in the peninsula, acting as a physical barrier for precipitation events. Sicily, instead, is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea. It is a predominantly hilly region (62 % of its territory), while 24 % is mountainous. In particular, while in eastern Sicily the Siculo Apennines can be recognized as the ideal extension of the continental Apennines, central and western areas are characterized by isolated massifs. The climatic conditions in this area demonstrate notable variability, predominantly influenced by the intricate orography. The climate can be broadly classified as Mediterranean, characterized by mild, rainy winters and hot, dry summers. However, this description primarily pertains to the coastal areas. In contrast, both precipitation patterns and temperature regimes can undergo substantial alterations moving towards inland areas and mountainous regions. Furthermore, the south-facing coastlines, especially in Sicily, can experience torrid summers due to hot winds blowing from the Northern African coast.  2.2 Rainfall databases The analyses are performed on monthly precipitation data acquired from ground-based monitoring networks and gridded datasets covering the period 1979–2019. The time frame is selected as the one commonly used to characterize the most recent climatological period (see WMO, 2017 ), and it represents a good compromise between maximizing data availability and consistency among datasets. While rainfall records were available before 1979 (or after 2019) over some of the selected stations, the adopted study period allows maximizing the spatial coverage without compromising data consistency. Although the data were recorded at least on a daily scale, nonetheless, many daily records are missing during the period when measurements were recorded manually (i.e., before 2000–2002). For example, in some cases, daily data from consecutive days were expressed as total values. On the other hand, recorded monthly data are more continuous, require only limited reconstruction of missing data, and are suitable for a range of applications related to water balance and drought studies. Further details on the characteristics of each dataset are reported in the following sections. 2.2.1 Observed data The dataset consists of monthly rainfall time series collected in a total of 264 stations distributed across the five regions of the study area ( Table 1 ). The rain gauge networks in the studied regions were managed by the Servizio Idrografico e Mareografico Nazionale  (SIMN) from 1918 to 1999 and, subsequently, the management was delegated to regional authorities. In many regions, the regional Civil Protection departments are responsible for rainfall data collection, but this is not always the case. As an example, in Sicily, the monitoring activities are supervised by the River Basin Authority of the Sicilian Hydrographic District (formerly “Osservatorio delle Acque ”), and in Calabria by the Regional Environmental Protection Agency. During the transfer of services between different authorities, most of the SIMN rain gauges were removed and relocated and/or replaced with new-generation instruments, resulting in discontinuous rainfall time series over time (Avino et al., 2024 ). Henceforth, the stations boasting the highest quantity of accessible data were chosen. Minor missing observations were reconstructed using the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation method (ASCE, 1996 ). IDW is a deterministic spatial interpolation approach that estimates missing data by calculating a weighted average of nearby measurements, where the weights decrease as the distance from the observation points increases. It is widely used in environmental data applications for its simplicity, computational efficiency, and reproducibility, making it ideal for spatial estimation (Bartier and Keller, 1996; Li and Heap, 2008 ). The effectiveness of IDW in reconstructing precipitation fields is well-documented in the literature (e.g., Caloiero et al., 2021 ). Studies such as Crespi et al. (2021)  and Avino et al. (2021)  demonstrated its utility in Italian conditions by interpolating precipitation data in the Trentino-South Tyrol and Campania region of Italy. Table 1  provides a detailed description of gauge observations and the corresponding missing/reconstructed data (see “Missing and Reconstructed observations'' column). The percentage of reconstructed monthly data was relatively low in Apulia, Calabria and Sicily, varying from 2 % to 6 %. In Basilicata and Campania, the percentage of reconstructed data was higher due to frequent changes in the gauging network, including relocations, equipment updates, and shifts in managing agencies. The full dataset of ground observations is available in the supplementary materials .  2.2.2 ERA5 and E-OBS datasets Over Europe, several gridded datasets are available based on rain gauge networks alone or merged with information provided by models. Amongst them, ERA5 and E-OBS are known as the two most recent and widely used pan-European gridded datasets (Bandhauer et al., 2022 ). Due to their widespread usage in climatic and hydrological studies, the analysis is focused on these two datasets. ERA5, the fifth-generation reanalysis of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF) over the past eight decades, utilizes a modern numerical weather prediction model (the Integrated Forecasting System Cycle 41r2, IFS, version from 2016) by means of a 4D-Var data assimilation system to integrate observations from different platforms (in-situ, radiosondes, satellite) (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). This dataset is made available from 1940 onwards. In the present study, ERA5 data was achieved on a regular longitude-latitude grid with a spacing of 0.25° and at a monthly resolution for the period of January 1979 to December 2019. Even if the ERA5 dataset has been successively extended back to 1940, a limited number of satellite data for assimilation were available before 1979. E-OBS, produced by KNMI (the Dutch weather service), is a gridded surface dataset of climate variables based on extensive archive observations from weather stations. This dataset is freely available from the C3S CDS (Buontempo et al., 2020 ), which makes it particularly appealing for climate and environmental-related studies over Europe (in the Scopus database, E-OBS dataset is retrieved in the article title, abstract or keywords of indexed papers almost 300 times in the last two decades - accessed on 10th July 2024). Monthly precipitation data are obtained on a 0.25° grid using cubic spline interpolation. Then, deterministic daily analyses are expected to derive via a generalized additive model (GAM) with square-root transformed observations and the introduction of the previously calculated monthly field as a covariate (Cornes et al., 2018 ). The dataset of stations used for the interpolation is regularly updated to ensure the best possible estimate for any given date. However, these continuous updates can also be the source of temporal inconsistencies and heterogeneity in the spatio-temporal coverage. Similarly to ERA5, gridded daily precipitation data from the E-OBS v28.0e platform were extracted for the period December 1979 - December 2019 and cumulated to monthly scale. The maps in  Fig. 2  show the spatial distribution of the average total annual precipitation for the period 1979–2019 according to the two gridded datasets (panels a-b) and the rain gauges (panel c). These maps highlight the large range of variability in rainfall within the study region, with lower values in all datasets in Sicily and Apulia and higher values (up to more than 1000 mm) along the Apennines. Fig. 2  (panel c) clearly shows that the wettest areas are those located along the Tyrrhenian side of the peninsula. This behavior is influenced by the interaction between the westwards moist currents and local orography dominated by the Apennines, and it is captured by ERA5 and partially by E-OBS. A cluster analysis performed using the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) highlights that southern Italy can be divided into four main regions concerning average total annual precipitation: a Tyrrhenian one, an Adriatic-Ionian one, an Apennine one and a Sicilian one (Fig. S1, supplementary material ). Significant correlations of the precipitation patterns in each of these zones to different exogenous variables can be detected (Table S1, supplementary material ). The same analysis performed on the gridded datasets led to similar results, especially for ERA5.    3 Methodology With the aim of detecting potential trends and change points in the rainfall climatic characteristics (average and inter-annual fluctuations) of the last 40 years, non-parametric trend tests, such as conventional and modified Mann-Kendell tests, and Pettit’s test were applied to analyze precipitation time series. Such analyses were performed on annual and seasonal total values derived from the monthly records. Four conventional seasons were considered: December-February (DJF), March-May (MAM), June-August (JJA), and September-November (SON). In addition, changes in the rainfall inter-annual variability were investigated using the coefficient of variation (CV, the ratio between standard deviation and mean) computed over a 10-year moving window. Nicholls and Wong (1990)  first introduced the concept of using CV as a metric to quantify the inter-annual variability of rainfall, and the approach has also been applied in Longobardi and Boulariah (2022)  over the Campania region. 3.1 Non-parametric trend test 3.1.1 Mann-Kendall test The Mann-Kendall test was originally proposed by Mann (1945)  as a non-parametric method for trend detection, while Kendall (1975)  provided the distribution of the test statistic for assessing non-linear trends and identifying turning points. In this test, each data point is compared to all subsequent data points, utilizing the ordered data samples. To address this issue, the modified Mann-Kendall test is employed to detect trends in hydrological and climatic data showing signs of serial correlation. This method incorporates a variance correction approach proposed by Yue and Wang (2004)  to mitigate the effects of serial correlation, enhancing the reliability of trend detection in such datasets. Using Eqs. (3), (6) and (7) , the modified test statistic can be obtained. This test is here used on the CV annual and seasonal records to account for the presence of autocorrelation in the datasets derived from the moving window approach.  3.1.3 Sen’s slope Using the method proposed by Sen (1968) , the magnitude of the slope of the trend is estimated as follows:(8) M  s   = Median ( x  j    −  x  i   )  ( j  − i )       ∀  i < j      If there are n   values in the time series, as many as N = n ( n − 1 ) / 2    slope estimates can be obtained. The median of these N   values, denoted as M  s     is used as the estimate of the trend slope. This approach leverages the median to provide a robust estimation of the trend slope, particularly effective in handling outliers or skewed data distributions.   3.2 Change point Pettitt's test The approach proposed by Pettitt (1979)  is frequently employed for the detection of a single change point in hydrological or climate series characterized by continuous data. This approach tests the null hypothesis that the variable follows one or more distributions with the same location parameter (indicating no change), against the alternative hypothesis that a change point exists. The results in Fig. 3 a highlight mostly positive trends in all the sites, with only a few locations with negative trends scattered across the domain (see also histogram in Fig. 3 a). Statistically significant (p < 0.05) trend values (demarcated by thick borders in both panels of Fig. 3 ) are observed in all regions, with clusters in northern Apulia and Campania. Changing points are mostly located between 2000 and 2005 (about 55 % of the stations, see insert in Fig. 3 b), with the spatial distribution of statistically significant results strongly resembling the one observed for the linear trend. A large cluster of changing points in the early 90 s can be observed in southern Apulia, mostly, however, corresponding to non-significant values. Data in  Table 2  summarize the results of the two tests for the different seasons on the rain gauge observations, highlighting how an overall smaller percentage of sites has statistically significant values. Most of the positive and significant trends are observed in SON, which is the rainiest season in the regions, and the same can be observed also for Pettitt’s test. Statistically significant negative trends are practically absent in all the regions and seasons for the analyzed rain gauge stations. Trends in CV ( Fig. 4 ) show an almost equal split between positive and negative values, with the former mostly clustered on the western side of the study area, in an area encompassing most of Campania region, western Basilicata and Calabria and northern Sicily. On the other hand, negative values gather in the eastern side, including the whole of Apulia, eastern Basilicata and Calabria and south-eastern Sicily. Furthermore, a cluster of stations with opposite values compared to the rest of the region can be observed in the northern coastal area of Campania, with statistically significant negative values lower than 0.5 % y−1 . As for the other tests, statistically significant values are not predominant, even though their frequency is not negligible (up to 45 % in Sicily).  4.2 Gridded datasets The Sen’s slope values obtained from the gridded datasets on total annual precipitation are reported in  Fig. 5  for ERA5 (Fig. 5 a) and E-OBS (Fig. 5 b), respectively. In both cases, trends are almost exclusively positive, with statistically significant values according to the Mann-Kendall test (p < 0.05) over most of the domain (hatched areas in Fig. 5 ). The only notable area with non-significant trends is Calabria region for E-OBS (Fig. 5 b), where a mix of slightly positive (< 2 mm y−1 ) and negative (> −2 mm y−1 ) values are observed. Overall, trends seem to be more marked in E-OBS compared to ERA5, with slopes greater than 6 mm y−1  in western Sicily, northern Apulia, Basilicata, and southern Campania. To integrate the results on the linear trend, the presence of potential change points is analyzed as summarized by the maps in  Fig. 6  for both ERA5 (Fig. 6 a) and E-OBS (Fig. 6 b), with statistically significant values (p < 0.05) according to the Pettitt’s test hatched. Also in this case, the two gridded datasets return similar results, with most of the statistically significant changing points located between 2000 and 2005 (96 % and 70 % for ERA5 and E-OBS, respectively; see inserts in Fig. 6 ). Results for both tests applied to seasonal data are reported in  Table 3  for ERA5 and E-OBS, summarizing the outcomes for each study region. Most of the data reported in Table 3  display strong similarities. In particular, positive trends are largely observed in all the regions and seasons, with the only notable exception being Calabria in DJF and MAM (for E-OBS). Trends are not significant during summer months (JJA) in both datasets and all regions (except Sicily for E-OBS), likely due to the low precipitation values observed during these months (corresponding to the dry period). Similarly, changing points are not significant in most of the regions during JJA (again, apart from Sicily in E-OBS), with a small percentage of statistically significant values in Calabria during all the seasons. Overall, the season with the most marked trends and changes is SON, which represents the period where a high fraction of the annual rainfall is concentrated. The outcomes of Sen’s slope analysis and Mann-Kendall’s test on the CV are summarized in  Fig. 7  for the annual rainfall data. Also in this case, the maps show consistent patterns in the trends in the two gridded datasets, with negative values mostly located in the eastern and southern areas facing the Adriatic and Ionian seas and positive trends elsewhere. Trends are more marked in E-OBS compared to ERA5, especially for the positive values (greater than 0.5 % y−1  in most of Campania and northern Basilicata and Apulia).   5 Discussion The climatology of a region is often defined by the average and standard deviation of its meteorological variables in a given reference period. The trend analysis on the mean and CV rainfall values reported in this study aims at contrasting how the behavior of these two quantities is reproduced by gridded datasets compared to station observations in the most recent 40 years. The mean temporal dynamic of annual rainfall is overall in good agreement for all three datasets, with a clear predominance of positive trends, which is particularly true when only statistically significant values are considered. Positive trends at the annual scale are mostly driven by analogous trends observed during the SON season, as consistently observed in all three datasets. This result is not particularly surprising, as a large fraction of the annual precipitation is concentrated in most of the analyzed regions during this season (Fratianni and Acquaotta, 2017 ). These positive trends may seem in contrast with several previous studies in the Mediterranean region highlighting a tendency toward a reduction in precipitation (Brunetti et al., 2011 ; Caloiero et al., 2021 ; Chiaravallotti et al., 2023 ; Polemio et al., 2004 ). However, it is worth pointing out how most long-term trend studies only barely overlap with our study period, and they are often based on longer past series. In this context, our results represent a complementary outcome to studies performed over longer time frames, highlighting how contrasting behavior can be observed if different sub-periods are analyzed. A more in-depth explanation of the observed positive trends can be given by investigating the results of the change point analysis, which highlights how significant discontinuities can be observed over large areas in both the gridded datasets and the local stations. Overall, there is a striking resemblance between the areas with significant trends and changing points, suggesting that the significance of the trend is likely mostly driven by the presence of a discontinuity rather than a continuous trend. Change points are mostly located in the early 2000s (between 2000 and 2005) in both ERA5 and E-OBS, underlining a certain consistency in this outcome. The presence of statistically significant change points around that period is confirmed in several ground stations as well. On the one hand, in the early 2000s, many ground stations were refurbished over most of the Italian territory as part of a renovation of the instrumentation. This can explain possible discontinuities in in-situ records, but also in the E-OBS dataset (as it is based on ground data interpolation). However, as ERA5 does not directly assimilate rain gauge data, it should not be affected by this factor. On the other hand, a multi-year drought period from the early 1990s to early 2000s (Mendicino and Versace, 2007; Mendicino et al., 2008; Spinoni et al., 2012 ) may also be the source of the detected discontinuities, which would be observed in all three datasets. As already mentioned, the fact that some previous trend studies investigating data up to the late 1990s show mostly negative trends may be ascribed to the same reason (Brunetti et al., 2000; Piervitali et al., 1998 ). In this case, the positive trends observed in this study can be seen as a return to the conditions pre-1990s rather than an actual increasing tendency in total precipitation. Beyond the overall agreement on the predominance of positive values, results of the trend analysis at the regional scale, summarized in the maps in  Fig. 8  and reporting both the percentage of the region with a certain sign in the trend (panel a) and the average (and standard deviation) slope values computed considering only the statistically significant values (panel b), provide additional insight on the behavior of the two gridded datasets at smaller spatial scale. Some differences can be observed when the data are analyzed at the regional scale, with E-OBS better in agreement with the observations over Calabria and Campania compared to ERA5. Both datasets seem to overestimate the percentage of positive and significant trends in Apulia, Basilicata and Sicily. A tendency of E-OBS to overestimate trends over Apulia was observed by My et al. (2022) , whereas a tendency to underestimate was observed for the CRU dataset. Here, ERA5 seems to perform similarly to E-OBS in terms of tendency, even if the ERA5 modeled slope values are closer to the observed ones in this region (see Fig. 8 b). Generally, ERA5 trends seem flatter, on average, over the entire Southern Italy area, with mean regional values of about +4 mm y−1  in all regions (see also insert in Fig. 5 a). While E-OBS shows more spatial dynamics, it reproduces the observed slope values only in Campania and Basilicata, but it overestimates the slopes in Apulia and Sicily. Flatness in ERA5 data may be related to the global scale data used to represent the terrain, which is one of the effects improved by the downscaling performed by ERA5-Land. In general, however, both gridded datasets underestimate some significantly high slopes emerging locally over Campania and Calabria, which are related to specific local climate conditions which cannot be captured at the scales used by both datasets. The large range of behaviors observed in E-OBS trend results can be ascribed to the considerable variability in space and time of the ground data used for performing the spatial interpolations. Since monitoring network management and consequent data delivery in Italy is handled at the regional level, the spatial density of observed data in southern Italy included in E-OBS is extremely heterogeneous, varying from 116 stations in Calabria (which were recently included in the dataset through the INDECIS project; Coll et al., 2019 ) to 38 in Campania, 8 in Sicily, 6 in Apulia and only 2 in Basilicata (see  Fig. 9 ). Also, while most of the Calabrian stations provide data for more than 80 % of the study period, data availability from stations in Apulia, Basilicata and Sicily generally ranges from 60 % to 80 % of the study period, and for Campania drops to less than 20 % (stations from Campania were included only from version v28.e). This issue can represent a general limitation of the dataset, as highlighted by Bandhauer et al. (2022) , which can hinder its use also in other geographical areas and larger spatial extensions than those analyzed here. Indeed, the two-stage process adopted to produce the daily fields relies on ground observations to capture long-range spatial trends in the data and modulate these trends locally (Cornes et al., 2018 ). Therefore, areas characterized by low station densities can provide contradictory or wrong information if the stations included in the dataset are not sufficiently representative of such areas. A possible high level of interpolation uncertainty in the gridded fields led to an ensemble approach for recent versions of E-OBS datasets (the term “e” in the version numbering stands for “ensemble”). In the version of the E-OBS database used in this study (i.e., v28.0e), a very high spatial density can be seen in the areas of Central Europe, whereas the Balkan area, the Iberian and Anatolian peninsulas and much of Eastern Europe are characterized by a very sparse distribution of measuring stations (KNMI, 2024 ). Concerning southern Italy, Fig. 9  clearly shows how each region in the area has a different spatial density of the stations. When we focus on the trends in the inter-annual variability, as captured by the CV, we can observe, again, an overall good consistency between gridded datasets and station measurements. The results at the regional scale ( Fig. 10 ) show a predominance of positive trends over Campania in all three datasets (Fig. 10 a), as well as an increase in the percentage of negative trends in the southern regions (Sicily and Calabria). Only a few previous studies focused on the trend in inter-annual variability, despite representing a key characteristic of climate. In Campania, such results were obtained by Longobardi and Boulariah (2022) . They investigated the inter-annual variability for 30 stations in the period 1918–2015, showing a large percentage of stations (about 60 %) presenting an increasing trend with an average slope of 0.035 %. By focusing on the slope values, a good agreement between ERA5 and ground data can be observed at the regional scale, whereas E-OBS tends to overestimate the slope in a few regions (e.g., Campania, Apulia, and Basilicata). Campania is the only region with a mean positive trend in CV for the observed dataset (0.2 % y−1 ), while negative trends are observed in Calabria and Sicily (of about −0.2 % y−1 ), as also confirmed by ERA5.
