An increasing trend in CV may be particularly concerning, as it translates into a larger inter-annual fluctuation in total precipitation that can cause increasing challenges in water resource management, even in the absence of significant changes in the total resource available on average. Finally, some similarities can be observed between the spatial patterns in the trends and the ones observed in the average annual precipitation in gridded datasets and observations (discussed in Section 2.2 ). In particular, the subdivision of the results in four macro clusters (see supplementary material ) is also partially noticeable in both CV and total precipitation patterns. This behavior may be worth of further investigations in future research studies.  6 Summary and conclusions Two gridded precipitation datasets, ERA5 and E-OBS, were compared against ground observations over southern Italy from 1979 to 2019. This roughly 40-year stretch is commonly used to characterize the current climate, so it is important to establish how reliable those gridded datasets are as a reference for future climate change analyses. Overall, both gridded datasets capture the major trends observed in ground-based data, with a vast majority of positive trends localized during the Autumn season (September to November). Considering that those datasets are designed for large-scale applications, this result can be considered encouraging for capturing the general trend over this key portion of the Mediterranean region. However, while ERA5 and E-OBS well capture the general behavior over Southern Italy, substantial differences can be observed when analyzed at a smaller scale (e.g., administrative region). Overall, ERA5 seems to return flatter results compared to the observed data, with good agreement with observations at the regional spatial scale over Sicily and Apulia. E-OBS is characterized by a larger range of variability, likely ascribed to poor station coverage in many areas, therefore it compares well with observations only over some of the regions (Campania, and partially Calabria and Basilicata). This result suggests that large-scale evaluation studies on the reliability of the datasets should not be used as an assessment of the local accuracy, which may vary significantly at the local scale. The scale of interest of the study should be then accurately evaluated before using these datasets. In particular, using E-OBS, the associated station coverage should be carefully checked. The presence of statically significant change points in all three datasets in the early 2000s suggests that the observed trends may be driven by a discontinuity rather than an actual continuous trend, with a return to precipitation levels similar to the 1980s after a relatively dry period in the 1990s. Following this result, it is clear how the conditions assumed to represent the current climate may change based on the adopted time window, and that a combination of different tools (trends, change points, etc.) should be used to evaluate the suitability of a particular period as a reference. In addition to the average behavior, we analyzed trends in the inter-annual fluctuations, quantified by CV values computed on a 10-year moving window. This analysis shows good consistency between gridded datasets and in situ observations, with contrasting trends in some of the regions (positive for Campania and negative for Calabria and Sicily). While both ERA5 and E-OBS are in good agreement with the observations in terms of spatial patterns, ERA5 seems to better capture the magnitude of the observed trends in CV. Analysis of the inter-annual fluctuations is particularly relevant for drought studies, and the obtained results encourage the use of ERA5 gridded data for such analyses over the region. The results of this study show how the two gridded datasets represent the dynamics in both mean and CV precipitation conditions over southern Italy reasonably well, returning a suitable depiction of the general patterns in the two quantities. In this regard, water balance and drought studies relying on these gridded datasets should return reliable outcomes when analyzed over the entire area. Further investigations on climate extreme indices, also related to temperature, could be an extension of the analysis reported in this study. The use of these gridded datasets at the local scale (i.e., region or finer) should be carefully evaluated, as significant discrepancies with local observations can be detected. Hydrological models forced with such large-scale gridded datasets may not be suitable for local scale applications, and the use of station data may still be preferable at regional or sub-regional scales. However, as in the most recent years mechanical stations were replaced (not only in Italy) with automatic stations, integrated analysis between local and gridded datasets can provide cross insights on data reliability.
1 Introduction Freshwater resources stored in rivers, lakes, and reservoirs are essential for human beings. However, the inherent variability of the water cycle contributes to significant uncertainties regarding inland surface water bodies. Throughout history, humans have implemented various water management techniques to enhance water-use efficiency and mitigate water-related disasters (Prigent et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2016; Cooley et al., 2021 ). Understanding of changes in water covered areas has become fundamental in adapting water strategies to dynamic environmental conditions (Piao et al., 2010; Koutroulis et al., 2013 ). The Yangtze River, the largest river in China, sustains a substantial population and economy. Although the total water resource of the Yangtze River Basin (YRB) is abundant, the per capita water resource amounts to only 2233 m3 , approximately one-quarter of the global average. Similar to many other major rivers worldwide, the YRB has experienced long-term water resources regulation practices. Since 1950, over 50,000 dams of varying sizes, from small-scale structures on farmers' fields to dams exceeding 100 meters in height, have been constructed across the basin (Yang et al., 2011 ). These dams play a crucial role in water supply, flood control, hydroelectric power production, and irrigation. The regulation of reservoirs has significantly altered the spatial and temporal distribution of water resources in the YRB (Dai et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2024a, 2024b ). Under the influence of changing climates, expansion of agricultural activities and urban developments, the distribution of surface water in the YRB has become more uncertain (Wu et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Song et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2022 ). Remote sensing data have been extensively used in the monitoring of land surface water. The surface water area (SWA) derived from multi-spectral satellite imagery is a robust indicator of the spatial and temporal distribution of water resources (Zhou et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018 ). As satellite data becomes increasingly accessible and cloud computing platforms advance, the analysis of these data are becoming more convenient (Pekel et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2022 ). Landsat imagery has been widely employed for surface water monitoring due to its extensive time-series archive (Wulder et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2019 ). However, missing observations still exist in the Landsat imagery before the year 2000, and many previous studies neglect to revise data of the early stage (Kovalskyy and Roy, 2013 ). Several studies have been conducted to examine the long-term changes in SWA in the YRB (Rao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022 ). Nonetheless, previous studies have either neglected to analyze the differences in changes among rivers, lakes, and reservoirs, or focused on one of them. Additionally, they pay less attention to the variations within different sub-regions. Zhu et al. (2020)  reported that aggregating the changes across various types of water bodies may obscure distinct patterns of change that are critical for identifying causality. Consequently, it is imperative to disentangle the variations in rivers, lakes, and reservoirs in order to comprehend the mechanisms behind the changes in land surface water within the YRB. The attribution of SWA changes in the YRB needs further research. Some studies considered lakes as the vital indicators of regional responses to climatic and anthropogenic influences (Cai et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019a ). Ma et al. (2010)  and Hou et al. (2020)  emphasized the significant role of reclamation activities for agricultural, aquaculture, and built-up lands, in causing the shrinkage of wetlands and lakes from the 1960s to the 2010s in the YRB. Xu et al. (2022)  had asserted that human activities have primarily driven changes in number of lakes, while climate change has predominantly influenced changes in lake area in 2000–2019. Other studies had also emphasized the impact of reservoir construction on lake area (Feng et al., 2016 ). Concerning the total SWA in the YRB, existing studies mainly focused on the impact of precipitation (Rao et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019 ). However, others had suggested that reservoir regulation, rather than precipitation, acts as the primary driving force behind recent changes in SWA (Zhu et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023 ). In summary, a comprehensive analysis of the driving forces at sub-basin scale remains lacking. The challenge of this study lies in decoupling variations of rivers, lakes, and reservoirs using remote sensing data, and elucidating the spatial heterogeneity in driving forces within each sub-basin. In this study, the SWA of the YRB was derived in both wet and dry seasons during every year spanning the time of 1990 to 2020. The driving forces behind these changes were explored. The main objectives of this study were: (1) to accurately extract water area from Landsat imagery utilizing a spatially differentiated method, and to fill in missing observations using an interpolation algorithm; (2) to identify the characteristics of the spatial and temporal variations in river, lake, and reservoir areas, and reveal the different changes of SWA in each sub-basin; (3) to quantify the influences of climate and human activities on long-term changes of the SWA. Many basins worldwide face similar environmental challenges such as climate change, reservoir construction, and rapid urbanization. Knowledges in SWA in the YRB can provide valuable insights for the development and management of other basins.  2 Study area The YRB encompasses a vast area of 1.8 million square kilometers, making it the third largest river basin globally. It constitutes approximately 18.8 % of China's land area, hosting 35 % of the nation's population and 45 % of the economy. Stretching over a length of approximately 6300 kilometers (Zhang et al., 2008 ), the Yangtze River traverses diverse geographical environments, ranging from the elevated Tibetan Plateau with an average elevation of 4000 meters to the lower stream plain at an elevation of 50 meters. Precipitation within the basin exhibits spatial variability, generally increasing from the northwest to the southeast, with an annual average of 1067 mm (Xu et al., 2010 ). The average temperature varies across the basin, ranging from −4℃ in the source region to 18℃ in the lower reaches. Water resources within the YRB are distributed unevenly. In the upper reaches, rivers tend to be narrow and fast-flowing, while in the lower reaches, they become wider and slower. As more tributaries join, the water surface area expands significantly in the lower reaches compared to the upper reaches. The YRB predominantly lies within the subtropical monsoon climate zone, subjecting it to complex hydrothermal conditions. Consequently, the region frequently experiences both floods and droughts, posing significant challenges to water supply, agriculture, shipping, hydroelectric power production, and the overall economy (Yang et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2024 ). The YRB comprises twelve distinct sub-basins, including the Tongtian River basin (TTR), Jinsha River basin (JSR), Minjiang River basin (MJR), Jialing River basin (JLR), Upper main stream basin (UMS), Wujiang River basin (WJR), Hanjiang River basin (HJR), Middle main stream basin (MMS), Dongting Lake basin (DTL), Poyang Lake basin (PYL), Lower main stream basin (LMS), and Taihu Lake basin (THL). The TTR serves as the source region of the Yangtze River, while the JSR, MJR, JLR, UMS, and WJR constitute the upper reaches. The HJR, MMS, DTL, PYL, LMS, and THL form the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River (see  Fig. 1 ). The source region is characterized by mountainous terrain, with snow cover persisting throughout the year. The upper reaches experience a noticeable decrease in elevation and contains many large reservoirs and hydropower plants, including the Three Gorges Dam. In contrast, the middle and lower reaches feature predominantly flat terrain. Notably, this region contains China's three largest freshwater lakes, namely Poyang, Dongting, and Tai Lake.  3 Data and method 3.1 Data 3.1.1 Satellite data To generate water maps of the YRB, all available surface reflectance images from Landsat-5 Thematic Mapper (TM), Landsat-7 Enhanced TM Plus (ETM+), and Landsat-8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) were acquired on Google Earth Engine (GEE). The Landsat-5 satellite was launched in 1984 and continued to operate until 2012, while the Landsat-7 satellite was launched in 1999 and the Landsat-8 satellite was launched in 2013, both of which remain operational to this day. The Landsat data provided long-term observations of the earth's land surface with a resolution of 30 meters and a repeat cycle of 16 days.  3.1.2 Reservoir and lake data set In this study, we have divided the total SWA into three distinct components, including reservoir area, lake area, and river area. The reservoir and lake area were separated from the total SWA by the boundary generated from maximum extent in last thirty years of each reservoir and lake. The Global Reservoir and Dam dataset (GRanD) (Bernhard et al., 2011 ) provided a comprehensive list of 7320 reservoirs globally, with a dam height of more than 15 meters or a capacity exceeding 0.1 km3 . In addition to offering location and boundary information, the GRanD dataset also provided critical reservoir information, including capacity, completion year, and function. The most recent iteration of GRanD, specifically version 1.3, included all big reservoirs completed before 2015 in China. However, for the purposes of this study, reservoirs constructed after 2015 were not considered, because they had little influence on surface water dynamic in past 30 years. The shapes of the reservoirs in GRanD were primarily derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) water body dataset completed in February 2000, which may not represent the maximum water area of the reservoir. To address this, we updated the reservoir boundaries using the max extent layer of the JRC Global Surface Water (GSW) dataset (Pekel et al., 2016 ). The GSW dataset contained pixels that indicate water presence anywhere detected by Landsat satellite imagery from 1984 to 2021. For the lake dataset, Zhang et al. (2019b)  delineated all major lakes (≥ 1 km2 ) in China using Landsat imagery. We combined all layers in this dataset to obtain the maximum extent of the lake.  3.1.3 Climate and human activity data To quantify the contributions of different factors to the SWA change, we collected climate and human activity data. The precipitation and temperature data of the YRB were obtained from the dataset generated by Peng et al. (2019) . The monthly precipitation and air temperatures at 2 meters were described by a 0.5 arc-minute (∼ 1 km) dataset. This dataset was spatially downscaled from the 30 arc-minutes Climatic Research Unit (CRU) time series dataset and evaluated using observations collected by 496 weather stations across China. To compute the reservoir capacity change in the YRB over the past decades, information from GRanD were used (i.e., capacity and time of completion). However, the Three Gorges Dam (TGD) had a very large capacity and impounded gradually over an extended period. The TGD began impounding water in June 2003, with the water level rising to 139 meters (about the water level of the conservation pool) by October 2003 and rising to 173 meters (about the water level of the normal pool) in November 2008 (Yang et al., 2014 ). Therefore, we added the conservation pool storage capacity (17.2 km3 ) in 2004 and the normal pool storage capacity (22.1 km3 ) in 2009. Additionally, we collected Nighttime Light (NTL), cropland area, and rice yield data to attribute SWA. The remote sensing NTL data was acquired from Li et al. (2020) , which characterized the intensity of the socioeconomic activities and urbanization. The NTL dataset was generated by integrating NTL observations from Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). The cropland area was generated from the China land cover dataset (CLCD) (Yang and Huang, 2021 ), and the rice yield was obtained from the AsiaRiceYield4km dataset (Wu et al., 2023 ), which both represented the influence of agriculture. The CLCD was an annual land cover product derived from Landsat with the overall accuracy of 79.31 %. The AsiaRiceYield4km was also a satellite-derived product, which provides the single, double and triple rice yield for the Asia.   3.2 Method 3.2.1 Algorithm for water mapping The availability of satellite data is often limited due to frequent cloud cover. For instance, as reported by (Wang et al., 2018 ), mean annual cloud frequencies ranged from 56.49 % to 89.81 % in the middle and lower reaches of the YRB from 2000 to 2014. In this study, water maps were generated for both the wet and dry seasons of the YRB over a 31-year period from 1990 to 2020. The wet and dry seasons were defined based on the annual hydrology cycle of the YRB, with the wet season spanning from May to October and the dry season spanning from November to April. To generate water maps, we employed water index methods, and the flow chart of the water extraction and classification is presented in  Fig. 2 . Two datasets of reservoirs and lakes were used for water bodies classification. The maximum area of reservoirs and lakes was up to 6451 km2  and 18880 km2 , respectively. Water indices have been widely used in water extraction from the satellite imagery, which separate water bodies from other objects based on the spectral absorption characteristic. Given the diverse land cover types in the YRB, including vegetation in the middle and lower reaches and snow/ice in the source region, different water indices must be applied. We utilized a method based on the modified normalized water index (mNDWI), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and enhanced vegetation index (EVI), denoted as (mNDWI-VIs), where (mNDWI > EVI or mNDWI > NDVI) and EVI < 0.1. The mNDWI-VIs approach significantly improved the separability between water and vegetation, achieving over 98.6 % accuracy in China, as reported by Wang et al. (2020) . However, the accuracy of mNDWI can be affected by reflective objects such as snow/ice or shadows from mountain (Li et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2022 ). In contrast, the normalized difference water index (NDWI) and the near-infrared band (NIR) performs well in differentiating water and snow/ice (Li and Sheng, 2012; Nguyen et al., 2021 ). Therefore, in regions with elevations over 3500 meters where snow and ice are prevalent, we utilized the method of NDWI and NIR to extract water bodies. The geographic slope less than 10° was also applied to eliminate mountain disturbance. Meanwhile, the mNDWI-VIs approach was used in regions with elevations less than 3500 meters (see Fig. 2 ). Prior to generating water maps, necessary preprocessing of satellite images was conducted. For each image, the quality assurance (QA) band based on the CFMask algorithm was used to remove bad-quality observations, including clouds, cloud shadows, and snow/ice.(1) mNDWI = ρ  green   － ρ  swir    ρ  green   + ρ  swir         (2) NDVI = ρ  nir   － ρ  green    ρ  nir   + ρ  green         (3) EVI = 2.5 × ρ  nir   － ρ  red    ρ  nir   + 6 × ρ  red   － 7.5 × ρ  blue   + 1       (4) NDWI = ρ  green   － ρ  nir    ρ  green   + ρ  nir         where ρ  blue    , ρ  green    , ρ  red    , ρ  nir    , ρ  swir     are blue, green, red, NIR, and shortwave infrared bands of Landsat images. The accuracy of water extraction can be affected by the seasonal variation of spectral indices due to changes in solar radiation and water sediment (Pan et al., 2010 ). Therefore, different thresholds must be set for the wet and dry seasons. To clarify the seasonal variation of water indices, we conducted an experiment in regions of elevation ≤ 3500 meters and elevation > 3500 meters. The specific steps involved sampling year-long water bodies and pure non-water objects (e.g., vegetation, bare soil), computing their EVI or NDWI, and determining the thresholds based on changes of indices in the wet and dry seasons (see Figure S1 ). The EVI of water and vegetation in the wet season was higher than that in the dry season, while the NDWI of water and bare soil in the wet season was lower than that in the dry season. Therefore, we set the threshold of EVI as 0.1 in the wet season and 0.0 in the dry season, while the threshold of NDWI was set as 0.0 in the wet season and 0.1 in the dry season, based on expert experience (see Fig. 2 ). The stratified random sampling approach was used to validate the accuracy of water maps in 2018. A grid of 0.5 × 0.5 degree was generated on the water map, and for each grid cell, a point was randomly generated within the surface water bodies. Subsequently, a total of 798 and 762 random points were selected during the wet season and dry season, respectively. Each point underwent visual validation, utilizing the very high spatial resolution images obtained from Google Earth.  3.2.2 Interpolation algorithm for long-term SWA series Despite our efforts, seasonal water maps still had missing observations in some areas of the YRB due to limited image quantity and availability. The missing observations mainly occurred in years before 2000 and in the year 2012, as the service time of Landsat satellites varied. On average, there were 1626 annually available Landsat images in 1990–2000, 2927 in 2001–2010, and 3173 in 2011–2020 in the YRB. The annual average number of sub-basins with missing observations were 7, 1.8, and 2.6 in 1990–2000, 2001–2010, and 2011–2020, respectively (see Figure S2 ). These defective data can cause underestimation of water area and show incorrect trends of inter-annual variations. Therefore, we replaced the water areas of sub-basins with obvious lack of data using an interpolation method before conducting trend analysis. The interpolation process was based on the nearest year without missing observations, describing in Eqs. (5) and (6) . We found that distribution of SWA was relatively consistent across sub-basins in different years. In the experiment in well-observed years, a strong correlation was identified between the SWA distribution in different years. Specifically, for the wet season, the correlation coefficient was 0.99, while for the dry season, it was 0.98 (see Figure S3 ). These results provided us great confidence in the ability to interpolate SWA values from poorly measured sub-basins using values from well-observed sub-basins.(5) SWA  ij   = β  i   × SWA  i  ′   j       (6) β  i   = ∑ j  ′   = 1  n   SWA  ij  ′       / ∑ j  ′   = 1  n   SWA  i  ′   j  ′            where i   is the year with missing observation, i  ′     is the nearest year without missing observation, j   is the sub-basin ID with missing observation in recent year, j  ′     is the sub-basin ID without missing observation in recent year, n   is the total number of j  ′    . A validation algorithm was designed to validate the accuracy of the interpolation algorithm. In well-observed years, a portion of the data was randomly designated as missing. Our interpolation method was then applied to these sequences and compared with the original sequences. The accuracy was represented by the correlation coefficient (r ) and the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Specifically, 1–7 out of all 12 sub-basins were designated as missing in every year, and the mean value of r  and NRMSE were calculated.  3.2.3 Attribution of changes in SWA In order to assess the influence of climate change and human activities on the changes in SWA within the YRB, we employed the multiple general linear model (GLM) regression. GLM can reveal the interactions among multiple independent variables, which is particularly useful for conducting quantitative analysis within complex phenomena. Non-parametric methods (such as decision trees and random forests) and machine learning methods (such as neural networks and support vector machines) are capable of capturing complex nonlinear relationships, but they often lack model transparency and interpretability. In contrast, GLM offers a clear framework for parameter estimation and interpretation (Ciulla and D'Amico, 2019 ). Given the extensive geographical coverage of the YRB, there were variations in climate conditions and human activity intensity across its sub-basins (Xu et al., 2010; Chai et al., 2020 ). To examine the spatially distinct impacts of climate and human activity, the GLM was established for each individual sub-basin. This approach allowed for a comprehensive assessment of the differential effects of these factors within the YRB. Prior to regression, all explanatory variables underwent z-score standardization to ensure normalization, and variables exhibiting variance inflation factors (VIF) exceeding 10 were excluded. The quantitative contributions were computed based on the normalized regression coefficients of the variables, disregarding the positive or negative signs of the coefficients (Chao et al., 2008 ). Nine variables that had been previously identified as potential factors influencing surface water were selected for the analysis in this study (Ma et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ). Climate factors included precipitation in the current year (P), precipitation in the previous year (Plast ), average temperature (Tave ), and maximum temperature (Tmax ). Anthropogenic factors included regional reservoir capacity (Capacity), Three Gorges Dam (TGD), Nighttime Light (NTL), cropland area (Cropland), and rice yield. Plast  typically influenced the preceding water storage in a basin, thereby affecting the surface water in the current year (Cheng et al., 2021 ). Anthropogenic factors represented the combined influence of land use change and surface water consumption. NTL change served as an integrative indicator of the societal demand for water consumption, and urbanization. The cropland area indicated the intensity of agriculture, which consumed surface water through irrigation or land reclamation from lakes. The cropland area had a significant impact on SWA, as irrigation accounts for 70 % of total water consumption (Dominik et al., 2008 ). Rice, being one of the most water-intensive crops, contributeed to 65 % of total agricultural water consumption. Given that the YRB is a major rice production region in China, rice yield also exerted a significant influence on SWA. Notably, the impact of TGD was limited to the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, as the dam was situated at the outlet of the upper reaches. The trends of these variables were depicted in  Fig. 3 . To visually illustrate the complex effects of climate change and human activities on reservoirs, lakes, and river water areas, we conducted redundancy analysis (RDA) (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2012 ). RDA is a statistical method used to assess the relationship between a group of variables and another group of multivariate data (Zhao et al., 2017; Shang et al., 2022 ). This method allows the relative importance of environmental variables (i.e., climatic and anthropogenic factors) to be determined considering variations in the SWA. The primary advantage of RDA lies in its ability to reduce the dimensionality of multidimensional data and express the correlations between different variables in a two-dimensional plane. The interaction effects of SWA and a certain environmental variable is approximated by the inner product of their respective vectors. The inner product between two vectors is calculated as the cosine of the angle between the two vectors, multiplied by the magnitudes (lengths) of the vectors. A positive or negative relationship depends on the cosine value.    4 Results 4.1 Spatial distributions of SWA  Fig. 4  illustrates the average distribution of surface water areas (SWA) in the YRB from 1990 to 2020. Water bodies covered approximately 1.37 % to 2.48 % of the total land area in the YRB, exhibiting significant changes between the dry and wet seasons. Notably, the Poyang and Dongting lakes experienced a substantial expansion in the wet season, with area reaching up to four times of that in the dry season. Conversely, the Taihu and Dianchi lakes, demonstrated minimal variation between the two seasons. The validation results presented in Figure S4  indicated that the water maps achieved high accuracies of 97.37 % and 93.96 % during the wet and dry seasons, respectively, which compared favorably to previous studies conducted in the YRB (Wang et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019 ). Validation of the interpolation algorithm shown high accuracy. Mean r  is 0.99 (0.95–1.0), and mean NRMSE is 2.8 % (0–13 %). The distribution of SWA within the YRB exhibited spatial unevenness, as depicted in  Fig. 5 . The middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River displayed larger SWA compared to the upper reaches and source region. The largest water area was observed in the LMS (>8000 km2 ), while the smallest water area was found in the WJR (<1000 km2 ). The types of SWA also exhibited spatial diversity within the YRB. In the source region, lakes and rivers dominated, with no reservoirs present. In the upper reaches, reservoirs and rivers constituted the primary types, accounting for 36 % and 50 % of the total water area, respectively. In some sub-basins, such as the UMS and WJR, reservoir area exceeded half of the total water area. Except the Dianchi lake in the JSR, lake areas in the upper reaches were relatively small. In the middle and lower reaches, lakes played a predominant role, accounting for 49 % of the local water area, while rivers and reservoirs accounted for 42 % and 9 %, respectively. The prevalence of lakes in the source region and middle and lower reaches of the YRB can be attributed to their flat terrain. Conversely, reservoirs were primarily located in the upper reaches, characterized by declining elevations.  4.2 Long-term changes in SWA 4.2.1 SWA change in the YRB  Fig. 6  presents the changes in SWA within the YRB from 1990 to 2020. The SWA during the wet season ranged from 31.98 × 103  km2  in 2011 to 44.33 × 103  km2  in 2020, while the SWA during the dry season varied from 24.48 × 103  km2  in 2006 to 31.13 × 103  km2  in 1993. Generally, the SWA exhibited greater interannual variation during the wet season compared to the dry season, and the annual average SWA was more influenced by the wet season SWA. Over the past three decades, there was no discernible trend in SWA for both the wet and dry seasons. The change in SWA during the wet season was −0.02 × 103  km2  year−1  (p >0.05), while the change during the dry season was 0.01 × 103  km2  year−1  (p >0.05). The annual average SWA exhibited a change of −0.01 × 103  km2  year−1  (p >0.05). Although no significant long-term trend was observed, the SWA in the YRB initially decreased from 1990 to 2006 and then increased from 2006 to 2020. The SWA reflected rapid transformations in wet and dry conditions in the YRB, including significant floods in 1998 and 2020, as well as severe droughts from 2000 to 2010 (Cao et al., 2018 ). The interpolation algorithm implemented in this study effectively addressed the issue of missing observations prior to the year 2000 and the year 2012. Additionally, it successfully rectified the erroneous upward trend in SWA during both the wet and dry seasons.  4.2.2 Changes in different components of SWA in different sub-basins At the sub-basin level, the inter-annual trends of reservoir, lake, and river area were examined. The analysis revealed similar trends in the total SWA during the wet and dry seasons ( Fig. 7 a and b). In the source region and upper reaches, most sub-basins exhibited significant increases in total SWA during both seasons, with the source region showing the most pronounced increase at a rate of approximately 30 km2  year−1 . In the middle and lower reaches, four sub-basins decreased, while two sub-basins (HJR and THL) increased. Notably, the highest decrease rates of SWA is in wet season in the PYL and LMS, approximately −30 km2  year−1 . Reservoir areas increased in almost all sub-basins during both wet and dry seasons, except for slight decreases in MMS (-1.22 km2  year−1 ) and DTL (-0.24 km2  year−1 ) in the dry season (Fig. 7 c and d). The JSR exhibited the highest increase rate of reservoir area (>14 km2  year−1 , p <0.05) in two seasons. Regarding the lake area (Fig. 7 e and f), the source region significantly increased with rates of 12.93 km2  year−1  and 17.77 km2  year−1  in the wet and dry seasons, respectively. In the upper reaches, the lake area remained relatively unchanged. However, in the middle and lower reaches, lake area showed a strong decline during the wet season. The decrease rates were up to −15.88 km2  year−1  and −19.15 km2  year−1  in DTL and PYL, respectively. Similarly, the lake area significantly decreased in DTL and PYL during the dry season, with rates of −20.97 km2  year−1  and −7.23 km2  year−1  (p <0.05). In terms of the river area (Fig. 7 g and h), the source region exhibited a significant increase in both wet and dry seasons. However, most sub-basins in the YRB experienced a decrease in river area. The JSR's river area significantly decreased in both seasons, showing an opposite trend to the reservoir area. The LMS's river area also experienced a significant decrease of over −20 km2  year−1  in both seasons, surpassing the increase in reservoir and lake areas, leading to an overall reduction in this area. Contrary to the conclusion at different sub-basins, the overall SWA at the whole basin scale had remained stable. Changes in the SWA at the sub-basin scale showed significant changes in the water area and types of the YRB over the past 30 years. This underscored the importance of discriminating changes in different water types and regions.  Fig. 8  summarizes the distinct patterns of changes in reservoir, lake, and river area within the YRB. Reservoir area exhibited a obvious increase from 1990 to 2020. Lake and river area displayed similar patterns, with an increase in the source region, no significant change in the upper reaches, and a substantial decrease in the middle and lower reaches. Overall, the increased water area in the entire basin demonstrated a rate of approximately 72.54 ± 20.05 km2  year−1 , with reservoir area contributing approximately 70 % of this growth. The decreased rate amounted to 78.22 ± 77.41 km2  year−1 , with lake and river area accounting for 45 % and 55 %, respectively. This study revealed significant changes in water types and spatial distribution of the SWA. Specifically, there was a shift of water area from lakes and rivers in the middle and lower reaches to reservoirs in the upper reaches. Reservoir area dominated the internal changes of SWA in the YRB during this period, with its proportion in the total SWA increasing from 10.5 % in 1990 to 14.6 % in 2018.   4.3 Attribution of SWA changes 4.3.1 Multiple GLM regression results The results of the multiple GLM analysis are presented in  Fig. 9 , showcasing the regression outcomes for SWA changes. The R2  ranged from 0.34 in the MMS to 0.85 in the WJR. Notably, the regression results in the source region and upper reaches exhibited higher significance (average R2  = 0.79) compared to the middle and lower reaches (average R2  = 0.54). This discrepancy can be attributed to the cumulative uncertainty that accumulates from upstream to downstream. In the entire YRB, the most significant contributors to the SWA changes were precipitation (P = 19 %, Plast  = 10 %) and reservoir construction (Capacity = 17 %, TGD = 7 %). Agriculture (Cropland = 12 %, rice yield = 11 %) followed behind, while temperature (Tave  = 8 %, Tmax  = 8 %) and NTL (8 %) had relatively less impacts. The YRB has experienced increasing influence from human activities and changing climate over the past 30 years, but these impacts have been spatially imbalanced. Attribution analysis revealed that climate predominantly drove SWA changes in the source region (74 %), while anthropogenic factor played a major role in the upper reaches (64 %). In the middle and lower reaches, climatic (51 %) and anthropogenic (49 %) factors had roughly equal effects on SWA changes. The SWA changes in the source region (TTR) were significantly influenced by the maximum temperature (Tmax ). In the upper reaches, the changes in SWA were driven by reservoir capacity (28 %) and agricultural (26 %), with cropland accounting for 11 % and rice yield for 15 %. Precipitation also played a significant role, contributing to 21 % of the changes. The GLM regression results varied across different sub-basins in the middle and lower reaches, which performed well in DTL, PYL, and LMS, but poorly in HJR, MMS, and THL. However, human activities had more intensive impacts on three major lake basins: DTL (69 %), PYL (60 %), and THL (71 %). In particular, the SWA changes in DTL were significantly influenced by agriculture, with Cropland and rice yield accounting for 12.7 % and 27.2 %, respectively. The SWA changes in PYL were significantly influenced by P and largely affected by the TGD. Overall, P (average 18 %), TGD (average 18 %), and Cropland (average 13 %) were the main drivers of SWA changes in the middle and lower reaches. Overall, the major driving forces varied in different sub-basins. Climate factors affected the SWA in all regions, but human activities, such as new reservoirs, agriculture, and the TGD, influenced the SWA changes in the upper reaches, and big lakes in the middle and lower reaches.  4.3.2 Redundancy analysis results The redundancy analysis (RDA) results, as depicted in  Fig. 10 , revealed the intricate correlations between the explanatory variables and the reservoir, lake, and river areas. The influence of climate change and human activities exhibited not only spatial variation but also differences among the water types of reservoirs, lakes, and rivers. In general, P exhibited a stronger positive correlation with river area, indicating that runoff generated from rainfall is the primary contributor to river flow. Factors such as Capacity, NTL, and TGD displayed strong correlations between each other and had significant positive impacts on reservoir area. Variables related to agriculture, such as Cropland and rice yield, had negative effects on all types of SWA in most sub-basins, particularly on reservoir and river area. Tave  and Tmax  had a negative effect on water area overall. However, the response relationship between these variables became less clear as we moved from the upper reaches to the middle and lower reaches. Table S1  listed the significant influence factors for lake, reservoir and river area in each sub-basin. Factors explained SWA changes well in upstream (most r  > 0.8), but their explanatory power is weaker in the middle and lower reaches (most r  < 0.6), which is similar with results of the GLM. The RDA results revealed the complex driving forces behind the changes in river, lake, and reservoir areas. Although significant driving factors varied in sub-basins (see Table S1 ). It highlighted that P primarily contributed to lake/river area increase, and human activities caused lake/river area to decrease. In most sub-basins, the negative influence of human activities had exceeded the positive influence of P on lake/river area. Reservoir capacity and NTL had a significant positive impact on reservoir area, while the agriculture and temperature had negative impacts. New reservoirs and social demand of water resources stimulated the increase of the reservoir area, which could be consumed by agriculture or in high temperature conditions. Overall, impacts of human activities on the SWA is increasingly obvious.    5 Discussion 5.1 Comparison of derived surface water map with other studies In this study, surface water maps were generated for the YRB at a frequency of every half year. The limited availability of Landsat images prior to 2000 posed significant challenges to creating reliable surface water maps (Figure S2 ). To address the missing observations, a simple but robust interpolation algorithm was employed to fill the gaps in the dataset. The revised SWA time series effectively corrected the erroneous upward trend in SWA in the YRB (Fig. 6 ). The time series of SWA from this study were compared with several existing studies. Rao et al. (2018)  utilized the random forests algorithm to extract water from MODIS satellite data, while Deng et al. (2019)  employed a multiple index water detection rule based on Landsat images in the YRB. In this study, a combination of multiple water indices was used to generate water maps of the YRB from 1990 to 2020. To facilitate comparison, the SWA series and Landsat image numbers in the YRB were normalized based on maximum and minimum values.  Fig. 11  illustrates the SWA changes and linear trends from the three different studies. The SWA of Rao et al. (2018)  and this study exhibited non-significant trends, whereas SWA of Deng et al. (2019)  showed a significant increasing trend at a confidence interval of p  < 0.1. Correlation analysis revealed a strong r  of 0.87 between the SWA of this study and Rao et al. (2018) , while the r  between this study and Deng et al. (2019)  was only 0.06. Furthermore, SWA of Deng et al. (2019)  had a r  of 0.70 with Landsat image numbers, while the SWA of this study (-0.10) and Rao et al. (2018)  (0.24) displayed poor r  with Landsat image numbers. This phenomenon can be attributed to the limited availability of Landsat images, which restricted the extraction of all water bodies in the basin in certain years. Additionally, Deng et al. (2019)  did not implement a correction process for this limitation. In contrast, the MODIS data, with its higher frequency and coverage, enabled the generation of complete water maps for the entire basin in a year. For instance, in 2012, when there were very few available Landsat data, SWA of Deng et al. (2019)  was lower than that of 2011, despite the severe drought that occurred in the YRB in 2011 (Lu et al., 2014 ). Therefore, the SWA estimates of this study and Rao et al. (2018)  were deemed more precise than those of Deng et al. (2019) , although study of Rao et al. (2018)  had a shorter time period. This study utilized an interpolation method to correct missing observations in the Landsat imagery, resulting in a more accurate estimation of the SWA in the YRB from 1990 to 2020.  5.2 Impact of reservoirs on spatio-temporal redistribution of SWA This study revealed the significant internal evolution of the SWA in the YRB, particularly highlighting the opposite trends in reservoirs and lakes/rivers. This was primarily achieved by discriminating changes in different types of water bodies. The construction of reservoirs, as a prominent form of human activity, plays a pivotal role in shaping the water area of the YRB. Over the past 30 years, new reservoir have contributed to a substantial increase in SWA by approximately 28 % in the upper reaches. Notably, the TGD, the largest reservoir on the main stream of the Yangtze River, has been proven to have significant impacts on the water area of Poyang and Dongting lakes (Hua et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Previous studies about reservoir constructions have primarily focused on their influence on stream flow (Ashofteh et al., 2016; Shakarami et al., 2022 ). From the perspective of stream flow in the YRB, it has been suggested that human activities were the dominant driving factors from 1970 to 1990, while climate change surpassed them from 1990 to 2010 (Cheng et al., 2019 ). However, this study places greater emphasis on the role of human activities, particularly reservoirs, in the period from 1990 to 2020 compared to previous studies. Impacts of reservoirs on the long-term distribution of SWA in a basin can vary between seasons. For instance, in the case of the WJR sub-basin, the reservoir area accounted for more than 60 % of the total SWA. Notably, the reservoir area experienced a significant increase during the wet season, while remained unchanged during the dry season over the past three decades. The imbalanced influence of reservoirs during these wet and dry seasons can introduce new challenges for regional flood control and drought relief efforts (Huang et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2020 ). To assess the influence of reservoirs in different season, the anomalies of SWA between the wet and dry seasons were computed by calculating the difference between the SWA values of the two seasons and dividing it by the annual average value. Figure S5  illustrates the changes in SWA anomalies across each sub-basin of the YRB from 1990 to 2020. The TTR and MJR exhibited a significant decreasing trend in SWA anomalies, while the WJR sub-basin showed a significant increasing trend. Interestingly, reservoir capacity had a substantial impact on the SWA anomalies of both the MJR and WJR, but they exhibited opposite inter-annual trends. This disparity in the changes of SWA anomalies between these two regions can be attributed to the different regulation schemes of the reservoirs. In the MJR sub-basin, 58 % of the reservoirs primarily serve irrigation purposes, while in the WJR sub-basin, 94 % of the reservoirs are primarily used for hydropower generation. Hydroelectric reservoirs generally have shorter hydraulic residence times compared to irrigation reservoirs (Maavara et al., 2020 ), which means that hydroelectric reservoirs tend to consume water more promptly, whereas irrigation reservoirs tend to store water from the wet season for use during the dry season. Therefore, it is crucial to further investigate the influence of reservoir types on the spatio-temporal variations of SWA and their resulting impact on water usage within the basin. In summary, the SWA in the YRB has undergone dramatic changes due to continuous reservoir constructions. This spatial redistribution of SWA has promoted equitable distribution of water resources throughout the basin and has provided opportunities for economic development in the upper reaches, as the reserved water can support local electricity generation, agriculture, and livelihoods (Albers et al., 2021; Randle et al., 2021 ). The redistribution of water resources has thus played a crucial role in the YRB.  5.3 Potential limitations This study explored the SWA variation in the YRB during past three decades based on the Landsat imagery. Although the Landsat imagery provides only 30 m spatial resolution images, which makes it ineffective in detecting rivers with width less than 90 m (Allen and Pavelsky, 2018 ), the Landsat is indispensable in studies aiming at long term surface water change. The bad data availability before 2000 is the main obstruction for studies. There are several methods to repair cloud contaminated images, such as by the water occurrence map (Zhao and Gao, 2018 ), or by the multidate information (Zhou et al., 2021 ). These methods either focus on single water body or need dense observations, which are not suitable for a large area. The interpolation algorithm proposed in this study depends on limited good observations. Limitation of this method lays in that it is not suitable in cases where the good observations is very little, such as less than 50 %. Few inputs can cause the algorithm to be unstable. In this study, 9 representative factors of climate and human activities were used to attribute changes of the SWA. These variables were tested by in-situ records or directly interpreted from satellite images, exhibiting good performance in large scale analysis. Biases may exist in these datasets, but the influence has been reduced by processing of normalization and multicollinearity elimination. In most sub-basins, inclusion of additional variables may not improve the explanatory power largely because the goodness of fit is larger than 0.6 (Fig. 9 ). But for the HJR, MMS and THL, extra factors may have bigger influence on the SWA change, as the goodness of fit is small. Human management and inter-basin water transfer may affect these region (Dai et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ), which are not included in this study. Models used for attribution of the SWA changes may bring uncertainties. The GLM may fail to discern the nonlinear relationship between changes in SWA and other influencing factors. Nonetheless, primary explanatory variables (such as rainfall and reservoir construction) are presumed to exhibit strong linear correlations with changes in SWA (Cai et al., 2016; Rao et al., 2018 ). Alternative models suited for nonlinear relationships might not substantially enhance performances. Influencing factors selected for attribution in this study have been demonstrated to affect water surface area, which is consistent with the findings of the majority of prior studies (Zhu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023 ).   6 Conclusion This study presents a comprehensive investigation of the alterations of river, lake, and reservoir areas in the YRB. By generating the seasonal series of surface water area (SWA) from 1990 to 2020 using Landsat imagery, this study provides a valuable insight into long-term dynamics of the SWA. The driving factors of changes of the SWA were attributed to 9 climatic and anthropogenic variables. Analysis at sub-basins scale revealed the spatially varied driving forces of climate and human activities on the changes in SWA in the YRB. The results reveal that the overall trend of SWA in the YRB remained stable over the past 30 years. However, significant changes have been observed in specific regions. The upper reaches have experienced a discernible increase in reservoir area, while the middle and lower reaches have witnessed a decline in both lake and river areas. Reservoirs have emerged as the dominant factor driving internal changes in SWA, with their proportion in the total SWA increasing from 10.5 % in 1990 to 14.6 % in 2018. They have contributed to 70 % of the overall increase in water bodies. The attribution analysis highlights a spatially uneven distribution of the impacts arising from climate change and human activities. Climate change primarily influences SWA in the source region, while human activities, particularly reservoir construction, play a significant role in the changes observed in the upper reaches. In the middle and lower reaches, both climate change and human activities contribute equally to the driving forces. Further analysis is suggested to conduct more detailed analysis in sub-basin scale, and evaluate the SWA changes under influence of different reservoir types. Accurate and continuous knowledge of surface water distribution is crucial for the sustainable strategy of water usage. The utilization of satellite data and extensive earth observation datasets in this study deepens our understanding of SWA changes in the YRB and provides a case study that can be easily applied to other regions. Overall, this study contributes to the advancement of our understanding of SWA dynamics and offers valuable insights for effective water resource management and conservation efforts.
1 Introduction The maturity of remote sensing science and algorithm developments for estimating the water balance components has given rise to multiple open-access remote sensing and reanalysis data sets with a wide range of spatio-temporal resolutions. These data sets have been widely used in several applications ranging from irrigation management (Melton et al., 2012 ), water accounting (Hessels et al., 2022; Karimi et al., 2013 ), and drought monitoring (Otkin et al., 2014; Sheffield and Wood, 2007 ), to reporting sustainable development (SDGs) (Vanham et al., 2018 ) and water footprint indicators (Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2011 ), thus providing valuable insights into hydrological processes (Lakshmi, 2016 ). Despite these data sets' widespread and extensive potential, all have various levels of systematic (bias) and random (noise) errors. Accordingly, there is a need to quantify and investigate the uncertainties in these data sets before their use in hydrological applications. Uncertainties in water balance data sets have been investigated in a multitude of scientific studies, either focusing on multiple water balance components simultaneously (Gao et al., 2010; Sheffield et al., 2009 ) or on specific water balance fluxes such as Precipitation (P) (Gehne et al., 2016 ; Herold et al., 2017 ; Sun et al., 2018 )), Evapotranspiration (ET) (Jaafar et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2020; Sriwongsitanon et al., 2020; Weerasinghe et al., 2020 ), soil moisture storages (SMS) (Albergel et al., 2012; Colliander et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2019 ) and total water storage (TWS) (Biancamaria et al., 2019 ; Scanlon et al., 2016 )). P is the most explored component among the water balance data sets due to its importance in weather, climate, and hydrological forecasting (Sarojini et al., 2016 ). SMS and TWS are the next most studied due to their importance in climate models (Koster and Suarez, 2001; Walker and Houser, 2001 ) and global change modeling (Henderson-Sellers, 1996; Taylor et al., 2013 ). ET was the least investigated component until recently, when an emerging focus on water management has given rise to a plethora of research and RS-ET product development (Anderson et al., 2015; Bastiaanssen et al., 1998, 1993; FAO, 2020; Feddes et al., 1993; Guerschman et al., 2009; Mu et al., 2011; Senay et al., 2013 ). Some studies show that among the water balance components, ET has the largest error, resulting in the deviation from water balance closure (Abera et al., 2017; Soltani et al., 2020 ), while other studies concluded that the largest errors are either caused by P (Sheffield et al., 2009; Wong et al., 2021 ) or TWS from GRACE (Aires, 2014; Long et al., 2014 ). These contrasting conclusions necessitate the assessment of the water balance component data sets prior to their incorporation in water balance analyses. While the hydrological community recognizes the significance of quantifying uncertainties in water balance data sets, there is currently no standardized method for error estimation. Bias and random errors in modeled water balance components are commonly quantified through direct validation against in-situ measurement reference data. Ground-based observations exhibit the greatest reliability, but even the most frequently and conceivably best-measured components – P from rain gauges, ET from Eddy Covariance (EC), lysimeters, or scintillometers, river discharge from stream gauges, TWS from well observations (in regions with extensive observations and where groundwater storage dominates the TWS signal) – still carry significant uncertainty due to unpredictable random errors (Kumar et al., 2017 ), and data errors (Massman and Lee, 2002 ). Other approaches quantify the relative uncertainties in water balance components by comparing them to a reference data set (Gao et al., 2010; Sheffield et al., 2009 ), other models (Koppa and Gebremichael, 2017; Scanlon et al., 2019 ), or by using inter-product comparisons (Parinussa et al., 2014; Weerasinghe et al., 2020 ), based on a triple collocation or three-cornered hat method (Alemohammad et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022 ). In addition, methods such as sensitivity analysis (Seo et al., 2010 ), uncertainty propagation (Cawse-Nicholson et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2006 ), and calculation of the coefficient of variation across multi-data sources of the same variable (Zhang et al., 2018 ) are also utilized. Another category of studies encompasses water balance closure methods developed to produce reliable and corrected water balance estimates, including approaches such as Proportional Redistribution (PR) (Abolafia-Rosenzweig et al., 2021 ), Constrained Kalman Filter (CKF) (Pan and Wood, 2006; Zhang et al., 2018 ), Multiple Collocation (MCL) (Abhishek et al., 2021 ), and probabilistic data fusion methods (Schoups and Nasseri, 2021 ). Some of the mentioned water balance closure methods have reduced uncertainties in input water balance data sets through bias correction before enforcing the water balance (Pan and Wood, 2006 ). Accounting for uncertainties in input data sets improves the accuracy of the corrected water balance estimates in water balance closure methods. Luo et al. (2023) , for instance, have considered using high-precision water balance components before enforcing the water balance closure, underscoring the importance of considering the uncertainties of input data sets for obtaining more reliable and accurate water balance closure results. This study expands on previous attempts to quantify and reduce uncertainties in the water balance components. The focus of this analysis is twofold. First, we develop and apply an expert-based prior uncertainty analysis framework for water balance variables. The term "prior" refers to the fact that our methodology does not rely on in-situ data, specifically river discharge data, which is often unavailable or inaccessible in many basins worldwide. Instead, we employ a combination of physical reasoning and uncertainty metrics to quantify and partially reduce prior uncertainties. This is achieved by evaluating (i) the prior plausibility of individual water balance variables using limited in-situ data, physical reasoning, and inter-product comparisons, and (ii) the prior plausibility of multi-variable combinations by assessing their representation of the long-term physically constrained seasonal water balance. Second, we apply the proposed approach to a monsoon-influenced and irrigated basin, the Hindon River basin of northern India – a tributary of the Yamuna River – that suffers from groundwater overexploitation and depends on external surface water imports. We present the first study on the Hindon basin, providing insights into the basin’s major hydrological processes and their associated uncertainties. To achieve the above goals, we structure the paper in the following manner: In Section 2 , we outline our methodology for quantifying and reducing prior uncertainties; in Sections 3  and 4 , we summarize the data sets used to apply the proposed framework to a case study of the Hindon Basin in Northern India, and in Section 5  we present and discuss the main findings. We conclude the paper with Section 6  by providing perspectives for future water balance analyses. The reader should note that as part of this multi-temporal analysis, all water balance variables, including the rate of changes in total water storage (TWS) and soil moisture storage (SMS), are expressed per unit of time at monthly, yearly, seasonal, and/or long-term scales. Throughout the paper, for ΔSMS/Δtime and ΔTWS/Δtime, we employ the abbreviated notations ΔSMS and ΔTWS to maintain conciseness, while the exact time period is indicated by the context in which they are used.  2 Prior uncertainty analysis In the following subsections, we outline the proposed framework for quantifying and partially reducing prior uncertainties associated with water balance component data sets in the absence of in-situ data (i.e., river discharge and external surface water imports). 2.1 Quantifying prior uncertainties The agreement between the various water balance components data sources is thoroughly evaluated through a combination of diagnostic plots to assess the temporal and magnitude consistency among the data sources for each variable (P, ET, ∆SMS, ∆TWS) at monthly and annual time steps. We use statistical metrics to quantify the uncertainty of these data sets along three dimensions ( Table 1 ): spatio-temporal consistency between product pairs, grid-scale inter-product uncertainty, and random errors in individual data products. We assess the spatio-temporal consistency between pairs of data products by the coefficient of determination (R2 ) of the linear regression between paired-pixel values for the long-term mean annual and monthly estimates of P and ET. Across all products, we quantify the grid-scale inter-product uncertainty for long-term mean annual estimates describing each water balance variable (P, ET, and ∆TWS) by calculating the coefficient of variation (CV, %) at each grid cell across the data sets. Given the dynamic nature of the ∆SMS component and its potential impact on the water balance at shorter timescales, we assess the inter-product uncertainty by computing the CV (%) at a grid-level for July, representing the onset of the monsoon season in the Hindon River Basin (Section 4 ). We further employ the triple collocation method (TC) (Stoffelen, 1998 ) to evaluate uncertainties in individual products. TC is interchangeably used with the intercomparison approach in the sense that both assess the data sets' relative uncertainties without presuming the superiority of one over the other. TC is a common error estimation technique that provides estimates of the random error variances (σ  2    ) associated with each data set in question, useful when the true value of the variable is unknown but multiple estimates are available. The TC error model assumes that each data set (e.g., A , B , C ) can be represented as a linear function of the true value (Θ  ) with additive (α  ) and multiplicative (β  ) biases, along with zero-mean random noise. Estimating the basic (classical) TC error is commonly done either through rescaling the data sets to a reference data set (removing α   and β  ) or based on the covariances between the data sets, with the former used in this analysis. The error variance for all possible triplet combinations of four P, six ET, five SMS, and four TWS products is calculated, and we report the final TC error (in mm/month) as the mean standard deviation (σ  ) for all possible triplets where a data set appears. A low (σ  ) for a specific data set denotes a small random error. In this analysis, achieving true independency in the water balance data sets was challenging due to data availability constraints. Some of the data sets may violate TC's major assumptions of data sets’ independence due to shared input data, modeling approaches, and parameterization, which can lower the TC error estimates (Yilmaz and Crow, 2013 ). Additionally, increasing the number of data sets typically increases the inter-model variability. However, using an ensemble of data sets for each water balance component (>3 data sets) helps overcome the potential impact of extreme individual triplets on the error estimation. In this context, we employ the basic TC to assess the relative uncertainties between the data sets, regardless of the magnitude of their random errors. A higher range of errors, even with potential bias due to violations of the TC’s major assumption, can still serve as an approximate measure and help reveal inconsistent data sets. TC is used here to complement/support conclusions drawn from the other statistical metrics (R2  and CV (%)). In R2  formula, A  i      represents values in data set A, B  i      represents values in data set B, A  ¯   i     is the mean of values in data set A, and n is the number of data points in the paired data set A and B. In the CV formula, s  i     and x  i    ̅    represent the standard deviation and mean of all evaluated water balance estimates for each variable (P, ET, ∆SMS, ∆TWS) at the ith grid cell. In the triple collocation error equations, the brackets represent the temporal mean, A, B, and C are the three data sets, A  s    , B  s    , C  s     are the three data sets scaled to the mean and standard deviation of the reference data set (Scipal et al., 2008 ). The rescaling procedure is applied to ensure the error orthogonality assumption of TC is preserved, and the system is solvable.  2.2 Reducing prior uncertainties We follow a proactive approach based on multiple lines of evidence to a priori exclude data sets with significant bias. The approach is applied to P and ET products to exclude the data set(s) that yield unrealistic individual water balance estimates and to combinations of all products (P, ET, ∆TWS) that yield unrealistic estimates of the seasonal water balance. The P products are evaluated against rain gauges using the point-to-pixel approach at a monthly temporal scale for the periods where the observed data are available. This approach assumes that the rain gauge observations are representative values over a corresponding grid cell (Baez-Villanueva et al., 2018; Zambrano-Bigiarini et al., 2017 ). The ability of the satellite-based P to capture the observed P at each weather station is assessed using three statistical indices: Pearson’s linear correlation (r), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and percentage bias (pBIAS). These indices are commonly used for rainfall evaluation (Ebert et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019 ). In addition to their relative performance against limited in-situ data, unreliable P products are excluded based on a comprehensive prior uncertainty analysis (Section 2.1 ). The ET products are evaluated by comparing them to a physically-based benchmark, which builds upon the expectation that realistic ET estimates should follow the temporal dynamics of irrigation water applications (i.e., high ET estimates when irrigation is conducted) and be higher for irrigated crops than other land use elements such as non-vegetated urban areas and rainfed crops. In support of this benchmark, exclusions of unreliable ET products are based on the consistency analysis (Section 2.1 ) and supporting literature. Additionally, we quantitatively assess the impact of excluding P and ET on the triple collocation error. Finally, the plausibility of product combinations is assessed by disaggregating and applying the water balance by season (dry vs. rainy) for a long-term period using unique combinations of P, ET, and ∆TWS. The combinations that don’t provide realistic estimates of the seasonal water balance are excluded from the analysis. At the basin level, the water balance can be expressed as:(1) 0 ≈ P − ET − Q  out   + Q  in   − ∆ TWS      where Q  out     represents total outflow across the basin boundaries, including river discharge at the basin's outlet and any groundwater outflow and Q  in     is total inflow across the basin boundaries, including groundwater inflows, as well as external irrigation water imports from outside the basin. The term ∆ TWS    is the change in total water storage (surface and subsurface). The seasonal disaggregation of the water balance is based on precipitation patterns. For example, for the case study (Section 4 ), we define a monsoon or wet season from June to September, and a non-monsoon or dry season from October to May. Based on this, Eq. 1  can then be rearranged as:(2) Q in  − Q out  ≈ ∆ TWS − P + ET = ε = Q net       Often, measurements of Q  in     and Q  out     are unavailable in data-scarce regions. Nevertheless, in conjunctively irrigated basins with strong seasonality (e.g., monsoon climate), it may be possible to put reasonable constraints on the seasonal value of the net flows (ε = Q  net   =   Q  in   − Q  out     ) (e.g., positive or negative), which in turn provides constraints on valid combinations of seasonal values for P, ET, and ∆TWS. In the non-monsoon season, we reasonably expect to have positive net inflows (i.e., Q  in     to exceed Q  out    ), suggesting that valid combinations of P, ET, ∆TWS products should satisfy the constraint that Q  in     > Q  out     or ε > 0   . Conversely, in the monsoon season we expect valid combinations of P, ET, and ∆TWS products to satisfy the constraint of Q  in     < Q  out     or ε < 0   . In reality, ε   combines uncertainties from P, ET, and ∆TWS. As such, we quantitatively study how the uncertainties of different combinations of P, ET, and ∆TWS control the value of ε   by analyzing the impact of excluding unreliable individual water balance components (P and ET) data sets on ε   per season. This is achieved through the computation of the ensemble of long-term average ε   disaggregated by season for the three scenarios, using (i) inputs of all water balance components data sets, before any exclusion, including 4 P, 7 ET, and 4 ∆TWS, resulting in 112 combinations, (ii) after excluding all combinations containing the identified unreliable P and ET data sets based on multiple criteria described above, (iii) after exclusion of combinations showing unrealistic ε  . Scenarios (i) and (ii) essentially serve as an alternative to a formal sensitivity analysis of excluding the individual P and ET data set(s). For the third scenario, we use seasonal constraints of ε > − 50    mm /non-monsoon and ε < 50    mm/monsoon rather than ε > 0    and ε < 0    to allow for some uncertainty in the computed value of ε   due to data errors. In the absence of ground observations on external water imports and river discharge in the studied basin to validate these thresholds, we consider them as reasonable approximations for guiding the combinations of products exclusion process.   3 Monthly gridded water balance data sets This section describes the water balance data sources and their general characteristics. The data sets are primarily accessed through the Google Earth Engine cloud computing platform or other public repositories. They are categorized into: remote sensing (RS), Ground-Based Measurements (GBM), Water Balance (WB) and Land Surface Models (LSM). All products were resampled to the same spatial resolution using bilinear interpolation for a consistent comparison.  Table 2  differentiates between each data set's original and resampled resolutions. Four gridded precipitation products are selected for evaluation, including the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) (Huffman et al., 2007 ), the NASA/JAXA Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM, IMERG) (Huffman et al., 2019 ), Climate Hazards Group Infrared Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) (Funk et al., 2015 ), and the Multisource Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP) (Beck et al., 2019 ). Each of these products merges a variety of ground- and satellite-based observations. Text A.1. and Table A.1. of the Appendix include detailed information on the different data sources and algorithms used to generate the studied precipitation products. Seven gridded ET products encompassing various ET calculation methodologies are used: pyWaPOR-ET based on the ETLook model (Bastiaanssen et al., 2012 ) (pyWaPOR v2.6 –authors’ generated product named similar to the open-access python package used to generate it), the operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop) developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) (Senay et al., 2013 ), Landsat Collection 2 Provisional Actual Evapotranspiration Science Product (Senay, 2018; Senay et al., 2023 ), the Surface Energy Balance Algorithm for Land (SEBAL) (Bastiaanssen et al., 1996, 1993; Bastiaanssen, 1995 ), the Atmosphere-Land Exchange Inverse model (ALEXI) developed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) (Anderson et al., 2007, 2015 ), the MOD16A2 V6 product supported by NASA Earth Observing System (Mu et al., 2011 ), and the CSIRO MODIS Reflectance-based Scaling ET model (CMRSET) (Guerschman et al., 2009 ). Although most of these products use MODIS satellite data as input (ALEXI, CMRSET, SSEBop, pyWaPOR, and MOD16), their ET modeling approaches are markedly different. Both pyWaPOR and MOD16 are Penman-Monteith (PM) ET mapping models. pyWaPOR-ET is based on the ETLook model (Bastiaanssen et al., 2012 ), which uses two parallel Penman-Monteith (PM) equations for both the canopy and soil to predict transpiration and evaporation. MOD16 is a three-layer PM model driven by RS data from the MODIS sensor and meteorological data from MERRA GMAO. MOD16 partitions ET between transpiration (T), soil evaporation (E), and Interception (I). The SEBAL ET model is a single-source energy balance model representing vegetation and soil in a combined energy balance. ET is calculated as a residual of the energy balance at a spatial resolution of 30 m. Thermal imagery from Landsat imagery is a crucial input to the SEBAL model. We developed a java-script Earth Engine-based implementation of the SEBAL model at 30-m resolution (eeSEBAL) with the ET product named similar to the script in its creation. On the other hand, SSEBop uses a simplified version of the surface energy balance. Like SEBAL, the estimation of ET with SSEBop is based on hot and cold pixels using differences between land surface and air temperature to determine the ET fraction (ratio of ET and ET0 ). ET is then calculated as the product of ET fraction and reference ET (ET0 ). We have collected and used two SSEBop-ET products. One is based on MODIS Land Surface Temperature, and the other uses the Landsat C2 Level-2 Surface Temperature as input, hereafter referred to as SSEBop (a) and SSEBop (b), respectively. The Landsat Provisional ET product (Landsat-based SSEBop, SSEBop (b)) also uses different inputs: auxiliary data for the temperature difference between hot and cold limits (dT) derived using meteorological data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis v5 (ERA5), the maximum air Temperature from the 1981–2010 climatological normal from the CHELSA Version 2 dataset (Thornton et al., 1840 ), and alfalfa-reference ET (ETr) derived using MERRA-2 which is in turn scaled and corrected via terrestrial ecoregions form OneEarth and scaled Worldclim ET0 (Abatzoglou, 2013; Dinerstein et al., 2017; Hobbins et al., 2022; Li et al., 2019a; Wang et al., 2010; Zomer et al., 2022 ). In comparison, CMRSET relies on shortwave infrared data to assess vegetation water content as a surrogate of ET fraction. CMRSET uses the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) and Global Vegetation Moisture Indices (GVMI). Both ALEXI and CMRSET use the Priestley-Taylor equation, valid for saturated land surfaces (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ), with one distinction: CMRSET utilizes the Priestley-Taylor equation for reference ET, while ALEXI uses it for potential crop transpiration. ALEXI’s algorithm is based on a 2-layer surface energy balance (TSEB) model, which separates latent heat flux (λE) into soil and canopy components. Since MOD16 product does not provide ET for non-vegetated grid cells (Running et al., 2017 ), we masked out these pixels from other ET products for consistent comparisons. All collected and generated ET products are used as provided globally without local calibration. More details on the studied ET products' data sources and theoretical background can be found in the cited references and Text A. 2. of the Appendix. We also compare soil moisture storage (SMS) data from various sources. The SMS (surface and subsurface) data comparison provides a complementary perspective to the total water balance analysis. We incorporate SMS data from remote sensing, water balance models, and land surface models (LSMs). The limited availability of the SMS from remote sensing compared to the widely available LSM-based SMS motivates a rigorous comparison between the different data sets. The thermal remote sensing SMS from pyWaPOR is derived using a two-step procedure. First, the relative soil moisture (%) is computed based on estimates of maximum temperature at dry conditions, the minimum temperature at wet conditions, and land surface temperature from MODIS using the pywapor script v2.6. Second, the relative soil moisture is converted into actual soil moisture by multiplying it by the subsoil saturated water content (θ sat  ) (0–100 cm) and the root depth (100 cm). We further use two NASA-USDA Root Zone SMS products: NASA-USDA SMOS and NASA-USDA SMAP products. These products are generated by assimilating SMAP Level 3 soil moisture observations and SMOS Level 2 soil moisture observations into the modified two-layer Palmer model using a 1-D Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) data assimilation approach. The subsurface depth of the two products depends on the depth of the effective root-zone calculated in the two-layer Palmer model (up to 100 cm). Additionally, we incorporate LSM-based SMS data sets from GLDAS driven by the Catchment land surface model (CLSM) (Rodell et al., 2004 ) and ERA5 driven by Hydrology Tiled ECMWF Scheme for Surface Exchanges over Land (HTESSEL) (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). GLDAS contains two depth intervals (0–2 cm and 2–100 cm), while ERA5 provides water storages of three soil layers (0–7,7–28, 28–100 cm). We summed the soil moisture across the layers for GLDAS and ERA5 to obtain the total soil moisture per pixel at a monthly timestep. Finally, we include the Terra Climate monthly soil moisture storage data set (at a 4 Km grid resolution) (Abatzoglou et al., 2018 ). Terra Climate is as an output of a single bucket modified Thornthwaite-Mather climatic water-balance model. The model combines high-spatial resolution climatological normals from the WorldClim dataset with coarser spatial resolution from CRU Ts4.0 and the Japanese 55-year Reanalysis (JRA55) along with extractable soil water storage capacity data from Wang-Erlandsson et al. (2016) . Compared to the multi-depth soil moisture data sets used in this study, the Terra Climate SMS product is a single-depth layer. Its depth depends on the spatially variable soil water storage capacity used in the modified Thornthwaite-Mather climatic water-balance model (up to 100 cm). For the total water storage variable, we use the GRACE Tellus (GRCTellus) Monthly Mass Grids composed of three spherical harmonic data sets produced by three centers: CSR (U. Texas / Center for Space Research), GFZ (GeoForschungsZentrum Potsdam), and JPL (NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory) (Watkins et al., 2015; Wiese et al., 2016 ), hereafter referred to as CSR, GFZ, JPL, respectively. We multiply the GRCTellus Land data by the spatially distributed scaling grid to counteract the effects of attenuation induced by sampling and post-processing GRACE observations. We compare these data sets to the GRACE Tellus (GRCTellus) Global Mascon data (Landerer and Swenson, 2012; Swenson and Wahr, 2006 ). The GRCTellus Mascon data set uses a-priori constraints in space and time to estimate the gravity fields in terms of Mascon functions to minimize the effect of measurement errors and produce better signal-to-noise ratios of the Mascon fields than the conventional spherical-harmonic solutions. We use the version that applies the Coastline Resolution Improvement (CRI) filter to separate the land and ocean contributions to mass changes (Wiese et al., 2016 ). A linear regression was used to fill the temporal gaps (approximately every 5–6 months) from 2011 onwards.
