1 Introduction Catchment memory refers to the dependence between past meteorological inputs and current hydrological variables in the catchment area, particularly preceding wet and dry spells, thereby influencing future runoff responses (Saft et al., 2015 ). In other words, a catchment’s memory of preceding conditions strongly influences its response to current hydrologic inputs (Nippgen et al., 2016 ). Benefiting from catchment memory, hydrological forecasts are usually more reliable than meteorological forecasts (Sutanto and Van Lanen, 2022 ). Hence, understanding the mechanism of catchment memory can greatly improve the skill of hydrological forecasting (Yossef et al., 2013 ). For instance, the level of moisture in the soil can influence the relationship between rainfall and runoff. When the soil is already highly saturated, it can lead to a significant increase in runoff. On the other hand, when the soil is relatively dry, it can help reduce the peak levels of runoff (Khanal et al., 2019 ). This fully demonstrates the impact of initial condition on hydrological forecast; the memory duration of the catchment for hydrological events can also serve as the identification of efficient lead times needed for hydrological forecast (Gu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022 ). There are also some studies on catchment memory focusing on the catchment recovery from climatic extremes, such as total storage change, streamflow, and soil moisture in response to the muti-year drought or the drought and heat wave (Creutzfeldt et al., 2012; Vega-Briones et al., 2023 ). Additionally, the prior experience obtained from catchment memory can help improve hydrological models to enhance the description of long-term climate impacts. For example, the upper and lower limits of the basin’s water storage determined by catchment memory can make the simulation results of hydrological models within a reasonable range (Fowler et al., 2020 ). According to different time scales, the catchment memory is divided into multi-year memory and seasonal memory (de Lavenne et al., 2022 ). The multi-year memory is also called long-term memory, which is calculated on an annual time step (Creutzfeldt et al., 2012 ). The seasonal memory is short-term, simulated on a monthly or daily time step (Alvarez-Garreton et al., 2021 ). This study mainly focuses on the seasonal catchment memory (SCM) effects, where the longest duration of catchment memory is considered to be less than one year. There are two main methods for studying seasonal memory: parametric method and graphical method. The parametric method mainly uses an indicator to quantify a certain characteristic of the catchment memory. The lagged correlation is the most common parametric method to study catchment memory. Iliopoulou et al. (2019)  calculated the lagged seasonal correlation between physical descriptors (including catchment, geological, and climatic descriptors) and the average river flow in the antecedent months and found that there is a traceable physical basis for catchment memory. Hughes et al. (2012)  used the Spearman's correlation to analyze linkages among precipitation, runoff and groundwater storage, and found that groundwater storage indicates the memory of a catchment, storing the water in wet years and releasing the water in dry years. Another popular parametric method is to calculate the potential parameter, which describes the capacity of water storage and discharge in a catchment (Sutanto and Van Lanen, 2022 ). However, this parametric method emphasizes an indicator to reflect the physical mechanisms associated with the catchment memory, giving minimal thought to characterize the dynamic of the catchment memory. Meanwhile, the graphic approach better represents the process of catchment memory. Gharari and Razavi (2018)  proposed a classic graphical method named hysteresis loops to visualize catchment memory and provided a tool for analyzing the relationships among different hydrologic variables, such as precipitation, runoff and water storage. The catchment memory curve is a graphical method to characterize the dynamic of catchment memory. In previous studies, Gamma distribution cumulative curve (de Lavenne et al., 2022 ) and the regression curve (Gu et al., 2023 ) are used as catchment memory curves. For now, there is no unified expression of catchment memory (Alvarez-Garreton et al., 2021 ), and even catchment memory has not been identified well. Firstly, the hydrological process of a closed basin on a seasonal scale can be simplified as the retention of incoming precipitation in various forms, including soil water, snow and ice, lake water, and groundwater, followed by the release of stored water as streamflow and evapotranspiration (ET). Therefore, terrestrial water storage (TWS) can be used as an indicator to indicate the water fluxes the catchment memorizes, which includes any type of natural or artificial water reservoir, such as ground water, soil moisture, rivers, lakes, snowpack, glaciers, land ice, and water stored in biomass (Humphrey et al., 2023 ). In a closed basin, precipitation is usually the main source of water storage, and the terrestrial water storage change (TWSC) within the basin can be seen as the final outcome of the precipitation memory process for the basin. As a result, the precipitation memory curve (PMC) can be used to connect TWSC and precipitation (Gu et al., 2023 ). Since the year of 2002, the Gravity and Climate Recovery Experiment (GRACE) satellite and its Follow-on (GRACE-FO) satellite have been used to monitor TWS anomalies (TWSA) (Lai et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2019a,2019b ). The data of GRACE TWSA have been widely applied in the field of hydrology as observed water storage, including seasonal streamflow forecasting (Khaki et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022 ), glacier ablation amount estimates (Chen et al., 2017; Yi and Sun, 2014 ), groundwater storage estimates (Li et al., 2019; Tangdamrongsub et al., 2020 ) etc. The introduction of GRACE data makes the description of catchment memory relatively reliable. However, the optimal form of PMC, which is the most critical function for connecting TWSC and precipitation, remains unknown. In this study, the impact of different forms of PMC on the performance of the precipitation-to-TWSC (PS) model is investigated. Taking the six main rivers in the Tibetan Plateau as the study area, this study analyzes the source of the uncertainty of the PS model, selects the optimal PMC function, and explains the physical meaning of the parameters of the model.  2 Study area and data The Tibetan Plateau is the highest plateau on the earth, located in the southwest of China, whose average altitude is above 4000 m (Liu and Chen, 2000 ). In this study, the SCM within six major rivers in the Tibetan Plateau is investigated, i.e., the upper Yarlung Zangbo River (YZR) basin, the Salween River (SWR) basin, the Lancang River (LCR) basin, the upper Yangtze River (YTR) basin, the upper Yellow River (YLR) basin, and the upper Tarim River (TRM) basin. The locations and control stations of these basins are shown in  Fig. 1 . Among the six rivers, the YLR basin has the least proportion of glacier area about 0.08 %; the TRM basin is most affected by glacier with the proportion of 9.62 %; the glacier areas in the remaining basins are relatively close in proportions, with about 1 %. The proportions of glacier area are calculated from the Second Glacier Inventory of China (Guo et al., 2015 ). Except for the TRM basin being influenced by westerlies, all other basins are dominated by southwest monsoon (Gu et al., 2023; Su et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the five southwest-monsoon-dominated basins and the TRM basin have different hydrological and climatic conditions.  Fig. 2  shows seasonal variations of runoff, precipitation, TWSA, and temperature. There are similarities between the runoffs of the southwest-monsoon-dominated basins and the TRM basin, where the runoff reaches its peak in July or August. The temperature also shows clearly seasonal fluctuations, with a higher temperature in the LCR due to its inclusion of more non-alpine area than other basins. The precipitation of southwest-monsoon-dominated basins is mainly concentrated from June to September, while the precipitation of the TRM basin is relatively uniform throughout the year. The differences in TWSA between the southwest-monsoon-dominated basins and the TRM basin are most pronounced. In the southwest-monsoon-dominated basins, TWSA reaches its peak in August or September closely following the precipitation, but at the same time, TWSA of the TRM basin is approaching its lowest point. In May and June before the peak of precipitation in the TRM basin, TWSA reaches its peak, while TWSA of the other five basins is at its lowest point. The GRACE data used in this study are GRACE RL06 Mascon solutions derived from Center for Space Research (CSR-M) and Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL-M). Adjacent month data interpolation is used to supplement missing data during the battery management period. The precipitation and temperature data used as the input of the PS model in this study are from the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD) (He et al., 2020; Yang and He, 2019 ), with a spatial resolution of 0.1°×0.1° and a temporal resolution of one day. In this study, the CMFD precipitation and temperature data are used as the input of the PS model. The actual evapotranspiration is from the monthly 0.01° terrestrial evapotranspiration dataset over the Tibetan Plateau (TED-TP) (Ma and Chen, 2021 ).The spatial and temporal resolutions are resampled to 0.25°×0.25° and one month respectively, consistent with those of GRACE data. The runoff data are from the China natural runoff dataset (CNRD) (Gou et al., 2020; Gou et al., 2021; Miao and Gou, 2022; Miao et al., 2022a, 2022b ), which provides monthly 0.25-degree natural runoff estimates from 1961 to 2018 over China. CNRD v1.0 is generated with the Variable Infiltration Capacity macroscale hydrological model (VIC), and shows well-calibrated parameters for most gauged catchments with an average Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.83 and 0.80 for calibration and validation, respectively. The Global Land Data Assimilation System dataset (GLDAS) is also adopted, which provides data of rainfall, runoff, and actual evapotranspiration. The GLDAS data used in this study has a temporal resolution of 1 month and a spatial resolution of 0.25°×0.25° from the GLDAS Noah land surface model products (GLDAS-Noah-M). All these grid-based data are used to calculate the surface data above the outlet stations in the six basins.  3 Methods 3.1 TWSC model based on seasonal catchment memory In this study, GRACE TWSA data used are the ensemble mean of two GRACE mascon solutions, i.e., CSR-M and JPL-M. Large earthquakes cause sufficient displacements of the Earth's lithosphere to generate a change in Earth's gravity field that GRACE measures, which results in measurement errors in TWSA (Rao and Sun, 2022; Yi et al., 2016 ). In this study, large earthquakes that occurred in October 2005, May 2008, and May 2015 are considered, with relaxation times of 8.8 years (Jouanne et al., 2011 ), 1.2 years (Diao et al., 2018 ), and 0.6 years (Diao et al., 2021 ), respectively. The signals due to these earthquakes are removed approximately following the approach of de Linage et al. (2009)  and Zhang et al. (2020) . The double difference time derivative of GRACE TWSA (Li et al., 2016; Ramillien et al., 2006 ) is used to estimate GRACE-derived TWSC. Due to the use of different solutions and parameters to calculate TWSA, there are certain differences between the CSR-M and JPL-M products (Xie et al., 2019a,2019b ). The uncertainty of CSR-M is recommended by the CSR website as 20 mm, whereas the uncertainty of JPL-M is calculated based on reference to Wahr et al. (2006) . As a result, the uncertainty of GRACE TWSA is obtained by the uncertainty of CSR-M and JPL-M using arithmetic synthesis method. The uncertainty of GRACE TWSC can also be estimated (Gu et al., 2023 ). The water budget approach (Lv et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2019a,2019b ) based on the principle of mass conservation is utilized to calculate TWSC at the watershed scale.(1) T W S C ( t )  = P ( t )  − E T ( t )  − R ( t )      Where R , P  and ET  are runoff, precipitation and evapotranspiration, respectively. In the previous study, Gu et al. (2023)  have developed the precipitation-to-TWSC (PS) model. According to the concept of SCM, a portion of precipitation directly contributes to runoff at the moment of its occurrence, whereas the remainder is reserved in the catchment as water storage, and subsequently convert into runoff over time. Thus, the precipitation within a month can be seen as the sum of water released over 0 to n  months, as shown in Eq. (2) :(2) P ( t )  = ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t   ( Δ t )  , Δ t = 0 , 1 , … , n     Where P (t ) is the precipitation within Month t; P t  (Δt ) means the amount of water released at the Δt  lag time, sourced from P (t ). Based on Eq. (2) , the concept of SCM can be expressed as the following:(3) R ( t )  = ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t − Δ t   ( Δ t )  − E T ( t )  + ε  t       Where R (t ) is the runoff at Time t , and ET (t ) is the evapotranspiration; ε t   denotes water flux contributions involved in the water budget beyond precipitation and ET, including processes such as the melting or repletion of ancient glaciers, the discharge or replenishment of deep groundwater, along with man-made water consumption or input, and so on; ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t − Δ t   ( Δ t )     in Eq. (3)  represents the water sourced from the precipitation within Month t . Combining Eq. (1)  and Eq. (3)  yields the TWSC estimation equation, as shown in Eq. (4) :(4) T W S C ( t )  = P ( t )  − ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t − Δ t   ( Δ t )  − ε  t         3.2 Precipitation memory curve Here, an index is used to relate P (t ) to P t  (Δt ) as the following:(5) P  t   ( Δ t ) = c  Δ t   P ( t )  ,  w h e r e   ∑ Δ t = 0  n  c  Δ t    = 1     Where c Δt   is the index with Δt  lag time at Time t , namely forgetting ratio. Assuming that c Δt   is a function related to Δt , the precipitation memory curve (PMC) is proposed in this study.  Table 1  presents the different functions describing the curve. When c Δt   is supposed to decay with time, the curves are constructed referencing the hydrograph recession function, i.e., Boussinesq (1903) , Maillet (1905) , Horton (1933)  and Drogue (1972) . When the temperature is low, precipitation may fall and be stored in the form of snow, and melt gradually in the following months. In this situation, the PMC doesn't conform to the assumption of monotonic decline, meaning that the first month's forgetting ratio may be lower than that in subsequent months. As shown in Figure S1 , the Gamma distribution density curve (de Lavenne et al., 2022 ) can exhibit a declining or single-peak form depending on changes in parameters, making it particularly suitable for verifying the shape of PMC. To satisfy Eq. (5) , it is also necessary to normalize the functions in Table 1  as the following:(6) c  Δ t   = f ( Δ t )  ∑ Δ t = 0  n  f ( Δ t )        Where f (Δt ) is the recession index at Time Δt . In this study, the value of n  is set as 11, representing a maximum SCM duration for precipitation of 1 year.  3.3 Temperature-introduced model PMC can vary with different temperature. For instance, PMC may demonstrate a recession curve at higher temperatures, whereas the curve may manifest a single-peak pattern at lower temperatures. Therefore, a segmented methodology is employed to improve the PS model as the following:(7) c  Δ t   = { c  Δ t  1     , T > 0    c  Δ t  2     , T ≤ 0           Where T  is the monthly mean air temperature; c  Δ t  1     and c  Δ t  2     are the forgetting ratios under different temperature conditions. In some basins, such as TRM, there is a large proportion of precipitation in cold season (Fig. 2 ), but it hardly turns into runoff. In warm season, glaciers and snow melts are one of the main sources of runoff. Therefore, it can be assumed that precipitation is not released in cold season, and in warm season, not only is there a process of precipitation release, but also the degree-day factor model needs to be introduced to describe the glaciers and snow melting (Chen et al., 2017; Su et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013 ). The improved PS model using the temperature-index module can be represented as the following:(8) T W S C ( t )  = { P ( t )  − ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t − Δ t   ( Δ t )  − δ T − ε  t    ′    , T > 0    P ( t )  − ε  t     , T ≤ 0           Where δ  is an empirical parameter; T  is the temperature; ε t   and ε’ t   represent additional fluxes involved in the water budget. The improved PS model shows that the precipitation is mainly converted into snow and ice in cold season (T  ≤ 0) and then gradually released as part of runoff in warm season (T  > 0).  3.4 Performance metrics Non-Dominated Sorted Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) (Deb et al., 2002; Tian et al., 2017 ) is utilized to calibrate the PS model. The calibration and validation periods are from 2003 to 2011 and from 2012 to 2016, respectively. Two metrics are utilized to evaluate the performance between simulated TWSC and observed TWSC (GRACE-derived TWSC), which are NSE (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) and the Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r ).(9) N S E = 1 − ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − S  i   )  2    ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   )  2         (10) r = ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   ) ( S  i   − S ¯   )   ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   )  2     ∑ i = 1  n  ( S  i   − S ¯   )  2           Where n  is the length of the TWSC series; O i   and S i   are the observed and simulated TWSC of the i th month, respectively; O ¯     and S ¯     is the mean value of the observed and simulated TWSC. Since the number of parameters differs for different PMC functions, the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (Akaike, 1974 ) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) (Schwarz, 1978 ) are further introduced for selecting the optimal curve function. AIC and BIC try to address the overfitting problem, seeking a balance between model complexity (number of parameters) and goodness of fit of the model.(11) A I C = 2 k + n  ln ( R S S  n  )      (12) B I C = k  ln ( n )  + 2  ln ( R S S  n  )      Where n  is the length of the TWSC series; k  is the number of model parameters; RSS  is the residual sum of squares between the observed TWSC and the simulated TWSC.   4 Results 4.1 Benchmark of simulated TWSC The CMFD precipitation data, the CNRD grid runoff data and TED-TP evapotranspiration data are used as inputs to simulate TWSC through Eq. (1) , where the CNDR data are obtained by the VIC model driven by CMFD and TED-TP data are estimated using the MOD16-STM model. This simulated TWSC is noted as CMFD-based TWSC. For further comparison, the monthly precipitation, surface runoff, baseflow runoff, and evapotranspiration from GLDAS-Noah products are used to calculated GLDAS-based TWSC. In this study, CMFD-based TWSC and GLDAS-based TWSC are used as benchmarks. The performances of these two types of TWSC against GRACE TWSC from 2003 to 2016 are shown in  Table 2 . In terms of the correlation coefficient, both GLDAS-based TWSC and CMFD-based TWSC match well with GRACE TWSC for the YZR, SWR, LCR, YTR, and YLR basins. As for the TRM basin, the correlation between GLDAS TWSC and GRACE TWSC is very poor, while CMFD TWSC and GRACE TWSC have relatively good correlations. From the perspective of NSE, only the LCR basin has a relatively good simulated TWSC, while the results for the other basins are rather poor. It can be noted that when calculating TWSC using the method combining the hydrological model with the mass conservation equation, the accuracy of the simulated components has a considerable impact on the simulated TWSC.  4.2 Hydrological factors primarily causing changes in TWS  Fig. 3  shows correlation matrix for GRACE TWSC, CMFD precipitation, CMFD temperature, and CNDR runoff in the six basins. In the YZR, SWR, LCR, YLR and YTR basins, there is a strong positive correlation between TWSC and precipitation. The positive correlations are also observed between TWSC and temperature, as well as between TWSC and runoff. However, the observed correlations may be spurious, due to the high correlation between precipitation and runoff in these basins, which is further compounded by the strong positive correlation between temperature and precipitation resulting from the basins’ concurrent periods of high precipitation and temperature. This leads to the manifestation of strong positive correlations between TWSC and temperature/runoff. In the TRM basin, the correlation between TWSC and precipitation is not statistically significant, while a strong negative correlation between TWSC and temperature is observed. As temperatures rise, the sign of TWSC shifts from positive to negative, while runoff gradually increases. Compared with the other five basins, the correlation coefficient between runoff and precipitation in the TRM basin is very low. This implies that the runoff and TWSC in the basins is mainly influenced by temperature. Although the relationship between temperature and runoff in the TRM basin exhibits similar patterns to those in the other five basins, the causes of its formation are quite different. This phenomenon occurs in the YZR, SWR, LCR, YLR and YTR basins due to the effects of rain and heat in the same season, while it occurs in this watershed due to the melting of the glacier and snow (Su et al., 2022, 2016 ). This can be clearly seen from the relationship between precipitation and temperature. Figure S2  illustrates the relationship between TWSC and precipitation/temperature in cold season (when average monthly temperature is less than zero) and warm season (when average monthly temperature is larger than zero). In cold season, a positive correlation exists between TWSC and precipitation, whereas there is no significant correlation with temperature. Conversely, in warm season, there is a significant negative correlation between TWSC and temperature, but no significant correlation with precipitation. This can primarily be attributed to the substantial influence of snow and glacier meltwater on TWSC in the TRM basin. In cold season, a considerable portion of precipitation is stored in the form of snow and ice, causing the magnitude of TWSC to be predominantly governed by the amount of precipitation. In warm season, melting snow and glacier play an important role in runoff, thereby TWSC mainly dependents on the volume of meltwater, which is controlled by temperature.  4.3 Uncertainty from different methods to identify seasonal catchment memory The precipitation-simulated TWSC is presented herein to analyze the uncertainty with different PMC methods. The performance of different methods is shown in  Table 3 . Performance of different methods in the same basin are close to each other. Considering that the number of parameters varies from method to method, AIC and BIC were introduced to evaluate the results. Although Horton gets superior results in the UBR and SWR basin in terms of r  and NSE,  Table 4  shows that the method with the best performance is either Boussinesq or Maillet. Generally, the Maillet function fits better than the other functions in the YZR and SWR basins, while the Boussinesq function gets the best performance in the LCR, YTR and YLR basins.  Fig. 4  shows the precipitation-derived TWSC simulated with the optimal PMC function in these five basins. The precipitation-derived TWSC demonstrates substantial proximity to GRACE TWSC compared to the benchmark. However, in the TRM basin, the model failed to simulate TWSC accurately with small value of r  and NSE.  Fig. 5  shows PMCs from different methods in the YZR, SWR, LCR, YLR and YTR basins, except the TRM basin, where the PS model has a good performance. Different methods acquired similar PMCs in the YZR, LCR, YTR and YLR basins. In the SWR basin, there are clear differences in the curves obtained by different methods. It is worth noting that the curves from Horton and Gamma function are very close to the previously assumed form of the curve for the cold season. The presence of different PMCs for different seasons interfered with the calculation of PMC. It can be posited that the SWR basin may possess distinct PMCs in the warm season and the cold season. This may cause large uncertainty in the PMC of the SWR basin.  4.4 Impact of temperature on seasonal catchment memory From the uncertainty in the PMC of the SWR basin in Fig. 5 , it can be found that the PMC may vary with seasons. It makes sense that cold season precipitation will directly freeze into ice and then melt slowly, while a large part of the warm season precipitation is directly converted into runoff. As shown in Fig. 2 , the Gamma function curve of the SWR basin is a possible form of the cold season PMC, which is consistent with our assumptions. Therefore, the PMC is represented using the segmented method, with one segment for cold season (average temperatures below zero) and another segment for warm season (average temperatures above zero). The Gamma function is used to describe the curve for cold season in the six basins. The Maillet function is used to describe the curve for warm season in the YZR and SWR basins. The Boussinesq function is used to describe the curve for warm season in the LCR, YTR and YLR basins. Since it has not been obtained the optimal PMC for the TRM basin in the previous section, the curves for both cold season and warm season are calculated with the Gamma function.  Table 5  shows the performance of the segmented method in all the six basins. Compared with Table 3 , both r  and NSE increase slightly in the SWR basin. In the YZR and LCR basins, there is no significant change in the performance on TWSC simulation. It is also found that r  and NSE in the YTR and YLR basins decrease slightly. The curves of the TRM basin still fails to be acquired, with a very poor performance on TWSC simulation.  Fig. 6  shows the PMCs of each basin in the cold and warm seasons in the YZR, SWR, LCR, YTR, and YTR basins. The curve consistent with the previous assumption appears in cold season in the SWR basin. In the other basins, similar phenomena do not appear, where the curves in cold season are very close to those in warm season, but relatively flatter in most basins. By only considering the Gamma function and without comparing multiple methods to select the optimal curve shape in cold season, the performance of TWSC simulation has declined as shown in Table 5 . However, because these basins experience low precipitation in cold season, the changes in the curve shape have minimal impact on the overall simulation performance. In terms of the PMCs in the warm season, the YZR, SWR and LCR basins show a relatively low precipitation forgetting ratio at the zero-month lag time but a long duration of precipitation memory. The YTR and YLR basins have precipitation memory of less than four months, shorter than the basins mentioned earlier. Due to the less impact of ice and snow in the warm season, it is supposed that the precipitation memory duration may have a certain relationship with other features of the basins, such as soil water holding capacity, water storage capacity of lakes, storage capacity of canopy interception, and so on. Here, the difference between the maximum and minimum values of TWSA during the study period is used to represent the potential water storage changeable amount in the basin, which is also called the amplitude of TWSA. The amplitude of TWSA can roughly represent how much water can be stored in the basin. Figure S3  implies that the YZR, SWR and LCR basins can store more water than thee YTR and YLR basins. Therefore, the difference in memory duration between these two categories of basins can also be explained. Basins with stronger water storage capabilities release water more slowly compared to basins with weaker storage capabilities. Neither the original PS model nor the segmented model achieves satisfactory TWSC simulation in the TRM basin. This could be because water supply in this basin is more dependent on glacier and snow melts. In this study, an improved model based on the temperature-index method is employed to simulate TWSC in this river basin. The applicability of this improved model within the TRM basin is discussed in the subsequent discussion section.  Table 6  shows the performance of different methods on TWSC simulation in the TRM basin. The improved model exhibits noticeable enhancement in simulating TWSC in the TRM basin. The simulation performance of different methods is comparably close. Specifically, the Maillet function exhibits slightly lower r  compared to other methods. However, it compensates with a higher NSE. Considering the evaluation based on AIC and BIC, the Maillet function is selected as the optimal method for the TRM basin.  Fig. 7 (a) shows the simulated TWSC using the Maillet function, which demonstrates substantial improvement compared to the benchmark. Fig. 7 (b) illustrates PMCs under different methods in warm season. The curves under different methods are basically in consistence, which signifies that there is less uncertainty in the shape of PMC. The PMC of the TRM basin has a shorter precipitation memory duration of approximately three months, similar to curves of the YTR and YLR basins.   5 Discussion 5.1 Applicability of the model with temperature-index method in the TRM basin Figure S2  shows that TWSC is dominated by precipitation in cold season and temperature in warm season in the TRM basin. Combined with Fig. 3 (f), it can be found that runoff is very small in cold season despite the large amounts of precipitation, whereas it displays a high linear correlation with temperature in warm season. This implies that the contribution of cold season precipitation release can effectively be disregarded, while meltwater assumes importance in the model in warm season. The assumptions made in the improved model with the temperature-index method hold true for the TRM basin. Moreover, since the calculated PMC in warm season approaches zero after two months as shown in Fig. 7 (b), it follows that warm-season precipitation exerts minimal impact on cold season. In the SWR basin, the model with segmentation methods can improve the performance of TWSC simulation. However, such approach does not result in notable improvements for TWSC simulation in the TRM basin. Hereby, Figure S4  provides multi-year average monthly snow depth for the six basins, which are calculated from snow depth data from 2003 to 2016 (Che et al., 2015, 2008; Dai et al., 2015, 2017 ). Compared to the YZR, LCR, YTR, and YLR basins, the SWR basin features deeper snow depths in cold season, therefore it makes sense that the basin exhibits more pronounced improvement when segmenting is considered. Meanwhile, except the TRM basin, snow depths drop to zero in July and August in these five basins, indicating that seasonal PMCs can describe the precipitation memory process of cold season. It is worth noting that snow persists through the whole year in the TRM basin, implying that the precipitation memory process in cold season extends beyond the seasonal scale. The PMC is not able to adequately capture the catchment memory process in the TRM basin. This explains the failure of TWSC simulation with the segmentation-based methods in the TRM basin.  5.2 Physical interpretation of parameters for PS model According to the PS model, the shape of PMC is determined by the curve function and the parameter b t  . In Section 4.4 , the five precipitation-dominated basins are categorized as follows: the YZR, SWR, and LCR basins (C1) exhibit long SCM with a low forgetting ratio of precipitation at zero-month lag time. In contrast, the YTR and YLR basins fall into the second category (C2), with a shorter SPM duration of less than four months. From  Table 7 , it can be observed that longer memory durations correspond to smaller values of b t  . Since this classification has a relationship with the water storage capability of basin, b t   also reflects the basin water storage capability, also known as the basin water storage elasticity. Interestingly, basins in C1 all have a positive additional flux, ε t  , which corresponds to decreasing TWSA. Meanwhile, basins in C2 have negative ε t   and increasing TWSA. This phenomenon can be explained. The cumulative water storage change (CWSC) (Hu et al., 2023 ), which is a calculated version of TWSA, can be expressed as the following:(13) C W S C ( t )  = T W S A ( 0 )  + ∑ t = 0  t  T W S C ( t )       Where CWSC (t ) represents the cumulative water storage change over a period of t  months. When replacing the item of TWSC with Eq. (4)  and considering ε t   as a constant, Eq. (13)  can be transformed into the following form:(14) C W S C ( t )  = T W S A ( 0 )  + ∑ t = 0  t  P ( t )   − ∑ t = 0  t  ∑ Δ t = 0  n  P  t − Δ t   ( Δ t )   − ε  t   t      Since TWSA can be inferred through TWSC with Eq. (14) , -ε t   represents the slope of the trend item. Table 7  summarizes Sen's slopes of TWSA, and the Mann-Kendall test results are also presented (Sen, 1968; Xie et al., 2018 ). The signs of ε t   and the TWSA trends are exactly opposite, but there is no strong correspondence between the value of ε t   and the slope of GRACE TWSA. Upon conducting an analysis utilizing the Mann-Kendall statistical test, it is found that a clear correlation between the magnitude of ε t   and the strength of the TWSA trend, with more significant trends corresponding to larger values of ε t  . Hence, ε t   can be used to investigate the long-term catchment memory.  5.3 Long-term changes in seasonal catchment memory With the impact of human activities and climate change on the basins, SCM can be affected to some extent. This impact is reflected in the changes of PMC on the one hand, and in the changes of ε t   on the other hand. In this study, the changes in PMC caused by climate change and human activities are not considered. It is supposed that PMCs are consistent between years during the study period. This is because the short length of GRACE TWSA will cause large uncertainties in the estimation of time-varying parameters. In future study, it may be considered to use reconstructed water storage data (Lai et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021 ) to study the changes of PMC under varying environment, for instance, the change patterns of SCM following extreme drought events, and the response of SCM to the construction of water conservancy facilities. From Fig. 4  and Fig. 7 , it is not difficult to find that precipitation-derived TWSC has a good description of seasonal variations, but there are still some errors compared to GRACE-derived TWSC. In order to further study the cause of this phenomenon, the empirical mode decomposition (EMD) method (Sang et al., 2014 ) is employed to analyze the trends of differences between GRACE-derived TWSC and precipitation-derived TWSC in the six river basins. In this study, the first three intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) are computed to remove the components with high frequencies and the residuals are considered as non-linear trends. As shown in  Fig. 8 , there are clearly trends existing in the differences between GRACE-derived TWSC and precipitation-derived TWSC, which implies that ε t   is not a constant, but varies interannually. Due to the small fluctuations in ε t  , the long-term trend of ε t   is difficult to observe in the TWSC simulation. However, calculating CWSC with a constant value of ε t   following with Eq. (14)  may produce a large error through the cumulative effect.   6 Conclusion In this study, the SCM was investigated with the terrestrial water storage data in six cold high mountain rivers. The PS conceptual model constructed in this study is a mathematical expression of SCM, and PMC is the key function connecting precipitation and TWSC. PMC can present the memory and forgetting process of precipitation in the basin through the form of a curve. It is beneficial for judging the future impacts of precipitation on the hydrological process of the basin. Therefore, a key possible application of these results can be the identification of efficient lead times needed for seasonal streamflow forecast. The following conclusions are drawn from this study:(1) In the YZR, SWR, LCR, YLR and YTR basins, there is a strong positive correlation between TWSC and precipitation. In the TRM basin, the correlation between TWSC and precipitation is not statistically significant, while a strong negative correlation between TWSC and temperature is observed. This correlation can be attributed primarily to the runoff resulting from the melting of glaciers and snow in the TRM basin.  (2) In the YZR, SWR, LCR, YLR and YTR basins, the two-parameter methods, i.e., Boussinesq function and Maillet function, can describe PMC, with which the proposed PS model can simulate more accurate TWSC results than the benchmark model. Meanwhile, the corresponding three-parameter methods, i.e., Horton and Drogue, have little improvement on the performance of TWSC simulation.  (3) In the SWR basin, there are different PMCs in the warm season and the cold season. The curve manifests a single-peak pattern in the warm season, which means that precipitation in the form of snow can be stored for a longer period of time. However, since the basin experiences low precipitation in the cold season, the PMC represented by segments have only a slight improvement on the TWSC simulation performance.  (4) The temperature-index method can improve the performance of the PS model in the TRM basin, which agrees with the fact that the basin is mainly affected by glacier and snow melting. The PMC of the TRM basin in the warm season exits and resembles those of the YTR and YLR basins, with a shorter precipitation memory duration of approximately three months.
1 Introduction Forests, covering approximately 31 % (4.06 billion hectares) of the world’s land area (FAO and UNEP, 2020 ), play a crucial role in the global water cycle. The evapotranspiration (ET) processes can mitigate global warming through negative radiative forcing (RF), which is achieved through evaporative cooling (Bala et al., 2007; Bonan, 2008 ). Climate change and associated extreme climate events, such as drought, wildfire, hurricane, and heavy snowfall, can alter the microclimate, energy balance, and carbon and water processing in forests, ultimately affect regional ET dynamics (Poon and Kinoshita, 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Numata et al., 2021 ). Many regions have experienced intense and frequent extreme climate events in recent decades (O’Halloran et al., 2012; Machado Nunes Romeiro et al., 2022 ), predominantly in the tropics and subtropics (IPCC, 2021 ). The long-term survival and effectiveness of ecosystems depend greatly on their resilience, which refers to their ability to resist and bounce back from forest disturbances (Dakos et al., 2015; Scheffer et al., 2009 ). For an ecosystem, the perturbations could be snowfall, fire, land-use change, or droughts (Gnanamoorthy et al., 2021; Boulton et al., 2022; Sharma and Goyal, 2018 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that extreme snow events can significantly impact vegetation through physical damages, causing changes in species composition, affecting plant physiological processes and altering microclimate conditions (Ge et al., 2015; Thadani, 2023 ). Several studies have utilized the temporal autocorrelation function (TAC) as a resilience metric with the loss of resilience exhibited by increasing values of TAC (Forzieri et al., 2022; Chakraborty et al., 2023 ; Knighton and Berghuijs, 2023 ). The resilience of tropical and subtropical forests has decreased due to increasing climate variability and frequent forest disturbances, and they may experience further degradation in the coming years (Forzieri et al., 2022 ). However, there is limited knowledge about the evolution of subtropical forest resilience in response to forest disturbance resulting from extreme climate events. Therefore, it is becoming increasingly important to investigate the vulnerability of forest ET and its partitioning and resilience driven by extreme snow events and the associated warming effect in damaged forests. Many studies have observed ET reduction in response to widespread forest disturbance, such as extreme snowfall, wildfire, bark beetle outbreaks, and drought, mainly due to the reduction of available water and stomatal closure (Diao et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020; Numata et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2013; Knowles et al., 2023 ). Others have showed that forest ET did not change or even increase after the events, likely due to the development of new seedlings, higher rates of soil evaporation (E), and transpiration (T) from surviving trees and deep rooting (Nolan et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2016; Diao et al., 2021 ). The different responses of forest ET to extreme climate events can be attributed to several factors such as tree species composition, climate type, timing of the event, and the magnitude and length of the extreme events (Sippel et al., 2016; Roche et al., 2018; Poon and Kinoshita, 2018 ). All these extreme forest disturbances influence not only ET but also forest carbon dynamics, vegetation, and species composition (Bowd et al., 2021; Gnanamoorthy et al., 2021 ). Generally, environmental changes induced by extreme events affect ET for a short period, typically up to a few months, whereas alterations in vegetation can have longer-lasting effects (Beaulieu et al., 2016 ). Vegetation changes can have both short-term and long-term effects on ET rates. In the short term, changes are mainly influenced by reduced rainfall events, seasonal variations in leaf area index (LAI), diurnal patterns in canopy conductance (Gc), and stomatal behavior. However, the long-term impact of vegetation changes on ET is primarily determined by factors such as the type, density, and distribution of vegetation, and the intensity of the disturbance (Anderegg et al., 2013 ). While the immediate impact of extreme events on ecosystem ET has been studied, their longer-lasting influences and underlying processes are less well understood. Therefore, more research is needed to investigate the responses of ET and its underlying processes over an extended period of time during the post-damage years to better understand the ecosystem functioning and its climate impacts. The changes in ET impact the ecosystem warming effects via radiative forcing from ET (RFET ) (Bonan, 2008; Beck et al., 2011; Naudts et al., 2016; Thom and Seidl, 2016 ). The changing climate and disturbance regimes of forest ecosystems have been shown to increase ET following forest disturbance, which can result in a cooling effect due to higher rates of ET (Zaitchik et al., 2006; Juang et al., 2007; Thom et al., 2017; Urban et al., 2017 ). Bonan (2008)  also found evidence of strong negative RFET  from higher rates of ET in tropical forests. Temperate forests had greater ET due to disturbance, which enhanced evaporative cooling (Bonan, 2011 ). The surface evaporative cooling effect from the higher ET rate offsets the warming over the Tibetan Plateau induced by vegetation growth (Shen et al., 2015 ). However, some studies suggest that climate-induced forest disturbances may have the opposite effect, reducing evaporative cooling and increasing positive RFET  (Bonan, 2008 ). This positive RFET  is largely due to a reduction in tree T and restricted water consumption (Lemordant et al., 2016; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2020 ). Drought disturbances in forests can result in reduced evaporative cooling leading to leaf heat stress and enhanced tree mortality (Muller et al., 2021 ). To our knowledge, only a few studies have investigated post-damage RFET  and its underlying processes in forests. Generally, a decrease in ET could strengthen the positive RFET , which is yet to be investigated in the subtropical forest ecosystem. In early January 2015, heavy snowfall occurred in subtropical regions in southwest China, with a maximum snow depth of 50 cm. This event resulted in significant damage to the vegetation and caused a considerable decrease in the annual carbon sequestration and albedo (α ) of that year in the subtropical forest ecosystem, which caused a positive net RF (warming effect) (Song et al., 2017; Gnanamoorthy et al., 2021 ). In the post-damage scenario, the components of ET and its partitioning may or may not recover to their pre-damage levels. The time frame, trajectories, and absolute magnitudes of recovery depend, in part, on the frequency and severity of damage (McDowell et al., 2023 ). However, the resilience of ET and its partitioning in the forest to such events remains highly uncertain. The present study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the response of water fluxes in the subtropical forest following the extreme snow event. Specifically, our objectives were as follows: (1) quantify the impact of the extreme snow damage on ET, T, E, and Gc using eddy covariance (EC) data in 2010–2019; (2) assess the changes in ET, T, E, and Gc corresponding to vegetation recovery during post-damage years; (3) investigate the RFET  changes after the snow damage; and (4) quantify the ecosystem resilience change patterns of ET, T, and Gc using TAC. We hypothesized that extreme snow damage can disrupt vegetation, resulting in a rapid decrease in ET, T, and Gc in subtropical forests. Although vegetation may eventually recover, the recovery of ET, T, and E would be expected to be faster compared to that of Gc. Our findings have important implications for understanding the impact of extreme snow damage on ecosystem processes in subtropical forests.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site The study area is located in the Ailaoshan National Nature Reserve Forest (24°32′N, 101°01′E, 2476 m above mean sea level) in Yunnan province, southwest China ( Fig. 1 ). This well-protected evergreen forest occupies an area of 5100 ha with stand age being more than 300 years (Yang et al., 2007 ). Fagaceae, Theaceae, and Lauraceae are the dominant species, and this includes 104 species belonging to 63 genera and 36 families (Wen et al., 2018 ). The most dominant were the subtropical evergreen broad-leaved species Lithocarpus chintungensis , Rhododendron leptothrium , Vaccinium ducluoxii , Lithocarpus xylocarpus , Castanopsis wattii , Schima noronhae , Hartia sinensis , and Manglietia insignsis  (Schaefer et al., 2009 ). At the genus level, the floristic composition was primarily represented by both tropical (46.0 %) and temperate (38.1 %) elements. The average annual air temperature (Tair) was 11.5°C with monthly mean values ranging from 5.4°C to 23.5°C. The average yearly rainfall recorded from 2010 to 2019 was 1693±140 mm, with 85 % of the rainfall taking place during the wet months of May and October, while the remaining occurred during the dry months of November–April. According to Liu et al. (2017)  and Schaefer et al. (2009) , the average values of canopy height, tree density, and mean diameter at breast height in the forest were 20 m, 2728 trees per hectare, and 65 cm, respectively.  2.2 Meteorological and leaf area index measurements The air temperature sensors (HMP45; Vaisala) were mounted at a height of 34 m. Soil water content (SWC) profiles were recorded at a depth of 5 cm (105 T-107_L Campbell Scientific Inc). Precipitation was recorded by a rain gauge positioned at the topmost level of the tower (Rain Gauge 52203 Young). A net radiometer (Kipp and Zonen CNR-1/CM11) was installed at a height of 26.5 m on the flux tower. This sensor measures the combined effect of incoming and outgoing short-wave and long-wave radiations. The vapor pressure deficit (VPD in kPa) was calculated using the measurements of Tair and relative humidity (RH, in %) obtained from the HMP45 meteorological sensor (Campbell and Norman, 1998 ). In evaluating the extent of atmospheric stress, we employed the calculation of atmospheric water potential (Ψatm, MPa), utilizing Tair and RH as outlined by Nobel (2009)  and Vasey et al. (2012)  studies. All these raw data were stored at a frequency of 1 Hz and subsequently averaged at 30-minute intervals by a data logger (CR1000; Campbell Scientific Inc.). A plant canopy analyzer (Model LAI-2200; Li-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, USA) was used to monitor the LAI every month. The average and standard deviations of LAI were calculated for each month across the 20 plots, covering an area of 1 ha around the flux tower. The measurements were conducted in the plots repeatedly throughout the study period. At each plot, LAI was estimated based on an average of 15 under-canopy records (which not includes understory vegetation) with reference to one record measured above the canopy at the top of the tower (34 m) under ambient light condition.  2.3 Eddy covariance sensor setup and measurements A rectangular steel tower was installed with EC flux sensors at 34 m on it, allowing measurements to be taken 14 m above the average canopy height of 20 m. The EC sensor setup included a 3D sonic anemometer (CSAT3; Campbell Scientific Inc.) and an open-path CO2  and H2 O infrared gas analyzer (LI-7500A, Li-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, USA). During the period from January 2010 to December 2019, we monitored the net ecosystem exchange (NEE; μmol m−2  s−1 ), latent heat flux (LE; W m−2 ), and sensible heat flux (H; W m−2 ). The raw data were stored at a frequency of 10 Hz by a data logger (CR3000; Campbell Scientific Inc.). Before calculating the half-hourly fluxes using EddyPro software version 6.2.0 (https://www.licor.com ), the raw EC measurements underwent quality control based on a set of recommended pre-processing recipes (Aubinet et al., 1999 ). Any erroneous values were removed after checking the half-hourly fluxes for outliers. The CO2  flux data were gap filled by means of the marginal distribution sampling (MDS) method, followed by the implementation of the nighttime algorithm to partition them into gross primary production (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (Reichstein et al., 2005 ). For our analysis, we used the latent heat flux (LE in Wm−2 ) as the measure of ecosystem-level ET. To obtain daily, monthly, and annual sums, a gap-filling routine needed to be applied (Falge et al., 2001 ). Generally, data gaps occurred at night, due to shortage of power supply or when precipitation obscured the sensors. An online program based on Reichstein et al.’s (2005) standardized methods, operated by the Max-Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry Jena (Germany) (www.bgc-jena.mpg.de/∼MDIwork/eddyproc/index.php ), was used to fill in missing data in NEE, ET, and micrometeorological measurements.  2.4 Transpiration estimation We utilized a unified stomatal conductance model (Yu et al., 2022 ) to estimate the transpiration fraction of evapotranspiration T / ET      as:(1) T  ET   = GPP  ET    C  a   P  a    1.6 VPD + g  1   VPD          ,     where, GPP ,  ET , C  a   ,  P  a     , and VPD    are commonly available output variables from EC flux towers and represent the gross primary productivity ( μ mol C O  2      m  − 2   s  − 1   ) ,   evapotranspiration μ mol H  2   O    m  − 2   s  − 1      ,    ambient atmospheric C O  2      concentration mol C O  2      mo l  − 1   air       ,   atmospheric pressure kPa    ,   and VPD kPa    ,   respectively. g  1    ( kP a  0.5   )    is a theoretical modeling parameter that varies for biomes as per a previously conducted study (Lin et al., 2015 ). This formulation assumes that the conductances of momentum and energy fluxes are the same (Mallick et al., 2016 ).  2.6 Radiative forcing calculation from evapotranspiration We calculated the RFET  on the basis of the study by Thom et al. (2017) . Latent heat flux is generated by the process of ET from the canopy or the forest floor and represents the transfer of energy from the surface to the atmosphere through evaporative cooling, resulting in a cooling effect or negative RF (Bonan, 2008 ). Calculated ET values were converted to represent ET per hectare on a daily scale, and we used annual sums to convert ET to RFET :(5) RF  ET   = − ET × 2.45  1000          where RFET  is the radiative forcing from the ET (GJ ha−1  yr−1 ), ET is the evapotranspiration (mm ha−1  yr−1 ), 2.45 MJ kg−1  is the latent heat of vaporization of water (Pereira, 2004; Grodsky et al., 2009 ), and 1000 is the factor to convert megajoule (MJ) to gigajoule (GJ).  2.7 Ecosystem resilience estimation We chose ET, T, and Gc as state variables for resilience analysis as per Forzieri et al. (2022) . We further obtained the TAC lagged by 1 month for ET (TACET ), T (TACT ), and Gc (TACGc ). To obtain the TAC, we first aggregated the daily time series of ET, T, and Gc into 5-day intervals. We further obtained the residual component of the time series by subtracting the seasonal cycle and the trends from the time series using local polynomial regression fitting curves (LOESS) (Cleveland et al., 1990 ). Furthermore, the Kendall tau-lagged 1-month TAC coefficient was obtained for the residual components for a moving window of 1 year. This methodology resulted in the TAC time series for ET, T, and Gc from 2011 to 2019.  2.8 Statistical analysis Daily trends in ET, T, E, and Gc were estimated by LOESS using the “ggpairs” function in the “Ggally” package in R (Schloerke et al., 2021 ). We constructed mixed-effect models to examine the differences in monthly ET, T, E, Gc, and LAI over the years, with the year as the independent variable. In the models, we grouped the years 2010–2014 together and labeled them as the “pre-damage years.” The random effect of month was incorporated in the model to account for seasonal variations. We utilized the R packages “lme4” and “lmerTest” to construct the models (Kuznetsova et al., 2017 ). To compare the dependent variables between post-damage years (2015–2019) and pre-damage years, we conducted post hoc Tukey honest significant difference tests by “emmeans” R package (Lenth et al., 2021 ). A random forest model (Breiman, 2001 ) was used to rank the importance of drivers for the water flux, including Tair, net radiation (Rn), SWC, and LAI. This analysis was done using monthly means to examine the importance of each driver as a random forest model estimates the relative contribution of each variable to the prediction of ET, T, E, and Gc. The random forest algorithm used was from the package “randomForest” R (Version 4.7–11; Liaw and Wiener, 2002 ). Further, partial dependence plots were used to compare the fluxes (ET, T, E, and Gc) with the top two main significant factors during the pre- and post-damage years. This analysis allowed us to examine the specific impact of Tair, SWC, Rn, and LAI on the observed fluxes. The partial dependence plots were performed using “partialPlot” function in “ggRandomForest” package. The R package “ggplot2” was utilized to generate the graphs (Wickham, 2016 ).   3 Results 3.1 Meteorological and vegetation changes As per long-term snow data from the study site, the extreme level of snow happened from 9 to 11 January 2015, and it fell to a maximum depth of 50 cm on the soil surface, which was heaviest on record since 1997 (Fig. S2). Only during the snow event days, Tair was −1.5±1°C, and 7 days of freezing conditions were noted after the snow event ( Fig. 2 a). In the pre-damage years, the Tair was recorded as 11.71±3.9°C, while during the post-damage years from 2015 to 2019, it was 11.34±3.98°C. The Rn was higher during the post-damage years when compared with that of the pre-damage years by 4.1 %. In 2019, the Rn was 10.1 % higher than the values of the pre-damage years (Fig. 2 b). During the study period, the mean annual precipitation was 1693±140 mm. The lowest recorded precipitation occurred in 2019 with 1406 mm, while the highest was observed in 2016 with 2359 mm (Fig. 2 c). Similar SWC levels were observed during the pre- and post-damage years. However, a notable difference was observed during 2019, with a 38 % lower SWC compared with that of the other years (2010–2018). As a result of extreme snow, LAI significantly reduced by 49 % (p<0.01) in 2015 than during the pre-damage years ( Fig. 3 ). Further, it exhibited a steady growth in the subsequent years (2016–2017), and finally, in 2018, it reached a similar level to that observed during the pre-damage period (p>0.05).  3.2 Variations in water fluxes after the snow damage According to the LOESS-based smooth trends, ET and T rates were mostly much higher during the wet seasons than in the dry seasons (Fig. S3a–b). By contrast, the Gc rate was always higher during the dry seasons than during the wet seasons (Fig. S3c). The annual average ET values were 762±44 mm yr−1  and 595±67 mm yr−1  for the pre-damage and post-damage periods, respectively. The annual ET in 2015 (534 mm yr−1 ), a post-damage year, decreased by 35 % (p<0.01) from the pre-damage level. During the post-damage years (2016–2017), ET continued to be significantly lower than that during the pre-damage period (p<0.05). In 2018, ET recovered to the levels of the pre-damage years (p>0.05;  Fig. 4 a). Similarly, the T exhibited a significant decline of 36 % (p<0.01) after the snow damage in 2015, as compared with the pre-damage level. In 2016, T rapidly recovered to the levels of the pre-damage years (p>0.05; Fig. 4 b). Following the damage, the annual E in 2015 experienced a 23 % decrease (p<0.01) compared with the levels in the pre-damage years. The E during the post-damage years remained significantly lower than that during the pre-damage period (p<0.05). However, in 2018, E showed signs of recovery, reaching levels comparable to those of the pre-damage years (p>0.05; Fig. 4 c). The Gc reduced by 33 % (p<0.01) after the snow damage in 2015 compared with the value during the pre-damage years. Importantly, the Gc showed an increasing trend from 2016 and reached the pre-damage status in 2018 (p>0.05; Fig. 4 d).  3.3 Effect of key controlling factors on water fluxes The random forest model identified the most influential variables affecting flux drivers, which varied between the pre- and post-damage periods ( Fig. 5 ). During the pre-damage period, Tair and SWC were the two most important factors influencing ET and T variability (Fig. 5 a–b). Additionally, Tair and Rn were the primary controllers of E and Gc (Fig. 5 c–d). In contrast, during the post-damage period, the model highlighted Tair and LAI as the most significant controlling factors for ET, T, and E. Furthermore, SWC and Tair emerged as the most important factors controlling Gc in the post-damage period. The shift in the dominant factors suggests that post-damage, the vegetation's physiological capacity, represented by LAI, along with Tair, became more critical in regulating these fluxes. Further, the partial dependence plots showing the marginal response of ET, T, and E increased with increases of Tair during both the pre- and post-damage periods ( Fig. 6 a–c, i–k). This suggests that higher temperatures consistently enhance the ET and T processes, likely due to higher energy availability for E. Interestingly, Gc decreased with rising Tair during the pre- and post-damage period (Fig. 6 d, p), indicating that higher temperatures might have led to stomatal closure, reducing Gc. This behavior could be a protective mechanism to prevent excessive water loss under high-temperature conditions. The influence of SWC on ET and T during the pre-damage period increased rapidly with rising SWC (Fig. 6 e–f). This indicates that sufficient soil moisture availability is crucial for maintaining high rates of ET and T, especially in periods before vegetation damage. Similarly, E and Gc during the pre-damage period increased with rising Rn (Fig. 6 g–h), emphasizing the role of energy availability from solar radiation in driving these processes. In the post-damage period, the partial dependence plots revealed that ET and E increased rapidly in response to rising LAI (Fig. 6 m, o). This indicates that as the vegetation recovered and leaf area increased, the capacity for ET and E also grew, likely due to enhanced photosynthetic activity and greater surface area for T. However, the relationship between T and LAI in the post-damage period was more complex: T increased until LAI reached 4.2 m² m⁻², then began to decline with further increases in LAI (Fig. 6 n). This non-linear response might reflect a threshold beyond which additional leaf area does not contribute to increased T, possibly due to shading effects or other limiting factors. The response of Gc during the post-damage years showed an decrease with rising SWC (Fig. 6 i), suggesting that soil moisture remained a critical factor for Gc even after the damage event.  3.4 Radiative forcing from evapotranspiration The pre-damage RFET  value was −18681.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  ( Fig. 7 ). After the snow event, the RFET  in 2015 reduced by 30 % from the pre-damage level. The RFET  showed a higher trend during post-damage years, which altered from −13082 GJ ha−1  yr−1  in 2015 to −14484 GJ ha−1  yr−1  in 2019. However, during the post-damage years, RFET  increased +5599.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  (2015), +4908.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  (2016), +4466.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  (2017), +1321.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  (2018), and +4197.4 GJ ha−1  yr−1  (2019) when compared with the values of the pre-damage years. Overall, this higher (less negative) RFET  reduced the ET cooling effect in the local forest ecosystem during the post-damage period.  3.5 Ecosystem resilience after snow damage The extreme snow damage resulted in significant increases in TAC, indicating an increasing loss of resilience during the post-damage period ( Fig. 8 ). The annual average TACET  values were −0.02±0.1 (pre-damage) and 0.15±0.1 (post-damage) (Fig. 8 a). Notably, TACET  exhibited a strong significant peak of 123 % in 2015 compared with that of the pre-damage period. Throughout the post-damage years (2016–2019), TACET  remained significantly higher than the pre-damage level (p<0.01). Similarly, TACT  during the post-damage period (0.12±0.2) showed a significant increase compared with that of the pre-damage period (0.05±0.05; Fig. 8 b). Over the post-damage years (2016–2019), TACT  values also sustained a significant increase compared with the values during the pre-damage period (p<0.05). The TACGc  also exhibited a significant increase of 115 % in 2015 compared with the value during the pre-damage period. Importantly, the TACGc  showed an decreasing trend from 2016 and had reached the pre-damage status in 2018 (p>0.05; Fig. 8 c).   4 Discussion The present study showed asynchronous responses of different water flux processes, E and T, to an extreme snow event during the post-damage period in an old-growth subtropical forest. The results suggest the important role of vegetation recovery in driving the water processes recovery during the post-damage period. Although ET is usually measured as a sum via the EC technique, our results highlight the importance of investigating them separately under the influences of environmental disturbance given the contrasting drivers underlying the processes. However, the specific decrease in ET led to higher (less negative) RFET  values. This increase in RFET  signifies a reduction in the cooling effect that ET typically provides, thus causing the forest to experience less evaporative cooling. Subsequent to the snow damage, there were substantial rises in TAC, suggesting a decrease in ecosystem resilience during the post-damage period. The predominant plant species listed at our study site are prevalent across Southeast Asia, the East Himalayan-Tibetan region, Northeast India, and a substantial portion of China (Schaefer et al., 2009; Gnanamoorthy et al., 2021 ). Extreme snow events are predicted to become more frequent, particularly in the northern hemisphere and high elevation regions in subtropics, due to significant changes in the hydrological cycle (O'Gorman, 2014; IPCC, 2021 ). Therefore, we propose that numerous forests in these regions, particularly at higher elevations, which share similar structural and climatic characteristics with our site, may exhibit analogous response patterns in water cycle when subjected to extreme disturbances. 4.1 Effect of vegetation damage and recovery process The reduction in water fluxes in the later months of 2015 could potentially be attributed to severe vegetation damage caused by the snow. The vegetation canopy was severely damaged due to the extreme snow event, leading to a decrease in LAI (49 %) during the snow year (2015). This severe vegetation disturbance caused significant declines in ET (35 %), T (36 %), E (23 %), and Gc (33 %), when compared with the monthly values during the pre-damage years (Fig. 4 ). This indicates that the snow damage had a substantial impact on the water fluxes of the studied area. In the post-damage years, there were signs of recovery, but the magnitude and pace of asynchronous recovery were observed across different parameters. For example, T experienced a rapid recovery in 2016, reaching pre-damage levels. However, ET, E and Gc recovery lagged and occurred 2 years later along with LAI in 2018. We found that changes in above-canopy vegetation (Fig. S4a–f) and rapid growth of understory biomass (Fargesia  sp; Fig. S5a–c) may have contributed to higher T from the understory vegetation, which explains the more rapid recovery of T compared with ET. Thus, T was relatively conservative even after severe forest damage because of the increase of understory T (Dore et al., 2012; Kasurinen et al., 2014; Nolan et al., 2014 ). The decreased E observed after snow damage contrasts with findings from other studies indicating an increase in E following disturbances such as fire, drought, hurricanes, and beetle attacks (O’Halloran et al., 2012; Biederman et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2020; Ohkubo et al., 2021 ). This discrepancy is attributed to the heightened E resulting from increased solar radiation reaching the ground. In contrast to the outcomes of prior studies, our research demonstrates a decrease in E due to reductions in forest foliage, changes in species composition, recruitment of new seedlings in response to an open canopy, and the rapid growth of understorey shrubby vegetation reaching a height of 5 m (Song et al., 2018 ). Additionally, the sparser tree canopy also contributed to recovery in T. This vegetation fills the canopy gaps created by the snow, which does not allow the soil to be exposed to solar radiation (Fig. S5a–c). Additionally, Ψatm or atmospheric water stress does not show any significant difference between pre- and post-damage periods, providing a possible reason for the observed lack of increase in E during the post-damage period (Fig. S6). These findings contribute to our understanding of the prolonged repercussions of extreme events on forest ecosystems, highlighting the complex interplay among vegetation, water fluxes, and recovery dynamics. Canopy conductance tends to be reduced during the wet season in high-altitude (2476 m) moist subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests for several reasons (Fig.S3d). Wet season conditions often involve frequent rain (85 % rain occurs during wet seson) and fog events in the site (Fig S7), which can lead to wet leaf surfaces. When leaves are wet, stomata (the pores on leaf surfaces) may partially close to prevent excess water loss (Choat et al., 2018 ). These results in lower Gc. Persistent wetness on the leaf surface can directly inhibit stomatal function. The water film over the stomata can physically impede gas exchange, thus reducing overall Gc. In the dry season, our forest canopy temperatures are generally lower than wet season. The combination of lower VPD and lower canopy temperatures can actually reduce the need for plants to open their stomata widely (Wehr et al., 2017 ), thereby lowering conductance (Fig.S8a-b). These factors together result in lower Gc during the wet season, despite the overall higher water availability, ET and T rates (Fig.S3).  4.2 Asynchronous recovery of E and T The reduction in ET following extreme snow damage is consistent with findings from previous studies that have reported reduced ET rates ranging from 24 % to 41 % following various extreme climate disturbances, such as drought, wildfire, snow damage, bark beetle outbreak, and windthrow, in forests (Hirano et al., 2017; Diao et al., 2021; He et al., 2022; Knowles et al., 2023 ). The decreased forest ET following extreme climate events may be due to both limited water supply and constrained water consumption by forests, which might affect post-damage recovery (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2020 ). Specifically, extreme climate events can contribute to relatively higher canopy loss and decreased shading in damaged areas, increasing surface E, decreasing T, and resulting in an overall decrease in ET, as observed in several post-disturbed forests (Bennett et al., 2015; Dore et al., 2012; Kasurinen et al., 2014; Nolan et al., 2014 ). By contrast, lower magnitude and short-term climate events generally increase or maintain forest ET through the utilization of deep water by deep rooting and increased T from intact stands (Barr et al., 2012; Hayat et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022 ). For example, undamaged bamboo shoots dramatically increased vegetation and maintained the ET rate following the snow damage in Moso bamboo forests in northwestern China (Xu et al., 2013 ), whereas in our site, the swift recovery of T to pre-damage levels within a year of damage suggests a capacity for adaptation and resilience within the vegetation. This also allows for a rapid restoration of water uptake and transport processes, such as seedling or understory regeneration and resprouting in surviving trees (Song et al., 2018 ). Furthermore, rapid increases in ET, T, and E were most pronounced during the initial 2–5 years post damage in many sites, including our own (Fig. 4 b). Our site, located in a warm, temperate subtropical evergreen broadleaved old-growth forest, has understory shrubs (Fargesia  sp.) that contribute to a year-round moist environment. This, combined with higher rainfall and dense foggy conditions, enabled the forest to recover quickly (i.e., a resilient ecosystem) after extreme snow disturbance. However, an earlier report has found a negative correlation between vegetation indices and ET, and the lack of T resulting from the burning of vegetation was sufficiently equalized by E in the presence of long-lasting precipitation (Ohkubo et al., 2021 ). Our study found that pre-damage ET was positively correlated with environmental factors, such as Tair and SWC, whereas the post-damage reduction in ET was more strongly correlated with post-vegetation changes, such as Tair and LAI (Fig. 6 ), suggesting vegetation recovery largely explained ET dynamics.  4.3 Decline evaporative cooling and ecosystem resilience The decreased ET rate led to higher RFET  trend following the post-damage period (Fig. 8 ), which dampened the evaporative cooling effect of the forest. Previous studies have also shown that evaporative cooling is suppressed (i.e., positive RFET ), leading to increased local temperatures (Hirschi et al., 2011; Mueller and Seneviratne, 2012; Teuling, 2018; O et al., 2022 ). The biogeophysical (radiative forcing from albedo (RFα ) and RFET ) and biogeochemical (radiative forcing from carbon (RFNEE )) effects and the net forcing (ΣRF) following ecosystem disturbance remain unclear and vary among tropical, temperate, and boreal forests (Bonan, 2008 ). For example, the post-damage ΣRF seen in different forests has positive and negative effects (Bonan, 2008; O’Halloran et al., 2012; Landry et al., 2017; Thom et al., 2017 ). We found ΣRF being positive under the post-damage period based on our previous and present results. Our previous study results found that albedo (α) dominated the positive forcing rather than those in NEE forcing (Gnanamoorthy et al., 2021 ). In this study, we found positive RFET  (warming effect) in feedback to the vegetation alteration and during the process of post-damage recovery in a subtropical forest (Fig. 7 ), while tropical and temperate forests studies highlighted that, overall, ΣRF forcing was most strongly driven by RFNEE  than by RFα  and RFET  forcing (Bonan, 2008; Thom et al., 2017 ). Overall, our results suggest an increased RF from NEE, albedo, and ET during the post-damage period, which can create further warming in the forest ecosystem during this period, but we need long-term studies to track this ΣRF forcing to draw a conclusion. After the snow damage, there were significant increases in TAC (Fig. 8 ), suggesting a decline in ecosystem resilience during the post-damage period. In particular, both TACET  and TACT  values showed a significant peak in 2015 compared with the values during the pre-damage period; from 2016 to 2019, they remained consistently higher than during the pre-damage period. Conversely, TACGc  experienced a significant rise in 2015 but exhibited a decreasing trend from 2016 onward and recovered to pre-damage levels by 2018. Recent studies confirm that up to 29 % of the global forests show symptoms of resilience loss across tropical, temperate, and arid regions, primarily due to water limitations and extreme climate events (Forzieri et al., 2022; Rocha, 2022 ). Our study also reveals a similar response, showing a decline in subtropical forest resilience function due to damaged vegetation and changes in understory composition during the post-damage period. The increased vulnerability of forests to natural disturbances and the rising tree mortality observed in much of Asia, the Americas, and Europe in recent decades serve as independent evidence of the ongoing decline in forest resilience (Forzieri et al., 2021; Rocha, 2022 ).   5 Conclusions The study reveals notable asynchronous recovery dynamics of T and E in a subtropical forest following an extreme snow event in 2015. While T swiftly recovered to pre-damage levels by the year 2016, ET, E, Gc and LAI experienced a lag, with recovery occurring in 2018. Our analysis underscores the crucial role of changes in above-canopy vegetation and the rapid growth of understory vegetation in accelerating the recovery of T, surpassing that of ET. This phenomenon suggests that the increased T from the understory vegetation played a pivotal role in the overall recovery process. Moreover, the decreased ET rate observed during the post-damage period resulted in a positive trend in RFET  (radiative forcing of evapotranspiration), leading to a decrease in the forest’s evaporative cooling effect. The study also noted significant increases in TAC, indicating a reduction in ecosystem resilience during the post-damage period. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationship between vegetation changes, water fluxes, recovery dynamics, and resilience in the aftermath of extreme weather events. While the study provides valuable insights into the recovery dynamics of water fluxes in a subtropical forest following an extreme snow event, there are several limitations to consider. First, the study is site-specific, and the findings may not be universally applicable to other forest ecosystems with different structural and climatic characteristics. Additionally, the study primarily focuses on short-term recovery dynamics, and long-term monitoring is necessary to fully understand the prolonged impacts of such extreme events on forest ecosystems. Future research should aim to explore the mechanisms underlying the observed recovery patterns in greater detail, potentially incorporating more diverse sites and longer observation periods. The findings of this study have significant implications for forest management and conservation strategies, particularly in regions susceptible to extreme weather events. By highlighting the lasting impact of vegetation damage and post-damage development on water fluxes, the study underscores the need for adaptive management practices that enhance ecosystem resilience. The insights gained from this research can inform policymakers and land managers about the potential ecological consequences of extreme weather events and guide the development of mitigation strategies. Additionally, the study's findings are relevant to broader scientific communities studying ecosystem responses to climate change, as they provide a framework for understanding how similar forests, especially those at higher elevations across Southeast Asia, the East Himalayan-Tibetan region, Northeast India, and China, might respond to extreme disturbances. Researchers in related fields can leverage these findings to explore analogous patterns in other ecosystems and develop cross-regional comparisons, ultimately contributing to a more holistic understanding of global forest dynamics in the face of climate change.
1 Introduction In arid and hyper-arid environments, the significance of groundwater resources cannot be underestimated. They play a vital role in fostering economic growth, maintaining social stability, and preserving the environment. With the availability and quality of groundwater being influenced by both natural processes and human interventions, it is crucial to prioritize their sustainable management (Bogardi et al., 2021; Lezzaik et al., 2018 ). An example of such areas is the United Arab Emirates, where about 50 % of the national water consumption comes from groundwater (https://water.fanack.com/uae/water-resources/). Currently, the UAE's groundwater resources are being impacted by a variety of factors, including climate change, population growth, groundwater overexploitation, and pollution. These interventions are directly linked to climate change, which has led to alterations in rainfall patterns, frequencies, and amounts, as well as changes in temperature cycles and land cover (Basarir et al., 2018; Ouarda et al., 2014; Shanableh et al., 2018 ). The UAE, for example, shows an increasing trend of surface air temperature (0.6–1.5°C) that further induced more evaporation which consequently placed extra pressure on conventional groundwater resources (Murad and Aldahan, 2019 ). Global warming and climate change is expected to cause further damage to the sensitive balance between water supply and demand which in turn expand the current water shortage (Lee et al., 2023 ). The situation demands a better understanding of the recharge mechanisms and quality of groundwater under natural and anthropogenic influences for better sustainable development of water resources in the country. For years, the field techniques including geophysical, hydrogeological, and geochemical measurements has emerged as a conventional approach for investigating the locations and rates of aquifer recharge (Dassi, 2011; Gouasmia et al., 2023; Kpegli et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016 ), as well as the responses of aquifers to natural and anthropogenic interventions (Cheng et al., 2022; Ciampi et al., 2022; Marques et al., 2021; Pujari et al., 2012; Soupios et al., 2008 ). These parameters are traditionally utilized for determining the groundwater table, quantifying storage volumes, mapping spatial regions of recharge and depletion, measuring recharge and discharge rates, and evaluating groundwater quality. Nevertheless, conducting country-wide measurements poses financial and logistical challenges due to the inaccessibility of many recharge areas.
