Stable isotopes of the water molecule provide unique “fingerprints”, which can be used to trace the movement of groundwater along the flow path. They have the ability to unveil insights into the groundwater evolution, recharge sources, runoff and discharge processes, as well as the groundwater and surface water interaction, which includes the identification of human-induced pollution (Murad et al., 2017a; Wood and Imes, 2003 ; Ji et al., 2020 ). Despite the crucial role of water's isotopic compositions, there is a lack of integrated studies in UAE that combine these measurements to provide a comprehensive dataset and identifying the spatial distribution for the different aquifer systems. Establishing such a database would not only optimize resources and efforts but also enhance the scientific community's understanding of the hydrogeologic system. Open access to these datasets would promote transparency, boost confidence in research findings, and stimulate collaboration among researchers, ultimately leading to groundbreaking discoveries. The spatial interpolation of isotope data has experienced a notable evolution through an innovative approach that combines an initial empirical model guided by independent parameters with residual kriging (Erdélyi et al., 2023 ). Traditional kriging interpolation has proven its superiority over alternative techniques in producing spatially continuous datasets of isotopic variability. It has established itself as claimed standard for mapping the spatial variability of precipitation isotopes, from global to regional scales (Erdélyi et al., 2023 ). However, the advent of machine learning approaches, such as artificial neural networks and support vector machines, has brought about a new era in analyzing geospatial data (Chitsazan et al., 2015 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Yoon et al., 2011 ). These techniques have demonstrated their value in extracting patterns and insights from vast amounts of data, revolutionizing the field of data-driven Earth system science. The current study involved the compilation of all country-wide isotopic composition data (newly unpublished and published) for groundwater resources in the UAE to establish an innovative and integrated dataset with web-based Geographic Information System (GIS) technologies. This dataset provides users with the ability to access, explore, showcase, and analyze the isotopic composition of any water sample. In addition, and a machine learning method to cluster groundwater isotopes and generate geographic decision areas with distinct groundwater zones. The study will help to solve the problem of the unclear boundary of groundwater zoning in the UAE and contribute to the sustainable management of groundwater resources.  2 Geology and hydrogeology The investigated region comprises the UAE, which has an arid to hyper-arid climate with topography, temperature and rainfall varying greatly in space and time ( Fig. 1 ). The annual average temperature is 28°C, with lower values in the eastern mountainous area, ranging from 22°C in the northeast to >30°C in the south (Fig. 1 a). The annual average precipitation is about 100 mm, but it is uneven, depending on the weather conditions, geographical location, local topography, and rainfall mechanisms (Fig. 1 b). The eastern and northeastern mountainous areas have higher rainfall than the average level, while this trend changes to less than average in the rest of the studied region. The source of moisture and rainfall varies between winter and summer times, with frontal rain occurring when the dry polar air mass meets the warm and humid air from the Gulf in winter. The summer rainfall is controlled by the monsoon retreat and is caused by the convective lifting mechanism (Doyle et al., 2021). The high average temperature of the region results in relatively high annual average evaporation at a level of more than 3300 mm. The topography of the region varies from the mountains in the east, the gravel plains, and wadis on both sides of the mountains with the sand dunes and the sabkha flats covering about 90 % of the region ( Fig. 2 a). The Hajar Mountains in the northern and eastern parts of the UAE, along with the lower-lying coastal areas, create a natural flow gradient for the groundwater toward the coast ( Fig. 3 ). In general, the regional groundwater flow in the UAE is influenced by topography, the aquifer system, and the amount of precipitation and abstraction. The UAE aquifer systems include the gravel plains, sand dune, carbonates, ophiolite, and coastal Sabkha (referred to here as coastal) aquifers (Industry, 2015). The interconnection among aquifer systems in the UAE may differ based on local geological and hydrogeological factors, as well as the characteristics of groundwater flow patterns. However, the targeted aquifer systems in this study represent only the shallow aquifers (<100 m depth). These aquifers are partly connected on the surface through the precipitation and flash flooding but at depth topography and geologic setting may affect the connection between aquifers. In the UAE, the main fresh groundwater reserve is located within the gravel alluvial deposits, as illustrated in Fig. 2 b. The sand dune aquifer covers around 74 % of the country's total area and is predominantly recharged from the western side of the mountain. The gravel plain aquifer is distributed on both sides of Hajar Mountains. The aquifer, characterized by its unconfined, porous nature, and variable productivity and thickness, consists mainly of sand, and gravels. The geological and environmental conditions in the vicinity of these aquifers play a significant role in affecting water quality, flow and evolution. It is evident that water salinity increased spatially and temporally along the regional flow direction from the mountains to the Gulf (Fig. 3 ). The groundwater depth varies from a few meters to more than 100 m in the dune areas. The sand dunes in the Liwa area surrounding Mzeerah village create an excellent shallow aquifer system, covering a significant 74 % of the UAE's total area. This aquifer level gradually rises to 250 m above sea level near Mzeerah, especially along the western coast. Moreover, the carbonates aquifers are extended in the northern region, as well as Jabal Hafeet catchment in Al-Ain region. The primary source of natural replenishment for the aquifer systems is derived from the infiltration of water from wadi flows originating in the mountainous areas. The carbonate aquifer at Jabal Hafeet is made of limestone and marl interbedded with gypsum, dolomite and evaporates of Lower Eocene to Miocene age. This aquifer is mainly confined and overlies a confining impermeable clay or anhydrite that delimits its water level. The total salinity ranges from less than 10,000 to more than 250,000 mg/L (Fig. 2 c), depending on the physiographic setting and the geographic location. The ophiolite aquifer is in the northwestern part of UAE. The tectonic elements control the potential storage and movement of groundwater in this aquifer. Despite its potential, the ophiolite aquifer is not yet fully studied and needs further investigations.  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Groundwater sampling and analysis Groundwater (141 samples) was collected from active wells in mainly farmed land that uses submersible pumps. All groundwater samples were taken 30 min to one hour after pumping to ensure groundwater flow. Temperature, pH and total dissolved solids (TDS) of the water were determined on site using the WTW-COND-3301 instrument at errors of ±0.3°C, ±0.05, and 5 % respectively. The groundwater was sampled in 10 ML glass bottles and sealed at 4°C for the analysis of stable hydrogen and oxygen isotopes. Analysis of the samples was done using Picarro 2120 and L2130-i. Each sample was tested at least three times with errors for δ18 O: 0.02 ‰ and δ2 H: 0.1 ‰. The stable isotope results are expressed in per mil (δ) values, referring to the Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) using Eq. 1 :(1) δ  sample   = R  sample   − R  standard      / ( R  standard   )  × 1000      where R  sample     and R  standard     represent the values of the collected samples and standards, respectively. Moreover, the deuterium excess (d-excess) has been applied to provide valuable information about the origin of the water. Deuterium excess is defined as: d-excess = δD - 8 * δ18 O (Craig, 1961; Dansgaard, 1964 ), Where δD and δ18 O are the stable hydrogen and oxygen isotope ratios, respectively, relative to a standard.  3.2 Isotope data compilation and Web-GIS platform construction In order to make optimal use of the stable isotopes composition of groundwater examined in this research, findings from 8 literature references, both published and unpublished, with 342 groundwater well are integrated into a geospatial dataset (  Table 1 ). The dataset includes various attributes such as sample ID, location, aquifer system type, δ18 O, δ2 H, TDS, pH, temperature, groundwater level, hydraulic connectivity, slope, land use, and literature source ( Fig. 4  and Table 1 ). The distribution of groundwater isotopes in the UAE has been made accessible by sharing the data as a web layer on the ArcGIS Online platform. This web-based application enables users to explore, edit, add and analyze scale the data as needed. Users can utilize various functionalities such as zooming, locating, and querying on the map, and access detailed information about each sample point and a summary table of sampling data through pop-up windows. To evaluate the internal consistency of groundwater isotope data collected from different literature sources and this study, Cronbach’s coefficient of reliability is applied as an evaluation indicator. Cronbach’s coefficient of reliability is a statistical method for measuring the correlation between multiple variables, ranging from 0 to 1. The closer to 1 indicates a higher correlation and the closer to 0 indicates a lower correlation. Reliability is defined as the ratio of the true score variance to the observed score variance. The formula for Cronbach's alpha is expressed in Eq. 2 :(2) α = (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - Σσ²i / σ²total )    Where: k is the number of items in the scale, σ²i is the variance of the individual items and σ²total  is the variance of the total scores. In the present study, we calculated the Cronbach’s coefficient of reliability between different data sources. Our data errors, in the Python environment and the Bootstrap confidence interval, for δ18 O and δ2 H from all collected data sources are recalculated to have a Cronbach's alpha coefficient (0.51–0.67), with a mean of 0.6. This range and mean value are reasonable considering the large set of collected isotope data.  3.3 Visualization of isotopic zones using machine learning The visualization of groundwater isotopic boundary map for the studied arid area was established, for the first time, to delineate decision boundaries for management of groundwater zones. Within the Python language environment, machine-learning functions from GeoZ and Scipy third-party libraries were utilized (ElHaj et al., 2023; Virtanen et al., 2020 ). The evaluation included an assessment of clustering methods from 9 different types of machine learning clustering algorithms(K-means, Affinity Propagation (AP), Agglomerative Clustering (AC), Birch, DBSCAN, Mean Shift (MS), OPTICS Spectral Clustering (OSC) and Gaussian Mixture (GM), using three commonly employed clustering evaluation indicators The three indicators include the Silhouette and the Calinski Harabasz methods with the higher scores, the better is the clustering effect and the Davies Bouldin method with the lower scores, the better is the clustering effect ( Table 3 ). We calculate a comprehensive score sum according to the formula.(3) Cos = Sis  ∑ 1  9   Sis   ̅    − Das  ∑ 1  9   Das   ̅    + Cas  ∑ 1  9   Cas   ̅        Where Cos is the comprehensive scores and Sis, Das and Cas are the Silhouette, Davies Bouldin and Calinski Harabasz scores respectively. The comprehensive scoring suggests the K-means (KM) to be the most suitable with an optimal number of 4 clusters (Table 3 ). The clustering model input included four features, longitude, latitude, δ18 O and D-excess as labels. By eliminating the need for predefined centroids or corresponding accuracy evaluation metrics, the spatial categories of the groundwater data are predicted. Our model was trained to create decision boundaries or regions (DZ) around each class. The K-means method serves as a valuable tool for preliminary judgment in administrative planning (Liu et al., 2015 ; Mohammadrezapour et al., 2020 ) while the use of regression equations to describe the characteristics and origins of local groundwater under different aquifer conditions can lead to significant discontinuities. The output of the clustering model was projected to the geographic coordinate system (GCS) and each cluster group was assigned a Thiessen polygon based on the previously obtained cluster label ID. The Thiessen Polygons boundaries were established on statistically equal-length boundaries using the ArcGIS toolbox Create Thiessen Polygons. The Thiessen Polygon method considered each sample point as a node and constructed an irregular polygon mesh. We assigned a different color to each polygon based on the cluster center that each node belonged to with a final spatial groundwater boundary zoning map.   4 Results and discussions 4.1 Isotopic composition of the aquifer system In general, the range of groundwater isotopic composition for all aquifer systems are spread between −13 to +8 ‰ for δ18 O and at −40 to+20 ‰ for δ2 H ( Fig. 5 a). This wide variation of isotopic composition reflects the effect of many factors such as different sources of water vapor, evaporation rate, latitude and altitudes and subsurface conditions such as rock-water interaction and mixing with different groundwater sources (Fig. 5 a). Groundwaters from the coastal region exhibit a wide range of variation, from −2.89–5.51 ‰, and from −42.29–22.65 ‰ for δ18 O and δ2 H, respectively (Fig. 5 b). This variation indicates different moisture sources of precipitation. The results indicate the occurrence of three groups of groundwater along the coastal region of UAE: Group 1 fall left to the LMWL which indicates evaporation before recharge, and/or mixing of water sources, Group 2 fits around the LMWL indicating that these groundwater samples are recharged from the modern precipitation and Group 3 falls right to the LMWL demonstrating water rock interaction or mixing of groundwater with surface water or waters from different aquifers (Fig. 5 a). In the coastal region, the current replenishment of precipitation is sustained by the geological and geomorphological conditions dominated at the mouths of large wadis temporary runoff. These wadis dissect the sedimentary rocks, collect rainfall and occasional flash floods, and then discharge into the coastal plains of the Arabian Gulf (Fig. 5 c and d). The δ2 H-δ18 O diagram indicates that isotopic composition is more depleted for some samples than the current rainfall, suggesting a contribution from leakage upward along the deep-seated faults, into the coastal aquifers (Fig. 5 d). Additionally, the deviation of the coastal groundwater samples from the Global Meteoric Water Line (GMWL) could be attributed to various natural and human-induced mechanisms, including isotopic enrichment from evaporative wadi flash floods, evaporation from the water table, intrusion of seawater, and potential input from salt marshes and lakes located along the coastal plains (Fig. 5 c). The isotopic composition of the groundwater in the carbonate aquifers ( Fig. 6 a) at the northern part indicates (δ18 O: −2.07–0 ‰, average −1.36 ‰; δ2 H: −10.44–0.1 ‰, average −6.05 ‰) and of Jabal Hafeet (δ18 O: −2.48–0.23 ‰, average −1.72 ‰; δ2 H: −15.65 to −9.5 ‰，average −14.25 ‰) which are below at or the LMWL. Groundwater from the carbonate aquifer in Jabal Hafeet is more depleted compared to those from the carbonate aquifer in the western areas of the UAE. These samples are mostly plotted to the right of the LMWL compared to those of samples of the carbonate aquifer along the line. This feature could be attributed to the mixing between the shallow and deep groundwater systems that were suggested to have deep-rooted migration of the groundwater that has also altered the oxygen and hydrogen isotopes (Gómez-Alday et al., 2022 ). Moreover, the enrichment of the isotopic composition of the groundwater in the western carbonate aquifer could potentially be attributed to significant inputs from recent precipitation that has accumulated over the high topographic features and subsequently flowed westward through the wadi channels into the carbonate aquifers (Fig. 6 b). Consequently, the variations in slopes and intercepts observed in carbonate aquifers across different setting of the UAE can be indicative of the influence of several precipitation moisture sources, evaporation patterns, and potential mixing with deep recharge sources. Among the groundwater investigated, the ophiolite aquifer has the most depleted characteristics (δ18 O: −4.2–1.14 ‰, average −2.14 ‰; δ2 H: −11.32–11 ‰, average −2.87 ‰). Overall, the isotope compositions of the eastern gravel, ophiolite, and northern carbonate aquifers were comparable, indicating the existence of a common source of recharge which is mainly modern precipitation (Fig. 6 ). The high 36 Cl in groundwater of the ophiolite aquifer compared to the eastern gravel plain was suggested to reflect the absence of seawater intrusion (Murad and Krishnamurthy, 2004). The δ2 H and δ18 O isotopic ranges in the gravel plains, eastern and western, are (δ18 O: −2.36–0.01 ‰, average −1.39 ‰; δ2 H: −6.74–0.19 ‰, average −3.43 ‰) for the eastern part and (δ18 O: −12.88–4.5 ‰, average −0.85 ‰; δ2 : −32.2–15.1 ‰, average −4.31 ‰) for the western part (Fig. 6 ). Based on the high d-excess (average of 7.7 ‰) for the eastern part, it can be inferred that precipitation is the main recharge source. The δ2 H and δ18 O isotopic distributions in the western gravel plains indicate values that suggest enrichment of the heavy isotopes in precipitation by evaporation before recharging the groundwater. A possible cause for this is both the relatively higher temperature in this aquifer region and the occurrence of muddy intercalations in the sediments that reduced the infiltration capacity of rainwater to be enriched before infiltrating into the groundwater. The range of δ2 H and δ18 O in groundwater of the Quaternary sand dune saquifer is (δ18 O: −3.86–7.72 ‰, average 0.91 ‰; δ2 H: −11.13–29.54 ‰, average 0.8 ‰). The groundwater is enriched in both heavy isotopes and is comparable to the gravel plain aquifer. ( Fig. 7 ), indicating the effects of evaporation before groundwater recharges. The 14 C activity in groundwater gave a rather old age (around 16–20 kyr; (Ji et al., 2020 ) for the most southern part of the sand dune system, suggesting a recharge source during the glacial age where the climate was relatively humid. Studies of lake sediments in Rub al Khali, southern Saudi Arabia, found that the paleoclimate during the late Pleistocene and early Holocene had two wet periods, one between 6000 and 9000 BP and another between 21000 and 30000 BP. It was predicted that the Holocene precipitation recharged groundwater in most southern sand dune system (known as the Liwa area) between 5500 and 9000 BP (Ji et al., 2020; Wood and Imes, 2003 ). Our data for groundwater in the sand dunes region show δ2 H/δ18 O slope value at 2.48 ‰, which were close to the results reported (slope of δ2 H/δ18 O was 2.19 ‰) in (Wood, 2011; Wood and Imes, 2003 ) for paleo-groundwater.  4.2 Tracing of the moisture sources The importance of deuterium excess in groundwater studies includes identification of water sources, tracing moisture sources and atmospheric processes, detecting evaporation and mixing processes, paleoclimate reconstruction and identifying groundwater flow paths and residence times (Ji et al., 2020; Wood, 2011; Wood and Imes, 2003 ). The UAE rainwater d-excess values range from −16.8–24.5 ‰, with an average of 8.7 ‰ (Ji et al., 2020 ). While the d-excess values of groundwater samples ranged between −32.2 and 21.9 ‰, with an average of 1.4 ‰ suggesting inputs from various sources and the evolutionary trend of the precipitation to the groundwater aquifer. The correlation between the oxygen isotope composition (δ18 O) of groundwater and the altitude of the groundwater recharge area is evident, with lower δ18 O values potentially indicating recharge from high-altitude areas, and higher δ18 O values suggesting recharge from lower-elevation areas ( Fig. 8 a). As groundwater moves downward, its isotopic composition can be altered by processes such as evaporation, water-rock interaction, and mixing with other water sources, resulting in a negative correlation between d-excess and δ18 O (Fig. 8 b). The relationship between δ18 O and TDS confirms the impact of evaporation, mixing, and dissolution processes on groundwater aquifers (Fig. 8 c). Furthermore, mineral dissolution resulting from rock-water interaction increases groundwater salinity and may adjust the stable isotopes fractionation of the groundwater to reach equilibrium conditions with the aquifer system, as indicated by the d-excess value (Fig. 8 d). The UAE, situated in the Arabian Peninsula, experiences a diverse range of air masses that shape the precipitation ( Fig. 9  and references therein). These include the Modified Maritime Tropical (MMT) air mass, originating from the Indian Ocean and Arabian Gulf, characterized by warm, moist conditions and higher δ18 O and δ2 H isotopic signatures. The Continental Tropical (CT) air mass, originating from the Arabian Peninsula, brings hot, dry weather with relatively prominent δ18 O and δ2 H due to evaporation. The Continental Polar (CP) air mass, originating from central Asia and Siberia, with cooler and drier conditions during winter with lower δ18 O and δ2 H values compared to other air masses. Lastly, the Mediterranean (MP) air mass, originating from the Mediterranean Sea, brings cooler, wetter conditions during winter with relatively lower δ18 O and δ2 H isotopic signatures. A continuous depletion of δ18 O associated with the increase in elevation has been observed in the samples collected along a cross section from the east to west. Moreover, the isotopic composition of groundwater can be altered by the occurrence of different flow systems or their mixing, leading to distinct cluster groups. Furthermore, it is essential to consider the potential mixing of the regional groundwater system with local systems. The mixing probably results from the effect of fracture systems, as well as surface water and groundwater. Rock water interaction also changes the salinity of groundwater which provides clues to pathways of isotopic fractionation. The low TDS of rainfall (less than 100 mg/L) is changed as it infiltrates and accumulates in the pores of aquifers.  4.3 Groundwater decision boundary delineation The different testing and evaluation algorithms outlined in Section 3.3  suggested K-means (KM) as the optimal clustering algorithm method. The clustering groups appear better separated in the d18 O-d2 H compared to d18 O-D-excess pairs, with two end members and two overlapping groups. The clusters spatial distribution (DZ 1–4: Fig. 9 ) largely follows the climatic spatial variability, where the rainfall in the eastern and northeastern mountainous area was higher than that in the western and southwestern desert areas. This is in turn reflected in the depletion of the groups 1, 2 and 4 which agreed with the average isotopic signatures of limestone, ophiolite and gravel plain aquifers ( Fig. 10 ). However, it is worth mentioning that DZ boundaries are inconsistent with the aquifer boundaries (Fig. 10 ). This indicates that, on a regional scale, the recharge mechanisms of groundwater were mainly controlled by climatic and topographic conditions rather than by the geological conditions of the aquifer. The DZ boundaries also indicate a spatial distribution consistent with the regional groundwater level distribution (Fig. 2 ). The eastern mountains, northeastern and southwestern regions all had shallow groundwater levels. Additionally, DZ 3 may have suffered seawater intrusion, and further data are needed to confirm this observation. DZ 4 corresponds to the location of the Jabal Hafeet aquifer and proximity to the recharge front (Hajar Mountains). However, DZ 1 encompasses the intersection of carbonates, eastern gravel, and ophiolite aquifers, further illustrating common groundwater recharge sources for the three aquifers. The boundary between DZ 3 and 4 was more westward than that of the lithological boundary of the western gravel aquifer. This may indicate the extension of the western gravel aquifer groundwater isotopic signature outside the aquifer system boundaries, which is due to the occurrence of these sediments along the mountain wadies below the sand dunes aquifer system. The boundary line between DZ 3 and 2 can be regarded as the hydraulic interactional boundary, with unpredictable dynamic exchange, between the western gravel aquifer and sand dune aquifer and beyond it. These aquifers may have a limited exchange of water volume and quality. This phenomenon is well illustrated by the temporal development of salinity due to the abstraction of groundwater and the increase in the salinity of groundwater in many areas.  4.4 Implication and constraints for the water resources management UAE, similar to arid areas, is currently exploring alternative sources of fresh water to tackle the challenges caused by the natural factors such as climate changes and human induced activities including population growth and the excessive extraction of groundwater. The development of sustainable management scenarios for groundwater resources in UAE is a priority for governmental agencies and research sectors. However, the collection of country-scale field measurements needed for sustainable management purposes is a challenge due to the limited accessibility and cost of these measurements. It is crucial to establish a database which integrates country-scale field measurements, and easy access for decision makers, researchers, and local communities. This database can play a vital role in guiding future field data collection efforts, reducing the resources and time required for field activities, and enabling researchers to address complex scientific questions at a country- and aquifer-scale. Among many data sets on groundwater, stable isotopes are vital for sustainable groundwater management. To ensure the web application remains current, researchers can easily add additional isotopic data as it becomes available. By downloading the current database for their specific area of interest and adding new data, researchers can save time, effort, and resources that would have been spent on collecting redundant field measurements. This tool will also assist in guiding field data collection by using available resources. Furthermore, by compiling historical isotopic composition data for water samples in UAE, a better understanding of the stable isotopic compositions of water resources at a country-wide scale will be achieved, leading to improved knowledge of recharge mechanisms throughout the country. This approach will allow the scientific community to address important scientific questions at both country and aquifer scales. Groundwater isotopes can also be used in the calibration of numerical groundwater models, as they are able to independently calculate groundwater flow rates (Ji et al., 2020 ). Monitoring stable isotopes in groundwater allows for assessing the efficiency of the temporary reservoir artificial recharge, determining the extent of seawater intrusion and the impact of farming and landscaping on groundwater. The challenge of accurate evaluation of groundwater sources in arid environments was further complicated by climate change. Consequently, the decision boundary delineation technology used here for the stable isotopic provides a reference for partitioning groundwater systems. Large-scale high-resolution isotopic sampling can deliver valuable indications for crucial locations in monitoring efforts, such as identifying or diagnosing sources of rapid recharge. It is important to acknowledge the constraints associated with creating and building the isotopic database of groundwater in the present research. One notable limitation is the distribution of isotopic data within the database, resulting in higher concentrations in certain regions and sparse data in others. Furthermore, the spatial resolution of the data may be coarse, lacking the level of detail required for comprehensive local-level investigations. Moreover, the temporal coverage of country-based database is often irregular, with data spanning diverse time periods in different regions. This inconsistency can present challenges in identifying and analyzing changes in isotopic signatures over time. Also, at the regional scale, databases might not contain comprehensive metadata, such as detailed chemical analysis, water level and lithologic logs. Without this essential related information, interpreting and comparing the data effectively could be challenging. In order to overcome these limitations, it is essential to apply some approaches such as supplementing country-level data with locally collected, high-resolution isotopic information; collaborating with international networks and initiatives to improve data sharing and harmonization; developing comprehensive, global-scale isotopic databases that can accurately capture the spatial and temporal variability of groundwater and precipitation isotopes. By addressing these constraints, researchers can enhance the reliability of isotopic data for water resources studies and applications, including the tracing of recharge sources and the reconstruction of past climatic conditions.   5 Conclusions We employed machine learning approach using stable isotopes of oxygen and hydrogen in groundwater to cluster spatial boundary regions in the arid climate region (UAE). The results indicated four major groundwater zones and isotopic landscapes that were mainly influenced by meteorological and topographic conditions, rather than by aquifer boundaries. We also identified some issues that need more attention and monitoring, such as the seawater intrusion, the unique fresh groundwater system, and the dynamic interaction between the different aquifer systems. Our results provide a new boundary clustering tool useful for the evaluation and management of groundwater resources in arid regions. This study also established, for the first time, an online sharing platform for UAE groundwater stable isotopes, providing data support and a cooperation platform for groundwater resource monitoring, management and innovation. We propose a stable isotopic “hot spots” recognition of groundwater with protection zones that can be vital for groundwater management in arid regions.
1 Introduction Vegetation constitutes a crucial link between the soil, water, and the atmosphere, serving as a fundamental component for sustaining ecosystem viability (Hoffmann and Jackson, 2000 ). Vegetation also plays an important regulatory role in hydrological systems; it can intercept precipitation and facilitate its evaporation into the atmosphere, thereby diminishing direct surface runoff into rivers and lakes and contributing to flood control (Bruijnzeel, 2004; Ellison et al., 2017 ). The subterranean root systems of vegetation absorb water and maintain groundwater levels, facilitating the provision of continuous groundwater resources and functioning as key elements of water resource management (Jackson et al., 2009 ). Moreover, vegetation greenery serves to augment local transpiration, thereby facilitating atmospheric moisture transport and stimulating precipitation in regions situated downwind; consequently, it assumes a pivotal role in the context of climate regulation (Cui et al., 2022 ). In summary, vegetation exerts a paramount influence on hydrological systems, aiding in the preserving of ecological equilibrium, reducing of flood and drought hazards, enhancing of water quality, safeguarding of water resources, and the supporting the sustainable human society development (Liu et al., 2020 ). Consequently, acknowledging the effect of vegetation on hydrological processes is imperative for ensuring the sustainability of water resources and ecosystems. The impact of vegetation alteration on hydrological variables has been extensively examined (Chen and Guan, 2021; Deng et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Zhang et al. (2022b)  empirically elucidated the bidirectional relationship between global vegetation productivity and soil moisture. Their findings underscored the considerable dependence of soil moisture changes on variations in vegetation productivity; this relationship is positive in approximately 88% of regions worldwide, while the remaining 12% exhibited a negative correlation. Xiao et al. (2023) highlighted the noteworthy negative correlation between changes in terrestrial water storage and shifts in vegetation within arid or semi-arid regions of China. Conversely, in more humid areas, a significant positive correlation between changes in terrestrial water storage and variations in vegetation was observed. It is evident that the impact of vegetation greening on hydrological variables may manifest differently within distinct climatic zones. Li et al. (2021) . quantified the ecohydrological consequences of large-scale afforestation in the semi-arid regions of China and established that vegetation restoration notably mitigates soil erosion and surface runoff within the Haihe River Basin. Likewise, a study in China's Loess Plateau also showed that greening vegetation can lead to reduced runoff and drying of top soil. The process of vegetation greening is inclined to amplify evapotranspiration (Jiao et al., 2017 ). In arid regions, given the limited availability of precipitation, increased transpiration can precipitate a decline in soil moisture and runoff, resulting in reduced terrestrial water storage (Chen et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023 ). Conversely, in more humid areas characterized by a relatively abundant supply of precipitation, the influence of vegetation greening on the water cycle is often mitigated by the profusion of available precipitation. Within humid regions, quantifying hydrological process responses to vegetation changes and differentiating between the effects of vegetation greening and climate change on the water cycle is very challenging. Hydrological models are indispensable tools for assessing the impacts of variations in vegetation and climate on hydrological processes. Models in this domain include the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC), Land Surface Models (LSMs), and Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) (Alvarenga et al., 2016; Dash et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2021; Uniyal et al., 2023 ). Renowned for its versatile modules and open-source code, SWAT has become the prevalent choice for watershed research in diverse geographical regions and environmental settings. Its adaptability is considerably enhanced by its capacity for user-driven secondary development (Arnold and Allen, 1996 ). However, in the traditional SWAT model, the growth cycle of vegetation is simulated based on temperature using the Environmental Policy Integrated Climate (EPIC) model, while tropical or subtropical vegetation growth is mainly controlled by precipitation. Traditional SWAT modeling methods encounter challenges in accurately capturing the real growth patterns of vegetation (Ma et al., 2019; Strauch and Volk, 2013 ). Moreover, they are unable to disentangle the distinct impacts of climate change and vegetation alterations on hydrological processes when climate variables are employed to simulate vegetation growth. In response to these challenges, Ma et al. (2019)  introduced an innovative approach that leverages the remote sensing-derived Leaf Area Index (LAI) to enhance the dynamic modeling of vegetation within SWAT. This refinement allows for a more precise representation of the effects of vegetation alteration on hydrological processes, which has enhanced the accuracy of the model, particularly in subtropical regions. Of paramount significance, this refined modeling approach can autonomously simulate hydrological processes influenced by climate change or variations in vegetation. Zhang et al. (2022a)  and Chang et al. (2023)  demonstrated the successful use of remote sensing-derived LAI to enhance the SWAT model for simulating ecohydrological processes within the East River Basin and Huxi Basin in China. These investigations provided compelling empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of integrating remote-sensing-derived LAI to enhance the precision of SWAT modeling within humid subtropical regions. We selected the Xiangjiang River Basin (XRB) as the study area. The XRB is a typical moist subtropical region that has experienced rapid vegetation changes over the past 20 years. Based on the improved SWAT model, we explored the impact of vegetation changes on hydrological processes in the subtropical basin. The objectives of this research were to: (1) enhance dynamic modeling of vegetation within the SWAT model through the integration of remote sensing-derived LAI, thereby enabling more precise simulations of hydrological processes in the XRB; (2) assess the sensitivity of hydrological variables within the XRB to vegetation change; and (3) disentangle the relative contributions of climate change and vegetation greening to the direct impacts of changes in hydrological variables within the XRB. This study is a foundational reference for informing water resource protection and management initiatives in subtropical regions.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study area is situated within the Dongting Lake system of the Yangtze River Basin in China. The XRB is geographically located in central south China (24°38′06″N–28°40′23″N and 110°10′34″E–114°15′00″E), and the basin has a drainage area of approximately 94,721 km2 . The topography within the basin is undulating, with elevated terrain in the southern regions and a gradual descent toward the north. The altitudinal range spans from sea level (0 m) to an elevation of 2100 m. The XRB is positioned within the subtropical monsoon zone, with an average annual temperature ranging between 16 °C and 18 °C, and average annual precipitation of 1300–1600 mm. The predominant land cover types in this basin are forest land (63 %), cultivated land (29 %), and grassland (4 %) (Liang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2022c ). The Xiangjiang River is the primary river in the region; it originates in Jingfengling before flowing northward and merging with Dongting Lake. The course of the river is traditionally divided into the upper, middle, and lower reaches, delineated by geographic landmarks such as Hengyang and Laobutou ( Fig. 1 ).  2.2 Data The input data for the SWAT model encompass various key components including topographical information, land use classifications, soil attributes, meteorological data, and vegetation parameters. In this study, the XRB sub-basins were delineated using a digital elevation model (DEM). Land use data from 2010 were reclassified to align them with the requisite SWAT categories. Soil data were used to ascertain pertinent soil properties within the basin, and daily weather records from 14 meteorological stations of the China Meteorological Administration from 2001 to 2020 were used to simulate the SWAT input meteorological data. The growth status of the vegetation was estimated based on remote sensing LAI data to replace the simulated vegetation growth data in the SWAT model. The SWAT model was calibrated and validated using monthly runoff data acquired from three observation stations spanning the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the XRB (Xiangtan, Hengyang, and Laobutou stations) and the observational data were from 2001–2020.  Table 1   2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Model description The SWAT distributed hydrological model has been extensively used to investigate water circulation and sedimentation within watershed areas (Arnold and Allen, 1996 ). This model is distinguished by its robust physical mechanisms, high computational efficiency, and capacity for continuous long-term simulations. By leveraging the spatial information sourced from remote sensing and geographical data, the SWAT model was used to simulate intricate hydrological processes, including watershed runoff and evaporation. The hydrological processes used in this study were based on the following fundamental water balance equations:(1) SW  t   = SW  0   +  ∑ i = 1  t   P  i    −  ET  i   −  Q  surf ,  i   −  Q  gw , i    −  W  seep , i           In this context, SW  (mm) represents the soil moisture content, where “i” designates the time step (with the daily time step set in this study), and “t” signifies the simulation time periods, and P , ET , Q surf  , Q gw  , and, W seep   represent precipitation, actual evapotranspiration, surface runoff, groundwater return flow, and soil water percolation, respectively (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). In the process of establishing the SWAT model for this study, 54 sub-watersheds were delineated based on the DEM of the study area with reference to existing studies (Liang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2022b ), using a threshold of 100,000 ha. These sub-watersheds were further subdivided using criteria such as slope grade, soil type, and land use type, with a uniform threshold of 10 %, resulting in 624 hydrologic response units (HRUs).  2.3.2 Model modification The simplified version of the EPIC model incorporated into SWAT was originally tailored for temperate regions, where it naturally simulates the growth cycle of vegetation primarily based on temperature. However, the growth of tropical and subtropical vegetation is mainly influenced by rainfall, making them less applicable to subtropical regions (Ma et al., 2019 ). The dynamic simulation of vegetation within a watershed system depends on key parameters found in the vegetation database, and the LAI is a pivotal component (Chang et al., 2023; Neitsch et al., 2011 ). Vegetation influences hydrological processes through its impact on variables such as evapotranspiration, precipitation interception, and soil water percolation. The remote sensing product LAI effectively captures the realistic dynamics of vegetation. With reference to the research of Ma et al. (2019)  and Chang et al. (2023) , remote sensing LAI observation data from various periods were used in this study to replace the EPIC vegetation parameters in the SWAT model. This enabled the effects of vegetation changes on hydrological variables to be evaluated. Using MCD15A2H data synthesized at a 500-m resolution every 8 d, and applying resampling and linear interpolation techniques, a continuous daily LAI dataset was constructed at a finer 30-m resolution within the study area. To implement this modification, the source code within the growth subroutine (grow.f) relating to LAI generation in SWAT was adapted to allow the integration of the observed LAI data into the corresponding HRUs (Luan et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2019 ).  2.3.3 Model calibration and validation The accuracy of SWAT simulations is significantly contingent on the calibration and validation processes. In this study, calibration was carried out using the auto-calibration feature of SWAT-CUP with the SUFI-2 algorithm (Jing et al., 2021 ). Monthly runoff data observed at three hydrological stations within the XRB (Xiangtan, Hengyang, and Laobutou) spanning the period from 2001 to 2020 were selected for the calibration and verification of the SWAT model. The calibration used 15 years of data (2001–2015), whereas the subsequent 5 years of data (2016–2020) were reserved for model validation. Owing to data limitations, Laobutou station only provided runoff data for the years 2016–2020 for model validation. In this study, 20 commonly used calibration parameters were considered and a parameter sensitivity analysis was conducted (Li and Fang, 2021; Zhu et al., 2022a ); specific details are provided in the Supplementary material  (Table S1 ). The model's performance was assessed using three key indicators: the coefficient of determination (R2 ), the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), and the percent bias (PBIAS). Generally, the acceptability criteria for these indicators are R2  > 0.6, NSE > 0.5, and PBIAS within ±25 % (Moriasi et al., 2007; Santhi et al., 2001 ).  2.3.4 Experimental design We selected factor separation methods with reference to previous research (Bai et al., 2019; Song et al., 2023; Stein and Alpert, 1993 ), and devised a set of 8 simulation experiments ( Table 2 ) to analyze the contributions of vegetation and climate to the hydrological processes in the XRB. In these experiments, we singled out three driving factors (LAI, potential evapotranspiration (PET), and precipitation (P)), which served as proxies for climate and vegetation impacts on hydrological variables. Precipitation is a pivotal driver of the global water cycle, and it plays a fundamental role in facilitating atmospheric water circulation. Potential evapotranspiration is a composite indicator that encapsulates the influence of temperature, air humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation on the atmospheric demand for evapotranspiration (Song et al., 2023 ). The LAI of vegetation characterizes the plant canopy structure and plays a central role in processes, such as radiation absorption, precipitation interception, water balance, and energy conversion (Cui et al., 2022 ). This study draws on the approach used by Song et al. (2023)  and uses the detrending method to remove linear trends from annual time series data while preserving seasonal variations. We devised distinct simulation experiments using the original driving data and the generated detrended driving data, and then executed the SWAT model. It should be noted that the observed forcing PET was determined by operating the SWAT model with observed data inputs, including temperature, humidity, solar radiation, and wind speed. The detrended forced PET was generated by employing a model driven by detrended temperature data, among other variables.  2.3.5 Statistical analysis This study calculated the single-factor effects and multi-factor interaction effects of LAI, P, and PET respectively. The formula for calculating a single factor effect, such as the LAI effect, is as follows,(2) E  LAI   = f LAI    − f ( control )      The interaction effect of the two factors is determined by subtracting the single factor effect from the combined effect of the two factors. For instance, the formula for calculating the interaction effect of LAI and P is as follows,(3) E  LAI * P   = f LAI , P    − f control    − E  LAI   − E  P        The interaction effect of the three factors is computed as the combined effect of the three factors, subtracting the single-factor effect, and further subtracting the pairwise interaction effect between the three factors. The formula for this calculation is as follows,(4) E  LAI * P * PET   = f LAI , P , PET    − f control    − E  LAI   − E  P   − E  PET   − E  LAI * P   − E  LAI * PET   − E  P * PET        Trend analysis: In this study, the Sen's slope and Mann-Kendall trend tests were employed to determine the annual variations in vegetation (LAI), climatic factors (P and PET), and hydrological variables (evapotranspiration (ET), soil water storage (SW) and flow depth (Q)). Z-values were used to ascertain the direction and significance of the observed trends (Kendall, 1975, 1948; Mann, 1945 ). Sensitivity analysis: The degree of response of hydrological variables (taking ET as an example) to changes in LAI is referred to as sensitivity. It is indicated in both sets of experiments, namely f LAI    − f control       and f LAI , P , PET    − f P , PET       that the changes in hydrological variables are caused by variations in LAI. In this study, a sensitivity assessment of ET to changes in LAI was achieved by constructing linear regression equations at an annual scale for ΔET and ΔLAI. Contribution analysis: Taking LAI and ET as examples, the proportion of the impact of LAI changes in the XRB or each sub-basin on ET to the combined effect of vegetation and climate change on ET was considered to be the contribution of LAI to ET (Song et al., 2023 ).    3 Results 3.1 Model evaluation Based on a comparative analysis of monthly runoff data between simulations and observations at three stations (Xiangtan, Hengyang, and Laobutou), we calculated the values of R2 , NSE, and PBIAS. During the calibration period, the R2  values for Xiangtan and Hengyang stations were 0.95 and 0.69, the NSE values were 0.93 and 0.63, and the PBIAS values were −6.4 % and 14.4 %, respectively. During the validation period, the R2  values for Xiangtan, Hengyang, and Laobutou stations were 0.95, 0.92, and 0.74, the NSE values were 0.91, 0.83, and 0.68, and the PBIAS values were −6.7 %, −11.6 %, and 13.1 %, respectively. All of the calibration and validation results indicate the reliability of the simulated data ( Fig. 2 ). Additionally, we compared the monthly ET simulated by SWAT with remote sensing products. The results demonstrated the reliability of the simulated ET (Fig. S1 ).  3.2 Dynamic changes in driving factors and hydrological variables The vegetation exhibited a consistent and significant greening trend in the XRB from 2001 to 2020. The LAI increased from 1.53 in 2001 to 2.20 in 2020, with an average annual growth rate of 0.04. Spatially, the LAI across all sub-basins within the study area exhibited an increasing trend, with upstream sub-basins displaying a more pronounced augmentation in LAI trends. The P within the XRB demonstrated a positive interannual trend characterized by a slope of 5.99 mm/year. Spatially, precipitation in 44 sub-basins followed an upward trajectory, whereas the remaining sub-basins experienced a decline in precipitation levels. Concurrently, the PET of the XRB indicated an interannual downward trend with a slope of −3.56 mm/year. Spatially, the PET of 38 sub-basins showed a downward trend, while the PET of the remaining sub-basins showed an increasing trend ( Fig. 3  and  Fig. 4 ). The hydrological cycle of the XRB showed an accelerating trend. At the interannual scale, ET, SW, and Q all exhibited upward trends, with slopes of 0.11 mm/year, 0.34 mm/year, and 6.69 mm/year, respectively. Spatial heterogeneity was evident at the rate of change of the hydrological cycle. More than half of the sub-basins exhibited a significant increase in ET. 44 sub-basins experienced a pronounced rise in SW, primarily concentrated in the middle and lower reaches of the basin. Additionally, 42 sub-basins demonstrated a significant increase in Q, with a focus on the upper and lower reaches of the basin (Fig. 3  and Fig. 4 ).  3.3 Sensitivity of hydrological variables to vegetation changes The slopes of the ΔET, ΔSW, ΔQ, and ΔLAI relationships represent the sensitivity of hydrological variables to changes in LAI. The sensitivity of hydrological variables (ET, SW, and Q) to changes in LAI for the entire XRB is shown in  Fig. 5 , and  Fig. 6  shows the sensitivity of the hydrological variables (ET, SW, and Q) to changes in the LAI for individual sub-basins. The ΔET and ΔLAI in the XRB exhibited a significant positive linear relationship, with an increase of 14.12 mm in ET for each unit increase in LAI (Fig. 5 a). All sub-basins showed a significant positive linear relationship between ΔET and ΔLAI (Fig. S2 ). The most sensitive area in the study was the downstream sub-basin 15, where each unit increase in the LAI resulted in an increase of approximately 27.75 mm in ET. The least sensitive area was the midstream sub-basin 27, where each unit increase in LAI resulted in only about a 7.38 mm increase in ET (Fig. 6 a and Fig. S2 ) ΔSW and ΔLAI in the XRB showed a significant negative linear relationship, with each unit increase in LAI leading to a decrease of approximately 2.47 mm in SW (Fig. 5 b). Looking at the sub-basins, ΔSW and ΔLAI showed a significant negative linear relationship in all 52 sub-basins. Only sub-basins 6 and 28 did not pass the significance test (P < 0.05) (Fig. S3 ). Among these, sub-basin 3 displayed the highest sensitivity of SW to LAI changes, with a slope of −3.93 mm per unit of LAI; while conversely, sub-basin 2 exhibited the lowest sensitivity of SW to LAI changes, with a slope of −1.25 mm per unit of LAI (Fig. 6 b and Fig. S3 ). There was a significant negative linear relationship between ΔQ and ΔLAI in the XRB. Each unit increase in LAI led to a decrease of approximately 13.96 mm in Q for the entire XRB (Fig. 5 c). At the sub-basin level, all 54 sub-basins exhibited a significant negative linear relationship between ΔQ and ΔLAI. All sub-basins passed the significance test (P < 0.05) (Fig. S4 ). Among these, sub-basin 15 showed the highest sensitivity of Q to LAI changes, with each unit increase in LAI resulting in a decrease of approximately 27.94 mm in Q. Conversely, sub-basin 27 displayed the lowest sensitivity of Q to LAI changes, with each unit increase in LAI leading to a decrease of approximately 7.60 mm (Fig. 6 c and Fig. S4 ).  3.4 Contribution of vegetation greening and climate change to hydrological variables This study assessed the responses of hydrological variables in the Xiangjiang River Basin to vegetation greening and climate change. The change ratios of ET, SW, and Q relative to the control simulations (driven by detrended forcing data) during the single-factor simulations (actual LAI, P, and PET) are shown in  Fig. 7 . Across the entire XRB, changes in LAI resulted in a 2.18 % increase in ET while causing a 2.55 % decrease in SW and a 1.73 % decrease in Q. Changes in P led to 1.37 %, 3.10 %, and 12.54 % increases in ET, SW, and Q, respectively; and variations in PET led to 0.20 %, 0.72 %, and 0.33 % increases in ET, SW, and Q, respectively. From a sub-basin perspective, changes in LAI uniformly increased ET in all sub-basins, with the largest increase of approximately 5.40 % observed in sub-basin 17 and the smallest increase of only 0.38 % observed in sub-basin 22. Furthermore, LAI variations uniformly led to decreases in SW and Q across all sub-basins, with SW decreases not exceeding 6 %. Changes in LAI resulted in decreases in Q in all sub-basins, with decreases not exceeding 3.10 %. Changes in P led to decreases in ET, SW, and Q in 17 sub-basins (these regions showed a decreasing trend in P), while the other 37 sub-basins experienced increases in ET, SW, and Q. Variations in PET resulted in increases in ET in 15 sub-basins, including sub-basin 7, and decreases in ET in the remaining 39 sub-basins. Simultaneously, PET variations led to decreases in SW in 15 sub-basins, including sub-basin 2, and increases in ET in the remaining 39 sub-basins. Additionally, PET variations resulted in decreases in Q in 24 sub-basins, including sub-basin 6, and increases in ET in the remaining 30 sub-basins. The relative contributions of LAI, PET, and P changes to the hydrological variables (ET, SW, and Q) are shown in  Fig. 8 . Across the entire XRB, LAI primarily influenced changes in ET, contributing to approximately 41 %, whereas P and PET accounted for 26 % and 4 % of the variations in ET, respectively. LAI and P jointly influenced SW with contributions of 23 % and 28 %, respectively. It is of note that LAI had a negative impact on SW. Furthermore, the combined effects played a significant role in the SW variations. P dominated the Q variations with an 81 % contribution, whereas LAI exhibited a negative influence on Q with an 11 % contribution. Considering all sub-basins, the average relative contributions of LAI, P, and PET changes to ET were 18 %, 27 %, and 40 %, respectively. In the upstream sub-basins, the contribution of LAI to ET was minor, whereas the contributions of P and PET were approximately equal. In some downstream sub-basins (14, 18, 20, 21, 24, and 26), P made a smaller contribution to ET, whereas LAI and P made approximately equal contributions. The remaining sub-basins showed a larger contribution from PET to ET. The average relative contributions of LAI, P, and PET to SW were 12 %, 30 %, and 32 %, respectively. LAI made a smaller contribution to SW, whereas P and PET made roughly equal contributions. The average relative contributions of the LAI, P, and PET changes to Q were 7 %, 62 %, and 18 %, respectively. In some sub-basins (6, 22, 28, 42, 45, and 46), PET made a major contribution to Q, whereas P made a substantial contribution to other sub-basins. In the study area, the single factor effect had a much greater impact on hydrological variables than the combined effect (Fig. S5 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Hydrological response to vegetation changes This study has highlighted the hydrological response of a subtropical watershed to vegetation changes through sensitivity analysis, which has substantial implications for water resource conservation and management. In the XRB, ET demonstrated a positive sensitivity to LAI changes, whereas SW and Q showed negative sensitivities to LAI variations. Prior studies have demonstrated the significant impact of vegetation on hydrological processes within terrestrial ecosystems. An increase in vegetation cover enhances canopy interception, evaporation, leaf litter interception capacity, and water storage, thereby reducing water infiltration. Additionally, the expanded canopy area leads to increased evapotranspiration, primarily drawing from soil moisture, which is predominantly supplied by precipitation, surface water, and groundwater. Under unchanged climatic conditions, an increase in the vegetation canopy intensifies evaporation, resulting in reduced soil moisture and watershed runoff, consequently accelerating the hydrological cycle within the basin (Rasouli et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022a ). The sensitivities of hydrological variables to LAI changes differ among the sub-basins, and this may be related to changes in the magnitudes of LAI or hydrological variables (Luan et al., 2022 ). Moreover, Fu et al. (2023)  conducted pixel-based studies that suggested that the sensitivity of hydrological processes to vegetation greening may be influenced by climatic variations. In addition, the study of Luan et al. (2022)  on the Loess Plateau indicated that the sensitivity of evapotranspiration and runoff to vegetation changes intensified with increasing aridity. However, this phenomenon was less pronounced (refer to Supplementary material Fig. S6 ). This could be attributed to the location of the XRB within the subtropical monsoon region, where there is ample moisture. On an interannual scale within small watersheds, significant drought events are less likely to occur, and variations in moisture do not substantially stress vegetation growth. The study of Hou (2019)  also showed that despite the increased sensitivity of hydrological variables to vegetation changes during the dry season, such correlations were not significant during the rainy season.  4.2 Hydrological response to climate change Climatic factors affect many aspects of the hydrological process. Q and SW mainly depend on precipitation, while climatic factors such as temperature and wind speed significantly influence the ET rate of the underlying surface (Jans et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2015 ). The spatiotemporal characteristics of Q are closely dependent on changes in precipitation (Jiang et al., 2022 ). Our time series analysis showed that the interannual change rates of Q and precipitation in the XRB were similar, and the interannual fluctuation characteristics were also relatively similar (Fig. 3 ). Judging from the spatial characteristics of the change trend, the spatial distribution of Q was similar to that of precipitation, showing a pattern of high values in the upstream and downstream areas and low values in the middle reaches (Fig. 4 ). This indicates that runoff in the Xiangjiang River Basin significantly responds to changes in precipitation both temporally and spatially, aligning with the conclusions of related studies (Zhu et al., 2022b ). Vegetation transpires through leaf stomata, converting soil moisture into water vapor and releasing it into the atmosphere. Vegetation factors have the most significant direct impact on the spatial variability of ET. At the same time, climatic factors control the ET process by affecting water availability and the energy supply (Ma et al., 2024 ). Interannual fluctuations in ET within the XRB are closely related to the LAI. Simultaneously, ET is limited by available water, and it fluctuates within the stable range of precipitation (Liu, 2022 ). Additionally, the change trend of ET is consistent with that of PET in terms of spatial characteristics, indicating that the spatial change of ET is strongly related to climatic factors. SW is mainly supplied by precipitation and runoff, and it is consumed by ET. Precipitation controls the recharge process of SW, while climatic factors such as temperature regulate the consumption rate of SW by affecting evapotranspiration.  4.3 Contribution of vegetation greening and climate change to hydrological variables, along with their spatial scale effects and spatial heterogeneity Based on the hydrological process simulations in this study, changes in the hydrological variables can be attributed to vegetation and climatic alterations. On the overall scale of the XRB, it is evident that vegetation changes are the primary driving factor for ET variations. This observation aligns with the findings of Cheng et al. (2021) , who emphasized the substantial impact of LAI and precipitation on ET changes in the Yangtze River Basin from 2001 to 2018 based on satellite data. They have noted that ET changes in the southeastern region of China were predominantly influenced by variations in vegetation, which corroborates the results of this study. The studies of conducted by Song et al. (2023)  and Zhai and Tao (2021)  have consistently highlighted that climate change, particularly alterations in precipitation, plays a leading role in influencing changes in runoff in China. These conclusions are consistent with the results of the present study. An increase in vegetation cover leads to increased soil moisture consumption, resulting in soil moisture deficits (Chen et al., 2008; Jiao et al., 2020 ). However, in humid subtropical regions such as those investigated in this study, soil moisture experiences timely replenishment from precipitation or runoff induced by precipitation (Thomas, 2000; Zohaib et al., 2017 ). Therefore, the increase in precipitation has a positive impact on SW, counterbalancing some of the negative effects of the increase in LAI on SW (Li et al., 2018; Song et al., 2023 ). When examined at a small watershed scale as opposed to the entire XRB scale, it is apparent that LAI has a diminished influence on changes in hydrological variables, while climate exerts a more pronounced impact. Taking ET as an example, the contribution of LAI to all small watersheds was consistently positive in this study, whereas the impact of PET on various sub-basins may be positive or negative. However, when aggregated on the XRB scale, the opposing effects of the PET tended to offset each other. The impacts of vegetation and climate on hydrological variables are subject to spatial-scale dependencies and have a high level of spatial heterogeneity (Zhang et al., 2022a ). The contribution of vegetation (climate) changes to hydrological variables depends on the sensitivity of the hydrological variables to vegetation (climate) changes and the changing trend of the vegetation (climate) itself (Xiao et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2020 ). The No. 28 sub-basin indicates that LAI changes had a greater impact on hydrological variables owing to the large LAI change trend. Compared to the No. 3 sub-basin, it indicates that the hydrological variables were highly sensitive to LAI changes, causing LAI changes to have a greater impact on hydrological variables. P in the upper reaches of the Xiangjiang River (sub-basins 49, 50, 51, 53, and 54) had a greater impact on the hydrological variables, and this was attributed to the larger changing trend of P in these areas. Compared with sub-basins Nos. 42, 45 and 46, the P change trend in the region was small, so that P had only a small impact on the hydrological variables in these small watersheds (Fig. 4 ).  4.4 Limitations This study has certain limitations. Given the difficulty in quantifying human activities such as reservoir water storage and agricultural irrigation, the model used in this study did not incorporate the impacts of anthropogenic activities on hydrological processes. This may have resulted in inaccuracies in hydrological simulations within regions with significant human activity. In addition, we assumed that all landscape attributes (except vegetation) remained constant during the study period. This assumption may introduce uncertainties in the hydrological simulations of regions with dynamic landscape changes. However, from 2000 to 2020, only a small portion of the study area experienced significant land use changes (refer to Supplementary material Table S2  and Fig. S7 ). Furthermore, given the constraints of the study area, we were unable to identify the patterns of hydrological variable sensitivity under different climate gradients. Exploring the impacts of different climate types and more complex landscape combinations on hydrological variable sensitivity is a potential topic for future research (Li et al., 2023 ). Given the intricate bidirectional interplay between vegetation and climate, it is challenging to completely decouple the effects of climate and vegetation change on hydrological cycles (Sheil, 2018; Song et al., 2023 ). The impact of climate change on vegetation greening is a well-established global consensus. Vegetation greening driven by climate change enhances atmospheric moisture transport, leading to increased precipitation in downwind areas (Cui et al., 2022 ). This indicates that climate change and vegetation greening have both direct and indirect effects on hydrological processes, but it is often too difficult to clarify the latter. Consequently, this study primarily estimated the relative contributions of climate change and vegetation greening to hydrological variables based on their direct effects.   5 Conclusions This study used remote sensing LAI data to enhance the SWAT model and then quantify the influence of vegetation greening and climate change on hydrological variables. The model's suitability for simulating hydrological processes in the region was assessed based on observed runoff data. An analysis of the linear regression equation showed that within the XRB, ET exhibited significantly positive sensitivity to changes in LAI, whereas SW and Q displayed significantly negative sensitivity to LAI changes. A contribution analysis demonstrated that vegetation greening and climate change jointly led to a 5 %, 2 %, and 10 % increase in ET, SW, and Q, respectively, within the XRB. Among these changes, changes in LAI resulted in elevated ET and decreased SW and Q, whereas increase in precipitation resulted in increased ET, SW, and Q. Alterations in potential evapotranspiration contributed to an increase in ET and a decrease in SW and Q. Hydrological variables exhibited a high level of sensitivity to alterations in vegetation within the subtropical region; however, with respect to their relative contributions, changes in Q were mainly dominated by changes in precipitation, changes in SW were dominated by the combined effects of climate change (P and PET), and changes in ET were mainly controlled by the LAI. Human activities are often difficult to quantify, and we therefore did not consider the possible impact of human activities on hydrological processes, which may have resulted in limitations. Therefore, clarifying the impact of human activities on hydrological processes is an important direction for future research. This study provides a thorough understanding of the impact of vegetation greening and climate change on the hydrological cycle of a subtropical basin, and it offers key insights into supporting effective regional water resource governance and promoting sustainable use. In particular, with respect to adaptation to climate variability and the enhancement of greening initiatives, the insights derived from this research will be instrumental in refining strategies for the allocation and optimized use of water resources. 1 Introduction An accurate quantification of the probability of exceeding extreme precipitation amounts on various temporal scales is fundamental in risk and resource management, city planning, hydraulic design and insurance as well as reinsurance business (Groenemeijer et al., 2015; Hailegeorgis and Alfredsen, 2017 ). For estimating extreme precipitation probability, long data records are usually needed, in order to have enough extremes for the extreme value statistics. Therefore, observations from station networks are commonly used to estimate design precipitation with defined return periods because such observations often span an observation period of several decades. In Germany design precipitation amounts are currently defined in KOSTRA-DWD-2020 (Shehu et al., 2023 ), an operational product that was recently updated to include more numerous and longer records from stations. The downside of using station data for estimation of design precipitation is the limited spatial representativeness of point measurements. Design values are determined at the location of the station and pertain the spatial scale of the rain gauge, which can be easily approximated with a point-scale. Therefore, design values derived from rain gauges need to be interpolated in order to cover the ungauged areas between stations. This interpolation process may lead to the smoothing of local gradients in precipitation climatology in case they are sharper than the typical inter-gauge distance. From radar observations, on the other hand, precipitation estimates with continuous coverage over regional to national, or even continental (Saltikoff et al., 2019 ) scales can be derived. They allow to capture spatial variability of precipitation extremes at scales comparable or smaller than the typical inter-gauge distance (Marra and Morin, 2015 ). For instance, Smith et al. (2024)  recently found that the spatial gradients in short duration rainfall extremes in the region of Baltimore can only be reproduced in radar data, but are not reflected in products based on rain gauge observations. Drawback of these products are the relatively short length of the available records, that cover up to a couple of decades, and the estimation biases that often accompany heavy precipitation values. An overview of the potential and challenges associated with using weather radar data to investigate extreme precipitation is given in Lengfeld et al. (2020)  and Marra et al. (2019a) . The most common approach to the estimation of design precipitation values consists in the collection of observed extremes, either the largest value of each year (block maxima approach) or the exceedances of a high threshold (peaks over threshold approach) and in the identification of a statistical model able to reproduce their probability distribution. Extrapolation from this distribution allows one to derive extremes with probabilities that are much smaller than the available time scale. Examples of applications of these methods to weather radar archives can be seen in Overeem et al. (2009), Eldardiry et al. (2015), Panziera et al. (2016), Goudenhoofdt et al. (2017) , and McGraw et al. (2019) . These approaches, however, were found to be subject to large uncertainties, due to the need to estimate the distribution parameters from a limited data sample and to the biases that typically characterise radar estimates (Berne and Krajewski, 2013; Marra et al., 2019a ). Different approaches were explored in the attempt to limit these issues. For example, Wright et al. (2013)  used stochastic storm transposition to increase the number of extreme events in the database, drastically reducing the uncertainty in their estimates. The approach is robust, but limited by the requirements in terms of spatial homogeneity. More recently, Srivastava and Mascaro (2023)  used a vast network of rain gauges to characterise bias and estimation variance in the high-order moment of the probability distribution in the study region and correct the estimates accordingly. The approach proved highly effective at the cost of requiring abundant long-recording rain gauges within a relatively homogeneous region. Alternative methods based on non-asymptotic statistics (Marani and Ignaccolo, 2015 ) can be used to estimate design precipitation amounts (Schellander et al., 2019; Miniussi and Marra, 2021; Poschlod, 2021; Marra et al., 2022; Shmilovitz et al., 2023; Siena et al., 2023; Dallan et al., 2024 ). These approaches rely on different assumptions with respect to extreme value theory. Specifically, they assume that the parent distribution of the process of interest is known, and consider extremes are rare samples from such distribution. This allows one to use a larger fraction of observations, thus providing reduced uncertainties in presence of short data records such as the ones of weather radars (Zorzetto et al., 2016; Marra et al., 2018 ). For example, Marra et al. (2022)  recently used such methods on an 11-year weather radar archive and, after adjustment with rain gauge statistics, obtained estimates of 100-year design precipitation with smaller standard error than those obtained using traditional approaches on long-recording rain gauge data. The next step towards robust design precipitation estimates would be a combination of the long records of station data with the spatially high-resolution radar data. Before such an approach can be implemented, a thorough investigation of the differences in design precipitation estimates from both data sources must be carried out. In this study, we evaluate the potential of the German weather radar network to derive design precipitation amounts at the national scale and test different statistical approaches. We assess the potential advantages of using a non-asymptotic approach, specifically, the Simplified Metastatistical Extreme Value (SMEV) (Marra et al., 2019b ) in comparison with established approaches in Germany. We address the following scientific questions: How well does the radar product reproduce the return levels with respect to the operational KOSTRA-DWD2020 reference product? What is the sensitivity of the used methods to the short available radar record? Can we reduce the uncertainty in radar-derived return levels using a non-asymptotic approach? What are its main advantages and disadvantages? After a brief description of the used data sets, the different methods to estimate design precipitation are provided in Sections 2 and 3 . Then the results are presented and discussed in Section 4 . A summary and outlook is given in Section 5 .  2 Data In this study we use precipitation data provided by the German Meteorological Service (Deutscher Wetterdienst, DWD): (i) measurements from DWD’s weather radar network; and (ii) observations from precipitation stations (Fig. 1 ).  The radar network consists of 17 C-band radars and covers nearly the whole domain of Germany (see Fig. 1 ). The data set RADKLIM_RW_2017.002 is a reprocessed climatological product (RW product) that spans from 2001 to 2022 and has a temporal resolution of 1 h and a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km ×   1 km. Radar observations are prone to several sources of error caused by the radar hardware and the surrounding climate, e.g. due to non-meteorological echoes, ground clutter, beam blocking or attenuation by heavy rainfall (Germann et al., 2006; Villarini and Krajewski, 2010; Borga et al., 2022 ). A reprocessing of the raw radar data with a set of correction algorithms is performed for the entire time period to ensure for a homogeneous data set. Detailed information about the weather radar dataset, including the algorithms used to address the sources of error and the evaluation of the overall quality of the estimates can be found in Winterrath et al. (2017) . The RADKLIM_RW_2017.002 data set is freely available for download at Winterrath et al. (2018) . The rain gauge data set consists of 155 stations with record lengths ranging between 29 years and 120 years. All stations cover at least the years 2001 to 2020 to maximise the overlap with the radar data set. We use hourly accumulated rainfall data in this study. A short description of the gauge data is given in Shehu et al. (2023) .  3 Methods In this study we compared two different statistical methods for determining design precipitation amounts using as a reference the current operational method for Germany. The two methods and the reference are described in the following sections. We focus on design precipitation for six return periods (2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 years) and five durations (1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 h). The estimation is done separately for each duration for both gauges and radar pixels. We then produce nation-wide maps. The design precipitation estimates derived at each station are compared with those of the collocated radar pixels. This assumes that potential differences between design precipitation at the rain gauge scale and at the radar pixel scale (1  km  2     ) are negligible, an assumption that we will find not always met. A discussion on the topic can be found in Peleg et al. (2018)  and Marra et al. (2019a) . To ensure a fair comparison between stations and radars, the statistical analyses of the gauge records are conducted for two time periods: (1) the entire station record, and (2) the 20 years covered by the radar network. Both investigated methods are applied to the full time series of the 155 precipitation stations, to the time series restricted to the years 2001 to 2020 and to the Germany-wide radar data set that also spans from 2001 to 2020. 3.1 DWA The first method is described in the guidelines for calculating extreme precipitation depending on return period and duration by the German Association for Water, Wastewater, and Waste (in German: Deutsche Vereinigung für Wasserwirtschaft, Abwasser und Abfall) (DWA, 2012 ). This method was used to determine design precipitation in Germany for decades before the new KOSTRA-DWD-2020 dataset was published in 2022. Before then, sewage systems, hydraulic structure and as well as the construction of rainfall hazard maps are based on design precipitation derived from the DWA method. Similarly, the catalogue of radar-based heavy rainfall events (CatRaRE, Lengfeld et al. (2021) ) used in several hydro-meteorological studies is also computed with the DWA method. Therefore, we chose to use the DWA method in this study to emphasise the improvement of the newly developed methods described below.
