The first method is described in the guidelines for calculating extreme precipitation depending on return period and duration by the German Association for Water, Wastewater, and Waste (in German: Deutsche Vereinigung für Wasserwirtschaft, Abwasser und Abfall) (DWA, 2012 ). This method was used to determine design precipitation in Germany for decades before the new KOSTRA-DWD-2020 dataset was published in 2022. Before then, the dimensioning of sewage systems, hydraulic structure and rainfall hazard maps were based on design precipitation derived from the DWA method. Similarly, the Catalogue of Radar-based Heavy Rainfall Events (CatRaRE, Lengfeld et al. (2021) ) used in several hydro-meteorological studies is also computed with the DWA method. Therefore, we chose to use the DWA method in this study to emphasise the improvement of the newly developed methods described below. The method uses a peak-over-threshold approach, assuming an exponential distribution (Generalised Pareto distribution with shape parameter set to zero), whose cumulative distribution function can be written as: (1) F  DWA   ( x )  = 1 − e  − x − u  w     .      The coefficients u   and w   are computed for each grid cell of RADKLIM_RW_2017.002 individually. The number of elements in the partial duration series depends on the length of the data set and is defined as twice the number of years in DWA (2012) . For the 20 years of radar data, the series consists of 40 elements per duration. The two parameters of the exponential distribution are first computed for each duration individually. It is not expected that the parameters will produce a consistent picture across all duration levels. Therefore, a linear regression of the parameters over all durations is applied. DWA (2012)  suggests three different approaches for the linear regression: (1) using logarithmic values of the duration, (2) logarithmic values of the duration and the parameters or (3) hyperbolic. The second approach with a double logarithmic regression of u   and w   over all durations has been proven to work best in our case. At the end the resulting function for calculating the return period is checked for monotone increase of the rainfall rate with increasing duration and return period to ensure for consistent estimates.  3.2 SMEV The second method we examine is the simplified metastatistical extreme value (SMEV) (Marra et al., 2019b ). SMEV assumes that annual maxima emerge from the finite sampling of identically-distributed ordinary events. Ordinary events are defined as the independent realisations of the process of interest. We use the codes freely available in Marra (2020) . Independent storms  are identified from the temporal series as periods with precipitation separated by at least 24 h of dry conditions. Ordinary events  of each duration are identified as the maximum intensities of the duration of interest observed within each storm . This is done using a moving window. Full details about the definition of storms and ordinary events and on the properties of ordinary and extreme events can be found in Marra et al. (2020) . Ordinary events are here described using a distribution with Weibull tail, following the theoretical derivation by Wilson and Tuomi (2005)  and the empirical observations by Marra et al. (2023) . Using a Weibull marginal distribution, the annual non-exceedance probability of precipitation intensities x   according to SMEV becomes: (2) G  SMEV   ( x )  = 1 − e  − x  λ      κ        n       where λ   and κ   are the scale and shape parameter of the Weibull distribution, and n   is the average annual number of ordinary events. The parameters of the distribution are estimated using a least-squares regression in Weibull transformed coordinates in which a left-censoring is included: the ordinary events not exceeding the 90th percentile are censored and only their weight in probability is retained. The choice of the left-censoring threshold is based on the objective test described in Marra et al. (2023)  (codes available in Marra, 2022 ). This value is in agreement with previous studies based on SMEV over Germany, both at short (Wang et al., 2020 ) and daily durations (Miniussi and Marra, 2021 ).  3.3 Reference method: KOSTRA-DWD-2020 As a reference data set we use the recently published new version of design precipitation maps (KOSTRA-DWD-2020) for Germany. The design precipitation maps are determined on the basis of more than 5400 stations. Approximately 4000 of these stations observe precipitation with daily temporal resolution and are disaggregated using a cascade model based on Olsson (1998)  to a temporal resolution of 5 min. This disaggregation may introduce biases in our reference. The annual maximum series is then derived from the 5 min time series for durations of 5, 10, 15 and 30 min, 1, 2, 6 and 12 h and 2, 3 and 7 days. The generalised extreme value (GEV) distribution is used to model the annual exceedance probabilities. The shape parameter is set to 0.1 and the location and scale parameters of the GEV are estimated from the annual maximum series for each station and duration individually, based on the L-moments method. The approach by Koutsoyiannis et al. (1998)  is then used to generalise the annual maximum series intensities over all chosen durations. The estimated parameters are interpolated independently with ordinary kriging with external drift to a 5 km ×   5 km grid. A detailed description of the KOSTRA-DWD-2020 dataset and the statistical methods used can be find in Shehu et al. (2023) . In addition to the station-based product, the GEV parameters of the KOSTRA-DWD-2020 algorithm are also provided at the radar pixels that include the stations without the regionalisation and for the time period from 2001 to 2020 matching the radar data.  3.4 Uncertainty quantification In order to quantify the uncertainty related to the design precipitation amounts estimated using the DWA and the SMEV methods from station and radar data, we use the bootstrap method (Overeem et al., 2008 ). We randomly sample, with replacement, M   years out of the M  -long record and we estimate parameters and design values based on the resampled record. A set of 1000 realisation is computed and uncertainty is quantified based on the dispersion of the obtained results. The codes are available in Marra (2020) . An analogous bootstrap approach is used to quantify the sensitivity of the methods to the length of the available data record. Based on the 1000 realisations the relative Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) in %   is computed for each station S   and each given duration D   and return period T  : (3) RMSE ( S , D , T )  = 1  1000   ∑  i = 1  1000   R R ( i , S , D , T )  − R R  ref   ( S , D , T )     2      R R  ref   ( S , D , T )    ∗ 100 ,     with i   being the realisation, R R    the design precipitation of the investigated methods and R R  r e f      the design precipitation from the official KOSTRA-DWD-2020 data set. As a second measure for uncertainty U   we calculated the median as well as the 5th and 95th percentile of the 1000 realisations (R R  P 5     , R R  P 95     ) of the bootstrapping and divided the range between 5th and 95th percentile by the median R R  P 50     : (4) U  rel   ( S , D , T )  = R R  P95   ( S , D , T )  − R R  P5   ( S , D , T )   R R  P50   ( S , D , T )    ∗ 100 .          4 Results and discussion 4.1 Analysis at station locations The first part of the analysis is based on the rainfall time series from 155 stations and from the corresponding radar pixels in which the stations are located. To ensure for a fair comparison the coefficients of KOSTRA-DWD-2020 for station data were provided by DWD for the same time period as for the radar data (2001–2020) and without regionalisation. Fig. 2  shows design precipitation based on these coefficients compared to KOSTRA-DWD-2020 estimates based on radar data at those 155 station locations. In addition design precipitation estimated with DWA and SMEV using radar data at the station locations are shown. This visualisation allows us to benchmark the DWA and SMEV methods with respect to the KOSTRA-DWD-2020 approach and, at the same time, to quantify the biases in the radar estimates. For all durations and return periods the KOSTRA-DWD-2020 (stations) shows the largest bias and RMSE compared to KOSTRA-DWD-2020 (radar). This bias indicates that the differences between the two data sets (systematic bias in the radar estimates) tend to be larger than the uncertainty in the statistical methods, contrary to the original assumption that potential differences between design precipitation at the rain gauge scale and at the radar pixel scale are negligible with respect to the estimation uncertainties. SMEV tends to underestimate the reference for all durations and return periods, while DWA tends to overestimate the reference for short durations and to underestimate daily precipitation with return periods of 20 and 100 years. Biases in SMEV tend to be smaller than the ones in DWA, with the exception of 6-h duration for 20-year and 100-year return periods. In general both, bias and RMSE, decrease with increasing duration and decreasing return period. For hourly precipitation, bias and RMSE are clearly larger for DWA compared to SMEV. For daily precipitation the two methods show similar results.          In the following analyses, we use the official KOSTRA-DWD-2020 data set based on station data with long time series and with regionalisation as the operational reference, because this is the official product to determine design precipitation and return periods in Germany. We extracted the estimated design precipitation at the KOSTRA- and the radar-pixels in which the stations are located. The relative bias between the design precipitation determined by KOSTRA-DWD-2020 for stations (reference) and DWA as well as SMEV is shown in Fig. 3  for all 155 stations combined in boxplots. The KOSTRA-DWD-2020 method applied to radar (orange colour) gives an impression of the differences due to the data source, station and radar, although the temporal disaggregation used to obtain station data of short durations may also play a role. As anticipated in Fig. 2 , the design precipitation estimated from radar data are lower than the ones estimated from station data, resulting in a negative bias in Fig. 3 . With increasing return period and decreasing duration the median of the bias also increases from −8.6% for a return period of 2 years and a duration of 24 h up to −25% for a return period of 100 years and a duration of 1 h. The inter-quantile range and the spread also increase with increasing return period, but remains almost constant for all durations. While SMEV (reddish colours) underestimates the reference data set KOSTRA-DWD-2020 for all durations and return periods, DWA (greenish colours) tends to overestimate the KOSTRA-DWD-2020 values for short durations. Both methods show higher design precipitation for the station than for the radar data set, corresponding to the bias between the design precipitation estimated with KOSTRA-DWD-2020 for station and for radar data and reflects the differences between the two data sets. The spread increases with return period and decreases with duration. Comparing the full station record with the station record overlapping with the radar record indicates that SMEV is less influenced by the length of the time series than the DWA method. In fact, the median and the inter-quantile range of the bias remains virtually unchanged when considering only 2001–2020 with SMEV, indicating no appreciable change neither in the bias nor in the uncertainty. Conversely, the inter-quantile range increases significantly for the short time series when using the DWA method, e.g. from −5 to 10% for a duration of 1 h and return period of 100 years for the whole data set to −10 to 20% for the short time series. The KOSTRA-DWD-2020 method applied to radar data (orange colour) lies in between DWA and SMEV for radar data for low return periods and gets closer to SMEV with increasing return periods. Another well-established measure for the quality of the estimated design storms is the Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE). To compute the RMSE at each station location, we performed a bootstrapping with 1000 realisation combining the years within the time series randomly. The relative RMSE is computed as the Root-Mean-Square Error from the 1000 realisations normalised over the reference value of the design precipitation (KOSTRA-DWD-2020 from station data) for each station. Fig. 4  shows largest values of the relative RMSE for durations of 1 h and a return period of 100 years and decreases with increasing duration and decreasing return period. For most durations and return periods, the relative RMSE is larger for SMEV than for DWA, with highest values for SMEV based on radar data. The influence of the length of the time series can be clearly seen for the DWA method. While the relative RMSE is smaller than 20% for most stations when using the long time series (dark green colour in Fig. 4 ), it is distinctly higher for design precipitation based on the short time series of station data and radar (lighter green colours in Fig. 4 ) up to more than 60% for a few locations. In contrast, when using the SMEV method the relative RMSE is nearly the same for the long and the short station time series, but distinctly higher for radar data.  4.2 Stability of the methods One important requirement of the methods for design precipitation estimation is a low sensitivity to the available data record. In order to examine this sensitivity for DWA and SMEV, we determined the uncertainty by computing the median as well as the 5th and 95th percentile of the 1000 realisations of the bootstrapping and divided the range between 5th and 95th percentile by the median. Fig. 5  shows that the uncertainty for the two methods and three different data sets increases with return period from ∼  20% for 2 years return period to more than 40% for 100 years return period. For the long station time series, the uncertainty is comparable for both methods, even though it is slightly higher for SMEV. Limiting the time series of the stations to only 20 years hardly influences the uncertainty in the SMEV method, but noticeably increases the uncertainty in the DWA methods for all durations and return periods. The uncertainty in estimation of design precipitation based on radar data is approximately 10% higher for both methods compared to long time series from stations. In the DWA method, however, the outliers are larger, which in combination with the distinct influence of the length of the time series, indicates that the DWA-method is more sensitive to statistical outliers from extreme precipitation events. The influence of statistical outliers is investigated based on the precipitation event in July 2021, which was one of the most extreme rainfall events in Central Europe in the last decades. Both methods, SMEV and DWA, are applied to the radar time series excluding and including the data from the year 2021 at the radar pixel with the largest amount of daily precipitation during the event. In Fig. 6  both methods show similar design precipitation with a duration of 24 h and return periods between 1 and 50 years (solid blue and red line). After including the data from 2021 the design precipitation increases for both methods (dashed blue and red line), but while the SMEV estimates are still within the confidence interval of the SMEV method, the DWA estimates increase up to 30% for a return period of 50 years. A detailed study about the impact of the July 2021 event on the return levels calculated with the DWA method can be found in Lengfeld et al. (2023) .  4.3 Nationwide analysis A nationwide comparison of the methods is only possible on the basis of the radar data, because the coverage with only 155 stations is too low to compute a reasonable composite. KOSTRA-DWD-2020 serves again as the reference. It should be, however, noted that this is an interpolation of station estimates and some differences with respect to this product are to be expected even if radar estimates were “perfect”. We focus on return periods of 5, 20 and 100 years and duration of 1, 6 and 24 h. The hourly design precipitation in Fig. 7  indicates large differences between all three methods. Design precipitation according to KOSTRA-DWD-2020 has higher intensity ranging from 20 mm at a return period of 5 years up to more than 60 mm once every 100 years. In comparison, design precipitation estimated with SMEV ranges between 12 mm (T =   5 years) up to 45 mm (T =   100 years). KOSTRA-DWD-2020 shows a gradient from lower values in the North to higher values in the South and seems much smoother than the radar based methods (note that KOSTRA-DWD-2020 has a spatial resolution of 5 km ×   5 km compared to 1 km ×   1 km for the radar data set). The spatial pattern of the design precipitation based on SMEV is smoother and generally lower than from DWA, especially for the lowest return period. This is highlighted by the relative difference between the methods that ranges between 0 and -50%. For higher return periods SMEV provides higher values than DWA in the Southern Alps, which is consistent with KOSTRA-DWD-2020. As shown in Fig. 8  the spatial correlation between SMEV and KOSTRA-DWD-2020 is significantly higher for SMEV than for DWA for all return periods while the overall bias is smaller for DWA. This is likely due to the larger uncertainties in DWA estimates, which manifest as spatial noise in Fig. 7 . At a duration of 6 h in Fig. 9  the influence of orography can be clearly seen in the design precipitation estimated with KOSTRA-DWD-2020 with largest values in the Alps, the Black Forest and Ore Mountains. To a lesser extent, this can also be seen in the radar-based design precipitation. In general, results from SMEV and DWA are more similar than for the hourly design precipitation. Differences between both methods range mostly between −20 and 10%, while both still underestimate KOSTRA-DWD-2020. In large parts of Germany SMEV still results in lower design precipitation than DWA, with an exception in the North-East. DWA estimates of 6-h design precipitation with longer return periods are better correlated with KOSTRA-DWD-2020 than SMEV ones (Fig. 8 ). The daily design precipitation is influenced by the orography in all three methods (Fig. 10 ). KOSTRA-DWD-2020 is still underestimated by the radar-based methods, but the patterns are very similar for all three methods and all return periods. The differences between SMEV and DWA are rather small (mostly between −10 and 10%) but there are some areas in the West and the East of Germany, where the DWA method suggests considerably higher design precipitation than SMEV that are not linked to the orography. In Fig. 6  it was already shown that the DWA method is more sensitive to statistical outliers from individual extreme events. In order to check whether those differences between the methods originate from extreme precipitation events, Fig. 11  shows the number of events that exceeded DWD’s warning level 4 for extreme precipitation with duration between 12 and 72 h from 2001 to 2020 taken from the Catalogue of Radar-based Heavy Rainfall Events CatRaRE (Lengfeld et al., 2021 ). A clear correlation between the areas of negative biases in Fig. 10  and the locations of the extreme events in Fig. 11  can be seen. This underlines the fact that the DWA method is more influenced by individual events than the SMEV method in case of short time series. SMEV estimates of daily design precipitation are correlated with KOSTRA-DWD-2020 slightly better than DWA estimates (Fig. 8 ). The overall bias is quite similar for both methods. Overall, both methods cannot account for the differences between the source of the data sets. Design precipitation estimated from the radar data set is generally lower than for the stations independent of the length of the time series. This is due to the differences in the measurement techniques: While a station measures the rainfall for an area of a few square centimetres, precipitation from radar data is averaged over a square kilometre. Therefore, the most extreme and mostly local precipitation amounts are smoothed by averaging over the larger area in the radar data leading to the underestimation of the design precipitation. In general the relative bias to the reference data set (KOSTRA-DWD-2020 applied to station data), the RMSE and the uncertainty increase with increasing return period and decreasing duration for both methods. For the long time series of station data the uncertainty in design precipitation estimation with DWA and SMEV is comparable. When applying both methods to shorter time series of only twenty years, SMEV leads to much more stable results. This is due to the inclusion of many ordinary events in the statistical inference, which leads to a decreased uncertainty in parameter estimation, and therefore in the design precipitation. The DWA method on the other side is highly influenced by individual extreme events. These events are physically possible realisation of climate, but represent statistical outliers when included in short time series. Therefore, the RMSE and the uncertainty is higher for DWA than for SMEV and the spatial pattern is more heterogeneous. However, design precipitation estimates determined from radar data with the SMEV method strongly underestimate those from KOSTRA-DWD-2020, especially for short durations by 50% and more, which cannot be explained by the different measurement principles alone. This underestimation is in agreement with the results by Wang et al. (2020) , and suggests that the Weibull tails used here to describe the largest 10% of the ordinary events could be too light to capture hourly extremes in Germany. This effect could be related to the presence of a mixture of processes, as highlighted for instance by Marra et al. (2019b)  (see Fig. 8 therein) and Mushtaq et al. (2023) , or to specific features of the local climatology (e.g., see Fig. S2 in Marra et al., 2024 ). Interestingly, this SMEV underestimation is stronger for shorter return periods (Fig. 2 ). According to the analyses by Marra et al. (2019b)  (see Fig. 1 therein), this may also suggest that the inter-annual variability considered in the full Metastatistical Extreme Value (MEV) formulation and neglected in SMEV (Marani and Ignaccolo, 2015; Zorzetto et al., 2016 ) could play an important role in this climate.   5 Summary and outlook Two different approaches for design precipitation estimation are applied to precipitation time series from 155 rain gauges and from the German radar network in order to assess their performance for data sets from different sources and with different lengths: (a) a method based on a peak-over-threshold approach and an exponential distribution, described in the guidelines for calculating extreme precipitation depending on return period and duration by the German Association for Water, Wastewater, and Waste (DWA, 2012 ) (DWA); and (b) the Simplified Metastatistical Extreme Value (SMEV) approach (Marra et al., 2019b, 2020 ) that relies on the analysis of ordinary events, described by a Weibull-tailed distribution, in a non-asymptotic formulation. The results are compared to the official design precipitation guidelines for Germany (KOSTRA-DWD-2020) (Shehu et al., 2023 ), which are based on station data only and use a Generalised Extreme Value distribution. Three main questions were answered in this study: (1) How well does the radar product reproduce the return levels with respect to the operational KOSTRA-DWD2020 station-based reference product? In general, design precipitation estimated from radar data are lower than from station data, because radar observations have a spatial resolution of 1 km  2      compared to point measurements from stations (e.g., see Peleg et al., 2018 ) and because of potential biases in the estimation of extremes with weather radars. It should also be noted that short duration estimates from KOSTRA-DWD-2020 are also obtained from the statistical disaggregation of daily time series, rather than from observations, and could, thus, be affected by biases. The difference between radar and stations tends to decrease with increasing duration and decreasing return period. SMEV underestimates KOSTRA-DWD-2020 based on stations to a larger extent compared to the DWA method, especially for shorter durations and shorter return periods. The application of the method used for KOSTRA-DWD-2020 on radar data at the station locations leads to similar results than SMEV. (2) What is the sensitivity of the used methods to the short available radar record? Can we reduce the uncertainty in radar-derived return levels using a non-asymptotic approach? The uncertainty in design precipitation estimates is clearly reduced when using SMEV compared to DWA. The DWA method is highly influenced by individual extreme events in the relatively short time series of the radar data, which is shown exemplary for the extreme precipitation event that occurred in Western Germany in July 2021. SMEV on the other hand is less influenced by the length of the time series and results in a smoother spatial pattern than the DWA method, especially for short durations. This allows for the estimation of design precipitation without spatial interpolation and smoothing that unavoidably introduces biases in situations in which the signal is not uniform in space. This is usually the case when using station data because the stations are not equally distributed over the studied domain. These situations are exactly the ones in which one would like to use a radar product. (3) What are the main advantages and disadvantages of SMEV? The most important advantage of the SMEV-method is its low sensitivity to statistical outliers and to the length of the time series which makes it a suitable tool for design precipitation estimates from radar data with comparably short record length. The main disadvantage is the clear underestimation of the estimated design precipitation compared to the DWA method and to the reference data set that could be due to the inclusion of ordinary events in the analysis. In the future a combination of station and radar measurements (e.g., see Marra et al. (2022)  for the case of SMEV) is sought, with the idea of using the advantages of the long term, accurate rain gauge records and the spatial information from weather radars.
1 Introduction Numerous models are available for simulating water and chemical transport through soil; however, they often demand extensive data, including hydraulic parameter information. While estimating hydraulic parameters through field or laboratory measurements is practical and essential, obtaining such large datasets can be time-consuming and costly. Pedotransfer functions (PTFs) offer a viable alternative, predicting hydraulic properties using readily-available or easily measurable soil characteristics like sand and/or clay content, organic matter content, and bulk density. However, PTFs are mostly based on historical datasets, which may not fully reflect current soil conditions due to ongoing changes in soil structure caused, for example, by the increasing mechanization in agriculture (Schjønning et al., 2015 ). This structural degradation can change pore architecture and hydraulic properties, potentially reducing the predictive accuracy of existing PTFs. Therefore, there is a need for updated datasets that accurately represent the current state of soil physical and hydraulic characteristics. Classical statistical regression (CSR) methods, such as multiple linear regression, have been widely used for PTF development. Despite their simplicity, they remain effective (Tóth et al., 2015 ). However, selecting an appropriate method is challenging due to numerous potential predictors and varying correlations between hydraulic properties and basic soil characteristics across different data subsets (Van Genuchten and Pachepsky, 2011 ). Nowadays, machine learning (ML) techniques have gained attraction for PTF development in the field of hydrology due to their flexibility and accurate predictive performance (Botula et al., 2013 ). These include artificial neural networks, random forests, support vector machines, k-Nearest Neighbors and etc (Botula et al., 2014; Van Looy et al., 2017 ). Later, De Pue et al. (2021)  introduced a Kriging-based Gaussian process into PTF development. Recently, Li et al. (2024)  tested various machine learning strategies and found extremely randomized trees and stacking ensemble models to outperform other methods. Machine learning can handle both linear and nonlinear relationships, and manage outliers better than CSR. However, there are few studies that explore the integration of CSR or ML with soil structure information to predict SWRC using updated databases. Soil structure information is a crucial yet often omitted factor in hydraulic parameter PTFs for Earth System Models (Fatichi et al., 2020 ). Including soil structure has been advocated to improve PTFs prediction accuracy (Nguyen et al., 2015; Rabot et al., 2018; Van Looy et al., 2017; Vereecken et al., 2010; Vereecken et al., 2019 ). Yet, it should be realized that this improvement is marginal and primarily observed in the wet range. Lin et al. (2022)  also found that soils with acceptable structural quality had 7 % higher water content at saturation, which reduced to 3 % higher at 100 hPa suction compared to degraded soils. To evaluate soil structure easily and quickly, visual soil evaluation and examination methods (VSEE, Pulido Moncada et al., 2021 ) can be employed. They allow semi-quantitatively assessment of soil structure, and are gaining popularity in soil surveys and monitoring of soil structural quality worldwide. For example, Cornelis et al. (2019)  demonstrated that soil quality scores (Sq) derived from VSEE methods are significantly correlated with the shape of soil–water retention curve (SWRC) in its wet range, where soil structure plays a significant role (Radcliffe and Simunek, 2010 ). Furthermore, Pulido Moncada et al. (2014)  showed that including Sq as a predictor variable did improve the prediction accuracy of saturated hydraulic conductivity. Soil strength, another key soil property, is linked to pore architecture. Soils showing higher strength and thus resistance to penetration at a given water content, are not only denser but also reflect soil deformation leading to a change in pore-size distribution, tortuosity and connectivity. Measuring penetration resistance (PR) with a penetrologger is easy and results in an immediate value of soil strength. It can therefore be easily applied to assess its spatial and temporal variability within field. If inclusion of PR in SWRC PTFs would lead to a higher prediction accuracy, measuring it in field studies at different positions and/or times could be useful to better grab spatial and temporal variation of hydraulic properties. When present in hydraulic databases, it then would of course also be a predictor worth considering. However, the effectiveness of including Sq scores and/or PR in improving the prediction accuracy of SWRC PTFs remains untested. Two primary approaches for developing SWRC PTFs are point and parametric PTFs. Point PTFs predict soil water content at preset matric suctions, while parametric PTFs predict parameters of models like the Van Genuchten model (1980), which provides a continuous curve (Cornelis et al., 2001 ). Although point PTFs are generally more accurate (Pachepsky et al., 1996; Vereecken et al., 2010 ), parametric PTFs remain popular for their direct applicability in simulation models. In order to further improve the prediction accuracy of hydraulic PTFs, data can be grouped according to different criteria, such as soil horizons, soil texture, and among others (Nguyen et al., 2015; Patil and Singh, 2016; Bruand, 2004 ). For instance, categorizing data into groups based on soil structure can enhance water content predictions within the capillary (intermediate) range of SWRC (Nguyen et al., 2015 ). However, further exploration is needed on whether grouping data by soil structure is a viable option for incorporating soil structure information in developing PTFs. The overall objective of this study was to evaluate the added value of soil structural or soil strength information in developing point and parametric PTFs for predicting SWRC of cropland soils. While such functions have been developed in the past, new in our study is that we used, at the time of writing, very recent soil data (2015–2019) from fields that show at least some degree of soil structural degradation and thus represent the current situation on most cropped fields in Western Europe and beyond. The specific objectives were i) to evaluate the performance of different regression methods, including CSR and ML, in developing PTFs to predict SWRC, and to assess the added value of using ii) a visually-assessed soil structural quality index (Sq) as additional predictor variable or for grouping data, or (iii) a soil-strength representing predictor variable (PR), in addition to or instead of ‘classical’ predictors. Besides, (iv) their performance was also compared with that of the PTFs by Weynants et al. (2009) , which are a revision of the well-known PTFs of Vereecken et al. (1989) . These existing PTFs have been shown to perform well in prior studies and are based on ‘older’ datasets from the same region as this study (Belgium). We hypothesize that including soil structural or soil strength information improves the prediction accuracy of SWRC PTFs, in at least the SWRC’s wet range, that ML performs better than CSR, and that PTFs derived from recent soil data are superior to existing ones based on older data, irrespective of the use of additional soil structure or soil strength information.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Sampling scheme for data collection Data were collected in the context of two regionwide projects on assessing the effects of soil compaction on soil hydraulic properties and water movement in Belgium. Field measurements were made and soil samples taken at 42 cropped fields. In each field, two locations with different degree of soil structural degradation resulting from different traffic intensity, this is, headland and in-field zones, were selected. At each location, six intact 250-cm3  (height: 50 mm, diameter: 80 mm) soil cores were taken with a METER Group’s Sample Ring Insertion Tool at three depths: in the ploughed topsoil (TOP) at ∼ 10–20 cm depth, TOP), in the compacted subsoil (CSUB) at ∼ 30–40 cm, and in the deeper subsoil (SUB) at ∼ 60–70 cm. Note that the depths of sampling could vary slightly depending on the soil profile description and penetration resistance measured to 80 cm depth. All cores were taken in a three-tiered stepwise manner by making a small pit in which the surface was levelled just above sample depth (Fig. 1  ). After having taken six cores at one depth, the pit was dug further till the following depth. In total, 252 soil horizons were sampled in six replicates totalling the number of cores taken to 1512. The goal of this sampling strategy was to encompass a wide range of soil textures and structures (i.e., with varying degree of soil structural degradation). The samples cover all seven major soil textural classes according to Belgian Soil Texture Classification Triangle (Dondeyne et al., 2012 ), that is sand (Z), loamy sand (S), light sandy loam (P), (heavy) sandy loam (L), silt loam (A), clay (E) and heavy clay (U). However, due to the nature of the Belgian temperate climate (Cfb according to Köppen; Brugger and Rubel, 2013 ) and geological conditions, E and U textures are scarce and are therefore underrepresented in the database (Fig. 2  ).  2.2 Soil analysis and data collection Soil-water retention curves were determined using the modified evaporation method (HYPROPTM setup, METER group; Schindler et al., 2010 ). First, a hermetian spline was fitted to the observed matric suction-water content datapairs, including water content at the tensiometers' air-entry point, extending observations to ∼ 8800 hPa. Tensiometer accuracy and offset were adjusted as needed to avoid calculation errors (Pertassek et al., 2015 ). SHYPFIT2.0 (Peters and Durner, 2015 ) was used for fitting the Peters–Durner–Iden (PDI) model (Iden and Durner, 2014; Peters, 2013; Peters, 2014; Peters et al., 2024 ) and the Van Genuchten (VG) model (Van Genuchten, 1980 ) to the data by a Shuffled Complex Evolution (SCE) optimization (Duan et al., 1993 ). The PDI model, a variant of the constrained VG model, considers capillary and adsorptive water retention, and shows greater flexibility than the VG model. It was used to calculate the water contents at 14 preset matric suctions for developing the point PTFs. The widely used VG equation was directly fit to the data and used to develop the parametric PTF. Matric suctions were expressed in terms of pF, that is log |h |, with matric suction head h  in cm. Matric suction values in units of hPa were converted to head values in units of m by dividing them by the density of water at 20° C and the gravitational acceleration; multiplying these values with 100 provided data in units of cm. The 14 preset matric suction heads for developing the point PTFs were well distributed along the SWRC (on a semi-log scale) and ranged from near saturation (pF = 0) to over wilting point (pF = 5). The corresponding water contents were the response variables. It is worth noting that the pF values of 4.0 to 5.0 in this study were extrapolated beyond the tensiometers’ cavitation limit. Additional observations using methods like the dew point method (WP4C) could have been beneficial, as Schelle et al. (2013)  found good correlation between water retention points obtained with WP4C and HYPROP. To develop the parametric PTFs, the four-parameter version of the VG equation was selected with response variables now being saturated water content (θs  ), residual water content (θr  ), a shape parameter related to air entry (α ) and a shape parameter related to pore size distribution (n ), and with m  = 1 – 1/n . The parameters were determined using the Hyprop-Fit software, now called LABROS SoilView-Analysis, after measuring the SWRCs with the HYPROP instrument. The data were imported into Hyprop-Fit for fitting, and the “Traditional Constrained van Genuchten-Mualem model” was selected to fit the data. The reason for using the (simple) VG equation was its popularity in a wide range of applications and simulation models, while previous studies showed its very good fits to SWRC data of soils in the same area as our study (Cornelis et al., 2005 ). We did not treat m  as a free parameter, because of its correlation with n  which would reduce their prediction potential, while not significantly affecting the model performance (Cornelis et al., 2005 ). Visual inspection of our SWRCs also did not show dual porosity. Bulk density (BD) was measured on the same cores as SWRC, following Grossman and Reinsch (2002) . Particle size distribution (sand: 0.05–2 mm, silt: 0.002–0.05 mm, and clay: < 0.002 mm) was determined using the pipette-sieve method (Gee and Or, 2002 ) and soil organic carbon (SOC) with the wet oxidation method of Walkley and Black (1934) . Soil depth was represented by a categorical variable, namely soil layer. Values of 1, 3, and 2, were assigned to the layers TOP, CSUB, and SUB, respectively, as the soil structural degradation was expected to be most pronounced in the compacted subsoil, followed by the deeper subsoil and the topsoil. The soil structural quality index was visually measured using the CoreVESS method (Johannes et al., 2017 ). Intact soil samples equilibrated at a matric suction of 100 hPa on a sand box (Royal Eijkelkamp) were broken by hand and evaluated on three attributes: (i) breaking difficulty, (ii) aggregate shape and size, and (iii) visible porosity. Scores of 1 to 5 were given to each of the three attributes, with 1 indicating very good and 5 poor structure (Johannes et al., 2017 ). The arithmetic mean of the scores given to the individual attributes yielded the (final) soil structural quality score Sq. Although CoreVESS was originally developed for topsoils, we applied it to subsoils using the same criteria. This approach is justified as we used it to quantify soil structure simply and easily, rather than for advising land users or consultants on soil management (Ball et al., 2007 ). Penetration resistance was measured to a depth of 80 cm using a Royal Eijkelkamp penetrologger with a cone top angle of 60° and a base area of 1 cm2 . Per position, measurements were done at four points. The arithmetic means of the four replications, averaged over a length of 5 cm corresponding to the core sampling depths, were taken for PTF development.  2.3 Regression methods for developing the PTFs Two classical regression and two machine learning methods were employed to develop the PTFs: multiple linear regression (MLR) and generalized additive model (GAM), and support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (KNN), respectively. 2.3.1 Description of methods Classical regression techniques have been widely used to derive the relationship between soil hydraulic and basic soil properties due to their simplicity, fast training, and well-interpretability (Van Looy et al., 2017 ). Multiple linear regression (MLR) is generally of the form:(1) y = a + ∑ i = 1  n  b i  x i  + ε     where constant a is the intercept, bi   is the regression coefficient and ε  is the error. Generalized additive models (GAM) allow fitting data with smooths or splines to handle non-linear effects, accommodating a wide variety of shapes (Gessler et al., 1995; Hastie and Tibsh, 1990 ). The flexible smooths in GAM are constructed of many smaller functions. Each smooth is the sum of several basic functions and each basis function is multiplied by a coefficient, each of which is a parameter in the model. To our knowledge, GAM has not been commonly used for PTF development, particularly for soil hydraulic PTFs. Support vector machines (SVM) is another popular method, originally developed by Cortes and Vapnik (1995) . SVM is a supervised learning model that is applicable to both classification and regression problems. The main idea of SVM is to find an optimal hyperplane that maximizes the margin between the hyperplane and the closest samples. Using a kernel function, SVM maps data to a space where a linear hyperplane can separate classes (Kalumba et al., 2020 ), efficiently handling both linear and non-linear relationships. The regression is formulated as:(2) f x    = ∑ i = 1  J  w i  Φ x    + b     where φ(x ) denotes non-linear transformation, wi   is a weight and b  is the bias term. SVM is already successfully used to develop soil hydraulic PTFs (e.g., Kalumba et al., 2020; Lamorski et al., 2008; Nguyen et al., 2015; Twarakavi et al., 2009 ). The k-nearest neighbors (KNN) is another machine learning method referred to as a lazy learning algorithm that uses a distance-based approach (Nemes et al., 2006 ). It is said to be lazy because it only uses the instance that is most similar to the target object from the neighborhood, based on their input attributes (Botula et al., 2014 ). The output of the target soil is the soil property value derived from the mean of input attributes of its k-nearest neighbors (Van Looy et al., 2017 ). The distance (di  ) of ith   soil from the target soil can be calculated as:(3) d i  = ∑ j = 1  x  Δ a ij  2        where Δαij   is the difference of the ith   soil from the target soil in the jth   soil attribute. The user defines the number of nearest neighbors (k ) to minimize the prediction error, and assigns a weight (wi  ) to each sample based on its distance (Van Looy et al., 2017 ). The wi   is defined as (Nemes et al., 2006 ):(4) w i  = ∑ i = 1  k  d i   d i      p  ∑ i = 1  k  ∑ i = 1  k  d i   d i      p        where p  is the power term which is dependent on the size of the Train dataset. KNN was also used earlier to develop soil hydraulic PTFs (e.g., Botula et al., 2014; De Pue et al., 2021; Nemes et al., 2006 ).  2.3.2 Development of the PTFs To evaluate the performance of the tested methods, all PTFs were initially developed by considering all predictor variables: sand content (Sand, %), clay content (Clay, %), soil organic carbon content (SOC, g kg−1 ), bulk density (BD, Mg m−3 ), soil depth (Layer), soil structural quality score (Sq), and soil penetration resistance (PR). For MLR, the best equation was selected by stepwise regression, while for GAM, the smoothing terms were represented using penalized regression spline. The construction of SVM PTFs relies on a selection of tuning parameters: cost (C ) determining the trade-off between complexity and the prediction error, radial basis kernel width (γ ) indicating the inverse of the radius of influence, and an insensitivity parameter (ε ) controlling the insensitive zone width (Lamorski et al., 2008 ). These parameters were optimized using a grid-based search, with C  ranging from 0.001 to 1000, γ  from 0.001 to 100, and ε  from 0.01 to 1 (Twarakavi et al., 2009 ). The set of C , γ , ε  giving the best cross-validation accuracy was chosen as a final model. Also KNN has tuning parameters, namely k  and p . The k  term decides the number of similar soil horizons in the reference data set to predict the desired attribute of targeted soil, while the p  term describes the weight-distance relationship. In this study, hyperparameter optimization via grid search adjusted k  from 1 to 15 and p  from 0.5 to 2.5. These values were based on formulas suggested by Nemes et al. (2006) , but optimized using a broader range for best results. For machine learning methods, Train data were standardized for a zero mean and unit variance to avoid bias to those attributes that have a broad value range (Twarakavi et al., 2009 ). Even though machine learning can handle both linear and non-linear relationships, redundant inputs can increase errors. Therefore, soil input attributes were withdrawn through an AIC (Akaike information criterion) feature selection, removing insignificant variables.   2.4 Data handling After having removed samples that missed info on Sq or PR, the number of soil horizons finally retained was 212. The dataset was then divided in two subdatasets, with a proportion of 70 % for the Train phase and 30 % for the Test phase. In doing so, textured-regulated splitting was employed to ensure that the data set was divided as such that all texture classes were proportionally distributed over the Train and Test phase with a ratio of 7:3. A preliminary test showed that this increased the prediction accuracy of the developed PTFs. Location, position and layer (depth) were also considered in order to, in as much as possible, achieve two well-balanced subdatasets. The Train dataset thus included 149 soil horizons and the Test dataset 63 soil horizons, the distribution of the indicators is shown in Fig. 3   and Table 1  . The accuracy of the PTFs was evaluated by cross-validation in four steps: (i) the data were partitioned into several subsets (k-fold), (ii) the model was trained using k-1 of the folds as the Train data, (iii) the resulting model was validated on the remaining part of the data, and (iv) the processes from ii to iii were iterated (as a loop) until each fold was used as validation data. The accuracy of the model thus corresponded to the average accuracy of each fold. Therefore, the data used for the Train phase were divided into two sets, a Train dataset and holdout cross-validation dataset. The size of the holdout-cross validation set depended on the value of k and a 10 fold-cross validation was applied throughout this research. The interrelationships among the set of variables/predictors was assessed by multivariate Principal Component Analysis (PCA; Bayat et al., 2013 ).  2.5 Testing the effect of including soil structural and soil strength information While the development of PTFs as described in section 2.3  could already shed a light on the importance of Sq and PR relative to the other predictor variables, their effect on improving the prediction of SWRC, was further tested in two ways. First, they were used as predictor variable in three additional PTFs that were developed by using the best of the four development methods and the simplest (point MLR). These PTFs had following predictors:• Sand, Clay, SOC and Sq  • Sand, Clay, BD and Sq  • Sand, Clay, SOC, BD and Sq    or.• Sand, Clay, SOC and PR  • Sand, Clay, BD and PR  • Sand, Clay, SOC, BD and PR    These PTFs were then compared with similar PTFs, but without Sq or PR:• Sand, Clay and SOC  • Sand, Clay and BD  • Sand, Clay, SOC and BD    The response variables Sand, Clay, SOC and/or BD are most widely used in PTFs worldwide. Secondly, Sq was used as discriminant for grouping data. Soils with Sq scores in the range of [1,3] were considered as of acceptable soil structure (Train phase: N = 86, Test phase: N = 36), and (3,5] as of degraded soil structure (Train phase: N = 63, Test phase: N = 27), based on findings of Lin et al. (2022)  using the same dataset. They found that grouping soils into these categories resulted in significant differences in SWRC, and that Sq was significantly higher at positions and depths that showed lower soil structural quality as indicated by indicators and an index of soil quality derived from traditional field- and laboratory-based methods of soil analysis. Selecting only two groups also kept the number of samples in each group reasonable. In order to verify whether the PTF performance depended on a soil structural effect or the effect of grouping data as such, we also grouped data according to texture, using groups of similar sizes as above. To do so, the texture classification used by Wösten et al. (1999)  was chosen: coarse-textured soil (Train phase: N = 68, Test phase: N = 25) and medium to fine-textured soil (Train phase: N = 81, Test phase: N = 38). Also here, the effect was tested by using the simplest method (point MLR) and the best performing method.  2.6 Model validation Both the Coefficient of Determination (R2 ) and the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) were selected as the primary statistics to evaluate and compare the PTFs. This is due to their widespread use and comprehensibility in predictive modeling. R2  indicates how well the model explains the variability of the response data and is easily interpretable. RMSE provides an average measure of prediction error with the same units as the dependent variable, offering a clear indication of model accuracy. To further enhance the evaluation, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) was also used to indicate the overall error of prediction. The performance indicators used in this study can be defined as:(5) R  2  = N ∑ i = 1  N  y i  y i  ^  - ∑ i = 1  N  y i  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  ^   N ∑ i = 1  N  y i  2  - ∑ i = 1  N  y i     2    N ∑ i = 1  N  y i  2  ^  - ∑ i = 1  N  y i  ^     2             (6) RMSE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  ^  - y i     2        (7) MAE = 1 N   ∑ i = 1  N  | y i  ^  - y i  |      where N is the number of observations, yi   is the measured value, and y i  ^     is the predicted value. The number of observations per SWRC for both the point and parametric PTF was 14, corresponding to the preset pF values.   3 Results 3.1 Performance of regression methods for SWRC PTF development 3.1.1 Point PTFs Table 2   shows the relationships between the water contents at 14 selected pF values and seven potential predictor variables. In the very wet range of the SWRC (i.e., till pF of 1.5), all the soil attributes were significantly related to different water contents. As matric suction increased, the influence of the predictors on water content became weaker, especially Layer, Sq, and then SOC and PR. The regression coefficients of the MLR and GAM point PTFs developed for each matric suction based on the Train dataset are presented in Table S1  and Table S2  in Supplementary materials . It can be seen that MLR and GAM successfully predicted the water retention curve from Layer, Sand, Clay, SOC, and BD. Note that these variables were also retained by SVM and KNN. Clay was always the best predictor, followed by BD. Soil organic content did not contribute much to the SWRC in the very wet range, but became significant from pF1.75, as was also the case with Sand. Layer was only accounted for between pF0.0 and pF1.5 under MLR, and even removed by GAM under all pFs. Though Sq was significantly correlated with water contents between saturation and pF 1.75 (Table 2 ), its effect was minimal in comparison with the other variables and it was only retained in MLR models between pF 2 and 3.5. It was similar to PR. The PCA shown in Fig. S1  indeed indicates small angles between the vectors of Layer, PR, BD and Sq, and shorter vectors for Sq in comparison with those three variables. This means that all four variables are well (positively) correlated, with Sq showing the smallest effect on this principal component (Dim). Clay and Sand vectors are at high angles as compared to these four variables and are relatively long. As expected, Sand is negatively correlated to Clay. SOC also shows a strong effect and is highly negatively correlated to Layer, PR, BD and Sq. Fig. 4   shows the R2  and RMSE values per point PTF (corresponding with the 14 pF values) for the four methods of PTF development using the Train and Test dataset. It can be seen that for most point PTFs, KNN was superior to the other methods showing the highest R2  values and lowest RMSE values for the Train dataset. Also SVM performed rather well, except for PTFs at pF 2.0–3.0. GAM was third best and MLR overall performed poorest. For the Test dataset, the trend seems not very clear, with overall mean values of R2  for the 14 point PTFs of 0.666, 0.674, 0.689 and 0.647 under MLR, GAM, SVM and KNN, respectively. The mean RMSE values were 0.030, 0.029, 0.028 and 0.030 m3  m−3 , respectively.  3.1.2 Parametric PTFs Table 3   shows the correlation between the VG parameters and seven potential predictor variables for the four parametric PTFs. Good relationships were observed between most predictors and parameters. For example, Sand was significantly correlated to all parameters, as were Clay and SOC except for θr  , and PR except for n . Layer and BD were significant only in relation to θr   and θs   or θs   and α , while Sq only had an effect on θs  . The regression coefficients for VG parameters derived by the MLR and GAM parametric PTFs in the Train phase are presented in in Table S3  and Table S4  in Supplementary materials . In MLR models, Sand and Clay were the most important predictors, followed by Layer and SOC. These were also the ones retained by SVM and KNN. PR and Sq were removed for almost all parameters. While in GAM, Layer was always removed; Sq remained but was not significant for the model. The performance of the different methods in developing the parametric PTFs for the Train and Test phase is shown in Table 4  . In the Train phase, KNN performed the best for θ s  and n , GAM was the best for θr   while, for α  SVM showed the best performance, with the highest R2  and lowest RMSE values (KNN also had the lowest RMSE for α ). Each parameter thus had its own most suitable model. The R2  and RMSE values were reasonable for θ s  and n , but less satisfactory for the other parameters and much lower in comparison to those of the point PTFs. Figure S2  shows the water contents predicted with these parametric PTFs at the corresponding 14 pF points for which also point PTFs were developed. The performance of the parametric PTFs was much worse than that of the point PTFs, in particular at the dry range of the SWRCs, with low R2  and high RMSE values. Overall, SVM gave the best predictive performance, MLR, GAM and KNN performed similar, with R2  values decreasing rapidly and RMSE values increasing rapidly from pF0.5 to pF1.5. In addition, especially for MLR, it had extremely high RMSE values at the dry range. The transformation of α  and n  as used in Weynants et al. (2009)  was also explored (Fig. 5  ), the parametric PTF performance was improved, especially in wet and dry range of the curves. KNN showed the best predictive ability in the very wet range followed by SVM in Train phase, while in Test phase, SVM was the best.   3.2 Effect of including soil structural or soil strength information The effect of including a predictor variable that captures soil structure or soil strength was tested with the point PTFs for the best performing method, which was KNN as demonstrated above. Fig. 6   shows the performance of incorporating Sq or PR in addition to the combination of Sand, Clay, and SOC as basic predictors. The predictive ability in the very wet region of SWRC was significantly improved by the addition information of Sq or PR, with R2  increasing and RMSE decreasing. However, their contribution disappeared from pF2.0 onwards. The performance of the combination of Sand, Clay, BD as basics predictors and the addition of Sq or PR is also shown in Fig. 6 . After the addition of PR, the predictive ability improved until pF1.25 with increasing R2  and decreasing RMSE when considering the Train dataset. On the other hand, the contribution of Sq was not clear; it resulted anyway in the highest R2  values between pF1.0 and pF2.0. Finally, the combination of Sq or PR in addition to Sand, Clay, SOC and BD as basic predictors was also tested as shown in Fig. S3 . Adding PR as an additional predictor improved PTF performance up to pF1.0 for the Train dataset, while this was not the case when Sq was included. When comparing Fig. 6  and Fig. S3 , it appears that Sq and PR had no to little effect on the prediction accuracy of the KNN-based point PTFs when added to Sand, Clay, SOC and BD. While they increased R2  and reduced RMSE in the wet range of the SWRC (till pF2.0) in the Train phase, the opposite was found in the Test phase. Nevertheless, Sq or PR substantially improved the performance of the PTFs till pF2.0 in case BD was not included as predictor (based on both the Train and Test dataset).  3.3 Effect of grouping data The effect of grouping data based on soil structural or soil textural quality was tested with the point PTFs for the simplest method (MLR) and the best performing method (KNN) based on the seven predictors mentioned above (Fig. 7  ). Grouping did increase the reliability of PTFs at all pF values for MLR as indicated by an increase in R2  and a decrease in RMSE, and with textural grouping being better than structural grouping. The effect of grouping was weaker after pF3.0. For the KNN PTFs, although grouping also increased the reliability of the PTFs in the range from pF0.5 to pF1.5 and pF2.5 to pF4.0, its effect was quite limited, and again, the textural grouping was slightly better than the structural grouping.  3.4 Comparison with existing PTFs The existing PTFs of Weynants et al. (2009) , which are revised PTFs of those by Vereecken et al. (1989)  and are based on soil data collected in the same study area as our research, were compared with the new point PTFs for the best performing method (KNN) based on seven predictors and the one with only Clay, Sand, SOC and BD as in Weynants et al. (2009) , and with the new VG parametric PTFs for the best performing method (SVM) based on seven predictors (Fig. 8  ) using both the updated Belgian Train and Test datasets. The new point KNN PTFs in our study performed better than that by Weynants et al. (2009) , both for Train and Test dataset, with higher R2  and lower RMSE values for the entire SWRC curve. However, the new seven-predictor point KNN PTF, performed somewhat poorer in the very wet range of in test dataset. The new parametric PTF only improved the predictive ability at the very wet range of SWRC from pF0.0 to pF1.5 in Train dataset and from pF0.0 to pF1.0 in the Test dataset; at higher suctions, it performed worse than the Weynants et al. PTFs. Fig. 9   shows the comparison of Weynants et al. (2009)  PTFs, new VG parametric PTFs for the best performing method (SVM) based on seven predictors, and new VG parametric PTFs with the transformation of α  and n . Using the transformation parameters clearly improved the parametric PTF performance, it was even better than Weynants et al. (2009)  PTFs, but except the very dry range of the curve. With R2  values above 0.65 in the Train phase and 0.58 in the Test phase (except for the very dry range), and with RMSE below 0.042 and 0.045 m3  m−3 , respectively, the PTFs can be considered as good. These values are also better than those of most PTFs evaluated by Vereecken et al. (2010) . Fig. 10   shows the scatter plots including water contents under 14 pF values with both Train and Test datasets. Overall, it shows that the new point KNN PTF based on four predictors (Clay, Sand, SOC and BD) was the best, with highest overall R2  and lowest overall RMSE value. The new point KNN PTF based on seven predictors did not result in an overall improvement. The new parametric SVM PTF performed even worse than that of Weynants et al. (2009) , in contrast with the new parametric SVM PTF based on a transformation of parameters α and n, which performed better than the original new parametric SVM PTF and that of Weynants et al. (2009) .   4 Discussion 4.1 Performance of different models 4.1.1 Point and parametric PTFs All the point PTFs used in our study are capable of predicting water retention curves, with a relatively high R2  ranging from 0.620 to 0.926, and relatively low RMSE from 0.017 to 0.035 m3  m−3 . The parametric PTFs, on the other hand, did not perform very well in our study, showing lower R2  and higher RMSE values, especially in the dry range of the SWRC. This could be because the predicted parameters sometimes showed negative values or were away from the reasonable range of values; moreover, for some samples’ water content increased with increasing pF values, which contradicts the theory. This was also observed by Cornelis et al. (2001)  when evaluating point PTFs. Also Du et al. (2022)  reported that the VG model is a complex nonlinear equation involving multiple related parameters, which made it difficult in their study to find optimal solutions for these parameters by inverse modeling. Our study shows the low predictive ability in the wet and dry ranges of SWRC, which has also been reported by several researchers who pointed out that VGM parameters have weaknesses in representing the wet and dry parts of SWRC (Khlosi et al., 2008 ). Vereecken et al. (2010)  found that the root mean square residuals based on the classical VGM model with fixed parameters are increasingly higher as the soil becomes drier. This could be due to the fact that water retention in the dry part of SWRC is no longer determined by capillary forces but by adsorption forces (Yu and Wardlaw, 1986; Lenormand, 1990; Nimmo, 1991 ). Khlosi et al. (2008)  also reported that measuring water content at high matric potential values is difficult, so there are fewer data sets that include tests beyond pF 4.2. Durner (1994)  noted that classical VGM parameterization even may fail for heterogeneous pore size zones. The deviations may be due to the presence of macro pores (Vereecken et al., 2010 ). On the other hand, it remains a challenge to predict the VG parameter α . It determines the 'height' of the SWRC, but also depends on n . Thus, α  is a real shape parameter that is less explained by the predictors. In contrast, point PTFs simply predict water content at a given matrix potential, which is generally higher with increasing clay content. In addition, Nimmo (1991)  and Vereecken et al. (2010)  found that residual water content was not easy to predict or determine. It was sometimes set equal to zero or excluded from the model during curve fitting process to avoid negative values (Weynants et al., 2009 ). Indeed, this was also observed in our study, were some soil samples had negative values, both for α  and θr  , especially for θr  , which weakens their prediction potential.  4.1.2 MLR, GAM, SVM and KNN techniques The assessment of various algorithms appears to have received limited attention over the past decade, only a few of machine learning studies examined three or more algorithms. Incorporating a comprehensive evaluation of diverse algorithms is deemed advantageous in the pursuit of PTFs development. The superior performance of the machine learning methods (i.e., SVM, KNN) for developing soil hydraulic PTFs is proved again in this study, and corroborates the findings of for example Haghverdi et al. (2012)  and Botula et al. (2013) . The main disadvantage of MLR is that it requires several stringent assumptions which are not always satisfied. This can explain why it performed the worst both for point and parametric PTFs in our study. GAM was developed to overcome this disadvantage, and can deal with both non-normal distributions and non-linear relationships. Thus, GAM performed better than MLR. However, it requires a large amount of data for developing the smooth terms. In contrast, SVM can work well with a small dataset. Moreover, the implementation of structural risk minimization in the SVM algorithm's optimization process makes its prediction more accurate than the classical regression methods. Nonetheless, SVM uses the kernel function to map the data and optimize the regression. The KNN method showed the best performance in predicting SWRCs in our study due to several factors. KNN is nonparametric and can be used for both classification and regression, allowing it to adapt flexibly to the data without assuming a specific functional form. This flexibility is crucial for capturing the complex, nonlinear relationships present in soil properties. KNN's ability to handle nonlinear decision boundaries and its localized approach, which considers only the nearest neighbours, helps accurately model the spatial variability and heterogeneity in soil characteristics. Additionally, the training step in KNN is much faster compared to other machine learning methods, making it computationally efficient. KNN is also robust to outliers and highly adaptable through its single hyperparameter, k , making hyperparameter tuning straightforward. However, while KNN offers these advantages, it can be computationally intensive during the prediction stage and its black-box nature can complicate the interpretation of predictor variables' effects on soil hydraulic properties. To mitigate these drawbacks, graphical interfaces like ROSETTA (Schaap et al., 2001 ) and the KNN Soil Water Retention Estimation software (Nemes et al., 2006 ) have been developed, making KNN more accessible and user-friendly for a broader audience. Ultimately, the predictive capability of PTFs derived by machine learning methods like KNN depends on the quality and similarity of the soils in the training phase to those for which hydraulic properties need to be predicted (Botula et al., 2013; Perkins and Nimmo, 2009 ). Despite the complexities, KNN’s flexibility, robustness, and localized learning make it a powerful and effective tool for predicting soil–water retention curves.   4.2 Importance of soil attributes for SWRC PTFs The basic predictor variables chosen in this study, that is, Sand, Clay, SOC, BD and to a lower extent Layer all showed useful for developing water retention PTFs, depending on the matric suction in case of the point PTFs or the VG parameter for the parametric PTFs. Overall, Clay statistically showed the highest contribution to the regressions. This is not surprising given that the affinity of soil for water by adsorption (due to hydrogen bonds and an osmotic effect) is function of the surface area of soil solids and their charge density (Jury and Horton, 2004 ), which typically increase with clay content. In addition, soils higher in clay content show a broader pore size distribution than more sandier soil (Jury and Horton, 2004 ) which affects the SWRC in its air-entry and capillary region. Finally, clayey soils generally show higher porosities and thus can retain more water at saturation. Bulk density was the second best predictor, and showed a high contribution to the regressions, except for the dry end of the SWRC (though it was still significant with GAM method in our study). BD is directly related to porosity, which determines the volume of water stored in the soil at low to moderate suctions. This makes BD an essential predictor in estimating the soil water characteristic (Arya and Paris, 1981 ). It is negatively correlated to soil water content in the wet range of the SWRC, as an increase in BD reduces both the volume and the size of the pores, leading to a reduction in water retention. However, in the drier (moist) range of the SWRC, the opposite is sometimes observed as the volume of smaller pores increases due to the destruction of the larger pores, and the relation between BD and hydraulic properties can there become positive (Alaoui et al., 2011; Richard et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2001 ). This was, however, not observed in our study, where overall the relation between water content and BD remained negative in the moist range. Though at matric suction higher than 1000 hPa (pF 3, i.e., in the dry range) capillarity and thus pore sizes have a minor effect on water retention (Tuller et al., 1999 ), a denser soil also increases the number of (negatively charged) particles within a given volume, and thus the volume of water bounded by adsorption forces which now prevail. Yet, we also found in this range soil water content to decrease with increasing bulk density. Soil organic matter content did not contribute as much to the very wet range of SWRC in our study, while it became significant above ∼ 50 hPa (pF 1.75). Beke and MacCormick (1985)  and Petersen et al. (1968)  also found that including information from SOC was useful for estimating water content at −1500 kPa, while this was not the case at –33 kPa. Salter and Haworth (1961)  on the other hand stated that SOC is an important factor for water content already at –33 kPa, while it may not really be an important predictor at lower suctions. The major effect of SOC on retention of water is through its increase in surface area and charge density (Rawls et al., 2003 ), though SOC can also modify the availability to water of adsorption sites on clay minerals (Christensen, 1996 ). In addition, SOC has a higher impact in sandy soils as compared to clayey soils (Rawls et al., 2003 ). On the other hand, being a binding agent, it affects aggregation, resulting in a change in pore size distribution (Dal Ferro et al., 2012 ). Overall, the impact of SOC to water retention is rather limited, especially when compared to the impact of clay content. Minasny and McBratney (2018)  observed by modelling that the greatest impact of SOC occurs within the range of 0 to 1 %, with diminishing returns as SOC increases further. In our study, the mean value of SOC exceeds 10 g kg−1  (Table 1 ), which suggests that the influence of SOC in our specific context is uncertain or less pronounced. The impact of Sand on the PTF performance was similar as that of SOC. Of course, sand content is typically well and inversely correlated with clay content (as was also demonstrated by the PCA, Fig. S1 ), and thus not add much extra value to the PTFs. Layer was not really withheld in our models. This could be primarily explained by the fact that it is well related to BD, and belongs to the same dimension according to the PCA biplot. That it was treated as a categorical variable ranging from 1 to 3 does not explain its low impact since a preliminary study where depth was considered as a continuous variable even showed a lower effect. Conversely, considering the sensitivity of soil hydraulic properties such as the SWRC, the incorporation of more complex soil attributes could potentially introduce a certain level of intricacy that might not be advantageous for PTFs. This added complexity can reduce model effectiveness, as it raises the risk of overfitting due to increased noise in the model structure, leading to weakened generalization. This aspect also warrants deeper investigation.  4.3 The contribution of including structural information As has been advocated by Vereecken et al. (2010), Van Looy et al. (2017)  and Vereecken et al., (2019) , a major challenge in the development of hydraulic PTFs is the inclusion of soil structural properties as predictor variable. Additionally, Pachepsky and Rawls (2003)  also propose that the structural attributes could serve as prospective predictors. In this study, we tested whether a visually assessed soil structural quality score Sq and a soil strength parameter PR could improve the prediction accuracy of SWRC PTFs. Their additional value as a new numerical predictor variable seemed not clear. In our study, adding Sq or PR as additional information clearly improved the predictive ability in the wet range of SWRC, primarily in case of a basic predictor combination of Sand, Clay, and SOC, and in the Train phase. This was in line with the PCA showing that Sq, PR and SOC did not provide similar information for predicting the SWRC. At pF values higher than 2, their contribution disappeared. Or et al. (2002)  stated that the effect of soil structure on SWRC is most prominent in the wet range of SWRC. This corroborates with findings of (Lin et al., 2022 ), who found that differences in water content between soils of acceptable and degraded structure were on average small (< 7%) and only till pF 2. When adding Sq or PR to a combination that included BD, the positive effect was only visible for PR, although it was small. The PCA also showed that PR, Sq, and BD contributed to the same principal component, implying that they contained similar information, while the vector length of Sq and PR was smaller than that of BD. Therefore, their contribution was limited. In addition, Sq was closer to BD compared with PR (the angle is smaller), so the improvement was even not clear. Given the rather marginal effects of including Sq or PR in SWRC PTFs, their use to for example better grab the SWRC spatial or temporal variability within fields might be limited, especially if BD is known. However, if (approximate) SWRCs are needed in field studies, both Sq or PR, which are rather easy and fast to determine, could be an alternative for taking samples and transporting them to the lab for BD (or SWRC) determination, given that Sand, Clay and SOC is known. Note that instead of using CoreVESS, Sq can also be derived from soil blocks in the field according to VESS, which should yield similar results (Cornelis et al., 2019 ).  4.4 The contribution of grouping Grouping soils increased PTF performance in our study, especially for the MLR. Nguyen et al. (2014)  also reported that after grouping, the accuracy of MLR PTFs was improved. However, textural grouping proved better than the structural grouping in the wet range of SWRC. After pF3.0 it was switched, this could be explained by the wet range of SWRC, which is more influenced by soil structure (Or et al., 2002 ). Grouping by soil structure would therefore limit the information in each subgroup. For the KNN PTFs, grouping soils only slightly improved the PTF performance in the SWRC range from pF 0.5 to pF 1.5. Nguyen et al. (2015)  also showed that grouping did not improve the PTF performance for the KNN method, which they partly attributed to their limited dataset after grouping. While our subgroups were larger in size than in their study, their size might still have been too low. As KNN is a highly data-intensive approach, it requires a large data set to obtain stable and accurate estimates (Hastie et al., 2009 ).  4.5 Comparison with existing PTFs The existing PTFs of Weynants et al. (2009)  were compared with the best performing methods for both the point PTFs and parametric PTFs, which were KNN and SVM, respectively. In addition, different predictor combinations were also compared. The new KNN point PTFs showed better predictive performance, the reason being similar to that mentioned in Section 4.1 , in that point PTFs seems superior to parametric PTFs. Also, the fact that we used recent soil data for developing our PTFs, while they were tested as well on recent soil data and thus contain soil information that is not necessarily reflected in the considered predictor variables could have played a role. With intensive mechanical tillage and inappropriate cultivation methods and techniques, soil structure degradation has become very common. Keller et al. (2019)  demonstrated a progressive increase in soil compaction due to intensified agricultural practices, particularly the use of heavy machinery such as tractors and combine harvesters, over several decades spanning from the 1950 s to 2020. Based on this evidence, it is reasonable to infer that Belgium has also experienced a similar trend of increased field traffic, resulting in soil degradation. The effect of this on SWRC is only to a limited extent enclosed in predictors like SOC or BD. While our SRWC were established using the HYPROP® modified evaporation method, and Weynants et al. (2009)  used SWRCs based on sandboxes and pressure plates, we do not believe that this had an impact on the results. Schelle et al. (2013)  for example showed that both methods result in similar SWRCs. However, for the new parametric PTFs developed in our study, the prediction performance was worse than that of the Weynants et al. PTFs. The main reason being its poorer predictive ability of the dry range of the SWRC. This is caused by our SVM PTF sometimes predicting n  values smaller than 1, resulting in m  values becoming negative, and thus in water contents that steadily increase as matric suction increases. This occurred in 6.13 % of the entire samples. Also, the θr   PTF predicted in 4.72 % of the cases negative values. Setting it equal to 0 as done by Weynants et al. (2009)  did, however, not result in an improvement. Moreover, transformation the parameters was also explored, it avoided problems which we mentioned above, thus the PTF performance was improved.   5 Conclusions To evaluate the large-scale influence of soil degradation on soil water flow with agrohydrologic models, collecting up-to-date input data and incorporating soil structure or strength information for developing new PTFs would be valuable. In this study, pedotransfer functions to predict soil water retention curves (SWRC-PTFs) were developed using various algorithms from classical regressions (multiple linear regression MLR and generalized additive model GAM) to state-of-the-art machine learning methods (support vector machine SVM and k-nearest neighbors KNN). In addition, both point- and parameter-based PTFs were considered. Furthermore, it was also investigated whether including soil structure or strength information or the grouping of dataset could improve the predictive performance of PTFs. The point PTFs performed much better than the parametric PTFs. Also, this study showed the superiority of the KNN approach over the other three selected model methods, while MLR performed the worst. After including soil structure or strength information, the prediction ability in the wet range of SWRC improved, and the contribution of penetration resistance was better than that of the CoreVESS Sq score.
