Moreover, grouping the dataset also improved the accuracy of the PTFs, with texture-based grouping performing better than structure-based grouping in the wet range of the SWRC. Finally, our new point PTFs showed a better performance in comparison with the existing PTFs Weynants et al. (2009)  developed on soil samples taken from the same study area. As a way forward, other predictors that could provide different soil information (e.g. including but not limited to pH) should be further explored. On the other hand, as the regression methods seem to affect the prediction accuracy of the PTFs, testing new emerging and advanced machine learning methods would be worth the investment. In order to finally evaluate the effect of soil management and remediation of soil structure degradation on the water regime, knowledge of hydraulic conductivity would also be needed. Given the high variability in hydraulic conductivity typically observed (e.g. Reynolds et al., 2000), we did not attempt to develop PTFs to predict it here, but rather suggest to measure it the field, as also concluded by Vereecken et al. (1990).
1 Introduction Runoff, evapotranspiration (ET), and other water fluxes, along with terrestrial water storage, are key components of the global water cycle and energy budget. A scientific understanding of hydrological cycle processes and effective management of water resources depend on accurate simulations of water stores and fluxes (Pokhrel et al., 2021 ). Hydrological models, when provided with reliable input data and appropriate parameters, can reproduce historical hydrological processes in regional water cycles and predict their future changes (Abbaspour et al., 2015; He et al., 2021 ). Ideally, distributed hydrological models should outperform conceptual models, as they incorporate more detailed physical mechanisms and provide a finer spatial representation of hydrological processes within a watershed. However, distributed hydrological models are often found to be inferior to conceptual models, due to issues such as lack of observational data, neglect of parameter spatial variability, and uncertainties in multiple parameters (Beven, 1993; Khakbaz et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ). To accurately simulate hydrological states and fluxes using distributed hydrological models, parameter calibration is an integral step in the modeling process and constitutes the crux of the issue at hand. The purpose of parameter calibration is to minimize discrepancies between simulated values and observed data, thereby enhancing the overall realism and accuracy of the model. Hydrological models are typically calibrated using observed streamflow, as it represents an integrated hydrological flux of the basin and can be measured more accurately and conveniently than other components. Conventional calibration is often limited to streamﬂow at the outlet, failing to capture the heterogeneity of spatial parameters in distributed hydrological models, which may result in poor simulations of other hydrological components (Blöschl et al., 2019; Garavaglia et al., 2017 ). To enhance the understanding of all hydrological processes, approaches focused on multiple hydrological processes and calibration strategies that integrate multiple data sources need to be developed (Clark et al., 2017; Yeste et al., 2023 ). In the past decade, many studies have used remote sensing-based ET, soil moisture, and terrestrial water storage data in addition to gauged streamflow in model parameter calibration (Herman et al., 2018; Immerzeel and Droogers, 2008; Sutanudjaja et al., 2014 ). The growing availability of data on ET, soil moisture, runoff coefficients, and other related variables has enriched hydrological modeling with valuable information and has effectively mitigated the inherent limitations associated with exclusively relying on discharge calibration, particularly in data-scarce areas (Crow et al., 2022; Li et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Employing multi-variable parameter calibration strategies to control multiple dominant processes contributes to improving the simulation of soil moisture, ET, and land surface water storage. However, many studies indicate that the use of additional variables besides gauged streamflow does not necessarily enhance the overall model performance, particularly in terms of streamflow prediction (Mei et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020 ). The presented multi-variable parameter calibration lack sufficient application of high spatiol and temporal information from datasets, typically using only one characteristic of the dataset to increase the number of calibration objective functions (Dembélé et al., 2020b; Efstratiadis and Koutsoyiannis, 2010; Guo et al., 2022 ), thereby constraining the feasible parameter ranges. This trade-off between multiple variables may lead the model to sacrifice runoff simulation accuracy to improve the simulation of other variables (Dembélé et al., 2020a, 2020b; Koppa et al., 2019 ). Constrained by the limitations of available data and caibration methods, it is hard to determine the spatial distribution of certain hydrological parameters for distributed hydrological model. Therefore, considering both temporal and spatial information from gridded datasets in parameter calibration is a potential optimization direction for distributed hydrological models. Evapotranspiration, as a key variable in the hydrological cycle, describes the moisture lost from surface water to the atmosphere through both biotic (e.g. plants) and abiotic (e.g. soils) sources. With the continuous advancement of satellite remote sensing, an increasing number of datasets can now provide spatiotemporally continuous and high-resolution evapotranspiration information (Chen et al., 2021; Miralles et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of calibrating model parameters based on evapotranspiration data. Satellite remote sensing data facilitate the representation of spatial variability, thus making parameter calibration of distributed hydrological models feasible at the grid scale (Dembélé et al., 2020a; Xie et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013 ). However, the accuracy of satellite-based products varies by region, and the direct use of unassessed and uncalibrated data can affect parameter estimation results and model performance. Satellite-based data are more readily available and have higher temporal and spatial resolution compared to field observations, but they do not typically measure hydrological processes directly, introducing a certain degree of uncertainty to any parameter estimation studies based on these data (Huang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2016 ). Some studies have assessed the uncertainty introduced by different datasets in parameter calibration and have applied bias correction to satellite remote sensing data to reduce the uncertainty associated with the datasets in hydrological modeling (Ehlers et al., 2019; Knoche et al., 2014 ). Additionally, merging certain products serves as a reliable method to reduce product uncertainty and obtain applicable data for specific regions (Xu et al., 2024 ). Therefore, before applying various satellite-based products to model parameter calibration, it is necessary and crucial to evaluate these products and reduce their uncertainties. To overcome the shortcomings of traditional calibration strategies based solely on observed streamflow data and to optimize the spatial heterogeneity of parameters in distributed hydrological models, this paper proposes a gridded-scale, hierarchical multi-objective parameter calibration framework using ET datasets and observed streamflow data. Before utilizing satellite-based ET products in calibration, using a triple collocation-based merging approach to integrate the daily ET from the three datasets to reduce data uncertainties. The merged ET data, along with observed streamflow data, are then used to calibrate parameters at the grid scale through a multi-objective genetic algorithm, and the results are compared with those of traditional single-objective calibration schemes. The proposed research is carried out in the Ganjiang River basin located in China, using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model over a period of ten consecutive years (2001–2010).  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area This study selects the Ganjiang River basin (GRB) as a case study ( Fig. 1 ), due to its relatively abundant observational data. The Ganjiang River, the seventh largest tributary of the Yangtze River in China, covers an area of 80,860 km2  upstream of the Waizhou hydrological station. The GRB experiences a subtropical humid monsoon climate, characterized by an average annual air temperature of approximately 17°C and annual precipitation ranging from 1400 to 1800 mm. The elevation across the basin ranges from 31 to 1183 m. The southern part of the basin features higher elevations with hilly terrain and rich vegetation, while the northern downstream areas have flatter terrain dominated by cropland and urban areas.  2.2 Datasets The datasets used for the 1999–2014 period (with 1999–2000 as the spin-up period, 2001–2010 as the calibration period, and 2011–2014 as the validation period) include the morphological data (e.g., elevation and land cover) and meteorological data (e.g., rainfall and air temperature). Topographic data are derived from commonly used existing gridded data, and meteorological data are sourced from the National Meteorological Science Data Center's stations. In situ soil moisture data from 28 evenly distributed stations within the basin are used to evaluate model performance at the point scale. The GRB also comprises 18 hydrological stations with observed streamflow data, facilitating their use for parameter calibration, model accuracy assessment, and ET datasets accuracy assessment. A description of these datasets, including their characteristics and sources, is presented in  Table 1 . In this study, three gridded satellite-based ET datasets, along with observed streamflow data, are considered for parameter calibration. These datasets include the surface energy balance-based global land evapotranspiration (EBET), the evapotranspiration product from version 2 of the Penman-Monteith-Leuning model (PML), and datasets containing various components of land evaporation from the global land evaporation Amsterdam model (GLEAM) v3.6a. EBET was derived from satellite data and a revised surface energy balance system model by Chen et al. (2014)  and was verified to perform better than Landflux, GLEAM, MOD16, GLDAS, and ERA-Interim products in irrigation areas (Chen et al., 2021 ). Based on the Penman-Monteith-Leuning model, PML is integrated with the gross primary productivity process, leveraging stomatal conductance theory. It utilizes the China meteorological forcing dataset and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) leaf area index (LAI), albedo, and emissivity as inputs, offering novel insights into monitoring crop water consumption and revealing characteristics of the planting system (He et al., 2022 ). GLEAM is a set of algorithms dedicated to the estimation of terrestrial evaporation and root-zone soil moisture based on satellite-observed soil moisture, vegetation optical depth, snow-water equivalent, reanalysis air temperature and radiation, and a multi-source precipitation product (Martens et al., 2017 ). The temporal resolution of these three datasets is at a daily scale, allowing for a more detailed depiction of the temporal dynamics of ET. To facilitate modeling, all gridded datasets are rescaled to a 0.05° spatial scale. A summary of ET datasets and further details are provided in  Table 2 .   3 Methodology In this section, the methodical steps for integrating ET datasets and observed streamflow into the distributed hydrological model parameter calibration are outlined. These steps are schematized in  Fig. 2  and described in the following subsections. The framework primarily comprises three main components. Firstly, it involves merging three gridded products using the triple collocation (TC) method to reduce uncertainty in evaporation products. Secondly, it employs a multi-objective parameter optimization method using the merged evaporation products and observed discharge data, implementing parameter calibration at the grid scale of distributed hydrological models based on the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm Ⅱ (NSGA-Ⅱ). Finally, the calibrated parameters and simulation results are evaluated using observed data. 3.1 Triple collocation-based merging of evapotranspiration datasets The TC analysis is a statistical technique used to estimate the error characteristics of three or more products in the absence of known true values (Stoffelen, 1998 ). Previous studies have merged multi-source soil moisture products via a least-squares framework based on constant error variances estimated by TC analysis to reduce uncertainty (Gruber et al., 2017; Yilmaz et al., 2012 ). This study references a TC-based soil moisture merging approach considering spatial and temporal non-stationary errors proposed by Zhou et al. (2021) , employing the TC-based merging approach to integrate the daily ET from the three datasets. (1994) . It has been widely used for simulating the terrestrial water cycle and applied to obtain simulated surface runoff, baseflow, evapotranspiration, and soil moisture dynamics at a grid scale for further data construction, evaluation, assimilation, and forecasting studies. The VIC model does not account for horizontal fluxes between adjacent grid cells, which are typically addressed by integrating a routing scheme during post-processing (Lu et al., 2015 ). In this study, the VIC model is established for the GRB as a case study at a temporal scale of daily and a spatial scale of 0.05°. The parameters of the VIC model can be categorized into climatic-geographic parameters, vegetation parameters, soil parameters, and hydrological parameters. The first three categories are primarily determined based on existing databases (Table 1 ) and are typically kept constant throughout the modeling process. Eight hydrological parameters are selected for the calibration process (two of which are typically set as constants and not subject to calibration), with their upper and lower bounds are shown in  Table 3 . These parameters are selected based on recommendations for calibrating the VIC model and are consistent with previous studies (Sepúlveda et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2007; Yeste et al., 2020 ). Sensitivity analysis is a key tool to provide information on which parameter values are the most influential for the dynamics of specific model responses. Especially in multi-objective parameter calibration, understanding the sensitivity of each parameter to the objective functions helps determine the priority of parameter calibration, thereby enhancing computational efficiency (Sun et al., 2020 ). In this study, the Distributed Evaluation of Local Sensitivity Analysis (DELSA) method is employed to investigate the sensitivities of six selected hydrological parameters concerning two metrics: ET and streamflow. DELSA is a hybrid local-global sensitivity analysis method introduced by Rakovec et al. (2014) , which can be applied at multiple points across the parameter space to reveal important parameter subregions at minimal computational cost. Although DELSA only examines first-order sensitivities, it has the potential to quantify parameter interactions (Zegers et al., 2020 ). Given a sample point θ  *    in the parameter space, the local sensitivity is measured by a modeled output ψ   relative to individual variations of a parameter θ  j     with a 1 % change:(7) ∂ ψ  ∂ θ  j     |  θ  *    = ψ ( θ  j   + 0.01 θ  j   ) − ψ ( θ  j   )   0.01 θ  j     .      The first-order sensitivity measure S  j  *     for each parameter j  at each sample point is calculate as:(8) S  j  *   = ( ∂ ψ  ∂ θ  j     |  θ  *     )  2  s  j  2    V  L   ( θ  *  )    ,     where s  j  2     is the priori parameter variance of parameter j  consistent with a uniform distribution with limits θ j ,max  and θ j ,min :(9) s  j  2   = 1 12   ( θ  j ,  max   − θ  j ,  min    )  2  ,      and V L  (θ *) is the linearized local variance of k  parameters:(10) V  L   ( θ  *  )  = ∑ j = 1  k  ( ∂ ψ  ∂ θ  j     |  θ  *     )  2   s  j  2   .      The range of first-order sensitivity values is from 0 to 1, and at each sampling point, the sum of all parameters' first-order sensitivities equals 1. In this study, 200 base runs are sampled based on the provided parameter boundaries, which is sufficient to sample the parameter space (Melsen and Guse, 2019 ). For these base runs, local sensitivity is determined by each parameter sampled 200 times with 1 % perturbation compared to the 200 base runs. To quantify the relative contributions of parameters within specific intervals, a moving average method is used to illustrate the local sensitivity of parameters.  3.3 Multi-variable parameters calibration The multi-variable parameter calibration (referred to as case Q+ET) is actually a multi-objective optimization problem aimed at optimizing multiple objectives at the same time. In this study, the merged ET and observed streamflow data are selected as target variables, with the Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) used as the evaluation metric. The objective (F  ) of the multi-objective calibration scheme is to maximize the objective functions (K G E  Q      and K G E  E T     ) for these two variables, with a maximum value of 1 for each.(11) F = K G E  Q   + K G E  E T        The KGE is proposed by Gupta et al. (2009)  and modified by Kling et al. (2012) . This comprehensive model performance measure comprises three components: correlation, bias, and variability. The objective function for streamflow measures the agreement between daily simulated streamflow and the observed data at the basin outlet. As for ET, the objective function is computed using the spatial average of the daily simulated ET compared to the merged ET data time series for each grid.(12) { K G E = 1 − ( R − 1 )  2  + ( β − 1 )  2  + ( γ − 1 )  2       β = μ  s    μ  o        γ = σ  s   / μ  s    σ  o   / μ  o           ,    (13) K G E  E T   = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  K G E  E T , i    ,     where R   is the correlation coefficient between simulated and observed (or reference) data; β   is the bias ratio of the mean of simulated data (μ  s    ) to the mean of observed (or reference) data (μ  o    ); γ   is the variability ratio; σ   represents the standard deviation of data series; n   is the total number of VIC model grids. The general outline of the multi-variable calibration process, which will be further detailed in the subsequent sections, includes initial random parameter sample generation, hierarchical optimization strategy based on parameter sensitivity analysis, and a multi-objective parameter calibration algorithm for grid-by-grid calibration. 3.3.1 Latin hypercube sampling and Monte Carlo simulation To obtain the base samples for sensitivity analysis and an initial population in multi-objective parameter optimization, a Monte Carlo simulation with Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) is employed in this study. Each parameter is uniformly sampled across the parameter space using the LHS method, and then the samples are randomly arranged to form a series of parameter sets. This method adapts to different dimensions and parameter spaces to obtain random samples, thereby avoiding dense sampling in some regions while being sparse in others.  3.3.2 Hierarchical optimization strategy Simultaneous grid-by-grid calibration of all parameters at the grid scale presents challenges such as high computational complexity and redundancy. Inspired by traditional manual calibration practices and a multiresolution and heterogeneous calibration strategy proposed by Sun et al. (2020) , this paper introduces a hierarchical calibration strategy based on parameter sensitivity. The main components of the strategy are outlined as follows:(1) The parameter range and calibration priority are determined based on the sensitivity of each parameter to the evaluation metrics of simulated ET and streamflow. Parameters sensitive to both ET and discharge simulation results are prioritized for calibration. The initial range of each parameter for each grid is presented in Table 3 . Using LHS and Monte Carlo simulation to obtain the distribution of parameters for each grid. Parameter ranges are narrowed based on parameter sensitivity, with less sensitive parameters having smaller ranges (ranging from half of the original range to the full range).  (2) In each iteration, only one parameter is calibrated for all grids by a multi-objective optimization algorithm, and optimized parameters from the best non-dominated fronts are retained for next iterations to calibrate other parameters, since the impact of each parameter on the model is not independent. A complete iteration of calibrating all parameters according to their priority is referred to as one cycle. This process continues until the optimization of all objective functions reaches a stable optimal state.     3.3.3 Multi-objective optimization algorithm: NSGA-II NSGA-II is a well-established multi-objective optimization algorithm based on genetic algorithms that has been wildely used in multi-objective parameter optimization (Bekele and Nicklow, 2007; Herman et al., 2018; Yeste et al., 2023 ). The NSGA-II algorithm sorts the population into different non-dominated fronts based on the concept of Pareto dominance and ultimately finds a set of Pareto-optimal solutions to resolve the problem of conflicting objectives (Deb et al., 2002 ). For this study, a NSGA-II algorithm with a hierarchical calibration strategy is employed to calibrate the hydrological parameters of the VIC model on a grid-by-grid scale. Firstly, the initial population is elected (with a size defined as 100 in this study) from randomly generated 1000 parameter samples (as described in Section 3.3.1 ) based on the concept of Pareto dominance. In each iteration, the values of the currently calibrated parameters in all grids serve as a solution set. Then, the offspring population is generated through selection, crossover, and mutation. Solutions from the best non-dominated fronts are preferred to replace the parent population and retain to participate in the calibration of the next parameter. The process continues iterating and cycling until a termination criterion is met (e.g., a maximum number of generations).   3.4 Model validation and evaluation 3.4.1 Evaluation methods for ET The hydrological water balance method was used to estimate the annual ET to assess the ET datasets and the merged ET at the basin scale. The water balance method assumes that the annual water balance closure in basins is primarily governed by precipitation (P), ET, streamflow (Q), and change in storage (ΔS):(14) E T = P − Q − Δ S .      On a multi-year scale, P (ET) serves as the only source (loss) of water within the basin, with no gains or losses through deep groundwater or inter-basin transfers, so the change in storage (ΔS) is typically negligible (Bai and Liu, 2018; Milly, 1994 ). Therefore, the multi-year ET can be obtained as the reference data through observed precipitation and streamflow.  3.4.2 Benchmark schemes: single-objective calibration This study establishes two benchmark schemes to compare with the multi-objective calibration scheme. The first benchmark scheme (case Q) is the traditional calibration strategy that constrains parameters using observed streamflow data at the basin’s outlet only. The objective function is calculated by maximizing the KGE between the observed data and the simulated streamflow. The parameters calibrated from this scheme do not have spatial heterogeneity.(15) F = K G E  Q        The second benchmark scheme (case ET) calibrate the VIC model parameters solely using the merged ET. Leveraging the spatiotemporal information from gridded ET data, the objective function is to maximize the evaluation metric KGE for all grid cells of ET, aiming to capture spatial heterogeneity in parameters. To reduce uncertainty introduced by algorithms, both benchmark schemes and the case Q+ET employ the NSGA-II algorithm. Unlike the multi-objective calibration, single-objective calibration schemes do not necessitate non-dominated sorting of objective functions based on the Pareto principle.(16) F = K G E  E T         3.4.3 Model performance metrics In addition to KGE, the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), reletive error (RE), Pearson correlation coefficient (R) and the root mean square error (RMSE) were also employed to assess the goodness-of-fit between model simulations and observed data. The NSE (Eq. (17) ) was evaluated the streamflow time series at both daily and monthly time scales. It is generally found to be highly sensitive to the large runoff values compared to KGE (Gupta et al., 2009 ). The range of NSE extends from negative infinity (no agreement) to 1 (perfect agreement). The RE (Eq. (18) ) was used to assess the magnitude of the simulated flow average relative to the observed flow average. The R (Eq. (19) ) describes the degree of linear correlation between two continuous sets of data. The RMSE (Eq. (20) ) measures the average magnitude of the errors between model simulations and observations. The last two metrics were applied to further evaluate the soil moisture outputs from the calibrated VIC model.(17) N S E = 1 − ∑ i = 1  t  ( Q  s , i   − Q  o , i   )  2    ∑ i = 1  t  ( Q  o , i   − μ  o   )  2     ,     (18) R E = μ  s   − μ  o    μ  o     × 100 % ,     (19) R = C o v ( X , Y )  V a r ( X )  ⋅ V a r ( Y )      ,     (20) R M S E = ∑ i = 1  n  ( x  i   − y  i   )  2    n    ,     where Q  s , i     and Q  o , i     are the simulated and observed streamflow at the time step i  , respectively; μ  s     and μ  o     are the average of simulated and observed streamflow series, respectively; X   and Y   are the reference data and simulated data, respectively.    4 Results 4.1 Assessment of ET datasets and merged ET The basin-average ET from three datasets and the merged ET during 2001–2010 are evaluated against the reference ET calculated by the water balance method from 18 GRB’s hydrological stations. The spatial distribution of the relative errors of each product compared to the reference ET is shown in  Fig. 3 . At the basin scale, GLEAM performs the best (RE=-0.7 %) among three products, followed by the merged ET (RE=-3.8 %). At the sub-basin scale, the annual average ET estimated by all datasets tends to be overestimated in the eastern part of the GRB and underestimated in the southern and western regions.  Fig. 4  shows the change (∆RE) in the absolute values of the RE for three products compared to the merged ET. A positive change in ∆RE indicates that the results of the merged ET are better, with the RE being closer to 0. It can be observed that the underestimation of ET in the western GRB and the overestimation in the eastern GRB have both been improved by the merged ET, performing better in these areas compared to the three individual products. Additionally, the RE from the merged ET is superior in at least 10 sub-basins compared to each individual product.  Fig. 5  shows the performance of all ET products across various sub-basins. From the box plot statistical results (Fig. 5 (a)), it can be observed that the PML product generally underestimates the multi-year average ET, while the GLEAM product generally overestimates it. The merged ET has the smallest mean absolute RE across all basins, outperforming the other three products in the sub-basins. Fig. 5 (b) provides a detailed display of the RE across sub-basins of varying sizes. The drainage area of sub-basins numbered 1–10 exceeding 5000 km2  (hereafter referred to as large sub-basins), while the remaining are classified as medium to small sub-basins. In large sub-basins, the RE is smallest for the GLEAM product, but overall highest in medium to small sub-basins. Conversely, for the PML product, the RE is smallest in medium to small sub-basins, but overall highest in large sub-basins. The EBET product falls between these two products, while the merged ET is superior to EBET. The merged ET is closest to EBET product, because the EBET exhibits the smallest temporal-spatial error variance to produce the largest merging weight. Overall, the merged ET not only performs best in terms of multi-year averages but also effectively captures the spatiotemporal uncertainties of the products.  4.2 DELSA sensitivity measures and calibration priority  Fig. 6  presents the sensitivity measures obtained by DELSA method to show the sensitivity of six hydrological parameters on streamflow and ET simulations. The DELSA first-order sensitivity measures range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater parameter sensitivity. To compare the relative influences of parameters and reflect the variability of parameter sensitivities across the objective function space, the moving average values are also calculated. The 200 parameter combinations randomly generated by LHS and Monte Carlo simulation exhibit a broad distribution space for both streamflow and ET evaluation metrics, with K G E  Q      mainly ranging between 0.36 and 0.90, while K G E  E T      fall between 0.42 and 0.67. The relative sensitivity among these parameters varies significantly across different subintervals of objective functions. Therefore, to comprehensively compare the sensitivity and priority of parameters, it is essential not only to consider the distribution of DELSA first-order sensitivity measures across the entire objective function space but also to emphasize their relative magnitude within the optimal objective function range. In Fig. 6 (a), four parameters (d3, Ds, d2, Dsmax) are identified as important across the whole objective function space. The parameter d3 elicited the strongest model response in terms of K G E  Q      within the optimal range, followed by Ds. In Fig. 6 ( b), whether across the entire space or optimal range of K G E  E T     , d2 is consistently identified as the most sensitive parameter. The parameters B and Ws are identified as the two least sensitive parameters with respect to the performance metrics of streamflow and ET. As a result, based on the sensitivity of parameters to the objective function, the calibration priority of parameters is determined as follows: d3, d2, Ds, Dsmax, B, Ws.  4.3 Model performance evaluation For streamflow,  Fig. 7  shows the daily and monthly streamflow evaluation results for different schemes. At the daily scale, the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme (case Q+ET) performed the best simulated streamflow results at the outlet section (KGE=0.92 and NSE =0.84), followed by the benchmark schemes case Q (KGE=0.91 and NSE =0.82) and case ET (KGE=0.87 and NSE =0.80). This improvement is likely due to the spatial-temporal information from the merged ET, which helped calibrate a reasonable parameter distribution and enhanced the accuracy of streamflow process simulations within the basin. From the daily streamflow simulation results of case Q, it can be observed that the simulation accuracy in medium and small sub-basins is poorer compared to larger sub-basins. The traditional parameter calibration strategy rely on using outlet streamflow processes to constrain parameters, aiming to make the simulated processes as close as possible to the observed processes, while often neglecting the internal hydrological processes of large basins. Although the spatial and temporal information provided by gridded ET products cannot completely match the true values, using only the corrected ET data by merging for parameter calibration (case ET) can still yield passable streamflow simulation results. In some sub-basins, the daily streamflow simulation results can outperform those of case Q. Therefore, using the merged ET for gridded parameter calibration in the VIC model shows potential for optimizing internal hydrological processes within the basin. At the monthly scale, the performance of streamflow form case Q+ET is better than that from case Q, and the improvement being more pronounced than in the daily results, with the average values of KGE and NSE across all sub-basins improved by 0.03.  Fig. 8  illustrates the monthly streamflow simulation results for several sub-basins with some improvements. It can be observed that the VIC model with traditional calibration scheme tends to overestimate the flow during wet months, whereas case Q+ET ameliorates this issue. The improvement in the results of case Q+ET can likely be attributed to the higher accuracy of ET products on a monthly scale. The results from case ET indicate that its performance on a monthly scale is generally comparable to that of case Q (with the average KGE and NSE being identical for both), and it surpasses case Q in some larger sub-basins (with more than half of the large sub-basins having a KGE better than the results of case Q). Additionally, the climatology of the merged ET, when evaluated using the water balance method, was found to be very close to the actual values. The inclusion of ET in the objective function further constrains the model from a water balance perspective, with the RE of streamflow from case ET is reduced compared to case Q in 10 sub-basins. The three evaluation metrics for monthly streamflow (average KGE, NSE, and the mean absolute values of RE from all sub-basins) all demonstrate that case Q+ET outperforms the two benchmark schemes, confirming the feasibility of the multi-objective calibration approach. For ET,  Fig. 9 (a) presents the performance of different schemes in simulating the annual area-average ET of all sub-basins. It can be observed that the daily and monthly area-average ET simulated by case Q+ET is very close to that of case ET, demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed multi-objective calibration framework in the algorithm. This calibration strategy effectively captures the spatiotemporal variability of the merged ET to obtain parameters with spatial heterogeneity, resulting in better model simulation outcomes. Fig. 9 (b) evaluates the accuracy of the multi-year average ET simulated by different schemes using the water balance method. It is evident that case ET optimizes the model-simulated ET, but it does not fully reproduce the ET process as the merged ET. This discrepancy arises partly due to the inherent errors and uncertainties in the ET data used for calibration and partly due to the systematic biases in the VIC model's structure regarding ET simulation. Nonetheless, it is reassuring that the inclusion of ET in the parameter calibration improves the VIC model's ET simulation. Enhancing the data accuracy of the variables used in the objective function is an effective method for further improving model simulation accuracy. The soil moisture content simulated by the calibrated VIC model was evaluated using in-situ observed soil moisture data at 28 sites from 0 to 40 cm depth. As shown in  Fig. 10 (a), the correlation of the soil moisture between observations and simulations from the VIC model using multi-objective calibration scheme improves compared to the results obatained from the benchmark scheme. The metric R from case Q+ET increase at 19 sites, with the median R rising by 0.03 and the average R increasing by 0.02 compared to that from case Q. Under the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme, the overall consistency between the VIC model's simulated soil moisture and the observed data has improved. However, there is no significant improvement in the errors. Compared to case Q, the overall correlation of simulated soil moisture with case ET increases while the errors become worse, further illustrating that the improvement in simulation with case Q+ET depends on the quality of ET used in parameter calibration.   5 Discussions Numerous studies have sought to improve hydrological model simulation accuracy by constraining parameters through joint calibration of multiple hydrological variables, yet they invariably face trade-offs among the objective functions. Typically, joint calibration sacrifices the simulation accuracy of one variable to enhance that of others. The NSGA-II algorithm used in this study avoids converting multi-objective problems into single-objective ones, thus reducing trade-offs among sub-objective functions. Additionally, by using the spatial distribution information from gridded products, the range of potential parameter combinations is expanded, imparting spatial heterogeneity. It should be noted that in the trade-offs between multiple objectives still exist in this study. The evaluation results of monthly streamflow and soil moisture indicate that the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme does not consistently outperform the two benchmark schemes across all sub-basins. The improvement in model accuracy compared to traditional calibration schemes is largely influenced by the accuracy of evapotranspiration. It is reassuring that the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme proposed in this study didn’t sacrifice streamflow accuracy to compensate for other hydrological processes, which has been challenging to achieve in previous studies (Herman et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2022; Mei et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2021 ). Gridded parameter calibration inherently introduces greater complexity, exacerbating the issue of equivalence and making it more uncontrollable, while also significantly increasing computational costs. Although the proposed multi-variable parameter calibration strategy demonstrates effective implementation in the GRB, its applicability should be further validated using more watersheds or other distributed hydrological models. Furthermore, there is considerable room for improvement in the multi-variable parameter calibration approach. For instance, enhancing computational efficiency by further constraining the effective parameter range for each grid and utilizing an increasing amount of multi-source data for multi-objective parameter calibration are potential directions for future studies.  6 Conclusions In this study, we explored a multi-variable parameter calibration framework based on satellite-based ET and observed streamflow to overcome the shortcomings of the traditional calibration strategy soly based on streamflow. Firstly, three sets of satellite-based datasets were merged and evaluated to reduce uncertainties. Then, the temporal and spatial information of the merged ET was used to calibrate six hydrological parameters of the VIC model at the grid scale. Finally, the results were compared with schemes that used only ET or only streamflow data for calibration to evaluate the improvements of the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme. The study was carried out in the Ganjiang River basin in China. The main findings are as follows:(1) The merged ET was obtained by three daily gridded ET datasets based on the TC method and evaluated by the water balanced method. The merged ET has an overall reduced relative errors compared to the three individual products used for merging, with the multi-year average ET estimates improved in more than half of the sub-basins. Given the limited evaluation data and methods, this merging approach emerges as a promising method for screening datasets and obtaining reliable data.  (2) Compared to the single-objective scheme calibrated solely with streamflow data, the results from multi-objective parameter calibration scheme not only ensures the accuracy of daily streamflow simulation but also improves the simulation of monthly streamflow processes. The improvement in area-averaged ET, soil moisture, and streamflow simulation results indicates that the spatially heterogeneous parameters obtained through proposed calibration framework are reasonable and enhance the model's capability to simulate internal hydrological processes.  (3) Compared to all single-objective schemes, the multi-objective parameter calibration scheme enhances model performance by the spatiotemporal information from products compensates for the inability of observed streamflow data to calibrate parameters with spatial heterogeneity. Simultaneously, the constraints imposed by observed data can mitigate the uncertainties introduced by the products.    In summary, this calibration framework provides a pathway for the application of multi-source remote sensing products in hydrological modeling, further optimizing distributed hydrological model parameters and improving model performance. It has the potential to enhance the simulation of various hydrological processes within large watersheds, providing valuable support for hydrological modeling under complex underlying surfaces and water resources management and decision-making in large watersheds. Future research could focus on improving the accuracy of satellite-based products, enhancing the efficiency of multi-variable parameter calibration computations, and further improving the accuracy and practicality of distributed hydrological models.
1 Introduction Aerodynamic resistance is affected by the rough surface generated by grassy plants in both horizontal and vertical directions. Grazing prohibition increases the cover and height of vegetation while grazing decreases it, affecting the surface roughness (Edwards et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b ). Heat transport from the surface to the atmosphere is limited by aerodynamic resistance via mechanical turbulence resulting from surface roughness (Brutsaert, 2013 ). The ascending turbulence has strengthened the energy transfer rate in the air (Smagin and Karelin, 2021 ). During the greening and senescence periods, the climate causes major changes in the canopy structure of vegetation (Richardson et al., 2018 ), which has a considerable impact on surface roughness. Strong monsoons accompany the greening season for grassland vegetation during spring in northern China. Surface water-heat fluxes are influenced by sufficient aerodynamics and different grassland management strategies (Shuttleworth and Wallace, 1985 ). A combination of natural and anthropogenic interventions affects the land surface energy balance by altering the sensible heat flux (H ) through changes in aerodynamic resistance. At the same time, energy and moisture in the spring influence vegetation growth throughout the year, and H  is the key to water and heat transport in the constituent grassland ecosystems (Moon et al., 2020 ). Thus, H  is highly influenced by the impact of spring grazing management on grassland aerodynamic resistance. Aerodynamic resistance and surface-air temperature can be used to estimate H , and modeling requires information on two crucial surface roughness parameters: roughness lengths for momentum and heat (Verhoef et al., 1997 ). The roughness length for momentum (Z 0 m  ) and the roughness length for heat (Z 0 h  ) explain the resistance of the surface to air flow and energy exchange. (Young et al., 2021 ). For heat transfer, Z 0 m   has a higher resistance effect on eddy diffusion, while the resistance generated by Z 0 h   is reflected in molecular diffusion, where the length of Z 0 h   is smaller than that of Z 0 m  . (Thom, 1972 ). Using an analogy to charge transfer described by Ohm’s Law, one can simulate turbulent transport near the surface of grassland vegetation by comparing H  and the force gradient (difference in vertical air temperature) to current and potential respectively, and connecting electrical resistance to aerodynamic resistance (Monteith and Unsworth, 2013 ). Determining the variable connection between air temperature and aerodynamics is thus crucial for determining H . In land-surface modeling, the parameter kB −1   (ln(Z 0 m   / Z 0 h  )) is used to quantify this excess resistance between Z 0 m   and Z 0 h   (Thom, 1972 ). The frictional resistance by plants on surface airflow is known as u*  (Shao, 2008 ). Due to Reynolds number Re  potentially describing the viscosity of the wind flow field and u*  being the frictional resistance of plants to surface airflow, they are frequently utilized to determine Z 0 h   and kB −1   (Wang et al., 2008 ). These eigenvalues can represent aerodynamic drag, but their relation to the time scale is often neglected. Short time scales (such as multi-hour and daily) and long time scales (such as seasonal and annual) have different relationships to meteorological factors (Ouyang et al., 2014 ). In a prior study, we discovered that as time scales increased, the connections between the hydroclimatic processes strengthened. Such as heat transmission, aerodynamic resistance controls wind speed, but sensible heat flux and wind speed have a seasonal and yearly positive and negative correlation, respectively. On a daily scale, compared to a monthly scale, the sensible heat flow is more closely tied to air temperature (Li et al., 2022 ). Although studies have been conducted regarding how H  responds to time scales and to the elements influencing it, there has been generally less focus placed on the impacts of time scales on estimations of H, and how to adequately explain the effect of time scale on pertinent parameters, particularly aerodynamic resistance. Employing the "big leaf" sensible heat model and Bowen ratio energy balance theory, the study investigated the effect of meteorological factors on H  across hourly and daily intervals in both grazing prohibited and grazed grasslands during spring in the Xilingol League. Our goals were to: (1) establish the significance of parameters related to aerodynamic resistance when estimating H  in grasslands; (2) examine the impact of time scale on each model parameter; and (3) compare the H  differences between grazing prohibited grasslands and grazed grasslands in the spring. These objectives will contribute to the understanding of the factors influencing the simulated sensible heat flux parameters under different grazing management practices and provoke consideration of most suitable time scales selected for modeling in light of their impact on model parameters.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Site description The study area was located in the Eritu pasture in the central part of the semi-arid steppe of Inner Mongolia, China (42°05′–43°02′N, 114°05′–115°37′E;  Fig. 1 ). Using Landsat data for 2021, we delineated the land use types in the Inner Mongolia region, with grassland being the dominant vegetation type in the region. The region has a mesothermal semi-arid continental climate with an average annual temperature of 1.9°C and a maximum temperature of 34.9°C. In the spring, winds are generally strong and focused. The species in this study area mainly include Stipa krylovii  Roshev., Leymus chinensis  (Trin.) Tzvel., Artemisia frigida  Willd., and Cleistogenes squarrosa  (Trin.) Keng. Since the 1960s, unreasonable land development and utilization such as reclaiming wasteland and overgrazing have caused severe damage to the ecosystem in this region. To ensure the survival and development of local people, the government has taken various measures to restore the grassland, with the main measure being the prohibition of grazing (Li et al., 2023a ).  2.2 Data collection We collected meteorological data for the most aerodynamic time period in the spring (April 8-June 8, 2022 and 2023), including five horizontal wind speeds at heights of 0.2 m, 0.4 m, 0.6 m, 1.2 m, and 2 m above the ground, which were measured using wind cups (014A-L, Campbell, America, 0.1 m/s). Air temperature and humidity were also recorded at 2 m and 0.4 m heights (HMP155A, Campbell, America). The upward longwave radiation (Rlu ) (SL-510-SS, Apogee, America, 0.01w/m2 ) and downward longwave radiation (Rld ) (SL-610-SS, Apogee, America, 0.01w/m2 ) probes were mounted at a height of 2 m above the ground. Observation equipment was the same for both prohibited and grazed grasslands, and all indicators were recorded at 1 min intervals. Data was collected by a data receiver (CR1000X, Campbell, America) and collected to a cloud platform using a 4 G network.  2.3 Basic theory The low vegetation in grasslands allows the H  model to neglect vertical variations within the canopy (Knauer et al., 2018 ). The "Big-Leaf" theory's modeling of H fully accounts for herbaceous traits and aerodynamic resistance to heat transfer (Rah ), which is appropriate for explaining variations in H  caused by grazing management:(1) H = ρ C  P   ( T  aero   − T  a   ) / Rah      where ρ  is air density (kg m−3 ) and C p   is a constant for the specific heat of dry air (1004.834 J K−1  kg−1 ). A computational method appropriate for semi-arid sparse grassland H was chosen based on the findings of previous studies since our objective is to explore the influence of hourly and daily scale input data on the results of model calculations (Martí et al., 2022; Platt, 1984; Wang and Ma, 2018 ). The Bowen ratio-energy balance (BREB) method, which is based on the energy balance of Bowen ratio at the surface (Angus and Watts, 1984 ), has been successfully applied to estimate surface energy fluxes, and we use it to verify the result of the Big-Leaf model for estimating sensible heat in grasslands. The final daily averages of the Bowen ratio give estimates of H .  2.4 Data analysis Our goal was to determine the difference between the hourly-scale daily variation of parameter eigenvalues (x_Dhour ) and the daily-scale parameters (x_Dday ) during model calculations. In simple words, the input data for the two types of time scales are same, but the daily changes in parameter values after the calculation are not:(17) x _ D h o u r = ∑ i 24   f ( x  i   )    24       (18) x _ D d a y = f ( ∑ i 24   x  i     24   )      where i  is the hour, x i   is the input data, and f(x)  is the operational equation for the parameter x  in the process of calculating the sensible heat flux. Ram  or Rbh  can be the cause of the variation of Rah  (i.e., Rah = Ram + Rbh ; Eq. (3) ), and knowing which one of both of them has a higher correlation will be crucial to determining the primary causes of Rah . In order to determine the variance of the sum of two random variables, we employ statistical properties (Pescott and Stewart, 2014 ):(19) V a r ( R a h  )  = V a r ( R a m + R b h  )       The variance and covariance functions are denoted by Var and Cov, respectively. We utilize Eq. (19) and Eq . Combinations of tree predictors known as random forests have all the trees in the forest having the same distribution, each parameter of which can be thought of as a tree and depends on the value of a randomly sampled random vector. The random forest method can converge to a limit as the number of trees in the forest grows. Each node is split using randomly chosen features, which results in an error rate that can illustrate how increasing the number of splits affects the number of features. Eigenvalues affect the variation of error rates and demonstrate their importance (Breiman, 2001 ). Z 0 m   and u*  are less influenced by the time scale, according to the correlation coefficients R 2   (Fig. 2 a and b), while Re  and kB −1   are influenced more strongly (Fig. 2 c and d). According to the probability densities, the aerodynamic characteristic parameters and their degree of dispersion were significantly greater in the grazing prohibited grassland than in the grazed grassland. Aerodynamic drag parameters were generally greater in grazing prohibited grasslands than in grazed grasslands. It is noteworthy that as the computational steps of parameters increase, the correlation between the two time scales gradually decreases. Specifically, when calculating from Z 0 m   to kB −1  , the correlation in the grazing prohibited grassland decreases from 0.98 to 0.67, and in the grazed grassland, it decreases from 0.84 to 0.71. Interestingly, the peak values of the distribution of each variable at the hourly scale are more pronounced compared to the daily scale.  3.2 Effects of grazing management and time scale on aerodynamic resistance On the grassland, the fluctuation of Rah_Dhour is more pronounced than that of Rah_Dday ( Fig. 3 , a∼d). Dhour was overall higher than Dday for Rah , Rbh , and Ram . As vegetation enters the growing season, Rah  exhibits an "s"-shaped trend, while the difference between Rah  and Ram  gradually diminishes. The variation trend of Rah  at hourly and daily time scales reaches its peak in mid-May, with Rah  in the grazing prohibited grassland being 57.8 s/m and 74.7 s/m, and in the grazed grassland being 63.2 s/m and 73.2 s/m, respectively. The gradual decrease of Re  in the grazing prohibited grassland indicates a transition of the wind flow field from turbulence to laminar flow; the stable variation of kB −1   suggests a relatively constant relationship between Z 0 m   and Z 0 h  . During the observation period, spring phenology exerted a significant influence on the aerodynamic characteristics of the grazing prohibited grassland. Attribution analysis can assist us in discerning the contributions of Ram  and Rbh  to Rah  by observing the variance ( Fig. 4 ). In the grazing prohibited grassland, the contributions to Rah_Day are as follows: synergistic action of Rbh  and Ram  (363.8) > Rbh_Day (321.9) > Ram_Day (124.5), while for Rah_Dhour, it is Ram_Dhour (24.5) > Ram_Dhour (18.2) > synergistic action of Rbh  and Ram  (-3.5). In the grazed grassland, the contributions to Rah_Day are similar to those in the grazing prohibited grassland: synergistic action of Rbh  and Ram  (121.0) > Rbh_Day (98.9) > Ram_Day (72.8). However, for Rah_Dhour, it is Rbh_Dhour (43.1) > synergistic action of Rbh  and Ram  (20.3) > Ram_Dhour (3.4). Interestingly, the variance of Ram , Rbh , and Rah  in daily data is significantly higher than that in hourly data. These results elucidate how grazing management and time scale effects influence the relationship among Ram , Rbh , and Rah .  3.3 Effects of grazing management and time scale on H H was highly correlated between both time scales ( Fig. 5 .a). H_Dhour increased by an average of 52.2 in grazed grassland and 25.9 in grazing prohibited grassland compared to H_Dday. The trend of increase in H_Dhour was greater than that of H_Dday. We considered the more straightforwardly operationalized Bowen Ratio Energy Balance Theory to explore H (Fig. 5 .b). In the cumulative values of H over time in grazed grasslands, the Bowen ratio estimates of H differed significantly from the macrophyte theory models at both time scales, with the differences becoming increasingly significant beginning in mid-April (20 DOY) (Fig. 5 .b). The fit between models was better in the grazing prohibited grassland, especially for H_Dday. Grazing management influenced the model simulating H, where the time scales of the parameters affected H. The time scales of the parameters were also affected by the time scales of the models.  3.4 Significance analysis of factors affecting H and Rah Z 0 h   has the highest impact on Rah , and its impact on Rah_Dhour  is especially obvious ( Fig. 6 .b). Molecular diffusion had a larger influence than momentum diffusion on the change of H . u * can be interpreted as a resistance to the wind, and u *_Dday  had a significantly higher importance than u *_Dhour  for both types of grassland. Re  responds to the flow characteristics of the air, and kB-1  reflects the synergistic changes of Z 0 h   and Z 0 m  . Re  and kB-1  showed smaller influence on Rah . We conclude that Rah  is less responsive to the turbulent state of the air flow and is independently influenced by Z 0 h   and Z 0 m  . The air heat transfer resistance parameter is more impactful for Dday than for Dhour when estimating H . Ta  and Taero  had significantly impact on H  than the heat transfer resistance (Rah , Ram , and Rbh ), with Taero  being most significant (Fig. 6 .d). When the time-scale effect of air temperature was not considered, H_Dday  and H_Dhour  were significantly different in the grazing prohibited grassland, suggesting that both grazing measures and heat transfer resistance were factors influencing the difference between H_Dday  and H_Dhour . In two types of grazing-managed grasslands, the hourly average of the difference (ΔRah) between adjacent days (Gg: 3.6 s m−1 , Gp: 2.7 s m−1 ) is greater than the daily average (Gg: 0.3 s m−1 , Gp: −0.4 s m−1 ). However, the hourly average of the difference (ΔH) between adjacent days (Gg: −7.8 W m−2 , Gp: 54.6 W m−2 ) is associated with grazing management, differing from the daily average (Gg: 6.8 W m−2 , Gp: 0.9 W m−2 ) ( Fig. 7 ). The rate of change in variables for grazing prohibition grasslands is smaller. The influence of temporal scale effect on Rah alters the trend of H, but temperature is the determining factor for H (Fig. 6 ). ΔRah_Dhour decreased by 116.5 % in grazed grassland and 89.9 % in grazing prohibited grassland compared to ΔRah_Day, while ΔH_Dhour increased by 98.2 % and 187.7 % compared to ΔH_Day, respectively.   4 Discussion Our research highlights the grazing management and plant greening processes in spring semi-arid grasslands that affect the estimation of sensible heat fluxes (H ), particularly the changes in estimations when modelling due to the time scales of parameters and aerodynamic resistance to heat transfer (Rah ). Specifically, the sensible heat flow was specifically impacted by changes in the plant canopy that changed the features of air turbulence. The influence of time scale effects on the simulation process can help to improve the prediction methods of sensible heat fluxes. These findings help us to think about how to select parameters that are appropriate for land surface flux modeling, such as particular time scales and potential anthropogenic impacts. 4.1 The effect of temperature on the emulation of H One may determine that H by combining the air temperature at a specific height with the Monin-Obukhov hypothesis (Wang and Bras, 1998 ). Although this method is of generalizable value, gradient variations in height above ground, surface roughness, and air temperature need to be considered. Our significance analysis reveals that the radiant air temperature at the surface (Taero ) is more impactful than both the air temperature at high altitudes (Ta ) and the resistance to air heat transfer (Fig. 6 . b), and that Taero  largely determines estimates of H  (Costa-Filho et al., 2021 ). Normally, air temperature decreases with increasing altitude, but nighttime air temperatures at high altitudes may be lower than at the surface. The inverse gradient change in H , or inverse temperature phenomenon, is caused by the alternating of positive and negative temperature differences at various heights (Jensen et al., 2015 ). Thus, the role of temperature differences for different heat transfer resistance simulations of H  enhances the difference between hourly and daily data, and the long-term cumulative effect of H  makes estimations highly dependent on the choice of time scale (Fig. 5 ). Canopy differences due to grazing practices (e.g., canopy height, density, leaf gaps, etc.) may also result in uneven spatial distribution of air temperature (Chen et al., 2019 ). In our previous research, we found out how grazing prohibition and grazing management in this area change vegetation characteristics (Lin et al., 2023 ). The patchy distribution of vegetation resulting from grazing in arid grasslands promotes a greater daytime warming amplitude than nocturnal cooling, thereby altering latent heat through changes in H  (Yunfei et al., 2020 ). Particularly evident is the sensitivity of climate response to the energy balance between H  and latent heat (Shao et al., 2017 ). Consequently, the diurnal variation temperature under different grazing management regimes emerge as significant factors contributing to the disparities in estimated results between daily and hourly data. For modeling H, irregular temperature swings are challenging. Studying simulations of H  requires the consideration of patterns of temperature change and vegetation features.  4.2 The effect of Rah emulation of H The flow of heat is reduced when Rah rises (von Randow et al., 2020 ). The fluctuation in Rah is presumably caused by plant roughness and the intensity of the monsoon, according to the shifting patterns in Z 0 m   and u*  (Young et al., 2021 ). In contrast, wind damage to stubble may have contributed to the drop that started later in the spring. We discovered that Rah was lowest early in the spring and gradually increased as grasses matured (Fig. 3 ). In grasslands, wind-induced leaf fall (Kinugasa et al., 2021 ) and grazing can diminish Z 0 m   (Fig. 2 ). In fact, the emergence of spring foliage effectively increases Z 0 m  . For example, the surface aerodynamic impedance of agricultural fields, scrub, mixed forests, grasslands, and evergreen coniferous forests all tend to increase with vegetation growth, resulting in a decrease in near-surface wind speeds (Moon et al., 2020 ). Changes in aerodynamic resistance affect Rah . Surface resistance is influenced by the phenological phase and vegetation when estimating H . However, the compact canopy structure of deciduous broadleaf woods creates a smoother surface, and the phenomena of higher heat transfer resistance is believed to be related to a drop in wind speed rather than surface roughness (Blanken and Black, 2004 ). Thus, estimating H  solely based on roughness may result in errors. In the middle to late spring, Rah  was similar for grasslands with varying grazing management, while Ram  and Rbh  were significantly different (Fig. 3 ). On the other hand, our attribution analysis revealed that grazing management and the temporal scale used in calculations determine whether Ram  or Rbh  contributes more to Rah  (see Fig. 4 ). Therefore, the effect of Ram  and Rbh  on Rah  can alter evapotranspiration by influencing H . We believe that in the early spring, more vegetation residue left by grazing reduces H  by increasing Rah . In late spring, wind action disrupts the residue and vegetation growth, altering the balance between Ram  and Rah  (Young et al., 2021 ). The estimation of H  is affected by both grazing management and the choice of aerodynamic measurements. Taking the Penman-Monteith equation as an example, when the average canopy resistance exceeds 200 s/m, the sensitivity of canopy resistance fluctuations is low, whereas when the average canopy resistance is less than 100 s/m, variations in resistance need to be considered (Lin et al., 2020 ). The lower Rah  in grazed grasslands has a more pronounced impact on H  compared to grazing prohibited grasslands. (Figs. 2 and 6 ). In semi-arid grassland ecosystems, evapotranspiration is predominantly governed by vegetation's stomatal configurations rather than external environmental forces, with temperature exerting a more substantial influence on the process than aerodynamic factors (Johns et al., 1983 ). Importantly, grazing management alters the canopy architecture of vegetation, thereby modifying the interplay between Rah  and H ; however, Rah  does not emerge as the critical factor driving the diurnal pattern of H  (Fig. 7 ). Solar radiation directly affects sensible heat and indirectly modulates sensible heat through its influence on latent heat via evaporation and transpiration (Ayoola O et al., 2022 ). In summary, the energy balance changes of sensible and latent heat in semi-arid grasslands, in response to Rah  and temperature, are related to grazing management, with the variation of H  being more significant in prohibited grazing grassland than in grazed grassland.  4.3 The effect of time scale on the simulation of H Suitable time scales are important for attribution analysis of heat transfer (Li et al., 2019 ). The choice of measurement time scale has been shown to influence the results of flux simulations. For example, hourly-scale data estimates for evapotranspiration by the Penman-Monteith model have been found to be 2 % greater than daily data (Sharma and Irmak, 2022 ). The accuracy of estimating canopy evapotranspiration using hourly versus daily data depends on the applied model (Rana et al., 1994 ). We found that the big leaf model provides more accurate estimates of sensible heat flux from daily data in grazing prohibited grasslands compared to hourly data, while grazing grasslands exhibit larger deviations (Gg:52.27w/m2 , Gp:25.95w/m2 ) (Fig. 5 ). Our time scale analysis encompasses not only the important phenological period of spring, but also hourly and daily variations in the factors linked with estimating H . In addition, the effect of Z 0 h   on Rah  is more significant than Z 0 m  . (Fig. 6 ). The daily mean value of Z 0 h   can fail to capture significant variations brought on by radiation during the day, while Z 0 h   has a strong influence on H  (Sun, 1999 ). In general, the relationship between wind speed and Z 0 m   is logarithmic and negative, and diurnal variations in wind speed amplify the discrepancy between daily and hourly data for predicting Z 0 m  . The final impact of Z 0 m   and Z 0 h   influences Rah . This finding raises the possibility that grazing-related differences in vegetation are what cause H  to exhibit a time scale effect. the differences between daily and hourly data of aerodynamic characteristics parameters result in changes in the grassland's "heat storage capacity" characteristics (Swenson et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the impact of temporal scale on simulating H is also related to grazing management. We found that grazing grasslands exhibit larger variations in Rah  compared to grazing-prohibited grasslands at both temporal scales, while the variations in H are relatively smaller (Fig. 7 ).  4.4 Differences between two models for simulating grass H The "Big-Leaf" sensing theory mainly considers the temperature gradient and the total aerodynamic resistance of the ground surface, while the traditional Bowen ratio sensing theory mainly considers the temperature and hydrobaric pressure gradients. Our study area belongs to semi-arid grassland, and the patchy distribution of grassland vegetation due to grazing makes the surface properties not uniform (Fig. 1 ). The Bowen ratio energy balance theory avoids errors caused by heterogeneous surfaces when estimating H (Raupach, 1995 ), and the unevenness of aerodynamic resistance parameters in grasslands results in lower applicability of the Big-Leaf model to grazing grasslands compared to grazing prohibited grasslands (Wilson et al., 2002 ). The climatic type and vegetation growth status of the grassland largely determine the heat transfer resistance. The two models exhibit good consistency in estimating H during the early growing season (until April 20th), but as vegetation grows, the differences in H between the two models in grazing grasslands gradually increase. This also indicates that grazing management is a key factor influencing model applicability. (Fig. 5 ). In summary, the choice of model for simulating grassland H is greatly influenced by the choice of heat transfer resistance. This is particularly true for short grasses (Ping et al., 2018 ), and our results further indicate that the values of resistance characteristic parameters are also related to the selection of temporal scale (Fig. 2 . and 3). The big-leaf sensible heat model, compared to the Bowen ratio energy balance equation, incorporates canopy resistance into the estimation of H. Future simulations of grassland sensible heat flux should focus on the variations in heat transfer resistance caused by grazing management differences.   5 Conclusions The "Big-Leaf" thermal model theory was applied in this work to compare hourly and daily data in prohibited and grazed grasslands to estimate important parameters of daily variations in H , and to examine the influence of these parameters on H  using attributional analysis and a random forest model. Employing the Bowen ratio energy balance theory, the applicability of the big-leaf model in semi-arid grasslands was validated. The results indicate: The values of the aerodynamic characteristic parameters (Z 0 m  , u* , Re  and kB −1  ) and their range of variation were smaller on the hourly scale than on the daily scale. The difference in momentum transfer resistance and residual resistance in grasslands under grazing prohibition is greater than in grazed grasslands, and this phenomenon is more pronounced on a daily scale. Air temperature was more significant than aerodynamic resistance to heat transfer for H  estimation and is more significant on an hourly scale than on a daily scale. In grazing prohibited and grazed grasslands, daily H  estimations exceeded hourly forecasts by 48.66 % and 26.37 %, respectively. Temperature largely determined the value of sensible heat flux, but the factor most responsible for the difference in time scales was the air resistance characteristics. The Bowen ratio energy balance equation validates that the Big-leaf model's daily H  estimates are more accurate than hourly data, with grazed grasslands exhibiting higher deviations (52.27 w/m2 ) than grazing prohibited grassland (25.95 w/m2 ). This research underscores the significance of the temporal scale of input model data on flux estimation outcomes, a consideration that should be integrated into hydrological models across diverse ecological regions.
