1 Introduction Drought represents a pervasive climatic phenomenon, exerting profound impacts on both human societies and natural ecosystems. Its primary impacts encompass agriculture, water resources, the ecological environment, and various socio-economic dimensions (Etienne et al., 2016 ). In China, drought disasters predominantly affect the northern and northwestern regions. Global climate change, along with sea surface temperature anomalies in the Pacific and Indian Oceans and various climate oscillations, are pivotal factors contributing to the frequent occurrence of droughts in China (Dixit and Jayakumar, 2021 ). In recent years, China has implemented a comprehensive suite of countermeasures to mitigate drought impacts. These include enhancing drought monitoring and early warning systems, advancing water-saving technologies and water resource management strategies, reinforcing infrastructure for farmland water conservation, optimizing water resource allocation, and promoting ecological preservation initiatives such as returning cropland to forest and grassland (Wilhite et al., 2000 ). These initiatives have somewhat alleviated the impacts of drought disasters, yet the issue of drought remains a significant challenge for China (Leng et al., 2015 ). Therefore, enhancing the predictive capabilities for drought disasters is crucial for relevant authorities to devise and implement effective response strategies (Yang, 2017 ). The degree of aridity is typically assessed using various aridity indices (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). Among the most widely utilized in meteorological drought studies are the Composite Aridity Index (CI) (He et al., 2015 ), the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) (Byun and Wilhite, 1999 ), the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) (Alley, 1984 ), and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) (Beguería et al., 2014 ). The application of SPEI data in drought prediction offers several advantages: primarily, SPEI integrates both precipitation and evapotranspiration, thereby providing a more comprehensive measure than indices solely based on precipitation data (Schreiner-McGraw and Ajami, 2021 ). This dual consideration allows SPEI to more accurately reflect the actual conditions of regional droughts, particularly in regions where drought is strongly influenced by evapotranspiration intensity, thereby yielding more reliable predictions. Furthermore, SPEI can be calculated over various temporal scales, ranging from short-term (e.g., 1 month, 3 months) to long-term periods (e.g., 9 months, 12 months) (Di Nunno and Granata, 2023; Xu et al., 2021 ). This versatility makes SPEI applicable to drought prediction across different temporal scales, thereby catering to a wide array of application scenarios. SPEI employs a standardized approach to convert precipitation and evapotranspiration data across various regions and temporal scales into a uniform standard distribution (Al Moteri et al., 2024 ). This standardization renders SPEI values comparable across different regions and temporal scales, thereby facilitating comprehensive comparison and analysis of drought conditions. The calculation of SPEI incorporates not only precipitation data but also leverages global meteorological observations, satellite remote sensing, and other data sources (Chang et al., 2021 ). This accessibility enhances the usability of SPEI data, facilitating its widespread application in drought prediction and monitoring. Currently, various methods are employed for drought forecasting, with the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model and the Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) neural network being among the most widely utilized techniques (Belayneh et al., 2014 ). The ARIMA model is known for its predictive accuracy and flexibility in handling linear time-series data, yet its reliance on linear relationships limits its performance (Kim et al., 2022 ). In contrast, the BiLSTM model excels in capturing nonlinear relationships within time series data and is particularly adept at managing long-term dependencies. The BiLSTM model extracts information from time series more comprehensively through its distinctive bidirectional structure, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy (Zheng et al., 2023 ). However, the performance of BiLSTM models is often influenced by data noise levels and sample size, and these models typically require significant time and computational resources for training (Dong et al., 2023 ). To overcome the limitations inherent in using a single model, this study integrates both approaches, leveraging the ARIMA model's strengths in modeling linear relationships and the BiLSTM model's capacity to capture nonlinear patterns. This hybrid model thus achieves superior prediction accuracy across diverse data characteristics. Compared to individual models, the hybrid approach demonstrates superior performance in drought prediction, effectively managing complex time series data and enhancing both the reliability and accuracy of forecasts (Shi et al., 2015 ). In recent studies, the variational mode decomposition (VMD) technique has seen a growing application in time series analysis, particularly in capturing data trends, variations, and periodicity (Zhou and Shi, 2024 ). VMD provides a detailed representation of signals in both time and frequency domains, elucidating the multilevel structure of the data. Relevant studies have demonstrated that VMD-based methods outperform traditional approaches in time series analysis (Loc et al., 2021 ). Currently, there is a relative paucity of studies applying VMD in drought prediction (Tran et al., 2021 ). However, the number of publications on the application of time series decomposition techniques in hydrology is on the rise (Jamei et al., 2024 ). This trend is becoming increasingly evident as more scholars integrate VMD techniques into the preprocessing of time series data to enhance model performance. This is attributable to the limitations of many traditional drought prediction models in effectively handling certain types of data. In this study, we employ the Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA) to optimize the VMD method (Zhang et al., 2023 ), thereby enhancing its efficiency in handling nonlinear and non-stationary signals, and to augment the model's capability in capturing drought signals by decomposing drought data and extracting features across multiple scales. The spatio-temporal cube is a modeling framework designed to integrate spatio-temporal data (Park et al., 2020 ), offering a holistic analysis of both temporal and spatial dimensions. It is predominantly utilized in fields such as urban planning and management, transportation, and healthcare, yet its application in hydrology remains limited (Cao et al., 2024 ). For drought prediction, this model can concurrently account for drought indicators across various temporal and spatial scales, thereby facilitating a nuanced understanding and forecasting of drought trends at distinct times and locations (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Spatio-temporal hotspot analysis is employed to detect significant changes at specific spatial and temporal scales, aiding in the identification of drought hotspot areas. The empirical kriging method represents an advancement over traditional kriging interpolation techniques. The advantage of empirical kriging over ordinary kriging lies in its explicit assumptions regarding the statistical properties of regional variability (Gribov and Krivoruchko, 2020 ). Moreover, empirical kriging produces a more rational spatial distribution of grids, thereby providing a more accurate explanation of regional variability. In this study, the integration of empirical kriging with spatio-temporal hotspot analysis not only enhances the intuitive understanding of the spatio-temporal distribution of drought but also innovatively improves the accuracy and reliability in identifying drought hotspots, thus synergizing the strengths of both approaches (Řehoř et al., 2023 ). Conversely, local anomaly analysis modifies traditional methods that detect anomalies over broad geographical areas and extended time scales, allowing for the detection and analysis of drought anomalies in localized regions (Li et al., 2020 ). These methodologies integrate spatial and temporal information, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding and prediction of drought occurrence and evolution (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Existing research methodologies exhibit significant potential for optimization in both the application of deep learning algorithms and the integration of temporal and spatio-temporal dimensions in drought analysis. The objective of this study is to address the limitations of current drought prediction techniques by introducing an optimized VMD method and a hybrid model combining ARIMA and BiLSTM, aligning with the prevailing trends in drought prediction (Di Nunno and Granata, 2023 ). Furthermore, this paper uniquely integrates the spatio-temporal cube model, aiming to offer a more comprehensive approach to drought prediction. By thoroughly analyzing data across both temporal and spatial dimensions, it sets a foundation for future research.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Located in northeastern China, Jilin Province spans between 121°38′-131°19′ east longitude and 40°11′-46°18′ north latitude, covering a total area of approximately 187,400 square kilometres (km2 ), constituting 1.95 % of China's land area. Jilin Province features relatively flat terrain, comprising primarily mountains and plains (Cao et al., 2019 ). To the west and south lie the Changbai Mountains and Changbai Mountain Hills, the central region encompasses the Songliao Plain, and in the east, there are the Jilin Hills and Liaodong Mountains. Jilin Province experiences a climate characterized by a temperate monsoon and continental monsoon. Summers are brief, winters are cold and prolonged, and spring and autumn are mild and enjoyable (Ma et al., 2023 ). The economy of Jilin Province is industrial-centric, with key sectors comprising automobile manufacturing, metallurgy, petrochemicals, chemicals, iron and steel, and machinery manufacturing. Agriculturally, Jilin Province predominantly cultivates crops, particularly soybeans and corn. Serving as a vital economic and natural resource hub in Northeast China, Jilin Province plays a crucial role in research on water resource utilization, climate change, and regional agricultural production. Concurrently, Jilin Province confronts the risk of natural disasters, notably drought. Conducting drought prediction research is crucial to safeguard local economic and social development (Liu et al., 2019 ) Fig. 1  . The data utilized in this study are sourced from the China Surface Climate Data Dataset (Xie, 2020 ) available at the National Meteorological Science Data Centre (https://data.cma.cn/ ). Due to varying amounts of missing historical data at some stations or their shorter establishment periods, meteorological data spanning 52 years (1960–2012) from 23 stations in Jilin Province were ultimately chosen. Following rigorous quality control, the data from the selected stations exhibit good quality. To ensure the completeness of meteorological station data, missing data at certain stations were filled using linear interpolation. The geographic elevation data for Jilin Province were obtained from the Geospatial Data Cloud (https://www.gscloud.cn/search ) (Zhang, 2014 ).  2.2 SPEI The research methodology used in this paper its main idea is shown in Fig. 2  . The standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) relies on the change in the difference between precipitation and potential evapotranspiration. Various methods exist for calculating potential evapotranspiration. Sheffield, Wood, and Roderick extensively studied different calculation methods (Ge et al., 2016 ), comparing them. Ultimately, we opted for the Penman-Monteith method (Hashemi and Sepaskhah, 2020 ) due to its greater accuracy, stemming from a stronger reliance on atmospheric evapotranspiration demand. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has affirmed the accuracy of the Penman-Monteith method by designating it as the standard for calculating potential evapotranspiration (PET). It combines the techniques of Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) and Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD), further optimized through a sparrow search algorithm. This method finds widespread use in the processing and analysis of time series data (Liu et al., 2018 ). The fundamental concept behind SSA-VMD is to decompose intricate time series data into multiple intrinsic modal functions (IMFs). Each IMF represents signal components of varying frequencies and amplitudes, enhancing the visibility of data characteristics. In contrast to traditional methods, SSA-VMD exhibits enhanced capability in handling nonlinear and nonsmooth signals. It is adaptive and does not necessitate pre-set parameters (Pandey et al., 2023 ). Optimization of the sparrow search algorithm enhances the efficiency of SSA-VMD in finding the optimal decomposition result, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of the decomposition. SSA-VMD has found extensive applications in diverse fields, including meteorology, biomedicine, and finance (Zhao et al., 2020 ). It empowers researchers to extract valuable information and features from complex time series data, supporting forecasting, analysis, and decision-making.(1) The parameters are initialized, and combinations of [ k , α ]    are randomly generated to serve as the initial position of the sparrow population. The magnitude of approximate entropy is unaffected by the quantity of data and exhibits robust stability for non-stationary nonlinear series. Therefore, it finds widespread application in engineering practice. Given that standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index data may encompass features in multiple time dimensions, approximate entropy aids in evaluating the regularity, periodicity, and predictability of data across different time dimensions. This capability facilitates the identification of potential patterns and evolutionary trends in drought events, thereby establishing a foundation for forecasting and early warning (Pincus, 1991 ). Originally proposed by Box and Jenkins et al. in 1976 (Makridakis and Hibon, 1997 ), the ARIMA model is extensively employed in time series analysis. The fundamental concept of the ARIMA model involves differencing the time series data to achieve smoother series. Subsequently, a model is constructed through a combination of autoregression (AR) and moving average (MA), which is then employed for forecasting. The strength of the ARIMA model lies in its ability to fully leverage historical information in time series data. It exhibits robust adaptability to all types of time series data and possesses a strong explanatory power. Nevertheless, the ARIMA model has certain drawbacks. Non-stationary time series data require differencing, and the parameter estimation process of the model is intricate. The model after multiple differencing can be expressed as follows:(24) H v  = τ 1  H v - 1   + τ 2  H v - 2   + ⋯ τ x  H x - 1   + e v  - θ 1  e v - 1   - θ 2  e v - 2   - ⋯ θ z  e z - 1           where H V     is the time series value; τ i     is the autoregressive coefficient; θ  i      is the sliding average coefficient; e v     is the white noise series, e v   N ( 0 , ρ  2  )    . The implementation process of this model is as follows:(1) Smoothness test: Initially, conduct a unit root test (Phillips & Perron, PP) or Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test (ADF) on the data series. If the series is non-stationary, it is essential to achieve data smoothness by applying d-differencing.  (2) Model identification: Determine the model parameters based on the Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF), Autocorrelation Function (ACF) of the data (Ramsey, 1974 ).  (3) Model ordination: Utilize the and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (Vrieze, 2012 ). Model testing: Examine whether the residual series is white noise and whether there is autocorrelation in the continuous residuals.  2.3.4 BiLSTM model The LSTM network model was introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997 (Gers et al., 2000 ) to address the issue of standard RNNs' inability to retain long-term information through the incorporation of a “gating” mechanism. The LSTM incorporates a memory unit for storing past information, and at each timestep, the model consists of three gates: forget gate, input gate, and output gate. The forget gate determines which information is discarded, the input gate determines which new information is merged, and the output gate determines which information will be sent to the next time step. Consequently, the LSTM excels in capturing dependencies between different time steps, enabling enhanced processing of sequence data(Granata and Di Nunno, 2023 ). Its architecture is depicted in Fig. 3  : The LSTM forward propagation formula is as follows:(27) f  t   = σ ω  f   h  t - 1   + μ  f   X  t   + b  f             (28) i  t   = σ ω  i   h  t - 1   + μ  i   X  i   + b  i             (29) C  t   = t a n h ω  c   h  t - 1   + μ  c   X  t   + b  c             (30) O t  = σ ω o  h t - 1   + μ o  X i  + b o             (31) h  t   = O  t   ⊗ t a n h ( C  t   )         where μ , ω , b    denote the parameter matrix of the model, the bias vector, ⊗    is the operator corresponding to the multiplication of values in the same position, h t     represents the state of the hidden layer at time t   , X t     represents the input at time t   , f t     is the output of the instant t    forget gate, the output of the first part of the input gate at time t    is i  t     , and Ct   is the state of the instant t    unit. The BiLSTM network model is an enhancement of the LSTM, primarily designed to enhance the capture of bi-directional contextual information in sequence data (Wang et al., 2023 ). BiLSTM consists of two LSTM layers: one processing from front to back (forward) and the other from back to front (reverse). At each time step, the forward short-term memory and backward short-term memory networks independently produce a hidden state, and the two hidden states are concatenated to obtain the corresponding temporal output. Consequently, BiLSTM can capture both past and future information, comprehensively understanding the context of sequence data. The bi-directional nature of BiLSTM enables better capture of contextual information in the input data, enhancing the accuracy of drought prediction. By simultaneously considering past and future information, the BiLSTM model can comprehensively analyze the factors influencing drought, improving the stability and reliability of predictions. The structure of BiLSTM is shown in Fig. 4  : Finally, the BiLSTM model will combine the outputs of the forward and backward LSTM layers to produce the final result.h n    (32) h  t  f   = LSTM  f   h  t - 1   , X  t        h  t  b   = LSTM  b   h  t + 1   , X  t                  (33) r  t   = w  f   h  t  f   + w  b   h  t  b   + b  y          w  f     is the weight of the forward LSTM layer, w  b     is the weight of the backward LSTM layer; b y     is the bias vector of the output layer.  2.3.5 BiLSTM hyper-parameter optimisation In this study, we employ the SSA to optimize the hyperparameters of the BiLSTM to enhance model performance in drought prediction. SSA is an optimization algorithm rooted in swarm intelligence, effectively addressing high-dimensional and nonlinear optimization problems(Lei et al., 2024 ). The specific optimization process involves the following steps:(1) Define the optimization problem: We define the key hyperparameters of the BiLSTM model as the optimization objectives, including the learning rate, the number of hidden units, the batch size, and the number of training epochs(Granata et al., 2022 ).  (2) Establish initial search ranges: We establish reasonable search ranges for each hyperparameter:    Learning rate: 0.0001–0.01; Number of hidden units: 50 – 200; Batch size: 16 – 128; Number of training epochs: 50 – 200.(3) Initialize the population: An initial population comprising various individuals (i.e., different hyperparameter combinations) is generated, randomly distributed within a predefined range.  (4) Fitness Evaluation: Each individual’s hyperparameter combination is used to train the BiLSTM model, with its predictive performance evaluated using a validation set. The fitness function employs mean square error (MSE) to assess model performance.  (5) Iterative optimization: In each generation, certain individuals explore new hyperparameter combinations through random exploration, while others perform local search based on the current optimal solution. SSA updates the population based on fitness values, continuously searching for superior hyperparameter combinations.  (6) Termination criteria: The algorithm terminates when the preset number of iterations is reached or when the fitness value no longer shows significant improvement, outputting the current optimal hyperparameter combination.     2.3.6 Joint model In this study, a novel model for drought prediction is proposed, and the specific workflow of the joint model is outlined as follows:(1) Calculate SPEIs at various time scales using meteorological data from the Meteorological Data Centre (MDC), selecting SPEI3 as the data input (Yin et al., 2022 ).  (2) Decompose the data using the SSA-VMD method to obtain multiple IMF vectors.  (3) Assess the complexity of the resultant components using the approximate entropy algorithm and arrange them in a sorted order.  (4) Feed the reorganized components into the ARIMA and BiLSTM models for individual predictions. Weighted combination of prediction results for each component to obtain the final prediction result (Du and Ma, 2018 ).      2.4 Predictive model evaluation metrics In this study, three statistical metrics, namely the coefficient of determination (R  2    ) (Nakagawa and Schielzeth, 2013 ), root mean square error (RMSE) (Chai and Draxler, 2014 ), and mean absolute error (MAE) (Willmott and Matsuura, 2005 ), are employed to assess the predictive performance of the model. Smaller values of MAE and RMSE signify improved model performance, and a value of R  2     closer to 1 indicates a better fit of the model to the data.  2.5 Time-space series model 2.5.1 Spatio-Temporal cube The spatio-temporal cube model is an analytical methodology utilized for multidimensional data analysis in geospatial terms, particularly for spatio-temporal data (Kraak, 2003 ). It is grounded in the concept of the data cube (a representation of a multidimensional dataset), enabling multidimensional analyses by considering the relationships between temporal, spatial, and other attributes. The model enhances our understanding and analysis of the drought situation at meteorological stations, integrating information from both temporal and spatial dimensions. It provides crucial support for drought monitoring, forecasting, and drought risk assessment. The model diagram is depicted in Fig. 5  . For meteorological data, especially climate index data such as SPI and SPEI, the spatio-temporal cube model can be employed to analyze the drought situation at various stations in geospatial space and achieve drought monitoring across diverse time scales. The spatio-temporal cube modeling of SPI and SPEI data from 23 meteorological stations in Jilin Province involves three main objectives:(1) analyzing the drought conditions at different meteorological stations and comparing their spatio-temporal characteristics.  (2) considering drought conditions at multiple time scales, encompassing short-term to long-term trends.  (3) providing drought prediction and monitoring based on spatio-temporal characteristics to offer data support for relevant decision-making.     2.5.2 Spatio-temporal hotspot analysis The spatio-temporal hotspot analysis model is a spatial statistical analysis method designed to detect clustered features in geospatial space, including outliers, hotspot areas, and spatio-temporal trends. This method integrates temporal and spatial information to identify clustering patterns, trends, or anomalies through the analysis of temporal variations and geographical distribution of data (Zhao et al., 2022 ). For drought visualization and analysis of meteorological stations, the spatio-temporal hotspot analysis model can assist in monitoring drought trends and identifying drought hotspots. The results of spatio-temporal hotspot analysis are subsequently visualized using tools like maps, trend maps, and hotspot maps. This facilitates the visualization of geographical locations and trends of drought occurrence and changes over time. A hotspot indicates areas that have not experienced drought in the past, where drought has been mild, or where drought has worsened compared to previous years, while a cold spot indicates the opposite (Zhang, 2021 ).  2.5.3 Local outlier analysis The local outlier analysis model is a spatial statistical method designed to detect outliers in a dataset that deviate from the surrounding data patterns (Alghushairy et al., 2020 ). This method focuses on outliers at a local scale rather than overall anomalies in the entire dataset. The model is primarily used to identify local clustering of anomalies in geospatial data. This is achieved by classifying the data into clusters and outliers, categorizing them into statistically significant high-value (high-high) clusters, low-value (low-low) clusters and high-value outliers surrounded predominantly by low-value (high-low), low-value outliers surrounded predominantly by high-value (low–high), no significance, and multiple types in six categories to discover local anomalies, clusters, and anomalous patterns in the data. Through local outlier analysis, we can identify anomalies in spatial data, such as clustering of high values, clustering of low values, or mutations in geospatial patterns. This analysis helps identify local outliers, providing deeper insights into specific patterns and potential issues in the data. Among these methods is Moran's I (Moran's Index) (Shahfahad et al., 2023 ): it is employed to test the spatial autocorrelation of the data and identify clustering patterns in the data.   2.6 Signal decomposition based on SSA-VMD Taking Ji'an city as an example, the computed SPEI-3 data are decomposed by SSA-VMD method, in this decomposition, the number of populations n = 10, the maximum number of iterations I MAX   =    20, the safety value is 0.6, the dimensionality is 2. The proportion of discoverers is 70 % of the population, the proportion of early warning is 60 % of the population, and the others are the joiners. The SPEI-3 time series data is processed by the SSA-VMD method to obtain the optimal k value of 7 for the SPEI signal and α    to be 22. The resulting time-domain plots of each modal component and the sample entropy fitness function plots are shown in Fig. 6  . The experimental results demonstrate that after applying the SSA-VMD method to decompose the signal, the center frequency of each mode is relatively independent, avoiding the phenomenon of mode aliasing and ensuring the purity of the eigenmodes. As depicted in Fig. 7  , the number of vectors post SSA-VMD decomposition is substantial. To reduce computational complexity and enhance efficiency, this paper comprehensively employs the approximate entropy (mode dimension m = 2, threshold r = 0.15), sample entropy (mode dimension m = 2, threshold r = 0.15), fuzzy entropy (mode dimension m = 2, threshold r = 0.15, weight w = 2), arrangement entropy (mode dimension m = 2, time delay p = 1), and time delay p = 0.15). A total of four algorithms are used to calculate the entropy value of each sequence, the resulting entropy values are shown in Table 2  . As this paper relies on four entropy values for the screening of IMF components, the calculated entropy values are initially standardized using Z-score (Bettahar and Şener, 2022 ). Subsequently, the four standardized entropy values are weighted and summed. The methodology in this paper emphasizes approximate entropy, assigning higher weights to it. Finally, a threshold is set to retain only the components with evaluation scores above the threshold and discard those with scores below the threshold. Component reconstruction is then performed on the resulting components, and the reconstructed components are illustrated in Fig. 8  .  2.7 Combined model prediction The recombined components were separately fed into the BiLSTM and ARIMA models for prediction. The dataset is partitioned into training sets、testing sets, choose the initial 80 % used for training and the remaining 20 % for prediction. The BiLSTM model is configured as follows: the initial layer of the neural network employs Bidirectional LSTM (Kheyruri et al., 2023 ) with 4 neurons, utilizing mean square error as the loss function. Gradient descent operates with a batch size of 1, employing Adam as the optimizer (Reyad et al., 2023 ). Training involves 60 epochs of Bidirectional LSTM (Kheyruri et al., 2023 ). The settings for the ARIMA model are as follows: due to the presence of two components post-recombination, and given their distinct data characteristics, parameter selection differs for each component. For illustration, Variable2 is considered, and the chosen parameters are (p, q, d) = (0, 0, 2).   3 Results and Discussion 3.1 Spatio-temporal cubes of SPI and SPEI In this study, the SPI and SPEI indices from 23 meteorological stations within the study area were visualized in three dimensions utilizing the spatio-temporal cube model. Five distinct time scales were selected for visualization and analysis, with results illustrated in Figs. 9-11    . As shown in Fig. 9 , the SPI1, SPEI1, SPI3, and SPEI3 indices reflect short-term drought conditions. The analysis indicates that droughts are predominantly concentrated in the central region of Jilin Province, with recent events showing increased severity. This finding aligns with Yu (Yu et al., 2014 ), who identified a high incidence of drought in central China. Given that SPI6 and SPEI6 can depict growing season drought conditions, the spatio-temporal visualization in Fig. 10  reveals a more extensive distribution of drought conditions in the eastern and northwestern regions. In contrast, the rest of the region exhibits a more even distribution. Additionally, drought durations in the western region are generally longer compared to other regions. The twelve and twenty-four-month time scales are effective in assessing long-term annual droughts (Zhang et al., 2024 ). The spatial analysis of SPI12, SPEI12, SPI24, and SPEI24 in Fig. 11  indicates that long-term droughts are largely absent in Jilin Province, with the exception of the western region. The spatial and temporal distributions of droughts are relatively uniform. A comparison of SPI and SPEI, along with historical drought data in Jilin Province, demonstrates that SPI is more accurate in identifying short-term droughts. This finding is consistent with Sun (Sun et al., 2015 ) analysis of long-term droughts in Northeast China. In contrast, SPEI exhibits a significant advantage in identifying long-term droughts, providing a more accurate reflection of drought conditions in the hydrological system as the time scale extends. Research indicates that the SPEI, which accounts for evaporation, offers greater reliability in identifying long-term drought conditions (Bai et al., 2020 ). A comparative analysis of the spatial visualization results for SPI and SPEI at equivalent time scales revealed that SPI tended to overestimate drought levels in specific areas, such as Jingyu and Donggang.  3.2 Spatio-temporal hotspot analysis of SPI, SPEI at different time scales The results from constructing the spatio-temporal cube are integrated with spatio-temporal hotspot analysis to examine the drought trends across 23 meteorological stations in Jilin Province over multiple time scales from 1960 to 2012. Fig. 12   presents a visualization of hotspots and coldspots, achieved with a 99 % confidence level using the hotspot analysis data for SPEI3, SPEI6, SPEI12, SPI3, SPI6, and SPI12, combined with empirical Kriging interpolation. Subsequently, the hotspot results are visualized using empirical Kriging interpolation, providing a clearer view of the overall spatial and temporal trends of drought over the past 52 years. The SPI and SPEI hotspot analysis results at various time scales, as depicted in the figure, reveal that hotspots are more pronounced in the central and eastern regions of Jilin Province, while coldspots are more evident in the northwestern and southern regions. Hotspots indicate a distinct increasing trend in drought severity within the corresponding time scales, whereas coldspots reflect the opposite trend. These findings are consistent with the impacts of climate change and human activities on drought trends, as outlined by Mukherjee (Mukherjee et al., 2018 ).  3.3 Local outliers Moran's I analysis Given the extensive dataset, this paper initially filtered the relevant site data, as detailed in Table 3  : A Moran’s I scatterplot was generated based on the results of local outlier analysis, with clustering outcomes categorized into four distinct quadrants: high-high value clustering in Quadrant I, low–high value clustering in Quadrant II, low-low value clustering in Quadrant III, and high-low value clustering in Quadrant IV. Table 3  reveals that the Local Moran’s I indices for most sites are significant. A positive Moran index indicates a spatial positive correlation, suggesting that these sites and their neighbors exhibit coordinated drought conditions. Conversely, a negative Moran index indicates a negative spatial correlation, where drought conditions in these sites negatively impact their neighbors. This spatial correlation highlights how the alleviation or exacerbation of drought conditions in one area influences adjacent regions(Abdi et al., 2018 ). Combined with Table 3  and Fig. 13  , this analysis further elucidates the spatial correlations among the study sites. Areas such as Baicheng, Qian'an, Tongyu, Qianguoerluosi, and Sanchahe are clustered in Quadrant I, indicating a high-high clustering relationship, where drought conditions exhibit a weakening trend and are relatively more humid. Conversely, Jingyu, Donggang, and Tonghua are situated in Quadrant III, showing a low-low clustering relationship, suggesting that drought conditions are worsening, aligning with the observed drought development in Jilin Province (Fu et al., 2024 ). Changling and Wangqing, located in Quadrant II, demonstrate a low–high clustering relationship, while Changbai, Changchun, and Dunhua, positioned in Quadrant IV, exhibit a high-low clustering relationship, indicating relatively higher SPEI values and greater humidity. This detailed analysis offers more refined statistics compared to previous studies by Yue (Yue et al., 2017 ).  3.4 Comparison of model prediction results Accurate and effective performance evaluation is crucial in drought prediction. This study developed prediction models for 23 meteorological stations across Jilin Province. Due to the extensive data, the analysis focused on three representative stations: Baicheng in the west, Changchun in the center, and Changbai in the east of Jilin Province. The prediction performance was evaluated based on statistical characteristics of evaluation indices and predictive curve plots comparing predicted and observed values. The R2 , MAE, and RMSE values for each model at these three stations are presented in Table 4  . For the R2 , MAE, and RMSE values of each model at each site, using Baicheng City as an example, the RMSE accuracy of the model proposed in this study improved by 93 %, 90 %, 85 %, and 30 %, respectively. Additionally, the correlation coefficient (R2 ) of the model showed improvements of 0.372, 0.131, 0.056, and 0.082, respectively. The prediction result plots in Fig. 14   reveal that BiLSTM and ARIMA models only approximate the time series patterns with significant numerical discrepancies, whereas models utilizing signal decomposition exhibit a closer numerical alignment with the actual values. This demonstrates that integrating signal decomposition techniques significantly enhances forecasting accuracy, with the SSA-VMD-ARIMA-BiLSTM combined forecasting model achieving the highest accuracy. This aligns with Ali (Ali et al., 2020 ), who highlighted the benefits of incorporating signal decomposition in time series forecasting. Fig. 15   presents the R2 , MAE, and RMSE boxplots for the combined model across all sites in Jilin Province. While some sites show anomalies, the R2 , MAE, and RMSE values for the remaining sites are 0.82, 0.15, and 0.083, respectively. Overall, the combined model demonstrates high prediction accuracy for most sites in Jilin Province, exhibiting strong performance with considerable regional stability and applicability.   4 Discussion In this study, we implemented the spatio-temporal cube model within the realm of meteorological drought prediction and integrated multiple forecasting models to conduct a comprehensive analysis of drought conditions in Jilin Province. We effectively elucidated the spatial and temporal distribution characteristics of both short-term and long-term droughts through 3D visualizations of SPI and SPEI indices from 23 meteorological stations across various time scales. The results indicate that short-term droughts are predominantly concentrated in the central region of Jilin Province, whereas long-term droughts exhibit a more uniform distribution across the entire province. These findings align with existing literature and further substantiate the validity and reliability of SPI and SPEI in drought monitoring (Ma et al., 2023 ). Notably, the SPEI results generally outperform those of SPI, likely due to the inclusion of additional factors such as evaporation. We employed the SSA-VMD-ARIMA-BiLSTM integrated model for drought prediction, and the results demonstrate that this composite model significantly surpasses individual models, particularly in addressing non-linear and non-stationary signals. Although other models occasionally yield superior results compared to the joint model, they generally exhibit less stability. This variability may be attributed to data characteristics that cause certain models to perform better during specific periods or tasks. Different models exhibit varying sensitivities to data, which can result in performance discrepancies. Additionally, the joint model may be susceptible to overfitting, particularly when dealing with relatively small datasets or high model complexity. Overfitting can result in excellent performance on the training set but poor generalization to the test set. In contrast, the joint model typically integrates valuable information from both linear and non-linear models, thereby leveraging their complementary strengths. Specifically, as illustrated by the boxplot analysis in Fig. 15 , the SSA-VMD-ARIMA-BiLSTM model exhibited substantial regional stability and applicability across the majority of sites. These findings align with Khan (Khan et al., 2020 ), who highlighted that models incorporating signal decomposition techniques offer considerable advantages in time series forecasting. In the realm of spatial analysis, Moran's I analysis of local anomalies elucidated notable variations in drought trends across different regions. Specifically, drought conditions in Baicheng, Qian'an, and Tongyu exhibited a weakening trend, suggesting potential improvements in drought severity in these areas. Conversely, Jingyu, Donggang, and Tonghua demonstrated an aggravating trend, indicating a need for increased attention and resources for drought risk mitigation. Such analyses of spatial heterogeneity yield critical insights for regional drought management, particularly in the context of climate change and anthropogenic impacts on water resources. The principal limitations in contemporary drought research encompass the complexity inherent in spatio-temporal analyses and the constraints of conventional spatial interpolation methods and model predictions. Traditional spatio-temporal analysis methods struggle to effectively manage large-scale and multi-dimensional datasets, leading to inadequate representation of the detailed spatio-temporal distribution of drought conditions. Conventional interpolation methods exhibit limited efficacy when applied to datasets with missing or incomplete information, failing to accurately capture the spatial distribution and temporal variations of drought conditions. Single prediction models exhibit suboptimal performance when addressing complex non-linear and non-stationary signals, resulting in insufficient accuracy and reliability in predictions. This study addresses these deficiencies by enhancing the spatio-temporal cube model, integrating hotspot analysis with empirical kriging interpolation, and employing a joint multi-model prediction approach. The spatio-temporal cube model offers more detailed and precise spatio-temporal dynamic information, thereby addressing the computational complexity and data processing challenges associated with traditional spatio-temporal analysis methods, particularly in handling large-scale and multi-dimensional datasets. The integration of hotspot analysis with empirical kriging interpolation enhances the accuracy and reliability of spatial interpolation, compensating for the limitations of traditional interpolation methods in handling missing and incomplete datasets, and yielding a more intuitive and precise spatio-temporal distribution map of drought. The proposed SSA-VMD-ARIMA-BiLSTM joint model markedly enhances the accuracy and reliability of drought prediction, overcoming the limitations of individual models in addressing complex non-linear and non-stationary signals, and delivering superior quality predictions. Moreover, the accuracy of the prediction model in this study is significantly influenced by factors such as the number of stations, the choice of model, the duration of the time series data, and issues related to missing data in both time series prediction and spatio-temporal analysis models. Despite the use of empirical kriging interpolation to minimize specific assumptions regarding the spatial context of the data points, the inclusion of additional meteorological and hydrological variables is essential to enhance prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the results of this study are primarily based on meteorological data from Jilin Province, which presents certain regional limitations. In summary, future research should focus on validating the model’s applicability to other regions and larger datasets, as well as exploring the use of additional optimization algorithms and both linear and nonlinear models to further enhance the accuracy and stability of drought prediction.  5 Conclusions This study conducted a detailed analysis of droughts in Jilin Province using the SPEI index alongside various spatio-temporal forecasting models. The results indicate that short-term droughts are predominantly concentrated in the central region of Jilin Province, with their frequency having increased by 20 % over the past decade. Over the long term, hotspots were predominantly located in the northeastern part of Jilin Province, whereas cold spots were concentrated in the northwestern region. Analysis of local anomalies reveals notable spatial correlations; for instance, drought trends in Baicheng and Qian'an exhibit a weakening pattern, whereas Jingyu and Donggang display a pronounced strengthening trend. In the model performance evaluation, the combined SSA-VMD-ARIMA-BiLSTM model demonstrates superior predictive capability, achieving a RMSE of 0.083 for drought event predictions—significantly lower than traditional models, which have RMSE values of 0.59 and 0.86. This finding suggests that incorporating the signal decomposition technique significantly enhances the prediction accuracy and reliability of the model when handling complex nonlinear and non-stationary data. This study not only offers a comprehensive framework for a nuanced understanding of drought trends in Jilin Province but also introduces novel methodologies and tools for advancing future drought prediction research.Specifically, the integration of the spatio-temporal cube model with hotspot analyses establishes a crucial scientific foundation for developing effective drought mitigation strategies and is anticipated to pioneer new research trajectories in the field of drought prediction. Future research should focus on further refining these models to address increasingly complex climate change scenarios and offer enhanced support for regional water resource management and agricultural production. 1 Introduction to Part 1: Homogeneous total density In this Part I we focus on situations with a homogeneous total density: a constant fluid density throughout the domain. We aim to provide a thorough description of the flow problem at hand, and therefore we first describe the most general problem setting of a 2D flow problem between two parallel drains (section 2 ), with simultaneously occurring upward seepage and downward recharge, and a discharging drain. This setting includes also the unsaturated zone and presence and mixing of solutes as is used in the numerical modelling for Parts I and II (SUTRA; Voss and Provost, 2002 ) and represents the current practice to model such systems numerically. We then have to constrain this general setting to allow for an analytical solution to the flow problem at hand (section 3 ). For this, we first consider only flow of water without any mixing, i.e. a sharp interface between the two flow regimes. Also, we consider only saturated flow, no head build-up between parallel drains, which, consequently, means no seepage face at surface level, and we employ the Boussinesq approximation. Next, we derive the stream function and interface position as function of distance to the drain in a steady state and consider a practical application regarding travel time and – depth analyses (section 4 ). In section 5 , we extend the analysis to transient conditions to find an analytical solution to the interface movement midway between the drains following oscillating boundary conditions representing seasonal fluctuations in recharge and seepage. The solution is based on a two-scale expansion which was found to correspond very well to numerical results of the general flow problem. Again, we show a practical application, in which we consider the fluctuation in concentration in the drainage water. Finally, in section 6  we also consider the mixing zone midway between two drains, and find an analytical approximation of the solute concentration as function of depth, matching reasonably well with numerical model results. Understanding these gradients and the factors influencing them is relevant for ecohydrological predictions. Overall, the analytical results give an excellent understanding of the general behaviour of shallow water lenses from a sound theoretical background, and provide ways to quickly assess potential effects of changes to the drivers of the shallow lenses. Sections 4 , 5 and 6  all provide relevant insights into practical, real-world situations, both for agricultural and natural systems.   2 Problem setting In this section the physical-mathematical model for describing flow of water and transport of solutes in saturated and unsaturated soil is introduced. In both Part I and Part II, the numerical finite element model SUTRA version 2.2 (Voss and Provost, 2002 ) is used to solve those equations. We consider a situation where a series of equally spaced drains (separated by a distance of 2L  [L], and positioned at depth D  [L] below soil surface) are present in a homogeneous, isotropic soil. Let the domain D ⊂ R  2     be described in x  and y , where x  denotes the horizontal direction perpendicular to the drain and y  denotes the vertical direction, positive when pointing upwards ( A). We assume no flow occurs in the third dimension (i.e. parallel to the drains). Choosing the coordinates such that a drain is located at {x  = L, y  = 0}, vertical water divides exist at x  = 0 and x  = L  due to symmetry of this flow problem. The domain in the numerical model SUTRA is given by (see also Fig. 1 A)(7) D n u m   = { ( x , y  )  : 0 < x < L ,  − H < y < D  }  ,     where H  [L] is the numerical model depth, chosen sufficiently far down from the interface and mixing zone to avoid a direct influence on their positions. In D n u m    , the unsaturated domain is considered in order to represent a real-world situation as closely as possible. This means that non-vertical flow through the capillary fringe, head buildup midway between the drains and a potential delay in flow due to the unsaturated zone are all accounted for. In SUTRA, half a drain is modeled explicitly within the element mesh by excluding half a circle with a radius of 3 cm centered at {x  = L, y  = 0}, as in van de Craats et al. (2021) . Mesh refinements are made in the proximity of the drain, to allow for multiple nodes on the drain circle. Top and bottom boundary fluxes are given by uniform recharge (N  [LT-1 ]) and seepage (K  [LT-1 ]) fluxes, respectively, which are defined positive into the domain. Both recharge and seepage are required to have a net positive contribution for a water lens to form. In addition, the fact that they are defined as uniform fluxes does not allow the presence of a seepage face at the soil surface. Hence, groundwater levels must remain below the soil surface everywhere at all times. Recharge and seepage are given a solute mass fraction of 0 and wK   [-], respectively, as given by(8) { w = w N  = 0 ,  q →  · e →  y  = − N  along   0 < x < L , y = D     w = w K  ,  q →  · e →  y  = + K  along   0 < x < L , y = − H    ∂ w  ∂ x   = q →  · e →  x  = 0  along   x = 0 , L  and   y < D      .      Along the drain boundary with a radius of 3 cm, fixed pressure nodes are prescribed in SUTRA based on the nodes’ vertical position, with a pressure ranging from 0 at the top node to 587.4 kg m-1  s-2  at the bottom node, according to a hydrostatic equilibrium within the drain, assuming a fresh water density of 998 kg m-3  within the drain and a fully saturated drain with no excess pressure. Water and solute move out of the domain via fixed pressure nodes, following the local pressure gradients and solute mass fractions.  3 Simplified mathematical model setting In this section we introduce a number of simplifying assumptions with respect to the physical problem and obtain a reduced setting that can be treated by (semi) analytical methods. Note that the horizontal discharge is zero for x  = 0 and x  = L , satisfying the properties of a vertical water divide. The maximum interface depth is reached midway between the drains at x  = 0. From (33)  we find(35) h ≔ I ( 0 )  = L π  ln ( K 2 N + K   )  . In order to compare analytical interfaces, determined with the sharp interface approach, with numerical model results of the fluid and solute mass balance, a definition of the interface is required for the numerical model. For this we use the (central) moments of the vertical solute mass fraction gradient, similar as in e.g. Eeman et al. (2011) , where the first moment gives the vertical position of the interface with respect to the drain, and the second central moment provides a measure of the mixing zone width. To account for the curvature in the groundwater table, which in SUTRA is situated at p (x, y ) = 0, lens thickness is obtained by subtracting the first moment from the groundwater table position. An interesting application of the steady state problem is related to average residence times and travel time distributions, which are relevant for e.g. the available time for a constituent to break down in the groundwater, before exfiltrating into the drain. The average residence time of water in the lens (Tres   [T]) is given as(38) T r e s   = η A l   N L   = η π N   ∫ 0 L  ( − ln ( sin ( K N + K   π x  2 L    )   sin ( 2 N + K  N + K   π x  2 L    )    )   )  d x ,     where Al   [L2 ] is the area of the water lens in the half strip. It is obtained by integrating (33)  from x  = 0 to x  = L . This integral can, in principle, be evaluated. However, as the resulting expression is lengthy and not straightforward to interpret, we do not show its evaluated form in (38) . Not only the average residence time, but also the travel time from any position at the top of the groundwater table towards the drain may be of importance. The flow path of a water droplet entering the domain at rent   = (x, y ) = (xent  ,0), with 0 < xent   < L , and leaving the domain through the drain at rdrn   = (x, y ) = (L , 0) is given as the streamline with value ψrent   = −Nxent  . For any point (x, y ) along this streamline the water flow velocity may be obtained from (30)  and (31)  and the porosity. The travel time Ttr   [T] of a water particle is then obtained as(39) T t r   = ∫ ψ x e n t    η | q ( r )   |    d s = ∫ r e n t    r d r n    η q x 2  ( r ( t )   )  + q y 2  ( r ( t )   )     | r ′  ( t )   |  d t ,     where r (t ) = (x (t ), y (t )) is the parameterization of the streamline and the integration bounds rent   and rdrn   form the points of entrance and exit of the domain. This expression is evaluated numerically. We can also obtain the maximum depth that a droplet, entering the domain at rent  , reaches while traveling through the domain. For each depth y  in h  < y  < 0 there exists one streamline originating from (x , 0) with a horizontal tangent at that specific depth. For any such point, this means that a flux of − ψ(x, y ) reaches to depths below y , whereas the remaining recharge (N  + ψ(x, y )) never reaches this depth. Denoting the coordinates of the deepest point of each streamline by (xd ,yd  ), we may find the horizontal position by considering qy  (xd ,yd  ) = 0. With (31) , we find for any vertical position in h  < yd   < 0 the corresponding horizontal position xd   as(40) x d  = L π  arccos ( − K + N  N  sin ( π y d   L  )  − cosh ( π y d   L  )   )  .      The stream function value corresponding to the coordinates (xd ,yd  ) can now be obtained from (29) , which can directly be used to find the point of origin of the water droplet at (xd ,yd  ), as ψrent   = −Nxent  .  4.2 Example results Steady state flow patterns for three situations are shown in Fig. 2  , with the middle panel corresponding to the reference situation (Table 1 ), and the other panels deviating in flux ratio only. Recharge water infiltrates uniformly at the top of the domain and flows towards the drain situated in the top right corner at ( x L  , y L   )  = ( 1 , 0  )    . Seepage water infiltrates at the bottom, flows in an upward direction and is then also diverted towards the drain. The streamline ψ = 0 separates negative stream function values (in blue) from positive stream function values (in red). It can readily be seen that this streamline indeed divides the domain D   in a recharge part (D N   ) and seepage part (D K   ), such that it acts as the interface as defined in (21) . The deepest part of the rainwater lens is found midway between the drains. Here, also the lowest flow velocities occur, with a stagnation point at the intersect between the vertical water divide and the interface. It follows directly from (33)  and (35)  that dividing both x  and y  by half the drain distance, the dimensionless lens thickness is a function of flux ratio only, as demonstrated in Fig. 2 . The larger the flux ratio, the smaller the (dimensionless) lens thickness. Agreement between the interface obtained with the analytical sharp interface approximation and the numerical flow and transport model SUTRA with regard to the interface position is very good (Fig. 2 ), especially away from the drain. A difference between the two methods can be observed close to the drain, for which we identified three causes. (i) For the numerical model results, we opted for the simple approach of obtaining the interface position in the vertical direction only, rather than obtaining the interface position perpendicular to the flow direction (as in Eeman et al., 2011 ). As the derivative of the interface with respect to x  is largest close to the drain, the largest errors present themselves in this region. (ii) The definition of the numerical interface is not identical to the definition used in the analytical model. Especially in case of skewed distributions, using the first moment of the concentration gradient to describe the interface position may result in different results. In addition, (iii) the groundwater table in the numerical results does not intersect the drain, but may be situated somewhat above the drain, such that a pocket of water exists above the drain. As lens thickness in the analytical model is, per definition, zero at the drain, this results in a relatively large difference between the two methods close to the drain. An example of the travel time of any water droplet entering between 0 < xent  /L  < 1 is given in Fig. 3  A, for three flux ratios. The travel time itself was non-dimensionalized, such that this graph holds for any drain system configuration, recharge rate and porosity when properly scaled. Clearly, increasing the flux ratio results in decreasing non-dimensional travel times, as the water lens becomes thinner (35) , which also immediately follows from the expression for the average residence times (38) . This is demonstrated in Fig. 3 B as well, showing the average residence time divided by half the drain distance, as function of flux ratio, for three different recharge rates. For a given flux ratio, an increase in recharge rate (and thus also seepage rate) results in a decrease in residence time, as water is required to move faster through the same lens area. Increasing flux ratios while maintaining the same recharge rate results in decreasing residence times due to shallower lenses. Returning to Fig. 3 A, for a flux ratio of 1, approximately 80% of the distance between 0 < x  < L  discharges faster than the average residence time, which may have important implications for the breakdown or formation of certain constituents (e.g., in the process of denitrification in the anaerobic environment) while traveling through the saturated zone and thereby affect the composition of drainage water. This percentage increases even further for decreasing flux ratios. In the reference case, with K /N  = 1, N  = 0.5 mm d-1 , η = 0.45 and L  = 5, the average residence time of a water droplet is approximately 1100 days. However, as much as 50% of the water infiltrating at the surface leaves the domain within 125 days, and 20% even within 4 days. In Fig. 3 C maximum travel depth of a particle entering the domain between 0 < xent  /L  < 1 is given (40) , for four flux ratios, including a situation in which only recharge occurs (Groenendijk and van den Eertwegh, 2004 ). The maximum depth reached by a particle originating midway between two drains at x  = 0 is determined by (35) , and reaches to minus infinity for the situation with K /N  = 0. Again, we see that the majority of the water is discharged through a rather shallow layer, corresponding with the short travel times (Fig. 3 A). Roughly 80% of the water is discharged through the layer between h /2 < y  < 0, with the remainder of the water reaching to larger depths. Dividing lens area Al   by maximum lens thickness, − h , and normalizing by drain distance gives a measure of convexity of the interface, with a more convex interface for larger numbers of this ratio (Fig. 3 D). A more convex interface can hold a larger volume of water in the lens for a given lens thickness. The ratio shows a decreasing trend for increasing flux ratios, with a horizontal asymptote given by ln(2). Therefore, with an increase in flux ratio, the storage of recharge water decreases not only due to a decrease in maximum thickness, but also due to a decrease in convexity of the interface. This is also a main explanation for the more strongly increasing average residence times for flux ratios decreasing below 0.5 (Fig. 3 A). For the purpose of comparison, also the ratio of lens area divided by thickness is shown for the situation described by Maas (2007) . It shows that, for a given maximum interface depth, the volume of water stored in the lens in an oceanic island is higher than for our current conditions. This may have implications for analyses in other work (Eeman et al., 2011 ; Stofberg et al., 2017 ), which apply the solution of Maas (2007)  to problems which actually involve the domain as presented in this paper.   5 Transient flow 5.1 Mathematical model description Even though the stream function (29)  responds instantaneously to changes in boundary fluxes for an incompressible fluid, this does not imply that the interface does so as well. Rather, the interface moves along with the local velocity at the interface itself, which does respond instantaneously to changes. As such, in case of transient boundary fluxes, i.e. N (t ), K (t ), the interface is no longer necessarily situated at the position where the stream function equals zero, and (21)  no longer holds. In the transient case, we obtain an equation for the movement of the interface by considering the seepage water balance in D K   . It reads(41) η ∂ I  ∂ t   + ∂ ∂ x   Q s  ( x , t  )  = K ( t )  ,     where Qs   is the horizontal seepage water flux(42) Q s  ( x , t  )  = ∫ − ∞  I ( x , t  )    q x  ( x , y , t  )  d y .      In terms of the stream function, (42)  becomes(43) Q s  ( x , t  )  = ψ ( x , − ∞ , t  )  − ψ ( x ,  I ( x , t  )  , t  )  = K ( t )  x − ψ ( x ,  I ( x , t  )  , t  )  .      Substitution of (43)  in (41)  yields the interface motion equation (Chan Hong et al, 1989 )(44) η ∂ I ( x , t  )   ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ x   { ψ ( x ,  I ( x , t  )  , t  )   }      subject to the initial condition I (x , 0) = Iinit  (x ). As the stream function reacts instantaneously to changes in the boundary fluxes, the right hand side term in (44)  follows directly from (29)  for situations without density differences. Clearly, the solution to (44)  depends on the nature of N (t ) and K (t ), such that no single unique answer exist. We may reformulate the interface motion equation into its dimensionless equivalent. For this, we define the reference values(45) x R  = L ;  ψ R  = N 0  L ;  T R  = T ,     where N 0  is characteristic recharge rate, for instance an average recharge rate, and T  is a characteristic time scale, for instance an oscillation period in case of sinusoidal boundary fluxes. Let us write any scaled parameter as e.g. x ^  = x x R     . Using this notation, the interface motion equation (44)  is written as(46) η x R  T R   ∂ I ^    ∂ t ^    = ψ R  x R   ∂ ∂ x ^    ψ ^  ( x ^  ,  I ^  , t ^   )   or   ∂ I ^    ∂ t ^    = ψ R  T R   η x R 2    ∂ ∂ x ^    ψ ^  ( x ^  ,  I ^  , t ^   )  .      Substituting the reference values (45)  in (46)  yields the dimensionless interface motion equation(47) ∂ I ^    ∂ t ^    = ε  ∂ ∂ x ^    { ψ ^  ( x ^  ,  I ^  , t ^   )   }  ,     where we introduced the dimensionless parameter ε  = N 0  T  η L     . For further analyses, we implemented a numerical solution scheme to solve (47)  using the Runge-Kutta method in time and central differences in space. In order to provide additional insights into this transient problem, we consider an example where the boundary fluxes follow a sinusoidal pattern. Such sinusoidal boundary conditions may be relevant when seasonality in both recharge and seepage fluxes occurs. The example problem is given by(48) N ( t )  = N 0  + A sin ( 2 π t  T  )     K ( t )  = K 0  − A sin ( 2 π t  T  )      ,     where A  [LT-1 ] is the flux amplitude, N 0  and K 0  [LT-1 ] are the average (positive) recharge and seepage fluxes, respectively, and T  [T] is the reference period. Flux amplitude A  may exceed both N 0  and K 0 , implying that N (t ) and K (t ) may become negative. This allows for seasonal evapotranspiration or downward seepage. Clearly, the parameters A, N 0  and K 0  should be chosen such that I (x, t ) < 0 for 0 ≤ x  < L  and for all times t  > 0. For this choice of boundary conditions, recharge decreases while seepage increases and vice versa, which resembles a real-world situation with a fixed aquifer head at sufficient distance from the groundwater table. In the summer period recharge may be low, such that phreatic groundwater levels are lower than heads in an underlying aquifer, resulting in increased upward seepage fluxes. Conversely, in winter more recharge results in higher phreatic groundwater levels, resulting in decreased upward seepage fluxes. When (48)  applies, the problem has two time-scales: the oscillation period T  in the boundary conditions and the transport time η L  N 0    . The ratio of the two, ε  = N 0  T  η L     , is the dimensionless parameter introduced in (47) . When the oscillation period is much smaller than the transport time, i.e. ε ≪ 1, we can follow van Duijn and van der Zee (2018)  and apply a two-scale expansion to obtain an approximation of the time dependent interface behaviour. This approximation can be handled by analytical techniques when x  = 0, i.e. at the location midway between the drains. The resulting expression is useful as benchmark for numerical simulations, and, more importantly, it gives insight in the roles of the two time scales. With h ( t ) ≔ I ( 0 , t  )    and h i n i t   ≔ h ( 0 )    , we derive in Appendix A  the approximation(49) h ( t )  = h 0  ( t )  + ε  A N 0   L 2 π    ( cos ( 2 π t T   )  − 1 + e  ( π h i n i t   L   )    1 + e  ( π h 0  ( t )   L   )     e  π 2 N 0  + K 0   2 ( N 0  + K 0   )    ( h 0  ( t )   L  − h i n i t   L  − K 0  t  η L    )     )  + O ( ε   2  )  ,     where O ( ε   2  )    [L] denotes the second and higher order terms with respect to ε. The function h 0 (t ) [L] is resolved from the algebraic equation(50) | e  ( π h 0  ( t )   L   )   − K 0  2 N 0  + K 0     |  e  ( − π 2 N 0  + K 0   2 ( N 0  + K 0   )     h 0  ( t )   L   )    = | e  ( π h i n i t   L   )   − K 0  2 N 0  + K 0     |  e  ( − π 2 N 0  + K 0   2 ( N 0  + K 0   )     h i n i t   L   )   e  ( − π K 0  ( 2 N 0  + K 0   )   2 N 0  ( N 0  + K 0   )     N 0  t  η L    )   .      In (49) , the first term denotes the slow variation of the interface position. From (50)  we deduce the following observations for the behaviour of h 0 (t ):• For any hinit   < 0, and with h  defined in (35) ,   h 0 (t ) → h  as t  → ∞, with exponential decay of order O ( e  ( − π K 0  ( 2 N 0  + K 0   )   2 N 0  ( N 0  + K 0   )     N 0  t  η L    )   )   ;   • If hinit   > h , then h 0 (t ) decreases towards h ;  • If hinit   < h , then h 0 (t ) increases towards h ;  • If hinit   = h , then h 0 (t ) = h  for all t  > 0.    The second term in (49)  involving the cosine is O ( ε  )    and oscillates with period T . Since ε  = N 0  T  η L   ≪ 1   , this is the fastly oscillating term. The third term in (49)  is O ( ε  )    as well and denotes the slowly decaying correction to the first term h 0 (t ). If hinit   = h 0 , then (49)  reduces to(51) h ( t )  = h 0  + ε  A N 0   L 2 π    ( cos [ 2 π t T   ]  − e  ( − π K 0  ( 2 N 0  + K 0   )   2 N 0  ( N 0  + K 0   )     N 0  t  η L    )    )  + O ( ε   2  )  .      As an example, we present solutions for time-dependent boundary conditions in the form of (48) . We follow the development of the interface depth over time, based on (i) the analytical approximation (49) , (ii) the numerical solution to the interface motion equation (47)  and (iii) the first moment of the vertical concentration change midway between the drains as calculated with SUTRA. To obtain lens thickness from SUTRA simulation results, we used the average groundwater level over one period to avoid fast groundwater level fluctuations obscuring the slower movement of the interface: the groundwater level is highest in times of highest recharge rates and responds quite fast. If we would obtain lens thickness including these fast groundwater level movements, this would obscure the slower interface movement, in accordance with de Louw et al. (2013) . We describe three cases, which only deviate in their initial conditions (IC), and one additional case with a different ratio ε of the characteristic time T  over the steady travel time η L  N 0    . For the parameters not specifically mentioned in this section, we use reference parameters given in Table 1 . The initial conditions are given by the steady state solution for K /N  ratios of 2, 1 and 0.5, respectively, of which their steady state solutions were already shown in Fig. 2 . The transient boundary conditions are given by (48) , with N 0  = K 0  = A  = 0.5 mm d-1 , and an oscillation period T  of 364 days. Given (35)  and (49) , the interface position moves from an initial state (given as h /L ) of -0.22, -0.35 and -0.51, respectively, to an equilibrium at -0.35 for all three situations. The reference parameters give ε =  0.081. The fourth situation also starts at -0.22, but has a four times larger value of ε (ε =  0.324) due to a decrease in porosity. As in our derivation of the analytical approximation we assumed ε ≪ 1, this parameterization may be already quite extreme.  5.2 Example results Calculated movement of the interface position midway between the drains by the analytical approximation (49) , as given by the solid sinusoidal lines in Fig. 4  , are hardly distinguishable from the numerical approximation of the interface motion equation (47)  (dotted lines) at that position. The second and higher order terms in (49)  therefore appear of minor importance and need not be evaluated for the given parameterization, even for the simulation with a higher value of ε. Results of our analytical approach also compare well to SUTRA (black dashed lines). There is a slight phase shift in the results of SUTRA as compared to our analytical approach. This may be caused by (i) a delay in response to changes in recharge due to the unsaturated zone, (ii) groundwater level fluctuations which are not accounted for in the analytical approximation, and (iii) oscillations in skewness of the mixing zone. The second and third term in (49)  are specific to the boundary conditions (48) . The effect of the third term in (49)  is clearly demonstrated for the situation with the initial condition given by K /N  = 1 (Fig. 4 , in green). In the first few oscillation periods, the sinusoidal line lies below the solid, non-sinusoidal line for the majority of time. This is a consequence of the definition and timing of the initial – and boundary conditions. As the boundary conditions are defined such that N (t ) > N 0  and K (t ) < K 0  for 0 < t  < T /2, during this time the interface is pushed downward from its initial, steady state position, and in the remainder of this period the interface is pushed upward again, only to end up slightly above its initial condition. Therefore, most of the time within the first period the interface is below its starting position. The analytical results match the results of SUTRA of this correction closely. The effect of the second term in (49)  is apparent in all simulations. In the analytical approximation, the amplitude of the oscillations itself is not influenced by the initial condition, as seen directly from (49) . It is solely driven by the value of ε and changes in boundary fluxes, of which the latter directly influences the stream function in time. In the SUTRA model the groundwater table itself may fluctuate, implying that lens thickness not only changes due movement of solutes, but also due to changes in thickness of the saturated zone. This effect appears to have little influence on the amplitude of the oscillation of the interface itself. Thus, for the parameterizations chosen, the analytical model also compares well to the SUTRA model in this respect. The first term in (49) , as given by the solid non-sinusoidal lines describes the change in average interface position rather well when compared to SUTRA. This slow term movement may be of special interest, as it not only applies to our specific boundary conditions, but also applies to situations with a sudden change in boundary conditions or may be used to model the effects of gradual changes in boundary conditions. Finally, Fig. 4  shows that the effect of an increase in the ratio of the oscillation period over steady travel time, ε, is three-fold. (i) The amplitude of oscillations increases, (ii) the response time to changes in N 0  and/or K 0  decreases and (iii) the time required for the correction term to diminish is shortened. Hence, a hydrological system with a relatively large value of ε is more sensitive to disturbances in boundary fluxes as compared to a system with smaller values of ε. It seems that even with a relatively high value of ε (0.324), the analytical approximation still aligns well with the numerical implementation of the interface motion equation as well as with SUTRA results. Hence, the contribution of the second and higher order terms in (49)  remain small. From the numerical implementation of the interface motion equation, we may not only derive the interface position midway between the drains, but also at any other location in 0 < x  < L . Obtaining the interface position sufficiently close to the drain, we may approximate the angle of the interface close to the drain with this numerical implementation. With (34) , this angle provides the relative contribution of both water sources (recharge and seepage) to discharge from the drain at any time t . Knowing the solute concentrations of both sources of water and the discharge volume, this relative contribution is easily converted to an estimate of concentration of the discharge water as well as solute load. SUTRA does, in itself, not distinguish between source of water, but with known input concentrations in the seepage and recharge water, we may use the model output of discharge volume and solute load to obtain an estimate of the relative contribution of both water sources to discharge at any time t . A comparison with estimates of the relative contribution obtained from the angle of the interface close to the drain with those obtained from SUTRA is shown in Fig. 5  , for the same situations as described in Fig. 4 . The resemblance between both models is remarkable, considering that SUTRA also takes mixing of solutes into account. The amplitude of the oscillation obtained with SUTRA is slightly larger compared to the amplitude obtained from the interface motion equation, but patterns and the speed at which the equilibrium value of the oscillation changes are very similar. The difference in amplitude may be related to the fact that in SUTRA, discharge volume also shows a slight oscillating behaviour due to changes in the groundwater level, whereas discharge volume is constant in the interface motion equation for the given parameterization. Clearly, the largest fluctuations in relative contribution, and thus solute concentration in the discharge water, are found for a larger value of ε. Comparing the evolution of the concentration over time with that of the maximum lens thickness (Fig. 4 ), it is evident that the oscillations in concentration move towards their final equilibrium more rapidly in the early stages. This is a consequence of the fact that the interface close to the drain adjusts more rapidly to the new equilibrium boundary fluxes compared to the interface further away. As time proceeds, the slower adjustment of the interface further from the drain becomes the main driver of the rate at which the discharge concentration moves towards its final equilibrium oscillation. Consequently, this rate becomes more in line with the rate of change in maximum lens thickness.   6 Mixing zone 6.1 Mathematical model description In this section we construct a steady state approximation for the concentration in the diffusive-dispersive mixing zone midway between the drains; i.e. at x  = 0. We use (3)  and (6)  at x  = 0, y  < 0 as starting point. In (3)  we assume the porosity and fluid density to be constant and we set qx  (0,y ) = 0, in accordance with (30) .
