The flux at the interface is obtained from the condition Cr  (0) = 0:(57) J ( h )  = − 1 R e [ A ( 0 )  + B ( h )  − A ( h )   ]    .      Expressions (53) - (57)  are derived in a dimensionless setting in Appendix B . It was found that, in the end, the characteristic dimensionless numbers that remain are D *, α L *    and K *, given as(58) D  *  = η D m   α L  N    and  α L *  = α L  L   and  K  *  = K N  .       6.2 Example results Concentration profiles in the vertical direction midway between the drains compare well between the analytical and numerical steady state solutions, especially below the interface position (Fig. 6  ). Above the interface, the mixing zone obtained with the numerical model extends slightly further towards the groundwater table. Two main reasons for this are (i) the fact that in the numerical model, solutes are allowed to enter the unsaturated zone, whereas in the analytical model we assume the concentration to be zero at y  = 0, and (ii) the upward curvature of the interface, and thus also the mixing zone, moving away from the position midway between drains. The latter implies that especially above the interface, mixing in the horizontal direction, which was deemed small in the analytical approach, and was ignored correspondingly, may result in some additional dispersion and spreading of the mixing zone. Fig. 6  shows the effects of changes of values of individual parameters. The effects on the mixing zone shape and extent are similar in both the numerical and analytical approach. These effects may also be interpreted in light of the dimensionless groups D  *  = η D m   α L  N     , α L *  = α L  L     and K  *  = K N    . A simultaneous increase in recharge and seepage rate, as well as a decrease in porosity, only affect D * and both do so by reducing its value. As a consequence the mixing zone width decreases (Fig. 6 ). An increase in drain distance affects only α L *   , resulting in a (relative) decrease in mixing zone thickness as well. The dispersion length influences both D * and α L *   , and does so in an opposite direction. For the parameterization in Fig. 6 , an increase in dispersion length results in an increase in mixing zone width as compared to the reference case, hence, for these parameters the effect of α L *    is dominant over D *. An increase in seepage rate, and thus only an increase in K *, leads to a decrease of the mixing zone width. Finally, an increase in recharge rate, reducing both K * and D *, also results in a decrease in mixing zone width, which is less pronounced as compared to the decrease with a change in seepage rate. We therefore conclude that D * is dominant over K * for the chosen parameters. These examples demonstrate the importance of individual parameters on the behavior of the mixing zone. We may also examine the response of the average mixing zone position (first moment) and width (as root of the second central moment) upon changes in the dimensionless groups D *, α L *    and K *. The first moment of the mixing zone as obtained with the analytical approximation presented here is given in Figs. 7  A and C, for varying combinations of the dimensionless groups. For increasing values of D * and α L *   , the first moment is situated deeper in the soil profile, and this effect is more pronounced for lower flux ratios. The reason for this shift is that the mixing zone spreads further into the seepage water part compared to the recharge water part; thus, the mixing zone becomes negatively skewed. This is a consequence of both the flow pattern and the solute boundary conditions, with higher velocity gradients in the recharge water part, and a prescribed concentration at y  = 0. Also note that for D  *  = α L *  = 0   , the first moment coincides exactly with the interface position as obtained with the sharp interface approximation. For any α L *  > 0    and D * > 0, the first moment is situated lower in the domain. With respect to the mixing zone width, for which we take the square root of the second central moment, we see in Fig. 7 B and D the following general behaviour. For increasing values of D * and α L *    the mixing zone width becomes larger. The width is smaller for increasing flux ratios, which is a consequence of the higher velocity gradients when the lens becomes shallower due to the increase in flux ratio. The numerical SUTRA results agree with these analytical results, although the obtained widths are consistently somewhat higher than obtained with the analytical model. This was observed in Fig. 6  as well.   7 Conclusions In this Part 1 of a series of two papers on flow in shallow water lenses subject to upward seepage and downward infiltration of recharge, we have obtained analytical expressions for steady state, transient and mixing zone problems, for the situation without density differences between the two types of water. Using the sharp interface approach, we have obtained an expression for the stream function in steady state, from which we obtain the interface between the two types of water, being either recharge or seepage water. This allows us to also calculate travel times of water in the shallow water lens, depending on the entrance location of water. For transient conditions, we obtained the interface motion equation., which can be solved by simple numerical techniques along the entire horizontal width of the domain. For a situation with specific oscillatory boundary conditions, we have demonstrated that the interface position midway between the drains can be handled accurately by analytical techniques. This allows for a simple evaluation of how parameters as porosity and drain distance affect the response of the interface upon changes in boundary conditions. The interface motion equation may also be used to estimate the relative contribution of both water sources to drain discharge at any moment in time. Finally, we developed an analytical approximation of the mixing zone in the vertical direction midway between the drains for steady state conditions. Based on this analysis we have identified three dimensionless parameter groups which determine the front width, which improves our understanding of the interaction between factors determining the mixing zone thickness. For all cases, we have shown that the results of our analytical expressions align very well with numerical model results of the model SUTRA, which solves convection, dispersion and diffusion in the two dimensions considered. The analytical expressions provided in this paper provide much more conceptual understanding of the flow of water and solutes in shallow water lenses as compared to numerical models, allows for simple exploration of the sensitivity of the shallow lenses to changing conditions, and may provide a basis for further studies on this subject.
1 Introduction Groundwater serves as a vital freshwater resource, playing essential roles in agriculture, industry, and daily life. However, rapid industrialization and urbanization have increasingly and severely polluted groundwater, threatening both the environment and human health (Lapworth et al., 2012; Famiglietti, 2014 ). Accurate GPSC is crucial for addressing this challenge. However, direct measurements of pollution sources are often exceedingly expensive, and data on this matter are scarce (Zhang et al., 2016 ). Consequently, inverse modeling methods have emerged as a popular approach, leveraging observed data to infer information about unknown pollution sources (Skaggs and Kabala, 1994; Xu and Gomez-Hernandez, 2016; Secci et al., 2022 ). GPSC is often an ill-posed problem and faces nonlinearity challenges. The PF(Gordon et al., 1993 ) offers a promising solution for state estimation in nonlinear and non-Gaussian systems. The PF approximates the probability distribution of variables using a set of random samples (particles) to estimate the variables. Based on observation information, the algorithm continuously resamples and state updates on the particles to approximate the posterior probability distribution of the variables (Field et al., 2016; Ramgraber et al., 2019 ). It is an implementation method of the Bayesian filter and has been widely used in dynamic systems (Mohseni et al., 2024; Song and He, 2024 ), target tracking (Xu et al., 2021 ), positioning (Adurthi, 2023 ), and other fields (Gustafsson, 2010 ). However, the general PF often encounters challenges related to particle degeneracy and a loss of diversity in GPSC tasks (Pan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023 ). As the iterations proceed, the weights of particles become highly heterogeneous, with only a small subset of particles carrying substantial weights while the majority have negligible weights. Resampling techniques can alleviate this issue by replicating high-weight particles and discarding those with low weights (Yu et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2024 ). Nevertheless, the resampling process sometimes over-emphasizes the current perceived optimal solution, potentially overlooking other promising solution spaces. In the end, the calculation results are predominantly influenced by high-weight particles, leading to a further loss of particle diversity (Li et al., 2015; Abbaszadeh et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2024 ). This can lead to inadequate approximations of the posterior distribution of variables and mislead the estimation results in GPSC (Yin and Zhu, 2015 ). Recent research has enhanced PF by integrating optimization methods with strong local search capabilities into the resampling step (Heris et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). A more accurate selection of resampled particles can be achieved by utilizing a nonlinear optimization model for resampling, thereby enhancing the algorithm's local optimization capability (Jamal and Linker, 2022 ). However, this integration approach may introduce additional computational burdens. Solving a nonlinear optimization model is required in each iteration, increasing computational complexity and time consumption. In addition, the choice of the optimization model solution method also affects the efficiency of resampling. The PF algorithm is also prone to getting stuck in local optima within complex search spaces. There remains a need to facilitate information sharing among particles to help them escape local optima regions, thereby enhancing the algorithm's ability to discover global optimum solutions. Balancing computational time and accuracy remains a challenging aspect in PF algorithm (Ito et al., 2024 ). This study proposes an IEPF method to tackle the limitations associated with general PF algorithm. First, we define a weight threshold by calculating the effective number of particles (N eff    ). Only particles with weights exceeding the threshold are selected as seeds for resampling, thereby preventing sample diversity loss while enhancing resampling efficiency. Second, we introduce an information transmission mechanism that enables low-weight particles to update their positions using information from high-weight particles and their neighboring particles. This mechanism facilitates greater information exchange among particles, enabling low-weight particles to gain more insights. As such, our approach enhances the contribution of low-weight particles to the characterization while effectively improving the algorithm's global search capability. Particles with low weights often represent suboptimal solutions in the PF algorithm. At this point, it is crucial to enhance these particles by introducing randomness and fostering diversity (Kuptametee and Aunsri, 2022 ). In GPSC, effective global exploration is crucial for identifying the globally optimal solution. Inspired by genetic algorithm(GA) in this study, we introduce crossover and mutation operations to enhance low-weight particles. The crossover operation generates new particles by randomly exchanging some of their features, thereby increasing population diversity. Meanwhile, the mutation operation randomly perturbs the positions of low-weight particles and introduces new solutions to improve the algorithm's global searchability. The crossover and mutation operations effectively enhance particle diversity, preventing their convergence on locally optimized solutions. This condition helps update and refine the entire particle set, ultimately enabling us to obtain more accurate GPSC. During the GPSC iterative search, numerical simulation models are repeatedly invoked to simulate and test various combinations of unknown variables. This undoubtedly induces a significant computational burden and lengthy computation time (Xing et al., 2019; Anshuman and Eldho, 2023; Guo et al., 2024 ). Surrogate models effectively solve this issue (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024 ). To enhance the fit to the complex nonlinear mapping relationship between the inputs and outputs of the simulation models, we apply ResNet to establish surrogate models. As an advanced deep learning technique, ResNet has powerful learning features and representation capabilities, enabling it to capture complex patterns and nonlinear relationships in data effectively. Training ResNet allows it to learn the mapping relationship between the inputs and outputs of simulation models, thereby significantly improving computational efficiency while maintaining high accuracy. The IEPF method proposed in this study enhances the algorithm's global search capability while maintaining particle diversity, leading to more accurate GPSC. Specifically, the main contributions of this research are as follows: (1) Introducing IEPF to address inefficiencies and susceptibility to local optima challenges in the PF algorithm. IEPF incorporates information transmission, crossover and mutation operations to adjust particle weights intelligently. Validation in two groundwater pollution cases demonstrates superior inversion accuracy compared to the general PF algorithm. (2) Employing ResNet as a surrogate model for the simulation model within the IEPF algorithm to alleviate computational burdens in GPSC. ResNet learns complex nonlinear mapping relationship between the inputs and outputs of the simulation model, which improves the approximation accuracy of the surrogate model to the simulation model, and further enhances the inversion accuracy.  2 Methodology 2.1 Numerical simulation model The governing differential equation of a two-dimensional phreatic aquifer is expressed as follows (Singh and Datta, 2006 ):(1) ∂ ∂ x i    ( K ij   ( H - B )  ∂ H  ∂ x j    )  + W = μ ∂ H  ∂ t   , ( x , y )  ∈ Ω , i , j = 1 , 2  , t ≥ 0     where K ij     is the hydraulic conductivity (L/T), x i  , x j     are the rectangular coordinate system, H   is the hydraulic head (L), W   is the volumetric flux per unit volume (L/T), μ   is the specific yield, Ω   is the range of the simulation area, and t   is the simulation time (T). The governing differential equation of groundwater pollution transport in a 2D aquifer is as follows (Pinder and Bredehoeft, 1968; Singh and Datta, 2006 ):(2) ∂ c  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ x i    ( D ij   ∂ c  ∂ x j    )  - ∂ ∂ x i    ( v i  c )  + I , ( x , y )  ∈ Ω , i , j = 1 , 2  , t ≥ 0     where c   is the groundwater pollutant concentration (M/L3 ), D ij     is the hydrodynamic dispersion tensor (L2 /T), v i    is the average velocity in groundwater (L/T), and I  is the change in solute mass per unit time per unit volume of liquid phase (only the volume of liquid phase is included, M / L 3  · T  ). The MODFLOW and MT3DMS modules in the groundwater modeling system (GMS) simulate the groundwater solute transport in this paper.  2.2 ResNet The typical structure of a deep neural network (DNN) comprises an input layer, multiple hidden layers, and an output layer. As the network's depth increases, introducing more layers, the number of parameters escalates, rendering the model more intricate (He and Sun, 2015 ). Consequently, DNNs are susceptible to challenges such as overfitting, gradient vanishing, and gradient explosion. Thus, ResNet emerged as a groundbreaking solution to these challenges. Generally, in DNNs, the network attempts to learn the mapping from inputs to outputs. Unlike general DNNs, ResNet (Fig. 1  ) adds a residual block that contains an identity mapping (i.e., the input is passed directly through the layer) and a residual mapping (Yan et al., 2021; Durga and Rajesh, 2022 ). The residual block structure enables the network to learn the mapping L ( d )  = G ( d )  - d     instead of directly learning G ( d )   . The shortcut connection can effectively reduce the impact of gradient vanishing. The residual structure can be represented as follows:(3) G = d i  + L d i  , w i        where G   and d i    are the outputs and inputs of the i -th residual block, respectively, and L   and w   are the residual functions and associated parameters of the i -th residual structure, respectively.  2.3 PF The basic idea of the PF is to use many particles with weights and obtain optimal estimates of the posterior probability distributions of random variables by mathematical statistics (Celik and Son, 2011; Ramgraber et al., 2019 ). Each particle can be viewed as an estimate of a set of random variables. In the PF, importance sampling and resampling steps are applied to constantly update the particles' positions and weights, allowing them to find the optimal estimates quickly. The generalized flow of the PF algorithm is as follows (Yin and Zhu, 2015 ):1) Initialization. N   particles are randomly generated in their initial estimated value interval according to the prior probability distribution of each random variable. Each particle has the same weight 1 / N   .  2) Importance sampling step. This step completes the update of the position and weight of each particle. The weights are reassigned by calculating the proximity between the simulated outputs values and the actual data observations, described as follows:   (4) w t i  = w t - 1  i  p Z t  | X t i    p X t i  | X t - 1  i     q X t i  | X 0 : t - 1  i  , Z 0 : t           The normalized weights (w t  i  ^   ) of each particle can be expressed as:(5) w t  i  ^  = w t  i  ∑ i = 1  N  w t  i        where N   is the number of particles, w t  i    is the weight of the i- th particle at moment t  , X t  i    is the position of the i- th particle at moment t  , Z   is the observation data, p ( Z t  | X t  i  )    is the likelihood function, p X t  i  |  X t - 1  i       is the transition probability, and q X t i  | X 0 : t - 1  i  , Z 0 : t       is the proposal distribution function.3) Resampling step. This step keeps and copies the particles with high weights and discards the particles with low weights. It is based on the normalized weights of the particles and follows the particle invariance principle.    After several iterations, the weight of the entire particle set is concentrated in a small number of particles, while most of the particles have extremely low weights. This phenomenon is known as particle degradation, and it is unavoidable. Particle degradation wastes most computing power on low-weighted particles, as the N eff     decreases continuously with iterations (Doucet et al., 2000; Li et al., 2014 ). The N eff     is approximated as follows (Liu et al., 2001 ):(6) N eff   = 1 ∑ i = 1  N  w t  i     2          where [] represents the rounding. Although the resampling operation can effectively alleviate the particle degradation problem, it reduces particle diversity, causing particle impoverishment.  2.4 IEPF 2.4.1 GA As an optimization algorithm, the GA (Holland, 1975 ) was inspired by natural evolutionary processes for solving search and optimization problems. It simulates biological evolution in nature, searching the solution space for an optimal or near-optimal solution to the problem through genetic, crossover, and mutation operations. Crossover and mutation are two critical operations in the GA that work together on individuals to help algorithms find a better solution in the search space. The crossover operation simulates gene exchange in organisms. Here, certain parts of two or more individuals are combined to generate new individuals. The mutation operation simulates the genetic mutations in organisms and introduces randomness to increase population diversity. Mutation helps to maintain population diversity, prevents premature convergence, and explores new regions in the search space. Mutation operations usually occur with a lower probability to avoid excessively disrupting the population stability.  2.4.2 IEPF This study introduces the crossover and mutation operators in the GA into the general PF algorithm to improve the algorithm's performance, i.e., the IEPF. The exact IEPF workflow is as follows:• Particle division:  A separation strategy was constructed to divide the high- and low-weight particles, represented as follows:   (7) X t  i  = P h  ,     w  t  i  > W t     P l  ,     w  t  i  ≤ W t             where P h    and P l    are the high- and low-weight particle populations, respectively. The partition of P h    and P l    is achieved by sorting the weights and calculating the weight threshold W t   . Particles closer to the observed data are given higher weights. The specific steps are as follows:(1) The weights (W ) of all particles are ranked in descending order.   (8) W =   w  t  1  ∼  ,  w  t  2  ,  ∼  ⋯ ,  w  t  N  ∼        (2) Determine N eff     and calculate W t   . N eff     is calculated by Equation (6).  (3) According to W t   , the indexes of high- and low-weight particles are divided.  • Threshold ( W t   ) definition:  This study refers to the threshold definition approach of Yin and Zhu (Yin and Zhu, 2015 ). We set the ( N eff   ) t h    particle weight as the threshold W t   .  • Information transmission:  We introduce neighborhood information and achieve information transmission by calculating the average neighborhood position of each particle and selecting a particle from high-weight particles. Interestingly, this transmission improves the synergy between particles so that the surrounding particles can guide the low-weight particles. Through neighborhood influence, the update of low-weight particles not only relies on high-weight particles, but also considers the state of surrounding particles, making the algorithm more characterized by global search and collaborative optimization.    For each low-weight particle, information transmission is performed with a certain probability, called the information transmission rate. When transmitting information, we calculate the average neighborhood position of the current low-weight particles as follows:(9) P n  =  X i  , X i + 1   , ⋯ , X i + k         (10) P avg   = 1 k + 1   ∑ j = i  i + k   X j      where X i    is the position of the i- th particle, and P n    is a set of neighborhood positions from X i    to X i + k    . A particle is randomly selected from a set of high-weight particles. We use the mixing factor to mix the high-weight particles with the neighborhood average position to get the new position. Then, the low-weight particle is updated to the blended position as follows:(11) P new   = a ∗  h p  + 1 - a   ∗  P avg       where h p    is the randomly selected location of the highly weighted particles, and P avg     is the average particle position in the neighborhood.• GA operations (crossover and mutation operations):  Crossover and mutation operations are performed on low-weight particles. Through crossover operation, low-weight particles can inherit some information from other low-weight particles, thus increasing diversity. Also, the mutation operation helps introduce randomness for better search space exploration.    Depending on the weight threshold, low-weight particles are subjected to crossover, mutation, and information transmission to improve the particles’ fitness. This renders them more likely to achieve higher weights and ultimately enhance the performance of the overall population. The area was divided into four hydraulic conductivity partitions. The AB and CD boundaries were generalized to the specified head boundaries, while the AD and BC boundaries were generalized to no-flow boundaries. The hydrogeological parameters of the aquifer are listed in Table 1  . The simulation time was five years and divided into five stress periods. There were two pollutant sources and six observation wells in the study area. The pollutant concentration was measured at the end of each stress period. The groundwater pollutant source continuously releases pollutant during the stress periods. The locations of the observation wells and the pollutant sources are depicted in Fig. 3  . In this case study, the pollution source release intensity in the five stress periods (Si Tj  , i  = 1,2; j  = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and the simulation model parameters (four hydraulic conductivity in four zones (K1, K2, K3, K4)) were simultaneously selected as variables to be identified. The actual values of the variables to be determined, the range of values, and the prior distribution are provided in Table A1  in the attachment file. The pollutant concentration at the end of each stress period in the six observation wells, along with pollutant transport, is depicted in Fig. A1 and A2  in the attachment file. Unlike practical problems, we first input the reference values of unknown variables into the simulation model. The observed pollutant concentration was obtained by running the model, which served as the actual concentration monitoring data.  3.2 Applying the surrogate model Our study involved iterative computations that entailed multiple repeated calls to the simulation model. This incurred a huge computational load and lengthy computation time. Thus, building a surrogate model based on ResNet solves this problem. When establishing surrogate models, the first step is to obtain training and test data. According to the prior probability distribution and value range of each variable to be solved, the Latin hypercube method is applied for sampling. The variables obtained from sampling are randomly combined, and 400 input datasets are obtained. We sequentially input the data into the model to obtain the outputs pollutant concentration data. Then, the dataset is divided into a training set (80 %) and a test set (20 %). The surrogate model is trained using the training set, and the test set verifies the model's performance. The mean squared error (MSE) was used as the loss function during model training. The MSE measures the average of the squared differences between the predicted and true values of the model, with smaller values indicating that the model fits the data better. Adjusting the depth, weight, and hyperparameters of the neural network structure can improve the approximation accuracy of the surrogate model to the simulation model. The surrogate model accuracy is evaluated using the determination coefficient (R  2   ), root mean square error (RMSE   ), and mean absolute error (MAE   ). The calculation formulas are as given:(12) R  2  = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y ^  i     2   ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y  ¯   i     2        (13) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y ^  i     2   n       (14) MAE = ∑ i = 1  n  | y i  - y ^  i  |   n      where n   is the number of samples, y i    and y ^  i    is the pollutant concentration outputs by the simulation model (M/L3 ) and surrogate model and y  ¯   i    is the average value of the simulation model outputs (M/L3 ). Larger values of R  2    and smaller values of RMSE    and MAE    indicate higher prediction accuracy of the surrogate model. After preprocessing the data, we determine the structure of ResNet. The ResNet model includes three residual blocks, leaky ReLU and GELU activation functions, batch normalization, and dropout layers, which can suppress overfitting. The numbers of neurons in the fully connected layer of the three residual blocks are 128, 128, 128, 128, 64, and 64, respectively. The specific residual network structure diagram is shown in Fig. 4  . In this study, we also employed a seven-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) to develop a surrogate model and compared its results with those obtained using ResNet. Through this comparison, we aim to gain the precision differences between two models in handling complex data. The training cost and accuracy of the surrogate models were compared and analyzed. The model's performance is shown in Table 2  . The training cost includes two parts, which are the time to obtain training and test data and the time to train surrogate model. The R2  of the ResNet surrogate model is 0.983, the RMSE is 36.483 mg/L, and the MAE is 20.695 mg/L. Table 2  shows that the ResNet surrogate model outperforms the MLP surrogate model in terms of approximation accuracy for simulation models. It is evident that the training time for the ResNet surrogate model is slightly longer than that of the MLP surrogate model. However, the significantly higher accuracy of the ResNet model makes this additional time investment worthwhile. Thus, the ResNet surrogate model has high accuracy and can be used as a substitute for the simulation model to complete subsequent iterative calculations.  3.3 IEPF method application The established IEPF method was applied to GPSC and compared with the general PF method to further verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. The state equation is expressed as follows:(15) E t + 1   = E t  + E t  ∗  R     where E t    is the position of the particle at time t  , R   means the search range of the particle in each search. The observation equation is expressed as follows:(16) y = S ( E t + 1   )     where S  is the ResNet surrogate model. The particle search process is performed by comparing the difference between the concentration at the current position and the observed concentration. The aim is to minimize the difference between the two. Therefore, the objective function of this study is expressed as follows:(17) m i n ∑ t = 1  5  ∑ m = 1  6  ( C m  t  ( t )  - C ^  m  t  ( 0 )  )  2        where t   and m   are the number of stress periods and the number of observation wells, respectively, C ^  m  t  ( 0 )     is the observed concentration (M/L3 ), and C m  t  ( t )     is the ResNet surrogate model outputs concentration for the m -th observation well at the i -th stress period (M/L3 ). The parameters of the IEPF method are given in Table 3   below. We started with a range of 200 to 1000 particles, an initial value range that performs well in many practical applications. Then we continuously adjusted the number of particles and observed the convergence of the algorithm with different numbers of particles. Therefore, the final particle counts for the case study were determined. The number of particles and iterations in the general PF method are the same as those in the IEPF method.  3.4 Identification results We determine the convergence of the algorithm by calculating the average deviation between the predicted value of each particle and the observed value. Specifically, at each iteration step, we record the concentration prediction value of all particles and compare them with the actual concentration monitoring data. We then calculate the mean of these deviations to serve as the error metric for the current iteration. When this mean deviation gradually decreases and stabilizes, we consider the algorithm to have converged. The convergence curve of the algorithm is shown in Fig. 5  . As the number of iterations increases, the loss curve stabilizes, suggesting that the algorithm converges. From the convergence curves of the algorithms, it is evident that the IEPF algorithm converges more rapidly during the initial iterations than the PF algorithm. Additionally, it achieves lower loss function values. At the end of the iteration, we take the weighted average of all particles as the final estimation result. To visualize the superiority of the IEPF algorithm, we provide relative error graphs for the PF and IEPF algorithms in Fig. 6  . The estimated results are shown in Table A2  in the attachment file. In the IEPF algorithm, the maximum relative error of the estimation results is 14.91 % and the average relative error is 6.66 %. In the PF algorithm, the maximum relative error of the estimation results is 43.71 %, and the average relative error is 16.44 %. Additionally, the computation time for a single run of the IEPF and PF algorithms are 106.52 s and 117.67 s, respectively. The results indicate that the IEPF method is more time-efficient and provides more accurate pollution source characterization, significantly improving computational efficiency. Fig. 6  shows that the IEPF algorithm has higher overall accuracy and smaller relative error in the estimation results. Additionally, we plotted the scatter plot of particles using the particle set from the final iteration of both algorithms (Fig. 7  ). In the plot, the size of each particle represents its weight, with larger and smaller particles indicating higher- and lower-weighted state estimates, respectively. Overall, the IEPF algorithm performs better in estimating variables than the PF algorithm.   4 Case study 2 4.1 Site overview The study area is characterized by a square shape, and the aquifer is generalized as a two-dimensional heterogeneous isotropic unconfined aquifer with steady flow. The state and observation equation are similar to the equation in Case study 1. The objective function of this study is expressed as follows:（18） m i n z ∑ j = 1  10  ∑ d = 1  5  ( C d  j  ( j )  - C ^  d  j  ( 0 )  )  2        where j   and d   are the number of stress periods and the number of observation wells, respectively, C ^  d  j  ( 0 )     is the observed concentration (M/L3 ), and C d  j  ( j )     is the ResNet surrogate model outputs concentration for the d -th observation well at the j -th stress period (M/L3 ). The parameters of the IEPF method are listed in Table 6  .  4.4 Identification results We calculated the mean absolute deviation between the observed values and the concentration predicted values of each particle to assess the algorithm's convergence (Fig. 9  ). As the number of iterations increases, the algorithm gradually converges. At the end of the iteration, we employ a weighted average of all particles to determine the final estimation. To visualize the IEPF algorithm's superiority, we plot relative error graphs for the PF and IEPF algorithms (Fig. 10  ), and the estimated results are presented in Table A4 . For a more comprehensive statistical analysis, the scatter plot of twelve variables based on the final iteration with 400 particles in both the PF and IEPF methods is included. Within the IEPF algorithm, the maximum relative error in the estimation results is 20.82 %, with an average relative error of 8.77 %. On the other hand, the PF algorithm exhibits a 38.42 % maximum relative error in the estimation results, coupled with a 17.5 % average relative error. Compared to the 6.66 % mean relative error in case 1, the mean relative error in case 2 is higher. This discrepancy might be attributed to the errors between the surrogate model and the simulation model. And the computation time for a single run of the IEPF and PF algorithms are 70.62 s and 69.03 s, respectively, with a negligible difference between the two. As a whole, the IEPF algorithm yields smaller relative errors in estimation results, indicating higher estimation accuracy. The weighted particle scatterplot for PF and IEPF methods is provided in Fig. 11  . Compared to case study 1 where 500 particles were set for estimating 14 unknown variables in the IEPF method, Case study 2 employed 400 particles to estimate 12 unknown variables. Consequently, the weight distribution was more uneven, resulting in a broader range of particle sizes (Fig. 11 ). Hence, the disparity in particle sizes was more pronounced.   5 Discussion The ResNet surrogate model performed well in Case study 1, achieving an R2  of 0.983 with an input variable dimension of 14. In Case study 2, with an input variable dimension of 12, the R2  was 0.954. This indicates that the accuracy of the surrogate model is not only related to the inputs-outputs dimensions but also significantly influenced by the types of unknown variables. The types of unknown variables in Case study 2 include pollution source characterization, model parameters, and boundary concentration. Typically, in previous GPSC studies, boundary conditions are assumed to be known variables. However, in many practical situations, boundary conditions are complex and cannot be accurately estimated in advance. The results of GPSC are influenced by multiple factors, including pollution source characterization, model parameters, boundary conditions, etc. Therefore, if the boundary conditions are inaccurately estimated, the characterization of other factors will also be inaccurate (Lauzon, 2024; Wang et al., 2024 ). This further demonstrates that the more types of unknown variables there are, the more complex the nonlinear relationships between inputs and outputs become. This complexity leads to errors between the simulation model outputs and the surrogate model outputs, resulting in errors between the true values of the unknown variables and the estimation results. In the future, researchers could explore integrating other surrogate models to improve approximation accuracy and reduce errors. Moreover, our study found that the location of observation wells significantly impacts accurate GPSC. The selection of observation well locations affects the quality and representativeness of monitoring data, which in turn affects the quality of the training data for the surrogate model. Future research will consider optimizing the design of monitoring wells in conjunction with GPSC to improve the accuracy of estimation results.  6 Conclusions In this study, we proposed an IEPF algorithm to address GPSC. The method effectively overcomes the limitations of the general PF algorithm with particle degeneration and loss of diversity. In addition, we employed a ResNet surrogate model to reduce the computational burden and time required for repeated calls to the simulation model. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, we set up various GPSC in two pollution scenarios. In case study 1, the unknown variables included pollution source characteristics and model parameters, while in case study 2, the unknown variables consisted of boundary concentration values, model parameters and pollution source characteristics. The conclusions are as follows:(1) The proposed IEPF algorithm offers more accurate GPSC than the general PF method. Mechanisms such as information transmission, crossover, and mutation operations effectively prevent particle diversity loss and enhance the algorithm’s global search capabilities. This scenario improves the search efficiency and accuracy of the algorithm in GPSC. By setting different types of GPSC in two scenarios, we demonstrated the significant advantages of the proposed algorithm over the general PF method.  (2) The ResNet surrogate model effectively captures the complex nonlinear mapping relationship between inputs and outputs of the simulation model. The ResNet model alleviates computational burdens and improves the approximation accuracy of the surrogate model to the simulation model. Coupling the ResNet surrogate model with the IEPF algorithm enhances the computational efficiency and accuracy of GPSC.    In the future, it may be worthwhile to consider applying the IEPF algorithm in more complex scenarios. More representative cases will also be explored in our future work. In addition, researchers may explore integrating other proxy models to enhance approximation accuracy and broaden the application scope of GPSC theory.
1 Introduction Pluvial flood hazards are escalating globally in urban areas due to intensified precipitation and runoff (Luo and Zhang, 2022; Mach et al., 2022 ). Recurrent flood occurrences have led to significant socioeconomic losses, hindering sustainable urban development and impacting the livelihoods of millions (Tellman et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, the frequency of flooding incidents is estimated to be further exacerbated by the combined impact of climate change and urbanization. It is essential to implement adaptive management measures for flood preparedness and mitigation to reduce the likelihood of flooding and facilitate recovery (Sanders et al., 2022 ). Identifying flood-prone areas for mitigation is an essential step in urban pluvial flood management and can be achieved through flood susceptibility mapping (Rahmati et al., 2020 ). Flood susceptibility describes an area’s flooding probability based on its physical characteristics, including climatic, terrain, and land-use conditions (Jacinto et al., 2015 ). These physical characteristics are represented by various flood conditioning factors such as rainfall pattern, elevation, slope, drainage density, and land use (Vojtek and Vojteková, 2019 ). Unlike flood risk, flood susceptibility focuses solely on an area’s flooding probability, without considering life or property losses (Dottori et al., 2018 ). Reliable flood susceptibility maps can effectively communicate location information to stakeholders and official agencies about sites with high flooding probability. These entities can then thoroughly analyze flood mechanisms at these locations to develop localized mitigation strategies. Conventional physically-based models can map flood susceptibility by simulating floodwater depths under different rainfall scenarios, but are typically restricted by their low computational speed and laborious construction processes. For efficiency, machine learning is increasingly used (Chen et al., 2020 ). Machine learning transforms flood susceptibility mapping into a flooded-nonflooded site classification task that require flood conditioning factors and flooded/nonflooded labels for training. The mapping relationship between inputs and their corresponding labels is automatically inferred through iterative optimization and then applied to other unlabeled sites to determine their probability of belonging to the flooded class, i.e., flood susceptibility (Zhao et al., 2019 ). To ensure the reliability of the flood susceptibility map and inform practical flood management, the machine learning model should, firstly, effectively fit the relationships between flood conditioning factors and flood susceptibility. Secondly, the model should also be capable of identifying key flood conditioning factors at historical and newly recognized flood-prone sites. Only by doing so can the accuracy and explainability of the results be guaranteed (Jones et al., 2023 ). However, current applications of machine learning models often prioritize fitting capability while neglecting the explainability (Rudin and Radin, 2019 ). Though machine learning models have already demonstrated accuracies exceeding 80 % across various spatial scales, their black-box essence hinders the local key flood conditioning factor identification (Bentivoglio et al., 2022 ). Aiming at systematic urban flood management, model explainability should be emphasized equally as their fitting capacity (Fu et al., 2022; Shin, 2021 ). The continuous development of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques makes it possible to unveil the black box of machine learning models (Lucas, 2020; Sudjianto and Zhang, 2021 ). Adopting inherently explainable models like logistic regression (LR) or random forest (RF) are one of the options (Giovannettone et al., 2018 ). These models quantify feature contributions based on their intrinsic structures. They rely on the internal parameters and hidden states to explicitly reflect the model’s input processing pattern. However, inherently explainable models are typically characterized by low structural complexity, which may potentially compromise fitting capability, making it challenging to adapt to highly heterogeneous urban environments (Petkovic et al., 2018 ). For example, LR, in particular, often performs poorest among different machine learning models in classifying flooded and nonflooded samples (Zhao et al., 2018 ). Additionally, inherent explanations are typically globally consistent. Therefore, the model can only provide a generalized analysis of flood formation mechanisms within the study area, rather than identify key flood conditioning factors for each site, contradicting the concept of adaptive flood management (Luo et al., 2023; Maragno et al., 2018 ). Model-agnostic methods constitute another XAI approach, which approximate complex machine learning models using simple, explainable models like linear regression (Ribeiro et al., 2016 ). They provide sample-specific (or so-called “local”) explanations and apply to various model structures without affecting the original model’s performance (Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ). Model-agnostic methods, such as Local Individual Model Evaluation (LIME) and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), have been frequently used to evaluate flood conditioning factor contribution by site in flood susceptibility mapping (Ekmekcioğlu et al., 2022; Seleem et al., 2022 ). However, model-agnostic methods are completely detached from the original simulation process. Their approximation of the original model’s behavior will necessitate additional computational resources. Moreover, model-agnostic methods rely solely on the original model predictions (Rudin, 2019 ). They may not undermine the original model’s performance, but they also cannot improve the model’s adaptability to heterogeneous urban environments. Consequently, the reliability of their explanations cannot be guaranteed if uncertainties already exist in the original predictions. Overall, machine learning methods that enable adaption to urban heterogeneous environments and robust local explainability still remain to be explored. To address the limitations of current machine learning models and XAI techniques, this study aims to synchronously enhance fitting capability and explainability. We proposed a novel inherently explainable machine learning model called Residual-Logistic Regression (RES-LR) for urban pluvial flood susceptibility mapping and key flood conditioning factor identification in each flood susceptible site. RES-LR follows the LR structure but incorporates neural networks as the explainability module, which outputs intermediate variables to replace LR’s globally consistent parameters. The explainability module generates weights for each flood conditioning factor at different sites. Residual connections then combine the flood conditioning factors and their corresponding weights for flood susceptibility calculation. Leveraging the residual structure, RES-LR’s fitting capability can be enhanced with increased structural complexity of the explainability module. Meanwhile, the model can flexibly generate flood conditioning factor weights according to local environment, facilitating an in-depth understanding of site-specific flood causes. We applied RES-LR in the Beijing Metropolitan Area and compared it with three conventional machine learning models: LR, RF, and artificial neural network (ANN) in terms of flooded-nonflooded sample classification, flood susceptibility mapping, and explainability. In addition, SHAP was adopted as the representative of model-agnostic methods and applied to all four models for comparison. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2  provides the descriptions of the study area and data for use; Section 3  demonstrates the method; Section 4  introduces the methodology; the detailed model results are presented in Section 5 . Section 6  further discusses the machine learning model’s fitting capability and explainability, as well as their values, and the conclusions are given in Section 7 .  2 Study area and data description 2.1 Study area description The Beijing Metropolitan Area was selected for research in this study. Beijing is located between 39°28′–41°05′N and 115°25′–117°30′E. The annual average precipitation of Beijing is approximately 580 mm, and 80 % of the precipitation occurs from June to September. The Beijing Metropolitan Area is located on the North China Plain and accommodates most population and critical infrastructures in Beijing, covering an area of 1085 km2  (Fig. 1  a). In the past, extreme rainfall events frequently occurred and resulted in various flood disasters in the Beijing Metropolitan Area (e.g., 30 July 1959, 8 August 1963, 5 July 1998, 23 July 2005, 13 June 2008, and 21 July 2012, 20 July 2016), causing severe life and property losses (Wang et al., 2021 ). Within this study area, the predominant local flood types include sewer overflows and waterlogging in depressions induced by pluvial floods.  2.2 Urban flood inventories The flood inventory data was acquired from the Beijing Water Authority’s official website (http://swj.beijing.gov.cn/ ). The inventory comprises 116 locations that have been consistently inundated during various rainfall events spanning from 2011 to 2021. These specific sites can be identified as the most susceptible areas to flooding within the study area and were selected as the flooded samples. Simultaneously, an equivalent number of sites were randomly chosen to constitute the nonflooded samples, based on the officially released Beijing flood inundation map, which was generated through the integration of simulations from various hydrodynamic and GIS-based models under typical extreme rainfall events. Specifically, we selected 116 locations as nonflooded samples with no simulated waterlogging observed in the map. Both the flooded and nonflooded samples were georeferenced onto a digital map using ArcGIS software, as depicted in Fig. 1 b. Each of these sites was converted into a 30 m × 30 m pixel and assigned a binary value of either 1 or 0 to denote flooded or nonflooded conditions, respectively. Subsequently, these sites were overlaid with their corresponding local flood conditioning factors and randomly partitioned to create the training, validation, and testing datasets. The distribution of sites within these three datasets was allocated as follows: 60 % for training, 20 % for validation, and another 20 % for testing.  2.3 Flood conditioning factor Flood conditioning factors depict the physical environment of a study area. The pluvial flood susceptibility in urban areas is generally related to four categories of flood conditioning factors: climatic, topographic, drainage and land use factors. As shown in Fig. 2  , eight flood conditioning factors were selected from the above four categories according to the characteristics of the highly-urbanized plain area. Referring to the review of previous studies in Beijing (Zhao et al., 2019, 2020, 2021 ), they are guaranteed the most relevant factors for flood susceptibility in the study area.A) Climatic factor    Precipitation is one of the driving factors of urban pluvial floods. Urban pluvial flood generally occurs when the rainfall intensity exceeds the capacity of urban drainage infrastructures. As the Beijing Metropolitan Area frequently experiences short-duration heavy rain, we selected the average of the annual maximum one-hour precipitation (PR) to represent the climatic condition.B) Topographic factor    The topographic factors used in this study includes elevation (EV), slope (SL), and topographic wetness index (TWI). The EV value was obtained directly from Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data. SL and TWI were computed based on EV. SL represents the maximum rate of change in EV value from a specific cell to its neighboring cells; As a commonly used index to quantify topographic influence on hydrological processes (Sörensen et al., 2006 ), TWI is a function of SL and the upstream contributing area per unit width orthogonal to the flow direction and is expressed as:(1) TWI = l n ( a tan b   )     where a   is the upslope area per unit contour length and tan b    is the local gradient in radians.C) Drainage factor    The drainage capacity significantly influences the extent of urban flooding within metropolitan areas. In urban settings, primary drainage pipes are typically constructed along roads and are extended towards water bodies. There is a well-established connection between the spatial distribution of urban surfaces and the capacity of drainage infrastructure, as noted in previous research (Chegini and Li, 2022 ). As a result, this study used factors related to roads and water bodies, which include road density (RD), distance to roads (DR), and distance to water bodies (DW), as proxy indicators for approximating drainage capacity. Road density (RD) was determined using the kernel density method, while the distances to roads (DR) and water bodies (DW) were computed based on the minimum Euclidean distance from each pixel to the nearest road or water body pixel.D) Land use factor    Various land uses present distinct hydrological processes, which result in differing susceptibility to flooding. This study used the annual average Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) (Guo et al., 2015 ) calculated from Landsat remote sensing images (2011–2021) to represent the impervious rate of the area so that the land use factor can be described.(2) NDBI = MIR - N I R  MIR + N I R       where MIR  and NIR  represent the middle infrared band and near infrared band of the Landsat images, respectively. The raw remote sensing images for use have already gone through atmospheric correction and were guaranteed to be not contaminated by cloud cover. All the raw flood conditioning factor data were projected onto a common coordinate system (WGS 1984 UTM 30N), resampled to 30 m × 30 m pixels, and normalized to a scale ranging from 0 to 1. Table 1   provides details regarding the data source, time period, and URL for accessing the flood conditioning factors.   3 Method 3.1 Logistic regression LR is a non-linear regression model for solving binary problems (Cox, 1958 ). It has been widely applied to flood susceptibility mapping with its ability to induce the dependency of the flooding occurrence on several variables (Zeng et al., 2020 ). Quantitatively, the relationship between the flooding occurrence and the flood conditioning factors can be expressed as:(3) p = 1 1 + e  - z         where p   represents the probability of the flooding occurrence, the probability varies from 0 to 1 on an S-shape curve, and z   is a linear combination that can be described as:(4) z = b + w 1  x 1  + w 1  x 1  + ⋯ + w n  x n      where b   represents the intercept of the model, x i    (i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )    denotes the flood conditioning factor, and w i    (i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )    denotes the corresponding weight of each factor. The training process of the LR model is equivalent to fitting an equation of the above form. The LR model is globally explainable with explicit expressions. The feature contribution can be quantitatively evaluated referring to its inner parameters that represent the weight of each flood conditioning factor, w i    (i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )   .  3.2 Artificial neural network ANN is a neuron-based machine learning model and comprised of input, hidden, and output layers. Each layer consists of at least one neuron, and the neurons in different layers are interconnected with some weights and run specific functions, namely activation functions that map the input to the output. During modeling, the underlying information in the dataset (flood conditioning factors) flows through multiple neurons from the model input to the output (flooding occurrence). The inner information flow forges the non-linear fitting capability, and enables the ANN to adapt to the complexity of the pluvial flood in urban areas (Zeng et al., 2020 ). The input to hidden layer and output layer is expressed as:(5) y i  = ∑ j = 1  N  w ji   x j  + b i 0       where N   is the total number of neurons in the former layer j  , x j    denotes the output from layer j  , w ji     represents the weight between layer j   and layer i  , and b i 0     is the added bias for fitting. y i    is the output of layer i  , and will then go through an activation function and be input to the next layer. The rectified linear unit (ReLU) was adopted as activation function, its expression is given as:(6) y i   ′  = m a x ( 0 ,   y i  )      where y i    and y i   ′    represent the original output and the activated output, respectively. The ANN used in this study was configured with two hidden layers. Model parameters were optimized through the back-propagation error-correction algorithm. The ANN is not inherently explainable and can only be explained using model-agnostic explainability methods, e.g., SHAP.  3.3 Random forest RF is an ensemble-learning technique that integrates multiple simple tree predictors for estimation (Breiman, 2001 ). In the context of flood susceptibility mapping, RF employs numerous decision trees to elucidate the spatial relationships between flooding occurrences and their associated flood conditioning factors. During the training phase, RF employs an iterative computational process to randomly select a subset of flood conditioning factors at each tree node, seeking the optimal split. All decision trees are grown to their maximum size without undergoing pruning. The final estimation is obtained by averaging the predictions generated by these trees. Aided by its ensemble-learning pattern, RF can be a potential method for analyzing complex and nonlinear hydrological interactions in urban pluvial flood scenarios (Lee et al., 2017 ). The explainability of RF lies in its inbuilt cross-validation by using out-of-bag (OOB) samples in parallel to the training process. During cross-validation, some training data are left out to constitute the OOB samples (Svetnik et al., 2003 ). The rest samples will remain for model training, while the OOB samples are used to test the model’s accuracy. The learning error is calculated by averaging the prediction error of each tree with their OOB samples (E OOB    ):(7) E OOB   = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  ( y i  - y i  ^  )      where n   is the total number of OOB samples; y i    denotes the observed output of OOB samples; y i  ^    is the output corresponding to the input factors for OOB. At the same time, each input variable in the OOB samples is permuted one at a time. These modified datasets are also predicted by the tree (termed E O O B 2    ). At the end of the training procedure, the feature importance is obtained through z-score standardization (Al Shalabi et al., 2006 ) on each factor’s difference between E O O B 1     and E O O B 2    .  3.4 Residual-Logistic regression model RES-LR is developed as an inherently explainable machine learning model. It aims to synchronously enhance fitting capability and explainability by integrating LR and ANN. LR enables explicit representation of the contribution of different flood conditioning factors through internal weight parameters, thus can be adopted as model framework (Yang and Wu, 2021 ). ANN, even when established on a single hidden layer containing a sufficient number of neurons, can approximate any continuous function with arbitrary precision (Cybenko, 1989 ). Accordingly, it is incorporated to ensure the model’s fitting capability. Specifically, RES-LR follows the LR structure and further introduces ANN as its explainability module for generating feature contribution scores as intermediate variables to replace LR’s original globally consistent parameter vector. With increasing structural complexity and explicit parameterization of the flood conditioning factor weight, the explainability module can aid in adapting to heterogeneous urban environments and identifying site-specific key flood conditioning factors. As illustrated in Fig. 3  , the flood conditioning factors (x 1  ,  x 2  , ⋯ ,  x  i   ) associated with each sample are transformed into a vector in i + 1    dimensions, which includes weights (w 1  ,  w 2  , ⋯ ,  w  i   ) and a bias term (b  ). This transformation is achieved using an ANN with a single hidden layer comprising j  neurons. The inclusion of neural networks for explainability offers increased flexibility in handling diverse inputs, potentially enhancing the model’s fitting capacity. Subsequently, with the addition of residual connections, the original flood conditioning factor input bypass the neural network and is subject to multiplication by the weights. The product is then combined with the bias, b  . Finally, a sigmoid function is applied to map the weighted sum to the numeric interval of 0–1, resulting in the flood susceptibility prediction. Classification as either a flooded or non-flooded site was determined by comparing the flood susceptibility with a specific threshold (in this case, 0.5). The above-mentioned weighted summation and activation function mapping process in the RES-LR model are consistent with the integration of flood conditioning factors and their corresponding weights by LR. In contrast to the traditional LR, the incorporation of distinct flood conditioning factor value distributions into the explainability module of RES-LR yields a diverse set of feature weights. Such characteristics facilitate the generation of site-specific explanations rather than providing a uniform explanation across the entire study area. The weight, w  , can be used to explicitly assess the contribution of each flood conditioning factor for each site. Therefore, local explainability can be achieved.  3.5 Shapely additive explanations method Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) was introduced as a representative model-agnostic explainability methods and applied to all four aforementioned machine learning models for comparison. SHAP is a game theoretic approach that explains the model prediction of an instance by computing the contribution of each feature to the prediction (Wang et al., 2024 ). SHAP connects optimal credit allocation with local explanations using the classic Shapley values from coalition game theory. The feature values of a data instance act as players in a coalition. Shapley values guide how to fairly distribute the “payout” (in our study, the probability of a site being flooded or nonflooded class), among the features. SHAP specifies the explanation as:(8) g z  ′    = ϕ 0  + ∑ j = 1  M  ϕ j  z  ′   j      Where g ( Â · )    is the simple explanation model (e.g., linear regression), z  ′  ∈ { 0 , 1 }  M     is the coalition vector, M   is the maximum coalition size and ϕ j    is the feature attribution for a feature j  , i.e., the Shapely values. Shapely values are equivalent to the importance of flood conditioning factors. Combined with the numeric distribution of the flood conditioning factor, SHAP can provide valuable insights into the positivity-negativity relationship between flooding occurrence and the factor (Arslan et al., 2022 ). Specifically, if the positive–negative distribution of the SHAP value aligns with the low–high trend of the flood conditioning factor value, it can be concluded that the factor has a positive effect on flooding occurrence, and vice versa. In cases where the trends of the two numeric distributions are not entirely consistent or are opposite, it indicates a non-monotonic influence of the factor on model estimation.   4 Methodology 4.1 Model training and evaluation In the case study, RES-LR and its comparison models, including LR, ANN, and RF, will be trained, validated, and tested based on the urban flood inventory constructed in Section 2.2 . All four models will use flood conditioning factors as inputs to output flood susceptibility maps and provide classifications of flooded/non-flooded sites. Meanwhile, LR and RF, due to their inherent explainability, will offer global flood conditioning factor weights. The RES-LR model, with its local explainability, will provide site-specific flood conditioning factor weights for detailed analysis. Additionally, SHAP will be applied to all models to obtain explanations by site for comparison. The workflow of the proposed methodology is illustrated in Fig. 4  . Hyperparameters were configured specifically for each model to guarantee its optimal prediction performances. The hyperparameter optimization was performed based on Optuna  framework using Bayesian mode sampler (Akiba et al., 2019 ). During the optimization, the training dataset was used for model training, while the model performances on validation dataset was used to supervise the optimization process. In the case of LR, no hyperparameter related to the model structure requires for setup. Based on the hyperparameter optimization results of the Bayesian model sampler, for ANN, the neuron numbers of its two hidden layers were set as 32 and 9, respectively, and the neuron number of the neural network-based module’s single hidden layer for RES-LR was set as 32. Four hyperparameters of RF including the number of estimators, minimum sample split, minimum sample leaf, and maximum depth of RF were optimized to 748, 2, 7, and 19 (Table 2  ). In model training phase, for all the four models, the maximum epochs of training were set as 1000. The learning rate for training LR, ANN, and RES-LR was 0.01. The model with the minor error on the validation dataset among all the training epochs was used for subsequent evaluation and analysis. Both the development of machine learning models and the implementation of Optuna  framework were coded in Python , executed on an Intel® Core™ i5 CPU  configuration.  4.2 Evaluation methods Four indicators, including accuracy (ACC ), precision (P ), recall (R ), and F-score (F ) were introduced to assess model’s flooded-nonflooded sample classification ability:(9) ACC = TP + T N  TP + F P + T N + F N       (10) P = TP  TP + F P       (11) R = TP  TP + F N       (12) F = 2 × P × R  P + R       where TP    is the true positive rate representing the proportion of sample that are actually flooded and judged as flooded, while TN    is the true negative rate representing the proportion of samples that are actually flooded but are judged as nonflooded. Similarly, FP    and FN    denote the false positive rate and false negative rate, respectively. The threshold value of flood susceptibility for determining whether a sample is assigned to the flooded or nonflooded class was set as 0.5. Besides the above four indicators, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and areas under the curve (AUC   ) were also used for evaluating model performance. The ROC curve is depicted by the true positive (TP   ) rate on the Y-axis and the false positive (FP   ) rate on the X-axis. The AUC    value is equivalent to the probability that a randomly chosen positive example is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative example. Determined by the properties of the ROC curve, the AUC    value ranges from 0.5 to 1, and a higher AUC    value indicates better model performance in the flooded-nonflooded sample classification task.   5 Results 5.1 Model evaluation The results of classifying flooded and nonflooded samples using RES-LR and the comparison models are summarized in Table 3  . RES-LR exhibited superior performance compared to LR and ANN across all evaluation metrics in the training, validation, and testing datasets. Although RF displayed higher precision in the training and validation datasets, RES-LR consistently outperformed RF in the testing dataset across all evaluation metrics. These findings indicate that RES-LR demonstrates a stronger fitting capability compared to LR and ANN. Furthermore, in comparison to RF, RES-LR demonstrated a more modest decline in performance from the training dataset to the testing dataset, thus avoiding overfitting phenomenon, which highlights its robustness and generalization capability. The ROC curves and AUC values for the four models led to a similar conclusion (Fig. 5  ). In the training dataset, the AUC value for RES-LR (0.90) exceeded that of LR (0.77) and ANN (0.87). Although RF achieved the highest AUC values in both the training and validation datasets (0.96, 0.80), RES-LR demonstrated superior performance among all the models in the testing dataset, with an AUC value of 0.82. Referring to the aforementioned results, RES-LR can be identified as the optimal model for the flooded-nonflooded sample classification task, outperforming LR, ANN, and RF. Particularly noteworthy were the substantial advantages of RES-LR over LR, indicating that incorporating the neural networks for generating site-specific feature importance significantly improved the model’s fitting capability.  5.2 Flood susceptibility map comparison For clearer characterization of flood hazard spatial patterns, the flood susceptibility maps of RES-LR and the comparison models were all classified into low, high, and very high areas, using threshold values of 0.5 and 0.75, respectively. As shown in Fig. 6  , the flood susceptibility maps derived from the four models presented different spatial patterns. Urban pluvial flood is typically dispersedly distributed at the city scale, and the terrain and drainage environment determines the local inundation extent (Van Dijk et al., 2014 ). According to the official Beijing flood inundation map, the disperse pattern also applies to the Beijing Metropolitan Area (http://swj.beijing.gov.cn/swdt/tzgg/ ). RES-LR and ANN provided flood susceptibility maps that more conformed to the dispersion of the urban pluvial flood (Fig. 6 b and d). In less urbanized peripheral areas of the Beijing Metropolitan Area, very high flood susceptibility sites aggregated into sparsely distributed clusters. These clusters were located in low-lying areas with insufficient drainage capacity, rendering them more prone to flooding. In the center of the study area, the intense urbanization has caused high rainfall intensity and low infiltration. Flooded sites exist in this area, and were generally small and scattered around the depression landscape. The local environments could not cope with extreme rainfall events though configured with relatively dense drainage networks. However, there were also differences between the maps generated by the two models. Specifically, the high flood susceptible areas identified by RES-LR displayed a more discrete pattern, whereas the ANN model tended to overestimate the flood susceptibility in the central region of the study area, particularly leading to clusters in proximity to roads. The outputs of the other two models, LR and RF, exhibited deviations from the typical spatial pattern of urban pluvial flooding. Referring to Fig. 6 a, LR has classified over 50 % of the study area as high or very high flood susceptible regions. Notably, a majority of these very high flood susceptibility areas were observed to cluster into several large-scale agglomerations, rather than being distributed discretely in space. On the other hand, in terms of RF’s results, most of the identified high and very high flood susceptibility areas were concentrated along roads (Fig. 6 c), which implies that RF tended to overestimate flood susceptibility in relation to road networks. The overestimation exhibited by RF is further highlighted by the following statistics related to the number of clustered patches and individual patches, as illustrated in Fig. 7  . Clustered patches refer to groups of adjacent very high flood-susceptible sites, and can be categorized into two groups: individual patches (comprising only one site) and clustered patches (comprising more than one site). For LR, ANN, and RES-LR, the count of clustered patches exceeded that of individual patches. However, the comparison relationship was reversed when using RF, which resulted in 3773 clustered patches and 3483 individual patches. Furthermore, RF displayed the lowest counts of both individual and clustered patches compared to all other models. It is worth noting that a substantial portion of the clusters of flood-susceptible sites identified by RF were connected, and aligned with the road network. This observation suggests an undue reliance of RF on road-related inputs. In summary, RES-LR emerged as the more robust model, consistently outperforming the other three models in terms of the rationality of the spatial pattern exhibited in the flood susceptibility map.  5.3 Model explainability 5.3.1 Global explanations We firstly compared RES-LR’s explanations with those of the other two inherently explainable machine learning models, LR and RF. RES-LR is able to quantify the contribution of each feature to flooding occurrence on a site-specific basis. In contrast, LR and RF can only yield globally uniform feature contribution results for the entire study area. To perform this comparison, we computed the average of the site-specific explanations provided by RES-LR for each flood conditioning factor and juxtaposed it with the global explanations generated by LR and RF. As depicted in Fig. 8  , factors related to drainage capacity and land use were identified as crucial features by all three models. Specifically, for RES-LR and RF, DR exhibited the highest importance, whereas NDBI was identified as the top-contributing feature by LR. Both LR and RF attributed the least significance to the climatic factor, PR, while PR ranked as the second most important feature for RES-LR. Regarding the topographic factors, EV was considered relatively important, whereas SL was seen as unimportant by all models. However, the models displayed conflicting results when it came to TWI. LR and RES-LR assigned similar or even higher absolute coefficient values to TWI compared to climatic and drainage capacity factors, while RF exhibited weak attention towards TWI. Overall, the models agreed on the importance of drainage capacity- and land use-related factors but displayed variations in their assessments of climatic and topographic factors. The explainability provided by RES-LR and LR allows us to further comprehend the positive or negative impacts of flood conditioning factors on flood susceptibility. Upon comparing the factor positivity or negativity, both models showed consistency in their assessments across different sites, except for RD. LR considered RD as a negative factor, whereas RES-LR indicated that flood susceptibility decreases with higher RD. Overall, RES-LR’s integration of different factors for flood susceptibility calculation conformed to the conventional understanding of urban pluvial flood mechanisms. The increase in PR and NDBI was found to enhance flood susceptibility, consistent with previous findings that higher precipitation and urbanization contribute positively to floods in urban areas (Song et al., 2019 ). Additionally, low elevation and slope or high TWI were associated with increased flood susceptibility, which is in line with prior knowledge regarding the influence of topography on surface hydrological processes (Pourali et al., 2016 ).  5.3.2 Site-specific explanations RES-LR possesses local explainability, enabling the quantification of the contributions of flood conditioning factors at each site, thereby revealing local flood causality. The local explainability serves as the basis for the RES-LR model to support the formulation of localized flood mitigation measures. Fig. 9  (a) demonstrates that RES-LR’s decision-making process exhibited a high degree of consistency across various factors and locations. The directionality (i.e., whether positive or negative) of the climatic, topographic, and land use factors remained unchanged across most sites. This consistency also extended to the factor DR. Nonetheless, the other two drainage factors, namely RD and DW, displayed varying positive or negative associations with the probability of being flooded depending on the specific site. These fluctuations can be attributed to the dual impact of these factors on flood susceptibility. In the study area, the central zone, characterized by an extensive drainage network, exhibited a higher density of manholes compared to other regions, thereby increasing the likelihood of overflow flooding events per unit area. Conversely, a higher drainage network density also improved local drainage capacity, consequently reducing flood susceptibility. Hence, the influence of RD on flood susceptibility is intricate and varies among different sites. Similarly, closer proximity to a water body may imply a shorter distance to the drainage outlet, but it could also result in potentially higher hydraulic stress downstream. These dual effects underscore the model’s adaptability and explainability across various sites. The RES-LR model excels in capturing the complex interactions among different factors at specific locations, offering site-specific insights into flood mechanisms. Fig. 9 (b) offers additional insights into the rank of feature contribution among the labeled sites. Within the study area, there were disparities in the rankings of absolute coefficient values across different sites. DR and RD emerged as the most pivotal factors, whereas SL exhibited the least significance among all the factors. The rankings of PR, EV, TWI, and NDBI displayed a broader range of variation, underscoring the imperative need for implementing a diverse array of flood preparation and mitigation measures tailored to the specific characteristics of each site within the study area. The fluctuating rank of these factors implies that one-fits-all approaches may not be efficacious in addressing flood susceptibility comprehensively. Instead, a site-specific approach that takes into account the unique combinations of influencing factors at each location would be more appropriate for formulating targeted flood management strategies. To gain a comprehensive understanding of the flood formation mechanism in the Beijing Metropolitan Area, we further visualized the spatial distribution of the dominant flood conditioning factor (the highest absolute coefficient value) among all sites with “high” or “very high” flood susceptibility levels. Fig. 10   illustrates that drainage-related features were identified as the most influential factors, with DR and DW being dominant in 57 % and 21 % of the study area, respectively. These sites tended to form clusters along the road network. Sites where flood formations were mainly dominated by TWI ranked third in terms of coverage, accounting for 14 % of the study area, but were sparsely distributed. Additionally, regions dominated by other terrain-related factors, such as SL and the land use factor NDBI, accounted for a lower proportion (4 %) than the aforementioned three variables. Areas dominated by EV and PR factors were extremely rare, making up less than 1 %. The spatial heterogeneity of dominant flood conditioning factors indicates the diverse formation mechanism underlying pluvial floods in the Beijing Metropolitan Area. Tailored local flood management measures are necessary at different sites based on the dominant factors. Meanwhile, the high proportion of dominant factors related to drainage capacity and terrain highlights the importance of optimizing drainage networks distribution and enhancing drainage capacity in conjunction with local topography. This should be the primary technical approach for reducing the probability of pluvial flooding occurrence and mitigating flood hazards in the Beijing Metropolitan Area.  5.3.3 Model-agnostic explanations SHAP was applied to all the four machine learning models. Fig. 10  illustrates that the SHAP values aligned with our previous analyses of flooded-nonflooded sample classification, flood susceptibility maps, and explanations. Specifically, the SHAP values confirmed our previous observations regarding RF’s overdependence on road data and ANN’s overestimation in central areas.
