(15) , which is more calibration-friendly for large-scale applications.(15) A D F = a × P sum   + A P I     m      where a is the parameter should be calibrated; P sum      is the total rainfall (mm); API is the antecedent precipitation index as in section 2.3.1; m is the total duration of the rainfall process as in Eq. (7) . Then, the corrected runoff can be estimated by adding the ADF to the initial runoff. This ensures the simplicity of the model parameters and reduces the systematic error to achieve better simulation results. The Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009 ) of simulated streamflow against observed streamflow was taken as the objective function and calculated as in Eq. (16) . The search ranges are custom-defined to exhaustively search for the optimal parameter.(16) K G E = 1 - r - 1    2  + σ s  σ o   - 1    2  + μ s  μ o   - 1    2        where r is the correlation coefficient between observations and simulations; σ s     and σ o     are the standard deviation values for the S i     and O i    ; μ s     and μ o     refer to the mean of the simulations and observations, respectively. To evaluate the agreement between simulated and observed streamflow time series, three metrics are employed: the KGE, percent bias (Pbias, %), and the correlation coefficient (R). Additionally, the probability of detection (POD) is used to assess the flash flood detection capability and normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE, %) is applied to the performance of peak flow simulations for a set of events. Pbias, NRMSE, and POD were calculated as in Equations (17)-(19):(17) Pbias = ∑ t = 1  T  O t  - S  t   ∑ t = 1  T  O t    × 100     (18) NRMSE = 1 T  ∑ t = 1  T  ( S t  - O t  )  2    O max   - O  min    × 100     Where S i     and O i     refer to the simulated and observed discharge at time t, respectively. O max      and O min      refer to maximum and minimum observations, respectively.(19) POD = Nhit  Nhit + N m i s s   × 100 %     where Nhit    is the number of events that are recognized as flash flood events by both simulation and observation; Nmiss    is the number of events that are observed to be flooding but not detected by the proposed method.  2.6 Storm rain selection We adopt the flash flood database published by Gourley et al. (2013)  derived from USGS stream gauge observations, to select flash flood events for evaluating the performance of the proposed TS-DUH method. The algorithm proposed by Tang and Carey (2017)  is used to identify rainfall-streamflow events from continuous time series data. In addition, we assume that the catchment routing time map is calculated accurately, and the catchment’s mean runoff process derived from phi(φ )   -index method (Chow et al., 1988; Chin, 2018 ) is used as the reference. The φ    index parameter is inferred from the observed surface streamflow and rainfall process by the trial-and-error method. Events exhibiting a KGE value greater than 0.4 for the hydrograph simulating from the convolution of the SDUH model and the mean runoff process are chosen to reduce the uncertainty of the precipitation data on the model evaluation findings. Further filtering criteria are implemented, including the requirement for continuous observations over time, the exclusion of likely human-intervened events with abrupt shifts in discharge series, and the cases where precipitation peaks substantially lagged behind observed streamflow peaks, or the cumulative precipitation was significantly lower than the total streamflow with less antecedent rainfall. All flood events that are likely not caused by rain are excluded, as we only focus on rain related flash floods in this study.   3 Study area and data In this study, we test the TS-DUH model in small to medium-sized catchments (i.e., upstream drainage area ranging from 100 to 3000 km2 ) widely distributed across CONUS with various hydroclimatic and topographic characteristics. In order to evaluate the performance of event-based flash floods, we carefully selected 6,324 flash flood events (1985–2016) from 281 United States Geological Survey (USGS) streamflow gauges for this study following the criteria: 1) each gauge has at least 2 years of hourly observed flow data; 2) the difference between the hydrologic model-derived catchment area and the USGS-reported area is within 10 % (Wu et al., 2011; Alfieri et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014 ); 3) no large impoundments exist in the upstream area to prolong cumulative routing time; 4) the observed flow events are matched with corresponding precipitation data; 5) at least 9 flash flood events recorded at each gauge. Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System NLDAS-2 (Xia et al., 2012 ) is utilized as rainfall input. We randomly selected 6 events for calibration for each gauge. The spatial distribution of the selected gauges is shown in Fig. 4   with a triangle marker. For the second scenario assessment, long-term hydrological simulation (2003–2020), we selected 803 stations based on the first three selection criteria described above and used runoff matched with the GFMS system to determine TS-DUH. The state-of-the-art IMERG-Early precipitation estimates (V06) from Integrated Multi-Satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Mission (IMERG) (Huffman et al., 2015; Huffman et al., 2020 ) is utilized as rainfall input. The spatial distribution of the selected gauges is shown in Fig. 4  with a circle marker. We use the DEM, upstream catchment area, and flow direction data at 90 m spatial resolution from the MERIT Hydro dataset (Yamazaki et al., 2019 ) and the 30 m resolution land cover data of 2019 from the National Land Cover Database (Dewitz and Geological Survey, 2021 ). The CN values to derive SCS-CN runoff are obtained from the published global dataset by Jaafar et al. (2019) , which was generated using three main data sources: a land use/land cover map, a hydrologic soil group map, and CN look-up tables created based on the USDA Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Runoff Curve Number (CN) method. In order to assess the flash flood detection capability, we adopt the action stage proposed by Gourley et al. (2013)  as the discharge threshold for identifying flash flood events. The DRIVE model is set to run at 1/8 degree resolution consistent with the GFMS routine runs, and the TS-DUH model is unified at 90 m resolution.  4 Results 4.1 The TS-DUH approach with the NLDAS-2 precipitation and hydrologically modeled runoff Assuming the NLDAS-2 precipitation product represent the “truth” over the study domains, the hydrographs determined by TS-DUH with CN-Runoff and DRIVE-Runoff as inputs (hereafter referred to as CN-TS-DUH and DRIVE-TS-DUH respectively) are carefully evaluated to justify the proposed TS-DUH approach, according to the observed flash flood events and hydrographs. According to the compiled flash flood events (Gourley et al., 2013 ), the POD for CN-TS-DUH and DRIVE-TS-DUH in the validation period is 0.88 and 0.91, respectively, showing an overall very good performance of both runoff-driven models, with slightly better performance value from the usage of DRIVE-Runoff for flash flood event identification. The simulated streamflow at the catchment outlet is evaluated against observed data using three skill metrics: KGE, R, and Pbias at the hourly scale. The detailed assessment results for all events in the calibration and validation periods of CN-TS-DUH and DRIVE-TS-DUH are visualized in Fig. 5  . According to statistical results, the CN-TS-DUH and DRIVE-TS-DUH models exhibit median KGE of 0.57, 0.64, median R of 0.85, 0.85, and median Pbias of 14.0, 11.3, respectively in the calibration period. The performance decreases slightly in the validation period, with median KGE of 0.49 and 0.59, R of 0.85 and 0.85, and Pbias of 14.0 and 11.5, respectively (Fig. 6  a1, b1, c1). CN-Runoff and DRIVE-Runoff lead to 90.7 % and 98.3 % of events with KGE > 0, and 60.7 % and 80.1 % of events with KGE > 0.4 in the validation period, respectively (Table 1  ). More than 98 % of events have a KGE > −0.41, which is comparable to an NSE > 0 (Knoben et al., 2019 ). These results show that CN-TS-DUH derives good performance in reproducing the observed flash flood hydrographs, while DRIVE-TS-DUH shows significantly better performance which is very encouraging for its global scale application with different precipitation inputs.  4.2 The performance of TS-DUH with satellite precipitation driven GFMS runoff without calibration A further step of the evaluation is focused on the application potential of the TS-DUH method in widespread un-gauged headwaters with satellite precipitation as near real-time inputs for the GFMS system to provide timely flash flood monitoring. This has been done by coupling TS-DUH with the GFMS system and comparing its performance in flash flood forecasting with the original GFMS. The runoff from the online GFMS output calculated using the near real-time IMERG-Early precipitation (at 3-hourly and 0.125° resolution) as the DRIVE inputs is taken to determine the TS-DUH. The streamflow simulated by TS-DUH with the GFMS runoff output (referred to as TS-DUH-Q) and the streamflow directly from the online GFMS (referred to as GFMS-Q) are evaluated against the observed data from the 803 USGS stream gauges (Fig. 4 ). The selected gauges are well located in the DRT derived river network at 1/8 degree resolution based on the aforementioned criteria (as in Section 3 ) and they are widely distributed in various hydroclimatic regions. The spatial distributions of the 3-hourly skill metrics for GFMS-Q and TS-DUH-Q without any calibration from 2003 to 2020 at the 803 gauges are displayed in Fig. 7  , indicating a better performance by TS-DUH-Q than GFMS-Q. The statistical analysis shows that TS-DUH-Q resulted in positive KGE values for 57.3 % of the gauges, with a mean positive KGE of 0.25, while the original GFMS (i.e., GFMS-Q) resulted in positive KGE values for 43.6 % of the gauges, with a mean positive KGE of 0.2 (Table 2  ). The median KGE of TS-DUH-Q is 0.07, while the original GFMS shows a negative median KGE metric (i.e., −0.08). The results, as shown in Figs. 7-8   and Table 2 , indicate that the TS-DUH integrated with GFMS can significantly improve the flash flood modeling and prediction capability of the GFMS. Note that the GFMS is running without the model calibration (a global calibration effort is on-going, which is expected to make further improvements). Given the GFMS global coverage, the evaluation indicates a great potential of flash flood prediction in un-gauged catchments across the globe by integrating the TS-DUH with GFMS in a real-time mode.  4.3 The performance of TS-DUH with calibrated satellite precipitation driven GFMS runoff As the TS-DUH is designed to be easy to calibrate for large-scale application, we further conduct the calibration of the GFMS-Runoff for this study with the calibration period set to 2014–2017 and the validation period set to 2018–2020 to further improve the TS-DUH performance. The results of the original GFMS-Q, TS-DUH-Q before calibration, and TS-DUH-Q after calibration are displayed in Fig. 9   (calibration period) and Fig. 10   (validation period). With calibration, the performance of the TS-DUH integrated GFMS can be further improved with 76.3 % of the gauges deriving positive KGE, with the overall median KGE value of 0.21. The over- and under-estimation in the GFMS-Q results are improved significantly as well (Table2 ). The change in R is not substantial indicating the improvements are mainly in the magnitudes while the temporal variations of precipitation input are consistent in both cases. The validation period results show only slight deterioration compared to the calibration period results with discernible improvements (Fig. 10 ) and 64.6 % of the gauges show positive KGE, with the overall median KGE value of 0.11. It is noteworthy that both the original GFMS-Q results and the TS-DUH-Q results demonstrate better performance in the humid regions of the CONUS than in arid areas, as indicated by both KGE and R values.  4.4 Case study We randomly selected four gauges to demonstrate the distinction between the calibrated TS-DUH-GFMS and the original GFMS in simulating flash flood events peak flow from 2014 to 2020 (Fig. 11  ). The drainage areas of the four gauges G1, G2, G3 and G4 are 2797.9 km2 , 2415.0 km2 ,1268.5 km2  and 1207.4 km2 , respectively. Hydrograph simulations in 2016 for gauge G3 and G4 are illustrated in Fig. 12  . Peak flows for G4 exhibit a considerable overestimation in the raw GFMS simulations, while G1, G2 and G3 exhibit a significant underestimation. The calibration of TS-DUH-GFMS at the four catchments shows significantly improved model performance adjusting the simulated flood peak toward the observations with a reduced NRMSE. However, an issue arises after the calibration of TS-DUH, where there is a significant increase in the overestimation of small peaks (Fig. 12 a). We suggest the possible reason is that the introduced parameter ADF focuses on the overall average of runoff, but fails to address the uncertainties within individual rainfall events. Despite this limitation, the ADF presents a promising solution by facilitating the low computational cost adjustment of runoff intensity, offering significant potential for global application. Moreover, regionalization of the calibrated parameters will be considered in the future for hydro-climatologically similar regions in un-gauged catchments.   5 Discussion and conclusions This study developed a Time-Space varying Distributed Unit Hydrograph (TS-DUH) to integrate the distributed hydrological model DRIVE for flash flood forecasting in large domains. We compared TS-DUH driven by two different, widely used excess rainfall methods to simulate runoff hydrographs, one estimated using the SCS-CN method (CN-Runoff) and the other based on the GFMS system (GFMS-Runoff) (with the DRIVE distributed hydrological model as its core). Overall, t he main results of the performance evaluation of TS-DUH in this study are as follows:(1) With the high-quality NLDAS-2 precipitation, both the SCS-CN method and DRIVE-Runoff driven TS-DUH perform satisfactorily in simulating the streamflow and flash flood event detection, while the DRIVE-Runoff driven TS-DUH can perform even better, i.e., 98.3 % and 80.1 % of the events have KGE values greater than 0 and 0.4, respectively, and a median KGE value of 0.59 and a probability of detection (POD) of 0.91.  (2) The long-term real-time GFMS driven TS-DUH shows better performance than the original GFMS, indicating that the hybrid approach has a great potential for un-gauged area flash flood monitoring and forecasting.    High-resolution hydrological and hydrodynamic models are effective at small scales but not efficient for large-scale flash flood forecasting. The TS-DUH model, a compromise between PDHM and RCM, is designed to be data and computing efficient, describing high-resolution characteristics of catchments and can be integrated with public GFMS-runoff data. To avoid the complexity of multi-parameter calibration processes, TS-DUH employs a single parameter, ADF, for calibration, which significantly enhances model performance and the model’s usability in large-scale applications. Compared to other unit hydrograph models (Melesse and Graham, 2004; Gironas et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2012b ), the TS-DUH integrated with DRIVE has the advantage of adapting to spatiotemporal variations in rainfall and soil moisture. The TS-DUH also emphasizes that the accuracy of runoff and dynamic soil moisture changes should not be overlooked in dynamic UH models (Du et al., 2009; Cho et al., 2018; Yi et al., 2022 ), as described by the better performance of DRIVE-TS-DUH than CN-TS-DUH. A comparison of the TS-DUH integrated with GFMS and the original GFMS in flash flood prediction is performed at 803 stations over the CONUS, to investigate the capability of the TS-DUH method with satellite precipitation inputs for large-scale application. The results show that the uncalibrated TS-DUH-GFMS already performs more efficiently than the original GFMS, with a median KGE improvement of 0.15. Our calibration efforts further improve the performance of TS-DUH by increasing the median KGE of GFMS from −0.19 to 0.21 with 76.3 % of gauges having positive KGE scores in the calibration period (2014–2017). Overall, the proposed TS-DUH demonstrates significant improvement in flash flood prediction with great flexibility in combining with distributed hydrological model, e.g., the DRIVE model of this study, which shows the promising global scale application through the widely used GFMS. The uncertainties of TS-DUH simulation arise from precipitation inputs, catchment subsurface feature extraction, and the structure and parameter estimation of the DRIVE model. The introduction of the parameter ADF helps to mitigate the inherent uncertainties in both the model and its inputs, including additional corrections of the catchment feature extraction and precipitation/runoff errors. Additionally, the model tends to work better in humid regions than arid regions, which likely due to the larger relative inaccuracies in precipitation forcing and modeling, as presented in previous studies, e.g., the IMERG product exhibits significant bias in dry climates and complex terrains (Pradhan et al., 2022 ). One would note that the coarse spatial resolutions of the precipitation data and the DRIVE model leads to a major challenge for the proposed TS-DUH to sufficiently describe the spatial variability of precipitation and runoff within small catchments. The TS-DUH model introduces a linear reservoir component to consider the storage diffusion effect to reduce, to some extent, the coarse resolution impacts on the hydrograph derivation. This warrants our next study to test TS-DUH with high-resolution radar precipitation which is expected to be able to provide further improved performance of upstream flash flood prediction in the GHS-F system for large to local scale applications (Wu et al., 2021 ).
1 Introduction Typically, hysteresis in hydrology is observed and studied at an event scale, such as rainfall-runoff or storage-discharge for one storm or across a single year (Ali et al., 2015 ). However, landscape hydrologic memory of antecedent conditions in some systems can form multi-year climate memory and hysteresis loops otherwise known as long‐range dependence, long‐term persistence, or the ‘Hurst’ phenomenon (Hurst, 1951 ). Understanding this long-term hydrologic memory, hereafter termed memory, is important due to the impact on the timing, magnitude and clustering of extreme events (Khanal et al., 2019; Bunde et al., 2005 ), and the increase in the uncertainty of related hydrological processes (Koutsoyiannis, 2005 ). Lakes can act as important storage bodies in the landscape and are indicative of the landscape response (hysteresis, non-linear, threshold) to meteorological cycles observed in specific climates. Lakes thus act as important test beds to examine core conceptualisations of hydrological memory that operate at a catchment scale over multi-annual to decadal time periods. Antecedent storage in lakes also represents an important regulator of catchment connectivity and thus also drives further non-linearity and hysteresis of the hydrological system (Spence, 2010 ). Geology impacts landscape memory by determining water storage and transmission capacities (Winter, 2001; Hokanson et al., 2019; Devito et al., 2023 ). The filling of depression storage (fill and spill) is a widely applied concept and form of memory in both the humid Boreal Shield and the semi-arid Prairie Pothole Regions. Within the Prairie Pothole Region this depression storage produces multi-year memory reflecting the balance of P to PET within isolated basins (Shook and Pomeroy 2011 ), whereas storage-driven seasonal responses in the Precambrian Shield bedrock lakes (Spence et al., 2019 ) are associated with variable connectivity processes such as gatekeeper lakes (Phillips et al., 2011 ). In contrast, water tables in coarse outwash lakes are driven by a range in local to large scale groundwater flows (Smerdon et al.,2005; Hokanson, et al., 2021a ), whereby memory is associated with lag, an autoregressive delay in response water level to climate, due to transit time through a catchment. While numerous studies have examined hysteresis responses in lakes, ponds and wetland water levels to climate (e.g. Hayashi et al., 2016; LaBaugh et al., 2018 ) or the influence of hydrogeological setting (Winter, 2001 ), few studies have attempted to characterise hysteresis characteristics (i.e. loop direction, shape, size) and their associated hydrological processes to assess the role of multi-annual memory across diverse hydrogeologic settings (Buttle, 2016 ). We assess the role of multi-annual memory on shallow lake water levels within the Boreal Plain. Shallow lakes are ubiquitous in the low relief glaciated Boreal Plains (BP) of Canada. They are critical aquatic habitats (Morissette et al., 2018 ) that require effective management in response to extreme landscape and climate mitigation pressures (Price et al., 2013; Ireson et al., 2015 ). But Boreal Plain lakes likely exhibit a diversity of responses to decadal weather patterns because of their varied hydrogeologic settings (Leader et al., 2024 ). Contrasts in storage and runoff result from thick glacial substrates that differ markedly in their texture, set within a sub humid climate with a strong and decadal climate signature (Devito et al.,2023; Hokanson et al., 2019 ). Lake responses to the climate signal result from spatially variable and interacting internal (lake) and external (landscape) controls on hydrology within the boreal plain (Leader et al., 2024 ; Plach et al., 2016; Smerdon et al., 2007 ). These controls suggest the prevalence of multi-annual hysteresis of water levels of varying periodicities across multiple types of Boreal and glacial lake systems. The aim of this paper is to evaluate how multi-year landscape memory of precipitation (P) varies spatially within shallow lake water levels (WL) across the range of lake-landscape types of the sub-humid Boreal Plains to address the following research questions:What are the general characteristics of precipitation-water level (P-WL) hysteresis and how do they reflect hypothesised hysteresis loops based on different conceptualised storage-threshold relationships between different lake-landscape characteristics?  The significance of memory is different at different temporal scales, ranging from seasonal to interannual and therefore what additional insights are gained by considering landscape memory at multiple temporal scales?  Does landscape memory cause temporally different short term lake level response to weather due to position within the long-term meteorological cycles?    Differences in interannual hysteresis loops between Boreal Plain lakes are conceptualized by considering different landscape/lake memories to meteorological cycles (represented by cumulative departures from the long term mean). This is considered in the context of a priori  conceptual understanding of the different response functions of surficial geologies typical of the BP (Table 1  ). We predict varying hysteresis loop types due to differing dominant sources of flow, transit times and storage-threshold mechanisms. Landscapes with a low storage capacity are hypothesised to produce a short memory of climate, with rapid recovery following drought conditions (Devito et al., 2023 ; Ferone and Devito, 2004 ; Lukenbach et al., 2017 ). However, complex feedback mechanisms, i.e. due to rates of drying varying as a function of drought length and severity within peatlands between wetting and drying periods (Kettridge & Waddington, 2014 ), may produce irregular figure-eight shaped hysteresis loops. Shallow lakes are hypothesised to exhibit frequent resetting of landscape memory as the lakes spill and dry out. This will produce parallelogram loops due to periods of no lake level change due to threshold exceedance (Hokanson et al., 2021a; Thompson et al. 2015 ). Difference in loop size is determined by the magnitude of lake level variability. High storage within closed fine textured lake basins connected to high storage catchments (Leader et al., 2024 ) are expected to produce the longest landscape memory and the large hysteresis loops (Shook and Pomeroy 2011 ). Whereas landscapes with larger scale groundwater flows (Hokanson et al., 2021a ) could produce consistent low magnitude WL responses and subsequently smaller hysteresis loops. However, receiving lakes in low landscape positions may display complex temporal variability due to gatekeeper processes (Winter 1999; Gibson et al., 2002 ), with changes in landscape connectivity at different points along the meteorological cycle (Mwale et al., 2011 ). Differences in precipitation WL responses between lake types are hypothesised to be amplified under dry conditions. This is due to i) larger differences in catchment storage capacities ii) larger differences in ratios of runoff generating landscape to lake proportions and iii) the influence of within lake feedbacks (Hayashi and van der Kamp, 2007 ). During extended wet cycles, WL responses may synchronise as landscape storage deficits are filled and spatial differences in antecedent conditions become less important (Buttle 2016; Devito et al., 2023 ). Characterising such landscape memory within the context of the long-term meteorological cycle, and across common lake types will not only provide a greater understanding of the impact of memory on extreme landscape responses (drought and deluge), but will also significantly improve integration of antecedent conditions and associated hydrological processes within hydrological modelling at multiple temporal scales.  2 Study area The study was conducted in the Utikuma Region Study Area (URSA; 56°N, 115°W; Supplementary Fig. S1 , Leader et al., 2024 ), situated within the sub-humid Boreal Plains (BP) ecozone of Alberta, Canada, where long term annual average PET (513 mm) exceeds annual average P (483 mm; Plach et al., 2016; NRC, 2006 ). The region is exposed to strong decadal meteorological cycles, with wet years occurring infrequently on approximately 20 year cycle (Mwale et al., 2009 ), in addition to a pronounced seasonal weather cycle with cold winters (January temperatures of −14.5 °C) and warm summers (July temperatures of 15.6 °C; Thompson et al., 2015 ). Peak vegetation growth and evaporative demand overlaps with the majority of annual precipitation, with 60 % falling in the three months of June to August (Devito et al., 2005 ). Although contributing a smaller proportion of total annual precipitation, snowfall and snowmelt and the occurrence of heavy spring rains provide a crucial component of the water balance by replenishing soils and recharging groundwater (Devito et al., 2012 ). The URSA is characterised by low relief deep (45–240 m) Quaternary deposits overlaying shale bedrock that limit regional groundwater interactions with streams and lakes (Hokanson et al., 2019; Plach et al., 2016 ). The surficial glacial deposits have been previously classified into three hydrologic response areas (HRAs) with similar storage and transmissivity properties: (1) coarse-textured glacial–fluvial outwash (CO); (2) fine-textured clay rich glacio-lacustrine plains (FP); (3) fine-textured hummocky moraine deposits (FH); (Leader et al.,2024; Hokanson et al., 2019 ). The overlying vegetation is characterised by a mosaic of forests, wetlands (peatlands), and ponds and shallow lakes that have been further discretized into hydrologic units (HU) representing contrasting soil-vegetation and hydrologic storage and transmission properties (Devito et al., 2012, 2017 ; Hokanson et al., 2020 ). Peatland wetlands are ubiquitous through the landscape and dominated by black spruce (Picea mariana) and tamarack (Larix laricina), whilst forestlands are characterized by trembling aspen (Populus tremuloides) or jack pine (Pinus banksiana) associated with surficial geology (NRC, 2006; Redding and Devito, 2011 ). This study comprises of 26 study lakes located along a 40 km transect that covers the three HRAs typical of the Boreal Plains (Devito et al., 2023; NRC, 2006 ). Lakes were selected strategically to include the diversity in surficial geology, land cover, topography, lake geometry and lake types observed within the URSA and the Boreal Plain. This larger synoptic lake series include four detailed study lakes that represent the range of lake types in the URSA, and were sampled year round and at a higher frequency (Leader et al., 2024 ). The lakes were classified and grouped previously by Leader et al. (2024)  based on the Hutchinson’s (1957)  glacial lake type and the dominant HRA of the connected catchment (Table 4 ). These include: (1) Outwash flow through lakes with the lake basin and associated surface and phreatic catchment located in coarse textured glaciofluvial HRA (Outwash-CO, includes detailed lake 16); (2) Closed basin lakes situated on HRAs designated as CO, but the headwater catchments have hummocky morphology fine-textured deposits overlaying (perched) coarse deposits not indicated on regional mapping (Hokanson et al., 2019 ) (Closed-FH, includes Lake 19); (3) Glacial moraine spilling lakes with basin and catchments on fine textured hummocky moraine HRAs (Moraine-FH; detailed lake 43); (4) peatland spilling lakes on glaciolacustrine clay plain with low relief catchments dominated by fine textured HRAs and large peatland coverage (Peat-FP, includes detailed lake 171); and (5) similar peatland spilling lakes on glaciolacustrine clay plain HRA but the connected catchments are dominated FH HRAs (Peat-FH). The areas of the lakes range 0.0005 to 3.2 km2  and topographic or phreatic catchments range from 0.08 to 90 km2  that vary from isolated headwater systems to large regionally connected systems and ranging in proportion of peatland and forestland cover (Leader et al., 2024 ; see Supplementary Information ).  3 Methods 3.1 Climate variables and climate-driven temporal study design for memory testing 3.1.1 Climate data and variables Daily precipitation and mean, maximum and minimum air temperatures have been monitored for 23 years (1995–2018) within the URSA and wider study region (see Supplementary Material  section 2.1; Leader et al., 2024; Devito et al., 2016 ). Study lakes are all within 40 km of each other and were subject to similar weather and climate conditions (Devito et al., 2016 ). Records from 4 meteorological stations along the 40 km lake survey transect from 1999 to 2018 were collected (Fig. S1 , Leader et al., 2024 ). Lag climate variables were devised to identify autoregressive responses associated with varying transit times, whereas cumulative climate variables are formulated to associate antecedent conditions and storage capacities with response. Precipitation lag value relative to the long-term mean (Lag P), and precipitation cumulative deviation from the long-term mean (CDM P) variables for memory periods of 0–5 years and 1–6 years respectively, were generated using the following equations (see Winter 2000; Hokanson et al. 2019 ):(1)  L a g  X y r  d =   ∑ d - X - 1 y e a r  d - X   P    - μ ;     (2)  C D M  X y r  d =   ∑ d - X  d  P    - μ × X    ;     where X  is the length of time for which the climate variable is calculated (in years), d  is the date of the calculated climate variable, P  is daily precipitation total (mm), μ  is the long-term mean of annual precipitation (November hydrologic year), given as 444 mm for the study region. CDM P (mm) for 1 – 6 years is presented in Fig. 1   for 1997–2019.  3.1.2 Lake water level data The elevation of water levels were measured at referenced staff gauges secured to the deep sediment with known elevation (m amsl) at the edge of all 26 lakes and used to estimate the depth of water at the centre during all sampling periods (see Supplementary Material  section 2.2 and Leader et al., 2024 ). In the earlier synoptic survey (1999–2004), instantaneous WL measurements were periodically measured between lake ice off and autumn conditions. In the later synoptic survey (2012–2018) at least one water level measurement was conducted in the final week of June or first week of July. Summer rainfall and runoff (small or large) represent a large portion of annual inputs to the BP lake water balance, thus the summer period represents relatively continuous high water levels or lower water levels for a given year. Therefore, maximum summer water levels derived from measurements taken June 1st to August 31st in the earlier survey were collated with single July samples during the later survey that have previously been shown to reflect interannual range in water levels for each lake during the two sampling period (see also Leader et al., 2024 ). For the four detailed study Lakes (lakes 16, 19, 43, and 171) representing four different lake-catchment classifications (see Supplementary Material Table S1 ), water levels were measured multiple times throughout the ice-free period, and also logged continuously by pressure transducers within stilling wells associated with staff gauges with known elevations. Mean daily water levels were calculated during periods with continuous records and augmented with instantaneous WL measurements when continuous records were not available. See Leader et al., (2024)  for further information.  3.1.3 Climate-driven temporal study design Analyses are conducted over four temporal scales for this study representing a trade-off between spatial and temporal scales (Table 2  ): 1) Interdecadal scales : World Satellite Imagery was obtained from Esri and combined with historical aerial photography of the URSA (8 images evenly disturbed across a 70-year period). Lake surface area was then delineated for each satellite image of Lake 19 and regression analysis conducted between lake area and CDM P 1–6 yr (mm) to determine the effects of memory at interdecadal scales. 2) Decadal scale : Interannual summer water levels of 26 study lakes across 19 years – the full field-based measurement period – is used to assess spatial variability in responses at the decadal scale. Higher frequency sampling is required to analyse shorter term cycles, and these were limited to the analyses of trends in WL of the four detailed study lakes. 3) Multi-year responses : Interannual summer water levels of four detailed study lakes across multiannual wetting drying cycles. Three multi-annual periods were identified representing dry (2000–2004), dry-mesic (2008–2012) and mesic (2013–2018) conditions within the long-term climate cycle based on the 1-year cumulative departure from the long-term mean (wet, >100 mm P CDM; mesic, −100 mm < P CDM<100 mm; dry, <−100 mm P CDM). 4) Intra-annual : For intra-annual analyses, 11 growing seasons (May 1st – September 30th) of the four detailed study lakes were identified and classified based on the directionality (wetting or drying) and value of the CDM P 1 yr (mm) (Table 3   ) providing their context within the long-term climate. The variability and wet-dry cycles at different temporal scales are evident in the time series illustrated in Fig. 1 .   3.2 Data analysis Autocorrelation and cross correlation were undertaken in R (R Core Team, 2021 ). Daily and annual climate records of URSA were tested to establish whether the cyclical meteorological patterns produced autocorrelation (Supplementary Fig. S1 ). For interannual summer water levels analyses, the average summer water level is correlated with precipitation and cumulative precipitation corresponding with the July 1 to June 30 hydrologic year, and a lag of 1 corresponds to 1 year. Where higher frequency water levels are tested, the cumulative precipitation (CDM P) relative to the long-term mean was correlated against water levels of the same day.   4 Results 4.1 Interdecadal memory Historic satellite imagery of the Closed-FH Lake 19 has revealed more than 4-fold change in lake surface area extent since 1951 due to interdecadal water level fluctuations (Fig. 2  ), ranging from 9674 m2  in 2011 to 38930 m2  in 1977, with perimeter varying two-fold between these records (476–933 m). Climate-lake water level correlation strength and significance were considerably greater with longer cumulative climate variables of CDM P 4 yr (r = 0.88, p = 0.004), CDM P 5 yr (r = 0.88, p = 0.0042) and CDM P 6 yr (r = 0.87, p = 0.0047) than one-year cumulative deviation from the long term mean in precipitation (CDM P 1 yr; 444 mm; r = 0.63, p = 0.093). Relatively low lake surface area occurred in 1951 despite above average rainfall for that year (74 mm CDM P 1 yr) as landscape antecedent conditions reflect a long-term precipitation deficit following 8 consecutive years of below average rainfall (CDM 6 yr P=-320 mm in July 1951). Similarly, 1965 surface water area is greater than expected for a CDM 1 yr P value of −88 mm. Instead, 1965 lake water levels reflect memory of ∼10 years of above average rainfall and thus a CDM 6 yr P value of +210 mm. This clearly demonstrates the importance of multi-annual memory of climate within this landscape, whereby clustering of wet or dry years propagate into extreme wetting and drying of the landscape.  4.2 Decadal scale – spatial variability in memory between different lake-landscape characteristics across 19 years Interannual summer lake water level response to annual precipitation totals (July 1 hydrologic year) produced hysteresis loops in all 26 study lakes (Fig. 3  ). Graphical comparisons reveal high variability in the shape, size and direction of hysteresis loops spatially among lakes (see summary in Table 4 ). The varied characteristics of hysteresis loops indicate that complex and spatially variable memory is present in the landscape in time and in space. A consistent response is observed across URSA in the dry year of 2002, where large decreases in water levels occur in all lakes (Figs. 3 and 4  ). However, the subsequent responses to wet conditions in 2003 vary substantially between lakes. This is exemplified by shallow Moraine-FH lakes, some of which dried out in 2002. These lakes could not dry further and produced parallelogram shaped loops. Peat-FP lakes display the greatest lake water level increases in 2003, producing elliptical or rapid-wetting figure-eight loops. In contrast, Outwash-CO lakes are the only class to display continued drying in 2003 in most lakes. Comparisons of loops for two of the 6-year cycles (period 1: 1999–2004 and period 3: 2013–2018) demonstrate consistent hysteresis responses between periods in some lakes and highly contrasting responses in others (Fig. 3 ). This occurs due to the similar CDM P 1 yr pattern for each period, enabling landscapes with low memory to produce consistent hysteresis loops (e.g. Moraine-FH or Peat-FP and Peat-FH lakes 122, 121, 118), whereas lakes associated with longer CDM P control display contrasting hysteresis loops between periods (e.g. Closed-FH lakes 7, 15, 19). Therefore, systems with greater memory produced larger hysteresis loops and shallower water levels or desiccation in the long-term dry period of 2000–2005. For each CDM P length (1–5 years), the cross-correlation function (CCF) value is displayed for the optimal lag (highest CCF) in Fig. 4 . The magnitude of CCF, the association with CDM precipitation periods and the variability in response between lakes differs between different lake-catchment classes. Cross correlation plots of Outwash-CO lakes demonstrate high similarity between lakes, with the exception of lake 1. Generally, Outwash-CO lakes produced highest CCF values for CDM P 1-3yrs with 0 lag, whereas the largest lakes (5 and 17) exhibit higher CCF for longer CDM variables. Closed-FH lakes that typically located in headwaters and/or perched above the CO HRA (Lake 11, 19, 15 and Moraine-FH lake 48) exhibit the poorest CCF values and longest lags, signifying poor association with climate at decadal scales due to interactions with antecedent moisture. Peat lakes with FP or FH catchments are positioned in plateau or extensive valley regions with low relief and with larger lake surface area for their fine-textured surficial geology class (39, 27, 42 & 121, 118) also exhibited low CCF and low synchronicity between lake types. In contrast, small and spilling, high landscape positioned Moraine-FH lakes (40, 43, 111, and peat-FP lake 171) produced high CCF values at 3 year CDM.  Of the peat lakes, lakes with catchments dominated by FH HRA’s (59, 112 and 122) produced high CCF values at varying CDM variables. In contrast, peat lakes with large catchments dominated by FP HRA and peatlands (168 and 205, Peat-FP) produces low CCF values, which could signal complex response patterns as a function of variable hydrologic connectivity with continuous wetland distribution.  4.3 Multi-year responses: placing shorter-term responses in context of the long-term climate Multi-year hysteresis loop plots for the four detailed study lakes (Fig. 5  ) demonstrate contrasting responses between each lake and between each 5/6 year time period. In each period, Closed-FH lake 19 produces the largest hysteresis loops due to the greatest water level declines with no recovery of water levels in 2000–2004 and continued drying in 2008–2012 (Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Moraine-FH Lake 43 produces similar limited recovery of water levels in 2000–2004 and 2008–2012, however the magnitude of responses is varied between years. Lower declines in 2002 and greater recovery was possible in 2003 due to the lake desiccation in summer 2002, whereas higher antecedent water levels within the dry/mesic period enables greater drying in 2009–2010. Similarly, Peat-FP lake 171, in low relief plateau landscape position and peatland dominated catchment, produces highly variable responses between periods, producing a large figure-eight hysteresis loop 2000–2004, and a linear, low magnitude response in 2008–2012. In contrast, the water levels in low landscape position Outwash-CO lake 16 do not decline to the same magnitude during dry periods, and also show an increase during dry years which could reflect lagged response to meteorological cycles. Regression analysis of high frequency detailed lake water level data against CDM P for 1 to 3 years (Fig. 6  ) generally indicates higher, but contrasting association with CDM 2 yr P across all lake types. For the Closed-FH lake 19 and Moraine-FH lake 43 CDM 2 yr P provides the highest association, whilst CDM 3 yr P provide the highest association for the Outwash-CO lake 16 and Peat-FP lake 171. Whereas other lakes display improved linear relationships, Closed-FH lake 19 produces a hockey stick shape, with low gradient response under precipitation deficit conditions but high response under above average cumulative precipitation. Fig. 6  also indicates individual years which have improved residuals when lake water levels are fitted within the regression analysis linearly to longer cumulative climate variables (e.g. 2001, 2003, 2014). Understanding which years fit poorly (high residuals) to CDM 1yrm which signifies presence of multi-annual memory supports interpretation from interannual analysis. Notably, CDM 3 yr P significantly improves the residuals of high lake water levels for Outwash-CO lake 16 during the long-term dry climatic conditions in 2001. Meanwhile, large negative residuals of low water levels in 2003 for Peat-FP lake 171 and 2003–2004 for Moraine-FH lake 43 signify memory of dry conditions which are better predicted with CDM 2/3yr P. High water levels during the dry summer of 2014 are also better represented by CDM 2/3yr P across all four lake types due to memory of wet conditions within 2013, as is also true for 2009 in Closed-FH lake 19 and Moraine-FH lake 43 following prolonged above average precipitation 2005–2009.  4.4 Intra-annual weather-lake WL responses Comparison of intra-annual weather and lake WL, grouped by different multi-annual weather classes (Dry, Mesic Dry, Wet to Mesic, Dry to Mesic, Mesic to Wet; Fig. 7  ), demonstrates differing annual lake WL responses between years that are driven by memory (Table 3 ). Similar short-term net precipitation totals in dry years 2002 and 2010 (pink ‘Dry’ segment; Fig. 7 ) produced comparable rates in lake levels decline through the year, however, lake water levels display greater magnitude rewetting responses to rainfall events in 2010 when in a wetter long-term meteorological cycle. Contrasting responses between lakes to rainfall events in 2002 reiterates the rapid post-drought recovery rate of peatland systems (Peat-FP lake 171) shown in 2003 and 2004 of Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7 . However, intra-annual data provides evidence for greater post-drought rewetting in Peat-FP lake 171 in late summer, when growing season evaporative demand is high but precipitation is typically low. Moraine-FH Lake 43 displays the greatest magnitude of water level declines within 2010, which implies lower retention of wet conditions 2005–2009 due to lake outflow generation during this period. Years 2003 and 2011 (green ‘Dry to Mesic’; Fig. 7 ) also have a comparable short term mesic climate and wet summer. Peat-FP Lake 171 continues to wet up the greatest in 2003 following the prolonged precipitation deficit, whereas under mesic long-term conditions, Moraine-FH lake 43 and closed-FH lake 19 display the greatest increases in lake levels, suggesting changes in the precipitation-lake water level gradients with CDM P value. Four short-term ‘wet to mesic’ years (light blue segment; Fig. 7 ) were identified within the study period, each with contrasting growing season P and long-term meteorological cycles. Within these years, both 2009 and 2014 represent dry summers following prolonged wet periods and lake outflow generation in spilling lakes, and produce near linear drying trends throughout the growing season in all lakes. Drier long-term conditions in 2014 than 2009 (111 mm drier CDM 3 yr P; 401 mm drier CDM 5 yr P) result in steeper gradients and greater magnitude decreases in lake water levels. Under these dry conditions we also observe a change in order of the gradient and magnitude response of each lake in comparison to mesic and wet years. Outwash-CO Lake 16 exhibits the lowest drying rate in 2009, but highest in 2014, which could reflect greater association with the long-term climate. Rates and patterns are similar between lakes 43, 19 and 171, however Peat-FP lake 171 water levels dry at a slow rate, diverging from closed-FH lake 19 and Moraine-FH lake 43 in mid-August, whereas lake Closed-FH 19 displays greater rates of water level decline in 2014 than Peat-FP lake 171 and Moraine-FH lake 43 throughout the whole growing season. In contrast to 2009 and 2014, mesic summers in the wet years of 2008 and 2012, frequent rainfall events produce several anticlockwise hysteresis loops in all lakes. In both 2008 and 2012, Outwash-CO lake 16 shows early season declines in lake water level while other lakes are stable or increasing, but also exhibits late summer increases when other lakes are drying. In both 2008 and 2012, Moraine-FH lake 43 displays the lowest lake level decline across the growing season and greatest wetting in response to rainfall events, whereas Peat-FP lake 171 produces larger anticlockwise loops towards a drier state.   5 Discussion Within this study, multi-annual hysteresis of precipitation-lake water levels clearly demonstrate the importance of understanding interannual landscape memory of climate within the sub-humid plains regions of the circumpolar Boreal Forest. Further, different insights are gained through analyses at different temporal scales, with memory evident from interdecadal to intra-annual scales (Table 2 ). The varied characteristics of hysteresis loops (Table 4 ) indicate that complex and spatially variable memory is present. These spatial variations in landscape memory are driven by differences in storage capacities (Table 1 ), which is in turn governed by landscape properties, such as surficial geology, landcover and landscape position (Leader et al., 2024; Devito et al., 2023 ). Thus, the propensity for drought years or wet years to persist or accumulate into extreme landscape drying or wetting varies significantly between different lake-landscape characteristics. Peatland lakes on fine plains (Peat-FP) HRAs demonstrated the rapid recovery following drought (Figs. 2 and 7 ) due to low storage capacities and subsequently short memory of dry conditions of connected peatlands within the lake catchment (Lukenbach et al., 2017; Hokanson et al., 2021b; Devito et al., 2023 ). In contrast, desiccation in many moraine spilling lakes in fine hummocky (Moraine-FH) HRAs restricted the magnitude of lake water level declines and memory of drought, but low water levels persisted one to two years following droughts (Figs. 2 and 7 ). This implies longer landscape memory of dry conditions within Moraine-FH systems, which fits with current conceptual understanding of deep hillslope soils, high infiltration rates, high evaporative demand and subsequent long runoff return periods (Redding & Devito, 2008; Hokanson et al. 2021b ). On the other hand, under mesic or wet climatic conditions Moraine-FH and Closed-FH lakes produced greater increases in lake water levels than Peat-FP lakes (Fig. 7 ), indicating non-linear precipitation-lake water level response functions with CDM 1 yr P value (Fig. 4 , Table 4 ). Small, high landscape positioned Moraine-FH lakes produced a strong cross correlation with CDM 3 yr P (Fig. 4 , Table 4 ) as spilling and desiccation frequently ‘reset’ memory. Closed basins (Closed-FH) produced poor cross correlations, and a hockeystick shaped response function with a near zero gradient response to CDM 1 yr P<0 mm, but high responses to above average long-term precipitation (Fig. 4 , Table 4 ). This echoes findings within the PPR, whereby depressional shallow lakes exhibit longer memory as they can only dry via evapotranspiration due to the absence of lake outflows (Hayashi and van der Kamp 2007 ). Within Outwash-CO lakes, high cross correlation with lagged and longer cumulative precipitation variables reflects the dominance of groundwater as a control on lake water levels within this glacial landform on the BP (Smerdon et al., 2007; Hokanson et al., 2021a , Fig. 4 , Table 4 ). As such, intra-annual patterns of Outwash-CO lake water levels often contrast with patterns in lakes on fine textured HRAs due lags in seasonal dynamics (snowmelt recharge) superimposed on to a lagged response to long term dry conditions (Carrera-Hernández et al., 2011 ). While some consistencies in precipitation-lake water level hysteresis characteristics and cross correlation were identified within lake classifications (Fig. 4 , Table 4 ), the generally poor cross correlation in a high number of lakes across the 18-year record could signify the complex interaction of lake basin memory and antecedent storage of the upslope catchment (Devito et al., 2023 ). Detailed investigative analysis comparing within year responses of similar short term climatic conditions (Fig. 7 ) demonstrate that seasonal climate is an important driver for within year water level patterns, but landscape memory of long-term climate and threshold runoff responses govern the magnitude and gradient of these patterns (Mwale et al., 2011 ). This echoes findings of short-term studies that specify that precipitation timing and magnitude relative to PET, rather than annual precipitation totals defined runoff (Devito et al., 2005; Redding & Devito, 2008 ). Yet slight differences in antecedent soil moisture or groundwater position can propel a hydrologically disconnected catchment into one that yields high proportions of annual runoff in one storm event (Devito et al., 2005; Devito et al., 2023; Hokanson et al., 2021b ). Thus understanding of antecedent conditions is crucial as proximity to storage thresholds results in disproportionate effects of precipitation events on discharge (Devito et al., 2023, Devito et al., 2023, Spence, 2010; Holecek 1988 ). Antecedent conditions also determines the connectivity between wetlands, modifying contributing area (Shaw et al., 2012 ). Consequently, it is difficult to directly define or infer hydrological processes from analysis that spans multiple climate cycles in landscapes with capacity for high memory. Simultaneously, it is challenging to gain a full understanding of a system’s hydrologic function without observing response under a range of climatic conditions where non-linearities exist. Instead, shorter term interannual or intra-annual analyses should be placed within the context of the long-term meteorological cycles, where comparisons of responses at different antecedent conditions will provide stronger evidence of landscape memory and associated hydrological processes. 5.1 Implications for land management A direct consequence of multiannual memory is that clustering of wet or dry climatic years can propagate into extreme wetting and drying of the landscape (Khanal et al., 2019 ). Multi-annual landscape memory of climate within the Boreal Plains demands greater understanding of the heterogeneity of glacial deposits and land covers and subsequent contrasts in storage and transmissivity processes governing antecedent moisture conditions of the connected catchment to accurately model lake water level responses, groundwater levels or landscape runoff over prolonged periods (multiannual to multidecadal), especially under drought or deluge (Devito et al., 2005, 2023 ; Holecek 1988; Hokanson et al., 2019 ). Thus, this knowledge is essential for land management practices at hydroclimatic periods when both uncertainty in hydrological processes is at its greatest (Koutsoyiannis, 2005 ) and water resource management is at its most critical. Yet one of the main limitations of previous BP research is the limited understanding of dynamic controls such as landscape memory (Devito et al., 2023 ). While research focusing solely on ‘static’ landscape characteristics controls such as landcover proportions, lake geometry and surficial geology have provided crucial knowledge for conceptualising hydrologic landscapes, static controls cannot fully explain temporal variations in both interannual and intra-annual water level patterns. The important control of storage in catchment hydrograph non-linearity has previously been recognised within the BP (Holecek 1988; Devito et al., 2005, 2023 ; Wells et al. 2017; Hokanson et al., 2021b ), and a plethora of concepts have been defined to describe these non-linear processes (e.g. Ali et al., 2013; Shaw et al., 2012; Spence, 2007 ). Approaches presented within this study to examine landscape memory could have applicability to many continental and plains Boreal regions globally. However, this is the first study to characterise landscape memory through both interannual and intra-annual water level analysis across heterogeneous hydrogeoclimatic settings typical of the Boreal Plains.
1 Introduction Since the Industrial Revolution, emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere have rapidly increased. This has led to changes in the energy balance and material cycling processes between the Earth's land and atmosphere (Alfieri et al., 2017 ).  One of the most significant impacts of global climate change is the intensification of the hydrological cycle, including the intensification of extreme rainfall (Franzke, 2022 ). Due to different driving factors, the spatial distribution of extreme rainfall also varies. In humid regions, the expansion of atmospheric water vapor convergence exacerbates the impact of extreme rainfall, while in arid regions, increased precipitation may be offset by evaporation (Zhu et al., 2022 ). The expansion of extreme rainfall leads to an increase in the intensity and frequency of floods (Garg and Mishra, 2019 ), and the unexpected relationship between the trends in extreme rainfall and extreme flow can be attributed to the influence of other flood generation mechanisms, such as soil moisture and snow dynamics (Tabari, 2020 ). Even if floods are triggered by extreme rainfall, the relationship between precipitation magnitude and flood magnitude may be nonlinear, as significant changes have occurred in the complex interactions of many variables, such as land cover, river channels, and evapotranspiration (Slater et al., 2021 ). The Luanhe River Basin, located in northeastern China, spans a broad range of latitudes, exhibits uneven spatial and temporal rainfall distribution, and is characterized by rapid fluctuations, high peak flows, and large discharge volumes in its floods, often leading to flood disasters. According to Gao et al. (2024) , extreme flood events in the Luanhe River Basin were primarily influenced by extreme rainfall and extreme high temperatures. Against the backdrop of intensified extreme rainfall, summer floods were becoming more complex, variable and destructive. However, current research in the Luanhe River basin mainly focuses on hydro-meteorological drought issues (Chen et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020 ), with a particular emphasis on the reduction in runoff volume under the context of global warming. When attributing changes in the runoff, these studies often consider the mean runoff rather than extreme discharge values (Jiang et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019 ). For instance, Zhang et al. (2018)  used the SWAT model to attribute changes in monthly runoff in the Luanhe River basin to climate change and land-use changes, finding that climate change was the main driver of reduced runoff across four sub-basins. Historical floods studies in the Luanhe River basin mainly focus on specific flood events for the purposes of downstream reservoir operation or flood risk management (Chen et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; He et al., 2024 ). However, the varying mechanisms for triggering floods with the context of climate change and human activities has not been thoroughly investigated. Feng et al. (2015)  developed a hydrological model based on the infiltration-excess and saturation-excess runoff mechanisms, examining the response of 16 flood peaks and volumes at the Lengkou hydrological station from 1956 to 2008 to land-use changes, but without considering the impact of climate change and the magnitude distribution of flood events. It can be envisaged that the response mechanisms behind 2-year flood versus 100-year flood can differ significantly, especially with long-term considerations of the climate change and changes in the underlying conditions of the basin caused by land use and land cover change. Although a drier climate has reduced the frequency of floods, the increase in rainfall and flood extremes still results in considerable economic losses in the study area. As the magnitude of flood events changes, understanding how response mechanisms will vary is important for implementing specific measures to mitigate flood risks. This study will address the research gaps in considering the historical characteristics of long-term floods and in the response of floods with different return periods to climate and land-use changes in the Luanhe River Basin, providing a research framework for studying regional flood response mechanisms. The objectives of this study include: (1) to analyze the distribution and characteristics of historical floods with different return periods in the Luanhe River Basin; (2) to examine the response patterns of floods with different return periods to typical scenarios of combined climate change and land-use changes; (3) to further analyze the response patterns of floods with different return periods to various land-use types. A generalized hydrological model, i.e. the SWAT model is utilized in this study to investigate the impacts of climate and land-use changes on floods. Its applicability has been widely confirmed for runoff simulation in the Luanhe River basin and ditto to its utility for long-term flood modeling and analysis. Eingruber and Korres (2022)  simulated future extreme floods by inputting future extreme rainfall into SWAT and statistically analyzed the return periods of floods using moving cycle GEV and Gumbel extreme value distributions. When tackling the hydrological extremes, the commonly used precipitation and flood extreme value distributions include Pearson Type III distribution (Tian and Wang, 2022 ), Generalized Extreme Value Distribution (GEV) (Yan et al., 2021 ), Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) (Gharib et al., 2017 ). The Annual Maximum (AM) method and Peak-Over-Threshold (POT) method are usually employed to select extreme events (Huguenin et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023 ). Unlike the AM method, which only considers the largest values in an annual series, the POT method considers all samples exceeding a threshold (Langousis et al., 2016; Agilan et al., 2021 ). The most prominent characteristic of the GPD is its ability to sample using POT, thereby increasing the sample capacity. Therefore, this study selects the POT-GPD method to obtain values of floods with different return periods. In this study, flood return values derived from the GPD method are used to identify and classify historical floods across different return periods. Flood behavior indicators are also employed to analyze the flood characteristics with different return periods. Various climate and land-use input scenarios are designed as inputs for the SWAT model to discuss the response of floods with different return periods to climate and land-use changes. The purpose of this study is to fully assess the impacts of climate change and land-use changes in the upper Luanhe River Basin on triggering floods with different return periods. The findings could provide important guidance for future flood risk assessment and management strategies, and serve as a reference for sustainable development planning and management in the Luanhe River Basin.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study area is the controlled watershed of the Sandaohezi hydrological station in the Luanhe River Basin (as shown in  Fig. 1 a), with a total area of 17,100 km2 . The Luanhe River Basin is located in the northeast of the North China Plain, characterized by a terrain that slopes from northwest to southeast, following a similar direction as the main course of the Luanhe River (as shown in Fig. 1 a). This geographic placement renders the Luanhe River Basin a protective barrier for the ecological environment of the “Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei” urban agglomeration, playing an irreplaceable role in influencing the climatic conditions and ecological environment protection of the cities in this region (as shown in Fig. 1 b) (Gao et al., 2023, Zheng et al., 2022 ). The northern and southern regions of the Luanhe River Basin experience considerable differences in climate and vegetation distribution. The northern region has an overall cold and arid climate, predominantly characterized by temperate semi-arid climates, with grass land being the dominant vegetation type (as shown in Fig. 1 c). In contrast, the southern region has a humid and warm climate, mainly characterized by a warm temperate semi-humid climate, fostering diverse vegetation such as forest-steppe, coniferous forests, mixed coniferous and broad-leaved forests, as well as deciduous broad-leaved forests (Wang et al., 2020 ). Additionally, the region boasts a variety of soil types, including marsh soil, saline soil, chestnut calcareous soil, black soil, meadow soil, and brown soil. The study area maintains a relatively pristine ecological environment with minimal human activities.  2.2 Datasets The meteorological data utilized is sourced from the China Meteorological Network (http://data.cma.cn/ ). Measured precipitation data from the rain station and daily runoff data from the Sandaohezi hydrological station are obtained from the Haihe River Conservancy Commission of the Ministry of Water Resources in China. The Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with a spatial resolution of 90 m is derived from Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) data collected by the US Space Shuttle Endeavour (https://www.gscloud.cn/ ). Soil type data is derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) - China Soil Dataset (https://gaez.fao.org/pages/hwsd ), which utilizes the FAO-90 soil classification system. The land-use data is provided by the Centre for Resource and Environmental Sciences and Data of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (https://www.resdc.cn/ ). The land-use data covers the years 1980, 2000, and 2018 and is reclassified into six categories: forest, grassland, cropland, urban land, water, and barren land. Runoff data is used to analyze flood events; DEM data, soil type data, land-use type data are used to construct the hydrologic model, with meteorological station data and rain station data as model inputs. This study focuses on flood events that mainly occur from June to September, thus the study period is selected from June 1st to September 30th.  2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Generalized pareto distribution (GPD) In extreme excess modeling, GPD is used to fit rainfall or runoff excesses above a properly selected threshold u (Langousis et al., 2016 ). The runoff distribution in the study area is uneven, with some years experiencing short-duration high peaks due to extreme rainfall events, while other years exhibit more stable runoff patterns. Therefore, this study employs the GPD to fit extreme runoff. On this basis, return values for different return periods are calculated. The cumulative probability distribution function (CDF) F(x) of GPD is given as follows (i.e., Eq. 1 ) (Lee et al., 2020 ):(1) F ( x )  = 1 - ( 1 + ξ x − μ  σ    )  - 1 / ξ       Where μ   is the location parameter，ξ   is the shape parameter，σ   is the scale parameter. One of the properties of GPD is that the shape and modified scale parameters remain constant with the increased threshold, and this property has been employed widely to verify the suitability of POT-GPD approach in frequency analysis (Pan et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2015 ). The mean residual life plot is one of graphical diagnostics to find a suitable threshold. When using the mean residual life plot for threshold selection, subjective visual inspection is often employed, leading to uncertainty. In order to reduce the uncertainty caused by subjective selection, this study combined the mean residual life plot with the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to choose the optimal threshold. (Pan et al., 2022 ). The model with the lowest AIC can be considered as the best model. The fitting to GPD is checked for statistical significance by using Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional test. In order to ensure the independence of POT excesses, observation data larger than the threshold should be set not to be consecutively selected. In this study, independent flood peaks are identified by criteria as follows (i.e., Eq. (2), Eq . (3) ) (Pan et al., 2022 ):(2) θ > 5 d a y s +  log ( A )      (3) Q  min   < 75 % M i n . [ Q  1   , Q  2   ]     Where θ   is separation period between two consecutive peaks, A is basin area (square mile), Q  min     is the intermediate flow value between two consecutive peaks, Q  1     and Q  2     are two consecutive peaks.  2.3.2 Flood behavior characteristic indicators Six flood behavior characteristic indicators are selected to evaluate floods, including flood characteristic indicators, flood dynamic indicators, and flood morphological indicators (as shown in  Table 1 ). Flood characteristic indicators depict peak characteristics and flood timing features. Flood dynamic indicators are used to characterize the rate of change of flood processes, and a higher value indicates a faster rise and fall velocity of floods. The coefficient of variation is used to describe flood morphology (Zhang and Chen, 2020 ).  2.3.3 Change point analysis Cluster analysis method is applied to identify the breakpoint in climate and hydrological series. Assuming a potential breakpoint as τ, the sum of squared deviations before and after the hydrological sequence breakpoint is expressed as (i.e., Eq. 4, Eq . 5):(4) V  τ   = ∑ i = 1  τ   ( x  i   − x  ¯   τ   )  2        (5) V  n − τ   = ∑ i = τ + 1  n   ( x  i   − x  ¯   n − τ   )  2        Where x  ¯   τ     is the mean of the hydrological sequence before the breakpoint τ, and x  ¯   n − τ     is the mean of the hydrological sequence after the breakpoint τ. The total sum of squared deviations is (i.e., Eq. 6 ):(6) S  n   ( τ )  = V   τ    + V  n − τ         When the condition S  = min S   n   τ        ( 2 ≤ τ ≤ n － 1 )    is met, the corresponding τ is identified as the optimal bisecting point, indicating it as the most likely breakpoint (Ma et al., 2021 ).  2.3.4 Extreme climate indices Considering that floods are directly influenced by extreme precipitation, eight extreme precipitation indices including R95p, R99p, Rx1day, Rx5day, PRCPTOT, SDII, R20, R10 are selected to determine the climatic breakpoints, which are commonly used indicators for detecting precipitation trends (Xing et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024 ). These indices serve as reference for identifying hydrological breakpoints. Extreme temperature indices are used to discuss the trend of temperatures, and four indices that most intuitively reflect extreme temperature changes are selected: TNn, TNx, TXn, TXx (as shown in  Table 2 ). The extreme climate indices adopted are based on the core climate indices defined by the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI) (Ozturk et al., 2021 ).  2.3.5 The SWAT model The SWAT model is one of the most widely used models worldwide and has been applied for an extensive suite of water resource issues across a broad range of basin scales and environmental conditions (Tan et al., 2020 ), which was developed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Agricultural Service Center in the early 1990s. SWAT is a process-based conceptual model with abstracted and empirical components. These different components result in a complex semi-distributed, eco-hydrological model (Pfannerstill et al., 2014 ). SWAT model uses the master water balance approach (i.e., Eq. 7 ) to compute runoff volumes and peak flows (Maghsood et al., 2019 ):(7) S W t = S W 0 + ∑ i − 1  t  ( R d a y − Q s u r f − E a − w s e e p − Q g w )      where S W t    and S W 0    are the final and initial soil water content for day i, respectively, R d a y    is rainfall that reaches soil surface, Q s u r f    is surface runoff, E a    is evapotranspiration, w s e e p    is interflow, and Q g w    is base flow. The SWAT model is based on DEM data to extract basin terrain parameters, setting a minimum drainage area and delineating sub-basins. It subdivides Hydrological Response Units (HRUs) by incorporating land-use types data, soil data, and slope characteristics.  2.3.6 Calibration and validation of the SWAT model SWAT-CUP has been widely applied as helpful tool to perform parameterization, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty analysis, calibration, and validation of hydrologic variables (Chen et al., 2023 ). The SUFI-2 algorithm from SWAT-CUP is adopted in this study (Bayat et al., 2023 ). P-factor (i.e. the 95PPU) is the percentage of observed data enveloped by modeling result. R-factor is the thickness of the 95PPU envelop. A P-factor of 1 and R-factor of zero is a simulation that exactly corresponds to measured data. The degree to which P-factor and R-factor are away from these numbers can be used to judge the strength of calibration (Naqash et al., 2023 ). For P-factor, a value of 70 % for discharge is suggested, while having R-factor of around 1. After meeting the P-factor and R-factor criteria, the SWAT model's performance is further evaluated using the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Percentage bias (PBIAS), Coefficient of determination (R2 ), and the Kling-Gupta efficiency coefficient (KGE). Previous studies (Maghsood et al., 2019, Osei et al., 2019, Li et al., 2023 ) suggest that a KGE greater than 0.5, an NSE greater than 0.5, an R2  greater than 0.5, or an absolute PBIAS less than 25 % indicate good model applicability. In this study, the calibration period and validation period are not continuous years but rather balanced combinations of high-flow and low-flow years. Using the traditional partitioning method, where the first 50–70 % of years are considered as the calibration period and the remaining 30–50 % are used for validation, may result in good performance during calibration but poor performance during validation, especially in cases of highly imbalanced runoff (such as several years of consistently high runoff followed by years of low runoff). This imbalance could lead to inaccurate portrayal of actual runoff dynamics by the model parameters. Balancing combinations based on hydrological conditions effectively addresses this issue, and this approach has been proven to lead to better calibration result (Houngue et al., 2023 ).    3 Results 3.1 Floods analysis with different return periods Before establishing a proper GPD model, a reasonable threshold u should be determined first. Mean residual life plot is drawn in Figure S1 , which shows that: when the threshold u is in the interval [50,160], the curve presents approximately linear increasing trend, and when u is in the interval [160,200], the linear relationship becomes unstable. When u>200, the vibration becomes severe because of few observations exceeding 200. The threshold should be chosen high enough that POT excesses are sufficient to approximate the GPD but a too high threshold can increase the error of the estimated values of model parameters by reducing the sample size (Lee et al., 2020 ). Multiple thresholds are selected within the range [50,160] to construct the GPD model, and the optimal threshold is determined to be 100 based on the AIC. Therefore, this study chooses 100 as the threshold of POT for GPD model. According to the GPD, flood discharges for different return periods are calculated (as shown in Table S1 ). Based on the flood discharges for various return periods, a total of 31 different return period flood events are identified from runoff sequences spanning the years 1961–2018, and their distribution is shown in the  Fig. 2 . These flood events are predominantly concentrated in July and August, accounting for 93.5 %. Flood events with return periods exceeding 20 years are mainly observed in the 1970s and 1990s. After the year 2000, there is a significant reduction in flood events. The flood behavior characteristic indicators with different return periods are statistically analyzed (as shown in  Fig. 3 ). Floods with return periods of 20 years and 2 years exhibit shorter peak appearance times, higher rising flood rates, and larger coefficients of variation, indicating they are both fast-rising single-peak floods. The 20-year floods show characteristics of large peak discharges and high destructiveness, reflected in the peak modulus and coefficient of variation, while the 2-year floods, with smaller peaks, have shorter duration, lower falling flood rate, and smaller coefficient of variation. Floods with return periods of 5 and 10 years exhibit wider peak time intervals, later peak times compared to other types of floods, longer durations, smaller rising and falling flood rates, and smaller coefficients of variation, particularly with the 5-year floods having the smallest falling flood rate and coefficient of variation, indicating they are mainly multi-peak floods. The floods with a return period of 20 years generally have longer overall durations. In the initial stage, when rainfall and soil moisture content are relatively low, intense short-duration rainfall events can result in large peak flows, leading to single-peak floods. Both the 10-year and 5-year return period floods, characterized by multi-peak floods, are also influenced by early rainfall. However, due to prolonged rainfall saturating or nearly saturating the soil moisture over time, subsequent rainfall events, even at relatively low levels, can trigger floods. Floods with a return period of 2 years, having smaller peak flows, which are easily triggered by short-duration intense rainfall events.  3.2 Breakpoint detection Breakpoints in runoff, precipitation, and temperature sequences are identified by using cluster analysis. The results indicate that breakpoints occur around 1980 and 1999, with additional breakpoints observed in the mid-1990s for temperature (as shown in Table S2 ). To further determine the breakpoints, considering that flood events are mainly caused by extreme rainfall factors, eight extreme precipitation indices are added to identify breakpoints (Zhou et al., 2015 ). The results show breakpoints in the hydro-meteorological environment around 1980 and 1999. This study divides the period from 1961 to 2018 into three stages for subsequent analysis based on the breakpoints: 1961–1980 as the baseline period, 1980–1999, and 1999–2018.  3.3 Calibration and validation of the SWAT Model This study run the SWAT model at a daily time step, a two-year period (1959–1960) is selected as a warm-up period. The calibration period and validation period are not selected as continuous periods but are based on hydrological conditions (high-flow years and low-flow years) to create balanced combinations. The years 1961–1968 and 1973–1980 are chosen as the calibration period. The baseline period is suitably extended and the years 1969–1972 and 1981–1984 are designated as the validation period. The SUFI2 algorithm in SWAT-CUP is utilized for multiple iterations and adjustments of sensitive parameters, aiming to bring simulated runoff values into close agreement with observed values. The SWAT model is well calibrated and validated according to the evaluative indicators (as shown in  Fig. 4 ). During the calibration period, the high-flow events in 1974 and 1976 have not been well simulated, which might possibly be due to the complex precipitation patterns in the mountainous region and the limitations of rain and meteorological station distribution, leading to inaccurate capture of actual precipitation. Based on the overall simulation results, the model is capable of reproducing most daily discharges with large magnitudes in the study catchment, and the simulated and observed discharges show relatively good agreement for both the calibration and validation periods.  3.4 Impacts of land-use and climate changes on runoff extremes Different scenarios are established based on the breakpoints identified in Section 3.2  (as shown in  Table 3 ). S0 is served as the baseline scenario, with meteorological data from 1961 to 1980 and land-use data from 1980. For S1 and S2, the climate inputs remain unchanged from S0, while land-use data are altered. Conversely, for S3 and S4, land-use data remains constant while climate inputs are modified based on S0. The differences between S1, S2, and S0 scenarios represent the effects of land-use changes during different periods, while the differences between S3, S4, and S0 scenarios denote the impacts of climate variations during different periods. According to the different return periods flood values calculated in Section 3.1 , the total amounts and total days of floods with different return periods under each scenario are statistically analyzed based on the model simulation results.
