Equations (4c) and (4d)  are for the unbiasedness requirement, where the secondary data makes zero net contribution to the mean of the primary variable. The pseudo-cross-semivariogram is needed because the AEM2020 data and the AEM2019 data are not collocated. The pseudo-cross-semivariogram for any two locations x  k     and x  j     is calculated as follows (Myers, 1991 ):(4) g 12  x  k  , x  j      = 1 2  Var R 1  x  k     - R 2  x  j             where Var is the variance operator. Given the large amounts of borehole data and AEM data, the IK and CoK from the gstat package (Gräler et al., 2016 ) were implemented using parallel computing in a supercomputer at Louisiana State University, High Performance Computing, to overcome the computing issue.  4.3 AEM Resistivity-to-Chloride concentration transformation This study used the “nearly collocated” USGS water quality data (see the inset figure in Fig. 3 ) to the AEM data within 500 m to establish the relationship between chloride concentration in groundwater and AEM resistivity data. In the study area, more than 450 chloride wells were found to be less than 500 m from their nearest AEM data location. Using the search radius of 500 m is acceptable because the resistivity and chloride concentration were estimated on 1-km NHG cells. However, correlating chloride samples from water wells collected over decades with recently collected AEM interval resistivity data can be challenging because of different spatial and temporal resolutions. Mean chloride concentration given an AEM resistivity value is suggested for that AEM resistivity value to cope with the issue. This approach can at least provide a general picture of salinity plumes for MRVA. MRVA is heavily pumped mainly for irrigation purposes. Therefore, salinity is likely to increase over the years. If an area showed high chloride concentration in the past, the area is likely to have high chloride concentration today. Fig. 5   shows the scatter plot of mean chloride concentrations versus the corresponding 45 AEM resistivity values, indicating a power law. Using SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020 ) and the Python-based Levenberg–Marquardt least-squares algorithm lmfit (Newville et al., 2016 ), a best-fit power-law equation is derived as follows(5) R = 223.04 Cl  - 0.531       where R   (ohm.m) is the AEM resistivity value, and Cl    (mg/L) is the maximum-likelihood estimated mean chloride concentration. The standard deviation of the natural log of the mean chloride concentration is 0.46. The uncertainties within Fig. 5  can come from many factors, including interbedded clays (Siemon et al., 2019 ), non-clean sands, AEM data inversion, etc. Nevertheless, delineating the MRVA sand in advance using a large amount of borehole data can significantly decrease the confusion on low resistivity being clay facies or salty water. This study set a low bound of AEM resistivity value for fresh water to be 11.9  o h m . m   , which corresponds to the chloride concentration of 250 mg/L. In general, brackish groundwater has a dissolved-solids content greater than freshwater but less than seawater. Based on USGS guidelines chloride ranges between 500 and 5,000 mg/L (corresponding to dissolved solids at concentrations between 1,000 and 10,000 mg per liter) are brackish groundwater (Stanton et al., 2017 ). The AEM resistivity value of 8.2 ohm.m (Cl = 500  m g / L   ) is chosen to be the upper bound for brackish groundwater. AEM resistivity values between 8.2 (Cl = 500 m g / L   ) and 11.9 ohm.m (Cl = 250  m g / L   ) indicate the transition from fresh groundwater and brackish groundwater. The brackish water threshold is similar to Gottschalk et al. (2020), Pozdnyakova et al. (2001) , and Schöniger et al. (2019)  for resistivity values between 0.3 ohm.m and 5 ohm.m. Moreover, Boaga et al. (2020)  set the electrical resistivity of less than 5 ohm.m and more than 10 ohm.m to be the upper and lower values for salt water and fresh water, respectively, in terms of the electro-lithological units.   5 Results and discussion 5.1 Semivariograms of the study area The experimental semivariograms and corresponding nested models for the IK and CoK methods are shown in Fig. 6  . The nesting semivariogram models integrate two random fields, small and large patches of lithofacies. The larger range indicates a random field with higher continuity and the lower range indicates a random field with lower continuity (Pardo-Iguzquiza and Chica-Olmo, 2008; Western et al., 1998 ). The nugget of the borehole semivariogram (Fig. 6 a) is small, which indicates low lithofacies variability over short distances between boreholes data (Equation (7) . The range is sufficiently large to ensure continuity of lithofacies over 1-km grid resolution. The experimental semivariograms of borehole data show a stationary spatial field. The low sill value indicates low variance among the data. A nested model of spherical and exponential functions was used to fit the experimental auto and pseudo-cross semivariograms for the AEM resistivity data (Fig. 6 b-d) as follows (Equation 8–10):(7) γ = 0.03 + 0.09 3 2  h 378.3   - 1 2  h 378.3      3      + 0.08 1 - exp - 3 h  3208.5               (8) γ 1  = 0.89 + 9.03 3 2  h 481.4   - 1 2  h 481.4      3      + 18.68 3 2  h 3043.5   - 1 2  h 3043.5      3      + 26.03 1 - exp - 3 h  22863.1               (9) γ 2  = 0.0 + 26.42 3 2  h 961.1   - 1 2  h 961.1      3      + 10.43 3 2  h 6281.7   - 1 2  h 6281.7      3      + 37.86 1 - exp - 3 h  5805              (10) g 12  = 24.49 + 7.55 3 2  h 2075.7   - 1 2  h 2075.7      3      + 21.80 3 2  h 73497.9   - 1 2  h 73497.9      3      + 16.97 1 - exp - 3 h  3170.0               where h  is the lag distance.  5.2 Aquifer characterization The MRVA sand is delineated by using indicator kriging to show the sand probability model in Fig. 7  a. The south of the Macon Ridge shows the potential surficial groundwater recharge zone for the MRVA in the study area, which corresponds to braided stream terraces. Most of the MRVA surface is capped by Quaternary fine-grained sediments with thicknesses that do not exceed 12 m (40ft) (Whitfield, 1975 ). Using a probability cutoff of 0.5, Fig. 7 b shows the sand and clay facies distributions. The lithofacies model matches with Hosman (1996), Vahdat-Aboueshagh and Tsai (2021), Weiss (1992), Whitfield (1975) , and Yin et al. (2021) . The MRVA base from the Pleistocene age consists of medium to coarse sand and gravel with a thickness of 6 to 41 m (20 to 135 ft) (Whitfield, 1975 ).  5.3 AEM Resistivity-to-Chloride concentration distribution in sand facies AEM resistivity distribution estimated by cokriging within the MRVA sand at different depths is shown in Fig. 8  . It is interesting to observe that the resistivity values in the sand facies decrease with depth, resembling saltwater stratification as saltwater is heavier than freshwater. Moreover, water quality data (see Fig. 1 ) confirm the presence of saline water in many areas. The predicted chloride concentrations at the MRVA base and in the middle of MRVA sand, using the resistivity-to-chloride concentration formula in equation (5) , are shown in Fig. 9  . The base of the MRVA shows relatively high chloride concentration (greater than 150 mg/L) in much of the study area. The salt domes in the North Louisiana Salt Basin and the Mississippi Salt Basin underneath the study area are the sources of saline water that reaches MRVA. The high chloride concentration zone (greater than 500 mg/L) coincides with the salt dome location in the Mississippi Salt Basin. The high chloride concentration zone also matches with the well water quality measurements (Van Biersel et al., 2008 ), the published water quality map for Louisiana (Van Biersel et al., 2008; Borrok et al., 2018; Tomaszewski, 1993 ), and the published water quality map for the MAP (Killian et al., 2023 ). However, the high chloride concentration zone also aligns with marine clays of the Vicksburg-Jackson Group, indicating that the low AEM resistivity at the MRVA base could also be affected by clay presence. On the other hand, there are good hydraulic connections between the MRVA and the underlying aquifers, which explain the source of freshwater in the MRVA base (see Fig. 9 ).  5.4 Saltwater Stratification, Upconing, and pumping wells Historically, several monitoring wells have shown salty groundwater in the MRVA. The monitoring wells listed in Table 1   (not used for Fig. 5 ) verify the resistivity-to-chloride transformation result with respect to the saltwater stratification shown in several cross sections in Fig. 10  . The stratified pattern indicates that (1) the source of saltwater is likely from deep formations and (2) upconing of saltwater is likely due to groundwater pumping. Most high chloride concentrations can be found at the MRVA base in Franklin and Madison Parishes. Most of the pumping wells were screened in the freshwater zone. However, saline groundwater approaches a few pumping wells through the upconing process. Saltwater upconing refers to the rising saltwater front locally below the well screen caused by pumping freshwater (Diersch and Prochnow, 1984 ). In response to the pressure depression around the well, the saltwater transports upward toward the well. This leads to a transition zone between freshwater and brackish water. Withdrawals of groundwater from the MRVA are primarily used for the irrigation of cotton, soybeans, and other crops. Heavy pumping has led to a substantial, widespread water-level decline in northeastern Louisiana (Yasarer et al., 2020 ) and aquifer salinization. However, prior to this study, there was no information regarding saltwater distribution in three dimensions. Taking advantage of the AEM data, this study reveals several potential saltwater plumes in the study area and their proximity to pumping wells.  5.5 Inference of River water quality impact Relatively higher chloride concentrations at the top of MRVA sand seem to have a good correlation with the rivers as shown in Fig. 11  a. Such a correlation is likely due to hydraulic connections between the rivers and the MRVA (Vahdat-Aboueshagh and Tsai, 2021; Yang et al., 2024 ). For instance, the Red River has much higher chloride measurements (DeGeer and Ball, 1968 ) compared to the estimated high chloride plumes in the adjacent groundwater, suggesting that these rivers are likely another source of salt to the MRVA. Conversely, knowing the significant hydraulic connections (Vahdat-Aboueshagh and Tsai, 2021; Yang et al., 2024 ), the low chloride measurements in the Mississippi River and low estimated groundwater salinity beneath the river, as depicted in Fig. 11 b indicate that the Mississippi River recharges freshwater to the MRVA. However, if both river chloride concentration and groundwater salinity are low, the interactions between the rivers and the MRVA cannot be conclusively inferred without prior knowledge of their hydraulic connections, as the salinity is generally low throughout most of the upper portion of the MRVA.  5.6 Implications of saltwater plume mapping for groundwater management This study identifies that the primary saltwater source in the MRVA is from deep formations. Saltwater migration upward due to intensive pumping is commonly seen in many aquifers in the U.S. This process renders groundwater wells unusable due to high chloride concentrations, significantly increasing costs and time for water treatment, and posing risks to human health and rural economies (Kingsbury et al., 2014 ). The lithologic model (Fig. 7 ) can delineate recharge zones for groundwater replenishment, such as managed aquifer recharge (Alam et al., 2021; Page et al., 2018 ), to dilute saltwater plumes and sustain aquifer health. The salinity model (Figs. 9-11 ) can inform decision-making on sustainable withdrawal rates to prevent over-extraction and further saltwater intrusion. For regions with significant saltwater presence, the salinity model can facilitate implementing mitigation strategies, such as effective monitoring network development, relocating existing or new pumping wells to freshwater zones, etc., to safeguard groundwater quality.   6 Conclusions The proposed framework for saltwater plume delineation in alluvial aquifers is efficient by utilizing airborne electromagnetic (AEM) surveys and borehole data. Using the borehole data to first produce a lithofacies model, and then using AEM resistivity data to construct resistivity architecture in sand facies avoids ambiguity in interpreting low resistivity values as salinity or clay facies. The cokriging method is an effective data-fusing method to integrate AEM resistivity data derived from two different airborne EM systems. This leads to predicting the overall spatial distribution of salinity and improves the prediction accuracy of groundwater salinity through resistivity-to-chloride regression analysis. The cokriging result shows stratified 3D resistivity architecture in the Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer (MRVA) in northeast Louisiana, resembling saltwater stratification. Areas with significantly low resistivity values align well with the Jurassic Mississippi Salt Basin. By using the resistivity-to-chloride concentration formula, a salinity model infers freshwater for the upper MRVA sand and brackish water at the MRVA base. However, the salinity model also shows a potential freshwater source from the underlying aquifers. The salinity model reveals saltwater upconing and its proximity to pumping wells. Moreover, the salinity model infers the surface water quality impact on near-surface MRVA water quality via surface water-groundwater interactions. Finally, the integrated framework has impactful applications for future MRVA groundwater management and other regions facing similar groundwater challenges. Prior to this study, the saltwater intrusion issue could only be inferred through a handful of chloride concentrations obtained from groundwater wells. Using borehole data, AEM data and chloride data to construct lithologic and salinity models, the study provides unprecedented information for decision-making, especially for the agriculture sector.
1 Introduction Evaluating the responses of hydrological processes to a changing environment is important for regional water resource management. Land use cover change (LUCC) is a crucial driver of hydrological processes in watersheds (Liu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024 ) by changing the land surface status, including vegetation coverage, surface roughness, and soil characteristics such as saturated hydraulic conductivity (Liu et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2023 ). LUCC at a large spatial scale alters surface albedo conditions and subsequently has considerable effects on regional energy balance and water cycles (Deng et al., 2015 ). Generally, climate change is the dominant factor in basin hydrological processes (Ahmed et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2017; Getachew et al., 2021; Li et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2015 ). However, the impact of LUCC cannot be ignored. LUCC effects on hydrological processes include alterations in canopy interception, soil infiltration capacity, evapotranspiration and surface and subsurface runoff generation (Chilagane et al., 2021; Getachew et al., 2021; Gwate et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2018 ), leading to changes in flood frequency and risk (Nayak et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2015 ). Therefore, a fully understanding of hydrological responses to changing land surfaces is essential for sustainable water resource management (Ahmed et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024; Narsimlu et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2018 ). Three methods are generally used to evaluate the effects of LUCC on watershed hydrological processes including paired watershed experiments, analysis using a time series of hydrological data, and assessment using hydrological modeling (Liu et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2018 ). For paired watershed experiments, it can be difficult to set a strict paired watershed and apply it to medium to large basins, and when using a time series of hydrological data, the physical mechanisms and detailed land surface information are often lacking (Yan et al., 2018 ). Therefore, hydrological modeling has become a major approach for studying hydrological process responses to LUCC. Some models, such as Soil and Water Assessment Tool, are widely used to evaluate LUCC effects on hydrological processes by forcing the model with land use and land cover data every five to ten years (Getachew et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2023; Nepal et al., 2023; Paul et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2024 ). A few studies have used the Budyko framework to investigate the impacts of vegetation cover change or ecological restoration on watershed water yield or streamflow by applying simple parameters linked to land surfaces (Feng et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2021 ). Temporal dynamic land use data could reasonably represent LUCC in watersheds and improve model accuracy (Nepal et al., 2023 ). However, only a few periods of land use cover data were used in these studies, and they mainly focused on vegetation type or area changes, without considering the growth status of vegetation (Ji et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2022 ). In fact, vegetation quality changes can have a more considerable impact on runoff dynamics than vegetation area changes (Yu et al., 2023 ). LUCC and its consequent hydrological impacts have aroused growing concern worldwide, and a more in-depth understanding is needed to separate and quantify the effects of vegetation area and its growth status changes on watershed hydrological processes. The source region of the Yellow River (SRYR) —the most critical runoff generation region of the Yellow River—accounts for 35 % of the total annual runoff for the entire basin, although it contains only ∼16 % of the total basin area (Wang et al., 2018 ). Grasslands occupy >72 % of the total SRYR area (Hu et al., 2014 ) and 50 % of the Yellow River Basin total area (Ji et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023 ), and play a critical role in ecological protection and soil water conservation (Wang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, grassland changes in the SRYR could have a notable impact on the water cycle of the entire basin, which could affect ecohydrological processes in the middle and lower reaches (Wang et al., 2023a ). Previous studies conducted in the SRYR report a decrease in high-cover grassland with concomitant increases in low- and medium-cover grasslands between 1975 and 2005 (Hu et al., 2014 ), in parallel with increases in the leaf area index (LAI) (Qin, 2018 ) and net primary productivity of vegetation (Zhao, 2021 ). Water use efficiency was consequently enhanced from around 2000 onwards (Liu et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023b ), indicating considerable changes in vegetation growth. Additionally, previous studies on how changes in land use affect runoff in the Yellow River Basin have analyzed the surface area of vegetation but not its state of growth (Iqbal et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b; Lu et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2021 ), even though the state of growth is an important determinant of runoff, at least in the middle reaches of the river (Li et al., 2020 ). Studies on the impacts of future land surface changes on runoff in the Yellow River Basin have also ignored changes in vegetation growth (Ji et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b ). Therefore, when studying the hydrological responses of LUCC in the SRYR, the area and growth status of grasslands should be considered, and it is necessary to further distinguish the contributions of these two aspects. Here, we applied the distributed hydrology soil vegetation model (DHSVM)—which considers parameters related to the soil, vegetation, and atmosphere as well as the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation and soil (Leroux et al., 2016; Wigmosta et al., 1994 )—to the SRYR in China to analyze how changes in grassland cover and growth status influence key hydrological variables during the period 1981–2020. Focusing on the SRYR over the past 40 years, the major objectives of this study were to quantitatively analyze grassland area trends and growth status; the hydrological responses to annual changes in grassland area and growth status; and the impacts of grassland growth status changes on critical hydrologic components in terms of runoff, soil moisture storage, evaporation, transpiration, and evapotranspiration.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The SRYR refers to the region of the Yellow River Basin above the Tangnaihai hydrological station (32° 9′ ∼ 36° 2′ N, 95° 59′ ∼ 103° 34′ E) in the northeastern part of the Tibetan Plateau, an area commonly represented as the headwater region of the Yellow River. The Tangnaihai hydrological station and 12 meteorological stations in the SRYR are shown in Fig. 1  . The source area covers 124,000 km2  and lies at altitudes ranging from 2842 to 6226 m. The terrain is high in the west and south but low in the east and north. The climate is inland alpine humid or semi-humid. Average temperatures range from −4 to 5 ℃, and average daily temperatures exceed 0 ℃ from May to September. Monthly minimum temperatures remain below zero for ∼seven months. The average annual precipitation ranges from 220 to 780 mm and varies substantially from year to year, with the precipitation falling unevenly throughout the year. Both temperature and precipitation gradually decreased from the southeast to the northwest. The multi-year average evapotranspiration of the SRYR from 2000 to 2014 was 538.61 mm (Ye et al., 2018 ). In general, the region experiences dry winters, spring droughts, and intense precipitation in the summer and autumn (June to September).  2.2 Model and data sources The DHSVM model (version 3.1.2) is a physically based, fully distributed, and time-continuous model developed at the University of Washington and the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (Wigmosta et al., 1994 ). It considers parameters related to soil, vegetation, and atmosphere, as well as the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation, soil, and other subsurface elements (Leroux et al., 2016; Wigmosta et al., 1994 ). The DHSVM model has been successfully utilized for addressing the hydrologic effects of land use change (Alvarenga et al., 2016; Thanapakpawin et al., 2007 ) and climate change (Cuo et al., 2009; Dickerson-Lange and Mitchell, 2014; Safeeq and Fares, 2012 ) with good performances. The DHSVM model can be applied over areas ranging from plots to large watershed spatial scales, and from hourly to daily timescales. It divides watershed areas into cells based on a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) grid, which is used to direct downslope water movement and extrapolate climate data. Each cell contains data on the slope, vegetation, soil, and river channels and can have up to two vegetation layers and a user-specified number of soil layers. The grid cells are hydrologically connected through surface and subsurface flow routing. At each time step, the model calculates the energy and mass balances in each cell using several modules (Wigmosta et al., 1994 ), including estimating evapotranspiration using a two-layer canopy model and Penman–Monteith equation; dividing interception by upper and lower vegetation as a function of LAI (Dickinson et al., 1991 ); simulating snow accumulation and melting on the ground using a two-layer energy balance model; describing vertical unsaturated water movement through multiple soil layers using a one-dimensional form of Darcy's Law; generating return flow and saturation overland flow using a quasi-three-dimensional method; routing lateral saturated subsurface flow through a cell-by-cell approach using either the kinematic or diffusion approximation; and simulating channel flow using a robust linear storage routing algorithm (Wigmosta et al., 2002; Wigmosta et al., 1994 ). Evaporation in the DHSVM model consists of two parts: evaporation from the interception for each vegetation layer (EInt) and evaporation from the upper soil layer (EvapSoil). The DHSVM model adopts monthly LAI as an indicator of grassland growth status, used as a multiplier in precipitation interception, canopy conductance, and turbulent energy flux attenuation calculations (Wigmosta et al., 2002; Wigmosta et al., 1994 ). Furthermore, LAI is widely used to describe the photosynthetic and transpiration surfaces of plant canopies (Chen et al., 1997 ). Therefore, we used LAI to reflect the grassland growth status in the SRYR to determine its relationship with hydrological responses. The model was run using the data described in Table 1   and according to the process shown in Fig. 2  . The raster input datasets listed in Table 1  were resampled with a consistent spatial resolution of 500 m, and processed into bin format using scripts provided by the DHSVM model. The major soil textures in the SRYR are silty loam and loam, with an area percentages of 66.5 and 27.3, respectively. Stream network data were generated for the SRYR at 500 m spatial resolution based on the DEM and region mask, along with the initial distribution of total soil depth in the SRYR, with values ranging from 0.76 to 1.278 m. A specific algorithm script provided in the DHSVM package (https://github.com/pnnl/DHSVM-PNNL ) was used to estimate soil depth based on slope, upstream catchment area, and DEM. The stream classification was based on the stream order and segment slope derived from the DEM. Channel geometric parameters were estimated from Google Earth satellite imagery data, and the parameters of Manning's friction coefficient and max infiltration were taken from the sample data (https://www.pnnl.gov/sites/default/files/media/file/DHSVM%203.1.2_0.zip ). The model tracked changes in the surface area of three grassland types: low (25–50 %), medium-(50–75 %), and high-cover (75–100 %). We ignored the negligible proportion of grasslands with < 25 % coverage. The model also tracked changes in monthly average LAI as a measure of grassland growth for each grassland type (Table A.1 ). The grassland changes were set in terms of grassland area and growth status, both of which were reflected in the land use data of the DHSVM model. Changes in the distribution of high-, medium-, and low-cover grasslands were used to reflect the hydrological response to changes in the grassland area, and changes in the LAI of high-, medium-, and low-cover grasslands were used to reflect the hydrological response to changes in the grassland growth status. The monthly zonal mean LAI was extracted for the three grassland types (Table A.1 ). The model was forced with meteorological input data at the site level (12 sites, Fig. 1 ), including air temperature, wind speed, relative humidity, shortwave radiation, longwave radiation and precipitation, obtained from the China Meteorological Data Service Centre (https://data.cma.cn/ ). The model was performed from January 1, 1981 to December 31, 2020, with a calibration period from January 1, 1981 to December 31, 2010, and a validation period from January 1, 2011 to December 31, 2020. Several simulations were conducted at a temporal resolution of 3 h and spatial resolution of 500 m (Table 2  ). Scenario S1 examined the hydrological responses of the SRYR to concomitant changes in grassland cover and growth, whereas scenarios S2 and S3 separated the influence of each type of change. Scenarios S4–S7 explored the responses against the background of three levels of grassland degradation and one level of grassland restoration. To study the effects of land use change, the same set of climate data was used for all scenarios. Because the proportion of low-cover grasslands was relatively small, the LAI in the scenarios varied only in high and medium-cover grasslands, giving rise to three degradation scenarios and one restoration scenario. We extracted model outputs in the SRYR, including streamflow, soil moisture storage, evapotranspiration, evaporation (including EInt and EvapSoil), and transpiration, for the period from January 1, 1981 to December 31, 2020. A three-month warm-up period was applied to each simulation. Here, the runoff response to grassland dynamics was represented by water volume changes at the outlet (Tangnaihai station) of the SRYR.  2.3 Calibration of model parameters and model validation The model parameters were calibrated based on scenario S0 by trial-and-error, as described for a similar environment in Northwest China (Zhang, 2017; Zhao, 2019 ). Calibration of the DHSVM model was a labor-intensive process performed using a two-step approach. First, the key sensitivity parameters were adjusted to approximate the simulated to the observed discharge at Tangnaihai hydrological station. Second, the parameters were adjusted using the control variable and iterative method to obtain the best simulation performance for discharge at Tangnaihai station. The adjustment of each parameter was limited by maintaining it within a known or assumed range. Regardless of the basin (tropical versus temperate) or land cover scenario (forest versus grassland), special attention should be paid to the following parameters during model calibration: lateral saturated hydraulic conductivity, exponential decrease in conductivity, porosity, vegetation height, LAI, and vapor pressure deficit (Cuo et al., 2011 ). When grassland is the dominant land cover, calibration efforts should place more emphasis on soil and understory vegetation properties (Cuo et al., 2011 ). Here, the calibrated parameters were divided into three categories: global, vegetation and soil. The final calibrated values of these parameters are listed in Table 3  . The Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), coefficient of determination (R2 ), and RMSE-observations standard deviation ratio (RSR) were used to assess the model performance. The NSE is defined as:(1) N S E = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s , i   - Q s i m , i      2   ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s , i   - Q o b s    ¯      2           The R2  is defined as:(2) R  2  = ∑ i = 1  n  Q obs , i   - Q obs    ¯     Q sim , i   - Q sim    ¯      ∑ i = 1  n  Q obs , i   - Q obs    ¯      2    ∑ i = 1  n  Q sim , i   - Q sim    ¯      2         2       The RSR is defined as:(3) R S R = RMSE  STDEV  obs    = ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s , i   - Q s i m , i      2    ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s , i   - Q o b s    ¯      2         where Q o b s , i    , Q sim , i    , Q o b s    ¯     and Q sim    ¯     are the observed, simulated, mean of the observed, and mean of the simulated discharges at the Tangnaihai hydrological station, respectively, and n is the total number of data points corresponding to the number of time increments over a given period. The NSE assumes values in the range of −∞ to 1, where the values close to one indicate better performance. R2  describes the proportion of the variance in the measured data explained by the model and ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating less error. RSR varies from an optimal value of 0 to a large positive value. The lower the RSR, the lower the RMSE, and the better the model simulation performance (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). The daily and monthly validation indicators were high for both the calibration period (1981–2010) and the validation period (2011–2020) (Table 4  , Fig. A.1 ), suggesting reliable model performance.   3 Results 3.1 Grassland dynamics in the SRYR During the study period (1981–2020), the grassland surface area in the SRYR decreased by 1110 km2  or 1.13 % of the area in 1981 (Fig. 3  a). Before 2000, the area fluctuated, but tended to decrease after 2000. This decrease was 2.5 % in high-cover grassland and concomitant increases were 7.05 % and 3.86 % in low-cover grassland and medium-cover grassland, respectively. In contrast, the state of growth in grasslands, based on LAI, remained fairly constant from 1981 to 2000 but tended to increase from 2000 (Fig. 3 b). These patterns were observed in all three grassland types.  3.2 Hydrological responses to grassland historical dynamics We examined the combined influence of changes in grassland area and growth on runoff, soil moisture storage, and evapotranspiration in the SRYR. For this purpose, we subtracted the output of scenario S1 from that of scenario S0. For all three hydrological variables, the effects of the grassland dynamics differed substantially before and after 2000. The intensity of negative effects on runoff increased throughout the study period with the trends becoming more severe after 2000 (Fig. 4  a). From 1981 to 2000 and 2000 to 2020, the negative effects of grassland dynamics on average annual water volume increased by 0.7 % (120 million m3 ) and 4.3 % (706 million m3 ), respectively—proportions calculated by dividing the annual average difference by the historical annual average of the corresponding hydrological variable. A positive effect of grassland dynamics was observed for the average annual soil moisture storage, with an increase of 1.2 % (2.7 mm) from 1981 to 2000 (Fig. 4 b). Meanwhile, the positive effect was strengthened gradually from 2000 to 2020 by increasing soil moisture storage by 2.9 % (6.1 mm) (Fig. 4 b). Grassland dynamics enhanced evapotranspiration during the study period (Fig. 4 c). From 1981 to 2000 and 2000 to 2020, the average annual evapotranspiration was enhanced by 1.7 % (2.7 mm) and 9.4 % (15.3 mm), respectively. The positive effects of grassland dynamics on evapotranspiration continued to increase, particularly after 2000. We examined whether particular months or seasons contributed more to the differences between scenarios S0 and S1 and found that July made the largest contribution (Fig. 4 d), which indicated that runoff changes during the grassland growing season contributed more to the water volume differences between the two scenarios than that during the non-growing season. After considering the joint contribution of changes in grassland area and grassland growth to hydrological processes, we examined the contributions of each separately. In both cases, the influence of each type of change showed substantially different trends up to, and after 2000. Comparing scenarios S0 and S2 to isolate the influence of changes in grassland surface area, we found that the influence was minimal from 1981 to 2000, with the average annual water volume remaining nearly constant at ∼3.1 million m3 ; however, after 2000, it decreased by 0.2 % (29 million m3 ) (Fig. 5  a). Changes in grassland area led to weak decreases in soil moisture storage until 2000, after which they led to stronger increases (Fig. 5 b). Grassland area changes slightly decreased evapotranspiration from 1981 to 2000, after which they strongly enhanced the process (Fig. 5 c). Comparing scenarios S0 and S3 to isolate the influence of changes in grassland growth state, we found that their influence was extremely strong throughout the study period, accounting for ∼95 % of the runoff variation caused by the combined effects of changes in grassland area and growth state. Changes in grassland growth on their own decreased runoff throughout the study period, but much more so after 2000—the decrease in water volume was 0.7 % (125 million m3 ) up to 2000, and 3.6 % (660 million m3 ) after 2000 (Fig. 5 d). The negative effects of grassland growth on runoff increased gradually during both periods, particularly after 2000. Conversely, changes in grassland growth enhanced soil moisture storage (Fig. 5 e) and evapotranspiration (Fig. 5 f) throughout the study period, particularly after 2000. In general, the positive effects of grassland growth on soil moisture storage and evapotranspiration continues to increase separately, both particularly after 2000.  3.3 Hydrological responses to grassland degradation and restoration We conducted various scenarios (S4–S7) to examine how grassland degradation and restoration may affect hydrological processes in the SRYR. Again, we found that degradation and restoration triggered substantially different trends in these processes before and after 2000. Degradation increased water volume throughout the study period with increases of 1.1, 2.8, and 7.3 % before 2000 and 2.6, 4.4, and 9.5 % after 2000 for mild, moderate, and severe degradation, respectively (Fig. 6  a, Table 5  ). The magnitude of the increase was proportional to the severity of degradation, with heavy degradation having a much stronger impact than light and moderate degradation. Opposing results were observed for the influence of degradation on soil moisture storage (Fig. 6 b, Table 5 ). Degradation decreased soil moisture storage throughout the study period with decreases of 0.8, 2.0, and 5.2 % before 2000 and 1.9, 3.2, and 6.8 % after 2000 for mild, moderate, and severe degradation, respectively. Similarly, the average annual evapotranspiration deceased by 2.9–21.6 % prior to 2000 and by 5.5–23.2 % thereafter (Fig. 6 c, Table 5 ). The magnitude of the decrease was proportional to the degradation severity. Grassland restoration had opposite effects on hydrological processes as that of degradation. It reduced the water volume throughout the study period, with a decrease of 0.4 % (73 million m3 ) prior 2000 and 0.9 % (155 million m3 ) thereafter (Fig. 6 a). The opposite results were observed for soil moisture storage with an increase of 0.3 % prior to 2000 and 0.7 % thereafter (Fig. 6 b). The average annual evapotranspiration increased by 0.9 % prior to 2000 and 1.7 % thereafter (Fig. 6 c). In the presence of such degradation or restoration, runoff was primarily affected between June and October, and particularly in August (Fig. 6 d). Changes in grassland area or growth due to degradation or restoration altered runoff more during the growing season than the non-growing season of grassland.  3.4 Analysis of evaporation and transpiration in each scenario Under the combined influence of changes in grassland surface area and in grassland growth, evaporation and transpiration increased by 1.4 % (1.4 mm) and 2.3 % (1.3 mm), respectively (Fig. 7  a) in the dynamically enhanced evapotranspiration of grassland from 1981 to 2000, while the increases from 2000 to 2020 were 8.4 % (8.3 mm), and 11.1 % (7.1 mm), respectively. EInt dominated the change in evaporation compared to EvapSoil (Fig. 7 b). The consistency of evaporation and transpiration changes was also reflected in the respective effects of grassland area and growth status on hydrological processes (Fig. 8  a, b). The change in grassland growth status had a greater impact on evaporation and transpiration (Fig. 8 a, b), and was mainly reflected in EInt (Fig. 8 c, d). Degradation reduced both evaporation and transpiration and subsequently evapotranspiration (Fig. 9  a, b). The reduction in transpiration contributed more to the decrease in evapotranspiration than the reduction in evaporation, particularly after 2000 (Table 5 ). The opposite trend was observed in the restoration scenario (Table 5 ). For evaporation, the results showed that the reduction in evaporation from canopy interception completely controlled the total decrease in evaporation under grassland degradation scenarios (Fig. 9 c, d), although the evaporation from soil surface showed slight enhancement (Fig. 9 d). In addition, the situation was contrary under the restoration scenario (Fig. 9 c,d). Overall, the evaporation from the canopy interception rather than from the soil surface dominated the variation of total evaporation.   4 Discussion Our study analyzed how changes in grassland surface area and growth affect runoff, soil moisture storage, and evapotranspiration in the SRYR. Our work suggests that although the total surface area of grassland decreased from 1981 to 2020 in the source area, grassland growth (represented by LAI) improved continuously. This positive development over the past 40 years was associated with a 2.03 % and 5.66 % increase in soil moisture storage and evapotranspiration, respectively, resulting in a 2.41 % decrease in runoff. As a result of the improvement in vegetation growth, the transpiration and evaporation of precipitation intercepted by the vegetation canopy increased. Our results also indicated that evaporation from canopy interception dominated the variation in total evaporation. A previous study also showed that an increase in LAI and evapotranspiration at the beginning of the growing season in the SRYR over the past 30 years caused the runoff coefficient to decrease (Qin et al., 2017 ). Our model results suggest that the increase in evapotranspiration and soil moisture storage during the study period explains the decrease in runoff because the meteorological conditions were kept consistent under different simulations. These hydrological changes appear to be responses nearly exclusively to changes in the grassland growth state, primarily during the major grassland growing season of summer, with minimal influences from changes in grassland surface area. We found that changes in grassland surface area or growth state influenced hydrological processes in the SRYR in substantially different ways before and after 2000. This may be related to the various ecological restoration policies that took effect throughout the year, including the return of pasture to grassland and the closure of mountains to grazing (Chen et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2021 ). The water conservation capacity of the SRYR improved during the process of restoration and reconstruction (Shui et al., 2017 ), and the efficiency of rainfall resource utilization was notably improved. LAI has positive effects on evapotranspiration and soil moisture and further reduces the water availability and runoff (Huang et al., 2019 ). Soil water content decreases considerably in moderately and severely degraded grasslands (Chen et al., 2020; You et al., 2015 ), due to the flat terrain of the grassland which is conducive to rainfall infiltration (Zhao, 2019 ). The water consumption of grasslands is low, and shallow root water consumption depths can be easily supplemented by rainfall (Wang et al., 2020 ). Over the last 40 years, the surface area of grasslands in the SRYR has not notably changed, whereas the growth state of grassland has improved. These results are broadly consistent with those of previous studies (Hu et al., 2014; Qin, 2018; Zhao, 2021 ). Land surface change is a comprehensive product of climate change and human activity (Cuo et al., 2009 ), and the reasons for enhanced grassland growth can be considered from these two aspects. Plant phenology is affected by climate warming, which leads to advanced spring and delayed autumn phenology (Piao et al., 2019 ). This validates our findings regarding increases in temperature and longwave radiation in the SRYR (Fig. A.2 ). Consequently, the length of the vegetation growing season of is extended (Menzel et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016 ), especially in the semiarid and semi-humid regions of China (Chen et al., 2022 ). Most studies have focused only on the changes in vegetation area while investigating the hydrological responses to land surface changes (Ji et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b ). Our results suggest that changes in the grassland growth status can influence hydrological processes in the SRYR to a much greater extent than changes in the grassland surface area. Indeed, we found that changes in grassland growth alone accounted for 95 % of the runoff changes caused by overall grassland dynamics in the SRYR. The much stronger influence of grassland growth than grassland area may help explain why, in our simulations, growth during the summer months influenced runoff more than growth during other months. Summer is the major growing season for grasses, during which evapotranspiration is at its peak. Our simulations—based on different scenarios of grassland degradation in the source area—showed increases in runoff and decreases in evapotranspiration and soil moisture storage. The decreasing evaporation was controlled by the reduction in evaporation from canopy interception due to grassland degradation, although evaporation from the soil surface was slightly enhanced with grassland degradation. Interestingly, we did not observe substantial hydrological differences between scenarios involving light and intermediate degradation, whereas the hydrological effects in scenarios involving heavy degradation were greater than the combined effects of light and intermediate degradation. Restoration reversed these trends, leading to greater evapotranspiration and lower runoff, consistent with studies based on other hydrological models (Hu et al., 2021 ). Refinement of our approach should consider the uncertainties involved in this study. First, for the input data, information on grassland area and growth status was retrieved from the LUCC and LAI datasets, respectively. The two datasets were produced from different remote sensing data sources, and there may be some uncertainties when considering the joint effects of grassland area and growth status. LAI data were extracted from two remote sensing sensor data sources to create a long-term series of growth statuses. In addition, there were only 12 meteorological stations in the SRYR, which may have introduced a certain level of uncertainty in the model simulation and also during the process of unifying the spatial resolution of the input data. Second, in the model calibration process, we only considered certain sensitive parameters, whereas others may have a notable impact. Moreover, the current parameter calibration process is based on a manual approach, which may make it difficult to determine the optimal combination of parameters. Finally, further studies are needed to consider the snowfall, freezing and thawing processes, which are also essential to the hydrological responses in the SRYR.  5 Conclusions In the SRYR, a negative effect of grassland dynamics on the average annual runoff was detected during the past 40 years, which was enhanced continuously, particularly after 2000. The major reason for this was the continuously increasing positive effects of grassland dynamics on evapotranspiration, transpiration, and evaporation, particularly after 2000. The warming climate in the SRYR has extended the growing season of grasslands, resulting in improved vegetation growth. Although the grassland area in this region showed a slight decreasing trend, the grassland growth status improved, enhancing the transpiration and evaporation of intercepted precipitation, particularly during the growing season. The results show that changes in the grassland growth state can influence hydrological processes in the SRYR to a much greater extent than changes in the grassland surface area. Further simulations under different degradation and restoration scenarios revealed enhanced and reduced runoff, respectively. Future grassland management in the SRYR should fully consider the sensitivity of hydrological responses to grassland growth and distribution.
1 Introduction Since the early 1990s, machine learning (ML) methods have received increasing attention from hydrological communities (Abbott, 1991; Hsu et al., 1995; Maier et al., 2023; Nearing et al., 2021; Satour et al., 2023; Shortridge et al., 2016; Solomatine and Dulal, 2003 ). Besides achieving more accurate predictions, many studies argue that the benefits of ML in hydrology go beyond improved predictions, as they may provide interpretable information about the underlying processes − i.e., information that is understandable by human users (Cannon and McKendry, 2002; Carlisle et al., 2009; Kratzert et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022b; Razavi et al., 2022 ). The knowledge learned from such interpretable information can serve several purposes such as helping us (1) understand how model predictions were made (Carlisle et al., 2009; Li et al., 2022a ), (2) identify model limitations to guide future model development directions (Fleming et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021a; Razavi, 2021; Sheikholeslami and Razavi, 2020 ), and (3) characterize the status and changes in watershed hydrologic regime, thus further facilitating water resources management (Wang et al., 2022a ). Various methods have been proposed to derive interpretable information from ML models, primarily under graphical or quantitative frameworks. For graphical interpretation of model behaviors, Friedman (2001)  proposed the partial dependence (PD) plot, which illustrates how changes in the value of an input variable are associated with changes in the prediction of the model, on average. Plate et al. (2000)  proposed the ‘effect plot’ for visualizing and interpreting variable importance, interaction strength, and nonlinearity of input–output relationships. Advanced upon PD plot, Goldstein et al. (2015)  proposed the individual conditional expectation (ICE) plot, which visualizes the dependence of the prediction on an input variable for each sample separately. More recently, Apley and Zhu (2020)  proposed the accumulated local effects (ALE) plot, which looks at how small changes in an input variable value (within a certain range) affect the model predictions. Graphical interpretation methods have been reported effective in hydrological studies; for example, Carlisle et al. (2009)  used PD plots to find potential thresholds in stream conditions and disturbances, and Cannon and McKendry (2002)  used effect plots to study variables operating under conditions of pre-monsoon phenomena. Fleming et al. (2021)  employed graphical analysis to investigate feature-target relationships, revealing nonlinear physical hydrological processes like climate elasticity. However, these graphical methods face limitations in handling large-scale cases, such as those involving hundreds of watersheds, where these methods can become overwhelming and less effective in capturing the whole picture across watersheds. Compared with graphical interpretation, quantitative variable importance is a more straightforward interpretation approach, which measures the contribution of individual input variables (e.g., precipitation and snowmelt) in explaining the predictive accuracy or variability of the response variable (e.g., streamflow). Quantitative variable importance can be classified as either local or global. Local variable importance (LVI) mainly focuses on the contribution of individual input variables (e.g., the contribution of rainfall, snowmelt, and soil moisture) on the predictive accuracy for a specific data point (e.g., a particular observed streamflow level at a given timestep). LVI is usually achieved by exploring models with various types of diagnostic tools (Nearing et al., 2021 ), such as integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017 ) and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) value (Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ). Unlike LVI, global (or average) variable importance (GVI) estimates the contribution of each input variable on the predictive accuracy across the entire dataset (e.g., streamflow values at all observed levels for the entire period). GVI has been implemented via both model-agnostic and model-specific approaches (Molnar, 2020 ). The most commonly used model-agnostic approach is the permutation feature importance (PFI) (Breiman, 2001 ), which treats the trained model as a black box, and evaluates its response by perturbing the inputs (Ribeiro et al., 2016 ). More recently, Sun et al. (2021)  applied the integral gradient (IG) method to quantify contribution of input variables to streamflow prediction over the contiguous United States. In comparison, model-specific approaches depend on the structure of specific interpretable ML models. For example, random forest (RF) (Breiman, 2001 ) uses mean decrease impurity (MDI) to measure the GVI of each variable in reducing the predictive error of the response variable, or extreme gradient boosting (Chen et al., 2015 ) measures the GVI based on the reduction in a loss function. The aforementioned quantitative variable importance methods have been reported effective in many hydrological studies, for example, to analyze runoff-generation driving factors (Wang et al., 2022a ), optimize the model input variables for monthly streamflow forecasting (Ahmed et al., 2021 ), and gain insights into flood generation mechanisms (Schmidt et al., 2020 ). However, most of these methods, which we refer to as ‘model-dependent approaches’, rely on specific predictive models and evaluation metrics (like mean squared error) to measure GVI. Consequently, the inferred relationship between input variables and model responses is inherently dependent on the chosen predictive model and its accuracy. This dependency may limit, even possibly obscure, the new knowledge gained through variable importance analyses, particularly in the field of hydrology, where models are not perfect and suffer from equifinality issues (Beven, 2006; Guillaume et al., 2019 ). This means that models with different structures and/or parameters can produce similar behaviors and fit the data comparably well, whether they are process-based (Beven, 2006 ) or data-driven (Schmidt et al., 2020 ). Under such conditions, different input variables may lead to similar model outputs, making interpretations difficult. To address this issue, very few methods have shifted focus from a model-dependent approach to direct analysis of hydroclimatic data without any assumptions about the underlying processes – this is referred to as the ‘model-independent approach’ here. An example method with this approach is Data-Driven Variogram Analysis of Response Surfaces (D-VARS), introduced by Sheikholeslami and Razavi (2020) , which is formally rooted in the concepts of global sensitivity analysis (Saltelli et al., 2021 ). D-VARS can perform sensitivity analysis on any data sample, regardless of how it is obtained, and thus does not require a predictive model to relate inputs and outputs. Essentially, the sensitivity index of an output to different inputs across the entire data space is a representation of GVI. Similarly, Li et al. (2021a)  proposed the Wilks feature importance (WFI) to measure the contribution of input variables in explaining the variability of the response variable(s) – a manifestation of GVI. This approach relies on statistical hypothesis testing and operates independently of any specific models or evaluation metrics. Both D-VARS and WFI have already shown robust performance in providing variable rankings in some test problems; however, their potential for gaining insights into hydrological processes remains largely unexplored. GVI can offer valuable alternative insights compared to those obtained from process-based models, which rely on intermediate state variables (such as soil moisture) to provide the rationales of the underlying mechanisms. ML models typically circumvent the direct representation of the relevant mechanisms by relying on ‘surrogate variables’. Such an approach is rooted in statistical hydrology techniques of the 1980s (Rao and Quillan, 1982 ), and has been a fundamental component of statistical flood forecast models since then. For instance, Shortridge et al. (2016)  and Ahmed et al. (2021)  used time-lagged (e.g., 1-month-lagged) precipitation and other climatic variables as surrogates to approximately represent antecedent catchment conditions for monthly streamflow simulations. The obtained GVI based on these surrogate variables will carry information on how antecedent catchment conditions influence monthly streamflow processes. However, the traditional use of surrogate information has limitations from the interpretation perspective. Firstly, the associated GVI primarily reflects the extent to which the variability can be explained by surrogates with specified lagged periods (Li et al., 2022b ), and further understanding between those surrogates and underlying processes (e.g., soil moisture and snowmelt) are limited. This limitation has been particularly challenging the existing ML approaches in modeling and interpreting hydrological processes in arid regions where soil moisture plays a critical role in surface runoff generations (Feng et al., 2020; Gauch et al., 2021; Hunt et al., 2022; Kratzert et al., 2018 ), and alpine regions where knowing the contribution of snowmelt and rainfall to streamflow generation has been a major concern to water resources management under changing climatic conditions (Avanzi et al., 2019; Frame et al., 2021; Konapala et al., 2020; Uysal et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022b ). In light of the above considerations, our objective in this study is to leverage the recently advanced model-independent interpretation methods, namely WFI and D-VARS, to gain insights into hydrological processes. This study entails (1) testing the variable ranking consistency of these methods through identifying the controlling factors influencing monthly streamflow variability over 600 catchments in the contiguous United States (CONUS); (2) qualitatively and quantitively investigating the effectiveness of surrogate variables of soil moisture and snowmelt, benchmarked against the reanalysis-based data on the original variables; (3) uncovering and addressing the ML challenges that may be encountered in monthly streamflow simulation over various runoff-generation mechanisms, including rainfall-runoff, snowmelt runoff, and the seasonal dominance of both processes. We anticipate the new insights gained in this study will cast new light onto the dynamics and controls of hydrological processes and inform future directions of streamflow modeling and data collection efforts, thus further facilitating water resources management.  2 Experimental approach 2.1 Interpretation method The main interpretation method used in this study is Wilks feature importance (WFI) (Li et al., 2021a ), which uses Wilks Ʌ statistics (Nath and Pavur, 1985; Wilks, 1967 ) to quantify the contribution of input variables on the variability of one or more response variables. WFI recognizes that the variability of the response variables can be quantified stepwise through a series of binary decisions based on the input variables (Li et al., 2021a ). These binary decisions recursively divide the data into smaller, more homogenous subsets, leading to a tree-like structure, termed an inference tree. Global variable importance (GVI) is then determined through the inference process of the tree. Binary decisions are a well-established practice that not only offers a balance between interpretability and computational efficiency, but also proves effective in capturing complex, non-linear relationships within the data (Breiman et al., 1984 ). WFI was successful in identifying the top-ranked input variables for achieving improved performance of the RF model when compared to top-ranked input variables identified by model-dependent methods such as PFI and MDI (Li et al., 2021a ). This positions WFI as a valuable variable selection tool in the initial stages of the modeling process. We use the following numeric case to illustrate WFI: suppose a dataset (Fig. 1  ) including 20 flood events (discontinuously sampled from a time-series) and 3 predictors as X1    (i.e., daily precipitation in mm), X2    (i.e., 3-day cumulative precipitation in mm leading up to present day) and X3    (i.e., daily temperature in degrees Celsius), and a response Y   (i.e., daily flow volume in m3 /s). It’s important to note that WFI is capable of handling multi-response problems, enabling the simultaneous consideration of multiple response variables (such as flood peak, volume, and water levels) in evaluating the contribution of input variables (refer to the dual-response case provided through the link in the “Data and Code Availability” section). For clearer and more direct hydrological interpretation, this case study employs WFI in a single-response scenario (i.e., flood peaks). The WFI evaluation starts with the following five steps: (1) Sorting the value of Xj    (j   indicates the column index of the predictors) in ascending order, and the Y   column will be reordered accordingly. (2) For each instance of Xj    from the top, we can use X  (z, j  ) to horizontally divide the predictor space (i.e., the three-column matrix in this case) into two subspaces as X1    and X2   , where X  (z, j  ) represents the z  th  element of j  th  predictor. Therefore, X1    = {x1,j   , x2,j   , …, xz,j   }; and X2    = {xz+1,j   , xz+2,j   , …, xk,j   } (where k   is the number of rows of Xj   ). The response space (i.e., the one-dimensional matrix in this case) Y   will be correspondingly divided into two subspaces as Y1    and Y2   , where Y1    = {y1   , y2   , …, yz   } and Y2    = {yz+1   , yz+2   , …, yk   }. (3) Then, the likelihood of whether Y1    and Y2    are sampled from populations with different means will be measured through the Wilks Ʌ statistics, which is defined as Ʌ = Det(W) /Det(B+W) , where Det  is the determinant of a matrix. The matrices W  and B  are analogous to ‘within-groups sum of squares’ and ‘between-groups sum of squares’ in a standard one-way analysis of variance, respectively. The W  and B  can be given by:(1) W = ∑ i = 1  z  Y 1  ( i )  - Y 1   ¯       ′  · Y 1  ( i )  - Y 1   ¯       + ∑ i = 1  k - z   Y 2  ( i )  - Y 2   ¯       ′  · Y 2  ( i )  - Y 2   ¯           (2) B = z · ( k - z )  z + k - z       ( Y 1   ¯   - Y 2   ¯   )  ′  · ( Y 1   ¯   - Y 2   ¯   )      where Y  1   ¯      and Y  2   ¯      represent the mean values of two subspaces Y1    and Y2   , respectively. z   and (k-z )  are the number of instances for the subspaces Y1    and Y2   , respectively. Y1  (i )  and Y2  (i )  are the i  th  element of Y1    and Y2   , respectively. The value of Ʌ is a measure of the extent to which Xj    can differentiate Y1    from Y2   . The smaller Ʌ value represents a more significant difference between Y1    and Y2   . (4) According to Rao’s F -approximation (Rao, 1952 ) and also the Supplementary material , Wilk’s Ʌ statistic under the above two groups of samples can be used to perform the F-test as follows:(3) F ( m , k - m - 1 )  = 1 - Λ  Λ  · k - m - 1  m      where m   is the number of predictands (in this case, m   = 1), and k   is the number of instances for both Y1    and Y2   . The null hypothesis would be H0 : Y  1   ¯       =  Y  2   ¯      versus the alternative hypothesis H1 : Y  1   ¯       ≠  Y  2   ¯     . (5) Let the significance level be α   (which is set as 0.05 in this study); if Fcalculated   ≥ F α   , we reject H0  , implying that the difference between the two subspaces is significant and thus they should be split (as illustrated in panel a   from level 1 to level 2). Otherwise (i.e., Fcalculated   < F α   ), we accept H0   and keep the two subspaces unchanged. Such a splitting process will be recursively repeated (as illustrated in panel a  ) until any newly generated subspace can no longer be split. Then, the merging process will be followed by examining any pairs of subspaces meeting the criteria of Fcalculated   < F α   . Such splitting and merging processes are iteratively performed until no node can be further split or merged. Once an inference tree is built, the initial WFI importance score for the variable Xj    is defined as:(4) W F I X j     = ∑ s  P s  · 1  -   Λ ( j , s )          where s   is the splitable nodes (i.e., ovels in Panel a  ), Ps    is the fraction of instances falling into s  , Ʌ (j, s  ) denotes the value of Ʌ obtained at the optimum splitting point of s   with predictor j  . The relative importance score for a particular variable is achieved by dividing the total initial importance score. The predictors with higher relative importance will lead to higher explanations for the variability of the response variable. To increase the robustness of the relative importance score, WFI is performed under the framework of the bootstrap ensemble, allowing the GVI to be estimated from the medians of hundreds of ensemble members. The ensemble of GVI is assumed to be more robust than any of the individual sets of GVI.  2.2 Hydrological interpretation from WFI inference processes WFI is more than a metric measuring the contribution of variables in explaining the variability of response; it is a summarization of the underlying hydrological processes. The inference process of WFI can be illustrated using the above numeric case in Fig. 1 : in the first node splitting process, entire flood peak values were split using criteria of a daily precipitation threshold of 94.6 mm. This threshold, which yields a Ʌ value of 0.17, effectively separates two distinct flood groups, indicating that such a precipitation threshold can strongly distinguish two groups of floods. Such numerical thresholding in flow generation agrees with physical processes governing flow generation observed in previous experimental studies (McDonnell et al., 2021; Tromp-van Meerveld and McDonnell, 2006 ). In the next step, the subgroup with lower flood magnitudes is further split using the criteria of daily precipitation volume of 58.6 mm, a threshold that moderately distinguishes small and moderate flood events with a Ʌ value equal to 0.36. When conducting the sub-node split further, daily precipitation is no longer the primary differentiator of flood events. Instead, 3-day cumulative precipitation of 37.5 mm becomes a threshold to differentiate two groups of flood events with Ʌ value equals 0.24, suggesting that the group with higher floods is contributed from higher antecedent soil moisture. Therefore, the cascade sequences of criteria throughout such an inference tree help explain the flow generation from a combination of events, demonstrating the interpretability of WFI from the perspective of model internal components. The GVI derived from WFI reflects the degree of hydrological behaviors that can be differentiated by corresponding input variables.  2.3 Benchmark method D-VARS was chosen as an alternative method to compare with WFI, particularly in terms of variable ranking consistency. Its selection is because of its model-independent nature, providing a comparable basis for analysis. The GVI calculation in D-VARS differs fundamentally from that in WFI. To measure the GVI, D-VARS assumes that there exists a response surface as a function of input variables. D-VARS seeks to empirically derive the directional variograms of this response surface in the direction of each individual input and then interprets them in terms of input importance (Sheikholeslami and Razavi, 2020 ) This novel approach is formally grounded in global sensitivity analysis (Saltelli et al., 2021 ) and is a data-driven version of the variogram analysis of response surfaces (VARS) framework (Razavi and Gupta, 2016a; Razavi and Gupta, 2016b ). A comprehensive explanation of D-VARS can be found in the methodology section of the publication by Sheikholeslami and Razavi (2020) .  2.4 Data preprocessing Catchment Attributes and Meteorological for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) (Addor et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2015 ) and ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ) are the datasets used to investigate the effectiveness of surrogate information in representing snowmelt and soil moisture dynamics. CAMELS contains ground observation-based meteorological forcings (Thornton et al., 2022 ) and streamflow data for 671 catchments across the contiguous United States, spanning from 1980 to 2014. The meteorological forcing data consist of basin-average daily weather parameters, including temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure, solar radiation, and day length. ERA5-Land is an improved version of the land component of the ERA5 climate reanalysis (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ), featuring greater accuracy for all types of land applications, including a higher resolution of 9 km compared to 31 km in ERA5. The renovated land surface model embedded in ERA5-Land improved the characterization of soil moisture and snowmelt compared with its predecessors (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ). In this study, four layers of volumetric soil water (m3 /m3 ) and snowmelt (m) from 1980 to 2014 were used in the modeling processes. These reanalysis variables were used to represent the benchmark data of soil water and snowmelt since they are the highest quality data available to us. The volumetric soil water data are estimated from a combination of data sources, including remote sensing data, in-situ measurements, and landcover information. The detailed representation of volumetric soil water data is represented in Fig. 6  of section 4.1 . Snowmelt in ERA5-Land is represented by the amount of snow water equivalent (SWE) that has melted over a specific period. To estimate the SWE, the land surface model in ERA5-Land uses a density parameter that relates the mass of snow to its volume. This density parameter varies with the temperature and age of the snow, and is updated as the snowpack evolves over time. The estimated SWE is then validated against available observations of snow depth and snow water equivalent from a variety of sources, including ground-based measurements and satellite data. Even though both datasets were available at daily resolution, spatial and temporal discrepancies exist due to various factors, such as original data sources, collection methods, spatial resolution, data processing algorithms, and assimilation techniques. Such discrepancies may potentially hinder interpretation and thus need to be addressed. To compensate for spatial discrepancy, the gridded ERA5-Land data were spatially aggregated based on catchment boundaries to match the CAMELS dataset. Then, both datasets were resampled into monthly resolution by averaging to compensate for the temporal discrepancy.  2.5 Evaluation of the effectiveness of surrogate information Two experiments were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of surrogate information compared to reanalysis data. In the first experiment, ten climatic input variables from CAMELS forcings, including minimum and maximum temperature (Tmin and Tmax), precipitation (Prcp), vapor pressure (Vp), and shortwave solar radiation (SRad) for the current and the previous one months, were analyzed using WFI and D-VARS to calculate the GVI in response of the streamflow variability. In this experiment, the previous-month (i.e., 1-month lagged) climatic variables served as surrogates for the antecedent catchment conditions. The second experiment replaced the five surrogates with five reanalysis variables from ERA5-land, including 1 to 4 layers of volumetric soil water (Swvl1, Swvl2, Swvl3, and Swvl4) and snowmelt (Smlt). The first dataset was referred to as the surrogate   dataset, while the second was referred to as the reanalysis   dataset. The motivation for this experiment design is that in real-world hydrological modeling, direct observations of snowmelt and soil moisture are often unavailable. Therefore, this experiment design assumes that previous-month climatic variables can function as approximations to reanalysis-based volumetric soil water and snowmelt. This experiment provides the basis to understand the limitations of surrogates in the ML modeling processes. Comparing the variable rankings from both datasets is expected to provide a qualitative understanding of how surrogate variables function in representing snowmelt and soil water of different layers. Modeling monthly streamflow with these two datasets allows us to quantitatively assess the efficiency of these surrogates in approximating soil moisture and snowmelt. Stepwise clustered ensemble (SCE) (Li et al., 2021a ) is used for streamflow modeling purposes. SCE has been reported effective in predicting and interpreting a complex non-linear system without the need for assumptions about input–output relationships (Li et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022b; Li et al., 2021b ). The evaluation process started by dividing both datasets into training (from January 1980 to December 2005) and testing (from January 2006 to December 2014) periods and evaluated with SCE. The training data were used to identify the GVI and associated streamflow performance, while the testing data were used to validate the reliability of the identified GVI and performance. To do this, two SCE models were trained using the training period (i.e., the first 26 years) from the two datasets, with an objective function of minimizing the root mean square error (RMSE). The testing period data (i.e., the remaining nine years) were used to assess the goodness of hydrological processes reflected by surrogate and reanalysis datasets.  2.6 Evaluation metrics To investigate the predictive accuracy, the resulting monthly streamflow values for the model testing period were evaluated against three metrics: KGE (Gupta et al., 2009 ), NSE, and log-NSE (Krause et al., 2005 ). The KGE is a combined measure of correlation, standard deviation, and mean squared error, which is sensitive to flow variability.(5) KGE = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( α - 1 )  2  + ( β - 1 )  2        where r  equals the square root of R2 , α denotes the measure of relative variability in the simulated and observed values (α = σ y  ∗    / σ y    , in which σ denotes the variance of samples; y  ∗      and y    denotes simulated and observed values, respectively), and β represents the ratio of simulated and observed flow means (β = y  ∗    ¯   / y  ¯     ). The NSE is the most commonly used metric to assess the predictive power of hydrological models. It ranges from −∞ to 1 and is defined as:(6) NSE = 1 - ∑ n = 1  N  y n  - y n  ∗      2  / ∑ n = 1  N  y n  - y  ¯      2      where y  ¯      is the mean of observed daily streamflow time series; y n  ∗      is the mean of simulated daily streamflow time series; N   is the number of observations.
