In general, the result shows that the overall pattern of these two methods aligns with each other. However, the WFI assessment is more assertive in what is more important compared to D-VARS. This is likely because the D-VARS measures GVI through directional variograms and tends to average out critical information in distinguishing low and high flows. In contrast, the iteratively produced inference tree in WFI may assign higher weights to such details, leading to more distinctive importance results. The top left panel shows that both methods identify precipitation and the third layer of soil water (Swvl3) as the top two dominant factors contributing to streamflow variability. It is not surprising that Swvl3 is the second dominant factor, as the water content in this soil layer (28 cm to 100 cm) plays a significant role in the interflow process, contributing significantly to streamflow. On the other hand, Swvl1 and Swvl2 are more likely to be associated with surface runoff processes, while Swvl4 is more related to baseflow, which will be discussed in section 3.3. Additionally, the panel highlights that snowmelt (Smlt) has the highest variation in importance score, ranging from about 0.03 to 0.35 for both methods. This is because of the strong variability in topography and snow dominance of catchments. The bottom left panel of Fig. 2  demonstrates that, without direct soil water information, precipitation is given more weight to explain the variability of streamflow. The 1-month-lagged climatic variables, labeled as lagged precipitation, serve as surrogates for antecedent soil moisture conditions in characterizing the streamflow process. To explore the robustness of variable rankings, we identified the top three variables from each catchment and each method. Then, these variables were used to fit the response variable through generalized linear regression (GLR) (Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972 ). The evaluation process started by selecting the top three important variables identified by WFI or D-VARS as input variables to fit the response variable through GLR. Suppose the linear combination of identified variables can lead to a better fit (i.e., R2 ) of the response variable. In that case, they contain more information explaining the variability of the response variable, inferring that the resulting variable ranking is more robust in reducing the dimension of input variables. The right column of Fig. 2  shows that the top three variables identified from WFI can lead to a higher fit (i.e., R2 ) of the response variable over the model testing period, suggesting that these variables are more effectively in explaining the variability of streamflow.  3.2 Interpretation consistency The right panel in Fig. 3   shows that the cross-correlations among importance scores for the reanalysis dataset reveal a high level of agreement between the two interpretation methods, evidenced by a Pearson correlation coefficient (R) of 0.91. This indicates that the hydrological interpretation obtained is robust. The strong positive correlation between the importance of Swvl1 and Swvl2 (R equals 0.78 and 0.77 for WFI and D-VARS, respectively) highlights the comparable influence of water content in the top two soil layers (0 cm to 7 cm and 7 cm to 28 cm, respectively) on streamflow. However, such correlation between the second and third soil layers, and between the third and fourth soil layers (28 cm to 100 cm and 100 cm to 289 cm, respectively), is significantly dropped due to the increased soil depth. This is because deeper soil contributes less to evapotranspiration as its connection to the external environment is limited compared to shallow soil. Another example showing the consistency of the two interpretation methods is that both methods show a positive correlation between Tmax and Tmin, with values of 0.66 and 0.47, respectively. The negative correlations highlighted in Fig. 3  (represented by red boxes in the left and middle panels) suggest the water and energy trade-offs for catchments. If a catchment achieves higher importance scores for evapotranspiration-related factors such as SRad, Tmax, and Tmin, then precipitation is more likely to evaporate before being stored in the soil (a water-limited condition), resulting in lower importance scores for precipitation and soil water layers (Swvl1, Swvl2, and Swvl3). Conversely, when evapotranspiration in a catchment is closer to potential evapotranspiration (an energy-limited condition), evapotranspiration-related factors will contribute less to streamflow variability, leading to an increased importance for precipitation and soil water layers.   4 Hydrological interpretation through surrogate and reanalysis datasets 4.1 Hydrological interpretation for interflow and baseflow To investigate the effectiveness of surrogate variables in representing sub-hydrological processes, specifically interflow and baseflow, this study analyzed the correlation between WFI-based importance scores and baseflow index. The baseflow index was calculated as the ratio of mean daily baseflow to mean daily discharge, which was determined using digital filter separation (Ladson et al., 2013 ). The geographic distributions of the baseflow index and the importance score of Swvl4 generally agree with each other, as depicted in the top panels of Fig. 4  . More accurately stated, the baseflow index appears to approximately follow Swvl4 with a root-square relationship with an R2  value of 0.31, as displayed in the bottom left panel of Fig. 4 . This result implies that the fourth soil water layer (100 cm to 289 cm) plays a significant role in determining baseflow. The bottom right panel of Fig. 4  shows that with the increment of soil depth (from soil layer 1 to 4), the correlation of importance between 1-month lagged precipitation and soil water shows an increasing trend (grey bars), while the correlation of importance between current month precipitation and soil water shows the decreasing trend (orange bars). These findings verified previous studies that in the absence of direct soil water information, variables with time-lagged precipitation could be effective surrogates for soil water (Meng et al., 2014; Tuttle and Salvucci, 2017 ). In particular, 1-month lagged precipitation has a stronger effect on deeper layers, while current month precipitation primarily affects shallow soil layers (the first and second layers). The results of the WFI analysis led to the classification of catchments into four groups based on the contribution of soil water layers, as depicted in the bottom right panel of Fig. 5  . The criteria for this classification are outlined in Table 1  . The lower-right map in the figure suggests that most of the basins fall into the first three categories. The “Other” category indicates that in some basins, the streamflow may not be significantly impacted by soil moisture but could be heavily influenced by precipitation, snowmelt, or both. The green rectangles in the map highlight two different clusters of catchments. The blue cluster, located in the southern Appalachian Mountains, indicates a high importance for the bottom soil water layer (Swvl4), suggesting a substantial contribution from baseflow. Meanwhile, the orange cluster, located in the northern Appalachian Mountains, demonstrates a high importance for the third soil water layer (Swvl3), which corresponds to a significant interflow contribution. These findings align with the findings of Olivero Sheldon et al. (2015) , who reported that perennial runoff with high baseflow regions is concentrated in the southern Appalachian Mountains, while perennial runoff with moderate baseflow regions is primarily located in the northern part of the mountains. Three representative catchments were selected based on their soil water classifications (Fig. 5 ), and their hydrographs are shown in Fig. 6  . In catchments with higher importance in the topsoil layer (i.e., Swvl1&2), precipitation is likely to contribute to overland flow rather than interflow and baseflow, resulting in flash floods during rainy seasons and little to no flow during dry seasons (top right panel of Fig. 6 ). In catchments with a higher importance in the mid soil layer (i.e., Swvl3), a significant amount of precipitation and snowmelt is stored in the third layer of soil, leading to consistent interflow and baseflow even during dry seasons. In catchments with a higher importance in the bottom soil layer (i.e., Swvl4), water could be abundant in such thick and highly permeable soil (as shown in the left panel of Fig. 6 ), leading to a high baseflow rate. The resulting hydrograph shows gradual rising and falling limbs.  4.2 Hydrological interpretation for snowmelt- and rainfall-runoff process To explore how surrogate variables characterize snowmelt- and rainfall-runoff generation mechanisms, the importance scores were correlated with snow fraction. Snow fraction is defined as the ratio of the number of snowing days to the total number of precipitation days. Snowing days are considered to be those on which precipitation occurs in the form of snow when the mean temperature is below 0 degrees Celsius. The top panels of Fig. 7   indicate that snow fraction and the importance of snowmelt are positively correlated with each other, with an R2  value of 0.59 (shown in the lower left panel), suggesting that the more precipitation that falls as snow, the greater the influence of snowmelt on the variability of streamflow. On the other hand, the significance of precipitation shows a negative correlation with snowmelt, with an R2  value of 0.61. This result implies that when snowmelt dominates the variability in streamflow, precipitation will be in less or merely no dominance, as most of it falls as snow, causing little to no immediate impact on streamflow. The lower left panel in Fig. 7  illustrates the two non-linear functions between snow fraction and snowmelt (represented by a blue line) and between snow fraction and precipitation (represented by a red line). The point of intersection (0.34, 0.14) between the two functions serves as a reference for catchment classification, which is further explained in Fig. 7  and Table 2  . The lower right panel of Fig. 7  indicates that when direct snowmelt information is unavailable, shortwave solar radiation (Srad) associated variables may partially explain the variability of streamflow. This is because Srad reflects the energy taken by the snowpack, thus further reflecting the snowmelt timing. Specifically, Srad for the current month (i.e., blue line) carries more snowmelt information than the 1-month-lagged Srad (i.e., red line). The map in the lower right panel of Fig. 8   shows the categorization of catchments based on the dominance of rainfall- and snowmelt-runoff. Catchments (shown as solid orange circles) located along the western coastal areas and in the Middle Eastern regions are predominantly governed by rainfall-runoff mechanisms. Meanwhile, catchments (shown as red stars) located in mountainous regions such as the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada are primarily governed by snowmelt runoff. Catchments (shown as light blue triangles) that are influenced by a mixture of rainfall- and snowmelt-runoff mechanisms are found in the boundary areas between the two categories. For example, the green rectangles in Fig. 8  highlight the transition of runoff generation mechanisms from being dominated by rainfall-runoff to being dominated by snowmelt. Specifically, on the coastal side of the Cascade Range, catchments are primarily dominated by rainfall due to the enormous moisture brought by the warm current. As atmospheric moisture (AM) elevated to the halfway of the mountain (indicated as black arrows in the top left panel), a fraction of precipitation will fall as snow, resulting in a mixed (seasonal) dominance of rainfall- and snowmelt-runoff. As the atmospheric moisture continues to elevate, most precipitation will fall as snow, leading to snowmelt domination in the corresponding catchments. Such a transition of runoff generation mechanisms highly agrees with the previously observation-based studies (Minder et al., 2008; Neiman et al., 2011 ). Catchments (shown as blue diamonds) that do not show strong dominance (i.e., importance scores less than 0.14) for either rainfall or snowmelt may be influenced by strong internal water storages such as interflow and/or baseflow. These catchments are primarily located around the Great Lakes and in low-elevation mountainous regions. Fig. 9   shows the importance scores and hydrographs for the representative catchments shown in Fig. 8 . For catchments governed by snowmelt-runoff mechanism (i.e., top row in Fig. 9 ), the flow spikes always appear in accordance with the snowmelt peaks. In such a case, the highest importance will belong to snowmelt with the reanalysis dataset. However, if direct snowmelt information is unavailable, concurrent and 1-month-lagged shortwave solar radiation may become the first and second highest in importance, as they reflect the timing of snowmelt. For catchments that are seasonally governed by snowmelt- or rainfall-runoff mechanism (middle row in Fig. 9 ), both snowmelt and rainfall will cause streamflow spikes. In such a case, snowmelt information and precipitation may achieve similar importance scores. For catchments primarily governed by the rainfall-runoff mechanism (bottom row in Fig. 9 ), precipitation and soil water contents (or 1-month-lagged precipitation) may achieve high importance.   5 Quantitative evaluation for surrogate and reanalysis datasets 5.1 Overall assessment of hydrological prediction Section 4  qualitatively explained the roles that surrogate information could play in characterizing hydrological processes. In order to quantitatively understand to what extent the surrogate dataset can explain hydrological processes compared with the reanalysis dataset, we examined the two datasets through the ML model, SCE. Fig. 10   indicates that the average NSE performance during the testing period decreased from 0.66 to 0.55, and the average KGE decreased from 0.65 to 0.56, when the surrogate dataset was used instead of the reanalysis dataset. These degradations suggest that better explanations of antecedent catchment conditions could have a significant potential for enhancing hydrological predictions.  5.2 Assessments over arid regions Fig. 11   illustrates how improved characterization of soil water and snowmelt can help facilitate prediction in basins with different aridity. In general, the accuracy of predictions is higher over wetter regions with both datasets. This pattern is more pronounced with the surrogate dataset (represented as the blue line in the figure). The improved soil water and snowmelt characterization in the reanalysis dataset greatly enhances the predictions in drier areas. The upper right panel demonstrates that the quality of low flow predictions (as measured by log-NSE) in drier catchments benefits from better characterization of soil water and snowmelt. This is because the sudden changes in soil water in drier regions can lead to more unpredictable runoff, making it more crucial to include accurate information on soil water and snowmelt. The light blue circle in the bottom panels of Fig. 11  shows that the majority of the catchments with significant improvements in prediction accuracy (indicated by green arrows) are highly arid. Here, aridity is defined by the ratio of mean potential evapotranspiration to mean precipitation.  5.3 Assessments over different Soil-Water classifications Fig. 12   depicts the potential for improved hydrological characterization for three selected catchments. The top left panel of the figure highlights catchment 11381500, where the 4th layer of soil moisture has facilitated the model to capture low flows (such as the red lines around the year 2014), leading to increased log-NSE and NSE by 0.19 and 0.12, respectively. This highlights the greater impact of soil water information on low flow predictions compared to overall streamflow. Such evidence can also be found at catchment 10396000 (top right panel in Fig. 12 ), where the log-NSE has increased by 0.25 while the NSE only increased by 0.09. The provision of 3rd layer of soil moisture information (with the highest importance scores for this catchment) has facilitated the model to better describe the interflows, leading to better agreement between the predicted and observed rising and falling limbs of the hydrographs (such as flows after the year of 2012). The bottom left panel of the figure showcases catchment 11148900, which has also seen improvement in low flow prediction, albeit not as significant (i.e., log-NSE increased by 0.1) compared to the other two catchments. Nevertheless, the NSE has seen considerable improvement (i.e., increased by 0.16), suggesting that better characterization of shallow soil water can help overland and peak flow simulation. Fig. 13   demonstrates that, compared with overall flow prediction, low flow predictions benefit more from soil water information, as indicated by the higher log-NSE values compared to NSE values. This finding indicates that surrogate information may have limitations in accurately characterizing streamflow that is heavily influenced by interflow. This is particularly challenging in areas with deep critical zones, where imprecise modeling could notably affect the accuracy of predicted streamflow in terms of both timing and volume.  5.4 Assessments over different runoff-generation mechanisms The top right panel in Fig. 14   highlights catchment 13011500 and demonstrates the potential for a better description of snowmelt processes in streamflow prediction. The result shows that substituting surrogate information into reanalysis snowmelt has substantially increased NSE, from 0.78 to 0.92. The simulation results provide evidence that flow peaks simulated using the surrogate dataset (grey lines) are significantly underestimated, while those simulated with the reanalysis dataset (red lines) show good alignment with the observed flow. This is because 1-month lagged precipitation data may not accurately reflect the amount of snow that accumulated during the winter. The top left panel of Fig. 14 , which depicts catchment 12189500, shows that both datasets accurately capture rainfall-induced flow spikes (such as those observed in 2006 and 2007), while snowmelt-induced spikes are mostly captured by the reanalysis dataset. The bottom left panel of Fig. 14 , which represents catchment 1114300, highlights that even snow-free catchments can see significant improvements in accuracy due to the better description of interflow and baseflow dynamics (evidenced by the good agreement between the predicted and observed rising and falling limbs of the hydrograph). At the CONUS scale, snow-free (i.e., as the category of rainfall) catchments have the greatest potential in improving low flow predictions (i.e., measured by log-NSE) compared with other catchment categories, as shown in Fig. 15  . This result implies that better characterization of soil water conditions can facilitate low-flow simulation in these catchments. In comparison, catchments with a mixed dominance (seasonal) have seen a greater potential in improving mid and high-flow predictions. This is because the snowmelt information can help the model better distinguish snowmelt- and rainfall-runoff mechanisms than the surrogate variables used. This is particularly the case for alpine catchments where streamflow is strongly affected by precipitation patterns (e.g., catchment 12189500 in Fig. 14 ). During winter, rain and snowfall may occur at the mountain foot and top, respectively, leading to rainfall-induced flood. During summer, the melting snowpack contributes to significant streamflow, leading to snowmelt-induced flood. This phenomenon challenges surrogate variables such as 1-month lagged precipitation to capture both rainfall and snowmelt-induced floods, as they may either emphasize characterizing soil water content or snowmelt. Such a dual role played by the surrogates may potentially lead to biased predictions either in favor of better agreement in rainfall-dominated processes or in favor of snowmelt-dominated ones.   6 Final remarks and outlook In process-based hydrological models, the partitioning of soil water in multiple layers is critical in capturing the evolution of water balance and representing the overland flow, interflow, and baseflow components. In this study, we extracted such knowledge directly from data to help explain hydrological processes in different types of catchments. Our findings revealed relationships between soil water layers and flow components, thereby enhancing our comprehension of sub-hydrological processes from an intuitive level to a quantitative level. Furthermore, the quantification of runoff-generation mechanisms at a continental scale offered valuable insights into the transition of mechanisms from rainfall-runoff dominance to snowmelt dominance. By comparing the results from the reanalysis and the surrogate datasets, we discovered that surrogate information, in most cases, may insufficiently describe soil water conditions and snowmelt processes. The insufficiency reduces for wetter catchments because when actual evapotranspiration is lower than precipitation (in wet catchments), the streamflow could be less sensitive to soil water. Thus, such insufficiency is likely to impact the predictive accuracy over drier basins more than wetter ones. In addition, the study found that compared with high flows, low flows were more likely to benefit from improved characterization of soil moisture. This finding suggests that the under-performed low flow predictions reported from previous studies (Feng et al., 2020; Gauch et al., 2021; Hunt et al., 2022; Kratzert et al., 2018 ) were likely due to the insufficient description of soil water conditions. By examining the effectiveness of surrogate information in characterizing snowmelt and soil moisture, the results revealed the limitations and potentials of surrogate information in ML models. In real-world hydrological practice, obtaining observed snowmelt and soil moisture information as model input could be difficult. In most cases, this information needs to be represented through models or surrogates. The limitations of surrogate information in modeling provided directions on what we should pay attention to for improving ML modeling in the field of hydrology. For instance, in this study, we found that snowmelt information played an irreplaceable role in capturing flow spikes for alpine catchments with a seasonal dominance of rainfall- and snowmelt-runoff. Unlike in snowmelt-dominated catchments, surrogate variables have limitations in effectively capturing flow spikes in catchments with mixed dominance. This is because surrogate variables may come short in describing both soil moisture and snow accumulation simultaneously, potentially leading to biased predictions in favor of either rainfall or snowmelt runoff generation mechanisms. Such limitations suggest that future modeling in watersheds with mixed dominance may benefit from improved characterization of soil moisture and snowmelt, for example by separating snowfall from other forms of precipitation in the modeling process. This study revealed controlling factors in hydrological predictions over the CONUS through an advanced ML interpretation method. The method can be used as an effective way to quantitatively examine hydrological processes, gaining insights into runoff-generation mechanisms and sub-hydrological processes. These insights are crucial not only for understanding watershed conditions but also for informing water resource management. The Supplementary material  includes a case study that demonstrates the use of this approach in tracking long-term shifts of dominant controls in monthly streamflow generation. This case study highlights the effectiveness of WFI in making informed decisions for water resources under evolving climate conditions.
1 Introduction Groundwater systems are key to the Earth's hydrological cycle, influencing both the availability and quality of water resources. Many agricultural regions experience significant depletion and contamination of this vital resource, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of groundwater dynamics. This is especially critical in areas heavily reliant on groundwater for agricultural purposes, as these are often the hotspots for the world’s most acute groundwater challenges. Regional strategies are essential for addressing these accelerating global problems of groundwater depletion (Aeschbach-Hertig and Gleeson, 2012; Canlon et al., 2007; Gleeson et al., 2010, 2012; Siebert et al., 2010 ). A prime example of this is the San Luis Valley (SLV) in Colorado. In this region, long-term groundwater extraction for agricultural activities causes depletion as well as seasonal variation in groundwater storage, a situation has been exacerbated by recurrent drought, as documented by McKee et al. (2000) . While traditional analysis of groundwater systems has relied primarily on in-situ measurements and hydrogeological modeling, the advent of remote sensing technologies enables larger-scale groundwater analyses. Among these technologies, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) has emerged as a robust tool for observing land subsidence with cm- to mm-scale accuracy, which can be related to a loss in groundwater storage (Reeves et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2023 ). Recent applications of InSAR have demonstrated its utility in estimating aquifer storage properties and for tracking changes over time (Miller et al., 2017, Li et al., 2021, Chaussard and Farr, 2019 ). Furthermore, advancements in InSAR analysis techniques, such as persistent scatterer analysis, have enhanced its capability to accurately retrieve ground deformation even over decorrelated agricultural fields, a challenge noted in earlier analyses (Chen et al., 2015 ). InSAR has been utilized previously to characterize groundwater in confined aquifers of the SLV (Chen et al., 2016 ).  Their study demonstrated that InSAR deformation measurements could be recovered over the vegetated groundwater basin by only considering stable pixels that are not affected by crop growth. Similarly, in a subsequent analysis, Chen et al. 2017  used multiple InSAR missions to infer the temporal and spatial variability of the confined aquifer head and storage properties in the SLV. However, despite these advancements, gaps in our understanding of the SLV's groundwater dynamics remain. Earlier analyses characterized deformation in the system as purely elastic, reflecting the ability of the aquifer to regain its original shape after stress is removed (Chen et al., 2017 ). However, the InSAR observation periods used in these analyses were either during periods of relatively high water availability when the aquifer heads remained stable, or had significant temporal gaps due to limited satellite coverage. A time period with dense InSAR data availability and drought-induced water level declines is needed to evaluate the potential for inelastic deformation, which causes a permanent change in the aquifer's structure, to occur. In this study, we present a dataset over the SLV spanning from 2015 to 2022. This period includes droughts in 2018 and 2020, and is the longest continuous period evaluated with InSAR data in the SLV to date, enabling us to see both seasonal and long-term trends in land deformation. We utilize a modified DS-interpolation algorithm to address unwrapping errors and decorrelation effects common in InSAR data in agricultural regions. To enhance data continuity, we also employ Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) analysis to fill a data gap in the ascending data for 2019. We validate our InSAR results using GPS observations; we then model groundwater flow and deformation in clay layers to estimate aquifer parameters and the elastic and inelastic components of deformation (Smith and Li, 2021 ) and characterize uncertainty using Bayesian methods. Our physical modeling approach allows us to estimate ground surface subsidence over a period when satellite data was not accessible, identify several periods of inelastic deformation and advance our understanding of the region's groundwater systems. By providing a detailed investigation of the interplay between groundwater extraction, aquifer system dynamics, and land deformation, our study provides knowledge and methods that can improve groundwater management practices in the region. Our methods can also be used in other regions with decorrelation issues or temporal gaps in water level measurements.  2 Hydrology of study area The hydrogeology of the SLV is complex and has been the subject of extensive research due to its unique characteristics and the importance of water resources for the region's agricultural economy. The SLV is a high-altitude basin with a desert climate, located in the south-central part of Colorado, near the border with New Mexico. It boasts a vibrant agricultural economy highly dependent on the effective management of limited water resources. Fig. 1   presents the geographic layout of the SLV within Colorado, highlighting distinct sub-basins and key monitoring locations. Specifically, the ALA6 and RGDSS08 wells, and the COA5 GPS station, all utilized in our study, are clearly indicated. The SLV consists of five distinct hydrogeologic layers as defined by Radutu et al. (2017) . Historical perspectives on Colorado droughts by (Henz et al., 2004 ) provide additional context to understaning how drought conditions influence these hydrogeologic layers. The top 15–40 m of the subsurface constitutes an upper unconfined aquifer. Layer 2 is a confining layer known as an aquitard, and the aquitard thickness diminishes at the edge of the SLV near the foothills. Layers 3–5 constitute a system of confined aquifers. The aquifer becomes more clay-rich and less productive as depth increases (Radutu et al., 2017 ). The SLV is underlain by an extensive blue clay layer deriving from ancient Lake Alamosa (Machette et al., 2013 ). The thickness of this clay layer varies throughout the base but is on the order of several hundred meters thick near the town of Alamosa and forms the primary confining unit for the confined aquifer in the SLV. The Closed Basin, situated to the north of the Rio Grande River and Costilla County, includes the northwest, ancestral sump, and northeast regions (Fig. 1 ), and is a crucial area in the SLV where significant groundwater pumping occurs, primarily from the unconfined aquifer. This area features a thick unconfined aquifer, which serves as a significant source of groundwater for the region. The unconfined aquifer here is characterized by its considerable thickness and high productivity, making it a crucial component for agricultural and other water-dependent activities in the San Luis Valley. South of the Rio Grande, particularly in the Conejos and Alamosa River Valleys, the hydrogeologic conditions differ markedly. This region is dominated by a shallow confining layer, primarily composed of clay, which lies near the ground surface. As a result, the unconfined aquifer in this area is relatively thin and less productive compared to its northern counterpart. Consequently, groundwater extraction in the southern regions predominantly occurs from the confined aquifer system. The State of Colorado's regulations mandate that confined aquifer head levels in the SLV stay within the historical range observed between 1978 and 2000 (Kuenhold, 2006 ). However, due to the interconnected nature of the confined and unconfined aquifers in the region, these regulations also indirectly affect the unconfined aquifer, promoting an integrated approach to groundwater management. To provide a clearer understanding of the subsurface geology, we have included a geologic cross section in the supplementary figures (Figure S10). This cross section, adapted from the Colorado Geological Survey's Groundwater Atlas, depicts the stratigraphy and structure of the San Luis Valley. The figure highlights key hydrogeologic features such as the Alamosa Formation (Qa), Santa Fe-Los Pinos Formations (Tlp), Vallejo Formation (Tfg/Tc/Tv), Pre-Vallejo; Blanco Basin Formation (pre-Tv), Fish Canyon-Carpenter Ridge Tuffs (Tsf/Tlp), and Precambrian crystalline rock (pC). Structural features such as the Monte Vista Graben, Baca Graben, and Alamosa Horst are also depicted, showing their impact on groundwater flow and storage. The groundwater divide within the San Luis Valley (SLV) indicates a region where groundwater flow diverges in different directions. North of this divide, unconfined groundwater generally flows towards the topographic low in the ancestral sump, while south of the divide, unconfined groundwater flows towards the Rio Grande (Huntley, 1976 ). This hydrological characteristic significantly impacts both unconfined and confined aquifers in the SLV. The Colorado Water Conservation Board and the Colorado Division of Water Resources have developed the Rio Grande Decision Support System (RGDSS) as detailed by Schreüder (2005) . This system includes a hydrogeologic database and a MODFLOW finite-difference groundwater flow model, crucial for monitoring and managing the SLV's groundwater resources. The RGDSS uses historical head measurements and stream gains or losses to calibrate its hydrogeologic model. The head data sets are available through the SLV Well and Water-Level Database (https://www.prinmath.com/rgwcd/ ). The SLV is also characterized by a complex system of faults, which can influence groundwater flow patterns, although their impact varies significantly across different regions. For instance, along the west side of the San Luis Hills, the smear zone of the Manassa fault enhances vertical flow, rather than acting as a barrier. However, in Costilla County, faults cause significant discontinuities in the heads over short distances (Bedrosian et al., 2015).  3 Data and method 3.1 InSAR data processing In this study, we employed Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) to derive surface displacements from two geometries: the ascending track (Orbit 04) and descending track (Orbit 142). We acquired Single-look Complex (SLC) SAR images from Sentinel-1A/B tracks in Terrain Observations with Progressive Scans SAR (TOPS) mode, operating at a C-band wavelength of approximately 5.6 cm. Figures S2 and S3 display the network of all available interferometric pairs generated in this study, with Figure S2 representing the ascending geometry and Figure S3 depicting the descending geometry. Fig. 2       outlines our workflow. Initially, we constructed SBAS networks of interferograms, constrained by maximum baseline thresholds for both time and space, set at 200 m and 200 days, respectively. This optimization aimed to increase the number of interferometric pairs while minimizing spatial and temporal decorrelation. Subsequent interferometric analysis of each pair involved co-registration, interferogram generation, removal of flat earth and topographic phases, filtering, and unwrapping, all performed using the InSAR Scientific Computing Environment (ISCE) software. Addressing the challenge of vegetation growth and motion, which often disrupts InSAR phase measurements in agricultural areas, we implemented a modified phase interpolation algorithm, as proposed by Chen et al. (2017) . This method, described in greater detail below, has been effective in mitigating vegetation decorrelation artifacts, a significant concern with C-band InSAR data, which is more prone to vegetation decorrelation than L-band data. Moreover, recent advances in SAR interferometry time series analysis, such as those described by (Hooper et al., 2012 ), have significantly improved the accuracy and reliability of measuring crustal deformation, especially in challenging environments like agricultureal fields. After initial processing, we found distributed scatterer (DS) pixels, based on their phase stability and spatial correlation. Our SBAS InSAR analysis was detected DS pixels in various settings, including locations along roads, buildings, and in unirrigated spaces between center pivots. DS pixels were selected based on the evaluation of each pixel's coherence, discarding those with coherence values below 0.2. Having identified these high-quality DS pixels and discarded all others, we proceeded to interpolate their wrapped phase values for each interferogram. This interpolation used pixels within a radius that varied based on nearby DS-pixel density. The radius thresholds were set between 500 m and 1 km. Specifically, if expanding the radius to 1 km did not yield at least 20 DS pixels within that radius, the location was not assigned a new value. Conversely, if sufficient DS pixels were found, a new phase value for the pixel was calculated using a weighted average. The weights were derived from an exponential decay function based on the square distance to each DS pixel, employing an Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) approach with an exponential decrease with distance. Figure S4 illustrates a comparison between the original wrapped and the interpolated wrapped interferograms, exemplified by interferometric pairs acquired between 21-Jun-2021 and 26-Sept-2021. This adaptive interpolation method, coupled with subsequent phase unwrapping, enabled us to maintain the integrity of our analysis despite the decorrelation challenges in irrigated fields. After the interpolation phase, we employed the Statistical-Cost, Network-Flow Algorithm for Phase Unwrapping (SNAPHU) to estimate the modified unwrapped phase map. While the above procedure reduced noise significantly, many pixels were removed due to low data quality. We used a modified SBAS time series analysis that constructs separate SBAS networks for each pixel, enabling us to create time series over pixels with some missing data, so long as the pixel had sufficient high-quality interferometric pairs. A pixel was deemed stable and included in the SBAS time series analysis only if its corresponding network maintained had no date (or node) with fewer than three connections. This criterion ensured that only pixels with high-quality, reliable data were considered. By applying this process to each pixel, we can identify a subset of pixels that exhibits high interferometric correlation and stability. Our methodology of conducting the SBAS analysis separately for each pixel offers a significant advantage, because an interferogram with low coherence in one region might still be usable in another. This selective approach prevents the complete discarding of these interferograms, enabling us to effectively utilize a larger portion of the available data. We implemented this workflow (Fig. 2 ) on both ascending and descending tracks, which allowed us to produce displacements along the LOS for the entire study area. Inherent to InSAR observations, we were able to observe deformation in only two different geometries, which consequently limited our ability to retrieve all three components of displacement. However, by integrating data from both the ascending and descending tracks, we were able to decompose the observed displacements into vertical and horizontal components along the satellite's flight direction. Given the constraint of having only two observations from these tracks, our analysis was naturally limited to extracting these two components: the vertical displacement, crucial for our groundwater-related deformation study, and a horizontal component corresponding to the satellite's flight direction in the descending orbit. Given our focus on groundwater modeling, which relies on head observations from observation wells and deformation data extracted from InSAR, distinguishing between east–west and north–south deformation was not necessary. Our primary concern was the extraction of the vertical component of deformation, as this is the strongest component of groundwater-related deformation in areas with regional groundwater pumping (Galloway and Burbey, 2011 ). Horizontal displacement occurs along the flight direction of the descending track from north (slightly toward east) to south (slightly to the west) and is generally less significant compared to the vertical displacement. Following the approach outlined by Hanssen (2001) , we considered an incidence angle (θ) and a satellite orbit with a heading (azimuth) of α h    . This led us to the equation:(1) d LOS   = d u  c o s θ    - d ALD   s i n θ    , d ALD   = d e  c o s α h     - d n  s i n α h          Where d LOS      represents the Line-of-Sight (LOS) displacement, de , dn   and du  , signify the east, north and upward (vertical) displacement, respectively, and d ALD      represents the projection of the multiple horizontal components on the azimuth look direction (ALD).  3.2 SSA for time series gap filling In order to estimate vertical and horizontal displacements from the ascending and descending data, observations from both look directions should be available simultaneously. However, the timing of the descending and ascending observations is not identical, as they have different temporal resolutions. Particularly, there was a data gap in the ascending observation between October 2018 and June 2019, during which no satellite data was acquired. To address this issue, we employed SSA for each pixel separately. This analysis is grounded in the principles of Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). However, SVD is not directly applicable to one-dimensional signals. To overcome this limitation, we transformed our one-dimensional signal into a two-dimensional format. This methodology is based on the principles outlined in the paper by [Vajedian et al, 2023 ]. The first step in this process was to define a window length. Given the seasonal behavior of the deformation signal extracted in our study, we set the window length to 365 days. This length was chosen as it adequately captured the signal spectrum, reflecting the seasonal variations in the data. We constructed a 2D matrix with each column representing a given year and each row corresponding to a day within that year. Starting from t0, we collected deformation values for first 365 days and placed them in the first column. We then shifted the window by one year to t = 365 days and collected the observations for the next 365 days, placing them in the second column. To address gaps in the dataset, including both the longer gap from October 2018 to June 2019 and daily gaps arising from observations being collected every 12 days, a cubic interpolation method was applied prior to performing SSA, ensuring a complete matrix for analysis. This process was repeated until the last observation, resulting in a 2D matrix where each column represented a given year and each row represented a day within that year. We then decomposed the matrix using SVD to obtain eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and reconstructed the signal using the largest three components, which explained 84.1 % of the variance. We validate our gap-filling process through correlation of ascending and descending time-series (see Supplemental Information Fig. S1).  3.3 Decomposition of seasonal and long-term components In our InSAR time series analysis over the SLV, we distinguished the seasonal and long-term components of the subsidence signal. The seasonal component typically reflects short-term, cyclical processes, such as variations in groundwater levels due to recharge and irrigation in the Valley. Isolating this component helps us understand these dynamics and their impact on ground deformation. The initial step in our analysis involved identifying pixels exhibiting seasonal behavior. Pixels affected by temporally decorrelated behavior, likely due to atmospheric influences or unwrapping noise, do not show this seasonal pattern. To differentiate between signals potentially affected by temporal decorrelation and those with significant seasonal behavior, we employed Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis enhanced with zero-padding to improve frequency resolution. This technique examines the dominant frequencies in the time series data, enabling us to isolate pixels that display a clear annual seasonal pattern. In our FFT analysis, we identified dominant frequencies by looking for peaks in the magnitude spectrum. We aimed to find the most prominent peaks in the frequency spectrum that clearly indicate a seasonal cycle. By setting criteria for peak significance and employing a narrow tolerance around the expected annual cycle of 365 days, we ensure that only the frequencies closely aligned with yearly cycle are considered. After identifying pixels with seasonal behavior, we applied the STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition procedure based on Loess) algorithm to decompose the time series signal into its seasonal and long-term components. The STL algorithm, introduced by Cleveland et al. 1990 , is an additive decomposition method based on locally-weighted regression. The algorithm fits multiple smoothing functions to the data, each capturing a different level of temporal granularity.  3.4 Gap filling of groundwater level observations using Theis Equation-Based interpolation In this study, we aimed to derive accurate estimations of groundwater head data by integrating observations from two observation wells, ALA6 and RGDSS08, located within the San Luis Valley. Given the proximity of ALA6 and RGDSS08—situated merely 150 m apart, as illustrated in Fig. 1 —and the significant correlation between their data sets, we consolidated their records to obtain a denser hydrograph. Despite the complementary nature of the data from ALA6 and RGDSS08, some gaps in the groundwater level records still existed. These gaps are due to the different frequencies and periods of data collection from each well (Fig. 7  ). The effort to interpolate these gaps using the Theis equation-based method, as opposed to simpler interpolation methods, is justified as this approach allows us to model the drawdown and recovery for each year separately. This modeling ensures that the interpolated head data closely follows the observed head.In  the next step of our study, we address the remaining gaps in the combined groundwater level observations from the ALA6 and RGSS08 wells (Fig. 8  ). To achieve this, we employed an interpolation method based on the Theis equation, a well-established solution to the groundwater flow equation that describes the drawdown or recharge within a well in a confined aquifer (Theis, 1935 ). The Theis equation is given below:(3) Δ h = Q 4 π T   W u        where Δ h    is drawdown, Q is the pumping rate, T is the transmissivity, and W(u) is the well function for u = r  2  S  4 T t     , with r being the distance to the pumping well, S the storativity, and t the time since the start of pumping. By using the Theis equation, we can interpolate the groundwater level data and fill in the gaps in our observations. We simplified the Theis equation following the work of Smith and Li, 2021  who introduced parameters c1  and c2 , to reduce the number of parameters needed for water level gap-filling. The parameters are defined as follows:(4) c 1  = Q 4 π T     , c 2  = r  2  S  4 T         Our approach begins with the division of the time series groundwater level observations into individual years within the span of the study. We then assume that each yearly subset includes both a drawdown curve, which corresponds to the decrease in groundwater level following the commencement of pumping when the irrigation season begins, and a recovery curve, which corresponds to the aquifer's recovery immediately after the cessation of pumping when the irrigation season ends. This detailed annual modeling, differing from Smith and Li, 2021 , aims to closely align modeled data with observed data. To estimate the parameters of the Theis equation for each curve, we utilize the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) optimization method. The parameters we aim to solve for include c1 , c2 , the start of pumping, and the duration of pumping. The MCMC method requires initial values and ranges for these values. To define these initial values, we overlay the drawdown-recovery curves observed for each separate year, as recorded by the observation wells, onto a single plot (Fig. S5). We then estimate the start date of pumping, which corresponds to the peak of the recovery curve (the maximum value of the groundwater level observation for each year), reflecting the effective start of the irrigation season given the varied operation times of wells. To refine our initial values for the MCMC method, we calculate an average effective start date of pumping after individually estimating this date for each year. Parameter c1 is defined as the amplitude of the seasonal groundwater fluctuation, which is calculated for each year by determining the difference between the minimum and maximum values of the head data. We compute an average amplitude across all observed years to establish a representative initial value for c1. Alongside c1, parameter c2, which describes how quickly water levels decline or recover, is also estimated within our model. We set an initial value of 0.3 for c2, and allowed it to vary between 0.1 and 0.8 to optimally fit the observed data This range was determined through an iterative process using MCMC simulations, which identified the bounds that consistently yielded the best fit to the observed data.We implemented MCMC using the MCMCSTAT Matlab package (Haario et al., 2006, Haario et al., 2001 ). The MCMCSTAT package uses the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, a type of MCMC method, with an adaptive scheme for adjusting the covariance matrix of the proposal distribution during the simulation. This adaptive scheme allows the algorithm to learn from the states that have been sampled so far and adjust the proposal distribution to improve the efficiency of the sampling process. In the case of Gaussian error model, the model error variance is sampled from the conjugate inverse chi-squared distribution. By using the Theis equation and the MCMC method, we can interpolate the head data and fill in gaps in our observations.  3.5 Inversion procedure for aquifer parameter estimation Building upon the interpolated head observations and the vertical time series deformation data for the area surrounding the ALA6 and RGSS08 observation wells, we developed a deformation model to better understand mechanisms driving seasonal and long-term deformation. The model is based on the work of Smith and Li, 2021 , who developed a model to simulate total surface deformation at a specific location with co-located yearly head measurements from an observation well and InSAR data processed from the Sentinel-1 satellites. The model assumes that the aquifer system is bounded by a thick, low permeability clay layer at the top, consistent with the confined nature of the aquifer. The aquifer system is composed of a number of interbedded clay layers within a permeable aquifer material. The total thickness of the aquifer system, and the number of clay layers within the aquifer system, are unknowns that the model solves for. We assume that within the permeable aquifer zone, the head remains consistent across different depths, represented by the data collected from the wells. The head in this zone of the aquifer was calculated from well data in section 3.4 . The less permeable clay layers, which are primarily responsible for deformation and exhibit dominant vertical flow, have unknown head that must be solved for. The head in these clay layers is estimated using Equation (5) :(5) ∂ h  ∂ t   = K v  S s      ∂  2  h  ∂ z  2       ,     where h  is the head, t  is time, Kv   is the vertical hydraulic conductivity, Ss   is the specific storage, and z  is the vertical location in the layer. Equation (5)   is solved for using finite differences with the boundary condition at the top and bottom of the layer set by the head in the permeable aquifer. Once the head within the clay layer is known, the change in head from one time step to the next can be used to compute the deformation in each discrete interval within the clay layer using Equation (6)  :(6) Δ b = Δ h b 0  S sk       where Δ b    is the change in thickness of the layer, b 0     is the original thickness of the layer, and S sk      is the skeletal specific storage. The skeletal specific storage varies based on the stress history of the material that is deforming as follows:(7) S sk   = S ske   f o r h t  ≥ h  min      S skv   f o r h t  < h min               where h min      is the lowest modeled head experienced at that location historically (the preconsolidation head). Thus, the parameters needed to model deformation in the clay layer are S ske     , S skv     , K v    , as well as the thickness and number of clay layers. An additional parameter indicating the thickness of the sandy intervals was needed to model coarse-grained deformation of the aquifer. This thickness was used as b 0     in Equation (6)  , with the head estimated from section 3.4  as Δ h   , to compute deformation of the coarse-grained aquifer. The deformation of both fine-grained and coarse-grained systems was then summed to get the total surface deformation, which can then be related to InSAR observations. As many unknown parameters needed to be solved for, an inversion procedure for these parameters was implemented. We used the MCMC method, which provided a robust estimate of uncertainty for each parameter. To initiate the MCMC method, we define initial values and ranges for all the parameters listed earlier. The initial range of values for hydrologic properties (K v    , S ske     , S skv      and S ske   m u l t   ) were set based on previous studies in similar regions ( Smith and Knight, 2019; Smith and Li, 2021; Lees et al., 2022; Smith, 2023 ) . For parameters representing geologic conditions of the study area (clay thickness, total thickness, and clay ratio), ranges were determined based on local geologic knowledge from drillers’ logs (Eric Harmon, personal communication). All initial ranges were very broad, so that the model was not limited by personal interpretation. Initial ranges are shown in Table S1. With these initial settings, we ran the MCMC method to estimate the optimized values for each parameter. The results of this inversion procedure provided us with a robust estimate of aquifer parameters, which we then used to model the aquifer system's deformation response to changes in hydraulic head.   4 Results 4.1 Signal decomposition Fig. 3  shows the reconstructed deformation signal for the point identified as P1 (also shown in Fig. 5 a). This graph shows the gap in observations starting from October 2018 until June 2019 (Fig. 3 b), and illustrates the application of our SSA-based gap-filling technique. The same time series is presented but with the data gap effectively filled. The continuity of the time series is restored, providing a complete dataset for the analysis period. To validate the SSA-gap filling process, we constructed a correlation plot between ascending and descending time series data (Fig. S1). The plot reveals a high correlation, with the scatter points aligning along a straight line that transitions into a curve at the end, where the deformation values are larger. This pattern uncovers a generally linear relationship. This indicates a strong linear correlation between the ascending and descending data for the lower (most common) deformation values. This alignment suggests that both datasets exhibit similar behavior within this range, affirming the effectiveness of the SSA-based gap-filling technique applied to the ascending data set. The linear portion of the plot validates our gap-filling analysis, reinforcing the integrity of our approach. At larger values there is a nonlinear relationship between the ascending and descending data. This curvature may reflect different sensitivities in the ascending and descending geometries, which become increasingly evident at higher deformation values ( Fig. S1).  To verify the results of our InSAR time series analysis, we utilized observations from a GPS station situated within our study area. The GPS observations do not provide continuous coverage for the entire duration of our InSAR study (2015–2022), with a notable gap occurring primarily in 2020 ( Fig. 3 . e and f ). Despite this, the observations still demonstrate a strong correlation between the InSAR findings and GPS measurements on both ascending and descending tracks. As depicted in Fig. 3 e  and f,  the InSAR and GPS observations closely align with each other.  4.2 Decomposition of seasonal and long-term components Fig. 4  illustrates the annual amplitude of seasonal deformation in the vertical direction, derived from the decomposition of seasonal amplitude observed in time series maps from both ascending and descending geometries (as shown in Fig. S5). As we move forward in time from 2015 to 2021, there is a noticeable increase in vertical seasonal deformation. This expanding pattern is observed in the spatial extent of the amplitude and is evident in both ascending and descending directions, as shown in Fig. S5. The red bullseye seen in Fig. 4  does not represent the overall distribution of pumping in the SLV. Instead, it highlights a specific area where the interaction of confined pumping and local aquifer properties creates conditions conducive to subsidence. Fig. 5 .b depicts the annual average pumping by individual wells, highlighting areas of higher pumping rates shown in red on the map. The data for this figure were sourced from the Colorado Division of Water Resources, which compiles records of groundwater extraction. These records include pumping from all aquifers in the San Luis Valley, both confined and unconfined. When compared to Fig. 5 .b, it becomes evident that subsidence is mainly attributed to the depletion of aquifer storage. Fig. 6  illustrates the variation of horizontal and vertical deformation along two profiles, AA' and BB', as indicated in Fig. 5 .a . Profile AA' traverses an area corresponding to an unconfined aquifer, while profile BB' crosses a confined aquifer. In profile AA', the observed subsidence over the study period is relatively modest, totaling 25 mm, whereas in profile BB', the subsidence is more pronounced, reaching 40 mm. The horizontal displacement along both profiles is minimal. Additionally, a profile illustrating changes in topography is also included. The lack of strong correlation between horizontal or vertical movements suggests that any effects from the troposphere have been effectively minimized.  4.3 Integration of InSAR-Derived vertical deformation and groundwater level observations We now present the results of our method for interpolating groundwater levels, as described in Section 3.4 , and compare these water levels with our deformation time series, which was produced using methods described in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 . Fig. 7  displays the combined groundwater level observations from wells ALA6 and RGDSS08. RGDSS08 offers near-daily measurements from 2001 to 2022, while ALA6 provides monthly data from 1998 to 2022. Despite their different measurement frequencies, the temporal coverage from both wells is complementary. Notably, data gaps in these wells occur at different intervals. For example, RGDSS08 lacks data for the recovery and drawdown curve (the period around the commencement of pumping) for 2002 and 2003, but ALA6′s records cover these gaps. In Fig. 8 , dashed lines indicate interpolated time series data, which we produced using the method described in Section 3.4 , and are particularly crucial for filling gaps like in 2008, a year with no observations. The adaptive Theis interpolator, proposed in this study, has enabled us to predict the variations in groundwater levels during these periods of data scarcity. We now compare the vertical surface deformation with our groundwater level time series. Utilizing data spanning from 2015 to 2022 with a temporal resolution of 24 days, we generate a time series plot to closely examine the relationship between surface deformation and groundwater levels in the vicinity of these wells. The time series plot (shown in Fig. 8 ) indicates a clear correlation between InSAR observed land subsidence and well observations of head variation from 2015 to 2018. However, the plot reveals a distinctive departure from this congruence after 2018. There is a dramatic drop in head in Fall 2018, which is accompanied by more pronounced subsidence. While the head recovers after 2018 and has no significant downward trend over the time period shown, the InSAR data reveals an increase in the long-term rate of land subsidence following this event. The divergence between the two data sets after 2018 is notable, with the InSAR demonstrating a considerably higher rate of long-term subsidence than suggested by the head observations. This continued subsidence, despite the recovery of the water levels, could be indicative of inelastic deformation, where the land surface does not rebound to its original state.  4.4 Aquifer parameter estimation The results of our deformation model and MCMC inversion procedure, described in Section 3.5 , provided us with a robust estimate of aquifer parameters (Table S1), which we then used to model the aquifer system's deformation response to changes in hydraulic head. Fig. 9   compares the observed deformation with the best-fit modeled deformation, represented by the maximum a-posteriori (MAP) estimate (black line), as well as a distribution of model runs (gray bars) sampled from the posterior of our MCMC results. A reasonably good fit is observed between observed and modeled data, indicating that the model is capturing the main deformation processes. Fig. 10   provides time series of the head variation observed over the time span from 1999 to 2023, as depicted by a blue line. This figure also shows the modeled deformation, which has been expanded to cover the entire time span. Because the model only requires head data as forcings and the parameters described earlier, we can reconstruct a deformation time series over any period where head data are available. Notably, the pronounced decrease in deformation observed in 2002–2003 aligns with the severe drought that ensued after a comparatively wet phase.   5 Discussion In our study, we aimed to evaluate the connection and discrepancies between InSAR-observed land subsidence and groundwater level fluctuations in the SLV as monitored by the ALA6 and RGDSS08 observation wells in the SLV. As noted in 4.3, the deformation and head data followed similar trends from 2015 to 2018, but diverged after a significant drawdown event in 2018 prompted several years of long-term subsidence, even after water levels rebounded. This observation is consistent with our understanding of inelastic deformation: when water levels drop below their historically lowest level, subsurface grains collapse inelastically. This process can take much longer than elastic deformation (Smith et al., 2017; Lees et al., 2022 ). Our observational evidence for inelastic deformation is reinforced by our model results (Figs. 9 and 10 ), which indicate multi-year periods of long-term subsidence associated with inelastic deformation following periods of large groundwater declines. This is most apparent over periods where groundwater levels recover, but the land surface does not recover, a clear indication of inelastic deformation. This observation is also consistent with other regions that experience significant elastic deformation coupled with long-term inelastic deformation (Li et al., 2023 ). To quantify the critical water table level below which inelastic deformation occurs, we analyzed long-term groundwater level records from the ALA6 well and modeled subsidence data. As shown in Fig. 10 , permanent subsidence begins around 2002 when the head is approximately 41 m. This level should be considered the preconsolidation head, as it represents the threshold below which significant inelastic deformation is triggered, leading to permanent subsidence. Maintaining groundwater levels above this preconsolidation head is essential to prevent irreversible land subsidence. Additionally, the preconsolidation head is not uniform within the clay layer. According to Smith and Li (2021) , the preconsolidation head varies at each point in a clay layer because the head in any given clay layer does not immediately equilibrate with that experienced in the aquifer. Thus, even if the aquifer head did not drop below the lowest level experienced during the 2002 drought, some parts of the clay could still be below their preconsolidation head, leading to inelastic deformation. Smith (2023)  further supports this by showing that inelastic deformation can occur in parts of the clay layer even while the head is rebounding, as the head in the aquifer might still be lower than the head in some intervals of the clay layer. This explains why subsidence continued after 2018 despite the recovery of the water table. While groundwater extraction remains the primary driver of land subsidence in the San Luis Valley (SLV), other factors such as the decomposition of organic carbon and natural soil compaction can also contribute. However, these factors play a secondary role compared to groundwater pumping, particularly because the SLV lacks significant amounts of peat, which is typically associated with more substantial subsidence due to organic carbon decomposition (Wösten et al., 1997 ). Natural consolidation of sediments likely occurs, but at a much smaller magnitude, similar to the minor subsidence observed in regions with soft soils, such as coastal Texas, where it is on the order of millimeters per year (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Previous studies show the dominance of groundwater extraction as the primary driver of subsidence in similar regions (Smith & Knight, 2019 ). This is consistent with our analysis and modeling. Previous studies in the SLV by Chen et al. (2016)  and Reeves et al. (2014)  reported only elastic deformation. The time periods those studies considered were generally periods dominated by elastic deformation (2003–2010), or had a sparse sampling of InSAR data, which limited time series analysis. By monitoring a longer period with robust temporal latency, including times when the head falls below its pre-consolidation level, we discovered that the groundwater level fully rebounds (black dots in Fig. 7 ), while InSAR (blue dots) only partially does so, revealing inelastic deformation in addition to the elastic behavior. This study is the first to identify such inelastic events in the San Luis Valley. While our observational and modeling results provide strong evidence for inelastic deformation, the episodes of inelastic deformation are relatively uncommon and are not associated with decades-long periods of long-term subsidence as in other subsiding regions (Lees et al., 2022 ). The primary reason for this is that even after periods of intense drought, water levels do not remain substantially below their previous levels. For example, the 2002 drought caused massive drawdown and our model estimates significant subsidence over that period (Fig. 10 ). However, water levels subsequently recovered, exceeding their pre-2002 levels by 2007. This recovery of water levels is not typically observed in regions with long-term subsidence due to a lack of groundwater management. Thus, the groundwater management in the San Luis Valley, which regulates withdrawals and requires that water levels are maintained above levels from 1970 to 2000 (Reeves et al., 2014 ), appears to be effective in mitigating land subsidence. The low rate of subsidence in the San Luis Valley relative to other agricultural areas with high subsidence potential is another indication of this effectiveness. As part of our study, we also estimate maps depicting the annual amplitude of seasonal deformation (dominated by elastic deformation) in ascending, descending, and vertical directions. This spatial representation provides a clear downward trend in the annual deformation of the LOS direction from 2015 to 2021 (Figure S6.a and S6.b). The noticeable increase in seasonal deformation and the expanding spatial extent of the amplitude is evident in both ascending and descending directions, with a clearer signal in the vertical direction. This apparent trend could be due to the relatively low seasonal fluctuation in head in the early years of our study (see for example the low head fluctuations from 2015 to 2017 in Fig. 10 ). Chen et al. (2017)  observed up to 10 cm of seasonal deformation from 2010 to 2011, a period when a large seasonal fluctuation in head occurred (Fig. 10 ). These observations are consistent with principles of elastic deformation: higher seasonal fluctuations in head will lead to higher seasonal deformation. The high seasonal deformation only occurs south of the Rio Grande, where pumping is almost exclusively from the confined aquifer. North of the Rio Grande, much more pumping occurs (see Fig. 5 ), but it is primarily from the unconfined aquifer. The unconfined aquifer south of the river, in contrast, consists of just a thin alluvial veneer atop blue clay, which significantly constrains its productivity in comparison to the large and productive unconfined aquifer in the Close Basin. Confined aquifers have a much stronger response in head to pumping and recharge due to their low storativity (Cherry and Freeze, 1979; Hasan et al., 2023 ), which is expressed in agricultural regions as a large seasonal decline during the growing season followed by a large rebound after pumping has ceased (see for example Fig. 3 a from Butler et al., 2013 ). Thus, the seasonal response of deformation to withdrawals can be an effective way to identify confined aquifer systems that are being produced. The application of InSAR methods in this study has proven to be effective for monitoring and modeling land subsidence and groundwater fluctuations in the San Luis Valley. Similar to the findings of (Navarro-Hernández et al., 2020 ), the ability of InSAR to provide detailed observations of ground deformation is critical for understanding the dynamics between land subsidence and groundwater levels. Our modeling approach can be used to effectively link deformation processes with groundwater processes, even in regions where limited groundwater level data are available or where InSAR signals are decorrelated. These models can also be used to forecast future scenarios (Smith and Knight, 2019 ).  6 Conclusions Our study has provided both a mechanistic model for deformation in the San Luis Valley, as well as a suite of methods that can be adopted in other regions to improve time series analysis of InSAR and head data. We have successfully addressed the challenges of phase decorrelation and data gaps, enhancing the utility of InSAR data in agricultural regions. Our use of a modified PS-interpolation algorithm and SSA-based gap filling technique has resulted in a complete dataset for the study period. Our SBAS InSAR time series analysis has revealed significant seasonal deformation and long-term subsidence within the confined portion of the SLV aquifer. The observed deformation is closely linked to the aquifer system's seasonal response, highlighting the critical role of effective water management in preventing further land subsidence. Interestingly, the presence of long-term deformation without a corresponding long-term head decline can be attributed to the inelastic deformation that occurs within the aquifer system. Even when the groundwater level rebounds to its pre-consolidation level, the inelastic deformation does not fully recover, leading to a lasting subsidence. Furthermore, our study has demonstrated the potential of advanced techniques, such as InSAR, in monitoring and predicting land subsidence due to groundwater extraction. Our findings underscore the importance of these techniques in informing water management strategies and planning for future land use, particularly in regions like the SLV where agriculture is highly dependent on groundwater resources. Future research should continue to explore the potential of these advanced techniques in other agricultural regions, and further refine the methodologies introduced in this study. This will help to improve our understanding of groundwater dynamics and associated land subsidence and contribute to the development of sustainable water management strategies.
1 Introduction Terrestrial evapotranspiration (ET) represents the sum of surface evaporation and plant transpiration, constituting a crucial component of the hydrological cycle. Annually, ET returns 60 % of precipitation to the atmosphere from the Earth’s surface, concurrently utilizing half of the solar energy absorbed by the land surface (Zhu et al., 2022 ). ET plays a pivotal role in linking ecosystem hydrological cycles, surface energy balance, and carbon cycling (Feng et al., 2021; Liu, 2022; Zhang et al., 2020a ). The components of ET encompass soil evaporation (Es), vegetation transpiration (T), and interception evaporation (I), with T being the dominant water flux in ET, constituting 60 %–80 % of the total terrestrial evaporation. In certain ecosystems, the proportion of T can be even higher, reaching up to 95 % of the total ET (Maes et al., 2020; Stoy et al., 2019 ). T involves the absorption of soil moisture by root systems and the vapor loss through plant stomata, thereby coupling climatic, vegetative, and soil-driven water and carbon dynamics through plant stomata (Shan et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the precise estimation of vegetation transpiration is of paramount significance for a comprehensive understanding of land–atmosphere water-carbon cycles and climate change. Nevertheless, due to the control exerted by surface heterogeneity and a myriad of complex biophysical processes, T is challenging to directly measure spatially, rendering it one of the most elusive hydrological variables at a global scale (Lu et al., 2018; Fisher et al., 2017; Dolman et al., 2014 ). The separation of T from ET is the most common approach to obtaining T. Currently, numerous methods have been developed for partitioning T from ET, encompassing scales ranging from plot-level to ecosystem-level and global-scale assessments. Methods for partitioning ET at the plot scale primarily include leaf gas exchange, lysimetry, psychrometry, soil heat pulse, liquid flow measurement, isotope techniques (Stoy et al., 2019; Kool et al., 2014 ), as well as recently developed approaches such as flux variance similarity method (Stoy et al., 2006 ) and eddy covariance method (Zahn et al., 2022 ). While these methods can accurately capture ET components at the plot scale, their application for partitioning ET components at the ecosystem or global scale introduces significant uncertainties. With the advancement of remote sensing technology, the partitioning of ET has been extended to larger regions and even global scales by integrating ecosystem observations and remote sensing techniques. This enables the quantification of water flux changes at various temporal and spatial scales, employing methods such as thermal imaging (Marshall et al., 2016 ), empirical or semi-empirical models based on vegetation indices and T/ET relationships (Schlesinger and Jasechko, 2014 ), and others. These methods simulate the T/ET by establishing empirical or semi-empirical relationships with the reflectance measured through optical remote sensing. However, the reflectance measured by optical remote sensing is not directly linked to the vegetation photosynthetic processes (Shan et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021 ). As a result, these methods can only indirectly estimate T/ET. Accurately obtaining regional or global-scale vegetation transpiration still presents significant challenges. The recently reported solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) measurements from satellites present new opportunities for accurately estimating regional or global-scale vegetation transpiration. Green plants absorb photosynthetically active radiation through photosynthesis, part of which is released as heat through non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), and a small fraction is re-emitted by chlorophyll at longer wavelengths (640–850nm). This emitted fraction is referred to as solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (Yang et al., 2022; Frankenberg et al., 2018 ). SIF is directly associated with photosynthesis and is considered a probe for photosynthetic activity (Meroni et al., 2009 ). Consequently, SIF has found extensive applications in monitoring photosynthesis, tracking gross primary productivity (GPP), and other related areas (Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Numerous studies have extensively documented the close relationship between SIF and GPP, providing evidence that, under natural conditions, SIF can serve as a viable surrogate parameter for GPP (Bai et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018a ). Plant stomata concurrently regulate T and GPP, with both linked through the water use efficiency (WUE=GPP/T) (Huang et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2023 ). Therefore, building upon the relationship between GPP and SIF, researchers have sought to establish a connection between T and SIF, aiming to unveil the coupling dynamics between SIF and T. Lu et al. (2018)  initially presented ground evidence of the potential of SIF to estimate T, demonstrating that the accuracy of SIF-based transpiration estimation is at least comparable to that of the traditional Penman-Monteith equation. Recent studies have further reported the close relationship between SIF and T at various temporal and spatial scales. The study conducted by Shan et al. (2019)  on T estimation across forest, farmland, and grassland ecosystems further demonstrates the potential of SIF in constraining T. Their research also indicates that SIF is an effective indicator of canopy stomatal conductance. This finding is significant for enhancing the understanding of uncertainties in T estimation arising from errors in simulating canopy conductance. Pagán et al. (2019)  explored the potential of constraining vegetation transpiration using SIF based on Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment-2 SIF data and site-monitored vegetation transpiration data. Maes et al. (2020)  demonstrated that T can be reliably estimated globally using observations of SIF by analyzing data from 83 global flux sites and two primary SIF datasets (Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment-2 SIF and Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 SIF). Feng et al. (2021)  incorporated SIF and T into two carbon–water coupling frameworks, demonstrating the physical correlation between SIF and T and successfully estimating T using SIF. Cong et al. (2022)  investigated the influence of meteorological and soil factors on the relationship between SIF and T. Gao et al. (2023)  successfully predicted T in Open Woodland using SIF and vegetation structure. Although numerous studies have demonstrated the significant relationship between SIF and T across different spatial and temporal scales, several challenges persist in this area of research. Firstly, ground-based SIF remote sensing has a limited monitoring range, typically effective only within a few hundred meters to a few kilometers. Within this limited range, most ecosystems are homogeneous (Liu et al., 2017a; Porcar-Castell et al., 2015 ).
