Additionally, existing studies utilizing ground-based SIF to monitor vegetation transpiration have predominantly been conducted within single ecosystems. Does the SIF-T relationship hold universally or vary across different time scales, land cover types, and photosynthetic pathways? To what extent is the SIF-T relationship influenced by environmental conditions? Such issues still require further in-depth investigation. Secondly, while satellite-based SIF remote sensing compensates for the limitations of ground-based SIF observations, SIF datasets derived from satellite retrievals originate from various sensors, wavelengths, and inversion algorithms. The substantial uncertainty inherent in these datasets may potentially obscure the relationship between SIF and T. Currently, satellite-retrieved SIF data face challenges such as coarse spatial resolution, high data noise, sparse global coverage, and limited record duration. Early satellites that acquired SIF datasets include the Greenhouse Gases Observing Satellite (GOSAT) (Frankenberg et al., 2011 ), the Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment-2 Satellite (GOME-2) (Joiner et al., 2013 ), and the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 Satellite (OCO-2) (Frankenberg et al., 2014 ). Both GOSAT and GOME-2 satellites offer fine temporal resolution (GOSAT: 3 days, GOME-2: 1.5 days) but have coarse spatial resolution (GOSAT: 10.5 km × 10.5 km, GOME-2: at least 40 km 40 km). In comparison, OCO-2 satellite exhibits a higher spatial resolution (1.29 km × 2.25 km), but lower temporal resolution (16 days) and spatial discontinuity. The Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) aboard the Copernicus Sentinel-5P mission provides superior temporal and spatial resolution (1 day, 3.5 km × 5.5 km) (Guanter et al., 2021 ). TROPOMI has demonstrated commendable performance in estimating global gross GPP and T (Liu et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, the TROPOMI time series is limited, with data available only from April 2018 onwards. The utilization of satellite-retrieved SIF has been demonstrated to exhibit a close relationship with T. However, limitations such as spatial resolution, spatial continuity, and data record duration hinder our comprehensive understanding of the SIF-T relationship. Hence, there is an urgent need for improved SIF data to delve deeper into the coupled dynamics of SIF and T. To overcome the limitations of satellite-measured SIF, researchers employ data reconstruction methods to acquire enhanced global gridded SIF datasets. These reconstructed SIF datasets are derived from one or multiple original SIF datasets, integrating various auxiliary data, such as MODIS surface reflectance data, PAR data, land cover data, ERA5 temperature data, among others. Subsequently, machine learning methods or light use efficiency approaches are employed for their generation (Zhang et al., 2018; Li and Xiao, 2019; Ma et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Duveiller et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022 ). In comparison to original SIF datasets such as GOME-2 SIF and OCO-2 SIF, the reconstructed SIF data exhibit superior performance in various aspects, including drought monitoring (Wei et al., 2022 ), vegetation phenology monitoring (Meng et al., 2021 ), and gross primary productivity (GPP) monitoring (Pastorello et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Among the numerous reconstructed SIF datasets, the CSIF (continuous SIF) dataset stands out for its elevated temporal resolution (4 days), fine spatial resolution (0.05°), and lower signal-to-noise ratio, showcasing significant potential in terrestrial ecosystem monitoring (Zhang et al., 2018 ). The excellent performance of CSIF data enables the robust elucidation of the inherent nature of the SIF-T relationship in a more resilient manner. However, it remains unclear whether reconstructed SIF data, which address issues of spatial resolution, spatial continuity, and data record duration, can also replicate the strong SIF-T correlations observed in original SIF data. In this study, a global analysis of the relationship between SIF and T was conducted using reconstructed SIF data and transpiration data obtained from 109 flux tower sites worldwide, encompassing 11 different land cover types. The primary research objectives are as follows: (1) to investigate the relationship between CSIF and site T by examining the CSIF-T relationship across various land cover types, temporal scales, and photosynthetic pathways, with the aim of elucidating variations in the SIF-T relationship under different conditions; (2) to compare the relationship between CSIF and vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) retrieved from MODIS with site T and assess the modeling potential of SIF for transpiration estimation; and (3) to analyze the impact of environmental factors (air temperature, vapor pressure deficit, net radiation, and leaf area index) on the relationship between SIF and T.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 FLUXNET2015 data The flux data (carbon flux and water flux) and meteorological data utilized in this study were sourced from the FLUXNET2015 dataset, graciously provided by the Global Flux Observation Network (https://fluxnet.org/ ). The Global Flux Observation Network (FLUXNET) is designed to advance the development of land surface models by furnishing them with high-quality validation datasets. Early versions of this network include the FLUXNET Marconi dataset from the year 2000 and the FLUXNET LaThuile dataset from 2007. The most recent iteration of this network, released in 2016, is the FLUXNET2015 dataset. Comprising over two decades of data records, the FLUXNET2015 dataset encompasses 10 land cover types. The data have undergone uniform preprocessing procedures, including quality control, interpolation, and partitioning, thereby rendering the FLUXNET2015 dataset the most comprehensive compilation of terrestrial ecosystem data available. The FLUXNET2015 dataset furnishes data at five temporal scales: half-hourly/hourly (HH/HR), daily (DD), weekly (WW), monthly (MM), and yearly (YY). The data utilized in this study pertain to daily fluxes and meteorological parameters, including net radiation (Rn, Wm−2 ), air temperature (TA,  °C), vapor pressure deficit (VPD, hPa), latent heat flux (LE, Wm−2 ). To address the issue of surface energy balance nonclosure, it is imperative to perform energy closure corrections on latent heat flux data.The FLUXNET2015 dataset, operating under the assumption of the correctness of the Bowen ratio, offers a corrected version of energy balance by applying an energy balance correction factor to the original latent heat flux, thereby rectifying the latent heat flux data (Pastorello et al., 2020 ). Due to the inconsistency between SIF data and flux tower observation footprints, it is imperative to assess the representativeness of flux sites for corresponding SIF pixels. Homogeneity within a 5-kilometer radius around each flux site was examined utilizing the 500-meter MODIS land cover product (MOD12C1). Given the gradual nature of land cover change, a 3-year time span of MODIS land use data (2001, 2006, and 2011) was selected to ascertain variations in vegetation cover types. Sites were retained if the predominant vegetation type within the 5-kilometer radius, as determined by MOD12C1, matched that of the flux site. Ensuring data quality necessitates the implementation of the following pre-processing steps for each site: (1) remove missing data and invalid values (−9999) to ensure data integrity, retaining only those instances where latent heat flux (LE) exhibits positive values; (2) exclude data from rainy days to mitigate the impact of rainfall interception; and (3) utilize only flux data with high confidence levels. The final dataset comprises flux data from 109 global sites spanning the years 2001 to 2014, encompassing 11 land cover types, including 16 cropland sites (CRO), 25 grassland sites (GRA), 13 deciduous broadleaf forest sites (DBF), 8 evergreen broadleaf forest sites (EBF), 22 evergreen needleleaf forest sites (ENF), 3 mixed forest sites (MF), 4 open shrubland sites (OSH), 2 closed shrubland sites (CSH), 6 savanna sites (SAV), 5 woody savanna sites (WSA), and 5 wetland sites (WET). The detailed information of 109 flux sites can be found in Table S1 . The spatial distribution of flux sites is illustrated in Fig. 1  . Aggregate the temporal scale of all daily flux data to 8-day and monthly scales. Data records with less than 5 days within an 8-day period or less than 20 days within a month will be excluded.  2.2 CSIF data The CSIF data, as developed by Zhang et al. (2018) , is derived from OCO-2-SIF data and MODIS surface reflectance data through a forward neural network (NN) algorithm. The model is constrained using instantaneous SIF data observed under clear-sky conditions, resulting in the generation of two consecutive SIF products with a temporal resolution of 4 days and a spatial resolution of 0.05°—namely, Clear-Sky Instantaneous SIF (CSIFclear-inst) and All-Day Average SIF (CSIFall-daily). CSIF, characterized by high temporal and spatial resolutions as well as a prolonged data record, is derived from OCO-2 SIF, offering reduced temporal and spatial gaps, enhanced signal-to-noise ratio, and superior accuracy compared to the original OCO-2 SIF data (Wang et al., 2023 ). In this study, all-day average CSIF data from January 2001 to December 2014 were selected for analysis (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.6387494) .  2.3 MODIS data This study utilized three MODIS data products, namely Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data, Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) data, and land cover data. NDVI and EVI are commonly employed for monitoring vegetation growth status and empirically estimating land evapotranspiration (Zhang et al., 2016; Zeng et al., 2022 ). In this study, we utilize NDVI and EVI for comparative assessment of the CSIF model’s performance in simulating vegetation transpiration. Utilizing the Google Earth Engine (GEE), NDVI and EVI data spanning January 2001 to December 2014 were synthesized from MOD09A1 (8 days, 500 m). Subsequently, all 500 m NDVI and EVI data were uniformly resampled to a 0.05° resolution for correspondence with CSIF pixels. Land cover data were obtained from the MOD12C1 dataset (https://ladsweb.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/ ), which is a 500 m annual land cover dataset. The MOD12C1 data for the years 2001 to 2014 were selected, and the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) classification scheme was employed to ascertain the vegetation cover types at flux sites.  2.4 Leaf area index data Leaf Area Index (LAI) data were derived from the Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS) LAI product dataset. This dataset is based on Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) reflectance data and was generated using a generalized regression neural network (https://www.glass.umd.edu/LAI/AVHRR/ ) (Xiao et al., 2017 ). The GLASS LAI data exhibit a temporal resolution of 8 days and a spatial resolution of 0.05°. The GLASS LAI data for the years 2001 to 2014 were selected to ensure temporal alignment with flux site data and SIF data.  2.5 The computation of T from eddy-covariance observations In recent years, various methods have been developed to partition vegetation transpiration from latent heat flux observations at flux sites. For instance, Zhou et al. (2016)  proposed a method based on the relationship between T and GPP, integrating the assumption from optimality theory that plants minimize water loss per unit CO2  gain, leading to the formulation of a water use efficiency approach (Zhou et al., 2016 ). However, these methods rely on GPP data and are subject to stringent data screening criteria, resulting in a limited number of effective records. In contrast, the transpiration partitioning method proposed by Wei et al. (2017)  is operationally straightforward, requiring fewer input variables. It only necessitates latent heat flux data, land cover data, and leaf area index data for the partitioning of evapotranspiration components. This method has undergone rigorous evaluation (Wei et al., 2017 ), and the computational formula is as follows:(1) T = a 1  LAI  a 2   × L E     In the equation, parameters a 1      and a 2     are fitting parameters for various land cover types. Wei et al. (2017)  collected values of variables such as vegetation transpiration and actual evapotranspiration from 64 published studies. These 64 studies were conducted at 64 different locations worldwide, encompassing six types of land cover (Broad leave forests, Needle leave forests, Mixed forests, Shrubs and Grasses, Crops, and Wetlands). Using these data, a stable regression relationship was established between LAI, T, and latent heat flux, thereby deriving the optimal empirical values of parameters a 1      and a 2     for different land cover types (Wei et al., 2017 ). LAI denotes the leaf area index data, sourced from the GLASS LAI dataset in this study; LE corresponds to latent heat flux data observed at flux sites. A comprehensive description of this method can be found in the literature (Wei et al., 2017 ). In this study, the aforementioned method was employed to compute vegetation transpiration data for each flux site.  2.6 Statistical analysis Utilizing vegetation transpiration data obtained from 109 global flux sites spanning 11 land cover types, along with CSIF data, this study assessed the relationship between SIF and site T at two temporal scales (8-day and monthly). Initially, the temporal variations in both SIF and T across the 11 land cover types were examined. This examination is crucial for establishing SIF as a key parameter for estimating transpiration, requiring not only a strong correlation between SIF and T but also consistency in their temporal patterns. Due to the opposite growing seasons in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, the 109 flux sites were grouped, and the temporal variations in SIF and T were separately analyzed for different land cover types in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Given the limited number of flux sites collected in the Southern Hemisphere (20 sites), the analysis focused solely on the temporal characteristics of SIF and T for five land cover types: CRO, DBF, EBF, SAV, and WSA. Subsequently, the correlation between SIF and T was examined. In evaluating the relationship between SIF and T, linear and exponential regression models were employed to represent the linear and non-linear associations of SIF and T (Lu et al., 2018; Shan et al., 2019; Shan et al., 2021 ), with the formulas for the linear and non-linear models presented in Equations (2) and (3) , respectively.(2) T = b 1 × S I F + b 2     (3) T = b 3 × e  b 4 × S I F       In the equations, b 1   , b 2   , b 3    and b 4    represent the fitting coefficients. When assessing the linear and non-linear relationships between SIF and T, the determination coefficients (R2 ) of both models were computed. The comparison of R2  values was employed to discern whether the relationship between SIF and T is linear or non-linear. The objective of this study is to assess the potential of SIF in modeling vegetation transpiration. Therefore, SIF is compared with the widely used vegetation indices to aid in evaluating the value of using SIF for modeling vegetation transpiration. Vegetation index data, derived from MODIS data, include NDVI and EVI. Due to the original spatial resolution of 500 m for NDVI and EVI, and to facilitate a fair comparison with CSIF data, the spatial resolution of the original NDVI and EVI was resampled to 0.05°. As SIF contains photosynthetic information, unlike the selected NDVI and EVI, which do not, this facilitates a contrasting comparison with SIF, highlighting its value in modeling transpiration. Similarly, linear and exponential regression models were employed to characterize the linear and non-linear relationships between NDVI or EVI and T. Thirdly, due to the varied biological characteristics across different land cover types, significant differences exist in the SIF-T relationships within distinct land cover types (Maes et al., 2020; Stoy et al., 2019; Shan et al., 2019 ). This variability can result in substantial uncertainty in regional or global estimates of vegetation transpiration. A thorough understanding of the SIF-T relationships in different land cover types and efforts to minimize the disparities in these relationships may lead to more accurate regional or global transpiration estimates. Is the relationship between SIF and T universally pervasive, or does it manifest specific characteristics contingent upon distinct land cover types? To address this inquiry, a comparative analysis of the association between SIF and T was undertaken across various land cover types. Due to the closer approximation to linearity in the relationship between SIF and T, as observed in Section 3.2 , emphasis is placed on investigating the linear association between SIF and T across diverse land cover types. To investigate the relationship between SIF and T across various land cover types, an examination of the determination coefficients and linear regression slopes of SIF and T was conducted by comparing different vegetation types. The imposition of a linear regression forced through the origin (intercept set to zero) aligns with the condition where SIF is zero in the absence of photosynthetic activity. This approach not only adheres to the premise that SIF is zero when there is no photosynthesis but also obviates the necessity for comparative analysis of intercepts in linear regression. Thus, the relationship between SIF and T across various land cover types can be effectively characterized solely through the examination of linear regression slopes. Utilizing one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), statistical differences in the SIF-T slopes among different land cover types were compared. Fourthly, prior research has documented variations in the relationship between SIF and GPP within C3 and C4 vegetation (Li et al., 2018b ). Due to the coupling of SIF, GPP, and T through stomatal function, does the relationship between C3 and C4 vegetation exhibit uniformity in both SIF and T? To address this, an analysis of the SIF-T relationship was conducted in agricultural fields and grasslands where either C3 or C4 vegetation predominates, aiming to elucidate whether the SIF-T association is universally applicable or contingent upon photosynthetic pathways. According to the descriptions of flux sites, data were gathered from 15 C3 sites and 7 C4 sites, drawn from a pool consisting of 16 CRO sites and 25 GRA sites. Finally, an exploration was conducted into the influence of various environmental factors on the SIF-T relationship. These environmental factors encompassed net radiation (Rn), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), air temperature (TA), and LAI. Rn is defined as the algebraic sum of the surface’s absorbed total energy and outgoing energy. It serves as a primary energy source for photosynthesis and evapotranspiration, and is also a crucial variable in the modeling of hydrological and climatic change models (Ghahreman and Rahimzadegan, 2022 ). VPD and TA regulate T and SIF through their effects on photosynthesis, while LAI, as a biological driver of T, is closely associated with both T and SIF (Tie et al., 2017; Wang and Dickinson, 2012; Wei et al., 2017 ). These environmental factors are derived from daily data collected at the flux tower sites and are similarly aggregated at 8-day and monthly temporal scale. Based on the distribution patterns of each environmental factor’s data, binning was employed, establishing diverse gradients to explore how environmental factors impact the SIF-T relationship. This endeavor aims to clarify under what environmental conditions SIF may potentially decouple from T, thereby providing valuable insights for mechanistically understanding the SIF-T relationship.   3 Results 3.1 Dynamics of the SIF and T at site scale Fig. 2   illustrates the seasonal dynamics of SIF and T across various land cover types in the Northern Hemisphere, as monitored by flux tower sites. Throughout the course of a year, both SIF and T in the Northern Hemisphere exhibit a similar temporal pattern, characterized by an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease. There are variations in the timing of peak values for SIF and T among different land cover types. In CRO, ENF, OSH, and CSH, the time at which SIF reaches seasonal peak values aligns with that of T, occurring at 185 DOY (Day of Year), 185 DOY, 217 DOY, and 129 DOY, respectively. Conversely, in DBF, EBF, MF, SAV, and WSA, the timing of SIF reaching peak values lags behind that of T, while in GRA and WET, the seasonal peak of SIF precedes that of T. Among the 11 land cover types, the maximum difference in the seasonal peak values of SIF and T occurs in DBF (48 DOY), followed by MF (24 DOY), WSA (24 DOY), and WET (16 DOY). In the remaining vegetation types, the disparity in the seasonal peak values between SIF and T is relatively smaller, ranging from 0 to 8 days. Overall, the seasonal dynamics of SIF and T exhibit a pronounced similarity across various land cover types in the Northern Hemisphere, displaying a concave-up (inverted U-shaped) trend. In the Southern Hemisphere, significant temporal disparities exist in the seasonal peaks of SIF and T between EBF and WSA vegetation types. Specifically, in EBF, the peak times for SIF and T are 353 DOY and 25 DOY respectively, whereas in WSA, these peaks occur at 305 DOY and 89 DOY respectively. Conversely, the seasonal peaks of SIF and T are relatively proximate among the remaining three land cover types, with variations ranging from 0 to 16 days. In contrast, when compared to the Northern Hemisphere, the seasonal dynamics of SIF and T in the Southern Hemisphere manifest an opposing pattern, collectively forming a convex-up (U-shaped) curve, as depicted in Fig. 3  . The results from Fig. 2  and Fig. 3  reveal that, at the site scale, SIF and T exhibit similar seasonal variation characteristics across various vegetation types. The analogous seasonal dynamics of SIF and T in different land cover types suggest that SIF effectively captures the temporal trends of Transpiration.  3.2 Comparisons between SIF and MODIS VIs with site T Across the 109 flux tower sites, each underwent a rigorous data quality control process. Notably, certain sites exhibited an excess of data, which could potentially impact the comparative analysis of the relationship between SIF and MODIS vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) with site-level T. Consequently, data from all sites were aggregated, and an investigation into the relationship between SIF, MODIS vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI), and site-level T was conducted at 8-day and monthly temporal scales (Fig. 4  ). The results in Fig. 4 (a1) and (b1) indicate that, whether at an 8-day or monthly scale, the linear relationship between SIF and T is stronger than the non-linear relationship (8-day: linear R2  = 0.59, non-linear R2  = 0.47; monthly: linear R2  = 0.65, non-linear R2  = 0.51). Furthermore, the aggregation from an 8-day to a monthly scale leads to an improvement in the relationship between SIF and T (linear relationship: R2  increases from 0.59 to 0.65, non-linear relationship: R2  increases from 0.47 to 0.51). To assess the potential of SIF in estimating T, a comparative analysis was conducted with two MODIS vegetation indices, NDVI (Fig. 4 (a2) and (b2)), and EVI (Fig. 4 (a3) and (b3). In general, at both the 8-day and monthly scales, MODIS vegetation indices exhibit moderate correlations with T, with R2  ranging from 0.35 to 0.50. Specifically, within NDVI, the non-linear relationship between NDVI and T is more pronounced (linear R2 : 8-day 0.35, monthly 0.43; non-linear R2 : 8-day 0.41, monthly 0.50), whereas in EVI, the linear relationship with T surpasses the non-linear relationship (linear R2 : 8-day 0.41, monthly 0.48; non-linear R2 : 8-day 0.38, monthly 0.44). Furthermore, akin to the SIF-T relationship, the relationship between monthly MODIS vegetation indices and T surpasses that at the 8-day scale. However, despite the moderate correlations between MODIS vegetation indices and T, the relationship between SIF and T excels over that of MODIS vegetation indices and T, both in terms of the 8-day and monthly scales, as well as in the linear and non-linear relationships. In summary, the relationship between SIF and T is more robust compared to MODIS vegetation indices, and the linear association better characterizes the SIF-T relationship. Consequently, the subsequent discussion will primarily emphasize the linear relationship between SIF and T.  3.3 The linear relationship between SIF and T across diverse land cover types To analyze the SIF-T relationship across different land cover types, data from 109 flux sites were aggregated according to 11 specific IGBP land cover types. Fig. 5   illustrates the linear relationship between SIF and T across 11 land cover types at both 8-day and monthly temporal scales. As depicted in Fig. 5 , a moderate to strong linear correlation is evident between SIF and T across the 11 land cover types at both temporal scales. Notably, variations in the linear relationship between SIF and T are observed across different land cover types. At the 8-day temporal scale, the linear R2  values for different land cover types range from 0.41 (OSH) to 0.84 (CSH). Notably, there is a higher correlation between SIF and T in GRA, MF, CSH, SAV, and WSA (R2  > 0.66), while the correlation is comparatively lower in CRO, DBF, EBF, ENF, OSH, and WET (R2  ranging between 0.41 and 0.59). At the monthly temporal scale, the range of linear R2  values varies from 0.32 (OSH) to 0.89 (CSH). Upon aggregation from an 8-day to a monthly scale, the linear R2  for the relationship between SIF and T improves for most land cover types, with the exceptions being EBF, MF, OSH, SAV, and WET. Linear regression slopes for SIF and T were further calculated across different land cover types at both temporal scales, as depicted in Fig. 5 . The slope is highest for OSH at 544.65 (W m−2 /W m−2  μm sr−1 ), and lowest for MF at 173.77 (W m−2 /W m−2  μm sr−1 ). The linear slopes for SIF and T in the remaining land cover types are as follows, in ascending order: SAV, WSA, WET, GRA, CSH, CRO, EBF, ENF, DBF. The differentiation in slopes across different land cover types was validated using ANOVA, as illustrated in Fig. 6  . In the ANOVA, land cover types with fewer than three site data points were excluded, and as such, CSH is not included in the analysis. The results of the ANOVA indicate that the linear relationship slopes between SIF and T for most land cover types do not exhibit significant differences from the slopes associated with their respective vegetation types. This finding suggests that the linear relationship between SIF and T is nearly universal across various vegetation types.  3.4 The linear relationship between SIF and T across various photosynthetic pathways To investigate whether different photosynthetic pathways result in distinct SIF-T linear relationships, a comparison of SIF-T linear relationships between known C3 and C4 sites was conducted at both 8-day and monthly scales, as depicted in Fig. 7  . From Fig. 7 (a) and (b), it is evident that at the 8-day scale, the linear correlation between SIF and T is stronger for C4 vegetation compared to C3 vegetation (C3: R2  = 0.60, C4: R2  = 0.80). Utilizing a linear regression model without intercept, the slope of the SIF-T relationship for C4 vegetation is higher than that for C3 vegetation, with the slope of C4 vegetation being 1.27 times the slope of C3 vegetation. At the monthly scale (Fig. 7 (c) and (d)), the linear relationship and slopes of SIF-T for C3 and C4 vegetation remain consistent with the patterns observed at the 8-day scale. As the temporal aggregation progresses from an 8-day scale to a monthly scale, the linear correlation between SIF and T strengthens for both C3 and C4 vegetation. Additionally, the disparity in SIF-T slopes diminishes, reducing from 1.27 times at the 8-day scale to 1.15 times at the monthly scale. Overall, the linear relationship between SIF and T is more robust in C4 vegetation compared to C3 vegetation.  3.5 Environmental effects on the SIF-T relationship The relationship between SIF and site T varies with changes in environmental factors (TA, VPD, Rn, and LAI) at both 8-day and monthly scales, displaying almost identical trends (Fig. 8  ). Under low and moderate temperature conditions (TA < 25 °C), the correlation between SIF and T strengthens with increasing temperature (8-day scale: R2  = 0.00 ∼ 0.63; monthly scale: R2  = 0.00 ∼ 0.67). When the temperature reaches a specific threshold, the R2  for CSIF-T reaches its maximum value. However, beyond this threshold (TA > 30 °C), the correlation between SIF-T significantly weakens (8-day scale: R2  decreases from 0.63 to 0.42, monthly scale: R2  decreases from 0.67 to 0.07) (Fig. 8 a and b). This suggests that moderate warming enhances the linear relationship between SIF and T, but when the temperature surpasses a certain threshold, it disrupts the coupling between SIF and T. For VPD, a high linear correlation is observed at low VPD, with the strongest linear correlation between SIF and T occurring within the VPD range of 0 to 10 hPa (8-day scale: R2  = 0.61; monthly scale: R2  = 0.68). As VPD exceeds 10 hPa, the correlation between SIF and T gradually weakens, reaching a significant decline when VPD surpasses 20 hPa. Beyond 30 hPa, the correlation reaches its minimum value. This indicates that the strong correlation between SIF and T is suitable for normal and humid conditions (Fig. 8 c and d). With the increase in Rn, the linear correlation between SIF and T steadily strengthens. However, when Rn surpasses a certain threshold (Rn > 100 Wm−2 ), the linear correlation between SIF and T begins to decline (Fig. 8 e and f). Under different LAI conditions, the linear relationship between SIF and T changes significantly. A strong linear correlation between SIF and T is observed at low LAI levels. When the LAI value exceeds 1.2 m2 /m2 , the linear correlation between SIF and T diminishes as the LAI increases (Fig. 8 g and h). As environmental conditions evolve, the slope (T:SIF) of the linear relationship between SIF and T also undergoes changes (Fig. 8 ). With the continuous increase in TA, the slope of the linear relationship between SIF and T steadily increases. This suggests that as the temperature rises, the proportion of T relative to SIF increases. Similar patterns are observed in VPD, Rn, and LAI, where the proportion of T in both SIF and T increases with higher VPD Rn, and LAI. In summary, the relationship between SIF and T is significantly influenced by environmental factors. A robust linear correlation between SIF and T is observed primarily under favorable environmental conditions. However, when environmental conditions exceed certain threshold values, the linear relationship between SIF and T deteriorates.   4 Discussion 4.1 The comprehension of the SIF-T relationship The investigation of the correlation between SIF and T was undertaken by leveraging T data acquired from 109 globally distributed flux tower sites, spanning 11 distinct land cover types, in conjunction with recently reconstructed SIF data (CSIF). Prior investigations have substantiated the close association between SIF and GPP (Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2021 ). The coupling relationship between T and GPP, mediated through stomatal functionality, affords an opportunity for the quantification of T through SIF (Stoy et al., 2019 ). The findings of this study demonstrate a robust linear correlation between SIF and site T across various temporal scales. Despite variations in the strength of the linear correlation between SIF and T across different land cover types (Fig. 5 ), a pervasive linear relationship between SIF and T is observed in diverse land cover types. It is important to note that differences in correlation strength do not necessarily imply substantial disparities in the linear relationship between SIF and T across various land cover types. Single-factor analysis of covariance across different land cover types further substantiates that the majority of land cover types exhibit no statistically significant differences in the SIF-T slopes when compared to other land cover types (Fig. 6 ). In essence, the relationship between SIF and T appears to be universally present. These research outcomes align with the conclusions drawn by Maes et al. (2020) , who utilized coarse spatial resolution OCO-2 SIF and GOME-2 SIF. However, the performance of the SIF-T relationship across different land cover types notably deviates from the findings reported by Maes et al. (2020) . For instance, the EBF land cover type in this study, resembling sparse shrub grassland land cover types (SAV, WSA), did not exhibit lower correlation and slope values. The potential reasons for these observed differences lie in the CSIF data employed in this study, generated from original OCO-2 SIF and additional environmental auxiliary data. The resultant data not only encapsulates photosynthetic information but also incorporates environmental information, thereby substantially mitigating the impact of environmental factors on the SIF-T relationship. Therefore, satisfactory results were obtained in ecosystems characterized by structural complexity, such as evergreen broadleaf forests that are challenging to monitor, and in ecosystems resembling sparse shrub grasslands where the influence of background information is significant. In addition, the strongest correlation was observed within the CSH, rather than in the CRO and DBF. This might be attributed to the fact that the selected CSH only includes two flux tower sites. If there were more observational data, the SIF-T linear relationship within the CSH could potentially undergo changes. The weaker SIF-T linear relationships in the CRO and DBF can be attributed to seasonal variations, and the practice of crop rotation in agricultural fields, which reduces the linear correlation between SIF and T. The association between T and SIF is established through the relationship of WUE between T and GPP (Huang et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2023 ), representing the fundamental basis enabling SIF to estimate T. The slope of the SIF-GPP relationship varies across different land cover types and is contingent upon factors such as photosynthesis, fluorescence quantum yield, and the probability of SIF photons escaping from the canopy (Li and Xiao, 2022 ). Indeed, the factors influencing the SIF-GPP relationship across various land cover types can be attributed to the intricate interplay of biological characteristics, canopy structure, and environmental conditions specific to different vegetation types (Lu et al., 2018; Damm et al., 2015 ). Similarly, these factors also determine the relationship between SIF and T in diverse land cover types. Most studies indicate that the relationship between SIF and T varies with vegetation types and environmental conditions (Shan et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2018 ). However, these studies often overlook the interactions among environmental factors both across different vegetation types and within the same vegetation type. Results obtained from leaf-scale observations at the hourly scale may not necessarily be applicable at larger spatial (ecosystem scale) and temporal scales (daily to monthly scale). The amplification of temporal or spatial scales tends to offset these influencing factors, thereby diminishing the differences in the SIF-T relationships across various vegetation types (Liu et al., 2022b ). Recent studies have also reported a reduction in the uncertainty of estimating T with the aggregation of time. Shan et al. (2021) , employing on-site SIF measurements and eddy covariance observations in three ecosystems (one forest and two croplands), accurately predicted T at both hourly and daily scales, with superior performance observed at the daily time scale for all three sites. Feng et al. (2021) , utilizing two independently developed methods (the water use efficiency method and the carbon–water coupled conductance method) to predict T at four different locations, demonstrated that both methods exhibited better performance at the daily scale (water use efficiency method: R2  = 0.67, conductance method: R2  = 0.78) compared to the hourly scale (water use efficiency method: R2  = 0.57, conductance method: R2  = 0.67). Similar conclusions were also obtained by Cong et al. (2022)  in a temperate evergreen needleleaf forest. In this study, we aggregated 8-day SIF data and site-level T to a monthly scale, revealing a more pronounced linear relationship between SIF and T at the monthly scale. These findings suggest that with the aggregation of temporal scales, particularly at larger temporal scales, the SIF-T relationship tends to become increasingly linear. This phenomenon mitigates the impact of nonlinear components within the SIF-T relationship, thereby simplifying the estimation of T based on SIF. While the linear relationship between SIF and T exhibits universality across various land cover types, our research findings indicate that the slope of the SIF-T relationship for C4 vegetation is approximately 1.27 times that of C3 vegetation (Fig. 7 ). The photosynthetic pathways of C3 and C4 plants differ, with C4 vegetation displaying a more intricate photosynthetic mechanism. Furthermore, C4 vegetation demonstrates greater adaptability under environmental stressors such as high temperatures and drought conditions (Gitelson et al., 2015 ). The disparity in photosynthetic processes between C3 and C4 vegetation can be elucidated through the electron transport rate model proposed by Guan et al. (2016) . In this model, the electron transfer rate (ETR) and GPP are linked through the electron utilization efficiency (EUE) equation (GPP = ETR × EUE). Research indicates a positive correlation between ETR and SIF, with the slopes of ETR-SIF relationships for C3 and C4 plants being remarkably similar (Guan et al., 2016 ). This indicates that ETR is not solely reliant on photosynthetic pathways, with the only distinction lying in EUE. EUE is determined by both maximum quantum yield and instantaneous quantum yield; due to the presence of photorespiratory losses in C3 vegetation (Edwards and Baker, 1993 ), the maximum quantum yield of C3 vegetation is smaller than that of C4 vegetation, while the instantaneous quantum yield is higher than that of C4 vegetation (Liu et al., 2017b ). Consequently, disparities in EUE between C3 and C4 vegetation lead to differences in the SIF-GPP relationship within these vegetation types. The substantiation of this perspective is further affirmed through field measurements or evidence derived from satellite and flux tower sites (Li and Xiao, 2022; Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2020b ). Due to the coupled relationship between GPP and T, the SIF of C4 vegetation may exhibit heightened sensitivity to T variations. Our research findings also demonstrate a more robust correlation SIF-T in C4 plants, aligning with the conclusions drawn by Maes et al. (2020)  and Liu et al. (2022b) . Hence, it is crucial to formulate different transpiration estimation strategies, considering the universality of the SIF-T relationship across diverse land cover types and the specificity within different photosynthetic pathways, in order to reduce the uncertainty associated with transpiration estimates.  4.2 The alterations in the SIF-T relationship under environmental stress Examining the variations in the SIF-T relationship under environmental stress contributes to a deeper understanding of the coupled mechanisms of SIF and T. Investigations into how environmental stress influences the SIF-T relationship have been actively pursued at hourly and daily scales (Feng et al., 2021; Shan et al., 2021; Cong et al., 2022 ). In contrast to prior studies, our research delves into the changes in the SIF-T relationship over a more extended temporal aggregation scale, thereby contributing to supplementary insights into the mechanistic understanding of the SIF-T relationship. In this study, four environmental factors, namely air TA, VPD, Rn, and LAI, were selected to investigate the impact of environmental stress on the SIF-T relationship. According to the Penman–Monteith equation, T is primarily controlled by radiation and aerodynamic stress, where TA represents aerodynamic stress information, and Rn represents radiation stress information (Maes et al., 2020; Brutsaert and Stricker, 1979 ). VPD serves as a key external physical driving factor regulating transpiration (Igarashi et al., 2015 ). LAI is associated with canopy conductance and serves as a biological driver of T (Wei et al., 2017; Wang and Dickinson, 2012; Wang et al., 2014 ). TA, VPD, Rn, and LAI are widely employed in land transpiration modeling (Tong et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020a ). To investigate how TA, VPD, Rn, and LAI influence the relationship between SIF and T, TA, VPD, Rn, and LAI were categorized, and linear R2  and slope (T:SIF) of SIF and T were examined under different environmental conditions. With the increase in temperature, the slope of the linear relationship between SIF and T becomes more pronounced. Higher temperature conditions result in a larger SIF-T linear slope, as depicted in Fig. 8 a and b. This indicates that under elevated temperature conditions, SIF and T exhibit a counter-directional development, wherein an increase in temperature leads to an augmentation in vegetation transpiration and a reduction in chlorophyll fluorescence released by vegetation. When both T and the SIF undergo variations within defined ranges (i.e., T increases within a specified range while SIF decreases within a designated range), the linear correlation between SIF and T initiates decoupling. The change of the linear relation R2  between SIF and T with temperature also proves this view. The impact pattern of Rn on the relationship between SIF and T is consistent with ambient air temperature, primarily due to solar radiation serving as the primary heat input source for temperature. For sites experiencing high water VPD, a weak correlation is observed between SIF and T. As VPD further increases, the SIF-T relationship gradually decouples. This decoupling phenomenon is predominantly attributed to the closure of stomata triggered by the need to maintain cellular water potential balance under high VPD conditions (Buckley and Mott, 2013 ), leading to a reduction in chlorophyll fluorescence and the release of vegetation transpiration. There is a close relationship between leaf size and stomatal density. Generally, larger leaves have higher stomatal density, resulting in increased evapotranspiration (Liu et al., 2023 ). However, as leaf size increases, canopy closure becomes more pronounced, and the structure of the vegetation canopy becomes more complex, making it difficult for optical satellites to monitor (Maes et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2017 ). Consequently, the linear relationship between SIF and T weakens with increasing LAI. Hence, under extreme environmental conditions, SIF may not serve as a direct substitute parameter for T.  4.3 Limitations and prospects From various temporal scales, land cover types, and photosynthetic pathways, this study globally analyzes the relationship between SIF and T exploring the impacts of environmental condition changes on the SIF-T coupling. The findings complement the understanding of the SIF-T coupling and provide a scientific basis for reliable vegetation transpiration estimation on a global scale. However, this study has several limitations. Firstly, the availability of ground observation data is limited, leading to some uncertainty in the study results. Although the FLUXNET2015 dataset used in this study provides data from over 200 flux sites worldwide, not all data can be used to verify the SIF-T relationship to ensure the reliability of the results. The data needs to undergo a strict quality control process, resulting in fewer available site data. While the 109 flux sites finally obtained in this study cover 11 land cover types, the limited availability of flux site data may introduce some uncertainty into the research results. With further development of the flux observation network, more available flux site data can be used in future to further verify the SIF-T relationship. Secondly, this study used CSIF data to obtain the corresponding SIF for flux sites. CSIF data is derived from OCO-2 SIF data through data reconstruction methods. Although CSIF data has significantly improved spatial resolution compared to the original OCO-2 SIF, with a spatial resolution of 0.05° (Zhang et al., 2018 ), it is still relatively coarse. Flux sites are typically monitored within a range of 1 km, and the mismatch between the monitoring range of flux sites and CSIF data can also introduce some uncertainty into the research results. In the future, more refined spatial resolution SIF data should be developed to better reveal the SIF-T relationship.   5 Conclusions Based on the reconstructed SIF data (CSIF) and vegetation transpiration data observed at 109 global flux sites, we investigated the relationship between SIF and site T. The main findings are summarized as follows: (1) In various land cover types, SIF demonstrates a commendable ability to capture the temporal dynamics of variable T. At different temporal scales (8-day and monthly scales), there exists a robust correlation between SIF and T. Notably, the correlation between SIF and T is found to be tighter compared to the association between SIF and conventional MODIS vegetation indices (EVI and NDVI). Furthermore, a linear relationship more aptly characterizes the association between SIF and T. (2) At both 8-day and monthly temporal scales, SIF and T exhibit moderate to strong linear correlations across diverse land cover types. With the exception of SAV and OSH, the slopes of the linear relationships between SIF and T among the nine major land cover types are relatively consistent. Univariate analysis of covariance of the SIF-T linear relationships reveals that the slopes are not significantly different across most land cover types, indicating that the relationship between SIF and T is nearly ubiquitous across various land cover types, rather than being specific to a particular land cover type. Consequently, SIF provides a means to directly quantify T variations in different land cover types, circumventing uncertainties associated with land cover-specific information. (3) At both the 8-day and monthly temporal scales, the slope of the SIF-T linear relationship in C4 vegetation is significantly higher than that in C3 vegetation. This underscores the heightened sensitivity of the linear relationship between SIF and T to photosynthetic pathways. (4) The SIF-T relationship is significantly influenced by environmental factors. Under normal environmental conditions, SIF can serve as a direct surrogate parameter for T. However, under environmental stress, the decoupling of SIF from T occurs. Therefore, caution is advised when employing SIF as a direct surrogate parameter for T in extreme environmental conditions.
1 Introduction Guaranteeing a sufficient availability of good quality water is becoming more and more challenging in various areas of the world as a consequence of climate change, population growth and increasing urbanization (Boretti and Rosa, 2019; Chu et al., 2013; Finkenbine et al., 2000; He et al., 2021; McGrane, 2016; Okello et al., 2015; Rose and Peters, 2001; Roy et al., 2012; Sordo-Ward et al., 2019 ). Ensuring an adequate supply and quality of water necessitates the implementation of management plans, as well as real-time monitoring, forecasting and control systems for water resource systems to avoid economic, environmental and social threats. This is particularly the case for surface water systems such as rivers and canals in highly urbanized areas, which are subject to various types of human activities and interventions (e.g. Wu and Tan, 2012; Yao et al, 2016 ). Climate change is expected to cause an increased occurrence of hydrological extremes such as floods and droughts (Hoang et al., 2016; Raymond et al., 2019; Tabari et al. 2021; Wasko et al., 2021 ). The increasing frequency of droughts can in turn lead to an increasing frequency of water scarcity due to lower water quantity and/or compromised water quality along many surface water systems (Asif et al., 2023; Delpla et al., 2009; Hordofa et al. 2023; Leta and Bauwens, 2018 ). Along river deltas and coastal areas, there is also a significant role of sea level rise and salt intrusion (Augustijn et al. 2011; Bertels and Willems, 2022; van den Brink et al. 2019; Zwolsman and Becker, 2012 ). Because of this water quality deterioration coinciding with the water quantity reduction, interactions between water quantity and quality require more consideration in the development of drought management plans and in real-time monitoring, forecasting and control systems. Real-time monitoring and forecasting of the state of a surface water system involves several sub-models, e.g. hydrological, hydrodynamic, water quality and pollutant transport models. While a variety of specialized models are available in the literature and used in water management and engineering practice, there is a need for a more practical framework for integrated surface water modelling both at the local and river basin scale. Such integrated models should be computationally efficient to provide quick updates on the surface water state after simulation of the different sub-models and their interactions, and to allow for rapid evaluations of possible management or control options. The models additionally require a good accuracy and reliability in their simulations to obtain trustful conclusions. High computational efficiency and high accuracy are, however, often contradictory objectives. This is especially the case for complex water systems in highly urbanized areas that involve several conflicting natural and anthropogenic controlling factors. A parsimonious model structure can achieve computational efficiency, and also facilitates an easy implementation by authorities and decision makers at various administrative levels. In response to these needs, the aim of this paper is to contribute to a more sustainable operational management of water resources during droughts by proposing, demonstrating and evaluating an integrated surface water modelling approach for the Campine Canals in Belgium. Studying the water availability in this complex system is interesting for a number of reasons. It has the highest water scarcity risk in Belgium due to the combined impact of three types of climate change impacts: higher frequency of low upstream water supply, salt intrusion in downstream reaches, and increasing water demand during dry seasons. There are several competing water users: drinking water supply, shipping, hydropower production, industrial and agricultural water use and several nature reserves, and a delicate interaction between water quantity and quality needs balancing during extreme droughts. Furthermore, it is a crucial water supply for the docks of Antwerp, the second largest port of Europe (Eurostat, 2022 ) and home to the second largest petrochemical cluster worldwide (AJOT, 2022 ). A wide range of spatial interactions, relevant time scales for the different water uses and temporal variations in boundary conditions need to be accounted for. Finally, the international Meuse Treaty places important constraints on these boundary conditions. Both the proactive system management as the reactive emergency actions during droughts need to consider these different system characteristics, user needs, and uncertain natural variations in boundary conditions. The Campine Canals are thus a complex water system in a highly urbanized area, controlled by several conflicting natural and anthropogenic factors, and thus an ideal test case for this study. The integrated surface water system modelling approach consists of the following three parts: 1) The set-up of a fast but reliable forecast scheme of the discharge of the river supplying the considered surface water system, with a lead time of several weeks in case of drought. 2) A framework for collecting and simulating data on water usage in the system, allowing to accurately evaluate the current state of the water system for water levels and discharges at key locations. 3) The set-up of a computationally efficient water quality state classifier that allows to take the water quality into account when modelling the behaviour of the canal network and make predictions of potential supply issues due to quality constraints. This study tests this methodology for the surface water system of the Campine Canals in Belgium. The approach can easily be adapted for other surface water systems in the region or even other cases in river deltas and canal networks worldwide after a tailoring of the methodology to the local application needs, subsystems and processes involved.  2 Description of study area The Campine Canals network of navigable waterways is situated in the north-east of Belgium, and bridges the Meuse river basin at Liège with the Scheldt basin in Antwerp. Its location and canal network structure are shown in Fig. 1  . The main waterway in the network is the Albert Canal, navigable by ships of CEMT class VI. The canal covers a height difference of 56 m and a length of 130 km which is divided by six lock complexes. The Meuse river supplies this network at Monsin (Liège) by a basin of around 16760 km2  (Lambert et al., 2017 ), mainly situated in the Belgian Walloon region. The river is mainly rain-fed and its discharge has a high temporal variability with high flows above 1000 m3 /s during wet winter periods and very low flows of only a few tens of m3 /s during droughts in summer periods. Bertels and Willems (2022)  provide a more detailed description of the study area. Drinking water is produced in the second most downstream canal reach between the Olen and Wijnegem lock complexes. One of two water inlets is situated in the canal reach itself at Broechem (see Fig. 1 ), while the second inlet is located in the Nete Canal side branch. The Albert Canal supplies this branch through the lock of Viersel. Combined, these two inlets account for 40 % of the total Flemish drinking water production (Flanders Environment Agency, 2019 ). Further, industry, agriculture and water inlets of nature reserves abstract water from the canal network. An adequate supply of water is additionally needed to ensure minimal water levels in the downstream docks of the port of Antwerp and to avoid a high salinity concentration. Salt water enters these docks through the large tidal locks between the Antwerp port and the Scheldt estuary. The Meuse river is the water source for this system and other shipping canals in the region, and has an important ecological function. To guarantee a fair division of the available water between canals in Flanders, the Netherlands and the river itself, an international treaty was signed in 1995 to regulate the water use during droughts (Meuse Treaty, 1995 ). This forces the canal operator in Flanders to use pumping stations at the Albert Canal’s lock complexes to compensate for water losses of the locks due to inland navigation. While this measure allows Flanders to comply with the treaty, it raised the question whether this focus on water quantity could threaten the canal’s water quality during extreme droughts, as the canal reach downstream of the Wijnegem lock consists of brackish water due to the interaction with the Antwerp port. When the water production company observes a conductivity of 1000 µS/cm, production is ceased. Bertels and Willems (2022)  studied this water management problem and concluded that although the movement of the salt water up to the critical locations of the water inlets for drinking water production is rare under current climate conditions, this may change in future climate conditions. For a high impact climate scenario, the water quality standards may be exceeded about every few years by 2100.  3 Methods This section describes the construction and calibration of the various components of the proposed integrated water availability – salt intrusion model for real-time management. The first component is the forecast of low/decreasing river discharge at the upstream boundary of the considered canal network. The second component combines the conceptual mass balance-water quality model with a semi-automated provision and retrieval of the data on water usage along the canal network, allowing to update the internal model states and identify potential shortages. The final component concerns the efficient prediction of the possible exceedance of water quality thresholds at key locations based on discharge simulations or observations. Combined, the model aims to operate as an early warning system during droughts, allowing decision makers to prepare adaptation measures. Further, these measures can be designed and optimized using the integrated model in scenario analyses. An overview of the integrated model is presented in Fig. 2  . 3.1 Low flow forecasting Hydrological models are available for the Meuse basin, but these were calibrated to reach an overall good accuracy for both high and low flows. In this analysis, however, the main objective is to predict the extreme low flows with high accuracy. Therefore, this work proposes a methodology to predict the Meuse discharge in the coming weeks during droughts. The main assumption of the discharge extrapolation is that the current Meuse discharge, as observed after several weeks without significant precipitation, mainly consists of the ‘slow flow’ or ‘baseflow’ (BF) component b ( t )   , and that this slow flow component is decreasing exponentially:(1) b t    = exp - 1 k     b ( t - Δ t )      Where k    [time] is the recession constant. Risva et al (2018)  successfully used this exponential decay function for low flow forecasting for up to six months ahead in the Mediterranean. Other authors used the same, or related models to predict the recession behaviour of river discharges during dry periods, e.g. Kadu and Biswal (2022), Reddyvaraprasad et al. (2020)  and Singh and Griffiths (2021) . In this study, the parameter k    is calibrated visually as the inverse slope of the (sub)flow in a ln q    - t i m e    plot (see Willems, 2009 ). The next step is the separation of the slow flow from the total observed discharge using the adjusted Chapman-filter as proposed by Willems (2009)  The discharge prediction for a continuous drought is made by assuming the exponential decreasing behaviour, starting from the filter results of the slow flow at the present time step, after applying the slow flow filter to the historical observed flows. To account for the influence of rain events, a fast flow (FF) component is added to the slow flow component. This fast flow component f ( t )    is computed based on the linear reservoir equation:(2) f t    = exp - 1 k f      f t - Δ t    + 1 - e x p - 1 k f         q in   ( t - τ )      Where k f     is the FF recession constant and τ    the time delay time of the incoming rainfall volumes q in     . The rainfall estimates are obtained as the mean of the precipitation observations in the Meuse basin, reduced by applying a FF runoff coefficient. The recession constants, delay time and runoff coefficients are calibrated to recent historical events.  3.2 Integrated conceptual water quantity and water quality model Bertels and Willems (2022)  constructed a reservoir-type conceptual model to simulate the discharge in the canal network as a function of the available upstream Meuse discharge. This model divides the canals in storage cells based on the lay-out of the shipping locks and calculates water exchanges between those reaches based on the operational rules of the canal. This model was combined with a detailed physics-based solute transport model of the two most downstream reaches of the Albert Canal (see Fig. 1 ), which serves to solve the 1D flow and solute transport equations using a detailed finite volume scheme. Discharge boundary conditions are provided by the conceptual water balance model. The upstream chloride ion concentration is fixed based on the long term average for the Meuse. The imposed downstream concentration was estimated using a monthly pollutant balance model of the Antwerp docks, where the salt concentration is mainly dependent on the concentration of the Scheldt river. Calibration and validation of the model makes use of high temporal and spatial observations along the canal network for the dry summer years 2019 and 2020. The water quality state influences the behaviour of the water use: if salt water reaches the Broechem inlet or the Viersel locks, respectively the Broechem and Notmeir-Walem water inlets will cease production until the canal reach is completely flushed, assessed by a sufficient quality at the Wijnegem locks. To integrate these management rules in the model simulations, a two-way coupling of the water quantity and water quality models was made by running the salt intrusion model every 12 h of the simulated water balance. The following section proposes a solution to accommodate the increase in computational complexity and calculation time. Data exchanges are set up with local authorities and stakeholders, in combination with publicly available datasets, in order to accommodate regular updating of the model database. This allows for daily or weekly assessments of the water availability and a proper initialization for making forecasts. An overview of this data is given in Table 1  . One cornerstone of this methodology is the automated retrieval of precipitation and discharge observations, through the KiWiS Web-Service, publicly available in Flanders and the Walloon region (KISTERS, 2023 ). This allows for easy execution of the data collection and forecasting steps using simple programming scripts. While the availability of such web-based data services is region-dependent, similar services are widely available for other regions worldwide (e.g. Delipetrev et al. 2014  or Demir and Krajewski, 2013 ).  3.3 Efficient water quality prediction The operation of the surface water system requires considering both water quantity and salt intrusion when controlling the usage of shipping locks, the combined hydropower-pumping stations and allowing abstractions, all in the context of temporally varying boundary conditions. However, detailed, physics-based water quality models can be computationally very demanding, making them unpractical in a real time or scenario analysis context where often only a binary classification of the quality state at relevant locations is needed. To accommodate this, a more efficient coupled mass balance and water quality model is proposed to predict the exceedance of a quality threshold, using computationally efficient classification algorithms. The aim is to let them operate as lightweight components of the integrated model. This work tests the method for the Campine Canals in the context of salinity risks for drinking water production where current management of the pumping stations takes into account the salinity at the Wijnegem locks, the Broechem inlet and the Viersel locks as discussed before. This data-based method can easily be adapted to include other pollutants or water quality indicators that are relevant for different case studies and water users, such as for example nutrients, suspended solids or water temperature. 3.3.1 Classification algorithms This study calibrates and compares a range of different classification algorithms. All of these methods are well established for (binary) classification and are hereafter only discussed briefly, and references for further reading are provided. All models are implemented in MATLAB (2020) . 3.3.1.1 Decision tree Decision trees are widely used classification methods that induce a number of rules on the input variables to segment the available training data into separate ‘branches’ and eventually end-nodes (Breiman et al., 1984 ). New instances are allocated to these end-nodes and are assigned a class based on the training instances. This assigned class can simply be the majority in that node, but other thresholds are possible as well, e.g. the assigned class is only positive if at least 80 % of all training instances in that node are positive. The main advantages of this technique are the interpretability of these induced rules by humans, and the high computational efficiency. This work applies the CART algorithm, using the GINI impurity measure (see a description in Liu and Wu, 2017 ). A 10-fold cross validation is applied to optimize the minimum number of training instances assigned to each leaf.  3.3.1.2 Bagged decision tree ensemble Bagging or bagged predictor-methods use a number of bootstraps of the training data to generate an ensemble of predictors (Breiman, 1996 ). The final decision of the ensemble can be the majority vote, or based on other thresholds similar as for the leafs in decision trees. This perturbation of the learning dataset can improve the accuracy and robustness of the ensemble, while retaining the advantages of decision trees. In this work, each ensemble contains 50 decision trees.  3.3.1.3 Multilayer perceptron Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) combine multiple connected transformations of the type of equation (3) , of an input-vector x    to a hidden state vector or output value h   . (3) h  = f x    = a c t ( W ∗ x  + b )      This study tests configurations with both one and two hidden layers. The hidden layer size of the MLPs is optimized by varying their number of neurons varying between 2 √ n + m    and 2 n + 1    where n    and m    represent the number of input and output nodes respectively (Fletcher and Goss, 1993 ).  3.3.1.4 LSTM model Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) introduce a feedback loop from the model output layer of MLPs to the input layer, allowing to model dynamic systems. Long short-term memory (LSTM) models are a specific form of recurrent neural networks, introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) . A designated ‘memory state’ is introduced in their architecture, allowing them to overcome some issues that plain RNNs face. LSTM-based models were successfully applied in a variety of environmental modelling studies, e.g. by Aslan et al. (2022), Kratzert et al. (2018) . The size of the memory state and the number of consecutive LSTM layers is optimized by training models with respectively 50, 100 and 200 hidden elements, and by testing both one and two LSTM layers.  3.3.1.5 Support vector machines Support vector machines (SVM), introduced by Cortes and Vapnik (1995) , are a popular machine learning technique used for classification and regression applications. The technique is based on the identification of the optimal n-1 dimensional hyperplane that separates n dimensional instances. In case the data is not linearly separable, it can be mapped in a higher dimensional space using appropriate kernel functions. This work uses the radial basis function kernel.   3.3.2 Predictor data The number of selected predictors is preferably low, and these data should be easy to collect by the canal’s managers or calculate by the water balance model with a high accuracy. Salt intrusion towards the water inlets is mainly driven by extensive pumping at the Wijnegem locks, combined with the high water demand of the inlets. Therefore, only four main water exchanges of the canal reach are selected as potential predictors: Olen, Wijnegem, Viersel and Broechem. (see Fig. 1 -c). The system is highly dynamic, as the salinization on a certain day depends not only on the discharges at the boundaries of the canal reach, but also on the extension of the salt wedge in the previous time step(s). Therefore, the set of potential predictors contains the mentioned fluxes at the current and previous time steps, with a maximum lag of 15 days to keep the computational burden of model training feasible. Additionally, a second approach combines the predictors at the ‘current’ time with their mean value over the past 15 days. Finally, a third approach uses the cumulative discharges at the current time starting from 1 to maximum 15 preceding days as potential inputs. These three approaches provide the tree-based classification methods discussed above, as those algorithms are designed to identify the predictor that leads to optimal splits in each node. The LSTM method uses the full time-series of all input-discharges as predictors, as the algorithm is capable of detecting temporal relations between predictors and predictands. To reduce the set of potential predictors in the MLP and SVM approaches and avoid using high dimensional input vectors of highly correlated variables, the partial mutual information (PMI)-algorithm is used (Sharma, 2000 ). This technique is suited for identifying non-linear dependence and does not require that a model has already been built (Fernando et al., 2009 ). Input data for the MLP, LSTM and SVM models are z-score normalized by subtraction with their mean value and division by their standard deviation.  3.3.3 Target data All training and testing data is generated using the combined mass balance and detailed physics-based models of the Campine Canals. The use of results from a 2100-high impact climate change scenario (developed by Tabari et al., 2015 ) ensures a sufficient number of summer periods with salinity threshold exceedances. To assure that the calibrated classifiers learn to predict the true behaviour of the salt wedge, this work uses both simulations in which the drinking water production does, as well as simulations in which it does not react to the simulated salinity. This avoids that the classification algorithms only learn that the threshold is exceeded whenever drinking water production is ceased. Training data consists of model simulations for the period 1970–1980 (without assuming water quality restrictions for drinking water production) and 1991–2010 (including water quality restrictions). In total, 18 years with an intrusion threshold exceedance are present in this training period. The period 2011–2020 is used for testing the models’ performance, in which salt intrusion occurs in 6 of the 10 years. Those salt intrusions vary from one/multiple short periods of intrusion, to longer periods of multiple weeks/months during more prolonged droughts.  3.3.4 Model evaluation A number of metrics are used to evaluate the trained binary classifiers. All of these are derived from the confusion matrix in Table 2  . Precision  is the ratio of the true positive instances to all instances predicted as positive. It indicates whether the values that are retrieved by the model are relevant. Its optimal value is 1.(4) Precision = T P / ( T P + F P )     The recall  ratio gives an indication of the fraction of the relevant instances (actual salinity threshold exceedances) retrieved by the prediction. Its optimal value is 1.(5) Recall = T P / ( T P + F N )     Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) / phi coefficient  (Matthews 1975 ) gives the correlation coefficient between real and predicted classes. It provides a good summary of the whole confusion matrix in a single value and has an optimal value of 1.(6) MCC = TP ∗ T N - F P ∗ F N  T P + F P   T P + F N    T N + F P    T N + F N           The F1-score  equals the harmonic mean of precision and recall, hence a value of 1 indicates a perfect prediction and the lowest value is zero (Sokolova et al., 2006 ).(7) F 1 = 2 T P  2 T P + F P + F N       ROC curves  depict the true positive rate TPR    (=recall) as a function of the false positive rate FPR   .(8) FPR = ( F P / ( F P + T N ) )     While these TPR    and FPR    rates are single numbers for a classifier, they are often dependent on a threshold chosen in the model to classify an instance as positive or negative. For example, in a decision tree, typically the majority of values in a leaf is chosen to designate a class, however, one could also set this limit at a value different than 50 %. Hence, a curve can be derived for all but the SVM-models described above. Optimal models are situated in the upper-left corner of the graph, indicating few false positive values and a good recall. To compare the different models in the ROC curve, an equal cost of false positive and false negatives predictions is assumed. One could argue that for the Broechem and Viersel inlets, a false positive prediction is more acceptable than a false negative, since the latter would overestimate the potential drinking water production. At Wijnegem on the other hand, operators want to know whether the threshold is no longer exceeded, indicating that water production at the water inlets can resume. Hence, false negatives might give an overly positive estimation of the water availability.    4 Results and discussion 4.1 Validation of model components 4.1.1 Low flow forecasting The baseflow and fast flow recession constants for the Meuse at Monsin were calibrated as 100 and 15 [days] respectively, based on the slope of the observed Meuse discharge on a log-scale versus time during the low flow recession periods. Fig. S1  of the Supplementary material s illustrates this process for the calibration of the baseflow recession constant. To evaluate the performance of the low flow prediction model, observed and predicted discharges during low-flow periods are compared using the NSE score (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) in Table 3  , for the Meuse discharge in the period 2010–2022. The low-flow period in each year is identified using an adapted version of the method proposed by Risva et al. (2018) . First, the observed discharge is smoothened using a Savitzky–Golay filter (Savitzky and Golay, 1964 ) with polynomial order 3 and a 7-day window. Second, the method assumes a preliminary low flow period to start on April 15 and end on October 15 of each year. This window is narrowed by removing the days after April 15 until the discharge of April 15 is no longer exceeded. Finally, the low-flow period ends on the first day on which the 15-day moving average discharge increases with more than 2 m3 /s. In Table 3 , 2012 is excluded due to missing values in the summer period. and 2014 is excluded as the procedure described above identified a low-flow period of only 2 days in this wet summer. The relatively high NSE coefficient values show that the low flow model has a good performance. Fig. 3   shows the comparison of predicted and observed discharges for the example of 2022, for which the NSE value is 0.89. The lower value for 2021 can be attributed to the unusually wet summer for that year, during which high precipitation amounts caused extreme floods in July, and the assumption of the strictly decreasing baseflow is not valid. The summer of 2016 was also characterized by rather high precipitation amounts and consequent runoff volumes. The lower NSE value for 2017 is caused by an underestimation of the discharge in April and May, while the prediction is better for the remaining part of the dry period, see Fig. 3 . It is concluded that the parsimonious model is able to accurately simulate the Meuse low flow behaviour, especially if one takes into account the high uncertainty in the mean basin rainfall estimates and predictions and the operational actions in the canalized Meuse river.  4.1.2 Integrated water quantity and water quality model The conceptual mass balance model of the Campine Canal network was evaluated in Bertels and Willems (2022)  using discharge observations at Kanne (located upstream in the canal network) and Grobbendonk (downstream of the Olen lock complex). Pearson correlation coefficient values of 0.92 and 0.82 between the 30-day averaged simulated and observed discharge were found for the two locations and for the periods 2016–2020 and 2018–2020 respectively. Evaluation for the more recent extreme dry summer period of 2022, indicates NSE values of 0.67 and 0.79 for the daily discharge at Kanne and Grobbendonk, and 0.92 and 0.90 for the weekly discharges. The physics-based salt intrusion model was calibrated and validated in Bertels and Willems (2022)  using high resolution observations along the canal network for the dry summers of 2020 and 2019 respectively, showing Pearson correlation coefficients higher than 0.8 after validation at several locations. No additional evaluation of the physics-based solute transport model was therefore made for this article.  4.1.3 Efficient conceptual water quality prediction Fig. 4   shows the ROC curves for all classification models, for their best performing configuration. The figure shows only the top-left part of the graphs to allow a better comparison. For the Broechem water inlet, the ROC graphs shows very comparable results for all approaches. However, it is clear that the (single) decision tree does not perform as well as the other techniques. The true positive rate for all of the models is high, indicating that almost all relevant (true exceedance moments) are detected by the models. The false positive rate of the best performing models lies around 0.15–0.2, thus remaining low enough to rely on these models for accurately predicting the actual period during which drinking water cannot be produced at the Broechem production centre. Performance of the prediction models at the Viersel lock is the lowest of all locations. Severe salt intrusion this far upstream is not as common compared to Broechem or Wijnegem as the lock is situated in the centre of the canal reach and the salt concentration is dependent on a complex interaction of up- and downstream water exchanges. However, all models still achieve acceptable results, and with very similar performance. All but the LSTM model achieve very good predictions at the Wijnegem lock complex. This was expected because any (significant) pumping at this lock complex will result in an exceedance of the threshold in dry periods as water in the downstream canal reach typically has a high salt concentration. The slightly poorer performance of the LSTM is likely attributed to the highly discontinuous behaviour of the canal system, where the pumps react immediately to an insufficient water supply from the Meuse, resulting in high concentrations upstream of the lock almost instantaneously. Table 4   presents results for all models at the three locations, for the testing period. Although all models perform very similar, the bagged decision trees achieve the highest performance at Broechem and Wijnegem when considering the MCC and F1 evaluation metrics. At Viersel, the MLP model performs slightly superior. Fig. 5   illustrates the predicted salinization at the Broechem inlet, calculated using the ensemble of bagged decision trees. This allows to put the goodness-of-fit metrics above in perspective and to assess the capability of the models to accurately predict the start and duration of the threshold exceedance. The figure makes clear that the precise moment of the first exceedance of the salinity threshold is predicted very well by the classifier and the duration of the exceedance period is satisfactory.
