For example, looking at the results for 2011, three distinct periods of salinization occurred and all three of their start and end dates are predicted accurately. The model results for the summer periods of 2019 and 2020 are less accurate, as illustrated in more detail in Fig. S2  of the Supplementary material . In 2019, the model does not predict the threshold exceedance by the end of August. The higher incoming discharge in the canal reach reduces the salinity concentration while the conductivity still remains slightly above the quality threshold. This false negative should therefore not be considered a gross violation of the quality limits, especially given the overall uncertainty of the various sub-models. The false positive in summer 2020 has a similar explanation: the conductivity is characterized by two peaks, and a longer period during which water production was ceased due to quality issues. In this period the incoming discharge of fresh water slowly reduces the overall salinity of the reach. The figure makes clear that the conductivity remains only very slightly below the threshold while the classifier still estimates an exceedance, hence the false positive. These good results are in line with the conclusions of other authors who predicted salt intrusion using similar data driven techniques. Both Nguyen et al. (2021)  and Tran et al. (2022)  successfully used a variety of machine learning approaches, including tree based techniques, SVMs and LSTM models for predicting salt intrusion in the Mekong Delta. Rohmer and Brisset (2017)  achieved a good performance of SVMs for predicting salt intrusion in the Comté River using river discharge and sea water level as predictors and the authors suggested that the model forecasts can be useful for warning local drinking water production operators. Most related studies focus on more natural surface water systems, i.e. river deltas or coastal waters. In this work, the results show that also in a completely human operated system, the data-driven approaches can be of added value for salt intrusion early warning. It should be noted that the focus of the data-driven techniques in this work is on classifying the local water quality in relation to quality thresholds of specific users. Using similar techniques for predicting actual salinity levels is not a straightforward step given the high complexity of salt wedge intrusion in river deltas. To mention just one aspect, modelling the salt concentration as averaged across vertical cross sections by Bertels and Willems (2022)  is acceptable in the rather shallow canal (with a constant 5 m water depth), while vertical concentration and related density gradients can play a significant role in salinity dynamics in other cases. Furthermore, while the canal network considered in this work is rather complex from an operational perspective, its boundary conditions such as operational rules and water users are well known, which might very well not be the case for natural river deltas. In order to apply such classification techniques for other study areas, robust and reliable physics-based models, or otherwise sufficient high-quality data need to be available. Still, the high flexibility of the different model components in the proposed framework should allow for an adaptation to other surface water systems.   4.2 Application of integrated model for 1976 drought To further illustrate the operation of the fully integrated model, the combined discharge forecast, mass balance and salt intrusion prediction models are applied to simulate the extreme drought of 1976. The drought of 1976 is a reference event in the region, characterized by high temperatures and extremely low precipitation amounts. It had a severe impact on water availability: Beersma and Buishand (2004)  estimated that the return period of the economic losses for that drought in the Netherlands exceeded 100 years in current climatic conditions. At Uccle (Belgium), the precipitation deficit reached 350 mm. The drought caused the Meuse to reach record low discharges (e.g. a minimum of 19 m3 /s for the 7-day averaged discharge at Monsin in 1976, compared to 28.2 m3 /s in the recent drought of 2020 (Bertels and Willems, 2022 ). The time series of observed Meuse discharge at Monsin during the period May-December 1976 is shown in Fig. 6  . In this simulation, the observed Meuse is imposed to the integrated model, starting from April 1st 1976, until the start of a forecast period. The first forecast is made on May 1st 1976, and it is repeated in weekly intervals until the final forecast of November 27, 1976. A total of 31 forecasts are made, each for a 60 day period. The objective of each prediction is to estimate whether and when a major event of salt water intrusion (defined here as an exceedance of the water quality threshold for drinking water production) will occur in the canal, under the assumption that no additional precipitation will occur in the following period. The bagged decision tree classifier is used as the method for predicting the quality threshold exceedance. Note that only the observed Meuse discharge is historical, while the canal’s characteristics and operational rules are based on the current condition. Hence the illustration is not a reconstruction of the historical water availability and water quality conditions, but a simulation of what can be expected when such a drought would occur today. Results of this analysis are presented in Fig. 6 . The area above the dotted line shows the simulation results when imposing the observed discharge and using the detailed, 1D physics-based model of salt intrusion, hence showing the ‘truth’. The individual bars per forecast show the predicted intrusion in case no precipitation is expected. Three separate dry periods are distinguished. The first largely coincides with the first three weeks of July, until summer storms at the end of the month caused a recovery in the discharge, sufficient to flush the salt wedge. The second period takes place from the last week of August to the end of September. By the first week of October, the discharge exceeds the water demand and no intrusion occurs for the rest of the season, except for a short period around the end of October. Comparison of the forecasted and ‘true’ intrusion shows that the prediction seems a bit conservative, which is expected due to two reasons. Firstly, no precipitation is taken into account and secondly, the classification algorithms’ precision evaluation showed a slight tendency to produce false positive predictions. However, the model predicts the first and most severe of the three drought periods with a high accuracy, given that the first forecasts correctly expect a severe intrusion in mid-June or July. This would allow the decision makers and drinking water production company to prepare for possible shortages by filling their reserves or making arrangements with high volume users. For the second period, the subsequent forecasts keep predicting an advanced intrusion for both locations, while the detailed model only simulates an intrusion up to the Broechem inlet, starting at the end of August. The simulation results show that the predicted Meuse discharges are close to the observations, as nearly no precipitation was observed in that period. However, the classification model overestimates the intrusion. When inspecting the conductivity simulated by the physics-based model (see Fig. S3  in the Supplementary material ), it can be seen that the salt wedge is not completely flushed from the canal reach, but still remains under the 1000 µS/cm threshold. This is consistent with the discussion above. The classification algorithms could be further refined. Another option is to run the detailed, physics-based models when the first estimate indicates a potential exceedance of the quality limits in the next weeks, as to better prepare for the coming period.  4.3 Limitations and future work The proposed methodology described above takes advantage of the systematic, public availability of a number of datasets. The most crucial of which is the continuous monitoring of the river(s) that supply the considered surface water system, and registered or estimated water abstractions. If such data sources are not publicly available, a good cooperation with the local data managers and authorities will have to be set up in order to obtain at least a semi-real time prediction model for management during droughts. The Meuse river and its main tributaries in the Walloon region are strongly canalized and it could be argued that assuming a ‘natural’ behaviour by the low flow model for its discharge at Monsin is not always valid. A potential improvement is the inclusion of the management of these canalized reaches in the conceptual mass balance model. One key aspect that requires further attention in this proposed method, is uncertainty. Errors and uncertainty likely arise in the various stages of the integrated model, and it might be beneficial to report this as probabilistic information on the forecast to decision makers. Amongst the sources of errors are input uncertainty (e.g. in the data of water use, mean basin precipitation estimates and predictions), the uncertainty in the calibration of the model parameters (e.g. flow recession rates), and the model structure uncertainty (e.g. validity of the parsimonious low flow prediction, the conceptual mass balance or the efficient water quality classification methods). A possible approach to obtain estimates of the final forecast uncertainty could be using an ensemble of models and input conditions, e.g. similar as the low-flow forecasting tool proposed by Nicolle et al. (2020)  who used five different hydrological models and 57 past years of meteorological observations to obtain multiple potential streamflow series. Other possibilities focus on predicting the model uncertainty by comparing model results with observations for historical data, as in the non-parametric method proposed by Van Steenbergen et al. (2012) . The quantification of the forecast uncertainty and its communication towards decision makers will be considered in subsequent work. Model simulations for the Campine Canals show that the system is vulnerable for water scarcity. For example, the current storage reserves for drinking water production can bridge a period of only 30 days, while advanced salt intrusion during droughts can easily exceed this in periods of extreme drought. Local authorities and stakeholders need to cooperate and invest in order to increase the system’s resiliency. A potential measure is the construction of additional storage reservoirs, but this is costly and not straightforward in the densely populated region. Use of existing reserves could be optimized using the integrated models by calculating the allowed additional water abstractions to refill the reservoirs when forecasts show that this is possible. Other potential measures include restrictions on ship traffic at the tidal locks of the Antwerp docks, e.g. limiting transfers during low tide to reduce water use and salt intrusion. Various users can also better coordinate available resources and align water quality needs of specific users with the available resources, e.g. the use of brackish and/or treated waste water in industry instead of drinking water when possible. The integrated model described in this paper is able to take all of these boundary conditions into account, and thus allows to make a complete assessment on the effectiveness of candidate adaptation measures. The potential of the proposed method was in fact already recognized by the local authorities and the models will serve as a key component in the new Flemish reactive assessment framework in the event of water scarcity and drought.   5 Conclusions Guaranteeing a sufficient availability of good quality water in urbanized areas can be a major challenge for authorities and decision makers. Especially if a limited supply is combined with a high demand and a large number of competing water users, as is the case in the urbanized river delta of the Scheldt, Meuse and Rhine rivers. As climate change and population increase are placing increasing pressure on the water system, it is crucial to develop efficient and reliable tools to assist decision makers in governing surface water systems for avoiding water shortages during extreme droughts. This paper proposes the use of parsimonious but accurate, integrated water quantity and water quality models of complex surface water systems to assist the management of canals and rivers during droughts. The work demonstrates and evaluates the method for the Campine Canals in Belgium, a complex water system fed by the Meuse river and governed mainly to accommodate shipping, while various other users are highly dependent on it for water supply. Parsimonious sub-models for different aspects of the integrated model are applied to achieve both a high computational efficiency and high accuracy. The first is a low flow prediction of river discharge during dry periods. Despite its simplicity, a good correspondence with historical discharge observations was found for the Meuse river. The second component is the integration of a conceptual water balance model of the considered waterway network with the semi-automated retrieval of necessary input data and boundary conditions from the local data managers. The final component is an efficient water quality state classifier, using a data-driven technique and trained on observations or training data generated by reference models. Five different classification algorithms were tested to predict the exceedance of salt intrusion thresholds for drinking water production. These achieved mostly a comparable performance, but bagged decision trees generally perform best. This allows to take water quality aspects into consideration while avoiding a two way coupling of the computationally efficient conceptual water balance model with highly detailed, physics-based water quality models. Advanced salt intrusion from the Scheldt river in the Albert Canal will occur occasionally in current climatic conditions. However, it will likely be more common in the future if climate change will decrease the Meuse’s discharge during summer months. Further research will focus on the integration of estimates of model errors and uncertainty and providing these as probabilistic results to stakeholders and decision makers.
1 Introduction Continuous global warming tends to accelerate hydrological cycles, leading to more extreme weather and climate events, like droughts, floods, heavy rainfalls, and heat waves, which have great influences on agriculture, ecosystem, and human lives (Allen et al., 2010; Ciais et al., 2005; Eggen et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019 ). It is termed as compound extremes when multiple extremes occur simultaneously. In general, the compound extremes may result in more severe impacts than any one extreme event (Zscheischler et al., 2018 ). The concurrent dry and heat waves over Europe in 2003 and Russia in 2010 are two high-profile examples of compound temperature and precipitation extremes which caused a heavy loss of life and substantial socio-economic impacts (Trenberth and Fasullo, 2012; Zhang et al., 2018 ). As the most important variables in hydrology and climate, extremes related to temperature and precipitation bring heat waves, floods, storms, and droughts frequently (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2012; Benestad and Haugen, 2007; De Luca et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2018 ). Therefore, an in-deep understanding of the changes in compound temperature and precipitation extremes is crucial for taking proper measures to reduce potential impacts on society and ecosystems. Numerous studies have confirmed the interaction and dependence between temperature and precipitation due to their thermodynamic relations (e.g., Fernandez-Montes et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2012; Trenberth and Shea, 2005 ). In cold season, there is a positive correlation between precipitation and temperature in high latitude areas, while a strong negative correlation in most global land areas in warm season (Adler et al., 2008 ). Due to the critical impacts, the extreme events of compound temperature and precipitation, termed as wet/warm, wet/cold, dry/warm and dry/cold, have been receiving an increasing attention. For example, Beniston (2009)  investigated the trends in the compound temperature and precipitation extremes across Europe and found significant increase in frequency of warm related combinations while sharp decrease in cold ones. Similarly, this kind of analysis has been conducted on the global scale (Bevacqua et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2021 ), Canada (Tencer et al., 2014 ), South Asia (Fan et al., 2022 ), Australia (Collins 2022 ) and South America (Olmo et al., 2020 ). These studies generally suggest that there are notable increases in warm related combinations. China, with a large population, characterized by a complex and diverse climate, and its economic and social development is susceptible to extreme weather. In past several decades, the extremes of temperature and precipitation across China have been widely explored (Li et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2019 ). Up to now, numerous studies have focused on univariate analysis of extreme temperature or extreme precipitation in China (e.g., Chen et al., 2021; Miao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2022 ), but increasing attention has been paid to compound temperature and precipitation extremes (Ning et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2016 ). These studies have also found a similar conclusion that the warm related compound extremes show significant upward trends while sharp decrease in cold combinations in most areas of China, which indicates that the long-term changes of compound extremes were significantly affected and controlled by regional climate warming. Previous studies showed that the atmospheric circulation factors, including ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation), AMO (Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation), NAO (North Atlantic Oscillation), AO (Arctic Oscillation), IOD (Indian Ocean Dipole) and PDO (Pacific Decadal Oscillation), are the main reason for the spatio-temporal evolution of temperature extremes and precipitation extremes in China (Cheng et al., 2019, 2021; Xiao et al., 2015; Yang and Lau, 2004 ). In the past decade, a few studies have analyzed the influence of atmospheric circulation factors on compound temperature and precipitation extremes. For example, Wu et al. (2019)  analyzed the relationship between compound temperature and precipitation extremes and multiple circulation factors in China and showed that AMO had significant correlations with the spatial extent of most compound temperature and precipitation extremes. While for the other circulation factors, significant correlations were only shown for limited modes for certain seasons. Subsequently, Yu and Zhai (2021)  pointed out that the compound temperature and precipitation extremes which occurred in multiple parts of the world in 2015/2016 formed mainly due to the changes in multiple driving factors/disaster causing factors caused by the extreme El Niño. These studies, focusing mainly on the effect of a single atmospheric circulation factor on compound temperature and precipitation extremes, have provided some useful information about why compound temperature and precipitation extremes vary spatiotemporally. However, the combined effects of multiple circulation factors at different time scales should be further explored considering that temperature and precipitation are affected simultaneously by multiple factors. In view of this, this paper focuses on systematically investigating the spatiotemporal variability of compound temperature and precipitation extremes in China and their relationship with atmospheric circulation factors. The novelty of this paper is to detect the combined effects of multiple circulation factors on compound extremes at varying time scales. Results of this study will provide a better understanding of the mechanism of the compound extremes and thus propose adaptive strategies. The structure of this paper is as follows. Section 2  introduces the data collection, definition of compound extremes events, and data analysis method. Section 3  studies the spatiotemporal changes of frequency in compound temperature and precipitation extremes for the period 1961–2020 in China and explores the relationship between compound extremes and circulation factors. The discussion and conclusion are presented in sections 4 and 5 , respectively.  2 Data and method 2.1 Data collection In this study, we employed monthly precipitation and temperature data for 1961–2020 from the China Meteorological Administration with a spatial resolution of 0.5°×0.5°, covering 2472 meteorological observation stations across the whole of China. The homogeneity and quality control were performed for these climatic observations by using the standard normal homogeneity test and the cumulative deviations test (Xu et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2015 ). This dataset can be obtained from https://data.cma.cn/data/detail/dataCode/SURF_CLI_CHN_PRE_MON_GRID_0.5.html  and http://data.cma.cn/data/detail/dataCode/SURF_CLI_CHN_TEM_MON_GRID_ 0.5.html. To facilitate the analysis of regional differences, we divide mainland China into three subregions: East China, Northwest China and Tibetan Plateau according to the elevation (Zhang and Zhao, 2019; Zhao et al., 2015 ). In addition, to examine the potential impacts of large-scale atmospheric circulations on compound extremes, AMO, AO, ENSO, IOD, NAO and PDO were employed because they have well characterized the China’s climate (Liu et al., 2018; Sang et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2015 ). Table 1   shows the specific definitions and sources of these climatic indices.  2.2 Definition of compound extremes events The individual extreme event is typically defined based on a threshold or percentile, which is then used to obtain the quantity of compound extremes based on the co-occurrence of individual extremes. Based on previous studies (Beniston, 2009; Hao et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2019 ), we used the 25 % and 75 % quantile thresholds of precipitation and temperature for each month to define compound extremes in order to capture a large number of events. For each month, specially, the wet (warm) extreme happens when the precipitation (temperature) exceeds the 75 % quantile thresholds, whereas the dry (cold) extreme happens when the precipitation (temperature) is below the 25 % quantile thresholds. Therefore, theoretically, there are four combinations of precipitation and temperature extremes: P75/T75, P75/T25, P25/T75 and P25/T25 (where P and T denotes precipitation and temperature, respectively), representing the compound extremes of wet/warm (WW), wet/cold (WC), dry/warm (DW) and dry/cold (DC), respectively. That is, the compound extreme event takes place when both precipitation and temperature extremes occur at the same month. The frequency of compound extremes is defined as the total number of months with concurrent extremes during the study period.  2.3 Data analysis The change trend of compound extremes was computed by the “robust fitting method” considering the effects of outliers and end points (Zhang and Zhao, 2019 ). The statistical significance of linear trend was tested by using the Mann-Kendall Tau nonparametric technique (Kendall, 1975; Mann, 1945 ). The Pearson correlation coefficient (r ) is used in order to examine the overall relationship between compound extremes and atmospheric circulation factors (Zhang et al., 2021 ). We examined the influence of a single or multiple atmospheric circulation factor(s) on compound extremes at different timescales, using the bivariate wavelet coherence (WTC) and multiple wavelet coherence (MWC) (Liu et al., 2017 ). The average wavelet coherence coefficient (AWC) and percent area of significant coherence (PASC) were employed to estimate the relations between compound extremes and climate indices. For MWC, the AWC may increase whereas the PASC may not necessarily increase with the increased number of independent variables (Hu and Si, 2016 ). Statistically, an increased PASC indicates that a significant increase in variations in compound extremes can be explained at 95 % confidence level. From a practical point of view, an additional factor is considered to be significant when it results in an increase of PASC by at least 5 % (Yang et al., 2020 ). For more information on the WTC and MWC, please refer to Hu et al. (2017) .   3 Results 3.1 Frequency of compound extremes Fig. 1   presents the frequency of four compound extremes (i.e., WW, WC, DW and DC) during warm and cold season for 1961–2020 in China. For warm season, the frequency of compound WW extremes in the Tibetan Plateau is more than 30 events and less than 10 events in other regions. The pattern of compound WC extremes is the opposite, and the frequency in the Tibetan Plateau is the smallest, not greater than 8 events. Except for some areas of the Tibetan Plateau and Huai River Basin, the compound DW extremes in most areas occur highly, exceeding 24 events, and even exceeding 30 events in some places, such as the southwest of Yunnan Guizhou Plateau, the central parts of Inner Mongolia Plateau. While the frequency of DC in most areas is less than 4 events. During the cold season, the frequency of WW and DW exceeds 16 events in most areas, while that of WC and DC are smaller, especially the frequency of DC is generally less than 4 events in most areas.  3.2 Spatiotemporal changes of compound extremes Then, we investigate the frequency change of compound temperature and precipitation extremes during warm season and cold season for 1991–2020 relative to 1961–1990 (Fig. 2  ). For warm season, the compound WW and DW extremes present an increase in almost the whole China. Especially, the increase of WW has exceeded 20 events in the Tibetan Plateau, and the increase of DW has exceeded 20 events in the western Northeast China and eastern Xinjiang Province. Conversely, the compound WC and DC extremes have decreased in most regions. The significant decrease of compound WC extremes is mostly shown in the Tibetan Plateau, Northwest and Southwest China, while that of the compound DC is shown in the northern Tibetan Plateau. For cold season, similar to the warm season, the compound WW and DW extremes increase for 1991–2020 relative to that for 1961–1990 in most regions, while for the compound WC and DC extremes, the pattern is the opposite. We further explored the interannual variations and computed the linear trends in the frequency of compound extremes during warm season and cold season for 1961–2020 in the whole China and three subregions (Fig. 3  ). The nonparametric Mann-Kendall test is employed in the linear trends test of compound extremes long-term change (at the 5 % significance level). The compound WW and DW extremes displayed significant increasing trends in all the regions for both warm season and cold season. Specifically, the increase rates of compound WW extremes in the warm and cold seasons are 0.04 ∼ 0.17 and 0.07 ∼ 0.09 events/decade respectively, especially in Northwest China and the Tibetan Plateau with the largest increases of 0.09 and 0.17 events/decade, respectively. For DW, the increase rates are 0.06 ∼ 0.14 and 0.03 ∼ 0.08 events/decade respectively, especially in the Northwest China and Tibetan Plateau with the largest increases of 0.14 and 0.08 events/decade respectively. However, the compound WC and DC extremes show a downward trend. Compared with WW and DW, the change range of these two compound extremes is much smaller, with the decreasing trends less than −0.04 events/decade, especially for DC, the change range is only about −0.01 events/decade in all the regions for both warm season and cold season. Additionally, the decreasing trend of WC in the warm season has passed the significance test (p < 5 %), and the decreasing range is greater than that in the cold season within insignificant change.  3.3 Connection between compound extremes and circulation factors This part first uses the Pearson correlation analysis to test the overall relationship between compound extremes and atmospheric circulation factors. Then, we apply the WTC and MWC methods to analyze the influence of a single or multiple atmospheric circulation factor(s) on compound extremes at different timescales. 3.3.1 Overall relationship with atmospheric circulation factors During the warm season, AMO is significantly positively correlated with the frequency of warm related combinations (i.e., WW and DW), but significantly negatively with that of cold related combinations (i.e., WC and DC) over most regions (Fig. 4   and Fig. 6 ). This suggests that more regions are influenced by compound WW and DW extremes with higher AMO values. Similarly, the correlation coefficients of the warm-related combinations and IOD have similar spatial distribution as AMO, but are relatively small compared with AMO. The NAO and WW, DW are negatively correlated in South and Northwest China, while the pattern is the opposite for WC and DC. The PDO and WW are positively correlated in West China, and negatively correlated with WC in the most regions. Although the correlation coefficients of AO, ENSO and compound extremes also have obvious regional differences, they have not passed the significance test in most regions. For cold season, WW is positively correlated with almost all atmospheric circulation factors in most regions (Fig. 5  , Fig. 6  ), especially the correlation coefficient with AMO and AO in some regions of Northeast China exceeds 0.5. The correlation coefficient between WC and AMO, ENSO, IOD, PDO is negative in Central China, and that between WC and AO, NAO is negative in Northeast China. DW and AMO show a general positive correlation. DW and AO, NAO show a positive correlation in Northeast China and a negative correlation in Southwest China. DC has a negative correlation with AO, ENSO, NAO, PDO in most regions, while a positive correlation with IOD except for Northeast China.  3.3.2 Relationship with atmospheric circulation factors at varying scales The best (combined) atmospheric circulation factor(s) influencing compound extremes based on bivariate (multiple) wavelet coherence analysis during warm season for the period 1961–2020 in the whole China and three subregions are shown in Fig. 7   and Table 2  . The wavelet coherence analysis suggested that compound extremes are closely related to atmospheric circulation factors with PASC and AWC ranging 17 %–42 % and 0.91–0.98, respectively, except for WC in Tibetan Plateau. The detected correlation between compound temperature and precipitation extremes and atmospheric circulation factors varied with scales over time. In specific, IOD-NAO, AMO-IOD-PDO, AMO-ENSO-NAO and AMO-IOD-NAO are the best combination that influenced WW in the Whole China, East, Northwest and Tibetan Plateau, respectively, mainly at time scales of ∼ 8 years in the 2000 s and > 12 years in the whole time period. Although WC is positively correlated to PDO in the Tibetan Plateau at time scales of < 8 years for 1975–2005, WC is influenced by the combination of AMO-PDO, ENSO-PDO and AMO-ENSO in the Whole China, East and Northwest regions. For DW, the greatest combination mainly influences at time scales of < 6 and 8–12 years in the East, and mainly > 16 years in the other regions. The combination of ENSO-IOD presents the best PASC (26 % and 19 %) and AWC (0.96 and 0.95) for DC in the whole China and Northwest at time scales of < 4 and > 12 years. Besides, AO-IOD and ENSO-IOD-PDO are the best combination that affected DC in the East and Tibetan Plateau mainly at large time scales, respectively. For the cold season, compound temperature and precipitation extremes are mainly affected by AO and PDO at large time scales (Fig. 8  ). Specifically, the combination of AO-ENSO-PDO mainly influences WW at time scales of >8 years in the Whole China, East and Northeast, and AO-IDO at time scales of >12 years in the Tibetan Plateau. AMO-AO is the best combination that affects WC at time scales of ∼8 years and >12 years in the Whole China and East while the combined AMO-AO-IOD and AMO-ENSO-PDO have great influence in the Northweat and Tibetan Plateau. For DW, AMO-NAO has the greatest influence at time scales of <8 years during 1961–1985 and >12 years during the whole time period in the Whole China and East, while IOD-PDO and AMO-AO-IOD at time scales of <6 years and >16 years in the Northwest and the Tibetan Plateau. Moreover, in the Whole China and East, DC has a negative correlation with AO at time scales of 6–12 years for 1961–1985 and >12 years for the whole period and also has a positive correlation at time scales of ∼4 years in the period of 2005–2015. In the Tibetan Plateau, DC is positively correlated to AO at time scales of 4–8 years in the period of 2000–2010 and negatively correlated at time scales of >12 years. The combination of AMO-AO presents the greatest AWC (0.92) and PASC (30 %) for DC and mainly influences at time scales of >8 years in the Northwest. It should be emphasized that for the combined effects of four circulation factors, since the added factor had no additional value compared with the three factors’ effect on compound extremes, there are no additional time scales based on the combined effects of three circulation factors.    4 Discussion Numerous studies have demonstrated that the interaction and dependence between temperature and precipitation is due to their thermodynamic relations (e.g., Fernandez-Montes et al., 2017; Trenberth and Shea, 2005 ). The correlation between temperature and precipitation can account partly for the spatial distribution of compound extremes (Zhou and Liu, 2018 ). The high (low) frequency of compound DW and WC extremes in southern China (Tibetan Plateau) in warm season is relevant to the positive (negative) correlation between temperature and precipitation (Fig. 9  a). Similarly, the high (low) frequency of compound WW and DC extremes in some regions of northern China and southeastern China (Tibetan Plateau and Sichuan Basin) in cold season is relevant to the positive (negative) correlation between temperature and precipitation (Fig. 9 b). A significant increase in the warm related combinations and a decrease in cold related ones suggest that the continuous rise in temperature may largely affect the compound extreme events change (Piao et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016 ). The spatial–temporal variations of compound extremes over China are greatly affected by the large-scale circulation factors. Our results showed AMO correlated significantly with the frequency of most compound extremes, especially for the warm season. After the mid-1990 s, AMO was mainly in the positive phase (Fig. 10  a-b), which may be responsible for the changes of the temperature extremes and precipitation extremes in north China (Li et al., 2017 ). Previous studies have also reported similar conclusions (Shi et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019 ). The positive (negative) phase of the AMO is consistent with warm (cold) temperature over China (Ding et al., 2014 ). Kang et al. (2014)  explored the mechanism related to the modulation of the ENSO amplitude stimulated by the AMO and found that the ENSO variability strengthened in the negative AMO phase and weakened during the positive phase. While for other climate indices, significant correlations are presented only for limited modes for some seasons. This may be because the variations of climatological mean state or extremes are mostly influenced by circulation factors at a regional scale (Wang et al., 2018; Zuo et al., 2016 ). The PDO, one of the interdecadal climate change signals, has far-reaching effects on the atmospheric circulation of East Asia. Previous studies have pointed out that the precipitation correlated strongly with PDO in Weihe Plain (Liu et al., 2017 ) and Huaihe Basin (Wei and Zhang, 2009 ). The NAO affects the winter climate variability in south-central China (Zuo et al., 2016 ). AO is also a major synoptic factor affecting the precipitation change in the northern hemisphere, which can reflect the intensity of the mid-latitude westerly (Sun et al., 2016 ). Fig. 10 c showed that AO was mostly in warm phase around the 1990 s and reached its maximum. The positive mode of AO lead to a stronger mid-latitude Westerlies, enhancing latitudinal water vapor gradient into central Asia (Yu et al., 2006 ). Additionally, AO can also increase the surface temperature and weaken the East Asian winter monsoon, which is conducive to the northward movement of warm and humid air (Zhou, 2011 ). As one of the most significant circulation factors affecting eastern China, ENSO affects temperature and precipitation by influencing the East Asian summer monsoon (Li et al., 2021 ). Meanwhile, ENSO can weaken the East Asian winter monsoon by causing abnormal anticyclonic circulation over the Northwest Pacific. Furthermore, the impact of ENSO on the East Asian Monsoon is regulated by PDO and IOD (Chakravorty et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2015 ). In addition, there are some complex interactions between some circulation factors, such as AO and ENSO (Cheung et al., 2012 ), PDO and ENSO (Shi et al., 2018 ). It should be emphasized that there is no unified definition for compound extremes. Previous studies have mainly two types: one is defined based on daily data, and the other is defined based on monthly data. The compound extremes in this study are defined using monthly data rather than daily data, because our study mainly focuses on long-term climate variability at the interannual and decadal scales influenced by atmospheric circulation factors.  5 Conclusions This paper studied the spatio-temporal variations of the frequency in compound temperature and precipitation extremes for the period 1961–2020 in China, and explored the relationship between compound extremes and circulation factors. Particularly, the individual and combined effects of circulation factor(s) on compound extremes were investigated for different timescales. The main conclusions are as follows.(1) For warm season, the frequency of compound DW and WW extremes have high values in most areas and the Tibetan Plateau, respectively, while for DC and WC, the patterns are opposite. During the cold season, the frequency of WW and DW exceeds 16 in most areas, while that of WC and DC are smaller. The compound WW and DW extremes showed significant upward trends in all areas for both warm and cold seasons. Specifically, the increase of the compound WW and DW extremes are particularly obvious in Northwest China and the Tibetan Plateau. However, for the compound WC and DC extremes, the linear trends are just the opposite, that is, showing a downward trend. Compared with WW and DW, the change range of these two compound extremes is much smaller.  (2) AMO significantly correlates positively/negatively with the frequency of warm/cold related combinations over most regions during the warm season. Similarly, the correlation coefficients of the warm related combinations and IOD have similar spatial distribution with AMO, but are relatively small. Other circulation indices can affect limited modes for some seasons. The detected correlation between compound temperature and precipitation extremes and circulation factors varied with timescales.    Results of this study will provide a better understanding of the mechanism of the compound extremes and thus propose adaptive strategies. However, as global warming continues, the intensified hydrological cycle will bring about more climate extremes. Meanwhile, the air-sea interaction will also change with the increase of sea surface temperature, which may cause changes in the coupling relationship between multiple atmospheric circulation factors, whether it is strengthened or weakened. Therefore, it is thus crucial to further investigate whether compound extremes will change with atmospheric circulation factors in the future.
1 Introduction Evapotranspiration (ET) is an essential variable in meteorology, hydrology, and ecology, and has been identified as a key process for centuries (Pimentel et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Mondal & Mishra, 2024 ). The actual ET is typically estimated by potential evapotranspiration (PET) representing the upper limit of ET under the unlimited water supply circumstance (Wang et al., 2023a ). PET has been extensively explored, resulting in several estimation techniques based on temperature, radiation, and combination approaches (Oudin et al., 2005 ). However, capturing accurate ET remains a challenge (Zhao et al., 2013 ). ET can be directly or indirectly measured through instruments such as lysimeters, the Bowen ratio technique, and eddy covariance tower at a field scale (Drexler et al., 2004; Alfieri et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2019 ). Although the eddy covariance, also known as eddy flux, is generally considered the gold standard for ET estimates (Anderson et al., 2015; Jimenez-Berni et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b ), it is only available at site scales and cannot be extended to larger areas due to landscape heterogeneity and economic infeasibility. All other methods for ET estimation are derived from simulations using various models. Remote sensing and hydrological modeling are the main methods currently used for obtaining ET on a basin scale (Yin et al., 2016 ). Remote sensing provides an unparalleled opportunity for global-scale ET coverage, achieving a scope impractical to attain through field measurements (Fang et al., 2012 ). However, despite the advantage, remote sensing data often falls short in fulfilling temporal resolution requirements and is susceptible to external conditions such as clouds (Kite & Droogers, 2000 ). Hydrological modeling can provide space and time continuous ET, where the ET is typically described as a function of PET and soil moisture (Zhao et al., 2013; Almorox et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2016; Peiris & Döll, 2023; Lian et al., 2023 ). Vegetation plays a crucial role in ET estimations, a factor often overlooked in traditional hydrological models (Gerten, 2013; Jasechko et al., 2013; Khtami et al., 2019; Rasouli et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2024 ). However, incorporating vegetation dynamics into hydrology modeling has been extensively studied in eco-hydrological models (Jayathilake & Smith, 2020 ), such as the HYMOD-BVM model (Tang et al., 2018, 2019 ). HYMOD-BVM is an integration of a conceptual Hydrological MODel (HYMOD) rainfall-runoff model (Boyle et al., 2000; Boyle, 2001; Wagener et al., 2001 ) and a modified bucked grassland vegetation model (BVM) (Istanbulluoglu et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2013 ). It is a conceptual, lumped eco-hydrological model with the model inputs being precipitation (P) and PET, and the outputs being streamflow (Q) and leaf area index (LAI). Like traditional conceptual hydrological and eco-hydrological models, PET is used as a classical model input while rare studies have considered using actual ET as a direct input (Guo et al., 2017a ). The ongoing global climate change may alter key components of the hydrological cycle, including precipitation, streamflow, soil moisture, vegetation, and evapotranspiration (Saharia & Sarma, 2018; Cramer et al.,2018; Gudmundsson et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023 ). Global Climate Models (GCMs) have been the most advanced tools currently available for simulating and predicting responses of the global system to increasing greenhouse gas concentrations (Mishra et al., 2020 ). The latest GCMs are under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) (Eyring et al., 2016 ), and offer significant improvements and robust simulations to its last version (Zhai et al., 2020; Aguayo et al., 2021 ). Under this circumstance, changes in ET driven by vegetation dynamics in response to climate change should be a concern. Given these considerations, the current study aims to revisit the traditionally dominant PET input and presents a novel look by introducing actual ET as a potential alternative to PET to incorporate vegetation impacts under climate change. The specific research questions are: (a) Can actual ET be used as a direct input in (eco-)hydrological modeling? (b) What are the effects of using PET versus ET inputs on model outputs? (c) How does model performance vary with PET and ET inputs across catchments with various hydroclimatic conditions (i.e., energy-limited and water-limited) under climate change? To address these, the traditional HYMOD-BVM (THV) is adopted as a benchmark model due to its simple structure and few parameters. This model exemplifies the classical usage of PET, a common practice in traditional hydrological or eco-hydrological models. A modified HYMOD-BVM (MHV) model is developed where the PET is replaced by actual ET as one of the direct model inputs. The actual ET is derived from (eco-)hydrological modeling. The THV and MHV models are applied to one energy-limited and one water-limited catchment in Australia. Both hydrological (expressed by Q) and vegetation (expressed by LAI) factors are simulated and projected under the latest CMIP6. This study provides insights into the evapotranspiration input under climate change.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area Two Australian catchments are studied (Fig. 1  ), the Florentine River (FR Catchment) in Derwent River Basin, Tasmania, Australia, and the Murray River (MR Catchment) at Biggara in Upper Murray Basin, Victoria, Australia. The two catchments are selected because (1) both are anthropogenically unaffected or less affected catchments (Turner, 2012; Ajami et al., 2017 ), allowing us to focus on the impact of climate change and vegetation change without interference from the effect of human activities. (2) both are humid areas with a UNESCO aridity index larger than 0.65 (Zarch et al., 2015 ), indicating they will adapt to the saturation-excess runoff mechanism in HYMOD. Note however, that the two catchments have different hydroclimatic characteristics with the FR catchment being an energy-limited environment (P>PET) while the MR catchment belongs to a water-limited environment (P<PET) (Table 1  ). (3) both are mainly covered by forest. As presented in Fig. 1 , forests cover 98.6 % of the FR catchment and 97.2 % of the MR catchment. The magnitude of LAI in the two catchments does differ: the maximum LAI value for the FR catchment is 4.47 (m2 / m2 ), while that for the MR catchment is 2.88 (m2 / m2 ).  2.2 Data 2.2.1 Observed data For historical observations, 6 variables covering the period 1980–2014 are collected for model calibration and validation, including daily precipitation (P), maximum temperature (Tmax ), minimum temperature (Tmin ), evapotranspiration (ET), streamflow (Q) and 8-day leaf area index (LAI) (Table 2  ). The Australian Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) provides gridded daily P, Tmax , and Tmin  data at 0.05° ×    0.05° resolution (about 5 ×    5 km) across Australia (https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/ ). These meteorological data were gridded from the station data using the Barnes successive correction method (Johnson & Sharma, 2012; Contractor et al., 2015 ). The Priestley-Taylor (PT) equation is adopted to estimate the potential evapotranspiration (PET) due to its modest data demand (Priestley & Taylor, 1972 ):(1) P E T  P T   = α × Δ Δ + γ   × R n  - G  λ      where α    is the Priestley-Taylor coefficient, Δ    is the slope of the saturation vapor pressure versus temperature curve (kPa °C-1 ), γ    is the psychrometric constant (kPa °C-1 ), R n     is the net solar radiation (MJm-2 day−1 ), G    is the daily soil heat flux density at the soil surface (MJm-2 day−1 ), and λ    is the latent heat of vaporization (MJkg−1 ). Typically, α = 1.26    and G can be ignored in daily cases. Details can be found in Guo et al. (2017b)  and Xiang et al. (2020) . While evapotranspiration is a key factor in the water cycle and energy balance, accurate global ET information or datasets, with spatially and temporally continuous coverage at moderate resolution, is still scarce (Zheng et al., 2022 ). Hydrological modeling is considered one of the effective approaches to estimate evapotranspiration continuously, therefore, in this study, ET simulated from the THV model is used as a proxy for observations. High-quality daily Q data are obtained from the Australian Hydrologic Reference Stations (HRS, https://www.bom.gov.au/water/hrs/ ). Long-term LAI series are provided by the Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS) at 0.05° resolution every 8 days (Yan et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017 ). GLASS is a combination product derived from Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) reflectance data (Liang et al., 2013 ). The LAI (starting from 1981, to be consistent with our study period, the data in 1980 is filled with null values) have been filtered after the Savitzky-Golay method (Savitzky & Golay, 1964 ).  2.2.2 CMIP6 data Six GCMs from the latest CMIP6 (Eyring et al., 2016 ) provide current simulations and future projections, including NorESM2-LM, ACCESS-ESM1.5, CMCC-ESM2, FGOALS-g3, GFDL-ESM4, and MPI-ESM1.2-LR, which can be downloaded from Earth Systems Grid Federation (ESGF, https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/ ). The six GCMs are chosen as they have a complete series of requiring data during both the current climate (1980–2014) and future climate (2021–2100) under r1i1p1f1 (r-realization, i-initialization, p-physics, f-forcing), details of the data used and GCMs are listed in Tables 2 and 3  . Most GCMs lack data in daily ET. To be consistent with eco-hydrological modeling, monthly ET is temporally downscaled into daily time series using the THV model, with detailed steps provided in Methods. The daily GCM PET is estimated using the Priestley-Taylor equation. For the future climate, only variables under the SSP5-8.5 scenario are considered to maximize the projected climate change signal (Dosio et al., 2019 ). The future period is further divided into the near future (2021–2050) and far future (2071–2100) for comparison.    3 Methods 3.1 Eco-hydrological model design 3.1.1 Hydrological model Hydrologic MODel (HYMOD), a lumped, parsimonious, conceptual rainfall-runoff model, is chosen as the base hydrological model to simulate streamflow in this study (Boyle, 2001; Wagener et al., 2001 ). HYMOD consists of two main components, i.e., runoff generation and runoff routing. Runoff is generated using a nonlinear soil moisture tank under the saturation-excess mechanism (Zhao, 1992; Harvey et al., 2023 ). The runoff is then distributed into quick and slow flow through a partitioning factor. Two series of linear reservoirs are used to describe the routing, where several reservoirs (usually 1–4) in series are used for quick flow (or surface flow) under the same routing rate Kq , and a single reservoir is used for slow flow (or baseflow) under another routing rate Ks . The two types of flow compose the total streamflow at the outlet of a catchment.  3.1.2 Vegetation model The Bucket Grassland Model (BGM) (Istanbulluoglu et al., 2012 ), a lumped, conceptual, dynamic vegetation model, is adopted to simulate biomass dynamics. The BGM model was initially developed for simulating biomass dynamics in grassland ecosystems, but its modified version can extend to woody ecosystems (e.g., trees and shrubs) (Zhou et al., 2013 ). Thus, the modified model can apply to grassland and woody ecosystems and is named the Bucket Vegetation Model (BVM) in this study. The BVM model is composed of a zero-dimensional land surface model with uniform soil moisture and biomass pools. The net primary production (NPP) is linearly driven by ET coupled with an ecosystem water use efficiency parameter (WUE): NPP = 0.75 × ( 1 - μ )  × E T × W U E × ρ v  × w   , where μ    is the ratio of nighttime to daytime CO2  exchange, ρ v     is water density, and w    is a factor converting CO2  to dry matter. The equation indicates that ET connects water and vegetation variables. Subsequently, green and dead plant biomass is updated using NPP and natural decay parameters for green and dead biomass. Green and dead LAI are simulated based on their respective biomass and specific leaf area respectively (Jayathilake & Smith, 2020 ). Detailed equations can be found in Istanbulluoglu et al. (2012)  and Zhou et al. (2013) .  3.1.3 Model coupling The HYMOD hydrological model is coupled with the BVM vegetation model via the replacement of BVM’s soil moisture dynamic with HYMOD’s soil moisture tank, which induces a lumped conceptual eco-hydrological model HYMOD-BVM (Tang et al., 2018 ). ET is an intermediate variable in the model, that bridges the hydrologic and vegetation models via a soil moisture tank. The modeled ET is expressed as a function of PET and available soil water storage. If sufficient water is available, the modeled ET is assumed to be equal to PET, otherwise, it equals the available soil water storage (Jayathilake & Smith, 2020 ). In this eco-hydrological system, HYMOD furnishes modeled ET to the BVM to estimate NPP, which is linearly derived from modeled ET and WUE. Additionally, BVM offers simulated LAI to HYMOD to adjust daily input PET relying on the function of LAI and a canopy interception capacity (Brolsma and Bierkens, 2007 ). This ultimately leads to interactions between hydrological and vegetation processes. To investigate the effects of evapotranspiration assumptions on future streamflow and leaf area index under climate change, two versions of the eco-hydrological model are used. The first version (Fig. 2  a1 + b + c) utilizes the traditional HYMOD-BVM (THV) where the inputs are daily P and PET, and outputs include daily Q and LAI. The second version (Fig. 2 a2 + b + c) is a modification of the THV model (MHV), where ET substitutes the conventional PET as a direct input. The inputs for the MHV model consist of daily P and ET, while the outputs are daily Q and LAI. The input ET is further regulated to the modeled ET through the soil moisture tank within HYMOD. The modeled ET is an adjustment of the input one as the actual ET should not exceed the available soil water storage in modeling. The ensuing NPP and LAI estimates in the BVM are derived using the modeled ET. The input ET can be perceived as a reflection of vegetation dynamics, implicating considerations of vegetation information. Consequently, vegetation processes are reflected in the input ET of HYMOD, while hydrological processes provide modeled ET for biomass estimation in the BVM. Interactions between the hydrological and vegetation processes are observed within the MHV model as well. Details of the parameters used in the THV and MHV models are presented in Table 4  , in all, eight parameters need calibrations.   3.2 Multivariate bias correction of GCMs GCMs provide insights into historical and future climate variabilities. However, the raw GCM outputs have biases in the simulation due to imperfect model parameterization, inadequate reference data, and incomplete knowledge, which limits its use in regional and hydrological catchment scales. Bias correction is a technique that removes the systematic biases of GCMs based on the observed and model-simulated data for the historical period. Various bias correction methods have been developed to correct the bias in GCM simulations before use, including univariate bias correction and multivariate bias correction methods. In this study, several variables such as precipitation, temperature, and evapotranspiration (which present some co-dependence in the eco-hydrological system) need to be bias-corrected. A robust multivariate bias correction (RoMBC) (Mehrotra & Sharma, 2021 ) method is adopted to correct the biases of multi-variables from raw GCMs. A daily time scale is used following the requirement of the THV and MHV models.  3.3 Temporal downscaling of the GCM ET data As we can see from Table 3 , most of the GCMs lack daily ET data. To be consistent with the eco-hydrological modeling, the monthly ET should be scaled into a daily series where daily ET is unavailable. For this study, the following steps are applied to obtain daily GCM ET based on monthly GCM data and the original HYMOD-BVM (THV) model:(1) Calibrate and validate the THV model using the Multi-objective Shuffled Complex Evaluation Metropolis (MOSCEM) method (Vrugt et al., 2003 ), the optimized parameter set is defined as parameter set θ   .  (2) Do multivariate bias correction (RoMBC) to daily GCM P and PET (current and future climate) simultaneously based on observed P and PET to obtain the bias-corrected GCM P and PET for the future climate.  (3) Input the bias-corrected daily GCM P and PET (future period) into the calibrated THV model with a parameter set θ    to get the daily model simulated ET (future climate) (ET-THV-day).  (4) Aggregate the model simulated ET into the monthly scale (ET-THV-mon), and calculate the scale factor expressed as the ratio of monthly GCM ET (ET-GCM-mon) and modeled ET (ET-THV-mon), i.e., scale factor (SF)=E T - G C M - m o n  E T - T H V - m o n     .  (5) Multiply the daily model simulated ET (ET-THV-day) by the scale factor (SF) to approximately estimate the daily GCM ET series (ET-GCM-day), i.e., ET-GCM-day = SF*ET-THV-day.  (6) The ET-GCM-day data was then coupled with GCM daily P and PET to do the bias correction for further use.     3.4 Model setup The Multi-objective Shuffled Complex Evaluation Metropolis (MOSCEM) algorithm (Vrugt et al., 2003 ) was adopted to calibrate the eco-hydrological THV and MHV models by maximizing the Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009 ) of Q and LAI simultaneously. For comparison, the single objective calibration method SCE-UA (Duan et al., 1992 ) is used to simulate Q or LAI based on their respective KGE. The KGE calculates correlation, variability, and bias parts, and is defined by:(2) K G E = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( s - 1 )  2  + ( e - 1 )  2        where r  is the linear correlation coefficient between simulations and observations, s  is a measure of variability determined as the ratio of the standard deviation of simulations and observations, and e  is the bias error calculated as the ratio of the means of the simulations and observations. A higher KGE (KGE ≤ 1   ) represents a better agreement between observations and model simulations (Knoben et al., 2019 ). Given that the THV and MHV are lumped and conceptual eco-hydrological models, catchment-average data were accessed through the clip for model simulation and projection. Data from 1980 to 2014 was used for model calibration and validation, which was further divided into the calibration period (1980–2010) and validation period (2011–2014), the first 2 years in the calibration period were allocated as a warm-up period. Once the calibrated parameters are optimized, the optimized parameter set θ    will be assumed to apply to both the THV and MHV models for the current and future climate.   4 Results 4.1 Model performance for the historical period The HYMOD hydrological and THV eco-hydrological models are implemented based on daily meteorological, hydrological, and 8-day vegetation data. Model inputs include P and PET, and the output of HYMOD is Q while the outputs of the THV model are Q and LAI. (Note that results for the MHV model are not presented for the historical period as its model input ET is derived from the THV model, leading to the same model performance as the THV model.) The SCE-UA and MOSCEM global optimization algorithms are applied to single-objective calibration and multi-objective calibration respectively. Data during the warm-up period is discarded from the following presentation of model performance. Table 5   summarizes the model performance for Q and LAI in the FR catchment and MR catchment under different models and calibration methods. For the HYMOD model, streamflow is the unique output, and the SCE-UA algorithm is used. As presented in Table 5 , the KGE(Q) for the energy-limited catchment (FR Catchment) is 0.90 and 0.87 during the calibration and validation period respectively, while for the water-limited catchment (MR Catchment), the KGE(Q) is 0.76 and 0.74. For comparison, the SCE-UA is applied to calibrate the THV model by focusing on Q solely. In this case, the KGE(Q) of the FR catchment is 0.89 and 0.87 (calibration and validation period) while that of the MR catchment is 0.82 and 0.80. The comparison between the single-objective calibrated streamflow performance illustrates that both the HYMOD and THV models perform equally well in the FR catchment when only Q is calibrated, while the THV model presents superior results in the MR catchment, which supports the reliability of the THV model. For the sole calibration of the Q case, the daily streamflow is well simulated by the THV model, however, the simulations are unable to reproduce the magnitude and variability in LAI which leads to low accuracy of LAI (Fig. 3   & Fig. 4  ). Similarly, for the sole calibration of the LAI case, the variations in LAI are well captured while the performance of Q is unsatisfactory (details about these metrics are presented in Table 5 ). The MOSCEM multi-objective calibration method provides a compromise between the two outputs. From the last row of Fig. 3  and Fig. 4 , the THV model using MOSCEM captures the variations of both Q and LAI for the FR catchment and MR catchment. For the FR catchment, the KGE(Q) is 0.84 and 0.83 while the KGE(LAI) is 0.51 and 0.49 in the calibration and validation period, respectively. For the MR catchment, the KGE(Q) is 0.76 and 0.75 while the KGE(LAI) is 0.39 and 0.35 in the calibration and validation period, respectively. The results indicate that compared with conventional calibration solely against one variable, the THV model calibrated by the MOSCEM multi-objective method can simultaneously capture satisfactory simulations of both Q and LAI in the study catchments.  4.2 Bias correction performance The RoMBC bias correction method considers the correlation between multiple variables, such as precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and actual evapotranspiration used in this study. Observed data coupled with GCM raw data during the current climate are used to train the RoMBC technique. Once the relationship between observations and GCM raw data is built, the calibrated relationship is assumed to be applied to future climate to correct the future outputs of GCM. Fig. 5   and Fig. 6   present a comparison of summary statistics (such as mean and standard deviation) between observed versus GCM raw or GCM bias-corrected data for the FR catchment and MR catchment respectively. The blue scatter points represent statistics of GCM raw data, while the red scatter points represent statistics of the bias-corrected GCMs. The result illustrates that the RoMBC technique is able to reproduce the daily distribution of observed P, PET, and ET for the two study catchments.  4.3 Model projections for future climate The bias-corrected precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and evapotranspiration from NorESM2-LM, ACCESS-ESM1.5, CMCC-ESM2, FGOALS-g3, GFDL-ESM4, and MPI-ESM1.2-LR GCMs under the SSP5-8.5 scenario are inputted into the calibrated THV and MHV models for streamflow and leaf area index projections. 4.3.1 Streamflow projection Fig. 7   and Fig. 8   present the annual and monthly distributions of streamflow during both the current and future climate for the FR catchment and MR catchment respectively. The color shades in Fig. 7 a1 and Fig. 8 a1 represent annual variations of streamflow at the 95 % confidence level, and the color lines denote the model ensemble mean of all 6 study GCMs. The MK trend test (Kendall, 1975; Mann, 1945 ) is applied to test the changes in annual streamflow. For the FR catchment, a significant decreasing trend (p < 0.05) of future ensemble-mean streamflow is projected with the decreasing rate being −37.1 mm/10a under the THV model and −35.4 mm/10a under the MHV model (Fig. 7 a1). The ensemble-mean streamflow projections decreased by −0.47 % and increased by 4.53 % in the near future, and decreased by −27.96 % and −21.56 % in the far future for the THV and MHV models respectively (Fig. 7 a2). For the MR catchment, a significant decreasing trend with a −8.6 mm/10a rate is projected by the THV model while no significant trend is detected under the MHV model (Fig. 8 a1). Compared to the historical period, it is likely that the ensemble mean streamflow projections will decrease during both the near future (−30.21 % in the THV model case, −14.51 % in the MHV model case) and far future (−43.61 % in the THV model case, −8.70 % in the MHV model case) (Fig. 8 a2). The future climate is further divided into the near future (2021–2050) and far future (2071–2100) to detect the variations in monthly streamflow. The monthly observed versus model projected streamflow for both the near future and far future are presented in Fig. 7 b and Fig. 8 b. Although the streamflow varies in different months, it presents an unimodal monthly distribution where high values are concentrated between June and November for both the study catchments. The high flow lies in the winter and spring of Australia, and flow in the two seasons takes up to 70 % and 75 % of the year for the FR catchment and MR catchment respectively. The peak monthly streamflow occurs in August for the FR catchment and in September for the MR catchment. Differences between the two models are small for the FR catchment but are substantial for the MR catchment, with higher differences shown particularly in the far future. Comparison between observations and projections indicates that the future streamflow will decrease significantly except for projections under the MHV model for the MR catchment which is consistent with previous analyses in time series data. The results compared between the THV and MHV models indicate that streamflow tends to be higher as estimated by the MHV model while being lower for the THV model. The differences between the two models are largely due to different ways of using ET. The PET is inputted into the THV model to derive the modeled ET through an empirical equation, while ET works as one of the direct inputs and is further adjusted in the MHV model. Comparing the FR catchment and MR catchment shows that the differences between the two models are more obvious in the MR catchment than in the FR catchment. This is probably related to catchment characteristics. As depicted in Fig. 2 , the streamflow projections are closely related to runoff generation. Following the saturation-excess runoff generation mechanism within HYMOD, runoff will not be generated until the soil water storage surpasses its capacity. Precipitation is the main source of water, which undergoes losses by interception, evapotranspiration, infiltration, and soil water absorption before being used for runoff. Changes in the evapotranspiration conditions will influence the water available for runoff generation. This relationship is particularly responsive in the MR catchment, where water shortage makes the area highly sensitive to alternations in water losses, which can significantly impact runoff and consequently streamflow. While in energy-limited catchments like the FR catchment, where P surpasses PET or ET, there will be sufficient water to respond to fluctuations in energy conditions.  4.3.2 Leaf area index projection Similarly, the temporal variations of leaf area index (LAI) are presented in Fig. 9   and Fig. 10   respectively for the FR and MR catchment. In contrast to Q, the variations in modeled LAI are mild due to the natural ranges of LAI. Tested by the MK trend approach, a significant change with a −0.011 /10a decreasing rate under the THV model and a −0.016/10a rate under the MHV model (ensemble mean) is obtained for the FR catchment, while no significant trend is tested under the THV model and a −0.015/10a decreasing rate is obtained under the MHV model for the MR catchment. Future LAI (ensemble mean) in the FR catchment are projected to be decreasing by −0.87 % and −2.32 % in the THV model, and by −2.42 % and −4.78 % in the MHV model during the near future and far future respectively. While LAI (ensemble mean) projected in the MR catchment indicates an increasing trend of 1.34 % and 1.12 % under the THV model and presents a decreasing trend of −1.18 % and −5.12 % under the MHV model for the two future periods. In all cases, the modeled LAI from the MHV model tends to be lower than that from the THV model, which indicates a trend contrary to streamflow. Monthly LAI is compared between the near future, far future, and historical period. As shown in Fig. 9 b and Fig. 10 b, (and different from the case with Q), low LAI occurs between June and August which lies in Winter while high LAI happens from December to February which lies in the Summer of Australia. The result is consistent with the plant phenology for trees (Tesemma et al., 2015 ). Differences between the THV and MHV models remain for the LAI, especially in the far future. Compared to the monthly observations, the future LAI mainly decreases from September to April, and increases from May to August in the FR catchment, while presenting a decreasing trend from November to April and an increasing trend from May to October in the MR catchment. This change decreases the differences between months, making the LAI stable for seasons in the future.   4.4 Shifts in the precipitation-streamflow relationship Gupta et al. (2015)  and Raymond et al. (2008)  point out that variations in streamflow can reflect the changes in precipitation and land cover to a certain extent, which induces shifts in the precipitation-streamflow relationship (P-Q relationship). Fig. 11   illustrates the P-Q relationship (ensemble mean) under the THV and MHV eco-hydrological models across various climate periods, where P is obtained from observations or bias-corrected GCMs, and Q is simulated or projected from the THV and MHV models. Under the THV model (Fig. 11 a1 & 11b1), the P-Q points for different study periods are all clustered around one curve. This indicates a consistent P-Q relationship maintained by the THV model. Notwithstanding, datasets in the near and far future present notable alterations within their corresponding point clusters (Fig. 11 a1 & Fig. 11 b1). Such changes are particularly evident in the FR catchment, indicating potential shifts in future climate, such as precipitation. Comparisons between the THV and MHV models are given in Fig. 11 a2, b2, a3, and b3 when the study period is fixed (near future or far future). Here, the P-Q curve under the THV model is almost parallel to that under the MHV model, but the distance between the two P-Q curves is shifting over time, especially for the MR catchment, indicating shifts in future P-Q relationships.   5 Discussion 5.1 Evapotranspiration comparison ET is usually estimated as a function of PET and soil moisture in traditional hydrological models. Rarely have conceptual hydrological and eco-hydrological models considered using actual ET as a direct input, likely because actual ET data is unavailable. While eddy covariance ET is considered the gold standard for ET estimates, it is only available at site scales. All other ET estimates are derived from simulations using various models. Although some simulated ET data, which consider vegetation information (e.g., remote sensing data), can be used directly as model input, there is still no actual ET data available for future predictions. Additionally, remote sensing data usually have coarse spatial or temporal resolutions (Fuentes et al., 2024 ). For example, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) MOD16A2 provides ET data on an 8-day interval, which may not be sufficient for daily eco-hydrological modeling. Hydrological modeling is another in-practice method to obtain ET, and spatially and temporally continuous ET can be acquired via modeling. Our study requires daily evapotranspiration data spanning from 1980 to 2100. We assume that ET simulated from the HYMOD-BVM eco-hydrological model can act as a proxy for direct. During the historical period, the modeled ET from the THV is taken as the actual ET and directly inputted into the MHV eco-hydrological model. During future climate, bias-corrected and temporal-downscaled ET simulations from GCMs are inputted into the MHV model. Both PET and ET inputs of the THV and MHV models are regulated to the modeled ET via its respective soil moisture tank. Fig. 12   presents the comparison of the modeled ET within the THV and MHV models for the future. In the two study catchments, despite the modeled ET demonstrating similar performance under the two eco-hydrological models, those derived from the THV model tend to present higher values. The finding suggests that the higher Q and lower LAI projected in the MHV model, as depicted from Fig. 7  to Fig. 10 , are not merely a consequence of smaller ET inputs relative to those in the THV model, but a result of comprehensive eco-hydrological processes.  5.2 Effects of climate change and vegetation change on streamflow Climate and vegetation are the most influential factors affecting catchment water balance (Liu et al., 2019 ). Previous studies have highlighted the importance of climate change in future water availability, however, vegetation change is not well understood in traditional hydrological models, especially its role in the future. The correlation between precipitation and streamflow can be indicative of future changes in a catchment. If the overall relationship between P and Q does not change in different periods (e.g. Fig. 11 a1 and 11b1 whereby the P-Q relationships remain unchanged during the current, near future, and far future climate), this suggests that shifts in streamflow are mainly induced by climate effects rather than changes in vegetation or terrestrial hydrologic properties (Gupta et al., 2015 ). Alternatively, a P-Q curve may show an upward or downward shift under a new climate regime or when analyzed with a new model. Fig. 11 a2, b2, a3, and b3 belong to this case, with the phenomenon especially obvious in the water-limited catchment. The THV and MHV models are used to predict future changes in streamflow, and different P-Q relationships are seen under the two models when the study period is the same. In this case, the P-Q relationship changes, land use effect would be the main inducer (Gupta et al., 2015 ). Considering the catchments are anthropogenically unaffected, vegetation is taken as the main driving force in this study. The comparison between the two models demonstrates that the THV model can well capture future climate change but cannot as effectively reveal changes in future vegetation, while the MHV model can capture both climate change and vegetation change. A different performance is obtained across the two study catchments. The FR catchment represents an energy-limited system while the MR catchment belongs to a water-limited system. The energy-limited catchment is more significantly affected by climate change while the water-limited catchment is more vulnerable to vegetation change (Fig. 11 ), and the effects are especially enhanced for the far future. This is likely because the energy-limited catchment is temporarily abounded in water, with the development of future climate, vegetation would not be severely affected given that sufficient available water (Sungmin & Park, 2023 ). In this case, variations in streamflow are mainly induced by climate change such as changes in precipitation. However, the water-limited catchment lacks water, and with the increasing future temperature and PET, plants may suffer from increasing water scarcity (Qin et al., 2017; De-Ville et al., 2024 ). In this condition, vegetation would be susceptible to future changes given the essential role water plays in vegetation growth (Porporato et al., 2001 ). A reduction in future vegetation is projected and further leads to increased streamflow in the MHV model compared to that in the THV model, which coincides with the previous analysis. The variations of streamflow in the MR catchment are dominated by vegetation change.  5.3 Limitation and outlook The THV and MHV models are studied to detect their PET or ET effects on model outputs. Our study indicates that the streamflow from the MHV model tends to be higher while the leaf area index is smaller than that from the THV model. The disagreements in future hydrology and vegetation projections indicate obvious challenges in the management of local water resources as well as for sustainable ecosystem conservation. However, this study highlights the significance of evapotranspiration input rather than suggesting which model is the best. For the historical period, both the THV and MHV exhibit the same model performance, while for the future climate, there is no observation for model outputs. Consequently, it highlights the importance of developing spatially and temporally continuous evapotranspiration data with high accuracy, satisfying hydrological/eco-hydrological modeling requirements in both the current and future climate.   6 Conclusion This study aims to provide insights into the impact of evapotranspiration estimates for use in eco-hydrological models as an alternative to traditionally used potential evapotranspiration. The HYMOD-BVM eco-hydrological model is used based on a conceptual rainfall-runoff model (HYMOD) and a bucket vegetation model (BVM). The inputs of the traditional HYMOD-BVM (THV) are precipitation and potential evapotranspiration. It is then modified into the MHV model where inputs are precipitation and actual evapotranspiration. A comparison between the two models is conducted over one energy-limited and one water-limited Australian catchment in the future. The main conclusions are drawn as follows:(1) In addition to the HYMOD rainfall-runoff model, the THV/ MHV eco-hydrological model is compared under single-objective and multi-objective calibration methods for the historical period. The results show that compared with the conventional calibration solely against streamflow, the multi-objective THV/ MHV models are more reliable when simultaneously describing the hydrological (in streamflow) and vegetation (in Leaf Area Index) features.  (2) The RoMBC multivariate bias correction method is performed on six GCMs from the latest CMIP6 under the high-emission scenario SSP5-8.5. Significant decreasing trends in annual Q (−37.1 mm/10a, −35.4 mm/10a) and LAI (−0.011/10a, −0.016/10a) are projected in the FR catchment based on the calibrated THV and MHV models. However, in the MR catchment, a significant decreasing trend of Q (−8.6 mm/10a) by the THV model and LAI (−0.015/10a) by the MHV model is obtained. Monthly mean LAI is distributed contrary to the general rules of streamflow where winter owns the least LAI but has the largest Q. A larger streamflow and smaller LAI are observed in the MHV model compared to that in the THV model, especially in the far future.  (3) The relationships between precipitation and streamflow for different climate periods are drawn for THV and MHV models. The result illustrates the potential of the MHV model in capturing future climate change and vegetation change.
