Among the two study catchments, the energy-limited (FR) catchment exhibits greater sensitivity to climate change, whereas the water-limited (MR) catchment demonstrates higher sensitivity to vegetation change.    Our study presented here is not intended to provide a new model, but to illustrate the importance of vegetation change and possible use of evapotranspiration in eco-hydrological modeling, especially for climate change studies. However, model performance is highly affected by the accuracy of ET, necessitating a better requirement of spatially and temporally continuous ET. Further studies will be conducted to account for the impacts of actual evapotranspiration over more catchments.
1 Introduction Soil moisture droughts (agricultural droughts) and hot events (heatwaves) typically coincide via land-atmospheric feedback (Barriopedro et al., 2023; Hsu & Dirmeyer, 2023; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Qiao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2021b ). Their combinations, i.e., Compound Agricultural Drought and Hot events (CADHEs), have more amplified disastrous impacts on water resources management, agricultural production, energy supply, and eco-environmental health in comparison with individual drought or hot extremes (García-García et al., 2023; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Otkin et al., 2016; Samaniego et al., 2018; Zscheischler et al., 2020 ). For instance, a once-in-800-years megadrought swept through southwestern North America in 2000–2021 (Williams et al., 2022 ), resulting in profound economic losses and environmental degradation; and the record-breaking extreme heatwave coupled with severe agricultural drought hit the Yangtze River basin in China in 2022 (Wu et al., 2023a ), leading to crop yield reduction, water scarcity, and energy stress. Investigations have demonstrated that the risks of compound extremes will intensify in a warmer climate, even though such risks have already been kept at a relatively higher level under the current climate (AghaKouchak et al., 2020; Bevacqua et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023a ). To mitigate the potential risks associated with droughts and hot events and to aid their reliable prediction, it is critical to understand the interaction between agricultural droughts and hot events. Due to water and energy exchanges between land and atmosphere (Humphrey et al., 2021 ), a long-lasting precipitation shortage (meteorological drought) and a continuous high-temperature anomaly (hot event) may reinforce soil moisture deficit (agricultural drought) (Miralles et al., 2019; Miralles et al., 2014; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2021b ). Furthermore, evapotranspiration excess is more likely to further deplete soil moisture, increase vapor pressure deficit, and elevate air temperature (Miralles et al., 2019; Miralles et al., 2014 ). These intercorrelated physical processes across a wide range of spatiotemporal scales may strengthen the likelihood of cascading effects between agricultural droughts and hot events (Miralles et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Qiao et al., 2023; Rajeev et al., 2022; Schumacher et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021b ). On the one hand, the positive temperature anomaly accelerates soil moisture depletion, resulting in the Hot-To-agricultural Drought (HTD) cascade event. On the other hand, with land–atmosphere feedback, a prolonged soil moisture deficit increases the sensible heat flux and decreases water for evaporative cooling, which in turn makes high temperatures more likely (Barriopedro et al., 2023; Miralles et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2021b; Yin et al., 2014 ), causing the agricultural Drought-To-Hot (DTH) cascade event. However, the cascading interactions between agricultural droughts and hot events are susceptible to the compounding influence of a multitude of confounders (drivers). For instance, Mukherjee et al. (2023)  leveraged the Cascade Modeling (CaM) framework to reveal the causal interactions between exposure (e.g., hot event) and outcome (e.g., agricultural drought) with the influence of different confounders (e.g., precipitation and vapor pressure deficit). Considering the compounding effects of distinct confounders on the DTH and HTD cascading events, therefore, how to simultaneously predict agricultural droughts and hot events may help improve the predictive capability of CADHEs. As the multivariate statistical methods can model complex statistical relationships and help reveal the causal interactions among different hydrometeorological variables, they have been widely utilized in drought, streamflow, and flood predictions and the response relationship simulations between water quality and drought (Abolafia-Rosenzweig et al., 2023; Bevacqua et al., 2017; Han & Singh, 2023; Jiang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021b; Wu et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2023d; Wu et al., 2022b ). However, these multivariate statistical methods primarily pay attention to single predictand variable (i.e., single-output prediction), while there are some multi-output models (e.g., multi-output neural networks and multi-output regression trees) that generally are the black-box models (i.e., cannot present explicit analytical expressions) and are prone to overfitting (Abbaszadeh et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022a ). Therefore, how to accurately predict multivariate compounding events (i.e., two or more predictand variables) is still a challenge (Pendergrass et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023a ). Although previous studies have directly predicted compound meteorological drought and hot events based on the meta -Gaussian model and logistic regression model (Hao et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2019a; Hao et al., 2019b ), the intrinsic link between drought and hot events have been overlooked. Noteworthy, much less is known about simultaneously predicting agricultural droughts and hot events based on a prediction model with multi-predictand variables. For high-dimensional situations, multivariate statistical models, such as vine copulas, can be employed to model complex dependence structures between response and contributing variables (Bevacqua et al., 2017 ). In particular, vine copulas decompose multidimensional variates into a series of combinations of bivariate copulas via pair copula constructions (Aas & Berg, 2009; Aas et al., 2009; Bevacqua et al., 2017; Czado & Nagler, 2022; Sévellec & Drijfhout, 2018 ). For example, Bevacqua et al. (2017)  used vine copulas to predict compound floods (i.e., joint storm surge and high river runoff) in Ravenna, Italy. Note that vine copulas comprise numerous tree (or vine) structures resulting from diverse ordering variables, especially for high-dimensional scenarios. As these vine structures may have a similar prediction performance, an optimal vine structure is selected to perform prediction that will inevitably lead to statistical bias (Liu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023b; Wu et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA), an ensemble prediction technique, has been leveraged to couple diverse prediction members with appropriate weights for reducing predictive uncertainty, hence, yielding more accurate predictions (Duan et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022 ), such as crop yield prediction (Abbaszadeh et al., 2022 ) and hydrological drought prediction (Wu et al., 2022a ). Thus, with consideration combining the merits of vine copulas in handling multiple variates and BMA in performing ensemble predictions, the prediction skills of CADHEs may be strengthened. The cascading effects of agricultural-Drought-To-Hot-event (DTH) and Hot-event-To-agricultural-Drought (HTD) may both have appeared within a specific period (e.g., warm season) due to the land-atmospheric interactions. The objectives of this study therefore were to: (1) assess the DTH and HTD cascading effects using a CaM framework; (2) propose a prediction model with multi-predictand variables that was developed by coupling a CaM framework with BMA and Vine Copulas (namely CaMBMAViC model); and (3) evaluate the performance of the proposed model for predicting agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: a brief description of the study area and datasets are given in Section 2 ; the methods are discussed in Section 3 ; the main findings of this study are reported in Section 4 ; and the discussion and conclusions are given in Section 5 .  2 Study area and data sets For the convenience of evaluating the spatial patterns of agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs, as shown in Fig. 1  , the whole of China (CHN) was divided into seven sub-climate regions (Zhao, 1983 ), including the temperate grasslands of Inner Mongolia (D1), the temperate humid and subhumid regions of northeastern China (D2), the temperate and warm-temperate northwestern China desert (D3), the subtropical humid regions of central and southern China (D4), the warm-temperate humid and subhumid regions of northern China (D5), the tropical humid regions of southern China (D6), and the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau (D7). For each sub-climate region, the combined temperature and moisture conditions are roughly similar, and the soil and vegetation types have a certain common characteristic. Details of the full names for each sub-climate region are shown in the bottom-left panel of Fig. 1 . The gridded monthly precipitation, maximum air temperature (T max ), and evapotranspiration (ET ) data with an equal 0.5° spatial resolution were obtained from the Climate Research Unit (CRU) observational datasets (available at https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/hrg/cru_ts_4.06/ ) for the period 1950–2021. The gridded monthly precipitation data at a 0.25°×0.25° spatial resolution was obtained from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) observational datasets (available at https://opendata.dwd.de/climate_environment/GPCC/full_data_monthly_v2022/05/ ) for the period 1950–2020. The gridded monthly soil moisture (SM) at three soil depths (i.e., 0–7cm, 7–28cm, and 28–100cm), 2m air temperature (Ta  ), 2m dew point temperature (Td  ), and surface air pressure (SP ) at a 0.25°×0.25° spatial resolution were obtained from the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ERA5 reanalysis datasets (available at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/dataset/ reanalysis-era5-single-levels-monthly-means?Tab=form ) for the period 1950–2021. Before all calculations, the CRU observational datasets were bilinearly interpolated to an equal 0.25° spatial resolution. Here, the monthly vapor pressure deficit (VPD) was calculated by leveraging monthly Ta  , Td  , and SP  obtained from the ERA5 reanalysis datasets (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ). The monthly average precipitation between CRU and GPCC was used to reduce the uncertainty from a single precipitation dataset. As most plant roots are found in the top 1m soil layer (Kumar et al., 2023 ), the monthly 0–100cm soil moisture was computed using soil moisture within three soil depths. Since droughts, hot events, and CADHEs are more likely to occur during the warm season (i.e., June-July-August) in China, this season was of primary interest.  3 Methods 3.1 Cascade Modeling (CaM) framework Detailed calculations for the drought indexes (including Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Standardized Soil moisture Index (SSI), Standardized Temperature Index (STI), Standardized Evapotranspiration Index (SEI), and Standardized VPD Index (SVPDI)) and compound events index (Blended Dry and Hot Index (BDHI)) can be found in Appendix A. Following the drought categories provided by Svoboda et al. (2002) , the specific classifications of the monitored droughts, hot events, and CADHEs using SSI, STI, and BDHI, respectively, are given in Table 1  . Here, the DEii  , CEii  , and HEii   (ii  = 0, 1, …, 4) indicate the specific categories of agricultural droughts, CADHEs, and hot events (see Table 1 ), respectively. The CaM framework (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ) was leveraged to detect the cascading effects of agricultural droughts on hot events (i.e., DTH cascade) and hot events on agricultural droughts (i.e., HTD cascade). For any given CaM framework, there are three components: exposure, outcome, and confounders (drivers). Here, we used the Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), a graphical representation of confounding effects, to illustrate the causal interactions in a dynamical system (Fig. 2  a). Taking the DTH cascade as an example, the exposure, outcome, and confounders were agricultural drought (Y 1 t  ), hot event (Y 2 t  ), and a set of antecedent hydroclimatic confounders (X  t–l  , including SEIt  – l  , SVPDIt  – l  , SPIt  – l  , SSIt  – l  , and STIt  – l  ; here, t  denotes the warm season, and l  represent a specific lag or lead time), respectively. Using the spatially averaged drought indexes in sub-climate region D4, we have provided an illustrative example for the cascade events (see the red arrows in Figure S1 ) and non-cascade events (see the blue and cyan arrows in Figure S1 ) between agricultural drought and hot event by considering the influences of the lagged confounders. The direct or indirect causal interactions between exposure and outcome, i.e., information propagation, can occur within a network of events; while the confounders control the causal interactions with both the outcome and the exposure variables (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ). Note that spurious relationships and endogeneity may be generated without consideration of confounding effects (Tuttle & Salvucci, 2017 ). As shown in Fig. 2 b, the event-to-event temporal network was applied to the CaM framework. With the DTH cascade as an example, this cascading event first was identified on the basis of the months of agricultural drought and hot event occurrences (i.e., SSI ≤ –0.5 and STI > 0.5) in the warm season for the period 1950–2021. Second, the months of the non-occurred/occurred agricultural drought (Y 1 t  ) and hot event (Y 2 t  ) were separately transformed into binary (0/1) time series. Third, considering the lagged effects of the previous confounders (X  t–l  ) on the information propagation between agricultural droughts and hot events, a logistic regression model (Equation (1) ) was used to fit the binary time series of Y 1 t   and Y 2 t   for a specific confounder Xi  , t–l  .(1) logit { Pr ( Y 2 t   = 1 | Y 1 t   = 0 , X i , t - l   )  }  = g ( Y 1 t   , X i , t - l   ; α  )      where g (∙) indicates an additive function of the variables Y 1 t   and Xi  , t–l  , that is, g (∙) = α 0  + α 1 Y 1 t   + α 2 Xi  , t–l  , here α   = [α 0 , α 1 , α 2 ] is the regression coefficient vector of the logit model. The exp(α 1 ) was defined as the Odd Ratio (OR), i.e., OR = exp(α 1 ). The OR > 1 and OR < 1 denote multiplicative increase and decrease (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ) in odds of an outcome for a given exposure and per unit increase in the lagged confounders (including SEIt  – l  , SVPDIt  – l  , SPIt  – l  , SSIt  – l  , and STIt  – l  ), respectively. For instance, for a DTH cascade, OR = 1.5 indicates that the odds of occurrence of an extreme hot event presumably increase by 1.5 times with per unit increment of the confounders given that an extreme agricultural drought has occurred. The Attributable Fraction (AF) was utilized to quantify the strength of causal interaction between agricultural droughts and hot events, it can be expressed as (Mukherjee et al., 2023; Sjölander, 2016a; Sjölander & Vansteelandt, 2011 ):(2) AF = 1 - Pr ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )  Pr ( Y 2 t   = 1 )   = 1 - Pr ( Y 2 t   = 1 | Y 1 t   = 0 , X i , t - l   = x i , t - l   )  Pr ( Y 2 t   = 1 )       where P r ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )    and Pr(Y 2 t   = 1) denote the counterfactual probability of outcome if the exposure Y 1 t   is eliminated (i.e., Y 1 t   is set to 0) and the factual probability of an outcome in the population, respectively; and xi  , t–l   indicates the observed level (standardized variables) of Xi  , t–l   (i  = 1, …, 5). As such, the AF represented the proportion of the binary outcome events (e.g., dry months) that could be prevented if the binary exposure events (e.g., hot months) were eliminated from the population for a predefined level of confounder Xi  , t–l   (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ). The magnitudes of AF can be classified into four different categories (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ): moderate (0 ≤ AF < 5%), severe (5% ≤ AF < 10%), extreme (10% ≤ AF < 15%), and exceptional (AF ≥ 15%). For instance, for any given DTH cascade, AF ≥ 15% implies that more than 15% of extreme hot events are caused by extreme agricultural droughts. To measure the risk ratios of outcome (Y 2 t  ) for the fixed level Y 1 t   = y 1 t   (here, y 1 t   = 0) at a given observed level of standardized variable Xi  , t–l  , a regression standardization method was employed in the fitted logistic regression model (Sjölander, 2016b ). If Xi  , t–l   is sufficient for cofounding control, then P r ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )    from the fitted logistic regression model can be defined as (Mukherjee et al., 2023; Sjölander, 2016b ):(3) Pr ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )  = E Pr ( Y 2 t   = 1 | Y 1 t   = y 1 t   , X i , t - l   )         (4) Pr ″  ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )  = ∑ i = 1  n  Pr ″  ( Y 2 t   = 1 | Y 1 t   = y 1 t   , X i , t - l   )    n      where P r  ″  Y 2 , t   = 1 |  Y 1 , t   = y 1 , t   , X i , t - l         is the estimation of Pr(Y 2 t   = 1|Y 1 t   = y 1 t  , Xi  , t–l  ). Accordingly, if we obtain P r ( Y 2 t  O  = 1 )   , the AF can be calculated via Equation (2) . Similarly, we can obtain the AF value for the HTD cascade by swapping the exposure and the outcome (that is, Y 1 t   and Y 2 t   correspond to the hot event and agricultural drought in that scenario, respectively).  3.2 CaM framework coupling Bayesian Model Averaging ensemble with Vine Copula (CaMBMAViC) model Two regular vine copulas, i.e., Canonical vine (C-vine) and Drawable vine (D-vine) copulas, have been widely used to decompose a multi-dimensional variate into a cascade of pair-copulas (Aas et al., 2009; Bedford & Cooke, 2002; Bevacqua et al., 2017; Kurowicka & Joe, 2011; Liu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2022a; Xiong et al., 2014 ). Regarding C-vine copula, its tree structure is comparatively simple, especially for high dimensional situations, and there is a key variable (i.e., root node) that manipulates interactions among different pair variables in contrast to D-vine copulas (Aas & Berg, 2009; Wang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022a; Xiong et al., 2014 ). The vine copulas used in this study therefore refer to the C-vine copula unless otherwise stated. Assume that we have n -dimensional random variables, r   = [r 1 , …, rn  ], the joint Probability Density Function (PDF), f (r 1 , …, rn  ), can be formulated via the C-vine copula as:(5) f ( r 1  , . . . , r n  )  = ∏ k = 1  n  f k  ( r k  )  × ∏ i = 1  n - 1   ∏ j = 1  n - i   c i , i + j | 1 : ( i - 1 )     F ( r i  | r 1  , . . . , r i - 1   )  , F ( r i + j   | r 1  , . . . , r i - 1   )          where fk  (rk  ) represents the marginal PDF of rk   (k  = 1, …, n ); and ci  , i+j  |1:( i  –1)  is the bivariate copulas density. F (·|·) denotes the conditional cumulative probability, which can be written as (Aas et al., 2009; Joe, 1996 ):(6) F ( r | u  )  = ∂ C r u j  |  u  - j     F ( r | u  - j   )  , F ( u j  | u  - j   )       ∂ F ( u j  | u  - j   )       where C. | .  indicates a cumulative probability of bivariate copula; u  = (u 1 , …, ud  ) is a d -dimensional conditioning variable vector; and u – j   denotes the vector u  after excluding one arbitrary component uj  . Additionally, Equation (6)  can be translated as an h -function (Aas et al., 2009; Kurowicka & Joe, 2011 ):(7) h ( r , u  ; ξ )  :  = F ( r | u  )  = ∂ C r , u    ( F ( r )  , F ( u  )  ; ξ )   ∂ F ( u  )       where ξ  indicates the parameter(s) of bivariate copulas for the variables of r  and u . For an n -dimensional C-vine copula with N cond  conditioning variables (1 < N cond  < n ), the number of decompositions is N cond !×(n  − N cond )!/2 for n  − N cond  > 1, and N cond ! for n  − N cond  = 1 (Bevacqua et al., 2017 ). There are n  − 1 trees and n ×(n  − 1)/2 edges for each decomposition (Aas et al., 2009; Bevacqua et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2021b ). Thus, the vine structures are more complicated if the number of the selected variables is large. For instance, for a five-dimensional C-vine copula with three conditioning variables (i.e., three explanatory variables) and two predictand variables, the number of decompositions is 3!×(5 − 3)!/2 = 6 (see Fig. 2 c-2h). In a CaM framework, the considered hydroclimatic confounders have previous meteorological drought (SPIt  – l  ; t  and l  correspondingly represent target month (e.g., t  = August) and lead times (e.g., l  = 1–3-months)), preceding atmospheric aridity (SVPDIt  – l  ), antecedent evaporative drought (SEIt  – l  ), prior agricultural drought (SSIt  – l  ), and antecedent hot condition (STIt  – l  ). Here, the three most important predictors that corresponded to three maximum OR values within a CaM framework were selected from these five hydroclimatic confounders. Note that the complicated vine structures may result in costly computation if a larger number of conditioning variables are used, especially for grid-wise predictions of droughts, hot events, and CADHEs using vine copulas. Taking the DTH cascade as an example, the three most important predictors (e.g., STIt  – l  , SEIt  – l  , and SVPDIt  – l  ) and two predictand variables (e.g., current agricultural drought (SSIt  ) and hot event (STIt  )) were assumed as random variables r 1 , r 2 , r 3 , r 4 , and r 5 , respectively. It should be mentioned that the vine structure decompositions (i.e., the combinations of ordered variables) are different among these five-dimensional variates, as shown in Fig. 2 c-2h. As an example by taking the ordering of variables “r 1 r 2 r 3 r 4 r 5 ” (i.e., first vine structure (V 1 ) in Fig. 2 c), a conditional C-vine copula distribution function of r 4  with the given conditions of r 1 , r 2 , and r 3 , based on Algorithm 1, can be determined by recursively applying the h -function as follows (Aas et al., 2009; Kurowicka & Joe, 2011; Wu et al., 2023b; Wu et al., 2022a ):(8) F ( r 4  | r 1  , r 2  , r 3  )  = ∂ C 43 | 12   F ( r 4  | r 1  , r 2  )  , F ( r 3  | r 1  , r 2  )       ∂ F ( r 3  | r 1  , r 2  )               = h h { h ( u 4  , u 1  ; ξ 14  )  , h ( u 2  , u 1  ; ξ 12  )  ; ξ 24 | 1   }     ,  h { h ( u 3  , u 1  ; ξ 13  )  , h ( u 2  , u 1  ; ξ 12  )  ; ξ 23 | 1   }  ; ξ 34 | 12              where uk  : = Fk  (rk  ) is the marginal Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of rk   (k  = 1, …, 4). Details of the multivariate conditional algorithm to simulate uniform variables r   = [r 1 , r 2 , …, rd  , rd  +1 , …, rn  ] from an n -dimensional C-vine copula and D-vine copula can be found in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm B1, respectively, in which the explanatory (predictand) variables are r 1 , r 2 , …, rd   (rd  +1 , …, rn  ). Note that different candidate vine structures (i.e., V 1 –V 6 ) may have diverse SSIt   and STIt   predictions due to the numerous decompositions of vine copulas (Wu et al., 2022a ). As BMA yields good skills in ensemble predictions, it has been widely used in the hydrology community (Duan et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Raftery et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2023b; Wu et al., 2022a ). Therefore, to obtain the ensemble SSIt   and STIt   predictions by merging these candidate vine structures with appropriate weights, the last step of the CaMBMAViC model was developed as follows:(21) p ( SSI   ¯    ¯   t  SSI t V 1   ,     … , SSI t V 6   , D )  = ∑ m = 1  6  p ( SSI t V m   D ) ·  p m  (  SSI   ¯    ¯   t  SSI t V m   , D )               (22) p ( STI   ¯    ¯   t  STI t V 1   ,     … , STI t V 6   , D )  = ∑ m = 1  6  p ( STI t V m   D ) ·  p m  (  STI   ¯    ¯   t  STI t V m   , D )               where S S I  ¯    ¯   t     represents the ensemble SSIt   prediction; p ( S S I  t  V m   | D )    signifies the likelihood of S S I  t  V m      prediction and satisfies ∑ m = 1  6  p S S I  t  V m   | D     = 1   , where the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm was used to estimate p ( S S I  t  V m   | D )    (Ajami et al., 2007; Raftery et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2022a; Fraley, C., Raftery, A. E., Sloughter, J. The meaning of symbols in Equation (22)  is the same as in Equation (21)  but for STIt   prediction. To further test the predictive capabilities of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs, the Averaged Vine Copula (AViC) model, i.e., the simple arithmetic mean among six candidate vine structures, was leveraged as a benchmark model under the same situations. The BDHIt   predictions in the warm seasons with different lead times were computed using the SSIt   and STIt   predictions that were obtained from the CaMBMAViC model, in which the SSIt   and STIt   predictions possessed the same dependency structure as their observations during the calibration period. Fig. 3   graphically displays the primary procedures for the CADHEs predictions based on the proposed CaMBMAViC model. More details about leveraging the proposed CaMBMAViC model to predict agricultural droughts (SSIt  ), hot events (STIt  ), and CADHEs (BDHIt  ) with 1–3-month lead times in the warm season for the period 1950–2021 in China were listed as follows: (1) The empirical CDFs of the 3-month (timescale) SPI, 3-month SVPDI, 3-month SEI, 3-month SSI, and 3-month SSI in the warm season for the period 1950–2021 were all calculated using the empirical Gringorten plotting position formula and the NQT method (see Fig. 3  and Equation A(1) ). Moreover, the whole paired SSI-STI series was divided into paired SSI-STI subseries with negative dependence and positive dependence via a threshold 0; and the BDHI observation series was calculated using these segmented SSI-STI subseries (see Fig. 3  and Equation A(2) ). (2) For the DTH and HTD cascades, the considered hydroclimatic confounders in the CaM framework comprised SEIt  – l  , SVPDIt  – l  , SPIt  – l  , SSIt  – l  , and STIt  – l   (i.e., X  t  – l   = [SEIt  – l  , SVPDIt  – l  , SPIt  – l  , SSIt  – l  , STIt  – l  ]). Taking the DTH cascade as an example, a logistic regression model (Equation (1) ) was implemented to fit these observed data, i.e., exposure (SSIt  , Y 1 ), outcome (STIt  , Y 2 ), and a specific hydroclimatic confounder Xi  , t  – l   (e.g., SPIt  – l  ) at a specific lead (lag) time (e.g., l  = 1-month), and we can correspondingly obtain the OR value for each confounder (see Fig. 3  and Equations (2)–(4) ). (3) Based on the maximum three OR values within the CaM framework (Fig. 3 ), we selected the three most important predictors from these considered hydroclimatic confounders at each grid point. Given that the three most important predictors, such as STIt  – l  , SEIt  – l  , and SVPDIt  – l  , and two predictand variables, SSIt   and STIt  , were as random variables r 1 , r 2 , r 3 , r 4 , and r 5 . The CDFs time series of r 1 , r 2 , r 3 , r 4 , and r 5  were (u 1 )t  – l  , (u 2 )t  – l  , (u 3 )t  – l  , (u 4 )t  , and (u 5 )t  , respectively. The observed datasets were divided into calibration period (1950–2007) and validation period (2008–2021), i.e., the proportion of samples for establishing and testing the CaMBMAViC model was about 80%:20%. (4) Given a 5-dimensional conditional C-vine copula, with the help of R package CDVineCopulaConditional  (Bevacqua, 2017 ), six different vine structures (i.e., V 1 –V 6 ; see Fig. 2 c-2h) were decomposed by using different ordered variables among r 1 , r 2 , r 3 , r 4 , and r 5 . An optimal bivariate copula function, based on the smallest AIC statistic, was selected from 39 copula families (see Table S1 ) for every pair of variables in each vine structure, and these copula parameters ξ  were correspondingly obtained. (5) Monte Carlo simulation was employed to generate 500 uniformly random numbers τ  over the interval [0, 1], and a sample of 500 (u 4 )t   and (u 5 )t   realizations for a specific vine structure (e.g., Equations (9) and (15) ) was determined. The 500 (u 4 )t   and (u 5 )t   realizations, based on the NQT method, were correspondingly transformed to SSIt   and STIt   realizations (see the thin grey lines in Fig. 3 ). The mean values of these SSIt   and STIt   realizations were targeted as the predictions of agricultural droughts and hot events, respectively. For each different vine structure of C-vine copulas for 5-dimensional scenarios at each lead time, we had six different SSIt   and STIt   predictions (see the thick colored lines in Fig. 3 ). (6) According to the assigned appropriate weights with the EM algorithm for six different vine structures (i.e., Equations (21) and (22) ), the ensemble predictions of agricultural droughts (i.e., SSIt  ) and hot events (i.e., STIt  ) were ultimately realized (see the thick black lines in Fig. 3 ). Accordingly, the negative and positive dependencies between SSIt   and STIt   ensemble prediction subseries were leveraged to calculate the predicted BDHIt   (see the cyan line in Fig. 3 ), in which the SSIt   and STIt   predictions possessed the same dependency structure as their observations during the calibration period. Similarly, for the HTD cascade, based on the above-listed steps, the STIt  , SSIt  , and BDHIt   predictions in the warm season over China for 1–3-month lead times were realized.  3.3 Performance measurement The Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE; Kling et al. (2012) ) and Percent Bias (PBIAS; Sorooshian et al. (1993)  and Wu et al. (2019) ) were utilized to measure the prediction performance of the CaMBMAViC model. Taking the evaluation of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting agricultural drought (i.e., SSI) as an example, these two performance metrics can be expressed as follows:(23) KGE = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( SSI p   ¯   SSI o   ¯    - 1 )  2  + ( σ SSI p   · SSI o   ¯    σ SSI o   · SSI p   ¯     - 1 )  2         KGE ∈ - ∞ , 1         (24) PBIAS = ∑ i = 1  N  ( SSI p , i   - SSI o , i   )   ∑ i = 1  N  SSI o , i      * 100 %     PBIAS ∈ - ∞ , ∞         where S S I  o   ¯      and S S I  p   ¯      denote the mean value of SSI observations and predictions over the entire calibration (or validation) period, respectively; σ S S I  p      and σ S S I  o      are the standard deviations of SSIp   and SSIo  ; r  indicates the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient between SSIp   and SSIo  ; SSIp  , i   and SSIo  , i   denote the i th predicted and observed values of SSI, respectively; and N  is the length of calibration (or validation) period. Similarly, based on KGE and PBIAS, we can correspondingly evaluate the prediction performance of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting hot events (i.e., STI) and CADHEs (i.e., BDHI). Here, a larger value of KGE (tending to 1) and an optimal value of PBIAS (close to 0) signify the perfect prediction performance of the CaMBMAViC model.   4 Results 4.1 Couplings between agricultural droughts and hot events We first used Kendall’s correlation coefficient (τk  ) corrected by the False Discovery Rate (FDR; Wilks (2016) ) to measure the coupling strengths between agricultural drought (SSI) and hot event (STI) in the warm season in China. As shown in Fig. 4  a, for the τk   from the global dependence of the paired SSI-STI series (i.e., τk  ± (SSI± , STI± )), we found a significant negative dependence (p  < 0.05) between agricultural droughts and hot events in most areas of China, except for arid Northwestern China (i.e., sub-climate region D3). A weak positive relationship was presented between agricultural droughts and hot events in this region primarily because the replenished soil moisture was sourced from the precipitation that lensed on the high-temperature season. However, for the segmented SSI-STI subseries via a threshold 0, the opposite signals of τk   were observed between the paired SSI-STI subseries with negative dependence (i.e., τk  – (SSI– , STI– )) and the paired SSI-STI subseries with positive dependence (i.e., τk  + (SSI+ , STI+ )) (Fig. 4 b vs . 4c). These phenomena indicated that agricultural droughts and hot events may not necessarily co-occur, e.g., the coincidence of wet and hot events as well as the consecutive dry and cool events (see the blue triangles in Figure A1 ). In comparison with the correlations of the unsegmented SSI-STI series, the negative and positive correlations for the segmented SSI-STI subseries were both larger, e.g., the correlations for τk  ± (SSI± , STI± ) was –0.21 on average (Fig. 4 a), while that for the τk  – (SSI– , STI– ) and τk  + (SSI+ , STI+ ) was –0.56 and 0.49 on average, respectively (Fig. 4 b and 4c). In the warm season, the mean probability of each percentile bin of SSI and STI across all grid points in China is exhibited in Fig. 4 d–4f. The bimodal distribution of the unsegmented SSI-STI toward both extremes, i.e., low SSI–high STI and high SSI–low STI, supported the importance of strong SSI-STI coupling for cooccurring agricultural drought and hot extremes (Fig. 4 d). Again, we found that the SSI-STI coupling was further strengthened after segmenting the SSI and STI series into diverse dry and hot combination conditions (Fig. 4 e and 4f). The high probability in the top-left bin in Fig. 4 d and 4e (the top-right bin in Fig. 4 f) demonstrated that the frequency of low SSI and high STI (high SSI and high STI) was much higher than that expected if SSI and STI were uncoupled. The Probability Multiplication Factor (PMF; Zhou et al. (2019) ) was used to measure the ratios of the coupled probability of SSI ≤ –0.5 (SSI > 0.5) and STI > 0.5 to their uncoupled probability (i.e., Pr = 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09); here, –0.5 (0.5) corresponds to 30th (70th) percentile roughly. Accordingly, the PMFs for the unsegmented SSI-STI series, paired SSI-STI subseries with negative dependence, and paired SSI-STI subseries with positive dependence were calculated as PMF±  = [0.3 – C ± (0.3, 0.7)]/0.09, PMF–  = [0.3 – C – (0.3, 0.7)]/0.09, and PMF+  = [C + (0.7, 0.7) – 0.4]/0.09, respectively; and C ± , C – , and C +  indicate the joint CDF of copulas for the unsegmented SSI-STI series, paired SSI-STI series with negative dependence, and paired SSI-STI series with positive dependence (Wu et al., 2023c ), respectively. As shown in Fig. 4 g–4i, we correspondingly estimated the relationships between τk  ± (SSI± , STI± ) and log(PMF± ), τk  – (SSI– , STI– ) and log(PMF– ), as well as τk  + (SSI+ , STI+ ) and log(PMF+ ) in the warm season across all grid points in China. For the more negative (positive) SSI-STI correlations, the CADHE extremes occurred more frequently, i.e., log(PMF) > 0 (Fig. 4 g–4i). Note that log(PMF) > 0 (i.e., PMF>1) denotes that the intercorrelated two events were closely coupled (Zhou et al., 2019 ). Besides, a good linear relationship between log(PMF) and τk  (SSI, STI) was exhibited for these three situations, e.g., log(PMF± ) = –3.55 × τk  ± (SSI± , STI± ) + 0.02 (p  < 0.001) for the unsegmented SSI-STI series, log(PMF– ) = –1.69 × τk  – (SSI– , STI– ) + 0.49 (p  < 0.001) for the paired SSI-STI subseries with negative dependency, and log(PMF+ ) = 1.21 × τk  + (SSI+ , STI+ ) + 0.85 (p  < 0.001) for the paired SSI-STI subseries with positive dependency (Fig. 4 g–4i). In comparison with the log(PMF+ ) > 0 and log(PMF– ) > 0, the more positive SSI-STI correlations (i.e., τk  ±  > 0) accompanied by the smaller log(PMF± ) (i.e., log(PMF± ) < 0) for the unsegmented SSI-STI series indicated that agricultural droughts and hot events may not tightly cooccur in certain situations (Fig. 4 g). Generally, by segmenting the paired SSI-STI series, the interaction between agricultural droughts and hot events will be further enhanced. This is a critical prerequisite for calculating the BDHI predictions at different lead times with SSI predictions and STI predictions.  4.2 Cascading effects of agricultural drought and hot event Since five confounders (i.e., SEIt  – l  , SVPDIt  – l  , SPIt  – l  , SSIt  – l  , and STIt  – l  ) were individually employed to fit a logistic regression model in the CaM framework, we have five AF values in each lag (lead) time for the DTH (or HTD) cascade event. Here, under the 1–3-month lag times, the maximum AF values were used to measure the magnitude of the DTH cascade and HTD cascade. These two cascade events were both tailored using SSI ≤ –0.5 and STI > 0.5 in the warm season for the period 1950–2021 in China. The spatial patterns of the maximum AF values for the DTH and HTD cascade events with 1–3-month lag times in the warm season are presented in Fig. 5  a–5f. Regarding the cascading effects of DTH or HTD, we found that the maximum AF values at different lag times were larger than 30% in most areas of China (see blue dashed vertical line for the insets in Fig. 5 a–5f), especially in sub-climate regions D1–D2 and D4–D6. By comparison, in sub-climate region D3, the cascading effects of HTD were stronger under 1–3-month lag times than that of DTH (e.g., Fig. 5 b vs . 5e). This demonstrated that the HTD cascade events occurred more prone than did the DTH cascade events in arid climate regions where the water-limited effects were larger than the energy-limited effects. The mean AF values in different sub-climate regions D1–D7 and the whole of China (CHN) (see the blue circle in Fig. 5 g and 5h) also indicated that the cascading effects of both DTH and HTD were all salient under 1–3-month lag times. Moreover, the cascading effects of DTH or HTD will both be further strengthened with the extension of lag times. These findings demonstrated that the occurrences of agricultural droughts could be reduced by approximately 30% in most regions of China if the hot events were eliminated from the population for a predefined level of a specific confounder, and vice versa.  Note that the cascading effect of the DTH event or HTD event in sub-climate region D3 was the smallest (but still occupied an extreme category, i.e., AF > 10%, based on its covered grid-point average values) in comparison with other sub-climate regions in China (Fig. 5 g and 5h). Since land evaporation or evaporative cooling is susceptible to limited soil moisture (Miralles et al., 2014; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2021b; Yin et al., 2014 ), especially during extreme drought and hot conditions, the progressively reduced soil water may result in elevated near-surface air temperature via land-atmospheric feedback that often morphs into the concurrent or consecutive drought and hot events. As demonstrated in Fig. 6  , for the DTH and HTD cascade events, the magnitudes of the OR value for different confounders exceeded 2 (at a 0.05 significance level) for 1–3-month lag times in the warm season in most areas of China; apart from arid Northwestern China (i.e., D3), these confounders showed a negligible influence (OR < 1). In each grid point, we found that one or more confounders displayed a dominant influence on DTH cascade events and HTD cascade events. For instance, at 1–3-month lag times, SPIt  –lag  and SSIt  –lag  showed a higher and pronounced positive influence (OR > 3) on the interaction between agricultural droughts and hot events in sub-climate region D1 (e.g., Fig. 6 c1–6d1, 6h1–6i1, and 6m1–6n1). Overall, these confounders had more positive compounding influences on the cascading effects of agricultural droughts and hot events in eastern China than in western China. To construct the CaMBMAViC model for a five-dimensional scenario, based on the three highest OR values within the CaM framework, we further selected the three most important predictors in the warm season with 1–3-month lag times for the DTH and HTD cascade events (Fig. 7  ). As expected, the agricultural drought persistence and previous meteorological drought (i.e., SSIt  – l   and SPIt  – l  ), with different lag times, were the 1st most important predictor for the predicted cascading events between agricultural droughts and hot events in most regions of China (Fig. 7 a, 7d, 7g, 7j, 7m, and 7p). This was attributed to the water-limited confounders (e.g., precipitation and soil moisture) being hugely beneficial for manipulating the occurrences of droughts and hot events. However, for 1–3-month lag times, the 2nd and 3rd most important predictors presented a relatively more spatially heterogeneous pattern than the 1st most important predictors. For example, with respect to the HTD cascade event for 3-month lag time, the 2nd (3rd) most important predictors in sub-climate regions D1 and D5 were primarily SPIt  – l   and SVPDIt  – l   (STIt  – l   and SVPDIt  – l  ), respectively (Fig. 7 q and 7r). Based on the above analysis, the agricultural droughts and hot events were tightly coupled, especially after segmenting the paired SSI-STI series, and these confounders (predictors) had considerable impacts on the cascading effects of agricultural droughts and hot events. Thus, these predictors were expected to provide more reliable information for predicting agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs in the warm season with diverse lead times.  4.3 Predictions of agricultural drought, hot event, and CADHEs using CaMBMAViC model Regarding a noteworthy example in the warm season of 2013, severe droughts and hot events swept southern China and the Tibetan Plateau (LeComte, 2014; Yuan et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2015 ), which resulted in disastrous impacts on water security, crop yield, and eco-environmental sustainability. Thus, we selected this typical extreme event to test the skills of the proposed CaMBMAViC model for predicting agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs with 1–3-month lead times in the warm season over China. For the agricultural drought predictions in the warm season of 2013 with 1–3-month lead times, neither for the DTH cascade nor for HTD cascade, the spatial patterns of the predicted SSI via the CaMBMAViC model were generally identical to that of the observed SSI (Fig. 8  a–8g); and the observed and predicted severe agricultural droughts were all mainly distributed in sub-climate regions D1, D4, and D6. As expected, the skill of the CaMBMAViC model in predicting agricultural droughts tended to slightly deteriorate for 3-month lead time in comparison with their observations, such as in southwestern China (e.g., Fig. 8 d vs . 8a). This implied that these predictors containing prediction information, with the prolonged lead times, would be undermined. Similarly, based on the CaMBMAViC model, we simultaneously predicted the spatial distributions of hot events at the same time (Fig. 8 i–8n). Intuitively, the 1–3-month lead STI predictions in the warm season of 2013 were in line with the corresponding STI observations in China; and the occurrence areas of the hot extremes (i.e., STI > 2; see red areas in Fig. 8 h–8n), e.g., sub-climate regions D4 and D7, were well predicted by the CaMBMAViC model. The BDHI indicated that the extreme CADHEs in the warm season of 2013 mainly appeared in southern China and the Tibetan Plateau (i.e., D4 and D7; Fig. 8 o). Moreover, under the conditions with the cooccurring extremes of agricultural droughts and hot events (e.g., SSI ≤ –2 and STI > 2; Fig. 8 a and 8h), we observed that the severity of CADHEs depicted with BDHI was more severe (BDHI ≤ –2; Fig. 8 o), such as in the western sub-climate region D4. Note that the bivariate predicted variables, (SSIp  , STIp  ), were used to derive the predicted BDHI. Herein, at each grid point, (SSIp  , STIp  ) possessed the same dependency structure as their observation variables (SSIo  , STIo  ). As shown in Fig. 8 p–8u, the spatial patterns of the 1–3-month lead BDHI predictions generally matched their observations in the warm season of 2013 in China. The 1–3-month lead predictions of agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs in the warm season of 2006 and 2019 in China can be found in Figures S2 and S3 . In the warm season of 2006, the observed and predicted agricultural droughts and CADHEs were mainly distributed in sub-climate regions D1, D4, D5, and D7, whereas the observed and predicted hot events almost hit the whole part of China (Figure S2 ). In the warm season of 2019, the observations and predictions of agricultural droughts and CADHEs were mainly distributed in sub-climate regions D1 and D5 as well as western parts of sub-climate regions D4 and D6, while the observed and predicted hot events almost swept throughout the whole part of China (Figure S3 ). Besides, at different sub-climate regions D1–D7, the spatially averaged BDHI predictions at the 1–3-month lead times via the CaMBMAViC model well matched their observations (Figure S4 ). Overall, these findings underscored that our proposed CaMBMAViC model yielded reliable predictions for agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs in the warm season with 1–3-month lead times in China. To verify the prediction ability of the CaMBMAViC model in diverse sub-climate regions, we further computed the area percentages of agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs in diverse categories (see Table 1 ), respectively. With the DTH cascade events as an example, under different lead times across sub-climate regions D1–D7 and CHN, a high R 2  value (R 2  = 0.86–0.99; p  < 0.01) was displayed between the predicted agricultural drought area percentages (DE0 or more severe, i.e., DE0–DE4) and the monitored agricultural drought area percentages (Fig. 9  a, 9d, and 9g); a high R 2  value (R 2  = 0.83–0.98; p  < 0.01) was found between the predicted hot event area percentages (i.e., HE0–HE4) and the monitored hot event area percentages (Fig. 9 b, 9e, and 9h); and a high R 2  value (R 2  = 0.88–0.98; p  < 0.01) was found between the predicted CADHEs area percentages (i.e., CE0–CE4) and the monitored CADHEs area percentages (Fig. 9 c, 9f, and 9i). With the magnitude of the severity intensified, R 2  between the predicted and monitored area percentages tended to degrade, e.g., for 3-month lead CADHEs prediction across CHN, R 2  = 0.97 for CE0–CE4 vs . R 2  = 0.89 for CE4 (Fig. 9 i). Compared to the area percentages of hot events and CADHEs, the area percentages for the predicted and monitored agricultural drought at each sub-climate region were all closely aligned with the 1:1 line (Fig. 9  and Figure S4 ). Accordingly, in comparison with agricultural droughts, the R 2  between predicted and monitored area percentages of hot event (CADHEs) was mostly sensitive to hot event (CADHEs) severity, e.g., R 2  ranging from 0.55 (0.59) to 0.98 (0.98) for hot events (CADHEs) (Fig. 9 ). As a result of the propagation rate of air temperature being faster than that of soil moisture, the hot extremes generally covered broader areas than agricultural drought extremes. The hot events and CADHEs were comparatively less predictable in contrast to agricultural droughts, as the CADHEs predictions were calculated based on the predictions of SSI and STI. From Figure S5 , we can obtain similar findings for the HTD cascade events with the DTH cascade events.  4.4 Prediction performance assessment of CaMBMAViC model During the validation period (i.e., 2008–2021) in the warm season for 1–3-month lead agricultural drought (SSI), hot event (STI), and CADHEs (BDHI) predictions, the KGEskill score  values (Knoben et al., 2019 ) were large than 0.684 and the PBIASCaMBMAViC/AViC  values (i.e., the ratio of PBIAS between CaMBMAViC model and AViC model) fell into the interval [–1, 1] over the majority areas of China (Figure S6 ), indicating that the predictive capabilities of our proposed model for predicting the DTH and HTD cascade events were consistently superior to the AViC model. Figs. 10 and 11    illustrate the prediction performance of the CaMBMAViC model assessed by using KGE and PBIAS for DTH and HTD cascade events during the validation period 2008–2021, respectively. For the DTH cascade events at a longer lead time (e.g., 3-month lead time), for example, these mean KGE (PBIAS) evaluations of SSI, STI, and BDHI predictions were 0.90 (1.84%), 0.89 (2.25%), and 0.84 (–0.95%) in China (see blue dashed vertical lines in Fig. 10 c, 10g, 10k, 10o, 10s, and 10w), respectively. In diverse sub-climate regions, the 25th percentile values of KGE for SSI, STI, and BDHI predictions all exceeded 0.82, 0.72, and 0.69 for different lead times (Fig. 10 d, 10h, and 10l), respectively. Interestingly, we found that the prediction performances of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting SSI were stronger than those for predicting STI and BDHI (Figs. 10 and 11 ). For example, in sub-climate region D3 with the 2-month lead time, the median (i.e., 50th percentile) KGE (PBIAS) values for the SSI, STI, and BDHI predictions were 0.95 (1.3%), 0.89 (2.1%), and 0.86 (0.2%) (Fig. 10 d, 10h, 10l, 10p, 10t, and 10x), respectively. This can be attributed to the persistence or memory effects of droughts (may last three months and even more) being longer than hot events (Bevacqua et al., 2022; Zscheischler & Seneviratne, 2017 ), i.e., the dry memory in soil moisture was stronger than heat memory in air temperature. As the predicted SSI and STI were used to calculate the predicted BDHI, i.e., BDHI was a transition prediction variable, the predicted uncertainty of SSI and STI may be propagated into the BDHI predictions. Furthermore, from the changes in median KGE values, we found that the performance of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting SSI (STI and BDHI) was slightly worsening (strengthening) with the increased lead times in most sub-climate regions of China (Fig. 10 d, 10h, 10l and 11d, 11h, 11l). Simultaneously, based on the box bounds of PBIAS for each lead time, the prediction uncertainty of the CaMBMAViC model for BDHI predictions was pronounced much larger than that for the SSI and STI predictions (Fig. 10 p, 10t, 10x and 11p, 11t, 11x). This implied that the severity of CADHEs, in comparison with the predictions of agricultural droughts and hot events, was a bit underpredicted by the CaMBMAViC model. Note that the uncertainties for the predictions of SSI, STI, and BDHI were still small (Fig. 10 p, 10t, 10x and 11p, 11t, 11x), e.g., the 25th/75th percentile values of PBAIS for BDHI predictions ranged from –12% to 7%. During the calibration period (i.e., 1950–2007) in the warm season with 1–3-month lead times, the performance assessment of the CaMBMAViC model for predicting DTH and HTD cascade events in China can be found in Figure S7 . These results indicated that our developed CaMBMAViC model yielded skillful predictions for SSI, STI, and BDHI for different lead times over most regions of China (Figs. 10 and 11 , and Figure S6 ). These findings increase our confidence in reducing the detrimental impacts of compound extremes on water-food-energy-ecology security via issuing compound hazard early warnings timely.   5 Discussion and conclusions Here, we proposed a reliable ensemble prediction model with multi-predictand variables, that is, the CaMBMAViC model, to simultaneously predict the agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs in the warm season in China for 1–3-month lead times. Based on the AF metrics within a CaM framework, we found that the cascading effects between agricultural droughts and hot events (i.e., DTH cascading event and HTD cascading event) were tightly coupled (Fig. 5 ). Besides, we leveraged the maximum three OR values to select the three most important confounders (predictors) for the DTH cascading event and HTD cascading event (Figs. 6 and 7 ), respectively. By leveraging our developed CaMBMAViC model in a five-dimensional scenario (Fig. 3 ), agricultural drought (SSI), hot event (STI), and CADHEs (BDHI) were simultaneously predicted in the warm season under diverse lead times over China. Two performance metrics, i.e., KGE and PBIAS, both indicated that the CaMBMAViC model yielded reliable 1–3-month lead agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs predictions in warm seasons over most areas of China (Figs. 10 and 11 ). Compound events were depicted using two or more variables with internal causal connections and they virtually are a second-hand variate. As such, directly predicting the compound event itself (e.g., to predict compound dry and hot events that were characterized using SCEI (Hao et al., 2019a )) may be problematic. On the basis of the linkages among exposure-confounder-outcome (Mukherjee et al., 2023 ), we first identified the most important confounders affecting the interactions between agricultural droughts and hot events via the CaM framework. Then, a prediction technique with multi-predictand variables (i.e., CaMBMAViC model) was used to simultaneously predict agricultural droughts and hot events to reserve their links as much as possible. Finally, based on the coupling relationship between observed agricultural droughts and hot events during the calibration period, we correspondingly calculated the CADHEs predictions in the warm season with diverse lead times. Heuristically, based on the developed processes of this model, other compound events can be correspondingly predicted, such as sequential flood–heatwave events (Chen et al., 2021 ), compound pluvial–hot events (Wu et al., 2023a; Wu et al., 2023c ), and compound lethal heat stress–drought hazards (Yin et al., 2022 ). Under the same conditions, when adopting the vine copulas to predict multivariate events, the tree structures of D-vine copulas are more complex than C-vine copulas, which will correspondingly increase the demands for computational resources (Bevacqua et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2022a ). This is one of the reasons why we selected the C-vine copulas to develop the CaMBMAViC model for predicting agricultural droughts, hot events, and CADHEs. Notwithstanding we have provided detailed procedures regarding the CaMBMAViC model for predicting multivariate compounding events (e.g., CADHEs), more research is necessary to further extend this model considering the potential influence of vine structure differences on prediction performance. It is noteworthy that the procedures of the proposed CaMBMAViC model were also suitable for the D-vine copulas (even though we only provided the sampling procedures of D-vine copulas for simulating the multivariate conditional distributions; see Appendix B). Because soil moisture plays a paramount medium in the soil–vegetation–atmosphere continuum, its variability controls the hydrological processes of land surface, water and heat exchanges, and biogeochemical cycles (Hsu & Dirmeyer, 2023; Humphrey et al., 2021; Miralles et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2023 ). The inter-implication between agricultural droughts and hot events propagates across the physical and human systems that will affect agriculture and human health (Huang et al., 2016; Mukherjee et al., 2023 ). Any associated effects of vegetation and atmosphere on soil moisture dynamics, such as vegetation-atmosphere coupling (Zscheischler et al., 2015 ) and ocean-atmospheric feedback (Barriopedro et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2023 ), probably influence the changes in soil moisture and temperature that may later affect the prediction accuracy of CADHEs. For instance, vegetation can alleviate drought stress and heat stress by absorbing the shallow or deep soil water in the initial period of droughts and hot events, which reduces the warming rate of air temperature caused by the increased surface albedo (Barriopedro et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2015 ). Ocean-atmospheric feedback may have longer lag effects on droughts and hot events via teleconnection modes (Barriopedro et al., 2023; Han & Singh, 2023; Zscheischler et al., 2020 ). Consequently, considering the vegetation conditions and teleconnection modes as potential predictors for predicting the CADHEs may further improve the predictive capability of the CaMBMAViC model, particularly in the extra-long lead times. Compared with traditional slow droughts, flash droughts (related to soil moisture at the pentad or weekly timescales), a rapid intensification drought type, have occurred frequently around the globe in a warming climate (Otkin et al., 2016; Pendergrass et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2023 ). Such flash droughts have severe impacts on crop yields, ecosystem health, carbon budget, and human health (Tyagi et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023; Zscheischler et al., 2020 ). In particular, Yuan et al. (2023)  underscored that flash droughts will be transited to a new normal under anthropogenic climate change. Additionally, the full assessments of predictive capability for a prediction model with multi-predictand variables across different timescales (e.g., from sub-seasonal scale to seasonal scale) are paramount for stakeholders and policymakers who timely issue the relevant adaptations for diverse lead times (e.g., from several weeks to months even to seasons). However, the limited predictability of CADHEs at shorter timescales has presented a new challenge for subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction (Pendergrass et al., 2020; Tyagi et al., 2022 ). Besides, the characteristics of CADHEs may have been changed due to the intensified impact of anthropogenic activities and climate change on the hydrological cycle (Milly et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021c ). As the stationary assumption may be restricted under the influence of warming climate change, especially for variables related to temperature, the CADHEs predictions under the nonstationary assumptions need to be considered, which will be explored in our next work.
1 Introduction Integrating unconventional water (UW) into the unified water allocation is essential for addressing climate change, mitigating environmental crisis and reducing the water-supply gap (Qadir et al., 2022 ). To deal with global water shortage and pollution (UN, 2023; WHO and UNICEF, 2021 ), alternatives such as reclaimed water and desalinated seawater have emerged as crucial solutions (Karimidastenaei et al., 2022; Musa, 2021 ). However, increased consumption of UW does not necessarily yield good outcomes (Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024 ). In fact, excessive UW consumption may pose threats to the environment, economy, and production (Cui et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019 ). In most developing countries, UW is insufficiently treated or accepted (Liao et al., 2021; Lyu et al., 2016 ), making it challenging for these nations to reach the level of UW development in Singapore (IWA, 2019 ) or the United States (IWA, 2022 ) in the short run. In view of this, UW utilization must adapt to the characteristics of each region, further deepening the need for the adaptability of conventional water (CW) allocation in the unified management of water resources (Wu and Xiang, 2022 ). In response to the requirements for sustainable development, this adaptability is crucial for guaranteeing water security and regional stability. One approach to achieving unified allocation of CW and UW is through reasonable water allocation (Li et al., 2022a ). It involves distributing the limited water resources in different forms to users within a certain basin or region in a fair and effective manner (Wei et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2018 ). On the other hand, fairness, efficiency, and sustainability principles of water allocation (Hu et al., 2016a; Li et al., 2022b; Wu and Xiang, 2022 ) implies the water allocation amount should tally with the local social development level, resource endowment, and water usage conditions to ensure efficient and spatially-balanced allocation. Therefore, this study proposes “adaptive allocation,” a multi-dimensional approach that aligns allocated water amount with the characteristics of water use of each industry or administrative region. These characteristics involve socioeconomic development level, water resource endowment, and water usage conditions (Li et al., 2022b; Wu and Xiang, 2022 ). Water resources encompass both CW and UW, so adaptive allocation includes both, with the amount of water serving as the basis for allocation. Unlike CW, the “low-quality” UW is often considered merely as an alternative to address water shortage in the context of social development (Karimidastenaei et al., 2022; Liao et al., 2021 ). However, UW also generates economic benefits comparable to CW, which leads to competition between the two water resources (Li et al., 2022a ). That means the adaptive allocation of water involves both cooperation and competition relationships (Li et al., 2022a; Wei et al., 2020 ). In addition, water allocation contains complex factors related to the economy, society, and ecology (Batisha, 2020; Yazdandoost et al., 2021 ). This raises two critical questions: How can the relationship between CW and UW be coordinated within a unified allocation system? How is the allocated water resource in line with local resource endowment, socioeconomic development level, and water usage conditions? The relationship between CW and UW within water allocation encompasses three aspects: cooperation, competition-and-cooperation, and independence. First, “cooperation” serves as the foundation of CW-UW coordination, but treats UW merely as a complementary water resource (Chai et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Second, “competition-and-cooperation” deems CW and UW as two separate systems which, while collaborating to meet each other’s needs, also compete for market share (Li et al., 2022a ). Third, “independence” refers to allocating UW separately from other water sources (Bo et al., 2022; Ghorbani Mooselu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2015; Yue et al., 2023 ). However, the fundamental goal of developing and utilizing UW necessitates a cooperative relationship with CW. At the same time, the pursuit of economic benefits from UW (Li et al., 2022a ) and its potential negative impacts (Cui et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019 ) establishes a competitive dynamic between CW and UW. In conclusion, competition-and-cooperation proves to be a comprehensive and suitable perspective for addressing the CW-UW relationship. Li et al. (2022a)  set two objective functions, maximum CW use benefit and maximum UW use benefit, to reflect the competition between CW and UW. Liu et al. (2024)  chose two different objective functions: minimization of the total amount of water retained in waterworks and maximization of the amount of UW supplied. However, neither considered the truth that CW always takes precedence over UW (Liao et al., 2021 ). Extensive use of CW and UW may yield negative impacts (Liu et al., 2024 ), so a balance should be stricken between the output and treatment volume at the most suitable supply amount (Kim et al., 2015 ). Currently, the Gini coefficient and water amount constraints are commonly used to match the allocation amount of multiple water resources with administrative regions or water users. The methods consider the matching from single indexes such as supply condition, population (Dai et al., 2018 ), economic output (Shen et al., 2021 ), and users’ satisfaction (Feng, 2021 ), but neglects the compound effect of multiple indexes (Chen et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2021; Lyu et al., 2016; Nkhoma et al., 2021 ), including the technological level of UW treatment and use (Lyu et al., 2016 ), and the characteristics and water-dependence of water users (Niu et al., 2023 ). Moreover, few studies have built models that match multiple heterogeneous factors affecting CW and UW utilization with water allocation and even fewer have explored how the advanced UW treatment technologies affect the water allocation decisions. Multiple-water-source allocation involves multiple objectives, water sources, and principles, making it a problem well-suited for multi-objective optimization (MOO) (Shen et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023; Han et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2019; Musa, 2021 ). While studies on multiple-water-source allocation consider the “competition-and-cooperation” between CW and UW, they mainly focus on maximizing UW allocation (Chai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2024 ). In fact, countries that do not face severe water shortages are often reluctant to invest in UW like reclaimed water (Liao et al., 2021 ). From the perspective of sustainable development, the practical way is to determine the most suitable UW supply amount while ensuring maximum CW utilization. Moreover, models that allocate water resources should follow two basic principles: fairness and efficiency (Zeng et al., 2017 ). The current MOO models use the Gini coefficient and match water allocation with single factors to achieve fairness (Dai et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2021; Feng, 2021 ). Efficiency is ensured by maximizing economic benefits (Li et al., 2022a; Shen et al., 2021 ). Additionally, Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) is employed to quantify the efficiency of sewage treatment facilities (Ayyildiz et al., 2021; Bellver-Domingo et al., 2023; Sala-Garrido et al., 2012 ) and rainwater recycling (Liao and Liu, 2017 ). However, the efficiency of UW allocation across three aspects of living, production, and environment is yet to be fully defined or measured. Incorporating UW into unified water allocation is one of China’s recent efforts in national water management. In 2023, the Chinese Government requested that UW allocation must “fully consider the practical conditions, including the socioeconomic development level, water resource endowment, and water usage conditions of each area.” Notably, China’s expansion of UW utilization is primarily driven by government intervention rather than market forces or natural resource demand (Lyu et al., 2016 ), leading to slow growth and low utilization level (Zhang et al., 2022b ). China’s commitment to establishing a system to integrate UW into unified water allocation is hindered by insufficient policy-making and public awareness of UW utilization. Current studies primarily explore the allocation of the total amount of water resources while overlooking the competition between CW and UW. For example, Zhang et al. (2022a)  only examined the application of brackish water in Guantao County, China. Additionally, most studies explore the allocation between water administrations and industries (Guo et al., 2023a; Han et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022a ), but there is a lack of studies on the UW allocation at the province level. This gap includes how to match UW allocation with the water usage characteristics of administrative regions. To address it, this study incorporates the concept of adaptive allocation of CW and UW into China’s unified water allocation system, addresses the competition and cooperation dynamics between CW and UW, and ensures a more equitable and efficient distribution of water resources. Synthesis of the above research, the adaptive allocation can be defined as follows: based on the principles of fairness and efficiency and constrained by the total regional water consumption, the amounts of CW and UW allocated to each sub-region will align with its socio-economic and environmental characteristics to ensure the overall optimal benefits for the region. The definition requires that the total amount of water resources should align with the characteristics of each sub-region. Specifically, the CW allocation amount matches the population distribution, resource endowment, economic advantages, and water-saving responsibilities of each sub-region, while the UW allocation amount matches the sub-region’s consumption level, supply capacity, and water scarcity. The details are shown in Fig. 1  . This study aims to offer a new perspective to address major concerns in China’s CW and UW allocation: how to reflect the “competition-and-cooperation” relationship between CW and UW? How to measure the adaptability via the multi-dimensional characteristics of factors influencing water use? And how to measure allocation efficiency? To achieve this, this study draws from previous research and develops an integrated adaptive allocation model based on multi-objective decision making (MODM) and Zero-Sum Gains DEA (ZSG-DEA). It is a common practice that the initial stage of water rights allocation, led by the government, prioritizes fairness, while trying to include efficiency (He et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2016b ). Our adaptive model involves two modules, the first module ensuring fairness and the second focusing on efficiency. Compared with previous research (Table 1  ), this study makes the following contributions:1. This study constructs four objectives to reflect the overall benefits of the region: Economic benefit, social benefit, environmental benefit, and maximum CW supply amount. Specifically, environmental benefit is represented by the minimum difference between UW substitutional rate and the government-mandated rate, meaning that UW utilization should be moderate within certain technological and acceptance levels. The maximum CW supply amount is represented as the maximum proportion of CW allocation amount in the total regional water use amount, highlighting the priority of CW supply. These two objective functions reflect the “competition-and-cooperation” relationship between CW and UW.  2. Given that CW and UW are influenced by multi-dimensional heterogeneous factors, we use the Technique for Order of preference by Similarity to Ideal solution (TOPSIS) to combine all the factors into a composite index of CW and another of UW. Next, we introduce the allocation amount and the composite indexes to the inequality index model, to construct a model that matches CW and UW allocation with the local water use characteristics, ensuring fair allocation.  3. Based on the current uses of UW in China, this study introduces, for the first time, the concept of UW allocation efficiency, encompassing living, production, and environmental aspects. Additionally, it extends the concept of CW allocation efficiency from these three perspectives. Finally, by constructing a model for measuring the allocation efficiency of water resources, this study expands the application of ZSG-DEA method to the field of UW allocation.  4. Considering the potential future water resource crises that may reduce available CW and exacerbate water scarcity, as well as the technological advances that can mitigate these impacts by lifting the maximum UW consumption capacity, this study conducts a comprehensive multi-scenario analysis. The analysis identifies optimal allocation plans for CW and UW under various scenarios, thereby enhancing the practical applicability of the integrated adaptive allocation model.     2 Methods 2.1 Allocation procedure Following the principle of prioritizing fairness while considering efficiency in administration-led water allocation (He et al., 2023 ), this study proposes an integrated adaptive allocation model for unified optimization of CW and UW resources. The model consists of two modules (Fig. 2  ): Module 1 ensures fairness. The initial model for adaptive allocation (Model I) was constructed with a constrained total water amount based on MODM. (1) Besides the socioeconomic benefits, we adopted the two objective functions to reflect the competition relationship between CW and UW: the minimum difference between the UW substitution rate and the government-mandated rate, and the maximum CW supply. (2) We combined multi-dimensional heterogeneous factors affecting CW and UW into two composite indexes of CW and UW use, and then introduced the allocation amount and the two composite indexes to the inequality index model that matches CW and UW allocation with the local water use characteristics, ensuring fair allocation. Module 2 focuses on efficiency. The optimization model for adaptive allocation (Model II) was constructed using the ZSG-DEA model. (1) We defined the CW and UW allocation efficiencies, and further built the Model II based on the ZSG-DEA model. (2) We used the genetic algorithm to generate the Pareto front of Model I. Then, using model II, we chose the set of noninferior solutions with the maximum efficiency (maximum sum of CW and UW allocation efficiencies) on the Pareto front of Model I as the initial plan for adaptive allocation. (3) If both CW and UW allocation of sub-region are on the efficient frontier of Model II, the plan is optimal. Otherwise, the plan should be modified via Model II until CW and UW allocation of all sub-regions are on the efficient frontier. (4) The plan is checked for consistency with the constraints in Model I. Otherwise, the previous modified plan will be adopted until it satisfies the constraints. An integrated adaptive allocation plan for CW and UW of the sub-region is then determined.  2.2 Initial model for adaptive allocation based on MODM 2.2.1 Notation While allocating water resources, the regional administration must ensure economic, social, and environmental benefits, guarantee the fairness of allocation, and consider the “competition-and-cooperation” relationship between CW and UW. In this section, we integrated these objectives to build an initial allocation model. The parameters of the model are shown in Table 2  .  2.2.2 Initial model for adaptive allocation 2.2.2.1 Objective function of economic benefit The regional economic benefit objective means that the unified allocation system for CW and UW must maximize GDP while maintaining sustainable economic development. To achieve sustainable development, the economy must aim for reasonable development under certain production relations and technological levels, rather than blindly pursuing maximum economic output. However, the inherent laws of economic development also seek to surpass the planned target of total economic output. To reflect both sustainable development and the inherent pursuit of economic output, we use the planned regional GDP as a benchmark for economic output. By maximizing the ratio of economic output to the planned regional GDP under certain constraints, we strive to balance sustainable development with economic output goals. The objective function of the economic benefit is as follows:(1) F 1  ( W ij   )  = max ( ∑ i = 1  2  ∑ j = 1  n  W ij   / a ij     )  / G      where W ij     is the amount of type i    water that the regional administration allocates to sub-region j ; a ij     is the water use intensity (m3 /10,000 yuan) of type i    water by sub-region j ; G    is the planned regional GDP in the planning year; F 1  ( W ij   )  ≥ 1    means the economic benefit of water use reaches and even surpasses the planned regional GDP, and F 1  ( W ij   )  < 1    means the economic benefit fails to reach the planned value.  2.2.2.2 Objective function of social benefit The regional social benefit is to make sure that the CW and UW allocated to each sub-region in the planning year match its socioeconomic and environmental characteristics, in line with the principle of fairness. To demonstrate the spatial matching of water, we introduced the composite indexes concerning both CW and UW use, and the inequality index (Xiong et al., 2019 ), to construct the composite inequality index, in a bid to measure whether the regional overall water allocation is fair. Therefore, this study adopted the expected UW substitution rate stipulated by the regional administration for the planning year as a benchmark. The closer the substitution rate is to the expected value, the more the environment benefits. The efficiency scores serve as a crucial criterion for evaluating the reasonableness of the initial plan for adaptive allocation. If the plan is deemed unreasonable, typically characterized by sub-regions getting lower efficiency scores in either CW or UW allocation, regional administration must make some adjustments within the capped total amount to ensure the plan is fair and effective for most sub-regions. This study drew from the ZSG-DEA model and constructed an optimal model of adaptive allocation accordingly. 2.3.1 ZSG-DEA BCC model In this study, sub-regions were treated as decision-making units (DMU). Thus, there were N (j = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , n   ) DMUs. Here, i = 1 , 2    represents CW and UW, respectively. The water input indicator was set as x i j      and the k    non-water input indicators were set as a matrix: X ij  = ( x ij  1  , x ij  2  , … , x ij  k  )  T    . Next, z output indicators were set as a matrix: Y ij   = ( y ij  1  , y ij  2  , … y ij  z  )  T    . This study constructed an input-oriented Banker–Charnes–Cooper (BCC) model in line with Zeng et al. (2016) , as sub-regions’ input, output, and technical efficiency differ against the assumption of constant returns to scale (CRS):(14) min θ i d     s . t . ∑ j = 1  n  λ i j   X ij   ≤ X id      ∑ j = 1  n  λ i j   x ij    ≤ θ i d  x id      ∑ j = 1  n  λ ij   Y ij    ≥ Y id      ∑ j = 1  n  λ ij   = 1    λ ij  ≥ 0    i = 1 , 2 ; j = 1 , 2 , 3 … , n ; d = 1 , 2 , 3 , … , n                  Suppose the DMU of inefficient input is DMU0  and the efficiency is θ i  0    .
