Certain DMUs, however, still cannot be on the efficient frontier. In this case, this study used the iterative method to keep modifying inefficient DMUs till all DMUs are on the efficient frontier.  2.3.2 Input and output indicators This study selected the amount of allocated CW obtained from Model I and the labor force (Zhao et al., 2017 ) as the inputs. China is a big agricultural country with over 60 % of the total water used for agriculture. So we considered the crop sown area as the output of water utilization in the production dimension. In light of previous studies, the medical condition (measured as the number of healthcare technicians per 1,000 people) was regarded as a social output (Zhao et al., 2017 ), and the amount of urban wastewater discharge as an undesirable environmental output (Chang and Zhu, 2021 ). This means that when keeping the CW allocation amount constant, a DMU is deemed more efficient if it exhibits higher agricultural production, better medical conditions, or less discharged wastewater. On the other hand, this study selected the initial allocation of UW as the input, and the cumulative investment in water-saving facilities during the sample period as capital input (Guo et al., 2023a ). In China, UW is mostly used for urban and rural greening, industrial cooling, construction, and secondary industry. As a result, this study chose green space per capita to measure the impact of UW use on people’s living standards. The environmental output was measured by the amount of wastewater discharge for a DMU in the planning year, while the economic output was represented by the output value of the secondary industry (including both the industrial and the construction sectors). Suppose industrial cooling and construction for a DMU completely use UW, then: when keeping the UW allocation amount constant, a DMU is deemed more efficient, if it has a larger green space per capita, a higher output value in the secondary industry, or less urban wastewater discharge. Given the negative correlation between the UW allocation amount and the amount of discharged urban wastewater, this study drew from the method of Scheel (2001) , converting the latter into a positive indicator to measure efficiency. The detailed input and output indicators are shown in Table 4  .   2.4 Integrated adaptive allocation model The integrated adaptive allocation model for unified optimization of CW and UW (Integrated Model) can be illustrated as follows: Module one (Model I):(20) F ( W ij   )  = opt F 1  ( W ij   )  , F 2  ( W ij   )  , F 3  ( W ij   )  , F 4  ( W ij   )         F 1  ( W ij   )  = max ( ∑ i = 1  2  ∑ j = 1  n  W ij   / a ij     )  / G     F 2  ( W ij   )  = min ∑ i = 1  2  w i  ∑ j = 1  n  2   2  ( W ij   / W i   - R ij   / R i   )      2  / n       F 3  ( W ij   )  = min ∑ j = 1  n  W 2 j    / ∑ i = 1  2  ∑ j = 1  n  W ij        / η  - 1        F 4  ( W ij   )  = max ∑ j = 1  n  W 1 j    / W goal  pro              s . t . The detailed equation is as follows:(22) W 2 j  S  = φ j  × ( ρ j  W D j  )  + ϛ j  W j  ra   + ψ j  P j mi  + W j de       where W 2 j  S     represents the UW supply capacity, reflecting how much UW generates; ρ j     represents the comprehensive sewage discharge coefficient; W D j     represents the water consumption, valued based on the planned annual total water use amount of sub-region in the planning year; ρ j  W D j     represents the sewage discharge of sub-region j   ; W j  ra      represents the precipitation in the planning year of sub-region j   , calculated based on the multi-year average value during the sample period; P j mi     and W j de      respectively stand for the amount of coal mining output and seawater desalination in the planning year of sub-region j   ; φ j    , ϛ j    , and ψ j     respectively stand for the average sewage treatment rate, maximum rainwater harvesting rate, and water yield per ton of coal of sub-region j    in the planning year.  2.5.2 Unconventional water consumption capacity According to the current UW use plans in China, this study assumed that in the planning year, UW that meets the water quality standard was used for six purposes (urban road washing, public toilet flushing, public greenery irrigation, construction, vehicle washing, and thermal power generation). This study investigated water allocation at the provincial / municipal levels (Wu and Xiang, 2022 ), with the provincial government as the regional administration. Jiangsu Province is a major UW user and an economic engine of China (Fig. 3  a-b). How Jiangsu allocates both CW and UW and how well it matches the allocated amount with the water use characteristics of each city determines the extent of its leading role. However, in light of statistics and surveys, Jiangsu Province currently faces several challenges in terms of UW development and use. (1) The adoption of UW is lagging (Fig. 3 c), with a low substitution rate of 2.10 % in 2021, slightly lower than the national mean (2.34 %). (2) Significant disparities exist among cities in terms of preparedness and extent of UW use. For instance, the annual UW substitution rate in Xuzhou was only 2.34 % during 2016–2021, compared to 6.24 % for Suzhou. (3) There are discrepancies between economic development and UW consumption among cities. For instance, in 2021, Zhenjiang’s GDP ranked 10th in the province while its per capita water consumption exceeded 1,200 m3 , ranking first in the province. The total amount of UW utilization was only 26 million m3 , the lowest in the province.  3.2 Data sources This study used 2012–2021 as the sample period to formulate the water allocation plan for Jiangsu Province in 2025 (2025 as the planning year). The data in this study were mostly collected from policies, water quotas, statistical yearbooks, and water resources bulletins.(1) Policy data were mainly obtained from the Notice on Issuing the “14th Five-Year” Targets for Total Water Consumption and Intensity Dual Control (Water Conservation [2022] No. 113) issued by the Ministry of Water Resources and the National Development and Reform Commission, 14th Five-Year Plan for Water-Saving Society Construction in Jiangsu Province, and the 14th Five-Year Plan for water conservancy development of each city. Data on mining were mainly obtained from the Xuzhou Overall Planning of Mineral Resources (2020–2025) and Overall Planning of Mineral Resources of Jiangsu Province.  (2) Data on water quotas were mainly obtained from the Water Use Quota for Forestry, Animal Husbandry, Fishery, Industry, Service, and Domestic Use of Jiangsu Province (Revised in 2019) and Sanitary Fixture for Water Saving (GB/T 31436–2015).  (3) Statistical data were obtained from the China Urban-Rural Construction Statistical Yearbook (2012–2021), statistical yearbooks of the cities in Jiangsu Province, such as the Statistical Yearbook of Nanjing (2013–2022), and water resources bulletins of cities in Jiangsu, such as the 2012 Suzhou Water Resources Bulletin.      4 Results 4.1 Range of conventional and unconventional water allocation amount Equations (22) and (23)  show that recycled wastewater and harvested rainwater are the major sources of UW supply in Jiangsu Province (Fig. 4  a-b). Coastal cities like Lianyungang and Yancheng are uniquely positioned to desalinate seawater, while mine water is mostly located in Xuzhou, a major coal-producing city of Jiangsu (Fig. 4 a). Meanwhile, cities differ greatly in their ability to consume UW, even the same type of water users may exhibit different potentials for UW utilization (Fig. 4 c). For example, public greening irrigation is a major UW user in Nanjing, with a much higher potential than in other cities. In the sample period, the real estate industry in Nantong took up about 35 % of the construction area of the whole province (Cai et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017 ), indicating a great potential for UW utilization. Generally speaking, every city of Jiangsu Province consumes much less UW than the locally available UW supply, highlighting a significant opportunity to improve UW consumption (Fig. 4 d). Therefore, based on Equation (8) , we denoted the UW consumption ability of each city as the upper limit of UW allocation amount in 2025. From the relevant planning and yearbooks, we obtained the upper and lower limits of CW and UW allocation amount for each city in Jiangsu Province in 2025 (Table 5  ). The total water use amount differs greatly among cities, with Suzhou ranking the first (10.3 billion m3 ) and Changzhou the last (2.784 billion m3 ). In terms of UW use, compared to UW use at the end of the sample year (2021) (W 2 j  h    ), each city can increase its UW use amount by at least 100 million m3 , with Nanjing and Nantong showing the greatest potential for increase. Overall, the range of CW and UW allocation amount of cities in Jiangsu Province demonstrates obvious spatial heterogeneity. Next, we combined all the factors affecting urban CW and UW use to demonstrate the differences in urban development characteristics. According to the ratings of the indicators in Table 3  by experts from administrative departments and the water management field, the weight in Equation (3)  can be obtained as w i k   = 0.10   0.30   0.15   0.15   0.20   0.10    0.15    0.13   0.20   0.10   0.25   0.17           . From Appendix Table A.1, we obtained the regional composite indexes of the urban development characteristics affecting CW and UW use, as shown in Fig. 5  . The characteristics affecting CW use show great spatial heterogeneity, while characteristics affecting UW use show minimal spatial heterogeneity, except for Suzhou.  4.2 Adaptive allocation plan for CW and UW 4.2.1 Initial plan for adaptive allocation According to water administrative authorities and experts, the weights in the initial model for adaptive allocation (Model I) were valued as w i  = 0.5 , 0.5        to demonstrate that the allocation of both CW and UW is of equal importance. Meanwhile, we set τ ′  = 90 %    and τ ″  = 115 %    to ensure sustainable economic development. Based on Table 5  and Fig. 5 , this study resolved Model I via genetic algorithm on Matlab2023 and got 80 sets of noninferior solutions (Fig. 6  ). Next, Model II was used to estimate the score of CW allocation efficiency under each set of noninferior solutions based. In the same way, the UW allocation efficiency score of each city was obtained. As per the principle of maximizing allocation efficiency, we chose the solution with the maximum sum (CW and UW allocation efficiency scores) as the initial plan for adaptive allocation, as shown in Table 6  . In detail, in the initial plan for adaptive allocation, F 1  (W ij  )     is 1.1236, and the provincial GDP is approximately 15.5365 trillion yuan, around 12.36 % higher than the expected GDP in 2025. F 2  (W ij  )     is 0.0095, meaning the CW and UW allocation in each city is relatively fair, as the amount of water generally matches the city’s composite indexes. F 3  (W ij  )     is 0.1963, and the relevant provincial UW substitution rate is 0.036, reaching the target of 0.03. F 4  (W ij  )     is 0.9463, and the relevant CW allocation amount is 49.7666 billion m3 . To sum up, in the initial plan for adaptive allocation, the amount of UW allocated to the province is 1.8526 billion m3 , exceeding China’s lower limit of UW use – 1.52 billion m3 ; the total amount of allocated water is 51.6192 billion m3 , higher than the lower limit – 42.7310 billion m3 , while lower than the provincial cap – 52.5900 billion m3 . As the results on the initial allocation of CW in Table 6  suggest, most cities (except Wuxi, Nantong, Yangzhou, and Taizhou) achieve an efficiency score of 1.0000, placing them on the efficient frontier. Among the four remaining cities, both Wuxi and Nantong have a relatively lower efficiency score of approximately 0.6500, whereas the two other cities score above 0.8000, indicating a relatively higher level of efficiency. In contrast, six cities fail to reach the target of 1.0000 for UW. Specifically, Lianyungang exhibits the lowest efficiency (0.7783). Xuzhou tends to be 0.9000, whereas Wuxi, Changzhou, Huai’an, and Yancheng exceed 0.9000. Thus, the cities exhibit relatively high efficiency in UW allocation compared to CW allocation. The initial plan for adaptive allocation, guided by the principle of fairness, results in highly efficient CW and UW allocation for each city, although the allocation amount of all cities on the efficient frontier is not ensured.  4.2.2 Optimal plan for adaptive allocation To further improve the allocation efficiency of CW and UW of each city under the principle of fairness, this study turned to Model II to, with the total allocation amount unchanged, slightly adjust the allocation amount of CW and UW of each city. As shown in Fig. 7  a-b, after three rounds of optimization, CW and UW allocation in each city almost approached the corresponding efficient frontier. However, it is imperative that the optimal allocation is within the constraints of the total water amount. Consequently, this study further compared the optimized CW allocation with that listed in Table 5 . The findings indicated that after one round of optimization, the amount of CW allocated to Xuzhou, Changzhou, Yancheng, and Suqian surpassed the cap of the total water use amount in 2025 by 647.6 million m3  in total. After three rounds of optimization, this amount increased to 736.1 million m3  (Fig. 7 c). Therefore, although the optimized plan improved the efficiency of CW allocation, it remained unfeasible. In this case, the initial plan should be deemed the optimal plan for adaptive allocation of CW. Meanwhile, the optimized allocation efficiency of UW was compared with the upper and lower limits of UW allocation in Table 5 . The results showed that the amount of allocated UW, after three optimizations, was lower than the cap (Fig. 7 d), such that the optimized UW plan was deemed optimal. Therefore, the initial CW allocation plan and the third optimized UW allocation plan were chosen as the optimal plan (Table 7  ). The results were then modeled into Equation (1)  and indicated that the GDP of Jiangsu Province in 2025 is approximately 15.543 trillion yuan, 12.40 % more than expected, with an annual growth rate of 7.26 %, lower than the rate during the sample period (9.08 %), but higher than the expected value of the 14th Five-Year Plan (5.5 %). It shows that the optimal plan for adaptive allocation is reasonable and feasible in terms of economic development. Fig. 8   presents an analysis of the rationality of water resource allocation in Jiangsu Province in 2025. The normalized composite index of CW and UW use is respectively consistent with the proportion of each city’s allocation in the total provincial CW and UW allocation (Fig. 8 a). As Fig. 8 b illustrates, the total water allocation for each city matches the cap in 2025, indicating that the optimal plan proposed in this study fits each city’s development characteristics. The UW consumption amount for each city was calculated based on the intended use of UW and China’s current technology for UW utilization. Thus, it may theoretically be lower than the actual amount in 2025. For each city, the UW allocation amount was below the consumption amount in 2025 (Fig. 7 d), also proving that the UW allocation plan proposed in this study is feasible.    5 Discussion 5.1 Comparative analysis with single-objective decision models Weighting is a common method in multi-objective optimization (MOO) of water allocation (Guo et al., 2023b ). Weights demonstrate decision-maker preference, implying the extent to which the decision-maker accepts the optimal value of the objective (Zhang et al., 2022c ). Using the linear weighted sum method, we turned the MODM Model (Model I) into a single-objective optimization (SOO) Model (Li et al., 2020; Wu and Wang, 2022 ) as follows:(24) min F ( W ij   ) =   - w 1  ( ∑ i = 1  2  ∑ j = 1  n  W ij   / a ij     )  / G  + w 2  ∑ i = 1  2  w i  ∑ j = 1  n  2   2  ( W ij   / W i   - R ij   / R i   )      2  / n       + w 3  ∑ j = 1  n  W 2 j    / ∑ i = 1  2  ∑ j = 1  n  W ij        / η  - 1     - w 4  ∑ j = 1  n  W 1 j    / W goal  pro       s . t . The weights of two objectives were kept equal to 0.25 to explore how changes in the weights of the other two objectives influence the final allocation plan, finally forming a total of 54 (6*9) combinations. Next, based on Equation (24) , the noninferior solution set of each combination was obtained, and put into Model II to identify the set with the maximum efficiency as the initial allocation plan. Furthermore, in line with the principle of efficiency, the initial plan was modified via Model II. The CW allocation amount, UW allocation, and total water allocation amount of each city after the first modification were denoted as W 1 j  r 1   , W 2 j  r 1   , W j r 1   ( j = 1 , 2 , … , 13 )    . After that, we checked if these values meet the constraints in Table 5 , and found that the modified plans of certain cities do not meet the constraints (Appendix Table A.2). That means the initial plan obtained through Equation (24)  cannot be optimized for efficiency. This indicates that the SOO model ensures allocation fairness at the expense of efficiency. Next, we used the total water use amount of each city in 2025 (W j goal     ) to represent water demand, measured the gap between demand and allocation plan, and roughly estimated the water shortage risk (Fig. 9  ). We found that although the total allocation efficiency of certain weight combinations with the SOO model in Fig. 9 b, c, and f is higher than that of the optimal plan obtained by the Integrated Model in the Results section, the corresponding water shortage risk is also higher than the latter. Overall, the total efficiency of the optimal plan obtained by the Integrated Model is higher than that obtained from most weight combinations. Last, using the coefficient of variation (Botta-Dukát, 2023 ), we analyzed the spatial heterogeneity of water shortage risk of Jiangsu Province under each weight combination. As shown in Fig. 10  , with the weights of two objectives fixed at 0.25 each, however the weights of the other two objectives change, the coefficient of water shortage risk is significantly higher than that of the Integrated Model in this study. In other words, the SOO model reveals a huge gap between water supply and demand, which threatens the fairness of water allocation. Therefore, based on the results of comparing the water allocation efficiencies and water shortage risks at the provincial level as well as the spatial heterogeneity of city-level water shortage, we came to a conclusion. Compared with the SOO model, the Integrated Model composed of the MODM and ZSG-DEA models offers greater potential for fairness and efficiency in the allocation of multiple water sources.  5.2 Scenario analysis 5.2.1 Influence of emergency incidents To measure the negative influence of possible emergency incidents (e.g., drought, warfare, nuclear pollution, and so on) on water allocation, we introduced the concept of available water supply into the initial model for adaptive allocation. “Available water supply” refers to unpolluted freshwater resources coming from rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and groundwater aquifers. The less the available water, the lower the upper limit of total water allocation amount and the lower the lower and upper limits of CW allocation. In Section 2.1 , we skipped the influence of emergency incidents. So, in this section, we reduced the three values by 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, and 25 % to represent the decrease in available water under different emergency incidents. The bigger the decrease, the more influential the impact of the emergency incident. We followed the measuring steps in Section 2.1 , and the results are shown in Table 8  . As shown in Table 8 , as the available water supply drops, the CW allocation of each city dwindles, while UW allocation increases significantly to meet the water demand. However, constrained by current technologies, the increase in UW utilization can never fully bridge the huge gap between water supply and demand. As a result, the water shortage risk at both provincial and city levels shows a positive correlation with the decrease in available water supply (Fig. 11  a-b). In the meantime, when the available water supply drops by over 20 %, the CW allocation of each city reaches the upper limit (Fig. 11 c). To meet water demand, the UW allocation amount gradually climbs up to the limit (Fig. 11 d). In other words, if the available water supply continues to decline, it would be unable to meet the city’s water demand due to limitations in water resource endowment and UW use technologies, further widening the supply and demand gap.  5.2.2 Technological breakthrough of UW treatment and use In the case of major emergency incidents affecting available water supply, improving the maximum UW consumption ability is supposed to be a critical means to bridge the supply and demand gap. How exactly does a higher level of UW treatment and use affect water allocation? In this regard, we assumed the extreme scenario of a 25 % drop in available water supply. The maximum UW consumption (W 2 j  max    ) was increased by 10 %, 20 %, 30 %, and 40 % to represent the improvement of UW treatment and use technology level, and introduced into Model I. We then followed the measuring steps in Section 2.1 , and the water allocation results of Jiangsu Province in 2025 are shown in Table 9  . The results show that no matter how much the technology level of UW treatment and use increases, the CW allocation of each city stays at the upper limit (Table 9  and Fig. 11 c). This is the result of the fourth objective in Model I, indicating that clean fresh water is always the top priority of socioeconomic development. Hence, when available water is in serious shortage, the supply and demand gap can only be narrowed by increasing UW supply. However, China’s scale of UW use is insufficient; even if the upper limit of UW consumption increases by 40 %, the total water allocation adaptive to Jiangsu Province in 2025 only reaches 49.158 billion m3 , significantly lower than the provincial red line “52 billion m3 .” Moreover, under this scenario, the total UW allocation reaches 5.826 billion m3 , much higher than the total UW utilization at the end of the sample period (1.17 billion m3 ). Overall, this plan is unlikely to be effective unless there is a significant breakthrough in the technology level of UW treatment and use. Furthermore, in the scenario of a 25 % drop in available water supply, if UW consumption does not improve, the UW allocation of most cities is constrained by their current consumption and cannot match the composite index of UW use. In other words, fairness cannot be fully guaranteed if the water supply gap needs to be filled. As the technology level increases, nonetheless, the UW allocation gradually aligns with the UW use composite index R2j   (Fig. 12  a) in terms of spatial evolution. This indicates that advanced technologies provide more flexibility for decision-making in UW adaptive allocation. Moreover, without considering the increase in technology level (−25 %, 0), cities face a greater water shortage risk. As the technology level increases, this risk gets alleviated (Fig. 12 b). When the technology level increases by 40 %, the water shortage risk of most cities drops to a relatively safe level.   5.3 Further discussion Generally speaking, compared with turning MODM into SOO via the method of weighting, this study solved MODM and ZSG-DEA models based on the Pareto front, achieving adaptive allocation of both CW and UW in a fairer and more efficient manner. In case of future emergency incidents affecting sustainable water use, efficiency needs to be compromised to meet the water demand due to constraints of water resource endowment and UW consumption. Only by increasing the technology level of UW treatment and use can we create more flexibility for decision-making in water adaptive allocation and comprehensively lower the risk of urban water shortage. Given that China’s current UW utilization is limited in both scale and proportion, a small increase in UW use cannot guarantee water use fairness and efficiency in the face of emergencies and disasters. Therefore, the key lies in achieving technological breakthroughs in UW treatment and use. For that, the Chinese Government needs to issue preferential policies and subsidies for institutes developing technologies, products, or services related to wastewater treatment. It should promote the integration of industry, academia, and research, and implement policies to guide and encourage factors and enterprises to marketize and industrialize their innovations in wastewater treatment and recycling. In addition, local governments can, based on the local water resource endowment and socioeconomic development needs, tighten the energy-related access to industrial parks, and require enterprises to recycle and reuse more water resources.   6 Conclusions Based on the concept of adaptive water allocation and the principles of fairness and efficiency, with fairness as the top priority, we combined the MODM and ZSG-DEA into an integrated adaptive allocation model consisting of two modules; the first module ensures fairness, and the second ensures efficiency. The first module, while reflecting the “competition-and-cooperation” relationship between CW and UW, ensures the precedence of CW use over UW use, aligning with real-world conditions. In the meantime, by constructing regional composite indexes and inequality indexes, we matched different water allocation amounts with regional development characteristics. The second module, based on actual conditions in China, defines CW and UW allocation efficiencies, and strives for allocation efficiency. Next, we applied the model to the unified allocation of CW and UW of Jiangsu Province in 2025, to test its validity and feasibility. Last, we ran a series of scenario analyses and discussions, and came to the following conclusions:(1) Compared with turning MODM into SOO, finding the Pareto optimal solution of the Integrated Model via genetic algorithm tallies with both fairness and efficiency principles of water allocation and narrows the spatial heterogeneity of water shortage risk.  (2) Available water supply determines water allocation. In the case of future emergency incidents (drought, warfare, nuclear pollution, etc.), available water supply drops by at least 20 %, and CW allocation would be the first to reach its upper limit. In this case, the fairness of UW allocation has to give way to the UW consumption capacity of each city.  (3) In the face of water crisis, constrained by the technological level of UW treatment, increasing UW utilization contributes little to filling the supply–demand gap. So maximum UW consumption must be improved to provide flexibility for decision-making in adaptive water allocation. As the UW consumption improves, the allocation plan changes and the spatial heterogeneity of water shortage risk narrows.  (4) At present, it is difficult for China to effectively address future water emergencies with its current scale and level of UW use. To better manage future water crises, China should prioritize making major technological breakthroughs in UW treatment and utilization.    The adaptive allocation method this study proposed fills a research gap regarding China’s efforts to incorporate UW into its unified water allocation system. It aligns the allocation results with local socioeconomic development, showing theoretical and practical significance. However, this study also has some limitations. Due to limited data availability, we assigned the same economic benefit per unit to CW and UW in the initial model for adaptive allocation. Additionally, we did not account for specific urban water demands while measuring water shortage risk; instead, we approximated this with the cap of total water use amount of cities. In future research, we will cover these deficiencies and adopt a more comprehensive and inclusive approach.
1 Introduction The increase in greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere, caused by human activities since the Industrial Revolution, has sparked global concern about of global warming. This concern is reinforced by empirical evidence of a recorded increase in average surface air temperature (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2019; Shivanna, 2022 ). The effects of global warming are evident through the rising frequency and intensity of extreme hydro-climatic events (Das et al., 2022 ), i.e.; heavy rainfall, droughts, floods, and heat waves have become more frequent and severe (Ali et al., 2019; Cannon et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2022; Gaur et al., 2021 ; Ge et al., 2021a; Tan et al., 2021 ; S. Wang et al., 2022; Wasko et al., 2021; Zittis et al., 2022 ). The adverse repercussions of hydro-climatic extremes go beyond their influence on crucial socio-economic sectors, encompassing areas such as food production, water security, and energy supply (Aghapour Sabbaghi et al., 2020; Lesk et al., 2016; Mehboob and Kim, 2021; Qin and Dai, 2022 ). Moreover, these extreme events can endanger human health and life by facilitating the dissemination of diseases and polluting the environment (Almudi and Sinclair, 2022; Aragão et al., 2016; Dai et al., 2022; Hondula et al., 2015 ). In Iran, climate change is already having a significant impact on hydroclimatic extremes, leading to more frequent and intense floods, longer and more severe droughts, and rising temperatures (Doulabian et al., 2021; Jahanshahi and Booij, 2024; Moshir Panahi et al., 2020; Shadmehri Toosi et al., 2019; Vaghefi et al., 2019 ) that are disrupting agricultural production, affecting water resources, and posing risks to human health and livelihoods (Abbaspour et al., 2009 ). In this context, the projection of future hydro-climatic extremes holds significant importance as it allows us to assess the potential impacts of climate change (Doulabian et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Pechlivanidis et al., 2017; Vaghefi et al., 2019 ). By offering critical insights into the most detrimental aspects, such projections can support policy and decision-makers in the design, development and execution of effective adaptation strategies. To study the effects of climate change on hydrological systems, a comprehensive projection framework needs three key components: climate downscaling, hydrological modeling, and statistical analysis (Dai et al., 2022 ).• Climatic downscaling involves the transformation of outputs from General Circulation Models (GCMs) to regional climate scales, typically at a higher spatial resolution (Dai et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Tabari et al., 2020 ). GCMs can simulate the global climate for historical, current, and future periods in response to various warming scenarios predetermined by the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project  (CMIP) (McBride et al., 2021 ). The process of dynamically downscaling global climate models (GCMs) to inform regional climate models (RCMs) serves the purpose of producing localized climate information that can be effectively applied in subsequent impact studies (Giorgi, 2019; Singh et al., 2019 ). Moreover, the use of RCMs typically increases the reliability of simulations of extreme climate events by reducing systematic errors through the application of a standard post-processing bias correction method, such as Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM). This approach increases confidence in the accuracy of the magnitude and direction of these extreme events (Cannon et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2021; Lehner et al., 2023; Qin and Dai, 2022; Sunyer et al., 2012 ).  • Hydrological modeling plays a crucial role in simulating the streamflow responses to climatological input (such as provided by RCMs), thereby being of significant importance to the overall process (Krysanova et al., 2018; Pandey et al., 2017 ). Its principal role is to generate time series runoff data, which facilitates the analysis of extreme streamflow and hydrological drought assessment.  • Statistical analysis relies primarily on the use of statistical indices that are specifically designed to accurately quantify the hydro-climatic attributes of the system under different conditions (Dai et al., 2022 ). Several statistical tools and indices can be used to investigate hydro-climatic extremes, including: (i) the annual minimum 7-day streamflow (Qn7day) used to assess low-flow extremes (Gaur et al., 2021 ), and (ii) the annual maximum 1-day streamflow (QX1day) and 5-day streamflow (QX5day) used to represent high-flow extremes (Arsenault et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017; Wang and Xuan, 2020 ).    Hydrological models, together with the integration of Extreme Streamflow Indices (ESIs), are extensively employed to project alterations in floods (high-flows) and droughts (low-flows) under changing environmental conditions (Dai et al., 2022; Galata et al., 2021; Hirabayashi et al., 2021; Iqbal et al., 2018; Stewart et al., 2015 ). In recent years, the abovementioned framework has been extensively used to investigate the effects of climate change on hydroclimatic extremes in catchments worldwide. For example, Galata et al. (2021)  used the SWAT model to assess the impact of future climate change on runoff in Hangar catchment, Ethiopia. Future projections indicated a rise in precipitation and temperatures compared to the base period (1987–2017). Under RCP 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios, average annual precipitation is expected to increase by 15.7–19.8 % (2025–2055) and 20.1–23.4 % (2056–2086) respectively. The SWAT model simulations demonstrated that this increase in precipitation positively influenced average runoff flow. Dai et al. (2022)  used an integrated assessment model to analyze the climate change effect on hydro-climatic extremes in Hanjiang river basin of China. Five RCMs under RCP 2.6 and 8.5 were employed, showing a slight precipitation increase, significant temperature rise, intensified precipitation events, and higher temperature extremes. Their study projected increased basin-wide streamflow indices for extreme 1-day maximum and 7-day minimum streamflows. Kay et al. (2021)  used the G2G hydrological model, which incorporated ensembles of 28 GCMs and 12 RCMs from the UKCP18 dataset. Their main objective was to calculate Return Period High Flow (RHQ) and Return Period Low Flow (RLQ) indices for both 5-year and 20-year periods and focused on assessing future changes in floods and droughts across Great Britain under the RCP8.5 scenario. RCM outputs directly influenced the hydrological model, while GCM outputs underwent pre-processing and downscaled using the delta change approach (Arnell, 2003 ). Lee et al. (2022)  used bias-corrected climate data from four RCMs for 2071–2095 under RCP 8.5 scenarios. They applied the SWAT and PRMS hydrological models, two Qn7day and Qn30day indices, to analyze the potential changes in extreme low flows due to global warming in the Chungju basin, South Korea. Previous research has focused predominantly on investigating the effects of climate change on either streamflow extremes or climatological extremes. However, Tegegne and Melesse (2020)  took a different approach by considering both aspects. They used outputs from GCMs to assess hydro-climatic extremes in a river basin in South Korea. In their study, a collection of 27 extreme climate indices (ECI), as outlined by the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI) in 2009 (WMO, 2009 ), was employed. Additionally, a selection of ESIs, including 7Q2 and HF2, were incorporated for analysis. The importance of concurrently assessing the impacts of climate change on both extreme hydrological and climatic responses is evident from that study. An integrated perspective aims to provide local decision-makers with a comprehensive understanding of the potential risks associated with future water-related events. However, to date, there have been only a limited number of studies of this nature. Currently, RCMs are commonly employed in climate change impact assessments for various climate variables, including temperature, precipitation, and cyclones (Byun et al., 2023; Giorgi, 2019; KhayatianYazdi et al., 2021; Tapiador et al., 2020; Xi et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021 ). However, there is a noticeable dearth of studies that employ RCMs to examine how hydro-climatic extremes may respond to the impacts of climate change, particularly in the context of Iran. In any such study, it is important that the effects of modeling uncertainties be taken into account. Downscaling techniques introduce uncertainties due to factors like the choice of method, representation of physical processes, and inherent GCM limitations (Chen et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2018; Lafferty and Sriver, 2023; Rastogi et al., 2022 ). These uncertainties can propagate through the modeling chain, affecting the reliability of hydrological projections (Chokkavarapu and Mandla, 2019; Senatore et al., 2022 ). Hydrological modeling also has its uncertainties and limitations, as simplifications and assumptions in the modeling process may not fully capture real-world hydrological systems. Parameterization of hydrological models, involving estimation or calibration of model parameters based on limited observations or expert judgment, adds further uncertainties (Ajami et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011 ). This study presents and demonstrates a comprehensive framework for integrated assessment modeling. This framework incorporates an ensemble of RCM outputs from the Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX), QDM method for bias correction, the HBV hydrological model, ETCCDI indices, and ESIs (specifically, QX1day, QX5day, and Qn7day). Our main goal is to comprehensively evaluate how climate change might affect hydro-climatic extremes across 576 catchments in Iran. The study utilizes the CORDEX RCMs, bias-corrected with the QDM method to develop future climate projections for both RCP 2.6 and 8.5 scenarios. Climate extremes are examined using ETCCDI indices, while hydrological extremes are appraised through ESI. The HBV model, in combination with RCM outputs, assesses both categories of indices, studying spatial and temporal changes in hydro-climatic extremes across the catchments over various periods in the 21st century. While our study focuses on the QDM method and HBV model, it is crucial to recognize the uncertainties and limitations in climate downscaling and hydrological modeling. Acknowledging these factors can enhance the transparency and robustness of assessments, contributing to the ongoing refinement of modeling practices in climate change impact studies.  2 Study area and data Our study area includes 576 catchments in Iran (see Jahanshahi et al. (2022b ; 2022a; 2021)) (Fig. 1  ). Iran experiences a wide range of climatic conditions due to its diverse topography and geographical features. The northern areas, including the Caspian Sea region, have a more humid and subtropical climate influenced by the Mediterranean climate. Compared to other regions within the country, this area receives more than average precipitation and experiences relatively mild temperatures. The central and eastern parts of Iran, including the vast deserts of the Dasht-e Kavir and Dasht-e Lut, are characterized by an arid or desert climate. These areas receive very little rainfall and are known for their extreme temperature variations, with scorching hot summers and cold winters. There are also some mountainous regions in Iran, particularly in the west, which experience a continental climate. These areas have colder winters and milder summers compared to the lowland regions (Jahanshahi and Booij, 2024, 2023 ). When classified according to the Koppen-Geiger climate classification, our study catchments fall into three groups: “Snow dry, warm summer (Dsb )”, “Warm temperate with dry, hot summer (Csa )”, and “Arid desert cold (BWk )” (Jahanshahi et al., 2022a ). They experience a broad spectrum of mean annual precipitation, ranging from 150 mm to over 2000 mm. Similarly, there is a substantial variation in mean annual temperature, varying from 5.3 °C to 36 °C within the study catchments. The study catchments cover a total drainage area of about 410,000 km2 , and exhibit diverse and complex topography, with the highest elevation reaching 4,583 m.a.s.l. About 34 % of the area consists of mountains that are located in the western, northern, and northwest regions. Moreover, 39 % of the study catchments are composed of hilly terrain located in the northeastern and western regions of the country, as well as within the valleys of the primary tributaries. The remaining 27 % are composed of plains, predominantly located in the far west, southwest, central, and southeastern parts of the country (Jahanshahi et al., 2022b ). Flood events are frequent between January and April (Jahanshahi and Booij, 2024 ). The western catchments have experienced maximum observed floods reaching as high as 2,200 m3 .s−1 . Significant variations in precipitation, temperature, and evapotranspiration are projected to occur in the study catchments due to climate change (Mansouri Daneshvar et al., 2019; Vaghefi et al., 2019 ). These changes are expected to have an impact on future hydrological processes. Consequently, investigating how the hydrological and climatic variables (i.e., precipitation and temperature) in Iranian catchments respond to climate change is of great interest and importance. Extensive hydro-climatic data has been gathered to support the implementation of the lumped HBV hydrological model for hydro-climatic analysis. Our study included the collection of daily meteorological data from 2663 meteorological stations, providing information on precipitation, evaporation, minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and mean temperature. Additionally, discharge data from 576 hydrometric stations were obtained (IEM, 2024; IRIMO, 2024 ). The historical data records used for hydrological modeling, cover the timeframe from 1993 to 2013. The Thiessen method was used to calculate areal precipitation (Jahanshahi et al., 2022a ), thereby accounting for the spatial distribution of climate stations. This method estimated precipitation values for different areas of the 576 study catchments. To obtain climate projection scenarios, data was sourced from the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) database, which stores outputs from CORDEX RCMs (Gaur et al., 2021 ). Five RCMs were employed: Had-REM, MPI-REM, Nor-REM, Had-Reg, and Nor-Reg (as outlined in Table 1  ). Had-REM, MPI-REM, and Nor-REM correspond to the REMO2015 RCM (Bento et al., 2023 ) driven by GCMs HadGEM2-ES, MPI-ESM-LR, and NorESM1-M, respectively. Had-Reg and Nor-Reg represent the RegCM4 RCM (Boulahfa et al., 2023; Giorgi et al., 2023; Pareja-Quispe et al., 2021 ) driven by GCMs HadGEM2-ES and NorESM1-M, respectively. Our daily time series of precipitation, temperature, and evaporation data, extracted from the RCM simulations, have an approximate spatial resolution of 25 km. Giorgi et al. (2012)  and Pietikäinen et al. (2018)  elaborate on the additional advantages of employing these RCMs. In this study, two emission scenarios, RCP 2.6 and RCP 8.5, were considered to represent climate change. The analysis focused on both the near future (2024–2050) and far future (2051–2080) for all RCMs. To establish a baseline for comparison with future indices, the control period from 1958 to 2020 was chosen as the reference period. While RCPs typically begin in 2006 with projected greenhouse gas concentrations, our aim was to incorporate a longer historical period to capture climate variability and provide a comprehensive context for our analysis. The selection of the control period was driven by several factors, including the availability and quality of historical climate data spanning multiple decades. By encompassing this extended timeframe, we were able to gain a better understanding of historical climate patterns, assess long-term trends, and account for decadal-scale climate variability.  3 Method An integrated assessment modeling framework, as illustrated in Fig. 2  , was employed to evaluate projected climate change impacts on hydro-climatic extremes across the study catchments. The first stage involved the calibration of the HBV model parameters using observed streamflow data, following the approach presented in Jahanshahi et al. (2022b) . Subsequently, the climate data obtained from the CORDEX RCMs, encompassing precipitation and temperature, was subjected to bias correction utilizing the quantile delta mapping (QDM) method (Cannon et al., 2015; Mehboob and Kim, 2021 ). The ECIs indices for different time periods were then computed using the bias-corrected climate data for the historical, RCP 2.6, and RCP 8.5 scenarios. The bias-corrected climate data was utilized to simulate daily streamflow time series using the calibrated HBV model. This simulation is essential for determining the ESI. 3.1 HBV hydrological model We used the TUW lumped conceptual version of the HBV model, developed at the Vienna University of Technology (Viglione and Parajka, 2019 ). This version follows the structure of the original HBV model (Bergström, 1992; Parajka et al., 2007a ), and has been applied in various studies for catchment-scale runoff simulation (Durgut and Ayvaz, 2023; Jahanshahi et al., 2022b ). The model uses three inputs (precipitation, temperature, and potential evapotranspiration (PET)) to simulate the hydrological processes of a catchment. The Hargreaves method was employed to calculate the PET values (Hargreaves and Samani, 1985 ). The TUW model has three main routines:• Snow accumulation and melt  : This routine calculates the accumulation of snow from snowfall and the melt of snow due to solar radiation and temperature.  • Soil moisture accounting  : This routine calculates the infiltration, evaporation, and transpiration of water from the soil.  • Runoff  : This routine calculates the runoff from the soil moisture and snowpack layers. The runoff is then routed through two distinct runoff routines (i.e., fast runoff and slow runoff) towards the catchment’s outlet.    The model has a total of 15 parameters that govern its behavior. These parameters are divided into three groups:• Snow routine parameters  : These parameters control the accumulation, melt, and water equivalent of the snowpack.  • Soil moisture routine parameters  : These parameters control the infiltration, evaporation, and transpiration of water from the soil.  • Flow routing routine parameters  : These parameters control how quickly water moves from the soil reservoir to the catchment outlet, simulating the timing of the discharge.    Model calibration using observed streamflow data was conducted to determine the optimal values for these parameters that most accurately represent the behavior of the catchment (Booij, 2005; Booij and Krol, 2010; Jahanshahi et al., 2022a; Parajka et al., 2007b ). The process involved adjusting the 15 parameters of the HBV model to maximize the NSE (Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency) (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) objective function, using the widely used and robust DEoptim (Differential Evolution optimization) algorithm proposed by Storn and Price (1997) , available through the DEoptim package in R (Ardia et al., 2011 ). The methos belongs to the class of genetic algorithms as described by Mitchell (1998) . In configuring the DEoptim algorithm, we used specific setting including itermax = 400, population size (NP) = 400, trace = FALSE, cross-over probability = 0.5, and step size = 0.8. The DEoptim algorithm was executed with various maximum function call settings, specifically 1,000, 2,000, 8,000, 10,000, 15,000, and 20,000. Through experimentation, it was determined that the best validation period results were obtained when the number of function calls ranged between 8,000 and 10,000, depending on the specific catchment. Notably, there was only slight variation in the final performance between catchments calibrated with 8000 and 15,000 function calls, and the results did not significantly deteriorate even when the number of function calls was reduced to 2000. The DEoptim algorithm, with carefully specified settings and an appropriate number of function calls, ensured an effective calibration process, resulting in reliable and accurate parameter values for the TUW model. The TUW model has previously been applied in several catchment-scale streamflow and water balance modeling studies in Iran (Jahanshahi et al., 2022b, 2022a, 2021; Jahanshahi and Booij, 2024, 2023 ). Simulations were conducted at a daily time step, aligned with the model settings for the historical period (1993–2013) in Jahanshahi et al. (2022b) ; more information on the input data, including historical meteorological and streamflow data, can be found there. The simulations demonstrate a reasonable reflection of spatiotemporal variations in simulated runoff across different climatic regions of Iran (Jahanshahi et al., 2022a ). Here, we extend the simulation period and leverage the model to project hydrological changes in Iran for future periods. Performance of the HBV simulation is assessed using the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta skill score efficiency (KGEss) (Gupta et al., 2009 ), a rescaled variant of the original KGE metric (Knoben et al., 2019 ), percent bias (PBIAS), and coefficient of determination (R2 ) metrics. These metrics provide further insights into the accuracy and bias of the rainfall-runoff model's simulation results (Moriasi et al., 2007 ).(1a) NSE  =  1  -  ∑ i  ( O i   -  S i  )  2   ∑ i  ( O i   -  O  ¯   i  )  2        (1b) R  2   =  1  -   SSR SST      =  ∑ i = 1  n  ( O i   -  O  ¯   )  ( S i   -  S  ¯   )    ∑ i = 1  n  ( O i   -  O  ¯   )  2    ∑ i = 1  n  ( S i   -  S  ¯   )  2         2      (1c) PBIAS  =  100   ×   ∑ i  ( O i   -  S i  )   ∑ i  O i        (1d) KGE  =  1  -  ( r  -  1 )  2   +  ( α  -  1 )  2   +  ( β  -  1 )  2      ,    α  =  σ S  σ o     ,   β  =  μ s  μ o           (1e) KGE SS   =   1  -  1  -  KGE  2         Here, Si  and Oi   represent the simulated and observed streamflow for the ith observation, respectively, while O  ¯      represents the mean value of Oi  . SSR (Sum of Squared Residuals) is the sum of the squared differences between the simulated runoff values and the observed runoff values. SST (Total Sum of Squares) is the sum of the squared differences between the observed runoff values and their mean. The coefficient α (=σs /σo ) measures the relative variability between observed and simulated variability, β  (=µs  /µo  ) is the ratio between simulated and observed mean, and r  is the linear correlation coefficient between Si  and Oi  (De la Fuente et al., 2023 ). When comparing R2 and NSE, it is important to note that R2 measures the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable(s), ranging from 0 to 1. A value of 1 indicates a perfect linear relationship between simulated and observed values. In contrast, NSE evaluates the model's predictive power by comparing the mean squared differences between observed and simulated values, normalized by the variance of the observed values. NSE values range from negative infinity to 1, with 1 indicating a perfect match. Unlike R2, NSE accounts for both systematic and random errors, offering a more comprehensive assessment of model performance (Krause et al., 2005 ).  3.2 Bias-correction approach To correct for systematic biases in RCM outputs (Teutschbein and Seibert, 2012 ) we use the QDM technique developed by Cannon et al. (2015) . This technique serves a dual function: preserving the projected climate data variability within the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and adjusting the systematic biases in the CDF of RCM outputs to align with the observed distribution. The QDM method is governed by the following equations.(2) S ∗   ( t )   =   F o , c  - 1    F m , p    [ S m , p   ( t )  ]      . δ r   ( t )  ,          for  precipitation    F o , c  - 1    F m , p    [ S m , p   ( t )  ]      + δ α   ( t )  ,      for  temperature                Here, Sm,p (t) is used in this study to represent the climate series simulated at time t during the projection period. The CDF of Sm,p , which varies with time, is represented by Fm,p , while F o , c  - 1      represents the inverse CDF obtained from the observed climate series during the control period. The bias-corrected Sm,p  is denoted as s *. The difference in quantiles between the control period and the projected time t for the precipitation series is expressed as δr (t) in relation to the relative shift, and as δα (t) in relation to the absolute shift. These values are obtained through the following process.(3a) δ r   ( t )   =  S m , p   ( t )   F m , c  - 1    F m , p    [ S m , p   ( t )  ]            (3b) δ α   ( t )   =  S m , p   ( t )   -  F m , c  - 1    F m , p    [ S m , p   ( t )  ]          The inverse CDF obtained from the modeled climate series during the control period is represented by F m , c  - 1      (Tong et al., 2021 ). To estimate the CDF, this study utilizes empirical distributions derived from monthly aggregated climate data using a rolling window methodology. Here, our methodology closely resembles that of Cannon et al. (2015)  in which several key considerations guide the preference for monthly data. By utilizing monthly data, we aim to reduce the noise and variability that are inherent in daily data, thereby improving the robustness of our analysis. Additionally, working with monthly data enhances computational efficiency, enabling more efficient processing and modeling. Moreover, aligning our data with the hydrological model entails accurately incorporating monthly climatic signals into daily data, ensuring consistency and enhancing the accuracy of our results. This methodological choice effectively facilitates comprehensive bias correction across short-term and long-term climatic variability.  3.3 Hydro-climatic extremes indices Two categories can be identified for the classification of hydro-climatic extreme indices: extreme climate indices (ECI) and extreme streamflow indices (ESI). Table 2   lists the ECI, offering a comprehensive overview of the distinct persistence, frequency, and amplitude characteristics exhibited by precipitation and temperature extremes. The indices encompass metrics such as the maximum 1-day precipitation (Rx1day), the count of heavy precipitation days (R25mm), and the number of summer days (SU) when the daily maximum temperature surpasses 25 ◦C. These have been chosen from a selection provided by ETCCDI (Ali et al., 2019; Brönnimann et al., 2018; Chapagain et al., 2021; Coppola et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022; Fathian et al., 2022 ; Ge et al., 2021b; Gupta et al., 2020; Jeferson de Medeiros et al., 2022; Pervin and Khan, 2022; Thomas et al., 2023; Tye et al., 2022; WMO, 2009; Zarrin et al., 2021 ). Our study aims to evaluate how climate change affects extreme climatic conditions by quantifying absolute changes in variables such as R10mm, R25mm, TXn, TNn, DTR, CDD, CWD, SU, TR, TXx, TNx, as well as relative changes in R95pTOT, R99pTOT, Rx1day, Rx5day, and SDII. The mean values within future timeframes (2024–2050, 2051–2080) will be compared to those in a control period (1958–2020). To complement these, we investigate three different measures of extreme streamflow. These include the annual maximum streamflow observed within a single day (Qx1day) and within a time span of five days (Qx5day) (Hu et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2023; Stewart et al., 2015 ). Additionally, the lowest cumulative streamflow over a period of seven days (Qn7day) is also examined (Dai et al., 2022; Gudmundsson et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022 ) (see Table 2 ). The streamflow indices Qx1day, Qx5day, and Qn7day are valuable for evaluating hydrologic extremes related to high flows over 1-day and 5-day periods, as well as low flows over a 7-day period. These indices offer valuable insights into potential occurrences of extreme drought and flood conditions. The evaluation of flood and drought risk levels in the face of climate change is essential, considering their potential to inflict significant harm on infrastructure, water resource management, and the delicate balance of aquatic habitats (Dai et al., 2022; Stewart et al., 2015 ). To calculate these indices, the daily streamflow data generated by the HBV model is utilized, incorporating both historical and future scenarios.   4 Results 4.1 HBV model calibration and validation We use the calibrated version of the HBV model reported in Jahanshahi et al. (2022b)  (Table 3  ). Fig. 3   (a-d) displays boxplots of HBV model performance during the calibration and validation periods. The HBV simulation matches the observed flows in the 576 study catchments well, with NSE (KGEss) values ranging from 0.50 (0.52) to 0.92 (0.94). These values indicate a reasonable degree of agreement between the simulated and observed values, suggesting that the model captures a significant proportion of the observed variability. Furthermore, R2  values, ranging from 0.78 to 0.96, demonstrate a robust linear relationship between the simulated and observed flows. These high R2  values reinforce the accuracy of the HBV model in explaining the variance in the dependent variable based on the independent variables. Moreover, the simulation demonstrates relatively low PBIAS values ranging from −1.14 to 6.05. The NSE (KGEss) values are 0.45 (0.48) and 0.88 (0.90), indicating a reasonable degree of agreement, while the R2  values are 0.74 and 0.92, and the PBIAS values are −1.42 and 7.83 indicating relatively low bias. Fig. 3  (e-f) shows a visual comparison of monthly observed and simulated streamflow series for four selected catchments during the calibration period of 1993–2008. The model performance in simulating daily streamflow in the evaluating period is shown in Fig. 4   for two of the sample catchments (2009–2013). Catchments 1 and 3 are situated in arid regions with mean annual precipitation of 238 mm and 264 mm, and mean annual temperatures of 25.7 °C and 24.9 °C, respectively. In contrast, catchments 2 and 4 are located in more humid areas with mean annual precipitation of 342 mm and 426 mm, and mean annual temperatures of 19.3 °C and 16.2 °C, respectively. The areas of catchments 1, 2, 3, and 4 are 1,882 km2 , 3,456 km2 , 793 km2 , and 974 km2 , respectively (four sample catchments are represented by red circles in Fig. 1 ). The HBV model performs well during calibration and demonstrates a satisfactory level of performance during evaluation for the provided sample catchments. Notably, during the evaluation period, the simulations in both catchments exhibit a tendency to underestimate peak flows, as is expected due to the nature of the calibration processes (see Gupta et al., 2009 ). Nevertheless, the simulations generally capture the peak flow behavior during both the calibration and evaluation periods across various other catchments. In general, the overall performance of the catchment-wide HBV simulation is deemed satisfactory, allowing for meaningful assessments of climate change impacts to be conducted. Table 4   shows the statistics of characteristics for 576 catchments.  4.2 Bias correction of climate variables To assess the efficacy of the QDM method, we performed a comparative analysis of the climate variables, including precipitation, minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and mean temperature, obtained for both the corrected and uncorrected RCM datasets. These variables were then compared with the observed climate variables for the period from 1958 to 2020, which served as a robust benchmark for our evaluation. The initial CDF curves of the RCM climate variables exhibit significant disparities between the observed and original data, prior to the implementation of bias correction. Implementation of the QDM correction method leads to a considerable reduction in this discrepancy. Figure S1  in the Supplementary Materials  provides a comprehensive comparison across 576 study catchments, focusing specifically on the month of January. The employed bias correction method demonstrates its effectiveness as the mean values for each month of the observed and corrected RCM climate variables (shown in Figures S2-S6 ) depict a nearly negligible absolute bias. Fig. 5   shows the Q-Q plots for the ECIs averaged at the catchment scale annually. The plots compare the observed values with both the corrected and uncorrected outputs of the Had-REM RCMs. The comparison reveals notable disparities between the uncorrected precipitation and temperature indices derived from the Had-REM RCM and the observed values. However, the corrected versions of the indices demonstrate improved agreement, as evidenced by their alignment with the 1:1 reference line depicted in Fig. 5 . An overestimation trend is evident in the Q-Q plot for the RX1day indices of both the corrected and uncorrected Had-REM RCM, particularly at higher quantiles, suggesting overestimation (Fig. 5 a). Additionally, the QDM method appears to be less effective for three indicators (namely SDII, CDD, and CWD) even after applying bias correction techniques (see Fig. 5 c, 5e, and 5f). The emphasis of the QDM method, as indicated by this observation, is primarily on capturing the overall distribution of the precipitation amount rather than specifically addressing the characteristics of wet and dry spells. The reliability of conclusions derived from using only the original RCM outputs for calculating ECIs or simulating a hydrological model is questionable. Despite a few shortcomings in accurately reproducing historical climate extremes, the QDM method is widely recognized as an effective approach for tackling such difficulties.  4.3 Future projections in temperature and precipitation We first assess the response of both temperature and precipitation to climate change, as they are used in calculating hydroclimatic indices. In Fig. 6  , the catchment-averaged annual climate series is visualized, incorporating data from 5 RCMs that have been corrected. The series covers the control period spanning from 1958 to 2020, as well as two future time windows: the near-future (2024–2050) and the far-future (2051–2080) for both RCP 2.6 and 8.5 scenarios. We observe that, despite fluctuations, the general trends in the RCM projections throughout the 21st century show similarities – in both the RCP 8.5 and RCP 2.6 scenarios:• Precipitation demonstrates relatively insignificant changes.  • Temperature undergoes a noteworthy and moderate rise.    The statistical variations resulting from the use of different RCMs and historical data are reflected in the boxplots presented in Fig. 6 e to 6 h, which depict the relative precipitation changes and absolute temperature changes between the control and future periods based on RCM outputs. Compared to the RCMs ensemble median, the RCP 2.6 scenario indicates that:• Precipitation is projected to decrease by 6.1 % in the near future, and by 8.3 % in the far future.  • Mean temperature is projected to increase by approximately 0.38 °C in the near future, and by 3.38 °C in the far-future period.    Conversely, the RCP 8.5 scenario indicates:• Precipitation is projected to decrease by 7.1 %. in the near future, and by 13.3 % in the far-future period.  • A substantial reduction in precipitation for the wettest RCM output, with a specific decrease of 14.1 % from 2051 to 2080.  • A substantial increase in mean temperature in the near future, with a projected rise from 0.76 °C to 4.28 °C in the far future.    Overall, the changes projected for the minimum and maximum temperatures display a certain level of consistency with the changes observed in the mean temperature. Similarities in precipitation changes between RCP2.6 and RCP8.5 scenarios can be attributed to spatial and temporal resolution limitations, inherent statistical variability, and the wide range of ensemble members. These factors lead to occasional similarities in precipitation patterns despite different scenarios. This conclusion aligns with findings by Doulabian et al. (2021)  and Taie Semiromi and Koch (2024)  in Iran.  4.4 Future changes in extreme climate indices The climatic extremes of the catchment-average were analyzed and compared for the near and far future periods, as depicted in Fig. 7  . These projections are based on the RCM ensemble from Table 1 , utilizing RCP2.6 and RCP8.5 scenarios, and we made a comparison with the control period (1958–2020). For both RCP scenarios, the ensemble median projections consistently indicate an upward trend in most extreme precipitation indices.• For instance, the projected changes show that SDII will experience a gradual rise of 10.7 % and 11.9 % for RCP 2.6, and 13.8 % and 15.2 % for RCP 8.5, from the near to far future.  • Under both RCPs, Rx1day and CDD exhibit a comparable gradual rise, similar to SDII. However, Rx1day under RCP 8.5 is projected to experience a considerable increase (37.6 %) in the far future.  • Under RCP 2.6, the R10 mm and R25mm indices experience a consistent increase of approximately 23.9 days and 17 days, respectively, across the two future periods, while the Rx5day index under RCP 8.5 gradually increase over time (e.g., when considering RCP 8.5, the projected rise in Rx5day is expected to be around 27.8 % in the near future, but this rise intensifies to 29.47 % in the far future).    When compared to the reference period, the projected CWD, reveals a consistent increasing trend, which translates to a decrease of approximately 11.1 days in the far future for both RCPs. Moreover, R95pTOT and R99pTOT exhibit an increase of 0.45 % and 0.6 %, respectively, in the far future for RCP 2.6 and a corresponding increase of 0.39 % and 2.1 % for RCP 8.5. According to the ensemble median estimates of multiple RCMs, a significant proportion of extreme temperature indices undergo an increase under both RCP scenarios for both future periods.• In the near future for RCP 2.6, there is a gradual increase in SU from 115.2 days to 122.4 days.  • Similarly, in the far future, TR is expected to rise from 49.9 days to 53.5 days.  • Likewise, in the far future for RCP 8.5, these indices are projected to experience a gradual rise from 117.7 days to 137.5 days for SU in the near future and from 51.66 days to 55.8 days for TR.    The larger rise in SU relative to TR indicates that climate change will have a more pronounced impact on the number of summer days compared to tropical nights. Moreover, for RCP 2.6 in the near future, the indices TXx, TNx, TXn, and TNn undergo increases of 31.1, 25.4, 13.6, and 3.7 °C, respectively. Under RCP 8.5, it is anticipated that these indices will experience increases of 32.3 °C, 27.7 °C, 14.7 °C, and 4.6 °C, respectively. By the year 2080, these increases are expected to become more pronounced, reaching up to 34.1, 29.5, 16.2, and 5.1 °C (far future, 8.5), respectively. Climate change seems to have less impact on the diurnal temperature range (DTR), as evidenced by the range of variation between −1.09 °C and 1.3 °C, indicating a relatively minor change in the median values. Looking ahead to the far future, there is a significant projection of increased extreme temperature indices for RCP 8.5. Furthermore, the majority of precipitation and temperature indices (excluding R25mm) are expected to experience a larger increase under RCP 8.5 when compared to RCP 2.6.  4.5 Future projections for extreme streamflow indices The assessment of climate change effects in this study is based on the comparison of relative changes in ESI derived from ensemble estimates of RCMs, specifically for the 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 quantiles (i.e., Q25, median, and Q75). The spatial pattern of the Qx1day index during the control period is depicted in Fig. 8  , along with the changes observed in this index due to climate change during two future period windows. Overall, there is notable variation in the spatial patterns of changes in ESI, as projected by different RCM scenarios. The observed Qx1day spatial distribution, representing the occurrence of extreme floods in Iran from 1989 to 2008, is illustrated in Fig. 8 a. The figure clearly illustrates a noticeable range, spanning from roughly 140–341 m3 .s−1  in the western to southeastern part of the country, to approximately 409–543 m3 .s−1  in the interior western and northern regions. Fig. 8 b to 8 m demonstrate a consistent pattern of both decreasing and increasing trends in the Qx1day index across the country, compared to the control period, for both RCPs and the two future periods. Fig. 8 b-e present the outcomes of the RCM ensemble analysis, specifically highlighting the changes in the Q25 quantile over the country. Under RCP 2.6, notable increases in the Qx1day index are anticipated in the western, central, northeastern, and southeastern regions. The projected increases range from 7.9 % to 30.9 % for the near future period and 9 % to 37 % for the far future period. However, in the northern part of the country, below and west of the Caspian Sea, there is a significant likelihood of a decrease in the Qx1day index. The projected changes ranges from approximately −18.3 % to −42.9 % for the near future period and 15.9 % to 48 % for the far future period. Projections indicate significant rises in Qx1day for the northeastern and southeastern parts of the country under RCP 8.5. The estimated increases are approximately 17.2–43.6 % and 10.4–33.5 % for the near and far future periods, respectively. Furthermore, there is a slight increase of 3.2 % projected in some catchments, located in the northwestern part of the country, for the far future under RCP 2.6. However, under RCP 8.5, this slight increase is expected to decrease to 1.55 % and shift to the catchments in a lower region than the near future, still situated in the northwestern part of the country. Fig. 8 f-i depict the outcomes from analysis of multiple RCMs conducted as an ensemble, illustrating the changes in the country through the median values. Under RCP 2.6, the Qx1day is projected to undergo a substantial increase between 15.3 % to 40.9 % for the near future period and −15.4 % to 43 % for the far future period in the southeastern part of the country. The Qx1day index is projected to experience significant increases, ranging from approximately 33.4 % to 46.9 %, in catchments of the central part of the country during the near future under RCP 8.5. In the far future, a notable shift is expected to occur, with the area experiencing a significant increase in the Qx1day index (by 50.6 %) shifting towards the southeastern end of the country. Fig. 8 j-m depict the results obtained from the RCM ensemble analysis, specifically depicting the changes in the Q75 index across the country. Consideration of RCP 2.6 reveals noteworthy increases in the Qx1day index in the southwestern and northeastern parts of the country, reaching approximately 36.4 % to 57 % for the near future and around 27.6 % to 49.8 % for the far future. The Qx1day index is expected to undergo a substantial increase of approximately 37.1 % to 46.2 % in the central catchments of the country in the near future under RCP 8.5. In the far future, a substantial rise of around 22 % to 54.2 % is projected in the northeastern and southwestern parts. Furthermore, Qx5day demonstrates a similar pattern as Qx1day regarding the relative change in future periods compared to the control period, although the magnitude of change is relatively smaller for both RCPs (see Fig. S7 ). Fig. 9   presents the spatial distribution of Qn7day, revealing how this index changes during the control period and the subsequent effects of climate change within two future time windows. Fig. 9 a presents the spatial pattern of Qn7day, which serves as an indicator of hydrological droughts, from 1958 to 2020 in the study catchments. Qn7day demonstrates a spatial variability comparable to that of Qx1day, with a variation from around 37–130 m3 .s−1  in the western, northwestern, central and southeastern parts of the country to approximately 160–240 m3 .s−1  in the northern part of the country. The RCM ensemble Q25 reveals changes in Qn7day, indicating a predominant decline across most of the catchments as depicted in Fig. 9 b–e. In the catchments located at the southwestern and right-bottom corner of the Caspian Sea, notable decreases, estimated at 21.8–34.8 % and 16.1–27.6 % for the near and far future, respectively, are expected to occur under RCP 2.6. Under RCP 8.5, notable declines in Qn7day are anticipated across the right-bottom corner catchments of the Caspian Sea in the far future, with reductions ranging from 30 % to 48.2 %. These decreases are significantly larger compared to the projected decreases for the near future, for the mentioned catchments where they range from 9.8 % to 17 %. Furthermore, there are slight increases projected for Qn7day in some regions of the country. For instance, under RCP 2.6, these increases are estimated to be around 7.6–26.6 % and 2.7–17.5 % in the near and far future, respectively. Under RCP 8.5 in the near and far future, the anticipated increases range from 4-11.8 % and 14.6–38.4 %, respectively. Fig. 9 f–i illustrates the Qn7day changes with respect to the control period, as indicated by the future RCM ensemble median. For the near future under RCP 2.6, noteworthy rises in Qn7day are projected for the western, center, southeastern, and northeastern regions. These increases are estimated to range from 2.8 % to 11.9 %. However, there is a slight decrease of up to 21 % in the catchments bellow the Caspian Sea. In the far future, Qn7day is projected to exhibit a catchment-averaged increase ranging from 4.2 % to 16 %. The most substantial increases are anticipated in the northeastern catchments of the country. The projections for Qn7day under RCP 8.5 suggest an increase ranging from 4.7 % to 18.3 % in the near future. For the far future, several central catchments are projected to experience an increase of approximately 6.5 % to 17 %. In Fig. 9 j to m, the changes in the Q75 of Qn7day over the catchments are presented. The analysis suggests that Qn7day is expected to exhibit consistent country-wide increases under RCP 2.6. The Q75 of Qn7day is projected to exhibit increases of approximately 4.8 % to 20.7 % in the near future and 6.4 % to 27.4 % in the far future. According to the projections under RCP 8.5, Qn7day is anticipated to undergo an increase of approximately 15.1 % to 30.1 % in the near future. Moreover, in the far future under RCP 8.5, there is a likely of increase in Qn7day in the northwestern and northeastern parts of the country. The northwestern part is projected to experience increases ranging from 0.4 % to 7.8 %, while the northeastern part may see increases ranging from 7.9 % to 28.1 %. However, most catchments are expected to experience a decrease in Qn7day. Notably, the catchments located in the eastern vicinity of the Caspian Sea are expected to undergo a substantial decline in Qn7day in the future for both RCPs.   5 Discussion 5.1 QDM procedures For bias correction of the original RCM precipitation output using the QDM method, it is important to undertake two pre-processing steps. The first step involves the selection of an appropriate CDF, and the second step addresses the issue of the overestimated number of wet days since RCMs are generating trace amounts of precipitation (Dai et al., 2022 ). Precipitation intensities are often modeled using two commonly used distributions: the Gamma distribution (Amburn et al., 2015; Hrachowitz et al., 2010; Volosciuk et al., 2017; Wilks, 2019 ) and the Empirical distribution (Demirdjian et al., 2018; Langousis and Kaleris, 2014; Maloku et al., 2023; Serrano-Vincenti et al., 2020; Themeßl et al., 2012; Wang and Xuan, 2020 ). Moreover, when addressing the substantial number of days with trace wetness in RCM precipitation data, a previously employed technique involves the implementation of two methods: the dynamic threshold method (DTM) (Cardell et al., 2019 ) and the random replacement method (RRM) (Cannon et al., 2015 ). Under the RRM method, a day is designated as wet if the precipitation exceeds a trace threshold (e.g., 0.5 mm.day−1 ), and as dry if the precipitation is less than this threshold. Prior to bias correction, any trace values (precipitation below 0.5 mm.day−1 ) are replaced with randomly generated values denoted as x (which follows a uniform distribution within the range of 0 to 0.5) in both the observed and RCM modelled precipitation datasets. Once the bias correction process is finished, any precipitation values less than 0.5 are set to 0. The DTM involves setting a threshold that dynamically determines whether a day is classified as wet or dry. The constraint on the threshold is implemented to maintain the consistency of the dry-days ratio between the observed series and the calibrated series when comparing future and control simulated raw data. Assessment of the QDM's effectiveness involves the utilization of precipitation data from observed and simulated Had-REM RCM cases during the control period. To provide a comprehensive evaluation, different pre-processing procedures were implemented, allowing for a thorough analysis of the QDM's efficacy. The Benchmark Case in this study is established by employing the QDM technique, which encompasses Empirical CDF and RRM pre-processing procedures. For Case 1, the QDM is utilized with a Gamma CDF and RRM pre-processing procedures, whereas for Case 2, the QDM applies an Empirical CDF and DTM pre-processing procedures. Upon comparison of Fig. 5 a-i and Figure S8 , it was noted that the QDM applied in both the benchmark Case and Case 1 showed similar performance when adjusting variables such as CDD, SDII, CWD, and R25m. However, the QDM applied in the benchmark Case showed a distinct superiority in accurately adjusting the R95pTOT, R99pTOT, Rx1day, Rx5day, and R10mm indices as compared to Case 1. When Fig. 5 a–i is compared with Figure S9 , it becomes evident that the QDM technique in the Benchmark Case demonstrates similar performance to the QDM technique in Case 2 when it comes to correcting the CDD, SDII, Rx1day, Rx5day, and CWD indices. However, the QDM implemented in the Benchmark Case displays a remarkable advantage when it comes to correcting the R10mm, R95pTOT, R25mm, and R99pTOT indices. Hence, according to our results, we recommended the RRM pre-processing procedures and an Empirical CDF as they prove beneficial for the bias correction of precipitation output when using the QDM.  5.2 Relationship between streamflow and extreme climate indices The relatively high Pearson correlation coefficients, which exceed 0.60, observed between the indices representing extreme high-flow events (Qx1day and Qx5day) and those for extreme precipitation (Rx1day, Rx5day, R95pTOT, and R99pTOT) (as displayed in Figures S10 a and b), indicate a substantial correlation between floods and intense precipitation in the study catchments. For instance, the correlation coefficients between the Qx1day and Rx1day in arid and warm temperate catchments, namely in western, northern, and northeastern areas, demonstrate a higher degree of statistical significance compared to those in the snow catchments (refer to fig. S11 ).
