This suggests that the influence of extreme precipitation events on local flooding is more prominent in selected catchments, and it varies depending on the specific location and climate conditions. Moreover, based on the information provided in Figure S10  of the Supplementary Materials , it is evident that the extreme high-flow and extreme temperature indices exhibit a minimal correlation. However, when examining the correlation between Qn7day and extreme precipitation indices, it becomes evident that the strength of this correlation is considerably weaker when compared to the correlation observed between Qx1day (or Qx5day) and precipitation indices (as shown in Figure S10 c). This is mainly due to the fact that changes in hydrological drought cannot be solely attributed to variations in precipitation; but they can also be impacted by additional contributing factors. For instance, increased evapotranspiration resulting from higher temperatures could lead to a reduction in streamflow. These results align with the findings of Dai et al. (2022) , who concluded that extreme precipitation indices demonstrate a more robust correlation with ESI compared to extreme temperature indices in a large river basin of China. Moreover, the impact of precipitation minus evapotranspiration changes on drought variability was found to be more substantial in a large river basin of Japan, as revealed by Hu et al. (2017) , in contrast to alterations in precipitation alone. Limitations . Two crucial aspects requiring further research are evident. First, uncertainties may be present in different modeling components, including scenarios of climate change, methods for bias correction, and hydrological models. Despite addressing uncertainties arising from RCMs through the use of ensemble quantiles (median, Q25, and Q75), we acknowledge that uncertainties associated with the QDM and HBV hydrological model have not been considered. Further, it is worth considering that the QDM method's capacity to handle changes in dry and wet periods is limited, which can lead to increased uncertainty in the corrected precipitation dataset. In addition, the HBV calibration and evaluation typically rely on comparing runoff data at a daily resolution, which may not offer a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics associated with extreme runoff events. To enhance the accuracy in assessing hydro-climatic extremes, additional HBV validation for low flows, peak flows, and ESI may be required to mitigate uncertainties. Second, the hydrological cycle is under significant pressure from three notable factors, namely continuous land use change and climate change (Arantes et al., 2021; Ekness and Randhir, 2015; El-Khoury et al., 2015; Goyal and Surampalli, 2018; Haleem et al., 2022; Lucas-Borja et al., 2020 ), and water withdrawals (Döll et al., 2012 ; L. Wang et al., 2022). Over the course of around 60 years into the future, as examined in this study, it is expected that intense human activities will bring about significant alterations in land use patterns, consequently influencing the occurrence of extreme runoff in the Iranian study catchments. Future studies are necessary to address this requirement.   6 Conclusions The primary focus of this study was a thorough assessment of potential climate change effects on hydro-climatic extremes within a large dataset of Iranian catchments. An integrated assessment modeling framework incorporating a range of components, including CORDEX RCM ensemble, the QDM method, the HBV hydrological model, ETCCDI indices, and extreme streamflow indices (QX1day, QX5day, and Qn7day), was used to conduct this evaluation. The QDM method was used to correct the temperature and precipitation data for both near and far future timeframes. Data from five CORDEX RCMs under RCP 2.6 and 8.5 scenarios were used for this purpose. The assessment of hydrological and climate extremes involved the use of extreme streamflow and ETCCDI indices, respectively. The projected climate data was linked with extreme streamflow indices using the HBV model. In the future, catchment-average precipitation is projected to decrease slightly, but with no remarkable declines in magnitudes, in relation to the control period. Under the RCP 8.5 scenario, temperature is anticipated to undergo a significant increase, by as much as ∼ 4.28 °C in the far future. Further, the projections indicate a rising trend for most of the extreme precipitation indices. Under both RCPs, a notable increase is projected for nearly all extreme temperature indices, albeit with varying magnitudes. These discrepancies in magnitude imply that the indices exhibit diverse responses to the influence of climate change. In particular, during the far period under RCP 8.5, the increase in the majority of extreme temperature indices is noteworthy, albeit with varying magnitudes. The study reveals that the catchments under investigation are expected to undergo a slight increase in wet conditions and a significant change in the future, involving more frequent and intense precipitation events, along with heightened temperature extremes under both RCPs. A substantial increase in the annual maximum 1-day streamflow is projected in the western, central, northeastern, and southeastern regions under RCP 2.6. During the far future and under RCP 8.5, on the contrary, this notable rise is projected to be observed in some catchments within the central region. Additionally, in the near future for RCP 2.6, the western, central, southeastern, and northeastern regions of the country are projected to experience substantial rises in annual minimum 7-day streamflow, while certain central catchments will be impacted in the far future for RCP 8.5. Our analysis of the link between extreme climate and streamflow indices indicates a strong relationship between the extreme high-flow indices and the Rx1day, Rx5day, R95pTOT, and R99pTOT indices. Of course, we recognize that certain limitations, as mentioned previously, require further investigation in future work.
1 Introduction In northern rivers, water becomes supercooled as the river loses heat to the colder overlying air during the late fall or early winter. Frazil ice particles form in the supercooled and turbulent water column, and anchor ice may form on underwater objects including the river bed. Anchor ice has been shown to be initiated through two processes: the nucleation of ice crystals and the accretion of frazil ice particles on submerged surfaces (Tsang, 1982 ). It then grows through continuous frazil accretion and in-situ growth of ice crystals (Kempema and Ettema, 2016 ). Anchor ice may be released from the bottom due to thermal or mechanical processes. Thermal release occurs as warm water weakens or melts the bond between anchor ice and the substrate. Mechanical release occurs when the buoyancy and hydrodynamic forces acting on the anchor ice overcome the resisting forces due to the ice-substrate bond and the submerged weight (Ghobrial and Loewen, 2021 ). Anchor ice formation can change river bed morphology (Stickler et al., 2010; Turcotte and Morse, 2013; Rødtang et al., 2023 ). This may cause rapidly varying water levels, impacting river hydrology during freeze-up (Turcotte et al., 2014 ), and posing a flood risk to riverine communities (Kempema et al., 2017; Kempema et al., 2019 ). Large anchor ice dams formed downstream of reservoirs may reduce the hydraulic head available for hydropower generation (Girling and Groeneveld, 1999 ). Fish habitats are also likely affected due to anchor ice formation, which forces fish to other areas, freezes fish eggs and juveniles, and reduces the transport of oxygenated flow into and through the substrate (Bergeron and Enders, 2013 ). Released anchor ice pans have been shown to contain a significant amount of sediment, contributing to the annual sediment budget of a river (Kempema and Ettema, 2011; Turcotte et al., 2011; Kalke et al., 2017 ). Anchor ice release may also generate anchor ice waves in rivers, which reduces the stability of the ice cover downstream, inducing the formation of freeze-up ice jams and potential ice jam flooding (Jasek et al., 2015 ). Laboratory experiments have been conducted to study the evolution and properties of anchor ice in a counter-rotating flume (Doering et al., 2001; Qu and Doering, 2007 ) and an open channel flume (Kerr et al., 2002 ). Kerr et al. (2002)  found that anchor ice initiation and growth occurred via frazil accretion and that the growth rates during the initial, transitional, and final stages became progressively smaller. They observed that tail, scale, and ball shaped accumulations formed during the initial stage as the Froude number F r    increased. The growth rates during the final stage ranged from 0.4 to 0.8 cm/h and increased with the increase of F r   . Doering et al. (2001)  demonstrated that a linear relationship described anchor ice growth during the entire growth period, with the observed growth rates varying from 0.3 to 0.7 cm/h and peaking when F r    was 0.27. Doering et al. (2001)  and Kerr et al. (2002)  found that anchor ice release was related to the Reynolds number R e   . Qu and Doering (2007)  observed that anchor ice released more easily when it formed on smaller gravels. They reported anchor ice densities that ranged from 160 to 400 kg/m3 , increasing with the increase of R e   , and anchor ice porosities that varied from 0.59 to 0.88. Comprehensive river ice process models include the simulation of anchor ice formation and release (Malenchak, 2011; Blackburn and She, 2019; Pan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021 ). The initiation of anchor ice in these models is through frazil deposition when the water becomes supercooled. Anchor ice growth and decay are simulated using an algorithm developed by Wang and Shen (1993) , which accounts for frazil accretion, thermal growth and decay due to heat exchange between anchor ice and the turbulent flow, and heating due to solar radiation. The models simulate thermal release of anchor ice when supercooling ends (Blackburn and She, 2019; Yang et al., 2021 ) or when the ice-substrate bond is weakened by the melting of the underside of anchor ice accumulation (Malenchak, 2011; Pan et al., 2020 ). The models assume that mechanical release occurs only when the buoyancy force acting on anchor ice exceeds the resistance forces. Anchor ice-related parameters in the models are typically set based on judgment or calibrated along with dozens of other ice-related parameters. The accuracy of anchor ice simulations is generally indirectly assessed by comparing modeled and observed water levels and discharges when anchor ice is predicted to be present (e.g., Pan et al., 2020 ). Yang et al. (2021)  simulated the anchor ice processes on the North Saskatchewan River during the 2019 freeze-up season using the River1D  model, and the modeled anchor ice thickness was directly compared with the field measurements. Observations and measurements of anchor ice have also been made in rivers. Anchor ice was found to form preferentially on coarse sediments (Wigle, 1970; Lind et al., 2016 ) and in steeper sections of the rivers (Turcotte et al., 2014 ). Tsang (1982)  found that anchor ice tended to form on clear cold nights with strong winds, low humidity, and lower flow rates, especially after a cold, windy, and cloudy day. Anchor ice that formed during the night usually released the next day during daylight hours when increasing solar radiation warmed the water to above 0 ℃ (Ghobrial et al., 2020 ). Multi-day anchor ice events have also been observed when cloudy skies prevented heating by solar radiation (Tremblay et al., 2014 ). Nafziger et al. (2017)  analyzed anchor ice formation and release indirectly from onshore photographs, hydrographs, and water temperature measurements in three rivers. They found that anchor ice initiation occurred when there was a net heat loss at the water surface and the river was supercooled, and most releases occurred when there was a net heat gain at the water surface and the air temperature was higher than −15 ℃. Terada et al. (1999)  found that anchor ice in Niuppu River, Japan only formed at locations where F r    ranged from 0.2 to 1 and when the air temperature was below −10 ℃. Anchor ice was observed at smaller F r    when the air temperature was lower. Stickler and Alfredsen (2009)  observed two anchor ice types in three northern streams. Type I formed in lower turbulence areas on top of the substrate, and Type II formed in higher turbulence areas in the interstitial spaces of the substrate. They found that Type II had a smoother surface and higher density, and R e    can be used to differentiate the two types of accumulations. The structure and porosity of anchor ice accumulations forming in rivers have been investigated. Hirayama et al. (1997)  observed that anchor ice accumulations in the Niuppu River consisted of platelets and needle-like crystals. Kempema and Ettema (2009)  stated that disc-shaped frazil ice crystals were never seen in the interior of anchor ice masses in the Laramie River, USA, and frazil crystals started to grow and change shape as soon as they attached to the river bed. Dubé et al. (2014)  used computed axial tomography (CAT) technology and the thin sections method to study the inner structures of anchor ice accumulations and anchor ice dams in the Montmorency River watershed, Canada. They also did not identify individual disc-shaped frazil ice crystals but observed large fixed-frazil ice crystals growing in situ in both anchor ice types. Anchor ice porosities reported in the literature vary widely from 0.02 to 0.84 (Parkinson, 1984; Stickler and Alfredsen, 2009 ), with most values ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 (Jasek, 2016; Kempema and Ettema, 2016; Pei et al., 2021 ). Only three studies directly and continuously measured anchor ice in rivers (Kempema and Ettema, 2016; Ghobrial and Loewen, 2021; Ghobrial et al., 2023 ). Kempema and Ettema (2016)  deployed an acrylic box with a wedge-weir screen mounted on one surface in the Laramie River, and they recorded images of anchor ice growing on the inside of the screen. They captured anchor ice growth on twelve nights, and in each event, anchor ice was initiated by frazil ice accretion. They found that the crystal growth rates were larger during the initial growth period, ranging between approximately 1 and 4 cm/h, and then decreased. Crystals stopped growing after anchor ice completely covered the screen, and the largest ice crystal reached ∼4 cm. Kempema and Ettema (2016)  concluded that anchor ice forming on the wedge-weir screen had a similar morphology to anchor ice that formed nearby on the river bed. Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  developed an underwater imaging system to monitor anchor ice formation, growth, and release on an artificial substrate in the North Saskatchewan River, Canada. They captured six single-day anchor ice events and found that anchor ice started to form when the solar radiation was negligible and released either prior to sunrise or in the early afternoon. Both in-situ crystal growth and frazil accretion were observed contributing to anchor ice growth, but these two mechanisms did not occur simultaneously. Anchor ice growth rates due to in-situ crystal growth ranged from 1.3 to 2.0 cm/h and from 0.3 to 0.9 cm/h due to frazil accretion. Anchor ice release always occurred while the water was supercooled, and three release modes were identified: lifting of the entire anchor ice accumulation, shearing of anchor ice layers, and rapid release of the entire accumulation. Ghobrial et al. (2023)  deployed a sonar to measure the anchor ice accumulation on a water intake in Mille-Iles River, Canada. They identified eight anchor ice accumulation events with durations varying from 7 to > 92 h. A threshold value of 4.5 °C.min of cumulative degree minutes of supercooling (CDMS) was determined to be a reliable indicator for the start of an event. The thickness of the accumulations was observed to increase at rates ranging from 0.46 to 4.0 cm/h and decrease at rates varying from 0.27 to 4 cm/h, and the release always occurred when supercooling had ended. These three field studies provided insightful knowledge of anchor ice evolution in rivers. However, because of the challenges typically encountered when conducting these types of measurements, the scope and volume of field data that have been collected are quite limited. In addition, the findings from these previous studies are not entirely consistent, particularly with regard to anchor ice growth mechanisms, growth rates, and the mechanics and timings of anchor ice release. Clearly, additional field measurements are needed to help resolve these inconsistencies and to supplement the existing datasets, and this was the motivation for the current study. In this study, simultaneous observations of anchor ice evolution and weather and flow conditions were conducted in two regulated Canadian rivers. The suspended frazil concentration was also measured in one of these rivers. A total of six anchor ice events were captured, and the in-depth analysis of the characteristics of each event, along with the corresponding hydrometeorological conditions, is presented. The mechanisms responsible for the growth and decay of each anchor ice accumulation and the temporal variations of the growth and decay rates are discussed. The simultaneous measurements of anchor ice growth and suspended frazil concentration during one event allowed the frazil accretion rate to be estimated with reasonable confidence for the first time.  2 Study sites The anchor ice measurements were conducted on two regulated rivers, the North Saskatchewan River (NSR) and the Kananaskis River (KR), as shown in Fig. 1  . The NSR is a large and irregular meandering river, and the measurement site on the NSR was adjacent to the EPCOR’s E.L. Smith water treatment plant (WTP) (53°28′30.1″N, 113°36′54.9″W). In the Edmonton reach of the NSR consisting of the study site, the mean annual flow rate is 220 m3 /s, the average channel width is 136 m, and the average bed slope is 0.00035 (Kellerhals et al., 1972 ). The NSR study site is ∼225 km and ∼415 km downstream of the Brazeau and Bighorn dams, respectively, and hydropeaking at the two dams typically causes water level fluctuations of 0.3–0.5 m during the wintertime (Ghobrial and Loewen, 2021 ). Freeze-up at the study site typically occurs from early November to late November or early December. The KR is a small-steep mountain river, and the measurement site was at the Fortress Bridge (50°47′14.1″N, 115°09′56.7″W), which was ∼10 km downstream of the Pocaterra dam. The average bed slope is 0.005 for the reach from Fortress Bridge to 10 km downstream (McFarlane et al., 2017 ), and the average channel width of the river is 32 m (Kellerhals et al., 1972 ). Daily discharge in winter varies between 1 and 20 m3 /s due to hydropeaking (Government of Alberta, 2023 ), which normally prevents the formation of intact ice cover at the KR study site.  3 Field measurements The anchor ice camera system originally developed by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  was modified to measure the anchor ice in this study, with the configuration shown in Fig. 2  . It was made by connecting an artificial substrate with an imaging system. Similar to the original setup, the imaging system consisted of a 36.3 MP Nikon D800 Digital Single Lens Reflex (DSLR) camera (equipped with a Nikon AF NIKKOR 35 mm f/2D lens) and a Nikon SB910 Speedlight flash. The camera and flash were housed in an Aquatica AD800 and a Subal SN-910 waterproof housings, respectively. The artificial substrate was created by attaching cobble-gravel-sized stones with sizes varying from 3.8 to 12.5 cm to a 50 cm × 50 cm (length × width) plywood base. An RBR temperature logger (accuracy: ±0.002 ℃) was mounted on the substrate to measure water temperatures every 1 min. More detailed descriptions of this anchor ice camera system are available in Ghobrial and Loewen (2021) . Three main alterations were made to the original setup: (1) The heat trace cable, wrapped around the two underwater housings to prevent ice from forming on their lenses, was extended using a long power cord and connected to a nearby 120-volt outlet at the NSR site. A portable gasoline generator was used previously, and this required frequent visits to the site to add fuel to the generator. However, for the KR deployment, the ice forming on the underwater housings was manually wiped away since no power source was available. (2) Scaling rods made of PVC tubes, each with a diameter of 1.3 cm and a height of 30 cm, were installed on the substrate to determine the pixel size of the captured images (i.e., μm/pixel). The front rod was removed in the later events since any visible anchor ice was almost always behind the front rod. (3) A Van Essen TD-Diver (accuracy: ±1 cmH2 O) was mounted at the bottom of the PVC frame to measure the local water depth every 5 min. Based on the laboratory test of the imaging system underwater, the aperture, ISO, and shutter speed of the camera were set to f/22, 5000, and 1/320, respectively. The distance from the camera lens to the midpoint of the depth of field on the artificial substrate was 53.8 cm, giving a pixel size of 59 μm/pixel and a field of view of 43 cm × 29 cm (width × height). TIFF format images, each with a dimension of 7360 pixels × 4912 pixels (width × height), were captured by the camera. Images on the NSR were taken every 3 min during the first two events and 4 min afterward, while the sampling interval of images was 10 min on the KR. These interval settings provided adequate memory card space and battery life for a 24-hour camera deployment. The anchor ice camera system was deployed on the NSR from November 9 to 20, 2021. The deployment location was approximately 60 m from the riverbank, where the water depth ranged between 0.5 and 1 m during the deployment. The imaging system was serviced daily on the NSR to change the camera batteries and memory cards. This process usually took about 40 min, during which no images were collected. The setup was deployed ∼5 m from the riverbank on the KR from 12:00 on January 30 to 15:00 on January 31, 2023, in water depth that varied from 0.4 to 0.8 m during the measurement. At the measurement sites on both rivers, a trail camera was mounted on the tree on the riverbank to monitor the surface ice conditions every 5 or 30 min at the KR and NSR, respectively. Meteorological data for the NSR was obtained from a weather station installed at the E.L. Smith WTP on October 7, 2021, approximately 90 m from the riverbank and 10 m above the water surface (see Fig. 1 a). The weather station measured the solar radiation, air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and direction, and atmospheric pressure every 1 min and logged the data every 10 min. A more detailed description of the station’s data logger and sensors can be found in Yang et al. (2023a) . An Apogee SN-500-SS net radiometer (accuracy: ±5% of readings) was installed on the riverbank at 7 m above the water surface on November 9, 2021. It measured downwelling longwave radiation with a sampling interval of 1 min and a logging interval of 10 min. The meteorological data for the KR deployment, including hourly air temperature, wind speed, and relative humidity, were obtained from the Alberta Agriculture and Forestry’s Kananaskis Boundary Auto station, which was ∼16 km from the measurement site (see Fig. 1 b). Hourly solar radiation data were obtained from the University of Calgary’s Barrier Lake Field Station (51°01′38.2″N, 115°02′02.0″W) (University of Calgary, 2023 ), approximately 28 km from the measurement site. The atmospheric pressure was assumed to be constant and equal to the value measured by a Van Essen TD-Diver before it was deployed into the river at 07:00 on January 31, 2023. Cloud fraction data with a 3-hour interval were downloaded from the Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC)’s Calgary Intl A weather station (51°06′50.0″N, 114°01′13.0″W; Climate ID: 3031092), which was ∼88 km from the study site. A 546 kHz Shallow Water Ice Profiling Sonar (SWIPS, ASL Environmental Sciences Inc.) was used to monitor suspended frazil ice, and a 2 MHz AquaDopp® (Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler, Nortek) was used to measure flow velocities during the NSR deployment. The SWIPS was set up with a pulse length of 34 μs, gain setting of 4, ping frequency of 1 Hz, and sound speed of 1403 m/s. The maximum sampling range of the SWIPS was set to 4 m with a vertical resolution of 1.1 cm. The AquaDopp® was programmed to collect 4 m long vertical velocity profiles with a cell size of 10 cm. Velocity profiles were recorded every 10 min and were used to calculate the time series of depth-averaged flow velocity. The SWIPS and AquaDopp® were initially deployed on the river bed ∼20 m from the imaging system on November 9, 2021 (see Fig. 1 a). The instrument platform was 2 m deep initially but was dragged by advecting ice pans to a shallower location with a depth of ∼0.7 m during the deployment. The depth-averaged flow velocity on the KR was estimated by measuring the flow velocity at 60% of the water depth from the water surface using a SonTek FlowTracker handheld Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter (ADV). The ADV was located ∼3 m from the imaging system and ∼2 m from the riverbank. The flow velocity was measured once on the KR at 09:10 on January 31, 2023, with a frequency of 1 Hz for a duration of 50 s. The SWIPS was not deployed on the KR to monitor the frazil ice.  4 Data processing 4.1 Anchor ice image processing Five anchor ice events were captured on the NSR (Events 1–5) and one on the KR (Event 6). This resulted in a total of 1624 anchor ice images recorded on two rivers. Each raw image underwent three processing steps to determine the anchor ice thickness. The raw anchor ice image (Fig. 3  a) was first imported into FastStone Image Viewer (version 7.5) to add a date and time stamp. The stamped image was then enhanced in Adobe Photoshop (version 23.0.1) using the Camera Raw Filter function by adjusting the exposure, contrast, brightness, and saturation, reducing the noise, and increasing the clarity (Fig. 3 b). Note that the criteria for image enhancement varied because the clarity of images was not constant. There were periods when anchor ice boundaries were still unclear after the image enhancement due to very weak lighting, murky water, or interference from underwater organic matter, and therefore, the anchor ice thickness was not determined during these periods. The enhanced image was then processed in Microsoft PowerPoint (version 1808) to delineate the boundaries of anchor ice accumulation (Fig. 3 c). The top boundary of the anchor ice accumulation was manually tracked using a red curve, and the approximate location of the bottom boundary was delineated for each event using a fixed green horizontal line. Lastly, a MATLAB algorithm was developed to detect the red curve and the green line to determine the anchor ice thickness in pixels. The thickness was calculated at one-pixel intervals, and the average values were presented in this study. The uncertainty of the image processing method was assessed by inviting three river ice researchers to process ten sequential anchor ice images independently, following the three steps outlined previously. It was found that the standard deviation of the calculated anchor ice thickness for an image was from 2.7%−4.8% of the mean thickness, with an average uncertainty of 3.4%. Seven objects, including the three scaling rods and four marked stones, were used to determine the pixel size at different locations in an image. Their distances to the camera lens are summarized in Table 1  . Note that the determined pixel size shown in Table 1  is larger than that of the original image. This is because the size of the images outputted from Photoshop was reduced to 1686 pixels × 1125 pixels to increase processing speeds. The pixel size used to obtain the thickness of an anchor ice accumulation (i.e., in centimeters) depended on how the accumulation was spatially distributed on the artificial substrate. If the anchor ice covered almost the entire substrate, the pixel size was set to the average at all seven object locations. This resulted in a maximum difference in thickness of approximately ±20% if the pixel size at the front or back rod was used. In cases where the anchor ice formed only on the part of the substrate between the locations of two adjacent scaling rods, the average pixel size at the locations of the two rods and the two stones in between was used. This gave a maximum difference in the calculated thickness of approximately ±10% compared to using the pixel size at either of these two rods. Note that the pixel size used for different images in an event was held constant. The start of an anchor ice event was defined as the time when anchor ice was first observed forming on the artificial substrate. The end of an anchor ice event was defined as the time when the anchor ice accumulation was observed to be completely released. Examination of the time series of anchor ice thickness computed for each event indicated that these were comprised of time periods during which the rate of thickness change remained relatively constant (i.e., there was a linear relationship between thickness and time). The median coefficient of determination R2  was calculated to assess how well a linear relationship fit the data, and it was 0.96. Anchor ice evolution rate (V an    ), formally defined as the rate of change of anchor ice thickness, was determined by the slope of each linear fit. Time periods when V an     ranged between −0.1 and 0.1 cm/h were defined as stable stages, time periods when V an     > 0.1 cm/h were classified as growth stages, and those with V an     < −0.1 cm/h were classified as decay stages. Accordingly, V an     was designated as the growth rate during growth stages and decay rate during decay stages. Note that certain stages necessitated the use of more than one linear relationship to characterize. For these cases, the stage-averaged evolution rate V an    ¯     was calculated as a duration-weighted average.  4.2 Analysis of heat flux at the water surface To assess the effect of thermal factors on anchor ice evolution, the net heat flux between the water and the air φ wa     was calculated using the full energy budget method:(1) φ wa   = - φ s  1 - α ws     - φ L w ↓   air   ( 1 - α wl   )  + φ L w ↑   water   + φ E  + φ H      where φ s    is the downwelling solar radiation; α ws     is the albedo of water surface to solar radiation, taken as 0.15 (Howley, 2021 ); φ L w ↓   air     is the downwelling longwave radiation emitted from the atmosphere; α wl     is the albedo of water surface to longwave radiation, taken as 0.03 (Raphael, 1962 ); φ L w ↑   water     is the upwelling longwave radiation emitted from the water; and φ E    and φ H    are the latent and sensible heat fluxes at the water surface, respectively. Negative heat fluxes in Eq. (1)  indicate heat gain into the river, and positive heat fluxes indicate heat loss from the river. For the NSR, φ s    was obtained from the weather station at the E.L. Smith WTP and φ L w ↓   air     was from the net radiometer. For the KR, φ s    was from the University of Calgary’s Barrier Lake Field Station while φ L w ↓   air     was calculated using Satterlund’s (1979)  clear sky emissivity formula and Konzelmann et al.’s (1994)  cloud effect formula (Yang et al., 2023b ). On both rivers, φ L w ↑   water     was calculated using the Stefan-Boltzmann law (Ashton, 2013 ), and φ E    and φ H    were quantified using Ryan et al.’s (1974)  formula, following Yang et al. (2023b) .  4.3 Determination of volumetric concentration of suspended ice Raw SWIPS data files were processed using IPS5Extract (ASL Environmental Sciences Inc.) software that extracted the time series of vertical profiles of digital counts, ranging from 0 to 65535. The acoustic pulse emitted by the sonar is reflected back from suspended ice in the water column, and the magnitude of the raw digital signal is a measure of the strength of the backscattered sound received at the sonar transducer. The raw count was converted to volume backscatter strength using the algorithm developed by Ghobrial et al. (2012) , and the depth-averaged volume backscatter strength was quantified from the minimum lookout distance of the sonar of 0.4 m to the bottom of frazil pans or the water surface (Ghobrial et al., 2013 ). The volumetric concentration of suspended ice C v    was then calculated from the depth-averaged volume backscatter strength using an empirical relationship developed by Ghobrial et al. (2012) .   5 Results 5.1 Synopses of anchor ice events In Fig. 4  , the time series of water temperature, air temperature, and solar radiation measured during the NSR deployment are plotted. Event 5 was unique in that it was the only multi-day event observed, and it was split into two events shaded and labeled 5a and 5b in Fig. 4 . Note that the time lapse video of Event 5 is provided at https://doi.org/10.5683/SP3/MGINHW  (Yang et al., 2024 ). This video shows that the camera captured images during the first 3 h of Event 5 before the camera batteries were depleted, but the image quality was quite poor due to the presence of organic matter in the water. As a result, the boundaries of the anchor ice accumulation could not be identified, but the start of the event was detected in the images. The camera batteries were first replaced ∼22 h later, and in the first image that was captured, an anchor ice accumulation with an average thickness of 2.6 cm was visible. The water temperature had briefly risen above zero just prior to the restarting of the camera (Fig. 4 a), and therefore, it was assumed that this accumulation was a remnant of one forming during the previous supercooling event that had decayed but not completely released. Anchor ice images were then continuously captured except for two short periods when the batteries were changed for a second and third time, and anchor ice was always visible in the images. Measurements in Event 5 stopped prior to anchor ice release because ice pans dragged the camera system downstream. Event 5a encompasses the time period between when the camera was restarted and when the second battery change occurred, and Event 5b is from when image capture restarted after the second battery change to the end of Event 5. Fig. 4 a shows that all anchor ice events on the NSR were associated with one or more supercooling events and that anchor ice was initiated once the supercooling had already begun, and this was also the case for the KR event. This is logical since the frazil production and in-situ crystal growth contributing to anchor ice formation and growth require supercooled water. Table 2   summarizes the timing and conditions for the six anchor ice events captured on the NSR and KR. It can be seen that anchor ice events started 0.3–3.7 h after the onset of supercooling, averaging 1.8 h later. At the start of supercooling that led to anchor ice events, the air temperature T a    was decreasing and the solar radiation φ s    was negligible or very low, as shown in Fig. 4 b and 4c, respectively. At the start of anchor ice events, T a    had decreased to between −11.8 and −3.6 °C and φ s    was between 0 and 46 W/m2 . Therefore, T a    lower than approximately −3 °C and φ s    less than 50 W/m2  might be useful preliminary thresholds for forecasting anchor ice formation. Table 2  shows that anchor ice formation began at times between 15:42 and 06:32 the next day, and the duration ranged from 6.4 to > 77 h, with five events less than 24 h. Anchor ice release occurred between 11:24 and 14:50, which was between 0.2 and 3.7 h after the end of supercooling. The air temperature and solar radiation were both relatively high when anchor ice released, with T a    ranging from −4.6 to 4.1 °C and φ s    from 111 to 352 W/m2 . Previous studies have shown that anchor ice processes are influenced by hydraulic conditions (Kerr et al., 2002; Stickler and Alfredsen, 2009; Lind et al., 2016 ), and therefore, the water depth, flow velocity, Froude number, and Reynolds number averaged for each event are presented in Table 2 . This data show that hydraulic conditions were relatively consistent across different anchor ice events on the NSR, with the mean water depth varying from 0.74 to 0.88 m and the mean depth-averaged flow velocity from 0.50 to 0.62 m/s. The water depth during the KR deployment was comparable to that on the NSR but the flow velocity was significantly smaller. The mean Froude number in all events was ≤ 0.17 and the mean Reynold number ranged from 45,000 to 721,000, indicating that the flow was subcritical and fully turbulent. Variations of water depth and flow velocity were observed during anchor ice events, mainly due to hydropeaking. The largest variations in the flow depth and the depth-averaged velocity in an event were 0.33 m and 0.30 m/s, respectively. However, these variations in depth and velocity did not have a significant influence on anchor ice evolution in this study.  5.2 Evolution of anchor ice thickness The three events plotted in Fig. 5   were selected to illustrate the temporal evolution of anchor ice thickness. Data gaps in Events 2 and 6 (Fig. 5 a, 5c) were caused by poor image quality or ice formation on the underwater housing that prevented the thickness measurements. At the start of Event 6, the water was quite murky due to hydropeaking, which prevented thickness measurements, but anchor ice could be observed forming starting at 18:10. Ice formed on the camera housing starting at 19:30, and anchor ice was observed on the substrate until 21:00 when the view became totally blocked. At 07:00 the next day, ice on the housing was manually removed and the image showed that the anchor ice was still present on the substrate, indicating that this was the same accumulation that had started to form at 18:10 the day before. Linear interpolation was required to calculate the anchor ice growth rate during the first 12.8 h of Event 6, while in Event 2, it was found that the growth rate during the gap period was similar to that during the subsequent period, and therefore, these two periods were combined for a single linear fit. The abrupt decrease in anchor ice thickness at ∼14:00 in Event 5b (Fig. 5 b) occurred because the anchor ice was disturbed when the camera batteries were replaced. Anchor ice evolution in Event 2 (Fig. 5 a) was the simplest but the most complete among all events, with sequential growth, stable, and decay stages. Event 5b (Fig. 5 b) was the most complex event, exhibiting the most temporal variability in anchor ice growth rates compared to the other events. It can be seen that after the first growth stage in Event 5b, there was a stable stage followed by another growth stage. Immediately after the stable stage, the increase in growth rate to 0.75 cm/h was likely caused by the wind speed increasing from 0.3 to 4.7 m/s and the air temperature decreasing by 1.2 °C. The higher growth rates that then followed coincided with the appearance of snowfall in trail camera images. Event 6, shown in Fig. 5 c, was unique since this was the only event in which anchor ice lifting was observed for a period of 2.2 h. The anchor ice lifted slowly in the first hour, and then part of the accumulation released, causing the thickness to decrease abruptly by 1.5 cm. After that, the lifting continued at a slightly larger rate and then more quickly right at the end of the 2.2 h, after which the part of the accumulation that was lifting broke free. This caused the thickness to decrease abruptly by 2.1 cm, and then the accumulation decayed for 1.3 h prior to the release. Table 3   summarizes the anchor ice thickness evolution data for all events, including duration D s   , range of evolution rate V an    , stage-averaged evolution rate V an    ¯    , and peak anchor ice thickness t p   . The duration of the stable stage in Event 5a was not measured since it was interrupted when the batteries were replaced. The anchor ice was still growing at the end of Event 5b, and therefore, the total duration of the growth stage and the peak anchor ice thickness were not measured. It can be seen from Table 3  that the growth stage was the longest stage in all events, ranging from 4.8 to > 21.1 h with an average of 11.8 h. Stable stages occurred in four events, with the duration varying from 2.8 to 5.6 h and averaging at 4.1 h. Decay stages were recorded in all events, lasting from 0.6 to 5.5 h and averaging 2.5 h. Anchor ice released following the decay stage in five events (Events 1–4 and 6). Table 3  illustrates that during the growth stage in a given event, the largest and smallest range in growth rates was 8.46 cm/h and 0.29 cm/h, in Events 1 and 5a, respectively. The growth rate during the initial growth period was on average 3.7 times larger than that during the subsequent period, except in Event 5a when it was slightly smaller. However, no images were captured in the first 0.6 h of the supercooling event associated with Event 5a, and as a result, the initial faster growth period may not have been recorded. The stage-averaged growth rate V an    ¯     in an event varied from 0.48 to 3.53 cm/h, with the largest occurring in Event 3 when snowfall was observed. This significantly larger average growth rate was 2 to 7.4 times larger compared to the other events. A single decay rate was observed during decay stages in all events except Event 3, which suggests that anchor ice decay was typically an approximately linear process. The fastest decay occurred during the snowfall influenced Event 3 when V an     was −6.57 cm/h, and it is interesting to note that this was followed by the slowest decay when V an     was −0.48 cm/h. Averaged over all events, the rates of growth and decay were 1.34 cm/h and −1.20 cm/h, respectively. This shows that on average anchor ice grows and decays at comparable rates. Table 3  also shows that peak anchor ice thickness t p    in an event varied from 8.2 to 17.2 cm. These corresponded to the events with the smallest and largest average growth rates, in Events 6 and 3, respectively. Interestingly, the thickest accumulation was formed in 4.9 h during snowfall, while the thinnest took over three times longer to form in 16.8 h.  5.3 Effect of the air–water heat flux on anchor ice evolution In Fig. 6  , the time series of anchor ice thickness t an     and the air–water heat flux φ wa     in Event 5a are plotted. It can be seen that the anchor ice growth stage occurred when the water was cooling (i.e., a positive upward heat flux). The average heat flux φ wa    ¯     during the initial growth period was 86 W/m2 , then increased to 187 W/m2 , which coincided with an increase in the growth rate from 0.42 to 0.71 cm/h. The stable stage that occurred next lasted 3.5 h when φ wa     decreased from 174 W/m2  to approximately zero. During the decay stage that followed, the water was warming and φ wa    ¯     was −50 W/m2 . A short stable stage, which was 0.7 h in duration, occurred next as the cooling heat flux increased, and the water began cooling again at the end of the event. The initiation of anchor ice and all subsequent growth stages in all events always occurred when there was a net heat loss at the water surface. During stable stages, the cooling heat flux always decreased. The average heat flux during all but one decay stage was negative, indicating that during this stage there was a net heat gain at the water surface. Anchor ice release was observed in five events (Events 1–4 and 6), and in four of these, the release occurred during a warming period (i.e., 0.7–2.8 h after the start of a warming period). In the other event (Event 4), the release occurred 1 h after a long warming period had ended. In Fig. 7  , the anchor ice evolution rate V an     is plotted versus the average air–water heat flux φ wa    ¯     during growth, stable, and decay stages for all events. It can be seen that φ wa    ¯     ranged from 30 to 331 W/m2  during growth stages, indicating that there was always a cooling heat flux during anchor ice growth. There are four data points that have relatively high V an     values but relatively low φ wa    ¯     values (< 100 W/m2 ), and during these four periods (two each in Events 3 and 5b), snowfall was observed. During stable stages, φ wa    ¯     varied from 73 to 139 W/m2  and from −30 to −100 W/m2  during decay stages (excluding Event 5b). However, the exception was the decay stage in Event 5b, which occurred when there was an average cooling heat flux of 87 W/m2 . Fig. 7  clearly shows that there is no significant correlation between the anchor ice evolution rate and the net air–water heat flux during any of the stages.  5.4 Estimation of frazil accretion rate A time series of vertical profiles of raw digital counts recorded by the sonar during Event 3 is presented in Fig. 8  a. This was the only event in which the sonar detected the suspended ice. Fig. 8 b shows the estimated volumetric concentration of suspended ice C v    during the same time period. The time period when snowfall was observed is denoted in Fig. 8 b, and it coincided with the time when suspended ice was present in the water. Fig. 8 b also shows that supercooling did not commence until 16.3 h after suspended ice was first detected. Water temperature measurements at a location ∼23 km upstream showed that supercooling never occurred there during the same time period and that the average water temperature was 0.41 °C. Therefore, it seems likely that the suspended ice detected by the sonar prior to supercooling at the study site was snow slush entrained into the water column and not frazil ice. Anchor ice in Event 3 began forming at 1.6 h after the start of supercooling, suggesting that newly formed active frazil ice crystals were being deposited onto the substrate. However, it is possible that once supercooling started, the suspended ice generated by snowfall became active, which also contributed to anchor ice growth on the substrate. Fig. 9   presents the times series of anchor ice thickness t an     and volumetric frazil concentration C v    in Event 3. The anchor ice growth rate V an     during the initial growth period was estimated to be 4.92 cm/h, calculated by the linear interpolation, and then it decreased to 2.89 cm/h. The thickness was not measured in the last 0.9 h of the event due to poor image quality, and the decay rate during this period could not be calculated since the thickness immediately prior to the release was unknown. The volumetric frazil concentration C v    during Event 3 varied from 1.28 × 10−4  to 1.99 × 10−3 , averaging 1.10 × 10−3 . The average C v    was 1.09 × 10−3  during the initial growth period, increasing to 1.48 × 10−3  during the following period. At the start of the decay stage, C v    decreased rapidly and was approaching zero when anchor ice was released. Examination of the images captured during Event 3 indicated that anchor ice growth was solely through frazil accretion. The equation typically used to estimate anchor ice growth in numerical models can thus be simplified to:(2) V an   = γ C v   1 - e a         where γ   is the frazil accretion rate; and e a    is the anchor ice porosity (Wang and Shen, 1993 ). The anchor ice porosity e a    was previously measured in the Edmonton reach of the NSR, and it ranged between 0.323 and 0.642, with an average of 0.523 (Pei et al., 2021 ). Using the simultaneous measurements of frazil ice concentrations and anchor ice growth rates in Event 3 and the average anchor ice porosity, the frazil accretion rate was estimated using Eq. (2) . The frazil accretion rate during the initial growth period was estimated to be 6.0 × 10−3  m/s, using V an     of 4.92 cm/h and average C v    of 1.09 × 10−3 , and was 2.6 × 10−3  m/s during the subsequent growth period, with V an     of 2.89 cm/h and average C v    of 1.48 × 10−3  (see Fig. 9 ).   6 Discussion 6.1 Hydraulic conditions during anchor ice events Anchor ice forms more easily in river reaches characterized by shallow water and high flow velocities, and therefore, the Froude number F r    was chosen in previous studies to relate anchor ice formation with hydraulic conditions (Bisaillon and Bergeron, 2009 ). Reported values of F r    when anchor ice was observed in rivers vary widely in the literature, ranging from ∼0.1 to 1.5 (Hirayama et al., 1997; Stickler and Alfredsen, 2009 ). Kerr et al. (2002)  conducted laboratory investigations and found that anchor ice grew faster as F r    increased. In this study, F r    recorded during anchor ice evolution varied from 0.05 to 0.2, which was at the lower end of the range documented in the literature. There was no significant relationship between the anchor ice growth rate and F r    found in this study. Previous studies have shown that anchor ice release was affected by the Reynolds number R e   . For example, Doering et al. (2001)  conducted laboratory experiments using R e    ranging from ∼14,000 to ∼84,000, and they found that the release occurred when R e    was less than ∼42,000. Kerr et al. (2002)  conducted experiments at two R e    values of 21,765 and 29,020 and only observed anchor ice release at the lower value. Stickler and Alfredsen (2009)  measured R e    up to 68,200, but anchor ice release was not related to a threshold value of R e   , and they concluded that release was controlled by solar radiation. In this study, the values of the mean R e    varied from 45,000 to 721,000, and no threshold value for anchor ice release was observed, which is in agreement with the previous field measurements by Stickler and Alfredsen (2009) .  6.2 Anchor ice evolution mechanisms Anchor ice evolution mechanisms in this study were analyzed by reviewing the time-lapse video of each event. These videos were created from sequentially captured anchor ice images after the enhancement, with a frame rate of 5 fps (frames per second) in Adobe Photoshop. Two example videos are provided at https://doi.org/10.5683/SP3/MGINHW , including a single-day event (Event 1) and the multi-day event (Event 5) (Yang et al., 2024 ). 6.2.1 Stages of anchor ice evolution Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  defined four stages of anchor ice evolution, including initiation by in-situ growth, transitional, linear growth, and release stages in their field study. The three stages defined by Kerr et al. (2002)  in their laboratory study are similar to the first three stages defined by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021) . In this study, it was observed during a number of events that the temporal evolution of anchor ice growth was more complicated than previously observed (i.e., the growth rate varied more frequently). In addition, there were a number of times when the growth rate was negligible (i.e., the thickness was approximately constant). Therefore, all time periods when an accumulation was growing significantly thicker were labeled growth stages, and time periods when growth was negligible were labeled stable stages. Note that the decay stage is equivalent to the release stage defined by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021) , except that it includes time periods of significant thinning or decay in addition to the actual release.  6.2.2 Growth mechanisms Three anchor ice growth mechanisms were observed in this study. The first mechanism, observed in five of the six captured events, was the result of the combined effect of frazil accretion and in-situ crystal growth. It should be noted that in-situ crystal growth in this study includes the growth of needle-shaped crystals on the substrate and the growth of frazil ice particles after they accreted onto the substrate or an existing anchor ice accumulation. At the start of these five anchor ice events, accreted frazil ice and large ice crystals both appeared in the images. As the growth stage progressed, more frazil particles accreted, some of which grew in situ, resulting in more large ice crystals in the images. Crystals significantly larger than frazil particles were always visible during the growth stage of these events, and their base was either attached to the substrate or to the top of anchor ice accumulations. This first mechanism is similar to anchor ice growth processes observed on the wedge-wire screen in the Laramie River by Kempema and Ettema (2016) . They found that frazil ice accretion always appeared first in an event, and anchor ice grew by a combination of frazil accretion and in-situ growth of attached frazil particles. Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  observed in-situ crystal growth first, followed by frazil accretion in three of six events on the NSR, but did not report observing them simultaneously. Anchor ice growth by only frazil accretion was defined as the second growth mechanism. This mechanism occurred when frazil accretion was observed, but there was no visible evidence of in-situ growth in the images. This mechanism was observed during snowfall in Event 3 and during part of Event 5 from 09:30 to 14:00 on November 20. The images presented in Fig. 10   show an accumulation growing through this mechanism during Event 5 that appears white and fluffy. Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  also observed anchor ice growth by only frazil accretion in three events, but no snowfall was reported. Anchor ice growth by only frazil accretion has also been observed in the laboratory (Kerr et al., 2002; Qu and Doering, 2007 ), although Qu and Doering (2007)  stated that in-situ crystal growth may also have occurred during their experiments based on an analysis of supercooling time series. The third growth mechanism is the deposition of fragments of anchor ice pans that had been released upstream, which was observed in Events 1 and 4. This mechanism is illustrated in Fig. 11   with three images captured during Event 4 on November 17. The first image in Fig. 11 a shows an original anchor ice accumulation captured at 00:30. The second image in Fig. 11 b, captured four minutes later, shows that a stone ∼10 cm in size has been deposited onto the accumulation. This stone originated from a released anchor ice pan, and just as it passed over the substrate, the stone became dislodged and fell onto the accumulation. The third image in Fig. 11 c, captured ∼1.5 h later at 02:10, shows a large fragment of anchor ice abruptly depositing onto the accumulation. The process is the same as for the stone, that is, the negatively buoyant fragment was deposited after it became dislodged from a released anchor ice pan passing above the substrate. This abrupt deposition caused the thickness of accumulation to increase by 4.4 cm. A smaller fragment was deposited during Event 1 (see video of Event 1), which increased the thickness by only 0.9 cm.  6.2.3 Decay and release mechanisms Fig. 12   shows a typical anchor ice decay stage observed in this study. The accumulation appeared to melt, thinning gradually, and abruptly released at 11:24, which was three minutes after the image in Fig. 12 d was captured. Decay stages were observed to start at times between 09:45 and 13:20, and the water was still supercooled at these times in six of seven cases. Solar radiation ranged between 76 and 113 W/m2  at the start, indicating that decay stages were initiated by heating due to solar radiation. Increasing air temperatures and solar radiation then typically caused supercooling to end, and anchor ice release occurred between 11:24 and 14:50, which was 0.2 to 3.7 h after the end of supercooling. The fact that the air temperature and solar radiation were both relatively high (T a    ranging from –4.6 to 4.1 °C and φ s    from 111 to 352 W/m2 ) at the anchor ice release times is clear evidence that thermal release occurred in all cases. Nafziger et al. (2017)  also concluded that thermal release was the dominant release mechanism in their field study. They observed that 98% of anchor ice accumulations were completely released on days when there was a net heat gain at the water surface and the air temperature was higher than −15 °C. However, Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  observed four anchor ice releases that all occurred while the water was still supercooled, and they concluded that the release due to the weakening of the ice-substrate bond was not likely to occur. Based on an in-depth analysis, they concluded that mechanical release due to buoyancy forces likely triggered the release of the two shallow water accumulations (∼0.6 m deep), but they were only able to state that solar radiation and/or buoyancy may have been a factor in the release of the deep water accumulations (∼1.6 m deep). It should be noted that Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  conducted their anchor ice measurements in close proximity to a bridge and relatively close to the right bank. As a result, shading from the bridge and trees along the bank may have significantly reduced the local solar radiation. The measurements in this study were conducted at an upstream location where there are no bridges nearby, and the anchor ice camera system was deployed relatively far from the left bank. As a result, shading was not a factor. This may explain why solar radiation appeared to play a larger role in triggering anchor ice release at this location, which resulted in thermal release in all cases.   6.3 Timing of anchor ice events The anchor ice initiation times in this study varied from 15:42 in the afternoon to 06:32 in the morning. These times are different from the observations by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021) , who reported that anchor ice started at times from 16:25 in the afternoon to 21:00 in the evening, with no events commencing overnight or in the morning. Anchor ice release in this study occurred between 11:24 and 14:50. Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  reported that the two shallow accumulations released before sunrise at 07:15 and 08:20, and the two deep accumulations released at 13:20 and 14:40. The duration of the single-day anchor ice events in this study (6.4 to 21.6 h) was comparable to observations by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  (13.3 to 22.2 h), and the duration of the multi-day event (> 77 h) was within the range observed by Tremblay et al. (2014)  (2 to 8 days). It is difficult to explain with any certainty why the start and release times vary as described above. However, variations in timing from one event to the next are likely influenced by temporal changes in conditions (e.g., heat fluxes, water temperature, etc.). Site-specific factors such as water depth, flow patterns, and shading may also influence the timing of events when comparing events at different locations.  6.4 Anchor ice growth rates Previous studies reported anchor ice growth rates when only frazil accretion or in-situ crystal growth was observed ranged from 0.3 to 0.9 cm/h and from 1 to 4 cm/h, respectively (Ghobrial and Loewen, 2021 ). In this study, the event-averaged growth rate when both frazil accretion and in-situ crystal growth were occurring ranged from 0.48 to 1.77 cm/h, averaging 0.94 cm/h. This shows that when frazil accretion and in-situ crystal growth are occurring simultaneously, the growth rate tends to fall between the values that were observed when growth was due to a single mechanism. The average frazil accretion growth rates during snowfall were estimated to be 1.64 cm/h and.3.53 cm/h in events 5b and 3, respectively. These values are approximately 2 to 12 times larger than the average growth rates during frazil accretion without snowfall, measured by Ghobrial and Loewen (2021)  on the NSR. In Event 3, the average volumetric concentration of frazil ice was 1.10 × 10−3 , which is considerably larger than the values measured previously on the NSR in the absence of snowfall, which varied from 1.0 × 10−6  to 2.0 × 10−4  (Ghobrial et al., 2013; McFarlane et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the larger anchor ice growth rates observed during snowfall are likely associated with higher concentrations of suspended frazil ice. The frazil accretion rates, estimated for the snowfall period, ranged from 2.6 × 10−3  to 6.0 × 10−3  m/s, which are larger, and in some cases orders of magnitude larger, than the values reported in the literature based on the calibration of river ice models ranging from 10−6  to 10−3  m/s (Malenchak, 2011; Blackburn and She, 2019; Yang et al., 2021 ) As was shown in Fig. 5 , anchor ice growth rates were found to vary frequently during an event. There was no correlation between growth rates and the air–water heat flux (see Fig. 7 ), and it is therefore logical to conclude that the growth rate is a function of multiple factors. Larger rates were observed during the initial growth period, and this often coincided with the principal supercooling period when the lowest water temperature occurred. An analysis of water temperatures during the initial growth period found that the supercooling temperatures were on average 2.3 times lower compared to the subsequent slower growth period. This is evidence that the larger initial growth rates are due, at least in part, to stronger supercooling temperatures. However, growth rates were observed to vary after the initial period when water temperatures were relatively constant in three events. Some of these rate changes in Event 5b were attributed to snowfall. Except for this special case, the specific reasons for why anchor ice growth rates varied during an event are unknown.   7 Conclusions In-situ continuous measurements of anchor ice evolution were conducted on two regulated rivers using an underwater imaging system and artificial substrate. Five single-day and one multi-day anchor ice events were monitored on two rivers. Measurements of suspended ice concentrations as well as meteorological and hydraulic parameters were also collected. Images of anchor ice events were analyzed, and the impact of hydrometeorological conditions on anchor ice evolution was investigated. The observations showed that anchor ice events coincided closely with river supercooling, and their initiation and release occurred after the start and end of the associated supercooling event, respectively. Anchor ice initiation occurred at times between 15:42 in the afternoon and 06:32 the next morning, and the release occurred between 11:24 and 14:50. Three stages of anchor ice evolution were defined in this study. These were the growth, stable, and decay stages, with the longest duration always being the growth stage. Anchor ice initiation and the subsequent growth stages were observed to occur during periods when there was a cooling heat flux at the water surface, stable stages during periods of decreased cooling heat flux, and most decay stages and anchor ice releases when there was a warming heat flux. There was no significant correlation found between the net air–water heat flux and anchor ice growth or decay rates during any of the stages. An analysis of hydraulic conditions showed that, unlike some previous studies, anchor ice evolution was not dependent on the Reynolds or Froude numbers. The anchor ice growth rate was generally larger during the initial growth period of an event when the supercooling temperature was on average 2.3 times lower than during the subsequent period. The average anchor ice growth rate in an event ranged from 0.48 to 3.53 cm/h. Anchor ice growth in the majority of the events occurred through a combination of frazil accretion and in-situ crystal growth, with event-averaged growth rates varying from 0.48 to 1.77 cm/h, averaging 0.94 cm/h. Anchor ice growth was monitored during snowfall for the first time, and it was observed that growth occurred only through frazil accretion. The growth rates during snowfall ranged from 1.64 to 3.53 cm/h, which are up to 12 times larger than previously reported rates for frazil accretion without snowfall. Anchor ice decay was the gradual melting of accumulations caused by solar radiation and above 0 ℃ water, with the average decay rate ranging from −0.48 to −2.52 cm/h. Estimates of the frazil accretion rate were made possible, for the first time, by using the simultaneous measurement of frazil ice concentrations and anchor ice growth rates. The calculated frazil accretion rates varied by just over a factor of two from 2.6 × 10−3  to 6.0 × 10−3  m/s. This is a significantly smaller range compared to the range of values previously estimated during the calibration of river ice models (10−6  to 10−3  m/s), which will help to simplify the calibration process and ultimately improve the accuracy of models. However, it should be noted that the frazil accretion rates calculated in this study were only for a single anchor ice event that occurred during snowfall, and an average value of anchor ice porosity was used based on the measurements in the previous year. The results from this study emphasize the need for future field or laboratory investigations focusing on several topics. For example, more simultaneous measurements of volumetric frazil ice concentrations, anchor ice growth rates, and anchor ice porosity under varying conditions would allow additional estimates of frazil accretion rates to be made. Secondly, there is no quantitative information currently available on the fate of anchor ice, that is, how much is ultimately incorporated into the ice cover and how much is melted prior to and after release. It would be very challenging to measure this, but it might be possible to do this using side scan sonar and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery. The side scan sonar could be used to measure the extent and depth of anchor ice accumulations and the UAV imagery to estimate the fraction of the ice cover comprised of released anchor ice pans.
1 Introduction Economic damage caused by droughts in the United States is estimated to be in the tens of billions of dollars annually (Smith and Matthews, 2015 ). Public perceptions and attitudes towards droughts – both pre- and post-drought – are indicators of public reception of water management and conservation measures (Campbell et al., 2004; Clarke and Brown, 2006 ). Adams et al. (2013)  found that public perception of the importance of water resources management significantly influenced water conservation outcomes. A study on the sociological impacts of drought perception in South-Central Nebraska revealed that crop and livestock producers were becoming increasingly concerned about water scarcity resulting from droughts (Woudenberg et al., 2008 ). Similar concerns were shared by farmers in a study conducted in the Jucar River Basin in Spain (Urquijo and De Stefano, 2016 ) and in South Africa (Bahta et al., 2016 ). After a record breaking drought in Texas in 2011, residents were significantly more concerned with water availability and water conservation (Gholson et al., 2019 ). A recent study on two cities in Alabama found that public awareness of drought is significantly dependent on geographic, physical, and social contexts (Shao et al., 2022 ). Understanding the complex relationship between droughts and people’s perception about droughts, offers key insights for decision makers who can leverage these insights for early warnings, public service announcements, or targeted water conservation initiatives. Such insights directly align with societal objectives, notably, reducing water consumption. Evaluating public responses to drought through traditional surveys can be costly and limited in scale and interpretability due to biases (McLafferty, 2016; Vaske, 2011; Fisher, 1993; Groves, 2006 ). The rise of internet and social media use, with 92% of U.S. households having computer access and 85% broadband subscriptions in 2018 (Martin et al., 2021 ), and the availability of these data open avenues for large-scale web-based studies. Previous research has effectively used large-scale online data, including Google Trends Search Interest, as a proxy for surveys in diverse fields such as epidemiology, mental health, political science, telemedicine, population health, etc. (Carneiro et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2010; Stephens-Davidowitz, 2014; Hong et al., 2020; Arora et al., 2019; Mellon, 2013 ). Previous studies, differing significantly in approach and scope of this study have also explored questions surrounding public awareness of droughts. Gonzales and Ajami (2017)  used the relative number of Google searches for the term ‘California drought’ as an indicator of public interest to suggest that multiple socio-political factors have contributed to growth in public awareness during and following droughts. Kam et al. (2019)  leveraged google trends data and standard precipitation indices and found that there was no detectable social response during the onset of the 2011–2017 California droughts. Kim et al. (2019)  they found that drought severity (as indicated US Drought Monitor (USDM) data) in most Northeastern and Southeastern U.S. states showed significant temporal correlations with corresponding Google search interest in droughts, while most Western and Central U.S. states displayed weaker or insignificant correlations. Despite these advancements, previous research has focused primarily on linear relationships. However, drought awareness intuitively presents non-linear characteristics which need to be considered in order to gain a more explicit understanding. To address this gap, we use computer vision models trained on lagged data to investigate the non-linear, heterogeneous relationship (and their drivers) between meteorological droughts and people’s search interest on the topic of “drought” - allowing for a more holistic view of the spatial and temporal variability (at state and regional levels) of drought awareness over Continental United States (CONUS). 1.1 Research questions In this paper, we address the following research question: • Is there a relationship between droughts and drought awareness, as measured by Search Interest, and what factors drive this relationship?      2 Methods In this section, we discuss the data-driven experimental approaches and methods that we used to address the research question outlined above. To address the research question, we broke it down into a set of sub-queries. We first looked at the averages, trends, and variances of the state-wise search interests and SPEI across CONUS within our study period (2004–2020). We also investigated any existence of statistically significant linear correlation among the corresponding variables. We then applied six computer vision (UNet) models trained on lagged drought (input) data and corresponding Search Interest (target) data to investigate the existence of nonlinear and heterogeneous dynamics between these variables. We then conducted a feature importance analysis to find out the most important drivers of this nonlinear relationship. We further compared these results with a Principal Component Analysis applied on the same dataset. We then explored the variability of these relationship aggregated at the state and regional levels and looked at the best lagged models per state and computed the sum of the R-squared (cumulative and population-weighted) per model predictions. 2.1 Data Table 1  summarizes the two data types used in this study, including where the data was sourced and their temporal scope.   2.1.1 Standardized Precipitation and Evapotranspiration Index (S P E I   ) We use the Standardized Precipitation and Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) (Beguería, 2022 ) as our meteorological drought index because it incorporates both precipitation and temperature data, making it a more comprehensive measure of drought conditions compared to indices that only consider precipitation, such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). The inclusion of temperature data in SPEI is crucial in the context of climate change because rising temperatures can worsen drought conditions by increasing evapotranspiration rates (Beguería et al., 2014 ). Intuitively, SPEI serves as a quantitative measure of droughts by providing a standardized index to assess moisture deficit over time and space. It is calculated by taking the difference between total precipitation and total potential evapotranspiration (PET) over a given period of time (e.g., monthly). SPEI is expressed in units of standard deviations calculated over local (per pixel) climatologies, allowing us to assess whether it is drier or wetter than expected conditions. Calculating SPEI involves the following steps: 1. Calculate the difference between precipitation (P  ) and reference evapotranspiration (E T 0   ) for each month or time step: (1) D  i   = P  i   − E T 0  i       where D  i     is the difference between precipitation and reference evapotranspiration for the i  th month or time step, P  i     is the precipitation for the i  th month or time step, and E T 0  i      is the reference evapotranspiration for the i  th month or time step.  2. Calculate the climatic water balance for each month or time step: (2) W B  i   = ∑  j = 1  n   D  i − j + 1       where W B  i      is the climatic water balance for the i  th month or time step, and n   is the time scale (e.g., 3, 6, or 12 months).  3. Fit a probability distribution, such as the three-parameter log–logistic distribution with the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) method, to the climatic water balance values: (3) F ( W B )  = 1  1 + W B − α  β      − γ         where F ( W B )     is the cumulative probability distribution of the climatic water balance, and α  , β  , and γ   are the distribution parameters that need to be estimated.  4. Calculate SPEI by transforming the fitted probability distribution to a standard normal distribution: (4) S P E I = Φ  − 1   ( F ( W B )  )      where SPEI is the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index, Φ  − 1     is the inverse standard normal cumulative distribution function, and F ( W B )     is the cumulative probability distribution of the climatic water balance.    SPEI can be calculated for a variety of time periods, ranging from 1 month to 48 months. We use monthly data in our analysis because Google Search Interest (target) data has the same temporal resolution. Positive SPEI values indicate wetter conditions, while negative values indicate drier conditions. We created images of monthly averaged SPEI over CONUS for each month from January 2004 to December 2020 to be used as input data for training and prediction for our analysis. Fig. A.6  shows an example of one of these SPEI maps.  2.1.2 Google Trends Search Interest (SI) We acquired Google Search Interest (SI) data from Google Trends using the Trends API. The Trends API allows programmatic access to Google trends data and track the popularity of different topics over time and place. We selected “Drought” as a topic. When a topic is selected, Google Trends aggregates all searches related to the concept of drought, regardless of the specific terms or phrases used. This includes searches in different languages and searches using related terms (e.g., “water shortage”, “dry weather”). The topic approach provides a broader view of public interest or concern about drought as a general subject. It captures the overall awareness and information-seeking behavior related to drought without being limited to a specific keyword. Given a specific topic, T  , and a time range from t  1     to t  n    , the search interest for T   at each time point, t  i    , is calculated as: (5) S I ( T , t  i   )  = S ( T , t  i   )   S  max   ( T )    × 100     where S I ( T , t  i   )     is the search interest for the topic T   at time point t  i    , S ( T , t  i   )     is the search volume for T   at t  i    , and S  max   ( T )     is the maximum search volume for T   within the specified time range. We use monthly state-wise S I    data on “Drought” topic from 2004 to 2020 to create maps over the CONUS. Fig. A.7  shows an example of a Google SI target map.   2.2 Analysis methods 2.2.1 Search interest and SPEI averages, trends, and variances Both droughts and people’s search interest in droughts varies spatially and temporally in a multi-directional (complex and nonlinear) manner rather than follow a steady trend. We first calculated the averages, trends (using linear regression), and variances aggregated by states for both search interest and SPEI. We then investigated for any statistically significant linear correlation between these corresponding variables.  2.2.2 Relationship between droughts and search interest We used machine learning models to investigate the non-linear relationship(s) between meteorological droughts and search interest over CONUS. Specifically, we trained U-Net models (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) to predict SI from SPEI maps. Details of our model architecture, training, and evaluation are in Appendix B  . In summary, we trained 6 models on 6 sets of lagged SPEI maps as inputs (from 0 months lag to 5 months lag) and the target data were their corresponding search interest maps. Correlation between (out-of-sample) search interest predictions made by these trained models and real search interest data is an estimate of the non-linear correlation between SPEI and SI at a given lag time. We evaluated the models on time periods not used for training (training period: 01/01/2004–07/31/2017 and test period: 08/01/2017–12/31/2020). This approach, aligning with the standard 80/20 training/testing data split, ensured a robust assessment of the models’ ability to generalize across different time frames and drought scenarios. We report the models’ performances based on the per pixel coefficient of determination (R  2    ) between the model predicted and observed search interest during the test period: (6) O  a , b   ( t )  = U ( T  a , b   ( t )  )      where O  a , b   ( t )     is the U-Net output for pixel ( a , b )    at time t  , T  a , b   ( t )     is the input data for pixel ( a , b )    at time t  , and U   is the U-Net model function. We then tested the model performance over time (using the coefficient of determination or R  2    ) for each individual pixel. (7) R  a , b  2   = R  2   ( O  a , b   ( t )  , G  a , b   ( t )  )      where R  a , b  2     is the coefficient of determination for pixel ( a , b )   , G  a , b   ( t )     is the ground truth (SI) data for pixel ( a , b )    at time t  , and R  2     is the coefficient of determination function. We then created a binary mask array based on the geometry of CONUS and constructed heatmaps of the R  2     values averaged over states and then aggregated to regions (as defined by the US Census Bureau) (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021 ). This approach allows us to observe overall model prediction performances over time across CONUS, and also by individual states and regions. We further evaluated the strength of correlation and significance of the statistical relationship between the model R  2     and corresponding averaged, trends, and variance of search interest and SPEI. For contrast, we applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the same dataset. The PCA served as a linear, dimensionality reduction technique to identify the major patterns of variance in droughts and corresponding people’s search interest state-wise and regionally. Our objective was to evaluate the strengths and limitations of nonlinear versus linear methods in capturing the dynamics of drought awareness.  2.2.3 Drivers of the relationship between droughts and drought awareness We investigated the most important drivers of the relationship between droughts and drought awareness.
