We first generated the histograms per state to visualize the distribution of (i) SPEI, (ii) trends of SPEI, (iii) variance of SPEI, (iv) length of droughts, and (v) severity of droughts. To calculate the length of droughts, we first selected a threshold of SPEI value of −1.0 and below to classify a drought occurrence based on commonly accepted standards in drought assessment (McKee et al., 1993; Svoboda et al., 2012 ). We recorded the number of consecutive months a pixel was in drought condition considering it as a continuous drought period and then aggregated the results by state. For drought severity, we identified all time points per pixel in drought conditions within the study period and computed the mean SPEI value. For each metric, we fitted an appropriate statistical distribution to the data. We assumed a Weibull distribution for drought lengths and normal distribution for rest of the metrics. We then extracted the parameters (for normal distributions: mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, interquartile range, and for Weibull distribution: form and scale) of these distributions. We then trained a Random Forest Regressor model using the parameters derived from the distribution fits as input features, with the R 2     values from our Unet models as the target variable. We then conducted a feature importance analysis to identify the drivers that most influence the relationship between droughts and drought awareness.  2.2.4 Best lagged model per state In our analysis, the term ‘lag’ refers to the time lag between variation in SPEI and corresponding changes in people’s search interest. We mapped the models (between 0 month lagged and 5 months lagged) which demonstrate the best overall predictive value per state. To perform this analysis, we followed these steps: First, we calculated the highest R  2     value for each model: (8) m a x _ r _ s q u a r e d  a , b   = max  k = 1  6   R  a , b , k  2       where m a x _ r _ s q u a r e d  a , b      is the highest R  2     value for pixel ( a , b )   , and R  a , b , k  2     is the R  2     value for pixel ( a , b )    in model k  . Then we assigned each pixel with the highest R  2     value: (9) b e s t _ m o d e l _ i n d e x  a , b   = arg max  k = 1  6   R  a , b , k  2       where b e s t _ m o d e l _ i n d e x  a , b      is the index of the model with the highest R  2     value for pixel ( a , b )   . We then aggregated these values to a state level. We also computed the sum of per model R  2     values and compared it with the population-weighted sum per model. The population weights were imparted by multiplying the averaged per-state per-model R  2     with the per-state population of 2020 according to the US Census Bureau.          3 Results and analysis In this section we address the research question laid out previously and discuss the results of our analyses. 3.1 Is there a relationship between droughts and drought awareness as measured by search interest, and what factors drive this relationship? In order to gain a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics between droughts and drought awareness, we break down this complex question into a subset of smaller questions. 3.1.1 How have drought conditions and drought awareness varied across CONUS from 2004 to 2020? We first look at the averages, trends, and variances of search interest on droughts and SPEI across CONUS (Fig. 1 ). Our objective with this analysis is to provide an overview of droughts and drought awareness and investigate any simple correlation between them within our study period of 2004–2020. The average search interest map (Fig. 1 (A)) demonstrates that drought awareness varied spatially across CONUS, with generally higher awareness in the western states and lower awareness in the eastern states. The most pronounced differences were observed between the southwestern and southeastern regions California and New Hampshire had the strongest increasing trend of drought awareness between 2004 and 2020, while the rest of the CONUS states demonstrated slightly increasing to stable trends (Fig. 1 (B)). We observed the highest degrees of variability in drought awareness (Fig. 1 (C)) in the western and central regions, particularly in the states located in the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain regions. The average SPEI map (Fig. 1 (D)) provides an overview of climatic tendencies in moisture balance (droughts) across CONUS states. The overall driest conditions were seen in the Southwestern and Southeastern regions whilst most Midwestern and Northeastern states had wetter conditions relative to the rest of the CONUS. The strongest increasingly dry to drought conditions were observed over Southwestern (e.g., Arizona, New Mexico, California, etc.), and Northeastern (e.g., Maine, Vermont and New Hampshire) states (Fig. 1 (E)). Conversely, strongest increasingly wet conditions were observed for Southeastern states (e.g., North Carolina, Virginia, Tennessee, etc.) The highest fluctuation in drought conditions was observed in the South-Central and Southeastern regions (Fig. 1 (F)), indicating the less predictable moisture conditions over these areas. These variances were also notable for California, Idaho, and Colorado while the least variances were seen for majority of the New England states. We found statistically significant inverse relationship (R  =   −0.64, p =   7.61e−07) between the trend in SPEI and search interest (Fig. 1 (H)), indicating that drought awareness has generally increased in states with increasingly dry to drought conditions. We did not find any statistically significant correlation between averages of and variances in SPEI and search interest.  3.1.2 Are there nonlinear relationships between droughts and drought awareness? As described in the methods section, we trained six UNet models (of the same architecture and hyperparameter settings but trained on 6 sets of lagged data) and tested their predictions for the period of June 2017 to December 2020. We measured the association (R  2    ) between the per-pixel values of target images and predicted pixel values by the U-Net models, and then aggregated and averaged them by individual states (Fig. 2 ). The U-Net’s capacity for capturing nonlinear relationships is a key in this analysis. Results highlight significant nonlinear and heterogeneous associations between variability in SPEI and corresponding changes in drought awareness. We elaborate on these nonlinear relationships and their drivers in the next section, where we discuss the results of our feature importance analysis. Although there is some degree of variability between the models, some of the common strongest nonlinear associations were seen for Colorado, Nebraska, and Arizona, suggesting heightened awareness in response to fluctuating drought conditions, while the least associations were observed over North Dakota, Mississippi, and New York.  3.1.3 What factors drive this relationship? As mentioned in Section 2.2 , we extracted a diverse range of parameters from the distributions fitted to SPEI, SPEI trends, SPEI variances, drought length, and drought severity data. We then trained a Random Forest Regressor using these parameters as input features and our UNet model R  2     as targets and carried out a feature importance analysis to identify the most important factors driving the nonlinear dynamics between droughts and drought awareness. Fig. 3  shows the results of the feature importance analysis. The interquartile range of the SPEI trend data (representing changes in drought severity over time) was the most influential feature, showing that middle 50% spread of SPEI changes over time is highly predictive of the UNet model R  2     - indicating that periods of moderate variability in drought conditions are significantly important to the shifts in public search interest on droughts. SPEI median was the second most important feature. Variability of SPEI trends (changes in drought severity) was another important feature indicating that both average fluctuations and mean fluctuations of drought conditions were key factors driving the dynamics between droughts and drought awareness. Drought severity range, drought mean, and drought trends mean were also important drivers. SPEI variance kurtosis and trend kurtosis were both key drivers in this relationship, suggesting that the ‘tailedness’ or the presence of extreme variability in drought conditions (outliers) significantly influenced the nonlinear dynamics between droughts and drought awareness. These findings suggest that people’s awareness of droughts is particularly sensitive to changes in drought conditions within a certain range of severity, rather than responding linearly to all levels of drought intensity. Moreover, the importance of drought severity range and extreme variability in drought conditions point towards potential threshold effects in people’s response to droughts. The relationship between droughts and public awareness is characterized by critical thresholds and potential saturation points, rather than a simple linear correlation. While our focus in this analysis was on the influence of extracted statistical parameters from SPEI data on the relationship between droughts and drought awareness, we did not account for potentially confounding variables, such as socioeconomic factors and media coverage which may introduce some bias.  3.1.4 How do the nonlinearity captured by the UNets and the PCA’s dimensionality reduction compare at the state and regional levels? We aggregated the UNet models’ average R  2     over states and regions (Fig. 4 ). We observed spatial variability of the average R  2     in both state and regional levels, with some degree of association found all over CONUS. The strongest relationships were observed for the Western region, followed by the Northeastern, Southeastern, and the Central regions. We additionally compared these results with the results of a PCA (a reductionist approach with two components) performed over our dataset (SPEI and Search Interest). The objective of the PCA was to identify the principal components (PCs) that captured the largest variances within our dataset. We found that PC1 had an explained variance of 25%, and PC2 had roughly 17%. We represent the spatial variability (by states and then aggregated by regions) of PC1 scores (indicating how regions relate to the patterns of variance captured by the principal component) in Fig. 4  and found the highest PC1 scores for California, South Dakota, and New Mexico while there was no to negative relationship for the other states. Regionally, we also saw some positive PC1 scores for the Western states with none or negative scores for the other regions. These findings further point towards significantly nuanced interactions between droughts and drought awareness - likely better captured by our UNet models (non-linear approach) which can account for the various dimensions and scales at which these interactions occur. Kim et al. (2019)  previously applied PCA to understand the spatiotemporal patterns of drought awareness over CONUS. Our findings are different to Kim et al. (2019) ’s. We designed our Computer Vision models to capture the complex nonlinear dynamics between droughts and drought awareness which linear and reductionist methods such as PCA might miss. Our method also allows pixel-wise prediction capability which is not possible with PCA. There are differences between their dataset and ours in terms of the periods of analysis as well as the drought indicators used, however, it makes sense that the complex interplay between any indicator of droughts and drought awareness would be better captured by nonlinear methods rather than linear ones.   3.2 Is there a time lag between droughts and changes in drought awareness? We mapped the models with the best overall R  2     values per state (color-coded to indicate the lag time from zero to five months) and found a very nuanced spatial distribution across CONUS (Fig. 5 ). We also quantified the overall and population-weighted sums of the models’ R  2     values to comparatively assess each model’s explanatory power across CONUS. We found that search interest tends to lag changes in drought conditions mostly between 1–3 months. There are multiple factors which could drive such observations, including for example, whether a region primarily relies on rain or water storage for agriculture. Several studies have discussed the diverse impact of droughts and ensuing water scarcity on public reactions and opinions. For example, AghaKouchak et al. (2014)  argued that concurrent droughts and extreme heatwaves from climate change have significant social implications, and they could influence public opinions and reactions. Drier conditions are increasingly linked to public health issues (Barrera et al., 2023; Moyo et al., 2023 ) and vegetation health as well (Chilakala et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2023 ), which impact people’s interest in droughts.   4 Conclusions & discussion We applied U-Net models and compared them with linear and reductionist approaches to understand the complex dynamics between droughts and drought awareness within CONUS. To do this, we leveraged S P E I    and Google Trends S I   . The primary findings of this study are (see the research question outlined in Section 1.1 ): • We found significant nonlinear and heterogeneous relationships between droughts and drought awareness as evidenced by the spatial variability of the UNet models’ R  2     values between predicted and observed drought awareness.  • We discovered that the most important drivers of this nonlinear relationship are the variability and extent of drought trends and severity, as well as climatic extremes.  • We also found that reductionist linear approaches, such as a PCA, might not be effective in capturing the nuanced relationship between droughts and drought awareness at various dimensions and scales.  • The strongest nonlinear associations were observed over the Western CONUS, followed by the Northeastern, Southeastern, and lastly the Central regions.  • We found that changes in drought awareness tends to lag changing drought conditions by around 1 to 3 months.    Our findings strongly underscore the nonlinearity and heterogeneity of the dynamics between droughts and drought awareness within the CONUS. By training the UNet models on a wide range of drought conditions and corresponding drought awareness data, we captured the intricate patterns and dependencies, adapting to the dynamic and nonstationary nature of the relationships. This approach allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the factors driving drought awareness, without relying on pre-defined thresholds or assumptions about the nature of the relationships. While dimensionality reduction with linear methods such as the PCA might provide some insights, our custom UNet models (with pixel-level predictions) were significantly better at capturing these interactions and explaining the variances of the variables involved. Our findings also provide significant insights into changes in human behavior with varying climatic conditions across the CONUS. We expect these findings to better inform the stakeholders at various levels making decisions on water resources management, conservation, policies, legislation, communication, and education. Future studies can build on our research by exploring (and modeling) the relationships between various natural and anthropogenic driven phenomena and anthropogenic responses. We particularly encourage future studies to understand meteorological droughts’ impact on agricultural, hydrological, and socioeconomic droughts and quantifying the multidimensional non-stationary interplay between these phenomena and their corresponding human responses at various scales. The results of our study boosts the feasibility of training large-domain drought prediction models in the sense that we provided the evidence that we can now better predict changes in drought awareness based on predicted drought conditions. As the impacts of anthropogenic-driven climate change become increasingly felt and realized by humans across the world, we expect future experiments to discover and decode more complex relationships between extreme weather events (such as droughts) with people’s engagement on different platforms across the global web. Given this scenario, computer vision models, such as our custom U-Nets, will continue to be significantly useful towards understanding (evolving) human-drought interactions.
1 Introduction Drought is one of the natural phenomena influencing many aspects of human activities like water scarcity, food production, agriculture, industry and ecological conditions of the environment. For decades, drought has caused huge financial losses in Europe and globally. As shown by Naumann et al. (2021) , in Europe drought damages could strongly increase with global warming and, in case no climate action is taken, annual drought losses in the European Union and the United Kingdom are projected to rise to more than €65 billion per year (currently they are €9 billion per year). Moreover, drought in southern and western parts of Europe could reduce regional agriculture economic output by 10 %. In the agricultural sector, the highest drought risk has been observed in southeastern Europe as well as northern and southern Africa (Meza et al., 2020 ). Counteracting the effects of drought is one of the main priorities of the European Union's climate policy. Already 23 years ago, the European Union developed the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) , which points the way forward for water management. Poland is characterised by low water resources compared to Europe. The amount of renewable freshwater resources per Polish inhabitant is nearly 1.6 thousand m3 , signalling a threat of water stress. Among European countries, only Czech Republic, Denmark and Malta have less water (SDG, 2020 ). Small water resources and a large share of light soils characterised by low water holding capacity make Poland particularly vulnerable to losses caused by agricultural drought (Stuczyński et al., 2007 ). In order to reduce drought losses for Poland, the Drought Effects Counteracting Plan (DECP 2021 ) for 2021–2027 has been developed in accordance with the guidelines of the Directive (2000/60/EC), as well as of national legislation (The Water Law Act 2017 ). This plan is a strategic document coordinating all activities concerning drought. A key action to prevent the effects of drought is to increase water retention (DECP 2021 ). The main practical course of action is to restore the natural conditions of the water cycle by enhancing natural retention and using technical solutions that contribute to slowing down water run-off from the environment, while agriculture is to contribute to increasing soil retention through appropriately selected agrotechnical treatments (DECP 2021 ). In central and northern Europe, the period 2018–2020 is referred to as a multi-annual drought period (Cammalleri et al., 2023 ). According to Barbosa et al., (2021)  from October 2019 to September 2020, dry conditions in central and Eastern Europe had a mild impact on agriculture with slightly reduced crop yields, while several local authorities ordered preventive measures. In case of an increase of temperature and a decrease in precipitation, drought influences land use changes. Within this context, the occurrence of extremely high air temperature values in the summer seasons at the turn of the 20th and 21st centuries deserves attention (Twardosz, 2009 ). For example, during the exceptional heat wave in Western Europe in 2003, there were significant precipitation deficits, which resulted in substantial agricultural losses and numerous fires (Trigo et al., 2005 ). De Jager et al. (2022)  evidenced an increase in the number of wildfires in Europe since 2010 during dry spells. Climate forecasts for the 21st century have predicted an increase in the occurrence of drought in a large part of Europe, especially Southern Europe, while drought decreases have been projected only for a limited portion of Northern Europe (Stagge et al., 2017 ). Although contemporary rainfall trends and scenarios for Poland at the end of the 21st century do not predict a reduction in rainfall, and indeed anticipate a small increase of about 5–10 %, it cannot be excluded that drought will not pose a threat. The drought caused by climate change is currently unfolding in Poland under the following conditions: rising air temperatures and an increase in the variability of rainfall. An increase in the coefficient of variation of precipitation will create conditions for an increase in the frequency of atmospheric drought, and subsequently agricultural and hydrological drought (Ziernicka-Wojtaszek and Kopcińska, 2020 ). The intensification of droughts, resulting from current climate change, manifests in more frequent occurrences of this phenomenon, in increased intensity, and in its spreading to more distant areas of the country. As an example, during the period 1951–1981, there were 6 drought events (about one drought every 5 years), whereas in the period 1982–2011, there were 18 drought periods (about one drought every 2 years) (Lorenc, 2011 ). In the area of the Polish and Ukrainian Carpathians, several periods with a deficit of rainwater have been detected (Cebulska, 2016, 2018, 2021 ), and it is a common trend that atmospheric droughts of varying severity can occur in this area at different times of the year. Cebulska (2018)  showed that the longest period without precipitation in the 21st century occurred between October and November 2011 and lasted between 26 and 40 days, covering the western and southern part of the Polish Carpathians. Kišš et al. (2022)  detected that the number of days with both meteorological and agricultural droughts is increasing in Slovakia. This trend can also be seen in the countries neighboring Slovakia, such as Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic, and thus monitoring drought phenomena also in regions where water resources seems to be sufficient is paramount. Bokwa et al. (2021)  performed a study on drought in the mountains areas of Polish Carpathians, and showed an increasing frequency of dry months especially in the cold half of the year. Anyway, only little research about the spatial and temporal variability of meteorological drought and the main mechanism determining its performance in Central Europe is currently available. Spatial and temporal monitoring of meteorological drought is a complicated process, and it has been developed over some decades using different indicators such as the Weighted Anomaly Standardized Precipitation Index (WASP) (Lyon, 2004 ), the Effective Drought Index (EDI) (Byun and Wilhite, 1999 ), the Relative Precipitation Index (RPI) (Kaczorowska, 1962, Przedpełska, 1971, Bokwa et al., 2021 ), the NOAA Drought Index (NDI) (Strommen and Motha, 1987 ).One of the most popular indictors is the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) proposed by McKee et al. (1993) , which is used to represent meteorological drought. The SPI has several advantages (Lloyd-Hughes and Saunders, 2002; Hayes et al., 1999 ) over many other drought indices. Firstly, it is based on rainfall only, so that in the absence of other hydro-meteorological measurements, drought assessment is still possible. Secondly, the SPI can be used to quantify precipitation deficit for multiple timescales, thus allowing the assessment of drought conditions in meteorological, hydrological and agriculture applications. On short timescales, the SPI is closely related to soil moisture, while at longer timescales, the SPI can be related to groundwater and reservoir storage. Finally, standardization of the SPI ensures that the frequency of extreme drought events at any location and any timescale is approximately constant. There are also some disadvantages in the use of the SPI. First, according to Wu et al. (2005)  it is best to use the longest possible time range to calculate the SPI, because short data sets may be subject to large errors in the estimated values (Osuch et al., 2016 ). Another disadvantage of the SPI is finding an appropriate way to implement standardization related to the identification of the theoretical probability function for modeling extremely different rainfall data (Lloyd-Hughes and Saunders, 2002; Pieper et al., 2020 ). Finally, the SPI does not consider the influence of temperature on the phenomenon of drought, being based on the amount of precipitation only. Despite these limitations, the SPI is generally used as good approximate of dry and wet periods because necessary data like precipitation have the longest time series and small number of gaps. Karavitis et al. (2011)  showed that the SPI can be useful for drought forecasting and warning. In fact, the SPI has been used to analyze and characterize the occurrence of droughts in several regional analysis (Brleković and Tadić, 2022; Minh et al., 2022; Achite et al., 2021; Caloiero et al., 2021 ). In Poland, an analysis of the frequency of drought occurrence was carried out, and results may support actions and decisions mitigating the negative effects of drought (Łabędzki and Bąk, 2014; Kalbarczyk and Kalbarczyk, 2022 ). Within this context, the aim of this paper is to analyze drought in a Central European area by means of the SPI. The innovative aspect of the work is the spatial and temporal analysis of drought, expressed as SPI, in a heterogenous area of the Polish Carpathians and a highland Region in East-Central part of Europe, based on long-term precipitation data. Moreover, in this work, for the first time the drought characteristics assessed have been discussed based on the atmospheric circulation calendar.  2 Study site The region under investigation is the Upper Vistula Basin located in the southern and south-eastern part of Poland. The area of this region is approximately 51,000 km2 , i.e. a quarter of the entire Vistula basin. This area is very diverse, as it includes various geographical regions (Carpathian Mountains, Subcarpathian basins, Lesser Poland Uplands). There are four climatic regions (Fig. 1  ) in the study area (Niedźwiedź and Obrębska-Starklowa, 1991 ): mountain with vertical climatic zones, Carpathian Foothills, foothill valleys, and highlands. In the mountain climate region there is a clearly marked climatic layering. Here, Hess (1965)  distinguished six climatic levels: moderately warm, moderately cool, cool, very cool, moderately cold and cold. The northern border of this climatic region is approximately the course of the annual isotherm of 7 °C, coinciding with the threshold of the Beskids. In the highest part of the Polish Tatras, the average annual air temperature drops to −4°C. In this area there are inter-mountain valleys: the Orawa − Nowy Targ Valley, the Subtatran Trench, and the Żywiec Valley. The boundaries of the climate region of the Carpathian Foothills are determined by the course of the annual isotherm of 7 °C from the south and 8 °C from the north. In this region there is the inland Sącz Valley, where temperature inversions also occur. The climate region of the foothill basins includes the Subcarpathian Basins with several areas with large urban, and industrial influences. The average annual temperature in this area is around 8 °C. The northern part of the study area constitutes the highland climate region with five sub-regions. Most of this area is within the scope of a warm temperate climate whose average annual temperature is about 7–8 °C; in the highest part of this region (Świętokrzyskie Mountains), there is a vertical cool climatic zone, with an average annual temperature below 6 °C. In the area of the upper Vistula river basin, there is great diversity of precipitation. The amount of precipitation depends not only on atmospheric circulation, but also on the altitude longitude, and landform. The area is characterized by a dense network of surface waters. At the same time, there is a constant development of settlement and changes in land use (multiple increase in covered area, including roads, at the expense of forests, and arable land). The consequence of such changes in the development of the catchment area is the systematic sealing of its surface, and thus changes in the hydrological cycle of the river basin (increase and acceleration of surface runoff, changes in the intensity of transpiration processes) (Niedźwiedź and Obrębska-Starklowa, 1991 ).  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Data and concept of the research Precipitation monthly data were collected from 55 meteorological stations (Fig. 2  ). The stations are located in the catchment area of the Upper Vistula river basin in the southeastern part of Poland. Meteorological data were obtained from the database of the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management of the National Research Institute in Warsaw. Only those stations for which the longest homogeneous sequences of monthly precipitation data were available were considered. In particular, for 28 meteorological stations, monthly precipitation data from 1961 to 2022 were obtained, for 17 stations from 1961 to 2014, and for 10 meteorological stations from 1961 to 2015 (Fig. 2 ). A double mass curve analysis (Searcy and Hardison, 1960, Gulmez et al., 2023 ) was performed to check the consistency of the data at the analyzed stations. The cumulative total annual precipitation was determined for each station and plotted against the cumulative total mean annual precipitation for the other stations. Two regression models, linear and linear with a breakpoint (Siegmund and Zhang, 1994 ), were then fitted to identify any abrupt temporal changes. Results showed that the precipitation time series analyzed in this study are consistent. The double mass curve analysis did not indicate any abrupt temporal changes at the stations analyzed. The long-term and annual course of the lowest monthly precipitation were examined. For this purpose, from the precipitation database of each station, the lowest monthly precipitation was selected for each year. Then, the frequency of the lowest precipitation occurrences in the annual course was determined, and the long-term trends of these precipitations were analyzed using the widely used Mann-Kendall test (MK) (Mann-Kendall, 1975, Banasik and Hejduk, 2012, Młyński et al., 2018 ). Subsequently, based on the monthly sequences of precipitation from the 55 considered stations, dry periods were identified using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) (McKee et al., 1993, 1995 ). The frequency of droughts of varying severity was examined, as well as the trend in SPI changes. In the study area, the frequency of the extremely dry (ED) 3-month periods was determined within the circulation types and air masses using the calendar of circulation types over southern Poland (Niedźwiedź, 1981 ).  3.2 Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is quite a simple index that can be linked with soil moisture (Ariyanto et al., 2020 ) and groundwater (Lorenzo-Lacruz et al., 2017, Secci et al., 2021 ), and depends on the time of aggregation. Both soil moisture and groundwater strongly influence water resources in the Upper Vistula Basin (Pociask-Karteczka, 2016 ). Due to the configuration of the research area, measurement stations (50 out of 55) which had a complete set of data consistent in terms of location and time of measurement were selected for analysis. These stations do not conduct measurements of climate elements necessary for determining SPEI. Only in 5 climatological/synoptic stations located in the research area are such measurements conducted, however, due to their small number, only SPI index was used to determine meteorological drought in the Upper Vistula Basin. The SPI is calculated based on the cumulative probability gamma distribution of precipitation data collected at the observation station (Edwards and McKee, 1997 ). The SPI computation involves fitting a gamma probability density function to the frequency distribution of precipitation totals for a specific station. The alpha and beta parameters of the gamma probability density function are estimated for each station and for each desired time scale (e.g., 3, 6, 9, or 12 months). The cumulative probability of gamma distribution can be presented as:(1) G x   = ∫ 0  x  g x   d x = 1 β ^   a ^   Γ α ^      ∫ 0  x  x  α - 1   e  - x / β   d x     where α  and β  are the shape and scale parameters respectively. x  is consecutive precipitation and Γ (α) is the gamma function. To allow for the possibility that the precipitation may be zero, a mixed probability distribution is used, for which the cumulative probability becomes(2) H x   = q + 1 - q   G x       where q  is the probability that the quantity of precipitation equals zero. The calculation of the SPI is based on the following equation (Llyoyd-Hughes and Saunders 2002):(3) SPI = - t - c 0  + c 1  t + c 2  t  2   1 + d 1  t + d 2  t  2  + d 3  t  3      f o r 0 < H x   ≤ 0.5    + t - c 0  + c 1  t + c 2  t  2   1 + d 1  t + d 2  t  2  + d 3  t  3      f o r 0.5 < H x   ≤ 1.0            where t is determined as(4) t = l n 1 H x      2       f o r 0 < H x   ≤ 0.5    l n 1 1 - H x      2       f o r 0.5 < H x   ≤ 1.0            and c 0 . c 1 . c 2 . d 1 . d 2  and d 3  are coefficients whose values are:(5) c 0  = 2.515517 .  c 1  = 0.802853 .  c 2  = 0.010328        (6) d 1  = 1.432788 d 2  = 0.189269  d 3  = 0.001308         According to McKee et al. (1993)  different categories and their associated approximate probabilities of wet and dry spells can be determined based on SPI for the desired time scale, as presented in Table 1  . SPI is expected to exhibit a nearly normal (bell curve) distribution, with SPI values close to 0 being the most frequent, and high positive or negative SPI values (indicating very wet or very dry periods, respectively) being rare. Drought frequency (Fi  ) is the chance of a station being in drought in a given year. This was estimated empirically based on the following formula:(7) F i  = n N  100 \%      where n  is the number of years of drought (SPI equal 0 or less) and N  is the number of analyzed years. In the paper, different time aggregation of SPI were used to deeply analyze of drought in the Upper Vistula Basin. SPI-3 can be used as an indicator for immediate impacts such as reduced soil moisture, snowpack, and flow in smaller creeks, which are in Upper Vistula Basin. In case longer time of aggregation, 6, 9 and 12 month, the SPI can be used as an indicator for reduced stream flow and reservoir storage and the SPI responds more slowly to changes in precipitation for longer time of aggregation which can be related to the global impact of drought on the water supply of the region. Moreover the choice of a longer accumulation period can reduce the uncertainty for the SPI (Laimighofer and Laaha, 2022 ).  3.3 Periodicity of extreme drought To decompose the complex time series, containing cyclic components, into several basic sinusoidal functions (sine and cosine) with specific “wavelengths”, the Fourier analysis was used (Wałęga et al., 2016 ). The analysis reveals a few periodic cycles of different wavelengths, which at first appeared in the tested time series to be more or less random walking. A general model of the spectral function may be described by the multiple regression function (Walega and Michalec, 2014 ):(8) X t  = a 0  + ∑ a k  cos λ k  t   + b k  sin λ k  t      f o r  k  ∊  ( 1 ,  q )      where: Xt  – random variable in time t, a0  – constant term, ak  and bk  – regression coefficients, λk  – frequency, t – time, q – number of variables in the model related to the number of data within the set. The results of the spectral analysis are presented as a periodograph, which was smoothed by the transformation of the weighted moving average using Hamming’s method to remove random fluctuations. The periodograph shows how the variance of the time series is decomposed into individual frequencies. Spectral analysis was performed using STATISTICA 13.0 software.  3.4 Calendar of atmospheric circulation types In the temperate zone, atmospheric circulation plays a significant role in shaping precipitation. The atmospheric circulation influences vertical air movements, which contribute to the occurrence of precipitation. Therefore, to determine the influence of circulation and air masses on the frequency of designated extremely dry (ED) 3-month periods in the study area, the calendar of circulation types over southern Poland was used. There are many classifications of circulation types, for example, for Central Europe “Grosswetterlagen” (Catalog of Grosswetterlagen…1993 ), for Great Britain Lamb (1972) , for Poland for example Lityński (1969), Osuchowska-Klein (1991) . However, due to the research area − the southern part of Poland − the authors adopted the circulation type calendar developed for this region by Niedźwiedź (1981, 2021) . This calendar was prepared based on synoptic maps of southern Europe at 00 and 12 UTC, as well as baric topography maps for the 700 hPa level. The classification, developed by Niedźwiedź (1981, 2021)  includes a list of 21 types of atmospheric circulation, atmospheric fronts, and air mass types. It comprises 20 types of synoptic situations, designated by letter symbols representing the direction of advection for both anticyclonic and cyclonic systems – see Table 2  . The classification was based on the atmospheric circulation typology developed by Hubert Horace Lamb (1972)  for the British Isles, with some modifications, particularly concerning non-advection situations. Based on synoptic maps of Europe, the direction of air mass advection (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) and the type of barometric system (a – anticyclonic situation, c – cyclonic situation) were determined. In addition to sixteen advection situations, two non-advection types were distinguished: Ca – central anticyclone situation and Ka – anticyclonic wedge or ridge of high pressure, as well as two cyclonic types with varied advection: Cc – central cyclonic, centre of low and Bc – cyclonic trough. Situations not classifiable into other distinguished types and baric saddles were marked with 'x' (Niedźwiedź and Łupikasza, 2019 ).   4 Results and discussion 4.1 The lowest monthly precipitation The lowest monthly precipitation (Pmin) showed significant variability not only over time but also in space. Over the years, there were periods with excessive rainfall as well as periods of rainfall deficit. In several stations, the lowest Pmin value was 0 mm (Fig. 3  ), while the highest one exceeded 60 mm in 4 meteorological stations located in the mountain climate region, above 400 m a.s.l. (Cisna, Rycerka Górna, Szczyrk, and Ustroń Równica Wieś). Anyway, in the long-term course of the Pmin, no statistically significant trends were observed at the 0.05 significance level in any station, only short-term fluctuations were noticed. As regards the no-rain intervals, during the observation period, there were months with no rainfall, especially in the colder half of the year. February 1976 was one such month with no precipitation at all in the meteorological stations of Grybów and Futory and precipitation not exceeding 10 mm in the other stations. Similarly, in April 2009, a lack of precipitation was observed in Bartków, Chrzanów, and Małogoszcz when, in the Eastern Carpathians, represented by the station in Cisna, the sum exceeded 50 mm. This period is particularly relevant because, in April 2009, a drought event mainly affected Central Europe due to high temperatures and high-pressure systems (Cebulska and Twardosz, 2010 ). Moreover, the extreme dry months also include November 2011, during which there was no rainfall in 7 meteorological stations (Bartków, Chrzanów, Goczałkowice-Zdrój, Grodzisk Dolny, Kraków, Piwnów, and Rajcza). In the other stations, the precipitation for that month did not exceed 4 mm, accounting for less than 6 % of the long-term average monthly precipitation. During the summer period, there were no months without rainfall in any of the considered stations. However, there were months with precipitation below 5 % of the long-term average.  4.2 Trends of SPI Given the strong autocorrelation in the SPI values, for each station, trend analysis was performed separately for the different months. Figs. 4–7      show the number of stations with statistical significantly values of Z statistics MK test (p value ≤ 0.05). Out of the 55 stations analyzed, 28 (50.9 %) showed statistically significant trends in the SPI values. For the 3-month SPI, the months with the highest number of stations showing significant trends were March, November, May, and January, with 8, 5, 4, and 4 stations, respectively. Only in July and September there were no trends detected in the analyzed stations. Significantly, in most cases, the SPI trend was positive. However, negative trends were observed in January (4 stations − 100 % of the stations with a significant trend in this month), February (1 station), June (1 station), and August (1 station) – Fig. 4 . For the 6-month SPI, the highest number of stations with statistically significant trends were observed in February (11 stations), May (6 stations), and March (4 stations). Only 1 station showed a negative trend, and that was in April – Fig. 5 . The number of stations with significant trends showed low variability for the 9-month SPI. In May and March, significantly positive trends were observed in 20 and 5 stations, respectively. Only 1 station showed a statistically significant negative trend in July and December – Fig. 6 . Regarding the 12-month SPI trend, a high number of stations with significant trends were observed between January and August, with the highest values in March and April, with 6 and 5 stations, respectively. All these detected trends were positive – Fig. 7 . These results agree with the ones of Hänsel et al. (2019)  who detected wetting trends in autumn and winter in the Central part of Europe. The highest number of months with statistically significant trends of the SPI values was observed at the Rozdziele and Koszarawa stations. Both the stations are located in the southern part of the analyzed region (Figs. 4–7 ). The Koszarawa station is situated in a mountainous area with an elevation above 580 m a.s.l., while Rozdziele is in a highland area with a main elevation of 545 m a.s.l.. In particular, at the Rozdziele station, statistically significant 3-months SPI trends were observed in 6 months (March, April, May, October, November, and December), 6-month SPI trends in 8 months (January, February, March, April, May, October, November, and December), 9-month SPI trends in 10 months (January, February, March, April, June, September, October, November, and December), and 12-month SPI trends in each of the 12 months. For all the analyzed cases, trends had positive values. At the Koszarawa station, statistically significant 3-month SPI trends were observed in November, 6-month SPI trends in 4 months (February, March, April, and May), 9-month SPI trends during 4 months (the same months as in 6-month SPI), and 12-month SPI during 9 months (January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, and December). As in the case of the Rozdziele station, all trends had positive values. Generally, in the majority of stations where statistically significant trends were detected, positive values of Z statistics were observed. The highest number of negative trends was observed at the Harkabuz station (3 cases) and Kańczuka station (2 cases). Overall, the highest number of cases of statistically significant trends was detected for the 12- and 9-month SPI, equal to 36 and 22 cases, respectively, while the lowest number of cases was for the 6-month SPI (14 cases). Generally, statistically significant trends were more frequently observed at stations located in the western part of the analyzed region – Figs. 4–7 . The results presented confirm the ones of Spinoni et al. (2015)  for which Central and Eastern Europe showed no clear tendencies in trends of droughts, and these regions acts like transition areas. Since the results of the trend analysis obtained for SPI-3 in dominant cases are not significant, trends associated with the inter-annual drought patterns were negligible. Based on the increasing rates of the ascending trends associated with the SPI-9 and SPI-12, the formation of the streamflow(s) and available water in catchments are expected to reduce a deficit. Also, Przybylak et al. (2020)  reported that the long-term frequency of droughts in Poland has been stable in the last two or three centuries. In most cases, positive trends confirmed the studies described by Caloiero et al. (2018)  with Central Europe dominated by positive SPI trends in winters and autumn–winter periods. The tendency and occurrence of drought in this part of Europe can be determined by combination of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and the eastern Atlantic/western Russia (EA/WR) circulation, as reported by Kingston et al. (2015) . The patterns are the most important drivers of the proportion of European land area experiencing drought on a monthly time scale.  4.3 Spatial variability frequency of periods of drought with different classes For all measuring stations during the years 1961–2022, based on the values of the SPI for 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month periods, MD, SD, and ED were identified. These periods occurred at each meteorological station but with varying intensities and frequencies of their occurrences (Figs. 8–11     ). The highest number of moderate drought (above 10 % of all years) occurred in the area below 300 m a.s.l. However, it is worth noting Węglówka (460 m a.s.l.) and Zakopane, located at an elevation of 844 m a.s.l., for which the period of moderate drought (3-month SPI) exceeded 11 % (Fig. 8 ). Much fewer 3-month periods of SD were observed, in the east part of the region. The least number of ED were observed in Rozdziele, Jakubowice, and Szczucin (below 10 cases) – in the central part of the region. Regardless of the location of the meteorological station, the number of 3-month periods of drought with different intensities varied only slightly among the stations, ranging from 14 to 18 % (Fig. 8 ). The highest, 18 % of drought periods, occurred in Szczucin and Czeladź. Slightly less, around 17 % of such periods were observed, especially in the central part of the Carpathian Foothills Climate Region, as well as in the eastern regions of the study area. The spatial variation of the study area does not significantly influence the number of drought periods with different durations. During the study period, 6-month periods of drought with different intensities occurred in all meteorological stations (Fig. 9 ). Only in 6 meteorological stations ED occurred in every month: in Chrzanów, Gorlice, Grodzisk, and Raków, located below 300 m a.s.l., in Wolbrom, located at 373 m a.s.l., located in the central and west part of the region, and in Żabnica at an elevation higher than 500 m a.s.l. (south-eastern part of the region). In the remaining meteorological stations, there were months during which extreme drought did not occur throughout the study period. Across the entire study area, the highest number of ED periods (i.e. 4) occurred in the eastern part of the region in December - 1973 and in 1983. During the same period, there were 2–4 times more periods of SD conditions in meteorological stations than extreme dry conditions. Throughout the year, months without SD drought occurred. However, the highest number of 6-month periods of SD drought, over 40 cases, occurred in Krakow, Małogoszcz, Szczawne, Szerzyny, Temeszów, Dynów, and Tylicz, in the southern part of the study area (575 m a.s.l.). Moderately dry periods occurred most frequently, in every month of the year. The highest number of moderately dry periods occurred in the Pilzno area, 91 cases (12.3 %). As regards the 1971 9-month period, extreme dry conditions occurred in every meteorological station (Fig. 10 ), but every month only in 3 stations (Raków, Szerzyny, and Wadowice) – central or west part of region. In June, July, and August, the ED period occurred sporadically, with up to 2 cases. However, the highest number of 9-month periods of ED, 5 cases, occurred in April in Żabnica (south-west part) in the years 1984, 1990, 1991, 1993, and 1994. There were 4 cases of ED periods in October 1964, 1973, 1976, and 1982, as well as in November in Krasna, in the eastern part of region, in 1976, 1982, 1986, and 2003. Similarly to ED, SD conditions occurred in every station. The number of SD periods in individual months throughout the year ranged from 5 to 7 cases. The highest number of 7 cases occurred in April in Sędziszów (northern part) and in May in Czeladź (western part). Moderately dry conditions constituted the largest percentage among the dry periods. The southern part of the study area, including the region of Zakopane (southern part of the region), is noteworthy, where the number of cases of these droughts amounted to 89 (12 %). Long-term drought of varying intensities, lasting for 12 months, occurred in the study area (Fig. 11 ) in every station during the study period, but not in every month. In the mountainous region, represented by stations such as Zakopane (844 m a.s.l.) and Białka Tatrzańska (700 m a.s.l.) (south part of the region), the ED drought occurred sporadically with 1–2 cases during the study period. In the rest of the area, the number of cases of ED drought did not exceed 4. Prolonged SD drought occurred much more frequently in the northern regions of the study area. Moderately dry conditions have not only been identified in the upland areas but also in the Carpathian region. For example, in Czeladź (west part of region), 95 cases of such drought were observed between 1961 and 2022. Long-term drought is particularly important because prolonged lack of atmospheric precipitation results in water deficiency in the lithosphere and lack of streamflow can lead to hydrological drought. The results indicate that the southern and the eastern part of the Upper Vistula basin are the most susceptible to drought occurrences due to the shift in climatic vertical zones caused by the rise in air temperatures. Bokwa et al. (2021)  reported an increase in air temperature in Polish Carpathian mountains from 0.5 to 0.7 °C per 10 years, and the highest increase is observed for Kasprowy where mean annual air temperature has exceeded 0 °C which means a shift from the “moderately cold” vertical climatic zone to “very cool”. Finally, an increase in air temperature caused an increased frequency of dry months express by SPI at about 15 % on an annual scale. Eini et al. (2023)  reported that severe meteorological droughts predominantly occur in eastern parts of Poland (Vistula region). This susceptibility is also observed in the foothills, as well as the basins situated at elevations ranging from 200 to 400 m above sea level. In these areas, the mean annual air temperatures are the highest across the vertical profile, and the annual precipitation totals vary significantly. Furthermore, the environmental conditions for beech trees are already unfavorable in these regions (Bokwa et al., 2021 ). Results also show high spatial variability of extremes and severe droughts in the analyzed region, as also confirmed by (Młyński et al., 2024 ). Kubiak-Wójcicka and Bąk (2018)  reported that in the period when meteorological drought was observed, the Vistula river basin was part of a much larger drought zone in Europe described by (Spinoni et al., 2015 ). In addition, the spatial variability of the drought is similar to the distribution of precipitation. Snow cover, mainly in the mountain areas, also contributes to determining the spatial variability of the SPI. An earlier snowmelt during winter or spring leads to earlier soil drying, thus increasing the likelihood of summer droughts (Szwed et al., 2017 ). Therefore, it seems justified to analyze dry periods of varying intensity and durations exceeding 6 months (e.g., SPI-9, SPI-12). As indicated by research such as Falarz (2004) , there is a slight downward trend in the number of snow-covered days and snow depth in Poland in the second half of the 20th century. Other studies show a lack of clear, statistically significant trends in snow cover thickness over longer periods (Szwed et al., 2017 ). The effects of climate change may influence the occurrence of more frequent droughts in the winter and early spring seasons, when snowmelt may decrease. As reported by Somorowska (2024) , as a result of warming in the cold-season, snow-dominated areas in Poland can be reduced from covering 86 % to covering 30 % of the country.  4.4 Intrannual temporal variability of SD and ED periods Throughout the year, SD and ED periods of different durations occur every month in the study area, and 3-month periods are significantly more frequent. Only in May and September more cases of prolonged 9-month drought were observed in this region (Fig. 12  ). The highest frequency of 3-month periods occurs in the winter months, when continental polar air (PPk) predominates. In these months the frequency is above 7 %, while in the other months is a little lower such as, for example, in May and July when it slightly exceeds 5 %. For the 6-month periods of SD and ED conditions, the highest number of such cases in the study area were observed in the months from January to April. Both short-term and long-term dry periods account for about 5 % in July. Over the course of the year, the 12-month period with insufficient rainfall occurred every month, but with the lowest frequency in April, equal to 5 % (Fig. 12 ). The results are consistent with the findings of Hänsel et al. (2021)  where increasing intensities of drought were observed in the northern part of Europe during the winter months, while a decrease was noted in the summer. In Poland, drought conditions are most frequently observed during the winter and autumn seasons in the southern part of the country (Kalbarczyk and Kalbarczyk, 2022, Przybylak et al., 2020 ).  4.5 Temporal distribution of SD and ED Atmospheric drought is characterized by irregular occurrence both in time and space. Its spatial distribution sporadically covers the entire study area. In the Upper Vistula River Basin, during the years 1961–2022, the 3-month period of SD and ED covered the entire area only in two years. This happened from February to April 1986 and from September to November 2011. During these periods, often precipitation did not exceed 50 % of the long-term average. In the years 1964, 1972 and 1984, SD and ED droughts covered over 90 % of the study area (Fig. 13  ). There were also years in which the dry period covered less than 5 % of the entire area. However, noteworthy are the years 1966 and 1998, during which the 3-month period of SD and ED did not occur. The 6-, 9-, and 12-month periods of SD and ED drought did not cover the entire study area. However, in 1984, the 6-month drought of SD and ED (November to April) covered 98 % of the study area. In the same year, the prolonged drought lasting for 9 and 12 months occurred in nearly 90 % of the Upper Vistula River Basin. The 3-month period of SD and ED drought more frequently (6–7 years) covered 80 % of the basin area compared to the prolonged drought (1–2 times in 62 years) affecting water resources in rivers. As reported in (Brunner and Chartier-Rescan, 2024 ), the drought extent increases during drought development from rainfall to discharge thanks to effects at the land-surface. High intensities of both short-duration (SD) and extended-duration (ED) droughts were observed in 2003, 2015, and 2018. This observation is supported by Tijdeman et al. (2022)  in southwestern Germany. The primary factor contributing to these phenomena was the simultaneous occurrence of high air temperatures, leading to a greater number of drought events and increased variability in their impacts. In the case of longer-term accumulation periods, a decreasing trend in the number of drought cases becomes apparent. Similar relationships were observed by Kubiak-Wójcicka et al. (2023)  in the northern part of Poland. Temporal distribution of drought strong depends on longest of analyzed period (Młyński et al., 2021 ) reported that in 1974–2017 period in two mountains catchments: Skawa and Dunajec, located in the Upper Vistula Basin, SPI classified years mainly as normal, but also was visible strong spatial variability of SPI.  4.6 Periodicity of extreme drought In Fig. 14  , the periodicity of the 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month SD and ED in the Upper Vistula Basin is shown. The analysis was performed for all stations. The analysis revealed a dominant 10-year periodicity for all analyzed variants of SPI. Additionally, Fourier analysis showed a 2-year periodicity for 3-, 6-, and 9-month SPI and a 31-year periodicity for the 12-month SPI. Gulmez et al. (2023)  reported that longest seasonality for longer time aggregation of SPI can affect groundwater. The similarity in the periodicity of SPI can be explained by the seasonality of monthly precipitations in the Upper Vistula Basin. The dominant 10-year periodicity of ED is caused by relatively higher precipitation in the Upper Vistula Basin, resulting in rarer extreme droughts compared to the middle or lower part of the Vistula Basin (Kubiak-Wójcicka and Bąk, 2018 ). According to Kalbarczyk and Kalbarczyk (2022)  meteorological drought occurs on average once every 7 years. A concerning trend is observed in the case of the 3-, 6-, and 9-month SPI, where a 2-year periodicity of extreme droughts is visible. This could be a result of climate change and increasing temperatures mainly in winter, spring, and summer seasons, along with a decrease in monthly precipitation mainly in spring and summer. Also Vaheddoost and Safari (2021) , reported that temporal correlation and seasonality of SPI can be determined by climate change. The precipitation deficit and high temperatures in Central Europe reported by Ionita et al. (2020)  may be triggered by a multiyear recurrent high-pressure system centered over the North Sea and northern Germany, along with a decline in the temperature gradient between the Arctic region and the mid-latitudes, diverting the Atlantic storm tracks northward. The results exhibit a typical behavior of climatic conditions in Poland with strong seasonality in precipitation and consequent drought indices (Karamuz et al., 2021 ). Moreover, periodicity of precipitation and drought depends on circulation changes (van Ulden and van Oldenborgh, 2006 ). In fact, long term periodicity can be ascribed to varying internal properties of some major circulation types (Beck et al., 2007 ). The short-term periodicity of extremes drought plays negative role on soil moisture and thus water deficit in agriculture (Orth and Seneviratne, 2012 ).  4.7 Influence of atmospheric circulation and air masses on the occurrence of extreme dry periods Atmospheric circulation plays an important role in climate dynamic. In many regions of the globe, it constitutes the most significant climatic factor (Niedźwiedź, 1981, Lhotka et al., 2020 ). Therefore, it is essential to understand the relationship between atmospheric circulation and periods of extreme drought by linking the frequency of drought days to circulation types. By understanding the relationship between atmospheric circulation and periods of extreme dryness, it is possible to forecast the occurrence of these periods based on specific atmospheric circulations types (Messeri et al., 2018 ). The frequency of atmospheric circulation types was examined in 149 3-month periods of ED. These types were adopted based on Niedźwiedź's circulation calendar (1981, 2021 ). As expected, the occurrence of ED periods is favored by anticyclonic circulation types. In all months with ED, the high-pressure ridge type (Ka) dominates (13.5 %). These results are confirmed by (Rehor et al., 2024 ), who detected in Central Europe more frequently episodes of fast drought were linked with anticyclonic situation. Moreover (Bartoszek et al., 2021 ) described atmospheric drought in the East-Central Poland and reported an increase in the frequency of high-pressure circulation types promoting more frequent drought events. The cyclonic trough type (Bc) also has significant importance (10.2 %), along with the western sector types Wc (8.5 %) and Wa (8.1 %) (Fig. 15  a). In all months with ED periods, one of the most common circulation types, Wa or Ka, is present. During the study period, 3-month periods were associated to ED conditions in over 50 % of the stations. This occurred in the years 1972, 1974, 1986, 1992, and 2011 when the dominant types were from the southern sector, SEa (13.5 %), Sa (9.5 %), and the high-pressure ridge, Ka (10.2 %) (Fig. 15 b). The ED period that occurred at 48 out of 55 meteorological stations is worth noting. It took place from September to November 2011. In the remaining meteorological stations, especially those located in the mountainous climate region, this period can be classified as very dry (SPI above −2.0). This period was favored by anticyclonic types, mainly from the western sector, Wa (17.3 %), high-pressure ridge, Ka (14.5 %), and southern anticyclonic, Sa (10.1 %). The anticyclonic situations, southern (Sa), western (Wa), and high-pressure ridge (Ka) also contributed to the occurrence of drought in the Polish Carpathians (Cebulska, 2018 ). Kingston et al., (2015)  reported that drought occurrence in Europe is linked to variations in the eastern Atlantic/western Russia (Ea/Wa) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) atmospheric circulation patterns, as partially confirmed in present study. In the future, an average shift to warmer and drier conditions in Central Europe could be observed across all circulation types in summer (Huguenin et al., 2020 ). For the long-term studies in the Upper Vistula Basin, the 3-month periods of ED were influenced by polar-maritime air masses (PPm), 52.3 % (Fig. 16  a), of which over 29 % of days were characterized by polar-maritime air masses in a stable, transformed state (PPms), 15.6 % by fresh polar-maritime air masses (PPm), and 7.3 % by warm polar-maritime air masses (PPmc) coming from the Atlantic south of the British Isles. 26.4 % of the days during the extreme drought periods were influenced by polar-continental air masses (PPk), which mainly came from the eastern sector, leading to hot and dry days in summer and cold and dry days in winter. The least frequent air masses (3.4 %) over the study area were tropical air masses (Fig. 16 a). In the case of the 3-month period that covered over 50 % of the meteorological stations affected by extreme drought, polar-continental air masses, 23 % played a role in causing the drought (Fig. 16 b). According to Niedźwiedź (1981) , there is a high probability of certain air masses flowing into the region − for instance, during the occurrence of the SEa situation in winter, polar-continental air masses flow in 89 % of the time, while in summer, the percentage drops to 68 %. Atmospheric circulation can on  influence the periodicity of drought described in Section 4.6 . This can be very important to provide potential recovery from an extreme drought period with moderate or severe drought (Antofie et al., 2015 ).  4.8 Influence of spatial and temporal variability of extreme droughts on the agricultural sector As regards the agricultural sector, the drought occurring during the growing season from IV to X is of greatest importance. This is the period when crops have high water needs. If prolonged atmospheric drought occurs during this period, its consequence is agricultural drought. According to literature, droughts (severe drought − SD and extreme drought − ED) are quite rare in the upper Vistula River basin. Drought is most frequently recorded for 3-month periods, in winter (X-IV), which accounted for about 7–8.4 %, while in summer it occurred 5–6.5 % on average (Fig. 14 ). In general, droughts are less frequent in the summer period (V-IX), which is more favorable for agricultural production. The results obtained allow us to assume that a 3-month drought occurs in the summer period once in 10 years on average. Similar results were obtained by Doroszewski et al. (2014)  according to whom, agricultural drought in the south-eastern part of Poland is very rare. In the northern region of the upper Vistula basin in the period 1961–2010, agricultural drought for the crops most sensitive to drought (spring cereals) occurs on average 1–2 times in 50 years. In contrast, in the mountainous region in the southern part of the upper Vistula basin, drought occurred occasionally 0–1. Compared to regions in Poland where drought occurs on average 5–6 times in a 10-year period in the central, north − western and central-eastern regions of Poland, the suitability of the upper Vistula river basin for agricultural production in terms of water resources is one of the best in the country. The high suitability of the region is also evidenced by the fact that during the period 1961–2022, the area was covered in its entirety only twice by a 3-month SD and ED period. The first drought which occurred in the spring period (II-IV) 1986. Due to the low water requirements of the plant during this period, this drought for agriculture did not cause much economic damage. On the other hand, the second drought in the autumn period (IX-XI) 2011 significantly reduced the emergence of winter cereals, as described in detail by Doroszewski et al. (2018) . Severe and extreme 3-months droughts occurrence 6–7 year covering a larger analyzed (80 % of the catchment area). Droughts, which occur cyclically every 10 years, do not pose a major threat to the stability of ecosystems and agricultural production. The high fragmentation of agriculture (diversification) makes agriculture in this region less vulnerable to adverse conditions. Drought can negatively affect forest conditions in the Upper Vistula Basin but, as reported by (Putzenlechner et al., 2023 ) the distribution of the impact depends on soil type, texture, stoniness, effective rooting depth, and available water capacity. More significantly, drought has a strong impact on the decrease in CO2  uptake in coniferous forests that are very often observed in mountain areas of the analysed region. As reported by (Jocher et al., 2021 ) the annual net ecosystem CO2  uptake at Rajec (Czech Republic) decreased by 50 % during the drought year. The upper Vistula river basin is characterized by a positive water balance (Jadczyszyn, 2022 ), which enables the retention of significant resources in this area. In connection with the implementation of Poland DECP (The Water Law Act 2017 ), mechanisms will be implemented in the future to support all water retention activities in the country in order to minimize the negative effects of natural phenomena (including drought prevention). The region is the most predisposed for the construction of larger water reservoirs in Poland. These can improve, on the one hand, the safety of agricultural areas against sudden river surges; on the other hand, the stored water can be used for agricultural purposes.   5 Conclusions In this study, we analyzed the spatial and temporal variability of extreme meteorological drought in the Upper Vistula Basin, Central Europe. The 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) were used as indicators of meteorological drought. For the 3-month SPI, the main climatic mechanisms determining extreme droughts were defined based on the calendar of synoptic circulations. We performed the analysis for 55 meteorological stations covering the period from 1961 to 2022. Our analyses revealed a high variability in the minimum sum of monthly precipitations. This variability is influenced by the topographic features of the analyzed region, which includes mountainous and lower areas. Regarding the trends of SPI, statistically significant trends were observed on 52.7 % of all analyzed stations, and in most cases, a positive trend was observed, indicating an increase in water resources in the Upper Vistula Basin. Statistically significant trends were more frequently observed in stations located in the western part of the analyzed region. The frequency of extreme drought events exhibited significant variability, with the highest number of extreme cases observed in the lower part of the study region, where a precipitation deficit was observed compared to the southern part of the Upper Vistula Basin, which experiences the highest precipitation in Poland. Long-term droughts, represented by the 12-month SPI, occurred in all stations but not in all years. Short-term droughts (3-month SPI) were most frequent in the winter season, 6 and 9-month SPI in winter and spring, and 12-month SPI in winter and autumn, respectively. The spatial distribution of droughts during the period 1961–2022 was highly diverse. For extreme events, 3-month SPI in the entire region was observed twice, in 1986 and 2011. The most intensive drought occurred in 1984, with the 6-month SPI covering 98 % of the analyzed region, and the 9 and 12-month SPI covering 90 % of the entire region. Droughts exhibit a seasonal pattern, with dominant 10-year periodicity for all analyzed variants of SPI. Additionally, Fourier analysis revealed 2-year periodicity for the 3, 6, and 9-month SPI and 31-year periodicity for the 12-month SPI. The results provide insights into the typical climatic conditions in Poland, with strong seasonality in precipitation. The study also highlighted that short-term extreme droughts, represented by the 3-month SPI, are often caused by anticyclonic situations with high-pressure wedges Ka and Wa, as observed in 52.3 % of cases. These findings are crucial for understanding the spatial and temporal variability of short and long-term extreme droughts in Central Europe, particularly for the agriculture sector dominant in the northern part of the analyzed region, where drought frequency is highest. Additionally, the study described the typical mechanisms generating short-term extreme droughts, which can be important for projecting future water deficits.
1 Introduction Coastal flooding incidents have emerged as the most significant and economically impactful natural disasters worldwide, driven by the increasing frequency of extreme weather events (Botzen et al., 2019; Neumann et al., 2015a ). Additionally, sea level rise (SLR) has compounded the severity of flooding cases and their frequency (Moftakhari et al., 2017; Nicholls, 2002; Vitousek et al., 2017 ). Coastal communities of the U.S. face flooding influences across multiple domains, including threats to coastal economies and property due to SLR and heavy precipitation events and resulting land losses, degradation of coastal environments or ecosystems, and exacerbation of existing environmental injustice and inequity due to heightened coastal flooding (Bremond et al., 2013; Fleming et al., 2018; Bates et al., 2021 ) Consequently, coastal flooding is now recognized as a critical national security concern, highlighting the urgent need for effective flood management strategies (House, 2015 ). Flood mitigation strategies require accurate estimation of flood inundation. Such estimations not only represent a distinct field of study but also provide indispensable data for a range of flood-related investigations, including the deployment of monitoring networks, evaluations of societal impact, assessments of urbanization trends, and the formulation of flood adaption and mitigation strategies (Council, 2015; Saulnier et al., 2017 ). Flood modeling for the flood risk and inundation analysis can be categorized into three main approaches: empirical, hydrodynamic (physical), and conceptual (Teng et al., 2017 ). The empirical method, rooted in the analysis of historical flood event data, offers advantages such as rapid computation and ease of replication (Segura-Beltrán et al., 2016 ). Recent advancements in computational capabilities, including machine learning (e.g., Xie et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022 ), have further enhanced this approach, allowing for the derivation of flood-causing factors and flood prediction based on historical data (e.g., Kabir et al., 2020; Lei et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2023; Purvis et al., 2008; Wagenaar et al., 2020 ). However, its reliability becomes less certain in scenarios not previously encountered, such as those involving SLR, global warming, and extensive urbanization. In contrast, hydrodynamic models provide a more detailed analysis of flood risk across various conditions, including scenarios with SLR and urbanization (e.g., Du et al., 2012 ; Gori et al., 2020 ; Grimaldi et al., 2013; Paiva et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2007 ). Nevertheless, these models heavily rely on the quality and quantity of input physical data, such as digital elevation and bathymetry, as well as hydraulic structures. The complexity and computational cost of these models can increase significantly when incorporating higher resolution and various hydraulic structures and complex bathymetric scenarios (e.g., Afshari et al., 2018; Bates and De Roo, 2000; Néelz, 2009; Nguyen et al., 2016; Teng et al., 2017 ). The third approach, conceptual models, employs a non-physical process of inundation, using conceptual methodologies such as cellular automata (Jamali et al., 2019 ) and the bathtub theory (Fereshtehpour and Karamouz, 2018 ). However, these models may lack accuracy and reliability in scenarios with rapidly changing water dynamics, such as surges or tsunamis. In addition to the conventional flood modeling approaches discussed above, the geostatistical approach (GA) based on spatial monitoring network data presents a potentially promising method for real-time flood modeling. Classical GA involves the spatial interpolation of time-invariant spatial properties, such as hydraulic conductivity and bathymetry, using a two-point spatial covariance (Guo et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2018; Zhao and Luo, 2020 ). When applying GA to dynamic systems like real-time flooding water levels, one must either assume the spatial covariance is time-independent or derive a time-changing spatial covariance for each interpolation time moment. Beyond interpolation, GA can also be formulated as an inverse modeling approach within the Bayesian framework to produce the best linear estimates while accounting for uncertainties in spatially correlated parameter fields. To efficiently compute GA with a large number of variables, Zhao and Luo (2020)  developed a reduced GA (RGA) for estimating latent variables, using dimension reduction methodology based on principal component analysis (PCA) (Eastman and Fulk, 1993 ). Similarly, Son et al (2023)  employed a related approach to assimilate real-time monitoring data and generate real-time water level maps. They used low-rank empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs) derived from a calibrated coastal flooding model. In this research, we introduce a comprehensive approach that integrates fluvial hydrodynamic models with RGA to provide both interpolation and inverse modeling capabilities for real-time spatial mapping of flooding. We name this approach the physics-informed geostatistical approach (PIGA), as it combines RGA (Zhao and Luo, 2020 ) with a method utilizing non-parametric spatial covariance derived from hydrodynamic (physical) models (Son et al., 2023 ). To demonstrate the effectiveness of PIGA, we apply this approach to the Savannah River, an area susceptible to coastal flooding and influenced by precipitation patterns. We develop a hydrodynamic model using the Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System (HEC-RAS), calibrated using historical monitoring data, to simulate fluvial floods. PIGA leverages spatial correlations computed from the physical HEC-RAS model and incorporates PCA along with a low-rank approximation of covariance matrices. Real-time water level maps can then be generated using either interpolation or inverse modeling techniques based on updated monitoring data. PIGA highlights the sensitivity of physical models to data quality and demonstrates how a Bayesian geostatistical approach can effectively complement these physical models. By integrating the strengths of both empirical and physical methods, while mitigating the weaknesses associated with each, PIGA offers a promising solution for real-time flood mapping.  2 Research domain and hurricane events Our research site is situated in Chatham County, Georgia, along the Savannah River, an area highly prone to flood hazards. The region has a history of frequent flooding events that pose significant threats to public safety and infrastructure. Several factors contribute to Chatham County's heightened risk of coastal flooding, including its low elevation, relatively flat terrain, and the absence of flood protection structures such as storm walls and weirs. Furthermore, the area is crisscrossed by numerous rivers and tributaries, further exacerbating its vulnerability. Given that coastal regions along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts face greater flooding risks compared to other parts of the country due to SLR and storm surge, conducting flood risk analysis in these areas is crucial for enhancing community sustainability and resilience (Gordon et al., 2014; Neumann et al., 2015b ). Fig. 1  A delineates our model domain, which is defined using the data from the Water Body Data (WBD) and NHDPlus HR datasets, covering the Savannah River and its associated catchments (Moore et al., 2019 ). Fig. 1 B showcases the distribution of 32 hurricane events that have affected this region between 2007 and 2023, displaying both overall precipitation and the maximum water stage for each event. Our selected test cases, Hurricanes Matthew (2016), Irma (2017), Dorian (2019), and Idalia (2023), were chosen based on several criteria, including data availability, the extent of flooding impacts such as precipitation and maximum water stage, the event timing, and documented flood damages. In specific, Hurricanes Matthew and Irma were chosen due to their severity and significant flood damage in the research domain. Dorian and Idalia, while less severe in this area, were selected to assess the stationarity or non-stationarity of geostatistical correlations over time.  3 Methodology The research methodology is structured into three key phases. Initially, it centers on constructing a physical HEC-RAS model using the Savannah River data to simulate fluvial floods. This involves integrating critical inputs such as river and catchment data, bathymetry, and hydraulic structures. The second phase entails the application of RGA, leveraging PCA for dimension reduction and creating low-rank approximations of non-parametric covariance matrices. In the final stage, spatial parameters and covariance matrices from the physical model are integrated into the RGA model, enhancing real-time flood mapping through interpolation and inverse modeling. This holistic approach yields a robust flood prediction model that adeptly combines detailed physical modeling with the flexibility of geostatistical analysis, ultimately aiming to deliver improved flood predictions and real-time water level maps. 3.1 HEC-RAS model To enhance efficiency and reduce computational time, we employed a 1D-2D modeling approach to develop a comprehensive fluvial model covering the entire watershed.
