Table 1   provides a detailed overview of the datasets utilized in constructing our model, with particular emphasis on the bathymetry dataset and the NHDPlus HD dataset. These datasets played a critical role in determining the physical configuration of the river model (Lee et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2019; USACE, 2016; Muthusamy et al., 2021 ). Additionally, the land use data obtained from the Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) consortium provided essential information for determining Manning's roughness coefficients for both the 1D and 2D components of the model. Fig. 2   provides a visual representation of our riverine model, illustrating the model domain and the fundamental structure of the river channel system. The model's boundary and domain were delineated using Water Body Data (WBD) datasets and catchment datasets from the NHDPlus HR datasets provided by the US Geological Survey (USGS) (Moore et al., 2019 ). It comprises 1D components tailored to simulate major channel routing including the Savannah River, Little Back River, and Middle River. The Savannah River system is interconnected via eight cuts as 1D channels. The channels, spanning 112 km, were digitized into 955 segments, considering the curvature of the main rivers, variations in width, and the locations of creeks and cuts to incorporate flow through the interface between the main channels and minor channels. Derived from the flow line data of the NHDPlus HR datasets and truncated using burnwater datasets, these segments underwent 2D surface routing analysis to distinguish them from floodplain areas. Additionally, USGS data collection points are labeled from Loc 1 to Loc 5 in the figure. The 2D component of the model, comprising 174,770 cells, is responsible for surface routing analysis across an area of 481 km2 , facilitating flow through the 1D-2D interface. To ensure precise simulation of surface water flow, we integrated surface hydraulic structures such as culverts, leveraging a hydro-enforced Digital Elevation Model (DEM) in conjunction with flow GIS data from the NHDPlus HR datasets. In the 2D segment, flow datasets from the NHDPlus HR data were incorporated as open channels with specific resolution, a critical step for accurate flow simulations, especially in areas with limited localized flow data for model calibration. The Lidar-derived DEM includes elevations of man-made structures like road fills and railroad grades, enhancing our simulation of hydraulic systems such as channels, culverts, and bridges, and providing essential bathymetric information and floodplain elevation. Portions of the DEM that were not processed were adapted following the methodologies recommended by Poppenga et al (Poppenga et al., 2010 ), with adjustments made using hydraulic datasets from SAGIS, a GIS data portal managed by the Savannah Metropolitan Planning Commission. To optimize computation, the 2D surface areas of the model were assigned varying scales based on factors such as elevation, slope, the presence of hydraulic structures, and road center data, which served as a reference for breaklines in the model to determine surface water transfer. For example, flat areas lacking hydraulic structures were assigned a coarser resolution of 50 m, while areas containing such structures were assigned a finer resolution of 15 m. To address backwater effects within coastal areas, dynamic wave computation was chosen as the most suitable numerical method, balancing model comprehensiveness with computational efficiency. Our 1D-2D modeling approach facilitated the creation of an extensive fluvial model covering the entire watershed with optimized computational costs. It is important to note that the model excludes urban stormwater infrastructure due to limitations in the HEC-RAS software's capability to simulate such features. Although the urban area constitutes approximately 14 % of the total model domain, we deemed the impact of urban flooding negligible for fluvial flood modeling. Consequently, the domain comprises multiple catchments from the datasets, focusing solely on surface water routing and excluding underground water transfer.  3.2 Reduced geostatistical approach 3.2.1 Low-rank non-parametric spatial covariance In classical geostatistics, spatial covariance is typically modeled as a function of the oriented or non-oriented distance between two points. Estimating spatial covariance, or more commonly, the variogram, typically necessitates measurements at numerous different locations. Nevertheless, this estimation process usually carries significant uncertainties, encompassing both model selection and hyperparameter estimations. Fig. 2  shows that the Savannah River has limited monitoring stations, which are considered sparse for estimating an accurate parametric spatial covariance or variogram model. In PIGA, we conduct simulations to generate time-series data to derive a non-parametric covariance function across the entire domain, mitigating the limitations associated with traditional variogram estimation methods. We start by considering the drift matrix X ∈ R  m × p     , where m   is the number of discretized elements, and p   is the number of drift functions, typically a small number. The detrending matrix P ∈ R  m × m      can be evaluated by:(1) P = I - X X  T  X    - 1   X  T      The simplest drift function is a constant mean, which is also used in our applications. For time series data Y ∈ R  m × K     ,  the detrended data can be computed from:(2) Y  ′  = P Y     where K   is the number of time moments simulated by the developed HEC-RAS model. In our application, the Savannah River channels were discretized into 955 segments, i.e., m = 955   . For a simulation spanning a 14-day event with a 15-minute time interval, K = 1 , 344    . The empirical, non-parametric approximation to the covariance Q ∈ R  m × m      can then be calculated by:(3) Q ≈ 1 K  Y ′ Y ′  T      For large-dimensional problems, Q   does not need to be expressed explicitly. By conducting a singular value decomposition of the time series data, the low-rank approximation of Q   can be expressed through the truncated eigen decomposition:(4) Q = V Λ V  T  ≈ Z Z  T      where V ∈ R  m × m      is the unitary matrix with m   linearly independent eigenvectors whose i   th column is the eigenvector v i    of Q  , also known as principal component axis, Λ ∈ R  m × m      is the diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are the eigenvalues, Λ ii   = λ i    , sorted in descending order, and Z ∈ R  m × k      is the matrix with truncated scaled eigenvectors. The eigenvalues λ i    indicate the variances along the corresponding principal component axes. The sum of all eigenvalues characterizes the total variance across all principal components. To determine the truncation rank k  , one can select a value of k   so that the ratio of the sum of all higher eigenvalues to the total variance exceeds a predefined threshold, such as 0.95, representing that 95 percent of variance can be described by the truncated principal components.  3.2.2 Interpolation for real-time flood mapping Given real-time monitoring data at several monitoring stations, the real-time water level map can be generated through spatial interpolation based on the low-rank approximate spatial covariance. The general cokriging form can be written as:(5) Q y y    X y    X y  T    0       γ  T    M        = Q y s     X s  T             where Q y y   ∈ R  n × n      is the covariance between observations, which can be obtained by extracting the elements from Q   corresponding to the monitoring stations, Q y s   ∈ R  n × m      is the covariance matrix between monitoring stations and estimation locations, which can also be extracted from Q  , X y  ∈ R  n × p      and X s  ∈ R  m × p      are trends at the monitoring stations and estimation locations, γ ∈ R  m × n      is known as the kriging weights assigned to the monitoring stations, and M ∈ R  p × m      is the matrix of Lagrange multipliers. For real-time mapping, the estimations at any time moment are a linear function of all monitoring data:(6) s = γ y     where s ∈ R  m × 1      represents the estimation at a specific time moment, and y ∈ R  n × 1      is the vector of measurements at the monitoring stations corresponding to those time moments. Eq. (6)  is evaluated sequentially following the time steps of monitoring. The associated estimation variance is given by:(7) V s  = Q - Q y s  T  γ  T  - X s  M     Eq. (5)  only needs to be solved for one time, while for each new set of data at different time moments, we can utilize Eq. (6)  to obtain the best estimates, and Eq. (7)  allows us to calculate the variance, enabling the efficient generation of real-time maps.  3.2.3 Inverse modeling for real-time flood mapping For inverse modeling of real-time water level mapping, we define the observation function describing the monitoring data based on the water level in the entire domain at a time moment:(8) y = H s + v     where s ∈ R  m × 1      is the water level variable vector over the entire domain, H  represents the matrix computation from the water level over the domain to the observation, composed primarily of ones and zeros indicating the presence or absence of direct measurement data, and v ∈ R  n × 1      represents a Gaussian noise vector with the covariance R   (often proportional to the identity matrix). For spatial random processes, the unknown variable s   is typically conceptualized and modeled by a deterministic mean with unknown drift coefficients and a stochastic process, which can be approximated by a linear combination of scaled principal components:(9) s = X β + Z α     where the latent variable α ∈ R  k × 1    N 0 , I      is the coefficient vector representing the projections of the stochastic fluctuations on the retained principal axes and β  ∈  R  k × 1      represents the unknown coefficient vector of the drift function. In our applications, a constant mean for each time moment is used as the mean drift function. The original inverse problem is thus converted to be a lower-dimensional problem of inverting α   and β  , which can be formulated in a Bayesian framework and obtained by solving the following linear equation system (Zhao and Luo, 2020 ):(10) H Z    T  R  - 1   H Z   + I   H Z    T  R  - 1   H X      H X    T  R  - 1   H Z     H X    T  R  - 1   H X          α   β        = H Z    T  R  - 1   y    H X    T  R  - 1   y            This is a k + p    linear equation system, which is independent of the number of observations. Substituting α   and β   into Eq. (9)  yields the best estimates of s   for the entire domain. After each update with new data, α   is revised for each iteration, regenerating WSE data for each time step. Essentially, WSE is considered as a linear combination of the PCs, Eq. (9) , at each time moment, and Eq. (10)  is used to calculate the coefficients of the PCs (i.e., latent variables) from measurement data at each time moment. Once these coefficients are determined, all WSE values over the entire domain at that moment can be evaluated. The interpolation method expresses the estimation as a linear function of measurement data, while the inverse modeling method estimates the latent variable by fitting the measurement data. These two approaches yield similar results because both are linear models assuming a Gaussian process (Kitanidis, 1986 ) and employ the same low-rank approximate covariance. However, their computation processes differ. In the interpolation method, the kriging weights are computed initially using Eq. (5) , and real-time mapping at any moment only requires implementing Eq. (6) . In contrast, the inverse modeling method estimates the latent variable for each time moment using Eq. (10) . The interpolation method may be more efficient for real-time mapping if the weights can be precomputed and stored. By contrast, the inverse modeling method may be more efficient in large-dimensional cases. In addition, the interpolation method takes the measurements as accurate data, whereas the inverse modeling method considers variations in measurement data within a Bayesian framework (Zhao and Luo, 2020 ).   3.3 PIGA algorithm The PIGA algorithm, as illustrated in Fig. 3  , consists of five main steps:1. Developing the 1D-2D flood model (Fig. 3 A)  2. Simulating water surface elevation (WSE) for a specific event (Fig. 3 B).  3. Generating reduced Principal Components (PCs) based on the WSE from step 2 (Fig. 3 C).  4. Determining the covariance matrix for monitoring stations and the cross-covariance matrix between monitoring stations and prediction locations.  5. Evaluating real-time WSE maps using RGA (Fig. 3 E) with real-time monitoring station data (Fig. 3 D).    For our model, boundary conditions are included in the dataset, and real-time monitoring datasets include boundary conditions for upstream and downstream, along with reference datasets within the model domain (5 USGS data stations). PIGA harmonizes spatial parameters and covariance matrices from the HEC-RAS physical model with the RGA model, enhancing real-time flood mapping through interpolation and inverse modeling techniques. This integration is pivotal for leveraging the detailed insights from physical modeling while benefiting from the efficiency of geostatistical analysis, resulting in more accurate and timely water level maps. A noteworthy aspect of this approach is its utilization of time series data in geostatistical methods and extending the time axis as correlated varying spatial information.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Fluvial model validation The HEC-RAS model underwent extensive testing for all four hurricane events. Fig. 4   shows the model performance specifically for Hurricane Matthew. Overall, the model results align closely with the monitoring datasets across all USGS data locations, particularly at Loc 2, 3, and 4. However, notable deviations are observed at Loc 1 and Loc 5. At Loc 5, the model tends to overestimate low water stages. This discrepancy is primarily attributed to inadequate bathymetry data, characterized by a flat bottom with an assigned elevation significantly higher than the minimum water stage values in the USGS datasets, resulting in discrepancies and potential instabilities in its simulation. Similar patterns were observed in other hurricane events, as detailed in the supplementary file . Table 2   presents a comprehensive quantitative analysis of model simulations for all hurricane events in comparison with the USGS datasets. It includes metrics such as differences in maximum water stages (DMWS), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), correlation coefficients (CC), and coefficient of determination (R2 ). Across Loc 2, 3, and 4, the quantitative measures consistently indicate high model performance, closely aligning with the observed data. Particularly noteworthy is the observation that all correlations and R2  values exceed 95 %, while DMWS, MAE, and RMSE remain minimal. However, the performance at Loc 5 exhibits a slight decline compared to other locations. For instance, the R2  values range from 0.66 to 0.86 at Loc 5, indicating a lower level of agreement compared to other locations. This discrepancy underscores the impact of limited input datasets in the vicinity of Loc 5, which led to performance degradation and computational instabilities. It highlights the model’s dependency on physical data quality and quantity.  4.2 Principal components for spatial correlations The HEC-RAS model provides a detailed representation of the Savannah River, along with its interconnected creeks and channels, through 956 cross-sectional analyses. For the events of Hurricane Matthew and Hurricane Irma, this model simulates a time series dataset for each cross-section, capturing water stage data over a span of 14 days for Matthew and 12.5 days for Irma, with observations recorded every 15 min. Fig. 5  A visually represents the HEC-RAS model's outcomes for Hurricane Matthew, with the x -axis plotting time and the y -axis depicting nodes (cross sections) along the river and its reaches. It's important to note that the model's assumptions are based on the relative, not absolute or physical locations of these cross sections, treating them as nodes within a networked riverine system. Fig. 5 B – D illustrate the spatial distribution of the most dominant principal components (PCs) for the spatial correlations of WSE derived from the PIGA model specifically for Hurricane Matthew. The first PC (Fig. 5 B) reveals a correlation pattern of high WSE along the coast, gradually decreasing towards the inland areas with a gentle decline near the coast. In contrast, the second PC (Fig. 5 C) depicts a similar decreasing trend, but with a rapid decline rate near the coast. The third PC (Fig. 5 D) illustrates smaller-scale variations, with peak WSE in the middle and decreasing values towards both the coast and further inland. The sum of these three eigenvalues, arranged in ascending order for these PCs, accounts for more than 98 % of the total cumulative sum of all eigenvalues. This high percentage underscores the significant variance captured by the leading PCs, indicating a strong underlying structure in the spatial data. To obtain the PCs, we tested three different datasets for each hurricane event: a time series of the non-hurricane period, during the hurricane events, and all-time series combined. However, the spatial reference from the separated datasets did not yield a noticeable difference. Therefore, the spatial PCs are assumed to be consistent over a hurricane event, including both non-hurricane and hurricane intervals within one hurricane event.  4.3 PIGA simulations for hurricane events After deriving the PCs (Fig. 5 ), the real-time WSE map was estimated using the RGA, incorporating the PCs and real-time monitoring data. The inverse modeling algorithm was employed to generate the WSE map. Utilizing the USGS datasets at Loc 2, Loc 3, and Loc 4, latent variables in the PIGA algorithm were estimated, leveraging measurements at these boundaries. Meanwhile, the remaining two USGS monitoring stations, Loc 1 and Loc 5, were utilized as reference data for validation. Fig. 6   compares the performance of PIGA and the HEC-RAS model. Fig. 6 A and 6B illustrate that PIGA significantly outperforms the HEC-RAS model at Loc 1 and Loc 5. Particularly, PIGA accurately describes the low WSE at Loc 5, a feature poorly captured by the HEC-RAS model. This improvement is further supported by quantitative measures, with R2  increasing from 0.88 to 0.94 and from 0.66 to 0.75 for Loc 1 and Loc 5, respectively (Table 3  ). Fig. 6 C displays all USGS datasets, HEC-RAS simulations, and the datasets in PIGA for estimating latent variables and predictions, highlighting the superior performance of PIGA. Additionally, three other locations without monitoring data were randomly selected for comparison between PIGA and the HEC-RAS model (Fig. 6 D to 6F). The close alignment between PIGA and the HEC-RAS model suggests that PIGA provides predictions as effective as those of the physical model, indicating the potential for PIGA to replace the physical model. Fig. 7   illustrates the maximum WSE generated from PIGA and HEC-RAS, along with their differences across the entire Savannah River during Hurricane Matthew. Fig. 7 A and 7B reveal that both WSE distributions exhibit similar overall patterns, with deviations particularly noticeable in the middle river sections. The mean difference in maximum WSE, as shown in Fig. 7 C, is 0.05 m. However, large deviations are observed in the upper branch of the Savannah River, with a maximum difference of 0.45 m, occuring in the areas characterized by deficient bathymetry data. Fig. 7 C suggests that the performance of PIGA closely matches that of HEC-RAS in data-sufficient areas, while major discrepancies occurred in data-insufficient areas. The outcomes from Figs. 6 and 7  indicate that PIGA shows the potential to provide accurate simulation results based on spatial correlations, particularly in areas where insufficient bathymetry data could significantly impact the physical model performance. Fig. 8   shows the PIGA simulation results for Hurricane Irma, employing the same algorithm applied in the Hurricane Matthew scenario. Updated PCs were estimated specifically using the HEC-RAS model simulations for Hurricane Irma. The results indicate that PIGA effectively predicts WSE with greater accuracy compared to its performance in the Hurricane Matthew application, demonstrating its consistency and reliability across diverse storm scenarios. In addition, PIGA outperforms the HEC-RAS, particularly in data-sparse areas such as Loc 1 and Loc 5 (Table 3 ), where it significantly enhances the accuracy and utility of hydrological modeling. These results emphasize PIGA's capability to accurately replicate overall spatial correlations in real-time, positioning it as an effective corrective tool tailored for challenging hydrological conditions. Overall, PIGA shows the potential to offer a robust and adaptable approach that may serve as a superior alternative to existing physical hydrological models for enhancing flood prediction.  4.4 Sensitivity of PIGA to data selection While PIGA effectively regulates the WSE from HEC-RAS based on reduced spatial correlations, its sensitivity to specific dataset selection remains uncertain. In the previous section, we utilized the USGS datasets at Loc 2, Loc 3, and Loc 4 to estimate latent variables in the PIGA algorithm and the USGS datasets at Loc 1 and Loc 5 for validation. To assess the sensitivity of PIGA’s performance to data selection, we intentionally excluded certain USGS datasets from the modeling process. We conducted a series of simulations, each using a unique combination of three datasets from the five available USGS datasets within the PIGA procedure, with the remaining two datasets for validation. Fig. 9   presents the performance results for all ten possible combinations. Two sets of statistical matrices were calculated: one comparing the PIGA simulation with the unselected USGS monitoring datasets, and the other assessing the overall performance of the PIGA simulation against the HEC-RAS simulation for the entire domain. The results indicate that all combinations yield good performance, with high R  2    values and low RMSE and DMWS values. However, performance varies among the ten selections. For example, Selection 3 includes the USGS dataset at Loc 4 presenting reliable performances of HEC-RAS while excluding the USGS dataset with poor performance of HEC-RAS at Loc 5 with less reliable performance of PIGA. By contrast, Selection 7 includes the USGS dataset at Loc 5 and excludes the USGS dataset at Loc 4. The R  2    values range from 0.83 to 0.99 for the unselected USGS datasets and from 0.93 to 0.98 for the entire domain. This variation indicates the influence of dataset selection on PIGA's efficacy. We further investigated the sensitivity of the model in terms of the number of reference datasets while keeping the number of principal components at three. Fig. 10   shows that as the number of reference datasets increases, the corresponding mean values of R  2    and RMSE improve, indicating overall model enhancement. This trend suggests that inverse models benefit from increased information (measurement data), which leads to better parameter estimates, reduced uncertainty, and greater robustness against noise and outliers (Acar and Vogel, 1994; Hansen, 2010 ). However, while the DMWS values remained low, their changes exhibited a more fluctuating pattern compared to RMSE. This difference arises because DMWS quantifies local behavior, whereas RMSE measures overall performance (Bishop, 2006; Huber and Ronchetti, 2011 ).  4.5 Stationarity and variability of spatial correlation The previous section confirmed the consistency of spatial correlations within a single hurricane event. Specifically, we derived PCs representing spatial correlations for Hurricane Matthew and Irma, respectively, and subsequently applied them in PIGA for simulations. However, a remaining question is whether the spatial correlations derived from analyzing one hurricane event can be applied to predict other hurricane events. For instance, can the spatial correlations observed in Hurricane Matthew be extrapolated to forecast Hurricane Irma and potentially similar events? If successful, this would enable PIGA’s application based on one hurricane event to predict others. Thus, it is necessary to evaluate the stability and variability of these spatial correlations across hurricanes of differing intensities. Our analysis includes comparisons among Hurricane Matthew, Irma, Dorian, and Idalia. PCs derived from one hurricane event are utilized to predict WSE for other hurricane events. Fig. 11   compares the simulations for hurricane events Matthew, Dorian, and Idalia using their respective PCs and the PCs derived from Hurricane Irma. These tests demonstrate that employing Hurricane Irma’s PCs yields results very close to the original spatial correlations, indicating the interchangeability of spatial references across different hurricane events. This transferability highlights the applicability of PIGA for predicting hurricane events using previously derived spatial correlations. Minimal differences between the PIGA simulation sets are evident, as indicated by the narrowly normally distributed differences. In the supplementary material , we summarize the statistical measures of all simulations, suggesting that the spatial reference from Irma represents the optimal alternative to the original spatial reference. This finding implies that the transferability of PCs from different hurricane events varies. Thus, for a specific site, it is crucial to investigate and select the most effective alternative spatial reference. Fig. 12   illustrates the performance of applying spatial references from different hurricane events, including Matthew, Irma, and Dorian, to Hurricane Idalia. Similarly, these simulations investigate how the variability of spatial references affects the performance of PIGA models and the transferability of derived PCs from different hurricane events. The PIGA model using PCs from Irma and Dorian yields results comparable to the original PCs of Idalia, underscoring the influence of spatial reference similarity on model outcomes. However, the application of the spatial reference from Matthew to Idalia shows underperformance. This observation is corroborated by the statistical data presented in the supplementary materials , which present comparisons with USGS monitoring locations (Loc 1 to Loc 5). These results further emphasize the importance of selecting the most effective alternative spatial reference for prediction. Fig. 13   depicts the first and most dominant principal component derived from different hurricane events. Across all test cases, the first PCs account for more than 85 % of the total variance. Notably, the first PCs for Hurricane events Irma, Dorian, and Idalia exhibit proximity to each other, indicating a high degree of similarity and correlation among the PCs. This observation supports the transferability of applying spatial correlations from one event to others, as demonstrated in Figs. 11 and 12 . Conversely, the magnitude of values differs for Hurricane Matthew, explaining the underperformance observed when applying the PCs from Matthew to other events, as shown in Fig. 12 . This analysis not only underscores the importance of careful spatial reference selection but also suggests the potential need for model adjustments or calibrations when applying PIGA across different flood events. Furthermore, Fig. 12  can be extended to other events to generate a library of PCs for conducting uncertainty analysis and investigating the impacts of climate and other drivers on spatial correlations. Fig. 14   presents a comparison of the statistical measures assessing the performance of the HEC-RAS model, PIGA using the original PCs for a specific hurricane event, and the best alternative PCs for that event. The analysis reveals that the physical model offers better results only for Hurricane Matthew in terms of DMWS, and PIGA consistently outperforms in all other measures, regardless of the event considered. Notably, while the original PCs may yield optimal performance for certain hurricane events, alternative PCs derived from other events also demonstrate satisfactory performance in various scenarios. Overall, the spatial reference derived from Hurricane Irma emerges as the most effective alternative PIGA reference, as demonstrated in Figure 10 . We note that the transferability of spatial correlation PCs is generally influenced by both the dynamic characteristics of hurricanes—such as their path, intensity, and rainfall distribution—and the relatively constant hydrological and topographical features of the Savannah River basin. While hurricane characteristics vary from one event to another, the latter features remain stable over time. Transferability is more reliable when hurricanes share similar characteristics, allowing PCs derived from one event to be applicable to another. In our study site and selected hurricane events, it is reasonable to conclude that the Savannah River Basin properties, such as bathymetry, may be the dominant factors controlling the spatial correlation, resulting in high transferability as shown in Figs. 11 to 14 . However, significant changes in land use or extreme events that deviate substantially from the norm can affect the applicability of PCs from one event to another. This necessitates the need for adaptive strategies or recalibration to enhance the transferability of spatial correlation PCs.  4.6 Sensitivity to the number of PCs In the above analyses, we chose three dominant PCs for approximating the spatial correlation and used them in the PIGA for conducting simulations. As illustrated in section 4.2  and Fig. 15  E, the three dominant PCs already accounted for more than 98 % of the total variance, which are considered sufficient to quantify the spatial variations. Fig. 15  shows the PIGA performance of using different numbers of PCs while setting the number of dataset selections as all five USGS monitoring stations. Fig. 15 A shows that the increase of PCs did not incur a meaningful change of computational time because the estimation of the latent variables and computation of the WSE for the domain are low-dimensional problems. There is no much computational difference for the reduced system. The increase in R2  (Fig. 15 B) and decrease in RMSE (Fig. 15 D) indicate that the model explains more variance with the inclusion of more principal components (PCs), thereby slightly improving PIGA performance. However, the addition of more PCs does not affect the improvement of DMWS (Fig. 15 C), as it reflects local behavior.   5 Discussion and conclusion We developed the PIGA method for estimating water surface elevations during fluvial flooding caused by hurricanes. PIGA integrates spatial correlations obtained from physical models and real-time monitoring data from limited stations with RGA for interpolating or inversely modeling water surface elevations across entire river channels and reaches. This integration addresses the computational cost and challenges of physical models in scenarios with limited data availability. Specifically, spatial correlations are derived by reducing the dimensionality of physical model simulation results. This approach describes spatial correlation using non-parametric Principal Components (PCs) rather than simplified two-point spatial covariance models found in classical geostatistics. RGA utilizes these reduced PCs for interpolation or inverse modeling, significantly enhancing the model's capacity to process and interpret large volumes of flood-related data. This reduction is not merely a statistical convenience but a critical improvement in computational efficiency. It enables a more manageable and accurate interpretation of dynamic flood data, making the model particularly valuable for real-time flood prediction scenarios by employing different references based on actual cases. We piloted our model application in the Savannah River basin, known for its susceptibility to riverine flooding during hurricane seasons. Specifically, we developed a 1D-2D HEC-RAS model to simulate coupled catchment hydrology and channel hydraulics. This model, along with PIGA, were applied to simulate four hurricane events, including Hurricane Matthew, Irma, Dorian, and Idalia. A comprehensive comparative analysis revealed PIGA’s enhanced performance in predicting water stages, especially in areas where the physical model faced limitations due to insufficient bathymetry data. Various statistical measures also underscored the significant improvement achieved by PIGA, confirming its effectiveness as a more accurate and reliable tool for flood prediction. Beyond its performance, the model offers substantial economic and computational advantages. For example, it took only a few seconds, in contrast to the extensive hours required for a physical model simulation spanning a 14-day hurricane event, making real-time updates and calibration challenging. PIGA demonstrates the potential to replace the physical model, providing real-time flooding maps based on real-time monitoring data. Our study explores the transferability of spatial correlations, specifically examining the feasibility of using principal components derived from one hurricane event to simulate others. Results demonstrate that it is indeed possible to simulate hurricane events using PCs from different occurrences, indicating the model's capacity to maintain accuracy across diverse scenarios. Notably, for the Savannah River basin and the investigated hurricane events, PCs derived from Hurricane Irma offer satisfactory predictions for other events when compared to their original counterparts. This discovery demonstrates the potential of PIGA for real-time water surface elevation forecasting based on spatial correlations obtained from historical hurricane events. Conversely, we also observed variability in spatial correlations among different hurricane events. For instance, PCs derived from Hurricane Matthew exhibited underperformance compared to others, highlighting the importance of selecting the optimal alternative spatial reference for prediction. Additionally, PIGA offers the advantage of convenience in updating PCs or creating a library of PCs for spatial correlations as new data becomes available. Through these consistent spatial correlations, PIGA could significantly improve computational efficiency compared to conventional physical models. This improvement is maintained with different options such as the number of dataset selections and PCs. Additionally, the transferability and relative stability of spatial correlations suggest that, in our tested cases and site, these correlations may not be significantly influenced by dynamic properties such as distinct hurricane characteristics. Instead, they appear to be dominated by relatively constant properties such as river bathymetry and the topographical features of the river basin. For instance, the successful application of the geostatistical reference from Hurricane Irma to the PIGA model for Hurricane Idalia, despite significant differences in precipitation and storm surge, supports this observation. Further research should investigate whether this transferability is valid for other sites and how to develop a methodology for selecting the most suitable reference hurricane event for new applications. Conversely, significant changes in bathymetry, the addition of hydraulic structures (e.g., weirs, dikes, additional wetlands, seawalls), land use changes, and extreme events that deviate significantly from the norm could affect the applicability of the developed method from one event to another. These scenarios indicate the need for adaptive strategies or recalibration to maintain the accuracy of the physical model for updating the spatial correlations for the PIGA analysis. PIGA is essentially a linear approach, assuming that water surface elevations can be approximated with a linear system. This assumption holds for the Savannah River basin, as observed in our study. However, it's important to acknowledge the potential limitations of PIGA in systems characterized by high nonlinearity, such as urban flooding scenarios influenced by both riverine flooding and drainage systems. Further investigations are warranted for such applications. Moreover, PIGA relies on a physical model to derive non-parametric spatial correlations. Except for the geostatistical aspect, the river system is a linked network responding dynamically to the surrounding environment. In this respect, there are different applications of reduced PCA in different fields such as wired network system analysis (Filho and Maia, 2010; Wang et al., 2012 ). While our field study demonstrated PIGA’s effectiveness in areas with limited data, enhanced performance can be achieved with a more accurate physical model, such as improved bathymetry data (Almeida et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018 ). Additionally, PIGA’s reliance on sample data for generating real-time maps highlights the importance of a reliable data portal system, such as the USGS Water Data for the Nation (Survey, 2001 ).
1 Introduction Human activity has considerably accelerated the nitrogen (N) cycle, increasing the availability and mobility of N worldwide (Vitousek et al., 1997 ). Although most N inputs meet human needs, such as agricultural and industrial production, their impacts on the environment are severe and long-lasting (Li et al., 2023; Van Meter et al., 2018 ). Large amounts of excess N are transported into surface water and groundwater, contributing to eutrophication and drinking water contamination (Basu et al., 2022; Greaver et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2024 ). Protecting water quality in the face of growing populations and increasing agricultural demands is crucial for ensuring water and food security for future generations (Basu et al., 2022 ). Various environmental management measures have been taken to improve the water quality, such as constructing centralized and decentralized water treatment facilities (Oakley et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2020 ), optimizing fertilization practices (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhuang et al., 2022 ), and implementing of water diversion projects (Qin et al., 2019; Zhang and Wu, 2020 ). Despite improvements in some water bodies, most water quality goals remain challenging to achieve. The gap between environmental management practices and water quality improvement exist not only in specific regions, but worldwide. For example, the U.S. aimed to shrink the Gulf of Mexico’s hypoxic zone to 5000 km2  by 2015, but it expanded to 16000 km2  (Basu et al., 2022; Van Meter et al., 2018 ). Similarly, despite China investing over 100 billion CNY (14 billion USD) in Taihu Lake’s treatment since 2007, the lake still faces severe eutrophication (Qin et al., 2019 ). Several obstacles can hinder the achievement of water quality goals, with time lags recently being identified as a key factor (Gao et al., 2023; Meals et al., 2010; Van Meter et al., 2018 ). In this study, a time lag was defined as the time elapsed between implementing watershed management measures and noticeable improvements in aquatic system water quality (Meals et al., 2010 ). Time lags vary among management measures. Previous studies found that the long-term accumulation of excess N fertilizer in the soil, known as N legacy, could impact water quality for decades (Gao et al., 2023; Van Meter et al., 2018 ). In addition to the direct impacts of human activities on aquatic N systems, human-driven climate change may alter the N cycle, especially in lakes (Greaver et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2024 ). Climate change will strongly affect lake N transport and transformation processes through spatiotemporal variations in temperature and precipitation (Adrian et al., 2009 ). These impacts are multifaceted, with some pathways increasing in lake N concentrations and others possibly resulting in decreases (Carpenter et al., 2022; Greaver et al., 2016 ). Generally, humans simultaneously discharge large amounts of N into lakes while implementing watershed protection measures. Meantime, the water quality response to these practices has different time lags. Climate change, especially the frequent occurrence of extreme weather events, has brought great uncertainty to the water quality of lakes (Donat et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2023 ). Under the combined influence of these factors, N concentrations in lakes change differentially. The shift in lake water quality has been particularly pronounced in China, where the rapid economic development over past few decades has been accompanied by severe water environmental issues. With years of watershed protection practices, some lakes improved significantly in N concentration, while others continue deteriorating. What causes this paradox between watershed management and lake N concentration response? This question has perplexed China’s watershed environmental managers for decades. Although some studies have attempted to explain the driving factors behind water quality changes, most have been based on qualitative correlation analyses and lacked quantification (Han and Bu, 2023 ). Moreover, these studies were based on individual lakes, and the overall changes in the water quality of China’s lakes were not well categorized and summarized. Therefore, in this study, (1) the different trends of N concentration changes in China’s lakes were summarized, (2) the drivers for different lakes at different stages were quantified, and, more importantly, (3) the response of lake N concentration changes to watershed management and climate change were analyzed.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area In this study, 13 typical lakes were selected, including six lakes in Yangtze River Basin (Taihu, Chaohu, Poyang, Honghu, Dongting, and Dianchi Lakes), one lake in Huaihe River Bain (Hongze Lake), one lake in Yellow River Basin (Wuliangsu Lake), one lake in Haihe River Basin (Baiyangdian Lake), one lake in Continental Basin (Bosten Lake), one lake in Southwest Basin (Erhai Lake), one lake in Pearl River Basin (Fuxian Lake), and one lake in Southeast Basin (Qiandao Lake) (Fig. 1  ). Among these lakes, Fuxian Lake has the deepest mean water depth (87 m), followed by Qiandao Lake (31 m) and Erhai Lake (11 m), while the others are shallow (mean water depth < 10 m). The lake watershed areas range from 691 to 261474 km2 . The climate of Bosten Lake and Wuliangsu Lake is temperate continental, while the others have monsoon climates. The annual precipitation of these basins ranges from < 200 mm to > 1500 mm (Table S1 , Table S2 ). The main water sources for all lakes are rivers or precipitation. This study focuses on total N (TN) as the main water quality indicator due to its significant role in eutrophication and the complex biogeochemical processes involved in N reduction compared to phosphorus (P) (Conley et al., 2009 ). The retention rate of N is lower than that of P, regardless of whether water treatment methods are centralized or decentralized (Tong et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2023a ). This highlights the greater challenges faced by watershed management measures in reducing N loads. This study presents long-term water quality data as comprehensively as possible to clearly illustrate the trends in TN concentration changes. The water quality data were extracted from published articles (see Table S1  for data sources). Based on the reports in the selected articles, multiple sampling points were used for each lake to ensure the representative of the sampling point data. In this study, environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) theory was used to explain water quality trends. According to the EKC, water pollution will show an inverted-U curve with the gross domestic product (GDP) per capita (or income level). At the first stage of EKC, the water environment deteriorates due to discharges from human activities, after which it improves with further increases in the income level (Shen et al., 2023b ). To depict the temporal trend of water quality more clearly, considering China’s rapid development over the past decades and the positive correlation between the socioeconomic index and time, time series was used as the horizontal coordinate of the EKC curve.  2.2 Driving forces analysis Eight driving forces of water quality changes were considered in this study and grouped into the following four categories: N cycle indicators (N use efficiency [NUE] and N surplus), climatic factors (temperature and precipitation), socioeconomic factors (GDP per capita and population density), and land use change (agriculture area percentage and urban area percentage). NUE, defined as the N input fraction harvested as a product, is an important indicator of the sustainability of crop systems (Shen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2015 ). N surplus (in kg N/ha), defined as the cropland N inputs (including fertilizer, manure, biological N fixation, atmosphere N deposition, and straw return) minus N outputs (including crop harvest), is increasingly being used to determine whether progress has been made in reducing agricultural inputs of reactive N into the earth system (Van Meter et al., 2023 ). Details on calculating N cycle indicator can be found in the reference Shen et al. (2024) . The data sources are shown in Table S1 , and the watershed parameters are summarized in Table S2 . Correlation analysis was conducted to qualitatively describe the relationship between water quality and the drivers (Fig. S1 ). The quantitative contribution of each driving force was identified using principal component analysis (PCA) and principal component regression (PCR). Using PCA, the input variables were transformed into a new set of variables known as principal components (PCs). The PCs were uncorrelated but still accounted for all the variation present in the data. Each component had a loading, which indicated the correlation between the PC and input variables. Subsequently, a multiple linear regression analysis was performed, taking the TN concentration as the dependent variable and the PC as the independent variable. This process is referred to as PCR analysis. Using PCR, the score for each variable was then calculated based on the PC weight coefficient, respective loadings of the PCA, and regression slope. Owing to constraints from the various data sources, the time series used for the driver analysis covered the period from 1995 to 2015. The details of the PCA and PCR calculation process are shown as follows. First, all variables were normalized into 0–1:(1) X nor   = X - X min    X max   - X min         where X    is the variable, X min      is the minimum value of the variable for the time period 1995–2015, X max      is the maximum of the variable for the time period 1995–2015, and X nor      is the variable after normalization. Thereafter, PCA was employed to convert the input variables into PCs:(2) PC  i  = α × N U E + β × N s u r + γ × T e m + δ × P r e + ε × p G D P + θ × P o p + μ × A g r + ρ × U r b a n     where Nsur   , Tem   , Pre   , pGDP   , Pop   , Agr   , and Urban    represent the watershed N surplus, annual temperature, annual precipitation, GDP per capita, population density, agriculture land proportion, and urban land proportion, respectively. α   , β   , γ   , δ   , ε   , θ   , μ   , and ρ    are the PC loading. In this study, four PCs were selected and collectively accounted for >90 % of the variance in all variables. The time span from 1995 to 2015 was segmented into three distinct periods: Period 1 (1995–2001), Period 2 (2002–2008), and Period 3 (2009–2015). Within each period, multiple regression analyses were performed using the lake TN concentration and PCs.(3) TN = ∑ i = 1  4  φ i  × PC  i  + ω i      where TN    is the lake TN concentration, and φ    and ω    are the estimated coefficients. Finally, the score of each driver was calculated, which (taking NUE as an example), can be defined as:(4) Score  NUE   = ∑ i = 1  4  α i  × φ i  × τ i         where τ    is the PC weight coefficient, and equals the variance contribution rate for the original variable. The contribution of each driver was determined by calculating its score relative to the total scores (Chen et al., 2023 ). Compared with correlation and factor analysis, the aforementioned method quantitatively analyzes the contribution of each factor (Ahmad et al., 2024; Hamma et al., 2024; Nagaraj & Masilamani, 2023 ). The PC-based regression analysis also avoids the multicollinearity found in traditional multiple linear regression.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Different stages of water quality changes The temporal trend of TN concentrations varied differently among the different lakes across China. These changes were divided into three clusters: inverted-U, linear, and non-trend (Fig. 2  ). Among the 13 lakes analyzed, five (Taihu, Chaohu, Dianchi, Hongze, and Baiyangdian Lakes) demonstrated inverted U-shaped curves that align with EKC theory (Fig. 2 a–c). In these lakes, the TN concentrations increased during the initial phase due to intensified human activities and subsequently decreased after peaking (Fig. S2 ). External N load changes were the primary reason for the improved of lake TN concentration. In this cluster, the maximum TN concentration values may differ substantially among lakes. Chaohu, Taihu, and Baiyangdian Lakes can reach maximum values exceeding 4 mg L-1 , whereas Hongze and Dianchi Lakes have much lower maximum values. Notably, crossing the EKC turning point, as some lakes such as Chaohu Lake did as early as the 1990s, does not necessarily mean that these lakes are already clean. Many lakes still face serious eutrophication issues, with TN concentrations exceeding China’s Class V surface water quality standard (Fig. 2 ) (Qin et al., 2019 ). Lakes in the linear cluster (including Honghu, Dongting, Poyang, Erhai, and Qiandao Lakes) are still in the first stage of the EKC, as the TN concentration has not yet reached the turning point (Fig. 2 d, e). Among these lakes, Honghu and Poyang Lakes are experiencing a rapid decline in water quality, with annual increases in TN concentrations of 0.05 mg L-1  and 0.04 mg L-1 , respectively. However, some lakes did not show a significant trend. Fuxian and Bosten Lakes have maintained a consistent water quality level, with average TN concentrations of 0.17 mg L-1  and 0.80 mg L-1 , respectively, over the years. Meanwhile, the water quality of Wuliangsu Lake experiences great interannual fluctuations, with TN ranging from 1.1 mg L-1  to 3.7 mg L-1  between 1999 and 2019 (Fig. 2 f).  3.2 Identification of drivers in lake water quality changes at different stages The differences in the driving factors for the lakes at various EKC stages (the first stage of the EKC, the second stage of the EKC, and non-trend) were further analyzed. Lakes in the second stage of the EKC had significantly higher contributions from N cycling indicators compared to those in the first stage (P <0.05). In contrast, the contribution from climatic factors was significantly lower for lakes in the second stage than for those in the first (P <0.05, Fig. 3  ). The contributions of socioeconomic factors and land use changes did not show significant differences across the three lake categories (P >0.05). Additionally, N cycling indicators had the most pronounced impact on water quality changes for lakes at the second stage of the EKC, while land use was the primary factor for lakes in the first stage and for those without a discernible trend. This result suggested that lakes in the early stages of human intervention are primarily constrained by watershed geography and economic characteristics such as land use, climate, and socioeconomic conditions. Once the deteriorating trend in water quality is under control, the influence of human management becomes more prominent and surpasses that of objective development patterns. These findings highlight the crucial role of human-led watershed agricultural N management, specifically increasing NUE and decreasing N surplus, in navigating passed the EKC turning point. Beyond this point, the influence of climatic factors on water quality recedes.  3.3 Differential responses of lake water quality to human activities In recent studies, N surplus has been considered an indicator of the human impact on agricultural N management (Basu et al., 2022; Van Meter et al., 2023 ). In this study, N surplus and the water quality trajectory were used to analyze the response of lake TN concentrations to watershed management measures. Three different patterns are summarized based on the different trajectories: lag (LAG), accelerate (ACCEL), and linear patterns (LIN) (Fig. 4  , Fig. S3 ). For LAG patterns, the watershed N surplus and lake TN concentration showed a counter clockwise (LAG1 in Fig. 4 ) or inverse linear hysteresis (LAG2 in Fig. 4 ) relationship. In this cluster, 4 out of the 13 lakes (Taihu, Dongting, Poyang, and Honghu Lake Basins) exhibited a significant time lag between water quality changes and N surplus. This means that the water quality did not improve immediately after the N surplus declined. Instead, it might have continued increasing after the N surplus peaked (Fig. 4 a–d). For example, the N surplus in Taihu Lake Basin has declined since 1995, but the TN concentration did not improve until 2004. This result indicates a time lag of at least 10 years in the response of water quality to agricultural N management practices in Taihu Lake Basin (Table S3 ). Indeed, the time gap between the maximum values of watershed N surplus and lake N concentration, signifying a potential time lag, could exceed two decades (Table S3 ). This lag suggests that the TN concentration is not only a function of the current year’s N inputs, but also depends on historical N inputs. Isotope-based methods can be used to measure time lags and include measuring deuterium levels in water or conducting N-15 labeled fertilizer experiments (Morgenstern et al., 2015; Sebilo et al., 2013 ). This study’s finding is consistent with previous studies conducted in the Gulf of Mexico (Van Meter et al., 2018 ) and the Songhua River Basin (Gao et al., 2023 ), which underscore the importance of long-term sustainable agricultural N management. Contrary to the LAG pattern, in the ACCEL pattern, the trajectories of N surplus and water quality exhibit a clockwise relationship, representing accelerated improvements in water quality. This pattern can arise in different circumstances. For example, in Chaohu Lake, the TN concentration peaked in 1995 at approximately 4.6 mg L-1 , after which it decreased by approximately 65 % over the next two decades (Fig. 2 b). However, the N surplus did not peak until the 2000s, indicating that point source or other improvements in N management dominated lake N reductions, independent of N surplus. Indeed, close to Hefei City (Fig. 1 f), the capital of Anhui Province, Chaohu Lake is strongly affected by point source pollution. With the rapid expansion of urban areas, large amounts of industrial wastewater and domestic sewage are being discharged into Chaohu Lake. The volume of wastewater discharged into Chaohu Lake is nearly ten times those of Poyang and Dongting Lakes (Shang and Shang, 2007 ). Since 1984, the Anhui provincial government has implemented watershed management measures for Chaohu Lake. The main control measures include building new wastewater treatment plants and reducing industrial point-source emissions (Shang and Shang, 2007 ). Owing to these pollution control measures, the water quality of Chaohu Lake began to improve from 1995 onwards. Another example of an accelerated pattern is with Dianchi Lake, one of China’s most eutrophic lakes (Fig. 4 f). Similar to Chaohu Lake, Dianchi Lake is located in a provincial capital city (Kunming), and high-intensity human activity is the main cause of water pollution in the Dianchi Lake Basin (Liu et al., 2015 ). To improve its water quality, the Niulan River to Dianchi Lake Water Diversion Project was implemented in 2013. Generally, this project diverts water from the Deze Reservoir to Dianchi Lake through the NiuLan River to dilute pollutants and shorten the water residence time (Zhang and Wu, 2020 ). This hydraulic project has proven effective. Before the project was implemented, the average TN concentration in Dianchi Lake was 2.2 mg L-1  (average over 2011–2013), and then it quickly decreased to 1.6 mg L-1  (average over 2014–2016) after implementation. However, it is of note that these results do not indicate that no time lags exist for hydraulic engineering or point source control measures. Theoretically, water quality has a time lag response to nearly all management measures (Meals et al., 2010 ). Compared to the time lag associated with agricultural N management, that linked to hydraulic engineering or point source control measures may be much shorter and is difficult be observe on annual scale data. Indeed, 24 % of U.S. river watersheds showed the ACCEL pattern; similarly, this study found that ACCEL watersheds were more likely to occur in high-population-density areas (Table S2 ) (Van Meter et al., 2023 ). Finally, two of the lakes showed a significant positive correlation between TN concentration and N surplus (P <0.01) (Fig. 4 g, h). For example, the TN concentration in Bosten Lake has not shown a significant trend over the past few decades, while the N surplus in the Bosten Lake basin has continued to increase. Therefore, the linear relationship between TN concentration and N surplus may not represent a linear response of water quality to N surplus. Longer time-series data are required for further analysis.  3.4 Uncertainty arising from climate change in watershed management Different driving factors contribute differently during different periods. For all lakes in this study, N cycle indicators, climatic factors, socioeconomic factors, and land use change contributed 24 %, 19 %, 28 %, and 29 % respectively in Period 1 (1995–2001). In the subsequent Period 2 (2002–2008), the contribution of climatic factors increased to 23 % and remained stable in Period 3 (2009–2015). Among the driving forces, climatic factors (including precipitation and temperature) had the most dramatic changes (Fig. 5  , Fig. S4 ). For example, during Period 1, the contribution of climatic factors to Hongze Lake was only 7 %, which rapidly increased to 33 % in Period 2, and then decreased to 10 % in Period 3. These drastic changes in climatic factors could be explained by the impact of extreme precipitation on water quality. The impact of precipitation on water quality is multifaceted. Precipitation and surface runoff transport more nutrients into lakes, especially when encountering nutrient-rich sources, such as farmland, which results in further nutrient transport (Coffey et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020 ). Although the contribution of climatic factors to water quality decreases after crossing the EKC turning point (Fig. 3 ), extreme weather events can still greatly affect water quality in the short term. Heavy precipitation can shorten the hydraulic retention time, disturb sediments, and release internal nutrients, which may increase TN concentrations (Shen et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, precipitation can dilute nutrient concentrations. In our correlation analysis, the results showed precipitation and lake TN concentration were mainly negatively correlated (Fig. 6  ), indicating that at the annual scale, the dilution effect of precipitation dominates the relationship with TN concentration. However, upon examining heavy precipitation—defined in this study as precipitation exceeding the upper quartile of the 1995–2005 period—it was found that the positive correlation dominated the relationship between strong precipitation and TN concentration (Fig. 6 ). This indicates that, once precipitation exceeds a certain threshold, a large quantity of pollutants can be introduced into lakes (Carpenter et al., 2022 ). The dilution effect sometimes ceased to be the prevailing factor. For example, during Period 2, Hongze Lake experienced two major floods (in 2003 and 2007), particularly in 2003, which had an annual precipitation of more than 40 % of the multi-year average. Therefore, the contribution of climatic factors rapidly increased during that period (Fig. 5 f). This result indicates that when extreme weather events occur, climatic factors may dominate water quality changes, potentially offsetting human efforts in watershed management. For example, the 2016 flood in Honghu Lake led to a doubling of the annual N concentration compared to that in 2015 (Fig. 2 d). Given the accelerating climate change, extreme precipitation events will become more frequent, great challenge future watershed management (Donat et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2023 ). This finding aligns with those of previous site-level lake studies (Han and Bu, 2023; Huang et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021 ), which indicate that following heavy precipitation or flooding events, lake water quality tended to decline. While most of the lakes showed a positive correlation between TN concentrations and heavy precipitation, there were still lakes where the negative correlation was stronger (Fig. 6 ). These lakes were divided into two categories. The first category included Bosten and Wuliangsu Lakes, which are located in China’s arid-to-semi-arid regions with an annual precipitation of < 200 mm (Table S2 ). For those regions, forming surface runoff is challenging even under heavy precipitation. The second category included Chaohu and Qiandao Lakes. Chaohu Lake is subjected to heavy point-source pollution (Zhang et al., 2022 ), while Qiandao Lake is an important drinking water source protection area mainly with grassland surroundings and a low intensity of human activity (Gu et al., 2016 ). Overall, for these two lakes, more precipitation did not lead to a rapid increase in N loads; therefore, the dilution effect of precipitation dominated. In addition to heavy precipitation, temperature increases due to climate warming affect TN concentrations in lakes in various ways. First, higher temperatures lead to lower concentrations of dissolved oxygen in water, which may affect nitrification. Second, higher temperatures promote algae growth, especially during warmer winters leading to earlier algal blooms, and the N-fixing capability of cyanobacteria may elevate N concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2021 ). Additionally, temperature affects the activity of plants and microorganisms, enhancing the capacity of water bodies for N removal (Duan et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2021 ). Similar to heavy precipitation, in this study, high temperature was defined as the temperature exceeding the upper quartile of the study period, and the correlation between TN concentration and high temperature was assessed. Compared to the correlation analysis using temperature, a stronger positive correlation was observed in 6 of the 13 lakes, whereas the remaining lakes exhibited a stronger negative correlation (Fig. 6 ). This result suggests that the dominant effect of temperature on TN changes varied across lakes. Furthermore, the effect of temperature on water quality varies seasonally (Qin et al., 2021 ), which might have been countered by the annual-scale data. Although the effect of temperature on TN concentration was not great in this study’s dataset, increased temperatures can accelerate harmful algal blooms, and previous studies have indicated that climate change may offset efforts made by humans to reduce nutrient loading in watersheds (Huang et al., 2020 ).   4 Implications and limitations This study, using 13 lake basins in China as a case study, explored the reasons why achieving water quality goals is challenging. The difficulty in reaching set targets is not limited to China; it represents a global challenge in improving water environments (Basu et al., 2022 ). Although this study focused on statistically analyzing two key factors hindering water quality goals (time lags and extreme weather), using water quality models to support decision remains pivotal in water environment management. Despite the significant uncertainty that climate change brings to water quality, it is important to acknowledge that human management measures can enhance the resilience of lakes to risks. Therefore, long-term and sustainable watershed management measures are always necessary. This paper delineates the relative contributions of N cycling factors, climatic factors, socioeconomic factors, and land use factors to the changes in TN concentration in lakes. However, it does not account for all potential influencing factors, such as interactions between surface water and groundwater. For specific lakes, some of the unaddressed water quality factors in this paper may be important, requiring further exploration in the future. Meanwhile, in addition to N, other water quality indicators, such as P and N: P ratio, require similar analysis to understand the reasons for their changes.  5 Conclusion Despite decades of watershed management practices in China, achieving water quality targets in watersheds has remained challenging. This study identified two factors hindering the attainment of these goals: time lags and extreme precipitation. Owing to watershed management measures, particularly those addressing non-point source pollution, time lags make it challenging to meet the set TN concentration targets in the short term. Furthermore, the increasing frequency of extreme precipitation events has led to a significant influx of pollutants into lakes through runoff, which can negate human watershed management efforts. However, compared to lakes at the early human intervention stage, lakes with a higher level of governance exhibit greater resilience to climate change. Faced with the challenges of future N pollution in water bodies, especially the uncertainty and risks associated with climate change, a more proactive approach that involves implementing multiple measures to reduce N load needs to be adopted. However, patience should also be maintained.
1 Introduction Urban sprawl is one of the most dramatic land surface processes. Liu et al. (2020)  reported an 80 % increase in urban area globally between 1985 and 2015, from 362,700 km2  to 653,400 km2 , and China’s urbanization is particularly impressive. However, urbanization, as a complex and large-scale anthropogenic process, is often accompanied by drastic underlying surface succession, which in turn affects local and even larger-scale hydrological processes (Carlson and Traci Arthur, 2000; Kaufmann et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2022 ). The Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei metropolitan area (BTH-MA) is one of the three world-class urban agglomerations in China, and studies (Shan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014 ) in recent years have found significant changes in the intensity of rainfall in the region, while the role of urbanization and driving mechanisms remain unclear. Studies (Changnon et al., 1971; Chen et al., 2011; Freitag et al., 2018; Tysa and Ren, 2022; Zhang et al., 2018 ) have shown that urbanization changes the distribution and magnitude of rainfall, based on the analysis of observational data and numerical modelling methods. However, due to the complexity of rainfall formation mechanisms and the limitations of observational data and numerical models, there are still different understandings of the laws, physical mechanisms and drivers of urban influence on rainfall. In Beijing alone, Yang et al. (2014)  found that the highest frequency of rainfall occurred in the city center and downwind, whereas Dou et al. (2015)  showed a decrease in rainfall downwind of the city. Regarding the reasons, Zhang (2010)  suggests that the increase in summer precipitation in Beijing is due to increased vertically mixed water vapor from rapid urbanization, while Miao et al. (2011)  found that the degree of change in rainfall in Beijing varies with the level of urbanization development and suggest that heat transport due to urbanization is more important for rainfall than momentum transport. Besides, Zhong et al. (2015)  concluded that the expansion of urban land type has the opposite effect to the increase in aerosols on rainfall, with the latter being more dominant. This shows that even in the same region, differences in the interaction between the atmospheric background, surface thermal effects and aerosol emissions at specific times may lead to different or even biased views of the effects of rainfall in cities, and a comprehensive study of the influence of urbanization from multiple perspectives is required. Furthermore, most existing studies of urbanization effects are based on typical heavy rainfall events, which not only fail to consider the influence of dynamic urbanization development, but also ignore the differential response of rainfall of varying intensities to urbanization (Li et al., 2013; Shem and Shepherd, 2009; Zhong and Yang, 2015 ). This study aims to clarify the extent of urbanization’s influence on rainfall of different intensities and the driving mechanisms behind it. First, we classify land use type in the BTH-MA using the GEE platform and the random forest algorithm, and the dynamic classification of urban and rural meteorological stations from 1965 to 2022 shows that there is a “Matthew effect” in rainfall in the BTH-MA. Then, the main driving factors are identified in combination with Geographical Detector model, and hypotheses are proposed accordingly. Finally, a total of 470 rainfall events during the flood season (Jun-Sep) of 1979–1981, 1999–2001 and 2019–2021 (representing different stages of urbanization) in Beijing are analyzed to further confirm the proposed hypotheses. We expect to provide scientific support for urban planning and regional water safety management through this research.  2 Study region and data The BTH-MA is located in northern China, with a total area of 218,000 km2 , and is the economic, political and cultural heart of China. The BTH-MA, which includes the two municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin and eleven prefecture-level cities in Hebei Province, is a world-class mega-urban agglomeration, the location distribution of which is shown in Fig. 1  . Since China promoted the coordinated development of BTH-MA as a national strategy in 2014, the total economic output of the BTH-MA has exceeded 10 trillion yuan in almost a decade, with a total population of nearly 110 million. Driven by rapid economic and social development, the built-up area of the BTH-MA has grown from 9,226 km2  in 1985 to 32,908 km2  in 2018, an increase of 2.6 times. And several studies (Dou et al., 2015; Miao et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2015 ) have shown that the rainfall in the BTH-MA has been greatly altered by the impact of urbanization. The daily rainfall observations used in this study were obtained from the China Meteorological Data Service Centre (https://data.cma.cn ). There are a total of 175 meteorological stations in the BTH-MA, but since most of the stations have measurement records after 1965, 124 stations were finally selected for the follow-up study by considering the completeness and consistency of the measurement series at each station, and their distribution is shown in Fig. 1 . Land use data is the basis for the division of urban and rural meteorological stations. Considering the accessibility of remote sensing imagery, this study divides the period 1965–2022 into a total of seven phases, and the phases and representative land use are shown in Table A.1  in Supplemental File S1 . Land use data for 2010 and earlier were obtained from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center of China (http://www.resdc.cn/ ), and land use data for 2018 were obtained from the global 10 m resolution land use results produced by ESRI based on Sentinel 2 data (https://livingatlas.arcgis.com/landcoverexplorer ). We found that the land use data from 1980 performed poorly in the northwestern part of the BTH-MA, mistakenly classifying non-urban areas as urban areas. Subsequently, we re-extracted the land use data for that period using the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform. During the image screening process, we discovered that only images from 1985 onwards met the selection criteria. Therefore, the land use classification results from 1985 were used to represent the land cover situation in the first stage. ERA5 is the fifth-generation reanalysis dataset of global climate and weather for the past 80 years by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). This study utilized its monthly and hourly reanalysis data from (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ ), and we assessed the accuracy of ERA5 data in Section 4.4 .  3 Methodology 3.1 Land use classification based on GEE and random forest Random forest is an integrated learning method based on multiple decision trees proposed by Breiman in 2001 (Breiman, 2001 ), which avoids the overfitting phenomenon to some extent because each tree selects some samples and some features. Moreover, since each tree chooses samples and features at random, it has good noise resistance and stable performance, and is widely used for land use classification research (Gislason et al., 2006; Tokar et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Google Earth Engine (GEE) is a remote sensing big data analysis platform based on Google’s cloud service infrastructure, which provides users with petabytes of publicly available Earth observation data and publicly available algorithms to analyze the data for free. In particular, the computations and analyses performed on the platform are based on the automated parallel processing of Google’s infrastructure, which greatly improves the computational and operational speed of the data and has been applied to a wide number of studies related to changes in the Earth’s surface in recent years (Kumar and Mutanga, 2018; Liang et al., 2020; Shafizadeh-Moghadam et al., 2021 ). Fig. A.1  in Supplemental File S1  shows the classification process used to classify land use in the BTH-MA based on Landsat 5 image from 1985. The total number of images that met the filtering requirements for that year was 69 views, all of which contained less than 2 % cloud cover. The images were then merged and cropped. In constructing the random forest classifier, we not only chose the B1-B7 bands that come with Landsat5, but also added the MNDWI, EVI and NDVI indices as additional feature variables, and used the B5 band as a texture feature to aid classification. We cyclically calculated the classification accuracy in the range of 5 to 50 decision trees, and finally found that the best classification effect was achieved when the number of decision trees was 25.  3.2 Dynamic identification of urban and rural meteorological stations In classifying meteorological stations, we calculated the proportion of built-up area within the buffer zone radius of each meteorological site based on the results of different stages of land use classification, thus taking into account the impact of dynamic urban development. In this study, 33 % (Luo and Lau, 2018; Yang et al., 2017 ) was used as the threshold for classification, and the proportion exceeding this value was considered an urban meteorological station, otherwise a rural station. In order to combine the urbanization development trend in the BTH-MA and then select the appropriate window radius, we conducted statistics on the proportions of urban stations corresponding to different window radii (2–10 km) based on the corresponding land use data in 2000, 2005, 2010, and 2018, respectively (see Fig. A.2  in Supplemental File S1 ), and found that the corresponding slopes under different land use scenarios are basically unchanged when the window radius is less than 4 km. This indicates that when the window radius is 4 km, the urbanization level reflected based on the sites is consistent with the urbanization level of the BTH-MA as a whole, and Han (Han et al., 2022 ) also used 4 km as a buffer zone.  3.3 Geographical detector model Geographical Detector model (GDM) is a spatial analysis method for detecting spatial dissimilarities and the driving factors behind them, proposed by Jinfeng Wang (Wang et al., 2010; 2016 ), and widely used in various fields (Chang et al., 2023; He et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2016; Meng et al., 2023 ). GDM include Factor detector, Interaction detector, Risk detector and Ecological detector. The Factor detector is designed to determine the extent to which each factor explains the spatial variance of the dependent variable, as measured by the q-value, calculated as shown in Eq. (1) . The Interaction detector is used to assess whether different factors, when acting together, increase or decrease the explanatory power of the dependent variable, based on the judgement shown in Table A.2  in Supplemental File S1 . The Risk detector is used to determine whether there is a significant difference in the mean value of an attribute between two sub-regions. The Ecological detector is used to compare whether there is a significant difference between the effects of two factors, X1  and X2 , on the spatial distribution of attribute Y.(1) q = 1 - ∑ h = 1  m  N h  σ h 2    N σ 2        where, h  is the stratification, i.e., classification or partitioning, of the dependent variable Y  or factor X ; Nh   and N  are the number of cells in stratum h  and the whole region, respectively; σ h     and σ    are the variance of Y  in stratum h  and the whole region, respectively.  3.4 Technical route The technical route taken in this study is shown in Fig. 2  .   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Urbanization and classification of urban and rural meteorological stations Based on high-resolution Google Earth images of 1985, we generated 9,100 sample points in the BTH-MA, and used 80 % and 20 % of the total sample points for training and verification, respectively. Then, combined with the land use classification process proposed in Section 3.1 , we successfully extracted the land use results for the BTH-MA in 1985 (see Fig. A.3  in Supplemental File S1 ), with an overall accuracy of 0.82 and a kappa coefficient of 0.77. Overall, the results of land use classification in the BTH-MA have a good performance compared to existing products. Then, we visualized the land use transfer at each stage from 1985-1995-2005-2018 (Fig. 3  ), and the results show that the built-up area in the BTH-MA increased from 9,226 km2  in 1985 to 32,908 km2  in 2018, an increase of 2.6 times, and was mainly converted from cropland. On the basis of the classification method of the urban and rural meteorological stations in Section 3.2 , we extracted the urban meteorological stations for each period (as shown in Fig. 4  ). In the first stage (1965–1989), there were 10 urban meteorological stations, accounting for only 8 % of the total number of meteorological stations. With the development of construction land, the number of urban meteorological stations has grown to 86 in the most recent period (2015–2022), accounting for as high as 69 %.
