Besides, the spatial distribution of urban meteorological stations has gradually expanded from the highly urbanized Beijing and Tianjin areas to other regions in the BTH-MA, reflecting the spatiotemporal characteristics of urbanization through the changes in meteorological station types.  4.2 Differential effect of urbanization on rainfall events of varying intensities The average annual rainfall amount in the urban and rural areas of the BTH-MA at different stages is shown in Fig. A.4  in Supplemental File S1 , and the differences in annual rainfall between the urban and suburban areas at the stages of 1956–1989, 1990–1994, 1995–1999, 2000–2004, 2005–2009, 2010–2014 and 2015–2000 are −40. 7 mm, 39.8 mm, 61.3 mm, 6.4 mm, 49.7 mm, 36.1 mm, and 5.1 mm, respectively. Only in the first stage, the rainfall in the rural area was higher than that in the urban area, and in the remaining stages, the rainfall in the urban area was higher than that in the rural area. The number of days with light rainfall and rainfall exceeding the moderate rainfall category is illustrated in Fig. A.5  in Supplemental File S1 . The results demonstrate a notable decline in the frequency of light rainfall occurrences across the study area, with an average of 77 days of light rainfall occurring annually during the initial period and a reduction to 56 days during the most recent period. In comparison to urban areas, rural areas exhibited a greater frequency of light rainfall during the same period. Conversely, the frequency of rainfall exceeding the moderate rainfall category was higher in urban areas than in rural areas during the same period. To further investigate the extent to which urban development affects rainfall of different intensities, we conducted a trend analysis (Fig. 5   and Fig. 6  ) of rainfall amount and frequency utilizing the Theil-Sen regression method (Dinpashoh et al., 2011; Vinod and Mahesha, 2024 ), which is robust to extreme values. The rainfall intensity classification criteria used in this study are derived from the relevant regulations of the China Meteorological Administration (https://www.cma.gov.cn/ ). Daily rainfall above 0.1 mm and less than 10 mm counts as light rain, above 10 mm and less than 25 mm as moderate rain, above 25 mm and less than 50 mm as heavy rain, above 50 mm and less than 100 mm as rainstorm and above 100 mm as extreme rain. As shown in Fig. 5 , the trends in annual rainfall amount in urban and rural areas are opposite, with an increasing trend in urban areas (slope = +0.6 mm/10a) and a decreasing trend in rural areas (slope = −13.6 mm/10a). Since the influence of the large-scale climatic background is nearly eliminated in the slope difference calculation (Han et al., 2022; Luo and Lau, 2019; Yu et al., 2022 ), it can be assumed that urbanization in the BTH-MA has increased annual rainfall by 14.2 mm/10a. In addition, we found that urbanization in the BTH-MA has an asymmetric effect on different rainfall intensities, i.e., it suppresses the amount of light rainfall (−1.7 mm/10a) and promotes the amount of moderate rainfall, heavy rainfall, rainstorm and extreme rainfall to varying degrees of + 5.2 mm/10a, +2.7 mm/10a, +4.7 mm/10a and + 3.5 mm/10a, respectively. In terms of rainfall frequency, urbanization significantly reduced the frequency of light rain (−1.6 d/10a) and increased the frequency of moderate rain (+0.3 d/10a), heavy rain (+0.1 d/10a), rainstorm (+0.07d /10a) and extreme rain (+0.03 d /10a). The p-values for the differences in slopes between annual rainfall, moderate rainfall, rainstorm and extreme rainfall in urban and rural areas are 0.0356, 0.0274, 0.0495 and 0.0137, respectively. Only the differences in slopes for light rainfall and heavy rainfall fail to meet the criteria for significance. With regard to rainfall frequency, the differences between the slopes of light rainfall, moderate rainfall, rainstorm and extreme rainfall in urban and rural areas also demonstrated statistical significance (p value < 0.05). The state of human health and well-being is inextricably linked to the phenomenon of climate change. A notable decline in rainfall days can result in the occurrence of droughts, which in turn exerts considerable pressure on water security and renders urban areas more susceptible to heatwaves. Zheng et al. (2020)  demonstrated that urban heatwaves in Beijing have become more prevalent since 1995, leading to an increase in deaths form cardiovascular and respiratory diseases (Dong et al., 2016 ). Conversely, the heightened incidence of heavy rainfall in urban areas, where property and population are concentrated, can result in more severe flooding. This has been evidenced by the experiences of Beijing in recent years (Wang et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2020 ). In light of the observed phenomena and existing studies, it can be concluded that the asymmetric impact of urbanization on rainfall is significant and far-reaching. Consequently, there is an urgent need to carry out relevant research to explore the impact of urban development on rainfall in the BTH-MA and the mechanism behind it. In this study, we refer to the phenomenon described above as the 'Matthew effect' of rainfall intensity.  4.3 Driving factors based on GDM and the propose of hypothesis 4.3.1 Driving factors based on GDM Previous studies (Inamura et al., 2011; Sun and Shu, 2007 ) have shown that the thermal effect and subsurface resistance generated by urban development are the main factors of urbanization affecting rainfall amount and its spatial distribution. In this section, we analyzed the degree of influence of net surface solar radiation (SSR), proportion of permanent urban residents (PPUR), urban–rural temperature difference (URTD), surface sensible heat flux (SSHF), potential evapotranspiration (PE), wind speed (WS), and surface latent heat flux (SLHF) on the urban–rural rainfall amount/frequency difference and the interactions between the above factors based on the Factor detector and the Interaction detector in GDM, the results are shown in Fig. 7   and Fig. 8  . The aforementioned SSR, SSHF, PE, and SLHF variables are derived from the ERA5 data set. The PPUR variable is calculated from the ratio of the resident urban population to the total population. The WS variable is derived from observed data. From the q-values characterizing the degree of importance, SSR (q = 0.42, p < 0.05), PPUR (q = 0.30, p > 0.05) and URTD (q = 0.23, p > 0.05) are the three main factors influencing the urban/rural rainfall amount difference, and GDP (q = 0.85, p < 0.01), URTD (q = 0.73, p < 0.01) and SSHF (q = 0.64, p < 0.01) are the three main factors influencing the urban/rural rainfall frequency difference. In addition, SSR, SSHF, PE and SLHF play a positive role on the difference in rainfall amount and frequency between urban and rural areas, while the other factors play a negative role. This is mainly because PPUR and GDP reflect the level of urbanization of a region in terms of economic and social development, and at high levels of urbanization, urban heat emissions from industrial production, cars, anthropogenic heat, etc. are higher, leading to uneven temperature distribution across the region, which in turn affects precipitation (Bornstein and Lin, 2000; Yu et al., 2022 ). Wind speed, on the other hand, alters the transport rate of air currents in the atmosphere and affects the rainfall distribution zone, while taller buildings in urban areas increase surface drag, which in turn slows down near-surface wind speed (Yang et al., 2014 ). Furthermore, the Interaction detector results showed different levels of interaction between each of the above driving factors. We list the top 5 strongest sets of interaction combinations affecting the differences in rainfall amount and frequency in Fig. 8 . In terms of rainfall amount, the interactions between PPUR∩SLHF, GDP∩SLHF, GDP∩URTD, and SSR∩SLHF are all nonlinearly enhanced, while the interaction between SSR∩PPUR is bi-enhanced, with the highest interaction q-value reaching 0.83. For rainfall frequency, GDP∩URTD, GDP∩SLHF, GDP∩SSR, SSR∩SSHF, and URTD∩SLHF are all bi-enhanced, and the highest interaction q-value reaches 0.95. And the interaction results not listed also all reached a bi-enhanced level, with no weakened interaction results. The above phenomena suggest that the thermal effect of urbanization in the BTH-MA and the resistance of the subsurface will jointly amplify the differences in rainfall amount and frequency between urban and rural areas.  4.3.2 Hypothesis Based on the results of the GDM, it can be seen that the factors of net surface solar radiation, surface sensible heat flux and PPUR have high q-values, but have different results (positive and negative correlation coefficients) on precipitation amount/frequency. Combined with the conclusion in Section 4.2  that urbanization suppresses the amount and frequency of light rainfall and promotes the occurrence of more intense rainfall events, we propose here the following hypothesis: compared to the outskirts, urban areas have higher temperatures, and according to the Clausius-Clapeyron theory (Wang et al., 2017 ), it is known that above the city is equivalent to an additional sponge that absorbs water, so that light rain events are more difficult to occur with weaker water vapor conditions. Due to the increased water holding capacity of urban areas as a result of higher temperatures, we suggest that heavy rainfall event is more likely to occur downwind of the urban fringe under more adequate water vapor conditions. In order to verify the validity of the above conjecture, we use the ERA 5-hourly reanalysis data to analyze the development process of rainfall events with varying intensities, and the specific conclusions are presented in Section 4.4 .   4.4 Explanations for the ‘Matthew effect’ of rainfall In the above analysis, we confirmed that urbanization has an asymmetric effect on precipitation of different intensities and proposed hypotheses based on the main drivers identified. To further confirm our proposed hypotheses and investigate the physical mechanisms behind the “Matthew effect” phenomena of rainfall, we analyzed a total of 470 rainfall events during the flood season (Jun-Sep) in the three phases (representing different levels of urbanization) 1979–1981, 1999–2001 and 2019–2021, based on the ERA 5-hourly reanalysis dataset, using Beijing city and its surrounding areas as the study object, of which 304 were light rainfall events, 90 were moderate rainfall events, 42 were heavy rainfall events, 25 were rainstorm events, and 9 were extreme rainfall events. First, the accuracy of the ERA5 reanalysis data was verified. We synthesized the rainfall of the ERA5 hourly scale reanalysis data of the flood season of the above-mentioned years to the daily scale and verified it together with the measured daily rainfall of the meteorological stations in the same period. The correlation coefficient reached 0.60, which indicates that the ERA5 reanalysis data has a better performance in the region and can be used for the subsequent analyses. By analyzing the development process of the 470 rainfall events, we can conclude the following pattern: 83 % of the light rainfall events in the Beijing occurred mainly in the suburbs around the city, while almost no precipitation occurred in the urban area. And 62 % of the rainfall distribution mainly in the upwind direction of the city, while 29 % of the precipitation falls mainly in the downwind direction of the city. For higher intensity rainfall events, 54 % of the precipitation centers occurred on the leeward edge of the city and 26 % of the rainfall events occurred mainly on either side of the windward edge of the city, a finding that was also confirmed in the study by Sun (Sun and Shu, 2007 ) on the phenomenon of rainfall bypassing. To better illustrate the specific mechanism behind the above phenomena, we take as examples two precipitation events with different intensities, whose spatial distribution of precipitation and average wind speed and direction during the precipitation period are shown in Fig. 9  . Rainfall event 1 was a light rainfall that occurred from 2000 to 06-15 T08:00 to T14:00, and rainfall event 2 was a rainstorm event that occurred from 2020-08-04 T20:00 to 08-05 T17:00, all in UTC and 8 h behind local time. Fig. A.6  in Supplemental File S1  shows the hourly evolution of rainfall event 1. It can be seen that the precipitation started to fall in the southwest of the region and then gradually moved towards the city, with the precipitation falling closest to the city Centre in the 6th hour after the start of the rainfall, with the maximum hourly rainfall being 3 to 4 mm. Fig. 10  a shows the distribution of the near-surface air temperature two hours before the start of precipitation event 1. The temperature difference between the city and the south was more than 10 °C, leading to a lower air pressure above the urban surface, and the warm air from the south flowed along the low altitude towards the city, while the frictional resistance in the city area increased due to the influence of the urban canopy, and the warm and humid airflow began to slow down in the upwind area close to the city, and the water vapor gradually became supersaturated, resulting in condensation and landfall. So why is there less precipitation in the city? To answer this question, as shown in Fig. 10 b, the water vapor deficit status of the region in the pre-event period is represented by the difference between the potential evapotranspiration and the actual evapotranspiration on the day before the rainfall event. It can be seen that there is a large water vapor deficit in the urban area in the pre-event period, and the maximum deficit can be up to about 10 mm compared to the northern mountainous area. In addition, the height of the boundary layer in the urban area is higher than that in the surrounding areas (as shown in Fig. 10 c), which leads to further diffusion of water vapor starting when it reaches over the city, making it more difficult to form the supersaturated water vapor conditions required for rainfall. Fig. 10 d shows the regional mean convective effective potential energy distribution during the precipitation period, from which it can be found that the strong convective activity mainly occurs on the southeast side of the city, which is close to the distribution of the rainy area. In case of rainstorm, it shows the opposite pattern to light rainfall. As can be seen from the above paragraph, the fallout areas for moderate rainfall and above are mainly located on the lee side of the city. An example of a rainstorm event (marked as rainfall event 2) is shown in Fig. A.7  in Supplemental File S1 . It can be seen that the moments of maximum precipitation on 5 August 2020 occurred at 10, 11 and 12o'clock (6 to 8p.m. local time), when the area of precipitation was mainly located in the south-central part of the city, and the area of high rainfall values at this time corresponded to the downwind areas of the interior and edges of the city. An analysis of the height of the boundary layer at the beginning of rainfall event 2 (Fig. 11  b) shows that when the rainstorm occurred, the height of the boundary layer is low (less than 250 m) over the whole region, and the whole region acts as a high-pressure convergence zone. At this time, the air carries a large amount of water vapor content, and after passing over the city, the air temperature increases (Fig. 11 a). According to the Clausius-Clapeyron theory (Wang et al., 2017 ), the atmospheric water-holding capacity over the city continues to increase, and as the water vapor content continues to increase, it becomes supersaturated with water vapor by the time it reaches the downwind edge of the city, leading to greater rainfall intensity compared to other regions. In addition, the Kx index (Fig. 11 c) for the period of maximum precipitation (3 h cumulative precipitation greater than 30 mm) and the mean CAPE (Fig. 11 d) during the precipitation period show that the thermal convective motion is very strong in the region of large precipitation, further supporting our hypothesis. In summary, under the combined effect of temperature and urban surface resistance, when a small rain event occurs, it tends to form a rain area upwind of the city and it is difficult to meet the weather conditions required for rainfall over the city, in which case both temperature and downwelling resistance play a dominant role. For higher intensity rainfall events, the increased temperature on the water vapor content of the air means that precipitation is more likely to form at the lower edge of the city, where temperature plays a dominant role.   5 Conclusion The “Matthew effect” of urbanization on rainfall, i.e., the suppression of light precipitation and the increase of higher intensity classes of rainfall, are clarified by the dynamic statistics of urban and rural rainfall over a long period of time in the BTH-MA from 1965 to 2022. The GDM shows that SSR (q = 0.42), PPUR (q = 0.30) and URTD (q = 0.23) have the greatest influence on the urban–rural rainfall amount differences. On the other hand, GDP (q = 0.85), URTD (q = 0.73), and SSHF (q = 0.64) are identified as the dominant driving factors influencing the urban–rural rainfall frequency difference. Additionally, varying degrees of interaction exist between different factors. In terms of rainfall amount, the intersection of PPUR and SLHF exhibits a non-linear enhancement effect with the highest interaction (q = 0.83), while the combination of GDP and HUE has the strongest interaction on rainfall frequency (q = 0.95), representing a bi-enhancement effect. Lastly, a substantial sample of rainfall events reveals that approximately 62 % of light rain occurrences in the Beijing area manifest on the windward side of the city, with a further 29 % intensification on the leeward side, whereas light rain is seldom produced within the urban area itself. For moderate rainfall or above, it is more likely to occur at the urban edge on the leeward side (accounting for 54 %). To summarize, the 'Matthew Effect' phenomenon of rainfall intensity is influenced by a combination of urban subsurface resistivity and temperature. In light rain scenarios, due to the scarcity of water vapor, precipitation is unlikely to occur within the city and tends to appear on the windward side influenced by urban surface resistance. Conversely, in heavy rain scenarios, the water vapor, intensified by the temperature above the city, is prone to form strong precipitation at the urban edge on the leeward side. Our results suggest that the phenomenon of building and population agglomeration associated with urban sprawl alters regional energy transfer processes, allowing heat to be absorbed and retained within the urban region, leading to higher temperature and boundary layer height. The above processes reduce the frequency of light rainfall and facilitate heat dome phenomena over cities, which in turn exacerbate urban heat wave events. Wang et al. (2023)  conducted a global analysis to identify potential future extreme heat wave risk zones and found that the frequency, duration, and intensity of heat waves are likely to increase under various emission scenarios. The projections presented by Marcotullio et al. (2022)  similarly indicate that, even under the sustainable scenario, 3.5 billion individuals will remain at risk of exposure to extreme heat waves globally during the period 2070–2099 (>42 °C). We recommend that more attention be paid to the role of green spaces and waterscapes in urban design to help cope with heatwave disasters that may be caused by reduced rainfall frequency. In addition, to prevent excessive run-off and flooding during heavy rainfall, more rainfall monitoring and warning devices should be installed in and around the city.
1 Introduction Several ice-dammed glacial lakes were formed during the decay of continental ice sheets during the last Ice Age (Clarke et al., 2004; Regnéll et al., 2023 ). When the ice dams failed, the impounded lake flushed out dramatically into the landscape downstream. These events are called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF) or jökulhlaups and hydraulic reconstructions of the events suggest that the floods may have had magnitudes exceeding 1 ×106  m3 /s = 1 000 000 m3 /s = 1 Sverdrup (Sv) (Alho et al., 2010 ; Denlinger and O’Connell, 2010 ; Lang et al., 2019 ; Winsemann et al., 2015 ). Contemporary GLOFs occur on the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, but also in numerous, glacierized mountain regions, where the consequences can be severe, threatening downstream communities, hydropower dams and infrastructure (Carrivick and Tweed, 2019; Engeset et al., 2005; Hewitt, 1982; Hewitt and Liu, 2013; Mir et al., 2018 ). More than 3100 GLOFs have been reported between 850 and 2022 according to a global GLOF database (Lützow et al., 2023 ). Glacial lake number and total area have increase by about 50 % between 1990 and 2018 according to an analysis of satellite images (Shugar et al., 2020 ). More than 110,000 glacial lakes currently exist (Zhang et al., 2024 ) and an estimated 10–15 million people worldwide are currently exposed to impacts from potential GLOFs (Taylor et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024 ). Ice-dammed lakes are the primary source for GLOFs in multiple locations such as Greeland, Scandinavia and Alaska (Zhang et al., 2024 , and references therein). A study compiling data from 20 countries with ca. 1350 glacier floods over the past ca. 1000 years showed that 70 % of recorded GLOFs were from ice-dammed glacial lakes (Carrivick and Tweed, 2016 ). Data on how downstream areas will be affected by potential ice-dam failures are often lacking, and investigation will be more important in a changing climate. Large prehistoric GLOFs have in many cases been landscape-defining events, carving out spectacular terrains in short timescales (Baker, 1973; Bretz, 1923; Gupta et al., 2007 ), mobilizing and depositing vast amounts of sediments (Komatsu et al., 2009; Maizels, 1997; Marren, 2005 ) and affecting climatic conditions (Carrivick and Tweed, 2013; Clarke et al., 2009; Teller et al., 2002 ). The most famous and well-studied example is perhaps the outburst floods related to the glacial lake Missoula in the USA (Baker, 1973; Bretz, 1923; Clarke et al., 1984; O’Connor et al., 2020 ), but other episodes have been investigated in glacierized and formerly glacierized regions elsewhere in the world (Benito and Thorndycraft, 2020; Herget, 2005; Margold et al., 2018 ). Reconstructions and hydraulic simulations of paleo outburst floods are challenging. It is not possible to calibrate the hydrodynamic model, as is standard practice for modern-day flood modeling, because there are no field measurements of discharge vs. water surface elevation for these particular flood events. Thus, the models rely primarily on geomorphological evidence to constrain the estimates of peak discharge. Very few studies have ample geomorphological evidence at multiple scales to properly constrain the estimates of peak discharges. It is for instance difficult to constrain the glacial lake volume – and the volume readily available during a GLOF – particularly when dealing with subglacial lakes (Björnsson, 2003 ). There are often few geological traces visible today that can be used to constrain maximum flood height during the GLOF, thus giving rise to considerable uncertainty of hydraulic reconstructions (Carrivick et al., 2013; Larsen and Lamb, 2016 ). Also, similar geomorphology can be produced by multiple processes, leading to the problem of equifinality during interpretation of the geomorphologic evidence (Wells et al., 2022 ). Lastly, the evolution of the flood is a concatenation of different processes, each having its own uncertainties, for instance related to routing through the remnant ice body, model resolution, hydrograph shape and terrain roughness. Many studies present a wide range of possible peak discharges, which highlights the challenges with constraining the input parameters and assumptions for the flood modeling (Alho et al., 2010; Lang et al., 2019; Winsemann et al., 2015 ). An informed reconstruction using multiple constraints on different parts of the process chain would provide enhanced robustness. Traces of glacial lakes and outburst floods from the late Pleistocene and Early Holocene are in some cases still well preserved in the landscape. This is particularly true where there have been one or few floods or where the subsequent floods are much smaller than the first GLOF, such that large-scale erosion and deposition of the GLOF has not been completely reworked on the same scale. The preservation of geological traces is also dependent upon additional factors such as tectonic stability and the type of substrate. One example of well-preserved landforms related to a glacial lake and the subsequent outburst flood is that of glacial lake Nedre Glomsjø in southeastern Norway, which formed at the retreating ice sheet margin during the Early Holocene (Berthling and Sollid, 1999; Høgaas and Longva, 2018; Holmsen, 1915; Longva, 1994 ). When the ice-dam ruptured around 10.4 cal. ka BP, a glacial lake outburst flood swept down the Rendalen and Østerdalen valleys and eventually out to the North Sea (Høgaas et al., 2023; Høgaas and Longva, 2016; Longva, 1994 ). The peak discharge of the flood has previously been estimated to ≤ 170,000 m3 /s (Berthling and Sollid, 1999 ) and ≤ 350,000 m3 /s (Longva, 1994 ) using the empirical equations of Clague and Mathews (1973) . The availability of new field observations combined with high-resolution mapping based on LiDAR data (Høgaas and Longva, 2016, 2018 ), as well as progress in hydrodynamic modelling now allow for more precise estimates of the available lake volume and peak discharge during the outburst flood. This paper combines thermodynamically-based ice tunneling simulations with the recomputed lake hypsometry and downstream hydrodynamic modelling – constrained by geomorphologic markers of the purported maximum flood level – to estimate the peak discharge of the glacial lake outburst flood.  2 Regional setting and geological background At the end of the last Ice Age, the ice divide was located in the interior of southern Norway (Mangerud et al., 2011 ). The ice sheet contracted rapidly in width across southeast Norway in the Early Holocene. As the northern ice sheet margin retreated south of the main drainage divide at ∼11 cal. ka BP, multiple glacier-dammed lakes formed and drained as progressively lower spillways became ice-free upon deglaciation (Garnes and Bergersen, 1980 ; Hansen, 1886 ; Holmsen, 1915, 1918 ). Meanwhile, the ice sheet thinned rapidly (Goehring et al., 2008 ), and meltwater corridors and associated landforms in the region indicate that large amounts of meltwater reached the glacier bed and locally altered the thermal regime of the ice sheet (van Boeckel et al., 2022 ). By ∼10.5–10.0 cal. ka BP it is believed that the remnant ice sheet had been reduced to a thin sector of glacial ice that extended from western Norway, across the large inland valleys and into Sweden (Høgaas et al., 2023; Hughes et al., 2016; Romundset et al., 2023 );  Fig. 1 . 2.1 Traces of the glacial lake Nedre Glomsjø Glacial lake Nedre Glomsjø formed as the lowermost regional spillway (at ∼660 m a.s.l.) toward the north became ice-free (Fig. 1 ). From mapping hanging shoreline features along Østerdalen, Rendalen and adjacent valleys, Holmsen (1915)  reconstructed the vast inland lake and proposed that it eventually covered 1500–1600 km2 . It has been debated whether the shoreline features reflected open glacial lakes or smaller lateral lakes along stagnant dead-ice (Gjessing, 1960 ; Hansen, 1886 ; Holmsen, 1915 ; Reusch, 1917 ; Høgaas and Longva, 2018  and review therein). However, the presence of recessional De Geer moraines in the basins – and the consistency between the moraines and shoreline features – show that the lake-terminating parts of the ice sheet retreated actively southward in the basins (Høgaas and Longva, 2018 ;  Fig. 2 ). It is believed that the ice-margin had retreated far south in Østerdalen and Rendalen when the ice-dam in Rendalen caved and a glacial lake outburst flood was funneled beneath the remnant ice sheet (Berthling and Sollid, 1999; Høgaas and Longva, 2016; Longva, 1994 ). This caused a sudden drainage of a large part of the lake from Østerdalen toward Rendalen across the Barkaldkjølen topographic saddle, forming, or reshaping, the spectacular, ∼2.5-km-long Jutulhogget canyon (Figs. 1  and 2 C).  2.2 Traces of the Nedre Glomsjø outburst flood Erosional and depositional features related to the Nedre Glomsjø outburst flood occur at multiple scales and are summarized in  Table 1 . The area between the southernmost mapped paleo shorelines and northernmost paleostage indicators (PSI) is assumed to be the potential extent of the remnant ice sheet during the GLOF. Based on characteristics of the paleostage indicators, Høgaas and Longva (2016)  suggested that the GLOF emerged from the ice sheet approximately 15 km north of Elverum (Fig. 1 ). There are substantial traces of the flood along the Glomma river valley and south of Kongsvinger, e.g. continuous erosive scarps, flood bars and sand dune deposits and ice-block obstacle marks (Fig. 3 ; Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ; Hansen et al., 2020 ). The erosive scarps mapped along the valley sides were interpreted as paleostage indicators by Høgaas and Longva (2016)  and the uppermost scarps were further used for reconstructing the maximum flood level during the event. Gravel extraction in the region has revealed sections with very coarse-grained material, e.g. stratified deposits containing colossal boulders (  Fig. 4 A, B). Sections through flood bars often show poorly sorted, yet stratified material that locally show thick foreset beds (Fig. 4 C). Deposits of a silty sediment termed the Romerike Silt Bed (no: Romeriksmjele ) are attributed to the Nedre Glomsjø GLOF. The silt bed, which is locally up to 1.5 m thick at Romerike, is present throughout the region from Romerike to Elverum (Longva, 1994 ). Conspicuous, elongated furrows in the clay plateaus on Romerike was interpreted by Longva and Bakkejord (1990)  and Longva and Thoresen (1991)  as iceberg ploughmarks formed during the Nedre Glomsjø outburst flood, implying that large icebergs were transported more than 130 km from the collapsed ice margin in the north to Romerike, where they were detained as the flood waned. Høgaas et al. (2023)  traced the Romerike Silt Bed in basin sediments records at different elevations in the region to reconstruct the maximum outburst flood level. They found that the flood level inferred from the sediments exceeded the landform-inferred flood level by several meters. Radiocarbon dates from the sediment cores indicate that the event took place between 10.5 and 10.3 cal. ka BP (Høgaas et al., 2023 ).   3 Methods and materials The evolution of the glacial lake outburst flood from Nedre Glomsjø must have been dictated by the dynamics of water release from the lake through the ice dam. We envisage that the flood developed by a self-enhancing mechanism where growth of an ice-walled channel due to dissipation of potential and thermal energy through the water flow caused a run-away process that quickly drained the lake (Clarke, 2003; Clarke et al., 2004; Nye, 1976 ). To test whether the inferred paleo discharges are consistent with this mechanism, both in terms of flood magnitude and possible duration, we employ a simple hydraulic model for an ice-walled channel through the remnant ice sheet that dammed glacial lake Nedre Glomsjø. Development of an ice tunnel beneath the ice sheet is simulated for a variety of tunnel lengths up to 70 km to gauge the uncertainty related to the exact dimensions of the subglacial drainage pathway. We then route hydrographs produced from the ice tunneling simulations through the Glomma valley and out to Skagerrak, the strait between Norway, Sweden and Denmark. The results in terms of simulated flood heights and water velocities are compared to geological traces for the glacial lake outburst flood. Our model area includes a 95 km stretch in the Rendalen and Østerdalen valleys, and a 31,140 km2  domain for hydrodynamic modeling, stretching from Rena southward to Skagerrak (Fig. 1 ). All model geometries are based on the 10 m digital elevation model (DEM) of the Norwegian national digital terrain model (NDH) based on LiDAR scanning (https://hoydedata.no/LaserInnsyn/ ). Vertical accuracy is +/- 1 m and locally +/- 2–6 m. The 25 m EU-DEM v1.1 is used for the terrain model coverage in Sweden (https://land.copernicus.eu/imagery-in-situ/eu-dem/ ). Vertical accuracy is +/- 7 m. 3.1 Nedre Glomsjø hypsometry reconstruction Distinct, continuous shoreline terraces in the valley sides reveal that large glacial lakes once existed in the region. Glacial lake Nedre Glomsjø is reconstructed by mapping shoreline terraces, beach ridges and perched deltas along the former lake shore using airborne LiDAR data. LiDAR point clouds for the entire Nedre Glomsjø palaeobasin were processed into 1 m DEMs and subsequently various hillshade images with different solar azimuths (45°, 315°, 360°), angles (30°, 45°) and terrain exaggeration (3x) to support landform identification. The landforms were mapped and compiled in geodatabases in ESRI ArcMap 10.8.1. Local 3D scene view in ArcGIS Pro aided the 2D mapping and was used for detecting delicate landforms along the Nedre Glomsjø paleoshores. The lake is divided into two primary basins: Østerdalen valley to the west and Rendalen valley to the east (Fig. 1 ). The two valleys are connected by the large canyon Jutulhogget and had a continuous water surface prior to drainage of Nedre Glomsjø. The lowest section of the Barkaldkjølen hills around Jutulhogget have an altitude of ca. 610 m a.s.l. between Rendalen and Østerdalen. We use a conservative estimate of 610 m a.s.l. as the threshold elevation to divide the bathymetry between the two valleys and assume no connection between the valleys below this level for reconstruction of the readily available lake volume. In doing so, we implicitly neglect the progressive downcutting of the canyon during the flood, which would have enabled drainage of a much larger water volume from the western Østerdalen part of the lake. The hypsometry of the glacial lake is developed by calculating the volume between mapped paleo shorelines down to the present-day topography by using the storage-area elevation-volume calculator in HEC-RAS 6.2 (Brunner, 2020 ). We have also constructed the lake hypsometry using a tilted, reconstructed paleo lake surface. The volume difference from this tilted surface considers differential isostatic uplift after deglaciation.  3.2 Ice tunneling simulations We construct a hydraulic model to describe the evolution of the flood from the glacier-dammed lake, propelled by self-enhancing tunnel enlargement. The model consists of three coupled equations, describing the evolution of a circular tunnel cross-section, the discharge in response to the prevailing hydraulic gradient and the mass balance of the lake water, respectively. All symbols are explained in  Table 2 . A water surface elevation of 670 m a.s.l. is assumed as a conservative starting water level based on the average height of mapped paleo shorelines (Høgaas and Longva, 2018 ; this study). The cross-sectional area S of the channel having length l evolves according to Eq.
