We apply the model equations to a profile line along the subglacial flood path, making assumptions about ice thickness of the remnant ice sheet, the endpoint of the tunnel and the temperature of the lake water at the onset of the flood. We assume the lake drained through a subglacial tunnel along the valley-axis between Åkrestrømmen and Elverum ( Fig. 5 ). While paleo shorelines provide good indications of minimum lake extent and thus constrain the start point of the channel, its end point is more uncertain. To explore the realm of possibility, we produced an ensemble of simulations by varying the downstream tunnel outlet location successively in 11 steps of 2.5 km each, the tunnel upstream entrance in four steps as well as varying the lake temperature in five steps between 2 and 6°C. In doing so, each of the 220 simulations is based on a unique combination of channel length, hydraulic gradient and lake temperature. The criterion of probable lake temperature between 2 and 6°C is based on data from proglacial lakes in Patagonia that are deeper than 100 m (Sugiyama et al., 2016 ) and ice-marginal lakes in Alaska, USA (Boyce et al., 2007; Josberger et al., 2006 ). Furthermore Alho et al. (2010)  estimated the water temperature for Glacial Lake Missoula as 5°C. The outlet position is varied between km 70 and km 95 (Fig. 5 ). The position of km 70 is upstream of mapped flood bars. The position of km 77 at Rena is the start of the first erosive scarps attributed to the glacial lake outburst flood. It is more likely that the tunnel exit was between km 85 to km 95, which is the transition zone where scouring is observed on the western valley wall, not just the eastern wall. The underlying terrain profile along the bottom of the subglacial pathway is generated by extracting the lowest elevation along a centerline drawn down the valley for a spacing of 1 km along the flow direction (Fig. 5 ). Average lake elevations (taken from www.norgeskart.no ) are used for the elevations of the three largest lakes along the pathway. For the mean ice thickness along the flood pathway we adopt a value of 500 m. Ice thickness greater than 500 m largely inhibited evolution of the outburst floods. For thick ice, closure rates of the channel cross-section (second term on the right-hand side of Eq. (1)  quickly dominate over the opening rates that are due to dissipation of potential and thermal energy, thereby inhibiting growth of the channel and flood evolution. Correspondingly, for ice thickness > 500 m, floods only developed in scenarios with the largest hydraulic gradients and highest lake temperatures, which are deemed unrealistic. The lake hypsometry input to the ice tunneling model uses the level pool assumption. Therefore, the readily available water volume and hydrostatic pressure at the tunnel entrance could be overestimated. To evaluate whether this assumption may have been violated by the rapid drawdown of the lake level as suggested by the ice tunnel simulation, we conduct a supplementary hydrodynamic simulation of the lake drainage using HEC-RAS v6.2. We used a cell resolution of 250 m, with refinement to 25 m around the Jutulhogget canyon. The Manning’s roughness coefficient is set to n = 0.03 s/m1/3 . The upstream boundary at the lake boundary farthest from the ice tunnel is set to a constant input rate of 100 m3 /s. The downstream boundary, i.e. at the ice tunnel entrance, is defined by the water level from the ice tunneling simulations for the hydrograph that is deemed most representative of the outburst flood.  3.3 Hydrodynamic modeling of the flood path Hydrographs calculated with the ice tunneling simulations are routed down the flood path using a two-dimensional (2D) hydrodynamic model, HEC-RAS version 6.2 (Brunner, 2020 ). HEC-RAS 2D is specifically selected for this study because of its prolific use in the scientific community for modeling floods. It is also selected for its ability to maintain volumetric accuracy despite a coarser modeling grid resolution as discussed below in Section 3.3.2 , which is advantageous when simulating a large model domain. The model is run with the PARDISO (direct) matrix solver. Water stage and velocity are calculated by simultaneously solving the continuity and momentum equations using a semi-implicit, Eulerian-Lagrangian finite-volume method (Brunner, 2020 ). The velocity is assumed constant throughout the vertical water profile for each modeling cell when solving the Saint Venant equations in two dimensions. The clearwater model assumes Newtonian fluid behavior and that the primary resistance to flow is surface friction between the bulk fluid and the terrain. The implications of using a clearwater model are discussed in Section 5.3 . The limitations of using a 2D instead of a three-dimensional (3D) hydrodynamic model are also discussed in Section 5.3 . A hydrodynamic model requires three basic input components: terrain, model geometry and boundary conditions. Additional model parameters are also described below. 3.3.1 Terrain model There is no preprocessing of the terrain model other than stitching the datasets from Norway and Sweden together. We use present-day topography, which is a simplification. There is currently not enough evidence to reconstruct a paleo topography. We assume that the volumetric difference between the paleo topography and the contemporary terrain used in the simulations is minor compared to the overall inundation along the pathway at peak discharge. Isostatic rebound could have a larger contribution to the error associated with using the contemporary terrain model compared to adjusting for pre-flood erosion and deposition. Erosion and deposition are not simulated in the hydrodynamic model; the terrain model remains static during the flood simulations. This means flood deposits are included as part of the terrain during the model. Whether this assumption leads to an overestimation or underestimation of the simulation results will vary from section to section, as it is dependent on when geomorphological processes have happened in relation to the discharge hydrograph. The thickness of flood deposits is small compared to the maximum water depth during peak discharge, so it is unlikely that the peak discharge is underestimated because flood deposits are included in the analysis. The U-valley topography is primarily formed by previous glaciation, and most erosion along the primary flow path would occur during the rising limb of the hydrograph, especially because the falling limb of the hydrograph is abrupt. There have been several large floods in the Glomma watershed since the Nedre Glomsjø GLOF (Engeland et al., 2020 ), but nothing in the same order of magnitude. Is it therefore unlikely that the simulation results overestimate the peak discharge because it assumes that the terrain is otherwise eroded down to modern elevations. The terrain model is not adjusted for bathymetry in lakes, rivers or the sea, such that the average water surface level is used as the terrain level. This approach has a negligible impact on the results, as the maximum peak discharge and/or the initial paleo sea elevation is already tens of meters above the modern-day water surfaces.  3.3.2 Model geometry The model domain extends from Rena to Skagerrak. The cell resolution is 100 × 100 m for 2325 km2  along the primary corridor of the flood path (Fig. 1 ). Finer resolutions are also tested, but 100 × 100 m was adequate for cell size convergence and run time constraints. The cell resolution is 1 × 1 km outside of the primary flow regions and 5 × 5 km in the paleo sea where the flood wave dissipates (Fig. 1 ). This decreases computation time for the 31,140 km2  model domain. Breaklines are used to orient the grid along the flow direction and to delineate flow obstacles. The minimum face length tolerance is set to 20 % to avoid small cell interfaces. In HEC-RAS 2D, the underlying terrain is represented by elevation-volume curves developed for all cells during model pre-processing, unlike most other hydrodynamic models that average the terrain under the cell and simulate with a constant elevation. This allows for larger cell sizes without compromising volumetric accuracy. Detailed cross-sections are constructed along all cell interfaces based on the underlying terrain model to compute conveyance between the cells (Brunner, 2020 ). This means that HEC-RAS 2D uses the underlying terrain model resolution for developing detailed hydraulic property tables used in the simulations even though the model cell resolution is coarser than the terrain model resolution. The streamline patterns for the peak discharge wave are checked for each simulation to ensure model accuracy in the primary flow regions. The calculation timestep is set to two seconds, which satisfies the Courant-Friedrich-Levy (CFL) condition for the chosen spatial resolution and resulting flow velocities.  3.3.3 Boundary conditions The upstream boundary condition is set at the approximate location of the ice margin at Rena (Fig. 1 ), corresponding to km 78 on the ice tunneling profile line (Fig. 5 ). This location is selected because it is immediately downstream of where the Rena valley joins the Østerdalen valley. The valley geometry is relatively homogenous directly downstream the confluence, aiding modeling stability for the upstream boundary condition considering the large flood discharges. Hydrographs from the ice tunneling simulations are used as input to the upstream boundary condition (discharge vs. time). The downstream boundary condition is set towards Skagerrak, farther than 150 km from the paleostage indicators. This ensures that the flood wave has ample room to dissipate in the downstream part of the model before reaching the downstream boundary. The boundary condition is set as a constant water surface elevation equal to the estimated relative sea level during the flood event, which corresponds to ca. 165 m a.s.l. in the current topography around Kongsvinger (Longva, 1994 ). This is referred to as the paleo sea level throughout this article, even though it refers to the contemporary sea level.  3.3.4 Roughness coefficient and eddy viscosity The Manning’s roughness coefficient and coefficients in the turbulence model are typically calibrated to velocity observations. Calibration is not possible for a paleo-GLOF. A Manning’s roughness coefficient of 0.03 s/m1/3  is selected, which is a typical value representative for flow in large rivers (Arcement and Schneider, 1989 ; Barnes, 1967 ; Chow, 1959 ). A sensitivity analysis is performed using a roughness coefficient of 0.05 s/m1/3 , which is a typical upper bound for large rivers. This range is also employed for other GLOF and paleo-GLOF studies, for example 0.3 – 0.5 s/m1/3 , glacial Lake Agassiz (Norris et al., 2021 ); 0.02 – 0.05 s/m1/3 , Himalayas (Westoby et al., 2014, 2015 ); and 0.3 & 0.5 s/m1/3 , Lake Bonneville (Abril-Hernández et al., 2018 ). The model is sensitive to the value used for the roughness coefficient. We therefore test the implication of assuming a constant Manning’s roughness throughout the simulation. The impact of the selected value on the results is discussed in Section 5.4 . Turbulent flow mixing is calculated as a gradient diffusion process, where the eddy viscosity represents the diffusion rate (Brunner, 2020 ). The conservative turbulence model is selected, where the mixing coefficient, D, is considered anisotropic and separated into a longitudinal (DL ) and transverse (DT ) component. The mixing coefficient represents turbulence produced by bottom friction and momentum dispersion (Brunner, 2020; Sanchez, 2022 ). Turbulence generated by sub-grid flows and horizontal shear is represented by the Smagorinsky coefficient, Cs  (Brunner, 2020; Sanchez, 2022 ). The Smagorinsky coefficient represents the fraction of the cell size that corresponds to the length scale of the average eddy diameter. Recommended values for Cs  range from 0.05 to 0.2 for the turbulence model employed in HEC-RAS (Sanchez, 2022 ). It is not possible to calibrate the turbulence model as the velocity distribution from the flood wave is unknown. Therefore, appropriate coefficients are estimated, and the results are compared to simulations with other coefficients and without the turbulence model. Coefficients representing moderate to strong mixing intensity (DL  = 1.0 and DT  = 0.3) are selected (Brunner, 2020 ). Cs  is set at 0.2 for comparison with paleo-GLOF hydrodynamic models (1 km grid, TUFLOW (Alho et al., 2010 ); 500 m grid, TUFLOW (Winsemann et al., 2015 )), even though this term is dependent upon cell resolution and mixing intensity. The impact of the eddy viscosity model on the results is discussed in Section 4.3.3 .  3.3.5 Initial conditions A hot start file is created for the initial conditions for all simulations. A model warm-up was performed using a constant discharge of 50,000 m3 /s over 48 hours in conjunction with the initial paleo seawater level, which is sufficient to establish an initial steady-state water elevation profile and wet the model. See Section 4.2  for more details. The hydrodynamic simulations of the ice tunnel hydrographs are then routed, each superimposed to this initial discharge of 50,000 m3 /s. This approach saves modeling time.   3.4 Geomorphological dataset for model validation Multiple landforms and flood deposits covering multiple spatial scales provide evidence for the Nedre Glomsjø flood pathway (see Section 2.2  and Table 1 ). Paleostage indicators (PSIs) in the form of erosive scarps are found along most of the floodpath between Rena and Magnor, except along the wide valley segments between Elverum and Kongsvinger. As the outburst flood re-enters more narrow valleys south and west of the bifurcation point at Kongsvinger, the erosive scarps reappear. The paleostage indicators do not always decrease in the downstream direction ( Fig. 6 ). Høgaas and Longva (2016)  suggested that these represent the uppermost erosive flood levels and not necessarily maximum flood stage. The paleostage indicators are compared to the maximum water surface elevation for each hydrodynamic simulation. The paleostage indicators are divided into three regions: Rena-Elverum, Kongsvinger-Magnor and west of Kongsvinger (Fig. 6 ). The paleostage indicator dataset between Rena and Elverum is the most reliable, as the valley geometry is relatively straight and wide, and the erosive scarps are more prominent. This section is also upstream of the contemporary marine shoreline. The paleostage indicator datasets around Kongsvinger and Magnor are used for rough comparisons of the maximum water surface elevation in the downstream section of the model. Flow patterns from the flood simulations are compared to flood bars attributed to the outburst floods (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ) and dune fields (Hansen et al., 2020 ). Surficial deposits attributed to the GLOF are mapped in the downstream section south of Elverum (1:50,000 scale, Longva and Østmo, 1986 ; Longva, 2004 ; Longva, 1991 ; Høgaas et al., 2020 ; Bargel, 1988 ) and are compared to the resulting inundation maps. Finally, the locations and elevations of attributed Nedre Glomsjø silt deposits in 15 lakes and bogs as described in Høgaas et al. (2023)  are compared to the maximum water surface elevation.   4 Reconstructed drainage of Nedre Glomsjø 4.1 Hypsometry We have mapped ∼1050 segments of shoreline terraces, ∼150 beach ridges and 12 perched deltas along Nedre Glomsjø. The reconstructed lake paleosurface ( Figs. 1  and 7 A) is based on 952 shoreline elevation readings and the lake’s extent is inferred from the presence of shorelines, which show that the proglacial lake extended far south in Østerdalen and Rendalen and occupied part of the present-day Femunden basin. The shorelines have been raised by differential isostatic uplift after they were formed. Subsequently, their contemporaneous elevations vary from 649 to 690 m a.s.l. depending on the closeness to the uplift center(s). The lake reconstruction shows that Nedre Glomsjø covered roughly 1250 km2 . There are no mapped shorelines beyond the southernmost end of the Femunden basin. Terrain profiles are constructed from the 10 m DEM along the southernmost mapped paleo shorelines, see Fig. 7 B. The outlet elevation in Østerdalen is ca. 320 m a.s.l., while the outlet elevation in Rendalen is ca. 260 m a.s.l. (Fig. 7 B). Liestøl (1956)  assumed the GLOF originated in the Rendalen valley, as the hydrostatic pressure was greater there than in the Østerdalen valley. There is also substantial geomorphological evidence for flow paths exiting Rendalen towards the Glomma valley near Rena (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ). The available lake volume in Rendalen alone is calculated as 65.7 km3 . The lake volume in Rendalen and Østerdalen available for the outburst flood is 103.9 km3  ( Fig. 8 A). This does not include the entrained lake volume in Østerdalen below the Barkaldkjølen hills at 610 m a.s.l. The polynomial representation of volume as a function of lake level h  above the lake bottom (260 m a.s.l.) is superimposed over the hypsometry curve (Fig. 8 B). The derivative dV/dH is readily derived from the polynomial for the ice tunneling simulations.  4.2 Ice tunnel hydrographs The primary set of hydrographs, simulated using the ice tunnel model, is generated by varying the lake temperature and location of the downstream outlet of the tunnel, as described above (Section 3.2 ). Larger peak discharges are attained when the tunnel outlet is closer to the starting point. This is because the shorter pathway creates a larger gradient as seen in  Fig. 9 A for simulations with a lake temperature of 4°C. There is more energy available to quickly develop the flood when the lake water temperature is higher. The diagonal contours in Fig. 9 C-H indicate there is a compensating effect between tunnel length and lake temperature: a higher temperature can compensate for a shallower gradient and vice versa. No floods are generated for situations when the lake temperature is low and the gradient is shallow. No floods at all are generated when the lake temperature is 2°C. Hydrographs with a peak discharge between 1 and 2 ×106  m3  s−1  are developed for lake temperatures between 3 and 5°C. A sensitivity analysis is conducted by varying the inlet position with a fixed outlet at km 75. Larger peak discharges are attained when the tunnel inlet is closer to the outlet, as this provides more energy for flood development (Fig. 9 B). A sensitivity analysis is also run for an ice thickness of +/- 50 m around the assumed Hi = 500 m using a fixed outlet position at km 75. For Hi = 450 m, all scenarios develop a flood (Fig. 9 E). The duration of the target flood peak (0.75 – 2 ×106  m3  s−1 ) gets longer. For Hi = 550 m, a large fraction of the considered situations does not develop a flood (Fig. 9 F). Only the high energy situations (large gradient and high temperature) develop a flood, which then has a very high and narrow peak. The effect of the roughness coefficient on the results is also tested by varying the Manning’s roughness coefficient. These scenarios are conducted for an ice thickness of 500 m and a fixed outlet position at km 75. The simulations using higher roughness (n = 0.05 s/m1/3 ) need more energy to initiate flood development (Fig. 9 G). Conversely, the simulations with a decreased roughness (n = 0.025 s/m1/3 ) produce floods for lower energy scenarios, as there is less energy needed to overcome roughness losses (Fig. 9 H). Six representative hydrographs are chosen for input to the hydrodynamic model based on lake temperature and peak discharge criteria ( Fig. 10  and  Table 3 ). The hydrographs are preprocessed for input in the hydrodynamic model to reduce simulation time, as the hydrographs have relatively low discharges for multiple days until a critical point is reached at which the discharge rapidly increases. Therefore, the input hydrographs are modified such that the starting discharge is at 50,000 m3 /s, which is a consistent threshold before rapidly increasing discharge for all scenarios. While this is a large discharge, it is still substantially below the peak discharge for all scenarios (Fig. 10 ). The starting discharge speeds up processing time and reduces errors in initial saturation of the model. This approach is compared against a simulation with the entire hydrograph for the 1.97 ×106  m3 /s peak discharge scenario. The resulting maximum water surface elevations for these two approaches are the same. The hydrographs from the ice tunneling simulations abruptly terminate when the lake volume above the spillway is emptied. This occurs 3 – 7.5 hours after the peak discharge, see Table 3 . Routing of the flood peak through the downstream model domain requires approximately six hours, so we extend the tunnel hydrograph to avoid prescribing a no-flow condition at the upstream boundary of the hydrodynamic model. This is achieved by following the falling limb of the hydrograph until it reaches a constant background discharge of 50,000 m3 /s (Fig. 10 ). The volumetric error introduced by extending the hydrographs in this manner is ca. 1–3.5 %, depending on the scenario.  4.3 Results from the hydrodynamic simulations The hydrographs are routed with a Manning’s roughness coefficient equal to 0.03 s/m1/3  and 0.05 s/m1/3 . Maps of the water surface elevation, velocity, water depth, etc. are generated for each scenario. A sensitivity analysis is also performed for the boundary conditions, initial flow conditions and turbulence model coefficients. 4.3.1 Inundation pattern All scenarios produce the same general inundation pattern ( Fig. 11 ). In the proximal floodplain, flow is restricted to the Glomma valley, which is 2.0–3.5 km wide north of Elverum. The cross-section along the valley is primarily wide and straight and acts as a large channel for the floodwater. The water surface elevation in this section is strongly controlled by the input hydrograph. The maximum water depth is up to 60–95 m, depending on the input hydrograph. The flood attenuates at Elverum, where opening of the valley and eventual flood routing through the eastern arm by Elverum decreases velocity and leads to an evening out of water stage. The water level is eventually high enough to spill over towards Mjøsa, ca. 8 km downstream / south of Elverum. The valley widens ca. 29 km south of Elverum, causing the channel velocity to decrease substantially by the time the flow reaches Flisa, which is approximately halfway between Elverum and Kongsvinger. The primary flow path is wider than 6 km in this section, with multiple side branches. The valley narrows considerably by Kongsvinger, 45.5 km south of Flisa. A few kilometers north of Kongsvinger, the valley narrows to less than 3 km wide, and the flow bifurcates around a bedrock outcropping to inundate lake Nugguren. At Kongsvinger, the flood splits into a branch that takes a 90-degree bend to the west and a branch that continues southward towards Magnor. The western branch at Kongsvinger narrows to 1.5 km wide, and the southern branch splits into two narrow arms ca. 1 km and 350 m wide. These constrictions cause a backwater effect that impact the maximum water surface elevation in the wide valley section north of Kongsvinger. The western branch has a series of expansions and constrictions along the present-day Glomma River, flowing to the Oslo fjord through multiple pathways. The southern branch widens at Magnor, at the Swedish border, and the flood wave dissipates towards Vänern in Sweden. There is an overall correspondence between mapped surficial deposits attributed to the GLOF downstream of Elverum as described in Section 3.4  and the inundation extent for all simulations. Only one simulation inundates the mapped deposits completely: hydrograph 2.11 x 106  m3 /s with n = 0.05 s/m1/3 .  4.3.2 Comparison to paleostage indicators and surficial deposits The maximum water surface elevation from each simulation is compared to the mapped elevation from the paleostage indicators determined from erosive scarps. The results for Rena-Elverum for n = 0.03 s/m1/3 and n = 0.05 s/m1/3  are shown in  Fig. 12 . Simulations are interpreted as valid reconstructions of the GLOF if the maximum simulated water surface elevation is at least as high as the paleostage indicator elevations (points to the upper left of the parity line in Fig. 12 ). The results show that:• For simulations with n = 0.03 s/m1/3 , the peak discharge needs to be > 2 x 106  m3 /s to produce water levels above the paleostage indicators for the Rena-Elverum dataset. The peak discharge needs to be > 1.6 x 106  m3 /s to produce water levels above the paleostage indicators for the Kongsvinger datasets.  • For simulations with n = 0.05 s/m1/3 , the peak discharge needs to be > 1.5 x 106  m3 /s to produce water levels above the paleostage indicators for the Rena-Elverum dataset. This is also the case for the Kongsvinger paleostage indicator datasets.    The maximum water surface elevations are also compared to the elevation of Romerike silt layer deposits in 15 lakes or bogs mapped by Høgaas et al. (2023) .• A peak discharge of > 1.5 x 106  m3 /s is required for overall correspondence to the field results (scenarios with n = 0.03 s/m1/3 ). Peak discharge must be > 1.3 x 106  m3 /s for overall correspondence to the field results for scenarios with n = 0.05 s/m1/3 .  • The simulation with a peak discharge of 2.11 ×106  m3 /s and n = 0.05 s/m1/3  is the scenario that has the best correspondence to the results from Høgaas et al. (2023) .  • Eight of the lakes or bogs have results that correspond very well to most of the simulations.  • Gørtjenn and Finnmyra, two basins that did not have evidence of a silt layer, are not inundated in the simulations (positive result).    Overall, the simulations have maximum water surface elevations ca. 5 – 50 m above the observed silt layer elevation. Lower energy regimes (lower velocity) are required to allow the silt to settle out of suspension. An overall analysis of the 1.97 ×106  m3 /s with n = 0.03 s/m1/3  simulation shows that the lakes/bogs are located in backwater areas or areas of generally lower velocity even during the peak discharge time interval, with one exception (Nordsetttjennet). Deposition of the silt layer could have occurred during the tail end of the hydrograph well after the initial peak discharge wave washed through. This is also the lake that has the largest difference between the silt layer elevation and the maximum water surface elevation, so there is ample time for the water level to decrease and the flow regime to be lowered while still maintaining inundation of the lake.  4.3.3 Sensitivity analysis of the hydrodynamic model The hydrodynamic simulation with the 1.97 x 106  m3 /s hydrograph and n = 0.03 s/m1/3  is used as a base scenario by which to compare the sensitivity analysis. 4.3.3.1 Upstream boundary condition The first few kilometers of the model are also impacted by the large discharge fluctuations from the hydrographs, such that the water surface elevation along the first ca. four kilometers from the upstream model boundary have more uncertainty. Therefore, there is more emphasis placed on matching the water surface elevation to the paleostage indicators that are < 275 m a.s.l. in elevation, which are not impacted by the upstream boundary condition. The upstream boundary is kept at a constant location for better comparison of the results, even though the simulated hydrographs represent different starting points for the flood wave. We justify this by noting that there is very little attenuation in the flood wave along the first 25 km of the flood path. This also provides more stable results for a majority of the valley upstream Elverum. The upstream boundary condition is adjusted for hydrograph 1.76 x 106  m3 /s, which has its exit point furthest downstream, to assess the impact on the resulting flood wave in the stretch between Rena and Elverum. The upstream boundary is moved to the 95 km profile as shown on Fig. 5 B. All other model parameters are kept constant. The results show:• The first ca. 2 km are impacted by the large discharge fluctuations from the hydrographs, such that the difference in the water surface elevation is locally more than a few meters. This section is impacted by the upstream boundary condition, such that only paleostage indicators < 260 m a.s.l. can be used for comparison to the maximum water surface elevation if this model geometry were to be used for primary analysis. The upstream boundary is also affected by being placed directly upstream a bend in the valley.  • From 2 to ca. 5 km downstream of the model boundary, the difference in the maximum water surface elevation is < 2 m and primarily < 1 m.  • From Elverum and throughout the remainder of the downstream model domain, the difference in the maximum water surface elevation is negligible (less than 0.20 m).    We conclude that using the same model boundary for all hydrographs is an adequate assumption at this stage in the research.  4.3.3.2 Downstream boundary condition and paleo sea level The location of the downstream boundary condition is tested by extending the boundary location 100 km downstream in all directions. The scenario with 1.97 x 106  m3 /s and n = 0.03 s/m1/3  is simulated for comparison. The difference in the maximum water surface elevation is less than 1 m and primarily 10–20 cm. There is no impact on the maximum water surface elevation for the paleostage indicators between Rena and Elverum. As an additional sensitivity analysis, scenario 1.97 x 106  m3 /s using n = 0.03 s/m1/3  is simulated for a paleo sea level of 160 m a.s.l. This has negligible impact on the maximum water surface elevation for the paleostage indicators between Rena and Elverum. The maximum water surface elevation for the paleostage indicators around Kongsvinger were ca. 1 m lower than the base scenario. The maximum water surface elevation at the most downstream paleostage indicators past Magnor was 5 m lower than the base scenario.  4.3.3.3 Initial flow conditions A simulation is run for the 1.97 x 106  m3 /s hydrograph without wetting the model (only initial sea level) to evaluate the accuracy of the warm-up approach. This had no impact on the maximum water surface elevation.  4.3.3.4 Turbulence model coefficients The coefficients for the turbulence model are in the upper bounds. Two models are run for comparison to the base scenario: turbulence model with coefficient values in the lower bound (DL  = 0.3, DT  = 0.1 and Cs  = 0.05) and without the turbulence model. Both cases introduce numerical instabilities. The difference in maximum water surface elevation from the base scenario varies from - 80 cm to + 70 cm, which is negligible compared to other uncertainty elements and considering the water depth. If sediment transport is modeled, the turbulence model becomes more important for simulating horizontal movement. The primary flood path is relatively straight and wide, and it is concluded that the eddy viscosity model in HEC-RAS has minimal impact on the results.     5 Discussion Cataclysmic megafloods, such as the Nedre Glomsjø glacial lake outburst flood, are substantially larger than floods observed today and lack contemporary observations. No floods of this scale have been observed and measured, including the turbulent regimes and flow composition as discussed in Miyamoto et al. (2006) . Additionally, compounding assumptions and equifinality contribute to the difficulty in reconstructing paleo glacial lake outburst floods (Wells et al., 2022 ). In this section, we highlight key assumptions made for our reconstruction and discuss their potential impact on the results. We further present our interpretation of the sequence of events, unifying hydrodynamic modeling and geomorphological evidence. 5.1 Lake hypsometry and drainage The high density of paleo shorelines, beach ridges and perched deltas provides an excellent constraint on the horizontal extent of the paleolake and its related volume available for drainage. The reconstructed lake hypsometry is likely a conservative estimate of the available lake volume, as it does not consider erosion of the Jutulhogget canyon down to its present altitude (approx. 450 m a.s.l.), thereby leaving a larger dead volume in Østerdalen, the western valley, that likely would have contributed to fueling the flood. In our model, we have used 610 m a.s.l. as the minimum level for drainage across Barkaldkjølen. A lower lying glacial lake shoreline (Berthling and Sollid, 1999 ) may imply that the canyon was eroded down to ∼570 m a.s.l., and thus that a larger water volume in Østerdalen was available for drainage. A threshold of 570 m a.s.l. as opposed to the threshold of 610 m a.s.l. used in this study would add 14.8 km3  to the lake volume that is readily available for drainage, resulting in a total lake volume of ca. 119 km3 . The hydrograph for the scenario with a peak discharge of 1.97 x 106  m3 /s is hydrodynamically routed in the glacial lake as described in Section 3.2 . This is done to test whether the lake is able to transport the necessary water volume to the lake outlet in concordance with the hydrostatic pressure necessary for the hydrograph development in the ice tunnel model. The hydrodynamic model results show that it is possible to drain the lake with this scenario without violating the level pool assumption. Very high velocities >> 30 m/s are reached in the Jutulhogget canyon and likely have caused erosion of the >100 m deep canyon. There are also high velocities at the ice tunnel entrance / downstream boundary of the lake in the Rendalen valley. Additional hydrodynamic simulations of the hydraulic gradient in the lake body during drainage remain a topic for future research.  5.2 Subglacial tunnel and implications for the ice sheet Given the existing uncertainties with respect to ice thickness and trajectory of the ice tunnel, we focus on the first-order controls and use a lumped-element approach to represent the tunnel through which the water escaped from the lake. This lumped approach assumes an average ice thickness over the entire tunnel pathway, which is why the ice thickness has a substantial impact on the results. In reality the ice sheet would be thinner towards the glacial lake and potentially thicker downstream; this would have a reducing effect on the hydraulic gradient. Lake Nedre Glomsjø is 410 m deep when the starting water level is 670 m a.s.l. An ice thickness of 500 m equates to an overburden pressure equivalent to a hydraulic head of 450 m, which means the difference in hydraulic head is only 40 m and a subglacial tunnel cannot close fast enough to inhibit drainage once it has been initialized. When the ice thickness is assumed to be 550 m, the difference in hydraulic head is 85 m. This scenario requires substantially more energy to counteract the pressure closing the subglacial tunnel. Conversely, an ice thickness of 450 m has a hydraulic head that is almost equal to the hydraulic head of the lake at the starting time, and a subglacial tunnel cannot be closed from ice pressure. The triggering mechanism for catastrophic draining of the lake is uncertain. Our current hypothesis is that a network of subglacial tunnels existed under the ice sheet, as the ice sheet probably had been climatically “dead” for one thousand years prior to the drainage event, i.e. that most of the ice body was situated below the equilibrium line after the Younger Dryas-Holocene transition (Hughes et al., 2016 ). This theory is supported by the extreme Early Holocene ice sheet thinning rates suggested by Goehring et al. (2008)  and Romundset et al. (2023) . Due to the amount of meltwater that must have been generated by the thinning, one would expect the existence of an active drainage network at the base of the ice. We also note that the ca. 310 m deep lake Storsjøen has its upstream boundary at the approximate location of the southernmost Nedre Glomsjø shorelines (Fig. 5 ). The lake bathymetry in Storsjøen is thereby ca. 310 m deeper than the lowest point along the cross-section at the lake outlet in Rendalen (Fig. 7 B). Lake Storsjøen is situated in an overdeepened basin and we speculate that it may have held a subglacial water reservoir at the end of the last Ice Age. This is consistent with the notion of a pre-existing drainage network that may have initiated the flood. When the water level in the lake reached a critical height, it produced the hydraulic gradient necessary for tunnel initiation and subsequent enlargement from the friction produced by the large volumes. Our results show that increasing the lake temperature aids tunnel formation, and even a 1°C increase can be the tipping point for certain scenarios. The glacial lake was formed during the retreat of the ice sheet, and it is possible that the lake would slowly increase in temperature over time. The subglacial tunnel would initially be composed of a network of smaller tunnels, not a singular large tunnel as assumed in the ice tunnel model. The maximum total tunnel cross-sectional area from the ice tunneling simulations varies from ca. 40,000 – 72,000 m2  (Table 2 ). This corresponds to a ca. 100 – 150 m radius for a circular cross-section and a ca. 160–210 m radius for a semi-circular cross-section. With the given peak discharge, this corresponds to peak flow velocities of 27–30 m/s. An analysis of three cross-sections directly upstream of Rena / upstream of the hydrodynamic simulation show that there is adequate space for the flood area just north of valley marker km 60 (Fig. 5 ). Just before the valley bends to the west (around km 65), there is less space to accommodate the maximum cross-sectional area and a smaller channel would branch off to the north. Directly upstream of the confluence at Østerdalen, the terrain to the north / northwest would have to be inundated to achieve a cross-sectional area of 70,000 m2 . This is consistent with mapped erosional and depositional features from Høgaas and Longva (2016) . It is thereby possible that the flood water spread out in multiple directions. The large tunnel area implies that the ice sheet could be unstable after such an event. It seems unlikely that this event would lead to a total collapse of an ice sheet that is over 50 km long (in linear flow direction) and 0.5 km thick. There could have been a local collapse of the ice sheet at the southern end / outlet of the ice tunnel. The location of the transition from orifice flow in the ice tunnel to open channel flow is uncertain. Høgaas and Longva (2016)  inferred the position of the southern ice margin in Østerdalen from mapping of GLOF-related scarps along the valley. The premise was solely based on the absence of high lying erosive scarps in an outer valley bend, however, despite mapping different flood-related bedforms north of this point. The presence of a large number of ice-block obstacle marks at Rena (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ) implies a subaerial environment and, if accepting the proposed ice margin position, may indicate a ∼20-km-large frontal ice sheet collapse during the event when considering an initial ice tunnel outlet located near Elverum. Also, the numerous traces of large icebergs arrested ∼140 km downstream at Romerike and Magnor during the event (Høgaas and Longva, 2016; Longva, 1994; Longva and Bakkejord, 1990; Longva and Thoresen, 1991 ), and the increased ice-rafted debris content tentatively tied to the event in a marine core ∼300 km downstream (Gyllencreutz, 2005 ), are clear indications of an ice sheet collapse. This has implications for modern environmental change, where the number and volume of ice-dammed glacial lakes increases as ice masses around the world shrink (Shugar et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ). An ice-dammed GLOF can impact the overall competence of an ice mass, and the rapidity and magnitude of the GLOF can accelerate other environmental changes locally and regionally.  5.3 Fluid composition and hydrodynamic model selection 5.3.1 Fluid composition The flood event is simulated as a clearwater model assuming Newtonian fluid behavior. It is unlikely that the fluid would behave as a hyper-concentrated flow or debris flow because of the gentle valley gradient and the large volume of freshwater in the lake. The valley geometry is relatively straight and U-shaped and has an average gradient of ca. 0.8 m/km between Rena and Elverum and ca. 0.3 m/km between Elverum and Kongsvinger. A lake volume of ca. 104 km3  emptying within a few days would be primarily composed of freshwater during the peak discharge. Flow would be highly turbulent in some regions, especially at the outlet of the ice tunnel. Fine sediments, large boulders, ice chunks, etc. would have been transported with the outburst flood wave. Therefore, stratified flow might have developed locally, but we assume that the clearwater model satisfactorily predicts the possible range of peak discharge given the many uncertainties in the reconstruction process.  5.3.2 Hydrodynamic model selection A two-dimensional (2D) model is selected for this study. The primary difference between a 2D and three-dimensional (3D) hydrodynamic model is the averaging of the vertical velocity component in the 2D model. Features such as helicoidal currents and stratified flow cannot be modeled with the depth-average flow velocities in a 2D model. Parameters such as turbulence and bed shear stress would be more accurately simulated by a 3D hydrodynamic model, but the large spatial domain of this study would result in excessive simulation times. The flood flow path has no sharp bends, except for the flow bifurcation at Kongsvinger and downstream of Elverum at high stages. The water depth is in the tens of meters for most of the flood inundation extent. Therefore, the inability of a 2D model to accurately model secondary currents should result in a negligible impact on overall calculation of maximum water surface elevations. A 3D model can be used in future studies for limited segments of the flood flow path using the discharges in this research as a baseline. Focus should be given to areas with ample geomorphological evidence for the flood and where there can be hydraulic features that could benefit from detailed modeling in 3D. Examples include the outlet of the ice tunnel / upstream segment of the flood path downstream of Rena and the flow bifurcation at Kongsvinger. 3D modeling would be most beneficial when coupled with sediment transport models and reconstruction of an estimated paleo topography, but this would introduce additional uncertainty that would not simply be resolved with a 3D model. The goal of this study is to constrain the probable range of maximum discharge, and therefore a 2D model is sufficient for this objective.   5.4 Manning’s roughness coefficient The primary resistance to flow is the friction between the fluid and the solid boundary in a clearwater model. This is represented by the Manning’s roughness coefficient, n , which was originally developed for one-dimensional, stationary flow and for smaller discharges than modeled for this GLOF. An increase in the manning’s roughness coefficient increases the water depth and decreases the velocity. Many assumptions inherent with the use of a constant n  are discussed in Smith et al. (2007) . Additional factors such as sediment transport, which consumes energy and thereby increases the apparent roughness to simulate the corresponding head loss, are also included in the roughness coefficient (Chow, 1959 ). The roughness coefficient represents not only the surface-bed roughness and flow obstacles with their resulting flow resistance, but also turbulence of the bulk fluid. The roughness coefficient varies as a function of flow depth, changing substrate composition, etc. but it is typically modeled as a constant value. A constant value is appropriate for a paleo-GLOF, as a variable roughness coefficient would introduce more complexity than necessary. A constant manning’s coefficient for the entire area allows for easier assessment of its impact on the results. The selection of the manning’s roughness coefficient is highly dependent upon the modeler and is not an exact value that can be calibrated without discharge vs. stage data from the actual flood event. Some paleo-GLOF studies run a suite of simulations for a range of manning’s values without varying other parameters and select the model with the lowest n  value that still produces a water surface elevation above the geomorphological evidence they are trying to match. This assumes a priori  validation of the input hydrograph, the other primary parameter impacting results, and can lead to selection of larger n values, for example n = 0.1 s/m1/3  for the Missoula floods (Alho et al., 2010; Miyamoto et al., 2006, 2007 ) and n = 0.1 s/m1/3  or n = 0.07 s/m1/3  for paleo-GLOFs in north-central Europe (Winsemann et al. (2015)  and Lang et al. (2019) , respectively). Most of these studies only have rough estimates of the available lake volume prior to discharge, adding additional uncertainty. The difference in maximum water surface elevation for scenarios with n = 0.03 vs. 0.05 s/m1/3  shows:• Ca. 15–20 m higher maximum water surface elevations for scenarios with n = 0.05 s/m1/3  in the upper section of the model.  • This decreases to ca. 5–10 m higher maximum water surface elevations for scenarios with n = 0.05 s/m1/3  towards Elverum.  • The scenarios with n = 0.05 s/m1/3  have maximum water surface elevations that are > 0–3 m higher downstream Kongsvinger towards Oslo.  • The scenarios with n = 0.05 s/m1/3  have maximum water surface elevations that are 1–7 m higher downstream Kongsvinger towards Magnor.    For comparison, the difference in the maximum water surface elevation from the difference in peak discharge (comparing the hydrographs 1.12 ×106  m3 /s and 2.11 x 106  m3 /s with n = 0.03 s/m1/3 ) is 15–20 m in the upper section and ca. 10–15 m towards Elverum. The difference is 1–15 m downstream of Kongsvinger. As an additional control on our Manning’s value selection, we have compared model results with critical velocity at point locations in Section 5.5 .  5.5 Critical velocity at point locations Velocity is negatively correlated to the roughness coefficient. Maximum velocity maps are compared to block diameter from deposits attributed to the outburst flood at Strandbygda ca. 3.5 km upstream of Elverum, where boulders greater than 2 m in diameter are observed in a coarse matrix (Fig. 4 A & 4B). The maximum water depth at this location needs to be at least 60 m above the valley floor to correspond with upstream paleostage indicators. The critical velocity needed to initiate transport for a 2 m diameter block is ca. 15 m/s for a water depth of 60 m according to Shields law (van Rijn, 1984; Shields, 1936 ). An increase in maximum water depth results in an increase in critical velocity. The minimum peak discharge required to produce an average velocity greater than 15 m/s for simulations with n = 0.03 s/m1/3  is 1.30 x 106  m3 /s. The simulations with n = 0.05 s/m1/3  fail to produce velocity values above 15 m/s. The scenario with the peak discharge of 2.11 x 106  m3 /s has a maximum velocity of ca. 14 m/s at this location, but the maximum water depth is greater than 70 m. Therefore 14 m/s is still below the critical velocity. Critical velocity is also determined for block deposits at Flomyra, ca. 4.5 km downstream of Elverum. Multiple large blocks with a minimum diameter av 1.5 m are observed at this location. The paleostage indicator that is near this location dictates that the maximum water surface elevation needs to be 30–40 m at Flomyra, depending on the measuring point. This would require a critical velocity of ca. 12–13 m/s to move the blocks. All scenarios fulfill this requirement within the vicinity of the block deposits. The conclusion based on this rough analysis is that the simulations with n = 0.03 s/m1/3  provide more appropriate critical velocity values based on the analysis at Strandbygda. In other words, n = 0.03 s/m1/3  appears to be a more appropriate roughness coefficient for this study than n = 0.05 s/m1/3 . Still, this is based on the assumption of a constant, depth-averaged Manning’s value, as discussed in Section 5.4 .  5.6 Probable peak discharge Given the assumptions in this paper, the peak discharge from the Nedre Glomsjø lake outburst flood lies between 1.5 ×106  m3 /s and 2.0 x 106  m3 /s. A ca. 2.0 x 106  m3 /s peak discharge is from the scenario that satisfies the most constraints provided by the geomorphological evidence. The rationale behind this peak discharge is discussed in the following two sections. Section 5.6.1  describes the results in the context of the geomorphological evidence that is outside of the bounds of the paleo sea and therefore less impacted by uncertainties associated with the paleo sea level. Section 5.6.2  describes the results that are directly impacted by the paleo sea level. Flow patterns are compared to attributed flood bar deposits (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ) and dune ridges where present for the following localities presented in Fig. 11 :• Rena-Elverum  • Pendant bar south of Elverum  • Drainage towards lake Mjøsa  • Downstream of Kongsvinger    As shown in Section 4.3.2 , there is an overall correspondence to mapped silt layer deposits in (or lack of deposits) in 15 lakes or bogs in the lower section of the model. Analysis of lake sediments in additional locations would help constrain the results. For example, Lake Midtre Rytjennet, ca. 11 km north of Kongsvinger, is inundated when the peak discharge is > 2 x 106  m3 /s with n = 0.03 s/m1/3  or 1.97 x 106  m3 /s with n = 0.05 s/m1/3 . The presence of GLOF sediment here would mean the peak discharge is truly closer to 2 x 106  m3 /s than 1.5 ×106  m3 /s. 5.6.1 Upper section of the flood pathway above the paleo sea level The upper section of the flood pathway is not impacted by the paleo sea level. The valley floor is ca. 40 m above the paleo sea level at the model boundary (Rena) and ca. 10–20 m above the paleo sea level at Elverum. The paleostage indicators are clearly marked in the terrain, and the valley geometry is wide and straight. The primary source of uncertainty in this upper section is the location of the ice tunnel outlet. The peak discharge of the hydrograph has a substantial impact on the maximum water surface elevations as discussed in Section 5.4 . Velocity at peak discharge and streamlines are compared to paleostage indicators, flood bars and dune fields in  Fig. 13  and described below. Rena-Elverum (  Fig. 13 A)   The valley north of Elverum is relatively straight with a U-shaped cross-section. There is therefore very little flood attenuation in the first 25 km of the model. Five longitudinal flood bars are mapped between Rena and Elverum (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ). The flood bars are streamlined with multiple kettle holes. A bedrock knoll projects from the eastern wall of the valley ca. 11 km upstream Elverum. A ca. 3 km-long, narrow pendant bar is located on the leeside of this protrusion immediately downstream of a valley bend (Fig. 3 C). The location of this bar is consistent with simulated hydrodynamics. A flood bar with uncertain delineation is located downstream of the pendant bar on the western side of the valley. The valley begins to widen at this location, resulting in a decrease in stream power. There are multiple wave-like features on the pendant bar, and crescentic-shaped features on the surface of the flood bar located just downstream (Høgaas and Longva, 2016 ). The rapid decrease in flood stage probably preserved these bars. The Strandabygda sections with the boulder sets (Fig. 4 A, B) are located just north of Elverum. They are probably a part of an expansion bar that was deposited due to the broadening of the valley. Pendant bar south of Elverum (  Fig. 13 B)   A large obstacle divides the flow path ca. 5 km south of Elverum, resulting in an increase in velocity. A back eddy is developed downstream of the obstacle, providing conditions for sediment deposition. A smaller topographic rise in the western arm around the obstacle also results in a section of decreased velocity on the leeward side. Both observations are consistent with mapped pendant bars from Høgaas and Longva (2016) . This flow pattern is observed in all simulations. Sections in the largest pendant bar reveal stratified, yet poorly sorted material with steeply dipping foresets (Fig. 4 C) and a large number of angular fragments. The latter may indicate high energy and internal smashing of clasts (Carling and Fan, 2020 ), which is supported by the high modelled velocity in the channel narrowing just north of the pendant bars. Drainage towards present-day lake Mjøsa (  Fig. 13 C)   The simulations show that the flood bifurcated ca. 9 km south of Elverum, with a small percentage of the discharge draining towards lake Mjøsa to the west. This is consistent with field observations. Peak discharge measured at the cross-section X-X’ in Fig. 11  is ca. 145,000 m3 /s (7.4 % of peak discharge) for the scenario with 1.97 x 106  m3 /s and n = 0.03 s/m1/3 . The variation is from ca. 11,300 m3 /s for 1.12 x 106  m3 /s to 177,000 m3 /s for 2.11 ×106  m3 /s (n = 0.03 s/m1/3 ). This corresponds to 1 % - 8.4 % of total peak discharge exiting the ice tunnel. The peak discharge is ca. 200,000 m3 /s for 1.97 ×106  m3 /s with n = 0.05 s/m1/3 . The discharge is greater towards lake Mjøsa when the maximum water elevation is higher in the primary flood pathway. A paleostage indicator is located at 230 m a.s.l. (Figs. 6 and 11 ). Scenario 1.52 x 106  m3 /s with n = 0.03 s/m1/3  has a maximum water surface elevation at 231 m a.s.l., but scenario 1.30 x 106  m3 /s reaches 228 m a.s.l. when measured at the inundation edge nearest the paleostage indicators. All simulations (> 1 x 106  m3 /s) with a mannings roughness coefficient of 0.05 s/m1/3  result in a maximum water surface elevation greater than 230 m a.s.l. A train of dune-like features are present ca. 18 km downstream from the bifurcation point, east of present-day lake Mjøsa (Fig. 3 D). The dunes are seen on a relatively even plain just west of where the topography suddenly drops 30–40 m, which may have led to decreased flow competence and subsequent deposition. Rapid deposition may also have been facilitated by the flood waters propagating into a marine environment here, as the contemporary sea level probably was situated around 160–170 m a.s.l. at the time. A canyon just east of the dune features was probably also formed during the event. The dune field's orientations correspond to the streamflow pattern for all simulations and deviate entirely from the orientation of the adjacent ribbed moraines. We have not found morphological traces of the outburst flood west of these features.  5.6.2 Lower section of the flood pathway affected by the paleo sea level The primary source of uncertainty in the lower section of the flood pathway is the relative sea level during the Nedre Glomsjø flood. The relative sea level is assumed to be ca. 170 m a.s.l. as described in Section 3.3.3 . There is an overall correspondence between the geomorphological evidence and the maximum water surface elevations and related inundation extent with the peak discharges simulated in this study. The contemporary sea level at Øyeren, ca. 24 km east of Oslo, was closer to 135 m a.s.l. such that the peak discharge would need to be greater than 2 x 106  m3 /s to have the same inundation in the lowest reaches of the model. It is possible that many of the narrower flow channels in the current topography between Kongsvinger and Oslo had reduced flow capacity during the Nedre Glomsjø flood (more erosion since the Early Holocene), forcing more water through the main flow arteries such as the Glomma valley and Øyeren. The initial relative sea level and its impact on the results is a topic for future research. The overall conclusion is that a peak discharge of 2 x 106  m3 /s is a conservative estimate when considering the lower section of the flood pathway. Velocity at peak discharge and streamlines are compared to paleostage indicators and flood bars in  Fig. 14  and described below. Flow bifurcation at Kongsvinger (  Fig. 14 A)   The flow path spilts at Kongsvinger, with a western branch making a ca. 90-degree bend from the mainstem and leading the flood wave out towards Romerike and the Oslo fjord. The other arm continues south towards Magnor and the Swedish border. The split in discharge is approximately 60 % / 40 % through the western and southern branches, respectively. The hydraulic gradient is greater in the western branch at this location, and higher channel velocities are reached. The maximum water surface elevations are also compared to the elevation of Romerike silt layer deposits in 15 lakes or bogs mapped by Høgaas et al. (2023)  and is discussed in Section 4.3.2 . South of Kongsvinger: Vrangselva and towards Magnor (  Fig. 14 B and C)   The southern branch towards Magnor is composed of two parallel valleys. The western valley in Fig. 14 B is covered in coarse sediments of glaciofluvial origin according to the 1: 50,000 Quaternary deposit map (Bargel, 1988 ). The gravely deposits at the downstream end of the western valley have a high concentration of boulders and are locally greater than 8 m thick (Bargel, 1988 ). The high velocities reached during peak discharge in this valley should leave multiple erosive scarps. This has not previously been mapped, but analysis of a 1 m DEM shows erosive scarps at ca. 200 – 225 m a.s.l. along this valley, corresponding with the elevation of paleostage indicators in the eastern valley. Farther south towards Magnor, the paleostage indicators correspond with the velocity patterns.   5.7 Large paleofloods and recommendations for future studies Integration of estimated discharges from paleoflood events can improve estimates of floods with low annual exceedance probabilities (Baker, 1987 ). Paleoflood data can be used to define the probable maximum flood, which is crucial for risk assessment for critical infrastructure such as dams and nuclear facilities (Benito and O’Connor, 2013; Harden et al., 2021 ). Paleoflood events can be correlated with estimated environmental change as recorded in geological and biological records, aiding future risk assessment as described in Harden et al. (2021) . Paleofloods assist in determining how climate variability can affect flood frequency, as demonstrated in an analysis of Norway’s largest river, Glomma (Engeland et al., 2020 ). Ice-dammed glacial lakes can have reoccurring floods, as the drainage is often subglacial, which can self-heal when the hydrostatic pressure decreases (Zhang et al., 2024 ). The methodology described in this paper can be applied to contemporary ice-dammed glacial lakes to better predict variability and frequency of GLOFs in a changing climate. It is imperative to emphasize that there is a large amount of uncertainty in estimation of peak discharge from megafloods. This is especially true for floods that occurred during the Middle Pleistocene, for example, where the topography can have changed drastically since the flood event. All megaflood studies will inherently have a large amount of uncertainty because no one has collected data from a megaflood and therefore there are no calibrated models or studies. Therefore the vast majority of inputs to the model are estimated based on extrapolation of modern-day flood processes. The lake volume and breaching mechanism are the two most important parameters for reconstruction of the discharge hydrograph for glacial lake outburst floods. The discharge hydrograph is then used to compare geomorphological evidence downstream. This is typically composed of a sparse dataset lacking in variety of evidence – over various scales and spatially. The two largest documented glacial lake outburst floods in the world are from the glacial Lake Missoula in the northwestern USA and the Kuray-Chuja lake in Altai, Russia. Both locations most likely had multiple lake drainages during the Late Pleistocene. Determination of peak discharge is a product of paleo shorelines, breach mechanism modeling and comparison of geomorphological evidence, leading to current estimates of 17 x 106  m3 /s for lake Missoula (Alho et al., 2010 ; Denlinger and O’Connell, 2010 ; O’Connor et al., 2020 ) and 10.5 ×106  m3 /s for the Kuray-Chuja lake basin (Bohorquez et al., 2019 ); building on work by Carling et al. (2010)  and Herget (2005) . The northwestern outlet of glacial Lake Agassiz, Canada, has been estimated with independent 0D gradual-incision modeling and 1D step-backwater modeling to have peak discharges of 1.8 – 2.5 x 106  m3 /s (Norris et al., 2021 ). However, the peak discharges in the study suffer from a lack of preserved channel cross-sectional profiles and paleostage indicators. Isostasy was included in the reconstruction of the lake bathymetry, but the lake volume was deduced from model results. An overview of selected paleofloods from the Late Pleistocene through the Early Holocene is presented in  Table 4 . We have not included outburst floods that were a result of subglacial volcanic activity. Many peak discharge estimates of GLOFs have been derived from empirical equations that relate lake volume to peak discharge (Clague and Mathews, 1973 ) or back-calculations of discharge from paleo-competence. Paleolake volume – and volume available upon potential ice-dam collapse – is a recurring, but pivotal issue when reconstructing paleofloods. Older studies and studies carried out in remote places have typically relied on aerial photographs, poor maps or terrain models to map paleolakes and calculate lake volumes (Benito and Thorndycraft, 2020; Herget, 2005; Holmsen, 1915; Jansson, 2003; Pardee, 1942 ). This may lead to large volumetric uncertainties. It may also be difficult to reconstruct paleotopography and accurately locate potential damming ice-margins and thus estimate the paleolakes’ extents. The lack of unambiguous evidence of maximum flood level when reconstructing paleofloods is problematic and may lead to the use of (often ambiguous) traces that tend to overestimate flood magnitudes (Carrivick et al., 2013 ). The use of bedforms as minimum floodstage indicators (Margold et al., 2018 ) on the other hand, may grossly underestimate flood magnitude. There is a whole range of features that have been used to infer maximum wash limits (Alho et al., 2005; Baker, 1973; Carrivick et al., 2004; O’Connor, 1993 ), but it is often difficult to interpret how well the landforms we can trace today actually reflect maximum paleoflow. The need of a robust geological dataset when estimating paleostage indicators was underlined by Jarrett and England (2002) . This was also highlighted by Høgaas et al. (2023) , who demonstrated that the Romerike Silt Bed related to the Nedre Glomsjø outburst flood is found significantly higher in the terrain than uppermost erosive scarps in the same area. Accordingly, assumed maximum paleoflow should preferably not be based on a few landforms alone, but rather a series of independent indications, both sedimentary and morphological. The use of continuous sediment records and different landforms to calibrate and reinforce the hydrodynamic reconstruction of the outburst flood, as carried out in this study, drastically reduces the uncertainty related to the flood magnitude and peak discharge estimates. The vast majority of megaflood and paleoflood studies are based on few constraints and one or two components of the process chain, however. As the model inputs often are estimates based on extrapolation of modern-day flood processes, study outcomes will inherently have a large amount of uncertainty, which the studies often fail to communicate. In order to provide trustworthy results, we accordingly believe that there is a need to include various geological traces to further minimize the number of unknowns prior to hydrodynamic reconstructions, in addition to assessing the various system components along the entire flood path.   6 Conclusion The methodology presented in this paper shows how uncertainties of estimated peak discharge of a (paleo) glacial lake outburst flood can be reduced by considering different geological constraints in a coherently coupled multi-component modeling framework. Our flood marker dataset comprises several landforms and flood traces at multiple scales, which adds to the robustness of our interpretation. The volume and quality of the flood marker dataset and its application throughout the entire flood domain are unique amongst paleoflood / megaflood simulations.• Nedre Glomsjø drained in a catastrophic mega-flood. The peak discharge must have been at least 1.5 x 106  m3 /s and probably closer to 2.0 ×106  m3 /s, exceeding previous estimates by an order of magnitude.  • The lake volume readily available for drainage is estimated to have been 103.9 km3 . The extent of the glacial lake is defined by ∼1050 segments of shoreline terraces and the paleo lake surface is reconstructed based on 952 shoreline elevation readings.  • A self-enhancing ice-tunnel model is used to create a suite of possible hydrographs that satisfy criteria for the lake drainage. The hydrograph form is consistent with glacial lake outburst floods, with a steep increase and decrease in discharge around the peak. The ice-tunnel cross-sectional area is estimated to have been greater than 50,000 m2 . Our ice drainage reconstruction also provides a constraint on average ice thickness for the ice dam, with ice thicker than 550 m effectively inhibiting development of the outburst. This has implications for understanding the demise of continental ice sheets.  • Routing of hydrographs with peak discharges of 1.5–2.0 ×106  m3 /s through the hydrodynamic model downstream of the ice sheet provides results that are consistent with various geological traces and critical velocity at point locations.    We recommend that paleoflood studies integrate a larger dataset prior to announcing an estimated peak discharge. Paleoflood studies should highlight the uncertainties associated with the analysis to a larger degree. The studies should also evaluate the different sections of the process chain. There should also be more focus on reevaluation of original sources for the underlying dataset to check if the old interpretations are still valid today.
