1 Introduction Research on flash droughts, including their identification, impact assessment, monitoring, and early warning, has recently received significant attention (Mohammadi et al., 2022; Zhang and Yuan, 2020; Zhong et al., 2022 ). Flash droughts have more severe environmental impacts and are harder to predict than conventional slow-developing droughts (Jin et al., 2019; Mohammadi et al., 2022 ). Historical occurrences demonstrate that flash drought events severely threaten global water resource availability, crop yields, and vegetation productivity (Xi and Yuan, 2022 ). With global warming, more regions are expected to frequently experience the impacts of flash drought events in the future (Christian et al., 2023; Sreeparvathy and Srinivas, 2022; Yuan et al., 2023 ). Consequently, developing effective management strategies for flash drought events is crucial for ensuring future food security and water resource sustainability. Understanding the differences and connections between flash and slow-developing droughts is a prerequisite for managing flash drought risk (Zhang et al., 2023a ). Incorrectly categorizing a flash drought event as a slow-developing drought can amplify the impacts of the flash drought, while overestimating a slow-developing drought event as a flash drought can lead to increased management costs for governments (Otkin et al., 2022 ). The distinction between flash droughts and conventional droughts lies in the rate of drought onset, but the connection between flash droughts and conventional droughts is rarely discussed (Wang and Yuan, 2018; Zhang et al., 2023a ). Interactions between multi-scale drought processes are often overlooked in existing flash drought identification frameworks (Minea et al., 2021; Yun-chuan et al., 2023 ). For example, the 2019 flash droughts in the Yangtze River Basin of China lasted more than three months, destroying crops on over 2.3 million hectares of farmland and resulting in direct economic losses exceeding $2.1 billion (Li et al., 2022b ). Therefore, clarifying the connection between flash droughts and slow-developing droughts is crucial for refining the definition of flash droughts. After reviewing the development of flash drought identification frameworks, it was noted that over 50 different methods and frameworks are used to define and identify flash droughts (Lisonbee et al., 2021; Rahim et al., 2023 ). Meteorological monitoring indices, remote sensing vegetation indices, and soil moisture percentiles are three indicators commonly used in the current flash drought identification framework (Ford et al., 2023; Wang and Yuan, 2018; Zou et al., 2024 ). The categorization of flash droughts based on meteorological indicator thresholds can serve to identify flash drought events on a large scale while explaining the meteorological driving mechanisms behind flash drought occurrences (Gerken et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2023 ). However, flash drought identification methods based solely on meteorological indicator thresholds overlook the rapid onset rate of flash droughts. Existing research suggests that such identification frameworks should be used less frequently in future flash drought studies (Otkin et al., 2016 ). Remote sensing vegetation indices utilize vegetation ecosystem functions to monitor flash droughts by observing vegetation responses (Liu et al., 2023a; Mohammadi et al., 2022; Xi and Yuan, 2022 ). Nevertheless, the temporal resolution of remote-sensing satellites, typically at 8-day or bi-monthly intervals, restricts the application of this method for analyzing the spatiotemporal evolution of flash droughts (Christian et al., 2022 ). Compared to the indicators above, soil moisture percentiles provide a more immediate and accurate reflection of the real-time status of a flash drought event (Liu et al., 2020a ). Moreover, the continuous variation in soil moisture percentiles during the progression of flash droughts makes it easier to delineate specific times for different stages of the drought than other disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and fires (Wang and Yuan, 2022 ). This means that the flash drought identification method based on soil moisture percentile dynamics can precisely monitor the full lifecycle evolution of flash drought events (Li et al., 2023a; McDaniel et al., 2017 ). During the full lifecycle of a flash drought event, the termination of flash droughts is determined either when their impact on crops and vegetation ceases or when lag effects are no longer caused by soil dryness being below a certain moisture threshold (Daryanto et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023a ). Conventional drought studies reveal that once a widespread drought occurs if soil moisture falls below the 40th percentile, the probability of the drought continuing increases by 50 % (Lloyd-Hughes et al., 2013 ). Furthermore, Yang et al. (2023)  demonstrated that the ecological impacts of flash droughts on vegetation ecosystems often continue for 16 days after soil moisture recovery above the 20th percentile. Therefore, whether the 20th soil moisture percentile in past flash drought identification frameworks adequately represents the termination of the ecological and environmental impacts of a flash drought event requires further analysis (Fang et al., 2019; McDaniel et al., 2017 ). Improvements in existing flash drought identification frameworks have primarily been achieved through multivariate statistical analysis, the construction of composite indices, and the application of remote-sensing indicators, thereby enhancing the performance of these frameworks in identifying spatiotemporal features and assessing environmental impacts (Chen et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b; Mukherjee and Mishra, 2022b; Zhang and Yuan, 2020; Zhao et al., 2023 ). However, few studies have evaluated the practicality of improved identification frameworks in flash drought risk management (Walker et al., 2024 ). The crisis lifecycle theory initially formulated by American management scholar Steven Fink was conceived to address corporate crises. In recent years, this conceptual framework has been widely adopted by scholars for research into risk management of natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods (Alhamid et al., 2023; Tabata et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2022a ). The crisis lifecycle theory posits that natural disaster progression mirrors biological organisms' lifecycles: natural disasters undergo distinct phases, namely, inception, growth, maturity, and termination (Li et al., 2022c ). From the crisis life cycle theory perspective, the entire process of a natural disaster from its onset to termination is delineated, effectively bridging the gap between risk assessment and risk management (Liu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2018 ). Summarizing the development of past flash drought identification frameworks, previous frameworks aimed to achieve a deep understanding of each phase in the flash drought lifecycle as outlined below: 1) In clarifying the distinctions between flash droughts and slow-developing droughts, scholars consistently introduced the concept of the onset phase (Liu et al., 2020b; Otkin et al., 2016; Wang and Yuan, 2022 ). 2) In evaluating the impacts of flash drought events on vegetation growth and crop yield, attention has shifted towards understanding the duration phase of the flash drought lifecycle (Jin et al., 2019; O and Park, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022 ). 3) When analyzing the driving mechanisms behind the recovery from flash droughts, the scholarly focus has turned to the recovery phase (Hain et al., 2019; Schwalm et al., 2017 ). 4) To construct effective early warning systems for flash droughts, scholars have specified parameters such as onset time, termination time, and the overall duration of flash drought events (Chen and Yuan, 2022; Pendergrass et al., 2020; Qing et al., 2022; Wang and Yuan, 2018 ). Although previous studies have not analyzed flash drought events from a complete lifecycle perspective, the findings from extant works suggest that a clear delineation of the distinct phases of flash droughts will facilitate systematic investigations into early warning forecasts, driving mechanisms, ecological and environmental effects, as well as future risk assessments (Lovino et al., 2024; Otkin et al., 2022 ). This study introduces the Full Life Cycle Flash Drought Identification Framework (FLCFDIF) that incorporates crisis lifecycle theory, emphasizing consistency between flash drought risk identification and risk management actions. The framework focuses on three critical elements: 1) distinguishing between flash droughts and conventional slow-developing droughts, 2) considering the classification of heat wave flash droughts and precipitation deficit flash droughts, and 3) linking flash droughts to seasonal droughts. Based on the FLCFDIF, we identified flash droughts' full lifecycle characteristics and meteorological driving mechanisms across various agricultural regions in China from 1980 to 2020. Additionally, we validated the advantages and uncertainties of FLCFDIF through historical flash drought cases and indicator sensitivity analysis. Compared to past flash drought identification frameworks, the improved FLCFDIF offers comprehensive information for systematically studying flash drought risk assessment and management.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Overview of the study area China is situated along the northeast coastline of Asia, adjacent to the Pacific Ocean, with geographic coordinates extending from a latitude of 3°51′ N to 53°34′ N and a longitude of 73°29′ E to 135°04′ E (Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023b ). China, influenced by the East Asian summer monsoon from the Pacific Ocean and the southwest summer monsoon from the Indian Ocean, is one of the most active regions for summer monsoon activity globally (Dai et al., 2020 ). The geographic distribution of the nine major agricultural regions across the monsoon and non-monsoon areas is depicted in Fig. 1  . The eastern monsoon region of China encompasses 46 % of the land area in China, 96 % of its population, and nearly all of its grain production zones (Tu et al., 2022 ). In recent years, severe flash drought events have frequently affected China's monsoon regions (Mahto and Mishra, 2023; Ran et al., 2020 ). Therefore, understanding the differences in the full lifecycle characteristics and meteorological driving mechanisms of flash droughts between China's monsoon and non-monsoon regions is crucial for future flash drought risk management.  2.2 Multisource datasets Apart from microwave remote-sensing datasets, this study employs four soil moisture datasets commonly used in recent flash drought research (Christian et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020b; Qing et al., 2022 ). Among the four datasets, the ERA5-Land dataset offers superior spatiotemporal resolution for soil moisture, initially at 0.1°×0.1° but later resampled to 0.25°×0.25° to ensure consistency with the other datasets (Wu et al., 2021 ). The GLEAM soil moisture dataset exhibits reliable accuracy when cross-validated with data from eddy covariance tower observations (Martens et al., 2017 ). Further, the robustness of the GLDAS dataset has been validated through its widespread application in examining soil moisture variations on both global and regional scales (Bi et al., 2016 ). Datasets of soil moisture from multiple sources demonstrate significant consistency in the depth of topsoil moisture (Wang and Yuan, 2018 ). In this study, the soil moisture data from the surface layer are utilized to validate the performance of a new FLCFDIF for identifying flash drought events in China. The selected datasets for surface soil moisture include ERA5-LAND with a depth of 0–7 cm, GLEAM with a depth of 0–10 cm, GLDAS–Noah with a depth range of 0–10 cm, and GLDAS–CLSM with a depth of 0–10 cm. To compare the sensitivity of identifying flash drought characteristics across the entire life cycle at different soil moisture depths, the middle soil moisture (0–40 cm) is determined by weighting the 0–10 cm and 10–40 cm layers with weights of 0.25 and 0.75, respectively. Similarly, the deep soil moisture (0–100 cm) is determined by weighting the 0–10 cm, 10–40 cm, and 40–100 cm layers with weights of 0.1, 0.3, and 0.6, respectively (Xu et al., 2021 ). The CN05.1 gridded meteorological observation dataset (https://ccrc.iap.ac.cn/) from the National Meteorological Center is selected to investigate the meteorological mechanisms driving flash drought events (Wu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2009 ). This dataset is derived from the interpolation of daily observation data from over 2400 national-level stations and has been validated for high spatial–temporal accuracy in multiple studies (Miao and Wang, 2020 ). The dataset includes seven daily meteorological variables: mean temperature, precipitation, maximum temperature, minimum temperature, mean wind speed, relative humidity, and evaporation. Atmospheric aridity has been demonstrated to be related to the development of flash droughts, and a shortfall in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) can lead to a rapid decline in soil moisture (Noguera et al., 2023 ). Therefore, daily VPD is calculated as the difference between saturation and actual vapor pressure, while potential evapotranspiration (PET) is determined using the Penman–Monteith equation introduced by the Food and Agriculture Organization in 1998 (Pereira et al., 2015 ). Consistent with the resolution of the soil moisture datasets, both the CN05.1 and ERA5 datasets have a spatial resolution of 0.25°. Detailed information on multi-source soil moisture and meteorological data is presented in Table S1 .   3 Methods 3.1 The Full Life Cycle Flash Drought Identification Framework The Full Life Cycle Flash Drought Identification Framework (FLCFDIF) divides a flash drought event into four phases: onset, duration, recovery, and termination. Fig. 2   presents a schematic that distinguishes among the various phases throughout the lifecycle of flash droughts. The construction workflow of the identification framework is illustrated in Fig. 3   and typically consists of the following seven steps:Step 1: Preprocessing of Soil Moisture Data and Meteorological Data     Data from different regions or seasons primarily reflect the soil moisture conditions at specific times, which complicates using such data for analyzing long-duration, large-scale drought events (Zhao et al., 2020 ). Therefore, this study transforms soil moisture datasets into pentad-mean soil moisture percentiles to eliminate weather-related noise and enhance the spatial–temporal comparability of the identification results. Similarly, daily meteorological data are converted into corresponding pentad time scales. Anomalies in pentad mean values for maximum temperature, precipitation, and evapotranspiration are calculated to identify meteorological driving mechanisms during the onset phase of flash droughts.Step 2: Identification of the Onset Phase     According to Yuan et al. (2019) , the onset phase of a flash drought is defined as the period during which soil moisture percentiles decline from the 40th percentile to the 20th percentile within a period not exceeding 4 pentads. The average soil moisture decline rate in each pentad is at least 5 % for 4 pentads.Step 3: Identification of the Duration Phase     When soil moisture percentiles drop below 20 %, both vegetation and crops experience significant growth inhibition (Mahto and Mishra, 2023; Zhang et al., 2023c ). Moreover, if soil moisture deficiency persists beyond the adaptive capacity of vegetation and crops, the ecosystem functions of vegetation and crop growth will be significantly impaired (Li et al., 2023a ). For the duration phase of a flash drought, we incorporate the concept of a peak point by Liu et al. (2020a,b) . The peak point refers to the lowest value of soil moisture percentiles below the 20th percentile after the onset phase.Step 4: Identification of the Recovery Phase     The endpoint of the recovery phase is often considered to mark the termination of a flash drought event. However, we argue that the recovery phase merely represents the initial stage of flash drought recovery, marked by the beginning of a decline in the event's environmental impacts (Yang et al., 2023 ). The recovery phase refers to the duration between the lowest peak point and when soil moisture recovers above the 20th percentile.Step 5: Identification of the Termination Phase     The termination period of flash droughts is considered the second stage of the recovery process. While the recovery and termination phases cover the transition of soil moisture content from a drought to a non-drought condition, the recovery phase pertains explicitly to the ascent above the 20th percentile. The termination phase covers the range from the 20th to the 40th percentile. This distinction makes it possible to detail the comprehensive ecological impacts of flash drought events (Yang et al., 2023 ).Step 6: Flash Drought to Seasonal Drought Shift     In previous studies, the duration of a flash drought was commonly considered a sub-seasonal drought event that lasted beyond three pentads (Otkin et al., 2021; Sreeparvathy and Srinivas, 2022; Wang and Yuan, 2018 ). However, when we connect flash droughts to conventional slow-developing droughts through the definition of the termination phase, flash droughts can evolve into long-term, seasonal-scale droughts in certain regions. Based on FLCFDIF, a flash drought leading to a seasonal drought is one lasting longer than 18 pentads.Step 7: Classification of Heatwave Flash Droughts (HWFDs) and Precipitation Deficit Flash Droughts (PDFDs)     The flash drought identification framework proposed by Mo and Lettenmaier (2016) categorizes flash droughts based on climate anomalies in precipitation, maximum temperature, and actual evapotranspiration. When integrated into our current framework for flash drought identification, Mo and Lettenmaier's framework does not serve as a requisite criterion for determining the onset phase and instead provides valuable insights into the meteorological drivers underlying the rapid decline in soil moisture during the onset phase. A flash drought is considered an HWFD if the Tmax anomaly exceeds one standard deviation, and the ET anomaly is positive. Conversely, a flash drought is classified as a PDFD if the Tmax anomaly exceeds one standard deviation, the ET anomaly is negative, and the precipitation is below the 40th percentile.  3.2 Gravity shift model By tracking the shift in the center of gravity of drought over time, the gravity shift model provides detailed insights into the movement and expansion of drought conditions across different regions (Guan et al., 2021 ). Over a long time series, the direction of the center of gravity shift in flash drought events can indicate potential future risk hotspots, emphasizing the importance of understanding the land–atmosphere–ocean driving mechanisms that lead to the occurrence of flash droughts in areas where the center of gravity is distributed (Weng et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022b ). The period of this study, which is 41 years (from 1980 to 2020), is further sub-divided into four periods: the 1980 s (1980–1990), the 1990 s (1990–2000), the 2000 s (2000–2010), and the 2010 s (2010–2020). The calculation formula of the center of gravity shift model is as follows:(1) X = ∑ i = 1  n  x i  × p i    ∑ i = 1  n  p i        (2) Y = ∑ i = 1  n  y i  × p i    ∑ i = 1  n  p i        In the formula, n  is the total number of grid cells in the flash drought occurrence area. Moreover, xi , yi ,  and pi   represent the longitude, latitude, and frequency, respectively, of flash drought occurrence in the grid cell.  3.3 Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope estimation The Mann–Kendall test, a non-parametric statistical testing method, does not require data to conform to any specific distribution and remains unaffected by outliers (Sa'adi et al., 2023 ). Additionally, Sen's Slope method quantifies the magnitude of trend changes, measuring the rate of change over time (Kumar and Middey, 2022 ). These two methods have been widely applied in the trend analysis of meteorological and hydrological time series to assess the degree and significance of changes (Atta ur and Dawood, 2016; Nury and Hasan, 2016 ). Therefore, this study employs a combination of the two methods to analyze spatiotemporal trends in the frequency of flash drought events in China from 1980 to 2020.  3.4 Triple collocation Selecting soil moisture data with lower uncertainty is crucial for assessing the sensitivity of the FLCFDIF, particularly in the absence of observational data (Mukherjee and Mishra, 2022a ). The Triple Collocation method, a technique for evaluating data quality without relying on actual measurements, has been widely used to compare the performance of various soil moisture datasets (Stoffelen, 1998; Yang et al., 2022 ). This study derived triplets by arbitrarily selecting three products from four soil moisture datasets (ERA5, GLDAS-Noah, GLDAS-CLSM, and GLEAM). Moreover, this research evaluated these triplets by calculating their correlation coefficients and noise standard error values. The detailed calculation process and formulas are available in McColl et al. (2014) . Based on the dataset with the lowest uncertainty in soil moisture simulations for China, the sensitivity of the FLCFDIF to different soil moisture depths and termination thresholds was compared.   4 Result 4.1 Spatial–temporal evolution characteristics of flash droughts in China The center of gravity shift path of flash droughts in China over the past few decades is shown in Fig. 4  . The centroid of flash droughts was mainly concentrated at the junction of monsoon and non-monsoon regions in China. The location of the centroid and the migration paths of flash droughts in China identified by the four soil moisture datasets show marked consistency. From 1980 to 2020, the center of gravity of flash droughts in China shifted from the southwest to the northeast. The spatial and temporal evolutionary trends of flash droughts in China were analyzed using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope estimation (Fig. 5  ). Although there are slight differences in the spatial performance of the four soil moisture datasets, the hotspots identified for the development of flash droughts in China over the past four decades remain consistent. From 1980 to 2020, there was a significant increasing trend of flash droughts in the monsoon regions of China, which mainly include the Northeast Plain, the Loess Plateau, and the Middle–Lower Yangtze Plain. For the non-monsoon zone, the evolutionary trends of flash droughts over the last few decades are not significant, and only the Gleam dataset identifies a significant downward trend of flash droughts. In summary, it is observed that both the southern and northeastern regions have experienced significant impacts from flash droughts over the past several decades. In contrast, the northwestern region appears to be comparatively less affected. With the projected northeastward migration of the locational centroid for flash droughts, the northeastern areas of China may encounter elevated risk levels for future flash droughts.  4.2 Full lifecycle characteristics of flash droughts in China The spatial heterogeneity of the entire life cycle of flash droughts in different agricultural sub-regions in China from 1980 to 2020 is represented in Fig. 6  , which shows the spatial distribution of the average total duration of flash drought events from onset to termination. Overall, the average duration of flash drought events in China ranges between 5 and 20 pentads, with few events lasting less than 5 pentads. Fig. 6 b–j shows the main characteristics of the four-phase flash drought evolutionary process using the multi-source soil moisture dataset. The performance of multi-source soil moisture datasets in identifying the full lifecycle characteristics of flash drought events in China is consistent. Across different agricultural sub-regions, the onset rates of flash droughts exhibit minimal variation, typically lasting approximately 2–3 pentads. In Southern China, the Loess Plateau, and the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, the duration phase of flash droughts often exceeds 6 pentads and is characterized by a high degree of uncertainty. This condition suggests that these areas are highly susceptible to prolonged exposure to deficient soil moisture levels when a flash drought occurs. The duration of the recovery and termination phases within flash drought events are not identical, with the recovery phase lasting approximately 2–5 pentads and the termination phase extending over approximately 2–3 pentads. The termination phase is an inherent stage in the lifecycle of flash drought events, and its delineation does not unnecessarily extend the duration of flash droughts. Fig. 7   details temporal trends in the characteristics of the full life cycle of flash droughts in different agricultural sub-regions of China. From a risk assessment perspective, the shorter the duration of the development phase and the longer the span of the duration, recovery, and termination phases of a flash drought event, the higher the future risk posed by flash droughts. Therefore, regions such as the Huang-Huai-Hai Plain, the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, the Middle–Lower Yangtze Plain, and the Northeast China Plain are expected to be severely affected by intense flash drought events. The full cycle characteristics of flash droughts in China's monsoon and non-monsoon regions show significant disparities. The shortening of the development stage and prolonging of the other three stages in monsoon regions imply that flash droughts have rapid onsets and last long. Therefore, the combined effects of increased frequency and duration of flash droughts might escalate the risk of crop yield reduction in monsoon regions in China.  4.3 Classification of flash droughts By analyzing anomalies in precipitation, maximum temperature, and actual evapotranspiration during the onset phase of flash droughts between 1980 and 2020, we accurately identified areas in China affected by HWFD and PDFD, as shown in Fig. 8  a–i. The impact range of flash droughts in different agricultural climate regions has significantly increased since 2000. HDFD has predominantly driven widespread flash droughts across various agricultural climate regions in China. In non-monsoon regions of China, such as the arid and semi-arid areas of northwest China and the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, precipitation deficits are also a major cause of widespread flash droughts during some years. It is noteworthy that the classification of flash droughts into HWFD and PDFD types does not fully capture the meteorological drivers behind the onset phase of each flash drought event. This failure to fully capture meteorological drivers is particularly evident in northeastern China, where the impact areas of the two identified types of flash droughts are much smaller than the actual affected areas. This outcome indicates that the singular criteria of a heat wave and precipitation-deficient flash droughts fail to comprehensively elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving flash drought occurrences. The probability of flash drought events evolving into seasonal droughts across various agricultural climatic zones in China over the past 40 years has been rigorously analyzed (Fig. 9  ). Across the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, Southern China, and the Middle–Lower Yangtze Plain, all datasets consistently indicate a 5–15 % likelihood of flash droughts progressing into seasonal droughts. The high proportion of seasonal flash drought events emphasizes the importance of not overlooking the connection between flash droughts and seasonal droughts in the flash drought identification framework. In China's major grain-producing regions, such as the Northeast and the Huang-Huai-Hai Plain, the proportion of seasonal flash droughts is approximately 5 %. In terms of agricultural production, while short-term flash droughts might not entirely compromise crop drought resistance and water supply capabilities, the concurrent occurrence of flash and seasonal droughts, especially in the absence of effective irrigation measures, can have devastating effects on crop yields (Mahto and Mishra, 2023 ). Hence, it is imperative to continuously monitor flash droughts so that policymakers can assess their potential evolution into seasonal droughts.  4.4 Key meteorological anomalies during different stages of flash drought evolution Existing studies have identified sensitive meteorological factors, including precipitation, temperature, actual evapotranspiration, potential evapotranspiration, and VPD (Ford and Labosier, 2017; Shah et al., 2023; Sreeparvathy and Srinivas, 2022 ). However, few studies have discussed the changes in driving mechanisms at different stages of flash drought evolution from a lifecycle perspective. The spatial distribution of the standardized climatic anomaly means at various stages of flash drought events in China from 1980 to 2020 is illustrated in Fig. 10  . Generally, the anomalies in key meteorological elements during the development and duration stages of flash drought progression align with previous analyses, demonstrating that the combination of precipitation deficits and high-temperature heatwaves has intensified the occurrence of flash drought events in China in the past (Christian et al., 2020; Mo and Lettenmaier, 2015 ). It is noteworthy that the duration phase of flash droughts exhibits more pronounced anomalies in potential evapotranspiration compared to the development phase, potentially serving as a key climatic driver for the decline in soil moisture to its peak point during the duration stage. The climatic anomalies driving the recovery from flash droughts primarily occur during the termination stage rather than the recovery phase. Compared to the other stages, the termination stage of flash droughts is marked by higher precipitation anomalies and reduced evaporation demand. Additionally, during the recovery phase of flash droughts, the northeast region of China exhibits stronger high-temperature and VPD anomalies than the development and duration phases. Positive anomalies in VPD have a more significant impact on crop and vegetation growth than soil moisture shortages, implying that the ecological and environmental effects of flash droughts persist into the recovery stage (Zhang et al., 2021 ). This outcome also confirms the necessity of improving soil moisture thresholds throughout the full lifecycle of flash droughts, highlighting the potential impact of the termination period on flash drought recovery.  4.5 Validation of FLCFDIF using a real-world flash drought event To substantiate the advantages of FLCFDIF, we examine the severe flash drought event of 2019 in the Middle–Lower Yangtze Plain to highlight the distinctions between our framework and earlier methodologies (Li et al., 2022b; Ma et al., 2020; Wang and Yuan, 2021 ). Fig. 11   is synthesized from four soil moisture datasets and presents soil moisture trends from mid-July 2019 to January 2020. Whereas many prior studies label the 2019 drought as an extreme slow-developing drought, our proposed FLCFDIF identifies this drought event as a seasonal flash drought lasting more than three months (Li et al., 2022b; Ma et al., 2020; Ran et al., 2020 ). Fig. S1  depicts the full evolutionary process of the 2019 flash drought in the Middle–Lower Yangtze Plain. In early August, the soil moisture in this region plummeted from a moist condition to an extreme drought within just two pentads, representing an essential characteristic of flash droughts. Notably, there was a rebound in soil moisture when it dropped below the 20 % soil moisture percentile, which correlates with low-intensity rainfall in early August. Using the 20 % percentile as the only criterion would indicate that this flash drought concluded by the end of August while misconstruing the subsequent soil moisture changes as a slow-developing drought. Therefore, while temporary precipitation events can disrupt the 20 % soil moisture percentile threshold during the progression of a flash drought, the drought may continue under a strong climatic background once these low-intensity precipitation events cease. Adjusting the soil moisture threshold used to determine the termination of a flash drought could prevent misinterpretations caused by a rebound in the soil moisture percentile. Fig. 12   illustrates anomalies in key meteorological factors during the progression of the 2019 flash drought event in the Yangtze River Basin. Comparing the changes in soil moisture percentile and climatic anomalies during the full life cycle of the flash drought, it can be concluded that the positive anomalies of actual evapotranspiration, potential evapotranspiration, VPD, maximum temperature, and surface net shortwave radiation have a contributing effect to the flash drought event. In contrast, negative anomalies of P_minus_PET, precipitation, and relative humidity contribute to flash drought events. Notably, flash droughts are particularly sensitive to positive anomalies in potential evapotranspiration. Research by Ford et al. (2020) indicates that flash drought events are more strongly linked to potential evapotranspiration than precipitation and temperature. Positive precipitation anomalies typically coincide with an increase in soil moisture percentiles. However, whether these anomalies can reach soil moisture thresholds during the recovery and termination phases depends on underlying surface conditions and the magnitude of effective precipitation (Zhao et al., 2017 ).   5 Discussions 5.1 Advantages of FLCFDIF The FLCFDIF emphasizes that the distinction between flash droughts and conventional droughts lies in the “flash”, while the connection is in the “drought”. This suggests that flash droughts develop more quickly than traditional slow-developing droughts, but it does not mean that flash droughts cannot last longer than slow-developing droughts (Wang and Yuan, 2018 ). Zhang et al. (2020)  pointed out that the average duration of flash droughts in China was approximately 43 days. However, the FLCFDIF framework identified several flash drought events lasting more than 90 days in both humid regions and arid and semi-arid areas of China. Liu et al. (2023a,b)  also confirmed that flash droughts can evolve into prolonged seasonal droughts after their initial rapid onset. Previous flash drought identification frameworks often overlooked such long-term flash drought events due to constraints on event duration (Lisonbee et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2019 ). Additionally, the FLCFDIF introduces the concept of a peak point to identify the inflection point where soil moisture continues to decline and then shifts to an increasing trend after the onset phase. Earlier frameworks often used the end of the onset phase as the inflection point to define the beginning of the flash drought recovery phase (Wang and Yuan, 2022; Yuan et al., 2019 ). Wang et al. (2023)  improved the initial identification framework by selecting the time point where the rate of soil moisture decline slows after the onset phase as the inflection point. However, the limitation remains that the continued decline in soil moisture below the 20th percentile should not be simplified as the recovery phase. Flash drought recovery is driven by effective precipitation events, and the FLCFDIF has confirmed that effective precipitation events in the past forty years typically occur in the termination phase (Wang et al., 2023 ). Liu et al. (2020a,b)  identified the inflection point by fitting a univariate polynomial function to the change in soil moisture percentiles, but this approach led to a high computational burden in large-scale studies and was often disrupted by low-intensity precipitation events. In contrast, the peak point provides a clearer distinction between the duration and recovery phases of a flash drought. The value of the peak point during the duration phase can reflect the ongoing developmental intensity of a flash drought event (Liu et al., 2020a; Lovino et al., 2024 ). The lower the peak point, the greater the severity of the flash drought event, indicating a need for strong driving forces for rapid recovery (Wang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2023 ). Therefore, incorporating the peak point into the flash drought identification framework can facilitate future research on the ecological and environmental impacts of flash droughts and the driving mechanisms behind flash drought recovery. Another key advantage of the FLCFDIF is its comprehensive delineation of the entire lifecycle of a flash drought from inception to conclusion. As noted by Lovino et al. (2024)  any attempt at predicting flash droughts requires a better understanding of their evolution and lifecycle. Building on the lifecycle concept, the FLCFDIF also integrates crisis lifecycle theory from management science, thoroughly considering the relationships between emergency response actions and risk management objectives across different stages of flash drought evolution (Zheng et al., 2021 ). Specifically, changes in soil moisture percentiles correspond to various stages of a flash drought's full lifecycle. Each stage (onset, duration, recovery, and termination) correlates with different elements of risk management, including warning, assessment, mitigation, and monitoring (Fig. 13  ). The onset stage of a flash drought event can distinguish whether a drought event is a flash drought or a slowly developing drought. The magnitude of the initial onset rate reflects the intensity of the climatic anomaly behind the flash drought event (Han et al., 2023 ). Analyzing climatic anomalies before the onset stage is crucial for providing early warning of flash drought risks (Das et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2023 ). Adequate early warning of flash droughts must ensure action is taken before soil moisture rapidly falls below the 20th percentile (Otkin et al., 2022 ). The duration phase of a flash drought occurs when soil moisture is at its lowest and the flash drought most severely impacts crop yields and vegetation ecosystem functions (Peña-Gallardo et al., 2019 ). This phase highlights the evaluation of exposure and vulnerability of areas affected by a flash drought (Dunne and Kuleshov, 2022 ). The recovery phase of a flash drought signifies that the drought has started to alleviate, which is typically triggered by a substantial increase in precipitation (Raposo et al., 2023 ). A flash drought frequently coincides with high-temperature heatwave events, leading to increased electrical load demands and shortages in hydroelectric power supply, and these conditions severely affect regional production and livelihoods (Cai et al., 2009a,b; Liu, 2020b ). Thus, analyzing the mechanisms driving the recovery of flash droughts offers key insights for devising strategies to allocate regional water resources and energy supplies (Schwalm, 2017; Zhang et al., 2018 ). The termination phase of a flash drought comprehensively considers the complete ecological and environmental impacts of flash droughts and determines the potential transition of a flash drought into a seasonal drought. Continuous risk monitoring during the termination phase is crucial in preventing policymakers from underestimating the irreversible impacts of a flash drought event.  5.2 Uncertainties of FLCFDIF The uncertainties in the framework for identifying flash droughts, which use soil moisture as a monitoring indicator, primarily stem from three sources: the soil moisture dataset, the depth of soil burial, and the thresholds for drought termination (Mukherjee and Mishra, 2022a ). Due to the lack of large-scale and long-term soil moisture monitoring data from stations, this study utilized multi-source soil moisture datasets from reanalysis and land surface models to compare the full lifecycle characteristics of flash droughts in China. To further explain the uncertainties in identifying flash droughts using these multi-source soil moisture datasets, a triple collocation was utilized to quantify the differences in soil moisture simulations among the four datasets (McColl et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2022 ). Fig S2  presents the correlation coefficients for each triplet computed using the triple collocation method, while Fig S3  shows the normalized bias values for each triplet. Summarizing the comparative results of the four datasets, the GLDAS_Noah and GLEAM datasets demonstrate high correlation coefficients for soil moisture simulation in the humid regions of China. However, the GLDAS_Noah dataset exhibits a low normalized bias, indicating a more accurate representation of soil moisture levels than the other datasets. Overall, the full lifecycle characteristics of flash droughts identified using the GLDAS_Noah dataset exhibit relatively low uncertainty. Poonia et al. (2022) also confirmed the superior performance of the GLDAS_Noah soil moisture dataset compared to other multi-source soil moisture datasets when assessing the response of India's terrestrial ecosystems to flash drought characteristics. The definition of flash drought identification frameworks, based on different soil moisture depths and drought termination thresholds, directly influences the lifecycle length of flash droughts and determines their relationship with seasonal droughts (Ford and Labosier, 2017; Li et al., 2020; Sehgal et al., 2021 ). Therefore, we utilized the GLDAS_Noah dataset to analyze the sensitivity of the FLCFDIF to soil moisture depth and termination thresholds. Moreover, to investigate the sensitivity of the framework to termination thresholds, Fig. 14  a–d illustrates experiments controlling the variation in termination thresholds using surface soil moisture data. Similarly, to examine the sensitivity of different FLCFDIF to soil moisture depth, Fig. 15  a–d depict experiments controlling the variation in root zone depth using the 40th percentile soil moisture threshold. Fig. 13 a indicates that from 1980 to 2020, the proportion of flash drought events with a duration exceeding 90 days is relatively low when using the 20th percentile soil moisture as the termination threshold. This outcome explains why previous studies have overlooked the connection between flash droughts and seasonal droughts (Yao et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020 ). When the soil moisture termination threshold is increased to the 30th and 40th percentiles, the FLCFDIF captures a higher proportion of seasonal flash drought events in the arid and semi-arid regions of northwestern China, southern China, and the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Additionally, the differences in seasonal flash drought risk over the past 40 years identified using the 30th and 40th percentile soil moisture termination thresholds are minimal. The 40th percentile threshold does not excessively extend the lifecycle of flash drought events, resulting in many flash droughts being classified as long-term seasonal droughts. This finding supports the rationale for selecting the 40th percentile soil moisture as the termination threshold in the FLCFDIF. Wang et al. (2016)  found that the differences in flash drought frequency caused by varying soil depths were far more minor than those caused by different percentile thresholds. Similarly, our FLCFDIF shows higher sensitivity to different percentile thresholds than to different soil depths. However, as soil depth increases, the proportion of seasonal flash droughts in southeastern China remains close to 20 %.  5.3 Potential extension for future studies Although the performance differences of multi-source soil moisture datasets in China were compared in this study, the uncertainty in soil moisture data still affects the results of identifying the full lifecycle characteristics of flash droughts in China over the past forty years. In future research, integrating advanced soil moisture satellite monitoring data from sources such as the Soil Moisture Active Passive, Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity, and Advanced Scatterometer systems along with the application of multi-source data fusion techniques can potentially reduce uncertainties in the FLCFDIF (Ford et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2023 ). Additionally, Applying the FLCFDIF in flash drought risk management is primarily a conceptual framework, and there is still a lack of detailed information on the various stages needed to formulate comprehensive emergency response plans (Roberts and Ottens, 2005; Zheng et al., 2021 ). If the FLCFDIF is to be applied to future flash drought risk management, further detailed analysis will be required that considers the full lifecycle characteristics of historical flash drought events. For example, 1) the coupled land–atmosphere–sea mechanisms preceding the onset stage of flash droughts in different agricultural climate regions need to be summarized, 2) the impact of the duration stage of flash droughts on crop yields and vegetation needs to be quantified, 3) and the adequate precipitation required to drive the recovery of flash droughts under different underlying surface conditions needs to be analyzed. Currently, some studies utilize various spatiotemporal clustering algorithms to propose improved three-dimensional flash drought identification frameworks for analyzing the spatiotemporal expansion of flash drought events (Chen et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a ). Thus, three-dimensional spatiotemporal clustering algorithms can be integrated into the FLCFDIF to construct an improved three-dimensional FLCFDIF. This will be crucial for deeply understanding flash droughts' evolution characteristics and occurrence mechanisms.   6 Conclusions In this study, we introduced the FLCFDIF to categorize the progression of a flash drought event into four phases: development, duration, recovery, and termination. Using this framework, the full lifecycle characteristics and key meteorological drivers of flash droughts in China over the past four decades were analyzed. Additionally, the sensitivity of the FLCFDIF to various soil depths and drought termination thresholds was assessed. The results indicate that: (i) over the past forty years, the risk of flash drought events in China's monsoon region has significantly increased due to faster onset, longer duration, and slower recovery; (ii) effective precipitation events driving flash drought recovery occur during the termination phase, rather than the traditionally assumed recovery phase; (iii) there is a 5–20 % likelihood of flash droughts evolving into seasonal droughts across different agricultural climatic zones; (iv) the FLCFDIF is more sensitive to different percentile thresholds than to soil depths, and using the 40th percentile of soil moisture as a threshold to determine the end of a flash drought aids in the comprehensive assessment of ecological and environmental impacts. To manage the potential cascading risks of flash drought events by integrating their full lifecycle characteristics, the FLCFDIF introduces the crisis lifecycle theory to explain how to apply information from different stages to flash drought risk management. As global warming intensifies, the FLCFDIF enables governments and agricultural producers to implement timely and practical strategies to address potentially more frequent and intense flash droughts.
1 Introduction Governments conduct quantitative and qualitative flood risk assessments at the administrative, basin, and district levels to efficiently reduce the flood risk with constrained disaster prevention budgets. Quantitative flood risk assessment has the advantage of showing the scale of flood damage quantitatively by calculating the damage amount to each asset type exposed to flood risk, such as buildings (residential and non-residential) and agricultural land (Reese and Ramsay, 2010; Scawthorn et al., 2006; MOIS, 2020 ). However, constructing the equations required to obtain accurate results is difficult, and the workload of the analysis becomes extremely large as the size of the target area increases. Expressing human losses such as death or injuries, in quantitative terms also poses challenges. In contrast, a qualitative flood risk assessment cannot show the scale of flood risk in concrete values, such as damage, but various types of indicators related to flood risk can be reflected in the flood risk index. Moreover, the workload required for analysis is less than that required for quantitative flood risk assessment. Therefore, if the accuracy of the flood risk index can be improved, it can be used as a decision support tool for disaster prevention projects. Recently, as the resolution of the analytical data used in qualitative flood risk assessment has improved, flood risk assessments using high-resolution grid data and flood risk maps have been conducted (Yu et al., 2018; Amadio et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2021 ). Qualitative flood risk assessments both domestically and overseas are mainly performed using an indicator-based approach (IBA) (Park et al., 2005; Van Westen and Yifru, 2016 ). In general, the IBA consists of four items (Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability, and Capacity) and item-specific indicators, and the flood risk index is calculated by applying weights to each indicator index (Benouar and Mimi, 2001; Han et al., 2015;NDMI, 2015; Lee et al., 2019 ). Currently, the traditional weighting methods applied to the indicator index for each item include entropy weight, Euclidean distance, Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), and Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS). However, flood risk indices calculated by applying existing weighting methods do not always yield the accurate results when validated using annual aggregated heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. First, the entropy weight is calculated using a statistical method, which has the advantage of obtaining objective results. However, depending on the mean and standard deviation of the raw data for each indicator, the weight can be skewed towards certain indicators (Al-Aomar, 2010; Lee et al., 2015; Seong and Byun, 2016 ). Second, Euclidean distance is used as an equal weighting method to calculate the weight of each indicator; however, the disadvantage of equal weighting is that the characteristics of certain items and indicators that are highly related to flood risk are not properly represented in the flood risk index. The AHP and TOPSIS use expert surveys to calculate weights; therefore, their results might be influenced by experts’ perspectives and biases. It is also costly and time-consuming to obtain results, and the disadvantage is that if new indicators are added or if there is a problem with the answers of experts, the weights must be recalculated by the survey. As a result, it is necessary to apply a new method that improves the shortcomings of the existing weighting method with optimization methods to show high accuracy when verifying flood risk assessment with annual heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. In the fields of hydrology and hydraulics, various studies have attempted to use optimization methods to efficiently manage water resources and reduce flood risk. In the model that simulates the water level and runoff of rivers, optimization methods have been used to optimize the parameters of the model to provide an optimal solution that minimizes the potential damage and cost associated with flood scenarios (Yazdi and Salehi Neyshabouri, 2012 ). In flood risk analysis using machine learning, hybrid models have been developed to predict the location of flood risk areas or the flood sensitivity of a target area by adjusting the parameters of the model using optimization methods (Panahi et al., 2021; Costache et al., 2022; Linh et al., 2022; Plataridis and Mallios, 2023 ). Moreover, optimization methods have been used to design an optimal flood evacuation plan that maximizes the number of victims rescued and minimizes the cost of flooding in the target area (Khalilpourazari and Pasandideh, 2021 ). In this study, an optimization method was applied not only to optimize the parameters of rainfall-runoff models and machine learning models, as in previous studies but also to optimize the flood risk index calculated by the IBA. For this purpose, we applied the weights calculated by the Genetic Algorithm (GA) to the indices of each indicator constituting the flood risk index. These are the optimal weights that minimize the absolute error between the flood risk index rankings of municipalities, such as cities and counties, and heavy rainfall and typhoon damage rankings. This allows for a more accurate flood risk assessment compared with the existing weighting method. This study aims to develop an improved flood risk assessment method that addresses the limitations of existing studies using grid data, flood risk maps, and GA. The flood risk index used for flood risk assessment consisted of four items (Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability, and Capacity) and 11 indicators. The indicators for the Exposure and Vulnerability items were reflected in the evaluation only for damaged targets directly exposed to flood risk, using grid cells overlaid on the flood risk map. In addition, to address the problem of bias in the distribution of the index by indicators, which distorts the evaluation results, we scored each quantile interval to index the statistical data by indicators. The GA was used to calculate the optimal weights for each indicator when calculating the flood risk index. To demonstrate the advantage of our proposed method in terms of enhanced accuracy, the results were compared with those obtained using existing methods, namely the entropy weight and Euclidean distance. Finally, an improved flood risk index was calculated for each year (2016–2021) for 161 Korean cities and counties to support decision-making for flood risk reduction by local governments.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Flood risk assessment process by cities and counties using the flood risk index To overcome the limitations of existing qualitative flood risk assessment, this study employed grid data and flood risk maps to construct statistical data for each indicator, developing a municipal-level flood risk assessment method using GA-based weighting. The municipal-level flood risk index using the IBA consists of four items (Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability, Capacity) and 11 indicators (Wang et al., 2023 ). Among the four items, the Hazard item consists of indicators related to the risk of flooding, and local governments with a high Hazard index for each year indicate a significant risk of flooding. The Exposure item consists of indicators, such as human and physical assets exposed to disaster risk, and the Vulnerability item consists of indicators that show the Vulnerability of the Exposure item. The Capacity item consists of indicators that contribute to reducing the risk in the target area, and the change in the index of each indicator that improves according to the disaster occurrence situation by year can be checked to determine whether the local government is making efforts to reduce damage. The flood risk index consists of 11 indicators: the Hazard item includes frequency-based rainfall (100-year frequency, duration 24 h, mm) and maximum rainfall (duration 24 h, mm); the Exposure item comprises the number of buildings (building), number of registered residents (people), official land value (1000 KW [Korean won]), and farmland area (m  2    ). The Vulnerability item consisted of the number of old buildings (more than 20 years after construction; building), number of dependent people (population aged seven years and under, 65 years and over; people), and field, greenhouse, and ginseng cultivation areas (m  2    ). Finally, the Capacity item consists of the disaster prevention facility density (pcs/km  2    ) and the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio (1000 KW/km  2    ). When selecting indicators to be reflected in the flood risk assessment, we first reviewed whether the indicators have the characteristics of each item, and then comprehensively evaluated whether the data is updated by year and whether it can be built with grid data. Below is the process of calculating the flood risk index, and Fig. 1   shows the research flow chart for calculating the flood risk index by cities and counties.1. Flood risk maps and grid data for each indicator of Exposure and Vulnerability were used for data selection.  2. Indexing by indicators through scoring each quantile interval.  3. Summation after applying GA-based weights to indices by indicators.  4. Applying min–max normalization to the indices calculated by cities and counties, the range of indices to 0–1.  5. Calculation of the flood risk index by cities and counties.     2.2 Construction of statistical data by indicators at the local government unit In previous flood risk assessments, basic statistical data built by local governments were utilized or extracted statistical values from land cover maps to establish data by indicators such as the number of buildings and farmland area (Fekete, 2009; Linh et al., 2022; Fernandez et al., 2016; Bakkensen et al., 2017; Joo et al., 2019; Chen and Alexander, 2022; Kim et al., 2022 ). However, owing to the characteristics of the data, the statistical data at the administrative district level used in previous studies cannot be used to select only those directly exposed to flood risk. In addition, polygon-based spatial analysis data require a high workload and time to select and edit the statistical data required for analysis. However, unlike polygon-based spatial analysis data, raster-based grid data have low workload requirements for spatial analysis, and the size of grid cells can be adjusted according to the purpose of the research. Therefore, it has the advantage of performing a time-series analysis using grid-level statistical values for each indicator without being constrained by administrative boundaries (European Forum for GeoStatistics, 2011; Steinnocher et al., 2011; Freire et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024 ). To overcome the limitations of existing studies, this study constructed raster-based grid data for each indicator using 500 m ×    500 m grid data provided by the National Geographic Information Institute (NGII) as the foundation. Among the Hazard indicators, frequency-based rainfall was gridded by applying kriging to point-wise rainfall data from 69 automated synoptic observing system (ASOS) stations nationwide with rainfall data retention periods of more than 30 years. In addition, the maximum rainfall was gridded by applying kriging to rainfall data from 579 stations to reflect not only typhoons but also localized torrential rains that cause flood damage in each region. Finally, the frequency-based rainfall and maximum rainfall at the municipal level were calculated by averaging the grid-level statistics within the administrative boundaries of each municipality. The statistics for each Capacity indicator were calculated based on annual municipal-level statistical data rather than on grid data. For disaster prevention facility density, the sum of the number of flood-related disaster prevention facilities per municipality, provided by the Korean Statistical Information Service, was calculated by dividing by the area of each local government. The cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio by municipality was calculated by accumulating the [025 Disaster Prevention and Civil Defense] budget and the [141 water resources] budget by city and county for each year from 2012 to one year before the base year, and then dividing it by the area of each municipality. Finally, the grid data for each indicator in the Exposure and Vulnerability items were overlaid with the national, local, and small river flood risk maps produced through R&D research by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety and the Ministry of Environment; only grid cells directly exposed to flood risk were selected and used. For the flood risk map, the grid-level flood damage rate (percentage of inundated area per grid) was converted into grid data with attribute values for the convenience of analysis (Ministry of Construction and Transportation, 2004 ). Therefore, the attribute values of the selected grid cells overlaid on the flood risk map were modified by multiplying the attribute values of the grid by the flood damage rate of the flood risk map. Fig. 2   shows the distribution of the number of registered residents by grid cell in Korea as of 2021 and the distribution of the national, local, and small river flood risk maps. By summing the number of registered residents selected by cities and counties, it is possible to identify the number of registered residents exposed to flood risk by the local government.  2.3 Scoring each quantile interval In general, the statistics of the indicators used in qualitative flood risk assessment have different units; therefore, in flood risk assessment using IBA, indexing methods such as min–max normalization or Z-score are applied to the statistics of the indicators (Cai et al., 2016; Lyu et al., 2018; Jelinek et al., 2021 ). However, for some statistical data, the distribution of the indices did not follow a normal distribution, even when the indexing method was applied, resulting in a bias in the distribution of the indices for each indicator and the final calculated flood risk index. To solve this problem, a root or log transformation is generally applied to statistical data before indexing. However, if there are very large extreme values in the statistical data or if the amount of data is small, the index does not follow a normal distribution, even after applying root or log transformation, as shown in Fig. 3  . Therefore, to solve these problems, this study applies the scoring of each quantile interval to calculate the index for each indicator. This method divides the statistical data of each indicator into ten equal parts based on the 10th decile and assigns scores to each part in the range of 0.1–1 with an interval of 0.1. Because this method assigns scores to sections with the same density, the distribution of the index does not follow a normal distribution; however, unlike min–max normalization and the Z-score, it can be indexed without skewing the distribution. In fact, when applying the scoring each quantile interval to the number of registered residents within the flood risk map in Fig. 4  , it can be seen that all sections have the same density. In this study, the statistical data for each indicator at the municipal level were indexed by applying the scoring of each quantile interval to the 11 indicators included in the four items.  2.4 Genetic algorithm-based weights calculation by indicators Flood risk assessments conducted in previous studies used weighting methods such as entropy weight, AHP, and TOPSIS to calculate the flood risk index (Chuansheng et al., 2012; Kafle and Shakya, 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Aroca-Jiménez et al., 2022; Chen, 2022; Mousavi et al., 2022 ). However, when applying these methods to calculate the flood risk index for each local government, there are limitations to reducing the absolute error between the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by year and the ranking of the flood risk index. Therefore, in this study, we developed a new weighting method for each indicator using a GA. A GA is a global optimization algorithm developed by imitating the evolutionary process of living organisms and is used in the fields of natural science and engineering to search for the optimal solution of parameters used in functional equations (Holland, 1992 ). In this study, we applied the weights derived from the GA to 11 indicator indices that comprise the municipal-level flood risk index to calculate the optimal flood risk index that minimizes the sum of absolute errors with the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. Fig. 5   shows the process of calculating the optimal weights for each indicator of the flood risk index using the GA. 2.4.1 Input data selection When selecting local governments that suffered flood damage due to river flooding caused by heavy rainfall and typhoons during the research period of 2016–2021 (six years), there were 751 local governments, including duplicates. Therefore, we organized the indices for each of the 11 indicators, which were calculated by scoring each quantile interval for local governments where damage occurred and the rankings of rainfall and typhoon damage by year.  2.4.2 Genetic algorithm-based fitness function setting To find the weights (a, b, c, d, e, ⋯ k) for 11 indicators that minimize the sum of the absolute errors between the ranking of the annual flood risk index and the ranking of rainfall and typhoon damage, the following fitness function was constructed.(2) F = ∑ { R A N K a x 1 2016   + b x 2 2016   + c x 3 2016   + ⋯ + k x 11 2016      - R A N K Damage  2016        +    R A N K a x 1 2017   + b x 2 2017   + c x 3 2017   + ⋯ + k x 11 2017      - R A N K Damage  2017       +    R A N K a x 1 2018   + b x 2 2018   + c x 3 2018   + ⋯ + k x 11 2018      - R A N K Damage  2018       +    ⋮    ⋮    R A N K a x 1 2021   + b x 2 2021   + c x 3 2021   + ⋯ + k x 11 2021      - R A N K Damage  2021       }            In the fitness function, x 1    , x 2    , x 3    , x 4    , …, x 11     are the indices of the 11 indicators calculated by municipalities for each year from 2016 to 2021, and damage is the amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage calculated by local governments for each year. The sum of the absolute errors was calculated by individually applying absolute values to the ranking deviations by year to prevent negative numbers from occurring in the ranking deviations aggregated by the local government units in the fitness function.  2.4.3 Generate and correct initial values that satisfy the conditions In the fitness function of the GA, we set each indicator weight (a, b, c, d, e, …, k) to genes, and generate 60 initial chromosomes consisting of these genes. At this time, the weights contained in each chromosome were set to satisfy the following conditions and were then randomly sampled:(3) 0 ≤ a ≤ 1 , 000  , 0 ≤ b ≤ 1 , 000  , 0 ≤ c ≤ 1 , 000  , ⋯ 0 ≤ k ≤ 1 , 000       The reason for implementing weights as integers rather than decimals is for the convenience of converting decimal numbers to binary numbers during the GA and then performing crossover between chromosomes. We also set the range of individual weights to a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1000 so that the weights could be implemented in three decimal places. Finally, because the sum of the chromosome-specific weights a, b, c, d, e, … k generated by random sampling should be 1000, the generated chromosome-specific weights were corrected by applying the following functional equation:(4) a  ′  = ⌊ 1000 × a ( a + b + c + d + ⋯ + k )   ⌋      (5) b  ′  = ⌊ 1000 × b ( a + b + c + d + ⋯ + k )   ⌋       ⋮ ⋮(6) j  ′  = ⌊ 1000 × j ( a + b + c + d + ⋯ + k )   ⌋      (7) k  ′  = 1000 - ( a  ′  + b  ′  + c  ′  + d  ′  + ⋯ + j  ′  )       To avoid decimals in the ten weights (a  ′    , b  ′    ,’ c  ′    , …, j  ′    ) corrected by the functional equations, decimal places were discarded, and the final weight k  ′     was calculated by subtracting the sum of the remaining corrected weights from 1000.  2.4.4 Calculation of fitness for each chromosome and selection of parent chromosomes When selecting the parent chromosomes to be inherited by the next generation in a GA, the chromosomes are typically selected based on their fitness. Methods for selecting the best chromosome include (1) Roulette Wheel selection, (2) Rank selection, (3) Steady-state selection, (4) Tournament selection, and (5) Elitism Preserving selection. In this study, the rank selection and elitism preserving selection methods were used together. In the rank selection method, the selection probability for each chromosome was calculated and applied in the same way as in Eq. (8) .(8) P R i     = 1 RANK ( F i  )   ∑ ( 1 RANK ( F i  )   )   w i t h P R i     ≥ 0 , ∑ i = 1  n  P R i     = 1     P R i       : Selection probability R i    : Rank positions  F i    : Fitness by chromosomes    Rank selection has a disadvantage in that, if the difference in selection probability according to the rank of each chromosome is not large, the work performance and time required to find the optimal solution are high. To solve this problem, a functional equation was constructed such that the selection probability of chromosomes with higher rankings was greater. Table 1   shows an example of the selection probability calculation results when rank selection was applied to the six chromosomes. It can be seen that the higher the rank of the chromosome, the larger the selection probability. In this study, the sum of the absolute errors corresponding to the fitness decreases as the results obtained using the fitness functional equation become closer to the optimal solution. Thus, the rank selection was applied after ranking the 60 chromosomes in ascending order so that the chromosome with the smallest sum of absolute errors could be selected. In addition, because 11 weights were used in the fitness functional equation in this study, the optimal weights derived from the previous generation may have been lost when moving to the next generation. Therefore, we also applied Elitism Preserving selection, which transferred the chromosomes with the highest fitness in the previous generation to the next generation.  2.4.5 Crossovers and mutations between chromosomes Once the 60 parent chromosomes with the highest fitness were selected by rank selection (allowing for duplicate selection), child chromosomes were generated by a crossover between the chromosomes. To perform the crossover, the weights (a, b, c, d, e, …, k) for each chromosome, which are in decimals, must be converted to binary, and using a binary for the crossover will cause a Hamming Cliff problem. In the Hamming Cliff problem, the distance between two numbers that are close or far apart in decimals is expressed differently in binary. For example, the difference between 7 and 8 in decimals is 1; however, when expressed as a 4-bit binary, it is expressed as 0111 and 1000, and the Hamming distance representing the bit difference is 4. Conversely, the difference between 0 and 8 is 8 in decimals but 0000 and 1000 in binary animals, with a Hamming distance of only 1. Therefore, in a GA, if crossover and mutation are applied as they are when the chromosomes are binary, a large difference in the scale of change may occur compared with decimals. As a solution, we converted the binary-to-gray code before performing crossover and mutation. The Gray code does not have problems during the crossover and mutation processes because the Hamming distance to neighboring numbers is one. When the weights for each chromosome, which are decimals, are converted to grey code, they are replaced with 10-bit of 0 and 1. The number of weights for each chromosome was 11; therefore, the total number of digits in the gray code was 110 (110-bit). In this study, for each of the 11 weights that comprise a chromosome, genes located at 1–5 positions from the right were crossed with genes from other chromosomes to generate child chromosomes. The crossover rate was set to 70 %; therefore, 42 of 60 parental chromosomes were randomly sampled and crossed. Once the crossover was completed, the child chromosomes were subjected to a 10 % probability mutation to convert the gray code for each weight that comprised the chromosomes. Fig. 6   shows the crossover process between the 42 parent chromosomes in the GA.  2.4.6 Correcting weights and performing iterations to calculate optimal weights When generating the initial values for each weight, the corrected individual weights ranged from 0 to 1000, with a sum of 1000. However, when the GA applied crossover and mutation and converted the 10-bit grey code to decimals, the individual weights ranged from 0 to 1023. Therefore, the same correction applied to the initial value is applied to the decimal generated by converting the grey code once again so that the sum of the weights is 1000. Finally, the GA was repeated for several generations to determine the weights that minimized the sum of absolute errors between the ranking of the flood risk index by cities and counties and the ranking of rainfall and typhoon damage. Subsequently, the derived weights were divided by 1000 to calculate the optimal weights, with a range of 0–1 for each indicator and a sum of 1.   2.5 Flood risk assessment by cities and counties Once the optimal weights for each indicator have been calculated through the GA, they were applied to the indicator indices for each municipality and summed up. Subsequently, min–max normalization was applied to the index derived by municipalities, and the municipal-level flood risk index in the range of 0–1 was calculated. Eqs. Geographically, it is a peninsula surrounded by the sea on three sides, and the Taebaek and Sobaek mountains are distributed in the east of the country; therefore, the elevation is higher in the east and lower in the west, as shown in Fig. 7  . The climate is divided into four seasons–spring, summer, fall, and winter–with large temperature differences between summer and winter. In particular, more than 50 % of the annual rainfall is concentrated in summer; therefore, the climate is hot and humid in summer, and significant flood damage occurs. In recent years, owing to the effects of global warming, Korea's climate has shifted to a subtropical climate, and the frequency of heavy rainfall and typhoons has increased. Fig. 8   shows maps of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage per year for each of the 161 municipalities from 2016 to 2021. On these maps, municipalities that did not experience any damage each year were classified into the lowest range (dark green, 0.1). Cities and counties that experienced flood damage were divided based on the nine quantiles and assigned scores in the range of 0.2 to 1.0 with an interval of 0.1. The amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by cities and counties was collected from the National Disaster Safety Portal of the Ministry of the Interior and Safety and was calculated by combining the damage to private and public facilities by cities and counties. In addition, damage to facilities such as ships, fishing nets, fishing gear, and ports that are not related to flooding was excluded. In South Korea, flood damages by local governments are systematically recorded annually, which is used to improve the accuracy of the GA-based weights. However, in other countries where statistics on flood damages are not well established, data on damages such as loss of life can be used instead. Considering the flood damage situation in cities and counties from 2016–2021, significant damage occurred in local governments that experienced heavy rainfall or were within the area of influence of typhoons that approached the Korean Peninsula. In 2016, damage from Typhoon Chaba and heavy rainfall occurred mainly in cities and counties within Gangwon-do and Gyeongsang-do provinces. In 2017, heavy rains in the central region caused significant damage to Cheongju City, Chungcheongbuk-do, and Incheon Metropolitan City. In 2018, typhoons such as Kong-rey, Soulik, and Prapiroon, and torrential rain caused damage to cities and counties within the Gyeonggi-do, Gangwon-do, Jeollanam-do, and Gyeongsang-do provinces. In 2019, owing to the impact of Typhoon Mitag, damage was limited to cities and counties adjacent to the coast within Gangwon-do and Gyeongsang-do provinces. In 2020, typhoons BAVI, MAYSAK, and HAISHEN, as well as heavy rains caused by a massive seasonal rain front, caused significant damage to most cities and counties across the country. Finally, in 2021, flood damage due to Typhoon Chanthu and localized heavy rainfall concentrated in the southern region occurred in cities and counties located in Jeollanam-do and Gyeongsangnam-do provinces. There are several characteristics of the flood damage caused by each of the 161 cities and counties during 2016–2021: First, large-scale flood damage occurred in two-year intervals (2016, 2018, and 2020) across the country. In addition, cities, and counties adjacent to the coast of Gangwon and Gyeongsang provinces, which overlapped with the typhoon's path of movement, experienced a high frequency and scale of flood damage. Furthermore, 2020 was the most damaging of the six years owing to the impact of multiple typhoons and seasonal rain fronts.  3.2 Calculation of indicator indices at the municipal level The Hazard item of the flood risk index comprised frequency-based rainfall and maximum rainfall. Frequency-based rainfall was calculated by applying the probability-weighted moment and Gumbel distribution to calculate point-level frequency-based rainfall (100-year frequency, duration 24 h, mm) using the 30-year maximum rainfall (duration 24 h, mm) data for each station. For maximum rainfall, we used the maximum rainfall data from the stations for each year. Subsequently, point-level frequency-based rainfall and maximum rainfall were gridded by applying ordinary kriging with an exponential variogram, and area-level frequency-based rainfall and maximum rainfall were calculated by averaging the rainfall grid cells within the administrative boundaries of each city and county. Finally, the frequency-based rainfall index and maximum rainfall index for 2016–2021 were calculated by scoring each quantile interval using ten quantiles. Fig. 9   shows the frequency-based rainfall index and maximum rainfall index at the municipal level for 2016–2021. Looking at the frequency-based rainfall index and maximum rainfall index by municipalities for 2016–2021, the frequency-based rainfall index was largely calculated in Seoul, northern Gyeonggi-do, Gangwon-do, and Jeju-do provinces, and the range of variation in the index by year was small. However, the maximum rainfall index showed a large variation over the years owing to the impact of heavy rainfall and typhoons. Typhoon Chaba in 2016, Typhoon Kong-rey in 2018, Typhoon Maysak in 2020, and Typhoon Chanthu in 2021 had significant impacts on the maximum rainfall index of the municipality. In addition, the localized heavy rainfall and seasonal rain fronts that occur in Korea also contribute to the large annual variation in the maximum rainfall index at the municipal level. For the Exposure item, the indicator index was calculated using the national 500 m × 500 m grid data built using indicators and statistical data for 161 municipalities selected by overlapping the national, local, and small river flood risk maps by grid cells. The grid cells for each indicator overlapped with the flood risk maps, and the grid-level flood damage rates were applied to the grid-level attribute values to aggregate statistics such as buildings, population, and area of farmland directly exposed to flood risk by municipalities. Fig. 10   shows the number of buildings, registered resident population, official land value, and farmland area indices by municipalities for 2016–2021. Unlike the maximum rainfall index for the Hazard item, the indicator indices for the Exposure item did not significantly change from year to year.
