In general, statistics on the number of buildings and registered residents, which are indicators of the Exposure item, cannot increase or decrease significantly in a short period of time; therefore, this feature was reflected in the indicator index. Compared to other indicators, official land values show a clear trend of yearly increase in the index, centered on municipalities with a high concentration of buildings and population. Similar to the Exposure item, the Vulnerability item was selected by overlapping the grid data for each indicator with the flood risk map, and the indicator index for each of the 161 municipalities was calculated. Fig. 11   shows the number of old buildings, number of dependent people, and index of fields, greenhouses, and ginseng cultivation areas by municipalities for 2016–2021. The indicators in the Vulnerability item are composed of those in the Exposure item that are more vulnerable to flood risk. The dependent people, who are the vulnerable registered residents, are under seven years old and over 65 years of age. The old buildings are composed of buildings that are more than 20 years old after completion of construction. In addition, fields, greenhouses, and ginseng are more vulnerable to flood risks among crops grown on farmland. Therefore, the statistical values of the indicators by municipality in the Vulnerability item were smaller than those in the Exposure item; however, the distribution of the indicator indices by municipality showed a similar pattern. In municipalities where the number of buildings and registered residents is large, the number of old buildings and dependent residents is also high. In addition, since the number of old buildings and dependent people (elderly population) exhibited an increase over time, the indices for each indicator increased significantly in many cities and counties in 2021 compared to 2016, in line with the recent phenomenon of a low birth rate and an aging population. The indicator index for the Capacity item was calculated based on yearly statistics at the municipal level, rather than grid data. In addition, the disaster prevention facility density and cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio indices were reversed before creating a statistical map. Fig. 12   shows the distribution of the indicator indices for disaster prevention facility density and the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio at the municipal level for 2016–2021. The density of disaster prevention facilities and the ratio of cumulative disaster prevention budgets at the municipal level showed trends of improvement over time. The cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index shows a noticeable change as disaster prevention budgets continue to accumulate in each municipality. In general, municipalities with a high density of disaster prevention facilities have a high density of buildings and population and a high frequency of flood damage; therefore, local governments have installed large-scale disaster prevention facilities to reduce flood damage. For the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index, the top and bottom municipalities were generally proportional to the disaster prevention facility density index. As these municipalities frequently install new disaster prevention facilities and maintain existing ones, the cumulative disaster prevention budget index is also large.  3.3 Calculation of weighting by indicators When conducting a municipal-level flood risk assessment using IBA, a genetic algorithm was applied to 11 indicators in four items to calculate the weight of each indicator. Entropy weights were calculated as a comparison group for the indicator weights calculated using a genetic algorithm. Genetic algorithm-based weights were calculated such that the sum of the weights of the 11 indicators was one. However, the entropy weight is characterized by separating the indicators by item, such that the sum of the indicator weights within an item is one. Entropy weighting has a different approach to weighting compared to genetic algorithms, because if the entropy weights of all 11 indicators are calculated simultaneously, the weight is skewed toward indicators with large coefficients of variation. Table 2   compares the entropy weights for each indicator used in the 2016–2021 flood risk index with the weights derived using the genetic algorithm. This shows that when the entropy weight is applied to all 11 indicators without separating the indicators by item, the weight is concentrated on the number of registered residents and the official land value, which have large coefficients of variation. In this case, the correct flood risk index at the municipal level could not be obtained, because the indicators in the Hazard item were not properly weighted. Therefore, entropy weights should be calculated by separating the indicators by item, as shown in the table, to properly distribute the weights by indicator. Because genetic algorithms are global optimization algorithms, the genetic-algorithm-based weighting method developed in this study can be applied to calculate the optimal flood risk index that minimizes the sum of absolute errors with the ranking of rainfall and typhoon damage by city and counties during 2016–2021. In this study, chromosomes with the best fitness among the chromosomes generated by the genetic algorithm through more than 30,000 generations of crossover and mutation were used. The results of the genetic algorithm-based weighting in Table 2  show that the maximum rainfall in the Hazard item is significantly weighted; the Exposure item is the number of registered residents and the official land value; the Vulnerability item is the field, greenhouse, and ginseng cultivation area; and the Capacity item is the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio. Table 3   shows the results of the genetic algorithm-based weighting calculation, which is divided into the highest and lowest sections based on the sum of the absolute errors. In the highest section, the sum of the absolute errors fluctuated slightly even if the weight of a particular indicator changed by only 0.001. In contrast, in the lowest section, the weights are concentrated on the number of registered residents, official land value, and number of dependent people, resulting in a very large sum of absolute errors of up to 32,859. Finally, to evaluate the performance of the optimally weighted flood risk index derived by the genetic algorithm, it was compared with the flood risk index calculated by applying the entropy weight and Euclidean distance. The flood risk index selected as the comparison group was calculated by applying entropy weights to the indicator indices to calculate the item indices and then applying the Euclidean distance with the same weighting concept. By comparing the accuracy of the two flood risk indices based on the amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage at the municipal level, the extent of improvement achievable through differences in weighting methods can be observed.  3.4 Flood risk index calculation results at the municipal level Fig. 13   compares the flood risk index calculated by applying entropy weights and Euclidean distances and the flood risk index calculated by genetic algorithm-based weights with heavy rainfall and typhoon damage for 161 municipalities in 2016–2021. In Fig. 13 , comparing the amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by city and county with the flood risk index, the flood risk index calculated by entropy weights and Euclidean distance has a small similarity and does not change significantly from year to year. This is attributed to the application of Euclidean distance, which represents an equal weighting concept, to the four-item indices. As mentioned previously, the indices included in the Exposure and Vulnerability items did not change significantly from year to year. Therefore, when the Euclidean distance is applied, the maximum rainfall index in the Hazard item and the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index in the Capacity item have less impact on the flood risk index. However, the flood risk index calculated by the genetic algorithm showed a high concordance rate compared with the amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by cities and counties. The difference in accuracy between the weighting methods was more pronounced when comparing the absolute error statistics for the rankings of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by year. Table 4   compares the absolute error statistics between the flood risk index ranking derived from each weighting method and the heavy rainfall and typhoon damage ranking. During 2016–2021, a total of 751 municipalities (including duplicates) experienced heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. For the annual flood risk index calculated using genetic algorithm-based weights, the average absolute error at the municipal level was a maximum of 37.450 and a minimum of 17.811. The average absolute error improved for all years compared to the flood risk index based on entropy weights and Euclidean distance. Specifically, in 2017 and 2020, when the GA-based weights were applied, the absolute errors were significantly reduced to 27.42 % and 38.99 %, respectively. Finally, compared to the municipal-level flood risk index calculated by applying entropy weights and Euclidean distance, the sum of absolute errors was reduced by 21.42 %, from 27,025 to 21,234, over the period of 2016–2021. Through this verification, when compared with the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by year, it was confirmed that the accuracy of the flood risk index using genetic algorithm-based weights was significantly improved compared with the conventional weighting method. Therefore, the flood risk assessment method that applies the new weighting method proposed in this study can be used as a useful decision support tool when conducting disaster prevention projects in cities and counties.   4 Discussion 4.1 Review of the causes for large absolute errors in each city and county Table 5   summarizes the statistics for heavy rainfall, typhoon damage, and GA-based flood risk indices for the top three municipalities with large absolute errors by year. Municipalities with large absolute errors can be divided into two types: the first is the case where the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage is high but the ranking of the flood risk index is low, and the second is the case where the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage is low but the ranking of the flood risk index is high. Among the top three municipalities each year, the first type was Yeoju and Bucheon City in Gyeonggi-do Province in 2016, Seoul Metropolitan City in 2018, Taean County in Chungcheongnam-do Province in 2019, Yesan County in Chungcheongnam-do Province in 2020, and Cheongsong County in Gyeongsangbuk-do Province in 2021. The common characteristic of these municipalities is that, except for Taean County in Chungcheongnam-do Province, they all suffered significant damage to public facilities such as rivers and erosion control facilities. However, the indicators in the Exposure and Vulnerability items, which are used to calculate the flood risk index at the municipal level, do not reflect indicators related to public facilities. Public facilities were not included as indicators because the details of river and erosion control facilities are not regularly updated and disclosed by year, making it difficult to build grid data. Consequently, the omission of public facility-related indicators from the flood risk index leads to a large absolute error. In the second type, where the absolute error is large, Jinju City, Gyeongsangnam-do Province, is a typical example of a city with a low ranking in terms of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage but a high ranking in terms of the flood risk index. Jinju City ranked first, with an absolute error of 141 in 2018, third with 102 in 2020, and third with 69 in 2021. In Jinju City, the Namgang River, a tributary of the Nakdong River, flows from west to northeast and has a basin-shaped terrain with plains surrounded by mountains. Therefore, there is a risk of large-scale flood damage in the event of heavy rainfall and typhoons in Jinju City, where downtown areas and farmlands are concentrated around the Namgang River, as shown in Fig. 14  . In 2018, Jinju City's maximum rainfall index was 1, the number of registered residents index was 0.8, and the field, greenhouse, and ginseng cultivation area index was 0.9, ranking it second, with a flood risk index of 0.945. However, the total amount of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage in Jinju City in 2018 was only 980,000 KW. The main reason for this difference is the Namgang Dam, which is a multipurpose dam located in southwestern Jinju. The dam not only provides water for irrigation to farmland downstream of the Namgang River but also contributes to hydropower generation and flood damage reduction. Therefore, even if large-scale heavy rainfall or typhoons occur in Jinju City, there is less risk of river flooding because the Namgang Dam regulates the water level and flow of the Namgang River. In addition, Namgang Dam is connected to Namhae by a Gahwacheon spillway, making it easier to control the amount of flooding compared with other multipurpose dams. However, the flood risk maps for the national, local, and small rivers used in this study were created without considering the flood control capabilities of the Namgang Dam located in Jinju City. Therefore, the area of the flood risk map applied to Jinju City was significantly larger than the actual flooded area, causing the flood risk index to be significantly calculated. As there were similar problems in other municipalities where the absolute error was largely aggregated, it is necessary to improve and supplement these problems in future studies.  4.2 Comparison and assessment of flood risk by municipalities under the same conditions The municipality-level flood risk index was calculated by applying genetic algorithm-based weights to the indices for each of the 11 indicators. Thus, it was possible to simulate the flood risk index if the index for a particular indicator was changed. Fig. 15   and Table 6   compare the flood risk index calculated by reducing the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index to the minimum value of 0.1 for all municipalities in 2020. With improvements in the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index, the flood risk index for all municipalities decreased to less than 0.9. Consequently, municipalities such as Damyang County in Jeollanam-do Province and Inje and Cheorwon County in Gangwon-do Province, which were previously among the top 10, dropped out of the ranking. In addition, as the disaster prevention capabilities of other municipalities improved, municipalities such as Gwangju Metropolitan City and Busan Metropolitan City, which previously ranked high in the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index, increased their flood risk index rankings. As a result, even though the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index was changed to 0.1, the local governments with the highest flood risk indices needed to take countermeasures because the indicator indices included in the other items were significantly calculated. Moreover, municipalities with a significant decrease in the ranking of the flood risk index compared to the previous one have insufficient disaster prevention capabilities; therefore, they need to strengthen their support for flood risk reduction. Fig. 16   and Table 7   show the changes in the flood risk index for the top 10 municipalities when the maximum rainfall index was changed to 1 for all municipalities in 2021. Under the existing flood risk index, the top 10 municipalities are all located in the southern region; however, changing the maximum rainfall index to 1 shifts the ranking of municipalities in various regions to the top. The most notable of these is Dangjin City in Chungcheongnam-do Province, which ranks first with a flood risk index of 0.975. Despite experiencing four heavy rainfall events and typhoon damages over six years (2016, 2019, 2020, 2021), Dangjin City has a highly accurate flood risk index with a sum of absolute error of 39. Looking at the situation In Dangjin City, as of 2021, the indicator indices of the Exposure and Vulnerability items were high, indicating that there were many damage targets directly exposed to flood risk. In addition, the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index (reversed) was 1, indicating a lack of disaster prevention Capacity against flood risk. Dangjin City did not experience any large-scale rainfall events from to 2016–2021, with the largest calculated maximum rainfall index of only 0.5. Therefore, if an extreme rainfall event with a maximum rainfall index of 1 occurs in Dangjin City, there is a risk of significant property and life damage. Thus, local government decision-makers in charge of flood prevention projects should utilize the results of comparing and evaluating the flood risk indices of each city and county under the same conditions to develop measures to reduce flood risk in their jurisdiction.   5 Conclusions In this study, we developed a new flood risk assessment method using a genetic algorithm to conduct a flood risk assessment using national grid data and flood risk maps. The flood risk index, derived by applying genetic algorithm-based weights to 11 indicators consisting of four items (Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability, and Capacity), was used to assess flood risks in 161 municipalities from 2016 to 2021. The analysis provides the following implications: First, a genetic algorithm-based weighting method can enhance the accuracy of municipal-level flood risk indices. In the existing qualitative flood risk assessment, weights were calculated using methods such as entropy weight, AHP, and TOPSIS; however, there were limitations in improving the accuracy of the assessment results during the validation process. In this study, a genetic algorithm was used to derive the optimal weights that minimize the errors between the Flood Risk Index and actual data on heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. As a result, compared to existing methods (i.e., entropy weight and Euclidean distance), the sum of absolute errors decreased up to 38.99 % on an annual basis, and overall 21.42 % during the period of 2016–2021. The GA-based weighting method developed in this study can replace traditional weighting methods in other qualitative risk assessments if reference data are available to evaluate the accuracy of the flood risk index, such as heavy rainfall and typhoon damage by municipalities. Second, our proposed method enables comparing and evaluating flood risk indices across municipalities under the same conditions to better identify their Exposure to flood risk and support decision-making for strengthening disaster prevention capabilities. In fact, when evaluating the flood risk index by municipality under the same conditions, such as the maximum rainfall index and the cumulative disaster prevention budget ratio index for a specific year, we found that certain municipalities, such as Dangjin City in Chungcheongnam-do Province, are more vulnerable to flood risks than others. By leveraging these findings, decision-makers can allocate resources more efficiently, prioritizing their investment in these more vulnerable municipalities to reduce flood risks. Third, we analyzed why absolute errors in some municipalities were high and identified the limitations of our flood risk index. Namely, the index did not reflect indicators related to public facilities; therefore, the flood risk index ranking was lower than the ranking of heavy rainfall and typhoon damage in municipalities with large public facility damage. Additionally, the flood risk map was created without considering the flood control capability of the dam, as in the case of the Namgang Dam in Jinju City, Gyeongsangnam-do Province. Therefore, in certain municipalities, the area of the flood risk map was much larger than the actual inundation area, causing the flood risk index to be too large relative to the heavy rainfall and typhoon damage. We plan to address these limitations in future studies by adding new indicators related to public facilities and revising the flood risk maps. Our municipal-level flood risk assessment method overcomes the limitations of existing studies by enhancing the accuracy and reliability of qualitative flood risk assessments. The flood risk assessment method, which uses the scoring of each quantile interval, damage target selection using flood risk maps and grid data, and a genetic algorithm-based weighting method, can support decision making for reducing flood risk in local governments.
1 Introduction Many coastal communities rely on the freshwater stored in coastal aquifers, which are threatened by seawater intrusion (SWI)—the displacement of fresh groundwater by the landward movement of seawater in coastal aquifers (Werner et al., 2013 ). Growing demands for freshwater, combined with sea-level rise induced by global warming, are aggravating SWI in many places (Michael et al., 2017; Gleeson et al., 2020 ). The invading seawater threatens the sustainability of fresh groundwater resources and can lead to adverse consequences for the environment (Werner, 2010; Mabrouk et al., 2013; Shi and Jiao, 2014 ). Therefore, effective countermeasures are necessary to mitigate seawater intrusion and its negative impacts. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate or reverse SWI. These can be grouped into two categories: water management approaches and engineering interventions (e.g. Werner et al., 2013 ). Water management approaches typically involve the regulation of groundwater extraction (e.g. Werner et al., 2011 ). Guidance may be provided through the application of optimization algorithms, which can inform the ideal locations, rates and timing of pumping to maximize freshwater extraction while minimizing SWI impacts (e.g. Dhar and Datta, 2009; Christelis and Mantoglou, 2019 ). Engineering strategies include artificial freshwater recharge (i.e. through surface infiltration or injection into wells) to create hydraulic barriers to SWI (e.g. Luyun et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2013 ), extraction of seawater from the aquifer (e.g. Kacimov et al., 2009; Pool and Carrera, 2010 ) and construction of subsurface physical barriers (Lu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020a; Yan et al., 2021 ). Among these, artificial recharge is the most prevalent in dealing with practical SWI problems (Werner et al., 2013 ). The scarcity of available freshwater in arid and semi-arid coastal settings, especially in dry seasons, limits access to freshwater for the purposes of developing hydraulic barriers to mitigate SWI. Treated wastewater has been used as an alternative to freshwater to develop hydraulic barriers in some areas (e.g. Foreman, 2003; Thomas et al., 2017 ), although this requires vigilant management to avoid threats to groundwater quality (Foreman, 2003 ). Sun and Semprich (2013)  proposed the injection of compressed air in coastal aquifers to mitigate SWI, thereby precluding the need for freshwater in creating a barrier to SWI. They compared the efficiency of freshwater injection and air injection (at the same injection pressure) for mitigating SWI, and they concluded that although injecting freshwater is more efficient in retreating SWI, air injection remains a viable approach, especially in regions where freshwater resources are limited. Recently, Zang and Li (2021)  explored air injection in a hypothetical unconfined aquifer, again using numerical simulation. Their results showed that although the efficiency of SWI mitigation in unconfined aquifers is reduced compared to its performance in confined aquifers (due to the release of air through the vadose zone), air injection may nevertheless be a viable approach to mitigate SWI in unconfined aquifers. Previous studies of coastal aquifer air injection were based almost entirely on numerical simulation, and no experimental or field studies on the effects of air injection in mitigating SWI have been published previously. To date, the work presented by Dror et al. (2004)  is the only relevant experimental study. They found that the formation of a low-permeability barrier after injecting air could reduce discharge by an order of magnitude or more, but the density effect of seawater was not considered in their study. In other words, they did not evaluate the effect of air injection in coastal scenarios. Thus, laboratory experiments or field tests are needed to explore the applicability of air injection for SWI mitigation, to overcome the uncertainties of numerical simulation, as pointed out by Zang and Li (2021) . Moreover, in a study of artificial freshwater recharge, Luyun et al. (2011)  found that more effective SWI mitigation can be achieved by selecting an appropriate location for the recharge well. Analogous to freshwater recharge, the efficiency of SWI mitigation by air injection can probably be improved by choosing the ideal location for injection. However, the impact of air-injection location on SWI mitigation remains unclear. The current study aims to verify the effectiveness of air injection for mitigating SWI through controlled laboratory experiments and to investigate the impact of the air-injection location on SWI mitigation. A laboratory-scale, two-dimensional (cross-sectional) sand tank was constructed to investigate the changes in saltwater distribution after injecting air. Sand tank experiments were used to validate a numerical model developed using TOUGH2. The model was subsequently applied to the field-scale simulation of air injection in hypothetical coastal confined aquifer scenarios. These were designed to investigate the impact of the air-injection location on SWI mitigation, including the effects of the location of air injection, to add to previous studies (e.g. Sun and Semprich, 2013; Zang and Li, 2021 ) that neglect this design aspect of air-injection barriers to SWI.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Laboratory experiments The experimental setup was intended to represent SWI scenarios in a confined aquifer. The experiments were conducted in a sand tank with internal dimensions: 1.2 m in length, 0.35 m in height, and 0.03 m in width (Fig. 1  ). The narrowness of the tank enabled the simulation of a two-dimensional, cross-sectional system. The sand tank consisted of a porous media chamber and reservoirs at each end. The tank walls comprised transparent acrylic plates. The porous media chamber was filled with quartz sand with a representative grain size (d 50 ) of 1.8 mm. The tank was packed carefully under saturated condition to avoid air-entrainment. Two stainless-steel fine meshes were used to prevent the quartz sand from entering the side reservoirs. The porosity (ϕ ) of the sand was 0.40, as measured by the water saturation method (Fetter, 2018 ). Darcy constant-head tests were conducted to obtain an estimate for the in-situ saturated hydraulic conductivity (K ), producing a value of 0.033 m/s, which is close to the value of 0.031 m/s obtained from applying the Kozeny-Carman equation (Freeze and Cherry, 1979 ). The left-side reservoir was filled with saltwater to represent the coastal boundary, while the right-side reservoir was supplied with freshwater to represent the inland boundary. Sodium chloride (NaCl) was used to produce the saltwater. The densities of the saltwater and freshwater were measured as 1025 kg/m3  and 999.5 kg/m3  using a density meter. The saltwater density was controlled throughout the experiments by monitoring the salinity and adding NaCl every ten minutes at amounts necessary to maintain the saltwater density. After adding NaCl, the water density in the saltwater reservoir was measured again to ensure that it was maintained at 1025 kg/m3 . To distinguish saltwater from freshwater, the saltwater was colored red using Allura Red AC, which has been used successfully as a tracer in previous studies (e.g. Wu et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2021 ). The saltwater boundary head (hs  ) and freshwater boundary head (hf  ) were set to constant values of 0.400 m and 0.414 m, respectively. The porous media chamber had an impervious base, while a removable acrylic plate was bolted to the top, serving as the upper confining layer. Silicone grease was smeared on the joint between the cover plate and sand tank to further prevent water and injected air from escaping. To investigate the effect of the compressed air in controlling SWI, a small hole was drilled on the back of the sand tank, simulating a horizontal well aligned parallel to the coastline. Its location is marked in Fig. 1 . The small hole was connected by a PVC hose to an air pump, which injected compressed air into the sand tank at a constant rate. The inner and outer diameters of the PVC hose were 5 mm and 7 mm, respectively. High-resolution photography of the experiments was undertaken every minute using a digital camera. Prior to the air-injection experiment, a steady-state interface was achieved by applying constant-head boundary conditions (using the above-mentioned heads) to both sides. It took about 5.5 h to reach steady-state conditions, which were verified by checking whether the interface position changed within an hour. The air-injection experiment was performed after the initial steady-state interface was reached. The air-injection rate was fixed at 900 L/h, and continued until a new steady-state condition was achieved. Based on preliminary experiments, it was found that this injection rate can effectively retreat seawater without causing instability near the injection location. Room temperature was 25 °C and remained effectively unchanged during the experimental process.  2.2 Numerical modeling Numerical modeling was undertaken using TOUGH2 (Pruess et al., 1999 ), which can simulate multiphase, multicomponent flow and transport in porous media. The EOS7 module of TOUGH2 was used to simulate two-phase flow with three components (i.e. air, water and brine), as discussed in the following subsection. We first tested the model by comparison to laboratory-scale air-injection barriers, which extended the evaluation of experimental processes from the direct laboratory measurements. Subsequently, a hypothetical field-scale confined aquifer model was developed to study the impact of the air-injection location on the mitigation of SWI. 2.2.1 Governing equations The mathematical model describing two-phase flow is based on mass conservation equations, which can be written as (Pruess et al., 1999 ):(1) d dt   ∫ V n   ϕ M κ    d V n  = ∫ Γ n   F   κ  · n    d Γ n  + ∫ V n   q κ  d V n      where ϕ  is the porosity, Vn   is the volume of the n th  subdomain of the flow system bounded by the closed surface Γn  , κ  is an indicator for the component (a -air, w -water and b -brine), Mκ   is the mass of component κ  (in every phase) per unit volume of porous medium, F  κ   is the mass flux of component κ  into Vn  , n   is the inward unit normal vector on surface element dΓn  , and qκ   denotes sinks and sources of component κ . The mass accumulation term, Mκ  , is:(2) M κ  = ∑ β  S β  ρ β  X β κ       where β  is an indicator for phase (l -liquid and g -gas), S β   is the saturation occupied by phase β , ρ β   is the density of phase β , and X β  κ   is the mass fraction of component κ  in phase β . The mass flux term Fκ    includes both advective and diffusive mass fluxes, which can be written as:(3) F  κ   = - ∑  β   X  β  κ    k k  r β   ρ  β    μ  β     ∇ P  β   - ρ  β   g    - ∑  β   ϕ τ  β   d  β  κ   ρ  β   ∇ X  β  κ       where k  is the intrinsic saturated permeability, kr  β   is the relative permeability of phase β , μ β   is the dynamic viscosity of phase β , P β   is the fluid pressure of phase β , g  is the acceleration of gravity, d β  κ   is the molecular diffusion coefficient of component κ  in phase β , and τ β   is a tortuosity factor related to the saturation of phase β  (S β  ). The second term on the RHS of Eq. (3)  accounts for the molecular diffusion, although its effect is weak in our simulations. TOUGH2/EOS7 does not consider velocity-dependent mechanical dispersion. As an alternative method suggested by Oldenburg and Unger (2004) , numerical dispersion in the model was used to account for velocity-dependent dispersion in our study, as discussed in detail in the next section. The tortuosity factor τβ  is based on the Millington and Quirk (1961)  model, which has been widely used for soil-gas and soil–water modeling (e.g. Jury et al., 1983; Yao et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2020 ), and can be expressed as:(4) τ β  = ϕ 1 / 3    S β 10 / 3       The relative permeability kr  β   is assumed to be a function of phase saturation (Fatt and Klikoff, 1959; Pruess et al., 1999 ):(5) k rl   = S e 3     k rg   = 1 - S e      3          where Se   = (Sl   − Slr  )/(1 − Slr  ), Slr   is the residual liquid saturation, and krl   and krg   are relative permeabilities of the liquid and gas phases, respectively. The fluid pressure of the liquid phase (Pl  ) and the gas phase (Pg  ) are related via the capillary pressure (Pcap  ), as:(6) P l  = P g  + P cap       Note that the capillary pressure is negative (Pcap   < 0). There are several models describing the relationship between capillary pressure and liquid-phase saturation. Here we use the Leverett’s empirical function (Leverett, 1941; Pruess et al., 1999 ) as suggested by Sun and Semprich (2013) , i.e.:(7) P cap   = - ϕ k     1 / 2    σ  1.417 1 - S e      - 2.120 1 - S e      2  + 1.263 1 - S e      3          where σ  is the water–air surface tension. The salt concentration is expected to have a negligible effect on the surface tension of the liquid phase (Jones and Ray, 1941 ), and thus a constant value of 7.2 × 10-2  kg/s2  was assigned to the surface tension in our simulations. The brine was modeled as a NaCl solution, and solid precipitation of NaCl was not considered. The liquid phase was modeled as a mixture of freshwater, brine and a very small amount of dissolved air, while the gas phase consisted of air and water vapor. The density of the liquid phase was calculated as the harmonic mean of freshwater and brine densities, as suggested by Herbert et al. (1988) :(8) 1 ρ l   = 1 - X l b   ρ w   + X l b  ρ b       where Xl b   is the mass fraction of brine in the liquid phase, and ρw   and ρb   are the densities of freshwater and brine, respectively. The liquid phase viscosity μl   is modeled with a polynomial correction that is a function of the viscosity of pure water (μ w  ):(9) μ l  = μ w  1 + 0.4819 X l b  - 0.2774 X l b     2  + 0.7814 X l b     3          where the polynomial coefficients are taken from Herbert et al. (1988) .  2.2.2 Numerical dispersion TOUGH2 uses an upstream weighting method in space and fully implicit discretization in time. This numerical scheme creates numerical dispersion on the order of one-half the grid size multiplied by the groundwater velocity (Oldenburg and Unger, 2004 ), although its value requires numerical testing, as described below. The velocity-dependent numerical dispersion of TOUGH2 provides an alternative method to model the mechanical dispersion (also typically represented as velocity dependent; Tang and Babu, 1979 ); a necessary approach given that TOUGH2 does not simulate mechanical dispersion. To estimate the numerical dispersion in TOUGH2 simulations, model outputs were compared to an analytical solution to calculate the effective mechanical dispersion caused by artificial dispersion, using the same approach as that of Werner (2017a)  who evaluated artificial dispersion in SEAWAT. The Ogata and Banks (1961)  analytical solution was adopted for one-dimensional advection-dispersive transport in a steady-state flow field to calculate solute breakthrough, which was also simulated using the numerical model, thereby inferring the numerical dispersion. The Ogata-Banks (1961) solution is given by:(11) C ′  x ,  t     = 1 2  erfc x - u  t  2 d l b  + α L   u     t        + exp x  u  d l b  + α L   u         erfc x + u  t  2 d l b  + α L   u     t                where αL   is the longitudinal dispersivity, u  is the groundwater velocity, and C ′ is the normalized concentration.  2.2.3 Tank-Scale and Field-Scale models The simulation of laboratory conditions using TOUGH2 involved parameters consistent with the laboratory conditions, including domain size, boundary conditions and hydrogeological parameters, as given in Table 1  . In addition to the tank-scale model, models were established to study the effect of air injection on the extent of seawater in confined aquifers at the field scale. The hydraulic properties of field-scale aquifers were typical of sandy loam (Carsel and Parrish, 1988 ). The parameters used in field-scale models are listed in Table 1 . The model domain of the confined aquifer was 1000 m long and 50 m deep, reflecting a similar aspect ratio to those adopted in previous coastal aquifer studies (e.g. Pool and Carrera, 2011 ). The model was assumed homogenous and isotropic. For the liquid phase, a constant head of 52.75 m was adopted at the inland boundary, while the sea level was assumed 50 m above the aquifer base. This hydraulic gradient is comparable to previous field-scale studies (e.g. Lu and Werner, 2013; Walther et al., 2020 ). For the gas phase, both the inland and coastal boundaries were assigned as fully penetrating water bodies, where the gas phase saturation was fixed as 0, serving as a sink of the injected air. Tidal fluctuations were not considered. The density of seawater was again taken as 1025 kg/m3 , reflecting a salt concentration in seawater of ∼ 35,000 mg/L. Both top and bottom boundaries of the confined aquifer were set to no-flow boundaries. To establish the initial condition, models were run without air injection to obtain the initial freshwater-saltwater distribution. This required about 130 years of simulation from an initially freshwater-filled aquifer. The inland limit of the model was assumed to be a constant-head boundary condition. Both options for the inland boundary (fixed-head and fixed-flux) are likely to deviate from the conditions of real-world systems, depending on various factors, such as the occurrence of surface water bodies (e.g. that might control the groundwater head), the inland limit of the aquifer (e.g. which may be treated as a no-flow condition), and other system characteristics. Model testing showed that a fixed-flux inland boundary may lead to a large, and possibly unrealistic increase of the inland hydraulic head after injecting air (from 52.75 m to 80.30 m). A detailed discussion of boundary effects is presented in Section 3.2.2 . Compressed air was injected into models at a single cell, representing a horizontal well parallel to the coastline (see Fig. 2  ), thereby avoiding the high computational burden of three-dimensional simulation (e.g. Sun and Semprich, 2013; Zang and Li, 2021 ). The sink/source term for air in Eq. (1)  (i.e. qa  ) was used to simulate the air-injection process with a constant rate of the laboratory experiments. In field-scale models, the wellbore diameter was assumed to be 1 m, consistent with the size of the injection cell. Eighteen different air-injection locations were examined to study the impact of injection location on the seawater extent. Table 2   lists the coordinates of air-injection sites. Note that the subscripts of these points represent the elevations. Point B10 , B20 , B30  and B40  have the same horizontal coordinates but different elevations (10, 20, 30 and 40 m, respectively) to analyse the impact of the vertical location of the injection well on SWI mitigation (the same goes for Points E10  to E40 , H10  to H40 ), while Points A10 , B10 , …, H10  and I10  have the same elevation (10 m above the aquifer base) but alternative horizontal location to study the impact of the horizontal position of the injection well. Air was injected at a fixed rate in laboratory experiments (consistent with the apparatus), whereas it was injected using a fixed air pressure in the field-scale models that was realized by fixing the pressure of the injecting cell. This is for reasons of practicality, in that it would be difficult in a real-world setting to ensure that air is injected at the same rate everywhere along a horizontal well. The air-injection pressure of field-scale models was set to 550 kPa (relative pressure). This ensured that it was higher than the initial steady-state maximum water pressure over the injected locations (i.e. 405 kPa at Point I10 ). The period over which air injection occurred was set to 1 year. The elevations of air-injection wells were selected to be higher than the aquifer base, rather than at the aquifer base, because otherwise a fully penetrating barrier formed (this was tested in preliminary experiments; results omitted for brevity). This reduced the flushing of seawater from the aquifer, causing seawater to be effectively trapped on the landward side of the air-injection well. This is, in part, a consequence of the two-dimensional model domain, whereby the flushing effect of fresh groundwater flow parallel to the coast (and the barrier axis) is omitted. The reduction of freshwater discharge also diminished the mitigation effect on the region of saltwater originally located on the seaward side of the air-injection well. This occurred because the flushing effect of freshwater discharge to the sea was effectively eliminated in the case of a fully penetrating air injection barrier. Moreover, Chang et al. (2019)  pointed out that a reduction of freshwater discharge toward the sea would lead to the accumulation of land-based pollutants. Therefore, we have avoided the situation of a full penetrating barrier to groundwater discharge given that these have shown reduced effectiveness in practical applications. The model adopted a variable grid spacing. For the tank-scale model, the grid size represented a balance between accuracy (i.e. the reduction of numerical dispersion) and computational burden (i.e. run times). The narrow mixing zones of the laboratory results indicated that dispersion effects were small, thereby requiring small grid spacings. After running some preliminary simulations, we found that the vertical grid spacing (Δz ) had a bigger impact on the width of the mixing zone compared to that of the horizontal grid spacing (Δx ). Thus, the tank-scale model domain was divided evenly into 100 layers (i.e. Δz  = 3.5 mm), while the finest horizontal grid spacing of 3.5 mm was applied near the air-injection well, with the remainder of the model domain discretised using larger spacings, up to a maximum spacing of 10 mm, resulting in a total of 12,500 cells. This led to model run times of up to 15 days on an Intel® Xeon® W-2102 CPU, which was a limiting factor in the grid design. For the field-scale models, the seawater wedge did not extend more than 400 m from the sea boundary, and thus, that region adopted a refined grid, with cells that ranged in size from 1 m × 1 m (around the air injection area) to 2 m × 2 m (see Figure S1  in the Supporting Information ). The model domain beyond 400 m from the sea boundary had horizontal grid spacings that increased gradually from 2 m to 5 m, with vertical discretization of 1 m to 2 m (consistent across the model). The total number of cells in the field-scale model was 10,991, leading to model run times of around 24 h on an Intel® Xeon® W-2102 CPU. It should be noted that the run time of TOUGH2 largely depended on the number of cells that underwent phase change from saturated to unsaturated conditions during the simulation. Although the number of cells in tank-scale models was comparable to those of the field-scale models, a larger proportion of cells in the tank-scale models underwent phase change, resulting in much longer run times. The evaluation of artificial dispersion used four one-dimensional numerical models to infer the longitudinal dispersivities (αL  ) in both directions (i.e. x  and z  directions) of tank-scale and field-scale models. The parameters adopted in these models are summarized in the Supporting Information  (Table S1 ). Because numerical dispersion depends on the model grid size, each one-dimensional model adopted the same grid resolution as that used along a flow pathway within either the tank-scale or field-scale models. For example, Model 1 (see Table S1 ) adopted the same grid spacing as the horizontal grid spacing of the field-scale model to estimate the numerical dispersion in the x -direction for the relevant grid resolution and scale. Boundary and initial conditions were consistent with the analytical model presented by Ogata and Banks (1961) , namely the aquifer was initially uncontaminated, with fixed normalized concentrations of 1 and 0 at the upstream and downstream boundaries, respectively. Based on the results from these models (see Figure S2 ; Supporting Information ), we inferred that αL   was 1 m in both directions of field-scale models, while αL   in the x -direction and z -direction of tank-scale models was 5.5 mm and 3.0 mm, respectively. The transverse dispersivity (αT  ) for the field-scale models was estimated as 0.166 m using the approach outlined in Section S1 (Supporting Information ). The grid Peclet number (Pe ), usually considered as an indication of the adequacy of the grid size for solute transport simulation, is defined by Voss and Souza (1987) , as:(12) Pe = u  Δ x 2  + Δ z 2     D H   = u  Δ x 2  + Δ z 2     d l b  + α L   u       where DH   is the hydrodynamic dispersion coefficient. In the current study, the value of Pe  taking into account the anticipated artificial dispersion in TOUGH2 ranges from 1.9 to 3.5 in tank-scale models (u  = 1 × 10-5  to 2 × 10-3  m/s, Δx  = 0.01 m, Δz  = 0.0035 m, dl b   = 1 × 10-9  m2 /s, αL  =3 to 5.5 mm) and 2.8 in field-scale models (u  = 1 × 10-7  to 1 × 10-5  m/s, Δx  = 2 m, Δz  = 2 m, d l  b   = 1 × 10-9  m2 /s, αL  =1 m), both of which satisfy the critical criterion of Pe  ≤ 4 for TOUGH2 (Javeri, 2003 ). Thus, the current schemes of grid spacing were considered acceptable for our study. In seeking to relate the tank-scale setup to field-scale parameters, three dimensionless parameters were defined, as in previous studies (Abarca et al., 2007; Meakin et al., 2000 ):(13) a = q f  K  ρ b  - ρ w   ρ w         (14) b = α L  B      (15) B o  = ρ l  - ρ g     g ε 2   σ      Here, a  is a mixed-convection ratio comparing the freshwater flux to the characteristic buoyancy flux (Abarca et al., 2007 ), b  is a form of the Peclet number (Abarca et al., 2007 ), and Bo   is the Bond number relating buoyancy forces to capillary forces (Meakin et al., 2000 ). Also, qf   is the seaward specific freshwater discharge, B  is the aquifer thickness, and ε  is the typical grain size of the porous medium (Meakin et al., 2000 ).    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Experimental results Fig. 3   presents photographs of the initial and final (following air injection) steady-state saltwater distributions from the sand tank experiment. Steady-state conditions were achieved 40 min after the start of air injection. The freshwater-saltwater mixing zone appears to be rather narrow, indicating that the effect of hydrodynamic dispersion was weak in the experiment. Air injection caused saltwater retreat to occur, whereby the saltwater toe shifted from 59.0 cm to 40.0 cm from the saltwater reservoir. Saltwater retreat following air injection is consistent with the modeling study of Sun and Semprich (2013) , who first showed the mitigating effects of air injection. The results of the sand tank numerical model are also presented in Fig. 3 . The green lines in Fig. 3  represent the 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 isochlors, which are normalized salt concentrations. The 0.5 isochlor is in good agreement with the experimental results, although the lower part of the 0.5 isochlor after injecting air was a little seaward of the experimental result. The 0.1 and 0.9 isochlors show a more dispersive mixing zone relative to that of the experiments, especially in the final steady-state condition after injecting air. The more dispersive mixing zone in the numerical model can be attributed to numerical dispersion, which was estimated to be equivalent to a longitudinal dispersivity (αL  ) ranging from 3 to 5.5 mm, as discussed in Section 2.2.3 . It is expected that the true longitudinal dispersivity would be lower, as the longitudinal dispersivity of the same sand was found to be 0.5 mm in previous studies (Yan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Although a narrower mixing zone would be possible with a finer grid, excessive model run times would be required (see Section 2.2.3 ). The landward extent of the 0.5 isochlor toe after injecting air in the numerical model was about 37.2 cm from the saltwater reservoir, which was shorter than the experimental result (i.e. 40.0 cm from the saltwater reservoir). Previous studies have shown that higher dispersion typically leads to shorter toe lengths (e.g. Badaruddin et al., 2017; Werner, 2017b ), and therefore, numerical dispersion in TOUGH2 is the likely cause of this mismatch. The volume of the initial saltwater wedge in our laboratory test was 775 cm3 , estimated by multiplying the area of the visible red zone, the width of the tank (i.e. 3 cm) and the porosity (ϕ  = 0.4). After injecting air, the saltwater volume changed to 509 cm3 , decreasing by 34.3 %. In our numerical model, volumes of the saltwater before and after injecting air were 790 cm3  and 527 cm3  (decreasing by 33.3 %), respectively, exhibiting a favorable agreement with the experimental results.  3.2 Field-Scale confined aquifer simulations 3.2.1 Initial conditions before air injection Fig. 4   presents the steady-state distribution of normalized salt concentrations before air injection in the field-scale simulation, which served as an initial condition for the subsequent air-injection simulations. Points for air injection in the various scenarios are also shown. The extent of seawater in the aquifer (i.e. the toe location according to the 0.1 isochlor) prior to air injection was 208 m from the coastal boundary, showing the classical buoyancy-driven wedge shape.  3.2.2 Impact of horizontal locations of Air-Injection wells on SWI mitigation Examples of the transient development of the saltwater distribution within the field-scale aquifer, following air injection, are given in the Supporting Information , Figure S3 . Results show that the volume of seawater continuously decreased as the air-injection time increased from 1 year to 10 years, while a growing portion of the aquifer domain became unsaturated. After injecting air for 10 years, most of the aquifer domain within 400 m from the seawater boundary was unsaturated (see Figure S3 b4). This is considered a disadvantageous effect of air injection, indicating that such an air-injection system may not be suitable for long-term operation, because otherwise, fresh groundwater extraction wells may be rendered inoperable by desaturation. Thus, the current study examines the development of the air-injection barrier and its performance in mitigating SWI, as a relatively short-term (1 year) intervention measure. Long-term operation of an air-injection system would need to ensure that desaturation did not impact production wells, likely requiring the cessation of air injection during periods of higher recharge and freshwater inputs. Otherwise, an air-escape well may be needed to allow continuous air circulation through the aquifer. These options are beyond the scope of the current study, partly due to the two-dimensional nature of the analysis that precludes assessment of the radial-flow effects of extraction wells. An evaluation of the transience of the field-scale saltwater wedge indicated that all cases in our study did not reach steady-state conditions after the 1-year simulation period, as expected given the 10-year results described above. Two quantitative indicators were selected to assess the effect of air injection: 0.1 seawater isochlor toe position and the total volume of seawater per unit length of coastline, which assisted in providing quantitative comparison (between modelling cases) of the conditions following 1 year of air injection. Another three quantitative indicators were used to evaluate the efficiency of air injection: total mass of injected air, air discharge ratio (i.e. the ratio of the mass of discharged air to the mass of injected air) and the total mass of discharged water through the inland boundary. All masses are given as cumulative values obtained during 1 year of air injection. The values of the indicators obtained from the different cases are summarized in Table 3  . Two representative cases (i.e. Cases B10  and E10 ) were selected to illustrate the impact of the air-injection location on the transient distribution of the seawater wedge during 1 year of air injection. The spatiotemporal variations in the seawater concentration and the liquid saturation in these two cases are presented in Fig. 5   (Case E10 ) and Fig. 6   (Case B10 ). In the early stages of air injection (see Fig. 5 b1, 5b2 and Fig. 6 b1, 6b2), the injected air flowed upwards due to buoyancy forces. Upward flow occur immediately downstream of the injection well, as a consequence of the ambient flow towards the sea. On reaching the upper boundary, the injected air displaced pore water within the upper part of the aquifer, creating downward flows of pore water in the upper aquifer towards both the left and right boundaries. The enhanced groundwater flow towards the sea boundary and the increase in the freshwater head resulted in retreat of the seawater wedge tip. As the compressed air continued to be injected, continuous bodies of gas formed barriers between the air-injection well and the top confining layer in both cases (see Fig. 5 b4, 5b5 and Fig. 6 b4, 6b5). The buoyancy-driven rise in air from the injection well allowed a region of the aquifer to remain saturated beneath the well, where substantial flow towards the sea occurred. In Case E10 , once the gas barrier was formed above the initial seawater wedge toe, the convergence of pore water discharge beneath the well drove the seawater wedge toe back rapidly towards the coastal boundary (see Fig. 5 a4 and 5a5). In Case B10 , the gas barrier was formed within the seawater wedge, creating a stronger response in the wedge to injection (and the displacement of freshwater in the upper aquifer), greatly reducing the total volume of seawater relative to Case E10  (see Fig. 6 a4 and 6a5). To test the influence of the specified-head inland boundary on the air-injection barrier performance, we obtained the flux at the inland boundary in the fixed-head case (without air injection) and adopted this as a distributed, fixed flux at the inland boundary. Case E10  was then re-run with a fixed-flux rather than fixed-head condition at the inland boundary. The distributions of the seawater wedge, gas saturation and water pressure after 1 year of air injection for the fixed-flux and fixed-head boundaries are shown in the Supporting Information , Figure S4 . The resulting toe location in the constant-flux condition was 167 m, similar to that obtained using the constant-head condition (i.e. 170 m). The air-occupied area in the constant-flux condition was smaller relative to the constant-head condition (see Figures S4a2 and S4 b2) due to the upstream-imposed influx boundary forcing the groundwater head to rise in response to the reduced transmissivity caused by the barrier. This is clearly apparent by comparing the hydraulic head distributions of the fixed-head and fixed-flux cases (Figures S4a3 and S4 b3). As shown in Figure S4 b3, the hydraulic head at the inland boundary increased dramatically from 52.75 m to 80.30 m. It is likely that in real-world (i.e. three-dimensional) situations, such a high hydraulic head would alter the regional groundwater flow field causing flow parallel to the barrier (i.e., parallel to the coast), which is not captured in cross-sectional models. A reduction in the rate of seaward freshwater flow would also be expected at the inland boundary due to the resistance to flow to the sea imposed by the barrier. Nevertheless, the considerable head increase at the inland boundary highlights the need to consider whether any wells installed in the aquifer may become flowing artesian (i.e. the head exceeds the land surface) during establishment of the air barrier. Fig. 7   shows the relationship between the seawater volume in field-scale aquifers and the horizontal locations of air-injection wells placed at 10 m above the aquifer base. Four cases were considered where the injection well was located inside the initial seawater wedge (i.e. Case A10 , B10 , C10  and D10 ; Fig. 4 ), as defined by the steady-state, pre-injection, 0.1 isochlor. The seawater wedge volume reduced in all cases compared with the initial condition. Apart from Case A10 , changes in the x -coordinate of the injection well led to a monotonic variation in the seawater volume, with a maximum value of 711 m2  (i.e. a decrease in the seawater volume of 46.7 % relative to the condition prior to air injection) in Case I10  and a minimum value of 405 m2  (decreased by 69.6 %) in Case B10 . Clearly, injecting air inside the initial seawater wedge had the beneficial effect of direct displacement of seawater (as shown in Fig. 6 a5) that led to stronger reductions in seawater volume. In Case A10 , the injection well was close to the seawater boundary, causing injected air to escape from the aquifer through the seaward boundary. This reduced the effectiveness of air injection in Case A10 , as evidenced by the larger seawater volume after 1 year relative to Case B10 . Thus, there appears to be an optimum lateral distance from the coast for placing the air-injection well. Fig. 8   presents a comparison of 0.1 seawater isochlors after 1 year of air injection in Cases A10  to I10 . The isochlors in Fig. 8  show consistent results with the seawater volumes given in Fig. 7 , whereby air-injection locations outside the initial seawater wedge (as shown in Fig. 8 b) caused the 0.1 seawater isochlors to be pushed back to the seawater boundary after injecting air for 1 year. Similarities in the 0.1 isochlor positions in Cases F10  to I10  indicate insensitivity to the injection location for injection positions landward of the initial toe location. The interface location in Case E10  is similar to that of Cases F10  to I10 , except the toe length retreated seaward in Case E10 . This is because the air barrier in Case E10  was formed above the initial toe location (as shown in Fig. 5 ), leading to a localized effect on the toe. For the cases in which air-injection occurred inside the initial 0.1 seawater isochlor, the resulting 0.1 seawater isochlors were modified substantially (see Fig. 8 a). In all cases, the 0.1 isochlor remained seaward of the initial condition, although in Case A10 , which was closest to the seaward boundary, the 0.1 isochlor toe was virtually coincident with the initial condition. The seawater wedge toe in Cases A10  to D10  (Fig. 8 a) was more landward for injection locations closer to the seaward boundary. The total mass of injected air during 1 year of operation decreased dramatically from 93.4 × 104  kg/m in Case A10  to 4.96 × 104  kg/m in Case I10  (see Table 3 ). This is because the closer the air-injection well is to the seaward boundary, the easier it is for the injected air to escape to the sea, as evidenced by the air discharge ratio which decreased from 99.6 % in Case A10  to 71.3 % in Case I10 . Although the seawater volume after 1 year of air injection in Case B10  was the lowest value of these cases (i.e. Cases A10  to I10 ), the total mass of injected air was several times larger than those cases where the air-injection well was placed farther from the seaward boundary. In practical applications, the economic viability of implementing air injection to mitigate SWI is a crucial aspect that demands further evaluation. In the study conducted by Zang et al. (2023) , a simulation–optimization framework was developed to ascertain the optimal design of an air injection system in a three-dimensional coastal aquifer. Their findings revealed that, in order to achieve a 30-m retreat of the 0.5 seawater isochlor, approximately 6.5 × 105  kg of air per unit length of coastline needed to be injected during the first year. Comparison with our study's results, as presented in Table 3 , suggests that the mass of injected air in the majority of cases have a similar order of magnitude. As the location of the air-injection well was shifted landward, more injected air was retained in the aquifer (rather than being released to the coastal boundary), and more freshwater was displaced and discharged from the landward boundary (Table 3 ). Whether this is advantageous or not depends on the extent of desaturation of the aquifer caused by the displacement of water by air, versus the location of pumping wells. That is, the region occupied by air within the coastal aquifer needs to be limited to sites where freshwater pumping does not occur, because otherwise, wells will become inoperable. Thus, from this perspective, there is an advantage to the coastal release of the injected air, in that the barrier can be maintained in the longer term without continuing to desaturate the aquifer. The same effect could likely be created by installing a gas-release well in the upper part of the aquifer. However, it is also important to consider the tradeoff between the effectiveness of reducing seawater volume and the potential loss of injected air. Injecting air closer to the sea boundary can reduce more seawater volume, but it also increases the loss of injected air and consequently the total mass of injected air (Table 3 ). This tradeoff needs to be carefully evaluated in conjunction with local groundwater management requirements to determine the optimal location for air injection.  3.2.3 Impact of vertical locations of air-injection wells on SWI mitigation Fig. 9   shows the distributions of soil-gas saturation and 0.1 seawater isochlors in Cases E10 , E20 , E30  and E40  after 1 year of air injection. As can be seen, continuous bodies of gas occupied the upper part of the aquifer, which constrained the groundwater to flow beneath the gas bodies. As the elevation of the injection well increased from 10 m to 30 m (see Fig. 9 a, 9b and 9c), the air-occupied area became larger. That is, more pore water originally stored in the aquifer was displaced by the injected air, promoting the retreat of the seawater wedge (marked as white lines in Fig. 9 a, 9b and 9c) and the outward discharge of freshwater through the landward boundary (increased from 105.8 × 104  kg/m in Case E10  to 183.0 × 104  kg/m in Case E30 ; see Table 3 ). As the applied air-injection pressure was fixed in these cases (i.e. 550 kPa), injection wells placed at higher elevations corresponded to a lower ambient water pressure, leading to larger masses of injected air due to the lower resistance from the ambient groundwater (see Table 3 ) and stronger air pressure gradient. In Case E40  (see Fig. 9 d), the air injection well was close to the top confining layer, and thus much of the injected air flowed laterally beneath the top confining layer, before exiting via the lateral boundaries, thereby limiting the extent of the air-occupied area. This highlights the need to moderate the injection pressure depending on the submerged depth (and therefore the ambient groundwater pressure) of the injection point. Fig. 10   shows the relationship between the seawater volume and the vertical locations of air-injection wells placed at three different distances from the seaward boundary (x  = 80 m, 200 m and 320 m) after injecting air for 1 year. Reductions in seawater volume differed with the vertical location of the air-injection well in a similar way for all three x -positions. That is, the seawater volume after 1 year differed significantly between 10 m and 20 m elevations, whereas the sensitivity of the seawater volume to the injection well elevation tended to decrease for injection wells of higher elevation. The resulting seawater toe lengths in the cases shown in Fig. 10  were consistent with the volume trends. That is, after 1 year of air injection, smaller toe lengths were obtained for air-injection wells of higher elevations (which led to larger air influxes), as shown in Table 4  . For a given vertical location of the injection well, the smallest seawater volume was obtained when injecting air at 80 m from the seaward boundary (i.e. red line in Fig. 10 ), but the 0.1 isochlor toe lengths in these cases (i.e. Cases B10  to B40 ) were further landward than the other cases (see Table 4 ). This is because air barriers formed on the seaward side of the seawater wedge toe in these cases (i.e. Cases B10  to B40 ), thereby displacing much more seawater than the other cases. However, the convergence of pore water discharge beneath the air barrier caused some of the seawater to be left on the inland side of the barrier (see Fig. 6 a5), reducing the beneficial effect of the barrier in terms of the retreat of the toe location. The mass of injected air of these cases increased in an approximately linear fashion with the elevation of the injection well when it was raised from 10 m to 30 m from the aquifer base. However, the injected air mass increased only slightly when the well elevation raised from 30 m to 40 m (see Table 3 ). This phenomenon can be attributed to the proximity of the injection well elevation to the top of the aquifer. As the well elevation raised from 30 to 40 m, the injected air reached the top boundary more rapidly, encountering greater resistance from the top boundary, which limited the further increase in the amount of injected air compared to the increase observed when the well elevation was raised from 10 to 30 m. The total mass of groundwater that flowed out of the model domain through the landward boundary during 1 year of air injection also increased significantly with the injection well placed at a higher elevation (Table 3 ). Given that lower air pressure would likely be applied to wells that are situated higher in the aquifer, an additional analysis using a fixed rate of air injection (rather than fixed air pressure) would enhance the current evaluation of the effects of well vertical placement on its performance as a SWI barrier.  3.2.4 Laboratory versus Field-Scale conditions The dimensionless parameters a , b  and Bo   allow for comparison of key controlling processes between the laboratory and field-scale conditions. Table 5   presents dimensionless parameters for both the laboratory case and field-scale conditions (Cases E10  to E40 ). Note that qf   and va   were time-dependent parameters during the air-injection process. We adopted final steady-state (after injecting air) values for the laboratory conditions, while values of the last time-step (i.e. after 1 year) were used in assigning values to dimensionless parameters for the field-scale conditions. The comparison of dimensionless numbers in Table 5  shows that the field-scale models involved higher seaward freshwater fluxes relative to buoyancy forces, on the basis of a . This arises because the buoyancy forces are the same in both field and laboratory scales and yet greater fluxes occur in the field-scale cases. The dispersive Peclet number b  in the laboratory condition was an order of magnitude lower than values arising from the field-scale models. This is consistent with the narrow mixing zone observed in laboratory experiments whereas the dispersion was higher in field-scale cases (because of the numerical dispersion that arose from larger cells, which is also consistent with higher dispersiveness arising from natural heterogeneities; Gelhar et al., 1992 ), which led to more dispersive plumes at the field scale. The Bond number (Bo  ) for the laboratory condition was one order of magnitude higher than for the field-scale conditions (Table 5 ), which is due to the relatively large grain size used in the laboratory experiments. The small value of Bo   for field-scale conditions indicates that capillary forces were dominant and the displacement of pore water was likely to occur in the form of capillary fingers (Liu et al., 2013 ). The capillary fingering in practical cases may result in a smaller air-occupy area and a lower displacement efficiency (compared to our simulation results). This may diminish the effect on SWI mitigation, as less groundwater may be displaced during barrier formation, but the barrier effect of air injection that constrained the seaward freshwater discharge to the lower part of the aquifer can still serve to mitigate SWI.    4 Conclusions Sand tank experiments undertaken in this study to explore the effects of air injection on the seawater wedge within a coastal confined aquifer showed that the saltwater toe retreated from 59 cm to 40 cm after injecting air, providing the first physical evidence, in the form of laboratory experiments, for the effectiveness of air injection in mitigating SWI. Numerical simulations provided a reasonable match to the laboratory observations of seawater wedge, offering evidence of the validity of both the numerical model and the laboratory experiments. Field-scale models provided new insights into the effect of the injection well location on the seawater wedge response to air injection. Field-scale simulations demonstrated that the efficiency of mitigating SWI by injecting compressed air varied considerably with injected location. The largest seaward shift in the seawater wedge toe was obtained when the air-injection well was above the original seawater wedge toe, while the optimal reduction in the seawater volume within the aquifer was obtained when the injection well was inside the original seawater wedge. Numerical simulations also showed that in confined aquifers, if the air-injection pressure was fixed, better seawater retreat was obtained when the injection well was installed at higher elevations. We find that although the method can be effective in mitigating SWI, careful operation of the system is needed to avoid extensive aquifer desaturation, the conversion of wells to flowing artesian conditions in the case of confined aquifers and potential damages to aquifer induced by air injection (e.g., changes on chemical properties and soil structures of the aquifer). These potential risks of air injection were raised for the first time, and should be systemically evaluated when planning air-injection systems. While the current study investigated air injection into homogeneous aquifers, natural geologic formations are virtually always heterogeneous. This is likely to create preferential flow paths for the injected air (e.g. Ji et al., 1993 ), which may impact the effectiveness of the method in real-world settings. Moreover, potential air leakage risks through the overlying layer as well as geochemical reactions and possible impacts on the ecological environment induced by introducing oxygen should be evaluated to ensure the safety of air injection. The efficiency of SWI mitigation by air injection under the impact of preferential pathways and other aquifer configurations are areas worthy of further investigation, as is the analysis of air injection within three-dimensional situations, to build on the two-dimensional analysis of idealized aquifers in the current study.
1 Introduction Chemical weathering regulates the global carbon cycle through a negative feedback mechanism, maintaining the long-term habitability of the planet (Walker et al., 1981; Berner et al., 1983 ). Silicate weathering was thought to be a long-term carbon sink on million-year scales, potentially contributing to global cooling since the late Cenozoic (Westerhold et al., 2020 ). In contrast, carbonate weathering can exert a significant impact on carbon budget at short time scales (102  to 104  years) (Beaulieu et al., 2012; Torres et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018 ) and is sensitive to tectonic, climatic and hydrological changes (Jacobson and Blum, 2000; Zeng et al., 2019 ), due to its rapid dissolution kinetics (Lasaga, 1984; Meybeck, 1986 ). It means that carbonate weathering may be a core mechanism of the Earth's Critical Zone in response to modern global change (Gaillardet et al., 2019 ). In the context of global warming, extreme weather and hydrological events have occurred frequently, such as droughts, storms, and debris flow (IPCC, 2022; King et al., 2023 ), significantly mobilizing the transport and cycling of surface materials. For example, Leyland et al. (2017)  revealed that extreme flood events driven by tropical cyclones during 2013 have caused a twofold increase in bank erosion volumes and a fourfold increase in suspended sediment volumes in the Mekong River. Moreover, Baynes et al. (2023)  reported that a 3-hour rainfall-induced extreme flood enhanced erosion in the upper Swale River catchment during 2019, with sediment production and export exceeding two orders of magnitude (∼100 times) more than the typical long-term average. Owing to intense hydrodynamic force during extreme flood events, extremely high runoff and erosion would facilitate rock denudation and weathering, especially for carbonate weathering (e.g., Galy and France-Lanord, 1999; Jacobson and Blum, 2000; Hren et al., 2007; Bufe et al., 2021 ). However, how carbonate weathering responds to extreme weather or hydrological events remains elusive, in particular at regions with high erosion as the marginal area of the Tibetan Plateau. Indeed, whether carbonate weathering flux increases with physical erosion is still in debate (e.g., Gaillardet et al., 1999; Hren et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2014; Bufe et al., 2021 ). Studies of high-temporal resolution variations of river water chemistry can minimize the uncertainties in tracing chemical weathering caused by spatial and lithological variability, allowing a more direct assessment of the response of chemical weathering to climatic parameters, in particular to storm events (Jin et al., 2011; Zhi et al., 2020; Gou et al., 2023 ). To date, examples of carbonate weathering in response to storm events are scarce based on high-temporal resolution sampling, thus hindering the understanding of carbonate weathering behaviors under extreme climate (Gaillardet et al., 2019 ). The main reason for this is that previous studies have used one-time spatial or low-temporal resolution samplings, often missing detailed observations of storm events. Therefore, high-temporal resolution flux of carbonate weathering and associated carbon budget need to be constrained in single catchments, in order to explore how carbonate weathering responds to storm events in the global warming scenario. The upper reaches of the Min Jiang are located in the tectonically active area on the eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, with steep topographic gradients, severe rock fragmentation, and strong physical denudation and chemical weathering (Qin et al., 2006; Yoon et al., 2008 ). In the region, a large amount of fresh minerals and rocks is exposed due to glacial abrasion and seismic landslides, releasing soluble elements into surface water through chemical weathering (Jin et al., 2016 ). Climatically, the upper Min Jiang is characterized by typical monsoon climate, more than 80% of the rainfall concentrated in the monsoon season (May to September). Storm events can result in large quantities of rocky materials entering the river, with significant impacts on the solute fluxes and the carbon cycling (Jin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016a; Baynes et al., 2023 ), especially for the upper Min Jiang in 2010 when intense monsoonal runoff drove high erosion and sediment transfer (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the upper Min Jiang is an ideal setting to explore the response of carbonate weathering to storm events. In this study, we investigated seasonal riverine ions and strontium (Sr) isotopes, as well as geochemistry and mineralogy of suspended particulate matters (SPM), by weekly sampling during 2010 at the Zhenjiangguan gauging station in the upper Min Jiang, which is unaffected by hydropower dams and far away from human activities, in order to explore the response of carbonate weathering and its CO2  consumption to the storm events, aiming to reveal the weathering behavior of carbonates at high denudation rates and provide new insights into the relationship among weathering, climate, hydrology, and the carbon cycling on short time scales.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area As the largest tributary of the Yangtze River, the Min Jiang originates from the eastern Tibetan Plateau and flows through the Sichuan Basin, with a total length of 793 km and annual water discharge (Q w ) of 842 × 108  m3 /yr (https://www.mwr.gov.cn ). The sampling site was selected at the Zhenjiangguan hydrological station in the upper reaches of the Min Jiang (Fig. 1  ), monitoring a drainage area of 4486 km2 , with coordinates of 32°17′46.78″ N and 103°43′37.39″ E. The climate of the upper Min Jiang is characterized by cold temperate monsoon climate, with annual temperature (T) ranging from –5℃ to 15℃ and with an average of 6℃ (1951–2016, https://data.cma.cn ). The annual precipitation at the Zhenjiangguan station is 560–904 mm/yr (1980–2016, https://data.cma.cn ), with more than 80% of rainfall concentrated between May and September during the monsoon seasons. The upper reaches of the Min Jiang stretch across the Songpan-Ganzi and the Longmen Shan fold belts (Burchfiel et al., 1995; Xiao et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2008 ), and are characterized by high mountains and deep valleys. The bedrocks are severely fragmented in the fracture zone and are easily transported into river channel by heavy rainfall, forming the debris flow and causing floods (e.g., Tang et al., 2011 ). As the upper Min Jiang is distant from the 2008 Wenchuan seismic landslide area (Jin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016a; Zhang et al., 2019 ), the response processes of river chemistry to natural hydrological changes can be better explored. The lithology is complex within the study basin, including sandstone, shale, granite, metamorphic igneous rocks with minor deposits of gypsum (Qin et al., 2006; Yoon et al., 2008 ), and carbonate rocks are distributed as isolated platforms in the reaches above the Zhenjiangguan station (Yoshimura et al., 2004; Qin et al., 2006 ).  2.2 Sampling and analysis A total of 56 river water samples were collected weekly throughout 2010 at the Zhenjiangguan station (Fig. 1 ), along with SPM samples. Two rainwater samples were collected during the monsoon season for atmospheric correction. The pH, T, and total dissolved solids (TDS) were measured in situ  using a water probe meter (Hanna HI98129). Each water sample was filtered with a 0.2 μm nylon membrane into pre-cleaned acidified (pH < 2) polyethylene bottles ready for analysis of major cations, Sr2+  concentrations, and Sr isotopic isotopes (87 Sr/86 Sr). Another group of the same water samples was also filtered and then transferred to unacidified bottles for anion analysis. All samples were stored in the dark at a 4℃ environment. Major cations (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , and K+ ) and Sr2+  concentrations of water samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer (ICP-AES), with analytical uncertainty less than 2% (2 SD).
