Anions (F− , Cl− , SO4 2− , and NO3 − ) were determined by Dionex ion chromatography (ICS 1200), and alkalinity (as HCO3 − ) was analyzed by Torch total organic carbon analyzer from Teledyne Tekmar, both with precision better than 1.5% (2 SD). All measurements were conducted at the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). For riverine Sr isotopes analyses, the Micro Eichrom Sr-Spec™ resins were employed to collect Sr using standard chemical separation technique (Jin et al., 2011 ). Water samples (∼400 ng Sr) were evaporated to dryness and then re-dissolved in 1 mL 3 M HNO3 , finally eluted with 3 mL Milli-Q H2 O. Riverine 87 Sr/86 Sr values were measured by Thermo-Fisher Neptune plus MC-ICP-MS at the Institute of Earth Environment, CAS (IEECAS). The international reference material NIST-NBS987 yielded an average 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio of 0.710265 ± 0.000012 (2 SD, n = 10). The SPM samples were removed from filter membranes with ultrapure water, dried and finely ground to below 200 mesh for subsequent geochemical and mineralogical analysis. About 50–100 mg powdered SPM samples were dissolved in a 4:2 (v/v) mixture of concentrated HNO3  and HF using the UltraCLAVE microwave digestion system, then dried and treated by 3 mL aqua regia, and finally dissolved in 2% HNO3  preparing for elemental analysis (Ca, Mg, Na, and Sr). The elemental analysis procedure for SPM samples is the same as that for river water samples and also at the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, CAS. Mineralogy of SPM was detected by an X-ray diffraction (XRD) method at the IEECAS. About 100 mg powdered SPM samples were placed onto glass slides, compacted evenly and parallel to the slide. XRD analysis was carried out by a PANalytical X’ Pert Pro diffractometer with continuous scanning at a range of 3–70° (2θ ) under the monochromated Cu Kα radiation (40 kV and 40 mA). The XRD spectra were processed using the JADE 6.0 software.  2.3 Data analysis and model calculations 2.3.1 Saturation indices (SI) and Ci  -Q w  relationship In order to evaluate the potential carbonate phases in equilibrium with solution thermodynamically, calcite and dolomite saturation indices (CSI and DSI) in river waters were calculated using the program PHREEQC (Parkhurst and Appelo, 1999 ). The PHREEQC is based on an ion-association aqueous model and has capabilities for speciation and SI calculations. The input parameters include water pH, T, ionic concentrations (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , Sr2+ , F− , Cl− , SO4 2− , NO3 − , and HCO3 − ). The saturation state of the solution relative to minerals is determined by SI value, i.e., SI = 0 is saturated, SI > 0 is supersaturated and SI < 0 is undersaturated. In this study, the relationship between the concentrations of major ions (Ci  ) and Q w  was used to assess whether riverine ion concentrations were influenced by dilution effect or compensation from rock weathering (Qin et al., 2006 ). The Ci  -Q w  relationship can be best fitted by a power function:(1) C i  =  a  Q w - b      where Ci   is the concentration of any ion i , a  and b  are coefficient and index respectively. Among them, b  is usually greater than 1 under dilution effect alone (Nkounkou and Probst, 1987 ), unless there is an additional source of compensation. The daily average Q w  and suspended sediment concentration (SSC) during 2010 at the Zhenjiangguan station (Fig. 2   and Table S1 ) were compiled from the Annual Hydrological Report P.R. China 2010 (Bureau of Hydrology, Ministry of Water Resources, P. R. China, 2011 ). In terms of hydrological measurement, the Q w  was measured using the current meter and Q w  was also measured using the buoy method during high water levels, and the SSC was measured by depth integration and full section mixing method.  2.3.2 Forward model The contributions of silicate, carbonate, and evaporite weathering to riverine chemistry in the upper Min Jiang during 2010 were evaluated using a forward method, given the stable sources of ions throughout the year (Fig. S1 ). The mass balance equations for cations are listed as follows:(2) X river   = ∑ i   X  i     (3) X i   =  Na i  × X Na   i     where X  refers to Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , and K+ , and the subscript i  denotes carbonate (carb ), silicate (sil ), evaporite (eva ), rain, and anthropogenic (anth ), respectively. A set of a priori  Na-normalized endmember constraints for different reservoirs was employed to solve the equations. Atmospheric input was considered only during the monsoon and was corrected using rainwater samples collected during the monsoon (Table S2 ). Detailed calculations of contributions from different sources to seasonal riverine chemistry in the upper Min Jiang were shown in the supplementary text (Appendix A) . In the forward modeling, we assumed that all SO4 2−  was derived from gypsum dissolution and that all Cl–  after atmospheric correction came from halite dissolution, assigning equivalent amounts of Ca2+  and Na+  to evaporite origin. Riverine NO3 –  was assumed to be entirely derived from agricultural activities to constrain anthropogenic inputs (mainly Na+ ), though human activities are limited in the upper Min Jiang. Compared with Na+  and K+ , riverine Ca2+  and Mg2+  are less sensitive to human disturbances and are more dominated and buffered by rocks weathering (Roy et al., 1999; Chetelat et al., 2008 ). The remaining riverine Na+  after evaporite, rain, and anthropogenic correction was considered to be from silicate weathering (Nasil  ), and then partitioning riverine silicate fraction with (X /Na)sil   molar ratios constrain by local lithology (Eq. (3) ). After the corrections for rain, anthropogenic, evaporite, and silicate fractions, the remaining Ca2+  and Mg2+  were taken to be originated from carbonate reservoir. Finally, sensitivity tests were performed to evaluate the reliability of the forward calculation results (please see supplementary text ).  2.3.3 Carbonate weathering flux (Φ CW ) and its CO2  consumption flux (Φ CO 2 carb    ) When driven by carbonic acid alone, the weathering reaction of carbonates is expressed as:(4) Ca x  ,  Mg  1 - x   C O  3  + C O  2  + H 2  O = xCa  2+  + ( 1 - x )Mg  2+  + 2HC O  3  -      where x refers to 1 or 0. Based upon the Eq. (4) , the Φ CW  and its associated Φ CO 2 c a r b     were calculated by the following equations, respectively (Hren et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2016b ):(5) Φ CW   = ( Ca carb 2+  + Mg carb 2+  ) × Q w  / A    (6) Φ CO 2 carb    = ( Ca carb 2+  + Mg carb 2+  ) × Q w  / A    where the Φ CW  is defined as total cation flux released from carbonate dissolution per square kilometer, Ca carb 2+    and Mg carb 2+    are the carbonate-derived cations based on the forward model results, and A  refers to the drainage areas. The Φ CW  and Φ CO 2 carb     are in units of t/yr/km2  in this study.  2.3.4 Kinetic partition coefficients Incongruent calcite dissolution (ICD) would produce a linear correlation of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) with a theoretical slope that is given by (Kd Sr  – 1)/(Kd Mg  – 1), where the partition coefficients for Sr (Kd Sr ) and Mg (Kd Mg ) in the kinetic system as following (Sinclair, 2011; Sinclair et al., 2012 ):(7) Kd Sr  = Sr Ca   crystal  / Sr Ca   solution     (8) Kd Mg  = Mg Ca   crystal  / Mg Ca   solution     where the subscripts crystal  and solution  denote quantities in crystals of host carbonate mineral and in river waters, respectively.    3 Results 3.1 Seasonal hydrology and storm events Detailed hydrological parameters at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang during 2010 are listed in Table S1 . Water T varied from –0.9℃ to +17.9 ℃ throughout the year, with the same trend as air T, showing an obvious seasonal variation (Fig. 2 ). During the pre-monsoon (January to April), river water exhibited a low T, with an average value of 3.9°C, and daily Q w  varied slightly (Fig. 2 ), ranging from 16.5 to 49.4 m3 /s (averaging 21.7 m3 /s). During the monsoon season (May to September), water T gradually increased due to rising air T, reaching a maximum of 17.9°C in early August (Fig. 2 ), followed by a slow decline in September. Under the prevalence of the summer monsoon, the Q w  rose rapidly in the monsoon season, reaching a maximum of 235 m3 /s and averaging 91 m3 /s, much higher than the pre-monsoon Q w  (Fig. 2 ). The Q w  during the monsoon in 2010 represents over 70% of the annual Q w , displaying a marked seasonal variation. During the post-monsoon (October-December), air T became cooler and water T gradually dropped to an annual minimum of –0.9°C. Similar to the pre-monsoon period, Q w  eventually declined to an average of 36.3 m3 /s (Fig. 2 ). It is noteworthy that the heavy rainfall during the monsoon in 2010 resulted in six rapid increases in Q w  up to 113, 141, 235, 171, 113, and 142 m3 /s, respectively (Fig. 2 ), which was 7 to 14 times higher than those during the pre-monsoon. We defined the six rapid increases in Q w  as storm events occurred in the upper Min Jiang during 2010 (9 days totally). Correspondingly, SSC during the storm events increased sharply in step with Q w  (Fig. 2 ), reaching a maximum value of 3380, 2180, 3150, 1780, 946, and 1010 g/m3  at each storm event, respectively. Compared with those of non-monsoon periods, SSC during the storm events were 10 to 40 times higher, indicating the extremely high erosion within the catchment. To facilitate the discussion below, six storm events were labeled as E1 to E6, respectively (shaded by light pink in Figs. 2 and 3  ).  3.2 Major ionic concentrations and Sr isotopic ratios The TDS at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang ranged from 239 to 366 mg/L in 2010, with relatively high TDS during the monsoon compared to the pre- and post-monsoons (Table S2 ). Concentrations of major cations and anions showed seasonal variations (Fig. 2 ), from 942.0 to 1650.8 μmol/L for Ca2+ , 455.8 to 988.7 μmol/L for Mg2+ , 143.4 to 360.2 μmol/L for Na+ , 13.9 to 23.7 μmol/L for K+ , 2870.8 to 4825.0 μmol/L for HCO3 – , 66.6 to 136.4 μmol/L for SO4 2– , 23.0 to 48.1 μmol/L for Cl– , and from 6.1 to 23.3 μmol/L for NO3 –  (Table S2 ), all exhibiting lower values during the monsoon than pre- and post-monsoons because of the dilution effect, especially for the storm events (Fig. 4  ). Both cations and anions were sensitive to the storm events. For example, Ca2+  concentrations decreased further in each storm event, reaching a minimum during the E3 with the highest Q w  over the year (Fig. 2 ). Like Ca2+ , the concentrations of Mg2+ , Na+ , HCO3 – , SO4 2– , and NO3 –  also showed similar responses to the storm events, whereas the K+  and Cl–  showed opposite responses to E1–E3, exhibiting increased concentrations (Fig. 2 ). Ca2+  + Mg2+  dominate the cations in river waters, accounting for more than 85 % of total cations over the year (Fig. S1 ), while HCO3 –  contributes over 96 % to the anions, followed by SO4 2–  and Cl–  (Fig. S1 ). It is worth noting that the relative distribution of both cations and anions is homogeneous without seasonal variation (Fig. S1 ), suggesting a stable source of ions throughout the year. The 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios of river waters at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang varied from 0.710199 to 0.711040 (Fig. 3 ), which is lower than those of the lower reaches of the Min Jiang reported by Yoon et al. (2008)  (0.71143–0.71265), Luo et al. (2014)  (0.711525–0.711694), and Xu et al. (2022)  (0.711345). Riverine 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios fluctuated steadily between 0.710432 and 0.710643 during the pre-monsoon, then increased rapidly to 0.710999 during E1 and 0.711040 during E2, respectively, and finally decreased to an average of 0.710330 during the post-monsoon (Fig. 3 ). Sr2+  concentrations varied between 2.3 and 3.9 μmol/L and were sensitive to the storm events, with 1/Sr exhibiting the same trend as 87 Sr/86 Sr (Fig. 3 ). River waters were alkaline in the whole year, with pH values between 8.31 and 8.84 (Table S2 ). CSI and DSI are 0.65–1.15 and 0.82–2.04 (Table S2 ), respectively, indicating that river waters are supersaturated with respect to both calcite and dolomite.  3.3 Mineralogy and geochemical compositions of SPM Mineralogically, XRD spectra of representative SPM samples at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang during 2010 are shown in Fig. S2 . Primary minerals identified in SPM for the whole year include quartz, albite, muscovite, and interstratified biotite/muscovite, with phyllosilicates such as kaolinite and vermiculite. In addition, carbonate minerals such as aragonite, calcite, Mg-calcite, and dolomite are abundantly presented in SPM. The fine and symmetrical diffraction peaks show that the minerals are highly crystalline, with insignificant differences between the monsoon and non-monsoons (Fig. S2 ). In terms of geochemistry, the elemental concentrations of the SPM samples in the upper Min Jiangrange from 46.71 to 138.46 mg/g for Ca, 9.12 to 15.22 mg/g for Mg, 4.23 to 8.06 mg/g for Na, and 0.17 to 0.25 mg/g for Sr, respectively (Table S3 ), with clear seasonal variations (Fig. S4 ).   4 Discussions 4.1 Carbonate weathering dominates riverine chemistry in the upper Min Jiang Based on the forward modelling (Eqs. (2) and (3) ), the results show that carbonate weathering dominates the seasonal riverine chemistry of the upper Min Jiang (Table S4 ), accounting for 71% to 81% of the total cations (averaging 76%, Fig. 5  ), which is consistent with the extremely high proportion of Ca2+  and Mg2+  in the total cations (averaging 89%, Fig. S1 ). In comparison, silicate weathering accounts for only 10–21% (averaging 14%), and evaporite input averaged to be 6%. The contribution of atmospheric input to total cations during the monsoon is limited, ranging from 6% to 9% (Fig. 5 ). Sensitivity tests show that when the ranges of the apportioned (Ca/Na)sil   and (Mg/Na)sil   varies by more than 80%, the maximum relative difference in the resulting contribution of carbonate weathering does not exceed 15% (Fig. S3 ), indicating that the contribution of carbonate reservoir is insensitive to changes in the a priori  endmembers. The high proportion of carbonate weathering in the total cations confirms that the fast dissolution kinetics of carbonate minerals (Lasaga, 1984; Meybeck, 1986 ) can rapidly dominate and buffer riverine chemistry (Roy et al., 1999; Chetelat et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2022, 2023 ). Riverine Sr2+  and Sr isotope ratios (87 Sr/86 Sr) were widely used as effective proxies for tracing continental chemical weathering, and for identifying the provenance of the dissolved load, since riverine Sr2+  and 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios generally behave distinct differences during weathering of carbonates (from 0.707 to 0.711 with high Sr2+  concentrations) and silicates (from 0.715 to 0.730 with low Sr2+  concentrations) but do not fractionate in secondary processes (Han and Liu, 2004; Chetelat et al., 2008; Jin et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2014 ). The 87 Sr/86 Sr versus 1/Sr mixing diagram (Fig. 6  a) for river waters demonstrates that the 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios in the upper Min Jiang are controlled by dissolution of carbonates, with limited contribution from silicate weathering. Moreover, the variations of 87 Sr/86 Sr against Mg/Ca molar ratio (Fig. 6 b) show different mixing trends for river waters between three rocks endmembers, i.e., silicates, dolomite, and limestone, all of which have been identified by XRD in the SPM samples (Fig. S2 ). The proportion of dolomite and limestone mixing trends accounts for more than 80% of these three endmembers mixing contributions (Fig. 6 b), indicating the dominant role of carbonate weathering on riverine 87 Sr/86 Sr, Ca2+ , and Mg2+  in the upper Min Jiang, which is consistent with the forward model constraints. It is noteworthy that Na-rich marine exchange pools have been shown to contribute significantly to the Na+  in modern rivers (Tipper et al., 2021 ), particularly in catchments with high erosion and sediment loads, which may also exist in the upper Min Jiang. Considering the possible contribution of exchangeable marine Na+  to riverine Na+ , the estimated Nasil   in the forward model may be overestimated, implying that the contribution of carbonate weathering to river water is underestimated (Tipper et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023 ). Although the influence of riverine exchange pools on seasonal riverine chemistry in the upper Min Jiang cannot be ruled out in this study, the dominance of carbonate reservoirs on the chemical compositions of river water is undoubtful. Although the ionic concentrations are sensitive to the storm events (Fig. 2 ) and rapidly decrease to a minimum with the increase of Q w  (Fig. 4 ), ionic concentrations (e.g., Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and HCO3 – ) cannot solely trace the response process of carbonate weathering to the storm events in the upper Min Jiang, considering that the riverine chemistry is dominated and buffered by carbonate weathering throughout the year (Fig. 5 ). In addition, Sr isotopes can only qualitatively, but not quantitatively, describe carbonate weathering sources and processes during storm events. For these reasons, a combination of weathering fluxes and the geochemistry of SPM is employed to explore the response of carbonate weathering to the storm events, as discussed below.  4.2 Enhanced carbonate weathering and CO2  consumption by the storm events The relationship between riverine Ci   and Q w  at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang during 2010 can be fitted by a series of power functions (Eq. (1) ), as shown in Fig. 4 . However, the index b  in this study is dramatically lower than 1 (Fig. 4 ), requiring an additional forcing that compensates for the dilution effect (Qin et al., 2006 ). It means that the increasing Q w  during the monsoon further intensifies water–rock reaction (mainly carbonate dissolution) in addition to dilution, releasing more carbonate-derived ions into river waters (Fig. 5 ). As a consequence, intensified carbonate weathering driven by sharply increasing Q w  and physical erosion rate (PER) during the storm events may be primarily responsible for the significant rise of Ca2+  + Mg2+  flux during the monsoon, showing a positive correlation between PER and Ca2+  + Mg2+  flux (r 2  = 0.90, Fig. 7  ). Riverine suspended sediments are the solid weathering products composed of secondary and residual primary minerals, with geochemical information on physical denudation and chemical weathering. Plots of Ca/Na versus Mg/Na and Sr/Na molar ratios for SPM display the mixing processes between carbonates and silicates (Figs. S4 a and c). Notably, a shift in the geochemistry of the SPM from near the carbonate endmember to the silicate endmember during the storm events (Fig. S4 ) may indicate two scenarios: (1) high runoff and physical denudation triggered by storm events delivered more silicates to the river (scenario-1); (2) fresh carbonate minerals were constantly exposed and dissolved more rapidly than silicates during the storm events, resulting in the carbonate-depleted SPM (scenario-2). For the scenario-1, we cannot rule out an increased production in silicates relative to carbonates during the storm events, though (1) the XRD mineralogy in SPM during the storm events and the monsoon were indistinguishable from that during the non-monsoons (Fig. S2 ), and (2) silicate weathering has a limited contribution to the riverine chemistry compared to carbonate weathering (Figs. 5 and 6 ). In contrast, the scenario-2 is more likely because river waters have higher proportions of Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and Sr2+  that are leached (relative to Na+ ) compared to their corresponding SPM samples (Figs. S4 b and d), especially during the storm events. Those high Ca2+ , Mg2+  and Sr2+  are a result of enhanced dissolution of carbonate minerals (Figs. 3, 5, and 7 ), behaving higher Mg/Na, Sr/Na, and Ca/Na molar ratios in the dissolved loads than those in the SPM (Figs. S4 b and d), indicating the preferential leaching of Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and Sr2+  (relative to Na+ ) from carbonate minerals. It means that seasonal variations in the geochemistry of the SPM may be caused by enhanced dissolution of carbonate minerals relative to silicates due to the rapid dissolution kinetics of carbonates during the storm events (scenario-2), rather than the increased silicates relative to carbonates (scenario-1). From this, enhanced carbonate weathering triggered by the storm events is simultaneously reflected by the coupled changes in the geochemical compositions of river waters and their corresponding SPM. The exposure and fragmentation of a large amount of fresh carbonate rocks during the storm events would increase the specific surface area of mineral particles and further promote weathering. As a result, carbonates would rapidly dissolve under high Q w  caused by the storms, resulting in a sharp increase in the flux of dissolved carbonates (Figs. 3 and 7 ), although the ionic concentrations show slight dilution effect (Fig. 4 ). According to the Eq. (5) , calculation results show storm events result in a 270% enhancement in the mean Φ CW  (46.84 ± 11.81 t/yr/km2 ) compared with those during the non-monsoons (12.65 ± 4.98 t/yr/km2 ), and a 54% increase compared with those during other periods of the monsoon(30.51 ± 9.16 t/yr/km2 , Fig. 3 ), indicating an enhanced response of carbonate weathering to the storm events. As mentioned above, the exposure and denudation of fresh carbonate minerals to increase the reactive specific surface area under highly erosion triggered by storm events (Fig. 7 ), as well as the rapid dissolution kinetics of carbonate under high runoff (Fig. S4 ) are the main mechanisms leading to Φ CW  enhancement. In addition, previous studies have shown that increased precipitation could promote soil CO2  emissions (e.g., Lee et al., 2002; Tan et al., 2021 ), which may provide more protons to enhance carbonate dissolution and Φ CW  during storms, as an additional mechanism (Eq. (4) ; Gaillardet et al., 2019 ). Since carbonate weathering is a dominant carbon sink at the centennial-millennial scales (Beaulieu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Gaillardet et al., 2019 ), it is worthy to assess the Φ CO 2 carb     accompanying the intensified carbonate weathering during the storm events. Before the assessment, sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering from sulfide oxidation is needed to be considered, because it would offset the CO2  consumption by silicate/carbonate weathering (Torres et al., 2016; Relph et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2023 ). Indeed, the contribution of sulfide oxidation to riverine SO4 2–  was suggested to be negligible in the upper Min Jiang, since (1) the concentrations of SO4 2–  (averaging 104 μmol/L) were much lower than those of HCO3 –  (averaging 3886 μmol/L), accounting for less than 3% of the total anions (Fig. S1 ), (2) the slope of scatter plot of Ca2+  + Mg2+  versus SO4 2–  (16.9, r 2  = 0.81, Fig. S5 a) is significantly higher than the theoretical slope of sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering (1 to 2; Calmels et al., 2007; Torres et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2023 ), and (3) the scatter plot of Ca2+  + Mg2+  versus HCO3 –  yielded a slope close to 1 (1.05, r 2  = 0.92, Fig. S5 b), indicating that carbonate-derived Ca2+  + Mg2+  are mainly driven by carbonic acid (Eq. (4) ). Accordingly, carbonate weathering in the upper Min Jiang acts as a net carbon sink, and the associated Φ CO 2 carb     was calculated by the Eq. (6) . The results show that a total of 1.21 × 105  t CO2  was consumed by carbonate weathering in the upper Min Jiang throughout the year of 2010 (Table S4 ). Specifically, total CO2  consumption during the monsoon period is 0.77 × 105  t, accounting for 64% of the year (Fig. 3 ). As shown in Fig. 8   and Table S4 , the calculated Φ CO 2 carb     during the non-monsoons is 16.8 ± 6.5 t/yr/km2  on average, and the average Φ CO 2 carb     during the storm events and other periods of the monsoon are 61.2 ± 15.1 and 40.1 ± 11.8 t/yr/km2 , respectively. It is worth noting that the storm events intensified the mean Φ CO 2 carb     with a 264% increase compared with those during the non-monsoons (Fig. 8 ), and a 52% increase compared with those during the common monsoon, with the intensifying Φ CW  (Fig. 3 ). These data indicate that storm events enhanced carbon sink by carbonate weathering over a hydrological year. Extending to global rivers, the enhanced Φ CO  2 carb     caused by the storm events in the upper Min Jiang is striking among river basins worldwide (Fig. 8 ). For comparison, we compiled the spatial Φ CO  2 carb     data deduced from global river basins (Gaillardet et al., 1999 ) and rivers originating from the Tibetan Plateau (Wu et al., 2008 ) (Table S5 ). As shown in Fig. 8 , the average Φ CO  2 carb     of rivers draining the Tibetan Plateau (17.8 ± 13.8 t/yr/km2 ) is comparable to that during the non-monsoon periods (16.8 ± 6.5 t/yr/km2 ) in the upper Min Jiang. Meanwhile, the Φ CO  2 carb     of rivers worldwide are lower than those of the Tibetan Plateau rivers (including the upper Min Jiang), but with a high degree of variability, ranging from 0.17 to 136.7 t/yr/km2  (averaging 12.1 ± 21.5 t/yr/km2 ). In comparison, the average Φ CO  2 carb     triggered by the storm events in the upper Min Jiang was 244% and 404% higher than that of the Tibetan Plateau rivers and global rivers (Fig. 8 ), respectively. This study highlights that the storm events play a significant role in enhancing surface material cycling and carbon sinks related to carbonate weathering, warranting further investigation.  4.3 Incongruent carbonate dissolution (ICD) triggered by the storm events The pH values of the river water at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang are higher than 8.30 throughout the year, with an average value of 8.57, indicating an alkaline water. Supersaturation in river water relative to calcite and dolomite suggests a possible tendency for carbonates to precipitate, which would inhibit further dissolution of primary carbonate. However, carbonate precipitation seems unlikely in the upper Min Jiang, since both CSI and DSI varied steadily all year and were not sensitive to the storm events (Table S2 ). Moreover, XRD mineralogy shows that the diffraction peaks of the identified calcite, dolomite, and aragonite are relatively fine and symmetrical (Fig. S2 ), indicating a highly developed crystalline primary mineral morphology. Therefore, the carbonates in the suspended sediments of the upper Min Jiang are mainly primary detrital minerals, with minor secondary carbonates, carbonate precipitation is not significant, though it might exist (Sinclair, 2011; Yang et al., 2015; Gou et al., 2023 ). A key scientific question is whether Φ CW  increases with high PER during the storm events. Is carbonate weathering controlled by physical erosion under active tectonic settings (i.e., supply-limited weathering regime)? Or is it controlled by climatic kinetic factors such as T and precipitation (i.e., kinetically-limited weathering regime)? A positive relationship between Ca2+  + Mg2+  flux and PER represents a steady state of Φ CW  under various erosion rates (Fig. 7 ), which cannot determine whether carbonate can continue to dissolve under high erosion rates, hindering us from deeply exploring the response of carbonate weathering to the storm events. Combining the geochemistry of SPM and river water, an ICD model, as a possible mechanism, was employed here to address the weathering behaviors of carbonates triggered by the storm events at an extremely-high erosion setting. ICD originally describes calcite-water interactions in speleothem and karst settings (Huang and Fairchild, 2001; Sinclair, 2011; Sinclair et al., 2012 ). Since not only calcite but also dolomite and aragonite were identified in SPM samples of the upper Min jiang (Fig. S2 ), ICD was defined as incongruent carbonate dissolution in this study. ICD is the process whereby Mg2+  and Sr2+  are released into solution in preference to Ca2+  during carbonate dissolution (McGillen and Fairchild, 2005; Sinclair, 2011 ). Therefore, an examination of Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca ratios in water and carbonate was usually used to diagnose the ICD between carbonates and water in speleothems and karst catchments (Sinclair, 2011 ). Moreover, Yang et al. (2015)  suggested that the possible trace dissolution of bedrock carbonates during exposure, erosion and even weak weathering conditions can significantly influence their Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca ratios. Then they proposed that the evolution of riverine Sr2+ , Mg2+  and Ca2+  compositions in the northeastern Tibetan Plateau can be explained by the carbonate fractional dissolution (i.e., ICD). As a result, the partial dissolution of carbonates has led to much higher Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca ratios in waters than when carbonate dissolution was significant, indicating that riverine geochemistry was controlled by the magnitude of carbonate dissolution (Yang et al., 2015 ). In our view, the ICD model can be used to depict the incongruent dissolution of carbonates during the storm events in the upper Min Jiang characterized by highly-erosion, where water availability is limited relative to the extremely high SSC (Fig. 2 ). There are two mechanisms for ICD, both of which potentially produce similar results but operate at different timescales and physical circumstances (Sinclair, 2011 ). The ICD model-1 is constructed as dynamic competition between a forward reaction (ion dissociation from the crystal surface) and a reverse reaction (re-precipitation of ions at the crystal surface) (Fig. 10 a). Net dissolution is represented by a dominance of the forward reaction over the reverse reaction from an undersaturated solution, and the ionic concentration in solution increases through time until a steady state is eventually achieved. In consequence, the solution becomes progressively more enriched in Mg2+  and Sr2+  relative to Ca2+  as more carbonate dissolves, producing an enrichment of Mg/Ca and Sr/Ca relative to the host rock, and the highest Mg/Ca and Sr/Ca ratios will coincide with the highest Mg2+  and Sr2+  concentrations (Sinclair, 2011 ). The ICD model-2 represents the preferential leaching of Mg2+  and Sr2+  from a thin layer of freshly exposed carbonate surface undergoing physical denudation (McGillen and Fairchild, 2005 ) (Fig. 10 b). In this case, lower partial dissolution would produce an enrichment of Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca in solution, the same as that produced by the ICD model-1, while the highest Mg/Ca and Sr/Ca ratios will coincide with the lowest Mg2+  and Sr2+  concentrations (Sinclair, 2011 ). As shown in Fig. 9   a and b, the Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca molar ratios in the river waters of the upper Min Jiang are higher than those of their corresponding SPM samples, indicating that the possible ICD leads to preferential leaching and enrichment of Sr2+  and Mg2+  relative to Ca2+ , which is consistent with the results simulated by ICD model (Sinclair, 2011 ). Specifically, the Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca molar ratios of most river waters and their corresponding SPM samples are positively correlated with Sr2+  and Mg2+  concentrations (including the storm events E3–E6), respectively, likely representing ICD scenario-1 (Fig. 9 a and b). In contrast, the negative correlation of Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca molar ratios with Sr2+  and Mg2+  concentrations for some water samples (i.e., E1 and E2) and their corresponding SPM samples, respectively, may represent ICD scenario-2 (Fig. 9 a and b). Our data show that ICD may control the riverine Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca variations throughout the year at the Zhenjiangguan station in the upper Min Jiang, particularly during the storm events under the exposure, high erosion and weak weathering conditions of carbonates, where limited supply of undersaturated freshwater and high carbonate fluxes could lead to incongruent dissolution of carbonates (Fig. 9 ). For the ICD scenario-1 (Fig. 10 a), the data points of river waters and their corresponding SPM samples during the storm events (e.g., E3–E6) are closer to each other relative to the non-monsoon seasons (Fig. 9 a and b), suggesting that storm events accelerated carbonate weathering towards congruent dissolution (but did not reach), shifting from a kinetically-limited regime to a supply-limited regime (West et al., 2005; Dellinger et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023 ). In terms of the ICD scenario-2 (Fig. 10 b), rapid physical denudation triggered by the storm events (e.g., E1 and E2) resulted in the exposure of a large amount of fresh carbonate minerals. The preferential leaching of Sr2+  and Mg2+  from the crystal surface led to higher Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca molar ratios in the dissolved loads than those of SPM, while the dissolved Sr2+  and Mg2+  concentrations were lower than those of SPM (Fig. 9 a and b), as predicted by Sinclair (2011) . In summary, both ICD scenario-1 and scenario-2 demonstrate that carbonate weathering is kinetically-limited under extremely high-erosion rates in the study area (Fig. 7 ), especially during the storm events. In order to verify the potential role of ICD in controlling the weathering behavior of carbonates in the upper Min Jiang, the slope of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) was employed to test the model. Modelling predicted that ICD would produce a linear correlation in the graph of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) with a theoretical slope (0.88 ± 0.13, Sinclair, 2011; Sinclair et al., 2012 ) that is given by (Kd Sr  – 1)/(Kd Mg  – 1), where the partition coefficients for Sr (Kd Sr ) and Mg (Kd Mg ) in the kinetic system were calculated by the Eqs. (7) and (8) . Here, the geochemical quantities of bulk SPM were assumed to be roughly representative of those of the host carbonates, given that the geochemical compositions of SPM are close to carbonate endmember (Figs. S4 a and c). As shown in Fig. 9 c, plot of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) of river waters and their corresponding SPM samples in the upper Min Jiang yields a mean slope of 1.02 ± 0.40, within error of the slope value (0.88 ± 0.13) predicted theoretically for ICD (Sinclair, 2011; Sinclair et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2015 ). The observed slope of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) with the theoretical slope defined by (Kd Sr  –1)/(Kd Mg  –1) is distributed along the 1:1 line (Fig. 9 d), supporting the potential ICD in the upper Min Jiang, especially under extremely-high erosion rate induced by the storm events during the monsoon.   5 Implications for carbonate weathering and carbon sink by the storm events under global warming Due to the kinetically-limited forcings such as runoff and precipitation, the carbonates would dissolve incongruently under extremely-high erosion rate (Figs. 9 and 10 ), causing riverine chemistry to rapidly reach supersaturation relative to the carbonate phases (Table S2 ). This means that more denudated solid carbonates are not immediately weathered, though the storm events promote the dissolution flux of carbonates (Fig. 11  ). Combined with the SSC data (Fig. 2 ) and relative abundance of identified carbonate phases in the SPM, the residual undissolved carbonate flux can be estimated (Table S4 ). We estimated that the ratios of Φ CW  to total carbonate fluxes were averaged ∼32% during the storm events (Fig. 11 ), implying that averaged ∼68% of undissolved carbonates would be likely carried downstream as suspended particles for further weathering. These particulate carbonates during the storm events require an average of ∼695 m3 /s of undersaturated freshwater to be completely dissolved, according to the relationship between observed Φ CW  and Q w  (y  = 0.31x  + 4.28, Fig. 11 ). Remarkably, these particulate carbonates delivered by storm events have the potential to consume an average Φ CO  2 carb     of ∼284 t/yr/km2  (if driven by carbonic acid alone, Eqs. (4)–(6) ), based on the observed relationship of Φ CO  2 carb     = 1.30 × Φ CW  + 0.46 (r 2  = 0.99, Table S4 ). This study shows that storm events not only intensify carbonate weathering in situ  and associated CO2  sequestration, but also deliver significant amounts of unweathered carbonates to the lower reaches, which have the potential for a CO2  sink. In the context of global warming, high-elevation catchments are thought to experience more rapid surface changes than low-elevation regions (Mountain Research Initiative EDW Working Group, 2015; Zhi et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, especially in the Tibetan Plateau known as Asia’s water tower, the stored water in glaciers and snow can be easily mobilized into runoff under warmer conditions (Kraaijenbrink et al., 2017 ), with high Q w  accompanying monsoonal precipitation. For example, Wang et al. (2021)  have estimated runoff increases of 1.0–7.2% during the wet season in all upper basins of the Tibetan Plateau under global mean warming of 1.5–4.0 °C above pre-industrial levels. Based on this prediction and our observations, the average Φ CW  and associated Φ CO  2 carb     in the upper Min Jiang would increase by 280–301% and 274–295% respectively during the storm events under the warming scenario, compared to those during the non-monsoon periods at the present (Table S4 ). With increasing monsoonal precipitation variability and the intensifying erosion under global warming (IPCC, 2022; Ombadi et al., 2023; King et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024 ), Φ CW  during storm events in the Tibetan Plateau rivers may be even higher than we predicted. In this case, the ICD will tend to be inhibited, potentially resulting in a shift of carbonate weathering from a kinetically-limited regime to a supply-limited regime (West et al., 2005; Dellinger et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023 ). Under the future global warming scenario, the Φ CW  and associated Φ CO  2 carb     due to storm events will be further enhanced. In addition, elevated river sediment loads by storm events may promote more efficient transfer, oxidative weathering and burial of particulate organic carbon (POC) in the downstream reaches (Wang et al., 2016a ), exerting a profound influence on the carbon cycle and climate change, which warrants further investigated.  6 Conclusions This study presents a high-temporal resolution dataset of ions and 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios for water samples collected weekly during 2010 in the upper Min Jiang, eastern Tibetan Plateau, as well as geochemistry and mineralogy of SPM, in order to explore the seasonal response of carbonate weathering to storm events under high erosion and global warming. The river waters remained alkaline and supersaturated relative to carbonates throughout the year due to the dominance of carbonate weathering in the seasonal cationic budget (averaging 76% estimated by the forward model). Riverine chemistry was sensitive to flooding and intense erosion triggered by the storm events. A strong positive correlation between dissolved Ca2+  + Mg2+  flux and PER (r 2  = 0.90) further indicated that the six storm events (9 days totally) enhanced carbonate weathering, behaving 270% and 264% increases in the average Φ CW  and associated Φ CO  2 carb     respectively during storm events, compared to those of non-monsoon seasons. In addition, storm events resulted in the preferential leaching of Mg2+  and Sr2+  relative to Ca2+  from the freshly exposed carbonates, which is supported by the mean slope of ln(Sr/Ca) versus ln(Mg/Ca) (1.02 ± 0.40) between river waters and their corresponding SPMs. Our data demonstrate the acceleration of catchment erosion rates, carbonate weathering and the associated CO2  sequestration during storm events, revealing that carbonate may undergo incongruent dissolution in a highly-erosion Tibetan Plateau river catchment.
1 Introduction Seawater intrusion and paleo–saltwater intrusion leads to severe ecological and environmental issues in coastal regions around the world. Modern seawater intrusion is defined as the migration of seawater into freshwater aquifers under the influence of intensive groundwater extractions and climate changes, which lead to deterioration of groundwater quality (Werner et al., 2013 ). In contrast, transgression and regression cycles are prevailing during the Quaternary period, together with the effects of evaporation and concentration and mixing with other water sources, which may affect groundwater salinity on a geological time scale. Under these conditions, the formed paleo–saltwater generally has higher salinity than modern seawater with TDS > 35 g/L (Delsman et al., 2014 ). Paleo–saltwater intrusion poses greater risks to ecosystems compared to seawater intrusion due to its higher salinity, as observed in Australia (Harrington et al., 2013 ), the United States(Panthi et al., 2022 ), the Netherlands (Post et al., 2016 ), and China(Li et al., 2021 ). Previous studies mainly focused on dynamic monitoring of the groundwater level and groundwater quality(Martinez-Perez et al., 2022; Sreekanth and Datta, 2015 ), identification of salt–freshwater interface (Russak and Sivan, 2010; Xu et al., 2022 ), exploring the evolution of hydrogeochemistry (Giambastiani et al., 2013; Tiwari et al., 2019 ), and numerical modeling for saltwater intrusion development (Abarca et al., 2013; Schiavo et al., 2023 ). Under influence of saltwater intrusion, the hydrogeochemical processes occurring in coastal aquifers mainly include cation exchange, mineral dissolution and precipitation, redox reactions, etc (Abu-alnaeem et al., 2018; Kushawaha et al., 2024 ). These hydrogeochemical processes often involve microbial metabolism. However, the microbial dimension, a crucial aspect of groundwater environments, has not received sufficient attention in the context of saltwater intrusion studies until recently. Microorganisms, as one of the most active factors in groundwater environments, play a catalytic role in facilitating various chemical reactions and elemental cycles (Anantharaman et al., 2016 ). Microbial actions have been widely applied in migration and transformation behaviors of contaminations in groundwater, microbial remediation, metal ore exploration, and other fields (Guo et al., 2016; Leslie et al., 2013; Li et al., 2020; Pearce et al., 2011 ). Recently, the variation in microbial community composition and diversity influenced by modern seawater intrusion has been studied. Chen et al. (2019)  investigated the principal components of microbial communities and their influencing factors within the salt–freshwater transition zone (TDS: 0.22–1.77 g/L) in Longkou City, China. In coastal aquifer systems, intensive anthropogenic activities and hydrological interaction could alter microbial community structure and further influence material circulation and biogeochemical processes. Xiong et al. (2023)  investigated the impact of modern seawater intrusion on the nitrogen cycling patterns by Bayesian isotope mixing model and microbial functional network. The salinity usually exerts inhibitory effects on the activity of microbes, and this inhibitory effect tends to intensify with increasing salinity (Vallero et al., 2003 ). However, recent studies in different regions (such as the Shandong Peninsula in China, the Pearl River Delta in China, and the Mallorca Island in Spain) have revealed that the microbial diversity in groundwater within the brackish–freshwater transition zones does not exhibit a continuous decline in response to rising salinity (Chen et al., 2019; Hery et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2020; Sang et al., 2019; Sang et al., 2018 ). Despite this, the influence of paleo–saltwater intrusion on microbial diversity and community composition has not been systematically studied, and the microbial biomarkers and functional profiles remain poorly understood. The Laizhou Bay Coast is the region most seriously affected by paleo–saltwater intrusion in China (Fig. 1  ). Previous investigates have established that three major brine aquifers (depth < 60 m) in the northern part of the study area are formed during the three marine transgressions and regressions since the late Pleistocene (Yao et al., 2014 ). Saltwater intrusion is attributed to excessive fresh groundwater exploitation during rapid development in the region since the 1970s, and has been recognized by local government since 1976 (Mei, 1997 ). Influenced by geological processes and anthropogenic activities, the groundwater in this region exhibits a complex chemical composition, encompassing freshwater, brackish water, saline water and brine (Han et al., 2014 ). As one of the representative paleo–saltwater intrusion areas in China, the process of paleo–saltwater intrusion and the background conditions have been well investigated (Han et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Previous studies had concluded that brines evolved from paleo–seawater diluted with water of paleo–meteoric origin; saline groundwater originated from brine mixed with seawater or fresh groundwater (Han et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2019 ). However, the impact of groundwater salinization on the diversity and structure of microbial communities and indicative significance of microorganisms for the sources of groundwater salinity remains unclear. Therefore, this study aims to (1) investigate the salinity evolution of groundwater along a typical profile form inland to the coast; (2) explore the variation characteristics of microbial community composition and diversity along salinity gradient; (3) reveal the role of microbial communities as indicators of salinization processes. This study will enhance the understanding of microbial succession in coastal groundwater system.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The study area is located in the northern part of Shandong Province, China, on the southern coast of Laizhou Bay (Fig. 1 ). Since the Late Pleistocene (85 ∼ 4 ka BP), it has experienced three major marine transgressions, forming several marine sedimentary layers and retaining paleo–seawater in the coastal area (Li et al., 2021 ). It has a warm temperate subhumid monsoon climate. The average annual rainfall is about 660 mm, significantly lower than the average evaporation of 1648 mm. Precipitation shows high inter–annual variability, with ∼50 % of annual precipitation occurring in the wet season (June–August). Topographically, the terrain of the study area inclines from south to north with a gently sloping gradient of 0.3–0.8 ‰ in the coastal plain. The Bailang River, one of the largest rivers in the study area, originates in the bedrock mountain area in the south of the study area and flows northward into Laizhou Bay. Geologically, the sedimentary layers gradually transition from alluvium and fluvial deposits in the south of the study area to marine sediments of the coastal plain in the north. The main aquifers in the study area are composed of Quaternary loose deposits, with a thickness of 30–50 m in the south, up to 360 m in the north (Xue et al., 2000 ). Close to the piedmont area, the aquifer is a single–layer structure, and the aquifer matrix is mainly composed of medium–coarse sand and gravel. Towards the coastline, aquifers change to a multi–layer structure and the strata are mainly medium–fine sand and silt sand (Han et al., 2011 ). Groundwater recharge, runoff, and discharge in this region are influenced by topography, lithology, and human factors. Precipitation and river infiltration are the main ways of shallow groundwater recharge, and evaporation and artificial mining are the main ways of shallow groundwater discharge. Under natural conditions, precipitation and river infiltration are the main ways of shallow groundwater recharge, and groundwater flows from south to north towards the sea. However, over exploitation of brine resources have resulted in changes of the natural groundwater flow field, forming depression cones of groundwater (Fig. 1 d). While there may be shallow groundwater discharge into the sea, it is currently difficult for the groundwater within the depths we investigated to flow towards the sea due to the hydraulic gradient.  2.2 Sample collection and analysis Eleven wells with depth of 40 m were drilled along Bailanghe river for monitoring groundwater, from July to November 2022 (Fig. 1 ). In December 2022, groundwater samples were collected from theses 11 monitoring wells. Before sampling, the wells were pumped for over half an hour to ensure the collection of fresh groundwater. Additionally, one seawater sample was collected in Bohai Bay, and one river sample close to GW3 was collected in Bailang River. In the field, groundwater was extracted by a submersible pump at 0.5 m below the water table. The groundwater temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), and electrical conductivity (EC) were measured using a Eureka–EasyProbe multi–parameter instrument. After these in-situ parameters had stabilized, groundwater samples were collected and then filtered through a 0.45–μm membrane filter. For trace element and major cation analyses, sample were acidified with HNO3  (pH<2), while samples without acidification were used for major anion and isotope analysis. All water samples were stored in portable ice–filled coolers at 4 °C and sent to the laboratory for analyses. Moreover, subsamples exceeding 3L of each water sample were filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and stored at − 20 ℃ in the field and then − 80 ℃ in the laboratory for subsequent DNA extraction. All hydrochemical analyses were conducted at the Water Quality Analysis Laboratory of the Institute of Hydrogeology and Environmental Geology, CAGS. Major cations (Na+ , K+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ ) were analyzed using inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (Avio 550 Max ICP–MS). Major anions (Cl− , SO4 2− , NO3 − ) and Br−  were determined by ion chromatography (DX–120, Dionex). HCO3 −  concentrations were measured through acid–base titration. Additionally, Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) was determined by gravimetric analysis. The analytical precision error of the ICP–MS and DX–120 instruments is less than 5 %. Moreover, the ion charge imbalances among most water samples were <5 %. The stable isotopes of water (δ 18  O    and δ 2  H   ) were analyzed using an isotope mass spectrometer, MAT 253. The δ 18  O    and δ 2  H    values are given hereafter in δ   –units calculated with respect to VSMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water) expressed in ‰. 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios were measured by the MC–ICP–MS (Neptune Plus). Table S1  presents the chemical and isotopic components for water samples.  2.3 DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and 16S rDNA sequencing DNA extraction utilized Protease K splitting and Phenolic chloroform extraction. The V4–V5 fragment of nuclear bacterial DNA was amplified using 515F (5′–GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA–3′) and (926R 5′–CCGTCAATTCMTTTGAGTTT–3′) primers. The primers also contained Illumina 5′overhang adapter sequences for two–step amplicon library building. PCR conditions included initial denaturation at 94 °C for 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 30 s, annealing at 55C for 30 s and extension at 72 °C for 30 s, with a final extension of 72 °C for 5 min. Barcoded PCR products were purified using a DNA gel extraction kit (Axygen, USA) and quantified using FTC–3000TM  real–time PCR (Funglyn Shanghai). The PCR products from different samples were mixed at equal ratios. The second step PCR with dual 8 bp barcodes was used for multiplexing. Eight cycle PCR reactions incorporated two unique barcodes to either end of the amplicons. Cycling conditions included one cycle of 94 °C for 2 min, followed by eight cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 56 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 30 s, followed by a final extension cycle of 72 °C for 5 min. The library was purified using a DNA gel extraction kit (Axygen, USA) and sequenced by 2 × 250 bp paired–end sequencing on the Novaseq platform using Novaseq 6000 SP 500 Cycle Reagent Kit (Illumina USA) at TinyGen Bio–Tech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.  2.4 Statistic analysis For alpha–diversity analysis, Coverage, Observed species, Chao, ACE, Shannon, Simpon, and PD_whole_tree indices were calculated using R software. Intergroup differences in microbial community were analyzed by non–metric multi–dimensional scaling (NMDS) based on Bray–Curtis. Redundancy analysis (RDA) tested the relationships between sampling characteristics and microbial community to extract principle environmental factors influencing microbial communities. LEfSe analysis identified different microbial biomarkers in fresh groundwater and salty groundwater with an LDA significance threshold of 4.0. To better understand the impact of groundwater salinization on microbial interactions, two different networks were established by the Molecular Ecological Network Analyses (MENA) (http://ieg4.rccc.ou.edu/MENA/ ) based on random matrix theory. Network visualization was constructed using the Gephi 0.10.1 platform. PICRUSt2 was applied to predict functional genes of the groundwater microbial community, obtaining results for functional gene abundance at each level.   3 Results 3.1 Physicochemical properties of groundwater profile The groundwater TDS concentrations exhibited a wide range, varying from 0.5 g/L to 144.6 g/L (Table S1 ), showing a gradual increase trend from south to north. Groundwater samples could be classified into five types based on TDS: fresh groundwater (<1g/L, GW1 ∼ GW5), brackish groundwater (1–10 g/L, GW6), saline groundwater (10–50 g/L, GW7 ∼ GW9), and brine (>50 g/L, GW10 ∼ GW11). Except for freshwater, the other four types can be collectively referred to as salty groundwater. As shown in Fig. 2  , the hydrochemistry of the fresh groundwater was mainly of the HCO3 –Ca type, while the hydrochemical components of saltwater were mainly Cl–Na. Salty groundwater samples were located close to the seawater sample in the piper diagram. Groundwater Br−  concentration presented large variation ranging from 0.24 to 156.40 mg/L and was positively correlated with Cl−  (r = 0.997) (Fig. S1 a). The bromine content in groundwater samples GW11 ∼ 15 was higher than that in seawater sample. The pH values ranged between 6.76 and 7.66 (mean: 7.28), demonstrating that the groundwater environment was neutral.  3.2 Stable isotopic characteristics in coastal groundwater Groundwater δ2 H ranged from −61 to −39 ‰ with an average value of −52 ‰, δ18 O ranged from −8.4 to −3.9 ‰ with an average value of −6.6 ‰, which was lower than seawater sample with δ2 H − 18 and δ18 O − 1.8 ‰. The δ2 H and δ18 O value in river sample was −43 ‰ and −5.5 ‰, respectively. The relationship between δ2 H and δ18 O was shown in Fig. 3  . The global meteoric waterline (GMWL: δ2 H = 8 × δ18 O+10) was referenced from Craig (1961)  and local meteoric waterline (LMWL: δ2 H = 7.4 × δ18 O+1.1) was referenced from Han et al. (2014) . All groundwater samples were plotted to the right of the GMWL and the LMWL, showing a trendline: δ2 H = 5.1 × δ18 O–18.7, R2  = 0.98, P < 0.01). The freshwater end–member (GW1–3, GW5) with the lowest values of water isotopes was close to the LMWL, indicating that they were mainly recharged by atmospheric precipitation. Saltwater and brine still had enriched water isotopes consistent with high Cl−  concentration. The distribution of salty groundwater samples deviates to the right from the LMWL, implying that mixing with seawater and the evaporation process are important factors controlling the salinity and isotopic (H and O) components of the study area (Pang et al., 2017 ). Remarkably, seawater end–member had the highest values of δ2 H and δ18 O. Overall, groundwater 87 Sr/86 Sr values ranging between 0.709598 and 0.712288 were higher than global seawater Sr isotope values (0.70924) (Veizer, 1989 ), but exhibit greater variability (Fig. 3 b). High 87 Sr/86 Sr in fresh groundwater (0.711575 to 0.712288) could result from water–rock interaction. The variations in 87 Sr/86 Sr values in salty groundwater distinctly depended on TDS. As TDS increased, 87 Sr/86 Sr decreased and approached the seawater strontium isotopes. GW11 presented the lowest 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios which close to that of present seawater.  3.3 Diversity and structure of aquatic microbial communities By quality filtering, each sample had an average of 51, 451 gene sequence reads. A total of 668,860 high–quality sequences were obtained, with sequences ranging from 246 to 422pb in length. A total of 5454 OTUs occurred in groundwater, river, and seawater samples, only 5 were identified common in all samples (Fig. 4  a). The brackish groundwater (GW6) had the lowest OTUs of 330 and the fresh groundwater (GW5) had the highest OTUs of 1408. Seawater sample exhibited strong uniqueness, with 329 out of 454 OTUs being exclusive in the seawater sample. The Chao, ACE, Shannon, PD_whole_tree indices jointly showed that the bacterial community diversity and evenness of salty groundwater were obviously lower than that of fresh groundwater (Fig. 4 b). At the phylum level, Proteobacteria  generally exhibited predominant relative abundance, varying significantly between 9.6 % and 78.5 % across the 11 groundwater samples (Fig. 4 c). The mean relative abundance of Proteobacteria  accounted for 50.9 % of all phyla bacteria, followed by Bacteroidetes , Firmicutes , and Cyanobacteria  accounting for 18.7 %, 9.2 % and 6.1 % of all phyla bacteria, respectively. Proteobacteria  is an extensive and diverse bacterial taxa, which is usually the most abundant species in coastal groundwater at the phylum level (McAllister et al., 2015 ). Previous reports have implicated that Bacteroidetes  is prevalent in marine environments, playing a crucial role in the decomposition of organic matter and contributing significantly to carbon cycling (Alonso et al., 2007; Tominaga et al., 2020 ). Cyanobacteria  can produce energy by photosynthesis, often playing a key ecological role in marine environments, such as nitrogen fixation (Andreeva et al., 2020; Schvarcz et al., 2022 ). Cyanobacteria  were a dominant bacterial taxon in the seawater sample and accounted for 43.2 % of all phyla bacteria (Fig. 4 c). The bacterial genera in different water samples showed significant differences (Fig. 5  ). For some bacterial genera, the relative abundance in the fresh groundwater was higher than that of salty groundwater, such as Candidatus_Nitrotoga  (2.5 %), Sulfuritalea  (2.6 %), and Pseudohongiella  (3.2 %). The difference was that Serratia  (13.5 %) and Kluyvera  (8.8 %) were enriched in brackish groundwater; Sulfurimonas  (36.7 %), Microcystis  (18.5 %), Vibrio  (5.3 %), Desulfuromonas  (6.6 %) were enriched in saline groundwater; Acinetobacter , Algoriphagus , Fusibacter , and Desulfopila  were enriched in salty groundwater and brine; Marinobacter  (12.0 %) and Gracilimonas  (8.8 %) were enriched in brine. NMDS results exhibited that salinity variation significantly altered the groundwater bacterial community structure (Fig. 4 d). Based on the intergroup difference of bacterial community, fresh groundwater and brackish groundwater could be grouped together, while saline groundwater and bring could be grouped together. In addition, bacterial community in modern seawater sample exhibited a significant difference compared to other samples.  3.4 Dominant environment factor of microbial community structure In coastal aquifers, water–rock interaction and anthropogenic activities generally result in dynamic variations in the physicochemical properties of groundwater, including temperature, salinity, pH, DO, nutrients (NO3 – , NO2 –  and NH4 + ) and so on (Han et al., 2011 ). In the Laizhou Bay coast, the marine–continental sedimentary environment has exerted great influence on groundwater quality since the late Pleistocene. Groundwater salinity gradually increased with the decrease of the distance from the coastline. The results of RDA based on bacterial OTU data with physicochemical parameters at the bacterial phylum level (Top 15) and genus level (Top 30) in water samples were shown in Fig. 6  . At the phylum level, the first axis explained 66.65 % of the community variations, while the second axis explained 19.72 %. Temp, pH, and DO were main factors in shaping ocean microbial community, whereas HCO3 – , salinity, and nutrients were important variables affecting groundwater community composition. For the microbial communities change at the genus level, TDS, SO4 2– , and NO2 –  were the dominant factors in the saline groundwater and brine; NO3 –  and H2 SiO3  were the dominant factors in the fresh groundwater; pH, Temp and DO were the dominant factors in the seawater; NH4 +  was the dominant factor in the river. The results suggested that salinity and nutrients have important influence on the microbial community, which is consistent with previous reports (Unno et al., 2015; Xiong et al., 2023 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Salinity origin of salty groundwater Notably, brine samples (GW10 ∼ 11) exhibit isotopic signatures (δ2 H and δ18 O) that are more depleted than modern seawater, despite having higher TDS concentrations. This suggests that the formation of brine cannot be solely attributed to the evaporation of paleo–seawater. Mixing with ancient meteoric water, surface runoff, or fresh groundwater during and after the formation of brine in a cold period may explain the hydrochemical characteristics with low isotopic values and high salinity in present brine (He et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2019 ). In the δ18 O vs. Cl−  plot (Fig. S2 ), saline groundwater samples (GW7 ∼ GW9) lie on a fresh–bring mixing line. This indicates that bring has a greater effect on salinization than modern seawater. Banner (2004)  and Saeed et al. (2021)  measured 87 Sr/86 Sr values of ancient marine authigenic sediments, and they concluded that the 87 Sr/86 Sr values in paleo–seawater from the Pleistocene and earlier periods are typically lower than those in modern seawater. However, the 87 Sr/86 Sr values in brines are higher than that in modern seawater (Fig. 3 b). The evaporation concentration of paleo–seawater and the mixing of paleo–seawater with other freshwater sources can precisely explain this isotopic characteristic. In addition, the saline groundwater samples (GW7 ∼ GW9) are plotted between fresh groundwater and brine, further suggesting a mixing scenario (Fig. 3 b). The Br/Cl ratio is commonly used to explain the origin of groundwater salinity (Li et al., 2019 ). A general linear relationship between the Br−  and Cl−  is evident, displaying substantial concentration variations in different samples (Fig. S1 a). The concentration of Br−  in fresh groundwater ranges from 0.24 mg/L to 0.32 mg/L, while in saline groundwater and Brine, it spans from 38.68 mg/L and 156.40 mg/L. The Br/Cl ratio in seawater remains relatively stable, with a value of 0.0034 (Fuge, 1988 ). As shown in Fig. S1 b, the Br/Cl ratios in rivers and most freshwater are significantly lower than that in seawater. Combined with the rock weathering analysis (Fig. S3 ), the results show that silicate and carbonate weathering are the primary hydrogeochemical processes in fresh groundwater. Conversely, the Br/Cl ratio of saline groundwater and brine (GW8 ∼ GW10) is close to seawater line, indicating that chemical components of groundwater are evidently influenced by the mixing of paleo–seawater, which agree with Han et al. (2011) . However, among the groundwater samples, GW11 exhibits the highest Br−  concentration and the lowest Br/Cl ratio, indicating the presence of another source with high Cl−  and low Br− . The results of rock weathering analysis suggest that the reduction in the Br/Cl ratios could be related to the dissolution of halite (Fig. S3 ). This indicates that the salinity in the brine not only comes from paleo–seawater but also from the dissolution of halite.  4.2 Response of microbial interactions to groundwater salination 4.2.1 Microbial biomarkers The results demonstrate substantial alterations in microbial community composition along the salinity gradient in groundwater. To identify distinct microbial biomarkers in fresh and salty groundwater, LEfSe analysis is conducted with an LDA significance threshold of 4.0 (Fig. 7  ). In fresh groundwater, the typical bacteria include classes Betaproteobacteria  and Sphingobacteriia , orders Rhodocyclale s, Nitrosomonadales , Burkholderiales , and Sphingobacteriales , and families Rhodocyclaceae  and Comamonadaceae . In salty groundwater, the typical bacteria are class Gammaproteobacteria , order Alteromonadales , family Alteromonadaceae , genus Marinobacter . Moreover, a significantly positive relationships between content of o_Alteromonadales , f_Alteromonadaceae , g_Marinobacter  and TDS are observed along the groundwater profile (Fig. S4 ). The microbial biomarkers identified in salty groundwater are prevalent in marine environments, specifically in seawater, deep-sea habitats, marine sediments, and on the surfaces of marine organisms (Green et al., 2013 ). Alteromonadales  play a crucial role in marine ecosystems and are closely associated with material cycling (López-Pérez et al., 2014 ). Marinobacter , commonly known as marine bacteria, belongs to the family Alteromonadaceae  within the order Alteromonadales . Marinobacter  species exhibit notable abilities in the degradation of hydrocarbons, particularly petroleum compounds (Gauthier et al., 1992 ). This capability is vital in environments impacted by oil pollution, as Marinobacter  plays a significant role in degrading and eliminating petroleum contaminants (Chernikova et al., 2020 ). Many Marinobacter  species exhibit adaptability to high–salinity environments (Saadaoui et al., 2023 ), and the relative abundance of Marinobacter  taxon in GW11 reaches up to 12.0 %. Their prevalence in the salty groundwater could further substantiate the occurrence of marine transgressions and seawater/ paleo–seawater mixing in the study area.  4.2.2 Microbial potential co–occurrence networks Microbial interactions play a vital role in shaping the structure and function of communities, and exploring the co–occurrence network among bacteria is crucial for revealing microbial response mechanisms to environmental changes (Zhang et al., 2023 ). To further investigate the mechanisms of microbial community response to groundwater salinization, two groups (fresh groundwater and salty groundwater) are used to construct empirical and random networks by random matrix theory. Distinct structural and topological characteristics of microbiome networks are obtained (Table S2 ). The fresh groundwater network displays a larger number of nodes (592) and edges (1256) compared to the salty groundwater network (nodes: 359, edges: 702) and constructs a more complex network (Fig. 8  a–b). In salty groundwater, a higher average clustering coefficient indicates a more closely connected microbiome, while lower average path lengths indicate a more efficient microbial information transfer. These results suggest that the microbial community structure in groundwater potentially tends to simplify but the network nodes become more closely connected with each other during groundwater salinization. Salinity is a key factor influencing the distribution of biota in aquatic systems, with most aquatic organisms adapted to either saltwater or freshwater environments (Herlemann et al., 2011 ). This reduction in diversity leads to a simpler network because there are fewer species or types of microbes present in the saline groundwater compared to fresh groundwater. While the overall microbial diversity may decrease in saline environments, the remaining species may exhibit stronger or more frequent interactions (Xiao et al., 2020 ). By forming a more interconnected community, microbes may be better able to withstand the stress of high salinity and other environmental challenges by sharing resources, forming cooperative relationships, or providing mutual protection (Ya et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023 ). Additionally, the potential keystone species are identified based on within–module connectivity and among–module connectivity values, which include module hubs, network hubs and connectors. In the network of fresh groundwater, several keystone species are mainly distributed in module hubs (intra–module interactions) (Zi > 2.5, Pi ≤ 0.62) (Fig. 8 c). The abundances of theses related OTUs (466, 496, 2271, 2838, and 3537) are less than 0.1 %, demonstrating that some low abundance bacteria may play a key role in maintaining microbial network stability. Previous studies show that microbes with similar ecological niches are closely associated (mainly cooperation and symbiosis) and result in a higher number of modular hubs (Wang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ), consistent with the higher average degree in fresh groundwater in this study area. In contrast, most of the nodes from the salty groundwater network are concentrated in peripherals (Zi ≤ 2.5, Pi ≤ 0.62). Only one module hub (OTU 235) is detected in salty groundwater. OTU 235 belongs to the genus Croceicoccus  in the family Erythrobacteraceae . Croceicoccus  microorganisms are primarily found in marine environments, particularly in seawater and sediments (Park et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2009 ). These results indicate that groundwater salinization markedly alters key microbial groups.   4.3 Functional profiles of the groundwater microbial communities Utilizing 16S rDNA sequencing data, PICRUSt2 is employed to predict the functional profiles of microbial communities in both fresh and salty groundwater. Microorganisms play pivotal roles in diverse functional pathways, mainly including cellular processes, metabolism, human diseases, genetic information processing, organismal systems, and environmental information processing (Fig. S5 ). At the level of secondary functional classification, the main functional features are membrane transport, amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, replication and repair, and energy metabolism (Chen et al., 2020 ). The comparative analysis between the fresh and salty groundwater shows that 9 of the 307 functional gene clusters are markedly different. The signal transduction mechanisms, replication, recombination and repair proteins, other ion–coupled transporters, and arginine and proline metabolism are predominant in salty groundwater (Fig. S6 ). We compare the results of PICRUSt2 with 23 KEGG Orthology (KO) identifiers involved in sulfur metabolism in the KO database. Abundant sulfur functional genes have been found in groundwater in the study area, encompassing assimilatory sulfate reduction (9 KOs), dissimilatory sulfate reduction (5 KOs), thiosulfate oxidation by SOX complex (6 KOs) (Fig. 9  ). Notably, the relative abundance of dissimilatory sulfate reduction genes (sat, met3, aprA, aprB, dsrA, and dsrB) in salty groundwater is significantly higher than that in fresh groundwater. Previous research has shown that sulfate–reducing bacteria exhibit a positive response to elevated concentrations of sulfate (SO4 2− ) by deriving energy through the reduction of sulfate to hydrogen sulfide (H2 S) (Nelson et al., 2015; Vizza et al., 2017 ). Elevated abundance of sulfur–reducing taxa (Desulfitispora  and Desulfopila ) has been found with groundwater salinization in the present study (Fig. S7 ). Desulfitispora  and Desulfopila  are characterized by halotolerant and halophilic taxa, and the related species have been cultivated from estuary, soda lakes and tidal–flat sediments (Gittel et al., 2010; Sabuda et al., 2020; Suzuki et al., 2007 ). These results indicate that groundwater salinization significantly alters sulfur cycling, showing an enhancement of sulfate reduction. The carbon cycle is closely interconnected with the sulfur cycle, especially in coastal systems (Niu et al., 2023; Nobrega et al., 2022 ). The existence of sulfate enables sulfate–reducing bacteria to outcompete methanogens for energy sources, thereby inhibiting methane production. (Egger et al., 2018; Poffenbarger et al., 2011 ). In turn, this can result in an increase in the abundance of sulfate reducers and a decrease in the abundance of methanogens (Mobilian et al., 2023 ). In this study, predicted methanogenic functional genes (such as mcrA and mcrB) in salty groundwater are virtually non–existent. In addition, sulfate reduction coupled with anaerobic oxidation of CH4  is a significant path for methane consumption in coastal environments (Egger et al., 2018 ), which plays a crucial role in the emission of greenhouse gases. Therefore, the salinization process of coastal groundwater caused by paleo–seawater has a significant impact on sulfur and carbon biogeochemical processes. However, these hypotheses or predictions require further evidence through future investigations and metagenomic analysis.   5 Conclusion This paper delves into the investigation of saltwater origin, explores the impact of groundwater salinization on microbial community composition and diversity, and reveals the indicative significance of microorganisms to groundwater salinization. Utilizing a comprehensive approach involving physicochemical parameters, stable isotopes, 16S rDNA sequencing, and bioinformation, the study yields key findings: (1) The concentration of TDS in groundwater across the study area spans a wide range, from 0.5 to 144.6 g/L. Groundwater undergoes a transition from freshwater to brackish water, saline water, and ultimately to brine as it moves from inland to the coast. Depletion in isotopes of H and O compared to modern seawater is observed in all groundwater samples. Notably, brine sample (GW11) exhibits the highest Cl–  concentration but the lowest Br/Cl ratio, akin to the Br/Cl levels observed in the river. This suggests that the salinity in the brine originates not only from paleo–seawater but also from the dissolution of halite. Saline groundwater may be the result of mixing fresh groundwater with brine. (2) Diversity indices such as Chao, ACE, Shannon, and PD_whole_tree suggest that bacterial community diversity and evenness are markedly lower in salty groundwater compared to fresh groundwater. Despite similar dominant phyla, including Proteobacteria  and Bacteroidetes , at the phylum level, significant differences in bacterial compositions emerge at the genus level along the groundwater salinity gradient. LEfSE analysis identifies class Gammaproteobacteria , order Alteromonadales , family Alteromonadaceae , and genus Marinobacter  as typical microbial taxa in salty groundwater. These microorganisms can serve as biomarkers for seawater or paleo–seawater sources. (3) Microbial sequencing and gene prediction reveal an enhancement in sulfate reduction during the groundwater salinization process. Following the salinity gradient, an increase in sulfate–reducing bacteria is noted, impacting sulfur and carbon cycling. Notably, dissimilatory sulfate reduction genes (sat, met3, aprA, aprB, dsrA, and dsrB) exhibit higher prevalence in salty groundwater compared to fresh groundwater. In summary, this study provides comprehensive insights into the origin and impact of salinity on groundwater, shedding light on microbial responses and the associated biogeochemical processes. The findings enhance our understanding of groundwater salinization and emphasize the importance of microbial indicators in evaluating this process.
1 Introduction to the SWAT model The SWAT model, developed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture-Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) in the 1990 s, is a powerful tool used to predict the impacts of land management practices on water quality, sediment, and chemical yields in large and complex watersheds. This semi-physically-based, continuous, semi-distributed hydrological model has gained widespread recognition and application across different climates and meso -scale watersheds worldwide. The model is described in detail in Neitsch et al. (2009) . To simulate hydrological processes in the SWAT model, Hydrologic Response Units (HRUs) are formed based on areas sharing similar characteristics in slope, soil type, and land use. These HRUs are assumed to have homogeneous hydrologic responses to changes in climate inputs (such as rainfall, temperature, wind speed). The hydrologic cycle of the SWAT model involves two phases: the land phase and the channel routing phase. During the land phase, the model controls the amount of water, sediment, nutrients, and pesticides in each sub-basin, directing them towards the main channel. In contrast, the channel routing phase manages the movement of water, sediment, and pollutants through the interconnected channel network of the watershed, guiding them to the outlet. To accurately capture the complexity of soil–water interactions, the SWAT model divides the soil profile into layers where various water recycling processes occur. Key soil properties, such as fractions of sand, clay, silt, and rock; thickness; BD; saturated hydraulic conductivity; available water capacity; and Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) equation soil erodibility, are required for each soil layer.  2.4.2 The setup of the SWAT model The SWAT model is set up as follows: using a 30 m resolution DEM, the Fengyu River watershed of 218 km2  is divided into 37 sub-basins to capture its hydrological characteristics. Subsequently, 440 hydrologic response units (HRUs) are defined, representing the unique combinations of land use, soil type, and slope category for each sub-basin. Within each HRU, the SWAT model uniformly simulated all hydrological, vegetation, and soil processes. To reduce the computational burden of the model, the ‘Multiple HRUs’ selection is utilized in HRU Definition. The thresholds for land use, soil, and slope are to be within a 5 % range (this means that patches of land with areas, soil types, and slopes less than 5 % are merged with adjacent larger patches). Daily climate data from 1980 to 2013, including daily temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation, are incorporated for model simulations. This enabled the model to generate daily and monthly output data at the HRU, sub-basin, and basin scales. To establish baselines for the watershed and minimize the impact of initial conditions on model simulations, the SWAT model is configured with a 2-year warm-up period (2009–2010) to establish baseline conditions, followed by a 2-year modeling period (2010–2012) for simulations and a 1-year validation period (2013) to verify accuracy. Meteorological data spanning from 1980 to 2009 proved advantageous for effective pre-warming of the SWAT model. A warm-up period in the SWAT model is essential for initializing components, achieving system equilibrium, and improving result accuracy, so that the results are minimized from being affected by inaccurate initial conditions. The parameters in the SWAT model are initially defined as the initial parameters at the model’s outset. For example, setting soil water content to 0.5 implies it starts at that level. Subsequently, soil water content varies over time due to factors like water infiltration, evapotranspiration, and runoff. Two cropping patterns were identified through field investigations within the watershed, including rice paddy-broad bean rotation and corn-broad bean rotation, distributed within specific land use areas for corn and rice paddy. Point source inputs of nitrogen and phosphorus are allocated based on sub-basin distributions, including fixed discharges from various sources such as livestock and poultry farms, factories, rural domestic waste, and wastewater.  2.4.3 Calibration of the SWAT model simulation results The SWAT-CUP (Calibration and Uncertainty Programs) calibration approach (Abbaspour et al., 2007 ) is used in this study.
