Prior to calibration, both single and global sensitivity analyses are conducted to identify the most important parameters for calibration purposes (Du et al., 2020; Faramarzi et al., 2017 ). Each parameter is assigned an initial range (Table S1 ) based on literature values and earlier research by the authors (Chen et al., 2023 ). These parameter sets are then input into SWAT-CUP, which generated output variables for comparison with the measured data using the Sequential Uncertainty Fitting algorithm (SUFI)-2 method (Panagopoulos et al., 2015 ). The Latin Hypercube Sampling technique in SWAT-CUP is used to sample input parameter ranges. During SWAT-CUP runs, parameter iterations are required. Therefore, this study conducted 300 simulations for each iteration and a total of 5 iterations (Panagopoulos et al., 2015; Ostad-Ali-Askari, 2022 ).  2.4.4 Evaluation of SWAT model simulation results In order to evaluate model performance, several widely recognized statistical criteria are used, namely the coefficient of determination (R2 ), Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) coefficient, and percent bias (Pbias). These measures are selected as they are the most commonly used in the literature (Chen et al., 2023; Amatya et al., 2022 ). As demonstrated in previous studies, there is a trade-off among these metrics in multi-objective calibration scenarios, as different metrics tend to focus on specific aspects of model performance (Du et al., 2020 ). The formulas for these measures are as follows:(4) R 2  = [ ∑ i  ( Q obs , i   - Q  ¯   obs  )  ( Q sim , i   - Q  ¯   sim  )   ]  2  ∑ i  ( Q obs , i   - Q  ¯   obs  )  2  ∑ i  ( Q sim , i   - Q  ¯   sim  )  2        (5) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  Q obs   - Q sim      2   ∑ i = 1  n  Q obs   - Q  ¯   obs      2        (6) Pbias = ∑ Q sim   - Q obs    Q obs    × 100      where Qobs  are the observed values, Qsim  are the simulated values, Q  ¯   obs    is the mean of the observed values, Q  ¯   sim    is the mean of the simulated values, and i  is the length of the simulation sequence. Moriasi et al. (2015)  defined performance measure values as ‘acceptable’, as follows R2  ≥ 0.60, NSE≥0.50, Pbias < ±15 % for streamflow, Pbias < ±20 % for sediment, and Pbias < ±30 % for nutrients.   2.5 Coupling of the SoLIM model and SWAT model This study investigates the adaptability and uncertainty of soil maps generated by the SoLIM model when integrated into the SWAT model. The simplified framework (Fig. 2  ) consists of the following steps: 1) Prepare basic data, including DEM, soil maps, soil properties, land use, meteorological data, point sources, and survey data on agricultural operations. 2) Generate environmental covariates, such as humidity index, slope, profile curvature, and contour curvature, using an automated model based on ArcGIS 10.2′s ModelBuilder function. The detailed model can be found in Supplementary Materials. 3 ) Execute the SoLIM model to generate spatial distribution maps of soils, soil properties, and their uncertainties. The uncertainty distribution map is automatically generated based on the SoLIM model, as detailed in Section 2.3 . Soil properties and uncertainty ratio generated by the SoLIM model are multiplied to obtain ranges for each soil attribute across soil types, which are used as non-fixed parameter inputs in the SWAT-CUP interface. As well, SWAT-CUP utilizes Latin hypercube sampling to randomly select values within parameter ranges, enabling automatic calculation of all HRUs based on the selected parameters. The soil parameters are uniformly distributed within the range of their maximum and minimum values. 4) Establish a necessary database for running the SWAT model. 5) Run the SWAT model to obtain desired model outputs. 6) Run SWAT-CUP for the first time. In this initial run, exclude parameters related to soil properties generated by the SoLIM model. This run, involving sensitivity analysis, calibration, and validation, focusing on fixing all parameters except those generated by the SoLIM model, is to ensure that other parameters do not interfere with the uncertainty analysis of the SoLIM-generated parameters in the SWAT model. 7) Run SWAT-CUP for the second time. In this run, both fixed parameters obtained from the first run and the parameters associated with the soil properties generated by the SoLIM model are included. This enables the calculation of the 95 % Prediction Performance uncertainty (95PPU) of the SWAT-CUP model (95PPU is obtained using SWAT-CUP for 1500 simulations, following a normal distribution), representing the sensitivity attributed to the soil generated by the SoLIM model as used within the SWAT model framework.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Obtaining SWAT parameters In the SoLIM model, there are two types of parameters: fixed and non-fixed. Fixed parameters include all variables except for soil properties generated by SoLIM. These parameters control variables and help uncertainty analysis within the SWAT model. These fixed parameters, derived from the initial run of SWAT-CUP, maintain consistent values in subsequent runs. They act as baseline values against which the effects of non-fixed parameters are assessed. On the other hand, non-fixed parameters consist of the pertinent parameters associated with SoLIM-generated soil properties along with their corresponding uncertainty ranges. These parameters form the input for the second SWAT-CUP run. Soil properties generated by SoLIM include sand, silt, and clay contents, soil bulk density, and soil water content. The uncertainty range for each of these soil properties is automatically determined by the SoLIM model using the exaggeration uncertainty algorithm outlined in Section 2.3 . This study ensures the accuracy of the determination of the effects of soil data uncertainty on SWAT model simulation results, since only non-fixed parameters differ while all other conditions remain constant. 3.1.1 Obtaining fixed parameters The initial run of SWAT-CUP is conducted to obtain fixed parameters, with detailed specific settings as described in Section 2.4 . Following a sensitivity analysis of parameters, 41 parameters are selected and grouped into four categories: streamflow, sediment, TN, and TP (Table 1  ). The automated iteration function in SWAT-CUP is used to derive ‘acceptable’ values for R2 , NSE, and Pbias. Subsequently, SWAT-Check is used to evaluate the accuracy of input data and output results from the SWAT model (White et al., 2014 ). Parameters are then adjusted based on empirical knowledge to achieve ‘acceptable’ values for R2 , NSE, Pbias, and SWAT-Check (Fig. 3  ). However, the Pbias value for sediment is 75.2 % and the NSE is 0.10, both of which are considered ‘unacceptable’ (Moriasi et al., 2015 ). Validation results showed a similar trend (Table S2 ). Despite attempting multiple methods, none successfully resolved this issue. The utilization of realistic soil types resulted in a sediment Pbias value of 15.3 %, which differed greatly from that of Chen et al. (2023)  (note: this is another study conducted by the authors using real soil types in the study area). Apart from the soil maps generated by the SoLIM model, all other data and methods applied in this study were identical to those used by Chen et al. (2023) . In addition, accurately predicting sediment properties in the SWAT model is inherently challenging. The uncertainties related to soil sand, clay, and silt content further complicate sediment prediction. Therefore, the discrepancy is attributed to the soil maps generated by the SoLIM model. Although the prediction of TP is acceptable, its accuracy is inferior to the results of Chen et al. (2023) . In other studies where the SoLIM model is coupled with the SWAT model, only hydrology is considered, making it challenging to establish reference points for comparison.  3.1.2 Obtaining non-fixed parameters and analyzing results of the SoLIM model The SoLIM model generates soil maps (Fig. 4  a), soil property maps (Fig. 4 b), and their uncertainties (Fig. 4 c) using environmental factors such as DEM, humidity index, slope, profile curvature, and contour curvature, along with point soil attribute data like sand, silt, and clay content; soil BD; and soil water content. Multiple soil types can be selected for the soil map. In this study, 11 soil types are ultimately chosen, denoted as SoLIMi, where i ranges from 1 to 12. The spatial distribution patterns of these 11 soil types align with the observed trends in the actual soil distribution within the Fengyu River watershed. However, SoLIM2 is a soil type present outside of the Fengyu River watershed, and is therefore excluded from the analysis. The integration of the soil map generated using the SoLIM model with the actual soil types in the Fengyu River watershed involves replacing SoLIMi with the corresponding real soil type. However, this replacement is not done in this study in order to align the soil map with the SWAT-CUP input parameters. The SoLIM model calculates the similarity vector for each pixel in the region based on established soil-environmental knowledge, indicating the similarity between the soil of a pixel and a specific soil type (Li et al., 2020 ). The model then represents this similarity as a fuzzy membership map (Zhu et al., 2010 ). Therefore, the soil map generated by the SoLIM model (Fig. 4 a) exhibits continuity consistent with the actual soil distribution. Furthermore, certain parameters influenced by soil data in the SWAT model, such as the Curve Number (CN) exhibit multicollinearity that cannot be eliminated. Additionally, the SoLIM model cannot directly use these parameters. Therefore, variables with multicollinearity are controlled to remain constant in this study to mitigate the influence of these parameters. The SoLIM model infers soil properties in the study area, taking into account environmental factors, which distinguishes it from methods such as kriging, inverse distance weighting, and spline functions. Unlike these other methods that simply rely on spatial distance calculations and disregard the environment (Qin et al., 2021 ), SoLIM integrates environmental context into its analysis. As shown in Fig. 4 b, the soil properties generated by the SoLIM model are more consistent with geographical conditions. In contrast to kriging and other interpolation methods that yield soil property data with spatial autocorrelation, the soil properties generated by the SoLIM model exhibit greater consistency with the surrounding environment than data with spatial autocorrelation. Currently, some studies, such as China’s third soil survey, prohibit the use of kriging and other interpolation methods for certain parameters like soil thickness due to the risk of significant errors (MARA, 2023 ). Therefore, in specific situations, soil properties inferred based on environmental factors, as done by the SoLIM model, are more in line with reality than kriging and other traditional interpolation methods. The SoLIM model generates an uncertainty map (Fig. 4 c) during the production of soil properties based on environmental and point attribute conditions. This map can provide a good indication of the uncertainty range at different locations. Uncertainty is a critical issue in both empirical and mechanistic models, leading to numerous studies on this topic. Typically, models require a comprehensive analysis of algorithm structure, parameter sensitivity, and input data to determine the range of uncertainty, which relies on the extensive experience of professional researchers. However, the uncertainty spatial distribution map provided by the SoLIM model can greatly reduce the amount of required uncertainty analysis. Soil properties and uncertainties of different soil types were transformed into parameters that can be recognized by SWAT-CUP (Table 2  ). In this table, ‘v’ represents the ‘assignment’ algorithm; ‘SOL_AWC’ stands for soil available water content (SOL_AWC, SOL_BD, CLAY, SILT, and SAND are the default parameter names in SWAT); ‘SOL_BD’ stands for soil bulk density; ‘CLAY’ indicates soil clay content; ‘SILT’ refers to soil silt content; ‘SAND’ represents soil sand content; ‘(i)’ denotes soil layer thickness, ‘1′ for ‘0–20 cm’, ‘2′ for ‘20–40 cm’, ‘3′ for ‘40–60 cm’; ‘____’ represents the SWAT-CUP recognition format; ‘SoLIM i’ refers to different soil types. While the uncertainty ranges (Min-Max) for each soil property in each soil layer are summarized in Table 2 , in practice, the specifics for each soil type and layer are inputted to SWAT-CUP. Due to the large amount of data, including a total of 206 parameters, a summary is given in Table 2 . The specific parameters can be found in Table S3 .   3.2 Sensitivity analysis of SWAT results to the uncertainty in soil properties generated by the SoLIM model 3.2.1 Uncertainty analysis of validation metrics with extreme input parameter values In the second round of running SWAT-CUP, the extreme values (minimum and maximum) of the soil parameters obtained from converting the results of the SoLIM model are used as inputs. The obtained R2 , NSE, and Pbias values from both the optimal and extreme parameters are organized and presented in Fig. 5  . Furthermore, the optimum values of 165 non-fixed parameters are included in Table S4 . These “optimum” values are not manually selected but are automatically chosen by SWAT-CUP through iterations within the given parameter range, based on metrics such as R2 , NSE, etc.). Interestingly, some of the optimal values in Fig. 5  fall outside the range of the minimum and maximum values. Additionally, the statistical result for the maximum value is smaller than that for the minimum value in some cases. This occurrence is expected because the study investigated the impact of the extreme parameter values on verification indicators. The results from different observation indicators are as follows: For streamflow, the R2  range is from 0.86 to 0.88, which is considered very good according to the criteria suggested by Moriasi et al. (2015) , This indicates a linear correlation between simulated and observed streamflow. The NSE values range from 0.72 to 0.75, which is classified as good, indicating a high level of agreement between simulated and observed streamflow. However, the Pbias is 19.7 (unsatisfactory range) when using optimum soil parameter values. This is much higher than the Pbias values when both the maximum soil parameter values (5.9, good range) and the minimum soil parameter values (10.1, satisfactory range). There is a significant cumulative deviation between simulated and observed streamflow, indicating poor fitting when using the optimum soil parameters. Additionally, there is uncertainty in the underestimation of this deviation with observed streamflow. For sediment, the R2  values range from 0.48 to 0.55 (satisfactory range), indicating a linear correlation between simulated and observed sediment. However, the NSE values range from 0.03 to 0.23 (unsatisfactory range), indicating a low level of fit between simulated and observed sediment. Additionally, the Pbias values range from 64 to 79 (unsatisfactory range), indicating a severe underestimation of the observed sediment. The unpredictable nature of sediment and the large number of influencing parameters (Table 1 ) likely contribute to errors and uncertainties associated with the modeling. Even in studies where the SWAT model was modified for sediment simulation, such as by Long et al. (2023)  the accuracy remained limited, with NSE values between 0.51 and 0.62, and PBIAS values between −13.3 % and 13.7 %. Therefore, the soil data generated by the SoLIM model introduces additional uncertainty to the SWAT sediment simulation. For TN, the R2  values range from 0.82 to 0.85 (very good range), indicating a linear correlation between simulated and observed TN. The NSE values range from 0.28 to 0.67 (unsatisfactory to very good ranges), indicating uncertain fitting between simulated and observed TN. The Pbias values range from 1.5 to 28.6 (very good to satisfactory ranges), indicating that the observed TN is underestimated and there is higher uncertainty. For TP, the R2  values range from 0.82 to 0.84 (very good rang), indicating a linear correlation between simulated and observed TP. The NSE values range from 0.64 to 0.67 (good to very good ranges), indicating a high degree of fit between simulated and observed TP. However, the Pbias values range from –23.5 to 69.8 (satisfactory to unsatisfactory ranges), indicating high uncertainty in prediction of observed TP. In this study, the accuracy of the SWAT model simulation for TN and TP, generally meets the criteria of Moriasi et al. (2015) , and is consistent with findings from other research and falls (Geza and McCray, 2008; Sharma et al., 2023; Nepal et al., 2023 ). After inputting the SoLIM result parameters into the SWAT model, the following observations can be made: 1) There is a linear correlation between the simulated and observed values for all model outputs. 2) When considering the fitting degree (i.e., the NSE), sediment exhibits greater uncertainty compared to streamflow, which affects the simulation of other SWAT model outputs. TN also demonstrates greater uncertainty, although it has a lesser impact on other model outputs. 3) Analysis of Pbias reveals significant uncertainty for all model outputs. Determining what constitutes an ‘acceptable’ Pbias value remains debatable. It would be argued that achieving “optimal soil parameters” yields an acceptable Pbias value. Streamflow, sediment, and TN produced positive Pbias, while TP produced both positive and negative Pbias. Overall, the variability of the SoLIM results on the SWAT model results is within an acceptable range.  3.2.2 Sensitivity analysis of SWAT parameters After applying SWAT-CUP, parameters with sensitivity p-values < 0.1 were selected. The corresponding soil layer, parameter name, t-Stat, p-value, SoLIM soil, slope, and land use are summarized in Table 3  . Higher sensitivity indicates greater uncertainty. The sensitivity analysis of the parameters was conducted from different perspectives as follows: For land use, the dominant land uses for sensitive parameters are rice paddy and pasture. Rice paddy and pasture exhibit rapid growth, and lifecycles are shorter than forest in regions with cold winters, making them more responsive to and dependent on environmental factors during their growth process (Zhang et al., 2020, 2022 ). Soil water is a crucial limiting factor for the growth of rice paddies and pastures, whereas cropland, forest, orchard, and villages have lower demands for soil water and minimal impact on model parameters (Wang et al., 2018 ). In terms of soil texture, rice paddies and pasture often grow in soils with fine texture, which have a strong capacity to retain water and nutrients (Du et al., 2021 ). Therefore, these land uses exert a significant influence on model parameters. Parameters with a sensitivity p-value < 0.1 show notable differences among soil layers. Specifically, 5 parameters are identified for the depth of 40–60 cm, 4 parameters for the depth of 0–20 cm, and only 2 parameters for the depth of 20–40 cm. The soil layers of 0–20 cm and 40–60 cm represent surface and deep soil layers, respectively. The properties and water status of these two depth ranges of soil layers are usually different compared to the soil layer of 20–40 cm, resulting in different responses to model parameters. Root distribution is concentrated in the shallow soil layer of 0–20 cm, where soil water content changes rapidly, and spatial variability in soil texture, organic matter is pronounced. Qi et al. (2019)  showed that this layer is usually affected by agricultural management measures, such as irrigation and fertilization, affecting distribution of soil water and nutrients. Even minor changes in soil parameters can have a significant impact on water movement and plant growth. In contrast, the deeper soil layer of 40–60 cm is usually less affected by human activities, allowing natural factors to contribute more to the systematic development of soil properties. Factors like groundwater level and physical soil properties are dominant in this deep layer. Additionally, absorption and release rates of water and nutrients are slower in this deep soil layer, resulting in longer time delays in effects on hydrological and ecological processes. Consequently, the model exhibits higher sensitivity to the soil parameters in this layer (Rajib et al., 2016 ). The soil layer of 20–40 cm is where the roots of shallow and deep crop roots intersect. This area exhibits less spatial variability in soil parameters, leading to a balanced distribution of roots. This would moderate water movement speed and thereby stabilizing the soil’s response to crop roots. As a result, the sensitivity of model output to the soil parameters decreases. Zhang et al. (2022)  showed that the soil layer of 20–40 cm acts as a turning point for nutrient distribution, with lower nutrient content below this layer and higher nutrient content above. Therefore, the nutrient content within this layer may not have as much impact on the model output as the soil layers above and below it. The physical and chemical properties of the soil in the layer of 20–40 cm may have a relatively smooth transition with the soil layers above and below it, minimizing the impact of changes in soil properties within this layer on the model output. Therefore, small changes in soil parameters in the layer of 20–40 cm have a limited impact on water and nutrient transport, resulting in a relatively low sensitivity to these soil parameters. Other watershed properties, including SoLIM soil and slope, have uniform distributions of sand, silt, and clay contents, as well as soil BD, and soil water content for each soil type. These properties do not show any significant correlation with the model output sensitivity. Specifically, none of the five parameters for soil BD demonstrate a p-value < 0.1. Generally, the model outputs have lower sensitivity to soil BD because these parameters are mainly used to calculate effective soil water and groundwater flow rates in the model, rather than directly impacting hydrological processes and pollutant migration (Neitsch et al., 2009 ). On the other hand, soil water content is one of the important input parameters in the model as it directly influences soil water changes, streamflow generation, and water pollution processes. Therefore, model outputs usually tend to be more sensitive to soil water content parameters than to soil bulk density parameters.  3.2.3 Uncertainty analysis over the output time series Fig. 6   illustrate variations in streamflow, sediment yield, TN load, and TP load across different temporal scales. The plot includes 95PPU and optimum values. It represents the uncertainty range of the SWAT model results, which arises from soil parameters generated by the SoLIM model. The optimum value for streamflow during the flood season typically falls towards the lower end of the uncertainty range. Conversely, the optimum value during the non-flood season is situated towards the upper end of the uncertainty range. The SWAT model calculates streamflow using the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) curve number equation (Neitsch et al., 2009 ) (Eq. S1). In the SCS, the storage parameter varies spatially based on soil type, land use, management practices, and slope, which vary with changes in soil water content (Eq. S2). During the flood season, frequent rainfall causes relatively high soil water content, leading to reduced infiltration and increased river flow. In contrast, during the non-flood season, soil water content is relatively low, thereby increasing water infiltration and storage in the vadose zones, and limiting flow into groundwater or rivers. Rainfall is partially absorbed and evaporated, resulting in relatively low streamflow (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Therefore, in this study soil water parameters generated by the SoLIM model introduce uncertainty into SWAT model simulations of streamflow. These parameters affect moisture retention parameters during both flood and non-flood seasons. Additionally, soil texture generated by the SoLIM model introduces uncertainty into the SWAT model streamflow simulations, affecting the effective infiltration coefficient, K. The same equation is used for streamflow calculation in both flood and non-flood seasons in the SWAT model. This can lead to overestimation of sensitivity of streamflow to soil water content during the flood season. Soil water content can exceed field capacity, resulting in an underestimation of optimal values within the uncertainty range. During the non-flood season, water scarcity reduces AWC below field capacity, neglecting effects of plant uptake and evapotranspiration and potentially overestimating optimum values within the uncertainty range. During the flood season, sediment yield, TN load, and TP load, display optimal values near the highest end of the uncertainty range, while during the non-flood season they tend to be at the lowest end of the uncertainty range. This pattern is contrary to the result for streamflow. This phenomenon can be attributed to abundant and saturated soil water capacity in the watershed during the flood season, facilitating sediment and nutrients (i. e., TN, and TP) running off into the river with streamflow. The flood season usually coincides with crop growth period. The land is intensively cultivated and fertilized, which further increases production of sediment, TN, and TP in the watershed. During the flood season, the rapid water flow rate enhances the transport capacity, effectively carrying suspended solids (such as sediment) and dissolved substances (such as TN and TP) downstream (Wu et al., 2023 ). This leads to the estimates of sediment yield, TN load, and TP load being near the highest end of the uncertainty range during flood season. In contrast, rainfall and fertilization are reduced during the non-flood season, resulting in the relatively slow water flow rates. This, coupled with the soil’s enhanced ability to retain and transform nutrients, leads to lower sediment yield, TN load, and TP load (Kang et al., 2021 ). In the SWAT model, soil texture only affects soil erodibility, which in turn affects the outputs of sediment, TN, and TP. Sediment affects the Enrichment Ratio of Phosphorus (ERORGP) parameter, while TP often adheres to sediment and is transported by non-flood season streamflow. Therefore, the optimal values of TP during the non-flood season tend to slightly exceed their uncertainty range compared to TN (Fig. 6 d). Overall, the uncertainty in parameters such as sand, silt, and clay contents; soil BD; and soil water content parameters generated by the SoLIM model affects the range of output values derived from the SWAT model. Specifically, during the flood season, the optimal value of streamflow tends to be at the lower end of the uncertainty range, while in the non-flood season, it tends to be at the upper end. Interestingly, this pattern is reversed for sediment yield, TN load, and TP load.  3.2.4 Sensitivity analysis for model output in space To assess the effects of soil data uncertainty generated by the SoLIM model on the sensitivity of SWAT model results, SWAT-CUP was used by inputting the maximum and minimum parameter values obtained from the SoLIM model. This process provided the spatial distribution data for sub-watersheds. By calculating the differences between these data sets, sub-watersheds that exhibited relatively high absolute values are identified, which marked in red in Fig. 7  . The corresponding land use and slope data for these sub-watersheds are listed in Table 4  . Sub-watersheds that exhibit high uncertainty in sediment yield, TN load, and TP load generally show consistent and high uncertainty for all these outputs. However, these sub-watersheds differ significantly from those displaying high streamflow uncertainty, which aligns more closely with the temporal uncertainty patterns. Specifically, sub-watersheds Nos. 1 to 4 in Table 4  are those with large uncertainty in sediment yield, TN load, and TP load, whereas sub-watersheds Nos. 5 to 7 are those with large uncertainty in streamflow. Sub-watersheds Nos. 5 to 7 are mainly covered by forest, while areas Nos. 1 to 4 have a balanced mix of pasture, forests, and rice paddy fields. Soil water in forests exhibits greater temporal and spatial variability compared to pasture and rice paddy fields. In contrast, the relatively uniform vegetation in pasture and rice paddy fields helps maintain stable soil water loss pathways, reducing uncertainty in streamflow (Du et al., 2021 ). In addition, the undulating terrain, abundant vegetation, and litter in forests can effectively store rainwater, gradually releasing it into the groundwater system or supplying it to rivers (Chen et al., 2020 ). This process can lead to localized water flow and increase streamflow uncertainty. A study by Wang et al. (2014)  shows that the conversion of forestland to cropland increases water flow. However, amount and transport of sediment, TN, and TP are mainly concentrated in rice paddy fields and pastures, leading to high uncertainty in these areas. Regarding slope, areas Nos. 5 to 7 mainly consist of steep slopes, whereas areas Nos. 1 to 4 have a more balanced proportion of slopes. Overall, areas with steeper slopes are associated with higher levels of uncertainty. Sime et al. (2022)  found that areas with steeper slopes exhibit higher uncertainties in both water and sediment measurements. This is because areas with steeper slopes usually have increased streamflow velocity and runoff, leading to more variable hydrological processes and non-linear responses. As a result, the estimation of parameters related to streamflow, sediment yield, TN load, and TP load in hydrological models becomes more uncertain (Lu and Chiang, 2019 ).  3.2.5 Uncertainty analysis of streamflow impact The SWAT model is run using the maximum and minimum soil parameter values generated by the SoLIM model. Subsequently, a SWAT-Check analysis is conducted on the SWAT model’s hydrological output, considering the optimal, maximum, and minimum soil parameter values (Fig. 8  ). Due to the limited availability of solar radiation data in the meteorological database, the Integrated Physical and Ecological Simulation Tool (IPET) in the ‘basins.bsn’ file of SWAT-CUP was set to ‘2 = Har’ (Hargreaves), as this setting provides a better simulation when solar radiation data is missing. The soil parameters, including sand, silt, and clay contents; soil BD; and soil water content, generated by the SoLIM model, do not affect potential evapotranspiration (PET), precipitation, average curve number, or evaporation from the shallow aquifer (revap). However, these parameters have an impact on evaporation and transpiration, surface runoff, lateral flow, return flow, percolation to the shallow aquifer, and recharge to the deep aquifer (Fig. 8 ). In the SWAT model, the estimation of evapotranspiration (ET) includes PET, evaporation, and transpiration. PET is determined using functional relationships between potential evapotranspiration and the leaf area index. There are three estimation methods commonly used: Hargreaves (Hargreaves and Samani, 1985 ), Priestley-Taylor (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ), and Penman-Monteith (Monteith, 1965 ). These methods are independent of soil attribute parameters. Evaporation is estimated by using an exponential function that takes into account soil depth and water content. Transpiration is estimated with a linear function that considers potential evapotranspiration and leaf area index. Therefore, the uncertainty of soil water content affects the accuracy of evaporation estimation. Revap from the shallow aquifer is related to soil texture and, to some extent, soil temperature (Wang and Melesse, 2006 ). However, in the SWAT model, this parameter is determined solely by a revap coefficient (βrev ) and potential evaporation (E0 ) (Eq. S3). Therefore, the values for revap from the shallow aquifer (wrevap ) are unaffected by changes in soil texture and soil temperature. Lateral flow, represented as the net outflow at the slope outlet cross section (Qlat ) in the SWAT model, is influenced by the thickness of the saturated zone perpendicular to the slope surface at the outlet cross section (H0 ) and the flow velocity at the outlet cross section (vlat ), as shown in Eq. S4. The value of H0  is determined by several parameters on a given day, including the soil water content (SWly ), total porosity of the soil layer (Φd ), and slope length (Lhill ), as shown in Eq. S5. Therefore, the soil water content and soil texture, as generated by the SoLIM model, introduce uncertainty into the results of the SWAT model by affecting SWly  and Φd . Among the fixed parameters, the value of ‘r__CN2.mgt’ has been fixed at 0.196, ensuring a stable average curve number. According to Eq. S2 and S6, changes in soil water content affect the retention parameter (S), thereby affecting the CN parameter. However, as the CN value remains fixed, uncertainty in surface runoff arises indirectly from the impact of lateral flow. Meanwhile, lateral flow affects various factors such as shallow groundwater recharge to the deep aquifer, return flow, percolation to the shallow aquifer, and recharge to the deep aquifer (Neitsch et al., 2009 ). In the SWAT model, the amount of water infiltration from the shallow to the deep groundwater layer (wdeep ) is mainly determined by the groundwater infiltration coefficient (βdeep ) and the total daily groundwater supply (wrchrg ), as shown in Eq. S7. The corresponding parameter, known as RCHRG_DP, is fixed in SWAT-CUP, ensuring stability without introducing uncertainty. Groundwater runoff and baseflow (Qgw ) are affected by the groundwater infiltration coefficient (Ksat ), the distance from the sub-watershed groundwater divide to the main channel (Lgw ), and the depth of the water table (hwtbl ), as shown in Eq. S8. Therefore, uncertainty in return flow is influenced by soil texture through its effect on Ksat . Overall, the soil properties (soil texture, soil BD, and soil water content) generated by the SoLIM model introduce uncertainty to the results of the SWAT model. This uncertainty stems from their influence on evaporation, SWly , Φd , and Ksat .   3.3 Coupling analysis of the SWAT model using soil data from the SoLIM model The application of the SoLIM model, in accordance with the third law of geography, uses existing soil data and topographic information to generate new soil data. This generated data supports simulation of key processes such as soil water and nutrient cycling in the SWAT model. Compared with traditional mapping methods, SoLIM-generated soil data offers higher spatial accuracy and improves the spatial continuity of SWAT model simulations. It can effectively fill data gaps, allowing the SWAT model to cover a wider area and improve its applicability across different regions. Furthermore, the SoLIM model enhances data consistency by consolidating similar soil types, reducing the number of HRUs, and easing computational burdens on the SWAT model, especially in large-scale watersheds. Additionally, the SoLIM model can reduce the cost and time required to obtain soil data, enabling faster data generation. However, there are limitations associated with SoLIM-generated soil data. Achieving accurate simulation of soil type distribution in reality always involves some degree of error, which poses a challenge in the field of soil science. This uncertainty can impact outcomes such as streamflow, sediment yield, TN load, or TP load, requiring careful consideration in management practices using SoLIM/SWAT data. Furthermore, the selection of environmental factors in the SoLIM model is critical. In this study, multiple environmental factors were selected, incorporating additional factors for soil attribute inference can further improve the SWAT model’s ability to simulate real natural conditions accurately. Despite these challenges, SoLIM-generated soil data generally provides reliable support for SWAT model applications.   4 Conclusion This study utilizes the Fengyu River watershed in Yunnan Province, China, as a case study. The Soil Landscape Inference Model (SoLIM), based on the Third Law of Geography, is employed to generate a soil dataset. This dataset serves as input for the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model to assess the impact of soil dataset uncertainty on performance of the hydrological model. The study showed that: 1) Despite introducing sensitivity in sediment yield, using SoLIM-generated soil data in the SWAT model maintain overall reliability. Therefore, soil datasets based on the Third Law of Geography can serve as input for semi-distributed hydrological models. 2) Uncertainty introduced by SoLIM-generated soil data affects specific model parameters such as evaporation, total porosity of the soil layer (Φd ), and groundwater infiltration coefficient (Ksat ), thereby influencing the sensitivity of SWAT predictions for streamflow and water quality. 3) Factors influencing model outcomes include steeper slopes in certain areas, which enhance streamflow velocity and flow rates, resulting in more dynamic and non-linear responses. Additionally, soil water dynamics exhibit higher temporal and spatial variability in forests compared to pasture and rice paddy fields, where vegetation tends to be more uniform, maintaining stable soil water loss pathways and reducing uncertainty in streamflow predictions. Compared to traditional methods of soil measurements, soil data generated by SoLIM offers higher spatial accuracy, enhancing the spatial continuity of SWAT model simulations and reducing computational load for large-scale watersheds by consolidating similar soil types. Nonetheless, accurately simulating soil type distribution poses challenges in soil science. Further research should focus on selecting suitable environmental factors in the SoLIM model to improve the SWAT model’s ability to simulate natural conditions more effectively. This study lays a foundation for addressing challenges in acquiring precise soil datasets for hydrological models.
1 Introduction Glaciers and snow meltwater provide water resources for more than 1.9 billion people living in or directly downstream of mountainous areas (Immerzeel et al., 2020 ). Glaciers regulate the discharge of many rivers (Wang et al., 2021b ), which plays a vital role in sustaining ecosystems and supplying fresh water for lowland areas (Nie et al., 2021 ). However, as the glacier melt is profoundly affected by temperature changes, these regions have become one of the most vulnerable environments to climate change (Barnett et al., 2005 ). A continuous loss of glacial storage is anticipated throughout the 21st century due to glaciers' strong responses to a warmer climate (Ragettli et al., 2013 ). As glaciers retreat, annual glacier runoff will typically increase until it reaches a maximum, beyond which runoff will decrease as the reduced glacier storage will no longer support increasing meltwater quantities (Huss and Hock, 2018 ), and subsequently it may greatly influence water resources in these regions. Glacier storage change's impact on runoff has recently gained much attention and has been assessed using different approaches. One profitable way is scenario analysis using hydrological models. Using the WASA hydrological model, Duethmann et al. (2015)  studied the impact of glacier geometry changes on runoff changes in the Aksu River and revealed that the annual runoff increases would be reduced by 14–23 % when glacier area and surface elevation decreased. However, the application of hydrological models requires the calibration of multiple parameters, which entails high uncertainty and considerable complexity in the process. Another way is the climate elasticity method based on the Budyko framework. By incorporating glacier mass balance and glacier fraction into the Budyko framework, Liu et al. (2022a)  investigated the glaciers' effect on runoff in 25 upstream basins in the Tarim River Basin (TRB) during 2001–2010. They found that a 1 % increase in glacier area fraction could lead to a 0.49 % increase in runoff. Similarly, by incorporating the ratio of glacier runoff into the Budyko framework, Xin et al. (2021)  revealed that the change in the proportion of glacier runoff is responsible for 49 % of the runoff change in the upper reaches of the Yarlung Zangbo River in the period between 1966 and 2015. Ning et al. (2021)  quantified the contribution of snowmelt runoff to streamflow in the Qilian Mountains using the Budyko framework incorporated with a degree-day model. Yang et al. (2024)  attributed the streamflow variation by incorporating glacier mass balance and frozen ground into the Budyko framework, they found that contribution of glacier mass balance to variation in streamflow varied between −2.42 % and 11.63 % in Qilian Mountains from 1982 to 2015. Those works demonstrated that the climate elasticity method based on the Budyko framework exhibits strong operability. However, it is noteworthy that, in those previous studies, both the hydrological modeling approach and the climate elasticity method require extensive glacier data. By now, it is difficult to obtain long-term time series of glacier data. Due to technical limitations, remote sensing images that can be used to invert relatively complete and accurate glacier data, such as ENVISAT (launched in 2002, https://earth.esa.int/eogateway/missions/envisat ), ICESat (Ice Cloud and land Welevation Satellite, launched in 2003, https://icesat.gsfc.nasa.gov ), and Sentinel (launched in 2014, https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel ) were unavailable until the last 20 years. Consquently, shortage of glacier data limits the researches on the impact of glaciers on runoff for a long period. It is urgently required to propose a method to quantify the impact of warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff without glacial data. Therefore, we aim to propose a simple and feasible elasticity method based on the Budyko framework to quantify the influence of warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff without glacier data. Furthermore, based on this method, we prepare to improve the attribution analysis framework for runoff change and conduct a comprehensive attribution analysis on 17 upstream glacier-covered catchments in the TRB from 1960 to 2019.  2 Methods and Data 2.1 Water balance and the Budyko framework In an enclosed catchment, the water balance equation can be expressed as R  = P  – AET – ∆S , with R  being runoff (mm/yr), P  being precipitation (mm/yr), AET being actual evapotranspiration (mm/yr), and ∆S  being the terrestrial water storage change (mm/yr). Wherein P  is the total precipitation including rain and snow that falls to ground surface. According to Li et al. (2020)  and Xu et al. (2009) , snowmelt has a minor influence on runoff increase in comparison to rainfall and glacier melt in the Tarim River Basin, coupled with the lack of snowfall data, we didn't distinguish between direct rainfall and snowfall in this study. ∆S  reflects the changes in the moisture storage in surface and subsurface stores, such as soil moisture and groundwater. According to Zhang et al. (2001) , the change of soil moisture and groundwater are frequently omitted over long periods because of lower anomaly, especially in regins with limited human activities. However, the glacier storage change ∆G  (mm/yr) is generally non-negligible under climate change in glacier-covered regions (Liu et al., 2022a ). Consquently, if ignoring storage changes in groundwater and soil moisture, ∆S  could be approximated as ∆G , and the water balance equation yields:(1) R = P − AET − Δ G      The glacier storage change ∆G  (mm/yr) can be expressed as ∆G= A  – L,  where A  (mm/yr) represents the accumulation of the glacier caused by processes such as snowfall, and L  (mm/yr) represents the loss of the glacier caused by melting and sublimation. Due to technical limitations, it is difficult to obtain long term data of ∆G . To explore the impact of glaciers on runoff in a long period, we make the following simplifications: (1) the accumulation and loss of glaciers are balanced under stable climatic conditions, denote the glacier loss in this situation as L B   (mm/yr),  then there is A  = L B  , thus ∆G  =0, which we refer to as the equilibrium state; (2) when temperature rise, the balance in the equilibrium state is broken, the amount of glacier melt will increase, denote this warming-induced glacier melt increase as L T   (mm/yr), then there is ∆G=A  – L B   – L T  , as A = L B  , ∆G  can be expressed as -L T  ; (3) since we focus on the warming-induced glacier storage change, we can assume that ∆G  is only affected by temperature in the following process and then indirectly express the change of ∆G  by the change of temperature thus to get rid of the limitation of lacking glacier data. AET can be estimated using the Budyko framework (Budyko, 1974 ), which refers to the ratio of actual evapotranspiration (AET) to precipitation (P ) as a function of the potential evapotranspiration (PET, mm/yr), precipitation and a parameter (n ) associated with catchment land surface characteristics, including vegetation, soil, and geographic properties, at a mean annual scale (Wang et al., 2021a ). Here, we use the Mezentsev–Choudhury-Yang equation (Choudhury, 1999, Mezentsev, 1955, Yang et al., 2008 ):(2) AET = P × PET  ( P  n  + PET  n  )  1 / n          where P  is the total available water supply, and PET is the available energy for evapotranspiration. Combined with Eq. (1) , mean annual runoff in glacier-covered regions can be estimated as follows:(3) R = P − P × PET  ( P  n  + PET  n  )  1 / n     − Δ G      In this study, we consider the parameter n  as a constant, it can be retrieved using multi-year average of runoff, precipitation, PET and ∆G  by Eq. (3) . ∆G  is about an order of 10 while P  is an order of 100 (Liu et al., 2006 ), thus we ignored ∆G  in the process of retrieving n .  2.2 Impact of Warming-Induced Glacier Storage Change on Runoff Based on Eq. (3) , the total differential of R  concerning temperature (expressed as T , ℃) can be given as:(4a) d R  d T   = ∂ R  ∂ PET   d PET  d T   + ∂ R  ∂ Δ G   d Δ G  d T   + ∂ R  ∂ P   d P  d T       or(4b) 1 R   d R  d T   = 1 R   ∂ R  ∂ PET   d PET  d T   + 1 R   ∂ R  ∂ Δ G   d Δ G  d T   + 1 R   ∂ R  ∂ P   d P  d T        As shown in Eq. (4a)  and Eq. (4b) , the impact of temperature on runoff can be divided into three parts, namely one through impacting PET, one through changing ∆G  and the other through impacting P.  The temperature elasticity of runoff is defined as ε  T     = 1  R   d R  dT      (%/℃). Similarly, it can be expressed as the sum of three elasticities: the temperature elasticity of runoff through potential evapotranspiration, ε  PET − T     = 1  R   ∂ R  ∂ PET   d PET   dT      (%/℃), the temperature elasticity of runoff through glacier storage, ε  ∆ G − T     = 1  R   ∂ R  ∂ ∆ G   d ∆ G  dT      (%/℃), and the temperature elasticity of runoff through precipitation, ε  P − T     = 1  R   ∂ R  ∂ P   dP  dT      (%/℃). Wherein ε  ∆ G − T     can quantitively reflect the impact of warming-induced glacier storage change on R  and can be denoted as:(5) ε  ∆ G − T    =  ε  T   – ε  PET − T    – ε  P − T        ε  T     can be assessed by the least squares estimator: ε  T   = 1  R  ̅    ∑  ( T − T  ̅  ) ( R − R  ̅  )   ∑  ( T − T  ̅  )  2        , where R  ̅    is multi-year average runoff and T  ̅    is the multi-year average temperature. We introduced the elasticities of runoff to precipitation and PET as ε  P    =P  R   ∂ R  ∂ P      (%/%) and ε  PET    =PET  R   ∂ R  ∂ PET      (%/%), respectively. Based on Eq. (3) , ε  P     and ε  PET     can be assessed by ε  P     = P  ̅   R  ̅    1 –  1 + P  ̅   n    PET  ̅   n        – n + 1  n           and ε  PET     = - PET  ̅   R  ̅    1 + PET  ̅   n    P  ̅   n        – n + 1  n       , where P  ̅    is multi-year average precipitaion and P ET  ̅    is the multi-year average potential evapotranspiration. Then ε  P − T     can be assessed by ε  P     along with the least squares estimator: ε  P − T   =  ε  P   1  P  ̅     ∑  ( T − T  ̅  ) ( P − P  ̅  )   ∑  ( T − T  ̅  )  2        . Expression of ε  PET − T      is shown in Text A1. Hence, ε  ∆ G − T      can be assessed by subtracting ε  PET − T     and ε  P − T     from ε  T    .  2.3 Improved Attribution Analysis Framework for Glacier-Covered Catchments In previous researches, runoff change is usually attributed to changes in precipitation and potential evapotranspiration (Roderick and Farquhar, 2011; Xu et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014 ; Zhang et al., 2016 ; Liu et al., 2022b ). However, in glacier-covered regions, ignoring the impact of glaciers on runoff changes would lead to deviation in attribution analysis. Here, we used the elasticity method to estimate the attribution of the variation in runoff. We combine Budyko framework and water balance equation in glacier-coverd regions in Eq. (3) , according to the Eq. (3) , the first-order differential equation of runoff can be expressed as the sum of driving factors of P , PET and ∆G :(6) dR = ∂ R  ∂ P   dP + ∂ R  ∂ PET   dPET + ∂ R  ∂ ∆ G   d ∆ G      As we mentioned in Section 2.1 , ∆G  is the warming-induced glacier storage change, thus we can assume that ∆G  is only affected by T , then there is d ∆ G   =d ∆ G  dT   dT    and the Eq. (6)  can be expressed as:(7) dR = ∂ R  ∂ P   dP + ∂ R  ∂ PET   dPET + ∂ R  ∂ ∆ G   d ∆ G  dT   dT      As expressed by elasticities of runoff that we mentioned in Section 2.2 , the runoff change can be separated as the impacts of precipitation change, potential evapotranspiration change and warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff:(8a) d R  R  = ε  P   d P  P  + ε  PET   d PET  PET   + ε  Δ G − T   d T     (8b) d R = ε  P   d P  P  R + ε  PET   d PET  PET   R + ε  Δ G − T   d T × R      Replaced differentials with differences, the change in catchment runoff can be expressed as the sum of three components:(9) Δ R = ε  P   Δ P  P ¯     R ¯   + ε  PET   Δ PET  PET  ¯     R ¯   + ε  Δ G − T   Δ T × R ¯     = Δ R  P   + Δ R  PET   + Δ R  Δ G − T         where ∆P , ∆PET and ∆T  are the changes in precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and temperature between two periods, and ∆R P  , ∆R PET  and ∆R ∆G   are the runoff changes caused by precipitation change, potential evapotranspiration change and warming-induced glacier storage change, respectively.  2.4 Estimate of accumulative glacier storage change The accumulative warming-induced glacier storage change can be expressed as:(10) Δ V  G   = R ¯   × ε  Δ G − T   × ∑ i = 2  m  ( T  i   − T  1   )  × S × ρ i = 2 , 3 , ⋯ , m     where ∆V G   is the warming-induced glacier storage change within the calculated period (km3 ), m  is the length of the calculated period (year), T i   is the mean annual temperature in a year i  (℃), and T 1  is five-year moving average temperature centered on the first year (℃), S  is the catchment area (km2 ), and ρ   = 0.9 is the density ratio of ice to water.  2.5 Study Area and Data The Tarim River Basin (TRB) has a drainage area of 1.02×106  km2  with a main stream length of 1321 km, surrounded by the TienShan, Eastern Pamir, Kunlun and Karakorum high mountains. Glacier and snow meltwater is considered the primary source of water for the basin, accounting for around 48.2 % of the total flow (Chen et al., 2007 ). This study selected 17 upstream catchments in the TRB ( Fig. 1 ,  Table 1 ). These catchments were chosen based on the following three criteria: (1) glacier-covered, (2) with runoff records longer than 40 years, (3) the direct influence of human activities such as damming, irrigation and water diversion is relatively low. In this study, monthly observed runoff data from 1960 to 2020 for 17 hydrological stations were collected from the local hydrographic bureau. Notably, all the annual data in this study are aggregated according to the hydrologic year, i.e., from October to next September, so in the following text, the research period is 1960–2019. ERA5-Land precipitation product was selected from CGDPA (Shen and Xiong, 2016 ), ERA5-Land (Muñoz Sabater, 2019, 2021 ) and AERA5-Asia (Ma et al., 2022 ) employing the extended double instrumental variable algorithms (EIVD) (Dong et al., 2020 ), which can effectively assess product errors without the need for true values, as further elaborated in Table A2. Besides, monthly meteorological data from 1960–2020, including potential evapotranspiration, air temperature, net radiation, wind speed, and relative humidity, are selected from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset (Muñoz Sabater, J., 2021 ). Potential evapotranspiration is computed by making a second call to the surface energy balance (for specific instructions, please refer to: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/dataset/reanalysis-era5-land-monthly-means?tab=overview . The glacier distribution used for Fig. 1  is based on the “mergy_product” from (He and Zhou, 2022 ) (https://doi.org/10.11888/Cryos.tpdc.272302 ). The glacier areas are based on the Second China Glacier Inventory (Guo et al., 2014 ) and Glacier Inventory of China Ⅲ Tianshan Mountain (interior drainage area of TRB in the southwest) (Xie et al., 1987 ). A climatic mutation to warm wet occurred in northwest China in the middle of 1987 (Shi et al., 2003 ). Since then, with the rise of temperature and precipitaion, glacial meltwater has increased rapidly, producing a profound impact on the water reserves of TRB. Therefore, the glacier storage change is evaluated from 1987, and the attribution analysis is also bounded by 1987 and divided into two periods, namely 1960–1987 and 1988–2019.   3 Results 3.1 Warming-induced glacier storage change We first obtained ε  ∆ G − T     for each catchment in the study area during 1987–2019 by using Eq. (5) . As shown in  Table 2 , ε  ∆ G − T     is accessed by ε  T     – ε  PET − T     – ε  P − T    . Then the warming-induced glacier storage change ∆V G   can be obtained as ε  ∆ G − T     based on Eq. (10) . As shown in Table 2 , the total glacier area inside the 17 studied catchments is 14,842 km2 , the calculated warming-induced glacier storage change is −91.05 km3 , so the mean glacier mass balance during 1987–2019 is −0.19 m w.e./yr. The glacier mass balance of this region was reported in two previous studies ( Table 3 ), namely −0.12 m w.e./yr during 1963–1999 by topographical maps and aerial photos in the whole TRB (Liu et al., 2006 ) and −0.14 m w.e./yr during 2000–2019 by high-resolution satellite images in all the 1°×1° tiles involving 17 studied catchment (Hugonnet et al., 2021 ) (He details of the glacier storage change for 2000–2019 in Hugonnet's was shown in Table A3). The glacier mass balance in the two studies are comparable with our result, which indicates that our proposed method has an acceptable estimate of warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff.  3.2 Attribution Analysis of Runoff  Table 4  exhibits the climate elasticity (ε  P    , ε  PET     and ε  ∆ G − T    ) for each catchements in 1960–2019. In the 17 study catchments, ε  P      ranges from 1.8 to 2.6 (1.9 on average), indicating that a 1 % change in P  causes a 1.8–2.6 % change in R ; ε  PET     is between −1.6 to −0.5 (-0.9 on average), implying that a 1 % increase in PET causes a 0.5–1.6 % decrease in R ; besides, ε  ∆ G − T      ranges from 5 % to 29 %/℃ (13 %/℃ on average), indicating that ∆G  change caused by a 1℃ increase in T  will produce a 5–29 % increase in runoff ( Fig. 2 (a)). Then we introduce ε  ∆ G − T      into attribution analysis framework to investigate the causes of runoff changes in the TRB. Multi-year average of meteorological variables (including temperature, precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, net radiation, wind speed at a height of 2 m, relative humidity and saturated vapor pressure) before and after 1987 are shown in Table A4. As shown in Table 4 , the average modeled runoff change for 17 studied catchments is 35.0 mm, close to 33.1 mm that observed, indicating a favorable performance of the proposed attribution method for most catchments. Thus, the method is deemed reliable for analyzing the relative contribution of each variable to the variation in annual runoff. Regarding the causes for runoff change in the two periods, namely 1960–1987 and 1988–2019 in the 17 catchments, precipitation change is responsible for 61.7–108.1 % (77.9 % on average), while warming-induced glacier storage change contributes 11.5–62.9 % (25.2 % on average) and potential evapotranspiration change leads to −39.8–12 % (-3.0 % on average). In the study region, precipitation change is the main factor and has a positive contribution of 77.9 % on runoff changes; warming-induced glacier storage change is also a significant and positive factor with a contribution of about 25.2 %. The contribution of warming-induced glacier storage change to runoff variations in 17 study catchments is shown in Fig. 2 (b).   4 Discussion 4.1 Warming-induced Impact of Glacier Storage Change on Runoff It is crucial to assess glacier changes and their influence on runoff in glacier-covered regions, which commonly require information on glacier volume in different periods. However, it is difficult to obtain long-term glacier data since many observations have just been using remote sensing for the lastest 20 years. In this study, we proposed a simple and feasible method based on the Budyko framework to obtain the warming-induced impact of glacier storage change on runoff without glacier data. To estimate ε  ∆ G − T    , we made an assumption that the influence of temperature on radiation, relative humidity and wind speed is neglectable. In other words, (∂  PET/∂  R n  )(dR n   /dT ), (∂  PET/∂  RH )(dRH /dT ) and (∂  PET/∂  U 2  )(dU 2  /dT ) are small enough so that d PET/dT  ≈ ∂  PET/∂  T  (Eq. (A.4) in Text A1). Wind speed is generally considered to be independent of temperature, i.e. dU 2  /dT  =0.  It can be found that (∂  PET/∂  R n  ) (dR n   /dT ) is about an order of 1 and (∂  PET/∂  RH) (d RH/dT ) is about an order of 0.01, which can be neglected comparing with ∂  PET  / ∂  T  having an order of 10 (more details were given in Text A2 and Table A1). It indicates that the assumption is acceptable. Based on this method, it was found that the glacier mass balance of the 17 upstream glacier-covered catchments in the TRB during 1987–2019 is about −0.19 m w.e./yr, close to −0.12 m w.e./yr and −0.14 m w.e./yr according to (Liu et al., 2006 ) and (Hugonnet et al., 2021 ) in this region during approximate time period, which are based on topographical maps, high-resolution satellite images and aerial photos. Besides, according to Brun et al.(2017) , the total glacier mass change of High Mountain Asia is about −0.18±0.04 m w.e./yr during 2000–2016 based on time series of digital elevation models derived from satellite stereo-imagery, it is also close to our results. It means that our method performs well in quantifying the warming-induced impact of glacier storage change on runoff. Compared with the hydrological modeling approach (Duethmann et al., 2015 ) and the climate elasticity method proposed by Liu et al. (2022a)  and Xin et al. (2021) , our method can reliably assess the impact of warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff without the need for glacier data or parameter calibration. This offers a new approach for studying the long-term impact of glaciers on runoff in situations where long-term glacier data is lacking. The vanishing glacier means a decreased water resource that can be utilized in the future. In our study region, the glacier reserve was 1807.61 km3  around 1985 (Shi, 2005 ) (Table A5), and 91.05 km3  has been melted over the past 30 years, as present in Section 3.1 . Consequently, the remaining glacier will be approximately 1716.56 km3  in 2020. According to Wang et al. (2006) , we assume that the ascending rate of annual mean air temperature in TRB is constant at 0.25℃/10 yr and ε  ∆ G − T     remains unchanged at 13.49 %/℃ (average value in the study area). The percentage of projected glacier storage loss relative to 2020 can be evaluated using Eq. (10) , and the result is shown in  Fig. 3 . Roughly half of the glaciers are projected to be lost in ∼99 years, that is, by the year 2119 (more details in shown in Table A6). Similarly, as projections presented by David et al. (2023)  using the Python Glacier Evolution Model (PyGEM) and Open Global Glacier Model (OGGM), the percentage of projected glacier storage loss by 2100, relative to 2015 is around 55 % in the same region. Based on the above results, the glaciers in this region will shrink to half their current size in the early 22nd century.  4.2 Attribution analysis considering the warming-induced impact of glacier change Our result shows that the warming-induced glacier storage change has contributed ∼25.2 % runoff variation during 1960–2019 in the TRB. In contrast, two previous studies reported the contribution of glacier mass balance to variation in streamflow in the adjacent regions, namely −2.42–11.63 % in 22 rivers in Qilian Mountains (Yang et al., 2024 ), and 31.0 % of the variation in runoff in the upper region of the Yarlung Zangbo River basin (UYZRB) (Xin et al., 2021 ). It should be noted that the glacier coverage was 0.08–7.62 % in the 22 rivers in Qilian Mountains (Yang et al., 2024 ) while that was 0.3–38.9 % in the TRB, thus the sensitivity of runoff to glacier in TRB can be strongly affected by glacier coverage (Liu et al., 2022 ), and in other words, lower glacier coverage can be the reason why the contribution of glaciers to runoff variation in the Qilian Mountains is smaller than that in the TRB. In the meantime, the UYZRB has an average elevation of ∼5000 m (Xin et al., 2021 ), while the TRB is at a much lower average elevation (∼3000 m), indicating a higher glacier coverage and subsequent stronger impacts on streamflow in the UYZRB. In summary, the large percentage of contribution from glacier change suggests that it is critical to consider the warming-induced impact of glacier change in attribution analysis on runoff change; meanwhile, the comparison with previous studies indicates that our proposed framework can provide a rational estimate of the contribution from the warming-induced glacier change.  4.3 Uncertainties and limitations There were still some uncertainties and limitations in this study. Firstly, in order to explore the impact of glaciers on runoff without glacier data, we focused on the increased glacier melting caused by temperature rising instead of the specific amount of glacier accumulation and loss, with the assumption that the loss and accumulation of the remaining part of glaciers are still balanced as in equilibrium state. However, in practical situation, with temperature rising, except for the increased warming-induced glacier melting, the loss rate and the accumulation rate of the remaining part of glaciers which we assumed to be balanced are actually changing. Secondly, since we didn't distinguish between direct rainfall and snowfall, in Eq. (5), we  ignored the reduction of runoff due to snowfall fraction decreasing caused by warming (Liu et al., 2022b ). In addition, we ignored the change of landscape (parameter n ) in this study, i.e. some possible factors, such as warming-induced vegetation change, were neglected. According to previous studies, vegetation dynamic indicated by NDVI in the TRB was generally stable in the past 40 years with a slight growth trend at 0.03 %/a from 1999 to 2019 (Li and Chen, 2014; Ma et al., 2023 ), and the effect of the rising temperature on vegetation change is not significant in most regions of the TRB (Yue et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2017 ). Therefore, despite more or less errors, the runoff change caused by underlying surface changes (embedded in parameter n ) is little in this region. Nevertheless, all these factors will have a certain impact on the hydrothermal equilibrium process, ignoring these factors may bring uncertainty to the conclusion. To obtain the temperature elasticity of runoff through glacier storage, ε  ∆ G − T    , the elasticity ε  T     was estimated using the least square method dependent on the time series of runoff and temperature. As shown in Table 2 , the linear relationship between R  and T  isn’t significant (p  < 0.05) in some basins. One of the possible causes is that the time series of R  and T  aren’t long enough to exclude the impacts from other factors. Another is the uncertainty in temperature data, especially in glacier-covered moutainous areas, where temperature generally have vary large spatial variation but there are lack of ground observations. Besides, the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset, used in this study, has the problem of overestimating precipitation in mountainous areas (Dalla Torre et al., 2024; Jiao et al., 2021 ) , resulting in some errors in attribution analysis. Further studies can use multi-source ensembled data to improve the accuracy of precipitation.   5 Conclusions In this study, we proposed a simple and feasible Budyko-based method to quantify the impact of warming-induced glacier storage change on runoff without requiring glacier data in glacier-covered catchments and further developed an improved attribution analysis framework. The application in 17 upstream glacier-covered catchments of the Tarim River Basin (TRB) shows that a 1℃ rise in temperature leads to a 5–29 % increase in runoff through glacier storage change, and on average, 25 % runoff change can be attributed to the warming-induced glacier storage change from 1960 to 2019. This novel and transparent approach can help us quantify the warming-induced glacier change and its impacts on runoff under a changing climate, enhancing confidence in water resource management and decision-making.
1 Introduction Floods significantly threaten human lives, impede sustainable socio-economic development, and inflict immeasurable damage on floodplains (Xu et al., 2022 ). Accurate flood forecasting can mitigate flood risks and provide timely and efficient environmental information for water resources management and decision-making (Waqas et al., 2023 ). Given that the flooding process is influenced by a combination of precipitation events, watershed characteristics, and geographic conditions, it exhibits complex nonlinearity, non-stationarity, and stochasticity (Dong et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023 ). Currently, flood forecasting employs a wide range of models, which can be categorized into two groups: process-driven hydrological models and data-driven models (Cui et al., 2021, 2022 , 2023). Data-driven models rely on statistical relationships between input and output data without considering the underlying physical mechanisms of hydrologic processes (Feng et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Luppichini et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2021 ). These models establish mathematical time series analyses and utilize samples to uncover statistical or causal relationships among hydrologic variables (Hauswirth et al., 2021; Sawaf et al., 2021 ). Early data-driven models include the Autoregressive model (AR) (Slutzky, 1937 ), the Vector Autoregression model (VAR) (Sims, 1980 ), the Autoregressive Moving Average model (ARMA) (Bartholomew, 1971 ), and the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average model (ARIMA) (Bartholomew, 1971 ). However, these models typically assume a linear relationship between inputs and outputs, disregarding the nonlinearity inherent in the rainfall-runoff generation and flow routing processes, ultimately hampering the model performance (Lin et al., 2021 ). In contrast, machine learning (ML) models, such as the Support Vector Machines (SVM) model (Boser et al., 1992 ), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) model (Rosenblatt, 1958 ), Random Forests (RF) model (Breiman, 2001 ), and Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM) model (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ), can effectively characterize the nonlinearity of rainfall-runoff relationship and have been increasingly used in recent years. In machine learning models, recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures are employed to process sequential data by updating the hidden state at each time step, thereby capturing temporal dependencies through a combination of current input and previous step information. While LSTM models with a multi-gate structure have gained significant popularity in runoff forecasting. Unlike RNN models, LSTM model can effectively mitigate issues such as gradient vanishing and explosion that arise due to the cyclic nature inherent in RNNs (Kratzert et al., 2018 ). The application of the LSTM model consists of two main aspects. The first is the direct application of the LSTM model for predicting or simulating runoff (Alizadeh et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020; Jamei et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023 ). The second is the indirect application, in which the LSTM models are used as post-processors for process-based hydrological models to improve their performance by learning simulation errors (Han and Morrison, 2022; Khatun et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ). However, due to the high computational complexity and lack of parallel calculations, the LSTM model and its variants are less efficient in the training and testing process with high computational cost (Meng et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2021 ). Convolutional neural network (CNN) based-models with a relatively small number of parameters and can realize parallel calculation, i.e., the simultaneous processing of different parts of the input data during the convolution and pooling operations, have better skills to overcome the above problems and produce better results in rainfall prediction (Pan et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Along with the development of deep learning technology, many variant models based on CNN are gradually derived, among which the Explainable Convolutional Neural Network (ECNN) model is a representative one (Altai et al., 2023; Fauvel et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The ECNN model retains the advantages of lightweight and parallel computation of the CNN while demonstrates outstanding performance in multidimensional time series tasks (Fauvel et al., 2021 ). The ECNN model has been successfully applied in the medical field, demonstrating its ability to predict joint moments and achieve remarkable outcomes accurately (Altai et al., 2023 ). In materials science, the ECNN model exhibits significant advantages in damage location classification of pressure vessels, and effectively reduces the computational costs and iterations. Moreover, it holds tremendous potential for guided wave-based damage detection techniques in structural health monitoring (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, within computer technology, the ECNN model enhances network intrusion detection effectiveness (O. Lopes et al., 2023 ). The ECNN model has been used for drought prediction (Jiang and Luo, 2022 ), while the implementation of this model in flood forecasting remains unrealized. The current state of research in deep learning models has yielded promising results. However, the interpretability of these models is often overlooked (Pradhan et al., 2023 ). The interpretability here is usually connected with the intuition behind the outputs of a model (i.e., the cause-and-effect relationships between the inputs and outputs) (Adadi and Berrada, 2018; Jiang et al., 2022b ). Despite their superior accuracy, deep learning models are commonly regarded as “black box” systems (Liu et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023; Yip et al., 2021 ). Recent advancements in interpretable methods include the Shapley Additional Interpretation (SHAP) method (Aydin and Iban, 2023; Park et al., 2023; Pradhan et al., 2023; Sushanth et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Yang and Chui, 2021 ), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) method (Başağaoğlu et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2022; Worland et al., 2019 ), Integral Gradient (IG) method (Jiang et al., 2022a, 2020 ), among others. The Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) method (Selvaraju et al., 2020 ) possess a concise structure and utilize gradient information to identify salient regions within input data that significantly contribute to the outcomes of the CNN model (Choi et al., 2022; Fauvel et al., 2021; Rajpal et al., 2021 ). Compared to other interpretability methods, the Grad-CAM technique does not require any modifications or retraining of the model structure and enables analysis of any layer within the convolutional neural network model, thereby providing a comprehensive global interpretation. The Grad-CAM method has garnered significant attention across various domains, including autonomous driving (Dworak and Baranowski, 2022 ), video image processing (Chao et al., 2023; Livieris et al., 2023 ), text processing (Zhang and Ogasawara, 2023 ), and medical applications (Jain et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024 ), yielding remarkable outcomes. For instance, in autonomous driving, Grad-CAM method aids in identifying crucial features during the decision-making process. Video processing facilitates the recognition of pivotal frames or segments to enhance comprehension of temporal dynamics. Employing Grad-CAM method in medical diagnostics empowers clinicians to pinpoint critical regions within an image that significantly influence CNN diagnostic results. Nevertheless, there remains a research gap concerning the application of Grad-CAM method for flood forecasting, particularly in identifying input data features. Based on the progress and shortcomings of previous research, the present study is motivated to achieve the following objectives: Firstly, this study introduces the ECNN for flood forecasting; Secondly, the Grad-CAM method is used to assess the importance of model inputs for temporal features quantitatively. Benchmark tests are conducted using LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models. The performance of the ECNN model and the benchmark models is evaluated from multiple perspectives using various evaluation metrics. An interpretable framework for ECNN models is proposed to improve the interpretability of deep learning. A comprehensive research investigation is conducted on the Lushui basin in China. The novelty of this work included (1) Proposing a novel framework of the ECNN model and specially designed with a 1D convolution kernel to extract time-related information in the input data; (2) Employing the Grad-CAM method to quantitatively evaluate the importance of input data and improve the interpretability of the ECNN model. All aspects of performance and applicable conditions for different marching learning models were analyzed and compared. Similar studies have not been reported in the literature till now. The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2  outlines the principles and structure of the ECNN model, the Grad-CAM method, and the benchmark models. Section 3  describes the Lushui basin and the data used to develop the models. Section 4  compares the results from both ECNN and benchmark models in forecasting floods and analyzes the interpretability produced by the Grad-CAM method. Section 5  discusses the main findings based on our ECNN model and Grad-CAM method, and finally, Section 6  summarizes the main conclusions.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The Lushui River is a first-class tributary of the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, encompassing a basin area of approximately 3,950 km2 , as depicted in Fig. 1  . The topography within the basin exhibits higher elevations in the southeast and lower elevations in the northwest. Located in the subtropical monsoon climate zone, this catchment experiences a warm and humid climate with an average annual temperature of around 15.5 ℃, an average annual rainfall of 1550 mm, and an annual runoff volume from the Lushui River reaching 3.03 billion m3 . Rainfall predominantly occurs within the Lushui basin from April to September, accounting for approximately 70 % of the annual precipitation. At the outlet of the river valley lies the Lushui Reservoir, which has a total volume of about 408 million m3 , while its flood control capacity is merely around 163 million m3 . Lushui Reservoir experienced a maximum flood event in early July 1995, with an inflow discharge of 4,500 m3 /s and a three-day flood volume of 500 million m3 . In 2017, there are six flood events with peak flows exceeding 1,000 m3 /s and maximum inflow flows reaching 4,400 m3 /s. Given its relatively limited flood control capacity and frequent flood events, accurate multilevel forecasts of incoming flows are critical for flood control scheduling and water resource management in Lushui Reservoir.  2.2 Data The present study collects data from the Lushui Reservoir during the abundant water period, from May 1 to October 31 of each year between 2012 and 2019. This dataset includes precipitation data recorded at three-hour intervals, pan evaporation measured at seventeen rainfall stations, and inflow data for the Lushui Reservoir. We employ the Thiessen polygon method on the three-hourly precipitation and evaporation data to determine the areal average precipitation and evaporation of the basin. The statistical characteristics of annual areal average precipitation and evaporation, daily inflow data series are listed in Table 1  . Table 1  also presents the variance inflation factor (VIF), which helps determine the presence of multicollinearity among variables (Farrar and Glauber, 1967 ). Table 1  shows that all VIF values range from 1.08 to 1.17, indicating no multicollinearity for these data sets. Correlation analysis reveals a positive correlation (0.33) between precipitation and inflow series and a negative correlation (−0.20) between evaporation and inflow series. The areal average precipitation and evapotranspiration, and reservoir inflow data series are normalized by the maximized and minimized method, and then used as input features for the models. The length of input data series (or the number of time-steps) was selected through trial-and-error method. We have conducted trial-and-error experiments to compare the impact of different time-steps on ECNN model performance. The experimental results demonstrated that ECNN model can achieve an optimal balance between prediction accuracy and computational complexity when the number of time-step for the input features is 80. Furthermore, a certain length of input variable is necessary for subsequent interpretability analysis to comprehensively examine feature contributions. This means that the areal average precipitation and evaporation, and observed inflow data from the past 80 time-steps (240 h) are used as inputs to the model. All model outputs will consist of multi-step forecasts ranging from one to four, representing forecast horizons from 3 h to 12 h, respectively.   3 Methods 3.1 The ECNN model Fauvel et al. (2021)  proposed the ECNN, a deep learning model for multivariate time series (MTS) problems based on the conventional network model. ECNN applies 1D and 2D convolutions and shows strong robustness and generalizability in various time-based signal classifications. The framework of the ECNN model and the Grad-GAM method is shown in Fig. 2  .
