The ECNN model primarily comprises 2D and 1D convolutions, wherein the 1D and 2D convolution processes consist of two convolutional layers. Despite their structural similarity, the 1D and 2D convolutions extract distinct information. The upper segment of the ECNN model (depicted as the blue part in Fig. 2 ) employs 2D convolution filters to capture unique features from each observed variable. Sliding the convolution kernel in a two-dimensional plane, the 2D convolution effectively captures relationships and local patterns among observed variables, which is crucial for understanding interrelationships within multivariate time series data. The lower half (the red part in Fig. 2 ) employs a 1D convolutional filter to capture time-dependent information and facilitate interactions among different temporal input sequences. By sliding the convolution kernel along the temporal dimension, 1D convolution efficiently extracts temporal features in a time series, making it particularly advantageous for processing signals that exhibit variations over time. It is worth noting that the design of the 1D convolutional filter incorporates similarities with the LSTM model, enabling it to capture long-term dependencies in time-series data effectively. The size of the convolutional kernel in the convolutional layer is determined by the hyperparameter window size, which specifies the window function's size for extracting temporal features from time subseries variables. After completing 2D convolutional processing, a feature map containing spatial features extracted from each observed variable is generated. The outputs of both 1D and 2D convolutions are combined into a unified feature map, serving as input for subsequent 1D convolution layers. The spliced feature map is fed into the 1D convolutional layer to extract the interplay between different features. This step involves sliding a 1D convolution kernel over the feature map, enabling the capturing of temporal relationships among diverse features and enhancing the model's capacity for recognizing intricate temporal patterns. Following the 1D convolutional layer, the resulting feature map represents extracted temporal characteristics and interaction information among variables. Finally, a 1D global average pooling layer is incorporated into the output feature map to address the risk of overfitting. This layer effectively reduces dimensionality and parameter count by globally pooling the entire feature map. Ultimately, the processed feature maps are subjected to prediction using the SoftMax  function, resulting in the final prediction (Lopes et al., 2023 ). The fully connected layer commonly used in traditional CNN model architectures may lead to overfitting phenomena and generate many parameters. To address this issue, the ECNN model uses 1D global average pooling to reduce the number of parameters and improve generalization (Altai et al., 2023; Fauvel et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The non-fully padded convolutional filters used in the CNN model may lead to inaccurate recognition of essential regions in the input data. Hence, the ECNN model uses fully padded filters, thus giving better results (Altai et al., 2023 ). In the ECNN model, the values of the hyperparameters are as follows: the size of the upper 2D convolutional kernel is windowsize × 1   , and the size of the lower 1D convolutional kernel is windowsize × D   ; where the windowsize    is 24, and D    is the number of feature variables of the input data, which is 3 in this study; and the step size of each convolutional kernel move is one. The number of convolutional kernels takes values in the range [32, 128] with an interval of 32, which can be determined by trial-and-error method.  3.2 Benchmark models We carefully selected three benchmark models to comprehensively evaluate the predictive capabilities of ECNN models for different flood types. Firstly, we chose the LSTM model due to its extensive application in flood forecasting and superior forecasting performance. Secondly, we included the CNN model as it is also based on convolutional neural networks, allowing us to highlight the distinctive advantages of the ECNN model compared to traditional CNN approaches. Lastly, we incorporated the LSTM-CNN model, combining the strengths of both LSTM and CNN architectures. Our research results ensure valuable references and applicability within flood forecasting by selecting these three models as benchmarks. The LSTM model consists of an input layer, LSTM layers, a dropout layer, and a dense layer. Hyperparameter selection for the LSTM neural network structure often involves trial-and-error experiments focusing on critical factors such as the number of hidden layers (ranging from 1 to 5 with an interval of 1) and the number of neurons (ranging from 32 to 128 with an interval of 32). The CNN model comprises an input layer followed by multiple layers of two-dimensional convolutional layers with pooling operations, a dropout layer, and a dense layer. Similar to the LSTM model, hyperparameters for the CNN neural network structure are determined through trial-and-error experiments considering essential factors like the number of layers (ranging from 1 to 5 with an interval of 1) and the number of filters (ranging from 32 to 128 with an interval of 32). Lastly, the LSTM-CNN model incorporates an input layer that feeds into an LSTM unit, which connects to another intermediate connection (or transformation) unit before being passed onto a subsequent 2D convolutional operation along with pooling and flatten layers similar to those found in the CNN architecture mentioned earlier. It also includes a final dropout layer and a dense output layer for forecast generation purposes. It should be noted that all parameter settings within these respective layers remain consistent with their counterparts from both the standalone LSTM and CNN models.  3.3 Grad-CAM method Selvaraju et al. (2020)  improved the original Class Activation Mapping (CAM) using the first gradient-based weighting scheme and proposed the Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) method. The (Grad-CAM) method is mainly used to interpret and analyze the forecast results of the convolutional network-based model (Choi et al., 2022 ). The introduced ECNN model is f X      , where X    denotes the time series matrix with T × D    input data (X    and D    represent the time series length and the number of variables, respectively). The model's outcome, y = f X      , is the value predicted using the input data X   . If A    denotes the feature map activations of the 2D convolutional layer in the ECNN model, we compute the gradient of the result y    to A  k    , i.e., ∂ y  ∂ A  k       with k ∈ [ 1 , ⋯ , F ]    the identifier of the feature map. These gradients are global-average-pooled over the time series length (T   ) and variable number (D   ) (indexed by i    and j   , respectively) to obtain the weight of each feature map. Thus, as regards the feature map k   , we calculate the weight as follows:(1) q k  = 1 T × D   ∑ j  ∑ i  ∂ y  ∂ A i , j  k         The q k     is used as the weight of the k    th feature map for the forecast result, and when the weights corresponding to all feature maps are calculated and then weighted and summed, the corresponding Grad-CAM value is obtained. It is shown as follows:(2) L Grad - C A M   = R e l u ∑ k  q k  A  k          To eliminate the effect of negative values on the results, the Relu    function is added to the linear combination. Since we are more concerned with the flood peak value, the L Grad - C A M      for forecastng the flood peak is calculated in this study. The derived L Grad - C A M      possesses the exact dimensions as the corresponding input variables (i.e., [80, 3]), representing the timewise feature importance scores for precipitation, evaporation, and previous inflow, respectively. The L Grad - C A M      was calculated and normalized between values of 0 and 1. The closer the value of L Grad - C A M      to 1, the greater the influence of a variable on the outcomes of the ECNN model at a given time. Overall, Grad-CAM is a gradient-based method that calculates the specific contribution of inputs by tracing the gradient relationship from the outcomes of the ECNN model to its inputs (Li et al., 2023 ). The ECNN model has five convolutional layers, where the variable features are extracted from the first 2D convolutional layer. Therefore, Grad-CAM is applied to this 2D convolutional layer.  3.4 Model calibration and validation This study employs a k -fold cross-validation approach for training and testing the ECNN models to mitigate overfitting and parameter uncertainty (Lei, 2020 ). The value of k  in k -fold cross-validation typically falls within the range of 5–10 (Lei, 2020 ). Fig. 3   shows schematic diagram of the k -fold cross-validation approach. The data series from 2012 to 2019 were collected to train and test the models, and the data series was divided into eight subsets (k  = 8) annually to ensure continuity and integrity. Each scheme selects seven subsets used to train the models, and the remaining one subset is used to test the models. The specific 8-fold cross-validation process as shown in Fig. 3  is illustrated as follows: For the first scheme, the first seven data subsets are used as the training folds, while the eighth data subset is used as the test fold. For the second scheme, the seventh data subset is used as the test fold, the remaining seven data subsets are used as the training folds, and so on. In total, there are eight schemes, i.e., 8-fold cross-validation used in this study. After completing all eight schemes, eight sets of results included both training and testing outcomes will be generated. Subsequently, the metrics are calculated for each scheme resulting eight sets of metrics. Finally, the average of these eight sets of metrics is used to evaluate the model performance. It should be clarified here that the schematic diagram shown in Fig. 3  is a conceptual representation of model evaluation rather than an ensemble model proposed in this study. The ECNN and three benchmark models are developed using Python programming language and open-source libraries, including TensorFlow and Keras. The optimization process utilizes the Adam algorithm with a recommended mean square error (MSE) loss function and a learning rate 0.001 per iteration. During training, we recommend a maximum number of epochs of 200 for a batch size of 64 to prevent overfitting problems. Additionally, our model employs an early stopping technique (Srivastava et al., 2014 ) and stores all relevant information throughout the learning process to further mitigate potential overfitting issues.  3.5 Evaluation of model performance The overall model performance is evaluated using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE   ) (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), the total flow relative error (RE   ) (Chen et al., 2022 ), and the root mean square error (RMSE   ) (Xiang et al., 2020 ), which are calculated using the formulas shown below:(3) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  ( Q o , i   - Q f , i   )  2   ∑ i = 1  N  ( Q o , i   - Q o   ¯   )  2        (4) RE = ∑ i = 1  N  Q f , i   - ∑ i = 1  N  Q o , i    ∑ i = 1  N  Q o , i     × 100 %     (5) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  N  ( Q f , i   - Q o , i   )  2   N        where N    is the number of samples, Q o     and Q o   ¯      denote the observed values of flow and their mean values, respectively, and Q f , i      denotes the simulated or predicted flow values. RMSE    is a metric with a theoretical range between 0 and ∞. The larger the RMSE    value, the larger the error. RE    measures the relative bias between the total observed runoff and predicted runoff and a zero value means no bias. NSE    ranges between negative infinity and 1, where 1 indicates a perfect match between predicted and observed flow. A value < 0 suggests that the model prediction is worse than the mean values of the observed flow. To further illustrate the performance of the model in predicting flood peak value, the relative error of flood peak (PRE   ) and the time difference between the occurrence of flood peaks (Δ T   ) metrics are also used in the study, which is calculated as follows:(6) PRE = Q f , p e a k   - Q o , p e a k    Q o , p e a k    × 100 %     (7) Δ T = T f  - T  o      where Q o , p e a k      denotes the observed peak flow of the flood and Q f , p e a k      denotes the simulated or predicted flood peak flow; T o     and T f     are the time of occurrence of the observed and the simulated or predicted flood peak flow, respectively. PRE    describes the relative bias between the predicted and the observed flood peak.   4 Result analysis 4.1 Comparison of model performance The NSE metrics for the validation period of 3–12 h forecast horizons are utilized to demonstrate the calculation results under different hyperparameters. It was observed from Table 2   that optimal forecasting performance is obtained by employing an ECNN with 128 filters, a two-layer LSTM neural network featuring 128 neurons, and a two-layer CNN with 128 filters for diverse foresight horizons. The prerequisite for extracting meaningful information from a model is reasonable and stable predictive accuracy (Jiang et al., 2022b; Murdoch et al., 2019 ). Table 3   presents the evaluation indicators of the four models used for predicting floods in the Lushui basin during the training period. It should be noted that a cross-validation approach, as mentioned in Section 3.4 , is employed in constructing ECNN model, resulting in eight sets of evaluation indicators for each scheme. Table 3  shows that the forecasting accuracy of the models decreases as the forecast horizon lengthens. However, the ECNN model demonstrates significantly better performance regarding NSE and RMSE indicators among all four models. Particularly at a forecast horizon of 12 h, LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models exhibit NSE values of 0.82, 0.75, and 0.86, respectively, significantly lower than that of ECNN (0.96). Additionally, RMSE values for the LSTM model (104.69 m3 /s), CNN model (124.71 m3 /s), and LSTM-CNN model (93.75 m3 /s) are higher than the ECNN mode (47.49 m3 /s). The evaluation indicators of the four models for flood forecast during the test period in the Lushui basin are presented in Table 4  . The performance of the ECNN model exhibits a much smaller degradation than other models as the forecast horizon increases. For instance, at a forecast horizon of 3 h, the NSE/RMSE value for the ECNN model (0.96/32.25 m3 /s) is slightly lower/higher than that of LSTM (0.98/25.48 m3 /s) and LSTM-CNN (0.98/23.35 m3 /s) models, respectively. However, the ECNN model consistently outperforms other models in terms of some metrics when the forecast horizon is beyond 6 h, meaning that the performance of the ECNN model is relatively stable with forecasting lead time. For example, the RE value of the ECNN model is significantly lower than that of the benchmark model during the 12 h forecast horizon. Meanwhile, the RMSE value of the ECNN model is reduced by 34.11 %, 48.41 %, and 33.14 % relative to the LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models, respectively. This highlights that the superiority of the ECNN model in flood forecasting primarily manifests itself over an extended foresight period. To illustrate the ECNN model results' correctness and accuracy, Tables 5 and 6    list the evaluation indicators obtained from the ECNN model during the k -fold cross-validation stage. To visually illustrate the difference between ECNN flood forecast results and those of LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models, are ploted in Fig. 4  . It is shown that a closer scatter plot to the black diagonal line indicates more accurate results. The blue points representing ECNN results are more centrally distributed on both sides of the diagonal than those of LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models. Particularly in the 12 h forecast horizon, ECNN performance is notably superior. This visualization highlights the advantages of the ECNN model in flood forecasting within these forecast horizons. Additionally, the most scatter plots of the LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models are located below the diagonal line in Fig. 4 , indicating that their predicted values are smaller than observed values, which explains why RE scores for these three models are negative, as presented in Table 3 .  4.2 Comparison of the effectiveness of peak flood forecast Four flood events in the Lushui basin were selected during the test period to validate the model performance in flood peak forecasting. These flood events encompass diverse flood processes, varying peak flow magnitudes, and distinct flood occurrence times, thereby facilitating a comprehensive evaluation of ECNN model forecasting capability with different flood types. Table 7   summarizes the evaluation metrics for the forecast horizons of 12 h in the Lushui basin for illustrative purposes. It is important to note that Table 7  presents evaluation metrics for individual schemes rather than combined metrics for all schemes. This approach avoids the fact that the model already has the context of the flood event in the training phase, and using the same flood event to test its performance may lead to inaccurate evaluation. Specifically, the flood event occurred from May 13 to 17, 2015 was evaluated using the ECNN model of the fifth scheme; the flood event occurred from July 1 to July 9, 2016 was assessed using the ECNN model of the fourth scheme; both flood events occurred from June 22 to June 29 and June 29 to July 5, 2017 were evaluated using the ECNN model in the third scheme. The metrics presented in Table 7  demonstrate that the ECNN model exhibits optimal performance across four evaluation indexes: NSE, RE, PRE, and ΔT. Specifically, the NSE values of the ECNN model consistently exceed 0.95, while the absolute value of RE remains below 10 %. Moreover, the absolute value of ΔT does not surpass 3 h, and only once does the absolute value of PRE exceed 10 %. These findings highlight the exceptional ability of the ECNN model to predict flood peak discharges. Conversely, both LSTM and CNN models and their combination (LSTM-CNN) exhibit subpar performance. To further visualize the model performance in predicting flooding process in the Lushui basin, we present the observed and predicted flood hydrographs with 6 h and 12 h forecast horizons for the four flood events in Fig. 5  , Fig. 6  , Fig. 7  , and Fig. 8   respectively. The flood hydrographs of the Lushui basin during the flood event from May 13 at 17:00 to May 17 at 23:00 in 2015 are presented in Fig. 5 . The presence of distinct peaks in flow and rainfall in Fig. 5  indicates a complex flooding process with multiple peaks. From Fig. 5 (a), it is evident that the predicted flood hydrograph generated by the ECNN model exhibits a higher level of consistency than the observed flood hydrograph. However, for the LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models, there are noticeable discrepancies between their forecasted flood hydrographs and the observed data, particularly during the flood-rising stage. In this stage, these models tend to underestimate the observed flood hydrograph, as depicted in Fig. 5 (b). It can be noted that the predicted flood hydrograph produced by the ECNN model maintains a better agreement with reality than other models. Furthermore, in Fig. 5 (b), both LSTM and LSTM-CNN models significantly overestimate the flood peak discharges. The flood hydrographs of the Lushui basin during the flood event from July 1 at 2:00 to July 9 at 11:00 in 2016 are presented in Fig. 6 . In Fig. 6 (a), all four models accurately capture the general trend of the observed hydrograph but underestimate the peak flow to varying degrees. In Fig. 6 (b), a noticeable delay is observed in the rising process of predicted flood hydrographs compared to the observed one, particularly for the LSTM and CNN models. Again, ECNN shows significantly better performance than other models. The flood hydrograph observation and forecast in the Lushui basin during the flood event from 2:00 on June 22 to 14:00 on June 29, 2017, are presented in Fig. 7 . In Fig. 7 (a), the predicted flood hydrograph by the ECNN model aligns well with the observed data, while the LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models underestimate the peak flow remarkably. In Fig. 7 (b), all four models yield suboptimal forecasts with a significant underestimation of the flood peak. Besides the ECNN model, there is a notable delay in capturing the rising phase of flooding among the other three models. Fig. 8  shows the observed and forecasted flood hydrographs of the Lushui basin by the four models for the flood event lasting from June 29 at 17:00 to July 5 at 17:00 in 2017. In Fig. 8 (a), the predicted flood hydrographs of the four models exhibit consistency with the observations, albeit underestimating the second flood peak by LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models. In Fig. 8 (b), while the ECNN model accurately reproduces the observed hydrograph, the other three models demonstrate a pronounced delay phenomenon with an underestimation of peak flow discharges.  4.3 Interpretability of the Grad-CAM In Fig. 9  , we present the box plots illustrating the overall feature importance scores of the input data obtained using the Grad-CAM method in the test period. It is important to note that during the test period, eight pre-trained ECNN schemes were utilized (as mentioned in Section 4.1 ). Thus, these feature importance scores represent their average values. The feature importance scores of Grad-CAM methods are used to quantify the relative contribution of input features to flood forecasts in the ECNN model. These score values, typically ranging from 0 to 1 after normalization, should be noted as non-negative. However, it is essential to emphasize that these scores represent relative contributions rather than probability values and thus may not necessarily sum up to 1. Fig. 9  shows that inflow exhibits consistently high feature importance scores, characterized by a relatively sizeable interquartile spacing (IQR) and a more significant number of outliers. These findings underscore the pivotal role played by inflow in flood forecasts. Additionally, precipitation demonstrates a notable feature importance score; however, its IQR is smaller than inflow, with outliers exhibiting a more concentrated distribution. This phenomenon suggests that precipitation is the second important in flood forecasting. Conversely, evaporation displays significantly lower feature importance scores along with the smallest IQR and the fewest anomalies detected, indicating its relatively minor contribution to model forecasts. Collectively, these results highlight inflow as the most influential feature in flood forecasting, followed by precipitation, while evaporation has limited influence. Applying the Grad-CAM method to the pre-trained ECNN models, we extract feature importance scores of the four flood peaks for the identical flood events, as discussed in Section 4.2 . For each target flood peak, the scores obtained from eight schemes (as mentioned in Section 4.1 ) with inputs at a specific time-step exhibit a consistent pattern of relative importance, albeit with slight variations due to cross-validated model training. Consequently, we computed an average of eight feature importance scores for each flood peak to facilitate further analysis. Given that the Grad-CAM method yields similar results for different forecast horizons, the 3 h forecast horizon is analyzed here. Fig. 10   illustrates the variations of the inputs and the importance of feature for flood peak forecasting. The feature importance scores of precipitations and inflow in Fig. 10  are significantly higher than those of evaporation, indicating that the ECNN model primarily relies on precipitation and inflow for flood peak forecasting. Although evaporation is included as an input variable in the ECNN model, it is observed that after training, the model can identify the empirical law governing flood peak formation, which states that the size of the flood peak is determined by precipitation and inflow. Consequently, the ECNN model predominantly utilizes precipitation and inflow rather than evaporation to achieve accurate forecasts. Specifically, Fig. 10 (b-Ⅳ) represents a typical compound flood with two peaks, where intervening precipitation events and the preceding flooding process play crucial roles in determining the flood peaks of this type. In Fig. 10 (b-Ⅰ), regions with more significant feature importance scores (indicated by sizable blue curve values) correspond precisely to two precipitation events. Similarly, In Fig. 10 (b-Ⅲ), prominent areas represent the last flood that does not recede entirely and the rising process of the current flood, respectively. The ECNN model effectively captures these critical processes for forecasting compound flood peaks, as shown in Fig. 10 (a) and 10(d). For single peak floods depicted in Fig. 10 (c), the ECNN model primarily focuses on precipitation events and the rising process leading up to each peak appearance. These findings illustrate that when flood peak forecasting using the ECNN model, regardless of flood type, emphasis should be placed on precipitation and inflow data changes due to their informative value for future forecasts (Choi et al., 2022 ).   5 Discussion The present study compares the flood forecasting performance of the ECNN model with the benchmark models, and analyses the interpretability of the ECNN model using the Grad-CAM method. The proposed ECNN model employs 2D convolution filters to directly extract features from observed variables (i.e., precipitation, evaporation, and inflow) in the input data. Simultaneously, 1D convolution filters are utilized to extract temporal information-related features (Altai et al., 2023; Fauvel et al., 2021 ). This contrasts the benchmark CNN model that sequentially arranges convolutional layers for information extraction (Pan et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). This parallel approach enables the comprehensive acquisition of all relevant information. Additionally, the ECNN model incorporates a window size  parameter to enhance the identification of local patterns and regularities within input time series data. As a result, the ECNN model improves flood peak forecasting accuracy, as evidenced by the evaluation indicators listed in Table 5  and Table 7 . Particularly striking is that the forecasted hydrographs shown in Fig. 5  are very close to the observed hydrographs, significantly better than the benchmark models. Regarding the LSTM model, which is extensively employed in hydrology studies (Kratzert et al., 2018, 2021 ), its performance degradation becomes prominent when predicting floods over longer forecast horizons (e.g., 9 h and 12 h as illustrated in Table 4 ). The suboptimal performance of the LSTM model in longer forecast horizons can be attributed to its recursive network structure, wherein the accuracy of subsequent predictions heavily relies on previous results, leading to evident error accumulation (Tang et al., 2022 ). Moreover, the confluence time of the Lushui basin is approximately 12 h (Cui et al., 2022 ), which moderately impacts the predictive efficacy of the LSTM model within a 12 h forecast horizon. Some studies have attempted to enhance flood forecasting performance for the LSTM model at extended horizons by incorporating exogenous inputs and attention mechanisms (Cui et al., 2022, 2023 ). However, this approach significantly escalates the computational cost of the model and complicates its structure, posing challenges for practical implementation. Furthermore, the LSTM network exhibits a high level of complexity due to its incorporation of multiple gates (input, forget, output) and state updates (Kratzert et al., 2018 ), necessitating numerous matrix operations at each time step. Consequently, this results in a linear increase in training time with sequence length. In contrast, the ECNN structure illustrated in Fig. 2  primarily relies on straightforward convolutional operations that can be efficiently parallelized (Fang et al., 2021 ). This inherent parallelism allows for a slower increase in training time with data size compared to LSTMs (Liang et al., 2022 ). Fig. 5 (b) and 7(b) show that the ECNN model outperforms the LSTM model when considering long-term foresight horizons. The ECNN model forecasts in Fig. 6 (b) exhibit a lag phase, wherein the predicted flood hydrographs are delayed compared to the observed flood hydrographs. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the flood hydrographs forecasted by benchmark models. Furthermore, similar lag phenomena have been reported in other studies (Chen et al., 2022; Cui et al., 2022 ). It should be noted that both the ECNN model and benchmark models display varying degrees of deficiencies when forecasting flood peaks. The reasons for these shortcomings can be analyzed as follows: firstly, it may be attributed to the limited number of input data features (precipitation, evaporation, and inflow in this study) used for flood forecasting. Secondly, the flood series demonstrates evident non-stationarity (Dong et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023 ), indicating that the probability distribution or statistical characteristics of the flood series change over time and do not adhere to assumptions of consistency or stationarity (Li et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Thirdly, The reason may be that the training data lack high flows, causing all models to underestimate high flows (Cui et al., 2022 ). The limitations of the model learning ability and the potential impact of manual adjustment of its hyperparameters are also factors in this study. Therefore, future improvements for deep learning models like the ECNN model could involve augmenting variable features within input data, adjusting model structure, introducing automatic optimization algorithms, and employing empirical mode decomposition on flood sequences. Several studies have identified three underlying mechanisms contributing to flooding: recent precipitation, historical precipitation, and snowmelt water (Jiang et al., 2022a, 2022b ). Considering the mountainous nature of the Lushui basin with rapid runoff confluence, floods in this basin are primarily driven by precipitation. Utilizing an analysis based on the Grad-CAM method, we observed that precipitation plays a crucial role in flood forecasting using the ECNN model in the Lushui basin. Therefore, it can be inferred that the ECNN model has successfully captured flood characteristics specific to this basin through training data acquisition, resulting in improved forecast accuracy and enhanced reliability. The Grad-CAM approach helps pinpoint critical regions and features in the CNN model that are crucial information for flood forecasting. Through Grad-CAM method, we identify specific features the model focuses on different flood processes, revealing their close relationship with flood formation and development. Our approach offers a more intuitive and quantitative analytical tool to simultaneously assess the contribution of input variable to flood forecasting results. This ability could enhance our understanding of model decision-making processes, and pave the way for new advancements in deep-learning models for flood forecasting. The performance of the ECNN model is superior to the benchmark models in the Lushui basin. It is essential to note that this disparity may be attributed to the unique characteristics of the basin. Generally, deep learning models exhibit varying capabilities for flood forecasting and depending on specific watershed attributes. Future research should further evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the ECNN model across different basins. Table 6  illustrated that the ECNN model performance was unstable and subject to significant fluctuations during the test period. One approach to overcome this limitation is employing cross-validation techniques as used in this study, where multiple schemes are trained and averaged to mitigate fluctuation effects.  6 Conclusions This study presents a novel ECNN model based on convolutional neural networks with a simple and compact structure. Firstly, the constructed ECNN model was applied to the Lushui basin for flood events forecast. Secondly, multiple evaluation metrics were used to compare the forecast results of the ECNN model with those of LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models from various aspects. Finally, the Grad-CAM method was employed to analyze the interpretability of the ECNN model in flood forecasting. The key findings of this study are as summarized as follows: (1) The proposed ECNN model outperforms benchmark models (LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-CNN models) according to evaluation metrics, particularly in the 12 h forecast horizon. (2) The precipitation and inflow data series play crucial roles in flood forecasting interpreted by the ECNN model and Grad-CAM method, which is consistent with flow generation and flood routing characteristics in the Lushui basin. (3) Compared to the benchmark models, the ECNN model utilizes a parallel approach to extract the information separately. The ECNN model has more accurate forecasts, an interpretable nature, and a compact network structure, which is up-and-coming in real-time flood forecasting. In the present study, the input data were processed as 1D vectors, disregarding the influence of spatial heterogeneity on model outcomes. Future investigations could explore the impact of incorporating satellite remote-sensing precipitation data with spatial information into flood forecasts using the ECNN model. Furthermore, considering parameter optimization algorithms (e.g., Bayesian Optimization) can be beneficial for handling hyperparameters to mitigate uncertainties arising from human adjustments.
1 Introduction Natural resources are the naturally occurring, direct material sources essential for human survival, including climate, water, land, vegetation resources (Bridge, 2009 ). Their dynamics are crucial for the human sustainable development agenda, especially in the endorheic basins of arid regions. Against the backdrop of rapid global economic development and significant climate change, human beings have engaged in exploitation of natural resources to meet the growing demands for material and cultural needs. This has led to a range of issues, including water scarcity, land desertification, and degradation of ecosystem services (Hopping et al., 2018 ). These problems not only hinder progress towards sustainable development but also exacerbate the impacts of climate change, leading to the degradation of the ecological environment (Sandifer et al., 2015 ). Natural resources have long been developed through separate monitoring and management activities (Nuwarinda et al., 2021 ), thus resulting in challenges in the protection and utilization of natural resources (Mucova et al., 2018 ). Recently, the management and analysis of natural resources have been developing from single to comprehensive perspectives (Blankenship et al., 2021 ). After the establishment of the Ministry of Natural Resources in 2018, China initiated a comprehensive natural resource survey aimed at obtaining information on the types, scope, quantities, distribution, development, utilization, and changes of natural resources (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The evolution of management policies has revealed a growing global interest in natural resource monitoring (Fancy et al., 2009 ) and assessment (Mahan et al., 2009 ). To realize the sustainability of natural resources (Ahmed et al., 2020 ) and conservation of the global ecosystems (Fu et al., 2021 ), it is essential to conduct intensive theoretical and practical investigations and systematic studies of multiple natural resources. The interactions among various climate resources have exacerbated the complexity of coordinating resource allocation and ecological security in arid and semi-arid areas. Water scarcity and the lack of coordination in the development of water and land resources are limiting factors for socioeconomic development in these areas. For example, insufficient irrigation water affects crop yields and quality, leading to lower agricultural income and food insecurity (Shi et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2024 ). Additionally, inadequate water supply for residents profoundly impacts human well-being and may spur population migration (Tra et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2020a ), intensifying regional economic pressures. Glacier shrinkage and permafrost thawing caused by climate warming have disrupted runoff patterns (Triplett and Condon, 2022; Zhan et al., 2014 ) and reduced the storage capacity of lakes (Li et al., 2019 ) in the Heihe River Basin (HRB), leading to vegetation degradation in the downstream area of the basin and impacting the stability of urban water supply. Additionally, rapid cropland expansion in arid areas has resulted in notable increases in water irrigation and groundwater exploitation (Cai et al., 2003; Fishman et al., 2011 ). Common land-use activities such as urbanization (Madlener and Sunak, 2011 ) and deforestation (Gibbs et al., 2010 ) can significantly alter the natural environment of an area. On the other hand, climatic conditions such as the temperature, precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration (ET) also influence vegetation distribution (Su et al., 2008; Fensholt et al., 2012; Uddin et al., 2022 ). The use of renewable energy sources (wind, water, and solar energy) can initially slow down, then reverse global warming, and provide energy sustainably (Jacobson et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018a ). Heat and precipitation resources are closely linked to phenology (Shen et al., 2011 ), and even food security (Kumar, 2016 ). For example, different precipitation patterns have varying impacts on vegetation growth and soil moisture, which directly affect agricultural production (Troy et al., 2015 ). All of these have shown that multiple natural resources interact and collectively impact the eco-environment (He et al., 2023; Piao et al., 2006 ). The HRB, a typical endorheic basin in arid and semiarid regions, is linked by water from upstream to downstream, forming diverse ice, snow, and frozen soil–forest–meadow–oasis (cropland and riparian forest)–desert–lake landscapes. The HRB is facing the issues of desiccation of terminal lakes and the disappearance of natural oases downstream since the 1960s. The implementation of the Ecological Water Diversion Project (EWDP) in 2000 has resulted in an increase in runoff and vegetation. Water scarcity in the downstream area has been alleviated, and remarkable improvements have been observed in the eco-environment (Cheng et al., 2014 ). In the face of these challenges and the implementation of ecological restoration, numerous researchers have conducted a series of field observations and remote sensing monitoring experiments in this basin (Li et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018, 2023 ), resulting in the release of numerous satellite–airborne–ground observation data, all of which have undergone rigorous quality control (Li et al., 2017; Che et al., 2019 ). Under the complexity of the eco-environment and the abundance of multivariate data, the HRB is an ideal field area for analyzing the spatio-temporal variations in water resources, as well as other natural resources. Many studies have explored precipitation and runoff variations, vegetation cover changes, and their impacts on the ecosystem (Hu et al., 2015; He et al., 2020; Paciolla et al., 2021; Triplett and Condon, 2022; Wu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015 ). While these studies provide valuable insights, they often focus on single resources. There is a need to enhance the integrated analysis of multiple natural resources. Such research is particularly critical in endorheic basins, where the allocation of water resources stands as the primary challenge for sustainable development (Zegeye et al., 2014; Samal and Gedam, 2021 ). Additionally, the temporal variation in natural resources is nonstationary and exhibits multi-scale periodicity, while their interactions vary at different spatial and temporal scales (Bai et al., 2016; Sebastian et al., 2019 ). Using the multiple factor analysis (MFA) method, our study reveals the scale-correlations among multiple natural resources from the perspectives of categories and variables, providing new insights and references for integrated resource management in basins. Taking the HRB as the study area, the scale-correlation relationships among multiple natural resources remain unclear, calling for further advancements in the integrated analysis of natural resources. To accomplish it, this study (1) analyzes the spatio-temporal variations of natural resources over the past four decades in the HRB, including climate, water, land, and vegetation resources; (2) reveals the multi-scale periodicity of natural resources; (3) quantifies the interactions among multiple natural resources at both interannual and interdecadal scales in different spatial scales. Knowledge from this study could offer comprehensive scientific support for eco-environmental protection in endorheic basins.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The HRB (37.7°∼42.7°N, 97.1°∼102.0°E) is the second largest endorheic basin in China ( Fig. 1 ), which is located in the arid and semiarid regions of northwestern China and extends across an area of approximately 143,200 km2 . The Heihe River flows through three provinces (Qinghai, Gansu, and Inner Mongolia) in China. With a wide range of elevations varying between 865 m and 5542 m, the mountain cryosphere and desert regions coexist in this basin. The landscape of the HRB is heterogeneous and diverse because of the significant climatic change and intensive anthropogenic activities. The upstream area is mainly covered by glaciers, frozen soil, alpine meadows, and evergreen needle leaf forests (Qinghai spruce). The oasis–desert landscape exists in the relatively dry midstream and downstream areas. The middle reach flows through the Hexi Corridor in Gansu Province, and the dominant vegetation type is irrigated cropland (artificial oases with corn, vegetables, and fruit trees). The lower reach ends in a terminal lake (Juyan Lake) in western Inner Mongolia, characterized by widespread deserts and riparian forests (natural oases with Tamarix and Populus euphratica). The HRB is an important food provision and storage area in Northwest China, and its limited natural resources support a population of 2.15 million people and secure local socio-economic development (Liu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020b ).  2.2 Data preparation The data used here include regional data and site observation data. The regional data mainly include grid meteorological data (air temperature, precipitation, wind speed, incoming shortwave radiation), glacier area, land cover types, soil organic carbon, leaf area index (LAI), gross primary productivity (GPP), and ET. The category, sources, and detailed information of the regional data are provided in Table A1  (supplementary material ). The site observation data are obtained from automatic weather stations (AWSs), eddy covariance (EC) stations, and hydrological observation stations. Table A2  provides a detailed summary of the information for the 23 stations, and Fig. 1  shows the locations. These stations cover all the land cover types in the basin.  2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Analytical scheme This study integrates the trend analysis, periodicity detection, and scale-correlation analysis into an analytical scheme that identifies the variations of climate, water, land, and vegetation resources in endorheic basins using multivariate data ( Fig. 2 ).  2.3.2 Trend analysis and statistical methods This study uses the ordinary least squares (OLS) method and the Savitzky-Golay (SG) filter to analyze the temporal variation and coefficient of variation (CV) to assess the spatial heterogeneity. Regarding the OLS method, a positive slope indicates an increasing trend, while a negative slope indicates a decreasing trend. The determination coefficient (R2 ) is used to evaluate the precision of the OLS method, and a higher R2  value indicates a better performance. The SG filter is adopted to smooth the annual temporal data series, which involves specifying two main parameters, window size and polynomial order (Chen et al., 2004 ). This study sets the window size to 7 and the polynomial order to 2. The CV is used to evaluate heterogeneity, and a higher CV value indicates higher heterogeneity.  2.3.3 Periodicity detection method The multivariate empirical mode decomposition (MEMD) method is employed to identify the multi-scale periodicity of multiple natural resources across four spatial scales (the whole HRB, upstream area, midstream area, and downstream area). The 10℃ accumulated temperature (10℃ AT), precipitation, runoff, LAI, GPP, and ET (defined as six natural resource elements for quantifying natural resources) in HRB from 1982 to 2018 are selected to form a multivariate data series and detrended. A description of the MEMD method and the reason for choosing these six elements could be found in supplementary material .  2.3.4 Scale-correlation analysis method This study employs the MFA method (Escofier and Pagès, 1994 ) in the FactoMineR package of R 4.0.3 software (Borcard et al., 2018 ) to simultaneously analyze correlations among categories (climate, water, and vegetation resources) and correlations among variables (six natural resource elements depicted in Section 2.3.3 ). MFA generates a partial axes plot that provides detailed insights into correlations, which have two distinct layers of meaning. Firstly, the coordinates of categories or variables (referred to as dimensions, similar to principal components in PCA) indicate the contribution (explained variance) of each category or variable to the overall dataset structure. Secondly, the angles between the categories or variables reflect the strength and direction of their relationships. The absolute cosine values of these angles represent the RV coefficient values (Josse et al., 2008 ), which generalize the Pearson correlation coefficient. RV coefficients range from 0 (indicating no correlation) to 1 (indicating perfect correlation): acute angles signify positive correlations, obtuse angles indicate negative correlations, and orthogonal angles suggest low or negligible correlations (Zhang et al., 2022a ).    3 Results 3.1 Spatio-temporal variations of natural resources 3.1.1 Climate resources This study carries out an analysis of climate resources from the perspective of solar energy, heat, wind energy, and precipitation resources in the HRB ( Fig. 3 ). The regionally averaged total solar radiation (TSR) in the HRB exhibits a decreasing trend, but this decrease is not statistically significant. The annual 10℃ AT and precipitation showed significant increases, with growth rates of 14.27℃ yr−1  and 1.26 mm yr−1 (R2 =0.70, 0.40), respectively. The temperature, wind speed, and precipitation significantly vary in different subbasins, while the radiation remains constant. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze these three resources in the three subbasins. Notably, the midstream of the HRB exhibits the highest growth rate in 10℃ AT (17.08℃ yr−1 ), followed by the downstream (15.49℃ yr−1 ) and upstream areas (3.92℃ yr−1 ). The precipitation in the midstream and downstream areas has remained relatively unchanged, while there is a noticeable increase in the upstream area (2.82 mm yr−1 ). The annual variation in the number of days when wind power density (WPD) (Eq. (A1)) exceeds 150 W m−2  is not notable in the upstream and midstream areas. Additionally, before 1989, there was a sharp decrease in the number of days when WPD exceeded 150 W m−2  in the downstream area. The decrease in wind speed is the primary factor contributing to the reduction in wind energy potential, consistent with the results of He et al. (2013) . The weakening of the East Asian winter monsoon leads to a decrease in windy days, thereby causing a reduction in wind energy (Ge et al., 2021 ). Seasonally, peak values for TSR, 10℃ AT, and precipitation typically occur in June and July, with the exception of WPD. The first peak, usually in April, is significantly higher than the second peak, usually in November or December. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the downstream area, which includes extensive desert regions.  3.1.2 Water resources (1) Surface water resources    This study examines the temporal variation in surface water resources using glacier area, long-term runoff, and lake storage data. The glacier area in the HRB has declined by approximately 47.47 % due to continuous temperature increases, reducing it to 259.00 km2  ( Fig. 4 a). As depicted in Fig. 4 b, there are distinct differences in the annual variation of runoff between two time periods: 1979–2001 and 2002–2020. Compared to the period from 1979 to 2001, a notable increase in runoff was observed from 2002 to 2020. The largest lake area of Juyan Lake (the terminal lake in the HRB) was only 23.50 km2  before the implementation of the EWDP (Fig. 4 c). The largest lake area has remained above 40 km2  in recent years and reached a maximum value of 43.20 km2  in 2020. The largest lake area has increased by 81.51 %, which can also be attributed to the increased water supply to the downstream area.(2) Soil water resources    The soil water content (SWC) (Eq. (A2)) in the 0–100 cm soil layers is used to evaluate soil water resources. Due to the limitations of available SWC data (the SWC observation began in 2014), this study focuses on analyzing the seasonal variation using daily-scale data in the study area. Affected by seasonal factors such as precipitation and snowmelt, the SWC exhibits consistent seasonal variation in multiple ecosystems in the upstream area ( Fig. 5 a). During the growing season, the SWC is higher, ranging from approximately 200 mm to 350 mm, while it remains low but stable at around 80 mm during the non-growing season. In the midstream area, the SWC in the Kalidium foliatum desert ecosystem (Huazhaizi site) ranges from 120 to 180 mm, while it varies from 200 to 450 mm in the cropland ecosystem (Daman site) (Fig. 5 b). This difference is primarily attributed to irrigation and climate factors. Typically, crops are irrigated four times during the growing season, with irrigation schedules closely matching fluctuations in SWC. In the downstream area, the SWC significantly differs among various ecosystems due to the spatial heterogeneity in moisture conditions (Fig. 5 c). The Reaumuria desert ecosystem (Desert site) relies on summer precipitation for soil water, with SWC ranging from approximately 40 to 60 mm. Influenced by spring irrigation and groundwater, peak SWC values in riparian forest ecosystems (Sidaoqiao site and Mixed forest site) occur earlier in March and are higher than those in the Reaumuria desert ecosystem, typically observed in August.(3) Groundwater resources    The groundwater depth in the grassland ecosystem (Heihe bridge site) of the midstream oases (Fig. 5 d) is very shallow, ranging from 1 to 3 m, due to its proximity to the river. In contrast, the groundwater depth ranges from approximately 10 to 20 m in the cropland ecosystem away from the river. It sharply declines in July, and the second valley appears in November. Irrigation is needed during these times (winter irrigation is in November), and a significant amount of groundwater is extracted to meet the demands of crop growth. This seasonal fluctuation in groundwater depth is primarily driven by the water demand for crop irrigation cycles. In the cropland ecosystem near the river, where groundwater depth ranges from approximately 3 to 6 m, variations are less obvious. This is because crop growth in these areas relies more on surface water from the river, supplemented by groundwater, rather than depending solely on groundwater reserves. The noticeable decline in groundwater depth in the cropland ecosystem (Cropland site) of the downstream oases (Fig. 5 f) from May to August can be attributed to the extraction of groundwater for irrigating melon fields, resulting in groundwater depletion and supporting agricultural activities during the growing season. In the riparian forest ecosystems (Sidaoqiao site and Mixed forests site), groundwater depth declines to approximately 2–3 m during the growing season (May to August) due to the reliance of riparian forests on groundwater for their growth. After the growing season, the groundwater depth gradually recovers as water demand decreases. Interestingly, there is a consistent pattern observed between groundwater depth and SWC in the downstream oases (Fig. 5 c and Fig. 5 f), indicating the significant impact of irrigation events on groundwater depth and SWC in regions with limited precipitation.  3.1.3 Land resources Land area and single land use dynamic degree (LUDD) (Eq. (A3)) are used in quantifying land resources. Soil organic matter (SOM) (Eq. (A4)) serves as an indicator for assessing land resources quality, given its crucial role in providing soil nutrients and supporting vegetation growth. The study area involves nine types of land resources. Dominant land cover types include bare land, grassland, and cropland, accounting for approximately 82.76 %, 9.14 %, and 4.68 % of the entire basin, respectively. Over the past four decades, the land cover types have undergone significant changes. Areas of grassland, wetland, cropland, shrubland, forest, built-up land, and bare land have all increased ( Fig. 6 a), with growth rates of about 11.72 %, 7.64 %, 6.61 %, 3.47 %, 1.74 %, 2.24 %, and 1.06 %, respectively. The most significant decrease has been observed in the snow/ice area, with a reduction rate of 61.42 %. There was a turning point in the area of water bodies between 1990–2000 and 2000–2010, closely related to the increased runoff recharge and lake storage after EWDP implementation in 2000. Some variations in land resource can be explained by the combination of area and LUDD (Fig. 6 b). For instance, the area of bare land has changed significantly over the past four decades, but the LUDD of bare land has remained low due to its large total area.  Table 1  presents the significant influence of different land resources on SOM content. Forests exhibit the highest SOM content, followed by grassland, wetland, cropland, built-up land, shrubland, and bare land. This is primarily due to the forest litter covering the soil surface, facilitating the transfer of organic matter into the soil through the activities of soil animals, microorganisms, and precipitation. Similar biological processes occur in grassland and wetland, leading to higher SOM contents compared to other land resources. Additionally, for all land resources, the SOM content in the surface soil (0–5 cm) is generally higher than that in deeper soil layers. This trend is consistent with Chen's findings on the Loess Plateau (Chen et al., 2007 ). In arid and semiarid regions, microbial crusts widely develop in surface soil and can produce abundant SOM. The organic matter content gradually decreases with increasing decomposition by soil microorganisms in deeper soil layers, resulting in lower SOM content. The variability of SOM can be analyzed using the coefficient of variation (CV). A CV value below 0.1 indicates low variability, while a value ranging from 0.1 to 0.9 indicates moderate variability. A value above 0.9 indicates high variability (Fang et al., 2012 ). For bare land, the CV of SOM in the 0–30 cm soil layer exceeds 0.9, indicating high variability in the shallow soil of bare land. With 81.76 % of the entire basin covered by bare land, the quality of land resources in the HRB is relatively low, and the distribution of SOM content exhibits a notable degree of heterogeneity.  3.1.4 Vegetation resources From the upstream to the downstream areas, the HRB exhibits distinct vegetation landscapes that are interconnected by water. Over the past four decades, the vegetation coverage area (areas of cropland, forest, grassland, and shrubland) has increased by 0.19 × 104  km2 , representing a growth of 9.28 %. The annual variations in the LAI and GPP show significant positive trends of 0.0016 m2  m−2  yr−1  and 1.69 gC m−2  yr−1  in the HRB, respectively. The growth rates of LAI follow the same order as GPP in the three subbasins ( Fig. 7 a and Fig. 7 b). Seasonal variations in LAI and GPP exhibit unimodal trends. In the upstream area with higher altitudes, the rate of organic matter accumulation decreases as the temperature gradually drops in August. Thus, the peak value of GPP in the upstream area occurs in July. However, vegetation remains lush in August, resulting in the peak value of LAI still appearing in August in the upstream area. In the midstream and downstream areas, both LAI and GPP reach their peak values in August. Grassland exhibits the highest LAI, followed by cropland and forest (Fig. 7 c). Forest attains the highest GPP, with an annual value of over 400 gC m−2  (Fig. 7 d). Shrubland, on the other hand, attains the lowest LAI/GPP, attributed to the dispersed leaf structure and relatively short growth cycle of shrubs. There is a noticeable increase in LAI/GPP values for cropland, forest, shrubland, and grassland, with growth rates of 17.52 %/131.41 %, 29.87 %/35.11 %, 68.03 %/63.06 %, and 45.14 %/55.43 %, respectively. Despite the relatively lower growth rate of shrubland area, it exhibits higher growth rate in LAI/GPP, indicating a significant improvement in the quality of shrubland resources. Overall, the increase in the LAI and GPP signifies a remarkable increase in vegetation resources over the past four decades, reflecting favorable hydrothermal conditions for vegetation growth.   3.2 Multi-scale periodicity of natural resources  Table 2  presents the calculated period values and variance contributions of the four intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) and one residual (displayed in Fig. A3). Smaller numerical values of the IMFs correspond to higher frequencies and shorter periods, implying that IMF1 to IMF4 values indicate increasing periods. The variance contribution quantifies the impact of the specific signal fluctuations on the variability of the original time series (Hu and Si, 2013 ). The mean periods of IMF1 and IMF2 for various natural resource elements are approximately 3 and 5 years, respectively, indicating interannual variation. Additionally, the mean periods of IMF3 and IMF4 range from 9.25 to 12.33 years and 18.50–24.67 years, respectively. IMF3 and IMF4 represent interdecadal variation. The similarity in period values indicates that these natural resource elements are influenced by specific climate rhythms or atmospheric circulation patterns (Lin and Sun, 2007 ). To further identify the heterogeneity of the periods of different natural resource elements, the CV is calculated. According to the CV, the periods of natural resource elements in the HRB and the midstream area tend to be consistent in interdecadal variation but inconsistent in interannual variation. This discrepancy may be related to the fact that the relationship among climate, water, and vegetation exhibits a more pronounced time lag in interannual variation. Chamaille-Jammes et al. (2006)  observed a stronger relationship between rainfall and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) during seasonal variation compared to interannual variation. This suggests that the time lag between natural resource elements changes with time scale. In addition, the variance contribution reveals that different IMFs have varying impacts on the variability of the original time series. This implies that the dominant periods of natural resource elements vary in different spatial scales. Overall, the short-term fluctuations represented by IMF1 and IMF2 typically account for approximately 60 % of the original time series. This indicates that the impact of interannual variation on the variability of the original time series of natural resource elements is more significant.  3.3 Interannual and interdecadal interactions of natural resources at different spatial scales The multi-scale periodicity of natural resources in different spatial scales complicates the interaction among elements. In order to analyze the correlation among the natural resources at different time scales, the time series are reconstructed (Mahecha et al., 2010 ). The specific methods of reconstruction involve adding up IMF1 and IMF2 (representing short periods) to describe the interannual variation and combining IMF3, IMF4, and the residual (representing long periods) to describe the interdecadal variation. Through the MFA method,  Fig. 8  presents “partial axes” plots of three natural resources (as categories) and six natural resource elements (as variables) at the interannual and interdecadal variations in four spatial scales. The first two dimensions (Dim1 and Dim2 shown in Fig. 8 ) explain about 70 % of the total variance in the global dimensions, indicating that the Dim1 and Dim2 capture most of the information from the original six natural resource elements. Precipitation and runoff are positively correlated with and greatly contribute to the Dim1, indicating that the Dim1 represents moisture condition. AT also has a certain positive correlation with Dim2, indicating that the Dim2 represents thermal condition. In the upstream area, LAI, GPP, and ET contribute notably to the Dim2 (thermal condition), suggesting that heat is the main controlling factor of vegetation growth in the upstream area. Additionally, LAI, GPP, and ET contribute notably to the Dim1 (moisture condition) in the midstream and downstream areas, indicating that moisture factors dominate vegetation growth here. By calculating RV coefficients, this study further reveals the interactions among three natural resources (Table A3 ) and six natural resource elements (Table A4 ) and finds that the magnitude and direction of the interaction among them vary in four spatial scales at different time scales. The 10℃ AT exhibits a negative correlation with precipitation (RV = −0.95, −0.57, and −0.98 in the three subbasins at the interannual scale, and RV = −0.73, −0.37, −0.39 in the three subbasins at the interdecadal scale). Thermal accumulation decreases on rainy days with more clouds and less radiation in the upstream area. The midstream and downstream areas experience less precipitation but relatively adequate heat, resulting in the feedback mechanism. This feedback mechanism between precipitation and heat is more significant at the interannual scale. In addition, there is a positive correlation between precipitation and runoff in the upstream area (RV = 1.00 at the interannual scale, and RV = 0.78 at the interdecadal scale). In the downstream area, there is a weak correlation between precipitation and runoff (RV = 0.67 at the interannual scale, and RV = 0.01 at the interdecadal scale). This phenomenon can be explained by the low precipitation and limited contribution to runoff in the downstream area, as well as the implementation of the EWDP. In regard to vegetation resources, precipitation is significantly positively correlated with LAI, GPP, and ET at the interdecadal scale (RV = 0.98, 0.91, 0.82) and slightly positively correlated at the interannual scale (RV = 0.19, 0.36, 0.45) in the HRB. Similar patterns are observed for the 10℃ AT as for precipitation. Our findings reveal that hydrothermal coupling provides favorable conditions for vegetation growth at the interdecadal scale. However, at the interannual scale, the lag between vegetation growth and the accumulated heat and precipitation weakens the correlation.   4 Discussion 4.1 Impact of climate and land resources variations on water resources The changes in the land cover types in the HRB over the past four decades are characterized by expansion of grassland, wetland, and cropland, alongside a considerable contraction in snow/ice area. During 1985–2000, the expansion of grassland, cropland, and wetland (Fig. 6 a) has resulted in a significant decrease in runoff at the Zhengyi Gorge station (−0.22 × 108  m3  yr−1  during 1979–2001) (Fig. 4 b), leading to severe ecosystem deterioration in the basin (Tan et al., 2024 ). Despite the continued expansion of grassland, cropland, and wetland after the implementation of EWDP in 2000, there has been a noticeable increase in runoff at the Zhengyi Gorge (0.28 × 108  m3  yr−1  during 2002–2020). Compared to other glaciers in western China, the HRB exhibits a higher rate of glacier retreat (Wang et al., 2011 ). Temperature directly influences glacier melting and accumulation rates, while precipitation has a relatively limited impact on these processes (Cai et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2021 ). Research by Jóhannesson et al. (1989)  has shown that despite a significant increase in precipitation, it is insufficient to compensate for the glacier melt loss caused by rising temperatures in a timely manner, which is the key factor contributing to glacier retreat. Another contributing factor to glacier retreat in the HRB is the prevalence of small glaciers, which are highly sensitive to climate change (He et al., 2019 ). The increase in runoff at the Zhengyi gorge station (0.28 × 108  m3  yr−1 ) is more prominent compared to that at the Yingluo gorge station (0.24 × 108  m3  yr−1 ). This phenomenon suggests that the rapid increase in precipitation and snowmelt caused by climate warming in the upstream area contributes to replenishing runoff (Qin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018b ). Additionally, a series of water resource management initiatives implemented in the midstream area, notably the EWDP in 2000, have also yielded noteworthy outcomes. The peak values of runoff at these two hydrological observation stations occurred in 1989, which could be attributed to the increased precipitation from 1985 to 1988 (Fig. 3 d) and the delayed response of runoff to precipitation events.  4.2 Scale effects on interactions of natural resources The relationships among different objects may change with spatio-temporal scale variation (Gurdak et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2022 ). This variation due to different scales is referred to as the scale effects (Wu, 2004 ). The relationships among natural resources become inconsistent as the scale changes. For example, there is a positive correlation between precipitation and runoff in the upstream area, while the correlation between precipitation and runoff in the downstream area is weak. Statistically insignificant correlations, positive correlations, or negative correlations among several natural resources occur arbitrarily and do not precisely reveal the substantial relationship. One possible explanation is that an insignificant correlation at a specific time scale may compromise a significant correlation on other time scales. This mechanism is also observed in positive and negative correlations. Due to factors such as data availability and quality, this study encounters uncertainties when analyzing spatio-temporal variations in natural resources. To ensure robustness and reliability in studying scale effects, the study maintained consistent temporal resolution and data quality in the selected datasets, aligning them where possible to analyze the multi-scale correlations among natural resources. The results of this study regarding scale effects are consistent with previous research on ecosystem services (Zhang et al., 2022b ) and sediment characteristics (Li et al., 2020 ), both emphasizing the importance of considering scale effects when examining the interactions among multiple factors.   5 Conclusions The study performs an integrated analysis to quantify the spatio-temporal variations and multi-scale correlations among climate, water, land, and vegetation resources over the past four decades in the HRB. The conclusions of this study include the following three parts:(1) Over the past four decades, heat (10℃ AT) and precipitation (precipitation) resources in the HRB have increased at rates of 14.27℃ yr−1  and 1.26 mm yr−1 , respectively. Affected by glacier melt and the implementation of the EWDP, the increase in runoff at the Zhengyi gorge station (0.28 × 108  m3  yr−1 ) is prominent, and the largest lake area of Juyan Lake has significantly increased. Land cover changes are characterized by the expansion of grassland, wetland, and cropland, along with a substantial contraction of snow/ice. The vegetation coverage has increased by 9.28 %, indicating that in recent years, the HRB has provided more favorable environmental conditions for vegetation growth.  (2) This study reveals the multi-scale periodicity of natural resources across different spatial scales using the MEMD method. The interannual variation significantly impacts the variability, accounting for 60 % of the original time series.  (3) This study quantifies the multi-scale correlations among natural resources using the MFA method. A negative feedback mechanism exists in the accumulation of temperature and precipitation, which is particularly evident at the interannual scale. Additionally, the effect of hydrothermal coupling on vegetation resources is more obvious at the interdecadal scale.    Insights from this study can guide ecosystem restoration and biodiversity conservation efforts in arid and semiarid environments. The analysis of natural resources suggests strategies to promote eco-environmental sustainability in the HRB, such as reducing cropland area and regulating groundwater extraction. Policies based on our findings can support sustainable development goals while mitigating the impacts of climate change and human activities. Currently, collecting long-term and multivariate data for assessing the quantity and quality of natural resources remains a challenge. Despite the need for refinement in data availability and indicator selection within this analytical scheme, integrated analysis and findings of this study can still serve as references for other endorheic basins along the “Silk Road”.
1 Introduction Significant progress in modern geodesy enables numerous unexpected hydrological applications, accelerating the development of an emerging applied scientific field–hydrogeodesy. Hydrogeodesy aims to mutate geodetic observations (e.g., Earth’s shape, orientation, and gravitational field) into hydrological variables (i.e., terrestrial water storage/fluxes) (White et al. 2022 ) based on relational theoretical models and inversion methods, which is beneficial for figuring out spatiotemporal characteristics of terrestrial water storage (TWS) and for enhancing our understanding of hydrology–climate interactions. Two widely-used Earth observation technologies (i.e., Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment and its Follow on (GRACE/GRACE-FO)) have advanced scientific progress in geophysics, hydrology, cryosphere, atmospheric science, oceanography, and climate changes (Bock and Melgar 2016; Chen et al. 2021 ), which provide critical foundational datasets for analyzing causality in the Earth system and for developing sustainable strategies to accommodate our changing planet. The GRACE missions open a revolutionary era to weigh the Earth from outer space by precisely measuring the variations in the orbits of two co-orbiting satellites and provide global time-varying gravity field data for the first time with unprecedented resolution and accuracy. The GRACE/GRACE-FO twin satellites have highlighted multitudinous discoveries and applications in geodesy, hydrology, oceanography, glaciology, and solid Earth science (Chen et al. 2022 ), which incentivize fruitful interdisciplinary geoscience studies and enable a better understanding of mass transport in the Earth system. In hydrological applications, the GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite missions profoundly facilitate water cycle science, such as investigating TWS anomalies at different temporal (interannual to seasonal) and spatial (global to regional) scales, inferring large-scale evapotranspiration estimates (Rodell and Reager 2023 ), tracking groundwater changes around the world (Famiglietti 2014 ), as well as supporting water resources decision-making, food security, and agricultural management. Another significant contribution of GRACE is improving our knowledge of interactions between different climate system components, which provides essential building blocks to understand complex interactions and transitions involved in today’s changing climate (Tapley et al. 2019 ). In addition, GRACE products are also used for characterizing hydroclimatic extremes (e.g., droughts and floods) by transforming GRACE-derived equivalent water height (EWH) products into drought indicators, including the water storage deficit index (WSDI) (Sun et al. 2018 ) and GRACE-based drought severity index (GRACE-DSI) (Zhao et al. 2017 ). There is a long-standing interest in the interactions between environmental fluid circulation (oceans, atmosphere, terrestrial hydrology) and solid Earth’s deformation, which is tiny but can be accurately measured by GNSS. As a cutting-edge research field, GNSS-based hydrogeodesy aims to obtain fine-scale water storage estimates from the inversion of GNSS-observed hydrological loading displacements. The mathematical model of this inversion problem is based on the mass loading theory that relates water height changes with GNSS-observed displacements (Farrell 1972 ). Two inversion schemes are generally applied: (1) using GNSS data in sparsely instrumented networks to estimate continental/regional-scale TWS variations based on spectral-domain Slepian basis functions (Han and Razeghi 2017; Jiang et al. 2021a; Li et al. 2023a ); and (2) inverting high-density GNSS observations for regional/local-scale water products based on the spatial-domain Green’s function method (Argus et al. 2014; Fu et al. 2015; Jiang et al. 2021b; Jiang et al. 2021c ). The main advantage of GNSS lies in the production of detailed TWS estimates in regionally/locally spatial and daily temporal scales, which is not simultaneously achievable with other widely-used geodetic tools (e.g., GRACE and Swarm satellites). Both GNSS-observed hydrological loading displacements and GNSS-inferred water height changes are used to characterize water storage deficits and surpluses during drought and pluvial periods (Chew and Small 2014; Fu et al. 2015 ). In addition, GNSS has also been proven to be an independent tool for drought characterization, for example, GNSS-DSI datasets are newly developed to quantify drought characteristics (e.g., onset, end, duration, magnitude, and severity) (Ferreira et al. 2018; Jiang et al. 2022a; Jiang et al. 2022b ). Although GRACE/GRACE-FO and GNSS showcase many fruitful applications in hydrological and climate communities, inherent drawbacks must be overcome to achieve the greater potential of these two geodetic technologies. For example, the coarse spatiotemporal resolution makes GRACE unable to effectively detect short-wavelength and short-duration water mass changes. Processing standards like empirical filtering and truncation in the post-processing of GRACE spherical harmonic solutions inevitably lead to signal leakage and suppression. The random (1–2 months) data missing and long-term (11 months) data gaps between GRACE and GRACE-FO missions also restrict the continuous analysis of some hydrological applications (Jiang et al. 2022b; Yang et al. 2021 ). Although GNSS has higher sensitivity in measuring small-scale mass changes, the resolving power of GNSS networks is heavily dependent on station density and coverage. Another issue that needs to be addressed is the contamination of non-hydrological loading signals, including systematic errors in data processing, mismodeling errors, unmodeled inelastic processes, and other non-geophysical signals such as draconitic errors (Han and Razeghi 2017; Jiang et al. 2022a ). To address the fact that individual geodetic techniques generally provide unilateral constraints on total TWS changes at specific spatiotemporal scales, joint inversion models of GNSS and GRACE data are implemented to maximize the respective strengths of these two geodetic techniques for hydrological applications (Adusumilli et al. 2019; Carlson et al. 2022; Li et al. 2023b; Yang et al. 2023 ). The above-mentioned joint inversion works are implemented in the spatial domain based on the widely-used Green’s functions and indicate that complementary effects are reachable in the recovery of more reliable water estimates using these two geodetic techniques (Yang et al. 2023 ). In this study, we design a spectral-domain joint inversion scheme that infers large-scale water height changes using Slepian basis functions and demonstrate that the joint inversion scheme with sparse GNSS data is still able to maximize their respective strengths. In our inversion model, we combine GNSS-observed and GRACE-derived vertical loading displacements to achieve the recovery of large-scale water height estimates. We also integrate the variational Bayesian principal component analysis (vbPCA) into our inversion model to largely improve the inversion efficiency and effectively address the data gaps in both GNSS and GRACE datasets. The jointly derived water height estimates are in comparison with other independent water measurements (e.g., GRACE, GLDAS) and are in conjunction with multi-source hydroclimatic datasets to quantify hydrological drought and pluvial periods. In addition, we harness geodetically inferred outcomes to characterize multifarious hydroclimatic patterns in response to normal climate oscillations and attribute interannual TWS changes using other hydrological and meteorological datasets. Our study aims to further broaden geodetic techniques in hydrogeodetic applications and explore more usage of geodetic observations for climate studies, contributing to unscrambling sophisticated hydrology-climate interactions and to coping with water security in a changing climate.  2 Study region and datasets 2.1 Study region The Australian mainland (Fig. 1  a) is the world’s flattest and smallest continent located between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, which consists of six distinct landform divisions: the eastern highlands, the eastern alluvial plains and lowlands, the southern highlands, the western plateau, the central deserts, the northern plateau and basins. Australia is ranked as the driest inhabited continent and ∼ 70 % of the territory belongs to arid and semiarid regions (James et al. 1999 ). Overall, extremely low precipitation falls on this continent and 80 % of the land receives an annual average precipitation of less than 600 mm, although that in the wet tropics reaches up to 1200–8000 mm (https://coastadapt.com.au/australias-climate-drivers-variability-and-extremes  (accessed on 1 July 2024)). Diverse climatic conditions are an important geographic feature due to the vast size of the continent, including six distinct climate groups: equatorial, tropical, sub-tropical, desert, grassland, and temperate. Australia’s weather and climate regimes are highly variable in different regions and periods, which continue to change due to global warming. This changeable climate pattern makes Australia’s water cycle highly variable both geographically and temporally. The hydrologic cycle also exhibits pronounced interannual variability in response to the highly variable precipitation, making Australia extremely vulnerable to droughts and floods.
