Four super-clusters (Fig. 1 b) are classified to report climate changes at a broader scale, including Northern Australia, Eastern Australia, Southern Australia and Rangelands (https://www.climatechangeinaustralia.gov.au/en/projections-tools/regional-climate-change-explorer/super-clusters/ ). The year-to-year changes in Australia’s water storage are mostly associated with multiple climate drivers (Fig. 1 c) such as the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), the Antarctic Oscillation (AAO), and the Australia monsoon (AUSM) (Xie et al. 2019 ). Geoscience Australia, a pre-eminent geoscience organization, maintains several continuously operating GNSS networks, including the Australian Regional GNSS Network (ARGN), South Pacific Regional GNSS Network (SPRGN), and AuScope Network. These continuous networks consist of more than 100 GNSS stations (Fig. 1 a) on geologically stable marks and offer an innovative means for investigating the spatiotemporal TWS changes. These high-precision deformation measurements in association with high-quality hydrological and meteorological observational datasets play a significant role in clarifying the hydroclimatic changes and interactions in Australia.  2.2 Data 2.2.1 GNSS vertical position time series The GNSS data are used in combination with GRACE Mascon solutions to jointly infer monthly TWS changes in the Australian mainland. The GNSS stations in our joint inversion model consist of 20 stations in ARGN and 94 stations in AuScope (Figure S1 ). The GNSS position time series aligned to the International GNSS Service (IGS14) frame are downloaded from the Nevada Geodetic Laboratory (NGL, https://geodesy.unr.edu/ ), University of Nevada, Reno, United States. These datasets are processed with a Precise Point Positioning (PPP) mode, which is implemented by using the GipsyX-1.0 software from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). The NGL GNSS data processing strategy (including parameter settings, prior models, and auxiliary files) is summarized in the document (https://geodesy.unr.edu/gps/ngl.acn.txt ) (Blewitt et al. 2018 ). To obtain water-induced vertical elastic deformation which upraises as water flows away and subsides when water loads, we correct the non-tidal atmospheric, oceanic loading effects, and thermoelastic deformation, which significantly contribute to the seasonal deformation signatures. The non-tidal oceanic and atmospheric loading predictions released by the German Research Centre for Geosciences (https://esmdata.gfz-potsdam.de:8080/repository ) are firstly subtracted from the raw GNSS vertical position time series. The thermoelastic deformation due to seasonal temperature changes is corrected using daily temperature products from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology according to the modified methodology of Fang et al. (2022)  (see more details in Text S1). To fit the postprocessing time series, a widely-used analytical expression is used to parameterize different signals (see Text S2 for more details), including an initial position (a constant term), a long-term rate (a linear term), seasonal variations (two sinusoidal terms with annual and semiannual cycles), and some necessary Heaviside terms (for instrumental and coseismic offsets) (Jiang et al. 2021c ). Note that postseismic movements are not considered since Australia is well away from epicenter areas of large tectonic earthquakes. After the removal of the constant, linear, and offset terms, the residual time series can be considered to be dominated by water-induced elastic deformations derived from seasonal and inter-annual hydrological changes. Fig. 2  a shows annual variations of GNSS-derived vertical crustal displacement (VCD) associated with water cycles. The non-tidal atmospheric loading effects (Fig. 2 b) significantly contribute to seasonal signals compared to non-tidal oceanic (Fig. 2 c) and thermoelastic (Fig. 2 d) mechanisms.  2.2.2 Independent water height products The monthly EWH products from GRACE Mascon solutions are considered as independent measurements to validate our joint inversion results. The new GRACE/GRACE-FO RL06.2 Mascon solutions are reprocessed at the Center for Space Research (CSR), the University of Texas at Austin. All necessary corrections are applied during the production of these Mascon products, i.e., C20 and C30 replacement, degree-1 corrections, and GIA and GAD corrections. The CSR RL06 Mascon solutions are estimated on the equal-area (120 × 120    km2 ) geodesic cells and are further represented on 0 . 25 °     lon-lat grids. It should be noted that both are likely not the resolution of GRACE Mascon solutions. Different from GRACE spherical harmonic solutions, users can directly obtain water height values without applying additional filtering or scaling factors. In our study, the short-term missing values (1–2 months) are filled using the cubic spline interpolation method, and the 11-month data gaps are not addressed in the data preprocessing stage. We also compare the GLDAS-based water contents with our water estimates jointly recovered from GARCE and GNSS. Both ground- and satellite-based measurements are involved to generate the optimal fields of land surface states and fluxes using state-of-the-art land surface modeling and data assimilation techniques (Rodell et al., 2004 ). Three water components at 0 . 25 °   × 0 . 25 °     grids, i.e., snow water equivalent, soil moisture of 0–2 m, and canopy water storage, are accumulated for GLDAS-based TWS changes. The monthly GLDAS Noah land surface model is considered in our study, which has spatial coverage of - 180 °     to 180 °     and - 60 °     to 90 °     and temporal coverage from 2000-01-01 to the present.  2.2.3 Meteorological products To characterize and attribute the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of TWS changes and hydroclimate extremes, we also consider the gridded meteorological products from the Bureau of Meteorology. Both gridded precipitation and temperature datasets are generated using discrete measurements from ground-based meteorological stations based on an optimized Barnes successive correction technique that applies a weighted averaging process to the station data (Jones et al. 2009 ). The gridded maps are generated using precipitation values from up to 3000 rain gauges and mean maximum temperature records at about 750 sites across the country. Both monthly precipitation and daily temperature datasets have spatial resolution of 0 . 05 °  × 0 . 05 °    , covering from 112.00  °     E to 156.25 °     E and 10.00  °     S–44.50  °     S. In addition, the daily temperature data are also used for modeling the thermoelastic deformation of monuments and bedrock.  2.2.4 Drought and teleconnection indices To characterize the hydrological extremes, we collect the self-calibrating Palmer Drought Severity Index (scPDSI, available at https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/drought/ ). The scPDSI is calculated using precipitation and temperature time series, together with some fixed parameters related to the soil/surface characteristics. To better understand Australia’s hydroclimatic patterns, various climate drivers (including the ENSO, IOD, AUSM, and AAO) are considered to attribute interannual TWS variability in Australia. Four teleconnection indicators associated with these climate drivers can be downloaded from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Climate Center (APCC, https://www.apcc21.org/ser/indic.do?lang=en ). The NINO3.4 index, measuring sea surface temperature anomalies in the equatorial Pacific, is a key to understanding the global impacts of El Niño and La Niña phenomena. The Dipole Mode Index (DMI) is calculated with the east–west temperature gradient across the tropical Indian Ocean and is used to assess the IOD’s influence on regional climate. The AAO index (AAOI) provides insights into the atmospheric dynamics of the Antarctic region, helping us to clarify wind patterns and climatic variations there. The AUS Index (AUSMI) captures the intensity and duration of monsoon activity in Australia, which is vital for understanding the region’s climatic patterns.    3 Methodology Our study aims to implement a joint inversion of GNSS and GRACE data for the recovery of monthly TWS changes in the Australian mainland. We firstly correct the far-field hydrological loading effects in GNSS vertical data using GRACE Mascon solutions and calculate the GRACE-predicted vertical elastic displacements at pseudo stations based on Green’s function method (Farrell 1972 ). Subsequently, a vbPCA-based inversion model is applied to handle the GNSS-measured and GRACE-predicted vertical displacements, which produces so-called temporal and spatial functions after this decomposition (Jiang et al. 2021c ). In the inversion model, the spatial functions of each principal component (PC) are converted into a group of spectral-domain Slepian EWH coefficients and are then synthesized into spatial-domain gridded EWH values of each PC. Eventually, total time-varying gridded TWS estimates are reconstructed by using spatial-domain gridded EWH values and corresponding temporal functions of all PCs. Fig. 3   shows a diagram of our joint inversion strategy in the spectral domain using GNSS and GRACE data for inferring monthly TWS estimates. 3.1 Calculating GRACE-VCD predictions The GRACE Mascon solutions are considered in our inversion model because GRACE also measures total TWS changes. The utilization of GRACE Mascon solutions aims to (1) calculate forward displacements at virtual stations, and (2) correct far-field effects due to water loads outside Australia at GNSS stations. The GRACE-VCD predictions at both GNSS and virtual stations are calculated based on the disk loading theory (Argus et al. 2014; Fu et al. 2015 ). The forward calculation of vertical loading displacement involves convolving gridded water mass loads with Green’s functions standing for the elastic response of vertical displacement at the locations of interest to the unit EWH changes. This forward process is summarized as the following formula:(1) d u λ , θ    = ∑ i = 1  n  d m λ i  , θ i     × G φ i         where d u λ , θ       represents the vertical displacements at stations with coordinates (longitude λ   , latitude θ   ), n    is the number of grid points, d m λ i  , θ i        denotes the EWH values at grid points λ i  , θ i      , G φ i        is the Green’s functions with angular distance φ i     between two locations ( λ , θ )    and λ i  , θ i      , which can be written as follows:(2) G φ    = R M  × ∑ i  l  h i  × P i  cos φ           where R    and M    are the averaged radius and mass of the Earth, respectively, h i     is the i    th- degree radial load Love numbers (LLNs), P i  cos φ          is the Legendre polynomial of degree i   . We use the LLNs calculated by Wang et al. (2012)  based on the Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM) (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981 ). In our study, the 0 . 5 °  × 0 . 5 °     EWH values within the Australian continent from GRACE/GRACE-FO RL06.2 Mascon solutions are used to predict vertical hydrological loading displacements at 2 . 5 °  × 2 . 5 °     virtual stations (see Text S3 for the selection criteria). To correct far-field loading effects at inland GNSS stations with high computational efficiency, the gridded EWH values outside Australia are resampled into 1 °  × 1 °    , 2 °  × 2 °    , and 3 °  × 3 °     grids divided by boundary buffers of 5 °    , and 20 °    . To align with the GNSS data, the 11-month data gap is reconstructed with seasonal and trend components of the GRACE-forward displacement time series, which can be considered as the first-order corrections.  3.2 vbPCA decomposition The PCA algorithm is widely applied for feature extraction in the GNSS network time series analysis, which compresses high-dimensional data into low-dimensional uncorrelated ones that retain the maximal amount of variance. To address that GNSS data routinely have missing values due to sensor failure, inconsistent sampling rates, and the removal of outliers, various extended versions of the PCA algorithm are developed. The vbPCA can effectively overcome the overfitting problem and locally optimal solutions compared to other existing methods such as unregularized approaches (e.g., imputation algorithm and alternating least-squares) and probabilistic models (e.g., probabilistic PCA) (Ilin and Raiko 2010 ), thus it works well in datasets with missing values and gives reasonable reconstruction results. For more details on the principles of vbPCA, readers can refer to previous studies (Ilin and Raiko 2010 ). In our study, we implement an inversion of GNSS-observed and GRACE-predicted vertical crustal motions for recovering monthly TWS changes in the Australian mainland. The daily residual time series dominated by hydrological loading effects are firstly resampled into monthly datasets. In total, GRACE-derived time series at 79 virtual stations are generated at 2 . 5 °  × 2 . 5 °     regular grids in our study area. We then build a sample-by-sequence observation matrix D mn  0     by placing each time series along its column (NaN for missing values), where m    and n    denote the numbers of stations (including 114 GNSS stations and 79 virtual stations) and epochs. Note that an equally weighted scheme is applied between these two datasets. The matrix D mn  0     is then processed using the vbPCA method integrated into a Matlab package (pcamv, available at https://users.ics.aalto.fi/alexilin/software/ ). After implementing the vbPCA decomposition, two matrices referred to as spatial U    and temporal V    functions are obtained (Jiang et al. 2021c ) and their product roughly equals the matrix D mn  0    . We can simplify the decomposition process as follows: D mn  0  ≈ U mr   ∗  V rn     , where r    is the number of selected PCs used for vbPCA reconstruction. To largely explain the variance of the matrix D mn  0     with a small number of PCs, the first ten PCs accounting for 84.4 % of the variance are chosen in our study (Table S1 ) and Figure S2  shows cumulative contributions of selected PCs to the explained variance of the filtered data.  3.3 Joint inversion modeling To achieve the recovery of large-scale TWS changes using sparsely distributed vertical deformation data, Slepian basis functions (or regional harmonic basis functions) are applied in our inversion modeling. These localized basis functions are orthonormal both across the entire sphere and within a specific spherical region. As an alternative to global spherical harmonic functions, this approach can significantly improve regional-scale modeling accuracy in the spectral domain and has resulted in widespread applications in geoscience, especially for analyzing and representing space-limited data (Han and Razeghi 2017; Harig and Simons 2012; Jiang et al. 2021a ). For a comprehensive understanding of the mathematical foundations of Slepian basis functions, we recommend readers consult pertinent literature (Harig and Simons 2012; Simons et al. 2006; Slepian 1983 ). The production of regionally specific Slepian basis functions depends on an open-source tool, SLEPIAN Alpha (https://github.com/csdms-contrib/slepian_alpha ), developed at the Princeton University (Harig et al. 2015; Harig and Simons 2012; Simons et al. 2006 ). Han and Razeghi (2017)  first give the detailed mathematical derivation of spectral-domain inversion using deformation data to infer TWS changes based on Slepian basis functions. In brief, the inversion process is firstly transforming spatial-domain discrete displacement to spectral-domain displacement coefficients, then converting them to spectral-domain EWH coefficients, and finally synthesizing spatial-domain EWH estimates. Here, we only list the key functional expression and the detailed inversion derivation can be referred to Han and Razeghi (2017) . The truncated data at discrete GNSS stations can be expressed in the form of Slepian basis functions as follows:(3) μ L  θ , λ , t    = a ∑ α = 1  L + 1    2   s α  vcd   t    g α  θ , λ       g α  θ , λ    = ∑ l = 0  L  ∑ m = - l  l  g α , l m   Y lm   θ , λ               where μ L  θ , λ , t       is the loading displacements in the vertical direction at specific geographic locations (longitude θ   , colatitude λ   ) and epoch t   , L    is the truncated degree of global Spherical harmonic functions Y lm   θ , λ      , g α  θ , λ       and s α  vcd   t       are the α    th Slepian basis function and corresponding VCD-related coefficients, and these two spherical harmonic functions can be linearly transformed into each other, g α , l m      is the l    th-degree m    th-order orthogonal localization coefficients of the α    th Slepian basis functions, a    is the Earth’s mean radius. After obtaining a set of zone-specific Slepian basis functions, the VCD-related Slepian coefficients are converted into EWH-related Slepian coefficients and spatial-domain EWH estimates can be eventually synthesized as follows (Han and Razeghi 2017 ):(4) s β  ewh   t    = ∑ α = 1  J  s α  vcd   t    ∑ l = 0  L  ∑ m = - l  l  ρ e  3 ρ w       2 l + 1  h l  ′   g α , l m   g β , l m      σ L  θ , λ , t    = a ∑ α = 1  J  γ α  s α  ewh   t    g α  θ , λ               where s β  ewh   ( t )     denotes the time-dependent EWH-related Slepian coefficients at the β    th degree, g α , l m      and g β , l m      are the VCD- and EWH-related localization coefficients, respectively. The term h l  ′     represents l    th-degree LLNs, ρ w     and ρ e     represent the density of fresh water and Earth, J    shows the truncated number for Slepian basis functions. The term σ L  θ , λ , t       refers to the time-varying EWH estimates at specific geographical coordinates, γ α     is the eigenvalue obtained when generating the Slepian basis functions, with its magnitude indicating the energy concentration ratio of the α    th Slepian basis function. According to the previous studies of Han and Razeghi (2017) , an eigenvalue-weighted scheme allows to obtain a robust synthesis of spatial-domain EWH estimates. In our study, the integration of vbPCA into our time-varying joint inversion model can markedly improve the computational efficiency. After obtaining the gridded EWH component from the inversion of spatial functions of each component at 114 GNSS stations and 79 GRACE virtual stations, the final time-varying gridded water estimates are reconstructed by cumulatively summing the products of temporal functions and gridded EWH components overall PCs (Fig. 3 ). In our study, we consider global spherical harmonic functions truncated with 70 degrees and Slepian basis functions with eigenvalues of ≥ 0.1    and a 250-km Gaussian filtering to avoid unstable results from Slepian coefficients corresponding to shorter wavelengths (see more details in Text S3, Figures S3–S6 ).  3.4 Calculating DSI datasets Multi-source water products (GNSS-, GRACE-, and GLDAS-EWH) are converted into DSI datasets to characterize hydroclimate extremes in Australia. Based on the knowledge of climate statistics, the DSI datasets are defined as standardized EWH anomalies, which are calculated by dividing EWH anomalies deviating from the climatological normal by the climatological standard deviation (Jiang et al. 2022b; Zhao et al. 2017 ):(5) DSI  i , j   = EWH  i , j   - μ j   σ j       where j    and i    denote the month and year indexes, respectively, EWH  i , j      indicates the monthly EWH values in the j    th month of the i    th year, and the j    th-month average and standard deviation among all years are μ j     and σ j    , respectively, the term EWH  i , j   - μ j     denotes EWH anomalies with negative values for deficits and positive values for surpluses. The DSI datasets are classified into 11 categories based on severity (Zhao et al. 2017 ) and Table S2  provides a detailed overview of the classification criteria.   4 Results 4.1 Water-induced vertical loading displacements The Earth’s lithosphere slightly deforms in elastic response to seasonal water loading and unloading. We investigate annual displacement amplitudes and phases to characterize seasonal water oscillations in the Australian mainland. As shown in Fig. 4  , annual hydrological loading displacement variations are examined by comparing the results derived from diversified datasets (i.e., GNSS, GRACE, and GLDAS). These three datasets consistently indicate that the most distinguishing seasonal alterations in TWS are located in north Australia (Fig. 4 a–c). On the contrary, the remaining vast territories, especially the arid to semi-arid interior geographical provinces, are manifested as insignificant annual amplitudes. It suggests that the water cycles in many Australian states experience minor seasonal variations and this mainland is extremely vulnerable to serious water scarcity. Most notably, GNSS detects relatively conspicuous but localized water-induced vertical deformation compared to GRACE and GLDAS along the southwest and southeast coast areas. This considerable departure is mostly owing to the inherent defects of the GRACE technique in the spatial resolution and the ignoration of other water contents (e.g., deep groundwater and surface water) in the GLDAS model. To examine the periods when water seasonally maximizes in storage, we calculate the annual displacement phases corresponding to the moment of peak surface subsidence. These three datasets simultaneously demonstrate a wide range of annual phases (Fig. 4 a–c), indicating that water storage in different geographical regions reaches a peak in different seasons within one year. The highly distinctive hydrological patterns are attributed to the multiplicity of climatic systems and landscapes in the Australian mainland. The most striking finding is that the annual phases in the northern regions are in the opposite direction to those in the southeast and southwest regions. It indicates a completely out-of-phase hydroclimatic condition, i.e., the water storage in north Australia peaks in the southern hemisphere’s summer and autumn (corresponding to the wet seasons) but that in south Australia maximizes in winter and spring (corresponding to the dry seasons). Compared to GRACE and GLDAS with relatively regular spatial variations in annual phases (Fig. 4 b–c), GNSS shows an unsystematized spatial pattern (Fig. 4 a). It mainly results from the strong sensitivity of GNSS to local- and regional hydrological mass transfer. In addition, the GNSS-measured results are also affected by other unmodeled signals, e.g., the poroelastic mechanism (especially in the vast aquifers of Australia’s sedimentary basins) features an opposite deformation pattern to the elastic loading effect. Fig. 4 d denotes the annual amplitudes and phases calculated using the vbPCA-reconstructed vertical displacement time series and we can conclude that using vbPCA to simultaneously decompose GNSS and GRACE data can balance the existing inconsistencies and reach a compromise result between these two datasets.  4.2 Spatial patterns of seasonal water oscillations Seasonal water storage changes generally inform seasonal forecasts of water availability in a region; thus, we investigate annual water oscillations derived from the joint inversion (Fig. 5  a), GRACE Mascon (Fig. 5 b), and GLDAS (Fig. 5 c). Overall, water height results derived from these three datasets demonstrate an accordant spatial distribution pattern in seasonal water oscillations. We can find that markable periodic features in annual water storage changes are distributed in the northern part of Australia closer to the equator. However, the hydrologic regime in other vast arid zones is characterized by inappreciable seasonal hydrological signatures (Fig. 5 a–c), indicating that Australia is confronted with persistent water scarcity and sustainable water infrastructure is necessary. Interestingly, some southeast and southwest coastal areas feature relatively moderate but local-scale variations in annual water oscillations. In the north geographical provinces, the GRACE Mascon solutions exhibit larger annual amplitudes (more than 150 mm) than those inferred from the joint inversion and GLDAS (smaller than 130 mm). The amplitude of seasonal TWS changes manifests a seaward increase and peaks along the coastline in the north, which is not in accord with the fact that TWS amplitudes near the coastline are generally reduced due to a low water storage capacity. The smoothing transition from land to ocean is observed along the Gulf of Carpentaria (Fig. S7 a) is closely related to the signal leakage problem that cannot be perfectly addressed even for Mascon solutions. It contributes to the overestimation of annual EWH oscillations in the coastal areas due to the infiltration of seawater signals with unusually large annual oscillations as well reported in previous studies (Tregoning et al. 2008; Zheng et al. 2023 ). Both joint-EWH and GLDAS-EWH results reveal comparable seasonal water oscillations in north Australia, which indicates that changes in soil moisture dominate the annual hydrological cycles since the other two water contents (i.e., snow water equivalent and canopy water storage) except for soil moisture almost have no seasonal changes (Fig. S7 b). Through this contrastive analysis, we can conclude that the joint inversion can balance the discrepancy between GNSS and GRACE data and decrease the signal leakage of GRACE to some extent. Fig. 5 d shows annual amplitudes of precipitation data and obvious seasonality is also observed in north Australia with a tropical monsoonal climate, spatially overlapping with the regions having peak annual water changes. It suggests that precipitation plays a key role in annual water cycles in North Australia. The other regions except for the coastal regions involve a low-amplitude annual precipitation due to the arid and semi-arid climate.  4.3 Time-varying hydrological signatures inferred from various datasets To examine the time-varying evolution characteristics of TWS changes, we investigate the basin-scale EWH changes calculated using an area-weighted scheme. Fig. 6   shows area-averaged TWS changes derived from the joint inversion model, GARCE Mascon, and GLDAS products in nine large river basins. The results illustrate that the jointly derived water height estimates generally temporally correspond to other two independent water products from GRACE Mascon solutions and the GLDAS model (Fig. 6 ). Two basins (i.e., CC (Fig. 6 a) and TTS (Fig. 6 b)) situated in north Australia exhibit marked periodic variations and annual EWH amplitudes can reach up to ∼ 80 and ∼ 60 mm, respectively. Very strong temporal correlations are found between these three datasets, with the correlation coefficient ranging from 0.84 to 0.96. In these two basins, the joint-EWH correlates well with GRACE-EWH compared to the consistency between joint inversion results and GLDAS water contents (Fig. 6 a and 6b). Besides exhibiting obvious seasonality in these two river basins, these three EWH time series are also characterized by prominent interannual variability with above- or below-normal water fluctuations. These year-to-year changes have strong linkages with hydrometeorological extremes (e.g., drought and pluvial episodes) which frequently occur in Australia. Strong to very strong linear relationships (0.6–1.0) also exist between these three water height estimates in other water-stressed regions (LEB, MDB, NEC, NWP, SWP) even though their hydrological cycles are characterized by no noticeable seasonal variations (Fig. 6 c-6g). It indicates that fluctuations in joint- and GRACE-EWH estimates are highly correlated with near-surface (0–2 m) soil moisture in GLDAS. These five basins show noteworthy interannual water storage variations, which are also attributed to the frequently occurring and long-lasting extreme events. In the southwest two regions (i.e., SWC and PG basins), the jointly inferred water heights have very weak-to-moderate temporal consistency with GRACE Mascon solutions and the GLDAS model. In contrast, GRACE-EWH is in good synchronization with GLDAS-EWH, with Pearson correlation coefficients of ∼ 0.70 (Fig. 6 h and i). In the SWC and SWP basins, significant inconsistencies between joint-EWH and GRACE-/GLDAS-EWH are observed during 2011–2012. The potential causes primarily include two aspects: (1) existing obvious differences both in seasonal displacement amplitudes and phases between GNSS and GRACE; (2) poor PCA reconstruction results in SWP due to that more than half (7 out of 15) of the stations lack data records from 2009 through 2012.  4.4 Quantification of regional hydroclimate extremes As indicated in Fig. 7  , various DSI datasets are calculated using jointly modeled, GRACE-derived, and GLDAS-output water estimates. In most river basins, there generally exists good correlations between these three dryness index datasets (referred to as joint-, GRACE-, and GLDAS-DSI). The linear relationships between joint-DSI and GRACE-DSI datasets are stronger than that between joint-DSI and GLDAS-DSI in eight river basins. In the MDB, NWP, TTS, and LEB, high Pearson’s correlation coefficients between joint- and GRACE-DSI datasets outweigh 0.90. The CC and NEC also feature strong to very strong linear associations (0.87 and 0.79) between joint- and GRACE-DSI. In the SWP, the Pearson’s correlation coefficient value is 0.63, which still indicates a strong correlation but is weaker than that in previous watersheds. However, bad consistency between joint- and GRACE-DSI is observed in the SWC and PG, because of the existence of low correlations between joint-EWH and GRACE-EWH estimates. Australia is a continent extremely susceptible to some extraordinary extreme weather events (e.g., droughts and floods), owing to the most variable precipitation climates. As shown in Fig. 7 , different watersheds experience different dry and wet characteristics, as well as multifeatured precipitation anomalies (green bars in Fig. 7 ). During the years of 2010–2011, much of the continent has undergone major devastating floods ending long-running drought periods, which is well documented in previous numerous studies (Pan et al. 2022; Xie et al. 2019; Yang et al. 2020 ). As clearly shown in our study, various DSI datasets show long-term positive values and reach a maximum during these periods, which also corresponds to the long-going precipitation surplus. Another rainy period (2016–2017) also occurred across most of Australia with a low intensity relative to the 2010–2011 extreme water event. After this event, a prolonged dry condition with precipitation persistently below average spans from 2017 to 2021. Starting in 2022, heavy rain gradually alleviated Australia’s drought-stricken regions and ended a years-long dry spell in north and east Australia. In places with abundant precipitation (e.g., NEC, CC, and TTS), short-term but significant precipitation deficiencies or surpluses frequently occur with durations of 2–3 months, which generally alleviate but cannot alter the long-term wet or drought conditions.   5 Discussion 5.1 Benefits from joint modeling for TWS changes In the hydrogeodetic community, multi-source geodetic observation data (especially GRACE and GNSS) are extensively utilized to quantify hydrological fluxes and storage, enabling us to better understand climate-driven and human-caused TWS changes. Nevertheless, the border-scale spatial resolution of GRACE results in some inevitable limitations in sensing high-frequency mass changes associated with terrestrial hydrological cycles. The GNSS-based inversion model also has inherent drawbacks including the contamination from non-hydrological signals and the strong dependency of station density and coverage. Therefore, joint inversion of GNSS and GRACE data are proposed to achieve the additional potential of these two geodetic techniques for hydrological applications (Adusumilli et al. 2019; Carlson et al. 2022; Li et al. 2023b; Yang et al. 2023 ). These joint inversion strategies are directed against the conditions with densely instrumented GNSS observations using Green’s function method. Differing from previous studies, our joint inversion model is designed to make it appropriate for sparsely distributed GNSS data using the Slepian basis functions. Admittedly, our joint inversion result does not significantly improve the spatial resolution due to the poor GNSS station coverage, which is an unavoidable defect but can be largely improved with the addition of more GNSS stations in the future. In this study, we demonstrate that the joint inversion model even with scarce GNSS observations can benefit the recovery of large-scale TWS changes and allow us to integrate the advantages of these two geodetic techniques. On the one hand, the joint inversion can compensate for the shortcomings in the spatial distribution of GNSS stations, which are distributed extremely unevenly in Australia, even with large-area vacancies in the NWP and SWP. If only using GNSS to infer TWS changes, a low bandwidth with 40–50 degrees can produce a stable inversion result due to the very poor spatial coverage (Figure S8 ), which is also confirmed in previous studies (Han and Razeghi 2017 ). On the other hand, the joint results can improve regional signal amplitudes to some extent where there is fine station coverage such as in southwest and southeast Australia (Fig. 4 d and Fig. 5 a), and reduce signal leakage along the northern marginal areas where conspicuous ocean signals are existing (Fig. 5 a and b). The joint inversion can also alleviate the effect due to other local non-hydrological signals in GNSS data as clearly seen in Fig. 4 a. In addition, the use of vbPCA can compensate for random data gaps in GNSS and GRACE, allowing us to implement a continuous analysis on TWS changes and related hydroclimatic applications (Figs. 6 and 7 ).  5.2 Various hydrographic features declassified by geodetic tools Australia experiences a variety of climatic conditions, ranging from a wet tropical climate in the North, a desert climate with seis-arid/arid conditions in central Australia to a temperate climate with four distinct seasons in the south. To characterize the broader-scale hydrological storage patterns responding to normal climate oscillations, we investigate the monthly EWH averages in four major climatic zones (or superclusters), including northern Australia, eastern Australia, southern Australia, and Rangelands. North Australia belongs to the monsoon-dominated regions and has two distinctive seasons classified by temperature and humidity properties, including the wet season (October to April) associated with tropical cyclones and monsoon rains and the dry season (May to September) with sunny and rainless weather (Fig. 8  a). The TWS seasonally peaks in the summer-autumn periods and reaches the lowest value in spring (black line in Fig. 8 e). The vast Rangelands contain varied landscapes and arid and semi-arid climates, which have a hot dry summer and a mild-to-cold winter and low precipitation patterns (Fig. 8 c). Seasonal water storage maximizes in early autumn (Fig. 8 e) and features the weakest annual oscillations due to the high evaporation and low precipitation throughout the year (Fig. 8 c). The terrestrial water manifests a fast increase in storage from December to next March and a slower subsequent decline in the remaining months after the rise to the peak value (Fig. 8 e). The Eastern Australian super-cluster has a range of climates, from sub-tropical in the north, through to temperate in the south, with a typically drier winter and wetter summer. The climate-controlled water storage seasonally peaks in the middle of this year (around July) (Fig. 8 b), corresponding to the mid-winter. This result indicates that more precipitation turns into water storage during a mild-to-cold winter in contrast to that relatively abundant precipitation is evaporated into the atmosphere or discharged into the ocean during the hot summer. The southern Australian super-cluster comprises southwest and southeast Australia and mainly has a predominantly Mediterranean climate, which has a dry and hot summer and a cool and rainy winter. As shown in Fig. 8 d, it shows higher winter precipitation and lower summer precipitation in southern Australia. Under the control of the subtropical ridge, a belt of high pressure that encircles the globe in the middle latitudes, it allows cold fronts to seasonally land to the south and to bring more precipitation here. The water storage increases rapidly as precipitation increases and temperature decreases during autumn and winter and reaches its maximum in winter and next spring (Fig. 8 e).  5.3 Attribution analysis of interannual TWS changes The water cycle in Australia is marked by high variability both in geography and seasonality due to a highly variable climate linked to changes in large-scale circulation systems. Spanning from 2009 to 2022, four moist years occurred in 2010, 2011, 2016, 2022, while 2012, 2014–2015, and 2017–2019 are three rainless periods (Fig. 9  a). The annual average temperature is in an opposite pattern with annual cumulative precipitation, namely that the wetter year has a lower annual temperature (Fig. 9 a). Fig. 9 b shows continental-scale EWH and precipitation anomalies and fluctuations in water storage anomalies are closely connected to precipitation deficits and surpluses. Ongoing precipitation deficits/surpluses resulted in long-term drier-than-average or wetter-than-average hydrological conditions and they generally cannot be altered with short-duration (1–2 months) precipitation anomalies. The continental-scale water storage anomalies can temporally correspond well with scPDSI, but a time lag of 2–3 months exists due to the propagation from meteorological to hydrological dry/wet periods. In addition, we can find that the joint-DSI shows more dry conditions in contrast to scPDSI derived from meteorological datasets during some extreme drought periods, which is most likely attributed to significant losses in groundwater and/or soil water (Fig. 9 b). Largely influenced by numerous climate drivers, Australia’s climates are variable and prone to extremes over different regions and seasons, e.g., droughts, heatwaves, fires, rainstorms, and floods. As a consequence, the continental-scale TWS changes manifest remarkable interannual alterations, and three increasing episodes and three decreasing stages are observed from 2009 to 2023 (Fig. 9 c). Adjacent to the Pacific and Indian Oceans, two ocean-related teleconnection mechanisms, i.e., ENSO and IOD (Fig. 9 c), perturb Australia’s hydrological cycles and water balance (Forootan et al. 2012 ). The ENSO-dominated region (orange shadows in Fig. 1 c) is prone to drought extremes when a prolonged El Niño brings drier conditions and warmer temperatures. In contrast, a La Niño would lead to above-average precipitation (sometimes flooding) attributed to the strengthened easterly trade winds across the Pacific. In the ENSO-dominated region (Fig. 9 d), the NINO3.4 index temporally corresponds to the monthly DSI time series, with a cross-correlation coefficient accounting for −0.36 and approximately 3-month lags during the study period. For example, the La Niña-induced wettest two-year period (2010–2011) (Fig. 9 d) caused continent-wide wetting episodes and damaging floods in several geographical provinces (Xie et al. 2019 ), which contributes to the drop in global sea level in this period (Boening et al. 2012; Fasullo et al. 2013 ). The IOD-related DMI index also yields a negative linear relationship with the joint-based DSI time series and the cross-correlation coefficient reaches up to −0.44. The IOD pattern dominates the parts of central and southern Australia (green shadows in Fig. 1 c), with lower precipitation during the positive phase and an increase in precipitation during the negative phase. Another climate driver is the Australian monsoon, which dominates the hydrological cycle in northern regions (red shadows in Fig. 1 c) and is influenced by ENSO, Madden-Julian Oscillation, and tropical depressions. Fig. 9 f demonstrates that good agreement (with a cross-correlation coefficient of 0.49 and a 2-month lag) exists between AUSMI and joint-DSI time series. During the active monsoon periods, heavy rainfall (e.g., 2010–2011, 2016–2017, and 2022–2023) is observed across much of northern Australia and hydrological wet conditions continuously maintain due to the long-duration rainfall surpluses. In contrast, the inactive monsoon phases (e.g., 2015–2016 and 2019–2020) are usually accompanied by evident rainfall deficits and reduced water storage. The AAO, also called Southern Annular Mode, can result in enhanced or attenuated precipitation in regions of southern Australia (blue shadows in Fig. 1 c). A positive correlation is found between the joint-DSI and AAOI datasets (cross-correlation coefficient of 0.21). It should be noted that the hydro-climatic patterns in southern Australia are also related to ENSO and frontal systems. In addition, we can find that different geographical regions exhibit varying degrees of dry and wet characteristics, and even contrasting dry and wet states according to precipitation anomalies and standardized water storage anomalies (Fig. 9 d–g).   6 Conclusion Our study aims to characterize multifarious hydroclimatic patterns using geodetic measurements in conjunction with multi-source hydroclimatic datasets in the Australian mainland. A joint inversion model that integrates the vbPCA to handle data gaps both in GNSS and GRACE measurements is implemented to infer monthly TWS changes. The joint inversion modeling strategy is capable of sufficiently utilizing the merits of multi-source geodetic data in measuring TWS changes. The inversion results are manifested as more spatial details compared to the GRACE Mascon solutions and good resistance to the non-hydrological mechanisms in GNSS data. We compare the jointly inferred water estimates with other independent water products (i.e., GLDAS, GRACE), and good consistency is found between these data datasets in temporal and spatial scales. These datasets reveal obvious yearly periodic variations in TWS changes in north Australia in contrast to inappreciable seasonal hydrological signatures in other vast arid zones. The TWS in north Australia seasonally peaks in the southern hemisphere’s summer and autumn, whereas it maximizes in winter and spring in the southeast and southwest regions. We convert multiple water estimates from the joint inversion, GRACE, and GLDAS into DSI datasets based on the knowledge of climate statistics and the joint-based DSI datasets are in temporal accordance with other two datasets in most watersheds. To characterize the broader-scale climate-controlled hydrological storage patterns, seasonal EWH characteristics responding to normal climate oscillations are analyzed in four major climatic zones. In addition, the attribution analysis on the interannual TWS variability is conducted using multi-source meteorological, hydrological, and climatological datasets and the large-scale TWS changes manifest remarkable interannual alterations dominated by numerous climate drivers (e.g., ENSO, IOD, AUSM, AAO). Our study illuminates more application prospects in the hydroclimatic and hydrogeodetic communities using space geodesy techniques (e.g., GNSS and GRACE), which would contribute to better measuring water cycles and understating climate changes.
1 Introduction Urban riparian zones play a crucial role in managing nitrogen pollution in urban rivers. They can intercept and filter nitrogen from surface runoff (Johnson and Wilby, 2015 ; Hénault-Ethier et al., 2017 ; Trauth et al., 2018 ), absorb nitrogen directly from rivers (Gomez-Velez et al., 2015; Hester et al., 2018; Man et al., 2024 ), and facilitate nitrogen removal through nitrification and denitrification processes (Fellows et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2019a,b ). Despite these benefits, urban riparian zones also contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, particularly nitrous oxide (N2 O), which has a global warming potential 298 times greater than carbon dioxide and is a major factor in stratospheric ozone depletion (Ravishankara et al., 2009 ; Stocker et al., 2014 ). Thus, while urban riparian zones are vital for nitrogen pollution control, they can also be hotspots for N2 O emissions. The expansion of urban areas has led to increased construction of revetments—barriers built between riparian zones and rivers. These revetments, categorized as natural (NR), permeable (PR), or impervious (IR), significantly influence soil properties and the thermal, moisture, pH, and nutrient dynamics within riparian zones (Man et al., 2022 ). Such modifications affect soil characteristics, which in turn impact the abundance of nitrifying (AOA amoA  and AOB amoA ) and denitrifying genes (nirK , nirS , nosZI , and nosZII ) that are critical for nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions (Xu et al., 2016, 2017; Taylor et al., 2017; Portilho et al., 2018; Mukhtar et al., 2019; Tzanakakis et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2022 ). pH plays a pivotal role in determining the effectiveness of nitrification and denitrification processes. Different microorganisms have distinct pH preferences, influencing the soil's dissolved organic matter, nutrient availability, and microbial activity (Zhang et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2019; Kou et al., 2021; Bárta et al., 2010; Herold et al., 2018 ). Additionally, the availability of substrates for nitrification and denitrification varies among microbial communities, affecting their efficiency and the associated N2 O emissions (Fu et al., 2020; Verhamme et al., 2011; Hink et al., 2017; Felgate et al., 2012; Juhanson et al., 2017 ). Temperature, vegetation biomass, water content, and soil porosity also influence the activity and abundance of these microorganisms by altering soil oxygen levels and other environmental conditions (Taylor et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2018; Man et al., 2022 ). For instance, AOA amoA  has a higher oxygen affinity than AOB amoA , which affects their survival in varying oxygen conditions (Du et al., 2022 ). Similarly, denitrifying microorganisms differ in their oxygen requirements and their efficiency in reducing N2 O emissions (Graham et al., 2010 ; Sun et al., 2022 ; Cai et al., 2013 ; Wu et al., 2017 ; Hou et al., 2018 ). However, current urban revetments only consider the nitrogen removal capacity or N2 O emission rate of the riparian zone and do not address the synergistic mechanism of nitrogen removal and N2 O emission reduction. Moreover, the contribution and mechanism of nitrifying (AOA amoA  and AOB amoA ) and denitrifying (nirK , nirS , nosZI , and nosZII ) microorganisms to nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in urban riparian zones are unknown, and the mechanism by which revetments affect the characteristics and distribution of nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in riparian zones is also unknown. Therefore, the current construction practices of urban embankments do not fully consider the synergistic effects on ecological restoration and greenhouse gas emissions, which are detrimental to the sustainable development of urban areas. In this study, three revetments (NR, PR, and IR) were set up in a single river section, and physical and chemical properties of the soil, vegetation biomass, nitrification and denitrification genes abundance, nitrification potential (NP), denitrification potential (DP), and N2 O emission rate were measured at the river-riparian interface (RRI), which is affected by frequent fluctuations in the river water level, and in the riparian zone area outside the RRI (RZ). This study assumes that revetments change the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying genes by affecting soil properties and vegetation characteristics, thereby leading to differences in the nitrogen removal capacity and N2 O emission characteristics and their distribution in riparian zones. The purpose of this study is to (1) analyze the significance of differences in nitrification and denitrification potentials and N2 O emission rates between different types of revetments to clarify the impact of revetments on nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions; (2) identify the dominant contributors to nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in riparian zones and their contributions to different revetments; and (3) explore the mechanism underlying the impacts of revetments on nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in the RRI and RZ. The results provide a theoretical basis and direction for the construction of urban ecological revetments.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area and field sampling The experimental site of this study is located in Shanghai, eastern China (31° 2′ 4′′ N, 121° 26′ 16′′ E), which has a subtropical monsoon climate with a mild and humid climate. The annual average temperature is 17.6 ℃, and the annual average precipitation is approximately 1200 mm. We set up three types of revetments (NR, PR, and IR) in a single river section to ensure the consistency of the river characteristics (pH=7, nitrate-nitrogen level=2.523 mg/L, ammonium-nitrogen level=0.439 mg/L, and nitrite-nitrogen level=0.042 mg/L) and initial properties of the riparian soil in the experiment, thereby resolving the problem of controlling the variables in the field experiment. Our experimental site was constructed ten years ago because sufficient time is required to realize the impact of revetments on the evolution of soil properties in riparian zones. The experimental site has the same vegetation type (Kalimeris indica (L.) Sch. – Bip ) and is less affected by human activities, and aquatic plants are not found in the river. RRI is a riparian zone area significantly influenced by fluctuations in river water levels. When the water level rises and either floods the surface or exchanges materials through the revetment, the RRI plays a crucial role in nitrogen removal from the water. It is a key functional area for ecological restoration of the riparian zone. In contrast, RZ is less affected by changes in river water levels and primarily serves a buffering and regulating role in riparian zone ecological restoration. At the experimental site, the riparian zone affected by frequent fluctuations in river water level (RRI) is 1.2 m away from the revetment, and a very clear dividing line is observed. We believe that the RRI denitrification capacity and N2 O emissions, which are frequently affected by river water, may differ from those of the RZ. Therefore, we set up quadrats at distances of 1 m（RRI） and 3 m（RZ） from each revetment, with three replicate quadrats in each group and five sample points in each quadrat, and the soil of the five sample points was evenly mixed into one sample to ensure the accuracy of the data. Soil samples at depths of 0–20 cm, 20–40 cm, and 40–60 cm were taken due to the high groundwater level and significant soil evaporation in the study area (there is typically more water in the soil below 50 cm of the RRI). Soil samples were collected in July 2022 (After ten consecutive days with temperatures above 30°C and no rain, two replicate experiments were conducted on the 11th and 12th days), and care was taken to ensure that the soil structure was not destroyed during sampling. A portion of the soil samples was used to measure the physical properties of the soil, while the other was used to measure the chemical properties, nitrifying and denitrifying genes abundance, NP, and DP. Thus, the samples used for measuring nitrifying and denitrifying genes abundance, NP, and DP were placed in a dry refrigerator and sent to the laboratory for real-time measurement. In this study, gas samples were collected first, followed by in situ collection of vegetation samples, and finally in situ collection of soil samples.  2.2 Soil physical and chemical properties Soil moisture and temperature were monitored using a three-parameter soil meter (DELTA-T, UK). Undamaged soil samples were analyzed and dried using a ring knife to measure the bulk density. The soil in the ring knife was immersed in water, and the soil volume was calculated after discharging air, and then the sample was weighed after drying. The ratio of dry soil mass to soil volume is the specific gravity of the soil, which was used to measure the soil texture after sieving the samples (Andrade et al., 2022 ). Total porosity was calculated based on the bulk density and specific gravity (Eq. 1 ). The ratio of capillary water volume to total soil volume is used to calculate the capillary porosity, whereas the difference between the total porosity and capillary porosity was used to calculate the air-filled porosity. We brought the collected soil samples back to the laboratory, the oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) was measured using an ORP meter (ORP-2096, Boqu, China) (Man et al., 2024 ). After mixing the soil and water at a 1:5 ratio, the pH of the soil was measured using a pH meter. Soil total nitrogen was measured using a soil nutrient detector (LD-GT4; Lynd, China). Ammonium nitrogen (NH4 + -N) and nitrate nitrogen (NO3 - -N) were monitored using an automatic discontinuous chemical analyzer (Smartchem200, Alliance Company, France). The amount of heated potassium dichromate required to oxidize the organic carbon in the soil samples was used to calculate the soil organic matter (SOM).(1) Tp = 1 − BD / SG    × 100       2.3 Plant biomass measurements Three 20 cm × 20 cm quadrats were chosen to measure the herbal biomass. The aboveground herbal parts were removed, cleaned, and stored in sealed bags. Similarly, a 60 cm deep soil block was excavated with a 20 × 20 cm quadrat as the boundary. Underground roots were cleaned and stored in sealed bags. The weight of the herbaceous plants' aboveground biomass and underground biomass was determined by drying to a constant weight at 105 °C (Man et al., 2019 ).  2.4 Nitrifying and denitrifying microorganisms The total DNA of each sample was directly extracted using a PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (Omega, cat: M5635–02) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was extracted using 0.8 % agarose gel electrophoresis and maintained at −80 °C for later use. A Funglyn Biotech TIB-8600 real-time PCR system was used to quantify the DNA. AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  were measured using the primer pairs amoAF  (STAATGGTCTGGCTTAGACG)/amoAR (GCGGCCATCCATCTGTATGT) and bamoA1F  (GGGTTTCTACTGGTGGT)/bamoA2R  (CCCCTCKGSAAAGCCTTCTTC), respectively (Mao et al., 2011 ). nirS  and nirK  were measured using the primers cd3Af  (GTSAACGTSAAGGARACSGG)/R3cdR  (GASTTCGGGRTGSGTCTTGA) and nirK1aCuF  (ATCATGGTSCTGCCGCG)/ nirKR3CuR (GCCTCGATCAGRTTGGTT), respectively (Palmer et al., 2012 ). nosZI  and nosZII  were measured using the primers nosZ2F  (CGCRACGGCAASAAGGTSMSSGT)/nosZ2R  (CAKRTGCAKSGCRTGGCAGAA) and nosZII-F  (CTIGGICCIYTKCAYAC)/nosZII-R  (GCIGARCARAAITCBGTRC), respectively (Zhao et al., 2018 ). The volume of the reaction mixture was 20 μL, which contained 10 μL of 2 × SYBR real-time PCR pre-mixture (Vazyme, China), 1 μL of template DNA (8 ng), and 0.8 μL of AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  primer (5 mM). Nuclease-free water was added to a total volume of 20 μL. The qPCR cycle was as follows: amoAF/amoAR  and bamoA1F/bamoA2R  (95 °C for 5 min and 40 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 60 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 1 min), cd3Af/R3cdR  and nirK1aCuF/nirKR3CuR  (3 min at 95°C, 35 cycles consisting of 30 s at 95°C, 30 s at 59°C and 1 min at 72°C), nosZ2F/nosZ2R  and nosZII-F/nosZII-R  (5 min at 95°C, 40 cycles consisting of 10 s at 95°C, 30 s at 57.9°C and 50 s at 72°C). The threshold cycle (Ct) result of each PCR run was compared to that of a known standard DNA concentration.  2.5 Nitrification and denitrification potential NP and DP are important indicators of the nitrification and denitrification rate and capacity. NP was determined as previously described (Yan et al., 2019a,b ). Briefly, 10 g of fresh soil was placed in a 50 mL culture bottle with 20 mL of an incubation solution (0.2 mol L−1  KH2 PO4 , 0.2 mol L−1  K2 HPO4 , and 0.05 mol L−1  (NH4 )2 SO4  in a volume ratio of 3:7:30; pH 7.2). The bottles were sealed with parafilm and shaken for 24 h at 25 °C (200 rpm). An automatic discontinuous chemical analyzer (SmartChem 200, Alliance, France) was used to measure the nitrate concentration before and after incubations. DP was determined using the acetylene inhibition method (Liu et al., 2016 ). Briefly, in a 50 mL culture bottle, 10 g of fresh soil was mixed with 20 mL of incubation solution (final concentrations of 1.0 g L−1  chloramphenicol, 0.1 g L−1  potassium nitrate, and 0.18 g L−1  glucose). The bottles were sealed and purged with N2  gas to create anaerobic conditions before adding acetylene gas in the headspace to a final concentration of 10 % (v/v). Bottles were then incubated for 24 h at 25 °C in the dark. The before and after N2 O concentrations were monitored using a gas chromatograph (Agilent 6890 N, Agilent Technologies, Inc., USA) equipped with an electron capture detector.  2.6 N2 O emission rate With three replication chambers at each site, the in situ N2 O emission rates were determined using closed-chamber techniques (Zhao et al., 2018 ). The N2 O flux was measured using a static chamber consisting of an upper chamber (The dimensions are 60 cm in length, 60 cm in width, and 100 cm in height) and a base. A fan for air mixing was placed in the upper chamber, and a probe was installed to monitor the air pressure and temperature during measurements. To create a sealed environment, the base was inserted into the soil for about 5 cm. From 9:00–10:00, every 20 min, a 200 mL gas sample was collected from the indoor environment using a glass syringe and then injected into a 500 mL gas-collecting bag (BKMAM, Hunan, China). The gas samples were immediately brought to the laboratory, where they were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC-2010) within a day. The gas collection was conducted simultaneously with the soil and vegetation sampling, and it was repeated for two days in July 2022.  2.7 Statistical analysis The data used in the significance analysis of the soil properties in this study were the average values of the three layers of data for each sample point, while the data used in the correlation, RDA and structural equation models were all original values. Before the statistical analyses, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was applied to check for the normality of all data. Repeated analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to determine the effects of the revetment type and distribution on the NP, DP, N2 O emission rate, nitrifying and denitrifying microbial abundance, soil physical and chemical properties, and plant characteristics. Pearson’s correlation analysis was used to analyze the correlation between the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying microorganisms in the RRI and RZ and the NP, DP, N2 O emission rate, and soil physical and chemical properties. All processes were statistically analyzed using Origin 2021 software. An RDA of the NP, DP, and N2 O emission rates was performed using CANOCO 5.15. To analyze observable explicit variables and unobservable implicit variables, we used the structural equation modeling (SEM) in Amos Graphics to establish, estimate, and test the causal models.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Revetment affects the soil properties and vegetation characteristics of the riparian zone Our previous study demonstrated that revetment types influence soil and vegetation characteristics related to RRI, affected by differences in material and energy exchange between river water and soil (Man et al., 2022 ). This determines the growth environment of nitrifying and denitrifying microorganisms. Therefore, we initially verified the significance of soil properties and their spatial distribution differences between revetments. As shown in   Fig. 2 , the difference in soil moisture between the RRI and RZ was significant. The soil moisture of NR relative to PR and IR was 1.26 times and 1.10 times higher in RRI, and 1.14 times and 1.01 times higher in RZ, respectively. This indicates that revetment type affects water exchange between the river and riparian zone. River water can supplement IR soil moisture only when the river water level is higher than that of the soil moisture (Man et al., 2022 ), reducing the frequency of river water replenishing IR soil moisture. However, the evaporation rate remains the same, resulting in the lowest soil moisture with the IR type. The difference in soil moisture between RRI and RZ was significant, with humidity in RRI significantly higher than in RZ. The difference in the RRI soil temperature was not significant between revetments. The difference in soil temperature in the RZ was significant between the revetments. The IR soil temperature (33.04 ± 0.02 °C) was 1.11 times and 1.01 times higher than that of NR and PR in RZ. This is because RRI soil moisture changes frequently in summer (due to repeated evaporation-supplementation), leading to frequent changes in the continuity of heat flow in the soil matrix, which weakens the effect of revetment or water on soil temperature (Amaludin et al., 2016 ). As shown in Fig. 2 , the difference between the total porosity and capillary porosity of the RRI was significant between the revetments and followed the order NR > PR > IR. Frequent dry-wet alternations can lead to the decomposition of soil aggregates and affect soil porosity (Zhang et al., 2018 ). The soil water exchange frequency of NR was higher than that of PR and IR (Man et al., 2022 ), resulting in the largest total porosity and capillary porosity of NR and the smallest in IR in the RRI. This indicates that the revetment type changed the total porosity and capillary porosity of the RRI by affecting the water exchange frequency. However, the difference in air-filled porosity in the RRI was not significant between the revetments. The differences in the total porosity, capillary porosity, and air-filled porosity of the RZ were not significant between the revetments, which shows that the dry-wet alternation of the RZ is not frequent. This finding highlights the particularity of the RRI in the riparian zone and provides an important reason for the significant differences in total porosity, capillary porosity, and air-filled porosity between the RRI and RZ.  Fig. 3  shows the significance of soil chemical properties and spatial distribution differences in the revetments. Differences in SOM, C/N, NH4 + , and EC were significant between revetments. However, significant differences were not observed in SOM, C/N, NH4 + , and EC between RRI and RZ. This indicates that revetments will affect SOM, C/N, NH4 + , and EC in the riparian zone but will not lead to significant spatial differences. As shown in Fig. 3 , significant differences in total nitrogen and ORP were observed between revetments in the RRI. However, the difference in total nitrogen and ORP between revetments was not significant in the RZ, and the difference in total nitrogen and ORP between the RRI and RZ was not significant. The differences in NO3 -  and pH were not significant between the revetments. The difference in NO3 -  between the RRI and RZ was significant, while the difference in soil pH was not. The difference in AN between the RRI and RZ was significant.  Fig. 4  shows the significant differences in vegetation biomass and spatial distribution between revetments. The difference in aboveground biomass is significant between revetments. The aboveground biomass of PR is 2.49 times and 1.05 times that of NR and IR in the RRI, respectively, and 2.49 times and 1.09 times that of NR and IR in the RZ respectively. The difference in the aboveground biomass between the RRI and RZ groups is also significant. The difference in the underground biomass of the RRI vegetation is not significant between revetments, whereas the difference in underground biomass is significant between revetments in the RZ.  3.2 Revetment type affects the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying genes in the riparian zone by changing the soil properties and vegetation characteristics Revetments affect the soil properties and vegetation characteristics of the RRI and RZ, which further affects the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying genes.  Fig. 5  shows significant differences in gene abundance and spatial distribution among nitrifying and denitrifying genes between revetments. The difference in AOA amoA  in the RRI was not significant among revetments; however, it was significant among revetments in the RZ, with significance observed between the RRI and RZ. The difference in AOB amoA  was significant between revetments, and it was also significant between the RRI and RZ. The abundance of AOA amoA  in the RRI and RZ was much higher than that of AOB amoA . This indicates that AOA amoA  is more suitable for the urban riparian in summer compared to AOB amoA . This could be related to the high temperatures during summer and the anaerobic conditions in the urban riverbank environment. (Treusch et al., 2005; Leininger et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2008; Yarwood et al., 2013; Du et al., 2022 ). As shown in Fig. 5 , the differences in nirS , nirK , and nosZII  were significant between revetments in the RRI and RZ; however, the differences in nirK  and nosZII  between the RRI and RZ were not significant. The difference in nosZI  was significant between revetments in the RRI, the difference in nosZI  was not significant between revetments in the RZ, and the difference in nosZI  between the RRI and the RZ was significant. The abundance of nirS , nirK , and nosZII  in PR was significantly higher than that in NR and IR. The abundance of nirK  was much higher than that of nirS . This may be because nirS  organisms prefer constant anaerobic conditions while nirK  organisms are not sensitive to oxygen (Desnues et al., 2007; Knapp et al., 2009; Graham et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2021 ). Moreover, the abundance of nirS  in the RZ was significantly higher than that in the RRI, which indicated that the lower frequency of dry-wet alternations in the RZ would improve the stability of the soil anaerobic environment and be beneficial to the growth of nirS .   Tables 1 and 2  show the correlations between nitrifying and denitrifying microorganisms and environmental factors in the RRI and RZ, respectively. AOA amoA  was positively correlated with soil temperature in the RRI and RZ, whereas AOB amoA  was negatively correlated with soil temperature in the RRI and RZ. This difference in AMO flexibility between AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  (Dela Torre et al., 2008; Hatzenpichler et al., 2008; Martens-Habbena et al., 2015; Kozlowski et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2022 ). Previous studies have suggested that soil temperature and pH are the main factors affecting the niche specialization of AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  (Verhamme et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2019; Prosser and Nicol, 2012; Hu et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017; Ying et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019 ). However, this study showed that AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  were not correlated with pH in the RRI and RZ, indicating that temperature had a greater impact on niche specialization than pH. Studies have shown that the affinity of AOA amoA  to oxygen is much higher than that of AOB amoA  (Jung et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Stewart et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Du et al., 2022 ); thus, the rich anoxic environment in the riparian zone may also be the reason why the abundance of AOA amoA  was higher than that of AOB amoA  (Treusch et al., 2005; Leininger et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2008; Yarwood et al., 2013 ). The correlation between AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  and the total porosity, capillary porosity, and air-filled porosity values was not significant in the RZ; however, the correlation between AOB amoA  and the total porosity and capillary porosity values was significant in the RRI. This shows that revetments can affect the abundance of AOB amoA  by changing total porosity and capillary porosity in the RRI, resulting in AOB amoA  abundance following the order NR > PR > IR because total porosity and capillary porosity affect the permeability of soil (Mentges et al., 2016 ). AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  were significantly positively correlated with SOM in the RRI and RZ, and AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  were also positively correlated with total nitrogen and AN in the RRI and RZ. This indicates that the higher the soil carbon and nitrogen content, the faster the nutrient mineralization rate and release and the more nutrients provided for AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  (Wessén et al., 2010, 2011 ). Although studies have shown that AOA amoA  and AOB amoA  have different biochemical mechanisms for ammonia utilization (Martens-Habbena et al., 2015; Kozlowski et al., 2016 ), AOA amoA  is less dependent on NH4 +  than AOB amoA  (Martens-Habbena et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Verhamme et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020 ); however, this phenomenon only occurs in the RRI. The correlations among AOA amoA , AOB amoA , and NH4 +  were not significant in the RZ. AOA amoA  and NO3 -  were significantly positively correlated with RRI and RZ; however, the correlation between AOB amoA  and NO3 -  was not significant in the RRI or RZ. This indicates that AOA amoA  play an important role in NO3 -  production. AOB amoA  were significantly negatively correlated with aboveground biomass in the RRI and RZ, which was related to the fact that the increase in the aboveground biomass was not conducive to soil oxygen supplementation (Man et al., 2022 ). AOA amoA  was not correlated with aboveground biomass in the RRI, although it was significantly negatively correlated with aboveground biomass in the RZ. This may be related to the fact that the aboveground biomass is significantly smaller in the RZ relative to the RRI, which again verifies that the affinity of AOA amoA  to oxygen is much higher than that of AOB amoA  (Jung et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Stewart et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Du et al., 2022 ). As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , nirS  and nirK  are significantly negatively correlated with C/N in the RRI and RZ. This is because most denitrifying bacteria are heterotrophic, and the C and N contents are highly significant in determining the abundance of nirK  and nirS  (Mosier and Francis, 2010; Liang et al., 2021 ). The lower the C/N ratio, the faster the decomposition of organic matter and release of N, which is conducive to the survival of nirK  and nirS  (Wu et al., 2020 ). This also explains why nosZII  and C/N are significantly negatively correlated with the RRI and RZ while nosZI  and C/N are only significantly negatively correlated with the RRI. The abundance of nirK  is significantly and positively correlated with moisture in the RZ, which is consistent with the findings of Szukics et al. (2010) . The abundance of nirK  increases with increasing water content until the nitrate content reaches the soil limit. nirS , nirK , nosZI , and nosZII  are negatively correlated with SOM, total nitrogen, and AN in the RRI and RZ. There are two possible reasons for this finding. (1) The decomposition of riparian plant residues leads to the accumulation of organic matter after flooding (Lima et al., 2008 ). Organic matter and other nutrients are very abundant and thus are not the main environmental factors affecting denitrifying bacteria in the RRI and RZ. (2) The dry-wet alternation in the riparian zone leads to the decomposition of soil aggregates and the release of nutrients, such as organic matter, into the soil. NirS , nirK , nosZI , and nosZII  are not related to NO3 -  in the RRI because the NO3 -  content in the study area is very small, the anaerobic environment is rich, NO3 -  has been consumed, and a NO3 - -limited environment is observed; however, these characteristics do not affect NO3 -  as a potential hotspot for denitrifying bacteria (O'Brien et al., 2007; Groh et al., 2019 ). The RZ had less NO3 -  in areas where nirK  and nosZI  were significantly negatively correlated with NO3 - . This may have been influenced by the surface soil data because the nitrification process is preferable in the surface soil and produces NO3 -  while the denitrification process is more suitable for deep soils. Both nirS  and nosZII  were significantly positively correlated with aboveground biomass in the RRI and RZ because of the large amount of evaporation in summer, which leads to a change in the anaerobic environment of the riparian soil. An increase in aboveground biomass reduces soil water evaporation and is not conducive to the supplementation of oxygen (Man et al., 2022 ). nirS  organisms prefer a constant anaerobic environment (Desnues et al., 2007; Knapp et al., 2009; Graham et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2021 ), and nosZII -encoding N2 O reductase may also be very sensitive to O2  (Thomson et al., 2012 ).  3.3 Revetment affects the spatial distribution of nitrogen removal and N2 O emission characteristics in riparian zones by changing the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying genes The revetment type altered the abundance of nitrifying and denitrifying genes by influencing the soil properties and vegetation characteristics of the riparian zone. We believe that the abundance of these genes is the primary factor influencing nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in the riparian zone.  Fig. 6  illustrates the significance of NP, DP, and N2 O emissions, as well as the spatial distribution differences between revetments. While the difference in NP between revetments was not significant, it was significant between the RRI and RZ. There was a significant difference in DP between revetments. In the RRI, the DP of PR (34.32 ± 1.17 mg/(kg·d)) was significantly higher than that of NR (31.53 ± 0.61 mg/(kg·d)) and IR (28.03 ± 0.42 mg/(kg·d)). In the RZ, the DP of PR (31.52 ± 0.72 mg/(kg·d)) was also significantly higher than that of NR (23.17 ± 0.72 mg/(kg·d)) and IR (27.14 ± 0.44 mg/(kg·d)). There was also a significant difference in DP between the RRI and RZ sites. There was a significant difference in N2 O emissions between revetments. In the RRI, the N2 O emission rate of NR (0.49 ± 0.01 mg/(m2 h)) was 1.10 and 1.41 times higher than that of IR and PR, respectively. In the RZ, the N2 O emission rate of NR (0.56 ± 0.02 mg/(m2 h)) was 1.06 and 1.24 times that of IR and PR, respectively. There was also a significant difference in N2 O emissions between the RRI and RZ. As shown in Fig. 6 , the denitrification potential of RRI was 20.95 % (NR), 16.17 % (IR), and 8.88 % (PR) higher than that of RZ, while the N2 O emission rate decreased by 12.67 % (NR), 15.51 % (IR), and 23.05 % (PR) respectively. As shown in  Table 3 , AOA amoA  is strongly positively correlated with NP in the RRI and RZ while AOB amoA  is only weakly positively correlated with NP in the RRI.  Fig. 7 (a) and (c) also show that AOA amoA  is the main factor influencing NP in the RRI and RZ. However, AOB amoA  has been suggested as the main driver of nitrification in neutral or alkaline soils (Lu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2013 ). We believe that this is related to high soil temperatures in the summer (Dela Torre et al., 2008; Hatzenpichler et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2022 ) and the more abundant anoxic environment in the riparian zone (Jung et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Stewart et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Du et al., 2022 ). Our results also show that the effect of revetment on NP is not significant in the RRI and RZ (Fig. 6 ) because the effect of revetment on AOA amoA  abundance is not significant. The difference in NP between the RRI and RZ was significant because the difference in AOA amoA  abundance between these zones was significant. As shown in Table 3 , nirK , nosZI , and nosZII  are significantly positively correlated with DP in the RRI and RZ. However, the correlation between nirS  and DP was not significant in the RRI but was significant in the RZ. This again suggests that nirS  microorganisms prefer constant anaerobic conditions (Desnues et al., 2007; Knapp et al., 2009; Graham et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2021 ); thus, the less frequent dry-wet alternation of the RZ may be more conducive to the growth of nirS . Fig. 7 (a) and (c) show that nirK  represented the main factor influencing DP. Therefore, the abundances of nirK , nosZI , and nosZII  in PR are significantly higher than those in NR and IR in both the RRI and RZ, resulting in a significantly higher DP in PR than in NR and IR in both the RRI and RZ. The DP of the RRI is significantly higher than that of the RZ (Fig. 6 ), which may be caused by the combined action of denitrifying bacteria. As shown in Table 3 , AOB amoA  and N2 O emissions were significantly and positively correlated in the RRI and RZ, whereas the correlation between AOA amoA  and N2 O emissions was not significant in the RRI and RZ. This is consistent with previous research results (Hink et al., 2018; Tzanakakis et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2020 ), indicating that the contribution of AOB amoA  to N2 O emissions is greater than that of AOA amoA  and that the nitrification process is an important driver of N2 O production in humid environments (especially riparian zones) (Huang et al., 2014 ). nirS  and nirK  were significantly and negatively correlated with N2 O emissions in the RRI and RZ. Although the abundance of nirS  was much lower than that of nirK , nirS  was more likely to achieve complete denitrification than nirK  (Jones et al., 2008; Graf et al., 2014 ). nosZI  and nosZII  were significantly and negatively correlated with N2 O emissions in the RRI, although the correlation between nosZI  and N2 O emissions was not significant in the RZ. This indicates that the affinity of nosZII  denitrifying bacteria to N2 O is higher than that of nosZI  (Yoon et al., 2016; Suenaga et al., 2018, 2019; Zhao et al., 2019 ). Our study found that denitrification reduces N2 O emissions in the RRI and RZ, while nitrification and abiotic factors may contribute significantly to N2 O production in these zones. Two reasons account for this dynamic. (1) RRI and RZ have high groundwater levels and soil moisture can be replenished by river water, leading to a rich soil anaerobic environment (Man et al., 2022 ). N2 O reductase is highly sensitive to O2  in the soil (Thomson et al., 2012 ). When oxygen is limited, denitrifying bacteria use nitrogen oxides as alternative electron acceptors, which results in complete denitrification and low N2 O emissions (Cai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017 ). (2) The nitrate-nitrogen content in the study area was very low. When nitrate is limited, denitrifying bacteria can optimize the use of all denitrification intermediates, which is conducive to complete denitrification and low N2 O emissions (Felgate et al., 2012; Juhanson et al., 2017 ). Therefore, the abundances of nirS , nirK , and nosZII  in PR were significantly higher than those in NR and IR in the RRI and RZ, resulting in significantly lower N2 O emissions from PR than from NR and IR. Fig. 7 (b) and (d) further indicate that nosZII  is the most important factor affecting N2 O emissions, which is explained by the fact that although nosZII  is usually genetically capable of reducing N2 O, it cannot produce N2 O (Jones et al., 2014; Graf et al., 2014; Domeignoz-Horta et al., 2016 ).
