Therefore, the abundance of nosZII  in the RRI was significantly higher than that in the RZ (Fig. 6 ), which is an important reason why the N2 O emissions of the RRI were significantly lower than those of the RZ.  3.4 Mechanism underlying the influence of revetments on nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in riparian zones The structural equation model further explains the mechanisms underlying denitrification and N2 O emissions in the RRI and RZ, and all models have passed the Chi square divided by degrees of freedom (CMIN/DF), P-value, Normed Fit Index (NFI), Comparative Fit Index (CFI), and Incremental fit index (IFI) tests. As shown in  Fig. 8 (a) and  Table 4 , in the RRI, nirK has the largest direct effect and total benefit on nitrogen removal, whereas C/N has the largest indirect effect on nitrogen removal. Underground root biomass promotes AOA amoA  growth by providing nutrients and improving air permeability (Bardgett et al., 2014 ; Jin et al., 2014 ; Lange et al., 2015 ; Bengough et al., 2016 ; Oburger et al., 2016 ; Pierret et al., 2016 ; Popova et al., 2016 ), thereby enhancing nitrification. Moreover, it provides a substrate (NO3 - ) for denitrification. Under the influence of soil C/N, NO3 -  is utilized by nirK  to complete the denitrification process, although lower NO3 -  content limits the denitrification process. As shown in Fig. 8 (c) and Table 4 , in the RZ, nirK has the greatest direct and total benefits on denitrification while C/N had the greatest indirect effect. Under the influence of AN and C/N, nirK  and nirS  in the RZ completed the denitrification process; however, nirK  is still the dominant DP and nirS  may compete for substrates in the soil. Compared with the RRI, the effect of nitrification on denitrification is reduced in the RZ. This indicates that nitrification and denitrification may primarily be distributed at different soil depths (Du et al., 2022 ). Soil moisture is lower in the RZ, resulting in limited nutrient migration, especially NO3 -  migration from the surface soil (the main site of nitrification) to the middle soil layers. In addition, competition with nirS  for substrates increased in the RZ because the RZ has less frequent dry-wet alternations and a more stable anaerobic environment. However, the content of NO3 -  is very low in the RRI and RZ (Fig. 3 ), which may weaken the contribution of nitrification to denitrification. Therefore, in the RRI, the C/N ratio of PR is significantly lower than that of NR and IR (Fig. 3 ), which leads to faster organic matter decomposition and greater N release, resulting in a significantly higher nirK  abundance (Wu et al., 2020 ) and nitrogen removal capacity compared with that of NR and IR(Figs. 5 and 6 ). In the RZ, the lower C/N and higher nirK  abundance of PR may also be the main reasons for the significantly higher nitrogen removal capacity of PR than that of NR and IR (Fig. 6 ). As shown in Fig. 8 (b) and (d) and Table 4 , the N2 O emission mechanisms of the RRI and RZ are similar. Under the influence of NO3 -  and aboveground biomass, nirS  promotes the reduction of nitrite, while nosZI  and nosZII  promote the reduction of N2 O. Interestingly, we observed a significant correlation between nirS  and nosZII  expression levels. This may indicate that microorganisms encoding the nirS  gene are likely to also encode the nosZII  gene. However, the following differences were also observed: (1) under the condition of NO3 -  limitation, RZ has less NO3 -  content and slower migration, which may lead to the limitation of the abundance and activity of nosZI , nosZII , and nirS , which eventually leads to significantly higher N2 O emissions in the RZ compared with that in the RRI (Fig. 6 ). (2) In the RRI, nosZII  had the greatest direct effect on N2 O emissions, while NO3 -  had the greatest indirect effect and total benefit on N2 O emissions. In the RZ, aboveground biomass had the largest direct, indirect, and total benefits on N2 O emissions (Fig. 8  and Table 4 ). This shows that under nitrogen and oxygen limitation, higher soil moisture facilitates substrate migration in the nitrification process, thereby reducing N2 O emissions. However, the contribution of N2 O produced by abiotic factors has not been considered, potentially weakening the understanding of N2 O production mechanisms. Therefore, aboveground biomass, nosZII , and nirS  of PR were significantly higher than those in NR and IR at both the RRI and RZ (Figs. 4 and 5 ), which was the main reason why the N2 O emissions of PR were significantly lower than those from NR and IR. It is noted that a few limitations exist in this study. To ensure the natural evolution of the experimental site, we did not intervene in vegetation growth. The vegetation at the experimental site consisted of herbaceous plants, lacking consideration of shrubs and trees, and did not attempt combinations of herbaceous-shrub-tree vegetation. Therefore, future research is recommended to explore the impact of different vegetation patterns on nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in riparian zones. These findings provide guidance for the ecological construction of urban waterfront spaces and offer theoretical references for urban ecological restoration and greenhouse gas emission reduction.   4 Conclusions This study investigated the impact of different types of revetments on nitrogen removal and N2 O emissions in riparian zones (RRI and RZ) by replicating natural, permeable, and impervious revetments in a single river section after ten years of natural evolution. The conclusions are as follows:(1) The nirK  genes have the greatest effect on the denitrification potential in summer, although the nitrification process could provide a substrate for denitrification in the RRI.  (2) Oxygen and nitrogen limitation in the riparian zone have led to complete denitrification. The abundance of nosZII  is the main factor affecting N2 O emission reduction in the RRI and RZ, and higher aboveground biomass is beneficial for N2 O emission reduction.  (3) Compared with the RZ, the RRI has a higher denitrification capacity and lower N2 O emissions.  (4) The riparian environment of the PR can significantly increase the abundance of nirK  and nosZII , which are conducive to efficient denitrification and N2 O emission reduction.
1 Introduction With ongoing urbanization and urban sprawl, ever more greenspaces in cities are replaced by buildings, roads, and other impervious areas, which results in the reduction of stormwater infiltration and the increase in surface runoff, very likely to cause urban waterlogging (Liu et al., 2018; Savi et al., 2015 ). Meanwhile, this process also leads to less evapotranspiration and causes stream erosion and incrase of pollutant loads. In turn, significant decline of stream habitats and water quality were found (Ercolani et al., 2018 ). Effectively managing stormwater has become a challenge due to aging gray infrastructure coupled with intensive population density and development. Due to gray infrastructure is expensive to install, repair, or replace, a solution frequently proposed to deal with extra runoff in urban development is to install green infrastructure (GI) which can provide multiple benefits such as reduced heat island effects, improved aesthetics, and other ecosystem services (Hoover and Hopton, 2019; Hoover et al., 2020 ). Rooftops, which account for up to 40 %-50 % of urban impervious areas, are a main source of runoff generation, contributing to urban water quality degradation and nuisance waterlogging or flooding (Berretta et al., 2014; Stovin et al., 2015 ). Moreover, rainwater can wash off and transport various nutrients and toxic metals from conventional roofs to receiving water (Gregoire and Clausen, 2011; Xu et al., 2020 ). Green roofs are a type green infrastructure and can correct or mitigate the disadvantages of conventional roofs by managing runoff and providing environmental, economic, and social benefits to cities simultaneously (Fu et al., 2021; Jung et al., 2016 ). For example, green roofs reduce the energy consumption of heating and cooling buildings, prolong the service life of the roof’s waterproof layer, and reduce damage to the roof from exposure to sunlight, especially ultraviolet radiation (Feitosa and Wilkinson, 2016 ). Green roofs also absorb pollutants and particulates from the air, provide habitat for wildlife, and help in biodiversity conservation (Voyde et al., 2010 ). Another advantage of using green roofs over traditional terrestrial or ground-based forms of GI is saving valuable spaces, especially in dense urban area (Fassman-Beck et al., 2013 ). Green roofs are generally divided into three types: intensive green roofs (IGRs), semi-intensive green roofs (SIGRs), and extensive green roofs (EGRs), according to the (International Green Roof Association 2008 ). Typically, a green roof consists of three major components: a vegetation layer, a lightweight substrate layer for plant growth, and a drainage layer (Carson et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2016 ). Most current green roofs adopt the lower-drainage method (i.e., no storage) to discharge rainwater from the outlet at the bottom of the drainage layer during the rainfall event (De-Ville et al., 2018; Seidl et al., 2013 ). The thickness of substrate layer of green roofs will decide which plant species can be supported. For example, IGRs have a thicker substrate layer (more than 150 mm) than semi-intensive and extensive ones and thus can be planted with a greater variety of plant species. IGR provides many ecological benefits and is very efficient at intercepting rainwater, but the heavy substrate layer requires additional structural support for the building and installation costs (Bus and Szelągowska, 2021 ). The higher installation and maintenance costs restrict the application of IGRs. By comparison, with the shallow substrate layer (less than 150 mm), EGRs are more economically efficient and tend to support plants with a lower need for irrigation, resulting in its widely acceptable all over the world (Deska et al., 2020; Fernandez-Cañero et al., 2013 ). Recent literature about the EGRs has focused on monitoring and simulating the effects of different structural and external factors of green roofs on runoff retention and water quality improvement. For example, it is commonly accepted that rainfall characteristics, season and climate, antecedent moisture of substrate, and structural factors of the green roof itself (e.g., substrate depth, substrate material, slope, vegetation type, etc.) are significantly related to runoff control performance (Dusza et al., 2017; Soulis et al., 2017; Pettersson et al., 2020 ). Rainfall intensity, materials, depth, and antecedent moisture of substrate layer of EGRs were critical to runoff retention capacity of green roofs (Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020 ), whereas the vegetation types are negligible in most situations. Although green roofs will initially capture and retain contaminants in stormwater, inevitably it will increase pollution because the substrate layer will accumulate nutrients and contaminants, or addition of nutrients added to the green roofs required for plant growth (Wang et al., 2017 ). For example, total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) levels in runoff from green roofs can be significantly higher (Beck et al., 2011 ). Water quality of runoff from green roofs is affected by a variety of factors, such as rainfall characteristics, season, temperature, and substrate materials (Buffam et al., 2016 ). Soil amendments with new materials, such as biochar and seaweed biomass, can help to reduce runoff pollutions and result in lower concentrations of TN, TP, organic carbon, and metal ions (e.g., aluminum, iron, and chromium) in runoff (Beck et al., 2011; Vijayaraghavan and Raja, 2015 ). In general, researchers are committed to enhancing the ability of green roofs to intercept and remove contaminants from rainwater and reduce pollution from runoff. Lower-drainage EGRs without rainwater storage is not suitable for installation in areas where the timing or frequency of storms is highly variable and irregular, either between or within seasons, because plants have specific habitat requirements for survival. Since the substrate layer of EGRs is thin, their runoff control effectiveness is greatly reduced in summer with the occurrence of heavy storms. For example, the average rainwater retention rate of EGRs is in the range of 40–60 %, and only about 30 % with heavy rain intensities (DeNardo et al., 2005; Dusza et al., 2017 ). On the campus of the University of Bologna. Italy, only rainfall depth less than 7.8 mm could achieve 100 % rainwater retention rate by the EGRs (Cipolla et al., 2016 ). But considering the structural load-bearing limits of buildings, it is not recommended to improve EGRs runoff control performance by increasing the depth of the substrate layer. To improve rainwater interception and retention, we newly designed the structure of the EGRs by adding or extending a rainwater storage layer (or storage space) and adjusting the vertical position of the drainage outlet to the top of the substrate layer, called the upper-drainage method. With the upper-drainage method, the infiltrated rainwater from the substrate layer no longer drains directly out of the EGR, but is stored in this storage layer. The upper-drainage method drains excess rainwater from the top of the substrate layer after the water storage space and the substrate layer are filled or saturated. In this study, we tested and evaluated the runoff control performance (runoff quantity reduction and water quality improvement) of EGRs with the upper-drainage, using an artificial rainfall simulator. We also explored the effects of slope, plant growth status, and model size of EGRs on runoff regulation. This study will provide detailed structural and characteristic parameters relevant to local climatic conditions to guide low-cost and high-adaptive design and construction of EGRs and planning strategies for urban vertical-greening practices. It also provides references for EGRs hydrological modeling (e.g., USEPA SWMM) and the experimental design of EGRs tested using a rainfall simulator.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 EGR model design and construction We designed and constructed four physical and portable models representing three types of green roofs and one conventional roof (CR) as comparison group. CR1 is a conventional roof model with a surface paved by concrete (5 cm thickness); LER2 is an EGR model utilizing a lower-drainage design (LEGR); and UER3 and UER4 are EGR models with upper-drainage designs (UEGR; Table 1 ;  Fig. 1  ; and Fig. 2  a). These models were made from 2 mm thick steel plates welded together to avoid deformation and leakage of water during the experiments. A hydraulic jack was installed under the model to adjust the slope according to the experimental design. Each model included a 30 mm thick textured polyethylene plastic drainage board to serve as the storage/drainage layer ( Fig. 2 b ), which supported to the planting substrate layer while leaving space to ensure storage of rainwater. A 2 mm thick permeable geotextile was used to separate the substrate layer and the storage/drainage layer and prevent the movement of small particles from the substrate layer into the storage/drainage layer. The LER2′s drainage outlet was positioned at the bottom of the storage/drainage layer and the UER3′s drainage outlet was installed flushing with the top surface of substrate layer, extending outward in a trapezoid shape with a splashing prevention device ( Fig. 2 a ). LER2 had the same structural design with UER3, except for the location of the drainage outlet. Based on the China National Standard Technical Specification of Planting Roof Engineering (JGJ 155–2013), widely used improved nutrient soil was selected as the substrate layer in all EGR models. This soil was a mixture of decomposing leaf matter, peat soil, vermiculite, and sand in a specific ratio (decomposing leaf matter: peat soil: vermiculite: sand = 2:2:1:1) designed to meet the growth needs of plants and the requirement of lightweight. Thickness of substrate layers usually is 50–150 mm (Soulis et al., 2017 ). Due to roof loading limits, it is not possible to build green roofs with ultra-thick substrates (Feitosa & Wilkinson, 2016 ). To represent a wider range of possible application of EGRs and to be suitable for different types of roofs, we set the thickness of substrate layer to 50 mm. When the models were completed and filled, they were placed outside for at least 7 days to receive natural rainfall and become compacted. The purpose was to compact the soil to the level/height of the upper-drainage outlet and guarantee approximate the same filling density across the model. EGRs require at least a 2 % slope to meet drainage needs, and most of green roofs are constructed within 10 % of slope (Getter et al., 2007 ). When the slope is more than 20 %, it requires implementation of anti-slip and stabilization devices on the top of the roof. Therefore, we selected three levels of slope, 2 %, 5 %, and 10 %, adjusted by the hydraulic devices in the experiments. We selected a typical sedum species, Sedum lineare , for the vegetation layer. It is local, highly adaptable, and soil-independent, and can grow in shallow soil conditions, widely used in green roofs installations (Vasl et al., 2017 ). Each model was planted at the same density (180 plugs/m2 ) and weeds were removed regularly. Experiments began when the plant reached 13–15 cm in height and vegetative cover was close to 100 %.  2.2 Experiment design The performance of EGRs in controlling runoff has been researched by monitoring green roofs under natural rainfall events or testing green roof models with artificial rainfall simulators (Fassman-Beck et al., 2013; Voyde et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2021 ). Although previous field-based (i.e., portable rainfall simulator) research may reflect better the real-world hydrologic performance of green roofs, they require a large site, expensive installation, and are influenced by the local climate and weather conditions (i.e., droughts, excessive precipitation, etc.). In addition, obtained data are often unevenly distributed in terms of seasons and rainfall intensities. This study used an artificial rainfall simulator that provided controlled experimental conditions, including rainfall intensities. The rainfall simulator is located in the Artificial Rainfall Simulator Hall of the Institute of Soil and Water Conservation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Yangling Demonstration Area, Shaanxi Province, China. The site is dedicated to rainfall simulation experiments, and it has a special console that can control the intensity and duration of rainfall. Experiments were conducted in the vertical spray area of the space ( Fig. 2 c).  The rainfall simulator can generate raindrops from a height of 16 m to mimic the natural raindrops’ terminal velocity reaching the ground in a natural process (Živanović et al., 2022 ). Rain intensities can be regulated in the range of 30–150 mm/h, with a rainfall uniformity of more than 80 %. To reduce the influence of factors such as season and temperature, all experiments were conducted during the summer months (June to September). We choose four rainfall intensities including 30 mm/h, 40 mm/h, 50 mm/h, and 60 mm/h, and a duration of two hours per event with constant precipitation pattern, which result in total rainfall 60 mm, 80 mm, 100 mm, and 120 mm, respectively. A rainfall event more than 50 mm/h is considered as heavy storm based on the definition from the National Standard of China Meteorological Administration (GB/T 28592–2012). We grouped all experiments into one of four groups (Table 2  ), and the four rainfall intensities were applied to each group. Each experiment was repeated three times, and there were total 48 rainfall events (Table 2 ). Due to operational limitations, CR1 and UER4 were tested separately, whereas LER2 and UER3 were tested at the same time. A two-day drying period was applied after each rainfall event to ensure the green roof substrate returns to its original water retention capacity (Liu et al., 2019 ). Experimental data of models LER2 and UER3 were compared to verify if the upper-drainage method affected the runoff control capacity of EGRs during heavy rainfall intensity. Group1 served as the control group and compared to the three treatment groups (Group2, Group3, and Group4) to explore the effects of slope and plant growth. In addition, comparing the experimental results of UER3 and UER4 with CR1 can reveal insights into the effect of model size.  2.3 Experiment process and analysis Before each experiment, a funnel-type rain barrel was used to measure and calibrate the rainfall intensity within the allowable range of error (±1mm/h). Models were positioned in the simulator hall and covered with a rain shelter during the calibration process. Experiments were timed by a stopwatch with accuracy of ± 1 s, beginning at the removal of the rain shelter. Runoff from models was collected every 60 s and weighed with an electronic balance that had an accuracy of ± 0.1 g (Meilen MTS600, China). Runoff samples for water quality testing were collected in 50 ml centrifuge tubes at three time points: 1) the model starting generating runoff, 2) the model reaching a stable rate of runoff, and 3) the end of rainfall simulation. Water samples were capped and tested on the same day of collection analyzed for TN, TP, and suspended solids (SS) concentrations. These nutrients can exacerbate eutrophication has become a global environmental pollution problem (Chiang et al., 2021; Jarvie et al., 2018 ), and high SS will make the water turbid decreasing oxygen transmission in the water and affect the survival of aquatic organisms (Badruzzaman et al., 2012 ). TN and TP were measured using the water quality tester (GL-200, Green Carey, China) with the accuracy of ± 5 %, which measures TN and TP following the alkaline potassium persulfate digestion method, and the potassium persulphate oxidation and the molybdenum antimony anti-spectrophotometric method, respectively (Jiang et al., 2019 ). The SS measurement was performed by vacuum filtration and microporous filter membrane (0.45um). Runoff starting time, runoff volume, and peak flow rate were collected or measured during the experiments. Runoff delay time refers to the different time from the rainfall starting time to the runoff starting time. We installed a foam panel extending outward and along the side edges of the drainage outlet to avoid splashing rainwater into the runoff outlet for improving accuracy of the runoff delay time measurement. Runoff retention rate was calculated to evaluate the performance of runoff quantity control (Zhang et al., 2015 ). The runoff retention rate was calculated following Eqs. (1) and (2) (1) V = R r  - R v     / R r  ∗ 1 00 %     (2) R r  = R ∗ A     where V is the runoff retention rate (%); Rr  is the rainfall volume received by the model (L); R is the depth of rainfall received by the models (mm); A is the area of the model; and Rv  is the runoff volume drained from the model (L). The statistical significance of measured differences in the runoff control performance for drainage method, rainfall intensity, slope, vegetation growth status, and model size were evaluated using Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA). The least significant difference (LSD) test was applied to further analyze the significance of the factors within their groups. All statistical analyses were performed using the SPSS (v25.0, IBM Inc., Armonk, NY).   3 Results 3.1 Runoff flow rate control of EGRs Runoff flow rates were different for each model under four rainfall intensities, but trends were similar. Hydrographs for the rainfall-runoff process of LER2, UER3, and CR1 under the highest rainfall intensity (60 mm/h) showed that the runoff rate continued to increase until it reached a relatively stable value (Fig. 3  ). CR1 generated runoff immediately after the start of rainfall, whereas runoff generation was delayed for both LER2 and UER3. Meanwhile, the LER2 and UER3 had lower peak flow rates (LER2 = 0.92 L/min; UER3 = 0.95 L/min) than the conventional roof during the two hours rainfall duration (CR1 = 0.99 L/min).  3.2 Effects of different factors on the runoff retention rate and delay time 3.2.1 The MANOVA analysis for different factors Statistical results of the MANOVA for runoff retention rate and runoff delay time are shown in Table 3  . The effects of drainage method, rainfall intensity, and slope on the runoff retention rate and runoff delay time were highly significant. Furthermore, the vegetation growth status and model size (two model sizes tested) did not have a statistically significant influence on the runoff retention rate and runoff delay time based on the designed rainfall events in the experiments.  3.2.2 Effects of rainfall intensity on runoff retention rate and delay time for LER2 and UER3 The average runoff retention rate of UER3 (61.82 %) was much larger than that of LER2 (23.94 %), and the variation among tests was greater in different rainfall intensities ( Fig. 4  ) . Both UER3 and LER2 runoff retention rate decreased with an increase in rainfall intensities and reached the largest values at the 30 mm/h; the mean values were 81.67 % and 31.9 %, respectively ( Fig. 5  ) . The runoff delay time of UER3 was larger than LER2 under the same rainfall intensity. Under the 30 mm/h intensity, mean runoff delay time of LER2 and UER3 were 28.75 min and 94.17 min. The mean runoff delay time shortened to 11.30 min and 44.33 min, respectively for LER2 and UER3 respectively at 60 mm/h rainfall intensity ( Fig. 5 ) .  3.2.3 Effects of slope on runoff retention rate and delay time for LER2 and UER3 The change of slope affected the runoff control performance for both LER2 and UER3 models. Increasing the model slope from 2 % to 5 % significantly weakened the runoff control performance for UER3. For example, the runoff retention rate decreased from 74.31 % to 54.48 % for UER3 with a change in slope from 2% to 5%, and further decreased to 40.14 % at the 10 % slope; and the runoff delay time decreased from 83.33 to 65.50 min for the UER3 with a change in slope from 2% to 5%, and further decreased to 40.17 min at the 10 % slope ( Fig. 6  ) . The runoff retention rate and runoff delay time for LER2 did not change significantly with increased slope ( Table 4  ) .   3.3 Effects of different factors of EGRs on runoff water qualities The results from the MANOVA for the runoff water qualities are shown in Table 5  . The effects of drainage method, rainfall intensity, and slope on the TN, TP, and SS concentrations in runoff were significant. The analysis results showed the vegetation growth status did not have a statistically significant influence on the TN, TP, and SS concentrations in runoff (p > 0.05). While the influence of the model size on the TN concentration was not significant, TP and SS concentrations in runoff were highly significant (p < 0.001; Table 5 ). 3.3.1 Effects of rainfall intensity on the runoff water quality for LER2 and UER3 Concentrations of TN and TP in runoff of LER2 increased with increasing rainfall intensities and reached maximum at the 60 mm/h, and SS reached maximum at 30 mm/h. However, the TP and TN contents in runoff of UER3 did not change proportionately with increasing rain intensity, and SS concentration was not significantly different under the four rainfall intensities (Table 6  ). Mean values of three pollutants in runoff from LER2 and UER3 models were compared. Their differences reflect the effects of the two drainage methods on runoff water qualities. Concentrations of TN, TP, and SS from rainfall water, CR1, LER2, and UER3 were monitored during the experiment and summarized in the Table 7  . There was no significant difference in TN and TP between the rainfall water and CR1 (LSD test, pTN =0.853 and pTP =0.810), but TN and TP from LER2 were significantly higher than the rainfall water (LSD test, pTN  < 0.001 and pTP <0.001). TN and TP of UER3 were slightly higher than that of rainfall water but the difference was not significant (LSD test, pTN =0.114 and pTP =0.265). The concentration of SS for CR1, UER3, LER2, and rainfall water, in descending order, were significantly different from each other.  3.3.2 Temporal variations of runoff water qualities for LER2 and UER3 Samples I, II, and III in the Table 8   represent water collected at three different time points in each experiment, such as, starting runoff generation, reaching stable runoff, and ending the rainfall. The water quality samples at three different time points for the LER2 and UER3 were not significantly different from each other. That means the runoff collection time for pollutants testing during the experiment was not timing sensitive.  3.3.3 Effect of slope on runoff water qualities for LER2 and UER3 Slopes had a significant effect on the runoff water qualities. The TN in LER2 and UER3 runoff decreased significantly when the model slope increased from 2 % to 5 %. When the slope of the model was increased to 10 %, the concentration of TN did not change significantly for either models compared to the slope of 5 %. However, the concentration of TP in runoff of LER2 and UER3 did not change significantly with the change of slope, but SS was significantly different for LER2. The variations of TN concentration was greatest when the slope of LER2 and UER3 is 2 %. The concentration of SS was the lowest value when the slope was 2 % for UER3 (Table 9 ) .    4 Discussion 4.1 The overall runoff control performance for EGRs In general, EGR models used in this study were more capable of intercepting rainwater from storms than conventional roofs, as demonstrated by increasing runoff retention rate and delaying runoff generation time. Compared with other studies which examined EGRs exposed to light rainfall intensities, the runoff control performance of LEGRs had poorer performance in this study. For example, the retention rate of LER2 ranged from 15.48 % to 36.31 % with a mean value of 23.94 % in this study, compared to other studies which had values around 50 % under low rainfall intensities (Cipolla et al., 2016; Carter and Rasmussen, 2006 ). For water quality, this study focused on the pollutants captured, introduced, or released by green roofs, and the type of pollutants mainly depended on the substrate material. The concentration of measured pollutants in runoff from the conventional roof was lower than values reported in other studies, because the conventional roof in our experiments was in a laboratory condition that did not include pollutants accumulation processes like a real outdoor conventional roof (Heusinger and Weber, 2015; Liu et al., 2016 ). Concentrations of TN and TP in the runoff of EGRs increased significantly compared to the conventional roof. This suggests the rainfall infiltrates through substrate layer and brings nutrients, such as TN and TP, while vegetation, geotextiles, and rainwater storage space will partially retain SS. Different rainfall intensities also affected the interception of rainwater by EGRs. The runoff retention rate and delay time decreased with the increase of rainfall intensities for storms of the same duration. Higher rainfall intensities will cause more rainwater entering into the EGR model, which lead to more rapid saturation of the substrate soil (Lee et al., 2013 ), and hinder infiltration of rainwater. Concentrations of TP and TN in runoff increased with increase in rainfall intensities, but the concentration of SS in runoff only had a slight increase. Green roofs with lower-drainage method can discharge large amounts of runoff with higher concentrations of TN and TP.  4.2 Advantages and disadvantages of the upper-drainage method for EGRs Compared to LEGRs, UEGRs did not have a significant functional improvement in controlling the peak flow rate of runoff, and the runoff peak flow rate for both were reached about 15–20 min after the start of runoff generation. However, the UEGRs could significantly increase the retention rate and better delay the time of runoff generation, because of benefits from the rainwater storage. The UEGRs would help delay the concentration time of the watershed or sewershed, and improve the ratio or duration of overloaded pipe networks in a city. In addition, the reduction of TN and TP concentrations in runoff for UEGRs could approximate the level of conventional roofs. Although the SS content in the runoff from UEGRs was higher than conventional roofs, this could be addressed by installing filtration devices (e.g., geotextiles, filters, etc.) at the outlet (Zhang et al., 2015 ). Strangely, there was also no significant change in runoff pollutants at different time points in one rainfall event, and this was inconsistent with some research that showed runoff pollutant concentration decreased with when rainfall duration was prolonged (Beck et al., 2011; Seidl et al., 2013 ). Overall, the upper-drainage method could effectively reduce the level of runoff containing pollutants discharged from the EGR itself during heavy rainfall events and delaying the runoff generation. It performed better in the runoff control performance than lower-drainage method.  4.3 Factors affecting runoff control performance of EGRs The size of the model did not have a significant effect on the rainfall control performance of EGRs in a relative flat slope condition. This is consistent with findings from other studies that showed area size had little effect on retention rate and runoff water quality control from green roofs (Gong et al., 2020; Hakimdavar et al., 2014 ). This also indicates using downscaled EGR models and an artificial rainfall simulator is effective to research the runoff control performance for EGRs. The runoff control performance of EGRs decreased with increasing slopes during low rainfall intensities (Getter et al., 2007 ). In this study, we found the effect of slope on LEGRs’ runoff retention rate was not significant at high rainfall intensities, whereas with the increase of slope, runoff retention rate and delay time of UEGRs decreased. This is because the water storage space of UEGR decreases with increasing slope. Although the area receiving rainfall will decrease when the slope increases (the area decreases by 0.12 % and 0.50 % when the slope increases from 2% to 5 % and 10 %, respectively), the change is minimal and could be ignored. Meanwhile, when the slope of UEGRs was increased from 2 % to 5 %, the TN in runoff decreased significantly, but there was no significant change from 5 % to 10 %. It is speculated because the increase in slope will increase soil erosion and reached a maximum level of release at the 2–5 % slope, but differences may have been missed due to small relatively sample size used in the statistical analysis. The increase of slope did not have a significant effect on runoff TP concentration in UEGRs, but the SS concentration increased significantly, perhaps because the upper-drainage method increased the washing off the surface soil as the slope increased. The pruning of vegetation changed the surface cover but did not significantly affect runoff control performance of EGRs, except for a slight decrease in peak flow rate for both drainage methods. This result is similar to other studies that found different vegetation types had little effect on the interception of rainwater in green roofs (Teemusk and Mander, 2011 ). But vegetation pruning can reduce biomass and evapotranspiration that results in the changes of antecedent soil moisture content (Nagase and Dunnett, 2010 ).  4.4 Limitations This paper explores the effect of vertical drainage locations on the runoff control performance of EGRs, which will provide much-needed guidance for the construction of EGRs, but still deserves further research in the following areas. UEGRs store more water than LEGRs, and as the amount of water stored increases, the increase in weight on the roof is an unavoidable problem. In other words, it puts higher demands on the load-bearing capacity of the roof. Although other improvements to EGR (e.g., increasing the thickness of the substrate layer or changing the material in substrate layer) may also place higher demands on the roof's load-bearing capacity, we are unable to measure at this time which of these improvements would result in a greater runoff control performance of EGRs. In addition, the vegetation growth status in this study was shown not significantly affecting the runoff control performance of green roofs, but due to the limitations of the experimental conditions, we were not able to test the effect of the vegetation growth status on the antecedent soil moisture content, which has been shown to affect the runoff control performance (Liu et al., 2020 ). Moreover, we did not test the hydraulic properties of the selected substrate, and therefore could not fully compare the differences for the substrates with other studies.   5 Conclusion EGRs are a widely-used low impact development technology to help manage extra runoff. Choosing different designs of EGRs, including changing vertical drainage positions, would be a tradeoff between runoff control performance and structural load-bearing of buildings. The runoff control performance of LEGRs can be greatly decreased during heavy storm events. Therefore, this study proposes to design and examine whether using the upper-drainage method for EGRs can provide a better rate of runoff retention and alleviate water pollution especially during the high rainfall intensities that occur during summer months. In total we conducted 48 rainfall experiments on conventional roof model and EGR models to compare the runoff control performance of two drainage methods by utilizing an artificial rainfall simulator. We also investigated the effect of rainfall intensities, slopes, vegetation growth status, and model size of EGRs on runoff control performance.(1) The upper-drainage method performed better than the lower-drainage method on runoff control performance. The application of upper-drainage EGRs not only increased the retention rate and delayed runoff generation, but also significantly reduced runoff water pollutants from EGR itself. In addition, we suggest existing EGRs can be retrofitted by equipping both upper and lower drainage outlets without changing the original EGR’s structure in practice, which can be switched in different seasons or weather, to adapt to periods of excessive dry or wet and save construction costs.  (2) The runoff retention rate of UEGRs gradually decreased as the slope becoming steeper. Thus, we recommend the slope of EGRs in practice should be kept as minimal as possible but match the minimum drainage slope requirement.  (3) The growth status of vegetation had no significant effect on the runoff control performance of EGRs. But dense growth of vegetation will provide more ecological benefits, such as, cooling effects, aesthetics, wildlife habitats, etc. UEGRs can help plants to survive during the dry season and ensure plants to provide ecological services across seasons and reduce maintenance cost of EGRs. Moreover, understanding the effect of vegetation structure and how it alters runoff process in shadow flow would be very interesting in future research.  (4) The size of the green roof models in a relative flat slope condition does not significantly influence the performance of runoff control measured as runoff retention rate or runoff delay time. That means decentralized, scattered, or small green roofs will contribute to runoff control in a watershed or sewershed. Moreover, EGRs are suitable for promotion for public participation or individual property installations. Whether this conclusion applies to other designs of green roofs deserves further study.    UEGRs provide more space for water storage on the roof but place more load on the roof’s structure, which is an unavoidable problem with application of the upper-drainage method. But the adjustment of structural factors such as increasing the thickness of the substrate layer and changing the material in substrate layer in LEGRs also will increase the load placed on the roof. In order to improve runoff control performance, the potential design for both drainage methods would increase weight, and finding solutions to reduce or adapt to the additional weight to improve of runoff control performance for EGRs is worth further investigation. In addition, rainwater accumulated in rainwater storage space and the SS accumulation can affect the growth of vegetation and runoff control performance of EGRs. How to choose the right discharge time and routine maintenance to align with irrigation demand, season, excessively dry or wet days are also deserved further research.  6 Disclaimer The research presented was not performed or funded by U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and was not subject to EPA’s quality system requirements. 1 Introduction Land subsidence refers to the settling of the Earth’s surface in response to various natural and human-induced factors and may occur over relatively small areas or cover large regions at various rates, from slow to rapid. One of the primary anthropogenic causes of land subsidence is the extraction of fluids from the subsurface. These activities are carried out commonly for purposes of fossil fuel and groundwater development. While groundwater resources can be found at any depth, their quality is suitable for domestic, agricultural, or industrial use normally when they are taken from shallower sedimentary formations, whose depth typically range from a few meters to a few hundred meters in depth. Excessive pumping of groundwater from aquifers is arguably the main cause of land subsidence worldwide (Gambolati et al., 1991; Holzer and Galloway, 2005; Erkens et al., 2015; Guzy and Malinowska, 2020 ). Land subsidence is the effect of a consolidation process that is triggered by groundwater abstraction, which causes a reduction in fluid pressure followed by an overall aquifer compaction, under the isostatic load exerted by burying materials. Such a deformation is then gradually transferred to the surface, where settlement is observed. This effect may pose significant environmental and infrastructural risks, which highlights the need for modelling and monitoring programs that can be used to assist sustainable water management practices that mitigate the risks. These may be particularly significant in coastal regions where the ground elevation is of the order of a few tens of centimetres above the mean sea level (Abidin et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2020 ) as it has the potential to significantly increase the vulnerability to sea level rise and coastal flooding (Kulp and Strauss, 2019 ). Mathematical models play a crucial role in forecasting land displacement caused by groundwater withdrawal. These models can be categorised into two types: numerical and analytical. The latter relies on solving the classical equations of poro-elasticity (Biot, 1941, 1955; Verruijt, 1969 ) through discretisation techniques like finite elements, finite differences, finite volumes, or their combinations. These models possess considerable power and flexibility, enabling simulation of intricate hydrogeological scenarios under various conditions of heterogeneity, elasticity, elasto-plasticity, and viscosity constitutive laws. As a result, they have led to unparallelled levels of sophistication and accuracy in simulations. For in-depth examinations of numerical models, one may refer to the works of Galloway and Burbey (2011), Gambolati and Teatini (2015) , and Guzy and Malinowska (2020) . Analytical models constitute the earliest group of mathematical tools for land subsidence assessment, and remain to these days an attractive solution for their ease of application, computational efficiency and low data requirement. One of the earliest and most renowned models for land subsidence was developed by Geertsma (1966, 1973)  to predict surface displacement caused by a disk-shaped reservoir embedded in a homogeneous, linearly-elastic, semi-infinite domain and subjected to a constant change in pore pressure. Geerstma used the “Nucleus of Strain” (NoS) equations (Mindlin, 1936; Mindlin and Chen, 1950 ), integrating them over the reservoir volume. These equations quantify both horizontal and vertical displacements resulting from a unit change in pore pressure within a unit volume at a specified depth underground. Following Geertsma ’s work, van Opstal (1974)  and, more recently, Tempone et al. (2010)  proposed analytical models to estimate the surface vertical displacement assuming the reservoir is positioned above a rigid basement. We should note that the NoS integration method can be extended to reservoirs with various shapes that experience a spatially distributed change in pore pressure, which typically requires numerical computation. However, under specific conditions, an analytical solution is feasible. For instance, Jayeoba et al. (2019)  introduced an analytical solution for the surface vertical settlement above a well that pumps at a constant rate from a cylindrical reservoir. In this case, due to the radial symmetry of the pore pressure change, the integration was carried out by utilising Geertsma ’s vertical surface displacement at the centre of a disk-shaped reservoir. For groundwater development applications, the studies of Bear and Corapcioglu (1981a, b)  and Corapcioglu and Bear (1983)  constitute the earliest examples of analytically based models for calculations of land subsidence due to pumping from shallow aquifers. Bear and Corapcioglu (1981a)  derived a closed-form solution for the compaction resulting from pumping in a confined aquifer. Their derivation relied on the integration of the 3D equation of groundwater flow across the aquifer’s thickness and the introduction, through Terzaghi’s effective stress principle (Terzaghi, 1923; Terzaghi and Peck, 1967 ), of a linear-elastic constitutive model between the vertical aquifer compaction and the average piezometric head, assuming horizontal flow and no horizontal displacements. Bear and Corapcioglu (1981b)  integrated the 3D classical equations of poro-elasticity (Biot, 1941 ) within the aquifer thickness, considering shear-free boundaries and conditions of plane stress, still under the assumption of horizontal flow and linear-elastic stress–strain relations. They thus derived closed-form equations for both vertical and horizontal displacements associated with flow to pumping wells in confined and partially confined aquifers. Corapcioglu and Bear (1983)  extended the approach of Bear and Corapcioglu (1981b)  to the case of unconfined aquifers. In this scenario, applying Terzaghi’s principle requires considering the variation in total stress to link changes in water level to effective stress variations. It is worth highlighting that the solutions presented by Bear and Corapcioglu  primarily focus on estimating the aquifer deformation (consolidation settlement) rather than directly calculating surface displacements. Indeed, the solutions are integrated over the saturated aquifer thickness, assuming a rigid basement beneath the aquifer. As a result, strains in the aquifer underburden and overburden are not taken into account, and the formation depth results to have no impact on the surface displacement. In the work of Xie et al. (2014) , Biot’s equations of poro-elasticity were solved analytically to determine radial symmetric analytical solutions for the land surface displacement induced by the deformation of an overburden layer sitting above a confined aquifer. Such a solution, however, did not account for the compaction of the aquifer, which was assumed merely as a rigid boundary where a time-dependent change in fluid pressure is imposed. Such a “drawdown” was given by the Theis solution (1935 ) for a single well pumping continuously in a laterally-infinite, horizontal and constant-thickness confined aquifer. Loáiciga (2013)  provided closed-form analytical solutions for the vertical consolidation settlement occurring within both confined and unconfined aquifers due to groundwater pumping, considering conditions of both steady-state and transient flow. These solutions were derived by integrating traditional aquifer drawdown solutions, such as in Thiem (1906)  and Theis (1935) , across the aquifer thickness. Loáiciga ’s approach enabled the estimation of effective stress variations that result in aquifer compaction, applicable to both normally consolidated and under-consolidated basins, and made use of linear superposition of solutions to simulate the effect of multiple wells. Of related interest is the work of Pujades et al. (2017) , who used a numerical approach to analyse the strain caused by groundwater pumping in overconsolidated, perfectly confined and partially confined aquifers. Their investigation employed a radial-symmetric conceptual model similar to the one used by Bear and Corapcioglu (1981b)  and addressed various aspects, including the influence of boundary conditions on displacements at the aquifer’s bottom and lateral boundaries. They also developed a closed-form solution for aquifer compaction in the case of confined flow, which significantly expanded upon the one proposed by Bear and Corapcioglu (1981b)  for three-dimensional consolidation. Zhang and Mehrabian (2020)  presented an analytical solution to the problem of underground fluid injection in a disk-shaped reservoir while accounting for strain-induced changes in permeability. While the focus of such a study was on aquifer injectivity rather than surface displacement, the rock stress was assumed to be a function of the pore fluid pressure change within the reservoir and was derived by integration of the NoS solution in an elastic half space. Wang et al. (2022)  presented a semi-analytical solution for the land subsidence due to pressure changes in a poro-elastic reservoir. Their method was based on the integration of a Green function derived as the solution of the coupled hydro-geomechanical system equation, multiplied to the reservoir pressure variation obtained from a flow simulator, either numerical or analytical. Aligned with the works reviewed above, this paper presents computationally fast semi-analytical models that can be used to assess land surface displacement due to aquifer pumping. These models effectively merge the NoS solution with the classic Theis solution for flow to wells in confined aquifers, following an approach that, to the best of the Author’s knowledge, is fully original. Despite both solutions being analytically based, their coupling results in integrals that can only be calculated numerically, which is computationally expensive. To overcome these limitations, two distinct models are proposed here, one employing lookup tables (LTs) and another relying on direct closed-form solutions, which furnish precise outputs for the horizontal and vertical components of the surface displacement. The closed-form solution relies on the fitting of the LT data with “hinge” models, that is, a particular type of piecewise-linear functions connected by smoothing curves around the intersection points. Both models share the same fundamental inputs, which are reduced to two dimensionless parameters, encompassing aquifer depth and thickness, surface location, well locations, time since pumping initiation, and critical hydro-geomechanical properties, including hydraulic conductivity, porosity, vertical compressibility and water compressibility. By adopting the NoS approach, these models enable a comprehensive analysis of 3D deformation effects across the aquifer, and the underburden and overburden formations. These models prioritise efficiency and scalability. By applying the principle of superposition, they enable the user to simulate land subsidence induced by multiple well pumping scenarios and varying pumping rates. These developments represent a notable step forward in the realm of land subsidence prediction, offering versatility and computational efficiency. This paper is organised as follows: Section 2  describes the fundamentals of the land subsidence model and the NoS solution; Section 3  presents the derivation of the semi-analytical land subsidence simulators, which rely on the integration of the NoS solution with the Theis equation over the aquifer volume, and the parameterisation of these integrals with respect to two dimensionless variables; Section 4  present the results of a number of numerical tests conducted for model testing purposes; in Section 5 , a discussion is provided concerning the model’s capabilities, along with a concise overview of its fundamental assumptions and an examination of the constraints imposed on the model’s accuracy and relevance; Section 6  includes concluding remarks on the models developed.  2 Land Subsidence Model Considered here is the case of a geomechanically homogeneous, linearly-elastic, semi-infinite system delimited by a traction-free horizontal surface, and subject to a spatially distributed pore pressure change Δ p    within a volume Ω   embedded in it. An alternative “hybrid” semi-analytical approach, is here devised in the case of the pore pressure change Δ p    produced by a single well, operating at a constant rate Q   within a confined, laterally-infinite, homogeneous, isotropic and horizontal aquifer. The well is positioned at the origin of the coordinate system ( x = 0 , y = 0 )    (Fig. 2 ) and is fully-screened through the aquifer, which is located at average depth c   and has a thickness b  . Note that the spatial and the temporal variables are accounted for in X  0     and β  , respectively. Since the double integrals (9) –(10)  cannot be solved analytically, they are calculated numerically using the iterative quadrature method developed by Shampine (2008a, b) . The results of these integrations are given in Fig. 3 , which shows a series of profiles of the scaled displacement components (u  h    ¯  , u  v    ¯    ) as functions of the spatial variable X  0    , for a discrete set of values of the temporal variable β  . A sensitivity analysis (not presented here) conducted on β = S  s    4 K   ⋅ c  2    t      indicates that such a variable typically takes values between 10−8  and 10, which is the range considered in Fig. 3 . In Fig. 3 , the scaled displacement components (u  h    ¯  , u  v    ¯    ) are seen to generally increase as β   decreases, that is, they become expectedly more pronounced at larger times, and for shallower aquifers, having lower c  . In addition, the displacements result larger for systems with lower values of the ratio S  s   / K   , that is, with low-compressibility c  M     (see Eq. (6) ) and high-permeability K  . This may seem counterintuitive at a first glance, but one must bear in mind that u  h    ¯    and u  v    ¯    are scaled with respect to the coefficient u  v  ∗     which is linearly proportional to c  M   / K   , thus what is true for the scaled displacement (Eqs. (9) ) is not necessarily true for the absolute displacement (Eqs. (8) ).   3.1 Lookup Table Numerical Model The substitution of Eqs. (9) –(10)  in Eqs. (8)  provides the mathematical model: (11) u  h   x  0   , t   = c  M   ⋅ ( 1 − ν )  ⋅ ρ  w   ⋅ g ⋅ Q  4 ⋅ π  2   ⋅ K   ⋅ u  h    ¯  X  0   , β      u  v   x  0   , t   = c  M   ⋅ ( 1 − ν )  ⋅ ρ  w   ⋅ g ⋅ Q  4 ⋅ π  2   ⋅ K   ⋅ u  v    ¯  X  0   , β        which simulates the surface displacement at the radial coordinate x  0     and at the time t   induced by a well pumping at the constant rate Q   from an aquifer of depth c  , thickness b  , hydraulic conductivity K   and compressibility c  M    . Since, as previously mentioned, the integrals (9) –(10)  can only be calculated numerically, which turns out to be computationally quite expensive, it is necessary to devise approaches to overcome this limitation. A first method presented here relies on the use of “lookup” tables (LT’s), compiled by numerical calculation of the functions u  h    ¯  X  0   , β      and u  v    ¯  X  0   , β      (Eqs. (9) –(10) ) over the points of a regular grid in the X  0   , β     space. LT’s are reported in Tables A.1 and A.2  of Appendix A , which contain the datasets employed to plot Fig. 3 . X  0    ’s and β  ’s are tabulated in the first column and in the first row, respectively, and the function values are in the table cells. Since X  0    , β  , u  h    ¯    and u  v    ¯    values may differ by several orders of magnitude, a logarithmic transformation is applied to all entries, which makes the data easier to interpret. Based on LT data, for any generic “input” point log X  0     , log β      , it is then possible to calculate approximate displacement components log u  h    ¯   ˆ     , log u  h    ¯   ˆ         by 2D interpolation. In this case, either cubic spline (de Boor, 1978 ) or cubic Hermite (Akima, 1974 ) algorithms can be adopted, both of which conserve continuity in the partial derivatives and closely adhere to the values of the original data points. Numerical tests, not presented here, indicate that a more simple bilinear interpolation method (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1964 ) is also viable but leads to results of comparable accuracy only if the grid resolution adopted in Tables A.1 and A.2  is at least doubled for the log β      “coordinate” (e.g. − 8 , − 7 . 5 , − 7 , … , 0 . 1 , 0 . 5 , 1 , 5 , 10   ).  3.2 Closed-Form Hinge Model An alternative to the LT model is to develop closed-form emulators u  h    ¯   ˆ   X  0   , β      and u  v    ¯   ˆ   X  0   , β      of u  h    ¯    and u  v    ¯    by regression of the LT “data”. Since all profiles in Fig. 3 , which are based on the data in Tables A.1 and A.2 , may be interpreted as contour lines of β   in the spaces of X  0   , u  h    ¯      (Fig. 3 a) and X  0   , u  v    ¯      (Fig. 3 b) and these exhibit a locally linear behaviour, it appears possible to construct semi-analytical models by fitting each profile to a “continuous hinge function”. A hinge function h ( x  ′   )     (x  ′     is a generic independent variable) is a type of 1D piecewise-linear function formed by merging together a generic number N   of straight lines using “sigmoids” to smooth out the discontinuity in the derivative at the intersection points (Sanchez-Ubeda and Wehenkel, 1998 ). Indicating with s  i   ( x  ′   )  = q  i   + m  i   x  ′      (i = 1 , … , N   ) the equation of the generic straight line, h ( x  ′   )     may be expressed as: (12) h ( x  ′   )  = q  1   + m  1   ⋅ x  ′   + ∑  i = 2  N   Δ m  i − 1 , i   ⋅ Δ  i − 1 , i   ⋅ log ( 1 + 1 0  x  ′   − x  i − 1 , i  ′    Δ  i − 1 , i       )      where Δ m  i − 1 , i   = m  i   − m  i − 1      is the slope variation between two consecutive segments “i − 1   ” and “i  ”, x  i − 1 , i  ′     is the abscissa of their intersection point (x  i − 1 , i  ′   = − q  i   − q  i − 1    m  i   − m  i − 1       ), and Δ  i − 1 , i     is a smoothness coefficient. A detailed derivation of Eq. (12)  is given in Appendix B .  The “goodness of fit” that can be achieved with the hinge model (12)  strongly depends on the selected number of segments N  . Based on the profiles in Fig. 3 , it appears reasonable, for any given β   value, to choose N = 3    for u  h    ¯    and N = 4    for u  v    ¯   . Fig. 4  shows hinge examples that mimic the profile shapes in Fig. 3 . Since Fig. 3  use a logarithmic scale on both axes, the variables in the hinge model (12)  need to be log-transformed (x  ′   = log X  0     , h = log u  ¯    ) prior to the fitting analysis. Here, these functions are “emulated” by fitting the models (13) –(14)  to each of the profiles in Fig. 3 a and b. This is carried out by implementing a two-stage regression procedure. The first stage consists of the calculation of parameter sets that provide a best fit of the hinge models (13) and (14)  for each of the 10 β   values selected in Fig. 3 . In practice, this requires minimising the square residuals between the hinge models (13) and (14)  and the scaled surface displacement calculated over N  s     points spanning the practical range of variability of X  0     (Fig. 3 ). These non-linear regressions are performed by using a “trust-region-reflective” algorithm (Coleman and Li, 1996 ) and produce 10 “training” data for each fitting parameter in θ  h     and in θ  v    . In the second stage, these training data are used to capture the relationships between the fitting parameters and the variable β  . The fitting model adopted in this stage relies either on logarithmic or double-logarithmic hinge functions (Eqs. (B.4) –(B.5)  in Appendix B ), given as: (15) g  1   ( β )  = ξ  1   + η  1   ⋅ log β + ∑  i = 2  N   Δ η  i − 1 , i   ⋅ δ  i − 1 , i   ⋅ log 1 + β  β  i − 1 , i        1  δ  i − 1 , i            g  2   β   = 1 0  ξ  1     ⋅ β  η  1     ⋅ ∏  i = 2  N   1 + β  β  i − 1 , i        1  δ  i − 1 , i          Δ η  i − 1 , i   ⋅ δ  i − 1 , i          The regression coefficients ξ  1   , η  1      , Δ η  1 , 2   , … , Δ η  N − 1 , N      , δ  1 , 2   , … ,   δ  N − 1 , N       , and β  1 , 2   , … , β  N − 1 , N       in Eqs. (15)  are determined by applying a non-linear least-square regression method based on the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Levenberg, 1944; Marquardt, 1963 ). Results of the two-stage process are presented in Tables 1 and 2  for the coefficients in θ  h     and θ  v    , respectively. Further details on the procedure may be found in Appendix B . Likewise, due to the hypothesis of linear elasticity and the boundary conditions to which the semi-infinite domain is subject, the principle of superposition can also be applied to the surface displacement fields associated with multiple overlapping Δ p    fields. Two well field scenarios are hypothesised. Well field #1 (Fig. 5 a) consists of a single large-capacity well operated continuously for 5 years at the extraction rate of 1000 m 3    /d from the location W  1 , 1    ≡   (10,000 m, 10,000 m). Well field #2 (Fig. 5 b), consists of 3 wells at the locations W  2 , 1    ≡   (13,535.53 m,13,535.53 m), W  2 , 2    ≡   (11 294.10 m, 5,170.3 m), and W  2 , 3    ≡   (5,170.3 m, 11 294.10 m), pumping continuously for 5 years at a flow rate of 333.33 m 3    /d each. The three wells form an equilateral triangle, with a distance of 5000 m from its center, which coincides with the location W  1 , 1     (Fig. 5 a). Note that Well field #1 and Well field #2 have the same cumulative extraction rate of 1000 m 3    /d.    4.1 Single-Well Scenario Fig. 6  shows the maps of the displacement fields u  x     (subpanels a-b), and u  z     (subpanels c-d) after 1825 days (5 years) of continuous operation of Well field #1 (u  y    -maps are not shown as they can be inferred from a 90° rotation of the u  x     maps). Subpanels 6 a and b present the comparison of the u  x     field obtained with the LT model and the hinge model with that determined using the FE approach as in Eq. (4) . The latter is considered the most accurate approach as it relies on a high-resolution discretisation of the aquifer domain (not shown here), in which the Δ p    field is calculated from the Theis analytical solution (Eq. (5) ) using linear superposition of effects, and the displacement components are calculated by spatial integration of the NoS Eqs. (2) . In Fig. 6 a, the horizontal displacement u  x     obtained with the LT model matches quite well that calculated with the FE model, particularly at “closer” distance, within about 2 km, from the pumping well, whereas some slight discrepancies are observed farther away. In Fig. 6 b, the horizontal displacement u  x     obtained with the hinge model still matches closely the one given by FE model, but the discrepancies become more significant, however not dramatic, away from the pumping well. Fig. 6 c and d pair the u  z     fields obtained with the LT and FE model, and the hinge and FE model, respectively. In Fig. 6 c, the LT model exhibits a close fidelity to the FE model in terms of u  z    . Fig. 6 d, shows that the hinge model is very accurate at closer distance (less than 2 km) from the pumping well, where u  z     is more pronounced, but such an accuracy tends to deteriorate, although slightly, away from the well, where the displacement becomes comparatively smaller. It is interesting to observe that, when compared the FE model, both the LT and the hinge models seem to mildly underestimate the horizontal displacement u  x    , and mildly overestimate the vertical displacement u  z    . The results presented in Fig. 6  relate to a single value of the time-dependent variable β   (5.38 × 10−4 ) so that the discrepancies between the LT and hinge models and the FE model can be explained in terms of the accuracy of the two approaches with respect to the spatial variable X  0     for that β   value. Overall, the LT model is generally very accurate where displacements are larger, that is, for smaller X  0    , and a bit less accurate where displacements are smaller, that is, for larger X  0    . This likely due to the accuracy in the numerical calculation of the integrals (9) –(10) , which is apparently close to perfect for low X  0    , but deteriorates — although quite slightly — for larger X  0    . The hinge model is apparently less accurate than the LT model because of the propagation of errors that arise from the numerical calculation of Eqs. (9) –(10) , as in the LT model, and from the hinge approximation, which is somewhat less accurate for larger X  0     values (Fig. B.12 ). The displacement profiles are shown for two observation points, one located at the center (O  2 , 1     in Fig. 5 b) of the well field, which is 5000 m away from each of the pumping wells, and another (O  2 , 2     in Fig. 5 b) located right at pumping well on W  2 , 1    . Subpanels 9 a and b present the comparison of the u  x     profiles obtained with the LT model and the hinge model with that calculated using the FE model. It is interesting to observe that all models show u  x   = 0    at O  2 , 1    . This is expected, since such a point is “central” and equidistant from the three pumping wells, and thus undergoes no horizontal displacement if the latter operate at the same pumping rate. On the other hand, the u  x     displacement at O  2 , 2     depends only on the effect of the wells at W  2 , 2     and W  2 , 3     (Fig. 5 b). In Fig. 9 a a reasonable match is observed between the LT model and the FE model, with the former overestimating u  x     at smaller times and underestimating it at larger times. These errors, however minor, can be linked to the numerical integration of Eqs. (9) –(10) . In Fig. 9 b a more significant discrepancy is observed between the hinge model and the FE model, with the former generally underestimating u  x    .
