However, it is worth mentioning that the relevance of these errors should be considered minor as the intensity of the horizontal displacement is indeed very small due to the large distance between the two wells W  2 , 2     and W  2 , 3    , and the observation point O  2 , 2    . Subpanels 9 c and c allow for the comparison of the u  z     profiles obtained with the LT model and the hinge model with those calculated using the FE model. The matching between the models is overall satisfactory, with a slightly better fidelity to the FE model of the LT model, rather than the hinge model. These discrepancies are more noticeable for observation points (e.g. O  2 , 1     in Fig. 5 b) that are situated at larger distance X  0     from the pumping wells. On the other hand, when observation points (e.g. O  2 , 2     in Fig. 5 b) are in close proximity to one of the pumping wells (e.g. W  2 , 1     in Fig. 5 b) approximation errors for both LT and hinge models are smaller because u  z     is due predominantly to the effect of that pumping well, and less to the contribution of the other pumping wells, which is potentially less accurate due to the large distance X  0     at which they operate from the observation point.      5 Discussion The LT and the hinge models rely on the coupling of the classical Theis equation (5) , which describes flow to a well, with the NoS equations, which quantify surface displacement caused by changes in effective stress. The assumption of linear elasticity forms the basis of the model, resulting in integral equations that can only be solved numerically, for example adopting a sufficiently resolved FE discretisation of the aquifer where pumping wells operate. However, it should be noted that FE-based methods often demand significant computational resources, and expertise to prepare model inputs and analyse results. To address these challenges, the LT and hinge model formulations proposed here aim to strike a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy and constitute approximations that can provide results comparable to the FE model. It is important to acknowledge that these models rely on idealised representations of the subsurface system. The aquifer is assumed to be laterally unbounded, perfectly confined, horizontal, constant thickness, and homogeneous in terms of hydraulic conductivity K  , vertical compressibility c  M     and porosity ϕ  . In addition, pumping wells are considered fully screened and point-like. While these assumptions (Theis, 1935 ) may not capture all the complexities of real-world aquifers, they are widely applied by practitioners for initial calculations, pumping tests, and other practical purposes for flow to pumping wells. Furthermore, the deformation of the subsurface is assumed to be caused solely by changes in effective stress, which are estimated to be equal and opposite to changes in pore pressure given by the Theis model (5) . This assumption relies on Terzaghi’s principle (Terzaghi and Peck, 1967 ) and assumes that the total stress remains constant during aquifer pumping, which is generally valid for confined aquifers. However, in the case of unconfined aquifers, the use of the Theis equation is not warranted, and the total stress does change. In these instances, it is necessary to determine how changes in effective stress can be quantified and corrected based on the changes in pore pressure, and analytical solutions distinct from Theis’s equation need to be applied. Another important matter of concern is the underlying assumption of laterally infinite aquifers. While these aquifers do not exist in reality, the models developed in this study should be applicable to aquifers of sufficiently “large” extent, that is, large enough that the cone of depression caused by groundwater pumping and the surface area affected by displacements remain within the physical boundaries of the system. Note that this does not depend on the boundaries alone, but also on the intensity of groundwater abstraction rates and the time horizon over which pumping occurs. Also, since the extent of the cone of depression is directly proportional to the hydraulic conductivity K   of the aquifer, and inversely proportional to the specific elastic storage S  s    , which depends on the vertical compressibility c  M     (Eq. (6) ), the boundary effects are expected to be less significant for aquifers having lower conductivity and larger storage properties, which imply smaller cones of depression and smaller surface displacement bowls. The models developed here can be applied under the assumption the aquifer is perfectly confined, that is, bounded above and below by perfectly impervious aquicludes. As such, they do not take into account of changes in fluid pressure that may occur in confining layers, and the consequent compaction, which may result results significant under particular conditions (Ferronato et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Last but not least, while it is important to acknowledge that the models presented here have certain limitations due to the simplifying conceptualisations discussed above, their computational efficiency makes them particularly suitable for obtaining fast initial estimates related to land subsidence caused by groundwater pumping from confined aquifers, what-if analyses, assessment of groundwater pumping based on displacement observations, risk assessment, decision-making, stochastic simulations requiring repeated model runs, and simulation–optimisation based groundwater management approaches.  6 Conclusions This paper presented innovative semi-analytical models designed for estimating land subsidence resulting from groundwater pumping in confined aquifers. Their derivation couples the NoS equations with the Theis solution, resulting in surface displacement components (horizontal and vertical) expressed as integrals that must be solved numerically, requiring significant computational effort similar to that of more advanced numerical models like FDs or FEs. The paper introduces two distinct models that aim to reduce such an effort: one utilising a lookup table (LT) containing results from numerical integration, and the other offering direct closed-form surface displacement solutions through the fitting of LT data with “hinge” models, that is, piecewise-linear functions connected by sigmoidal curves. Such solutions depend on two dimensionless spatio-temporal variables, which account for aquifer depth and thickness, well locations, pumping schedules, and essential hydro-geomechanical properties like hydraulic conductivity, porosity, vertical compressibility of the porous skeleton, and water compressibility. Emphasising computational efficiency and scalability through the superposition principle, these models can simulate land subsidence caused by various well pumping scenarios. To validate their accuracy, a confined aquifer with specific dimensions was considered for testing, and the model results were rigorously compared with those obtained with a finite-element-based integration of the NoS solution and Theis equation. Impressively, these models provide quite accurate predictions of land subsidence, with errors below 5% when compared to more complex models, while resulting computationally much more efficient. However, one must be aware that these models remain analytically-based and thus should be applied only within the limitations of the NoS and Theis solutions, which rely on simplified subsurface conceptualisations. As such, these models are ideally suited for swift initial assessments, what-if analyses, assisting groundwater management decisions, and stochastic simulations for risk assessment. Under these real-world settings, they offer a robust toolset for assessing and mitigating the impacts of groundwater pumping in confined aquifers, with scalability ensuring applicability across diverse hydrogeological conditions.
1 Introduction  Understanding how a watershed responds to a rainfall event holds great significance across various hydrological and hydraulic studies, ranging from water resource management issues, like irrigation, to designing hydraulic infrastructure and flood-control planning. Gericke and Smithers (2014)  noted that a significant portion, up to 75 %, of errors in estimating peak flow on a watershed scale stems from inaccuracies in predicting watershed response times. Such inaccuracies in temporal parameters can lead to either over- or under-designing of hydraulic structures, with socio-economic repercussions (Sultan et al., 2022 ). Estimating response time is also crucial for developing flood forecasting models, implementing flood warning systems (Alfieri et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016 ), and executing urban drainage projects (Grimaldi and Petroselli, 2014 ). Therefore, delving into the time it takes for runoff to occur after a rainfall event lies at the heart of practical hydrological studies (Allnutt et al., 2020 ). Determining time parameters reflecting watershed responses has been a focal point in recent decades. Essentially, time variables characterize individual events depicted on either a hyetograph or hydrograph, while a time parameter is defined by the difference between two interconnected time variables. The most frequently used time parameters that measure how quickly a watershed responds to precipitation are the time of concentration, lag time, and time to peak. It is well-known that, for a given basin, the time of concentration is usually greater than the lag time. The relationship between these characteristic times is supported by a wide literature (Gericke and Smithers, 2014; Allnutt et al., 2020; Evangelista et al., 2023 ). Though these parameters are widely used as input to common hydrological design tools in the context of everyday engineering applications, their definitions are not unique. For example, McCuen (2009)  shows at least six different lag time definitions, among which two of the most widely used are (1) time to centroid: time interval between the centroid of the effective rainfall and the centroid of direct runoff, and (2) time to peak: time interval between the centroid of effective rainfall and peak of direct runoff. A large number of equations for estimating response times have been published. A comprehensive list of traditional formulas can be found in Gericke & Smithers (2014), Almeida et al. (2022) , and Evangelista et al. (2023) . The interest in these kinds of equations is still substantial, as evidenced by several recent research studies (de Almeida et al., 2017; Salimi et al., 2017 ; Ravazzani et al., 2019; Sultan et al., 2022; Alamri et al., 2023; Nam et al., 2024 ). Most equations are derived using geographical features, such as the basin area, characteristic lengths (e.g., river length and width), and the basin slope. However, catchment response time is also intricately linked to and influenced by climatological variables and catchment characteristics (e.g., land cover, soils, and storage). For example, Yu et al. (2000)  and Loukas and Quick (1996)  pointed out the importance of the roughness coefficient in rivers for lag time estimations, whereas Sultan et al. (2023)  demonstrated the effects of land-use change on response times. Even the river network type (e.g., parallel, pinnate, braided, dendritic) has a direct impact on the time of concentration (Jung et al., 2017 ). Gericke and Smithers (2014)  stated that there is no single method of estimating response times that is superior to all others, considering the wide variety of climatological, geomorphological, and hydrological responses encountered in practice. For this reason, Evangelista et al. (2023)  proposed not to judge formulas based on their ability to reproduce observed travel time parameters. Instead, they suggested using simple hydraulic reasoning to calculate implied velocities from wave celerities and assessing how velocity varies with catchment size and whether this aligns with observations. Considering the different estimations of this parameter, resulting in very different design values, response times remain ambiguous, and uncertain concepts of modern hydrology (Grimaldi et al., 2012; Michailidi et al., 2018; Beven, 2020 ). In particular, the major inconsistency is represented by considering them as constant parameters of the basin rather than hydraulic variables, thus neglecting the role of flow velocities that may be particularly different if extreme or usual flood events are considered (Michailidi et al., 2018 ). Indeed, Minshall (1960)  derived response functions for certain small catchments, which showed a pronounced dependence of lag time on the intensity of rainfall excess. The value of response time has been proven to be decreasing with increasing rainfall intensity by many authors since (Askew, 1970; Loukas and Quick, 1996; Saghafian et al., 2002; Szilagyi, 2007; Zhang et al., 2007; Kjeldsen et al., 2016; Mathias et al., 2016; Meyersohn, 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Michailidi et al., 2018; Cuevas et al., 2019; Nagy et al., 2022; Barbero et al., 2022 ). A different approach to estimating response time using the measured precipitation and discharge time series has been proposed by Giani et al. (2021) . They applied the Detrending Moving-average Cross-correlation Analysis (DMCA) to determine response times both for long observed time series and at the event scale, resulting in a set of values for each catchment. The strength of the DMCA method is that it can find the timescale at which two time series are linked even when they exhibit different frequency spectra and are nonlinearly related. Their method has been further developed and applied in several papers since then (Gnann et al., 2021; Giani et al., 2022; Nagy et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023 ). The DMCA method was successfully applied to 61 Hungarian catchments at the event scale since it yielded similar values to the two lag time definitions mentioned above (Nagy et al., 2022 ). A new trend in the catchment response definition and analysis of the river networks is the use of 2D hydraulic models based on the Shallow Water Equations (SWEs), where the rainfall and infiltration rates are considered as source terms (see, for example, Caviedes-Voullième et al., 2012; Cea and Bladé, 2015; Fernández-Pato et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2019; Costabile et al., 2023; García-Alén et al., 2023; Costabile et al. 2024 ). 2D models are potentially able to describe both overland and channel flow, evaluating velocities and water depths throughout the watershed, and only require the estimate of roughness coefficients and the computation of net rainfall rate if compared to hydrological models. Recent examples of the potential of this approach can be found in Garzon et al. (2023) , who used a 2D hydrodynamic-based rainfall/runoff simulation to explore the effect of the watershed morphometry on the lag time, and Zolghadr et al. (2022) , who proposed this method to estimate the time of concentration in a watershed. Another relevant study on this topic can be found in Barbero et al. (2022) , who analyzed response times in terms of hydrodynamic response simulated by an integrated 2D-SWEs model running on high-resolution digital elevation models (DEMs). Specifically, four formulas were introduced, proving their ability to predict lag time variability simulated for three small ungauged basins. These four formulas may be considered: 1) physically-based, as they were able to reproduce the results of a physically-based numerical approach and, consequently, the simulated wave celerities, and 2) event-based because they use information extracted from the considered event. However, these formulas were calibrated using synthetic rainfall from a few specific watersheds and were only tested using observed rainfall/runoff time series in a very limited number of small, mountainous catchments. Consequently, there is insufficient evidence to suggest that they can reliably produce accurate results in different climatic and orographic conditions. Therefore, the main goals of this work can be summarized as follows: 1. to determine the extent to which these formulas accurately represent lag time estimations in watersheds with geomorphic and climatic features different from those considered during their calibration and verification; 2. to reduce uncertainty to enhance their practical use, providing further simplifications in their formulations; 3. to evaluate their performances in respect to an event-based approach, the DMCA method, discussing potential and limitations of both approaches; 4. to evaluate the robustness of these formulas analyzing the magnitude and basin scale dependence of the inferred velocities with the values observed in the literature, following the approach recently proposed by Evangelista et al. (2023) . These issues are discussed with reference to 60 rainfall events occurring in 27 watersheds in Hungary and Italy, having substantially different geomorphic and climatic features. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2  delineates the methods employed for deriving lag time estimation, the event-based approaches considered in this paper, the possible sources of uncertainties, and some empirical formulas used for further comparisons. Section 3  presents the available data. Section 4  encompasses the results and discussion. Finally, the most significant conclusions of this work are summarized in Section 5.  2 Methods 2.1 DMCA method The response time of a catchment can be estimated using observed precipitation and runoff time series. However, the existence of numerous definitions casts doubts on the objective evaluation of such calculations (Nagy et al., 2022 ). Moreover, defining rainfall-runoff events necessitates either manual determination or the application of a rainfall-runoff event selection procedure. Recently, Giani et al. (2021)  proposed a novel methodology in hydrology called the Detrending Moving-average Cross-correlation Analysis (DMCA) method. This procedure can be applied to long observed rainfall and runoff time series, as well as to short data segments, i.e., pre-defined rainfall-runoff events. While the former approach yields a characteristic value, the latter provides event-specific response times. Giani et al. (2021)  successfully applied the DMCA method to directly estimate the response time of a catchment from rainfall and streamflow observations. As they state, this method’s strength is “to find the timescale at which two time-series are linked even when they exhibit different frequency spectra and are nonlinearly related.” The DMCA-based correlation coefficient (ρDMCA   [-]) for time series with length T  and applying a window length L  can be calculated as:(1) ρ DMCA  L  = ∑ t = 0.5 L + 1    T - 0.5 L - 1     R t  - R t , L   ^    Q t  - Q t , L   ^     ∑ t = 0.5 L + 1    T - 0.5 L - 1     R t  - R t , L   ^    2  ∑ t = 0.5 L + 1    T - 0.5 L - 1     Q t  - Q t , L   ^    2    ,   w i t h  - 1 ≤ ρ DMCA  L  ≤ 1    where Rt   and Qt   are the cumulative time series of the rainfall (r ) and streamflow (q ) data, while R t , L   ^    and Q t , L   ^    are the centered moving averages of the cumulative rainfall and streamflow time-series, given as:(2;3) R t  = ∑ i = 1  t  r i    ;  Q t  = ∑ i = 1  t  q i    f o r  t  =  1 , 2  , ⋯ , T     (4) R t , L   ^  = 1 L  ∑ t - 0.5 ( L - 1 )  t + 0.5 ( L - 1 )    R t      (5) Q t , L   ^  = 1 L  ∑ t - 0.5 ( L - 1 )  t + 0.5 ( L - 1 )    Q t       The rainfall and streamflow time series must have the same length and time step. The original study of Giani et al. (2021)  employed hourly time series. The window length L  must be defined in units of time steps (in this case, hours) and must have an odd value since a centered moving average is calculated. The value of Tr   can be estimated as half of Lmin  -1, where Lmin   is the window length, resulting in the minimum value of ρDMCA   (ρmin   [-]). In order to find this optimum, several window lengths need to be applied. The maximum possible value of Tr   (Tr,  max  [h]) can be attributed to the maximum tested window length (Lmax   [h]). This Lmax   value can be considered as the only parameter of this approach. This parameter limits the maximum value of Tr   as (Lmax  -1)/2 = Tr,  max . The numerator in Equation (1)  represents the bivariate fluctuation of streamflow and runoff, while the denominator contains the squared fluctuations of the rainfall and streamflow time series. The sign of the rainfall and streamflow fluctuations carries physical meaning: the center of mass is preceded by a negative fluctuation and followed by a positive one (Giani et al., 2021 ). Therefore, ρmin   is achieved when the value of L  is closest to the time between the centers of masses. A detailed, step-by-step introduction to the original DMCA-based method is presented by Giani et al. (2021) , along with a detailed description of the calculation steps’ interpretation. At the event scale, the application of the DMCA-based method requires generating an artificial time series that includes several copies of the event’s precipitation and runoff time series. Both of the latter need to have a series of constant values in between the copies, longer than the maximum length of the tested time window (Lmax  ). The constant value can be zero in the case of the precipitation time series, while it can be the last value of the observed discharge in the case of the runoff time series, or the values can change linearly between the last and first observed values. The number of required repetitions is not clarified in the original text by Giani et al. (2021) , but through experiments, we found that five repetitions are sufficient. The DMCA method was previously applied at an hourly temporal resolution and is now also tested for Italian catchments at a higher (10-minute) temporal resolution, with results compared to differently derived reference values.  2.2 Physically-based formulas based on regressions of 2D SWE model results Barbero et al. (2022)  used a physically-based approach based on the 2D SWEs numerical model developed by the authors (see, for example, Costabile et al., 2013; Costabile et al., 2019; Costabile and Costanzo 2021 ) to provide evidence on the variability of the lag time in small basins. In particular, a clear influence of the return period in the lag time estimations was observed, meaning that the characteristics of the rainfall events are among the main variables influencing the lag time. The variability of hydrologic response time observed in the numerical rainfall-runoff scenarios was described by a combination of characteristic times influencing the hydrodynamic response of a basin to rainfall events. Specifically, four formulas were introduced that proved to be able to predict the lag time variability observed for three small ungauged basins. The regressive formulas provided results in reasonably good agreement with the estimations of the lag time related to the observed events, showing errors of the order of 30 %. Their performances have been further highlighted in the light of the variability of the predictions based on the applications of several empirical literature formulas, proving to be very competitive and encouraging. The characteristic times were deduced using two approaches: the first one is based on a conceptual model, whereas the second one is essentially empiric. The conceptual approach takes advantage of the kinematic wave theory (see characteristic times X 1  and X 2  shown in Eqs. (6) and (7) . In the empirical approach, attention is devoted to finding relations where relevant variables that may influence the hydrodynamic response of the watershed (Eqs. The morphometric variables were defined in QGIS based on 1-meter and 5-meter resolution DEMs, applying a threshold to define the channel network equal to 0.05 % of the basin area. As regards the calculation of the Manning coefficient, we used values usually suggested in the literature (see, for example, Papaioannou et al., 2018 ). 2.2.1 Source of uncertainties in the application of Barbero’s et al formulas and their simplification for practical applications The formulas proposed by Barbero et al. (2022)  require information about specific geomorphic features of the river network, such as the length of the maximum flow path and drainage length. These values can be derived from Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) through various methods (Bárdossy & Schmidt, 2002 ). It is widely acknowledged that the source of the DEM, data resolution and the threshold values for flow accumulation can affect these estimations, thereby influencing the prediction of the hydrological response of the watersheds, particularly when employing stream-network dependent models like the geomorphological instantaneous unit hydrograph (GIUH) (Al-Wagdany et al 2020 , Akai & Koçyiğit 2021, Chavan & Srinivas 2015 ). Specifically, one parameter that significantly impacts results is the threshold area, which can be computed as a fixed value or as a percentage of the watershed area. Akay and Koçyiğit (2021)  demonstrate the influence of threshold area on hydrological modeling based on 13 different papers, covering basins ranging in area from 13 km2  to 127 km2 , with DEM resolutions ranging from 10 m to 1000 m. To explore their effects on the results, one approach could involve experimenting with different threshold area values. However, we chose to address this issue within the framework of one of the most renowned scaling laws governing river networks, which elucidates the relationship between the length of the longest channel of a river basin (L ), measured from outlet to drainage divide, and the area (A ) of the basin itself. This scaling relation is known as Hack’s law (Hack, 1957 ) and can be expressed as shown in Eq. (14) :(14)  L = α · A β       For drainage areas lower than 100 km2 , Hack determined β to be 0.6, while α is approximately 1.5 but ranges between 1.1 and 2.7 (with L  and A  expressed in km and km2 , respectively). From this pioneering study, Hack’s parameters have been estimated in various contexts. From extensive studies based on datasets spanning several orders of magnitude in the basin area, Mueller (1972)  found that the length–area relationship is best fitted using β = 0.55, whereas Montgomery and Dietrich (1992)  obtained Hack’s coefficient and exponent of 2.02 and 0.49, respectively (again with L  and A  expressed in km and km2 , respectively). Other studies have indicated greater variability in these parameters, indicating that β ranges between 0.45 and 0.7, and α ranges between 1 and 6, depending on regional estimates (Willemin, 2000; Walcott and Summerfield, 2009; Shen et al., 2017 ). A modification of Hack’s law has been proposed by Sassolas-Serrayet et al. (2018) , who emphasized that the coefficient α depends on the basin shape. In this paper, the structure of the Hack’s law is incorporated into the Tlag-3 equation of Barbero’s et al. (2022)  formulas. Specifically, the computation of the variable θ2  relies on the ratio between A  and L,  whereas the variable θ1  depends on the value of L . Therefore, the variable X3  is influenced by the coefficient and the exponent of the scaling law. Specifically, the variable X3  can be expressed as follows (Eq. (15) ):(15) X 3  = α · A β   R max   · n S  · A α · A β     1 3     0.5     After performing some algebraic manipulation, Eq. (16)  can be derived:(16) X 3  = α 1 3   · n S · R  max     0.5  ·  A 2 β + 1  6      Therefore, the Tlag-3 formula can be simplified as:(17) T lag - 3 s   = K · n S · R max      0.41  ·  A c     where K  and c  represent two constant parameters determined by the values of α and β, which are considered to be more representative of the specific watershed being analyzed based on user experience. The structure of Hack’s law is first verified through the Hungarian and Italian watersheds, estimating the related values of K  and c.  Then, α and β values suggested by Willemin (2000), Montgomery and Dietrich (1992) , and the original values provided by Hack (1957)  are used to estimate values of L  for a given watershed area. This approach will enable us to roughly examine the potential impact of the user’s choice in deriving the value of L  from a DEM and to highlight the effects on lag time estimation by means of the simplified Eq. (17) . The related values of K  and c  will be shown in the results section.   2.3 Accuracy of the predictions and comparison with literature formulas The reliability of estimated lag time values by both the DMCA method and the Barbero’s et al. (2022)  formulas have been initially compared to the results obtained through a hydrological approach (HEC-HMS). Then, they were further analyzed in light of the results of some literature formulas. 2.3.1 Estimation of the lag time from the events: HEC-HMS approach The lag time, defined as the distance between the center of mass of the net rainfall and the center of mass of the direct runoff, was evaluated for all the considered events through the HEC-HMS software (Fieldman, 2000 ), which is still a widely used model (see, e.g., Theochari & Baltas 2024 ). It should be observed that this approach is very similar in nature to the ones applied by Giani et al. (2021)  and Nagy et al. (2022)  to determine the observed values for the catchment response time at the event scale. All these applied approaches are hydrology-based, including the separation of effective precipitation and direct runoff. The difference is that the HEC-HMS approach is evaluated within modeling software using well-established calculation procedures, while in the other two cases, the hydrological model is much simpler. Hence, the calculations were self-programmed. Starting from the observed rainfall and runoff hydrographs, the software HEC-HMS was used first to assess the net rainfall through the original Conservation Service Curve Number method (SCS-CN, now NRCS-CN) (Soil Conservation Service (SCS), 1975 ). The CN values were calibrated to determine the time series for effective rainfall and direct runoff. Subsequently, the duration between the centroid of the effective rainfall and the centroid of the direct runoff was computed. Two different runoff series were considered: the observed series and the one simulated by the Clark hydrological model. In both cases, the direct runoff was obtained by subtracting the base flow from the discharge hydrograph. Accordingly, two different lag times were then defined as reference values: the distance between the centroid of the net rainfall and the centroid of the net runoff simulated by the Clark model (TlagA ) and the observed (TlagB ) runoff, respectively. Fig. 1   shows an application of the HEC-HMS software to two of the considered events, where the two lag times obtained with HEC-HMS are compared. The difference between the two estimations may be recognized for the second event, whereas no substantial variation can be noted for the first one. TlagA  is initially used as the reference value for evaluating model performances (Section 4 ), whereas TlagB  is considered for further verifications (see Section 4.3 ). The metrics used for comparative purposes are the percentage errors (Ej  ) related to the generic event j  and the mean absolute errors (MAE), defined as in Eqs. (18) and (19) , respectively:(18) E j  = T lag , c   j   - T lag , e   j    T lag , e   j         (19) MAE = ∑ j = 1  N  E j     N      where T lag,e,  and T lag,c  refer to the lag time estimated using the HEC-HMS-based procedure and the computed ones by the DMCA and the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas (or DMCA method), respectively; N  is the total number of events considered in this paper (see Section 3 ).  2.3.2 Comparison with literature formulas The predictive capabilities of the two approaches analyzed in this work will be compared with well-known literature formulas that employ the same lag time definition (time to centroid). Among the plethora of existing ones, the equations listed in Table 2   have been selected. Specifically, formulas based on the watershed area (Corradini et al., 1995 ) and on the length of the main channel (Haktanir and Sezen, 1990 ) are considered. These formulas provided reliable results using data previously published by the author (Barbero et al., 2022 ), while the Haktanir and Shezen (1990) formula performed well for the Hungarian catchments (Nagy et al., 2016; Nagy et al., 2021 ). Moreover, a third formula (Watt and Chow, 1985 ) is also considered since, according to the approach developed by Evangelista et al. (2023) , it is hydraulically consistent and respects the observed growth rate between velocity and basin area. It should be noted that this latter formula estimates lag time, defined as the time difference between the centroid of net rainfall and the hydrograph peak (tp  ). We used the conversion factors proposed by Evangelista et al. (2023)  to transform Tp  -values into Tlag  -values. The formulas listed in Table 2  provide lag time in hours for A  in km2  and L  in km.   2.4 Robustness of lag time predictions: Analysis of inferred velocities based on Evangelista’s et al. (20)  for the analysis of the implied velocities from wave celerities under the simplified hypotheses of the validity of the Chézy formula wide rectangular channel:(20) v = L 1.5 t c        where the average velocity v  is evaluated as the ratio between the length of the longest drainage path L  and the time of concentration tc  . (21) , introducing a conversion factor of 1.42 between lag time and time of concentration (Evangelista et al., 2023 ):(21) v = 0.47 L t lag         Response time formulas have been considered as robust or not depending on their consistency with the observations. Specifically, average velocities increase with watershed size, according to a power law-type relation v  = p·Am  , with a growth rate m  around 0.1. In particular, Evangelista et al. (2023)  suggested that formulas showing m  = 0.1 ± 0.025 can be considered consistent with observations. The analysis of the growth rate values for both the DCMA results and the Barbero’s et al. (2022)  formulas will be shown in Section 4.3 .   3 Available data The study area spans across two European countries, Italy and Hungary, each characterized by unique hydrological and geographical features (see Table A1  – Appendix ). To ensure the representativeness of the results, the catchments were selected to cover a wide range of sizes, with different geographical locations and topographic and land use characteristics. In Hungary, there were a total of 18 catchments, while in Italy, nine catchments (Fig. 2  ) were chosen based on their diversity and data accessibility for a total of 60 events. The delineation of the Hungarian catchments was previously performed using the Copernicus Land Monitoring Services’ EU-DEM v1.1 digital surface model (Nagy et al. 2021 ) with a spatial resolution of 25 m in raster format (Copernicus, 2016 ). The main characteristics of the Hungarian catchments and considered rainfall events are presented in Table 3  , which shows a notable variability. For instance, watershed areas range between 28 km2  and 432 km2 ; the total length of the channel network ranges between 108 and 591 km. The observed discharge and precipitation time series of the Hungarian catchments were provided by the local water directorates and the Hungarian Meteorological Service (HungaroMet, Meteorological Database). Data from 22 stations were used, which were within or near the basins. During the preparation of the data, the Thiessen polygon method was applied in the case of three basins (Béci, Ronyva, Völgységi). In the matter of five rainfall events, there were no reliable data available from the Meteorologic Database. In these cases, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) reanalysis of precipitation data was applied for modeling. From the time series data for 18 catchments and their 39 events were selected. In terms of duration and rainfall intensity, complex and highly variable rainfall events have been examined. Within Italy, nine basins were considered, located in Northern Italy and in Sicily. The basins of Northern Italy are part of the Po River basin, while the Sicilian basins are located on Sicily Island, in the southwest of Italy. The elevation characteristics of the basins were derived in QGIS 3.14 using a high-resolution DEM with a spatial resolution of 5 m and Corine Land Cover geo-referenced database. As before, the main characteristics of the Italian catchments and considered rainfall events are presented in Table 3 . The Italian catchments also show prominent diversity, for example, their areas range between 9 km2  and 1627 km2 ; basin slope range between 17.4 and 47.0 %. The observed discharge and precipitation time series applied were available from the official websites of regional agencies for the protection of the environment. The time resolution of the data was 10 min, and the data was prepared with Excel and MATLAB software. From the time series data of the 9 Italian catchments, we identified 21 events for analysis with notably diverse rainfall characteristics, as shown in Table 3 . According to Natural Environmental Research Council (NERC) (1975) , the areal reduction factor (ARF) was computed for all events (Italian and Hungarian) for all the considered events. Comparing the Hungarian and Italian basins and the related rainfall events, the differences are remarkable. The basin slope differs notably as the minimum slope of the Italian basins is 17.4 %, while the same value is 3 % in the case of the Hungary catchments. The average basin slope is 5.5 % for the Hungarian catchments, while it is 26.6 % for the Italian catchments. It should be noted that the range of basin slope is the only characteristic which does not overlap in the case of the two datasets. Regarding the rainfall characteristics, the mean net and the maximum rainfall intensities tend to be higher in the case of the Italian rainfall events. The dissimilarities of the catchments and rainfall characteristics can further improve the reliability of the results using novel methods.  4 Results and discussion In the dataset under consideration, 18 watersheds had more than one event. Overall, the larger the rainfall intensity, the smaller the lag time found for the considered events. Table 4   shows the variability in estimated lag time values for each watershed. In some cases, the maximum lag time exceeded twice the minimum lag time. These results confirm that lag time cannot be regarded as a constant parameter for a watershed but rather depends on the specific rainfall event. Fig. 3   illustrates the performance metrics related to the predictions obtained using the DMCA method and the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas. Specifically, Fig. 3 a portrays the distribution of errors generated by various formulas, presented in the form of box plots, highlighting the effectiveness of these formulas in producing reliable results. The interquartile range emphasizes the relatively low variability of errors. For both the DMCA method and the formulas proposed by Barbero et al. (2022) , a few outliers can be identified, resulting in significant overestimations of the observed lag time. Fig. 3 b offers additional insights into the performance metrics, specifically focusing on the mean absolute errors (MAE). Of particular interest is the Tlag-3 formula, which exhibits the smallest errors among the examined methods. The error rates hover around 37 % across the dataset. The predictions made using Tlag-2 and, especially, Tlag-4 formulas show slightly higher errors. The predictions related to the Tlag-1 formulas can be considered fairly good, but they provided the worst results among the Barbero’s et al. (2022)  equations. The DMCA results are slightly better than those yielded by the Tlag-1 formula but slightly worse than the outcomes obtained by the other three formulas. However, the median value of the distribution is very close to homologous ones computed by Tlag-2, Tlag-3, and Tlag-4 equations (Fig. 3 a). The DMCA results, though characterized by reliable predictions, perform worse than the formulas proposed by Barbero et al. (2022)  but slightly better than the equations proposed by Haktanir and Sezen (1990)  and Corradini et al. (1995) . Overall, the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas and the DMCA method produce more accurate predictions compared to the relationships that neglect the contribution of rainfall rate. The comparison between observed and computed lag time is further represented in Fig. 4  , which shows the variability of the predicted values around the line of perfect agreement. Percentage error bands are included in Fig. 4  to provide a visual indication of the range within which predictions may deviate from the ideal line. While the general trend in the plots follows a reasonable pattern, deviations from the line of perfect agreement indicate that certain data points exhibit significant discrepancies from the overall trend. This is particularly evident for the predictions based on the Tlag-1 and Tlag-2 formulas (Fig. 4 b and c), whereas it seems to be reduced for the rest of the estimations (Fig. 4 a, d, and e). Overall, the errors in all the considered approaches are rarely greater than 75 %. Table 5   reports the percentage of events falling in the error bands shown in Fig. 4 . Table 5  highlights that both the Tlag-3 and Tlag-4 formulas perform very well, with errors lower than 25 % for half of the events and lower than 50 % in more than 80 % of the cases. 4.1 Methods’ performances as a function of watershed area and slope As mentioned in Section 3 , the dataset considered in this work is characterized by heterogeneous watersheds, having, in particular, different slopes, ranging between 0.017 and 0.47, and sizes (from 10 to 1627 km2 , approximately). Searching for correlations between the method’s performances and the morphometric parameters of the watersheds could be useful from a practical point of view. Therefore, the analysis of the predictive performance of the methods examined here is now carried out considering the influence of watershed slope and area. Attention is first focused on mild and steep watersheds, roughly identified here by introducing a slope threshold equal to 0.15. This choice allowed for the dataset to be halved into two subsets, each containing approximately the same number of watersheds. Fig. 5   displays the mean absolute errors associated with the formulas utilized in the paper as a function of the mean slope. In particular, when analyzing catchments with milder slopes (Fig. 5 a), the DMCA method yielded the best results. Conversely, the estimations obtained using the formulas proposed by Barbero et al. (2022)  produced results worse than the DMCA method, substantially equal to each other, and similar to the results obtained from applying the Watt & Chow (1985)  equation. When transitioning from the analysis of mild to steep catchments, the performance metrics undergo substantial changes. In particular, the DMCA method yielded the worst results, while the estimations obtained using the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas performed better than other formulas found in the literature (Fig. 5 b). Specifically, Tlag-3 and Tlag-4 exhibited the lowest MAE, approximately equal to 0.33. The good prediction of the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas for steeper catchments is expected in part, considering that they were originally deduced from the analysis of steep watersheds. The reason why the DMCA performs better for mild slopes will be discussed later in this work. Attention is now focused on watershed areas. The analysis has been organized by splitting the database according to the threshold area (150 km2), and the results are shown in Fig. 6  . Specifically, Fig. 6 a suggests that predictions based on the DMCA method are particularly reliable for watersheds with areas greater than 150 km2, with errors lower than 30 %. The predictions by Tlag-3, Tlag-4, and Tlag-2 also provided good results (MAE approximately equal to 0.35) and produced the most accurate predictions for smaller ones (Fig. 6 b), even though the associated errors are not so different from other formulas (Watt and Chow, Tlag-1). Interestingly, Fig. 6 b highlights that the DMCA method's performance worsens when considering smaller catchments.  4.2 Application issues for the DMCA method The lag times yielded by the DMCA method compared to the estimated lag time values (TlagA ) are presented in Fig. 7  . In the case of the Italian catchments, the DMCA method resulted in a lag time equal to one time step of the used input time series in many cases, which is much shorter than the observed lag time. Based on the shape of the correlation coefficient (ρDMCA   [-]) curve, the original output equal to one time step was not accepted as an actual value for the lag time. In these cases, the precipitation time series was shifted backward one time step at a time, while the DMCA method was re-applied in each case. The lag times larger than one time step resulting from the smallest shift possible are plotted for these events in Fig. 7 . 8 out of the 21 Italian events (35 %) had to be manipulated this way. Such an example is given in Fig. 8  . The unsatisfactory operation of the DMCA method appeared in cases where the peaks of the total precipitation and discharge were close to each other. Hence, the lag time values were compared with the time elapsed between the maxima (Fig. 9  ). It can be seen that except for two events, the resulting lag time is equal to the time elapsed between the peaks applying the minimum shift. It is also visible that the linear regression is more robust between the lag times yielded by the DMCA method and the time elapsed between the peaks than the observed values, which denote the time elapsed between the centers of masses. The presented results highlighted two major application issues for the DMCA method. First, the DMCA method tends to yield values closer to the times elapsed between the peaks of the total precipitation and runoff rather than the centers of masses, despite Giani et al. (2021)  stating that the method should yield the latter. Although the time between the peaks might be close to the time elapsed between the centroids, it should be further clarified, which might be expected from the DMCA method. Second, the DMCA method tends to operate insufficiently when the peaks are close to each other. This behavior might be related to the fact that the DMCA method seems to put more weight on the peaks than on the centers of masses. This might be a substantial disadvantage for strongly asymmetric hyeto- and/or hydrographs, as for smaller catchments with very short response times. This is clearly highlighted by the presented results, where the DMCA method could be used without any restriction for the generally milder Hungarian catchments. In comparison, 35 % of the events were problematic in the case of the steeper Italian catchments. The influence of two essential catchment characteristics, i.e., catchment slope and area, on the observed lag time is visualized in Fig. 10  . In this case, only the catchment-wise average lag time is plotted for each catchment. The Italian catchments where there was at least one problematic event when applying the DMCA method have higher slopes and smaller areas. The apparent effect of the catchment slope on average lag time is also visible. From the dataset used in this study, it seems that catchments with a slope higher than 20 % might have very short response times, resulting in the problems discussed above when applying the DMCA method. This is strongly related to the findings presented in Fig. 5 . where it was shown that the DMCA method performs significantly better for catchments having slopes milder than 15 %.  4.3 Consistency with velocity observations Using the Hungarian-Italian database considered in this work, the grow rates m  (section 2.3.2 ) obtained by the DMCA method and the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas are reported in Table 6  , considering both the average lag time for each watershed and the event-based lag time. Table 6  shows that all the grow rate values computed by the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas, using the event-based estimation of lag time, are substantially in the range suggested by Evangelista et al. (2023)  and, therefore, can be considered consistent with observations. Interestingly, even the coefficients “p”  are close to the values that fit the Leopold and Maddock (1953)  and Jowett (1998)  data, respectively equal to 0.22 and 0.33. These values confirm the robustness of the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas when reproducing velocity values, as they were obtained through regressions of results from two-dimensional shallow water model results. The growth rate predicted by the DMCA method exceeds the target range. This discrepancy may stem from catchments with slopes higher than 20 % and very short response times, for which the DMCA has previously indicated application issues discussed in Section 4.2 . When considering the average lag time, the growth rates are greater than the previous values. Both the DMCA and the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas provided substantially similar results, which, however, are slightly out of the target range. However, it is important to bear in mind that the velocity values are estimated using Eqs. (19) and (20)  are affected by all the simplifications and assumptions introduced for its derivation (validity of the Chézy formula, wide rectangular channel). Consequently, these factors unavoidably introduce a degree of uncertainty that is quite challenging to quantify. Our point of view is that the higher values of m  reported in Table 6  are not far from the target range and, considering the uncertainty associated with the use of Eqs. (19) and (20)  can be reasonably considered consistent with the observed values in the literature.  4.4 Uncertainty due to the estimated lag time The estimation of the lag time from rainfall/runoff series is associated with some uncertainty. To address this issue, we have provided two estimations of the lag time, as mentioned in Section 2.3.1 . Specifically, the center of mass of direct runoff has been computed using both the simulated discharge yielded by the Clark hydrological model (TlagA ) and the observed one (TlagB ). While the results shown previously refer to the first parameter, we now consider the second estimation as the reference value to compute the errors in order to understand to what extent the previous results still hold. In Table 7  , the mean absolute error is shown and compared to what was computed before. Table 7  highlights that the errors are slightly greater than those computed previously, but the ranking and the order of magnitude of the results are not affected by the approach used for the lag time estimation.  4.5 Results of the Barbero’s et al. (2022)  simplified formulas based on the structure of the Hack’s law Regarding the 27 watersheds considered in this study, the structure of Hack’s laws is confirmed, with coefficient and exponent values that align well with the papers mentioned in Section 2.2.1 . Specifically, as illustrated in Fig. 11  , an excellent correlation has been obtained (R2  = 0.94). The numerical parameters of the regression law, α = 1.56 and β = 0.56, closely resemble the values found by Willemin (2000)  (α = 1.6 and β = 0.58). The values of K  and c  (see Eq. (17)  related to both this study and suggested values of literature are reported in Table 8  . These values should be employed when A  is expressed in km2  and Rmax   in mm/h. The comparison between the lag time estimated using the original and the simplified Tlag-3 formula is depicted in Fig. 12  . The remarkable agreement between the two sets of predictions is evident from the regression law, which closely aligns with the line of perfect agreement. Considering that different values of α and β result in different values of L  for a given watershed area, the utilization of Eq. (17) , with the values of K  and c  provided in Table 8 , enabled us to examine the potential impact of the user’s choice in deriving the value of L  from DEM. To illustrate, for watersheds with a size of 300 km2 , the values listed in Table 8  may lead to variations up to 25 % in channel length estimation. The mean absolute percentage errors computed using the original Tlag-3 and the simplified Tlag-3 s formulas, using the values reported from Table 8 , are presented in Table 9  . No significant variations are observed with the use of the simplified formulas. These findings underscore that there is no need to extract information on the main channel length, as the simplified formulas can yield similar results to the original ones. The methodology employed to streamline the Tlag-3 formula can be similarly extended to the Tlag-4 equation, thereby circumventing the necessity of generating the channel network. As far as the authors are aware, there is a dearth of studies demonstrating an analogous relation to the Hack law concerning the total length of the channel network. The pairs of data, Lt   and A , pertaining to the Hungarian and Italian watersheds examined in this study, can be characterized by the power law relation delineated in Eq. (22) , exhibiting a notably high coefficient of determination (Fig. 13  ).(22) L t  = 19.3 · A 0.56     where Lt   is km, and A  is km2 . After applying similar algebraic manipulation as done for the Tlag-3 equation, Eq. (22)  can be integrated into the Tlag-4 equation, deriving the simplified version “Tlag-4 s”, as illustrated in Eq. (21) :(23) T l a g 4 - s   = 5.44 · n S · R max     0.425  ·  A 0.301     where R max  is in mm/h and A  in km2 . It should be noted that deriving Eq. (23)  requires both Eq. (22)  and Eq. (17)  to properly evaluate the variables θ1  and θ3 , respectively. Specifically, Eq. (16)  has been utilized with the values of α and β obtained in this study. The comparison between Tlag-4 s and Tlag-3 s formulas shows very limited differences in the values assumed by the exponents and the coefficients characterizing the formulas themselves. This explains the substantial closeness of the predictions obtained using these two formulas (Figs. 3 and 4 ).   5 Conclusions and recommendations The paper focused on exploring the predictive capabilities, robustness, and uncertainty of event-based approaches for lag time estimation in natural watersheds, specifically analyzing two recent methods: the formulas proposed by Barbero et al. (2022) , derived from regressions of results from two-dimensional shallow water modeling and the DMCA approach, that is a statistical method developed by Giani et al. (2021) . To ensure the robustness of the findings, the study selected catchments representing a diverse range of sizes, geographical locations, topographic features, and land use characteristics across Italy and Hungary. Moreover, the hydraulic consistency of the results has been assessed by calculating implied velocities and assessing how velocity varies with catchment size, following the suggestions by Evangelista et al. (2023) . Overall, both approaches yielded reliable predictions of the lag time estimated in the catchments, as reproduced using the HEC-HMS software, and were found to be more accurate than the literature formulas considered in this work, which neglect the role of the storm event. However, each method has specific potential and limitations. Key insights from the research can be summarized as follows.1) The Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas produced fairly accurate predictions in watersheds with geomorphic and climatic features different from those considered during their calibration. This finding is quite surprising, given that they were calibrated using synthetic rainfall data in a limited number of mountain watersheds. This shows the robustness of the overall approach proposed by Barbero et al. (2022) , which is based on regressive formulas derived from results obtained through an integrated physically-based model at the watershed scale. Nonetheless, significant variations in estimated lag time were observed, as expected;  2) the DMCA method provided the best results for milder (slope lower than 15 %) and bigger (area greater than 150 km2 ) catchments but struggled when the peaks of total precipitation and runoff were closely aligned, typical for steeper catchments with very short response times;  3) lag times predicted by both approaches were evaluated in terms of inferred velocities, with the growth rate values between velocity and basin areas showing a fairly good agreement with the suggested ranges by Evangelista et al. (2023)  based on observations, particularly for the Barbero et al. (2022)  formulas, which confirm their physically-based nature. Overall, the predictions provided by the event-based approaches analyzed here may be considered robust, as they demonstrate consistency with velocity observations.  4) notably, the Tlag-3 formula demonstrated superior performance across the entire dataset, with errors not exceeding 35 %. For the steepest and the smaller catchments, Tlag-2, Tlag-3, Tlag-4 formulas provided the most accurate results;  5) the Tlag-3 and Tlag-4 formulas can be further simplified based on the structure of Hack’s law. These simplified formulas provided comparable results to the originals and eliminated the need to estimate the longest flow paths or drainage lengths, enhancing practical usability.    While this study has highlighted the potential of event-based approaches, further research is necessary to enhance them. Specifically, more efforts are required to address the application issues identified for the DMCA method in the steepest watersheds with very short response times. Additionally, although the physically-based formulas considered here have shown accurate results consistent with observations, they could benefit from further refinement through the comprehensive methodology proposed by Barbero et al. (2022) , which relies on the application of the integrated 2D shallow water modeling. To establish more reliable and representative relationships, this methodology should be extended to a larger dataset that encompasses watersheds with even more diverse geomorphic and climatic characteristics. These issues cannot be fully addressed within the scope of this paper and represent avenues for future research development.
1 Introduction Global climate change caused by anthropogenic CO2  emissions potentially stresses terrestrial vegetation and affects carbon–water cycle processes (Reichstein et al., 2013; Reyer et al., 2013 ). Higher atmospheric CO2  concentration acts as a positive radiative forcing which reduces net primary production by changing the global climate (O’Halloran et al., 2012; Zhao & Running, 2010 ). Despite this positive feedback, an increase in atmospheric CO2  concentration also increases vegetation productivity through a process known as the CO2  fertilization effect (CFE) as revealed by both observational and modeling studies (Ainsworth & Long, 2005; Friedlingstein & Prentice, 2010 ). This has negative feedback on the atmospheric CO2  concentration because plants act as a carbon sink by capturing CO2  from the atmosphere (Liu et al., 2019 ). Literature highlights such feedbacks of elevated CO2  (Frank et al., 2015a; Reichstein et al., 2013 ), however, there is limited understanding regarding the impacts of CFE on the water cycle specifically on soil moisture (SM) and drought. The inter-annual variation (IAV) of vegetation productivity is governed by several factors, including CFE, SM, temperature (T), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), etc. (Gentine et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2019; Zscheischler et al., 2014; Li et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016 ). On a global scale, total water storage (TWS) including SM is the major driver of IAV of CO2  growth rate (Humphrey et al., 2018; Humphrey et al., 2021 ). Low SM often accompanies high VPD due to low moisture generation from the soil. SM-atmosphere feedback amplifies T and VPD anomalies that further aggravate water stress (Humphrey et al., 2021 ). Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021 ) assessed that the terrestrial carbon sink will become less efficient under SM limitations (Green et al., 2019 ) in a high-warming scenario. However, there is uncertainty in the direction of changes in the plant carbon uptake from the atmosphere due to the role of CFE and increased water use efficiency (WUE), in a low-warming scenario. WUE is the amount of carbon gained by plants per unit of water loss (El Masri et al., 2019 ). It is a physiological parameter based on the theoretical argument that stomata should act to minimize the amount of water used per unit of carbon gained. It is based on the hypothesis that plants have a certain amount of available water storage at any given time and should spend it as efficiently as possible (Cowan & Farquhar, 1977; Medlyn et al., 2011 ). A few studies showed that the CFE (Li et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016 ) resulted in improved WUE, alleviating plant water stress. Plants regulate stomatal conductance to maximize the photosynthesis capacity of the leaf while using the least amount of water (Medlyn et al., 2011 ). However, the role of WUE in mitigating SM stress under enhanced plant growth is not clear. SM saving due to increased WUE can be nullified by SM losses due to increased transpiration (TRAN) under a high leaf area index (LAI) (Singh et al., 2020 ). Moreover, stomatal conductance is also sensitive to T and VPD, which may cause stomatal closure (Grossiord et al., 2020 ). Several studies suggest that WUE can ameliorate plant water stress (Farrior et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2016; Swann et al., 2016 ), but its impact is uncertain during extreme drought conditions (Li et al., 2023; Menezes-Silva et al., 2019 ) when SM stress governs the stomatal conductance (Anav et al., 2018 ). The resultant of (1) increased plant growth and water uptake from soil and (2) increased WUE, due to CFE, determining changing patterns of SM. The response of SM to CFE in India under different climatic conditions is not addressed in scientific literature. In India, a concurrent increase in CO2  emissions (Peters et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2017 ) and vegetation greenness (Chen et al., 2019 ) make the carbon and water cycle interaction complex. With a large population (Coale and Hoover, 2015 ), India has a high food demand and corresponding water demand (Garg et al., 2022 ). The majority of the water demand is met by precipitation, with the rest being fulfilled by region-specific irrigation techniques (Chiarelli et al., 2020 ). In India, the interactions between the carbon and water cycles are region-specific due to high human interventions, higher cropland coverage, and distinct irrigation methods (Verma et al., 2022 ). The number of studies in this direction is limited and they do not explicitly consider the impacts of CFE. In the present study, we aimed to analyze the impact of CFE on SM through plant physiological effects. We have analyzed the same at a country scale and separately for 5 agroecological regions. We used land surface model simulations available in the Land Use Model Inter-comparison Project (LUMIP), which is part of a coupled model inter-comparison project phase 6 (CMIP6) (details in the Methods section). A detailed description of LUMIP experiments was provided by Lawrence et al. (2016) . Meteorological factors like precipitation, temperature, etc. play a crucial role in the variations of SM. However, the research question we are addressing is how the widespread vegetation greening due to CO2  fertilization impacts SM. Therefore, we selected experiments appropriate for analyzing the historical impact of CO2  fertilization on land and vegetation, keeping the meteorological factors the same. Earlier studies used 2 ×   CO2,  an abrupt change in CO2  concentration to investigate the impacts of enhanced LAI and stomatal conductance (Kergoat et al., 2002; McDermid et al., 2021 ). Similarly, the Free-Air Carbon Dioxide Enrichment (FACE) experiment investigated CFE under doubled or quadrupled CO2 , but present ecosystems are subject to a gradual increase in atmospheric CO2  (Ueyama et al., 2020 ). Although the FACE experiment has improved process-based models to represent ecological responses to CFE (Medlyn et al., 2015 ), the limitation lies in the abrupt rise in CO2  concentration. Here, we are using a Land-hist experiment forced with observed CO2  concentration, climate, and all other forcings relevant to land models and reflect more realistic conditions compared to an abrupt increase in CO2 . The impact of CO2  fertilization is isolated by comparing Land-cCO2  experiments with Land-hist. Land-cCO2  is the same as Land-hist, except that CO2  is held constant at the preindustrial level in 1850 (285 ppm). The comparison between Land-hist and Land-cCO2  simulations describes the impacts of WUE and plant growth on land processes due to atmospheric CO2  (increased) only effect.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Land use model inter-comparison project simulations In the present study, we used the Land Use Model Intercomparison Project (LUMIP) (Lawrence et al., 2016 ). LUMIP experiments are explicitly designed to investigate the effects of land use and land cover change on climate and biogeochemical cycling. It also simulates how higher atmospheric CO2  concentrations influence vegetation productivity. The land simulations allow for the assessment of trends and variability in SM, carbon stocks, vegetation dynamics, and the effects of climate change. The primary control experiment of LUMIP is “Land-hist“. Land-hist is a historical land-only simulation that uses historical climate forcing data from the global soil wetness project version 3 (GSWP3). For spin-up, climate mean and variability from the two decades 1831–1850 are recycled and data is available from 1850 to 2014. Land-cCO2  is the same as the Land-hist experiment except that CO2  concentration is held constant at the preindustrial (1850) level of 285 ppm. We analyze CO2  only effect by comparing Land-hist and Land-cCO2 . We used the LAI to represent plant growth. WUE is calculated as the ratio of gross primary productivity (GPP) and TRAN. GPP (kg m−2  s−1 ) is the carbon mass flux out of the atmosphere due to photosynthesis. TRAN (kg m−2 ) is water loss by plant stomata in the atmosphere. WUE is the proxy of plant physiological effect which shows carbon gain per unit loss of water. We selected total SM content (kg m−2 ), which is the SM summed over all soil layers present within the model. In this study, our initial selection process involved choosing five models based on the availability of GPP, LAI, and SM. The CESM2 model is excluded from the analysis due to the disparity between CESM2 GPP and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) GPP (Supplementary Fig. S5 ). Table 1   describes a summary of 5 LUMIP models which provides the outputs for Land-hist and Land-cCO2  simulations. Out of five models, only three (CMCC, CNRM, IPSL) models provide TRAN.  2.2 Observed and reanalysis datasets In India, the limited observations of SM have been explicitly highlighted in the literature (Mishra, 2020; Sebastian et al., 2023 ). We use SM provided by the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM v3.6a: root zone SM) (Martens et al., 2017; Miralles et al., 2011 ) and the European Space Agency's Climate Change Initiative (ESA-CCI: combined active and passive SM product) (Dorigo et al., 2017; Gruber et al., 2019 ) to check the consistency between observations and model outputs. GLEAM data is derived from satellite and reanalysis radiation and temperature data, satellite-based vegetation optical depth data, and a combination of gauge-based, satellite, and reanalysis precipitation data. GLEAM and ESA-CCI SM datasets have been widely used in previous studies to validate simulated SM over the Indian subcontinent, confirming their reliability for the region (Kushwaha et al., 2021; Mishra, 2020; Nair & Indu, 2019; Pal & Maity, 2021 ). Notably, Vangala & Chandrasekar (2022)  compared GLEAM data with SM data obtained from the advanced scatterometer (ASCAT) and reported consistently low differences with higher correlation (r ∼ 0.5–0.9) and lower root mean square error than other reanalysis products across different climatological regions in India. Furthermore, Joy & Satheesan (2023)  demonstrated that GLEAM effectively captures temporal variations in SM in India, supporting the suitability of the dataset for our analysis. Both GLEAM and ESA-CCI SM datasets are available at a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° and a daily temporal resolution. Spatial means for these datasets are computed for both India and its agroecological regions. Additionally, monthly means are calculated for comparison with simulated SM data. The entire analysis is conducted over a period of 35 years (1980–2014). To ensure the consistency of simulated GPP and precipitation data, we use the proxy of observed GPP data from the MODIS (Running, 2015 ) and FLUXCOM (Jung et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2020 ), along with precipitation data from the India Meteorological Department (IMD) (Pai et al., 2014; Rao et al., 2009 ). Agroecological regions are obtained from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research-National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (ICAR-NBSS&LUP), which provides 20 agroecological zones based on climate, growing period, soil type, etc (Sehgal et al., 1990 ). We aggregated 20 agroecological zones into 5 climate regions (Supplementary Fig. S1 ): arid, semi-arid, sub-humid, humid, and coastal.  2.3 Standardized precipitation index To understand the impact of precipitation deficit and surplus periods, we use precipitation from LUMIP. Standardized precipitation index (SPI) is calculated following Mckee et al. (1993) . We used 35 years (1980–2014) of continuous monthly precipitation data and calculated the 6-month moving sum of precipitation for SPI6. This data is fitted to a gamma distribution, which is then transformed into a standard normal distribution (μ   = 0, σ   = 1) using the inverse normal of the probability of precipitation. It provides the deviation of precipitation (SPI) from the standard normal distribution. Using SPI6 values, we divided SM into 3 periods: dry (SPI<-1), normal (−1 ≤   SPI ≤   1), and wet (SPI>1).  2.4 Peter Clark Momentary conditional independence The most widely used correlation analysis gives an idea about the association. Two variables X and Y may be associated through a third variable (Z), a common driver (Z ⟶    X and Z ⟶    Y), or a mediating variable (X ⟶    Z ⟶    Y) (Reichenbach & Morrison, 1956 ). In complex dynamical systems like Earth, where real experiments are not feasible, observations and model outputs open up the data-driven causality approaches (Runge, et al., 2019a ). Peter Clark Momentary Conditional Independence (Runge, 2018; Runge et al., 2019b ) (PCMCI) is well well-established causal discovery approach that removes the spurious links due to a common driver or mediating variable. In the variable set X  ¯    = {X ,  1  X ,  2  X ,  3  ⋯ X  n    }, where n denotes the total number of variables within the system, PCMCI computes the causality among these variables, forming a network in which arrows denote causal links and nodes represent individual variables. It involves two steps: PC and MCI. PC step starts by initializing a parent set for each variable using the entire past. If ( X  t  j  )     represents distinct variables at time t, the initial parent set includes:(1) P ( X t  j  )  = { X t - 1 ⋯ t - τ ,  1  X  t - 1 ⋯ t - τ ,  2  X t - 1 ⋯ t - τ ,  3  ⋯ X t - 1 ⋯ t - τ  n  }      where τ   indicates the maximum number of lags. After initializing the preliminary parent set, PC step assess the conditional independence between of X t  j    with each variable within the parent set P ( X t  j  )    as follow:(2) PCstep : X  t  j    ⫫  X  t - τ  i   | S     where ⫫   represents the independence, and S   is the condition set which represents a subset of P X t  j    \  X t - τ  i     comprising ρ   elements. We keep on increasing ρ   and test whether X t  j    is independent of X t - τ  i   . If X t  j    is independent of X t - τ  i   , we eliminate X t - τ  i    from the parent set of X t  j   . During the initial iteration (ρ   = 0), uncorrelated variables are eliminated from P X t  j      . In second iteration (ρ   = 1), variables that become independent after conditioning on the most highly correlated variable from the previous iteration are removed. This process continues, where variables that become independent after conditioning on the ρ   strongest drivers from the previous iteration are eliminated from P X t  j      . The algorithm converges when we cannot expand the condition set S  , indicating that ρ   has reached the number of elements in the parent set P X t  j      . PC step reduces the parent set as small as possible so that it contains only relevant variables. Intuitively, it escapes the curse of high dimensionality, by removing the irrelevant variables in the parent set, which can reduce the strength of the link and even give a spurious link. PC step chooses the parents based on a significance value (α PC    ). However, for unspecified α PC     (α PC   = n o n e   ), it determines the optimal value of α PC     based on the Akaike Information criterion. The MCI step uses the parents set obtained in the PC step and determines the strength of the causal link between the variables (Equation (3) .(3) MCIstep : X  t  j    ⫫  X  t - τ  i   | P X  t  j     \   X  t - τ  i   , P X  t - τ  i    ∀  X  t - τ  i   ∈  X ¯     MCI step also includes real-time variables (τ = 0) so that any real-time association can be identified. However, this link will be unidirectional because the cause must precede the effect in time. The difference between the PC step and MCI step is that the PC step considers only the parents of X t  j    in conditioning set S   but the MCI step also includes parents of X t - τ  i   . Hence, MCI helps us to control the false positive rate by accounting for autocorrelation, which may lead to spurious links. This step assigns the strength and significance value to each link. Before applying PCMCI, time series data is detrended and deseasonalized. We use partial correlation and gauss-process distance correlation as conditional independence tests and show only the consistent links with a maximum lag of 3 months and a significance level of 0.05.   3 Results 3.1 Comparison of model simulations with observed data To understand the ability of LUMIP models in simulating SM, we compare the spatially averaged total SM content in India, simulated by Land-hist (SMLand-hist ), with spatially averaged root zone SM obtained from GLEAM (SMGLEAM ). Fig. 1  (a-e) shows normalized anomalies of SMLand-hist  and SMGLEAM . The Mann-Kendall test reveals a slightly increasing trend (p-value < 0.05) in both simulated and observed SM from 1980 to 2014, except for CNRM and IPSL, which exhibit a decreasing trend. Moreover, Land-hist effectively captures the observed country averaged SM interannual variability. The time series of SMLand-hist  and SMGLEAM  (Supplementary Fig. S2 ) show minor trends in the five agroecological regions. SMGLEAM  shows an increasing trend in all agroecological regions whereas SMLand-hist  shows a slightly increasing trend in arid, semi-arid, and coastal regions, and a minor decreasing trend in sub-humid and humid regions. All the simulations captured the variability of the SMGLEAM  in all the regions, and, hence, can be used to evaluate SM changes due to CFE. We also compared the simulated SM with the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (ESA-CCI) SM and found similar results (Supplementary Fig. S3  (a-e)). The scatter plots indicate a significant positive correlation between SMLand-hist  and SMGLEAM  (Fig. 1 (f-j)), ranging from 0.770 to 0.873, and with SMESA-CCI  (Supplementary Fig. S3 (f-j)), ranging from 0.408 to 0.548. Since the Land-hist simulations are forced with observational meteorological data from the global soil wetness project, there is a good match with the observations for SM. Precipitation is kept the same in both Land-hist and Land-cCO2  which is taken from the global soil wetness project (GSWPv3) reanalysis data. We compared the simulated precipitation with the IMD (Rao et al., 2009 ) precipitation. The spatial mean (Supplementary Fig. S4  (a-e)) exhibited a good agreement between model simulations and observed data. The higher precipitation amounts observed in western ghats and northeast India and low precipitation in western India are well represented in the models. The mean seasonal cycle of modeled data follows the exact pattern of observed data except for a slight overestimation in the monsoon season (Supplementary Fig. S4  (f-i)). Scatter plots show a very good correlation between the observed and modeled data (r values varying from 0.85 to 0.93 as shown in Supplementary Fig. S4  (j-m)). Supplementary Figs. S5-S6  compare simulated GPP with observed MODIS (Running, 2015 ) and FLUXCOM (Jung et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2020 ) GPP datasets. The spatial mean indicates that CESM2, CMCC, and IPSL exhibit close agreement with MODIS data (Supplementary Figs. S5 (a-f)), while the spatial patterns of CMCC, CNRM, and IPSL align with FLUXCOM (Supplementary Figs. S6 (a-f)). The spatial mean plot suggests that MPI overestimates GPP compared to observed data (Supplementary Figs. S5 (f) and 6(f)). The mean seasonal cycle of CESM2 (Supplementary Figs. S5 (g)) exhibits a peak in April due to the model-generated high irrigation in the pre-monsoon season, which is not the case in reality (Jha et al., 2022 ). Irrigation during the key crop season in India, the summer monsoon, potentially contributes to the observed change in late-season monsoon characteristics (Devanand et al., 2019 ) and, consequently, impacts vegetation patterns. CNRM and MPI follow the mean seasonal cycle of MODIS (Supplementary Figs. S5 (i and k)), whereas CMCC and IPSL show a peak earlier than MODIS (Supplementary Figs. S5 (h and j)). All models exhibit a peak occurring later than the FLUXCOM GPP data, as illustrated in Supplementary Figs. S6 (g-k). The state-of-the-art models used in LUMIP are still inadequate to address the India-specific irrigation and crop practices (Joseph & Ghosh, 2023 ). Uchale et al. (2023)  also observed this variation in the maximum and minimum values of the mean seasonal cycle, resulting in a phase difference among them. We found that the mean seasonal cycle of most models tends to overestimate GPP compared to observed data, which can be attributed to the CO2  fertilization effect that is not captured by the satellite datasets (De Kauwe et al., 2016 ). The alignment between observed and modeled GPP is noteworthy, showcasing a correlation of −0.26 to 0.62 with MODIS and 0.42 to 0.66 with FLUXCOM data. Notably, CESM2 simulations display a negative correlation (−0.26) with MODIS due to a seasonal pattern mismatch. This discrepancy has been explicitly highlighted, leading to the decision not to use CESM2 for further analysis. The correlation coefficients indicate that MPI has the highest correlation with MODIS GPP, while CNRM has the highest correlation with FLUXCOM GPP (Supplementary Figs. S5 (p) and 6(n)).
