The MODIS and FLUXCOM GPP also show some differences, e.g. the mean seasonal cycle of MODIS GPP shows higher values in the post-monsoon season due to the high SM from monsoon recharge acting as a soil-vegetation capacitor and also due to the rabi cropping season (Das et al., 2023; Sebastian et al., 2023 ). The mean seasonal cycle of FLUXCOM GPP does not capture this pattern. The FLUXCOM is based on time-varying meteorological data together with the mean seasonal cycle of the remote sensing data of plant growth (Tramontana et al., 2016 ). The FLUXCOM product primarily captures the impact of instantaneous climate variability on GPP, omitting the influence of the current vegetation state. The vegetation state is influenced by both concurrent climate conditions and past vegetation growth, but this aspect is not accounted for in the FLUXCOM product (O’Sullivan et al., 2020 ). The Supplementary Fig. S7  illustrates the spatial trends in LAI using MODIS data and Land-Hist model simulations. Supplementary Fig. S7  (a) shows a widespread increase in LAI across India, with the exception of the Northeast forests and Western Ghats. According to Chen et al. (2019) , agricultural expansion is the primary contributor to this greening trend in India. Most models accurately captured this pattern, showing a decreasing trend in the Northeast Forests and Western Ghats. However, the CESM2 model did not accurately capture the decreasing trend in these regions. The Supplementary Fig. S7  indicates that models generally overestimate the trends in LAI, although CESM2 exhibits a similar magnitude of trend to that of MODIS LAI. Similarly, Supplementary Fig. S8  shows trends in GPP. Supplementary Fig. S8 (a) reveals an increasing trend in GPP across most of India, except in the Northeast Forests, Peninsular India, and the Indo-Gangetic plains. We observed that in Peninsular India and the Indo-Gangetic plains, GPP is decreasing despite an increasing trend in LAI. Das et al. (2023)  also reported the spatial variation between MODIS LAI and GPP trends and attributed it to increased warming over these regions. We found that all models accurately captured the spatial pattern of increasing and decreasing trends in MODIS GPP. However, the models tend to overestimate GPP trends compared to MODIS GPP. Singh et al. (2020)  and Wieder et al. (2019)  found that models often overestimate vegetation greening and productivity due to high photosynthesis sensitivity to increasing CO2 . On the other hand, De Kauwe et al. (2016)  and Keenan et al. (2023)  argue that satellite datasets underestimate the impact of elevated CO2 . Most satellite-based estimates, whether machine learning or algorithmically based, do not account for the observed direct effect of increasing CO2  on the light-use efficiency (LUE) of C3 vegetation leaves. This is because the direct effect of increasing CO2  on LUE cannot be directly observed from space. Therefore, reconciling these discrepancies between models and satellite data necessitates comparing both with eddy-covariance flux tower measurements. Overall, the analysis of spatial trends in LAI and GPP reveals that while models generally capture the broad patterns of vegetation change across India, they tend to overestimate these trends when compared to MODIS observations. We are constrained to use only the satellite observations to evaluate model performances due to the limited availability of in situ measurements. Nevertheless, it is imperative to validate satellite products through ground-truthing. This highlights the essential need for a robust eddy covariance flux tower network across India. In summary, the models exhibit a good agreement with observed data in terms of interannual variation after the removal of trends and seasonality. It is important to note that we performed both the correlation and causal analysis by removing the trend and seasonality present in the dataset, and thereby we can say that our results from the causal analysis will not be affected by differences in trend and seasonality between observed and modeled data. Supplementary Fig. S9  illustrates the difference in SM between the historical (land-only) simulation and three simulations with constant climate, constant CO2 , and no land use change. Supplementary Fig. S9 (a) highlights the impact of climate on SM. Most models indicate an increase in SM, with the arid regions experiencing the largest impact from climate change, while the coastal regions show the least impact among the different agroecological zones. Supplementary Fig. S9 (b) shows the impact of elevated CO2  on the SM. We observed that in most models, the arid and semi-arid regions exhibit the largest decrease in SM. This is primarily due to the dominance of increased LAI over enhanced WUE. It should be noted that arid and semi-arid regions exhibit less SM compared to sub-humid and humid regions. Therefore, the decline in SM in these regions makes them more vulnerable to elevated CO2  levels. Supplementary Fig. S9 (c) shows the impact of land use change on SM. It suggests a mixed response among the models, CESM2 and MPI show an increase in SM, CMCC and IPSL indicate a near-zero impact, while CNRM shows a decrease in SM. Overall, the models suggest an increase in SM as a response to climate, a decrease in response to elevated CO2 , and a mixed response to land use change. It is important to note that the impact of CO2  fertilization depends on the relative roles of increased LAI and WUE, which can partially offset each other. This is why the change in SM in response to CO2  differs from the impacts of climate and land use change. Although climate and land use have more prominent effects on SM, the impact of CO2  fertilization should not be overlooked, as it may become more significant in the future. Therefore, the present study investigated the influence of CFE on SM using the Land-Hist and Land-cCO2 .  3.2 Mean seasonal cycles and interannual variations Fig. 2   presents the mean seasonal cycles of GPP, TRAN, WUE, LAI, and SM as simulated by Land-hist and Land-cCO2  experiments. All the simulated variables in both experiments have strong seasonal patterns associated with the seasonal climate of the Indian sub-continent and are consistent with monsoonal rain. The mean seasonal cycle for GPP (Fig. 2  (a-d)) begins to rise in June, the starting of the Indian summer monsoon, peaks in August-September (end of monsoon), and then starts declining. The SM (Fig. 2 (q-t)) peaks in August (peak monsoon) and September (end of monsoon) due to the seasonal patterns of monsoon rainfall. TRAN (Fig. 2 (e-h)) peaks during the end of the monsoon, with a high SM availability as increased plant water availability leads to more water loss. Monsoon rainfall drives the seasonal patterns of the simulated LAI (Fig. 2 (m-p)). WUE (Fig. 2 (m-p)), the ratio of GPP to TRAN is dominated by the seasonal pattern of GPP and exhibits a similar pattern as GPP. High GPP during the monsoon season is due to high water availability (Fig. 2 (a-d)). We also found a high TRAN due to the same factor. While GPP endeavors to enhance WUE, TRAN exerts a counteracting influence on the same ratio during the monsoon season. Our findings indicate an increase in WUE in the monsoon, signifying a predominant role played by GPP in this dynamic. Had TRAN exerted a more substantial impact, it could have led to a reduction in WUE during the monsoon. A comparison between the two experiments shows the impacts of CFE on increasing GPP that is consistently visible across all the models (Fig. 2 (a-d)). The GPP dominates in the WUE ratio which leads to increased WUE ((Fig. 2 (i-k)). Ideally, CFE results in a reduction in plant water use (Ukkola et al., 2016 ); however, higher LAI due to CFE (Fig. 2 (m-p)) leads to higher TRAN ((Fig. 2 (e-g)). Supplementary Fig. S10  illustrates the comparison between two components of evaporation: (1) TRAN and (2) soil evaporation. The difference in spatial mean of soil evaporation between Land-hist and Land-cCO2  shows an increase in TRAN and a decrease in soil evaporation in Land-hist simulation compared to Land-cCO2  (Supplementary Fig. S10 (a-f)). This is also evident in mean seasonal cycles (Supplementary Fig. S10 (j and l)) of the soil evaporation except for CNRM, where the opposite pattern is observed (Supplementary Fig. S10 (k)). The increase in TRAN and decrease in soil evaporation can be attributed to the increase in LAI. The greater leaf surface area leads to increased TRAN in Land-hist as more leaves are actively involved in plant water use. This increase in LAI surpasses the impact of improved WUE, which would typically reduce TRAN per unit of carbon gained. A higher LAI not only increases TRAN but can also provide more shade to the soil surface, reducing direct exposure to sunlight. This shading effect can decrease soil evaporation by limiting the energy available for evaporation from the soil surface. Notably, the increase in TRAN is higher than the decrease in soil evaporation. As a result, SM has slightly decreased in Land-hist compared to Land-cCO2 , indicating the dominance of LAI. The decrease in SM is not visible in monthly mean seasonal cycles. Therefore, we analyze the two experiments at an annual scale (Fig. 3  (a, c, e, and g)), revealing a distinct decline in Land-hist SM. This reduction is also evident in the difference in mean seasonal cycles illustrated in Fig. 3 (b, d, f, and h). We found similar results in 5 agroecological regions as shown in Supplementary Figs. S16-S17 . Although the model agrees on the reduction of SM, there is limited consensus regarding the amount of reduction (Fig. 3  and Supplementary Figs. S16-S17 ), showing uncertainty across model simulations. The precipitation forcing is the same in Land-hist and Land-cCO2  simulations; hence, the differences in TRAN between the simulations mainly depend upon the differences in LAI and WUE. The dominance of either LAI or WUE determines the direction of the change in TRAN. Our results show that the combined effect of increased LAI and enhanced WUE is a net increase in TRAN, which in turn reduces SM (Fig. 2 ). While our results imply that enhanced LAI inhibits the translation of increased WUE to SM in India during the historical period (1980–2014), it is important to note that despite the decline in SM (Fig. 2 (q-t)), there has been a positive increase in GPP (Fig. 2 (a-d)), and hence an increase in the WUE (Fig. 2 (i-l)). The mean seasonal cycles for five agroecological regions, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S11-S15 , exhibit similar patterns to those shown in Fig. 2 , with minor deviations due to regional climatological conditions. A comparison between the two experiments shows that in arid regions (Supplementary Fig. S11 ), there is a clear reduction in monthly mean seasonal cycles of SM in IPSL, and MPI models. In contrast, CMCC and CNRM exhibit minimal alterations in TRAN, consequently resulting in less pronounced declines in the mean seasonal cycles of SM when compared to other models. In the arid region, the baseline LAI remains low due to water limitations. Vegetation in these water-limited regions has evolved to withstand dry conditions and sustains its productivity through effective water utilization. Under high CO2  concentrations, increased CFE and WUE help the plants to maintain GPP and LAI. This, in turn, leads to an increased water demand and results in a subsequent decrease in SM. Similarly, in semi-arid regions (Supplementary Fig. S12 ), the decrease in SM is visible in mean seasonal cycles in all the models. In water-limited regions, vegetation predominantly consists of shallow-rooted species that primarily rely on upper SM, in contrast to deep-rooted forests, which extract groundwater. In comparison to water-limited regions (arid and semi-arid) (Supplementary Figs. S11-S12 ), energy-limited regions (humid and coastal) (Supplementary Figs. S14-S15 ) demonstrate a substantial increase in LAI, with the most pronounced increase occurring in humid regions. However, the corresponding decrease in SM is not evident, even within the annual time series of humid regions (Supplementary Fig. S14 ). This phenomenon can likely be attributed to the limited or absent representation of deep soil layers and groundwater within the models (Fan et al., 2017; Scanlon et al., 2018 ). In humid regions, deep-rooted forests are significantly influenced by deep groundwater reservoirs. The comparative analysis reveals a more pronounced difference in WUE between the two experimental scenarios in arid and semi-arid regions, whereas the difference in LAI is more prominent in humid and coastal regions. This indicates the distinct mechanisms within water and energy-limited regions. In water-limited regions, the optimization of water utilization comes at the expense of productivity, while in energy-limited regions, the focus is on maximizing LAI, even if it results in water consumption from deep layers of soil (Requena-Mullor et al., 2023 ). These findings highlight the necessity for enhancing the representation of deeper soil layers, CFE, and plant physiological traits within land surface models, which would contribute to a more accurate simulation of SM.  3.3 Causal analysis We performed statistical analysis to understand the processes associated with changes in SM due to CFE through plant growth and the physiological effect. We focus on causal inferences to the differences in the simulated variables between both the simulations, Land-hist and Land-cCO2.  First, we applied lagged correlation to understand the spatial association between the differences of variables from the two simulations for individual models. All models agree that changes in lagged LAI have negative correlations with changes in SM (Supplementary Fig. S18 ). Interestingly, the strength of the correlation is less in the northeast and western forest regions. It implies that deep-rooted forests extract water from deeper groundwater without impacting surface SM, as opposed to shallow-rooted vegetation that relies on surface SM. A negative relationship between lagged LAI and SM most likely indicates the causal direction from LAI to SM but does not confirm causality. Higher LAI leads to higher water extraction and lower SM. We also computed the spatial correlation between the lagged WUE and SM (Supplementary Fig. S19 ). We found mixed signs of correlation across the country; however, there is a slight dominance of positive correlations. A positive correlation between WUE and SM does not imply causation, but it suggests the potential for increased SM with higher WUE. The positive correlation between WUE and SM is intuitive; however, the absence of a positive correlation over many regions in India, clearly indicates the role of other factors, such as changing LAI. Indeed, the increased WUE promotes SM by regulating TRAN. A lower TRAN indicates a lower demand for water by vegetation, increasing the SM. Such impacts of CFE on SM were also reported in the literature for different regions across the globe (Kergoat et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2020 ). If the LAI remains constant, CFE will typically increase SM by reducing TRAN (increasing WUE). The other pathway of CFE impacts is the increased LAI that increases the collective TRAN at an ecosystem level. Since correlation does not imply causality (Runge, et al., 2019a ), we applied a causal discovery approach to the same simulations. To ascertain the causal direction, we investigated the impact of CFE on SM variability using a well-established causal discovery method known as Peter Clark Momentary Conditional Independence (PCMCI) (Runge, 2018; Runge et al., 2019b ). Before applying PCMCI, any seasonality or trend in the data is removed. We used the differences in the variables, WUE, LAI, and SM between the simulations for the causal inference method. Since we are interested in drivers of SM variations, we only showed the incoming links to SM from WUE and LAI. We considered a memory of up to 3 months (3-lags). Fig. 4   (a) shows the causal network between LAI, WUE, and SM for the CMCC model. LAI sends a negative causal link to SM at the lag of 1 and 2 months. More LAI leads to more TRAN increasing the plant water demand and reducing SM. Simultaneously, plant physiology attempts to reduce water demand while maintaining carbon gain. This is accomplished by partially closing the leaf stomata, which reduces TRAN and increases WUE. WUE has a positive causal link to SM at 1 and 2-month lags. Causal networks for CNRM and IPSL show similar results as CMCC (Fig. 4 (b-c)). Both models show a negative link from LAI and a positive link from WUE to SM. Hence, we conclude that increased LAI offsets the effect of enhanced WUE on SM during the historical period in India. To understand the variability of the CFE on SM across different agroecological regions, we performed causal analysis separately for 5 agroecological zones. For the arid regions (Supplementary Fig. S20 ), LAI is sending a negative causal link to SM at a lag of 1 to 2 months, whereas WUE is real-time associated with SM (except IPSL). Arid regions typically have limited water availability, and plants need to efficiently use the available water to survive. Therefore, any improvement in WUE immediately affects SM because it directly impacts how much water plants retain and transpire. WUE exhibits a positive causal link in semi-arid, sub-humid, humid, and coastal regions, except for IPSL, which shows a negative causal association in the humid region with a 3-month lag and no link in the coastal region. Overall, the causal relationship remains the same across the agroecological regions, with a negative link from LAI and a positive link from WUE to SM, except in the arid region. It implies that vegetation in arid regions exhibits distinct plant physiological characteristics compared to other regions.  3.4 Responses to dry, normal and wet conditions We further attempted to understand the relative impacts of WUE and LAI on SM during meteorological drought. We used the standardized precipitation index (SPI) (Mckee et al., 1993 ) as an indicator for meteorological drought. We examined the processes under three meteorological conditions derived using SPI6: dry (SPI<-1), normal (−1 ≤   SPI ≤   1), and wet (SPI>1). Fig. 5   shows the probability density functions (PDFs) of SM for both the simulations from LUMIP, based on the availability of all data required for the analysis. We found that the PDFs of SM in all three meteorological conditions are bimodal which is due to seasonality. The first peak, characterized by lower SM values, indicates the driest period of the non-monsoon season, while the second peak denoted by higher SM values, represents the monsoon season. Supplementary Fig. S21  shows the probability density functions of SM, LAI, and WUE for monsoon (June-September), and non-monsoon (October-May) seasons. India receives more than 80 % of annual rainfall in the period from June to September. The abundant precipitation in the monsoon season leads to increased SM, which increases the photosynthesis activity, and a subsequent rise in the LAI. The high LAI during non-monsoon seasons in CNRM and MPI models suggests non-monsoon agriculture practices. The seasonality of the photosynthesis activity or GPP leads to the seasonal variations of WUE. In the monsoon season, plants are less likely to experience water stress due to sufficient water availability. The comparison of Land-hist and Land-cCO2  reveals that increased CO2  leads to high LAI and WUE, regardless of the season, whether monsoon or non-monsoon. This implies that a rise in CO2  positively impacts vegetation activity during both seasons, enhancing productivity in the monsoon and improving WUE in the non-monsoon period. Consequently, the improved WUE helps to maintain plant growth during non-monsoon periods. Moreover, the reduction in SM observed in both monsoon and non-monsoon seasons suggests that the increased LAI has exerted a higher impact than the improved WUE. The mean of SM (dashed line) is lower in dry conditions (Fig. 5 (a, d, and g)) and higher in wet conditions (Fig. 5 (c, f, and i)), but the relative differences between the simulations are small. CFE resulted in a slight decrease in SM, as evident from modest negative shifts in the mean of Land-hist relative to Land-cCO2  under all conditions. While the differences between Land-hist and Land-cCO2  SM are not substantial in terms of the mean and shape of PDFs for SM under dry, normal, and wet conditions, there is a slight decrease in SM attributed to the increased LAI. It can be inferred that the resultant of opposing impacts of an increase in LAI and WUE in response to CFE (Supplementary Fig. S22-S23 ) determines the change in SM. Supplementary Figs. S22-S23  show an increase in the mean of both LAI and WUE. However, the increase in WUE does not increase SM, owing to the enhanced LAI leading to increased TRAN. In Supplementary Fig. S23 , we show WUE for two models due to the unavailability of TRAN data in the MPI model. Similar to Fig. 5 , we plotted the cumulative density function in Supplementary Fig. S24 , which also indicates a decrease in SM, particularly under dry conditions. In arid regions, SM remains usually less, and plant physiological effects due to CFE tend to be more advantageous under such circumstances. Plants maximize photosynthesis when they have enough water, but in case of water stress, they should use water optimally. Fig. 6   shows the PDFs of SM, LAI, and WUE for the arid region. As compared to other agroecological regions, SM has substantially decreased in arid regions, with a more pronounced decrease during the dry period. Interestingly, even after the reduction in SM, the arid region shows an increase in WUE. This could be because of plant adaptation to water stress conditions or very low TRAN. Even if SM reduces, plants still maintain their growth, resulting in an increased GPP and subsequent increased WUE. These findings align with Gonsamo et al. (2021) , who showed the increasing response of LAI to SM, consistent with the CFE on WUE in water-limited ecosystems. WUE is beneficial when plants need to cope with drier conditions, where water scarcity may limit growth. However, WUE is not able to sustain SM due to increased LAI. One potential pathway could involve a reduction in the critical SM threshold (Fu, et al., 2022a ), indicating a relaxation of plant water stress. With the same meteorological forcing, thus, under the same amount of precipitation, plants tend to close their stomata earlier compared to conditions with higher CO2 . While this helps plants capture more carbon (Supplementary Fig. S25 ), the increased carbon uptake leads to increased water demand, subsequently lowering SM. The causal network for the arid region shows similar results with a real-time association between WUE and SM, suggesting that they interact in real time. However, we cannot comment on the causal direction between them. When SM falls below a certain level, stomatal closure occurs, resulting in a reduction in TRAN cooling and exacerbating the heat stress/dry period (Buckley, 2019 ). The SM limit refers to the critical SM threshold and the wilting point. When SM falls below the critical SM threshold, vegetation experiences water stress. In arid regions, plants are generally adapted to water stress and partially close their stomata to reduce water loss. However, if SM drops below the wilting point, complete stomatal closure occurs. Thus, under severe water stress conditions, the increased WUE does not add value in sustaining plant growth. PDFs of GPP (Supplementary Fig. S25 ) support this conclusion, in dry conditions, GPP does not change much, but under normal and wet conditions PDFs of GPP show a significant increase in Land-hist as compared to Land-cCO2 . WUE maintains plant growth in normal and wet conditions, but in dry conditions, plant growth is limited by water stress. While the most significant decline in SM occurs in water-limited regions (arid and semi-arid), there are minor changes in SM within water-surplus regions (humid and coastal) as shown in Supplementary Figs. S26-S29 . This could be because, regions with limited water resources frequently encounter droughts and stomatal closure, making them more susceptible to a decrease in surface SM (Chaves et al., 2016; Orth et al., 2020 ). Conversely, regions with ample water resources typically experience water surplus, and increased WUE in response to elevated CO2  helps to sustain SM (Liu et al., 2020b ). Another possible explanation could be that in water-surplus regions, deep-rooted trees utilize groundwater (Humphrey et al., 2018 ). Therefore, the increase in WUE and LAI due to increased CO2  in these areas might not significantly affect surface SM, but rather the groundwater levels. The weak correlations observed between LAI and SM in Northeastern forests and the Western Ghats indicate similar findings (Supplementary Figs. S18-S19 ).   4 Discussion and conclusions The interaction between the climate, carbon, and water cycle is a complex dynamic process that is influenced by a multitude of factors (Gentine et al., 2019; Humphrey et al., 2021; Seneviratne et al., 2010 ). In recent years, there has been a growing interest in understanding the role of the CO2  fertilization effect (CFE) in shaping these interactions (Chen et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023 ). Our study contributes to this understanding by investigating the impacts of CFE on SM variations in India. Previous research has highlighted the significant influence of climate and land use on the terrestrial water cycle (Dai, 2012; Trenberth et al., 2013 ); however, there is uncertainty regarding the role of CFE. In this study, we use LUMIP simulations to investigate the role of CFE on SM in India. We hypothesize that elevated CO2  concentrations lead to increased plant growth, which in turn raises transpiration demands and potentially reduces SM. This reduction may be somewhat mitigated by enhanced WUE. The objectives of this study are: (1) to examine how simulated SM changes in response to CFE driven by plant physiological adaptations; (2) to analyze the roles of two key factors—enhanced WUE and increased plant growth—under elevated CO2  levels across different agroecological regions in India; and (3) to evaluate SM responses under varying precipitation conditions (dry, normal, and wet) using the standardized precipitation index. 4.1 Influence of plant growth, and WUE on SM under increased CO2  First, we compared SM simulated by models (Land-hist simulations) for historical period (SMLand-hist ) with GLEAM data (SMGLEAM ) and satellite data (SMESA-CCI ). We found that Land-hist simulations capture the interannual variability of observed SM well. We analyzed the impact of CFE on GPP, WUE, LAI, and TRAN using the mean seasonal cycles. CFE increases GPP, which dominates the WUE ratio, leading to increased WUE. The higher LAI resulting from CFE increases TRAN, and this increase in TRAN outweighs the reduction in TRAN due to increased WUE, resulting in a slight reduction in SM in the Land-hist simulation compared to Land-cCO2 . Using the PCMCI method, we investigated the causal relationships between LAI, WUE, and SM. The results indicate that increased LAI has a negative impact on SM, while enhanced WUE has a positive impact on SM. Our findings show that CFE plays a crucial role in driving SM variations in India. Higher CO2  concentrations have been shown to stimulate photosynthesis, leading to increased plant growth and higher LAI (McDermid et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2020 ). This enhanced plant growth, while contributing to enhanced water demand for TRAN, is counteracted by the partial closure of stomata and improved WUE (Buckley, 2019; Evans & von Caemmerer, 1996; Lawson & Vialet-Chabrand, 2019 ). The combined effect of increased plant growth and improved WUE has resulted in a slight decrease in SM during the historical period (1980–2014). Our results are in agreement with Singh et al. (2020) , who found that plant growth nullifies the effect of increased WUE on streamflow under elevated CO2  in the Southeastern United States. However, they observed a net zero combined effect of WUE and plant growth on streamflow which suggests the complex interplay of regional factors, climate conditions, and ecosystem characteristics, highlighting the need for region-specific investigations. Further, we extended our analysis to various agroecological regions within India. We found similar results in all agroecological regions, an increase in LAI and WUE along with a decline in SM, with a particularly pronounced decrease within arid regions. Although dry regions exhibit less vegetation activity, they show a distinct response due to plants' adaptive strategies to water stress and elevated CO2 . Zhang et al. (2022)  indicate that elevated CO2  decreases precipitation sensitivity by reducing leaf-level TRAN, particularly in wet regions. In drylands, however, this leaf-level TRAN reduction is overridden at the canopy scale by a large proportional increase in leaf area. The increased sensitivity for global drylands implies a potential decrease in ecosystem stability and greater impacts of droughts in these vulnerable ecosystems under continued global change. Kong et al. (2023)  found that WUE has a significant increasing trend in the arid and semi-arid areas of Northwest China with rising CO2  concentrations, but SM showed a significant drying trend. In contrast, WUE and SM showed an increasing trend in humid areas, suggesting an enhanced sensitivity of elevated CO2  to SM in arid and semi-arid areas. Additionally, Lu et al. (2016)  compared soil water content under ambient and elevated CO2  treatments, finding an 11 % increase in soil water availability under elevated CO2  in both drylands and non-drylands, with a statistically stronger response in drylands (17 % vs. 9 %). Ukkola et al. (2016)  also showed that in the dry regions of Australia, runoff declines are amplified by CO2 -induced greening, which leads to increased vegetation water use.  4.2 Agroecological variability in SM dynamics with increased CO2  concentration SM carries the long-term memory of precipitation. To check the impact of precipitation, we evaluated SM under dry, normal, and wet conditions. While we observed marginal shifts in mean SM across all agroecological regions, the arid regions exhibited the most substantial changes. This emphasizes the importance of stomatal limitation under plant water stress conditions, particularly in arid regions. In comparison to arid regions, water-surplus areas (humid, coastal) may exhibit lower WUE due to reduced stomatal resistance resulting from abundant water availability. However, the higher vegetation density in these regions leads to high WUE. Our findings indicate that water-surplus regions exhibit high WUE, primarily due to their dense vegetation. Furthermore, the increase in WUE under elevated CO2  levels can be attributed to the increase in GPP resulting from CFE (Sun et al., 2023 ). It implies that under increased CO2 , plants use less water to assimilate the same or increased amount of carbon. Theoretically, WUE is beneficial under drier conditions when plants need to cope with water stress, but it is less important when ample water is available (Eamus, 1991; El Masri et al., 2019 ). However, recent Free-Air Carbon Dioxide Enrichment (FACE) experiments (Obermeier et al., 2016 ) show that CFE is more prominent under normal conditions and even reduced in drier conditions. Such a finding is in contrast with the classic view that WUE is generally high under drier/hotter conditions. The reason is that the plants are adapted to normal conditions. In water stress situations, resource limitations, e.g., nutrient limitations in dry soil, high T, and VPD, limit plant growth and stomatal conductance (Fu et al., 2022c ). The incomplete knowledge of plant physiological responses to elevated CO2  for different climatic conditions leads to uncertainty in the modeling of terrestrial water and carbon cycle interactions (Frank et al., 2015b; Ueyama et al., 2020 ). In humid and coastal regions, the deep-rooted forests may not extract water from surface SM, but deeper layers of groundwater. An increase in LAI depletes groundwater, which is not captured by the models. Models only provide information about surface root-zone SM (Scanlon et al., 2018 ). It is one of the limitations of our work which requires data for deep layers of groundwater. Some satellite observations provide groundwater data (Save et al., 2016 ), but they underestimate CFE on vegetation productivity (Keenan et al., 2023; De Kauwe et al., 2016 ). Moreover, we cannot separate the effect of climate and CFE directly in observations, and hence, we have to rely on models. We use land-only simulations to separately analyze the mechanism of CFE on SM which is not possible with observed data.  4.3 Water stress adaptation and stomatal behavior in response to CO2  enrichment The literature indicates that SM transitions through three distinct stages: drainage (abundant water in the soil), energy limitation (high SM with energy-constrained evapotranspiration), and water limitation (low SM leading to water-regulated evapotranspiration) (Akbar et al., 2018 ). Additionally, WUE depends upon the ability of plant species to cope with water stress. Recent studies (Fu et al., 2022a,b ) showed that during water stress conditions plants follow two adaptation strategies. In arid and semi-arid ecosystems that experience frequent dry periods, plants partially close their stomata and maintain photosynthesis but after a critical threshold, a rapid stomatal closure occurs to prevent hydraulic failure (McDowell, 2011 ). However, in humid and sub-humid ecosystems, a more gradual stomatal closure takes place in response to a decrease in SM, which enhances plant growth, but under severe drought conditions, they are more susceptible to hydraulic failure (McDowell et al., 2008 ). To comprehensively assess the influence of CFE on critical SM threshold, a more thorough analysis is necessary. Furthermore, certain plant species (such as Crassulacean acid metabolism , like Cacti) in dry areas adopt a strategy of closing their stomata during daylight hours to prevent water loss, while opening them at night when temperatures are cooler (Black & Osmond, 2003 ). This suggests that the region-specific and plant-level investigation will be helpful to get more insights about CFE on SM.  4.4 Synthesis of key findings and implications The increasing atmospheric CO2  concentration increases the photosynthetic carbon uptake and enhances the WUE as revealed by both satellite and global ecosystem models (Ruehr et al., 2023; Walker et al., 2021; El Masri et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2016 ). Global satellite datasets show a prominent greening pattern over India, which is largely attributed to land use management activities (Chen et al., 2019 ), CFE (Zhu et al., 2016 ), and improved WUE (Cheng et al., 2017 ). However, the resulting net impact of CO2  fertilization on SM is poorly understood. CO2  fertilization influences SM by two conflicting pathways. The first involves decreased stomatal conductance as WUE increases, leading to reduced TRAN (Keenan et al., 2013; McDermid et al., 2021 ). Conversely, the second pathway involves an increase in the LAI, resulting in increased plant water uptake. Thus, the plant response to CO2  fertilization may increase or decrease the TRAN, which introduces complexity to the regulation of SM. The model outputs show an increase in LAI and GPP in response to CO2  fertilization, which is also observed from the satellite records (Chen et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2016 ). While satellite records show widespread greening in India, the implications of this greening on SM are not clear. Our analysis provides evidence for the increasing impact of LAI on interannual changes in SM in India since the 1980 s. Using LUMIP model outputs, we show that increased LAI reduces SM by dominating the response of TRAN. Moreover, our results highlight that after the reduction in SM, even under drought conditions, WUE maintained LAI, emphasizing the essential role of WUE in vegetation activity. The future response of SM to CO2  will depend upon the extent of warming and land use management practices, and therefore future studies should focus on these aspects.  4.5 Challenges and prospects for future research The primary limitation of our study arises from the unavailability of observed vegetation and SM data, compelling us to rely on satellite products. Consequently, our dependence on satellite observations to evaluate model performance is a notable constraint. Another limitation stems from the uncertainty present across the models, such as the misrepresentation of the crop cycle in the CESM2 model, resulting in different seasonal variations of GPP from observations and other models. Lastly, the coarse-resolution model simulations restrict our ability to accurately capture plant-specific traits, especially in small shrub forests or vegetation patches. The coarse-resolution averages out the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation, soil, and topography, resulting in the loss of critical local-scale processes and variability essential for accurately modeling vegetation and SM dynamics. Additionally, coarse resolution is insufficient for studying highly diverse large forests, like those in the Western Ghats. This inadequacy hampers a thorough understanding of CFE induced changes in vegetation and SM within these ecosystems. However, fine-resolution models, while capable of addressing these issues, demand significant computational power and extensive ground-based observations. In India, the unavailability of flux tower measurements and observed SM data leads to reliance on these models. While we focused on the impact of greening and plant physiological effects on SM, future research should explore the combined impact of elevated CO2  through multiple pathways, including atmospheric dryness and temperature changes. Regional land surface modeling efforts, along with investigations into plant-level responses, are essential to enhance our understanding of these complex interactions and their implications for ecosystem sustainability and water resource management.
1 Introduction Floods are natural hazards having high frequencies of occurrence and causing significant harm(Hu et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2021). According to an estimate by Tellman et al. (2021) , the global flooded area reached 2.23 million km2  from 2000 to 2018 and the number of the directly affected people reached 255–290 million. With the intensification of global climate change and the agglomeration of urban populations, urban flooding has become increasingly frequent worldwide, causing serious losses to people’s lives and property(Mudashiru et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024 ). Taking China as an example, many cities are facing threats resulting from heavy rainfall and floods and, according to the China Flood and Drought Disaster Bulletin, more than two-thirds of Chinese cities have experienced severe urban flooding events. Moreover, during the period of 2010–2017, the number of cities affected by floods reached an average of 176 per year, with as many as 258 cities affected in 2010. The annual disaster-stricken population reached 113 million, and the annual direct economic loss was as high as 1.98 × 1011  yuan (China Flood and Drought Disaster Bulletin, 2018 ). Some cities are experiencing a compound flooding impact as a result of multiple drivers, such as typhoons, astronomical tides, floods from the upstream watershed, and sea-level rise(Fang et al., 2021; Hsiao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2019 ). During many urban flooding events, the surging floodwater is often accompanied by strong wind, hail, and thunder and lightning(Spencer, 2023; Wang and Marsooli, 2021 ). These compound effects have led to more serious impacts on pedestrian safety in high-density cities than single flooding events(Fang et al., 2022; Nicholls et al., 2021 ). Taking the accompanying wind as an example, Hurricane Sandy in 2012 hit the United States and especially the low-lying coastal regions in New York City, causing $ 1.9 × 1010  USD in damage and 43 fatalities, for which the strong wind played a crucial role according to post-event surveys and analyses(Wang and Marsooli, 2021 ). Recently, strong convective weather including sudden local short-term heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and strong winds occurred on March 31, 2024, in the city of Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi Province, China. This event affected 313,000 people, and 115 households with 263 houses were seriously damaged, causing a direct economic loss of 400 million yuan. More seriously, the strongest wind speed in this event reached 35.3 m/s at 4 a.m. on March 31, resulting in the falling deaths of three residents (Chinanews, 2024). These disasters highlight that performing pedestrian risk assessments under the joint effect of surging floodwater and strong winds is of importance in many urban flooding events. Wind flows are complicated in densely populated cities(Blocken et al., 2016; Mittal et al., 2020 ). In research examining the wind environment and air pollution dispersion within urban blocks, some studies have investigated the effects of multiple geometric factors (urban morphology) on wind comfort and associated pollution concentration(Blocken et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2021; Toparlar et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2021). These factors include the urban density (planar and vertical), urban heterogeneity, and urban enclosure degree on the neighborhood scale and the height aspect ratio, building opening, and viaduct on the street scale(Chen and Mak, 2021; Cui et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2023; Jiang and Gao, 2021; Lee and Mak, 2021 ). For example, Lam et al. (2009)  explored the impact of the size of the cavity on the dynamic wind load performance of the building in the H-shaped high-rise buildings. The results highlighted the role of the existence of the cavity in the dynamic loads of the building, and have indicated that the wind field environment around a single building is greatly affected by the shape of the building and the inflow wind direction. Based on the wind tunnel datasets of high-rise rectangular buildings with wings, Paulla and Dalui (2022) optimized the location of the wings of the building from the aerodynamics perspective, implying that both of the structure of the isolated building and the angle of the wind incident have a significant impact on the distribution of wind fields around the building. The study of You and Ding (2024) have demonstrated that the wind field distribution around the twin buildings is affected by many factors, such as wind direction, wind speed and the building spacing. In current microscale urban flooding studies, numerical simulations and/or physical experiments have been performed to investigate the flow characteristics through elements such as an ideal building, building clusters of various layouts, urban street valleys, intersections, sewers, and flows inside buildings(Liang and Guan, 2024; Mignot et al., 2019 ; Taylor et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2023 ). For example, Liu et al. (2018)  have performed a dam-break experimental study, and have demonstrated that the locked/unlocked condition of the front door of a simplified building plays an obvious role in affecting the water depth difference around and within the building and associated impact force characteristics. The numerical study of Percy et al. (2023)  has showcased that the layout and configuration of buffer blocks along the coast greatly affects the attenuation of tsunami-like flow (flow depth, flow velocity, momentum flux, pressure distribution, Tsunami forces). A recently study performed by Liang and Guan (2024)  focused on the effect of urban drainage inlet layout on surface flood dynamics, and the results have shown that both the distribution configuration and the spacing of drainage inlets have influences on the drainage efficiency and the surface flood discharge. However, because urban buildings often have a complex morphology, the correlation between building configurations and wind/floodwater flow characteristics is not fully explored or understood. Furthermore, studies on the pedestrian risk around complex buildings under the joint impact of floodwater and wind are deficient and require more detailed examination. Therefore, this study examines the effect of the building configuration on the pedestrian risk within an urban block under the joint effect of floodwater and wind. An individual building model is adopted in this study to represent an ideal urban building with different configurations, heights, and orientations to explore the role of these factors with respect to pedestrian safety. A double-building model is also used to investigate the effect of an upstream building on the pedestrian risk around a downstream target building. In this study, we chose three types of complex building configurations for the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. These are “2″–shaped, “﹞”-shaped, and “ョ”-shaped buildings (Fig. 1  ), which are typical building configurations, especially in humid and hot high-density cities such as Hong Kong(Chen and Mak, 2021; Lee and Mak, 2021 ). Although there are also other complex building configurations in some actual urban blocks, such as “I”-shaped, “H”-shaped, “+”-shaped, “C”-shaped and “D”-shaped buildings, they are merely chosen as typical examples to explore the relationship between the building configuration and the characteristics of floodwater spreading and wind blowing in this study based on the following considerations: (1) Three kinds of buildings adopted in the current study contain an axisymmetric configuration (the “2″–shaped building) and also symmetrical configurations along the horizontal direction (the “﹞”-shaped, and “ョ”-shaped buildings), which can demonstrate more fully the impact of irregular building configurations on both floodwater routing and wind blowing around the building in actual urban blocks. (2) Each of these building configurations is comprised of many regular building segments, which can also constitute other types of irregular buildings. The analysis results toward them could also offer insights on the physical mechanism regarding the interaction between the floodwater/wind and the building configuration for other kinds of the complex buildings, for example, the impact of building height, and the influence of the wind/floodwater direction. The remainder of the paper is arranged as follows. Section 2  introduces the methodology adopted in the study, including the case description, the CFD simulation information, the assessment method for the pedestrian risk, and the laboratory flume experiment. In Section 3 , the numerical simulation scheme is validated against existing dam-break and wind-tunnel experimental datasets. The results and discussions regarding pedestrian risk under single- and double-building configurations are presented in Section 4  and Section 5  respectively. Finally, Section 6  explains the limitations of the study and provides concluding remarks. The novelty of this study can be summarized as follows: (1) for an isolated building, synthetically considering the impacts of building configuration, building height and converging and diverging flows on pedestrian safety beneath the building using both CFD technique and the laboratory experiment method when floodwater and wind coexists in urban regions; (2) for an double building configuration, comprehensively considering the effects of many factors on the pedestrian risk around the target building, including the distance of upstream building, the upstream building height, the upstream building length, the upstream building interspace, and the reduced ratio of the upstream building. These research results could shed lights on the physical mechanism regarding the interaction between the building and the inflow floodwater/wind conditions, which offers some references for administrators and stakeholders when implementing tailored measures against direct impacts of surging floodwater and strong wind in the context of resilient city management.  2 Methodology The workflow of the present study for quantifying the impacts of the building configuration and an upstream building on pedestrian risk around ideal buildings under a joint floodwater–wind effect includes (i) considering different scenarios of building configuration and upstream buildings, (ii) validating the CFD results with existing experimental datasets, (iii) conducting simulations for different case studies, (iv)assessing pedestrian risk for various cases, and (v) qualitatively verifying the results via a laboratory experiment. Each of these steps is explained in the following subsections. 2.1 Case descriptions Referring to the Standard for Urban Residential Area Planning and Design in China (GB50180-2018) and numerous actual building layouts in Hong Kong(Chen and Mak, 2021; Lee and Mak, 2021 ), as well as previous studies(Dai et al., 2022; Du et al., 2018a; Hang and Chen, 2022 ), the geometric dimensions of the single- and double-building models are illustrated in Fig. 2  (a)–2(c). Here, the x  −, y  −, and z  −coordinate axes in the Cartesian coordinate system denote the stream-wise, lateral, and vertical directions, respectively, and the x  −coordinate direction is aligned with the input floodwater/wind direction. In Fig. 2 (a) and 2(b), for each of the “2″-shaped, “﹞”-shaped and “ョ”-shaped single buildings, the length and width are 70 m and 35 m, respectively. The “2”-shaped building is comprised of two “L” segments in opposite directions (an axisymmetric configuration), each of which has a length of 30 m and a width of 25 m, and between the two segments there is a column with a length of 10 m and a width of 35 m. The “﹞”-shaped building comprises a center trapezium (with a width of 10 m) and two symmetrical trapeziums with widths of 35 m on its two sides, with an intersection angle of 120°. The “ョ”-shaped building is symmetric along the horizontal direction and consists of two semi-open column groups, each of which has a length of 35 m and a width of 35 m. Choosing the “2″-shaped building with a height H T    of 35 m as the target building, an upstream building was added upstream of it to form the double-building models in Fig. 2 (c). The upstream building is a rectangular-plan building model, with its length and height labeled L U    and H U   , respectively, and the distance between the upstream building and the target building is D T   . As illustrated in Fig. 2 (c), the area of interest is a rectangular area around the target building with a length of 100 m and a width of 70 m, where pedestrians could engage in recreational activities (Chen and Mak, 2021; Liu et al., 2019 ) and where their safety is of concern under a joint floodwater–wind effect. Herein, the inflow wind direction is set to be perpendicular to the building surface for both single- and double- buildings as did by many researchers (Tamura et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023; Chen and Mak, 2021 ), which is different from the typical channel winds that flow primarily along the street within highly dense urban areas (Du et al., 2018b; Huang et al., 2022 ). This is to investigate the impact of wind that directly hits the isolated building on the pedestrian safety beneath within the interest precinct since the focus of this study is on an isolated and irregular building not the building groups (so-called street scale) in urban regions. A reviewing work regarding the urban heterogeneity on street scale (the height aspect ratio and building opening/separation, etc.) in the context of urban pollution dispersion can be found in Li et al. (2021). Table 1   provides a summary of the tested cases. In the upper panel, “A”, “B”, and “C” denote the “2”-shaped, “﹞”-shaped, and “ョ”-shaped single buildings, respectively, and “+” and “−” indicate that the floodwater/wind direction is consistent and opposite to the x  −axis direction, respectively. For example, Case [AM+] indicates a “2”-shaped single building with a moderate height of 35 m under a floodwater–wind effect along the x  −axis direction. The heights of the single buildings range from 20 m (low-rise), 35 m (moderate-rise), to 50 m (high-rise), corresponding to 6-, 10-, and 14-story buildings, which are typical in Hong Kong(Chen and Mak, 2021; Du et al., 2018a ), to investigate the impact of building height on pedestrian risk around the target building. Cases with varying input floodwater/wind direction are included to explore the effect of the inflow direction on pedestrian safety. In the lower panel of Table 1 , we set an upstream building with a length of 60 m, a width of 10 m, and a height of 35 m together with a “2″-shaped building (length of 70 m, width of 35 m, and height of 35 m) as the target building to form a benchmark case to facilitate the following case comparisons; this case is labeled Case [Basic]. Case [D40] and Case [D60] are included to investigate the impact of the horizontal distance between the upstream building and the target building on the pedestrian risk. Six cases (Case [H20], Case [H25], Case [H30], Case [H40], Case [H45], and Case [H50]) are used to explore the possible effects of the height of the upstream building on the pedestrian risk. Four cases (Case [L40], Case [L50], Case [L70], and Case [L80]) are included to examine the effect of the length of the upstream building. Following real-world building configurations(Lee and Mak, 2021 ; Mejía-Morales et al., 2021a, 2023), we divided the upstream building into two and three segments while fixing the total length and changed the interspace distance of the segments to examine the possible effect on the downstream pedestrian risk; these cases are labeled Case [2d10], Case [2d20], Case [3d5], and Case [3d10]. In addition, we adjusted both the length and height of the upstream building to be 0.6, 0.8, 1.2, and 1.4 times the reference case to explore their effect on the pedestrian risk around the target building; these cases are denoted Case [R0.6], Case [R0.8], Case [R1.2], and Case [R1.4].  2.2 CFD simulation information To reduce the necessary computational resources without decreasing the simulation accuracy, this study adopted the reduced scale ratio (1:100) of the wind-tunnel experiment provided by the Architectural Institute of Japan (AIJ)(Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2021; Mittal et al., 2020; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). A wind-tunnel experimental dataset validation study is presented in Section 3 . However, for the floodwater inundation modeling, because the water depth is much smaller than the horizontal dimension of an urban building, there will only be a small number of meshes in the vertical direction or a massive mesh distribution in the horizontal direction if a fixed reduced scale ratio (1:100) is applied to both the horizontal and vertical directions. Geometrically distorted model technology is often proposed to overcome this problem(Li et al., 2020 ). Following such studies and several guidelines regarding urban flooding processes(Biscarini et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2021; Soares-Frazão and Zech, 2008 ), we set the vertical reduced scale ratio to 10 for the floodwater inundation modeling in this study, yielding a geometric distortion ratio (the ratio of the horizontal reduced scale to the vertical reduced scale) of 10. A validation study using existing experimental datasets of urban flooding is presented in Section 3 . 2.2.1 Turbulence model and grid arrangement The Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations with a standard k  –ε   turbulence closure model are employed in this study to model the wind movement and floodwater inundation processes around the buildings(Biscarini et al., 2010; Fondelli et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2021 ). The standard k  –ε   model was chosen based on the validation study in Section 3 . When modeling the wind field around urban buildings, the domain size and grid arrangement obeys the practical guidelines of CFD simulations provided by AIJ(Franke et al., 2012, 2011; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). Referring to the validation study in Section 3  regarding the sensitivity of the simulation results to the grid configuration, the grid size around the surface of the building was set to 5 mm and the grid on the ground around the building was set to 10 mm with a wall layer encryption; the maximum grid size was 160 mm within the rest of the studied domain. For the floodwater inundation modeling around the urban buildings, also referring to the validation study in Section 3 , the grid size around the building and on the ground was set to 25 mm, while the grid size for the rest of the domain was set to 50 mm. Three-layer adaptive grid technology (5 mm) was used for local refinement to ensure the accuracy of the numerical simulation results. This study adopted poly-hexcore volume mesh generation technology based on “mosaic” technology, which can realize node sharing between the hexahedral mesh configuration and the polyhedral mesh configuration without any additional manual mesh settings(Gou et al., 2024 ). Under the premise of full automation, this method increases the number of hexahedrons in the grid configuration, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of the CFD simulation. The grid convergence index (GCI) is estimated to be 1.83 % (if a velocity magnitude relative error of 0.01 m/s is used) and 0.24 % for the floodwater and wind modeling, respectively(Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2021, 2020; Huang et al., 2022 ). The Y+values at the building surfaces for the floodwater and wind modeling are estimated to be 79.39 and 1335 for the wind and floodwater modeling, respectively. These values lie within the recommended values for CFD simulations and are in accordance with several previous modeling studies(Franke et al., 2011; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020; Zhang et al., 2023, 2022 ).  2.2.2 Computational domain and boundary conditions Taking Case [Basic] as an example, Fig. 3   shows the geometric configurations of the computational domain. Following previous studies and practical guidelines regarding CDF models in urban flood and wind modeling studies(Biscarini et al., 2010; Franke et al., 2011; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020; Peng et al., 2021 ), the geometric dimensions of the computational domain are arranged as follows. Let the building height H T    be equal to the characteristic length. The distance between the inlet flow boundary and the upstream building is set to 5 × H T    such that the wind/floodwater routing process can fully develop, whereas the outlet boundary has a long distance of 10 × from the target building to avoid possible effects of return flow(Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020 ). Each side boundary has a distance of 5 × H T    from the target building to minimize the blocking effect resulting from the existence of solid side boundaries(Zhou et al., 2016 ). At H T    = 20 m, 35 m, and 50 m, the total blockage ratio becomes 1.67 %, 2.08 %, and 2.98 %, respectively; these values are lower than the recommended value (3 %) according to best practice guidelines(C Biscarini et al., 2010; Blocken, 2015; Franke et al., 2011 ). In addition, the top of the domain has a vertical distance of 7 × H T    from the top of the target building for the wind modeling, which yields a total number of grids for the computational domain of 2.2–2.70 × 106 . For the urban floodwater modeling, the computational domain is set to have a height of three times the water depth to reduce the required computational resources following previous modeling studies(Biscarini et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2019 ), leading to a total grid number of 8–10 × 104  for the entire domain. Referring to previous CFD modeling studies(Blocken, 2015; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2021, 2020; Mittal et al., 2020 ), to model the urban wind environment, a free outflow condition was set at the outlet boundary of the computational domain, a symmetric boundary condition was applied to the two lateral boundaries and the top boundary of the domain, and the non-slip condition was employed at the bottom boundary of the domain and at the surface of each building (Fig. 3 ). Herein, the symmetrical boundary condition for the wind modelling refers to the fact that there is zero normal velocity and normal gradients of all variables, which has been frequently used by many researchers in the urban wind environment modelling (e.g., Chen and Mak, 2021; Lee and Mak, 2021 ; You and Ding, 2020). At the inlet boundary, a logarithmic wind profile was adopted because it can yield a better horizontal homogeneity of the wind speed distribution within the urban canopy(Zhang et al., 2023, 2022 ). Specifically, the wind profile V w  z      at a vertical position z   and the vertical distribution of the turbulence quantities can be expressed as(Zhang et al., 2023 )(1) V w  z   = V w ∗   κ  ln z + z 0   z 0         (2) κ = V w ∗  2  C μ        (3) ε z   = V w ∗  3  κ z + z 0           where V w ∗     is the friction velocity in m/s, κ   is the von Karman constant (=0.41), z 0    is the roughness height, C μ    is a constant (=0.09), and ε   is the turbulence dissipation rate. The friction velocity V w ∗     can be estimated using the following equation:(4) V w ∗   = κ V w - r e f   ln z ref   + z 0   z 0           where V w - r e f     is the reference wind speed at a reference height of z ref    . In general, z ref     is taken as 10 m, as measured at many meteorological stations(Blocken, 2015 ; Li et al., 2021; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). Here, we use a reference wind speed V w - r e f     of 7 m/s, which represents the condition of a moderate breeze according to the Beaufort wind scale. For the floodwater routing modeling, the boundary settings were as follows (Fig. 3 ). A pressure outlet condition was adopted for the outlet boundary and the top boundary of the computational domain, and symmetry conditions were adopted for the lateral boundaries. A non-slip wall function was used at the bottom of the domain and on the surface of each building. There were two components at the inlet boundary. Referring to real-world urban flooding circumstances and laboratory experimental datasets(Chanson and Brown, 2018 ; Mejía-Morales et al., 2021a; Mignot et al., 2013, 2020; Soares-Frazão and Zech, 2008 ), a steady floodwater condition was used in the lower component with a velocity V f    of 1.2 m/s and a water depth h   of 1 m, yielding a Froude number Fr    of 0.383, which presents a typical urban flooding scenario(Chanson and Brown, 2018; Mignot et al., 2020, 2013 ). In the upper component, an air pressure inlet condition was implemented.  2.2.3 Solution technique and computation processing The volume of fluid (VOF) method can be employed to capture the free surface during floodwater inundation simulations(Biscarini et al., 2010; Fondelli et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2021 ). This method can model both air and water by solving a single set of momentum equations, and the accurate tracking of the water–air interface is realized by solving a continuity equation for the volume fraction of each fluid phase within the computational domain(Gou et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2021 ). The governing equations are discretized using the finite volume method for the spatial variation terms and the forward Euler method for the temporal variation terms(Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020 ). For the wind environment modeling, the SIMPLE (semi-implicit method for pressure-linked equations) algorithm was adopted for the coupling between the pressure and velocity terms in the governing equations. The relaxation factors for the pressure term, momentum terms, the k   equation, and the ε   equation were 0.3, 0.7, 0.8, and 0.8, respectively. The calculation iterations were continued until the residual errors for the continuity, momentum, k  , and ε   equations were below a given small value of 10−5  (Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2021, 2020; Huang et al., 2022; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). For the floodwater modeling, the coupling between the velocity and pressure was performed using the PISO (pressure-implicit with splitting of operators) algorithm. Because the floodwater modeling was toward the transient state of floodwater routing within the urban blocks, we simply chose the simulation results at a simulation time t   of 20 s, at which time the floodwater could reach the outlet boundary of the domain(Biscarini et al., 2010; Gou et al., 2024; Soares-Frazão and Zech, 2008 ). In this study, the CFD software ANSYS Fluent was adopted. Herein, it is worth pointing out that as stated in the study of Venier et al. (2017) , the SIMPLE algorithm and its numerous derivation are mainly used to solve steady state flows, whereas the PISO algorithm was conceived as a transient state flow solver. Since we modeled the wind blowing and floodwater routing within the research domain separately in this study, the SIMPLE algorithm was adopted to model the steady wind speed distribution and the PISO algorithm was utilized to model the transient state of the floodwater inundation around the buildings here. The numerical simulation results can be transformed to a real-world prototype scale following their Froude similarity(Postacchini et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2014 ). The water depth h   has the relationship h p  h n   = e vn     , while the velocity has the relationship V p  V n   = e vn      , where the subscripts p   and n   denote the prototype scale and the model scale, respectively, and e vn     is the geometric ratio used in this study. As for the Reynolds similarity for the wind field modeling within the research domain, the calculated reference Reynolds number Re  is approximately 156,051 if the reference wind speed V w - r e f     is 7 m/s at a reference height z ref     of 10 m, which is much larger than the value of 11,000 needed to satisfy the requirement of Reynolds number similarity between the simulation and the prototype(Lin et al., 2021; Snyder, 1972 ). Finally, because there is a mismatch in the grid configurations between the wind environment and floodwater inundation modeling along the vertical direction because the grid size for the former is much larger than that for the latter, we simulated the wind movement and floodwater routing processes around the buildings using different grid arrangements separately. The modeled inundation depth and floodwater velocity were adopted to represent the floodwater condition, and the wind speed at the pedestrian level (i.e., z   = 1.5 m) was used to represent the wind conditions for pedestrians(Du et al., 2018b; Liu et al., 2019 ). A simple superposition of the modeled floodwater and modeled wind conditions at the same grid position within the research domain during the numerical simulation was used to yield the final results for assessing the pedestrian risk.   2.3 Assessment method for pedestrian risk Some observations have demonstrated that pedestrians on streets or roads are prone to losing their stability in terms of sliding and toppling when surging floodwater hits them within urban regions(Abt et al., 1989; Xia et al., 2014 ). The floodwater velocity and inundation depth are two important variables that can be adopted to characterize the impact of urban floodwater on pedestrians. Strong wind can often hinder the normal walking or running movement of pedestrians in a windy environment. With respect to pedestrians subject to the joint effect of floodwater and wind, Gou et al. (2024)  observed the toppling of a human body model representing a pedestrian in a quasi-natural state when floodwater and wind conditions reached a so-called threshold in a laboratory flume. They derived a theoretical formula to characterize the threshold condition in terms of the floodwater velocity V f   , inundation depth h  , and wind speed V w    at pedestrian level:(5) V w 2  = λ 1  m p  - ρ f  a 1  h h p     2  + b 1  h h p        ∗ a 2  m p  + b 2      h p  - h    h p    - λ 2  V f 2  1 + β    2  h 2   h p  - h    h p    h p  h    2 β       where m p    and h p    are the mass and height of the human body; λ 1   , λ 2   , and β   are three coefficients to be calibrated; ρ f    is the floodwater density; and a 1   , b 1   , a 2   , and b 2    are four empirical coefficients that depend on the physical characteristics of the human body introduced by Xia et al. (2014) . For a typical Chinese person, a 1    = 0.633, b 1    = 0.367, a 2    = 1.015 × 10−3  m3 /kg, andb 2    =  − 4.927 × 10−3  m3 . To obtain the values of λ 1   , λ 2   , and β  , Gou et al. (2024)  performed a reduced scale laboratory flume experiment examining the instability of a dummy; they then adopted these experimental datasets to find λ 1    = 2.31, λ 2    = 12916.60, and β   =  − 0.7038. The accuracy of the dummy against the pedestrian will be discussed in the following subsection (section 2.4 ). Using Eq. (5) , we can adopt the compound hazard rating (CHR ) index to quantify the pedestrian risk within urban blocks under a joint floodwater–wind effect; this facilitates comparisons of the different scenarios.(6) CHR = V w  V w , c        Here, V w    is the modeled wind speed at pedestrian level from the CFD simulations and V w , c     is the wind speed calculated using Eq. (5)  based on the floodwater velocity and water depth from the CFD simulations. This method is simple and straightforward, and a similar method has been widely adopted to quantify the pedestrian risk in urban floodwaters by many scholars, such as Kvočka et al. (2016), Musolino et al. (2020) , and Wang and Marsooli (2021) . Furthermore, following such studies, to facilitate a quantitative comparison for divergent urban building scenarios, we classified the pedestrian risk given the different building scenarios into five classes: Class I (0 < CHR <0.2); Class II (0.2 ≤ CHR <0.4); Class III (0.4 ≤ CHR <0.7); Class IV (0.7 ≤ CHR <1); and Class V (CHR ≥1). It can be seen from Eq. (6)  that, as CHR  exceeds unity, the pedestrian experiences a loss of stability resulting from the combined impact of the floodwater and wind, threatening their safety. Conversely, as CHR  approaches zero, there is little effect on the pedestrian safety. Therefore, these types of pedestrian risk levels can be qualitatively denoted such that Class V is extreme risk, Class IV is remarkable risk, Class III is moderate risk, Class II is low risk, and Class I is safe. This classification of risk rating was used in previous studies(Gou et al., 2024 ). When using Eq. (5) , we adopted the physical characteristics of a typical Chinese male(Xia et al., 2014 ): h p    = 1.7 m and m p    = 70 kg. For areas with CHR ≥1, it is important to identify the dominant factor between the floodwater and wind that triggers the toppling instability of pedestrians to implement tailored measures to protect pedestrians, for example, flood control measures and/or wind-proofing measures. To this end, we directly compared the moment induced by the drag force of the floodwater (M df    ) to that induced by the drag force of wind (M dw    ) using Eq. (5) , as well as the moment induced by the floodwater (M f   ) and that induced by the wind (M w   ), to determine the dominant role of the floodwater or wind for various urban building scenarios. Here, M df     is a part of M f    (which also includes the effect induced by buoyancy), whereas M w    is the same as M dw    . In addition, for areas with CHR <1, the evacuation speed (walking or running) of the pedestrian is an important parameter in emergency evacuations when urban flooding impacts a crowd(Shirvani and Kesserwani, 2021 ). Regarding the movement speed of a pedestrian in floodwater, using a laboratory test, Ishigaki et al. (2008) found that the walking speed of a pedestrian has a power function relationship with the specific force per unit width F  , that is,V f 2  h  g  + h 2  2    . Bernardini et al. (2020)  further proposed the following formula to estimate the walking (V p _ w a l k    ) and running (V p _ r u n    ) speeds of pedestrians in floodwater: V p _ w a l k    ,V p _ r u n    =k 1  V f 2  h  g  + h 2  2     k 2     , where k 1    and k 2    are two empirical coefficients depending on the ages and movement forms of the pedestrians (walking or running). Here, we chose an age range of 21–28 years from Bernardini et al. (2020) , i.e., k 1    = 0.36 and k 2    =  − 0.13 for walking and k 1    = 0.48 and k 2    =  − 0.19 for running. Because there are few studies that report the declining effect of wind on the movement speeds of pedestrians, we used the Beaufort wind scale in China to assess the quantitative relationship between the reduction coefficient φ V w       for the movement speed of a pedestrian and the wind speed V w    via a linear interpolation method: φ V w       = 0.8997 − 0.062 × V w   , with a coefficient of determination of 0.9724. Finally, the evacuation speeds of a pedestrian under a joint floodwater–wind effect can be obtained via a simple multiplication of the floodwater and wind effects: V p _ w a l k    ,V p _ r u n     = φ V w    ∗ k 1  ∗ V f 2  h  g  + h 2  2     k 2     .  2.4 Laboratory flume experiment for dummy stability/instability To qualitatively examine the CHR  distribution within an urban block based on the CFD simulations, a laboratory flume experiment of the stability/instability of a dummy under a combined floodwater and wind effect for various block configurations was performed, as shown in Fig. 4  . The flume was 25 m in length, 0.8 m in width, and 0.8 m in depth (Fig. 4 (a)). The maximum design discharge was 240 L/s (the error in the discharge adjustment lies in a range of ± 1 %), and the maximum water depth within the flume can reach 0.65 m in actual manipulations (due to a limitation in the water supply and regulation system in the flume system after pre-experiments) (Shu et al., 2021 ). During the experiment, the water discharge was monitored by an electromagnetic flowmeter and the water depth was read from a dividing rule that was stuck on the side wall of the flume. Therefore, the cross-section averaged velocity of the floodwater within the flume was equal to the water discharge divided by the area of the cross section. As shown in Fig. 4 (b), the dummy was made of a resin material using 3D printing technology; therefore, its density (1130 kg/m3 ) is close to that of an actual human body. The dummy had a width of 0.05 m and a height of 0.25 m, close to a reduced ratio of 1:5 compared with the actual physical characteristics of a human body. This scale is also devised based on the relative dimension of the dummy and the building physical model, as well as the convenience for observing its behavior under different inflow conditions. The dummy standing in floodwater within the flume was adopted to approximately represent a pedestrian in a quasi-natural state on a street or road in a real-world urban flooding event(Postacchini et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2014 ), although this also leads to a discrepancy. A mobile fan (type: STF-300) together with a speed adjustor device was used to generate the desired wind flow (Fig. 4 (a)). A long aluminum foil tube with a length of 3 m was installed with the fan to direct the wind flow in front of the building models. The wind supply outlet had a large diameter of 30 cm, and the distance between it and the building model was set to 80 cm to allow the wind turbulence to fully develop. During the actual experiment, the building model was completely impacted by the wind. An anemometer (type: DLY-1602C) was used to measure the wind speed in front of the building model, and its measurement range was 0.7–30 m/s, and it accuracy is ± 0.7 m/s when the speed is smaller than 1 m/s, and ±(2.0 % +0.5 m/s) when the speed varies from 1 m/s to 30 m/s. Herein, it should state that there is a difference in the boundary conditions between the numerical model and the experimental design: the former is the rectangular wind inflow, whereas the latter corresponds to the circular inflow wind condition; however, this discrepancy could not affect the qualitative validation of experimental results against the numerical simulation results since there is a distance of 80 cm between the wind outlet and the building, which could be enough to render the wind turbulence develop fully along the width direction. In our actual manipulations during the pre-experiment, the wind blowing near the building can be also felt by hand more evenly along the width direction of the flume. Considering the representativeness of the CFD simulation results and the physical building models, we chose three groups of single buildings (Case [AM+]/[AM−], Case [CM+], and Case [CM−]) and nine groups of double buildings (Case [Basic], Case [D40], Case [D60], Case [H25], Case [H50], Case [L40], Case [L80], Case [2d10], and Case [3d5]) in Table 1  to build physical models. By considering the blockage effect of the side wall of the flume and the relative ratio of the geometrical dimension of the building models and flume width(Mignot et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2016 ), the horizontal dimension of each building model was designed at a reduced scale ratio of 4:5 compared with the scale in the numerical simulation. All of the building models were made of a white nylon material and had a certain resistance against the impact of the floodwater and wind during the experiment. Table S1  in the supplementary material  A lists all of the geometrical dimensions of the prototype, the numerical model, and the experimental physical model adopted in this study. Figure S1  in the supplementary material  A shows pictures of all the tested building models within the flume. Taking Case [AM+] as an example, Fig. 4 (c) shows the locations where the stability/instability of the dummy was observed. All of these points were distributed around the target building, and their number was sufficient to clearly identify spatial variations in the pedestrian risk within the area of interest. After a series of pre-arranged experiments, we chose two types of input floodwater conditions, i.e., input discharges of 10 L/s (small discharge) and 15 L/s (large discharge), and three types of wind conditions, i.e., no wind, a wind speed of 3.50 m/s (low wind condition), and a wind speed of 4.40 m/s (high wind condition), to perform observational experiments. A wind speed of 4.40 m/s was found to lead to a toppling instability when the dummy was placed at a distance of 40 cm from the building model at a water discharge of 15 L/s in our pre-arranged experiments(Gou et al., 2024 ). During the actual manipulation, given a small water discharge without any wind, we observed the stability/instability of the dummy within the flume at different positions. Then, while adding the low wind and high wind conditions successively, the stability/instability state of the dummy was detected again. Finally, while increasing the input floodwater discharge, the above observation procedure was repeated.
