Three states were observed and recorded for the dummy in our experiment (Fig. 4 (c)): “stable” indicates that the dummy could maintain its stability under the joint floodwater–wind effect; “instability” implies that the dummy experienced toppling instability as a result of the impact of the floodwater and wind; and “critical” indicates that the dummy experienced a shake state in the position before toppling when being subjected to both the floodwater impact and the wind impact. In general, the “stability” state corresponds to the Class I pedestrian risk level, the “instability” state corresponds to Class V, and the “critical” state corresponds to Class IV or even Class III. Herein, it is worth pointing out that observational results obtained in this experiment merely provides a qualitative comparison against the numerical simulation results regarding the impact of different building configurations on pedestrian safety since the dummy and the horizontal dimension of each building model have different reduced scale ratios relative to the actual pedestrian and the numerical configuration. Regarding the accuracy of the stability/instability of the dummy within the flume against the safety of actual pedestrian in floodwaters, the center of gravity of the dummy adopted in this study has an approximate height of 14 cm, and it was placed at some designed places around the target building during our experiment (see Fig. 4 (c)). During the experiment, the dummy was standing on the bottom of the flume to wait the floodwater impact without any support. Indeed, actual pedestrians do not always act like the dummy: people can adjust the posture and the orientation accordingly against the surging floodwater and the strong wind; people can also use some supporting devices (e.g. holding onto the pillar or unwashed trees, and using handrails and the building facades to move cautiously) to protect themselves from the floodwater/wind; the coordination and mutual help among the crowd can enhance the pedestrian safety; there is also heterogeneity in demographic characteristics of pedestrians (e.g. the older, children, adult) and also factors (friction condition, outer floodwater environment (daytime or nighttime)). However, to the best of our knowledge, it seems difficult to incorporate such factors into a simple quantification method for pedestrian safety. Toward this problem, on one hand, some authors have organized some volunteers to carry out the instability experiment (Abt et al., 1989; Foster and Cox, 1973; Karvonen et al., 2000 ; Martinez-Gomariz et al., 2016). These experimental results show a large data scattering since their test object and test environment are different, but each of them has indicated that the floodwater velocity decays with the inundation depth when the instability of people occurs. On the other hand, some scholars have adopted a simple dummy (has a reduced scale ratio relative to the prototype) to experimentally investigate its hydrodynamic instability in floodwaters (Xia et al., 2014; Postacchini et al., 2021 ), together with the hydrodynamic forcing analysis relating to the human body. After upscaling to the prototype scale and calibrating some empirical coefficients, these results were found to agree with those observational results from the actual volunteers in terms of the instability threshold relationship between floodwater and inundation depth (Xia et al., 2014 ). Thus, it seems practicable to adopt the dummy to perform the vulnerability analysis, even though it has a discrepancy with the actual pedestrians.   3 Validation study 3.1 Floodwater experiment and wind-tunnel experiment descriptions The validation of the numerical simulation scheme against existing experimental datasets in terms of the turbulence model chosen, grid arrangement, and grid size is necessary for later CFD simulations(Biscarini et al., 2010; Chen and Mak, 2021; Mittal et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). At present, there are few experimental datasets regarding the flow field around an urban building under the combined effect of floodwater and wind. Accordingly, we validated the numerical model against experimental datasets for wind flow and floodwater flow around a building separately. Of the many wind-tunnel experiments, a group of complete experimental datasets regarding the wind flow around an idealized urban building conducted by AIJ is adopted here(Franke et al., 2011; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2021, 2020; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). As shown in Fig. S2 (a) in the supplementary material  A, the building block has a length of 20 cm, a width of 5 cm, and a height of 20 cm, which corresponds to the prototype scale (length of 20 m, width of 5 m, and height of 20 m) with a reduced scale ratio of 1:100. As the wind flow was injected, the mean wind speeds were measured at nearly 115 positions around the block at a vertical height of 12.5 mm (1.25 m in the prototype scale). As presented in Fig. S2 (b), the input wind profile provided by AIJ approximates a power-law function; therefore, the following fitting function was adopted to characterize the input boundary condition for the numerical simulation(Huang et al., 2022; Tominaga et al., 2008 ):(7) V w  z   = V w - r e f   z z ref      0.25       where V w - r e f     is the reference wind speed (=7.84 m/s) at a reference height z ref     of 10 m. Of the existing floodwater experiments, a simple dam-break flow experiment conducted at the Maritime Research Institute Netherlands (MARIN) by Kleefsman et al. (2005)  was used to validate the numerical model in this study, as also adopted by many researchers (Jiang et al., 2023; Kim and Park, 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Percy et al., 2023 ). As shown in Fig. S3 (a) and S3(b) in the supplementary material  A, the experiment adopted a water tank with a length of 3.22 m, a width of 1 m, and a depth of 1 m (its top was an open roof and its bottom was horizontal). On the left side of the tank, there was a water body column with an initial depth of 0.55 m, whereas on the right side of the tank, a solid box with a length of 0.403 m, a width of 0.161 m, and a height of 0.161 m was placed to represent an isolated urban building. When the door between the left side and the right side is open, the dam-break flood can flow downstream and impact the building. During the experiment, Kleefsman et al. (2005)  set up four vertical probes to detect the instantaneous water depths at different sections: H1 was placed in the reservoir and H2, H3, and H4 were placed successively downstream. Experimental datasets regarding the water depth were extracted to validate the numerical scheme in this study. In the validation study, three common turbulence closure models, i.e., the standard k  –ε   model, the RNG k  –ε   model, and the realizable k  –ε   model, were compared against the experimental datasets. For the mesh configurations, following previous modeling studies and best practice CFD guidelines(Du et al., 2018b; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020; Peng et al., 2021 ), three types of meshing configurations (fine, medium, and coarse) were compared. As shown in Figure S4  in the supplementary material  A, for the wind modeling (Fig. S4 (a)), the mesh size around the surface of the building and that on the ground around the building were set to 2.5 mm and 5 mm (fine mesh), 5 mm and 10 mm (medium mesh), and 10 mm and 20 mm (coarse mesh), respectively. This results in total cell numbers of 1.11 × 106 , 2.99 × 105 , and 8.84 × 104 , respectively, for the total computational domain. For the floodwater modeling (Fig. S4 (b)), the mesh size around the building (and on the ground) and that for the rest of the domain were 12.5 mm and 50 mm (fine mesh), 25 mm and 50 mm (medium mesh), and 50 mm and 50 mm (coarse mesh), respectively. This results in total mesh numbers of 1.02 × 105 , 4.92 × 104 , and 3.23 × 104 , respectively, for the domain. Herein, three-layer adaptive grid technology (5 mm) was implemented for local refinements.  3.2 Validation results Fig. S5  (a) in the supplementary material  A compares the measured wind speed from the wind-tunnel experiment and the simulated wind speed using different turbulence models. The statistical parameters between the two, including the root-mean-square error (RMSE), correlation coefficient (CC), and percent bias (PBIAS), are given in Table S2  in the supplementary material  A. The calculation iterations were continued until the residual errors for the continuity, momentum, k  , and ε   equations were below a given value of 10−5  (Biscarini et al., 2010; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020, 2021; Tominaga et al., 2008 ). In general, each of the three turbulence models led to good agreement with the measured data. However, in terms of RMSE, CC, and PBIAS, the standard k  –ε   model is superior to the other models. Using the standard k  –ε   model, Fig. S5 (b) in the supplementary material  A shows a comparison between the measured wind speed and the simulated wind speed using various meshing configurations, and the statistical parameters between the two are listed in Table S2  in the supplementary material  A. Overall, there is a small discrepancy between the three different meshing techniques. To better capture the variation in the wind speed at the pedestrian level (close to 1.5–2 m), Franke et al. (2004)  suggested that the vertical position of 1.5–2 m (15–20 mm in the reduced scale) should be designed to be in the third to fourth mesh from the ground when developing a numerical mesh configuration in the vertical direction. Considering this aspect and the trade-off between the computational efficiency and the computational accuracy, the medium meshing configuration, where the mesh size around the surface of the building is 5 mm and that on the ground is 10 mm, was chosen for subsequent CFD simulations, as previously mentioned in Section 2.2.1 . Figure S6  in the supplementary material  A compares the simulated and measured water depths from the dam-break flood experiment at four cross sections at different simulation times, and the calculated values of RMSE, CC, and PBIAS are listed in the upper panel of Table S3  in the supplementary material  A. It can be seen that each of the three turbulence models can capture the variation in the water level within the tank. There is a deviation between the RNG k  –ε   model simulated values and the measured values; however, both the standard k  –ε   model and the realizable k  –ε   model show good agreement with the experimental data points, especially at H4. In particular, when the simulation time reaches 5 s at H3, both models underestimate the water depth, as found in previous studies(Akkerman et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019 ). In terms of RMSE, CC, and PBIAS, the standard k  –ε   model shows the best performance. Using the standard k  –ε   model, Figure S7  in the supplementary material  A shows a comparison between the simulated water depths using the three different meshing configurations and the measured values. The statistical parameters are provided in the lower panel of Table S3  in the supplementary material  A. By and large, there is a small discrepancy between the three meshing configurations: the medium mesh configuration leads to a small PBIAS value but marginally decreases the CC value. This indicates the grid independence of the solution to a certain degree; furthermore, the GCI is estimated to be also 1.83 % if a velocity magnitude relative error of 0.01 m/s is used, which also lie within the recommended values and the range adopted in previous modeling studies (Franke et al., 2011; Hadavi and Pasdarshahri, 2020; Zhang et al., 2023, 2022 ). After comprehensively considering the balance between the computational cost and the computational accuracy, as well as the practical CFD guidelines(Biscarini et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2021 ), the medium meshing configuration was adopted to simulate the floodwater inundation process around the buildings, as previously mentioned in Section 2.2.1 .   4 Results and discussion: An isolated building To accurately describe the flow field, especially for wake regions under different urban building scenarios, the contours of the water depth, floodwater velocity, and wind speed at the pedestrian level were plotted in a rectangular-plan area with a length of 200 m and a width of 240 m (at the prototype scale). Conversely, the CHR  for the pedestrian risk was calculated within an area of interest of 100 m in length and 70 m in width around the target building(Chen and Mak, 2021; Lee and Mak, 2021 ), as previously introduced in Section 2.1  and shown in Fig. 2 (c). The calculated CHR  values are shown in Fig. 5  for all of the single-building cases. It can be seen that the building configuration, building height, and the direction of input floodwater/wind conditions play a role in affecting the pedestrian risk to different degrees, which is discussed in the following subsections. 4.1 Effect of building configuration Taking Case [AM+], Case [BM+], and Case [CM+] as examples, Fig. 6  (a)–6(c) shows the modeled contours of the water depth, floodwater velocity, and wind speed at the pedestrian level and CHR , respectively. In each sub-figure, the area marked by the white dashed line is the area of interest. In general, as the floodwater impacts each of the “2″-shaped, “﹞”-shaped, and “ョ”-shaped buildings, there is a deep water accumulation zone in front of the buildings with a slow velocity. On the two sides of the buildings, the floodwater is accelerated by compression. However, there is a large wake zone behind each building, where the inundation depth is shallow and the routing velocity is low. In Fig. 6 (a)–6(c)(ii), the wake zone even extends significantly downstream. Regarding the wind flow in Fig. 6 (a)–6(c)(iii), as the wind approaches the building, there is a low-speed zone in front of the building, as well as behind the building, and two accelerated wind speed zones exist at the side corners of the building as a result of the Venturi effect. In terms of the corner zones, there are small discrepancies for various cases. In Fig. 6 (a)(iii), because of the asymmetric nature of the “2”-shaped building, there is a small wind speed acceleration band at the right-side corner of the building (following the input wind direction) whereas the acceleration zone becomes large at the left-side corner. However, for both the “﹞”-shaped and “ョ”-shaped buildings, there is a symmetric distribution of enhanced wind speed zones at both corners of the buildings because these buildings are strictly symmetrical along the central stream-wise direction. There is a high-speed zone embedded in the low-speed zone in front of the “﹞”-shaped building but not the “ョ”-shaped building; this may be due to the existence of the middle segment in the “ョ”-shaped building, which hinders the movement of high-speed airflow streams. These characteristics lead to somewhat different CHR  distributions for the various building configurations in Fig. 6 (a)–6(c)(iv). Focusing on the area of interest in Fig. 7  , it can be seen that, on both sides of the building, pedestrians experience a dangerous state in terms of toppling and there is a large safe/low risk zone in front of the building as well as behind the building because of the blocking effect against the floodwater/wind. In particular, for Case [BM+] and Case [CM+], the area with Class IV or Class III is small such that there seems to be an abrupt transition between Class V and Class II in front of the building compared with the findings in Case [AM+]; this implies a large discrepancy in the pedestrian risk. For Case [AM+], Case [BM+], and Case [CM+], the areas with CHR ≥1 occupy 26.40 %, 21.32 %, and 23.72 %, respectively, of the area of interest whereas both the safe and low risk zones account for 50.76 %, 60.72 %, and 47.84 %, respectively (Fig. 5 (a)–5(c)), implying that the building configuration affects the pedestrian risk to some degree. Experimental studies of Soares-Frazao and Zech (2007)  and Postacchini et al. (2019)  have revealed the impact of building orientation on the flow characteristics (water level, floodwater velocity, and impact force, as well as pressure) around an isolated building when a dam-break flow impacts it. Using a three-dimensional numerical model, Peng et al. (2021)  have also showcased the impact process of a dam-break induced flood on an idealized and isolated building. These are consistent with our findings that different building configurations lead to divergent floodwater routing characteristics around them. In the urban wind environment studies, both Mittal et al. (2019) and Thordal et al. (2020)  highlighted the role of corner modification of the high-rise building in affecting the wind flow around it (such as chamfered and rounded corner); furthermore, the numerical study of Agrawal et al. (2022)  focused on the aerodynamic performance of unconventional building shapes. Lee and Mak (2021)  showed different wind flows and pollutant distributions for the “L”- and “U”- building shapes. These characteristics are in accordance with the finding in this study that building configuration is an important factors in affecting the wind flows around the building for the pedestrian safety assessment. We plot the measured CHR  of the dummy within the laboratory flume for Case [AM+] and Case [CM+] in Figure S1  in the supplementary material  B at a water discharge of 15 L/s and a wind speed of 4.4 m/s as an example. It can be seen that the dummy experiences a toppling instability on both sides of the buildings and that an instable/shaking state exists near the side corners in front of the buildings. This characteristic is consistent with the modeled CHR  contours in Fig. 7 , validating the CFD simulation results. We also compared the relative importance of the floodwater and wind effects for these dangerous areas and calculated the evacuation speeds of pedestrians within the areas with CHR <1 in Figure S2  in the supplementary material  B. Regardless of the building configuration, floodwater plays a dominant role over wind in threatening pedestrian safety. This indicates that, for such building configurations, flood control measures can be effective to protect pedestrians against the impact of floodwater and wind in the context of urban flooding prevention and mitigation. In terms of the evacuation speed of pedestrians around a building, the walking speed and the running speed in front of and on the two sides of the building are below 0.5 m/s and 1 m/s, respectively, for either of these cases; however, behind the building, the walking speed increases up to 0.5–1 m/s, or even 1–1.5 m/s, and the running speed increases up to 1–1.5 m/s, or even over 1.5 m/s.  4.2 Impact of building height Variations in the building height could influence the pedestrian risk via the wind flow field around the building but does not affect the floodwater routing around the building. Therefore, Fig. 8  (a)–10(b) only shows the contours of the wind speed for Case [AL+] and Case [AH+] as examples. Compared with the findings in Case [AM+] (Fig. 6 (a)), as the building height increases, both the wind speed in front of the building and that behind the building exhibit a slight decreasing trend. However, at the two corners of the building, the two wind speed acceleration zones expand remarkably with increasing building height, as also shown in Chen and Mak (2021), Huang et al. (2022) , and Du et al. (2018b) . Therefore, the total wind speed within the area of interest shows a slight increasing trend. As shown in Fig. 9   in terms of the CHR  distribution, the Class V areas for Case [AL+], Case [AM+], and Case [AH+] account for 26.40 %, 26.40 %, and 26.43 % of the area of interest, respectively, and both Class I and Class II occupy 47.56 %, 50.76 %, and 50.33 % (Fig. 5 (a)), respectively. This implies that the building height plays a small role in affecting the pedestrian safety. As also shown in Fig. 5 (b) and 5(c), the Class V areas for Case [BL+], Case [BM+], and Case [BH+] become 21.41 %, 21.32 % and 21.35 %, respectively, and those for Case [CL+], Case [CM+], and Case [CH+] are 23.72 %, 23.72 %, and 23.80 %, respectively. This indicates a minor effect of the building height on pedestrian risk regardless of the building configuration. It is worth noting that in the urban wind environment studies, some authors have shown the influence of the urban building height variability on the wind speed and pollutant dispersion (Hang et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2017; Tamura et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2022 ); especially, a high-rise building leads to a large corner speed-up zone of the wind. This characteristic is also obvious in our study, as shown by Fig. 8 . We also plot the pedestrian evacuation speeds for Case [AL+] and Case [AH+] in Fig. S3 (a) and S3(b) in the supplementary material  B, respectively, as well as for Case [AM+] in Fig. S2 (a) in the supplementary material  B. By and large, there is no obvious discrepancy in the evacuation speeds because of the changing building height: the walking speed is below 1 m/s, while the running speed can reach 1–1.5 m/s in a portion of the area.  4.3 Influence of converging and diverging flows Because the “2″-shaped building is axisymmetric, we compared Case [BM+] and Case [BM−], as well as Case [CM+] and Case [CM−], to explore the possible effect of the input floodwater/wind direction on the pedestrian risk around the building. Fig. 10  (a) and 10(b) shows the contours of the water depth, floodwater velocity, wind speed at pedestrian level, and CHR  for Case [BM−] and Case [CM−], respectively. Pairwise comparing them with Case [BM+] in Fig. 6 (b) and Case [CM+] in Fig. 6 (c), we see a large discrepancy in the water depth, floodwater velocity, and wind speed because of the converging /diverging flow. Moreover, within the area of interest, Class V for Case [BM+], Case [BM−], Case [CM+], and Case [CM−] has area proportions of 21.32 %, 53.14 %, 23.72 %, and 22.55 %, respectively, whereas both the safe zone and the low risk zone for these cases account for 60.72 %, 33.46 %, 47.84 %, and 53.96 %, respectively. For the “﹞”-shaped building, an adverse floodwater/wind direction leads to a strong diverging flow when impacting the protruding segment of the building (Fig. 10 (a)), whereas, as for the following floodwater/wind direction, there exists a large converging flow (Fig. 6 (b)). However, for the “ョ”-shaped building, because there is a uniform cross section for the floodwater and wind movement, floodwater accumulates around the two corners in front of the building, yielding almost equal extreme risk zone areas (Fig. 10  (b) and Fig. 6 (c)). Therefore, it can be concluded that the extent to which the floodwater/wind direction plays a role in affecting the pedestrian risk depends on the building configuration. Although the building configurations adopted in this study differ from that in Chen and Mak (2021) , both studies highlight the importance of the input wind direction on the wind speed at pedestrian level around the building. We plot the measured CHR  of Case [CM−] from the laboratory flume experiment as an example in Figure S4  in the supplementary material  B. Compared with the findings in Case [CM+] in Fig. S1 (b) in the supplementary material  B, a reversal in the floodwater/wind direction leads to different risk positions. Under the effect of an adverse floodwater/wind direction, pedestrians experience a dangerous state at the two sides of the building and at some locations in front of the building, whereas they are safe behind the building because of the blocking effect. These observational results resemble the modeled CHR  in Fig. 10 (b)(iv). Fig. S5 (a) and S5(b) in the supplementary material  B shows the evacuation speeds of pedestrians for Case [BM−] and Case [CM−]. Pairwise comparing this with Case [BM+] in Fig. S2 (b) and Case [CM+] in Fig. S2 (c) in the supplementary material  B, we see some variations within the area with CHR <1. (i) There are only a few areas where pedestrians can walk at a speed greater than 1 m/s for Case [BM+], whereas for Case [BM−], the allowable walking speed of pedestrians in more than half of the safe areas exceeds 1 m/s. (ii) For Case [CM+], the running speed of pedestrians in most safe areas is 0.5–1 m/s, while for Case [CM−], the running speed of pedestrians exceeds 1 m/s in nearly half of the safe areas. This indicates that differing inflow directions have a significant impact on the speed and efficiency of pedestrian evacuation.   5 Results and discussion: Double-building configurations The integrated effects of an upstream building on the pedestrian risk around the target building were analyzed from five perspectives: the horizontal distance between the upstream building and the target building; the height of the upstream building; the length of the upstream building; the interspace between segments in the upstream building; and the reduced ratio of the upstream relative to the reference case. These cases are compared with Case [Basic], and their modeled CHR  contours are shown in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. Fig. 11  (a)–11(d) shows the modeled water depth, floodwater velocity, and wind speed at pedestrian level and CHR , respectively, for Case [Basic]. In comparison with the isolated building (Case [AM+]) in Fig. 6 (a), both the floodwater flow field and the wind flow field are changed by the impeding effect of the upstream building against the inflow. The extreme risk zone is located at the two side bands of the target building, occupying 16.33 % of the total area within the area of interest. The area proportions of Class IV, Class III, Class II, and Class I are 0.77 %, 6.99 %, 27.68 %, and 30.45 %, respectively. In comparison to Case [AM+], the extreme risk zone is reduced by 10.07 %, whereas the safe/low risk zone is improved from 50.76 % to 58.13 %, implying that the existence of an upstream building increases the safety of pedestrians. We plot the measured CHR  of the dummy within the laboratory flume for Case [Basic] in Figure S7  in the supplementary material  B; the dummy primarily loses its stability along the two sides of the building, as in Case [AM+] in Fig. S1 (a) in the supplementary material  B, and there is little toppling of the dummy observed near the corners in front of the building, which differs slightly from Case [AM+] in Fig. S1 (a) in the supplementary material  B. This is again attributed to the blocking of the upstream building in Case [Basic]. The measured CHR  of the dummy is consistent with the modeled CHR  in Fig. 11 (d). In addition, as illustrated in Fig. S8 (a) and S8(b) in the supplementary material  B, floodwater occupies a leading role in triggering the pedestrian risk along the two sides of the building; the walking speed of pedestrians in most safe areas is less than 0.5 m/s, the running speed is between 0.5 m/s and 1 m/s, and only a small number of safe areas have a pedestrian running speed greater than 1 m/s. 5.1 Effect of the distance between the upstream building and the target building Fig. 12   shows the proportion of CHR  for Case [D40], Case [Basic], and Case [D60], and their CHR  contours are presented in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. With increasing distance between the upstream building and the target building, the extreme risk zone with CHR >1 shows an increasing trend from 16.20 %, 16.33 %, to 19.07 %, whereas the safe and low risk zones reduce in terms of the area proportion. This implies that a close upstream building can better protect the pedestrian safety around the target building, as expected, because a larger area in the area of interest is affected by the wake zone behind the upstream building. The measured CHR  distributions for both Case [D40] and Case [D60] are plotted in Figure S9  in the supplementary material  B, and that for Case [Basic] is plotted in Figure S7  in the supplementary material  B. It is obvious that pedestrians experience a dangerous state at the two sides of the building for all cases, which validates the numerical simulation results regarding CHR  (Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B); however, more toppling instabilities of the dummy can be observed, especially behind the target building in Case [D60] when comparing with either Case [D40] or Case [Basic]. We plot the heat-maps based on the transition matrix between Case [D40] and Case [Basic] and between Case [D60] and Case [Basic] in Fig. 13  (a) and 21(b), respectively. Compared with the findings in the reference case (i.e.D T    = 50 m), only 1.49 % of the area has deteriorated into an extreme risk area with CHR >1, whereas 1.61 % of the area becomes safer as D T    is shorten to 40 m. Nevertheless, as D T    increases to 60 m, 3.29 % of the area transforms into an extreme danger zone with CHR >1, and only 0.55 % of the area becomes safe with CHR <1 in comparison to the case with D T    = 50 m. These results indicate that the horizontal distance between the upstream building and the target building affects the pedestrian risk to some extent. In urban flooding studies, Li et al. (2021), Zhu et al. (2023)  and Percy et al. (2023)  have showcased that a less dense building layout leads to a different floodwater flow field from a highly dense block. Whereas in the urban wind environment studies, both of Chen et al. (2017)  and Hadavi and Pasdarshahri (2020)  pointed out the role of building packing densities in affecting the wind flows within the buildings. These conclusions can agree with our modeling results well herein.  5.2 Effect of the upstream building height Fig. 14  (a)–14(f) depicts the wind flow fields at pedestrian level for Case [H20], Case [H25], Case [H30], Case [H40], Case [H45], and Case [H50], respectively. Comparing them, and Case [H35] in Fig. 11 (c), we see that an increase in the height of the upstream building causes a large area of speed-up flows around the two corners of the upstream building because the down flow from a high vertical position to a low vertical position in front of the building can transfer a higher wind speed to the pedestrian level, as revealed by several previous studies on urban wind environment fields (Chen and Mak, 2021; Gou et al., 2024; Tamura et al., 2019 ). In addition, a tall upstream building leads to a somewhat decreasing trend in the wind speeds around the target building. However, note that, in Fig. 15   in terms of the proportions of the CHR  for these cases, this does not give rise to an obvious variation in the extreme risk zone because this effect may be not sufficient to trigger the toppling of pedestrians under such circumstances. We show the heat-maps based on the transition matrix between Cases [H20]–[H50] and Case [Basic] in Fig. 16  (a)–16(f) and the changes in the CHR  for these cases in Fig. 16 (g). Note that, when the upstream building is shorter than the target building, the geometrical area of the region that becomes dangerous shows a decaying trend. When the upstream building is taller than the target building, both the region that becomes more secure and the region that becomes more dangerous are expanded with the increasing upstream building height; however, the former is dominant over the latter, thus yielding a safer environment for pedestrians within the area of interest because a taller upstream building better hinders the wind in the downstream direction. The measured CHR  for pedestrians from the laboratory flume experiment is illustrated for Case [H25] and Case [H50] in Figure S10  in the supplementary material  B. It is evident that there are two extreme risk bands along the two sides of the building, which is consistent with the CFD simulation results in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B.  5.3 Effect of the upstream building length The length of the upstream building is predicted to exert an influence on both the floodwater and wind flow fields around the target building. Fig. 17   shows the proportion of CHR  for Case [L40], Case [L50], Case [Basic], Case [L70], and Case [L80], and their CHR  contours are provided in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. As the length of the upstream building increases, the area of the extreme risk zone decreases from 25.54 %, 24.97 %, 16.33 %, and 8.98 % to 1.82 %, whereas the safe and low risk zones show an increasing trend. This suggests that a long upstream building hinders both floodwater and wind flow, better protecting the safety of pedestrians downstream. The measured CHR  distributions for both Case [L40] and Case [L80] are shown in Figure S11  in the supplementary material  B. By comparing them and Case [Basic] in Figure S7  in the supplementary material  B, it can be seen that, for either case, there are extreme risk zones at the two sides of the building, which is consistent with the CFD simulation results (Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B); nevertheless, it is obvious that, as the length of the upstream building L U    increases up to 80 m, some points at the two sides of the building decrease to remarkable or moderate risk state from the extreme risk state at L U    = 40 m and 60 m. The heat-maps based on the transition matrix between Cases [L40]–[L80] and Case [Basic] are shown in Fig. 18  (a)–18(d), and the final changes in the CHR  in Cases [L40]–[L80] relative to Case [Basic] are depicted in Fig. 18 (e). In comparison with the reference case (L U   =60 m), a shorter upstream building (L U   =50 m → 40 m) leads to a more dangerous pedestrian state within the domain; as L U    increases to 70 m and 80 m, the overall domain becomes safer: the area of the zone becoming more dangerous decreases significantly and the area of the zone getting safer increases significantly. These results highlight the importance of the upstream building in protecting the pedestrian safety within urban blocks under a joint floodwater–wind effect.  5.4 Effect of the upstream building interspace Regarding the role of the interspace between segments in the upstream building on the downstream pedestrian risk, Fig. 19   shows the proportions of CHR  for Case [Basic], Case [2d10], Case [2d20], Case [3d5], and Case [3d10] and their CHR  distributions can be seen in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. For Case [2d10], Case [2d20], Case [3d5], and Case [3d10], the extreme risk zone (Class V) occupies 8.19 %, 23.86 %, 2.60 %, and 17.20 % of the area of interest, respectively, whereas the safe and low risk zones (Class I and Class II) have proportions of 70.47 %, 55.64 %, 77.12 %, and 61.80 %, respectively. This implies a differing influence of the interspace configuration in the front building on the pedestrian risk. Specifically, as shown by Fig. 20   in terms of the heat-maps based on the transition matrix between Cases [2d10]–[3d10] and Case [Basic], we observe the following. (i) Compared with the findings in Case [Basic], 6.24 % of the area of interest degrades to an extreme risk state with CHR >1, whereas 14.38 % of the area becomes safer with CHR <1 from an extreme risk state with CHR >1 in Case [2d10]. (ii) For Case [2d20], although 19.90 % of the area becomes an extreme risk zone, 12.37 % of the area evolves into other states with CHR <1. (iii) In Case [3d5], 14.03 % of the area becomes safer with CHR <1 from the previous extreme risk state; however, 0.31 % of the area deteriorates to an extreme risk state. (iv) For Case [3d10], 13.07 % of the area transforms to an extreme risk zone; in contrast, 12.20 % of the area, previously in the extreme risk state, becomes safer. These phenomena can be explained by comparing the variations in the flow fields in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B (in terms of the CHR  contour), as well as Fig. 11 (d) for Case [Basic]. As shown in Fig. 11 (d), when the upstream building is impervious, the extreme risk zone within the area of interest originates from accelerated flows (floodwater or wind) around the two corners of the upstream building because of the blocking effect. Because the upstream building has a horizontal interspace, as in Case [2d10] in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B, the area of the accelerated flow decreases greatly within the area of interest because both sides of the upstream building extend along the y  −direction (30 m → 35 m). Although there is a jet flow (either floodwater or wind) from the gap between the segments of the upstream building that impacts the target building, it cannot offset the former effect; consequently, the extreme risk zone becomes smaller than in the reference case (Case [Basic]). However, if the interspace of the upstream building increases to 20 m in width (in the prototype scale), as in Case [2d20] in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B, there is a strong jet flow with a large discharge that hits the target building, leading to a large scale extreme risk zone for pedestrians, even though a further extension of the two sides of the upstream building in Case [2d20] (35 m → 40 m) also decreases the area of the extreme risk zone. A similar explanation can be found by comparing Case [Basic], Case [3d5], and Case [3d10] in cases with a double-gap configuration in the upstream building. In addition, it is of interest to pairwise compare Case [2d10] and Case [3d5], as well as Case [2d20] and Case [3d10], because they have the same ensemble and gap width for the upstream building in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. In comparison to the single-gap configuration, the double-gap configuration has a dispersion effect against the intruding floodwater and wind, forming narrow water passages and ventilation channels. Together with the interference between the two jet flows, this decreases the impact on pedestrians around the target building. These points could be of value when implementing tailored measures against the joint impact of floodwater and wind to protect pedestrians when planning and managing urban building clusters. Mejía-Morales et al. (2023)  and Mejía-Morales et al. (2021b) highlighted the impact of the porosity of an urban block (representing the lateral flow exchange between the surrounding streets and the block) on the pedestrian risk during urban flooding. Mignot et al. (2020)  showcased the influence of flow intrusion towards building areas on flow hydrodynamics in the street. Although we have a different gap configuration, both studies demonstrate that orifice jet flows have a non-negligible effect on pedestrian risk assessments. Furthermore, Zhou et al. (2016), Liu et al. (2018)  and Wüthrich et al. (2018)  highlighted the impact of the opening of the building on the flow characteristic and the forces exerted on it by a dam-break flow. Similarly, numerical studies of Hadavi and Pasdarshahri (2020)  and Zhang et al. (2022)  showed the wind blowing process around and within the buildings with different opening configurations. Although there is a different opening configuration between these studies and this study, all of them stressed the impact of the building opening on the floodwater routing and wind blowing around the target building. We plot the measured CHR  of the dummy from the laboratory experiment for Case [2d10] and Case [3d5] in Figure S12  in the supplementary material  B. There are toppling points at the two sides of the building; in particular, there exists extreme or remarkable risk points in the middle part for Case [2d10] and near the middle part for Case [3d5] in front of the building because there are two and three jet flows, respectively, in these cases. These characteristics are consistent with the modeled CHR  contours for both Case [2d10] and Case [3d5] in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B, which validates the numerical simulation results.  5.5 Effect of the reduced ratio of the upstream building Keeping the same length to height ratio of the upstream building as the reference case, Fig. 21   shows the proportions of CHR  for Case [R0.6], Case [R0.8], Case [Basic], Case [R1.2], and Case [R1.4] and the modeled CHR  contours for these cases are illustrated in Figure S6  in the supplementary material  B. A long and tall upstream building leads to a small extreme risk zone and large safe/low risk zones for pedestrians around the target building because it better hinders both the floodwater inundation and the wind flow protecting pedestrians downstream. Fig. 22  (a)–22(d) presents heat-maps based on the transition matrix between Cases [R0.6]–[R1.4] and Case [Basic], and the final changes in CHR  for these cases in relation to Case [Basic] are depicted in Fig. 22 (e). Compared with the findings in the reference case (Case [Basic]), a reduced ratio of the upstream building (Case [R0.6] and Case [R0.8]) leads overall to a more dangerous situation for pedestrians, whereas an amplified upstream building (Case [R1.2] and Case [R1.4]) facilitates the safety of pedestrians around the target building.  5.6 Local sensitivity analysis Regarding the CFD simulation results for the double-building configurations, we performed a local sensitivity analysis to estimate the impact of each input variable of the upstream building, including the horizontal distance D T    from the target building, the height H U   , the length L U   , and the reduced ratio R   relative to the reference case, on the pedestrian risk within the area of interest. The local sensitivity analysis method is relatively straightforward and simple and is based on the one-parameter-at-a-time method; it can provide a qualitative description of the impact of each input parameter on the output response(Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The shortcoming of this method lies in the fact that it cannot interpret the non-linear relationship between each input variable and the output results or the interactions between the different input variables. Here, we use a sensitivity coefficient (SC ) to quantify the importance of each input variable of the upstream building for the output results (here, we chose the proportion of the extreme risk zone as the output variable because it is of greatest concern when designing effective measures against floodwater and wind) as follows(Liu et al., 2020 ):(8) SC = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  Δ o p  o p i  + o p i + 1    2     / Δ i p  i p i  + i p i + 1    2            where Δ i p    and Δ o p    are the changes in the input and output values, respectively; i p i     and i p i + 1      are two input values; o p i     and o p i + 1      are two corresponding output values; n   is the total number of increments for an variable; and i   is the increment adopted in this study. This parameter was adopted by Liu et al. (2020)  and Zhang et al. (2023)  to estimate the effectiveness of passive design strategies in responding to further climate changes for residential buildings and the effects of trees on the cross-ventilation of an isolated building, respectively. In addition, we calculated the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) for the correlation between the input variable and the output results (a perfect linear relationship often has an R 2  value close to 1). Table 2   lists the sensitivity coefficient (SC ) for the horizontal distance of the upstream building from the target building, the height of the upstream building, the length of the upstream building, and the reduced ratio relative to the reference case, as well as the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) between each variable and the output results. The length L U    of the upstream building has the highest SC  value of 4.031, keeping the strongest linear relationship with the area of the extreme risk zone with an R 2  value of 0.956. The reduced ratio R   of the upstream building relative to the reference case has the second highest SC  value of 3.809 with the second largest R 2  value of 0.947. However, the height H U    of the upstream building has a low SC  value of 0.02 and a weak relationship with the output response with an R 2  value of 0.441. This indicates that the length of the upstream building plays a key role in triggering the toppling of pedestrians around a downstream building because floodwater is the driving factor in causing pedestrian toppling and a longer upstream building can better hinder the floodwater impact and the wind flow, as discussed in Section 4.2.3. The horizontal distance D T    from the target building has a moderate influence (SC =0.444) as well as a moderate linear relationship (R 2  = 0.782) with changes in the extreme risk zone around the target building. This is because, as D T    increases, the blocking effect of the upstream building (especially against the floodwater impact) for the target building becomes weaker, as mentioned in Section 4.2.1.   6 Limitations of this study and concluding remarks In this study, the integrated impacts of the building configuration and an upstream building on the pedestrian risk around a target building were investigated using CFD simulations and laboratory flume experiments. Some concluding remarks for the single-building case are as follows. • For “2″-shaped, “﹞”-shaped, and “ョ”-shaped buildings, pedestrians experience a dangerous state in terms of toppling at both sides of the building and there is a large safe/low risk zone in front of the building as well as behind the building because of the blocking effect. The building configuration affects the pedestrian risk. Floodwater plays a dominant role over wind in threatening pedestrian safety regardless of the building configuration. The evacuation speeds of pedestrians within the area of interest were also estimated. • Although increasing the building height leads to larger areas of the two speed-up zones at the two corners of the building, it yields a minor effect on the pedestrian safety regardless of the building configuration. Both converging and diverging flows lead to different pedestrian risk distributions within the area of interest, and the extent to which the floodwater/wind direction plays a role in affecting the pedestrian risk depends on the building configuration. There are some discrepancies in the pedestrian evacuation speeds depending on the converging/diverging flow. For the double-building configuration, our concluding remarks are summarized below. • With increasing horizontal distance between the upstream building and the target building, the extreme risk zone shows an increasing trend, whereas the proportions of the safe and low risk zones decrease, implying that a close upstream building can better protect pedestrians around a target building. A tall upstream building leads to large areas of speed-up flows around the two corners of the upstream building but does not give rise to an obvious variation in the extreme risk zone because these flows might not be sufficient to trigger the toppling of pedestrians under such circumstances. • As the length of the upstream building increases, the area of the extreme risk zone decreases significantly, whereas the safety and low risk zones show an increasing trend, which is attributed to the fact that a long upstream building hinders both floodwater routing and wind movement, thus better protecting downstream pedestrians. Similarly, a long and tall upstream building leads to a small extreme risk zone and large safe/low risk zones for pedestrians around the target building because it better hinders both floodwater inundation and wind movement to protect downstream pedestrians. • The number and length of the interspace between the segments of the upstream building have an obvious effect on pedestrian risk around the downstream target building. This can be explained by the relative importance of the blocking effect of the upstream building and the impact effect resulting from the jet flow(s) from the gap(s). The local sensitivity analysis performed in this study confirmed that the length of the upstream building plays a key role in triggering the toppling of pedestrians, followed by the reduced ratio relative to the reference case and the horizontal distance from the target building. The height of the upstream building has the smallest effect on the pedestrian risk response. These results can be referred to by administrators and stakeholders when implementing tailored measures against the direct impact of floodwater and strong wind in the context of resilient city management. The methods adopted in this study encompassed both of the CFD simulations and laboratory flume experiments. Compared to the theoretical analysis and the experimental studies, the CFD simulations are advantageous in terms of greatly decreasing the time cost and rapidly modeling many divergent engineering scenarios (hydrodynamic or aerodynamic). The CFD method established in this study can fast provide flow fields of floodwater and wind around the target building for any given inflow conditions and boundary conditions (Fondelli et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2023; Nkwunonwo et al., 2020; Toparlar et al., 2017 ), which facilitates a rapid estimation of spatial distribution of compound risk of pedestrians (where is the dangerous zone and where is the safe zone) (Gou et al., 2024 ). The disadvantages of the CFD method lie in the computational cost and the reliability. In contrast, the laboratory experimental method can provide an intuitive and full picture regarding the pedestrian stability/instability within the interest precinct as both the floodwater and wind impact the building. It is straightforward and meaningful, which can offer a qualitative comparison against the CFD simulation results (Li et al., 2020, 2021; Mejía-Morales et al., 2021, 2023 ). The disadvantages of this method lie in some limitations in geometrical dimensions and test objects that replicate the actual engineering cases and limited experimental samples, as well as the labor cost. Simultaneous utilization of the CFD simulations and the laboratory flume experiment can overcome these shortcomings, and provides some insights into the physical mechanism regarding the interaction between the building(s) and the inflow floodwater/wind conditions when both surging floodwater and strong wind occur. This study offers insights into how the building configuration and upstream buildings affect the pedestrian risk downstream. The accuracy of the findings was ensured by validating the CFD simulations of the floodwater and wind movement around ideal buildings. First, we carefully chose the numerical settings and boundary conditions for the CFD simulations. Second, we conducted grid sensitivity analyses and validation tests for the CFD simulations of divergent cases by comparing them with existing dam-break and wind-tunnel experimental datasets. Finally, a series of laboratory flume experiments testing the stability/instability of a dummy at the reduced scale were performed to validate some of the CFD simulation results. Despite this, this study has a few limitations that should be considered when interpreting and applying the results to future studies and engineering applications, as discussed below. • One limitation of the CFD modeling is that interactions between the wind and floodwater are not covered in the current study. In fact, surface wind can accelerate floodwater, especially on the top layer along the downwind direction, which might have an effect on the floodwater velocity and pressure gradient but will not have a large effect on the wind environment because the vertical scale of the wind is much larger than that of the floodwater inundation. Future studies should address this multiple-phase flow problem to achieve an accurate assessment of the pedestrian risk around urban buildings(Gou et al., 2024 ). In addition, there are inherent uncertainties associated with the CFD simulations resulting from the grid configuration, the convergence of the solution technique, and the usage of the numerical calculation scheme(Biscarini et al., 2010; Blocken, 2015; Blocken et al., 2016; Nkwunonwo et al., 2020; Toparlar et al., 2017 ). • There are several uncertainties associated with the laboratory flume experiments because of the limitation in the geometrical dimensions of the dummy and the building in relation to the flume and the wind generating equipment (Blocken et al., 2016; Gou et al., 2024; Mignot et al., 2019 ), also including the different geometrical ratios among the prototype, the numerical modelling setting, and the laboratory flume experiment. Especially for the wind effect study, the adopted laboratory wind tunnel experiment has the potential to reproduce the wind turbulence characteristics of the boundary layer flow within the urban canopy(Blocken et al., 2016; Tamura et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017 ): for example, air in wind tunnel is predominantly sucked rather than pushed, as observed in this experimental study, and the wind tunnel apparatus can generate the more uniform wind inflow condition when impacting the buildings for the laboratory experiment. Additionally, the dummy is simple adopted to replicate human behaviors in this experiment, neglecting a comprehensive consideration of many factors on the pedestrian instability. The behavior of actual pedestrians in the joint environment of the floodwater and the wind is worthy of investigation in future studies. In addition, although the single- and double-building configurations adopted in the current study are representative of typical urban buildings in urban flooding events, it is necessary to perform pedestrian risk assessments toward more generalized urban configuration, such as “I”-shaped, “H”-shaped, “+”-shaped, “C”-shaped and “D”-shaped buildings, and around real-world, complicated building configurations within urban blocks(Du et al., 2018a ; Li et al., 2021). Further studies regarding the pedestrian risk assessment in a floodwater-wind joint environment could be carried out in the following ways: (1) more physical mechanisms relevant to the impact of both floodwater and wind on the buildings, either idealized (which is a generalization of some actual urban buildings) or real world ones, need to be revealed. These results could provide some insights about how the geometrical characteristics of the building(s) affect the wind/floodwater dynamics and associated with pedestrian safety in urban regions. (2) the estimated CHR  distribution maps can be referred to by administrators and stakeholders when implementing effective measures against floodwater and wind in urban flooding events via either engineering measures (such as flood control measures and wind-proof measures) (Bernardini et al., 2021a ) or non-engineering measures (such as emergency evacuation planning and management) (Bernardini et al., 2021b; Du et al., 2023 ).
1 Introduction A spatially and temporally explicit representation of global terrestrial evaporation (E ) is vital for understanding the Earth’s energy, water and carbon cycles (Zhang et al., 2023; Volk et al., 2024 ). While the widely-used eddy-covariance (EC) flux towers greatly boosted our understanding of E  at the plot scale (Shao et al., 2024; Kannenberg et al., 2024 ), estimating E  with a global coverage is still held back by difficulties in parameterizing the biophysical and biochemical processes controlling the water movement across the soil–vegetation–atmosphere continuum for a heterogeneous landscape (Katul et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2022 ). These problems give rise to the observed substantial uncertainties in global evaporation values estimated by a wide array of existing models (see e.g., Fig. 9 in Ma et al., 2021  and Fig. 1 in Ma et al., 2024 ). In this context, it is worthwhile to further develop novel approaches for an improved estimation of globally distributed E  rates. The complementary relationship (CR), first proposed by Bouchet (1963) , is a powerful tool for estimating terrestrial evaporation as it employs only standard meteorological variables without resorting to land use/land cover, vegetation and/or soil information, illustrated in recent studies where E  was estimated at a continental-scale (e.g., Ma and Szilagyi, 2019; Ma et al., 2019; 2020 ). The CR derives E  of the drying or wet land from the oasis effect, i.e., from the local evaporation-boosting influence of horizontal air advection over a wet land of regional extent. While the wet region evaporates at a spatially averaged rate of Ew  , temporally averaged over a week or longer time interval under a similarly averaged net radiation (Rn  ) term, its upwind wet boundary zone (a width of the order of ten meters) evaporates at an elevated rate, Ep  , due to the aforementioned advection of potentially drier and warmer air blowing from the drying land (see Section 2.1  for a detailed description of Ew   and Ep  ). Naturally, when the drying land is as wet as the wet region downwind then E  = Ew   = Ep  , while in general E  ≤ Ew   ≤ Ep  . It follows that the larger the difference between Ep   and Ew  , the drier is the land, thus the smaller E  has become over it, hence the complementarity between Ep   and E . Early works related deviations of E  and Ep   from Ew   directly, such as Ep   – Ew   = Ew   – E , which became known as the symmetrical CR (e.g., Brutsaert and Stricker, 1979; Morton, 1983 ) or as Ep   – kEw   = Ew   – kE , termed the asymmetrical CR (e.g., Kahler and Brutsaert, 2006 ), k  being a constant. Both have been extensively used in estimating E  at varying temporal and spatial scales (e.g., Ma et al., 2015; Huntington et al., 2011; Szilagyi and Jozsa, 2008 ). Inspired by Brutsaert’s (2015)  seminal work on the nondimensional form of the CR, Szilagyi et al. (2017 ; see also Crago et al., 2016 ) formed nondimensional variables, such as y  = E Ep  -1  and X   = ws  Ew  Ep  −1  –where a dynamic wetness scaling coefficient, ws   (−), is defined as ws   = (Ep max   – Ep  ) (Ep max   – Ew  )−1  –and derived first a polynomial (Szilagyi et al., 2017 ) and later a generalized power-function complementary relationship (PCR) formulation (Szilagyi et al., 2022 ) of the CR (Fig. 1  ) as(1) y = 2 X  b  - X  2 b - 1   , b ≥ 1     which, with the b  = 1 choice, yields the linear nondimensional CR of Crago et al. (2016) , while with b  = 2, the polynomial CR of Szilagyi et al. (2017) . Ep max   in Eq. (1)  is the maximum achievable rate of Ep   when the drying land is completely devoid of moisture (i.e., the vapor pressure becomes zero) and the air in this way attains a temperature of Ta dry  . Ta dry   can be obtained from Ta dry  = Ta   + ea  γ −1  (Szilagyi, 2021 ). Eq. (1)  contains only one parameter, b , that needs to be calibrated, since the Priestley-Taylor parameter can be found from a universal formulation that requires only the wet-environment air temperature (see Section 2.1 ). Szilagyi et al. (2022)  argue that b  is a necessary correction factor for E  due to the effect of moisture advection over the drying land. Such advection is especially significant over warm and arid regions along the sea where the moisture-laden air blowing toward the dry land not only cools the air above it but also raises its moisture content. Advection in closed warm and arid basins surrounded by mountains with ample moisture at high elevations may have a similar effect but to a lesser degree due to adiabatic warming of the descending air. In either case, this increased moisture and the cooler air then effectively lowers the vapor pressure deficit. The steep slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve at high temperatures allows the reduction in vapor pressure deficit by cooling to be highly effective. This depresses the Ep   value prompting a necessary reduction in E  since the drop in Ep   came not from an increasing E  rate of the land but rather from external sources. For a given value of X  , Fig. 1  shows that y  = E Ep  −1  can be lowered by increasing b . Thus a warm, dry region with moisture advection should have an elevated value of b . Note that the linear relationship of y  = X  in Fig. 1 , when b  = 1 in Eq. (1) , describes ideal conditions of clear adiabatic (plus isobaric thus isenthalpic) cooling/warming of the land by surface fluxes of water vapor (Szilagyi et al., 2022 ) without the effect of any external energy/moisture advection. While the effect of energy advection (in the form of drier, warmer air) is most important during wet conditions of the land and reflected in the increasing Priestley-Taylor parameter value with dropping temperatures (see Section 2.1 ), the effect of moisture advection is most significant when the land is dry and produces the sagging curves of Fig. 1  as b  increases. With the help of the Budyko (1974)  hypothesis on the long-term regional water-energy balance, Kim et al. (2024)  presented an intriguing approach of estimating b  globally at a spatial resolution of 0.25° using the PCR of Eq. (1) . Quite surprisingly the resulting b  values attained their highest values in the wettest tropical regions of the continents, contrary to expectations from the above argument and data presented by Szilagyi et al. (2022) . Such a contradiction thus motivated the current study. Kim et al. (2024)  derived b  from an inversion of Eq. (1)  that yielded the same E  ¯     as the classical empirical relationships (f ) that predict the long-term mean annual evaporation ratio, E ¯   P ¯   - 1    , as E ¯   P ¯   - 1     = f (E ¯  w   P ¯  - 1    , n ), where P  ¯     is the long-term mean annual precipitation, and n  is a constant (Mezentsev, 1955; Pike, 1964; Choudhury, 1999; Yang et al., 2008 ). Kim et al. (2024)  further related n  empirically to an aridity index of E p  ¯   P ¯  - 1    . Here, we propose a different route for the derivation of the b  value to see if it produces the same unexpected results. The present study is guided by three primary objectives: i) develop an isenthalpic index for estimating b  directly without resorting to any a priori  global model estimates of E  (as in Kim et al., 2024 ); ii) explore the spatial distribution of the b  values constrained by its phyical meaning across the continents; and finally; iii) improve the PCR with updated b  values for a more accurate estimation of E  globally.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Deriving Ep   and Ew   In the present study, Ep   (mm d−1 ) is expressed by the Penman (1948)  equation as(2) E p  = Δ Q n   Δ + γ   + γ f u  e  ∗   T a    - e a     Δ + γ       where Qn   (expressed in water-depth equivalent of mm d−1 ) is the available energy (=Rn   – G ) at the surface. Rn   (mm d−1 ) is the net radiation at the surface, while G  (mm d−1 ) is the ground heat flux, the latter typically negligible at a temporal averaging of a day or longer. Δ  [= 4098e* (Ta   + 237.3)−2 ] denotes the slope of the saturation vapor pressure (e* ) curve (hPa °C−1 ) at the measured air temperature, Ta  . The empirical wind function, fu   (mm d−1  hPa−1 ), is traditionally formulated (Brutsaert, 1982 ) as fu   = 0.26(1 + 0.54u2  ). Here u2   (m s−1 ) is the horizontal wind speed at 2-m above the ground/canopy surface and can be estimated by a power function (Brutsaert, 1982 ) from measurements (uh  ) at h  meters above the surface/canopy as u2   = uh   (2 / h )1/7 , and γ  [= cp  p  (0.622L )−1 ] is the psychrometric constant (hPa °C−1 ) where cp   (J kg−1  °C−1 ) the specific heat of air under constant pressure, L  (J kg−1 ) the latent heat of vaporization and p  atmospheric pressure (hPa). ea   (hPa) is the actual vapor pressure equal to e*  taken at the dew-point temperature (Td  ). The e* (Ta  ) – ea   difference is called the vapor pressure deficit (VPD ). The wet-environment evaporation rate, Ew  , is often expressed by the Priestley and Taylor (1972)  equation as(3) E w  = α Δ ( T w  )  Q n   Δ ( T w  ) + γ       where α  (>1) is the dimensionless Priestley-Taylor parameter and accounts for the fact that even under perfectly wet conditions (i.e., over the oceans) the air rarely stays saturated over a daily or longer period, therefore the second term in Eq. (2)  does not vanish. The wet-environment air temperature, Tw  , in Eq. (3)  (when applied during drying conditions) can be estimated by the wet-surface temperature, Tws  , provided the latter is capped by Ta  , as the wet-environment air temperature cannot be higher than Ta   (under the same Qn  ) due to the cooling effect of evaporation, while Tws   can (Szilagyi, 2014 ). The implicit equation (Szilagyi and Jozsa, 2008 ) for Tws   can be written as(4) Q n  - E p   E p   = γ T ws   - T a   e  ∗   T ws     - e a        requiring some iterations. The α  in Eq. (3)  was found to be related to Tw   (Andreas et al., 2013 ) as(5) α = Δ T w    + γ  Δ T w    + c γ       where c  is a universal constant value. Szilagyi et al. (2014) , unaware of the work of Andreas et al. (2013) , specified a polynomial relationship between Tw   and α , which overlaps almost perfectly (Szilagyi and Crago, 2023 ) with the curve of Eq. (5)  in the 15–25 °C warm season Tw   range when evaporation rates may be the highest, provided c  = 0.55 in Eq. (5) . In this study a c  value of 0.55 is kept throughout.  2.2 Model inputs The present CR model inputs include Ta  , Td  , uh   and Rn  . Here the first three came from ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020 ), in which the 10-m wind speed was transformed into 2-m value by the power-function relationship of Brutsaert (1982) , discussed above. The Rn   values came from the Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2.1 Noah land surface model output (GLDAS v2.1, Beaudoing and Rodell, 2020 ) with a correction to match the climatological mean monthly values of the Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System product (Kato et al., 2018 ). All these monthly inputs are at 0.25°, the same spatial resolution for estimating E  by the PCR of Eq. (1)  globally. Because GLDAS v2.1 is only available since 2000, the PCR model was run for the 2000–2016 period at a monthly time step in the present study.  2.3 Reference datasets To test the models, the reference datasets of E  used in this study include water-balance-based evaporation (ETwb  ) and eddy-covariance (EC) measurements from the FLUXNET2015 Database (Pastorello et al., 2020 ), both regarded as “ground-truth” information for model calibration/verification. Annual ETwb   is calculated as the annual precipitation (Prec ) less runoff (Q ) less change in water storage (dS ), either on a cell-by-cell or basin-wide basis. The latter is determined mainly by the format of the Q  data since gridded observation-based Prec  (Sun et al., 2018 ) and dS  (Tapley et al., 2004 ) are available across the continents, but station-observed Q  is only available at the outlet of gauged basins. Thus, to derive gridded ETwb   values, two gridded global runoff datasets available at 0.5° were employed for deriving Q  as the arithmetic mean of the two values in the present study, which included the Global RUNoff (GRUN) reconstruction database by Ghiggi et al. (2019)  and the Linear Optimal Runoff Aggregate (LORA) from 11 land surface models by Hobeichi et al. (2019) . The Prec  values come from the Global Precipitation Climatology Center (GPCC) Full Data Monthly Version 2018 at 0.25° (Schneider et al., 2018 ), while dS  is derived from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory Mascon RL06 Version 2.0 Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) at 0.5° (Watkins et al., 2015 ). After resampling GPCC to 0.5°, annual ET wb  was obtained for the overlapping period of these datasets, i.e., 2003–2012, at the same spatial resolution. Note that while this sort of gridded ETwb   can be derived for the globe, calibrating the b  values in the PCR on a cell-by-cell basis for the entire world would have entailed a great amount of computation time. Therefore, this study restricts the cell-by-cell calibrations to Australia only as this continent enjoys a diverse climate from tropical, to savannah, to semi-arid, to Mediterranean and temperate, reflected in the wide range (Fig. 2  ) of an impromptu wetness index, wi   = P ¯   E w  ¯   −1 . Note also that estimation of E  by the PCR across Australia is also performed at 0.5° to match the spatial resolution of above gridded ET wb  data. While the above gridded ETwb   data provide terrestrial evaporation information for each grid-cell, the possible error in gridded runoff data (Hou et al., 2023 ) may be propagated into such ETwb   estimates. Therefore, the present study also employs the basin-scale ETwb   estimates of globally distributed 56 large river basins (Fig. S1 ) of Ma et al. (2024) , where observed runoff from the hydrological station of each basin outlet were used. These basins were selected based on the following criteria: i) basin area is larger than 105  km2 ; ii) glaciers cover less than 0.5 % of the basin area; iii) water bodies account for less than 7 % of the basin area, and; iv) continuous monthly Q  data is available for 1983–2016 with a maximum permitted gap of 1 %. To reduce possible error in precipitation measurements that can impact the accuracy of ETwb  , the typical undercatch in the precipitation gauge measurements were corrected, thus mitigating the underestimation of ETwb   particularly in mid- and high-latitudes. For further details on the ETwb   values of the 56 basins, refer to Ma et al. (2024) . In the FLUXNET2015 dataset (Pastorello et al., 2020 ), the monthly meteorological variables required by Eq. (1) , together with ground-truth latent (LE ) and sensible heat (H ) fluxes potentially came from altogether 171 stations (for a complete list, see Table S2 ) around the globe. After necessary data processing and filtering, summarized in Szilagyi and Crago (2023) , only those months and stations were consequently kept when/where the uncorrected monthly LE  and H  values were within 10 % of the Qn   value in order to avoid the application of often arbitrary/complicated energy-budget closure techniques (Mauder et al., 2020 ), which thus left altogether 124 stations (Fig. S2  and Table S2 ) for a practical evaluation of the gridded b  values.  2.4 Development of an isenthalpic index In this study, the b  values are calibrated over Australia by a numerical inversion of Eq. (1)  (via a systematic trial-and-error process as it cannot be inverted algebraically) to approach the multi-year mean annual gridded water-balance evaporation, E wb    ¯    , as much as possible. Notice that the relatively dry cells in the southern and western edges of the continent (Fig. 2 ) attain higher b  values that decrease with distance from the sea. The wetness index, wi   (= P ¯   E w  ¯   −1 ), in itself does not contain information of the relative  significance of moisture advection into the area similar to another, so-called evaporative aridity index, ai   (−), here defined as ai   = (E p  max    ¯   - E w   ¯     )(E p  max    ¯   - E p   ¯     )−1 . However, when combined (the latter first raised to a certain power, d ), the product, i.e., ai d wi  , named an isenthalpic index, Ii   (−), does so. As Fig. 2  demonstrates, the lower the value of Ii   the higher b  becomes, and vice versa. The exponent of ai   in Ii   (=ai d wi  ) was obtained by a systematic trial-and-error optimization where the objectives were to find a best-fit curve that i) approaches unity (i.e., the theoretical minimum of b ) as Ii   increases to 5 while at the same time reaching a b  value close to 10 at Ii   = 0; ii) yields b  values that minimize the root-mean-square-error (RMSE) between Eq. (1) -predicted basin-averaged multi-year mean (2000–2016) annual evaporation (E  ¯    ), and water-balance derived E wb    ¯     values over the 56 large river basins across the globe (Fig. S1 ). The optimization yielded a value of 2.4 for d . A plot of ai   versus wi   and the relative magnitudes of Ii   are included in Supporting Information  (Fig. S3 ) along with Table S1 , which summarizes conditions associated with large and small values of wi   and ai  . Large wi   corresponds to good moisture availability while large ai   corresponds to dry air. The reason that Ii   can respond to the relative  strength of moisture advection lies in the fact that wi   indicates general water availability of the land mainly via the measured precipitation for which proximity to a sea in itself does not guarantee more abundance (see Fig. 2  or consider the Peruvian or Namibian coastline). At the same time ai   measures the aridity of the air and reacts to moisture source proximity (as long as the prevailing wind brings that moisture into the land area in question). Namely, the larger the long-term mean Ep   value deviates from a similar mean of Ep max  , due to sustained or frequent moisture import to the area, the smaller ai   becomes. So a dry land with minimal external moisture import produces small wi   and large ai   values (and thus large Ii  ), while over a wet region ai   is already close to unity, almost independently of any moisture import, and wi   is large (Fig. S3 ), altogether yielding a large Ii   value again in comparison to the arid seashore with significant moisture advection from the sea, as seen in Fig. 2 . Ii   can be called an isenthalpic index because the higher its value the weaker the relative influence of any external moisture advection on the isenthalpic cooling/warming of the land. As seen, this index is the highest in the monsoonal region of Australia because during the wet season the land is almost as wet as the sea the winds arrive from, so the relative importance of such moisture import is low, while during the dry season the winds arrive from the already dry center of the continent (Szilagyi et al., 2022 ), so overall, the relative influence of external moisture advection remains low throughout the year in that area, which may not be trivial at first sight. Fig. 3   displays the heat-scatter plot of the b  vs Ii   values over Australia. Single, double, and triple-term composite exponential functions were tested for curve-fitting (for each test value of d  in Ii  ), the last one producing the best results for d  = 2.4 (Fig. 3 ) in the form of(6) b = 3.259 e  - 6.689 I i    + 0.1975 e  - 0.3626 I i    + 2.848 e  - 1.058 I i    + 1      As the scatter in the b  vs Ii   values is significant, especially toward large b  values above the densest, warm-colored ridge of the scatter plot (Fig. 3 ), therefore a simple fitting (i.e., considering all data points in the scatter plot) would yield elevated b  values (and thus underestimation of E ) since the fitted curve would be above this ridge. In order to force the best-fit curve onto the ridge, the fitting had to be restricted to (b  ± 0.1, Ii   ± 0.1) interval blocks in which the number of value pairs exceeded a prescribed minimum limit value. Naturally, the larger this limit value, the more the curve would sink downward to trace the ridge ever more tightly but then requirement i) above would frequently be violated, plus the curve would yield ever larger ensemble mean 〈 E  ¯   〉    values across the 56 test basins as a consequence of the suppressed b  values (see Fig. 1 ) produced by the “low-lying” curve. Eventually, an optimal limit value of four was found by trial-and-error combined with a visual inspection of each curve.   3 Results and discussions 3.1 Global distribution of I i  and b  As the b  values are tightly related to the isenthalpic index, Ii  , it is worthwhile to take a look at the global distribution of the latter (Fig. 4  ), calculated from the 0.25° global data for 2000–2016. The higher the value of Ii  , the less influence external moisture import is supposed to exert on the isenthalpic cooling/warming of the land surface. Such areas are marked by warm colors in Fig. 4  and generally found in high latitudes, and in cold/warm humid regions. Interestingly, in the Sahel of Africa mostly isenthalpic conditions exist probably because in the dry season not much external moisture reaches the region, similar to what is found in the monsoonal part of Australia. The lowest Ii   values in turn are found in the Sahara, around the Horn of Africa and the Gulf of Oman, in the arid regions of western China, and in general along the western shore of the continents where the climate is dry due to strong cold ocean currents. The spatial distribution of the b  values (Fig. 5  ) is almost a mirror image of that of Ii  : low values in high latitudes, and in humid regions, in general. In the contrary, the hot/warm and dry regions of the world are generally characterized by high b  values, as the relative importance of external moisture import is significant in these areas and often is the only source of water for the desert flora and fauna (e.g., in the Atacama, Namib, and Taklimakan Deserts). In a comparison with the b  values of Kim et al. (2024) , the warm/humid regions of the tropics (especially the Amazon and Congo basins, but most of Indonesia as well) stand out where the current b  values are significantly lower (Fig. 6  ). The current b  values are lower than those of Kim et al. (2024)  in general, by about one in their mean, and by about half of that in their median value (Fig. 7  ). The reason for this discrepancy must be found in the different approaches taken for deriving them, as the input data are very similar in the two studies.  3.2 Performance evaluation of the PCR employing Ii  -based b  values The PCR-predicted mean annual evaporation rates of Eq. (1) , employing Eq. (6)  for the b  values, are depicted in Fig. 8  . Naturally, the largest evaporation rates are found in the tropics, while the smallest in the Sahara and over Greenland, reminding one that deserts are not necessarily connected with hot regions of the world. The global terrestrial mean (without Antarctica) is 583 mm yr−1 , which is almost identical to the state-of-the-art atmospheric reanalysis, ERA5 (586 mm yr−1 ), and land surface model, Noah, from GLDAS v2.1 (582 mm yr−1 ) calculated by Ma et al. (2024)  covering roughly the same period (i.e., 2000–2016 in this study vs 2003–2019), and 13 mm yr−1  more than what a constant value of b  = 2 produces (i.e., 570 mm yr−1 ). The difference in the two PCR estimates comes from the mean (and median) grid-b  value of 1.77 which, being lower than two, yields higher evaporation rates (Fig. 1 ). In comparison, the global terrestrial mean is 539 mm yr−1  by the method of Kim et al. (2024)  for the same period. In general, the spatially varying b  values improve the performance of the PCR (Fig. 9  ) when assessed over the 56 large basins of the world (Fig. S1 ), raising the explained variance (R2 ) by about 4 %, the NSE value by ∼6 %, while reducing the RMSE value by about 23 mm yr−1  for the mean annual basin-averaged E  values. As the 56 basin E wb    ¯     values were employed during determination of the ai   exponent in Ii  , an independent evaluation of the grid-b  values maybe necessary to see how they perform in regions not covered by the basins. Since the water-balance derived E  values may contain relatively large uncertainties in basins with somwhat sparse precipitation gauges (Ma et al., 2024 ), the eddy-covariance (EC) measurements of the global FLUXNET2015 network (Pastorello et al., 2020 ) could serve as an independent data source for checking the reliability of the derived b  values. If the grid-b  values are correctly derived the way described above then Eq. (1)  (combined with Eqs. (5) and (6)  should improve over the constant, b  = 2, case when applied with the FLUXNET2015 stations’ input data and employing the grid-cell b  values that overlap the stations. This is indeed the case (Fig. 10  ), as the explained variance (R2 ) increased from about 80 % to 82 %, the NSE value from ∼78 % to 79 %, while the RMSE value dropped from 17.76 mm mo−1  to 17.16 mm mo−1 .
