Approximately 80 % of the study regions demonstrated a negative deformation rate, indicating subsidence (Fig. 9 b). The average deformation rate and distribution suggest that the study region is experiencing a trend of subsidence due to climate warming and extreme rainfall events, which aligns with previous research findings (Chen et al., 2021 ). Fig. 9 c illustrates the distribution of TLS on the deformation rate map in the study area. More than 90 % of TLS occurrences were observed in regions with a negative deformation rate (i.e., subsidence region). About half of the observed TLS cases exhibited deformation rates ranging from −5 to −10 mm/year. The overall deformation trend (Fig. 9 a), deformation distribution (Fig. 9 b), and distribution of TLS on the deformation rate map (Fig. 9 c) strongly validate the reliability of the improved SBAS method. Furthermore, by examining the changes in deformation rates of historical landslide points from 2015 to 2022, we have analyzed the trends in deformation rate over the past eight years, as depicted in Fig. 10  . The graph reveals that while the deformation rate for historical landslide points with an average rate exceeding −5 mm/year has exhibited some fluctuations, it has overall maintained a stable trend. In contrast, the deformation rate for landslide points with an average rate below −5 mm/year has experienced a noticeable upward trend over the same period, with this trend becoming more significant when the average rate falls below −10 mm/year. This analysis suggests that landslide points with lower deformation rates are typically stable, whereas those with higher rates are classified as unstable. Over the past eight years, the deformation rates of these unstable points have progressively increased. Given the warming and humidifying climate in the QTP (Wang et al., 2023 ), the rising temperatures and enhanced precipitation could potentially exacerbate the deformation rates of these unstable landslides. Should the rates reach a critical threshold, there is a risk of further collapse. Particularly, it is crucial to focus on the instability of landslide points in the vicinity of the Qinghai-Tibet Railway and Qinghai-Tibet Highway, as their reactivation could lead to substantial damage to the infrastructure, including embankments, road surfaces, and culverts (Luo et al., 2019 ).  4.2.3 TLS map using the ITM We generated the TLS map using the ITM, as shown in Fig. 11  . The classification of TLS based on both the IM and ITM was generally consistent. TLS in the VH and H categories primarily concentrated along fluvial banks. These regions exhibited abundant vegetation coverage, heavy precipitation, and low ground surface temperature, resulting in noticeable development of underground ice and a high potential for TLS occurrence (Luo et al., 2019 ). The ITM achieved an AUC value of 0.98 when using validation data (Fig. 11 c), indicating that its accuracy surpassed that of the IM. When comparing the TLS maps generated by the IM and ITM, we observed an increase in the areas classified as VH, H, and M, with a significant rise in VH and H susceptibility primarily concentrated along fluvial banks (Fig. 11 a, d). The standard deviation (STD) is widely recognized as a reliable indicator for identifying active regions (Ciampalini et al., 2016; Novellino et al., 2021 ). Consequently, regions with a ground surface deformation rate of less than −5 mm/year were classified as unstable areas. In Fig. 11 a, five regions marked with black lines and labeled A, B, C, D, E were identified as having a high potential for tidal land subsidence (TLS) occurrence based on the deformation rate. To evaluate the performance of the ITM, the TLS of these five regions was compared with the results obtained using the IM, as shown in Fig. 12  . The comparison revealed a significant increase in TLS for regions A, B, C, D, and E. This suggests that regions exhibiting high negative deformation rates have a greater potential for TLS occurrence. The results were deemed satisfactory and indicated that the enhanced susceptibility map offered a more rational assessment compared to the original version.  4.2.4 Assessment of the ITM Landslide susceptibility model (LSM), a crucial instrument for evaluating landslide risk, had been effectively employed to mitigate the impact of landslide hazards (Panahi et al., 2022 ). The division method of mapping units, which mainly contain grid cells and slope units, affected the accuracy of LSM. Although lacking a direct connection to the topography, grid cells units which had computational advantage over slope cells was obtained to generate the TLS map in this study. Integrating landslide susceptibility evaluations with InSAR deformation was a hot research topic. Scholars mainly used a contingency matrix and weighted overlay to integrate the results (Shen et al., 2019; Devara et al., 2021 ). In this study, we utilized a contingency matrix to combine the IM with ground surface deformation rates, resulting in the development of an integrated TLS model. The percentage and count of recorded TLS in various TLS classifications were calculated to evaluate the reliability of the integrated model, with the results depicted in Fig. 13  . The integrated TLS model revealed that approximately 95 % of TLS were distributed in H and VH classifications, a significant increase from the 87 % observed in the original TLS model. This finding suggests that the integrated model more accurately depicts the distribution of TLS in the research area.    5 Discussion 5.1 Assessment of atmospheric error correction The STD of the deformation rate reflects the internal precision of the linear deformation rate and serves as an index to evaluate the effectiveness of atmospheric error correction in the SBAS process (Kang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, we analyzed the disparity in the standard deviation of deformation rates between the enhanced SBAS and the conventional SBAS methods. The conventional method employed a quadratic model for correcting topography-related atmospheric errors (tropospheric delay) without segmentation. The comparison of STD results is presented in Fig. 14  . The analysis revealed that the STD based on the enhanced SBAS was lower than that of the conventional SBAS in the majority of the study regions, with the mean STD of the improved SBAS results reduced by 59 %. This suggests a substantial enhancement in the mean internal precision of the rate for the enhanced SBAS. To further evaluate the performance of the enhanced SBAS method, this paper established integrated TLS models using deformation rates obtained from both the enhanced and traditional SBAS methods, based on the contribution matrix. The ROC curves and AUC areas were utilized to assess the accuracy of both models, with the results depicted in Fig. 15  . The AUC areas of the two integrated TLS models were 0.94 and 0.98, indicating the higher accuracy of integrated TLS model with improved SBAS. This finding highlighted the reliability of the result obtained through the improved SBAS, supporting the establishment of the integrated TLS model.  5.2 Validation of TLS results The permafrost region of the QTP is characterized by limited transportation infrastructure, particularly in the highly vulnerable areas identified in this study, which are predominantly situated in uninhabited regions devoid of transportation facilities. Conducting on-site investigations in these high-risk areas poses significant challenges. To address this, high-resolution remote sensing images from the GF-6 satellite were employed to validate the TLS result. Four representative regions, which marked in Fig. 10 , namely a, b, c, and d were chosen due to their high deformation rates and TLS. We utilized high-resolution Gaofen-6 optical remote sensing imagery to analyze the geomorphological features of these regions, thereby validating TLS results. Our analysis identified newly developed TLs in regions a and c (Fig. 16  a, c). Historical TLS data were derived from remote sensing images captured in 2020. The optical remote sensing images referenced in the text were acquired in 2023, indicating the emergence of newly developed TLs in these two areas post-2020. TLs that emerged after 2020 are associated with climate change. Both precipitation and landsurface temperature play crucial roles in the initiation of TLs. Fig. 17   illustrates the variations in annual mean landsurface temperature and annual accumulated precipitation from 2010 to 2022 in regions A and C, where recent TLs have occurred. Notably, both regions exhibit a distinct upward trend in temperature and precipitation between 2019 and 2022, which has created favorable conditions for the formation of landslide events. Although no newly developed TLS were observed in regions b and d (Fig. 16 b, d), surface features such as gullies, erosion patches, and freeze–thaw folds resulting from slow creep suggest a high likelihood of TLS occurrence (Niu et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019 ). These findings from the geomorphological survey underscore the reliability of the TLS results obtained through the integrated model.  5.3 Influencing factors of the TLS The q-index and interaction detectors on each factor for the TLS based on GD were conducted (Fig. 18  ). TDD and PRE were the two most important factors to TLs occurrence, and this result was consistent with previous studies that climate was a determinant of occurrence and spatial distribution for TLs (Lewkowicz, 2007; Luo et al., 2019 ). Our results also indicated that NDVI and DEM with q-index of more than 0.1 also provided important roles in the occurrence of TLs, whereas these factors were not considered to establish the TLS model in the previous study (Luo et al., 2019 ), which was unreasonable. In addition, we conducted interaction detection on the impact factors, which evaluates whether the explanatory power of the dependent variable increases or decreases when factor 1 and factor 2 act together (Wang et al., 2010 ). By calculating the similarity between the newly formed polygon distribution of the two independent variables stacked together and the spatial distribution of the dependent variable, we can determine the impact of the interaction. It could be observed from the results of interaction detector that the q value between any two impact factors is greater than that for a single factor (Fig. 18 ), which suggested that any combination of two impact factors had higher important contributions to the occurrence of TLs. We exemplify the interaction between TDD and PRE by noting that their combined effect yields an impact q-value of 0.68 on the TLs (Fig. 18 b), which exceeds the sum of their individual q-values. This indicates that the spatial distribution resulting from the overlay of TDD and PRE exhibits a higher similarity with the spatial distribution of TLs. TDD influences the active layer's ground ice melting, while PRE augments the water content at the sliding surface attachments. These factors significantly impact the occurrence of TLs (Wang et al., 2023 ). Consequently, the spatial distribution resulting from the overlay of TDD and PRE layers is anticipated to exhibit a higher similarity with the thermal thaw slumping distribution, thus increasing the q-value.  5.4 Distribution features of TLS A statistical analysis was carried out to examine the distribution features of TLS (Fig. 19  a-f). These features were primarily evident in the fact that the regions with high TLS had a tendency to occur in areas with a gentle slope, fine-grained sediments, high PISR, moderate precipitation and low TDD. The reasons for these distribution features were as follows: 1) The gentle slopes were more susceptible to occurrence of TLs due to the accumulation of power water pressure caused by inadequate drainage conditions (Rudy et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2021 ), 2) Although precipitation contributed to the accumulation of power water pressure in the active layer and increased the risk of TLs occurrence, the low land surface temperatures in the heavy precipitation areas of the study area (Fig. S1 ) were not conducive to underground ice melting, and therefore TLs were unlikely to occur in these areas (Lewkowicz, 2007; Lewkowicz and Harris, 2005; Luo et al., 2019 ), 3) The soils with fine-grained sediments were inclined to the increase of water-holding capacity and segregated ice production (Kokelj and Burn, 2005; Chen et al., 2021 ), 4) the areas with high PISR were generally in the south-east and south-west facing slope, which were relatively ice-rich (Luo et al., 2019 ), 5) despite TDD being the primary source of heat flux in the active layer, areas with low TDD values were more susceptible to the occurrence for TLs due to the poor development of ground ice for areas with high ground surface temperature. This paper also analyzed the effects of NDVI, WC, VT, ALT and DEM on the distribution features of TLS, and the results showed that regions with high TLS were prone to occur in the areas with high NDVI and water content, moderate DEM and ALT and the vegetation cover type of alpine steppe. The increasing NDVI was related to the increasing water content of the upper part of the active layer (Hu et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021 ), which may result in the occurrence of TLs. The areas with high elevation were not prone to the occurrence of TLs due to steep slope and low ground surface temperature, which had restrictions for the growth of ground ice. The regions with deep active layer were also unfavorable to the development of ground ice due to this region with high ground temperature frequently (Chen et al., 2021 ).  5.5 Limitations of the integrated model The study aimed to enhance the TLS model by integrating SVM approach with the improved SBAS technique. The integrated model demonstrated improved accuracy, with TLS results exhibiting enhanced rationality and comprehensive coverage. However, several limitations were identified: 1) Atmospheric errors, which may introduce potential errors in the SBAS result, were challenging to eliminate entirely, despite the application of a segment processing technique to mitigate atmospheric errors. 2) The low spatial resolution of certain factors (TDD, PRE, Soil, and ALT) at 1000 × 1000 m could lead to potential errors in the SVM model result due to the limited area of TLs within the permafrost region. Therefore, future research should focus on acquiring more precise and comprehensive data to improve the overall accuracy of the model. 3) The integrated model, effective in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) alpine valley region, was not suitable for areas with dense vegetation due to potential errors in the InSAR process caused by vegetation cover. It is crucial to refine this integrated model using technological advancements and explore its applicability across various topographic landscapes.   6 Conclusion This study introduced a novel model for TLS by incorporating a conventional machine learning approach and an improved SBAS technique. Nine influencing factors were selected using the q-index to assess the susceptibility of TLs in the IM. The TLS of IM suggested that some regions with high negative deformation rates had relative low susceptibility, although this result was not sufficiently precise to reflect real susceptibility. The comparison between STD and field monitoring data has demonstrated the reliability of the surface deformation obtained through the enhanced SBAS method utilized in this study. After integrating the ground surface deformation, the TLS of ITM were characterized by enhanced rationality and greater accuracy (the AUC value was 0.98, larger than that of the initial method which was 0.92). This was demonstrated by the TLS in some areas with a high negative deformation rate that changed from L to H, M to H, and H to VH. Moreover, more historical TLs distributed in H and VH, and fewer TLs distributed in L and VL, were in favor of this argument. Through the analysis of factors influencing TLS, we discovered that climate is the predominant factor for TLS occurrence (with an integrated contribution for susceptibility of 0.68), followed by NDVI, DEM, Soil, and Slope. This finding aligns with the observed distribution characteristics of TLS and further validates the high predictive accuracy of our integrated model. The proposed methodology overcame the constraints of conventional machine learning approaches in assessing TLS and demonstrated more comprehensive performance in predicting the occurrence likelihood of TLs. This approach had the potential to be implemented in permafrost regions and to serve as a foundation for the prevention and mitigation of disasters.
1 Introduction Soil water content (SWC) as a key variable in hydrology and agriculture affects a wide variety of land-atmospheric interactions at a range of spatial and temporal scales. Soil moisture is highly spatially and temporally variable, and knowledge of the characteristics of this variability is important for understanding and predicting the terrestrial phase of the hydrologic cycle, terrestrial-atmospheric interactions, and many other environmental processes. The spatio-temporal variability of SWC is controlled by processes at different spatial scales from centimeters to thousands of kilometers (Western and Grayson 1998 ). As a result, soil moisture variability has different patterns depending on the scale, which needs to be considered when designing the sampling scheme for quantifying SWC evolution dynamics. According to Bloschl and Sivapalan (1995) , the scale consists of three elements: spacing, extent, and support. The spacing is the distance between measurements or data points, the extent is the total size of the spatial domain, and the support is the effective area or volume represented by the measurement. Small-scale variability will not be captured if the spacing is too large, while large-scale variability will not be captured if the extent is too small. And if the support is too large, variability within the support will be ignored. Therefore, a proper scale for measurements is needed to obtain the dataset that can best suit the requirement of a process at interest. The relationships between the SWC statistics of variability, such as standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV) with mean SWC are important topics for studying SWC spatio-temporal variability (e.g. Brocca et al., 2010; Burns et al., 2016; Choi and Jacobs, 2011; Famiglietti et al., 2008; Molina et al., 2014 ). The results regarding the change in SD with mean from previous studies were inconsistent depending on different settings. Some studies have found an increase in SD as mean soil moisture decreased (Famiglietti et al. 1999, Hupet and Vanclooster, 2002 ), while others have documented an increase in SD as mean soil moisture increased (Famiglietti et al., 1998; Western and Grayson, 1998; Williams et al., 2009 ), although mean SWC was within in the similar range between 0.20 cm3  cm−3  to 0.45 cm3  cm−3 . With a wider range of mean SWC that included drier soils with mean SWC less than 0.2 cm3  cm−3 , an upward convex curve of SD versus mean SWC was proposed, with standard deviation peaking at about 0.2 cm3 /cm3  of mean soil moisture (Choi and Jacobs, 2007; Famiglietti et al. 2008; Owe et al., 1982; Penna et al., 2009 ). For the relationship between CV and mean SWC, most studies found an exponentially decreasing CV as the mean SWC increased, while others reported a linear decrease with the increasing mean SWC (Bell et al. 1980, Famiglietti et al. 1999, Famiglietti et al. 2008, Li et al. 2020, Owe et al. 1982 ). Quantifying the relationship of the SWC statistics between different scales is valuable for determining the controlling factors, upscaling or downscaling SWC, and validating and better utilizing remotely sensed SWC products (Famiglietti et al., 2008; Korres et al., 2015 ). Famiglietti et al. (2008)  analyzed several datasets covering spatial scales from 2.5 m to 50 km and found that SD, CV, and skewness of soil moisture increased with increasing spatial extent scale. They also reported that SD∼mean had a upward convex relationship for scales beyond 1.6 km, while there was no clear trend for scales less than 100 m likely due to a narrower range of mean SWC and a smaller number of samples than at larger scales. However, Korres et al. (2015)  reported that there was no clear relationship between SWC variability with extent scales (spatial extent and support) based on measured or modelled data for various land use types at different scales. They attributed the difference to the large SWC variability within a spatial scale from natural processes that were not scale-dependent, such as varying evapotranspiration rates of different plants, overwhelmed the variability between scales. Shehata et al. (2022)  found that lower spatial resolution, i.e. larger spacing between sampling points led to smaller SD and CV for 0–25 cm soil depth within an alfalfa field. Most previous studies on spatio-temporal variability of SWC have been conducted for surface soils. Limited studies on deeper soils have shown that the spatial variability of soil moisture generally decreases with increasing soil depth, largely because surface soils have highly variable inherent properties, and are susceptible to external influences such as meteorological conditions, soil biology, compaction, and other physical disturbances (Owe et al. 1982; Bell et al. 1980; Choi and Jacobs 2007, Choi et al., 2007, Korres et al., 2015, Rao and Ulaby, 1977 ). Other studies reported opposite results that deeper soils had larger variability than the surface soils (Gao and Shao, 2012; Penna et al., 2009 ). Penna et al. (2009)  found that SWC at 0–6 cm was wetter and had less spatial and temporal variability than at 0–12 cm and 0–20 cm, especially during dry periods. They also found that SD, CV, and skewness were highly depth-dependent, with SD and CV increasing from 6 cm to 12 cm depth. Choi and Jacobs (2007)  also found that SD and skewness of SWC were less depth-dependent, with SD tending to decrease with increasing depth of the soil layer. Korres et al. (2015)  found that CV decreased with deeper soil layers under forest, while in the farmland, CV in the 0–20 cm was equal to or even slightly lower than that of 20–40 cm. The authors attributed the apparent difference to the homogenization of the topsoil layer by agricultural management practices (e.g., tillage and harrowing) and variable plant water uptake intensity in the root zone during different periods, which led to lower CV in the surface layer than in deeper layers. In contrast, CV of SWC was found to be similar in the surface and deep layers, i.e. CV was more dependent on moisture levels, relative to soil depth (Bell et al., 1980 ). As mentioned above, there have been many studies on SWC variability at different scales. However, most of those results were obtained at scales larger than an agriculture field, and also many of them were on natural landscapes, such as grass and forest fields. As Scaife et al. (2021)  have noticed, SD∼mean relationships at field or plot scale might be more complex than those at larger scales. At present, few studies have examined the variation of SWC statistics, such as spatial mean, SD, and CV at different extent scales of farmland and for different hydrologic years. Further, although spatio-temporal variability of SWC has been studied with a variety of approaches, such as descriptive statistics, geostatistics, and temporal stability analysis, few studies have attempted to quantify the relative magnitude of spatial and temporal variability. Understanding the patterns of SWC statistics including the spatial mean, SD, and CV changing with scales, are essential for determining a proper spatial scale for setting up either a manual sampling or automatic monitoring network in an agriculture field. Therefore, the objectives of this study were to investigate the variation of SWC statistics including mean, SD, and CV, the relationships between CV and mean, and to quantify the contribution of spatial variance over the total variance at different scales for different soil layers during three growing seasons within an intensively irrigated vineyard.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Experimental site description and data collection The experiment was conducted at Huangtai vineyard located at Wuwei, Gansu Province of China (37°52′20 “'N, 102°50′50″E, and altitude of 1581 m). The area has a typical temperate arid continental climate with dry and hot summer and cold winter. At the area, the mean annual temperature is 8.8℃ and the mean annual precipitation is about 164 mm. The groundwater table at the site is over 25 m deep. The whole vineyard was flat with the elevation of the sampling region ranging from 1573 to 1577 m, and the mean slope < 0.07°. The soil at the site was classified as an Aridisol (USDA definition) with a sandy loam texture. The mean bulk density of 0–100 cm soil is 1.47 g cm−3 , and there is an impermeable layer at a depth of 1.2 m. The vines were established in 1999, and the grape variety was Vitis vinifera  L. cv Merlot Noir. The vine rows were oriented in east–west direction roughly 270 cm apart, and the spacing between vines was about 100 cm. The vineyard was furrow-irrigated 4 times during the experiment period of each year, and for each irrigation event usually lasting for one to two days, about 70 mm of water was applied. The furrows were about 30-cm deep, and given the amount of irrigation used, the vineyard was like flood-irrigated visually during an irrigation event. The irrigation dates in each year are presented in Table 1  . Soil volumetric water content was measured using a portable device with a capacity type sensor (Diviner 2000, Sentek Environmental Technologies, Stepney, South Australia) at regularly-spaced points with 25-m apart in both east–west and north–south directions during the growth period of 2012–2014, and details about sampling locations and dates could be found in Hao et al. (2020) . The measured soil volumetric water content was calibrated using the gravimetric one through soil sampling at each location during the sampling period. At each location, 0–60 cm was measured in 2012, while in 2013 and 2014, 0–100 cm was measured. As Diviner measures SWC at a 10-cm interval, we took the average of two adjacent intervals from the soil surface to represent the SWC for each 20-cm interval, i.e. the average of 0–10 cm and 10–20 cm were reported as SWC of 0–20 cm, the average of 20–30 cm and 30–40 cm for 20–40 cm, and so on. As a result, three depths of 0–20 cm, 20–40 cm, and 40–60 cm in 2012, and five depths with two additional depths of 60–80 cm and 80–100 cm in 2013 and 2014 were analyzed in the study. Soil water content was measured about every 10 days, and there were 17, 15, and 18 times of measurements in total in 2012, 2013 and 2014 respectively. The accumulated rain from April to September was 128, 72, and 234 mm in2012, 2013 and 2014, respectively, and dates with rainfall greater than 5 cm are shown in Table 1 . For this study, three sets of SWC data were constructed to represent three different scales, and Fig. 1   shows the sampling grids of 25-m, 50-m and 75-cm scales. The sampling region was about 0.5, 2.25, and 5.06 ha for 25-m, 50-m, and 75-m scales, respectively. There were 16 points for each extent scale.  2.2 Data analysis For each scale, the spatial mean, SD, skewness and CV of SWC were calculated for different depths in the three years, based on the 16 sampling locations of each sampling day. The relationship of CV and mean SWC was fitted with a linear equation for each combination of scale, depth and year. The critical SWC, at which SD reaches its maximum was calculated based on the linear regression equations between CV and mean SWC. Given CV = a + b*mean SWC, we can get SD = a*mean SWC + b*mean SWC*mean SWC. Consequently, SD is at its maximum when mean SWC equals −a/(2*b). Spearman’s correlation coefficient was calculated between any two sampling days for each scale, layer, and year combination. According to Sun et al. (2010) , the total variance of a variable with both spatial and temporal characteristics could be partitioned into its spatial and temporal components, and two schemes were proposed in their study, i.e. space-first formulation and time-first formulation namely. In the space-first formulation, the total variance or grand variance could be partitioned into the average of the spatial variance of different measurement times, and the temporal variance of spatial means. Similarly, In the time-first formulation, the total variance was the sum of the average of the temporal variance of different locations and the spatial variance of temporal means. Given that the relative importance of spatial to temporal variance was the focus of this study, the space-first formulation was employed to calculate the spatial and temporal components for each case. Specifically, spatial and temporal variance were calculated as (Sun et al., 2010 ):(1) V s  = m n - 1     m × n - 1     ∑ i = 1  m  σ s  2  i     m      (2) V t  = n m - 1     m × n   - 1   σ t  2  ( u )      (3) σ s  2  i    = ∑ j = 1  n  ( θ ij   - u s  ( i )  )   2  / ( n - 1 )      (4)  σ t  2  u    = ∑ i = 1  m  ( u s  i    - μ g  )   2  / ( m - 1 )      where V s  and V t  are spatial and temporal variance, m  and n  are number of sampling days and points, respectively. σ  s  2  i        is the spatial variance of i th day, σ t  2  ( u )     is the temporal variance of the spatial mean, θ ij      is the observed SWC at j th point on i th day, u s  i       is the spatial mean at i th day, ug   is the grand mean of SWC. The total variance equals to the sum of V s  and V t , and the fraction of spatial variance was obtained by dividing V t  by (V t  + V s ). ANOVA test was conducted to compare the difference of mean, SD, skewness, CV, total variance, V s , V t , and the fraction of spatial variance between different scales, soil depths and years. All statistical analyses in this study were conducted using R software, and specifically “aov” and “TukeyHSD” function were used for the ANOVA analyses (R core team, 2019; Korres et al., 2013; Brocca et al., 2007 ).   3 Results 3.1 Mean, standard deviation, skewness and CV of soil water content at different scales Fig. 2   displays the description statistics of mean, SD, and CV of SWC for different layers at the three scales. For most cases, mean SWC was similar between the three scales with the difference less than 0.05 cm3  cm−3 , except that the mean SWC of 25-m scale was found significantly greater than that of 50-m and 75-m scale for 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm in 2013 and 2014 with the difference larger than 0.10 cm3  cm−3  (p  < 0.01, Table 2  ). In general, the range of mean SWC increased with larger scales. The greatest difference was found in 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm depth in 2013 when the range of mean SWC was about 0.05 cm3  cm−3  for 25-m scale, and about 0.06 and 0.10 cm3  cm−3  for 50-m and 75-m scale respectively. Standard deviation was found significantly different between the three scales for most cases except for the surface soils in 2012 and 2013 and 20–40 cm in 2012 and 2014. For soil layers of 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm, 50-m scale tended to have the lowest mean SD averaged over different measurement dates than the other two scales in all three years, while the difference between 25-m and 75-m scales were relatively smaller and mostly insignificant. Among different layers, 40–60 cm or 60–80 cm tended to have larger SD than the other layers. The pattern of CV changing with soil depths and scales was similar to SD. For 0–20 cm in all three years, CV was found similar between the three scales, while in 40–60 cm layer, 50-m scale tended to have a lower CV than the other two scales. Similar with SD, CV tended to increase with deeper soil depth from the surface to 40–60 cm, then decline with the further increase in soil depth in 2013. In 2014, there was no apparent trend regarding the change of CV with soil depth. Fig. 3   shows the correlation coefficients between the mean SWC of different time intervals for the three scales. In general, significant correlations were found for all scales, depth and years, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.37 to 0.98. Difference in correlation between scales was more pronounced for 0–20 cm than the other layers in both 2012 and 2014, while the difference was greater for soil layers of 40–100 cm in 2013 than the same layers in 2012 and 2014. For 0–20 cm, correlation coefficient was larger at 50-m scale in 2012, while for 2013 and 2014, 75-m scale had the largest correlation coefficients. Overall, correlation of SWC between different times was weaker for 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm in 2012 than in 2013 and 2014.  3.2 Relationship of SD and CV versus mean soil water content Fig. 4   shows scatterplots between mean and SD for different scales in the three years. For surface soils of 0–20 cm, SD fluctuated within a narrow range with a seemingly random fashion for all scales in the three years, and correlation analysis confirmed that there was no significant correlation for the surface layer in all three years (p  > 0.05). Apart from 0 − 20 cm soil, the change pattern of SD versus mean varied depending on the scale, as well as different layers in different years. For the third layer in 2012 and all subsurface layers in 2014, SD apparently increased with the increase in mean, and the correlation between mean and SD for all scales was found mostly significant with a correlation coefficient larger than 0.7. For all depths in 2013, there was no apparent relationship between SD and mean, and SD changed within a narrow range with the change of mean. Table 3   shows the linear regression equations, R 2 , and p -values between CV and mean, separately for each combination of soil layers, scales, and years. For 0 – 20 cm, CV decreased with the increased mean at all scales in the three years, with R 2  ranging from 0.12 to 0.68. The slope was found to vary with different scales and years ranging from −1.7 to −0.44, with 50-m scale having smaller absolute value of slope than the other two scales. For all subsurface soil layers, CV decreased in 2012 and 2013, but increased in 2014 with the increased mean at the three scales except for 80–100 cm at 75-m scale. The regression was largely insignificant for subsurface soils beyond 40 cm at 50-m scale. For the same soil layer in the same year, the slope was similar between 25-m and 75-m scales. Fig. 5   shows the change of CV with the mean for different depths with the three-year data combined, along with the fitted linear equation. Overall, the change of CV with mean SWC for the same layer in different years could be described by a linear equation except for 20–40 cm layer. Both slopes and intercepts of the linear regression equations varied depending on different scales and layers. For the subsurface layers beyond 40 cm, the absolute value of slope was smaller for 75-m scale than the other two scales, while it was similar between 25-m and 50-m scales. For the surface layer, 75-m scale had the largest absolute value of the slope, and the largest intercept, indicating the magnitude of variation when the soil was extremely dry. For subsurface soil beyond 40 cm, the intercept decreased with the increase of the scale. In terms of the difference between soil layers, the intercept was found much greater for 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm than that of 0–20 cm and 80–100 cm for all scales. For 25-m and 50-m scales, the absolute value of slope for 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm were similar, and larger than 0–20 cm and 80–100 cm, while the slopes were similar between those three layers for 75-m scale. Apparently, the relationship between CV and mean showed a different pattern for 20–40 cm with the other soil layers. With three-year data combined, there was no significant CV∼mean linear relationship for the layer as the other layers have shown, because of the different pattern but a similar mean SWC range in 2014, relative to the other two years. For the other subsurface soil layers, mean SWC was greater, and CV was lower in 2014 than those in 2012 or 2013, leading to better overall regression when combining the three-year data, although the regression slope with 2014 data alone had the opposite sign with the other two years. Table 4   presented the calculated values of (−a/2b) from the fitted linear equation of CV = a + b* mean, considered as the critical SWC at which SD reaches its maximum for different soil scales and depths. The critical SWC in the study ranged between 0.17 and 0.36 %. There was no consistent pattern in terms of the critical SWC change with scales for different layers. For 0–20 cm, the critical SWC was similar between the three scales while it was greater at 75-m scale than the other two scales for deeper soil layers than 40 cm.  3.3 Partition of soil water content variability between space and time Fig. 6   shows the spatial and temporal variance obtained from partitioning the total variance for the three different scales in the three years. The total variance varied with scales, soil layers, and years. ANOVA test indicated that there was no significant difference in the total variance between scales for the three layers of 0–20 cm, 20–40 cm, and 80–100 cm, while for both layers of 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm, the total variance of 50-m scale was substantially lower than 25-m and 75-m scale. In terms of interannual variation, the total variance in 2014 on average was substantially lower than the other two years for all scales. Overall, the total variance for 25-m, 50-m, and 75-m scale was 54.8, 33.3, and 44.2 (×10−2  cm3  cm−3 )2  in 2012, 60.3, 43.3, and 54.7 (×10−2  cm3  cm−3 )2  in 2013, and 45.4, 31.9, and 50.6 (cm3  cm−3 )2  in 2014. Apparently, spatial variance dominated the temporal variance, accounting for more than 57 % of the total variance for all cases, more than 75 % for subsurface soils, and more than 85 % for soils deeper than 40 cm excluding 80–100 cm of 2013. On average, spatial variance accounted for 86.1 %, 82.8 %, and 84.5 % of the total variance for 25-m, 50-m, and 75-m scales, respectively. As a result, the variation of spatial variance with scales, years, and layers had a similar pattern with the total variance. Relative to spatial variance, temporal variance fluctuated within a relatively narrower range between 1.7 and 10.6 (×10−2  cm3  cm−3 )2 , and 50-m scale resulted in lower temporal variance on average than the other scales. Temporal variance for the surface 0–20 cm was substantially larger than the deeper soil layers in both 2012 and 2013, while there was no significant difference among subsurface layers in 2012 and 2013, and all layers in 2014. The fraction of spatial variance over the total variance was apparently smaller for the surface layer than the other layers for all scales in the three years. The fraction was mostly similar between the three scales for different years and layers, with exceptions of 0–20 cm where 50-m scale had much smaller fraction than the other two scales.   4 Discussions 4.1 Descriptive statistics at different scales for different soil layers As the same number of samples with different spacing between samples were used for different scales, the effect of scales observed in the study resulted from the combined effect of both spacing and extent. Considering that the number of samples might have a great effect on the calculated statistics, we presented the results using the same number of samples for each scale (extent) to minimize the effect. To better analyze the effect of extent scale, we also calculated and compared the statistics of the mean, SD, and CV, as well as the relationships between mean vs. SD, and mean vs. CV based on the data with the same spacing (25 m) between samples for each scale (Figs. S1-S3 ). In that case, there were 16, 49, and 100 samples for 25-m, 50-m, and 75-m scales, respectively. The results showed that the differences in SWC statistics and relationships of mean with SD, and CV between scales were found similar between using the data with the same spacing and those with different spacing but the same number of samples. Therefore, the conclusions of the study regarding the effect of scales were mainly from the extent, rather than spacing. Spatial mean SWC did not differ significantly between the three extent scales for the surface soil, which was consistent with previous findings at comparable scales. Famiglietti et al. (2008)  reported that mean SWC changed within a narrow range and the range was similar for different extent scales from 2.5-m to 1.6 km from one-year measurement. However, this was not the case for some subsurface soil layers in the study. The discrepancy between the surface and subsurface layers was attributable to the homogenizing effect from external forces, such as agricultural management practices, precipitation, irrigation, and evaporation on the surface soil (Famiglietti et al., 2008; Korres et al., 2015 ). Relative to surface soil, mean SWC for subsurface soil might depend more on plant root water uptake, inherent soil properties, and the particular settings of the grid points of different scales. Therefore, if only the evolution of mean was the interest, the spatial extent or resolution of the sampling grid would not make great difference for the top soil layer (0–20 cm), while for subsurface soils, sampling in different extent scales would likely result in different mean depending on the specific setting of the field. It is generally agreed that SWC variability, often represented by its SD and CV at observed points on a given sampling time, increases with the increase in the extent scale (Famiglietti et al., 2008; Koyama et al., 2010 ). Famiglietti et al. (2008)  reasoned that different controlling factors for soil water dynamics determined the SWC variability at different scales. In their case, spatial variability of soil texture, vegetation, and evaporation were the dominant factors at 500-m scale, while at the larger scale of 5 km, heterogeneity in rainfall became the dominant factor under wet conditions, which combined led to the increase of SWC variability at larger scales. At much smaller scales as in this study, it was expected that spatial variability in soil properties, particularly soil texture, would control SWC variability. Indeed, CV of SWC for 0–20 cm soil was found similar to CV of soil clay content of the surface layer at the three scales, with the difference less than 5 % between CV of SWC and clay content. In this study, CV of soil clay content at grid points of 25-m, 50-m and 75-m was 20 %, 13 %, and 22 % respectively for 0–20 cm, and 17 %, 11 %, and 23 % respectively for 20–40 cm (Table 5  ). The order of CV corresponded to that of soil texture, i.e. 75-m > 25-m > 50-m for 0–20 cm in the three years. The results suggested that the variability of SWC for surfaces soils at different scales would depend largely upon soil texture, thus knowledge of the variability of soil texture is expected to provide a good estimate of the variability of SWC for surface soils at field scale. Kim and Barros (2002)  found that spatial variability of surface SWC in the SGP97 field was closely associated with spatial distribution of soil sand and clay contents, as soil texture was a proxy measure tor of soil hydraulic properties, such as permeability and water holding capacity. Noticeably, the differences in SWC variability between scales in the layer of 20–40 cm were smaller than the counterparts of soil clay content in both 2013 and 2014, indicating that factors other than soil texture played an important role in shaping SWC dynamics. The homogenization effect from precipitation and agricultural management (e.g. plowing) was considered the main factor leading to overall lower variability of surfaces soil than deeper soil layers (Korres et al., 2013; Korres et al., 2015 ). While for subsurface soils in agricultural fields, heterogeneity in root distribution (root water uptake) likely increased the overall magnitude of spatial variability of SWC, but reduced the difference between scales in 2013 and 2014. Moreover, the larger variability for soil layers from 20 to 80 cm than that in the surface soil and 80–100 cm also indicated that plant root water uptake contributed to the overall larger variability of SWC and smaller difference between scales. Indeed, a study conducted at the exact vineyard showed that grapevine roots were mostly distributed in 10–80 cm soil, with the largest root biomass and surface area found at 30–40 cm (Zhang et al., 2012 ). With the further increase in soil depth from 30 to 40 cm, grapevine root biomass and surface area linearly decreased to the soil depth of 100 cm. Lin et al. (2023)  reported that SD and CV were generally larger for soil layers of 20–40 cm and 40–60 cm than those for 0–20 cm in a cotton field. Korres et al. (2015)  stated that relatively larger variability from some natural processes within the scale, such as root uptake mentioned above, could dominate the overall SWC variability, thus diminishing the difference in variability caused by scales. As mentioned above, irrigation, especially with such large amount of water for one event, might be one of the factors leading to the lower level of spatial variability for the surface soil layer than the subsurface soil layers. Given that the observation points were at the similar positions concerning the flow direction of a furrow for the three scales, it was not expected that the possible non-uniformity in irrigation along a furrow or between furrows would lead to different conclusions on the effects of scales on the spatial variability of SWC. However, a lack of irrigation uniformity might contribute to the overall spatial variability of SWC. There was no obvious SWC distribution pattern along a furrow or between furrows, suggesting that there was no structural influence of irrigation uniformity on SWC spatial distribution in this study. Therefore, irrigation inconsistences might affect SWC spatial distribution randomly, leading to the larger SD or CV. Unfortunately, the extent to which irrigation uniformity contributed to the overall spatial variability could not be quantified, as irrigation uniformity was not measured in this study. The change pattern of the calculated spatial variance with the scales was similar with mean SD, as they both reflect the overall spatial variability. The statistical analysis for SD and spatial variance was slightly different mainly because the number of samples in the statistical analysis of ANOVA was different for SD and V s. For SD, the number of samples was the number of SWC measurement times in that year while it was only one for each combination of scale, year, and layer in V s analysis because V s basically was the average value of spatial variance over different measure times. As a result, the degree of freedom in ANOVA analysis was different for the two variables. Interestingly, there was no difference in the temporal variance between the scales for each soil layer, indicating that the mean SWC of different scales had similar evolution trend during the growth period of each year, although the absolute mean for a given day was different.  4.2 The relationship of SD and CV vs. mean at different scales for different soil layers Previous results on the relationships of SD and CV with mean SWC showed that SD in general first increased, then decreased with increasing SWC while CV decreased continuously with larger SWC (Famiglietti et al., 2008; Brocca et al., 2010 ). Some studies showed that SD increased continuously with mean, and the narrow mean range and short study period were considered as the main reason as the very dry state of soil condition was not captured in their studies (Brocca et al., 2007; Molina et al., 2014 ). Molina et al. (2014)  showed that there were three stages in which SD changed with increasing mean for upper 30-cm soil on a Mediterranean terrace. First, SD increased slowly with the mean increasing from 0.18 to 0.32 cm3  cm−3 , then there was a faster increase when the mean changed from 0.32 to 0.38 cm3  cm−3 , and decreased when the soil was near saturation. The results in this study in general agreed with the findings of previous studies. For most cases, SD either increased (for most subsurface layers) or changed little (for surface soils) with the increase in mean. Given that the mean fluctuated within a relatively narrow range at field scales, especially with a single growth season, the pattern of SD changing with mean was more of a segment of the overall SD or CV∼mean relationship. The nearly constant SD with mean for 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers, and linear increase of SD with mean for deeper layers in 2012 and 2014 were similar to the first stage of slow increase, and the second stage of fast increase respectively described in Molina et al. (2014) . Although many studies employed exponential function to fit the relationship between CV and mean (Choi and Jacobs, 2011; Famiglietti et al., 2008 ), linear regression was used in the study for better interpretation considering that there was no particular dry state during the study period and for most cases, R 2  between linear regressions were slightly larger than those of exponential regressions. Overall, the results that CV decreased linearly with mean were consistent with those from different scales and vegetations, and the slopes from the regressions in this study (−2.5 to −0.55) were comparable with those obtained based on modeling and observations at scales from field to catchment scale (−1.5 to −0.6) (Korres et al., 2015 ) and winter wheat (−0.63) and sugar beet (−0.65) field (Koyama et al., 2010 ). Apparently, the decrease in variability with a larger mean was faster for smaller extent scales of 25-m and 50-m than 75-m for subsurface soils, which agreed with the previous results on surface soils (Famiglietti et al., 2008). In their study, exponential function (CV=k 1 exp(−k 2  mean)) was used to fit the relationship, and k 2  was found to decrease with the increase in the extent scales. Therefore, soil moisture tended to become more homogeneous in a short time for smaller areas when the soil was becoming wetter, leading to a faster decline in variability. Previous studies on the relationship of variability with mean were mostly conducted on surface soils and at relatively larger scales, and a few studies compared the change of variability with mean for different soil depths. Burns et al. (2016)  found that the relationship of SD and CV with mean was different between 5-cm depth and 20-cm and 50-cm depth soils in an agriculture-dominated region. The rainfall effect was considered as the main reason for the difference as surface soils were more sensitive to rainfall events. Similarly, irrigation probably was the main factor leading to the difference between the surface and deeper layers in this study. Meanwhile, the absolute value of slope was greater for 40–60 and 60–80 cm layers than 0–20 cm layer, which agreed with the results of Choi and Jacobs (2011) . They reported that the k 2  in exponential function mentioned earlier was found to increase with soil depth from 5 – 25 cm at a watershed scale. The consistent trend of CV decreasing with a larger mean for the layers of 40–60 cm and 60–80 cm was partially attributed to the large mean difference between the three years. In general, there was no overlap between the range of means in the three years, and the wider range of means by combining all three-year data contributed to a better fit and larger R 2  in the linear regression for the two layers. On the contrary, the range of means was similar for 20–40 cm in the three years, and the narrow range of means and also the distinct pattern of CV∼mean in the three years led to non-significant linear regressions with three-year data combined. The different pattern in the change of SD with mean led to the distinct pattern of CV vs. mean for subsurface soils in 2014, when compared to the other two years. The change of SD with mean was relatively smaller in 2012 and 2013 than in 2014. In 2013, SD changed minimally with the change in mean for the same layer, which led to CV decreased linearly with mean for the layer, while in 2014, there was an notable increase of SD when mean SWC was within a narrow range, and SD remained fairly stable when mean SWC exceeded the range. Consequently, the relatively greater increase in SD with a smaller increase in mean led to the increase CV with larger mean, i.e. positive slopes from the regressions of CV∼mean for 2014. Molina et al. (2014)  had pointed out that inconsistent relationships between SD vs. mean found in different studies was probably the result from varying control factors on soil water dynamics in those studies. Similarly, the inconsistency of CV∼mean relationship between 2014 with the other years could be attributed to the differences in the controlling factors between different years and scales. Unlike the surface soils where one or two factors might dominate, the subsurface layers were influenced by many forces, such as precipitation, irrigation, evaporation, transpiration, and drainage, which all could contribute comparably to SWC dynamics. The relative importance of those factors might be variable at different times within each year, as well as in different years. It was suspected that in 2012 and 2013, the layer was predominantly in drying process during which the decline in mean dominated the change of CV, leading to the continuous increase in CV with a decreasing mean. In 2014, soils in subsurface layers went through wetting processes more frequently, during which the increase of SD was a dominant factor influencing the change of CV, resulting in an increase of CV with mean. The results obtained in the study have important implications for setting up a monitoring network at an agricultural field or assimilating the monitored SWC data at the field into hydrological models when both mean and variability of SWC are needed. Specifically, when only mean and overall SD of surface soils of 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm in a given field were needed, setting up a monitoring network at any extent scale within a reasonable range in the field is probably fine, given that there was not much difference in mean and SD of SWC between the three scales in the study. However, when statistics of deeper soil layers were concerned, the extent at interest needed to be specified for setting up a monitoring network, as the mean and variability for deeper soils would be different depending on the extent scale used. Meanwhile, for surface soils of an agricultural field, SD of soil texture could be used to estimate SD of mean SWC at different scales, while one set of mean vs SD could be used in modeling between different years at the same scales. However, the pattern is fairly different between surface and subsurface soils. For the layer immediately below the surface layer, the overall variance of SD and CV might be similar for different scales, but its change pattern with mean would be different depending on scales and years.   5 Conclusions For the surface soil layers of 0–20 cm, the average SWC was generally similar between different scales, while SD of SWC was similar to SD of soil clay content of those sampling locations at corresponding scales in the three years, suggesting that the magnitude of soil texture variability to a great extent determined the magnitude of SWC variability, rather than scale itself. There was no consistent pattern regarding the change of SD and CV with scales for subsurface soil layers. For soil layers with relatively large root density, the heterogeneity in root water uptake increased the overall magnitude of SWC variability, but led to a smaller difference in variability between extent scales, relative to the variability of soil texture. The relationship of CV vs. mean was generally consistent in different years, but variable between scales, for all soil layers except for the layer 20–40 cm. For subsurface soil layers, the relationship of CV vs. mean was found to be distinct between the wet and dry years, suggesting that forces dominating SWC dynamics in the layers were variable depending on environmental conditions, precipitation in particular. Spatial variance was found to dominate temporal variance at all scales and layers in the three years from the variation partitioning analysis, while temporal variance was similar between scales for subsurface soils. Therefore, caution should be taken in applying the patterns derived from surface soils into subsurface soil, especially the root zone. The findings in the study are expected to shed some light on how SWC statistics of different soil depths changed with extent scales during different hydrological years in agricultural fields, which would be useful in designing soil water monitoring networks, and parameterizing soil moisture variability and assimilating observed soil moisture data into in field soil water modeling.
1 Introduction The conventional definition of the water quality volume (WQV) is the volume of runoff resulting from a specified percentile of runoff-producing rainfall events. Typical percentiles are in the range of 85%–95%. The WQV is the basis for designing the water-quality-control components of stormwater control measures (SCMs). In this context, the WQV represents the volume of runoff that is afforded full treatment, with larger runoff events being afforded only partial treatment. Treatment of the WQV typically consists of either retention with infiltration, or detention with release through an outlet structure. In both cases the storage basin is designed to have a specified drain time, which is the time required to either infiltrate or discharge the WQV from the storage basin. Typical drain times are in the range of 24–72 h, and these times are traditionally associated with the average time interval between rainfall events, although assumptions regarding interevent durations are seldom validated. Separation of rainfall events. Independent rainfall events are usually extracted from long-term rainfall records using an automated algorithm. The parameter that underlies the extraction procedure is the minimum interevent time, δ  min    , and non-zero rainfall measurements separated by more than δ  min     are deemed to be within independent rainfall events. As δ  min     is increased, rainfall measurements interspersed with longer dry periods become lumped into the same rainfall event, which results in the extraction of larger composite rainfall events that subsume multiple independent rainfall events. Runoff-generating rainfall events are defined as events with magnitudes exceeding a given threshold, the water quality rainfall (WQR) is defined as a given percentile of runoff-generating rainfall events, and the WQV is defined as the runoff generated by the WQR. Increasing δ  min     increases the magnitude of the extracted WQR and the consequent magnitude of the WQV. In relating the WQV to the WQR there is an underlying assumption that the rainfall percentile associated with the WQR is the same as the runoff percentile associated with the WQV, and hence treating the WQV in a water-quality-control basin corresponds to treating the runoff from a known percentile of independent runoff-generating rainfall events. The key challenge here is to identify the value of δ  min     that realistically separates sequential independent rainfall events. Using values of δ  min     that are too small will break individual rainfall events into intra-event bursts of rainfall, while using values of δ  min     that are too large will lump sequential independent rainfall events into combined larger events. Hence, appropriate selection of δ  min     is of critical importance in identifying the percentile rainfall amounts associated with independent rainfall events. It is known that δ  min     varies with geographic location (e.g., Driscoll et al. (1989) ) and therefore appropriate values of δ  min     and associated values of WQV for any given location should be established based on local rainfall records. However, it is a common practice for regulatory agencies to only state percentile runoff-generating rainfall amounts (WQRs) or percentile runoff amounts (WQVs) without also stating the associated value of δ  min     and supporting validation. In the absence of such validation any assertion that treating the WQV is equivalent to treating the runoff from a given percentile of independent rainfall events becomes questionable.  The role of drain time. Water quality basins used to treat runoff are conventionally designed to store and completely drain the regulatory WQV within a specified drain time. The drain-time specification combined with the given regulatory WQV fixes the average design discharge rate from the basin. For a given WQV, as the drain time increases the required basin storage also increases, since with increasing drain time the basin becomes less likely to fully drain between runoff events. Consequently, to provide adequate treatment the basin must accommodate both the undrained storage as well as runoff from the subsequent event. In conventional designs, water-quality basins are sized to accommodate the WQV and neglect carryover storage, however, when drain time is taken into account the required storage could be greater than the conventional WQV that is typically used in sizing a basin, leading to inadequate basin designs.  Scope of present paper. The present paper proposes a novel and robust methodology for determining the appropriate minimum interevent time, δ  min    , that should be used in the automatic separation of rainfall events. This paper also proposes a methodology for determining the appropriate water quality control basin volume that takes into account the drain time. Both methodologies are demonstrated in detail within a study area containing multiple rain gauges, and are further demonstrated at three locations that are far removed from the primary study area.   2 Background Restrepo-Posada and Eagleson (1982)  asserted that random occurrences of storm events at any given location can be represented as a point Poisson process that yields interevent times, δ  , having an exponential probability distribution. Based on this hypothesis, the appropriate value of δ  min     is the one that yields the best fit of the δ  ’s to an exponential distribution. Representation of the occurrence of rainfall events as a point Poisson process generally assumes that the durations of rainfall events are much shorter than the interevent times, which is usually the case but should be generally be validated in any particular application. A feature of the exponential distribution is that the mean is equal to the standard deviation, which makes the coefficient of variation (COV) equal to 1. Finding the value of δ  min     that makes COV = 1    is commonly used as the basis for separating a rainfall record into independent events. Previous studies. Driscoll et al. (1989)  used the COV = 1    test of the interevent times as a basis for separating independent rainfall events and found that the optimum value of δ  min     varied with geographic location, with δ  min   = 6  h    being optimum at a rain gauge in New Jersey, δ  min   = 18  h    at a rain gauge in Texas, and δ  min   = 300  h    at a rain gauge in Los Angeles. Driscoll et al. (1989)  ultimately recommended that δ  min   = 6  h    was the most statistically defensible value and should be standardized for the sake of having a common basis for comparison of rainfall statistics across all geographic regions of the United States. Seminal results from the National Urban Runoff Program (NURP) were based on fitting interevent times to exponential distributions using the COV = 1    test and recommended using δ  min   = 6  h    (USEPA, 1986 ). Several subsequent studies have followed suit in using δ  min   = 6  h    without further validation (e.g., Guo and Urbonas, 2002; Urbonas et al., 2011 ). Wang et al. (2019)  investigated appropriate values of δ  min     in eastern China based on δ   having an exponential distribution and found δ  min     to be in the range of 7.6–16.6 h. Wang et al. (2019)  further noted that 10–15 years of data was sufficient to obtain a stable value for δ  min    , and the derived value of δ  min     was insensitive to rainfall-measurement intervals in the range of one minute to one hour. The Urban Watersheds Research Institute (UWRI) reported that values of δ  min     typically cited in the literature are in the range of 6–24 h, and suggested considering 6–12 h with 6 h being recommended for general use (UWRI, 2020 ). In an earlier study, Huff (1967)  also used δ  min   = 6  h    as a basis for separating rainfall events. Cao et al. (2023)  studied rainfall measurements at two rain gauges in China (in Hangzhou and Jinan) and reported that using δ  min     in the range of 10–12 h with a runoff threshold of 3 mm was optimum. Essien et al. (2023)  investigated the separation of rainfall events in the UK and assumed a priori that δ  min   = 6  h    was an appropriate value for event separation.  Limitations of conventional approach. The main limitation of the conventional approach is that it is predicated on the assumption that the occurrence of rainfall events can be characterized as a point Poisson process, in which case interevent times have an exponential distribution and the appropriate value of δ  min     is that which yields COV = 1   . In reality, the property of COV = 1    is not unique to the exponential distribution and the conventional method for finding δ  min     does not address cases in which the probability distribution of interevent times is significantly different from an exponential distribution. Further, the widespread practice of taking δ  min   = 6  h    without local validation cannot generally be justified since rainfall characteristics can vary substantially with geographic location (e.g., Chin, 2020 ). These limitations are avoided by applying a procedure for determining δ  min     that does not depend on the assumption that interevent times are exponentially distributed.  Daily-rainfall approach. As an alternative to separating incremental rainfall measurements into independent rainfall events based on a specified value of δ  min    , USEPA (2009)  suggested that the 95-percentile daily (24-h) rainfall depth be used in establishing the WQR. Based on the results of Shrestha et al. (2014) , percentile values of daily rainfall can sometimes be on the same order as the corresponding percentile values of event magnitudes, where the events are separated based on δ  min   = 6  h   . In using daily rainfall amounts it must be realized that one is no longer dealing with rainfall events, since event durations can be shorter or longer than 24 h. In New York, the WQR is defined as the 90-percentile daily rainfall amount (New York, 2022 ).  2.1 Water quality depth The water quality depth (WQD) is the depth of runoff generated by the water quality rainfall. Methods of estimating the WQD from the WQR include the rational method which uses a constant volumetric runoff coefficient, the curve-number (CN) method, or a method that explicitly accounts for infiltration within the catchment, such as the ϕ  -index method. When a volumetric runoff coefficient is used, the runoff coefficient is commonly taken to be equal to the impervious fraction of the catchment, when the curve-number method is used a maximum catchment storage (which is related to the curve number) is specified, and when an infiltration method is used the infiltration capacity of the catchment is specified or derived from the curve number (Chin, 2021, 2018 ). Some jurisdictions bypass the rainfall-runoff calculation altogether and directly state a WQD without explicitly relating the WQD to the WQR. In this approach, the most common value of WQD is 2.5 cm. This value likely originated from an earlier perception (USEPA, 1983c. ) that the highest concentrations of pollutants are contained in the first 2.5 cm of runoff, which is sometimes referred to as the “first flush”. In present practice, it is still generally expected that the concentration of pollutants are higher in the initial runoff that is still generically called the first flush. However, in current practice, the WQD at any particular location is defined as a given percentile of runoff depths, which is determined primarily by the rainfall and catchment characteristics at the location and hence cannot be taken as a fixed value such as 2.5 cm. For example, for a paved catchment in Miami, Florida, 2.5 cm of runoff might correspond to 80% of the runoff amounts, while for a paved catchment in Las Vegas, Nevada, 2.5 cm of runoff might correspond to 98% of the runoff amounts. Therefore, taking 2.5 cm as the WQD at both locations would not provide the same level of water-quality control. In principle, the WQD is determined based on a fixed percentile of runoff-generating rainfall events (WQR), and extraction of the WQR is fundamental to estimating the WQD which is a basis for designing stormwater control measures.  2.2 Drain time The drain time, also known as the drawdown time or evacuation time, is the average time for a water quality storage basin to discharge the WQD. The drain time is typically specified based on the type and function of the basin. Longer drain times (up to 72 h) are typical of extended detention basins, while shorter drain times (on the order of 24 h) are typical of bioretention cells. Treatment of the WQD usually involves providing basin storage to accommodate the WQD and infiltrating or discharging the stored volume over a specified drain time. For a given storage volume, the average outflow rate decreases with increasing drain time and this can lead to an increase in the required storage due to carryover storage requirements between events. Hence, drain time can sometimes be a controlling factor in determining the required storage to treat the WQD. A proposed procedure to determine the required basin storage is described and demonstrated in this paper.   3 Proposed procedure Determination of the required basin storage to fully treat the runoff from a given percentile of runoff-producing rainfall events requires a representative rainfall record and specification of: (1) the minimum interevent time to separate independent rainfall events, (2) the threshold rainfall amount for producing runoff, and (3) the drain time for the water quality volume to be discharged from the storage basin. A sequence of steps for incorporating these considerations into the determination of the required basin storage is given below. 3.1 Step 1: Separation of a rainfall record into events A rainfall record generally consists of a sequence of incremental rainfall amounts, Δ P   , over fixed time increments, Δ t   , as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Separate rainfall events can be identified by lumping non-zero incremental rainfall measurements that are spaced less than δ  min     apart, as shown in Fig. 1 (b). Implementation of this rule transforms the rainfall record into a sequence of events, with each event having a definitive start time, end time, and rainfall amount. Three random variables associated with the extracted sequence of rainfall events are: (1) rainfall amount, P  , (2) duration, d  , and (3) interevent time, δ  . The probability distributions of P  , d  , and δ   depend on the imposed value of δ  min    . Functional dependency of the percentile rainfall.  Consistent with the aforementioned formulation, it is expected that the magnitude of a particular β  -percentile of event magnitudes, P  β    , will depend on the value of δ  min     as illustrated in Fig. 2 . For shorter values of δ  min    , corresponding values of P  β     will increase with increasing δ  min     as closely spaced rainfall measurements are lumped into rainfall events; this is shown as Region A in Fig. 2 . As δ  min     exceeds the characteristic size of the rainfall events, only sporadic measurements that are typical of interevent rainfall are incorporated into the rainfall events which results in a smaller rate of increase in P  β     with increasing δ  min    . This type behavior starts to occur at δ  min  ∗    , and the region in which this behavior occurs is designated as Region B in Fig. 2 . As δ  min     becomes sufficiently long, subsequent independent rainfall events begin to be incorporated into the lumped rainfall events and consequently the rate of increase of P  β     with δ  min     increases substantially. This type of behavior begins to occur at around δ  min  +    , and the subsequent behavior is shown as Region C in Fig. 2 . As δ  min     continues to increase, it is expected that this pattern will repeat itself. The pattern described here and illustrated in Fig. 2  is one in which there is a range between δ  min  ∗     and δ  min  +     where the slope of the P  β     versus δ  min     remains approximately constant before subsequently increasing. If the behavior described here is confirmed with field measurements, then δ  min  ∗     will be clearly identifiable as the appropriate minimum interevent time that should be used in separating rainfall events. Once δ  min  ∗     is determined, the rainfall events can then be automatically extracted by lumping incremental rainfall measurements that do not include dry periods longer than δ  min  ∗         3.2 Step 2: Runoff producing rainfall events Runoff from a given rainfall event is assumed to occur whenever the rainfall amount exceeds a given initial abstraction amount. USEPA (2009)  recommends using 2.5 mm as the threshold for identifying runoff-producing rainfall events at most sites, and associates this threshold value with depression storage within the catchment. In reality, this depth of depression storage is typical of paved surfaces (Chin, 2021 ), and it might be prudent to use larger threshold values for pervious areas where the threshold rainfall will likely depend on the catchment soil, cover types, and topographical characteristics. If the initial abstraction is taken to be the same as that used in the conventional curve number method, then the threshold rainfall, P  0     (in cm), is related to the curve number, CN, of the catchment by (1) P  0   = 508  CN   − 5 . 08     The sequence of runoff-producing rainfall events is then obtained by deleting all rainfall events extracted in Step 1 that have magnitudes less than or equal to the assigned initial abstraction, P  0    .  3.3 Step 3: Determination of the runoff from each event A variety of methods can be used to estimate the runoff from a given rainfall event. Such methods include the rational method, the curve-number method, and the ϕ  -index method. These are all one-parameter methods, with the respective parameters being the volumetric runoff coefficient, the curve number (or, equivalently, the maximum catchment storage), and the ϕ  -index. The utilization of these parameters and their associated methodologies are described below. Rational method. The rational method is based on the assumption that the ratio of the runoff depth to the rainfall depth is a constant. The runoff-to-rainfall ratio is called the volumetric runoff coefficient (Guo and Urbonas, 2014 ). Using the rational method, the total runoff from the i  th event, Q  i    , is estimated as (2) Q  i   = C  v   P  i   ,   for P  i   ≥ P  0     0 ,   for P  i   < P  0            where C  v     is the volumetric runoff coefficient, and P  i     is the event rainfall amount. Incremental runoff, Δ Q  j     , within the j  th time interval of a runoff producing rainfall event (where P  i   > P  0     ) is estimated as (3) Δ Q  j   = C  v   Δ P  j       where Δ P  j      is the incremental rainfall within the j  th time interval. Incremental application of Eq. (3)  within an event leads to Eq. (2) .  Curve number (CN) method. The CN method can be used to estimate both the total runoff and the incremental runoff within a rainfall event (Natural Resources Conservation Service, 2004 ). The total runoff from the i  th event, Q  i    , is estimated as (4) Q  i   = ( P  i   − 0 . 2 S )   2    P  i   + 0 . 8 S   ,   for P  i   ≥ 0 . 2 S   0 ,   for P  i   < 0 . 2 S          where P  i     is the total rainfall in the i  th event, and S   is the maximum catchment storage. In this formulation, the threshold rainfall, P  0    , for generating runoff is equal to 0 . 2 S   . Incremental runoff, Δ Q  j     , within the j  th time interval of an event is estimated as (5) Δ Q  j   = ( ∑  j  ′   = 0  j   Δ P  j  ′     − 0 . 2 S )   2    ∑  j  ′   = 0  j   Δ P  j  ′     + 0 . 8 S   − ( ∑  j  ′   = 0  j − 1   Δ P  j  ′     − 0 . 2 S )   2    ∑  j  ′   = 0  j − 1   Δ P  j  ′     + 0 . 8 S       where Δ P  j  ′        is the incremental rainfall within the j  ′    th time increment, and the cumulative rainfall terms in Eq. (5)  must exceed 0 . 2 S    to generate nonzero runoff.  ϕ  -Index method. The ϕ  -index is a constant infiltration capacity that when applied within an event yields a given total event runoff. In time increments where the rainfall intensity is less than the ϕ  -index, the runoff is equal to zero. To estimate the ϕ  -index, total runoff for the i  th event, Q  i    , is first estimated using the curve-number equation given by Eq. (4) , and then ϕ   is determined by solving the relation (6) Q  i   = ∑  j = 1  J  i     max ( P  j   − ϕ Δ t , 0 )      where J  i     is the number of rainfall increments in the i  th event. After solving Eq. (6)  for ϕ  , the runoff in each increment can be estimated by (7) Δ Q  j   = max ( P  j   − ϕ Δ t , 0 )      Using this formulation, the ϕ  -index method will generally give the same event runoff as the CN method, but the runoff sequence will be different, which will affect the required basin storage for water quality control.   3.4 Step 4: Determination of the water quality depth The water quality depth, WQD, is defined as the runoff depth produced by the water quality rainfall, WQR, where the WQR is equal to a specified percentile of runoff-producing rainfall events that are extracted in Step 2. For the three rainfall-runoff models considered in this study, the WQD is calculated from the WQR as follows: (8) WQD = C  v   ⋅ WQR ,   for the rational method   ( WQR − 0 . 2 S )   2    WQR + 0 . 8 S   ,   for the CN and ϕ -index methods          Determination of the WQD as described here fundamentally depends on the specification of the minimum interevent time, δ  min    . In contrast defining the WQD in terms of percentile rainfall amounts in independent rainfall events, the WQD is sometimes defined as a given percentile of daily rainfall amounts which does not require specification of δ  min    . However, in using the daily-rainfall approach considerations of the WQD being associated with a rainfall event, and the relation between drain time and interevent durations are lost.  3.5 Step 5. Incorporating the effect of drain time Incorporating the effect of drain time on the storage requirement of a water quality basin requires routing the runoff through the basin as illustrated schematically in Fig. 3 .
