The specified drain time, T  d    , and water quality depth, WQD, determine the average outflow rate, O  d    , for which the basin is designed, where O  d     is defined by (e.g., Urbonas et al., 2011 ) (9) O  d   = WQD  T  d         The basin storage during each rainfall event can then be estimated using the following recursive routing relation: (10) S  j + 1 , i   = S  j , i   + Q  j , i   − O  d   Δ t     where S  j , i     and S  j + 1 , i     are the storage at the beginning and end, respectively, of the j  th time interval of duration Δ t    within i  th rainfall event, and Q  j , i     is the runoff entering the basin during the j  th time interval of the i  th event. All the terms in Eq. (10)  are expressed as a depth, and the corresponding volumes are obtained by multiplying the terms by the catchment area. The basin storage at the beginning of the subsequent runoff event, S  0 , i + 1    , is calculated as (11) S  0 , i + 1   = max ( S  e , i   − O  d   δ  i   , 0 )      where S  e , i     is the storage at the end of event i  , and δ  i     is the duration of the dry period following the i  th event. Application of Eq. (10)  within each runoff event and application of Eq. (11)  to the dry period following the event leads to a time series of storage values represented by S  j , i    . The storage volume required to fully detain or retain the runoff from the i  th event, V  i    , is the maximum storage within the i  th event and is calculated as (12) V  i   = max  j  ∈  J  i     ( S  j , i   )      where J  i     is the number of time intervals within event i  . The required water quality depth, RWQD  , corresponds to the storage volume that fully treats a β  -percentile of the runoff events, and therefore is calculated as the β  -percentile of V  i    . It is apparent from Eq. (10)  that O  d    , and hence T  d    , is a key factor in determining the required water quality depth to treat a given percentile of runoff events.     4 Field demonstrations The main focus of this study was to compare the conventional water quality depth, WQD, determined in Step 4 with the required water quality depth, RWQD, as determined in Step 5 and influenced by the imposed drainage time, T  d    . Determination of the design WQD fundamentally depends on the value of δ  min     that is used to automatically separate rainfall events in long rainfall records, and determination of the appropriate value of δ  min     is an issue that is also addressed in this paper. The proposed procedures are demonstrated in detail within a region of South Florida containing 149 rain gauges, and further demonstrated at particular locations in Athens (Georgia), Roanoke (Virginia), and St. Louis (Missouri). 4.1 Study areas The study area in South Florida is delineated by the South Florida Water Management District (SFWMD). To assess the applicability of the proposed analyses to other areas, data collected at three other locations were also analyzed and the results compared with the results obtained in the SFWMD. The locations of all the study areas are shown in Fig. 4 , and the characteristics of these study areas and their data properties are described below. South Florida.  Analyses were performed using data collected at 149 rain gauges distributed throughout the SFWMD. The SFWMD covers an area of approximately 46 600 km 2     in the southern half of Florida, and includes about 31% of the area of the entire state. The location of the SFWMD within the United States and the distribution of rain gauges within the SFWMD are shown in Fig. 4 . Rainfall in the SFWMD is seasonal, with the wet season nominally being May–October, and the dry season being November–April. The average annual rainfall is around 152 cm, and approximately 70% of the annual rainfall typically occurs during the wet season. The 149 rain-gauge stations used in this study were selected based on the high quality and time resolution of the rainfall measurements collected at these stations. These data were quality-controlled by the SFWMD professional staff, each had a temporal resolution of 15-min, and each had continuous records between October 2007 and June 2023 for a record length of approximately 15.5 years. These data were downloaded from the DBHYDRO database which is maintained by the SFWMD. Although a longer record would have been desirable, albeit not available, using these available data was partially justified by results reported by Wang et al. (2019)  who showed that 10–15 years of data was sufficient to obtain a stable value for δ  min     to yield an exponential distribution of interevent times. Using these data was further justified by having 149 separate rain gauges, where results from nearby rain gauges reinforce the results obtained at individual rain gauges. For each of the 149 stations in the study area, the rainfall measurements at 15-min intervals were aggregated to at 1-h intervals, and subsequent analyses were based on the 1-h data.  Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis. Hourly rainfall data from Athens (Georgia), Roanoke (Virginia), and St. Louis (Missouri) were used to compare outcomes of the proposed methodologies at different locations. Since these three locations have seasonal climates with cold winter months, only the summer months of June-September were considered. The coordinates of the station locations along with the rainfall totals and average temperatures during the summer months are shown in Table 1 , where the climatic data were obtained from Weather Spark (2024) . All the rain-gauge locations are at airports, specifically Athens-Ben Epps Airport, Roanoke Blacksburg Regional Airport, and St. Louis Lambert International Airport, and the elevations at these locations are 239 m, 347 m, and 162 m, respectively, relative to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988. It is apparent from Table 1  that the average rainfall amounts and average temperatures during the June-September study periods are fairly close between locations, with rainfall amounts in the range of 31–34 cm, and temperatures in the range of 23–25 °C. For each of the three locations, hourly rainfall data were obtained from the National Center for Environmental Information (NCIS, 2024 ) and these data generally covered the period of 1948–2013. There were some missing data in these hourly time series, so the records was cut so as to include only continuous data without missed measurements. The length of continuous data sets varied with location and were 56 yr, 59 yr, and 28 yr for Athens, Roanoke and St. Louis, respectively.     4.2 Separation of rainfall events All rainfall records used in these analyses were continuous at 1-h intervals, and at each station these 1-h measurements were automatically separated into events based on an imposed value of δ  min     as described in the methodology section. Based on the separated events, the corresponding sample values of event magnitude, P  , event duration, d  , and interevent time, δ  , were determined. For the South Florida study area, the analysis protocol was extended to accommodate this region having multiple rain gauges and two rainfall seasons. Specific considerations are given below. South Florida. To investigate the regional rainfall properties in the SFWMD study area, the station data were combined from all stations to yield single sample sets of P  , d  , and δ   that are representative of the SFWMD as a whole. This was done separately for the wet season and the dry season. These regionally combined data sets are relevant to the objectives of the present study since uniform regulations relating to the design of stormwater control measures (SCMs) within the SFWMD are applied over the entire SFWMD. This includes a single quantification of the water quality rainfall.  Other locations. Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis locations only had one station each, so there was no lumping of data, and single-station analyses were taken as representative of these station locations and their immediate surroundings.   4.3 Identification of minimum interevent time The main study area was South Florida, with additional analyses done at other locations to assess the variability of outcomes that could be expected due to geographic and climatic differences. The USEPA (2009)  recommended threshold of 2.5 mm was used as a basis for identifying runoff-producing rainfall events, with the recognition that this threshold value is mostly characteristic of paved catchment areas. 4.3.1 South Florida Using the 90-percentile magnitude, P  90    , of runoff-producing rainfall events as a reference water quality rainfall, the relation between P  90     and δ  min     for the wet and dry seasons are shown in Fig. 5 (a), with the corresponding incremental changes in P  90     with δ  min     shown in Fig. 5 (b). It is apparent from Fig. 5  that the behavior of the P  90     versus δ  min     relation is consistent with the expected behavior as postulated previously and illustrated in Fig. 2 . For the wet season, Region A extends to around δ  min   = 6  h   , Region B occurs for δ  min     in the range of 6–8 h, and Region C extends beyond around δ  min   = 8  h   . Hence, in terms of the parameters shown in Fig. 2 , δ  min  ∗   = 6  h    and δ  min  +   = 8  h   . For the dry season, δ  min  ∗     can still be taken as around 6 h, however, there is no subsequent increase in slope of the P  β     versus δ  min     relation, which indicates that typical interstorm durations are likely long relative to the minimum interevent duration of 6 h. Distribution of interevent times.  A histogram showing the distribution of occurrences of interevent times, δ  , resulting from using δ  min   = 6  h    to separate rainfall events is shown in Fig. 6 (a) for the wet season and shown in Fig. 6 (b) for the dry season. Considering the wet-season distribution of δ   shown in Fig. 6 (a), the distribution has local peaks at 17.5 h, 45.5 h, 69.5 h, and 94.5 h, as well as subsequent peaks at around 20 h intervals. Using δ  min   = 6  h    leads to an average rainfall event having a duration of around 6.5 h, and combining this with the results shown in Fig. 6 (a) indicates that wet-season rainfall events are typically separated by dry-period durations in the range of 17.5–21.5 h. This is consistent with the common occurrence of daily afternoon rainfall events in South Florida during the summer wet season. In contrast to the wet-season results, the distribution of interevent times during the dry season, as shown in Fig. 6 (b), does not show local peaks in the distribution of interevent times that are characteristic of wet-season rainfall. The probability distribution of dry-season interevent times has more of an exponential distribution that is characteristic of a point Poisson process. Based on the data shown in Fig. 6 (b), the average interevent time during the dry season is around 38 h. It is relevant to note that the distribution of interevent times during the wet season does not follow an exponential distribution due to the occurrence of local peaks in the probability distribution, and hence the conventional approach of finding δ  min     based on the best fit to an exponential distribution of using the COV = 1    criterion would not be appropriate for the wet season.     4.3.2 Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis The 90-percentile runoff-generating rainfall amounts during the months of June–September as a function of the minimum interevent time at Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis are shown in Fig. 7 . It is apparent that the constant slope range that can be used to identify the appropriate value of δ  min     is present at all three locations, although at varying strengths. Based on the results shown in Fig. 7 , appropriate values of δ  min     to be used for event separation can be estimated as 6 h, 12 h, and 9 h and Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis, respectively. It is also apparent in Fig. 7  that beyond the aforementioned values of δ  min     there are also longer values of δ  min     that correspond to a flattening of the P  β     versus δ  min     relation. The presence of these second-tier values of δ  min     indicate the elevated likelihood of occurrence of multiple events within the time frame of the higher values of δ  min    . The higher values of δ  min     shown in Fig. 7  are 17 h, 20 h, and 20 h for Athens, Roanoke and St. Louis, respectively, which could correspond to elevated probabilities of daily rainfall during the June–September study period. This elevated-probability assertion is subsequently confirmed by the distribution of interstorm durations at these locations. Distribution of interevent times.  Interevent times were calculated for Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis for events that were separated using the appropriate values of δ  min     for each location. The results of these analysis are shown in Fig. 8 . These distributions of interevent times show the same key feature that was found for the wet-season stations in South Florida: the presence of distinct peaks within the occurrence distribution of interevent times. This result confirms that it would generally be inappropriate for δ  min     to be determined based on the fundamental assumption that the interevent times have an exponential distribution. The peaks of the occurrences shown in Fig. 8  generally show approximate-daily event activity with peak interevent times in the range of 16.5–21.5 h. Specifically, for Athens there is a peak at 21.5 h for Roanoke at 19.5 h, and for St. Louis at 16.5 h. There are also other peaks as well reflecting other frequencies of rainfall occurrence.      4.4 Effect of drain time Incremental rainfall measurements at each rain-gauge location were converted to runoff using the rational method, curve-number method, and ϕ  -index method. A runoff threshold of 2.5 mm was used, which is typical of the depression storage in paved surfaces as these are the types of surfaces for which water quality control is most appropriate. For the rational method, C  v   = 1    was applied to rainfall events with magnitudes greater than 2.5 mm, for the curve-number (CN) method the corresponding catchment storage is S = 2 . 5 / 0 . 2 = 10  mm   , which corresponds to a curve number of 95, and the ϕ  -index was determined on an event-by-event basis to give the same event runoff as the CN method. For each rainfall record, the incremental (1-h) runoff amounts were calculated from the incremental rainfall amounts using the aforementioned methods, and these runoff amounts were routed through a water quality storage basin using Eq. (10) . The outflow rate from the basin was calculated using Eq. (9) , where the water quality depth, WQD, was calculated by applying the rainfall-runoff method to the water quality rainfall (WQR), and T  d     values of 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h were considered. The basin storage that would completely detain or retain a given percentile of the runoff events from a catchment area at each rain-gauge location was determined, and this is referred to as the required water quality treatment depth, RWQD. 4.4.1 South Florida The required water quality storage depth, RWQD, for various drain times and percentile runoff events that are fully retained or detained are shown in Table 2 . These depths are contrasted with the conventional water quality depth, WQD, which is typically defined either as a percentile of the event runoff depths or as a percentile of the daily runoff depths. The preferred WQD is based on the event runoff depth, and the volume of the water quality storage basin is normally be taken as the WQD multiplied by the catchment area. For each runoff method and each season, 85-, 90-, and 95-percentile storage requirements were determined using the routing procedure given by Eq. (11) , and cases in which the RWQD exceed the corresponding WQD based on either event or daily runoff amounts are shown in bold. It is apparent from Table 2  that a specified drain time greater than or equal to 24 h would not generally be adequate within the SFWMD, with the only exception being for 95-percentile quantities. However, drain times greater than or equal to 48 h would generally be inadequate without exception. The results in Table 2  also show that the WQD based on event rainfall amounts is greater than or equal to the WQD based daily rainfall amounts for the same percentile. This means that assigning the WQD based on daily rainfall amounts is not an appropriate benchmark to assess the percentile adequacy of required storage amounts. Collectively, the results in Table 2  show that (1) a rule of using a design drain time of 24 h is not generally adequate for providing water quality treatment for a given percentile of runoff events, and (2) using daily runoff percentiles can underestimate the event runoff percentiles which are usually considered the benchmarks of water quality basin design. Results for other values of C  v    .  The results presented in the previous section used the rational method with C  v   = 1    which is characteristic of paved areas. Using a lower-limit value of C  v   = 0 . 4    in the analyses does not change any of the conclusions for the rational method, with the required storage depths for the given drain times and seasons being equal to the reduced C  v     times the storage depth required for C  v   = 1    as shown in Table 2 , and the conventional water quality depth being equal to the reduced C  v     times the water quality depth for C  v   = 1   , as shown in Table 2 . Consequently, the inadequacies cited for C  v   = 1    also translate to lesser values of C  v    .  Inter-station rainfall variation. The percentile values of WQD based on daily rainfall that are given in Table 2  for the rational method with C  v   = 1    are equal to the percentile values of runoff-producing daily rainfall. For example, the 90-percentile of all the runoff-producing daily rainfall measurements within the SFWMD is equal to 3.81 cm. This value is based on the combination of all rainfall measurements at all stations, and the percentile values of daily rainfall at individual measurement locations will generally be different. To illustrate this point, the distribution of 90-percentile runoff-producing daily rainfall values over the 149 rain-gauge stations in the wet season is shown in Fig. 9 (a), and these values are referenced to the overall 90-percentile value of the combined events in the wet season given in Table 2  and shown in Fig. 9 (a) as P  ˆ    90   = 3 . 86  cm   . Using this reference value, it is apparent from Fig. 9 (a) that there are several measurement locations with 90-percent runoff-producing rainfall magnitudes greater than P  ˆ    90    , which means that the overall 90-percentile value would not be an appropriate WQR based on daily rainfall at several locations. Therefore, it might be appropriate to take the WQR for daily rainfall as the 90-percentile value of the 90-percentile values at rain-gauge locations, which in this case is equal to 4.23 cm and is represented in Fig. 9 (a) as P  90 , 90    . Since there are 149 measurement locations used in this study, then approximately 15 stations have 90-percentile event rainfall amounts greater than P  90 , 90     and the locations of these stations are shown in Fig. 9 (b). It is notable that there is a cluster of nine of these stations in the southern part of the SFWMD around the Miami area, which could prompt more stringent design standards at these locations.     4.4.2 Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis The rainfall-runoff analyses that were done for the lumped 1-h data in South Florida were also done for the three other study locations (Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis) and the results are shown in Table 3 . It is apparent that a drain time of 24 h would generally be adequate, a drain time of 48 h would also be adequate at St. Louis, and a drain time of 72 h would not generally be adequate. The difference in performance for drain times of 24 h between South Florida and the locations considered here can be at least partially attributed differences in rainfall characteristics, with shorter durations between rainfall events and lesser rainfall amounts contributing to the increased adequacy of shorter drain times such as 24 h. The lumping of data from different locations within the South Florida region might also be a factor in the difference. The results listed in Table 3  also show that the percentile event rainfall amounts are generally greater that the percentile daily rainfall amounts so, as was the case for South Florida, basing water quality designs on percentile daily rainfall amounts will not accurately reflect the performance of a water quality basin in terms of the percentile of runoff events that receive full treatment in the basin.      5 Summary and conclusions This paper presents and demonstrates methodologies for separating incremental rainfall measurements into independent rainfall events, and sizing water quality storage basins in stormwater control measures based on the event statistics. Inadequacies in existing methodologies are highlighted by contrasting the demonstration results with those based on existing methods. Separation of rainfall into events. The minimum interevent time, δ  min    , is the basic parameter that is used to transform incremental rainfall measurements into discrete rainfall events, and a novel method is presented for determining the appropriate value of δ  min    . The proposed method is based on a relation between a percentile rainfall magnitude and δ  min     that does not rely on assuming that the occurrence of rainfall events is a point Poisson process with a consequent exponential distribution of interevent times. The approach is demonstrated in South Florida and also at three locations in other parts of the United States. For South Florida, the results obtained support the proposed methodology, and also provides an example case in which the interevent times do not follow an exponential distribution, and therefore it would not be appropriate to implement the conventional approach of determining δ  min    . The appropriate value of δ  min     in the wet season is shown to be around 6 h, and the appropriate value in the dry season is around 8 h. The sample distributions of interevent times are substantially different between the wet and dry seasons, with dry-season interevent times having more of an exponential distribution than the wet season. The proposed approach was also validated for the summer months at selected rain-gauge stations in Athens (Georgia), Roanoke (Virginia), and St. Louis (Missouri), where the appropriate values of δ  min     were found to be 6 h, 12 h, and 9 h, respectively. The probability distribution of interevent times at these stations have multiple peaks which represent various frequencies of rainfall occurrence, which further supports the assertion that finding a δ  min     that yields an exponential distribution of interevent times is not an appropriate approach for finding δ  min    .  Assessing drain-time limitations. The design drain time of a water quality basin influences the required basin storage to retain the runoff from a given percentile of runoff producing rainfall events, since the design average discharge rate from a water quality basin is generally taken as being equal to the conventional water quality depth divided by the design drain time. Using incremental runoff depths resulting from incremental rainfall depths, and routing the runoff through a storage basin with the design discharge rate yields the required storage for each runoff event from which the storage required to detain or retain the runoff from a given percentile of runoff-producing rainfall events can be determined. Without using this routing approach, the conventional methodology of sizing the water quality basin to simply be equal to the water quality depth is inadequate since it neglects the potential carryover storage between events. This limitation is exacerbated in cases where the design drain time is long relative to the interevent times. The proposed approach was demonstrated using multiple rainfall-runoff models (rational, curve number, and ϕ  -index models) for a threshold runoff-producing rainfall of 2.5 mm. For South Florida, it was shown that using a maximum design drain time of 24 h with a basin sized for the water quality depth (WQD) will not always treat the same percentile of runoff events as the percentile associated with the WQD, which is an inadequate design relative to the treatment objective. In contrast, at the selected locations in Athens, Roanoke, and St. Louis it is shown that a maximum design drain time of 24 h would lead to adequate performance of water-quality basins, however, maximum design drain times of 48 h would not lead to adequate performance. Another useful finding from these analyses was that percentile daily rainfall amounts were typically less than percentile event rainfall amounts, which means that sizing water quality basins based on percentile daily rainfall amounts will typically correspond to treatment of a lesser percentile of runoff events and hence the design objective for water quality basins might not be met in these instances.  Practical applications. The results reported in this paper potentially have profound implications on the design of water quality storage basins. Then proposed methodology for separating rainfall events does not rely on the conventional limiting assumption that the rainfall process is a Poisson process with the associated exponential distribution of interevent times. Hence, an opportunity for a broader range of application as well as standardization of the event-separation approach is provided by the proposed methodology. It is further demonstrated that the exponential distribution assumption for interevent times is not generally valid for appropriate values of δ  min    , including the conventional value of δ  min   = 6  h   . The second implication of the results presented here is an alert to designers of the importance of drain time in controlling the water quality storage requirements of stormwater control measures. The magnitude of the drain time relative to the probability distribution of interevent times influences the percentile of runoff events that are fully detained or retained in the water quality basin, and the methodology described in this paper facilitates quantitatively assessing this influence.
1 Introduction Runoff simulation can effectively determine the variation patterns of hydrological elements, providing a scientific foundation for water resource management and water environment protection (Merz et al., 2021 ). However, the runoff process's inherent nonlinearity and randomness pose challenges to accurate estimation (Eini et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022 ). Conventional runoff simulation methods heavily depend on ground observation data, which usually assume uniform precipitation distribution without considering spatial variations due to terrain characteristics (AL-Areeq et al., 2023 ). Moreover, these methods generally require using physical models that entail intricate calibration processes and computational procedures, resulting in poor generalization and adaptability (Li et al., 2023 ), and cannot accurately simulate runoff in all situations (Mei et al., 2023 ). In conclusion, conventional methods may fail to capture the dynamics of runoff generation and flow paths accurately. To address these constraints, it is necessary to consider solutions from the perspectives of data substitution and method optimization. Precipitation plays a pivotal role in runoff simulation, directly impacting the runoff generation. Utilizing remote sensing technology to acquire satellite precipitation product (SPP) has become an important alternative to ground-based precipitation observation. A distinctive characteristic of SPP is its ability to provide valuable information regarding large-scale rainfall patterns, including areas where ground observations are sparse. The current SPP dataset can support hydrological process modeling and analysis (Pang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021a; Yu et al., 2022a ), which aids in addressing some limitations of conventional runoff simulation methods (Zhang et al., 2019b ). Consequently, it is worth attempting to gradually enhance the reliability of SPP data within the hydrological modeling process through an understanding of the associated physical mechanisms (Wang et al., 2021b ). Neural network models exhibit adaptive learning capabilities, autonomously learning to extract multidimensional features from the nonlinear relationship between SPP and runoff observations (Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021 ). Various neural network structures can enhance runoff simulation information processing and are suitable for modeling complex hydrological systems (Kratzert et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022 ). It should be noted that the data-driven nature of neural networks often obscures the interpretability of underlying physical relationships during prediction (Yu et al., 2021 ). Current research increasingly focuses on integrating neural network algorithms with conventional hydrological models (CHMs) to reconcile this limitation (Zaherpour et al., 2019 ). Researchers have attempted to delegate intensive and repetitive operations to neural networks while preserving a comprehensive physical model (Essenfelder and Giupponi, 2020; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2023 ). This method aids in optimizing inputs based on the interactions among the feature variables rather than depending exclusively on the neural network's output. Besides utilizing neural network models, examining spatial element features and their integration in the runoff computational process represents a crucial advancement. Previous studies on spatial element feature models have focused on constructing spatial distribution models (Tran et al., 2018 ). Such models segment the study area into multiple spatial units and simulate the hydrological process of each unit (Cherkauer et al., 2003; Gassman et al., 2014; Lampert and Wu, 2015 ). Implementing spatial distribution models necessitates the prior definition of spatial elements' size, typically discretizing them into numerous sub-basins or reach sections based on the hydrological network and nodes (Lu et al., 2017 ). This treatment is feasible for conventional meteorological-hydrological data, assuming homogeneity in each spatial unit's terrain and soil characteristics. However, difficulties arise in identifying fine-grained feature representations between grid cells when gridded data, such as remote sensing data, are used as inputs (Huang et al., 2020 ). The spatial variability of parameter information may lead to unreliable identification and updating features within grid flow paths. In summary, the current research challenge is to develop multi-scale spatial element modeling techniques for hydrological processes and to optimize the modules that enhance the runoff estimates accuracy influenced by remote sensing data. Combining process-driven and data-driven methods can potentially enhance application through the integration of hydrological physics and machine learning (Xia et al., 2017 ). Furthermore, improvements can be made to the current spatial partitioning methods to address the characteristics of SPP or remote sensing meteorological data. For instance, using variable-scale spatial partitioning methods to represent feature differences between grid units may adapt to data across varying detail levels (Zhang et al., 2019a ). Spatial correlation features are utilized for spatial partitioning and pattern recognition of the data, thus enhancing the confidence in runoff estimation. Additionally, in the process of refining spatial partitioning and flow path identification, neural networks can be incorporated to calibrate and validate model parameters. This study aims to integrate the physical process description of spatial element dynamics with the nonlinear fitting capabilities of neural networks, and to fully exploit the spatiotemporal information of remote sensing data, aiming to achieve accurate depiction and effective simulation of runoff processes. The specific content includes two facets: (1) the development of a fine-resolution grid scale runoff estimation module to realize spatial element-based runoff processes, and (2) the design of a neural network-based runoff estimation method that meets the scale requirements of SPP data. The integration of spatial distribution information and remote sensing data-driven techniques has the potential to improve the accuracy of runoff estimation. Distinct from conventional hydrological process studies, this study emphasizes the analysis and discussion of heavy precipitation runoff processes, employing fuzzy classification and modular refinement tools to enhance practical applicability.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Conceptual framework and design This study presented a multi-scale runoff estimation framework, encompassing fine (resolution) grid, SPP grid, and basin unit, with distinct objectives realized at each scale. At the fine grid scale, runoff generation-confluence of spatial elements and hydrodynamic modeling were implemented. At the SPP grid scale, a fuzzy classification process combined with neural networks was employed for confluence computation. At the basin scale, the scheme results were outputted and validated. The study scheme and workflow of the runoff simulation modeling are shown in Fig. 1  . In the preparation phase, the study area was delineated, and a multi-scale transformation methodology was developed. This framework enhanced the runoff process by optimizing and synthesizing it with a computational module that incorporates surface, soil, and subsurface elements. The hydrodynamic confluence analysis was conducted by combining spatial element information, necessitating the construction of dynamic evolution simulation operations to acquire key parameters such as flow velocity. Runoff estimations were derived through fuzzy clustering and long short-term memory (LSTM) model, facilitating runoff process optimization. The primary parameters of this scheme were subsequently analyzed, encompassing those related to runoff generation, confluence processes, and optimization techniques. Simultaneously, quantitative indices evaluated the scheme's performance, and a comparative analysis was conducted against established models cited in the relevant literature.  2.2 Study area and data 2.2.1 Study area The study area is located in the Songhua River basin in northeastern China. Given its significance as a major waterway in the Far East and a vital grain-producing region, the Songhua River basin is crucial in shipping logistics and food security. The basin experiences a temperate continental monsoon climate. During the study periods, which encompass the calibration (2011–2015) and the validation (2017 and 2018) periods, the average annual precipitation was recorded at 640 mm. Summer (June to August) saw the majority of rainfall, contributing over 65 % of the total with 420 mm. Winter had minimal precipitation at 20 mm, while spring and autumn averaged around 100 mm. Runoff in the Songhua River basin, predominantly derived from precipitation, shows pronounced seasonal fluctuations. The runoff during July and August can comprise up to 40 % of the annual total, whereas it accounts for merely 15 % from October to April of the following year.  2.2.2 Study data Precipitation data were sourced from the IMERG (Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement)) final run satellite product, provided by NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) and its international partners. This global precipitation dataset is regarded for its comprehensive assimilation of data from various satellite sensors, rendering a highly accurate representation of precipitation patterns (Pradhan et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2020 ). The study employed the daily IMERG version V07 dataset with a spatial resolution of 0.1°. Runoff data were extracted from the Hydrological Yearbook of the People's Republic of China , with observations from six hydrologic sites categorized into two sets: one for the main channel of the Songhua River (Tonghe, Yilan, and Jiamusi sites) and another for its tributaries (Qinjia, Yanshou, and Shitou sites). The DEM data, with a spatial resolution of 90 m, were acquired from the SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) system (Rabus et al., 2003 ). Soil texture data, indicating sandy, silt, and clay textures at a 1 km resolution, were obtained from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Soil organic matter content data were obtained from the National Tibetan Plateau Science Data Center, with a spatial resolution of 1 km. Land use data, offering annual classifications at a 30 m resolution, were derived from the CLCD (China Land Cover Dataset) with production and accuracy evaluation details documented by Yang and Huang (2021) .   2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Fine grid scale runoff estimation based on antecedent precipitation The SPP-Fine Grid Runoff Estimation (SFGRE) module comprised surface, soil, and subsurface operators. In the design of the surface operator, a distinction was made between surface I and Ⅱ operators to enhance the runoff estimation capability from the fine grid to the SPP grid scale. To characterize the influence of precipitation on cumulative runoff variation, daily SPP data were converted to antecedent precipitation index (API) (Li et al., 2021 ), and the value selection consideration was discussed in the discussions section. The SFGRE module initiates the runoff estimation by classifying the API into heavy or non-heavy categories by a predefined threshold. This classification dictates whether precipitation data are processed by the surface I (non-heavy) or II (heavy) operator. For the surface I operator, precipitation is adjusted for losses including vegetation interception, evapotranspiration, and depression storage to form net precipitation. For the surface Ⅱ operator, canopy and surface losses are deemed negligible; precipitation primarily produces horizontal surface runoff, while the remainder aids in the vertical recharge for the I operator. The calculation procedure for these surface operators is detailed in the appendix. Thus, the total surface runoff Q t  can be expressed under the combined effects of surface I and Ⅱ operators.(1) Q t  = ( P 0   + (1 -   a ) P 0 ′  - ( I a  + b )  )  2  S d  + P 0   + (1 -   a ) P 0 ′  - ( I a  + b )    + a P 0 ′  + b      where P 0  and P '0  are the initial rainfall for the surface I and Ⅱ operators, I a  is the initial water loss. The a  and b  are the linear relationship between the P '0  and the surface runoff generation, and S d  is the surface storage. For the soil and subsurface operators, runoff simulation employs the nested water tank concept (Song et al., 2019 ), using infiltrated water as input to simulate soil and base flow. The soil operator utilizes a tank model with multiple outflow orifices to regulate the flow, reflecting the actual runoff process with delay characteristics. The subsurface operator employs a dual-layer outflow system to represent the generation of stable base flow.(2) y s  = 0 , x ≤ h 1     y s  = K x - h 1    , h 2  < x ≤ h 1      y s  = K h 2  - h 1    + α 1  x + β 1  , x ≥ h 2             (3) y g  = α 2  ( x - h 3  )  , h 3   < x ≤ h 4     α 2  ( x - h 3  )  + β 2  ( x - h 4  )  , x > h 4               where h 1  and h 2  are the heights of the first and the highest outflow orifice of soil operator's water tank. K  is a constant for the exponential function, while α 1  and β 1  are linear coefficients correlating with the water level. The h 3  and h 4  are the heights of the outflow orifice and the water tank for the subsurface operator, while α 2  and β 2  are coefficients for segmented linear changes. The variable x  represents the water depth.  2.3.2 Runoff optimization through spatial elements and fuzzy classification To analyze the runoff evolution process, it was essential to quantify the flow direction and velocity. The neighborhood-equivalent partitioning technique was employed to label flow direction in this study, which required adjacent DEM grids sharing the same attribute to be merged into a unified spatial element. Assuming a uniform flow within each spatial element, we derived the flow velocity as follows (Yi et al., 2022 ).(4) V c  = C R 2 / 3   T 1 / 2    n       where C  is the conversion coefficient, R  is the hydraulic radius, T  is the energy gradient line, and n  is the roughness coefficient. The calculation of the hydraulic radius R  required extracting the width W  and depth H  from the spatial elements. H  could be expressed by the Q t  and the spatial element area A . The energy gradient line T  was defined by the relative slope between upstream and downstream spatial elements.(5) R = WH  2 H + W   = W Q t   2 Q t  + W ∑ i = 0  n  A i        (6) T ij  = Z i  - Z j   d       where d  is the distance along the centerline, and Z  is the average elevation. For the confluence results within a unit SPP grid, a fuzzy classification method was adopted to optimize the computational process. Fuzzy processing combines fuzzy classification functions with affiliation judgment methods to determine the classification process system's transfer characteristics to assign the confluence range's probability. Here, based on the information on flow velocity, volume, and distance of the spatial elements, fuzzy classification was achieved by labeling the confluence. The construction of the fuzzy classification matrix and fuzzy affiliation function is as follows (Sahraei et al., 2022 ).(7) F ( w i  , u hj  , s hi  )  min  = ∑ j = 1  n  ∑ h = 1  c  u hj  w i  ( r ij  - s hi  )        2       (8) μ ( x )  = 1 1 + ( x f 2   )  ± f 1           where F  is the feature function, u  and s  are the fuzzy clustering matrix and the centroid matrix, r  is the affiliation function, and ω  is the weight. The f 1  is the divergence, and f 2  is the midpoint,which was defined as the boundary point between probability affiliation based on the set samples.  2.3.3 Runoff adjustment strategy based on LSTM and surface Ⅱ operator The operation of the LSTM network relies on input derived from the surface I, soil, and subsurface operator's results generated by the SFGRE module. The LSTM utilized a forget gate to control the information discarded from the cell state at the previous time step, while an input gate to manage the incorporation of new information into the cell (Wu et al., 2023 ). This process necessitates a decision regarding the information to preserve or eliminate, which in turn requires updating the state variables of the memory cells. Subsequently, the output gate was engaged to generate the estimated runoff (Kratzert et al., 2018 ).(9) Q lstm   = σ [ W o  ( h t - 1   , x t  )  + b o  ]       where W  is the weight matrix, b  is the offset vector, σ  is the sigmoid activation function, and h  is the hyperbolic tangent activation function. Upon the LSTM output, the surface Ⅱ operator was incorporated as an adjustment parameter to simulate the final runoff results. If this component was zero, no adjustment was made to the runoff estimation. In contrast, a non-zero component prompted the application of an empirical relationship between rainfall intensity and runoff to adjust the LSTM-derived estimates. This adjustment accounts for the correlation between runoff and peak flow, enhancing runoff simulation accuracy within the SFGRE module.(10) Q a  = J × F × Q lstm  k  + E      where J  is the runoff coefficient, F  is the basin area, k  is an empirical coefficient, and E  is the error term.  2.3.4 Evaluation indices In addition to the correlation coefficient (CC), root mean square error (RMSE), and standard deviation (STD), the scheme's accuracy was evaluated using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) coefficient, the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) coefficient, the water balance (WB), and the peak percentage error (PPE). The NSE is a widely recognized metric of the goodness-of-fit for hydrological models. The KGE is also extensively employed to evaluate the performance of hydrological models; it incorporates the correlation, the bias ratio, and the variability between simulated and observed data. The WB quantifies the cumulative discrepancy between simulated and observed runoff. A value of WB greater or less than one indicates underestimation or overestimation of the cumulative simulated runoff in comparison to observations. The PPE measures the relative error between the simulated and observed peak flows. Table 1   shows the expression, value range, and ideal value for the NSE, KGE, WB, and PPE.    3 Results 3.1 Four operators results of the SFGRE module Within the SFGRE module's framework, runoff production was calculated through analysis of process components associated with different hydrological operators. Here, runoff depth was employed to quantify outcomes of the surface I, soil, and subsurface operators for two site sets, encompassing both the main channel and tributaries, during the calibration period from 2011 to 2015 (Fig. 2  ). The module revealed a gradient in mean values among the three operators, decreasing from the surface to the subsurface layer. The surface I operator exerted the most significant influence, showing a pronounced peak between April and September, reflecting the basin's overall precipitation patterns. The soil operator exhibited tighter clustering with peak values exceeding those of the surface I and subsurface operators, indicating its sensitivity to heavy precipitation through infiltration. The subsurface operator was the least influential of the three operators and reflected the basin's overall base flow. During the calibration period, the results for the surface Ⅱ operator were computed (Table 2  ). The surface II operator components displayed a monthly unimodal pattern, approaching zero from December to March and peaking from June to August, aligning with frequent and intense precipitation seasons. The annual average component value was 7.16 mm for the tributary set and 7.25 mm for the main channel set. Statistical analysis was conducted on runoff conditions associated with heavy and non-heavy precipitation samples. The runoff results for heavy precipitation samples were significantly higher than those for non-heavy precipitation across all sites. Specifically, the average multiplier difference was 2.51 for the main channel set and 3.23 for the tributary set. Runoff from heavy precipitation elicited a more robust response, thereby having a more pronounced influence on the estimated results of the tributary set. To evaluate the effectiveness of the surface Ⅱ operator's independent classification operation for heavy precipitation, a control experiment using a single surface layer without considering differential changes in precipitation intensity was designed. Fig. 3   shows the runoff errors for the surface Ⅱ operator and the control group during the calibration and validation periods. During the calibration period, runoff error for the tributary sites exhibited minimal reduction, ranging from 0.33 to 0.85 m3 /s. Conversely, the main channel sites experienced a significant decrease in runoff error, from 41.63 to 62.03 m3 /s. During the validation period, runoff error for the tributary sites decreased by 1.30–8.74 m3 /s, with a relative error reduction of 21.34 %. The runoff error for the main channel sites decreased by 132.46–152.21 m3 /s, with a relative error reduction of 29.62 %. These findings suggest that integrating the surface Ⅱ operator within the SFGRE module, which allows for more refined delineation of precipitation scenarios, can improve runoff estimation accuracy.  3.2 Multi-scale dynamic-fuzzy confluence results The confluence information for each SPP grid cell was calculated using the spatial element dynamics method. Fig. 4  (b) displays all grid elements corresponding to the IMERG data in the Songhua River basin. By selecting an SPP grid north of the Qinjia site, Fig. 4 (a) depicts the internal flow accumulation within the fine grid based on DEM data. It presents a typical flow accumulation pattern featuring a prominent catchment line with high cumulative values, which allows for determining flow direction based on the accumulated amount. In the fine grid scale analysis presented in Fig. 4 (c), four cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north) were defined for movement to reflect the conversion of confluence information from the fine grid to the SPP grid. The primary direction (P) for each SPP grid was determined by assessing the flow accumulation at each cardinal outlet. Subsequently, the other three directions were labeled as secondary directions (C1, C2, and C3) clockwise. Statistical analysis revealed that the primary directions for the SPP grids were north, south, east, and west, with respective proportions of 43.65 %, 31.96 %, 7.83 %, and 16.56 % (Fig. 4 (b)). Fig. 4 (c) illustrates the flow direction information in the fine grid before and after spatial element processing. Without this processing, the flow direction for each grid must be computed individually, followed by cumulative statistics to identify the catchment line. While this approach may be suitable for small-scale applications, it is redundant and time-consuming for the extensive dataset in this study, which encompasses over two thousand SPP grids and six test regions. Spatial element processing merges adjacent grids with the same attributes into a single entity eliminates repetitive computations, and efficiently identifies catchment lines for each SPP grid, thereby laying the groundwork for calculating confluence parameters. The confluence information was normalized to facilitate the comparison across main channel and tributary site sets. This approach allowed for the acquisition of dimensionless discharge and velocity to improve confluence analysis considering hydrodynamic properties. The basin extent corresponding to each site was partitioned into uniform distance intervals. Confluence information at the fine grid scale was compiled within these intervals, and the area proportion was calculated (Table 3  ). The analysis revealed varying trends and magnitudes in discharge and velocity changes relative to the distance across different test basins. In the tributary set, a typical pattern emerged, with maximum discharge and velocity values occurring at a normalized distance of 0.1–0.3 from the outlet, while minimum values were consistently found beyond the 0.9 distance threshold. This trend was only consistent at the Yilan site within the main channel set, while the trends at the Tonghe and Jiamusi sites were complex. The standard deviations for discharge and velocity in the main channel set were 0.05 and 0.07, respectively, indicating more stable variations than the tributary set, with standard deviations of 0.16 and 0.17. Furthermore, statistical analysis showed a weak correlation between discharge and velocity at the fine grid scale, suggesting that a simple linear model does not adequately capture their relationship. At the SPP grid scale, fuzzy classification was applied to the velocity, discharge, and distance data from the fine grid, resulting in a comprehensive distribution of fuzzy classification certainty values (Fig. 5  ). The given velocity and discharge parameters were utilized to express the affiliation information of different sets and to allocate weights based on the relationship between fuzzy classification and spatial element distance. Overlaying the hydrography layer revealed a noticeable alignment between regions of high fuzzy classification values and the locations of river channels. SPP grids at river crossings displayed elevated fuzzy classification certainty values, indicating the pronounced influence of these critical network nodes on confluence calculations. The fuzzy mean values ranged from 0.26 to 0.35 for the tributary sites and 0.24 to 0.29 for the main channel sites. A robust correlation between velocity and discharge was observed at the SPP grid scale, with CC surpassing 0.998. In the linear coefficients, the slopes ranged from 0.98 and 0.99, and the intercepts approached zero. The velocity and discharge maintain a positive linear relationship at the SPP grid scale with no significant systematic bias effects.  3.3 Analysis of runoff simulation for the proposed scheme The proposed scheme was validated during the calibration period, demonstrating satisfactory simulation performance for tributary and main channel site sets. The performance at tributary sites outperformed that of the main channel sites, as shown in Fig. 6  . At the tributary sites, the CC ranged from 0.94 to 0.98, indicating a strong correlation between the simulated and observed runoff. The NSE averaged 0.90, and the KGE ranged from 0.87 to 0.94, confirming high accuracy and reliability in runoff simulation. The WB averaged 0.97 and simulated cumulative runoff slightly exceeding observations, and the RMSE ranged from 8.74 to 20.33 m3 /s. A flood disaster occurred along the Songhua River in 2013, resulting in elevated runoff at the main channel sites. During this period, the CC averaged 0.95, and the RMSE averaged 196.93 m3 /s. The large runoff volumes at these sites accounted for the relatively greater errors but within a reasonable range. The NSE averaged 0.84, and the KGE ranged from 0.84 to 0.86, demonstrating good simulation performance with stable reliability. The WB ranged from 0.89 to 0.95, with an average of 0.92, indicating that the simulated cumulative runoff was slightly higher than observed. Analyzing the ability to simulate high-value runoff is critical for evaluating model performance, particularly in accurately simulating peak runoff during heavy precipitation events. We evaluated the performance of the proposed scheme against the CHM using the top 1 %, 5 %, and 10 % of observed runoff data (Fig. 7  ). In these high-value runoff zones, the proposed scheme closely matched observed values, whereas the CHM consistently underestimated runoff. Specifically, within the top 1 % interval, the CHM's underestimation was considerable, while the proposed scheme effectively captured runoff variations. For the top 5 % and 10 % intervals, the proposed scheme provided slightly higher but more stable estimates compared to the CHM's severe fluctuations. Conventional models often face stability issue when simulating high-magnitude runoff, while the proposed scheme solves it with acceptable simulation accuracy. In the top 10 % runoff interval, the proposed scheme's PPE10%  was 14.56 % for the tributary set and 15.84 % for the main channel set, significantly better than the CHM's average PPE10%  of 23.35 %. In the top 5 % runoff interval, the PPE5%  of the proposed scheme was 9.84 % for the tributary set and 10.93 % for the main channel set, compared to the CHM's average PPE5%  of 19.85 %. In the top 1 % runoff interval, the proposed scheme achieved a PPE1%  of 5.15 % for the tributary set and 7.42 % for the main channel set, while the average PPE1%  for the CHM was 14.52 %. Considering these evaluation results, this study scheme significantly outperforms conventional hydrological models in simulating high-magnitude runoff. During the validation period, the scheme's performance was examined (Fig. 8  ). At tributary sites, the CC consistently exceeded 0.90, the NSE ranged from 0.88 to 0.91, the KGE averaged 0.89, and the PPE10%  averaged 16.21 %. The scheme underestimated the simulated cumulative runoff at the Qinjia and Yanshou sites, with WB of 1.03 and 1.05, while the WB for the Shitou site was 0.93. The STD at tributary sites ranged between 14.61 and 21.85 m3 /s, and the RMSE averaged 15.37 m3 /s. At main channel sites, the CC averaged 0.89, the NSE ranged from 0.77 to 0.81, the KGE averaged 0.80, and the PPE10%  averaged 18.26 %. The scheme overestimated the simulated cumulative runoff at these sites, with a mean WB of 0.97. The STD and RMSE progressively increased for Tonghe, Yilan, and Jiamusi, averaging 216.81 m3 /s and 204.68 m3 /s, respectively. The results from both the calibration and validation periods collectively affirmed the proposed scheme's robust generalization capability, satisfying the criteria for its intended application. Moreover, as illustrated in Fig. 6  and Fig. 7 , the scheme performed better at tributary sites than at main channel sites. This difference may be due to the tributary sites' increased sensitivity to runoff error changes, stemming from their relatively lower flow magnitudes. Additionally, the scheme demonstrated good peak flow representation for smaller basins while having a propensity to overestimate for larger basins. The superior performance at tributary sites, as shown in Fig. 8 , further underscores the scheme's suitability for small to medium-sized basins.   4 Discussions 4.1 Optimal selection of scheme parameters The API exerts an important influence on runoff calculations within the SFGRE module. The selection of different combinations based on antecedent days induces variations in API results. As the number of antecedent days increased, the API captured fewer details but emphasized the critical information. For the Qinjia and Yanshou sites, the correlation peaked with an API based on a 15-day threshold after initially increasing and then declining with the number of antecedent days. In contrast, for the other sites, the correlation consistently increased with the number of antecedent days, though the rate of increase slowed after the 15-day threshold. The 15-day API was deemed the most effective and was thus selected for driving the SFGRE module. The schematic diagram of the API's variation over the days, along with the correlation table between the API and runoff, was shown in the appendix. In applying the SFGRE module for runoff generation, the sensitivity of undetermined parameters requires examination to ascertain optimal solutions across diverse test basins. Within the surface runoff process, five parameters including the physical variables C  and S v , which represent canopy loss, and the coefficients a , b , and k  required calibration. For soil and subsurface runoff processes, four parameters α 1 、β 1 、α 2 , and β 2 , needed to be determined. These parameters were fine-tuned through optimization, using the trend and magnitude of correlation changes. Fig. 9  (a) and (b) reveal that the sensitivity of surface runoff parameters S v  and k  was comparatively low, with minor correlation fluctuations, culminated at values of 0.05 and 3, respectively. Parameter C 's correlation sharply increased and then stabilized after a maximum change of 0.06. The correlation for the parameter a  increased linearly to a maximum change of 0.03 then declined, while b  reached a peak change of 0.04 at the value of 1. For the soil operator, parameters α 1  and β 1  decreased the correlation changes by 0.09 and 0.07, respectively, as values rose from 0.1 to 1.0. In the subsurface operator, β 2  slightly increased the correlation change at higher values, and α 2  peaked at 0.02 when valued at 1. Optimal values were identified using a local search strategy, validating the evaluation index's robustness by varying these values within specified ranges. This iterative process resulted in the determination of optimal parameters for the targeted basins. In the local search, the optimal values of the surface runoff parameters C , S v , k , a , and b  were 0.05, 0.6, 3, 0.6, and 1, respectively. The optimal values of the soil and subsurface runoff parameters α 1 , β 1 , α 2 , and β 2  were 0.1, 0.1, 1, and 1, respectively. The optimal parameter values for the six test basins are shown in Fig. 9 (c).  4.2 Comparison and limitation of the scheme simulation effect This study derived the runoff generation process through hydrological mechanism methodology and estimated the confluence flow using neural networks. The proposed scheme focused on spatial elements, enabling effective integration with satellite precipitation data. The advantage of this scheme is particularly evident in a watershed appearing multiple localized heavy precipitation. Utilizing average precipitation data as input would obscure the detail in runoff estimations, while gridded remote sensing data effectively captures the variability in regional runoff prompted by such localized precipitation events. In the evaluation stage, the proposed scheme's accuracy was assessed against conventional hydrological models, and here, the performance of existing models was reviewed. Empirical models such as PRSS and TPHM demonstrated limited precision and applicability, with CC of 0.84 for PRSS and NSE of 0.65 for TPHM (Song et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2022b ). In contrast, the CC and NSE for this study's scheme averaged 0.90 and 0.84, respectively, surpassing these models. The physical model of rainfall interception-infiltration runoff (RIIR) proposed by Tao et al. (2023)  achieved an average NSE of 0.89. The tributary sites evaluated in this study exhibited an NSE of 0.90, comparable to the RIIR model. Machine learning models such as SA-MGGP (Mehr and Nourani, 2018 ) and RR-Former (Yin et al., 2022 ) reported an NSE of 0.84 and 0.79, respectively. The PHY-LSTM (Xie et al., 2021 ) model presented an average KGE of 0.68, whereas this study's scheme indicated an average KGE of 0.85. In the numerical model, the peak runoff error range for the FRBM method (Reshma et al., 2018 ) spanned 9.13 % to 16.63 % (three sample cases), which is similar to the PPE10%  (ranging from 9.51 % to 18.15 %) of this study (six sample cases). The analysis revealed that adopting the surface Ⅱ operator within the SFGRE module effectively enhanced estimation accuracy. The introduction of this operator was grounded in a heavy precipitation adjustment mechanism to mitigate errors in high runoff simulations. The surface Ⅱ operator's pronounced efficacy in error reduction at tributary sites relative to main channel sites highlights its suitability for small to medium-sized basin runoff estimation. Compared to conventional hydrological models, the study scheme equipped with the SFGRE module provides a more effective solution for accurately simulating high-value (peak) runoff. However, this study has limitations that future research should address. The accuracy of the proposed scheme is contingent upon reliable input data, yet acquiring high-quality data for all critical variables proves challenging. The runoff data were daily records from hydrological yearbooks, failing to capture variations on an hourly or sub-hourly scale. Moreover, to align with the unit grid of the remote sensing data, the DEM spatial resolution was sampled at the hectometer scale, potentially leading to an insufficient representation of fine-scale hydrological processes. We tested the scheme's reliability in six sample basins within the Songhua River basin; however, its applicability to other regions, given variations in climate, topography, and hydrological behavior, requires further validation.   5 Conclusion This study advances the understanding of hydrological evolution processes and addresses the necessity for accurate runoff estimation in complex scenarios. By leveraging remote sensing precipitation data, the study employs the developed SFGRE module and integrates spatial element evolution, fuzzy classification, and neural network algorithms. These integrations are designed to improve runoff estimation during heavy rainfall events and refine the spatial representation of hydrological information. The implementation of the surface Ⅱ operator for precipitation intensity adjustment within the SFGRE module has been shown to enhance runoff estimation accuracy. During the validation period, errors were diminished by 21.34 % at tributary sites and 29.62 % at main channel sites. Capturing the relationship between flow discharge and velocity on a fine grid scale presents challenges; however, this relationship becomes apparent when analyzed at the SPP grid scale across diverse sample basins. SPP grids with higher fuzzy certainty values more frequently coincided with river crossings, suggesting a pronounced influence of these critical nodes on confluence computation. The study's scheme achieved CC of 0.95 and 0.90, and NSE of 0.87 and 0.84 during the calibration and validation periods, respectively. Furthermore, the scheme showed superior simulation results for the tributary site set compared to the main channel site set, with the KGE differing by 0.05 and 0.09 for each period. The proposed scheme effectively mitigated the common issue of peak runoff underestimation found in conventional hydrological models. The PPE10%  of this scheme for the tributary and main channel site sets was 14.56 % and 15.84 %, respectively, it compares favorably to the average PPE10%  of 23.35 % for the conventional model. This scheme demonstrates considerable advantages in runoff simulation, providing an effective solution for runoff modeling that utilizes remote sensing precipitation data.
1 Introduction Geologic media (soils and rocks) are physically heterogeneous; that is, their pore micro-structural properties (e.g., pore size, geometry, alignment, connectivity) can vary greatly in space (Blunt et al., 2013; Bacher et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Meyer and Bijeljic, 2016; Bultreys et al., 2016; Vogel and Roth, 2001 ). Pore-scale interactions between fluids and geologic media influence numerous subsurface phenomena, including the transport of groundwater contaminants (Zheng et al., 2011 ), biogeochemical cycling of nutrients (Briggs et al., 2015 ), storage of CO 2     (Pereira Nunes et al., 2016 ), extraction of oil from reservoirs (Ishutov et al., 2018b ), colloid filtration (Scheidweiler et al., 2020; Bordoloi et al., 2022 ), and bioclogging (Kurz et al., 2022 ). The impact of such microscopic physical heterogeneity on macroscopic processes is well documented and recognized for influencing flow distribution (Muljadi et al., 2016; Heyman et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2014 ), transport behavior (Tompson and Gelhar, 1990; Berkowitz et al., 2000; Morales et al., 2017 ), mixing dynamics (Werth et al., 2006; Anna et al., 2014; Sole-Mari et al., 2020 ), fluid partitioning (Benzhong et al., 2019; Ferrari et al., 2015; Bandara et al., 2011 ) and effective reactions (Meakin and Tartakovsky, 2009; Valocchi et al., 2019; Gramling et al., 2002 ) that differ substantially from homogeneous media. Nevertheless, a direct and formal relationship between a medium’s microscopic structure and its resulting flow and transport dynamics is still elusive. While image-based numerical simulations have been central to elucidating this relationship (e.g., from microtomography scans of the sample), high-quality experimental data is needed to validate and complement the numerical models for flow and transport. Using undisturbed samples for repeatable experimentation is out of the question, as no two natural samples are exactly alike. Methods capable of replicating identical soil/rock pore structural analogues accurately, at high-resolution, in 3D, and at the 1:1 scale, would enable conducting repeatable and well-controlled laboratory experimentation under realistic structural heterogeneity. Significant progress has been made in the last decade to convert digital soils/rocks into 3D printed analogues for geoscience. Resolution and scale are the two most challenging factors for current 3D printing methods aiming to replicate the pore network of natural porous media (Bacher et al., 2015; Otten et al., 2012; Dal Ferro and Morari, 2015; Ishutov et al., 2015, 2021; Kong et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2017 ). The resolution of 3D printing approaches is restricted by the printing technique and the printing material properties. Increasing the scale has been routinely used to capture more details of the structure (e.g., Otten et al., 2012  used 1:3, Ishutov et al., 2018a  used 1:15, 1:23, and 1:30, and Song et al., 2021  used 1:10, 1:20, 1:30, 1:60 scale magnification to reproduce 3D printed soil/rock prototypes). An added benefit of upscaling the print is the reduced difficulty in removing residual/support materials from the complex pore network during post-processing, although no reported approach has shown to be fully successful. The latest printing formats like low force stereolithography and digital light synthesis do away with the need for support material altogether, thereby circumventing the issue of pore clogging from inefficient post-processing. Few studies have successfully reconstructed their undisturbed sample analogues at the original 1:1 scale, albeit with notable limitations. For example, work by Dal Ferro and Morari (2015)  printed soil samples at the real 1:1 scale with multijet technology, but reported measured hydraulic conductivity discrepancies from the original soil model of 88%–1400%. Bacher et al. (2015)  created reprints of undisturbed soils at their original scale with selective laser sintering, stereolithography, and polyjet approaches, but only reproduced the percolating macropore. Most recently, Ishutov et al. (2021)  proposed a two-photon lithography approach that can resolve porous medium features in the order of ∼ 100  nm   , with the explicit stipulation about size limitations of the nano-printed model being <  1 mm in each direction for a printing job that requires several days of labor. As of yet, a substantial trade-off exists between achieving accurate pore structures and realistic surface properties in 3D printed soil/rock analogues due to the availability of materials used to print. On the one hand, powder-based printed rock proxies with wettability or reactive surface properties that mimic natural samples suffer evident printing defects with regards to the complex pore structure (Ferrari et al., 2022; Anjikar et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021 ). On the other, resin-based prints show superior performance at reproducing the complex pore structure but differ in wettability (are typically less hydrophilic) from natural rocks (Song et al., 2021; Dal Ferro and Morari, 2015; Bacher et al., 2015; Ishutov et al., 2021 ). Recently, different chemical treatments (silanization) have been used to manipulate the wettability of printed porous media with remarkable success in pseudo-2D samples (Catterton et al., 2021; Bacha et al., 2021 ) or 3D samples with highly homogeneous, and well connected structures made of large pores (> 250  μ m   ) (Hodder and Nychka, 2019; Vogelsang et al., 2022 ). Alternative protocols must be developed for complex samples with structural heterogeneity and micron-sized pores to work around mass diffusion limitations that prevent homogeneous functionalization of the printed surface. This study explores the quality performance of four low-cost 3D printing technologies to reproduce the heterogeneous pore structure of an undisturbed soil sample at its original 1:1 scale for fluid flow experimentation. We propose specific measurements to benchmark the characteristics that define accuracy  and repeatability  in 3D prints from a combination of structural and hydrologic properties obtained from analysis of tomographic images of the printed products and image-based simulations, respectively. The paper is organized as follows. First, we describe the soil model used as the basis for 3D printing, the printing technologies chosen, as well as structural and hydrologic properties considered for evaluating the goodness of the prints. Second, we summarize our evaluation of accuracy and repeatability for the four technologies. Third, wettability of the prints is assessed prior to and post plasma treatment. Finally, we discuss performance trade-offs between the 3D printing technologies evaluated, make recommendations for achieving the most accurate and repeatable porous media analogues, and summarize the limitations of replicating key properties in soils/rocks by 3D printing that are of paramount importance for fluid flow and mass transport.  2 Materials & methods 2.1 Soil model from 3D μ  CT image An undisturbed sample of sandy loam Cambisol from an agricultural experimental plot at the James Hutton Institute, Invergowrie, Scotland (established in 2003) was selected as the basis for 3D printing, from here on forth referred to as soil Computer Aided Design (CAD). Characterization of the internal pore geometry was achieved by scanning the sample with 3D micro-computed tomography (μ  CT) in a Metrix X-Tek X-ray (Nikon, UK) at a resolution of 35 μ m   . For more details, the reader is referred to Pérez-Reche et al. (2012) . A subsample of the segmented scan (size: 14 mm ×   14 mm ×   18 mm) was selected and pre-processed to remove isolated pores that encumber 3D printing and analysis of the prints. A mesh file of the cleaned soil image was generated with Fiji (Fiji is ImageJ) (Schindelin et al., 2012 ), an open source image processing software, and exported as a stereolithography (.stl) file for 3D printing.  2.2 3D printing of soil samples The four additive technologies considered for 3D printing soil analogues include (1) digital light synthesis (DLS), (2) PolyJet with gel support material (PJ Gel), (3) low-force stereolithography (LFS), and (4) Polyjet with water-soluble support material (PJ WS). The authors note that selective laser sintering (SLS) with nylon powder and stereolithography (SLA) with dual resin were also tested, but were excluded from this study because it was impossible to remove unsintered powder and support resin, respectively, from the pore space (data not included). As a result, the choice of techniques here presented is motivated by the requirement to fabricate a soil analogue with an open pore space  with as much resolution as possible and at its original scale. Neither DLS nor LFS require a support resin to be used in the void space during printing due to the light sheet used to cure the printing material and their gravity-inverted extraction process (see Fig. A.6  for a schematic). Conversely, both PolyJet approaches (PJ Gel and PJ WS) require the use of a support material for the void space, which require heat and water treatments during post-processing, respectively, to be removed from the pore space. Despite these advantages over solid resin support (e.g., from SLA), gel and water soluble support materials can still be difficult to remove completely. To evaluate improvements in support resin removal, replicates of these techniques were also printed at 1.5×   magnification. Samples generated by LFS were printed at two orientations of 45 °    rotation over an edge or a corner. It is worth noting that LFS prints at the default face (0 °    rotation) did not generate connected pore networks from the sample’s top to bottom, suggesting that rotation during printing is required with this technique. A summary of the technologies and materials used in each case is provided in Table 1 . Details about the principles behind each printing process and a photograph of the produced prints are also included in the appendix (see Appendix A and Fig. A.7 ). All four techniques here evaluated employ plastic resin as the primary printing material because it provides the best resolution for the final product (Ishutov et al., 2021 ) and surface finishes (Kafle et al., 2021 ). Resin is also the most commonly used material for 3D printing (Arrieta-Escobar et al., 2020 ). Polyjet was chosen because it is one of the most commonly used printing technologies for producing models in the soil science domain Arrieta-Escobar et al. (2020) . LFS from FormLabs was chosen because it is a high-quality, high-precision desktop printer found in many classrooms and labs. DLS was chosen for its proclaimed accuracy. Identical printing conditions were used for printing at least two replicates for each technology to evaluate repeatability at 1×   magnification of the original soil CAD. The cost for fabricating the samples in this study ranged from 50–160 US dollars per unit. All 3D printing services used (three of which are commercial) proposed cost advantages for jobs with 10 or more identical prints, making the technology broadly accessible and affordable for researchers.    2.3 Image analysis of 3D printed soils 2.3.1 3D microtomography imaging: 3D X-ray microtomography images of each printed sample were collected at a voxel resolution of 25 μ m    with a MicroXCT-200 (ZEISS Xradia). Scanning settings included 8 W of X-ray power source, 40 kV of energy and 1600 projections covering the full sample at 360°. An LE1 source filter of 0.03 mm thickness was used to reduce beam hardening artifacts (ZEISS X-ray Microscopy, Oberkochen, Germany). Reconstructed images were processed in Amira (Thermo Fisher Scientific), a commercial software for CT image analysis, according to the following protocol for increasing signal-to-noise ratio with a non-local mean filter, registration, rescaling, and segmentation. Given that the microtomography images of the original undisturbed soil and each printed soil analogue varied slightly in scale, orientation, and resolution, two important image pre-processing steps were performed. First, all tomograms were aligned to a common spatial reference by way of image registration . Second, all images were matched in resolution by way of image rescaling  so as to obtain the same voxel size. Finally, watershed thresholding was used to segment the image into solid and pore voxels. The authors note that any support material or residual resin that was not removed by post-processing of the prints was here classified as part of the solid phase. By matching the orientation and resolution of all images it is possible to equitably compare structural properties between and across samples. Identification of the percolation path (PP) and its morphological characteristics for all sample images was carried out with the Particle Analyzer plugin of the software Fiji (Domander et al., 2021b ). Briefly, the Particle Analyzer plugin identifies individual particles  in the binary image stack, and computes their volume and bounding rectangle dimensions. Here, particles  correspond to isolated pores that do not necessarily connect all the way through the sample in the z  -direction (from the top to the bottom). Only those pores with the largest volume and a bounding rectangle that spans the full length of the sample are taken as the percolation path (PP) (see Fig. B.8 ). Analyses related to the permeability, specific surface area, connected porosity, and pores size distribution are carried out only on the PP, as it is expected that pores that are not connected to it will not significantly contribute towards flow and mass transport (Sirivithayapakorn and Keller, 2003 ).  2.3.2 Quantitative image analysis: The following describes the five quantitative metrics used to evaluate the accuracy and repeatability of the 3D printing technologies because they play important roles in the description and understanding of flow and transport through porous media. The choice of metrics is motivated by the need to balance hard-line criteria for microscopic defects with effective macroscopic performance metrics of hydrologic relevance.
