Match/mismatch volume:  Voxel-by-voxel comparison between registered and rescaled images is used to provide a volumetric approximation of the accuracy  across 3D printing technologies (comparing images of 3D printed samples against the reference soil image) and of the repeatability  within each technology (comparing replicate images of 3D printed samples against one another). Mismatched voxels in analyses for accuracy can be classified in one of two ways. First, solid voxels in the reference soil image that appear as pore in the printed soil are considered missing . Second, pore voxels in the reference soil image that appear as solid in the printed soil are considered excess . Mismatched voxels in analyses for repeatability have only a single classification, mismatch , since there is no reference. Matched voxels for both accuracy and repeatability analysis have the same classification (solid or pore) in the two images being compared and are considered match . Permeability:  Permeability defines the ability of the medium to transport fluid. The permeability of each printed soil is calculated from steady-state pore-scale flow simulations (by solving the Navier–Stokes equations) within the porous medium’s detailed geometry. The pore geometry provides the local boundary conditions that control the flow field. Direct numerical simulations are then performed with the FlowDict module in Geodict, a commercial solver for porous materials (Math2Market, Germany). Briefly, a mean approach fluid velocity of 25 mm/h (corresponding to a creeping flow with Reynolds number of roughly 10−2 , typical infiltration rate for sandy loam soils) is specified in FlowDict (Brouwer et al., 1988 ). The software adjusts the pressure drop until the calculated water velocity matches the one specified by the user. Then, during post-processing, the software applies Darcy’s principle to compute the sample permeability from the simulated mean flow velocity, the water viscosity, simulated pressure drop, and the media thickness (Hilden et al., 2019 ).  Specific surface area:  The specific surface area (SSA) of the pore space is an informative metric for reactive transport problems where reactions occur at the fluid-solid interface (e.g., colloid filtration, mineral precipitation). The SSA is estimated as the surface area to volume ratio of the percolating path, as determined from morphological analysis of this region of interest using the Particle Analyser plugin in Fiji (surface resampling = 1) (Domander et al., 2021a ). Consistent and limited resampling on the registered and rescaled images allows a fair comparison of the meshed surface area across samples. Connected Porosity:  Connected porosity is a fundamental metric that describes the fraction of voids in the medium that control the transport of fluids. The connected porosity is computed according to the pore space volume associated with the percolating path, relative to the total sample volume. Pore size distribution:  The pore size distribution is a basic characteristic of porous media that describes its structural heterogeneity and signals the system’s propensity for anomalous transport (Xiong et al., 2016 ). Porosimetry is used to estimate the pore size distribution in each sample with the PoroDict module in Geodict. With this method, the intrusion of a non-wetting fluid is simulated into the pore space and the volume of the intruded fluid is then used to calculate the pore size distribution. To quantify the level of pore size distribution dissimilarity between the reference soil and the printed soils (for accuracy) or between multiple printed soils (for repeatability), we use the Earth Mover’s Distance method (EMD), which provides a measure of the minimum amount of work required to change one distribution into the other (Rubner et al., 1998 ).  2.3.3 Wettability measurements and treatment: Static water contact angles were measured to quantify the wettability of the printed analogues. Briefly, a 10 μ L    droplet of Milli-Q water was pipetted on a smooth, flat face of the printed analogues and its profile imaged after 10 s by a handheld digital microsope MicroDirect 1080P HDMI (Celestron). The images of the contact angle were then analyzed with Fiji with the drop shape analysis plugin Stalder et al. (2010) . To improve the wettability of the printed analogues, the samples were subjected to standard plasma cleaning for soft-lithography, which is traditionally used to impart hydrophilicity on Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic reactors. First, the samples were thoroughly soaked in isopropanol to clean their surface from dust. Compressed air was then used to dry them out completely. Next, the samples were exposed to 1 min and then 2 min treatments by air plasma (Harrick Plasma, Inc. Ithaca, NY). Immediately following each treatment, the contact angle was measured on two different surfaces.    3 Results The following section presents the results from all five quantitative metrics to assess accuracy and repeatability in all 3D printed technologies herein evaluated. The soil structure used here is considered to be a reasonable representation of “typical” soil characterized by its broad pore size distribution, multitude of interconnected pores, and intricate topology, as explicitly determined by Pérez-Reche et al. (2012) .   3.1 Accuracy: similarity between printed analogues and reference soil Qualitative comparison of pore structure:  A visual inspection of the rendering of the original soil design and the porosity produced by the 3D printing techniques under evaluation is shown in Fig. 1 a. The pore space of the soil CAD is shown in white, while the pore space of the printed soil analogue replicas are shown in different colors. Qualitatively, the soil CAD displays a complex structure with interconnected pores of diverse sizes that is most closely recreated by DLS (green) and PJ Gel (yellow) approaches. Analogues made by LFS (red) and PJ WS (magenta) lack much of the details of the pore structure by comparison. Match/mismatch volume:  Voxel-by-voxel comparisons of the soil CAD against the printed soil analogues are shown as stacked bar plots in Fig. 1 b. Missing  volume (shown as the black portion of the bar) represents portions of the solid that are missing in the printed soil (i.e., incorrect pores). Missing is consistently below 3% for all technologies, with even smaller percentages for DLS and LFS. One possible source for this structural error is infiltrated air bubbles during the drop injection process for traditional stereolithography, which can generate undesirable micropores in the final print (Patpatiya et al., 2022 ). Nevertheless, their contribution to printing errors is considerably low across all forms of 3D printing. Excess  volume (shown as the gray portion of the bar) represents portions of the void that are missing in the printed soil (i.e., clogged pores). The percent of excess printed solid ranges from 11%–20%, with DLS at the lowest end. This structural defect can be attributed to printing error in the cases of DLS and LFS, and to incomplete removal of the support material in the cases of PJ Gel and PJ WS. Match  volume (shown as the line shaded portion of the bar) represents portions of the sample (solid or void) that are correctly created in the printed soil. The percent of matched structure ranges from 75%–86%, with DLS and PJ Gel as the technologies that most closely resemble the CAD. Fig. 2  illustrates three cross-sections at different sample depths for each technique where details of the matched/missing/excess volume are indicated. In general, the image suggests that the smallest pore features are the hardest to reproduce for all printers. Overall, the outcomes of the voxel-by-voxel comparison are in agreement with the visual inspection of the 3D printed pore spaces (Fig. 1 a). From the combined qualitative and quantitative analyses, the 3D printing techniques would rank as follows DLS >   PJ Gel >   LFS ∼   PJ WS. Permeability, specific surface area, connected porosity:  Relative percent differences in permeability, SSA, and connected porosity between the CAD and each digitized print are reported in Fig. 3 a (refer to the Table B.2  in the appendix for measured absolute values). In this analysis, properties reported from the soil CAD are taken as the reference point. The simulated permeability of the soil CAD was found to be 8 . 62 × 1 0  − 10    m  2     , which is within the upper range reported for typical Cambisol (Pawlowska and Pawlowski, 2014; Gonçalves-Maduro et al., 2020 ). All printed analogues had lower simulated permeability values than the CAD, with DLS differing by only −23.9%, while the other three techniques differed between −85.6 and −99.8% (see solid bars in Fig. 3 a). Considering the importance of permeability for all hydrologic processes, DLS substantially outperforms the other approaches for the porous structure here tested. Despite the substantial differences of the other printing techniques to recreate the desired permeability, fabricating realistic printed porous media analogues with permeabilities of O ( 1 0  − 10   )     to O ( 1 0  − 12   )    m  2     is already a great advance, bearing in mind previous studies of reported printed soil-like sample permeabilities in the range of 10−18  or 1 0  − 21    m  2      (Kong et al., 2019 ). While the analysis here presented is from image-based simulations, it permits an equitable comparison of the permeability of the soil and the prints at identical resolutions, which cannot be done with laboratory measurements because the soil sample no longer exists. Nevertheless, the interested reader is advised to work with cylindrical 3D prints (rather than the cubic samples here used) to create a proper seal at the interface between the printed analogue and the permeameter when applying fluid flow in the lab to measure permeability experimentally. It is recommended that the soil analogue and the flow through cell (if also 3D printed) are generated as independent pieces and assembled prior to experimentation and not printed as a single integrated unit. This will ensure maximal efficacy of the porous medium’s post-processing (i.e., cleaning of the pores with water at high pressure), which is especially important for anisotropic samples. The SSA of the soil CAD was found to be 5.69 ×  1 0  3    m  − 1     . Most printed samples had lower SSA values than the CAD, with a narrow range of differences from −17.0% to −26.9%. Only PJ Gel produced a greater SSA of similar discrepancy magnitude (see dotted bars in Fig. 3 a). This small difference suggests that SSA can be easily reproduced by 3D printing. Discrepancies of this structural property can be understood as the imbalance between reduced pore surface area, which results in lacking SSA, and the inevitable reduction in porosity, which leads to enlarged SSA during 3D printing. The connected porosity of the soil CAD was estimated at 0.29. All printed samples exhibited lower connected porosity than the CAD, with variations between −32.4 to −80.3% (see stripped bars in Fig. 3 a). For this structural property a clear trend emerges among the printing methods tested, where DLS shows the smallest discrepancy at −32.43%, followed by PJ Gel at −49.7%, then LFS with much greater difference at −71.09%, and PJ WS as the worst performer with −80.27% deviation. These quantitative results are consistent with the renderings in Fig. 1 a, which illustrate that DLS most closely matches the desired porosity, while LFS and PJ WS exhibit the largest differences from the soil CAD. The above comparative analysis of the pore structure between the prints and the soil CAD demonstrates that none of the 3D printing techniques can perfectly match the permeability, SSA, or connected porosity of the original design. However, the structural features that can be achieved are closer to a natural porous medium than a typical bead pack and are still useful for experimental work. Moreover, one 3D printing technique clearly outperforms the others in accuracy of these particular metrics. As such, ranking of the approaches from this analysis follows the order DLS ≫   PJ Gel ≥   LFS ∼   PJ WS.  Pore size distribution:  The cumulative pore size distribution for the original soil CAD and the 1×   magnification printed soil samples is presented in Fig. 4 a. Consistently, the pores in the printed samples are larger than the original design, yet this shifted pore size is not sufficient to increase porosity as shown in Fig. 3 a. The largest pore size in the soil CAD (gray line) was found to be ∼ 2400  μ m   , while the maximum pore size of all printed soils (colored lines) was larger (between ∼ 2700  μ m    and ∼ 3400  μ m   ). The smallest pore size is dictated by the resolution of the soil scan (35 μ m    voxel size), which is comparable to the resolution of the printers (between 16 and 75 μ m   , as specified by the manufacturer). The soil CAD distribution increases most sharply between 244 μ m    and 944 μ m    (0.2 and 0.8 cumulative probability, respectively), indicating a large proportion of pores within this specific size range. The print distributions for all samples increase somewhat less sharply in this size range, except for prints made by PJ Gel. This suggests that a broader size distribution is typically produced with 3D printing of complex porous media. It is worth noting that only in samples from PJ Gel (yellow line), a substantial fraction of the pores (up to 0.6) tend to be smaller (< 600  μ m   ) than those of the CAD. The distribution dissimilarity (through Earth Mover’s Distance analysis) quantifies the absolute differences between the prints and the CAD distributions, as shown in Fig. 4 b. As the figure shows, PJ Gel has the smallest dissimilarity from the CAD, followed closely by DLS and LFS. PJ WS had the largest dissimilarity. One important limitation of 3D printing analogues of geologic porous media is the difficulty in reproducing the smallest of pores, as is evident in the cumulative pore size distributions. On the one hand, for techniques that require support resin, the main challenge is removing this material from the smallest pores. On the other hand, support-free techniques are limited by both the resolution of the laser and the high viscosity of the resin that makes harder the removal process of the non-cured material. Successful cleaning of the pore space during post-processing is challenging, especially for complex geometries with structural features equal to or smaller than the printer resolution (Quan et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2024 ) (refer to Table 1  for details of the printers here used). Importantly, the technology that most closely recreated the CAD’s pore size distribution was not the same as that which produced the closest permeability, SSA, and connected porosity. Thus, it is imperative that the user evaluates the trade-offs of matching the pore size distribution at the expense of properties like permeability. From a pore size distribution analysis, the ranking of the 3D printing technologies follows the order PJ Gel >   DLS ∼   LFS ≫   PJ WS.    3.2 Repeatability: similarity between like-printed analogues Qualitative comparison of pore structure:  A visual evaluation of replicate pore structures pairs fabricated by the four 3D printing approaches is presented in Fig. 1 a. Qualitatively, each soil analogue exceptionally resembles its replicate counterpart (compare pore structures of the same color top vs. bottom). While each printing type has obvious deficiencies in accurately recreating the soil CAD, the imperfections in each printing technique are very consistent. In the sample produced by DLS (green), only minor variations at the front boundary are apparent between the two replicates. Of note, is the upper left region, which is more connected for the bottom sample. This defect is in excess from the CAD and is here classified as a printing artifact. In addition, the bottom right corner for both replicates is similarly missing a small region of the pore space in the original design. This opening is missing from the CAD and can be considered to be a structural feature that is particularly difficult to recreate with DLS. The remaining details of the pore network are captured remarkably well in both prints. For the sample produced by PJ Gel (yellow), similar trends emerge: the upper left region has slight variations in connectivity between the two prints, and a small gap at the center of the sample shows up equally. Although samples made by LFS (red) and PJ WS (magenta) deviate the most from the soil CAD (e.g., final prints were unable to recover the dainty portions of the pore network), these techniques are still capable of duplicating the same imperfections from print to print. Thus, comparing replicate analogues (top and bottom) for the four additive manufacturing techniques under scrutiny demonstrates that whatever 3D printer is used will yield highly reproducible, albeit imperfect, soil analogues. Match/mismatch volume:  Voxel-by-voxel comparisons replicate pairs printed by the same technique are shown as stacked bar plots in Fig. 1 c. Similar to the above section evaluating printing accuracy, here mismatched  volume (shown as the black portion of the bar) indicates an inconsistent representation of the solid/void at identical locations of the replicate prints. That is, we group together missing/excess type errors since there is no reference structure. Mismatched volume is consistently below 5% for all approaches. Match  volume (shown as the remaining line shaded portion of the bar) represents the proportion of the sample that is consistently classified (solid or pore) at identical locations of the replicate prints. The matched structure across replicates for all printing techniques is over 95%, a quantity that is in agreement with the rendering of the pore space shown in Fig. 1 a. Of note, PJ WS exceeds the other three techniques in this evaluation with the lowest error (< 1 %   ) and greatest match (> 99 %   ) for replicate prints, but this trait should be taken into consideration with the other metrics herein presented when choosing a 3D printing technique. Permeability, specific surface area, connected porosity:  The differences in permeability, SSA, and connected porosity between replicate pairs printed by the same technique are reported in absolute percent in Fig. 3 b. In terms of permeability (see solid bars in Fig. 3 b), the choice of printing approach distinctly affects how similar this property will be for like-printed analogues. Our findings show that permeability differences among replicates range from 10% for DLS up to 36% for PJ WS. While the permeability differences for repeatability are important, they are considerably lower than those for accuracy. For SSA (see dotted bars in Fig. 3 b), all printing approaches reproduce this property to a similar and faithful degree; differing by < 11 %   . Our findings reveal that SSA is a structural feature that is the easiest to generate both accurately (as prescribed in the original design) and reproducibly across identical printed replicates. On the basis of connected porosity (see stripped bars in Fig. 3 b), only DLS succeeded at matching this property closely between the two printed analogues (with the smallest difference of ∼ 7 %   ). All other printing approaches differed by ∼ 20 %    in connected porosity. For pore networks that are structurally complex, it is crucial to identify the 3D printing approach that offers the closest corresponding permeability and connected porosity with each batch of prints. In this regard, DLS is the prominent performer for repeatability. Pore size distribution:  Pore size distributions of two replicate prints (A and B) are shown in Fig. 4 c in dark/light coloring. Unfailingly, all four printing technologies under evaluation are capable of reproducing nearly identical pore size distributions in replicate analogues, for the given undisturbed soil design. This observation is quantitatively confirmed by the distribution dissimilarity analysis for like-fabricated analogues, which is very low (<  0.04) across the board for all technologies (see Fig. 4 d). This crucial finding demonstrates that, even when one of the evaluated 3D printing techniques falls short to accurately recreate the pore size distribution of the CAD, any imperfections in the pore network will be rendered in near identical ways for every print.  3.3 Surface wettability 3D printing resins are strongly hydrophobic, producing water contact angles > 86 °    (see Fig. 5  circles). Through this measurement, is it evident that contact angle variability is substantial among all printing techniques, with PJ WS being the most erratic. Plasma treatment is traditionally used to render polymer substrates temporarily water wet. Here, we expose our 3D printed soil analogues to air plasma as per standard soft-lithography protocols because it is an approach to modify the surface wettability of substrates that does not suffer from the mass diffusion limitations of liquid silanization. Two tests were conducted to understand how the plasma exposure influences the wettability of the resin prints. The first treatment (1 min plasma exposure) diminished the contact angle for all samples to span a range of 30–66° (see Fig. 5  triangles). The second treatment (2 min plasma exposure) produced mixed results in improved wettability, whereby one resin became more wettable (DLS), some resins stayed similarly wettable (PJ Gel and LFS), and another became slightly less wettable (PJ WS) (see Fig. 5  diamonds). Such a reversion to hydrophobic surfaces is not uncommon with plasma treatment and must be fine-tuned for each resin type. In general, for 3D printed soil analogues we recommend the shorter plasma treatment which guarantees an improved wettability, even if the contact angle is at an intermediate value (30–60°) of the normal reported range in real soils (0–120°) (Morales et al., 2010; Woche et al., 2005; Bachmann et al., 2000a,b; Leelamanie and Karube, 2013 ). Because the longest distance to permeate plasma into the pore space from any external sample surface is short (here, ∼  5 mm), we expect that this treatment improves the wettability of the pores inside the sample in a similar way as the sample’s measured exterior. Verifying wettability changes to the internal pore network surface, however, is beyond the scope of this work.     4 Discussion 4.1 Recommendations for best 3D printing with maximal accuracy and repeatability While each soil structure is one of a kind, we are confident that the recommendations made here for soil/rock analogue fabrication with 3D printing will hold for other complex porous media. The authors invite the readership to contribute to expand the assessment of accuracy and repeatability of any of the 3D printing approaches here presented (with priority placed on DLS) for alternative soil structures. The thorough evaluation here presented reveals that the best printing technology to fabricate soil analogues that accurately capture the pore structural complexity of real soils/rocks is plainly DLS. This approach dominantly outperformed the others in terms of accuracy for most similar by visual inspection, greatest voxel-by-voxel match, and least difference in permeability, SSA, and connected porosity from the CAD. Although pore size distribution was best captured by PJ Gel, DLS came in at a close second for this criterion. All three other approaches performed similarly worse, especially in terms of permeability and connected porosity, which are at the center of all hydrologic processes that these analogues would be used for studying. Both PolyJet-based technologies had pore clogging issues that affected the quality of the prints. Our analysis suggests that gel (SUP705) is more easily removed than water soluble (SUP706) support material in intricate pore networks like the soil one here tested. Attempts to artificially boost the pore space accuracy by increasing the sample’s printing magnification did not sufficiently improve the recovered pore features to achieve better results than DLS, which has excellent performance at the original 1:1 scale. Parallel evaluation for the best printing technology to fabricate identical soil analogues indicates that all considered approaches are very good for replication, with a moderately better performance by DLS over the rest. Replicates made by the same approach are alike in visual similarity, resemble one another in high voxel-by-voxel match, and show nearly identical matches in pore size distribution. The largest difference between the four tested technologies is seen in the absolute difference in permeability, SSA, and connected porosity for which DLS produces prints that are objectively almost exactly the same. For all technologies, no clear issues emerged in reproducing the same imperfect pore structure from one printing batch to the next. With the exception of DLS, all analogues were produced and post-processed in back to back batches. The samples from DLS were produced by two different providers (UC Davis TEAM and Diversified Plastics) with a time gap of two years, which is a further testament to this technique’s exceptional repeatability. This suggests that whatever difficulties exist during the printing process and sample post-processing (e.g., removing the support material), the final outcome is a nearly identical copy from print to print. Moving forward, the authors encourage future 3D printing users to adopt the quality control metrics herein proposed to better cross evaluate 3D printing approaches with other pore network samples.  4.2 Limitations and remaining qualities to optimize for 3D printing geologic porous media The latest advances in high-resolution 3D printing are finally capable of reproducing key characteristics of porous media, including geometry, permeability, specific surface area, porosity, and pore size distribution at the original size  with a single material in a repeatable manner. Wettability and surface texture, however, are geologic properties that cannot yet be perfectly matched in addition to the above listed physical features. Resin-based printers can accurately fabricate the pore geometry, but the wettability is different (even after plasma treatment) from what might be expected of natural porous media (Ishutov et al., 2021; Bacher et al., 2015; Otten et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2017; Dal Ferro and Morari, 2015 ). Powder-printing technologies enable the fabrication of 3D prints with surface texture and wettability that can more closely resemble soils and rocks, but the geometry of pore systems is poorly replicated (Ishutov et al., 2021; Anjikar et al., 2020; Ferrari et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020 ). Nevertheless, for research that requires fabrication of identical copies of a natural pore structure, functionality and accuracy are paramount, even if they lack certain surface properties. The workflow herein presented can be applied to replicate the physical micro heterogeneity of permeable soils and rocks within the dimensional limit of resin-based printers. Improvements made to the wettability of the soil analogues show that this surface property can be adjusted through plasma treatment to closely approach measurements from real soils, which the literature reports span between 0–120° (Morales et al., 2010; Woche et al., 2005; Bachmann et al., 2000a,b; Leelamanie and Karube, 2013 ). Yet, the longevity of its effect and its efficacy to uniformly increase the wettability of the entire pore network must still be evaluated in greater detail. Nanoporosity can be introduced by use of powder-based printers at the expense of reproducing the intricate microstructure blueprinted in the CAD. The authors recommend that 3D printed geologic analogues for applications in fluid flow should choose an optimal size and resolution of the printed samples by “reverse engineering” the system. This implies selecting the smallest physical size of the analogue that can be used for laboratory experimentation (e.g., minimum 10 mm diameter ×   20 mm length), using this sample size to obtain the maximum image resolution of the original sample, and selecting a 3D printer whose accuracy and resolution can support the detail required. Omission of these three considerations may render a sample that is too small for fluid flow experimentation, or a microstructure that is unrecognizable by the imaging technique or unprintable at the original scale. The authors note that the sample herein analyzed is dominated by large pores (≥ 500  μ m   ), which contain a pore size that is suitable to the printer resolution. The applicability of this method to soils with pores dominated by even finer textured grains requires reviewing the resolution of the image of the original soil sample and the printer resolution to ensure the finest details are both visible for CAD construction and printable in the final product.   5 Summary and conclusions In this work we present one of the most detailed descriptions and measurements of structural and hydrologic properties in 3D printed heterogeneous porous media. In doing so, we shed light on the quality of 3D printing to produce identical soil/rock analogues, which has been an elusively revolutionary technique for investigating subsurface processes due largely to the improper removal of support material from the pore space, a longstanding bottleneck. We have surveyed the capability of four different 3D printing technologies for producing soil analogues through direct comparison of microtomography imaging of their pore space. Typical metrics were used for quantifying the recovered pore morphology to evaluate how well each technique can relate their print to the complex soil design they were crafted from (accuracy), as well as how close the prints are to one another (repeatability). One particular technology emerged as the best–DLS. No trade-off was required between accuracy and repeatability. Strategies to overcome accuracy limitations are unique to each printing strategy here investigated. Generally, we recommend avoiding approaches that require the use of support material in the voids during fabrication (PolyJet) because its removal from intricate pore networks is notoriously difficult. For LFS, tilting the sample by 45° on edge or corner during printing greatly and similarly improved the final product. To alleviate the extreme hydrophobicity of resin printing, we propose plasma treatment. While some limitations remain to be resolved (e.g., printing the smallest of pores and treating the polymer surface to change its wettability and surface texture), we are optimistic that the soil/environmental science community could be on the verge of moving past using glass beads and sand for performing controlled transport experiments in the laboratory. The adoption of a new generation of model porous media with realistic pore structures can take advantage of the large databases of microtomography images of undisturbed soils/rocks representative of myriad systems, land uses, and applications. High quality 3D printed soil/rock analogues can open up many yet unexplored opportunities to investigate the impacts of pore structural characteristics on flow, transport, and reactions in environmentally relevant media.
1 Introduction Over the past six decades, more than 16 million reservoirs have been built to meet urban and agricultural water demands, facilitate navigation, and bolster power generation (Lehner et al., 2011 ). However, such reservoir developments have significantly altered natural flow regimes, leading to prolonged residence time of water in rivers, reduced seasonal variability, and the emergence of artificial hydropeaking (Chalise et al., 2023; Döll et al., 2009; Graf, 2006; Poff et al., 2007; Ruhi et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Numerous studies have underscored the adverse impacts of such alterations on riverine and riparian ecosystem functions and services, manifesting in the decline in fish productivity and the loss of species diversity (Humborg et al., 1997; Nilsson et al., 2005; Poff & Schmidt, 2016; Ruhi et al., 2018; Ziv et al., 2012 ). Despite the evident environmental repercussions, there is a surge in the proposal and construction of over 3,700 new hydropower dams in developing economies, primarily due to their perceived advantages as clean and cost-effective energy alternatives (Hadjerioua et al., 2012; Zarfl et al., 2015 ). To optimize the operation and management of reservoirs for sustainable development, there is an urgent imperative to deepen our understanding of the flow regime alterations induced by these hydraulic structures. However, the impact of reservoirs on flow regime is often intertwined with climate variability and other human activities, including irrigation and water extraction. This complexity poses a challenge in disentangling the specific impacts attributable to reservoirs. (Dey & Mishra, 2017; He et al., 2017; Juez et al., 2023 ). To address this issue, scholars have made numerous attempts, with hydrological modeling being one of the methods employed. Many researchers have sought to integrate reservoir modules into hydrological models to account for the impact of reservoirs (Burek et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2022; Hanasaki et al., 2008; Turner et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Yassin et al., 2019; Zajac et al., 2017 ). When analyzing the effects of reservoirs using hydrological models, it is necessary to simulate scenarios that consider both reservoir operation and the absence of reservoir operation. The comparison of different simulation results is crucial for extracting insights into the reservoir's influence. This method's advantage lies in its ability to eliminate impacts from climate and other human activities. However, its drawback stems from the substantial uncertainty inherent in the model. Even traditional hydrological models, which exclude considerations of human activities, still exhibit a certain degree of uncertainty stemming from the input data, model structure, and parameters (Liu & Gupta, 2007; Schewe et al., 2014 ). With the incorporation of reservoir parameterization, this uncertainty is further magnified. On one hand, this is due to the limited availability of publicly accessible reservoir operational data (Brown et al., 2015; Ehsani et al., 2016 ), compelling scholars to rely on remote sensing data to infer reservoir operational information (Dong et al., 2023; Du et al., 2022; Otta et al., 2023; Vu et al., 2022 ). On the other hand, even with knowledge of operation rules, the flexible adjustment of spillage strategies in special conditions proves challenging to represent in the model (Salwey et al., 2023 ). Hence, the modeling approach is subject to limitations in detecting hydrological impacts of reservoirs, especially for multiple-basin or multiple-reservoir cases. In addition to modeling approaches, scholars have sought to analyze the impact of reservoirs solely based on observed data. These methods involve identifying corresponding observational data unaffected by reservoir’s influence for comparative analysis. One such method is the “upstream–downstream” approach, where runoff observations from the upstream of a reservoir serve as a reference for analyzing the reservoir's impact (Brunner, 2021; Chalise et al., 2023; Haghighi et al., 2021; Rangecroft et al., 2019 ). However, the effectiveness of this method relies on the proximity of the two gauging stations; otherwise, nonlinear relationships may emerge due to influences from intermittent inflows between the stations (Van Loon et al., 2019 ). Additionally, the availability of hydrological data restricts the use of this method for large-scale and extensive sample implications. Another approach is the “pre-post-disturbance” method, which uses pre-reservoir construction runoff observations as a baseline for assessing the reservoir's impact (Gao et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2021; Poff et al., 2007; Singer, 2007 ). The limitation of this method lies in its inability to distinguish the reservoir's effects from climate variability and non-stationarity (Penas et al., 2016 ). A third category is the “paired-catchment” approach, which was initially an experimental method applied in forest hydrology (Bates, 1928; Bathurst et al., 2018; Bosch & Hewlett, 1982; Brown et al., 2005, 2013; Hewlett, 1971; McCulloch & Robinson, 1993 ). In this method, one catchment serves as a control while another undergoes specific treatments, allowing hydrologists to assess the treatment impacts on flow dynamics. Over time, it has evolved into a statistical analysis tool widely used to quantify the effects of land cover changes (e.g., bushfires, deforestation, urbanization, agricultural practices) on local hydrological regimes (Cheng et al., 2017; Pathiraja et al., 2016; Bart & Hope, 2010; Folton et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2012 ). The method necessitates that the climate and underlying surface characteristics of paired catchments remain as similar as possible during undisturbed periods. Initially, the runoff characteristics between paired catchments are statistically related during a baseline period, typically through linear regression modeling. This relationship is then used to simulate runoff characteristics in the disturbed catchment during the disturbance period. The disparity between simulated and observed runoff characteristics quantifies the impact of the specific disturbance (Zégre et al., 2010 ). Van Loon et al. (2019)  pioneered the application of the paired-catchment approach to analyze the direct influence of human activities on hydrological drought. They identified a catchment devoid of human influence but with similar physical characteristics to serve as a reference for evaluating human impacts. The paired-catchment approach offers distinct advantages for analyzing the impact of human activities: (a) It relies entirely on observational data, bypassing uncertainties associated with hydrological modeling. (b) By directly comparing two similar catchments over the same period, it effectively mitigates the impacts of climatic variability and non-stationarity. However, this method currently faces significant limitations: (a) Selection criteria for paired catchments often involve subjective judgments. (b) Difficulties in meeting matching conditions and data requirements constrain the identification of suitable pairs, thereby limiting the method's application predominantly to case studies. To more effectively leverage the strengths of the paired-catchment approach, we plan to improve it based on the framework of Van Loon et al. (2019) . Specifically, we aim to quantify the screening criteria throughout the pairing process to enhance objectivity and make the method more suitable for large sample applications. Additionally, we will implement modifications to better adapt the approach for analyzing reservoir impacts. In recent years, the rise of the big data era has given rise to a prominent avenue in hydrological research known as large-sample hydrology (Gupta et al., 2014 ). Numerous studies have explored the impact of human activities on hydrology through large-sample comparisons (Salwey et al., 2023; Tijdeman et al., 2018a; Tijdeman et al., 2018b ). The advantages of employing a large sample include improved statistical reliability, enhanced representation of hydrological variability, and increased robustness in characterizing overall hydrological patterns (Addor et al., 2020; Janssen & Ameli, 2021 ). In this study, we integrate the improved paired-catchment approach with the large-sample comparison method, this integration will provide us with statistically more reliable conclusions while also offering more insights into the details of reservoir impacts. The objectives of this study are outlined as follows: (a) To refine the existing paired-catchment method by implementing appropriate modifications for detecting reservoir impacts on flow regime alterations, creating an automated procedure suitable for large-sample implications and free from empirical judgment. (b) To investigate the influence of reservoirs on the flow regime in large-sample catchments from three perspectives: statistical distribution, spectral structure, and hydrological signature. This exploration seeks to assess how reservoirs, with different functionalities and diverse regulatory capacities, influence the flow regime.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Hydrometeorological data Global daily and monthly streamflow observations were collected from 12 national or international institutions (see Table S1  in the supplementary material ). Catchment boundaries were delineated using the flow direction map of HydroSHEDS 15 s (Lehner et al., 2008 ) and the Automatic Outlet Relocation Algorithm developed by Xie et al. (2022) . For all hydrological stations, we conduct a preliminary screening based on the following rules:(a) We maintained stations that have published catchment area information and those with catchment areas between 100 and 100,000 km2. This is because if the catchment area is too small, the subsequently extracted attribute data will be less dependable. Conversely, if the area is too large, the catchment becomes heterogeneous with numerous factors influencing the flow regime, making it challenging to isolate the reservoir's impact.  (b) We preserved stations for which the catchment boundary extraction error is limited to ± 20 %. The extraction error is quantified by the discrepancy between the extracted catchment area and published catchment area:   (1) e x t r a c t i o n  e r r o r  ( % )  = e x t r a c t e d  a r e a  -  p u b l i s h e d  a r e a  p u b l i s h e d  a r e a   × 100     (c) Due to the overlap of stations between different data sources, for stations within 100 m of each other, we retained those with longer observational records, in alignment with Yin et al. (2023) .  (d) Considering that our analysis is primarily based on monthly data, yet the majority of the data obtained is recorded at a daily scale, it is necessary to compile the daily data into monthly aggregates. The prerequisite of this data aggregation necessitates a minimum of 20 days of observations for each month. Ultimately, only those stations with a continuous monthly record of at least 30 years and a missing data rate of less than 5 % were retained (Van Loon et al., 2019 ).    Following above rules, we filtered a total of 12,132 stations that satisfied the requirements. Thereafter, these 12,132 catchments were utilized for attribute extraction. We extracted monthly precipitation data using delineated catchment boundaries from the TerraClimate dataset. TerraClimate, which combines high-spatial resolution climatological normals from the WorldClim dataset with coarser spatial resolution but time-varying data from CRU Ts4.0 and the Japanese 55-year Reanalysis (JRA55), was designed to provide a high-spatial resolution dataset covering a more extensive temporal record (Abatzoglou et al., 2018; Fick & Hijmans, 2017; Harris et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2015 ). This dataset features a spatial resolution of 1/24 degree and spans the period from 1958 to 2020. We utilized it to assess the similarity of precipitation variability between catchment pairs and to compute runoff elasticity.  2.2 Catchment attributes and reservoir data We extracted static catchment attributes from the HydroATLAS dataset (Linke et al., 2019 ) using the “Caravan” software developed by Kratzert et al. (2023) . The HydroATLAS dataset contains 56 hydro-environmental variables and 281 individual attributes. We meticulously chose a subset from it focusing on four fundamental dimensions: climate, land cover, soil, and geology. These dimensions are acknowledged as pivotal for the runoff generation process (Jencso & McGlynn, 2011; Nanda & Safeeq, 2023 ), and the variables associated with them were carefully selected. In terms of climate, our selection includes average annual precipitation and average annual potential evaporation, aligning with the approach outlined by Van Loon et al. (2019)  for characterizing climatological similarity. Regarding land cover, HydroATLAS distinguishes 22 land cover classes based on the GLC2000 database (Bartholomé & Belward, 2005 ). To enhance clarity and facilitate analysis, we consolidated these classes into 9 broader categories: forest, crop, shrub, grass, barren, impervious, wet, snow & ice, and unclassified (specific aggregation rules are listed in Table S2  in the supplementary material ). We examined the proportion of each land cover category within the catchment as a measure of land cover similarity. Concerning soil properties, we individually considered the fractions of clay, sand, and silt to represent soil similarity. In terms of geology, factors such as lithology and dissolution degree significantly influence runoff characteristics, with karst topography being a typical manifestation that expedites the rapid transport of groundwater (Luo et al., 2023; White, 2002 ). We calculated the proportion of karst areas within the catchment to briefly represent geological similarity. To obtain specific catchment-scale attributes, a spatial join computation was performed between the level12 polygons (constituting the highest resolution shapefile available in the HydroATLAS dataset) and catchment boundaries (most of our catchments are bigger than the level12 polygons with an average area of 130.6 km2 ). Subsequently, the catchment attributes were computed as an area-weighted aggregate. It is acknowledged that perfect alignment between our catchment boundaries and HydroATLAS polygons may not be achieved. However, the associated mismatch effect is considered acceptable for catchments larger than 100 km2 , according to Kratzert et al. (2023) . Kratzert et al. (2023)  also introduced an index called “area_fraction_used_for_aggregation ”, which presents the proportion of the polygon area utilized for aggregation relative to the total catchment area, to quantify the area mismatch. In our study, all area_fraction_used_for_aggregation  values exceed 0.95, with 94 % surpassing 0.99, indicating minimal boundary mismatch. We employed two datasets to gather information on reservoirs within the catchment. The first dataset, GRanD v1.3 (7,320 records), provides comprehensive attributes of reservoirs but excludes many small to medium-sized ones (Lehner et al., 2011 ). The second dataset, GeoDAR v1.1 (21,515 records), covers the majority of reservoirs but only offers location information without detailed reservoir attributes (Wang et al., 2022 ). Our analysis primarily focuses on reservoirs documented in the GRanD dataset, while the GeoDAR dataset serves the purpose of excluding catchments impacted by reservoirs not documented in GRanD. The procedures can be delineated as follows: Initially, utilizing catchment boundaries, dam sites corresponding to reservoirs in both the GRanD and GeoDAR datasets were extracted. Subsequently, catchments were categorized based on the presence of dam sites in either the GRanD or GeoDAR dataset. Those with documented GRanD dam sites were labeled as regulated, while those with dam sites exclusively in the GeoDAR dataset, lacking corresponding entries in GRanD, were excluded. Catchments without dam sites identified in both datasets were classified as unregulated. Ultimately, we identified a total of 10,213 catchments for subsequent pairing, comprising 6,296 unregulated catchments and 3,917 regulated catchments.  2.3 Catchment pairing Each of the 6,296 unregulated catchments was systematically paired with each of the 3,917 regulated catchments, generating a total of 6,296*3,917 candidate pairs. Following this, a rigorous filtration process was implemented for these catchment pairs, considering factors such as climate similarity, geographical characteristics, and runoff similarity (dividing streamflow by catchment area yields runoff) (Fig. 1  ). Firstly, we assessed climate similarity by examining both annual values and variability for each catchment pair. Following the criteria established by Van Loon et al. (2019) , we limited the differences in average annual precipitation (Δ P mean     ) and potential evapotranspiration (Δ PET  mean     ) between unregulated and regulated catchments to within ± 10 %. Δ P mean      and Δ PET  mean      were calculated using the following formulas:(2) Δ P mean   ( % )  = P unregulated   - P regulated    P regulated    × 100     (3) Δ PET  mean   ( % )  = PET  unregulated   - PET  regulated    PET  regulated    × 100     where P unregulated      and P regulated      denote average annual precipitation of unregulated and regulated catchment, respectively, and PET  unregulated      and PET  regulated      denote average annual potential evapotranspiration of unregulated and regulated catchment, respectively. To ensure concordance in precipitation variability, we set controls on the linear regression slopes and R2  values of yearly and monthly precipitation series between each catchment pair. The linear regression equations are expressed as follows:(4) P yearly , r e g u l a t e d   = α 1  P yearly , u n r e g u l a t e d   + β 1  + ε 1      (5) P yearly , u n r e g u l a t e d   = α 2  P yearly , r e g u l a t e d   + β 2  + ε 2      (6) P monthly , r e g u l a t e d   = α 3  P monthly , u n r e g u l a t e d   + β 3  + ε 3      (7) P monthly , u n r e g u l a t e d   = α 4  P monthly , r e g u l a t e d   + β 4  + ε 4      P yearly , r e g u l a t e d      and P monthly , r e g u l a t e d      represent the yearly and monthly precipitation series for the regulated catchment, whereas P yearly , u n r e g u l a t e d      and P monthly , u n r e g u l a t e d      represent the corresponding yearly and monthly precipitation series for the unregulated catchment. The corresponding illustration is provided in Fig. 1 b. Next, we conducted a further filter on catchment pairs based on geographical similarity. We constrained the differences in each land cover fraction, each soil type fraction, and karst area proportion to be within ± 25 %. They are expressed by the following equations:(8) - 0.25 < L C  i , u n r e g u l a t e d   - LC  i , r e g u l a t e d   < 0.25     (9) - 0.25 < S o i l  j , u n r e g u l a t e d   - Soil  j , r e g u l a t e d   < 0.25     (10) - 0.25 < K a r s t  unregulated   - Karst  regulated   < 0.25     where LC  i , u n r e g u l a t e d      represents the fraction of the i th land cover type in the unregulated catchment, Soil  j , u n r e g u l a t e d      represents the fraction of the j th soil type in the unregulated catchment, and Karst  unregulated      represents karst area proportion in the unregulated catchment. The corresponding values are represented by LC  i , r e g u l a t e d     , Soil  j , r e g u l a t e d      and Karst  regulated      for the regulated catchment, respectively. Recognizing the inherent uncertainty associated with the data products used for extracting these attributes, these constraints are relatively loose. We consider that imposing excessively stringent standards at this stage would be less meaningful, potentially resulting in a reduction in effective sample size. More precise control conditions were implemented in subsequent stages. In the final stage, we further honed our selection of catchment pairs based on runoff similarities. Despite meticulous control for climate and geographical similarities, as mentioned earlier, uncertainties in the data and unaccounted factors, such as human activities beyond reservoir regulation, present challenges in ensuring complete similarities among the retained catchment pairs beyond the mere presence of reservoirs. Consequently, in our deductive process, we operated under the assumption that, given fundamental similarities in climate, land cover, soil, and geology characteristics, the hydrological response of two catchments is considered similar if their runoff patterns exhibit resemblance. Our filtering approach aligns with this rationale: if the runoff of two catchments is comparable before reservoir construction but diverges after reservoir implementation, we attribute the disparities in post-reservoir stage runoff between the two catchments to reservoir regulation. However, this approach raises two key issues. First, there is the challenge of determining the metric for the similarity or dissimilarity of runoff between two catchments. Second, establishing the breakpoint for catchments with multiple reservoirs poses another consideration. To tackle the first issue, we followed the methodology outlined by Betterle et al. (2018) , utilizing Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) as a metric for measuring runoff similarity. Runoff is considered dissimilar when NSE is less than 0.5. To assess runoff similarity, we employed five thresholds: 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, and 0.9, conducting filtering and analysis for each threshold. NSE is calculated as follows:(11) N S E = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  ( R regulated , i   - R unregulated , i   )  2   ∑ i = 1  n  ( R regulated , i   - R regulated    ¯   )  2        where R regulated , i      and R unregulated , i      are the runoff (in mm) for the regulated catchment and unregulated catchment in the i th month, respectively. R regulated    ¯      is the average monthly runoff in the regulated catchment. Addressing catchments with multiple reservoirs involves the following breakpoint determination process: all reservoirs within the catchment were arranged in descending order of storage capacity. We identified the top n  reservoirs, where the cumulative storage capacity just exceeds 80 % of the total catchment storage. The construction years of these n  reservoirs were considered potential breakpoints. Subsequently, using each of these n  years as a breakpoint, we conducted calculations of NSE both before and after the breakpoint. If the NSE value before the breakpoint exceeds the established similarity threshold, and the NSE value after the breakpoint is less than 0.5, we deem the breakpoint acceptable. In cases where none of the potential breakpoints meet this criterion, the corresponding catchment pair was excluded from consideration. In situations where multiple potential breakpoints meet the criterion, we selected the one with the highest NSE value before the breakpoint. The decision to exclusively consider the top 80 % of reservoirs, determined by storage capacity percentage, was made with the aim of excluding reservoirs with relatively small capacities, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, a deliberate choice was made to refrain from designating the year of construction for the largest reservoir as the breakpoint. This decision is based on the acknowledgment that the reservoir with the maximum capacity may not necessarily have the most significant impact on the flow regime, considering variations in distance to the outlet and distinct functional characteristics among reservoirs. In summary, our approach not only ensures comparability of two catchments but also identifies the construction year of the reservoir that significantly influences the flow regime, termed the “transition point” – the year when the flow regime began to change. Two prerequisites for implementing this approach are that the shared data span for both catchments must exceed 30 years, and there should be a minimum of 5 years of data both before and after each breakpoint for NSE calculations. Failure to meet these conditions will result in the exclusion of the corresponding catchment pairs or potential breakpoints from consideration. While this approach is tailored for catchments with multiple reservoirs, it is equally applicable to single-reservoir catchments where the reservoir's storage capacity constitutes 100 % of the total catchment storage, exceeding the 80 % threshold. The retained catchment pairs, following the screening (Fig. 1 ), are now poised for analysis. However, some pairs contain duplicated regulated or unregulated catchments compared to others. To ensure sample independence, we retained only the pairs with the highest pre-transition NSE. This refinement yielded 177, 139, 98, 62, and 28 pairs when employing NSE similarity thresholds of 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, and 0.9, respectively. In the subsequent sections, our focus will predominantly center on the analysis results employing a threshold of 0.7. To investigate the varied impacts of reservoirs, we systematically classified regulated catchments based on different functionalities and regulatory capacities. Initially, we computed the proportions of reservoir capacities associated with various functionalities within the regulated catchment. If the capacity proportion for a specific functionality exceeds 60 %, we categorize the catchment under that functionality. Conversely, if the proportions for all functional types fall below 60 %, we classify the catchment as having multiple functionalities. Simultaneously, drawing inspiration from Salwey et al. (2023) , we employed the Normalized Upstream Capacity (NUC) as a metric to assess the overall regulatory capacity of reservoirs within the catchment. NUC is determined by dividing the total reservoir capacity within the catchment by the overall precipitation in that catchment.(12) N U C = t o t a l  u p s t r e a m  r e s e r v o i r  c a p a c i t y ( m m  3  )  t o t a l  c a t c h m e n t  a r e a ( m m  2  )  ∗  a v e r a g e  a n n u a l  c a t c h m e n t  p r e c i p i t a t i o n ( m m )          2.4 Improvements to the paired-catchment approach We summarize our improvements to the paired-catchment approach in the following aspects: (a) Quantification of catchment similarity criteria. Previous work by Van Loon et al. (2019)  provided a framework for selecting paired catchments to analyze human influence. However, their determination of similarity relied heavily on expert judgement. We have automated the pairing process by quantify the screening criteria, thereby enhancing its objectivity and scalability. (b) Adoption of a “Before-After-Control-Impact” (BACI) setup. Unlike the 'Control-Impact' (CI) setup employed by Van Loon et al. (2019) , which directly compared benchmark catchments with human-influenced catchments in the post-disturbance period, the BACI setup involves controlling for runoff similarity during the pre-disturbance period, thereby enhancing the reliability of our comparisons after the disturbance. (c) Adaptation for reservoir impact analysis. We tailored the paired catchment approach to make it more suitable for reservoirs. Specifically, we introduced a breakpoint determination process to effectively handle multiple reservoirs within a catchment, ensuring the identification of period with the most significant reservoir impact.  2.5 Flow regime analysis We commenced our investigation by analyzing the statistical distribution of monthly runoff. Subsequently, we utilized continuous wavelet transform (CWT), in conjunction with three hydrological signatures, to scrutinize the influence of reservoirs on the flow regime. These analyses collectively aim to underscore the effectiveness of the improved paired-catchment method in capturing the effects of reservoirs. 2.5.1 Statistical distribution According to the definition by Vogel and Fennessey (1994) , a flow duration curve (FDC) illustrates the relationship between the magnitude and frequency of daily, weekly, monthly (or another specified time interval) streamflow. It quantifies the percentage of time during which the flow equaled or exceeded a specified value (Shu & Ouarda, 2012 ). In this study, we employed a curve like the FDC to represent the statistical distribution of monthly runoff. The runoff within each catchment pair was normalized and used as the x-axis for plotting the cumulative probability distribution curve. This normalization was conducted because our analysis focuses on comparing the impacts of reservoirs within the same catchment pairs. After normalization, all catchment pairs can be plotted together, facilitating mutual comparison to derive general patterns.  2.5.2 Continuous wavelet transform Unlike the Fourier transform, which decomposes signals into non-decaying sinusoids of varying frequencies, the wavelet transform dissects a time signal into a combination of wavelet basis functions, each exhibiting some decay across time. This characteristic enables the analysis of the time–frequency properties of signals (Brown et al., 2023 ). The CWT of a discrete time series x n     (for n = 0 , 1 , ⋯ , N - 1   ) at a given temporal scale s   , denoted as W n  ( s )    , is the convolution of x n     with a wavelet function Ψ   :(13) W n  ( s )  = ∑ n  ′  = 0  N - 1   x n  ′   Ψ  ∗   n  ′  - n   δ t  s         where N    denotes the length of the time series, Ψ  ∗      denotes the complex conjugate of Ψ   , δ t    denotes data sampling interval. The wavelet function Ψ    is obtained by normalizing a mother wavelet function Ψ 0    . We utilized the Morlet wavelet as the mother wavelet function, chosen for its effective trade-off between time and frequency resolution, as demonstrated by Rezaei and Gurdak (2020) . The Morlet wavelet function, Ψ 0  ( η )    , is mathematically expressed as:(14) Ψ 0  ( η )  = π  - 1 / 4   e  i ω 0  η   e  - η  2  / 2       where i    is the imaginary unit, ω 0  = 6    is the non-dimensional frequency parameter (Farge, 1992 ), and η = n  ′  - n   δ t  s     is the non-dimensional time parameter. The amplitude of W n  ( s )    , denoted as W n  ( s )      , serves as a measure to quantify the wavelet power. Finally, the wavelet power spectrum (WPS) can be defined as:(15) W P S  n  s    = W n  s       2      where W n  s       2     represents the wavelet power at time n    and scale s   . To calculate the average wavelet power for each regulated and unregulated catchment during both the pre- and post-transition periods, we utilized the “analyze.wavelet” function from the R package “WaveletComp v.1.1”. To enhance the robustness of our wavelet analysis, we implemented an additional criterion regarding data length. Specifically, we required a minimum of ten years of data for both the pre- and post-transition periods in both catchments. Out of the 177 pairs of catchments, 110 pairs met this criterion. Subsequently, we conducted a wavelet power examination at monthly, seasonal, annual, and interannual time scales using these 110 pairs of catchments.  2.5.3 Hydrological signatures Reservoirs are often operated to sustain a consistently pre-defined discharge over extended periods to achieve specific objectives. In this study, we selected three signatures closely associated with reservoirs to quantify their influence: segmentation of FDC (Seg_FDC), low flow variability (LFV), and runoff elasticity (E) (Salwey et al., 2023 ). In natural settings, the daily FDC typically exhibits a sigmoidal shape. However, reservoir operations can introduce abrupt changes and flat segments in the daily FDC. Therefore, the Seg_FDC can be employed to capture the reservoir's influence. To calculate the Seg_FDC, the first step is to fit a sigmoidal function to the observed cumulative distribution to represent the “natural” shape, The formula for the sigmoidal function is as follows:(16) f ^  = - a ∗  l o g 1 1 - x      + b     where a    and b    are optimized individually for each catchment and period through a nonlinear least squares regression applied to the daily FDC between the 5th and 95th percentiles. The variable x    represents the flow exceedance probability. The deviation of the observed FDC from the natural shape is calculated as follows:(17) S e g _ F D C = ∑ i = 1  N  l o g Q i     - f ^  i     2   N    ∗ 1 σ      where N    is the length of the data records, Q i     represents the daily flow value at the i   th position of the observed FDC, f ^  i     is the associated flow based on the sigmoidal function, and σ    represents the standard deviation of the (log) flow timeseries. A higher Seg_FDC value indicates a more pronounced alteration to the natural flow variability. The LFV can assess the intra-annual variations in low flow regime, and its calculation formula is as follows:(18) L F V = 1 - max  m = 1 , ⋯ , 12   Q 80 , m      - min  m = 1 , ⋯ , 12   Q 80 , m       Q      where Q 80 , m      denotes the 20th flow percentile in month m    across all years within the analysed time series, and Q    is the mean daily discharge. Reservoir construction is often undertaken to address the uneven temporal distribution of water resources, with the goal of mitigating peak flows and enhancing low flows. Concurrently, to safeguard downstream ecological environments, reservoirs typically adhere to a minimum discharge standard known as “ecological flow” (Rudra, 2018 ). These two factors may contribute to a reduction in intra-annual variations in low flows, resulting in a higher LFV. E describes the sensitivity of runoff to precipitation variations and can be calculated as follows:(19) E = m e d i a n Δ R year-on-year     Δ P year-on-year         ∗ P R      where P    and R    denote the average precipitation and runoff within a catchment, whereas Δ P year-on-year       and Δ R year-on-year       represent the year-on-year change in annual precipitation and runoff within the available time series. Due to the function of reservoirs to store and subsequently redistribute precipitation, they may act as buffers, reducing the sensitivity of runoff to precipitation. It is noteworthy that, in computing the three signatures, different sample sets were utilized. The Seg_FDC and LFV necessitate the use of daily runoff records. To ensure the reliability of the results, we meticulously selected catchment pairs from the pool of 177 that met the following criterion: a minimum of 10 years of daily runoff data both before and after the transition point, with missing values not exceeding 5 %. A total of 80 catchment pairs satisfied this condition and were employed for calculating the Seg_FDC and LFV. As for the E, the calculation of this signature inherently eliminates the influence of inconsistent rainfall, obviating the need for a pre-transition comparison. Additionally, as the precipitation data utilized here is available only from 1958 onwards and does not cover the pre-transition period for most catchments, our consideration was focused solely on the post-transition period. In computing this signature, our data prerequisite was as follows: a minimum of 20 years of concurrent monthly precipitation and runoff data after the transition point. Out of the 177 catchment pairs, 120 pairs met this criterion and were used for calculating E.    3 Results 3.1 Selected catchment pairs With a similarity threshold set at NSE=0.7, we identified 177 pairs of catchments from a pool of 12,132 catchments with ample monthly runoff data. The distances within these catchment pairs span from 2.9 km to 328.5 km, with a median distance of 71 km. When pairing the catchments, we did not set a distance criterion; instead, we relied on the similarity of meteorological and geographical conditions. The resulting catchment pairs exhibited closely matched distances within each pair, aligning with the first law of geography – “Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related to each other.” (Tobler, 1970 ). This, to a certain extent, validates the rationality of our selection criteria. From the spatial distribution of catchment pairs (Fig. 2  ), they are predominantly located in the United States, southeastern South America, and Europe – regions characterized by rich hydrological data and dense reservoir distribution. Effective catchment pairs in Asia, Africa, and Australia are scarce, with sporadic occurrences. Despite the uneven global spatial distribution of catchment pairs, this represents the largest sample we could identify with publicly available data. Among the 177 regulated catchments, over half are primarily influenced by flood control and hydroelectricity reservoirs (29.9 % for flood control, 28.8 % for hydroelectricity). The proportions influenced by irrigation, water supply, multiple functionalities, and unknown functionalities are 13.6 %, 11.9 %, 7.3 %, and 8.5 %, respectively. The reservoir regulatory capacity (NUC) within these 177 regulated catchments ranges from 0.01 to 2, with the majority (79.7 %) having a NUC between 0.01 and 0.4.  3.2 Alteration in statistical distribution of monthly runoff To evaluate the impact of reservoirs on the statistical distribution of runoff, we plotted cumulative distribution curves for normalized runoff across all catchment pairs, encompassing both pre- and post-transition periods (Fig. 3  a). In the figure, dashed lines and their surrounding shaded areas represent conditions during the pre-transition period, where both catchments were unaffected by the reservoir, serving as a reference. It reveals a high similarity in the statistical distribution between the unregulated catchment in the post-transition period and both catchments in the pre-transition period, with their median lines nearly overlapping. However, runoff under the influence of the reservoir (regulated catchment in the post-transition period) exhibits a different distribution, with runoff below the 50th percentile being larger and runoff above the 50th percentile being smaller. This implies that the operation of the reservoir augments low flows while mitigating high flows, resulting in a more concentrated statistical distribution of runoff. Fig. 4   illustrates the changes in cumulative distributions of runoff under different classifications of reservoirs (functional and NUC classification). We did not present the results for the “Multiple” and “Other/Unknown” categories due to their relatively small sample sizes (13 and 15 pairs, respectively). Notably, Fig. 4 a reveals that reservoirs with different functionalities exert distinct influences on runoff distribution. Reservoirs designed for hydropower generation exhibit the most pronounced peak-shaving and drought-supplementing effects on monthly runoff, whereas the corresponding effects for flood control reservoirs are relatively less apparent. Reservoirs for irrigation and water supply primarily manifest as peak-shaving without substantial drought-supplementing effects. It is crucial to emphasize that these results represent a synthesis across all catchment pairs. If there is a clear pattern, it can be construed as a general trend for that type of reservoir. However, even in the absence of a clear pattern, it should not be interpreted as an indication that the impact of reservoirs of that type is generally inconspicuous. Instead, it should be interpreted as the impact of reservoirs of that type being diverse, with effects becoming less apparent when averaged. The observation that reservoirs for irrigation and water supply mainly exhibit peak-shaving without drought-supplementing aligns with our common understanding. These two types of reservoirs primarily serve consumptive water uses, leading to an overall reduction in runoff. The histograms in Fig. 4 a illustrate that there is no significant difference in the distribution of reservoir regulatory capacity among samples with different functionalities. Therefore, the variation in runoff distribution is primarily attributed to the differing functionalities of the reservoirs. From Fig. 4 b, it can be observed that reservoirs with stronger regulatory capacity also exhibit enhanced capability in redistributing water resources, with catchments having an NUC greater than 0.2 showing a more pronounced peak-shaving and drought-supplementing effect.  3.3 Alteration in streamflow periodicity To explore the modifications in streamflow periodicity resulting from reservoir operations, we compared the average wavelet power spectrum between regulated and unregulated catchments (Fig. 3 b). It is evident that reservoirs significantly modulate the annual periodicity of streamflow signals while amplifying their low-frequency components (with lower average wavelet power at 12 months and higher average wavelet power at 16–64 months). This is because reservoirs are primarily designed to address the uneven temporal distribution of water resources, aiming to ensure sustained and stable release over the long term. The regulation of streamflow periodicity by reservoirs with different functionalities did not reveal pronounced differences, except for hydroelectricity reservoirs, which exhibited a greater suppression of the annual periodic signal compared to other types (Fig. 5  a). Upon scrutinizing the outcomes based on the classification of NUC (Fig. 5 b), as anticipated, reservoirs with greater regulatory capacity exhibited a higher degree of attenuation for streamflow periodic signals (catchments with NUC>0.4 displayed lower annual signals and higher multi-year signals). This phenomenon is attributed to the prolonged residence time of reservoirs with higher NUC, thereby enhancing their capacity for streamflow redistribution.  3.4 Alteration in hydrological signatures Fig. 6   presents a comparison of Seg_FDC and LFV signatures between regulated and unregulated catchments before and after the transition point. The boxplot illustrates a notable similarity in the distribution of Seg_FDC and LFV between the two catchment types before the transition point. However, following reservoir operation, the values of these signatures consistently exceed those in unregulated catchments. Specifically, the LFV in regulated catchments exhibits a significant increase compared to unregulated catchments (p = 0.002, determined through a Wilcoxon test). From a pairwise perspective, during the pre-transition period, 53.8 % of regulated catchments demonstrate higher Seg_FDC values than their unregulated counterparts, while 38.8 % of regulated catchments exhibit higher LFV values than their unregulated counterparts. In the post-transition period, these proportions escalate to 60 % and 68.8 %, respectively. This observation suggests that reservoir operations significantly alter the shape of the daily FDC while also reducing the variability in low flow throughout the year. When comparing the signatures across different functional types (Fig. 7  a and 7c), it becomes evident that flood control reservoirs exhibit the most significant rise in the Seg_FDC, while water supply reservoirs demonstrate the most notable increase in the LFV. Flood control reservoirs may need to employ varied flow release strategies at different time intervals to adapt to rainfall and flood predictions. This irregular discharge behavior can introduce fragmented features on the FDC. In contrast, the primary design objective of water supply reservoirs is to ensure a consistent water supply throughout the year, emphasizing stability relative to other types of reservoirs. In terms of NUC classification, reservoirs with a strong regulatory capacity exhibit a more substantial increase in both the Seg_FDC and LFV, as these signatures show a significant difference between catchment pairs with NUC>0.2 (Fig. 7 b and 7d). As illustrated in Fig. 8  b, runoff elasticity in regulated catchments is markedly lower than that in unregulated catchments, with 62.5 % of regulated catchments exhibiting lower elasticity compared to their unregulated counterparts. This discrepancy is attributed to the capacity of reservoirs to independently regulate downstream flow regardless of precipitation. Although the differences in elasticity within each category are not statistically significant after classification based on reservoir functionality and regulatory capacity (NUC), the overall elasticity of regulated catchments consistently remains lower than that of unregulated catchments (Fig. 8 a and 8c).   4 Discussion 4.1 Impacts of different thresholds for catchment paring To ensure runoff similarity within paired catchments before the transition point, it is essential to establish a predefined standard. Various thresholds were tested using NSE values ranging from 0.7 to 0.9. Clearly, as the standard increases, the number of effective samples significantly decreases. Specifically, for every increment of 0.05 in the NSE threshold, there is an approximate reduction of 40 pairs of samples. From the analysis results, it is evident that with the increase in the standard, certain patterns become clearer. For instance, as the NSE threshold increases from 0.7 to 0.9, it becomes increasingly apparent that water supply reservoirs reduce both high-flow and low-flow values, indicating water consumption by these reservoirs (Fig. S2 a, S8a, S14a, and S20a in the supplementary material ). Furthermore, the amplification effect of reservoirs on multi-year periodic signals becomes more pronounced (Fig. S1 b, S7b, S13b, and S19b). However, the decrease in sample size may lead to the transformation of initially statistically significant findings into non-significant ones. For instance, when NSE≥0.8, the disparity in runoff elasticity between regulated and unregulated catchments shifts from being statistically significant to non-significant (Figure S12 b, S18b, and S24b). Throughout the main text, emphasis is placed on discussing outcomes derived from an NSE threshold of 0.7. This preference is rooted in the assertion that samples selected with this threshold align with our stipulated requirements, effectively capturing the influence of reservoirs on various facets of the flow regime. Meanwhile, the relatively large sample size employed ensures the robustness and reliability of the findings. We posit that this threshold is judiciously chosen through a careful balance between sample quantity and accuracy.  4.2 Effectiveness of the improved paired-catchment approach Through an examination of the statistical distribution of monthly runoff, we have confirmed that irrigation and water supply reservoirs facilitate consumptive water use through water abstraction or diversion, thereby reducing the flow magnitude across the entire range of the flow duration curve. In contrast, flood control and hydroelectricity reservoirs primarily serve to homogenize the variability of runoff, resulting in increased low flows and decreased high flows. These observed patterns align with prior research findings (FitzHugh & Vogel, 2011; Singer, 2007 ). Due to short-term flow releases for hydropeaking in hydroelectricity reservoirs, previous scholars have predominantly emphasized their impacts on shorter timescales (daily or sub-daily) (Ashraf et al., 2022; Chalise et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2015 ). Our study confirms that hydroelectricity reservoirs bring about equally substantial changes in the flow regime at longer temporal scales (monthly and yearly). They significantly diminish the annual periodic signal of streamflow, with the extent of attenuation even surpassing that observed in other types of reservoirs. Additionally, our findings indicate that the multi-year periodicity (>16 months) of reservoir-impacted streamflow is slightly higher than that of natural streamflow, consistent with results from Chalise et al. (2023)  and Hwang et al. (2021) . Regarding hydrological signatures, our study echoes the conclusions drawn by Salwey et al. (2023) , illustrating that reservoirs induce more flat segments and abrupt changes in the daily flow duration curve, ensuring a more even distribution of low flows throughout the year and a lower sensitivity of catchment runoff to precipitation. Despite both our approach and the method employed by Salwey et al.
