(2023)  involving comparisons between regulated and unregulated catchments, the clarity and statistical reliability of our results are enhanced by our meticulous filtering and one-to-one matching of catchment pairs. Collectively, these findings affirm the effectiveness of our improved paired-catchment approach in detecting reservoir impacts on flow regime across various aspects.  4.3 Limitations and future work Although we have effectively captured the impacts of reservoirs on flow regime using the improved paired-catchment approach, it is important to acknowledge several limitations in our study. Firstly, despite the significant distribution of reservoirs in Asia and Africa, accounting for approximately 42 % of the global total storage capacity (according to GRanD) (Lehner et al., 2011 ), the limited availability of streamflow data led to the selection of only a few catchment pairs in these regions. As a result, the generalizability of our results to a global scale is constrained. Secondly, due to the multifunctional nature of most reservoirs, the largest impact on specific aspects of the flow regime may not necessarily align with their primary functionality (Chalise et al., 2023 ). Our classification based on primary functionality alone may obscure nuanced distinctions in their impacts in certain analyses (e.g., Fig. 5 a). Furthermore, the influence of reservoirs on rivers is not solely reflected in the flow regime but also extends to water quality, water temperature, sediment transport, and nutrient dynamics (Maavara et al., 2020; Olden & Naiman, 2010; Wohl et al., 2015 ). Therefore, future investigations should encompass a more comprehensive consideration of these facets, which play a pivotal role in preserving the ecological integrity of rivers and optimizing their ecosystem services. Finally, while our conclusions regarding reservoir impacts are to some extent well-recognized, the enhanced utility of our improved paired-catchment approach underscores its practical significance. Moving forward, we plan to extend the application of this method to assess the influence of reservoirs on extreme hydrological events, such as droughts and floods. Additionally, we aim to investigate the impact of reservoirs on various aspects of rivers beyond runoff. This endeavor will furnish us with additional insights for the operation and management of hydraulic structures in the Anthropocene era.   5 Conclusions In this study, we introduced an improved paired-catchment approach to systematically elucidate the impacts of reservoirs on various aspects of the flow regime. The improved approach refines the original version by implementing more rigorous controls for catchment similarity and creating an automated procedure suitable for large-sample implications and free from empirical judgment. Our findings suggest that reservoirs can homogenize variations in runoff over time, introduce more flat segments and abrupt changes to the daily flow duration curve, and lead to decreased sensitivity of runoff to rainfall. The degree of alteration in the flow regime due to reservoirs is also related to their functionalities and regulatory capacity. From a statistical perspective, flood control and hydroelectricity reservoirs can effectively reduce peak flow and supplement low flow, while irrigation and water supply reservoirs almost exclusively reduce peak flow without supplementing low flow. Flood control reservoirs differ the most from natural conditions in their daily flow process, while water supply reservoirs exhibit the most uniform distribution of low flow within a year. When considering the impact of reservoir regulatory capacity, the influence of reservoirs on various aspects of the flow regime becomes more pronounced when the normalized upstream capacity (NUC) of the basin exceeds 0.2, indicating a stronger regulatory capacity of the reservoir. In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness and enormous potential of the improved paired-catchment approach in the context of climate change. The improved approach can be further employed in the future to investigate the impact of reservoirs on extreme hydrological events such as droughts and floods, as well as their impacts on aquatic ecosystems. Particularly, in situations where hydrological data is abundant, it has the capability to capture more nuanced patterns.
1 Introduction Rivers are vital conduits for water, sediment, and organic carbon (OC) transport along the Land-to-Ocean Aquatic Continuum (LOAC) (Meybeck, 1982; Milliman and Farnsworth, 2011; Regnier et al., 2022 ). An estimated 0.17–0.20 Gt/yr (1 Gt = 1 × 109  t) of particulate organic carbon (POC) and 0.13–0.21 Gt/yr of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) are delivered to the ocean annually by river systems, providing an essential linkage between terrestrial and marine systems (Ludwig et al., 1996; Dai et al., 2012; Galy et al., 2015; Fabre et al., 2020 ). Riverine DOC can be quickly returned to the atmosphere by oxidation while POC can be buried in sediments over long-term timescales, resulting in carbon sequestration (Bianchi, 2011; Galy et al., 2015 ). Hydrological processes and water–sediment export in global rivers have been significantly altered by climate change and human interventions, especially dam construction (Nilsson et al., 2005; Best, 2019; Dethier et al., 2022; Syvitski et al., 2022 ). Changes in riverine hydrologic condition and biogeochemical processes will further impact the transport and transformation of OC from land to the ocean (Bianchi and Allison, 2009; Bauer et al., 2013; Regnier et al., 2013 ). The global rivers have been under fragmentation due to extensive dam construction since the 1950s, causing significant alterations on riverine hydrology (Grill et al., 2019; Dethier et al., 2022 ). With >50 % of rivers worldwide fragmented by dams and reservoirs, the global sediment exported to the ocean has decreased by 49 % and ∼ 3,200 Gt of sediment has been retained by large reservoirs since the 1950s (Nilsson et al., 2005; Milliman et al., 2008; Syvitski et al., 2005, 2022 ). Consequently, these hydrological changes are strongly impacting OC cycling in rivers (Bauer et al., 2013; Maavara et al., 2017; Mendonça et al., 2017; Regnier et al., 2022 ). Asian rivers are some of the most impacted systems by damming in the world, shifting the global dominance of sediment supply to the ocean from Asia to South America (Dethier et al., 2022 ). In fact, the sediment load, from East Asian rivers to the sea, has decreased from 2.0 Gt/yr since 1,000 yr BP to 0.6 Gt/yr today, resulting in significant impacts on OC transport and composition (Liu et al., 2022; Park et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2011 ). Asian rivers contributed approximately 76 Mt/yr (1 Mt = 1 × 106  t) of POC and 69 Mt/yr of DOC to the ocean, with typically high POC to DOC export ratios (POC/DOC) (Milliman and Meade, 1983; Ludwig et al., 1996 ). However, POC/DOC ratios in East Asian rivers have significantly decreased due to river damming in the past fifty years (Zhang et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015; Le et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022; ). Thus, determining the variations in POC and DOC delivery in the LOAC, driven by dam regulation, is essential for understanding the global carbon cycle. The Yellow River is one of the most human-impacted large rivers in the world, much of it due to dam construction and regulation (Best, 2019; Wang et al., 2006, 2007b ). Historically, the Yellow River was the major sediment contributor to the western Pacific Ocean, with sediment fluxes reaching as high as 1.08 Gt/yr, accounting for 6 % of the global riverine flux (Milliman and Meade, 1983; Milliman and Syvitski, 1992 ). In the 1980s, these fluxes were characterized by a high POC flux (4.5–6.1 Mt/yr) and a low DOC flux (0.1–0.2 Mt/yr), resulting in POC/DOC ratios (i.e. 30–75) far greater than other major global rivers (Amazon [0.2], Yangtze [1.0], Mississippi [0.2], Mekong [1.1] and Nile [1.3] Rivers) (Bianchi et al., 2002; Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Coynel et al., 2005; Le et al., 2007; Meybeck and Ragu, 1996; Moreira-Turcq et al., 2013, 2003; Wang et al., 2012 ). However, the sediment flux in the Yellow River has decreased by > 90 % to 0.15 Gt/yr since the 2000s, mainly because of dam construction and land-use change (Wang et al., 2007b ). Since 2000, the Xiaolangdi (XLD) reservoir has impounded ∼ 246 Mt/yr of sediment and ∼ 0.6 Mt/yr of POC (Lu et al., 2022 ). As a result, the flux of POC from the Yellow River to the sea has declined from approximately 4.5 Mt/yr in the 1980s to less than 0.6 Mt/yr today (Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Ran et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2022 ). Dam regulation, particularly during the Water and Sediment Regulation Scheme (WSRS) by the XLD reservoir, has changed OC transport from river to the sea − across annual and seasonal timescales (Tao et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2013 ). Approximately 35 % of DOC and 56 % of POC are periodically exported to the sea during the WSRS within 20 days (Zhang et al., 2013 ). Previous studies much focused on the delivery and composition of POC or DOC separately, at only one or two gauging stations in the Yellow River (Li et al., 2024; Ran et al., 2013; Tao et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020a; Xue et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2019a,b; Zhang et al., 2013, 2015a–d, 2022 ). Thus, a systematic examination of dam-related POC and DOC delivery along the reservoir-river continuum has yet to be explored. In this study, we focused on the controlling mechanisms of dam regulation on POC and DOC delivery from middle to lower reaches of the Yellow River. POC and DOC datasets were examined during the WSRS in 2020, sampled at station Lijin (LJ) – the last gauging station in the river. Water-sediment records were compiled with corresponding OC measured and reconstructed datasets on daily-monthly-annual timescales, from middle to lower reaches from the 1980s to the 2010s. These combined datasets, with high spatio-temporal scales, were used to examine the alteration of OC delivery modulated by dam regulation along the reservoir-river continuum. This study provides a comprehensive exploration of how extensive and increasing river damming impacts OC delivery along the LOAC in the Yellow River, and how that compares with other global major rivers.  2 Study area The Yellow River is the second largest river in the world (after the Amazon River) in terms of sediment load for ∼ 1.08 Gt/yr in history, which represents 6 % of global riverine sediment load to the ocean (Milliman and Syvitski, 1992 ). The sediment flux in the Yellow River has recently decreased to just 0.2 Gt/yr because of dam impoundment and changes in land use (Wang et al., 2007b ). Compared to the high sediment flux, the water discharge in the Yellow River is only ∼ 48 km3 /yr, much lower than other large rivers worldwide, such as Amazon (∼6,600 km3 /yr), Yangtze (∼800 km3 /yr), Mississippi (∼500 km3 /yr), Mekong (∼500 km3 /yr) and Nile (∼80 km3 /yr) Rivers (Bianchi et al., 2002; Coynel et al., 2005; Le et al., 2007; Meybeck and Ragu, 1996; Moreira-Turcq et al., 2013, 2003; Wang et al., 2012 ). The Yellow River has experienced extensive dam construction (e.g., Sanmenxia (SMX), Wanjiazhai (WJZ), and XLD reservoirs) over the past fifty years (Fig. 1  a-b). The WSRS, implemented by the above three reservoirs, has significantly altered the hydrological regime and OC delivery in the downstream (Lu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2013 ). The WSRS included two phases with specific purposes: the Water-regulation and Sediment-regulation stages (Fig. 1 b). Clear water was released from the XLD reservoir in order to scour the siltation in the lower reaches during the Water-regulation stage. In the Sediment-regulation stage, the flooding water was released from the SMX and WJZ reservoirs to scour the siltation in the XLD reservoir, thus forming an artificial hyperpycnal flow with high suspended sediment concentration (SSC) exported from the XLD reservoir (Wang et al., 2017 ). Approximately 30 % of the annual water discharge and 50 % of the annual sediment load were periodically exported to the sea during the WSRS (Wang et al., 2017 ).  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Sampling and measurement The WSRS in 2020 was conducted in June-August with two stages. The initial Water-regulation stage was conducted from 28 June to 8 July, followed by the Sediment-regulation stage from 9 July to 12 August. In 2020, daily sampling was conducted from 20 June to 12 August in 2020 to cover the entire duration of the WSRS at station LJ, the last gauging station in the river (about ∼ 110 km to the river mouth) (Fig. 1 a). Water samples were filtered on site through pre-weighted and pre-combusted (450℃ for 5 h) glass filters (GF/F, 0.7 μm pore size, Whatman) for POC and DOC analyses. All the samples were stored at temperature of −20℃ prior to further analyses. Water samples were acidified with HCl to pH<2 and then DOC concentrations were determined by a total organic carbon (TOC) analyzer (isoTOCcube, Elementar) (Ming et al., 2023 ). The freeze-dried sediment was removed from the filter and acidified with HCl to remove inorganic carbon and oven-dried at 60℃ for 24 h. Then, the POC contents were determined using a Vario EL Elemental Analyzer (Ran et al., 2013 ). Samples for grain-size analysis were pre-treated with 30 % H2 O2  and 1 mol/L HCl to remove organic matter and carbonates before dispersion and homogenization. Grain size of the suspended sediment was determined using a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000).  3.2 Hydrological records and OC datasets The hydrological datasets of water discharge, sediment load, SSC, and water level were supplied by the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (YRCC). Hydrological records were collected, in daily-monthly-annual timescales along the main-stem of the river, and included the following gauging stations: Toudaoguai (TDG); Longmen (LM); Tongguan (TG); Sanmenxia (SMX); Xiaolangdi (XLD); Huayuankou (HYK); Gaocun (GC); Sunkou (SK); Aishan (AS); Luokou (LK); and Lijin (LJ) (Fig. 1 a). To analyze the impact of dam regulation on organic carbon transport along the river, we compiled datasets of POC and DOC concentrations, measured with simultaneously sampling from historical literatures (Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Liu, 2010; Qiu et al., 2013; Ran et al., 2013; Su, 2005; Sun, 2007; Wang et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2020a; Xue et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 1992, 2013, 2015a–d ). We calculated fluxes of POC and DOC on daily and monthly timescales (Fig. S1 a-d), following the method by Wang et al. (2012) . During the flood season, POC and DOC fluxes are strongly correlated with sediment and water discharge, which are augmented by allochthonous sources (Hu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2013 ). Based on hydrological and OC datasets, we reconstructed OC fluxes during the flood season in 2011–2012, using the relationship between OC and sediment flux (or water discharge) (Fig. S1 a-d). The POC/DOC ratios in the Yellow River showed a significant correlation with SSC during both the flood and non-flood seasons. Therefore, we calculated the riverine POC/DOC ratios on daily, monthly, and annual timescales (Fig. S1 e).   4 Results 4.1 Downstream hydrologic regime and OC transport during the WSRS 4.1.1 Water and sediment export The WSRS in 2020 was implemented from 25 June to 12 August at station XLD. The water discharge at station XLD increased from ∼ 2000 m3 /s before the WSRS to > 4000 m3 /s during the Water-regulation stage. Correspondingly, five days later, the water discharge increased to ∼ 4000 m3 /s at station LJ (Fig. 2  a-b). Although no sediment was released from the XLD reservoir, the SSC maintained at ∼ 10 kg/m3  at station LJ in the Water-regulation stage, due to downstream riverbed erosion. During the following Sediment-regulation stage, the hyperpycnal flow was released from the XLD reservoir and the SSC increased to > 200 kg/m3  and > 20 kg/m3  at stations XLD and LJ, respectively (Fig. 2 a-b). Daily sediment flux at station XLD, during the Sediment-regulation stage (8.4 Mt/d), was nine times higher than the Water-regulation stage (0.9 Mt/d). Total sediment load and water discharge to the sea were 134 Mt and 10 km3  during the WSRS in 2020, accounting for 43 % and 28 % of the annual fluxes, respectively.  4.1.2 DOC and POC export The hydrological regime controlled by the XLD reservoir had a substantial effect on the delivery of organic carbon to the coastal ocean. During the Water-regulation stage, POC concentrations at station LJ remained at ∼ 13 mg/L and DOC concentrations were ∼ 4.8 mg/L (Fig. 2 c). With minimal sediment released from the XLD reservoir at this stage, the primary sources of POC and sediment were erosion from the downstream riverbed, characterized by a coarse grain size (∼28 μm) and a low POC content (∼0.2 %) (Fig. 2 d). In the Sediment-regulation stage, POC concentrations increased to 43 mg/L on average with a maximum > 100 mg/L at station LJ, owing to inputs from dam-released muddy waters (Fig. 2 c). POC content increased to 0.3 % corresponding to fine-grained sediment particles (∼19 μm). DOC concentrations, during the Sediment-regulation stage, decreased by half to 2.5 mg/L on average, in comparison to the Water-regulation stage. During the Water-regulation stage, POC/DOC ratios were ∼ 3 on average and DOC represented 25 % of the total OC, due to a reduction in POC export from the reservoir (Fig. 2 d). In the Sediment-regulation stage, the dam-derived muddy flood waters increased POC/DOC ratios to ∼ 18 on average, with a maximum reaching > 40. Daily DOC fluxes, during the Water-regulation stage, averaged ca. 1.6 kt/d (1 kt = 1 × 103  t) and decreased to ca. 0.5 kt/d during the Sediment-regulation stage. Daily POC flux increased from 4.1 kt/d in the Water-regulation stage to 7.9 kt/d in the Sediment-regulation stage, due to higher sediment fluxes and POC concentrations. Total POC and DOC loads were 310 kt and 35 kt during the WSRS in 2020, respectively.   4.2 Basin-wide hydrologic regime and OC transport modulated by the WSRS 4.2.1 Water and sediment delivery The WSRS in 2012 was a normal (e.g., sufficient water to implement the WSRS in a flood year) Water-Sediment Regulation across multi-reservoirs (Lu et al., 2022 ). The Water-regulation stage was implemented from 20 June to 3 July at station XLD (Figs. S2 a-c). Upstream from the XLD reservoir, daily water fluxes remained < 0.05 km3 /d, which reflected natural conditions for June (Fig. 3  a). In contrast, the XLD reservoir released clear water, for flood prevention, with a flux on average of 0.3 km3 /d. During the Water-regulation stage, erosion of the downstream riverbed resulted in increased sediment loads, that ranged from 4 Mt, at station XLD, to 37 Mt at station LJ. During the Sediment-regulation stage, the SMX reservoir released an artificial flood, with water fluxes > 0.4 km3 /d, which allowed for desilting the XLD reservoir (Fig. 3 a-b and S2a-b). At this stage facilitated by the multi-reservoir regulation, a hyperpycnal flow with SSC>150 kg/m3  was released from the XLD reservoir (Fig. S2 b). The dam-orientated sediment-laden flood was efficiently exported to the downstream, with sediment flux at 8.4 Mt/d on average and maximum over 14 Mt/d (Fig. 3 b). During the Sediment-regulation stage (<6 days), a large quantity of sediment load of 51 Mt was exported from the reservoir, which allowed 28 Mt to be delivered to the sea (Fig. 3 b).  4.2.2 DOC and POC transport During the Water-regulation stage, DOC flux was < 0.2 kt/d at station SMX and increased to > 0.7 kt/d at stations XLD and HYK (Fig. 4   a-c). The POC fluxes, at stations XLD and SMX, remained low (∼2 kt/d) due to minimal sediment export from the reservoirs (Fig. 4  a-b). The dam-released clear water resulted in effective riverbed erosion, thereby increasing POC fluxes to ∼ 4.3 kt/d at station HYK (Fig. 4 c). During the Sediment-regulation stage, DOC flux increased to 1.0 kt/d at station SMX, while DOC flux at station XLD remained at 0.2 kt/d (Fig. 4 a-b). The joint operation of the SMX and XLD reservoirs set off a hyperpycnal flow with extremely high POC concentrations (∼691 mg/L) at station XLD (Fig. S2 a-b). Daily POC flux at station XLD increased to 72 kt/d in 5, July, with mean value at 39 kt/d (Fig. 4 b). Correspondingly, daily POC flux increased to 23 kt/d at station HYK (Fig. 4 c). The WSRS resulted in widely different OC proportions along the mainstream spatially bounded by the XLD reservoir (Fig. S1 f and 4d). During the Water-regulation stage, the XLD and SMX reservoirs retained sediment and POC, while releasing DOC in clear water. POC/DOC ratios at stations XLD and SMX were < 0.3 and DOC was the dominant OC pool at 70 % (Fig. 4 d). Downstream of the reservoir, POC/DOC ratios increased from 4 to 12 along the downstream channel, due to enhanced erosion of the riverbed. During the Sediment-regulation stage, an artificial hyperpycnal flow, with high SSC (150 kg/m3 ), was released from the XLD reservoir (Fig. 4 e). The corresponding POC/DOC ratios increased sharply to 80 in average, with maximum > 200 at station XLD (Fig. 4 d). POC/DOC ratios increased to 37 and 20 at stations HYK and LJ, respectively.   4.3 Seasonal hydrological regime and OC transport under dam regulation 4.3.1 Water and sediment delivery The hydrological year from November 2011 to October 2012 was representative of a flood year with standard dam regulation. The hydrological regime, upstream the SMX and XLD reservoirs, was basically in a naturally seasonal pattern driven by monsoon, with concentrate sediment-water export during the whole flood season (Figs. 5  and S3). During the flood season of 2012, water discharges from stations TDG to SMX exceeded 5 km3  per month, with peak values occurring in September as a result of significant precipitation events (Fig. 5  a and S4). Three months prior to the natural flood peak, the XLD reservoir began to release water artificially downstream in June to avoid possible flooding (Figs. S3 a-f). The water discharge in June increased by 70 % spatially to 6 km3 /month at station XLD, occupying ∼ 15 % of the annual runoff (Fig. 5 a). In the late flood season (August-October), water discharge spatially decreased by ∼ 30 % via the XLD reservoir, due to dam impoundment (Fig. 5 a). During the flood season in 2012, sediment fluxes displayed a sharp increase from 14 Mt/month at station TDG, to 110 Mt/month at station SMX, due to sediment input from the Loess Plateau (Fig. 5 b). The “natural” delivery of sediment, upstream from the XLD reservoir, displayed significant changes compared to that downstream of the XLD reservoir. During the Water-regulation stage in June, artificial clear water was released from the XLD reservoir for downstream desilting and flood prevention (Fig. S3 d-f). Consequently, sediment flux increased to 24 Mt/month at station LJ, three times higher than that at station HYK (Fig. 5 b). During the Sediment-regulation stage in July, the XLD reservoir released hyperpycnal flow with high sediment flux in 2012 (96 Mt/month). In the late flood season, most of sediment (∼80 %) was impounded by the XLD reservoir (Fig. 5 b). In July 2011, during the WSRS, the sediment flux was just 33 Mt/month due to inadequate precipitation and water for dam regulation, making a 66 % decrease compared to July 2012 (Fig. 5 b and S4). Water and sediment distribution over two hydrological years reflected patterns influenced by both anthropogenic and natural forces.  4.3.2 DOC and POC transport During the flood season in 2012, DOC fluxes were 12–15 kt/month on average upstream the XLD reservoir, with peak values in August-September (>17 kt/month) (Fig. 6  a-c). Downstream the XLD reservoir, DOC delivery was largely dam-controlled during the WSRS. Peaks in DOC fluxes occurred in June-July, from station XLD to LJ, approximately three months earlier than that upstream from the XLD reservoir (Fig. 6 d-f). During the Water-regulation stage in June, DOC fluxes increased to ∼ 16 kt/month, at stations XLD and HYK, and increased to 20 kt/month at station LJ in July. During the flood season, the average POC flux at station SMX was > 400 kt/month in July-September (Fig. 6 c). Downstream the XLD reservoir, the POC flux at station XLD displayed a peak value of 364 kt/month in July stimulated by the WSRS (Fig. 6 d). Correspondingly, POC flux rose sharply to 237 kt/month and 168 kt/month at stations HYK and LJ in July, respectively (Fig. 6 e-f). During the late flood season, a large quantity of POC (>290 kt/month) was retained by the XLD reservoir, accounting for ∼ 80 % of upstream input (Fig. 6 d). The fluxes of POC (or DOC) increased during the flood season, driven by the delivery of concentrated water and sediment. These fluxes were highly correlated with sediment (or water) fluxes, with a coefficient of determination R2  > 0.9 (Fig. S1 c-d and 6). In July 2011, the POC and DOC fluxes, at station XLD, were 68 % and 47 % lower than that in 2012, respectively, owing to insufficient precipitation and water discharge (Fig. 6 d and S4). The POC/DOC ratios at station TDG remained at 3 to 5, reflective of typical DOC fractions (e.g., 20–30 %) of the total OC pool (Fig. 6 g). In the middle reaches, the POC/DOC ratios increased sharply to 11 at station TG during the flood season. The relatively “natural” OC delivery in the upper and middle reaches were altered by dam regulation downstream the reservoirs. The SMX and XLD reservoirs impounded sediment with POC and released water with DOC during the non-flood season and were characterized by low SSC<0.5 kg/m3  (Fig. 6 h). Consequently, POC/DOC ratios at stations SMX and XLD were < 0.5, indicating the dominant component of DOC (∼70 %) during the non-flood season. The WSRS in June-July made a key time point for transformation from DOC to POC (Fig. 6 g and S1f). The POC/DOC ratios, at station XLD, increased sharply from 0.4 in June to 36 in July, due to dam-released muddy flood waters (SSC>15 kg/m3 ) (Fig. 6 g-h). The POC/DOC ratios were the highest during the Sediment-regulation stage (>10), and decreased to < 1 during the dam impoundment and Water regulation stage (Fig. S1 f and 6 g).    5 Discussion 5.1 Impact of dam regulation on organic carbon delivery in the reservoir-river continuum The OC delivery displayed a widely different pattern upstream and downstream of the XLD reservoir. Upstream of the XLD reservoir, natural muddy waters were concentrated in the flood season, thereby enhancing the OC export in the middle reaches. Correspondingly, the OC mainly transported in July-September and displayed seasonally “natural” patterns induced by rainfall driven by the East Asian Monsoon (Fig. 6 a-c; Qian and Lee, 2000; He et al., 2017 ). This is the typical seasonal variability of many subtropical rivers in the world (Ming et al., 2023; Duan and Bianchi, 2006 ). Dam regulation, however, has influenced the hydrology and OC delivery, altering their seasonal and decadal variability (Liu et al., 2022; Imtiazy et al., 2023 ). Downstream of the XLD reservoir, the dam-oriented WSRS created an artificial water–sediment discharge in June and July, as opposed to the natural flood season in the middle reaches (Zhang et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2022 ). This artificially induced muddy flood pulse accounted for 56 % of the annual flux of POC and 35 % of DOC to the coastal ocean, occurring three months earlier than the natural peak upstream of the reservoir. During the flood season, the POC and DOC were mainly contributed from allochthonous sources due to severe erosion on the Loess Plateau, indicative of highly correlated relationship between OC fluxes and sediment (or water) fluxes (Fig. 6 and S1a-d ). Phytoplankton production is limited in the flood season, due to light limitation from enhanced turbidity in the muddy flood waters (Hu et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012 ). Consequently, the Chl-a concentrations were low (<2 μg/L) and POC/Chl-a ratios reached as high as ∼ 4000 in the mainstream, reflective of dominant allochthonous sources (Huang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013 ). During the non-flood season, the XLD reservoir impounded sediment with POC, while releasing clear water that contained DOC. Consequently, the dam impoundment resulted in extremely low SSC concentration and POC/DOC ratios (< 0.5), much lower than typical non-flood seasons in the 1980s (Fig. 6; Zhang et al., 1992 ). Thus, the seasonal POC/DOC ratios showed a pattern that was largely controlled by dam regulation (Fig. 6 g). The XLD reservoir was not only a modulator of OC fluxes, but also served as a filter and driver of OC composition. The Yellow River was characterized by old radiocarbon ages of DOC (∼1500 year) and POC (∼4000 year), older than most of large rivers in the world (Marwick et al., 2015; Tao et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2021 ). Owing to soil-derived OC input from the Loess Plateau, the POC and DOC ages displayed a sharp increase upstream of the XLD reservoir (Xue et al., 2017; Qu et al., 2020 ). Downstream of the XLD reservoir, however, the 14 C age of downstream POC was 2400 years younger than that in the middle reaches. This is because the reservoir impounded coarse-grained POC with old radiocarbon age, while releasing fine-grained POC with younger age (Lu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2019b ). Moreover, the decreasing turbidity by dam impoundment has stimulated the phytoplankton production, contributing to younger OC into the downstream (Lyu et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2017 ). As a result, the DOC also showed an increase in Δ14 C, via the XLD reservoir, from −221 ‰ in the middle reaches to −177 ‰ in the downstream, largely due to phytoplankton inputs (Wen et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2017 ). Although phytoplankton production was limited during the flood season, Chl-a concentrations increased to 10 μg/L within the XLD reservoir during the dam impoundment (Huang et al., 2020 ). The construction of reservoirs has resulted in low turbidity in the river water and promoted the contribution of autochthonous OC sources (Lyu et al., 2023 ). As a result, with low turbidity in the non-flood season, OC fluxes were less correlated with sediment/water fluxes (Fig S1 c-d), reflective of higher phytoplankton inputs in the river and reservoirs (Huang et al., 2020; Maavara et al., 2020; Shao et al., 2023 ). In fact, higher phytoplankton inputs in the XLD reservoir has become an important source for POC in the downstream during the Water-regulation stage (Zhang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2023 ). The interface between the reservoir and river played a crucial role in regulating hydrodynamics and organic carbon delivery. However, additional research is required to more accurately define the intricate carbon budgets and cycling in aquatic environments during the Anthropocene.  5.2 Delivery dynamics of organic carbon to the sea: Dam regulation and climate change Based on OC and hydrological datasets, we found that inter-annual OC export during the flood season is regulated by both dam regulation and El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events in the Yellow River. The precipitation and water discharge in the Yellow River are closely teleconnected with climate oscillation and ENSO events (Wang et al., 2006 ). El Niño events can lead to droughts in the Yellow River basin, whereas La Niña events may increase the likelihood of floods (Li et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2018 ), which regulates OC exports from terrestrial to aquatic carbon pools (Qu et al., 2020; Raymond and Saiers, 2010 ). During the flood years (e.g. 2007, 2010, 2020) with the La Niña events, the XLD reservoir regulated sediment-laden water and OC periodically into the coastal ocean (Fig. 7  a-e; Hu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017, 2006 ). The WSRS resulted in effective downstream erosion, indicative of higher seaward sediment flux than that released from the XLD reservoir (Fig. 7d; Bi et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020b ). Although the XLD reservoir has impounded POC at 0.60 Mt/yr, the WSRS has contributed POC flux at 0.56 Mt/yr from riverbed erosion (Lu et al., 2022 ). Thus, the WSRS enhanced OC export and offset low water discharge in years with El Niño events (e.g. 2002, 2006, 2009). In 2002–2014 with the WSRS, the average POC and DOC fluxes were 194 and 10 kt/month in the flood season, respectively (Fig. 7 e). The super El Niño event in 2015–2016 resulted in low precipitation and water discharge and resultant interruption of the WSRS (Fig. 7 a-c; Wang et al., 2006 ). During the flood season in 2015–2017 (without the WSRS), DOC fluxes decreased by 4 times to 3 kt/month, compared to flood years and POC fluxes decreased by one magnitude to only 10 kt/month (Fig. 7 e). The POC/DOC ratio decreased to 4 in 2015–2017, lower than that in 2002–2014 (∼20), due to the termination of the WSRS (Fig. 7 e; Ran et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2020a ). This lowest OC fluxes and POC/DOC ratios were linked with both climate changes and dam regulation (Ran et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2007b, 2017 ). The XLD reservoir unprecedentedly cut off the sediment from the middle reaches in 2015-2016, which resulted in riverine fragmentation (Fig. 7 d; Ministry of Water Resources, 2015 ). Due to dam impoundment in 2015–2017, the seaward annual POC flux decreased by > 90 % to 0.09 Mt/yr, and the DOC flux decreased by > 70 % to 0.03 Mt/yr, one magnitude lower than that in the 1980s (Fig. 8a; Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Wu et al., 2020a; Xue et al., 2017 ). Since 2018, the XLD reservoir restarted the WSRS as “muddy flood releasing”; the WSRS in 2018–2020 was prolonged to over a month in July-August for reservoir desilting (Fig. 2; Kong et al., 2022; Ministry of Water Resources, 2020 ). Consequently, the sediment flux released from the XLD reservoir, was higher than the seaward flux at station LJ in recent years (Fig. 7 d). Combined with the dam regulation, the La Niña event in 2020 enhanced the OC export to the sea, with an OC flux even comparable to that in the 1980s (Figs. 2 and 7 e; Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Zhang et al., 1992 ). Dam regulation has changed OC transport and hydrodynamics in the river, which has further induced alteration of biogeochemical condition in the coastal sea (Wang et al., 2017 ). The variations of long-term nutrient concentration and structures has been triggered by dam regulation in the Yellow River, resulting in nutrient imbalance in the coastal sea (Liu et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2021 ). The concentrations of PO4 -P and SiO3 -Si, in the Bohai Sea, have gradually decreased in the past few decades and nutrient limitation has changed from nitrogen to phosphorus and silicon limitations at present (Wang et al., 2019 ). Under hydrological and biogeochemical impacts by dam regulation, the seasonal distribution of phytoplankton in the Bohai Sea has been significantly altered, with only one peak in spring-summer since 2002, rather than general two peaks in spring and autumn in history (Zhang et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2020 ). This dam orientated hydrological and biogeochemical alteration will further impact the OC sources, fluxes and transport from river to the coastal sea. Dam regulation, teleconnected with ENSO events, has driven the long-term OC delivery and hydrodynamics into a highly dam-modulated pattern, along the Yellow River-coast continuum (Fig. 7 ). Human activities, especially dam operations, have altered the transport and transformation of OC from rivers to the ocean (Regnier et al., 2013; Imtiazy et al., 2023; Bianchi et al., 2024 ). However, there is limited consideration of anthropogenic perturbation in terms of OC fluxes in the carbon budget or model (Regnier et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Kandasamy and Nagender Nath, 2016 ). The traditional river pipeline conceptual model provided an integrate global OC budget, which has been used by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and Global Carbon Project (Climate Change, 2013; Friedlingstein et al., 2022 ). Regnier et al. (2022)  has pointed out this traditional model for OC budget has neglected the anthropogenic perturbation on OC transport and induced uncertainties on the estimation of OC fluxes along the LOAC. Actually, there remain large differences between field and model output datasets for the estimation of OC fluxes and POC/DOC ratios, which led to the problem of “missing terrigenous carbon” in the global cycle (Hedges and Keil, 1995; Hedges et al.,1997; Kandasamy and Nagender Nath, 2016 ). Future empirical and modeling approaches need to account for variations in OC sources, fluxes, and composition caused by human activities. This will help us refine our understanding of the global carbon budget and cycle.  5.3 Dam-orientated organic carbon export in the Yellow River: Regional significance and global perspective Erosion and weathering on the Earth regulate the global carbon cycle, controlling the production of POC and DOC in the river basin (Hilton and West, 2020; Zondervan et al., 2023 ). The riverine POC/DOC ratios, as an indicator of OC proportion and transport, displayed an increasing trend with the increasing sediment yield in major rivers on a global scale (Fig. 8  b; Wu et al., 2007; Ran et al., 2013 ). The low sediment yield can result in low turbidity, thus stimulating the growth of phytoplankton, and the decomposition of POC could provide more DOC into the aquatic system (Bianchi, 2011; Butman et al., 2007 ). As a result, the tropical rivers (e.g. Congo and Murray Rivers) and artic rivers (e.g. Yenisey and Ob Rivers) are characterized by low sediment yields (<100 t/km2 /yr) and resultant low POC/DOC ratios (<1) (Fig. 8 b). In contrast, intense erosion can mobilize deep-soil horizons and that can result in export of more refractory POC to the sea (Hilton et al., 2011; Milliman et al., 2017; Bianchi et al., 2024 ). With sediment yields ranging from 100 to 1000 t/km2 /yr, the POC/DOC ratios in the Yellow, Yangtze, and Ganges-Brahmaputra rivers were 53, 2.9, and 0.8–1.2, respectively. These ratios were higher than the Mississippi River's ratio of 0.6, despite both being in the same latitude region. Actually, the Asian rivers are characterized by high POC/DOC ratios (>1), as > 70 % of terrestrial sediment to the ocean was delivered by Asian rivers in history (Ludwig et al., 1996; Milliman and Meade, 1983 ). However, with > 50,000 mega-dams constructed worldwide, there have been 60 Mt/yr of OC and 2 Gt/yr of sediment currently buried in worldwide reservoirs, especially for Asian rivers (Mendonça et al., 2017; Syvitski et al., 2005 ); this have further changed the original OC delivery and proportion in the global river system (Maavara et al., 2020; Dethier et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022 ). The OC delivery in the Yellow River provides a typical dam-impacted illustration for global rivers. With less anthropogenic impact in the 1980s, the historic POC and DOC fluxes in the Yellow River were averaged at ∼ 5.3 Mt/yr and 0.13 Mt/yr, accounting for 2 % and 1 % of global seaward fluxes, respectively (Fig. 8 a; Zhang et al., 1992; Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Ludwig et al., 1996 ). Although the sediment flux (639 Mt/yr) in the Yellow River, in the 1980s, was comparable to the Amazon River (600–1150 Mt/yr) and Yangtze River (480 Mt/yr), the POC flux was lower than that in the two large rivers (>6 Mt/yr) (Moreira-Turcq et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017 ). The low POC flux in the Yellow River is due to the dilution by mineral particles eroded from the Loess Plateau (Zhang et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2015 ). The historically high sediment yield (∼1,000 t/km2 /yr) in the Yellow River drove POC/DOC ratios maintaining at 53, much higher than the global average (1.4) (Ludwig et al., 1996; Ran et al., 2013 ). The elevated POC/DOC ratios in the Yellow River resemble those found in small mountainous rivers, such as the Lanyang Hsi River. In the Yellow River, this is attributed to erosion on the Loess Plateau, whereas in the latter, it results from storms or earthquakes (Kao et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2022; Milliman et al., 2017 ). Over the past seventy years, the Yellow River has undergone significant anthropogenic perturbations especially for land usage and dam construction (Wang et al., 2007b ). The seaward sediment flux in the Yellow River decreased to 126 Mt/yr in the 2010s, only 20 % of the historic sediment flux in the 1980s (Wang et al., 2007a ). The sediment load, from the Loess Plateau, has decreased from 1.58 Gt/yr in the 1950s to 0.27 Gt/yr in the 2000s, due to Soil Conservation Practices and Grain For Green Project (Wang et al., 2007b, 2016; Fu et al., 2017 ). Moreover, dam impoundment has led to ∼ 30 % of decrease of sediment load in the Yellow River in the past 50 years (Wang et al., 2007b; Peng et al., 2010 ). The POC fluxes in the 2010s in the Yellow River decreased by almost one magnitude to 0.42 Mt/yr than that in the 1980s, comparable to the Lena, Rhone and Nile Rivers at present; while the DOC fluxes displayed a slight decrease to 0.06 Mt/yr (Fig. 8 a-b; Coynel et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2015 ). Driven by the dam regulation, the POC/DOC ratios decreased from 53 in the 1980s to 8 in the 2010s with the WSRS, indicating an increasing proportion of DOC from ∼ 1 % to ∼ 10 % (Cauwet and Mackenzie, 1993; Ran et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 1992 ). Nevertheless, the POC/DOC ratios in the Yellow River are still higher than the most of large rivers, owing to the effective dam-orientated Water-Sediment Regulation (Fig. 8 b; Ludwig et al., 1996; Wu et al., 2007 ). During the drought years (e.g., 2015 and 2017), with the absence of the WSRS, the impoundment by the XLD reservoir led to fragmentation of the river system. Consequently, water discharge and sediment flux in the Yellow River dropped to 11 km3 /yr and 20 Mt/yr, respectively (Ministry of Water Resources, 2015; Ministry of Water Resources, 2017 ). Compared to the 1980s, the POC flux in 2015–2017 dropped by over 90 % to 0.09 Mt/yr, and the DOC flux decreased by more than 70 % to 0.03 Mt/yr (Xue et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020a ). In 2015, as impacted by a super El Niño event, the POC/DOC ratio was only 1.3 − similar to the Nile and Pearl Rivers under dam impoundment (Fig. 8 b). Dam regulation and impoundment have profoundly changed the OC proportion and formed a dominant DOC delivery in the Yellow River (Fig. 6 g and 8). Global rivers have increasingly been fragmented in recent decades due to the continued construction of dams (Bianchi, 2016; Grill et al., 2019, 2015; Mulligan et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). The OC delivery have been significantly altered by damming in global rivers, such as the Mississippi, Amazon, Yangtze, Red, Mekong and Nile Rivers (Ellis et al., 2012; Bianchi et al., 2015; Le et al., 2017; Sadaoui et al., 2018; Hecht et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022; Ming et al., 2023 ). The dam construction in the Mississippi River has led to three-fold reduction of OC export to the Gulf of Mexico (Bianchi et al., 2015 ). Similarly, the OC burial in the Amazon River basin has been estimated to increase by 38 times until 2030, owing to newly constructed ∼ 200 dam reservoirs (Maavara et al., 2017 ). Since the 1950s, the major rivers in East Asia, which were once the primary contributors of sediment and organic carbon to the ocean, have become the most anthropogenically impacted river systems by damming (Wang et al., 2011; Park et al., 2018; Dethier et al., 2022 ). For example, the Three Gorges Dam (TGD) reservoir in the Yangtze River has impounded 2.1/yr Mt of POC and 172 Mt/yr of sediment, accounting for 3 % and 9 % of the global burial fluxes, respectively (Li et al., 2015; He et al., 2020; Lyu et al., 2023; Ming et al., 2023 ). The POC flux in the Red river has decreased by ∼ 50 % in the last fifty years, induced by the dam construction (Le et al., 2017, 2018 ). Over the past few decades of dam construction, the major rivers in China, including the Yangtze, Yellow, Pearl, and Liao rivers, have experienced a gradual decrease in their POC/DOC ratios (Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2022 ). The construction of dam reservoirs has surged during the Anthropocene, significantly altering global hydrological patterns and organic carbon transport (Mendonça et al., 2017; Maavara et al., 2017 ). The Yellow River is now the most impacted river system globally due to human activities, featuring the highest historical levels of sediment and organic carbon exports, though these levels have significantly decreased since the 1950s (Ludwig et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2011; Dethier et al., 2022 ). Due to the extensive river damming, the global sediment flux from rivers to the ocean has decreased from 20 Gt/yr to 7.2 Gt/yr (Dethier et al., 2022; Syvitski et al., 2022 ). Dam impoundment has induced a sharp decrease in sediment and OC export to the coastal sea, thus resulting in sinking deltas and loss of OC burial in the coast (Syvitski et al., 2009 ). Worldwide, these types of changes in hydrological and biogeochemical conditions have altered the global OC delivery in the LOAC (Maavara et al., 2020, 2017; Mendonça et al., 2017 ).   6 Conclusion Based on the hydrological records and OC fluxes on daily-monthly-annual timescales, we illustrated the spatio-temporal OC delivery under dam regulation in the Yellow River. We found that the “naturally” seasonal OC delivery, driven by monsoon upstream of the XLD reservoir, has turned into a highly dam-controlled pattern downstream of the XLD reservoir. The dam-orientated Water-Sediment Regulation enhanced OC export periodically to the sea in June-July downstream of the XLD reservoir, 2–3 months leading to the “natural” OC peak in September upstream of the reservoir. The OC was impounded by the XLD reservoir in the late flood season, rather than delivered in the whole flood season upstream of the XLD reservoir. Dam regulation has redistributed water–sediment and OC export from the Yellow River to the sea, teleconnected by the ENSO events. The Yellow River, with dominant POC export over DOC in the history, has lost the feature of high POC/DOC ratios in the past thirty years, driven by dam regulation and climate change. The redistributed pattern of the hydrological regime, via dam regulation, will further impact the delivery and transformation of OC from the Yellow River to marginal seas. The evolution of OC delivery in the Yellow River provides an emblematic case for global rivers under dam construction.
1 Introduction Stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen have been widely used for tracing plant water (Barbeta and Peñuelas 2017; Brooks et al., 2010; Dawson and Ehleringer 1991; Sprenger et al., 2018 ), including the origin, spatial source, and age of transpiration (Evaristo et al., 2019; Mennekes et al., 2021; Nehemy et al., 2022b ). Traditionally, this tracing approach involves sampling and extracting water from plants. The most sampled plant tissue for source investigation is the xylem – the vascular tissue that conducts water from roots to leaves (Brooks et al., 2010; Brunel et al., 1995; Zhao et al., 2024 ). Xylem water can be sampled in roots, stems, branches, and leaves (Benettin et al., 2021; Peters and Yakir 2008; Song and Barbour 2016; Vega-Grau et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2016 ), and other tissues (e.g., the phloem) are also sampled for water dynamics of the entire plants (Nehemy et al., 2022a; Treydte et al., 2021 ). Although in situ sampling of xylem water is possible and provides data in higher temporal resolution (Kühnhammer et al., 2022; Marshall et al., 2020; Volkmann et al., 2016 ), there are still significant limitations with it being widely applied across sites (e.g., access to power at the site, high cost of dedicated field-based laser spectroscopy analyzer) and plant growth forms (i.e., it is limited to mature plants and straight branches) (Duvert et al., 2024 ). Therefore, the traditional destructive sampling methods are still the most widely used. In these approaches, the collected plant materials are stored in vials in the field, and then water is extracted subsequently from the samples in laboratory. Several techniques are available to extract water from vascular tissue in the laboratory, such as cryogenic vacuum distillation (CVD) (Koeniger et al., 2011; Orlowski et al., 2013 ), azeotropic distillation (Revesz and Woods 1990 ), centrifugation (Bowers et al., 2020; Edmunds and Bath 1976 ), centrifugation using Cavitron (Barbeta et al., 2022 ), and high-pressure mechanical squeezing (Mazurek et al., 2015 ). All of these techniques were developed for soil pore water extraction and then adapted to plant water extraction, except the Cavitron method (Barbeta et al., 2022 ), which is specifically tailored to plant tissue. As for soils, most studies still use the CVD extraction method to extract water from plants, given the ability to collect and store samples for later analysis, which enables research in remote field sites. Several protocols are reported in the literature for CVD extraction method (e.g., Table S1 ) but still without a clear, unified approach (Millar et al., 2022 ). The early study by Araguás-Araguás et al. (1995)  investigating CVD extraction of soil under distinct extraction times and temperatures showed that different protocols yielded accurate isotope results for sandy soils when more than 98 % of water was extracted but not for soils with higher clay content. They recommended clayey soil extraction approach to be tailored to the research question. Later, West et al. (2006)  investigated CVD extraction time protocols for soil and plant samples using the same temperature (boiling water; ∼100 °C) and showed that the isotopic value of extracted water increased with extraction time until reaching a certain threshold depending on the investigated material. Following Araguás-Araguás et al. (1995) , an extraction efficiency of 98 % has been used as a standard threshold during the cryogenic extraction of plant samples, which means that 98 % of the water in the sample (bulk xylem water) is extracted, assuming that no fractionation is introduced during the extraction process. We simply do not know if these sorts of findings now made for soil and their CVD extraction applies to plants in terms of its impact on the isotopic results for xylem water following different CVD protocols (i.e., extraction temperature and time, Table S1 ). The CVD method for plant water extractions has indeed been questioned recently regarding the possible bias it introduces to the observed plant water isotopic composition (Chen et al., 2020 ), and correction protocols have been discussed (Allen and Kirchner 2022; He et al., 2023 ). Additionally, while cryogenic techniques aim for higher extraction efficiency, it is possible that the bulk water in the xylem may not represent the water actively moving within conduits and contributing to transpiration. In contrast, other techniques, such as centrifugation and Cavitron, do not prioritize high extraction efficiency; rather, they specifically target the more mobile water within xylem (Barbeta et al., 2022; Duvert et al., 2024; He et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2023 ). Theoretically, the Cavitron approach is thought to extract water that would participate in the transpiration stream by applying a centrifugation force equivalent to –2 MPa to –6 MPa, without extracting potentially intracellular water like the CVD method. The applicability of Cavitron to extract water for plant water source analysis has been shown experimentally in controlled conditions (Barbeta et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2023 ) and in the field (Duvert et al., 2024; He et al., 2023 ). Barbeta et al. (2022)  showed that isotopic values of Cavitron-xylem water were similar to labeled water used in pot irrigation experiments. Wen et al. (2022)  demonstrated that Cavitron-xylem water closely matched the water used to rehydrate wood stems. Duvert et al. (2024)  and He et al. (2023)  showed Cavitron-xylem water was located on the source water line. While confirming the applicability of Cavitron, they also pointed out that CVD-xylem water was more depleted in deuterium compared to the reference water (source water). However, no studies that we are aware of have compared the different CVD extraction protocols and Cavitron methods aimed at determining whether their performance differs due to different CVD protocols. Here, we investigate the isotopic signature of xylem water using various CVD protocols to determine the effect of the CVD extraction protocol on the comparison with the Cavitron method. The specific research questions were thus: i) what is the effect of CVD extraction protocol (in terms of extraction temperature, time, and efficiency) on plant water isotopic values? and ii) how do the results obtained from the Cavitron method compare to those waters extracted via CVD, considering varying extraction protocols?  2 Material and methods 2.1 Site description The field sampling was conducted in Changwu Tableland, located in the southeastern part of the Chinese Loess Plateau. The site has an elevation of 1200 m above mean sea level and a continental monsoon climate. The mean temperature of the site is 9.4 °C, with annual precipitation of 585 mm, and potential evapotranspiration of 897 mm per year. Approximately 53 % of the annual precipitation occurs between July and September. Grasslands and steppe forests dominated the Loess Plateau during the Holocene periods (Shang and Li 2010 ). However, intensive farming during the last 2000 years severely depleted grasslands and forests (Wang et al., 2006 ). To tackle the ecosystem degradation issue, the “Grain to Green” program was implemented by the Government of China in 1999, and apple orchards became the predominant land use type in this region. We selected a healthy apple tree in a 21-year-old apple orchard, planted in 2001, to conduct our experiment. The tree was 3.2 m tall and 23.4 cm in diameter at 130 cm height.  2.2 Sampling We commenced the experiment by collecting soil samples at a distance of 1.5 m from the tree stem on July 29th, 2022. The soil sampling was conducted using a hollow-stem hand auger with increments of 20 cm to a depth of 10 m. Upon approaching the desired depth, we immediately sampled the soil by filling three-quarters of each 12 mL glass vial (737 W, Labco Ltd., UK). Following the initial background sampling, we irrigated the apple tree daily at evening until August 6th, 2022, totaling an amount equivalent of 160 mm. Irrigation was provided using tap water (–11.04 ‰ for δ18 O and –78.40 ‰ for δ2 H, originally pumped from groundwater), and a drip irrigation system was placed around the stem of the apple tree. During the experiment, one 9 mm precipitation event occurred on August 3, 2022 with isotopic values of −4.67 ‰ and −27.17 ‰ for δ18 O and δ2 H, respectively. On August 7th, 2022, we repeated collection procedures for soil samples following the identical protocol mentioned above and we collected branch samples from the south-facing side of the selected tree after sunset at about 7 pm to prevent potential evaporation during sampling processes. We collected straight branches that were ∼ 1 cm in diameter and longer than 28 cm. The branches used for cryogenic extraction were quickly processed in the field by removing the inner barks, cutting the xylem into small pieces, and placing them into 12 mL glass vials (737 W, Labco Ltd., UK; n = 10 per protocol). We also collected an additional set of 10 branches adjacent to the sampled branch for Cavitron analysis (referred to as Cavitron samples hereafter), which were wrapped with parafilm and stored in a cooler with ice packs following the procedures of He et al. (2023)  and Wen et al. (2022) . Subsequently, the Cavitron samples were transported to the laboratory where water was extracted within 24 h. The vials with samples were securely sealed with parafilm before being stored in a cooler with ice packs in the field and transferred to a refrigerator at 4 °C in laboratory on the same day.  2.3 Laboratory analysis We used a capillary and vial-style CVD extraction system (Koeniger et al., 2011 ) to extract xylem and soil water. Briefly, the sample vials were frozen using liquid nitrogen and then connected to another empty vial (collection vial) through a capillary tubing, depressurized to less than 0.01 mbar, and then heated at a predetermined temperature for a specific duration time. Within this closed system, the water evaporated from the sample vials and condensed into collection vials. The extracted water was transferred into a sealed 2 mL screw glass vial using a cap and parafilm for storage. The extracted sample vials were oven-dried at 105 °C for 24 h to assess extraction efficiencies. Fifteen distinct CVD protocols (Table 1  ), with 10 replications per treatment, were used to extract the plant samples. For soil samples, we used 200 °C and 30 min for the CVD extraction. We used a Cavitron (H2100R; Xiang Yi Lab Instr. Co., Ltd.) for water extraction. In the laboratory, we trimmed the branches to 27.4 cm by removing small portions from both ends. Then, we peeled off the bark from around 4.5 cm on both ends, inserted the bark-free ends into cuvettes, and wrapped the cuvettes and branches with parafilm. Subsequently, we set the rotation speed in the Cavitron to 7636 rpm, which is equivalent to a centrifugal force of −6 MPa (Alder et al., 1997; Cochard 2002; Du et al., 2019 ), set the temperature to 10 °C, and used a rotation time of 2 min to collect enough water (Duvert et al., 2024; He et al., 2023 ). On average, 0.4 g water was obtained via Cavitron. The extracted water was collected into two cuvettes and immediately transferred to a 2 mL screw-capped glass vial for isotopic analysis.  2.4 Extraction efficiency For the CVD method, we weighed empty sample vials, sample vials with samples, and collection vials both before and after xylem water extraction. The sample vials were weighed again after oven-drying the extracted samples. The weight difference between a collection vial before and after water extraction represents the amount of water actually collected. The weight difference between the sample vial pre- and post-extractions indicates the amount of water extracted from the sample (i.e., sample-extracted water). The difference in weights between a sample at pre-extraction and post-oven-drying reflects the total water present in the sample. Typically, extraction efficiency is calculated by dividing the sample-extracted water by the total water. However, we calculated extraction efficiency by dividing the collected water by the total water. This approach provides a more realistic measure termed ‘total extraction efficiency’ hereafter.  2.5 Isotope measurements and data analysis Plant-water samples were analyzed using a mass spectrometer (253 Plus; Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Bremen, Germany) attached to an elemental analyzer (EA Isolink; Thermo Fisher Scientif Inc.) at Ludong University, China. Soil-water, irrigation, and precipitation water samples were measured using a laser spectrometer (IWA-45EP; Los Gatos Research, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA) at Northwest A & F University, China. The measured isotopic values of hydrogen and oxygen were normalized to the Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water and Standard Light Antarctic Precipitation (VSMOW-SLAP) scale via the co-measured standards. The isotopic compositions were expressed in per mil (Equation (1) .(1) δ 2 H o r 18 O   = R sample   R standard    - 1   × 1000 ‰      where Rsample  and Rstandard  denote the ratio of number of heavy isotopes to that of the light isotopes in the sample water and standard water, respectively. To compare the difference of Cavitron-xylem water and CVD-xylem water to the source water, following previous approaches that compare Cavitron and CVD, we calculated the deuterium offset, Equation (2) , based on the soil water line (De la Casa et al., 2022; Duvert et al., 2024 ).(2) δ  2  H offset   = δ  2  H Cavitron - o r C V D - x y l e m w a t e r   - a δ  18  O Cavitron - o r C V D - x y l e m w a t e r   + b        where a and b are the slope and intercept of the soil water line, respectively. We used the Kruskal-Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952 ) and post hoc Dunn’s test (Dunn 1964 ) to assess statistical differences in isotopic composition among different CVD extraction protocols and to compare the deuterium offset of Cavitron-xylem water and CVD-xylem water with zero, the offset to the soil water line. Non-parametric statistical tests were used due to the non-normal distribution of the isotope data. The normalities were evaluated with the quantile–quantile plots, histograms, and Shapiro–Wilk test. We then compared the cryogenic isotope results with those obtained from Cavitron-xylem water. We calculated the relative water content of stem samples by dividing the total amount of water by the weight of wet material, which is the difference in weights between the empty sample vial and the pre-extraction sample-filled vial. We used the relative water content and total water amount to address isotopic bias caused by CVD that was reported by Chen et al. (2020)  due to H-exchange with cellular during the extraction and by Diao et al. (2022)  due to the water amount issue for the extraction.   3 Results 3.1 Comparison of cryogenic extraction across different protocols Generally, when comparing extraction approaches under the same temperature, we found that longer extraction time produced more positive isotopic values (Fig. 1  ). When comparing extraction approaches under the same extraction time, higher temperatures produced more positive isotopic values (Fig. 1 ). At 100 °C, the isotopic values became fairly stable when extraction time was longer than 60 min, implying that there was no isotopic difference between xylem waters for CVD-100–60 (approach-temperature–time), CVD-100–120, and CVD-100–240 (p > 0.05). At 140 °C, the isotopic values of xylem water became fairly stable when extraction time was longer than 30 min, implying that there was no isotopic difference between xylem water for CVD-140–30, CVD-140–60, CVD-140–120, and CVD-140–240 (p > 0.05). Xylem water δ2 H and δ18 O extracted at CVD-200–30 showed no difference with those extracted at 100 °C with extraction time longer than 60 min (Figure S1 ) and those extracted at 140 °C with extraction time longer than 30 min (p > 0.05). Generally, the isotope values of xylem water extracted under shorter extraction time protocols (e.g., CVD-100–30, CVD-140–15, and CVD-200–15) were not noticeably different from xylem water extracted at 60 °C (p > 0.05). Conversely, the isotope values of xylem water extracted at temperature ≥ 60 °C with shorter extraction times (i.e., CVD-100–30, CVD-140–15, and CVD-200–15) were significantly different from those extracted at higher temperatures with longer extraction times (p < 0.05). However, a few samples did not follow this general pattern; for example, δ2 H of xylem water extracted at CVD-200–15 showed a significant difference from that extracted at CVD-60–60 (p < 0.05) but no difference from the other protocols (p > 0.05). Additionally, δ2 H of xylem water extracted at CVD-140–15 showed no difference from that extracted at CVD-100–240 (p > 0.05).  3.2 Xylem water signature as influenced by CVD extraction temperature and extraction efficiency Total extraction efficiency varied across the methods compared (Fig. 1 c); higher temperatures and longer extraction times provide higher total extraction efficiency. Generally, the higher the temperature, the lower the extraction time needed to reach the total extraction efficiency above 98 %. For 60 °C extraction temperature, extraction efficiency was below 98 % at all extraction times investigated. For 100 °C extraction temperature, total extraction efficiency was also below 98 % for extraction time of 30 min, while for 60 min extraction time, total extraction efficiency showed some variability. Extraction times longer than 60 min at 100 °C extraction temperature resulted in total extraction efficiency ≥ 98 %. For 140 °C extraction temperature, total extraction efficiency was below 98 % for 15 min extraction time, fluctuated close to 98 % for 30 min extraction time, and exceeded 98 % for 60 min or longer extraction time. For 200 °C extraction temperature, the extraction efficiency was below 98 % for 15 min extraction time but was above 98 % for longer extraction times (Fig. 1 c). Xylem water δ18 O and δ2 H values were more positive when total extraction efficiency exceeded 98 % compared to lower than 98 % (Fig. 2  ). Xylem water δ18 O ranged from –103.9 ‰ to –50.3 ‰, and δ2 H ranged from –13.8 ‰ to –7.4 ‰ with < 98 % total extraction efficiency. Total extraction efficiency > 98 % yielded xylem water isotopes ranging from –70.3 ‰ to –55.5 ‰ for δ2 H and from –9.1 ‰ to –6.9 ‰ for δ18 O. With total extraction efficiency exceeding 98 %, longer extraction time did not yield an isotopic difference compared to shorter times at the same temperature (Fig. 3  ). However, after combining the data from different extraction times at the same temperature, we found that low extraction temperatures were significantly more depleted in deuterium (p < 0.05) than those resulting at higher extraction temperatures with a mean δ2 H value of –64.4 ‰, −62.7 ‰, and –59.3 ‰ for 100 °C, 140 °C, and 200 °C, respectively (Fig. 4  ). Nevertheless, this trend was not observed for δ18 O with a mean value of −8.1 ‰, −8.2 ‰, and −7.9 ‰ for 100 °C, 140 °C, and 200 °C, respectively. There was a significant linear relationship between δ2 H of CVD-extracted water and total extraction efficiency at each extraction temperature (p < 0.01) (Fig. 5  ). The slope of the regression line decreased with the increase in extraction temperature and was 0.57, 0.53, 0.51, and 0.37 for 60 °C, 100 °C, 140 °C, and 200 °C extraction temperature, respectively. In contrast, the intercept of the regression line increased with increasing extraction temperature; the intercept was −126.87, –116.90. –113.01, and –97.38 for 60 °C, 100 °C, 140 °C, and 200 °C extraction temperature, respectively. δ18 O of CVD-extracted water exhibited a similar pattern with δ2 H.  3.3 Comparison between Cavitron-xylem water and CVD-xylem water The total amount of CVD-extracted xylem water sample varied from 1.15 g to 2.67 g, with an average of 1.99 g. The relative water content of CVD-xylem sample varied from 44.8 % to 62.3 %, averaging 51.7 %. The total amount of xylem water obtained with Cavitron was 0.4 g. On average, Cavitron-xylem water was more depleted in heavy isotopes when compared to CVD-xylem water, with total extraction efficiency > 98 % (Fig. 1 ). Cavitron overlapped with xylem water extracted by CVD with extraction efficiency < 98 %. Cavitron-xylem δ2 H and δ18 O were statistically distinct from CVD-xylem water extracted (Fig. 1 ) at 100 °C with extraction time > 60 min, and also from 140 °C and 200 °C extraction temperatures with extraction time > 15 min (p < 0.05); but Cavitron-xylem water was statistically similar to CVD-xylem water extracted at 60 °C for all extraction times, 100 °C for 30 min extraction time, 140 °C for 15 min extraction time, and 200 °C for 15 min extraction time. In dual-isotope space, the mean Cavitron-xylem water plotted below the LMWL, soil water line, and CVD-xylem water (Fig. 2 ); although, some cavitron samples plotted within the soil water distribution. Furthermore, mean Cavitron-xylem water showed significant differences from the source water (Fig. 6  ), i.e., the offset from the soil water line was significantly different from zero (p < 0.05), with the extraction efficiency above 98 %, the isotopic values of CVD-xylem water were closer to that of source water with the increasing extraction temperatures and showed no difference from the source water at 200 °C (p > 0.05).   4 Discussion 4.1 Influence of CVD protocols on xylem water isotopic composition Our results revealed that isotope values of CVD-xylem water obtained by using protocols that provided high extraction efficiency (>98 %) were statistically higher than those that provided low extraction efficiency (<98 %) (p < 0.05). At the same temperature, longer extraction time yielded more positive isotopic values with increasing extraction efficiency. Once extraction efficiency reached 98 %, there was no isotopic difference with longer extraction times (p > 0.05). With extraction efficiency > 98 %, lower extraction temperature resulted in deuterium depletion when compared to higher temperature protocols (p < 0.05), but not for δ18 O. Thus, studies using different extraction temperatures and times in CVD (e.g., Table S1 ) are comparable for δ18 O when extraction efficiency is > 98 %. But studies that use lower extraction temperatures (e.g., the “glass and manifold CVD system” and its derivatives) might show generally lower δ2 H values. Note that not all studies in the literature report extraction efficiency. In some studies, extracted samples were pre- and post-extraction weighted, but the adopted extraction efficiency was not always reported. Our observations for xylem water are similar to what Araguás-Araguás et al. (1995)  first reported for sandy soils, where extraction efficiency < 98 % resulted in extracted water more depleted in heavy isotopes, and those were statistically different from water obtained with extraction efficiency > 98 %. This result indicates that xylem water extraction follows the Rayleigh distillation process (Gat 1996 ), where the extracted water is depleted in heavy isotopes compared to the remaining bulk water, and the isotopic difference between extracted water and bulk water decreases with the increasing percentage of extracted water (with increasing extraction efficiency). During Rayleigh distillation process, another key factor is temperature, which controls isotopic fractionation (Gat 1996 ). We also observed temperature differences in the slopes and intercepts of regression lines between extraction efficiency and isotopic composition. Higher temperatures produced a smaller isotopic difference of extracted water from bulk water. Therefore, under the same extraction efficiency, lower temperature yielded higher depletion in heavy isotopes than higher temperature extraction protocols. During the cryogenic extraction of xylem samples, an additional process takes place beyond Rayleigh distillation that could explain the isotopic observations, i.e., deuterium depletion with lower temperatures compared to higher temperatures with extraction efficiency > 98 %. In xylem tissues, there is a large quantity of exchangeable hydrogen on the hydroxyl groups of wood cellulose and hemicellulose (Feng et al., 1993; Pettersen, 1984 ), which can rapidly exchange with xylem water during extraction (Frilette et al., 1948 ). During the extraction, water with lighter isotopes preferentially evaporates from the sample, and water with heavier isotopes stays behind in the sample. The exchangeable hydrogen actively equilibrates with water remaining in the xylem. Therefore, at the end of extraction, xylem tissues contain more heavy hydrogen compared to pre-extraction xylem tissues. According to isotope mass balance, the extracted xylem water would be more depleted in deuterium than the “real” xylem water. The heavy isotope depletion effect can be reduced by increasing the extraction temperature (Younger et al., 2024 ). With higher extraction temperature, the isotopic difference between evaporated water and remaining water becomes smaller (Horita and Wesolowski 1994 ) and eventually decreasing the isotopic difference between xylem tissue and extracted xylem water. Higher temperature led to an enrichment of heavy isotopes in extracted water from clayey soils (Araguás-Araguás et al., 1995 ) and wheat samples (Millar et al., 2018 ). Higher temperature extraction may co-extract volatile organic compounds from plant samples (West et al., 2010 ), which affects the subsequent isotopic analysis, especially for isotope ratio infrared spectrometry (Brand et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2021; Martín-Gómez et al., 2015 ). However, in our study, isotope ratio mass spectrometry was employed. The possibility of organic contamination producing the positive isotopic values for higher temperatures is small. Generally, it is believed that oxygen on hydroxyl sites in xylem tissue does not exchange with oxygen in water (Cohn and Urey 1938 ), which our results support as there was no δ18 O difference among various extraction temperatures with extraction efficiency > 98 %. Recently, several studies reported deuterium depletion in xylem water caused by CVD extraction (Chen et al., 2020; Wen et al., 2022 ) and acknowledged the water amount issue during CVD extraction (Diao et al., 2022 ). For the water amount issue, the xylem water amount in our study was always above 1.15 mL, which is higher than the threshold of 0.6 mL indicated by Diao et al. (2022) . Therefore, our results were not affected by the water amount issue. Moreover, the studies reporting a deuterium depletion employed CVD systems using low extraction temperatures, ranging from 60 °C to 105 °C (Chen et al., 2020; Barbeta et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2023; He et al., 2023 ). Based on our data, the deuterium depletion caused by CVD may be due to employing lower temperature protocols. Employing higher temperatures for CVD could decrease the δ2 H bias and make the δ2 H within acceptable ranges. Recent research showed that δ2 H bias can be eliminated by increasing CVD temperature to values near 170 °C and potentially completely eliminated when increasing it to 229 °C (Younger et al., 2024 ).  4.2 CVD-xylem water differs from Cavitron-xylem water Cavitron has been proposed as an alternative to using CVD systems when extracting plant water for water source investigations (Barbeta et al., 2022; He et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2023 ). While we do not disagree that Cavitron is a useful approach, the reality is that many studies might still continue to use CVD given its accessibility. And perhaps with some adjustment, CVD could indeed be used effectively going forward with revised protocols for extraction. Our data showed that Cavitron-xylem water was more depleted in heavy isotopes than CVD-xylem water with > 98 % total extraction efficiency. But, Cavitron-xylem water was statistically similar to all CVD-xylem water with < 98 % total extraction efficiency. Cavitron-xylem water showed similar δ2 H values to CVD that followed 60 °C for 240 min and 100 °C for 30 min protocols. CVD-xylem water was slightly more depleted in deuterium than Cavitron-xylem water in two scenarios only, with extraction temperature of 60 °C and extraction time of 60 min and 120 min. Compared with Cavitron-xylem water, the CVD-xylem water extracted at 200 °C with extraction efficiency > 98 % was closer to the source water (i.e., soil water line). Our results differ from all previous Cavitron studies, i.e., Barbeta et al. (2022), Duvert et al. (2024), Wen et al. (2023) , and He et al. (2023) . Their studies showed CVD-xylem water was more depleted in deuterium than Cavitron-xylem water. While their Cavitron system and its applied protocol are similar to our studies, their reported CVD protocols used lower extraction temperatures. Their employed protocols were: 80 °C for 150 min, 100 °C for 90 min, 100 °C for 120 min, and 105 °C for 180 min for Barbeta et al. (2022), Duvert et al. (2024), Wen et al. (2023) , and He et al. (2023) , respectively. Barbeta et al. (2022)  and Duvert et al. (2024)  used a cryogenic system described by Orlowski et al. (2013) , while other investigators have used the capillary and vial system of Koeniger et al. (2011) . Barbeta et al. (2022)  and Duvert et al. (2024)  did not report extraction efficiency, but Wen et al. (2023)  and He et al. (2023)  used 98 % extraction efficiency. As their reported δ18 O was similar between Cavitron-xylem water and CVD-xylem water, we speculate that the deuterium depletion was not caused by lower extraction efficiency but by the lower temperature used by the earlier studies. Moreover, in our study, Cavitron-xylem water was not only different from CVD-xylem water in δ2 H but also in δ18 O. In dual-isotope space, our Cavitron-xylem water was located below the CVD-xylem water with total extraction efficiency above 98 %. Cavitron and CVD exhibit notable differences in their water extraction approach. Because of the methodological design employed during Cavitron, both the outer and inner bark are maintained in the branch sample (Barbeta et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2023 ) to avoid evaporation during centrifugation. There is potential extraction of water from elastic tissues, such as the phloem. This phenomenon can be understood through two distinct mechanisms. First, the xylem and inner bark are radially connected through parenchyma rays and during extraction when negative pressure is applied through centrifugation, phloem water can be released into the xylem, mimicking the transpiration process with the release of water of elastic storage at lower xylem water potentials (Du et al., 2019; Pfautsch et al., 2015; Venturas et al., 2017 ) as the potentials become extremely low (–6 MPa) during Cavitron centrifugation. Second, the phloem is exposed on the ends of the branch with the transversal cut and water can be easily extracted along with xylem water since the sieve cells are exposed. Recent studies have shown that phloem water can be significantly more depleted in deuterium than xylem water (Nehemy et al., 2022a; Treydte et al., 2021 ), but not always (Nehemy et al., 2022a ). Our offset of Cavitron-xylem water from the source water (i.e., soil water line) is at odds with the published Cavitron-related papers, i.e., Barbeta et al. (2022), Duvert et al. (2024), Wen et al. (2022), Wen et al. (2023) , and He et al. (2023) . There are a few reasons that could explain this. One reason could be the definition of the true source, such as irrigation water signatures or bulk soil water lines used in previous studies. While we heavily irrigated the tree and sampled xylem water after estimating its travel time, xylem signatures did not reflect this new source. Thus, we used the bulk soil water line as others (De la Casa et al., 2022; Duvert et al., 2024; He et al., 2023 ). However, this soil water line isotopic signatures can also be impacted by its own extraction protocols (e.g., temperature). Another possibility is the time of sampling that might impact xylem water isotopic signatures. He et al. (2023)  did their experiments on the same field site as us, and we followed the same operational procedures. The main difference is the sampling time, i.e., after sunset in our study, and in the afternoon for He et al (2023) . Sampling the branches after sunset reduced the risk of evaporation during the highly evaporative time of day; however, in the evening, the reduced transpiration rates and trees refilling of internal water storages could have influenced xylem water isotopic composition due to the potential internal fractionation process during phloem refilling (Nehemy et al., 2022a ). The difference could also be a result of other physiological processes linked to bark conductance that might lead to evaporative enrichment depending on the conditions (i.e. relative humidity and temperature) related to the time of the day sampled. We acknowledge that there might be other reasons for these differences as well. Clearly, more research is needed to tease out these potential effects.
