In total, the δ2 H discrepancy when comparing CVD and Cavitron-xylem water observed in this study and others (Barbeta et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2023; He et al., 2023 ) might be due to an effect of lower extraction temperature used in CVD in previous studies and, the potential influence of phloem water during the extraction that could be more depleted (Nehemy et al., 2022a; Treydte et al., 2021 ) or more enriched (Cernusak et al., 2005 ) in heavy isotopes than xylem water, and the different sampling times that might influence other physiological processes. We understand that some laboratories are currently updating the Cavitron protocol to decrease the extension of the bark and phloem covering the branch prior to extraction and several papers are being prepared. However, the results reported in the literature still reflect the previous practice of using the branch with bark and phloem. Clearly, an updated Cavitron protocol with sampling time, comparison between with and without the bark and phloem, and supporting data  is urgently needed. Further investigation is also needed to understand this across different species and wetness conditions.  4.3 Limitations and future research We acknowledge that our results are limited to only one species and single sampling period, but the investigation of the use of distinct CVD protocols and comparison with different methods like Cavitron is crucial given the varieties of protocols present in the literature and the urgent need for standardization (Millar et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, xylem water from other plant species should be tested using CVD protocols and Cavitron systems, especially those growing in environments where the deuterium fractionation is known to occur (Ellsworth and Williams 2007; Lin et al., 1993; Poca et al., 2019 ), such as xerophytes and halophytes. Future research should also compare the same species under distinct soil texture, water content, and salt stress conditions.   5 Conclusion Cryogenic vacuum distillation (CVD) was used to extract plant water under different extraction protocols (i.e., temperature and time) to determine these effects on stable isotope values of the extracted water. The isotopic compositions of CVD-xylem water were intercompared and compared with Cavitron-xylem water. Our results showed that Cavitron-xylem water was close to CVD-xylem water with total extraction efficiency below 98 % but was more depleted in heavy isotopes than CVD-xylem water with total extraction efficiency above 98 %. With total extraction efficiency above 98 %, isotopic compositions of CVD-xylem water extracted using different protocols are similar but higher extraction temperatures yielded more positive δ2 H. Cross-comparisons of the Cavitron- and CVD-xylem water at different temperatures for more plant organs, tree species, and water-stress conditions are strongly suggested for future research to determine the robustness of CVD extractions for plant water in future studies.

1 Introduction With the ongoing urbanization process, disaster prevention has become an essential concern, especially for coastal cities where floods pose a serious threat (Hallegatte et al., 2013; Muis et al., 2016 ). In August 2017, Typhoon Hato caused severe floods and storm surges in Macao and Hong Kong, which caused severe damage and huge losses to Macao (Takagi et al., 2018 ). The situation can even be aggravated by the combined effects of climate change, urbanization, and insufficient stormwater drainage systems (Fang et al., 2021; Collins et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2022 ). Therefore, real-time prediction and early warning of the flooding hazards in urban areas are particularly crucial for mitigating flood risks and enhancing urban public safety (Aerts et al., 2014; Krajewski et al., 2017; Piadeh et al., 2022 ). Obtaining sufficient measurements is a challenge for developing effective flood prediction and mitigation strategies, as limited monitoring equipment and potential malfunctions during floods further constrain data availability. Physics-based models like SWMM (Rossman et al., 2004 ), LISFLOOD-FP (Bates and De Roo, 2000 ), and MIKE (Danish Hydraulic Institute, 2017 ) are widely used to simulate urban floods. However, their extensive computational demands hinder real-time forecasting applications (Bermúdez et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, densely populated urban areas require flood prediction results with high accuracy and fast computation speed. Hence, a resolution of less than 5 m is needed to consider the impact of buildings and to capture flood processes in urban areas further (Xing et al., 2018 ), which is a considerable computational burden. To address the computational demand associated with physics-based models in simulating urban floods, studies have been carried out to enhance computational efficiency, such as GPU-based acceleration (e.g., Liang et al., 2015; Xia and Liang, 2016; Xia et al., 2019, Su et al., 2022 ) and simplified models (e.g., Guidolin et al., 2016, Cao et al., 2020 ). Alongside these advancements, surrogate models incorporating techniques such as machine learning have gained increasing attention (Bentivoglio et al., 2022; Fraehr et al., 2022 ; Li and Willems, 2020 ). Surrogate models leverage machine learning methods to reproduce the output of the physics-based model without simulating the underlying physical processes (Seleem et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2022 ), which greatly shortens simulation time. Machine learning models have advantages, such as diverse and flexible forms, high computational efficiency, and straightforward implementation. According to previous studies (Contreras et al., 2020; Jhong et al., 2017; Kabir et al., 2020; Löwe et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2023 ), the machine learning-based surrogate models have been proven successful in predicting pluvial or fluvial flood events. Nevertheless, the current use of machine learning surrogate models is still limited in predicting high-resolution floods in coastal cities that are frequently affected by storm tides and rainfall compound events (Zahura and Goodall, 2022 ). The combined effects of storm surge and rainfall increase the flood risks in low-lying coastal areas (Hsiao et al., 2021 ). Therefore, it is crucial to consider both factors when developing flood prediction models for coastal cities. In addition, the drainage system also plays an essential role in flood processes for highly urbanized cities (Ogie et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2022 ). However, existing studies on flood prediction using surrogate models often consider only the static indicators, such as drainage network density, and therefore fail to capture the dynamic drainage flow processes. The outlet discharge of drainage network system (drainage outflow) is an important factor that not only indicates the discharge rate of urban waterlogging but also reflects the efficiency of the drainage system (Liu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023 ). In addition, the intrusion of seawater backflow into the drainage system under extreme conditions can affect areas further inland from the coastline (Sangsefidi et al., 2023 ). However, how to take into account the dynamic contribution of drainage flow into a coastal flood simulation tool has seldom been discussed. A surrogate model of high accuracy and low computational cost, which can yield real-time results with comprehensive consideration of the combined effects of storm tides, rainfall, and drainage outflows still needs to be built up. In this study, hybrid machine learning techniques were implemented to enable rapid and event-based flood forecasting. To be specific, LSTM network was used to predict drainage outflows by leveraging forecasted or observed storm tide and rainfall time series data. The integration of storm tide, rainfall, and predicted drainage outflow data was subsequently processed through a CNN model, which generated water depth outputs for the entire area. The temporal and spatial prediction accuracy of the proposed hybrid model was then assessed, and the sensitivity of the drainage network data was analyzed. This study offered a novel rapid forecasting method for compound storm surges and rainfall flooding in coastal cities.  2 Study area and data processing 2.1 Study area As shown in Fig. 1  , Macao is located on the southeast coast of the Chinese Mainland, on the west bank of the Pearl River Estuary. It is bordered by Zhuhai City to the north. It is a heavily populated, densely built, and economically developed coastal city. Macao is composed of Macao Peninsula, Taipa, and Coloane. Due to the geographical location of Macao, it is mainly affected by the subtropical high and monsoon over the Northwest Pacific. Tropical cyclones mainly affect Macao from May to November each year. Due to the existence of the central depression of tropical cyclones and strong wind shear, abnormal sea level rise and a large amount of rain often occur at the same time. As one of the most densely populated areas in the world, Macao has a population density reaching 20,700 people per square kilometer, a per capita GDP of about 80,000 US dollars, and an urbanization rate of 100 %. Considering the low-lying terrain and dense population in Macao, the combined impact of severe tropical cyclones and rainfall is likely to bring huge economic losses to Macao (Lau et al., 2021 ). Macao Peninsula is selected as the study area, with an area of about 9.3 km2 . Since it has been badly affected by the storm surges and floods, 12 surface water depth stations and 2 tide level stations are set up. The Macao Meteorological and Geophysical Bureau (SMG) collects the data so that the water level can be monitored and released to the public on time. To further inspect the inundation simulation results on Macao Peninsula, 3 virtual stations are selected.  2.2 Compiling datasets for coastal urban flood prediction 2.2.1 Storm tide The SMG and the Marine and Water Bureau provided historical data on total tidal levels and the corresponding rainfall records in this study. Information about historical events with storm surge and rainfall records was listed in Table 1  . The tidal measurements of the related typhoon events were provided by SMG. Due to the failure of the tidal observatory during the period of Typhoon Hato and Mangkhut, the missing data from these two typhoons were supplemented by related studies (Yang et al., 2019 ). Design storm tides were also considered in addition to the historical records. The storm tide was composed of astronomical tide and storm surge. Macao has a semi-diurnal tidal pattern, with two high tides and two low tides daily. The peak of each tide lasts around one hour, with high tide generally 0.51 m higher than the daily average and low tide around 0.31 m lower than the daily average, according to the Barra Tidal Station (SBR) observations from 2017 to 2020. To describe the change in storm surge level over time, Zhong et al. (2013)  presented the following Eq. (1)  after summarizing a large amount of storm surge events.(1) h s  t    = h smax   ∙ cos  2  ( π ∙ t  T S   )      where h smax      stands for the peak value of the storm surge; T S     is the duration of the storm surge. The design of storm surge level is to determine the values of h smax      and T S    , with T S     set as 24 h. The h smax      was obtained according to the storm surge level across varying return periods. To ensure the designed scenario is on the safe side, the astronomical high tide is assumed to coincide with the peak of the storm surge, which means the peak of storm tide is equal to the peak level of storm surge plus 0.51 m. The Pearson type II frequency curve fitting approach was employed to obtain the maximum storm tide levels for various return periods (Shan et al., 2018 ). As a result, peak levels of storm tides corresponding to return periods of 10-, 50-, 100-, and 200- years are 2.33, 3.14, 3.50, and 3.85 m, respectively. Therefore, the storm tide time series can be obtained by the determined values of h smax      and T S    .  2.2.2 Rainfall A rainfall design method was proposed in addition to historical events to consider more rainfall conditions. Hourly rainfall data covering a period from 1984 to 2015 were provided by the Macao SMG. The precipitation concentration index measures the degree of rainfall concentration over a specific period (He et al., 2022 ). The calculation of a precipitation concentration index used in this study is shown in Eq. (2) .(2) PCI = ∑ i = 1  n  r i  2   ∑ i = 1  n  r i     2   × 100 %     where n  is the total rainfall duration; r i  is rainfall intensity at each moment. The closer the value of PCI is to 100 %, the more concentrated the rainfall is. The PCI has three concentration levels: low (PCI ≤ 25), medium (25 < PCI ≤ 30), and high (PCI > 30). By reference to rainfall records at geographically similar locations such as Guangdong province (He et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021 ), four rainfall patterns were selected in this study, which were unimodal, bimodal, and uniform, covering high, medium, and low temporal PCIs. Table 2   summarized the corresponding hourly rainfall percentages for each pattern. A duration of 12 h was chosen to cover the dangerous periods associated with storm surges, ensuring a conservative design. Rainfall intensity was determined using the multi-year Intensity-Duration-Frequency curves provided by SMG (Macao SAR, 1996 ), and the total rainfall amounts for 10-, 100-, and 200-year return periods for each pattern were obtained using the maximum intensity method. Consequently, 12 rainfall scenarios were designed by combining the 4 PCI rainfall patterns with the 3 return periods. The rainfall was assumed to be uniformly distributed across the entire study area.  2.2.3 Drainage outflow Drainage outflow data is an important source of information for flood forecasting, risk assessment, and mitigation strategies. The flow hydrograph at drainage outlets can reveal trends in network flows, helping to identify abnormal flow increases associated with flooding. Peak flow values can also reflect the hydraulic impact of flood events on the drainage system. Unlike rural fields, impervious surfaces such as roads and buildings in cities make most of the water flow out of the drainage network. To incorporate the capacity of the drainage system, drainage outflow was selected as a key feature in this study. Given the difficulty in monitoring and collecting drainage outflow data, the physics-based numerical model was used to simulate drainage outflow data, which served as the ground truth. An LSTM model was trained based on the simulated drainage outflow data and then applied to predict drainage outflow under testing scenarios. This approach ensured that the hybrid surrogate model can predict floods using a combination of readily accessible storm tide and rainfall data. The total value of drainage outflow in the southeast of the study area was chosen in this study.  2.2.4 Synthetic compound scenarios In addition to the 7 historical events (Table 1 ), the other 48 synthetic compound scenarios were generated by combining 4 storm tide time series with 12 rainfall scenarios. For example, under the scenario T10R100P1, T10 represents a storm tide with a 10-year return period, and R100P1 indicates a 100-year return period for the P1 rainfall pattern. Among all synthetic compound scenarios, T10R100P1, T10R100P2, T50R10P4, and T50R200P1 scenarios were selected as testing scenarios, while the remaining scenarios were used for training purposes.    3 Methodology 3.1 A framework that combines LSTM and CNN for real-time urban flood inundation prediction As shown in Fig. 2  , the framework comprises three main components: data processing, physics-based modelling, and hybrid surrogate modelling. The physics-based numerical model is adopted to simulate surface runoff and drainage flow processes, yielding spatially distributed flooding flow depth and velocity. In addition, it provides flow data within the drainage network. The storm tide and rainfall data then accompany the simulated results to generate the training and testing data for the hybrid surrogate model. The hybrid surrogate model consists of an LSTM network and a CNN. LSTM networks excel in handling long time-series problems by quickly processing nonlinear mapping relationships in time series data and mitigating gradient vanishing and exploding issues in traditional Recurrent Neural Networks. Recent studies have applied LSTMs to enhance the prediction and management of urban water levels, demonstrating significant accuracy and efficiency in various applications within urban drainage systems (Zhu et al., 2023; Palmitessa et al., 2021; Huang and Lee, 2023 ). The LSTM network was adopted to predict drainage outflow in areas lacking monitoring data. CNN-based methods can extract features directly from the raw data through the learning process, avoiding the need to preprocess fixed features, which often involve high computational complexity. The 1D CNN architecture, introduced by Kiranyaz et al. (2016) , successfully predicted urban flood inundation (Kabir et al., 2020; Löwe et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2023 ). The CNN was leveraged to generate the flood inundation processes. Overall, in the hybrid surrogate model, storm tide and rainfall data serve as input features, while the simulation results (to be specific, the water depth of each cell over time) are the target variables. After the hybrid surrogate model is trained and optimized, it can be utilized by inputting observed or predicted rainfall and storm tide situations to predict the flood inundation process. The performance assessment evaluates the spatiotemporal outcome of the hybrid surrogate model, comparing it with the physics-based simulation outputs and observations.  3.2 Physics-based numerical model for flood simulation A physics-based numerical model that couples 1D drainage and 2D overland flow components (Gao et al., 2019; Long and Gao 2023 ) was adopted to simulate flood inundation processes. The model can simulate flow interactions between the drainage pipe network and surface water systems. The 1D pipe flow component was utilized for modelling flow dynamics within urban drainage networks and pumping stations, while the 2D hydrodynamic component can simulate coastal floods and surface overflow processes. The simulation results can be used to derive the relationship between the 1D drainage and 2D overland flow components by accounting for flow interchanges through manholes and outfalls. To validate the numerical model, the simulated water depth time series were compared with the measurements at water level monitoring stations LMF, LHK, and LPM during Typhoon Mangkhut. The physics-based model was implemented using a coupled MIKE 21 and MIKE Urban framework (Danish Hydraulic Institute, 2017 ). As shown in Fig. 3  , the simulated curve matches well the observed curve. The Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency coefficient (NSE) values for stations LPM, LMF, and LHK are 0.939, 0.842 and 0.887, respectively. Higher NSE values closer to 1 indicate better model performance. The numerical model adopted herein perform well in simulating the flooding process in Macao Peninsula. Therefore, the flood simulation results produced by the physics-based model were used to train and assess the hybrid surrogate model.  3.3 Hybrid surrogate model 3.3.1 LSTM model for drainage outflow prediction The LSTM model was designed to transform input sequences X = x 1  , x 2  , . . . , x t s      T  ∈ R  t s  × n s       into outputs sequences Y = y 1  , y 2  , . . . , y t s      T  ∈ R  t s  × n d      , where x i     and y i     are the i -th element within the time series data (i  = 1, 2, …, t s ), respectively, and t s  denotes the number of time steps in the series. The subscript “s ” in”n s    “represents the number of features in each input element, while the subscript “d ” in”n d    “represents the number of features in each output element. In this study, the i -th element of X    and Y    are constructed as x i  = s i - 8   , s i - 7   , . . . , s i  , r i - 8   , r i - 7   , . . . , r i       , and y i  = o i       , in which s i    , r i     and o i     represent the i -th element of the time series storm tide, rainfall, and drainage outflow data, respectively. The structure and specific data format of the LSTM model used in this study are illustrated in Fig. 4  . The LSTM model can be trained offline using numerical simulation results, with substantially lower computational costs than traditional hydrodynamic simulation. The model predicts drainage outflow, which is difficult to monitor directly, using more easily monitored storm tide and rainfall data. The predicted outflow data from the LSTM model and the corresponding storm tide and rainfall data were then used as inputs to the 1D CNN model.  3.3.2 1D CNN for flood inundation prediction The 1D CNN model was designed end-to-end to learn the mapping from input layer features W = w 1  , w 2  , . . . , w t s      T  ∈ R  t s  × n p       to output water depth maps Z = z 1  , z 2  , . . . , z t s      T  ∈ R  t s  × n o      , where w i     and z i     is the i -th element within the time series input and output data (i  = 1,2, …, t s ). The value of n p     corresponds to the number of input features, while n o     corresponds to the number of cells in the study area, as the target outputs are the flood inundation depth for every cell at every time step. In this study, the i -th element of W    and Z    were constructed as w i  = s i - 8   , s i - 7   , . . . , s i  , r i - 8   , r i - 7   , . . . , r i   , o i - 8   , o i - 7   , . . . , o i       , andz i  = z i  ( 1 )   , z i  ( 2 )   , . . . , z i  ( n o  )        , where z i  ( j )      represents the water depth of the j -th cell in the study area at the i -th time step. The input features w i     include storm tide, rainfall, and drainage outflow data with eight antecedent time steps (the time step interval is 15 min, corresponding to 2 h of physics-based model initialization time), resulting in 27 input features. The structure and specific data format of the CNN model used in this study were illustrated in Fig. 4 . The size of each cell in the study area was 4 × 4 m, and the entire study area was divided into 1,263,185 cells. To reduce training costs and improve training accuracy, cells with water depths that never exceeded 0.05 m under any scenario were excluded after simulating all scenarios with the physics-based model, resulting in a final count of 213,297 cells. Key hyperparameters, such as filter size and number of filters in the convolutional layers, number of nodes in the dense layers, and dropout rate, need to be tuned during training for optimal performance.  3.3.3 Model training and hyperparameter tuning for the hybrid surrogate model In this study, the hybrid surrogate model was developed and trained utilizing the Keras (https://keras.io ) library with the TensorFlow (https://www.tensorflow.org ) backend in Python (Abadi et al., 2016 ). Among the 55 scenarios (7 historical scenarios and 48 synthetic compound scenarios), 49 scenarios were used for training and 6 for testing. In addition, a scenario with no storm surge and no rainfall was included in the training set to represent non-inundation condition. Each scenario generated samples every 15 min over 24 h, resulting in 89 samples per scenario (excluding the first 2 h). The total number of training samples was 4,361, and the testing samples totaled 534. The LSTM network (in Fig. 4 ) included six layers: the input layer, two LSTM layers, dropout layer, dense layer, and output layer. Each LSTM layer consisted of 50 units. The dropout rate was 0.2. The GridSearchCV function from the Scikit-learn module was used (Pedregosa et al., 2011 ), performing 10-fold cross-validation over all predefined hyperparameter values to determine the best combination of hyperparameters. The loss function was Mean Squared Error (MSE). The optimized batch size was 40, the epoch number was 100, and the optimizer was Adam. The CNN (in Fig. 4 ) followed a similar optimization process to the LSTM network, and the optimal structure and hyperparameters were identified using MSE as the loss function and GridSearchCV for 10-fold cross-validation. The two convolutional layers extracted features, while the three dense layers acted as a multilayer perceptron network for nonlinear fitting. Each node in the output layer corresponded to a cell in the simulation domain (i.e., 213,297 for the current case study). The optimized convolutional layer 1 and layer 2 had 32 and 128 filters, respectively. The three dense layers had 32, 256, and 512 neurons, respectively, with a dropout rate 0.2. After optimization, the batch size for the 1D CNN was set to 30, with 500 training epochs, using the Adam optimizer.   3.4 Performance metrics To assess the precision of the predicted flood inundation time series, the following model performance metrics were employed: root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and mean error (ME).(3) RMSE ( P , R )  = ∑ i = 1  N  P i  - R i     2   N        (4) MAE ( P , R )  = ∑ i = 1  N  a b s P i  - R i      N      (5) ME ( P , R )  = ∑ i = 1  N  P i  - R i      N      where N    denotes the sample size, P i     and R i     represent the predicted and reference values, respectively. When the prediction perfectly aligns with the reference data, the values of RMSE    and MAE    will be 0. MAE    quantifies the average absolute difference between the predicted and reference values, while RMSE    is the square root of the mean squared difference between predicted and reference values. The former treats all errors equally, while the latter gives more weight to large errors compared to small ones. ME    can show whether the predicted flood depth is overestimated or underestimated. To assess the accuracy in predicting flood inundation extent, the precision, recall, and F1 metrics were also considered to demonstrate how precisely the models predict ‘true positives’ in comparison to the total predicted positives and to the total actual positives over the entire domain:(6) Precision = Ture  positive  Total  predicted  positive       (7) Recall = Ture  positive  Total  actual  positive       (8) F 1 = 2 × Precision × R e c a l l  Precision + R e c a l l       where Ture  positive    refers to the cell accurately classified as flooded by the predictive models, Total  predicted  positive    refers to the sum of cells predicted as flooded, whether correctly or erroneously, and Total  actual  positive    refers the cells identified as flooded by the reference model over the entire domain. Precision    represents the proportion of correctly predicted flooded cells to all cells classified as flooded by the model, whereas Recall    represents the proportion of correctly predicted flooded cells among all actual flooded cells in the reference model. The F 1    score, calculated as the harmonic mean of Precision    and Recall   , offers a balanced assessment for the performance of the model. The ideal precision, recall, and F1 score value is 1, indicating perfect performance.   4 Application of the hybrid surrogate model in the study area 4.1 Performance comparison of hybrid and physics-based models in simulating water depth for test flood scenarios Fig. 5   illustrates a comparison of the performance of the hybrid surrogate model with the physics-based model in simulating water depth during compound scenarios at eight representative locations. The upper part of the figure shows the scenario name and corresponding storm tide level, rainfall, and outflow data under each testing scenario. The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) coefficients of the predicted outflow data under the 6 testing scenarios are 0.423, 0.622, 0.934, 0.931, 0.936, and 0.912, indicating that the LSTM-based component effectively captured the drainage outflow dynamics in the study area. The lower part compares the water depth predictions of the hybrid surrogate model and the simulated water depth values from the physics-based model under each testing scenario. MAE and RMSE were employed to quantify the performance of the hybrid surrogate model. For the Mangkhut event, the hybrid surrogate model demonstrates good accuracy at each location, although some differences are noted, such as an over-prediction of 0.296 m at the peak for the water level monitoring station LIV (As shown in Fig. 1 ) and flood peaks at water level monitoring stations LMF and LRR predicted by the hybrid surrogate model occurring about one hour earlier than those calculated by the physics-based model. Despite these differences, the hybrid surrogate model effectively captured the overall surge and retreat of the flooding process simulated by the physics-based model. In terms of quantitative performance, the MAE and RMSE values at all locations do not exceed 0.066 and 0.114 m, respectively. Regarding the Higos event, the water depths predicted by the hybrid surrogate model largely match those simulated by the physics-based model, with the peak predicted value at the LSI water level monitoring station only 0.137 m less than the reference value. The flood inundation depth of this event is relatively small due to the low tidal levels and rainfall. The rainfall pattern exhibited a roughly bimodal distribution, with the first rain peak coinciding with the tidal peak, resulting in two water accumulations. Both LIV and M1 stations reflected this tendency. The MAE values at all locations did not exceed 0.056 m, while the RMSE values were less than or equal to 0.066 m, indicating the solid predictive ability of the hybrid surrogate model. Under the T50R10P4 scenario, the rainfall exhibited a temporally uniform distribution, resulting in no obvious peaks in water depth due to rainfall. The hybrid surrogate model accurately predicted flooding onset, peak, and retreat timing. However, slight errors occurred at the LIV, LMF, and M1 locations. At the LIV station, the hybrid surrogate model overestimated the peak water depth by 0.199 m. For the LMF station, the hybrid surrogate model predicted the retreat time to be one hour earlier than the physics-based model. At the M1 station, the hybrid surrogate model predicted peak values that were 0.141 m larger than the simulated peak water depth. The remaining three synthetic scenarios (T10R100P1, T10R100P2, and T50R200P1) exhibited distinct flood peaks caused by rainfall, demonstrating location-based sensitivity to storm tides and rainfall. The LIV, LRR, M1, and M3 stations showed greater sensitivity to rainfall, while the LSI, LPF, and M2 stations responded more to storm tides. The other stations displayed intermediate behavior, influenced by both factors. With reference to Fig. 1 , locations near the northwestern sea area reflected tidal changes more than rainfall peaks due to their low elevation and proximity to coasts. In contrast, inland sites represented rainfall peaks better due to their greater distances from the shore. This finding is consistent with previous research in this study area (Gao et al., 2023b ). However, the drainage system was overwhelmed during intense rainfall, resulting in wide waterlogging. Under the T10R100P1 scenario, the physics-based model results showed tidal flooding peaks at LMF, LSI, and LPF. The hybrid surrogate model underestimated the peaks at these three locations by 0.018 m, 0.083 m, and 0.102 m, respectively. As LIV, LRR, and M3 were more sensitive to rainfall, the hybrid surrogate model captured the rainfall peaks, although there were some discrepancies in the timing of the surge and retreat compared to the physics-based model. M1 shows the largest errors among locations (RMSE 0.077 m, MAE 0.045 m). Under the T10R100P2 scenario, the occurrences of three water level peaks at the LMF station caused by rainfall and storm tides could be captured by the surrogate model, with an overestimation of the first peak by 0.142 m. The water level at LIV, LRR, and M3 stations were more sensitive to rainfall, and the deviations between the predicted and simulated peaks ranges from 0 to 0.164 m. The result simulated by the physics-based model showed two rainfall peaks at location M1, while the hybrid surrogate model prediction had three peaks, resulting in the largest RMSE and MAE among all the locations, which were 0.09 m and 0.062 m, respectively. Under the T50R200P1 scenario, the 50-year tidal level was relatively high, and each location showed the high water depths caused by the high tidal level. The average RMSE and MAE were 0.056 m and 0.033 m, respectively. Overall, the simulation results showed that different locations exhibited varying sensitivities to rainfall and storm tides. The areas close to the sea are more likely to be affected by storm tides, while the inland areas with higher altitude are more likely to be affected by rainfall. To further show the accuracy of the overall prediction, the mean RMSE of all cells during the 6 testing scenario was calculated. The mean RMSE ranges from 0.014 to 0.028 m, and the overall mean RMSE is 0.019 m. The RMSE under Mangkhut scenario was the highest, as it was the most severe compound scenario within the test dataset. Fig. 6   presents the inundation areas for different water depth intervals and the corresponding histograms of ME under each testing scenario. The simulated and predicted inundation areas show good agreement, particularly for water depths greater than 1 m. The negative ME values indicate underestimation of mean water depth, while positive ME values indicate overestimation. Across all testing scenarios, more than 99.5 % of the ME values fall between −0.03 m and 0.03 m, which suggests that the hybrid surrogate model accurately predicted flood volumes within the testing scenarios. Overall, the results indicated that the hybrid surrogate model could reproduce the outputs from the physics-based model. Despite some discrepancies between the hybrid surrogate model and the physics-based model at some locations, the surrogate model demonstrated high precision in forecasting the timing and magnitude of peak water depths, as supported by the low overall RMSE, MAE, and ME values.  4.2 Spatial prediction accuracy of the hybrid surrogate model under different flood scenarios To assess the pointwise performance, four levels of flood severity were defined: no flooding (0–0.1 m), minor flooding (0.1–0.5 m), severe flooding (0.5–1.0 m), and extreme flooding (greater than 1.0 m). Two-dimensional histograms were used to compare the predicted values against simulated values based on these flood severity levels. The greater the values of the diagonal cell frequencies, the better performance of the model was. In Fig. 7  , the hybrid surrogate model accurately predicted the peak water depths, and the spatial distribution of the inundation area matches. The absolute deviations between the prediction of hybrid surrogate model and the simulation results of physics-based model were in general less than 0.1 m. Figs. 8 and 9    show the hybrid surrogate model predictions for flood peaks due to storm tides and rainfall under synthetic scenarios. The model generally captured the spatial distribution of inundation extent. The two-dimensional histograms in Fig. 9  show more off-diagonal frequencies than those in Fig. 8 . This indicates that the model performed better in predicting the spatial distribution of water depth under the condition that the storm tides dominate. Table 3   displays the precision, recall, and F1 scores for the hybrid surrogate model in predicting maximum inundation extents during various flood scenarios. Cells with water depths greater than 0.1 m were classified as inundated, while those with less than or equal to 0.1 m were assumed to be non-inundated. The precision scores range from 0.901 to 0.957 across the different flood scenarios, indicating that more than 90.1 % of the cells predicted as flooded by the hybrid model were inundated in the physics-based model simulations. The recall scores ranged from 0.823 to 0.992, indicating the hybrid surrogate model emulated above 82.3 % of the flood cells from the physics-based model simulation. The F1 scores, ranging from 0.865 to 0.968, demonstrated a consistent balance between precision and recall, confirming its overall accuracy in flood extent prediction. To be specific, the recall score of the Higos event was the lowest among the testing scenarios, but it maintained a score higher than 0.82. The spatial distribution of the hybrid surrogate model predictions is mainly consistent with the results of the physics-based model, as shown in Fig. 7 . This discrepancy is likely due to the slight floods, and the physics-based model identified 10.9 % of cells as flooded. As per the formula for recall calculation in Eq. (7) , a smaller denominator (actual inundated cells) means that even minor discrepancies in the numerator (correctly predicted inundated cells) can lead to a more pronounced variation in the recall metric. In future studies, oversampling the training data with water depth ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 m could potentially enhance recall scores. However, increasing recall values may decrease precision because of the inherent trade-off between these two metrics (Buckland & Gey, 1994 ). Balancing these two metrics depends on which is more important: avoiding false alarms (high precision) and ensuring all potential flood locations are identified (high recall).  4.3 Computational cost The computational cost for simulating a specified flood event using different models could vary significantly according to different solutions and computing schemes (Liang et al., 2015; Xia and Liang, 2016; Xia et al., 2019; Su et al., 2022 ). The resolution could also affect the computational time. For example, the HiPIMS model (Xia et al., 2019 ) was applied to simulate a flood event with a duration of 96 h in a specific region with a total area of about 2500 km2 . It took 37.5 h for a computation domain of about 100 million elements with a resolution of 5 m × 5 m. If the resolution was adjusted to 40 m × 40 m, the number of elements reduced to about 1.56 million, and the running time could be reduced to 0.15 h. Table 4   lists the computational times required for training the proposed hybrid model and for simulating the Mangkhut event using the trained model. The proposed hybrid surrogate model is user friendly and demonstrates remarkable efficiency, requiring only 9.69 min for training and only 2.86 s for prediction of one 24-hour event (4 m × 4 m resolution, 1.26 million cells). In this study, this efficiency makes the model highly suitable for real-time prediction and particularly beneficial for probabilistic flood forecasting that leverages ensemble numerical weather predictions.   5 Discussion 5.1 Sensitivity analysis of drainage outflow Sensitivity analysis was undertaken to investigate how drainage outflow variations impact model performance. The perturbation-based method was adopted to evaluate the effect of drainage outflow variation on water depth prediction using the hybrid surrogate model. In this case, the influence of the drainage outflow (o i  = o i - 8   , o i - 7   , . . . , o i       ) on the water depth (z i  = z i  ( 1 )   , z i  ( 2 )   , . . . , z i  ( n o  )        ) of each cell was considered. The modified Morris screening method (Lenhart et al., 2002; Song et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2023a ) was adopted, and the sensitivity index was calculated for every cell using Eq. (9) :(9) S = ∑ α = 0  m - 1   ( Y α + 1   - Y α  )  / Y 0   ( C α + 1   - C α  ) / 100   / m     where S    is the sensitivity index, Y α     is the water depth output by the model on the α -th run, Y 0     is the result of the model run with the initial input value, C α     is the percentage change in the target input value compared to the initial value for the α -th model run, and m    is the number of model runs. A higher absolute value of S signifies a greater sensitivity of the model to variations in the corresponding input. In this study, Y 0     was selected as the highest water depth of a cell, and the drainage outflow group values were tested in ±10 % and ±20 % perturbation steps. Other input values and model parameters were kept constant during each perturbation step. Fig. 10   illustrates the variations in the sensitivity analysis results of each cell under combinations of storm tides and rainfall scenarios across different return periods. Overall, the range of the sensitivity coefficient is from −1.741 to 1.985. The figure shows two spatial categories: positive values in the southeastern area and negative values in the northwestern area. Because the southwestern area is elevated, it is unlikely to be inundated by storm surges, and rainfall dominates. Most of the maximum water depth occurrences in this area coincide with rainfall peak periods, when the drainage network flow reaches ultimate capacity. When the drainage outflow increases, the predicted water depth for the southeastern area increases, resulting in positive sensitivity indices. The northwestern area has low elevation, and storm tide dominates. When the storm tides rise to the critical level, the drainage system becomes entirely overwhelmed, potentially leading to seawater backflow into the drainage outlets (Gao et al., 2023b ). When the drainage outflow was adjusted to increase, the predicted water depth for the northwestern area decreased, resulting in negative sensitivity indices. The absolute values of the sensitivity index decrease as the return periods of rainfall increase, while it changed slightly as the storm tide level was altered. The southeast area is dominated by rainfall, and the sensitivity index does not change significantly as the peak storm surge level changes. For the northwest area, the maximum water depths escalate with rising tidal levels. Yet, the impact on water depth from altering the drainage network flow is small when the drainage network reaches its ultimate capacity. Thus, the absolute value of the sensitivity index is also small. From the results, when the rainfall return periods are relatively small, the impact of drainage network flow on water levels is significant and cannot be ignored. This is consistent with actual situations because as rainfall or tidal levels continue to increase, the drainage network gradually loses effectiveness, and the influence of outflow data diminishes.  5.2 Method limitations and future work More water depth measurements during storm scenarios should be adopted for better validating the flood models. Furthermore, the monitoring techniques of drainage outflows are underdeveloped, and further flow monitoring facilities are needed. The current choice of drainage outflow shows promise, but the methodology used is relatively simple and could be explored to refine the fitting parameters to represent the capacity of the drainage system better. The physics-based model setting also has shortcomings. For example, the permeability coefficient for urban surfaces is set to be essentially impermeable, meaning that some puddles with uneven surfaces have water that can neither drain nor infiltrate through the drainage system. The underground pipe network should be further refined and set up in the physics-based model to better represent the actual condition. While the hybrid surrogate model has demonstrated remarkable efficiency and accuracy, the potential for further improvement exists by incorporating a more diverse set of training scenarios. Expanding the range of scenarios to include a wider variety of climatic conditions would enhance the robustness and adaptability in different and potentially more extreme climate states, ensuring more reliable predictions. Another concern is that the geographical differentiation of each cell was not considered in this study. Although different cells correspond to different parameters in the hybrid surrogate model, they still share some features and parameters, making some of the predicted values for cells that differ from the general environment (such as those located in a pump-affecting area) inaccurate. More in-detail features and geographical information should be incorporated into the model. In addition, the model can be used further in other areas, such as inland cities or more complex urban systems.   6 Conclusions In this study, a hybrid surrogate model was developed to provide real-time, event-based prediction of storm tides and rainfall compound floods in the Macao Peninsula, China. The hybrid surrogate model consists of an LSTM-based component for predicting drainage outflow data and a 1D CNN-based component for predicting flood inundation distribution in the study area, using input data including storm tide, rainfall, and the predicted drainage outflow. Based on the study, the following conclusions can be drawn:(1) The hybrid surrogate model demonstrates strong performance in predicting water depth and extent across all testing scenarios, with average RMSEs ranging from 0.014 to 0.028 m and high precision, recall, and F1 scores for spatial distribution. The proposed hybrid surrogate model can yield reliable results with fast computational time, which can be used to support real-time flood prediction.  (2) The distribution of water depth reflects the response of different areas to rainfall and storm tides. The model performed more accurately in flood peaks dominated by storm tides than in those dominated by rainfall.  (3) The sensitivity analysis results reveal that drainage network flow significantly influences flood water depth when rainfall return periods are relatively small, emphasizing the importance of considering drainage outflow in flood modelling. The sensitivity indices vary, with positive values corresponding to rainfall-dominated area and negative values corresponding to storm tide-dominated area. This pattern provides valuable insights into the dominant flood drivers in different parts of the study area.
1 Introduction Drought is a complex natural phenomenon that persists and recurs at multiple scales, characterized by high frequency of occurrence, long duration and widespread impacts (Mishra and Singh, 2010; AghaKouchak et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020 ). It severely affects water resources systems, agricultural systems, ecosystems and socio-economic systems (Tu et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019 ). The IPCC Sixth Climate Change Assessment Report indicates that the frequency, duration and severity of droughts are increasing globally in response to global climate change and land change (IPCC, 2019; Jiang and Wang, 2021 ). Therefore, it is important to monitor and assess regional drought conditions and improve the capacity to address drought risks. However, characteristic variables such as the intensity and extent of drought occurrence are generally difficult to observe directly and are usually described by drought indices based on measured or modelled hydrometeorological information (Lloyd-Hughes, 2014 ). The selection of an applicable drought index is fundamental to the accurate monitoring and assessment of regional drought conditions (Wu et al., 2021 ). At present, hundreds of drought indices have been proposed by scholars from different countries and regions. They can be broadly classified into three categories according to the type of drought characterized by various indices: (1) Meteorological drought indices. It is generally used to describe precipitation shortages, such as the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI; Palmer, 1965 ), the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI; Mckee et al., 1993 ) and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), which are now widely used globally. Vicente-Serrano et al. (2015)  indicated that SPEI is more sensitive to reference evapotranspiration (ET0 ) than PDSI, and therefore it is more appropriate to use SPEI as a drought index in the applications most relevant to ET0  changes. Tirivarombo et al. (2018)  compared SPEI and SPI for drought monitoring in the Kafue Basin and found that SPEI was more sensitive than PDSI in considering evapotranspiration and that SPEI was more suitable for drought monitoring in applications where ET0 changes were most relevant. Wang et al. (2018)  used SPEI to analyze the spatial and temporal evolution pattern of drought in the YRB for the past 55 years in detail, providing a scientific basis for drought prevention and drought mitigation in the basin basis for decision making. Numerous studies have shown that SPEI combines the advantages of PDSI and SPI, with spatial comparability and multiple time scales, and has good prospects for application (Alam et al., 2017; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). (2) Hydrological drought indices. It mainly describing surface water deficiencies, are commonly available as standardized runoff index (Standardized runoff index, SRI; Standardized streamflow index, SSI or SSFI; Described uniformly as SRI later in this paper). Shukla and Wood (2008)  adopted the concept used by Mckee et al. (1993)  in SPI and defined SRI as the unit standard normal deviation associated with the percentile of hydrological runoff accumulated over a given duration. The results of the comparative analysis with SPI showed that SRI is a valid indicator for describing hydrological drought and can be a useful complement to SPI. It has subsequently been widely used in different research areas by national and international scholars and has been well validated (Damberg and AghaKouchak, 2014; Ding et al., 2021; Mishra and Singh, 2011; Peña-Gallardo et al., 2019; Rivera et al., 2017 ). (3) Agricultural drought indices, which are generally based on soil moisture data to reflect soil and crop water deficits. Common agricultural drought indices such as the standardized soil moisture index (SSMI or SSI, described in the following paper as SSMI) are used. SSMI (Das et al., 2021; Hao and Aghakouchak, 2014 ) is defined in a similar way to SPI and SRI. Oertel et al. (2018)  detected the drought propagation characteristics of semi-arid basins in Latin America by analysing the interdependence of three standardized drought indices, SSMI, SPEI and SRI. Quintana-Seguí et al. (2020)  used soil moisture data simulated by land-surface models (LSMs) to construct an SSMI and applied it to the Spanish mainland to investigate the evolution of drought, and showed that soil moisture combines the effects of effective precipitation and actual evapotranspiration. Inocêncio et al. (2021)  applied various standardized drought indices, including SSMI, to a semi-arid region in northeastern Brazil and validated the ability of SSMI to describe drought. The drought indices mentioned above are mostly used for monitoring a particular type of drought and do not reflect the multi-scale characteristics of drought events and the multiple impacts they bring in an integrated manner. For a severe drought event, the development process often corresponds to different types of droughts, and there is a link between drought propagation and progression. Meteorological drought caused by a persistent lack of precipitation acts on the subsurface and affects soils, vegetation and water bodies to different degrees, thus triggering agricultural drought and hydrological drought (Mishra and Singh, 2011 ). Assessing drought conditions based only on a certain type of drought index is prone to misreporting and underreporting of drought conditions. In order to monitor and assess drought conditions more accurately, an increasing number of studies have started to develop integrated drought indices that incorporate information from multiple sources, i.e., to characterize the spatial and temporal evolution of drought and its impact magnitude in an integrated framework. At present, domestic and foreign scholars have proposed various integrated drought indices, but there is no consensus on the understanding of this concept in academic circles. Niemyer (2008)  classified drought indices that integrate multidisciplinary data into two categories: (1) comprehensive drought indices that consider multiple hydrological, meteorological and agricultural drought factors; (2) combined drought indices that are based on multiple single drought indices. Hao and Singh (2015)  defined the drought index as multivariate drought index (MDI) by combining several drought-causing factors or indices, and introduced the research progress of MDI index from the perspective of index construction methods. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) refers to the results obtained by combining different drought indices based on weighting or modeling methods as composite (or hybrid) drought indicators. Wu et al. (2021)  summarized that the current common methods for constructing comprehensive drought indices are weight combination, joint distribution and machine learning methods. The key of the weight combination method is the selection of index components and the reasonable assignment of weights. The joint distribution method derives the joint cumulative probability of multiple drought indices by constructing a joint distribution function. The machine learning method is based on the training of a large amount of drought base data to explore the fuzzy spatial correlation between drought indices and drought conditions. The derivation of joint distributions of drought variables based on Copula functions is currently considered a better way to characterize drought than weight combination methods and machine learning methods (Mishra and Singh, 2011; Wang et al., 2020 ). As an important agricultural production base in China, the YRB is a sensitive and vulnerable area affected by climate change, with frequent and severe droughts throughout its history. In particular, over the last 60 years, the YRB has experienced a significant increase in temperature and frequency of droughts due to climate change and human activities (She and Xia, 2013; Zhang et al., 2016 ). The degree of impact has become increasingly intensified, bringing great risks to the food, energy, water security and ecological environment in the basin. For this reason, in order to improve the accuracy of understanding the impact of drought on the Yellow River, many scholars have constructed different composite drought indices based on univariate drought indices for the YRB. However, most of the existing indices are bivariate indices combining meteorological, hydrological and agricultural droughts, such as the Integrated Drought Index (IDI) and the Nonparametric Multivariate Standardized Drought Index (NMSDI), which combine SPI and SRI (Huang et al., 2015 ); Nonlinear Joint Hydrological Drought Index (NJHDI) (Li et al., 2020 ), which integrates surface water and groundwater; Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Streamflow Index (SPESI), which integrates SPEI and SRI (Wang et al., 2020 ), etc. Dracup et al. (1980)  pointed out that a comprehensive analysis of drought events requires a combined analysis of rainfall, evapotranspiration, runoff, and soil moisture conditions. Therefore, the above mentioned bivariate comprehensive drought indices are not yet comprehensive for the assessment of drought in the YRB. In this study, we proposed a comprehensive drought index (SPERSI) that combines three standardized climate indices, SPEI, SRI and SSMI based on trivariate Copula functions for a more comprehensive and reliable assessment of drought characteristics. And SPERSI is used to verify the rationality and evaluate the drought characteristics in the YRB where drought disasters are prone to occur. The main objectives of this study are to: 1) propose a new comprehensive drought index SPERSI based on SCI framework and trivariate Copula functions; 2) reveal the spatial and temporal characteristics of drought in the Yellow River Basin reflected by SPERSI, and 3) disclose the relationship between SPERSI and multiple teleconnection factors by using multiple cross wavelet transform.  2 Materials 2.1 Study area As shown in Fig. 1  , the Yellow River Basin is selected in the study area of this study. The whole basin was divided into seven sub-basins on the basis of the Chinese sub-basin boundaries, including above Longyangxia (AL), Longyangxia to Lanzhou (LL), Lanzhou to Hekou (LH), Hekou to Longmen (HL), Longmen to Sanmenxia (LS), Sanmenxia to Huayuankou (SH) and below Huayuankou (BH).  2.2 Data The data used in this study are mainly rainfall, temperature, runoff and soil moisture data. The rainfall and temperature data were obtained from the National Meteorological Information Centre of the China Meteorological Administration (CMA), and a total of 123 meteorological stations were selected for the period 1961–2019, on a monthly time scale (https://data.cma.cn/ ). As can be seen from Fig. 1 , the 123 meteorological stations selected for this study are evenly distributed in the YRB. In addition, the homogeneity and reliability of the meteorological data were checked by the CMA prior to release, and the data showed good homogeneity under strict quality control. Monthly runoff data for 1961–2019 from seven typical hydrological stations (Tang Naihai, Lanzhou, Toudaoquan, Longmen, Sanmenxia, Huayuankou and Lijin) on the main stream of the Yellow River Diversion provided by the Hydrological Bureau of the Yellow River Conservancy Commission were used. The seven selected hydrological stations are located downstream of each catchment, so they can reflect hydrological information from different catchments (AL, LL, LH, HL, LS, SH and BH) (Wang et al., 2020 ). The soil moisture data is selected from the Profile soil moisture (PSM) (0 ∼ 100 cm) in the Catchment Land Surface Model (CLSM) product of the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS), with a spatial resolution of 0.25° and a temporal resolution of 1 day, corresponding to the time frame of meteorological data and runoff data (https://disc.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov/hydrology/data-holdings ). In addition, monthly remote correlation data from 1961 to 2019 were used to analyse the influence of selected remote correlation factors on the evolution of droughts in the YRB, using indicators such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Arctic Oscillation (AO) and sunspot data (Su et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020 ). Table 1   describes the abbreviations, time periods and sources of teleconnection factors used in this study.   3 Methodology 3.1 Standardized drought indices Standardized indices have become very popular in drought management since Mckee et al. (1993)  introduced the Standardized precipitation index SPI to detect drought events. A key feature of Standardized indices is comparability across time, space and variables, allowing for better quantification of drought events (Slette et al., 2020 ). Research on Standardized indices as drought detection tools is multifaceted and they provide a solid basis for the application of drought analysis (Heim, 2002; Mishra and Singh, 2011; Quiring, 2009; Wood and Sheffield, 2012 ). The calculation procedure is the same, independent of the input variables used, i.e., precipitation, soil moisture, flow rate. The main steps in the calculation are (Guttman, 1998; Mckee et al., 1993; Sivakumar et al., 2011 ): (1) Obtain a time series of the desired variables at a given time step (e.g., monthly); (2) Fitting the probability distribution function to monthly data aggregated using different cumulative periods (e.g., 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months); (3) Converting to a cumulative distribution function; (4) Using the inverse function to obtain normalised Gaussian values (i.e., values that obey a normal distribution and have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1). Three standard drought indices, SPEI, SRI and SSMI, were selected as the three variables for the construction of the composite drought index. They can effectively characterize meteorological drought, hydrological drought and agricultural drought respectively. All of the indices were calculated using the Standardized Climate Indices (SCI) package in R (Gudmundsson and Stagge, 2016 ). According to past applications, the most suitable probability distributions are log-logistic for SPEI (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ), and generalized extreme value for SRI (Shukla and Wood, 2008 ) and SSMI (Oertel et al., 2018 ).  3.2 Construction of the SPERSI Trivariate Copula functions were used to connect the standard drought indices SPEI, SRI and SSMI to construct the SPERSI composite drought index. The flow chart is shown in Fig. 2  . Step 1:  Collect rainfall data, temperature data, runoff data and soil moisture data in the catchment and pre-process the data, including interpolation of missing data from stations and synthesis of monthly scale soil moisture data. Step 2:  Based on the measured data from 123 stations, use the Thiessen polygon method to calculate the monthly scale mean of rainfall and temperature for each sub basin by weighted average; By combining the vector range of sub watersheds with monthly soil moisture grid data, calculate the monthly mean soil moisture for each sub watershed using partition statistics. Step 3:  Using the Standardized Climate Indices (SCI) package in R to calculate SPEI, SRI and SSMI. Step 4:  Calculate the edge distribution of SPEI, SRI and SSMI. This step is mainly calculated using Gringorten's formula (Gringorten, 1963; Hao and Aghakouchak, 2014 ).(1) P r  = r - 0.44  n + 0.12       where r  is the ranking of the data when sorted in descending order and n  is the sample size. Step 5:  Five types of Copula functions, namely Clyton, Frank, Gumbel, t and Gaussian, were used as the linking tool for the marginal distribution functions to construct the trivariate joint distribution functions of SPEI, SRI and SSMI respectively. The goodness-of-fit (GOF) of the Copula functions was also tested based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) between the empirical and theoretical distribution functions, and the results of the best-fitting Copula function were selected as the joint distribution function of the three indices. The structure of the five Copula functions is shown in Table 2  . Step 6:  Calculate the composite drought index SPERSI, which is calculated using the formula:(2) SPERSI = φ - 1   ( p )      where φ    is the normal distribution function and p  is the cumulative joint probability. This step mainly converts the cumulative joint probability of SPEI, SRI, and SSMI into values with the same distribution as SPEI, SRI, and SSMI. The resulting SPERSI index has the same statistical framework as SPEI, SRI, and SSMI, and can be classified into drought levels using the same threshold, which is beneficial for comparing drought events in different regions and time scales. It is worth noting that the variables SPEI, SRI and SSMI used to construct SPERSI have multi-scale characteristics. Therefore, different scales of SPERSI can be obtained by constructing standard drought indexes at different scales and using the above calculation process. This paper takes the time scales of 1,3 and 12 months as an example, which is very important for us to grasp the drought information in time and make reasonable responses. The drought index on a 1-month time scale can sensitively reflect the beginning and end of drought events, providing timely information for drought monitoring and early warning. The drought index on a 3-month time scale can better reflect seasonal drought, which is related to the agricultural growth season, while avoiding the influence of short-term weather changes. The drought index at a 12-month time scale can reflect interannual drought changes and match the time scale of hydrological cycle and water resource management, which is beneficial for conducting interannual drought assessment. SPERSI is graded using the same criteria as SPEI, SRI and SSMI, as shown in Table 3  .  3.3 Run theory Run theory (Yevjevich, 1967 ) can be used to calculate drought characteristic variables such as drought duration and drought severity, revealing the fundamental properties of drought (Chang et al., 2016 ). In the past, when using run theory to study drought events, a single threshold level was usually set to identify drought characteristic variables. However, in practice, some more severe drought events may be mixed with individual short duration non drought events. Setting a single threshold may cause one severe drought event to be divided into multiple general drought events, thereby weakening the severity of actual drought. Therefore, in order to improve the reliability of drought identification process, this study optimized the truncation level of drought identification. Three truncation levels X0  (index value of 0), X1  (index value of −0.5) and X2  (index value of −0.8) are used (Wang et al., 2019a ；Hou et al., 2023 ). The process of identifying drought events is as follows. (1) When the index value is less than X1 , it is tentatively determined that there is a drought in the month. (2) When the drought event lasts for only one month and the corresponding index value is greater than X2 , it is considered that there is no drought in the month. (3) When the time interval between two adjacent drought events is only one month and the corresponding drought index value for that month is less than X0 , the two adjacent drought events can be combined into one drought event. The drought duration is the sum of the duration of the adjacent drought event and one month, and the drought severity is the sum of the severity of the adjacent drought events. Otherwise, they are two separate drought events.  3.4 Evaluation metrics In order to verify the performance and reliability of the new SPERSI drought index, this study first used the correlation coefficient method (CC, Pearson correlation coefficient) to calculate the correlation coefficients between SPERSI and SPEI, SRI, and SSMI. In addition, a set of categorical skill indicators were used to explore the applicability of SPERSI for detecting drought events, including probability of detection (POD), false alarm rate (FAR) and critical success index (CSI). More specifically, the CC is used to assess the degree of correlation between SPERSI and SPEI, SPI, and SSMI. POD describes the proportion of occurrences of the three types of drought events, SPEI, SPI, and SSMI, that are correctly detected by SPERSI. FAR indicates the proportion of occurrences of drought events that are actually not detected by SPERSI. CSI measures the overall performance of SPERSI to determine the correct detection of drought events (Das et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022 ). It is important to note in particular that the classification skill indicators are highly correlated with sample size, which may affect the assessment results, especially in arid areas, and therefore this paper focuses on the assessment of SPERSI at the monthly scale. The equations related to the above indicators are shown in Table 4  . The main steps for calculating POD, FAR, and CSI are as follows: ① Extract drought events from monthly time series of SPEI, SRI, and SSMI using Run theory and treat them as benchmarks. In this step, we set the same threshold for all drought indices, as detailed in section 3.3 . ② Extract drought events from monthly time series of SPERSI using the same threshold criteria. ③ Accurately identify the number of events (HIT), missed reports (MISS), and false reports(FALSE) using the SPERSI index. Taking SPERSI's monitoring of meteorological drought as an example: HIT is the number of drought events detected by both SPERSI and SPEI; FALSE is the number of drought events detected by SPERSI but not by SPEI; and MISS is the number of drought events detected by SPEI but not by SPERSI. ④ Calculate the POD, FAR, and CSI of SPERSI for different drought events based on the formula in Table 4 .  3.5 Modified Mann-Kendall (MMK) trend test The Mann-Kendall (MK) trend test method is a non-parametric test method used to identify monotonic trends in data sequences. It is commonly used in time series analysis in fields such as environmental science, meteorology, hydrology and water resources. The MK test does not require data to follow a specific distribution and is not affected by a few outliers. Therefore, it can be used for independent and identically distributed sample sequences, as well as for non-independent or differently distributed sequences (Khambhammettu, 2005 ). However, caution should be exercised when using the MK test for non-independent or differently distributed data. If there is autocorrelation between data or if the variance of the sequence changes over time (heteroscedasticity), this may affect the efficiency and efficacy of the MK test. Hamed and Ramachandra Rao (1998)  proposed a modified Mann-Kendall (MMK) trend test, which can eliminate the autocorrelation component of the series and significantly improve the test power of the Mann-Kendall method, and is widely used in the field of hydrometeorology (Wang et al., 2019a; Guo et al., 2019 ). Based on SPERSI, this paper will use this method to reveal the drought trend characteristics of the Yellow River basin and its sub regions from 1961 to 2019.  3.6 Bivariate and multivariate cross wavelet transform technology The cross wavelet transform technique is a commonly used method for detecting multi-scale relationships between two variables in fields such as hydrology, meteorology and soil science. The multivariate cross wavelet transform is an improvement on the traditional bivariate cross wavelet transform and can be used to analyse relationships between multiple variables and can characterise local features of non-stationary signals in both the time and frequency domains (Hu and Si, 2016; Nalley et al., 2019; Ng and Chan, 2012 ). For more detailed information on cross wavelet transform techniques, see Nalley et al. (2019) .   4 Results 4.1 Performance of the SPERSI The copula function modeling results between SPEI, SRI, and SSMI at different watersheds and time scales are detailed in Appendix I . The GOF results (Appendix I ) show that there is no fixed type of optimal Copula for the construction of SPERSI on different scales in different regions. In general, the Gaussian-type Copula function performs better on the monthly scale, the gumbel-type Copula performs better on the annual scale, and the t Copula is not suitable for the construction of SPERSI. Fig. 3   shows the monthly, quarterly and annual values of SPERSI, SPEI, SRI and SSMI for the YRB from 1961 to 2019. As can be seen from Fig. 3 , the trend and variation of SPERSI at different scales in the YRB are basically consistent with the variation patterns of SPEI, SRI and SSMI, which indirectly verifies the effectiveness of the calculated SPERSI, and the index can reliably reflect the information of various types of drought at different scales. Further analysis of the variation of SPERSI with SPEI, SRI and SSMI at different scales according to Fig. 3  reveals some differences between the four indices. It is generally accepted that the onset of drought is usually due to a persistent lack of rainfall, therefore SPEI is very sensitive in capturing the onset of drought while due to the complex process of sink production. There is a delay in the response of hydrological and agricultural droughts to meteorological droughts, so SRI and SSMI are effective in identifying the duration and end of droughts. As shown in the black rectangular boxes b, c, d in Fig. 3 , the values of SPERSI and SPEI fall to −0.8 before SRI and SSMI, indicating that the SPERSI is comparable to SPEI in its ability to capture the onset of drought. At the same time, the values of SPERSI and SRI and SSMI rise to −0.8 later than SPEI, as shown in the black rectangular boxes c, f, g in Fig. 3 , indicating that the SPERSI captures the end of drought comparable to the SRI and SSMI. This is because SPEI takes meteorological drought characteristics as the main reference, and meteorological drought develops suddenly and rapidly. The SRI index is based on the characteristics of hydrological drought, and the SSMI is based on the characteristics of agricultural drought, while the hydrological drought and agricultural drought a considerable delay and a long duration. SPERSI can include the beginning and end of drought captured by SPEI, SRI and SSMI to a large extent. SPERSI can capture the onset of drought as well as SPEI, and the duration and end of drought as well as SRI and SSMI. Whether only a single type of drought event occurs or multiple types of drought events occur simultaneously, SPERSI can capture the onset and end of the complete drought event to a greater extent. These results provide strong evidence that SPERSI is a combination of precipitation, temperature, runoff and soil moisture information that is more sensitive to capturing the onset, duration and end of droughts, and is therefore a reliable and effective tool for drought monitoring and prediction. In addition, we can see from Fig. 3  that although SPERSI can capture the onset, duration and end time of the vast majority of drought events, there are also some cases of under-reporting, mis-reporting, early reporting and late reporting. In order to quantitatively assess the ability of SPERSI to characterize drought, we used CC to assess the correlation between SPERSI and SPEI, SRI and SSMI. Then, we used Run theory to extract drought events from monthly SPEI, SRI, SSMI and SPERSI time series of the YRB and its seven subbasin from 1961 to 2019, and used POD, FAR and CSI to evaluate the comprehensive ability of SPERSI to capture drought events. The results are shown in Fig. 4   and Fig. 5  . Fig. 4  shows the CC of SPERSI and SPEI, SRI and SSMI for the YRB and its seven subbasins on monthly, seasonal and annual scales. The CCs of the YRB SPERSI and SPEI, SRI and SSMI were 0.63, 0.74 and 0.67 on the monthly scale, 0.71, 0.82 and 0.71 on the seasonal scale, and 0.86, 0.87 and 0.72 on the annual scale, respectively, all of which passed the 95 % confidence interval test. Of these, SPERSI and SRI are the most closely related on all time scales, with a maximum CC value of 0.75 (LS) for both on the monthly scale, 0.82 (YRB) on the seasonal scale, and 0.89 (LS) on the annual scale. SPERSI has the worst correlation with SSMI, only outperforming SPEI and SRI on the monthly and quarterly scales of BH, with values of 0.70 and 0.74 respectively. The correlation between SPERSI and SPEI at the monthly scale is lower than that between SRI and SSMI in the whole YRB. However, as the time scale increases, the correlation between SPERSI and SPEI at seasonal scale is generally higher than that of SSMI, and the correlation between SPERSI and SPEI at annual scale is already comparable to that of SRI, and the CC values of four divisions, AL, LH, HL and BH, are higher than that of SRI, with CC values of 0.80, 0.85, 0.75 and 0.80 respectively. In general, the correlation between SPERSI and SPEI, SRI and SSMI increases significantly with increasing time scale, and even at the monthly scale, the correlation between SPERSI and the three standard drought indices is above 0.6 (p < 0.05). This result meets the expectations of our designed SPERSI index modeling scheme. The good correlation between SPERSI and indices such as SPEI, SRI, SSMI, etc. gives this index a certain degree of ability to comprehensively express meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural drought. Fig. 5  shows the results of three indicators of SPERSI's ability to detect drought on a monthly scale for the YRB and its seven subbasins. The first is to assess the ability of SPERSI to detect meteorological drought, hydrological drought and agricultural drought respectively. As shown in Fig. 5 , SPERSI captures meteorological drought with POD, FAR and CSI of 0.91, 0.26 and 0.69 respectively, hydrological drought with POD, FAR and CSI of 0.79, 0.08 and 0.74 respectively, and agricultural drought with POD, FAR and CSI of 0.9, 0.29 and 0.67 respectively in the YRB. Among them, SPERSI is better at detecting meteorological drought and hydrological drought in the YRB, with POD>0.84, FAR<0.26 and CSI>0.69 for meteorological drought and POD>0.78, FAR<0.23 and CSI>0.73 for hydrological drought. In addition, it can be seen from the Fig. that the FAR value of SPERSI detection of agricultural drought events is significantly higher than that of meteorological drought and hydrological drought, and the CSI value is significantly lower than that of meteorological drought and hydrological drought. The FAR values of SPERSI detection of agricultural drought events in seven regions are 0.4 (AL), 0.15 (LL), 0.25 (LH), 0.39 (HL), 0.35 (LS), 0.44 (SH) and 0.47 (BH), respectively. CSI values were 0.55 (AL), 0.73 (LL), 0.7 (LH), 0.48 (HL), 0.5 (LS), 0.5 (SH), 0.46 (BH), respectively, indicating that SPERSI had weak ability to capture single agricultural drought. However, due to the inconsistent occurrence time of different types of drought events, the response of hydrological drought and agricultural drought to meteorological drought is delayed, and the intensity of some meteorological drought events is low, which may not necessarily lead to hydrological and agricultural drought events. Therefore, the drought events captured by SPERSI include more single drought events such as meteorology or hydrology, which is the main reason for the high FAR and low CSI of agricultural drought events detected by SPERSI. For this reason, a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of SPERSI's ability to assess drought requires that the drought events identified by SPEI, SRI and SSMI respectively be combined and then analysed in comparison with the drought events identified by SPERSI. The results are shown in Fig. 5  for the combined drought assessment results (green area). SPERSI detects integrated drought events in the YRB with POD>0.75, FAR<0.04 and CSI>0.73, indicating that the ability of SPERSI to characterize integrated drought events is reliable. To further verify the applicability of SPERSI, two remote sensing drought indices, the Vegetation Health Index (VHI) and the Normalized Vegetation Supply Water Index (NVSWI), were selected to verify the correlation between SPERSI and vegetation, and the results are shown in Fig. 6  . From the results, it can be seen that the correlation between the composite drought index SPERSI and VHI and NVSWI has a significant increase compared to the standardized drought indices SPEI, SRI and SSMI.  4.2 Temporal changes and spatial features of drought Fig. 7   shows the characteristic values of monthly, seasonal and annual temporal trends in SPERSI based on the MMK trend test method. Zs > 0 indicates a decreasing trend in drought and Zs < 0 indicates an increasing trend in drought. It can be seen that the temporal variation of drought is clearly different for different sub-regions at different scales. Firstly, looking at the sub-divisions, the Zs values of the two sub-divisions AL and LL, which are located in the upper reaches, are basically greater than zero at all time scales, indicating that the drought in these two sub-divisions as a whole tends to ease, while the drought in the remaining sub-divisions tends to intensify, and the drought in the YRB as a whole tends to intensify. On monthly scale, the Zs values for each month in the YRB are −0.47, −0.57, −1.22, −1.12, −0.53, −0.26, −0.88, −1.02, −0.88, −1.14, −1.10, and −0.62. It can be seen that the YRB shows an increasing trend in all months, with the most obvious increase in March.
