For instance, the values below zero indicate the presence of water while values nearing zero indicate an absence of green leaves on the surface. Conversely, positive NDVI  values signify the existence of green vegetation, with higher values corresponding to denser vegetation cover. For missing pixels in any images, we calculated the average of the preceding and following one-month window. When high-quality data were unavailable, the missing values were initially replaced with the historical eight-day average, and if this was unavailable, with the historical monthly average. Subsequently, the median NDVI  value was computed for each pixel per month and assigned as the representative value. The obtained monthly NDVI  datasets had a 30 m resolution.(3) Estimation of the leaf area index (LAI)    Correlations between the reflectance of near infrared and red light and LAI  have been reported in past research (Sobrino et al., 2008 ). Assuming a uniform distribution of leaf inclination in vegetation, LAI  can be estimated as (Carlson et al., 1995; Carlson and Ripley, 1997; Choudhury et al., 1994 ):(8) LAI = - 2 I n 1 - f NDVI          where f NDVI     represents the Fraction Vegetation Cover (FVC ). In this study, FVC  is retrieved according to the linear relationship between NDVI  and FVC  (Gutman and Ignatov, 1998 ):(9) f NDVI   = ( NDVI - NDVI  0   NDVI  1  - NDVI  0    )       where NDVI  1    corresponds to the NDVI  value entirely covered by vegetation, and NDVI  0    signifies the NDVI  value devoid of vegetation. Here, we prescribe NDVI  0    = 0.04 and NDVI  1    = 0.8 (Gutman and Ignatov, 1998; Sobrino and Raissouni, 2000 ).(4) Estimation of the land surface emissivity (LSE)    In this study, land surface emissivity (LSE   ) was calculated from NDVI   . Sobrino and Raissouni (2000)  have proposed an operational NDVI    threshold method for estimating LSE    from remote sensing data (Sobrino et al., 2008; Sobrino and Raissouni, 2000 ). This method presupposed that: (1) the surface consisted solely of soil and vegetation, (2) the emissivity of bare soil had a linear relationship with the surface emissivity in the red channel, and (3) the land surface emissivity had a linear relationship with the FVC   . Hence, the LSE    can be calculated as follows:(10) ε λ  = ε v λ   f NDVI   + ε s λ   ( 1 - f  NDVI   ) +  C λ      where ε v λ     and ε s λ     represent the emissivity of vegetation and soil, respectively, C λ    is a measure of the surface cavity effect. It should be noted that LSE    estimated via NDVI    threshold exhibits discontinuity due to consideration of the cavity effect and the implementation of diverse methods to calculate LSE    across various NDVI    ranges. Disregarding the cavity effects, the calculation can be summarized via the simplified method proposed by Sobrino et al. (2008) , as shown in equation (11) :(11) ε λ  = ε s λ   ,    ε s λ   + ε v λ   - ε s λ     f NDVI   ,    ε v λ   ,        N D V I < NDVI  0      NDVI  0  ≤ N D V I ≤ NDVI  1      Here, ε s λ     and ε v λ     denote the emissivity of bare soil and vegetation, with values suggested 0.96 and 0.985, respectively (Valor and Caselles, 1996 ). As in the estimation of LAI   , the NDVI    datasets, derived from harmonized Landsat dataset with a resolution of 30 m, were used to obtain the FVC , which was subsequently used to estimate LSE   .(5) Estimation of surface albedo    Surface albedo was retrieved from remote sensing data dependent on the surface and atmospheric conditions. Liang (2001)  provided simple formula for calculating surface albedo from various satellite sensors. Furthermore, Smith (2010)  normalized the Landsat formula to calculate surface albedo. This study employed the methods by Liang (2001)  and Smith (2010)  to estimate surface albedo:(12) albedo = 0.356 ρ 1  + 0.130 ρ 3  + 0.373 ρ 4  + 0.085 ρ 5  + 0.072 ρ 5  - 0.0018  1.016       where ρ 1  , ρ 3  , ρ 4  , ρ 5  , ρ 7     correspond to bands 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7 of Landsat dataset, respectively. The derived monthly albedo had a spatial resolution of 30 m. For missing data, we interpolated values by averaging the temporal windows immediately before and after the gap.   3 Datasets and methods 3.1 Inputs for the PML_30 model The input variables of the PML_30 model included meteorological data, monthly atmospheric C O  2    concentrations, land cover, and surface parameters. The meteorological forcing was obtained from GLDAS-2.1 with 3-hour resolution and 0.25˚ encompassing precipitation, air temperature, vapor pressure, shortwave downward radiation, longwave downward radiation, and wind speed. This data was interpolated to 30 m resolution via the bilinear interpolation, following the original process in PML-V2, to minimize footprint effects and yield smoothed data (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Similarly, land cover data obtained from MCD12Q1.006 were resampled from 500 m to 30 m using bilinear interpolation. Monthly atmospheric C O  2    concentrations were obtained from NOAA globally averaged marine surface monthly mean data and downloaded from the Global Change Information System (GCIS) website (https://data.globalchange.gov ). The surface parameters were retrieved from Landsat satellite images. Here, we selected GLDAS-2.1 instead of other reanalysis datasets such as ERA5-Land (ERA5L) or station-interpolated meteorological data for the following reasons. Firstly, previous research indicated that GLDAS-2.1 provided more stable meteorological drivers in arid regions than ERA5L (Valipour and Dietrich, 2022; Wu et al., 2021 ). Secondly, the PML_30 model used calibration parameters derived from GLDAS-2.1 data (Zhang et al., 2019 ), necessitating re-calibration if different drivers were used. Thirdly, although meteorological observations were available at selected flux sites, continuous data was missing in the Yarkand River basin. Hence, we used GLDAS-2.1 for consistency. Additionally, He et al., (2022)  found that ET simulation results based on PML using CMFD (2000–2018) and GLDAS-2.1 (2019–2020) in China showed good continuity, indicating the reliability of GLDAS-2.1. In future work, we can explore using higher-resolution datasets such as ERA5L, re-calibrate the parameters, and analyze if this improves the results.  3.2 Observations from FLUXNet sites Global validation was conducted at 42 flux sites from FLUXNet-2015 across arid and semi-arid regions. The following criteria are required for each site, including: (i) the flux site has at least 2 years of continuous ET data (since 2000); and (ii) the site with overall energy balance ratio (EBR) value greater than 70 % (Wilson et al., 2002 ). Locations of the selected sites are shown in Fig. 2  .  3.3 Observation over the Yarkand oasis The Yarkand oasis in southwestern Xinjiang, northwest China, constitutes a major part of the Yarkand basin (Fig. 3   (a)), which is one of the headstreams of the Tarim River. The oasis covers about 16,000 km 2   , with a research area of 2600 km 2    along the 150 km lower river, dominated by sparse Populus euphratica (Fig. 3  (b)). To validate the model at the regional and the field scales, we collected monthly streamflow and precipitation data from hydrological stations (Kaqun, Yuzimenleke, Ailiketamu, and Heiniyazi) between 2000 and 2020. Additionally, groundwater level observations were collected at the Heiniyazi, the outlet of the region. The locations of the sites were shown in Fig. 3 . In this highly heterogeneous downstream region, globally available ET products failed to capture the variation patterns of surface information, often missing ET values such as MOD16A2 or mapping ET that was clearly inconsistent with the patterns of land cover type such as PML-V2 (Mu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019 ) as shown in Fig. 4  . The resolution of PML-V2 was insufficient to accurately depict the forest regions along both sides of the downstream riverbank. Higher and more precise estimation of ET was still in need.  3.4 Model validation (1) Site-scale validation against FLUXNet sites    Model validation was conducted using data from 42 flux sites within arid and semi-arid regions globally. The model-derived monthly ET was compared with latent heat-derived monthly ET. Evaluation metrics include coefficient of determination (R  2   ), root mean square error (RMSE   ) and bias   .(13) R  2  = ∑ i = 1  N  ( X sim , i   - X  ¯   sim   )  ( X obs , i   - X  ¯   obs   )   ∑ i = 1  N  X sim , i   - X  ¯   sim      2  X obs , i   - X  ¯   obs      2        2      (14) RMSE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  (  X sim , i   - X obs , i     )      (15) bias = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( X sim , i   - X obs , i   )      where X sim     and X obs     represent the simulated and observed ET, respectively. N   is the length of the datasets.(2) Regional validation over the Yarkand oasis    To ascertain the robustness of the PML_30 model, a regional validation was undertaken. The water balance method was deployed to derive a multi-year average ET as reference. Relevant research on groundwater changes in the area found that the groundwater levels have remained relatively stable (Chen et al., 2016 ). Therefore, we assumed that the effects of groundwater changes and domestic water usage are negligible. Under such assumption, the water balance equation was presented as:(16) ET  =  R in    +  P  -  R out        In the equation, R in     refers to the basin input runoff depth, P   denotes the basin precipitation, and R out     is the basin output runoff depth. The inflow and outflow runoff data were sourced from hydrological stations. Our study regions, characterized by a typical arid continental climate, experienced strong evaporation, low precipitation, and dry air. Multi-year hydrological data indicated an annual precipitation of about 65 mm, much of which evaporates immediately upon contact with the ground. As this instantaneous evaporation cannot be accurately quantified, the annual rainfall in the region was disregarded. Hence, the annual runoff was employed as the annual ET derived from the water balance and adopted as the reference value. Observation at the Heiniyazi station showed no inflow and virtually no rainfall in 2020. Therefore, changes in groundwater levels (Δ G W L   ) were assumed to directly represent regional water consumption (WC   ) (WC ≈ Δ G W L   ). Hence, the change in groundwater level in 2020 was used to validate the water consumption estimated by the PML_30 model in the nearby area. For this purpose, a random point, referred to as Point1 (location given in Fig. 5  ), was selected in the vicinity. This region primarily consisted of silty soil with a specific yield of 0.1 (a parameter that indicates the amount of water released due to drainage), based on the recommendation of local engineers who have observed groundwater levels for years. Therefore, multiplying the decline in groundwater level by 0.1 provided an estimate of the water consumption of the neighboring Populus euphratica.(3) Spatial comparison with other ET products    To reveal the improvement of the PML_30 in ET mapping, we compared its spatial distribution patterns of ET with widely used ET products, focusing on areas with high heterogeneity. These comparisons involved ET products such as PML-V2 and MOD16A2 obtained from GEE platform.   4 Results 4.1 Validation against FLUXNet sites The model's monthly ET estimations were evaluated against the observed monthly ET values for all 42 flux sites. Fig. 6   illustrated the scatter plot between observed ET and PML_30 simulation. The datapoints, clustering around the 1:1 dashed line, suggested a high degree of model accuracy. For the mean ET of available data at each site, PML_30 performed well, with an R  2    of 0.79, an RMSE    of 0.52 mm/day, and a bias    of 0.39 mm/day. Overall, the model also performed well, with an R  2    of 0.82, an RMSE    of 0.78 mm/day, and a bias    of 0.38 mm/day, though it slightly overestimated ET. Fig. 7   showed the performance of PML_30 over different biomes, identified as the plant functional types (PFTs). The model performed best for ENF, GAR, and OSH sites in terms of R  2    and RMSE   , while it performed poorly for SAV and WSA sites. This variation may be related to the different accuracies of surface parameters retrieved from remote sensing inversion on diverse land types. Additionally, the accuracy of the evaluation was influenced not only by plant types but also by other factors, including the geographic location and the quality of observation data. For instance, the RMSE    at one of the CRO sites was significantly higher than all other sites, likely due to its proximity to the coastline.  4.2 Validation in the Yarkand oasis (1) At the regional scale    Fig. 8   delineated the boxplot of annual ET estimates from 2000 to 2020 in the Yarkand oasis, using water balance method, PML_30 model, and PML-V2 model. The PML_30 model projects slightly elevated ET values compared to the PML-V2 model. The water balance analysis averaged an ET of 380 mm/year over the 21-year period for the basin region, while the PML_30 model calculated 344 mm/year, corresponding to a relative error of 9 %. The PML-V2 model, on the other hand, projected a multi-year ET average of 304 mm/year with a relative error of 20 %. These findings implied the PML_30 model's enhanced accuracy and reliability for estimating ET in the study area.(2) At the field scale    Table 2   compared water consumption derived from groundwater measurements with estimates using the PML_30 model in 2020. The groundwater level change at the Heiniyazi station receded by 2.4 m in the year 2020, inferring an annual water consumption of approximately 240 mm/year by Populus euphratica. In contrast, the PML_30 model projected an annual water consumption of 236 mm/year at this point in 2020, with a marginal relative error of 1.67 %.(3) Finer spatial patterns of ET    The PML_30 model, PML-V2, and MODIS were used to display monthly mean ET distributions in the sparsely vegetated downstream area of the Yarkand River. A randomly selected summer month, August 2017, was chosen for comparison. Fig. 9   (a)-(c) displayed the results from the three products. Fig. 9  (d), which aligned with the land cover type reported by (Yang and Huang, 2021 ), showed that the highest ET values were found in cropland, followed by river-adjacent areas, with ET decreasing further from the river. While in Fig. 9  (b), PML-V2 results revealed a clear demarcation in the downstream area, with similar ET values on both sides of the line except for a few distinct pixels. This abrupt ET shift appeared incongruent with the land cover type distribution. Fig. 9  (c) confirmed that MODIS products neglect surface information in sparsely vegetated areas, indicating non-null values for individual pixels only. The coarse resolution of PML-V2 and MODIS products failed to precisely simulate the region's spatial distribution, primarily due to their oversight of surface information changes in highly heterogeneous regions. In contrast, higher spatial resolution results provided more accurate ET distribution maps that closely aligned with actual land cover types and the river seepage pattern of the lower Yarkand River. Our study not only enhanced the accuracy of ET measurements but also yielded a more refined spatial distribution. At a spatial resolution of 30 m, a more distinct ET pattern became evident. Fig. 10   (a) showed the variation of mean annual ET with the distance from the river of the cross-section was selected randomly for a given year (2018). The mean ET decreased by 0.16 mm/day/km as the distance from the river increases. Beyond about 1.5 km from the river channel, ET markedly decreased, indicating a lower impact of fluvial seepage. Additionally, Fig. 10  (b) presented a temporal increase in the vegetation ET to total ET ratio downstream between 2000 and 2020, suggesting ecological improvement.   5 Discussion (1) Effective harmonization of Landsat images.    Harmonizing Landsat data was essential to ensure continuous 30 m inputs in this study. Therefore, we first analyzed the effects of harmonizing different Landsat satellite images. Recent advances in data assimilation, such as temporal interpolation, multi-sensor fusion, and machine learning applications, enabled more consistent analysis (Chen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2018, 2018; Zhu et al., 2010 ). Yet, the higher resolution of remote sensing images and the more extended period increase the difficulty of calculation since more pixels need to be processed in the same area, limiting the application of Landsat data on a large scale. Harmonizing multiple satellites may effectively improve the frequency and availability of sufficient Landsat images, ensuring longer-term data acquisition (Roy et al., 2016 ). Here, we first presented the average number of available pixels per year within the region in Fig. 11  , including data from TM, ETM+, and OLI, as well as the total number of available satellite images. The figure demonstrated significant variability in the number of available images from different satellite sensors. Relying on images from a single satellite would result in insufficient information for analysis. Therefore, we utilized images from all available satellites for each pixel in this study to ensure sufficient data input. Furthermore, Fig. 12   illustrated the spatial distribution of aggregated satellite images available in the arid region for the period from 2000 to 2020 after harmonization. For each satellite, the image availability for each satellite was markedly limited, with the quantity of TM satellite images ranging between 0 and 200, while the highest count for ETM+satellite images does not exceed 600. After harmonization, the number of accessible images within this study area had markedly increased, with the maximum count in some regions approaching 1000.(2) Advantages over other high-resolution ET products    Our results showed that the PML_30 model had promising accuracy and applicability. This model increased the spatial resolution of ET from 500 m to 30 m compared with the original PML-V2, providing detailed information on terrestrial water consumption. It provided key insights into water usage across sparse vegetation near riverbanks and cross-sectional water consumption patterns, which were particularly vital for studies on ecological restoration and riverine water loss. This finer ET information enabled the provision of constructive suggestions regarding water use across different land surface types, which is crucial for sustainable water management in arid and semi-arid regions. In contrast to ET products derived from just a single Landsat satellite or other satellites (Fisher et al., 2020a; Melton et al., 2022 ), the model offered an extended ET estimate series from 2000 to 2020, enabling a deeper understanding of hydrological changes, ecological restoration, and climate-induced drought challenges. Compared with other regional ET products (Comini de Andrade et al., 2024; Melton et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2012a ), the PML_30 modeling approach proposed in this study was validated at 42 global flux sites and study area, and was implemented on the GEE cloud platform, facilitating broader application in arid and semi-arid regions worldwide.(3) Uncertainty and future enhancements    Nevertheless, there are some uncertainties in this study. Firstly, Landsat images are significantly affected by clouds and cloud shadows in the study area. The filtered data is sparse, and the median value of all image values on a grid may not adequately represent the monthly average for the grid. Certain grids may not include any images in a month. Secondly, for grids with missing data, the method of averaging one time circle sliding at the point introduces uncertainty due to the non-linear month-to-month variation. In addition, our model employed the 0.25 deg GLDAS-2.1 meteorological data and the 500 m MCD12Q1 land cover data. The coarse spatial resolution inputs may bring some uncertainties. Regarding the model, its parameters were given from the original PML-V2 model without new calibration. which can lead to some uncertainty. Moreover, our focus here was on arid and semi-arid regions, where cloud contamination was fewer compared ewith humid regions (Cai et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2016 ). In humid and sub-humid regions, cloud cover and cloud shadowing may result in less available imagery data, and thereby make it more challenging to estimate continuous and accurate ET (Zhu et al., 2018 ). Future work can expand the PML_30 model to a global scale, complementing the results in humid and sub-humid regions and further validating the stability of the model across. In this study, we analyzed the total ET and achieved promising results. However, among the components of ET, soil evaporation accounts for a large proportion of total ET in arid and semi-arid regions, while transpiration dominates in vegetated regions (Yang et al., 2023 ). Although the PML model can calculate different components, this study, similar to previous studies (He et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019 ), primarily focused on the estimation accuracy of total ET. This was because direct observation of each ET component at the site scale was not feasible, and various methods used to decompose ET can introduce uncertainties. Additionally, the PML model employs empirical formulas to calculate soil evaporation, which still requires further improvement. Overall, the PML_30 model demonstrates good accuracy in estimating total ET, but the accuracy of its component estimates needs to be assessed in further research.  6 Conclusion This research (1) retrieved long-term monthly 30 m resolution Leaf Area Index (LAI   ), Land Surface Emissivity (LSE   ) and albedo, by harmonizing data from three satellite products, namely TM, ETM+and OLI, on the GEE platform; (2) constructed a 30 m resolution monthly ET model based on PML-V2 model; (3) evaluated the model at global 42 flux sites; and (4) applied the model to estimate monthly ET from 2000 to 2020 in the Yarkand oasis, an arid region in Northwest China. The PML_30 model had a good estimate of ET with R  2    of 0.79 and RMSE    of 0.52 mm/day against observations from the flux sites. In the Yarkand oasis, the estimated mean annual regional ET is 344 mm/year, which was close to the calculated (380 mm/year) by the water balance method, with a relative error of 9 %. At the field scale in the region, the water consumption estimated by PML_30 model in 2020 at Heiniyazi was assessed with 1.67 % errors. Overall, the ET products at 30 m resolution appeared plausible. The PML_30 model can well depict the spatial distribution of ET in the downstream of the Yarkand River. Daily ET predominantly exceeded 0.5 mm/day within a 1 km distance from the river. The mean annual ET decreased at a rate of about 0.16 mm/day/km as the distance from the river increased. The proposed PML_30 model, with its straightforward structure and computations conducted on the GEE platform, is easily scalable and suitable for regions with high heterogeneity. The long time-series ET estimate based on PML_30 is also valuable for investigating hydrological processes and environmental shifts, especially in arid and semi-arid regions.
1 Introduction In recent years, flood disasters have occurred more frequently and caused greater losses, accounting for approximately 40 % of all losses caused by natural disasters globally (Jamali et al., 2018; Wang and Shen, 2023 ). An urban environment is a complex system formed by the interaction between natural and human systems (Arosio et al., 2018 ). Urban flood disasters not only directly cause large areas of water accumulation but also induce landslides, debris flows, building collapse, and road traffic accidents. In this study, urban flood disasters, and natural geological disasters and social accidents triggered by urban floods are referred to as disaster events, namely urban flood cascade compound disaster events (UFCCDEs). The occurrence of these disaster events has significant cascade, superposition, and amplification effects (Bermúdez et al., 2021; Girgin et al., 2019; He et al., 2024 ). If the disaster chain cannot be cut off rapidly when an urban flood disaster occurs, it will bring serious economic losses and casualties. Therefore, only studying the impact of a single disaster event has made it difficult to handle the current risks caused by urban floods (Dunant et al., 2021 ). It is urgent to study the development process of urban floods and determine the interactions between UFCCDEs to scientifically and effectively realize risk mitigation (Cutter, 2018; Hilly et al., 2018 ). Considering various factors, such as meteorological conditions, underlying surface characteristics, and socio-economic activities, flood risk assessment is a scientific method to assess the threat and loss caused by flood disasters from aspects such as hazards (severity of the flood), exposure (people, buildings, and infrastructure in the area that may be affected by the flood), and vulnerability (the possibility of damage to the exposed elements) (Li et al., 2022; Maranzoni et al., 2023 ). Most scholars have used mathematical statistics methods (Li et al., 2022 ), multi-criteria index system methods (Ma et al., 2021 ), remote sensing and geographic information system coupling methods (Tang et al., 2018 ), scenario simulation assessment methods (Zhao et al., 2021 ), and machine learning methods (Du et al., 2022 ) to assess the flood disaster risk. These methods primarily evaluate the severity of flood disasters, as well as the losses and impacts resulting from them, without considering the interactions between disaster events caused by floods. Thus, the risk of flood disasters is underestimated, especially in urban areas, because the cascade, superposition, and amplification effects are ignored. Considering the interactions between disaster events, we constructed a UFCCDE network (UFCCDEN) of Guangzhou to identify the key disaster events and causal chains for assessing the vulnerability of the UFCCDEN. Because natural and human systems are involved, the impacts of urban flood disasters are complex, inherently correlated, and nonlinear (Arosio et al., 2018 ). Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of applying complex network theory to represent and analyze the complexity and nonlinearity of flood disaster systems (Fang et al., 2023 ). Complex networks are topological structures composed of nodes and edges connecting these nodes, which can characterize complex systems in the real world (Zou et al., 2019; da Costa et al., 2007 ). The difficulty of applying complex network theory to urban flood disasters is the construction of the UFCCDEN. This is because official publications, such as disaster investigation reports and infrastructure location data, are sometimes difficult to obtain and generally do not cover the complete processes of disasters (Noguchi et al., 2021 ). Social media data can solve this problem due to its accessibility and comprehensive content. For example, Sina Weibo (Weibo), one of the most commonly used social media platforms in China, not only has many official social media accounts but also has a large number of users. When flood disasters occur, they feed news and specific events related to flood disasters on Weibo, which can offer sufficient data to construct a UFCCDEN. Furthermore, social media data also has the advantage of instantaneity. Real-time updated data makes it possible to rapidly construct and assess disaster event networks. However, it is challenging to extract effective information from social media data because these data are unstructured and have a low information density and a large sample size (Noguchi et al., 2021; Sedlakova et al., 2023 ). An event evolutionary graph (EEG), an important development direction of the new generation of knowledge graphs, is a suitable tool for constructing a UFCCDEN using social media data. An EEG is a logical, directed graph of event process evolution, which is used to describe the sequential and causal relationships between events (Li et al., 2017 ). The main research objects of an EEG are predicate events and their logical relations, aiming to construct an event logic knowledge base to reveal the evolution of events and the relationship between events (Guan et al., 2023 ). Recently, EEGs have been widely applied in many fields, such as epidemiology (Chen et al., 2021b ), finance (Cheng et al., 2020 ), emergency response (Zhang et al., 2023a ), and text generation (Colas et al., 2022 ). However, few studies have applied EEGs to flood disasters. Apparently, EEGs have great application potential in the field of flood cascade compound disasters. To construct a UFCCDEN rapidly, we leveraged an EEG to integrate social media data, successfully applying complex network theory for the vulnerability assessment of disaster event networks. Therefore, this study has two primary objectives: 1) based on an EEG, using social media data to rapidly construct a UFCCDEN that represents the development of UFCCDEs; and 2) applying complex network theory to assess the vulnerability of disaster events and causal chains in the UFCCDEN to mitigate the risk of flood disasters. The megacity of Guangzhou was selected as an example. First, we used flood-related data in Weibo from 2018 to 2022 to analyze the spatio-temporal distribution of UFCCDEs and construct a UFCCDEN based on an EEG. Then, we applied complex network theory to evaluate the importance of disaster events and the vulnerability of disaster causal chains in the constructed UFCCDEN. Finally, we calculated the global efficiency of the network to assess the propagation efficiency of the UFCCDEN before and after implementing disaster mitigation strategies based on the assessment results to demonstrate the performance of the assessment framework. The details of the assessment framework are shown in Fig. 1  .  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong Province, is one of the most economically developed and urbanized cities in China. By the end of 2023, the permanent population of Guangzhou was 18.8270 million, with an urbanization rate of 86.76 % according the People's Government of Guangzhou’s website. Guangzhou is located in the Pearl River Delta on the southeast coast of China with complex topography, which decreases from northeast to southwest, as shown in Fig. 2  . The northeastern part of Guangzhou features mountains, the central region consists of hills and basins, and the southern part is characterized by coastal alluvial plains, which are a part of the Pearl River Delta. Guangzhou has climatic characteristics of simultaneous heat and precipitation with abundant rainwater resources. The average annual temperature is between 21.7 and 23.1 °C, and the average annual precipitation is about 1923 mm. Affected by climate, topography, and human activities, flood disasters occur frequently in Guangzhou. There are some major reasons for the frequent flood disasters in Guangzhou: (1) uneven distribution of precipitation, in that the precipitation in Guangzhou is concentrated in the flood season from April to September, and the area is prone to flooding; (2) complex topography, in that the northern region is prone to flash floods, while the southern region is prone to multiple attacks from typhoon rainstorms, astronomical tides, and storm surges; and (3) rapid urbanization, in that the urbanization process leads to the rapid reduction of permeable land, which increases the storm runoff and flood peak runoff. In addition, the lack of construction and protection of water conservancy facilities in the early stage of urbanization intensifies the pressure of flood control and drainage. Therefore, we selected Guangzhou as an example to construct and assess the UFCCDEN.  2.2 Data collection and processing We chose Weibo as the data source because of its accessibility, high comprehensiveness, and immediacy. First, Weibo not only has a large number of people sharing what they see and hear but also has many official media sources reporting news and current events, such as People’s Daily Online and China Daily Online. Second, the update speed of Weibo is high, and its real-time hot spots, i.e., the discussions or events that gain significant attention and engagement on the platform, are updated every minute. Furthermore, previous studies have demonstrated the reliability and representativeness of Weibo data for urban flood disasters through comparing Weibo flooding points with official flooding points (Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023b ). 2.2.1 Data collection Because the number of requests for the Weibo APIs is limited, we used web crawler technology with high degree of freedom to collect Weibo data through flood disaster keywords. Keywords can quickly retrieve the Weibo data related to flood disasters. Referring to relevant literature, the keywords of flood disasters used in this study are shown in Table 1   (Please see Table S1  for Chinese version). We crawled the text and post time of Weibo based on those keywords.  2.2.2 Data processing The collected data contained duplicates and noise that needed to be removed. In addition, the disaster-inducing factors, hazard-prone environments, and disaster-bearing bodies of flood disasters in different cities are different, so their UFCCDENs also have certain differences. It is necessary to eliminate the data outside the study area when constructing a UFCCDEN. Therefore, we filtered out data that did not contain the place names of the studied cities in the text. Comprehensive details for de-duplication, de-noising, and geolocation extraction can be found in a previous publication (Chen et al., 2023 ), and therefore, only a brief introduction is provided as follows.(1) De-duplication and de-noising: When more than one keyword appeared in a single piece of Weibo data, it would be retrieved repeatedly. Thus, only one piece of data needed to be retained. There are two main sources of noise. First, some irrelevant data were incorrectly collected due to Chinese ambiguity. For example, although Weibo data containing the phrase “Pulmonary edema” were not related to urban floods, they were collected because “Pulmonary edema” and “Water accumulation” have the same characters in Chinese. Second, there were some data related to stars in Weibo, which also interfered with the results.  (2) Geolocation extraction: We extracted the location names mentioned by users in the text of the Weibo data as the geographic locations of disaster events. If the geographical location appearing in the text of Weibo was within the studied city, the piece of data was considered eligible. The Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers–Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory–Conditional Random Fields (BERT-BiLSTM-CRF) model based on deep learning methods is widely used in the field of named entity recognition (Dai et al., 2019 ), and it can effectively extract geographical location names in text. It has the advantages of a high accuracy and generalization ability (Liu et al., 2023 ). The input of the model is a sentence, and the output is the optimal tag sequence with the highest score of the sentence. The geolocation names are the words formed by the Chinese characters extracted from the optimal tag sequence.    We acquired the data highly related to urban floods by de-duplication and de-noising, and then we used the extracted place names to determine whether the data were located in the study area. Finally, the UFCCDE dataset of the study city was obtained.   2.3 UFCCDEN construction UFCCDEs consist of urban flood disasters, and natural geological disasters and social accidents triggered by urban floods in this study. When the urban flood disaster comes, these disaster events often occur in succession or at the same time, resulting in cascading and compound effects. To better understanding the occurrence mechanism of UFCCDEs, we constructed a UFCCDEN based on an EEG, where the nodes represent disaster events, and the directed edges represent the causal relationships of disaster events, that is, causal chains. Therefore, the construction process of the UFCCDEN included four steps, which were event causality extraction, event representation, event merging, and event storage and visualization. 2.3.1 Event causality extraction The UFCCDEN had causal relationships between its components, so the first step was to extract event causality. Event causality extraction consisted of cause events, effect events, and causal connectives. Causal connectives are the words or phrases that represent causal relationships between events. Based on the properties of causal connectives, causality can be categorized into implicit and explicit causality (Xu et al., 2020 ). At present, the methods of causality extraction mainly include statistics (Yang and Mao, 2014 ), pattern matching (Ittoo and Bouma, 2011 ), and deep learning (Liang et al., 2022 ). Explicit causality is usually extracted by pattern matching methods because it has explicit causal connectives. Implicit causality is difficult to extract because of implicit causal connectives, and thus, it is often extracted by deep learning methods. Therefore, we used pattern matching methods and deep learning methods to comprehensively extract event causality. Regular expressions are templates consisting of a sequence of characters and special characters, which are used to describe the text patterns to be matched (Thomo, 2012 ). We extracted event causality by a pattern matching method based on regular expressions. The causal patterns used in this study are shown in Table 2  . Note that different patterns needed to be prioritized in order to improve the accuracy of event extraction. For example, single causal connective patterns with higher priority can interfere with double causal connectives patterns. The Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration (ERNIE) model is a pre-training model for continuous-learning semantic understanding based on knowledge enhancement (Sun et al., 2019 ). ERNIE combines pre-training with multi-source knowledge and evolves through continuous learning technology to obtain a better performance (Sun et al., 2021 ). We also used deep learning based on the ERNIE model to extract event causality. Three layers of fully connected neural networks were added to the ERNIE model to perform three tasks to identify the attributes of words. The three tasks were to determine whether the word was located in the causality region, identify whether the word belonged to a causal event, and classify it as a subject, predicate, causal connective, or none of the above. Through multi-task learning, the cause subjects, cause predicates, causal connectives, effect subjects, and effect predicates were successfully identified.  2.3.2 Event representation The cause-and-effect events extracted by the event causality extraction still have noise, so the main part of the event should be extracted to represent the information of the event. Event representation generally uses the methods of semantic role labeling (SRL) and dependency parsing (DP). SRL focuses on the predicate of the sentence and analyzes the relationship between the components of the sentence and the predicate, including core semantic roles (such as agent and patient) and subsidiary semantic roles (such as time and place) (Lim et al., 2013 ). DP analyzes the dependency relationships between the components of the sentence to reveal syntactic structures (Ouchi et al., 2016 ), which mainly include the subject–verb relationships, verb–object relationships, and verb–complement structures. The process of the event representation method in this study was divided into two steps. 1) Based on SRL, the subject–verb–object triple of the event was extracted if it existed. Otherwise, the event was represented by the subject–verb structure and the verb–object structure in turn. If the extraction result was empty, step 2 was executed. 2) Based on DP, the subject–verb–object triple of the event was extracted if it existed. If not, whether the subject–verb–object relation, verb–object relation, verb, and noun existed in turn was judged, until the representation was completed.  2.3.3 Event merging The extracted disaster events focused on a single case. For example, the expressions “water accumulation in multiple road sections” and “water accumulation on the road surface” both convey the meaning of water accumulation. A single case is one-sided for understanding disaster events, and thus, the extracted disaster events need to be generalized. The main objective of the event merging was to merge similar events to avoid duplication and optimize the presentation of events. The K-means cluster algorithm is a classical unsupervised machine learning algorithm used for text clustering. It can group large amounts of text data according to their similarity, ensuring that texts within the same group have a high degree of similarity (Singh et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2022 ). In this study, we first converted the texts into vectors, and then measured the similarity between texts by calculating the Euclidean distance between their respective vectors. Finally, we generalized the similar disaster events into one class through continuous iterative calculation, which could greatly reduce human workload. Therefore, we merged the disaster events with high similarity by combing the K-means cluster algorithm with manual judgement to better understand the structural characteristics of the UFCCDEN.  2.3.4 Event storage and visualization An EEG has a directed cyclic graph structure and needs to be stored in a graph database. Neo4j, a high-performance open-source graph database based on Java, is one of the mainstream graph databases that can effectively organize, store, and update data, in addition to supporting query, backup, and other functions (Zhu et al., 2019 ). Neo4j excels in storing and updating data, while its capability for visualizing data is not as strong. Gephi is an open-source software for network analysis and visualization that provides rich visualization functions to clearly present the network structure (Bastian et al., 2009 ). Therefore, we utilized Neo4j and Gephi to store and visualize data, respectively.   2.4 Vulnerability assessment of UFCCDEN based on complex network theory Complex network theory is one of the important branches of graph theory, which can be applied to many network systems in real life. Complex systems with a large number of constituent elements can be studied as complex networks. The elements and relations between elements of complex systems are regarded as the nodes and edges of complex networks, respectively (da Costa et al., 2011 ). In this study, we applied complex network theory to identify the key disaster events and causal chains, quantifying their respective importance and vulnerability. First, the degree centrality, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and eigenvector centrality of the nodes were calculated to evaluate the importance of disaster events in the network. Second, both the edge betweenness centrality and connectivity were considered to assess the vulnerability of disaster casual chains. Finally, the global efficiency metric was used to evaluate the global propagation efficiency of the network to demonstrate the performance of the assessment framework. 2.4.1 Importance of nodes Degree centrality is the most direct metric to reflect the centrality of nodes in network analysis. For directed networks, the degree of a node includes the in-degree and the out-degree (Borgatti and Halgin, 2011 ). The in-degree refers to the number of other nodes that point to the given node. The out-degree refers to the number of other nodes to which the given node points. Therefore, for the disaster event network, the larger the in-degree value of a disaster event is, the more difficult it is to control. The larger the out-degree value of a disaster event is, the more losses are caused by it. Degree centrality synthesizes the in-degree and out-degree, so a disaster event with a high value of degree centrality indicates that it plays an important role in the UFCCDEN. The degree centrality is calculated as follows:(1) C D  i    = 1 N - 1   ( d in   ( i )  + d out   ( i )  )      where C D  i       is the degree centrality value of disaster event i   , N    is the number of disaster events in the UFCCDEN, and d in   ( i )     and d out   ( i )     are the in-degree and out-degree of disaster event i   , respectively. The betweenness centrality is a metric that measures the controlling and restricting effect of a node on other nodes in the network (Brandes, 2008 ). A disaster event with a high value of the betweenness centrality means it is more important as a bridge in the network. If the disaster event can be effectively controlled, the connection between disaster events will be quickly inhibited or even blocked. The betweenness centrality is calculated as follows:(2) C B  i    = 1 ( N - 1 ) ( N - 2 )   ∑ s ≠ i ≠ t ∈ I   n s , t    i )   n ( s , t )       where C B  i       is the betweenness centrality value of disaster event i   , n ( s , t )    is the number of shortest paths between disaster s    and t   , n s , t    i )     is the number of shortest paths between disaster s    and t    passing through i   , and I    is the set of disaster events of the UFCCDEN. The closeness centrality is a measure of the ability of a node to influence other nodes in the network through the network, indicating the closeness between the node and other nodes (Freeman, 1978 ). The larger the closeness centrality value is, the shorter the average shortest distance between the node and other nodes is. Similar to the degree centrality, both the inward and outward distances should be considered. A disaster event with a high closeness centrality value indicates that it plays a significant role in the risk propagation. The closeness centrality is calculated as follows:(3) C c  i    = N in   ( i )   ∑ j  N in   ( i )    L ( j , i )    + N out   ( i )   ∑ j = 1  N out   ( i )    L ( i , j )        where N in   ( i )     is the number of other nodes that can reach node i   , N out   ( i )     is the number of other nodes that node i    can reach, L ( j , i )    is the inward distance to node i   , and L ( i , j )    is the outward distance to other nodes. Eigenvector centrality involves the importance of the node and its neighboring nodes. Its core idea is that the centrality of a node is positively related to the importance of its neighboring nodes (Bonacich, 1987 ). That is, the eigenvector centrality value of a node is positively correlated with the sum of the centrality scores of its neighboring nodes. The eigenvector centrality value of a disaster event represents the importance of itself and its neighboring nodes. The formulas for calculating the eigenvector centrality are given as follows:(4) Ax = λ x ,   x = [ x 1  , x 2  , x 3  , ⋯ , x N  ]  T      (5) C E  i    = x i      where A    is the adjacency matrix of the network with eigenvector x    and eigenvalue λ   .  2.4.2 Vulnerability of edges The causal chains in the UFCCDEN represent the interactions of the disaster event. Assessing the vulnerability of causal chains can control the propagation of disaster risk and suppress the cascading effect of disaster events. Similar to the betweenness centrality of nodes, the betweenness centrality of edges indicates the role of the edge as a bridge in the network, and it is calculated as follows:(6) EC  B  e    = 1 N ( N - 1 )   ∑ s , t ∈ I   n s , t    e )   n ( s , t )       where EC  B  e       is the betweenness centrality value of causal chain e   , and n s , t    e )     is the number of shortest paths between disaster s    and t    passing through e   . The larger the betweenness centrality value is, the more vulnerable the causal chain is in the disaster network. Connectivity indicates the reachability between disaster events in the network. A causal chain plays an important role in the network connectivity if the connectivity value of the network becomes smaller after removing it. The smaller the connectivity value after removing the causal chain is, the more vulnerable the causal chain is in the disaster network. Therefore, the vulnerability of causal chains is given as follows:(7) E V e    = EC  B  e     EC  B max     ∗ ECN  ECN ( e )       where E V e       is the vulnerability of causal chain e   , EC  B max       is the maximum value of the betweenness centrality of all causal chains in the network, E C N    is the number of reachable nodes in the network, and ECN ( e )    is the number of reachable nodes after removing causal chain e   .  2.4.3 Network propagation efficiency It is necessary to deeply understand the propagation path and efficiency of the disaster network from the overall network level to control and suppress the propagation of disaster events in the network in time. Generally, the average path length and global efficiency metrics are used to evaluate the overall network propagation level. The average path length of the network is the average of the shortest path lengths in the network. In directed unweighted networks, the shortest path length is the number of edges in the shortest path from one node to another node. The propagation efficiency of the network is positively correlated with the inverse of the shortest path length, and the global efficiency is given as follows (Chen et al., 2021a; Latora and Marchiori, 2001 ):(8) GE = 1 N ( N - 1 )   ∑ s ≠ t ∈ I   1 L ( s , t )       where GE    is the global efficiency of the network, 0 ≤ GE ≤ 1   ; L ( s , t )    is the shortest path length from disaster event s    to t   . When two nodes are disconnected, the shortest path length between them is infinite, and the global efficiency is zero. Thus, the global efficiency is more suitable for quantifying the propagation efficiency of the disaster event network (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010 ). The larger the global efficiency value of the disaster network is, the faster the disaster events spread in the network. The global efficiency of the UFCCDEN reflects the efficiency with which the disaster events spread through the disaster event network. Therefore, we removed the nodes and edges of the UFCCDEN and then recalculated the network global efficiency to analyze the performance of the proposed framework. Node removal refers to preventing the occurrence of disaster events. We removed the nodes in descending order based on the results of the degree centrality, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality and eigenvector centrality, respectively. Because the network structure would respond simultaneously when the nodes were removed, we removed the nodes one by one according to the respective centrality metrics which were recalculated after every removal. Edge removal refers to cutting off the propagation between disaster events. We removed the edges in descending order based on their vulnerability, and the removal process was similar to that of node removal. Moreover, we randomly removed the nodes and edges as the controls.    3 Results 3.1 UFCCDEs of Guangzhou In order to construct the UFCCDE dataset, the data in Weibo from 2018 to 2022 based on keywords were collected and processed, as explained in Section 2.2 . Fig. 3   shows the number distribution of the Weibo data that were highly related to flood disasters from 2018 to 2022. The amount of data from April to September was significantly greater than that in the other months. This is reasonable because the flood season in Guangzhou is from April to September. When a severe flood cascade compound disaster occurs, the amount of data related to flood disasters in social media is greater than usual, and thus, it can reflect the magnitude of the disaster risk. As shown in Fig. 3 , Guangzhou usually has a high risk of UFCCDEs from May to July, which is in the flood season, and the risk is the highest in June. This may be due to the Dragon Boat Water, the high-accumulation, wide-spatial-coverage, and long-duration rainfall (Sheng et al., 2023 ), appearing from May 21 to June 20 in Guangzhou. The locations of the UFCCDEs can reflect the distribution of UFCCDE risks. We drew the thermal map of the UFCCDEs of Guangzhou from 2018 to 2022 based on kernel density analysis method. As shown in Fig. 4  , the density of UFCCDEs in the areas along the river network and transportation network was higher than in other areas. The risk of UFCCDEs is the highest in the urban center of Guangzhou where UFCCDEs are prone to occur (Yuexiu, Tianhe, Liwan and Haizhu districts).  3.2 UFCCDEN vulnerability of Guangzhou We processed the UFCCDEs of Guangzhou from 2018 to 2022, as demonstrated in Section 2.3 , to construct the UFCCDEN. Based on the methods of the EEG construction we carried out, 81 disaster events and 220 disaster causal chains were obtained. Fig. 5   shows the UFCCDEN of Guangzhou, and the description of each node is presented in Table S2 . 3.2.1 Assessment of important nodes Four centrality metrics of the UFCCDEs in Guangzhou were calculated to identify important disaster events from different perspectives. Fig. 6   shows the calculation results of four centrality metrics. There were three types of disaster events with a high degree centrality (Fig. 6 a). One type was the disaster events with high values of the out-degree, such as Node 3 (fluvial flood or coastal flood), Node 1 (waterlogging), Node 14 (water accumulation), Node 2 (flash flood), Node 4 (landslide), and Node 5 (debris flow). These events are highly hazardous because they can trigger numerous other disaster events. In contrast, the disaster events with high values of the in-degree, such as Node 79 (economic losses), Node 80 (casualties), and Node 81 (people trapped), are easily triggered by other disaster events, thus having high values of the in-degree. Disaster events of the third type—such as Node 23 (road damage) and Node 51 (power facility damage)—have high degree centralities in both the in-degree and out-degree, and they can be triggered by the first type and can trigger the second type. In terms of the betweenness centrality (Fig. 6 b), Node 1 (waterlogging) has the highest betweenness centrality, indicating that it is in the most central position of the disaster network. Meanwhile, Node 14 (water accumulation), Node 53 (drainage facility blocked), Node 65 (water pollution), Node 63 (non-point source pollution), and Node 51 (power facility damage) also have relatively high betweenness centralities, which tend to amplify the cascading effect generated by the disaster events with high values of the out-degree in the disaster event network. Node 79 (economic losses), Node 3 (fluvial flood or coastal flood), Node 1 (waterlogging), Node 2 (flash flood), and Node 14 (water accumulation), with high closeness centralities, were close to other disaster events in the disaster event network. The eigenvector centrality values of Node 3 (fluvial flood or coastal flood) and Node 79 (economic losses) were much higher than those of other disaster events. The different centrality metrics represent different attributes of disaster events, so we equally divided disaster events into five levels based on each centrality metric separately to further understand the UFCCDEN structure. The higher the value of the centrality metric is, the higher the level of the disaster event is. Fig. 7   shows the proportions of each level of the four centrality metrics. As expected, the different centrality metrics had different level distributions of disaster events. Table 3   shows UFCCDEs with at least one centrality metric level greater than 3. Some disaster events ranked high in certain centrality metrics while ranking low in others. However, it is interesting to note that for all the centrality metrics, most disaster events were distributed at level 1, and a few had levels greater than 2 (Fig. 7 ). For each centrality metric, the proportion of disaster events exceeded 0.66 at level 1 and was less than 0.18 with levels greater than 2. This demonstrated that only a few disaster events in the UFCCDEN were at high risk.  3.2.2 Assessment of vulnerable edges We calculated the vulnerability of the disaster causal chains by Equations (6) and (7)  and divided them into five levels based on the calculation results, as shown in Fig. 8  . Similar to the assessment results for the nodes, the vulnerability distribution of disaster causal chains in the UFCCDEN was not uniform, and the causal chains with a high vulnerability accounted for a small proportion. Table 4   shows causal chains with vulnerability levels greater than 1. The causal chains at levels greater than 1 accounted for 0.055. The disaster causal chain with the highest value of the vulnerability was drainage facility blocked → waterlogging, which exacerbated the risk caused by urban floods. Most of the disaster causal chains with levels greater than 1 involved waterlogging, indicating that it played an important role in the UFCCDEN of Guangzhou. Furthermore, the causal chains of the non-point source pollution → water pollution and power facility damage → power outage also promoted the propagation of disaster events.   3.3 Performance of disaster mitigation strategies The risk of disaster can be mitigated by preventing the occurrence of disaster events or cutting off the propagation between disaster events. We removed the nodes and edges as demonstrated in Section 2.4.3  to demonstrate the performance of the assessment framework. Note that Node 1 (waterlogging), Node 2 (flash flood), and Node 3 (fluvial flood or coastal flood) were not removed during node removal because the main research objects were UFCCDEs. Fig. 9  a and 9b show global efficiency trends of the UFCCDEN of Guangzhou implementing mitigation strategies for disaster events and disaster causal chains, respectively. The original global efficiency of the UFCCDEN was 0.0765. After removing nodes based on the degree centrality, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and eigenvector centrality, the final values of the global efficiency were 0.0287, 0.0310, 0.0481, and 0.0434, respectively. They were all lower than the global efficiency value of the control (0.0539). Furthermore, after removing edges based on the edge vulnerability, the global efficiency value decreased from 0.0765 to 0.0430, which was lower than the control value (0.0730).   4 Discussions This study proposed a new framework for the rapid vulnerability assessment of the UFCCDEN based on the EEG. The principal contributions of this study are as follows. 1) A UFCCDEN was constructed rapidly by leveraging an EEG that integrates social media data, addressing the challenges of data acquisition and the lack of detailed data. 2) The UFCCDEN vulnerability was assessed comprehensively from a network perspective, which considered the interactions between disaster events caused by urban floods. We demonstrated the proposed framework on a megacity of Guangzhou in China using Weibo data from 2018 to 2022. The effectiveness of using social media data to construct a UFCCDEN based on an EEG is reflected in both temporal and spatial aspects. In terms of temporal distribution, the high-risk period of UFCCDEs in Guangzhou is part of the flood season, especially during the Dragon Boat Water period. In this period, UFCCDEs often occur due to the high occurrences of flood disasters caused by factors such as rainstorms, astronomical tides, and storm surges. Regarding spatial distribution, the areas along rivers and transportation networks have higher UFCCDE risk than other areas because of the high frequency of floods and the strong cascade effect of floods, respectively. The urban center areas in Guangzhou have the highest UFCCDE risk. Those areas have dense rivers and impervious surfaces, which easily lead to fluvial floods and pluvial floods in the increasingly frequent extreme weather. The low discharge ability of drainage makes them more vulnerable to floods (Meng et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, flood disasters have greater cascading effects in urban centers due to the dense populations and complex underlying surfaces. Moreover, the areas with high UFCCDE densities in Guangzhou seem to be consistent with the areas with high risks of flooding assessed by Lyu et al. (2018) , demonstrating the high performance of social media data. The application of an EEG can model the development process of urban floods as completely as possible due to the high comprehensiveness of social media data. Furthermore, Chen et al. (2023)  found that social media data can reflect the spatio-temporal changes of urban waterlogging at the hourly scale. Thus, UFCCDENs can be updated on demand at any time, which facilitates the rapid assessment of UFCCDENs for disaster mitigation. Waterlogging, flash floods, fluvial floods, coastal floods, landslides, and debris flow have high out-degrees, indicating that natural disasters often induce other disaster events. It is difficult to mitigate the impacts caused by urban floods because economic losses, casualties, and people trapped have high in-degrees, which should be prevented and controlled from many aspects. Waterlogging is not only in the most central position of the disaster network but also one of the constituent nodes of causal chains with a high value of vulnerability. This is because Guangzhou is located in the Pearl River Delta on the southeast coast of China, which is often affected by waterlogging due to factors such as rainstorms, river flows, tides, and storm surges (Chan et al., 2024 ). Based on the results of the degree and betweenness centralities, it was found that water accumulation, power facility damage, road damage, and drainage facility blocked have significant cascade effects, amplifying the impact of urban floods. Thus, it is necessary to promptly remove water accumulation on roads and near power networks to cut off the propagation of disaster events. Drainage facilities play an important role in the disaster event network due to their self-cyclic disaster chain formed with waterlogging (waterlogging → drainage facility damage → drainage facility blocked → waterlogging). The prominent characteristic of self-cyclic disaster chains is the sustainable development of disasters, which can constantly self-reinforce if not impeded by external intervention. Therefore, UFCCDEs will cause continuous adverse effects for cities without effective prevention and control, which emphasizes the significance of the UFCCDEN vulnerability assessment. Furthermore, only a small fraction of the disaster events and causal chains have high values according to the equidistant quintile results. The results signify that the UFCCDEN risk of Guangzhou will be greatly alleviated, as long as the small fraction of disaster events and causal chains are curbed. In fact, the propagation efficiency of the UFCCDEN decreased significantly after removing important disaster events and vulnerable causal chains. Based on the assessment results of disaster events and causal chains, the global efficiency of the UFCCDEN decreased by 37–62 % and 44 %, respectively, after implementing mitigation strategies. The performances of both were greater than those of the controls, highlighting the necessity of UFCCDEN vulnerability assessment. The proposed framework realizes the rapid vulnerability assessment of the UFCCDEN based on the EEG, and thus, it has great potential for mitigating the impact of flood disasters on cities in a timely manner. However, there are several limitations which should be improved in this study. First, the construction of the UFCCDEN only considered disaster events caused by urban floods and their relationships, while the occurrence probability of causal chains was neglected. In fact, the probability of the cause event leading to the effect event is generally different. Second, although social media data has comprehensive contents that can cover most specific disaster events, a few disaster events are likely missed due to a lack of attention. Third, the reliability of social media data should also be considered. An analysis of the spatio-temporal distribution of UFCCDEs in Guangzhou reveals that social media data can provide effective information about UFCCDEs. Nevertheless, there are still a few points need to be considered. Certain disaster events that attract substantial public interest are often mentioned repeatedly by various users. These repeated mentions affect the detection of high-risk periods and increase the data volume processed during the UFCCDEN construction. In addition, the density of the data may be affected by population or mobile device users due to the source of social media data, resulting in excessive or insufficient data in some areas. Further research can construct a weighted directed network to better model the disaster event network. Furthermore, ongoing advancements in deep learning have facilitated the rapid development of multi-modal models in recent years (Stefanini et al., 2023 ). Multi-modal models can perfectly achieve the image captioning task that describes the visual content of an image in natural language (Alsharid et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2016 ). Therefore, combining EEGs with multi-modal models can make full use of multi-modal data in social media, such as images and videos, which are able to offer more information to construct UFCCDENs.  5 Conclusions In the context of global climate change and rapid urbanization, it is urgent to study reliable methods capable of assessing UFCCDEN risk for dealing with increasingly frequent flood disasters. The framework proposed in this study assesses the UFCCDEN vulnerability effectively from a network perspective by leveraging an EEG that integrates social media data. An EEG allows for social media data to be used as a data source, which can achieve the rapid construction of a UFCCDEN. Complex network theory is applied to quantify the importance of disaster events and the vulnerability of disaster causal chains, allowing the interactions between urban floods and the compound disaster events caused by them to be explored. The decreases in the network global efficiency demonstrated the excellent performance of the proposed framework. We apply the proposed framework to Guangzhou, a coastal megacity located at the Pearl River Delta in China, which suffers from urban floods due to factors such as rainstorms, astronomical tides, and storm surges. The main conclusions can be summarized as follows. 1) Social media data can provide detailed and valid information about UFCCDEs, which can be used to construct the UFCCDEN based on the EEG. 2) Waterlogging is found to be the most important disaster event of the UFCCDEN in Guangzhou. Furthermore, the power facility, drainage facility, and road should be given top priority in the prevention and mitigation of urban floods due to their significant cascading amplification effects. 3) The proposed framework can markedly decrease the propagation efficiency of the UFCCDEN. Based on the assessment results of disaster events and causal chains, the global efficiency of the UFCCDEN decreased by 37–62 % and 44 %, respectively. Overall, this study provides a new framework to mitigate urban flood risks, which considers the interactions between disaster events caused by floods from a network perspective. This could help governments and communities better deal with increasingly frequent urban floods with a convenient and effective framework.
1 Introduction With the intensification of human activities and the continuous demand for energy resources, growing numbers of reservoirs are constructed worldwide (Mishra & Jain, 2022; Zhou et al., 2023 ). As of 2021, China alone built over 98,000 reservoirs, encompassing nearly 40 % of the world’s largest reservoirs (Song et al., 2022 ). However, while reservoir construction can promote economic and social development, it might also introduce geologic hazards (Dun et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Vassileva et al., 2023 ). For example, a tragic history event was a huge landslide that occurred on the southern slope of the Vajont reservoir in Italy in 1963, killing about 2,600 people (Zangerl et al., 2010 ). Additionally, since the construction and operation of the Three Gorges Reservoir, the periodic fluctuation of the reservoir water level has triggered many landslides, causing disastrous effects on its surroundings (Jiang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Song et al., 2024 ). Hence, the precise identification of landslides distributed around reservoirs, coupled with an in-depth study of the response of different types of landslide deformation to the triggering factors, becomes particularly vital in landslide risk management. The steep topography and complex geological conditions surrounding hydropower stations contribute to the widespread distribution, strong concealment, and inaccessibility of reservoir landslides (Dun et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Particularly, under the influence of water level fluctuation and rainfall, the unstable slopes just show signs of deformation, which are often ignored by traditional monitoring methods (Du et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b ). Addressing this challenge, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) emerges as the preferred solution for identifying reservoir landslides, leveraging its advantages of high precision, wide coverage, and weather independence (Liu et al., 2021; Vassileva et al., 2023 ). Multi-temporal InSAR (MT-InSAR) has been successfully applied in identifying potential landslides in various places such as the Rules Reservoir in Spain (Reyes-Carmona, et al., 2020, 2021 ), the Jinsha River basin (Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022 ), the Three Gorges Reservoir (Zhou et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023b ), and the upper reaches of the Yellow River (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2023 ). These case studies demonstrated the potential of InSAR technology in an early identification of reservoir landsliding. Nevertheless, the application of this technology faces some technical challenges that cannot be ignored. First, due to limitations in wavelength and acquisition frequency, InSAR is more suitable for monitoring slow-moving landslides (Du et al., 2024 ). Second, owing to the geometric mode of side-looking imaging in SAR, geometric distortion occurs, leading to blind areas in landslide identification and, hence, landslide omission (Zhu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b ). Furthermore, current InSAR technology is constrained by its ability to capture only one-dimensional deformation information, falling short in comprehensively revealing the actual kinematic behavior of landslides (Hu et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2022 ). To overcome these limitations, an approach that combines ascending and descending data was applied. It not only effectively reduces the impact of geometric distortion on monitoring results, but also solves the two-dimensional deformation, thereby enabling an evaluation of information on landslide deformation in multiple directions. The Baihetan Hydropower Station, the second largest in China, began impounding water on 7 April 2021, raising concerns about landslide risks in the surrounding area (Dai et al., 2023 ). Hence, studies included the early detection of landslides before the impoundment (Dun et al., 2021 ), landslide inventory and characterization analysis (Li et al., 2022 ), assessment of landslide susceptibility (Xue et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2023 ), time-lag response of landslide to water level changes during the impoundment (Yang et al., 2023c ), automatic identification of active landslides (Liu et al., 2024b ), and an in-depth investigation of the deformation characteristics and mechanism of the Wangjiashan landslide (Wu et al., 2022; Yi et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b ). Although these studies provided valuable insights into the formation and dynamics of landslides in the Baihetan Reservoir region, research on the response relationships between deformation of different types of landslides and triggering factors is still insufficient. Moreover, while existing studies, based on short-term single-point monitoring data, did classify the landslides into steady-type, exponential-type, convergent-type, and step-like (Miao et al., 2018; Du et al., 2020 ), most of them were only qualitative assessments. In this study, a quantitative analysis of the displacement–time curve obtained by the InSAR technique was performed, which provided a robust foundation for accurately evaluating different deformation types. Meanwhile, the combination of wavelet analysis, a powerful signal analysis tool, can reveal the non-linear displacement–time series characteristics of landslide motion at different time scales (Jiang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024 ), which provides a new perspective on studying deformation and its triggering factors of different landslides types. In this study, we conducted an early identification of geological hazards and a quantitative study of deformation patterns in the Baihetan Reservoir region based on ascending and descending Sentinel-1A datasets, using the MT-InSAR method. By combining Line-of-sight (LOS) deformation velocity from both datasets, we extracted two-dimensional deformation velocity and comprehensively analyzed the deformation characteristics of landslides. Furthermore, we performed a quantitative analysis of the normalized displacement curves for four types of landslides and combined with the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) field investigation to deeply analyze the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of landslides. Eventually, we explored the relationship between landslide deformation and rainfall as well as reservoir water levels. This study provides a basis for the early identification and monitoring of landslides at reservoirs.  2 Study area The study area covers the Baihetan hydropower station reservoir and its surroundings between Ningnan County and Qiaojia County, China (Fig. 1  a). It is situated in the transition zone from the eastern margin of the Tibetan and Sichuan-Western Plateau to the Yunnan-Gui Plateau and Sichuan Basin (Liu et al., 2024b ). The climate is mainly subtropical, with a mean annual temperature and precipitation of 21℃ and 822.7 mm, respectively. Affected by the southeast ocean monsoon, rainfall is mainly concentrated in summer between June and August (Li et al., 2022 ). Proterozoic to Quaternary strata make up the region and form outcrops (Dai et al., 2023 ). The region is tectonically quite active and traversed by many faults such as Xiaojiang, Daliangshan, and Zemuhe (Fig. 1 b). Earthquakes, erosion, rainfall, and reservoir water level fluctuations have triggered numerous reservoir landslides (Dun et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2023 ), representing a severe geologic hazard, particularly in relation to several engineering activities.  3 Materials and methodology 3.1 MT-InSAR analysis In this study, both ascending and descending Sentinel-1A datasets covering the study region were selected (Table 1  ). SAR images were co-registered and resampled, assisted by the POD Precise Orbit Ephemerides and the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data at 30 m-resolution (Fig. S1 ). The interferometric processing follows the principle of generating two interferometric pairs for each data (Fig. 2  ). Meanwhile, precision baselines were obtained using the high-quality unwrapping phase and DEM data to mitigate the error effects of initial baselines. Subsequently, a spectral diversity criteria threshold of 0.42 and a low temporal amplitude variation criteria threshold of 2.2 were used to select the single-look phase (Liu et al., 2022 ). A multi-looking ratio of 12:3 was used to select the multi-look phase that was adaptively filtered to obtain the optimal phase. After combining single- and multi-phase elements, regression analysis was used to process the differential interferometric phases to obtain linear deformation, topographic residuals, and residual phases (Wegmüller et al., 2021 ). During this process, to correct the topographic residual phase, a linear model based on the perpendicular baseline was used (Shi et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a ). Given the complex topography in mountainous regions, the atmospheric component is primarily divided into topographic and turbulent atmospheres. Topographic atmospheric estimation relied on a linear relationship with elevation-related phase components (Liu et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2022 ), while spatiotemporal filtering techniques were applied in turbulent atmospheric extraction (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Ultimately, after removing the error phases, the least squares method was used for the inversion of time-series displacements and deformation velocities.  3.2 Two-dimensional deformation velocity decomposition While InSAR can obtain LOS one-dimensional deformation information utilizing single-orbit SAR data, this approach only partially reflects on deformation details (Shi et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022 ). To address this limitation, data from multiple orbital tracks are combined in extracting two-dimensional motion information (Hu et al., 2014; Du et al., 2023 ). Hence, we employed ascending and descending orbit data from Sentinel-1A. Studies indicated that the contribution of the north–south component to the overall deformation is relatively minor and can be reasonably disregarded (Shi et al., 2019 ). To describe the vertical and east–west landslide deformation, a two-dimensional deformation decomposition was conducted based on Equation (1)  (Motagh et al., 2017; Aslan et al., 2019 ):(1) d LOS  asc   = cos θ asc   · d U  - sin θ asc   cos α asc   · d E     d LOS  de s   = cos θ des   · d U  - sin θ des   cos α des  · d E          where θ asc      and θ des      are the incidence angles of ascending and descending orbit data, respectively; α asc      and α des     are the heading angles of ascending and descending orbit data, respectively. Moreover, the cumulative displacement in the east–west and vertical directions can be calculated by numerical integration (Shi et al., 2022; Du et al., 2023 ).  3.3 Wavelet analysis Wavelet analysis is a common signal analysis tool. In this study, wavelet transform correlation (WTC) and cross wavelet transform (XWT) were utilized to reveal the non-linear displacement time series characteristics of landslide motion at different scales (Du et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024 ). XWT can measure the distribution pattern of different time series over time in a given period, assuming two different time series are x n     and y n    , then XWT is defined as:(2) W n  xy   ( s , t )  = W n  x  ( s , t )  ∗ W n  y ∗   ( s , t )       where W n  y ∗   ( s , t )     represents the complex conjugate W n  y  ( s , t )    , and cross wavelet spectrum W n  xy   ( s , t )     describes the correlation of two time series at scale s and in time t. WTC is used to analyze the correlation between two time series:(3) R n  xy   = | S [ W n  xy   ]  S [ W n  y  ]  S [ W n  y  ]     |      where, S    is the smoothing operator, and R n  xy      represents the wavelet coherence between time series x n     and y n    .
