The value of wavelet coherence ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 means no correlation and 1 means perfect correlation.   4 Results 4.1 The reservoir landslides detected by MT-InSAR Fig. 3   illustrates the LOS deformation velocity for the study area retrieved from ascending and descending Sentinel-1A datasets. While positive values (blue) indicate motion toward the satellite, negative values (red) denote motion away from it. For Sentinel-1A data, when the absolute value of the LOS deformation velocity of a slope is greater than 10 mm/yr, the slope is considered to be in an unstable state (Zhu et al., 2023 ). About 94 % of the measured displacement velocities obtained from the ascending and descending datasets were distributed between −10 and 10 mm/yr (Fig. 3 c, d), with a median of −1.94 mm/yr for the ascending and of −1.08 mm/yr for the descending data, indicating that the region is generally stable. The observation data collected by two Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) continuous stations (Fig. 3 b) were projected into the LOS direction of the descending orbit Sentinel-1A dataset (Fig. 4  ). The root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of the GNSS observations and InSAR monitoring results were calculated to be 1.69 mm and 5.2 mm, respectively, demonstrating a good consistency between both and, hence, validating the reliability of InSAR monitoring. The LOS deformation velocities detected for the ascending and descending data were inconsistent (Fig. 3 a, b) as they ranged from −190.74 to 70.95 mm/yr for the ascending data and from −137.19 to 79.41 mm/yr for the descending data. In addition, a total of 44 unstable slopes with significant deformation were detected from the average LOS deformation velocity maps (Fig. 5  ), of which 31 were identified from ascending data, 25 from descending data, and 12 from both ascending and descending data. These results illustrate that the use of ascending and descending datasets to detect regional unstable slopes can serve to complement and validate each other, making the monitoring results more reliable. We further decomposed the LOS deformation velocity obtained from the ascending and descending data to generate a two-dimensional deformation velocity map (Fig. 3 e, f). Positive values denote eastward and vertical upward movement. From the two-dimensional deformation results, the deformation velocity in the east–west direction ranges from −97.61 to 142.42 mm/yr (Fig. 3 e), indicating that the motion of the unstable slopes is faster to the east than to the west. The vertical deformation velocity is between −91.97 and 50.14 mm/yr (Fig. 3 f), illustrating that the movement of unstable slopes in the vertical direction is dominated by subsidence, while it locally shows uplift due to soil accumulation, construction and other factors. The deformation velocity decomposition in the east–west and vertical directions requires that both ascending and descending data are based on sufficient measurement points. Nevertheless, due to the geometric distortion of side-looking imaging (such as shadowing, foreshortening and layover), the measurement points obtained from ascending and descending data in the same region are usually not completely consistent, i.e., the density of measurement points in the east–west direction and the vertical direction will be lower than that in the LOS direction.  4.2 Motion dynamics of selected landslides According to previous studies on deformation patterns of reservoir landslides and based on our results of displacement deformation characteristics in the study area, we classified selected landslides as follows: Yiwan (L27) as of convergent-type, Dadou (L39) as of steady-type, Xiaomidi (L38) as of exponential-type, and Tianjiapingzi (L15) as of periodic-type. To better understand landslide motion, we combined the results from InSAR analysis with those from UAV and field surveys (Fig. 6  ). The Yiwan landslide is a large complex (red solid line) with a smaller active portion on its right side (Fig. 6 a(i)), where a collapse of loose material damaged the road (Fig. 6 a(i)). The landslide deformation at the foot is larger than at the top, probably indicating retrogression. We found a crack in the building at the back end of Dadou village (Fig. 6 b(i)). Many smaller collapses are scattered across the landslide (Fig. 6 b(i)), and their loose material was deposited in mountain gullies, which presents a potential hazard of debris flows during the rainy season. The landslide surface significantly changed after deformation with a maximum velocity of –33.47 mm/yr (Fig. 6 b(ii)). There is a collapse deformation on the surface of the Xiaomidi landslide, exposing red clay, and a few small collapses were observed the landslide’s surroundings, where loose material was deposited in narrow channels at the bottom by the river (Fig. 6 c(i)). This typical gully topography comprises also loose sediments that can evolve into debris flows during rainstorms and may increase the silt load of the river, impacting economic activities. Fig. 6 c(ii) demonstrates that the deformation is more severe on the left side of the landslide, where the deformation velocity reaches –22.49 mm/yr. The Tianjiapingzi landslide is a large landslide complex with a small landslide at its surface (Fig. 6 d(i)). The small landslide gradually expands in width from top to bottom and accumulated a larger amount of loose material at the foot of the slope. To prevent further movement, retaining walls have been constructed. During field investigation, we noticed that the original road in the center of the landslide had been destroyed by the deformation and a new one had been constructed. Furthermore, several collapses were observed on both sides of the road (Fig. 6 d(i)), particularly at the foot of the landslide where loose material slid into the river and safety warning signs have been placed. Fig. 6 d(ii) illustrates the significant landslide surface deformation with the maximum velocity of −107.58 mm/yr. 4.2.1 Convergent-type landslide deformation Time series points P1 and P2 (Fig. 6 a(ii)) were selected to further study the relationship between landslide displacement and velocity in relation to daily rainfall and reservoir water level from 19 February 2017 to 29 June 2022 (Fig. 7  ). The LOS displacement curves of P1 and P2 exhibit initially high velocity, and then gradually become stable (Fig. 7 a). The cumulative displacement was −151.34 mm at P1 and −153.3 mm at P2. We normalized the displacement data to eliminate the interference by errors or other factors, and performed exponential fitting on the normalized displacement time curve to quantitatively describe the deformation trend of this convergent-type landslide (Fig. 7 b). We found that the fitting improved the results, with a R2   of 0.96 for P1 and 0.98 for P2. Thus, it can be concluded that the convergent-type landslide is first displaced at a higher velocity, before it gradually stabilizes in agreement with an exponential fit. We further analyzed the two-dimensional time series displacement of the landslide (Fig. 7 c), and found that it was dominated by vertical motion with a vertical displacement of −155.71 mm at P1 and −148.46 mm at P2. Notably, the deformation trend of the displacement in vertical direction was similar to that in the LOS direction, which further confirms the evaluation of the landslide deformation pattern. Fig. 7 a exhibits that the movement velocity at P1 and P2 was almost consistent except for larger fluctuations on 14 May 2017, 18 March 2021, and 9 August 2021. The acceleration of the landslide on 14 May 2017, occurred at the beginning of the rainy season, presumably due to the impact of the earthquake on 5 January 2017, the severe ground shaking produced ground cracks, and the infiltration of rainwater reduced the shear strength, thus promoting the accelerated movement of the landslide (Bayer et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021 ). Although rainfall remained stable in the following rainy seasons and heavy rainfall occurred on 30 June 2020 (Fig. 7 c), the movement velocity remained relatively stable, suggesting that the movement may be weakly related to rainfall. However, on 18 March 2021, the velocity suddenly increased again. We noticed that concurrently the Baihetan reservoir was filled for the first time and its water level rose rapidly, which suggest may have caused the acceleration of the landslide. This dynamic relationship occurred again on 9 August 2021, when the movement velocity again increased (Fig. 7 c). In summary, these results suggest that there is a significant correlation between reservoir water level fluctuations and the movement velocity of landslides.  4.2.2 Steady-type landslide deformation We further studied the evolution of landslide displacement and velocity at the time series points P3 and P4 (Fig. 6 b(ii)) in connection with daily rainfall and reservoir water level from 19 February 2017 to 29 June 2022 (Fig. 8  ). The LOS displacement curves exhibit a trend of steady growth, with cumulative displacements of −158.58 mm at P3 and −128.99 mm at P4 (Fig. 8 a). Linear fitting was conducted to quantitatively describe the variation in the steady-type landslide displacement curves, revealing robust fits with R2   of 0.96 for P3 and 0.95 for P4 (Fig. 8 b). Therefore, the displacement curves of steady-type landslides not only demonstrate a consistently increasing trend but also agree with linear fitting. Moreover, the time series displacements in the east–west and vertical directions showed that landslide moved similarly in the both directions (Fig. 8 c): the vertical displacements were −111.79 mm at P3 and −100.11 mm at P4, while the east–west displacements were −114.28 mm at P3 and −83.04 mm at P4. Furthermore, the displacement curves of the landslides indicate distinct linear characteristics in both directions, providing a reference for understanding the deformation patterns of steady-type landslides. Fig. 8 a shows that during the 2017–2022 rainy season, the landslide movement velocity at P3 and P4 fluctuated significantly. Several events of accelerated landsliding occurred mostly during the annual rainy season, especially after an event of heavy rainfall on 30 June 2020 that was followed by fast movement for seven subsequent days (Fig. 8 c). These results suggest that the events of accelerated landsliding were likely triggered by short high-intensity rainfalls. Note that the landslide acceleration event of 28 July 2021 occurred not only during the rainy season, but also during a period of falling water levels that are prone to cause landslides, so it can be inferred that the acceleration may have been determined by the combination of rainfall and water level fluctuations.  4.2.3 Exponential-type landslide deformation The link between landslide displacement and velocity in relation to daily rainfall and reservoir water levels was further investigated at P5 and P6 for the period from 19 February 2017 to 29 June 2022 (Fig. 9  ). The displacement curves for both points show a trend of increase, with cumulative displacements of −110.14 mm for P5 and −105.61 mm for P6 (Fig. 9 a). To quantitatively depict the exponential-type landslide displacement curves, exponential fitting was adopted, revealing good fits with R2   values of 0.98 for P5 and 0.97 for P6 (Fig. 9 b). Therefore, the displacement curve of exponential-type landslide not only shows an increasing trend, but also conforms to exponential fitting. Fig. 9 c displays the two-dimensional time series displacement of the landslide, showing significant deformation in the east–west direction and relatively minor deformation in the vertical direction. However, despite the small vertical deformation, the displacement curve in the vertical direction exhibits a similar deformation trend to that of the LOS displacement curve, which provides a new perspective for understanding the deformation pattern of landslides. Fig. 9 a illustrates that the movement velocity of P5 and P6 fluctuates significantly during the rainy season each year and generally follows the seasonal cycle. However, landslide acceleration on 8 April 2017 occurred before the start of the rainy season, while landslide acceleration occurred after the onset of the rainy season from 2018 to 2021. It can be assumed that the 2017 event was caused by the earthquake on 5 January 2017 (Bayer et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021 ). In contrast, the 2018 to 2021 events follow the rainfall cycle, indicating a correlation between the slow movement of landslides and precipitation. Nevertheless, the 2021 event occurred not only during the rainy season, but also during a significant rise in reservoir water levels (Fig. 9 c). Thus, further in-depth analysis and discussion are needed to determine whether this acceleration was influenced by rainfall factors alone or by a combination of rainfall and reservoir water level fluctuations.  4.2.4 Periodic-type landslide deformation Through the analysis at time series points P7 and P8 (Fig. 6 d(ii)), the relationship between landslide displacement and velocity and daily rainfall and reservoir water level from 1 March 2017 to 27 June 2022 was further studied (Fig. 10  ). The displacement curves at P7 and P8 exhibit periodic fluctuations, with cumulative displacements of 239.46 mm and 154.44 mm, respectively (Fig. 10 a). To quantitatively characterize the trend of the periodic-type landslide displacement curve, we perform Fourier fitting and find that the fitting trend of two points is better, with R2   of 0.98 and 0.96, respectively (Fig. 10 b). Thus, the displacement curve of periodic-type landslide not only manifests periodic fluctuation, but also conforms to Fourier fitting. Furthermore, the two-dimensional deformation characteristics in the east–west and vertical directions were further explored (Fig. 10 c). It was found that significant cumulative east–west displacements of −435.21 mm at P7 and −489.15 mm at P8. Meanwhile, the vertical displacement curve exhibited periodic fluctuations similar to the LOS displacement curve, with cumulative displacements of −190.50 mm at P7 and −123.26 mm at P8. Analyzing displacement data in both directions contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the deformation patterns of periodic-type landslides. Fig. 10 a presents the dynamic changes of the velocity at P7 and P8, revealing the ongoing motion of the landslide. Notably, when the displacements of P7 and P8 increase, it corresponds to the non-rainy season, whereas decreases in displacement coincide with the rainy season (Fig. 10 c). This phenomenon suggests that there is a negative response between rainfall and the continuous motion of the landslide. These findings underscore the correlation between rainfall and slow landslide movement. Based on the above findings, the LOS time series displacement data of the remaining 40 landslides were normalized (Fig. S2 ). There are 6 convergent-type landslides, 27 steady-type landslides, 3 exponential-type landslides, and 4 periodic-type landslides. Detailed information on location, aspect, slope, velocity, and deformation pattern of these landslides can be found in Table S1 . This supports the idea that the normalized time series displacement curve analysis adopted in this study can be applied to active landslides in other reservoir regions.   4.3 Deformation response to rainfall and reservoir water levels The described results and conclusions (see Figs. 7–10 ) found a correlation between four types of landslides in the study area and rainfall and/or reservoir water levels, that deserve further investigation. Landslide displacement is mainly affected by geology and trigger factors (Jiang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024 ). To describe the relationship between landslide displacements and trigger factors, linear fitting was used to remove the trend term displacements, thereby separating the non-linear displacement (Fig. S3 ). Previous studies concerned with the correlation between landslides and rainfall considered an antecedent rainfall period of over 30 to 40 days depending on the specifics of the location (Guzzetti et al., 2007; Bayer et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2023 ). Consequently, it was of interest to explore the relationship between landslide displacement and rainfall under different rainfall cycles. The correlations between landslide non-linear displacement and rainfall are displayed in Fig. 11  . Prior to any rainfall event, there is no significant correlation between the non-linear displacement of the Yiwan landslide and rainfall (Fig. 11 a). Despite abundant rainfall during the period of 2018–2022 (Fig. 7 c), the increase in landslide displacement remains relatively small, suggesting a limited impact of rainfall on landslide dynamics. When lead-up rainfall beyond twelve days is aggregated into the effective rainfall, the Dadou landslide and rainfall showed a correlation of 0.19 with a p-value much lower than 0.05, and even in case of longer antecedent rainfall cycles, the p-value remained relatively low (Fig. 11 b). This implies that longer rainfall periods may trigger this type of landslide. When rainfall lasts between 36 and 47 days, the Xiaomidi landslide and rainfall showed a correlation higher than −0.11 with a p-value well below 0.05 (Fig. 11 c). The Tianjiapingzi landslide and rainfall showed a relatively high correlation with a p-value of around 0.01 when rainfall exceeds two days, which indicates a relatively short response time (Fig. 11 d). Given that the peak correlation coefficients were reached when preceding rainfall lasted between 2 and 47 days, the non-linear displacement of four landslides were compared with the previous 36 days of rainfall (Fig. 12  ). No correlation was found between the non-linear displacement of the Yiwan landslide and rainfall (Fig. 12 a). The non-linear displacement of the Dadou and Xiaomidi landslides showed relatively weak correlations with rainfall (Fig. 12 b, c). The non-linear displacement of the Tianjiapingzi landslide exhibited a moderate correlation with rainfall (Fig. 12 d). To further verify these findings, an in-depth study was conducted using wavelet analysis on the time series non-linear displacement of the landslides and rainfall. WTC results further confirmed that there is no correlation between the Yiwan landslide and rainfall (Fig. 13  a(i)), while the other three landslides showed varying degrees of correlation with rainfall (Fig. 13 b(i), c(i), d(i)). XWT results revealed a certain lag between non-linear displacement and rainfall for the Dadou, Xiaomidi, and Tianjiapingzi landslides (Fig. 13 b(ii), c(ii), d(ii))). Additional investigations based on wavelet analysis examined the relationship between the east–west and vertical non-linear displacements of these four landslides and rainfall (Fig. S4 ). The results showed that the non-linear displacements of the Yiwan landslide in both east–west and vertical directions were not correlated with rainfall, while the non-linear displacements of the other three landslides showed a correlation with rainfall for both directions. Notably, WTC results for both the east–west and vertical directions of the Dadou landslide were similar to those in LOS direction (Fig. S4 b(i)). WTC results for the vertical direction of the Xiaomidi and Tianjiapingzi landslides also coincide with those in LOS direction (Fig. S4 c(i), d(i)), further confirming the above findings (Figs. 7–10 ). The wavelet analysis was then used to study the relationship between non-linear displacements in LOS direction and rainfall for the remaining 40 landslides (Figs. S5 , 6). The results show that 25 of the steady-type landslides were associated with rainfall and 2 were unrelated to it. One of the convergent-type landslides was related to rainfall, and 5 were unrelated. Two exponential-type landslides were related to rainfall, and 1 was unrelated. All 4 periodic-type landslides were correlated with rainfall. Therefore, in the Baihetan Reservoir region, steady-type, exponential-type and periodic-type landslides are mainly affected by rainfall, while most convergent-type landslides have no significant relationship with it. These observations provide useful insights into the relationship between a specific landslide type and rainfall. Furthermore, the relationship between displacement and reservoir water level was explored (Fig. 14  ). There is a strong correlation between non-linear displacement of the Yiwan, Dadou, and Xiaomidi landslides and reservoir water levels (Fig. 14 a–c). Conversely, the non-linear displacement of the Tianjiapingzi landslide showed no apparent correlation with reservoir water level (Fig. 14 d). Moreover, the relationship between LOS non-linear displacement and water level for the remaining 40 landslides revealed that 20 steady-type, 5 convergent-type, and 3 exponential-type landslides were correlated with water level fluctuations (Figs. S7 , 8). Among the 4 periodic-type landslides, only one landslide showed a correlation with water level fluctuation. This implies that convergent-type, steady-type, and exponential-type landslides are significantly affected by reservoir water level fluctuations during impoundment.   5 Discussion 5.1 Normalized displacement curves of four landslide types Under the influence of external factors such as water level fluctuation and rainfall, landslides undergo different deformation processes, resulting in significant differences in their deformation patterns (Wu et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2024 ). Surface displacement monitoring has become a crucial basis for accurately identifying landslide deformation patterns (Intrieri et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023a ). Therefore, surface displacement monitoring systems are usually established to monitor landslides, and the monitoring results are often described by displacement–time curves (Intrieri et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019 ). Scholars, based on these monitoring data, have classified the deformation patterns into steady-type, exponential-type, convergent-type, step-like, etc., and have detailed the morphological characteristics of displacement–time curves for each type, aiding in the interpretation of landslide deformation patterns (Miao et al., 2018; Du et al., 2020 ). Intensified by extreme rainfall events and human activities, landslides are significantly affected by external factors, resulting in more complex displacement deformation curves (Guo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023a; Zhu et al., 2023 ). This may make it difficult for the actual displacement curves to simply conform to the previously established patterns (Chen et al., 2021 ), thus posing challenges to the accurate judgment of landslide deformation patterns. To eliminate errors and mitigate the influence of external factors, the acquired displacement data were normalized. After normalization, we conducted a quantitative analysis of the normalized displacement curves, revealing that convergent-type landslides conform to an exponential function, manifesting initial rapid movement that gradually stabilizes (Fig. 7 ). Steady-type landslides follow a linear function, demonstrating consistent movement speed over a prolonged period (Fig. 8 ). Exponential-type landslides exhibit characteristics of an exponential function, a slow initial velocity that gradually accelerates (Fig. 9 ). Periodic-type landslides agree with a Fourier periodic function, displaying periodic fluctuations in displacement (Fig. 10 ). Based on these findings, we created a morphological characteristic schematic of the normalized displacement–time curve for each of the four landslide types (Fig. 15  ). This schematic, consistent with previous research findings, confirms the accuracy of our study. Hence, utilizing normalized displacement–time curve schematic for interpreting landslide deformation patterns can not only effectively eliminate external influences on landslide curves, but also help to accurately judge landslide types, providing a scientific basis for taking corresponding prevention and control measures.  5.2 Regulation mechanism of rainfall and reservoir water levels on landslide movement Through the analysis of the time series behavior of four landslide types, we found that the movements of steady-type, exponential-type, and periodic-type landslides are all influenced by rainfall (Figs. 7-10 ). Comparisons with antecedent rainfall reveal that steady-type and exponential-type landslides are primarily affected by accumulated rainfall in the preceding 12 to 47 days (Fig. 11 b, c). This may be due to the gradual saturation of landslide bodies under continuous rainfall, leading to a gradual reduction in shear strength, thereby affecting overall stability and eventually triggering landslide movement (Bayer et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021 ). In contrast, the periodic-type exhibits a more rapid response to rainfall, showing signs of movement with approximately two days after rainfall (Fig. 11 d). This phenomenon may be attributed to differences in their physical properties, topographic conditions, and landslide depths (Bayer et al., 2018 ), resulting in significant differences in the sensitivity of their response to rainfall. The Baihetan Hydropower Station first started to store water on 7 April 2021, and its water level rose to 825 m by 24 October 2022 (Dai et al., 2023 ). Significant fluctuations in water levels during this period potentially adversely affected the surrounding area, leading to landslide destabilization (Vassileva et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Our findings document that convergent-type, steady-type, and exponential-type landslides are affected by water level fluctuations (Figs. 7, 8, 9 ). Notably, changes in reservoir water levels may affect landslides through two different mechanisms (Tang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022 ). When the reservoir water level rises significantly, the pore water pressure also increases, and this change in pressure may trigger or accelerate landslide movement (Tang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023a ). The convergent-type and exponential-type landslides in the study area are closely related to this phenomenon (Figs. 7, 9 ). Conversely, during the process of reservoir water level drop, pore water pressure decreases, resulting in seepage pressure gradually pointing to the surface of the landslide, increasing the sliding force, and thus accelerating the landslide movement (Yin et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2021 ). In the study area, steady-type landslides conform to this characteristic (Fig. 8 ). Additionally, during the operation of the reservoir, the periodic changes in water level ‘rise-drop’, trigger repeated wet-dry cycles for reservoir landslides. This cycle may cause changes in the movement state of landslides, thereby affecting their stability (Zhou et al., 2023 ). However, relying solely on remote sensing data, we found it challenging to accurately reveal the relevant processes of the landslides studied. Therefore, we emphasized the necessity of conducting in-depth field investigations and simulation studies to gain a more comprehensive and profound understanding of the complex mechanisms involved in landslide evolution.  5.3 Limitations and improvements Reservoirs cover wider areas, and complex and changeable natural environments are a challenge in landslide monitoring (Dun et al., 2021 ). While traditional measurement techniques, such as precise leveling, GNSS, and inclinometers, have high accuracy in the monitoring of known landslides, they are not useful in identifying landslides (Du et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023c ). Although optical remote sensing images are suitable for landslide identification in larger areas, image quality is susceptible to disturbances such as clouds cover (Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022 ). UAVs offer convenience in operation but have limited coverage and higher operating costs, making them unsuitable for large-scale and high-frequency landslide identification and monitoring. They are more suitable for rapid response in emergency situations (Du et al., 2024 ). However, InSAR technology, with its advantages of all-day and all-weather monitoring capabilities, has demonstrated great potential in identification and monitoring of landslides at reservoirs (Ye et al., 2024 ). Compared with the performance of traditional time-series InSAR in the Baihetan Reservoir region, the time-series InSAR analysis of single- and multi-look phases in this study showed that the method has significant advantages. (i) Except for the area with geometric distortion and average coherence less than 0.1, the measuring points almost cover the entire study area. (ii) The extraction of multi-look phase avoids the use of complex algorithms for DS point identification, allowing the method to be applied in the identification and monitoring at a large scale. (iii) The combination of single- and multi-look phases allows for a much faster processing speed when compared with the method that combines PS and DS. However, this method also has some limitations. The spatial resolution of the multi-look phase is about 40 m, which is not suitable for the identification and monitoring of small landslides (Liu et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the water vapor content in the surrounding of the reservoir is high, which negatively impacts traditional atmospheric phase removal methods; hence, additional meteorological data such as ERA-5 or GACOS are needed (Zhang et al., 2022; Du et al., 2023 ). Thus, next steps to improve the here presented method should include the enhancement of spatial resolution and introduction of additional atmospheric data. This should allow for even more accurate and reliable landslide identification and monitoring in reservoir areas.   6 Conclusions The vulnerability of a reservoir area environment requires rigorous monitoring. We conducted an early detection study of unstable slopes in the Baihetan reservoir area employing the MT-InSAR analysis approach. When quantitatively analyzing the normalized displacement curves of four landslide types, results demonstrated that the convergent-type landslide exhibited a rapid initial displacement, followed by gradual stabilization, fitting an exponential model. In contrast, steady-type landslides exhibited a steady growth trend, but also conformed to linear fitting. Exponential-type landslides displayed displacement growth conforming to an exponential model. Periodic-type landslides showed periodic fluctuation, but also conformed to Fourier fitting. Moreover, through wavelet analysis between non-linear displacement and antecedent rainfall in the preceding 36 days, along with reservoir water levels, we confirmed that water level fluctuations significantly affect convergent-type landslides. Meanwhile, steady-type and exponential-type landslides are subject to an impact from both rainfall and water level fluctuations, whereas periodic-type landslides are primarily influenced by rainfall. This study provides critical insights into the evolution of landslides in the reservoir area, thereby establishing a scientific foundation for the development of effective monitoring and mitigation measures.
1 Introduction Global landscapes (10–15 %) are covered by numerous bedrock outcrops worldwide. These bedrock outcrops form a variety of surface habitats such as fissures, ditches, and pits, which are widespread in rocky environments (Ford and Williams, 2007; Peng and Wang, 2012; Yue et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2022 ). Bedrock outcrops are a visual indicator of karst desertification and a characteristic karst region feature (Yuan, 1997; Jiang et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2020 ). The surface morphology of these bedrock outcrops is quite different from that of other landforms. In addition to influencing soil physical and chemical properties and promoting topographic heterogeneity, bedrock outcrop surface morphology can influence rainfall infiltration and surface runoff processes, ultimately promoting the development of complex hydrological systems (Göransson et al., 2014; Sohrt et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020b ). This is attributed to the fact that outcrop surfaces with weak or un-weathered bedrock are prone to water flow when receiving rainfall because of their weak permeability. In previous studies, we referred to this flow as rock surface flow (Gersper and Holowaychuk, 1971; Wilcox et al., 2007; Kidron and Starinsky, 2012; Fu et al., 2015 ). Rock surface flow is a type of runoff that drives surface erosion and underground leakage in rocky desertified areas. Previous studies have shown that the runoff formed by rainfall collected from bedrock outcrop rock surfaces with different morphologies has different effects on soil erosion on the slopes below (Ao et al., 2024 ). However, it is unclear whether there are differences in the effects of bedrock outcrops with different rock surface morphologies on slope runoff production. In addition, outcropping rock alters slope soil permeability and runoff behaviour (Zhao et al., 2020a ), of which the rock–soil interface (CRSI) is an important factor influencing this behaviour. The majority of previous studies on the in situ monitoring of runoff processes on karst slopes were based on the excavation section, simulated rainfall, dye tracers, soil moisture monitoring, ground penetrating radar, and other test techniques and methods (Fu et al, 2016; Peng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020 ). These results show that the CRSI is an important pathway for the development of soil preferential flow. As a result, the rock surface flow or surface runoff can preferentially flow downwards at the CRSI with a higher infiltration rate (Sohrt et al., 2014 ), in which such a infiltration rate potentially even exceeds the regional maximum rainfall intensity. However, others have shown that soils at the CRSI are less permeable than soils away from them (Yang et al., 2023 ). Regardless of CRSI permeability, the ability of the rock surface flow to produce surface runoff at the soil surface is entirely dependent on the soil infiltration rate and water storage capacity at the CRSI, where the rock surface flow first permeates. Therefore, it is necessary to quantify and determine whether surface runoff could be produced through the soil infiltration rate and water storage capacity at the CRSI. Based on this, it can help quantify the influence of outcrop bedrock surfaces on surface runoff formation and hydrological behaviour from rock surfaces. An increase in bedrock outcrops can lead to a shallower soil profile or lower soil amount, and further result in a decrease in soil water storage per unit area and an increase in water leakage at the CRSI (Chen et al., 2022 ). Previous studies on runoff generation in karst areas have highlighted the important role of bedrock outcrops and CRSI. Runoff from bedrock outcrops is often attributed to the excess infiltration mechanism and can contribute significantly to peak flood flows (Burns et al., 2001 ). Moreover, discontinuities in infiltration rates at bedrock outcrops can drive surface runoff through an excess infiltration runoff process (Meng et al., 2023 ). Nonetheless, it is currently unclear how the bedrock outcrops and CRSI affect the surface runoff through what mechanism of runoff generation. Currently, studies of surface runoff in karsts have generally suggested that excess saturation and infiltration runoff can occur simultaneously on karst slopes or even be dominated by excess saturation runoff, but the specific trigger mechanism has not been well explained. Researchers have primarily studied slopes, watersheds, and simulated rainfall experiments (Peng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023 ). These studies are important for understanding how flow and hydrological processes occur in karst areas. Nevertheless, the role of outcrop bedrock in the runoff process and mechanism on the karst slope is still unclear. Although some studies have investigated the effects of outcrop bedrock on the spatial distribution of soil moisture, preferential flow at the CRSI, and infiltration processes (Li et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2018; Shen et al.,2019; Zhao et al., 2020a ), how the input of rock surface flow derived from outcrop bedrock affects the original conditions of runoff generation, especially at the CRSI where the rock surface flow directly flows and closely follows the outcrop bedrock. More importantly, can the surface runoff formed around outcrops benefit from rock surface flow? By what mechanism? This is important for understanding hydrological processes in karst environments. It is worth noting that in addition to soil infiltration and water storage capacity determining whether surface runoff is generated in the two mechanisms as excess saturation and excess infiltration runoffs, the ability of the soil at the CRSI to regulate the rock surface flow, determined by the effective outcrop rock surface catchment area size and rainfall combined, is also a prerequisite for surface runoff generation. Therefore, two typical bedrock outcrops with different hydrological rock surface paths were selected in a rocky karst area of China. This study aims to 1) quantify surface runoff generation influencing factors and relationships around bedrock outcrops, 2) propose conditional equations for two types of runoff production mechanisms for an in-depth understanding of the hydrological processes around bedrock outcrops, and 3) analyse their water storage and infiltration capacities and explore whether surface runoff can be generated by rock surface flow from bedrock outcrops. The results of this study provide a new understanding of the hydrological processes influenced by outcrops in karst areas.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Site description The study area was located in Ganhe Village, Changshun County, Guizhou Province, China. It is a renowned county with a total rocky desertified area of 1220 km2 , accounting for 77.9 % of the county’s total area. The sampling area is located at 26°1′30″N, 106°29′59″E with an altitude of 1250–1579 m. The area has a subtropical monsoon climate with an average annual rainfall of 1250–1400 mm and an average annual temperature of 13.5–18.5℃. The regional soils are yellow, purple, limestone, and paddy (classified by Chinese Soil Taxonomy). Four sites with outcrop bedrock were selected in the study area: grassland (GL), shrub grassland (SL), garden land (GAL), and slope farmland (SF). The GL was undisturbed by agricultural activity (ploughing) and recovered naturally in April 2020. SL was naturally restored in early 2016. GAL was no longer planted with fruit trees as of May 2020. After conducting agricultural operations on the SF in April 2021, no further farming activity was undertaken, which is considered the control. At the selected sites, the soil type was limestone soil (classified as Calcisols in the FAO taxonomy), and the bedrock was primarily weak or un-weathered limestone (Fig. 1  ).  2.2 Experimental design and sample collection Four sites with notable bedrock outcrops were selected to avoid specificity of the results obtained from a single plot. Two shapes of rock surfaces with different hydrological paths, straight and concave (two replicates for each form), were selected at each site because they are more capable of collecting rainwater and producing rock surface flows. The fundamental information for all bedrock outcrops with selected rock surfaces, such as outcrop height, outcrop rock surface effective catchment area, and track length, are provided in Table 1  . The rock track length is the length of rock surface that touches the soil and reflects the width of the water flow entering the soil via rock surface flow (not all rainwater runs off the entire outcrop bedrock surface). The soil sampling points for the two rock surface shapes were located at the CRSI middle and concave sites, based on the rock surface confluence characteristics. The cutting ring method was used to collect the undisturbed soils closely adhere to the CRSI and far from the outcrops horizontally (>20 cm, FRSI) in each layer (0–10 cm and 10–20 cm), respectively. These samples were used to determine the soil water infiltration rate and soil water storage performance. Specific sampling details are detailed in Yang et al. (2023) .  2.3 Soil water infiltration rate and storage performance determination The methods used to determine the soil hydrology indicators such as the soil water infiltration rate and storage performance were similar to those reported by Yang et al. Surface runoff is generated on the soil surface once soil infiltration and water storage is satisfied by the rock surface flow and rainwater. There is no doubt that only part of the rainfall forms the rock surface flow at the outcrop bedrock surface (Zhao et al., 2020 ) with a conversion coefficient (a). In this study, all rainwater received in the effective catchment area of the rock surface was assumed to form the rock surface flow (a = 1). A RS  (cm2 ) was used as the efficient catchment area for the measurable exposed rock surface. R I  (mm/min) and R A  (mm) were the intensity and amount of precipitation, respectively. In addition, it is assumed that the rock surface flow will flow within a certain range upon permeating the soil surface at the CRSI (Fig. 2  ). The flow width was taken as W (cm) and the forward distance of this flow on the soil surface as L  (cm). The former can be obtained based on the rock surface shape or the width of the water flow outlet of the effective catchment area, whereas the latter is an unknown parameter.
