Overall, CRSI soil infiltration was generally lower than that of FRSI for all land-use type straight and concave shapes, except for GL. Moreover, the soil water infiltration rate at the 0–10 cm and 10–20 cm soil layers of both rock surface shapes of different land-use types decreased with increasing duration, and the infiltration process of the 0–10 cm FRSI was greater, indicating that FRSI has advantages in infiltration runoff regulation ability compared to that of the CRSI. Regarding the rock surface shapes, the concave shape total infiltration capacity was greater than that of the straight shape, and the total infiltration was greatest at the 0–10 cm FRSI for both the straight and concave shapes, whereas the lower infiltration rates at the 0–20 cm CRSI and 10–20 cm FRSI resulted in the promotion of surface runoff. Regarding land-use types, the CRSI and FRSI infiltration rates were relatively low for SL, and the total infiltration amount was the lowest for GAL. The straight and concave shape initial, average, and stable infiltration rates for the different land-use types are shown in Fig. 4  . Overall, the initial, average, and stable infiltration rates for the different soil layers and the CSRI and FSRI of both rock surface types did not differ significantly. The initial, average, and stable infiltration rates at the 0–10 cm FRSI were higher significantly than those at the 0–10 cm CRSI, 10–20 cm CRSI, and 10–20 cm FRSI for both straight and concave shapes. Regarding specific soil layers and CSRI (or FRSI), no notable differences were observed in the initial, average, and stable infiltration rates; for example, no notable differences were observed in the three infiltration rates at the 0–10 cm CSRI. For the same rock shape and soil layer, the three infiltration rates were highest for the SF and GL straight and concave shapes.  3.2 CRSI and FRSI soil water storage capacity variations Straight and concave shape soil reservoir capacities under different land-use types are shown in Fig. 5   and Table S1  (Supplementary Material ). Except for SL, the CRSI total soil storage capacity was slightly less than that of the FRSI for the straight and concave shapes (Fig. 5 ), suggesting that the outcropping rock affects the ability of the periclinal soils to store the rock surface flow. The total storage capacity is the maximum soil capacity to store water; the greater the total reservoir capacity, the more it reflects the soil's ability to regulate water cycling and soil conservation. At soil depths of 0–10 and 10–20 cm, the CRSI had a TS  of > 500 mm and a US  of > 250 mm. This indicates that the CRSI soil reservoir capacity has substantial space for storing and regulating water and superior ability for soil and water conservation. Additionally, TS , US  and FS  were greater at the 0–10 cm soil depth than at the 10–20 cm depth, indicating that the surface soil had greater runoff regulation ability. In addition, the soil storage capacity at the CRSI was in the order of US>FS>DS . Furthermore, SL had the largest TS  and US , suggesting that vegetation may influence soil properties around outcrops. The SF TS  for both CRSI and FRSI straight and concave shapes was lower than that of the other land-use types, suggesting that human activity affects soil properties and indirectly affects soil water storage capacity. FS  characterises the ability of the soil to temporarily store water and regulate surface runoff from heavy or prolonged rainfall over a short period of time. Overall, the CRSI FS  was less than that of the FRSI, and the concave shape FS  was greater than that of the straight shape, suggesting that the CRSI had a weaker temporary water storage capacity.  3.3 Critical conditions for surface runoff generation around outcrops 3.3.1 Excess surface runoff infiltration generation A surface runoff model that considers the excess surface runoff infiltration mechanism occurring near outcrops is shown in Fig. 6  . The corresponding R I  and A RS  values within the coloured areas did not produce surface runoff. Overall, for a specific outcrop with an A RS , the stronger the R I , the easier it was to produce surface runoff. For a specific rainfall event with an R I , the larger the A RS , the greater the surface runoff produced. The relationship between these two can be described as an inversely proportional function.  The straight GL CRSI shown in Fig. 6  was used as an example to explore the relationship between A RS  and R I  (Fig. 6 a). As shown, the R I  critical threshold was 37.96, 52.93, 60.93 and 65.92 mm/min for the patchy soil near outcrops with an I  of 87.38 mm/min and an A RS  of 325.5 cm2  measured when the L  was 5, 10, 15 and 20 cm respectively. Therefore, the A RS  was determined as 325.5 cm2 , the L W was 250, 500, 750, and 1000 cm2  respectively, and the rock surface flow derived from the above R I  flowed on the rock surface. Once the A RS  or corresponding R I  is exceeded, surface runoff is produced. Conversely, if the R I  is less than the above value, surface runoff will not be produced. A similar critical R I  threshold can also be obtained for other rock surface shapes and land types (Fig. 6 b–6 h). For an FRSI with a specific I  (Fig. 7  ), surface runoff generation on the soil surface depends on the R I . The R I  must exceed the measured I  of 87.74 mm/min to produce excess infiltration runoff (Fig. 7 a). These results suggest that the rock surface flow input alters the conditions for surface runoff formation near outcrops (CRSI), but that of FRSI depends solely on R I .  3.3.2 Excess saturation surface runoff generation The surface runoff model, which considers the excess saturation surface runoff generation mechanism occurring near outcrops, is shown in Fig. 6 . The corresponding R A  and A RS  within the coloured area did not produce surface runoff. Overall, for a specific outcrop with an A RS , the greater the R A , the easier it was to produce surface runoff. For a specific rainfall event with an R A , the greater the A RS , the greater the surface runoff produced. The relationship between the two can also be applied as an inverse proportional function.  The straight GL CRSI shown in Fig. 8   was usen as an example to explore the relationship between A RS  and R A  (Fig. 8 a). As demonstrated, it can accommodate 23.68, 33.02, 38.02 and 41.13 mm of precipitation in the patchy soil near outcrops with a TS  of 54.52 mm and an A RS  of 325.5 cm2  measured when L  was 5, 10, 15, and 20 cm, respectively. Once the above A RS  or corresponding R A  values were exceeded, surface runoff occurred. Conversely, if the R A  is less than the above value, surface runoff will not be produced. A similar critical R A  threshold can also be obtained for other rock surface shapes and land types (Fig. 8 b–8 h). For FRSI with a specific TS  (Fig. 9  ), whether surface runoff can be generated on the soil surface depends on the R A . An R A >55.12 mm will produce excess saturation runoff (Fig. 9 a).    4 Discussions 4.1 Surface runoff generation conditions 4.1.1 Excess infiltration surface runoff generation conditions The current study was designed to determine the discriminatory conditions for whether the rock surface flow generated surface runoff near the outcrops. The conditional equations present an inversely proportional function between rainfall intensity and rock surface catchment area. As the rock surface catchment area increased, the critical rainfall intensity required to generate surface runoff gradually decreased. Using the straight-shape GL CRSI as an example, the A RS  is 325.5 cm2 , and the L W is 250 cm2  when L  is 5 cm; if it exceeds this critical value of 37.96 mm/min, then excess infiltration runoff generation may occur. The excess infiltration runoff used in this study is shown schematically in Fig. 10  . For the FRSI, where there is no rock surface flow input, when rainfall intensity is greater than the soil infiltration capacity, the soil is unable to absorb and infiltrate the rainfall rapidly, resulting in the generation of surface runoff on the soil surface. For the CRSI, nevertheless, this is not the case as there is input from rock surface flow. In this case, at the sites adjacent to the CRSI, if the intensity of the rains with moderate rainfall intensity combined with the rock surface flow caused by these rains exceeds the soil infiltration rate, excess infiltration runoff will occur on the surface. Meanwhile, the areas of FRSI will not form excess infiltration surface runoff. Therefore, excess runoff usually occurs when the soil infiltration capacity is low, rainfall intensity is high, or the rainfall duration is short (Loague et al., 2010 ). Gregory et al. (2009)  studied the soil infiltration rates in limestone karst landscapes and found that they were high, resulting in very low surface runoff coefficients (<5%), which altered the runoff-producing mechanisms in the area. In addition, bedrock outcrops play an important role in influencing rainfall-runoff generation. Bedrock outcrops not only increase the surface impermeable area, which helps rainfall runoff to collect on the rock surface, thus increasing surface runoff generation (Peng and Dai, 2022 ); bedrock outcrops also reduce the surface erodible area, thus increasing the ability to intercept surface runoff (Arnau-Rosalén et al., 2008; Gan et al., 2020 ). When the rock cover reached 70 %, the amount of water from the rock was equal to the amount of rainfall received by the soil patches (Wang et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020b ), indicating the effect of the rock surface catchment area on infiltration when the rainfall intensity was certain. In karst areas, bedrock outcrops play an important role in water infiltration and surface runoff generation (Li et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2018; Zhao and Shen, 2022 ). The bedrock outcrop rock surface shapes and catchment areas affect the rock surface flow output and have different degrees of influence on soil physical and water-holding properties around the rock (Conn and Snyder-Conn, 1981; Nobles et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016 ). Shen et al. (2019)  showed that the exposed rock heterogeneity significantly influenced water and runoff heterogeneity from the surrounding soil patches. In this study, the CRSI infiltration capacity was generally lower than that of the FRSI, which is contrary to the results of Zhao et al. (2020a) . The reason may be that, on the one hand, rainwater catchment by outcrop rocks has exposed CRSI soils to a lengthy period of scouring and wet conditions, resulting in greater soil bulk weight and less soil porosity relative to the FRSI. On the other hand, the CRSI infiltration capacity here is the soil closely adhering to the rock–soil interface, not the interface itself, which is also a key factor affecting infiltration capacity. This is also a limitation of this study. Therefore, more attentions should be paid to the infiltration capacity of the CRSI itself and further explore how the CRSI affects the conversion of rock surface flow to surface runoff.  4.1.2 Excess saturation surface runoff generation conditions In this study, the conditional equations was established based on the relationship between the rainfall amount and rock surface catchment area by considering the total soil storage capacity as the rainfall infiltration amount. It presents that the critical rainfall amount required to generate surface runoff gradually decreased with increasing rock surface catchment area, and the same applies to the inverse proportional functional relationship.  Using the GL straight-shape CRSI as an example, the A RS  is 325.5 cm2  and the L W is 250 cm2  when L  is 5 cm; if it exceeds this critical value (23.68 mm), excess saturation runoff generation may occur owing to soil saturation or the inability to infiltrate further. Tani (1997)  studied rainfall thresholds on steep forested hillslopes with thin soil layers and showed that the total runoff was negligible when the total rainfall was < 20 mm. Wang et al. (2022a,b)  identified an initiation threshold of 36 ± 2 mm for surface runoff rainfall depth generation on a karst hillslope in a peak-cluster depression and concluded that surface runoff was generated by the Dunton mechanism. The results of the thresholds for generating FRSI surface runoff in our study showed that they were all > 45 mm, indicating that soil moisture content has a strong influence on runoff (Penna et al., 2010 ). The excess saturation runoff in this study is schematically shown in Fig. 11  . Overall, excess saturation runoff usually occurs when the soil is saturated or unable to allow rapid permeation. Hence, the generation of surface runoff is influenced by factors such as rainfall amount, soil saturation, and topography. In addition, the results of this study showed that the CRSI total soil storage capacity was slightly less than that of the FRSI, suggesting that the CRSI soil has a weaker ability to intercept water than the FRSI, which is a side effect of the fact that CRSI has a small water deficit and thus is more likely to fill with water first and produce runoff. With the addition of input from rock surface flow, the soil surface is easily filled with rainwater at the sites adjacent to the CRSI, resulting in excess saturation surface runoff. Related studies have proven this point that the runoff generation on karst slopes with dolomite is dominated by excess saturation runoff (Zhang et al., 2022 ), which preferentially occurs at the interface between overlying soil layer and bedrocks because of the thinner soil layer and weaker soil water holding capacity.   4.2 Influence of the rock surface flow from outcrops on water leakage Soil water loss spatial characteristics in karst areas are closely related to the geological environment (Wilcox et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2022a,b; Fonseca et al., 2023 ). In rocky desertified areas dominated by outcrop bedrock, the outcrop bedrock surface acts as a medium and tends to form a rock surface flow after receiving precipitation (Kidron and Starinsky, 2012 ). This flow is exported to the soil around the bedrock and promotes soil water transportation at the CRSI, which has an important effect on the changes in hydrological processes in the soil around the bedrock. Studies have also shown that bedrock outcrops play an important role in rainfall redistribution and soil infiltration, primarily because a fact that the CRSI plays a significant influence on infiltration and groundwater recharge processes, resulting in the rapid infiltration of water into the deep subsurface (Sohrt et al., 2014 ). Relevant studies have shown that soil infiltration rates can be extremely high at certain locations around bedrock outcrops, often exceeding the maximum natural rainfall intensity (Calvo-Cases et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2019 ). Studies have predominantly used simulated rainfall methods to explore the effects of bedrock outcrops on water leakage from karst areas. Li et al. (2011)  studied the hydrological processes controlling infiltration rates and runoff generation in the mountainous karst areas in Spain. They concluded that, at the plot scale, bedrock outcrops play a dominant role in controlling infiltration rates and runoff generation in karst landscapes. Through simulated rainfall laboratory studies, Rodrigo-Comino et al. (2017)  and Dai et al. (2017)  showed that large areas of rock fragments can effectively reduce the rate of soil erosion. However, the runoff amount increases with the bare rock rate, and the soil loss amount has a decreasing trend. Moreover, some studies have shown that bedrock outcrops can increase the surface runoff infiltration rate, thereby reducing soil erosion by suppressing flow production and soil erodibility (Gong et al., 2018 ). In addition, the outcrop bedrock affected the karst slope surface runoff, which largely depended on bedrock occurrence. The rocks parallel to the slope left a flow channel for surface runoff, whereas the horizontal rocks impeded surface runoff and reduced flow velocity (Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018 ). Overall, the influence of bedrock outcrops on rainfall infiltration is accompanied by uncertainty and complexity, related to the size of the bedrock, its orientation, exposure height, surface roughness, karst nature, slope, and soil type and nature, etc. Furthermore, water leakage from the rock perimeter is driven by the action of the outcrop bedrock surface flow due to the presence of the CRSI. The results from Sohrt et al. (2014)  showed that rainfall runoff on bare rock surfaces shows clear signs of preferential flow along the CRSI, as the fractures are the primary pathway, thereby promoting infiltration and reducing runoff. Li et al. (2011)  showed that rock fractures acting as surface runoff sinks and rock fragments embedded within the topsoil effectively prevent runoff in karst landscapes. Surface karst seepage on slopes has also been shown to occur through discrete pipes and fractures, mostly at soil–bedrock interfaces and above barrier layers (Gombert, 2002; Chen et al., 2018; Berthelin and Hartmann, 2020 ). Many studies have shown that the runoff generated from karst surfaces is transported to the bedrock, where it is lost along fractures and conduits. The presence of bedrock at the surface affects surface runoff continuity and increases the contact time between surface water and soil (Zhao et al., 2020a ). Ao et al. (2023)  studied the effects of three cave rock surface morphologies on the flow production characteristics of karst slopes. Their results indicated that all three rock surface morphologies significantly increased the surface runoff coefficient of the slope. The main reason is that, compared with no bare rock, part of the rainfall is intercepted by the bare rock surface, converges on the rock surface to form rock surface flow, after which part of the rock surface flow combines with the surface runoff on the slope below the bare rock together with the rainfall on the slope, causing scouring. Moreover, because the 'cave' plays the role of the CRSI preferential conduit, rock surface flow through the 'cave' infiltrates rapidly into the soil. Owing to the abrupt contact at the CRSI, the rock surface flow can easily enter the CRSI (Fu et al., 2015 ), and most of the rock surface flow can infiltrate directly into deeper soils, causing them to reach saturation quickly and generate surface runoff earlier. In general, the surface flow of bedrock outcrops creates a complex environment around the bedrock, leading to different soil infiltration properties that have a more complex effect on water leakage in karst areas, resulting in different hydrological study results in different karst areas.   5 Conclusions The conditions for judging the rock surface flow derived from bedrock outcrops that generate surface runoff were established by considering the infiltration and saturation excess surface runoff generation mechanisms. We found that the input of rock surface flow changed the conditions for surface runoff formation near outcrops (CRSI), however, that at the FRSI depended solely on the R I  or R A . The CRSI is more prone to causing surface runoff than the FRSI. This is due to the fact that the soil infiltration capacity of the CRSI with straight and concave shapes was overall less than that of the FRSI except for the straight-shape GL. The CRSI is more likely to promote surface runoff formation because it receives input from rock surface flow. Moreover, outcrops with concave rock surface shapes, influenced by the hydrological path of the rock surface and high soil infiltration capacity, are more likely to promote surface runoff than those with straight shapes. The comparison of an inversely proportional functional relationship between the R I  or R A  and the A RS  to the soil infiltration and soil water storage at the CRSI constituted the discriminatory conditions for whether the rock surface flow generated surface runoff near the outcrops. In addition, we introduced the A RS  of the four sites into the discriminant condition and obtained the R I  or R A  critical threshold for rock surface flow to promote surface runoff formation near outcrops. For instance, the critical R I  and R A  for the straight-shape GL (A RS , 325.5 cm2  and L, 5 cm) were 37.96 mm/min and 23.68 mm, and those for the concave-shape GL (A RS , 4289.25 cm2  and L, 5 cm) were 0.80 mm/min and 2.83 mm, respectively. This indicates that the R I  and R A  are smaller for a concave shape with a given A RS . Therefore, it is important to be aware of the effect of concave shapes on surface runoff generation in rocky desertified karst areas. This discriminant condition provides useful information for accurately predicting the surface runoff in desertified areas with multiple outcrops.
1 Introduction The “dragon-boat water” (DBW) refers to a substantial and concentrated precipitation event in South China that occurs after the onset of the South China Sea summer monsoon (SCSSM) from mid-May to mid-June each year, coinciding with the Dragon Boat Festival and earning its evocative name. The intensity and duration of DBW bear significant relevance to atmospheric circulation and various weather systems (Sheng et al., 2023 ). The balanced occurrence of DBW is advantageous for the growth of early rice and other crops. Conversely, abnormally intense rainfalls, including torrential, heavy, or extremely heavy rainfalls, can result in substantial economic losses and human injuries. These repercussions stem from annual flash floods, urban flooding, landslides, lightning, and other disasters in southern China, making DBW an essential focus of atmospheric research (Cheng et al., 2023 ). Notably, under ongoing global warming, DBW has exhibited a significant increase in the rainfall amount, the number of rainy days, and rain intensity (Wang et al., 2018 ). Therefore, a profound comprehension of DBW mechanisms is essential for safeguarding human life, and property, as well as ensuring the resilience of industrial and agricultural production, aligning with the imperatives of sustainable social development. The SCSSM onset typically signals the start of a major rainy season in south China (Wang et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2005 ). Very often, an abnormal SCSSM onset could result in severe flood and drought events (Xu et al., 2022a ). The SCSSM introduces warm and humid air masses from tropical oceans to the region. Upon encountering the region’s complex topography, these air masses become unstable, resulting in convective precipitation. Such conditions set the stage for DBW season, characterized by prolonged heavy storms (Jiang et al., 2003 ). DBW seasons are primarily influenced by large-scale atmospheric circulation systems during monsoon season, including the shear line, subtropical jet, Western Pacific subtropical high, South Asia high, and low-level southwest jet in the subtropics, as well as the East Asian trough and northeastern cold vortex in the mid-high latitudes (Li et al., 2019; Miao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2023 ). Additionally, DBW seasons are affected by other forcings such as tropic sea surface temperature (SST) and sea ice and snow (Qin et al., 2023 ). A typical DBW season involves multiple episodes of prolonged heavy storms, which necessitate an active circulation system. Previous studies have largely focused on the overall DBW season (Liu et al., 2020; Nie and Sun, 2022 ), but often overlook the crucial aspect of convective processes within individual precipitation events in DBW. Therefore, understanding the convective processes during DBW is essential for comprehending the underlying thermo-dynamic processes associated with DBW rainfall. Precipitation stable isotopes (δ2 H, δ18 O, and d-excess), rich in climatic and environmental information, have been widely utilized in climate and hydrological studies (Dansgaard, 1964; Araguás-Araguás et al., 2000 ). These isotopes are frequently used to trace atmospheric circulation (e.g., Fousiya et al., 2022; Gou et al., 2022 ), precipitation types (e.g., convective precipitation and stratiform precipitation) (e.g., Aggarwal et al., 2016; Braun et al., 2017 ), and moisture sources for precipitation and their transport processes (e.g., Tan, 2014; Ruan et al., 2019; Zhan et al., 2023 ). However, previous studies have largely focused on longer time scales, ranging from daily, months to decades, with limited attention to the controlling factors within individual precipitation events. Recent studies have demonstrated that high-resolution isotopic data can provide more detailed insights into isotopic evolutionary characteristics (He et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2022b, 2023 ). Precipitation δ18 O within individual events exhibits various evolution patterns, including both descending or increasing trends (Celle-Jeanton et al., 2004; Munksgaard et al., 2012; Li et al., 2021 ), as well as periods of decrease followed by increase or stabilization (Celle-Jeanton et al., 2004; Coplen et al., 2008; He et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2021 ). The δ18 O variations within precipitation events could be remarkably substantial, with fluctuations of up to 10 ‰ (Munksgaard et al., 2012; He et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2021 ). Various factors could influence isotope evolution during an individual event, including the type of precipitation (Aggarwal et al., 2016; Han et al., 2021 ), mesoscale subsidence in stratiform zone (He et al., 2018a; Risi et al., 2008, 2010; Kurita, 2013 ), upstream cumulative convection (He et al., 2018b; Sun et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023 ), changes in moisture sources (Munksgaard et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015 ), and rain re-evaporation (Aemisegger et al., 2015; He et al., 2018a ). However, despite the importance of understanding the intra-event dynamics of DBW δ18 O, no studies have investigated the precipitation isotope evolution during individual DBW events. This gap in research holds significant limitations for comprehending regional hydrology and climate in the southern China region. Between 11 May and 20 June 2022, Fuzhou experienced extreme DBW rain events due to an unusually active cold vortex compared with the normal year and the southeastward position of the Western Pacific subtropical high (Fig. S1 ). This period saw a total rainfall amount of 548 mm, the second-highest recorded since 1951. During this time, we collected hourly precipitation samples for isotope stable analysis, in addition to samples collected before the SCSSM onset. Our primary aim is to explore the influence of SCSSM onset on DBW rainfall and the underlying microphysical processes and mechanisms driving these events. The major objectives of this investigation are to (1) assess the effect of the SCSSM on precipitation δ18 O and (2) examine the control factors influencing the evolution of precipitation δ18 O during individual DBW events.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 DBW events in 2022 According to the China Meteorological Administration, during the 2022 DBW season, certain areas in southern China (Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, and Fujian Provinces and their surrounding areas) experienced the most severe rainstorms in the past 60 years. In these areas, the regionally averaged rainfall during the 2022 DBW reached up to 518 mm, 1.6 times the climatological mean value of 322 mm for the DBW season over the region, making the highest record since 1979 (Cheng et al., 2023 ). The 2022 DBW season has seen high cumulative rainfall, uneven spatial distribution, frequent heavy precipitation processes, and a large number of days of heavy rainfall. Numerous areas experienced basin floods, widespread urban and rural flooding, and geological hazards, prompting the General Administration of Pearl River Control to raise the flood control emergency response to level I, surpassing historical records.  2.2 Sampling site and its climatology Our sampling site is located on the campus of Fujian Normal University, Fuzhou, southeastern China (26°05′ N, 119°30′ E) (Fig. 1 ). Fuzhou has a typical subtropical monsoon climate, featuring hot and rainy summers and mild and dry winters. According to the instrumental meteorological data from the Fuzhou meteorological station, the average annual temperature is 20 °C, with an average annual precipitation of 1390 mm. More than 80 % of average annual precipitation is concentrated in the rainy season from March to September. Bounded by the onset of SCSSM, Fuzhou has two primary rainy seasons: spring persistent rain and the DBW season. In 2022, the SCSSM occurred from May 11 to May 15 as expected, coinciding with the DBW season lasting from May 11 to June 20. During this period, Fuzhou received a total precipitation of 548 mm, nearly 40 % of the annual average. This amount is 60 ∼ 70 % higher than the same period in a normal year and significantly surpasses historical records, making it the second-highest amount recorded since 1951 (Fig. 1  ). Furthermore, several extremely heavy rainfall events accounted for about half of the total rainfall amount, with the highest hourly rainfall exceeding 30 mm. In addition, the number of rainy days during this period in Fuzhou amounted to 35 days, breaking historical records and exceeding normal years by 30 ∼ 50 %.  2.3 Precipitation sampling and isotopic analyses Rainwater sampling was conducted on open ground in front of the School of Geographical Sciences building, which houses the school’s Stable Isotope Laboratory. We collected rain samples from both events before the SCSSM, and DBW events between May 11 and June 20, 2022. For rain sample collection, we used large containers with a funnel placed at the top opening. To prevent possible contamination and rain sample evaporation, a ping-pong ball was positioned at the funnel opening. A new dry container with a fresh funnel was used for each sample to ensure that no sample residue from the previous sampling remained. The collection intervals varied based on rainfall intensity, ranging from an hour to two hours. In total, we collected 268 samples during the study period. All sample vials were capped and sealed with a Parafilm membrane and stored in a refrigerator at 4℃ before analysis. The stable isotopic compositions of the rainwater samples were measured using a Picarro water analyzer L2140-i at Stable Isotope Laboratory, Fujian Normal University. Each sample was analyzed six times and only the average of the last three measurements was used to minimize memory effects. The analytical results are reported in the δ-notation (i.e., δ18 O and δ2 H) relative to Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW). Calibration employed three in-house reference standards (GBW04458, GBW04459, and GBW04460) with δ18 O values of − 0.15 ‰, −8.61 ‰ and − 19.13 ‰, and δ2 H values of − 1.70 ‰, −63.40 ‰ and − 144.00 ‰, respectively. The analytical precisions were ± 0.5 ‰ for δ2 H and ± 0.08 ‰ for δ18 O.  2.4 Meteorological data On-site hourly meteorological parameters including temperature (T) and relative humidity (RH) were recorded at 30-minute intervals using a HOBO Temp/RH data logger, and the precipitation amount was measured using a tipping-bucket rain gauge with a resolution of 0.2 mm. Both the data logger and rain gauge were installed in an open area on the roof of the School of Geographical Sciences building. Hourly outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), above-ground RH, total precipitation, and convective precipitation data were obtained from the ERA5 re-analysis dataset (0.25° × 0.25°) provided by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Copernicus Climate Data Store (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ ) (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). Using ERA5 precipitation data, the fraction of stratiform precipitation is calculated by subtracting convective precipitation from total precipitation, divided by the total (Tian et al., 2023 ):(1) Fst = Pt - P c  Pt       where Fst refers to the fraction of stratiform precipitation, Pt refers to the total precipitation, and Pc refers to the convective precipitation.  2.5 HYSPLIT moisture source diagnostic To trace moisture sources and assess their relative contributions, we performed the air mass backward trajectory (240 h) for each rainy hour using the Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model software from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) at the Air Resources Laboratory. The background meteorological data for HYSPLIT model calculations were obtained from the Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) at 850 hPa with a spatial resolution of 1°×1° (ftp://arlftp.arlhq.noaa.gov/pub/archives/gdas1/ ). By examining the changes in specific humidity of these air masses, which indicated either moisture input from evaporative sources or depletion due to rainfall, we can measure the contributions from various moisture uptake sites. This enables us to trace the rainfall at Fuzhou back to its origin while accounting for moisture loss during transport (Zhan et al., 2023 ). Following the approach described by Zhan et al. (2023)  for dividing moisture sources and combining the spatial distribution of moisture uptake locations and regional geographic units, we categorized moisture sources into five major regions and quantified their regional moisture contributions. Additionally, we calculated the weighted mean of upstream rainout to account for the accumulated convective activities, incorporating meteorological information along the trajectories (Sun et al., 2022 ). For this calculation, the backward trajectories were initialed at each rainy hour at seven levels (e.g., 500 m, 1000 m, 1500 m, 2000 m, 3000 m, 4000 m, and 5000 m above ground level, AGL) (Zhan et al., 2023 ), and moved back for 240 h. We employed the Python-based function PySPLIT to operate the HYSPLIT software, enabling the generation of trajectories in clusters (Warner, 2018 ).   3 Results 3.1 General variations in precipitation isotope during the study period Both precipitation δ18 O and d-excess show large variations during the study period (Fig. 2  ; Table S1 ). In general, δ18 O tends to be higher before the SCSSM onset, with a narrower range of variability compared to values after SCSSM commencement. δ18 O values of the pre-SCSSM samples range from − 4.6 ‰ to − 9.6 ‰, with a weighted mean of − 5.7 ‰, and d-excess ranges from 5.2 ‰ to 13.9 ‰, with a weighted mean of 8.5 ‰. In contrast, the samples collected during DBW events after the SCSSM onset exhibit a much larger range of δ18 O values, spanning from − 3.5 ‰ to − 15.6 ‰, with a weighted mean of − 9.7 ‰, notably lower than those of pre-SCSSM samples. The d-excess of SCSSM samples ranges from 1.2 ‰ to 18.3 ‰, with a weighted mean of 11.5 ‰, obviously higher than that of pre-SCSSM samples.  3.2 Precipitation isotopes during individual events One distinct feature of the 2022 DBW season following the onset of the SCSSM is the occurrence of numerous sudden rainstorms. In this study, we only reported 19 precipitation events, including moderate rain events and above, with the rainfall amount exceeding 10 mm per day or 2.6 mm per hour (Table S2 ). A notable negative shift in δ18 O values occurred during most events, especially in instances of heavy rainfalls, with the rainfall amount exceeding 25 mm per day or 8.1 mm per hour. In most events, this shift, i.e., the difference between the initial and the lowest values, does not exceed 4 ‰, although it can reach up to 8 ‰ in three event (Table S2 ). Interestingly, the initial δ18 O shows a strong positive correlation with both the lowest and average δ18 O (Fig. 3  ), consistent with the findings of He et al. (2018b) . During a typical event, δ18 O shows a V-shaped pattern; its value is relatively higher at the beginning, gradually decreases as the event progresses, and returns to a higher level at the end of the events (Risi et al., 2010; He et al., 2018a ). This V-shaped pattern is commonly observed in the rain events investigated in this study (Fig. 4  a, b, Fig. S2 ). In these events, both stratiform and convective precipitation were present, with a gradual shift from mainly convective precipitation to mainly stratiform precipitation. Typically, a relatively low δ18 O value is observed corresponding to stratiform precipitation or near the transition zone between convection and stratiform zones (Fig. 4 a, b). Additionally, a temperature drop (about 1 to 5 °C) accompanies the decrease in δ18 O, corresponding to the arrival of the cold pool associated with convection (Tremoy et al., 2014; He et al., 2018a ). Initially, RH is relatively low, but it increases as the events progress and then remains consistently high thereafter. Although a simple V-shaped pattern is commonly observed, not all events follow this trend. Some events exhibit different patterns, such as a W-shaped with large fluctuations observed during the events on May 15 and June 11 (Fig. 4 c, d). This W-shaped pattern is likely associated with the passage of multiple convection cells over the sampling site (He et al., 2018a ). As a result, the lowest δ18 O values are not necessarily observed exclusively in the stratiform zone. During some rain events, where only a partial convection system passes by the sampling site, δ18 O patterns may only partially resemble the usual V-shape or W-shape. For example, a “L” shape (Fig. 4 e) likely reflects the presence of the convection rain, while a reversed “L” shape (Fig. 4 f) represents stratiform rain only.  3.3 Correlation analysis of δ18 O with on-site T, RH, and precipitation amount We conducted a correlation analysis between δ18 O and precipitation amount as well as between δ18 O and on-site meteorological parameters (T, RH, and rainfall amount) during DBW rainfall events. On daily scales (Table S3 ), we observed a strong positive correlation between T and δ18 O. This correlation is likely due to downdraft bringing in cooler air from high levels, causing an on-site T drop and resulting in a spurious correlation between T and δ18 O (He et al., 2018a ). In contrast, no correlation was found between δ18 O and RH or between δ18 O and precipitation amount. At event scales, a positive correlation was also observed between T and δ18 O, for example, during the 15 May and 9 June events (Table S4 ). However, we found no regular correlation between δ18 O and RH at event scales. Similarly, no correlation was found between δ18 O and precipitation amount, except for the 8 June event. This observation is consistent with the previous studies demonstrating that the amount effect can only be detected in monthly and annual precipitation, but not in daily or event precipitation in the mid-low latitudes (Kurita et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2019; Jackisch et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023 ). The general low correlation of δ18 O with meteorological parameters may suggest that the ambient environmental conditions on the ground only partially represent those in the atmosphere below the cloud-base (He et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2023 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Factors influencing the temporal variation of precipitation isotopes The variation pattern in rainfall δ18 O over time (Fig. 2 ) is closely tied to the regional convection activities, which are significantly influenced by various atmospheric circulation systems. With the onset of the SCSSM, the Western Pacific subtropical high moved eastward, transporting water vapor from the South China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean to the southern China. Simultaneously, unstable atmospheric conditions above the southern China led to the formation of other large atmospheric circulation systems (Charney and Stern, 1962 ), such as shear lines, characterized by the convergence of different directional air masses. Additionally, in the northern region, the cold vortex system also remained active, facilitating the southward movement of cold air masses. These large atmospheric systems collectively contributed to intensive convection in our region after the onset of the SCSSM, leading to various rainfall events (Fig. S3 ). For example, the events on May 13 are associated with the cold vortex (Fig. S3 a) that there is a low-pressure center in the middle and high latitudes while the events on June 8 and June 9 originated from multiple low vortices (Fig. S3 b). The association between precipitation isotopes and regional convection is manifested in the distribution of regional OLR and the positive correlation between precipitation δ18 O and regional OLR (Fig. 5  ). OLR serves as a proxy for deep convection, displaying a negative correlation with convection; low OLR values signify heightened convection intensity (Wang and Xu, 1997; Gao et al., 2013 ). Relatively high OLR over the study site before the onset of the SCSSM (Fig. 5 a) indicates low cloud coverage and weak convection, while the low OLR over the site during the SCSSM implies high cloud coverage and strong convection. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a positive correlation of precipitation δ18 O at our site with regional OLR (Fig. 5 c) in the northern SCS, the major moisture source region (Fig. 6  ), but a negative correlation with regional precipitation in the same region (Fig. 5 d). Therefore, low δ18 O values at our site correspond to strong convection with low regional OLR and high regional precipitation. This suggests that with increased convective activities, precipitation stable isotopes tend to shift towards lower values, reflecting the influence of intense convection processes on precipitation isotopes. A comparison of the δ18 O time series with Hovmöller diagram of OLR in our study area demonstrates that extensive cloud coverage persisted for most of the study period, with OLR levels consistently below 240 W/m2  (Fig. 7  ). Notably, the negative shifts in δ18 O largely correspond to the presence of large spatial cloud coverage characterized by extremely low OLR, lower than 210 W/m2 . This observation strongly suggests that the isotopic composition of precipitation is influenced by the intensity and spatial extent of convection, with lower δ18 O values indicative of regions experiencing more vigorous convection and greater cloud coverage. Moreover, over the observation period, we identified multiple moisture sources and calculated their fractional contribution (Fig. 6 ). This variability is also reflected in d-excess, which exhibits frequent fluctuations rather than a clear trend (Fig. 2 ). Before the onset of the SCSSM, the water vapor was mostly sourced from the SCS and inland areas, with very little contribution from the neighbouring oceanic regions (Fig. 6 a). In contrast, after the onset of the SCSSM, water vapor primarily originated from the oceanic regions. Although water vapor from the SCS remained comparable, there was a significant increase in water vapor from distant areas such as the Indian Ocean and the Western Pacific Ocean and a decrease in water vapor from inland areas at higher latitudes (Fig. 6 b). The prolonged convergence of high-latitude and low-latitude water vapor in southern China has led to persistent rain bands in the region, one of the requirements for the occurrence of extreme DBW in 2022. Although water vapor contribution from the SCS was almost constant before and after the SCSSM onset, convection in the study area and the northern part of the SCS was significantly stronger after the SCSSM onset (Fig. 5 a and b), which lowered δ18 O values. In addition, the transport distance of water vapor determines the extent of Rayleigh distillation on water isotopes; when water vapor originates from more distant regions, the prolonged rainout process could have enhanced the isotopic depletion in rainfall, lowering δ18 O values (Cai and Tian, 2016 ). Both increasing convective activities and moisture transport distance after the onset of the SCSSM led to the lower δ18 O values in precipitation. To further explore the relationship between upstream rainfall and precipitation δ18 O, we calculated total precipitation along backward trajectories following the method described by Sun et al. (2022)  and Zhan et al. (2023) . A significant correlation between δ18 O and total precipitation along the backward trajectory was observed, with the most pronounced correlation occurring at 96 h (Fig. 8  ). This indicates that precipitation δ18 O is significantly affected by integrated upstream processes associated with Rayleigh distillation of water vapor (Tang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2019; Zhan et al., 2023 ). Our findings align with recent studies highlighting the significance of integrated convective activities on rainfall isotopes (Wei et al., 2018; He et al. 2018b; Ruan et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2023 ). Specifically, accumulative convective activities along water vapor transport trajectories influence precipitation isotopes and can lead to isotopic depletion in both water vapor and rainfall.  4.2 Evolution of precipitation isotope during individual events In general, as rain events progress (Fig. 4 ), δ18 O becomes gradually more negative. This decrease corresponds to an increase in the relative proportion of stratiform precipitation, and thus, the most negative δ18 O values largely occur in the stratiform zone. This phenomenon is consistent with observations made during tropical rain events by Risi et al. (2010)  and He et al. (2018a) . Previous studies have also revealed the negative correlation between δ18 O values and the relative proportion of stratiform precipitation (Kurita, 2013; Aggarwal et al., 2016; Sánchez-Murillo et al., 2019 ). Lower δ18 O values observed in stratiform zones can be attributed to the mesoscale subsidence (Kurita, 2013; He et al., 2018a ). The mesoscale subsidence involves the descent of cold air below the cloud-base, driven by the cooling of ambient air in the mid-troposphere through the melting of ice particles and evaporation of precipitation. The descent of the cold air brigs isotopically depleted vapor into the sub-cloud layer, where it undergoes recycling for convective precipitation. This process leads to precipitation with more negative δ18 O values as convection progresses (Risi et al., 2010; Kurita, 2013; He et al., 2018a ). Furthermore, stratiform precipitation largely occurs in elevations well above the 0 °C level and contains ice particles (Houze, 2014 ). The ice particles grow through the direct deposition of vapor and possibly some riming while drifting slowly downward. They also undergo aggregation when approaching the melting layer, producing large particles. Under low-temperature conditions, the ice particle growth with vapor deposition involves a kinetic isotopic effect due to supersaturation (Jouzel and Merlivat, 1984 ), leading to lower isotope values. When falling below the elevation of the freezing point, these ice particles will melt into small raindrops (Houze, 2014 ), with lower δ18 O values. These processes also likely contribute to lower isotope values observed in stratiform rain (Fig. S4 ). Convection activities generally decrease the precipitation δ18 O during rain events but this decrease at the sampling site, i.e., on-site convection effect, is limited. For most events in this study, the difference (Δδ) between their initial and lowest δ18 O values varies ranges from 0.3 to 4 ‰, with only a few exceptions with a Δδ above 4 ‰ (Table S2 ). In this investigation, events with very low δ18 O values mostly exhibit corresponding low initial values, and as a result, the lowest and initial δ18 O values are positively correlated, as demonstrated in Fig. 3 . Take, for example, the event on June 14, where we recorded the lowest δ18 O values of − 15.2 ‰, along with a notably low initial δ18 O of − 13.8 ‰. Low initial precipitation δ18 O values in this rain event suggest that the vapor already had very low δ18 O values upon arrival at the sampling site. This observation suggests that accumulative convection, i.e., upstream rainout, along vapor transport trajectories, has significantly decreased vapor δ18 O values before precipitation. Therefore, upstream rainout remains an important factor influencing inter-event variations of precipitation isotopes. As rain slows down and humidity drops below the cloud-base, especially in the late stage of stratiform or near their end, raindrop re-evaporation becomes prevalent. The evaporation facilitates kinetic fractionation, causing an increase in precipitation δ18 O but a decrease in its d-excess. For example, at the late stage of the May 15 event, RH below 700 hPa consistently remained low, between 70 ∼ 80 % (Fig. 9  a). Such low humidity conditions favor rain evaporation, resulting in higher precipitation δ18 O and lower d-excess values. A similar evolution pattern in precipitation δ18 O and d-excess was also observed in the June 8 event (Fig. 9 b), characterized by a low RH zone below 750 hPa. Consequently, a negative correlation is often observed between δ18 O and d-excess during many events, especially in the stratiform zone (Moerman et al., 2013; He et al., 2018a ). The changing trend of precipitation δ18 O due to rain evaporation contributes to the formation of the V-shape or W-shape evolution pattern observed (Fig. 4 ). However, in some events, for example, those on 15 May and 11 June, there are no clear trends in the change of both δ18 O and d-excess values, and no correlation between them (Fig. 4 c, d, Table S4 ). This lack of correlation can be attributed to the presence of multiple convective systems that blur the relationships. On certain occasions, our site only captures a part of the convection system, as seen in the event at noon on May 13, which represents only the convection zone without the stratiform zone. During this event, both δ18 O and d-excess decrease and exhibit a positive correlation instead of a negative one.   5 Conclusion In this study, we collected pre-SCSSM rain samples and hourly rain samples during DBW rain events after the SCSSM onset and analyzed them for stable isotopes. These samples exhibit significant variation in their δ18 O values, ranging from − 3.5 ‰ to − 15.6 ‰. Generally, DBW rain samples have notably lower δ18 O values, with a weighted mean of − 9.7 ‰, compared to the pre-SCSSM samples, with a weighted mean of − 5.4 ‰. This long-term temporal variation pattern of precipitation δ18 O over the study period can be attributed to regional convective activity associated with large atmospheric circulation systems during the SCSSM, such as the Western Pacific subtropical high, shear line, and the cold vortex in the northern region. These large atmospheric circulation systems became more active during the SCSSM, leading to more intensive convective activities and thus lowering precipitation δ18 O values. This conclusion is supported by the strong positive correlation of precipitation δ18 O values at our site with regional OLR and the negative correlation with regional precipitation. Furthermore, the negative shifts in the δ18 O time series largely correspond to the presence of large spatial cloud coverage characterized by extremely low OLR, lower than 210 W/m2 . The seasonal fluctuation in moisture sources also has a significant influence on the long-term temporal variation pattern of precipitation δ18 O observed. Before the SCSSM, the water vapor primarily originated from nearby inland areas with short transport distances. After the onset of the SCSSM, water vapor mainly came from distant oceanic areas, with longer transport distances compared to the pre-SCSSM. The long transport distance of the moisture suggests a greater degree of Rayleigh distillation, which lowered precipitation δ18 O. This is exemplified by the negative correlation between upstream rainfall and δ18 O values, with the most pronounced correlation occurring at 96 h. Therefore, accumulative convective activities along water vapor transport trajectories influenced precipitation isotopes. In general, δ18 O during individual rain events shows a “V” shape, with higher values at the beginning and near the end but the lowest values in the middle of events, largely in the stratiform zone. A “W” shape is observed in some events, likely due to multiple convection cells captured at our sampling site. Occasionally, only a partial convection system passes by our site, and thus δ18 O evolution pattern only resembles a part of the V-shape or W-shape, such as a “L” shape or reversed “L” shape. Different from the long-term variations, the evolution of precipitation δ18 O during individual rain events is largely controlled by microphysical processes, including mesoscale subsidence, vapor deposition of ice particles in stratiform, and below-cloud rain-vapor interactions (e.g., rain re-evaporation). While mesoscale subsidence and vapor deposition tend to lower δ18 O values, rain evaporation increases δ18 O values. We noticed that those rain events with lower δ18 O values also have lower initial values. This suggests that accumulative convection or upstream rainout along vapor transport trajectories had significantly decreased vapor δ18 O values before precipitation, and the influence of on-site convection on precipitation δ18 O is limited. This observation further suggests that upstream rainout is also an important factor influencing inter-event variations of precipitation isotopes.
1 Introduction Groundwater Contaminant Source Identification (GCSI) is vital for controlling and remediating groundwater pollution (Ayvaz, 2010; Secci et al., 2022; Xu and Gómez-Hernández, 2016 ) by identifying the spatial and temporal characteristics of contaminant entry into aquifers (Khan et al., 2004; Lapworth et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2022 ). As highlighted by recent reviews by Gómez-Hernández and Xu (2022)  and Moghaddam et al. (2021) , the research on GCSI has grown exponentially in number over the past four decades. The GCSI methods include the direct method, and Simulation/Optimization (S/O) method (Atmadja and Bagtzoglou, 2001; Sun, 2007 ). The direct method often employs the footprint method, which utilizes isotope and geochemical techniques (Han et al., 2020 ). While this method has seen broader application in surface water (Chen et al., 2017; Miglietta et al., 2017 ), its application in identifying soil pollution sources remains less developed (Han et al., 2020 ), and it may yield inaccurate results under specific conditions (Stout et al., 1998 ). On the other hand, the S/O method has gained widespread popularity due to its demonstrated effectiveness (Ayvaz, 2010; Ayvaz and Karahan, 2008; Datta et al., 2011; Mirghani et al., 2009 ). In practical terms, the S/O method integrates contaminant transport simulation with optimization algorithms: numerical simulation to model contaminant transport in the aquifer, and optimization techniques to calibrate model parameters by aligning simulated results with observed temporal variations of contaminant concentrations in monitoring wells (Singh and Datta, 2006; Sun, 2007; Xia et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2007 ). This calibration process ensures that the calibrated model parameters offer valuable insights into the true conditions of the contaminant source. Some studies even note that GCSI is a typical groundwater inverse problem (Wang et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2007 ), this suggests that the S/O is so popular that when researchers mention GCSI, they may refer to the S/O method by default. Various optimization algorithms have been utilized for GCSI. There are the pre-existing optimization techniques adopted for GCSI, including Genetic Algorithm (GA) (Han et al., 2020 ), particle swarm optimization (Anshuman and Eldho, 2022; Li et al., 2020 ), heuristic optimization algorithms (Zhao et al., 2020 ), ensemble Kalman filter (ENKF) (Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021 ), Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm (Secci et al., 2022 ), Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (Xing et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2019 ), iterative local update ensemble smoother (ILUES) (Zheng et al., 2023 ), ensemble smoother method (Chang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ), Multiverse Optimization (Anshuman and Eldho, 2023 ). There are also new optimization methods developed specially for GCSI. These methods typically adopt a hybridization strategy, to combine the strengths of individual algorithms for improved accuracy, convergence speed, and search efficiency. These methods include the hybridization of Metropolis-Hasting algorithm with Kalman filter algorithm by (Luo et al., 2023 ), Ensemble Kalman Filter with ant colony algorithms by (Wang et al., 2022a ), a binary genetic algorithm with generalized reduced gradient method by (Ayvaz, 2016 ), particle swarm optimization with Markov chain method by (Pan et al., 2021 ), etc. Implementing these methods, especially the hybrid ones, requires considerable effort from researchers. Moreover, the optimization process requires thousands of iterations of the forward model to achieve effective convergence, causing high computation costs for GCSI. Faced with the prohibitively high computation costs, recent studies in GCSI have emphasized the necessity of surrogate models. Besides the iterative simulations in the optimization process, another reason for the high computation cost is the transient nature of contaminant transport simulation models: the simulation involves calculations at each time step, significantly increasing the overall computational workload. Surrogate models offer a more computationally efficient alternative by approximating the essential features of these complex simulations (Asher et al., 2015 ). The surrogate methods that have been utilized in GCSI research include Kriging (Anshuman and Eldho, 2022; Chang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022a; Yan et al., 2019 ), Support Vector Regression (Anshuman and Eldho, 2022 ); Radial basis function (RBF) (Li et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2019 ), Extreme learning machine (Li et al., 2021, 2020; Zhao et al., 2020 ), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) model (Pan et al., 2021; Secci et al., 2022 ), LSTM (Anshuman and Eldho, 2022; Li et al., 2021 ), temporal convolutional network (TCN) (Luo et al., 2023 ), convolutional neural network (Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2023 ), ensemble surrogate model (Xing et al., 2019 ). Notably, Zheng et al. (2023)  proposed an enhanced CNN specifically for GCSI surrogates. From the above-mentioned methods, we observe that the ANN model (and its variants CNN and LSTM) has been applied in GCSI. As a crucial part of artificial intelligence, the ANN models often exhibit satisfying accuracy for GCSI surrogates (Asher et al., 2015; Li et al., 2021 ). Another significant advantage of ANN surrogate models is the low computational demand after the initial training phase, because their calculations primarily consist of matrix operations like multiplication and addition. The ANN model can model complex non-linear relationships, thus used in various fields, including image, speech recognition, and hydrological modeling. Despite the success, the ANN models in GCSI have been used in an inversed manner with the typical practice of using the ANN models in various fields. Examining the use of ANN models across various domains, we find that the typical practice of using the ANN models involves inputting the model with raw data collections and it functions to output the desired outcomes. However, when the ANN models are used to construct the surrogate models in GCSI, desired outcomes (specifically contaminant release properties and aquifer parameters) are used as the input, and the estimated real-world data collections (contaminant concentrations at observation wells) are used as the output. This unconventional use of ANNs in GCSI inspired us to propose a novel GCSI approach that employs the ANN model in its classical manner. Specifically, for the new approach, we input monitored contaminant concentration data into the ANN model and let the model directly output the desired contaminant release properties and aquifer parameters. This novel GCSI approach eliminates the need for optimization algorithms and thus offers three distinct advantages. First, it removes the effort required to select an optimization algorithm from various options and to implement it. Second, it increases estimation efficiency because its estimation only requires a single pass through the neural network model (approximately 0.001 to 0.01 s), thus avoiding the high computational costs of traditional S/O methods, which often need thousands of iterations of the forward models. Third, it eliminates the issue of equifinality, an intrinsic limitation in all optimization inversion processes that can impact the accuracy and reliability of inversion results (Bohling and Butler, 2010; Wang et al., 2020, 2022 b; Younes et al., 2016 ). To the best of our knowledge, it remains unexplored to propose such a new GCSI method based on a machine-learning model, which takes monitored contaminant concentration BTCs as inputs and directly generates groundwater contaminant properties as outputs. In this work, we realize this new concept in GCSI by developing two novel GCSI methods: the Direct Forward Machine Learning (DFML) method and the Direct Forward One-Hot Machine Learning (OHML) method. Here, “Direct” signifies that these methods can directly estimate GCSI properties using available monitoring data collections, while 'Forward' emphasizes the absence of an inverse optimization algorithm. Both methods employ the ANN model in the field of machine learning. The first method DFML can estimate eight properties about the contaminant location, release history, and aquifer characteristics. The second OHML method incorporates the One-Hot encoding concept to provide the spatial distribution probability of the contaminant source, thereby enhancing the reliability of predictions. The feasibility and accuracy of the proposed approaches are tested. The new approaches provide novel and unconventional practices in the realm of GCSI. Through this exploration, we hope to contribute valuable perspectives to the evolving field of GCSI methodologies. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2  introduces the utilized methods. Section 3  introduces the setup of the simulation model and the construction of the two direct forward methods. The estimation results are verified and evaluated in Section 4 . Discussions and conclusions are provided in Section 5 .  2 Methodology 2.1 Numerical simulation model    We simulate the flow and solute transport process by a 2-D EPM model.
