The Baseline (S1) Scenario was designed to directly optimize the solution for the projected multi-regional input–output tables for the years 2020, 2025, and 2030. The Load Limiting (S2) Scenario was designed to restrict the scope of industrial restructuring and water use in the lower-rated areas. The key coefficient δ  in Scenario S2 denoted the spatial equilibrium adjustment coefficient, which was expressed as a relative value. The magnitude of the δ  value was determined by the ratio of the city’s overall evaluation score to the highest score attainable. Within Scenario S2, the constraints of spatial equilibrium were manifested in the imposition of limitation on the city’s aggregate output and the scope of interprovincial trade, as well as in the corresponding reduction of the city’s maximum total water usage. Further, the Water Intensity Mitigation (S3) Scenario is intended to reflect the potential impacts of future technological advances and water restriction policies on the optimization and regulation based on the Scenario S2.     4 Results 4.1 Quantification of virtual water 4.1.1 Inter-regional net virtual water transfer in the BTH region Virtual water transfers dependent on the industrial chain represent a potential avenue for mitigating spatial disequilibrium in regional water resources. The net virtual water flow of 13 cities in the BTH region was shown in Fig. 4  . Shijiazhuang, Tangshan, Tianjin and Handan were the net virtual water outflow cities, while the remaining 9 cities were in the state of net virtual water inflowing, including Baoding, Beijing, Qinhuangdao, Langfang, Hengshui, Cangzhou, Xingtai, Zhangjiakou and Chengde. Among them, Baoding and Beijing had the most significant net virtual water inflow, 3692.51 × 106  m3  and 3025.54 × 106  m3  respectively, which indicated that the economic development of these regions requires a large number of virtual water-intensive products. In contrast to previous studies, Tianjin played the role of a net virtual water inflow city in the BTH region (Zhao et al., 2017 ). However, after excluding the effects of imports and exports, its virtual water outflow exceeded the inflow, and were mainly toward Beijing. Shijiazhuang and Tangshan accounted for most of the net virtual water outflow, with 6132.89 × 106  m3  and 5102.18 × 106  m3  respectively. These relatively underdeveloped regions seeked economic growth mainly through the water-intensive products export, which made water scarcity worse in regions with water shortage. Although virtual water trade could regulate the disequilibrium distribution of water resources among regions in certain degree, the spatial difference of water resources endowment and the regional economic development degree limited the effect of virtual water transfer. The inter-regional virtual water transfer in the BTH region was shown in Fig. 5  . Tangshan transferred 1382.18 × 106  m3  virtual water to Baoding and 969.91 × 106  m3  virtual water to Cangzhou. Shijiazhuang transferred 1200.70 × 106  m3  virtual water to Baoding and 895.74 × 106  m3  virtual water to Cangzhou. In terms of water resources, Shijiazhuang and Tangshan were scarcer than Baoding and Cangzhou. It can be explained that the two cities used the already insufficient water resources for production to be consumed by other cities with relatively sufficient water resources, which were driven by socio-economic relations. These indirect impact on local water stress, resulting from economic linkages, required decision makers to manage it under the synergic judgment of economic measures and environmental policies.  4.1.2 Revised water resources stress index In the face of increasingly severe water scarcity, RWRSI could provide a more accurate classification of water resource stress and incorporate the challenges of regional industrial linkages to water resources in a manner more consistent with actual conditions. As depicted in Fig. 6  , a comparison of water consumption levels before and after the adjustments reveals that the water consumption of cities which virtual water was net outflow had all decreased. The water consumption of Shijiazhuang, Tangshan, and Handan had all reached a negative value after revision. The water resources stress of Beijing and Tianjin had no significant change before and after the revision, and the water resources were still under extreme stress. The water resources stress of Qinhuangdao, Baoding, Langfang, and Hengshui had changed from no stress to extreme stress immediately after revision. Also, these four cities were heavily dependent on the water resources of others in the BTH region. On the contrary, Shijiazhuang and Tangshan which had moderate and mild water resources stress respectively became water-rich cities without stress after revision. Among the cities with water resources stress, Xingtai, Beijing, Tianjin, Qinhuangdao, Baoding, Langfang, and Hengshui all belonged to the extreme stress state, while the others were in the no stress state. The RWRSI in the BTH region was relatively polarized except for Xingtai city. When the city was not in extreme stress state, it was in no stress state, and vice versa. The coordinated development of the BTH region had contributed to the inter-regional sharing of water resources stress. However, nearly half cities with extreme water stress would have drastic changes of the water resources stress index before and after the revision. To some extent, this suggested that the water stress across the BTH region could no longer be adequately mitigated by the existing economic trade relationships and industrial structures within the region. While guaranteeing water demand for each city, it is imperative to explore alternative industrial adjustment strategies or to seek water resource support from external sources. However, this approach may entail the transference of additional challenges, such as inefficient water resource utilization and water quality contamination.   4.2 Spatial equilibrium evaluation of water resources load As shown in Table 2  , the comprehensive index weights of the four dimensions of water resources consumption, water pollution discharge, water space crowding and water flux interference were 0.4634, 0.2541, 0.1674, and 0.1151 respectively. The Proportion of water quality above class III, the proportion of inferior class V water quality, and the proportion of water area were the indicators with weights greater than 0.1 in the evaluation system, accounting for a total weight of 0.3942. At the same time, the water quality index was greatly affected by the subjective weight, which increased from 0.1799 to 0.2541. In order to respond to the demand of high-quality development, the water quality requirement was artificially and subjectively raised, which was the direction measure to comply with the high-quality development. Proportion of water area acreage index in the area criterion was greatly affected by the objective weight, which decreased from 0.2069 to 0.1401. The Proportion of water area acreage was mainly determined by the water area of a city and the scope of the administrative area. In actual regulation and control, the measures implemented may be relatively large or difficult to achieve. The results of proximity degree in each criterion shown in Fig. 7   also clearly exhibited the disorganized “quantity-quality-area-flow” relationship among cities in the BTH region. In terms of space, equilibrium is even more out of the question. The evaluation scores of the four criterions were mostly concentrated in the range of 0.2–0.6, which indicated that the water resources load capacity of the BTH region was mostly at a medium or low level. As shown in Fig. 8  , the spatial equilibrium capacity of water resources load in Chengde was in the first echelon, while Baoding, Tianjin, Qinhuangdao, Zhangjiakou, Tangshan, Cangzhou and Handan were in the second echelon. Langfang, Hengshui, Beijing, Shijiazhuang and Xingtai were in the third echelon. From a spatial planning standpoint, the hierarchical urban structure of the BTH region was delineated as follows: The primary tier, led by Chengde, predominantly constitutes the ecological conservation zone. The secondary tier, with Tianjin at its core, encompassed the central region’s key functional and coastal development areas. The third tier included the central core area, anchored by Beijing, along with the functional expansion zones in the southern part of the region.  4.3 Multi-dimensional equilibrium optimal allocation of water resources This section outlined the resolution of the multidimensional equilibrium optimization model for water resources, conducted using Lingo 12.0, and grounded in the input–output tables derived from projections for the years 2020, 2025, and 2030. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of the outcomes across the three scenarios, S1, S2, and S3, was performed to discern the key nodes and sectors. 4.3.1 Water resources optimization under basic Scenario As shown in Fig. 9  , Tangshan and Qinhuangdao were the main net virtual water outflow cities in the BTH region under the Scenario S1, and the amounts of outflow gradually increased. Although Chengde, Zhangjiakou, and Beijing were net virtual water outflow cities, whose virtual water inflow and outflow were relatively close, they were not obvious in the figure. Over time, the virtual water outflow from Langfang gradually increased, resulting in Langfang becoming a net virtual water outflow city by 2030. On the contrary, the others were the net virtual water inflow cities in the BTH region. Notably, Shijiazhuang displayed the most significant net virtual water inflow, which surged to 298.10 × 106  m3 , 413.02 × 106  m3 , and 578.48 × 106  m3  in 2020, 2025, and 2030, respectively, starkly contrasting with the pre-optimization net outflow. In general, the net virtual water inflow in Shijiazhuang increased rapidly, while the net virtual water outflow of Tangshan rose sharply. It could also be expressed that the water resources stress in Shijiazhuang would increasingly spill over, which limited the overall spatial equilibrium of regional water resources. In contrast, Tangshan would make a great contribution to achieving the spatial equilibrium of water resources in the BTH region. The transfer of various sectors among cities after the optimization under the basic scenario was shown in Fig. 10  . Among the cities with net virtual water outflow, the agricultural sectors of Xingtai, Qinhuangdao, Tangshan, and Beijing emerged as the primary outflow sectors. In Shijiazhuang, PM and CPM were the main recipients of virtual water inflow, whereas the outflow from its AGR sector constituted a significant portion. Over time, the virtual water outflow from Tangshan’s AGR and MIN increased progressively, while its MM’s virtual water outflow diminished and approached nil by 2030. In Langfang, the virtual water inflow of CPM and the virtual water outflow of SER were increasing by degrees. The virtual water inflow of its PM was about 48.38 × 106  m3  in 2020 and 2025, while suddenly dropped to 28.56 × 106  m3  in 2030, and that made Langfang become a net virtual water outflow city. When the volume of virtual water transfer associated with the PM diminished to a critical level, Langfang City could attain an equilibrium in the allocation of virtual water transfer among regional sectors by augmenting the volume of virtual water outflow amount within the SER. In general, the net virtual water outflow cities were mainly reflected by the increase of the AGR outflow. In the net virtual water inflow cities, except for Shijiazhuang, the virtual water outflow of the SER was increasing with the year.  4.3.2 Identifying key nodes in the BTH region By comparing the optimization outcomes of Scenario S2 with those of Scenario S1, the variations in water resources optimization and regulation strategies, accounting for spatial equilibrium of water resources load, can be discerned. Similarly, when contrasting the optimization outcomes of Scenario S3 with those of Scenario S2, it becomes evident that: following the initial attainment of spatial equilibrium, and in the context of technological breakthroughs in water conservation and the enforcement of water restriction policies, the regional water resources system would be further optimized and directed along a specific trajectory, as depicted in Fig. 11  . With respect to the nature and direction of virtual water transfer, the optimization outcomes under the S2 align closely with those of the S1, manifesting a clear direction for spatially equilibrium regulation. Nevertheless, significant variability is observed in the before-and-after comparisons, highlighting the dynamic nature of the adjustments. In summary, it could be deduced that the spatial equilibrium of water resources was achieved through the enhancement of virtual water transfers from cities such as Shijiazhuang, Tangshan, Qinhuangdao, Handan, and Baoding to Langfang and Cangzhou. Compared with the Scenario S3 and the Scenario S2, the virtual water transfer changes were only displayed at three nodes: Shijiazhuang to Cangzhou, Shijiazhuang to Langfang, and Tangshan to Langfang. The key transfer nodes for virtual water spatial equilibrium in the BTH region could be discerned through an analysis of the patterns of change in the optimization results across the three target years. In general, the regulation of spatial equilibrium within the water resources system of the BTH region primarily occurs among the cities in Hebei Province, with limited involvement of the two economic core cities, Beijing and Tianjin. This aligns largely with our anticipated outcomes, as the load limiting coefficient δ  is represented in percentage terms, and both Beijing and Tianjin exhibit significantly higher levels of total city output and the volume of inter-city trade compared to the other cities. Consequently, they would be subject to more stringent constraints. In the figure, key nodes were denoted by circles, with different colors signifying various temporal changing trends in virtual water transfer: red for surging nodes, blue for growth nodes, green for fluctuating nodes, purple for unchanged nodes, and yellow for decreasing nodes. The transfer changes were mainly concentrated on Shijiazhuang of row direction as well as Cangzhou and Langfang of column direction, encompassing the majority of surging nodes (80 %) and a substantial proportion of the growth nodes.  4.3.3 Regulation guidance of key nodes’ industrial transfer The nodes identified were most pronounced in the year 2030, hence the results for that year were used as an example for demonstration. The regulation guidance of inter-sectoral virtual water transfer in surging nodes was depicted in Fig. 12  . Shijiazhuang, Handan and Cangzhou were classified as net virtual water inflow cities, with the transfer control in these surging nodes primarily achieved through the virtual water embedded in agricultural products and services. Langfang, on the other hand, was a net virtual water outflow city, while Baoding was a net virtual water inflow city. The inflow to Langfang was predominantly concentrated in the manufacturing and service sectors. Simultaneously, the virtual water outflow from Langfang was mainly from the manufacturing sector, thus the virtual water inflow it primarily accepted was only reflected in the transfer to its service sector, while most of its manufacturing sectors served as transfer stations. The regulation guidance of inter-sectoral virtual water transfer in growth nodes was presented in Fig. 13  . The guidance from Cangzhou to Tangshan primarily involved the virtual water transfer from Cangzhou's chemical product manufacturing to Tangshan's mining sector. However, under the Scenario S1, the virtual water transfer from Tangshan’s mining sector exceeded the incremental transfer to Cangzhou’s chemical product manufacturing, resulting in a net reduction in the transfer in this direction. Similarly, in the regulation of net inflow cities (from Shijiazhuang to Baoding and Hengshui), the inflow of primary manufacturing from other cities to local chemical product manufacturing promoted its outflow. In the regulation among net outflow cities, it was predominantly the transfer of the same or similar industries in Xingtai's manufacturing, service, and electrical and gas industries to Langfang. In the regulation from net outflow cities to net inflow cities (Tangshan to Baoding, Qinhuangdao to Cangzhou), the primary focus was on increasing the net virtual water inflow to the chemical products manufacturing sector. The regulation guidance of inter-sectoral virtual water transfer in fluctuating, unchanged, and decreasing nodes was illustrated in Fig. 14  . The transfer of virtual water in the nodes from Langfang to Tangshan and from Qinhuangdao to Xingtai has shifted, with a notable increase in the transfer of agricultural virtual water from the source cities to the primary manufacturing sectors of the destination cities. The notion of unchanged nodes suggested that these nodes have converged towards spatial equilibrium as a result of the optimization within the Scenario S1, while the load limitation could be largely avoided through regulatory measures. The equilibrium was achieved through virtual water transfers such as those from Shijiazhuang’s primary manufacturing sector to Tangshan’s agricultural sector, from Tangshan’s chemical product manufacturing sector to Shijiazhuang’s own chemical product manufacturing sector, and from Qinhuangdao’s advanced manufacturing sector to Handan’s transportation sector. In the decreasing node, Qinhuangdao and Langfang, which were both net virtual water outflow cities, were governed primarily by the intercity transfer of metal manufacturing and other advanced manufacturing sectors. This transfer of industries between cities served to counterbalance the overall decline observed in the node. In reality, water intensity mitigation generally refers to the technological advancements in the secondary industry and the water restriction policies in the tertiary industry. The data presented in Fig. 15  , demonstrated the effectiveness of the regulation in reducing virtual water transfer. The observed effects were predominantly manifested in the inter-transfer of chemical products manufacturing sectors between Shijiazhuang and Tangshan, indicating that the impact was directionally constrained. Given the practical challenges of reducing water intensity, this regulatory approach requires the collaborative efforts and cooperation of the entire society.    5 Discussion This investigation quantified virtual water transfers within the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, assessing not only the volumetric flow of water resources but also pinpointing the underlying sources of water stress in each urban. The revised water resources stress index delineated the cities that were most at risk, suggesting that virtual water transfers within industrial networks could either mitigate or exacerbate local water stress. Evaluating the spatial equilibrium of water resource loading revealed a pronounced disequilibrium within the region, necessitating a strategic approach to the development, and siting of water-intensive industries. A multi-dimensional equilibrium optimal allocation model of water resources was employed, solved under spatial equilibrium constraints, to tackle this critical decision-making challenge. Within the intra-city, prioritizing agriculture to satisfy internal virtual water demand and curbing non-essential construction were key to achieving water resource equilibrium. Within urban agglomerations, the migration of virtual water through the chemical manufacturing sector represented a significant strategy for mitigating water stress impacts. In the context of the Scenario S3, it was noteworthy that the expedited transfer of virtual water from the chemical products manufacturing sector in Shijiazhuang to its counterpart in Tangshan constituted the immediate and principal strategy. The biomedical sector in Shijiazhuang stands as a key economic support for the city. To effectively tackle the issue of spatial imbalance in water resources and to reduce water intensity, it is imperative to harness the industry’s current scale. This can be achieved by fostering the growth of the chemical products manufacturing sector. Additionally, reinforcing inter-industry connections within the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region will play a crucial role in this strategic approach. Tangshan, with its steel industry as a primary growth engine, has seen optimization strategies that highlighted the importance of increasing virtual water inflows from other cities into its mining sector. Langfang, as a crucial transit point, has achieved a reversal in the net direction of virtual water transfer by enhancing the outflow of virtual water associated with its service industries. As the political and economic epicenter of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei urban agglomeration and China, Beijing enjoyed a central role in industrial development. What can be foreseen is, Certain firms would opt to maintain their headquarters in Beijing while shifting production to cities with lower water stress, such as Shijiazhuang, Tangshan, Handan, Zhangjiakou, Chengde, and Cangzhou. This strategy would allow companies to leverage Beijing’s status while reducing the capital’s water consumption and indirectly facilitating virtual water transfers from Hebei province to Beijing. The Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region’s core objectives were to foster integrated development and governance among its cities, facilitate industrial structural transformation, and promote an equilibrium allocation of water resources. Whereas existing policies predominantly concentrated on curbing direct water consumption and enhancing water use efficiency, this paper offered novel perspectives on water management and governance through the regulation of spatial equilibrium in water resources, contingent upon industrial interconnections.  6 Conclusion Utilizing the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region as a case study, this research employed an integrated IOAAPO framework to systematically investigate the spatial distribution and evolutionary dynamics of water resources. The spatial equilibrium of regional water resources was scientifically evaluated, and the BTH region was initially divided into three water resources carrying layers. Finally, a multi-dimensional spatial optimization and integrated management method for regional water resources was designed, and key nodes and sectors for water resources transfer were precisely located. The following main conclusions were drawn: (1) The flow of virtual water within the BTH region has been delineated, and the consumption of water resources for each city have been revised, thereby providing a more accurate depiction of the actual regional water stress conditions. (2) The spatial equilibrium of water resource loading in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region was evaluated across four dimensions: water quantity, water quality, water area, and water flow, with cities categorized into three tiers based on their functional orientations. (3) The future industrial structure of the BTH region was forecasted utilizing the Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) model, and the multi-dimensional equilibrium allocation of water resources was optimized accounting for the heterogeneity of regional water resource endowments. This study provided an important perspective and enlightenment for the comprehensive urban agglomeration level joint prevention control of water-saving policies and environmental resource elements management in the trade system. It has expanded and enhanced the traditional research scope of water resources accounting in urban agglomerations, which had important practical significance for promoting the adjustment and sustainable development of high water consumption industries. Furthermore, this study provided essential guidance for decision makers to formulate more comprehensive urban agglomeration water conservation policies, and presented novel insights and methodologies for governing the trade system with environmental ecological factors. The optimization model employed in this study categorized regions based on input–output tables, which may not always align with the actual hydrological boundaries of water resources. Consequently, the optimization results and regulatory strategies derived from administrative divisions may introduce some degree of bias. In our future research, water environmental considerations should be integrated to redefine these boundaries more accurately. Due to limitations in data availability, this paper only considered the transfer of virtual water within the BTH region in 2015, and did not incorporate detailed international trade data. The increasingly interwoven import–export trade is exerting a growing influence on the water resource system of the region. Incorporating these factors in future studies would yield more precise regulatory directions and policy guidance.
1 Introduction In recent decades, extreme precipitation events have become more frequent and of greater magnitude, particularly in urban areas (Burian and Shepherd, 2005; Fowler et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021 ), threatening the lives and property of inhabitants. For example, in 2021, the 7.20 heavy rainstorm disaster in Zhengzhou City affected 14.78 million people in Henan Province, with a direct economic loss of 120.6 billion CNY. Therefore, the spatiotemporal variability of extreme precipitation and its influencing factors have been extensively explored in various regions of the world (Zhang et al., 2013; Zeder and Fischer, 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). The average annual precipitation in China has been increasing by 0.8 %/decade, with the annual cumulative rainstorm (daily precipitation ≥ 50 mm) increasing by 4.2 %/decade (China Meteorological Administration, 2023 ). Regional differences in the variability of extreme precipitation are present and studies on the Yangtze River Basin showed a greater upward trend in extreme precipitation in the eastern region (Wu et al., 2023 ). Changes in the intensity and duration of precipitation extremes are attributed to both global climate change (Westra et al., 2013; Millán, 2014; Wang et al., 2020a ) and urbanization (Fowler et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2022 ). Global warming intensifies the hydrological cycle (Fowler et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021 ), leading to a more variable hydro-climate on different time scales. Human activities unequivocally caused global warming, and global surface temperatures were 1.1°C higher in 2011–2020 than in 1850–1990 (IPCC, 2023 ). In China, the warming rate from 1961 to 2022 was about 0.16 °C/decade, higher than the global average over the same period (China Meteorological Administration, 2023 ). The responses of extreme rainfall to the warming climate differ in different regions of China and are more sensitive in the lower Yangtze River Basin (Wang et al., 2020a ). The impact of urbanization on precipitation is more complex. Urbanization is accompanied by intense human social and economic activities, resulting in changes in the underlying surface characteristics, local weather, and climate (Zhao et al., 2023 ), such as urban heat islands (Wu and Yang, 2013; Wu et al., 2021 ) and urban moisture islands (Hao et al., 2018 ; Du et al., 2019 ; Luo et al., 2021 ), which affect the generation and intensity of precipitation (Fletcher et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, changes in land use and building spatial forms alter the energy balance in urban areas, affecting winds, storm characteristics, and precipitation distribution, intensity, and frequency (Ntelekos et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2016; Huszar et al., 2020 ). The effects of urbanization on precipitation have mainly been investigated using the urban-rural comparison method (Lokoshchenko, 2017; Tang et al., 2022 ) and the comparative analysis between different periods in the same region (Burian and Shepherd, 2005; Wu et al., 2023 ). Tang et al. (2022)  found that both high urbanization level and speed are conducive to summer hourly extreme precipitation in central China. Zhao and Wu (2017)  found that warming associated with urbanization, particularly in urban clusters, influenced large-scale circulation and precipitation, leading to an average increase in precipitation of 0.016 mm/day over China. However, the specific causes of the changes in extreme precipitation at different temporal and spatial scales remain controversial. Compared with an individual city, urban agglomerations have multiple highly urbanized centres with radiation-leading roles and are subject to a wide range of anthropogenic influences that affect regional extreme precipitation and other environmental factors (Sun et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020 ). Therefore, this study focused on the urban agglomerations in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River (MRUA) and explored the influence of the spatially uneven development of urban areas using distributed urbanization indicators (population and impervious surface morphology indicators, etc.) rather than the overall statistics of administrative regions. The MRUA is the largest urban agglomeration located in central China, spanning 31 prefecture-level cities in three provinces, with a total area of over 350,000 km2 . It is a key area of urbanization in China and occupies an important position in its development patterns. Owing to the large size and data availability, trend analyses tend to focus on a specific city or sub-basin, with fewer studies on the entire urban agglomeration. Dai et al. (2023)  used daily meteorological data from 89 stations and analyzed the spatial and temporal characteristics of summer extreme precipitation in the Wuhan Urban Agglomeration, which is part of the MRUA. The increasing trend in short-term precipitation was also observed in the Poyang Lake Basin in the southeastern part of the MRUA (Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Liu et al. (2022)  explored the spatiotemporal variation of extreme precipitation during 1970–2017 in the MRUA using daily data from 27 meteorological stations and revealed an increase in extreme precipitation. However, the low resolution of data from meteorological stations, together with the use of different stations and periods by different researchers, lack uniform conclusions for trend analyses and spatial heterogeneity within the entire region. Therefore, selecting high-precision precipitation product data in combination with distributed urbanization indicators can fill the gaps in the study of extreme precipitation trends and the impacts of urbanization in the MRUA. The MRUA includes areas with uneven levels of urbanization, allowing for comparative studies at multiple spatial scales between cities, and between centres and rural areas of the same city. This study aims to reveal the spatiotemporal variation characteristics of extreme precipitation and the cluster effects of different urbanization indicators on a large scale. Based on high-resolution precipitation and urbanization data, the key impact indicator of extreme precipitation at the urban agglomeration scale was explored using regression models, and the contributions of urbanization were quantitatively analyzed by urban-rural comparison method. The influence mechanism and spatial scales of urbanization are further discussed in Section 3.4 . These findings are highly relevant for meteorological disaster prevention in economically developed and densely populated regions such as the MRUA and provide a solid foundation for the impact mechanism analysis of extreme precipitation in the context of rapid large-scale urbanization.  2 Data and material 2.1 Study region The MRUA, a pillar of the Yangtze River Economic Belt, is a super-large urban agglomeration comprising the Wuhan Metropolitan Area (WHM) in Hubei Province, the Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan City Group (CZT) in Hunan Province, and the Poyang Lake Metropolitan Area (PLM) in Jiangxi Province ( Fig. 1 ). Located between 110.25° to 118.48° E and 25.98° to 32.64° N, the MRUA is the largest urban agglomeration in China, accounting for approximately 3 % of the national territorial area. The region has a typical subtropical humid monsoon climate with four distinct seasons, and rainfall is mainly concentrated in summer. Abundant and intricate river-lake networks flow through the MRUA and provide rich water resources. Over the past twenty years, the MRUA has experienced increasingly accelerated urban expansion (approximately 250 km2 /year) (Zheng et al., 2020 ), covering a large latitude and longitude span with differences in the overall urbanization process, including the megacity of Wuhan, the big cities of Changsha and Nanchang, and medium-sized cities and small towns. High population concentrations (more than 130 million people by 2022) and high regional GDP (10,959 billion CNY in 2022 from the Provincial Bureau of Statistics) make the region highly vulnerable to extreme climate risks. Therefore, it is of practical importance to explore the influence of urbanization on extreme precipitation in this region, and an increased knowledge will help understand the effects of large-scale urbanization on extreme climate events worldwide.  2.2 Data processing Based on daily rainfall data from 53 national meteorological stations (locations shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 ), the applicability of multiple precipitation products (CMFD, MSWEP, and CN05.1) was evaluated on daily, monthly, and yearly time scales (accuracy assessment metrics and results are shown in Supplementary Table 1 ). The accuracy assessment results showed that the errors in the annual precipitation and annual maximum 1-day precipitation were relatively small (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). The daily precipitation correlation coefficient, normalized root-mean-square error (NMSE), and probability of detection (POD) calculation results were 0.72, 0.69, and 0.98, respectively. The China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD) was created through the fusion of remote sensing products, reanalysis datasets, and in-situ station data (He et al., 2020 ). This dataset has been widely used for the construction of hydrological models and downscaling of global climate models in China (He et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ), including the Yangtze River Basin (Jin et al., 2022 ), and can capture spatiotemporal patterns of extreme precipitation indices. This study used four meteorological elements of the CMFD (daily precipitation, temperature, specific humidity, and wind speed) to analyze historical changes and serve as natural factors that may affect extreme precipitation indicators (O’Gorman, 2015 ). To analyze the influence of spatially uneven urbanization, various urbanization indicators, including residential population, degree of urbanization, and impervious surface area dynamics, were used in this study. Data for these indices, which reflect the development patterns, were obtained from global public raster datasets and clipped to the study area. The data list and specific sources are listed in  Table 1 . The definition and classification of “Degree of Urbanization” by GHS-SMOD are based on the population and building surface (Schiavina et al., 2022 ); the complete workflow logic is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 . Data pre-processing was performed to unify the spatial resolution of the raw data; grids were generated based on the 0.1° resolution of meteorological data, and the population and impervious area were summed in each 0.1° × 0.1°grid. On this basis, a subsequent series of indices (in Sections 2.4 and 2.5 ) was calculated. Then, the influence of urbanization on the evolution of precipitation characteristics was explored using regression models and urban-rural comparison method.  2.3 Mann-kendall trend test The Mann-Kendall (M-K) test is a common method for the trend analysis of hydro-meteorological variables (Gocic and Trajkovic, 2013; Gong et al., 2023 ), which assumes that variables are independent and uniformly distributed. If the length of the data series n  > 10, the test statistic S  and standard normal test statistic Z  are calculated using Eqs. (1) and (2) . When the absolute value of the calculated Z -value is greater than the standard normal distribution threshold value under the confidence level, the data series shows a statistically significant positive or negative trend. In this study, the trend significance test of the precipitation index was performed at the 95 % and 99 % confidence levels, and the corresponding thresholds were 1.96 and 2.58, respectively.(1) S = ∑ i = 1  n - 1   ∑ j = i + 1  n  s g n ( x  j   -   x  i   )     (2) Z = { S - 1  V A R ( S )    ( S >  0 )    0 ( S = 0 )    S + 1  V A R ( S )    ( S <  0 )           where n  is the length of the data; x  i    and x  j    are the values in time series i  and j  (j  > i ); VAR(S)  is the variance.  2.4 Urbanization index calculation This study quantified the urbanization process of the MRUA from two dimensions: population growth and changes in the underlay. The raster data from GHSL were used to calculate the corresponding population of each grid by the “Zonal statistic” tool in ArcGIS. The annual, seasonal, and extreme precipitation indicators of 2914 grids from 1979 to 2018 were calculated, and the change trends over the past 40 years were statistically analyzed.  2.6 Regression model Regression analysis is an effective way to explore and simulate the relationship between variables and test the significance of this relationship and has been widely used in econometrics, urban planning, ecological environment, and other fields (Ariken et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Mollalo et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020b ). In this study, global and local regression models were applied to explore the spatially varying associations between important urbanization factors and extreme precipitation. The regression model was implemented using the MGWR 2.2 software (https://sgsup.asu.edu/sparc/multiscale-gwr ). Ordinary least square (OLS) is a classical linear regression model, regardless of the influence of spatial weights of variables; the basic equation is shown below (Eq. 7 ).(7) y  i   = β  0   + ∑ k = 1  m  β  k    x  i k   + ε  i   , i ∈ [ 1 , n ]     where y  i     is the response variable, referring to the extreme precipitation indices in Table 2 ; x  i k     is the value of the k  th independent variable in the i th sample, including the meteorological elements and urbanization indicators mentioned in Section 2.4 ; β  k     is the corresponding coefficient; ε  i     is the error term; n  is the number of samples; m  is the number of dependent variables. The geographically weighted regression (GWR) was proposed (Fotheringham et al., 2016 ) to address the problem of the OLS model ignoring the spatial relationship of variables and the non-stationarity of spatial location. The spatial position of the variable is embedded in the regression equation as shown in Eq. (8) .(8) y  i   = β  0   ( u  i   , v  i    )  + ∑ k = 1  m  b  k    ( u  i   , v  i    )  x  i k   + e  i   , i ∈ [ 1 , n ]     where ( u  i   , v  i    )    are the spatial coordinates of the i th sample. The major difference between the two models is that GWR is a local regression model, which assumes that the contribution of each sample is weighed according to its proximity to the local sample points. The space weight is calculated using the Gaussian function, as shown in Eq. (9) .(9) ω  i j   = e x p ( - ( d  i j    b   )  2   )      where ω  i j     is the weight of the j th data point to the i th observation point; d  i j     is the distance between the j th data point and i th observation point; b   is the bandwidth, determined by the criteria of the Akaike information criterion(AICc) (Fotheringham and Oshan, 2016 ). To avoid bias in the regression analysis caused by multicollinearity of the dependent variables, the variance inflation factor (VIF) was used to test the linear correlation of the independent variables (Ma et al., 2020 ). It is generally believed that if the VIF value > 10, the variable has multicollinearity and should be removed. The VIF equation is given in Eq. To separate the contributions from urbanization and climate change, with reference to the urban heat island effect (Hu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2021 ), the urban-rural comparison method was used. Based on the GHS-SMOD, whether the raster belongs to urban (including urban centre and urban cluster) or rural by the major type in the grid can be determined (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). Rural grids can reflect the background values of climate change, and the effect of urbanization can be determined by the difference between the urban and rural grids. To reduce differences in atmospheric conditions due to regional and inter-annual variations, the intensity of the urban heat island effect (UHII  ) is expressed as a relative value of the difference between urban and rural temperatures (Δ T   ).(11) UHII = T  u r b a n   - T  r u r a l    T  r u r a l         where T  u r b a n     is the mean temperature in urban area; T  r u r a l     is the mean temperature in rural area. The effect of urbanization on the variable X  is defined as:(12) Δ X = X  u r b a n   - X  r u r a l       where X  u r b a n     is the mean value in urban; X  r u r a l     is the mean value in rural area.   3 Result and discussion 3.1 Urbanization characteristics of the MRUA 3.1.1 Urbanization characteristics of the underlying surface and population As shown in  Fig. 2 (a), the impervious surface in the MRUA expanded significantly from 1972 to 2019, with the total area increasing from 1356 km² to 14,509 km². The three capital cities, Wuhan, Nanchang, and Changsha, had the densest distribution of impervious surfaces, with the proportion of impervious surfaces excluding water bodies in Wuhan reaching 15.23 % in 2019. The surrounding areas showed a multi-center decentralized expansion pattern, and the total impervious area (urban area) accounted for a relatively small proportion (< 0.5 %) in 2019. The urban agglomeration area was evenly divided into 2914 grids (grey grids in Fig. 2 (a)) with a spatial resolution of 0.1°. The growth trends of the total IA and total population (POP) are different in the MRUA (Fig. 2 (b)), where the growth rate of the IA continues to increase with time, whereas the population growth rate slowed after 1995. The different trends in these two variables reflect the inconsistency of multiple dimensions of urbanization, which should be considered in the construction of the urbanization indicator system. In this study, the three classifications of urban degree (urban centre, urban cluster, and rural cluster, representing high, moderate, and low urbanization, respectively) and water body were used for trend analysis. Over the past forty-five years, the urban center and urban cluster areas have experienced an increase in the MRUA, whereas the rural cluster area has decreased (Fig. 2 (c)). Combining statistical results and regional development policies, the urbanization process in the MRUA can be categorized into three stages: a) the rapid development stage (1975–1990). In 1978, China's reform and opening up was implemented. It improved people's well-being and promoted the modernization of China; therefore, the regional population and rural cluster areas are rising rapidly; b) the fluctuation stage (1990–2000), when the urbanization development mode changed and the overall rate of urban expansion slowed down; c) the new stage of urbanization development (2000–2020), implementing the new concept of "insisting on the coordinated development of large, medium, and small cities and small towns".  3.1.2 Urbanization process of three metropolitan areas Considering the three development stages and time series of the collected data, this study divided the historical period into four periods: S1 (1979–1989), S2 (1990–1999), S3 (2000–2009), and S4 (2010–2018). The violin plot ( Fig. 3 ) shows the changes and variations in urbanization indicators at various stages of development in the three metropolitan areas.(1) Population density (Fig. 3 (a)) was obtained by dividing the total population of each grid by the grid area. The population densities of the three urban agglomerations showed an increasing trend, and the mean values were always the highest for WHM (500 persons/km2  in S4) and lowest for PLM (344 persons/km2  in S4). There were several extreme points in Wuhan that were much higher than the other regions of the city clusters.  (2) The changes in the IA and IAE exhibited similar patterns (Fig. 3 (b-c)). WHM has the highest average IA and IAE in the three urban agglomerations, with mean values of 0.03 and 0.13 km2 /year, respectively, for the historical period. CZT and PLM exhibited some peaks (in the provincial capital city center area), and the overall distribution had a growth trend.  (3) The spatial morphology of impervious surfaces was reflected by IPD and SI, as shown in Fig. 3 (d-e). The expansion of impervious surfaces was accompanied by a decreasing IPD trend (representing fragmentation), which was most pronounced in the CZT. The mean values of SI in the three metropolitan areas showed an increasing trend, indicating a greater spatial complexity of the impervious surface.     3.1.3 Relationship among urbanization indicators To explore the relationship among the different urbanization indicators, the mean values of four periods and change values from S1 to S4 (represented by ∆X) of 2914 grids were calculated. The 3D scatter plot of IA-POP-∆POP ( Fig. 4 (a)) shows that most of the grids are less urbanized and clustered in the lower left corner (IA < 0.1, POP < 200,000 persons/grid, and ∆POP around 0). Then, analyzed from three projection coordinates: the orange dots indicate a positive correlation between IA and POP in highly urbanized areas (IA > 0.4); the green dots show that when IA > 0.2, the ∆POP > 0, indicating that the permanent population has the willingness to migrate from areas with low urbanization to other areas with high urbanization; the blue dots show that population decline (∆POP < 0) occurs only in areas with small resident populations (POP < 200,000 persons/grid), whereas population growth is linearly positive when the number of permanent residents is large. SI is a landscape index reflecting the spatial distribution of impervious surface in each grid, and the relationship among its change (ΔSI), IA and its change (ΔIA) were explored (Fig. 4 (b)). The analysis is based on the entire region and the three projection coordinates: on the whole, the impervious area in all the grids showed an expanding trend (ΔIA > 0), except for some grids with the impervious area always equal to 0; the orange dots indicate that IA and ΔIA are linearly positive in the less urbanized area (IA < 0.3), whereas the change amplitude decreased in the highly urbanized area; the green dots indicate that in the highly urbanized area (IA > 0.4), the SI decreases (ΔSI < 0) with the expansion of impervious area. The reason may be that when the impervious area is sufficiently large, its overall spatial continuity is higher, and its complexity is reduced.   3.2 Temporal and spatial changes in precipitation 3.2.1 Long-term temporal change trends of precipitation The average annual precipitation and summer precipitation (June to September) during the period from 1979 to 2018 were 1479.44 mm and 606.11 mm, respectively, without evident change trends. However, as shown in  Fig. 5 , some extreme precipitation indices (Pmax1d, PF95, and R20) showed significant upward trends at 95 % confidence level and slope values of 0.43 mm/year, 2.46 mm/year, and 0.11 day/year, respectively, indicating that the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation have increased over the past forty years in the MRUA.  3.2.2 The spatial distribution of precipitation indices  Fig. 6  shows the distribution of the changing trends in annual and seasonal precipitation and extreme precipitation indices. The spatial distributions of annual and summer precipitation were similar, showing a gradually increasing trend from northwest to southeast. In the southwestern part of the urban agglomeration, mostly near Poyang Lake in Jiangxi Province, winter precipitation showed a significant increasing trend over time (Fig. 6 (c)). Fig. 6 (d) and (e) show that the maximum 1-day and 3-day precipitation (Pmax1d and Pmax3d) had local peaks in Wuhan and Changsha, indicating that the spatial distribution of extreme precipitation was related to urbanization. For Pmax1d, the points with a significant upward trend were concentrated near Changsha and Nanchang. Regarding Pmax3d, only a few points on the fringes exhibited a significant increasing trend. In most regions of the MRUA, R50, PF95, and PR95 (Fig. 6 (g-i)) exhibited increasing trends that were more pronounced in the southwestern region. In general, the spatial distribution of extreme precipitation trends varied across the MRUA, with a more pronounced upward trend in the southeastern region. These findings are consistent with those of Liu et al. (2022)  based on 27 rainfall stations in the MRUA, where extreme precipitation was mainly characterized by a gradual increase from west to east.   3.3 Influence of urbanization on extreme precipitation 3.3.1 Regression models construction and results In this study, four extreme precipitation indicators (Pmax1d, R20, R50, and PF95) with significantly increasing trends were selected as dependent variables for the regression model construction. The independent variables included annual mean temperature (T), wind speed (WIN), specific humidity (SH), annual precipitation (P), impervious area ratio (IA), impervious surface expansion index (IAE), impervious patch density (IPD), and landscape shape index (SI). Multicollinearity tests showed that SH and IA had VIF values > 10 ( Table 3 ). Based on the OLS correlation coefficient, SH was significantly positively correlated with P, T, and WIN, and IA had a significant positive correlation with IAE. In addition, IA is an important indicator of the degree of urbanization and the change in IA can be substituted for IAE to reflect the average expansion rate. Therefore, the variables SH and IAE were removed, and the adjusted VIF values (Adj. VIF in Table 3 ) were all < 10. Therefore, three meteorological elements (P, T, and WIN) and four urbanization indicators (POP, IA, IPD, and SI) were used as inputs for the subsequent construction of the regression model. Extreme precipitation events often exhibit strong randomness, and are affected by climate change and human activity. To reduce the uncertainty in the study and explore the differences in the impact of urbanization at different stages, the historical period (1979–2018) was divided into four stages: S1 (1979–1989), S2 (1990–1999), S3 (2000–2009), and S4 (2010–2018), with each stage roughly corresponding to a decade. In addition, the change values of each variable between periods S1 and S4 (S1–S4) were also calculated and are represented by ∆X  in subsequent figures to identify the contribution of the intensity of urbanization change in the change of extreme precipitation. The accuracies of the regression models are shown in Supplementary Table 3 . From the values of Adj.R2  in the OLS models, the performances of the R20 and PF95 OLS models were better than that of the other indicators, with the Adj.R2  of four historical periods > 0.85. The Pmax1d OLS had the lowest values of Adj.R2 , ranging from 0.204 to 0.525 during the historical periods, and the reason for the poor simulation effect may be that the maximum daily precipitation is usually due to an ultra-high magnitude rainstorm affected by typhoons, which is uncertain and difficult to capture. The simulation effect of the R20 OLS model was better in S2, S3, and S4 than in S1. For the GWR model, all Adj.R2  values were > 0.9, and the AICc values of the GWR were much lower than those of the OLS model, which means that the effect of local regression models was better than that of the global regression. The fitting coefficients (β) of the various extreme precipitation indicators OLS models in different periods are shown in  Fig. 7 , which can reflect the strength and type of relationship (positive or negative) between independent and dependent variables. The fitting coefficient of each index showed no clear increasing or decreasing trend over time. However, overall, a significant positive correlation between the extreme precipitation indices (Pmax1d, PF95, R20, and R50) and the annual precipitation (P) was observed (Fig. 7 (a-d)), with β ranging from 0.42 to 0.98, indicating that the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall events can contribute to the annual rainfall to some extent. Regarding the urbanization indicators (Fig. 7 (e-h)), the IA and SI had large positive fitting coefficients. In particular, SI always exhibited a positive effect on Pmax1d and R50 during different historical periods. An increase in the complexity of the regional distribution of impervious areas promotes an increase in the frequency and total amount of extreme precipitation. Based on the results of OLS models, the fitting coefficients of IA and SI of GWR models were selected to explore the process of urbanization spatially varying relationship with extreme precipitation indexes ( Fig. 8 ). The white vacant areas in the figure are the grids with impervious area always equal to 0; 58 grids in total were removed to avoid the problem of a singular matrix in the operation of the GWR models. Fig. 8 (a-d) show the spatial distribution of changes in extreme precipitation indicators (Pmax1d, R20, R50, and PF95) with the urbanization process (from the 1980s to the 2010s), indicating that the significant increase in heavy rainfall is concentrated in the southeast of the urban agglomeration, especially in Jiangxi Province. Fig. 8 (e-h) shows the spatial distribution of the positive fitting coefficients of IA in the GWR models for different dependent variables, and different colored dots represent the size of the coefficients. In highly urbanized areas, including west of Wuhan and northwest of Changsha, an increase in IA was shown to promote short-duration rainstorms (Fig. 8 (e)). For heavy rainfall (PF95), the increase in IA had greater positive effects in almost the entire region (Fig. 8 (h)). Fig. 8 (i-j) shows the spatial distribution of the positive fitting coefficients of SI in the GWR models, which have one feature in common: they are not concentrated in highly urbanized areas, such as the center of the provincial capital city, but in suburban areas or surrounding towns. This may be related to the complex relationship between urbanization indicators, as shown in Fig. 4 (b), where, in more urbanized areas (IA > 0.4, centres of capital cities), the SI decreases as impervious surface continues to expand. In contrast, in suburban areas or other small cities, the impervious area ratio was small in the last century. However, with the expansion of the impervious area from S1 (1979–1989) to S4 (2010–2018), it was essentially fragmented with a significant increase in SI. In other words, both urban impervious area growth and spatial morphological complexity affect extreme precipitation, with reduced morphological complexity of impervious surfaces in urban centres resulting in a less significant contribution of SI to extreme precipitation. These results suggest that there is not a simple linear relationship between the increase in urban impervious areas and subsurface morphological complexity, whereas there is a spatial correlation between these changes and an increase in extreme precipitation.  3.3.2 Urban-rural comparison results To separate the impacts of climate change and urbanization, the impacts of urbanization were further analyzed using the urban-rural comparison method for the same period. The relative differences in temperature (UHII), extreme precipitation indicators, and urbanization indices (IA and SI) between the urban centres and rural areas of each prefecture-level city for four periods were assessed. The correlation coefficients ( Fig. 9 ) revealed that urban-rural differences in temperature and extreme precipitation indicators were not significantly correlated with urbanization differences during the early development stage (S1 ). In S2–S4 , the differences in SI of urban and rural impervious surfaces showed a significant positive correlation with UHII, with impervious surfaces altering albedo and heat transfer capacity. A correlation between all extreme precipitation indicators, such as Pmax1d, pmax3d, and PF95 was identified. Except for S1  (after 1990), a positive correlation was present between UHII and urban-rural extreme precipitation difference values. The three provincial capitals, Wuhan, Changsha, and Nanchang, are the most densely populated, economically developed, and urbanized areas of the MRUA. The Urban-rural differences in extreme precipitation indicators of these three cities are shown in  Table 4 . In the four periods, Pmax1d and R50 were greater in urban centres than in rural areas, with one exception, indicating that short-duration rainstorms occurred more frequently and with greater intensity in urban centres. Tang et al. (2022)  also found that higher levels of urbanization benefited precipitation intensity, but not accumulated precipitation, based on hourly summer rainfall data from five meteorological stations in Hubei Province. However, no increasing or decreasing patterns in the differences in the same variable over time owing to the complexity of the influence mechanisms of urbanization on extreme precipitation.   3.4 Discussion 3.4.1 Influence of impervious surface morphology changes on precipitation This study found two key urbanization indicators, IA and SI, promoting the increase in extreme precipitation. These metrics can measure form and patterns of urban areas (Wahyudi et al., 2019, Yu et al., 2021 ) and have spatial heterogeneity in the MRUA (Supplementary Fig. 5 ). As analyzed in Section 3.1 , the WHM urban area was expanded with reduced patch density, consistent with the finding that the merging of existing urban patches and adjacent expansion to existing urban developments led to reduced complexity in the WHM (Zheng et al., 2020 ). Liu et al. (2022)  also revealed urbanization has a greater impact on extreme precipitation non-stationarity than climate change in the MRUA, particularly the largest patch index and SI. The increased proportion of impervious surfaces affects weather systems by reducing local evaporation and increasing sensible heat flux, whereas the increased density and shape complexity of urban buildings also affect the urban canopy structure by increasing aerodynamic roughness and altering thermal and convective conditions, thereby affecting the magnitude and duration of local rainfall (Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2016; Souma et al., 2013 ). In addition, urban-rural comparison method revealed that differences in SI had a significant positive correlation with UHII (Fig. 9 ). Greater urban-rural differences in impervious surfaces indicate a more compact urban footprint distribution. Compact urban footprints lead to more pronounced urban-rural thermal contrasts and aerodynamic perturbations, with a greater increase in the frequency of extreme rainfall in city centres (Yang et al., 2024 ). The increase in impervious surfaces and complex morphology change surface properties and capture more solar radiation, and together with the influence of anthropogenic heat dissipation, the urban heat island effect is one of the prominent features of the local climate of urbanization (Zhao et al., 2014; Zhong et al., 2017 ). Other studies also found that the size and perimeter of urban clusters are important variables in explaining changes in UHII (Sun et al., 2019 ), and the relationship between city size and UHII is complex and non-linear (Zhang et al., 2023 ). The urban heat island effect is conducive to the generation of localized weak precipitation processes, increasing the intensity and duration of precipitation in urban areas (Xu et al., 2023 ). Thus, the influence mechanism of urbanization on extreme precipitation is complex, and there is also a non-linear relationship between the two main influences, subsurface change and the urban heat island effect.  3.4.2 Urban agglomeration effects with multiple spatial scales The urban agglomeration gathers a group of cities with compact spatial organization and close economic ties. As distances between cities decrease, statistical indicators and geographical analyses based on administrative divisions have difficulty in reflecting the cross-border linkage caused by socio-economic activities. Therefore, in this study, the extreme precipitation and urbanization data statistics were at a spatial scale of 0.1°, and the non-uniform urbanization degree in the region and the effects of urbanization across administrative districts are taken into account. The adaptation bandwidths of extreme precipitation GWR models were between 52 and 60, indicating that the local regression model for each point contains about 2 % of the sample points. Different grid scales affect the results of the regression model analysis. Chen et al. (2023)  used 10 grid scales (from 60 to 600 m) to explore the influence of urban spatial morphology on surface temperature and its scale effect, and 60 m was identified as the appropriate size. Huang et al. (2023)  used the percentage of impervious area within the 2-km circular buffer to reflect the degree of urbanization for weather stations and found that the urbanization in MRUA enhanced the intense rainfall and the trend of increasing intense rainfall was more pronounced at higher urbanization levels, which is consistent with the findings of this study. The population distribution and spatial pattern of impervious surfaces in urban agglomerations reflect regional socioeconomic activities to some extent. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 5(a) and 6(a) , the POP and IA are distributed in a ring shape linking the three provincial capital cities. The nine cities in the south-central region with yellow border in Supplementary Fig. 6 (b) accounted for 33.5 % of the total area, whereas impervious area and GDP accounted for 43.6 % and 48.5 %, respectively. Emissions from industrial production and human activities also have spatial spillover effects, affecting neighboring cities (Zhou et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2024 ). This may be the reason for a significant increase in heavy rainfall in the central and southeastern regions (Fig. 8 (a-d)). Thus, there are multiscale effects of urban agglomerations on extreme precipitation that need to be further explored.  3.4.3 Limitations and future work This study focused on the dynamic population distribution and spatial patterns of impervious areas and used regression models and urban-rural comparisons to explore the influence of urban agglomeration on extreme precipitation at both the urban agglomeration and city scales. Subsequent studies could include more data on human activities, such as infrastructure and gridded enterprise data, to better explore the impacts of human activity. Meanwhile, to investigate the thermodynamic and kinetic mechanisms of the effects of impervious surface expansion and morphological changes on precipitation, future work could combine localized and finer-resolution data for model simulations at different spatial scales. In addition, this study concluded that there are multiscale effects in the influence of spatially uneven development on precipitation in the MRUA. Climate models can be used to further evaluate the spatial scales of their effects in other urban agglomerations to reach new and more thorough conclusions.    4 Conclusion The changes in both extreme precipitation and urbanization indicators of the MRUA were quantitatively analyzed, and regression models (OLS and GWR) were used to explore the impact of uneven urbanization on the spatiotemporal variation of extreme precipitation. Simultaneously, the urban-rural comparison method was used to separate the impacts of urbanization. The main conclusions are as follows:(1) There was spatial heterogeneity in the degree of urbanization in the MRUA. Overall, WHM was the most urbanized. The relationship between the IA and SI is not simple or linear but has a threshold value of 0.4, which can reflect different stages and patterns of urban development. When less urbanized, the SI increased with increasing IA; when IA > 0.4, urban area expanded with reduced patch density and shape complexity.  (2) The frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation have increased in the MRUA with slope values of 0.43 mm/year, 2.46 mm/year, and 0.11 day/year for regional average Pmax1D, PF95, and R20 over the past 40 years. Increasing trends were more pronounced in the central and southern parts of the urban agglomeration.  (3) Based on OLS and GWR regression models, IA and SI were the key urbanization indicators that played a positive role in promoting the increase in extreme precipitation, particularly for the spatial positive correlation with PF95 and Pmax1d.  (4) The urban-rural comparison revealed that the urban-rural difference in the SI was significantly and positively correlated with the UHII, thus affecting extreme precipitation. Pmax1d and R50 in the three provincial capital city centres were greater than those in rural areas, indicating that short-term rainstorms occurred more frequently and with greater intensity in urban centres.    In summary, increased variations in extreme precipitation events were observed particularly in the central and southern parts of the MRUA. IA and SI were positively correlated with the amount and frequency of extreme precipitation, and the influence of spatially uneven urbanization on precipitation has multiscale effects.
1 Introduction Subterranean formations like saline aquifers, depleted oil and gas reservoirs, and coal seams provide suitable carbon dioxide (CO2 ) storage options due to their inherent properties. These formations typically possess porous rock structures capable of trapping the injected CO2  through various mechanisms, including physical trapping, dissolution, and mineralization. Several pilot projects worldwide are actively testing and refining CO2  sequestration in subterranean formations. The Petra Nova project in Texas, USA, captures CO2  from a coal-fired power plant and injects it into a deep saline formation (Jenkins, 2015 ; Shimokata, 2018 ). Similarly, the Sleipner project in Norway stores CO2  captured from a natural gas processing plant in a saline formation beneath the seabed (Ringrose, 2023 ; Bashir et al., 2024 ). Compared to other geological formations, deep saline aquifers boast the most significant storage potential, estimated to hold centuries' worth of global CO2  emissions (Ismail and Gaganis, 2023 ). This vast capacity makes them crucial for large-scale mitigation efforts. These aquifers possess inherent properties that favor long-term CO2  containment. The dense brine readily dissolves the CO2 , while impermeable caprock formations act as a natural barrier, preventing escape into the atmosphere. Over time, the CO2  can transform into stable mineral carbonates, further securing its permanence. Deep saline aquifers are widely distributed across the globe and available in many geographical regions with high-emission sources (Qin et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). The solubility of CO2  in brine results in an acidic solution with a wide range of pH depending on the pressure, temperature, and salinity (Diamond et al., 2003 ; Hemmati-Sarapardeh et al., 2020 ). Greater pressure increases the solubility of CO2  in brine, leading to a larger concentration of carbonic acid and, hence, lowering the pH (Mohammadian et al., 2023 ). The impact of temperature on CO2  solubility in brine is inversely proportional. This means that as the temperature increases, the solubility of CO2  in brine decreases, and the pH increases (Deng et al., 2018 ). Greater salinity leads to a larger decrease in CO2  solubility and hence larger pH. The relationship between salinity and pH is nonlinear and depends on the specific ions present. For instance, salts with common ions like Cl-  or Na+  have a relatively minor impact, while divalent ions like Ca2+  or Mg2+  have a more significant impact due to their stronger interactions with water molecules. Calcite, the main component of limestone, reacts with carbonic acid to create larger pores and increase permeability. This ongoing reaction even carves out channels through the rock called wormholes. Wormholes potentially aid fluid injection but raise concerns about the rock's structural integrity. The generation of wormholes is not possible in sandstone formations which are mainly made of quartz; however, studies showed that it might impact the rock wettability and petrophysical properties (Wang et al., 2020 ; Kou et al., 2023 ). Few studies have explored how CO2  injection affects wormhole development and rock properties. Madland et al. (2006)  reported a significant decrease in chalk strength after injecting CO2 -saturated brine. Al-Ameri et al. (2016)  observed a long-term reduction in Young's Modulus (a measure of stiffness) in limestone samples soaked with CO2 . Finally, Zhang et al. (2020)  compared the effects of dry CO2 , CO2 -saturated brine, and dead brine (i.e., brine that does not contain CO2 ) on wormhole formation. While dry CO2  caused some dissolution, only CO2 -saturated brine created continuous wormholes with the most significant impact on rock properties. Al-Dhafeeri et al. (2023 , 2024 ) studied the impact of temperature and salinity on wormhole efficiency due to the injection of CO2 -saturated brine. Their findings suggest that higher temperature and salinity required larger CO2 -saturated brine volume to create a continuous wormhole within a limestone sample. This is because higher temperatures and salinity decrease the CO2  solubility in the brine, making it less acidic and less effective at dissolving the rock. The slow creation of wormholes, however, results in more reduction in the rock strength. In the context of acid stimulation, the impact of acid injection velocity on wormhole propagation was thoroughly studied. Researchers found that there is an optimum velocity to create an efficient wormhole with the minimum volume of acid. The injection of acid above that optimum velocity results in branched wormholes with high acid consumption. Similarly, injection below the optimum velocity results in thick wormholes or face dissolution (Wang et al., 1993 ). Bujise and Glasbergen (2005)  found that the efficiency curve is steeper below the optimum velocity. Meaning it is better to avoid lower velocities as the acid stimulation is significantly less efficient. Fredd and Fogler (1998)  related this phenomenon to the Damköhler number that is the ratio between acid reaction rate and fluid transport. They found that the optimum Damköhler number is 0.29 based on numerous experimental data exceeding one hundred. Snippe et al. (2020)  collected data from the literature on CO2 -saturated brine injection at different velocities and fitted them with a simulation model to find the optimum injection velocity. The data collected are not consistent as they are from different sources of different rock types, rock properties, and experimental conditions. The literature is lacking consistent experimental data to reveal the impact of CO2 -saturated brine injection velocity on wormhole efficiency. These data could be suitable to describe the dissolution at a specific location of a saline limestone aquifer where the brine is fully saturated with CO2 . Also, it might be suitable in the application of water alternating gas injection (WAG) for enhanced oil recovery or injectivity improvement of a disposal well. Acid stimulation could also be conducted with CO2 -saturated brine instead of HCl acid, where the understanding of optimum injection velocity is of paramount importance. In-situ capturing of calcite dissolution due to CO2 -saturated brine injection at reservoir pressure and temperature was conducted previously (Menke et al., 2014 , 2018 ). However, the previous studies failed to represent the reservoir stresses while conducting the experiments. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the reactive transport of CO2 -saturated brine into limestone samples at high temperature, pressure, and stresses while continuously capturing the wormhole propagation using X-ray computed tomography (CT). The experiments were conducted at various injection rates to reveal its impact on efficient dissolution. The analysis was supported by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) T2  measurements, coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) analysis, and high-resolution micro-CT images. This research focused on the reaction and potential changes in rock petrophysical near the wellbore region, which might not be applicable deep into the reservoir.  2 Methodology 2.1 Materials Three cylindrical Indiana limestone samples that are 1 inch in diameter and 1.7 inches in length were used. The samples are similar in terms of porosity, permeability, and mineralogy as they were cut from the same core. Notice that the coreholder dimensions determined the sample's diameter and length. The samples consist of 99.1 % calcium carbonate with an average porosity of 14 % and permeability of 13 mD and they were cut from the same long core. The samples were prepared by applying different layers of shrink-fit tubing and a Viton sleeve to prevent CO2  leakage during the experiments (Al Shafloot et al., 2021 ). CO2  was used for the preparation of the carbonated brine while N2  was used for the confining fluid. A high salinity brine with 40,000 ppm was prepared for all experiments, as shown in Table 1  .  2.2 Coreflooding experimental setup The experimental setup is designed to image continuously the rock samples using an X-ray computed tomography scanner while coreflooding at high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) conditions (Glatz et al., 2018 ). The samples were placed in the pressure chamber (see the middle part of Fig. 1  ) and were connected to the N2  confining line at a pressure of 1950 psi. The setup consisted of a Parr reactor to mix the brine with CO2  before injection, ISCO pumps, pressure gauges, and a temperature-controlled heater. The detailed experimental procedures are addressed later. An ISCO pump is connected to the Parr reactor to inject the CO2 -saturated brine into the sample through the inlet, and another ISCO pump was connected to the outlet as a back pressure regulator (BPR) at 1480 psi. An additional ISCO pump was connected to the actuator to apply a constant 725 psi deviatoric axial stress to the sample (Al Shafloot et al., 2021 ). The pressure transducers, with 0.15 % accuracy, were used to monitor the pressure of the reactor, confining line, and inlet and outlet streams. The reactor, flow lines, and the sample's temperatures were fixed at 60 °C during the experiments using a heat controller. The GE HiSpeed CT scanner was operated at 120 mA current and 140 kV voltage and gave 195 × 195 × 625 µm voxel resolution. The temperature at different locations of the setup was monitored using thermocouples. Table 2   summarizes the conditions of the experiments.  2.3 Auxiliary measurements The samples’ porosity and pore-size distribution were characterized using a helium gas porosimeter and NMR. The measurements were conducted both before and after CO2 -saturated brine injection. The NMR T2  relaxation measurements provide insights into the dynamics of fluids confined within porous media. The T2  value reflects the time it takes for the NMR signal to weaken to a specific fraction of its starting intensity. When a porous sample is exposed to a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses, the decay of the NMR signal, also known as relaxation, is influenced by the mobility and distribution of fluids within the pore spaces. This decay directly relates to the characteristics of the fluid, pore size, and how pores are connected. The conventional Car-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse sequences are employed to acquire T2  relaxation time measurements. The effluent brine composition was analyzed using ICP-OES. This technique uses ICP to excite atoms in a sample that then emit light at specific wavelengths characteristic of each element. By measuring the intensity of this light, the concentration of each element can be determined. Calcium concentration was tracked in this study as an indication of the dissolution magnitude between CO2 -saturated brine and limestone samples. X-ray micro-computed tomography scan images (micro-CT) of the core samples after CO2-saturated brine injection were taken to capture the dissolution volume and pattern. It was taken through a Zeiss VersaXRM-500 X-ray micro-CT scanner with 47 µm resolution.  2.4 Experimental procedure A confining pressure of 1950 psi was applied in the pressure chamber after installing the sample, where it was monitored overnight to detect any potential gas leakage. Then, the sample was vacuumed for two hours, after which it was saturated with a dead brine. CT scan images were taken for both the dry and brine-saturated samples to estimate the rock porosity (Akin and Kovscek, 2003 ). Then, the sample permeability was measured using Darcy's law by measuring the differential pressure across the sample at three different injection rates. The brine and scCO2  were injected into the 500 cm3  Parr reactor at 1500 psi and mixed overnight to ensure the equilibrium condition was achieved. Notice that the brine was injected first and then followed by the scCO2  at a 70/30 ratio. After that, the heat controller was set at 60 °C for 2–3 hrs before starting the injection. The deviatoric stress of 725 psi was applied axially to the sample through the actuator. Then, 700 cm3  of CO2 -saturated brine was injected through the sample at different injection cycles, where each cycle was conducted on a different day. The injection in cycles was due to the limitation of the Parr reactor size and the need to take CT scan images manually. CT scan images were taken every couple of minutes to monitor the changes in the rock structure. Through the experiments, the effluent brine was collected in 50 cm3  tubes to monitor the reactivity. Notice that in each sample, a different injection rate of CO2 -saturated brine was applied to study the impact of injection velocity (see Table 3  ). The observed porosities and permeabilities on each sample are almost identical. It is of note that gas porosity and NMR measurements were taken before and after the experiments, while a micro-CT scan was taken post-treatment.   3 Results 3.1 Coreflooding and in-situ CT scanning In all experiments, a 700 cm3 vol of CO2 -saturated brine was injected at the same conditions but at different flow rates. At 0.5 cm3 /min, the injection happened in three cycles (i.e., 3 days) due to the low injection rate, where the injection is stopped overnight between the cycles. On the other hand, the injection for the other two experiments occurred in two cycles. Fig. 2   shows the differential pressure profile at different pore volumes (PVs) across IL1 due to CO2 -saturated brine injection.
