The pressure drop during the first cycle was around 10–15 psi and stayed almost constant except at 2–10 PVs, where a sudden pressure drop was encountered due to an issue with the pump that was immediately fixed. A large pressure drop was encountered during the start of the second cycle, which might be attributed to the precipitation of salts during the static conditions at 60 °C. The breakthrough of a wormhole across the sample happened at 160 PVs as indicated by the sudden drop in pressure to almost zero. Although a third cycle of CO2  injection did occur, it was not shown in the figure, as the pressure drop profile stayed constant and around zero. This small pressure drop was attributed to the fluid flow within the wormhole. Fig. 3   shows the CT scan images of IL1 versus PV injected, starting from the top left and ending at the bottom left. The CT scan images clearly show the wormhole initiation, propagation, and breakthrough during the experiment. At breakthrough (160 PV), the CT scan image showed a wormhole that did not reach the sample's outlet. This was attributed to the CT scan resolution, which could not detect the thin portion of the wormhole. However, after several PVs, the wormhole thickness increased, and hence, a continuous wormhole was detected at 201 and 251 PV. The differential pressure profile during the injection into IL2 at 1 cm3 /min is shown in Fig. 4  .  This experiment showed excessive pressure drop due to a smaller upstream line diameter. This, however, did not impact the detection of breakthrough that occurred at 48 PV as indicated by a zero pressure drop. Notice that less than one-third of the volume was needed to create a continuous wormhole, as compared to the 0.5 cm3 /min experiment. This clearly indicates that the injection velocity has a significant impact on reactivity and wormhole propagation. CT scan images of wormhole initiation, propagation, and breakthrough during the 1.0 cm3 /min experiment are shown in Fig. 5  . The closest image to the breakthrough moment is the image at 42.8 PV. The image shows localized dissolution but does not show a continuous or partially continuous wormhole. This is again attributed to the resolution of the CT scan that is lower than the wormhole thickness at the time of breakthrough. The CT scan could show a partially continuous wormhole at 84 PV while the wormhole length and thickness kept increasing as more PV of CO2 -saturated brine were injected. Fig. 6   shows the differential pressure profile at different PV during CO2 -saturated brine injection at 2 cm3 /min. The profile shows an increase in the pressure drop until reaching a peak of 40 psi, and then it dropped to zero at 36 PVs. At 16–24 PVs, there was a sudden pressure drop encountered due to an issue with the pump that was immediately fixed. The concaved-down profile is a common profile in acid injection into carbonate rocks. As the increase is usually attributed to the acid increase in viscosity, localized dissolutions that temporarily restrict flow and the release of CO2  decrease the brine's relative permeability. The drop in pressure is attributed to the generation of a low-resistance path. The pore volumes required to break through at 2 cm3 /min are lower than those at 1 cm3 /min. This observation provides additional evidence of the injection velocity impact on reactivity. Notice that the breakthrough happened during the first injection cycle, and hence, there was no need to provide the injection profile of the second cycle. Fig. 7   shows the CT scan images at different PVs of CO2 -saturated brine injection into sample IL3. The closest images to the breakthrough moment are at 30.2 and 44.5 PV and they show no indication of a wormhole. A clear partial wormhole is shown at 82.1 PV, where it becomes clearer at larger PV due to the enlargement of wormhole diameter. The CT scan images cannot be used to detect the wormhole breakthrough moment during CO2 -saturated brine injection. Scanning, however, was a useful tool to monitor the pattern of dissolution and wormhole evolution during the experiment. Based on the conditions of this study, a larger injection rate resulted in faster wormhole propagation. At a larger injection rate, the wormhole was thin at breakthrough as indicated by the inability of the CT scan to detect it. The smaller injection rate resulted in a thicker wormhole at the breakthrough moment that could be partially detected with the CT scan resolution. Therefore, a faster breakthrough of the wormhole resulted in a thinner wormhole at the breakthrough moment.  3.2 Reactivity and wormhole efficiency Effluents were collected during the experiments to measure the concentration of calcium ions using the ICP-OES analysis. The saturation of brine with CO2  results in an acidic solution that reacts with the limestone's main constituent (i.e., calcium carbonate). The reaction results in the release of calcium ions into the brine, adding to those already existing in the solution. The calcium concentration is used in this context to indicate the magnitude of dissolution. The ICP-OES analysis was done in the two extreme experiments of 0.5 and 2 cm3 /min, ignoring the intermediate 1 cm3 /min. Fig. 8   shows the calcium ions concentration at different PVs during the 0.5 cm3 /min experiment. It is observed that the concentration of calcium ions throughout the experiment was above the calcium ion concentration of the dead brine. This result indicates that the dissolution reaction is more prevalent than any potential precipitation. The calcium concentration increased during wormhole propagation until breakthrough, as indicated by the orange triangle data point, after which it declined. The increase in the concentration of calcium ions before breakthrough indicates an enhanced dissolution as the wormhole progresses through the sample. After the breakthrough, the CO2 -saturated brine channeled through the wormhole, creating dissolution in the periphery of the wormhole. Therefore, the calcium ions concentration declined due to the lower surface contact area between the brine and the rock. Fig. 9   shows the ICP-OES analysis of the experiment conducted at 2 cm3 /min, showing the same behavior as the results reported in Fig. 8 . The calcium concentration increased until the breakthrough, as indicated by the blue triangle data point, followed by a sharp decline. Comparing Figs. 8 and 9 , the effluent calcium ion concentration during the 2 cm3 /min experiment was greater than that at 0.5 cm3 /min. This indicates that the injection at 2 cm3 /min resulted in a faster acid/rock dissolution and, hence, the lower pore volume of CO2 -saturated brine needed for the wormhole to go through. Finding the optimum injection rate is a common practice in acid stimulation studies as it minimizes the required acid volume to achieve a specific wormhole penetration target. Fig. 10   shows the efficiency curve of CO2 -saturated brine injection into the Indiana limestone samples. It clearly shows the reduction of pore volume to breakthrough (PVBT) as the injection rate increased. This agrees with the ICP-OES analysis, as the calcium concentration was larger at a higher injection rate, indicating a faster dissolution. However, the PVBT curve should reverse direction once the optimum injection rate is reached, as depicted through the dashed black curve. The reverse in the curve direction happens because fluid convection through the wormhole is larger than surface reaction kinetics, not allowing enough residence time for acid/rock dissolution. The dashed fitting line drawn inFig. 10  is speculative and based on a common behavior of acid injection into carbonate rocks (Mirzayev et al., 2024 ). The optimum injection rate should be known in order to draw a more precise fitting line based on semiempirical models, which needs further experiments to reveal.  3.3 Changes in rock petrophysical properties A precise quantification of the wormhole size is possible through the higher-resolution micro-CT images. Fig. 11   shows the wormholes created at 0.5, 1, and 2 cm3 /min, illustrating different wormhole shapes and sizes. The wormhole shape is dependent on the inherent rock sample heterogeneity as well as the injection conditions (Wang et al., 2023 ). The largest wormhole size was that created at 1 cm3 /min, as it represents 2.5 % of the sample size, while the others represent 1.26 % and 1.33 % at 0.5 and 2 cm3 /min, respectively. Notice that these are the final shapes after injecting the 700 cm3  of CO2 -saturated brine and do not represent the wormhole size at breakthrough. As indicated previously from the CT scan images, the wormhole size was larger at lower injection rates at the breakthrough moment. Different methods were used to quantify the incremental change in porosity, including helium gas, micro-CT scan, NMR, and medical CT scan. The most accurate methods were the gas and micro-CT scan porosities, as their values were more reasonable and closer to each other (see Table 4  ). The CT scan method overestimates the porosity due to the image resolution and the continuous change of the brine CT number during treatment. The estimation of porosity post-dissolution using NMR is a challenge due to the difficulty of water containment within the wormhole, which might affected the resolution.. Fig. 12   shows the impact of the injection rate on the incremental change in porosity. Gas and micro-CT scan porosities showed that the largest increase was achieved at 1 cm3 /min. Hence, there is no clear trend of the impact of injection rate on the change in rock porosity based on the reported three experiments. The NMR T2  measurements were used to characterize the pore-size distribution where a shorter relaxation time corresponds to a smaller pore size (Gallegos and Smith, 1988 ). Fig. 13   shows the T2  relaxation time distribution before and after injecting the CO2 -saturated brine into the IL1 sample. The sample contained both micro (<100 ms) and macro pores (100 to 2000 ms) before and after the treatment (Lawal et al., 2020 ). The injection of CO2 -saturated brine resulted in the generation of a new larger pore system (i.e., wormholes), as indicated by the distributions greater than 2000 ms. Also, it resulted in the creation of a new smaller micro system (<2 ms) that might be attributed to salt precipitation. Notice that it took a long time to inject the 700 cm3  in the 0.5 cm3 /min experiment. That is, there were three cycles at three days separated with a shut-in period and this might explain the precipitation. Similarly, micro and macro pore systems existed before and after the injection of CO2 -saturated brine for IL3, as shown in Fig. 14  . The treatment caused the enlargement of both pore systems, as indicated by the complete shift of the curve to the right. Also, the generation of a larger pore system (i.e., wormholes) is observed from the T2  distribution above 2000 ms. Notice that the CO2 -saturated brine was injected four times faster in this experiment at 2.0 cm3 /min. Therefore, no indication of salt precipitation can be inferred from the NMR T2  distribution for this experiment.   4 Discussion According to Fredd and Fogler (1998) , the optimum wormhole velocity in acid/rock reaction corresponds to an optimum Damköhler number (NDa  ). Damköhler number compares the timescale of reaction to the timescale of transport phenomena. If the timescale of the reaction is much slower than that of the transport, the wormhole is inefficient, resulting in large PVBT and ramified wormholes. On the contrary, large NDa   corresponds to a greater reaction to fluid transport ratio and hence large PVBT with a thick wormhole or a face dissolution. It is necessary to understand the optimum wormholing conditions at which the CO2 -saturated brine can be injected. For instance, a smaller skin factor can be obtained in the context of acid stimulation if the injection occurs at the optimum conditions. Also, the sequestration of CO2  at the optimum injection rate could mitigate the excessive reaction near the wellbore by avoiding a face dissolution. The acid reaction can be described as either mass transfer limited in strong acids or surface reaction limited as the case in weak acids. Carbonated brine can be described as a weak acid with a pH in the range of 3–4. Therefore, we suspect that the reaction in this study was limited by the surface reaction where the NDa   can be described through the following equation (Fredd and Fogler, 1999 ):(1) N D a   = π v d L k r   q        Where v  is the stoichiometric ratio between reactants and products of reactions, d  is the wormhole diameter, L  is the wormhole half-length, kr   is the reaction rate constant, and q  is the injection rate. According to Peng et al. (2015) , the reaction rate constant of the CO2 -saturated brine with calcite is 6.5 × 10–5  cm/s at 60 °C and 1500 psi. Fig. 15   shows the generalized curve proposed by Fredd and Fogler (1988), suggesting that NDa   = 0.29 is the optimum for a wide range of acids and carbonate rocks. Based on this study, the experimental data did not fit the generalized curve, and hence, the assumption of the same optimum NDa   may not be valid. Fredd and Fogler investigated single-phase incompressible acids, while the system utilized in this study is more compressible due to the dissolved CO2 . Therefore, more extensive experimental work should be done on CO2 -saturated brine injection into carbonate to find an optimum NDa   number. Based on the initial data provided in this study, we speculate that the optimum NDa   is smaller than 0.29. Fig. 12  did not provide a conclusive understanding of the injection rate impacts on porosity increase. More data might be required to establish such a relationship. Another parameter that could be related to the porosity increase is the PV needed to achieve breakthrough (PVBT). The intuition is that the remaining CO2-saturated brine volume after the breakthrough increases the wormhole diameter, indicating that lower PVBT has the potential to create a larger wormhole diameter after the breakthrough. Fig. 16   shows that the PVBT, according to the data from this study and Al-Dhafeeri et al. (2023 ; 2024 ), did not show a clear relationship with the porosity increase. Notice that all the experiments were based on an injection of 700 cm3  of CO2 -saturated brine into Indiana limestone. It might be concluded that the sample's heterogeneity has an impact on the relative change in porosity. A limitation of this study is the injection of CO2 -saturated brine in cycles instead of the continuous injection of the full volume. A reaction between the acidic brine and the rock sample during the static condition was not accounted for in the efficiency study. Future studies should focus on conducting larger sets of coreflooding experiments examining a wider range of injection rates in order to clearly identify the optimum injection rate and, therefore, the optimum NDa  .  5 Conclusions This study assessed the reactive transport of CO2 -saturated brine in limestone samples at three different injection rates: 0.5, 1, and 2 cm3 /min through coreflooding and in-situ CT scanning. The experiment simulates a deep limestone aquifer at 60 °C, 1480–1500 psi pore pressure, 2000 psi confining pressure, 725 psi deviatoric axial stress, and 40,000 ppm brine salinity. The speed of dissolution is monitored through the in-situ images, pressure drop data across the sample, and ICP analysis of the effluents. The changes in rock petrophysical properties were evaluated through the gas porosimeter, NMR, and micro-CT scan. At the experiment conditions, wormholes were created in the samples during the injection of 700 cm3  of CO2 -saturated brine. The speed of wormhole generation was the fastest at 2 cm3 /min with 36 PV at breakthrough, while 160 and 48 PV at breakthrough at 0.5 cm3 /min and 1 cm3 /min, as detected from the pressure drop data. The ICP-OES analysis confirmed by tracking the calcium ions concentration that the highest dissolution occurred at 2 cm3 /min. The ICP-OES analysis showed that the dissolution speed increased before the breakthrough. This result was attributed to the propagation of the wormhole; however, the dissolution rate declined after the breakthrough due to the channeling of the fluids within the wormhole that increased its diameter. The x-ray CT scanning resolution was not fine enough to detect the wormhole breakthrough time accurately. The increase in wormhole diameter after breakthrough allowed for clear images of the wormhole shape. The CT scan images confirmed that the more efficient the wormhole is (i.e., smaller breakthrough time), the less the wormhole diameter at breakthrough. This indicates that the ratio of reaction to fluid convection is closer to the optimum at 2 cm3 /min, allowing the acid greater contact time with solid in the flow direction, increasing the wormhole length rather than increasing the diameter. The optimum injection rate changes if the rock properties (i.e., porosity, permeability, lithology) or experimental conditions (pressure, temperature, and salinity) are changed. Therefore, the optimum wormhole speed is related to an optimum Damköhler number in a generalized approach. We found that the Fredd and Fogler generalized efficiency curve was not applicable in the cases of CO2 -saturated brine reaction with limestone. The wormhole diameter from micro-CT images or the change in gas porosity as per 700 cm3  of CO2 -saturated brine injection did not show a correlation with the injection rate or the PV injected at breakthrough. The NMR T2  distribution showed a significant change in the pore-size distribution after the treatment. In general, the existing pores were enlarged due to the dissolution with minor precipitation that occurred in the 0.5 cm3 /min experiment. In the context of CO2  storage, the dissolution occurs due to CO2  solubility in brine that should be reflected in the petrophysical properties such as the porosity, relative permeability curves, and capillary pressure. Hence, a better assessment of CO2  storage capacity and CO2  distribution within the aquifer can be obtained.
1 Introduction Due to increased vulnerability caused by climate change and population growth, many dryland areas are exposed to desertification and land degradation risk and ensuing contradiction between humans and land (Sun et al., 2023 ). To achieve land degradation neutrality −which is one of the sustainable development goals (SDGs) and enhance carbon sequestration, many dryland areas are undergoing extensive reforestation/afforestation (Arneth et al., 2021; Schulze et al., 2021 ). Considering the vulnerability of the Sahel to desertification and land degradation (Mbow et al., 2017 ), the region is currently undergoing vast reforestation through the Great Green Wall Initiative (GGWI) (Mbow, 2017 ). The objective of the GGWI is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land through reforestation, sequester 250 million tons of carbon and create 10 million green jobs by 2030 (Mbow, 2017; Goffner et al., 2019 ). Whilst many studies have been conducted in other regions undergoing reforestation to understand the factors influencing actual evapotranspiration (ET) variability (Teuling et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ), such studies are generally lacking in the Sahel. ET is an important component of regional energy cycle representing the complex interaction between vegetation, climate, and landscape characteristics (Zhang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021 ). It is also an important component of the water cycle with a strong influence on runoff and soil moisture availability and groundwater recharge (Guo et al., 2017; Yinglan et al., 2019; Condon et al., 2020 ). Therefore, to achieve consistent, evidence-based allocation and management of water resources in the context of the GGWI, it is crucial to identify and quantify the climatic (abiotic) and environmental (biotic) factors influencing ET variability in the Sahel. Such information may be crucial for adopting climate-smart reforestation policies to support the implementation of the GGWI, enhance water management given the strong links between water scarcity and violent conflicts in the Sahel (Nkiaka et al., 2024 ) and improve our knowledge of vegetation-hydrology-climate interactions in the Sahel. Several studies have assessed the climatic and environmental factors influencing ET variability at different scales. For example, Feng et al. (2020)  showed that ET is strongly influenced by precipitation at the global scale, while potential evapotranspiration, terrestrial water storage, and catchment characteristics influence ET variability in energy-limited environments, arid and humid regions respectively. Yang et al. (2022)  reported that precipitation, temperature, and vegetation cover are the dominant factors influencing ET variability in northwest China. Li et al. (2022)  found that precipitation, net radiation, and vapour pressure deficit exert greater control on ET variability in dry climates, tropical regions, and boreal mid-latitude regions respectively. Land use change, precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration were found to be the main factors influencing evapotranspiration across Europe (Teuling et al., 2019 ). Changing precipitation patterns and land cover have been reported to be the dominant factors affecting the components of the hydrological cycle in the Amazon (Heerspink et al., 2020 ). Different approaches have been used to study the effects of climatic and environmental factors influencing ET. For example, Zheng et al. (2022)  used the partial least squares structural equation model to explore the relationship between ET and climatic and environmental factors. Other studies adopted the Budyko framework (Teuling et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ), the elasticity concept (Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022 ) and the complementary relationship (Brutsaert, 2015; Li et al., 2021 ) to analyse the effects of climate and vegetation changes on ET. Adeyeri and Ishola (2021)  applied the time–frequency wavelet decomposition method and partial correlation analysis to reveal the factors influencing ET in West Africa. Ndehedehe et al. (2018)  used the independent component analysis to explore ET dynamics in sub-Saharan Africa. Overall, most of the methods used for studying the relationship between ET and climatic and environmental factors are data-driven analytical methods. Analytical methods use mathematical equations based on the assumption that the catchment water balance remains under steady-state over a long period of time (Dey and Mishra, 2017; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Advantages of analytical methods include: (1) simple model structure and (2) require minimum input data to produce results that are practically useful for most hydrological applications (Hasan et al., 2018 ). Despite the high sensitivity of Sahelian vegetation to climate variability and environmental change (Leroux et al., 2017 ), very few studies have investigated the factors influencing ET variability in the Sahel while existing studies have focused mostly on the western Sahel. Meanwhile, the effects of vegetation on ET are conspicuously ignored in exiting studies. For example, Adeyeri and Ishola (2021)  showed that precipitation and atmospheric evaporative demand (AED) had a greater influence on ET in the western Sahel. Ndiaye et al. (2021)  revealed that ET in the western Sahel is more sensitive to relative humidity, maximum temperature, and solar radiation. Ndehedehe et al. (2018)  attributed ET variability in the western Sahel to changes in precipitation, soil moisture and temperature. The limited number of studies addressing this issue in the Sahel suggests that there is a dearth of knowledge on the vegetation-hydrology-climate interactions which hampers the development of climate-smart reforestation practices in the context of the GGWI and regional water management. To overcome the challenge of widespread in situ data scarcity in the region, this study leverages on the availability of a wide range of satellite-derived and reanalysis data. The main advantage of such data is that they can provide high spatial resolution and long-term homogeneous data for previously unmonitored regions at scales that are suitable for studying changes in the hydrological cycle (Sheffield et al., 2018 ). From the above, the objectives of this study are to: (1) analyse trends in annual ET, climatic and environmental (soil moisture and vegetation cover) variables, (2) identify the main climatic and environmental factors influencing ET and, (3) quantify the impact of climate and vegetation changes on ET across the Sahel.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Sahel stretches from Senegal to Eritrea with a length of about 8,000 km. It is a transitional zone located between the Sahara Desert to the north and the Sudanian-savanna to the south covering ten countries with a population of about 150 million (Fig. 1  ). It is one of the world’s largest water-limited environments and ranked amongst the most fragile ecosystems in the world (Ghins et al., 2022 ). The Sahel is remarkable because of a mega drought that affected the region from the 1970 s to mid-1990 attracting much media coverage because of the humanitarian crisis that ensued from the drought (Nicholson et al., 1998; Dai et al., 2004 ). Precipitation estimates from Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS) over four decades (1982–2021) show that annual precipitation varies from 71-200 mm/year in the north to about 700–1000 mm/year in the south. The present study covers 45 watersheds nested within six major hydrological basins including Senegal, Volta, Niger, Lake Chad, Nile, and Red Sea (Fig. 1 ). The total surface area covered by all the watersheds is about 3,021,412 km2  ranging in size from 4095 km2  (Senegal 4) to 541,267 km2  (Dallol Bosso). Most of the watersheds lie between Latitudes 12°N and 20°N. A full list of the watersheds and their characteristics is available in Appendix A . Shapefiles of the watersheds are collected from HydroSHEDs which provides a seamless global coverage of consistently sized and hierarchically nested sub-basins using the high-resolution Shuttle Radar Topographic Mission digital elevation model (Lehner and Grill, 2013 ). HydroSHEDs shapefiles have been used in several studies e.g., (Gebrechorkos et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Nkiaka and Okafor, 2024 ).  2.2 Data and aggregation Table 1   summarises the characteristics of the different datasets used in the study. The ET data used in the study has been validated in previous studies e.g., (Nkiaka et al., 2022 ) and also used in several studies in the Sahel e.g., (Gbohoui et al., 2021; Hernández et al., 2021 ). CHIRPS, AgERA5, GLEAM Soil moisture and NDVI data from MODIS have been validated and also used extensively in other studies in the region e.g., (Fensholt et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2023; Asante et al., 2022; Dembélé et al., 2020 ). A complete description of the different datasets is available in their respective references provided in Table 1 . The climatic and environmental variables were downloaded at annual timescale at their respective native spatial resolutions using the Climate Engine research App [https://app.climateengine.com  ] (Huntington et al., 2017). Watersheds shapefiles can be uploaded to Climate Engine directly from a computer folder or using the Google Earth Engine interface through a custom user account. Soil moisture data are downloaded from GLEAM and processed using OriginPro software. All the data were downloaded as spatial average over each watershed.  2.3 Trend analyses The non-parametric Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator are used respectively for trend analysis and to quantify trend magnitude and significance. The Mann-Kendall test and Sen slope estimator are widely used for detecting the presence of statistically significant increasing or decreasing trends in hydroclimatic time series and have been used in several studies in the region e.g., (Nkiaka et al., 2017 ). Although several different Mann-Kendall tests exist, e.g., (Güçlü, 2020 ), the study adopted the classical Mann-Kendall test. The period 1982–2021 is adopted for climate variables while 2000–2021 is used for vegetation change (NDVI). Trend analyses are conducted at the 5 % significance level.  2.4 Identifying the factors influencing evapotranspiration (ET) variability The study uses three statistical methods to assess the factors influencing ET in the Sahel. Considering that collinearity and interactions among the different independent variables cannot be overlooked, partial correlation coefficient (PCC) is used to determine the relationship between each independent variable (climate and environmental variables) and the dependent variable (ET) while controlling for the effects of all the other independent variables. PCC is calculated using the following equation (Engström and Ekman, 2010 ) and has been used in several studies e.g., (Yang et al., 2022; Adeyeri and Ishola, 2021 ).(1) ρ X , E T ( Y )   = ρ X , E T   - ρ X , Y ρ Y , E T    1 - ρ X , Y 2     1 - ρ Y , E T 2           Where ρ X , E T ( Y )     is the partial correlation coefficient between X & ET considering the effect of variable Y; ρ X , E T     and ρ Y , E T     are the correlation coefficients between ET and X & Y, respectively, and ρ X , Y     is the correlation coefficient between X and Y. In the second step, Pearson correlation was used to establish how change in the independent variable affects the dependent variable. In the third step, multiple linear regression analysis is conducted between the rate of change of each independent variable and the rate of change of the dependent variable to determine the relative contributions of each independent variable on the dependent variable. This was achieved using multivariable regression at 5 % significance level using equation (2) . The relative contributions of the change in each independent variable to the rate of change in ET was then estimated from the multivariable regression coefficients using equation (3) . Equations (2) and (3)  have been used in several previous studies to estimate the relative contribution of independent variables on the dependent variable e.g., (Chen et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022 ).(2) Y = aX  1  + bX  2  + cX  3  + ⋯ dX  n      (3) r x  = a   a   + b   + c   + ⋯ d     X 100 %     Where Y  is the standardized dependent variable (ET), X1, X2, X3,  and Xn  are the standardized independent variables (precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, windspeed, net radiation, humidity, vapour pressure, AED and NDVI); rx   is the relative contribution of each independent variable to ET and a, b, c , …. & d  are the regression coefficients of the independent variables.  2.5 Quantifying the effects of climate and vegetation changes on evapotranspiration Analytical method based on the Elasticity concept was used to quantify the effect of climate and vegetation changes on ET. 2.5.1 Attribution of ET change The elasticity concept is useful for quantifying how a relative change in one variable affects the other variable (Ahiablame et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2020 ). The elasticity concept is widely used in hydrology due to its clear physical meaning and simple formulation (Sankarasubramanian et al., 2001 ). Due to its limited input data requirements, the elasticity concept has been extended to investigate the sensitivity of runoff, baseflow and ET to climate and vegetation changes (Ahiablame et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2020 ). Since its original formulation, several other elasticity models have been proposed such as the least square elasticity model (Zheng et al., 2009 ), the multivariable double logarithm, and multivariable transformation analyses models (Tsai, 2017 ). This study adopts two elasticity models: (1) the least square elasticity (LSE) model because it can overcome the problem associated with small sample size and (2) the double logarithm elasticity (DLE) model which has previously been used exclusively for quantifying the impact of climate and vegetation changes on streamflow (Tsai, 2017; Khan et al., 2022 ). The aim of using the two elasticity models is to ensure that our results are robust. The LSE model is expressed as:(4) ε = X  ¯   ET   ¯    · ∑ ( X i  - X  ¯   )  ( E T i  - ET   ¯   )    ∑ ( X i  - X  ¯   )  2    = ρ X , Q   · C Q  / C X      Where ET  is evapotranspiration and X  represent the annual climate or environment variable (precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, solar radiation, windspeed, specific humidity, AED and NDVI) and X  ¯     and ET  ¯     represent the multiyear annual mean climatic/environmental variable and ET values respectively. ρ X , Q     is the correlation coefficient between the climatic/environment variable and ET and CX   and CET   are coefficients of variation of climatic and environmental variables and ET, respectively. The DLE model is built on the premise that evapotranspiration (ET) is influenced by multiple factor elasticities in the form of regression coefficients of a multivariable regression model. The multivariable function describing the influence of climatic and environmental variables on ET is expressed as:(5) ET = f P , S M , T , H , S , W , V P , A E D , N D V I       Where P, SM, T, H, S, W, VP, AED, NDVI  represent precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, solar radiation, windspeed, specific humidity, AED and NDVI. We then modify equation (5)  using the approach proposed by Tsai (2017)  as follows:(6) ET = P  β 1   SM  β 2   T  β 3   H  β 4   S  β 5   W  β 6   VP  β 7   AED  β 87   NDVI  β 9       Taking logarithm of both sides of equation (6)  produces the following equation:(7) LogET = β 1 L o g P + β 2 L o g S M + β 3 L o g T + β 4 L o g H + β 5 L o g S + β 6 L o g W + β 7 L o g V P + β 8 L o g A E D + β 9 L o g N N D V I     Where βn   is the elasticity coefficient of the different climatic and environmental variables. In our approach, we estimated the elasticity coefficient of each independent variable on ET separately. The elasticities are then estimated as coefficients of the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis between ET and each of the independent variables. In running the regression analysis, the intercept term was left unadjusted (i.e., assumed to be zero). After estimating the elasticity coefficients using the two methods, we used linear correlation analysis to measure the strength of the relationship between the elasticity coefficients obtained using the two models. To determine which elasticity model to be adopted for further analysis and interpretation, we conducted a linear regression analysis between ET and the different independent variables. We conducted the same analysis for their log-transformed counterparts (ET and climatic and environmental variables). Lastly, we used the adjusted R2  values obtained from both linear regression models to assess the regression goodness of fit for the log transformed and least square elasticity models (Tsai, 2017; Khan et al., 2022 ). We adopted the adjusted R2  because it provides a better overall performance of a regression model by considering the number of predictors in the model. We estimated the mean of the adjusted R2  obtained from both models and adopted the model with highest mean adjusted R2 .    3 Results 3.1 Trend analysis Fig. 2   shows the mean annual ET estimates and trends across Sahelian watersheds over a period of 4 decades (1982––2021). It can be observed that there is a strong spatial variability in mean annual ET across the study area varying from 50-850 mm/year. High annual ET occur mostly in the southern fringes of the Sahel while low annual ET occur in watersheds around the central and eastern Sahel (Fig. 2 a). Trend analysis also shows a strong spatial heterogeneity with statistically significant increasing trends visible around watersheds in the western and central Sahel (0.5–4.5 mm/year) and statistically significant decreasing trends observed in the far eastern Sahel (Fig. 2 b). Mean annual estimates of all the climatic and environmental variables are shown in Fig. 3  . There is a strong spatial heterogeneity in precipitation and soil moisture across the study area (Fig. 3 a & b). Mean temperature is quasi uniform in the western and central Sahel but shows strong spatial heterogeneity in the eastern Sahel (Fig. 3 c). Windspeed and net radiation are higher in the northern Sahel compared to the south while relative humidity appears to be uniform across the region with a strong spatial heterogeneity observable around the far eastern Sahel (Fig. 3 d, e, & f). There is also a strong spatial heterogeneity in vapour pressure and AED across the study area (Fig. 3 g & h). NDVI scores are higher in watersheds located in the southern fringers of the Sahel compared to those in the north and eastern Sahel (Fig. 3 i). Fig. 4   shows the results of trend analysis for all the other climatic variables over a period of four decades (1981–2021) and NDVI over two decades (2000–2021). Trend analyses show statistically significant increasing trends in annual precipitation, soil moisture and mean temperature across the region (Fig. 4 a, b & c). Other climate variables show both statistically significant increasing and decreasing trends, however, there is a strong spatial heterogeneity in trend magnitudes. For example, increasing and decreasing trends in windspeed are perceptible in the eastern Sahel and western Sahel respectively (Fig. 4 d). Decreasing trends in net radiation are also perceptible around the central Sahel (Fig. 4 e). Statistically significant increasing trends in specific humidity are visible in the western and central Sahel while decreasing trends occur in the eastern Sahel (Fig. 4 f). Decreasing trends in vapour pressure occur in the eastern Sahel while increasing trends are clearly visible in the central and western Sahel. There is also a strong spatial heterogeneity in AED trends with statistically significant increasing trends clearly visible in the eastern Sahel (6 mm/year) while statistically significant negative trends occur in the western Sahel. (Fig. 4 h). There is a consistent increase in NDVI across all watersheds with statistically significant trends occurring in a few watersheds (Fig. 4 i).  3.2 Factors influencing ET Table 2   shows the results of PCC between ET and each independent variable while controlling for the effect of all the other variables. PCC scores show that precipitation, mean temperature, net radiation, specific humidity, vapour pressure and NDVI have statistically significant correlations with ET. Results of Pearson correlation between the rate of change in each independent variable and the rate of change in the dependent variable (ET) are also available in Table 2  and in Fig. 5  . Multivariable regression indicate that the independent variables contributed about 80 % of the ET variance (R2  = 0.80 and adjusted R2  = 0.75). The relative contributions of soil moisture, mean temperature, windspeed, AED and vapour pressure were 21.12 %, 20.46 %, 15.39 %, 13.72 % and 12.49 % respectively suggesting that these are the main variables influencing ET in the Sahel (Table 2 ). Pearson correlation analysis also indicate that a positive change in precipitation, soil moisture, specific humidity, vapour pressure and NDVI lead to a positive change in ET (Fig. 5  a, b, e, f, & i). In contrast, a positive change in mean temperature, windspeed, and AED leads to a decline in ET (Fig. 5  c, d, & h). Among the climatic variables, vapour pressure has the strongest positive Pearson correlation coefficient (r = 0.67, p < 0.05 ) while mean temperature, windspeed and AED have the strongest negative Pearson correlation coefficients (r > -0.70, p < 0.05 ) with ET.  3.3 Quantifying the effects of climate and vegetation changes on ET The LSE and DLE models were used to calculate the elasticity coefficients of the independent variables on ET. Results of the Pearson correlation between the elasticity coefficients from both models are shown in Fig. 6  . Pearson correlation coefficients between the elasticity coefficients produced by both models are substantially high (r > 0.91, p < 0.05 ) for all variables suggesting that both models have similar performance (Fig. 6 ). To determine which of the models to be adopted for further analyses, we used the adjusted R2  values obtained from the linear regression analysis between ET and the different independent variables, and their log-transformed counterparts as explained in the methods section. Adjusted R2  values obtained from LSE and DLE models are available in Fig. 7   for all the watersheds. Analyses indicate that the mean adjusted R2  from the DLE model is (0.31) while that from the LSE is (0.22) (Fig. 7 ). Since the adjusted R2  from DLE is higher than that of LSE, the elasticity coefficients from DLE are presented and discussed throughout the rest of this paper. Fig. 8   shows the elasticity coefficients of climate and environmental factors on ET. Results from the analyses show that precipitation, soil moisture, and vapour pressure produced positive elasticity coefficients on ET across all the watersheds while mean temperature and NDVI produced positive elasticity coefficients in about 80 % of the watersheds (Fig. 8 a, b, g & i). Other independent variables produce mixed scores (positive and negative elasticity coefficients) across the watersheds. Elasticity coefficients range from (0.17 to 165), (1.03 to 3.75), (8.55 to −5.65), (−5.25 to 5.35), (−26.92 to −0.61), (1.46 to 1.36), (0.19 to 5.49), (−9.92 to 1.13) and (−1.65 to 4.09) with corresponding means of 0.78, 1.90, 0.08, −1.48, −9.58, −0.18, 2.52, −3.41, & 0.57 for precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, windspeed, net radiation, specific humidity, vapour pressure, AED and NDVI, respectively. Elasticity coefficients obtained suggest that climatic factors produced higher elasticity coefficients on ET than environmental factors (Fig. 8 ). Furthermore, vapour pressure has a greater positive influence on ET than soil moisture and precipitation (Fig. 8 a, b & g). Conversely, net radiation shows a greater negative effect on ET compared to other climate variables (Fig. 8 e).   4 Discussion 4.1 Mean annual estimates Generally, higher AED values recorded around the central Sahel may be attributed to higher mean temperature, windspeed, net radiation and vapour pressure which all have different modulating effects on AED. On the other hand, higher NDVI values observed in watersheds around the southern fringes of the Sahel may be attributed to higher annual precipitation and soil moisture availability.  4.2 Trend analysis The results of trend analysis are consistent with those from other studies around the Sahel. For example, Ndehedehe et al. (2018)  and Adeyeri and Ishola (2021)  found increasing trends in annual ET across the western and central Sahel using data derived from MODIS and GLEAM respectively. Using reanalysis data obtained from the Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA), Ndiaye et al.  (2020) also reported increasing trends in solar radiation, and specific humidity and decreasing trends in windspeed in the western Sahel. Cook et al. (2022)  reported increasing trends in mean temperature across the Sahel, reduced (increased) windspeed in the western (eastern) Sahel and increased specific humidity in the central Sahel and our analysis are consistent with their results. Declining trends in ET in parts of the Sahel are also consistent with results from a global study which attributed the decline to changes in specific humidity (Yang et al., 2019 ). Increasing trends in precipitation and mean temperature follow results reported in several studies in the region e.g., (Nkiaka et al., 2017; Ilori and Ajayi, 2020; Dembélé et al., 2022 ). Increasing trends in annual precipitation in the Sahel have been attributed to changes in global circulation patterns such as sea surface temperatures and increased moisture recycling in the region (Yu et al., 2017; Biasutti, 2019 ). Increasing mean annual temperature follow a global pattern that has been attributed to global warming (Hegerl et al., 2019 ). Decreasing trends in incoming solar radiation around the central Sahel may be due to increasing precipitation which increases cloud cover over the region which in-turn reduces incoming solar radiation at the surface (Giannini, 2010; Cook et al., 2022 ). Increasing specific humidity in parts of the Sahel have been attributed to increasing surface temperatures and stronger monsoon winds carrying more moisture from the Gulf of Guinea (Cook et al., 2022 ). Increasing trends in AED parts of the Sahel reflect the increasing trends in mean temperature in those areas which is also consistent with results from another study in the region (Abiye et al., 2019 ). Many studies in the Sahel attributed increasing trends in NDVI to precipitation increase (Yu et al., 2017; Ogutu et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022 ). However, there is a strong spatial heterogeneity in the distribution of NDVI trends across the region. Overall, our analyses suggest that increasing trends in annual ET across the Sahel may be attributed to different climatic and environmental factors. This is the first study to assess the effects of vegetation cover on ET in the Sahel and as the GGWI is still under implementation, it not yet known how increasing tree cover in the Sahel will affect the vegetation-hydrology-climate interactions especially as the trees become mature in the decades to come. As such, more studies are needed in the region to understand vegetation-hydrology-climate interactions under different alternative scenarios.  4.3 Factors influencing ET 4.3.1 Climatic (abiotic) factors The study uses several climatic variables including precipitation, mean temperature, windspeed, net radiation, specific humidity, vapour pressure and AED to assess the factors influencing ET variability in the Sahel. The three statistical methods including PCC which considers the collinearity and interactions among the different independent variables revealed that precipitation, vapour pressure and humidity are climatic variables with the strongest influence on ET. Multivariable regression analyses show that the climatic factors contribute about 75.11 % of the ET variance with mean temperature, windspeed, vapour pressure and AED contributing the highest to ET variance. Results from our analyses are consistent with those from previous studies in the western Sahel (Adeyeri and Ishola, 2021; Ndiaye et al., 2021 ). Multivariable regression analyses also indicate that mean temperature and windspeed have a greater negative influence on ET than AED because of their higher relative contributions to ET variance. It is worth highlighting that AED reflects the atmospheric drying power and is influenced by all the other climate variables except precipitation. This implies that the different climate variables have varying modulating effects on AED which may influence the relationship between ET and AED. Nevertheless, the strong negative Pearson correlation between ET and AED suggest that there may be a complimentary relationship between them as suggested in a previous study (Brutsaert, 2015 ). This has been attributed to the fact that AED in dryland areas is higher than precipitation and ET combined, and as such, ET is limited by water availability (Yang et al., 2019 ). Positive Pearson correlations between ET and precipitation, net radiation and specific humidity and the negative relationship between ET and mean temperature and AED have also been observed in other dryland regions e.g., (Li et al., 2022 ). Precipitation is the main supplier of water for ET consumption while net radiation provides the energy needed for ET to occur. The negative correlation between mean temperature and ET may be attributed to rising global temperatures which in-turn enhance soil moisture depletion leading to limited water for soil evaporation and vegetation growth which both influence ET in water-limited environments (Jung et al., 2010 ).  4.3.2 Environmental (biotic) factors Results of our analyses indicate that biotic factors (soil moisture and NDVI) have less influence on ET compared to abiotic factors (climatic variables) with a relative contribution of 24.79 % to ET variance. The PCC between ET and NDVI shows a weak score (r = 0.28, p < 0.01 ) even though statistically significant at 1 % significance level (Table 2 ). This is consistent with results obtained in other dryland regions (Chen et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ). The low relative contribution of vegetation cover to ET may be attributed to the fact that vegetation covers varies seasonally and also depends on the characteristics of the vegetation structure such as leaf area index (LAI), root depth, vegetation coverage, physiology, age and vegetation type e.g., forest, agriculture, or grassland (Odongo et al., 2019 ). The present study was conducted at an annual timescale which may mask the strong seasonal correlations between ET and NDVI in the rainy season when ET is not limited by water supply. Nevertheless, Pearson correlation between ET and NDVI shows that a positive change in NDVI leads to a corresponding positive change in ET which is in-line with results from other studies e.g., (Chen et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ). This suggest that as vegetation cover increases in the Sahel, this may likely increase the rate of ET in the region. The low PCC score between ET and soil moisture may be attributed to increasing global temperatures which depletes the amount of soil moisture available for soil evaporation and transpiration.   4.4 Quantitative attribution of ET change The impact of climate variability and vegetation change on ET in the Sahel was quantified using the double logarithm elasticity model. Mean elasticity coefficients were 0.78, 1.90, 0.08, −1.48, −9.58, −0.18, 2.52, −3.41, & 0.57 for precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, windspeed, net radiation, specific humidity, vapour pressure, AED and NDVI, respectively. This implies that a 10 % increase in precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, vapour pressure and NDVI will increase ET by approximately 8 %, 19 %, 0.8 %, 25 % & 6 % respectively. Vapour pressure contributes substantially to ET variance and also produced the highest positive elasticity coefficient on ET which is consistent with results obtained from other dryland regions (Ma et al., 2019 ). The greater positive effect of vapour pressure on ET in water-limited environments may be attributed to the fact that this variable can influence plant stomatal activity and canopy photosynthesis (Yang et al., 2022 ). In contrast, a 10 % increase in windspeed, net radiation, and AED leads to a decline in ET by approximately 15 %, 95 %, & 34 %, respectively. This is consistent with results from another study in the region which showed that net radiation, and mean temperature had a negative impact on ET (Yang et al., 2019 ). Vapour pressure, soil moisture, precipitation and NDVI produced the highest positive elasticity coefficients while net radiation and AED had the highest negative elasticity coefficients on ET. NDVI also produced positive elasticity coefficients across most watersheds suggesting that increasing vegetation greenness in the Sahel may enhance ET. However, increasing vegetation greenness in the Sahel may lead to water scarcity as more water may be lost to the atmosphere through the ET. Additional research is needed to investigate vegetation-hydrology-climate interaction in the Sahel as suggested at the end of section 4.2  above. This is very crucial considering that enhance vegetation greenness has been shown to exacerbate water scarcity in some regions (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2021 ). Although results from previous studies reported that precipitation is the dominant climatic factor controlling ET in many regions (Feng et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022 ), results from the present study show that soil moisture has a stronger positive effect on ET than precipitation with a higher mean elasticity coefficient (1.91) compared to precipitation (0.78). Moreover, the Pearson correlation coefficient between soil moisture and ET is stronger (0.51) than that between precipitation and ET (0.38). Furthermore, soil moisture had a higher relative contribution (21.12 %) to ET variance compared to precipitation (4.61 %). This is in-line with results from a previous study showing stronger positive correlations between soil moisture and ET compared to precipitation (Yinglan et al., 2019 ). In contrast the PCC between soil moisture and ET is (0.06) when controlling for precipitation and other variables. This suggests that although precipitation is the main source of water supply for ET, it would appear that across the Sahel, most of the precipitation is lost through infiltration into the soil and therefore contributes indirectly to ET through transpiration (Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). In fact, several studies have attributed the decline in ET in many areas to limited soil moisture, thereby highlighting the fact that soil moisture is an important variable driving ET in many regions (Jung et al., 2010; Ndehedehe et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, moisture recycling in the Sahel has been identified as an important factor influencing ET in the region (Yu et al., 2017 ). Results of the different analyses conducted in this study suggest that the mechanisms controlling ET variability in the Sahel are complex and could transcend natural climate variability and vegetation change. Whilst all the datasets used in the study have been validated and used extensively in previous studies in the Sahel, we wish to acknowledge that satellite-derived and reanalysis data have inherent uncertainties which may influence the results of the analyses reported in this study. Therefore, we wish to caution that results from this study should be regarded with a bit of caution. We also wish to acknowledge that the number of climatic and environmental factors analysed in the study are non-exhaustive. However, the different factors are selected based on the results from previous studies conducted around the world and in other dryland regions as highlighted in the introduction section of this article. We acknowledge that there may be other important factors that may have been inadvertently left out which could influence the results of the analyses reported herein which is another weakness of the study.   5 Conclusions The present study used analytical methods to assess the effects of climate and environmental changes on ET in the Sahel over the period (1981–2021) for climate variables and (2000–2021) for vegetation cover change. Results from our analyses show increasing trends in annual ET in the western, central and parts of the eastern Sahel. Precipitation, soil moisture, mean temperature, and NDVI also show increasing trends across the whole region while the other variables show both increasing and decreasing trends in the different watersheds with a strong spatial heterogeneity in trend magnitudes. Multivariable regression analyses show that both climatic and environmental factors contribute about 80 % of the ET variance. However, the relative contribution of climatic variables is 75.11 % while that of environmental variables is 24.71 %. Vapour pressure had the highest mean positive elasticity coefficient (2.58) while net radiation had the highest mean negative elasticity coefficient (−9.58) on ET. Taking together, results from the different analyses carried out in the present study suggest that the mechanisms controlling ET variability in the Sahel are complex and may transcend climate and environmental changes. The LSE and DLE models produced similar elasticity coefficients with strong Pearson correlations coefficients (>0.91) between the elasticity coefficients from both models. This suggest that both models may be used to quantify the impact of climate variability and vegetation change on ET in other regions. Results from the present results may be crucial for adopting climate-smart reforestation policies and enhance water resources management in Sahel. This is the first study to assess the effects of vegetation cover on ET in the Sahel. As the GGWI is still ongoing, it not yet fully known how increasing tree cover will affect the vegetation-hydrology-climate interactions especially as the trees become mature in the decades to come. Therefore, more studies are needed in the region to disentangle the relationship between vegetation-hydrology-climate under different alternative scenarios.
1 Introduction As the water towers of the world, the mountainous areas provide as much as 95 % of the total freshwater available in arid and semi-arid watersheds to support ecosystem services such as food production, biodiversity, and energy (Messerli et al., 2009; Immerzeel et al., 2010; Makino et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023a ). In recent decades, under the dual pressures of global warming and intensification of human activities, eco-hydrological processes in mountainous areas have changed markedly, threatening ecological and water security, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions (He et al., 2012; Luce et al., 2013; Immerzeel et al., 2019; Vereecken et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021). Infiltration is a critical water flow process that controls runoff generation, groundwater recharge, flooding, soil erosion, landslide, and ecosystem water use efficiency (Chen et al., 2021a; Liu et al., 2022; Shadab and Hesse, 2022; Vereecken et al., 2022 ). The advance of soil wetting front, directly related to the transformation of the limited precipitation to soil moisture that impact the availability of water for plant roots (Wang et al., 2008 ), plays an important role in hydrological process in arid and semi-arid regions (Mei et al., 2018; Zhou and Zhao, 2019 ). However, owing to the lack of a large-scale, in-situ monitoring network to analyze soil wetting patterns after rainfall, most previous studies have focused mainly on the infiltration capacity under different vegetation types (e.g., Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022 ). The distribution patterns and mechanism of the wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types are poorly understood. In recent years, several studies have analyzed the movement of wetting front via infiltration experiments (Young et al., 1999; Chu et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2022; Rubio et al., 2022 ). For example, Rubio et al. (2022)  observed the non-linear nature of the wetting front velocity in laboratory infiltration experiments, the value was highest near the water source and gradually decreased with the advance of the wetting front. During a field-scale infiltration experiment, Young et al. (1999)  found that mean local wetting front velocities varied substantially with depth, while effective wetting front velocities were statistically stable and the variance decreased with increased soil wetting depth. Chu et al. (2018)  demonstrated that the soil matrix potential drives soil water horizontally towards adjacent drier soil during the early wetting phase, and soil water flow gradually becomes dominated by gravity (i.e., vertical movement) as the wetting front moves deeper into the soil during the later wetting phase. In reality, soil water movement after rainfall under natural field conditions is an extremely complex process, e.g., the occurrence of preferential flow (PF), a process whereby water largely bypasses the soil matrix and flows rapidly into deeper soil in a non-uniform manner (Flury et al., 1994; Jarvis, 2007; Hardie et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2017; Guo and Lin, 2018; Demand and Weiler, 2021 ). For example, Ma et al. (2022)  reported that the relationship between wetting front depth/velocity and the infiltration rate is a positive linear relationship under matrix infiltration, but the relationship between wetting front depth and infiltration rate is non-linear under preferential infiltration. Although laboratory infiltration experiments are easy to implement, the original microstructure of the soil was destroyed (Wen and Yan, 2014 ), and it cannot accurately represent the soil wetting process in the natural state (Guo, 2020; Ma et al., 2022 ). In field infiltration experiments, artificial rainfall cannot accurately represent real natural rainfall and monitoring results are not continuous bringing some uncertainty to the representativeness of such results. With recent developments in monitoring technology, high temporal resolution in-situ soil moisture monitoring can now be used to study soil water movement, which provides an opportunity to solve the aforementioned dilemma (Song and Wang, 2019; Liu et al., 2020 ). Vegetation as a pivotal factor influencing the soil wetting process by regulating the amount of rainfall that enters the soil through interception, throughfall, and stemflow above the ground (Wang et al., 2013 ), and through natural preferential flow channels formed by root systems (Beven and Germann, 2013 ), water uptake, and alteration of soil hydrological properties under the ground (Singh et al., 2021; Qiu et al., 2023 ). Previous studies based on high temporal resolution in-situ soil moisture observation have indicated that vegetation type significantly affects the soil wetting pattern and PF in arid and semi-arid regions (Chang et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022 ). However, most of these studies mainly focused on the infiltration capacity under different vegetation types (He et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020 ), only a few studies qualitatively described the wetting front depth and velocity at a few observation sites and several rainfall events under different vegetation types. Jin et al. (2018)  reported that compared with grassland, forestland at an uphill-slope exhibited a deeper wetting front depth and faster wetting front velocity. Dai et al. (2022)  found that the wetting front depth in shrub was greater than that in alpine meadow. Wang et al. (2008)  indicated that barren was prone to infiltration beneath a depth of 40 cm. However, a systematic quantification of the spatiotemporal distribution patterns and mechanisms of wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types at large-scale are hardly reported. In this study, we investigated the distribution patterns of wetting front depth and velocity, as well as PF effects across different vegetation types based on a large-scale, long-term (7 years), high temporal resolution (30-min intervals) in-situ soil moisture observation network located in the northwest of China. Our work addresses the following specific questions concerning the Qilian Mountains and other similar arid mountainous areas: (1) What are the characteristics of the spatiotemporal distribution of soil wetting depth and velocity at the rainfall events scale under different vegetation types? (2) What are the effects of PF on wetting front depth and velocity? (3) What are the critical environmental factors influencing the transport process of the soil wetting front? Our results will provide important information for vegetation restoration projects and hydrological model improvement in the Qilian Mountains and other similar areas.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Description of the study area As the second-largest inland river watershed in China (Cheng et al., 2014 ), the Heihe River Basin (HRB) is located in the middle of the Hexi Corridor and divided into upper, middle, and lower reaches by the Yingluo and Zhengyi Gorges (Cai et al., 2023 ). The upper reaches of the HRB (UHRB) are the main runoff-producing areas of the basin, situated in the middle part of the Qilian Mountains (37°43′–39°39′ N, 97°29′–101°32′ E), covering 2.75 × 104  km2  (Fig. 1  ) and accounting for 21.15 % of the total basin area. The terrain slopes from southwest to northeast and the elevation ranges between 1719 and 5544 m above sea level (a.s.l.). It is characterized by a continental alpine and semi-arid climate, with the average annual temperature is about 0.5℃ and annual precipitation is 323 mm (Hu et al., 2022 ). The UHRB provide approximately 88 % of the total runoff for the entire watershed (Rogger et al., 2017 ), with an average annual runoff of 16.76 × 108  m3  from 1960 to 2019. The main sources of runoff are atmospheric precipitation and snowmelt in mountainous areas. Therefore, the UHRB plays a significant role in providing water resources to support the sustainable development of the basin. Owing to the complex topography, there are evident temperature and precipitation gradients in mountainous areas, leading to strong spatial heterogeneity and vertical zonation of soil and vegetation with changing altitude. The soil textures mainly include silt, silt loam, and sandy loam (United States Department of Agriculture classification) (Tian et al., 2017 ), and the land-cover types are mainly alpine meadow (AM), grassland, shrub, barren and forestland (Luo et al., 2017 ).  2.2 Data sources 2.2.1 Soil moisture network Soil moisture data were obtained from a continuous long-term monitoring network consisting of 32 monitoring sites established in July 2013 in the UHRB. Soil volumetric water content sensor (ECH2O-5TE, Decagon Devices Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) was installed at depths of 5, 15, 25, 40, and 60 cm below the soil surface, and the volumetric water content with a temporal resolution of 30 min was continuously recorded on a data logger (EM50, METER Group Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) at each monitoring site, and the measurement accuracy is ± 0.03 m3 /m3 . To fully restore the soil to its natural state and avoid the effects of the freeze–thaw process on soil moisture, we selected the growing season (from May 1 to October 15, 2014–2020) for data collection (Liu and Lin, 2015; Kang et al., 2022 ) and a detailed data quality control steps can be found in Kang et al. (2022) . During the installation of the soil moisture sensors, soil samples were collected and transported to the laboratory at Lanzhou University to determine soil hydrological properties, including bulk density (BD), particle size distribution (sand, silt, and clay content), soil organic carbon (SOC), saturated hydraulic conductivity (KS ) and soil water characteristic curve (SWCC) for each layer at each monitoring site. Detailed soil properties measurements can be found in Tian et al. (2017) . In addition, we also obtained detailed monitoring sites information, including elevation, slope, and root depth. To investigate the process of wetting front transport under different vegetation types, based on the combination of different vegetation types, but similar soil texture and small slope, we selected 11 soil moisture monitoring sites in the monitoring network, including barren (2 monitoring sites), grassland (6 monitoring sites), alpine meadow (2 monitoring sites), and shrub (1 monitoring site); details of the selected monitoring sites are shown in Table 1  .  2.2.2 Precipitation and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) data Owing to the lack of ground-based meteorological observation stations close to soil moisture sites for rainfall observations, precipitation data were obtained from a long-term (1979–2020) high-resolution (1/30°) precipitation dataset for the Third Polar region (TPHiPr) (Zhou et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023 ). In addition, normalized difference vegetation index data were obtained from a high spatiotemporal resolution (30 m and 8 d, respectively) NDVI time-series dataset covering the period 2000–2020 for the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau (QTP-NDVI30) (Chen et al., 2021b; Cao et al., 2022 ). Precipitation and NDVI data were downloaded from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC) (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/ ).   2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Determination of an infiltration event In this study, we adopted the infiltration event identification method used by Tian et al. (2019)  and Kang et al. (2022) . As shown in Fig. 2  (a), this method defines an infiltration event as the period from the start of the increase in soil moisture (SMinit  ) to the end of the increase in soil moisture (SMmax  ), and if the gap between two events is less than 6 h, they are combined into one event (Lozano-Parra et al., 2015, 2016 ). Events with soil moisture increment greater than 1 % were selected for analysis (Wiekenkamp et al., 2016; Demand et al., 2019 ), and a total of 1234 events were selected from 2014 to 2020. The identification of infiltration events was automatically selected using Matlab scripts; the total number of infiltration events at each monitoring site is shown in Supplementary material Fig. S1 .  2.3.2 Calculation of infiltration metrics (1) Wetting front depth (Zf  ). The wetting front depth of an infiltration event is considered to be the maximum depth of the soil layer where an increase in soil moisture. The ECH2O-5TE probes were installed at depths of 5, 15, 25, 40 and 60 cm, so the wetting front depth was 5, 15, 25, 40 and 60 cm when infiltration occurred in the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth layers, respectively. This can also be expressed as (Moran et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2019 ):(1) Z  f   = 60  c m ,  ASWI  5   > 1 %   40  c m ,  ASWI  4   > 1 %   25  c m ,  ASWI  3   > 1 %   15  c m ,  ASWI  2   > 1 %   5  c m ,  ASWI  1   > 1 %           with(2) ASWI  j   = ∑  ST  ET   Δ S M  t +  j       (3) Δ S M  t +  j   = Δ S M  t  j   ,  Δ S M  t  j   > 0   0 ,  Δ S M  t  j   ≤ 0          (4) Δ S M  t  j  = SM  t + Δ t  j  - SM  t  j       where, SM  t  j     is the soil water content (vol. %) at time t  during the j-th  infiltration event, Δt  is the time interval (30 min), ST  and ET  are the start and end moments of the j-th  infiltration event, and ASWI  is the cumulative soil moisture increment of a layer of soil for one infiltration event. (2) Wetting front velocity. The wetting front velocity of profile for an event can be expressed as:(5) VC  p  = Z f  - H 0   Δ T        where, VC  p     indicates the profile wetting front velocity (cm/h), Z f     is the wetting front depth of the infiltration event (cm), H0   is the distance of the first layer probe from the surface (H0   is 5 cm in this study), and ΔT  is the time taken for the wetting front to reach the maximum depth from the first layer (h). The wetting front velocity between two soil layers can be expressed as:(6) VC  i - i + 1   = H i + 1   - H i   t i + 1   - t i         where, VC  i - i + 1      represents the wetting front velocity between two adjacent layers (i  = 1, 2, 3, 4), H i     represents the depth at which the probe is located in layer i  of the soil profile, H i + 1      is the depth at which the probe is located in layer i  + 1 of the soil profile, t i     is the moment when the wetting front reaches layer i , and t i + 1      is the moment when the wetting front reaches layer i  + 1. (3) Other related indicators. To further explore the detailed effects of precipitation and rainfall intensity on the wetting front depth and velocity at rainfall event scale, we calculated soil water storage increment (SWS ) (Tian et al., 2019 ) and maximum variation or slope of the soil moisture (Smax  ) (Lozano-Parra et al., 2016 ) to substitute for precipitation and rainfall intensity, respectively. The calculation formula is as follows:(7) SWS = d i  × ∑ ST  ET   Δ SM  t  j       with(8) Δ SM  t  j   = Δ SM  t  j   ,  Δ SM  t  j   > 0   0 ,  Δ SM  t  j   < 0           where, SWS  is the soil water storage increment, Δ SM  t  j     is the change in soil moisture for the j-th  infiltration event in the i  layer (vol. %), and d i     is the soil thickness of the i-th  layer.(9) S max   = max SM  t + Δ t   - SM  t   Δ t      × 2      where, Smax   is the variation or slope of the soil moisture wetting curve (vol. %/hour), SMt   is the soil moisture value in the time t , and Δt  is the measurement interval (30 min). In addition, to identify the effect of initial soil moisture conditions on the wetting front depth and velocity, we calculated the initial soil water storage deficit degree, calculated as follows:(10) SWSD  0  = FC  0  - SWS  0   FC  0   × 100 %      where, SWSD0   is the initial soil water storage deficit degree in the first soil layer, FC  0     is the field capacity in the first soil layer (mm), and SWS  0     is the soil water storage in the first layer (mm).  2.3.3 Classification of infiltration events Based on the start time of the infiltration event at two adjacent layers, infiltration events were divided into three main categories, as shown in Fig. 2 (b):(1) NR: No response includes events where soil moisture increased only the first layer and there was no response in deeper soil layers, i.e., an infiltration event where the wetting front depth was 5 cm;  (2) MF: Matrix flow includes events where there was a sequential soil moisture response from the soil surface to deeper layers;  (3) PF: Preferential flow includes events where at least one deeper soil layer responded earlier than or simultaneously with a shallower soil layer.     2.3.4 Random forests Random forest (RF) is an ensemble of un-pruned regression trees grown on bootstrap samples (Koestel and Jorda, 2014; Gao et al., 2018 ). Because individual trees are randomly perturbed, the forest allows for a broader exploration of the prediction space of all possible trees, which tends to have better predictive performance in practice (Genuer and Poggi, 2020 ). Variable selection and importance calculation were implemented in the R package VSURF (Genuer et al., 2015 ). Detailed steps can be found in Tian et al. (2023) . In this study, RF were used to identify the controlling factors influencing the profile distribution of wetting front depth and velocity.  2.3.5 Statistical analysis One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to identify the differences in wetting front velocity of profile among different vegetation types and between matrix flow (MF) and PF velocities under the same vegetation type. Pearson’s correlation was used to assess the significance of the relationships between soil properties, moisture conditions, vegetation, infiltration pattern and wetting front depth and velocity. The significance level of all statistical tests was set at P<0.05. Structural equation models (SEM) (Bollen, 1989 ) were established to analyze the effect of environmental factors on the temporal dynamics of wetting front depth and velocity. We selected a final model based on an overall goodness-of-fit (Eldridge et al., 2018 ), including the Chi-square (χ2 )/ degree of freedom (df ), comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). Favorable model fits were indicated by no significant difference when using the χ2 -test (P>0.05), high CFI and TLI (>0.9), and low RMSEA (<0.08) and SRMR (<0.08) (Liu et al., 2017 ). The standardized total effect was calculated according to direct plus indirect effects (Li et al., 2020). Structural equation model has emerged as a synthesis of factor analysis along with path analysis and are now widely used in ecological studies as a causal inference tool (Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022 ). The SEM analysis was carried out using Mplus Version 8.3.    3 Results 3.1 Profile distribution characteristics of wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types The proportion of surface events (5 cm) was largest in barren, grassland, and alpine meadow, and gradually decrease with soil depth. In contrast, in shrub, there was a pattern of increase, followed by decrease, and then a further increase with depth, with the largest value occurring in the fifth soil layer (51.43 %). Among all vegetation types, the maximum proportion of events in the first (5 cm), the second (15 cm), the third (25 cm), the fourth (40 cm) and the fifth (60 cm) soil layers appeared in alpine meadow (42.38 %), barren (34.35 %), alpine meadow (17.62 %), grassland (11.47 %) and shrub (51.43 %), respectively (Fig. 3  (a)). In addition, the cumulative event proportions of the first three layers were all higher than 80 % in alpine meadow (92.22 %), barren (90.77 %), and grassland (80.56 %), but only accounted for 43.80 % in shrub (Fig. 3 (b)–(e)). Furthermore, the averages of wetting front depth for all events were 15.70, 18.95, 14.31 and 39.81 cm in barren, grassland, alpine meadow and shrub, respectively (Fig. S2 ). Evidently, the wetting front depth of shrub was the largest, followed by grassland, barren, and alpine meadow. To explore wetting front depth and velocity in more detail, we divided the events into three categories: NR, MF, and PF. The highest proportions of NR and MF events were in barren (39.69 % and 59.61 %, respectively), followed by grassland (38.09 % and 50.40 %, respectively), alpine meadow (21.07 % and 42.38 %, respectively), and shrub (8.57 % and 39.05 %, respectively). For PF events, the highest proportion occurred in shrub (52.38 %, more than half of all events), followed by alpine meadow (36.55 %), grassland (11.51 %), and barren (0.70 %) (Fig. 4  ). Therefore, the largest proportion of PF events occurred in shrub, followed by alpine meadow and grassland, with very few in barren. There were significant differences in profile wetting front velocity among the four vegetation types. The mean value of profile wetting front velocity in shrub was the largest (11.42 cm/h), followed by alpine meadow (4.96 cm/h), grassland (2.32 cm/h), and barren is the smallest (1.16 cm/h), and the profile wetting front velocity of shrub was 9.84 times greater than that of barren (Fig. 5  (a) and Fig. S3 ). In addition, the velocity values of MF and PF events in grassland were 2.24 and 7.13 cm/h, respectively, i.e., the profile wetting front velocity of grassland with PF occurrence was 3.18 times higher than that of grassland without PF occurrence. In shrub, the profile wetting front velocities of MF and PF events were 7.45 and 14.67 cm/h, respectively, i.e., the profile wetting front velocity of shrub with PF occurrence was 1.97 times higher than that without PF occurrence (Fig. 5 (b)). This evidences the effect of PF in accelerating the profile wetting front velocity. In MF events, the trend of wetting front velocity between adjacent layers with soil depth in barren and alpine meadow initially decreased, then increased, and finally decreased again. In contrast, the trend in grassland and shrub decreased initially, followed by an increase (Fig. 5 (c–f)). Fig. 5 (g) shows the wetting front velocities of MF and PF in the shallow (5–25 cm) and deep (25–60 cm) soil layers in shrub, the vegetation type with the highest proportion of PF. The mean wetting front velocities of MF and PF in shallow soil layers were 8.01 and 16.34 cm/h, respectively, with the PF wetting front velocity being 2.05 times higher than that of MF. The minimum and maximum values of MF wetting front velocity were 0.56 and 13.33 cm/h, and the minimum and maximum values of PF wetting front velocity were 0.83 and 40 cm/h, respectively; hence, the wetting front velocity of PF ranged from 0.06 to 71.43 times higher than that of MF in the shallow soil layers. The mean values of MF and PF wetting front velocities in the deep soil layers were 6.65 and 25.69 cm/h, respectively, with the PF wetting front velocity 3.86 times higher than that of MF.
