The minimum and maximum values of MF wetting front velocity were 1.03 and 11.67 cm/h, and the minimum and maximum values of PF wetting front velocities were 0.30 and 67.96 cm/h, respectively; hence, the PF wetting front velocity ranged from 0.30 to 68 times higher than that of MF in the deep soil layers. In other words, the MF wetting front velocity in shallow soil layers was greater than that in deep soil layers, while the PF wetting front velocity exhibited the opposite pattern. The mean PF wetting front velocity was 2.05 times (range 0.06–71 times) and 3.86 times (range 0.3–68 times) that of MF in the shallow and deep soil layers, respectively. In summary, the profile wetting front velocity of shrub was the largest, followed by alpine meadow, grassland, and barren; this is consistent with the proportion of PF ordered by vegetation type, demonstrating the effect of PF in accelerating soil profile wetting front velocity. There was a similar trend in the wetting front velocity with soil depth for MF events in barren and alpine meadow, the trend in grassland and shrub were also similar to each other, with the former took the form of an ‘S’ shape and the latter a horizontal ‘U’ shape. Finally, the wetting front velocity of PF in deep soil layers was greater than that in shallow soil layers.  3.2 Monthly distribution characteristics of wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types In barren, the wetting front depth was mainly located in the upper two soil layers in May and September, and in the upper three layers from June to August, the proportion of third layer events was highest in July (5.57 %), while the maximum of wetting front depth was only 15 cm in October. There was little difference in the proportion of monthly events in grassland, which mainly distributed across the upper four layers from May to July, in the upper three layers in August and September, and the proportion of fourth layer events was highest in July (3.94 %). The wetting front depth of alpine meadow was primarily located in the upper three layers from May to September. The proportion of events in the upper two layers showed an increasing trend from May to July, reaching a maximum (11.03 %) in July, before decreasing, and the maximum wetting front depth was only 5 cm in October. In shrub, the wetting front depth was mainly concentrated at 60 cm, and the proportion of 60 cm events tended to increase from May to July, reaching a maximum (13.33 %) in July, after which the proportion decreased, and reaching a minimum in October (2.86 %). In summary, the monthly distribution pattern of wetting front depth across different vegetation types showed a maximum (deepest) in July, and minimum (shallowest) in October (Fig. 6  ). The wetting front velocity showed a single peak distribution in barren and alpine meadow, with both reaching their peak value in July (0.69 cm/h in barren and 5.00 cm/h in alpine meadow) (Fig. 7  (a) and (c)). A double peak distribution was observed in grassland and shrub, with the former reaching peak values in July (1.36 cm/h) and September (1.67 cm/h), and the latter in June (9.58 cm/h) and September (9.38 cm/h) (Fig. 7 (b) and (d)). These distributions may be caused by seasonal differences in precipitation, vegetation, soil moisture, and proportion of PF (Fig. S4 ). It can also be seen that NDVI, initial soil moisture content, and proportion of PF show similar trends in barren and alpine meadow (Fig. S4 ). Furthermore, the maximum PF proportion in grassland and shrub occurs in July and June, respectively (Fig. S4 ), this appears to be the main explanation for the first peak of wetting front velocity under these two vegetation types. In addition, Fig. S4  shows that higher initial soil moisture content may be the main reason behind the wetting front velocity reaching the second peak in grassland and shrub. Therefore, the wetting front velocity is highest in barren and alpine meadow in July, shrub in June, and grassland in September.  3.3 Profile control factors of wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types Random forest analysis was applied to identify the factors controlling the profile distribution of wetting front depth and velocity (Fig. 8  (a) and (c)). We found that the critical factors controlling the profile wetting front depth were PF, NDVI, θr , and α. Further analysis revealed that the factors controlling wetting fronts at different depths varied with soil layers. In the first layer, wetting front depth was controlled by θs  and α; in the second layer, it was controlled by n; in the third layer, θr  played a significant role; in the fourth layer, it was controlled by BD and PF; and in the fifth layer, it was controlled by NDVI (Fig. 8 (a)). The results of the Pearson correlation analysis were shown in Fig. 8 (b). In other words, PF plays a pivotal role in determining the wetting front depth, with the upper three layers primarily influenced by soil properties (especially SWCC, θs , α, n and θr ), while the lower two layers are mainly controlled by preferential flow through macropores formed by vegetation roots. This also reflects the soil characteristics of the study area, where the first three layers are mainly for water storage functions, while the last two layers are more conducive for infiltration. Moreover, Tian et al. (2023)  also reported that parameter of SWCC (α and n) were the most important infiltration factors in the upper three layers, this is mainly because the SWCC reflects the soil water-holding capacity, which is closely related to the soil pore structure and soil water conductivity, significantly affecting the soil hydrological processes (Yang et al., 2014 ). Fig. 8 (c) and (d) shows that SOC had the greatest influence on profile wetting front velocity, followed by SM, Pre , NDVI, and PF; these are most significantly positively correlated with the profile wetting front velocity. Generally speaking, vegetation with higher coverage has deeper root systems, more SOC, and stronger biological activity, promoted by the formation of soil aggregates and macropores (Beven and Germann, 2013; He et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2023 ); this is conducive to water infiltration and affects the soil water holding capacity, and is thus reflected in the properties associated with the SWCC. In summary, PF is the most critical factor influencing the wetting front depth, and the control factors vary across different soil depths; in the upper three layers, the wetting front depth is primarily controlled by soil properties (especially SWCC, θs , α, n and θr ), while in the deeper two layers, it is influenced by vegetation. Furthermore, the most critical factor affecting the wetting front velocity is SOC.  3.4 Temporal control factors of wetting front depth and velocity under different vegetation types The temporal dynamics of the wetting front propagation process are influenced by a combination of rainfall characteristics, vegetation, initial soil moisture status, and infiltration pattern. Here, precipitation (SWS) had the most significant positive impact on wetting front depth, followed by rainfall intensity (Smax ), vegetation (NDVI), and PF. Initial soil moisture status (SWSD0 ) had a negative effect on wetting front depth in all events (Fig. 9   (a–d)). This result is similar to those of Hao et al. (2008)  and Liu et al. (2015) . In other words, the primary factor influencing the temporal dynamics of wetting front depth was precipitation, followed by initial soil water content, and the third was rainfall intensity. It is worth noting that PF also played an important role in the migration of wetting front depth in shrub (Fig. 9 (e) and S5(d)). Fig. 9 (f) and S6(a–d)) show that precipitation (SWS) also had the most significant positive effect on wetting front velocity, while initial soil moisture status (SWSD0 ) exhibited a negative effect on wetting front velocity. The first determining factor of wetting front velocity was initial soil water content in barren, and precipitation in grassland, alpine meadow and shrub. In addition, PF also played an important role in the wetting front velocity in shrub. In summary, the most critical factor for the temporal variation of wetting front depth and velocity was precipitation and initial soil moisture conditions, and PF played an important role in the transport process of the wetting front in shrub.   4 Discussion 4.1 Effect of PF on soil wetting front under different vegetation types Vegetation type markedly influenced the proportion of PF, the largest proportion of PF occurred in shrub, followed by alpine meadow, grassland, and finally barren. Mei et al. (2018)  reported that PF in patches of shrubs and woods was significantly greater than that in grassland in semiarid hillslopes. Hu et al. (2016)  also found that deeper and longer macropores were developed in shrub compared with other vegetation types in Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. In addition, the wetting front velocity was consistent with the order of PF proportion. The wetting front depth was deepest in shrub, followed by grassland, barren, and shallowest in alpine meadow (Fig. 10  ). In other words, with an increase in the proportion of PF, the wetting front velocity increased, and the wetting front depth also increased except in alpine meadow. This indicates that PF has the effect of increasing the wetting front depth and accelerating the wetting front velocity (Mei et al., 2018; Worthington, 2019 ). In alpine meadow, there is a thick mattic epipedon layer composed of dense sedge roots in the top 30 cm of the soil (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b ), which facilitates infiltration and increases the soil water-holding capacity (Biskop et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023b ). Kang et al. (2023)  also reported that PF was mainly concentrated in the top soil layer in alpine meadow. This is mainly because the mattic epipedon accounts for above 90 % of the roots and 80 % of the soil organic matter of soil profile (Miehe et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023b ), with a large number of macropores (Hu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019 ), which is conducive to PF (Beven and Germann, 2013 ). Therefore, PF has the effect of increasing the wetting front depth and accelerating the wetting front velocity, while PF in alpine meadow mainly occurs in the surface mattic epipedon layer, which is conducive to runoff production.  4.2 Wetting front depth under different vegetation types Vegetation is the key factor that determines the soil wetting process after rainfall. Different vegetation types have different coverage, root depths and densities, and soil hydraulic properties, which influence the processes of infiltration and PF (Ge et al., 2022 ). Our results showed that the wetting front depth varied among different vegetation types. Huang et al. (2013)  indicated that wetting front depth increase significantly with vegetation cover, this study confirms the above finding, converting barren to grassland or shrub will generally enhance the wetting front depth. Specifically, the average wetting front depth was as follows: alpine meadow (14.31 cm) < barren (15.70 cm) < grassland (18.95 cm) < shrub (39.81 cm). In other words, after converting barren to alpine meadow, to grassland or shrub, the average soil wetting front depth would change by −8.86 %, 20.67 %, and 65.13 %, respectively (Fig.S7 ). This is mainly because alpine meadow has a thick mattic epipedon layer in the topsoil that contains > 90 % of the plant roots (Zhang et al., 2023c ), while other vegetation types with higher vegetation cover generally have deeper root systems. These plant roots promote soil structure through physical–mechanical and biochemical action (Fan et al., 2022 ), producing more PF paths (Qiu et al., 2023 ), which facilitate the movement of soil water to deeper soil layers. Thus, vegetation restoration can promote soil structure, decrease soil bulk density, and increase organic matter content and soil porosity through enhanced plant root systems and faunal activities; this alters soil hydraulic properties and greatly contributes to PF pathway connectivity and runoff–infiltration partitioning (Jarvis, 2007; He et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2023 ). The wetting front depth changes temporally as well as spatially (Hao et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2015; Rossi et al., 2018 ). In our study, precipitation was the main factor affecting the temporal dynamics of wetting front depth, followed by rainfall intensity, and initial soil moisture conditions, but these factors varied across different vegetation types. Precipitation is the main source of soil moisture in arid and semi-arid regions (Ge et al., 2022 ). Higher intensity rainfall events often tend to result in more PF, and even small precipitation events may reach deeper soil layers through PF paths (Halihan et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2021; Liu and Lin, 2015 ). Barren, grassland, and shrub all exhibited high soil moisture conditions favoring infiltration to deeper layers. The different manifestations in alpine meadow can be attributed to the “mattic epipedon”, whereby water could not be transported to deeper soil layers even under high soil moisture conditions (Dai et al., 2022 ); the mattic epipedon is key for maintaining surface runoff. In summary, the factors controlling the spatial distribution of the wetting front are vegetation and soil properties, whereas the temporal control factor is precipitation.  4.3 Wetting front velocity under different vegetation types Our study showed that the slowest profile wetting front velocity occurred in barren (1.16 cm/h), followed by grassland (2.32 cm/h), alpine meadow (4.96 cm/h), and shrub (11.42 cm/h), consistent with the change in proportion of PF (Fig. S4  and Fig. 10 ). This indicates that although the mattic epipedon on the surface of alpine meadow prevents the propagation of the wetting front to deeper soil layers, PF paths exist within it, which can promote wetting front velocity (Zhang et al., 2023c ). Hu et al. (2016)  also found that a large number of macropores in the soil surface layer in alpine meadow, verifying our results herein. Hence, revegetation can markedly accelerate the profile wetting front velocity. Specifically, the average soil wetting front velocity increased by 0.99, 3.26, and 8.80 times after converting barren to alpine meadow, grassland, and shrub, respectively (Fig.S8 ). Singh et al. (2021)  reported that the wetting front velocity gradually increased with soil depth during MF; in contrast, we found that the wetting front velocity in grassland and shrub showed a horizontal ‘U’-shaped trend, and that in barren and alpine meadow showed an ‘S’-shaped trend with soil depth. These differences are attributed to the inability of in-situ monitoring to completely distinguish the occurrence of MF and PF. In other words, a MF event may also encompass PF occurrence, and a PF event also includes the MF, but these are not accurately detected and distinguished. This also fully reflects the complexity of soil water flow under natural conditions. Meanwhile, our study showed that profile wetting front velocities varied widely, ranging from 0.06 to 55 cm/h across different vegetation types. The profile wetting front velocity of PF events was 1.97 times that of MF events; notably, in shrub, the mean wetting front velocity of PF was 2.05 times (range 0.06–71 times) and 3.86 times (range 0.3–68 times) that of MF in shallow and deep soil layers, respectively. Halihan et al. (2023)  reported that PF velocity can reach 174 cm/h, this being nearly two orders of magnitude higher than MF velocity. Germann and Hensel (2006)  based on 215 observed values at various depths, suggested that the maximum value of wetting front velocity could reach 198 cm/h, and PF velocity was 10–100 times faster than MF velocity. Our results are evidently lower than those obtained in the above studies. The main reasons for this are as follows: first, in-situ monitoring could not completely distinguish between MF and PF, and the presence of MF in PF events weakened the accelerating effect of PF on infiltration; second, the study area is located in an alpine mountainous region with complex topography and harsh environment, and the battery life and capacity of the data logger limited the monitoring time step to a maximum of 30 min, potentially leading to some calculation errors and differences in the results. For example, when PF occurred, water may have moved through the soil profile too fast for the instrument to record the wetting front; the highest velocities may not have been captured, only a minimum for the fastest value.  4.4 Implications for water resource management Located on the northeastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, the Qilian Mountains serves as an important water source area and ecological security barrier in China (Xue et al., 2023 ). Our study showed that the wetting front velocity was lowest in barren, followed by grassland, alpine meadow, and shrub; the wetting front depth was the deepest in shrub, followed by grassland, barren, and finally alpine meadow. This demonstrates that vegetation restoration helps to accelerate the wetting front velocity, and increase the wetting front depth (except for alpine meadow). Furthermore, the presence of a thick mattic epipedon in alpine meadow is a critical component of the ecological security barrier of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau; it is key for maintaining surface runoff, which is considered to be the most critical ecological service function of alpine meadow (Wu et al., 2020; Niu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022 ). However, existing studies have shown that alpine meadow are experiencing rapid degradation (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023a ), potentially leading to a series of ecological and environmental problems (Rodriguez-Iturbe et al., 2019; Asner et al., 2008; Normile, 2007; Hibbard et al., 2001; Schlesinger et al., 1990 ). Therefore, future ecological restoration programs should prioritize the protection of alpine meadow to ensure runoff generation, which in turn ensures water and ecological security of the entire basin. Although this study provides new insights for understanding soil water movement processes, the measurement interval of soil moisture could only be set at 30 min owing to the harsh mountainous environment, making it difficult to completely distinguish between MF and PF. In addition, there was no in-situ rainfall observation owing to the vulnerability of the instrument to damage, destruction, and theft by wild animals and humans in the study area, which brings some uncertainty to the influence of rainfall on the wetting front. Future research should take these into account, and should also discriminate the influence mechanism of roots on soil hydraulic properties to better determine the relationships between vegetation and infiltration in arid and semi-arid mountainous areas.   5 Conclusions In this study, a large-scale long-term in-situ soil moisture monitoring network was used to investigate the wetting front propagation process under different vegetation types at the rainfall event scale. The proportion of PF is highest in shrub, followed by alpine meadow, grassland, and barren. With an increase in the proportion of PF, the wetting front velocity increased, and the wetting front depth also increased except in alpine meadow. PF had the effect of increasing the wetting front depth and accelerating the wetting front velocity, especially in shrub, thus, its important role PF should not be ignored in shrub when simulating rainfall-runoff processes in mountainous areas. The factors controlling wetting front depth vary by soil depth. Soil properties (especially SWCC, θs , α, n and θr ) dominate the wetting front depth in the upper three layers, while vegetation mainly influences the process in the two deeper layers. SOC is crucial for wetting front velocity, and precipitation drives temporal variations in wetting front depth and velocity. Furthermore, since the function of the surface mattic epipedon layer in the alpine meadow is crucial to maintaining surface runoff, measures should be taken to strengthen its protection. These findings provide new insights for vegetation restoration and water resource management in arid and semi-arid regions. Further work needs to distinguish the influence mechanism of plant roots on soil hydraulic properties to better understand the influence of vegetation on infiltration process in arid and semi-arid areas.
1 Introduction Climate change exerts particularly strong effects on coastal areas (Richardson et al., 2024 ). In this context, our focus is specifically on the risks associated with rising aquifer levels (Rotzoll and Fletcher, 2013 ). With sea levels rising by a few millimeters to a few centimeters per year depending on climate change scenarios (Rignot et al., 2011 ), the levels of coastal aquifer are also increasing. This poses a threat to buried and low-lying infrastructures, nearshore ecosystems, and amplifies the risk of flooding (Habel et al., 2017; Knott et al., 2017 ). Fluctuations in aquifer level traduce the variations of groundwater storage, and consequently the difference between recharge and discharge. For this reason, varying seasonal rainfall and evaporation can lead to temporary increased or decreased aquifer levels, depending on discharge conditions. Both marine and continental forcings, as well as the geometry of the coastline, distance from the coast, geologic depositional environments, and regional stream network contribute to groundwater-induced flood-risk evolution in coastal areas (Knott et al., 2019 ). Aquifer hydraulic properties were found to be a dominant factor in groundwater-rise vulnerability, with propagation projection of 10 km from the coast and main rivers in Netherlands (Oude Essink et al., 2010 ). Diffusive aquifers extend the zone of tidal influence and their associated high levels (Jacob, 1950; Nielsen, 1990 ). They also moderate the influence of recharge, with reduced head gradients and limited aquifer levels. Conversely, less diffusive aquifers mitigate marine influences but increase the vulnerability to groundwater rise from the continental side. This initial qualitative analysis becomes significantly more complex for heterogeneous aquifers. This is particularly true for coastal areas where Quaternary sand deposits next to the shoreface separate inland less diffusive bedrock formations from marine boundaries, a common configuration found in coastal areas like on the Western Normandy coast (France) (Dupret et al., 1989 ). The dune ridge shields the adjacent low-lying area from most of the marine submersion risks but does not protect it from increasing groundwater levels. A few hundred meters to a few kilometers away inland, the bedrock rises significantly, protecting more distant coastal areas from any marine risk, but increasing the vulnerability to flooding induced by aquifer outlets. To assess vulnerability to groundwater-induced flooding, one of the major challenges lies in characterizing hydraulic properties and their heterogeneity. Information derived from the aquifer's response to the tidal signal has been widely employed to determine these properties (e.g. Aguila et al., 2023; Fischer et al., 2020; Goyetche et al., 2022; Jha et al., 2008; Slooten et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021 ). They provide basic to advanced constraints on aquifer properties and flow structures (Rogers et al., 2023 ). For homogeneous aquifers, piezometric tidal effects decrease exponentially with shore distance as a function of diffusivity (Ferris, 1952 ). Diffusivity can thus be determined by comparing the amplitude of piezometric head variations with that of tides (Carr and Vanderka, 1969; Slooten et al., 2010 ) and, for greater precision, by analyzing both signals together (Jha et al., 2008 ). Heterogeneous aquifers also exhibit spatial variations with hydraulic conductivity increasing linearly with the distance from the coastline in some cases (Monachesi and Guarracino, 2011 ), or vertically in other cases (Li and Jiao, 2003 ). Mapping these variations in diffusivity often requires several monitoring wells (Carol et al., 2009; Rogers et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2021 ). A review of methods also emphasizes the necessity to develop original approaches to independently estimate hydraulic conductivity and specific yield for water resources management (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Here, we propose an alternative and innovative approach to characterize subsurface hydraulic properties (hydraulic conductivity and specific yield) and their heterogeneity, based on hydraulic head measured on a single piezometer. The method uses three aspects of aquifer response to marine and continental forcings: i) average head, which filters out the temporal variability and is linked to average recharge, sea level and hydraulic conductivity; ii) high-frequency head variations linked to tidal effects; iii) seasonal variations, which respond to hydrological cycle of aquifer recharge and discharge. We propose to characterize heterogeneous subsurface hydrodynamic properties by analyzing these three piezometric signal components, associated to characteristic time scales of weeks (spring and neap tides), months (hydrological cycle) and years (average recharge). We show that coastal aquifers may respond specifically to each of those forcings using data obtained on a coastal aquifer in Normandy, France (section 2 ). We propose a step-by-step approach to constrain the subsurface hydraulic properties relying on analytical and simplified 1D numerical models without considering any groundwater seepage (section 3 ). We compare the results obtained with a more advanced 2D numerical model, investigate the effects of seepage and of the distance of the observation piezometer to the lithological interface (section 4 ). We then discuss the most adapted identification method depending on the encountered conditions, and its domain of applicability. We eventually illustrate our methodology by presenting an application to groundwater-induced flooding in a coastal area (section 5 ). We believe that this is one of the key applications of our methodology, as this latter is specific to coastal areas, which are often prone to groundwater flooding as water table is likely to be shallow in such contexts.  2 Response of coastal hydraulic heads to tidal and recharge variations Starting from a classic coastal context (2.1), we demonstrate the dual influence of continental and marine forcings on hydraulic head variations (2.2) and propose a quantification of their main characteristics (2.3). 2.1 Geological and hydrogeological contexts The study area is a coastal site located in the south-western part of the town of Gouville-sur-Mer, in western Normandy, France (Fig. 1  , insert). It is located in the downstream part of the Moulin-de-Gouville river catchment, the source of which lies 10 km to the East. The modelled area is 1 km wide and 3.3 km long (frame in Fig. 2  ). This site is representative of coastal areas made up of a dune ridge, a retro -littoral palaeo-cliff and, between these two groups, a sea-marsh. The palaeo-cliffs of Normandy are polygenic structures, whose formation began in the Neogene (Pedoja et al., 2018 ). They contain different levels of marine terraces, most often masked by periglacial cover (Bigot, 1897; Coutard et al., 2006; Elhaï, 1960; Lautridou, 1989 ). The most recent of these terraces is the Eemian (124,000 to 119,000 years ago), which is located in the basal parts of the paleo-cliffs and consists of perched fossil beaches of pebbles or sand (Dupret et al., 1989 ). Within the studied site, the dune belt reaches a maximum elevation of 20 m. To the West, it overlooks a sea marsh, whose elevation is close to that of the sea at high tide. The paleo-cliff has a gentle profile, a result of erosion of the last ice age. The highest points of the modelled area, located to the East of the paleo-cliff, reach approximatively 25 m above sea level. Note that all elevation including hydraulic head are referenced as meters above sea level shortened as “m”. The study site is located in a complex geological context, both from a lithological and structural point of view. It is located in the heart of the Cadomian island arc of Coutances (Dissler et al., 1988; Dupret et al., 1990 ), whose main geological formations are of magmatic origin (Dupret et al., 1987; Dupret et al., 1989 ). In the environment of the site, sedimentary formations of detrital origin are also present, of lower and upper Brioverian age. Some Cambrian sandstones also crop out to the north and on the rocky flat off the site, on the foreshore. The geological bedrock at the study site is covered by more or less ancient Quaternary rocks, generally sandy (zone 1 in Fig. 2 ). They are of continental or marine origin depending on the case. Under the dunes, the bedrock was reached by various drillings at a height of around ten meters. This Brioverian bedrock outcrops on the foreshore and in the paleocliff (zone 2 in Fig. 2 ). The description of the rocks reached by the drilling does not make it possible to precisely characterize the composition of the bedrock located under the dunes, in the vicinity of the study site. Understanding its structure in detail would require high-precision geophysics coupled with close-up surveys. Nevertheless, this environment is that of a strongly faulted site. It is likely that the paleocliff originated from the presence of these structural discontinuities. The lithological differences observed between the rocks outcropping on the foreshore or in the paleocliff can only be conceived in the presence of a bundle of faults and folds masked by the dune massif and the sea marshes which border it at the foot of the paleocliff. Fig. 2  synthetizes the site geological setup, with a well-marked heterogeneity characterized by two juxtaposed distinct formations. In the western part (zone 1 on Fig. 2 ), the site consists of recent, loose rocks, mainly marine and eolian sands, up to 10 m thick. These sands are partially interbedded with solifluction deposits or sandy clay peat. They are referred to as Quaternary sands in the next sections. In the eastern part, the outcropping rocks (zone 2 on Fig. 2 ) belong to the local Cadomo-Variscan bedrock (Brioverian sequence). They are designated as Brioverian shales in the next sections. They consist of variably metamorphosed sandstone and shale, as well as granite, showing fissures and surface alteration. This bedrock forms the basement of the unconsolidated rocks in the western part of the site. There is no clear discontinuity or impervious layer between the ancient rocks and the overlaying unconsolidated formations, due to a weathering layer affecting the upper part of the bedrock. It is therefore not possible to clearly distinguish an upper aquifer from a lower, confined aquifer. As a whole, the aquifer extends to a thickness of over 35 m.  2.2 Piezometric, sea-level and recharge data The Gouville piezometer (red dot on Fig. 2 ) has been monitored at a daily frequency since 2005. It is part of the French national network of groundwater measurements, whose information is accessible online on the ADES database (Winckel et al., 2022 ). The piezometer is 11 m deep, drilled through sands within the Quaternary formation, and located 420 m east of the shoreline. The recorded head data is shown in dark blue on Fig. 3   for the 2009–2017 period. It reacts to both spring-and-neap tide and seasonal recharge forcings. The high frequency variations of the head data are to compare with the tidal signal (light blue curve on Fig. 3 ). It is obtained from the nearest oceanographic station of Saint-Malo operated by the Hydrographic and Oceanographic Marine Service, which produces oceanographic data at several coastal stations along the French shore (SHOM, 2020 ). Hourly levels were translated in daily levels to focus on the bimonthly tidal fluctuations, which are the only ones observed in the piezometric data. The high frequency variations of head data (dark blue) are well marked and have logically a significantly smaller amplitude than the sea level ones (light blue). The head lower frequency variations are well phased with aquifer recharge (red curve on Fig. 3 ), obtained from the SURFEX national climate model (Le Moigne et al., 2020 ), produced by the French meteorological institute. In SURFEX, aquifer recharge values are resulting from the exchanges of mass and energy between the soil, the surface, the biosphere and the atmosphere accounting for the wide diversity of surfaces.  2.3 Main characteristics of the hydraulic head signal The head data displays three main components: the mean pluriannual value, the amplitude of seasonal recharge-induced variations, and the amplitude of weekly tidal variations. Using the value of K 1  previously determined, we obtain a value of Sy 1  of 10 % (Sy  1  = 0.1   ). As for K 1 , this approximation is subject to several assumptions.
