The hydraulic properties of the Brioverian shales are more difficult to assess as they will influence the seasonal head fluctuations for which, to the best of our knowledge, no analytical solution is available for heterogeneous aquifers in transient state. We thus use a simplified numerical model to constrain the hydraulic properties of Brioverian shales (K 2 , Sy 2 ).  3.2 Constraints on Brioverian shales hydraulic properties with a 1D numerical model To complete the identification, we set up a simplified 1D free aquifer perpendicular to the shoreline having the same characteristic as the one presented in the previous subsection. The head is fixed at the coast by the tidal signal (Fig. 3 , light blue curve). The recharge applied uniformly on the top of the model is taken from the SURFEX reanalysis (Fig. 3 , red curve). A no-flow boundary condition is applied upstream at x  = L  to represent the groundwater divide at the watershed limit. The minimal aquifer thickness is set at its value at the coast (h sea  = 20  m). The free-flow model is carried out using MODFLOW NWT (Harbaugh, 2005; Niswonger et al., 2011 ) with 1-meter-wide mesh cells and daily time steps. The initial head values are set to the steady-state solution obtained from the mean recharge and sea level. We first and synthetically evaluate the quality of the approximations given by the previous analytical solutions with a homogeneous numerical model with the values of K 1  and Sy 1  obtained previously by the analytical solutions. Results give values of α =    0.014 and β t  =    0.013, showing indeed close agreements. Calibrating directly with the numerical model instead of the analytical solutions following the same procedure would lead to close values K 1  = 18.33  m.d−1  and Sy 1  = 7.1 %. The relevance of the analytical solution was expected for the mean head. It is more conclusive on the confined assumption for the tidal fluctuations. Even though the homogeneous model captures well the mean head and the tide-induced signal (red curve), it remains far from the observed signal (blue curve, Fig. 5  ). Seasonal variations are too large. For some of the later years (2013–2017), winter levels are overestimated by 0.2–0.5 m. For the earlier years (2009–2012) and the last year 2018, summer recessions are underestimated by around half a meter. It shows that the model calibrated on the mean level and on the tidal variations displays too large seasonal variations. In other words, the response to the tidal fluctuations and the mean level imposes that the aquifer is not capacitive enough to buffer the seasonal variations of recharge shown by the observations. We provide additional details in Section 5  regarding the utilization of the earlier identification and comparison as a homogeneity test. We set up a heterogeneous model, derived from the homogeneous model, to accurately capture seasonal variations while maintaining the calibration of the mean hydraulic head and tidal fluctuations. To this end, we perform a sensitivity analysis of the recharge variations criterion βr  as a function of K 2  and Sy 2  at fixed values of the Quaternary sands hydraulic properties K 1  and Sy 1 , those values obtained with the analytical solutions (Fig. 6  ). The range of values of K 2  is limited to a minimum value of 20  m.d−1  to restrain the piezometric values below the topography and avoid any significant seepage not accounted by this simplified model. Results do not show a well-targeted minimum but a zone of lower βr  values. Using a limit of 0.3 for βr , the top right corner of Fig. 6  limited by the blue line corresponds to a narrow range of specific yield (Sy 2  = 23–30 %) and a large range of hydraulic conductivities (K 2  = 20–103  m.d−1 ). For this range of values, the values of α and βt  remain smaller in absolute values to 0.1 (more precisely α = 0.02–0.05 and βt  = 0.08–0.1), justifying the approach to first determine K 1  and Sy 1  before looking for constraints on K 2  and Sy 2 . Seasonal variations are thus reduced when Sy 2  is significantly increased to 23–30 % while the hydraulic conductivity is not limiting as long as it remains larger than 20  m.d−1 . Variations are thus reduced thanks to the creation of an upstream aquifer that is sufficiently capacitive to buffer the recharge signal as strongly as possible. Even with the highest values of specific yield, however, βr  does not converge to zero. The upstream aquifer is too far from the piezometer (600  m) to exert a strong influence on the seasonal variations. This and the specific yield values found in the most upper part of possible values for shales indicate that the interface between the geological units might be effectively closer to the piezometer than shown by the geological map.  3.3 Role of the position of the geological interface between Quaternary sands and Brioverian shales We repeat the previous method with an interface between Quaternary sands and Brioverian shales no longer at x i  = 1000  m but at x i  = 500  m to determine to what extent such a configuration would enable a better calibration of the piezometric signal with lower shale specific yield values. K 1  and Sy 1  are kept equal to their previously determined values. β r     is shown in Fig. 7   as a function of K 2  and Sy 2 . It shows a better-defined range of minimal values close to 0. It also leads to smaller specific yields Sy 2  of 10–15 % more in agreement with fractured shales. The hydraulic conductivity K 2  remains poorly defined. The absolute values of α and βt  remain smaller than 0.1 (more precisely α = 0.02–0.05 and βt  = 0.08–0.1). Even closer to the piezometer, the upstream aquifer has only a minor influence on the average head and tidal fluctuations. It still justifies the approach to first determine K 1  and Sy 1  before looking for constraints on K 2  and Sy 2 . Seasonal variations in hydraulic head also suggest that the upstream aquifer is closer than indicated on the geological map (Dupret et al., 1989 ). These results are surprising since, first, Quaternary sands are expected to be more porous and permeable than Brioverian shales and second, the lithological interface is indicated further away from the piezometer. Nonetheless, additional informations support the potential existence of highly permeable formations East of the Quaternary sands. First, several boreholes at the study site show the existence of coarse sands containing pebbles beneath Quaternary eolian sands (Borehole file BSS000KUVT, 2017 ). Those coarse sands are probably Eemian sands (Dissler et al., 1988 ; Dupré et al., 1990), potentially extending further East and forming a more capacitive aquifer upstream. Second, a fault was observed and mapped 1.5 km east of the piezometer (Dupret et al., 1987; Rolet et al., 1994 ), oriented towards it and probably extending in its direction. This fault facilitates hydraulic connection between the low-permeability Brioverian shales and the lower Brioverian formations, which are known to be much more weathered and permeable. The presence of this fault in our study site, extending towards our observation point, could also explain the results indicating a closer interface. Finally, three boreholes drilled in the study area close to the coast show shales at depths averaging 6 m, contributing to explain the lower specific yield in zone 1 (Borehole file BSS000KUVT, 2017 ). Moreover, hydraulic tests performed in these boreholes give hydraulic conductivities of 7.5 to 22  m.d−1  and specific yields of 4 to 15 % confirming the ranges of values globally obtained for both formations (Table 2  ).   4 Effects of spatialization and surface–subsurface interactions We investigate the specific effects of spatialization and of surface/subsurface interactions on the flow structures and identification process. To this end, we develop a more comprehensive 2D model, identify the hydraulic properties, and determine the similarities and differences with the properties identified in the previous section. 4.1 2D model characteristics and implementation The 2D model geometry is extracted from a 25-meter resolution DEM using HydroModPy, a Python toolkit allowing building MODFLOW models from GIS files (Gauvain et al., 2024 , in prep.). The modelled area is a rectangular zone of 1 km North-South width, extending 3.3 km East perpendicular to the shoreline (black rectangle, Fig. 2 ). The model has a square mesh configuration, a lateral resolution of 25 m, and a single layer. Bottom of the model is at the constant elevation of −20 m. Elevation of the model is ranging from 0 to 25 m, corresponding to the DEM topography (Fig. 1 ). Flows are computed with MODFLOW NWT using the same initial and boundary conditions as in the previous 1D model case at a daily time step. Initial conditions are defined after running the model in steady state using the mean recharge over the two years preceding the calibration year. Recharge is imposed homogeneously to the whole domain. Seepage is modelled using the DRAIN package (Harbaugh, 2005 ) and allows water to flow out of the aquifer when hydraulic head intersects topography. We take two assumptions for the location of the interface between hydrogeological zones of Quaternary sands and Brioverian shales. The first one is based on the geological map and cross-section (Fig. 2 ) at a distance x i  = 1 000  m from the coast. The second one is set closer to the coast at x i  = 500  m, based on the previous section findings.  4.2 Hydraulic conductivities as determined by the mean hydraulic head We first analyze the dependence of the α performance criterion (5) for the original position of the interface (x i  = 1000  m) with the hydraulic conductivities of Quaternary sands and Brioverian shales K 1  and K 2 . Instead of the mean hydraulic head, we use as a proxy the hydraulic head obtained in steady state. Indeed, complementary analyses show only marginal differences of α values between them for the range of K1  and K2  values investigated. Results are obtained by an exploration on a 30 by 30 grid of regularly spaced value for K 1  and K 2  taken in the range of values identified by the 1D model (Fig. 8  ). Optimal values of α (white cells) are composed of two sections. The first section of optimal α values is obtained for values of K 1  = 18  m.d−1  and K 2  higher than 8  m.d−1 . For those simulations, it has been checked that seepage only occurs marginally in the modelled area. This domain of (K 1 , K 2 ) solutions is thus identified as the “no-seepage conditions” (Fig. 8 ). It matches the solutions obtained for the analytical and 1D numerical models. K 1  is close at 10 % to the analytical solution, a good approximation given the coarse resolution of the exploration. K 2  remains unconstrained as long as it is high enough. The steady-state piezometric level allows to identify the Quaternary sands hydraulic conductivity K 1 . In the second section identified as the “seepage conditions” (Fig. 8 ), the steady-state piezometric level depends not only on the Quaternary sands conductivity K 1  but also on the Brioverian shales conductivity K 2 . K 1  values range from 10 to 18  m.d−1  and K 2  from 1 to 8  m.d−1 . Any reduction in K 1  must be matched by an equivalent reduction in K 2 . To keep the same hydraulic head at the observation piezometer, the lower capacity of the Quaternary sands to transmit the incoming flows to the sea should be matched by lesser incoming flows and more seepage in the Brioverian shales. In such cases, the mean hydraulic head constrains a relation between both hydraulic conductivities, which happens to be linear in this case. A similar pattern is obtained regarding the spatial distribution of α values for the closer interface location (x i  = 500  m). In this case, no-seepage conditions are restricted to K 1  = 22  m.d−1  and K 2  higher than 15  m.d−1 . The seepage conditions are obtained for lower K 1  values ranging from 5 to 22  m.d−1  and K 2  values ranging from 1 to 15 m.d−1 . Lower K 1  values are explained by the larger groundwater seepage area occurring in the zone of Brioverian shales that is made 500  m wider. Indeed, this extension causes more seepage and thus less water income to the zone of Quaternary sands where the piezometer is located. Lower K 1  values are needed to counterbalance this smaller upstream groundwater flow.  4.3 Specific yields as determined by tidal fluctuations and seasonal variations Simulations are run in transient state to explore the dependence of βt  and βr  with Sy 1  and Sy 2 . Hydraulic conductivity K 1  and K 2  are set to their values identified in the previous step at the places identified by crosses in Fig. 8 . For the no-seepage conditions in the x i  = 1 000  m case, we explore βt  and βr  over a 7 by 7 grid of specific yield values Sy 1  and Sy 2 . Results are qualitatively similar to those obtained with the 1D model. βt  remains independent of Sy 2  and leads to a Sy 1  value of 8 %. For this value of Sy 1 , the simulation of the seasonal fluctuations imposes values of Sy 2  in the higher range of values (27–30 %) with associated absolute βr  values ranging from 0.42 to 0.46. Comparison with the 1D model (Table 2 ) shows that the identified values are close at 12 % for Sy1   and 15 % for Sy2  . In the absence of significant seepage, the 1D model can thus be used for the hydraulic parameter identification. In the seepage conditions, we analyze the 3 cases marked by the crosses for the x i  = 1000  m interface case. As diffusivity of the Quaternary sands has been reported to be conserved in all previous cases (Table 2 ), we set Sy 1  to keep this same diffusivity (D 1  = 4.5 103  m2 .d−1 ). The resulting models still match the tidal fluctuations whatever the investigated values of Sy 2 , with βt  remaining lower than 0.28. With Sy 1  respecting this constraint, the seasonal variations remain large whatever the value of Sy 2  (β r  < - 0.5   ) and even quite larger than in the absence of seepage (Fig. 9  a). The head variations remain far from the observed ones especially in the recession and flooding periods (Fig. 9 b). The occurrence of seepage limits even more the reduction of the seasonal variations. This can be explained by a partial disconnection of the upstream and downstream zones by the seepage process, which limits the influence of the hydraulic properties of the Brioverian shales. To counteract this effect, the interface should be positioned even closer to the piezometer than in the no-seepage conditions. The closer interface case (x i  = 500  m) gives better results, with β r     values closer to zero (Fig. 9 a). In this latter configuration, the 3 performance criteria α , β r     and β t     can still be met simultaneously, allowing to represent the main trends of the hydraulic head chronicle (Fig. 9 b, pink curve). Several types of geological information can explain our hypothesis of a closer interface. As presented in section 3.3 , this can be due to lithological variations (Dissler et al., 1988 ; Dupré et al., 1990) or fault hydraulic connection (Dupret et al., 1987; Rolet et al., 1994 ). Indeed, the bedrock of the study site is polyphase and abundantly faulted, and uncertainties persist as to the precise characteristics of its depth and nature.   5 Discussion We propose to synthesize the parameter identification methods previously illustrated on the Gouville hydraulic head chronicle. The aim is to show how these methods can be applied to piezometric signals exhibiting both tidal fluctuations and seasonal variations in cases where (i) heterogeneity occurs between two geological formations separated by an interface globally aligned with the coast and (ii) the topographical gradient does not change much along the coast. The first step is to determine whether the aquifer formation is heterogeneous, by means of a homogeneity test (section 5.1 ). If heterogeneity is confirmed, the subsequent step is to define an identification method based on approaches that are as accessible as possible without requiring time-consuming calibration operations (section 5.2 ). We conclude by analyzing the significance of heterogeneity on the coastal vulnerability to groundwater flooding (section 5.3 ). 5.1 Homogeneity test The homogeneity test is designed to determine whether the three components of the piezometric signal (mean hydraulic head, tidal fluctuations and seasonal variations) can be obtained simultaneously with a homogeneous model. The test can only be carried out in cases for which the interactions between surface and subsurface are sufficiently limited and do not require advanced spatial representation of the seepage. The test is performed in two steps, based on the decomposition of the piezometric signal into its three components using Eqs. (1)–(4) . In the first step, hydraulic conductivity and specific yield are obtained respectively from mean hydraulic head and tidal fluctuations, using the two analytical solutions given by Eqs. (9) and (11) . In the second step, a 1D numerical model is developed with these two values of hydraulic conductivity and specific yield. The analytically calibrated model then undergoes a validation procedure, based on available sea-level and recharge data. The simulated seasonal variations are compared with the observed signal using the ratio of their variability given by βr . If βr  is sufficiently close to 0, the homogeneity test is positive and the hydraulic parameters (conductivity and specific yield) as provided by the two analytical solutions can be applied to the whole domain to simulate hydraulic head variations.  5.2 Identification of the heterogeneous hydraulic properties When the three components of the piezometric signal cannot be properly simulated using a homogeneous model, the identification method depends on whether seepage is significant. If seepage is not significant, the hydraulic conductivity and specific yield of the geological formation close to the coast can be approximated by their values provided by analytical solutions, based on average head and tide-induced fluctuations. As the hydrodynamic properties determined this way allow proper simulation of mean value and tidal fluctuations of hydraulic head, they can be assigned to the near-shore aquifer formation. The calibration of the seasonal variations (using βr  performance criterion) offers a way to identify some constraints on the hydraulic properties of the far-from-shore aquifer formation. Several identification methods can be used to explore the two-dimensional parameter space formed by its hydraulic conductivity and specific yield. If solutions can effectively be found, it makes sense to get a relationship between properties rather than a single pair of values, since only one constraint is available. In the absence of clear optimal solutions provided by parameter exploration, several causes can be investigated. As for the case presented above, the interface may have been misplaced, making the simulated piezometric signal too insensitive to the far-from-shore geological formation. Interactions with the surface can impose boundary conditions that limit or, on the contrary, increase seasonal variations. This is especially the case when groundwater seepage occurs. In such cases, the identification method is different since the mean hydraulic head depends on hydraulic conductivity of both proximal and distal geological formations. Indeed, low upstream hydraulic conductivity values can cause important seepage, leading to reduced downstream heads, which can in turn be counterbalanced by reduced hydraulic conductivity values, as shown in section 4.2 . The relation between hydraulic conductivities can be obtained from the average hydraulic head using a transient model or a steady-state model if the steady-state hydraulic head can be shown to be close to the steady-state solution. For each identified valid couple of hydraulic conductivities (providing low α values), the specific yields can be determined by using the tidal and seasonal variations as shown in section 4.3 , assuming that their effect on the mean hydraulic head remains limited.  5.3 Seepage areas and vulnerability to aquifer-induced flooding From a single piezometer data, we infer the possible values of hydraulic conductivity of both Quaternary sands and Brioverian shales. Those values define two main flow regimes, associated to variable groundwater seepage occurrence. In this section, we discuss to what extent our methodology of heterogeneous aquifer property investigation can provide insights on a major issue of some coastal areas that is groundwater-induced flooding. To this end, we use the MODPATH particle tracking module (Pollock, 2016) to analyze the spatial variability of seepage areas. Seepage area location is controlled by time-variant boundary conditions (sea-level, recharge), as well as aquifer properties. Fig. 10   shows the resulting flow lines and seepage areas for steady-state simulations using mean observed values of sea-level and recharge rate, and implementing previously inferred values of aquifer properties. The first simulation (A.) corresponds to the no-seepage conditions (black cross on Fig. 8 ). Associated results show seepage areas only at the shoreline. Groundwater flowlines go straight from the Brioverian foothill to the sea, indicating no surface/subsurface interaction. The second simulation (B.) corresponds to the seepage conditions as defined in section 4.2  (orange cross on Fig. 8 ). Due to the lower hydraulic conductivity K 2 , the water table rises up to the topographic surface. While shoreline seepage areas are maintained (with lower rates), additional seepage areas show up along the low-lying points of the sea marsh. Some of the groundwater pathlines end up in these seepage areas, instead of flowing straight to the sea. The third simulation (C.) corresponds to seepage conditions with a lithological interface located at x i  = 500 m, i.e. closer to the shoreline. In this configuration, a larger zone of the modelled area is associated to low K 2  values, leading to new seepage areas extending West and reinforcing surface–subsurface interactions. Land vulnerability to aquifer-induced flooding can be described as the likelihood of terrains to be part of seepage areas (i.e. to be subject to flooding due to the groundwater rise), or to show high groundwater levels (i.e. having water table at small depths). This analysis shows that a proper identification of hydrodynamic parameter values is necessary to assess this vulnerability. Indeed, if coastal groundwater level is linked to recharge rate, sea level and geomorphology, it is eventually controlled by aquifer hydraulic properties. Our work shows that, in a heterogeneous aquifer made up of two zones, the hydraulic conductivities of both zones control the mean hydraulic head. Hydraulic conductivity controls the aquifer capacity to drain incoming recharge to the sea, and thus the average groundwater level. Low hydraulic conductivity values in the upstream zone can cause significantgroundwater rise, leading to seepage areas and increasedvulnerability. In association to hydraulic conductivity, specific yield also impacts land vulnerability, as it controls the amplitude of the water table variations. Lower conductivity increases the water table fluctuations and its probability to generate seepage areas. Close to the shore, lower specific yield values also lead to increased diffusivity and thus to higher tide-induced water table rise (Haehnel et al., 2023 ). Identifying hydraulic parameters is essential to assess coastal vulnerability to aquifer saturation and the induced risks on several types of infrastructure, even before reaching the surface. Buildings can crack if water table fluctuations reach swelling clay, and water can rise up the walls by capillary action, producing saltpeter (by bringing minerals from the soil, and drying back) and potentially leading to sanitary issues. Farmlands can also be impacted by groundwater rise, with various effects such as lowered bearing capacity of the soil, or disturbed root systems. Buried networks are also vulnerable to groundwater rise, with damage such as electric wires corrosion, water supply breaking, or groundwater intrusion into sewage networks leading to water treatment plant bypass. In some cases, analytical and numerical solutions can yield various combinations of hydrodynamic properties, both in terms of values and spatial heterogeneity. In such configurations, seepage areas can be an efficient complementary observation to calibrate the models, as proposed in previous works (Abhervé et al., 2023 ).   6 Conclusion We propose a new method for identifying the hydraulic conductivity and specific yield of heterogeneous coastal aquifers using time series of hydraulic heads observed in an isolated piezometer showing clear sensitivity to both marine and continental stresses. The method is based on the interpretation of three components of the hydraulic head signal: weekly fluctuations, seasonal variations and multi-year average level. In order to calibrate hydraulic conductivity and specific yield values of the two zones that make up the main aquifer terrains, we define new performance criteria. We show that the average hydraulic head depends on the hydraulic conductivity of terrains and on the recharge rate. Weekly fluctuations are essentially determined by the diffusivity of formations between the coast and the piezometer. Seasonal variations are mainly controlled by the hydraulic properties of the upstream zone further away from the coast. In the absence of groundwater seepage, this method uses analytical solutions and numerical models. In the case of significant seepage, more advanced models must be used to separate the effect of heterogeneity from the effect of surface-subsurface interactions. Our method fundamentally relies on time-series approaches and multistress analyses to enhance characterization of groundwater systems in coastal areas with limited availability of hydrogeologic information. While other approaches analyze hydraulic response to multiple stresses to better understand groundwater level fluctuations (Bakker and Schaars, 2019; Yang and Mccoy, 2023 ), we analyze this response to infer some essential information on hydrodynamic properties heterogeneity. Our method can be applied to any coastal site with an observation piezometer sensitive to both continental and marine stresses, and an identified lithological interface defining the heterogeneity location. Depending on the occurrence of surface-subsurface interactions, hydraulic properties can be identified using simplified 1D models or more complex spatialized 2D models. If the data does not allow to fully constrain hydraulic properties, a complementary calibration procedure can be performed using the seepage areas, assuming that they can be identified in the field. Conversely, if head data allows to identify hydraulic properties, seepage areas can be modelled using our method. This approach can have useful applications linked to surface-groundwater interactions in coastal contexts, such as groundwater flooding of low-lying areas or seawater intrusions.
1 Introduction Regional climate models (RCMs) are used routinely to generate high-resolution climate projections by dynamically downscaling global climate model (GCM) outputs. For instance, in Australia projections from the Conformal Cubic Atmospheric Model (CCAM) and the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) RCMs have been widely used in scientific impact assessments (Di Luca et al., 2018; Grose et al., 2019; Herold et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2016, 2020 ). In theory, the greater spatial and temporal resolution offered by RCMs should better represent thermodynamic and dynamical processes as radiative forcings change, offering additional information on future climate at the regional scale (Rummukainen, 2016 ). In practice, whether RCMs add value to GCM projections is controversial (Lloyd et al., 2020 ). Some studies, including over Australia, demonstrate clear benefits of RCM downscaling. Many of these focus on the ability of RCMs to improve spatial representation of mean quantities, which RCMs tend to do well (Di Virgilio et al., 2019; Evans et al., 2012; González-Rojí et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2014 ). Projecting trends is perhaps the most important function of RCMs (Li et al., 2018; Panda et al., 2013; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2020 ), yet verifying trends in RCMs tends to be much less common than verifying spatial correlations in the literature. In studies that do so, the benefits of RCMs are mixed. RCMs have been found to provide added information in projected climate change signals in high elevation areas and coastal regions in southeast Australia (Ciarlo et al., 2020; Di Virgilio et al., 2020; Grose et al., 2019 ). Ayugi et al. (2020)  appraised the performance of ten RCMs over East Africa and showed that the RCMs were able to moderately simulate some of the recent trends in precipitation and adequately simulate inter-annual and seasonal variations. Conversely, Racherla et al. (2012)  found that WRF did not reproduce observed historical trends over North America, concluding that “it is indeed hard to discern holistic improvement after dynamical downscaling” and that “RCM skill is strongly limited by the skill of the [forcing] GCM”. Similarly, Guo et al. (2018)  evaluated the Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX) RCMs in simulating temperature and precipitation over the Tibetan Plateau, and concluded that the RCMs fail to reproduce the observed spatial patterns of temperature and precipitation trends, and on average produce greater trends in temperature and smaller trends in precipitation than observations. Racherla et al. (2012)  found that the forcing GCM strongly influences RCM performance, giving some indication of the difficulty of assessing whether RCMs add value without introducing confounding errors. We aim to establish the benefit of the RCM without being penalized or rewarded by the performance of the forcing GCM. One approach to this is to use ‘ideal’ forcings, for example from more coarsely resolved reanalysis products (Gu and Wang, 2020; Teutschbein and Seibert, 2013 ). Reanalyses are strongly constrained by observations, so we assume that when reanalysis is used to force RCMs both the values and trends of individual forcing variables and inter-variable correlations are realistic. This isolates the performance of the RCM and allows us to measure performance against concrete observed trends, rather than speculating on how well RCMs might simulate future trends. It is also not a straightforward test for RCMs to pass: Teutschbein and Seibert (2013)  compared precipitation and temperature simulations from 15 different RCMs driven by ERA40 for five Swedish catchments, and found that for precipitation simulations even the ensemble median often deviated considerably from observations and was not able to capture the variability in the observations. However, a more recent study showed more promise for RCMs: Gu and Wang (2020)  noted that annual precipitation trends from ERA-Interim-forced RegCM4 simulations show a better agreement with the observations than the ERA-Interim reanalysis over the Tibetan Plateau. There have been other studies that investigated the performance of reanalysis data driven RCMs (Fantini et al., 2018; Moalafhi et al., 2017a; Moalafhi et al., 2017b ), but none of these assessed the RCM’s ability to reproduce trends. The lack of consensus on whether RCMs add value to GCM projections, especially in their ability to project trends, means that it is still necessary to assess this question 1) over the region of interest and 2) for the specific RCMs being used. In this study, we are concerned with southeast Australia, a region that includes a significant portion of the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia’s most economically significant agricultural region (Pittock and Finlayson, 2011 ). In the past several decades, rainfall has changed significantly in southeast Australia, with substantial rainfall declines in the cool season (April-October) (Liu et al., 2021; Murphy and Timbal, 2008 ). This decline has had far-reaching consequences for agricultural productivity, ecosystems, cultural uses of water, and water management in the basin (Prosser et al., 2021 ). Our study assesses the ability of RCMs to improve simulations of precipitation over southeast Australia. These RCMs will ultimately be used to generate projections of runoff, so we are concerned with trends in the mean state as well as trends in extreme values, which disproportionately influence runoff. We are particularly concerned with trends that have had significant impacts on agricultural production and water management: specifically the decline in cool season rainfall over southeast Australia. We also assess the ability of the RCMs to simulate the spatial patterns of means and variances. To make these assessments we use ERA-Interim to force WRF and CCAM, with two different configurations of each RCM. The use of multiple RCMs will allow us to make more general conclusions of RCM added value over southeast Australia. The outcomes of this research provide suggestions on where new research needs to be focused for the development of RCMs and implications for the next generation of Australian hydro-climate projections generated from CMIP6.  2 Study area and data Fig. 1   shows the coverage of the validation data (Australian Gridded Climate Data or AGCD – see Section 2.3 ) and modelling domains of the RCMs used in this study. The validation and comparison are carried out for the smallest overlapping domain (CCAM VCP-19), which encompasses Victoria, New South Wales and part of South Australia. It is surrounded by coastline in the east and south. The southern end of the Great Dividing Range, including Australia’s highest mountain – Mt Kosciuszko (2,228 m above sea level), is nestled in the southeast of the domain. The models are assessed only for grid cells over land. 2.1 RCMs RCM outputs were sourced opportunistically from existing projects. These runs have a common period of 1980 to 2013 (34 years), which serves as our evaluation period. All trends and other statistics were calculated for this period. Key characteristics of the RCMs, ERA-Interim and AGCD are summarized in Table 1  . 2.1.1 CCAM The Conformal Cubic Atmospheric Model (CCAM) is a global atmospheric model with a stretched grid (i.e., a variable resolution grid) that simulates a finer spatial scale over a study region. Hence when referring to the CCAM domain, we are describing the high-resolution region of the CCAM global grid. CCAM simulations have been found to perform well in simulating precipitation and temperature when assessed at the continental scale for Australia (Di Virgilio et al., 2019 ). The ERA-Interim-downscaled CCAM runs used in our comparison were both forced by sea-surface temperature (SST) and sea-ice concentration (Thatcher and McGregor, 2009 ). The two runs differ in both resolution and some aspects of the downscaling design. The Victorian Climate Projections 2019 (VCP-19) simulations where initially downscaled to 50 km resolution using bias-corrected SSTs and no atmospheric nudging (following an approach from Hoffmann et al., 2016 ), then a second downscaling was performed to reduce the resolution to ∼5 km VCP-19 (Clarke et al., 2019 ). The initial 5 km domain was over Victoria only; for this study we have expanded the domain to that shown in Fig. 1 , which necessitated interpolating the ∼5 km projections to ∼10 km. The bias-corrected SSTs are required for downscaling GCMs that contain significant biases (e.g., a cold bias in the Pacific ocean). Only changes in the SSTs predicted by ERA-Interim are passed to the CCAM simulation, where the SSTs are designed to preserve the observed climate during the historical time period. CCAM is then free to simulate other prognostic variables consistent with the corrected SSTs (e.g., air temperature, precipitation, etc), so that the bias-correction is consistent with CCAM’s physics parameterisations. In this way the VCP-19 CCAM simulations are only constrained to agree with ERA-Interim SSTs and are otherwise free to change atmospheric behaviour consistent with CCAM'’s dynamical and physics parameterisations. Conversely, the ESCI-12 CCAM runs (Electricity Sector Climate Information Project, 2021 ) use spectral nudging of air temperature, winds and surface pressure from ERA-Interim, as well as being forced by uncorrected SSTs directly from ERA-Interim. The ESCI-12 simulations are therefore more constrained to agree with ERA-Interim in terms of air temperature, upper-level winds and surface pressure at large length-scales than the VPC-19 simulations. The ESCI-12 simulations have a similar resolution of ∼12 km. These two runs also differ in their land surface scheme. The VCP-19 land surface scheme is from the Community Atmosphere–Biosphere Land Exchange (CABLE) model version 2.5 (Haverd et al., 2018 ). Finally, there are also differences in the version of CCAM used in the ESCI-12 and VCP-19 runs (version v1704 used for VCP-19 and version v1911 used for ESCI-12). The most relevant changes in CCAM from VCP-19 to ESCI-12 have been an update to the convection parameterization (i.e., adjustments to entrainment and detrainment rates) and improved aerosol emissions (i.e., improved simulated aerosol burden).  2.1.2 WRF The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations used in this study were obtained from the second generation of the NSW and Australian Regional Climate Modelling (NARCliM1.5) project (Nishant et al., 2021 ). Two configurations of WRF, designated WRF-R1 and WRF-R2, were used in NARCliM1.5. The two RCMs used two physics scheme combinations of the WRF V3.6 model (Skamarock and Klemp, 2008 ), which were selected from 36 physics scheme combinations based on model performance and independence of errors (Evans et al., 2013, 2012; Ji et al., 2014 ). They used the same planetary boundary layer, surface layer, cloud microphysics, shortwave/longwave radiation and land surface physics but different cumulus physics: Kain-Fritsch (KF) was used in WRF-R1 and Betts-Miller-Janiac (BMJ) was used in WRF-R2. As with CCAM, the WRF model’s resolution is too coarse to simulate convection. All WRF RCM simulations were carried out at ∼10 km resolution over southeast Australia. This high-resolution domain was nested within a ∼50 km resolution outer domain that covers the CORDEX Australasia region (Evans et al., 2020b ), which provided boundary conditions for the ∼ 10 km inner domain.   2.2 Forcing: ERA-Interim The RCMs were driven by the ERA-Interim reanalysis (Dee et al., 2011 ). ERA-Interim is a global atmospheric reanalysis at 0.75° horizontal resolution (∼80 km) produced by European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF). ERA-Interim was established as an upgrade over the ERA-40 reanalysis and offered improvements in the data assimilation of satellite data, which improved the representation of the hydrological cycle. ERA-Interim was, however, always viewed as a stepping-stone to a higher resolution reanalysis, which has now been released as ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). We relied on existing RCM simulations for this study, and none were available with ERA5 forcing. However, even if such runs were available, it is doubtful they would have been instructive for this study. This is because we are specifically interested in downscaling coarse resolution reanalysis to finer resolution with ERA5′s resolution (∼30 km) too close to that of the RCMs used in our study.  2.3 Observations: Australian Gridded climate data (AGCD) The Australian Gridded Climate Data (AGCD) (Evans et al., 2020a ) (previously known as the Australian Water Availability Project or AWAP) are used in this study as observations to validate the RCM simulated trend and interannual variability. Unlike reanalysis, AGCD interpolates only surface-level gauged observations, available from 1900 onwards, to produce daily and monthly time series. AGCD is thus independent of ERA-Interim, so serves as an objective test of both ERA-Interim and the RCMs. The rainfall characteristics used in this study were calculated from the daily time series, referred to as AGCD hereafter.   3 Method 3.1 Indices assessed We assessed RCMs on three key rainfall indices that are critical for runoff generation in southeast Australia (informed by Fu et al. (2021) ): annual rainfall, cool season rainfall and maximum 30-day rainfall. In addition, we evaluated a range of climate extreme indices based on daily precipitation as defined by the Expert Team on Sector-specific Climate Indices (ET-SCI; Alexander and Herold, 2015; Herold and Alexander, 2016 ). We used the ClimPACT version 2 software (https://climpact-sci.org/ ) to calculate the indices summarised in Table 2  . We calculated these at two spatial resolutions:1) At the resolution of AGCD (∼5 km), by regridding all RCMs and ERA-Interim to the AGCD grid;  2) At the resolution of ERA-Interim (∼80 km) by regridding all RCMs and AGCD to the ERA-Interim grid.    To resample the indices to AGCD resolution (downscaling), the “nearest neighbour” interpolation method was used. This method maintains the “blockiness” from the coarser resolutions, enabling us to discern if higher resolution RCMs outperform the lower resolution ERA-Interim solely due to their finer resolution. Higher spatial resolution is known to provide a better representation of topography, enhancing the simulation of orographic rainfall and coastal effects. The resampling to ERA-Interim resolution (upscaling) was performed on the daily time-series using “bilinear” interpolation. By assessing at the coarser resolution, the RCMs lose their finer resolution advantage, ensuring that any superiority of RCMs over ERA-Interim could be attributed to the added value of the RCMs themselves.  3.2 Statistical tests performed The statistics we have calculated on all the above indices were mean, trend and variance. The variance was calculated on the annual timeseries to represent inter-annual variability. To assess variance, we used the standard deviation of log-transformed variables:(1) s log  = σ log v             where σ    is the standard deviation and v    is the timeseries of a given index (i.e. annual rainfall, cool season rainfall or Rx30day) at each grid cell. The log transformation is effective at normalising the (skewed) distribution of rainfall variables (not shown for reasons of brevity), allowing easy comparison between grid cells. Normalising the data also allowed us to ignore bias in our comparison of variance. The rainfall indices we analysed have a negligible number of zero values in the evaluation period, so no special treatment of zero values was required in the log-transform. We estimated linear trends with Sen’s slope (Sen, 1968 ):(2) m = m e d i a n M          where M    comprises the slopes of all pairs of values in a time series x  = x 1  , x 2  , … , x T         :(3) M n  = x i  - x j   i - j     n = 1 , 2 , . . . , N         where x i     and x j     are the data values at times i    and j   , respectively, such that i > j   , and N = T T - 1    / 2    is the number of pairs. Sen’s slope is insensitive to outliers near the beginning or end of time series, and thus offers robust estimates of linear trends. In addition, we tested the statistical significance of these trends using the well-known Mann-Kendall test (Kendall, 1975; Mann, 1945; Zarei and Eslamian, 2016 ). The test used the statistic:(4) S MK   = ∑ i = 1  T - 1   ∑ j = i + 1  T  s g n x j  - x i          The null hypothesis was approximated by a normal distribution. We used a two-tailed test with a significance threshold of 20 % to denote a statistically significant trend.  3.3 Evaluation metrics applied To summarise the performance of RCMs, we compared simulated mean values, coefficients of variation and trends to observations with Pearson’s correlation coefficient (R) and root mean squared error (RMSE) calculated across all grid cells. R indicates the ability of a model to simulate general spatial patterns in the data, without considering bias; RMSE considers the ability of the model to simulate spatial patterns and magnitude (including bias). Here we standardized RMSE to bring it to the same data range as R (0–1)(5) RMSE  std   = 1 - RMSE - RMSE  min    RMSE  max        where RMS E min     and RMS E max     are the lowest and highest values, respectively, of RMSE from any of the model runs. Note that a value of RMS E std   = 1    does not indicate zero errors, but rather that the model achieved the lowest RMSE in relation to other model runs. A higher value of RMS E std      thus signifies better performance relative to other models runs. We were also interested in testing how significant and impactful trends in RCMs agree with observations. In southeast Australia, the most hydrologically relevant of these trends is the decline in cool season rainfall. When the RCM predicts a negative and statistically significant trend in cool season rainfall in a grid cell (we will call this an ‘event’), we can check this against any significant negative trend in observations at the same grid cells with a standard contingency table (Table 2 ). We then aggregated these across all grid cells using categorical verification scores. We used two scores: 1) the success ratio and 2) event bias. The success ratio and event bias are:(6) Success ratio =   S R = a a + b       (7) Event bias =   Δ = 1 - 1 - a + b  a + c           where all terms are defined in Table 3  . Both scores have a maximum (best) value of 1. The success ratio describes the number of hits given the number of predicted events, while the event bias calculates the difference in the number of events predicted and the number of events observed. The two measures should be assessed in tandem: it is possible to get a high success ratio even if the number of events is strongly underestimated; conversely, it is possible to perfectly predict the number of events (zero event bias), but not score a single hit (i.e. the events are predicted in the wrong locations). In neither of these cases should a model be considered to perform well. We were thus looking for scores closer to 1 for both event bias and  the success ratio.   4 Results 4.1 Spatial correlations in mean indices and coefficients of variation Fig. 2   summarises spatial correlations of ERA-Interim and the four RCMs at AGCD (∼5 km) resolution. For all three rainfall indices – annual rainfall, cool season rainfall and Rx30day – all models represent general spatial patterns well, with R > 0.9    for all RCMs and ERA-Interim. However, ERA-Interim is substantially more positively biased than the RCMs, tending to overestimate rainfall along the eastern coast. This results in substantially worse RMSE scores than all four RCMs for all rainfall indices. As noted in the introduction, RCMs are generally quite good at improving the spatial representation of mean quantities, and this is the case here: the higher spatial resolution of the RCMs offers better spatial representation of mean rainfall, including lower biases. Both CCAM models tend to perform similarly, and both outperform the two WRF models for these indices. The WRF models tended to overestimate all rainfall metrics over much of the north-eastern domain. This was particularly true of WRF-R1, which therefore tended to perform worse than WRF-R2 in RMSE. RCMs and ERA-Interim accurately represent the general spatial patterns of variance, as defined by s ln    , for all three indices with high correlations (R > 0.9   ) (Fig. 3  ). However, the RCMs tend to systematically underestimate s log     over much of the domain, leading to poorer RMSE scores for s ln     than ERA-Interim. We note that the models also generally tend to overestimate observed variance along the southern coast. The CCAM models again tend to outperform the WRF models for all indices. Indeed, for cool season rainfalls, CCAM performed nearly as well as ERA-Interim in RMSE of s log    . WRF-R1 tended to perform worse than WRF-R2 for s log    , especially in annual and cool season rainfall.  4.2 Spatial correlations of trends Observed trends in rainfall vary substantially in space and with index (Fig. 4  ). Trends in AGCD annual rainfall tend to be negative in the southern parts of the Great Dividing Range – evident as a slender red crescent in the southeast – and positive in the northern and western parts of the domain, particularly on the north-east coast. As noted, observed cool season rainfall has declined in most areas in this domain. Rx30day rainfalls have generally tended to increase, except for small regions in the southern Great Dividing Range. Observed spatial patterns of trends (correlations) are not always well represented by either ERA-Interim or the RCMs. ERA-Interim performs at least as well as the RCMs in spatial correlations of trends. It does not replicate the spatial pattern of observed trends in Rx30day rainfalls well, though this is also true of the RCMs. Of the RCMs, CCAM ESCI-12 produces the highest spatial correlations. It is particularly notable that CCAM ESCI-12 outperforms CCAM VPC-19, particularly for correlations in annual rainfall trends and Rx30day trends. This can be explained by the improved land surface model in ESCI-12. RCMs offer lower RMSE values for all trends in rainfall indices than ERA-Interim. Lower RMSE in trends occurs both at AGCD resolution (∼5 km) and at the coarser ERA-Interim resolution (∼80 km). We illustrate the latter with trends in cool season rainfall in Fig. 5  , including measures of statistical significance. These show the wide area of statistically significant cool-season rainfall declines in AGCD observations. CCAM not only represents the magnitudes of these trends more accurately than ERA-Interim, it also improves the spatial representation of statistically significant trends, as shown in the signal detection statistics. While ERA-Interim and CCAM have similar success ratios (SR > 0.6   ), event bias (Δ   ) shows the tendency of ERA-Interim to over-estimate spatial range of significant rainfall declines compared to CCAM. Both WRF models improve RMSE of cool-season rainfall trends, particularly the WRF-R1 model. But there are substantial differences in the performance of the two WRF models in representing significant cool-season rainfall declines: WRF-R1 exhibits similar success ratios to ERA-Interim, but WRF-R2 has much lower success ratios. Both WRF models substantially underestimate the spatial extent of significant rainfall declines, leading to poor event bias. We present trends in other extreme indices measured in units of mm. Trends in indices measured in units of days are also included in the supplementary materials . In both Rx5day and Rx1day (Fig. 6  ), the areas of negative observed trends decrease compared to Rx30day, with a large proportion of the domain showing increases in Rx1day (supplementary materials ). Trends in Rx5day and Rx1day tend to be poorly spatially represented by all models, including ERA-Interim, with spatial correlations <0.3 for Rx5day and <0.2 for Rx1day. ERA-Interim gives higher spatial correlations than any of the RCMs, but poorer RMSE values than all RCMs. WRF-R2 and CCAM ESCI-12 were the best performed of the RCMs, and performed similarly to ERA-Interim at both the AGCD resolution (∼5 km) and ERA-Interim resolution (∼80 km; see supplementary materials ), while CCAM VCP-19 performed markedly more poorly than ERA-Interim. The more extreme the rainfall percentile (R90p, R95p, R99p), the more likely observed trends would be positive, with R99p trends largely positive over the domain (Fig. 7  ). Similarly for the Rx indices, ERA-Interim offered the highest spatial correlations with observed trends, but the lowest RMSE. All models (including ERA-Interim) gave low correlations for R99p (<0.2). This is similar to the poor simulation of trends in Rx1day (and R10mm, R20mm, CDD and CWD, see supplementary material ). For very extreme rainfall indices like these R99p and Rx1day, the poor performance may be because the models are not capable of actively simulating convection. Interestingly, WRF-R1 tended to simulate trends in R90p and R95p (Fig. 8  ) indices better than other RCMs, with CCAM ESCI-12 also offering good simulations. ERA-Interim tended to dramatically overstate the instances of statistically significant negative trends in R90p and R95p compared to observations. For trends in the other extreme indices (see supplementary materials ), ERA-interim generally showed stronger spatial correlations with AGCD trends than the RCMs but performed much poorer at matching the magnitude of trends (as represented by RMSE, Table S1  in supplementary materials ). Trend spatial correlations can sometimes be misleading for these indices because ERA-interim tends to overestimate negative trends in most extreme indices, and substantially overestimates the number of statistically significant negative trends in most indices, especially RX1Day, R90p and R99p. The overall ability of RCMs to match these indices is also somewhat mixed and not clearly superior to ERA-interim. However, it is important to note that these indices are of secondary importance in this study, which focuses on trends in runoff-generating indices such as Rx30day, mean annual rainfall, and especially mean cool-season rainfall.   5 Discussion 5.1 Differences in model performance We summarise RCM performance by categorizing RCMs as ‘outperforming’, ‘performing similarly to’ or ‘underperforming’ ERA-Interim in Table 4  . The categories are qualitative and the categorization, whilst based upon our quantitative results, is somewhat subjective. The RCMs consistently outperform ERA-Interim in the spatial representation of the means of all three rainfall indices. This result is expected because improvements in the spatial representation of topography improve the spatial representation of rainfall averages and Rx30day. Conversely, we found that the RCMs were not able to represent variance as well as ERA-Interim, tending to underestimate observed variance of all rainfall indices. The exceptions were the two CCAM models for cool season rainfall, where they offered similar performance to ERA-Interim. It is possible to correct variance (Berg et al., 2012 ) under the assumption that the RCMs represent underlying changes to variance adequately. This assumption is difficult to test as it would require a much longer time series than the 34 years considered here. In general, trends can be well represented by the RCMs, though there are differences between variables and between RCMs. The CCAM ESCI-12 outperforms or performs similarly to ERA-Interim for all variables, notably outperforming CCAM VCP-19 in the representation of trends in annual rainfall, all Rx indices and the R95p index. This is likely because CCAM ESCI-12 is nudged by the ERA-Interim atmospheric variables while CCAM VPC-19 is not. This forces CCAM ESCI-12 to more closely agree with ERA-Interim’s atmosphere than CCAM VCP-19, allowing it to better represent trends in rainfall. WRF-R1 generally outperformed WRF-R2. Overall WRF-R1 represents trends in annual rainfall and RX30day as well as or better than ERA-Interim, and performs similarly in representing cool season rainfall (e.g. RMSE, success ratios), even though it underestimates the spatial extent of significant cool season rainfall declines. WRF-R1 also performs similarly to ERA-Interim in representing Rx5day, R90p and R95p trends. WRF-R2 performs worse than ERA-Interim in representing trends in annual and cool season rainfall, notably underestimating the spatial extent and significance of the crucial cool season rainfall decline. This highlights the strong influence convection parameterization can have on rainfall trends. As already noted in the introduction, we gave special weight to the cool season as it has had substantial impacts on water management in the region. The ability of CCAM to generally outperform WRF in both the representation of variance and trend in cool season rainfall is not straightforward to explain. Subtle differences in parameterizations and the design of the downscaling experiment are all likely to be contributing factors (i.e., stretched grid compared to limited area). Changes to CCAM in upgrading the CABLE land-surface, improved aerosol emissions that reduced the aerosol burden to more realistic levels and changes to the convective parameterization (i.e., adjustments to the rates of entrainment and detrainment) could all have contributed to general improvements in CCAM performance compared to previous versions of CCAM used (i.e., CCAM v1704 compared to v1911). CCAM’s CABLE may be particularly important, as the Unified Noah land surface model used in WRF is known to overestimate soil moisture in the top soil layer, leading to underestimation of surface temperatures and a tendency to overestimate rainfall (Yang et al., 2011 ). A conclusive result will require a more systematic study to isolate the relative benefits of these changes, relative to changes in convection and aerosols.  5.2 Study limitations We have assumed the statistically significant cool season rainfall decline in southeast Australia for the period 1980–2013 is emblematic of the kind of responses Reanalysis-forced RCMs should reproduce. We note, however, that the degree to which this decline is a result of natural variability or a result of human-induced changes to radiative forcing is not clear (Rauniyar and Power, 2020 ). This is a constraint to earth-system modelling validation generally: it is very difficult to produce controlled experiments that isolate only the response of local climate to changes in external forcings. In this study we have sought to isolate the performance of RCMs, and therefore ignored interactions between GCMs and RCMs. For example, biases in GCM forcing variables, or unrealistic correlations between forcing variables, may have substantial deleterious impacts on the ability of RCMs to represent significant rainfall trends. It is difficult to generalize about the effects of such plausible although difficult to identify interactions; they are likely to vary for each combination of GCM and RCM. Nonetheless, we recommend that the effects of these interactions be explored in future research. As canvassed in the introduction, studies assessing the value of RCMs can vary substantially with region, RCM and variable. We therefore caution against generalising our findings to other RCMs or regions (even within Australia), or to other variables.   6 Recommendations A primary aim of this study was to provide suggestions on where new research should be focused for the development of RCMs over southeast Australia for use in hydroclimate projections. The analyses here show that RCMs do add value in simulating rainfall for this region, notably in the representation of mean values and trends of key rainfall indices that drive runoff generation. Accordingly, we recommend that studies projecting future hydroclimate variables in this region can benefit from the use of RCMs. This could include, e.g., using trends simulated by RCMs along with delta-change/scaling methods, bias-correction methods, or stochastic generators to force downstream (e.g., hydrological) models. The RCM simulations under historical and future conditions are of course dependent on, and limited by, the boundary conditions provided by the GCMs. From our comparison between CCAM and WRF, it is likely that the updated CABLE land-surface model in CCAM has been an important factor in CCAM’s overall enhanced performance. The improvements to the simulated aerosols in CCAM and the associated changes in direct and indirect feedbacks on radiation and precipitation could have also made some contribution to the improved simulation results. These aspects of the RCM development deserve more attention in the future. In particular, a systematic study of the impact of changes into the land-surface, convection and aerosol indirect feedback on cloud microphysics is required to isolate the most important contributors to these changes (e.g., between CCAM VCP-19 and ESCI-12). The atmospheric nudging used for CCAM ESCI-12 also seems to be beneficial, as demonstrated by CCAM ESCI-12 outperforming CCAM VCP-19. However, atmospheric nudging is likely to require biases to be removed from forcing data, as noted by Moalafhi et al. (2017a,b)  and Wamahiu et al. (2020) . In addition, because atmospheric nudging ties CCAM more closely to the forcing data, nudging may make CCAM more prone to underlying problems in GCM forcing variables, for example unrealistic inter-variable correlations, which are more difficult to correct than univariate biases. WRF-R1 outperformed WRF-R2, with the only difference between the two being their cumulus physics. This emphasizes the importance of the parameterization of convection. Indeed, one of the main reasons for RCMs to underestimate variance would be underpredicting extreme events, which need to be addressed by better parameterization of convection or resort to finer resolution, convection permit models. The long-standing ‘drizzle effect’ may be another reason why RCMs underestimate variance, which is generally dealt with by post-processing such as ‘dry-day correction’ (Berg et al., 2012 ). We suggest that future RCM development seek to improve both tails of the rainfall distribution as one of the priorities. The systematic underestimation of variance in rainfall indices in the RCMs, even with ‘ideal’ forcings, indicates that some form of variance inflation may be needed if projections are used to force hydrological models. It is possible to apply static variance corrections (e.g. Berg et al., 2012; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020; O’Reilly et al., 2020; Rocheta et al., 2017 ), while preserving trends (Hempel et al., 2013 ). This is particularly so if the projections are used to force downstream models (e.g., hydrological models) that require such realistic statistical properties in their inputs. We therefore recommend that any bias-correction scheme that may be applied also explicitly correct for variance. We see from the range of trends shown in the different RCMs, even when forced with the same ‘observed’ forcings, that uncertainties in RCMs are substantial. For this reason, we recommend assessing a range of RCMs for future downscaling studies projecting changes to hydroclimatic variables. Further, we note that the two CCAM models are closer to each other in performance than the WRF models, indicating that a greater range of uncertainties is sampled by considering different RCMs than different configurations of a single RCM. For this reason, if computational budgets do not extend to running multiple versions of multiple RCMs, we recommend the use of different RCMs rather than the use of a single RCM with multiple configurations. We recommend using a range of RCMs despite the CCAM ESCI-12 model performing better than the other RCMs used in this study. We have seen that relatively minor changes in model physics (e.g. WRF-R1 vs. WRF-R2) can lead to large changes in the simulated trends. RCMs undergo constant development, so it is likely that the versions of CCAM and WRF used in future projections studies will differ from the model versions used in this study. It is thus important to understand the drivers of uncertainty inherent in these models. Some of the key sources of uncertainty in RCMs include: model physics, boundary conditions, initial conditions, parameterization schemes, emission scenarios. However, it is likely that the largest amount of uncertainty could still be sourced from the driving GCM (Maslin & Austin, 2012; Teng et al., 2012 ).  7 Concluding remarks This study investigated if RCMs add value in reproducing means, variances, and trends in three rainfall indices that are important for runoff generation over southeast Australia. We found that RCMs were valuable in improving mean values and can be beneficial in producing trends (esp. CCAM), but systematically underestimated inter-annual variability. Whilst the ability to reproduce historical observations is no guarantee for extrapolation into the future, there is good reason to have more confidence in the projections of rainfall indices where the Reanalysis-driven models can reasonably reproduce historical trends. Based on these findings, we suggest that future RCM development focus on improving both tails of the rainfall distribution. It would be advantageous to use the change signals from the RCMs that performed better in producing trends (such as CCAM in this study) in top-down hydrological impact studies. Variance-correction and a multi-RCM approach should be considered when using these RCMs to inform changes in rainfall inputs to produce future runoff projections. Although these conclusions may not be directly transferable to the use of RCMs in other regions, given the model- and domain-specific nature of RCM simulations, the methodology applied in this study could benefit climate impact studies worldwide. Reanalysis-driven RCM simulations can help build confidence in the model, and the statistical tests and evaluation metrics used in this study can offer valuable insights for enhancing RCM performance in different regions globally.
1 Introduction Despite its simplicity, the Green-Ampt model (GAM) is a widely used infiltration model that does not require tediously measured soil characteristic curves. The GAM has been adopted in hydrological models, such as SWAT, HEC-HMS, and WEPP (Gassman et al., 2007; Dun et al., 2009; Zema et al., 2017 ), and has been applied in irrigation system management (Kale & Sahoo, 2011 ). Similar to other infiltration models, the GAM is used to characterize soil hydraulic properties (Mohammadzadeh-Habili & Heidarpour, 2011; Angulo-Jaramillo et al., 2016 ). The classical GAM assumes a sharp wetting front with a constant effective suction head, which can be determined from water retention curves (Ogden & Saghafian, 1997 ). However, the capillary pressure–saturation relationship (i.e., the water retention curve) changes with the saturation rate (Hassanizadeh & Gray, 1993; Manthey et al., 2005 ). A linear approximation proposed by Hassanizadeh & Gray, 1993 , expresses the dynamic capillary pressure (P c  d y n    ) as a function of the saturation rate (∂ S / ∂ t   ) as follows:(1) P c  d y n   - P c  e q   = - τ d  ∂ S  ∂ t       where P c  e q     is the capillary pressure at equilibrium and τ d    is the damping or relaxation coefficient. During the infiltration process, a high infiltration rate or fast-moving wetting front should result in a fast saturation rate, and therefore lead to a suction head that is smaller than the static suction head. The dynamic capillary pressure or dynamic effective suction head in the GAM is velocity-dependent and varies during infiltration (Weitz et al., 1987; Geiger & Durnford, 2000; Siebold et al., 2000; Hilpert, 2012; Baver et al., 2014 ). Using column experiments, Weitz et al. (1987)  found that the dynamic capillary pressure was proportional to - α  C a  β    , where α   and β   are fitted constants, and Ca is the capillary number. According to Weitz et al., β = 0.5 ± 0.1   . With the power-law relationship, Annaka and Hanayama (2005)  obtained β = 0.3    for 400 μ m    glass bead sand and β = 0.79    for 30/50 sea sand. Since the effective suction head is a function of the contact angle and the geometry of the pore space, one potential origin of the dynamic suction head (DSH) can be attributed to the dynamic contact angle (DCA, ϑ d   ), a velocity-dependent apparent contact angle. DCA can be expressed as a function of Ca. Various expressions have been used to describe the relationship between ϑ d    and Ca (Hoffman, 1975 ;1983; Cox, 1986; Seebergh & Berg, 1992; Wallach et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2018 ). Based on “molecular kinetic theory,” Hoffman (1983)  derived Eq. (1979)  are suitable for Hoffman’s experimental data. Hsu and Hilpert (2011)  extended the concept of the pore-scale effective DCA by parameterizing the velocity-dependent DSH using the “power-law” and modifying the classical GAM by incorporating the DSH into the classic GAM. The modified GAM (MGAM) improves the description of the upward and downward wetting processes (Hsu & Hilpert, 2011; Pellichero et al., 2012; Hsu et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2018 ), especially during the early transient stage (Hsu et al., 2017 ). Huang et al. (2023)  showed that by prescribing β = 1   , the MGAM fit experimental data well; however, the prescribed values changed the optimization of other parameters. Zhang et al. (2019)  applied a similar MGAM with a modification in the water content distribution and obtained simulations that were consistent with their experiments. Wang and Wallach (2021)  modified the MGAM based on Hsu and Hilpert (2011)  by including time-dependent contact angles, and provided simulation results close to the experimental results using subcritical water-repellent soils. The suction head in the GAM can be modified using different DCA expressions as described by Hsu and Hilpert (2011) ; nonetheless, few studies have been performed to compare different parameterizations and determine the most suitable or convenient expression for parameter fitting and simulation. The fitting parameters rely on infiltration experiments; however, the influence of experimental data, such as data length and inaccuracies in recoding timing, which may alter the fitting value of parameters, has not been widely explored. Additionally, previous studies (Huang et al., 2023; Pellichero et al., 2012; Hsu and Hilpert, 2011 ) often explained the dynamic suction head in the GAM based on the dynamic capillary pressure–saturation relationship, although none compared the dynamic effects of the capillary pressure–saturation relationship and dynamic suction head. In this study, we constructed DSH formulas based on the abovementioned DCA formulas, including the power law, Jiang’s law, Hoffman’s law, and Cox-Voinov law. Additionally, we applied a linear expression based on the power-law with β = 1   . The MGAMs based on these five expressions were named MGAM-PW, MGAM-Jiang, MGAM-Hoff, MGAM-CV, and MGAM-LN. To validate and evaluate the performance of these formulas, we performed a series of 1-D downward infiltration experiments with three types of sands and fitted the simulations from the MGAMs to the experiments. The dynamic effects between the sand columns were compared based on the fitted values of the parameters. The influences of data length and shifts in recoding time on estimated suction head are also discussed. Moreover, based on the experimental and analyzed results, the relationship between the dynamic capillary and saturation rate during downward infiltration is discussed.  2 Methodology 2.1 Infiltration data The infiltration data were obtained from Huang et al. (2023) . These experiments were conducted using sand columns consisting of glass cylinders measuring 60 cm in length, filled with B35, B60, and B150 glass sands (Table 1  ). The infiltration experiments were performed at constant ponding heads (h ( t )  = h 0    ) of 10 and 20 cm, whereas the bottom of the sand columns was open to air. For each combination of h 0    and sand column, at least three repeated experiments were performed. Fig. 1   shows the experimental infiltration depth, l f  ( t )    , determined by the weight loss (with a recording frequency of 1 Hz) of the water-supplying bottle. Table 1  lists the mean particle size D e f f    , porosities ∊  , water content change Δ θ   , and hydraulic conductivity K s   .  2.2 Theory 2.2.1 Green-Ampt model (GAM) The GAM, a 1-D infiltration model, describes a sharp wetting front that displaces air and saturates the porous medium with a constant ponding height h 0    (cm). The initial water content of the porous medium is θ i    (m  3  / m  3    ). The water content behind the sharp front is assumed to be saturated water content θ s    (m  3  / m  3    ) with a saturation hydraulic conductivity K s    (cm/s). For vertical downward infiltration at a constant ponding height h 0    (cm), the driving heads include the h 0   , suction head (h s  > 0    for the wetting phase), and potential head (l f   , cm). Based on Darcy’s law, the wetting front position l f    can be described by an ordinary differential equation expressed as(6) Δ θ  K s   d l f   dt   l f  = h 0  + l f  + h s      The water content change Δ θ    is θ s    minus θ i   . The effective suction head (h s    cm) is constant in classical GAM and velocity-dependent in MGAMs. When assuming a constant suction head, the suction head is usually considered to be the equilibrium suction head (h s 0    ), which is the maximum rising height in the vertical upward infiltration. As mentioned in the Introduction, h s    is not constant during infiltration experiments and depends on the saturation rate, time-dependent wettability, and velocity-dependent contact angle. In this study, we assumed that h s    is a function of the wetting front velocity, as demonstrated previously (Huang et al., 2023; Pellichero et al., 2012; Hsu and Hilpert, 2011 ), and approaches h s 0     when the infiltration rate is low (Huang et al., 2023 ). For the convenience of drawing an analogy between DSH and DCA, we non-dimensionalize Eq. (6)  using the scaling parameters L 0    (cm) and t 0    (s), which are determined by(7) L 0  = 2 γ  ρ w  g R 0        and(8) t 0  = Δ θ L 0   K s       In Eq. (7) , γ   is the interfacial tension; and ρ w    is the water density. The effective pore radius, R 0    is determined by Eq. (9)  as proposed by Glover and Walker (2009) .(9) R 0  = D e f f   2 a m  2   8 ∊  2 m            where the effective particle size D e f f     applied in this study was the mean partical size (μ m   ). The applied values of a   and m   were 8 / 3    and 1.5, respectively, which are recommended for spherical particles (Glover & Walker, 2009 ). Letting ζ = l f  / L 0    , τ = t / t 0    , ψ s  = h s  / L 0    , and ψ = h 0  / L 0    , the nondimensionalized Eq. (6)  can be expressed as(10) ζ ̇  ζ = ψ + ζ + ψ s      For the classical GAM, ψ s    is replaced by the the dimensionless effective equilibrium suction head (ψ s 0   = h s 0   / L 0    ) which is independent of the infiltration rate. In MGAMs, ψ s    is paramterized by different expressions based on the DCA formulas.  2.2.2 Dynamic suction head (DSH) formulas Hsu and Hilpert (2011)  expressed h s    as follows:(11) h s  = γ ρ g D   E ∊ , θ i    cos ϑ     h s    depends on the effective contact angle (ϑ  ), porosity (∊  ), grain size (D), and initial water content (θ i   ). The non-dimensional function E ∊ , θ i       represents the effect of ∊   and θ i    on the suction head. The term γ ρ g D   E ∊ , θ i       represents the capillary length with zero contact angle and is a constant during infiltration. Applying a straight capillary tube model and zero θ i   , γ ρ g D   E ∊ , θ i       is only related to the tube radius, which represents the effective pore radius of porous media, and is equal to L 0   . Therefore, we replaced γ ρ g D   E ∊ , θ i       with L 0    because θ i    was zero. The h s    value is proportional to cos ϑ   . The evolution of ψ s    along C a    is similar to that of cos ϑ d     along C a   . Hence, we postulated that the expression of ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     can be constructed based on DAC formulas by replacing cos ϑ d    , cos ϑ s    , and Ca    with ψ s   , ψ s 0    , and C a 0  ζ ̇    , respectively. Here, DSH formulas were constructed based on the four DCA formulas (power-law, Jiang’s law, Hoffman’s law, and Cox-Voinov law) listed in Table 2   and the linear velocity-dependent suction head (LN). (10)  (i.e., simulated ζ ( τ )   ) to the experimental one by applying the “nlinfit” function in MATLAB. The performance of each infiltration simulation was quantified using the root-mean-square error (RMSE).(18) R M S E = ∑ i = 1  N  O i  - P i     2   N       where, N   is the number of pairs of observed (O i   ) and simulated (P i   ) values.    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Experimental effective suction head from Green Amp analysis By rearrange Eq. (10) , we have(19) ψ s  = ζ ̇  ζ - ζ - ψ     With Eq. (19) , ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     can be calculated from the experimental data, although the noises in l f  ( t )     resulted in a scattered ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     as shown in Fig. 2  a-c. Nevertheless, the experimental ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     from Eq. (19)  clearly changed during infiltration. During infiltration, ζ   increases and ζ ̇    decreases. Meanwhile, ψ s    increases. Despite different h 0    experiments, the ψ s    value tended to approach a certain value about 0.3 ∼ 0.4 as ζ ̇    approached 1 (Fig. 2 a-c), which has been discussed in Huang et al. (2023) . The experimental evolution of ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     is similar to the DCA. According to the DCA formula, the cosine of the DCA is small when the advancing rate of the fluid–fluid interface is high. A decrease in the advancing rate led to an increase in the cosine of the DCA. The DCA approached the equilibrium value when the moving rate approached zero. Fig. 2 (d) shows the ψ s  C a      from our experiments and Jiang’s law (black solid line). The black solid line is plotted with parameters (α = 4.96   , β = 0.702   ) suitable for Hoffman’s data (Hoffman, 1975 ) and cos ϑ s  = 0.3   . The solid black line shows a plateau region (x-axis on the log scale) when Ca is greater than 1. However, this plateau region does not exist in our experimental ψ s  C a     . The experiment result shows a plateau region of ψ s    at a small Ca that is similar to DCA. The curve of ψ s  C a      can be suitably described using the power-law model (Fig. 2 d). The Ca value in our experiment was less than 0.01, at which point the DCA could be described using a power-law model. However, the effective suction head in our experiments was more sensitive to the wetting front than that predicted by the DCA. Fig. 2 (d) shows that the ψ s  C a      from the infiltration experiments follow the red solid curve. The red solid curve’s α = 198    is considerably larger than 4.96, which is used for the black solid line. Moreover, despite using the same sand, the ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     curves were different at different H 0    (Fig. 2  a-c). The slope of ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     at h 0  = 20    cm was smaller than that at h 0  = 10    cm. Therefore, the dynamic effect of the effective suction head may not be solely caused by the DCA. Huang et al. (2023)  found that the parameters of the MGAM-PW can be empirically expressed as a function of ponding height.  3.2 Prescribed values of β   for MGAM-PW and MGAM-Jiang In the literature, β   is often prescribed as a constant rather than a fitting parameter. A previous study indicated that a suitable β   value is less than 1, of which 0.3 was often applied (Pellichero et al., 2012; Hsu et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2018; Wang & Wallach, 2021 ). However, Huang et al. (2023)  indicated β = 1    resulting in a reasonable optimized ψ s 0     from MGAM-PW. Therefore, the β   value was provided rather than a fitting parameter and needed further evaluation. We prescribed the same β   value for MGAM-PW and MGAM-Jiang because the power-law formula approach to Jiang’s law at small Ca applies the same β   and α   values. The fitting parameters α P W     and α J A     are used to quantify the effect of the DSH in MGAM-PW and MGAM-Jiang, respectively.
