To determine a suitable β   value for our experiments, six β   values (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, and 1) were considered and applied in the MGAM-PW simulation. The modeling performances with different β   values were quantified using RMSE and are shown in Fig. 3  . Fig. 3  shows the RMSE from the classical GAM simulations. All MGAM-PW simulations performed better than the classical GAM. The RMSE decreased rapidly when β   increased from 0.1 to 0.3. When β   was between 0.3 and 1, the decreases in RMSE were minimal. For the B150 and B60 sand column experiments, the smallest RMSE resulted from simulations with β = 1   , although the RMSEs were very close when β   was between 0.3 and 1. For the B35 sand column experiment, β = 0.7    resulted in the best simulation performance. A β   value of 0.7   , which is different from and less than 1, was prescribed for MGAM-PW and MGAM-Jiang in our study.  3.3 Model simulation performances and comparison Fig. 4   shows the RMSE of the simulations for the different MGAMs and the classical GAM. All MGAMs obtained RMSEs less than 0.15 cm, which were considerably smaller than the RMSE of the classical GAM performance (RMSE=1.47 cm). Despite using different expressions for ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )    , the decrease in RMSE showed improvement when additional parameters were introduced. For the B150 experiments at h 0  = 10    cm, the smallest RMSE was obtained using MGAM-LN, whereas the largest RMSE was obtained using MGAM-CV. At h 0  = 20    cm, MGAM-Hoff resulted in the smallest RMSE, whereas MGAM-PW resulted in the largest RMSE (Fig. 4 a). For all of the B150 experiments, MGAM-Hoff resulted in the smallest RMSE (0.13 cm), whereas MGAM-Jiang resulted in the largest (0.14 cm) RMSE. For the B60 experiments at h 0  = 10    cm, the smallest RMSE was obtained using MGAM-Jiang, whereas the largest was obtained using MGAM-CV. At h 0  = 20    cm, MGAM-LN resulted in the smallest RMSE, whereas MGAM-Jiang resulted in the largest RMSE (Fig. 4 a). For all the B60 experiments, MGAM-LN resulted in the smallest RMSE (0.14 cm), whereas MGAM-CV resulted in the largest RMSE (0.15 cm). For the B35 experiments at h 0  = 10    and 20 cm, the smallest RMSE was obtained using MGAM-PW, whereas the largest was obtained using MGAM-CV (Fig. 4 a). Consequently, for all the B35 experiments, MGAM-PW resulted in the smallest RMSE (0.16 cm), whereas MGAM-CV resulted in the largest RMSE (0.22 cm). Fig. 4 b shows the RMSE calculated from all the experiments. Overall, MGAM-Hoff performed slightly better than the other MGAMs, with an RMSE of 0.14 cm. MGAM-CV resulted in the largest RMSE (0.15 cm). As shown in Fig. 4 a, the best MGAM changed under different experimental conditions; however, the RMSE of the MGAMs exhibited only a slight difference. The small difference indicates that despite applying different perameterizations of the DSH, those expressions can describe the ψ s  ( ζ ̇  )     during downward infiltration. Additionally, it is notable that MGAM-LN resulted in a small RMSE, which implies the applicability of the analytical solution of MGAM-LN (Eq. (14) ). Eq. (14)  is an implicit function that can be solved efficiently and quantitatively to demonstrate the curve of infiltration depth and time (Huang et al., 2023 ).  3.4 Fitting parameters of MGAMs The optimized values of the MGAM parameters are listed in Table 4  . Among the fitting parameters, ψ s 0     and ϑ s    are related to the equilibrium suction head. In all MGAMs except for in MGAM-CV, ψ s 0     represents the dimensionless suction head as the wetting front velocity approaches 0. In MGAM-CV, this equilibrium suction head is represented by cos ϑ s    . The parameter ψ s 0     and cos ϑ s     indicate the same physical interpretation as the dimensionless equilibrium suction head. The equilibrium suction head determined the maximum height increase in the vertical capillary-raising experiment. Other parameters (α P W    , α LN    ,  α JA     ,  α HF     , k  , and α CV    ) indicate the sensitivity of the DSH to the advancing rate of the infiltration wetting front. The fitted ψ s 0     values from the MGAMs and classical GAM are compared in Fig. 5  . The classical GAM assumes a constant suction head equaling the static suction head. Because of this assumption, the estimated ψ s 0     from the classical GAM should be notably different from that of MGAMs, each of which includes an additional parameter representing the dimensionless suction head at an extremely slow infiltration rate. The MGAMs resulted in similar optimal values of ψ s 0    , which were larger than those obtained using the classical GAM. As shown in Fig. 5 , for the B150 sand column experiments, MGAMs result in ψ s 0     of approximately 0.45, whereas the classical GAM results in a smaller ψ s 0     of approximately 0.2. For the B60 sand column experiments, MGAMs result in ψ s 0     of approximately 0.33, whereas the classical GAM results in a smaller ψ s 0     of approximately 0.13. For the B35 sand column experiments, MGAMs result in ψ s 0     of approximately 0.77, whereas the classical GAM results in a smaller ψ s 0     of approximately 0.14. We examined the difference between ψ s 0     from different GAMs using one-way ANOVA. The probabilities of the null hypothesis (no difference between t h e  ψ s 0       from different GAMs) being true were 19 %, 6 %, and 0 % for B150, B60, and B35, respectively. When hypothesis testing was conducted using ψ s 0     from MGAMs (without classical GAM), the probabilities increased dramatically to 91 %, 87 %, and 40 % for B150, B60, and B35, respectively. Statistical testing showed that the estimation of ψ s 0     was considerably changed by considering the effect of the DSH. In this study, there were no fitted ψ s 0     and experimental ψ s    values outside the ideal range of −1 and 1. The value of ψ s    is affected by the application of L 0   . Using the L 0    value may cause ψ s    to fall outside of the ideal range. In this study, the L 0    value was determined using the mean particle size, with the assumption that the sand particles were spherical. Therefore, instead of constraining the range of ψ s    and ψ s 0    , a free ψ s    and ψ s 0     range that is appropriate for the simulation and fitting process is used. The expressions of ψ s    and ψ s 0     in MGAM-PW, MGAM-LN, MGAM-Jiang, and MGAM-Hoff are not bounded by any lower or upper limit, whereas the MGAM-CV limits ψ s    ranged from −1 to 1 inclusive. If a large effective pore size is used, the optimal ϑ s    may be bound by ψ s  < 1   , resulting in an underestimated equilibrium suction head. Careful determination of the effective pore size, or a further approach to determine the effective pore size, is required for MGAM-CV. The parameters β  , α P W    , α LN    ,  α JA     ,  α HF     , k  , and α CV     play a similar role that indicates the sensitivity of ψ s    to ζ ̇   . MGAM-LN and MGAM-CV require only one parameter to describe this sensitivity. MGAM-PW, MGAM-Jiang, and MGAM-Hoff use two parameters to describe this sensitivity. For MGAM-PW, the β   value could be prescribed using a value within 0.3 to 1 (Fig. 3 ). The same β   value could be used in MGAM-Jiang and remarkably improve the simulation results. For MGAM-Hoff, there is no similar suggestion to prescribe α HF     or k   as a fixed value. According to the comparisons, all MGAMs were capable of describing downward infiltration. The estimates of the ψ s 0     values were similar among MGAMs. MGAM-CV limits the optimizing range of ψ s 0     (represented by cos ϑ s    ). MGAM-CV has two fitting parameters: α CV     and ϑ s   . Similarly, MGAM-LN has two fitting parameters: α LN     and ψ s 0    . In contrast, MGAM-Hoff, MGAM-PM, and MGAM-Jiang each have three fitting parameters. However, the β   values in MGAM-PM and MGAM-Jiang can be prescribed based on the results of previous studies. Therefore, MGAM-Hoff typically requires more fitting parameters than do the other methods. The number of fitting parameters was smallest in MGAM-LN and MGAM-CV, whereas MGAM-LN had an analytical solution. MGAM-LN is more convenient and efficient for model fitting than are the other MGAMs.  3.5 Influence of data length on optimalψ  s  0     Compared to the ψ s 0     based on the capillary raising experiments, the optimal ψ s 0     of MGAMs seems to be overestimated, especially for the B35 experiments. Compared to B150 and B60 sand columns, the B35 sand column has higher hydraulic conductivity, resulting in short data length and less data at the small ζ ̇   . Fig. 5  shows that the ψ s 0     values based on the capillary raising experiments were approximately 0.3–0.4, which were similar to the ψ s    at the later stage of infiltration (i.e., ζ ̇  → 1   ) shown in Fig. 2 a-c. These similarities indicated that the effective suction head approached the equilibrium suction head during infiltration. However, Figs. 2 and 5  imply that the length of infiltration data affects the optimal value of ψ s 0    , and the lack of infiltration at a later stage of infiltration might result in an overestimated ψ s 0     when using MGAMs. Fig. 6   shows examples of how the optimal ψ s 0     of MGAM-PW changes with the length of applied data. Each of the different-length data points represents an infiltration process from the beginning of the infiltration experiment to a certain time point. In other words, a shorter length indicates infiltration at an earlier stage. For B150 experiments with h 0  = 20    cm, when the data length increases, the optimized ψ s 0     value decreases and approaches a certain value (Fig. 6 a). Fig. 6 b and c demonstrate examples of the B35 and B60 experiments (both at h 0  = 10    cm). From Fig. 6 b and c, the fitting ψ s 0     does not always decrease with longer data lengths. Nevertheless, Fig. 6  shows that the length of the data influences optimization, and an optimization using only the data from the early stage of infiltration often overestimates the equilibrium suction head.  3.6 Influence of time delay of measurement on optimalψ s 0     A delay may have occurred during the experiment. The digital balance measuring rapid weight change might be affected by the sampling process of the apparatus, force balance, or damping effect, and therefore does not accurately or immediately reflect the true weight. In addition, the measurement time resolution was 1 Hz; therefore, there may have a delay of less than 1 s in the measurement. Taking the infiltration in the B35 sand column at h 0  = 10    cm as an example, Fig. 7   shows that the original experimental ζ τ      and experimental ζ τ      shifts left by 0.008 (denoted by ζ τ + 0.008     ). The shifting amount of 0.008 of τ   corresponded to 0.47 s (approximately a half of the recording period). The experimental ζ τ + 0.008      was closer to the GAM simulation than the experimental ζ τ     . Fig. 7  shows the MGAM-LN simulations with ψ s 0   = 0.67   , 0.3   , and 0.4 where α L N     values are the optimal values for the experimental ζ τ     . Although the three MGAM-LN simulations were similar when τ   was large, at the early stage of infiltration, a larger ψ s 0     resulted in a larger τ   at the same ζ  . Conversely, a measurement of infiltration with a time lag could result in an optimal ψ s 0     higher than that for a measurement without any time lag or time shifting.  3.7 Comparisons between dynamic effect of the capillary pressure–saturation relationship and DSH Previous studies (Manthey et al., 2005; Das & Mirzaei, 2012; Li et al., 2018 ) on dynamic capillary pressure–saturation found that τ d    is not a constant. Instead, τ d    is influenced by the domain scale, permeability, saturation, capillary force, fluid properties, and porous media properties. High saturation and high permeability usually result in a lower τ d   . A lower τ d    was obtained at a faster flow rate. τ d    increased as the domain size increased. Regarding the aspect of infiltration with a sharp wetting front, as assumed in GAM, we consider an adjacent small segment with a length Δ L    below the wetting front l f  ( t )     (Fig. 8  ). The saturation change rate (dS / d t   ) in Δ L    is dominated by the wetting front velocity (l f  ̇   ) when the wetting front passes through Δ L    from time t to t + Δ t   . During this period, the inflow of Δ L    is Δ θ l f  ̇    , and the outflow is 0. Because of the conservation of mass,(20) dS  dt   = Δ θ  ϕ  l f  ̇  Δ L       By substituting Eq. (20)  into Eq. (1) , the capillary pressure–saturation relationship for Green-Ampt infiltration is expressed as(21) P c  d y n   - P c  e q   = - τ d  Δ θ  ϕ  l f  ̇  Δ L       The length Δ L    may be taken as the spatial domain of the sensors (e.g., soil moisture meter) or the representative elementary volume. The capillary term P c  d y n   - P c  e q      can be determined by ψ s  - ψ s 0     , which is expressed as α P W   ψ s 0   + 1   ζ ̇   β     by Eq.(12); that is, the power-law model. Thus, the damping coefficient (τ d   ) considering the dynamic effect of suction head is expressed as(22) τ d  = ρ g L 0  ψ s 0   + 1   α ϕ Δ θ   η γ     β  Δ L l f  ̇   β - 1       Eq. (22)  indicates that τ d    is proportional to the domain size (Δ L   ), and is associated with the flow rate, texture of sand column (related to L 0    and α  ), and saturation (related to Δ θ   ). The α   (or α P W    ) value is positive. The β   value is positive and is usually less than 1. If β   is less than 1, an increase in the flow rate results in an increase in τ d   . A coarse-textured sample usually has a high permeability (or K s   ) and a small L 0   . Additionally, its α   is slightly small (Tsai et al., 2018 ). These properties imply that τ d    is small for the high K s    sand column. An increase in θ i    results in a decrease in α   (Hsu et al., 2017 ). Hsu et al. (2017)  found that the order of decrease in α   was larger than that in Δ θ   . Therefore τ d    should be small in the moisture sand column. The abovementioned properties of τ d    are consistent with the findings in previous studies (Manthey et al., 2005; Das & Mirzaei, 2012; Li et al., 2018 ). This shows the similarity between the dynamic effects of capillary pressure saturation and DSH.   4 Conclusions A series of vertical downward infiltration experiments at a constant ponding height demonstrated that the suction head changed during infiltration and approached the terminal value. The terminal value was close to the maximum capillary rising height, that is, the equilibrium suction head. The dynamic suction head in the experiment was more sensitive to the capillary number than to the dynamic contact angle. Five modified Green-Ampt models (MGAMs), namely MGAM-PW, MGAM-Jiang, MGAM-Hoff, MGAM-CV, and MGAM-LN, were constructed based on the formulas for the dynamic contact angle: power-law, Jiang’s law, Hoffman’s law, Cox-Voinov law, and a linear approximation, respectively. Our simulations showed that all modified Green-Ampt models could describe downward infiltration to a satisfactory degree. The modified Green-Ampt models resulted in a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of less than 0.15 cm in the all experiments, whereas the classical Green-Ampt Model resulted in an RMSE of approximately 1.47 cm. The modified Green-Ampt models exhibited similar fitted ψ s 0     values, indicating the non-dimensional equilibrium suction head. However, MGAM-CV has a limited ability to optimize ψ s 0    . Both MGAM-CV and MGAM-LN each have two fitting parameters. MGAM-Hoff, MGAM-PM, and MGAM-Jiang each have three fitting parameters. However, the values of parameter β in MGAM-PM and MGAM-Jiang can be prescribed based on results of previous studies. Therefore, MGAM-Hoff typically requires more fitting parameters than do the other methods. MGAM-LN had the smallest number of fitting parameters. MGAM-LN can be solved more efficiently than can other modified Green-Ampt models because of its analytical solution and smaller number of fitting parameters. The fitting ψ s 0     were close to the capillary rising result and non-dimensional suction head (ψ  ) with dimensionless infiltration rate (ζ ̇   ) approaching to 1 for the B150 and B60 glass sand experiments, whereas the modified Green-Ampt models overestimated ψ s 0     for the B35 glass sand experiment. We found that the data length influenced the optimal parameter values. A lack of infiltration at a later stage of infiltration can result in overestimation of ψ s 0    . This length effect may explain the overestimation of ψ s 0     in the B35 experiment. In addition, measurement delay can result in overestimation of the equilibrium suction head. We linked the dynamic capillary-saturation relationship and dynamic suction head based on the infiltration rate. The damping coefficient τ d    is proportional to the domain size and saturation rate. A decrease in permeability or initial water content resulted in an increase in the damping coefficient. The behavior of the capillary pressure–saturation relationship during the infiltration process indicated by the modified Green-Ampt models is similar to that reported in the literature.
1 Introduction As one of the primary threats to soil erosion and the decline of land fertility (Amundson et al., 2015; Ballabio et al., 2017; Panagos et al., 2016 ), the pervasive process of water erosion affects the physicochemical mechanisms of stabilized carbon in soils profoundly, resulting in the horizontal movement of soil carbon and dynamic changes in soil carbon storage (Bouchoms et al., 2017; Lal, 2005; Li et al., 2023; Van Oost et al., 2007 ). Thus, strengthening the understanding of soil erosion's potential effect on soil organic carbon (SOC) characteristics—mediated by the interconnected actions of soil particle separation, transport and deposition—is imperative for providing empirical data pertinent to the influence that erosion exerts on global carbon cycle for the scientific community, the details of which are subject to debate (Meyer et al., 1975). The concentrated flow along rills during rill erosion is the main reason for soil particles or aggregate migration. It is generally believed that the sorting of sediment in rill erosion does not exist or is not obvious, as well as with consideration of SOC (Schiettecatte et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2019 ). Raindrop impact is the major cause of the detachment and migration of soil aggregates during inter-rill erosion. The direct detachment transport of sediment by sheet flow can be neglected without raindrop impact (Kinnell, 2005; Wang et al., 2020; Zhang and Wang, 2017 ), leading to the sorting characteristic in the sediment of inter-rill erosion. Compared with coarser fractions such as soil aggregates and sand particles, finer soil fractions are transported greater distances and are the main medium for SOC redistribution (Martinez-Mena et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014 ). Therefore, elucidating the potential fate of SOC in inter-rill erosion in complex field environments is a prerequisite for a full understanding of the intricate function of soil erosion in the global carbon cycle (Maïga-Yaleu et al., 2015; Müller-Nedebock et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013 ). To date, researchers have extensively explored the dynamics of sediment separation and transport mechanisms during inter-rill erosion (Zhang et al., 2022, 2019, 2018 ; John. Zhang et al., 2020 ), as well as the selective loss characteristics of SOC with or without cover by vegetation (Jiang et al., 2019; Müller-Nedebock et al., 2016; Müller-Nedebock and Chaplot, 2015; Quijano et al., 2020; Simplício et al., 2021 ). However, these studies have predominantly focused on the influence of runoff, sediment and organic carbon loss, with little attention given to the fraction loss. In fact, vegetation can have a great impact on runoff and erosion reduction by direct mechanical protection of soil particles (Casermeiro et al., 2004; Duan et al., 2022; Li et al. 2022a, b; Liu et al., 2022, 2021; Ma et al., 2022; Zuazo et al., 2004 ), as well as indirectly improvement of physical–chemical properties in soils, along with flow hydraulic properties (Aranda and Oyonarte, 2005; Ding et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2020 ). By mitigating the erosive force of rainfall by diminishing the kinetic energy transferred by raindrops to soil surfaces, vegetation not only exerts a great impact on soil and water loss, but also can transform aggregates and soil particles, which are the primary transport carriers of SOC and its fractions during inter-rill erosion (Wang et al., 2021; Guy et al., 1987; Kinnell, 2005; Zhang and Wang, 2017 ). This has the potential to lead to disparities in the mechanisms of loss for different SOC fractions. This difference may have a lasting and profound effect on the carbon cycle in subsequent transportation and deposition (He et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023 ). Thus, research about vegetation on inter-rill erosion, sediment particle size distribution (PSD), and SOC loss, especially the study of SOC fractions, provides a vital perspective for global carbon cycle modeling. Since the implemented the “Grain for Green Project” (GGP) on the Loess Plateau in 1999, the local landscape has undergone significant changes, and the natural slopes covered by vegetation have increased rapidly (Fu et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2021 ). Concurrently, intensified erosion has been observed during the rainfall period (typically from July to September), coinciding with the peak growth season for vegetation (Fang et al., 2008; Li et al. 2022a, b ). The dynamic nature of vegetation coverage, which fluctuates with the varying growth stages of plants, presents a challenge: research fixated on static coverage values may not capture the full scope of erosion and SOC loss mitigation afforded by vegetation throughout the entire rainy season. Moreover, previous related research mainly focused on the reducing effect of vegetation on erosion and SOC loss, without further consideration of the variability and complexity of SOC fractions under the complex natural evolution process on the field, such as vegetated hill slope. Therefore, more long-term and detailed in-situ  monitoring studies are urgently needed to explore the influence of the dynamic change of vegetation coverage in such a complex erosion environment on SOC loss, especially from the fractions perspective. To address the aforementioned scientific challenges, the current study focuses on the characteristics of inter-rill erosion, sediment PSD, and the content and loss of SOC fractions. On-site monitoring data were gathered at micro-runoff plots with different vegetation coverage ranges that were set up for the study. The specific objectives were to (1) explore the variation of inter-rill erosion factors (runoff, sediment yield and concentration), PSD, as well as the content and loss of SOC fractions across different vegetation coverage ranges; (2) quantitatively assess relationships between varying levels of vegetation coverage and the corresponding changes in inter-rill erosion, sediment PSD, as well as SOC fraction loss; and (3) comprehensively analyze the causal links between rainfall characteristics, dynamic vegetation coverage, inter-rill erosion processes, sediment PSD, and SOC and its fractions loss. The insights garnered from this research will enhance the current understanding of the mechanisms of SOC loss on vegetated slopes during inter-rill erosion events, and provide foundational support for studying the underlying impacts of sheet erosion on the dynamic variation of SOC stocks and the broader carbon balance in natural environments.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Site description Field experiments were conducted in Ansai County, located in the northern Loess Plateau of China (109°19′23″E, 36°51′30″N). This region experiences a warm and semi-arid climate. The mean precipitation for years is 510 mm, most of which occurred between July to September, corresponding to the growth season of plants in this area (Li et al. 2022a, b ). The mean temperature is approximately 8.8℃, and the mean annual pan evaporation is between 1500 to 1800 mm. The area features a complex and diverse topography, sloping downward from northwest to southeast, and primarily characterized by herbaceous vegetation. Species prevalent in the region include Medicago sativa , Sorghum bicolor , and Agropyron cristatum  (Li et al. 2022a, b ). The dominant soil is Calcaric Cambisols  (sand ranges from 4.59 % to 8.53 %, silt ranges from 52.83 % to 55.69 %, and clay ranges from 8.23 % to 10.13 %, FAO), with bulk density = 1.2 ± 0.1 g cm−3  and SOC=2.99 g kg−1 .  2.2 Experimental design Four relatively uniform micro-runoff plots (1 m length × 0.6 m width) were set up at a representative slope adorned with local herbaceous vegetation, including species such as Artemisia capillaris Thunb., Sorghum bicolor, Cirsium arvense  var. integrifolium,  etc. The gradient of these plots was 15°to maintain uniformity. The size of the plots was determined based on the WEPP model and years of field monitoring data in the study site to ensure the type of soil erosion they exhibit is inter-rill erosion. To eliminate the influence of spatial variability, all plots were positioned on the same slope and placed adjacent to one another. Consequently, potential initial spatial variations induced by environmental factors were not accounted for in this study, such as slope location, altitude, and soil properties. The digital camera was used to capture the plot data at intervals, and the supervised classification method was used to extract vegetation cover information from the photos. The initial vegetation coverage levels of the four plots were set as 0 % (bare), 15 %, 25 % and 35 %. Vegetation and weeds in the bare plot were pulled up manually to ensure the surface remained bare during the whole study period. Care was taken to avoid damage to the topsoil. Due to the difficulty of controlling vegetation coverage, as a fixed value in the field environment, which may not reflect the comprehensive role of vegetation growth on inter-rill erosion, the vegetation coverage of plots was kept within a certain range manually (except for in the bare plot). After the rainy season, the vegetation coverage of the plots was measured as 35 %, 55 % and 70 %, respectively. Therefore, during the monitoring period, the vegetation coverage range of the four micro-runoff plots corresponded to 0 % (bare), 15 ∼ 35 %, 25 ∼ 55 % and 35 ∼ 70 %. Iron fences were installed as borders to prevent infiltration from outside sources and to minimize disturbances from human activities. Additionally, at the lower end of the plot, an iron stream path was constructed, connecting the plot to a tank designed for runoff and sediment collection. According to local rainfall data, which were provided by the Ansai Research Station of Soil and Water Conservation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, the capacity of the tank was determined to match the maximum runoff and sediment expected during individual rainfall events. Following each erosive event, the runoff and sediments were collected from individual plots and measured by weight. Yields of runoff and sediment were then calculated by dividing the weight by the respective plot area. Furthermore, the concentration of sediment was determined by sediment yield divided by runoff yield. The sediment samples collected from the tanks were placed for at least 24 h to facilitate particle deposition. Subsequently, the water was drained, and dried in an electric oven at 60 °C until the dry weight was constant. The dried samples were then sent to analyze the PSD and SOC fraction content. The field experiment period was from May 2019 to November 2020, with a total of 14 erosive rainfall events. During the monitoring period, a total of 56 samples, including sediment and runoff, were collected. Due to the limitation of the site, repeated plots were not set up in this experiment. The monitoring of repeated erosive rainfall events can diminish the deviation of the experiment, and ensure the reliability of the experimental data as much as possible. Before the micro-runoff plots were set, a surface soil sample was obtained using a soil auger (diameter = 2 cm). The sample was taken from a depth of 10 cm at a location corresponding to the midpoint of the plot. The sampling was done as carefully as possible to avoid damage to the growth of vegetation, ensuring an original soil sample was obtained to establish the background value for the plot. After sampling was complete, the holes were carefully filled with prepared original soil taken from a location near the plots.  2.3 Laboratory procedures Particle size analysis of both the sediment and surface soil samples was performed using a laser (Mastersizer 2000, Malvern Instruments, Malvern, UK). To accurately assess the PSD of both sediment and surface soil, reflecting their conditions and transport status during erosion, samples underwent different treatments. For the effective PSD, samples were screened by a 2-mm sieve and directly analyzed by laser diffraction without pretreatment. However, the ultimate PSD samples were treated with hydrogen peroxide to eliminate organic matter after sieved through a 2-mm sieve. Subsequently, they were chemically dispersed with sodium hexametaphosphate, and physically dispersed by agitate ultrasonically before analysis. SOC fractions in this study were categorized as particulate organic carbon (POC, 53 ∼ 2000 μm) and mineral-associated organic carbon (MOC, <53 μm), according to Cambardella and Elliott (1993) . Prior to measuring organic carbon content, the samples underwent treatment with hydrochloric acid to eliminate inorganic carbon, ensuring the accuracy of the determination results. Subsequently, the soil samples (about 20 g each, free from impurities) were treated with 100 ml of a 5 g/L sodium hexametaphosphate and shaken at a velocity of 90 revolutions per minute for 18 h by shaker, following the method described by Cambardella and Elliott (1993) . Afterward, the samples were sieved through a 53 μm sieve and washed with deionized water until clear. An elemental analyzer (Elementar Vario MACRO cube, Germany) was used to measure SOC concentration in the well-prepared samples. The SOC was assumed to be equal to the sum of POC and MOC.  2.4 Calculation of PSD parameter Soil and sediment were categorized as sand particles (d > 0.05 mm), silt particles (0.002 mm ≤ d ≤ 0.05 mm), or clay particles (d < 0.002 mm). The aggregation ratio (AR) was employed to assess the degree of particle aggregation. It is calculated by dividing the percentage of effective particles by the percentage of ultimate particles, expressed by the equation:(1) A R i  = E f f i  / U l t i      Where: ARi   represents the aggregation ratio in the i -th size class. Effi   represents effective particles in the i -th size class, %. Ulti   indicates ultimate particles in the i -th size class, %. Each size class was individually assessed. When the AR value is 1, it suggests the particle size is transported as primary particles during the erosion process, while AR≠1 suggests that the size class is in the form of aggregate during transportation (Weltzin et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The closer the AR value is to 1, the more likely it is for sediment to be transported as individual particles. Conversely, when the AR value deviates from 1, it indicates a tendency for the sediment to be transported as aggregates. The enrichment ratio (ER) is applied to measure the particle's selectivity. It is determined by calculating the ratio of effective particle percentage in the i -th size class in sediment to the percentage in undisturbed soil (it refers to the undisturbed surface soil collected before plots were set up). The formula for the enrichment ratio is as follows:(2) E R i  = S e d i  / S o i l i      Where: ERi   represents the enrichment ratio of the i -th size class. Sedi   represents the effective particle of the i -th size class in the sediment, %. Soili   represents the effective particle of the i -th size class in undisturbed soil, %. Each size class was individually assessed. ER values greater than 1 indicate that the particle size has a higher content in sediment, suggesting enrichment compared to the undisturbed soil. ER values less than 1 indicate a lower content in sediment, indicating deposition. When ER values are equal to 1, the particle size neither enriches nor deposits during inter-rill erosion (Martínez-Mena et al., 2002 ). Similarly, the calculation method of the ER in SOC fractions is consistent with the particle size.  2.5 Statistical analyses One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and independent samples t-tests were adopted to explore significant differences in study factors, such as runoff, sediment, particle content, and others, across various vegetation coverage in IBM SPSS software at a significance level of 0.05. In correlation analysis vegetation coverage levels were treated as categorical variables, using a non-parametric test method. To assess the causal effects of rainfall characteristics and vegetation coverage on inter-rill erosion, PSD, SOC fraction content, and loss, structural equation modeling (SEM) was applied by Amos 22.0. Figures were produced by Origin 2021. The reported value, in the absence of a special note, is the average of 14 erosive rainfall events over a two-year monitoring period.   3 Results 3.1 Variations of inter-rill erosion under different levels of vegetation coverage The higher the vegetation coverage in the plots, the less sediment, runoff and sediment concentration were collected for the same rainfall scenario (Fig. 1  a, c and e). It's also worth noting that sediment and runoff yield were comparatively higher in the early period of the rainy season (roughly from June to July), which corresponds to the early period of vegetation growth. Specifically, when averaged across all the rainfall event data (Fig. 1 b, d and f), the highest sediment yield was observed under the bare plot with a significant difference between the yield of the bare plot and the plots with vegetation coverage in the range of 35 ∼ 70 %, while no statistically significant was found for the runoff yield between all treatments. The correlation analysis result showed that, on the whole, vegetation coverage was correlated with sediment yield and sediment concentration significantly, with a correlation coefficient of −0.33 and −0.30, respectively, and most rainfall characteristics, especially parameters related to rainfall intensity, correlated with sediment yield and runoff yield significantly (Fig. 2  a). When partitioning the vegetation coverage into different ranges, sediment yield only correlated with I (mean rainfall intensity) when vegetation coverage was in the range of 25 ∼ 55 %, while runoff yield correlated with I30  and EI30  (Fig. 2 b ∼ e), indicating vegetation coverage played a regulatory role between rainfall and inter-rill erosion.  3.2 Variation of PSD in sediment under different levels of vegetation coverage For effective particles, the content of clay decreased with the increase of vegetation coverage, while the content of silt was relatively stable (Fig. 3  ). The lowest content of clay was observed under a vegetation coverage range of 35 ∼ 70 % (4.80 %), followed by 25 ∼ 55 % (6.07 %), bare (6.08 %) and 15 ∼ 35 % (6.50 %), with significant differences between 35 ∼ 70 % and other treatments, while the lowest content of silt and sand were was observed when the range was 25 ∼ 55 % (52.76 %) and 15 ∼ 35 % (38.70 %) without significant differences between all treatments. For ultimate particles, the content of clay, silt and sand all fluctuated with the increase of vegetation coverage, with the clay displaying similar trends to the silt, and the opposite tendency to the sand. The highest content of ultimate clay and silt were both observed under the vegetation coverage range of 25 ∼ 55 %, while the peak of ultimate sand was in the scenario of the range of 35 ∼ 70 %. No significant differences for all the ultimate particles between all vegetation coverage were found. For the aggregation ratio, although no significant difference was observed for all three particle sizes between treatments, the clay in all treatments was less than 1.0, and the silt in the bare plot and the treatment with a coverage range of 15 ∼ 35 % was close to 1.0, while the sand was all greater than 1.0, indicating silt and sand particles were aggregates during transportation process for high coverage conditions (25 ∼ 55 % and 35 ∼ 70 %) (Fig. 4  ). For enrichment ratio, the clay was mainly greater than 1.0 except for the coverage range of 35 ∼ 70 %, while the ratio was close to 1.0 for the slit and sand fraction when the vegetation coverage range was over 25 ∼ 55 %, indicating there was great enrichment for clay fraction for most conditions. On the whole, there was no significant correlation between vegetation coverage, effective particles and ultimate particles, while the effective particles in sediment were significantly correlated with most rainfall characteristics except for the rainfall duration (Fig. 5  a). Interestingly, the correlation between rainfall characteristics and sediment particles varied with different vegetation coverage scenarios (Fig. 5 b ∼ e). For example, the effective particle of silt was only correlated with EI30  when the plot was bare, then the correlation coefficient between the effective particle of silt and I30  increased with the increase of coverage range, indicating the increasingly important role of I30  in regulating PSD of sediment under increasing levels of vegetation coverage.  3.3 Variation of SOC under different vegetation coverage Overall, the content of SOC, which was synchronized to the change of MOC, decreased when the vegetation coverage changed from bare to the range of 25 ∼ 55 %, then increased slightly when the range was within 35 ∼ 70 %, while POC content showed the opposite trend with slight increase first and then decrease (Fig. 6  ). No markedly significant was found for the content of SOC, POC and MOC between all vegetation coverage circumstances. The SOC fractions loss showed an interesting pattern, that is, the loss of all fractions declined by different degrees under different vegetation coverage, with the highest loss under the bare condition and lowest under the vegetation coverage range within 35 ∼ 70 %. For the loss of SOC and MOC, significant differences were observed between vegetation coverage of bare and the range of 35 ∼ 70 %, while there was no significant difference in POC between different vegetation coverage situations. For the content and the loss, SOC fractions ratio under different vegetation coverage both showed a similar trend, with no significant difference between all treatments (Fig. 7  ). The ratio of POC to SOC first grew and then declined when the coverage increased, while the MOC content to SOC content showed the opposite trend, with the highest/lowest ratio found in the range of 15 ∼ 35 %. The ratio of MOC to POC was greater than 1.0 for all treatments, and it decreased and then increased sharply with the increase in coverage, indicating MOC was the essential fraction for SOC content and loss in inter-rill erosion sediment. For SOC, the average enrichment ratio was greater than 1.0 for the bare treatment and the vegetation coverage range of 35 ∼ 70 %, indicating SOC was depleted slightly for the coverage ranges of 15 ∼ 35 % and 25 ∼ 55 %, although there was no significant difference (Fig. 8  ). On the other hand, the enrichment ratio of POC showed the opposite trend, with slight enrichment for the coverage ranges of 15 ∼ 35 % and 25 ∼ 55 %. For MOC, enrichment was observed for all treatments, except for the range of 25 ∼ 55 %, indicating MOC on the plots was transported into the sediment in most situations. Overall, vegetation coverage was correlated with the loss of SOC and MOC markedly, and the intensity-related characteristics of rainfall correlated with SOC content and loss (Fig. 9  a). However, when partitioning vegetation coverage into different ranges, the loss of SOC fractions had different responses to rainfall characteristics (Fig. 9 b ∼ e). For example, the loss of MOC only correlated with rainfall characteristics when the vegetation coverage was in a relatively high range (25 ∼ 55 % and 35 ∼ 70 %), while POC showed no significant correlation for the vegetation coverage range of 35 ∼ 70 %.  3.4 The causality between rainfall characteristics, vegetation coverage, inter-rill erosion, PSD, and SOC fractions and their loss Fig. 10   illustrates the significant impact of rainfall characteristics and vegetation coverage on content and loss of SOC fractions in sediment through the adjustment in sediment PSD during the inter-rill erosion process. The structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis indicated a good fit of the data based on fitting indices (χ2 /df  = 0.55, GFI=0.51, and SRMR=0.50). The models showed that rainfall characteristics directly influenced inter-rill erosion, PSD, the content and loss of SOC with path coefficients of 0.41, 1.10, −0.01 and −0.47, respectively. Vegetation coverage affected inter-rill erosion, PSD, the content and loss of SOC directly with coefficients of −0.81, −0.07, −0.01 and 0.06, respectively. Compared to the content, the loss of SOC was more susceptible to other factors, and affected by inter-rill erosion and PSD directly, by vegetation coverage indirectly through the regulation of inter-rill erosion, and by rainfall characteristics both directly and indirectly through the regulation of inter-rill erosion and PSD.   4 Discussion 4.1 The dynamic effect of vegetation coverage on inter-rill erosion and PSD in sediment Sediment and runoff yield under the first few rainfalls in 2020 were higher than in 2019 in our study, when there was more rainfall precipitation, which may be due to the inter-annual difference in soil water content and the development of surface soil crust (Hu et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2014 ). It is worth noting that for multiple consecutive rainfall events in a short period, such as rainfall events on 8/04, 8/12, and 8/15 in 2020, the yield and concentration of sediment show a decreasing trend, even for the bare plot (Fig. 1 a and e). The erodibility of soil is predominantly determined by the degree of affinity between soil particles and water, and a higher degree of affinity results in easier disintegration of soil into suspended particles, as well as increased susceptibility of soil aggregates to breakage (Luk and Hamilton, 1986; Poesen et al., 1999 ). When the soil moisture content reaches a certain threshold, the attraction between soil particles intensifies, leading to enhanced erosion resistance and a reduction in soil erosion. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent during intermittent wetting events with low runoff. Furthermore, the sediment in inter-rill erosion primarily originates from the detachment of soil particles (Mermut et al., 1997; Sutherland et al., 1996; Van Dijk et al., 2003 ). In intermittent rainfall events, the formation of soil crusts limits the detachment capacity of the thin sheet flow, resulting in a reduction of splash erosion (Moore and Singer, 1990 ; Zhang et al., 2019b). Sediment, runoff yield and sediment concentration were controlled by precipitation, and subjected to vegetation coverage, supported by the correlation analysis that rainfall characteristics, especially for the mean rainfall intensity and rainfall duration, correlated with sediment yield and runoff yield significantly. Such results are in accordance with previous studies from indoor simulated experiments (Wang et al., 2018 ) and micro-plots under degraded grassland conditions (Dlamini et al., 2011 ). The observed erosion reduction can be attributed to the reinforcement of the vegetation root system (Gyssels et al., 2005; Li et al., 2017 ) and the protection offered by vegetation (Hoffman et al., 2013; Saco and Moreno-De Las Heras, 2013 ), with the former leading to increased soil infiltration and stability, and the latter intercepting raindrops to prevent their impact from detaching soil particles. The effect of the vegetation’s roughness is a reduction in the erosive energy of the rain splash and the overland flow volume. Meanwhile, a significant correlation was established between vegetation coverage and both sediment yield and concentration, yet no such relationship was observed with runoff (Fig. 2 ), suggesting vegetation predominantly curtails inter-rill erosion by capturing sediment as opposed to reducing runoff. One potential reason for this could be that the micro-plot size (0.6 m2 ) used in the study may be inadequate for substantial interception and infiltration of runoff on-site. In the present study, the effective particle content of clay/sand decreased/increased with the increase in coverage, while the ultimate particle content of clay/sand was the highest/lowest in the vegetation coverage range of 25 ∼ 55 % (Fig. 3 ). This pattern can be attributed to the selective transport process that occurs during inter-rill erosion under varying degrees of vegetation coverage. The aggregation ratio of sediment confirmed that the effective particle content of silt and sand was mainly as primary particles in transportation when plots were bare or the coverage was 15 ∼ 35 %. When coverage was over 25 %, the effective particle content of silt and sand tended to be migrated in the form of aggregates (Fig. 4 ). When plots were bare or sparsely vegetated, the continuous and strong influence of rainwater causes soil aggregates to separate and break into primary particles, then carried away by surface flow (Wei et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020 ). In plots with relatively high vegetation coverage, the energy of raindrop splashing is weakened by the vegetation canopy, which is not enough to separate soil particles (Bochet et al., 2006; Geißler et al., 2012 ), and the surface soil aggregates were strengthened by roots system (Li et al., 2017 ). Additionally, surface soil crust, bolstered by plant biomass, further reduced soil detachment, infiltration, and surface soil hydraulic conductivity significantly (Bajracharya and Lal, 1998; Hu et al., 2020; Maïga-Yaleu et al., 2015 ). Moreover, the enrichment ratio of sediment showed effective particles of clay were enriched for all vegetation coverage plots (including the bare plot) except in the highest range scenario (35 ∼ 70 %), while the effective particles of sand were slightly depleted when plots were bare and in the vegetation coverage range of 15 ∼ 35 % (Fig. 4 ). This indicates that most clay particles in the surface soil were transported into the sediment, which seems to be inconsistent with the depletion of SOC (Fig. 8 ), since clay particles were the major factor of SOC fractions loss in the inter-rill erosion. This discrepancy may be ascribed to the relatively low content of SOC in sediment (Fig. 6 ). A previous meta -analysis study about vegetation restoration on SOC in the Loess Plateau found a decline in SOC during the initial years after restoration (Zhao et al., 2023 ). This trend is particularly prominent in grassland ecosystems (He et al., 2022 ). The complexity and spatial heterogeneity of plant species composition, as well as the variation in vegetation types, contribute to the heterogeneity in resource efficiency, communities of soil microbial, and cycling of SOC (De Deyn et al., 2008; He et al., 2022; McGonigle et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2015 ). For instance, litter quality, quantity, and soil-litter interfaces play a crucial role in controlling litter decomposition rates and SOC accumulation, especially in water-limited ecosystems (Aranda and Oyonarte, 2005; Cossu and Gazzale, 1986; Virginia and Jarrell, 1983 ).  4.2 The dynamic effect of vegetation coverage on the content and loss of SOC The SOC content in sediment, as well as MOC, with the increase of coverage, showed a trend of decreasing first and then increasing, while POC exhibited the opposite trend; the loss of MOC also followed the same tendency of SOC loss, with a significant difference between the bare plot and the plot with a coverage range of 35 ∼ 70 %, while no statistical differences were found between all treatments for POC loss (Fig. 6 ). These findings suggest that MOC is the dominant fraction in SOC loss during inter-rill erosion, significantly influencing the overall trend of SOC content and loss in the sediment (Hua et al., 2016; Li et al., 2023 ), and that vegetation plays a crucial role in mitigating organic carbon loss, particularly in scenarios of high coverage. The enrichment ratio of SOC fractions in sediment showed that MOC was enriched in all treatments except for the vegetation coverage range of 25 ∼ 55 %, indicating MOC in the surface soil was transported into the sediment (Fig. 8 ). MOC corresponded to the fractions with diameters less than 53 μm in the SOC, which is in accordance with the size of clay (d < 0.002 mm) and silt (d < 0.05 mm) particles. Thus, the enrichment of clay and silt particles provided ample transportation potential for the loss of MOC in inter-rill erosion (Fig. 4 ) (Koiter et al., 2017 ). With the negative correlation observed between vegetation coverage and the losses of SOC and MOC (Fig. 9 ), it is evident that vegetation overall has a favorable impact on the prevention and minimization of SOC loss. Although vegetative cover may facilitate the coarse particles deposition on the soil surface, potentially accelerating the downslope movement of fine particles—which are major carriers of MOC (Issa et al., 2006; Martínez-Mena et al., 2012; Schiettecatte et al., 2008 )—the overall result is a reduction in organic carbon loss. This outcome can be linked to the reduced erosion and sediment quantity in areas with vegetative cover. Since the loss of organic carbon is heavily dependent on the SOC fraction content and soil loss, which is significantly decreased by vegetation (Fig. 1 ), the enrichment of MOC due to the transport of fine particles does not translate into substantial SOC loss. Ultimately, this underscores the importance of sediment control as a direct means of mitigating SOC loss (Hua et al., 2016 ). Vegetation coverage affects both the detachment process of the surface soil and the dynamic change of runoff, both causing great implications for the separation, transportation and deposition of SOC and its fractions. However, it is difficult to separate and distinguish their individual effects under the limitations imposed by traditional research methods since these two processes happen simultaneously in the same erosive rainfall events. Therefore, we call for the adoption of innovative methods, such as 7 Be measurement or well-designed rain simulator experiments, which in forthcoming research could help isolate the effects of sub-processes on organic carbon loss from composite erosion events. The structural equation model revealed that rainfall characteristics are the primary drivers influencing inter-rill erosion dynamics, PSD, and SOC fractions loss in the sediment, both directly and indirectly (Fig. 10 ). This aligns with previous studies that identified rainfall as a critical factor in initiating soil erosion, mobilizing particles, and contributing to SOC loss (Gholami et al., 2021; Hancock and Wells, 2021; Li et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2021 ). Moreover, the highest path coefficients involving vegetation coverage were related to its impact on inter-rill erosion. This indicates that vegetation coverage primarily influences PSD and SOC fraction loss indirectly through its modulation of the inter-rill erosion process. A possible explanation is that the erosive force derived from rainfall, after being impaired by the weakening of vegetation, undermines the sediment yield in inter-rill erosion significantly, contributing to the reduction of SOC loss which is dominated by MOC, even though such a process may still result in the enrichment of MOC and particles smaller than 53 μm by exacerbating the selective transport process (Ding and Huang, 2017; Hao et al., 2016; Kiani-Harchegani et al., 2018; Koiter et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021 ). The relative proportion of MOC in organic carbon fractions showed consistency in the content and loss, that is, it decreased with the increase of coverage when the range was under 55 %, then surged for the coverage in the 35 ∼ 70 % condition (Fig. 7 ), indicating the response of different SOC fractions to inter-rill erosion varied with different vegetation coverage levels. Thus, our study highlights that the causality between the loss of SOC fractions and the alterations associated with soil erosion is complex and multifaceted, particularly under the conditions of natural environments. Although there is a downward trend in SOC loss, substantial changes may have transpired in the loss mechanisms of its fractions. This result offers a novel research perspective for further understanding the controversial function of soil erosion in the carbon cycle under complex environmental conditions (Lal and Primentel, 2008; Sanderman and Berhe, 2017 ; Van Oost et al., 2008). From the perspective of natural evolution, a barren plot will experience vegetation growth, typically of herbaceous plants, starting in spring. As the plants grow throughout the rainy season, vegetation coverage increases, eventually reaching a high and stable state. Our study demonstrates that the interactive relationship between rainfall characteristics, vegetation coverage, inter-rill erosion, PSD and the loss of SOC fractions is complex and mutable throughout this evolutionary process (Fig. 2 , Fig. 5  and Fig. 9 ). While vegetation generally reduces soil erosion and lessens organic carbon loss overall, the interaction between various factors evolves with the range of vegetation coverage, ultimately resulting in differences in the mechanisms of organic carbon fraction loss. Accordingly, we suggest that prevention and control strategies for inter-rill erosion and organic carbon loss on natural slopes must specifically and comprehensively take into account the condition of surface coverage, in order to optimize the ecological benefits. In the meantime, in the context of the warm and semi-arid climate in the Loess Plateau, we advise against sustaining overly high levels of vegetation coverage. Excessive vegetation density may lead to soil drought, hinder plant growth, and impede the natural succession of plant species (Cao et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2008 ). Our study further underscores, from the perspective of fractions, the dynamic influence of vegetation coverage on lateral movement of SOC during inter-rill erosion, providing a robust empirical basis for understanding the interconnection between erosion and SOC dynamics. This contributes to enhancing the precision of global carbon cycle models by providing the possibility of incorporating insights from organic carbon fractions and vegetation cover dynamics into carbon budget estimations.   5 Conclusion In this study, we investigated the variation in inter-rill erosion, PSD, and loss of SOC fractions under different levels of vegetation coverage, and explored the causal relationships among these variables. In terms of inter-rill erosion, vegetation coverage mainly affects sediment concentration in inter-rill erosion by regulating sediment yield instead of runoff, with a better reduction effect under the higher coverage. For the PSD in sediment, the content of effective particles in clay decreased, while the sand increased, with the increase of vegetation coverage, and the highest content of ultimate particles in clay and silt both occurred in the case of the coverage range of 25 ∼ 55 %. Clay particles were mainly aggregates in transportation, with enrichment for all coverage conditions except for the range of 35 ∼ 70 %, while silt and sand were primary particles during migration when the plot was bare and at the coverage range of 15 ∼ 35 %. The content of SOC in sediment was dominated by MOC content, and the loss of SOC fractions decreased as vegetation coverage increased, with a slight enrichment of MOC. The proportion of MOC in sediment organic carbon content and loss decreased first and then increased with the increase of coverage. The loss mechanisms of organic carbon fractions on slopes were regulated by rainfall characteristics both directly and indirectly, and by vegetation coverage indirectly. We highlighted the importance of exploring the complicated interaction between vegetation coverage and SOC loss from the perspective of fractions, providing new insights for carbon cycle modeling. Despite the study confirming the important role of vegetation in sediment interception, erosion reduction and SOC fraction loss prevention, the dominant mechanisms of SOC fraction losses under natural erosion environment remains to be learned, such as the influence of plant roots and the input of plant organic carbon.
1 Introduction Uranium is the fundamental element for the development of the nuclear industry and holds undeniable importance. It has been used extensively for nuclear power generation, nuclear medical and scientific research, and plays indispensable roles (Singh et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2014 ). Globally, approximately 7.918 million tons of uranium ore are commercially available for mining; however, China's accessible uranium reserves amount to only 223,000 tons. With the rapid advancement of the nuclear industry, the demand for uranium resources is increasing daily. Therefore, because of the limited reserves of uranium, improving the efficiency of uranium mining has become imperative. Uranium minerals in nature commonly coexist with gangue minerals (Van Lien et al., 2020 ), and economically important uranium minerals include tetravalent uranium ore, pitchblende, uraninite, silver uranium ore, and a minor proportion of oxidised hexavalent uranium ore (Bhargava et al., 2015; Kaksonen, 2020 ). Currently, the extraction of uranium primarily relies on chemical or biological methods with acid leaching, alkaline leaching, and neutral leaching (Li et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023 ). Acid leaching is widely used because of its effectiveness, and sulfuric acid is typically used as the solvent and hydrogen peroxide, ferric sulfate, or manganese dioxide is used as the oxidising agent. The efficiency of acid leaching is influenced by various factors, such as the mineral composition of uranium, the physical and chemical properties of the rocks and water, and the hydrodynamic conditions (Bhargava et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2020a,b ). The specific reasons are as follows: Uranium minerals are often encapsulated by gangue minerals, which inhibits contact between the leaching agent and uranium (Fan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2018a,b; Liu et al., 2023 ). During the leaching process, most of the leaching agent migrates along well-connected pore channels, while only a small portion of the solution flows at a lower rate into the micropores or remains stagnant in dead zones (Zeng et al., 2022 ). Additionally, chemical blockage during the leaching process is also an important factor limiting the leaching efficiency. Researchers have enhanced the uranium leaching efficiency through various approaches, such as alkali pretreatment + dilute acid leaching. This method is based on the principle of first selectively crushing gangue minerals with weakly alkaline solutions to increase the contact area between the dilute acid and uranium minerals (Fan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2018a,b ). In addition, microwave (Liu et al., 2023; Madakkaruppan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021a,b ) and low-frequency vibrations (Su et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2022 ) have been effective at increasing the permeabilities of uranium minerals, thereby increasing the uranium leaching efficiency. Surfactants have also been used to improve the permeability and molecular diffusion of leaching agents in low-permeability uranium ores (Du et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2014 ). In response to calcium sulfate precipitation during sulfuric acid leaching of uranium ores, which leads to clogging of the ore-bearing strata, CO2  + O2  leaching technology was tested in laboratory and field uranium mining tests, the results of which indicated that this technology inhibited the clogging of the ore strata (Su et al., 2020 ). These findings of increased leaching efficiency for uranium ore processing have important research implications. However, certain limitations exist: The alkali pretreatment + dilute acid leaching method necessitates using an additional alkaline solution, thereby exerting a considerable environmental impact; microwave and low-frequency vibrational treatments are challenging to implement in the field; surfactants have limited abilities to increase the permeability and fail to address the fundamental issue of poor ore permeability; and CO2  + O2  leaching technology currently exhibits low leaching efficiency. Because of the high efficiency and environmental friendliness of electrokinetics, its principles are now well documented and widely used in leaching valuable metals and soil remediation (Acar et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2018; Rosestolato et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021a,b; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Applying a suitable potential gradient in heavy metal-contaminated soil enhanced the migration rates of the heavy metal ions in the contaminated soil (Abou-Shady et al., 2023; Reynolds et al., 2008 ). Usually, the application of a potential gradient of 1.0 V/cm-2.0 V/cm enables the removal of heavy metal ions from contaminated soils (Rosestolato et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015 ; H. Zhou et al., 2020a,b ). Martens et al. (Martens et al., 2021, 2018; Ortega-Tong et al., 2023 ) investigated the use of electric fields to extract target metals by solubilising leachants, and the results showed that the application of a constant potential gradient generated more uniform solute transport that overcame the effect of preferential flow and successfully extracted the target metal. Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2017 ) used an electric field to enhance manganese leaching from low-grade manganese dioxide ores, and their results showed that an applied electric field increased the leaching efficiency of manganese and reduced the amount of reductant needed. In rare-earth ore mining, the use of electrokinetics increased the recovery efficiency of rare-earth elements by approximately 2.6 times, reduced the dosage of the leaching agent by approximately 80 %, and reduced the metallic impurities in the obtained rare-earth elements by approximately 70 % compared with the conventional method. The main reason for this difference was the difference in the mobilities and reactivities of rare-earth elements and metallic impurities under an electric field (Wang et al., 2022a,b ). Li et al. (Li et al., 2020 ) designed an electroassisted leaching method for low-grade uranium tailings. The results showed that an electric field facilitated the migration of the ions and reduced the probability of precipitation, which in turn considerably improved the uranium leaching efficiency. Moreover, the power consumption of the process was only approximately 1.5 W/h. Although electrokinetics has been widely used with heavy metal-contaminated soils and solid wastes, reports of its use in leaching uranium from sandstone uranium ores are still scarce. In this study, we used electrokinetic-enhanced sulfuric acid leaching of uranium from sandstone uranium ores to investigate the effects of different potential gradients on the leaching of sandstone uranium ores. The conductivities, pH and Eh values, the U concentrations and concentrations of other ions in the pregnant solution were monitored. Finally, a five-step sequential extraction experiment and characterisation analysis of sandstone uranium ore before and after the experiment were carried out to provide solid theoretical support for electrokinetic −enhanced sulfuric acid leaching of sandstone uranium ore.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental setup and materials 2.1.1 Experimental setup Fig. 1   shows a diagram of the experimental device used for electrokinetic horizontal column leaching. This device consisted of a cylindrical container made of Plexiglas and measured 3 cm × 8 cm. The dimensions of the sample chamber were 3 cm × 5 cm, and the dimensions of the filtration layer were 3 cm × 1.5 cm. Cylindrical titanium electrodes with diameters of 6 mm and lengths of 5 cm were placed between the sample chamber and the filtration layer. The anode and cathode of the device were connected to a DC power supply (KA6002D DC digital control power supply, Shenzhen KORAD Technology Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China). The current in the system was measured with a microammeter (WDCU3003 High Precision Voltammeter, Xiamen Yunlifang Electronic Technology Co., Ltd., Xiamen, China).  2.1.2 Experimental materials Sulfuric acid (95 %-98 %, analytically pure) and ferric sulfate (analytically pure) were purchased from Xilong Science Co., Ltd. (Shantou, China). Ultrapure water was obtained from Hetai-S10 equipment (Beijing, China). The uranium ore samples used in the experiments were obtained from a sandstone uranium mine in Inner Mongolia.   2.2 Experimental process The experimental procedure is shown in Fig. 2  . First, the sandstone uranium ore was sampled by shrinkage, and 15 g of the sandstone uranium ore sample was taken for each set of experiments. Four groups of experiments were performed, and potential gradients of 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm were applied. Before the potential gradient was applied, tap water was pumped into the experimental setup with a peristaltic pump (BT100-3 J constant-flow peristaltic pump, Baoding Lange Constant-Flow Peristaltic Pump Co. Ltd., Baoding, China) at a flow rate of approximately 5 mL/h to establish saturation equilibrium. After one day of saturation, a potential gradient was applied, and simultaneous electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments were conducted with H2 SO4  at a concentration of 10 g/L and Fe2 (SO4 )3  at a concentration of 1 g/L as the leaching agent. The pH, conductivity, and Eh of the collection solution were measured every hour with a Mettler Toledo multiparameter tester (S400-B, Mettler Toledo Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). Moreover, inductively coupled plasma emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) (Avio200, PerkinElmer, USA) was used to determine the concentrations of the major elements in the collection solution, and the sulfate ion concentration in the collection solution was tested with an ion chromatography (IC6200, Anhui Wanyi Science and Technology Co., Ltd., Anhui, China). After 20 h of experiments, the uranium ore in the sample chamber was collected, washed three times with ultrapure water, and then dried in a blast drying oven at 80 °C for 48 h. The uranium leaching efficiency of the experiment was determined with the following expression:(1) R = ( C 1  + C 2  + . . . . . . . . + C 19  + C 20  ) V  M  × 100 %     where R  is the uranium leaching efficiency, C1   to C20   are the uranium concentrations in the collected solutions per hour (mg/L), V  is the volume of the collection solution (L), and M  is the total mass of uranium in the ore sample (mg).  2.3 PHREEQC calculations PHREEQC is a computer program developed with the C and C++ programming languages and is designed to perform various geochemical calculations (Charlton and Parkhurst, 2011; Zhang et al., 2019 ). This approach is particularly useful for calculating hydrogeochemical reactions, such as simulating solute transport in fractured bedrock (Lipson et al., 2007 ), modelling leaching (Wu et al., 2021 ), and calculating species equilibria in solution (Catrouillet et al., 2014 ). The LLNL.dat database in PHREEQC software was used to simulate and calculate the ion morphologies in the pregnant solution of the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment and to assist in analysing the ionic migration states during leaching.  2.4 Analytical methods The surface micromorphology and mineral composition characteristics of the sandstone uranium ore were determined using field emission scanning electron microscopy energy spectrometer (SEM-EDS) (Pharos G2, Phenom, Netherlands). The mineral structures of the sandstone uranium ore were determined using X-ray diffraction analysis (D/max-2500, Rigaku, Japan). The chemical composition were determined with a high-resolution multipass X-ray fluorescence trace element analyser (S4 T-Star, Bruker, Germany). Sequential extractions were used to separate different chemical fractions from the uranium-containing minerals (Chen et al., 2023 ).   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Variation in the conductivity, pH, Eh and current with time Fig. 3   shows the conductivity, pH, Eh and current values with time in the pregnant solution of the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment. As shown in Fig. 3 (a), under different potential gradients, the overall conductivity in the pregnant solution exhibited a rapid increase, followed by a slow increase, and finally stabilisation. After 1–8 h, the conductivity of the pregnant solution in each group of experiments increased rapidly, and the conductivities at 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm were 591,984 µs/cm, 583,856 µs/cm, 605,041 µs/cm, and 646,183 µs/cm, respectively. After 9–20 h, the growth rate of the conductivity in the pregnant solution slowed and then stabilised, and the conductivities in the experiments run with 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm potential gradients stabilised at approximately 661,017 µs/cm, 677,511 µs/cm, 686,103 µs/cm, and 716,862 µs/cm, respectively. During the leaching process, the interactions between the leaching agent and gangue minerals led to substantial generation of cations, including Mg2+ , Al3+ , K+  and Ca2+ . The applied electric field expedited the migration of these cations, thereby resulting in enhanced conductivity within the pregnant solution. Additionally, a higher applied potential gradient led to faster ion migration and increased conductivity within the pregnant solution. Notably, a decreasing trend in conductivity was observed during the 7–10 h of the experiment for both the 1 V/cm and 2 V/cm potential gradient experiments. This decline can be attributed to an accelerated rate of ore dissolution, resulting in an increased surface area of the ore(Wang et al., 2024 ). Consequently, this enhanced surface area is likely to promote the temporary adsorption capacity of the ore, leading to a greater amount of ions being adsorbed on its surface during the leaching process. Therefore, after the adsorption capacity stabilized of the sandstone, the leaching efficiency of uranium continued to growth again. As depicted in Fig. 3 (b), the applied potential gradient did not have a substantial influence on the pH of the pregnant solution. The pH of the pregnant solution in each experimental group initially decreased rapidly to approximately 1.5 and then stabilizsed, indicating that all of the groups had similar acid reaction rates and that sufficient H+  was provided. As displayed in Fig. 3 (c), the Eh of the pregnant solution in each group increased rapidly during 1–2 h after reaction initiation. Specifically, for potential gradients of 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1 V/cm, and 2 V/cm, the corresponding Eh values were 419.7 mV, 459.6 mV, 453.8 mV, and 464.3 mV, respectively. Injection of the leaching agent provided a considerable amount of Fe3+ , while the electric field facilitated the migration of Fe3+  out of the experimental column. Notably, higher potential gradients resulted in faster migration rates and higher Eh values in the pregnant solution. From 3 to 20 h, a slow decrease in the Eh was observed for the pregnant solutions with potential gradients of 0.5 V/cm, 1 V/cm, and 2 V/cm, stabilising at final values of 442.0 mV, 437.1 mV and 433.9 mV, respectively. However, for the 0 V/cm potential gradient, the Eh gradually increased, eventually reaching 454.3 mV. The redox reaction between tetravalent uranium and Fe3+   led to a decrease in the Eh of the pregnant solution. An applied potential gradient accelerated product migration in this reaction. Notably, a higher potential gradient applied at both ends of the column led to accelerated ion migration, resulting in enhanced reaction kinetics and increased consumption of Fe3+ . Consequently, the elevated potential gradient corresponded to a greater decrease in Eh within the pregnant solution. In the experimental group with a 0 V/cm potential gradient, the amount of injected Fe3+  ions exceeded their consumption because of sluggish reaction kinetics. As shown in Fig. 3 (d), the initial current values in the experiments with 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm potential gradients applied were approximately 0.82 mA, 1.15 mA, and 4.42 mA, respectively. After leaching for a duration of 20 h, the currents reached approximately 0.73 mA, 1.00 mA, and 4.07 mA, respectively. This continuous decline in the system current occurred because numerous cations migrated out of the experimental column because of the applied electric field. Moreover, higher applied potential gradients resulted in faster ion migration and consequently greater reductions in the system current.  3.2 Characteristics of the uranium leaching efficiency with time The characterisation results by XRF analysis are listed in Table 1  . The sandstone uranium ore is mainly composed of SiO2  and Al2 O3 , where the uranium content is 0.042 wt%. Fig. 4  (a) shows the uranium leaching efficiency versus time for the pregnant solutions with different potential gradients. In the first 1–3 h, the reaction rate of each experimental group was slow, and the uranium leaching efficiency was only approximately 10 %. With continuous injection of the leaching agent, the uranium leaching efficiency in the pregnant solution continued to increase. After 20 h of leaching, the uranium leaching efficiencies for the 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm potential gradients were 54.9 %, 56.36 %, 67.33 %, and 82.04 %, respectively. The uranium leaching efficiency with the 2.0 V/cm potential gradient was 27.14 % greater than that with the 0 V/cm potential gradient. Fig. 4 (b) shows the percentages of the species of uranium in the pregnant solution, as calculated with PHREEQC simulations, and at pH 1.5, the species of uranium in the pregnant solution were mainly UO2 SO4 , UO2 2+  and UO2 (SO4 )2 2– , with percentages of 65.81 %, 17.92 % and 16.15 %, respectively. The sum of the UO2 SO4  and UO2 2+  percentages was 83.73 %. In the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment, the reactive transport of sandstone uranium ores is a complex process. The equations for the electromigration, electroosmosis, advection, diffusion, and reaction transport are described as:(2) ∂ C i   ∂ t   = - ∇ ( J M  + J EO  + J A  + J D  )  + R i      where Ci   is the molar concentration of the species i (mol/m−3 (−|-)); JM   is the electromigration flux (mol m−2  s−1 ); JEO   is the electro-osmotic flux (mol m−2  s−1 ); JA   is the advection flux (mol m−2  s−1 ); JD   is the diffusion flux (mol m−2  s−1 ); and Ri   is the rate of chemical reactions (mol/m−3 (−|-) s−1 ). The electromigration flux JM  , electro-osmotic flux JEO  , advection flux JA  , diffusion flux JD   are described by(Martens et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022a,b ):(3) J M  = - D i  z i  C i  F RT   ∂ V  ∂ x       (4) J EO   = - K EO   C i  ∂ V  ∂ x       (5) J A  = C i  v     (6) J D  = - D i  ∇ C i      where Di   is the diffusion coefficient in the free solution at infinite dilution of the species i  (m2 /s), zi   is the valence of the species i , F  is the Faraday constant (C/mol); R  is the gas constant (J mol−1  K−1 ); T  is the temperature (K); V  is the electric potential (V); and KEO   is the electro-osmotic permeability or conductivity (m2 /s V−1 ); and v  is the average velocity of the pore water (m/s). The rate of chemical reactions Ri   is described by Zhang et al.
