As revealed in Fig. 4 (c), the ore surface was negatively charged, and the surrounding liquid was positively charged because of electrostatic attraction, and an electric double layer formed at the liquid–solid interface. When a direct current electric field was applied and induced electromigration was induced, the positively charged ions at the liquid–solid interface moved towards the cathode and dragged the liquid through viscous force, which is called electroosmosis. Based on the PHREEQC simulation of the species of uranium in the pregnant solution, combined with the analysis of the mathematical model of uranium reaction transport in the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment, the UO2 SO4  and UO2 2+  in the experimental column migrated to the negative electrode because of flow, electromigration and electroosmosis to enable dissolution of additional uranium minerals and increase the uranium leaching efficiency. Experiments showed that the leaching efficiency increased with the increase of the potential gradient. Furthermore, in the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment, the dissolving leaching agent reacted chemically with the uranium minerals to produce various uranium compounds, and uranium mineral dissolution equilibrium was reached at a certain point. However, when the products migrated, the original dissolution equilibrium was disrupted, and the uranium minerals continued to dissolve until a new equilibrium was reached.  3.3 Changes in the contents of other ions in the pregnant solution In addition to the known key factors affecting uranium leaching, such as temperature and acid concentration (Wang et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019 ), other parameters, such as the concentration of trivalent ferric ions in solution, also affect the uranium leaching process. The trivalent ferric ions in solution were mainly used to oxidise the insoluble tetravalent uranium in the ore (Manaa, 2021 ). Therefore, the content of trivalent ferric ions in solution was crucial for uranium leaching. As shown in Fig. 5  (a), the total ferric content in the pregnant solution increased with increasing applied potential gradient, and the total ferric contents at the 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm potential gradients were 24.99 mg, 27.83 mg, 29.05 mg, and 39.74 mg, respectively. This comparison indicated that the electric field had a considerable effect on the content of ferric ions in the pregnant solution. Fig. 5 (b) shows the percentages of the ferric species in the pregnant solution calculated with PHREEQC simulations. At pH 1.5, the species of ferric in the pregnant solution were mainly FeSO4 + , FeHSO4 2+ , Fe(SO4 )2 - , and Fe3+ , and the percentages were 69.77 %, 13.37 %, 12.53 %, and 3.94 %, respectively. Clearly all of the ferric ions in the pregnant solution were trivalent ferric, of which 87.08 % of which were cationic. The applied potential gradient promoted the migration of these ferric complex cations to the negative electrode, increased the total ferric content in the pregnant solution, and increased the efficiency of tetravalent uranium oxidation. Fig. 5 (c–f) shows the changes in the elemental contents of Mg, Al, K, and Ca in the pregnant solution under the different potential gradients. As the applied potential gradients increased, the elemental contents of Mg, Al, K, and Ca in the pregnant solution also increased, with Ca showing the greatest increase. In the process of leaching uranium ore, the sequence of uranium leaching proceeded as follows: initial leaching targeted the portion adsorbed on the ore surface, followed by subsequent leaching of the uranium present in pores and microcracks and ultimately targeting uranium encapsulated within gangue minerals (Zhou et al., 2020a,b ). However, to extract the uranium coated with gangue minerals effectively by leaching, it is imperative to decompose these gangue minerals and enhance contact between the leaching agent and the ore while minimising the precipitation of ions such as calcium. In the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment, the electrokinetic action initially enhanced the dissolution and exposure of gangue minerals, thereby increasing the contact area between uranium minerals and the leaching agent and subsequently improving the uranium leaching efficiency. As electrokinetic leaching progressed, the degree of gangue mineral dissolution increased, leading to continuous increases in the Mg, Al, K, and Ca contents in the pregnant solution. This result ultimately contributed to additional improvement in the uranium leaching efficiency. Furthermore, by driving Ca ion migration out of the experimental column, the electrokinetic action prevented calcium sulfate precipitation within the column and reduced the risk of chemical blockage. In brief, the potential gradient facilitated gangue mineral dissolution from the uranium ore, which increased the uranium mineral exposure and improved the uranium leaching efficiency while reducing the probability of chemical blockage.  3.4 Discussion of the analytical results 3.4.1 Analysis of the uranium chemical fractions The chemical fractions of uranium in the ore directly affect the difficulty of leaching and are a key natural factor determining the uranium concentration during leaching (Li et al., 2018a,b ). Fig. 6   and Table 2   show the percentages and contents of uranium in the different chemical fractions of the sandstone uranium ore before and after leaching in the five-step sequential extraction method. As shown in Fig. 6 (a), the content of the exchangeable fraction of uranium (F1) in the original sandstone uranium ore was 55.52 µg/g, which accounted for 8.6 % of the total; the acid-soluble fraction of uranium (F2) showed the highest content of 321.46 µg/g, a 50.1 % share; the acid-soluble fraction of uranium (F3) comprised 108.10 µg/g, which accounted for 16.9 %; the oxidisable fraction of uranium (F4) had a content of 119.44 µg/g, with a share of 18.6 %; and the lowest uranium abundance among the residual soluble forms (F5) was 36.92 µg/g, with a share of only 5.7 %. According to the five chemical fractions of uranium, the uranium in the ore was classified into three major categories: easily leachable, leachable, and hardly leachable uranium (Chen et al., 2023 ). The easily leachable uranium contained an exchangeable fraction, an easily acid-soluble fraction and an acid-soluble fraction. The latter fraction of uranium was adsorbed on clay mineral sediments and coprecipitated with carbonate minerals. Leachable uranium was the oxidisable fraction with a percentage of 18.6 %. This portion of uranium was mainly the tetravalent uranium in the uranium ore. Hardly leachable uranium showed residual solubility and referred to the uranium encapsulated in the lattices of silicates and primary and secondary minerals, etc., and its percentage content was the smallest at only 5.7 %. The above analysis indicates that this sandstone uranium ore showed good leachability. After the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments, the uranium contents of the five specific fractions were decreased at the different potential gradients, as shown in Fig. 6 (b) and Table 2 . In the experiments in which 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm potential gradients were applied, the contents of easily leachable uranium decreased by 305.61 µg/g, 320.3 µg/g, 359.01 µg/g, and 405.46 µg/g, respectively; the contents of leachable uranium decreased by 38.97 µg/g, 47.16 µg/g, 65.52 µg/g and 78.57 µg/g, respectively; and the contents of refractory leachable uranium decreased by 16.54 µg/g, 20.85 µg/g, 25.19 µg/g, and 27.29 µg/g, respectively. The content of easily leachable uranium decreased the most, while the leachable and refractory leachable uranium contents also showed substantial reductions. Overall, the applied potential gradient facilitated the leaching of easily leachable uranium as well as leachable and hardly leachable uranium to a certain extent.  3.4.2 XRD analyses Fig. 7   shows the XRD data for sandstone uranium ore over the 2θ range of 10-80° before and after the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments. By comparing the data with those of the PDF standard cards, it was determined that the sandstone uranium ore consisted of quartz, sodium feldspar, and plagioclase feldspar minerals before and after the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments. However, the peak intensities for sodium feldspar at 2θ = 27.47°, 2θ = 36.51°, and 2θ = 42.39° and for plagioclase feldspar at 2θ = 20.81° and 2θ = 68.11° were lower after leaching. This result indicated that some of the sodium feldspar and plagioclase feldspar dissolved during the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments. In addition, the peak intensities at 2θ = 20.81°, 2θ = 68.11° and at 2θ = 42.39° decreased gradually with increasing applied potential gradient, suggesting that the applied potential gradient enabled the dissolution of sodium feldspar and plagioclase feldspar in the sandstone uranium ore.  3.4.3 SEM-EDS analyses Fig. 8   shows SEM-EDS images of the uranium ore before and after the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment. The original uranium ore exhibited a cohesive structure with attached detrital particles, as depicted in Fig. 8 (a). In the potential gradient experiment with 0 V/cm applied, the surface of the leached uranium ore became smooth, and some holes appeared (Fig. 8 b), indicating that a portion of the sandstone uranium ore was dissolved during the leaching process. When a potential gradient of 2.0 V/cm was applied for leaching, the uranium ore disintegrated into smaller granules (Fig. 8 c), indicating that the applied potential gradient dissolved some of the sandstone uranium ore. In addition, Fig. 8 (d, e, f) shows a map of the uranium ore before and after the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments, which revealed changes in the elemental composition of the sandstone uranium ore. O, Si, Mg, Al, K, and Ca were uniformly distributed in the original uranium ore, and their contents were reduced after the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment. Notably, as the applied potential gradient increased, the reductions in the elemental contents increased. This behaviour suggested that the potential gradient promoted mineral dissolution.   3.5 Analysis of energy consumption The energy consumed during electrokinetic horizontal column leaching of sandstone uranium ore in industrial applications is a key indicator (Oladipo et al., 2022 ). According to the current values and corresponding potential gradients in Fig. 3 (d), the energy consumed in the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiment was calculated with Equation (8)  (Ghobadi et al., 2021; Pedersen et al., 2015 ):(8) Energy consumpton   = ∫ 0 t  U t  I t  d t     where Ut   is the applied potential gradient, It   is the corresponding current, and t  is the leaching time. Under laboratory conditions, the energy consumption levels for the experiments with applied potential gradients of 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm, and 2.0 V/cm were 0.038 Wh, 0.101 Wh, and 0.796 Wh, respectively. Overall, the energy consumed with different potential gradients was low, even though higher potential gradients resulted in higher energy consumption. Therefore, electrokinetic-enhanced sulfuric acid leaching of sandstone uranium ore resulted in better uranium extraction with lower energy consumption.   4 Conclusion The mechanism of action for electrokinetic-enhanced sulfuric acid leaching of sandstone uranium ore was investigated. The following conclusions were obtained according to the experimental and characterisation results: (i) In a sulfuric acid leaching system, the application of a potential gradient improved the efficiency of uranium leaching. In the experiments with potential gradients of 0 V/cm, 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm and 2.0 V/cm, the uranium leaching efficiencies were 54.90 %, 56.36 %, 68.33 % and 82.04 %, respectively. The uranium leaching efficiency increased with increasing potential gradient. (ii) The applied potential gradients facilitated solute transport during the leaching process, thus accelerating the leaching efficiency of adsorbed uranium, tetravalent uranium, and uranium encapsulated in lattices comprising silicates, primary and secondary minerals, etc., in the sandstone uranium ore and reducing the number of leaching cycles needed. (iii) In the electrokinetic horizontal column leaching experiments, the energies consumed at potential gradients of 0.5 V/cm, 1.0 V/cm and 2.0 V/cm were 0.038 Wh, 0.101 Wh and 0.796 Wh, respectively. In general, the energy consumed by the experiments with different potential gradients was low, which indicated good application prospects. In future work, more leaching agent systems, different types of uranium ores and practical field uranium mining will need to be tested to obtain a deeper understanding of the electrokinetic-enhanced uranium leaching process and its feasibility and limitations in practical field applications. In addition, in the process of electrokinetic −enhanced leaching, solute transport involves diffusion and convection, as well as electromigration and electroosmotic effects. The contributions of diffusion, convection, electromigration and electroosmosis to uranium leaching need further research. In the present study, electrokinetic-enhanced technology promoted the leaching of more uranium and gangue mineral metals. In the in-situ leaching of practical uranium ore mining, the pregnant solution is pumped from the underground to the hydrometallurgical plant to separate and recover of uranium and gangue mineral metals, which has less impact on the environment. 1 Introduction Coastal zones exhibit some of the highest population densities globally, with almost half of the global population residing in these areas (Small and Nicholls, 2003; Klassen and Allen, 2017 ). Fresh groundwater serves as the primary water source for domestic, industrial, and agricultural purposes in coastal cities (Yang et al., 2015; Huizer et al., 2017; Elsayed & Oumeraci, 2018 ). Nevertheless, seawater intrusion (SWI) occurs frequently in coastal areas (Flynn et al., 1995 ). SWI can lead to the salinization of fresh groundwater, polluting valuable freshwater sources and thus adversely affecting social production activities. SWI is commonly classified into two types: lateral saltwater intrusion (LSWI) and vertical saltwater intrusion (VSWI). LSWI is over-exploitation of groundwater or extreme weather events that disrupt the balance between freshwater and saltwater in coastal aquifers, resulting in a landward movement of the saline plume-freshwater interface (Geng and Michael, 2020; Walther et al., 2020 ). VSWI is primarily caused by sea level rise (GMSL) or storm surge events that result in vertical intrusion of saltwater from the surface into aquifers, disrupting subsurface freshwater systems (Kulp and Strauss, 2019; Nauels et al., 2017; Song et al., 2022 ). LSWI has been extensively studied over many decades, focusing on the effects of pumping and sea level rise (Bosserelle et al., 2022; Heiss et al., 2022; Huyakorn et al., 1987; Werner et al., 2013 ). Nevertheless, the detrimental impact of VSWI on aquifers has only recently gained recognition. Storm surge-induced VSWI phenomena exhibit significant risks in coastal areas around the globe, which can trigger salinization of coastal groundwater in a short period of time (Guimond and Michael, 2021 ). In recent studies, surge-induced VSWI has received increasing attention. Storm surge-induced VSWI generally includes three phases (Song et al., 2022 ): (1) rapid infiltration of saltwater in the unsaturated zone during a storm surge event; (2) infiltration of saltwater into the saturated zone with finger-flow pattern after sea level recedes; and (3) gradual dilution and flushing of saltwater driven by precipitation recharge and inland recharge. Liu and Tokunaga's (2019)  numerical simulations of aquifer recovery processes under the tsunami scenarios at Niijima Island, Japan, found that the volume of the unsaturated zone and the structure of the base of the aquifer control the rate of aquifer salinization. Paldor and Michael (2021)  calculated the effects of surge events with different recurrence times on the anisotropic coastal aquifer, showing that the total salt load in the aquifer increases due to repetitive vertical salinization. Yu et al. (2016)  explored the effect of topography on groundwater salinization caused by surges, and they found the amount of saltwater in the surface depression and connectivity of overland flow are primary controlling factors on salinization and recovery processes of coastal aquifers. Yang et al. (2018)  modeled ocean-surge inundation on coastal aquifer under the influence of permeability, hydraulic gradient and recharge rate, and assessed aquifer vulnerability and recovery time. However, these studies mainly focus on homogeneous aquifers (e.g., Liu and Tokunaga, 2019; Yu et al., 2016 ) and aquifers with anisotropic permeability (e.g., Yang et al., 2018; Paldor and Michael, 2021 ), and without addressing the impact of complex geological heterogeneity on VSWI. In heterogeneous beach aquifers, pore water flow and solute transport exhibit more complex spatial and temporal variations. The study of heterogeneous aquifers consists of two main categories: the spatial heterogeneity assumption (i.e., permeability coefficient (K) follows a lognormal distribution) and the layered geological structure assumption. Weeks & Sposito (1998)  showed that significant spatial variability in K can produce chaotic velocity fields similar to turbulent flow fields. Therefore, in recent years, attention has been paid to the effect of spatial heterogeneity on VSWI. Mahmoodzadeh and Karamouz (2019)  studied the combined effects of stochastic hydraulic conductivity fields on SWI, and their research unveiled that heterogeneity amplifies the volume of mixing and expands the area of the mixing zone. Song et al. (2022)  investigated the effects of connected heterogeneity on the recovery process of coastal aquifers. They found that connected heterogeneity, compared to the equivalent homogeneous scenario, increased the range of salinization; however, it also resulted in a reduction of the maximum salinized volume, while shortening the overall aquifer recovery time. Layered heterogeneous structures, as one of the most common forms of heterogeneous in realistic aquifer systems, have been commonly used in past studies on coastal aquifer systems to model heterogeneous conditions. Numerous studies have demonstrated that layered heterogeneity significantly affects groundwater flow and solute transport (Abdoulhalik et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2022 ). On this basis, some studies have explored the VSWI under layered heterogeneous conditions. Chui et al. (2013)  investigated the damage and recovery of freshwater lenses in a layered atoll aquifer (with a low-K layer present above a high-K layer) after a storm. Gingerich et al. (2017)  investigated the rainfall recharge and artificial recharge on the recovery of freshwater lenses on low-lying islands (aquifers are multilayered systems) after saltwater flooding events. Vithanage et al. (2012)  investigated the effects of continuous and intermittent low-permeability layer (LPL) on salinization plume migration and flushing time at the laboratory scale. Their study demonstrated that a continuous LPL resulted in a 40 % increase in the aquifer recovery time, but when an opening was introduced in LPL, the aquifer recovery time decreased. Previous studies have revealed the recovery processes of heterogeneous and homogeneous aquifer systems after storm surge events, as well as the differences between these two types of systems. However, past researches on VSWI had primarily been based on geological systems formed under natural conditions. With the development of coastal areas, various subsurface engineering measures have been proposed and constructed to prevent LSWI and safeguard coastal freshwater resources. Changes in water flow paths and groundwater levels by subsurface structures are likely to have a significant impact on the behavior and time scales of VSWI, particularly in heterogeneous aquifers, where the effects may be more pronounced. Therefore, the combined effects of the heterogeneity of coastal aquifers and subsurface structures on VSWI recovery mechanisms make accurate assessment of VSWI challenging, which creates significant uncertainty in coastal groundwater management. Among the many engineering measures to safeguard coastal freshwater resources, subsurface physical barrier stands out due to low operating costs, low post-maintenance, high stability, and ability to store fresh groundwater resources (Wu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021 ). Commonly used physical barriers include subsurface dam, cutoff wall and semi-permeable subsurface barrier (SPSB). Previous studies have shown that subsurface dam may truncate the saltwater wedge and large amount of saltwater could be trapped upstream the dam. Complete desalination of the residual saltwater in field scale may take several decades. Therefore, cutoff wall is becoming increasingly popular for controlling LSWI. However, as a permanent subsurface structure, the cutoff wall can impede the seaward flow of groundwater and may affect the process of the VSWI during high-intensity storm surge. Yang et al. (2021)  and Song et al. (2022)  are among the few studies that have considered the influence of subsurface structures on aquifer recovery processes. Yang et al. (2021)  investigated the impact of cutoff wall on the surge inundation process of islands. They found that the presence of cutoff wall accelerated the recovery of the aquifer on islands with low and medium permeability, but prolonged the recovery time on islands with high permeability. Song et al. (2022)  investigated the combined effects of physical barrier (subsurface dam and cutoff wall) and connected heterogeneity on the recovery of coastal aquifers after storm surge. Their study demonstrated that the presence of a physical barrier led to an increase in the salinized volume and total salt mass, thus prolonging the recovery of aquifers in both the connected heterogeneity and gaussian heterogeneity scenarios. However, physical barrier also decreased the accumulated salinized volume and accelerated the removal of saltwater in unconnected heterogeneity scenario. Geologic evidence has revealed that the frequent pattern of layered heterogeneity in coastal aquifers is a LPL situated between two high permeability layers (HPL) (i.e., the HLH-pattern) (Capaccioni et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2006; Oki et al., 1998; Rathore et al., 2018; Ratner-Narovlansky et al., 2020 ). Past studies have demonstrated that the transport behavior and removal timescales of contaminants in HLH-pattern aquifer systems will be significantly different from homogeneous systems (Abdoulhalik & Ahmed, 2017; Zhang et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2022 ). Although studies by Song et al. (2022)  and Yang et al. (2021)  revealed the combined effects of cutoff wall and aquifer characteristics (including permeability coefficient variations and spatial heterogeneity features) on aquifer recovery after storm surge events. However, to the best of our knowledge, the combined effect of typical layered heterogeneity (one LPL confined between two HPL) and cutoff walls on VSWI remains uncertain (Fig. 1  ). The research on recovery processes of coastal aquifer subject to storm surge combined with the typical layered heterogeneity and cutoff wall is of great importance for the assessment of coastal aquifer vulnerability and management. Previous studies have focused on the effects of layered heterogeneity or cutoff wall on aquifer recovery after storm surge events, respectively (Vithanage et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2021 ), which leaves a knowledge gap in understanding their combined effects. Consequently, our research aims to bridge this gap by developing advanced numerical models. This study employs numerical simulations to investigate the combined impact of typical layered heterogeneity and cutoff wall on the salinization and recovery processes of coastal aquifers following a single storm surge event. The surge-driven VSWI process and its salinization mechanism are explored through 2D numerical simulations using a range of different cutoff wall structures and heterogeneity distributions. A quantitative analysis of the effects of layered heterogeneity and cutoff wall in coastal aquifers on the extent of salinization and total salinity is presented. Our study provides significant insights into the interactions between storm surge-driven saltwater intrusion, geologic layered heterogeneity, and cutoff wall. These insights will help decision-makers select appropriate engineering measures for coastal groundwater management to address future risks from storm surges.  2 Methods 2.1 Governing equations We employed SUTRA, a model developed by Voss and Provost (2008) , to investigate the flow and solute transport processes in a coastal unconfined aquifer following a storm surge event. SUTRA is a suitable model for solving problems related to variable-saturation, variable-density groundwater flow and single-species solute transport. Fig. 2   shows the configuration of a two-dimensional layered aquifer cross-section with a cutoff wall installation. The boundary conditions of the groundwater flow and salt transport model were established to represent the natural forces acting on the beach aquifer, which include seaward, surface recharge, and landward flux boundaries. As in previous studies (Song et al., 2022; Mahmoodzadeh & Karamouz, 2019; Yu et al., 2016 ), we assumed that inland fluxes and net rainfall evaporation fluxes were kept constant in order to study the combined effects of layered heterogeneity and cutoff wall on the recovery of the coastal aquifer after a single storm surge event. Although the settings of inland flux and net rainfall evaporation flux are critical for numerical simulations of groundwater flow and solute transport in coastal aquifers (Chang et al., 2020 ), systematic comparisons of specific flux boundaries for aquifer recovery after storm surge events influenced by cutoff wall and LPL are outside the scope of the purpose of this study. Therefore, simulations were conducted at the corresponding specified boundaries (i.e., using the parameter values of the specified inland flux and net rainfall evaporation flux in this study). The model assumes that the calculation area is situated on bedrock, and the aquifer basement DE is treated as an impermeable no-flow boundary and a zero-salt flux boundary. Considering the net groundwater recharge from precipitation and evapotranspiration, the top boundary AB is assigned as a specified flux boundary with a flow rate of Qr   = 0.03 m3 /d·m2 . The landward boundary AE is specified as a constant fresh groundwater flux (Qf   = 0.7 m3 /d·m2 ) and constant salt concentration (CL  =0 ppt) boundary condition. To facilitate the formation of a stable salinization plume-freshwater interface within the layered aquifer in a short simulation period, as proposed by Lu et al. (2013) , the seaward boundary BCD was set as a pressure boundary with external pressure related to sea level, and also as a concentration boundary with external concentration equal to the salinity of seawater. Firstly, a steady-state preheating period with a constant sea level of 24 m was simulate, which intended to establish a quasi-steady-state saltwater wedge in the aquifer (Song et al. 2022 ). The final results of the preheating phase were used as the initial conditions for the simulation of vertical saltwater intrusion (VSWI), which spanned 30 years. The sea level variation curve during the VSWI simulation phase was developed based on the studies by Cardenas et al. (2015)  and Yang et al. (2021)  (see Fig. 3  ). A single surge event lasting for 8 h, with a maximum surge height of 3.5 m, was considered. During the storm surge event, the sea level increased to its maximum surge height based on the surge curve (2 < t < 6h) and then returned to the mean sea level (MSL) according to the surge curve (t > 6h) (Fig. 3 ). When the seawater level declines, the groundwater level in the aquifer also decreases, but at a slower rate than the sea level. This leads to the creation of a seepage surface at the beach boundary above the seawater level. According to the research conducted by Wilson & Gardner (2006)  and Xin et al. (2009) , there are two scenarios for the boundary nodes above the sea level: (1) if these nodes were saturated in the previous time step, they are treated as seepage surface nodes and assigned atmospheric pressure (P=0); (2) if these nodes were unsaturated in the previous time step, no flow is assumed. Correspondingly, for salt transport, nodes with inflow to the beach aquifer were assigned a seawater concentration (35 ppt); however, a zero-concentration gradient was applied to nodes with outflow from the beach aquifer. This process follows Eqs. (9)  and (10) .(9) C = C sea   n f  · u < 0     (10) - n f  · D ∇ C = 0 n f  · u ≥ 0      This study compared the effects of low-permeability layer and cutoff wall on groundwater salinization by considering homogeneous aquifer without cutoff (Case H), layered aquifer without cutoff wall (Case L), homogeneous aquifer with cutoff wall (Case C), and layered heterogeneity aquifer with cutoff wall (Case CL). Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was conducted based on Case- CL to explore the effects of variations in the cutoff wall depth (Hc), distance between the cutoff wall and the seawater boundary (DL), thickness of LPL (TL), distance from LPL centerline to the aquifer base (LL) (it can also be called the elevation of LPL), and hydraulic conductivity of LPL (KL) on VSWI. Fig. 2  illustrates the dimensions of the simulated aquifer area, where the physical barrier was modeled by designating the cutoff wall installation area as an inactive unit and setting the thickness of the cutoff wall to 1.0 m. The model domain was discretized into a grid with a constant size of 0.8 m in the x -direction and a variable size in the y -direction, with grid sizes ranging between 0.2 and 0.6 m. The lattice space discretization scheme meets the Péclet number criterion, for avoiding numerical oscillations. The hydraulic conductivity of the aquifer is isotropic, with a hydraulic conductivity (K) of 1.447 × 10-4  m/s for the highly permeable soils at the top and bottom, and a hydraulic conductivity (KL) of 1.447 × 10-5  m/s for LPL in the basic model (Zhang et al., 2021 ). As with past studies, to simplify the model, the study made an assumption the values of other hydrological parameters, e.g., porosity (ɛ ), longitudinal dispersivity (αL  ), transverse dispersivity (αT  ), and water retention parameters (Swres  , n , and α ) were fixed for both low-permeability and high-permeability layers (Zhang et al., 2021; Gao et al. 2022 ). The effect of these parameters on VSWI is negligible compared to permeability (Yang et al.,2021 ).  2.3 Measurable diagnostics In this study, two measurable metrics were used to compare the numerical results: (1) volume of salinization plume with salt concentration exceeds 0.5 ppt; and (2) total salt mass of salinization plume with salt concentration exceeds 0.5 ppt. At the initial state (year 0), the lateral intrusion distance of LSWI (calculated from the 50 % salinity contour) was reduced by the presence of LPL and cutoff wall. During the initial stage (0.25 years) of VSWI occurrence, the vertical intrusion process of seawater exhibited similarity across all four cases. In this stage, saline water infiltrated the unsaturated zone rapidly and permeated the saturated zone in a finger-like pattern. After 1.0 years, LPL and cutoff wall have a significant influence on the evolution of VSWI resulting from storm surges. Comparing Case H with Case L, the vertical intrusion distance of VSWI in Case L is shortened and the saline plume cannot penetrate LPL due to the fact: 1）the low permeability of LPL inhibits the downward infiltration of the saline plume; and 2) LPL enhances the groundwater flow rate in the upper high-K layer, which makes saltwater diffusion in the horizontal direction dominate. Compared to Case H, the inland freshwater fluxes in Case L are more unevenly distributed due to LPL, with larger fluxes in the upper and bottom layers than in LPL. Consequently, larger pore water velocities accelerated the discharge of saltwater from the upper high-K layer under Case L conditions (years 3 to 5 of Fig. 3 ). The small amount of salinization plume in Case L that enters LPL will be retained for a longer period (years 3 to 5 in Fig. 3 ), which is attributed to reduced flow velocities within LPL, resulting in a gradual release of the retained salinization plume. Compared with Case H, the vertical intrusion distance of the salinization plume in Case C is longer and almost reaches the bottom of the aquifer. On the one hand, it is because the cutoff wall hinders the horizontal transport of the salinization plume. On the other hand, it is because the cutoff wall slows down the flow of water behind the wall, which enhances the finger-flow effect under the density gradient, and the salinization plume can reach deeper into the aquifer. Years 3 to 5 of Fig. 3  show that the recovery time of the aquifer will be prolonged by the cutoff wall. This is related to the fact that the cutoff wall impedes upstream and downstream hydraulic connections and lengthens the path of saltwater transport. The vertical invasion distance of the saline plume in Case CL was both inhibited by LPL and enhanced by the cutoff wall. Thus, the vertical invasion depth of saline plumes in Case CL was intermediate between Case L and Case C and comparable to Case H. From the perspective of aquifer recovery rate, the discharge of saline plume in Case CL is significantly slower than the other three cases for two reasons. Firstly, on the one hand, the cutoff wall hinders the horizontal transport of saltwater in the upper high-K layer and lengthens the path of saltwater transport. Secondly, on the other hand, the cutoff wall allows more saltwater to enter into LPL, which is slow to transport salt, and saltwater therein takes a longer time to be completely removed.  3.2 Measurable diagnostics of salinization plume Fig. 5   compares the temporal trends of measurable metrics (M , VS ) to evaluate the progression of the salinization plume generated by VSWI. 3.2.1 Time-varying process of m  In Fig. 5 a, the total salt mass for all cases initially increases rapidly to its maximum value and then gradually decreases. Maximum M  (Mmax  ) follows the order of Case H>Case L>Case C>Case CL (Fig. 5 d). The varying reductions in maximum M  observed in the other cases, as compared to Case H, are due to the presence of LPL and cutoff wall, which raise the groundwater level in the aquifer prior to the storm surge event (as shown in Fig. 5 c). The effect of the cutoff wall on the groundwater table is in general agreement with the results of Chang et al. (2023) . The rise of groundwater level inhibits the vertical intrusion of seawater, resulting in a lower maximum M  (as the higher the groundwater level, the lower maximum M ). As can be seen in Fig. 5 d, under the combined influence of LPL and cutoff wall, Mmax   of Case CL decreases more (relative to Case C) than the sum of the effects of the single LPL (Case L) and cutoff (Case C). This corresponds to the degree of initial groundwater level increase for Case L, Case C, and Case CL relative to Case C in Fig. 5 c. The M  values for Case L were consistently lower than Case H. The recovery time of aquifer (Tre  ) was 6.59 and 5.88 years in Case H and Case L, respectively, with Case L recovering 10.77 % faster than Case H (Fig. 5 f). This seems to be contrary to the results obtained by Vithanage et al. (2012)  at the laboratory scale. We suspect that there are several reasons for this result. Firstly, when the same density of seawater is used (same pressure gradient due to density change), saltwater is more likely to enter LPL in the middle of the aquifer because the experimental flume has a much smaller scale in the vertical direction compared to a field-scale aquifer (More saltwater getting into LPL may make recovery slower). Secondly, Vithanage et al. (2012)  used a head-control boundary on landward side, so LPL inhibits the total amount of freshwater inflow to the flume, which ultimately lengthens the aquifer recovery time. Thirdly, we use a flux control boundary on landward side so that the total amount of freshwater flowing into the aquifer is not reduced. Therefore, LPL does not extend the recovery time of the aquifer under certain conditions. Fourthly, the location of LPL directly affects the amount of saltwater entering LPL, and the higher LPL is located, the more saltwater enters LPL and the more likely it is that aquifer recovery will be delayed. Finally, storm surge intensity is also an important influence. The greater the storm surge intensity, the greater the degree of VSWI, which means more saltwater is likely to enter LPL. A comparison of Case H and Case C reveals that M  in Case C gradually exceeds that of Case H after about year 1.3. Between the 2nd and 6th year, the total salt mass of Case C significantly surpasses that of Case H. The recovery time of aquifer (Tre  ) in Case H is 6.59 years, while the corresponding time for Case C is 8.58 years. Even though Mmax   was less in Case C than in Case H, the recovery rate of Case C was 30.20 % slower than that of Case H (Fig. 5 f). This is apparently the result of the cutoff wall increasing the depth of vertical saltwater intrusion and impeding the horizontal transport of saltwater. For Case CL, which considers the combined effects of LPL and the cutoff wall, its M  is the smallest in the early stage (0–1.2 years), and then gradually exceeds that of the other three cases. In particular, between year 4 and year 8, the M  of Case CL is significantly larger than that of the other three cases. Although the Mmax   of Case CL was reduced by 14.31 %, 11.21 %, and 9.45 % compared to Case H, Case L, and Case C, respectively, its recovery was 95.14 %, 118.71 %, and 49.88 % slower than that of Case H, Case L, and Case C, respectively. The reason is that the cutoff wall hinders the discharge of the salinization plume from the upper high-K layer, and almost of the salinization plume has to bypass LPL in order to be discharged from the aquifer, which greatly reduces the natural recovery capacity of the aquifer.  3.2.2 Time-varying process of VS  Fig. 5 b illustrates a time-varying process of VS  that is comparable to M , but the differences in VS  among the four cases differ from M . The response time of the maximum VS  significantly lags behind that of the maximum M , indicating the predominant accumulation of salinity in the unsaturated zone initially, followed by gradual spreading until reaching the maximum salinized volume due to rainfall recharge and terrestrial groundwater discharge. Maximum VS  (VSmax  ) follows the order of Case C>Case CL>Case H>Case L (Fig. 5 e). The vertical transport of the salinization plume is restricted by LPL, resulting in a notably lower maximum VS  in Case L compared to Case H, and the VS  of Case L is always lower than that of Case H. Case L reaches the maximum VS  slightly earlier than Case H. This is because the obstruction of LPL in the vertical direction leads to the majority of the salinization plume being discharged through the upper high-K layer, and LPL increases the flow velocity in the upper high-K layer, resulting in faster horizontal dispersion of the salinization plume. A comparison of Case H and Case C shows that the VS  of Case C has been consistently larger than that of Case H from year 0.6 onwards. For example, between year 1 and year 5, the average VS  of Case C is 300 m2  larger than that of Case H. This observation suggests that the construction of the cutoff wall will result in an expansion in the salinized volume. It is clear that this increase in the area of salinization is primarily the result of an increase in the depth of invasion in the vertical direction. Compared to the other three cases, Case CL experiences a slightly delayed maximum VS  and exhibits a significantly slower decline rate. For example, from year 3.8 to year 10, Case CL maintains a notably higher VS  compared to the other cases. This is because the cutoff wall enables the majority of the salinization plume to enter LPL with slower water-flow velocity, resulting in a prolonged time for Case CL to reach its maximum VS  and a decelerated rate of VS  decline. The presence of LPL restricts the vertical dispersion of the salinization plume within the aquifer, resulting in a lower maximum VS  in Case CL compared to Case C. Conversely, the cutoff wall facilitates the migration of a portion of the salinization plume across LPL towards the lower high-K zone, leading to a higher maximum VS  in Case CL compared to Case L. The maximum VS  of Case CL was slightly larger than that of Case H, suggesting that the inhibitory effect of LPL on the vertical depth of saline intrusion at this time was slightly weaker than the facilitatory effect of cutoff wall.    4 Sensitivity analysis Based on Case CL, we further explored the effects of cutoff wall depth (Hc), cutoff wall location (DL), thickness of LPL (TL), elevation of LPL (LL), and hydraulic conductivity of LPL (KL) on VSWI in coastal aquifer. The evaluation metrics used in the sensitivity analysis include: maximum M  (Mmax  ), maximum VS  (VSmax  ), and recovery time of coastal aquifer (Tre  ). 4.1 Influences of cutoff wall depth Fig. 6  a shows the impact of cutoff wall depth on Mmax   in a layered heterogeneous aquifer. The homogeneous case (Case H) without cutoff wall construction exhibits a higher Mmax   compared to the other cases. Mmax   is expected to decrease as Hc increases (Fig. 6 a), which correlates with the initial groundwater level of the aquifer before the storm surge event (a higher initial groundwater level results in a smaller Mmax  ). As depicted in Fig. 6 c, in Case H, the initial groundwater level is the lowest, while it increases with rising Hc. When Hc = 14 and 16 m, the differences in their Mmax   is minimal (varying by only 0.63 kg) due to the proximity of the initial groundwater levels. Fig. 6 b shows the impact of cutoff wall depth on VSmax  . Unlike Mmax  , VSmax   showed a non-monotonic relationship with Hc. As Hc increases, VSmax   first increases (from Hc = 0 ∼ 14 m) then decreases (from Hc = 14 ∼ 16 m) and then increases (from Hc = 16 ∼ 18 m). Overall, however, VSmax   maintains a gradual increase as Hc increases. The changes in VSmax   are significant when Hc increases from 0 to 14 m. However, the changes become relatively small when Hc increases from 14 to 18 m. This suggests that VSmax   is insensitive to changes in Hc as Hc increases to a certain value. Fig. 6 d shows that construction of the cutoff wall lengthened the recovery time of the layered heterogeneous aquifer, suggesting that the saline plume is flushed more slowly than it would be without the barrier. As Hc increases from 10 m to 18 m, Tre   does not increase but gradually decreases. The superficial reason for this counterintuitive phenomenon (i.e., Tre   decreases with increasing cutoff wall depth) lies in the disparity in the rate of saltwater removal within LPL. Saltwater migration within LPL is very slow; at the same time, some of the saltwater that enters the underlying high-K layer needs to re-pass through LPL before it can exit the aquifer. Therefore, the removal time of saltwater within LPL essentially determines the recovery time of the entire aquifer. As can be seen from the course of saltwater mass (Mlpl  ) in LPL under different Hc conditions (Fig. 11 a), the pattern of change in the clearance time of Mlpl   with Hc is basically the same as that of the corresponding Tre  . For example, Tre   will be unusually large at Hc = 10 m, which also corresponds to the presence of a very slow decline in Mlpl   at this time. Of course, the deeper reasons for the differences in saltwater mass removal rates can be attributed to differences in total saltwater intrusion and aquifer flow rate variations. On the one hand, a deeper cutoff wall will effectively reduce the total amount of saltwater intruding into the aquifer after a storm surge event, which is to some extent conducive to accelerating aquifer recovery. For example, when the bottom of the cutoff wall belows the lower surface of LPL (Hc = 16 and 18 m), the Mmax   at Hc = 18 m is smaller, and therefore the recovery period will be shorter. Similarly, compared to the case where the bottom end of the cutoff wall insides LPL (Hc = 14 m), when the bottom end of the cutoff wall enters the lower high-K zone (Hc = 16 m), Mmax   shows a decline and therefore recovers more quickly. This is also clearly reflected in the changes in the Mlpl   curves: at Hc = 14 and 16 m, both Mlpl   curves have essentially the same rate in the descending phase, but the peak of the Mlpl   at Hc = 16 m is smaller, and therefore the recovery period is shorter. On the other hand, the change in flow rate due to cutoff wall may be an important reason for the difference in Tre   (Figure S1 ). Firstly, compared to the case where the bottom end of the cutoff wall fails to enter LPL (Hc = 10 m), when the bottom end of the cutoff wall locates within LPL (Hc = 12 and 14 m), flow velocities within LPL, particularly in the area of the freshwater discharge channel downstream of the cutoff wall, will be significantly higher. Increased flow velocity accelerates the dispersion and transport of the salinity plume within LPL and freshwater drainage channel areas, and this is also reflected in the rate of decline of the Mlpl   curve. Secondly, for the case where the bottom of the cutoff wall is within the LPL (Hc = 12, 14 m), although the peak Mlpl   at Hc = 14 m is higher than that at Hc = 12 m, the slightly higher velocity within the LPL at Hc = 14 m results in a faster decay of the Mlpl   curve, thus shortening the overall recovery time. Finally, when the bottom end of the cutoff wall is below the lower surface of LPL, all of the saline water must pass through the lower high-K zone before it can be discharged. Although the peak Mlpl   at Hc = 18 m was higher than the peak Mlpl   at Hc = 16 m, the rate of decline of Mlpl   in the former was greater in the earlier and later periods, which may be related to the increased flow velocity in the bottom high-K zone (Figure S1 ).  4.2 Influences of cutoff wall location Fig. 7  a illustrates the impact of varying the distance of the cutoff wall from the seawater boundary on Mmax  . In Case H, Mmax   is significantly higher than the other cases. Mmax   does not follow a monotonic relationship with DL: it initially decreases and then increases as DL increases, and the maximum and minimum Mmax   are observed at DL equal to 55 and 70 m, respectively. Furthermore, the distribution of the initial groundwater level (Fig. 7 c) provides additional evidence that supports the relationship between Mmax   and DL: the groundwater level reaches its lowest point when DL is equal to 55 m and its highest point when DL is equal to 70 m; additionally, the groundwater level demonstrates a pattern of initially increasing and then decreasing with the increase in DL. VSmax   for different DL cases is depicted in Fig. 7 b. It is observed that VSmax   shows a pattern of initially increasing, then decreasing with increasing DL. Interestingly, this is the exact opposite of the law for Mmax  . We suspect there are two main reasons for this phenomenon. Firstly, unlike the other cases, the groundwater flow rate upstream of the cutoff wall does not weaken at DL=55 m, but rather strengthens, implying that there is a saltwater discharge zone on the beach surface behind the cutoff wall (Figure S2 ). A large amount of saltwater exits the drainage channel behind the cutoff wall, only a small fraction of the saltwater enters the interior of LPL (Fig. 11 b), and intrusion of the saline plume in the vertical direction is also limited by LPL. Therefore, on the whole, at DL=55 m, the saltwater is almost entirely concentrated in the upper high-K layer, and the area of saltwater pollution is greatly reduced (Figure S3 ). Secondly, after DL >= 70 m, the salinization plume needs to bypass the cutoff wall before being discharged out of the aquifer. At this point, the effects of LPL and cutoff wall on the dispersion of the salted plume in the vertical direction are essentially the same across DL scenarios, i.e., DL does not significantly affect the dispersion of the salted plume in the vertical direction (Figure S3 ). However, in terms of diffusion in the horizontal direction, a larger DL means that the spatial area behind the cutoff wall for the salinization plume to diffuse in the horizontal direction is smaller. Therefore, VSmax   gradually decreased when DL was increased from 70 to 100 m. Fig. 7 d shows that the location of the cutoff wall has a huge impact on the recovery time (Tre  ) of a layered heterogeneous aquifer, and the location of the cutoff wall too close to the marine boundary may greatly prolong the recovery time. As DL increases from 55 m to 100 m, Tre   decreases in steps. VSmax   and Mmax   at DL=55 m are smaller than Case H, but its Tre   nearly tripled. The reason for this is that the clearance of saline in LPL at this time is very slow, and Mlpl   undergoes an extremely long decay period (Fig. 11  b). The deeper reason for this phenomenon is that the cutoff wall compresses the freshwater discharge channel (Figure S2 ), and the area of increased flow velocity within LPL triggered by the cutoff wall is significantly smaller, which in turn leads to slower overall recovery. As the DL increases from 70 m to 100 m, although Mmax   gradually increases, Tre   gradually decreases, in the same way that the clearance time of Mlpl   is related to DL. The reason for this pattern is that as DL increases, the freshwater discharge channel will be closer inland, especially in the zone of increased velocity in LPL (Figure S2 ). This means that saltwater can be discharged earlier from LPL, which will greatly reduce the removal time of the saline plume. This is also corroborated by the Mlpl   curves in Fig. 11 b: as DL increases, the Mlpl   curves can start to decrease earlier.  4.3 Influence of the thickness of LPL Different LPL thicknesses were used to investigate the impact of LPL thickness on the natural recovery of VSWI in layered aquifers with installed cutoff wall. Fig. 8  a illustrates the impact of TL on Mmax  . Mmax   of Case H is 3486.42 kg, exceeding that of the other cases. Mmax   reduces with increasing TL (Fig. 8 a), which is due to the variance in the initial groundwater level (Fig. 8 c) —Case H displays the lowest initial groundwater level, while the initial groundwater level increases with the growth of TL. The drop in Mmax   during the increase in TL from 4 to 5 m (50 kg), which is significantly smaller than the drop in TL from 5 to 14 m (174 ∼ 210 kg), and this also corresponds to the difference in the initial groundwater level (Fig. 8  c). Fig. 8 b illustrates the impact of TL on VSmax  . The highest VSmax   was observed in the case of TL equal to 0 m (Case C). VSmax   decreased monotonically as TL increased from 0 m to 14 m (Fig. 8 b). This is related to the decrease in Mmax   and the inhibition of salinization plume diffusion by LPL. Fig. 8 a, Fig. 8 b and Fig. 8 d shows that the presence of an intermediate LPL reduces the total amount of saltwater intrusion, but significantly increases the recovery time of aquifer. Relative to the case with TL=0 m, the average increase in Tre   for the other cases (TL over 0 m) was 49.07 %. There was no monotonic relationship between Tre   and TL as TL increased from 4 m to 14 m. Tre   showed a tendency to increase and then decrease. The course of saltwater mass (Mlpl  ) in LPL under different TL conditions shows (Fig. 11 c) that there is also no monotonic relationship between the removal times of Mlpl   and TL. The effects of cutoff wall and LPL on groundwater flow rates (Figure S5 ) and total saltwater intrusion lead to differences in the peaks of Mlpl   as well as the rate of decline, which ultimately affects aquifer recovery. Overall, an increase in TL does not necessarily lead to an increase in aquifer recovery time.  4.4 Influence of the elevation of LPL We simulated four additional scenarios (LL=8、10、14、16 m) to study the sensitivity of LL. As shown in Fig. 9  a, Mmax   in Case H is still greater than in the other cases; moreover, as LL increases, Mmax   exhibits a pattern of decreasing before increasing. The relationship between Mmax   and LL is consistent with the difference in initial groundwater level (Fig. 9 c). The groundwater level rises as LL increases from 8 to 12 m. Subsequently, the groundwater level gradually decreases as LL increases from 12 to 16 m. Fig. 9 b shows the impact of LL on VSmax  . VSmax   exhibits a pattern of initially increasing, and then decreasing. From the recovery time under different LL conditions in Fig. 9 d, as LL increased from 8 m to 16 m, Tre  increased by an average of 7.3 years relative to Case H. As LL increases from 8 m to 16 m, Tre   shows a general trend of increasing, but deviates at LL=10 m. The course of saltwater mass (Mlpl  ) in LPL under different LL conditions shows (Fig. 11 d) that the relationship between the removal time of Mlpl   and LL is consistent with that between Tre   and LL. At LL=8 m, although Mmax   is larger, most of saltwater will flow out of aquifer from the top high-K layer due to the large spacing between the bottom of the cutoff all and the LPL (Figure S5 ); moreover, only a small portion of saltwater will enter the LPL (Fig. 11 d). Therefore, the saltwater removal is faster at this time (compared to the scenarios with LL=10, 12, 14, and 16 m). Relative to other scenarios (LL=12, 14, 16 m), the Mmax   at LL=10 m is not the highest, but the Tre   at this point is significantly greater than that of other scenarios, which is related to the rate of saltwater clearance within the LPL. As can be seen in Fig. 11  d, the peak Mlpl   for LL=10 m is smaller compared to the peak Mlpl   for other scenarios (LL=12, 14, 16 m), but the rate of descent is on the small side. The deeper reason for the smaller rate of decline in Mlpl   is when LL=10 m, there is not a significant zone of increased flow velocity within LPL (Figure S5 ), which slows down the removal of saltwater from LPL. As LL exceeds 12 m, the increase in the peak Mlpl   (Fig. 11 d) and decrease in the degree of increase in flow velocity within LPL (Figure S4 ) are the main reasons for the gradual increase in Tre  .  4.5 Influence of the KL of LPL Numerical experiments were conducted on LPL with varying hydraulic conductivity (KL) to investigate the influence of hydraulic conductivity on VSWI. The KL used in each scenario was obtained from the model of Zhang et al. (2021) . LSWI was found to be unstable when KL equaled 4.576 × 10-6  m/s and 1.447 × 10-6  m/s (Fig. S6 ). The reason for this phenomenon is that LPL and cutoff wall inhibit groundwater discharge to the ocean. As a result, the gravitational fluid velocity surpasses the background fluid velocity, thus creating unstable flows (Menand and Woods, 2005 ). At this point, Eq. (12)  to Eq. (19) cannot account for the influence of an unsteady saltwater wedge, and the calculated total salt mass, and salinized volume cannot accurately reflect the impact of VSWI. Based on the temporal and spatial variations of salt concentration during the VSWI process, it can be seen (Figure S6 ) that saltwater intrusion caused by storm surge inundation mainly occurs behind the cutoff wall. As a result, the amount of saltwater intrusion in the area to the right of the cutoff wall basically reflects the total amount of saltwater intrusion in the aquifer. At the same time, if the location of the cutoff wall is used as the dividing line, when the saltwater in the area to the right of the dividing line is completely removed, it can basically be considered that the saltwater in the aquifer is completely removed (Figure S6 ). Therefore, we used the location of the cutoff wall as a dividing line to evaluate the effect of LPL permeability on VSWI by calculating Mmax  , VSmax  , and Tre   for the saline plume in the region to the right of that line. In Fig. 10   a, Mmax   gradually decreases as KL decreases, which is consistent with the initial groundwater level conditions on the right side of the cutoff wall (Fig. 10 c), where the groundwater level rises as KL decreases. As KL decreases, VSmax   initially decreases, then increases, and then decreases again; moreover, the maximum and minimum VSmax   occur at KL values of 4.576 × 10-5  m/s and 1.447 × 10-6  m/s, respectively (Fig. 10 b). From the recovery times under different KL conditions in Fig. 10 d, relative to Case H, although Mmax   decreased to different degrees under different KL conditions, Tre   increased significantly, with an average increase of 67.6 %. The non-monotonic characterization between KL and Tre   suggests a complex relationship between them. Compared to the case where KL is large, Tre   instead decreases when KL is low enough. This result suggests that a decrease in the permeability coefficient of LPL does not necessarily increase the recovery time of aquifer when the bottom of the cutoff wall locates in LPL.   5 Discussion This study emphasizes the importance of typical stratification heterogeneity (low permeability layer located between two high permeability layers) and cutoff walls for VSWI processes in coastal aquifers triggered by a single storm surge. By conceptualizing a typical two-dimensional beach dip profile, we investigated the combined effects of cutoff wall and layered heterogeneity on the natural recovery of a coastal aquifer after a single storm surge event. Our results show that cutoff wall and LPL is effective in reducing seawater infiltration but prolonging the recovery time of the aquifer. 5.1 VSWI due to storm surge inundation in layered aquifers Vithanage et al. (2012)  found, based on laboratory tank experiments and numerical simulation methods, that the slower flow of saltwater in low-permeability layer (LPL) resulted in a 40 % increase in the complete flush-out time of saltwater. We believe that the experimental and numerical simulation approach of Vithanage et al. (2012)  suffers from two shortcomings. First, in their simulation of aquifer salinization due to storm surge inundation, saltwater intrusion was not created by natural infiltration from the surface due to seawater inundation, but rather took the form of applying saltwater at a constant rate flux through a drip tube with the drip tip immediately below the water table. This ignores both the problem of declining total saltwater intrusion due to the uplifting effect of LPL on the water table, and the fact that saltwater intrusion due to seawater inundation is spatially and temporally inhomogeneous on the beach. Second, LPL leads to changes in freshwater drainage pathways, but they do not consider the lateral saltwater intrusion that would have been present at the same time, which is likely to affect saltwater drainage. Contrary to the results of Vithanage et al. (2012) . Our study shows that under certain conditions, LPL not only reduces the amount of seawater infiltration and the area of salinization, but also effectively shortens the recovery time. This is partly because LPL reduces the total amount of saltwater intrusion and the amount of saltwater that enters within LPL is so small that LPL does not have a large impact on recovery time. On the other hand, it is because the presence of LPL makes the inland freshwater flux distribution more heterogeneous, with increased fluxes in the top and bottom layers, and therefore, the larger groundwater flow rate in the top layer accelerates the discharge of saltwater from the top layer. Based on Case L, we further explored the effect of the thickness (TL) and elevation (LL) of the LPL in a layered aquifer on Tre. Calculations show that both TL and LL maintain a non-monotonic relationship with Tre, and that the presence of LPL does not necessarily lead to an increase in aquifer recovery time (Figure S8 ). This phenomenon is the result of a number of factors: (1) the stratification pattern significantly affects the total amount of saltwater intrusion during storm surges; (2) the amount of saltwater that enters the LPL also varies considerably from case to case, which will also affect the recovery time; and (3) the presence of the LPL results in a more heterogeneous distribution of inland freshwater fluxes, which has a significant impact on the discharge of saltwater.  5.2 Feasibility of constructing cutoff wall Past studies have demonstrated that cutoff walls significantly increase groundwater flow time (Lu et al., 2019 ). Our studies have also shown that although the cutoff wall reduces the amount of seawater that infiltrates into the aquifer from the surface (in the sense that the cutoff wall not only prevents lateral intrusion of seawater, but also inhibits the degree of vertical intrusion of seawater from the surface of the beach), it also drastically slows the rate of recovery of the aquifer. This is because the cutoff wall increases the extent of vertical intrusion of saltwater, more saltwater is carried into LPL and deeper areas of the aquifer, and saltwater will be more difficult to flush, thus slowing recovery. Past research on cutoff wall for recovery of homogeneous aquifers after storm surges remains deficient. For example, the study by Yang et al. (2021)  did not consider inland freshwater recharge, and the effect of cutoff wall length variation was not considered in the homogenized case of the study by Song et al. (2022) . To address these issues, we further explore the effect of cutoff wall length variation on Tre   in a homogeneous aquifer considering inland freshwater recharge. Calculations show that Hc maintains a non-monotonic relationship with Tre  . Specifically, as Hc increases, Tre   first increases (Hc = 10 m to 16 m) and then decreases (Hc = 16 m to 18 m) (Figure S9 ). Construction of the cutoff wall will slow the recovery of the homogeneous aquifer by 16.84 % to 142.33 %. In conjunction with our results, for coastal aquifers that can be approximated as homogeneous, an appropriate increase in the length of the cutoff wall may be more conducive to accelerated aquifer recovery when the threat of other contaminants is not considered. Most of the previous studies have focused only on the role of cutoff walls in mitigating LSWI and exacerbating nitrate contaminant accumulation in layered heterogeneous aquifers, while neglecting their compounding effect on the recovery process of aquifer salinization caused by extreme hazards such as storm surges. When LPL locates in the middle of the aquifer, the greater the depth of the cutoff wall, the lesser the seawater intrusion and the faster the aquifer can recover. Conversely, if the depth of the cutoff wall is too small at this point, it may instead result in a surge in aquifer recovery time and significantly reduce the performance of the cutoff wall against lateral seawater intrusion. In other words, at this point, the cutoff wall should go through at least the top of the LPL in order to be able to prevent severe VSWI and LSWI. A study by Gao et al. (2022)  showed that nitrate contamination increases with cutoff wall length in the scenario where the LPL is located in the middle of the aquifer. Combining Gao et al. (2022)  and our results, when the base of the cutoff wall is located near the centre of the LPL, a balance can be struck between the prevention effect of lateral seawater intrusion, the recovery rate of vertical seawater intrusion, and the enrichment effect of nitrate pollution. When the bottom end of the cutoff wall is placed within LPL, the location of the cutoff wall installation can have a significant effect on the salinization process in the aquifer. Cutoff wall is too close to the ocean for there to be limited change in lateral seawater intrusion distance; however, there will be a significant increase in aquifer recovery time after a storm surge. From the numerical simulation results, the further the cutoff wall is from the ocean, the more the aquifer recovers. According to Sun et al. (2021) , if the barrier location is closer to the seashore, the greater the degree of nitrate accumulation. In this sense, the construction of cutoff walls away from the seashore is encouraged. Layering pattern is a key factor controlling aquifer recovery. From the relationship of Tre   with TL, LL and KL, the effect of LL on Tre seems to be more significant. When the LPL is located near the top of the aquifer, the construction of a cutoff wall would greatly extend the recovery time of the aquifer, and in that sense, the construction of a cutoff wall is not encouraged. In terms of the relationship between Tre   and TL, although the increase in LPL thickness significantly reduces the saline area and the total amount of saline water, Tre   increases by 34 % to 60 %. In this sense, the construction of cutoff walls needs to be particularly careful when the LPL thickness is large. The relationship between permeability and Tre   shows that when the LPL has a high permeability level (KL>10-5  m/s), the Tre   is greater than when the LPL has a high permeability level (KL<10-5  m/s). Therefore, from this perspective, the construction of cutoff walls is encouraged when the permeability of the LPL is low enough. In addition, from the results obtained for cases 5 and 17 in Table 2 , we find that Tre   is substantially increased when the spacing between the bottom of cutoff wall and the upper surface of LPL is very small. Therefore, when constructing a cutoff wall in a stratified aquifer, it is important to ensure sufficient space between the bottom of cutoff wall and the upper surface of LPL if the cutoff wall is not required to penetrate the LPL for specific reasons. It is important to note that, as in the study by Yang et al. (2021) , we did not consider the effect of the rebalancing process of the saltwater wedge on aquifer recovery after the cutoff wall construction was completed. Gao et al. (2021)  showed that after the cutoff wall is built, the toe of the saltwater wedge initially advances forward and then gradually recedes from the aquifer behind the wall. Therefore, the aquifer recovery process in this study is modeled under the assumption that the saltwater wedge reaches a new equilibrium after the construction of the cutoff wall.  5.3 Initial exploration of 3D systems This study uses a two-dimensional cross-sectional model perpendicular to the shoreline, which has been frequently used in past studies (Cardenas et al., 2015; Song et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021 ); however, this seems to ignore the effect of the presence of spatial inhomogeneities in the VSWI in a three-dimensional system. To this end, further three-dimensional analyses based on Case H, Case C, Case L, and Case CL were conducted to show that the results of this paper can be applied to predict the recovery time of the aquifer after a single storm surge event in a three-dimensional system. The mathematical model setup of the 3D system is shown in Text S1 of the Supporting Information . Comparison of Figure S11  and Fig. 5  (d ∼ f) shows that the results of the 3D numerical model and the 2D cross-section numerical model have a consistent pattern. This suggests that the results and laws obtained from the 2D cross-section model (perpendicular to the coastline) are equally applicable to the 3D system.  5.4 Model simplifications and limitations Seasonal groundwater level fluctuations have a large impact on fresh groundwater flux and contaminant migration, and enhanced mixing effects due to seasonal flow conditions may lead to wider spreading of the salinization plume, thus affecting the timescale of aquifer recovery. In this case, the combined effects of seasonal flow conditions on storm surge inundation-induced groundwater salinization need to be further investigated. In this study, a 2D cross-section model perpendicular to the coastline was used, and although a preliminary exploration was carried out concerning the 3D system, it should be noted that we did not consider the influence of the beach topography, and therefore further three-dimensional analyses are necessary. Our results are based on the concept of a typical three-layered layered aquifer with an intermediate low-permeability layer, and VSWI analysis triggered by a single storm-surge event may be extended to multilayered aquifers due to the greater complexity of real-world heterogeneity. The occurrence of recurring storm surges is unavoidable, especially during high-frequency storm surge events driven by climate change, and the mechanisms of salinization of the aquifer will be more complex, so the current models will need to be appropriately refined to provide a better understanding of real-world configurations.   6 Conclusion This study investigates the combined effects of layered heterogeneity and cutoff wall on storm surge-induced VSWI in coastal aquifers using variable saturation-variable density groundwater flow and salt transport simulations. We quantify the spatial and temporal evolution of VSWI resulting from a single storm surge event by calculating the total salt mass, salinized volume, and recovery time of coastal aquifer. We perform a single-factor analysis to evaluate the effects of cutoff wall depth, cutoff wall location, LPL thickness, LPL elevation, and hydraulic conductivity of LPL on the salinization and recovery process of groundwater in the aquifer. From this study, the following conclusions can be drawn:(1) Compared with the homogeneous case, groundwater levels will be elevated by the combination of LPL and cutoff wall (which reduces the vertical component of the hydraulic gradient), resulting in a reduction of total vertical saltwater intrusion of 3.5 % to 35.0 % during a single storm surge. The cutoff wall impedes the horizontal transport of salinization plume and prolongs the saltwater discharge path, while the flushing rate of the trapped salinization plume within the LPL is slower. Their combined effects result in varying degrees of prolongation of aquifer recovery time.  (2) LPL would limit vertical transport of salinization plume and reduce depth of intrusion of salinization plume in vertical direction, so LPL prefers to reduce salinized area in the aquifer following a storm surge event. In contrast, the obstructive effect of cutoff wall in horizontal direction increases depth of invasion of salinization plume in vertical direction, therefore, cutoff wall prefers to increase salinized area.  (3) In coastal layered heterogeneous aquifers, the location and length of cutoff wall control the aquifer recovery time after a storm surge event, and the recovery time shows a nonmonotonic trend with the cutoff wall parameter.  (4) The thickness, elevation, and hydraulic conductivity of LPL can dramatically alter VSWI processes (including maximum mass of saltwater intrusion, maximum salinized area, and aquifer recovery time). In addition, saltwater removal within the LPL essentially determines the recovery time for the entire aquifer.  (5) The feasibility of constructing a cutoff wall may significantly depend on the location and thickness of LPL in aquifer. Generally, constructing a cutoff wall (i) is recommended on aquifer when LPL near the base of aquifer because cutoff wall increases freshwater storage and also has a relatively weak impact on natural recovery capacity of aquifer, (ii) requires special caution on aquifer with higher LPL thicknesses, because cutoff wall can not significantly improve the control of LSWI, however, it is likely to substantially slow down aquifer recovery time after a storm surge event, and (iii) is recommended on aquifer when the permeability of LPL is small enough.    Overall, our study improves the understanding of the effect of cutoff wall in layered heterogeneous aquifer on vertical seawater intrusion caused by a storm surge. With the intensity of extreme events such as storm surges expected to increase as global sea level rises, the results of the study are useful for cutoff wall design and groundwater management in coastal areas at risk of storm surge inundation. Due to certain assumptions and limitations, future work should also consider the combined effects of other factors, including spatial stochastic heterogeneity, changes in inland recharge, sea level fluctuations and so on.
