These severe droughts have profound effects on terrestrial ecosystems, leading to the depletion of water resources and adversely affecting vegetation and crops, thereby posing a critical threat to food security in the context of a burgeoning global population (Roy, 2022; Shi et al., 2023 ). Meteorological droughts are commonly characterized by the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) introduced by Vicente-Serrano et al. in 2010 (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). This index offers a more comprehensive assessment of the "climate water balance" by incorporating potential evapotranspiration, presenting a more holistic measure compared to the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI). In contrast, monitoring hydrological droughts has traditionally faced challenges due to the limited availability of runoff data from hydrological stations. Historically, hydrological drought monitoring relied on hydrological models and observations, which suffered from restricted accuracy and spatiotemporal continuity. However, the advent of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) in 2002 has revolutionized hydrological drought monitoring (Yan, 2021; Zheng et al., 2023 ). Unlike traditional hydrological drought monitoring that included both streamflow and groundwater droughts, groundwater drought is now studied independently, primarily due to the reduction in groundwater recharge (Zhang et al., 2021 ). A significant advantage of GRACE is its unique ability to monitor groundwater storage anomalies through data such as soil water content from hydrological models like GLDAS. Utilizing these GRACE-retrieved anomalies, researchers can calculate a groundwater drought index, enabling more precise assessments and overcoming previous limitations. This method, pioneered by Thomas et al. (Thomas, 2017 ) and applied to California's Central Valley, has proven its efficacy in the region. Subsequent studies, such as those by Wang et al. (Wang, 2020 ), have employed GRACE data to identify severe drought cases and their primary causes on the North China Plain. Additionally, Han et al. (Han, 2021 ) explored the threshold at which meteorological droughts propagate into groundwater droughts and developed a probabilistic model to determine this propagation threshold. The complex relationship between vegetation response and drought is attributable to the inherent physiological properties of vegetation that confer drought resilience. This resilience manifests as reduced vegetation productivity, primarily through inhibited water transpiration and stomatal closure (Zhang, 2023 ). Consequently, shifts in water availability do not align immediately with changes in vegetation but exhibit a lagged response, underlining the gradual accumulation and the delayed impacts of drought as critical factors influencing vegetation growth (Yao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The conceptual distinction between the cumulative effect and the lag effect lies in that the former assesses the impact of a prolonged water deficit on current vegetation status and is utilized in evaluating drought resistance of vegetation, whereas the latter measures vegetation sensitivity at a specific temporal juncture (Zhan, 2022; Zhao et al., 2020 ). As the world's highest per capita crop producer, Argentina's agricultural and livestock sectors contribute approximately 7.3 % to the national GDP, with exports of food commodities and soybean oil ranking in the global top ten (Maydana et al., 2020; Rótolo, 2022 ). Over recent decades, the country has faced several severe droughts—in 2004, 2009, and 2012—which led to significant river depletion, reduced wheat production, and adversely affected soybean and corn exports (Sgroi et al., 2021 ). Given Argentina's substantial dependence on agriculture, it is imperative to understand the impacts of seasonal droughts on regional crop and vegetation cover. Although numerous studies have investigated the effects of meteorological and groundwater droughts on vegetation, there remains a limited understanding of how these drought types concurrently influence vegetation. Moreover, existing research has primarily focused on the immediate occurrences and physiological or biochemical impacts of droughts on vegetation, with less attention paid to the cumulative and lagged responses of vegetation to these events. To address these deficiencies, this study examined the cumulative and lagged effects of the SPEI and the Grace Groundwater Drought Index (GGDI) on the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). This analysis aimed to elucidate the response of different vegetation types in Argentina to meteorological and groundwater droughts. The primary research objectives were to: (1) validate the accuracy of GRACE application results in Argentina, (2) delineate the temporal patterns of drought occurrences from 2002 to 2022, (3) characterize the accumulated and delayed impacts of seasonal drought conditions, and (4) clarify how different vegetation types respond to the cumulative and lagged effects of SPEI and GGDI. The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights for policy formulation and the development of strategies for effective vegetation management and protection in response to various drought conditions.  2 Study area, data, and methodology 2.1 Study area and datasets The study area encompasses mainland Argentina, the eighth largest country in the world, located on the South American continent. According to the 2010 national census, Argentina has a population of 40,117,096. The National Institute of Statistics and Censuses of Argentina (INDEC) categorizes the country into five principal regions as shown in  Fig. 1 . The considerable geographic expanse of the study region results in a diverse climate ranging from subtropical in the north to polar in the south, with average annual temperatures of 25°C and 5°C, respectively (Beck et al., 2018). Precipitation varies dramatically across the country, ranging from as little as 150 mm annually in the driest areas to over 2000 mm in the western and northeastern regions. Agriculture, crucial to the national economy, utilizes approximately 30 million hectares of cultivated land, supporting Argentina's status as the global leader in per capita crop production (FAO, 2018 ). The reclassification using the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) reveals that northern Argentina predominantly comprises forests, central and eastern areas are largely croplands, the southern regions feature shrublands and grasslands, and the western section includes the high topography of the Andes Mountains ( Fig. 2 ). This detailed characterization underpins the study's examination of diverse environmental interactions. 2.1.1 GRACE gravity satellite The GRACE Gravity Satellite, a collaborative initiative between the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and NASA, monitors variations in Earth's gravitational field to detect changes in global terrestrial water storage (TWSA) (Tapley et al., 2004 ). For this study, we accessed the latest version of the GRACE dataset, known as RL06, provided by the Center for Space Research. This dataset, available from April 2002 to December 2022, features a monthly temporal resolution and a spatial resolution of 0.25°×0.25°. We employed the CSR mascon solution, which is favored over traditional spherical harmonics due to its reduced error rates and improved signal resolution (Scanlon, 2016 ). To address data gaps in the GRACE datasets, we utilized Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (mSSA) for grid time-series imputation (Agarwal et al., 2022 ).  2.1.2 Hydrological models We utilized the GLDAS Noah version 2.1 hydrological simulations dataset (https:// disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GLDAS_NOAH025_M_2.1/summary), which offers a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° and extends from 2000 to the present. This dataset includes critical variables such as soil moisture, canopy water content, snow water equivalent, and surface water storage anomalies, all of which are essential for large-scale hydrological assessments (Jing, 2020; Liu et al., 2023 ).  2.1.3 MODIS landuse (MCD12C1) The study employed the MCD12C1 dataset, which was reclassified using the IGBP methodology (Grekousis et al., 2015 ). The reclassification included grouping Croplands and Cropland/Natural vegetation under the Cropland category, while various forest types and Woody Savannas were categorized as Forest. Grasslands and Savannas were classified under Grasslands, and Closed and Open shrublands were labeled as Shrublands. The original data, with a 0.05° spatial resolution, was resampled to 0.25° to maintain consistency across datasets.  2.1.4 MODIS NDVI (MOD13C2) The MOD13C2 version 6.1 dataset was selected to calculate the NDVI, which is widely used to assess vegetation growth, coverage, and biomass. Like other datasets, the original monthly data with a 0.05° spatial resolution was resampled to 0.25° for analysis.  2.1.5 Meteorological data We sourced temperature, precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration data from the Climate Research Unit Time Series version 4.07 (CRU TS4.07) dataset to compute the SPEI. This dataset combines observed station records and climate model outputs that have undergone rigorous quality control (Sun, 2017 ). The acquired variables were resampled from a 0.5° spatial resolution to a 0.25° resolution, employing the nearest neighbor interpolation method (Liu et al., 2023 ).   2.2 Framework for vegetation response to drought  Fig. 3  illustrates the framework utilized to examine how vegetation responds to drought conditions. Initially, we computed two drought indices, the GGDI and the SPEI, using data from GRACE, GLDAS, and CRU datasets. Subsequently, we analyzed time-series data of GGDI, NDVI, and SPEI to identify drought events and assess changes in vegetation. Further, we examined vegetation's sensitivity to drought and its resilience, considering both the cumulative and lagged effects of GGDI, SPEI, and NDVI.  2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Calculation of groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) We isolated specific variables from the GLDAS dataset to compute the GWSA for Argentina. Additionally, the Total Water Storage Anomaly (TWSA) derived from GRACE data was incorporated into the calculation as follows (Ali, 2022; Xu et al., 2021 ):(1) GWSA = TWSA − SMSA − CWSA − SWEA − SWSA     where SMSA is the soil moisture storage anomalies, CWSA represents canopy water storage anomalies, SWEA indicates snow water equivalent anomalies, and SWSA denotes surface water storage anomalies.  2.3.2 GRACE groundwater drought index (GGDI) Groundwater drought in Argentina was identified using the GRACE data through the dimensionless GGDI (Zhao et al., 2022 ). The index is calculated as:(2) Ci =  1  n   ∑ 1  n   GWSi      (3) GSDt = GWS − Ci     (4) GGDI =  GSDt − μ GSD  σ GSD        Here, Ci   represents the monthly climatology, GSDt   is the groundwater storage deviation, and GGDI   is the Groundwater Drought Index. By quantifying GWSA and introducing GGDI as a dimensionless indicator, this study provides crucial insights for sustainable water resource management (Zhao et al., 2022 ).  2.3.3 Standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) The SPEI serves as a pivotal meteorological drought indicator, employed to evaluate the severity and duration of droughts. This study calculated the monthly SPEI for Argentina using precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PET) data sourced from the CRU TS version 4.07 dataset. SPEI indices from SPEI-01 to SPEI-12 were computed using the R programming language. These indices represent the SPEI calculated over timescales ranging from 1 to 12 months, respectively. SPEI-01 captures short-term (1-month) drought conditions, whereas SPEI-12 indicates long-term (12-month) drought conditions. By utilizing various SPEI timescales, this study assesses drought conditions over differing periods. For analyzing drought characteristics in Argentina, SPEI-03 was selected because it effectively captures variations in shallow groundwater levels (Li et al., 2021; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). Drought classifications are detailed in Table S1 .  2.3.4 Characterization of drought events The characterization of drought events typically relies on Run Theory (Eini et al., 2023; Yevjevich, 1967; Zha et al., 2023 ). This theory facilitates the assessment of drought frequency, severity, and intensity by identifying drought events when specified variables consistently fall below a predetermined threshold (González and Valdés, 2006 ). The operational details are depicted in Figure S1  (Le et al., 2019 ). The duration of a drought is defined as the number of consecutive months that the SPEI remains below a critical threshold. Frequency is calculated as the ratio of the total duration of drought episodes to the total observation period. Severity quantifies the cumulative values of SPEI and GGDI during a drought event, thus measuring the drought’s intensity and impact.  2.3.5 Cumulative and lagged effects of drought on vegetation Through Pearson’s correlation analysis, this study quantified both the cumulative and lagged effects of drought on vegetation response. The cumulative effect denotes the correlation between monthly NDVI and SPEI over 1–12 months. This analysis focused on identifying the maximum correlation of cumulative effects, denoted by r  i    , and the month corresponding to this maximum correlation, denoted by r  max _ cum    . The equations used are as follows (Xu, 2023 ):(5) r  i   = corr NDVI , SPEI  i       1  ≤  i  ≤  12     (6) r  _SPEI _ cum   = max r  i        1  ≤ i ≤  12     where r  i     represents the maximum correlation of the cumulative effects, i   is the time scale of cumulative effects from 1–12 months and r  _SPEI _ cum     is the month corresponding to the maximum cumulative correlation. The lagged effect is distinct from the cumulative effect, referring specifically to the influence of a past drought event on the present growth of vegetation (Zhao et al., 2020 ). This effect is quantified by correlating monthly NDVI data with lagged SPEI-01 and GGDI. Typically, this involves holding NDVI data constant while advancing SPEI-01 data by 1–12 months, thereby producing a relative lag in NDVI. For instance, with NDVI data spanning from April 2002 to June 2022, to study a one-month lag, SPEI-01 data are shifted from April 2002 to March 2002, resulting in a one-month lag represented by the data mismatch. However, due to the availability of GRACE datasets only from April 2002 to December 2022, this study adapts the traditional method by delaying NDVI data instead, aligning it with corresponding changes in SPEI-01 and GGDI. For example, for a one-month lag, SPEI-01 data from April 2002 to May 2022 correspond to NDVI data from May 2002 to June 2022, ensuring maximum data integrity. The correlations calculated are as follows:(7) r  s   = corr NDVIs , SPEI    ,  0 ≤ s ≤ 12     (8) r  _ SPEI _ lag   = max R  s        ,  0 ≤ s ≤ 12     (9) r  g   = corr NDVI  g   , SPEI    ,  0 ≤ g ≤ 12     (10) r  _ GGDI _ lag   = max R  g        ,   0 ≤ g ≤ 12      Here, r  s     represents the maximum correlation between NDVI and SPEI across different time lags, s   denotes the time scale from 1 m to 12 months, and r  _ SPEI _ lag     identifies the month showing the maximum correlation. Similarly, r  g     indicates the maximum correlation between NDVI and GGDI across time lags, g   is the time scale of cumulative effects from 1 m to 12 months, with r  _ GGDI _ lag     identifying the month of maximum correlation. Furthermore, the study utilized the annual average SPEI-12 from 2002 to 2022 as a measure of the water balance, defining the water balance gradient in 0.1 intervals. Regression analysis focused on the relationships between the mean maximum cumulative and lagged correlations and the response months with respect to the water balance gradient.  2.3.6 Cumulative and lagged effects of drought on vegetation A sliding window analysis method was introduced, employing a three-year interval mechanism to systematically explore the dynamic changes in the cumulative and lag effects of drought (Han, 2019 ). This approach factors in key environmental variables such as precipitation, temperature, and soil moisture, aiming to elucidate the intricate relationships between these variables and the impacts of drought on vegetation.    3 Results 3.1 Dynamics and verification of terrestrial water reserves To effectively utilize GRACE-TWSA data in Argentina, we validated it against the GLDAS hydrological model (Spennemann et al., 2020; Wang, 2020; Zhao et al., 2023 ). Our analysis revealed general consistency in terrestrial water storage trends between GRACE-TWSA and GLDAS-TWSA from 2002 to 2022, as depicted in  Fig. 4 . However, discrepancies were observed in the Cuyo region from 2009 to 2016, and in the Northwest from 2017 to 2021. These divergences may stem from the inclusion of components such as GWSA, SWSA, SMSA, and SWEA in the GRACE-TWSA, which are absent in the GLDAS-TWSA (Akhtar, 2022 ). Correlation analysis between GRACE-TWSA and GLDAS-TWSA from 2002 to 2022 demonstrated significant positive correlations across various provinces, underscoring the robustness of GRACE-TWSA data for hydrological assessments in Argentina. Despite regional variations, all correlations were significant (p < 0.001), with Patagonia showing the highest correlation coefficient of 0.67, indicating the strongest agreement. Notable outliers, attributed to discrepancies in GWSA between the two datasets, were identified, particularly in the Pampas region where a significant increase in GRACE-TWSA was noted in 2017, predominantly due to GWSA as illustrated in  Fig. 5 . These results affirm the reliability of GRACE-TWSA data for monitoring and managing water resources in Argentina's diverse hydrological environments. The significant correlations, even amidst notable regional differences, highlight the value of integrating GRACE data into hydrological models to enhance accuracy and support effective water management strategies.  3.2 Vegetation and drought trends As evidenced in Fig. 5 a-c, meteorological droughts in Argentina exhibit a declining trend across most regions, with the exception of the Northwest, Northeast, and parts of southern Pampas, where an increasing trend is observed. Conversely, groundwater drought shows a decrease across the entire Cuyo region and the southern part of Patagonia, while other areas experience an increasing trend. Similarly, NDVI indicates a declining trend in the Pampas, northern Cuyo, and most parts of Patagonia. The temporal patterns of SPEI, GGDI, and NDVI from 2002 to 2022 resemble a horizontal "S" shape, initially decreasing, then increasing, and subsequently decreasing again (Fig. 5 ). The vegetation in Argentina demonstrates high consistency with SPEI, both in spatial slope changes and in the time series analysis. For instance, in the Cuyo region, both NDVI and SPEI reached their respective nadirs in 2009, with SPEI at −2.30 in April and NDVI at 0.16 in October. In the Pampas, SPEI recorded its lowest value of −1.88 in June 2009, while NDVI reached its minimum of 0.34 in August 2009. These observations suggest that vegetation responds to meteorological drought with a discernible lag. In  Table 1 , the Run Theory is applied utilizing the SPEI index to identify drought events. We adopt the drought threshold as defined by previous researchers to characterize drought events (Ali, 2022 ). The analysis of SPEI across Argentine provinces reveals distinct patterns. The Northeast experienced the highest number of one-month drought occurrences, totaling 19 events. In contrast, both the Northwest and Patagonia recorded 17 instances of droughts lasting longer than three months each. The longest continuous droughts were observed in Cuyo and Pampas, each enduring for 17 months. Moreover, the most severe drought occurred in Cuyo, with an intensity of −1.84. These findings indicate that the Northeast predominantly encounters short-duration droughts, while regions such as Cuyo, Pampas, and Patagonia experience longer-lasting and more intense meteorological droughts. In comparison, the GGDI indicates fewer drought events but with longer maximum durations. For instance, the Northwest region recorded the highest number of one-month droughts, with eight occurrences, while the Northeast experienced the most extended droughts exceeding three months, with 11 instances. The longest continuous drought, as measured by the GGDI, occurred in the Pampas, lasting for 32 months and reaching an intensity of −32.58. These data suggest that meteorological droughts in Argentina tend to be of shorter duration but occur more frequently than groundwater droughts. Moreover, the intensity of meteorological droughts is generally higher than that of groundwater droughts. With the exception of the Pampas and Northwest regions, the severity of meteorological droughts in other provinces also surpasses that of groundwater droughts.   3.3 The cumulative and lagged effects of drought on vegetation growth  Fig. 6  illustrates the correlation between maximum cumulative effects and their corresponding months. Overall, 93.76 % of Argentina shows statistical significance, with 89.94 % exhibiting a significant positive correlation, covering nearly the entire study area. Conversely, 3.82 % of the area demonstrates a significant negative correlation, primarily concentrated in the western Andes and the southernmost part of Argentina (Fig. 6 a). Considering the cumulative effect of SPEI on vegetation, the most substantial impact is observed at the 3-month interval, affecting 35.44 % of the area. This is followed by 13.99 % at the 4-month interval and 13.56 % at the 5-month interval (Fig. 6 b). It is evident that the cumulative effect of SPEI on vegetation primarily occurs within short calendar periods, predominantly from February to May. Spatially, the Pampas and Northwest regions typically experience shorter cumulative drought periods, ranging from the first to the fourth month. In contrast, regions such as Patagonia and the western areas along Cuyo experience prolonged droughts, exceeding five months in duration. Notably, regions along the Andes and in the southern highlands are characterized by prolonged cumulative drought events.  Fig. 7 a illustrates the relationship between the mean maximum cumulative correlation of SPEI and the mean annual SPEI, functioning as a water balance gradient. The mean SPEI-12, which integrates both precipitation and potential evapotranspiration over a 12-month period, serves as a comprehensive climatic index. It effectively reflects the overall wetness or dryness of a region, proving essential for assessing long-term climatic trends and their impact on water resources (Zhao et al., 2020 ). As the water balance gradient increases, so too does the cumulative effect, indicating a more pronounced impact on vegetation in the semi-humid areas of Argentina. Fig. 7 b depicts the relationship between the month of maximum SPEI accumulation and the water balance gradient. Notably, the months of maximum accumulation decrease significantly as the water balance gradient increases, demonstrating that vegetation in arid areas has a longer response time to the cumulative effect, whereas vegetation in semi-humid areas responds more swiftly. The lagged response of vegetation to drought offers insights into the sensitivity of vegetation to drought conditions. The significant lagged correlation between NDVI and SPEI covered 93.71 % of the study area, with 87.06 % showing a significant positive correlation and 6.65 % exhibiting a significant negative correlation ( Fig. 8 a). Areas with higher values of positive correlation were predominantly located in the Pampas and Northeast regions, characterized mainly by croplands and forests. Conversely, areas of significant negative correlation, mirroring the earlier cumulative effect analysis, were primarily concentrated along the Andes in western Argentina and the southern highlands. The percentage of areas affected by lagged effects peaked at 66.99 % for a 1-month lag, followed by 7.93 % for a 2-month lag (Fig. 8 b). The 1-month lag predominantly affected the entire Pampas and Northeast regions, as well as eastern Cuyo and the eastern Northwest regions, while lags exceeding 9 months were mainly concentrated along the Andes in western Argentina and in some northern regions. These findings suggest that drought impacts vegetation growth rapidly after its onset across most of Argentina. The SPEI lagged effect exhibits a similar relationship to water balance as the cumulative effect ( Fig. 9 ). The lagged effect shows a more pronounced impact in sub-humid areas and reveals that vegetation is highly sensitive to drought, mostly within 2 months. The lagged effect of NDVI on groundwater drought is delineated in Fig. 11 . The significant maximum correlation encompasses 49.72 % of the entire Argentine region, with 20.76 % indicating a significant positive correlation and 28.96 % showing a significant negative correlation ( Fig. 10 a). The significant positive correlations are predominantly found in the northern part of the Pampas, eastern Northeast, and along the Andes in western Argentina. Meanwhile, significant negative correlations are concentrated in the central and southern regions. Fig. 10 b illustrates the monthly spatial distribution of the maximum lagged correlation. The most prevalent maximum correlation, occurring with a 1-month lag, accounts for 23.40 %, followed by a 12-month lag at 12.89 % and a 2-month lag at 10.31 %. Lags of 1–4 months, accounting for 47.59 %, are mainly distributed in the Pampas and Patagonia, where vegetation responds rapidly to the onset of groundwater drought. Spatially, the maximum correlation for lags of 10–12 months is primarily concentrated in Cuyo and along the Andes. The average maximum lagged correlation of the GGDI demonstrated a positive trend with water balance. However, in arid and semi-arid regions, the correlation values were predominantly negative, indicating an adverse vegetative response to groundwater drought conditions in these areas. For water balances ranging from −0.9–0.3, the average lag months for the GGDI generally spanned between four and seven months.   3.4 Predominant influence of cumulative and lagged drought effects on vegetation Analysis of the mean values of maximum cumulative effect correlations and maximum lag effect correlations across different land use types has elucidated the varying responses to drought. As illustrated in  Fig. 12 a, the cumulative effect of the SPEI is the primary driver of vegetation dynamics in Argentina, particularly affecting grasslands, followed by croplands. In contrast, shrublands show a minimal response to both the cumulative and lagged effects of meteorological drought. The lagged response to groundwater drought is most significant, with croplands exhibiting the shortest average time scales for both effects, highlighting their pronounced vulnerability to drought conditions. Shrublands, on the other hand, display the longest response period to the cumulative effect, at 5.95 months, which suggests a higher resilience to drought. Forests show longer time scales for lagged effects of both SPEI and GGDI than other vegetation types, indicating their reduced sensitivity to both meteorological and groundwater droughts.  3.5 Dynamic changes in cumulative and lag effects of drought on vegetation To further analyze the dynamic changes in the cumulative and lag effects of drought on vegetation, we present figures depicting the maximum cumulative correlation, maximum lag correlation, and their corresponding monthly sliding three-year time scales ( Fig. 13 ).  Fig. 14 a illustrates these dynamic changes in maximum correlation, revealing no significant trends in r  _SPEI_cum     and r  _SPEI_lag    , while the correlation of R  _GGDI_lag     increases following an initial decline, aligning with the water surplus detected by the GGDI. The dynamics of maximum correlation months are depicted in Fig. 13 b, showing a gradual decrease in r  _SPEI_cum_months     and r  _SPEI_lag_months    . This trend indicates a progressive shortening of the vegetation response time to meteorological drought, reflecting both cumulative and lag effects, which suggests an accelerating impact of drought on vegetation—a phenomenon that necessitates closer scrutiny. Additionally, our findings reveal that in years of severe drought, such as 2006–2009, 2007–2010, 2018–2020, and 2019–2021, the cumulative and lag effects of meteorological drought correlate more strongly with vegetation impacts, and the duration of impact is shorter.   4 Discussion 4.1 Characteristics of regional drought and vegetation changes in Argentina Meteorological drought significantly impacts agricultural and hydrological conditions, and a thorough understanding is crucial for providing theoretical support for agricultural and regional economic development (Shiau, 2023; Wang, 2023 ). In Argentina, droughts are generally characterized by high frequency and moderate severity, although there are instances of more severe drought events. For example, a meteorological drought in the Pampas lasted for 17 months from April 2008 to August 2009, and in Patagonia, a drought spanned 12 months from October 2008 to September 2009. These observations are consistent with the drought characteristics identified in prior research (Müller et al., 2014 ). Groundwater droughts, while less frequent and intense, tend to persist longer, likely due to the inherent stability of groundwater resources (Peters et al., 2005 ). Notably, in the Pampas, a prolonged drought lasted 32 months from September 2010 to April 2013, and in Cuyo, a drought persisted for 21 months from July 2012 to March 2014. These events may have been exacerbated by severe marine heatwaves in the western South Atlantic, which elevated sea surface temperatures by 3°C above the climatic average, impacting the region during the summer of 2013–2014 (Rodrigues et al., 2019 ). Temporally, NDVI trends exhibit a horizontal S-shaped pattern reflecting the drought dynamics in Argentina. Spatially, the consistency of meteorological drought trends with NDVI changes underscores the critical role of precipitation as the primary determinant of vegetation growth and development (Bento et al., 2018 ). Initial analyses concluded that significant NDVI variations in the Argentine region are closely linked to drought occurrences, a conclusion further supported by correlation analysis that revealed a robust relationship between vegetation and the cumulative effect of SPEI, indicating the drought-resistant characteristics of vegetation (Guo, 2023 ).  4.2 Response of vegetation to drought The most pronounced correlation between the NDVI and the cumulative SPEI is observed at a three-month interval, primarily in the lush, vegetation-rich areas of the Pampas and Northwest, characterized by a humid subtroical climate. Linear regression analysis of the average maximum cumulative correlation and the water balance gradient reveals that the cumulative impact on vegetation in arid and semi-arid regions is less pronounced compared to that in humid and semi-humid regions. Prior research has demonstrated that vegetation in humid regions exhibits a stronger correlation with SPEI-03, whereas in arid and semi-arid regions, a higher correlation exists with long-term accumulated SPEI (Xue, 2022; Zhang, 2022 ). When examining the hysteresis effect, both the response of vegetation to meteorological drought and to groundwater drought predominantly occur within one month, indicating a high sensitivity of most Argentine vegetation to drought conditions. The maximum lag correlation of the average SPEI closely aligns with the cumulative effect, further confirming that vegetation in arid and semi-arid areas of Argentina is minimally impacted by the lag effect, whereas vegetation in humid and semi-humid areas shows a strong response to this lag effect of drought. Notably, Argentina's humid and semi-humid zones, which are central to the country's agriculture, exhibit pronounced drought sensitivity (Sgroi et al., 2021 ). The maximum lag correlation of the average GGDI diverges from the aforementioned trend, displaying a negative correlation with groundwater in arid and semi-arid areas, possibly due to the prevalence of shallow-rooted vegetation in these regions. Excessive groundwater does not facilitate the growth of such vegetation (Chui et al., 2011 ). The study also explored the differential responses of various vegetation types to both cumulative and lag effects of SPEI. Croplands and grasslands showed significant reactions to these effects, with croplands particularly sensitive, evidenced by an average cumulative response time of 2.94 months and an average lag response time of 1.14 months. These findings indicate that agricultural areas in Argentina possess limited drought resilience and heightened sensitivity to arid conditions, likely due to their shallow root systems which impede deep groundwater absorption, thus enhancing their correlation with meteorological drought (Shi, 2021 ). Conversely, shrublands displayed considerable resilience to drought, with an average cumulative response time of 5.95 months to SPEI, marking them as the most drought-resistant among the studied vegetation types. This resilience in shrublands can be attributed to adaptive strategies such as the synthesis of secondary metabolites, including flavonoids, which are essential in mitigating oxidative stress and enhancing drought resistance (Varela et al., 2016 ). Moreover, Fig. 10  illustrates that Argentine vegetation is more significantly influenced by the cumulative effects of meteorological drought than by its lag effects. Groundwater drought lag effects have the least impact on vegetation changes in the region. These observations underscore the importance of focusing on both cumulative and lag effects of meteorological drought in research examining the interplay between drought and vegetation in Argentina.  4.3 Dynamic characteristics and causes of vegetation response to drought Historically, the dynamic changes in the cumulative and lag effects of drought on vegetation have been underexplored. Our research fills this gap by indicating that these effects demonstrate dynamic variations, particularly during severe drought years when their impact intensifies (Fig. 13 ). We hypothesize that these variations may be linked to changes in water availability or temperature. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted regression analyses examining the relationships between precipitation, temperature, soil moisture, and both dynamic cumulative and lag effects of drought (Fig. 14 ). The analysis reveals that precipitation and soil moisture are the primary drivers of variations in both cumulative and lag effects. Specifically, precipitation exhibits a significant negative correlation with the maximum correlation of cumulative effects, suggesting that higher precipitation levels result in a reduced impact of drought on vegetation. Similarly, increased precipitation prolongs the response time of vegetation to the lag effects of meteorological drought. A comparable pattern is observed with soil moisture, which likely serves as a critical water source for vegetation, mitigating the adverse effects of drought. Past research supports this, indicating that the availability of soil water significantly influences the adaptive capacity of vegetation (Hoover et al., 2021 ). Concerning the lag effects of groundwater drought, increases in both precipitation and soil moisture lead to a more pronounced negative correlation with vegetation's lag response to groundwater drought. This finding is consistent with earlier studies suggesting that excessive water availability can inhibit the development of fine roots, thereby adversely affecting vegetation growth (Huang et al., 2020 ).  4.4 Limitations and prospects This study acknowledges certain limitations, particularly with respect to the completeness of data, notably those derived from the GRACE satellite missions. Enhancing the validation of our results and a deeper consideration of uncertainties would bolster the robustness of our findings. Furthermore, the integration of machine learning approaches to predict vegetation responses, alongside further exploration of long-term trends and the impact of seasonal variations on vegetation, could significantly enhance the applicability of our research. Such improvements would contribute to the development of more effective drought management strategies within the region. To propel this research field forward, future studies should investigate more detailed temporal and spatial variations in the interactions between drought and vegetation.   5 Conclusion This study examines the response of vegetation to meteorological drought (SPEI) and groundwater drought (GGDI) in Argentina. Key findings highlight the effectiveness of GRACE data in analyzing trends in terrestrial water storage, which closely mirror observed patterns of vegetation change and drought impacts. Meteorological drought in Argentina is characterized by greater duration, intensity, and severity compared to groundwater drought. Vegetation in the humid zones, particularly croplands, displays lower drought tolerance and a strong correlation with the short-term cumulative effects of SPEI. In contrast, vegetation in arid regions, especially shrublands, shows higher drought resilience and a stronger correlation with the longer-term cumulative effects of SPEI. All vegetation types demonstrate increased sensitivity and a strong correlation to the lagged effects of SPEI, with croplands and grasslands being particularly susceptible to these delayed impacts of meteorological drought. Overall, the cumulative effects of drought are more pronounced than the lagged effects in Argentina, underscoring the stronger influence of meteorological conditions on vegetation compared to groundwater availability. The limitations identified in this study pave the way for further research. Primarily relying on remotely sensed data, the incorporation of in-situ data to validate our findings could yield invaluable insights. Additionally, examining the roles of other environmental factors such as surface temperature or land management practices could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the responses of vegetation to drought. Furthermore, the coarse spatial resolution (0.25 degrees) of the datasets might mask finer details, suggesting that future research could benefit from incorporating higher resolution or downscaling techniques to validate the findings of this study. The complex relationship between different types of drought and vegetation responses enhances our ability to improve drought preparedness, mitigation, and water management practices. Thus, the impacts of this research extend to both the scientific community and policymakers. The comprehensive analysis of vegetation response to drought presented here provides valuable guidance for land management strategies and water resource allocation, not only in Argentina but also in other regions facing similar challenges.
1 Introduction Fluid flow through porous media controls the transport of dissolved chemicals, pollutants, and biological compounds in a wide range of natural and industrial porous systems (Dentz et al., 2011; Rolle and Le Borgne, 2019 ). The complex network of interconnected pores can lead to highly non-uniform flow patterns and, consequently, heterogeneous distributions of chemical concentrations (Dentz et al., 2023 ). Understanding the dynamics of mixing at the pore level and its influence on reaction kinetics on larger scales is important for applications such as the prediction of contaminant migration in groundwater (Rolle and Le Borgne, 2019 ), production of oil-wet reservoirs by CO 2     injection (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2016 ), designing effective remediation strategies in subsurface environments (e.g., Kitanidis and McCarty, 2012 ), and the optimization of transport processes in engineered porous media (e.g., Johnson and Locascio, 2002 ). Solute mixing brings reactants together in a fluid, allowing chemical reactions to occur. Since this process can be relatively slow in porous media, a range of chemical reactions have kinetics with characteristic times significantly shorter than typical mixing times (Li et al., 2006; Valocchi et al., 2019 ). Such mixing-limited reactions result in a reaction zone confined to an interface that acts as a boundary between segregated reactants (e.g., Rolle et al., 2009; Bauer et al., 2008; Willingham et al., 2008; Cirpka et al., 1999; Eckert et al., 2012; Hidalgo et al., 2015; Perez et al., 2019 ). A range of reactive transport problems are characterized by steady-state or slowly moving plumes, where mixing occurs predominantly transverse to the flow direction in narrow mixing fronts, typically on the millimeter scale (Rahman et al., 2005; Benekos et al., 2006; Shafabakhsh et al., 2024a; Nambi et al., 2003; Jose and Cirpka, 2004 ). The localization and size of such transverse mixing zones are greatly influenced by the heterogeneous nature of geological formations (Cirpka et al., 2015 ). At Darcy scale, most numerical studies of reactive transport employ a continuum-based approach in which solute concentrations are integrated within a representative elementary volume (e.g., Katz et al., 2011; Molins and Knabner, 2019; Porta et al., 2013, 2016; Boso and Battiato, 2013 ). This approach uses hydrodynamic dispersion to represent the effect of unresolved pore-scale fluctuations in fluid velocities. Although this macrodispersion framework is useful in describing the spread of solute plumes, it tends to overpredict the rates of mixing-limited reactions because of the persistence of incomplete mixing at the pore scale (Raje and Kapoor, 2000; Gramling et al., 2002; Liedl et al., 2005 ). This highlights the need for methodologies that can accurately capture these pore-scale processes. Substantial progress has been achieved to simulate the resulting pore-scale concentration gradients by using different Lagrangian and Eulerian simulation methods (Benson et al., 2017; Oostrom et al., 2016 ). Lagrangian methods, which involve tracking individual solute particles, have been applied in investigating mixing phenomena in single- and multiphase flow systems (Guida et al., 2012; Minier et al., 2014; Voronov et al., 2011; Sternagel et al., 2021; Klimenko, 2009; Benson and Bolster, 2016; Ding et al., 2017; Benson et al., 2019; Engdahl et al., 2019 ). A key benefit of Lagrangian methods is their ability to accurately capture advection-dominated transport processes, characterized by high Péclet number Pe   (the ratio of diffusive to advective fluxes), without introducing numerical dispersion (Salamon et al., 2006; Boso et al., 2013 ). However, the limitation is the requirement for a large number of particles to effectively resolve concentration gradients, leading to high computational costs (Noetinger et al., 2016 ). Moreover, interpolation methods for computing concentrations based on particle positions introduce a risk of over-smoothing concentration fields, potentially degrading accuracy (Fernàndez-Garcia and Sánchez-Vila, 2011 ). Eulerian simulation methods, on the other hand, solve the advection–diffusion equation directly in a discretized domain Sole-Mari et al. (2022), Baek and Seo (2017, e.g.,) . To avoid spurious oscillations in the resulting concentration fields, various stabilization approaches have been proposed (Hughes, 1979; Brooks and Hughes, 1982 ). These may again introduce non-physical numerical dispersion and smear out concentration gradients unless the spatial and temporal resolution is high enough. While mixing dynamics can be well resolved at the pore scale in two-dimensional simulations (e.g., Acharya et al., 2007; Du et al., 2023; Hejazi and Azaiez, 2013; Oostrom et al., 2016 ), this task is much more challenging in three-dimensional porous media (e.g., Sole-Mari et al., 2022 ). The additional degree of freedom induces chaotic stretching and folding at the pore scale, which sustains concentration gradients and incomplete mixing (Lester et al., 2014, 2016; Heyman et al., 2020; Souzy et al., 2020; Heyman et al., 2021; Aquino et al., 2023; Sanquer et al., 2024 ). Therefore, the transition towards three-dimensional simulations is essential to capture the spatial variability and heterogeneity of porous media, which cannot be adequately represented in two-dimensional models. The effects of chaotic mixing on reactive processes are best evidenced when considering transverse mixing in steady state mixing fronts (e.g. (Sanquer et al., 2024 )). Yet, there is, to our knowledge, currently no method or studies that directly address how to properly and practically resolve chaotic mixing in 3D pore-scale flows. Eulerian methods suffer from numerical dispersion and numerical instabilities, while Lagrangian methods require a large amount of particles to accurately resolve concentration gradients in three dimensions. Methods that rely on temporal integration of the governing equations (both Lagrangian and Eulerian) require a long time to converge to the steady state of transverse mixing between two continuously injected solutions. Using time-dependent solvers such as OpenFoam, with a spatial resolution Δ x    and time step Δ t   , requires Δ x ∼ Δ t ∼ Pe  − 1 / 2      for stability as discussed e.g. by Martínez-Ruiz et al. (2018) . Considering that the diffusion time in the transverse direction is t  D   ∼ Pe   , this leads to the number of time steps N  t   ∼ t  D   / Δ t ∼ Pe  3 / 2      and problem size N ∼ Δ x  − 3   N  t   ∼ Pe  3     , resulting in high computational costs for advection-dominated transport. Hence, there is a critical need for methodologies that can balance computational efficiency with the ability to accurately capture the pore-scale gradients for simulating mixing and reactions in 3D porous media. To effectively resolve sharp concentration gradients, adaptive mesh refinement strategies have been widely used for the transport of solutes in porous media (Mansell et al., 2002 ), primarily in the context of transient flow at the Darcy scale (Nilsson et al., 2005; Pau et al., 2009; Cusini et al., 2019; Dell’Oca et al., 2018 ). Refinement criteria may be based on both local gradients (Cusini et al., 2019 ) and a posteriori  error analysis (Dell’Oca et al., 2018 ). For advection-dominated conditions, robust refinement strategies based on the Streamline-Upwind Petrov–Galerkin method (Hughes, 1979; Brooks and Hughes, 1982 ) have been developed (John and Novo, 2013 ). These techniques may provide new opportunities to resolve sharp chemical gradients in complex three-dimensional flow fields that arise at the pore scale in realistic porous media. Here, we introduce a new methodology for simulating steady-state mixing and reaction at the pore-scale in three-dimensional porous media. The approach relies on accurately solving steady conservative scalar transport in a porous domain, given a mesh representation of the pore space and a steady velocity field within it. To simultaneously achieve numerical stability and physically valid concentration fields, a key step is the combination of numerical stabilization (using the Streamwise-Upwind Petrov–Galerkin approach) and iterative refinement based on local concentration gradients. This methodology offers enhanced spatial resolution to capture detailed transverse mixing processes, and accurate representation of concentration gradients, which the existing modeling frameworks fail to adequately resolve at the pore-scale. Based on the proposed refinement criterion, we provide scaling estimates for the number of computational nodes needed to resolve the mixing zone, which is qualitatively different in two and three dimensions. We evaluate instantaneous reactions by post-processing the resulting conservative concentration fields. The adaptability of this methodology allows us to resolve pore-scale mixing in a wide range of porous media systems, including chaotic flow through a bead pack and flow in a natural rock sample of Berea sandstone.  2 Physical model In the following, we present the considered physical model and the modeling assumptions used. We describe both conservative and reactive transport, as well as to how the two modes of transport can be linked assuming instantaneous reaction kinetics.   2.1 Porous domain and velocity field We consider a fluid domain Ω ⊂ R  3     , schematically displayed in Fig. 1 , which represents the pore space within a solid porous matrix. This pore space is filled with single-phase fluid. Ω   is contained within a box of size L  x   × L  y   × L  z     . The boundary of Ω   is comprised of the inlet boundary Γ  in     (at z = 0   , ref. Fig. 1 ), the outlet boundary Γ  out     (at z = L  z     ), and the pore wall boundary Γ  wall    , i.e. the surface of Ω   that separates fluid and solid. A steady fluid velocity field u ( x )     is defined within Ω  . Here, x = ( x , y , z )  ∈ Ω    is the spatial coordinate and the velocity field is that of an incompressible fluid, such that ∇ ⋅ u = 0   . Furthermore, we assume that the solid is impermeable, i.e. u ⋅ n  ˆ   = 0    for x ∈ Γ  wall     . Here, n  ˆ     the outward normal of Ω  . For creeping flows typical to porous media, the velocity field u ( x )     will generally be well represented by the solution of the Stokes equations (Feder et al., 2022 ) (see Appendix B ).  2.2 Advection–diffusion equation We now consider the concentration c  i     of a given chemical species C  i     dissolved in a fluid that flows through a porous medium. The evolution of c  i   ( x , t )     in space x ∈ Ω    and time t  , is described at the pore-scale by the advection–diffusion equation (1) ∂ c  i    ∂ t   + u ⋅ ∇ c  i   − D  i   ∇  2   c  i   = 0 ,     where D  i     is the diffusivity of the species. A Dirichlet boundary condition is supplied at the inlet boundary as (2) c  i   ( x , t )  = C  i , 0   ( x )   for  x ∈ Γ  in   ,     where the precise function C  i , 0   ( x )     will be specified later. For the pore walls, we also take the boundaries to be impermeable for the chemical species, which when n  ˆ   ⋅ u = 0    is expressed by n  ˆ   ⋅ ∇ c  i   = 0    for x ∈ Γ  wall     . To close the equations, we also choose the boundary condition n  ˆ   ⋅ ∇ c  i   = 0    for x ∈ Γ  out     , in this case representing no diffusive solute flux at the outlet. For constant injection rates, a steady transport regime will eventually be established. Here we consider a co-injection of two fluids with different solute concentrations (e.g., Acharya et al., 2007 ) leading to a non-trivial steady-state concentration c  i   ( x )     described by removing the time-dependence in Eq. (1) : (3a) u ⋅ ∇ c  i   − D  i   ∇  2   c  i   = 0 , for  x ∈ Ω ,    (3b) c  i   ( x )  = C  i , 0   ( x )  , for  x ∈ Γ  in   ,    (3c) n  ˆ   ⋅ ∇ c  i   = 0 , for  x ∈ Γ  wall   ∪ Γ  out   .        2.3 System of advection–diffusion–reaction equations When chemical reactions take place within the fluid, the concentration fields c  i     of the different species C  i     become coupled to each other. Eq. (1)  then generalizes to the advection–diffusion–reaction equation: (4) ∂ c  i    ∂ t   + u ⋅ ∇ c  i   − D  i   ∇  2   c  i   = R  i   .     Here, the chemical species C  i    , i ∈ { 1 , … , N }     interchange mass through the reaction terms R  i    . In principle, these terms could result from several reactions taking place in a complex reaction network (De Simoni et al., 2007a ). However, to demonstrate our approach, we consider a simple bimolecular reaction for which pore-scale mixing plays an important role (Valocchi et al., 2019 ).  2.4 Irreversible bi-molecular reaction The simplest fluid–fluid reaction involving more than one species is the irreversible bimolecular reaction: (5) A + B ⟶ C .     This reaction has been well studied in porous media both in simulations (e.g., Borgne et al., 2014; Kim, 2019 ) and in experiments (e.g., Willingham et al., 2008; Izumoto et al., 2023; d. Anna et al., 2014 ). Here, mixing between two reactants A and B yields product C upon contact between the two miscible fluids. The local reaction rate expressing the creation of product C can be expressed by: (6) R = k a b ,     where k   is the reaction rate constant. The steady advection–diffusion–reaction system corresponding to reaction (5)  can be described by Eq. (4)  and becomes: (7a) u ⋅ ∇ a − D ∇  2   a = − R    (7b) u ⋅ ∇ b − D ∇  2   b = − R    (7c) u ⋅ ∇ c − D ∇  2   c = R ,       where a  , b  , and c   are the concentrations of the involved species, and we have taken the diffusion coefficient D   to be equal for all species. 2.4.1 Inlet boundary conditions We consider the idealized scenario of two miscible fluids containing, respectively, species A and B, which mix within the porous domain Ω   (see Fig. 1 ). This scenario fixes the inlet boundary condition (2)  for the reaction (5) . Both species have the same initial concentration (normalized to 1, for simplicity), and the fluids are injected from two different locations at the inlet boundary Γ  in     (i.e., co-flow injection). The concentration of species C is equal to zero at the inlet boundary, meaning that all production of C by construction occurs within the domain. The boundary Γ  in     can be split into two subdomains separated by a sharp interface, where either (8) ( a , b , c )  = ( 1 , 0 , 0 )   or  ( 0 , 1 , 0 )  .     In particular, in this work, we will approximate the inlet boundary condition (9) a ( x , y , 0 )  = Θ ( x )  ,    (10) b ( x , y , 0 )  = 1 − Θ ( x )  ,       where Θ ( x )     is the Heaviside step function, (11) Θ ( x )  = 0   for  x < 0 ,   1   for  x ≥ 0 .            2.4.2 Simplifications by identifying conserved and non-conserved quantities From Eq. (7c) , we identify two conserved  quantities δ , ψ    and a non-conserved  quantity ρ  : (12a) δ = a − b ,    (12b) ρ = a + b ,    (12c) ψ = c − ρ / 2       The reaction rate (6)  can then be expressed as (13) R = k  4   ρ  2   − δ  2     .     Accordingly, Eqs. (7a) and (7b)  can be expressed as: (14a) u ⋅ ∇ δ − D ∇  2   δ = 0 ,    (14b) u ⋅ ∇ ρ − D ∇  2   ρ = k  2   ( δ  2   − ρ  2   )  ,    (14c) u ⋅ ∇ ψ − D ∇  2   ψ = 0 .       The evolution Eqs. (14a) and (14c)  for δ , ψ    are linear and do not depend on any other field but themselves, and can be solved independently. Further, the evolution Eq. (14b)  for ρ   depends only on the found solution for δ  . Hence, Eqs. (14a)–(14c)  can be solved sequentially, with the only constraint that Eq. (14b)  must be solved after Eq. (14a) . This approach is computationally beneficial, as it reduces the size of the linear system resulting from a finite element discretization (see Section 3.2 ) compared to a coupled solution of Eq. (7c) . Following Eqs. (8) and (12c) , we find for the composite concentrations at the inlet boundary: (15) δ ∈ { − 1 , 1 }  ,  ρ = 1 ,  ψ = 1 / 2  for  x ∈ Γ  in   .     For the specific inlet conditions considered herein, which divides the inlet into two halves along the x   direction, we obtain from Eq. (10) : (16) δ ( x , y , 0 )  = 2 Θ ( x )  − 1 ,     where Θ   is the Heaviside step function defined in Eq. (11) . Eq. (14a)  shows that δ   will stay within the interval [ − 1 , 1 ]    in the entire domain, while Eq. (14b)  shows that ρ   will tend to decay with the distance away from the inlet boundary (as ρ ≥ | δ |    ). Finally, with the inlet condition ψ = 1 / 2   , the only solution that can satisfy Eq. (14c)  is a trivial one, ψ = 1 / 2    everywhere in the domain. Hence, the concentration of product C can be calculated explicitly by solving (17) c = 1 − ρ  2   ,     and henceforth Eq. (14c)  can be neglected.  2.4.3 Instantaneous reaction Mixing-limited reactions are characterized by a high Damköhler number (Da  ), defined as the ratio between the characteristic time of fluid motion to that of the chemical reaction. Considering a reaction with a first-order-kinetic constant (k  ), the Damköhler number is (18) Da = k d  2    D       where d   is a characteristic pore size. We now assume that the reaction occurs on time scales much smaller than the diffusive and advective time scales, which corresponds to the limit of large Damköhler number Da → ∞   , i.e. instantaneous reaction. Taking k → ∞    in Eq. (14b) , we then obtain: (19) ρ = | δ |  .     The concentration of reactants A, B, and product C can be readily calculated using Eqs. (19) and (12c)  as: (20a) a = | δ |  + δ  2   ,    (20b) b = | δ |  − δ  2   ,    (20c) c = 1 − | δ |   2   .       Thus, given that the reaction (5)  is instantaneous and irreversible, the system expressed by Eq. (7c)  is completely specified once the solution δ   of Eq. (14a)  is known. This property will be exploited in the ensuing sections; in particular, we will solve the steady advection–diffusion Eq. (14a)  and use Eq. (20c)  to calculate the distribution of the species involved in the reaction (5) .   2.5 Metrics of mixing and reaction We investigate mixing and reaction at different Péclet numbers, which characterizes the ratio of the diffusive and advective time scales at the pore scale, (21) Pe = U d  D   ,     where d   is a characteristic pore size and U   the average flow speed. Fluid mixing can be quantified by measuring different quantities related to the concentration field, flux, transported mass, and reaction rate of the product, as explored in previous studies (e.g., de Dreuzy et al., 2012; Rolle et al., 2009; d. Anna et al., 2014; Alhashmi et al., 2015 ). Here we summarize the main quantities used for measuring mixing and reaction in the present study. For quantifying conservative mixing, we use the scalar dissipation rate, which has been used in several studies of fluid mixing in porous media as a proxy for the mixing rate (e.g., Luo et al., 2008; Le Borgne et al., 2010; Bolster et al., 2010; Chiogna et al., 2011; Jha et al., 2011; Engdahl et al., 2013 ). Using δ   as a conserved quantity, the conservative scalar dissipation rate is defined as (22) I = ∫  Ω  ⊥   ( z )    D | ∇ δ |   2   d x d y ,     where the integral is taken over a cross section Ω  ⊥   ( z )     of Ω  . We quantify effective reaction rates using the total reaction rate in each cross-section. The latter can be estimated as (see Appendix D ), (23) R  c   = d J  c    d z   .     where J  c     is the total flux of c   through a cross-section Ω  ⊥   ( z )     of Ω  , (24) J  c   ( z )  = ∫  Ω  ⊥   ( z )    z  ˆ   ⋅ j  c   d x d y ,     and the local flux j  c     is the sum of the advective and diffusive fluxes, (25) j  c   = u c − D ∇ c .     The total produced mass of C in each cross-section can be calculated as (26) M  c   = ∫  Ω  ⊥   ( z )    c ( x )   d x d y ,     which is directly proportional to the evolving volume of the mixing zone.   3 Computational method 3.1 Overall workflow The workflow consists of four distinct steps, as shown schematically in Fig. 2 . The prerequisites for the workflow are a computational mesh representing the fluid domain and a well-resolved velocity field within it. Specifically, we assume that we have a three-dimensional computational mesh representation of the pore space Ω   (as discussed in Section 2.1  and shown in Fig. 1 ). Computing pore-scale velocity fields is in itself an active research topic and is not the focus of this paper, and we refer to other resources for more specialized literature on this topic (Indelman, 2001; Siena et al., 2015; Aramideh et al., 2018 ). In this work, we primarily computed the velocity field by solving the Stokes equations with no-slip conditions on the solid boundaries and slip conditions on the lateral side walls (see Appendix B ). The main step of the workflow is to solve the advection–diffusion Eq. (14a)  to calculate the concentration field of conserved species δ   (Fig. 2 ). As a consequence of the nonuniform concentration field that we impose on the inlet boundary in the advection–diffusion equation, we obtain nontrivial steady concentration distributions within the porous media. These distributions form the basis for subsequent analyses. Accurate determination of δ   is achieved through an iterative adaptive refinement procedure, which is described in Section 3.3 . Finally, in the post-processing phase, the conserved scalar field δ   is used to compute the spatial distribution of chemical species involved in Eq. (5)  within the porous media by solving the local Eq. (20c) .    3.2 Finite element scheme The finite element method (FEM) offers a powerful approach for solving partial differential equations like Eq. (14a) . In the limit of large Pe  , Eq. (14a)  becomes singularly perturbed (Roos, 2008 ) and naive discretization approaches will typically fail to converge or lead to unphysical oscillatory solutions unless very fine meshes are used (Elman et al., 2014 ). To obtain meaningful and convergent results, various stabilization techniques have been proposed (Roos, 2008 ). One such technique is the Streamwise-Upwind Petrov–Galerkin method (Brooks and Hughes, 1982; Hughes, 1979 ), which modifies the standard Galerkin finite element method by adding numerical diffusion in the streamline direction (John et al., 2018; Elman et al., 2014 ). The variational formulation corresponding to Eq. (14a)  with Streamwise-Upwind Petrov–Galerkin stabilization is given by the following. Find δ ∈ V    such that for all test functions v ∈ V   : (27) ∫  Ω   ( u  h   ⋅ ∇ δ )  v  d  3   x + ∫  Ω   D ∇ δ ⋅ ∇ v  d  3   x + ∫  Ω   τ ( u  h   ⋅ ∇ δ )  ( u  h   ⋅ ∇ v )   d  3   x = 0 .     Here, we consider the function space V ⊂ H  1   ( Ω )     and τ   is a space-dependent stabilization parameter. The latter is modeled according to Elman et al. (2014, Eq. 3.44) : (28) τ = h  2 | u  h   |    Θ 1 − Pe  h  − 1     ,     where h   represents the local mesh size, | u  h   |    is the local magnitude of the velocity vector u  h     interpolated from the input velocity field u  , and Θ ( x )     is the Heaviside step function defined in Eq. (11) . Further, the element Péclet number is defined by Pe  h   = | u  h   |  h / ( 2 D )    . As discussed below in Section 3.3 , u   is typically defined on a coarser mesh than u  h    . In practice, we solved u   once with a higher-order (P  2    ) finite element basis and used a piecewise constant representation (P  0    ) of u  h    , which we found to give the most robust convergence. With adaptive mesh refinement in the interface region, the P  0     representation u  h     on the finer mesh approaches the P  2     representation u   on the coarser mesh. In our simulations, we used piecewise linear (P  1    ) elements for δ   for robustness. Note that the form of Eq. (27)  assumes this; for higher-order elements, a diffusive term must be added to Eq. (27)  (Elman et al., 2014 ).  3.3 Refinement criteria To obtain accurate solutions of the scalar field δ  , it is critical to combine the stabilization discussed above with mesh refinement. In our case, the interface between the fluids is of particular interest as it will form a layer of sharp change in δ  , and to extract physically valid results it is imperative to add as little numerical diffusion as possible to this zone. Thus we need a refinement strategy where we identify the regions where δ   exhibits significant variations and iteratively refine this region. The large fraction of the mesh where δ   is relatively constant, even though the velocity field u   is complex, may remain coarse. In the regime of pore-scale flows we are interested in, corresponding to the Batchelor regime (Haynes and Vanneste, 2005; Heyman et al., 2023 ), the length scale of velocity fluctuations is typically larger than the length scale of concentration variations. Hence, we only need to refine the mesh used for computing δ  , which justifies computing u   only once and using an interpolated u  h     (on a progressively finer mesh) as discussed in Section 3.2 . We adopt a simple refinement criterion employed for mesh refinement based on the product of the local mesh size h   and the magnitude of the concentration gradient, | ∇ δ |   , expressed as (29) h | ∇ δ |  < Δ  δ   .     where Δ  δ     is a user specified tolerance that limits how much δ   can change over an element. In the simulations presented in Section 4 , we used a tetrahedral mesh representation of the domain and chose h   as the longest edge in the associated tetrahedron. Every cell of the mesh wherein the criterion Eq. (29)  is not met, is marked for refinement and subsequently divided according to the algorithm of Plaza and Carey (1996)  as implemented in FEniCS (Alnæs et al., 2015 ) (see Section 3.4 ). We found the value Δ  δ   = 0 . 2    to strike a good balance between computational efficiency and the accuracy of the solution, effectively placing most of the degrees of freedom in regions where the concentration field changes drastically over short length scales.  3.4 Implementation  We solve the advection–diffusion Eq. (14a)  in the form of Eq. (27)  using the FEniCS/DOLFIN framework (Alnæs et al., 2015 ). FEniCS is a software collection for automating the solution of differential equations using the FEM, and DOLFIN functions as the primary user interface to FEniCS. Our FEniCS-based solver, named AdDiCTIF ,1  1 Ad vection-Di ffusion-C hemistry in a T ime-I ndependent F ramework.   is implemented in Python and C++, and available for use and further development in a dedicated Git repository (Shafabakhsh and Linga, 2024 ). The code is structured into distinct modules as shown in Fig. 3  for easy code reuse: • The module ade_steady  solves the advection–diffusion equation given the mesh and velocity field. To solve the linear system resulting from discretizing Eq. (27) , we use the (iterative) bi-conjugate gradient method (bicgstab ), with the Hypre Euclid implementation of the ILU preconditioner (hypre_euclid ).  • After solving the advection–diffusion equation and obtaining the concentration field of δ  , the mesh may be refined by using the module refine . This task may be repeated by executing ade_steady  and refine  iteratively to progressively refine the solution. The iteration is stopped at the latest when the criterion Eq. (29)  is met everywhere, and thus no cells are marked for refinement.  • Subsequently, post-processing steps can be performed to analyze and visualize the results. With the module postprocess_abc , we compute the concentration fields of the components a  , b  , and c  , based on sets of Eq. (20c) .  • Following this step, the module analyze_data  interpolates the solution into a Cartesian grid. This step enables easy analysis of different cross-sections.  • Lastly, with module compute_averages  we can compute the averages of different indicators presented in Section 2.5  in each cross-section.      4 Numerical simulations To assess the performance of the method, we apply it to three representative cases. To establish the validity of the approach, we first consider the case of uniform flow, where approximate analytical solutions can be obtained. This benchmark reveals differences between refinement when going from two to three dimensions. Second, we consider mixing and reaction through a three-dimensional monodisperse spherical bead pack, which is a well-studied model system for porous granular media (Heyman et al., 2020 ). Lastly, we consider mixing and reaction in a three-dimensional natural porous rock sample. These simulations highlight the ability of the model to effectively resolve and quantify mixing in a broad range of domains. Notably, variations in pore-scale geometry are known to impact the mixing dynamics, making such evaluations crucial. 4.1 Uniform flow To establish the convergence of the method with mesh refinement, we first consider the case of uniform flow, for which approximate solutions are available (Abramowitz et al., 1968; Sale and McWhorter, 2001; Kumar et al., 2009 ). For clarity, we give a brief derivation of these solutions in the Appendix A . The uniform flow field is given by u = U z  ˆ     , where U   is a constant. To numerically approximate the inlet boundary condition Eq. (16)  on a discrete mesh, we use (30) δ ( x , y , 0 )  = erf x  ϵ     ,     where ϵ   is a smoothing length. In our simulations, we used ϵ = 1 0  − 3     . As presented in Appendix A , for a simple one-dimensional diffusion equation, where z   assumes the role of a time coordinate, the solution subject to Eq. (30)  is given by (31) δ ≃ erf x  4 α z       ,     where α = D / U    and the approximation is valid for ϵ → 0   . We consider a cubic domain of side lengths L = 1   , with an initial mesh contained 2400 nodes. In Fig. 4 a and Fig. 4 b, we show the calculated δ   obtained for the uniform flow case when α =    0.01 in a refined mesh containing 489,024 nodes, achieved after eight refinement iterations. The comparison between different iterations of refinement is presented below. With the choice of α   and system size, we expect longitudinal diffusion to be negligible everywhere except for a small neighborhood around the inlet (x = 0   ) so that the analytical expression (31)  above should be applicable. Fig. 4 a shows the steady-state concentration distribution of conserved species δ  . In Fig. 4 b, the concentration profiles along the x  -direction at various heights are shown. The numerically obtained profiles (indicated by points) are compared to the approximate theory (31)  (represented by continuous lines). The agreement between the numerical data and theory is very good, which serves as a first validation of our simulations.  As a second test, we consider the conservative scalar dissipation rate (Le Borgne et al., 2010 ) which is approximated in Appendix A  for the depth-averaged expression (32) I  x   ( z )  ≃ 2 2   D  π ( 4 D z + ϵ  2   )      .     In Fig. 4 c, we compare the calculated depth-averaged dissipation rate for the uniform flow scenario with α ∈ { 0 . 01 , 0 . 0025 , 0 . 001 , 0 . 00025 }     for both our numerical models (represented by points) and the analytical solution (32)  (represented by continuous lines). The numerical data closely follow the theoretical curves, particularly as α   is lowered. The agreement between the model and the analytical solution can be attributed to the fact that under conditions of low diffusivity (characterized by low α   values), the longitudinal component of diffusion has a vanishing contribution to the transport, in accordance with the assumptions made in the analytical calculations above. To achieve the desired level of precision, we performed an iterative refinement process until no element were marked for refinement according to our selected criterion Eq. (29) . For all values of α  , convergence was reached after eight iterations, as shown in Fig. C.13 a. The detailed refinement process and its dependence on the smoothing scale of the inlet profile, as well as the differences observed between two and three dimensions, are discussed in detail in Appendix C . Fig. 5 a shows the convergence of the numerical dissipation rate towards the analytical value with different iterations for the case of α = 0 . 001   , demonstrating the convergence of our numerical solution towards the analytical solution with mesh refinement. We note that the points for iterations larger than four are virtually indistinguishable, despite an order of magnitude smaller mesh size. This result is due to excessive refinement near the inlet having negligible effects downstream, and suggests that our refinement criterion could be limited, for example, by increasing the inlet smearing scale ϵ   or stopping the refinement at a specified smallest mesh size h  min    . In Fig. 5 b and Fig. 5 c, we analyze the cross-sectional properties of the product C for uniform flow with α =    0.001 for different mesh refinement iterations. The integrated mass, M  c    , is shown in Fig. 5 b and Fig. 5 c shows the reaction rates R  c     calculated by Eq. (23) . Both cases are shown to approach the analytical solutions presented in Appendix E . The results confirm the importance of sufficient refinement, showing that in this case sufficient resolution is achieved after around 4 refinement iterations. A slight decrease is noticeable near z = 1    in the numerical solution for reaction rate compared to the analytical solution (Fig. 5 c), which we interpret as a relic from an initially coarse mesh, where the refinement procedure fails to identify that further refinement is needed near the outlet.  The excellent match between the numerical results of this section and analytical solutions under uniform flow conditions shows the robustness of our approach in resolving concentration gradients. This validation supports expanding our simulations to more complex porous media.  4.2 Flow through a bead pack We investigate conservative and reactive transport through a random bead pack, which is an archetypical example of a granular porous medium (Heyman et al., 2020; Turuban et al., 2019 ). The bead pack was generated using the discrete element method code Yade (Smilauer et al., 2023 ) to approximate a random close packing. 149    beads of radius d = 0 . 2    were placed inside a periodic box (in order to suppress effects that may cause order in the bead pack), which was shrunk until all the beads were locked in place and the linear size of the box was L = 1 ± 0 . 001   . This procedure resulted in a porosity of 38%. To avoid resolving extremely small elements near the cusp-shaped contacts between beads (Turuban et al., 2019 ), smaller beads of diameter 0 . 2 d    were also inserted at bead contacts, mainly overlapping with the large beads. The pore space between these grains was then meshed with tetrahedral elements using gmsh  (Geuzaine and Remacle, 2024 ), resulting in a mesh containing approximately 465,000 nodes. To approximate the sharp inlet boundary condition (16)  by a smooth function to avoid over-refinement in the inlet region, we used (33) δ ( x , y , 0 )  = tanh x  2   ϵ     ,     with ϵ = 1 0  − 2     . This profile closely resembles that used for the uniform flow (Eq. (30) ). We verified that results are insensitive to the choice of inlet profile as long as the gradient at the inlet is significantly higher than gradients downstream. Fig. 6 a shows the steady velocity field obtained by solving the Stokes equations (see Appendix B ) within the domain. We computed the concentration distribution of conservative species (Fig. 6 b), and the reactive product (Fig. 6 c) for Pe ∈ { 1 . 3 ⋅ 1 0  1   , 1 . 3 ⋅ 1 0  2   , 1 . 3 ⋅ 1 0  3   }    , estimated from Eq. (21)  where the characteristic length scale is taken as the bead diameter d   and the mean velocity U   is normalized to 1. From Fig. 6 b it is clear that the mixing region within the bead pack, indicated by intermediate values of δ  , narrows as Pe   increases. This result highlights the relatively higher influence of diffusion at lower Pe  .  A representative part of (a) the initial mesh and (b) the mesh at the final iteration for the flow in a sub-sample of the bead pack is displayed in Fig. C.14 , showing how mesh refinement captures the narrow mixing zone. Fig. 7 a shows the evolution of the total number of computational degrees of freedom (mesh nodes) as a function of mesh refinement iteration. For each value of Pe  , the mesh refinement process culminates at a specific iteration, i.e. when the criterion (29)  is met in all cells. The refinement stops after three, five, and six iterations for the three considered Péclet numbers in increasing order. The number of nodes at which the refinement process saturates (N  sat    ) as a function of Pe   values is shown in Fig. 7 b, consistent with a linear scaling N  sat   ∼ Pe   . This relation can be rationalized in light of the Batchelor scale that sets the mixing scale in chaotic flows (Heyman et al., 2020 ). Stretching and folding of fluid elements in the pore space lead to an exponential elongation of fluid elements (Lester et al., 2016; Turuban et al., 2019; Souzy et al., 2020 ) ρ ∼ e  λ t / t  a       , where λ   is the dimensionless Lyapunov exponent and t  a   = d / U    is the advection time. The resulting constant stretching rate implies that diffusion and compression equilibrate at the Batchelor scale s  B   ∼ D d / ( λ U )      . Thus, the width of the mixing interface is expected to scale with s  B   ∼ d Pe  − 1 / 2     . As detailed in Appendix G , a fixed number of nodes N  ⊥     is required to satisfy the refinement criterion Eq. (29)  in the direction perpendicular to the interface, leading to h ∼ s  B   / N  ⊥     . Assuming roughly isotropic elements yields a total number of nodes N  sat   ∼ N  ⊥   A / h  2     , where A   is the area of the interface, which for large Pe   will only increase weakly with Pe  . Thus, we find N  sat   ∼ N  ⊥  3   Pe   , in particular N  sat   ∼ Pe   , explaining the result of Fig. 7 b. This scaling highlights the effect of pore scale chaotic mixing on the enhancement of concentration gradients and of the resulting required mesh refinement.  On a physical level, the steady Eq. (14a)  reflects mass conservation, i.e. the flux of a conserved species δ   is the same through each cross-section Ω  ⊥   ( z )     of the domain transverse to the flow direction. To ensure that our results are valid, this fundamental property should be respected also numerically. Fig. 8  shows the average flux of δ  , denoted as J  δ    , for different iterations of mesh refinement for the three considered Péclet numbers. The flux J  δ     is here relatively constant, fluctuating around J  ̄    δ   ≃ − 0 . 04   , which is different from 0 because the domain is not symmetric. The fluctuations in J  δ     are of the order < 0 . 005   , which must be compared to the total flux of velocity, which by construction is J ≃ 1    (since the mean velocity U = 1   ). The relatively consistent values of the average J  δ     for each value of Pe   demonstrate that mass conservation is well respected. Furthermore, the fluctuations in J  δ     decay with increasing refinement for all Pe   values. This result suggests that the deviations from mass conservation originate from an imperfect input velocity field due to the fact that the solution method (FEM) only weakly satisfies the divergence-free condition (Eq. (B.2) ). Altogether, these results establish confidence in our simulations.  To further investigate mixing-limited reactions inside the bead pack, we examine the distribution of the reaction product C for different refinement iterations within the bead pack for flow with Pe = 1 . 3 ⋅ 1 0  3     . Figs. 9 a and 9 b show the integrated mass M  c     (Eq. (26) ) and reaction rate (Eq. (23) ) of product C in each cross-section along the z  -direction, respectively. We verify that refinement iterations increase the accuracy of the distribution of c   and its reaction dynamics in the bead pack. In Supplementary Information (Movies S1–S6), we provide videos of the spatial distribution of δ   and c   in cross sections moving along the z  -direction in the bead pack.  The simulations of this section provide insights into the behavior of solute mixing under conditions of chaotic flow through a bead pack. The adaptive mesh refinement method successfully captures the intricate patterns of mixing and reaction at the pore scale, demonstrating its efficiency in handling complex geometries.
