Unlike the WaterGAP model, which employs a single curve for prediction, our approach provides a more accurate portrayal of regional differentials in water use efficiency in relation to economic development. If the analysis reveals that the IWUE indicators are difficult to reach via the current match mode of IWUE and EDL, the rank match level between IWUE and EDL must be increased. The department of water resource management should increase its investment in IWUE control methods, such as reducing industries with high water consumption and promoting the use of water-saving technology, and it should keep the rank match degree of IWUE and EDL at a higher level, thereby increasing the marginal benefits of economic development for water use efficiency. The model can be used to anticipate regional industrial water demands. As a result, estimating industrial water demand requires knowledge of both the economy index (such as industrial added value and GDP per capita) and the IWUE index (such as water use per 10,000 yuan of industrial added value) in order to provide an accurate estimate. WaterGAP2 follows this same idea, with the exception that it measures the total industrial water use by multiplying the industrial water use intensity by the country's total electricity output. Therefore, the proposed conceptual model can reveal and predict IWUE by EDL which is more accessible. The IWUE model comprises three stages if it is to be used to calculate regional industrial water demands. The economic model predicts the GDP per capita and industrial added value first. Then, the GDP per capita is substituted into the conceptual model of IWUE to determine the water use per 10,000 yuan of industrial added value. The prospective total industrial water demand in a region is calculated by multiplying its industrial added value by the water use per 10,000 yuan of industrial added value.  4.2 Potential improvements of the conceptual regional IWUE model This study investigated the relationship between the EDL and the IWUE at the prefecture-level city scale. The findings indicate that the two indices exhibit a hyperbolic pattern, the parameters of which is determined by their rank match level. There is an expectation that this regulation can be employed in the projection and analysis of global IWUE comparisons, provided that its validity is proven at the national level. The prediction of regional IWUE necessitates the assumption that the city will maintain the same rank match level between years, or that the rank match level can be estimated beforehand. In mainland China, the rank match level has remained constant in 102 of 336 cities between 1998 and 2017. Given that cities' rank match degrees may change over time, predicting rank match degree will be the focus of future research. If the rank match degree of cities in the following year can be anticipated, the model's accuracy will improve, making it more practical. Furthermore, using an ensemble prediction approach, which includes all possible matching level hyperbola equations, may provide a broader perspective of future IWUE. A prediction with a confidence interval can improve our understanding of future IWUE dynamics. For decision-makers of water resources management, maximize the marginal advantages of economic development for water efficiency, it is necessary to improve the rank match level as part of the regulation measures for improving regional IWUE. Therefore, in future research, it is essential to determine the factors that affect the rank match level. The water resources per capita, the urbanization rate, the industrial output value per capita, the proportion of industrial employees, the percentage of the total industrial output value that comes from high-water-consumption industries, the percentage of the total industrial output value that comes from high-tech industries, the industrial water price, the industrial wastewater discharge rate, and other related variables are all possibilities to affect the rank match level. In future investigations, it is crucial to do additional research on prospective aspects that may have an impact, and afterward integrate them into a more comprehensive set of components. This will provide a strong basis for the development of a more accurate scenario model for IWUE. This process will entail the refinement of the model framework, which will enable water resources management to effectively govern the various aspects that influence regional IWUE, hence facilitating its improvements. The conceptual model presented in this study has the potential to serve as a beneficial foundation for future prediction and regulation of IWUE in various regions and countries.   5 Conclusion The conceptual model established in this study is derived from three key findings. The stable categorical hyperbolic correlation between the log-transformed EDL and IWUE indices forms the foundation for employing similar model structures in different rank match levels. Second, the shape of the hyperbola remains constant throughout different years, implying that the model’s shape parameter a i   remains stable and can be effectively calibrated using multi-year data samples. Furthermore, the hyperbola's location exhibits a linear relationship with the progression of the year, which lays a foundation for predicting regional IWUE in the coming years. The model is trained using data from 336 administrative cities in China from 1998 to 2014 and validated using data from 2015 to 2017. The precision demonstrates the practicability of using the model to simulate the annual variation of regional IWUE. Given the assumption that the unit maintains a constant rank match level, the model is capable of predicting the regional IWUE based on the projection of EDL. Subsequently, a number of water resources management measures can be evaluated to determine their effect on increasing the rank match level in order to achieve the regional IWUE control objective. The factors that influence the rank match level remain an unanswered question that requires additional investigation to resolve. After the model is built using data sets encompassing various regional units, the IWUE prediction results for a single region may be produced. This parsimonious model thus provides a useful analysis tool for the prediction and regulation of regional IWUE. While China currently lacks objective methods for determining regulatory targets for regional industrial water efficiency, this model provides a new quantitative analysis technique for improving the country's Most Stringent Water Resources Management System, which is based on the control of water use "quantity, quality, and efficiency" red lines. This study can be used as a starting point for more research into the correlation between IWUE and other socioeconomic characteristics in different nations and as an outline for improving regional and possibly worldwide IWUE model construction and parameterization.
1 Introduction Groundwater resources are globally preferred as a source of water for drinking, agriculture and industry, and often considered more reliable and accessible than surface water (Guppy et al., 2018; Gleeson et al., 2020; Nawaz et al., 2022 ). With population increase and the advert threats of climate change, groundwater has become increasingly threatened, with depletion due to an escalating demand, and pollution due to rising volumes of wastewater, and increased use of chemicals in agriculture practices (Abbasi et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2018; Noori et al., 2019; Bera et al., 2022 ). Pro-active groundwater protection actions are undoubtedly essential to support groundwater quality protection strategies (Banda et al., 2019; Simaubi et al., 2023 ). Aquifer vulnerability assessment to pollution is an important component in the development of groundwater quality protection strategies and provides a basis for practical guidelines and policies that will minimize groundwater pollution and thus allowing sustainable resources management (Chande and Mayo, 2019 ). To effectively institute any groundwater quality protection measures, it is necessary to delineate the groundwater zones vulnerable to contamination. Aquifer vulnerability lacks a standard and specific definition (Vrba and Zaporozec, 1994; Fannakh and Farsang, 2022 ) as it is not an absolute indicator but rather a complex indicator. Nevertheless, it is basically a measure of the sensitivity of groundwater quality to contaminant load. It is based on the intrinsic characteristics such as the inherent geology, hydrology and geohydraulics of the aquifer system. Aquifer vulnerability can be regarded as intrinsic or specific; the former is the vulnerability based on the aquifer properties, whereas, in the latter both the nature of the contaminant and aquifer are considered. Several methods to quantify these vulnerabilities exist, which can be put into three basic groups: overlay index-based (qualitative methods), statistical and process-based method (quantitative methods) (Taghavi et al., 2022 ). The quantitative methods, which include simulation modeling are intended to determine the “specific vulnerability” of groundwater, whereas the qualitative methods aim to examine “intrinsic vulnerability”. Overlay index-based methods are commonly used for groundwater vulnerability due to their simple and easy data handling protocols. The parameters used for the analysis can be adapted based on site conditions and data availability. DRASTIC (Depth to water table [D], Net recharge to the aquifer [R], Aquifer media [A], Soil media [S], Topography [T], Impact of vadose zone [I], Conductivity [C]) (Aller et al., 1987 ), AVI (Aquifer Vulnerability Index) (Stempvoort et al., 1993 ), GOD (Groundwater Occurrence [G], Overall lithology of aquifer [O], Depth of groundwater level [D]) (Foster, 1998 ), SINTACS (Civita and De Maio, 2004 ), modified SINTACS method (Awawdeh et al., 2020 ) are some of the most commonly used overlay index-based methods. Among the overlay index-based methods, the most widely used and popular method is DRASTIC (Fannakh and Farsang, 2022; Taghavi et al., 2022 ). DRASTIC method provides a better visualization of spatially varied results and is best suited for regional-scale vulnerability assessments (Abbasi et al., 2013; Bera et al., 2022 ). Through a process of assigning appropriate ranking and weight on the scale of one to ten and a GIS based weighted overlay, vulnerable zones are obtained (Taghavi et al., 2022 ). In the conceptualisation of the DRASTIC model, Aller et al. (1987) , made important assumptions that include: (a) at the earth’s surface, the pollutant is released (through the use of fertilizers, burning of coal and leaching of metals from coal-ash tailings etc.), (b) the pollutant is transferred into the groundwater by rainfall, (c) the pollutant moves simultaneously with water, and (d) the affected area should be at least 100 acres (0.4 square kilometres). These assumptions limit the application of DRASTIC when some or all of the factors are invalidated (Saha and Alam, 2014 ). Vulnerability mapping using the DRASTIC technique has a number of shortcomings, despite its ease of use and popularity. The biggest disadvantage is its subjective nature, which raises questions about the selection of specific factors and the exclusion of others (Panagopoulos et al., 2006 ). Several researchers have disagreed with parameter weights and ranks thus proposed modifications in DRASTIC (Saha and Alam, 2014; Mogaji and Lim, 2017; Ahmed et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2022; Saranya and Saravanan, 2023 ). DRASTIC has been criticized for the following reasons in its application as detailed by Patel et al. (2022) : (a) by giving equal rates and weights to parameters, it ignores the effect of regional characteristics (b) a standard validation approach is not used in this procedure. (c) the parameters were chosen based on qualitative assessment rather than quantitative research. As a result, a number of researchers have worked to improve the DRASTIC model so that a more accurate vulnerability assessment may be obtained. Several methods have been developed to enhance the ranks and weights used in the DRASTIC method. For example, Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) has been adopted when the problem statement involves several influencing factors, and used to find the weights of the parameters used in DRASTIC (Thirumalaivasan et al., 2003; Bai et al., 2012; Lad et al., 2019 ). Similarly, other methods include Fuzzy Logic technique (Saranya and Saravanan, 2022; Nourani et al., 2023 ), Artificial Neural Networks (Agoubi and Kharroubi, 2019 ). Also, some of the statistical bivariate models like the Linear Regression model (LR), Frequency Ratio model (FR), Weight of Evidence (WofE), Shannon Entropy (SE) aims at determining the risk of groundwater contamination by assessing the statistical dependency of parameters with the contaminant (Khoshtinat et al., 2019; Taghavi et al., 2022 ). Additionally, machine learning methods such as decision tree (DT), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), naïve Bayes (NB), Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) and adaptive neuro fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) have also been used to optimise rankings and weights thus better accuracy in groundwater vulnerability assessments (Nadiri et al., 2018; Moazamnia et al., 2020; Barzegar et al., 2021; Elzain et al., 2022; Nourani et al., 2024 ). Machine learning algorithm, even though new and robust, require large and high resolution data for accuracy. In data scarce regions, the effective use of the foregoing methods are constrained, thus a dependency on overlay methods, especially DRASTIC or numerical models (Roy et al., 2024 ). An innovative approach to overcome data challenges, has been to use Bayesian Probability algorithms such as Weights of Evidence (WofE). WofE though a relatively simple tool, has been documented to have superior prediction power compared to other objective methods such as SE, Logistic Model Tree (LMT) and Bootstrap Aggregating (BA) (Sorichetta et al., 2011; Abbasi et al., 2013; Khosravi et al., 2018 ). WofE in some cases has produced better accuracy than machine learning options like RF and BRT (Rahmati and Pourghasemi, 2017 ). To the best of our knowledge, the application of WofE has been on a local scale catchment. The aim of this study is to evaluate the reliability of the DRASTIC approach by comparing its results to the Weights of Evidence (WofE) modelling approach at a regional scale. The Tuli-Karoo Aquifer System, a transboundary aquifer system (TBA) shared among South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana, was selected as there is a disproportional availability of data on the aquifer system. The South African side is well monitored, with data on groundwater quality and quantity regularly collected. The TBA also has several hotspot threating groundwater quality. The outcomes of this research provide a basis for regional transboundary aquifer governance.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area Tuli Karoo Transboundary Aquifer is a transboundary aquifer system within the Limpopo River Basin ( Fig. 1 ). The surface area is over 12,000 km2 , with a population just over 120,000. The Tuli Karoo is shared among Botswana, South Africa and Zimbabwe. The biggest proportion of the aquifer’s surface area is contained within Zimbabwe; whereas the smallest part was contained in South Africa. 2.1.1 Geography and climate Overall, the Tuli-Karoo Catchment is predominately dry. The 1999–2000 season at Botswana's Bobonong Rainfall Station recorded the greatest annual rainfall total of 1074 mm, while Tshokwe Station recorded the lowest annual rainfall total of 5 mm (International Water Management Institute, 2019 ). High inter-annual rainfall variability in the recent decades has resulted in significant droughts and floods. Stations in and near the Tuli-Karoo have mean annual maximum temperatures between 29 and 33 0 C. According to Siebert et al. (2013) , the Tuli-Karoo Catchment was predominately arid to semi-arid. Topography varies from 817 to 474 m and slopes towards the south-east (International Water Management Institute, 2019 ).  2.1.2 Geology and hydrogeology of the study area The Tuli-Karoo Aquifer straddles Botswana, South Africa and Zimbabwe. It is part of the Karoo Supergroup Formation composed of mudstones, siltstones, sandstones and grits overlain by aeolian sandstone, which are in turn overlain by basaltic flood lavas (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). The lowest stratigraphic unit contains a conglomeratic sandstone embedded in a fine-grained silty matrix. The upper units are generally homogenous, red bedded clastic sediments and aeolian deposits. In parts of the unit, the sandstone is poorly sorted suggesting that, at least in part, the sediments were deposited under fluvial conditions. The more extensive upper unit are basalts, whereas the lower unit are olivine tholeites and limburgites (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). Tuli-Karoo is a multilayer aquifer composed of four different aquifers ( Table 1 ). The intergranular aquifer type in the form of unconsolidated sediments occurs around the Limpopo River channel as alluvium hosts has groundwater yields (Unconsolidated sedimentary aquifers/Alluvium aquifers in Table 1 ). It is extensively developed, having many boreholes with shallow water strikes and some are considered artesian, as they do not require a pump to bring water to the surface. The total groundwater resource using the average aquifer thickness of 20 m has been estimated at 750 million m3  (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). Basalt Aquifer (Karoo Igneous Aquifer) is often overlooked as a potential aquifer due to absence of primary porosity, however, it has secondary porosity that is well developed along linear fracture zones associated with faulting and contact between individual basalt flows. The transmissivity varies according to the amount of secondary porosity the basalt has developed and thus it can range from as little as 0.1 to as high as 100 m2 /day. Tsheung/Forest Sandstone aquifer is laterally extensive and generally hydraulically continuous. The main sandstone aquifer has a dual porosity with the primary and fracture porosity being limited (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). The aquifer is overlain by Karoo basalts and underlain by mudstones and fine grained formations with low permeability (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). As consequence, the aquifer is confined and unconfined at different parts of the basin. Furthermore, its basalt sandstone contact is a secondary porosity that is well developed at the indurated-basalt contact. Transmissivities from this aquifer range from 9 to 121 m2 / day, whereas storativity ranges from 0.00006 to 0.03, albeit for the Sandstone only (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). In the Madikana beds, hosts undifferentiated rocks and diverse lithologies in the form of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks are characterised by low to mid water yields. Drilling data in the area showed evidence of sandstone intercalations within the basalt with thickness of 1–10 m. They were encountered as shallow as 49 mbgl (metres below ground level) and as deep as 193 mbgl with 5–15 m of basalt between the beds (Water Surveys Botswana Ltd, 2007 ). Transmissivity has been calculated within a range of 5–23 m2 /day. The aquifer area is similar across the three countries, thus the Water Surveys Botswana Limited developed a conceptual model of groundwater flow. The current understanding is that the Tsheung/Forest sandstone is locally disconnected from the other hydrogeological units. Groundwater flow is mainly recharged around the edges of the aquifer system through the sandstone or near the basement-basalt contact. Recharge also occurs within exposed and weathered/fracture basalt outcrops. However, it is isolated and does not interact with the main groundwater flow existing as perched aquifers. Once, it enters the aquifer area it flows towards the centre of the aquifer area, then flows in the south-eastward direction to discharge along the edge of the aquifer area. The discharge is in the form of artesian flows in the basalt, whereas in the Tsheung/Forest Sandstone, it is ultimately lost to evapotranspiration.  2.1.3 Groundwater quality threats It is important to emphasise that possible sources of contamination may lie outside of the Tuli-Karoo Aquifer Region but inside the larger Limpopo Basin. This is because the area's geology is very heterogeneous, with certain places having extensive fracture densities that allow for higher potential connection. There are mines, factories, abattoirs and wastewater treatment plants in the region that are hotspots for pollution. The location of pollution hotspot areas in Botswana include Bamangwato Concessions Ltd (BCL) Mine, Water Utilities Corporation Mambo Water Treatment Plant, Nortex textiles, B and M textiles, Botswana Breweries Limited, Botswana Meat Commission Abattoir, Richmark Chicken Abattoir, Bobbsies Chicken Abattoir and Botswana Breweries Limited (International Water Management Institute, 2019 ). In South Africa the hotspot areas include Vele Coal Mine (closed), Venetia Diamond Mine and wastewater treatment in Weipe Town and from Zimbabwe part of the aquifer area, the areas include wastewater treatment near Beitbridge, Manama area (Tuli Coal Mine - closed opencast coal mine due to poor coal) and Shigwangana area (new coal mine opening soon). Commercial agriculture using fertilisers containing nitrates is also of concern especially in South Africa. Natural occurrence of nitrates has also been reported in several studies (Vogel et al., 2004; Stadler et al., 2008; Gemmell et al., 2021 ).   2.2 DRASTIC method DRASTIC approach to vulnerability assessment has been used widely since its development by the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) and the National Water Well Association (NWWA) during the mid-1980s (Aller et al., 1987 ). The method is relatively simple in concept and is particularly popular due to its ease of use and strong compatibility with GIS software. DRASTIC includes weighing the contributions from seven parameters to calculate an index value ( Table 2 ). The parameters are: D  – depth to water; R  – net recharge; A  – aquifer media; S  – soil media; T  – topography (slope); I  – impact of the vadose zone media; and C  – conductivity (hydraulic) of the aquifer. The index is calculated as follows:(1) V =  ∑ i = 1  7   ( W  i    x  R  i   )   … … … … … … … … … …     Where V  is the calculated index value, W i   is the weighting coefficient for parameter i , and R i   is the rating value for parameter i . The weighting coefficients range from 1 to 5, depending on their relative importance, and D  (depth to water) has a high weighting coefficient of 5. Higher index values indicate more susceptibility than lower ones, and the derived index offers a relative indication of the aquifer's potential vulnerability to pollution (Javadi et al., 2011 ). Many researchers have tried to improve the DRASTIC algorithm through various refinements (e.g. Thirumalaivasan et al., 2003 ; Noori et al., 2019 , Bera et al., 2021 ), but the standard DRASTIC approach is still used routinely as the primary approach to vulnerability assessment.  2.3 Weights of evidence method Among the various statistical methods, the WofE modelling technique has been chosen for its reliability in performing meaningful and scientific defendable groundwater vulnerability maps, which has been proved by various authors (e.g. Arthur et al., 2007 ; Uhan et al., 2011 ). Groundwater vulnerability was evaluated using the Weights of Evidence (WofE) approach, which established relationships between a variety of contributing hydrogeological parameters and measured groundwater nitrate concentrations. The WofE method has been widely used in mineral resource evaluation and landslide vulnerability (Bonham-Carter, 1989; Porwal et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2002; Chakrabortty et al., 2022 ). Since its first application in the 1990s to assist US Superfund investigations, it has gained popularity in risk assessments related to ecology and environmental health (Linkov et al., 2009; Hope and Clarkson, 2014; Suter et al., 2020 ). There are still limited cases of the application of WofE in hydrogeology (Corsini et al., 2009; Abbasi et al., 2013; Ozdemir, 2015; Khoshtinat et al., 2019 ). The range of values that affects the concentration of water quality may be identified by using the WofE approach, which assesses the significance of each individual factor class. It can also be used by combining two or more classes that are associated with distinct parameters that have a high association with a contaminant (Masetti et al., 2008 ). The WofE is a statistical method based on Bayes’ theorem. If a causal factor is represented by B , the classes in it are Bi , and the supporting evidence is denoted by s ; then, as stated by Corsini et al. (2009) , Bayes’ theorem can be used to calculate the conditional probability to have s  given the class B i   according to Eq. 2 :(2) p s  |  B  i      = p    B  i    |  s     ×  p s      / p B  i      … … … …     Where p s  |  B  i         is the conditional probability to have B i  , given s ; p(s ) is the prior probability to find s  within the study area (AS); and p(Bi ) is the prior probability to find the class Bi  within the study area AS (Eq. 3 ). The conditional probability to have s  when the class Bi  is not given is:(3)  p s  |  B  i    Ʌ      = p    B  i    Ʌ    |  s     ×  p s      / p B  i    Ʌ          Where p(Bi ˆ|s ) is the conditional probability not to have the class Bi , given s ; and p(Bi ˆ) is the prior probability not to find the class Bi  within the study area AS. All these calculations are possible using various GIS platforms because of the spatial nature of the data. In this study, the ArcSDM extension to ArcGIS 10.3 was used (Sawatzky et al., 2009 ). Using map-crossing functions, all the members of Eqs. (2) and (3)  can be calculated as follows (Corsini et al., 2009 ):p s    = area s  / area AS       p B  i      = area B  i     / area AS       p B  i    Ʌ      = area B  i    Ʌ     / area AS       p s  |  B  i      = area s ∩ B  i     / area B  i        / p B  i          p s  |  B  i      = area s ∩ B  i     / area B  i        / p s        p s  |  B  i    Ʌ      = area s ∩ B  i    Ʌ     / area B  i    Ʌ        / p B  i    Ʌ          p B  i    Ʌ    |  s    = area s ∩ B  i    Ʌ     / area B  i    Ʌ        / p s         In the WofE analysis, the weight of every class of causal factors can be calculated by combination of positive and negative correlation values (W +  and W −) and by the difference (or “contrast” C ) between them, as follows:W  +    = ln p B  i    |  s     |  p B  i             W  −    = ln p B  i    Ʌ    |  s     |  p B  i    Ʌ             C =  W  +   −  W  −        The weights W + and W − are zero, such that C  becomes zero where a map pattern has a distribution that is spatially independent of the points. For a positive spatial association, C  will have a positive value, usually in the range 0–2; and C  would assume a negative value in a similar range for a negative association.  2.4 Data acquisition Data availability is poor in the TBA with no groundwater monitoring data on the Zimbabwean side. Some data on production boreholes was available across the three countries but with gaps on aquifer properties, water quality and hydraulics. Data acquisition was therefore from global datasets and remote sensing products to fill the gaps. A summary of the input datasets and spatial resolution are provided in  Table 3 .  2.5 Data analysis 2.5.1 Sensitivity analysis In general, sensitivity analysis measures the uncertainty and the robustness of the output results obtained from model-based outputs. In this study, the single-parameter sensitivity analysis is implemented to assess the effect of each parameter on the vulnerability index, by comparing its assigned (theoretical) weight with the real (effective) weight (Napolitano and Fabbri, 1996; Ouedraogo et al., 2016; Kirlas et al., 2022 ). This technique helps to evaluate the importance of subjectivity elements in the vulnerability method. The effective weights for all parameters were calculated using Eq. 4 :(4) W = ( P  r   P  w    V   )  × 100      Where W is the effective weight of each parameter, Pr  and Pw  are the rating value and the weight of each parameter, respectively, and V denotes the overall vulnerability index (Ouedraogo et al., 2016 ). When a parameter has an effective weight greater than the theoretical value, it has a higher significance on the results of the groundwater vulnerability model.  2.5.2 Model evaluation with receiver operating characteristic Model evaluation is a crucial step to determine the quality of the achieved maps. In this study, we use the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) method. ROC method is the well-known and most popular method of evaluation based on visual attractiveness. This performance metric, developed by Swets (1988) , considers the accuracy of diagnostic systems. The result of the diagnostic system and an event are divided into four groups, which comprise True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False-Positive (FP), False Negative (FN) to prepare the ROC curve. The ROC curve displays the FP variations versus TP at various threshold settings. The model with higher performance has the ROC curve with a deviation toward the left upper corner. The Area under the Curve (AUC) quantifies this deviation as the ratio of the area under the ROC curve to the total area, which varies between 0.5 and 1. The AUC values close to 0.5 indicate a random signal in the model, whereas the AUC value close to 1 indicates a significant signal.    3 Results 3.1 Depth to the water table The depth to the water table was facilitated by 250 production boreholes that have been drilled in the area and analysed for this study. The boreholes intersect different aquifer systems at different depth.  Fig. 2 , shows that the groundwater level varies from 3.6 m to more than 28 m. Generally, the groundwater water table is shallow on the eastern side and deepens towards the west. This suggests that groundwater flows from the east (Zimbabwe area) to the west (Botswana). The ranking of the classes are shown in Fig. 2  as well.  3.2 Net recharge due to rainfall Net recharge indicates the amount of water per unit area of land penetrating through the ground surface and reaching the water table (Bhuvaneswaran and Ganesh, 2019 ).  Fig. 3 , shows the net recharge of the Tuli-Karoo Aquifer. High recharge occurs around the edges of the aquifer through the sandstone or near the basement-basalt contact. Recharge data was obtained from the WHYMAP database (https://services.bgr.de/grundwasser/whymap_gwr ).  3.3 Aquifer media The Tuli-Karoo Sedimentary succession consists of a series of mudstones, siltstones, sandstones and conglomerates overlain by aeolian sandstones, with basaltic flood lavas overlying everything. The intergranular aquifer type occurs at the northern part of the aquifer along the Limpopo river channel and was generally high water yielding. Datasets were obtained from the SADC-GIP (Groundwater Information Portal) database and aquifer types were plotted and ranked as per  Fig. 4 . Dolomites and limestone were ranked highly (10) whereas poor permeability rocks were ranked poorly (3).  3.4 Soil media Soil significantly impacts the amount of recharge that can infiltrate into the ground and have the ability of a contaminant to move vertically into the vadose zone. Lithosols / leptosols are the predominant soil media, followed by calcic luvisols and vertic cambisols ( Fig. 5 ). Cambic arenosols were ranked the highest (6), whereas, the rest of the classes were relatively poor conduits for infiltration thus ranked low (3).  3.5 Topography Topography was converted to slope as shown in  Fig. 6 . Generally, the slope was flat (0 – 2 %) as shown in Fig. 6 . Higher slopes were observed in the central interior region of the basin. Given that the shallower slopes allow for ponding of water compared to steep slopes, a high ranking of ‘10’ was allocated to shallow slopes and ‘1’ to the steepest.  3.6 Impact of the vadose zone The type of material in the vadose zone determines the pollution attenuation. Most soils are coarse-grained sandy and clayey loam soils with generally good permeability and drainage. They are primarily from granites, gneisses and sandstone parent material; hence their coarse and gravely texture over the Tuli-Karoo Sub-Basin TBA. Given that the soil media and impact of the vadose provide similar inputs, we disregard the impact of vadose zone.  3.7 Hydraulic conductivity The hydraulic conductivity over the entire aquifer thickness, thus, transmissivity is given in  Fig. 7 . Data were obtained from the British Geological Survey database (Africa Groundwater Atlas) taken from the work of MacDonald et al., (2012) . The highest ranking (‘10’) was allocated to the zone with transmissivity 44–50 m2 /d and lowest ranking (‘1’) for the range 13–26 m2 /d.  3.8 Vulnerability maps The generic DRASTIC map, in  Fig. 8 , shows low (41−89), medium (89.1 – 101) and high vulnerability (102 – 132). WofE vulnerability classification ( Fig. 9 ) based on the posterior probability, shows high probability vulnerability of 0.005 – 0.022, medium (0.002 – 0.004) and lowest vulnerability of 0 – 0.001. DRASTIC high vulnerability area covers 52 % compared to 40 % for the WofE map. In addition, DRASTIC medium vulnerability covers 25 % against 44 % medium vulnerability for the WofE. Furthermore, 23 % and 16 % area coverage for the low vulnerability area in the DRASTIC and WofE vulnerability, respectively. The two maps tend to capture high aquifer vulnerability well but vary in the spatial variability of low to high vulnerability. Specifically, the DRASTIC approach has a large proportion in the west with low vulnerability and high vulnerability in the east. WofE has a large proportion of medium vulnerability in the central region. Nitrate concentration values were from 22 mg/L to 631.4 mg/L and were predominately from the South African side (Fig. 8 ). No water quality datasets were available on the Zimbabwe side. The potential impacts on groundwater protection and performance of the two models are discussed in the subsequent sections.  3.9 DRASTIC sensitivity analysis  Table 4 , shows the sensitivity of the DRASTIC model used for the Tuli-Karoo Aquifer system. Generally importance of parameters range as follows D > I > A > R >T > C > S, compared to the theoretical D ∼ I > R > A ∼ C > S > T. The aquifer media (14.8 %) and topography (10.2 %) have higher weights than the theoretical weight indicating high sensitive to the generic DRASTIC vulnerability map.   4 Discussion 4.1 Vulnerability assessment The DRASTIC vulnerability, Fig. 8 , was likely geologically controlled, with high vulnerability within the intercalated shales and sandstones, and fractured basalts. This is in agreement with other DRASTIC based assessments where the geological character (lithology) strongly influenced the vulnerability (Li et al., 2018; Udosen et al., 2024 ). In contrast, WofE vulnerability seems to be controlled by the soil media and topography using nitrate as evidence. Several studies have shown that the extent of contamination within regional aquifers is dependent on regional hydrology, soil properties, climate, land use patterns, and nature of contaminators (Vrba and Zaporozec, 1994; Lahjouj et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2024 ). These parameters facilitate the ease of toxicant exudation into the vadose zone thus rendering aquifers susceptible to contamination. The WofE approach to vulnerability assessment produces specific vulnerability that takes into account the role of the contaminant (nitrate in this case study), whereas the standard DRASTIC method uses the geological and hydrogeological characteristics of the media to produce a measure of intrinsic vulnerability that is independent of the contaminant. This is in agreement other authors (Corsini et al., 2009; Abbasi et al., 2013; Ozdemir, 2015; Khoshtinat et al., 2019 ) who have demonstrated similar finding although with a larger dataset available for validation.  4.2 Comparison of DRASTIC and WofE The two vulnerability models were compared using the Receiver Operating Curve (ROC) ( Fig. 10 ). Based on the area under the curve (AUC), WofE and DRASTIC have performance values of 0.61 and 0.63, respectively, interpretated as being comparable. According to Yesilnacar and Topal (2005) , an AUC between 0.6 – 0.7 indicates satisfactory performance. DRASTIC, although a simpler method, captures the high groundwater vulnerability well compared to WofE as discussed in Section 3.8 . Ouedraogo et al. (2016)  conducted a pan-Africa scale groundwater vulnerability assessment showed that DRASTIC was sensitive to the depth to water. Sorichetta et al. (2013)  compared different data-driven groundwater assessment method and demonstrated that WofE was affected by the soil protection cover. Under data scarcity conditions, WofE would therefore be an appropriate model to use over DRASTIC.   5 Limitations The nitrate data points were not homogenously distributed across the catchment. An assumption was therefore made that the available dataset for validation was sufficient as the lithological information was generally homogenous throughout the basin.  6 Conclusion and recommendations The study investigated the reliability of the DRASTIC approach by comparing its results to vulnerability assessments obtained using the Weights of Evidence (WofE) approach with elevated nitrate, in the Tuli-Karoo Transboundary Aquifer. The study revealed that the generic DRASTIC vulnerability model results were comparable to the WofE, if you considered elevated nitrate concentration. Therefore, one would conclude that DRASTIC performs well and was reliable in data scare regions to predict vulnerability. However, there are differences in spatial variability comparing DRASTIC and WofE vulnerability maps. Given that groundwater vulnerability is not a measured quantity in the field like landslides, the usefulness and the focus should not only be in zones classified as high vulnerability, but also in low/medium vulnerability. WofE was therefore superior in capturing spatial variability of groundwater vulnerability. Considerations must therefore be provided, under data scarcity, to incorporate proxies that include landuse-landcover and population density as evidential layers. This study recommends that more studies should focus on validation approaches that use high predictive models like WofE to support effective environmental planning and groundwater protection strategies in data scarce region. 1 Introduction Nowadays, contaminants in subsurface environments are reasonably likely to have an adverse effect on human health. Therefore, it is crucial to implement a robust long-term health risk assessment system (Wenning and Apitz, 2024 ). This system would facilitate the detection and monitoring of hazardous substances in subsurface environments, helping to ensure that public exposure remains at safe levels. Groundwater flow is the most likely pathway for the transport of contaminants released from source regions into the subsurface environment (Banaei et al., 2021 ; Bourg, I. C., 2010 ). Various theoretical and experimental studies have been carried out to understand the fate and transport of contaminants in groundwater system, aimed at developing appropriate and accurate mathematical models for calculating the concentration of contaminants. The advection-dispersion equation (ADE) is a crucial tool for understanding the transport behavior of contaminants in groundwater. Analytical approaches to ADE are often more efficient than numerical models for evaluating contaminant distribution over extensive spatial and temporal scales (Lin et al., 2022 ). This efficiency arises because numerical solutions usually demand a substantial number of grids and time steps, leading to significant computational loads. In contrast, analytical solutions do not necessitate discretization of the temporal and spatial domains, enabling rapid calculations. A number of analytical models have been developed that can be used for describing the transport of a single contaminant in saturated and homogeneous geological media (Chen et al., 2017 ; Gao et al., 2013 ; Liang et al., 2016 ; Mustafa et al., 2022 ; Pérez Guerrero et al., 2010 ; Qiu et al., 2022 ; Shaikh and Eldho, 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2009 ). Contaminants decay into other elements or stable species, called the daughter or progeny species. These decay chain reactions have a profound effect on the plume migrations of decaying contaminant (Chen et al., 2018 ). However, the process of transformation from the parent species to daughter element has generally been neglected in the previously developed single-species analytical models. Thus, such models will produce inaccurate predictions of transport behavior for all progeny members of a sequential decay chain. Over the past several decades, progress has been made towards developing multispecies analytical transport models in which a set of ADEs is coupled to a series of decay reactions for evaluating the transport of coexistence of a decaying contaminant and its sequential products (Carr, 2021 ; Chaudhary and Singh, 2020 ; Chen et al., 2016 , 2023 ; Liao et al., 2021 , 2022 ; Mieles and Zhan, 2012 ; Pérez Guerrero et al., 2009 , 2010 ; Quezada et al., 2004 ; Srinivasan and Clement, 2008a , 2008b ; Sudicky et al., 2013 ; Suk, 2013 , 2016 , 2022a , 2022b ; Yu et al., 2019 ). Most of the aforementioned multispecies transport analytical models consider equilibrium sorption between the dissolved and sorbed phases. With the equilibrium sorption assumption, the mass transfer of contaminants is considered to occur more rapidly than the time scale required for groundwater flow through geological media. Numerous studies have shown that nonequilibrium sorption significantly influences the transport of sorbed contaminants (Hansen and Vesselinov, 2018 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ; Kaleris, 2002 ; Clement et al., 2004 ; Shupe et al., 2011 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2019 ). When the sorption mass transfer reaction is not sufficiently rapid compared to the solute travel time, the local equilibrium assumption becomes invalid, and its impact can be substantial (Hansen and Vesselinov, 2018 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ). In such flow conditions, the sorption process should be represented as a first-order reversible kinetic reaction (Zheng and Bennett, 2002 ). Efforts have thus been made to develop analytical models that solve ADEs linked with first-order reversible kinetic sorption reaction with consideration of rate-limited mass partitions of contaminants between the dissolved and sorbed phases (Goltz and Oxley, 1991 ; Haggerty and Gorelick, 1995 ; Valocchi, 1986 ). However, relatively few analytical models have been derived for multispecies transport of sequentially decaying products subject to nonequilibrium sorption process. In Kaleris (2002) , a numerical model is developed to investigate the cleanup time on different influence parameters, as well as the conditions under which nonequilibrium sorption is important for the cleanup of formations. Clement et al. (2004)  presented a numerical approach for modeling multispecies reactive transport subject to nonequilibrium sorption using the three-dimensional RT3D technology (Clement, 1997 ). In the practical application, Shupe et al. (2011)  used a rate-limited sorption model to simulate pump-and-treat remediation at a contaminated site in Fernald, Ohio. The experimental results could only be satisfactorily simulated with the rate-limited sorption model. Therefore, it can be concluded that a rate-limited sorption model, rather than an equilibrium sorption model, must be applied to more accurately simulate the behavior of contaminant transport (Yang et al., 2023 ). Chen et al. (2019)  has successfully developed a semi-analytical model for investigating the multispecies transport of degradable contaminants subject to rate-limited sorption. They demonstrated that the kinetic sorption rate constants of the contaminants have a significant impact on the migration of degradable contaminants. However, the decay reaction in the sorbed phase, which might have important implications for transport of degradable contaminants, has been ignored in the study due to complexity in derivation of the solution. To the best of the author's knowledge, no one has derived a semi-analytical model to simulate the multispecies transport of decaying contaminants, considering nonequilibrium sorption and decay in both dissolved and sorbed phases. Therefore, the objective of this study is to develop a novel semi-analytical solution to simulate the multispecies transport of decaying contaminants subject to nonequilibrium sorption undergoing decay in both the dissolved and sorbed phases. Indeed, this study is an extension of Chen et al. (2019) , overcoming the limitations of Chen et al. (2019) . A novel solution strategy is proposed to overcome the difficulty in deriving the analytical solution, which is expressed as recursive relations among parent and daughter species in both the dissolved and sorbed phases. It begins with using the Laplace transform to remove the temporal derivative and the generalized integral transform to eliminate the spatial derivatives, thus reducing the partial differential equation to an algebraic equation. We first solve for the dissolved concentration of the first species and then apply the kinetic sorption equation to determine the sorbed concentration of the first species. Subsequently, by solving the ADE for the second species, we express its dissolved concentration in terms of the dissolved and sorbed concentrations of the first species. Solving the kinetic sorption equation for the second species allows us to represent its sorbed concentration using the dissolved concentration of the second species and the sorbed concentration of the first species. By repeating this iterative procedure, we obtain the solutions for both the dissolved and sorbed concentrations for all species in a recursive form. The newly developed semi-analytical solution will be verified by comparing it with the equivalent numerical solution and the existing analytical model of Chen et al. (2019) . The derived model will be applied to investigate the effects of decay in the sorbed phase and kinetic sorption rate on the multispecies nonequilibrium transport of a radionuclide decay chain, respectively. The model has the capability to comprehensively and effectively simulate the transport of decaying contaminants, addressing the critical concern in managing contaminants in subsurface environments.  2 Mathematical model A novel recursive analytical model is developed to describe the multispecies transport of a decaying contaminant and its daughter element generated during the process of decay subject to nonequilibrium sorption in a uniform field. The transport mechanisms of the decaying contaminant and its progenies are governed by the advection, longitudinal dispersion, first-order reversible kinetic nonequilibrium sorption as well as the first-order decay reactions of species of their ingrowth generated from the parent element. Based on the above conceptual description, Fig. 1   schematically represents the complicated reaction network of a reactive decay chain undergoing the rate-limited sorption and decay reaction processes in both the dissolved and sorbed phases. Incorporation of the decay reaction in the sorbed phase into the governing equations leads to extra reaction pathways, that is, the first sorbed species will decay into second sorbed species which could then desorb as second dissolved species and complicated pathways form sequentially for the daughter species in the decay chain. The extra reaction pathway will significantly add mathematical complexities for finding the analytical solutions. A set of ADEs for members in the sequential decay chain takes the following form:(1a)  D ∂  2  C i  ( x , t )   ∂ x  2    − v ∂ C i  ( x , t )   ∂ x   − λ i  C i  ( x , t )  + λ i − 1   C i − 1   ( x , t )  − β i  θ  ( C i  ( x , t )  − S i  ( x , t )   K i   )       = ∂ C i  ( x , t )   ∂ t     i = 1 , . . . , N    in    0 ≤ x ≤ L , λ 0  = 0 ;        (1b) ρ b  ∂ S i  ( x , t )   ∂ t   = β i  ( C i  ( x , t )  − S i  ( x , t )   K i   )  − γ i  ρ b  S i  ( x , t )  + γ i − 1   ρ b  S i − 1   ( x , t )     i = 1 , . . . , N    in    0 ≤ x ≤ L , γ 0  = 0 .     where Ci  (x,t ) represents the concentration of species i  in the dissolved phase [ML−3 ]; Si  (x,t ) represents the concentration of species i  in the sorbed phase [MM−1 ]; x  denotes the spatial coordinate [L]; t  is the time [T]; θ is the porosity [-]; D  is the longitudinal dispersion coefficient [L2 T−1 ]; v  is the average uniform pore-water velocity [LT−1 ]; ρb   is the bulk dry density of the solid grains [ML−3 ]; βi   is the kinetic sorption reaction constant between the dissolved and sorbed phases of species i  [T −1 ]; Ki   represents the partition coefficient of species i  [M −1 L3 ]; N  is the total number of the species involved in the decay chain; L  represents the length of the transport system [L]. The coefficients λi   and γi   are the first-order decay constants of species i  [T −1 ] in the dissolved and the sorbed phase, respectively. In the governing equations, D, v, L , θ, and ρb   are used as transport parameters to describe the aquifer properties, whereas other Greek letters are used to describe the contaminant characteristics. The subscripts i  refers to sequence of the species in the decay chain. These two rate constants will have different values for both microbiological and chemical degradation. However, for the case of radioactive decay, we should assume them to be identical. In Eq. (1b) , incorporation of S i  − 1 (x, t ) means that S i  − 1 (x, t ) decays into Si  (x,t ) and Si  (x,t ) desorbs onto Ci  (x,t ), thereby creating more complicated reaction network caused by a series of decay/ingrowth and sorption/desorption processes. The complicated reaction network significantly adds the mathematical complexities for the development of the analytical solution. Prior to the release of decaying contaminants in the source area, the groundwater system is assumed to be free of contaminants in both the dissolved and sorbed phases, thus, the initial conditions for the elements in the decay chain in both two phases follows:(2) C i  ( x , t = 0 )  = 0    i = 1 , . . . , N    0 ≤ x ≤ L ;     (3) S i  ( x , t = 0 )  = 0    i = 1 , . . . , N    0 ≤ x ≤ L .      In this study, the contaminant is assumed to be released as an inflow source boundary condition with a constant concentration. Based on the continuity of the concentration flux for each species through the inlet boundary, the third-type boundary conditions should be used, which are mathematically expressed as follows:(4) − D ∂ C i  ( x = 0 , t )   ∂ x   + v C i  ( x = 0 , t )  = v c i , 0      i = 1 , . . . , N .     where c i ,0  is the constant source concentration of species i  applied at the inlet boundary [ML−3 ]. To derive the analytical solution, the Laplace transform with respect to t  and generalized integral transforms with respect to X are applied, converting Eqs. (7)  and (8)  into algebraic equations. The work procedure of model developing in this study is shown in Fig. 2  . The recursive analytical solutions and associating derivations are explained in a detailed manner in Appendix A . The developed solutions provide as a robust tool for assessing spatial concentration distribution of the decaying contaminant and its daughter element. It needs to be noted that the model requires a recursive solution rather than an explicit one, meaning that daughter species concentrations must be evaluated sequentially after obtaining the concentrations of all parent species.  3 Results and discussion 3.1 Verification of the developed semi-analytical model A computer program is built using FORTRAN language to evaluate the solutions based on Eqs. (27)-(28) expressing the recursive relations among Ci  LV G , Si  LV G , C i − 1  L V G    , and S i − 1  L V G    . The inversions of the integral transform described in solution derivations involve the mathematical expression of the sum of infinite series expansions. Theoretically, the evaluation of the infinite series expansion can be dealt with straightforwardly; however, it is important to understand the convergence behavior of the infinite series expansion, thereby determining an optimal value for the numerical evaluation The convergence investigation considers the hydrogeological transport of a four-member radionuclide decay chain comprised of 238 Pu→234 U→230 Th→226 Ra released from a high-level waste (HLW) repository as first described by Higashi and Pigford (1980) . The parameters used for the convergence investigation are adopted from van Genuchten (1985)  and are summarized in Table 1  . It's noteworthy that βi   is an important parameter, which represent the sorption reaction rate, tested in this study. The higher βi   value indicates the faster sorption between the dissolved and sorbed phases would be expected. The convergence behaviors from the numerical evaluation on the spatial concentrations of the four nuclides with various values of Pe  using the derived solutions are shown in Fig. 3  , where N  defines the number of terms summed up for an infinite series expansion of the inverse generalized integral transform. To provide a completeness relating to tests of convergence behaviors, the raw data of exact spatial radioactivity concentrations for the four nuclides are collected in Table S-1 ∼ S-4 in the Supplementary material. It is observed that for larger values of Pe , which means that advective transport is dominant in the groundwater system, the solution evaluation must be executed with a larger number of terms when summing up the infinite series expansion. Moreover, the number required for summing up the series expansion with desired accuracy decreases as the serial number of the nuclide in the radionuclide decay chain increases. A numerical evaluation of the proposed model is then executed based on the results of convergence investigation. To confirm the correctness of the newly derived models and verify the corresponding computer program code, we conducted comparisons between the recursive analytical solutions and numerical results obtained using the Laplace transform finite difference (LTFD) method. Additionally, we cross-verified the results from our new model with those obtained from an analytical model previously derived by Chen et al. (2019) . Essentially the same simulation conditions and parameters used in the convergence evaluation is considered for the verifications. Fig. 4   depicts the results which have good agreements between the new recursive analytical model and the equivalent numerical model, for the four nuclides in the radionuclide decay chain. Fig. 5   depicts the spatial concentrations for the four nuclides along the distance at t  = 1000 years computed with our newly developed model and Chen et al.’s (2019)  model. On the other hand, since Chen et al.’s (2019)  ignored the decay reaction in the sorbed phase, the first-order decay rate constants in the sorbed phase for all nuclides are set to zero in the newly developed model. It can be seen that there is excellent agreement between two models for four nuclides. Drawing from outcomes of the verifications, it clearly demonstrates the correctness of the derived semi-analytical model and its associated computer code.  3.2 Effects of decay reactions in the sorbed phase on the dissolved phase concentrations The newly derived recursive analytical solution is applied to investigate the effects of decay reactions in the sorbed phase on nonequilibrium transport of a radionuclide decay chain. The four-member radionuclide decay chain is comprised of 238  Pu→234 U →230  Th→226  Ra. The issue of assessing health risk of radionuclides in the subsurface environment requires our urgent concern and wide attention, since in recent years, widespread use of nuclear technology makes it inevitable that we face the potential risk of exposure to radionuclides in the environment as well as deal with the problem of nuclear waste disposal. Through the application of the newly developed model, accidental release and subsequent transport behavior of radionuclides in groundwater system can be investigated. For radionuclides, the decay reactions in the dissolved and the sorbed phases are identical, suggesting that the decay reaction in the sorbed phase should be seriously considered in nonequilibrium multispecies transport of a radionuclide decay chain. It should be noted that the decay reaction in the sorbed phases can be safely ignored for an organic contaminant decay chain because the degradation rate of organic contaminants is much faster in the dissolved phase than that in the sorbed phase (Guo et al., 2000 ). As compared to Chen et al.’s solution (2019), the major advantage of the derived recursive analytical model is that the chain-decay reactions in both the dissolved and sorbed phases can be more realistically considered, which is of great importance in assessing the transport and fate of radionuclides. The effects of decay reactions in the sorbed phase on multispecies nonequilibrium transport can be investigated by comparing the results obtained with our newly developed recursive analytical model against those obtained from Chen et al.’s (2019)  model, which ignores decay in the sorbed phase. The simulation scenario considers similar conditions and transport parameters for the convergence investigation and the verification comparison but replacing the zero values for decay rate constant in the sorbed phase (γi  ) with the values for the decay rate constants for the dissolved phase (λi  ). Fig. 6   shows the spatial radioactivity concentration profiles along the groundwater flow direction of the four nuclides in the decay chain, given different values of sorption reaction rate constants (β = 5, 50 and 500 year−1 ) obtained from our new model with decay in the sorbed phase and Chen et al.’s model without decay in the sorbed phase for a time period of t  = 1000 years. The concentrations of 238 Pu predicted by our new model is obviously lower than the those obtained with Chen et al.’s (2019)  model. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that, without decay in the sorbed phase, as in Chen et al.’s (2019)  model, the radioactivity concentration of 238 Pu in the sorbed phase will be overestimated in comparison to that predicted by our newly derived model with the consideration of the decay in the sorbed phase. The smaller difference in concentration between the dissolved and sorbed phases leads to less mass transfer from the dissolved phase into the sorbed phase, thus leading to the higher radioactivity concentration of 238 Pu in the dissolved phase for Chen et al.’s (2019)  model. In contrast, the radioactivity concentration of 234 U, 230 Th and 226 Ra predicted by our newly developed model are higher than those computed with Chen et al.’s (2019)  model. A higher 234 U radioactivity concentration in the sorbed phase is predicted due to radioactivity accumulation resulting from the decay of the parent nuclide 238 Pu in the sorbed phase, leading to a smaller predicted radioactivity difference between the dissolved and sorbed phases with our newly developed model. As a consequence, less 234 U is transferred from the dissolved phase to the sorbed phase, meaning that a higher 234 U radioactivity concentration remains in the dissolved phase (as compared to that obtained with Chen et al.’s (2019)  model with no decay in the sorbed phase). The results predicted for the other daughter species in the decay chain, such as 230 Th and 226 Ra, can also be explained because of the same trend of nuclide transport behavior. The large differences found in the dissolved radioactivity concentration between the decay and no decay are required to revive the health risk assessment conducted in the radioactive waste disposal site.  3.3 Effects of rate-limited sorption on dissolved phase concentrations Unlike the equilibrium-controlled sorption model which conventionally describes the kinetic sorption reaction rate as infinite, our new model has the capability to consider arbitrary kinetic sorption rate constant values. The assumption of equilibrium-controlled sorption simplifies the description that the concentration partition of decaying contaminants between the dissolved and sorbed phases occurs much more rapidly than the time required for contaminant migration through the groundwater flow system. When the concentration partition of contaminants between the dissolved and sorbed phases is not sufficiently rapid compared to the groundwater flow velocity in porous media, the process should instead be described by rate-limited sorption. Based on the same application case, we are thus interested in understanding the impact of the kinetic sorption rate constant on the transport of the radionuclide decay chain. A simulation is conducted considering the same descriptive conditions and transport parameters as those applied for investigating the effects of decay reactions in the sorbed phase on the nonequilibrium transport. Four different values of first-order kinetic sorption rate constant (βi   = 5, 50, 500 and 5000 year−1 ) are considered. Fig. 7   depicts the spatial concentration profiles of the four nuclides along the x  direction at t  = 1000 years subject to different values of sorption reaction rate constants, obtained from our new model. Obviously, higher concentrations in the dissolved phase can be observed when the sorption rate constant is smaller. The differences impacted by the sorption rate constant increase while the distance of nuclide plume migration is larger. To measure the relative importance of reaction rate, a dimensionless parameter called Damköhler number is addressed here. The Damköhler number is defined as the ratio of groundwater flow rate to the reaction rate. In our study, there are two types of reaction considered in the model: kinetic sorption and decay reaction. Therefore, we have Damköhler numbers in this study for both kinetic sorption and decay reaction. To avoid confusion between the two cases, we use Da s,i   to describe Damköhler number relating to kinetic sorption and Da d,i   relating to decay reaction, for species i  respectively. Da s,i   is applied to compare radioactivity partition caused by sorption against radioactivity advective transport. A small Da s,i   indicates that the sorption rate is relatively small in comparison to the advective transport and vice versa. For the parameters described in this section, the values of Da s,i   are set to be 5, 50, 500 and 5000 (when βi   = 5, 50, 500 and 5000 year−1 , respectively). Moreover, as shown in Fig. 7 , we also include the spatial concentration profiles obtained from the multispecies equilibrium transport model developed by Chen et al. (2016) . The spatial concentration profiles predicted by our new model with Da s,i  =5000 coincide well with those obtained with the Chen et al.’s (2019)  equilibrium sorption model. Therefore, Da s,i   acts as an important parameter to determine if the assumption of equilibrium sorption is appropriate. For the conditions with small Da s,i  , which implies that instantaneous sorption equilibrium is not attained, the equilibrium sorption model will significantly underestimate the concentrations in the dissolved phase. The results of this investigation clearly show the vital role of the kinetic sorption rate constant in governing multispecies transport of a radionuclide decay chain.   4 Summary and conclusions This study presents a novel recursive analytical model for describing the nonequilibrium multispecies transport of a sequential decay chain in the presence of decay in both the dissolved and sorbed phases. The developed solutions, which are expressed in a recursive mathematical formulation, can efficiently calculate the spatial and temporal concentration of decaying contaminant as well as of any species in the sequential decay chain. The reliability of the model is confirmed by the excellent agreement between the spatial concentration distributions obtained from the our newly developed semi-analytical model and an existing analytical model for nonequilibrium transport developed previously. The derived model is also applied to investigate the effect of decay in the sorbed phase on the multispecies nonequilibrium transport of a radionuclide decay chain. A lower radioactivity concentration is estimated for the first nuclide of 238 Pu, whereas higher radioactivity concentrations are predicted for the progeny products such as 234 U, 230 Th and 226 Ra with our new model. These results demonstrate that decay in the sorbed phase should be taken into accounts for accurately simulating multispecies nonequilibrium transport of a radionuclide decay chain. Furthermore, the impact of the kinetic sorption rate constant on multispecies transport is analyzed. The equilibrium sorption model significantly underestimates the radioactivity concentrations of a decay chain for low values of the kinetic sorption rate constant, and on the other hand, it has excellent agreement with the nonequilibrium sorption model with high values of the kinetic sorption rate constant. The results suggest that equilibrium sorption model could lead to an inaccurate prediction of radioactivity concentration. It is concluded that as a recursive analytical solution, the newly derived model is an effective and realistic tool for simulating nonequilibrium transport of decaying contaminant in subsurface environment, more importantly, providing a good assessment of the potential risks to human health at a radioactive disposal site.
1 Introduction The current study is motivated by the fact that flow in porous media has extensive applications in diverse fields, including chemical catalytic reactors, industrial cross-flow filtration processes, transpiration cooling, the design of solid-matrix heat exchangers, oil recovery in the petroleum industry, and flow transport in fractured geological media (Allen, 1984; Berkowitz, 2002 ). Apart from the industrial applications, such flow configurations are recently getting more attention from researchers for exploring the transition from laminar flow to turbulence on a macroscopic scale. More specifically, the idea came up because of the advent of hyperporous materials, which allow us to apply the Forchheimer equation to describe fluid flow in a porous medium with a high flow rate. Furthermore, treating the submerged aquatic vegetation as a permeable medium could make such a flow model relevant in deciphering shear flow instability at the canopy-water interface of an aquatic flow. In particular, the friction drag entrained by the submerged canopy generates a shear layer that is similar to the hydrodynamic mixing layer and dominated by the Kelvin–Helmholtz-type vorticity structures, which grow further downstream due to instability and eventually turn into turbulence (Raupach et al., 1996; Ghisalberti and Nepf, 2004; Defina and Bixio, 2005; Ghisalberti and Nepf, 2006 ). In addition, the current flow arrangement could be useful in aiding the development of an accurate numerical and mathematical model that optimizes the transport of contaminants in ground water contaminant systems (Ewing and Weeks, 1998 ). The study of fluid flow in a porous medium was initiated a few decades ago. In the macroscopic perspective, one can use the one-domain continuum approach to deal with fluid flow in a porous medium (Goyeau et al., 2003 ). In this approach, the primary goal is to precisely formulate the macroscopic governing equations for describing fluid flow in the composite medium. From a microscopic point of view, flow occurs through pores, which means we can only enforce the Navier–Stokes equations in the fluid phase, not in the solid phase. Hence, it is imperative to develop a modified version of the Navier–Stokes equations that will be valid in fluid and solid phases. In this context, Whitaker (1986)  derived a steady form of Darcy’s equation to govern fluid flow in a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium using the method of volume averaging (Whitaker, 1999 ). In fact, he omitted inertia terms, so Darcy’s equation is applicable to a very dense porous medium where the flow rate is very low. However, in the situation of a high flow rate in the porous medium, i.e., including inertia terms, he further developed the volume-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, which are adequate for general porous media (Whitaker, 1996 ). In the context of a plane Poiseuille flow overlying a porous medium, Sparrow et al. (1973)  began both numerical and experimental studies. In fact, they conducted temporal stability analysis and validated their findings with the experimental results. Using similarity solutions, Deng and Martinez (2005)  also carried out temporal stability analysis for fluid flow in a porous channel. Chang et al. (2006)  provided a detailed linear stability analysis for a fluid flow overlying a porous layer when the Reynolds number is large. They mainly investigated two-dimensional disturbances of arbitrary wavenumbers under the framework of the Orr–Sommerfeld-type boundary value problem. They employed an unsteady Darcy’s equation in their study to describe fluid flow in the porous medium and investigated the effect of depth ratio on shear mode instability. The same flow model was revised by Hill and Straughan (2008, 2009)  to analyze the impact of viscous diffusion on the momentum exchange at the fluid-porous interface, and therefore, an unsteady Darcy–Brinkman’s equation was used to govern fluid flow in the porous medium. They also conducted their study in the large Reynolds number regime, exploring the effects of depth ratio and porosity on shear mode instability. After that, Samanta (2017)  took the flow model of Chang et al. (2006)  to incorporate the slip effect on the upper wall. His results predict that wall slip has a destabilizing role in the fluid layer mode but has a stabilizing role in the porous layer mode. Wu and Mirbod (2019)  introduced advective inertia terms in the momentum equation. Therefore, an unsteady volume-averaged momentum equation was implemented to describe fluid flow in a porous medium without taking the Forchheimer quadratic drag term into account. Clearly, their equation is appropriate for a large flow rate in porous media. Again, the effects of porosity and depth ratio are deciphered on shear mode instability. After that, Samanta (2020a)  and Hooshyar et al. (2022)  explored how the Couette flow component affects the linear stability of a pressure-driven channel flow overlying a porous medium. As mentioned by them, the upper wall velocity has a stabilizing effect on the primary instability. Tilton and Cortelezzi (2008)  unraveled the linear temporal stability of a Poiseuille flow in a channel when the Reynolds number is large. Both the upper and lower walls of the channel were partially occupied by a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium in their study. They showed that permeability destabilizes the unstable shear mode. The above study was further extended by Samanta (2022)  for the channel flow bounded by an inhomogeneous and anisotropic porous medium. In particular, he performed both modal and nonmodal stability analyses. His study predicts that the anisotropy parameter stabilizes shear mode instability. Furthermore, it reduces transient disturbance energy growth and, consequently, delays the transition from laminar flow to turbulence. It was Breugem et al. (2006)  and Samanta et al. (2015)  who used the one-domain continuum approach to do direct numerical simulations of fully developed turbulent flow in a porous channel. According to their findings, streamwise turbulence intensity significantly decreases when a porous wall is present. Samanta et al. (2013)  also employed the one-domain continuum method to investigate the surface mode instability of a gravity-driven fluid flow over a homogeneous and isotropic porous substrate. To explore the dynamics of the nonlinear traveling wave solution in the low to moderate Reynolds number regime, they developed a depth-averaged two-equation model based on the local flow rate q ( x , t )     and the local film thickness h ( x , t )    . They came to the conclusion that an increase in the Darcy number amplifies the amplitude of the steady-state traveling wave. Recently, Samanta (2023)  executed a modal stability analysis for the free surface flow over an inhomogeneous and anisotropic porous medium at low and high Reynolds number regimes. His numerical simulation identified both shear and surface modes due to the fluid surface. According to his findings, as the coefficient of inhomogeneity increases, surface mode instability becomes stronger, whereas shear mode instability becomes weaker. Furthermore, in the case of flow problems involving the asymptotic suction boundary layer, Wedin et al. (2015), Wedin and Cherubini (2016)  demonstrated that changing the plate permeability can significantly alter the stability characteristics for both linear and nonlinear solutions. For instance, for large values of the plate’s permeability, the lower limit for the existence of linear and nonlinear solutions shifts to significantly lower Reynolds numbers than the zero permeability case (Milinazzo and Saffman, 1985 ). Additionally, Li et al. (2014)  conducted a linear temporal stability study of a Poiseuille flow in a channel that had one porous layer inserted in the center. As discussed by them, one porous layer inserted in the middle is more stable than the structure of two porous layers placed at the upper and lower walls. After that, Dai et al. (2015)  showed how the fluid-saturated multi-layer porous media in a parallel-plate channel affects the stability of the flow. They reported that the flow becomes less stable as the number of porous layers increases. In parallel, Nield (2003)  pioneered the study of the temporal stability of two-dimensional disturbances for the fluid flow in a channel occupied by a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium. In fact, he conducted a numerical study in the high Reynolds number regime and used a hyperporous material when the porosity of the material was very high. To govern fluid flow in the porous medium, he employed an unsteady Darcy–Brinkman equation. As Nield stated, the critical Reynolds number for the onset of shear mode instability increases as the Darcy viscous drag force induced by the solid matrix in the porous medium intensifies. Avramenko et al. (2005)  further revisited the above flow model to account for the Forchheimer quadratic drag term in the momentum equation. As a result, they reported an accurate value of the critical Reynolds number for the onset of shear mode instability when the Forchheimer number is non-zero. Indeed, the inertial Forchheimer term is necessary for high Reynolds number flow in a porous medium. Subsequently, Makinde (2009)  adopted the same porous channel flow model as (Nield, 2003 ) to numerically predict the behavior of an unstable region and the temporal growth rate for shear mode instability when the permeability of the porous medium varies. In fact, his findings corroborated Nield’s conclusion. More recently, Basavaraj and Kumar (2024)  revisited the flow model of Nield (2003)  again to numerically assess algebraic growth for two-dimensional disturbances of fluid flow in a porous channel. Therefore, they employed the same unsteady Darcy–Brinkman equation as proposed by Nield, rather than the Forchheimer equation, to describe fluid flow in a porous channel. Kapen et al. (2021a, b)  used an unsteady Darcy–Brinkman-type equation to study the linear temporal stability of a hybrid nanofluid flow between two parallel plates that were filled with a porous medium. In one flow configuration, the plates were stationary, while in the other, the upper plate was moving at a specific velocity. They reported that the Darcy number affects the stability of the porous channel flow, while the volume fraction dampens the infinitesimal disturbances. After that, Ketchate and his co-workers (Ketchate et al., 2021, 2023; Kapen et al., 2022 ) performed a linear temporal stability analysis for the non-Newtonian blood flow through a porous medium containing hybrid magnetic nanoparticles. They concluded that the Casson and mechanical anisotropy parameters destabilized the primary instability. Ketchate et al. (2022, 2024a, b)  also explored the linear temporal stability of mixed convection for both Newtonian and nanofluid in a fluid-saturated porous channel in the presence of a magnetic field and viscous dissipation. According to their discussion, the Richardson number and the Prandtl number have a destabilizing effect on mixed convective flow. The literature survey above highlights the fact that studies on the stability of channel flow filled with a porous medium only confine to two-dimensional disturbances of arbitrary wavenumbers. In particular, the temporal stability analysis was executed numerically in the high Reynolds number regime for fluid flow with streamwise and cross-stream directions. The spatial stability analysis was not discussed. The impact of the spanwise wavenumber on shear mode instability was ignored. Furthermore, there was no information on the nonmodal stability of three-dimensional disturbances. To fill these extensive gaps, we have conducted a detailed study of three-dimensional channel flow occupied by a homogeneous and isotropic hyperporous medium in the high Reynolds number regime. We have used the generalized Forchheimer equation as proposed by Avramenko et al. (2005)  to govern fluid flow in a porous channel. Both temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths are examined numerically. It is found that base flow velocity decelerates in comparison with a plane Poiseuille flow once the Darcy viscous drag force is introduced, which is further decelerated if the Forchheimer quadratic drag force is activated. As a result, we see that both temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths weaken with increasing values of the Darcy viscous drag force. Furthermore, the critical Reynolds number, above which shear mode instability begins, rises with increasing values of porosity. These findings indicate a strong dependency of temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths on the geometrical properties of a porous material. As a consequence, the scalings of temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths with R e  2      will not be the same as those found for a plane Poiseuille flow (Reddy and Henningson, 1993 ). In addition, as the parameter M   increases, shear mode instability suppresses, causing a delay in the transition from laminar flow to turbulence. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 , the governing equations and associated boundary conditions are provided for the current porous channel flow configuration. In Section 3 , the temporal evolution equations are developed. Modal stability analysis is performed in Section 4 , while nonmodal stability analysis is carried out in Section 5 .
