Summary and concluding remarks are presented in Section 6 .  2 Governing equations  Consider the three-dimensional laminar Poiseuille flow of an incompressible Newtonian viscous fluid in a homogeneous and isotropic hyperporous medium bounded by impermeable rigid parallel plates. Hence, the permeability κ   and the porosity ϵ   are constants for a given porous material. Suppose the laminar flow in a parallel-plate porous channel occurs under the action of a constant streamwise pressure gradient. Assuming that the porous medium is saturated by the same Newtonian fluid with constant density ρ   and constant dynamic viscosity μ  . The schematic diagram of the present porous channel flow configuration is shown in Fig. 1 , where 2 L    is the length between parallel plates. We prefer the Cartesian coordinate system, where we place the origin at the center of the parallel-plate channel and label the axes x  , y  , and z   in the streamwise, cross-stream, and spanwise directions, respectively. The main purpose of this study is to expand previous research works on two-dimensional modal stability analysis by Nield (2003)  and Avramenko et al. (2005)  in the direction of three-dimensional nonmodal stability analysis. More specifically, our aim is to unravel temporal and spatial transient disturbance energy growths for the porous channel flow, which generally occur in wall-bounded shear flows (Schmid, 2007 ). The motivation stemmed from the desire to explore the transition from laminar to turbulent flow in hyperporous media, which was pioneered by Nield (2003)  and later extended by Avramenko et al. (2005)  to include the Forchheimer quadratic drag term. Accordingly, we select the same set of governing equations for describing fluid flow in the porous medium, as suggested by Nield (2003) . However, in an analogous fashion with the work of Avramenko et al. (2005) , the Forchheimer quadratic drag term is also added to the momentum equation for accurate prediction of the onset of primary instability. As mentioned by Nield, if the porosity and permeability of a porous material are very high or, equivalently, if the parallel-plate channel is occupied by a hyperporous material, then one can model a pressure gradient-driven macroscopic flow whose governing equations will be the same as those proposed in the study of Nield (2003) . Furthermore, there is an advantage that the current flow configuration is akin to the Hartmann flow in the presence of the transverse magnetic field (Hartmann, 1937; Takashima, 1996 ) if the Forchheimer quadratic drag term is removed from the governing equations. Therefore, the current results can be easily compared with those of the Hartmann flow. On the basis of the above discussion, we employ the following modified form of the volume-averaged Navier–Stokes equations to govern fluid flow in a channel packed by a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium (Whitaker, 1996; Antohe and Lage, 1997; Nield, 2003; Avramenko et al., 2005 ) (1) ∇ ⋅ u = 0 ,     (2) ρ ( ∂  t   u + u ⋅ ∇ u )  = − ∇ p + μ ∇  2   u − ( μ  ϵ / κ )  u − ( ρ  c  F    ϵ  2   / κ   )  | u |  u ,     where the second term in the RHS of the volume-averaged momentum equation represents the Brinkman viscous diffusion term, the third term represents the Darcy viscous drag term, and the fourth term represents the Forchheimer quadratic drag term. Here, t   is the time, p   is the volume average intrinsic  pressure, and u   is the volume average intrinsic  velocity vector defined by u = ( 1 / Ω  f   )  ∫  Ω  f     u  ̃    d Ω  f     , where u  ̃     is the fluid velocity vector, Ω  f     is the volume of fluid, and Ω  s     is the volume of solid in a unit volume Ω   (Ω = Ω  s   + Ω  f     ) inside the porous medium. It should be fruitful to mention here that we have enforced the Dupuit–Forchheimer relationship, u  D   = ɛ u   , between the superficial  Darcy volume average velocity vector u  D   = ( 1 / Ω )  ∫  Ω  f     u  ̃    d Ω  f      and the intrinsic  volume average velocity vector u  . The effective viscosity is also written in terms of the dynamic viscosity as μ  eff   = μ / ϵ   . Here, c  F     is the Forchheimer coefficient, and | u |    is the absolute value of the intrinsic  velocity vector. For a given porous material, the permeability κ   and the Forchheimer coefficient c  F     can be estimated by using the following Kozeny–Carman and Ergun equations if the porosity ϵ   and the average pore diameter d  p     are known (Nield and Bejan, 1999; Whitaker, 1996; Hsu and Cheng, 1990; Alazmi and Vafai, 2000 ) (3) κ = ϵ  3   d  p  2    a ( 1 − ϵ )   2     ,  c  F   = b  a   ϵ  3 / 2     ,     where a   and b   are the Ergun constants. The volume-averaged Navier–Stokes equations are closed by the following no-slip and no-penetration boundary conditions at the impermeable parallel plates: (4) u = 0 ,    at   y = ± L .     Since we are interested in deciphering the nonmodal stability of a steady laminar parallel flow through a porous channel, we require its solution. For this reason, we consider a model of a steady constant streamwise pressure gradient-driven unidirectional flow in a parallel-plate channel occupied by a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium, which is also called the base flow. Therefore, we must have V = W = 0   , where V   and W   are the cross-stream and spanwise velocity components of the base flow. The above assumptions simplify the volume-averaged Navier–Stokes equations into the following forms: (5) μ D  2   U − d p / d x − ( μ  ϵ / κ )  U − ( ρ  c  F    ϵ  2   / κ   )  | U |  U = 0 ,     with boundary conditions (6) U = 0 ,   at   y = ± L .     Here, D = d / d y    represents the differentiation with respect to y  . It should be noted that the base flow momentum equation (5)  cannot be solved analytically because of the Forchheimer quadratic drag term. For this reason, we will solve Eq. (5)  numerically. However, if the Forchheimer quadratic drag term is ignored, the base flow momentum equation can be solved analytically with the aid of boundary conditions (6) , and the non-dimensional form of its solution can be expressed as follows: (7) U ( y )  = cosh ( M )  − cosh ( M y )   cosh ( M )  − 1   ,     where the parameter, M = ϵ  κ     L = ϵ  D a       , is analogous to the Hartmann number in magnetohydrodynamic flow (Takashima, 1996 ), and D a = κ  L  2        is the Darcy number. To non-dimensionalize the governing equations, we have preferred the maximum velocity of base flow, U  m a x   = − κ  ϵ  μ   d P  d x   [ cosh ( M )  − 1 ]   cosh ( M )      , in the porous channel flow as the characteristic velocity scale, the channel half-height, L  , is the characteristic length scale, and L / U  m a x      is the characteristic time scale. As per the discussion of Avramenko et al. (2005) , if we use the Kozeny–Carman equation, we can show that M   is simply proportional to ( 1 − ϵ )  / ϵ   . Therefore, small values of M   imply a hyperporous material, and large values of M   imply a dense porous material. Obviously, the analytical solution (7)  coincides with that obtained by Nield (2003) . How the base flow velocity varies in the cross-stream direction is demonstrated in Fig. 2(a)  for different values of M   when the Forchheimer coefficient c  F     is equal to zero. We can perceive that the boundary layers that are generated on both impermeable plates extend uniformly from both sides and meet at the center of the channel when M = 0   . In fact, this is the situation of a plane Poiseuille flow. However, this event no longer prevails for the porous channel flow as long as M   increases because the variation of streamwise base velocity in the cross-stream direction becomes almost zero after a certain height from both plates. This fact was earlier reported by Vafai and Kim (1989)  and Avramenko et al. (2005) . To investigate the effect of porosity on base flow variation, we set a fixed large value for the Darcy number (D a = 0 . 1   ). In fact, we produce the results for various Kelvin foams with high porosity values (Jobic and Médale, 2024 ), as depicted in Fig. 2(b) . Unlike the parameter M  , increasing porosity precludes the formation of boundary layers on the rigid impermeable plates, but it affects them mildly. In particular, for a fixed value of the Darcy number, the value of parameter M   increases as porosity increases. As a result, varying porosity yields a similar result on the base flow velocity as the parameter M  . Instead of U  m a x    , if we select U  P   = − L  2    μ   d P  d x      as the characteristic velocity scale, which can be procured by balancing the viscous friction term μ D  2   U    and the streamwise pressure gradient term − d P  d x      for a plane Poiseuille flow, the non-dimensional form of the base flow momentum equation becomes (8) D  2   U + 1 − M  2   U − M  F o | U |  U = 0 ,     which is subjected to the following boundary conditions: (9) U = 0 ,   at   y = ± 1 ,     where F o = ρ U  p   L  c  F    ϵ  3 / 2    μ   = R e  c  F    ϵ  3 / 2      can be called the Forchheimer number and R e = ρ U  p   L  μ      is the Reynolds number. It should be noted that the nonlinear equation (8)  and the boundary conditions (9)  are the same as those rendered in the study of Avramenko et al. (2005) . The solution of (8)  is computed numerically by using the software AUTO 07p (Doedel et al., 2007 ) and shown in Fig. 2(c) . The numerical results are also compared with the results of a plane Poiseuille flow and the results of a porous channel flow (Nield, 2003; Avramenko et al., 2005 ). Clearly, we have excellent agreement among them for the same set of parameter values. Moreover, we observe that the base flow velocity decelerates in comparison with that of a plane Poiseuille flow if the Darcy viscous drag term is introduced (M ≠ 0    and F o = 0   ) because it inhibits fluid flow in a porous medium. It is further decelerated if the Forchheimer quadratic drag term is added (M ≠ 0    and F o ≠ 0   ) to the momentum equation. This result is expected because the Forchheimer quadratic drag force also prevents fluid flow from happening in a porous medium. In Fig. 2(d) , we have unveiled the variation of d U ( y )   d y     in the cross-stream direction for the distinct sets of parameter values. We can see that the base flow shear stress, specified by a dotted line, approaches zero after a certain distance from both plates for the higher values of M   and F o   . This observation concludes that the existence of a porous medium prevents boundary layers that develop on the rigid impermeable plates from reaching the center of the channel. Indeed, this result differs from that of a plane Poiseuille flow, in which boundary layers grow from the plates uniformly and intersect at the center of the channel where d U ( y )   d y   = 0   .    3 Temporal evolution equations This section deals with the formulation of temporal evolution equations corresponding to perturbation normal velocity and perturbation normal vorticity for three-dimensional fluid flow through a porous channel. Thereby, we impose an infinitesimal perturbation on base flow and decompose each flow variable into two parts: one pertains to base flow, while the other pertains to perturbation flow (10) s ( x , y , z , t )  = S ( y )  + s  ′   ( x , y , z , t )  ,     where S ( y )     stands for base flow quantity and s  ′   ( x , y , z , t )     stands for perturbation flow quantity. After the insertion of Eq. (10)  in the mass conservation and momentum equations, we linearize them with respect to the base flow solution. Finally, we obtain the following non-dimensional linearized perturbation equations: (11) ∂  x   u  ′   + ∂  y   v  ′   + ∂  z   w  ′   = 0 ,     (12) R e ( ∂  t   u  ′   + U ∂  x   u  ′   + v  ′   D U + ∂  x   p  ′   )  = ( ∂  x x   u  ′   + ∂  y y   u  ′   + ∂  z z   u  ′   )  − M  2   u  ′   − 2 M  F  o    U u  ′   ,     (13) R e ( ∂  t   v  ′   + U ∂  x   v  ′   + ∂  y   p  ′   )  = ( ∂  x x   v  ′   + ∂  y y   v  ′   + ∂  z z   v  ′   )  − M  2   v  ′   − M  F  o    U v  ′   ,     (14) R e ( ∂  t   w  ′   + U ∂  x   w  ′   + ∂  z   p  ′   )  = ( ∂  x x   w  ′   + ∂  y y   w  ′   + ∂  z z   w  ′   )  − M  2   w  ′   − M  F  o    U w  ′   .     It should be useful to report here that the maximum velocity, U  m a x    , for the porous-channel flow is chosen as the characteristic velocity scale and ρ U  m a x  2      is chosen as the characteristic pressure scale to non-dimensionalize the perturbation equations. As a result, the Reynolds number R e    and the Forchheimer number F  o     can be redefined in terms of U  m a x     as R e = ρ U  m a x   L  μ      and F  o   = ρ U  m a x   L  c  F    ϵ  3 / 2    μ     . The associated boundary conditions are (15) u  ′   = v  ′   = w  ′   = 0   at   y = ± 1 .     The following step is to assume the solution of the linearized perturbation equations (11) –(15)  in the normal mode form: (16) u  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    v  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    w  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    p  ′   ( x , y , z , t )       = u  ̃   ( y , t )    v  ̃   ( y , t )    w  ̃   ( y , t )    p  ̃   ( y , t )       e  i ( α x + β z )    ,     where α   and β   represent the streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers of the infinitesimal perturbation, and the variables with “tilde” notation stand for the amplitudes of perturbation quantities. Now, we introduce the perturbation normal vorticity component η  ′   = ( ∂  z   u  ′   − ∂  x   w  ′   )    . Injecting the normal mode solution (16)  in the linearized perturbation momentum equations and eliminating pressure terms, we can derive the following forms of the temporal evolution equations for perturbation normal velocity and perturbation normal vorticity, respectively: (17) ( D  2   − k  2   )  ∂  t   v  ̃   = 1  R e   [  ( D  2   − k  2   )   2   v  ̃   − M  2   ( D  2   − k  2   )  v  ̃       +  ( 1 / k  2   )  M  F  o    U { α β D η  ̃   − α  2   D  2   v  ̃   − k  2   ( D  2   − k  2   )  v  ̃   }      +  ( 1 / k  2   )  M  F  o    D U { α β η  ̃   − ( α  2   + k  2   )  D v  ̃   }  ]      −  i α { U ( D  2   − k  2   )  v  ̃   − D  2   U v  ̃   }  ,      (18) ∂  t   η  ̃   = 1  R e   [ ( D  2   − k  2   )  η  ̃   − M  2   η  ̃   − ( 1 + β  2   / k  2   )  M  F  o    U η  ̃   + ( α β / k  2   )  M  F  o    U D v  ̃   ]   −  i α U η  ̃   − i β D U v  ̃   ,      where η  ̃   ( y , t )     is the amplitude of the perturbation normal vorticity component, and k = α  2   + β  2        is the total wavenumber of the infinitesimal perturbation. At y = ± 1   , the associated boundary conditions can be written as (19) v  ̃   = 0 ,   D v  ̃   = 0 ,   η  ̃   = 0 .     The above two coupled differential equations (17) and (18)  can be recast into the following temporal matrix initial value problem: (20) B ∂  t   Q = A Q ,     with temporal initial condition Q  0   = Q ( y , t = 0 )    . Here, Q = [ v  ̃   , η  ̃   ]   T      is a column matrix, where the superscript “T  ” indicates transpose, and the forms of the square matrices A   and B   are given by A = L  O S    L  C 1     L  C 2    L  S Q         and   B = L  D    0   0  1      ,     where L  D   = ( D  2   − k  2   )  ,    L  O S   = 1  R e   [ ( D  2   − k  2   )   2   − M  2   ( D  2   − k  2   )  ]  −  ( 1 / k  2   )  M  F  o    R e   [ U { α  2   D  2   + k  2   ( D  2   − k  2   )  }  + D U ( α  2   + k  2   )  D ]  −  i α { U ( D  2   − k  2   )  − D  2   U }  ,    L  C 1   = 1  R e   [ ( α β / k  2   )  M  F  o   ( U  D + D U )  ]  ,    L  C 2   = 1  R e   [ ( α β / k  2   )  M  F  o    U  D ]  − i β D U ,    L  S Q   = 1  R e   [ ( D  2   − k  2   )  − M  2   − ( 1 + β  2   / k  2   )  M  F  o    U ]  − i α U .       Prior to investigating nonmodal stability, we have generated some important results regarding modal stability that remain unexplored in the published literature.  4 Modal stability analysis To delve into modal stability, we assume the solution of perturbation temporal evolution equation (20)  in the following form: (21) Q ( y , t )  = Q  ̃   ( y )  exp [ − i ω t ]  ,     where ω = k c    is the angular frequency and c   is the wave speed. In the following, we are interested in exploring the temporal stability of basic parallel flow corresponding to an infinitesimal perturbation. As a result, we will assume that ω = ω  r   + i ω  i      is complex or, equivalently, c = c  r   + i c  i      is complex, but k   is real. After substitution of Eq. (21) , we can turn temporal evolution equation into the following generalized matrix eigenvalue problem: (22) A Q  ̃   = − i ω B Q  ̃   .     The boundary conditions (19)  are also plugged in the matrices A   and B  , respectively. From the solution (21) , one can state that the infinitesimal perturbation will grow exponentially with time and the parallel laminar flow in a porous channel will be linearly unstable if the imaginary part of ω   is positive, i.e., if ω  i   > 0   . Otherwise, it will be linearly stable to infinitesimal perturbations if ω  i   < 0   , while ω  i   = 0    will provide the neutral stability condition. The next step is to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem (22)  numerically using the Chebyshev spectral collocation method (Schmid and Henningson, 2001 ). To this end, we expand each perturbation amplitude function in the column matrix Q  ̃     as a truncated series of the Chebyshev polynomials, T  i   ( y )    , of the first kind, as shown below: (23) v  ̃   ( y )  = ∑  i = 0  N   v  ̃    i   T  i   ( y )  ,   η  ̃   ( y )  = ∑  i = 0  N   η  ̃    i   T  i   ( y )  ,     where v  ̃    i     and η  ̃    i     are unknown coefficients that need to be computed numerically. Inserting Eq. (23)  in the generalized matrix eigenvalue problem, the Chebyshev functions are calculated at the Gauss–Lobatto collocation points y  j   = cos ( π j / N )    , where j = 0 , … , N   . To ensure the desired accuracy of the numerical results, we have kept at least a hundred Chebyshev polynomials (N ≥ 100   ) in each numerical simulation. This produces matrices A   and B   with dimensions 200 by 200 or higher and takes a maximum of 10 min on a powerful computer per numerical simulation involving modal stability analysis. However, we observe that the computational cost increases as N   increases. Additionally, the computational cost increases significantly for each numerical simulation involved in the nonmodal stability analysis discussed in the next section. Moreover, to justify the accuracy of the present numerical code, we have compared our numerical results with the existing findings of a two-dimensional porous channel flow (Nield, 2003; Avramenko et al., 2005; Makinde, 2009 ). First, we have reproduced the results of Nield (2003) . To do this, we have deleted the Forchheimer quadratic drag term from the momentum equations and the Darcy viscous drag term from the y  -momentum equation. Accordingly, we have set F o = 0    and β = 0    in numerical simulation. Table 1  illustrates the variation in the critical Reynolds number and critical streamwise wavenumber for the onset of shear mode instability as the parameter M   rises. The results show a close match with those of Nield (2003) . Here, we perceive that the critical Reynolds number increases with increasing values of M  , and it indicates a stabilizing impact of the parameter M   on shear mode instability. Secondly, we have recreated the results of Avramenko et al. (2005)  when F o = 0    and β = 0   . But in this case, we have retained the Darcy viscous drag term in the y  -momentum equation. As before, Table 2  demonstrates how the critical Reynolds number and critical streamwise wavenumber for the onset of shear mode instability vary against the parameter M  . Again, we observe that the critical Reynolds number increases with increasing M  , but at a slightly faster rate than the result of Nield (2003) . Finally, we have validated our numerical results with those of Makinde (2009)  when F o = 0    and β = 0   . The details can be found in Appendix . Even though we have figured out that the parameter M   stabilizes shear mode instability, we do not know anything about the unstable region that the neutral stability curve generates in the neutral diagram. We will decipher this thing soon. Fig. 3  depicts the spectrum of the matrix eigenvalue problem (22)  when R e = 1 0  4     , α = 1   , and β = 0   . First, the temporal eigenvalues, specified by the red circle symbols in Fig. 3 , are computed numerically for a plane Poiseuille flow (M = 0    and F o = 0   ). It is evident that there is only one unstable mode, designated by mode 1, because ω = k c = 0 . 2375 + i 0 . 0037397   , with ω  i   > 0   . Hence, the plane parallel Poiseuille flow is linearly unstable to infinitesimal disturbance for the selected data set. To examine eigenvalues for the porous channel flow, we increase the value of the parameter M   gradually from M = 0    to M = 4 . 605   , but F o    is kept constant at F o = 0   . We see that mode 1 no longer resides in the unstable region but crosses the real axis (ω  i   = 0   ) and moves down to the stable region with ω = 0 . 2611 − i 0 . 0574    (ω  i   < 0   ). The green diamond symbol specifies the new location of mode 1. Hence, the laminar parallel porous channel flow is linearly stable to infinitesimal disturbances when M = 4 . 605    and F o = 0   . This result is expected because the parameter M   has a stabilizing influence on shear mode instability (Nield, 2003; Avramenko et al., 2005 ). Finally, to analyze the effect of the Forchheimer number, we repeat the numerical experiment and calculate the spectrum of the eigenvalue problem (22)  when M = 4 . 605    and F o = 1   . We notice that mode 1 slightly moves up from its prior location but still lies in the stable region with ω = 0 . 2729 − i 0 . 0386    (ω  i   < 0   ). The blue star symbol specifies its new position. Clearly, the stability feature of a porous channel flow does not alter in the presence of the Forchheimer number. As discussed by Avramenko et al. (2005) , the critical Reynolds number for the onset of shear mode instability emerges at a very large value of R e    in the presence of the Forchheimer number and the parameter M  . That is why we have not demonstrated results for higher values of the Forchheimer number and the parameter M  . To explore the unstable region corresponding to the shear mode for a three-dimensional porous channel flow, we compute the neutral stability curve for various sets of flow parameters. First, we reproduce the neutral stability curve for a plane Poiseuille flow (M = 0   , F o = 0   ), which creates a tongue-like shape in the neutral diagram [see Fig. 4(a) ]. As soon as the parameter M   is introduced in numerical simulation (M ≠ 0   , F o = 0   ), the neutral stability curve exhibits a similar tongue-like shape, but the unstable region attenuates significantly in comparison with that of a plane Poiseuille flow. Moreover, the critical Reynolds number for the onset of shear mode instability increases with increasing M  . This result implies a stabilizing role for the parameter M   in shear mode instability like a two-dimensional porous channel flow. For further confirmation, we compute the temporal growth rate for shear mode instability when R e = 1 0  4     . We observe that the temporal growth rate becomes weaker as the parameter M   increases [see Fig. 4(b) ]. This fact is fully consistent with the stabilizing impact of M   on shear mode instability. Physically, with increasing M  , the Darcy viscous drag force that inhibits fluid flow in a porous channel intensifies and causes a stabilizing effect. To decipher the sole effect of porosity on shear mode instability, we vary porosity in numerical simulation at a fixed value of the Darcy number. As porosity increases, Fig. 4(c)  shows noticeable changes in the unstable region caused by the shear mode. In particular, the unstable region that corresponds to shear mode instability shrinks significantly, and the associated critical Reynolds number, above which instability initiates, increases rapidly. We can attribute this fact to the rise in M   as porosity increases. For further confirmation, we compute the temporal growth rate for the shear mode and plot it in Fig. 4(d) . It is clear that the temporal growth rate attenuates very quickly with an increase in the value of porosity. On the basis of these results, one can also deduce that the transition from laminar flow to turbulent flow will be significantly delayed in the presence of a porous medium in a parallel-plate channel. Fig. 5  illustrates the spectrum of the matrix eigenvalue problem (22)  for a three-dimensional porous channel flow when R e = 1 0  4     , α = 1   , M = 0 . 5   , and F o = 0   . In this case, the spanwise wavenumber β   is varied in numerical simulation. The temporal eigenvalues, specified by the red circle symbols in Fig. 5 , are evaluated when β = 0   . Again, we can observe that there is one unstable mode, designated by mode 1, because ω = k c = 0 . 2377 + i 0 . 0027381    with ω  i   > 0   . Hence, the laminar parallel porous channel flow is linearly unstable to infinitesimal perturbation for the given data set. As soon as, the spanwise wavenumber β   is increased gradually, the unstable mode crosses the real axis (ω  i   = 0   ) and moves down to the stable region with ω = 0 . 2688 − i 0 . 0750    (ω  i   < 0   ) at β = 4   . This result indicates that the spanwise wavenumber stabilizes shear mode instability. To strengthen our numerical results, the neutral stability curve and the temporal growth rate are calculated for the shear mode when β   changes. In Fig. 6(a) , we find that the unstable region diminishes as long as the spanwise wavenumber rises. This event is followed by the successive increment of the critical Reynolds number for the onset of shear mode instability. In Fig. 6(b) , we notice that the temporal growth rate and the unstable range of shear mode instability shrink with increasing β  , which is completely in favor of the stabilizing influence of the spanwise wavenumber on shear mode instability. In fact, the stabilizing impact of β   agrees well with the statement of Squire’s theorem that the two-dimensional infinitesimal disturbance is more unstable than the three-dimensional ones. Fig. 7  reveals the contours of the temporal growth rate for the shear mode in (α  , β  ) plane. In Fig. 7 , the thick line indicates the contour for ω  i   = 0   . Hence, it is nothing but the neutral stability curve in (α  , β  ) plane. Comparing Figs. 7(a) and 7(b) , we can discern that the temporal growth rate and the unstable ranges of the streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers corresponding to shear mode instability amplify with the increase in the value of the Reynolds number. On the other hand, the opposite phenomena take place when we compare Figs. 7(b) and 7(c) . In this case, the temporal growth rate and the unstable ranges of the streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers corresponding to shear mode instability condense with the increase in the value of the parameter M  . In view of these results, we can come to the conclusion that the transition from laminar flow to turbulence will be significantly delayed in the presence of a porous medium in three-dimensional parallel-plate channel flow. However, this transition can be made faster by increasing the Reynolds number or, equivalently, the flow rate in a porous channel.          5 Nonmodal stability analysis 5.1 Temporal transient disturbance energy growth    This section concerns the nonmodal stability of fluid flow in a parallel-plate channel packed by a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium. Both temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths will be discussed. At the outset, we shall deal with temporal transient disturbance energy growth, as the modal stability analysis supplies asymptotic behavior of the operator exponential, where the linearized perturbation equations ensue a nonnormal matrix operator (Butler and Farrell, 1992; Schmid and Henningson, 2001 ). To comprehend the short-term behavior of disturbance, in numerical simulation, we will set the Reynolds number below its critical value, i.e., in the subcritical zone. The first step is to write the general solution of the temporal matrix initial value problem (20)  as follows: (24) Q ( y , t )  = exp [ ( B  − 1   A )  t ]  Q  0   = C Q  0   ,     in which C = exp [ ( B  − 1   A )  t ]     is the temporal matrix operator exponential. On the basis of the operator C  , the temporal initial condition Q  0     evolves forward in time. The next step is to introduce the kinetic energy density norm, as it is a physically relevant quantity for measuring the growth of disturbance in a channel flow. Hence, in accordance with the studies of Butler and Farrell (1992) , Reddy and Henningson (1993) , and Schmid (2007) , we define the kinetic energy density norm in the following form: (25) E ( Q )  = ‖ Q ‖  E  2   = 1  2 k  2     ∫  − 1  1   ( | D v  ̃   |   2   + k  2   | v  ̃   |   2   + | η  ̃   |   2   )  d y = 1  2 k  2     ∫  − 1  1   v  ̃     η  ̃         H   ( k  2   − D  2   )   0   0  1      v  ̃     η  ̃        d y = 1  2 k  2     ∫  − 1  1   Q  H   M Q = 1  2 k  2     ∫  − 1  1   Q  H   F  H   F Q = ‖ F Q ‖  2  2   ,      where M = F  H   F    is the positive definite energy weight matrix and the superscript “H  ” denotes the conjugate transpose. After that, we quantify the optimal temporal energy amplification function G  T   ( t )     in the following way (Barkley et al., 2008 ): (26) G  T   ( t )  = max  Q  0   ≠ 0   E ( Q )   E ( Q  0   )    = max  Q  0   ≠ 0   ‖ Q ‖  E  2    ‖ Q  0   ‖  E  2     = max  Q  0   ≠ 0   〈 C Q  0   , C Q  0   〉   〈 Q  0   , Q  0   〉    = λ  m a x T   ( C  ∗   C )  ,     where C  ∗     represents the conjugate transpose of C   and λ  m a x T   ( C  ∗   C )     represents the largest eigenvalue of C  ∗   C   . Here, G  T   ( t )     is maximized over all admissible initial conditions Q  0    . In Figs. 8(a) , 8(b) , 8(c) , and 8(d) , we have depicted the eigenvalue spectra, boundary of the numerical range, and boundaries of pseudospectra for four diverse sets of parameter values, where the boundary point of the numerical range is determined by the following complex number (Schmid and Henningson, 2001 ) (27) Z = Q  m a x  H   ( B  − 1   A )  Q  m a x    Q  m a x  H   Q  m a x     ,     in which Q  m a x     is the principal eigenvector. The outcomes manifest two distinct scenarios of spectrum in (ω  r    , ω  i    ) plane: case I (R e = 2000   , α = 1   , β = 0   , and M = 0 . 6   ) and case II (R e = 2000   , α = 1   , β = 0 . 25   , and M = 0 . 6   ) have an asymmetric shape, whereas case III (R e = 1000   , α = 0   , β = 2   , and M = 0 . 3   ) and case IV (R e = 1000   , α = 0   , β = 2   , and M = 0 . 9   ) have a symmetric shape with respect to vertical damped modes. Comparing Figs. 8(a) and 8(b) , we see that the numerical abscissa (Schmid, 2007 ), i.e., the maximum hump at the boundary of the numerical range that enters the unstable region (ω  i   > 0   ), increases if the spanwise wavenumber is included in the initial temporal perturbation. However, from Figs. 8(c) and 8(d) , we can say that the maximum hump at the boundary of the numerical range decreases with an increasing value of M  . In these four cases, the interesting outcome is that all temporal eigenvalues, specified by dot points, remain in the stable region (ω  i   < 0   ), as the values of the Reynolds number do not exceed the critical value, i.e., they belong to the subcritical zone. However, the boundary of the numerical range, specified by the thick solid curve, crosses the real axis (ω  i   = 0   ) and enters the unstable region (ω  i   > 0   ). This fact ensures the appearance of transient disturbance energy growth over time in all cases. To corroborate our argument, we numerically compute the optimal temporal energy amplification function G  T   ( t )     with time for the same set of parameter values when M   alters. Figs. 9(a) , 9(b) , and 9(c)  reveal that transient disturbance energy growth exists and grows over time, and ultimately decays monotonically as time progresses after attaining a maximum value at t = t  m a x     . It should be noted that temporal transient disturbance energy growth is strongly dependent on M  , and it weakens as the parameter M   rises. This result is expected because the parameter M   or, equivalently, the Darcy viscous drag force induced by the solid matrix of the porous medium, stabilizes disturbed flow. Another important result is that temporal transient disturbance energy growth becomes stronger if the initial temporal perturbation includes only a spanwise wavenumber (α = 0   , β = 2   ) rather than the oblique perturbation that includes both streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers (α = 1   , β = 0 . 25   ) and the perturbation that has only a streamwise wavenumber (α = 1   , β = 0   ). Fig. 9(d)  illustrates the variation of temporal disturbance energy growth when porosity alters. Similar to the case of M  , we observe weaker temporal transient disturbance energy growth as porosity increases. This is because the parameter M   is a monotonically increasing function of porosity. Physically, increasing porosity makes the viscous drag force stronger [see also Eq. (2) ]. This slows down fluid movement in a porous channel, lowering the kinetic energy of the disturbed flow. Additionally, the current numerical results arrest those of a plane Poiseuille flow (Schmid, 2000; Schmid and Brandt, 2014 ) once the Darcy viscous drag term and the Forchheimer quadratic drag term are omitted from the momentum equations (M = 0    and F o = 0   ). Now, we activate both the Forchheimer number F o    and the parameter M   in numerical simulation, and we see that temporal transient disturbance energy growth reduces significantly [see Fig. 10(a) ]. Conversely, increasing the Reynolds number leads to a successive amplification of the temporal transient disturbance energy growth, which is strongly reliant on R e    [see Fig. 10(a) ]. Following the study of Reddy and Henningson (1993) , we rescale G  T   ( t )     with R e  2      and t   with R e    and replot our numerical findings again in Fig. 10(b) . We can clearly see that all temporal energy growth curves merge into a single curve. Hence, unlike a plane Poiseuille flow, the scalings of G  T   ( t )     with R e  2      and t   with R e    remain valid for a porous channel flow when the parameter M   and the Forchheimer number F o    are fixed. Furthermore, we can state that the maximum value of G  T   ( t )     increases by approximately 1 . 6 × 1 0  − 5   R e  2     , and the time t  m a x    , at which the maximum temporal transient growth is achieved, increases by approximately 1 . 3 × 1 0  − 2   R e    with increasing R e    when M = 4 . 605    and F o = 1   . However, if the parameter M   or the Forchheimer number F o    alters, we can speculate that the scalings of G  T   ( t )     and t   will no longer be the same as those of a plane Poiseuille flow due to the dependence of G  T   ( t )     on M   and F o   . In this case, we have figured out the scalings of G  T   ( t )     and t   for the initial temporal perturbations that include only a spanwise wavenumber (α = 0   , β ≠ 0   ). To support our claim, we have created two numerical results for two different values of β   when the parameter M   varies. Figs. 11(a) and 11(b)  show that all temporal growth curves collapse on a single curve if we rescale G  T   ( t )     with g  M   R e  2      and t   with R e / [ 1 + 2 M / ( 10 β )  ]    , where g  M     is the ratio between the maximum temporal transient disturbance energy growth at a given M   and the maximum temporal transient disturbance energy growth at M = 0   . Hence, for a porous channel flow with varying M  , the maximum temporal transient disturbance energy growth is proportional to g  M   R e  2      and the time t  m a x    , at which the maximum temporal growth occurs, is proportional to R e / [ 1 + 2 M / ( 10 β )  ]    . To decipher the behavior of the temporal transient disturbance energy growth in wavenumber plane, we calculate the contours of the maximum temporal energy amplification function G  m a x  T   = m a x  t > 0   G  T   ( t )     on a logarithmic scale and display them in Fig. 12  for different values of the Reynolds number. Comparing Figs. 12(a) and 12(b) , we can report that the contours of G  m a x  T     are remarkably similar when R e = 8000   . For instance, the maximum value of G  m a x  T     arises close to the spanwise wavenumber β  -axis, and its minimum value arises in the vicinity of the streamwise wavenumber α  -axis. Hence, we can opine that the initial temporal disturbance, which contains only a finite spanwise wavenumber (α = 0   , β ≠ 0   ), generates the largest temporal transient growth in comparison with initial temporal disturbances including both streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers (α ≠ 0   , β ≠ 0   ) or only a streamwise wavenumber (α ≠ 0   , β = 0   ). This result completely endorses the result reported in Fig. 9 . Moreover, we can see that a shaded zone appears in both Figs. 12(a) and 12(b)  when R e = 8000   . In particular, this shaded zone represents the unstable region for shear mode instability, where we can expect an exponential growth of the shear mode. As the Reynolds number, R e = 8000   , belongs to the supercritical zone, it is greater than its critical value for the onset of shear mode instability predicted from the modal stability analysis. That is why an unstable region emerges in wavenumber plane. In addition, we see that the shaded zone diminishes in Fig. 12(b)  due to an increase in parameter M  , which raises the critical Reynolds number necessary for the onset of shear mode instability. As a result, the unstable region of exponential growth of shear mode instability reduces. In contrast, if the Reynolds number is kept in the subcritical zone, the shaded zone disappears [see Figs. 12(c) and 12(d) ]. In fact, the Reynolds number, R e = 1000   , is less than its critical value for the onset of shear mode instability, and for this reason, the unstable region no longer emerges in wavenumber plane. From the level curves of G  m a x  T    , we can also report that the maximum of optimal temporal transient disturbance energy growth for a porous channel flow arises approximately at α = 0    and β ≈ 2    when R e = 1000   . To access the shape of the optimal initial disturbance that triggers the largest temporal transient disturbance energy growth and leads to the optimal final response, we demonstrate optimal input and optimal output in Fig. 13(a)  at t = t  m a x      when R e = 1000   , α = 0   , β = 2   , M = 0 . 6   , and F o = 0   . Obviously, the optimal temporal initial condition consists of a pair of counter-rotating streamwise vortices spanning the entire channel height, which are similar to those of a plane Poiseuille flow (Butler and Farrell, 1992 ). On the other hand, the optimal final response corresponding to streamwise perturbation velocity generates two sets of alternating high-speed and low-speed elongated streaks in the streamwise direction, which can be clearly understood from the isosurface plot depicted in Fig. 13(c) . Moreover, these streaks are anti-symmetric with respect to the centerline of the channel. To examine the effect of the streamwise wavenumber on the shape of the optimal final response, we repeat numerical simulation for an optimal initial perturbation that has both non-zero streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers (α = 0 . 25    and β = 2   ). Figs. 13(b) and 13(d)  show how the shapes of the optimal input and optimal output are affected by the streamwise wavenumber. Clearly, the optimal output corresponding to streamwise perturbation velocity generates two sets of alternating high-speed and low-speed oblique elongated streaks, which are no longer orthogonal to the cross-stream z y   -plane [see Fig. 13(d) ], but have a finite inclination with respect to the streamwise direction. The reason can be attributed to the Orr-type vortex-tilting mechanism discussed by Butler and Farrell (1992)  for a plane Poiseuille flow. In particular, if an initial perturbation characterized by a flow pattern is placed in a mean flow, it opposes the mean shear direction. As time evolves, it is tilted in the mean shear direction, which results in transient disturbance energy growth.      5.2 Spatial transient disturbance energy growth    To unravel the spatial transient disturbance energy growth for a parallel-plate porous channel flow, we invoke the three-dimensional linearized perturbation equations and the associated boundary conditions: (28) ∂  x   u  ′   + ∂  y   v  ′   + ∂  z   w  ′   = 0 ,     (29) ∂  t   u  ′   + U ∂  x   u  ′   + v  ′   D U = − ∂  x   p  ′   + ( ∂  x x   u  ′   + ∂  y y   u  ′   + ∂  z z   u  ′   )  / R e − ( M  2   / R e )  u  ′   − 2 ( M  F  o   / R e )  U u  ′   ,     (30) ∂  t   v  ′   + U ∂  x   v  ′   = − ∂  y   p  ′   + ( ∂  x x   v  ′   + ∂  y y   v  ′   + ∂  z z   v  ′   )  / R e − ( M  2   / R e )  v  ′   − ( M  F  o   / R e )  U v  ′   ,     (31) ∂  t   w  ′   + U ∂  x   w  ′   = − ∂  z   p  ′   + ( ∂  x x   w  ′   + ∂  y y   w  ′   + ∂  z z   w  ′   )  / R e − ( M  2   / R e )  w  ′   − ( M  F  o   / R e )  U w  ′   ,     (32) u  ′   = 0 ,   v  ′   = 0 ,   w  ′   = 0 ,  at  y = ± 1 .     The next step is to formulate the spatial matrix initial value problem. Therefore, we assume the solution of the linearized perturbation equations (28) –(32)  in the normal mode form (Schmid and Henningson, 2001 ): (33) u  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    v  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    w  ′   ( x , y , z , t )    p  ′   ( x , y , z , t )       = u  ˆ   ( x , y )    v  ˆ   ( x , y )    w  ˆ   ( x , y )    p  ˆ   ( x , y )       exp ( i β z − i ω t )  ,     in which ω   is the angular frequency of the infinitesimal perturbation. Obviously, there is spatial oscillation only in the spanwise direction. After inserting Eq. (33) , we can cast the linearized perturbation equations (28) –(32)  into the following forms: (34) ∂  x   u  ˆ   = − ∂  y   v  ˆ   − i β w  ˆ   ,     (35) ∂  x   p  ˆ   = i ω u  ˆ   − U ∂  x   u  ˆ   − D U v  ˆ   + ( ∂  x x   u  ˆ   + ∂  y y   u  ˆ   − β  2   u  ˆ   )  / R e − ( M  2   / R e )  u  ˆ   − 2 ( M  F o / R e )  U u  ˆ   ,     (36) ∂  x x   v  ˆ   = − i ω R e  v  ˆ   + U R e  ∂  x   v  ˆ   + R e  ∂  y   p  ˆ   − ( ∂  y y   v  ˆ   − β  2   v  ˆ   )  + M  2   v  ˆ   + M  F o  U v  ˆ   ,     (37) ∂  x x   w  ˆ   = − i ω R e  w  ˆ   + U R e  ∂  x   w  ˆ   + i β R e  p  ˆ   − ( ∂  y y   w  ˆ   − β  2   w  ˆ   )  + M  2   w  ˆ   + M  F o  U w  ˆ   ,     (38) u  ˆ   = 0 ,   v  ˆ   = 0 ,   w  ˆ   = 0 ,   y = ± 1 .     Finally, we convert the above set of Eqs. (34) –(37)  into a spatial matrix initial value problem: (39) ∂  x   S = P S ,     with spatial initial condition S  0   = S ( x = 0 )    . Here, S = [ u  ˆ   , v  ˆ   , ∂  x   v  ˆ   , w  ˆ   , ∂  x   w  ˆ   , p  ˆ   ]   T      is the column matrix and the matrix P   has the form: P = 0  − D  0  − i β  0  0   0  0  1  0  0  0   0  − R e  T  U R e  0  0  R e  D   0  0  0  0  1  0   0  0  0  − R e  T  U  R e  i β  R e   T − ( M  F o / R e )  U  − D U + U  D  − D / R e  i β  U  − i β / R e  0      ,     where T ≡ ( D  2   − β  2   )  / R e + i ω − ( M  2   / R e )  − ( M  F o / R e )  U    is the differential operator. To discuss spatial stability, we assume the solution of spatial matrix initial value problem (39)  in the following form: (40) S ( x , y )  = S  ˆ   ( y )  exp [ i α x ]  ,     where α   is the streamwise wavenumber. After plugging Eq. (40)  into the spatial matrix initial value problem, we obtain the following spatial matrix eigenvalue problem: (41) P S  ˆ   = i α S  ˆ   .     As we are interested in exploring the spatial stability of a basic parallel flow corresponding to an infinitesimal perturbation, the angular frequency ω   is assumed to be real, but the streamwise wavenumber, α = α  r   + i α  i     , is assumed to be complex. Fig. 14(a)  displays the spectrum of the spatial matrix eigenvalue problem (41)  when R e = 2000   , ω = 0 . 2   , and β = 1   . Initially, we calculate the spectrum for a plane Poiseuille flow (M = 0    and F o = 0   ). We perceive that all spatial eigenvalues with different α  r    , which are specified by circular symbols, lie in the upper-half plane (α  i   > 0   ). Therefore, the plane parallel Poiseuille flow is linearly stable to downstream propagating disturbances (x > 0   ). However, it will be linearly unstable for upstream propagating disturbances (x < 0   ). To examine the result for a porous channel flow, we first take M ≠ 0   , but F o = 0    in numerical simulation. As before, the spatial eigenvalues are computed and demonstrated by dot points in Fig. 14(a) . Obviously, all spatial eigenvalues move up with increasing M  , and they remain in the upper-half plane (α  i   > 0   ). We have specified their new locations with diamond symbols when M = 4 . 605    and F o = 0   . Hence, the laminar parallel porous channel flow becomes more stable to downstream propagating disturbances for a non-zero value of M  . Finally, we also choose a non-zero value of the Forchheimer number (M = 4 . 605    and F o = 1   ). In this case, we see that the spatial eigenvalues slightly move down from their previous locations, but they still reside in the upper-half plane (α  i   > 0   ). Therefore, the stability characteristic of a porous channel flow does not change in the presence of the Forchheimer number. On the other hand, if the spatial eigenvalues are evaluated for a steady disturbance (ω = 0   , β = 2   ), a nice scenario is found [see Fig. 14(b) ]. In this case, all spatial eigenvalues lie on the α  i    -axis, with α  r   = 0    and α  i   > 0   . Although the other features are the same as before, they move up with increasing values of M   and stay in the upper-half plane (α  i   > 0   ). Hence, the porous channel flow is linearly stable to downstream propagating disturbances (x > 0   ) when ω = 0    and β = 2   . Next, we have unveiled the spatial growth rate, − α  i     , when the angular frequency ω   varies [see Fig. 15(a) ]. First, we have shown the result for a plane Poiseuille flow when R e = 5772   , β = 0   , M = 0   , and F o = 0   . Clearly, the maximum value of the spatial growth rate curve touches the line − α  i   = 0    at ω ≈ 0 . 2692   . This is because the selected Reynolds number is the onset of shear mode instability for a plane Poiseuille flow. Using the definition of angular frequency, we further determine the phase speed, c  r   = ω / α  r   ≈ 0 . 2637   , of the neutral shear wave. The numerical value of phase speed matches very well with the result of a plane Poiseuille flow (Orszag, 1971 ). If the numerical simulation is continued for a porous channel flow (M ≠ 0    and F o = 0   ), the maximum value of the spatial growth rate curve no longer touches the line − α  i   = 0   , but decreases successively with increasing M  . In particular, the critical Reynolds number necessary for the onset of shear mode instability rises due to an increase in parameter M  , which causes a reduction in the spatial growth rate. This fact also implies that the parameter M   plays a stabilizing role in shear mode instability. In contrast, if the Reynolds number is increased for a porous channel flow when the parameter M   is kept constant, we can see that the spatial growth rate, − α  i     , is no longer negative but becomes positive in a certain range of angular frequency [see Fig. 15(b) ]. In fact, this unstable range emerges because the chosen Reynolds number exceeds its critical value for the onset of shear mode instability. Furthermore, this unstable range of spatial instability magnifies as long as R e    increases because the Reynolds number has a destabilizing influence on shear mode instability. Our next aim is to decipher spatial disturbance energy growth when the Reynolds number lies in the subcritical zone. To accomplish this, we write the general solution of the spatial matrix initial value problem as follows: (42) S = exp ( P x )  S  0   = N S  0   ,     in which N = exp ( P x )    . Clearly, on the basis of the spatial matrix operator exponential, the spatial initial condition evolves in space. To quantify spatial disturbance energy growth, we define the optimal spatial energy amplification function G  S   ( x )     in the following way (Schmid, 2000; Samanta, 2020b ): (43) G  S   ( x )  = max  S  0   ≠ 0   E ( S )   E ( S  0   )    = max  S  0   ≠ 0   ‖ S ‖  E  2    ‖ S  0   ‖  E  2     = max  S  0   ≠ 0   〈 N S  0   , N S  0   〉   〈 S  0   , S  0   〉    = λ  m a x   ( N  ∗   N )  ,     where N  ∗     denotes the conjugate transpose of N   and λ  m a x   ( N  ∗   N )     denotes the largest eigenvalue of N  ∗   N   . Here, the optimal spatial energy amplification function G  S   ( x )     is maximized over all admissible spatial initial conditions S  0    . To check the existence of a spatial disturbance energy growth corresponding to stable spatial eigenvalues (α  i   > 0   ) or, equivalently, for the downstream propagating disturbances, we create numerical results for the optimal spatial energy amplification function G  S   ( x )     when the Reynolds number R e    increases, but the parameter M   and the Forchheimer number F o    are fixed. It should be noted that the values of the Reynolds number are preferred from the subcritical zone. Fig. 16(a)  displays the results corresponding to a porous channel flow for a steady disturbance (ω = 0   ) when the spanwise wavenumber β = 2   . It is observed that spatial disturbance energy growth strongly depends on the Reynolds number because it amplifies significantly as R e    increases. In accordance with the study of Biau and Bottaro (2004) , if we rescale G  S   ( x )     with R e  2      and x   with R e    and replot numerical outcomes again in Fig. 16(b) , all spatial energy growth curves collapse on a single curve. Therefore, unlike a plane Poiseuille flow, the scalings of G  S   ( x )     with R e  2      and x   with R e    also hold for a porous channel flow when the parameter M   and the Forchheimer number F o    are fixed. Moreover, we can see that the maximum value of G  S   ( x )     increases by approximately 2 . 3 × 1 0  − 4   R e  2     , and the streamwise coordinate x  m a x    , at which the maximum spatial transient growth arises, increases by approximately 5 . 4 × 1 0  − 2   R e    with increasing R e    when M = 0 . 3    and F o = 0   . Instead, if we increase the value of the parameter M  , an opposite event occurs, as observed for temporal transient disturbance energy growth. Fig. 17(a)  shows that spatial disturbance energy growth appears and exhibits a double-hump shape curve rather than a single-hump shape curve, while its maximum value arises at the first hump. We can explain the appearance of a double peak curve in Fig. 17(a)  in the following way: As the spatial transient disturbance energy growth is evaluated for stable spatial eigenvalues when R e = 2000   , ω = 0 . 2   , and β = 1   , all the spatial eigenvalues do not lie on the α  i    -axis with α  r   = 0    [see also Fig. 14(a) ]. As a result, the spatial growth rates, − α  i     , for the least stable eigenvalues contribute more to the spatial energy amplification function than the other stable eigenvalues. Since α  r     values are non-zero for these dominant spatial eigenvalues, we find an oscillatory nature or a double peak on the curve of the spatial energy amplification function. Obviously, spatial disturbance energy growth also decays successively as the parameter M   rises. It should be noted that numerical results are produced for an unsteady disturbance, i.e., for a non-zero value of angular frequency. As soon as we set the zero value to angular frequency, spatial disturbance energy growth intensifies significantly and generates a single-hump shape curve rather than a double-hump shape curve [see Fig. 17(b) ]. However, the spatial disturbance energy growth reduces in the presence of the parameter M  . In addition, the current results recover those for a plane Poiseuille flow when the parameter M   vanishes (Schmid, 2000; Biau and Bottaro, 2004 ). The reason for the appearance of a single peak curve in Fig. 17(b)  is the consequence of the zero values of α  r    . Specifically, in this case, all spatial eigenvalues remain on the α  i    -axis with α  r   = 0    [see also Fig. 14(b) ], and only the least stable spatial eigenvalues contribute to the spatial energy amplification function. As a result, an oscillatory nature or a double peak curve is not found in Fig. 17(b)  when R e = 2000   , ω = 0   , and β = 2   . As the parameter M   alters, we can expect different scalings of G  S   ( x )     and x   from those of a plane Poiseuille flow because G  S   ( x )     depends on M  . The scalings of G  S   ( x )     and x   are retrieved only for steady initial perturbations (ω = 0   , β ≠ 0   ). Accordingly, numerical results are shown for two separate values of β  , where the optimal spatial energy amplification function G  S   ( x )     is scaled by s  M   R e  2      and the streamwise coordinate x   is scaled by R e / [ 1 + M / ( 10 β )  ]    . Here, s  M     is the ratio between the maximum spatial transient disturbance energy growth at a given M   and the maximum spatial transient disturbance energy growth at M = 0   . In both cases, all spatial energy growth curves almost merge into a single curve [see Figs. 17(c) and 17(d) ]. Therefore, for a porous channel flow with varying M  , the maximum spatial transient disturbance energy growth is proportional to s  M   R e  2      and the streamwise coordinate x  m a x    , at which the maximum spatial transient growth arises, is proportional to R e / [ 1 + M / ( 10 β )  ]    . Next, we examine the effect of porosity on the optimal spatial energy amplification function. As a result, we compute it numerically and plot it in Fig. 18  when porosity varies. Similar to the effect of M  , the optimal spatial energy amplification function depletes as porosity rises. Furthermore, as before, we see a double peak when R e = 2000   , ω = 0 . 2   , and β = 1   , and a single peak on the curve of the optimal spatial energy amplification function when R e = 2000   , ω = 0   , and β = 2   . To know the nature of optimal spatial disturbance energy growth in angular frequency versus spanwise wavenumber plane, we further evaluate the contours of the maximum optimal spatial energy amplification function G  m a x S   = m a x  x > 0   G  S   ( x )     when the parameter M   changes. From the level curves of G  m a x S     [see Fig. 19(a) ], we can assert that the maximum value of spatial transient disturbance energy growth can be achieved in the vicinity of the spanwise wavenumber β  -axis for a steady disturbance (ω = 0   ). This fact is consistent with the result reported in Fig. 17 . In particular, we notice that the maximum value of G  m a x S     appears approximately at ω = 0    and β ≈ 2   . To access the shape of the optimal spatial initial disturbance that generates the largest spatial transient disturbance energy growth and yields the optimal final response, we determine optimal input and optimal output at x = x  m a x      and illustrate them in Fig. 19(b)  when R e = 2000   , ω = 0   , β = 2   , M = 0 . 6   , and F o = 0   . We observe that the optimal spatial initial condition consists of a pair of counter-rotating streamwise vortices, which are similar, but their directions are opposite to those found for the optimal temporal initial condition. On the other hand, the optimal final response corresponding to streamwise perturbation velocity generates two sets of alternating high-speed and low-speed streaks in the streamwise direction, like the optimal final response induced by the optimal temporal initial condition. However, the positions of high-speed and low-speed streaks are replaced by each other in comparison with the temporal final response [see also Fig. 13 ].         6 Summary and conclusions A nonmodal stability analysis is accomplished for the three-dimensional nonstratified flow through a parallel-plate channel filled with a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium. The volume-averaged Navier–Stokes equations are employed to describe fluid flow in a porous channel. The base flow solution is determined for the linear stability analysis. Moreover, both temporal and spatial evolution equations are formulated to investigate temporal and spatial disturbance energy growths, respectively. Additionally, we have executed modal stability analysis by analyzing the eigenvalues of the temporal matrix exponential operator and the spatial matrix exponential operator, respectively. Based on the current study, we can draw the following key conclusions: • The base velocity decelerates compared to that of a plane Poiseuille flow due to the presence of the viscous drag force induced by the solid matrix in the porous medium.  • The Forchheimer quadratic drag force further decelerates the base velocity.  • As the channel is occupied by a porous medium, the base flow shear stress approaches zero after a certain height from the plates for higher values of the parameter M   and the Forchheimer number F  o    , which prevents boundary layers that develop on the rigid impermeable plates from reaching the center of the channel. This result is fully different from that of a plane Poiseuille flow, where boundary layers grow uniformly from both sides and meet at the center of the channel.  • According to the modal stability analysis, the viscous drag force stabilizes the unstable porous channel flow. This is because the dominant shear mode shifts from the unstable upper-half plane to the stable lower-half plane as the parameter M   rises.  • The presence of the Forchheimer number does not alter the stability characteristic of porous channel flow.  • The spanwise wavenumber stabilizes shear mode instability because the unstable region caused by the shear mode diminishes. This fact agrees with the statement of Squire’s theorem.  • The spatial growth rate corresponding to the downstream propagating disturbances becomes stronger as the Reynolds number increases, but it becomes weaker as the parameter M   increases.  • Shear mode instability weakens as porosity increases.  • The nonmodal stability analysis demonstrates that both temporal and spatial transient disturbance energy growths attenuate if the impact of the viscous drag force is strengthened. However, they significantly intensify if the Reynolds number is increased.  • If temporal transient disturbance energy growth is scaled by R e  2      and time t   is scaled by R e   , all temporal growth curves merge into a single curve, resembling a plane Poiseuille flow. The same scalings are also valid in the case of spatial disturbance energy growth when the porous material remains fixed. However, these scalings no longer prevail for varying porous materials.  • For different porous materials, temporal transient disturbance energy growth is scaled by g  M   R e  2     , and time t   is scaled by R e / [ 1 + 2 M / ( 10 β )  ]     only for spanwise perturbations. Similarly, we employ the scale s  M   R e  2      for spatial transient disturbance energy growth and the scale R e / [ 1 + M / ( 10 β )  ]     for spatial coordinate x   solely for steady disturbances.  • Temporal transient disturbance energy growth becomes larger for a spanwise perturbation than for oblique perturbations, which incorporate both streamwise and spanwise wavenumbers, and for a perturbation that includes only streamwise wavenumber.  • The maximum temporal energy amplification emerges at α = 0    and β ≈ 2   .  • The initial spanwise perturbation, for which the largest temporal transient growth occurs, yields an optimal response that consists of two sets of alternating high-speed and low-speed streaks for the streamwise perturbation velocity.  • Spatial transient disturbance energy growth becomes larger for steady initial perturbations that exclude the angular frequency.  • The maximum spatial energy amplification emerges at ω = 0    and β ≈ 2   .  • The optimal spatial input generates an optimal output, which consists of two sets of alternating high-speed and low-speed streaks for the streamwise perturbation velocity, as observed for the temporal initial condition. However, the positions of the high-speed and low-speed streaks are replaced by each other in the case of optimal spatial response.    As the current study deals with the nonmodal stability analysis of an isothermal channel flow filled with a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium, it offers some potential future directions: (i) The investigation of the nonmodal stability of a non-isothermal porous channel flow. (ii) The investigation of the nonmodal stability of an isothermal porous channel flow when the porous medium is nonhomogeneous and anisotropic. These studies will be considered in future attempts.
1 Introduction In the context of frequent extreme climate events, climatic variability has significantly impacted vegetation productivity and the water cycle in terrestrial ecosystems (Huang et al., 2015 ). Water use efficiency (WUE) is defined as the ratio of gross primary productivity (GPP) to evapotranspiration (ET), representing the rate of water loss per unit of carbon absorbed (Huang et al., 2016 ). WUE links carbon and water cycling processes in ecosystems, serving as a crucial parameter to quantify the response of ecosystem productivity to water availability (Wang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, a thorough analysis of spatiotemporal variations in WUE and its driving factors contributes to understanding the processes of carbon and water cycling processes in ecosystems and their responses to climatic variability. In recent years, extensive research on the spatiotemporal variations of ecosystem WUE based on remote sensing data has been conducted at various scales. Tang et al. (2014)  found an increasing trend in WUE from the subtropical to northern high latitudes, peaking around 51°N, followed by a declining trend. Zou et al. (2020)  observed that WUE in Central Asia showed overall little change, but the trends varied significantly across different ecosystems. Sun et al. (2018)  noted that from 1979 to 2012, WUE in China exhibited a growing trend, with concentration in the northeastern, southwestern, and eastern regions, while declining areas were concentrated in the western region. Ma et al. (2022)  demonstrated a fluctuating upward trend in WUE on the Loess Plateau, with substantial variations in WUE change rates across different seasons. Wang et al. (2023)  investigated the trend of WUE in Southwest China and identified favorable areas for artificial carbon sequestration. Southwest China is the world's largest continuous karst region. Due to extensive rocky desertification and soil erosion, its ecological environment is highly sensitive to external disturbances and is susceptible to the influences of climatic variability (Lu et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2023 ). It is a typical ecologically fragile area. In recent years, the Chinese government has undertaken a large number of ecological restoration projects, resulting in improvements to the ecological environment, with trends of increasing vegetation coverage and carbon storage (Fang et al., 2014; Li et al., 2022 ). The geomorphologic differences between karst and non-karst ecosystems have led to significant variations in the ecological environment. Qiao et al. (2020)  found that lithology and topography dominate the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation change. Jiang et al. (2020)  demonstrated that the impact of temperature rise on vegetation drought stress is higher in karst than in non-karst ecosystem. In addition, there is evident heterogeneity in the spatial distribution of meteorological elements in Southwest China (Wang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, a deep investigation into the differences in WUE between karst and non-karst ecosystems is crucial for enhancing our understanding of the carbon and water cycling processes in Southwest China, with significant implications for achieving sustainable development goals. Changes in WUE are highly sensitive to non-climatic factors, including human activities. Land cover changes (such as deforestation, afforestation, etc.) and land management practices can directly alter carbon absorption (Tian et al., 2011 ). Mei et al. (2022)  pointed out that WUE changes in Inner Mongolia from 2001 to 2020 were significantly influenced by human activities, with positive effects being more pronounced than negative ones. Zhang et al. (2023)  found that ecological restoration projects in Southwest China from 2003 to 2017 led to a rapid increase in WUE, with human activities being the dominant factor in WUE changes. In addition to human activities, WUE is also influenced by climatic variability. Against the backdrop of frequent extreme climate events, climatic variability can have a significant impact on the carbon and water cycling processes in global ecosystems. Du et al. (2019)  explored the impact of climatic variability and afforestation programs on WUE changes in northern China, and the results indicated that climatic variability is the primary driving factor for WUE changes in northern China. Fan et al. (2022)  pointed out that WUE in the Yellow River Basin showed an increasing trend from 2003 to 2017, with climatic factors being the dominant driver of WUE growth in the Yellow River Basin. Wang et al. (2015)  showed that in the Yangtze River Delta region, WUE decreases with the increase of vapor pressure deficit, and this phenomenon is most significant in broad-leaved forests. However, the impact of complex climatic variability on the trend of WUE and the differences in the dominant climatic factors between karst and non-karst ecosystems have not been fully explored. Therefore, we aim to explore the differences and characteristics of the impact of complex climatic change on WUE in different ecosystems using PML-V2 data and variable climate data from 2000 to 2020. The specific objectives of the study are as follows: (1) Explore the spatiotemporal patterns of GPP, ET, and WUE in karst and non-karst ecosystems; (2) Reveal the persistence characteristics of WUE in karst and non-karst ecosystems; (3) investigating the correlation between climatic factors and WUE; (4) Quantify the impact of climatic factors on WUE and identify the dominant ones.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Overview of the study area The study area was located in the southwestern part of China, with geographical coordinates between 20°54′∼34°19′N and 97°21′∼112°04′E, composed of Sichuan, Chongqing, Guizhou, Yunnan, and Guangxi ( Fig. 1 ). The terrain slopes from west to east, and the topography is complex, including the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, Zoige Plateau, Hengduan Mountains, Sichuan Basin, and Guangxi Hills. It is one of the world's three largest contiguous karst areas, with a karst area of 5.5×105  km2  (Li et al., 2002 ). The region is dominated by a monsoon climate, with an average annual temperature mostly above 15°C. The rainfall is abundant, exhibiting significant wet and dry season differences. The period from May to October is the wet season, with more than 80 % of the annual precipitation occurring during this time. The dry season has less rainfall but higher evapotranspiration (Nie et al., 2012 ). Influenced by the typical monsoon climate and karst topography, Southwest China is prone to soil erosion and drought events, making the vegetation growth environment highly vulnerable.  2.2 Data sources In this study, GPP and ET utilized to calculate ecosystem WUE are derived from the PML-V2 product with a spatial resolution of 500 m. This product has been proven effective in coupling GPP and plant transpiration, providing a reliable estimation of ecosystem WUE (Gan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019, 2016 ). The Google Earth Engine platform was utilized to acquire the PML-V2 product for the growing season (May to October) from 2000 to 2020. Complex climatic conditions have caused changes in vegetation growth characteristics. For example, thermal conditions determine the growth rate of vegetation, while water conditions are a crucial factor affecting the available water content of vegetation (AghaKouchak et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2021; Farooq et al., 2009 ). Additionally, atmospheric conditions can impact vegetation photosynthesis and transpiration (Durand et al., 2021; Novick et al., 2016 ). Therefore, to comprehensively express the complex climatic conditions in Southwest China, precipitation (PR) is utilized to represent water conditions; average temperature (Temp), minimum temperature (Tmin), maximum temperature (Tmax), and downward surface shortwave radiation (SRAD) are utilized to represent thermal conditions; while relative humidity (RH), vapor pressure (VAP), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and wind speed (VS) are utilized to represent atmospheric conditions. Among them, Monthly average temperature, monthly average minimum temperature, monthly average maximum temperature, and monthly total precipitation from 2000 to 2020 are sourced from the dataset provided by the Third Pole Environment Data Center (TPDC) (Peng et al., 2019 ), with a spatial resolution of 1 km. This dataset is generated by downscaling based on climate data from CRU and the high-resolution climate dataset released by WorldClim. Downward surface shortwave radiation, vapor pressure, vapor pressure deficit, and wind speed are obtained from the TerraClimate dataset (Abatzoglou et al., 2018 ) with a spatial resolution of 1/24°. Relative humidity is sourced from the ERA5-Land dataset (Munoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ) with a spatial resolution of 0.1°, and is calculated from temperature and dew point temperature (Simmons et al., 1999 ). Bilinear interpolation is applied to all meteorological data to achieve a resolution of 500 m (Li et al., 2020 ), consistent with the ecosystem WUE, and synthesized into annual data. The climatic variables used in this study and their data sources are listed in  Table 1 .  2.3 Methodology In this research, Theil-Sen Median trend analysis, Mann Kendall significance test and Hurst index were used to explore the spatiotemporal variation trends of the ecosystem WUE. To reveal the impact of climatic variation on WUE, principal component analysis (PCA), residual analysis, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used ( Fig. 2 ). Each method will be introduced comprehensively in subsequent sections. 2.3.1 Water use efficiency calculation The WUE in Southwest China was calculated using the total value of GPP and ET data during the growing season, using the following formula:(1) WUE = GPP  ET           Where WUE represents the water use efficiency during the growing season (gC mm−1  m−2 ); GPP is the total value of primary productivity (gC m−2 ); ET is evapotranspiration (mm).  2.3.2 Theil-Sen Median trend analysis and Mann-Kendall significance test Using Theil-Sen Median trend analysis, the spatiotemporal variation trend of WUE in Southwest China from 2000 to 2020 was calculated. Theil-Sen Median trend analysis is a non-parametric statistical method that calculates the median of a data sequence, mitigating the impact of outliers on the trend slope. It possesses advantages in determining the change trends in long-time series data (Sen, 1968 ). The slope calculation formula of Theil-Sen is as follows:(2) β  WUE   = Median WUE  j   − WUE  i    j − i      , 2000 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ 2020 #       Where WUE j   and WUE i   represent the values of WUE in years j  and i , respectively; β  WUE     represents the slope of variation trend in WUE from 2000 to 2020. When β  WUE     > 0, it indicates an increase trend in WUE. When β  WUE     = 0, it suggests that the WUE is essentially stable. When β  WUE     < 0, it implies a decrease trend in WUE. The Mann–Kendall significance test, a nonparametric statistical test, is generally employed to identify the significance of variation in long-term time series data (Almazroui and Şen, 2020; Güçlü, 2020 ). The Mann–Kendall significance test was utilized to determine the significance of WUE variation trends in Southwest China from 2000 to 2020. Based on the results, the variation trend was classified into significant changes (P < 0.05) and weak changes (P ≥ 0.05).  2.3.3 Future water use efficiency dynamics trend analysis The Hurst index is an index that quantitatively expresses the long-term memory process of time series (Hurst, 1951 ). In recent years, the Hurst index has been widely applied in ecological and environmental research (Lu et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2022 ). In this study, the Hurst index is used to assess the persistence characteristics of WUE variation. The detailed calculation steps can be found in (Zhong et al., 2022 ), as follows: Divide the time series WUE  τ    ¯       (τ = 1, 2, …, n) into τ sub-series V(t), and for each sub-series, t = 1, 2, …, τ. A mean WUE of the time series was specified as:(3) WUE  τ    ¯  = 1  τ   ∑ t = 1  τ   WUE  t      , ( τ = 1 ,  2 ,  … ,  n ) #        The accumulated deviation from mean WUE was specified as:(4) V ( t , τ ) = ∑ t = 1  τ   WUE  t     − WUE  t      ¯     #        A range series of R was specified as:(5) R  τ     = max V  ( t , τ )   − min V  t , τ     ,  ( 1 ≤ t ≤ τ ; τ = 1 ,  2 ,  … ,  n ) #        A standard deviation series of S was specified as:(6) S  τ   = 1  τ   ∑ t = 1  τ   WUE  t        − WUE  t    2    ¯     1  2     #        The Hurst exponent was specified as:(7) R  τ      S  ( τ )     = ( c τ )  Hurst   #        Among these, Hurst denotes the variation trend of time series in values of 0–1. When 0 ≤ Hurst < 0.5, it indicates that WUE changes exhibit anti-persistence, meaning the overall trend in future WUE is opposite to the past. A Hurst index closer to 0 suggests stronger anti-persistence characteristics. When Hurst = 0.5, it signifies that WUE is independent, and there is no dependence, implying that past overall trends do not influence future changes. When 0.5 < Hurst ≤ 1, it indicates that WUE changes exhibit persistence, meaning the overall trend in future WUE is the same as the past. A Hurst index closer to 1 suggests stronger persistence characteristics.  2.3.4 Principal component analysis and residual analysis PCA is a multivariate statistical method for reducing the dimensionality of redundant datasets. It orthogonalizes data containing potential correlations, reducing a large amount of data to a set of mutually orthogonal or uncorrelated new variables (principle components, PCs), and uses them to explain the original dataset (Abdul-Wahab et al., 2005; Ul-Saufie et al., 2013 ). Residual analysis quantitatively expresses the influence of independent variables on dependent variables and is widely used in studies on the impact of climatic variability and other factors on vegetation changes (Wessels et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2022b ). In this study, to mitigate the effects of collinearity among complex climate factors on residual analysis, and to retain the characteristics of complex climate conditions optimally, PCA was employed as a pre-step for residual analysis to construct a framework for evaluating the impact of climatic change on WUE. The specific construction process of this framework is as follows: (1) Based on the various climatic factors shown in Table 1 , a redundant dataset representing complex climatic conditions was constructed. (2) The robust principal component analysis with varimax rotation was employed to obtain principal components with eigenvalues greater than 1 in the dataset, and the three principal components with the highest variance interpretation rate were selected as PC1, PC2, and PC3. (3) These principal components (PC1, PC2, PC3), considered as independent predictive factors explaining complex climatic conditions, were used to construct a multivariate linear regression model between WUE observed values (WUEobs ) and climatic variables for each pixel, obtaining WUE predicted values (WUEpre ) time series representing the impact of climatic variability only. (4) The difference between WUEobs  and WUEpre  time series was calculated as the residual values (WUEres ) time series representing the impact of other factors on WUE. (5) Significance testing are performed on the WUEres  time series. If the change in WUEres  is insignificant, it indicates that climatic change is the dominant factor affecting WUE. Conversely, if the change in WUEres  is significant, it indicates that the impact of climatic change on WUE is less than the impact of other factors on WUE (Herrmann et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 2017 ). (6) The significant level of WUEres  and the variation trend of WUEobs  were superimposed to evaluate the spatial variation characteristics of WUE affected by climatic change. The formula for residual analysis is as follows:(8) WUE  pre   = a * PC 1 + b * PC 2 + c * PC 3 #       (9) WUE  res   = WUE  obs   − WUE  pre   #       Where WUE p  re   represents WUE under the influence of climatic variability; WUE res   represents WUE under the influence of other factors; WUE obs   represents the observed WUE; PC1 , PC2 , PC3  represent the three principal components explaining complex climatic conditions.  2.3.5 Correlation analysis The Pearson correlation coefficient is utilized to explore the correlation between WUE and various climatic factors at the pixel scale, aiming to evaluate the impact of different climatic factors on WUE in Southwest China (Karimi et al., 2022 ). The calculation formula for the Pearson correlation coefficient is as follows.(10) R  xy   = ∑ i = 1  n    x  i   − x  ̅     y  i   − y  ̅      ∑ i = 1  n    ( x  i   − x  ̅  )  2     ∑ i = 1  n    ( y  i   − y  ̅  )  2       #       Where R xy   represents the correlation coefficient between WUE and climatic factors; n  represents the total length of the research period; x i   and y i   represent the WUE value and climatic factor value in the i th year, respectively; x ¯    and y ¯    represent the average values of WUE and climatic factors during the study period, respectively. When the correlation coefficient is significant at a confidence level of 0.05(p < 0.05), WUE is considered significantly correlated with the candidate factor. Otherwise, it is considered insignificantly correlated.  2.3.6 Feature importance To delve into whether there are differences in the potential relationship between climatic factors and WUE changes, the importance of each climatic factor in non-karst and karst ecosystems was analyzed to determine the primary driving factors. XGBoost is a machine learning algorithm based on the gradient boosting decision concept (Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ), known for its high prediction accuracy and computational speed. It has been widely applied in ecology and environmental studies (Michael et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022a ). SHAP is a method based on game theory for interpreting machine learning models (Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ). Its core idea is to calculate the marginal contributions of features to the model's output and then explain the "black box model" at both global and local levels. In this study, the XGBoost algorithm was utilized to uncover potential nonlinear relationships between climatic factors and trend in WUE. The SHAP model was introduced to quantitatively express the importance of climatic factors in the model, aiming to identify the dominant climatic factors in WUE trend.
