The specific approach is as follows: (1) Build XGBoost models for karst and non-karst ecosystems separately, with the independent variables including the trends of various climatic factors (PR, RH, Temp, Tmax, Tmin, SRAD, VAP, VPD, VS), and the target variable being the trend in WUE. (2) Use the SHAP model to interpret the XGBoost models for karst and non-karst ecosystems, obtaining importance scores for each climatic factor, and clarify the degree of influence of different climatic factors on WUE trend.    3 Results 3.1 Multi-year average of GPP, ET, and WUE The spatial distribution of the multi-year average of GPP, ET, and WUE from 2000 to 2020 are shown in  Fig. 3 . From the spatial distribution, GPP in Southwest China exhibits significant spatial variability, with the multi-year average mainly concentrated between 400 and 2000 gC m−2  year−1 , low values distributed in Sichuan and Guizhou, and high values mainly distributed in Yunnan and Guangxi. Similar spatial distribution differences are also observed in ET, with the multi-year average concentrated between 300 and 700 mm year−1 , low values distributed in Sichuan and Guizhou, and high values mainly distributed in Yunnan and Guangxi. Like GPP and ET, due to differences in climate, geological conditions, vegetation types, and other factors, there are significant differences in WUE across Southwest China, with the multi-year average concentrated between 0.5 and 3 gC mm−1  m−2 , low values distributed in Sichuan, and high values mainly distributed in Guangxi. From an ecosystem perspective, there are differences in the three parameters in different ecosystems. In non-karst ecosystem, the multi-year average GPP is 914.35 gC m−2  year−1 , ET is 451.75 mm year−1 , and WUE is 2.01 gC mm−1  m−2 . In karst ecosystem, the multi-year average GPP is 897.18 gC m−2  year−1 , ET is 429.68 mm year−1 , and WUE is 2.08 gC mm−1  m−2 . Overall, in Southwest China, the multi-year average GPP and ET in non-karst are higher than those in karst ecosystem, while the multi-year average WUE is lower than that in karst ecosystem.  3.2 Temporal variation in GPP, ET and WUE The temporal trends of GPP, ET, and WUE during the growing season from 2000 to 2020 are shown in  Fig. 4 . Overall, during the study period, GPP, ET, and WUE in Southwest China showed an overall fluctuating upward trend. The GPP growth rate was 4.543 gC m−2  year−1 , reaching its maximum value in 2013 at 1017.993 gC m−2  year−1 . The ET growth rate was 1.408 mm year−1 , reaching its maximum value in 2011 at 495.88 mm year−1 . The WUE growth rate was 0.005 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 , reaching its maximum value in 2016 at 2.239 gC mm−1  m−2 . From an ecosystem perspective, non-karst and ecosystems areas exhibited similar variation characteristics. The multi-year average GPP in non-karst ecosystem was slightly higher than that in karst ecosystem, and the GPP growth rate in non-karst ecosystem (4.746 gC m−2  year−1 ) was also slightly higher than that in karst ecosystem (4.079 gC m−2  year−1 ). In comparison to the differences in GPP changes, the differences in ET changes between the two ecosystems were more significant. The multi-year average ET in non-karst ecosystem was generally higher than that in karst, and the ET growth rate (1.711 mm year−1 ) was also higher than that in karst ecosystem (0.715 mm year−1 ). In contrast to GPP and ET, the multi-year average WUE in non-karst ecosystem was generally lower than that in karst ecosystem, and the WUE growth rate (0.004 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 ) was also lower than that in karst ecosystem (0.007 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 ). Overall, during the growing season from 2000 to 2020, GPP, ET, and WUE in Southwest China showed an upward trend, with GPP and ET increasing more rapidly in non-karst ecosystem compared to karst ecosystem, while WUE increased more slowly in non-karst ecosystem than in karst ecosystem.  3.3 Spatial variation in GPP, ET and WUE This study assessed the spatial trends of GPP, ET, and WUE in Southwest China from 2000 to 2020, and the results are shown in  Fig. 5 . From a spatial perspective, the area of GPP increase in Southwest China is greater than the area of decrease. Significant increases are mainly found in the eastern part of Sichuan and the border areas of each province. Regions such as Guangxi, Guizhou, and the southwestern part of Chongqing show a significant decrease in GPP. There is significant spatial heterogeneity in ET changes in Southwest China. The regions with a significant increase in ET are mainly distributed in the western part of the study area, while regions with a significant decrease are mainly distributed in the eastern part of the study area. We found that from 2000 to 2020, WUE in Southwest China underwent significant changes (Fig. 5 ). Overall, the area of increase in WUE is greater than the area of decrease, indicating an upward trend in WUE in Southwest China from 2000 to 2020. The regions with a significant increase in WUE are mainly concentrated in Sichuan, Chongqing, and the border areas of Guizhou and Yunnan. The regions with a significant decrease in WUE are scattered, with large areas of significant decrease in Guangxi, Yunnan, and Guizhou. It can be seen that overall, GPP, ET, and WUE in Southwest China showed an increase trend from 2000 to 2020. It is shown in  Table 2  that the proportion of significantly increased and significantly decreased (p < 0.05) areas by ecosystem. From the perspective of ecosystems, there is no significant difference in GPP changes between different ecosystems, and the areas with significant increases are significantly higher than the areas with significant decreases. The significant decrease trend in ET shows no significant difference between the two ecosystems, but there is a difference in the significant increase trend. The non-karst area has a higher proportion of significant increase area (44.5 %) than the karst area (29.74 %). The differences in WUE between different ecosystems are mainly in the areas with a significant decrease trend, with the non-karst area having a higher proportion of significant decrease area (13.31 %) than the karst area (9.06 %). Overall, the non-karst area has a higher proportion of significant increase area in ET and a higher proportion of significant decrease area in WUE than the karst area.  3.4 Persistence characteristics of WUE As shown in  Fig. 6 , the temporal persistence characteristics of WUE and its coupling with temporal trends were assessed. The Hurst index of WUE in Southwest China ranges from 0.05 to 0.95, with an average value of 0.43, indicating an overall anti-persistent behavior of WUE. In terms of temporal persistence features, the area percentage of anti-persistent WUE in Southwest China is 77.02 %, while the persistent area percentage is 22.98 %. The overlay analysis results of the temporal trends and persistence characteristics of WUE are shown in  Table 3 . The area percentage of future increasing trends in WUE in Southwest China is 46.21 %, with a dominance of decreasing-anti-persistence, accounting for 34.28 % of the area, mainly distributed in the western part of the study area. The area percentage of future decreasing trends in WUE in Southwest China is 53.79 %, with a dominance of increasing-anti-persistence, accounting for 42.74 % of the area, mainly distributed in the eastern part of the study area. From an ecosystem perspective, the area percentage of future increasing trends in WUE in non-karst ecosystem is 47.86 %, with an increasing-persistent area percentage of 12.08 %. In karst ecosystem, the area percentage of future increasing trends in WUE is 42.47 %, with an increasing-persistent area percentage of 11.6 %. Overall, the future changes in WUE in Southwest China are dominated by decreases, with most areas transitioning from increasing to decreasing trends, and a relatively small proportion of persistently decreasing areas. The area percentage of future increasing trends in non-karst ecosystem is higher than that in karst ecosystem, with a similar proportion of persistently increasing areas compared to karst ecosystem.  3.5 Spatial characteristics of complex climate impacts on WUE The spatial variation trends in WUE affected by climatic change is shown in  Fig. 7 . In Fig. 7 , colored areas represent the dominance of climatic change over changes in WUE, while gray areas represent a less significant impact of climatic change on changes in WUE compared to other factors. The proportion of regions where changes in WUE are dominated by climatic change in Southwest China is 66.59 %, with 35.26 % of regions experiencing an increase in WUE due to climatic change, mainly distributed in Chongqing, eastern Sichuan, and western Guizhou. The proportion of regions with decreased WUE due to climatic change is 31.33 %, mainly distributed in the mountainous areas of western Sichuan and Yunnan. The proportion of regions where the impact of climatic change on change in WUE is less significant compared to other factors is 33.41 %. From an ecosystem perspective, climatic change is the dominant factor in 69.43 % of karst areas, slightly higher than in non-karst areas (65.36 %). Specifically, in non-karst areas, climatic change increased WUE in 33.51 % of regions and decreased WUE in 31.85 % of regions (Fig. 7 a). In karst areas, climatic change increased WUE in 39.28 % of regions and decreased WUE in 30.15 % of regions (Fig. 7 b). Overall, climatic change is the main factor affecting WUE in Southwest China, and regardless of whether the areas are karst or non-karst, WUE is mainly increasing under the influence of climatic change.  3.6 Effects of climatic factors on WUE Through the correlation analysis between WUE and climatic factors, it is indicated that there is significant spatial differentiation in their relationship across Southwest China ( Fig. 8 ). WUE demonstrates primarily positive correlations with PR, RH, SRAD, Tmax, and VAP, with proportions of positive correlation at 61.26 % (PR), 51.25 % (RH), 51.45 % (SRAD), 52.57 % (Tmax), and 64.09 % (VAP), respectively. Among them, the area with a significant positive correlation (p < 0.05) with PR has the highest proportion (11.95 %), and the area with a significant positive correlation with Tmax has the lowest proportion (5.37 %). The spatial distribution of WUE exhibits positive correlations with PR, RH, and VAP, predominantly observed in Chongqing, Yunnan, and eastern Sichuan. Conversely, regions exhibiting positive correlations with SRAD and Tmax are primarily founded in Guizhou and western Sichuan. WUE demonstrates predominantly negative correlations with Temp, Tmin, VPD, and VS, with proportions of negative correlation at 51.76 %(Temp), 56.98 %(Tmin), 58.11 %(VPD), and 59.52 % (VS), respectively. Among them, the region significantly negatively correlated with VPD (p < 0.05) has the highest proportion at 6.99 %, and the region significantly negatively correlated with VS had the lowest proportion at 3.61 %. The spatial distribution of WUE exhibits negative correlations with Temp, VPD, and VS, predominantly located in Chongqing, Guangxi, southern Yunnan, and eastern Sichuan. The regions with a negative correlation between WUE and Tmin mainly distributed in Guangxi, Guizhou, and western Sichuan.  Table 4  presents the correlation between WUE and climatic factors in different ecosystems. In non-karst ecosystem, the region with a positive correlation between WUE and VAP is the largest, accounting for 63.2 %, and the region with a negative correlation with VS is the largest, accounting for 60.53 %. In karst ecosystem, the positive correlation area of VAP is still the largest, accounting for 66.12 %, and the region with a negative correlation with Tmin is the largest, accounting for 60.61 %. It is noteworthy that significant differences exist in the correlation between WUE and RH, SRAD, Temp, and Tmax in the two ecosystems. In non-karst ecosystem, WUE is predominantly positively correlated with RH, whereas it is predominantly negatively correlated with SRAD, Temp, and Tmax. Conversely, in karst ecosystem, WUE is predominantly negatively correlated with RH and positively correlated with SRAD, Temp, and Tmax. The difference in these correlations is particularly significant for SRAD and Tmax. It is evident that the unique geomorphic conditions in karst ecosystem can result in differentiated impacts of climatic factors on WUE. XGBoost and SHAP models were employed to capture the potential relationship between WUE and climatic factors, and plotted a scatter plot of SHAP values to illustrate the impact of various climatic factors on the changes in WUE in Southwest China ( Fig. 9 ). In Fig. 9 , climatic factors are ranked from top to bottom based on their impact on the changes in WUE, with the top row representing the highest importance and the bottom row representing the lowest. The horizontal axis represents the SHAP value, indicating the extent to which the climatic factor affects the changes in WUE. Each scatter point represents a sample, with colors ranging from red to blue indicating the climatic factor values of the sample from high to low. When there are more points with the same SHAP value, the height of the scatter plot is greater. In non-karst ecosystem, PR is the most important factor affecting the changes in WUE, whereas VS is the least important. As SHAP values change from negative to positive, the scatter plot colors for PR and SRAD gradually transition from blue to red (Fig. 9 a). This indicates that as PR and SRAD increase, their impact on the changes in WUE shifts from negative to positive, demonstrating that PR and SRAD significantly positively affect the changes in WUE. Conversely, as VPD and Temp increase, SHAP values transition from positive to negative, indicating that VPD and Temp have a negative effect. Similar to non-karst ecosystem, PR and SRAD positively affect the changes in WUE in karst ecosystem, while VPD and Temps have a negative effect (Fig. 9 b). Additionally, although VAP has not demonstrated significant positive or negative effects, it remains the most important climatic factor affecting the changes in WUE, while VS remains the least important. It is noteworthy that Tmax in non-karst ecosystem exhibits a significant negative impact, indicating that when the maximum temperature is too high, the changes in WUE are significantly inhibited. This effect is not observed in karst ecosystem. To visually demonstrate the importance of climatic factors on the changes in WUE across different ecosystems, the average importance of climatic factors was calculated based on the absolute average value of SHAP ( Fig. 10 ). In non-karst ecosystem, PR is the most important factor, followed by VAP, with VS being the least important. Similar to non-karst ecosystem, VAP is the most important factor in karst ecosystem, followed by PR, with VS being the least important. Notably, Temp and Tmin have similar importance in changes in WUE across different ecosystems, but the importance of Tmax in non-karst ecosystem is significantly higher than in karst ecosystem. Overall, the dominant climatic factor affecting the changes in WUE is PR in non-karst ecosystem, while it is VAP in karst ecosystem. PR and SRAD have a significant positive impact on the changes in WUE in Southwest China, whereas VPD and Temp have a significant negative impact. The negative effect of Tmax on the changes in WUE is significantly greater in non-karst ecosystem than in karst ecosystem.   4 Discussion 4.1 Spatiotemporal variations and persistence of WUE in Southwest China In recent years, a series of ecological restoration projects have impacted the dynamics of vegetation and carbon-water exchange processes in Southwest China. In this study, we analyzed the spatiotemporal trends of WUE in Southwest China based on strongly coupled GPP and ET data. The multi-year average of WUE is mainly concentrated between 0.5 and 3, and the overall trend of WUE shows a fluctuating upward trend over the years, consistent with other research results (Shi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In addition, this study also explores the differences in changes between karst and non-karst ecosystems. The variation trend of WUE is similar in both ecosystems but with some differences. Specifically, the WUE in karst ecosystem is generally higher than that in non-karst ecosystem, and the rate of increase is slightly higher than in non-karst ecosystem. At the same time, the proportion of the area with a significant decrease trend in WUE in karst ecosystem is significantly lower than in non-karst ecosystem. This difference is similar to the results of Wang et al. (2021) . It is noteworthy that the results of this study indicate that the GPP in karst ecosystem during the growing season (May to October) is at the same level as in non-karst ecosystem, but ET is lower than in non-karst ecosystem, leading to slightly higher WUE than in non-karst ecosystem. This result is consistent with the study by Zhou et al. (2023) . This phenomenon differs from the WUE observed at the annual scale ( Table 5 ). We believe that there are two reasons for this difference: (1) During the growing season, Southwest China receives abundant rainfall. Fu et al. (2019)  confirmed that the higher average phosphorus concentration and leaf thickness of vegetation in karst ecosystem result in higher leaf photosynthetic rates, leading to higher individual vegetation WUE than in non-karst ecosystem. (2) Due to the shallow soil layer in karst areas, water is easily lost from the karst conduits, making plants more susceptible to drought stress. Under frequent drought stress, plants reduce their transpiration to prevent excessive water loss (Huang et al., 2019 ), resulting in lower ET in karst ecosystem than in non-karst ecosystem. In the future, the areas where WUE in Southwest China continues to rise are mainly distributed in the eastern part of Sichuan, the southern part of Guangxi, and the border areas of various provinces. On the one hand, these areas, with the implementation of projects such as returning farmland to forest, karst rocky desertification control, and other ecological protection projects (Ding et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019 ), have gradually improved their ability to resist disasters, and the ecological environment continues to improve. On the other hand, the above-mentioned areas all have good meteorological conditions, with sufficient sunshine and abundant rainfall, which is conducive to vegetation growth (Jiang et al., 2021 ). The areas where WUE continues to decline in the future are mainly distributed in the southern part of Yunnan, the northern part of Guangxi, and the surrounding areas of major cities. It can be seen that urban expansion and unreasonable land use will have a sustained negative impact on WUE. The proportion of Southwest China where WUE transitions from rising to falling in the future is 42.74 %. It is necessary to continue to pay attention to the areas where WUE transitions from rising to falling, and formulate environmental protection measures based on local conditions to improve the effectiveness of ecological restoration projects in Southwest China.  4.2 Impact of complex climate on WUE In this study, we evaluated the impact of various climatic factors—including temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and others—on WUE in Southwest China. The results indicate that climatic factors predominantly influence changes in WUE across most regions (Fig. 7 ). Specifically, WUE is primarily positively correlated with PR, RH, SRAD, Tmax, and VPD, whereas it is predominantly negatively correlated with Temp, Tmin, VPD, and VS (Fig. 8 ). However, previous studies have demonstrated that the response of vegetation to climatic change varies under different geographical conditions (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2015 ). Therefore, Southwest China is divided into non-karst and karst ecosystems to explore the differences in WUE responses to climatic factors across different ecosystems. Our results indicate a significant difference in response, especially in the relationships between WUE and RH, SRAD, Temp, and Tmax. Non-karst and karst ecosystems exhibit completely opposite correlation relationships (Table 4 ). This result indicates a significant difference in the impact characteristics of the different ecosystems on thermal conditions, which has not been found in previous studies. In addition, interpretable machine learning was utilized to capture potential relationships between WUE and climatic factors, aiming to determine the importance of changes in climatic factors to WUE. The results showed significant differences in the importance of various climatic factors between karst and non-karst ecosystems. Interestingly, in the karst area, the most important factor affecting WUE changes is VAP, while in the non-karst area, the most important factor is PR. Wang et al. (2020)  demonstrated a positive correlation between air pressure and WUE in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region. PR and SRAD have significant positive effects on WUE, while VPD and Temp have negative effects on WUE. Previous studies have shown that water content plays a crucial role in GPP in semi-arid and arid regions (Bai et al., 2008 ). The increasing trend in precipitation will alleviate water limitations, effectively sustaining plant growth and thereby increasing GPP and WUE (Khalifa et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2016 ). In contrast to the positive effect of precipitation, under conditions of rising temperatures, stomatal closure is a factor causing a decrease in GPP, and increasing temperatures do not significantly affect ET (Niu et al., 2011 ), leading to a decrease in WUE. Under the backdrop of climate warming, VPD causes stomatal closure and a decrease in vegetation transpiration, resulting in a negative impact on WUE (Grossiord et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2010 ). The phenomenon where the influence of climatic factors on WUE is lower than that of other factors has only been observed in certain regions. This phenomenon is related to vegetation restoration and desertification control projects. The large-scale ecological governance projects implemented in Southwest China have effectively increased vegetation greenness and coverage, leading to growth in GPP and WUE (Tong et al., 2017 ).  4.3 Research gaps and future prospects Due to the numerous factors and complex processes influencing the spatial variation of WUE, there are still some issues and limitations in this study that need further improvement and exploration in future research. (1) This study used PCA to transform the various climatic factors (PR, RH, Temp, Tmax, Tmin, SRAD, VAP, VPD, VS) into three uncorrelated principal components, which were then used in residual analysis as climatic factors influencing WUE changes. Although this method can maximize the explanation of complex climatic situations, it still loses some variance explanatory power, i.e., the principal components cannot fully explain the information contained in all climatic factors. (2) Different lithological conditions can lead to differences in vegetation conditions. Future research could delve into the distribution differences in WUE under different lithological conditions.   5 Conclusions There exists widely karst topography in Southwest China, and the ecosystem is extremely fragile. WUE is an important indicator for understanding the carbon and water cycling processes in karst ecosystem. A long-term time series study on WUE was conducted in the karst and non-karst ecosystems of Southwest China. The main research findings are as follows:(1) Temporally, the WUE during the growing season in Southwest China exhibits a fluctuating upward trend, increasing at 0.005 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 . Specifically, WUE in the karst ecosystem increases at 0.007 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 , while in the non-karst ecosystem, it increases at 0.004 gC mm−1  m−2  year−1 . Spatially, 20.28 % of the karst ecosystem showed a significant increasing trend, while 9.06 % showed a significant decreasing trend. 19.45 % of the non-karst ecosystem showed a significant increasing trend, while 13.31 % showed a significant decreasing trend.  (2) The persistence characteristics of WUE changes in Southwest China are mainly characterized by anti-persistence. The area in karst ecosystem that will transition from rising to falling in the future is the largest, accounting for 48.77 %, with increase persistence of 11.6 %. In non-karst ecosystem, the area that will transition from an increase trend to a decrease trend in the future is the largest, accounting for 40.09 %, with increase persistence accounting for 12.08 %.  (3) Spatially, climatic change dominates WUE in 66.59 % of Southwest China. WUE is predominantly positively correlated with PR, RH, SRAD, Tmax, and VPD, with PR and SRAD having a significant positive impact. WUE is predominantly negatively correlated with Temp, Tmin, VPD, and VS, with VPD and Temp having significant negative impacts.  (4) The response of WUE to climatic factors varies significantly between different ecosystems. The correlation between WUE and RH, Temp, Tmax, and Tmin is completely opposite in the different ecosystems. Additionally, the dominant factor affecting changes in WUE is VAP in the karst ecosystem, while the dominant factor in the non-karst ecosystem is PR. The negative impact of Tmax on the non-karst ecosystem is significantly higher than that on the karst ecosystem. 1 Introduction Groundwater (GW), as the critical natural resource, plays fundamental role in supporting human societies and ecosystems. GW serves as the primary source of drinking water, irrigation and industry. Moreover, it sustains ecosystems by replenishing surface water bodies, supporting aquatic habitats, and maintaining ecological balance. Recognizing the immense importance of GW, it is imperative to understand its characteristics, monitor its quality and quantity, and implement sustainable management strategies to ensure its long-term availability for present and future generations. Evaluating GW quality (GWQ) is essential to ensure the safety and suitability of water for human consumption and to protect ecosystems from potential contamination. In coastal aquifers, the intrusion of seawater into freshwater GW is a significant concern. This saltwater intrusion occurs when the interface between the saline seawater and the freshwater aquifer shifts landward. It is primarily driven by natural processes such as tidal fluctuations, as well as human activities such as excessive GW pumping and coastal development. The intrusion of seawater can have detrimental effects on the quality and availability of freshwater resources in the coastal areas. As seawater infiltrates the freshwater aquifers, it contaminates the previously potable GW, rendering it unsuitable for various uses, including drinking water supply and irrigation. The increased salinity levels can also have adverse impacts on ecosystems and agricultural productivity. Understanding the availability, recharge rates, and extraction rates of GW helps prevent overexploitation and depletion of this valuable resource. Accurate assessments of both GWQ and quantity are effective for managing water resource, ensuring the long-term availability of clean and sufficient water for various uses. The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite presents unique opportunity for accurately measuring spatial variations in GW storage at large basin scale with high precision at monthly resolutions. Utilizing GRACE data allows continuous monitoring of GW storage at regular intervals, surpassing the limitations posed by the scarcity and uneven distribution of piezometers in the study area. The quantification of changes in total water supplies by GRACE data proves crucial in hydrological studies, particularly in investigating drought conditions. Water within large watershed plays pivotal role in the hydrological cycle and exerts significant influence on the local climate system. Previous studies have successfully employed GRACE data to calculate GW anomalies, highlighting the applicability and effectiveness of this dataset (Foroumandi et al., 2023; Sabzehee et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). Like all hydrological process, GW quantity and quality is affected under climate change. The hydrological cycle is strongly influenced by climate change, as any alteration in climate has substantial implication for the hydrological cycle. Furthermore, climate change impacts the accessibility of water by changing water sources (Sivarajan et al., 2019 ). Various methodologies have been used to assess the impact of climate change on GW recharge and its repercussions on GW level (GWL) (e.g., see Nourani et al., 2022a ). To predict subsurface water region, prevalent approach involves utilizing data obtained from general circulation models (GCMs). Multiple studies applied GCMs for climate change impacts assessments in hydrology (e.g., see, Baghanam et al., 2019 ; Nourani et al., 2018 ; Nourani, et al., 2019 ). Due to the complexity of GW modeling, the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based methods both of Shallow learning (Nourani et al., 2018 ) and deep learning (Emmert-Streib et al., 2020; Nourani et al., 2022b ) were successfully applied for GWL modeling via employing different inputs. AI methods have ability to establish non-linear connections between input parameters and targets. These methods do not necessitate any preconceived assumptions about the underlying physical system being modeled. Hence, these statistical techniques are effective in uncovering associations within the data. According to the provided literature review, the majority of previous studies focusing on GWL modeling overlooked the influence of anthropogenic activities and neglected the prediction of future GWL and GWQ conditions. To address this research gap, the current study utilized a combination of remote sensing and GCMs datasets to model and project GWL and GWQ. This approach enabled a more comprehensive analysis, considering the impact of human activities and providing insights into the future states of GWL and GWQ. In this study, the GWL and GWQ in Miandoab aquifer, which play vital role in supporting agricultural activities in the region were modeled and predicted under climate change scenarios. For this purpose, shallow, ensemble and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) AI methods were used for GWL modeling. Based on the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study that used GCM, GRACE, and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) (as representative of anthropogenic activities) for prediction of the GWQ. On the other hand, the abundance of piezometers within the aquifer makes it an arduous task to assess each one individually. To simplify this process, clustering techniques could be employed to group piezometers with similar patterns together, allowing for the selection of a representative piezometer (centroid member) from each cluster. This approach facilitates more efficient and manageable assessment of the piezometers, ensuring that their characteristics and behaviors are adequately captured. Thus, clustering ensemble (Link-Clue) was also used for clustering GW piezometers. This study aimed at following 3 main objectives:i. GWL modeling and projection for future via application of the GCMs, GRACE and NDVI data,  ii. Using clustering ensemble for clustering the piezometers and the aquifer zoning,  iii. Projection of GWQ parameters and the Hydro-chemical Facies Evolution (HFE) diagram for investigation of seawater intrusion into the aquifer.     2 Materials and methods 2.1 Proposed methodology The overall applied methodology in this paper for modeling and prediction of GWL and GWQ is depicted in  Fig. 1 . At the first step, the appropriate GCM is selected based on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). In the second step, for determination of the representative piezometers of the aquifer, all piezometers are clustered via the proposed ensemble clustering method. The bias corrected precipitation and temperature of the GCM, and also, GRACE and NDVI data are considered as inputs of the modeling. These data are then projected for future via the Markov chain method. Then, shallow, ensemble and deep learning methods are applied for GWL modeling and projection for the future under climate change scenarios. At the final step, Fourier equation is used to estimate GWQ for 2050 and 2100 and to plot the HFE diagram.  2.2 2.2 Case study The Miandoab basin, situated in the northwestern part of Iran, is a sub basin of the Urmia Lake (refer to  Fig. 2 a). Urmia Lake is located in the northwestern region of Iran, with its latitude ranging from 37°4′ to 38°17′ and longitude spanning from 45°13′ to 46°. In recent years, the water level of the Urmia Lake has experienced a significant decrease, as well as soil degradation and desertification of its watershed. These environmental crises have been attributed to both climate change and anthropogenic activities, which have played significant roles in exacerbating these issues. According to Javadzadeh et al. (2020) , there exists a reverse relationship between the GWL of the Miandoab aquifer and the water level of the lake. This suggests that as the lake level increases, the GWL in the aquifer tends to decrease. The Miandoab area features diverse geological formation. The climate can be characterized as semi-arid to arid. The yearly average of rainfall in the region ranges from 200 to 500 mm, with the majority occurring during the winter season. The arid climate in the area contributes to high rates of evaporation, intensifying the challenge of water scarcity. The Miandoab basin holds great agricultural importance, with the cultivation of crops such as wheat, barley, and fruits (Es’ haghi et al., 2022 ). Unfortunately, excessive exploitation of GW and inadequate implementation of irrigation techniques have created to challenges in Miandoab. In Fig. 2 b the geological map of study area is presented. The study area encompasses different geological formations described completely by Norouzi and Moghaddam, (2020) .  2.3 Applied data The GRACE data used for investigation of the GWL fluctuation impact; different GCMs applied for climate change impact assessment on GWL, and Landsat data were used as representative of anthropogenic activities in the modeling process (see  Table 1 ). The GRACE mission employs two satellites for calculation of the gravitational properties of the Earth and explore its water storage. GRACE provides valuable data on variations of terrestrial water storage anomaly in monthly scale. GRACE was launched in 2002 and operated until its end of mission in 2017. Following its launch in 2018, GRACE-FO serves as a successor mission aimed at sustaining the important data collection efforts initiated by GRACE. GRACE-FO guarantees the uninterrupted continuity of the dataset, enabling the monitoring of long-term trends and changes over time. The vertical water model is used to extract the GW storage anomalies (GWSA), which is influenced from SWSA (surface water storage anomaly), SMSA (soil moisture storage anomaly), SWEA (snow water equivalent anomaly) based on Eq. 1 :(1) TWSA = GWSA+SWSA+SMSA+SWEA    According to Foroumandi et al. (2023) , surface water storage anomalies are negligible in arid and semiarid regions because the TWSA is significantly controlled by GWSA (Eq. 2 ) and SMSA:(2) GWSA = TWSA - (SMSA+SWEA)    The auxiliary data used to calculate GWSA  for SMSA  and SWEA  in this study were collected from the Famine Early Warning Systems Network Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS) dataset in monthly scale (see Table 1 ). To facilitate the incorporation of climate change effects, GCMs could be employed in GWL and GWQ modeling. GCMs are essential tools used in climate science to simulate and understand the Earth's climate system. The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) represents the latest generation of GCMs developed by the international climate modeling community. CMIP6 aims to provide comprehensive assessment of past, present, and future climate conditions by simulating various components of the Earth system, including the atmosphere, oceans, land surface, and cryosphere. CMIP6 GCMs simulate important climate variables such as temperature, precipitation, winds, and sea ice extent, enabling researchers to study climate change impacts, understand underlying mechanisms, and inform policy and decision-makers. The CMIP6 project facilitates model intercomparison and evaluation, allowing for the assessment of uncertainties and improving our understanding of climate projections, ultimately contributing to more accurate and robust climate predictions. In this paper, the historical and Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP585) data were used for modeling and projection of GWL. The historical dataset in CMIP6 represents the observed or simulated climate conditions from the past. The SSP scenarios are alternative pathways that describe potential socioeconomic developments and their associated greenhouse gas emissions and climate outcomes. SSP585 presents Fossil-fueled Development - Pathway with high population growth, rapid economic growth driven by fossil fuel use, and limited environmental policies. For consideration of anthropogenic activities in the modeling, NDVI was employed in this study. NDVI is employed as a quantitative measure of vegetation greenness, providing valuable insights into vegetation density and facilitating the assessment of changes in the plant health. The calculation of NDVI involves determining the ratio between the values of red and near infrared spectral bands, for Landsat 7 and Landsat 8.  2.4 DTW method The selection of an appropriate GCM (compatible with observed hydro-climatological data of case study) is crucial to achieve accurate and reliable model performance in regional climate studies. The DTW technique is specifically designed to assess the similarity between two sequences of data, such as time-series data. By employing dynamic programming approach, DTW identifies the optimal alignment of two signals. DTW aims to match the patterns exhibited by two signals via identifying the best path through grid mapping, connecting elements of one signal to elements of the other in one-to-many fashion, resulting in minimum distance metric. As a result, DTW provides detailed information regarding differences in signal amplitudes and temporal variations. This method utilizes the Euclidean distance as measure of similarity between the two temporal sequences. Given two time series sequences U = {u 1  , u 2  , …, u n  } and V = {v 1  , v 2  , …, v m  } with lengths n  and m , a n -by-m  matrix, Dbase  = (d base  (u i  ,v j  )) n×m   stores the Euclidean distances between u i  ∈ U ∀ i = 1,2 , … , n    and v  j   ∈ V ∀ j = 1,2 , … , m    as (Belgiu et al., 2020 ):(3) d  base ( i , j )   = u  i   − v  j           The d  i , j     is calculated as:(4) d  i , j   = d  base ( i , j )   + min { d  i − 1 , j   , d  i − 1 , j − 1   ,  d  i , j − 1   }      A warping path, W, is a contiguous set of matrix elements that defines a mapping between U and V. The k th   element of W  is defined as w k   = (i ,j )k  , W =w 1 , w 2 ,…,w k , …, w K . DTW  is as follow:(5) DTW U , V    = min 1  K   ∑ k = 1  K   w  k           max m , n    ≤ K < m + n − 1      the path which minimizes the warping cost (Eq. 5 ) is considered in the modeling process.  2.5 Markov chain In this study to use NDVI and GRACE data, Markov chain was employed for projection of future values. Markov chain has the ability to forecast future time series data and through analyzing the current state of a system and its transition probabilities, Markov chain can make probabilistic predictions about the future states of the system (Stepchenko and Chizhov, 2015 ). The Markov chain assumes sequence of discrete states, allowing for the calculation of transition probabilities between these states. It is random process that undergoes transitions within state space, characterized by the property of "memorylessness". This property implies that the probability distribution of the next state solely depends on the current state and is independent of the past sequence of events. A stochastic process X = {Xn ; n = 0, 1, …} with discrete state space S  is considered first-order discrete-time Markov chain if the following condition holds for every j ∈ S  and n = 0, 1, …, N :(6) Pr { X  n + 1   = j X  0   = i  0   , … , X  n   = i  n   } = Pr { X  n + 1   = j X  n   = i  n   }            For any given set of states i0 ,…,in  within the state space, the values of X i   are derived from a finite or countable set S  known as the chain's state space. Moreover, Markov chain is said to possess stationary transition probabilities if:(7) Pr { X  1   = j X  0   = i } = Pr { X  n + 1   = j X  n   = i  n   }            In stationary probability scenario, the process can be fully described by the initial conditions, specifically the one-step transition probabilities. To represent these probabilities, square matrix is utilized and typically denoted by P  as follow:(8) P = P ( 1 , 1 )  P ( 1 , 2 )  …  P ( 1 , r )   P ( 2 , 1 )  P ( 2 , 2 )  …  P ( 2 , r )   .  .  .  .   .  .  .  .   .  .  .  .   P ( r , 1 )  P ( r , 2 )  …  P ( r , r )           Where(9) P i , j    = Pr { X  1   = j X  0   = i }         The number of states, denoted as r , determines the dimensions of matrix P . As P  represents probabilities, it is always nonnegative, and the sum of the elements in each row is equal to one. A matrix that satisfies these conditions, where all entries are nonnegative and the row sums are equal to one, is referred to as Markov matrix.  2.6 Clustering Due to the presence of numerous piezometers in the aquifer, considering all piezometers into the modeling process can be exhausting work. To address data redundancy, clustering techniques can be employed to identify a representative piezometer for each region. This study utilized well-known clustering methods, including K-means (Boongoen and Iam-On, 2018 ), Self-Organizing Map (SOM) (Kohonen, 1984 ), Fuzzy c-means (FCM) (Bezdek et al., 1984 ), and hierarchical clustering (Murtagh and Contreras, 2012 ). These methods were combined using the LinkCluE clustering approach. Sharghi et al. (2022)  highlighted that employing an ensemble clustering could lead to precise outcomes compared to using a single clustering method. Although the mentioned classic clustering methods can be reasonably effective, they may demonstrate varying performance levels when applied to the identical data. Consequently, ensembling could improve the overall performance of clustering. Proposed ensemble method introduced by Iam-on and Garrett (2010)  was utilized in this study. The initial stage of the cluster ensemble involves creating a cluster ensemble. П = π  1   , … ,  π  M         , which is a collection of M base clustering results. The output E produced from this function is an N ×   M matrix of cluster labels for N data points from M base clusters. The objective of this method is to enhance the effectiveness of the traditional pairwise similarity approach by incorporating link-based similarity metrics. By doing so, it aims to improve the evaluation of similarity measures between various data points. The LinkCluE method provides three functions for creating such similarity matrix: the connected-triple-based similarity (CTS), the SimRank-based similarity (SRS) and the approximate SimRank-based similarity (ASRS). Their main input argument is a matrix of cluster ensemble E. A similarity matrix S, acquired as the output of CTS, SRS or ASRS, is used together with any similarity-based clustering algorithm to generate the final result. The computation of the CTS involves (Iam-on and Garrett, 2010 ):(10) CTS x  i   , x  j      = 1  M   ∑ m = 1  M   S  m   x  i   , x  j           where S  m   x  i   , x  j         is the similarity between data points x  i   ,  x  j    ∈ X   .
