FFNN, ANFIS, SVR as shallow learning methods and their ensemble were applied in the modeling. The performance of each shallow learning model can vary across different conditions and case studies. In this study, the individual performance of each shallow learning model was examined. Additionally, an ensemble model was employed to enhance overall performance. FFNN is a widely used and accessible AI modeling tool, while ANFIS is capable of managing uncertainty, and SVR helps mitigate the probability of overtraining. FFNN has gained popularity due to its capability to address problems that are not linearly separable. In practical applications, a three-layer FFNN is often sufficient. The first layer represents the input variables, the second layer serves as the hidden layer, and the third layer functions as the output layer. Connections between layers are established through weights, and each unit calculates the sum of its inputs, incorporating a bias or threshold term, followed by a non-linear activation function that transforms the sum into an output (Bebis and Georgiopoulos, 1994 ). ANFIS, initially introduced by Jang (1993) , is a hybrid model that combines elements of fuzzy logic and artificial neural networks. This model employs a feed-forward network architecture in which the nodes in different layers handle fuzzy parameters, similar to distributed parameter fuzzy inference systems. ANFIS-based modeling commences by initializing a model using a dataset comprised of input-output pairs. The ANFIS system utilizes the entered membership function and input-output data to optimize membership functions through hybrid and backpropagation algorithms. Once the ANFIS system generates a model, it undergoes validation against predefined criteria. SVR is an enhanced version of Support Vector Machines specifically designed for regression tasks (Cheng and Shiu, 2014 ). Unlike traditional regression algorithms that aim to minimize error rates, SVR focuses on fitting the errors within a defined threshold. SVR can be employed with both linear and nonlinear regression models. It introduces a region known as a "tube" around the function being optimized, aiming to identify the tube that provides the best approximation of the continuous-valued function while minimizing prediction errors. SVR utilizes an ε-insensitive loss function that penalizes predictions that deviate beyond a certain ε threshold from the desired output. In addition to shallow learning methods, recently deep learning models gained attention in modeling hydrological process, but higher number of parameters in their structure is their disadvantages. GRU is one of the deep learning methods, that used in this study. GRU is a type of recurrent neural network. GRU is developed to address challenges such as long-term memory and gradients in backpropagation (Fu et al., 2022 ). The memory block of GRU is the key feature, which consists of two gates (reset gate and update gate) and a memory cell. The cell state, represented by a horizontal line on top of the block, acts like a conveyor belt that controls the transfer of information to the next moment through the following formulas (Fu et al., 2022 ):(14) r  t   = σ ( W  r   . h  t − 1   , X  t      )      (15) z  t   = σ ( W  z   . h  t − 1   , X  t      )      (16) h  t   =  = σ ( W  z   . h  t − 1   , X  t      )      Where σ   is the sigmoid function. W  r   ,  W  z      are weight matrices. z  t     is the update gate at time step t, which determines how much of the new candidate activation should be incorporated into the hidden state. X  t     is the input at time step t, r  t     is the reset gate at time step t, which determines how much of the previous hidden state should be forgotten. GRU includes reset and update gates in its architecture. These gates take the current time step input x and the previous time step's hidden state h  t − 1     as inputs, and their output is calculated by a fully connected layer with a sigmoid activation function. By using the sigmoid function, the values of the elements in the reset gate and update gate are constrained between 0 and 1. As a result, each element in the reset gate and update gate has a value within the range of [0,1]. The GRU model calculates candidate hidden states to assist with later hidden state calculations. Specifically, the candidate hidden state h  ̃   t     at time step t  and hyperbolic tangent function (tanh )    is computed as:(17) h  ̃   t   = tanh ( W  h  ̃    . r  t   . h  t − 1   , X  t      )       The reset gate determines how the hidden state from the previous time step is incorporated into the candidate hidden state of the current time step. The hidden state at the last time step may contain all the historical information of the time series up to that point. W  h  ̃     , and W  O     are weight matrices. Thus, the reset gate can be used to discard irrelevant historical information. The hidden state h  t     at time step t is expressed as (Fu et al., 2022 ):(18) h  t   = 1 −  z  t      . h  t − 1   +  z  t   . h  ̃   t       (19) y  t   = σ ( W  O   . h  t      )     where h  ̃   t    is the candidate activation at time step t  , which is a combination of the previous hidden state and the new input. The final output is y  t    , which is the result of the σ   activation on the hidden layer states h  t    . GRU networks have a simpler architecture compared to Long short-term memory (LSTM). They also have memory cells, but each cell contains only two gates: reset gate and update gate. Due to its simpler architecture with fewer gates and parameters, GRU is generally computationally more efficient compared to LSTM. GRU networks can be quicker to train and require fewer computational resources, making them suitable in scenarios with limited computational power. Given the well-established effectiveness of modeling ensembles in previous studies, an opportunity arises to enhance the regionalization process by applying ensemble learning to shallow networks, enabling a parallel learning approach. By combining the outputs of single models, along with an ensemble kernel (any AI model can be used as kernel), it will be feasible to develop a precise and adaptable model that demands less data. In this regard, the outputs of the single models are utilized as inputs for a new network, depicted in  Fig. 3 , with the GWL as the target variable. Since deep learning has many parameters, it was not considered in ensemble learning. Ensemble works as parallel processing, with lower parameters, because at first the models are calibrated and then are used in the ensemble technique, but deep learning models have numerous parameters must be trained by larger size of data set.  2.8 Detrended quantile mapping Detrended quantile mapping is a statistical technique used in climate and hydrological modeling to correct the biases of the variables, such as temperature or precipitation (Cannon et al., 2015 ). It is particularly useful when comparing and reconciling climate model outputs with historical or observed data. The main goal of detrended quantile mapping is to adjust the shape and spread of the distribution of the modeled variable to match that of the observed or reference data, while preserving any existing trend in the data. It is an extension of the traditional quantile mapping method, which is commonly used for bias correction. Quantile mapping equates cumulative distribution functions F  o , h     and F  m , h    , respectively, observed data x  o , h    , denoted by the subscript o , and modeled data x  m , h    , denoted by the subscript m , in a historical period, denoted by the subscript h  as follow:(20) x  ˆ   m , p   t    = F  o , h  − 1   F  m , h   x  ̅   m , h   x  m , p   ( t )  x  ̅   m , p   ( t )         x  ̅   m , p   ( t )  x  ̅   m , h         Where x  ̅   m , h      and x  ̅   m , p   ( t )   , respectively, involve estimations of the long-term output average, based on historical data projections in the future period p   for time t.   2.9 Hydro-chemical facies evolution (HFE) diagram The HFE diagram serves as an effective tool in GWQ assessment, as it provides visual representation of the complex relationships between different hydro-chemical parameters. It aids in identifying potential water quality factors, such as salinization, pollution, or changes in GW recharge patterns. By tracking HFE, scientists and water resource managers can make informed decisions regarding GW management, protection, and remediation strategies. Gimenez Forcada (2010) proposed HFE as convenient method for assessing the status of coastal aquifer in terms of intrusion or freshening phases occurring over time. These phases can be identified by analyzing the distribution of anion and cation percentages in the square diagram ( Fig. 4 ). The HFE diagram focuses on the major cations (Ca2+  and Na+ ) and anions (HCO3 - , SO4 2- , and Cl- ) percentages, which are the key factors determining the dynamics of saline/saltwater intrusion. During the intrusion stage, two almost simultaneous processes affect the aquifer. Firstly, there is an increase in salinity (line I), leading to reverse exchange reactions (line II). This results in the characteristic Ca-Cl facies. Subsequently, the composition of GW evolves (line III) towards saline/saltwater facies (Na-Cl). In the freshening process, the introduction of freshwater recharge induces direct exchange reactions (lines I’  and II’ ), leading to the formation of a Na-HCO3 -  facies. Finally, the water evolves along line III’  towards the composition of freshwater, allowing for the recovery of the aquifer. The diagram consists of three sections: (A) Mixing between end members, specifically freshwater and seawater; (B) HFE evolution during the intrusion period; and (C) HFE evolution during the freshening period. There are also labels (I) and (I′) representing the initial process of mixing in the intrusion and freshening stages, (II) and (II') representing reverse and direct base exchange reactions, and (III) and (III') representing mixing during the later stages until reaching equilibrium with the dominant flow's chemical facies.  2.10 Modeling evaluation metrics The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) were applied in this study as modeling evaluation metrics. Hybrid Validity Index (HVI) was considered for assessment of the clustering performance. NSE metric is applied to assess the performance of models and it is between− ∞    to 1. It quantifies the agreement between observed and modeled values, with values closer to 1 indicating a better fit and values below 0 indicating poor model performance (Nourani et al., 2019 ):(21) NSE = 1 − ∑ i = 1  N   ( R  i   − Z  i   )  2     ∑ i = 1  N   ( R  i   − R )  ̅   2          where R  i    , Z  i     and R  ̅    are the actual values, modeled values and mean of the observed values, respectively. N  is the number of the observations. RMSE measures the standard deviation of the residuals, which are the prediction errors, serves as an indicator of the dispersion. RMSE  is calculated as follow:(22) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  N   ( R  i   − Z  i   )  2     N          Choosing the most appropriate clustering method can be challenging because of presence of numerous cluster assessment criteria that utilize diverse methodologies to evaluate the model efficiency. To streamline the investigation, this study utilized the HVI. The HVI is based on combination of multiple clustering assessment criteria, providing a comprehensive and efficient assessment of clustering performance (Sharghi et al., 2022 ) as:(23) HVI = 0.5 CH + 0.5 SI  DB       Where CH, SI and DB are respectively Calinski-Harabasz (Caliński and Harabasz, 1974 ), Silhouette Index (Rousseeuw, 1987 ) and Davies- Bouldin (Davies and Bouldin, 1979 ) metrics. Superior clustering performance is indicated by greater CH and SI, as well as lower DB metric. Consequently, the overall clustering performance can be quantitatively assessed by evaluating the HVI, where a higher HVI value signifies better clustering performance.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Results of clustering Given the existence of multiple piezometers within study aquifer, including all in the modeling process can be a challenging endeavor. To overcome data redundancy, clustering was employed to identify representative piezometers. In this study, among 153 GWL piezometers, the data from 50 piezometers that cover longer time period were considered. For clustering purposes at first, single clustering methods were employed independently then ensemble of clusters was used for final clusters identification. In the k-means and FCM methods, respectively five and three clusters were considered by examination of different values. In the FCM method, the iterations were set up to 100, and a minimum improvement of 1e−5  in the objective function between consecutive iterations was considered. For the SOM method, a 2 × 2 grid was used to define the dimensions. In hierarchical clustering, the weighted linkage method was chosen to calculate the distance between clusters, and the Euclidean distance metric was employed to measure the dissimilarity between data points. The final number of clusters obtained by k-means, hierarchical, SOM, and FCM methods were 5, 3, 5, and 3, respectively. Consequently, a total of 17 piezometers, representing multiple clusters, were considered by removing duplicate piezometers and excluding clustering methods with subpar performance. These representative piezometers were utilized as inputs for the proposed approach. The output of ensemble resulted in three clusters, with 1, 8, and 6 piezometers assigned to clusters 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Cluster 2 housed the majority of the piezometers, indicating a higher concentration in that particular cluster. The evaluation of clustering methods was conducted using predefined metrics, and the corresponding results are summarized in  Table 2 . According to the evaluation metrics presented in Table 2 , the ensemble method LinkCluE exhibited superior performance compared to the individual techniques. The LinkCluE approach takes into account the collective merits of multiple clustering methods, concurrently. The LinkCluE approach effectively mitigates the influence of biases and errors inherent in individual models, resulting in a more comprehensive and accurate representation of cluster structures. The location of three clusters is depicted in  Fig. 5 . The piezometers in clusters 1, 2 and 3 are located in Southern, North and East parts of the Miandoab aquifer, respectively. Cluster 1 located utmost distance from the Urmia Lake (see Fig. 2 ) and also in higher elevation compared to the piezometers in clusters 2 and 3. The piezometers in cluster 2 are in the proximity of the coastline and in lower elevation of the aquifer. The majority of the piezometers in cluster 3 located at the east part of the aquifer.  3.2 Results of the GCM selection In order to assess the impact of climate change on GWL and GWQ, GCMs were considered as input of the modeling. From multiple GCMs, in order to select the appropriate GCM, DWT was applied in the modeling. Since precipitation is the most influential parameter in GW modeling, the DTW values were calculated for precipitation data from different GCMs (precipitation of the nearest grid point to the case study was used in analysis) and the observed time series of precipitation in the case study and the results are tabulated in  Table 3 . The GCM with lower DTW distance from the observed precipitation was selected for further analysis and applied in the modeling process. In this way, the DWT was lowest for KACE-1, so its data were used for the subsequent modeling process across all clusters. The parameters of GCM from the nearest grid point to the case study were considered as inputs of the models (see  Fig. 6 , grid point 1). Since GCMs are subject to uncertainties and potential sources of error due to various factors like the inherent complexity of the Earth's climate system, computational constraints, thus the bias correction of GCMs is essential before to be used in the modeling. In this study, detrended quantile mapping was used for bias correction (Cannon et al., 2015 ). Then bias corrected precipitation and temperature were then used for GWL modeling.  3.3 Results of modeling via AI models The importance of input selection in AI models cannot be overstated, as it directly impacts the performance, efficiency, and interpretability of the modeling. The correct selection of relevant and representative input features is crucial for capturing the essential patterns and relationships in the data, reducing noise and irrelevant information, and improving the model's ability to be generalized to the unseen data. The precipitation and temperature affect the evapotranspiration; thus, they have significant impact on GW and multiple studies have used these parameters as inputs for GWL modeling (e.g. see, Foroumandi et al., 2023 ). Therefore, these two parameters from KACE-1 were used in input layer of AI models after bias correction. GRACE and GRACE-FO data as the representative of the GW storage anomaly and GWL with 1-month lag time were the other inputs. Incorporating a one-month lag time in the modeling of GWL has demonstrated the potential to enhance modeling accuracy. Moreover, the time series of GWL with a one-month lag exhibits a higher correlation with the primary GWL time series. This approach has been previously employed in studies such as Javadinejad et al. (2020) , where a one-month lag was considered in GWL modeling. Furthermore, Tao et al. (2022)  emphasized that fluctuations in GWL serve as a direct indicator of the impact of GW development and provide valuable insights into aquifer dynamics within GWL time-series data. Consequently, there is a high possibility to accurately forecast future GWL from its previous data. Moreover, NDVI inputted to the model as the representative of the anthropogenic activities. During the modeling process, 70 % of the data were assigned for training purposes, while the remaining 30 % were allocated for the verification. The optimal epoch number was determined through iterative examination. The applied data were from 2002 to 2012 for the modeling as the KACE-1 GCM was available up to 2012 and for the recent years (as the observed values were available) the model was reconfirmed. The Levenberg–Marquardt and Tansig were considered as learning algorithm and active function, respectively (Nourani et al., 2019 ). The kernel function of the SVR was radial basis. The layer and unit number in the GRU method set as one. This adjustment was found to be effective in optimizing the model's performance. Deep learning is generally more suitable for time series data with longer lengths, and minimum layers and units may enhance the efficiency when dealing with shorter datasets. The sigmoid function was determined to be the most suitable activation function in training GRU. The mean squared error was employed as the loss function, and the Adam optimizer algorithm was utilized as the learning algorithm. Fine-tuning of the hyperparameters within the GRU model was performed to determine the optimum parameters. Parameters such as the number of GRU layers, the number of hidden units in each layer, the learning rate, batch size, dropout rate, and number of epochs, as well as the window size, were investigated, with values ranging up to 5, 10, 5, 5, 5, 1000, and 4, respectively. The outcomes of the applied methods and the ensemble approach are presented in  Table 4 . Investigation of the results shows that for among shallow learning models, in all cases, the performance of ANFIS was more accurate (up to 6 %) than the performance of the FFNN. ANFIS demonstrating its superior performance compared to FFNN due to its more versatile and adaptable structure, which considers the strengths of neural networks and fuzzy logic. ANFIS flexible structure allows to adapt its architecture and parameters to accommodate a broader range of problems by leveraging the input data.  Fig. 7  illustrates the output of the individual models. The analysis of Fig. 7  reveals that ANFIS displayed superior performance in certain instances, while SVR exhibited better results in others. This observation underscores the importance of employing ensemble learning techniques, as they enable the final model to leverage the strengths of all three individual models. Consequently, an ensemble of models was incorporated into the modeling process to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of the shallow learning models. The parallel processing approach was used to ensemble the results of the applied individual models and the outputs of the individual models were regarded as inputs for modeling of ensemble model. For training the ensemble method, ANFIS was utilized as the kernel due to its satisfactory performance compared to other individual methods. It should be noted that, alternative models can be employed as the kernel for the ensemble. The findings demonstrated that the ensemble of models could significantly enhance the efficiency of individual models by up to 35 %. The collective power of an ensemble lies in its ability to capture a wide range of distinctive data characteristics that may not be able to effectively detected by the individual models. Also, overfitting can be mitigated through ensembling, resulting in improved performance. Furthermore, ensembling contributes to the enhanced generality of the model by leveraging the advantages of multiple individual models. Every individual model within the ensemble possesses the capability to detect distinctive patterns, and when combined, patterns are integrated effectively to enhance the final outcome. In  Fig. 8 , the Taylor diagram of the applied methods is depicted. As shown in Fig. 8 , the ensemble of shallow learning models is closer to the coordinate origin, which shows better performance. Moreover, evaluation of the modeling performance indicated that the ensemble learning outperformed deep learning up to 41 % based on the NSE metric. The modeling conducted in this study was on a monthly scale, and given that the historical data from GCM are only available up to 2012, the time series were relatively short. Consequently, deep learning methods did not exhibit optimal performance as they typically require extensive data to effectively calibrate their numerous parameters. On the other hand, ensemble, which is a parallel learning process and it is independent of large dataset, models individually and the obtained results are more accurate.  3.4 Projection of GWL and quality for future Once the model (ensemble of shallow learning) and GCM (KACE-1) with optimal performance were identified, they were utilized to forecast the future state of GWL and GWQ. To validate the constructed model, it was applied to simulate the states for 2020 and consequently, and compare to the presently accessible observed values of 2020. To forecast the future state, bias corrected precipitation and temperature parameters of the GCM’s SSP585 that represent high-emissions scenario were used to project GWL for 2050 and 2100. To find out the NDVI and GRACE data values for 2050 and 2100, the Markov chain method was used and its results imposed as inputs of the projection model. The predicted monthly values of NDVI and GRACE data for future via the Markov chain are shown in  Fig. 9 . The time series of the GWL for the average of the modeling period (2000–2012), and predicted values of the GWL for 2020, 2050 and 2100 are depicted in  Fig. 10 . For revalidation of the constructed model, the model was performed for 2020 and the results was compared with the observed values in 2020, which are available now (see, Fig. 10 ). According to Fig. 10 , for central piezometers of clusters 1, 2 and 3, the GWL may decrease down to 11.74 m, 11.64 m and 1.53 in 2050 and 8.23 m., 8.59 m and 1.19 m in 2100, respectively; however, there may be an increase in GWL for cluster 1 in wet seasons. The value of the precipitation and temperature for average of historical period (2000–2012), 2050 and 2100 are presented in  Fig. 11 . It is worthy to mention that projected values are based on high-emissions scenario, moreover the GCMs data consist of uncertainty and in this study only bias correction was applied and downscaling was not used for the GCMs data. Furthermore, the scenarios used for future projections involve inherent uncertainty. The applied scenarios rely on extreme and pessimistic assumptions, which means that the resulting future temperature and precipitation values may appear to be exaggerated. Changes in temperature and precipitation patterns can have impact on GWL. Higher temperature and lower precipitation can lead to increased evaporation rates, which can cause decrease in the GWL. When temperatures rise, evaporation rates increase, resulting in greater water loss from the aquifer. Additionally, reduced precipitation means less recharge to the aquifer, further contributing to decline in GWL. The results showed decreasing and increasing trends for precipitation and temperature, respectively. Moreover, Nourani et al. (2019)  conducted downscaling of precipitation and temperature data for the years 2050 and 2100, leading to the conclusion that there will be a decreasing trend in precipitation and an increasing trend in temperature in the future for the area. Dehghanipour et al. (2019)  expressed that GW head in the Miandoab aquifer has dropped over time due to a reduction of precipitation as well as an increase of GW withdrawal for agricultural purposes. The positioning of the piezometers within cluster 1 indicates a considerable distance from Urmia Lake. The Urmia Lake (refer to Fig. 2 ) has a mitigated impact on the piezometers within its vicinity, resulting in lower variation in response to the lake level fluctuations. Additionally, cluster 1 is situated in the higher altitude lands compared to the remaining clusters, which can influence the wells within cluster 1 to exhibit increase in GWL. Furthermore, in elevated regions, agricultural activities and the presence of wells are usually limited. Cluster 1 consisted of only two piezometers, whereas most of the wells were distributed across clusters 2 and 3, which exhibited a declining GWL. This observation leads to the conclusion that the study aquifer is experiencing a significant concern regarding the decline of GWL. In addition, Javadzadeh et al. (2020)  mentioned that the water level in the observation wells close to the lake, especially in the eastern and southern coasts of the lake (e.g. Miandoab aquifer) experience lower GWL than the ecological water level. The aquifer type throughout the entire region is consistent, being unconfined. Therefore, it seems that the variation in GWL was not influenced by the aquifer type. In order to investigate GWQ, HFE diagram was plotted for the average parameters during the modeling period (2000–2012) as well as for predicted parameters for future (2050 and 2100). GWQ parameters were predicted by establishing correlation between GWL and GWQ parameters. Correlation analysis was used here instead of modeling via the AI models because GWQ data were reported only twice a year, therefore the length of GWQ time series were too short to be modeled via the AI models. The GWL time series were in monthly scale while GWQ time series were 6 monthly data, so the GWL time series were adjusted to match the 6-month interval. To establish the GWL-GWQ relationship using historical data, Curve fit toolbox was used for the modeling and among multiple equations of the Curve fit toolbox, the Fourier model outperformed the other equations. The GWQ modeling parameters was calibrated and verified via Fourier model. The better performance of the Fourier equation could be due to its sin and cos kernel functions, proves to be more effective in modeling hydrologic processes exhibiting seasonality. Subsequently, the predicted GWL values were used to estimate GWQ parameters. Additionally, to consider the Urmia Lake water quality parameters, based on assumption that the current condition of the lake would be stable, linear regression was employed to project the data related to the quality parameters of the Lake for 2050 and 2100. The HFE diagrams for average of the modeling period (2000–2012), 2050 and 2100 are presented in  Fig. 12  and the facies are tabulated in  Table 5 . Based on Fig. 12 , the cluster 1 for average of the historical data (2000–2012) in both wet and dry seasons has refreshing facies (located in part 10 in Fig. 12 ). This may be due to the far distance of the cluster 1 from the shoreline. The extent of saltwater intrusion is directly correlated with the perpendicular distance from the coast. It is evident that the maximum level of saltwater intrusion occurs when the aquifer is in close proximity to the shore and favorable hydrogeological conditions exist for transmission. However, the hydraulic conductivity is high in this part of the case study, but its more distance and higher GWL prevent seawater intrusion. The hydraulic conductivity of the aquifer plays critical role in determining the vulnerability of GW to seawater intrusion, as it governs the ease with which saltwater can infiltrate and contaminate the freshwater aquifer. As tabulated in Table 5 , in wet seasons there is Mixed Ca–Cl water type, which is compatible with study of Amiri et al. (2016)  expressing that in wet period most of the samples show water type of Mixed Ca–Mg–Cl. The hydraulic conductivity map of the case study is presented in  Fig. 13 . The extent of the saline waterfront's spread under constant hydraulic pressure is directly associated with the hydraulic conductivity of the GW system. Due to the aquifer's high hydraulic conductivity, the cone of depression during pumping expands, leading to an increased likelihood of saltwater up-coning. The representative point of cluster 2 with Mg-Cl facies indicates simple binary mixing with little or no intervention of base exchange reactions. However, it is near the coastline and the lower hydraulic conductivity of this part decreases the seawater intrusion effect. The representative point of cluster 3 placed in the right and beneath line A and below the horizontal line at 33.3 %, which is initial process of mixing in intrusion. During the phase of seawater intrusion, there is an initial increase in salinity and rapid and marked reverse exchange of Na+ \Ca2+ , which is recognized by the characteristic Ca-Cl facies. This might be due to the high hydraulic conductivity of the area of cluster 3 (see, Fig. 13 ). GWL below sea level holds significant importance as it increases the vulnerability to seawater intrusion. The GWL plays critical role in maintaining hydraulic pressure along the coast, which helps prevent the intrusion of saltwater. Water level in representative well of cluster 2 is the highest and for cluster 3 it is the lowest. As the freshwater level decreases, the intrusion of the saltwater front extends further into the aquifer, thereby increases the risk of aquifer vulnerability. The likelihood of saltwater intrusion is low in an aquifer where the freshwater level is significantly higher than sea level. In the HFE diagram of 2050 for dry season, representative well of cluster 1 became near the mixing line (part 12 in Fig. 12 ); this might be due to the decline of GWL in which discharge is minimal in dry season in both 2050 and 2100 as presented in Fig. 10 . The position of representative well of cluster 1 doesn’t change in wet season and the Fig. 10  shows increase in GWL for wet season. For representative points of clusters 2 and 3, both points moved to right and left parts of the mixing line, which indicates the intrusion in both dry and wet seasons. Moreover, the GWL in these two clusters in both 2050 and 2100 shows decreasing trend. Therefore, it could be concluded from the obtained results that there is a chance to the saltwater intrusion into the aquifer under the influence of climate change and anthropogenic activities. The obtained results in this study are compatible with the results of Jeihouni et al. (2018)  which stressed that high drop rate in the water table leads to reduction of freshwater pressure in the transition zone, and accordingly the saltwater penetrates into the surrounding plains aquifers in the Urmia Lake area. Regarding the obtained results of this study, the GW table has a downward trend at surrounding aquifers of the Urmia Lake. However, the water level of Urmia Lake has a descending trend during the study period, but the downward trend of water table is more expressed than the one for the water level of the Lake. This pressure change caused saltwater intrusion from saltwater aquifers beneath the lake to surrounding plains freshwater aquifers. The importance of the results of this research is about prediction of the GWL and GWQ for future under consideration of the climate change impacts and scenarios and also anthropogenic activities. The findings of this study provide valuable information and insights to policymakers and decision-makers, enabling them to effectively manage GW resources and regulate their utilization. By considering intrusion probabilities in the aquifer, appropriate measures can be implemented to control and safeguard GW resources.   4 Conclusions In this study, GWL and GWQ were modeled and predicted for future under climate change effects. For this purpose, the shallow learning methods and their ensemble, and deep learning model of GRU were applied. Among different GCMs DTW method selected KACE-1 as the most appropriate GCM for GWL modeling. Clustering ensemble method of Link-Clue was used for clustering the piezometers of the case study leading to three clusters. The precipitation, temperature of KACE-1 GCM, NDVI, GRACE data and GWL with a lag were used as inputs of modeling GWL and GWQ for representative (centroid) piezometers of the clusters (one for each cluster). Evaluation of the modeling performance indicated that ensemble learning outperformed the deep learning up to 35 % based on the NSE metric. In addition, it was concluded that the ensemble model improved the performance of individual models up to 23 % in this study. For future projection, NDVI and GRACE data were predicted for 2050 and 2100 via the Markov chain. Projection of the GWL under the SSP585 showed that in 2050 and 2100, there will be decline in GWL down to 20.2 m, especially for the piezometers of clusters 2 and 3. The trained model was used for prediction of GWL for future. Then the Fourier model was used to make relationship between the GWL and GWQ and HFE diagram was plotted for quality parameters in 2050 and 2100. Results indicated that in 2050 and 2100, GW may have intrusion facies especially near the shoreline. Comparison of the obtained results of this study with the results of other researchers showed that there was agreement about the saltwater intrusion in the regions near the Urmia Lake and also GWL decreasing trend in Miandoab aquifer due to reduction of precipitation and anthropogenic activities. In addition, in wet seasons there is Mixed Ca–Cl water type which is compatible with previous studies. As suggestion for future studies, for improvement of the modeling performance under climate change, future studies can fill the gap in GCMs data. Currently, GCMs provide data only until 2012, resulting in 10-year gap in historical data and the training process. In addition, the uncertainty associated with the modeling of GWQ and GWL can be quantified via different methods of uncertainty quantification. Future studies can investigate the factors influencing GWQ, such as land use practices, industrial activities, and agricultural inputs, and develop models to predict changes in GWQ under different scenarios.
1 Introduction The derivation from the linear Darcy's law is defined as non-Darcy flow. The high-speed non-Darcy flow through porous media is of great essence for unconventional oil and gas reservoir development, nuclear waste treatment, water resources management, environmental protection, carbon dioxide geological sequestration etc. (Barree and Conway, 2004 ; Sharma et al., 2017 ; Shin, 2022 ). In addition to high-velocity non-Darcy flow, the nonlinear relationship between volumetric flow rate and pressure gradient is also observed in low-velocity fluid flows (Xiong et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2022 ). As the flow rate increases, the pressure gradient indicates a non-linear relationship with the seepage velocity (Li and Engler, May 2001 ; Huang and Ayoub, 2008 ). To account for the inertial losses in the high-speed non-Darcy flow, the Forchheimer equation established by experiment test is one of the most widely used equation to quantitatively characterize the pressure gradient along the flow direction (Forchheimer, 1901 ).(1) ∇ P = μ K F   u s  + α ρ u s 2       The Forchheimer permeability (KF  ) is close to but not equal to Darcy permeability (KD  ). The non-Darcy coefficient (Forchheimer coefficient) α  is generally determined by laboratory experiments and multi-rate well tests. However, there are currently no accurate theoretical expression available to predict the non-Darcy flow coefficient. The available theoretical models and empirical formulas for the non-Darcy coefficient are summarized in Table 1  . The capillary model has been commonly applied to describe the high-speed fluid flow through porous media and determine the theoretical formulas for the non-Darcy coefficient. Ergun and Orning (1949)  assumed that a porous medium is made up of a bundle of parallel and straight capillaries with uniform size, and proposed the parallel capillary model to develop a theoretical formula for the non-Darcy coefficient. While Scheidegger (1974)  put forward a serial capillary model to get another theoretical non-Darcy coefficient, where all the pores with different pore size are serially lined up and the capillary tortuosity was taken into account. Huang et al. (2020)  employed the fractal capillary model to characterize the flow path through a porous medium, and they proposed an explicit function for the non-Darcy coefficient. These theoretical formulas demonstrated that the non-Darcy coefficient is inversely proportional to the permeability and porosity of the porous media, which are only validate for isotropic porous media with simple idealized microstructures. Therefore, various empirical formulas were proposed by fitting experimental and numerical results to predict the non-Darcy coefficient for various types of porous media. Pascal et al. (1980) , Jones (1987)  and Friedel and Voigt (2006)  used the data from low-permeability hydraulically fractured well, sandstone, limestone, tight-gas reservoir and fracture proppant pack, to obtain an empirical model for the non-Darcy coefficient. They took the non-Darcy coefficient as a power function of permeability, where the exponent varies from 1.11 to 1.55. It is widely accepted that the non-Darcy coefficient is a power function of permeability and porosity. The exponent value of permeability and porosity are in range of [0.5,1.8] and [0.48,6.67], respectively. In order to determine the empirical equation for the non-Darcy coefficient, Ergun (1952)  carried out 640 sets of gas flow (carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane, and hydrogen) through filled spheres, sand and coke powder. Janicek and Katz (1955)  correlated the data from sandstone, limestone and dolomite. Geertsma (1974)  analyzed the data obtained from unconsolidated sandstones, consolidated sandstones, limestones, and dolomites. Li et al. (2001 , 2002 ) performed experiment on single-phase nitrogen gas in a heterogeneous Berea sandstone wafer, and combined analysis of results from analytical and numerical methods to get a general correlation of non-Darcy coefficient. Khaniaminjan and Goudarzi (Khaniaminjan and Goudarzi, 2008 ) performed experiments on unconsolidated porous media made of sand packing of different grain size with liquids. Yao et al. (2015)  conducted high-velocity non-Darcy seepage experimental studies on artificial sand-packed models. Shi et al. (2020)  used a self-designed apparatus to study the non-Darcy flow through granular limestone with a wide range of porosity, the particle size of which ranges from 0.075 to 4.75 mm. Furthermore, a few researchers introduced the tortuosity into the empirical correlations for the non-Darcy coefficient. By considering the effect of tortuosity, Liu et al. (1995)  got a better regression fit correlation of non-Darcy coefficient using a wide variety of data from consolidated and unconsolidated porous formations. Thauvin and Mohanty (1998)  proposed a pore-level network model to obtain a non-Darcy coefficient correlation. Veyskarami et al. (2016)  solved one-dimensional steady state Navier-Stokes equation for single-phase incompressible fluid in a representative model of porous media made up of converging/diverging capillaries with various curvature, to evaluate non-Darcy coefficient as a function of morphological parameters of the porous medium. Wang et al. (1999)  studied non-Darcy flow through anisotropic porous media by using pore-scale network models. Elsanoose et al. (2022)  performed experiments on water flow through seven large artificial sand samples to study non-Darcy flow and non-Darcy coefficient. The empirical equation for the non-Darcy coefficient is a power function of permeability and porosity as well as tortuosity, the exponent value of which are in range of [0.5,1.2404] and [0,4.4] as well as [0.6,3.35], respectively. While, the particle and fracture size are generally included in the non-Darcy coefficient for granular and fractured material, respectively. Sidiropoulou et al. (2007)  proposed the non-Darcy coefficient is function of porosity and particle size. Kundu et al. (2016)  investigated the incompressible single-phase fluid flow through homogeneous and mixed isotropic porous glass bed. However, the constant in their non-Darcy coefficient depends on the particle size, which decrease from 1.199 to 0.58 when the particle size increases from 2.5 mm to 5.0 mm. By using laboratory test and finite element method, Sedghi-Asl et al. (2014)  and Zhang et al. (2022)  argued that the non-Darcy coefficient can be expressed with a power function of particle diameter. Based on the water flow test through granite fracture samples with different roughness, a double-parameter expression for the non-Darcy coefficient was obtained by Chen et al. (2015) . Zhou et al. (2015)  used a critical Reynolds number model to fit the data from a single natural fracture, and determined the constant in the power function of non-Darcy coefficient. Xing et al. (2021)  carried out experimental and numerical study on the non-Darcy coefficient in rough single fractures. They found the influence of geometric attributes is the dominant factor compared that of inertial effect of fracture flow, and introduced roughness characteristics in the non-Darcy coefficient equation. In addition to these common formulas in Table 1 , there are a lot of different expressions for non-Darcy coefficient. It can be observed that the non-Darcy coefficient is an empirical value whose physical meaning has not yet been accurately defined, but it represents the inertial resistance and strongly depends on the structure and morphology as well as property of porous media including porosity, pore/fracture/grain size, tortuosity, specific surface area, permeability etc. The available formulas for the non-Darcy coefficient are different from each other and generally contain one or more empirical constants. Although the values of these constants in non-Darcy coefficient can be determined based on experimental and numerical results, the values of constants obtained by different researchers often vary considerably. Therefore, there is an urgent need for a reasonable and accurate prediction model of non-Darcy coefficient. Since most natural porous media have been proven to indicate fractal scaling law (Yu, 2008 ; Xu, 2015 ; Cai et al., 2020 ), fractal geometry is applied in the present work to characterize the irregular and complex microstructures of porous media. A new fractal pore-throat chain model (FPTCM) for non-Darcy flow through porous media is developed, and the analytical expressions for the apparent permeability and non-Darcy coefficient are derived accordingly. Furthermore, numerical simulation is also carried out on an equivalent 3D pore-throat structure by finite element method to validate the proposed theoretical model and explore the local flow field. The influence mechanisms on the non-Darcy coefficient and apparent permeability are also analyzed in detail.  2 Fractal pore-throat chain model 2.1 Pore-throat chain model The fluid flow through porous media strongly depends on the microstructures (Liu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2024 ). Both the pore size distribution and pore-throat morphology majorly affect the relationship between values of non-Darcy coefficient and other parameters in porous media (Barree and Conway, 2004 ; Sharma et al., 2017 ; Li and Engler, May 2001 ; Veyskarami et al., 2016 ). Therefore, a FPTCM as shown in Fig. 1   is proposed to characterize the multiscale pore structure and tortuous flow path based on the statistically fractal scaling laws of the isotropic porous media. The fluid flow paths in a representative volume element (REV, Fig. 1 a) of the porous media are represented by a bundle of pore-throat chain shown in Fig. 1 (c). Each pore-throat chain is composed of multiple concatenated pore-throat structure (Fig. 1 d) with same pore-throat ratio (β ). The size distribution of pores/throats (Fig. 1 b) is assumed to follow the fractal scaling law (Yu, 2008 ; Xu, 2015 ; Yu and Cheng, 2002 ):(2) f ( λ )  = D f  λ min  D f   λ  − ( D f  + 1 )        If the fractal probability density function (PDF) satisfies the normalization condition, then the ratio of the minimum to the maximum pore diameter should have ( λ min  / λ max   )  D f   = 0   . That is, the area and volume porosity can be written as ϕ = ( λ min  / λ max   )  2 − D f       and ϕ = ( λ min  / λ max   )  3 − D f      , respectively. According to Eqs. The tortuousness of fluid flow paths strongly depends on their size (Wheatcraft and Tyler, 1988 ; Xu et al., 2020 ). It can be found that the value of the porosity is ϕ =1 when the pore-throat ratio β =1, and it approaches to 0 when the pore-throat ratio tends to be infinity.  2.2 Darcy flow model The steady-state laminar flow of incompressible Newtonian fluid through porous media is assumed, and the inner wall of pore-throat chain is taken as smooth surface without slip interface. According to the Hagen-Poiseuille equations and conservation of mass, the flow rate through a throat and its concatenated pore in a pore-throat chain equals to each other.(13) q p t   = π 128  λ  4  μ  Δ  p t   l t   = π 128  ( β λ  )   4  μ  Δ  p p   l p        The pressure difference along a pore-throat unit is the sum of the pressure difference along a throat and its concatenated pore, Δppt   = Δpt   + Δpp  . The dimensionless Darcy permeability can be calculated by K D +  = K D  / λ max  2     .  2.3 Non- Darcy flow model The high-speed fluid flow through the pore-throat structure results in local energy loss (Morison et al., 1982 ; Shichikha et al., 2013 ).(18) h = ∑ ξ u  2  2 g        where the local kinetic energy loss coefficient for the sudden enlargement and contraction structure in a pore-throat unit are ξ = ( 1 − 1 / β  2    )  2     and ξ = ( 1 − 1 / β  2    )  / 2    , respectively. Since the pore-throat ratio depends on the porosity (Eq. 12 ), the non-Darcy coefficient is a function of porosity, maximum pore size and fractal dimensions for pore and tortuosity. That is, the non-Darcy coefficient depends on the pore structure alone. According to Eq. (17) , the Darcy permeability depends on pore structures, thus, the apparent permeability (non-Darcy permeability) is a function of porosity, maximum pore size, Reynolds number and fractal dimensions for pore and tortuosity. Fractal dimension for pore and tortuosity are introduced to characterize the irregular and complex microstructures of porous media, and both viscous energy loss and local kinetic energy loss for the high-speed fluid flow are taken into account. It is clear that each parameter in the proposed non-Darcy coefficient and non-Darcy permeability has specific physical meaning.   3 Numerical simulation The single-phase fluid flow through an equivalent pore-throat unit is numerically simulated by the finite element method (FEM). As shown in Fig. 2  (a), the pore-throat unit is generated by the spherical solid particles arranged uniformly according to the principle of tight filling. The pore-throat ratio can be changed by adjusting the particle diameter. The particle diameter is 49.5, 45, 40, 30, 20 and 10 μm, while the porosity is 0.494, 0.620, 0.734, 0.888, 0.967 and 0.996, respectively. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (b), the size of pore-throat unit is 100 μm × 100 μm. The k -ε  turbulence model in COMSOL Multiphysics is applied to model the incompressible gas flow through the pore-throat unit. The density and viscosity of gas phase (oxygen) are 1.429 kg/m3  and 2.05506 × 10–5  Pa·s, respectively. While the density of solid phase (sandstone) is 2600 kg/m3 . A smooth no-slip interface is applied on the inner wall of porous media, the upper and lower boundaries of the pore-throat unit are set to be symmetrical. An initial flow velocity of 5.76 × 104  m/s is used on the inlet, and the outflow boundary is set on the outlet. The mesh is controlled by the physical fields (Fig. 2 c). Ignoring the effect of gravity, the conservation equations of fluid mass and momentum are:(27) ρ ∇ · u = 0     (28) ρ ( u · ∇  )  u = ∇ · ( − P I + K  )  + F     where ρ  is the fluid density, u  is the velocity vector, P  is the pressure, I  represents the unit diagonal matrix, F  is the volume force vector, K  = (μ  + μ tur )[∇u  + μ (∇u )T  ] is viscous stress tensor. The transport equations for the turbulent kinetic energy and dissipation rate are:(29) ρ ( u · ∇  )  k = ∇ · [ ( μ + μ tur  σ k    )  ∇ k  ]  + J − ρ ε      (30) ρ ( u · ∇  )  ε  = ∇ · [ ( μ + μ T  σ ε     )  ∇ ε   ]  + C ε  1   ε  k  J − C ε  2   ρ ε   2  k      where k  is turbulent kinetic energy, ε  is turbulent dissipation rate, μ tur  = ρ C μ  k  2   / ε      is turbulent viscosity, J = μ tur  [ ∇ u : ( ∇ u + ( ∇ u  )   T   )  − 2 3  ( ∇ · u  )   2   ]  − 2 3  ρ k ∇ · u    is the production term. The model constants determined by experimental data (Wilcox, 1998 ) are Cμ  =0.09, Cε  1 =1.44, Cε  2 =1.92, σk  =1.0, σ ε =1.33. The PARDISO is used to solve fluid flow equation in the pore-throat unit.  4 Results and discussion In order to validate the present fractal pore-throat chain model, the predicted Darcy permeability was firstly compared with seven sets of experimental data (Lei et al., 1998 ; Scholz et al., 2012 ; Ehrenberg and Nadeau, 2005 ; Baker et al., 2019 ; Rust and Cashman, 2004 ; Klug and Cashman, 1996 ; Farquharson et al., 2015 ) and Kozeny-Carman equation as well as classic capillary bundle model (Xu and Yu, 2008 ). According to Eq. (4) , the pore fractal dimension can be calculated by D f  = 2 − ln ϕ  ln ( λ min  / λ max   )      with given area porosity and ratio of minimum to maximum pore size. In order to evaluate the tortuosity fractal dimension with Eq. (6) , the average tortuosity is firstly determined by τ ave  = 1 2  [ 1 + 1 2  1 − ϕ   + 1 − ϕ   × ( 1 / 1 − ϕ    − 1  )   2  + 1 / 4    / ( 1 − 1 − ϕ    )   ]    , which is an analytical expression for tortuosity (Yu, 2008 ; Xu, 2015 ; Cai et al., 2020 ). In Fig. 3  , predicted Darcy permeability by the present FPTCM was compared with classical Kozeny-Carman equation (Xu and Yu, 2008 ) and capillary bundle model (Xu, 2015 ) as well as experimental data for different types of porous media (Lei et al., 1998 ; Scholz et al., 2012 ; Ehrenberg and Nadeau, 2005 ; Baker et al., 2019 ; Rust and Cashman, 2004 ; Klug and Cashman, 1996 ; Farquharson et al., 2015 ). It can be clearly seen that the present FPTCM indicates better agreement with experimental data compared with Kozeny-Carman equation and capillary bundle model. In Fig. 4  , the predicted Darcy permeability by the present FPTCM was also compared with the fractal models by Thompson et al. (1987)  and Cai et al. (2019) . The statistical fractal characteristics of pores were taken into account in the percolation model by Thompson et al. While, the hydraulic properties of the reservoir rocks were predicted with the capillary bundle model with variable pore size by Cai et al. However, the tortuosity and connectivity should be determined by empirical equation. It is clear that the predicted Darcy permeability by the present FPTCM shows good agreement with measured Darcy permeability. As shown in Fig. 5  , the relationship between flow velocity and pressure in the high-velocity non-Darcy flow deviates from a linear correlation. The fluid flow through porous media is influenced by many factors including structural parameters of porous media, fluid properties, viscous force, capillary pressure, gravity, pressure gradient due to non-Darcy effect etc. Yao et al. (2015)  carried out a steady pressure gradient-flow rate core displacement experiment on sand-packed models and artificial cores with the controlling flow rate of 0.25–42.0 ml/min. While, Liu et al. (2020)  carried out a physical experiment on a single fracture with different apertures with water flow rate of 2–97 ml/s. The present FPTCM shows better agreement with experimental data (Yao et al., 2015 ; Liu et al., 2020 ), compared with Ergun equation (Ergun and Orning, 1949 ). The dimensionless non-Darcy coefficient and dimensionless apparent permeability can be calculated by α + =αλ max  and K app   +  = K app   / λ max  2    , respectively. The values of non-Darcy permeability by FPTCM and FEM were compared in Fig. 6  . It is found that the Darcy permeability is much higher than the non-Darcy permeability. And the predicted apparent permeability agrees well with the numerical results. Table 2   shows the turbulent velocity field in the pore-throat model with different pore structure. The flow velocity increases when the porosity increases, and the velocity around the throat part is significantly higher than that near the pore part. And the local kinetic energy loss of pore-throat structure increases as the flow velocity increases. As shown in Fig. 7  (a), the non-Darcy coefficient decreases with the increase of Darcy permeability, which is consistent with experimental results (Geertsma, 1974 ; Shi et al., 2020 ). It can be seen in Fig. 7 (b) that the variation tendency of the predicted non-Darcy coefficient by the present FPTCM with porosity is close to the empirical formulas (Pascal et al., 1980 ; Jones, 1987 ; Friedel and Voigt, 2006 ; Ergun, 1952 ; Janicek and Katz, 1955 ; Geertsma, 1974 ; Li et al., 2001 ; Li, 2002 ; Khaniaminjan and Goudarzi, 2008 ; Yao et al., 2015 ; Shi et al., 2020 ), however, the difference between the predicted non-Darcy coefficient of empirical formulas is evident. It can be deduced from Eqs. (17) , (25)  and (26)  that both Darcy and non-Darcy permeability and non-Darcy coefficient strongly relate to the microstructures of porous media (porosity, pore size, fractal dimension). Fig. 8   illustrates the influence of porosity, Darcy permeability, pore and tortuosity fractal dimensions on the dimensionless non-Darcy coefficient under different pore size range (10–2 ∼10–4 ). Similar to most available theoretical and empirical formulas for non-Darcy coefficient (Table 1 ), it is negatively related to porosity and Darcy permeability (Fig. 8 a and b). As shown in Fig. 9  , the fractal dimensions for pore and tortuosity increases and decreases with the increase of porosity, respectively. And the pore fractal dimension approaches to 2.0 as the porosity increases from 0 to 1.0. While the tortuosity fractal dimension tends to be 1.0 when the porosity approaches to 1.0. Thus, it can found in Figs. 8 (c) and (d), the non-Darcy coefficient is negatively and positively correlated to pore and tortuosity fractal dimensions, respectively. Furthermore, the pore size range (ratio of minimum to maximum pore size, λ min /λ max ) shows significant influence on the non-Darcy coefficient. Under certain porosity, the enlarged pore size range (decreased λ min /λ max ) induces the pore fractal dimension to increase, while it lowers the tortuosity fractal dimension simultaneously. This can be attributed to the more complex pore structure with increased portion of small pores caused by enlarged pore size range. Accordingly, the non-Darcy coefficient increases as the pore size range enlarges. The porosity takes predominant role in the permeability of porous media. It can be clearly seen in Fig. 10   that both Darcy and non-Darcy permeability increases with the porosity. However, the rising extent of Darcy permeability is much more significant than that of non-Darcy permeability. Both Darcy and non-Darcy permeability decrease as the pore size range enlarges. However, the non-Darcy permeability is much more sensitive to the pore size range, compared with Darcy permeability. As shown in Figs. 10 and 11  , the apparent permeability is positively correlated to Darcy permeability. And the value of non-Darcy permeability is generally much smaller than that of Darcy permeability.  5 Conclusion Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulation were carried out to understand the high-speed non-Darcy flow through porous media. A pore-scale FPTCM has been developed based the statistically fractal scaling laws of pore phase, and the analytical expressions for Darcy and non-Darcy permeability as well as non-Darcy coefficient were deduced accordingly. The finite element method was also performed on an equivalent pore-throat unit to explore the local flow field. The present FPTCM has been validated by comparing the permeability and non-Darcy coefficient with available experimental data. The results indicate that FPTCM shows better agreement with experimental data, compared with commonly used semi-empirical formulas including Kozeny-Carman equation, Ergun equation and capillary bundle model. It has been found that both Darcy and non-Darcy permeability as well as non-Darcy coefficient strongly relate to the pore structures of porous media. The non-Darcy permeability is positively correlated to porosity, pore fractal dimension and Darcy permeability, while it is negatively related to tortuosity fractal dimension and pore size range. On the contrary, the non-Darcy coefficient increases with the increase of tortuosity fractal dimension and pore size range, and it decreases with the enhancement of porosity, pore fractal dimension and Darcy permeability. The results are of great significance for understanding the flow mechanisms of multi-scale porous media, and provide important theoretical basis for unconventional oil and gas exploration, porous phase transition energy storage composites, CO2  geological sequestration, nuclear waste treatment etc. Compared with available theoretical models for the high-speed non-Darcy flow, the proposed FPTCM is more in accordance with the actual pore-throat characteristics of porous media. And each parameter in the proposed non-Darcy coefficient and non-Darcy permeability has specific physical meaning. In most existing models for the non-Darcy coefficient, the value of which depends on both the permeability and porosity. However, it is well accepted that the Darcy permeability is a function of pore structures. In this sense, the non-Darcy coefficient depends on the pore structure only, which is also confirmed by the proposed analytical expression for the non-Darcy coefficient. It is worth noting that only single-phase flow through saturated porous media was focused on, and a few complications such as dead-end pores and pore shape were neglected here. Further work may be carried out to improve the accuracy of FPTCM by taking these into account.
1 Introduction Lakes play an indispensable role in maintaining the ecological balance and ensuring the sustainable development of human society. They serve vital functions, such as regulating the climate and providing sufficient fresh water for industrial and domestic use (Cooley et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2014 ). The United Nations regards protecting lake ecosystems as one of the sustainable development goals (SDG 6.6) (https://www.un.org/ ). However, a large number of lakes worldwide have experienced dramatic changes (e.g., size, shape, edge wetlands, water quality) over the past decades, as a result of global warming and intensified human interferences (Donchyts et al., 2016; Pickens et al., 2020 ). Accompanying these changes are multifarious issues threatening the water ecological environment, such as algae bloom, biodiversity loss, and degradation of wetlands (Hou et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2020 ). In particular, studies have proved that the ecosystem of inland lakes at mid and high latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere were more fragile to climate changes, as the region is warming almost twice the rate of the global average level (Peng et al., 2020; Screen and Simmonds, 2010 ). This emphasizes the need for a comprehensive understanding of the changes in lakes and driven forces at the mid to high latitude regions, which is of significant guiding importance for regional lake management. With the rapid development of remote sensing technology since the 1970s, satellite remote sensing, capable of large-scale and periodical observations, has been extensively employed to monitor changes of lake area at global and regional scales (Dai et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2021; Yue and Liu, 2021 ). Numerous satellite datasets, such as the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Landsat and Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), have been utilized in lake area studies (Hou et al., 2022; Hu, 2009 ). Yue and Liu (2019)  used 329 Landsat images to define the boundaries of Hongjiannao Lake in Shaanxi, China, from 1986 to 2018. Gao et al. (2023)  analyzed surface water area changes in the Mongolian Plateau from 1991 to 2021 based on Landsat-5/7/8 surface reflectance observation data. Additionally, global surface water map products, such as Global Surface Water Occurrence (GSWO) and Global Lake Maximum Boundary dataset (GLAKES), have greatly facilitated the monitoring of lake characteristics (Pekel et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2022 ). Ma et al. (2024)  selected the GLAKES dataset as mask data and integrated it with multi-source remote sensing data (ICESat-2, Cryosat-2, Jason-1/2/3, and Sentinel-3A/3B) to obtain water levels of 988 lakes with area > 10 km2  in China from 2002 to 2023. Zhao et al. (2022)  combined the Global Surface Water Occurrence (GSWO) dataset with the HydroLAKES shapefile to reconstruct the monthly time series of water area for 1.42 million lakes from 1985 to 2018 and quantified their evaporation volume. The Amur River (Heilongjiang) Basin is located in northeast Asia, and the Amur River is a transboundary river flowing through China, Russia, and Mongolia. The basin is of great ecological significance as it has densely distributed lakes and wetlands, providing habitats for more than 1000 kinds of plants, fish, and birds (Nikitina et al., 2020; You et al., 2020 ). Meanwhile, the geographic location and wide coverage have made the area vulnerable to the changing climate and anthropogenic interferences. The air temperature in this region was reported to warm faster than the global average level due to Arctic amplification phenomena (Cohen et al., 2014 ). Hence, the hydrological budget of lakes may be affected by accelerating the glacier melting, permafrost degradation, water evaporation, etc. Moreover, the basin has a distinct gradient in population density and anthropogenic intensity from the north to south areas, driven by different regional policies, and economic and social development levels in different countries (Yan et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the spatial/temporal changes of lakes in the basin is urgent, which can help comprehend the influences of climate change and anthropogenic activities on these lakes. Many previous studies have endeavored to analyze changes in lakes and the underlying mechanisms driving these changes within the ARB. Li et al. (2020)  investigated the changes of lakes in the southwest of Songnen plain based on Landsat images during 1985–2015, and found that the lake shrinkage was more pronounced in the east and northeast. Tao et al. (2020)  revealed the changes of lake area (>10 km2 ) on the Mongolia Plateau (MP) and Northeast Plain between the mid-1980s and 2015, showing that precipitation, irrigation, grazing, and mining contributed to the rapid loss of lakes. Zhou et al. (2019)  explored the changes in lakes with area larger than 1 km2  on the Mongolian Plateau using Landsat images from 1991 to 2017. They found that both natural (precipitation and temperature) and anthropogenic processes (irrigation, mining, and grazing) caused a shrinkage of lakes before 2009, while precipitation played a key role in promoting the recovery of the lakes after 2009. Ma et al. (2010)  revealed changes in China's lakes during two periods, the 1960s–1980s and 2005–2006, and found that a large number of lakes in Northeast China and Inner Mongolia have undergone dramatic changes. Despite these valuable progresses made by previous studies on lake dynamics and underlying driven mechanisms, limitations still exist regarding the study region, duration, and selection of lakes. Existing research tends to focus primarily on large lakes (e.g., over 10 km2 ), overlooking the ecological significance of small lakes. Zhou et al. (2019)  demonstrated that the small (1–10 km2 ) lakes accounted for 33.6 % to lake area growth on Mongolian Plateau, and the number of lakes increased by 124/32 in Inner Mongolia/ Mongolia during 2009–2013. The lakes with areas <1 km2  have also been proved to dominate the variability in total lake size in half of the global inland lake regions (Pi et al., 2022 ). Therefore, ignoring these small-size lakes could potentially result in the loss of crucial information and incomplete assessments regarding lake dynamics. In addition, previous studies have often focused on specific regions or individual lakes, thereby restricting our comprehensive cognition of lake dynamics in response to the gradients of climatic factors and varying levels of anthropogenic activities across large river basins, especially those spanning different countries. In view of the above issues, this study aims to obtain a comprehensive understanding on the changes of lakes over the whole ARB and the underlying driven mechanisms behind them. Multi-source remote sensing datasets (e.g., global surface water dynamic (GSWD), GLAKES, precipitation, and soil moisture) from 1999 to 2021 were used to provide the latest information. The main objectives of this study were: 1) to extract the extent of lakes in the ARB from 1999 to 2021 using the GSWD and GLAKES, 2) to elucidate the spatial and temporal changes in area and number of lakes larger than 1 km2  in the whole ARB and in sub-regions, and 3) to analyze the primary driving factors (climatic and anthropogenic factors) affecting lake changes and demonstrate their influencing mechanisms in different sub-regions of ARB. This study offers vital insights on lake changes in climate-sensitive regions with varying levels of human activities, which is crucial for crafting effective conservation strategies, managing lake ecosystems, and adapting to future climate change.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Amur River Basin (ARB) is situated in northeast Asia, spanning a latitude from 41.72° N to 55.90° N and a longitude from 108.05° E to 141.17° E ( Fig. 1 ). Being one of the largest transboundary river basins in the world, it has approximately 48 % of its total area in Russia, 43 % in China, and the remaining 9 % in Mongolia (Mao et al., 2021 ). The elevation varies from 0 to 2678 m, featuring mountains and plateaus in the western region and plains in the middle and eastern regions. The annual mean air temperature (AMT) exhibits geographic diversity, ranging from −8℃ in the northernmost region to 6℃ in the southernmost region. The AMT of the entire ARB experienced an increase at a rate of 0.34 °C per decade from 1975 to 2004 (Zhou et al., 2021 ). The annual mean precipitation (AMP) also shows noticeable geographic variation, varying from 250 to 800 mm across the basin. The eastern coastal area, which is influenced by the Pacific monsoon climate, receives higher levels of precipitation ranging from 570 to 800 mm annually. As a result, this region features abundant trees and wetlands. On the other hand, the western area receives less precipitation of 250–300 mm annually due to the influence of Siberian continental monsoon climate (Wen et al., 2021 ). It has been reported that the Northeast Plain region has experienced rapid population growth and an increase in food demand, which resulted in the expansion of cropland and urbanization in the area. However, such activities have been less noticeable in other regions, such as the Siberian Federal region. (Fig. 1 b).  2.2 Datasets This study used the GSWD dataset to provide detailed visualizations of interannual surface water dynamics. The GSWD dataset was originally generated based on Landsat images (5/7/8) with a spatial resolution of 30 meters and was developed by the Department of Geographical Sciences, University of Maryland (https://glad.umd.edu/ ) (Pickens et al., 2020 ). The GSWD dataset records the location and frequency of water occurrence from 40°S to 90°N over the past two decades (1999–2021), and the mapped permanent water exhibited high accuracy levels with the user's and producer's accuracies of 97.8 (±1.8)% and 85.8 (±2.4)%, respectively (Pickens et al., 2020 ). The GSWD was used in this study as a base information of the presence of open surface water bodies. In total, we obtained 176 images from GSWD covering the entire ARB from 1999 to 2021. In each image, the values of pixels indicate the probability of water presence, which is the percentage of times that a pixel was inundated over all observations from Landsat 5/7/8 for that year. Further, the global lake maximum boundary dataset named GLAKES by Pi et al. (2022)  was employed to mask the lake extents from the identified water pixels based on GSWD. Compared with previous global lake datasets, the GLAKES dataset has a significant improvement in terms of wider global coverage (60°S-80°N), finer spatial resolution (30 m), and higher spatiotemporal consistency (Pi et al., 2022 ). The dataset allows for the identification of a minimum lake area of 0.03 km2 , making it highly reliable and supportive for lake change analysis. To identify the major driving factors behind lake changes, relevant hydro-climatic data and socio-economic variables were collected. Precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff data were downloaded from an enhanced global dataset for the land component of the fifth-generation of European Reanalysis (ERA5-Land) released by European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ ). ERA5-Land is a reanalysis dataset with a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1° (∼10 km at the equator), known for its strong applicability in interpreting large-scale regional hydro-climatic change patterns (Dee et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2022 ). The monthly released data were further integrated into annual mean values for each pixel within the drainage area of ARB, which were used to analyze the hydro-climatic impacts on lake changes. Water availability (WA) is calculated as the difference between precipitation and evapotranspiration. Soil moisture data were obtained from the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM, version 3.5) (https://www.gleam.eu/ ), which provides global soil moisture datasets from 1980 to 2021 at a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° (∼25 × 25 km at the equator). The soil moisture data were resampled to the same spatial scale as the ERA-5 land dataset. Anthropogenic impacts were primarily assessed by considering grazing (number of sheep and goats), irrigation (area of irrigated croplands), and population density. These factors were considered to have a strong impact on lake area changes (Blanc et al., 2014; Yue and Liu, 2021 ). Irrigation water use may lead to a reduction in ecological flow in rivers and lakes, thus reducing the water supply to lakes (Tao et al., 2020 ). On the other hand, the soil infiltration caused by irrigation can enrich the groundwater, which in turn replenish the lake (Scott et al., 2011 ). Excessive grazing could disrupt surface vegetation, accelerate soil moisture loss, and consequently impact the water supply to lakes (Xu et al., 2022 ). Regions with higher population densities may exert greater pressure on surrounding lakes due to the substantial water demands for industrial production and residential use (Carmichael and Boyer, 2016; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The grazing and irrigation data from 1999–2021 were sourced from the National Bureau of Statistics, China (http://www.stats.gov.cn/ ), and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (https://www.fao.org/faostat/ ). Population data were obtained from the LandScan Global Population Database (https://landscan.ornl.gov/ ), with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km.  2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Lake area extraction Based on the GSWD and GLAKES datasets (Section 2.2 ), the lakes were extracted using the following processes. First, the regions of interest (ROIs) for all lakes within ARB were delineated based on GLAKES, and they were utilized as the maximum extent of lakes from 1999 to 2021. Secondly, water pixels were identified based on the GSWD dataset. Considering that some pixels in GSWD may have false water area detections, pixels with probabilities of water presence below 5 % in one year were excluded. All remaining pixels of GSWD were considered as water bodies, including rivers, lakes, and reservoirs. Third, to determine the water extents of lakes, the remaining water pixels extracted from the second step were masked with the ROIs of lakes identified from the first step, thereby yielding the annual lake maps within ARB. The corresponding number and area of lakes were then counted for each year. The flowchart for extracting lake maps is depicted in Figure S1 .  2.3.2 Statistical analysis A linear regression was employed to analyze the interannual changes in lake areas and lake numbers from 1999 to 2021. The associated slope of regression was used to represent the long-term change rates. To characterize the influence of environmental variables on lake area changes, correlations between lake area and these variables were calculated, and the correlation significance levels were defined as significant (p <0.05) and nonsignificant (p> 0.05). To identify the relative contributions of hydro-climatic and anthropogenic factors to changes in lake area, the General Linear Model (GLM) was applied in this study. GLM is a common method in mathematical statistics and is widely used to deal with multi-variable dependencies (Tong et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012 ). A multiple regression model was used as follows:(1) Y = β  0   + ∑ i = 1  k   β  i   X  i    + ε     where Y   is the dependent variable β  0     is a constant, X  i     and β  i     are the i -th independent variable and its regression coefficients; ε   represents the random error term. The relative contribution of each independent variable is defined as the proportion of its variance in the total variance, as shown in formula (2)(2) C  i   = F  i    / ( ∑ i = 1  k   F  i    + F  ε   )       where C  i     is the contribution of the i -th independent variable, F  i      is the variance of the i -th independent variable and F  ε     is the variance of the random error term. All statistical analyses were conducted using Excel version 2016 and R version 4.0.4.    3 Results 3.1 Interannual changes of lake area and number Lakes with surface area greater than 1 km2  were considered in our analysis. To better understand the lake dynamics, we categorized all lakes into four classes based on the range of their surface areas: small (1–20 km2 ), medium (20–50 km2 ), large (50–100 km2 ), and giant lakes (> 100 km2 ).  Table 1  presents the total area and number of lakes in ARB for the four classes in 1999 and 2021. In 1999, the total number of lakes was 1138 and the surface area was 16 858 km2 . Among these, the small-sized lakes accounted for 93.9 % (1069) in number, while for 21.2 % (3578 km2 ) of the total lake area. The medium-, large-, and giant-sized lakes collectively accounted for nearly 80 % of the total lake area, with lake numbers of 69 in 1999 and 77 in 2021. The total number of lakes in ARB increased from 1138 in 1999, to 1268 in 2021 with an increase of 11.4 %, and the total lake area increased from 16858 to 17598 km2  with an increase of 4.4 %. Notably, the large-sized lakes experienced a significant change from 1999 to 2021, with an increase of 3 in number and a 22.9 % expansion in area. At the same time, giant-sized lakes experienced a slight increase of 0.6 % in lake area change.  Fig. 2  further presents the annual total area and number of lakes from 1999 to 2021 in ARB. The total lake area exhibited a slightly increasing trend of 32.72 km2  yr−1  (p >0.05), with a minimum of 14 663.4 km2  in 2008 and a maximum of 17152.7 km2  in 2013 (Fig. 2 a). An abrupt increase was observed between 2012 and 2013, primarily due to an extreme precipitation event occurred in a large part of the ARB (Trubetskova et al., 2019 ). It is evident that the changing trend of total lake area was not constant, which showed a notable mutation in 2009. Specifically, the total lake area significantly decreased at a rate of 143 km2  yr−1  (p <0.05) from 1999 to 2009, while increased at a rate of 145.57 km2  yr−1  (p <0.05) from 2010 to 2021. The total number of lakes revealed a similar long-term trend as the area change (Fig. 2 b), which decreased at a rate of −12.9 yr−1  (p <0.05) by 2009 and then increased at 16.8 yr−1  (p <0.05) afterward. Notably, there is a statistically high correlation between the total number and total area of lakes (R 2 : 0.87, p <0.05). The recent recovery trends in both the area and number of lakes demonstrated an overall improvement in the ecological functionality of lakes, with a gradual enhancement in water conservation capacity.  3.2 Spatial variation of lake changes Considering the broad geographical extent of ARB and its diverse natural and human-induced gradients (Section 2.1 ), it is essential to reveal lake changes in different sub-regions to account for these influences. The entire ARB was divided into four sub-regions, namely Northeast Plain region, Mongolian Plateau region, Siberian Federal region, and Far East Federal region (Fig. 1 b), and their annual lake area and number changes are plotted in  Fig. 3 (a)–(d), respectively. At the same time, the spatial distribution of 69 giant-, large-, and medium-sized lakes detected in 1999 (see Table 1 ), along with the lake area change of each individual lake over the study period, are shown in  Fig. 4 .
