These 69 lakes were selected because they collectively accounted for nearly 80 % of the total lake area in ARB in 1999 (i.e., 13 280 km2  of the giant-, large- and medium-sized lakes versus total lake area of 16 858 km2 , Table 1 ). Detailed information of these 69 lakes is given in Table S1  in the supplementary materials . It can be seen that both the Northeast Plain, Siberian Federal, and Far Eastern Federal regions had overall increasing trends in lake areas and numbers, among which the Northeast Plain and Far Eastern Federal region showed significant increasing trends at rates of 48.7 km2  yr−1  and 29.6 km2  yr−1  for lake area, and 5.8 yr−1  and 2.4 yr−1  for lake number, respectively. In the Northeast Plain, the lake area accounted for 30.63 % of the total lake area in ARB in 1999. Among its 41 large and medium-sized lakes (Fig. 4 ), 2/18 lakes exhibited significant decreasing/increasing trends in lake area (p <0.05). In the Far Eastern Federal region, 7 lakes increased significantly (p <0.05). Inversely, the Mongolian Plateau region exhibited a decreasing trend in both lake area and number, particularly before the year 2012 (Fig. 3 b). The significant decrease in 3 giant-sized lakes (Lake Buir, Lake Khukh, and Lake Zuun Tooroi) ultimately revealed the shrinking trend of lakes in this region. There is only one medium-sized lake in Siberian Federal region with area increased (Fig. 4 ). Indeed, in the four sub-regions, the number of lakes is highly correlated with the area of lakes, particularly in the Northeast Plain region, Siberian Federal region, and Far Eastern Federal region (R >0.90); while the correlation is relatively weak in Mongolia Plateau region with R =0.62.  3.3 Driving forces To analyze the potential driving mechanisms of the interannual changes of lake areas in ARB, the impacts of several hydro-climatic and anthropogenic variables were examined. Precipitation, water availability (WA), soil moisture, and runoff were selected as indicators of regional climate conditions, while irrigation, grazing, and population density were indicators of anthropogenic activities. The annual mean air temperature was not considered as a dependent variable due to its effect being involved in WA. Given the statistically high correlation between the number and area of lakes (see Section 3.2 ), we only focused on analyzing the driving mechanism behind lake area changes. The impacts of hydro-climatic factors were firstly analyzed. Because of the different patterns of lake area change pre- and post-2009 mentioned in Section 3.1 , we investigated the driving forces of lake area change separately during 1999–2009 and 2010–2021. The annual mean precipitation within the ARB significantly decreased by 6.4 mm per year (p <0.05) before 2009 and then increased at a rate of 2.34 mm yr−1  (p >0.05) afterward ( Fig. 5 a). The variation of interannual precipitation is statistically correlated with lake area changes, with R 2  of 0.55 (p <0.05) and 0.56 (p <0.05) for the two time periods, respectively. Fig. 5 (b) showed a statistically significant correlation (p <0.05) between WA and lake area, with R 2   of 0.62 in the period 1999–2009 and 0.46 in the period 2010–2021. Since the inclusion of evaporation (i.e., between precipitation and WA) did not significantly alter the impacting level on lake area change, subsequent analysis will only focus on the effects of precipitation. Fig. 5 c shows the significant correlations between soil moisture and lake areas in two periods with R 2   of 0.53 and 0.83, respectively (p <0.05). The improved soil moisture may percolate downward, eventually entering the groundwater layer, which in turn increases the water supply to the lake (Niu et al., 2019 ). The correlation between runoff and lake area were found to be weak in both time periods (Fig. 5 d). Considering the diverse hydro-climatic conditions across different sub-regions (Section 2.1 ), we further analyzed the correlations in four sub-regions during the two different periods, as detailed in Table S2 . Overall, soil moisture was identified as the most correlated impacting factor to the sub-regional lake area changes. A significant positive correlation was found between soil moisture and lake area change during 1999–2009 (R 2  =0.40, p <0.05) and during 2010–2021 (R 2  =0.90, p <0.05) in the Northeast Plain, and during 2010–2021 in the Siberian Federal region (R 2  =0.46, p <0.05) and in the Far Eastern Federal region (R 2  =0.65, p <0.05). Also, precipitation was found to be significantly correlated with lake area change in Mongolia Plateau during 1999–2009 (R 2  =0.45, p <0.05), and in Far Eastern Federal during 2010–2021 (R 2  =0.45, p <0.05). Runoff was found to be insignificantly correlated with lake area changes in any of the sub-regions. To delve deeper into the influences of these hydro-climatic factors on lake area changes, correlation analysis (R , Pearson correlation coefficient) was conducted for each individual lake. Similar to Section 3.2 , a total of 69 medium-, large- and giant-sized lakes detected in 1999 were illustrated for this analysis, as they collectively accounted for nearly 80 % of the total lake area in ARB in 1999 (Table S1 ). Soil moisture was found to be positively correlated with lake area expansion in 38 lakes, with R  value exceeding 0.43 (p <0.05) ( Fig. 6 a). Precipitation and runoff were found to significantly affect the lake area change of 31 lakes and 10 lakes, respectively (Figs. 6 b and 6 c). Among the 69 examined lakes, the area changes of 43 lakes were found to be significantly correlated with at least one of the three hydro-climatic variables (p <0.05), and 32 lakes were found to be statistically correlated with more than one factor. To further elucidate the influencing mechanisms of different lake sizes, the R  between hydro-climatic factors and lake area was examined for the small-, medium-, large- and giant-sized lakes, as shown in Fig. 6 d. Overall, the interannual precipitation and soil moisture were found to be significantly correlated with the lake area changes of the small-, medium-, and large-sized lakes (R >0.7, p <0.05), while runoff had significant correlations with small- and medium-sized lakes. This means that as the size decreased, the lake area change is more likely to be explained by the examined hydro-climatic variables. However, the area changes of grant-sized lakes were not strongly correlated with any of these hydro-climatic factors. In addition, lake changes may be largely affected by human activities (Tao et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021 ).  Fig. 7  presents the correlations between lake area and irrigated area, grazing number and population density in four sub-regions for periods 1999–2009 and 2010–2021, respectively. From 1999–2009, significant correlations were only detected between the irrigated area (R : −0.95, p <0.05) and the grazing number (R : −0.97, p <0.05) with the lake area changes in the Mongolian Plateau. Meanwhile, the irrigated area was found to have a significant positive correlation with lakes in the Northeast Plain between 2010 and 2021. The irrigation activities may pose different impacts on the lake area. On the one hand, irrigation withdraws water from rivers or lakes, leading to a reduction of ecological flow in both rivers and downstream lakes (Tao et al., 2020 ). On the other hand, irrigation water infiltration could increase soil moisture content and groundwater recharge, leading to an increase in lake water volume (Scott et al., 2011 ). Excessive grazing will disrupt surface vegetation, accelerate soil moisture loss, and consequently impact the water supply to lakes. The growth of population may excessively consume water resources for living and industries (Yue and Liu, 2021 ). However, the population density was found to be insignificant to lake area change in any of the four sub-regions.  Fig. 8  further shows the relative contributions of the six explanatory variables (i.e., precipitation, runoff, soil moisture, irrigation, grazing, and population density) examined above to lake area changes using GLM. It is obvious that the driving mechanisms were different across the four sub-regions. In the Northeast Plain, changes in the lake area were predominantly influenced by soil moisture, accounting for 78.4 % of the variance. In the Mongolian Plateau, the human activities showed dominant influences, with irrigation accounted for 80.8 % and grazing accounted for 9.3 % of the lake area changes. In the Siberian Federal region, the examined hydro-climatic and anthropogenic factors were found to explain 75.1 % and 14.6 % of the lake area changes, respectively. In the Far Eastern Federal region, hydro-climatic factors were the main driver, explaining 44.9 % of lake area changes, with additional 37.4 % contribution from anthropogenic factors.   4 Discussions 4.1 Uncertainty of the extracted lake area change It is widely recognized to apply the single-band data (red band, NIR band) or water index (NDVI, NDWI) to separate land and water, based on the differences in their signal absorption intensities (Pi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020 ). However, it is impractical to determine a fixed threshold for delineating water surface for large numbers of lakes with thousands of images. The thresholds may differ considerably in different images due to the disparities of illumination condition, water turbidity level and shadow occlusion. Fortunately, several global surface water products have been developed in recent years (Pekel et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2022; Pickens et al., 2020 ), which offer a fine spatial resolution of 30 m, enabling precise distinction between water bodies and land. In this study, the GSWD, providing base information of the presence of open surface water, and GLAKES, delineating lake extents, were jointly employed to identify lake changes. The annual lake area change in this study was compared with those from Feng et al. (2023) . Despite slight differences in the magnitude of areas due to the discrepancies in data sources and extraction thresholds (see Text S1 for details), the consistent trends of lake area change (R 2  > 0.91, p <0.01) indicated the validity of using GSWD and GLAKES products in this study. In addition, an uncertainty analysis of water extraction was conducted by adjusting the threshold values of water presence probability (Sections 2.3.1) to 2 %, 5 %, 8 %, 10 % and 15 %, for distinguishing water bodies from land ( Fig. 9 ). The modification of threshold values certainly resulted in discrepancies in lake areas, which emphasized the importance of carefully choosing thresholds when focusing on the magnitude of lake area. However, the long-term changing trends of lake area were rather consistent under different thresholds, with R2 >0.94. This suggested that the changes of lake areas, as well as the subsequent driving mechanism analysis in this study were reasonable and reliable, which were less affected by the selection of threshold value.  4.2 Potential impacts of other possible driving factors on lake area change The six hydro-climatic and anthropogenic explanatory factors examined in this study could effectively interpret 82.3–98.7 % of the variation in lake area across the four sub-regions (Section 3.3 , Fig. 8 ). However, it is important to recognize that there are other factors influencing the lake dynamics, such as mining, permafrost degradation, Gross Domestic Product (GDP), and Gross Industrial Product (GIP) (Yue and Liu, 2019; Zhang et al., 2017, 2020 ). Mining processes not only consume a significant amount of water resources (Palmer et al., 2010 ), but also interrupt rivers and damage underground aquifers (Lyv et al., 2023 ), thereby affecting the water supply to lakes. The roles of permafrost degradation in affecting lake area were diverged. On the one hand, it may increase the regional runoff and recharge lakes (Lamontagne-Hallé et al. 2018 ). On the other hand, permafrost degradation will cause a drop in regional groundwater levels, which may lead to a decline in regional soil and water conservation capacity (Zheng et al., 2019 ). GIP and GDP are considered as alternative indicators of industrial water consumption, while high water consumption in industrial sectors may lead to the overexploitation of water resources (Kang and Yan, 2017; Tan et al., 2010 ). Nevertheless, the current paper lacks detailed information regarding the specific influences of these factors on changes in lake area, primarily due to limitations in data availability. Future considerations can delve deeper into the impacts of these factors on lake dynamic using numerical/physical models with sufficient hydro-climatic, economic and social data.  4.3 Implications for safeguarding lake ecology Given the variations in lake area changes and underlying factors across diverse regions (Sections 3.2  and 3.3 ), it is imperative to implement region-specific strategies for lake governance. This study demonstrated that hydro-climatic factors were the primary drivers of lake area change in the Northeast Plain (total contribution 79.4 %) and Siberian Federal region (total contribution 75.1 %), while human activities were the dominant factor influencing lake changes in the Mongolia Plateau (total contribution 93.7 %) (section 3.3, Fig. 8 ). Therefore, strategies such as rotational grazing, regulating grazing intensity, soil conservation, and curbing the encroachment of irrigation areas can contribute restoring soil permeability and water retention capacity in Mongolia Plateau (Cai, 2008; Shen et al., 2006 ). Preserving the ecological integrity of the lake surroundings is crucial for ensuring the sustainability and robust development of the lake ecosystem. In addition, implementing efficient water management practices can help conserve and optimize water resources utilization in the surrounding lake basins, which can effectively address the impacts of climate change on the lake ecology. These include efficient irrigation techniques, storage facilities, vegetation restoration and regulations on water abstraction, land use planning, etc. Furthermore, given the intricate human activities and vulnerability to climate change in ARB (Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2020 ), it is crucial to conduct frequent and ongoing monitoring of lake ecology. This type of surveillance is essential for early detection of shifts in the lake ecosystem and the identification of possible risk factors, enabling prompt implementation of appropriate management and protection strategies (Dai et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2019 ). At the same time, enhancing international collaboration and managing transboundary water resources are crucial strategy for safeguarding lake water resources (Mao et al., 2021 ). The analytical framework of this study and its implications for protecting lake ecology can be referable and extendable to other densely distributed lake regions.   5 Conclusion This study used the GSWD and GLAKES products to extract the annual lake surface maps from 1999 to 2021 in the Amur River Basin (ARB). The area and number of lakes in the whole ARB showed a decreasing trend from 1999 to 2009, followed by an increasing trend from 2010 to 2021. From a sub-regional perspective, lake shrinkage is mainly intensified in the Mongolian Plateau, while lakes in the Northeast Plain and the Far Eastern Federal region showed an overall significant trend of expansion. Moreover, results indicated that hydro-climatic factors (precipitation, runoff, soil moisture) and human activities (irrigation, grazing, and population density) jointly affected the lake dynamics within ARB, and the driving mechanisms differed among sub-regions. The changes of lake area in the Mongolian Plateau were mainly affected by anthropogenic factors, while those in the Northeast Plain and Siberian Federal region were largely affected by hydro-climatic factors with relative importance exceeding 75 %. This research improves our understanding of the ecological changes of lakes in ARB, and also provides a scientific basis for lake ecological governance in other large basins that have densely distributed lakes.
1 Introduction Climate change and natural hazards are among the most pressing issues of the twenty-first century. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021 ), global surface temperatures from 2011 to 2020 were approximately 1.09°C higher than pre-industrial levels (1850–1900). This temperature rise has significantly impacted the hydrological cycle, leading to an increase in water-related hazards such as droughts and typhoons (Javadinejad et al., 2019a; Mamalakis et al., 2021 ). Human activities are the primary drivers of climate change. The burning of fossil fuels and the transformation of forests into agricultural land are significant contributors. Besides, the construction of many factories and the burning of fossil fuels lead to an increase in greenhouse gases. These is causing a range of severe weather events, including heavy rainfalls, droughts, and tyhoons (Trenberth, 2018; Javadinejad et al., 2019b ). These events are becoming more frequent and intense, leading to significant societal and environmental costs (Trenberth, 2018 ). Typhoons, also known as tropical cyclones (TCs), are particularly significant in this context due to their potential to cause devastating hydrological disasters, such as flooding and landslides (Huang and Wang, 2015; Liou et al., 2019 ). Understanding the characteristics of TCs, including their precipitation patterns, interactions with other weather systems, and environmental triggers, is crucial for mitigating their impact (Wang et al., 2011; Liou et al., 2016; Liou and Pandey, 2020; Ditchek et al., 2023 ). Typhoons can result in immediate and severe impacts, such as infrastructure damage and loss of life, as well as long-term effects on the environment and economy. Conversely, droughts represent another extreme of the hydrological cycle, characterized by prolonged periods of insufficient rainfall. The immediate impacts of drought include dry vegetation and reduced water levels in lakes and reservoirs, while long-term effects can lead to land subsidence, seawater intrusion, and ecosystem damage (Chang and Bonnette, 2016 ). Both typhoons and droughts significantly affect human life, industry, environment, and agriculture. In the case of Taiwan, the impact of typhoons and droughts is particularly pronounced. Typhoon Morakot, which struck Taiwan in August 2009, exemplifies the severe consequences of such natural disasters. The typhoon brought approximately 3000 mm of rainfall within four days, destroyed 61,163 houses completely or partially, killed over 619 people, and caused more than 76 people missing, and resulted in an economic loss of 16.4 billion New Taiwan Dollars (NTD) in agriculture (Wu and Ming-Jen, 2011 ). In contrast, Taiwan has also experienced several major drought events over the past 40 years, with significant occurrences in 1983, 1993, 1995, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2010, 2014, 2017, and 2020 (NCDR, 2018 ). A particularly severe drought occurred from September 2020 to mid-2021, worsened by the lack of typhoons in 2020. Given that over 70 % of Taiwan’s water supply comes from typhoon-related rainfall (Hale, 2021 ), the absence of typhoons can lead to significant water shortages affecting households, agriculture, and industry. There are numerous studies examining the relationship between drought and TCs. Early research suggested a positive relationship, indicating that storms can help alleviate drought conditions (Maxwell et al., 2012; 2013; Kam et al., 2013 ). Conversely, a negative relationship has been observed between typhoon frequency in the WNP and drought severity in East Asia, including Korea, China, and Japan (Choi et al., 2016 ). Various methods have been employed to demonstrate the relationship between TCs and droughts. These include identifying TCs that end droughts and using logistic regression to investigate teleconnections (Maxwell et al., 2012; 2013 ), employing the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) land surface hydrologic model with and without TC-related precipitation (Kam et al., 2013 ), and applying Vegetation Supply Water Index (VSWI) and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) to monitor drought relief before and after typhoons (Jing et al., 2014 ). Regarding drought analysis, Yoo et al. (2015)  proposed a hidden Markov chain model-based drought analysis (HMM-DA) tool for analyzing the spatiotemporal drought patterns in Korea. Choi et al. (2016)  used the drought index (EDI), as well as VSWI and NDVI (Jing et al., 2014; Guo and Weng, 2017 ), and the weekly Standardized Soil Moisture Index (Song et al., 2022 ). Multiple timescales of drought index can be used to assess the drought status. For typhoon impact assessment, most research uses frequency as an indicator for typhoon impact, such as in Choi et al. (2016)  and Song et al. (2022) . Additionally, landfall time and location of typhoons were also used to define the impact of typhoons (Ortegren and Maxwell, 2014; Misra and Bastola, 2016 ). This study aims to achieve three main objectives: (1) to utilize multiple timescales of the Standard Precipitation Index (SPI) to measure drought severity in Taiwan and estimate typhoon parameters such as frequency, length, duration, and intensity – where previous studies used only one parameter, this study uses multiple – across four distinct zones, namely the Taiwan boundary, 100 km buffer, 500 km buffer, and the WNP basin for the period 1981–2020. Unlike previous studies that used rectangular boundaries, this study employs buffers that match the shape of Taiwan's boundary; (2) to determine the correlation and coherence between typhoon parameters and drought severity in Taiwan; and (3) to investigate seasonal variations and trends in both drought events and typhoon activities. The findings of this research could be beneficial in developing and implementing effective policies to better comprehend and manage the disruptive effects of hydrometeorological extremes in the region.  2 Study area, data, and methodology 2.1 Study area Taiwan locates in the WNP, one of the regions with the highest frequency of typhoon activity. Taiwan is situated between longitudes 119°18′E and 124°34′E and latitudes 21°54′N and 25°34′N. Taiwan is an island surrounded by water and lies on the primary typhoon routes in the WNP as shown in  Fig. 1. The climate is subtropical in the north and tropical in the south, with a distinct typhoon season. Taiwan is impacted by an average of 3.7 typhoons each year, with the typhoon season usually lasting from May to November (Chang et al., 2018 ). They also reported that more than 60 % of Taiwan's water supply comes from rainfall generated by typhoons.  2.2 Data collection and preprocessing 2.2.1 Rainfall data The rainfall data was collected from the Climate Hazards Center Infrared Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS V2, https://www.chc.ucsb.edu/data/chirps/ ) over a period of 40 years (1981–2020). CHIRPS V2 is developed and maintained by the Climate Hazards Group of the University of California-Santa Barbara. CHIRPS provides rainfall estimation (in millimeters) on daily, 5-day, 10-day, and monthly timescales, starting from 1981 and spanning 50°S-50°N at 0.05° (and all longitude bands). CHIRPS has a higher spatial resolution than other satellite rainfall products, such as Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP, 0.1°) and Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG, 0.1°). This enables us to investigate rainfall variations in small regions (Katsanos et al., 2016; Rivera et al., 2018 ). CHIRPS rainfall estimation was calibrated using Multi-satellite Precipitation Analysis (TMPA) pentadal precipitation product (Funk et al., 2015 ). Therefore, CHIRPS is highly recommended for trending analysis and seasonal drought monitoring. It has been successfully used in the spatiotemporal assessment of drought in Argentina (Rivera et al., 2018 ), Ethiopia (Liou and Mulualem, 2019 ), India (Prakash, 2019 ), and Peru (Torres-Batllo ´ and Martí-Cardona, 2020 ). In the case of Taiwan, CHIRPS copes with the certainty of sparsely and unevenly distributed rain gauges (Wu et al., 2016 ) for climatology research and has been validated by Hsu et al. (2021) . To extract rainfall information over Taiwan, the administrative boundary of Taiwan was initially utilized. According to CHIRPS data, Taiwan receives an average annual accumulated precipitation of over 2500 mm per year (as depicted in  Fig. 2 ). Rainfall patterns generally decrease from east to west across Taiwan, with higher amounts of rainfall occurring in the central mountain range. The northern region experiences more rainfall compared to other areas, and the upland regions receive more rainfall than the western lowland areas.  2.2.2 TCs best-track dataset The original TCs data of Regional Specialized Meteorological Centers (RSMC) – Tokyo Typhoon Center was retrieved indirectly from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship Version 4 (IBTrACS V4, https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/index.php?name=ib-v4-access ) from 1981 to 2020. The National Climatic Data Center (NCDC) and the World Data Center (WDC) for Meteorology collaborated on its development and management. The latest version 4 is available in three different formats, all of which are free (namely netCDF, CSV, shapefiles). This version introduced new features, such as basin assignment, TCs translation speed, and direction. The TCs data contains information about TC center’s location (longitude and latitude), categorization, maximum sustained wind speed (in knots), and the minimum central pressure (in hPa) of typhoons every 6 hours (Knapp et al., 2010 ). In this study, we only consider records in the WNP during the mature typhoon phases (with a maximum wind speed ≥ 35 knots) and exclude weaker depression phases. All typhoon tracks across the WNP are represented by the grey lines in Fig. 1 . From 1981–2020, there were 970 typhoons formed in the WNP, and out of them, 74 typhoons made landfall in Taiwan.   2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Drought identify The Standard Precipitation Index (SPI) is a drought indicator established to evaluate the drought severity by McKee et al. (1993) . The SPI estimate is based on standardizing rainfall to calculate the rarity of a current drought (McKee et al., 1993; McKee, 1995 ). The SPI is determined using the likelihood of precipitation for any timescale, as represented by Eq. (1) :(1) SPI = x  i   − x  ̅     σ       where x  i     is precipitation for the i  cell; x  ̅    is the mean precipitation; and σ   is the standard deviation. The long-term mean average precipitation was calculated using monthly precipitation data from 1981 to 2020. The calculation requirement of at least 20 years of data was met by using 40-year CHIRPS data (McKee et al., 1993 ). This long-term record is fitted to a Gamma probability distribution, which is subsequently transformed into a normal distribution (Edwards and McKee, 1997; Lloyd-Hughes and Saunders, 2002 ).  Table 1  shows the SPI categories and its corresponding SPI values (McKee et al., 1993 ). The range of SPI fluctuates from 2.00 to −2.00, indicating dry and wet periods, respectively. In this paper, multiple timescales of SPI were calculated at each of the 2652 grid points from the CHIRPS rainfall dataset’s produced time series (1981–2020). The SPI has been utilized to assess the characteristics of meteorological drought in Taiwan. In this study, SPI values on different timescales (SPI-12 for 12 months, SPI-6 for 6 months, SPI-3 for 3 months, and SPI-1 for 1 month) were distributed between 1981 and 2020. The different SPI timescales interpret and represent four major types of droughts (McKee et al., 1993; McKee, 1995 ). SPI-1 is a short-term value that is useful for determining the association between soil moisture and crop stress during the growing season. Therefore, SPI-1 is sensitive and can result in inaccurate detection of meteorological drought. SPI-3 measures short- and medium-term moisture conditions and provides an estimation of precipitation seasonality. Evidence from SPI-6 may possibly begin to be associated with anomalous stream flows and reservoir levels. Likewise, the 12-month SPI timescale reflects long-term rainfall patterns (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). Multiple SPIs, except SPI-1, are used for additional analysis to explore the connection with typhoon parameters.  2.3.2 Definition of typhoon-influence zones and typhoon parameters Buffers are useful for analyzing the proximity and potential impact of typhoons. To enhance the accuracy of our study, we delineated four specific typhoon-influence zones. These zones are crucial for understanding the spatial distribution and frequency of typhoons affecting Taiwan and the surrounding WNP basin. The zones are defined as follows:• Taiwan Boundary (TW): This zone encompasses the entire geographical boundary of Taiwan, providing a fundamental area for baseline comparisons.  • 100 km Buffer (TW_100km): This zone includes a 100-kilometer radius buffer extending from the coastline of Taiwan. It captures typhoons that come very close to the island, allowing for a precise assessment of direct impacts on coastal regions.  • 500 km Buffer (TW_500km): Extending to a 500-kilometer radius from the Taiwanese coastline, this buffer encompasses a broader area, capturing typhoons that are near enough to potentially affect Taiwan indirectly through wind, rain, or subsequent storm systems.  • Western North Pacific Basin (WNP): This larger zone includes the entire WNP basin, which is a critical area for the genesis and development of typhoons. It provides a broader context for understanding the origin and movement patterns of typhoons before they approach Taiwan.    Previous studies have utilized rectangular boxes to define regions influenced by typhoons. For examples, Liang et al. (2017)  defined the “Taiwan Box” that covered 116°–126°E, 18°–29.5°N, while Hung (2013)  delineated a study area encompassing 117°-125°E, 19°-28°N. However, our approach employs buffer zones centered on Taiwan’s coastline, providing a more nuanced understanding of proximity impacts. Specifically, a 5-degree radius buffer (approximately 500 kilometers) was used, as recommended by Nogueira and Keim (2010)  and Chen et al. (2019) . Additionally, a zone that encompasses Taiwan island and is located within 100 kilometers of Taiwan’s nearest coastline is also an ideal zone for quantifying the typhoon approaching Taiwan (Chang et al., 2013 ). In this study, we have four specific regions: the Taiwan boundary (TW), 100 km buffer (TW_100km), 500 km buffer (TW_500km), and WNP basin (see Fig. 1 ). To calculate the values for each of the four defined regions (TW, TW_100km, TW_500km, and WNP), we performed the following steps:(1) Count the total number of typhoons passing through each region annually from 1981 to 2020, and calculated the average number by dividing the total by 40 years.  (2) Sum the track lengths (in km) of all typhoons within each region using Vincenty's formula (Vincenty, 1975 ) to obtain the total track length. The average track length was then calculated by dividing the total by 40 years. The first landing location of typhoons was determined based on where the typhoon paths intersected with the boundary lines of each zone.  (3) Calculate the duration (in hours) for each typhoon's passage through a region by dividing the track length within that region by the translation speed. The total and average durations were obtained by summing and averaging these values respectively, with the average calculated by dividing the total by 40 years.  (4) Extract the maximum sustained wind speed (in knots) and minimum central pressure (in hPa) for each typhoon, then noted the overall maximum wind and minimum pressure across all typhoons in each region.  (5) Derive the percentage values by dividing the TW region averages (number, length, duration) by the corresponding averages for TW_100km, TW_500km, and WNP, then multiplying by 100.    All data were processed and compiled on an annual timescale using R Software version 3.6.3 and ArcGIS version 10.4.1. The integration of these tools allowed for sophisticated spatiotemporal analysis, leveraging geospatial techniques that have proven more effective than conventional methods in recent natural hazard research (West et al., 2019 ). By defining these specific typhoon-influence zones and utilizing advanced geospatial methods, our study provides a comprehensive and detailed assessment of typhoon activity and its impacts on Taiwan.  2.3.3 Anomalous and statistical analysis (Pearson’s correlation test and Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope) The Absolute Anomaly Index (AAI) was employed as a straightforward method for anomaly analysis, measuring deviations from the multi-annual average values. In the context of typhoon tracking analysis, an anomaly indicates the deviation from the normal, which is defined as the average condition over a multi-year period. For this study, AAI values were calculated by subtracting the mean value of a fixed 40-year period from the annual values of typhoon parameters. The formula used is described in Eq. (2)  as follows:(2) AAI =  X  i   −  X  ̅      where X  i      is the annual value for a given year and X  ̅    is the average value over the 40-year period. Years with no or fewer typhoons than the long-term average are classified as below-normal conditions, while years with a higher number of typhoons are considered above-normal conditions. Anomaly analyses were conducted on yearly data for three key typhoon parameters: the number of typhoons, maximum wind speed, minimum central pressure, track length, and duration. Additionally, AAI calculations can be extended to compare typhoon parameters with drought indices, facilitating a broader understanding of climatic interactions. Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) is used to examine the level of correspondence between typhoon parameters and drought indices (Kirch, 2008 ). This statistical test measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables, ranging from −1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation). The correlation between typhoon parameters (such as the number of typhoons, maximum wind speed, minimum central pressure, track length, and duration) and drought indices (e.g., SPI) was assessed to understand how variations in typhoon activity might relate to periods of drought in Taiwan. For example, the analysis might reveal whether years with fewer typhoons correlate with higher drought indices, indicating drier conditions. The long-term trend of drought in Taiwan was assessed by Sen’s slope and Mann-Kendall, with a 95 % confidence level (p-value <0.05). The Mann-Kendall non-parametric test (Kendall, 1938 ) is used to detect trends in time series data without assuming any particular distribution. It assesses whether a monotonic upward or downward trend exists. Sen’s slope (Sen, 1968 ) calculates the magnitude of the trend. It provides a robust estimate of the linear rate of change over time, complementing the Mann-Kendall test by quantifying the trend. These methods were applied to 6-month SPI data, which reflects cumulative precipitation anomalies over a six-month period and can indicate meteorological drought. By examining trends in the SPI, we can infer changes in drought severity and frequency over time. This is particularly important for understanding hydrological impacts, such as anomalous stream flows and reservoir levels, which are critical for water resource management in Taiwan. The R software packages “raster” and “rtk” were used to perform Pearson’s correlation and trend analysis. The combination of these statistical methods with remote sensing and meteorological data enhances the robustness and reliability of the findings. Previous applications in similar fields (Chu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Liou and Mulualem, 2019 ) have demonstrated the effectiveness of these methods in analyzing environmental and climatic trends.  2.3.4 Wavelet coherence analysis The wavelet coherence method is a powerful tool for analyzing the relationships between two time series in both time and frequency domains simultaneously. It is particularly useful for studying non-stationary signals and identifying localized intermittent features. The wavelet coherence method computes the cross-wavelet transform and wavelet coherence between two time series, providing a measure of the local correlation between them as a function of time and frequency (Grinsted et al., 2004 ). One of the main advantages of the wavelet coherence method is its ability to capture the time-varying nature of the relationship between two signals. Unlike traditional correlation or coherence analyses, which assume stationarity, the wavelet coherence method can reveal how the correlation between two signals changes over time and across different frequency bands (Torrence and Compo, 1998 ). This makes it particularly valuable for analyzing complex non-stationary processes, such as those encountered in fields like climate science, geophysics, and biomedical signal processing. The Morlet wavelet, favored for its precise localization in both time and frequency domains, is the chosen tool for conducting wavelet coherence analysis, ensuring a fine balance between temporal and spectral accuracy. To gauge the statistical significance of our findings, we employ Monte Carlo methods with 1000 realizations, generating synthetic time series that closely resemble the original data. This approach allows us to confidently evaluate coherence patterns against null hypotheses, such as red noise, thereby strengthening the validity of our results.    3 Results 3.1 Drought severity in Taiwan To assess the severity and frequency of droughts in Taiwan, we analyzed the SPI across different timescales (SPI-12, SPI-6, SPI-3, SPI-1). This approach provides a detailed view of both short-term and long-term precipitation anomalies, which are critical for understanding the temporal dynamics of drought events.  Fig. 3  illustrates the temporal evolution of the spatial mean of multiple SPI values in Taiwan from 1981 to 2020, highlighting the drought periods identified by the NCDR. The orange shaded areas correspond to significant drought years, including 1983, 1993, 1995, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2010, 2014, 2017, and 2020, during which all SPI lines dip below zero, indicating severe drought. Notably, the major drought occurred between 2002 and 2007, marked by a prolonged and severe lack of precipitation. During this period, the SPI values consistently dropped near −3 across multiple timescales, indicating a substantial and sustained precipitation deficit. This extended drought had significant impacts on water resources, agriculture, and ecosystems in Taiwan. The recent drought event occurred around 2020, where the SPI values again fell sharply, reflecting a marked decrease in precipitation. This recent drought underscores Taiwan's continued vulnerability to extreme hydrological events and highlights the need for ongoing monitoring and adaptive management strategies. The longer-term SPI-12 (red line) shows sustained drought trends, while the shorter-term SPI-1 (yellow line) captures more immediate changes. This figure demonstrates the coherence among different SPI timescales during drought periods and provides a comprehensive view of Taiwan's drought history, aligning with NCDR data and underscoring the SPI's effectiveness as a drought indicator. To confirm the occurrence of drought in Taiwan, a two-day field trip was conducted to central and southern Taiwan on April 10th and 11th, 2021, during one of the worst drought events in Taiwan as shown in Fig. S1 . The field observation provided visual evidence of the severe drought conditions. At Tsengwen reservoir, which supplies water for irrigation, hydropower, and flood control in southern Taiwan. In the upstream area, the ground was exposed, allowing us to walk on the cracked surface, where soil moisture was relatively low, and no water had been provided for a long time (Fig. S1  a). The water level in the upstream region had significantly dropped, and there was a visible shoreline (Fig. S1b ). In the downstream area, the water level at the spillway had not reached the normal level required to supply local residents (Fig. S1c ). Sun Moon Lake in central Taiwan, which belongs to Nantou County, was also suffering from a water shortage (Fig. S1d ). The Itathao pier had been at a low level for a few months, and the soil at the bottom was cracking. All floating systems near the port were currently in poor condition and could not operate normally. Typically, the water level at Sun Moon Lake can reach 7–7.5 m above the ground. This drought event was considered the worst drought in Taiwan in the past six decades, mainly due to the absence of typhoons hitting Taiwan in early 2020. The drought posed a threat to semiconductor production, especially for the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest contract chip maker.  3.2 Typhoons in Taiwan To better understand the impact of typhoons on Taiwan, we analyzed the characteristics of typhoons affecting Taiwan from 1981 to 2020. Despite the fact that yearly number of typhoons reaching Taiwan varied in the timeframe of 1981–2020, no trends were observed. Over this period, there were 77 landfalling typhoons in Taiwan, 111 within 100 km, 311 within 500 km, and 970 in the WNP. On average, 1.85 typhoons made landfall in Taiwan, 2.78 typhoons entered the 100 km buffer zone, 7.78 typhoons entered the 500 km buffer zone, and 24.25 typhoons occurred in the entire WNP basin annually ( Table 2 ). The total and average lengths of typhoon tracks, total and average durations, maximum wind speeds, and minimum central pressures are reported for each zone. This data highlights the significant variability and impact of typhoons on Taiwan across different buffer scales. The number of typhoons that make landfall in Taiwan accounts for a small proportion of the total number in the WNP basin, specifically 7.94 percent of the total number and around 0.36 percent of the track length and duration ( Table 3 ). This implies that while Taiwan is affected by typhoons, it experiences a relatively small fraction of the overall typhoon activity in the WNP region. The study also examined the intensity of typhoons, as represented by their maximum wind speed and minimum central pressure. As expected, these intensity parameters showed increasing values with wider zones around Taiwan. For instance, the maximum wind speed ranged from 115 knots for landfalling typhoons to 125 knots for typhoons within the 500 km buffer and the entire WNP basin. An interesting observation is that Taiwan did not experience any landfalling typhoons for four years (1983, 1985, 1993, and 2020) during the studied period. However, in only one year (1993), no typhoons entered the 100 km buffer zone around Taiwan. To further understand the relative impact of typhoons on Taiwan compared to the surrounding regions, Table 3  presents the percentage ratios of various typhoon parameters. On average, the number of landfalling typhoons in Taiwan was 69.37 % of those entering the 100 km buffer zone and 24.76 % of those entering the 500 km buffer zone. Additionally, the track length and duration of landfalling typhoons in Taiwan accounted for approximately 22.34 % and 21.37 %, respectively, of those within the 100 km buffer zone, and only 3.50 % and 3.00 %, respectively, of those within the 500 km buffer zone.  3.3 The relationship between typhoons and droughts Pearson’s correlation analysis revealed two significant relationships between typhoons and droughts in Taiwan.  Fig. 4  illustrates Pearson's correlation between typhoon parameters and drought indices in various buffer zones across Taiwan and the WNP, with color intensity indicating the strength and direction of the correlation at a 95 % confidence interval (p-value <0.05). In Taiwan (Fig. 4 a), there are significant positive correlations between typhoon parameters and drought indices, suggesting that increased typhoon activity generally alleviates drought conditions. Notable correlations include total duration with SPI-3 (0.42) and SPI-6 (0.46), total length with SPI-3 (0.41) and SPI-6 (0.46), and number with SPI-3 (0.43) and SPI-6 (0.46). The Taiwan buffer within 100 km (Fig. 4 b) shows similar patterns, with total duration correlating positively with SPI-3 (0.48) and SPI-6 (0.43). In the 500 km buffer zone (Fig. 4 c), the positive correlations with total duration, total length, and number are not significant. The 500 km buffer zone serves as a transition zone between typhoons in the WNP and approaching Taiwan, and the relationship between typhoons and drought appears to be insignificant within a 500 km buffer around Taiwan. Even though the number of typhoons in the WNP has no significant relationship (r = −0.2) with Taiwan’s drought index (SPI-12), the total duration and length throughout this region have contributed a negative correlation (r = −0.44 and r = −0.43 at a moderate level, respectively) (Fig. 4 d). This figure highlights the varying impact of typhoon parameters on drought conditions across different regions, with more direct positive effects seen in Taiwan and its immediate surroundings. Also, the time series of drought indices and anomalous typhoon parameters from 1981 to 2020, comparing the AAI estimation of typhoon factors including typhoon frequency, total length, total duration, and intensity in conjunction with drought indices (Fig. S2 ). The left panels show typhoons approaching Taiwan, while the right panels show typhoons in the WNP. The analysis highlights two diametrically opposed relationships between typhoons and droughts. Wavelet coherence analysis reveals relationships between various typhoon parameters (number, duration, length, maximum wind speed, and minimum pressure) and drought indices (SPI-6 and SPI-12) from 1981 to around 2020 at different time scales ( Fig. 5 ). Higher coherence (warmer colors) is seen between typhoon parameters and SPI-6 at longer 8–10 year periods compared to shorter scales. Coherence patterns vary across typhoon characteristics, with duration, length, and maximum wind showing stronger associations with drought conditions over certain periods. Coherence is generally higher and more persistent from the late 1990s to 2010s across most variables, except minimum pressure which exhibits somewhat different patterns. In particular, typhoon duration and length in the WNP exhibit strong coherence with SPI-12 drought intensity, especially at lower multi-year to decadal frequencies, suggesting links between prolonged typhoon events and extended droughts. Other parameters like frequency, wind speed, and pressure show moderate to weaker drought coherence, with higher coherence during specific periods. The analysis indicates potential connections between various typhoon characteristics and regional drought patterns, primarily manifesting on multi-year to decadal timescales, warranting further investigation into causality and mechanisms.  3.4 Seasonality of drought events and typhoons This section illustrates the seasonal variation of typhoons and their tracking.  Fig. 6  shows the total monthly frequency of drought events and typhoons in Taiwan during this period. The number of drought events varied from 5 to 11 between July and March. The frequency of typhoons in each of the four zones is represented by different colored bars. Most typhoons made landfall in Taiwan between May and November, with the highest number occurring in August. The seasonal fluctuation of typhoon frequency in the WNP is visible from May to November, peaking in August, despite the fact that there is no significant feedback on the SPI-12. The majority of drought events occurred during late winter to early spring, specifically in February to March, with the numbers of events being 10–11, respectively. The number decreases during summer, with a minimum value of five in July. There are two peaks per year in March and September, but the number of drought events between March and July is gradually decreasing.  Fig. 7  depicts the composite distribution of typhoon track (typhoons hitting Taiwan) and drought severity in Taiwan for four seasons: March-April-May (MAM), June-July- August (JJA), September-October-November (SON), and December-January-February (DJF). During the MAM season (Fig. 7 a), moderate to severe wet conditions dominate the large region in northern and eastern Taiwan, while lowland areas in the southern and western regions are nearly normal. In contrast, during the JJA season (Fig. 7 b), southern and western Taiwan become drier, and there is a slight increase in number of drought events from July to September. During the JJA season, the highest number of typhoon tracks that make landfall in Taiwan is around 59 (73 %), while in the SON season, the maximum number of typhoon landing is approximately 21 (26 %) (b). In the JJA season, the moist conditions dominate through Taiwan, especially in the northern and central regions, while drought conditions are moderate in a small portion of southern Taiwan. As the number of typhoons slowly drops in SON (Fig. 7 c), more regions, such as southwestern and eastern Taiwan, become drier. There are no typhoons in the DJF season (Fig. 7 d), which has enabled the spread of severe drought areas throughout more than 65 % of Taiwan. In MAM, the number of drought events reduces substantially, and typhoons begin to reach Taiwan during this season, making the entire island wetter.  3.5 Landing typhoon points and its linkage with droughts over Taiwan The Mann-Kendall test demonstrates long-term trend of drought (e.g., SPI-6) during the timeframe of 1981–2020 ( Fig. 8 ). Panel (a) shows the spatial distribution of the SPI-6 trend across Taiwan, where a positive SPI-6 slope value (green areas) indicates a rising trend in precipitation, and a negative SPI-6 slope value (red areas) denotes a declining trend. This map highlights regions that are becoming wetter or drier over time. Inset within the map, typhoon landfall points along Taiwan's coast are marked, showing where typhoons have historically made landfall. Panel (b) displays the total typhoon frequency for landfall locations at 0.5° latitude intervals. The bars represent the number of typhoons making landfall at each interval, with color coding for different proximity zones: 0 km (blue), 100 km (orange), 500 km (gray), and the Western North Pacific (WNP, yellow). The linear trend lines indicate overall trends in typhoon frequency for each zone. Panel (c) similarly shows the total typhoon frequency for landfall locations at 0.5° longitude intervals, with the same color coding and trend analysis as in panel (b). The result revealed that the drought increased in central and southern Taiwan, while it is decreased in northern Taiwan and southern central mountain range. The long-term trend in lowland areas near the coastal region is increasing, especially in the central and southern coastal regions. The annual growth rate is approximately 0.15. The no-trend areas are scattered throughout Taiwan. The dispersion of the landing points and hitting points into three zones are also presented in small circles. According to the results, 48 % of overall typhoons hitting Taiwan had a northward tracking movement when approaching Taiwan and making landfall (b). These landing locations in Taiwan are closely linked to the long-term drought severity distribution for the whole island. Beyond the path of typhoons, the landing point is concentrated in northern Taiwan where dryness is on the declining trend. The data also shows a west-east distribution for all typhoon-influence zones (panel c).   4 Discussion The findings highlight the significant impact of typhoon activity on drought patterns in Taiwan. Drought occurrences were most frequent during late winter to early spring (December to March), contrasting with the peak typhoon season from July to September. This study offers a novel approach by employing spatially differentiated buffer zones in Pearson’s correlation analysis to explore the dynamic relationship between typhoons and droughts in Taiwan. A positive correlation between short-term drought indices (SPI-3 and SPI-6) and typhoon parameters was observed for typhoons within a 100 km buffer (TW_100km), indicating that even typhoons not making direct landfall contribute to drought relief. This relationship becomes insignificant for typhoons passing within a 500 km buffer, showing a diminishing influence on drought conditions. Moreover, the stronger correlation with six-month SPI (SPI-6) compared to the three-month SPI (SPI-3) suggests that typhoon effects extend over longer periods, with a lag time of approximately six months for water to recharge reservoirs and groundwater systems. For example, typhoons in August can signal sufficient water in March of the following year. Additionally, SPI-6 indicates seasonal to medium-term trends in precipitation and may also be associated with anomalous streamflows and reservoir levels depending on the location and time of year (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). Interestingly, the 100 km buffer shows a stronger positive correlation between typhoon maximum wind speed and drought indices than the Taiwan region, suggesting that the intensity of typhoons approaching Taiwan, even if they do not hit Taiwan, is crucial for drought relief contribution. Although some typhoons did not directly hit Taiwan, they still bring a significant amount of rainfall to the island. These results suggest that the fewer typhoons passing through the 100 km buffer or hitting Taiwan’s mainland, the lower SPI value, and the greater the risk of drought in the current and subsequent year. Additionally, typhoons with a longer duration, greater length, and higher intensity may bring more water to the island, ensuring sufficient water availability. Several probable causes for such northward shifts and typhoon-induced rainfall intensity have been associated with drought severity distribution in Taiwan during the last decade. One of those is the increased water vapor supplies induced by global warming (as measured by variations in sea surface temperature in the western Pacific) has likely caused more typhoons to travel poleward on their route to mid-latitude East Asian nations rather than the South China Sea (Chou et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011 ). Besides, Wang et al. (2013)  proposed a coupled-model experiment to conclude that the impacts of Mega-El Nino Southern Oscillation (Mega-ENSO) and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) are more powerful than global warming in generating more typhoons. Chang et al. (2013)  and Kuo et al. (2017)  hypothesized that terrain (the consequent convective heating pattern) might slow down the tracking of northward typhoons. One last possibility is the longer duration of typhoons, the weakening of easterly steering flow, and increasing track frequency (or track length) are all proposed as explanations for the rise in typhoon-related rainfall intensity hitting Taiwan (Tu et al., 2009; Chu et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2017 ). Our research innovatively utilizes boundary-based buffering methods tailored to Taiwan's geographical contours. Previous studies used rectangular boxes to count or assess typhoons hitting not only Taiwan (Liang et al., 2017 ) but also another region (Wu et al., 2024 ). In contrast, this study creates buffers based on the actual boundary of Taiwan, leading to a more accurate representation of typhoon effects. This boundary-based buffering method captures the true geographical influence of typhoons, considering the island's shape and area, thus providing a more precise analysis of how typhoons contribute to drought relief. The effectiveness of this buffer method is evident in the improved correlation analysis and the more nuanced understanding of typhoon impacts. By aligning the buffers with Taiwan's actual boundary, the study accurately reflects the areas affected by typhoon-induced rainfall, offering a clearer picture of water resource distribution and drought conditions. The seasonal analysis of drought events and typhoon occurrences reveals a clear temporal pattern. Typhoon impacts are more significant over longer periods, with a lag time of about six months for water to recharge reservoirs and groundwater systems. For example, typhoons in August can signal sufficient water in March of the following year. Most drought events occur in late winter to early spring, peaking in March, while typhoons predominantly occur from May to November, peaking in August. This seasonal discrepancy suggests that drought conditions in Taiwan are primarily a result of the absence of typhoons during critical periods. The composite distribution of typhoon tracks and drought severity across different seasons highlights the spatial variability of drought impacts. The transition from wet conditions in northern and eastern Taiwan during MAM (March, April, May) to drier conditions in the south during JJA (June, July, August) and SON (September, October, November) indicates a shift in drought vulnerability zones, which is crucial for regional water resource planning. The seasonal fluctuation of typhoon frequency in the WNP, peaking in August, shows no significant impact on the SPI-12, suggesting that typhoon frequency in the WNP has an insignificant effect on drought severity in Taiwan. Long-term trends analyzed through Mann-Kendall tests indicate increasing drought severity in central and southern Taiwan, while northern regions showed a decreasing trend. This trend aligns with historical shifts in precipitation patterns, suggesting that climate change may be influencing these trends. The findings are consistent with previous research using a rain gauge dataset (Chen et al., 2009 ). One possible explanation is that the precipitation series shifted dramatically around the 1960s (Yu et al., 2006 ). The analysis of typhoon landing points reveals that typhoons making landfall in northern Taiwan are associated with regions experiencing a decreasing trend in drought severity. The data also reveals a west-east distribution for all typhoon-influence zones. Most typhoons reaching Taiwan originate in the WNP rather than the East Sea. Typhoons tracking westward, however, contribute to long-term drought relief in southeastern Taiwan. This spatial correlation between typhoon tracks and drought trends underscores the importance of typhoon pathways in influencing regional drought patterns. Two factors might contribute to the uncertainty in this research. First, due to the differences in timescales and temporal distributions between droughts and typhoons, we had to compromise and use an annual timeframe to address this issue. To do so, we aggregated monthly rainfall data (CHIRPS) and typhoon parameters (IBTrACS) into a yearly timeframe. Somehow, the aggregated approach could convey slight uncertainties for the total duration and total length of typhoons and drought magnitude. Secondly, the proximity analyses in this work are based on the conceptual idea of typhoon effect to Taiwan within 1°-radius (Chang et al., 2013 ) and 5°-radius (Nogueira and Keim, 2010 ). It is possible that the frequency, duration, and length of typhoons will alter somewhat. While the study identifies a correlation between typhoon characteristics and drought occurrence, it does not establish causation or rule out other influential factors. Additionally, the analysis is limited to the study period (1981–2020) and may not fully capture long-term climate variability or future changes due to global warming. There may be underlying factors or mechanisms that influence both typhoon behavior and droughts, which are fully explored in the future research. We may overlook other important factors that contribute to drought occurrence, such as local topography, land use changes, human activities, oceanic conditions, atmospheric circulation patterns, or climate change impacts. Additionally, further research could explore the potential impact of climate change on the frequency, intensity, and tracks of typhoons affecting Taiwan, and how this may influence future drought patterns and water availability. The boundary-based buffering method employed in this study offers insights that can be generalized to other regions facing similar climatic conditions and geographic features. By aligning buffers with Taiwan's geographical boundaries, our analysis not only enhances the accuracy of correlation assessments but also supports the applicability of this method to other areas susceptible to typhoon-induced droughts. This approach provides a more nuanced understanding of how typhoons interact with local topography and meteorological conditions to influence drought dynamics. Regions with comparable coastal geography and seasonal typhoon patterns, such as parts of East and Southeast Asia, could benefit from adopting similar boundary-based methodologies. Furthermore, the method's adaptability allows for tailored assessments that consider specific regional variations in typhoon tracks and local hydrological conditions, thereby improving the precision of drought prediction models and enhancing resilience strategies against climate-related hazards. As climate change continues to alter precipitation patterns and typhoon behaviors globally, this approach stands poised to contribute valuable insights into the evolving dynamics of water resource management under changing environmental conditions.  5 Conclusion This study investigates the relationship between typhoon parameters and drought occurrences in Taiwan. Utilizing datasets including tropical cyclone best-track and satellite-based precipitation data from 1981 to 2020, we conducted analyses on anomalies, correlation matrices, and wavelet coherence. The key findings are:− A positive correlation exists between typhoon characteristics (frequency, duration, length, wind speed) approaching Taiwan and short-term drought indices (SPI-3, SPI-6), indicating increased drought risk with fewer typhoons affecting the region.  − Conversely, a negative correlation was observed between typhoon duration and length in the WNP and the long-term drought index (SPI-12) over Taiwan, suggesting that prolonged typhoon activity in the broader region reduces the likelihood of drought.  − Seasonally, drought events were most frequent during late winter and early spring, coinciding with lower typhoon activity. Central and southeastern Taiwan experienced higher drought intensity during the dry winter months (DJF season) — a period characterized by minimal typhoon activity. In contrast, the JJA season, marked by a high frequency of typhoons making landfall in Taiwan, experiences relatively rainy weather, mitigating drought conditions.  − Spatially, increasing drought trends were identified in central and southern Taiwan, while northern regions exhibited decreasing dryness, potentially linked to the concentration of typhoon landing points in the north.    These findings highlight the crucial role of typhoons in modulating water availability and drought patterns across Taiwan, both locally and through regional influences. The positive and negative correlations, along with the seasonal and spatial variations, offer insights for improving drought forecasting and water resource management strategies. This climatological study provides a foundation for further investigating the influence of typhoons on drought severity in Taiwan and the broader East Asia region, contributing to enhanced preparedness and resilience against these natural hazards.
1 Introduction The challenge of water security is increasing globally due to rising water demand resulting from population growth, water quality degradation, climate change, and the need for economic development (Sadoff et al., 2015 ). Due to the uneven distribution of water resources in space and time, approximately half of the global population lives in countries that experience water scarcity for at least one month of the year (Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2016 ). Consistent with these global challenges, southern Africa faces high inter-annual rainfall variability and strong seasonal cycles (Ambrosino et al., 2011; Mason and Jury, 1997 ). Inter-annual rainfall variability in southern Africa has significantly increased since the late 1960s, and droughts have become more intense and widespread (Fauchereau et al., 2003 ). Botswana suffered severe droughts from 1981 to 1987, 1990–1995, in the 1998/99 season, from 2002 to 2006, and from 2011 to 2013 (Batisani, 2020 ), for example, and Zimbabwe encountered drought events between 1991 and 1992, 1994–1995, 2002–2003, 2015–2016, and 2018–2019.1  1 World Bank, (2014) . Drought Resilience Profiles Zimbabwe https://www.ciwaprogram.org/wp-content/uploads/SADRI_Drought_Resilience_Profile_Zimbabwe.pdf .   One way to cope with seasonal and inter-annual climate variability and enhance resilience to climate change is to store water. In recent decades, water storage has been closely linked with grey infrastructure, such as large dams. However, there is growing recognition of the need and opportunity to draw on and integrate storage in both natural and built infrastructure, namely soil, aquifers, lakes, and wetlands, as well as small and large reservoirs, ponds, and sand dams2  2 Sand dams can be seen as a hybrid storage option. Natural water storage exists without a sand dam, but the construction of sand dams increases the volume of sand accumulated behind the dam, enhancing the storage volume.   (GWP and IWMI, 2021; McCartney and Smakhtin, 2010; World Bank, 2023 ). Different water storage types can manage short-term, seasonal, and inter-annual variability in water availability and provide a buffer for uncertainty and variability (GWP and IWMI, 2021 ). Unfortunately, given sedimentation and environmental deterioration, water storage is decreasing in the face of growing demand (World Bank, 2023 ). Despite the growing need to expand storage and potentially abundant opportunities to roll out integrated storage approaches, practical implementation of integrated storage planning is not widespread (McCartney and Smakhtin, 2010 ). Basin plans, for example, often contain detailed estimates of large dam potential yet only provide limited detail of the storage potential in aquifers and soil (Kazbekov et al., 2016 ). One of the key barriers to rolling out integrated storage is understanding the relative potential of different storage types in particular geographies. Indeed, while there is a growing body of literature on the benefits of integrated storage (GWP and IWMI, 2021; McCartney et al., 2022; McCartney and Smakhtin, 2010; World Bank, 2023 ), besides the work by Johnston and McCartney (2010) , there is scant guidance on how to evaluate the relative potential of different storage options so that their potential can be optimized in integrated planning. Specifically, determining the temporal and spatial distribution in the volume of water stored in different storage types would provide a key basis for planning. This paper develops an approach to assess and compare water storage volumes in natural and human-made water storage options and analyze their temporal and spatial variability. The approach has been applied to the Shashe catchment of the Limpopo River Basin to generate a set of results that can be used to support integrated planning. This paper addresses the following research questions:1. What is the total water storage in the Shashe catchment?  2. How much water (volume) is in different water storage types (i.e., nature-based (e.g., soil moisture, groundwater) and grey infrastructure (e.g., small and large reservoirs, sand dams)?  3. How does water storage in different storage types vary in time and space? How much storage, at what time, and where (i.e., both seasonal variation and long-term trends)?     2 Study area The Shashe catchment is one of the sub-basins of the Limpopo River Basin shared by Botswana and Zimbabwe. It has an area of approximately 30,000 km2  ( Fig. 1 ). In terms of area, it is the second largest sub-basin of the Limpopo River Basin, after the Changane sub-basin (Aurecon, 2013 ). About 64 % of the Shashe catchment is in Zimbabwe, and 36 % in Botswana. It is home to an estimated 430,000 people (WorldPop, 2020 ); see Section S1  and Figure S1  of the Electronic Supplementary Material  (ESM). Its elevation ranges from 509 to 1564 m above mean sea level (amsl) (Section S2  and Figure S2  of the ESM). The average annual rainfall ranges from 224 to 604 mm/a (Section S3  and Figure S3  of the ESM). Rainfall is highly seasonal, and about 95 % of the rain occurs between October and April. The average temperature in the area is 21.0 °C. Annual potential evapotranspiration ranges from 514 to 3067 mm, and the basin-wide average is about 1954 mm. Geologically, about 79 % of the study area is characterized as hard rock. The hydraulic conductivity of basement complex or hard rock aquifers relies on secondary fracture and weathering processes (See Section S4  and Figure S4  of the ESM). The study area includes one of the most important aquifers shared by Botswana, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, i.e., The Tuli Karoo Transboundary Aquifer. However, only 20 % of the Tuli Karoo Transboundary Aquifer is within the Shashe catchment and covers only 8 % of the Shashe catchment. The dominant soil texture is sandy soil (77 %), and the dominant soil type, luvisols covers about 67 % of the study area (See Section S5  and Figures S5 and S6  of the ESM). The catchment area is mainly covered by shrubs (See Section S6  and Figure S6  of the ESM). The Shashe catchment contributes 12.3 % of the mean annual runoff of the Limpopo River Basin. This makes it the third-largest contributor to the Limpopo River Basin, after the Olifants (32.7 %) and Luvuvhu (13.1 %) sub-basins (Love et al., 2010 ). Water availability in the Shashe catchment is highly seasonal due to high seasonal rainfall variability (Sutcliffe and Knott, 1987 ). The seasonality as well as inter-annual variability, causes shortfalls (demand exceeds the average water availability) in certain months and years. Storage is needed to bridge the seasonal water availability “gap” and mitigate the deficits in drought years, i.e., inter-annual variability (Briscoe, 2009; Brown and Lall, 2006 ). Based on crude calculation, the total current water demand in the Shashe catchment is approximately 240 Mm3  (See Section S7  and Table S1 of the ESM). Nonetheless, water demand in the Shashe catchment is expected to grow significantly in the coming decades due to irrigated area expansion in the Zimbabwean portion of the Shashe catchment, population growth, and climate change. In the face of increasing climate variability and change, diversifying water storage options in the Shashe catchment is key to meeting future water demand. To this end, the Shashe catchment presents a key opportunity to assess the value of integrated storage options to increase resilience and capacity to help manage climate variability and demand. In the Shashe catchment, there are five water storage types: soil, groundwater, large dams, small dams/ ponds, and sand dams. There are no known wetlands or natural lakes in the study area. Soil water storage, also known as soil moisture, refers to the water held in soil pores, typically in the upper 2 m of the soil profile (Liu et al., 2010; McCartney et al., 2022 ). Groundwater storage is a term that refers to the volume of water that is present in an aquifer. A large dam is a dam with a height of 15 m or greater from the lowest foundation to the crest or a dam between 5 and 15 m impounding more than 3 million cubic meters (ICOLD, 2023 ). Large reservoirs can retain several months of water flow or have multiyear storage capacity (Lindström and Grani, 2012 ). Sand dams are impermeable concrete structures constructed across ephemeral rivers to harvest water (Lasage et al., 2008 ). Small dams are water storage structures less than 15 m high and have a reservoir capacity of less than 0.75 Mm3  (Keller et al., 2000 ). Small dams are associated with small streams and drainage areas of a limited extent (United States Bureau of Reclamation, 1987 ). They store relatively small amounts of water and often empty every year (McCartney et al., 2013 ). For instance, small dams in Zimbabwe are not enough to supply water year-round (De Hamer et al., 2008 ). Ponds are often constructed by individuals or communities to capture and store surface runoff (McCartney et al., 2013 ).  3 Methods The methodological framework for storage assessment in the Shashe catchment is presented in  Fig. 2 . Dam storage volumes were estimated based on observed reservoir volume time-series data. Sand dam storage was estimated based on the sand volume behind the sand dam and the hydraulic properties of the sand. Soil and groundwater storage were estimated using an integrated SWAT-MODFLOW model. Soil storage estimated with the SWAT-MODFLOW model was compared with Soil Moisture Active-Passive (SMAP) remotes sensing soil moisture data. The estimated total water storage was compared with Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Total Water Storage data (GRACE-TWS). Details about each method are presented in the subsequent sections. 3.1 Surface water storage estimation As time-series of reservoir volume are available for all ten dams in the Shashe catchment, we used the observed time-series data for our integrated storage assessment. Reservoir volume data were obtained from the Zimbabwe National Water Authority (ZINWA) and the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS), Botswana. The spatial frequency of water occurrence map for the period January 2016 – June 2021 for the Limpopo River Basin was purchased from the South Africa National Space Agency (SANSA). The water frequency map is developed based on Sentinel-2, 20 m x 20 m pixel resolution and it shows the number of times a given grid cell on the satellite image contains water. The total number of months for the data period January 2016- June 2021 was 66. The frequency is calculated by simply summing the number of monthly occurrences over the full-time period. This map was used to map small dam reservoirs and ponds with a surface area greater than 1 ha. Based on the empirical area and storage volume power relationship developed for small dams for small catchments in Zimbabwean portions of the Limpopo River Basin (Sawunyama, 2005 ) (Eq. 1 ), the volume of water storage was calculated.(1) V = 0.0231  × A  1.3272       Where V is water stored volume (m3 ) and A is reservoir surface area (m2 ) Assuming small dams will be full throughout the wet season (October-March) but then empty gradually so that they are dry at the end of the dry season (September), the monthly distribution of the total small dam storage was calculated.  3.2 Sand dam storage estimation In the Shashe catchment, there are 30 sand dams (Section S8 , and Figure S8  and S9 of the ESM). The volume of water stored in sand dams was estimated based on the sand storage volume and sand hydraulic properties (i.e., specific yield (Sy)). The sand volume was calculated based on the sand dam height, river width, and sand accumulation behind the dam, which were obtained for 14 sand dams surveyed by Dabane Trust, a local NGO (Non-Governmental Organization). The Sy value was estimated based on sediment grain size analysis data for Mtshelele River, Zimbabwe, and literature values (Borst et al., 2006; Love et al., 2011; Moyce et al., 2006; Owen and Dahlin, 2005 ), See Section S9  and Fig. S10  of the ESM. In the present study, storage volumes were calculated for 14 sand dams using Sy of 15 % (i.e., the more conservative estimate). The total sand dam storage in the Shashe catchment was calculated by multiplying the average storage of the 14 sand dams by the total number of known sand dams in the Shashe catchment as identified by the NGO, Dabane Trust (i.e., 30 sand dams).  3.3 Soil and Groundwater storage estimation To estimate soil and groundwater storage for the Shashe catchment, an integrated SWAT-MODFLOW model was developed. SWAT-MODFLOW is a loosely coupled model of SWAT and MODFLOW (Bailey et al., 2016 ). SWAT is a physically based model that simulates continuous-time landscape processes at a catchment scale. MODFLOW is a three-dimensional finite-difference hydrogeological model for simulating and predicting groundwater conditions and groundwater-surface water interactions. In the coupled SWAT-MODFLOW model, the SWAT groundwater module is replaced by the MODFLOW model. In SWAT, the watershed was divided into 12 sub-basins, which were then further subdivided into 458 hydrologic response units (HRUs) based on land use, soil, and slope (Section S10  and Figure S11-S13  of the ESM) without defining any threshold. The input data used in the SWAT-MODFLOW model, and the data sources are presented in Section S10  and Table S2  of the ESM. The SWAT model was calibrated and validated using streamflow data at the B85 gauge station in sub-basin 9 of the Shashe catchment, as there is no gauging station at the Shashe catchment outlet and a lack of reliable time-series data for model calibration and validation in other gauging stations ( Fig. 3 ). Sub-basin 9 accounts for 27 % of the Shashe catchment area. Measured monthly flow data at the B85 gauging station were obtained from ZINWA. The B85 gauging station is no longer functional; hence, the data are limited to the period from 1982 to 2003. The Mtshabezi dam was constructed in sub-basin nine in 1997 and started storing water from 22 January 1996. Therefore, the data from 1996 to 2003 were not used as it is assumed to be affected by the dam operation. There is also a lot of missing data in 1995, so this year was also removed from the analyses. The SWAT model was calibrated from 1985 to 1991 and validated for 1992–1994 using streamflow data at the B85 gauge station. Three years (1982–1984) were used as a warmup period to prepare the model for calibration. The calibration was carried out using SWAT CUP (SWAT Calibration and Uncertainty program) with the SUFI-2 (Sequential Uncertainty Fitting version 2) algorithm (Abbaspour, 2015 ). Parameter ranges and calibrated values are presented in Section S11  and Table S3  of the ESM.  Fig. 4  shows the observed and simulated monthly streamflow hydrograph for the calibration and validation period. The calibration performance statistics show good calibration for a data-scarce basin, the Nash-Sutcliffe coefficient (NSE) is 0.64. NSE is slightly lower during the validation (NSE = 0.50). Since, NSE > 0.5 the model calibration performance is satisfactory (Moriasi et al., 2015 ). The groundwater flow system was modeled using MODFLOW-NWT using the ModelMuse user interface (Winston, 2009 ). Based on the conceptual model of the hard rock aquifers (Dewandel et al., 2006; Durand et al., 2017 ), the model was divided vertically into two layers; the top layer representing the weathered zone and the bottom layer representing the fractured rock aquifer. The total aquifer thickness was assumed to be 100 m because hard-rock aquifers develop mainly within the first 100 m below ground surface (Lachassagne et al., 2021 ).
