The weathering profile is generally 15–30 m thick and may be thicker where faults or fracture zones have permitted the weathering processes to penetrate more freely (Chilton and Smith-Carington, 1984 ). The upper aquifer system (the top 0–30 m) was simulated as an unconfined aquifer, while the second aquifer layer (30–100 m) was simulated as a convertible aquifer (See Section S12  of the ESM). Spatially, the model area was discretized into a uniform grid size of 400 m x 400 m. The 40-year simulation period (1982–2021) was divided into 458 monthly stress periods. The three years 1982–1984 were used as model warmup. A watershed boundary with no flow along all sides of the model was assumed. General Head Boundary (GHB) was used at the catchment outlet to simulate the head-dependent flux boundary. Groundwater pumping (irrigation, domestic, and Livestock uses) was estimated based on well yield data from the SADC-GMI GIP (Groundwater Information Portal)3  3 https://sadc-gmi.org/resource-centre/sadc-groundwater-information-portal/    and assumed to be constant throughout the simulation period. Evapotranspiration extinction depth was determined based on Shah et al. (2007)  for a given soil type and land cover and was set to be 3 m (See Section S12  of the ESM). The steady-state MODFLOW model was calibrated using long-term average static water level data [January 1990 and Feb 1991] measured in 46 wells (irrespective of the date). The initial value of hydraulic conductivity was estimated based on the literature (Chilton and Smith-Carington, 1984; Makungo et al., 2021; Wright, 1992 ). The vertical hydraulic conductivities (Kz) were estimated to be an order of magnitude smaller than the corresponding horizontal hydraulic conductivity (Kx) values, Kz= Kx/10. (Lachassagne et al., 2021 ). The initial and calibrated parameter values for the MODFLOW model are presented in Section S13  and Table S4  of the ESM.  Fig. 5  shows a scatter plot of the measured and observed groundwater levels. There is a good correlation between observed and simulated water levels, and the residuals are randomly distributed across the catchment (not shown) in agreement with recommendations by Hill (2000) . The simulated water level contours also agree with the regional groundwater flow direction. The mean absolute error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) between the observed and simulated water levels were 10 and 13.7 m, respectively. A Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE), i.e., Root Mean Square Error divided by a Range of Observations of less than 10 %, is considered acceptable for the regional groundwater model (Anderson et al., 2015; BMRR, 2020 ). Since the observed groundwater level ranges from 170 to 1256 m, an acceptable RMSE is 54 m using 10 % as a criterion (Anderson et al., 2015 ). Due to a lack of time-varying water level time-series data, calibration of the transient MODFLOW model was not possible. Therefore, the transient MODFLOW model was developed based on literature values of storage parameters (Sy of 0.05 (MacDonald et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013 ) and specific storage of 10−6  (Boisson et al., 2014 ; Kaehler and Hsieh, 1994 ; Kuang et al., 2020 )). The transient simulation used water levels generated from the steady state model as an initial condition. The independently calibrated SWAT and MODFLOW models were coupled following Bailey and Park's (2019)  approach without further calibration, similar to Chunn et al. (2019) . In the water budget of the coupled model, the difference in inflow and outflow during the model simulation is within 1 %, as ASTM (2010)  recommended, signifying the water balance's closure. The coupled SWAT-MODFLOW model was run monthly for the period 1982–2021, 40 years, including the three-year warmup period.  3.4 Comparison of soil moisture estimate with remote sensing data Soil moisture storage simulated using the SWAT-MODFLOW model was compared with subsurface soil moisture estimate based on the SMAP Global soil moisture data. The NASA-USDA Enhanced Soil Moisture Active-Passive (SMAP) Global soil moisture data provides surface (the top ∼5 cm) and sub-surface soil moisture (root zone soil moisture generally considered to be the upper 200 cm of the soil) information globally at 10 km spatial resolution. SMAP was launched in January 2015 and started operation in April 2015. Data is available every three days (Entekhabi et al., 2014 ). In the SMAP, the subsurface soil moisture was generated by integrating satellite-derived SMAP soil moisture observations into the modified two-layer Palmer model using a 1-D Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) data assimilation approach (Mladenova et al., 2020 ). The surface and subsurface soil moisture data for the present study were obtained from the SERVIR website https://climateserv.servirglobal.net/map .  3.5 Long-term trends in the storage We tested the existence of trends in the storage volume time-series. A freely available trend/change detection software, TREND V1.0.2, provided by eWater CRC (www.toolkit.net.au/trend ), facilitated statistical testing for trends. The non-parametric Mann-Kendall test was used to test trends in storage volumes. Data used for trend analyses for each storage type are presented in Section S14  and Table S5  of the ESM. Since trend tests require continuous data to be meaningful, continuous data periods were carefully chosen for each analysis.   4 Results 4.1 Surface water storage The total full storage capacity of the ten large dams in the Shashe catchment is nearly 700 Mm3  . Three Botswana dams and seven Zimbabwe dams store a total of 514 Mm3  and 184 Mm3 , respectively (See Section S15  and Figure S16  of the ESM for dam locations).  Table 1  presents dam height, storage capacity, year of construction, and purpose of each dam. The historical evolution of dam construction in the Shashe catchment is presented in Figure S17  of the ESM. The Dikgatlhong dam in Botswana stores nearly 57 % of the aggregate capacity of dams in the Shashe catchment. The total long-term mean monthly dam storage volume in the Shashe catchment for the analysis period 2015–2020 ranges from 505 Mm3  in November to 599 Mm3  in April. ( Fig. 6 ). For the analysis period 2015–2020, the total storage capacity of dams in Shashe reached approximately full capacity in March 2018 (679 Mm3 ). However, the total storage fell as low as 58 % of the capacity in November 2020 (i.e., 397 Mm3 ). The average seasonal variations in large dam storage are very low. This is because the storage volume of the dams is more than the mean annual runoff, indicating that reservoirs don’t empty and fill on an annual basis. For example, the ratio of storage volume to mean annual runoff for the Dikgatlhong dam is 6.5, and for the Shashe dam in Botswana is 3.5 (Water Utilities Corporation, 2021 ), indicating that these dams are designed to able to cope with extremely dry years and multiyear droughts. The total full storage capacity of small dams and ponds in the Shashe is 45 Mm3 . Based on the surface area threshold of 1 ha, 412 small water bodies were identified with surface area ranging from 0.01 to 1.07 km2  (see Section S16  and Figure S18  of the ESM). Figure S20  of the ESM presents large dams and small dams/ponds in the Shashe catchment. It would be anticipated that most of these small (and shallow) reservoirs and ponds will fill and empty each year. A significant proportion of the water will be lost through evaporation.  4.2 Sand dam storage Total sand dam storage is approximately 0.13 Mm3  . The total storage volume for 14 sand dams in the Shashe catchment, on which we have data, is about 0.06 Mm3  (See Section S17  and Table S6  of the ESM). On average, a single sand dam can hold 0.0043 Mm3 . The total storage volume for the 30 sand dams in Shashe is estimated at 0.13 Mm3 . The storage here represents the sand dam water storage at full capacity. To distribute the total storage into monthly storage volume, sand dams were assumed to be full throughout the wet season but empty at the end of the dry season, a similar assumption to small dams.  4.3 Soil water storage -temporal dynamics Soil storage is 1500 Mm3  . The monthly soil water storage for the Shashe catchment for the simulation period 1985–2021 ranges from 0 to 121.6 mm, with a mean of 14.6 ± 21.2 mm ( Fig. 7 ). The long-term mean monthly soil moisture storage for 2015–2020 ranges from 0.1 to 61 mm ( Fig. 8 ). The maximum soil moisture storage occurs in February, with a minimum in August and September. The soil moisture estimate compares reasonably well with the remote sensing-based soil moisture estimate.  In general, there is a good agreement between SWAT-MODFLOW soil moisture and SMAP soil moisture estimates. For the analysis period 2015–2020, the correlation between the SWAT-MODFLOW simulated soil moisture and SMAP soil moisture is 0.9 ( Fig. 9 ). The annual total soil moisture storage obtained from SMAP for the analysis period 2015–2020 is 1760 Mm3 . This is higher than the annual total soil moisture storage computed by SWAT-MODFLOW, which is 1500 Mm3 . The reason is the soil moisture storage estimate using SMAP accounts for the total soil water storage, including the residual water content unavailable for plants. In contrast, SWAT-MODFLOW simulated soil moisture content represents the plant's available water (DeLiberty and Legates, 2003 ). The plant's available water is calculated as the total soil moisture minus the wilting point. Therefore, SWAT-MODFLOW simulated soil moisture cannot be directly compared with SMAP (Rajib et al., 2016 ). Water held at the wilting point was calculated and added to the SWAT-MODFLOW soil water storage to make them comparable (Rajib et al., 2016 ). Water held at the wilting point was calculated for each HRU for two soil layers and weighted by HRU area to obtain the catchment-wide value. The average water content at the wilting point for the two-soil layer as a fraction of total soil volume was found to be 0.11, which is equivalent to 20 mm of soil water for the Shashe catchment. Considering the residual soil water content, the annual soil water computed by SWAT-MODFLOW is 2080 Mm3 , which is higher than the SMAP estimated total soil moisture storage (See Section S18  and Figure S21  of the ESM).  4.4 Soil water storage -spatial variability There is high spatial variability in soil moisture storage.  A spatial map of seasonal soil moisture storage developed for the four southern hemisphere seasons, consisting of Summer (December-January-February), Fall/Autumn (March-April-May), Winter (June-July-August), and Spring (September-October-November), is presented in  Fig. 10 . The catchment average available soil moisture for summer and autumn is 45.2 and 31.6 mm, respectively. During the winter and spring seasons, the catchment average available soil moisture is 2.2 and 5.4 mm, respectively. During the dry season, there is less available water than residual soil water. The spatial variability of soil moisture storage is a function of soil characteristics, vegetation types, evaporation rate, and rainfall. The soil moisture spatial distribution generally followed the rainfall pattern, with the greatest soil moisture occurring in the wet northeast region and less soil moisture in the drier lowland areas of the catchment.  4.5 Groundwater storage-temporal dynamics Groundwater storage is approximately 42,000 Mm3  . The groundwater storage for 1985–2021 ranges from 40,960 Mm3  to 42,900 Mm3  ( Fig. 11 ). The average groundwater storage for the analysis period 2015–2020 is approximately 42,000 Mm3  ( Fig. 12 ). This storage represents the maximum volume of water that could be recovered if the basement complex aquifer is completely emptied. However, all the groundwater storage in the aquifer cannot be fully utilized due to physical, environmental, legal, and regulatory restrictions. The long-term mean annual recharge for the period 1985–2021 is 20.2 ± 40.1 mm (See Section S18  and Figure S21  of the ESM). There is significant inter-annual variability in groundwater recharge. In volumetric terms, the annual recharge 1985–2021 is 585 ± 1277 Mm3 . Recharge occurs predominantly in a few wet years ( Fig. 13 ). The annual recharge in 1988, 2000, 2017, and 2021 is 2693, 3579, 4497, and 5246 Mm3 , respectively. The mean annual groundwater recharge for the analysis period 2015–2020 is 35.8 mm or 1038 Mm3  ( Fig. 14 ). Groundwater recharge is maximum from March to May. However, due to delay in groundwater recharge it was observed that groundwater storage increased during the dry season and remains stable until the end of the year.  4.6 Groundwater storage-spatial variability Groundwater storage in the Shashe catchment is spatially variable . The groundwater potential is higher in the lowland or low-lying areas and along the rivers ( Fig. 15 ). Across the model domain, the average groundwater storage per grid cell is estimated to be 0.232 Mm3 . With 180,866 active grid cells, this translates to a total storage capacity of approximately 42,000 Mm3  for the 2015–2020 period. The spatial variability is due to a combination of topography, rainfall, soil type, aquifer properties, recharge, and land use/land cover. This spatial variability has implications for groundwater development and management.  4.7 Total water storage in the Shashe catchment Total water storage in the Shashe is approximately 44,000 Mm3  . Groundwater storage is the largest component of the total water storage in the Shashe catchment and would be even greater if the Tuli Karoo Transboundary aquifer storage was included. It is estimated that groundwater makes up approximately 95.0 % of the total storage in Shashe, while soil storage, accounts for about 3.4 %, and large dams and small dams/ponds together account for about 1.8 %. The ratio of total large dam storage (i.e., 698 Mm3 ) to the mean annual runoff (i.e., 318.7 Mm3 ) of the Shashe catchment is 2.2. This means that the storage in large dams is about 220 % of the mean annual runoff and provides multiyear water carryover. This is particularly important here, as in the Shashe, flow varies considerably from year to year, and prolonged dry periods are common. Groundwater storage dominates throughout the year. There is relatively little variation but storage in large dam reservoirs is maximum from March to May. Soil storage is maximum in February ( Fig. 16 ). From July to September, soil storage is very low. Though groundwater recharge varies significantly, the total storage in the basement complex varies relatively little between seasons and years. The lack of temporal dynamics in both the groundwater storage and the large dams is due to the large storage capacity and currently relatively little demand. The total water storage anomalies in this study agree reasonably well with GRACE TWS (data not shown).  4.8 Long-term trends in storage There is a trend in groundwater storage, but no trends have been detected in the large dam or soil storage volumes . The soil storage in the Shashe catchment [1985–2021] showed no statistically significant trend at α = 0.05. However, the monthly rainfall trend test based on the Chirps rainfall time series [1981–2021] at the grid close to the centroid of sub-basin 9 showed a statistically significant increasing trend (α = 0.05) from December to February (rainy season). Groundwater storage in the Shashe catchment [1985–2021] shows a statistically significant increasing trend at α = 0.1. The observed trend in rainfall could be due to long-term climatic or anthropogenic impacts.   5 Discussion Integrated water storage has long been discussed but has rarely been systematically assessed in a particular geography. This paper assessed the different storage types for the Shashe catchment by combining remote sensing and integrated modelling approaches. This is believed to be the first quantitative analysis to apply an integrated storage assessment in a specific catchment. The analysis has generated seven key findings. First, total storage greatly exceeds current demand . While both calculations of total water storage as well as demand are admittedly approximate, what is clear is that there is far more storage than demand for it. Demand is indeed unlikely to exceed 1 % of the water stored in the catchment. Further, there has been no depletion of any of the water stores. While both points suggest substantial opportunity, it is critical that the practical use of water storage is constrained by the capacity to extract and distribute water to communities. A service perspective i.e., the ability to provide different services (drinking and irrigation services, ecosystem functions, flood and drought protections, etc) at a particular place and time within a given level of assurance (GWP and IWMI, 2021 ), may help to rationalize the utilization of high storage volumes. Second, groundwater is the main water storage in the Shashe catchment . Approximately 95 % of the total storage in the Shashe catchment is housed in the ground. While this reality points to abundant potential, many factors – e.g., legal, environmental, and impracticality of placing a network of production boreholes that extract all the groundwater stored in the aquifer – restrict or limit the amounts that can be abstracted. In the Shashe catchment, groundwater is by far the most significant store and, though concentrated along river valleys, is widely dispersed across the sub-basin. At the catchment level, it is less variable than other water sources. Currently, there is no evidence that groundwater is being depleted or polluted. As the percentage of total groundwater abstraction to total recharge is low (i.e., only 4 %), signifying the potential for expansion of groundwater use in the area. Investment is needed in wells, boreholes, and pumps to access it, though sustainable financing and mechanisms for operation and maintenance are also needed to ensure that such investment continues to function (United Nations, 2022 ). Related, key efforts can be made to ensure groundwater opportunities are put on the table in planning discussions, which can help ensure they attract investment. Third, soil provides the second largest water store in the Shashe catchment . The total annual soil water storage in the soil is more than 1500 Mm3 , approximately 3.4 % of the total storage in the Shashe catchment. This is contrary to what many people assume. People usually think surface storage in dams is the major storage. People usually appreciate what they see. Soil and groundwater stores, on the other hand, are invisible and hence often given limited attention by water resources planners and decision-makers. Soil moisture is critical for supporting agricultural production. Soil moisture information is of great value in water resources management, especially drought management (Lettenmaier et al., 2015 ). It controls the water and energy flux exchanges between the land and atmosphere by regulating the evapotranspiration flux (Lettenmaier et al., 2015 ). The capacity of soil to regulate the terrestrial freshwater supply is a fundamental ecosystem service (McCartney et al., 2022 ). Soil moisture is depleted relatively quickly through evapotranspiration during the growing season (McCartney et al., 2022 ). Although, soil moisture is important for agriculture and ecology, it is not accessible for other uses. In-situ rainwater management techniques and other soil management agronomic practices can enhance infiltration and water retention in the soil profile to stabilize and increase crop yields, and this is very important, especially in rainfed agriculture (Hatfield et al., 2001 ). Fourth, large dams provide the third largest water storage in the Shashe catchment . Storage in large dams is about 700 Mm3 , approximately 1.7 % of the total storage in the Shashe catchment. Large dams in the Shashe catchment are mainly used for large-scale irrigation and domestic and industrial water uses. They have the advantage of greater yield than small reservoirs, and their yield is generally more reliable (Keller et al., 2000 ). However, their operations are more complex than small reservoirs and the construction and operation of these dam reservoirs may impact the downstream ecosystems, which also needs to be considered. Although small compared to the natural stores, the large dams store significant volumes of water and are designed to cope with multiyear droughts. Currently, a relatively small proportion of the total large dam storage volume is being utilized for irrigation and water supply. Almost certainly, more of the water stored in large dams could be utilized safely if there is demand and the water can be accessed (e.g., via pipes and canals). Fifth, the aggregate volume of water storage in sand dams at full capacity is negligible . Relative to other storage types, the storage in sand dams is minimal. This suggests that their environmental impacts, as well as their potential impacts on downstream users, are unlikely to be significant. Nonetheless, although total storage is low, sand dams provide a water source for some communities living in remote, rural areas. Because of their low capital costs, sand dams have relevance to poor communities. As such, sand dams serve as the main domestic water supply source for several rural communities in the Shashe catchment. In low-lying areas close to rivers, careful consideration needs to be given to the relative cost and reliability of sand dams and groundwater boreholes operated conjunctively. Sixth, natural water storage can be measured and considered alongside storage in dams, to provide a basis for utilizing and jointly managing different storage options together . Water storage volumes in natural water storage (soil moisture and groundwater) far exceed water storage volume in grey infrastructure (e.g., small and large reservoirs, and sand dams). The small-scale storages (small reservoirs and sand dams) and the soil moisture are nonetheless variable, with limited or no flexibility over the way the water can be used. Given the high temporal dynamics of smaller volume water storage options, accounting for temporal variability, as well as the evolving nature of demand on their use, is essential. Finding the optimal pathways for integrating the different water storage options is thus important. Total storage must be thoroughly compared with water demand to identify the water storage gaps in the current and future water demands. Seventh, the management of different storage options can be integrated according to several options . It is important to consider complementary opportunities among different types of storage systems that exploit seasonal variations in their water availability. Indeed, seasonal variation in soil moisture, small reservoirs, and sand dams is significant with these stores emptying over the course of the dry season each year. By comparison, volumes in large dam reservoirs and groundwater vary relatively little, because demand is low compared to the water stored. Many communities in the basin are (seasonally) water insecure as water is only available part of the year (e.g., small reservoirs, sand dams). As such, a first option could center on maximizing the use of available soil moisture from December to February by planting crops more suited to short rainy seasons or by early planting to increase the chance of crops reaching maturity before the rain ends ( Table 2 ). The second option could be increasing groundwater abstractions to supplement dry season irrigation. The third option could be to maximize surface water use in high flow periods while allowing groundwater to remain in storage and drawing on groundwater resources during the dry season to maintain a steady supply. The fourth option could be to utilize techniques to enhance groundwater recharge during the wet season. Before concluding this discussion, it is worth noting the limitations of this study. The known sources of uncertainties in the present study are: 1) due to a lack of discharge measurement at the main stem of the Shashe River, the SWAT model is calibrated in a sub-basin of Shashe; 2) the SWAT model was calibrated using streamflow data only; hence the soil moisture simulation was not constrained with field-measured data; 3) due to a lack of groundwater level time-series data, transient calibration of the MODLFOW model was not possible; 4) as the information for the dead storage is unavailable we did not attempt to estimate live storage which is the total dam storage less any dead storage built into the reservoir, 5) storage of dam reservoirs presented in the present paper does not take into account rigorous assessment of sediment accumulations in each dam over time which reduces the storage capacity of reservoirs. The annual sedimentation rate of the Tuli Makwe dam in Shashe catchment was reported to be 0.87 % (Mupfiga et al., 2016 ). With the assumed annual sedimentation rate of 0.87 % uniformly to all large dams the total storage lost due to sedimentation is about 130 Mm3  (approximately 19 % of the total dam storage), 6) our assessment does not consider water quality issues, 7) small dam storage capacity was estimated using empirical formula due to lack of small dams’ storage characteristics, and 8) the present analysis does not include an estimate of groundwater storage of the more productive sandstone aquifer of the Tuli Karoo Transboundary Aquifer as it is deeper than the model thickness considered in this study, and the groundwater storage is likely considerably more than estimated.  6 Conclusions Water storage is a key vehicle to achieve water security, enhance resilience, and accelerate progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6). Maximizing the benefits derived from water storage can benefit from considering all storage types. However, existing approaches to water storage tend to place greater emphasis on grey options, and integrated evaluations of all storage types in a particular geography have not been undertaken previously. This study conducted an integrated evaluation of all storage types in a specific geography, providing an important basis to advance integrated storage planning. One key point worth noting is that the level of investment required to evaluate water volumes in different storage types ranges widely. Estimating storage in dams, for example, is straightforward. Assessing storage in aquifers, however, can be longwinded. Aquifers are poorly mapped, characterized, and understood. The relative dearth of knowledge reflects the relatively limited attention that groundwater receives. This variation may predispose planners and managers to utilize those storage options for which information is more readily available. As such, to counteract this reality and lay a basis for integrated storage, it may be necessary to consciously direct more resources toward those storage types that are historically under-represented. Related, a central finding of this paper is that the Shashe catchment indeed possesses ample storage—primarily in the ground but also elsewhere. Coupling this finding with the realities of seasonal water scarcity and periodic interannual droughts suggests more emphasis can be placed on expanding the utilization of existing storage by fostering more investment in extraction and distribution infrastructure. A key foundation for this, in turn, is putting natural storage such as groundwater on the development agenda and making the investment case for infrastructure that expands access. Coupling evidence suggests that the storage in groundwater within the Shashe catchment is immense, But in reality that groundwater is not always recognized as a storage mechanism, which may suggest that this resource is somewhat overlooked. Nonetheless, a significant portion of groundwater is not readily accessible. The practical limit on usable groundwater is often dictated by the rate at which the aquifer is naturally refilled through recharge, not by the total volume of water it holds. Therefore, caution must be exercised to avoid over-extraction of groundwater resources, which can lead to depletion or negative environmental impacts. A holistic approach is required. This study examined the role and relative importance of the various storage options in the Shashe catchment. By optimizing different storage options, storage planning and management can be improved. To further advance integrated storage approaches in a management context, the next steps may include: i) understanding how the different storages can best be integrated, in partnership with concerned stakeholders, ii) identifying demand for storage in order to enable identification of the gap between existing (and possibly diminishing) supply and growing demand, and iii) demonstrating the benefits of integrated storage planning and management compared to the business–as–usual approach, in order to motivate change toward integrated approaches. As such, further research is recommended to assess gaps between demand for storage and access to it in the Shashe catchment (evaluating the different storage options in terms of key performance indicators, i.e., reliability, resilience, and vulnerability of storage options), and addressing the uncertainties listed in this study. We conclude with four recommendations to advance integrated storage approaches in the Shashe, and other geographies:• Undertake integrated assessments of water storage to understand the relative potential of different storage types. Given disparities in time requirements to estimate water volumes in less conventional storage options, allocate disproportionately greater resources to evaluating water stored in the ground and soil. This should help offset the historic emphasis on surface water and lay a stronger basis for integrated planning.  • Critically compare existing storage mixes with alternative options (e.g., soil moisture conservation and watershed management techniques to enhance soil moisture and groundwater recharge) presented through integrated storage assessments to identify if there may be ways to enhance benefits.  • Explore ways to integrate storage options to mitigate risk and enhance resilience. Various options may present themselves for integration and it may make sense to evaluate integration options technically, but also to discuss with stakeholders to respond to their needs/preferences.  • Demand as well as storage are potentially vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Hence, future storage planning and management should consider what makes sense now, but also what makes sense going forward in the context of climate change.
1 Introduction 1.1 Background Flooding is an inevitable and costly climate-driven hazard, incurring annual average losses of US $106 billion globally (UNISDR, 2015 ) that is predicted to increase further with continuing economic growth, urbanization, and climate change unless preventive measures are implemented (Blöschl et al., 2019; Winsemius et al., 2016 ). Although climate change significantly contributes to increased flood risks in Asian and African regions (Batibeniz et al., 2023; Hirabayashi et al., 2013; IPCC, 2023, 2014; Mori et al., 2021 ), flood losses are often dwarfed by socioeconomic growth. The nation of Sri Lanka is impacted by severe flood damage. Sri Lanka is an island located in the Indian Ocean with a land area of 65,510 km2  in which climate-related hazards are governed by monsoon rainfall. Although Sri Lanka is on the path toward becoming a middle-income country, a quarter of its population is considered poor or vulnerable to poverty (UNDP, 2020 ). More than 64 % of the population was affected by flooding of major rivers, including the Gin River, during the period 2005–2015 (Ministry of Disaster Management Sri Lanka et al., 2017 ). Floods represent the most significant cause of average annual disaster losses in Sri Lanka, with costs amounting to approximately 140 million USD per year (The World Bank Group and Asian Development Bank, 2020 ). Alahacoon et al. (2018)  reported that over the past five decades, Sri Lanka has experienced 1500 flood events, resulting in approximately 1438 deaths. During 2002–2012, floods impacted 16–23 of the country’s 25 districts. The districts of Kegalle, Ratnapura, Kalutara, Kandy, Colombo, and Galle have been identified as the country’s most flood-prone areas, among which the western and southwestern slopes, including the Gin River basin, face the highest flood risk (Zubair et al., 2006 ). Moreover, from 2006 to 2016, the Southern province, where the Gin River basin is located, experienced significant inundation (Alahacoon et al., 2018; Fernando et al., 2023 ) but has received less research attention than other flood-prone regions such as the Kalu (Nandalal, 2009; Rasmy et al., 2019 ), Kelani (Manawadu and Wijeratne, 2021; Samarasinghe et al., 2022 ), and Mundeni Aru (Yoshimoto and Amarnath, 2018 ) river basins. This discrepancy highlights the urgent need for comprehensive flood risk assessment in the Gin River basin to mitigate future damages. The Gin River is the main water source of drinking water for the Galle district, located in the downstream part of the basin, which contains the UNESCO world heritage city of Galle (Boxem et al., 2012 ). This district is home to more than 1 million people and the recurrence of flood disasters will significantly affect their livelihoods and the economic development of the area. Therefore, detailed flood studies should be conducted in this region to identify effective adaptation measures. General circulation models (GCMs) are pivotal for projecting climate variables, as they are integral to regional- and continental-scale climate impact assessment. Various statistical and dynamic downscaling approaches have been employed to bridge the resolution gap between GCM projections and the hydrological model inputs required for climate impact assessment at the fine catchment scale. Previous studies have tested and compared the pros and cons of various statistical bias-correction methods within different scopes, demonstrating that the use of such methods should be carefully assessed depending on study objectives. These studies have used methods ranging from simple linear factor statistical bias correction methods (Aryal et al., 2019; Hay et al., 2000 ) to nonlinear or power law corrections that address either the mean difference error or both the average and variance (Leander and Buishand, 2007; Terink et al., 2010; Teutschbein and Seibert, 2013 ). Statistical downscaling methods are widely preferred over dynamical downscaling due to their lower cost and computational power requirements (Lee et al., 2021; Nyunt et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2011 ). GCM projections that are downscaled to finer resolutions via either method will retain biases that require correction prior to application in hydrological models (Galavi and Mirzaei, 2020; Illangasingha et al., 2023; Piani et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2004 ). Downscaled, bias-corrected GCM outputs obtained using suitable methods can be employed in climate impact studies and to develop decision-making tools for efficient water resource management at the river basin scale. In addition, uncertainties stemming from GCM selection, unknown climatic forcing factors, or random variability of climate models affect projected variables (Gao et al., 2019; Lawrence, 2020; Lee et al., 2021 ), complicating GCM selection. Although no standardized guidelines have been defined for the selection of GCMs, the use of multi-model ensembles has been recommended to minimize the uncertainties inherent to the GCM structure and generate reliable projections, especially at the river basin scale (Bosshard et al., 2013; Jose and Dwarakish, 2020; Lee et al., 2021; Masson and Knutti, 2011; Zhang et al., 2011 ). Land-use change is an environmental issue that requires continuous rigorous monitoring. Rapid population growth and unplanned urbanization lead to land-use changes, which have significant impacts on hydrological processes, especially runoff generation and the flood response, ultimately increasing potential flood damage (Aghsaei et al., 2020; Blöchl et al., 2007; De Roo et al., 2001; NOAA, 2020 ). Therefore, assessment of the combined effects of climate and land-use changes on flooding is crucial to the development of effective adaptation strategies (Winsemius et al., 2016 ). The conventional approach to flood modelling involves hydrological simulation with a rainfall–runoff model followed by inundation simulation using a hydraulic model (Jayapadma et al., 2022b; Nkwunonwo et al., 2020; Van Drie et al., 2011 ). Flood simulation techniques that couple rainfall–runoff models with hydraulic models that directly use rainfall data are becoming popular, including the Rainfall Runoff Inundation (RRI) model (Sayama et al., 2012 ). Previous research has employed similar modelling approaches, applying direct rainfall on a two-dimensional grid to simulate and route catchment runoff using shallow water equations across various catchments (Caddis et al., 2008; David and Schmalz, 2020; Hall, 2015; Johnson, 2013 ). Hall (2015)  developed a flood model for the relatively flat, serpentine area of the sandy Swan Coastal Plain in southwest Western Australia using the direct rainfall flood modelling approach. That work detailed the advantages and disadvantages of the method, outlining its key benefits including the replacement of hydrological models for direct rainfall flood modelling and more accurate representation of minor overland flow paths, which facilitate cross-catchment flows during high rainfall events, compared to conventional models. A recent study of a small rural catchment in Hesse, Germany, compared conventional modelling and integrated (direct rainfall method) approaches using the HEC-HMS and HEC-RAS models, demonstrating that the integrated approach yielded more detailed flood inundation maps within subcatchments while the conventional approach produced better hydrographs. In addition, the integrated approach captured the highly dynamic and interconnected flow processes of runoff formation, concentration and routing in the small catchment and thus was recommended for urban, pluvial, and flash floods in small catchments (David and Schmalz, 2020 ). Furthermore, the simultaneous simulation of rainfall–runoff and flood inundation processes provides significant advantages, particularly in scenarios where floods occur at multiple locations within a basin or where separating rainfall–runoff from inundation processes is challenging (Sayama et al., 2012 ). This approach can overcome common issues inherent to the conventional approach, such as inaccurate representation of catchment parameters (e.g., roughness) during the calibration of hydrological models (Van Drie et al., 2011 ). Therefore, the RRI model was employed to simulate flood flows in this study based on the model’s structure (detailed in Section 2.2.1 ) and its demonstrated capacity to produce reliable results at a reasonable computational cost (Perera et al., 2017; Rasmy et al., 2019; Sayama et al., 2017, 2015, 2012; Try et al., 2020 ). Although the impact of climate change has been studied for some river basins in Sri Lanka (Selvarajah et al., 2021; Sirisena et al., 2021 ), the individual and combined effects of future climate and land-use changes have not been evaluated. Therefore, this study explores the impacts of climate and land-use changes on future floods while considering both flood flow and inundated extent in the Gin River Basin, which is located in the humid tropical monsoon region, using a multi-GCM ensemble based on the climate impact assessment of Jayapadma et al. (2024) . This integrated approach aims to support sustainable management and minimize the adverse effects of floods.  1.2 Study area The Gin River is a fast-flowing river 113 km in length located in southwestern Sri Lanka. This river originates in the Gonagala Hills, approximately 1300 m above mean sea level, and empties at sea level at Gintota, which is a few kilometres north of Galle ( Fig. 1 ). The basin has a catchment area of 932 km2  and receives a mean annual rainfall of over 2500 mm. Its average annual discharge into the sea is approximately 2000 million cubic meters (Wickramaarachchi et al., 2012 ). Land use in the Gin River basin is mainly natural and plantation forests, agricultural areas, and settlements. Agricultural areas include paddy and export-oriented crops such as tea, rubber, and cinnamon. The catchment lies at approximately 80°08′E to 80°40′E and 6°04′N to 6°30′N, encompassing four districts, namely, Galle, Matara, Kalutara, and Rathnapura. Nearly 83 % of the catchment area belongs to the Galle district, and the district’s water supply system depends mainly on the water resources in the Gin River basin (Wickramaarachchi et al., 2012 ). A map showing the Gin River basin, its topography, and the locations of river gauges and rainfall gauging stations is provided in Fig. 1 .   2 Materials and methods 2.1 Climate data 2.1.1 GCM selection The Data Integration and Analysis System (DIAS) developed by the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) and partner universities was used for the acquisition of Climate Model Inter-comparison Project 5 (CMIP5) data (Kawasaki et al., 2017 ). Although various plausible emissions scenarios are defined in CMIP5 data, we employed General Circulation Model (GCM) projections based on Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 4.5, recognized as a stabilization scenario. In this pathway, greenhouse gas emissions are projected to peak before declining in the latter half of the 21st century (IPCC, 2014; Taylor et al., 2012 ). This scenario is considered plausible as it assumes moderate efforts to mitigate emissions and limit global warming (Falkner, 2016; Farinosi et al., 2019; Rogelj et al., 2016 ). Five GCMs from the CMIP5 dataset were selected based on a scoring system that evaluates the ability of GCMs to simulate major regional-scale climate variables through comparison with a reference dataset of basin-scale inter-seasonal precipitation for the period of 1981–2000 in the study area. The monthly mean spatial correlation (Scorr ) (Eq. 01) and the root mean square error (RMSE ) (Eq. 02) of climate variables including precipitation, outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) in the local domain, sea-level pressure, sea surface temperature (SST), air temperature at 850 hPa geopotential height, specific humidity, and zonal and meridional winds in a regional domain were calculated using the tools available in DIAS. The reference datasets for precipitation, SST, and OLR were obtained from the Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) (Adler et al., 2003 ), Hadley Centre (Rayner et al., 2003 ) and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (Liebmann and Smith, 1996 ), respectively, while Japanese 25-year ReAnalysis (JRA-25) data (Onogi et al., 2007 ) were used as reference datasets for other climate variables. The key meteorological elements evaluated, domains considered, and reference datasets are summarized in Table S1.(1) S  corr   = ∑ i = 1  N   x  i   − x  ̅     ( y  i   − y  ̅  )   ∑ i = 1  N   x  i   − x  ̅     2   y  i   − y  ̅     2            (2) RMSE = 1  N   ∑ i = 1  N   x  i   − y  i      2           In equations 01 and 02, x i   refers to the GCM simulation, x  ̅    is the zonal mean of that simulation, y i   is the reference data, y  ̅    is the zonal mean of the reference data, and N  represents the total number of time series. Both RMSE  and Scorr  values were averaged over the evaluation period (1981–2000) and across the whole set of models analyzed. Thus, Scorr total average  and RMSE total average  were obtained. Then, an index score of 1 was assigned if the individual Scorr  of a particular model for simulation of a particular climate variable was greater than the overall average of Scorr  (IndexScorr  =1; Scorr model  ≥ Scorr total average ), and a score of 0 otherwise. Similarly, models were assigned index scores of 1 or 0 based on their individual RMSE  values (IndexRMSE  =1 if RMSE model  ≤ RMSE total average  and IndexRMSE  =0 if RMSE model  > RMSE total average ). If the index scores for both Scorr  and RMSE  for a particular model simulation were 1, a total index value of 1 was assigned (Indextotal =1; if IndexScorr  =1 and IndexRMSE  =1) while a value of 0 was assigned if only one index score for Scorr  or RMSE  was 1 (Indextotal =0; if IndexScorr  =1 and IndexRMSE  =0, or IndexScorr  =0 and IndexRMSE  =1). If both index scores were 0, models were given a total index value of −1 (Indextotal  =−1; if IndexScorr  =0 and IndexRMSE  =0). Finally, the scores calculated for each model corresponding to all climate variables were summed and models were ranked based on the total index values obtained. The scoring system employed in this study for model selection is summarized in supplementary Figure S1. The highest priority was given to the selection criteria for precipitation, as GCMs should be capable of simulating the seasonal and inter-annual variability of precipitation with reasonable accuracy over the study area and this value is the main input for the flood model.  2.1.2 Downscaling and bias correction GCM simulations tend to underestimate extreme rainfalls, show poor accuracy for seasonal variation, and overestimate the frequency of wet days. The three-step statistical bias-correction method described by Nyunt et al. (2013), (2016)  and available in DIAS was used in this study with reference to observed rainfall data obtained from the Asian Precipitation – Highly Resolved Observational Data Integration Towards Evaluation of Water Resources (APHRODITE) project (Yatagai et al., 2012 ). This study employs extreme rainfall bias correction based on the partial duration series (PDS), which uses events above a threshold considering both intensity and frequency. This bias correction method allows for the inclusion of more than one extreme event per year, as opposed to the traditional method based on the annual maximum series (AMS), which may neglect extremes exceeding the annual maximum rainfall of another year. Simple rank-order statistics of the entire time series were used to obtain the total frequency of wet days to correct for the wet day frequency error of GCM projections. Then, the same frequency of wet days was applied to the historical GCM outputs, and the rank of the last rainfall event from the observed data was defined as the threshold for correction. All rainfall intensities between the extreme and total rain day correction thresholds were classified as normally distributed for both GCM and observed time-series data in rank order, and a two-parameter gamma distribution was employed to correct biases in seasonal precipitation. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of monthly normal daily rainfall at a particular grid point is assumed to follow the gamma distribution function. Daily GCM and observed historical rainfall data are then fitted to a two-parameter gamma distribution for the 12 months of the year. Supplementary Section S1 provides a detailed explanation of the downscaling and bias correction methodology implemented in this study. Bias-corrected rainfall data at 16 points were resampled to the resolution of the RRI model grid (15-arcsec) using the Thiessen polygon method.   2.2 Flood modelling using the RRI model 2.2.1 Model structure Flood simulations were conducted using the two-dimensional RRI model, which can simultaneously simulate rainfall–runoff and flood inundation (Sayama et al., 2012 ). This model’s governing equations were derived from the mass balance (Eq. 03) and momentum (Eq. 04) equations, where h  is the height of the water from the local surface, q x   and q y   are the unit-width discharges in the x and y directions, r  is the rainfall intensity, f  is the infiltration rate, H  is the height of the water from the datum, ρ w   is the density of water, g  is gravitational acceleration, sgn  is the signum function, k a   is the lateral saturated hydraulic conductivity, d  is the soil depth times the effective porosity, and τ x   and τ y   are shear stresses in the x and y directions, respectively (Sayama, 2017 ). When inertia terms in the momentum equations for gradually varied unsteady flows were neglected under the diffusion wave approximation, Eqs. 05 and 06 can be obtained. The model considers slopes and river channels separately. The model assumes that both the slope and river are positioned within the same grid cell where a river channel is located. The channel is modelled as a single line vector along the centreline of the corresponding slope grid cell and serves as an additional flow path between grid cells aligned with the actual river course. Water exchange between the slope and river is determined from the water levels of the slope, river, levee crown, and ground. Four overtopping formulas, detailed by Iwasa and Inoue (1982)  and Sayama (2017) , are used to calculate this exchange. A crucial distinction between the RRI model and other inundation models is that it employs multiple discharge and hydraulic gradient relationships, enabling the simulation of both surface and subsurface flows using the same algorithm (Sayama et al., 2012 ). This model describes saturated subsurface flow using Darcy’s law, given by the first expressions of Eqs. 07 and 08 (when h ≤ d ), while the second expressions (d < h)  explain the combination of saturated subsurface flow and surface flow. In addition, the river geometry is assumed to be rectangular, and river geometry parameters along with other model parameters were set and optimized through a trial-and-error approach that considered saturated lateral subsurface flows to be dominant in the catchment, as described by Jayapadma et al. (2022a) . Further details about the model structure are available from Sayama et al. (2012) .(3) ∂ h  ∂ t   + ∂ q  x    ∂ x   + ∂ q  y    ∂ y   = r − f     (4a) ∂ q  x    ∂ t   + ∂ uq  x    ∂ x   + ∂ v q  x    ∂ y   = − gh ∂ H  ∂ x   − τ  x    ρ  w         (4b) ∂ q  y    ∂ t   + ∂ uq  y    ∂ x   + ∂ v q  y    ∂ y   = − gh ∂ H  ∂ y   − τ  y    ρ  w         (5) q  x   = − 1  n    h  5  3     ∂ H  ∂ x       sgn ∂ H  ∂ x          (6) q  y   = − 1  n    h  5  3     ∂ H  ∂ y       sgn ∂ H  ∂ y          (7) q x  = − k a  h ∂ H  ∂ x    ,  h ≤ d   − 1 n  h − d    5 3   ∂ H  ∂ x     sgn ∂ H  ∂ x    − k a  h ∂ H  ∂ x    ,  d < h         (8) q y  = − k a  h ∂ H  ∂ y    ,  h ≤ d   − 1 n  h − d    5 3   ∂ H  ∂ y     sgn ∂ H  ∂ y    − k a  h ∂ H  ∂ y    ,  d < h           2.2.2 Model settings and input data First, the model’s ability to simulate major flood events that occurred in the basin during the periods of May 2003, May 2016, and May 2017 was tested through an event-based calibration and validation process (Jayapadma et al., 2022a ). Then the RRI model subjected to event-based validation was optimized for long-term simulation incorporating evaporation data and APHRODITE rainfall data for the period of 1981–2000, as the same model was used for climate impact analysis (Jayapadma et al., 2024 ). Observed hydrometeorological data and river cross-sections at 10 locations along the river were obtained from the Department of Meteorology and the Department of Irrigation of Sri Lanka. The digital elevation model (DEM), and flow accumulation and flow direction data, were obtained from the United States Geological Survey, and hydrological data and maps were based on Shuttle Elevation Derivatives at multiple Scales (HydroSHEDS) with 15-arcsec (approximately 500 m) resolution (Lehner et al., 2008 ). Daily evapotranspiration data at 0.25° resolution were obtained from the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) (Rodell et al., 2004 ). For future flood simulations, we used CMIP5 monthly evaporation projections from the Copernicus Climate Data Store (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2018 ). Land-use maps were obtained from the Land Cover project of the European Space Agency’s Climate Change Initiative (ESA CCI-LC) (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2019 ). The input data used in this study and their sources are summarized in Table S2.   2.3 Land-use change assessment The land-use maps generated by ESA CCI-LC for 1992–2018 were obtained to assess temporal changes in the basin. Then the land-use map for 1992 was compared to the land-use projection from ESRI for the year 2050, which is based on the ESA CCI-LC dataset, to evaluate possible future changes in land use. The ESA land-use maps are based on the PROBA-V and S3-OLCI satellites and have spatial resolution of 0.002778° (approximately 300 m at the equator and around 200 m at mid-latitudes) (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2019 ). These maps can be used at various temporal and spatial scales and comply with the United Nations (UN) Land Cover Classification System (LCCS), making them compatible with the concept of plant functional types defined in many models (Di Gregorio, 2016 ). The land-use projection for Sri Lanka for the year 2050 with horizontal resolution of 300 m was downloaded from ESRI. This projection is based on the land cover maps from ESA CCI-LC. Land use in 2050 was projected by ESRI based on the patterns present in ESA land-use maps from 2010 to 2018 using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network (Esri and Clark Lab, 2021 ). Quantitative variables such as biomass, crop suitability, distance to airports, distance to cropland (2010), distance to primary roads, distance to railroads, distance to secondary roads, distance to settled areas, distance to urban areas (2010), elevation, gross domestic product, human influence, index population, density of precipitation, regions, slope, and temperature were used to create models to project past anthropogenic land-cover changes to the year 2050. Using the land-use maps described above, temporal changes in land use in the basin from 1992–2050 were calculated based on the four dominant land-use types in the basin (i.e., agricultural land, forest, shrubland and urban/built-up areas). The land-use map of the year 1999 and the projected land-use map for the year 2050 are shown in supplementary Figure S2. Across the Gin River basin, a slight reduction in forest area is expected in 2050 compared with the past (1992), when more than 50 % of the total area was covered with forest. Similarly, agricultural lands constituted 22.5 % of the basin area in 1992 and are expected to shrink to 17.5 % in 2050. In contrast, urban areas and shrublands are expected to expand by 2.75 % and 3.15 % in 2050, respectively. Supplementary section S3 summarizes the temporal changes in land use in the basin from 1992–2050 based on ESA land-use maps. To evaluate the potential impact of land-use changes on the inundated area in each subcatchment, land-use changes were studied at the subcatchment scale by dividing the basin area into three subcatchments: upstream, midstream, and downstream. These subcatchments were divided based on the locations of river gauging stations and have contrasting demographic and geographical characteristics. According to ESRI projections, each will be subjected to significant changes in terms of land use, as summarized in  Fig. 2 . The agricultural area in the upstream subcatchment is predicted to decrease by 18.75 % compared to 1992. Similar reductions of 20.14 % and 26.39 % are expected in agricultural land area in the mid- and downstream subcatchments, respectively. Apart from that, the most significant expansion was projected for shrublands, which increased in the upstream subcatchment by 28.80 %, and by 9.70 % and 7.32 % in the mid- and downstream areas, respectively. In the RRI simulations, slope parameters for soil depth, Manning’s roughness coefficient, porosity (gamma), and lateral saturated hydraulic conductivity (k a  ) for each land-use class were defined. These parameters incorporate potential changes in the dominant flow processes within the catchment resulting from the changes in land use.  2.4 RRI model performance assessment The simulated hydrographs at two river gauging stations, Baddegama and Thawalama, were compared to observations. Model performance was evaluated based on Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE ), volume ratio (V r  ), mean bias error (MBE ), and root mean square error (RMSE ), as defined in equations 09–12.
