Here, the historical climate corresponds to the period of 1980–2000, while 2040–2060 is the future time window considered. The simulation scenarios are summarized in  Table 1 . The results obtained from these simulations were compared with the historical simulations (HC-HLU) to assess possible changes in river discharge and inundation extent due to climate and land-use changes and to differentiate the changes associated with those causes.   3 Results 3.1 Flood model setup The river and slope parameters summarized in supplementary Tables S3 and S4 were optimized through a trial-and-error approach based on the model validated by Jayapadma et al., (2022a) . Table S5 presents the slope parameters defined for each land-use class, while Table S4 shows aerial weighted average of slope parameters across the floodplain. The calibrated parameters are in accordance with those used in previous studies (Rasmy et al., 2019; Sayama, 2017; Sayama et al., 2012; Yoshimoto and Amarnath, 2018 ). The validation of RRI simulation conducted by Jayapadma et al. (2024)  is summarized here. Simulated hydrographs based on daily APHRODITE rainfall, daily evaporation from GLDAS, and the land-use map for 1992 were compared with observed data from two gauging stations for the historical period 1980–2000. The model performance indices for the simulated river discharge at the downstream gauging station (Baddegama; NSE  = 0.72, V r  =0.778, MBE  = −13.08 m3 /s, RMSE  = 46.32 m3 /s) indicated reasonable agreement with the observed river discharge for the period 1980–2000 based on the high NSE  value (NSE  > 0.7), although the peak flows were underestimated (Gauch et al., 2023; Moriasi et al., 2007 ). The model performance indices at the upstream gauging station (Thawalama) indicated that the model underestimated both peak and low flows (NSE  = 0.41, V r  =0.684, MBE  = −13.47 m3 /s, RMSE  = 30.58 m3 /s). These discrepancies may stem from the coarser resolution of rainfall, evaporation, and topographic data in areas where catchment peak flow is predominantly generated through the dominant saturated subsurface and saturated excess overland flows as elaborated by Jayapadma et al. (2022a), (2024) . Despite the discrepancy in the upstream area, model performance was sufficient for application to climate impact assessment, particularly in the heavily flooded downstream portion of the basin (NSE  = 0.72) (Merz et al., 2011 ).  3.2 Impact of climate change on rainfall 3.2.1 GCM selection and bias correction Five GCMs, namely, ACCESS 1.0 (Bi et al., 2013 ), CESM.CAM5 (Neale et al., 2012 ), CMCC.CMS (Scoccimarro et al., 2011 ), CNRM-CM5 (Voldoire et al., 2013 ), and MPI.ESM.LR (Giorgetta et al., 2013 ), were selected based on the scoring system described in Section 2.1.1 . A summary of the GCM selection procedure and its results are provided in Supplementary Section S3. The GCMs projected rainfall over the area from 80°E to 80.5°E and 6°N to 6.5°N in 0.25° grid cells (16 points). The three-step bias correction method effectively corrected biases in the raw GCM projections according to APHRODITE data at all points.  Fig. 3  compares GCM projections before and after correction of extreme rainfall biases at a location (80.25° E, 6.25° N) near the Hiniduma gauging station. Although all GCMs except the CNRM.CM5 model underestimated extreme values (ranked in descending order based on comparison with the observed data), these biases were effectively removed through generalized Pareto model fitting, especially for the highest ranks. Similarly, biases for inter-seasonal rainfall were corrected effectively at the Hiniduma gauging station. All GCMs appear to underestimate monthly rainfall and fail to simulate the seasonal variation of rainfall between the two monsoon seasons. This deficiency could be due to the poor representation of the topography of Sri Lanka by models with coarse resolution, as it lies in the middle of the Indian Ocean (Nyunt et al., 2016 ). Despite the minor discrepancy in seasonal rainfall variability, the three-step bias correction method used in this study effectively eliminated biases at all stations, producing an appropriate precipitation projection for climate impact analysis from the GCM ensemble mean.  3.2.2 Temporal changes in rainfall A comparison of bias-corrected future monthly rainfall projected using the GCM ensemble mean with historical rainfall is shown in  Fig. 4 . The basin is predicted to receive increased rainfall with higher variability in the months of August to November (toward the end of the southwest monsoon season and the beginning of the second inter-monsoon season) in the future under the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario. On the other hand, extreme rainfall exceeding the 95th percentile of daily rainfall projected by the GCM ensemble mean under the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario is expected to increase significantly from 15.5 to 16.8 mm/day. In addition, the number of daily rainfall events exceeding the 95th percentile of historical daily rainfall is predicted to increase to 514 from 367 in the past. The GCM ensemble mean projected an increase in seasonal rainfall in the future except during the first inter-monsoon rain season from March to April, as shown in supplementary Figure S3. A very small increase (0.85 %) in rainfall was predicted for the northeast monsoon season, while increases of 9.7 % and 15.7 % were predicted for the southwest monsoon and second inter-monsoon seasons, respectively. Rainfall in the second inter-monsoon season is expected to decrease by 5.2 % compared to the past. Thus, rainfall during the southwest monsoon season, when the basin previously received the heaviest rainfall, will intensify further, continuing until the end of second inter-monsoon season. On the other hand, the northeast monsoon season showed no significant change in rainfall under the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario.   3.3 Temporal changes in land-use The assessment of land-use change dynamics produced interesting land-use conversions in the basin ( Fig. 5 ). Almost half of the agricultural land (42.03 km2 ; 48.24 %) in 1992 is expected to remain agricultural land in 2050, while 27.07 % will be converted to shrubland. A share of 18.90 % of the historical agricultural land will be converted into forest, and 5.79 % is projected to become urban areas. Accordingly, 171.63 km2  of the historical forest area (82 %) will remain forested in 2050. Although the conversion of forest into built-up areas is negligible, 11.65 % of forest area is projected to become shrublands. In addition, 16.67 % of urban areas will be converted to shrublands, with the rest remaining urban from 1992 to 2050. In contrast, shrublands appear to be a flexible land-use type, as 17.08 % will be converted to forest and 14.41 % to agricultural land. A significant expansion of shrubland was projected in the mid-stream catchment at the expense of 21.42 km2  of agricultural land and 14.58 km2  of forest. Similarly, urban areas in the mid-stream area will expand at the expense of 1.89 km2  of shrubland and 1.44 km2  of agricultural land. A total of 23.76 km2  of agricultural land is expected to become shrublands in the downstream subcatchment, which is 32.28 % of the total historical agricultural land area in 1992. Similarly, 34.50 % and 20.00 % of the historical forest and urban areas will be converted into shrublands in 2050, respectively. On the other hand, 10.53 km2  of historical shrublands and 7.83 km2  of agricultural lands are projected to undergo conversion to urban areas in the downstream subcatchment, as shown in Fig. 5 (c).  3.4 Impact of climate change on river flow The results obtained from the simulation scenarios HC-HLU and FC-HLU were compared to evaluate the possible impact of climate change on river flow. Both scenarios consider land use in 1992, while HC-HLU considers the 1980–2000 climate and FC-HLU considers the 2040–2060 climate. The flow duration curves ( Fig. 6 ) comparing historical and future daily discharge corresponding to the rainfall projected by the GCM ensemble mean revealed that high flows, defined as those exceeded by 5 % of recorded flows (Q5 ), are projected to increase by 5 % at the downstream gauging station and by 16 % at the upstream gauging station. In contrast, mean annual discharge (Qm ) is projected to decrease by 34 % and 25 % at the downstream and upstream gauging stations, respectively. This reduction in Qm  may affect water availability in the basin. The monthly river discharge corresponding to the rainfall projected by the GCM ensemble mean predicted decreased streamflow throughout the year except in October at the downstream gauging station (Baddegama;  Fig. 7 ). On the other hand, monthly river flow is expected to increase from August to October at the upstream gauging station (Thawalama). The month of maximum river flows is expected to shift from November in the past to October in the future at both gauging stations. This could be due to increased rainfall expected in the basin from the end of the southwest monsoon until the end of the second inter-monsoon season, as shown in Figure S3. In addition, future monthly river flow is expected to decrease significantly through the end of July at the downstream gauging station, even though no notable change in rainfall is expected relative to the historical climate. An increase in evapotranspiration in the future appears to drive this reduction as the daily average evapotranspiration projected by the GCM ensemble mean is 1.23 mm/d and 4.22 mm/d for past and future time windows, respectively.  3.5 Impact of climate change on future inundation The historical (scenario HC-HLU) and future (scenario FC-HLU) 20-year averages of annual maximum inundation extent generated using RRI were compared to identify possible changes, as shown in  Fig. 8 . The 20-year average annual maximum inundation area in the future projected using the GCM ensemble mean was 185.71 km2 , for the whole basin. This average was 179.23 km2  in the past, indicating an increase of 3.5 %. Of the total inundation extent predicted in the future using the GCM ensemble mean projections, 34.82 km2  was in the upstream subcatchment, 96.45 km2  in the midstream subcatchment, and 54.05 km2  in the downstream subcatchment. The upstream area of the basin is expected to experience a greater increase in inundation than the mid- and downstream areas of the basin, as the inundated area is to grow by 14 % in the upstream subcatchment, as shown in Fig. 8 . Inundated areas in the mid- and downstream are expected to increase by 2 % and 1 % on average compared to the past. This increase may be due to the increase in river flow expected during the southwest and second inter-monsoon seasons in the future in upstream areas of the basin. Although the upstream areas of the basin are mainly forested, this amplification of river flow and inundation may affect the mid- and downstream areas containing larger human settlements. Therefore, the expected increase in inundation extent driven by the increased high flows in the basin should be considered in basin planning and management. Furthermore, the ratios of mean (F(µ)) and variance (F(σ2 )) (Eq. 13 and Eq. 14 ) of the maximum inundation extent maps indicate that inundation extent will increase in the future, as summarized in Table S9, if the climate changes as projected by the GCM ensemble mean, in accordance with the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario.(13) F μ    = μ  future    μ  historical         (14) F σ  2      = σ  future  2    σ  historical  2           3.6 Impact of land-use change on river flow Quantile–quantile plots of future daily discharge distributions simulated under all simulation scenarios (HC-FLU, FC-FLU, FC-HLU) against the historical daily discharge distribution (HC-HLU) were constructed to compare and differentiate the impacts of climate and land-use changes on projected river flow, as shown in  Fig. 9 . From the comparison of scenarios considering the past climate with land use in 1992 (HC-HLU) and 2050 (HC-FLU), the change in land use does not appear to impact the river flow distribution at the two gauging stations investigated. In addition, the future river flow distributions will be similar if the climate changes according to the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario, despite the projected land-use changes. Thus, climate variability plays a greater role in altering surface rainfall–runoff processes in the Gin River basin than changes in land use.  3.7 Impact of land-use change on future inundation The RRI simulations indicated slight expansion of inundated area in the downstream part of the basin, which could be due to the predicted increase in human settlements in the future in the lower part of the downstream subcatchment ( Fig. 10 ). In addition, an area of 2.25 km2  that was flooded in the past will not be flooded in the future according to the RRI model simulations using GCM ensemble mean projections. The temporal change in inundation extent with only the land-use change projected by ESRI and no change in climate (comparison between scenarios HC-HLU and HC-FLU) is summarized in Fig. 10 . The total annual inundated area projected for the scenario HC-FLU is 174.23 km2 , while an extent of 179.23 km2  is projected for scenario HC-HLU, indicating a decrease of 2.8 %. The summary statistics of the maximum inundation extent maps verified this result, indicating no significant change in inundated area in the future under these conditions (F(µ)=1, F(σ2 )=1). If land use in the catchment changes with no change in climate, the inundated area is expected to decrease in the upstream, midstream, and downstream areas by 0.3 %, 0.68 %, and 6.83 %, respectively. The expansion of forests and shrublands converted from agricultural areas in the up- and midstream areas of the basin appears to increase the roughness of the floodplain, slowing the flood waters, reducing peak flows, and ultimately reducing inundation extent. Although the urban areas in the downstream portion of the basin are expected to expand, the effect of the expansion of shrublands appears to play the dominant role in reducing the downstream inundated area (discussed in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 ).  3.8 Impacts of changes in climate and land use on future river flow and inundation The river discharge projected with the GCM ensemble mean when the land-use projections for 2050 were incorporated into the RRI simulation along with the future climate (scenario FC-FLU) was similar to the discharge simulated under scenario FC-HLU considering only climate change (Fig. 9 ). This finding suggests that the land-use changes projected for 2050 will not significantly alter streamflow generation, whereas climate change is expected to impact streamflow. High flows are expected to increase (+2.68 %), along with a decrease in mean flows (−33.74 %), similar to the river flow prediction of scenario FC-HLU. Although the expansion of urban areas in the downstream portion of the basin is expected to increase runoff due to the increase in impervious area (Bronstert et al., 2002 ), the expansion of forests and shrublands will decrease the total runoff generated in the basin. The inundated area simulated by RRI using the GCM ensemble mean projections for scenario FC-FLU was 183.06 km2 , while this area was 179.22 km2  for scenario HC-HLU, indicating a 2.14 % increase. This amount is smaller than the increment projected due to the change in climate alone (i.e., the change from scenario HC-HLU to FC-HLU of 3.5 %). The RRI simulations projected an increase in maximum inundation area across the entire basin, as indicated by the summary statistics (F(µ)=1.07, and F(σ2 ) =1.42). The total inundated area predicted through RRI simulations corresponding to the GCM ensemble mean projections (scenario FC-FLU) in the downstream subcatchment was 50.20 km2 , whereas the equivalent area was 53.50 km2  in the past (scenario HC-HLU), indicating a decrease in inundated area by 6 % in the downstream subcatchment ( Fig. 11 ). On the other hand, the inundation extent is projected to increase from 94.72 km2  to 97.32 km2  (2.76 % increment) and from 30.55 km2  to 35.11 km2  (14.84 % increment) in the mid- and upstream areas, respectively. The predicted increase in inundated area in the upstream sub-basin may be due to the elevated discharge predicted at the upstream gauging station. The conversion of agricultural land into shrublands and the reduction of river discharge in the mid- and downstream areas appear to reduce flow velocity. This reduction in velocity will ultimately reduce the inundation depth, despite the expansion of urban areas in downstream areas.  3.9 Impact of land-use management on future inundation under a changing climate  Fig. 12  shows the variation in inundated area if land use is managed as per the ESRI projections, with the climate changing in accordance with the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario (comparison between scenarios FC-HLU and FC-FLU). The total inundated area in the basin will be reduced from 185.54 km2  to 183.07 km2  (1.34 %), as predicted by the RRI simulations corresponding to GCM ensemble mean projections. Although significant reductions cannot be achieved in the up- and midstream areas, the inundated area in the downstream subcatchment can be reduced by 7.11 %, from 54.05 km2  (scenario FC-HLU) to 50.20 km2  (scenario FC-FLU). The downstream inundated area can be reduced if land-use changes in the basin are regulated in accordance with the ESRI projections, particularly the conversion of agricultural land into shrublands.   4 Discussion 4.1 Temporal changes in rainfall Considering the results presented in Section 3.2 , the projected intensification of rainfall during the monsoon seasons, excluding the first inter-monsoon season, corroborates recent climate impact assessments across various climate zones and the mountainous region of Sri Lanka (Asian Development Bank, 2022; Illangasingha et al., 2023 ). Although a decrease in rainfall on the southwestern slope of the central hills (where the Gin River basin is situated) is anticipated during the first inter-monsoon season under the RCP 8.5 emissions scenario according to the same study, our findings indicate a negligible change in rainfall for this period. This difference may be due to the different modelling approaches and emissions scenarios considered in the assessments. The impact of the projected intensification of rainfall during monsoons on river flow was studied in detail, as river flow affects water availability and the occurrence of extreme flood events (discussed in Section 4.2 ).  4.2 Impacts of climate change on future river flow and inundation According to the results presented in Sections 3.4 and 3.5 , high flows are expected to increase by 5 % at the downstream gauging station and by 16 % at the upstream gauging station in the Gin River basin. Although climate impact assessments in neighbouring river basins in Sri Lanka have documented similar trends of increasing rainfall during monsoon and inter-monsoon seasons (Asian Development Bank, 2022; Illangasingha et al., 2023; Selvarajah et al., 2021; Sirisena et al., 2021 ), no definitive pattern (increase or decrease) of changes in river flow has been reported. However, discharge in the upstream portion of the Nilwala river basin, which is adjacent to the Gin River basin, is projected to increase through the end of 2099 under the RCP 4.5 emission scenario (Chathuranika et al., 2022 ). This increase may influence and intensify the flood hazard in both river basins, a finding that our results support. Furthermore, the shift in the timing of maximum monthly river flow observed in our study corresponds with their findings, providing valuable insights for the agricultural and water resource management sectors. This information, coupled with data on reduced mean river flow, will support informed decision-making (Chathuranika et al., 2022 ).  4.3 Temporal changes in land use and their impact on future river flow and inundation In summary, significant expansion of shrubland was predicted throughout the basin, and concurrently, built-up areas were projected to expand in the densely populated mid- and downstream subcatchments (Section 3.3 ). These changes will affect inundation extent and vulnerability to flooding according to the results presented in Sections 3.6 and 3.7 . We identified a notable decrease in inundated area following the transformation of agricultural land into shrubland, potentially due to enhanced floodplain roughness. This observation is in accordance with prior research indicating that conversion of natural vegetation into agricultural land reduces flood plain roughness, changing river morphology and resulting in increased runoff and accelerated sediment transport, thereby ultimately destabilizing river systems (Bekele et al., 2019; Horton et al., 2021; Ibitoye, 2021; Langat et al., 2019; Prokop et al., 2020 ). Although we did not directly evaluate the effects of land-use changes on surface and groundwater flows within our flood simulations, our observations suggest that transitioning back to more natural vegetation may mitigate these impacts, highlighting the potential of vegetation restoration as a sustainable land-use management strategy to reduce flood inundation (Maaß et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, the increase in impervious area in the downstream region may lead to higher velocities of inundation flow and greater inundated area, as the transformation of natural vegetation into unvegetated landscapes typically reduces surface roughness, which in turn accelerates flow velocity (Bekele et al., 2019 ). Despite limited direct evidence of the transition from agricultural land to shrublands impacting flood flow and inundation, previous studies have shown that agricultural expansion at the expense of natural vegetation such as woodlands and bushlands results in reductions of infiltration and canopy interception. These reductions subsequently increase surface runoff. On the other hand, restoring vegetation cover has been linked to a significant decrease in surface runoff, illustrating the protective role of natural vegetation against flooding (Gebremicael et al., 2019; Nyssen et al., 2010 ). Additionally, the transformation of tropical forests into non-forested areas may considerably heighten flood risks due to the exposure of compacted, bare soil to intense rainfall, leading to greater and more rapid discharge. The mechanisms underlying this change include decreased infiltration and interception, increased surface runoff, and markedly decreased evapotranspiration and groundwater recharge (Horton et al., 2021; Szwagrzyk et al., 2018 ).  4.4 Impacts of changes in climate and land use on future river flow and inundation According to the results described in Section 3.8 , the impact of climate change on runoff generation is demonstrated to be more significant than the combined effect of climate and land-use changes in the basin (Fig. 9 ), similar to previous reports (Barlage et al., 2002; El-Khoury et al., 2015; He et al., 2019 ). Although the combined effects of climate change and land-use changes did not significantly impact runoff generation (Fig. 12 ), the combined impacts of climate and land-use changes appear to significantly alter the predicted inundation area. The projected conversion of forest and agricultural lands into shrublands appears to drive this change in inundation area, which may be aggravated by static land use. Determining whether climate change or land-use transformation is the primary driver behind changes in river flow and flood extremes is a challenge. This difficulty arises from a multitude of factors related to both the processes being investigated and the methodologies employed for their assessment. Key factors include the size of the catchment, the climate (e.g., tropical or humid), the nature of rainfall processes, the dominant flow processes (such as subsurface flows), the scale at which changes are evaluated, and the inherent uncertainties of the assessment methodologies. Each of these elements plays a crucial role in influencing observed hydrological changes, complicating efforts to isolate the impacts of climate change from those of land-use transformation (Blöchl et al., 2007; Cuo, 2016; Davies-Barnard et al., 2015; Kayitesi et al., 2022; Ranzi et al., 2017 ). Specifically, climate change (in terms of precipitation and temperature) directly impacts runoff and flood levels, whereas changes in land use modify the response of the watershed to precipitation by changing hydrological processes such as interception, infiltration, and evapotranspiration (Davies-Barnard et al., 2015; Kayitesi et al., 2022; Petchprayoon et al., 2010 ). Moreover, these changes in land use can cause changes in river morphology, such as floodplain roughness, as detailed in Section 4.3 . Therefore, the reduction of inundated area despite increased discharge in upstream areas resulting from elevated rainfall induced by climate change can be attributed to increased flood plain roughness. This increase in roughness is a consequence of changes in riparian vegetation, illustrating the complex interdependencies between climate dynamics, land-use practices, and hydrological responses.  4.5 Possible flood adaptation measures Considering the results shown in Section 3.9  and the discussion in Section 4.3 , the conversion of agricultural land into shrublands can be encouraged as a sustainable flood mitigation measure worldwide, as this change will support the restoration of riparian forests (Dixon et al., 2019; Nakamura, 2022; Taki, 2022 ). Soft engineering solutions, such as the restoration of riparian forests ( Fig. 13 ) at the subcatchment scale, have been reported to reduce flood wave velocities, ultimately significantly reducing the flood peak magnitude (Dixon et al., 2016 ). Furthermore, riparian forests are a traditional flood mitigation practice historically employed in Japan, along with open and ring levees. These forests represent functional green infrastructure that effectively utilizes local ecosystem services for disaster prevention (Nakamura et al., 1997; Taki, 2022; Yoshimura et al., 2005 ). Abandoned agricultural lands are more easily converted into urban areas than into riparian forests without proper management. Therefore, strict administrative and management plans are required for conversion of abandoned agricultural lands into riparian forests. The effects of riparian forests depend on the scale at which the riparian forests are restored and the maturity of the riparian forests. Generally, 40–50 years are needed for full restoration and maturity of a riparian forest, when it will have the significant impacts on flood peak reduction that are expected. Some studies have proposed engineering interventions such as log jams until the riparian forests are fully restored (Dixon et al., 2019 ). The primary mechanism through which this reduction occurs is an increase in roughness in the flood plain through the creation of obstacles that the water must flow around. These obstacles cause the water to slow down and spread out, which can reduce the flood peak, enhancing flood storage (Thomas and Nisbet, 2012, 2007 ). Additionally, by increasing habitat complexity, riparian forests can attract fish and other aquatic organisms, which can in turn reduce erosion and stabilize the channel, enhancing the ecological, hydrological, and geomorphological functions of the river and further reducing flood peaks (Nakamura, 2022 ). Therefore, the newly expanded shrublands in the up- and midstream subcatchments of the Gin River basin could be converted into riparian forests, which would reduce flow velocities and inundation extent in the downstream subcatchment despite climate change increasing river flow at the upstream gauging station. Traditionally, flood management practices have focused on controlling or reducing the flood hazard through structural defences such as dams, levees, and retention basins, which are designed for a specific flood event (Merz et al., 2010b ). However, such measures have limitations and may not protect against extreme floods, potentially even exacerbating flood risks (Di Baldassarre et al., 2013; Merz et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ). Consequently, these structural approaches are now being supplemented with non-structural strategies under on broader, risk-based flood management policies that account for complex human–flood interactions as well as ecological considerations. Flood risk is defined as the combination of the likelihood of a flood event and its potential impacts on human life, property, and the environment. It includes three main components: hazard (the physical flooding event, characterized by discharge, duration, and inundated area), exposure (people, property, and assets located in flood-prone areas), and vulnerability (the susceptibility of these elements to damage from flooding) (Merz et al., 2010a ). Given the increasing intensity of flood hazards, strengthening or expanding structural defences (e.g. heightening levees) is becoming unsustainable (Lallemant et al., 2021; Merz et al., 2021; Nakamura, 2022 ), and thus a shift toward non-structural measures to effectively mitigate flood risks is essential, as suggested by this study.  4.6 Limitations and future directions One major limitation of this study is that the changes in evapotranspiration parameters were not fully modelled. The conversion of forests and agricultural lands into shrublands appears to reduce runoff while increasing evapotranspiration, as reported in previous studies, influencing catchment hydrology in various ways (Kayitesi et al., 2022; Li et al., 2009 ). Changes in soil water content and evapotranspiration may affect the runoff generation process due to changes in land use, especially the expansion of shrublands, and these changes should be modelled in future research. Given the limited data available on RRI model parameters for each land use class (especially the slope parameters), the parameters were chosen on a trial-and-error basis, referring to similar studies conducted in comparable river basins. This approach could introduce bias into the final predictions. Therefore, it is recommended to conduct a comprehensive sensitivity analysis for all parameters for each land use class to minimize this uncertainty. This will help verify the optimal parameter combinations for each land use class and further validate the temporally defined slope parameters in this study. Moreover, some studies have found that land-use change dominates or is equally responsible for the runoff alteration process compared to climate change (Priyambodoho et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016 ), contrary to our observations. Therefore, we must deepen our understanding of the factors driving flood disasters (both climatic and anthropogenic) through interdisciplinary research to seek effective adaptation strategies. Because we used the average of GCM ensemble projections, the uncertainties propagated by each GCM into the discharge and inundation simulations were not evaluated. Differences in assumptions regarding GCM structure, natural variability, parameterization approximation, and numerical methods for solving climatic equations can lead to variation in outputs among GCMs, even when the same initial boundary conditions and emission scenarios are used (Altamirano del Carmen et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2019; McFarlane, 2011 ). This variation highlights the critical need to address uncertainties in GCM projections and select the best overall models through the use of GCM ensembles for each specific application, as no single model can achieve superior performance at both historical climate simulation and future climate projection (Gu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, we utilized a statistical downscaling method to bridge the resolution gap between raw GCM outputs and to correct biases due to the scope of the study and the limited computational resources available. The primary limitation of statistical downscaling methods lies in the assumption of a stationary statistical relationship between large-scale and local-scale climate variables over time, including both past and future periods. This assumption may not hold, considering the nonlinear and nonstationary nature of the evolving climate. Additionally, statistical downscaling methods require long-term observational data to establish robust statistical relationships for a specific region (Johnson and Sharma, 2015; Lafon et al., 2013; Maraun, 2016; Piani et al., 2010; Smitha et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Dynamic downscaling is preferred by researchers for its capacity to accurately capture systematic characteristics related to topography, climatic dynamics, and other factors at high resolution (Adachi and Tomita, 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Therefore, we recommend dynamic downscaling using a suitable regional climate model based on the recommendations of Souma et al. (2013b), (2013a)  in future work. This approach will facilitate detailed assessment of the climatic conditions specific to the study area at a high resolution, as well as the potential impacts on flooding, providing valuable insights for comparative analysis. We also recommend that future research focus on quantifying the uncertainties originating from each stage, namely, GCM selection, downscaling, and bias correction, and their impacts on future flood simulations. In addition, the use of scenario-based land use projections based on ground data in future studies may help reduce uncertainties that could stem from the ESRI land use predictions used in this study. Further research directions may also include evaluation of the impacts of climate and land-use changes on flooding under alternative emission scenarios, such as RCP 8.5 or the new shared socioeconomic pathways defined in the CMIP6 dataset, and assessing the associated flood risks.   5 Conclusions The impacts of climate and land-use changes on future flooding in the Gin River basin were investigated using the RRI model and GCM predictions. The RRI model was calibrated, validated, and verified to simulate flood flow and inundation in the Gin River basin with reasonable accuracy, as indicated by model performance indices (NSE > 0.7 at the downstream gauging station), despite underestimation of peak flows at Thawalama gauging station. Overall, the results demonstrate that the model simulated flood flows in the basin with good accuracy. The main conclusions drawn from the flood simulations using the validated RRI model and bias-corrected GCM projections are summarized below.(1) The Gin River basin will receive increased rainfall throughout the year, except from March to April. Rainfall during the southwest monsoon and second inter-monsoon will increase by 9.7 % and 15.7 %, respectively, in the future under the RCP 4.5 emission scenario.  (2) Comparison of land-use maps from 1992 to 2050 indicated that human settlements will expand in the downstream areas of the basin, while a significant portion of the agricultural land (27 %) in the basin will be converted into shrubland by 2050.  (3) Flood simulations that consider only the effect of climate change using the validated RRI model indicate that high flows will increase by 16 % and 4 % at Thawalama and Baddegama, respectively, relative to historical data. On the other hand, mean river flow in the basin is expected to decrease by 25 % and 34 % on average compared to past levels at the upstream and downstream gauging stations, respectively. In addition, monthly river flow is expected to fall at the downstream gauging station and rise at the upstream gauging station under the projected climate.  (4) The simulated annual maximum inundation extent averaged over 20 years under the future climate is 3.5 % greater than the corresponding extent over the past due to climate change under the RCP 4.5 emission scenario.  (5) Climate change appears to be the dominant factor affecting runoff generation in the Gin River basin, rather than land-use changes. However, the combined effects of climate and land-use changes compensate for the impact of climate change on inundation. Total inundation extent in the basin could be reduced by 1.3 % if land-use changes are regulated in accordance with the ESRI projections, compared to a scenario where land use remains static under the RCP 4.5 emission scenario. In particular, the conversion of agricultural land into riparian forests drives this reduction.  (6) Riparian forests can reduce flood velocities by enhancing flood plain roughness, which can in turn decrease both the inundated area and flow velocities downstream. The implementation of sustainable land-use management plans may reduce the inundated area in the downstream subcatchment by 7 %, despite the expansion of urban areas. Therefore, restoration of riparian forests in the basin is recommended as an adaptation measure to minimize the damage associated with climate change.    Our study emphasizes the significance of integrated assessment of the impacts of climate and land-use change on water resource management, particularly for water supply and flood management. Our findings highlight the potential to mitigate damage from increased frequency of high flows, which are projected to grow by 16 % at Thawalama (upstream) and 4 % at Baddegama (downstream) due to climate change, through facilitating the conversion of agricultural areas into riparian forests. This change could reduce the inundated area in the basin by 1.3 %, with a 7 % reduction in downstream areas. These findings provide a thorough explanation of the interactions between climate and land-use changes and their impacts on future flood flows and inundation, which will aid in the development of effective flood mitigation and adaptation strategies. 1 Introduction Shale gas is stored as free, dissolved, and adsorbed under in-situ  conditions (Le et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ). The Klinkenberg effect increases the Kapp   of porous media to gases at low pressures (Chen et al., 2020a , b , 2021 ). This non-Darcy phenomenon occurs because the gas mean free path is similar to the pore size in low-permeability rocks like shale. Consequently, gas molecules collide more often with pore walls than with each other. This apparent increase in permeability differs significantly from the interaction between liquids and the pore surfaces (Chen et al., 2021 ; Qin et al., 2018 ). The dimensionless Knudsen number (Kn  ), representing the ratio of gas mean free path to the macroscopic length scale of a physical system, classifies flow regimes in a nanopore system, as shown in Fig. 1  : (1)  continuum flow regime (Kn   < 10−3 , Fig. 1(a) ) – the gas flow follows Darcy's law, driven by filtration without any major impacts from gas molecules' interactions with the adsorption layer or the pore surfaces; (2)  slip flow regime (10−3  < Kn   < 10−1 , Fig. 1(b) ) – both collisions with the pore walls and other gas molecules are significant, such that the velocity at the pore walls matches that inside the pore space; (3)  transitional flow regime (10−1  < Kn   < 10, Fig. 1(c) ) – both slip flow and Knudsen diffusion are substantial; (4)  Knudsen diffusion regime (Kn   > 10, Fig. 1(d) ) – gas molecules move through the pores by diffusion, with significant collisions with pore walls (Knudsen, 1909 ); theses flow mechanisms are considered as the non-Darcy flow behaviours in our study (Cui, 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Roy et al., 2003 ; Yan et al., 2016 ; Zhong et al., 2015 ). Gas transport mechanisms are strongly pressure-dependent, as lower pressures increase the mean free path of gas molecules, leading to more interactions with pore walls and altering the flow dynamics (Chen et al., 2020a , b ; Wang and Li, 2004 ). The effects of non-Darcy flow physics on pore network conductivity can be described by Kapp   (Cui et al., 2018 ; Guo et al., 2015 ; Wu and Olson, 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Many experimental studies showed that Kapp   increases with decreasing pressure, attributing this change to gas slippage rather than compaction alone (Heller et al., 2014 ; Moghadam and Chalaturnyk, 2015 ; Yang et al., 2018 ). Darcy's permeability does not describe flow behaviour in nanopores, leading to the development of numerous Kapp   models (Table 1  ). However, these models are not readily available in most commercial or open-source flow simulators. Few recent studies have presented strategies for considering the effects of non-Darcy flows. For instance, the numerical analysis of Shen et al. (2016)  modelled only gas diffusion via a set of embedded functions in a commercial simulator, ignoring other flow mechanisms like slip flow due to the lack of a comprehensive Kapp   model. Wang and Marongiu-Porcu (2015)  presented a mathematical framework for coupling a Kapp   model (albeit Knudsen diffusion was ignored). Their approach was limited to their own 2D shale-gas reservoir simulator and did not apply to other typical flow simulators. Guo et al. (2014)  also developed mathematical models where Kapp   was incorporated into the 2D flow calculations of their in-house codes. This work aims to formulate a Kapp   modelling scheme that is efficient and compatible with the 3D UDFM method. The strategy can be readily implemented in other simulators. Integrating Kapp   modelling and 3D DFN is challenging (Rocha et al., 2017 ; Srinivasan et al., 2018 ). Rubin et al. (2019)  conducted a numerical study that updated the matrix Kapp   based on an empirical model but ignored Knudsen diffusion and modelled only a limited number of evenly-spaced natural fractures. Wang and Marongiu-Porcu (2015)  incorporated a randomly distributed DFN and Kapp   modelling in their mathematical model; however, despite the issues mentioned earlier, their model is limited to 2D. Our previous work (Zhong and Leung, 2019 , 2020a , b ) incorporated 3D stochastic DFNs and a Kapp   updating scheme in a commercial simulator. However, the DFN model is upscaled into a dual-porosity dual-permeability (DPDK) model for flow calculations. One challenge with the traditional DPDK approach is that connections between adjacent fracture cells may not be captured correctly during upscaling if the fracture plane is not aligned with the grid axes (Xu and Leung, 2022 ). Other studies demonstrated that DPDK is inadequate for simulating long fractures orthogonal to the grid axes (Lee et al., 2001 ; Moinfar et al., 2011 ). The method in this study mitigates this issue by generating unstructured Voronoi mesh cells. A correction algorithm is also implemented to refine flux calculations for off-axis fractures (Sweeney et al., 2020 ). Fluid flow and mass transfer in fractured subsurface environments occur in both the porous matrix and the embedded fracture networks (Robinson et al., 2015 ). The matrix provides storage capacity for long-term processes, while fractures offer rapid flow pathways (Neuman, 2005 ; Johnson et al., 2021 ). Modelling the interaction between these two physical systems is crucial (Sweeney et al., 2020 ). Models for fractured porous media fall into three categories: discrete fracture network models (DFN), discrete fracture-matrix models (DFM), and continuum/multi-continuum models. In the DFN approach, 2D lines or 3D planar polygons explicitly represent fracture properties and geometry (Hyman et al., 2019 ). The fracture network is meshed for transport and flow simulations, but the matrix is not modelled, limiting DFN's application to scenarios with ultra-low permeability or very short time scales (Delay and Bodin, 2001 ; Painter et al., 2008 ). In contrast, DFM models explicitly represent the matrix and fracture network using unstructured meshes, but they are computationally challenging with complex fracture networks (Berre et al., 2018 ; Chen and Leung, 2020 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Srinivasan and Leung, 2022 ). Continuum modelling offers a viable alternative (Hartley and Joyce, 2013 ; Lichtner et al., 2015 ; Moinfar et al., 2013 ; Neuman, 2005 ). This technique involves upscaling properties (Hadgu et al., 2017 ; Jackson et al., 2000 ; Oda, 1985 ). It captures matrix and fracture flow while handling complex, stochastically generated fracture networks, though it may lose small fracture details during upscaling. DFNWORKS, developed at Los Alamos National Laboratory, is a parallelized suite for creating 3D DFN and simulating flow and transport, crucial for studying fractured media from millimetres to kilometres (Hyman et al., 2015a ). Its DFNGEN module combines FRAM (Feature Rejection Algorithm for Meshing) with the LAGRIT meshing toolbox to stochastically generate 3D DFNs and high-quality meshes optimized for high-performance computing (Hyman et al., 2014 ). Another component, DFNFLOW, uses PFLOTRAN for simulating flow, and DFNTRANS, though not used in our study, offers a Lagrangian approach for transport simulation. PFLOTRAN, addressing nonlinear partial differential equations for multiphase, multicomponent flow in porous materials (Hammond et al., 2011 , 2014 ; Lichtner et al., 2015 ), works on various platforms and leverages PETSc (Portable Extensible Toolkit for Scientific Computation) libraries for parallelization (Balay et al., 1997 ). It handles diverse processes, including the Richards equation, two-phase flow and complex reactive transport, offering fully implicit Newton-Raphson and operator-splitting methods for equation solving. DFNWORKS and PFLOTRAN have been implemented in various recent studies, including CO2  sequestration (Lu et al., 2015 ; Makedonska et al., 2015 , 2018 ), nuclear waste repositories (Hammond and Lichtner, 2010 ; Hyman et al., 2015b , 2016a , b ) and gas reservoir energy extraction (Lovell et al., 2018 ; Makedonska et al., 2020 ; Mudunuru et al., 2020 ; Karra et al., 2015 ; Valera et al., 2018 ), as well as fractured reservoir characterization and production history matching (Jaysaval et al., 2023 ; Johnson et al., 2017 ; Redoloza et al., 2023 ). In terms of modelling hydraulically fractured shale reservoirs, Karra et al. (2015)  integrated DFN modelling with a residence-time particle-tracking approach to capture gas diffusion effects in the matrix, successfully reproducing production decline curves and investigating several physical mechanisms. Lovell et al. (2018)  extended this model to predict gas travel times through diffusion from matrix to tributary fracture zones (TFZ) and advective travel times from TFZ to larger fractures. However, both studies did not physically model matrix pressure distribution and fluid flow, omitting mechanisms like gas slippage and considering only single-phase flow. Thus, there is potential to enhance the modelling framework of DFNWORKS to capture the dynamic processes transpiring within both the matrix and fractures. The Upscaled Discrete Fracture Matrix model (UDFM) is an innovative computational geometry-based upscaling approach designed to capture dynamic interactions within and between subsurface fracture networks and their surrounding porous matrix (Sweeney et al., 2020 ). It can be directly implemented within the DFNWORKS framework. UDFM upscales key fracture attributes and integrates them with matrix properties. These integrated attributes are then represented within an unstructured, spatially variable continuum mesh. The resolution of this mesh is adjusted around fractures to preserve the geometric and topological integrity of the fracture network while enhancing the accuracy of matrix-fracture flow approximation. The UDFM approach employs the Delaunay mesh and its dual Voronoi mesh, making it compatible with existing multiphysics simulators. However, the existing UDFM workflow presents several notable limitations. Firstly, the upscaling process overlooks rock properties (e.g., density, thermal properties) and rock-fluid functions (e.g., relative permeabilities) within the upscaled "fracture" cells that encompass both fracture and matrix elements. Secondly, the well package function in DFNWORKS is currently not compatible with systems developed using UDFM. Finally, limited research has employed UDFM within DFNWORKS for modelling hydraulically fractured shale gas reservoirs, where gas flow within the nanopores of the matrix is notably complex. Srinivasan et al. (2021)  presented a novel workflow for shale gas reservoirs that combines reduced-order models and machine learning to address real-time reservoir management challenges. However, this study primarily focused on enhancing the modelling of fracture networks and did not improve matrix flow modelling. It is essential to capture the variations in overall conductivity within the matrix resulting from pressure changes (Klinkenberg effect). In this study, we aim to explore the full potential of UDFM and enhance its capability to accurately capture the dynamic processes occurring within and between fractures and matrix when modelling fractured shale gas reservoirs. 3D stochastic DFNs representing the secondary fracture (SF) networks are generated, upscaled into octree-refined continuum meshes using the UDFM method, and then subjected to multiphase flow simulations in DFNWORKS. The existing DFNWORKS framework has several limitations when computing upscaled parameters. Therefore, novel upscaling equations are formulated to assign appropriate rock properties and rock-fluid functions to the octree-refined meshes. In addition, an innovative coupling scheme facilitates updating Kapp   and captures the effects of non-Darcy flow. A new well model representation ensures our UDFM formulation is compatible with the octree mesh. All these modifications are implemented directly in the DFNWORKS source codes. The proposed strategies are particularly flexible and can be adopted in other commercial/open-source reservoir-simulation frameworks or packages.  2 Methodology DFNWORKS 2.5 is used to generate stochastic 3D DFN models and conduct complex flow simulations. In this study, it runs on an open-source, Debian-based Linux operating system – Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS. 2.1 Discrete fracture network 3D stochastic DFNs are generated using the FRAM (Hyman et al., 2014 ), as shown in Fig. 2  . Fracture networks with multiple families, multiple regions/layers with various fracture densities, in-fracture aperture/transmissivity variability, stochastic distributions (i.e. lognormal, truncated power law, exponential distributions), geometries (i.e. elliptical, rectangular), sizes, orientations and intensities are permissible.  2.2 Upscaled discrete fracture matrix modelling The UDFM (Sweeney et al., 2020 ), as implemented in DFNWORKS, creates a 3D, spatially variable and octree-refined continuum mesh of the generated DFN and its surrounding matrix. Upscaled equivalent parameters are derived for the matrix-fracture system (Figs. 3(c)   and (d )). The octree-refined mesh, created in the near-fracture regions, maintains the fracture network's topological and geometric integrity while improving the accuracy of the dynamic gradient at the matrix-fracture intersection. 2.2.1 Upscaling of rock properties Suppose only a matrix exists in the control volume; the cell is labelled a "matrix" cell, with its porosity and permeability assigned using the matrix properties (ϕM   and kM  ). It is important to note that the upscaling model for relative permeability has been simplified to reduce computational efforts. A justification is that this aspect is not the primary focus of this paper. The idea is to incorporate the influence of the matrix in the cells that contain both fractures and matrix and not simply modify the associated fracture properties. We intend to explore and implement more elaborate models to enhance the upscaling process in future work. 2.3.2 Workflow of the upscaling method Multiple (n ) sets of upscaled rock-fluid functions corresponding to different fracture volume fractions are created: ϕF   is adopted as an indicator to determine which set of rock properties should be assigned for a cell. The entire workflow, as shown in Fig. 4  , is implemented externally by a code written in MATLAB (MathWorks, 2021 ).   2.4 Well representation A production well representation in the octree-refined continuum mesh is implemented using the well package function of DFNWORKS. A modification is made to be compatible with the UDFM method (Fig. 5  ). Well coordinates are converted to a polyline and expanded to a volume with a radius, where the nodes are tagged as “well nodes” in the continuum mesh. The source code is modified in Python 3.6 in the Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS system (Van Rossum and Drake Jr, 1995 ).  2.5 Flow simulation PFLOTRAN 3.0 (Hammond et al., 2011 ; Lichtner et al., 2015 ) is an open-source, parallelized, multiphysics, subsurface flow and reactive transport code integrated with DFNWORKS. It uses a fully implicit backward Euler method with Newton-Krylov iteration to solve the flow and heat equations and a two-point flux-based finite volume scheme for discretization. A two-phase liquid water-gas flow simulation mode is used here. The governing mass conservation equation is shown in Eq. (2012)  and originally developed by Javadpour (2009)  is adopted; it incorporates slip flow and Knudsen diffusion. Darabi et al. (2012)  state that the model is scale-invariant (i.e., the form of the equation remains valid even upscaling from one scale to another) and applicable over a broad range of the Knudsen number. Many previous studies demonstrated reliable results with the model (Naraghi and Javadpour, 2015 ; Singh et al., 2014 ; Wu et al., 2015a , b ; Zhong and Leung, 2019 , 2020a , b ).(15) K a p p   =  μ M  R T ρ a v g     ϕ M  τ  ( δ ′  )   D f  − 2   D k  + k D  ( 1 + b P   )   ,     (16) D k  =  2 R a v g    3  ( 8 R T  π M   )   0.5   ,     (17) b = ( 8 π R T  M  )   0.5   μ R a v g    ( 2 α  − 1  )   ,     where,(18) α = 1 − log 10  ( 1 + K n 0.7   )  ,     (19) K n  = B T  2  π R a v g   ( R m c   )   2  P   ,     (20) δ ′  = R m  2 R a v g     ,      Eq. (15)  incorporates the contributions of Knudsen diffusion and slip flow (Javadpour et al., 2007 ). In this model, Kapp   [m2 ] is a function of pore pressure (P  [Pa]), assumed to be the gas phase pressure in this study. µ  [Paˑs] denotes gas viscosity; M  [kg/kmol] is the molar mass of gas (methane); R  [J/mol/K] refers to the universal gas constant; T  [K] denotes temperature; ρavg   [kg/m3 ] is average gas density; τ  denotes tortuosity; δ'  refers to the ratio of normalized molecular size to local average pore diameter. Df   indicates the fractal dimension of the pore surface and captures the effect of surface roughness; its value ranges between 2 (smooth surface) and 3 (space-filling surface) (Coppens, 1999 ; Coppens and Dammers, 2006 ). Dk   is the Knudsen diffusion coefficient. kD   [m2 ] = Ravg  2 /8 refers to Darcy permeability. b  is a symbolic representation for Eq. (17) , derived from a theoretical dimensionless coefficient F  developed for correcting slip velocity in tubes (Brown et al., 1946 ; Darabi et al., 2012 ). Ravg   [m] denotes average pore radius; α  refers to the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient, and it is a function of gas compositions, pressure, temperature and wall surface smoothness; it takes a value between 0 (specular accommodation) and 1 (diffuse accommodation) (Arkilic et al., 2001 ). B  [J/K] denotes the Boltzmann constant; Rm   [m] is the molecule diameter of methane; Rmc   [m] is the collision diameter of methane. During our simulation, parameters, such as α, µ, ρavg   and Kn  , are also dynamically updated at each time step according to P . Comprehensive sensitivity analysis regarding the impact of these parameters on gas permeability, along with parameter ranges, is detailed in Javadpour (2009)  and Darabi et al. (2012) . The impact of incorporating these non-Darcy effects using this particular apparent-permeability formulation (Eqs. 15-17 ) on gas-production is analyzed in Zhong and Leung (2019 , 2020a , b ).  2.6.2 Permeability corrections for "Fracture" cells At the "matrix" cell, Eq. (15)  updates kM  . At each "fracture" cell, KF   (Eq. (3) ) is replaced with Eq. (21)  to account for Kapp  . It is assumed that the flow is laminar at each "fracture" cell, and fluid flow in the fracture and matrix portions is mutually non-interfering. Additionally, τ , the gas mean free path, and Kn   remain constant and unaffected by the presence of the fracture network.(21) K F c o r r e c t e d   =  ( 1 − ϕ F  )  * K a p p   + k F  ,      KF corrected   [m2 ] is the corrected upscaled permeability after updating the Kapp   of the matrix portion. Then, Eq. (22)  is obtained by subtracting Eq. (3)  from Eq. This "permeability correction term" is added to the upscaled permeability at every "fracture" cell in the Kapp   updating workflow.  2.6.3 Dynamic updating of apparent permeability Simulations with multiple restarts are accomplished by modifying the part of the source code that is used for calling and using PFLOTRAN in DFNWORKS. A MATLAB script creates multiple restart files with incremental checkpoint times, different restart command lines, and flow/boundary conditions (MathWorks, 2021 ). A novel, explicit coupling strategy is formulated to achieve the dynamic updating of Kapp  , as presented in Fig. 6  . The periodic updating of Kapp   balances computational efficiency and model accuracy. A UDFM output file with a Boolean index of cells determines if fractures intersect the cell at each updating time step. At a "matrix" cell, its permeability is updated to a new Kapp   (Eqs. 15-17 ); at a "fracture" cell, Eq. (22)  is used to update KF  . The updated permeability at every cell is written into an input file for the next simulation. The computation continues until the next updating step. This coupling scheme is achieved by modifying the source code of DFNWORKS. Multiple output files are generated from numerous restarts. They are post-processed in MATLAB to generate a single production profile.    3 Results and discussions This section presents and analyzes several cases. Reservoir, fluid, and fracture properties are collected from field data sets or previous studies on the Horn River shale reservoir (Table 2 , Appendix A). Parameters for Kapp   modelling are summarized in Table 3 , Appendix B. 3.1 Model validation Following the proposed methodology, a 3D shale-gas production base model (Case A) is constructed in DFNWORKS and compared with a similar model built with a commercial black-oil simulator, IMEX (CMG, 2016 ), as shown in Fig. 7  . Both models feature a cubic domain (1 m  × 1 m  × 1 m) with one vertical fracture plane (main hydraulic fracture, HF) and three horizontal planes (SFs), as shown in Fig. 7(a) . In DFNWORKS, the domain is refined into 32,745 octree-refined mesh cells, with the refinement level being 2 and the level-0 mesh element size being 0.1 m (Fig. 7(b) ). A well is located at the center to model a vertical producer's perforation (Fig. 7(c) ). The IMEX model is discretized into 40 × 40 × 40 grid blocks (Fig. 7(d) ) with a similarly sized and shaped producer (Fig. 7(e) ). All six surfaces are assigned as no-flow boundaries, with the producer defined as the only outflow boundary. In both models, Kapp   is dynamically updated. The IMEX model employs an updating scheme we developed for the commercial software package (Zhong and Leung, 2020a , b ). Production profiles and pressure distributions are compared in Fig. 8 and Fig. 9   , respectively. The DFNWORKS predictions agree with those from the IMEX model, with slight discrepancies due to differences in computational meshes. This indicates that our model yields reliable multiphysics two-phase flow simulation results, and the adopted approach has been validated. Regarding computational cost, the DFNWORKS model demonstrates higher efficiency, taking only 2 min and 35 s to complete the simulations, compared to the IMEX model's 18 min and 45 s.  3.2 Effects of non-Darcy flow behaviours and apparent permeability modelling Two 3D, reservoir-scale, hydraulically fractured shale-gas production models (Case B and C) are constructed, both with a domain size of 1024 m  × 100 m  × 120 m (Fig. 10  ). Case B is the same as Case C, except that the Kapp   modelling is not incorporated. Each model consists of a single HF located at the center with a half-length of 340 m along the x-z plane and a DFN of 50 fractures. The DFN represents the SFs generated stochastically from two random fracture sets (details in Table 4 , Appendix C). The domain is refined into 10,868 continuum mesh cells, with an octree-refined mesh in the near-fracture regions (Fig. 10(b) ). Three sets of upscaled rock properties are computed and assigned to the "fracture" cells. A vertical production well (perf) representation is located at the center. Based on sensitivity analysis of updating frequency, Kapp   is updated every 14 production days, resulting in 300 restarts over a simulation duration of 600 weeks. One way to simulate an initial state post-hydraulic fracturing is to inject a certain amount of fracturing fluid into a pre-defined HF (Agrawal and Sharma, 2015 ; Ghanbari and Dehghanpour, 2016 ; Wang and Leung, 2015 , 2016 ). However, such an approach overestimates the fluid leak-off during the injection stage. We adopt an alternative approach by Liu et al. (2018 , 2017 , 2019 ) – instead of modelling injection, the pressure in the HF is set to the minimum horizontal stress (55,000 kPa) and a porosity of 0.99, and it is filled with water. This models the in-situ  condition immediately after injection (Fig. 11(a)  ). Then, an 80-day shut-in period with no outflow boundary allows water to redistribute into the nearby areas (Fig. 11(b) ). The shut-in period is followed by a flowback and production period at a constant bottom-hole pressure. In summary, this model simulates the shut-in, flow-back and production stages immediately after the hydraulic fracturing, while the injection and fracture propagation are ignored. The modelling of these operations is implemented by running multiple restarts while updating the boundary conditions at the well accordingly. Results of the Kapp   updating are shown in Fig. 12  , where the upscaled cell permeability distribution is plotted. Incorporating Kapp   leads to an increase in cumulative gas production by 6.55 %, as shown in Fig. 13  . This is also evidenced by an overall lower gas mass density (i.e., lower gas saturation) in Case C (Fig. 14  ). The discrepancies are more pronounced at the later stage. This is because non-Darcy flow mechanisms are more important at a lower pore pressure, since Kapp   is inversely proportional to P . Additionally, as production continues, matrix storage becomes more important. Higher water recovery is observed in Case C (Fig. 13(b) ), attributed to the increase in matrix permeability.  3.3 Impacts of fracture network connectivity, pressure interference, water retention and shut-in duration 3.3.1 Effects of isolated and disconnected fractures Not all SFs contribute equally to flow. For example, natural fractures may be isolated from the main HF and not reactivated (Chen et al., 2021 ; Wang and Leung, 2016 ). Induced SFs may close and disconnect from the network during the flow-back period (Zhong and Leung, 2020b ). A previous study by Wang and Leung (2016)  indicated that these fractures could still benefit flow by providing pathways for fluids to access the HF. However, their study modelled only a few oversized orthogonal microfractures. In this work, two cases are constructed (Case D and E). Case E is the same as Case D, except for the inclusion of 19 isolated/disconnected SFs (Figs. 15(a)   and (b )). The corresponding gas productions are compared in Fig. 15(c) . In contrast with previous work, our results illustrate that isolated/disconnected fractures have negligible impacts, with only a slight enhancement of production observed in Case E. Two possible explanations could explain the different observations. First, the DFN configuration here differs from previous studies. Most disconnected fractures here are far from the wellbore, limiting their impact on the wellbore performance and the early-stage flowback. This setup is valid as induced SFs and reactivated NFs far from the wellbore tend to close earlier in proximity to the wellbore due to lower fluid pressure (Zhong and Leung, 2019 ). Disconnected fractures have a slightly greater impact on production at the later stage (> 2500 days), as illustrated in Fig. 15(c) . Second, the increase in Kapp   enhances the overall conductivity of the system, minimizing the effects of disconnected fractures located far away from the perforation. Previous studies have also shown that poorly interconnected fractures behave similarly to a slightly more permeable host rock (Philip et al., 2005 ; Olson et al., 2009 ).  3.3.2 Effects of initial pressure distribution in the near-well region Two cases (Cases F and G) are tested to examine the impacts of initial pressure distribution in the near-well region. Cases F and G are the same as Case C (homogenous initial pressure distribution), except that Case F's near-well region is initialized with high pressure. In contrast, a lower initial pressure is set in Case G (Fig. 16  ). These cases aim to examine the interference of other existing wells. Also shown in Fig. 16  are the gas production profiles. The results illustrate that gas production increases with initial pressure near the perf. Higher pressure means that more frac-fluid (i.e., water) remains inside the HF during shut-in, which is produced quickly during the flow-back. In addition, less water is redistributed to the nearby regions, resulting in higher gas relative permeability. Figs. 17(a)   and (b ) compare water mass densities between Cases F and G at the end of the shut-in period, illustrating differences in water redistribution. Additionally, higher pressure in the near-well area creates a larger pressure gradient for flow into the wellbore.  3.3.3 Effects of water retention in the near-well region Case H is identical to Case C, except that the near-well region is initialized with a higher water saturation of 0.85 (Fig. 18(a)  ). In contrast, Case C has a lower value of 0.25. We aim to investigate how redistributing fracturing fluid (water) from a nearby well may influence the current treatment well/cluster. Fig. 18(b)  compares the production profiles. The results show that more water near the well improves gas production. Due to water's near-incompressibility, fluid pressure surrounding the perforation increases rapidly in Case H during fluid redistribution. Therefore, higher pressure is observed in Case H at the end of shut-in, as depicted in Figs. 19(a)   and (b ). During the subsequent flowback, this elevated pressure gradient increases the gas production, as discussed in Section 3.3.2 .  3.3.4 Effects of shut-in durations Two additional cases, Case I and Case J, are tested to examine the impacts of different shut-in durations. Cases I and J are identical to Case C, except for their shut-in duration. Fig. 20   illustrates the flowback profiles for Case C (80-day shut-in), Case I (160-day shut-in), and Case J (40-day shut-in). Fig. 21   shows the distributions of liquid pressures immediately after shut-in and following a period of production. The results illustrate that shut-in durations have minimal impact on gas production, contrary to findings from several previous studies. However, these studies often overlooked or simplified the modelling of the complex fracture networks (e.g., Cheng, 2012 ; Fakcharoenphol et al., 2013 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Our results demonstrate that water predominantly distributes to the highly conductive fracture network during the shut-in period, evidenced by the high fluid pressure observed in the fractures in Figs. 21(a) , (c ), and (e ). Only for a very long shut-in period (Case I) is a slight matrix pressure increase, yet the fluid volume entering the matrix remains minimal. Upon production, water is rapidly produced through the conductive network, mitigating its negative impact on gas mobility. This observation is supported by the pressure maps early in production, shown in Figs. 21(b) , (d ), and (f ). They illustrate an identical fluid pressure distribution regardless of the shut-in durations. A shorter shut-in period enhances water recovery (Fig. 20(b) ) by keeping more fracturing fluid near the wellbore (Fig. 21(e) ).    4 Conclusions This work presents a set of numerical simulations of hydraulically fractured shale gas reservoirs using an open-source suite, DFNWORKS, and a computational geometry-based upscaling method, UDFM. 3D DFNs are upscaled into octree-refined continuum meshes using UDFM modelling and subjected to multiphase-flow simulations. Several improvements have been made to the existing DFNWORKS framework. First, an innovative and feasible coupling scheme is created to update the pressure-dependent matrix Kapp   and capture the effects of non-Darcy flow behaviours in the matrix nanopores. Second, the UDFM technique was extended to upscale equivalent rock-fluid functions and rock properties to the octree-refined mesh cells. Third, the well-modelling module is modified to ensure compatibility with the octree mesh. Fourth, the code is modified to facilitate multiple restarts, which are needed to simulate varying operational strategies and dynamic updating of Kapp  . These proposed flexible strategies can be integrated into other commercial/open-source reservoir-simulation frameworks or packages. The presented model is validated against results from other commercial flow simulation packages. The results revealed that neglecting the influence of non-Darcy flow behaviours could lead to underestimating gas and water production, while the effects are more significant later. The results also demonstrate that the connectivity of the fracture network, pressure interference, water retention near the well, and the shut-in period significantly impact flow performance. This study introduces a practical framework for modelling shale gas reservoirs with complex, arbitrarily distributed fracture networks and nano-sized pore structures, where non-Darcy flow phenomena notably influence matrix flow. The proposed method is computationally efficient and widely applicable, enabling detailed analysis of fracture network distributions, connectivity, and matrix flow dynamics. It provides valuable insights for assessing stimulation efficiency and forecasting production. In future work, we will explore using alternative flow-based hydraulic upscaling techniques. 1 Introduction As one of the world’s largest organic carbon reservoirs, the oceanic dissolved organic matter (DOM) is essential for the carbon cycle and marine ecosystems (Bonelli et al., 2021 ). The Arctic Ocean is the world’s largest longitudinal ocean and rivers discharge massive amounts of freshwater and DOM every year (Cooper et al., 2005; Dittmar and Kattner, 2003 ). As the climate warms, river runoff and thawing permafrost depth increase in the Arctic region. As a result, the amount of DOM discharged into the Arctic Ocean by rivers has increased, which has a range of effects on the physical, chemical, and biological environments of the Arctic continental shelf waters (Stedmon et al., 2011 ). In the coastal area, river water is the main source of DOM, and the absorption coefficient of colored dissolved organic matter at 443 nm (a CDOM (443)) provides a good indication of DOM (Vantrepotte et al., 2015 ). When DOM is discharged into seawater, its fate and transformation are not well known. The spectral slope of the CDOM absorption in the 275–295 nm wavelength range (S 275–295 ) is a reliable indicator of dissolved lignin in riverine-influenced waters, which can indicate the proportion of terrigenous dissolved organic carbon (tDOC) and is a reliable proxy for land-based sources of tDOC (Fichot and Benner, 2012 ). In addition, S 275–295  is a good indicator of photobleaching and microbial alteration of DOM upon entry into coastal sea (Fichot and Benner, 2012 ). Simultaneously, S 275–295  is an important parameter that limits the variability between CDOM and DOC in the ocean and can improve the reliability of the CDOM-DOC empirical algorithm for DOC inversion (Brewin et al., 2023 ). S 275–295  can be inverted from remote sensing data. Fichot et al. (2013)  proposed an empirical algorithm, which performed well in the S275–295  inversion in the open seas of Arctic Ocean. In addition, Vantrepotte et al. (2015)  indicated that S 275–295  can be retrieved based on the absorption coefficients of CDOM in river-influenced waters. Empirical algorithms are susceptible to water optical properties variation, suggesting that retrievals in different waters may require different settings according to the water characteristics (Lee et al., 2002 ). Owing to the complexity of the optical composition in coastal waters, the performance of the empirical model is unlikely to be satisfactory. Therefore, new methods were desired to improve the accuracy of the inversion of S 275–295  in coastal waters. Recently, machine learning models have been developed to effectively connect the internal and hidden relationships among different parameters. Owing to their powerful computational capabilities and ability to efficiently connect intrinsic and hidden relationships between different parameters, machine learning models have yielded satisfactory results for the retrieval of aquatic environmental variables such as CDOM (Aurin et al., 2018 ) and chlorophyll a (Cao et al., 2020 ). A multilayer backpropagation neural network (MBPNN) is a commonly used machine learning method that can approximate complex nonlinear relationships while exhibiting self-learning, self-adaptation, self-organization, and high robustness (Sun et al., 2011 ). The gradient descent method can calculate the difference between the retrieved and expected values in the output layer, which is the main characteristic of the MBPNN. The weight and bias values are then modified based on error backpropagation until the errors reduce to minimum (Ma et al., 2021 ). The MBPNN model has been successfully applied in many environmental and hydrological remote sensing studies (Chen and Hu, 2017; Liu et al., 2021 ) and has the potential to retrieve water optical properties accurately. The Laptev Sea is located in the western part of the Arctic East Siberian Shelf and is connected to the East Siberian Sea through the straits between the Novosibirsk Islands (Dmitry Laptev Strait, etc.) and to the Kara Sea through the Velikitsky Strait between the Northland Islands. The Laptev Sea is a vast shelf surrounded to the north by a deep-water Arctic Ocean basin. The Lena River flows into the Laptev Sea and is the primary source of DOM (Vantrepotte et al., 2015 ). Previous studies focused on CDOM inversion in the Laptev Sea (Juhls et al., 2019 ). However, as a riverine-influenced sea, studying the spatiotemporal distribution of S 275–295  is essential for understanding the carbon cycle in the Laptev Sea, which remains unclear. In this study, a machine learning model was used to retrieve S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. The proposed model was then applied to the MODIS (Moderate-resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) images to map the spatiotemporal distribution and variation of S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea during the ice-free period (July-September) from 2002 to 2022. Factors influencing S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea, such as river discharge, sea ice, salinity, permafrost, vegetation, and wind speed are discussed, and the contribution of each factor is calculated.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 In-situ data The in-situ data in this study was obtained from the open sea and coastal area of Laptev Sea and channels of the Lena River between 2010 and 2019 ( Fig. 1 ), which can be freely downloaded from website of PANGAEA (https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.898813 ). All cruises took place during the ice-free period from late June to mid-September, except for LD14, which was conducted during the flood flow after ice breakup of Lena River, from late May to late June.  Table 1  summarizes the sampling dates and statistic data of in-situ CDOM, salinity and S 275–295  used in this study. The details of measurement and process can be referred to Juhls et al. (2019) . S 275–295  can be calculated as following:(1) a  CDOM   λ    = a  CDOM   ( λ  0   ) · e  − S ( λ − λ  0   )       where a CDOM (λ0 ) is the absorption coefficient at the reference wavelength λ0 , and S  is the spectral slope of a CDOM (λ) for the selected wavelength range (275 – 295 nm, i.e. S 275–295 ). The in-situ S 275–295  data varied in the range of 0.012–0.0275 nm−1  with a mean value of 0.0174 nm−1 .  2.2 Remote sensing data MOD09 is a seven-band level 2 product derived from MODIS bands 1–7. MOD09GA provides daily surface reflectance data at a resolution of 500 m, and MOD09A1 is a level 3 composite of MOD09GA. For each pixel of MOD09A1, the best possible level 2 granule observations from all ensembles were selected over an 8-day period based on high observational coverage, low viewing angle, absence of clouds and cloud shadows, and aerosol loading (Vermote, 2015 ). MODOCGA is a 7-band remote sensing product derived from MODIS bands 8–16, which provides the surface reflectance data at a resolution of 1 km. In this study, MOD09A1 data were used to assess the long-term changes in S 275–295  in the offshore region of the Laptev Sea. To reduce the time window between in-situ and remote sensing data, the daily MOD09GA data was used for data matching (Wang et al., 2020 ). In this study, surface reflectance was corrected to remotely sensed reflectance (Rrs) by subtracting the minimum of the 3 bands in near-infrared and shortwave infrared, and then being divided by π, following the correction method proposed by (Li et al., 2016 ). A quality attribute banding algorithm (StateQA) was used to mask the clouds and cloud-shaded pixels in the MOD09 data. To match the in-situ data with satellite data, this study followed these steps: 1) obtaining a 3 × 3 matrix of pixels centered at each sampling location from all satellite images within 24 h before or after the in-situ sampling time, 2) discarding matches with < 5 valid pixels out of 9 possible pixels, and 3) computing the median Rrs(λ) of the extracted pixels for each site. There were two datasets in this study: Dataset I for MOD09GA images and Dataset II for MODOCGA images. Owing to the small number of matches in Dataset II, the time window between the in-situ data and remote sensing data was relaxed to three days. Finally, there were 95 pairs of MOD09GA Rrs vs. in-situ S 275–295  for the training and testing of machine learning algorithms in Dataset I and 105 pairs of MODOCGA Rrs vs. in-situ S 275–295  for the development of the empirical algorithm in Dataset II.  2.3 Ancillary data The Lena River discharge (m3 /s) at Kyusyur Station was obtained from the Arctic-GRO and PARTNERS projects (https://arcticgreatrivers.org/data ) (Shiklomanov et al., 2021 ). Monthly and yearly averaged river discharge data were calculated based on daily river discharge data. Arctic Sea Ice News and Analysis (https://nsidc.org/arcticseaicenews ) provided monthly ice extent dataset (Schweiger et al., 2011 ).
