Permafrost active layer thickness data were obtained from the European Space Agency (ESA) Permafrost Climate Change Initiative (Permafrost_CCI) v3.0, which provided the maximum permafrost active layer thickness in July and August from 2002 to 2019, which was equivalent to subsequent permafrost thaw depth data (Obu et al., 2021 ). The subset of Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM) data on GEE provided the monthly salinity data in this study, which were interpolated to 40 standard z-levels (Cummings and Smedstad, 2013 ). Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were obtained from MODIS product of Google Earth Engine, which provided monthly mean NDVI for the Lena River Basin.  2.4 Algorithm development for S 275–295  The in-situ data were classified into two water types according to salinity: coastal waters with salinity <16 psu and open-sea waters with salinity >16 psu. As a CDOM (443) was strongly correlated with S 275–295  (r =0.95) in both water types with different salinities ( Fig. 2 ), the regression relationship was as follows:(2) S  275 − 295   = 0.0243 + 0.0208 * a  CDOM   ( 443 )  1 + 1.518 * a  CDOM   ( 443 )        The structure of the MBPNN model consisted of one input layer, one output layer, and two hidden layers containing 17 and 6 neurons, respectively. Rrs(469), Rrs(555), Rrs(645), Rrs(469)/Rrs(555), and Rrs(555)/Rrs(645) were used as inputs and S 275–295  was used as the output of the MBPNN model. Based on the regression relationship between S 275–295  and a CDOM (443), Eq. (2)  was added to the output layer as a customized function of the MBPNN model. Each layer of neurons is fully connected to the subsequent layer of neurons, and there are no same-layer or cross-layer connections between neurons. The rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function was used between the layers, except for the output layer, which used a customized activation function. The Rrs-S 275–295  dataset was divided into training and testing groups, and 70 % were used for modeling, leaving the rest as the testing group. All values were normalized and scaled to a range of 0–1, guaranteeing that all feature information was in the valid domain of the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function. When the error value was small enough and the curve flattened, the number of training iterations can be determined, with mean square error (MSE) as the loss function.  2.5 Comparison of models In this study, five algorithms were selected as benchmark algorithms: one empirical algorithm and four machine learning algorithms. The empirical algorithm used five bands of Rrs(443), Rrs(488), Rrs(531), Rrs(555), and Rrs(667) to invert S 275–295  as described by Fichot et al. (2013) , and the empirical coefficients were adjusted with the measured data of this study as follows:(3) Ln S  275 − 295      = − 3.817 − 0.094 * Ln Rrs 443       + 0.503 * Ln Rrs 488       − 0.693 * Ln Rrs 531       + 0.485 * Ln Rrs 555       − 0.139 * Ln Rrs 667            The four machine learning algorithms were Random Forest (RF), extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Machine Regression (SVR), and a Mixture Density Network (MDN). After selecting the best segmentation method on account of all feature subsets, RF integrates the generated multiple decision trees into a single forest and averages the regression predictions produced by all trees as an outcome (Al-Mukhtar, 2019 ). XGBoost improves the gradient-boosting decision tree by adding a regularization term to the cost function and performing a second-order Taylor expansion. Both methods are based on the principle of improving learning outcomes over a single learner by integrating the results of each weak learner. All regression trees of XGBoost have different weights and they are strongly correlated rather than independent (Nguyen et al., 2021 ). The main goal of SVR is to identify a hyperplane in multidimensional feature space that separates the data with a maximum margin (Tang and Huang, 2021 ). The input data is converted to higher dimensional space with a nonlinear kernel function. As a result, a linear regression is implemented in a high-dimensional space, solving the problem of data dimensionality (Kim and Ahn, 2022 ). The MDN obtains a more complete probabilistic distribution of the data in the space of the target value by learning the distributional parameters (e.g., mean vectors, covariance matrices, and mixing coefficients) of the input features in the given situation and finally superimposes the output distributions according to certain weights. The same dataset (Dataset I) was used to train and test the 4 machine learning algorithms. As the MOD09GA product (Dataset I) did not meet the band requirements of the empirical algorithm, so Dataset II of the MODOCGA product was used instead. For a fair comparison, Dataset II was also used to train and test the best machine learning model for comparison with the empirical model.  2.6 Analytical methods All model statistical analyses were performed using the Python software. Statistical analyses were performed using the coefficient of determination (R2 ), root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and mean absolute error (MAE). These metrics are computationally more robust for evaluating algorithms and are defined as follows:(4) RMSE = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   E  i   − M  i      2           (5) MAPE = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   E  i   − M  i      M  i        * 100 %     (6) MAE = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   E  i   − M  i            where n  is the number of the data, and E i   and M i   denote the retrieved and measured S 275–295  values, respectively. As a method of model post-hoc explanation, the SHapley Additive explanation (SHAP) can be used to characterize the marginal contribution of features (Zhu et al., 2024 ). In this study, SHAP was used to explain the contributions of the five features to the MBPNN model with a customized function. The random forest regression model (RFM) is widely used to quantify the effects of various influencing factors (Xu et al., 2019 ), which was also used to quantify the influencing factors’ contribution to the S 275–295  variation in the Laptev Sea. The relative importance of individual influence factors in RFM represented their contribution to S 275–295 , and was calculated based on the effect of each feature on the mean square error of the RFM (Song et al., 2021 ). The result is statistically significant when the p -value is less than a significance level, and common significance level values are 0.1, 0.05, and 0.01 (Ritter and Muñoz-Carpena, 2013 ). Therefore, p <0.01 and p <0.1 were used as the basis for the significance level in this study.   3 Results 3.1 Algorithm performance evaluation  Fig. 3 (a)–(f) show the model performance evaluations of the machine learning models with Dataset I, and (g) and (h) show the model performance evaluations of the MBPNN with a customized function and the empirical model with Dataset II. The MBPNN model performed the best among all the models, with R2 , MAPE, RMSE, and MAE values of 0.60, 7.45 %, 0.0017 nm−1 , and 0.0012 nm−1 , respectively (Fig. 3 (a)). The other four machine learning models demonstrated similar performances, with R2  varying from 0.42–0.53, and RMSE varying from 0.0019–0.0022 nm−1 . In comparison, the MBPNN model with a customized function in Fig. 3 (f) showed an obvious performance improvement, with R2 , MAPE, RMSE, and MAE values of 0.81, 6.12 %, 0.0012 nm−1 , and 0.0010 nm−1 , respectively. The MBPNN model (R2 =0.64, MAPE=6.20 %, RMSE=0.0013 nm−1 , and MAE=0.0010 nm−1 ) surpassed the empirical model (R2 =0.45, MAPE=8.84 %, RMSE=0.0018 nm−1 , and MAE=0.0014 nm−1 ) (Fig. 3 (g) and (h)). According to the results of both datasets, the accuracy of the MBPNN model with a customized function in S 275–295  prediction was significantly better than that of the empirical algorithm and other machine learning algorithms. The MBPNN model with a customized function built with Dataset I outperformed the one built with Dataset II. Furthermore, Dataset I had a higher quality 8-day synthetic product, making it better suited for long time series analysis. Therefore, the MBPNN model with a customized function constructed using Dataset I was chosen for the subsequent inversion.  3.2 Spatial and temporal variations of S 275–295  The spatial distribution of S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea was retrieved using MOD09A1 data.  Fig. 4  shows the results during the ice-free period (July–September) from 2002–2022. However, owing to ice and clouds, only the first half of September’s results was used. To understand the variation of S 275–295  from the coastal region to the open ocean, this study plotted a section line as shown in Fig. 4 . The S 275–295  of the Laptev Sea ranged between 0.014 and 0.022 nm−1 , initially decreasing and then gradually increasing from coast to open sea. Influenced by river input, lower S 275–295  values were concentrated in the estuarine and littoral regions, consistent with a previous study (Pugach et al., 2015 ). Owing to strong influence of rivers, the S 275–295  changes were more pronounced in offshore areas than in the open sea. In addition, there was an anomalous area around 134° E, 74°N, which is marked with a red box in Fig. 4 (e). S 275–295  in the abnormal areas was low (Fig. 4 (f)). Section 4.2  discusses the possible caused of the abnormal areas. The annual mean S 275–295  of the Laptev Sea varied between 0.0185 nm−1  and 0.0190 nm−1  during 2002–2022 ( Fig. 5 (a)). In comparison, the monthly mean S 275–295  within one year showed an increasing trend (Fig. 5 (b)), with the lowest value in July and the highest value in September. It was worth noting that the low S 275–295  in July 2008 was due to the influence of clouds and ice, and only pixels with low S 275–295  values assembling in the near-shore region were valid and calculated. To further study the variation in S 275–295 , the Laptev Sea was divided into small sections with 0.5° increments and 4.5° ranges, and the annual mean S 275–295  was calculated for each section ( Fig. 6 (a)). The S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea was low in coastal areas affected by river runoff. The interannual anomalies of S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea were also calculated and are depicted in Fig. 6 (b). The percentage anomalies in the Laptev Sea ranged from −8–6 %, with obvious variability concentrated near the mouth of the Lena River.  3.3 Influence factors of S 275–295  The S 275–295  of the Laptev Sea is influenced by factors such as Lena River discharge, the melting of sea ice, permafrost, vegetation, and wind speed, while the relationship between S 275–295  and salinity is crucial for the fate of CDOM from land-based sources into the Laptev Sea (Juhls et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Wickland et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2023 ). The regression analysis was first conducted between influencing factor and the year to find out variation trend of each influencing factor. The annual mean river discharge and NDVI fluctuated during the study period without a significant variation trend (Fig. 5 (a)). While ice extent (r =-0.58, p <0.01) and salinity (r =-0.69, p <0.01) had a significant decreasing trend, and the average thaw depth of permafrost in the Lena River basin increased significantly (r =0.69, p <0.01). 3.3.1 Spatial-temporal analysis of influencing factors This study analyzed the relationship between the annual mean of the above factors and the S 275–295 . Furthermore, permafrost data of 2004 were removed because the permafrost thaw depth was extremely low and its contribution to tDOC in the Laptev Sea was erratic. Fig. 5 (a) demonstrates a significant negative correlation between S 275–295  and the Lena River discharge (r =-0.41, p <0.1) and permafrost thaw depth within the basin (r =-0.42, p <0.1). To understand the relationship between the influencing factors and S 275–295  on a monthly scale, the relationships between monthly mean S 275–295  and Lena River discharge, wind speed, ice extent, NDVI, were also analyzed (Fig. 5 (b)). The wind speed was divided into southward and northward winds for analysis. The Lena River discharge and ice extent decreased from July to September. Significantly negative correlations between monthly mean S 275–295  and Lena River discharge (r =-0.37, p <0.01), monthly mean S 275–295  and NDVI (r =-0.46, p <0.01), and monthly mean S 275–295  and ice extent (r =-0.55, p <0.01) were observed. Meanwhile, there was a significant negative correlation between the monthly mean S 275–295  and the north wind (r =0.46, p <0.01). This study used in-situ data from the Laptev Sea to investigate the spatial distribution of the relationship between S 275–295  and salinity. In addition, the retrieved S 275–295  and the corresponding HYCOM salinity were extracted and analyzed  Fig. 7 (a) demonstrates a significant positive correlation between in-situ salinity and S 275–295  (r =0.86, p <0.01). The retrieved S 275–295  and the corresponding HYCOM salinity data exhibited a similar trend (r =0.81, p <0.01; Fig. 7 (b)). Both Fig. 7 (a) and Fig. 7 (b) show that high salinity correlates with high S 275–295  and vice versa in the spatial distribution. Fig. 7 (b) shows two high-density areas; one in coastal waters with lower salinity and the other in open seas with higher salinity. The distribution of scatter points showed a convergence trend from the coastal waters to the open sea.  3.3.2 Contributions of influencing factors to S 275–295  The maximum permafrost thaw depth in July and August was used as the annual maximum thaw depth for RFM. The first line of  Fig. 8  depicts the annual-scale contributions, which were calculated using the mean values of the Lena River discharge, ice extent, salinity, NDVI in July, August, and September. Owing to the lack of monthly permafrost thaw depth data, the other factors were used to analyze the monthly scale contributions. To assess the contribution of wind speed to the monthly S 275–295  variation, the Lena River discharge, sea ice extent, wind speed, salinity, and NDVI of the months when north winds prevailed were analyzed. On an annual scale, the Lena River discharge was the most important factor affecting the S 275–295  variation, with a total contribution of 25 %. The thaw depth of permafrost was the second most influential factor, contributing 23 % of the S 275–295  variation, follow by ice extent (22 %), salinity (15 %), and NDVI (15 %). On a monthly scale, the contribution of sea ice extent was 34 % in July, followed by NDVI (24 %), Lena River discharge (23 %), and salinity (19 %). In August, the Lena River discharge made the greatest contribution (29 %) to the S 275–295  variation, followed by the sea ice extent (28 %), NDVI (23 %), and salinity (20 %). In September, the four factors contributed similarly to the S 275–295  variation. When the north wind prevailed, the Lena River discharge made the greatest contribution (27 %) to the S 275–295  variation, followed by the ice extent (24 %), NDVI (20 %), wind speed (18 %), and salinity (11 %).    4 Discussion 4.1 Customized function As described in Section 3.1 , the accuracy of MBPNN model was obviously improved by incorporating known functional relationships into the output layer and assigning them as activation functions. To evaluate the performance improvement caused by the customized function, two MBPNN models with (Fig. 3 (f)) and without (Fig. 3 (a)) a customized function were trained concurrently and compared. The MBPNN model with a customized function performed significantly better than the MBPNN model without it (R2 =0.60 RMSE=0.0017 nm−1 , MAPE=7.45 %, and MAE=0.0012 nm−1 ). The addition of the customization function significantly improved the MBPNN’s performance in the range of 0.015–0.020 nm−1 , which corresponds to the variation range of S 275–295  at the river-ocean intersection. There is an urgent need to better understand the transition and fate of terrestrial organic carbon in the sea (Fichot and Benner, 2012 ). The customized function not only acted on the forward transmission but also on reverse transmissions errors from the training process, adjusting the weights and biases of each layer to improve the model’s prediction accuracy. In addition, a customized function was added to the model as a constraint, reducing the model’s dependence of the amount of data. However, using empirical relationships as a customized function reduces the model’s portability. Therefore, further application of the proposed MBPNN model with a customized function should be used with suitable regional empirical relationships.  4.2 Performance of different models The S 275–295  empirical algorithm proposed by Fichot et al. (2013)  has been widely used in previous studies and was chosen as the benchmark algorithm in this study. In addition, the RF, XGBoost, SVR, and MDN models were also chosen for comparison. The empirical algorithm’s parameter adjustment used the MYDOCGA data instead the MOD09GA data since the later did not meet the empirical algorithm’s band setting requirements. Consequently, there were two datasets in this study: Dataset I for MOD09GA images and Dataset II for MODOCGA images. As described in Section 3.1 , the RF, XGBoost, SVR, and MDN models showed unsatisfactory prediction accuracy, particularly in the high-value section. This could be attributed to the complexity of the water characteristics in the Laptev Sea as well as the small amount of data used for training. Although machine learning can theoretically fit the functional relationship between Rrs and S 275–295  well, it relies on a large number of in-situ data as inputs. The method proposed in this study can utilize known empirical relationships to improve the prediction accuracy of a model with limited data. SHAP could elucidate the impact of each feature on S 275–295  predictions by quantifying their contribution to the model outputs (Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Rrs(645) contributes the most to the MBPNN model with a customized function ( Fig. 9 ), followed by Rrs(555)/Rrs(645), Rrs(555), Rrs(469)/Rrs(555), and Rrs(469), with similar noncritical contributions. Previous studies have shown that the red band is effective at retrieving water color parameters in coastal waters (Huang et al., 2017 ). Griffin et al. (2018)  found that atmospheric effects tended to be largest in the blue region; however, the MBPNN model was less affected by atmospheric correction because of the low contribution of the blue band and its ratio. Simultaneously, the band ratio was less affected by aerosols than a single band as an input variable (Cao et al., 2023 ). Consequently, the proposed MBPNN model with a customized function can effectively capture subtle variations in S 275–295 . Previous studies have shown that S 275–295  is lower than 0.02 nm−1  when the proportion of tDOC is higher than 50 % (Fichot and Benner, 2012 ). According to the spatial distribution of S 275–295  in Section 3.2 , most S 275–295  of the Laptev Sea was lower than 0.02 nm−1 , which is consistent with previous results that DOM in the Laptev Sea was mainly from terrestrial DOM (Juhls et al., 2019 ). In addition, there was an anomalous area with an obviously low S 275–295  around 134°E, 74°N, which is labeled with a red box in Fig. 4 (e). This anomaly was also clearly observed along the section line in Fig. 4 (b, d, and f). Interestingly, this anomaly was absent in July but reappeared in August. In September, the anomaly was most pronounced and could be explained by the salinity anomaly observed by Sukhanova et al. (2017)  on September 8–14, 2015, in the same region. The localized salt levee layer was uplifted to the surface near this region, reducing the depth of the upper quasi-homogeneous layer causing surface river water pooling, creating a river-like flow effect (Sukhanova et al., 2017 ). The mutual corroboration between the anomaly area of retrieved S 275–295  and the in-situ salinity anomaly demonstrated the MBPNN model’s inversion accuracy. Although the MBPNN has a relatively simple structure, it performs better in simulating and solving complex nonlinear problems between Rrs and water parameters (Zhang and Zheng, 2018 ). In this study, the MBPNN outperformed four other machine learning models and one commonly used empirical model for S 275–295  retrieval. This study demonstrates that the ability to solve complex water parameters can be enhanced by adding customization features. The integrated use of MODIS images and MBPNN with a customized function can be used to obtain spatial and temporal changes in S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. Although the MBPNN model with a customized function can reduce the dependence on the number of in-situ data, the difference in acquisition time between MODIS imagery and the in-situ data may lead to uncertainty in Rrs, which may affect the inversion accuracy of the machine learning model (Hu et al., 2013 ). At the same time, although SHAP can explain the contribution of the input variables to the prediction, the internal operating mechanisms of the MBPNN model remain unclear.  4.3 Analysis of influential factors Large river discharge has a significant impact on the Laptev Sea’s carbon cycle and physical properties (Fahl et al., 2001 ). The Lena River delivers a large amount of land-based organic carbon to the Laptev Sea each year, and global warming has a significant impact on river runoff, decomposition, and transportation of organic carbon in the catchment and shelf seas (Cauwet and Sidorov, 1996 ). The average annual discharge of the Lena River is 542 km3  Discharge in June and July accounted for 56.6 % of the total discharge, and only 11.9 % in September (Juhls et al., 2019 ). Therefore, Lena River discharge is one of the most important factors influencing S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. As discussed in Section 3.3 , there is a significant negative correlation between river discharge and S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. Previous studies have shown significant changes in the Arctic Sea ice cover over the past three decades (Meier et al., 2014 ). Since 1979, the sea ice has been declining in all months, with an even greater decline in the last decade, resulting in more sea ice melting and a one-month reduction in ice cover duration (Comiso and Hall, 2014; Pefanis et al., 2020 ). Huang et al. (2024)  showed the water from melting sea ice contains less CDOM than the subsurface waters, and decrease the relative proportion of terrigenous CDOM by diluting the surrounding seawater. As discussed in Section 3.3 , there is a strong negative correlation between the ice extent and S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. The melting of sea ice dilutes of terrigenous CDOM. High values of S 275–295  usually correspond to marine waters, whereas low values of S 275–295  are indicative of river water (Fichot and Benner, 2012 ). As a result, sea ice melting leads an increase of mean S 275–295  by diluting terrigenous CDOM. Aalto et al. (2018)  indicated that Arctic surface permafrost stores large amounts of soil organic carbon, accounting for nearly half of the estimated global soil carbon stock, which exceeds the amount of carbon currently in the atmosphere. Simultaneously, the surface temperature in the Arctic is gradually rising, and a warming climate could lead to further melting of permafrost (Biskaborn et al., 2019 ). Thus, there may have been an increased release of organic carbon from the melting permafrost. These results suggest that thawing permafrost caused more terrigenous CDOM to flow into the river and Laptev Sea, resulting in a significant negative correlation between permafrost thaw depth and S 275–295  (Fig. 5 ). Fichot and Benner (2012)  found that the photodegradation of CDOM in the ocean and protein-rich planktonic CDOM led to elevated S 275–295 . As described in Section 3.3 , the significant positive correlation between salinity and S 275–295  suggests that the freshwater discharged from the Lena River was conservatively mixed with the seawater of the Laptev Sea. Li et al. (2018)  showed that wind speed is an important factor that influences the spatial distribution of S 275–295  by increasing or inhibiting the spread of low S 275–295  to the open ocean. North winds can inhibit the spread of low S 275–295  from coast to the open sea, and the decrease in dispersal extent of low S 275–295  would lead to an increase in averaged S 275–295  of Laptev Sea. As a result, the increase in north wind speed and decrease in dispersal extent of low S 275–295  showed a positive effect on S 275–295 . However, the insignificant correlation between S 275–295  and wind speed when the south wind prevailed may be because the diffusion of low S 275–295  was controlled by a number of factors. Fichot and Benner (2012)  showed that lignin was an important component of CDOM and exclusively biosynthesized by land vascular plants. The S 275–295  was negatively correlated with lignin in river-influenced ocean margins. Wickland et al. (2007)  indicated that vegetation was an important source of CDOM for rivers. Thus, CDOM from land vegetation being transported to the sea will cause a decrease of S 275–295 . This was well demonstrated by the significant negative correlation between NDVI and S 275–295  in Section 3.3 . From the annual results of the RFM (Fig. 8 ), the Lena River discharge had the most important influence on the annual S 275–295  change, followed by permafrost, sea ice, salinity, and NDVI. According to the monthly scale RFM, sea ice was the main factor influencing the change in S 275–295  in July, probably because of the large amount of sea ice melting. S 275–295  was more sensitive to changes in the Lena River discharge in August owing to the absence of sea ice. In September, the four factors were at a low value; therefore, discharge, sea ice, salinity, and vegetation all played a role in the S 275–295  variation. When the north wind prevailed, wind speed had a significant impact on S 275–295  by inhibiting the diffusion of low S 275–295 . The deepening of the permafrost thaw led to more terrigenous CDOM entering the Laptev Sea through the Lena River, whereas a large amount of melting sea ice diluted the terrigenous CDOM. This is a reasonable explanation for the fact that S 275–295  did not change significantly between 2002 and 2022.   5 Conclusions In this study, a new MBPNN model with a customized function was combined with MODIS images to perform remote sensing inversion of S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. The customized function significantly improved the performance of the MBPNN model to retrieve S 275–295 . The temporal and spatial distributions of S 275–295  from 2002 to 2022 were obtained. During the study period, there was no significant annual variation in S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea. The monthly mean S 275–295  increased from July to September. The spatial distribution of S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea showed a gradual increasing trend from the coastal waters to the open sea. The S 275–295  was mainly affected by Lena River discharge, sea ice, permafrost melting, salinity, and vegetation in the Laptev Sea. RFM quantitatively analyzed the influence of various factors. Although the proposed model could effectively monitor long-term changes in S 275–295  in the Laptev Sea, using empirical relationships as a customized function still reduced the model’s portability. In the future, the application of transfer learning or meta learning to quantitative retrieval may improve the generalizability and accuracy of S 275–295  inversion algorithms. The use of regional empirical relationships in machine learning model could provide new ideas for the further studies on water optical parameters retrieval in complex waters. Our results also provide access to sources of CDOM in the Laptev Sea and improve the reliability of the CDOM-DOC empirical algorithm for DOC inversion in the Laptev Sea.
1 Introduction River systems are valuable natural legacies and play important roles in ecosystems and human society, such as the distribution of water resources, maintenance of aquatic ecosystems, and flood control (Chin, 2006; Cooke et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2018a; Napieralski and Carvalhaes, 2016 ). Over the past 50 years, urban river systems have been greatly affected by significant human interference worldwide (Han et al., 2016; Julian et al., 2015; Pringle, 2003; Stammler et al., 2013; Vorosmarty et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ). Specifically, many rivers have undergone the fate of being buried, channelized, culverted, or even further excavated in urban areas, which in turn has affected their function of flood regulation, nutrient cycles, and water quality (Cui et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2016; Ha et al., 2023 ). Therefore, an increasing number of studies have emphasized the importance of investigating changes in river systems (Elmore and Kaushal, 2008; Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Considerable numbers of studies have been performed on changes in the quantity and morphology of river systems worldwide. Horton (1945)  first proposed the concept of river order, which was revised by Strahler (1952)  and then widely applied in the analysis of river systems. Subsequently, various quantitative indicators of river structure, such as river density, water surface ratio, branching ratio, river sinuosity, and fractal dimension, have been proposed (Deng et al., 2018b; Nikora, 1991; Schumm, 1979 ). Using these indicators, many studies of the structural and morphological characteristics of rivers have been conducted. Steele et al. (2014)  investigated river systems in 100 metropolitan areas and found that the water surface ratio in developed areas decreased by 89 % in comparison with undeveloped land. Similarly, the river density in Baltimore City was reduced by 66 % because of rapid urbanization (Elmore and Kaushal, 2008 ). Moreover, river systems also experienced drastic degradation in several Chinese delta plains (e.g. the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing–Tianjin region) over the past 30 years (Zhao et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2006, 2008 ). Han et al. (2016)  also reported that reductions in river lengths in areas with a high level of urbanization were greater than those in areas with a low level of urbanization across the Yangtze River Delta. Generally, research findings about changes in urban river systems are abundant, but studies about the effects of such changes on flood regulation capacity have been rather limited. River systems are important carriers of water resources, as well as play vital roles in flood relief (Chin, 2006 ). The flood regulation capacity of rivers is a critical function for flood discharge and storage in river networks in urbanized plain regions. In recent years, the flood regulation capacity of urban rivers has significantly declined with the degradation of river systems in China (Lei et al., 2022 ). As reported by Xu et al. (2018) , the flood regulation capacity of the Taihu Plain decreased by 40.61 % from the 1980s to the 2010s because of a reduction in river density. Similar phenomena occurred in Ningbo city (Yang et al., 2016 ) and Shanghai city (Yuan et al., 2005 ). Furthermore, some researchers have found that river structure also has irreplaceable effects on urban floods (Anderson et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2018b; Wang et al., 2016 ). Previous studies mainly analyzed the responses of flood regulation capacity to changes in river quantity but seldom focused on its responses to changes in river structure. Moreover, previous researchers paid more attention to the annual average flood regulation capacity and seldom focused on it at the flood event scale. As we know, the amount of water that can be stored in rivers directly determines the risk of urban floods. Once the flood storage capacity of rivers is smaller than the flood yield, urban areas may face a flood disaster. Therefore, how to identify the distribution of flood storage capacity at the event scale is significant for flood management. The Taihu Plain contains one of the most complicated river networks in the world. Its river system provides almost half of the total flood regulation capacity (Wang et al., 1999 ). Owing to rapid urbanization, the quantity and structure of rivers exhibited downward tendencies during the last 30 years, which posed great challenges for flood management (Chen et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2016; Han et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2019 ). This study aimed to provide an event-based approach for assessing the impacts of changes in rivers on their flood regulation capacity. The Changzhou Plain, which is located in the northern part of the Taihu Plain, was selected as an example. The specific objectives of the study were to: (1) quantify the changes in river systems from the 1980s to the 2020 s; (2) establish a coupled flood model based on hydrological and hydrodynamic methods; and (3) assess the effects of changes in rivers on their flood regulation capacity at the event scale.  2 Study area and materials 2.1 Study area The Changzhou Plain covers a total land area of 1731 km2  and is 3–5 m above sea level. As shown in  Fig. 1 , it is characterized by the presence of many rivers and lakes linking the Yangtze River and Taihu Lake. Twelve trunk rivers are mainly responsible for water exchange, flood drainage, and shipping. For instance, the Jinghangyunhe River, which forms a southern section of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal, is a link between different hydrological regions within the Taihu Plain. As a core city of the Su-Xi-Chang (i.e. Suzhou–Wuxi–Changzhou city) economic zone, Changzhou underwent processes of rapid urbanization during the past few decades. Its river system has been severely disturbed, for example by river landfill, channelization, and curve cut-off (Deng et al., 2015 ). These changes in the river system caused alterations in river functions, such as flood regulation capacity and self-purification ability.  2.2 Data description The data used in this study comprised two parts. The first part corresponded to the river system and was extracted from topographic maps with a scale of 1:50,000. The topographic maps from 1988 are in paper form, and all the rivers are delineated manually. The maps from 2020 are digital line graphics displaying all the rivers, which were also checked and updated according to Google images with a resolution of 2 m. The second part, including hydrometeorological data (rainfall, water level, and discharge), river cross-sections, and flow regulation by pumps, was obtained from the Changzhou Hydrological Bureau. Among these data, hydrometeorological data with intervals of 5 min were converted into data with intervals of 1 h. Land use data with a resolution of 30 m were obtained from the Chinese Resource and Environmental Science Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn/ ). More detailed information about the data is summarized in  Table 1 . Considering the characteristics of plain river systems, rivers are divided into three orders (Han et al., 2016 ). Rivers with widths of greater than 20 m are defined as first-order rivers. Second-order and third-order rivers are those with widths of between 10 and 20 m and below 10 m, respectively. For this study, first-order rivers were viewed as main rivers and second-order and third-order rivers were considered to be tributary rivers. The second part of the data involved the basic data of the hydrological model (Nedbør-Afstrømnings-Model [NAM]) and the hydraulic model (MIKE 11), which mainly included the river network, river cross-sections, and rainfall, as well as boundary conditions (water level and discharge). Among these data, observations of historical flood events at three hydrological stations (Sanbaojie [SBJ], Changzhousan [CZS], and Cailinggang [CLG] shown in Fig. 1 ) were used to calibrate and validate model parameters.   3 Methodology 3.1 Indices for quantifying changes in river systems Two indices are used to represent changes in river systems, namely, river density (Rd ) and box dimension (D ), which are used to describe the quantity and complexity, respectively, of a river network (Horton, 1945; Zhang et al., 2015 ):(1) Rd  = L /S    (2) D = − lim  r → 0   lg N  r       lg r         where L  is the total length of rivers, S  is the total land area, r  is the length of the measurement lattice, and N (r ) is the number of grid cells of size r  needed to cover the river. For this study, 20 lattice sizes were used to analyze the fractal dimensions of the river system. These ranged from 50 m to 1000 m with intervals of 50 m.  3.2 Indices for assessing flood regulation capacity In previous studies, the flood regulation capacity of rivers was represented by the volume of the river cross-section between the annual average water level and the warning water level. For this study, we analyzed the flood regulation capacity at the event scale. Two indicators were developed based on the results of river modeling, namely, flood storage capacity (FSC ) and remaining flood storage capacity (RFSC ). FSC  and RFSC  represent the ability of the river system to provide flood discharge and flood protection, respectively. As illustrated in  Fig. 2 , FSC  refers to the total water volume between the initial water level and the flood water level, whereas RFSC  is defined as the space between the flood water level and the river bank elevation. They can be calculated using the following formulae:(3) FSC = S  1   × L    = W − 2 k H − h  1         + W − 2 k H − h  2          2   h  2   − h  1      × L       (4) RFSC = S  2   × L    = W − 2 k H − h  2         + W  2   ( H − h  2   ) × L       where S 1   and S 2   are the average cross-sectional area of the river, L  is the total length of rivers, W  is the width of the river, k  is the slope coefficient of the river, and h 1  , h 2  , and H  are the initial water level, flood water level, and river bank elevation, respectively. Of these, the h 2   value of each river is an important parameter that can be obtained by coupled flood modeling.  3.3 Establishment of coupled flood model A coupled flood model was established using the DHI MIKE platform (DHI, 2009 ). It included hydrological and hydraulic models. Hydrological processes were calculated using the NAM, and hydrodynamic processes were calculated using MIKE 11. Water exchange between the two models was achieved through a shared storage space (Thompson et al., 2004 ). Details of the technique can be seen in  Fig. 3 . 3.3.1 NAM The NAM, which is a combined rainfall-runoff model, was developed by Nielsen and Hansen (1973) . It splits runoff conceptually into overland flow, interflow, and baseflow components. This model can be applied independently, as well as to catchments generating lateral inflow. It was difficult to divide sub-basins according to a digital elevation model because of the flat terrain in the Changzhou Plain. Therefore, sub-basins were delineated based on the spatial pattern of rivers. The Euclidean distance method (Leeuw and Pruzansky, 1978 ) was used to perform this task in ArcGIS 10.3. The study area was divided into 99 sub-basins.  3.3.2 MIKE 11 model The MIKE 11 model is widely used for computing unsteady flow, discharge, and water levels in river channels and usually uses an implicit finite difference method for numerical solutions. It is especially suitable for flood plains with complex river systems. There are four modules in MIKE 11, namely, river network, cross-section, hydrodynamic, and boundary. The river network is the key linkage between all the module files. We generalized the river network according to the following criteria (Zhou, 2013 ): (1) main rivers with flood discharge functions remained unchanged; (2) tributary rivers with water transport functions could be merged with other nearby rivers; and (3) tributary rivers (e.g. terminal rivers and ponds) without water transport functions were merged with nearby main rivers as water storage areas. A total of 66 branches were generated in the model.  3.3.3 Calibration of coupled flood model The performance of the model was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R 2 ), Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE ; Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), and percentage error (PE ):(5) R = ∑ i = 1  n   h  obs  i   − h  obs  i    ̅     × h  sim  i   − h  sim  i    ̅       ∑ i = 1  n   h  obs  i   − h  obs  i    ̅     2    × ∑ i = 1  n   h  sim  i   − h  sim  i    ̅     2            (6) NSE = 1 − ∑ i = 1  n   h  obs  i   − h  sim  i      2     ∑ i = 1  n   h  obs  i   − h  obs  i    ̅     2          (7) PE = h  simp   − h  obsp    h  obsp         where h  obs  i     and h  sim  i     are the measured and simulated water levels at time i , respectively, h  obs  i    ̅    and h  sim  i    ̅    are the mean values of the measured and simulated water levels, respectively, and h  obsp     and h  simp     are the flood peak values of the measured and simulated water levels, respectively. Normally, performance ratings are categorized based on NSE and R² values: when 0.50 < NSE  (R ²) < 0.65, 0.65≤NSE  (R ²)< 0.75, and NSE  (R ²)≥0.75, indicating satisfactory, good, and very good model performance, respectively (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). We selected three flood events (20150602, 20161018, and 20170806) for parameter calibration and one flood event (20150616) for parameter validation. As shown in  Table 2 , heavy rainfall with different rainfall intensities occurred during the four selected flood events, which could represent various rainfall scenarios in the study area. Ten parameters were calibrated, namely, nine hydrological parameters and one hydrodynamic parameter (the Manning number n ), and the calibrated results are shown in  Table 3 .  Fig. 4  illustrates that simulated water levels during flood events closely matched measured hydrographs in the calibration period. The R 2  and NSE  values for the three selected flood events exceeded 0.95 and 0.91, respectively. The PE  values for these events were below 2.0 %. During the validation period, the selected flood event also demonstrated a precise agreement between simulated and measured water levels, with R 2  and NSE  values exceeding 0.90, and PE  below 1.5 % ( Fig. 5 ).    4 Results and discussion 4.1 Changes in the river network Changes in the spatial pattern of the river network from the 1980s to the 2020 s are illustrated in  Fig. 6 . As shown in Fig. 6 (b), there were no significant changes in main rivers during the last four decades except for locations A and B. The right branch of the Wunanhe River (location A) was excavated to connect it to the Wujingang River (location D) in 1996, and another canal named the Xinjinghangyunhe River (location B) was built to connect the Jinghangyunhe River (location E) and the Wuyiyunhe River (location C). These two new rivers strengthened the passage of floods from east to west and from north to south in the Changzhou Plain. In contrast, tributary rivers were heavily altered and reduced in scale and complexity; in particular, the rivers close to the city center, where the level of urbanization is higher, underwent a greater reduction. As shown in Fig. 6 (a), in areas such as locations A, B, and C, many rivers disappeared from the 1980s to the 2020 s. As shown in  Table 4 , the total length of the rivers in the study area decreased from 3311.46 km to 3061.47 km. The length of main rivers slightly increased by 3.05 % whereas the length of tributary rivers declined by 11.14 % from the 1980s to the 2020 s. Therefore, the decreases in total river length and river density in the Changzhou Plain could be attributed to the great reduction in the length of tributary rivers. Moreover, the complexity of the river network (D ) decreased from 1.71 in the 1980s to 1.58 in the 2020 s. As shown in  Fig. 7 , the Changzhou Plain experienced rapid urbanization with a significant increase in urban land as well as rapid decreases in agricultural land and water areas in the last three decades, which indicates that the river system in this region was hugely disturbed because of urban development. Fig. 7  reveals a trend where numerous tributary rivers disappeared between the 1980s and the 2020 s, replaced by urban land, particularly pronounced in urban centers. There was a slight increase in main rivers to facilitate flood discharge in these urban areas. Agricultural land experienced comparatively fewer losses of river networks compared to urban areas. This suggests a tradeoff between expanding urban impervious surfaces and preserving river networks, resulting in sacrificing small channels for urbanization in recent years (Deng et al., 2015; Han et al., 2020 ).  4.2 Effects of changes in rivers on their flood regulation capacity Flood regulation capacity serves as a critical indicator of how rivers adapt to flood disasters. The findings demonstrate significant changes in the river network of the Changzhou Plain over the past 40 years. The main rivers act as crucial conduits for flood drainage due to their strong connectivity, while tributary rivers provide ample space for water storage (Lei et al., 2022 ). Three scenarios were developed based on the evolving characteristics of these rivers during each period ( Table 5 ). S1 represents the current river network, while S2 and S3 depict alterations in tributary and main rivers, respectively. Using data from the regional river network and water level parameters derived from the integrated flood model, both FSC  and RFSC  were computed for each river. The flood event 20150616, which experienced heavy rainfall (213 mm) over a brief duration (36 h), was selected for assessing flood regulation capacity.  Fig. 8  illustrates the results of FSC  and RFSC  across three scenarios. In scenario S1, notable spatial variations in FSC  were observed among different rivers, with higher values concentrated predominantly in central and northern river systems. Among these, the FSC  in the Xinjinghangyunhe, Deshenghe, and Cailinggang rivers was higher than 10.0 × 104  m3 /km, which indicates that these rivers had a strong ability for flood drainage. In contrast, the FSC  in the southern rivers and rivers in the urban center was lower than 5.0 × 104  m3 /km, which represents a small capacity for discharging floods. As for RFSC  in scenario S1, the rivers in the eastern and southern parts had higher RFSC  values than the others in the event of a flood peak. The RFSC  in the Xinjinghangyunhe, Taigeyunhe, and Zhihugang rivers was above 15.0 × 104  m3 /km, which indicates that the areas along these rivers had strong abilities to resist flood risk. Notably, the Xinjinghangyunhe River was excavated as an important channel for flood drainage in the Changzhou Plain after 2000 and has played important roles in regional flood discharge and drainage (Wang, 2020 ). In comparison, the spatial distribution of FSC  and RFSC  in scenario S2 was similar to that in scenario S1 but rather different from that in scenario S3. This suggests that main rivers played more important roles than tributary rivers in terms of flood regulation capacity. To analyze changes in FSC  and RFSC  under different scenarios, we used the differences in indices between scenarios S1 and S2 (S3) in rivers. In comparison with scenario S1, the FSC  in central and southern rivers exhibited slight decreases under scenario S2, which was associated with the great reduction in tributary rivers along these rivers. Among these, the largest decrease in FSC  reached 0.27 × 104  m3 /km, which occurred in the case of the Cailinggang River. In comparison with scenario S3, the connectivity of the river network was further improved by excavating the Xinjinghangyunhe and Wunanhe rivers under scenario S1, which led to a notable change in flood discharge. As shown in  Fig. 9 (b), the FSC  in southern and eastern rivers under scenario S3 was lower than that under scenario S1. Especially, the difference in FSC  in southern rivers (i.e. Wuyiyunhe, Zhihugang, and Taigeyunhe) was higher than 1.0 × 104  m3 /km, which indicates that flood water was more easily transferred to southern and eastern areas with the help of the optimized river network under scenario S1. This implies that the optimized structure of main rivers has played a more important role in regional flood control than that of tributary rivers (Deng et al., 2018a ). The differences in RFSC  between scenarios S1 and S2 (S3) in each river are shown in  Fig. 10 . The RFSC  in most rivers under scenario S2 was higher than that under scenario S1, but the differences, which ranged from 0.05 to 0.3 × 104  m3 /km, were rather limited. This indicates that there were only slight effects on RFSC  from the decrease in tributary rivers. As shown in Fig. 10 (b), the spatial distribution of RFSC  significantly changed when the main rivers were altered. In comparison with scenario S1, RFSC  exhibited slight decreases in northern rivers and great increases in southern rivers under scenario S3. This suggests that the optimized structure of the river network can balance the spatial distribution of flood regulation capacity. The regional total FSC  and RFSC  under the three scenarios were calculated and are shown in  Fig. 11 . Among these, the highest regional FSC  of 5.02 × 104  m3 /km and RFSC  of 5.27 × 104  m3 /km occurred in scenarios S1 and S2, respectively. This indicates that scenarios S1 and S2 have the strongest ability to provide flood discharge and flood protection, respectively. Both FSC  and RFSC  had the lowest values under scenario S3. On comparing scenarios S1 and S2, FSC  increased by 1.62 % and RFSC  decreased by 1.74 % because of the reduction in tributary rivers. On comparing scenarios S2 and S3, FSC  and RFSC  increased by 6.70 % and 3.74 %, respectively, because of the improvement in the connectivity of the main rivers. This indicates that the effects of changes in main rivers on flood regulation capacity were stronger than those of changes in tributary rivers. However, there were increases of 8.42 % and 1.97 % in the regional FSC  and RFSC , respectively, from the 1980s to the 2020 s, which indicates that the capacities for both flood discharge and flood protection are improved under the current condition of rivers. Above all, the increases in flood regulation capacities from the 1980s to the 2020 s are mainly attributed to the improved connectivity of main rivers.  4.3 Discussion 4.3.1 Comparison with previous studies Owing to urbanization, both the quantity and the morphology of rivers have been marked by human interference in many cities across China (Han et al., 2016 ). From this study, Rd  decreased by 7.55 % in Changzhou from the 1980s to the 2020 s, which is similar to the results from other cities that Rd  in Shenzhen and Ningbo decreased by 10.1 % and 22.6 %, respectively, from 1980 to 2010 (Wu et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2008 ). In Baltimore, USA, Rd  in urban areas decreased by 66 %, but this value fell to 18 % in suburbs (Elmore and Kaushal, 2008 ). It can be inferred that rapid urbanization has been the main reason for the degradation of river systems, although the degree of reduction in Rd  varies between different cities. In terms of methodology, previous studies calculated flood regulation capacity mainly via statistical approaches (Lei et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2018 ). In this study, we combined a coupled flood model and a statistical approach. A coupled flood model, integrating hydrological and hydraulic components, was developed and demonstrated effective performance in the Changzhou Plain. This model facilitated the determination of the initial water level (h 1  ) and peak water level (h 2  ) for each river. Both of them are crucial variables for calculating flood regulation capacity and reflect temporal and spatial variations in water levels during flood events (Zhou et al., 2013 ). Previous studies typically considered only static regulation capacity, defined as the total volume of water between average and warning levels for the entire region (Yang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2005 ). Thus, the water level variables obtained in this study are more precise compared to those utilized in previous studies. Additionally, RFSC  was defined as the potential space between peak water level and river bank elevation, serving to evaluate the flood protection ability of rivers. These two event-based indicators have become useful tools for determining flood regulation capacity in urbanized plain river networks because such areas will face losses of tributary rivers and optimization of main rivers in the future (Wheater et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2013 ).  4.3.2 Implications for regional flood mitigation and river planning River systems play a positive role in flood control in urbanized plain river networks via their flood regulation capacity (Wang et al., 1999; Yuan et al., 2005 ). In the past few decades, most cities in the Taihu Plain have experienced reductions in river quantity and simplification of river structure, which have resulted in profound changes in the flood regulation capacity of rivers (Lei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018 ). Flood management is one of the most important issues in regions with urbanized plain river networks because of their huge population and wealth (Wang et al., 2020 ). For this study, two flood indices, namely, FSC  and RFSC , for different river systems were calculated with the help of the coupled flood model. A meaningful result that was found is that the effects of changes in main rivers on flood regulation capacity were stronger than those of changes in tributary rivers in the Changzhou Plain. Flood regulation capacity was improved, with increases of 8.42 % and 1.97 % in FSC  and RFSC , respectively, although Rd  declined by 7.55 % from the 1980s to the 2020 s. From further inspection of changes in rivers, the structure of the main rivers was improved, although many tributary rivers disappeared from the 1980s to the 2020 s. This implies that reductions in flood regulation capacity due to the loss of tributary rivers can be compensated by optimization of main rivers (Cui et al., 2009 ). Owing to rapid urbanization, river disappearance has become an indisputable fact that is irreparable, especially in the case of the large number of disappeared tributaries. Therefore, river planning based on structure optimization has become an important task for urban managers (Bahrami et al., 2021 ). This study has indicated that the flood control function of rivers could be improved by optimization of main rivers. Two main rivers (i.e. the Xinjinghangyunhe and Wunanhe rivers) were excavated to connect five other main rivers (shown in Fig. 6 (b)), which was beneficial for transferring upstream floods bypassing the city center and opened a new flood channel to Taihu Lake. This implies that more flood discharge channels through connecting main rivers should be considered during river planning in regions of urbanized plain river networks. Cui et al. (2009)  and Schmadel et al. (2018)  also reported that regional flood control could be improved by optimizing the structure and connectivity of rivers. Therefore, a river system with high flood safety should comprise main rivers with good connectivity for flood drainage and dense tributary rivers for water storage (Deng et al., 2018b; Napieralski and Carvalhaes, 2016 ).    5 Conclusions and limitations River systems in areas of urbanized plain river networks have changed dramatically during the last 40 years, which has altered their flood regulation capacity. In this study, we took the Changzhou Plain as an example and then analyzed the effects of changes in rivers on their flood regulation capacity using a coupled model at the flood event scale. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) From the 1980s to the 2020 s, there were remarkable changes in the river system in the Changzhou Plain, with a reduction in total river length of 7.55 %. In detail, the length of main rivers increased by 3.05 % and that of tributary rivers decreased by 11.14 %. The complexity of the river network tended to decrease, with a reduction in box dimension of 7.60 %. The structure of the main rivers was improved by the excavation of the Wunanhe and Xinjinghangyunhe rivers. (2) A coupled model was established based on the NAM and MIKE 11 model at the flood event scale. Two indices (FSC  and RFSC ) were developed to assess changes in the flood regulation capacity of rivers. Changes in tributary rivers had slight effects on flood regulation capacity, with an increase in FSC  (maximum value of 0.27 × 104  m3 /km) and a decrease in RFSC  (maximum value of 0.23 × 104  m3 /km). By contrast, changes in main rivers had great effects on the spatial pattern of FSC  and RFSC . At the regional scale, both FSC  (8.42 %) and RFSC  (1.97 %) increased from the 1980s to the 2020 s, which was mainly attributed to the improvement in the connectivity of main rivers. Based on the above analysis, we believe that this approach provides a practical method for assessing the flood regulation capacity of river systems in urbanized plain river networks. Moreover, the mechanisms of the impact of river structure on flood regulation capacity can be examined using the coupled flood model by flood managers. However, some limitations and uncertainties still existed in this study. As for the coupled flood model, more flood events are needed for validation, although four different flood events were selected for parameter calibration. Moreover, the coupled flood model performed rather well, yet there are still uncertainties in terms of hydrological parameters. Owing to the lack of measurements of runoff in the Changzhou Plain, only water level data were used for parameter calibration. In future work, we will select more flood events with different magnitudes, as well as obtain rainfall-runoff data based on hydrological experiments in urban basins, for validation of the coupled model.
1 Introduction Conceptualization of the media as a pore network (rather than a bundle of capillaries) goes back to the work of Fatt (1956)  and Broadbent and Hammersley (1957) , further advanced by the seminal works of Wilkinson and Willemsen (1983), Wilkinson (1986), Lenormand et al. (1983) . In its simplest form, a porous medium is conceptualized as a lattice of conductors, disregarding the pore shape. More complex (and realistic) pore network models relate the bond geometry to their conductance (Sahimi, 2011 ) and map out the pore structure obtained from pore space partitioning (Blunt, 2017 ). Depending on the complexity of the pore space, the resulting pore network may be characterized by subnetworks or clusters that are hydraulically isolated, that is, clusters that are not connecting the inlet and outlet of the pore network (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2010 ). Isolated sites cause numerical problems for the solution of flow in networks because they lead to singular system matrices. For example, the dilution of a pore network (Hunt and Sahimi, 2017 ) by randomly assigning zero conductances to connections between sites may lead to isolated subnetworks. This is a general issue for flow problems in media characterized by isolated clusters. Such media can result from the dilution of regular networks (Hunt and Sahimi, 2017 ), from networks patterns generated by invasion percolation, or from pore networks derived directly from image analysis of porous and fractured media characterized by unconnected porosity. The singularity issue can be addressed by preprocessing of the network image and removing isolated clusters before the flow solution. Algorithms for the cluster identification include the methods of Sheppard et al. (1999)  and Raoof and Hassanizadeh (2010)  and Guo et al. (2021) . In this note, we propose a robust algorithm based on singular value decomposition (SVD) of the system matrix in order to both solve the linear flow problem and identify isolated clusters in the network. SVD decomposes a matrix into the product of a diagonal and two orthonormal matrices (Golub and Van Loan, 2013 ). It is used, for example, to determine the pseudoinverse of a singular matrix and calculate low-rank approximations of a matrix. SVD finds broad applications in data-driven science and engineering (Brunton and Kutz, 2019; Bisgard, 2020 ). The idea here is to use SVD to identify nodes belonging to isolated clusters by solving for single-phase flow in the PNM using the pseudoinverse of the Laplacian matrix. The internal nodes of zero pressure belong to isolated clusters. The proposed method is general and applies to the identification of isolated clusters in networks. In this technical note, we first evaluate the accuracy of the SVD pseudoinverse approximation, then demonstrate its robustness.  2 Methods 2.1 Graph Laplacian The graph Laplacian is a representation of the graph underlying the PNM (Bapat, 2010 ). The Laplacian is weighted by the conductances of its bonds of the graph. The conductance or weight matrix G   contains the conductances between G  i j     between sites i   and j  . If all non-zero conductances are unity, G   is equal to the adjacency matrix of the graph. The weighted degree matrix is a diagonal matrix that contains the sum of the conductances of the bonds adjacent to a node, that is, D  i j   = δ  i j   ∑  [ k i ]    G  i k     , where ∑  [ k i ]      denotes summation over all sites k   that are connected to site i  . With these definitions, the weighted graph Laplacian is given by L  ′   = D − G   . The continuity equation for single-phase flow through the PNM can then be written as (1) L  ′   ⋅ P = 0 ,     where P   is the vector of pressures at all sites of the network. Following Poiseuille law (Poiseuille, 1839 ), the flow rate between sites i   and j   is (2) Q  i j   = G  i j   ( P  i   − P  j   )  ,     which is a statement of momentum conservation. Notice that the pressure at the unconnected site does not affect the flow field as G  i j   = 0    on all bonds in the unconnected cluster periphery. Also note, that Q  i j   = − Q  j i     . Continuity, or mass conservation, is expressed by (3) ∑  [ j i ]    Q  i j   = 0 .     The latter is equivalent to Eq. (1) . The flow rates at sites are defined by (4) Q  i   = 1  2   ∑  [ j i ]    | Q  i j   |  .     From the mass conservation statement (3) , it follows that the graph Laplacian has the eigenvector ( 1 , … , 1 )    with the eigenvalue zero, which is the trivial solution of equal pressure at all sites. Thus, the determinant of the graph Laplacian is zero, i.e., L  ′     is not invertible. The multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue is equal to the number of isolated clusters in the graph, or equivalently, the rank of the graph Laplacian is equal to the number of sites minus the number of connected components (Bapat, 2010 ). Note that the sites belonging to an isolated cluster do not contribute separately to this count, that is, an isolated cluster, even though it may contain multiple sites, counts as one. We seek a solution to Eq. (1)  for prescribed pressure at the inlet and outlet nodes. To this end, we define the modified graph Laplacian L   such that L  i j   = δ  i j      for all sites i , j    that are in the inlet or outlet boundaries and L  i j   = L  i j  ′      for all other sites. With this definition, the boundary value problem can be written as (5) L ⋅ P = b ,     where the vector b   on the right side of Eq. (5)  contains the boundary conditions with b  i   = p  0      for the sites j   at the inlet boundary and b  i   = 0    else. For networks that consist of a single connected cluster, the modified Laplacian L   is an invertible (non-singular) matrix. The trivial zero eigenvalue proper to the graph Laplacian is eliminated by specifying non-trivial boundary conditions. Only in the presence of isolated clusters has the modified graph Laplacian L   a zero eigenvalue and thus is not invertible. This can be interpreted by the example of a single isolated internal site of the network. In this case, a row in the modified Laplacian is zero, and thus, its determinant is zero as well. In order to solve the flow equation (5) , and to determine the sites belonging to isolated regions, we propose to use the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the modified graph Laplacian. In the following, we provide a brief summary of SVD.  2.2 Singular value decomposition The singular value decomposition of L   is the decomposition of the matrix L   into the product of two orthonormal matrices U   and V   and a diagonal matrix Σ   with positive real entries σ  i     as (Golub and Van Loan, 2013 ) (6) L = U Σ V  T   ,     The entries σ  i     are called the singular values of L  . The number of non-zero σ  i     is defined as the rank of the matrix L  . The columns of V   (termed the right singular vectors of L  ), and the columns of U   (the left singular vectors), always form an orthogonal set with no assumptions on L  . If L   is an invertible matrix, its inverse is given by (7) L  − 1   = V Σ  − 1   U  T   .      If L   is a singular matrix (i.e., at least one σ  i   = 0   ), its pseudo-inverse L  +     is determined as follows (Golub and Van Loan, 2013 ). First, the pseudo-inverse Σ  +     of the diagonal matrix Σ   is determined by inverting every non-zero element on the diagonal and leaving the zero elements unchanged. In the numerical calculations, elements are inverted if they are larger than a given threshold and set equal to zero if they are smaller. The pseudo-inverse L  +     is then given by (8) L  +   = V Σ  +   U  T       Once the pseudo-inverse is obtained, the pressure distribution is determined by a matrix multiplication as (9) P = L  +   b .     The sites i   belonging to isolated clusters have zero pressure P  i   = 0    because they are not connected to inlet and outlet. This approach does not require matrix preconditioning and can be used for singular and invertible matrices. At the same time, it is robust and accurate.  2.3 Pore network from a partially saturated medium We compare the proposed SVD-based method to a method that uses first a pre-processing step in order to identify and remove isolated clusters, and then solve the flow problem by standard inversion of the system matrix. To this end, we consider a pore network characterized by isolated regions that is obtained by pore space partitioning of an image of the fluid phase of a two-dimensional millifluidic device under partially saturated single-phase flow conditions. Fig. 1  shows the fluid phase (in white) distribution in a milifluidic device before (Fig. 1 a) and after (Fig. 1 b) processing the image to exclude the non-percolated disconnected fluid clusters. The experimental setup and device specification are described in Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2017) . In this work, we only use the image to construct a relevant pore network and do not address the physics arising from the experiment. The original image (Fig. 1 a) contains many disconnected regions of different sizes. The small regions are formed by wetting liquid phase films surrounding the grains, while the larger clusters are formed by the entrapment of the liquid phase by the non-wetting gas phase. The processed image (Fig. 1 b) does not include isolated fluid clusters. The pre-processing of the pixelized image was conducted using the MATLAB image analysis toolbox (The MathWorks Inc., 2022 ) using the 8-connectivity criterion to identify isolated clusters. The pore-scale partitioning, both in the original and pre-processed images, is performed following the methodology presented in Ben-Noah et al. (2024a) . This method uses information about the curvatures of the distance map (obtained from the binary image) to separate distinct pores (small plot in Fig. 1 b) and to evaluate the pore body and throat sizes. The construction of the detailed network follows the methodology presented in Ben-Noah et al. (2024b) . A parabolic parameterization of the pore geometry is assumed to evaluate the bond conductivities in the resulting pore network models. For laminar flow, the bond conductance is evaluated by the harmonic sum of the local conductivities along the pore channel with variable width by using Boussinesq (1868)  equation for rectangular apertures. The pore sizes and conductance distributions and additional information about the milifluidic device and pore partitioning are provided in Figure SF1 in the supplementary material. The results of this analysis are presented in Section 3.1  below.    2.4 Diluted pore networks We use the SVD method to solve the steady flow equation on two types of diluted networks based on two-dimensional hexagonal and square lattices at different degrees of dilution. In short, networks are diluted by randomly assigning zero conductances to connections between sites. The network properties, such as the probability of a cluster connecting inlet and outlet, can be determined by percolation theory based on the occupation probability (p  ) of either lattice bonds or lattice sites and their conductances (Berkowitz and Ewing, 1998; Broadbent and Hammersley, 1957; Hunt and Sahimi, 2017; Stauffer and Aharony, 2018 ). We compare the percolation properties determined from the SVD-based flow solution to theoretical values from percolation theory. We consider two types of diluted lattices based on two-dimensional hexagonal 2D lattices with coordination number Z  s   = 3    and a two-dimensional square 2D lattice with coordination number Z  s   = 4   . For simplicity, we use a uniform conductance field (G  i j   = 1    for all i , j   ), unit bond length of ℓ = 1   , N = 100    sites along each face of the lattices, and a unit pressure gradient Δ P / L   . The domain length is L = N ℓ    for the square lattice, and L = 3 N ℓ / 4    for the hexagonal lattice, which is oriented with the long diagonal in the main flow direction. The total number of sites in the regular network is denoted by N  s    . Starting from a regular lattice with coordination number Z  s    , the network is diluted to obtain a target occupation probability (10) p  b   = 〈 Z 〉   Z  s     ,     where 〈 Z 〉    is the mean coordination number of the diluted network. The dilution method applied here is a simplification of the protocol described in Raoof and Hassanizadeh (2010) . Each bond is randomly assigned a dilution or elimination number between zero and one. Then, all bonds with an elimination number larger than p  b     are assigned zero conductivity. In this way, N  R   = 50    network realizations are generated for each p  b     value. Then, for each realization, the flow Eq. (5)  is solved using the pseudoinverse given by Eq. (8) . We determine for each target p  b     value the number of realizations for which a percolating cluster prevails. A percolating cluster exists if the permeability defined by Eq. (15)  is larger than 0. The percolation frequency p  p     for a given p  b     is defined as the ratio of the number N  p     of realizations with percolating clusters and the total number N  R     of realizations, (11) p  p   = N  p    N  R     .     For p  b     smaller than a critical value p  c    , the bond percolation threshold, there is no percolating cluster, that is, p  p   = 0   . The theoretical random bond percolation threshold for an infinite hexagonal lattice is p  c   = 1 − 2 sin ( π / 18 )  ≈ 0 . 6527   , and for an infinite square lattice it is p  c   = 1  2      (Hunt and Sahimi, 2017 ). These synthetic media are used to evaluate the robustness, that is, the ability of the SVD method to solve the flow equation of a media with many singular points and isolated clusters. The results of this analysis are presented in Section 3.2  below.   3 Demonstration and validation In this section, we demonstrate and validate the proposed SVD approach. First, in Section 3.1 , we evaluate the accuracy of the method. Then, in Section 3.2 , we demonstrate the robustness of the method. 3.1 Pore network from a partially saturated medium In this subsection, we consider a pore network obtained by pore space partitioning of an image of the fluid phase of a two-dimensional millifluidic device under partially saturated single-phase flow conditions (see Section 2.3 ). The results are compared in terms of flow rate and pressure statistics to assess the accuracy of the proposed method. The total flow rate (Q  m    ) is defined by the sum of the flow rates at the network’s inlet sites. (12) Q  m   = ∑  i   Q  i   ,      We determine the probability density function (PDF) of the flow rate at the sites through areal sampling from the network flow simulations and image pore space partitioning (13) f ( Q  k   )  = ∑  i   I ( Q  i   , Q  k   )  A  i    Δ Q  k   ∑  i   A  i     ,     where A  i     [L 2    ] is the area of pore i  , and Q  i     is the flow rate at the i  th site. The indicator function I ( Q  i   , Q  k   )     is one if the flow rate Q  i     is within the interval ( Q  k   , Q  k   + Δ Q  k   ]    and zero otherwise. The pore area (A  i    ) is evaluated by summing the number of pixels in the image belonging to each pore and multiplying it by a single pixel area (1 0  − 3    mm  2     ). The distribution of the pressure at the sites is determined in analogy to the distribution of flow rates as (14) f ( P  k   )  = ∑  i   I ( P  i   , P  k   )  A  i    Δ P  k   ∑  i   A  i     ,      For the network constructed from the original image, the flow Eq. (5)  is solved using the pseudoinverse (8)  obtained from SVD, which gives the pressures at all sites through Eq. (9) . For the network obtained from the pre-processed image, the flow equation is solved both by direct inversion of Eq. (5)  and by using the pseudoinverse from SVD.  Fig. 2 a and b show the spatial distribution of flow rates in the pore networks obtained from the original and pre-processed images. The singular disconnected regions attain a zero pressure value. In the network resulting from the original image, the solution using SVD assigns zero pressure to the isolated clusters. The clusters obtained from the SVD analysis on the original image coincide with those identified from the pre-processing step of the binary image. The spatial flow rate distribution in the two networks is essentially identical. This is confirmed by the probability density function of bond flow rates and pressures for both networks, shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 2 . Moreover, the device flow rate Q  m     defined in Eq. (12)  for the networks from the original and pre-processed images differ by about 0.2% further confirming the performance and accuracy of the proposed SVD-based method. In order to assess whether this difference is a result of the solution of the flow equation by different methods (SVD versus direct inversion) or due to the pre-processing, we use also the SVD method to solve for the flow on the pre-processed image, even though the pre-processed image does not have any singularities. The difference in the total flow rates obtained by the two methods is smaller than 10−11 , that is, they are essentially identical. This implies that there is a slight difference in the identification of isolated clusters by the SVD method on the pore network extracted from the direct image and by the connectivity-based method on the pixel image. In other words, the connected percolating clusters in the pore networks extracted from the direct and pre-processed images are not exactly the same. Thus, the SVD-based method provides an accurate method for the identification of isolated clusters and solution of single phase flow in the network obtained from the direct image without the need for pre-processing, which may introduce some inaccuracies.  3.2 Diluted pore networks In this section, we evaluate the ability of the SVD-based method to solve the flow equation and identify isolated clusters at bond occupation probabilities close to the percolation threshold (see Section 2.4 ). In addition to the percolation thresholds, the results for this media, are compared in terms of relative conductivity, which is defined in terms of the total flow rate relative to the total flow rate in a corresponding regular network as (15) k  r   = Q  m    Q  m  ( 0 )      ,     where the superscript 0   denotes to the flow rate for the corresponding regular network. From the SVD-based numerical flow simulations in the diluted networks, the percolation threshold p  c     is estimated as the bond occupation probability p  b     for which 50% of the lattice realizations percolate (Friedman and Seaton, 1998 ). As shown in Fig. 3 a, the numerical values obtained for p  c     are in very good agreement with the theoretical values both for the hexagonal (p  c   ≈ 0 . 6527   ) and square (p  c   = 0 . 5   ) lattices. A slight deviation of the numerical from the theoretical values can be attributed to the finite size of the lattices with N = 100   , and the finite number of realizations with N  R   = 50   . Fig. 3 b shows the dependence of permeability on p  b    . For p  b   < p  c     , permeability tends to zero, then for p  b   > p  c      it increases monotonically toward k  r   = 1   , which is the value for the non-diluted lattices. For p  b     far from p  c    , the evolution is approximately linear. These behaviors are in accordance with the literature (Kirkpatrick, 1973; Friedman et al., 1995 ). The variability of the k  r     values between realizations, illustrated by the width of the error bars, is not linear, with zero variance for p  b   = 1    and p  b   ≪ p  c      and a large variance for intermediate values. These results demonstrate the robustness of the proposed SVD method.     4 Conclusion We have shown that SVD is a robust, easy-to-implement, and accurate method to identify sites belonging to isolated clusters in heterogeneous networks. Isolated clusters render the modified graph Laplacian non-invertible. Thus, we use the pseudoinverse determined from SVD to solve for single-phase flow in the heterogeneous networks, which assigns zero pressure to sites belonging to isolated clusters. The SVD method is demonstrated and validated for pore network models, which are characterized by singular points and isolated clusters. The time complexity for algorithms to identify isolated clusters such as the one proposed in Sheppard et al. (1999)  is of order N ln N   , where N   is the number of sites, while the time complexity for matrix inversion is of the order of N  3    . The proposed SVD method, which provides at the same time the flow solution and delineates the isolated clusters, is of order N  3    . This shows that SVD provides a robust alternative to combined algorithms that identify isolated clusters and solve for single phase flow sequentially.
1 Introduction It is anticipated that East Asia will experience an increase in both the intensity and frequency of extreme precipitation events due to climate change (IPCC., 2021 ; Do et al., 2023 ). Consequently, this will increase the severity and frequency of damages caused by floods and landslides (Blanchet et al., 2016; Ghanmi et al., 2016; Thomassen et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022 ), major infrastructure failures (Papalexiou et al., 2016; Pregnolato et al., 2016; Nissen and Ulbrich, 2017 ), degradation of ecosystems (Ummenhofer and Meehl, 2017; Walsh et al., 2020 ), and socioeconomic disruption (Singhal et al., 2022; Sanders et al., 2023 ). Hence, it is imperative to gain an accurate understanding of the magnitude, duration, and frequency of extreme precipitation by conducting spatiotemporal analyses on historical observations. This knowledge is crucial for effectively designing, planning, and managing systems that can cope with for the challenges posed by extreme events.
