A common approach to quantifying significant extreme precipitation is through the concept of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP). PMP is defined as the maximum depth of precipitation that is physically possible for a given duration and geographic location (Hand et al., 2004; Cerveny et al., 2007; Johnson and Smithers, 2019 ). There are three primary methods used to estimate PMP: (1) the meteorological method, which calculates PMP based on the maximum moisture capacity of the atmosphere. The method is advantageous for its physical realism and adaptability to various regions, but it is data-intensive and complex if climate model simulation is employed; (2) the statistical method, which infers PMP by assuming that observed extreme rainfall follows a specific probability density function. This method relies on available historical data, yet it is constrained by the length of records and the assumption that past patterns will continue; and (3) the envelope method, which involves plotting the relationship between the maximum observed precipitation depth (y) and the corresponding duration (x) on a graph and then drawing an envelope line below which all data points are encompassed (Hershfield, 1965; Paulhus, 1965 ; WMO, 1986 ; WMO, 2009 ; Lee, 2010 ). This method is visually straightforward and robust if estimated with extensive data, though it can be heavily reliant on past extremes. Jennings (1950)  employed the envelope method to establish the PMP values for durations spanning from one minute to two years on a global scale. Subsequently, Paulhus (1965)  updated the extreme precipitation records compiled by Jennings at durations ranging from 9 h to 8 days. Paulhus demonstrated a power law relationship between PMP and precipitation duration, as expressed in Eq. 1 .(1) PMP = a D  b        Here, D represents the duration of precipitation (e.g., hours), PMP denotes the probable maximum precipitation (e.g., mm), while the parameters a and b capture the temporal scaling behavior between these two variables. Various studies have estimated the PMP envelopes for different regions across the world over an extended time period (Paulhus, 1965 ; Dyck and Peschke, 1995 ; Zhang et al., 2013 ; Gonzalez and Bech, 2017 ; Pöschmann et al., 2021 ; González-Herrero et al., 2023 ).  Fig. 1  illustrates some of the PMP envelopes derived from these investigations. In the case of the Republic of Korea, distinct formulas are utilized based on a threshold duration of 1-day (Lee, 2010 ). For both global and Korean analyses, the exponent of the power law is around 0.5, while Antarctica and Germany exhibit the exponent values of around 0.6 and 0.2, respectively. Notably, Antarctica demonstrates remarkably low y-intercept values, indicating low PMP during short duration periods. Conversely, the high exponent of the power law of Antarctica suggests a substantial increase in PMP with the increase of durations (González-Herrero et al., 2023). Conventional ground-based observations, traditionally used for estimating extreme precipitation and Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP), have inherent limitations. They offer localized information and fail to account for extreme values that may occur between observation points, as noted by Chaubey et al. (1999) . For this reason, recent efforts have been made to overcome these limitations by incorporating precipitation data obtained through remote sensing techniques such as weather radars (Goudenhoofdt et al., 2017; Marra and Morin, 2015 ) and satellites (Zhou et al., 2008; Rajulapati et al., 2020 ). Comparing Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE) based on weather radar data with surface precipitation gauges, Goudenhoofdt et al. (2017)  found that QPE generally fell within the confidence interval of surface precipitation gauges when assessing extreme precipitation values over 1- and 24-hour durations in Belgium. Marra and Morin (2015)  utilized radar data to derive Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves for the Eastern Mediterranean region and compared them with those derived from ground-based precipitation data. They observed that radar-based annual maximums and IDF curves tended to be slightly overestimated but 70 % of them remained within the 95 percent prediction interval of the ground-based IDF curve. Notably, weather radar data with high temporal and spatial resolution have proven more valuable than point observations for capturing short-duration heavy rainfall events (Tilford et al., 2003 ). Marra and Morin (2015)  demonstrated that weather radar data can provide distributed precipitation estimates with enhanced spatial and temporal resolution, thus mitigating the typical limitations associated with point precipitation data, especially in regions characterized by significant seasonal precipitation fluctuations. Pöschmann et al. (2021)  analyzed the PMP envelope based on radar data from Germany and revealed significant deviations from the power law. They identified three distinct scaling characteristics at the threshold durations of 1 h and 1 day, attributing these differences to the merit of the radar data to capture entire precipitation depth as grid format across the observation domain. In this research, we employ radar-ground composite precipitation data to investigate the temporal scaling behavior of the PMP envelope of the Republic of Korea (South Korea). Diverging from prior studies (Marra and Morin, 2015; Goudenhoofdt et al., 2017; Pöschmann et al., 2021 ), our study takes a distinct approach by: (1) utilizing radar-ground synthetic precipitation data to construct an envelope based on a more accurate spatiotemporal representation of the precipitation field; (2) identifying various factors that influence the shape of the envelope through spatiotemporal analysis of precipitation data; and (3) independently examining the impacts of East Asian rainy seasons and typhoons, which play crucial roles in shaping the characteristics of summer extreme precipitation events in the Republic of Korea. The primary aim of this study from practical perspective is to analyze the differences in extreme precipitation measured from ground-based observations and radar-based observations in terms of precipitation amount and observation locations. Through this, we aim to demonstrate how these differences, resulting from various observation methods, can significantly impact flood risk and design criteria for major hydraulic structures related to flood management.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Study area The study area of this research encompasses South Korea, as depicted in  Fig. 2 . South Korea is situated on a peninsula extending from the eastern edge of the Eurasian continent, characterized by approximately 70 % mountainous terrain. It is geographically located between 33° and 38° north latitude and 126° and 132° east longitude (Fig. 2 ). Within South Korea, Jeju Island stands as the southernmost volcanic island, receiving an average annual precipitation of approximately 2000 mm. This value is approximately 1.5 times higher than the average precipitation recorded in the rest of the country, which amounts to 1300 mm. Considering this distinction, our study initially focuses on analyzing the behavior of PMP specifically for the Korean Peninsula. The analysis involving Jeju Island will be presented separately in the Discussion section.  2.2 Rainfall data This study uses data from 547 Automatic Weather System (AWS) ground-based precipitation stations (blue circles in Fig. 2 ) and quality-controlled (QC) radar (red circles in Fig. 2 ) across Korea provided by the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) for the period 2009–2018. The radar precipitation data has a spatial resolution of 1×1 kilometer and a temporal resolution of 10 min. The radar data used here consists of one Dual-Polarization radar (Baengnyeongdo) and ten Single-Polarization radars. The Myeonbongsan radar and the Incheon radar operate in the C-band, while the rest operate in the S-band. Currently, all radars except for Incheon radar have been replaced with S-band dual-polarization radars. Radar data is provided in Binary format in Plan Position Indicator (PPI) after undergoing Radar Product Generator (ORPG) Quality Control (QC) (https://data.kma.go.kr/resources/html/en/aowdp.html ). Typically, studies involving radar precipitation data for hydro-meteorological applications in the Korean Peninsula employ CAPPI (Constant Altitude Plan Position Indicator) data due to the region's terrain and the radar locations, which are predominantly situated on hilltops near the coast (Yoo et al., 2016 ). Instead of CAPPI data that tends to underestimate precipitation observed on the ground (Kim et al., 2008; Yoon et al., 2014 ), our study employs CMAX (Column MAXimum) radar reflectivity data. CMAX data records the highest reflectivity value within each vertical column of the radar volume observation data. This choice is particularly useful for analyzing short-term summer precipitation (Lee and Ryu, 2009 ). Raw reflectivity data was converted to precipitation intensity according to the relationship between radar reflectivity (Z , mm  6    /m  3    ) and ground precipitation (R ,mmh  − 1    ): Z = 200 R  1.6      (Marshall and Palmer, 1948 ). A detailed description of the radar data generation process can be found in Suk et al. (2013) . The reliability of weather radar data has been a subject of ongoing improvement (Wilson and Brandes, 1979; Habib and Krajewski, 2002 ; Moore et al., 2004 ; Krajewski et al., 2010 ; Biggs and Atkinson, 2011 ). The radar equipment used in this study has been officially operated by the South Korean government for many years to provide real-time public services, so its network was carefully designed with its installation location at high altitudes to minimize terrain blockage. However, numerous outliers in the raw radar data still arose, the causes of which could not be clearly identified. To address these outliers, the authors developed a custom algorithm specifically designed to remove such anomalies. This algorithm iterates the process of identifying and replacing the outliers based on local spatiotemporal statistics until no outliers are present. The algorithm has been published as a separate paper (Kim et al., 2024 ), ensuring the reliability of the data of this study. The algorithm for detecting outliers based on a simple 3-sigma rule in a spatiotemporal context and the algorithm for detecting rapid changes between adjacent radar cells in a spatial context were both iterated at the local scale, effectively improving the quality of radar rainfall data (RMSE: reduced from 17300 to 3.77, hit rate: increased from 0.25 % to 62 %; Kim et al., 2024 ). To further enhance the accuracy of the radar data after outlier removal, the conditional merging (CM) method was employed (Pegram, 2002; Ehret, 2003; Sinclair and Pegram, 2005 ). The CM method corrects the original radar precipitation field by estimating the spatial field of residuals between the radar data and ground observation data that is obtained by performing a Kriging-based spatial interpolation (e.g., Ordinary Kriging applied in this study) based on the radar pixel precipitation values at the location of the ground gauges. This residual field is then added to the original radar data, thereby correcting the bias of the original radar data (Sinclair and Pegram, 2005; Berndt et al., 2014 ). Here, it is noteworthy that conditional merging calculates the residuals between radar grid data and point data for each location, spatially interpolates these residuals to create a spatial field of residuals, and then uses this field to correct the radar spatial field. Therefore, the resulting precipitation field represents the point data values that would likely be observed at the locations of the radar grid. Thus, it is reasonable to consider that the difference in precipitation due to the spatial scale difference between the radar grid (1 km) and the point scale is already accounted for in the results of this study. However, the interpolated residuals may not accurately reflect the residuals of CMAX values at locations without ground data. To address this issue, this study validated the radar-gauge merged product using data from 100 Automatic Synoptic Observing System (ASOS) stations operating independently of the precipitation data utilized in this research. The comparison results are presented in Appendix A1. According to the analysis, there was a significant difference between the ASOS observations and the radar-gauge merged product for very short duration (e.g. 10 min). However, for longer durations, the differences between the two variables began to decrease significantly, and no systematic bias was identified for high precipitation amounts. The CM method has been successfully applied to enhance the quality of radar-based precipitation (Dao et al., 2020 ), as well as satellite-based precipitation (Baik et al., 2016 ) and soil moisture (Kim et al., 2016 ).  2.3 Calculate the relationship between precipitation depth and duration The radar-ground precipitation synthetic data was generated in the form of a three-dimensional cube with dimensions of 525,888 (t) × 371 (x) × 613 (y). Here, x and y represent the spatial extent of 1 km pixels covering the entire region of Korea, while t represents the number of two-dimensional radar precipitation fields recorded at 10-minute intervals over the period from January 1, 2009, 00:00 to December 31, 2018, 23:50. Within this dataset, there are 35 different durations considered, ranging from 10 min to 86400 min (corresponding to 2 months). The maximum precipitation and extreme quantile values for each grid point were calculated using the rolling-window summation method.  Fig. 3  describes the process of estimating maximum rainfall data points used to draw the scaling behavior plots:(1) Extract the 10-minute rainfall time series for each grid cell (Fig. 3 a).  (2) Apply the rolling sum to this rainfall time series for the desired duration. For example, if a part of the 10-minute rainfall time series has values of …10, 50, 70, 30, 10, 0…, and then the 30-minute rolling sum would be …130, 150, 110, 40…. The highest value among these is considered the maximum rainfall for that grid cell (Fig. 3 b).  (3) Repeat steps (1) and (2) for all grid cells to calculate the maximum rainfall for each grid cell (Fig. 3 c). The highest value among these is determined as the maximum rainfall for the given duration.  (4) Repeat steps (1) through (3) for different durations to obtain the scatter points (x: durations, y: maximum rainfall) in the scaling behavior plot.      3 Results 3.1 Depth-Duration scaling behavior  Fig. 4  presents the temporal scaling behavior of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) in South Korea, based on data from Automatic Weather System (AWS) ground observations (represented by black triangles) and radar observations (represented by blue circles). For reference, the behavior based on the German radar-based maximum precipitation values shown (asterisks), and the past PMP envelope line of South Korea (Lee, 2010 ) is depicted by the red line. Most extreme precipitation values derived from AWS data are higher than values based on traditional envelopes. Specifically, there is a difference of over 100 mm between the duration of 2 h and 10 h, as well as for durations of 1 month or longer. It is important to note that these results are based on observations made only in the last 10 years. This could imply differences in the density of observation networks, but it also warrants cautious consideration of the influence of climate change (Najibi and Devineni, 2018; Zhu et al., 2021 ). Therefore, it suggests an increased risk of flooding in urban areas heavily affected by short-duration heavy rainfall. Radar precipitation consistently exhibits higher PMP values compared to the conventional envelope throughout the durations ranging from 10 min to 2 months. Moreover, the radar based PMPs are higher than those based on ground gauge precipitation for durations shorter than 1.5 h, between 10 h and 1 day, and beyond 5 days. Notably, these observations are predominantly observed in mountainous areas where ground observations pose challenges. In contrast, for durations of 2–6 h and 1.5–2 days, both AWS and radar exhibit similar maximum precipitation values in regions with a dense ground gauge network. See  Fig. 5 , a histogram illustrating the distribution of elevations for maximum precipitation based on duration, comparing data from ground observation stations (AWS) and radar data. Each column in the histogram is color-coded, with blue representing shorter durations and red representing longer durations. The histogram reveals that a higher frequency of maximum precipitation tends to occur at mountainous area with elevations higher than 1000 m in radar observations as opposed to AWS in which maximum precipitations tends to occur at low area with elevations lower than 400 m. The observed disparity in extreme precipitation measurements between one-dimensional point-based and two-dimensional plane-based concepts underscores the critical influence of orography on precipitation events. This discrepancy also highlights the potential of remote sensing technologies like radar and satellites for a better understanding of the spatial distribution of precipitation. Furthermore, in Fig. 5 a, heights between 800 m and 900 m show the typhoon Nakri, which reaches its maximum precipitation at durations of 16 h to 1 day. In Fig. 5 b, heights above 1000 m show typhoon Bolaven with maximum precipitation at durations of 8 h to 1.5 days, and typhoon Malou with durations ranging from 5 days to 15 days. Here, the maximum rainfall for a 10-minute duration in Fig. 5 a is attributed to convective rainfall patterns, as the location is adjacent to the sea and consists of steep mountain terrain. When using ground observation stations only, this location may appear as a short-duration maximum rainfall event. Therefore, when examining the duration according to altitude, it can be observed that rainfall events, such as typhoons, which carry significant rainfall, encounter higher altitudes, resulting in even more precipitation and longer durations. Radar-derived maximum precipitation values at durations ranging from 12 h to 1.5 days are similar with each other. This phenomenon makes the PMP behavior deviate from the power law relationship, as depicted by the regime of flat slope in the graph. It signifies a scenario where the extreme rainfall that would typically be distributed over an extended period (1.5 days), occurs more intensively within a significantly shorter timeframe (12 h). This unusual extreme rainfall within a short duration of 12 h was observed in Mt. Deogyusan, Jeollabuk-do, caused by Typhoon Bolaven. This observation highlights the ability of typhoons to gather water from the ocean on a larger spatial scale and transport it to the Korean Peninsula within a compressed timeframe, surpassing the capabilities of local convective systems and frontal systems. The maximum precipitation exceeding 10 days in duration, as indicated by both AWS and radar data, resulted from multiple heavy rainfall events with different generation mechanisms, including the East Asian rainy season, local intense rainfall, and typhoon activities. Regarding the flat surface interval (10 h - 2 days) caused by Typhoon Bolaven in Fig. 4 , the interaction between the terrain and the typhoon can be identified as the most plausible physical cause. The typhoon, which could receive unlimited moisture from the North Pacific, lost its moisture source as it passed the Korean Peninsula, the eastern end of the Northeast Asian continent. If the typhoon had veered to the right of the peninsula and received more moisture from the sea between Korea and Japan, the scaling curve for the interval between 10 h and 2 days would have shown a consistent increase. In the case of Germany, indicated by asterisks in Fig. 4 , an extended regime of flat slope in the depth-duration relationship is observed, unlike the South Korea. Considering that the characteristic duration of each precipitation generation mechanism, such as orographic systems, typhoons, frontal systems, and local convective systems, is unique, it is speculated that the flat slope regime in Germany is attributed to extreme precipitation being caused by less diverse mechanisms compared to Korea. If this conjecture holds true, it can be inferred that as the spatial and temporal domain of the analysis expands, with an increased likelihood of observing extreme precipitation triggered by various mechanisms across multiple durations, the relationship between the two variables will converge towards the power-law pattern. In addition to the diversity of precipitation mechanisms, the proximity to the ocean may also contribute to differences in scaling behavior between the two regions. The Korean Peninsula, located at the end of a continent with active meteorological activities over the ocean, can receive continuous moisture supply from the sea, allowing extreme events to maintain consistent intensity (especially in the case of typhoons). In contrast, Germany, being inland, does not benefit from such continuous moisture supply. The limitation of moisture supply leads to the dissipation of extreme precipitation events, resulting in plateaus in the scaling behavior despite increased duration. To clearly prove this hypothesis, it would be necessary to utilize precipitation data observed on a global scale including oceans, or to conduct simulations using climate models. The reason for including the German study results is that it utilizes a methodology similar to ours (estimating PMP using the envelope method from radar data), and it is a recent study. Additionally, comparing the results of two countries with different climatic systems is intriguing.   4 Discussions 4.1 Scaling behavior for high-quantile rainfall Although considerable efforts have been devoted to ensuring the accuracy of the radar precipitation data utilized in this study through the implementation of non-precipitation echo removal, and conditional merging, it is important to acknowledge that the vast amount of pixel precipitation data analyzed in our estimations, totaling 119,599,026,624 (525,888 × 371 × 613), cannot be assumed to have undergone flawless correction (Biggs and Atkinson, 2011; Yang et al., 2020 ). To address this limitation, we computed four high quantile precipitation values (0.99999, 0.9999, 0.999, and 0.99) for each pixel location and duration, following the methodology employed by Pöschmann et al. (2021) , and examined their scaling behavior ( Fig. 6 ). In this analysis, only the inland area was deemed to have significant value. Consequently, the radar area (x, y) was spatially reduced from the total of 227,423 pixels (371 × 613) to 97,463 pixels (n) corresponding to the inland area. Subsequently, the depth-duration of total precipitation was calculated from the maximum value to the 975th greatest per duration according to each quantile. Our analysis reveals the presence of a flat regime, defying the power law, up to the 0.999 quantile, while at the 0.99 quantile, we observe a convergence to a power-law relationship between duration and precipitation.  Fig. 7  depicts the geographical locations where high-quantile precipitations occurred, whereby the duration is denoted by the color of the circles. Owing to overlapping locations of precipitation occurrences, not all circles corresponding to all durations are shown. Remarkably, higher quantile precipitations tend to occur at similar locations across the durations, thereby contributing to the flat slope regimes of the scaling curve caused by unusual short-duration extreme events. Conversely, lower quantile (e.g., 99th percentile) precipitations tend to occur at diverse locations caused by distinct mechanisms. These findings support the notion that the diversity of precipitation mechanisms further strengthens the power-law relationship between precipitation duration and accumulated depth.  4.2 Scaling behavior based on ground gauge density In previous studies (Paulhus, 1965 ; WMO, 1994 ; Dyck and Peschke, 1995 ; Lee, 2010 ; Zhang et al., 2013 ; NWS, 2017 ; Gonzalez and Bech, 2017 ; González-Herrero et al., 2023 ), it has been commonly assumed that a power-law relationship exists between maximum precipitation depth and duration. It has been conjectured that deviations from this power law could be attributed to the limited density of observation stations. To investigate these assumptions, random sampling locations were selected from the original radar precipitation data, and extreme precipitation values were extracted only from those locations. This allowed for an examination of the influence of gauge density onto the power-law scaling behavior. The analysis involved 30 iterations of extracting maximum precipitation by durations, using different set of randomly drawn sampling locations, specifically 10, 100, 1000, and 10,000. The outcomes of these analysis are presented in  Fig. 8 . The analysis of Fig. 8  reveals an interesting trend. Generally, as the number of sampling pixels decreases, the relationship between duration and maximum precipitation tends to align more closely with a power law (as observed in Figs. 8 a and 8 b). In contrast, as the number of sampling locations increases, there is a higher likelihood of capturing unusual short-duration extreme precipitation events, resulting in a deviation from the expected power law relationship (as evident in Figs. 8 c and 8 d). These findings also emphasize the significance of ensuring an adequate density of the ground gauge network to accurately observe genuine extreme precipitation events. This is particularly crucial for estimating Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) and designing precipitation values to ensure public safety, specifically in mitigating risks associated with the failure of critical infrastructures like dams and nuclear power plants. In other words, power-law scaling behavior of PMP had better be considered as many alternatives to define design standard, but not as a universal scientific law, at least in the field of design practices.  Fig. 9  further supports this argument. On the x-axis, the duration of accumulated precipitation is represented, while the y-axis illustrates the error in extreme precipitation observations for each sampling frequency (the difference between the top dotted line and the lower lines in Fig. 8 ). Even with observations utilizing 1000 grid cell points, the average underestimation bias for durations of 1 h, 6 h, 1 day, and 7 days is significant, reaching 50 mm, 53 mm, 150 mm, and 560 mm, respectively. On the other hand, as stated in the methodology, the precipitation data used to derive results in this study are radar rainfall data corrected by point data, which approximate the values of point rainfall observed at radar cells. These point rainfall values are generally higher than areal rainfall values. Since PMP is typically applied in practice to large watersheds, such as those used for major multipurpose dams, the values derived in this study should be attenuated by multiplying by the Areal Reduction Factor (ARF). For this purpose, one can refer to radar data-based research results (Kim et al., 2019 ). Additionally, it is noteworthy that grid-based precipitation data, such as reanalysis data (referencing ERA5) and satellite-based data (Global Precipitation Mission), have spatial resolutions around 10 km. PMP derived from these datasets should also be attenuated by applying ARF considering watershed area.  4.3 Scaling behavior due to summer rainfall events (East Asian rainy season, typhoons) South Korea is located within the East Asian monsoon region, which experiences a significant portion of its annual precipitation, approximately 70 %, during the summer months of June to August. This precipitation is primarily influenced by two major weather phenomena: the East Asian rainy season and typhoons. The East Asian Rainy Season (EARS hereafter) is characterized by a large-scale cyclonic rainfall pattern caused by a stationary front that moves up and down the Korean Peninsula over an extended period, often lasting several weeks to two months. This season typically affects South Korea from mid-June to early August, contributing to a substantial portion of the annual rainfall. Typhoons, on the other hand, are tropical cyclones originating in the tropical Pacific Ocean. These weather systems can impact South Korea multiple times a year, with an average frequency of three to four occurrences. Typhoons can occur as early as June and persist until October, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds to the Korean Peninsula. In this study, the scaling behavior of these two influential factors, the EARS and typhoons, is analyzed separately. To provide further insights,  Table 1  and  Table 2  summarize relevant information on the EARS and the typhoons that have affected South Korea during the study period from 2009 to 2018.  Fig. 10  illustrates the scaling behavior of extreme precipitation for EARS and typhoons, analyzed separately. The results show distinct patterns: for durations shorter than 6 h, the East Asian rainy season records higher peak precipitation compared to typhoons, whereas for durations longer than 6 h, typhoons exhibit higher peak precipitation than the East Asian rainy season. These findings suggest that the East Asian rainy season, known for its association with riverine flooding in large watersheds, can also have a substantial impact on urban flooding. There are two main reasons for this: (1) The EARS can generate more extreme short-duration precipitation events that are highly associated with urban flooding than those caused by typhoons. (2) The prolonged duration of precipitation during the EARS can significantly influence the water levels of large rivers, which are interconnected with urban drainage systems. On the other hand, considering that major rivers in large watersheds are particularly susceptible to prolonged heavy rainfall, it can be inferred that typhoons have even greater potential to cause more severe flooding compared to the EARS, especially the four major rivers in South Korea. The analysis reveals distinct patterns in the behavior of extreme precipitation for the EARS and typhoons. During the EARS, maximum precipitation demonstrates a steady increase with longer durations. Notably, there are intervals with relatively flat slopes observed at various durations, including 6–12 h, 14–18 h, 1.5–3 days, and 1.5–2 months. These intervals are a result of the EARS front, which is formed through east-west axis and undergoes irregular yet repetitive movements in the north-south direction. The front tends to remain stationary at specific locations in South Korea, leading to unusually short-duration intense extreme precipitation. In contrast, the maximum precipitation depth associated with typhoons exhibits a steep increase with increasing duration until 6 h. Following this initial steep increase, there are three intervals with relatively flat slopes caused by three specific typhoons: Typhoon Bolaven in 2012, Typhoon Kompasu in 2010, and Typhoon Malou in 2010. The dissipation and movement of typhoons are faster compared to the EARS fronts, resulting in lower peak precipitation values for sub-daily durations. However, as the duration increases, the maximum precipitation associated with typhoons surpasses that of the EARS. This is attributed to the cumulative effect of multiple typhoons included in the calculation of the moving sum. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that a significant number of maximum precipitation values induced by typhoons were observed in the southern part of the country. This because this region often lies within the path of typhoons. 양식의 맨 위  4.4 Scaling Behavior with Jeju Island The results in the previous sections were based only on precipitation data for the South Korea, excluding Jeju Island. This was because extreme precipitations for most of the durations were observed on Jeju Island, which is characterized by a strong maritime climate, making it difficult to perform an analysis of factors affecting the scaling behavior. In this section, we analyze the scaling behavior by including Jeju Island as part of the study area along with South Korea.  Fig. 11  shows the results based on both AWS (black triangles) and radar (blue circles) data. The maximum precipitation for all durations except the sub-hourly duration was greater than the maximum precipitation on the Korean Peninsula, by as much as 1500 mm. For the supra-hourly duration, all maximum precipitation observed on Jeju Island was caused by typhoons. This is because unlike the Korean Peninsula, Jeju Island is located closer to the main path of typhoons (Lim et al., 2023 ) receiving more rain from the same typhoon compared to the Korean peninsula. Considering the projected increase in the intensity (Kim et al., 2006 ) and frequency (Lim et al., 2023 ) of typhoons near the Korean Peninsula, as well as the anticipated northward shift in their migration paths (Seol, 2010; Park, 2022 ) due to climate change, it becomes imperative to enhance the existing understanding of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP).  4.5 Analysis on the uncertainty caused by the measurement through radar All radar-based precipitation products, including the radar-gauge merged product of this study, are exposed to significant uncertainty due to the indirect measurement of precipitation using the reflection of electromagnetic waves off raindrops. Considering that the ultimate aim of this study is to improve within flood risk management or design specifications in a quantitative manner, it is necessary to quantify the extent of uncertainty inherent in radar observations. Therefore, this study validated the gridded precipitation product by using rainfall data from Automatic Synoptic Observation Stations (ASOS), which operate independently of the original precipitation data used in this study. The comparison results between the two variables are presented in Appendix A1. The following points were analyzed: (1) For short durations of 10 min, there is a significant difference between radar-based data, which scans raindrops in the sky, and ground-based data. However, as the duration increases to 1 h, the difference between the two variables decreases rapidly; (2) The uncertainty of the radar-based product in this study, which merged ground data, is significantly lower than that of the unmerged product. This highlights the importance of merging ground precipitation data in producing accurate gridded precipitation products. For all durations used in drawing the scaling plot, trend lines and 95 % prediction intervals between the two variables (ASOS rainfall (y) versus conditionally merged radar (x)) were calculated and shown in  Fig. 12  with blue shading. For reference, results from the unmerged radar product were also shown in red shading. Even considering that the y-axis scale is logarithmic, the uncertainty of the conditionally merged product in this study was determined to be small, significantly smaller than that of the unmerged product. Additionally, it was observed that the scaling trend in short-duration ranges resembled that of ground observation data. This difference is likely due to the disparity between sky and ground precipitation amounts and is one of the major discoveries of this study.   5 Conclusion This paper investigates the temporal scaling behavior of extreme precipitation in South Korea using radar precipitation data, aiming to overcome the limitations of ground gauge networks. The analysis reveals several important findings that contribute to our understanding of extreme rainfall and its implications for flood defense and infrastructure design. Firstly, the study demonstrates that the PMP values estimated based on radar data are significantly higher than those estimated using ground gauge observations. This highlights the importance of radar precipitation data in capturing true extreme rainfall events that may be missed by ground-based networks. The difference in PMP values emphasizes the need to consider radar data for accurate estimation and design of precipitation-related parameters. Secondly, it was revealed that unusual short-duration extreme rainfall events that would normally occur over longer durations contribute to the deviation of the scaling behavior from the power law. These unusual short-duration extreme rainfall events are better captured by weather radar, which is the reason why the deviation from the power law is greater for the case of radar rainfall. The power law was held better for the case of lower quantile (e.g. 99 %) rainfall values. This was because this low quantile rainfall values were caused by various types of precipitation generation mechanisms with distinct characteristic time scale. These findings also suggest that, with an increase in spatial and temporal domains, the relationship between PMP and duration may converge toward a power law. This is because a larger spatiotemporal domain allows for the inclusion of extreme rainfall events generated by various mechanisms. Furthermore, the study reveals that the East Asian rainy season and typhoons play distinct roles in the temporal scaling behavior of precipitation. The East Asian rainy season tends to generate greater extreme rainfall for shorter durations, while typhoons contribute more significantly to extreme rainfall for longer durations. This highlights the importance of considering both these weather phenomena in flood defense strategies, with urban and riverine environments being particularly vulnerable. Additionally, the inclusion of Jeju Island in the analysis reveals that typhoons have a significant impact on extreme precipitation scaling behavior of the entire South Korea. With the anticipated northward shift of typhoon paths due to climate change, it is crucial to implement appropriate flood defense measures, especially in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. Radar precipitation data provides extensive spatial coverage, making it an effective approach for monitoring rainfall. This study specifically utilized combined radar-ground precipitation data, demonstrating that this approach can overcome the limitations of point measurements and reduce the uncertainties associated with radar data. Overall, this study underscores the significance of radar precipitation data in understanding the temporal scaling behavior of extreme rainfall and its implications for flood defense and infrastructure design. Paradoxically, it also emphasizes the need for a dense ground gauge network to monitor and analyze true extreme precipitation events. These findings provide fresh insights for policymakers, engineers, and researchers working in the field of precipitation analysis and flood management, contributing to improve resilience and preparedness in the face of changing precipitation patterns. 1 Introduction Interests in accurately predicting groundwater flow and contaminant transport in the subsurface have prompted many studies on the high-resolution characterization of aquifer heterogeneity. The hydraulic Tomography (HT) surveys, as demonstrated in various studies (Gottlieb and Dietrich, 1995 ; Yeh and Liu, 2000 ; Liu et al., 2002 ; Zhu and Yeh, 2005 ; Soueid Ahmed et al., 2015 ), consist of sequential cross-hole interference tests using a well field. HT produces many sets of aquifer responses (i.e., scanning a heterogeneous field from different perspectives), and the assimilation of these responses using an inverse model yields a high-resolution image of the spatial distribution of hydraulic conductivity (K ) and specific storage (S s ). The HT survey requires an appropriate mathematical inverse modeling technique to analyze HT data. The geostatistical inverse models are most suitable since they adopt spatial statistics of the properties to be estimated as soft prior information to constrain the inversion. Among many geostatistical inverse methods, the Successive Linear Estimator (SLE) (Yeh et al., 1996  and Xiang et al., 2009 ) derives the conditional effective parameters and their uncertainty. These effective parameters honor the measured parameters (if available), and the observed heads during each HT test (Gao et al., 2021 ). They also yield unbiased conditional mean heads at locations where data are not available in HT surveys. Unlike other geostatistical inverse models (e.g., Maximum a-posteriori ), the SLE successively updates the linear estimates and their covariance functions at every iteration. Another technique is the Quasi-Linear Geostatistical Inversion (QLGI), developed by Kitanidis (1995)  and co-workers (e.g., Nowak and Cirpka, 2004 ; Fienen et al., 2008 ), which treats the parameters to be estimated as spatial random fields that need to be conditioned given the head or/and conductivity data. In the second stage of QLGI, the corresponding estimation of parameters is similar to SLE, except the prior covariance is kept unchanged during Bayesian updating steps. Over the past decades, numerical simulations (Yeh and Liu, 2000 ; Cirpka and Kitanidis, 2000 ; Zhu and Yeh, 2005 ; Xiang et al., 2009 ; Zha et al., 2018 ; Mao et al., 2013 ; Liu and Kitanidis, 2011 ; Sun et al., 2013 ; Tso et al., 2016 , and many others), laboratory experiments (Liu et al., 2002 ; Illman et al., 2007, 2008, 2010, 2012 ; Liu et al., 2007 ; Pollock and Cirpka, 2010, 2012 ; Jiang et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ; Zhao and Illman, 2017 , and many others) and field surveys (Bohling et al., 2007 ; Illman et al., 2009 ; Brauchler et al., 2011 , 2013 ; Berg and Illman, 2013, 2015 ; Cardiff et al., 2012 ; Zha et al., 2017 ; Wen et al., 2020 , and many others) have confirmed the usefulness of HT surveys and the geostatistical inverse models. However, HT robustness depends on the number of observations and pumping wells. Yeh and Liu (2000)  remarked that the optimal horizontal well spacing is about half of the correlation scale, and the vertical spacing should be as small as possible. Illman et al. (2015)  further advocated using additional data from multiple pumping tests and prior information as additional soft constraints. In addition, SLE is a stochastic estimator based on the Bayesian statistical method, which requires the specification of the mean and covariance of the random field. Many laboratory and field experiments (Illman et al., 2015 ; Zha et al., 2017 ; Jiang et al., 2017 , and others) have proven HT with SLE robust if many observed responses are available. However, if only a sparse dataset is available, HT yields reasonable but insufficiently detailed hydraulic heterogeneity distribution. Acquiring large-scale prior information in aquifer characterization thus becomes valuable and critical. Many studies (Zhao et al., 2016 ; Zhao and Illman, 2017 ; Tso et al., 2016 ; Zha et al., 2017 ; Soueid Ahmed et al., 2015 ; Hermans et al., 2015 ) discussed inverse modeling based on a regularization approach, which incorporates the geologic structures and some direct measurements of K  (i.e., hard data) as prior information. For instance, Zha et al. (2017)  introduced a general statistical framework, including site-specific spatial patterns of large-scale geologic structures using geology and borehole data for SLE to improve estimates. This framework used conditional mean and covariance to represent site-specific large-scale geologic information. That is, this information was cast as a kriged mean at a coarse-scale grid using qualitative borehole log data with a large-scale covariance function (nest-variogram), and the small-scale variability within the large-scale structure is represented by a zero mean and a small-scale covariance function. The approach, however, has not been tested in a field situation. Zhao et al. (2016)  and Zhao and Illman (2017)  demonstrated that the SLE inversion using heterogeneous geological models with assigned K  values obtained from permeameter tests, combined with geological conceptual models as an initial trend model, led to improvements in a small-scale field experiment. Extending their approach to basin-scale problems invites new approaches because of the uncertain conceptual models (i.e., qualitative geology information) and the number of slug tests. To obtain site-specific geologic prior models and to reduce model uncertainty in a hydrogeologic inverse model, geophysical data (Slater et al., 2000 ; Yeh et al., 2008 ; Soueid et al., 2014 ; Hermans et al., 2012 ; Hermans et al., 2015 ; Mao et al., 2015 ; Singha et al., 2015 ; Xu et al., 2019 ) could be an another solution to this problem. For example, Soueid Ahmed et al. (2015)  proposed an image-guided inversion using structural information obtained from a geophysical survey. Pollock and Cirpka (2012)  determined the K  distribution using a fully coupled hydrogeophysical inversion of time-lapse ERT of a salt tracer movement and hydraulic head measurements. Jardani et al. (2013)  developed a stochastic joint inversion of Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT), self-potentials, and measurements of the salinity of a salt tracer test to reconstruct the K  field. Their paper used a linear model to relate solute concentration to electrical conductivity. Wang and Illman (2023)  used borehole geophysical logs to construct zonation models as the initial guess of spatial variability in the geostatistical inversion of HT analysis. Although joint inversion of ERT and hydrological data has shown some promise for mapping geologic patterns and K  distribution (Hermans and Irving, 2017 ), directly converting geophysical features to hydrologic properties (e.g., K , moisture content, and concentration) via some local-scale hydrogeophysics relationships (e.g., Archie's law) adds uncertainty to the inverse problem or data fusion (Slater et al., 2002 ; Slater, 2007 ; Slater and Lesmes, 2002 ). The local-scale relationships are empirical, spatially/temporally varying, and controlled by many factors (Slater, 2007 ). Therefore, deriving site-specific geologic and hydrologic information translated from resistivity models through petrophysical relationships remains a challenge at field-scale aquifers and needs further exploration. In this study, we propose a practical approach that uses relatively inexpensive and easy-to-operate ERT to detect geological structures. This approach was commonly believed to require a precise relationship between resistivity and hydraulic properties, which could be highly uncertain due to many unknown factors. To cope with this issue, we hypothesize that so long as the ERT survey can cost-effectively yield reliable information about the structure of the aquifer, a general relationship without a precise K -resistivity formula would be sufficient. This large-scale structure helps to constrain HT analysis, and HT, in turn, can progressively correct the estimated K  field in each zone according to observed hydraulic heads. Our proposed approach is detailed as follows.1) It starts with ERT surveys with the SLE inverse modeling to obtain an estimated electrical conductivity (or resistivity) field.  2) Next, we collect hydraulic conductivity  samples from the vertical profiles in a limited number of wells. We find a general relationship between the electrical and hydraulic conductivities from the estimated electrical conductivity field at these sample locations.  3) This general relationship converts the estimated resistivity field into HT's prior K  field. This prior field provides information on the stratigraphy (i.e., large-scale geological structures and their connectivity), the intralayer spatial variability of K , and the contrasts among each layer, even though this prior K  field may be inaccurate in detail.  4) Last, the approach adopts the prior K  field and statistical correlation scales as the prior information for the HT calibration.    This paper is organized as follows: Section 2  briefly reviews the forward problems of groundwater flow, solute transport models, and electric potential models (Sections 2.1 and 2.2 ). After that, we present SLE algorithm for ERT surveys (Section 2.3 ). Section 3  describes numerical and physical sandbox experiments to investigate the detection of layer structures under saturated and drainage conditions using ERT. Sections 3.1 and 3.2  discuss the correlation between electrical resistivity and moisture content. Finally, we test the proposed approach under unsaturated conditions and validate the results of this method using synthetic independent pumping and tracer tests (Section 3.3 ). Discussions and conclusions are given in the final Sections 4 and 5 .  2 Methodology 2.1 Groundwater flow and solute transport models This study assumes that the steady-state groundwater flow field in a saturated and heterogeneous porous media can be expressed as the following equation:(1) ∇ · [ K ( x )  ∇ ϕ ( x )   ]  + Q ( x p  )  = 0      with boundary conditions(2) ϕ |  Γ  D    = ϕ  *     [ K ( x )  ∇ ϕ ( x )   ]  · n |  Γ  N    = q  *          where ϕ(x ) is the hydraulic head or total head (in m), K (x ) is the saturated K field in m/s, and Q (x ) is the source/sink term at the location x p  . The SLE approach first conceptualizes the parameter field (i.e., K  or σ field) as a collection of an infinite number of random variables (i.e., a spatial random field characterized by a joint normal probability distribution, the mean and covariance function). Within this distribution, an infinite number of unconditional realizations not affixed to any observations exist, and the distribution is the prior probability distribution in Bayesian statistics. That is, SLE imposes the mean and covariance of the possible solutions as soft constraints before solving the inverse problem. (Yeh et al., 2015a  and 2015b ). A highly parameterized inverse problem often has more unknowns than the data. The problem is not well-defined (or under-determined) and has infinite possible solutions. One stochastic approach to resolve this problem is to conduct a Monte Carlo simulation using many realizations of hydraulic or electric conductivity fields to simulate the subsurface's response and then filter out those realizations that do not reproduce the observed hydraulic heads or electric potentials at sample locations. After the filtering, many conditional realizations remain, characterized by the posterior probability distribution. Taking the expected value of these conditional realizations yields one conditional mean K  or σ field (e.g., Hanna and Yeh (1998)  and others for geohydrology applications). Then, SLE derives the conditioned effective K  or σ field that could honor the observation data and yield the statistically best-unbiased predicted head or potential field (Yeh et al., 1996 ,2006 ; Gao et al., 2021 ). Mathematically, using ERT as an example, we illustrate the mathematical rationale of SLE. First, since σ is a random field, the electrical potential field u  becomes a random field. They can be expressed as a mean and perturbations:(10) σ ( x )  = σ  ‾  + σ  ′  ( x )   and  u ( x )  = u  ‾  ( x )  + u  ′  ( x )          The terms with overhead bars denote the unconditional mean, and primes indicate the unconditional perturbation.
