SLE conditions the estimates using the measured electric potential at receiver locations to estimate the parameters of a highly parameterized heterogeneous model. After conditioning, the potentials at the measurement locations agree with the observed with zero perturbations (i.e., no uncertainty). On the other hand, the u ¯  ( x )     at the unmeasured locations become the average of the remaining conditional realizations. As a result, the cross-covariance σ ′  ( x )  ∇ u ′  ( x )   ‾    in Eq. (14)  changes and, in turn, the σeff   in Eq. (14)  is(15) ∇ · [ σ C e f f    ∇ u ¯  C  ( x )   ]  + I δ ( x − x s   )  δ ( z − z s   )  = 0      where σCeff   is the conditioned effective electrical conductivity, and u ¯  C    is the conditioned mean electrical potential field, which is the observed potential at the sample location and the unbiased mean potential at other locations. If only sparse potential measurements are available for conditioning, σCeff   is a conditional effective conductivity field that produces the unbiased potential field at locations where no potentials are measured and yields the observed potentials at the sample locations. This conditioned effective parameter field is the objective of the SLE algorithm (Yeh et al., 1996 ). Suppose we discretize the estimation domain into M  elements and N  nodes, where parameters (i.e., K  or σ) will be estimated, SLE estimates the natural logarithm of parameters lnF , where F with a dimension of M  × 1. SLE starts with the unconditional mean F ¯   . Then, it incorporates the observed responses D  (heads or electrical potentials, with a dimension of N  × 1) collected during the ERT or HT surveys. The estimated parameter vector, conditioned on the measured data D  is F c   (subscript c denotes conditional), is iteratively determined using the following successive linear estimator (Yeh et al., 1996 ,2002 ; Xu et al., 2019 ):(16) F c ( r + 1  )   = F c ( r )   + ω   T  [ D − G d  ( F c ( r )   )   ]      where r  is the iteration index; Gd  ( · ) denotes forward model (i.e., Eqs. (1)  and (7) ), which simulates the responses, using the estimated parameters, F c  , at iteration r . Note that r  = 0, F c ( 0 )   = F  ‾     (the unconditional mean value). The coefficient matrix, ω   T   , has a dimension of M  × N , and the superscript T  denotes the transpose. The coefficient matrix ω   T    is determined by solving the following equation:(17) [ R d d  ( r )   + θ  ( r )   Maxdiag ( R d d  ( r )   )   ]  ω   ( r )   = R  d f  ( r )       where R d d  ( r )     is the covariance of the responses at measurement locations. The term R d f  ( r )     is the cross-covariance between measured responses and the parameters to be estimated. The term θ ( r )     is a dynamic stability multiplier, and Maxdiag(R d d  ( r )    ) is the maximum value of the diagonal elements of R d d  ( r )    . Mathematically, the dynamic stability term is the Marquardt or damping factor and constrains the updated coefficient matrix values, known as the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm combining the gradient descent method and the Gauss-Newton method. Note that R d d  ( r )     changes and, in turn, its conditional number during each iteration. The product of these two terms controls the stability of the solution to Eq. (17) . A first-order numerical approximation (Zhu and Yeh, 2005 ) derives the auto-covariance R d d  ( r )     and cross-covariance R d f  ( r )    :(18) R d f  ( r )   = J d ( r )   R f f  ( r )   ,    R d d  ( r )   = J d ( r )   R f f  ( r )   J d ( r )  T          where r  again is an iteration index; R f f  ( r )    (M  × M ) is the auto-covariance of the conductivity. J d ( r )    (N  × M ) is the sensitivity (Jacobian) matrix of heads/potentials to the element-wise parameters, evaluated using the estimates at the current iteration. An adjoint state variable approach is adopted to compute the sensitivity matrix (Li and Yeh, 1998 ; Sykes at el., 1985 ; Zhu and Yeh, 2005 ; Mao et al., 2013 ). At iteration r  = 0, R f f  ( 0 )     is the unconditional covariance of parameters, which is an exponential spatial covariance function. Considering that this study is a 2D case, the R f f  ( 0 )     can be written as:(19) R f f  0  ( P , P ′  )  = σ  2  exp [ − ( x − x  ′   )   2  λ x 2   + ( z − z  ′   )   2  λ z 2      ]  .      In Eq. (19) , σ2  is the parameters' variance, λ x    and λ z    are the correlation scales in x  and z  directions, respectively. The unconditional mean field and unconditional covariance functions were generally derived from geologic facies, outcrops, or borehole logs via kriging approach or variogram analysis in SLE, which is different from the QLGI method using a maximum likelihood approach for prior structural parameters analysis (Kitanidis, 1995 ; Soueid Ahmed et al., 2015 ). The auto-covariance implies the correlation relationship between the parameters at a point P (x, z ) and that at the point P ′(x ′, z ′). In addition, these prior parameters are soft constraints to the inverse problem in a statistical sense; the effects of the prior model will be overridden once measurements become abundant (Yeh et al., 2015b ). For iteration r  ≥ 1, the model covariance function R f f  ( r )     is updated to represent the conditional (or residual) covariance of the conductivity according to(20) R f f  ( r + 1  )   = R f f  ( r )   − ( ω   ( r )   )   T  R d f  ( r )   .      This update of the residual covariance is designed to reflect the improvement (i.e., reduction of the uncertainty) of the estimates due to more information about the heterogeneity is extracted from the measurements (e.g., heads and electrical potentials) during each iteration. Two convergence criteria are used to terminate the iteration: (1) if a change in the spatial variance of the estimated conductivity field between the current and last iterations is smaller than a specified tolerance. (2) If a change of simulated potentials between successive iterations is smaller than a given tolerance. Once one of the two criteria is met, the estimates are optimal, and the iteration procedure is terminated (Xiang et al., 2009 ).   3 Results 3.1 ERT & HT sandbox setup Jiang et al. (2021)  constructed a physical heterogeneous sandbox to study the joint inversion of HT and natural gradient flow surveys. The box is 80 cm long, 90 cm high, and 10 cm thick, with 19 layers made of five different types of sand (Fig. 1  a and 1 b). Table 1   lists the grain size, K,  and porosity values of the five types of sand (Jiang et al., 2017 ,2021 ). Before we conducted the ERT survey using physical sandbox experiments, a numerical sandbox mimicking the physical one was created to test our hypothesis. In the numerical sandbox, we set 96 copper electrodes for the ERT survey at 5 cm vertical spacing along 6 columns with 30 cm horizontal spacing (black dots in Fig. 1 c). A pole-pole array was used with constant potential boundaries along the top, and the left and the right sides of the sandbox during the ERT experiments. A continuous copper wire, connected to the current source, facilitated this boundary condition (see red line in Fig. 1 c). The electrical current was injected individually at eight locations (i.e., the solid black rectangles in Fig. 1 c, A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, and A8). During each current injection, the remaining 95 receiving electrodes were scanned at different times during the experiments. In order to inspect the effectiveness of this step, we conducted a standard dipole-dipole survey with no current flow boundaries along the four sides of the sandbox. The inverse results of these two arrays are consistent except around boundaries. We use the pole-pole surveys for simplicity and to better estimate boundaries (Xu et al., 2019 ). The numerical HT setup was identical to the sandbox HT survey experiments by Jiang et al. (2021) . Fig. 1 d shows the design, in which 40 horizontal ports (red dots) were installed between the electrode columns (i.e., x  = 40, 70, 100, 130, and 160 cm, respectively) with 10 cm vertical and 30 cm horizontal spacing. These 40 ports were utilized for pumping and injecting water and pressure monitoring. The HT tests were implemented by pumping water from one port with a constant pumping rate and monitoring the drawdown at the other 39 ports. The top, left, and right sides were kept as constant head of 95 cm (indicated by two inverted triangles in Fig. 1 d). The bottom of the sandbox was a no-flow boundary.  3.2 Numerical sandbox experiments In this numerical sandbox, we assumed that the sandbox was fully saturated and that the resistivity of the 19 layers of the five materials follows Archie's law (Archie, 1942 )(21) σ = σ w  ϕ  m      where σ is the electrical conductivity of the saturated sand (in S/m), σw   the solution's electrical conductivity in porous media (0.03 S/m), and ϕ is the porosity of five materials, as listed in Table 1 . The exponent is the cementation factor m  (1.5), reflecting rock pore structures' consolidation degree. In this numerical sandbox, a constant electrical conductivity value for each of the 19 layers was created by Eq. (21)  with a value of 0.03 S/m for σw  , a uniform cementation factor of 1.5, and the porosity of five materials as listed in Table 1  (Jiang, 2017 ). Fig. 2  a shows the generated layered electric conductivity field (the reference σ field). During the ERT survey, we simulated eight current transmissions (white rectangles in Fig. 2 b) to yield 780 electrical potential measurements. With these measurements, an estimated σ field was derived from SLE with a uniform mean of 0.0065 S/m, a horizontal correlation scale of 60 cm, and a vertical correlation scale of 5 cm. The estimated (Fig. 2 b) is in excellent agreement with the reference field (Fig. 2 a). Next, along the two vertical boreholes (red lines in Fig. 2 a and 2 b), we sampled the σ values from the estimated fields with a fixed interval (2.5 cm). We then averaged them to obtain the average σ value for each layer encountered along the boreholes. Fig. 3  a is the plot of the natural log of averaged electric conductivity vs. the natural log of the K  value of each layer, listed in Table 1 . Notice that the K  values are measured for materials in the physical sandbox. The figure's best-fit line (red dashed line) suggests that natural log K  is negatively related to the natural log σ with a slope of −49.74 and an R2  of 0.276. This low R2  value is evident from the plot in which some layers have a negative, and some have a positive relation between K  and σ (e.g., the upper high K  data in the figure). Such a relationship reflects that the porosity in Eq. (21)  is not the main factor controlling the K  values. This fact is also evident from Table 1 , where the K  is more related to the grain size than the porosity. Despite this low R2  value, using the overall regressed line (Fig. 3 a), we translated the estimated σ field (Fig. 2 b) into a K  field (Fig. 3 b) as prior information for HT analysis. We aimed to test whether such an inappropriate prior K  filed can improve HT's K  estimates. For this purpose, Fig. 4  a displays the HT estimates based on six monitoring points from two pumping events and a uniform K  value without any site-specific layer structure as prior information. Meanwhile, Fig. 4 b illustrates the K  estimates based on the translated K  field in Fig. 3 b as the prior information for the HT with the same pumping tests. A visual comparison of Fig. 4 a and 4 b to the layer structures (white outlines of the layers and Fig. 1 b) reveals that the translated proxy model for HT produces high and low K  layers, closely resembling the layered field, even though each layer's K  values were inaccurate. Fig. 4 c shows a slightly better-estimated field than in Fig. 4 b when eight pumping tests and eight observation ports were used. The result using eight pumping tests and sixteen observation ports is displayed in Fig. 4 d. Although increasing pumping locations may only provide partially non-redundant information (Wen et al., 2020 ), the estimated K  field in Fig. 4 d demonstrates more heterogeneity than previous estimates. Besides, the pattern of heterogeneity becomes consistent with the layer model. Scatterplots of estimated K  fields for each scenario (Fig. 5  a, b, c, and d) reach the same conclusions (e.g., Fig. 5 d with highest R2  and lowest L 1 , L 2  norms). In summary, the results of the numerical experiments confirmed the feasibility of our proposed fusion approach of ERT and HT, even using a rough or inconsistent K  and σ relationship. In essence, the dense but relatively inexpensive ERT surveys provide crucial geometric information about the K  general distribution from which the incorrectly interpreted K  field could be improved by HT even though only a few pumping tests and observation data are available.  3.3 Results of physical sandbox for ERT The results from the above numerical sandbox experiments under fully saturated conditions neglecting noise, measurement and model errors, and other factors, were significant, prompting us to authenticate them using physical experiments. For these reasons, the physical sandbox experiments were conducted and discussed next. 3.3.1 ERT surveys and inversion The ERT setups are the same as the numerical ones. Surprisingly, the results of the physical experiments told a different story—ERT surveys with identical setups could not reveal the layer structure (Xu et al., 2019 ). The high electrical conductivity of tap water, little contrast in the porosity of different sands, measurement noises, and, more importantly, the limitation of the source strength are likely the reasons. Subsequently, the sandbox underwent a drainage process such that the contrast in σ was increased due to the five materials' different water retention characteristics (pore-size distributions). This decision was based on coarse-textured sand having a relatively uniform pore-size distribution (dominated by large pores). During drainage, large pores are drained first and rapidly; only a tiny amount of water is retained in interfacial spaces between grains. On the other hand, fine-textured sands have smaller pores, as they are drained, most of the water remains in small pores due to the capillary pressure. Thus, the contrasts between the σ of different layers could be enhanced so that ERT can detect the shape of different layers. The estimated σ distribution based on the ERT survey of the sandbox at 2.5 h after drainage is illustrated in Fig. 6  a. As we expected, the layer structure becomes apparent. The white lines in the figure outline the shape of 19 layers based on visualization. The ERT inversion used the initial mean electrical conductivity of 0.05 S m −1 ; the variance lnσ of 0.5; a 5 cm for the vertical correlation scale, and a 60 cm for the horizontal correlation scale of the covariance functions, refer to Xu et al. (2019) . As Yeh et al. (2015b)  pointed out, the exact correlation scales are helpful but not essential since they are soft constraints to the inversion. The effects of inexact correlation scales will be overridden once measurements become abundant, such as in this ERT survey. Details of this ERT investigation and corresponding uncertainty analysis are available in Xu et al. (2019) . Fig. 6 a reveals that the layer structures from ERT estimates do not entirely agree with those observed in the sandbox. This result is expected since many factors affect the electric conductivity distribution, as discussed in Section 3.2 , in addition to estimation errors. For example, the lower boundary of the sandbox exhibits high electrical conductivity, likely due to undrained water at the boundary. Nonetheless, the ERT estimates capture the major features of the layer geometry: the coarse-textural layers exhibit low σ, while the fine-textured layers display high σ due to water content differences from the pore-size distribution.  3.3.2 Translation of σ to K field Similar to Section 3.2 , we assume that the K  values of and lithofacies type along the two boreholes (the two vertical red lines in Fig. 6 a) are known. We sampled the σ values from the estimated fields at an interval of 2.5 cm along the boreholes and then averaged them to obtain the average σ value for each layer. The plot of the natural log of averaged σ values against the natural log of the K  values of all layers (based on Table 1 ) is shown in Fig. 6 b. In this figure, the red dashed line is the best-fit relationship between the K  [cm/s] and σ [S/m], indicative of a power-law relationship with an exponent of −1.28 and a coefficient of determination (R2 ) of 0.85.(22) K = 0.00008 σ  − 1.2772        The match of the power-law relationship with the data is more satisfactory than that in Fig. 3 a of the numerical sandbox experiments under a fully saturated condition. Because Archie's law considers the porosity of different layers and neglects the effects of other factors, such as the radius of pores and tortuosity (Carman, 1937 ), a definitive K -σ relationship does not exist. On the other hand, during the drainage experiment, the high and low σ values of the layers correlate well with their high and low moisture contents, indicating the validity of extended Archie's law, which describes the relation between resistivities of fully and partially saturated rocks as a function of water saturation S (Archie, 1942 ; Cassiani et al., 2006 ):(23) σ u n   = σ w  ϕ  m  S  d      where σun   is the electrical conductivity of the medium under the partially saturated conditions in the absence of surface electrical conductivity; σw   is the solution's electrical conductivity; S  is the degree of saturation, d  is saturation index (e.g., 1.3–2 for unconsolidated sands). If m  = d , we have σeff   = σw  θd  , typically used in soil science (Looms et al., 2008 ; Lesmes and Friedman, 2005 ). We could take the Brooks and Corey  (1964)  model for the water retention curve to derive the relationship between water saturation degree S  and saturated hydraulic conductivity K :(24) S = ( ψ a  ψ c   )   λ      where λ is the pore size distribution index, ψa   is the air entry pressure and ψc   is the capillary pressure. Compared to the van Genuchten model (1980) , we have the following relation between soil parameter α and ψa  :(25) ψ a  = 1 α  .      The air entry pressure is the threshold pressure head at which air displaces water in the largest pores. The scaling between air entry pressure ψa   and saturated K  can be deduced as (Leverett, 1941 ; Thomas et al., 1968 ; Guarracino, 2007 )(26) α ∝ K     ψ a  ∝ 1 K   .         Thus, Eq. (24)  becomes(27) S ∝ ( 1 ψ c  K    )   λ  .      Substituting eq. (27)  into extended Archie's law (Eq. (23) ) yields:(28) σ u n   = σ w  ϕ  m  S  d  ∝ ( 1 ψ c   )   d λ   K  − d λ  2         Eq. (28)  suggests a power law relationship between saturated K  and bulk electrical conductivity under unsaturated conditions, given a constant capillary pressure and pore size distribution index. However, this relationship could not be verified directly from our physical sandbox experiment. Generally, the unsaturated moisture contents in the layers result from the water release process dictated by the water retention curves of the layers, which reflect their pore-size distributions. The moisture content distributions reflect the effects of porosity, pore sizes, and tortuosity, leading to the high and low moisture content in different layers under drainage. These factors also control K.  Therefore,  fitting the power-law relationship to saturated K  and σ under unsaturated condition data is logical as Eq. (22) . Using this rough relationship, we next converted the σ estimates (Fig. 6 a) to a K  field (Fig. 7  a). While the converted K  distribution does not yield the exact values of the layers, it carries more site-specific prior information about the hydraulic parameter patterns than general spatial statistics (mean, variance, and correlation scales) of K  values of sparse core samples.  3.3.3 Synthetic HT analysis The next logical step is to use the ERT-detected structure or K  fields as prior information to conduct HT analysis to estimate the K  distribution of the physical sandbox and validate it for predicting flow and solute transport. Unfortunately, data governance and copyright issues forbid using the HT data from the physical sandbox for this purpose. Specifically, the investigators of HT using the same physical sandbox declined to share their data. As such, this study has to rely on synthetic HT data presented previously to test and validate the new findings. Under such an unfortunate situation, we explored the benefits of integrating ERT and HT surveys using two boreholes (the two vertical red lines in Fig. 7 a) in the synthetic sandbox to conduct HT surveys. In the synthetic HT surveys, the first pumping test used Port No. 14 as the pumping location, and steady drawdowns were collected from Ports 10, 12, 16, 26, 28, 30, and 32 (the white circles in Fig. 8  ). Then, Port 28 was used as the pumping location, and steady drawdowns were sampled at Ports 10, 12, 14, 16, 26, 30, and 32 in the second test. Afterward, these data sets were used in SimSLE, with different types of prior information (Cases 1, 2, and 3 as explained below) to estimate the K  field. In Case 1 , the prior K  distribution (Fig. 7 a) for the HT's analysis was translated from ERT with the K  - σ relationship (i.e., Fig. 6 b). The correlation scales used were the anisotropic model from the variogram analysis of ERT estimates. Case 2  used geometric mean and covariance functions in Section 3.1  as the prior K  for HT analysis. Case 3  used a kriged K  field conditioned with 40-point samples of K  as the prior information of the HT analysis. Fig. 7 b, 7 c, and 7 d show the estimated K  fields of the three cases. Fig. 7 b shows slight differences between the estimated K  field in Case 1 and the prior K  field translated from the ERT result (Fig. 7 a). The estimated K  field in Case 1 resembles the layer model more than that in Case 2 and Case 3, indicative of the importance of site-specific prior layer structures for HT when data are insufficient. The K  field in Fig. 7 d (Case 3) exhibits layer patterns, but the statistics of Case 3 estimates are better than those of Case 1 and 2, as shown in Figs. 5 a and 8 . However, such a dense sample network for Case 3 is impractical and rare in a real field. Overall, these sandbox experiments of ERT and synthetic HT suggest that better knowledge of site-specific prior K  distribution via ERT surveys could improve K  estimates for HT when the well or K  sampling network is sparse. The findings are consistent with previous sandbox and field studies by Zhao and Illman (2017) .  3.3.4 Validation Validation of our proposed approach by predicting head distributions induced by independent pumping tests at different locations and forecasting tracer distribution in a tracer test is most appropriate. Note that the independent pumping test means that the observation wells and pumping wells were not used in HT calibrations. In other words, the validation avoids previously used data (Illman et al., 2015 ; Wen et al., 2020 ). Independent Pumping Tests.  The validation results are presented in Fig. 9  a, b, and c as scatter plots for Case 1 (HT with translated K  field based on ERT), Case 2 (HT with the geometric mean and covariance function), and Case 3 (HT with kriged K  with 40 sampled K  values), respectively. The well setup for the validation is the same as the HT experiments discussed previously (Section 3.3.3 ). Pumping at q  = 18.336 cm3 /s was initiated at Ports 3, 6, 19, 22, 35, and 38 (not used in the HT) to reach a steady flow field. Each scatter plot compares the predicted steady flow heads and the observed at all the observation ports, excluding Ports 10, 12, 14, 16, 26, 28, 30, and 32. These figures also show the linear regression line, R2 , L1 , and L2  values. Based on the visual inspection and the statistics, we rank the performance of the models as Case 3 first, Case 1 next, and Case 2 last. Note that Case l and Case 3 perform almost equally well: the slope of the regression line of Case 1 is 1.0 with an intercept of 0.17, but data points scatter slightly wider than those of Case 3, as indicated by slightly lower R2  and higher L1  and L2  values. The results again indicated that the knowledge of the layer structures in HT is essential, and the ERT in our proposed approach can provide that information. Tracer Validation.  The independent pumping test is one way to evaluate the robustness of our proposed approach. However, the diffusive nature of heads generally smoothes out the errors in the estimated K  fields. Evaluation of improvements on the predicting velocity field is relevant, as articulated below. Characterization of fluid velocity plays a vital role in solute transport in environmental science and engineering. For example, our inability to depict velocity variation at the molecular scale has led to the diffusion concept. The shear flow dispersion concept has been created to overlook the velocity variation in the pipe (e.g., Fischer et al., 1979 ). Similarly, the concept of dispersion in porous media (Bear, 1979 ) overcomes our incapacity to detail the pore-scale structure and velocities. The macro-dispersion theories were formulated to avoid characterizing large-scale aquifer heterogeneity and upscale lab-scale solute transport principles to field-scale problems (e.g., Gelhar, 1986 ). Without recognizing ensemble mean and ergodicity embedded in Fickian dispersion concepts, many had proposed dead-end pores, mobile/immobile zones, or non-Fickian dispersion models over the past decades. As high-resolution aquifer characterization technology has advanced, these non-Fickian dispersion theories become convenient artifacts aiming to avoid high-resolution characterization. Moreover, these theories failed to address their inherent ensemble mean nature and uncertainty at the scale of our interests (Yeh et al., 2023 ). This study shows that our proposed approach is a possible high-resolution technology that can reduce uncertainty in our prediction of solute transport in aquifers. Here, we present synthetic tracer tests to validate HT's estimated K  and velocity field with different prior information. These numerical tests involved a dipole solute tracer test using sodium chloride (4 g/L in TDS) as a tracer. The saline water was continuously injected at well No. 27 using a fixed rate, and water was extracted at well No. 15 at the same rate (see Fig. 1 d). Then we used VSAFT2 (Yeh et al., 1993 , available at http://tian.hwr.arizona.edu/downloads/ ) to simulate the solute transport experiment using the layered K  model to create the reference concentration field for comparisons with the others from the three different K  models. VSAFT2 solves the advection-dispersion equation using the modified method of characteristics designed for advection-dominant transport processes. The simulation domain was discretized into 180 vertical and 360 horizontal elements with a dimension of 0.5 cm (length) × 0.5 cm (width). The boundary conditions for the three cases were the same as the HT experiments, i.e., constant head and zero concentration around the left, the right, and the top sides, and no flow and concentration flux at the bottom. The effective porosity was 0.38 for all three cases (since its variability is small, Table 1 ). The longitudinal and transverse dispersivity values were zero to simulate pure advective transport. Numerical dispersion always exists if the element size is not infinitesimally small since the concentration must be extrapolated and interpreted from node to node. Fig. 10  a is the simulated solute distribution 35 min after the tracer was released, using the layered reference K  model. This figure is the reference tracer field in the following comparisons. Fig. 10 b, 10 c, and 10 d are those from Cases 1(the proposed approach), Case 2 (HT using the geometric mean, no layer structure prior information), and Case 3 (HT with kriged K  field conditioned on 40 K  samples), respectively. The smear zones around the red concentration areas in all figures are numerical dispersion. These figures also illustrate the streamlines as white lines, velocity vectors as yellow arrows, and injection and extraction well as black circles. Visual comparison of the reference and other tracer distributions suggests that the performance of the proposed approach (Case 1) is the best. Next is the HT with the kriged prior with 40 samples (Case 3), and the last is the HT results without any site-specific prior information (Case 2). The plots of the streamlines and velocity vectors explain these outcomes. In Case 1, HT with ERT prior large-scale structures closely captures the effects of the structures on the velocity field between the injection and withdrawal wells. In Case 2, HT with the geometrical mean and covariance function produces smooth streamlines and velocity fields, omitting the effects of layerings. On the other hand, HT using the kriged field based on 40 K  samples (Case 3) yields streamlines and velocity patterns closer to the reference one than in Case 2. Notice that kriging is a conditional mean estimator, smoothing out heterogeneity estimates unless a significant number of K  samples are used to condition the estimates. Again, all these results confirm the importance of the site-specific layer structure in our sandbox experiment and support our hydrogeophysics hypothesis.    4 Discussions Many previous studies have reported that ERT or other geophysical surveys can reveal geological features in aquifers (Clifford and Binley, 2010 ; Mastrocicco et al., 2010 ). Our numerical experiments confirm that ERT can depict the layer structures in the fully saturated synthetic layered sandbox, mimicking layerings in an actual sandbox packed with different sandy materials. Using the detected layer structure with the inconclusive relationship between K  and σ samples to construct a prior K  field for HT, HT can yield an estimated K  field closer to the true one than the estimate without any site-specific structure. The agreement between the estimates and the true ones is improved when the number of pumping and observation wells increases in HT. Such a result indicates that once the large-scale structure in a domain is identified, HT can progressively correct the detailed guess of K  values within the large-scale structures. While the numerical sandbox experiments confirm our intuition, to our surprise, ERT surveys in the real sandbox under fully saturated conditions could not detect the layer structure in the sandbox packed with different sands without clays. The accuracy of the ERT survey technique and equipment may be the issue. However, the same technique and equipment detected the coarse and fine sand layer structure after draining the sandbox. This result indicates that more water was trapped in the fine sands after drainage of the sandbox than the coarse ones, enhancing the contrast in electrical conductivity of layers of different sizes of sands such that ERT can detect the differences. The pole-pole-based sandbox ERT survey aims to estimate boundaries with lower uncertainty. A conductive wire connected to the current source facilitated this boundary condition. To us, the boundary conditions are merely heterogeneity of the parameters. One way to resolve this issue is to implement a known boundary in the domain, as we did in the sandbox experiments. These perfectly conductive boundary conditions do not exist in real-world cases. However, utilizing some unconventional ERT configurations, such as 'fluid-flow tomography' (Ho, 2009 ), long electrode ERT (Ronczka et al., 2015 ), and borehole-to-surface array (Power et al., 2015 ) to improve the accuracy of characterization may be necessary. Again, since the suitability of an ERT array depends on many factors: its sensitivity to the target, signal-to-noise ratio, depth of investigation, and data collection efficiency (Loke et al., 2013 ), we emphasize that our results are limited to the sandbox experiments, and more ERT configuration research is necessary for field applications. Based on the identified sand layer structure, we again validate the importance of the prior large-scale structure information on HT inversions from the independent pumping and tracer tests. These tests' results confirm our hypothesis that the large-scale layer structure can assist HT when the HT data are limited. On the other hand, we show that conditioning the HT survey inversion with a large number of point K  measurements without using an ERT survey can lead to similar results. Of course, draining an aquifer to allow ERT to reveal the large-scale structures as we did in the sandbox is impractical. It is a convenient method to increase the difference in resistivity for the sand-only sandbox. The electrical resistivity of a water-saturated formation depends on the distribution of grain size and the quality of the water that is saturating the formation (Patra et al., 2016 ). ERT surveys still play a vital role in delineating large-scale structures and solute plumes (Mézquita González et al., 2021 ; Han et al., 2024 ) since the resistivity contrasts in field applications are much larger than our sandbox setup (i.e., sand-only). As for tidal aquifer applications, the ERT survey could cost-effectively detect the saturation variation in time and offer valuable information (i.e., layer structures and hydraulic properties) for coastal Tidal Tomography to estimate the hydraulic diffusivity (Ma et al., 2024 ). Similarly, ERT surveys may detect large-scale subsurface heterogeneity from the groundwater variation induced by river water level changes as prior information to improve Riverstage Tomography (Wang et al., 2017 ). We believe that assimilating a broad range of hydrologic, geologic, and geophysical information is essential to make the parameters more representative of reality. Another relevant issue explored by this paper is: "Is it worthwhile to establish a precisely local-scale hydro/geophysical property relationship, which could vary spatially or temporally in large-scale problems?" Or shall we exploit one survey's unique ability for some characterization and let the other survey do the rest? For example, as demonstrated in this paper, we use less expensive ERT to capture the large-scale structures and let HT self-correct the effects of incorrect K  and σ relationship at the local scale. It is well-known that hydraulic tests are more suitable for characterizing hydraulic conductivity than ERT since the processes are different, and hydraulic properties are our primary interest in this case. This fact may further suggest that the selection of the weights in calibrating the joint inverse modeling of hydrogeophysical data should consider the parameters of the interests. The weight for hydrologic data should be heavier than geophysical data to reach final K  estimates for hydrogeological investigation because the physical processes of groundwater flow and contaminant transport are different from those of the electrical current. Without this consideration, a fully joint inversion (Binley et al., 2010 ; A. 2015 ; Camporese et al., 2015 ) may lead to more uncertainty in the hydrologic parameter. Undoubtedly, comparisons between the fully coupled inversion and our approach could be an exciting research topic in the future. Notice that our results stress the importance of using the ERT-detected large-scale structure for HT even without a clear K -σ relationship. Specifically, once the large structures of the geological media are captured, even though their hydraulic properties are unknown, HT can modify the incorrect hydraulic values in each zone to match the observed hydrologic processes, indicating the importance of large structures in HT analyses. Combining other helpful information, such as borehole logs, with ERT would allow ERT to detect large-scale geological structures with low uncertainty.  5 Conclusions From this study, we draw the following conclusions:1. Our numerical experiments in a fully saturated numerical sandbox showed that the ERT survey could map the layer structures. However, the ERT survey with an identical setup in actual lab experiments could not identify the structure. We attributed the failure to the dominance of tap water, little contrast in the porosity of different sands, measurement noises, and the limitation of the source strength.  2. Using dense but relatively inexpensive ERT surveys in the sandbox under unsaturated conditions, our proposed approach has detected the large-scale layer structure close to the true one. With this layer structure and a pragmatic approach, which derived an approximate power-law relationship, we then translated the estimated electrical conductivity field to the approximate K  field as prior information for the inversion of a sparse HT survey. The estimated K  field from this approach yielded excellent predictions of heads during independent pumping tests and tracer migration of the tracer injection test.
1 Introduction In the Alpine region, natural and artificial lakes are essential elements of the water cycle, e.g., in terms of habitat, water retention and release, nutrient cycling or flood retention. Their hydrologic and limnologic regime is highly likely to be impacted by climate change in most world regions due to modifications in water input (streamflow) and output (evaporation; Zajac et al., 2017 ; Fan et al., 2020 ), but also due to alterations of chemical and physical conditions related to climate warming (Fink et al., 2016; Woolway et al., 2020 ) and CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere (Perga et al., 2016 ). Most climate change impact studies on lakes focus on limnologic aspects, i.e., how climate warming modifies temperature (O’Reilly et al., 2015 ), mixing regimes (Råman Vinnå et al., 2021 ) or nutrient cycles (Moss, 2012 ). Some ecological studies analyse how lake level management impacts littoral habitats (Aroviita and Hamalainen.., (2008); Cifoni et al., (2022) ). The work by Zohary and Ostrovsky (2011)  discusses that the ecosystem functioning of lakes ”respond(s) adversely to excessive lake level fluctuations”, even for deep lakes. Large perialpine lakes, the focus of this study, are susceptible to climate change due to its pronounced effect on snow and glacier melt (Muelchi et al., 2021 ). Numerous water resources studies, therefore, focused on the cryosphere’s role in modulating how climate change impacts streamflow (François et al., 2018; Hanus et al., 2021; Horton et al., 2022 ). Besides the few modelling studies that specifically target the interplay of streamflow (lake input) and lake levels (Gibson et al., 2006a; Veijalainen et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2022 ), the vast majority of hydrological modelling studies do not explicitly address the effect of lake level variations or management on streamflow, even for catchments including large lake systems (e.g. in the works of Bosshard et al., 2014 ; Jasper and Ebel, 2016 ; Zischg et al., 2018 ; Legrand et al., 2023 ).Despite growing anthropognic pressure on the European large perialpine lakes (Salmaso et al., 2018 ) and the importance of lake level variability for ecology and socio-economic activities, hydrologic analyses of lakes in terms of lake level variability are rare (e.g. Hingray et al., 2007 ; Veijalainen et al., 2010 ; Hinegk et al., 2022 ). This represents a critical knowledge gap, given that the lake level of many large perialpine lakes is heavily regulated to meet numerous natural resources and hazards management goals related to drinking and irrigation water supply, fishery, shipping, energy production, nature conservation, tourism and flood protection (Clites and Quinn, 2003; Hingray et al., 2007; Hinegk et al., 2022 ). These manifold objectives are generally implemented through lake level management rules that mitigate high and low extremes (Veijalainen et al., 2010; AWA, 2014 ). For perialpine lake systems which are influenced by snow and glacier melt in spring and summer, the lake level management typically consists of raising the winter levels (when there is little inflow due to snow accumulation in the catchment) and of lowering the lake levels before the melt period onset to avoid flooding (Gibson et al., 2006b; Hinegk et al., 2022; FOEN, 2023a ). Additional provisions can be formulated, e.g. a recurring exceedance of a flood limit for ecological purposes or preventive lake level lowering to avoid flood events. The question of how climate change impacts the resulting lake level variability and management naturally arises: ongoing climate change alters streamflow seasonality (Addor et al., 2014; Rössler et al., 2019; Muelchi et al., 2021 ) and thereby affecting the seasonal water input to lakes. Additionally, evaporative losses can increase the outflow from lakes (Gibson et al., 2006b ). As one of the few studies, Gibson et al. (2006b)  investigate how climate and lake level management have influenced lake level variability in the Great Slave Lake (Canada) from the mid-20th century. They employ a comparison of pre-regulated and naturalised simulations to disentangle the individual impacts of these factors. Due to limited lake level observations, several studies have used satellite data to analyse anthropogenic influence on lake level variability (Cooley et al., 2021; Kostianoy et al., 2022 ), such as hydropower generation (Sinyukovich et al., 2024 ) or lake level management (Aminjafari et al., 2024 ). Further studies have investigated the impact of evaporation on lake levels, both in arid regions (La Fuente et al., 2022 ) and worldwide (Zhao et al., 2022 ), as this impact is projected to increase in this century. Most conceptual hydrologic models operate on a physical basis (Paiva et al., 2011 ); however, the large perialpine lakes were often omitted or modeled in a simplified manner in such hydrologic studies. The high computational costs associated with hydrodynamic models can probably explain the omission of lake level management, as mentioned in several studies (Paiva et al., 2011, Hoch et al., 2017; Papadimos et al., 2022 ). To overcome corresponding limitations, the lake system is often considered as the control point (outlet) of the hydrologic model (e.g. Hicks et al., 1995 ; Dembélé et al., 2022 ). Other studies include the effect of large regulated lakes with a simplified reservoir approach (e.g. Hingray et al., 2007 ; Legrand et al., 2023 ). These simplified flow routing methods can adequately represent flood wave delay and attenuation but cannot handle other hydrodynamic processes, such as backwater or floodplain water retention effects (Lohmann et al., 1996; Paiva et al., 2011 ). For our study, we selected four Swiss lakes with different degrees of lake level management. We combine the hydrologic model PREVAH and the hydrodynamic model MIKE11 to investigate lake level variability. Our analysis is based on a modelling framework that uses existing streamflow simulations from a catchment-scale precipitation-streamflow model (PREVAH; Viviroli et al., 2009 ; Speich et al., 2015 ) for 39 climate change modelling chains as input to a hydrodynamic model (MIKE11; DHI, 2003 ), for which we developed a specific methodology to account for lake level management rules. The expansion with a 1D hydrodynamic flow routing model, represented with cross-sections, can provide information on flow variables (e.g., river geometry, roughness, river stage, velocity, slope), which could be relevant for transport or diffusion processes (Cox, 2003; El kadi Abderrezzak and Paquier, 2009; Haghiabi et al., 2012; Mesman et al., 2020 ). Hydrodynamic models can incorporate lakes, considering stage-area relationships (Mesman et al., 2020; Papadimos et al., 2022 ) and built-in lake level management rules to account for the effect of lakes in the simulations (DHI, 2003 ). In this context of missing climate change studies on natural perialpine lake levels, we address the following research question: How does climate change impact lake level variability, and how do varying levels of lake level management modulate these impacts? Compared to previous work (Hingray et al., 2007 ), the focus on regulated and unregulated lakes allows for analysing climate change impacts on lake level management. To our knowledge, the present study is the first climate change impact assessment on perialpine lake level variability, analysing lakes with different degrees of lake level regulation. The national focus has the main advantage of building upon a coherent set of climate change simulations (FOEN, 2021 ), resulting in a modelling framework readily transferable to other perialpine lakes. The relevance of this study is threefold: (i) the large Swiss lakes are significant reservoirs at a supraregional level, with several lakes spanning across the Swiss borders (Lanz, 2021 ); (ii) climate-induced impacts depend on the degree of lake level management, which we can analyse here based on the selected case studies; (iii) lake level management also means an anthropogenic intervention in nature, which alters hydrologic patterns and affects the connectivity of aquatic habitats (Stanford and Hauer, 1992 ) and urgently needs to be studied to understand further how climate change threatens biodiversity.  2 Material and methods 2.1 General change assessment framework The analysis framework of our study is based on comparing the current conditions of daily lake levels and outflows with future conditions under climate change. As current conditions, we define the reference period, Tref : 1981 – 2010, and as future conditions, the three future periods: 2035: 2020 – 2049, 2060: 2045 – 2074, 2085: 2070 – 2099. These periods are typically used in studies with CH2018 data (NCCS, 2018 ). To analyse climate change impacts on different degrees of lake level management, we assume unchanged regulatory practices. The change analysis compares the simulations resulting from an ensemble of climate model chains (combinations of a Global Circulation Model and Regional Climate Model) for the reference period and for the selected future periods. The change analysis does not consider observed hydrologic variables (streamflows, lake levels) or simulations obtained with historical meteorological data. It compares climate-data-driven simulations for the reference period and for the future periods. This is a standard procedure in climate change impact analysis (Schaefli, 2015 ) to discount potential biases of the climate-data-driven simulations with respect to historic data. Potential climate change impacts are further analysed in terms of simulated monthly average lake levels (averaged over the above 30-years period); direct comparison of the simulated daily lake levels (reference and future) is impossible given that they do not represent the same years. Changes in extremes are assessed based on indicators such as the frequency of reaching the drought and flood limits.  2.2 Selected case studies We selected four perialpine lakes in Switzerland ( Fig. 1 ) representative of different levels of lake level management: one lake is unregulated, two are fully regulated with line diagrams, and one is semi-regulated. The four selected lakes are located in pairwise nested catchments: catchment I contains the two connected lakes Walen (unregulated) and Zurich (regulated). Catchment II contains the two connected lakes Brienz (semi-regulated) and Thun (regulated). A channel connects the two lakes in catchment I and II, but the flow direction in the channel is unidirectional, due to the disparity in elevation between the two lakes. The lakes cover between 2 % and 5 % of their hydrologic catchment area ( Table 1 ). The corresponding catchments show glacier covers between 1 % and 16 %. Catchment I, with 1 %, has a lower glacier cover than catchment II, with 9 % (Table 1 ). Part of the differences in lake levels and outflows between the two lake systems can be attributed to the hydrologic regime of the rivers feeding the lakes. However, both systems will continue to be fed by snow-influenced regimes in the future, resulting in high inflows during spring/early summer (FOEN, 2021; Stahl et al., 2022 ). Both lake systems have experienced flooding in the recent past (e.g., in the years 1999, 2005 or 2021 Hilker et al., 2009 ; FOEN, 2023d ). The unregulated Lake Walen had very low levels during the recent 2018 drought year (Blauhut et al., 2022; FOEN, 2023d ) when the level dropped down to the 97.5 % exceedance percentile. The lowest observed August and September lake levels of Lake Walen occurred in the drought year 2003. All lakes show consistently lower lake levels in winter than in summer ( Fig. 2 ). For all four lakes, the monthly lowest observed levels date back to the late 1940s and early 1950s (FOEN, 2023c ), i.e., before the onset of modern lake level management (Table 1 ). Further details are described in the Appendix.  2.3 Lake level regimes and management Lake level management reduces the seasonal lake level fluctuations, as clearly visible by comparing the within-year lake level fluctuations of the four studied lakes (Fig. 2 , top row). The unregulated Lake Walen shows the most natural lake level dynamic, which is, however, slightly impacted by the seasonal change of streamflow distribution resulting from the hydropower production along the main tributary (Figure SI 4). The lake level of the regulated Lake Zurich is artificially lowered in late winter to provide retention capacity for the melt period in spring. It is kept artificially high in summer for tourism purposes and fishery. The current management rules lead to annual lake level fluctuations that are narrower for Lake Thun than for Lake Brienz. All lakes analysed here are large enough to dampen daily inflow variability but small enough not to (naturally) dampen the seasonal inflow variability. Accordingly, the annual streamflow pattern, with high flows in summer and low flows in winter, is visible in all outflow regimes (Fig. 2 , bottom row). Lake level management imprints, however, a modification on the outflow regimes in spring: the melt-related increase in outflow is less steep for the downstream regulated lakes than for the upstream semi-regulated or unregulated lakes. This results from the artificial lake level lowering in winter to provide additional retention capacity for snowmelt in spring. The two lakes Brienz and Thun (catchment II) show a higher and longer-lasting summer outflow peak due to the more snow and glacier melt influence inflow regime (see Table 1  and Stahl et al., 2016 ). Finally, it is important to note that highly dampened lake level dynamics do not necessarily translate into similarly dampened outflow dynamics (see Lake Zurich and Lake Thun in Fig. 2 ). This depends on the stage-discharge relationship and the underlying lake level management rules. In Switzerland, lake levels are regulated by floodgates according to specific management diagrams. These so-called line diagrams (Spreafico, 1980 ) define a target lake outflow as a function of the calendar day and of the current lake level ( Fig. 3 ). Nowadays, the actual lake level management is done by automatic regulators, with occasional manual intervention during exceptional situations such as flood or drought situations (FOEN, 2023a ). The line diagrams result from compromises between level management targets formulated by different stakeholder groups for different periods of the year. Some of them were elaborated based on modelling (Spreafico, 1980 ). Lake level management targets, e.g., maintaining sufficiently high lake levels during winter to guarantee access to harbors or sufficiently high lake levels during fish spawning periods to ensure habitat availability for selected species (Neumann, 1983 ). Downstream river flow targets consist of maintaining river flow below flood limits at selected river cross sections (e.g. FOEN, 2020a ). A line diagram can be completed by a set of exceptions, e.g., a preventive lake level lowering to avoid flood events, a temporary minimum lake level to ensure navigability or a certain minimum lake level fluctuation to satisfy ecological needs (Spreafico, 1977; Kaderli, 2021 ).  2.4 Hydrologic climate change scenarios The transient daily streamflow scenarios used in this study were derived from the latest downscaled and de-biased Swiss climate change Scenarios CH2018 (NCCS, 2018 ), which are based on the EURO-CORDEX dataset (Jacob et al., 2014 ). For emission scenarios, different frameworks are currently employed: the RCPs (Representative Concentration Pathways), which delineate greenhouse gas concentrations and their effect on radiative forcing, and SSPs (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways; IPCC, 2023 ), which narrate societal evolution and its impact on climate change. In this study, we consistently adopt the RCPs as provided by the publisher of the CH-2018 climate scenarios. The climate model ensemble CH2018 contains a total of 39 model chains for three RCPs: RCP2.6 (concerted mitigation efforts), RCP4.5 (limited climate mitigation) and RCP8.5 (no climate mitigation measures). The CH2018 ensemble consists of different combinations of Regional Climate Models (RCMs) and General Circulation Models (GCMs), and the ensemble chains are listed in Table SI 3. The model ensemble provides daily air temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, global radiation and near-surface wind speed (Brunner et al., 2019 ). The climate change scenarios were translated into streamflow scenarios (FOEN, 2021 ) with the conceptual hydrologic model PREVAH (PREcipitation streamflow EVApotranspiration HRU related Model; Viviroli et al., 2009 ) in its spatially explicit version (Speich et al., 2015 ).  2.5 Hydrologic and hydrodynamic models Combining the hydrologic and hydrodynamic models allows us to assess the climate change impacts on water-level-outflow dynamics, which expresses a complex balance of stakeholder interests. The conceptual hydrologic model PREVAH computes streamflow by solving the water balance equation (Speich et al., 2015 ). The hydrodynamic model MIKE11 1D routing model allows for the modelling of river systems (Doulgeris et al., 2012 ), including reservoirs and lakes (Papadimos et al., 2022 ), and their associated regulation structures. The detailed model description is provided in the Appendix. MIKE11 is run at a one-minute time step (a numerical choice related to its use in real-time applications), which we aggregate to daily values. We assess the model performance (Section 4.1 ) by comparing daily observed lake levels and outflows to simulated values (Table SI 2), where the simulations are obtained with observed meteorological data from the reference period (rather than with the climate model outputs). We assume the model developed with observed input data remains valid with the downscaled climate model outputs as input, a standard assumption in comparable studies. The two models are not dynamically coupled as, e.g., in the work of Papadimos et al. (2022) ; for the present CC impact on lake-level assessment we apply a loose one-way coupling. The hydrologic model provides input to the coupled lake system’s boundary; the flow within and out of the system is simulated with MIKE11, ensuring mass is conserved.  To assess the added value of using an actual hydrodynamic model, simulated and observed lake levels are compared for the used set of models (PREVAH and MIKE11) and for a simplified case where lake levels are obtained by simply solving the water balance equation for the filling of a reservoir. In this simplified case, the lake levels are obtained from the simulated storage volumes based on interpolated stage-area relations. The stage-discharge relation of the regulated lakes is interpolated without accounting for management rules. For the hydrodynamic simulations with MIKE11, we use the stage-area relations of all lakes, the stage-discharge relation of the unregulated lake and the lake level management rules for the regulated and semi-regulated lakes. The management rules for the regulated lakes specify a corresponding outflow for each day of the year and lake level (as illustrated in Fig. 3 ). In the case of a semi-regulated lake, there are no inherent management rules for different days of the year. The outflow follows a stage-discharge relationship but is influenced by controlled outflow, resulting in a dampened lake level fluctuation compared to an unregulated lake. The stage-discharge relations and the management rules are available in the provided data set (Wechsler et al., 2023 ). The stage-area relationships were determined for different elevations and areas by the FOEN, which we then linearly interpolated. For the unregulated Lake Walen, the observed stage-discharge relation is parameterised by constructing a median observed lake level for observed outflows and then extrapolating the relation between discharge and stage with a polynomial function (degree 3). The cross-sections used for the hydrodynamic simulations (Section 2.5 ) are surveyed by the FOEN every ten years (FOEN, 2023e ). This data is assumed to remain constant throughout the entire simulation period.   3 Calculations The assessment of simulated changes is based on daily time steps but compares aggregated future monthly (m) mean lake levels (h m,fut ) to the reference period (h m,ref ):(1) Δ h  m    =  1  n  m , fut      ∑ ∀ i  ∈  m   h  i , fut     −  1  n  m , ref      ∑ ∀ i  ∈  m   h  i , ref     =  h  m , fut    ̅   −  h  m , ref    ¯   ,     where Δh m  [m] is the future monthly lake level change of month m, computed based on the daily simulations h (t ). nm is the number of daily simulation steps within a month over the 30-year period. However, short-duration extreme events, such as flash floods, have less significant impacts on large lake systems.
