In the western part of the Hayakawa River Basin, there are steep, 3,000-m-high mountain ranges (i.e., the Akaishi Mountains) formed by rapid uplift over the past million years (World Natural Heritage Registration Council of the Southern Alps, 2010 ). Owing to these characteristic lithological and topological properties, excessive sediment inputs from slope failures and landslides after storms, typhoons, and earthquakes frequently occur in the basin. Because the sediment yields are high, instream gravel mining and extraction from river channels are important industries in the area. The Amehata River—a subtributary of the Hayakawa River system—has a hydroelectric dam (i.e., Amehata Dam; Fig. 1 b). After the historic heavy rainfall in 2011, a huge amount of sediment was transported from the upstream basin and deposited in the dam’s reservoir, exceeding 90 % of the dam’s total storage capacity (Shizuoka Shimbun, 2022 ). Because such massive sediment accumulation in the reservoir has often caused overflowing waters during storm events and eventually floods in nearby villages, the sediments accumulated along the water course have been continuously dredged and carried out of the reservoir to date. Nevertheless, to date, there is not efficient strategy for mitigating such sediment-filled conditions.  2.2 Field sampling and data collection Field sampling was conducted at 23 sites in the middle and lower reaches of the Fuji River system, including the Hayakawa and Amehata River tributaries (Fig. 1 b). The sampling sites were longitudinally established in the upstream reach of the Hayakawa River (St.1–4; hereafter “upstream Hayakawa River”), the Amehata River (St.5–8), and the downstream reach of the Hayakawa River (St.9–13; hereafter “downstream Hayakawa River”), which is located in the downstream of the confluence point between the Amehata and upstream Hayakawa Rivers. These study reaches generally feature fast-flowing pool-riffle channels in deeply incised valleys. In the main channel of the Fuji River, the sampling sites were established in both the upstream (St.14–15; hereafter “upstream Fuji River”) and downstream (St.16–23; hereafter “downstream Fuji River”) reaches of the confluence point of the Hayakawa River. The study reaches in the main channel of the Fuji River are characterized by fast-flowing, gravel-bed morphology with pool-riffle sequences and alternating bars. At each sampling site, river water and SS samples were collected once or twice a month, and fluvial sediment samples were collected every three to four months from January 2021 to June 2022. River water samples were collected from the bridge over the area of thalweg by lowering a plastic container on a rope, filtered through 0.2 μm cellulose acetate membrane filters (DISMIC series; ADVANTEC, Tokyo, Japan) and stored in 50 mL polyethylene bottles with 0.1 mol L−1  HNO3 . SS were collected by passing the river water samples (collected in 2 L polyethylene bottles) through 0.2 μm cellulose acetate membrane filters (C020A047A; ADVANTEC, Tokyo, Japan). The polyethylene bottles used for river water sampling were cleaned with 6 mol L−1  HCl for 24 h and then rinsed with Milli-Q water before the sampling. Fluvial sediment samples were collected from the surface of alluvial deposits accumulated adjacent to active wetted channels using a plastic scoop and stored in plastic bags. The fine sediment fraction (< 1 mm grain size) was obtained by sieving the air-dried sediment samples in the laboratory. The total concentrations of SS in the river water were determined following Standard Methods 2540 D (American Public Health Association, 1998 ) by weighing the dried residues after filtration. In order to know the timing and variability of both rainfall and runoff events during the study period, we collected the hydrological data from a gauging station at St.19 (Nanbu Station of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport, and Tourism, Japan, http://www1.river.go.jp/ ), which is located in the middle part of the study reaches. Water level data (commonly used as a proxy for discharge) were obtained from the gauging station. Daily precipitation data were also collected from a nearby meteorological station (Nanbu Observatory of the Japan Meteorological Agency, https://www.jma.go.jp/jma/index.html ).  2.3 Sample analysis The concentration of Sr was determined using a quadrupole inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (ICP-MS) (7500cx; Agilent Technologies), and Sr isotopic composition was determined using a multi-collector double-focusing ICP-MS (Neptune, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at the Research Institute for Humanity and Nature (RIHN) in Kyoto, Japan. River water samples were evaporated in Teflon vials on a hotplate and dissolved in 3.5 mol L−1  HNO3 . Approximately 50 mg of SS and fluvial sediment samples were soaked in a mixed acid of 1.0 mL HF, 0.5 mL HNO3 , and 0.5 mL HClO4  (Yokoyama et al., 1999 ) and completely digested in microwave vessels at 200 ºC. The resulting digested solutions were passed through Eichrom Sr-specific resin to separate and extract the dissolved Sr fraction. The measured 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio was normalized to the 86 Sr/88 Sr value of 0.1194. The 87 Sr/86 Sr value of the NIST SRM 987 standard throughout the analyses was 0.710275 ±0.000024 (2σ, n = 81). The precision of the analysis was within ±0.000015 in the 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio. All measurements were normalized to the recommended 87 Sr/86 Sr value of 0.710250 (Faure, 2001 ).  2.4 End-member mixing analysis using Sr isotope ratios and concentrations When the two source components (A  and B ) have different Sr isotope ratios and concentrations, the Sr isotope ratio of the mixture (M ) can be determined using an isotope mass-balance model as follows:R  M   = R  A   f  A   C  A    C  M        + R  B   1 − f  A      C  B    C  M            where R  and C  denote the 87 Sr/86 Sr and Sr concentrations, respectively, for the mixture M , the source A , and the source B . f A  refers to the fraction of source A  in mixture M  in terms of mass. The equation indicates that the 87 Sr/86 Sr of the mixture (R M ) is a linear function of the inverse of the Sr concentration of the mixture (1/C M ) (Faure and Mensing, 2005 ), implying that the mixture M  is plotted on the straight line connecting the two points (A  and B ) in the 87 Sr/86 Sr−1/Sr concentration plot. From the above equation, the fraction of component A  in the mixture (f A ) was calculated as follows:f  A   = R  M   C  M   − R  B   C  B    R  A   C  A   − R  B   C  B         which was used to estimate the source contributions of SS, riverbed sediments, and river water.   3 Results 3.1 Seasonal variations of river flow and riverine SS concentration In this study, the flow of the Fuji River was represented by the water level monitoring data (at St.19) because the public data of discharge is unavailable, although the river water flow is non-linearly related to water level. The river water flow varied seasonally and was associated with frequent runoff events ( Fig. 2 a). Rainfall–runoff events tended to occur frequently during the high-water season from spring to autumn, whereas stable and low river water flow was observed during the winter season. The SS concentrations in the Fuji River also varied seasonally and tended to be high during runoff events (Fig. 2 b). During the low-water period in winter, the SS concentrations tended to be low (<20 mg L−1 ) at most sampling sites (Fig. 2 b). Spatial variations in riverine SS concentrations were also observed at the sampling sites (Fig. 2 b). In particular, the sampling sites in the Amehata River (St.6 and St.8) showed the highest SS concentrations during runoff events (>1000 mg L−1 ), followed by those in the upstream Hayakawa River (St.1 and St.4). In the downstream Hayakawa River (St.13), the SS concentrations ranged between those of the Amehata River and the upstream Hayakawa River (Fig. 2 b). In contrast to the high SS concentrations in the Amehata and Hayakawa River tributary systems, the SS values in the upstream Fuji River (St.15) were the lowest among the sampling sites. The SS values did not generally exceed 200 mg L−1 , even during high water level periods. However, SS concentrations in the downstream Fuji River (St.19 and St.22) increased after the confluence with the Hayakawa River.  3.2 Sr isotopic composition of river water The Sr isotopic composition and concentrations of river water showed distinct values in the Fuji River system (Tables S1 and S2 ;  Fig. 3 ). The two sampling sites (St.8 and St.4) are located just upstream of the confluence point of Hayakawa River with Amehata River. Therefore, Sr concentrations and 87 Sr/86 Sr values of river water collected at these sites can be end-members for those values of the downstream Hayakawa River (see Fig. 1 ). Likewise, St.15 is located upstream of the confluence point of Fuji River with Hayakawa River. This sampling site can also be an end-member for Sr concentrations and 87 Sr/86 Sr values of river water in the downstream Fuji River. Therefore, we calculated the average Sr concentrations of river water as 284 ±56, 182 ±62, and 67 ±9 μg L−1  for St.8, St.4, and St.15, respectively (Table S1 ). The average 87 Sr/86 Sr values of the river water were 0.70981 ±0.00012, 0.70881 ±0.00010, and 0.70579 ±0.00014 for St.8, St.4, and St.15, respectively (Table S2 ). In the Fuji River system, the river water samples exhibited an isotope mixing line of Sr between the major geologic source components. On the plot of 87 Sr/86 Sr−1/Sr concentration, the 87 Sr/86 Sr values of almost all river water samples were distributed between the values of two end-member study reaches, i.e., the Amehata River (St.8) and the upstream Fuji River (St.15) (Fig. 3 ). Regarding the Hayakawa River system in the plot, the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) was distributed between two end-points, namely the Amehata River (St.8) and the upstream Hayakawa River (St.4) (Tables S1 and S2 ; Fig. 3 ). Similar to the river water of the main channel, the downstream Fuji River (St.16–23) generally fell between two end-points, namely the downstream Hayakawa River (St.13) and the upstream Fuji River (St.15), although some downstream data points (i.e., St.22 and St.23) deviated slightly from the mixing line (Fig. 3 ). The isotope mixing pattern of the river water was consistently observed irrespective of the hydraulic conditions. The fractions of Hayakawa River water to Fuji River water (f HAY ) and Amehata River water to Fuji River water (f AME ) were estimated by the Sr isotope mass-balance model. The median f HAY  and f AME  values of river water were 0.15 (range = 0.05–0.61) and 0.06 (range = 0.01–0.16), respectively (Table S3 ). During no runoff periods, the median values of f HAY  and f AME  were 0.13 (range = 0.08–0.23) and 0.04 (range = 0.01–0.09), respectively (Table S3 ), and thus almost comparable to the values that would be expected from the catchment areas at the confluence point (Hayakawa River Basin: 503 km2 ; Amehata River Basin: 104 km2 ; Fuji River system: 3025 km2 ). However, under rainfall–runoff events, the median f HAY  and f AME  values increased to 0.24 (range = 0.05–0.61) and 0.10 (range = 0.02–0.16), respectively (Table S3 ), indicating that the contribution of river water derived from the Hayakawa River system became disproportionately large in the Fuji River during runoff events.  3.3 Sr isotopic composition of riverine SS The Sr isotopic composition and contents of riverine SS differed among the major river systems. Therefore, Sr concentrations and 87 Sr/86 Sr values of riverine SS collected at St.8, St.4, and St.15 can be end-members for the values of the downstream Hayakawa River and the downstream Fuji River likewise river water. The average Sr concentrations in the riverine SS were 102 ±9, 138 ±13, and 155 ±19 mg kg−1  for St.8, St.4, and St.15, respectively (Table S1 ). The average 87 Sr/86 Sr values of the riverine SS were 0.71297 ±0.00059, 0.71020 ±0.00064, and 0.70626 ±0.00039 for St.8, St.4, and St.15, respectively (Table S2 ). Similar to the isotope mixing line of river water, the 87 Sr/86 Sr values of almost all riverine SS samples were distributed between the values of the Amehata River (St.8) and the upstream Fuji River (St.15) on the 87 Sr/86 Sr−1/Sr plot ( Fig. 4 ). For the Hayakawa River system, the data points of SS samples collected from the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) were plotted between two end-points: the Amehata River (St.8) and the upstream Hayakawa River (St.4). For the main channel of the Fuji River, the data points of SS samples from the downstream Fuji River (St.16–23) were generally distributed between the two data points of the downstream Hayakawa River (St.13) and upstream Fuji River (St.15), although some downstream data points (i.e., St.22 and St.23) slightly deviated from the mixing line. The Sr isotope mass-balance model estimated the median values of f HAY  and f AME  of riverine SS as 0.65 (range = 0.56–0.71) and 0.29 (range = 0.05–0.71), respectively (Table S3 ). During no runoff periods, no estimates of f HAY  and f AME  values for riverine SS were obtained because of insufficient sample amounts for 87 Sr/86 Sr analysis due to low turbidity or were calculated incorrectly due to the deviation of data from the isotope mixing line for both the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) and the downstream Fuji River (St.17–23) (Table S3 ).  3.4 Sr isotopic composition of fluvial sediments Fluvial sediments also showed distinct Sr isotope values and concentrations for each river system. The average Sr contents of the sediments were 94 ±4, 137 ±9, and 165 ±34 mg kg−1  at St.8, St.4, and St.15, respectively (Table S1 ). The average 87 Sr/86 Sr values of the fluvial sediments were 0.71187 ±0.00048, 0.70939 ±0.00011, and 0.70502 ±0.00007 for the Amehata River (St.8), the upstream Hayakawa River (St.4), and the upstream Fuji River (St.15), respectively (Table S2 ). On the plot of 87 Sr/86 Sr−1/Sr concentration ( Fig. 5 ), most data points of sediment samples collected from the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) were distributed between the two data points of the samples of the Amehata River (St.8) and the upstream Hayakawa River (St.4). Similarly, in the main channel of the Fuji River, the data points of sediment samples showed an isotope mixing line of Sr between the two end-points of the downstream Hayakawa River (St.13) and the upstream Fuji River (St.15); however, some data points collected from the most downstream reaches (St.23) deviated slightly from this line (Fig. 5 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Pattern of turbidity in the Fuji River and its tributaries High SS concentration in the Fuji River system was observed when the river water level was high because of heavy rainfall in the basin (Fig. 2 ). In particular, the SS values of the Hayakawa River system, especially the Amehata River tributary, were relatively high (Fig. 2 b) compared to those of the upstream Fuji River (upstream of the confluence point between the Fuji River and the Hayakawa River). These results indicate that SS transported from the Amehata and Hayakawa River tributary systems are likely a major cause of increased turbidity in the downstream reaches of the Fuji River. The Amehata River has high turbidity and hydroelectric dams, such as the Amehata Dam, in the basin. Due to landslides associated with the historic heavy rainfall in 2011, a huge amount of sediment was deposited in the dam’s reservoir, exceeding the 90 % of the dam’s total storage capacity (Shizuoka Shimbun, 2022 ). After this massive sediment deposition, SS leakage through water outflow from the sediment-filled reservoir has been pointed out to be a cause of turbid conditions in downstream reaches. The sampling sites at St.6 and St.8 were located upstream and downstream of the dam, respectively (Fig. 1 b); however, their SS values showed no significant differences during rainfall–runoff events. Moreover, the downstream site (St.8) frequently exhibited lower SS values than those of the upstream site (St.6) during low water level conditions (Fig. 2 b), even though the dam gate was generally opened to lower the water level because the reservoir capacity had been very low due to the presence of sediments. Therefore, sediment leakage from the Amehata Dam may have contributed less as a source of the strongly turbid water in the Amehata River. In the downstream reach of the Amehata Dam, illegal dumping of industrial waste, such as sludge, occurred during the period 2009–2019, and it has also been revealed as a potential source of turbid water in the Fuji River (Nihon Keizai Shimbun, 2020; Shizuoka Shimbun, 2021 ). Although a part of the industrial sludge was removed from the Amehata River bank after the local government order in 2019, most of the illegally dumped sludge was reportedly flushed to downstream areas by storm events. Therefore, no sludge samples are currently available to examine the chemical and physical characteristics for tracing the fates of sludges in the river. Nevertheless, considering that no significant increase of the SS at that site of the Amehata River occurred, such an illegal source is unlikely to contribute at least to the “current” turbid condition in the basin, although it potentially might have contributed to riverine SS before the public concern halted the illegal sludge dumping.  4.2 Contribution of tributary river water to the Fuji River The isotope mixing line of river water Sr on the plot of 87 Sr/86 Sr−1/Sr concentration (Fig. 3 ) confirmed that river water was composed of a mixture of those transported from major tributary systems. The river waters in the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) were plotted on a straight line between the upstream Hayakawa River (St.4) and the Amehata River (St.8) (Fig. 3 ), suggesting that the Hayakawa River waters originated mainly from these two major tributary basins. Similarly, the downstream Fuji River (St.17–23) was plotted on the line between St.13 and St.15, suggesting that the river water in the downstream Fuji River can be largely considered a mixture of those derived from the Hayakawa River system and upstream Fuji River (upstream of the confluence point of the Hayakawa River). However, some sampling sites in the downstream reaches located close to the estuary (St.22 and St.23) deviated slightly from the line, suggesting the contribution of other tributary water sources (e.g., Shibakawa River) in the lower reaches of the Fuji River. The Sr isotope mass-balance model revealed the contributions of tributary river water to the Fuji River, that is, the f HAY  and f AME  values of river water. The disproportionately large values of f HAY  and f AME  under rainfall–runoff events are probably because the high terrain of the Akaishi Mountains often enhances precipitation, thereby increasing the flow of the Hayakawa River. In fact, the mean annual precipitation (2000−2300 mm) in the Hayakawa River Basin (World Natural Heritage Registration Council of the Southern Alps, 2010 ) is higher than that in the entire Fuji River Basin (1100−2100 mm).  4.3 Contribution of tributary SS to the Fuji River The Sr isotope mixing line of the SS showed that the riverine SS of the downstream Fuji River can also reflect the contribution of riverine SS derived from the Amehata and Hayakawa River systems (Fig. 4 ). Similar to the river water, the SS in the downstream Hayakawa River (St.9–13) was a mixture of riverine SS derived from the Amehata River and upstream Hayakawa River. In addition, the SS transported downstream of the Fuji River mainly originated from the downstream Hayakawa River and upstream Fuji River. The estimated median values of f HAY  and f AME  of riverine SS (0.65 and 0.29, respectively) were significantly higher than the f  values of the river water, suggesting that the riverine SS derived from the Hayakawa River system could be a major source of strong turbidity in the Fuji River. Moreover, the riverine SS derived from the Amehata River often account for more than half of those in the downstream Hayakawa River system, indicating that they are an important source of turbidity. Because there is no strong evidence showing the contribution of SS leaked from the dam reservoir and the resuspension of illegally dumped SS in the downstream reaches of the Amehata River, other sources, such as the massive sediment production from deep-seated landslide areas (e.g., Oikenosawa and Yashio-Kuzure landslides) occurring in the upstream reaches of the Amehata River, were possibly a major cause of the current strong turbidity in this tributary system. For the source of SS under low turbid conditions, no reliable estimates for f HAY  and f AME  values were obtained (Table S3 ). Moreover, the deviation of data (St.9–13 and St.17–23) from the isotope mixing lines suggests that other effects, such as bedload transport of SS or the contribution of SS transported from other tributaries, may have influenced the mixing of SS in the study area. Accordingly, the riverine SS from the Hayakawa River system may contribute less to the turbidity in the Fuji River, except during rainfall–runoff events. Another important point is that the size of suspended particles could influence the Sr isotopic compositions and concentrations because the size of suspended particles may depend partly on the lithological source (Haddadchi et al., 2015; Le Gall et al., 2017 ). Therefore, further studies using the 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio across multiple particle size fractions and/or other sediment fingerprint parameters are necessary to evaluate the SS source materials and dynamics more accurately.  4.4 Fluvial transport and deposition of riverine SS Riverbed materials are supplied by sediment transported through streamflow (Colby, 1963 ). We estimated the f HAY  and f AME  values of the fluvial sediments using the Sr isotope mass-balance model with average values at each sampling point. The estimated values for sediments in the main channel of the Fuji River (f HAY  = 0.11; f AME  = 0.01) were considerably lower than the riverine SS f  values (median f HAY  = 0.65; median f AME  = 0.29). This result implies that most of the riverine SS derived from the Hayakawa River system flowed into Suruga Bay without much accumulation of riverbed sediment in the Fuji River, although it should be noted that the particle size of sediments was slightly larger than that of SS. This argument is supported by the Sr isotope values per se . Sediments in the downstream Fuji River (St.17–23) had lower 87 Sr/86 Sr values than those of riverine SS in the corresponding sites ( Fig. 6 ). However, the sediment 87 Sr/86 Sr values in the downstream Fuji River overlapped with the SS 87 Sr/86 Sr values of the upstream Fuji River (St.15; Fig. 6 ). These results suggest that SS derived from the upstream Fuji River (i.e., upstream of the confluence point of the Hayakawa River) may be the predominant source of riverbed materials in the downstream reaches. However, because the particle size of sediments was slightly larger than that of SS in our measurement samples, which may affect Sr isotope values (Le Gall et al., 2017 ), a careful discussion about the fate of riverine SS is necessary. Based on these results, it can be concluded that the riverine SS derived from the Hayakawa River system significantly contributes to the high turbidity of the Fuji River, whereas most of the SS are likely to be transported into Suruga Bay without accumulating much on the riverbed. These findings suggest that strong turbidity caused by the Hayakawa River SS can affect aquatic organisms in the Fuji River (Lively et al., 1983; Lloyd, 1987; Japan Fisheries Resource Conservation Association, 1994; Bilotta and Brazier, 2008 ), while it seems likely that such turbid water does not significantly modify riverbed and sediment characteristics in the river. Furthermore, in Suruga Bay, the inflow of massive amounts of riverine SS has raised concerns regarding its inhibitory effect on the survival and growth of marine organisms, such as Sakura-Ebi shrimp (Lucensosergia lucens ) (Alam et al., 2022 ). Therefore, proper soil management is required to prevent the harmful effects of turbidity on aquatic organisms in rivers and coastal ecosystems. The Sr isotopic composition (i.e., 87 Sr/86 Sr) showed great potential regarding fingerprinting individual tributaries in the Fuji River system due to heterogeneous geology in the catchment, in accordance with studies conducted in other watersheds (Goldstein and Jacobsen, 1988; Andersson et al., 1994; Martin and McCulloch, 1999; Gingele and De Deckker, 2005; Le Gall et al., 2017 ). Although it was used for estimating sediment sources derived from the major tributaries in the present study, 87 Sr/86 Sr can be applied to estimate multiple sources derived from other tributaries in the lower reaches of the Fuji River with more detailed investigation. Other fingerprinting methods, such as the additional use of geochemical properties (i.e., major and trace element concentrations) in mixing models (Olley and Caitcheon, 2000; Douglas et al., 2003; Evrard et al., 2011; Navratil et al., 2012 ) and/or radioisotopic approaches (e.g., fallout radiocesium) (Evrard et al., 2020 ), may also be applicable to estimate the contributions of soil erosion sources and human activities that were not detectable in this study.   5 Conclusion The present Sr isotope analyses revealed that riverine SS derived from the Hayakawa River system are likely a major source of strong turbidity in the Fuji River. However, most of the Hayakawa River SS seem to be scarcely deposited on riverbed sediments and therefore transported into Suruga Bay. Due to the ongoing increase of extreme rainfall events caused by climate change in Japan, the effect of turbidity on the riverine and coastal ecosystems is expected to become greater in the future. Considering that it is indeed difficult to control SS production from slope failures and landslides, the river manager and stakeholders may need to adapt to the changing environment, such as the modifications of fishery management plans and more strict resource protection than before, rather than mitigating the turbid condition in rivers. The Sr isotopic composition (i.e., 87 Sr/86 Sr) can be a robust tracer of riverine sediment dynamics, including production, transport, and deposition processes in an isotopically heterogeneous basin because the 87 Sr/86 Sr values of transported materials depend on the basin rock type (Nakano et al., 2020 ). In the case of isotopically homogeneous basins or to estimate the contributions of soil erosion sources and human activities to river turbidity more accurately, fingerprinting methods employing other geochemical elements (e.g., radiocesium, rare earth elements, etc.) should also be adopted. These findings improve our understanding of fluvial sediment transport and the cause of river turbidity, enabling more proper soil erosion controls in river-to-ocean continuum systems.
1 Introduction Coastal communities worldwide are increasingly experiencing tidal flooding as a recurring phenomenon. In the past, the extent of inundation typically associated with major coastal storms now frequently transpired during high tides and under fair weather conditions. This form of coastal flooding, commonly known as high tide flooding (HTF), sunny day flooding, or nuisance flooding, generally yields minor ramifications, such as submerging streets and sidewalks (Dusek et al., 2022 ; Jacobs et al., 2018 ), congestion in storm drainage systems (Obeysekera et al., 2011 ), the intrusion of saltwater (Sukop et al., 2018 ), and the deterioration of wastewater treatment facilities (Hummel et al., 2018 ). Nonetheless, with the ongoing increase in relative sea level (RSL) along the majority of coastlines in the world, the frequency of high-tide flood events per year is rapidly increasing and, in numerous locations, has even accelerated over time (Burgos et al., 2018; Sweet et al., 2018; Thompson et al., 2021 ). Concurrently, coastal disturbances resulting from high tide flood events, such as disruptions in transportation and commerce, are becoming more prevalent (Hino et al., 2019 ). The HTF can cause significant damage to coastal communities, particularly during storms or other weather events that coincide with high tides. The risk of HTF varies depending on many factors, including the coast's location, the land's topography, the coastline's shape, the strength and frequency of storms, and sea level rise. Coastal low-lying and flat areas, or those with steep slopes leading into the ocean, are particularly vulnerable to the HTF. Climate change, such as sea-level rise (SLR), is expected to increase the risk of HTF inundation in many coastal areas as more frequent and intense storms and rising sea levels merge to create more frequent and severe flooding events (Hauer et al., 2021; Shokouhifar et al., 2022 ). For instance, the anticipated escalation of coastal flooding consequences throughout Europe is closely associated with escalating sea levels (Vousdoukas et al., 2018; Maul and Duedall, 2019 ). Recent investigations utilizing water level data from NOAA tide gauges have demonstrated that sea level rise plays a significant role in the increased occurrence and prolonged duration of tidal flooding compared to previous decades (Ezer et al., 2014 ; Moftakhari et al., 2015 ; Sweet et al., 2014 ). This means that HTF occurs more frequently every year as sea levels continue to rise and is increasingly disrupting coastal community life. Since the HTF has led to concerns about the long-term sustainability of coastal development and the need for effective adaptation strategies to minimize flooding risks, coastal communities should take steps to prepare for and mitigate HTF risks, including investing in infrastructure that can withstand flooding, developing emergency response plans, and encouraging residents to relocate to safer areas. In addition to the immediate consequences experienced by individuals and their properties, the impairment of a stormwater management system resulting from events related to HTF can have vast implications for the entire coastal community. Even minor HTF events can disrupt transportation networks by impacting emergency response, the flow of goods and services, and the mobility of residents. The accumulation of stagnant floodwaters, which cannot infiltrate or drain properly, can further exacerbate public health impacts. The ability of a coastal community to deal effectively with such events is contingent upon event frequency. Persistent flooding, even from minor events, can substantially alter how people live and affect businesses and the community. Consequently, adverse economic effects can arise, such as the depreciation of real estate values, a decline in tourism, and other detrimental consequences for local businesses. Neumann et al. (2015)  highlighted Asia's high concentration of coastal residents, particularly in China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Vietnam, rendering them vulnerable to coastal hazards. They projected stable coastal population exposure trends since 2000, with rising sea levels expected to heighten global susceptibility to coastal hazards, posing significant risks to coastal populations (Dada et al., 2023 ). Assessing economic loss and population impact due to sea-level rise (SLR)-induced high tide flooding (HTF) is crucial for academia and policymaking. Coastal regions face escalating inundation risks attributed to climate change-induced sea-level rise, leading to significant socioeconomic challenges. Analyzing potential economic losses and at-risk populations provides valuable insights into vulnerabilities and consequences, aiding decision-makers, researchers, and stakeholders. This evaluation process enables a comprehensive understanding of direct and indirect outcomes, informing targeted interventions and adaptation strategies. Additionally, assessing socioeconomic loss and the affected population is essential for designing equitable policies and measures that consider the needs and rights of affected communities (Lai et al., 2023 ). Currently, extensive research has been conducted to examine the relationship between SLR and HTF frequencies (Dahl et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Taherkhani et al., 2020; Vitousek et al., 2017 ). However, an increased focus on investigating the impacts and damage resulting from SLR-induced HTF events, including coastal inundation, affected populations, and economic losses, is needed. These aspects have received limited attention in existing studies, although many studies have focused on storm surge-generated coastal inundations (Chen and Liu, 2014; 2016; Piecuch et al., 2022 ) In this study, we aimed to assess the potential impact of sea-level rise (SLR)-induced high tide flooding (HTF) on the southwestern coast of Taiwan by quantifying the affected population and economic losses resulting from coastal inundation caused by SLR-induced HTF. The methodologies developed in this research can be applied globally to estimate local coastal flood risks, particularly in regions experiencing significant SLR. Section 2  describes the study's coastal region, while Section 3  outlines the data sources and coastal flood modeling approaches utilized. In Section 4 , the study presents estimates for annual HFTs, the extent of coastal inundation, the population at risk, and the associated economic losses under various SLR scenarios, accompanied by a discussion of the uncertainties involved. Finally, Section 5  concludes the study and summarizes the findings.  2 Coastal region for the present study The southwestern coastal area in Taiwan (within the white solid-line box, as shown in  Fig. 1 a), which comprises Yunlin, Chiayi, Tainan, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung Counties, has experienced increased susceptibility to flooding due to the detrimental effects of groundwater overextension and resulting land subsidence caused by intensive aquaculture activities. Taiwan has more than 40,000 ha of land-based aquaculture farms, and the southwest coast accounts for more than 30,000 ha, approximately 80 %. The rapid growth of the aquaculture industry in this coastal region has led to excessive groundwater pumping for various operational needs. Unsustainable practices have disrupted the hydrological balance and resulted in adverse consequences. The over-extraction of groundwater has led to a decrease in water levels in the underlying aquifers, gradually causing the land to subside (within the white dashed-line box, as shown in Fig. 1 b). The geological composition of this coastal area, characterized by clay and unconsolidated sediments, exacerbates the subsidence phenomenon. The compaction of these soft and compressible materials under excessive groundwater drawdown further lowers the land surface area, causing the regions to be more prone to flooding. Subsidence-induced topographical alterations have disrupted natural drainage patterns, reducing the capacity of waterways to carry excess water effectively. As a result, even minor precipitation events, combined with high tides, storm surges, or heavy rainfall, can lead to waterlogging and inundation of low-lying areas. The highest astronomical tides along the study coastline range from 1.0 m to 2.5 m, depending on the coastal location (Yu et al., 2019 ).  Fig. 2  depicts a site within the study area where the road is (Fig. 2 a) inundated at flood tide and (Fig. 2 b) emerged at ebb tide (Fig. 2 c) at present due to decades of land subsidence. The combination of land subsidence and rising sea levels further intensifies the risk of flooding, posing a significant threat to the affected coastal communities in southwestern Taiwan.  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Categories of high tide flooding As the relative sea level rises, coastal flooding no longer solely depends on solid storms or hurricanes. HTF emerges due to sea level rise and localized factors pushing water levels beyond the customary high tide mark. Alterations in prevailing winds, shifts in ocean currents, and intensified tidal forces during full or new moon phases can all contribute to high tide flooding, resulting in street inundation even on clear days. According to the definition from the National Ocean Service of NOAA in the U.S., HTF can be categorized into three levels of severity: minor, moderate, and major. These classifications are based on the extent to which water levels surpass the mean higher high water (MHHW) at a particular location.• Minor high tide flooding occurs when water levels rise to approximately 0.55 m (1.8 feet) above the MHHW. This level of flooding primarily disrupts normal activities, causing stormwater system backups and road closures in coastal communities.  • Moderate high tide flooding is characterized by water levels approximately 0.85 m (2.8 feet) above the MHHW. This level of flooding can lead to further disruptions and damage to residential and commercial properties in coastal communities.  • Major flooding encompasses water levels exceeding 1.20 m (3.9 feet) above the MHHW. Floods of this magnitude are highly destructive, often requiring evacuations and significant repairs to infrastructure and private properties in coastal communities.    Since the MHHW refers to the mathematical mean of the elevations corresponding to the higher high waters within a mixed tide pattern observed over a defined 19-year period, we analyzed the 20-year (from 2003 to 2022) tide measurements recorded at five tide-gauging stations deployed by the Central Weather Agency, Taiwan. The locations of these five tide-gauging stations in the study coastal region are shown in Fig. 1 a, and the corresponding names, coordinates, MHHWs, and minor, moderate, and major high tide flood thresholds are listed in  Table 1 . The MHHWs in the coastal study area decreased from north to south. The maximum MHHW was 1.44 m for the No. 1 tide-gauging station, Boziliao. In contrast, the No. 4 tide-gauging station, Kaohsiung, had a minimum MHHW of 0.610 m for the five tide-gauging stations. Therefore, the minor HTF occurs once astronomical tide superposes SLR exceeding 1.99 m. Table 1  can be used for further details by analogy. These long-term tide measurements were also used to ensure the model was well-calibrated and validated, enabling accurate projections of future coastal inundation risks due to sea-level rise.  3.2 Land use and socioeconomic data for the study area According to the 2020 statistical report published by the Council of Agriculture, Taiwan, southwestern Taiwan's agricultural and aquaculture regions constitute more than 50 % and 80 % of the country, respectively. Groundwater is recognized as a reliable water source for rice cultivation due to its significant irrigation requirements. Moreover, freshwater aquaculture has flourished in the coastal areas of southwestern Taiwan, necessitating substantial water resources that can only be supplied through groundwater. However, intensified groundwater extraction in the southwestern coastal regions of Taiwan has resulted in significant land subsidence, exacerbating water stress in agriculture and fisheries.  Fig. 3 a illustrates the details of land use in the study area provided by the Department of Land Administration, Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan, in 2022. The minimum statistical area (MSA) is a geographical unit commonly employed for statistical and analytical purposes. It represents a small-scale geographic region that is typically smaller than administrative divisions such as cities, counties, or areas and possesses specific boundaries and population statistical data. The definition of MSA may vary depending on the country or organization. Nevertheless, it is generally used to collect and analyze specific statistical data such as population census data, employment statistics, crime rates, and education indicators. These regions can be delineated based on different objectives and requirements, such as population density, geographical features, or community divisions. The size and shape of the MSA can be determined as needed to ensure the accuracy and comparability of the statistical data. They are usually regarded as unique areas and are considered independent units in the collection and analysis of statistical data. Using MSAs can assist researchers, policymakers, and businesses in further understanding and analyzing the characteristics and trends of specific regions, thereby providing valuable information for relevant decision-making. The Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan defines the MSA as the smallest spatial unit for collecting and aggregating population or socioeconomic data, and it possesses the following characteristics: (1) Data within the region should exhibit as much uniformity as possible, such as levels of economic activity and population counts. (2) The spatial distribution characteristics of the original data should be preserved to the greatest extent possible. (3) It should possess discernible and relatively stable boundaries on the ground, such as streets, rivers, and roads. (4) It should have connectivity and a subordinate relationship with other publishing levels. The latest MSA population data released by the Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan in June 2022 are shown in  Fig. 4 . The study area comprised 33,889 MSAs, and the spatial distribution of the population by each MSA in this region is shown in Fig. 4 a. Most MSAs contained a population of less than 500, except for two coastal metropolitan areas (as shown in Figs. 4 b and 4 c), and the population of certain MSAs could reach 2000. Figs. 4 b and 4 c are enlarged maps that distinctly exhibit the coverage of each MSA.  3.3 Projection of rising sea level for the study area The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is an intergovernmental organization established under the auspices of the United Nations, with the primary objective of providing policymakers with comprehensive and up-to-date scientific assessments on climate change. Its mandate involves regularly evaluating and communicating scientific knowledge about climate change and its potential future risks, facilitating informed decision-making processes. By extensively surveying the scientific literature, the IPCC generated consensus-based projections regarding future sea-level changes across global regions, considering a spectrum of plausible future scenarios. The most recent publication by the IPCC was the 6th Assessment Report (AR6), made available on August 9th, 2021. It served as the latest authoritative document produced by the IPCC, encompassing various scientific contributions and findings. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a sea level projection tool (SLPT) to aid researchers in evaluating future coastal inundation risks. The SLPT enables users to visualize and download sea-level projection data derived from the IPCC AR6. Within the integrated climate change assessment community, the quantification of anthropogenic emissions aligns with diverse shared socioeconomic pathway (SSP) scenarios, each representing a distinct combination of socioeconomic and political circumstances envisaged for the future. Under these SSP scenarios, sea-level changes can be projected, albeit with moderate confidence. The SLPT provides sea-level projections for five specific SSP scenarios, namely, SSP1–1.9, SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5, which cover each decade from 2020 to 2150. These projections are relative to a baseline period spanning from 1995 to 2014. The CO2 concentrations projected for these scenarios range from 393 to 1135 ppm (parts per million) by 2100, corresponding to the lowest (SSP1–1.9) and highest (SSP5–8.5) emission scenarios, respectively (Meinshausen et al., 2020 ). The SSP5–8.5 scenario, characterized by low confidence, incorporates representations of low-likelihood yet high-impact ice sheet processes, which are also integrated into the SLPT. The projections concerning sea-level changes are derived through an assessment considering multiple uncertainties. These uncertainties encompass the temperature changes associated with emission scenarios, the relationships between temperatures, and various drivers of projected sea-level change, such as thermal expansion, ocean dynamics, and glacier and ice sheet mass losses. Typically, the likely ranges of sea-level projections are determined based on the 17th to 95th percentiles, with results in this range interpreted as likely. The term "probably" denotes a probability threshold of at least 78 %. For this study, we adopted sea-level rise (SLR) projections for a specific tide-gauge location, namely, Kaohsiung II. The decision to use the 95th percentile values was primarily driven by the need to assess the potential worst-case scenarios for SLR-induced high tide flooding impacts in a highly vulnerable coastal region. The 95th percentile values provide a critical upper bound that helps policymakers and stakeholders understand the maximum possible extents of inundation and the consequent socioeconomic losses under the most extreme yet plausible SLR scenarios. This approach aligns with risk management practices, prioritizing understanding and preparing for extreme events to ensure robust coastal resilience planning. By utilizing 95th percentile values of SLR derived from SSP1–1.9 (representing the lowest-emission scenario), SSP2–4.5 (representing the medium-emission scenario), and SSP5–8.5 (representing the high-emission scenario), we obtained the necessary inputs for estimating the HTF-induced maximum inundation extents (MIAs) in the designated coastal region.  Fig. 5  shows the projected SLR from 2040 to 2100 under the SSP1–1.9 (Fig. 5 a), SSP2–4.5 (Fig. 5 b), and SSP5–8.5 (Fig. 5 c) scenarios. The shaded areas in Fig. 5  represent the range between the 17th and 95th percentiles of SLR. Based on the estimations from AR6, the projected 95th SLR increments in Kaohsiung II by 2100 were estimated to be 0.837 m, 1.084 m, and 1.391 m under the SSP1–1.9, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.8 scenarios, respectively. These findings highlighted the substantial disparity in projected SLR depending on the underlying emission scenarios and associated socioeconomic pathways. The lower-emission SSP1–1.9 scenario exhibited relatively modest SLR projections, whereas the higher-emission SSP5–8.5 scenario entailed more significant uncertainty and indicated substantially greater SLR estimates. These results highlighted the importance of considering various scenarios and their implications for future coastal inundation risks.  3.4 Implementation and configuration of the coastal flood model for the study area The SCHISM model (Zhang et al., 2016 ) is an advanced numerical model for simulating hydrodynamic processes in various water bodies. It utilizes a semi-implicit finite-element/finite-volume method with the Eulerian Lagrangian algorithm and unstructured grids to efficiently and accurately solve the Navier Stokes equations, capturing interactions across different scales of motion within a single computational domain. Additionally, it incorporates features for simulating sediment transport and water quality processes and has been validated against field observations and laboratory experiments. Developed at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, the SCHISM model is widely adopted for studying hydrodynamic processes globally, offering distinctive features such as a semi-implicit scheme, unstructured grids, cross-scale interaction capabilities, sediment transport, and water quality simulations. When applied in diverse environments, it has been crucial for investigating circulation patterns and coastal inundations induced by sea-level rise and storm surges (Chen and Liu, 2014; 2016; Hsiao et al., 2022 ). We used the SCHISM-COAST-2D model to project sea-level rise-induced coastal inundations in southwestern Taiwan and the Taiwan Strait. The SCHISM-COAST-2D model utilizes digital elevation data (DEM) provided by the Department of Land Administration, the Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan. This DEM was acquired in 2022 and has a spatial resolution of 1 m and an accuracy of 0.01 m. The computational domain covered approximately 10,847 km2  (white line in Fig. 2 ), utilizing refined meshes in the terrestrial areas and coarser meshes in the ocean boundary regions. The most refined meshes, with a 5-m resolution, were distributed on the terrestrial area, while the coarsest meshes, with an approximately 1000-m resolution, were arranged on the oceanic regions. The model employed a 60-second time step interval and incorporated geographic data (Figs. 3 a and 3 b) and tidal harmonic constants as boundary conditions. A 60-second time step is derived from prior research findings (Hsiao et al., 2022 ), allowing the coastal inundation model developed in this study to achieve a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. The SCHISM-COAST-2D model utilized eight major astronomical tidal variables (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, P1, and Q1) extracted from a regional inverse tidal model (Egbert and Erofeeva, 2002; Zu et al., 2008 ) as input data for the open boundary conditions.  Fig. 6  represents a flowchart of the implementation process in the present study.   4 Results 4.1 Sea level rise-induced potential for high tide flooding    Figs. 7–9  illustrate the projections of minor, moderate, and major annual HTF events for seven decades from 2040 to 2100 under low-, medium-, and high-emission scenarios, and the red, yellow, and blue shades refer to minor, moderate, and major HTFs, respectively. The annual days with minor annual HTFs ranged from 40 to 50 for Boziliao (Fig. 7 a) in 2040 under low- to high-emission scenarios. For Dongshi (Fig. 7 b), Jiangjun (Fig. 7 c), Kaohsiung (Fig. 7 d), and Donggong (Fig. 7 e), the number of minor HTF days increased significantly by 2060; except Jiangjun, the number of minor annual HTF days exceeded 40 even under the low-emission scenario. By 2090, minor HTFs are likely to occur between 280 and 360 days per year on the southwestern coast of Taiwan, depending on location. A moderate HTF tended to be more frequent by 2060 for Boziliao (Fig. 8 a) under low- to high-emission scenarios, but a similar phenomenon was observed by 2080 for Dongshi (Fig. 8 b), Jiangjun (Fig. 8 c), Kaohsiung (Fig. 8 d), and Donggong (Fig. 8 e). However, the number of annual moderate HTF days surpassed 320 on the southwestern coast of Taiwan by 2090 under the medium- and high-emission scenarios. A major HTF event did not occur on the southwestern coast of Taiwan until 2070–2080, even under a high-emission scenario (as shown in Figs. 9 a–9 c). There were more than 40 major annual HTF days by 2090 under the medium- and high-emission scenarios, and rapid growth exceeded 240 days by 2100 under the high-emission scenario (Figs. 9 a–9 c). Because of rising sea levels, the trend of high tide flooding will become more frequent in the southwestern coastal communities along Taiwan. Predictions from the present study show that minor high tide flooding might be more common beginning in 2040 and occur every day in 2010. As sea levels continue to rise, conditions that cause minor and moderate high tide flooding today will cause moderate and major high tide flooding by 2070 and 2080.  4.2 Coastal inundation caused by high tide flooding It is imperative to validate and calibrate the numerical model using present-day field-observed data before conducting scenario simulations to ensure accurate future inundation projections in coastal areas. This study identified sea-surface elevation variations as the primary factor influencing inundation in the coastal transition zone. Therefore, sea-surface elevation data recorded at five tide-gauging stations (Boziliao, Dongshi, Jiangjun, Kaohsiung, and Donggong) along the coast of the computational domain were employed for validation and calibration of the tidal simulation performance of the SCHISM-COAST-2D model. A one-month simulation was conducted from January 1 to January 31, 2023, encompassing spring and neap tide periods. The first 15 days were dedicated to the calibration phase, while the remaining 16 days served as the validation phase.  Fig. 10  compares the simulated and observed sea-surface elevation time-series data collected at the Boziliao (Fig. 10 a), Dongshi (Fig. 10 b), Jiangjun (Fig. 10 c), Kaohsiung (Fig. 10 d), and Donggong (Fig. 10 e) tide-gauging stations in January 2023. The maximum tidal ranges in January 2023 were approximately 3.5 m, 3.0 m, 2.0 m, 1.3 m, and 1.4 m at the Boziliao, Dongshi, Jiangjun, Kaohsiung, and Donggong tide gauging stations, respectively. The evaluation metrics indicated a correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.95 for the Donggong and Jiangjun stations and 0.98 for the Boziliao, Kaohsiung, and Donggong tide-gauging stations, and the root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) ranged from 0.07 to 0.12 m (as shown in Fig. 10 ). The SCHISM-COAST-2D model demonstrated favorable agreement with the observed sea-surface elevation time series, accurately reproducing tidal dynamics. In addition to quantitative analysis, qualitative assessments were essential for evaluating the model's applicability.  Fig. 11  illustrates a site within the study region (Fig. 11 a) where the road is inundated at flood tide (Fig. 11 b) and emerges at ebb tide (Fig. 11 c) due to severe land subsidence. This figure compares the field survey and modeled results (Figs. 11 d and 11 e). These results demonstrate substantial agreement between the simulated and observed current high-tide flood extents, confirming the effectiveness of the SCHISM-COAST-2D model. Here, we must provide some information. According to the WRA report, the rate of land subsidence along the southwestern coast of Taiwan in 2023 ranges between 3.7 and 6.4 cm per year. If we disregard constraints on ground compaction, the land subsidence in this area will exceed 3 m over the next 50 years, significantly surpassing the rate of sea-level rise. Consequently, the low-lying areas of this coast are already temporarily inundated by seawater during exceptionally high astronomical tides. Since the SCHISM-COAST-2D model has been quantitatively and qualitatively examined, the present study can superpose the various SLR increments on astronomical tidal heights to represent the total tidal levels at open boundaries. The SLR magnitudes at the 95th percentiles of the low- (SSP1–1.9), medium- (SSP2–4.5), and high- (SSP5–8.5) emission scenarios from 2040 to 2100 (as shown in  Fig. 12 a) were imposed on the SCHISM-COAST-2D model to project the most severe HTF inundated coastal extents resulting from SLRs rising from low-, medium-, and high-emission scenarios. The present study used the 95th percentile values of SLR derived from the SSP1–1.9, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.5 scenarios. The SLR magnitudes for each scenario were imposed on the SCHISM-COASTAL-2D model by superposing astronomical tides generated from eight primary harmonic constants. By integrating these SLR scenarios into the SCHISM-COASTAL-2D model, the study projected the maximum inundation extents and analyzed the potential impacts of HTF under different emission scenarios. Moreover, we must clarify that this study primarily aims to estimate the permanent inundation impact caused by sea level rise in the study area. Given that the western coastal waters of Taiwan are relatively shallow, wave heights are usually quite small. The annual average wave height in the nearshore area of the study region is approximately 0.9 m. Therefore, this study does not consider the influence of wind waves on coastal inundation. Fig. 12  presents an overview of the SLR magnitudes (Fig. 12 a) and the corresponding extents of coastal inundation caused by the HTF (Fig. 12 b) in the present study. Before 2070, the projected extents of coastal inundation resulting from SLR closely resembled those of the three scenarios. However, beyond 2070, the variations in SLR magnitudes between the scenarios lead to increasingly divergent estimations of coastal inundation areas. Specifically, by 2100, the estimated extent of coastal inundation was approximately 220 km2  for the low-emissions scenario and approximately 400 km2  for the medium-emissions scenario. Notably, the high-emissions scenario indicated a significantly greater projected coastal inundation extent of approximately 600 km2  by 2100 (Fig. 12 b).  Fig. 13  portrays the anticipated scope of coastal inundation resulting from the HTF under distinct SLR scenarios derived explicitly from a high-emissions scenario, i.e., SSP5–8.5. When juxtaposed with present-day flood tide conditions (Fig. 13 a), the projected inundation extents exhibited a noteworthy expansion inland, owing to the implementation of higher SLR magnitudes within the SCHISM-COAST-2D model (Figs. 13 b–13 h). Notably, the most extensive inundation was observed to propagate landward by up to 9.0 km, aligning spatially with regions of comparatively lower elevations in the southwestern coastal area of Taiwan (as is evident in the comparison between Fig. 13 h and Fig. 1 b). The projected most severe inundation extents under different emission scenario SLRs by 2100 were 220 km² for the low-emission scenario (SSP1–1.9), 400 km² for the medium-emission scenario (SSP2–4.5), and 600 km² for the high-emission scenario (SSP5–8.5). These projections indicate that higher emission scenarios result in significantly greater coastal inundation extents due to sea-level rise.  4.3 Socioeconomic loss exposure to coastal inundation Evaluating socioeconomic loss, including population impacts and economic loss, from exposure to SLR-induced coastal inundation serves as a foundation for evidence-based decision-making, sustainable development planning, and the formulation of policies to protect and enhance the well-being of coastal communities. We used the latest MSA-based population data (Fig. 4 ) distributed within the study area and released by the Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan in June 2022 to assess how many people live in the coastal communities that various SLR-induced HTFs might inundate. The projected extents of HTF-caused inundation overlapped with the MSA-based population distribution map. Then, the total population was obtained by summarizing the number of MSA-based populations covered by the projected extents of HTF-caused inundation.  Figs. 14 a–14 c show the total populations impacted by various SLRs from low- (Fig. 14 a), medium- (Fig. 14 b), and high- (Fig. 14 c) emission scenarios. Each bar represents an impacted population corresponding to an SLR (on the horizontal axis) and inundation extent (red line with black circle). The impacted population increased with increasing SLR and inundation extent. The least impacted population was 41,177 under an SLR of 0.263 m and an inundation extent of 30.25 km2  (Fig. 14 a). In comparison, the largest impacted population was approximately 490,000 under an SLR of 1.391 m and an inundation extent of 609.75 km2  (Fig. 14 c). Notably, the impacted population rose 1.77 times, from an SLR of 1.141 m to 1.391 m, because the more populated areas next to the coast were inundated with an increase in SLR of only 0.178 m (1.391–1.141=0.178). The economic losses caused by SLR-induced HTFs were estimated using an approach derived from the loss assessment by flood disasters proposed by the Water Resource Agency (WRA), Taiwan, in 2019 (Water Resource Agency, 2019 ). Each kind of land use has lower and upper limit values, depending on the types of agriculture and aquaculture, and the total economic losses can be estimated by summing the values of each land use inundated by the SLR-induced HTF. Notably, according to the open data from the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, Taiwan, the average inflation rate in Taiwan over the past four years (2019–2022) has been 1.31 %. Therefore, the estimated total economic losses in this study are approximately 1.05 times the multiplier of the price increase caused by inflation during these four years.  Figs. 15 a–15 c illustrate the total economic loss caused by various SLRs in the low- (Fig. 15 a), medium- (Fig. 15 b), and high-emission (Fig. 15 c) scenarios. Each bar represents a low (light pink bar) and upper (light blue bar) limit of total economic loss, corresponding to an SLR (in the horizontal axis) and inundation extent (red line with black circle). Similar to the impacted population, the total economic loss also increased with increasing SLR and extensive inundation. The upper limit total economic loss was approximately 3.25 million US dollars under an SLR of 0.263 m and an inundation extent of 30.25 km2  (Fig. 15 a); however, the upper limit total economic loss was approximately 35.31 million US dollars under an SLR of 1.391 m and an inundation extent of 609.75 km2  (Fig. 15 c). In general, the rise in SLR will majorly affect populations, ecosystems, and infrastructure in coastal areas. Flooding will displace people more often and severely, causing socioeconomic issues and challenges in relocation. Vulnerable communities, especially in low-lying regions, are at higher risk of health problems and livelihood loss. Coastal ecosystems like wetlands, mangroves, and coral reefs will suffer habitat loss, impacting biodiversity and natural protection against storms. Their decline will lead to species loss and weakened coastal defenses, worsening flooding and erosion. Infrastructure will face more flooding and storm damage, increasing maintenance costs. Critical infrastructure like roads, bridges, water treatment plants, and power grids will be particularly at risk, resulting in economic losses and service disruptions.  4.4 Population dynamics in high-vulnerability coastal regions However, an analysis of MSA-based population data for the years 2008, 2013, 2018, and 2022, as provided by the Ministry of the Interior of Taiwan, conducted in the present study revealed a gradual decline in population within the coastal areas vulnerable to SLR under the SSP5–8.5 scenario in southwestern Taiwan over the past 15 years (2008–2022). This decline could be attributed to demographic challenges in Taiwan, such as population aging, population migration, and declining birth rates. Notably, within the regions encompassed by the projected maximum inundation range, the population at risk decreased from approximately 0.52 M in 2008 to approximately 0.49 M in 2022, representing a decline of approximately 5.8 % over the 15-year period examined (as shown in  Fig. 16 ). These findings emphasize that population decrease could be an alternative solution within this environmentally sensitive coastal zone, effectively addressing the consequences of SLR from climate change.   5 Discussion The projection of the SLR-induced HTF was subjected to several uncertainties that must be considered. First, the accuracy of future SLR projections relies on the reliability and comprehensiveness of climate models used to estimate global and regional changes (Lotfirad et al., 2023 ). These models incorporate factors such as greenhouse gas emissions, ice sheet dynamics, and oceanic processes, which introduce uncertainties in predicting the magnitude and rate of SLR. Additionally, uncertainties arise from the inherent variability and complexity of coastal systems, including local topography, coastal erosion, and land subsidence, which can modify the impact of SLR on high tide flooding. Moreover, formulating warning thresholds of minor, moderate, and major according to local geographical characteristics is essential for accurately projecting the potential of SLR-induced HTFs in a regional coastal region. One key source of uncertainty in projecting the extent of coastal inundation resulting from SLR-induced HTFs lies in future SLR projections (as mentioned above). Furthermore, the interaction between SLR and local coastal conditions, including topography, geomorphology, and tidal variations, adds another layer of uncertainty to the projection process. Variations in coastal erosion rates and human interventions further contribute to the uncertainty in predicting coastal inundation intensity. Moreover, uncertainties could also arise from the limitations of numerical coastal flood models that simulate SLR-induced HTF-caused inundation events, which rely on assumptions and simplifications of complex physical processes. This work excludes the contributions of land subsidence and bathymetric changes to coastal inundation since straightforward linear extrapolation of land subsidence and bathymetric changes may entail considerable uncertainty (Wang et al., 2018 ). Accurately estimating the future population affected by SLRs relies on various demographic factors, such as population growth, migration patterns, and land-use changes, which are challenging to anticipate accurately over long-term periods. Similarly, assessing economic losses requires integrating numerous socioeconomic variables, such as property values, infrastructure investments, and business activities, which are subject to change due to evolving societal and economic dynamics. Based on the abovementioned reasons, the present study assessed the effects of HTF-induced inundation on socioeconomic losses under present-day conditions. Despite the limitations of such an assessment approach, helping coastal engineering and social science researchers better understand whether the current coastal defense infrastructure is adequate for mitigating coastal inundation caused by SLR remains insightful. Additionally, this study provides valuable insights into the potential impacts and losses faced by present-day socioeconomic aspects due to varying degrees of coastal flooding. Reassessing these assumptions is crucial for several reasons. It enhances awareness of the heightened risks, enabling more effective preparation and response. Accurate assumptions are essential for improving planning and adaptation strategies, including engineering solutions and nature-based approaches. Understanding the potential extent of flooding helps estimate economic losses and plan for social impacts, thereby mitigating disruptions. The present study emphasizes that coastal regions must update their SLR assumptions to ensure they are adequately prepared for future HTF events' increasing risks and impacts. Applying the NOAA-classified HTF criteria to assess the future impacts of HTF on the southwestern coast of Taiwan under the threat of sea-level rise is not an optimal approach. However, the coastal management authorities have not yet established the classification for the HTF in Taiwan. Therefore, this study temporarily adopts NOAA's classification system. Despite this, our analysis of the MHHW at five tidal stations, which is essential for classifying HTF, to some extent reflects region-specific characteristics. Ideally, the best approach would be for Taiwanese coastal management authorities to promptly establish suitable classification thresholds for HTF in Taiwan. The adaptations required to mitigate SLR-induced coastal inundation necessitate a comprehensive and multifaceted approach encompassing engineering and nature-based solutions. Engineering adaptations involve constructing or enhancing coastal defense structures such as seawalls, breakwaters, and levees to provide immediate protection against inundation. These measures aim to strengthen coastal areas and minimize the adverse impacts of rising sea levels on human settlements, critical infrastructure, and economic activities. Nevertheless, within the realm of sustainable coastal protection, there is considerable emphasis on implementing nature-based solutions to evaluate the merits of ecosystem services, thereby fostering additional economic and social advantages (Sutton-Grier et al., 2015; Schoonees et al., 2019; Moraes et al., 2022; Unguendoli et al., 2023 ).  6 Conclusions The present study utilized long-term tide measurements recorded at five tide-gauge locations to analyze the potential for HTF resulting from future SLR under low-, medium-, and high-emission scenarios. The study found the following regarding the potential for HTF under different emission scenarios. Minor HTF: By 2040, minor HTF events (0.55 m above me MHHW) are projected to occur 40–50 days annually under low to high-emission scenarios. By 2090, minor HTF events are likely to occur between 280 and 360 days per year, depending on the location along the southwestern coast of Taiwan. Moderate HTF: Moderate HTF events (0.85 m above MHHW) will become more frequent by 2060, especially in locations like Boziliao. By 2090, moderate HTF events could occur more than 320 days annually under medium and high-emission scenarios. Major HTF: Major HTF events (1.2 m above MHHW) are expected to occur in 2070–2080, even under high-emission scenarios. By 2090, major HTF events could occur more than 40 days annually, exceeding 240 days by 2100 under high-emission scenarios. Inundation Extents: By 2100, the projected extent of coastal inundation ranges from 220 km² under low-emission scenarios to 600 km² under high-emission scenarios. The study highlights that rising sea levels will significantly increase the frequency and severity of HTF events, posing substantial risks to coastal communities in southwestern Taiwan. This work acquired minimum statistical area (MSA)-based population data and land use data distributed in the study area provided by the Ministry of the Interior in Taiwan in June 2022 to estimate the population and economic loss due to HTF-caused coastal flooding. The estimations revealed that a population of approximately 490,000 people living in the southwestern coastal area of Taiwan could be impacted if the sea level rises to 1.391 m, i.e., the 95th percentile of the SSP5.85 scenario (high-emission scenario), under the present-day population data. Considering the total economic loss from coastal flooding damage, if the extent of HTF-caused coastal inundation exceeds 600 km2 , i.e., an SLR of 1.391 m is present, the upper and lower limits could reach approximately 35.31 million and 10.69 million US dollars, respectively, according to the present-day land-use data. Based on the analysis conducted in this study, it was found that the population residing within the area affected by the most severe flooding scenarios due to rising sea levels decreased by 5.8 % over 15 years from 2008 to 2022. This population decline could be attributed to population migration and declining birth rates in the southwestern coastal region of Taiwan. The methodologies introduced in the study demonstrate global applicability through their comprehensive and adaptable approach to assessing coastal flood risks. Firstly, using Minimum Statistical Area (MSA)-based population data and detailed land use information allows for precise and scalable assessments of population and economic impacts in various coastal regions worldwide. By overlaying projected inundation extents with the local population and land use data, the methodology can be applied to different geographic areas with varying levels of data granularity. Secondly, the study employs a loss assessment approach developed by Taiwanese Water Resource Agency (WRA). These models can be tailored to other regions by incorporating local economic and land use variables. This approach ensures that the economic loss estimations are relevant and accurate for diverse coastal contexts; additionally, using the SCHISM-COAST-2D model for projecting sea-level rise (SLR)-induced coastal inundations is based on robust hydrodynamic simulations. These simulations can be calibrated and validated with local tide measurements, ensuring the model's flexibility and accuracy for global applications. The present study makes significant contributions to flood mitigation and coastal resilience strategies. It provides detailed estimates of population and economic losses under various sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios, offering valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders. The study underscores the need for a comprehensive approach to enhance coastal resilience by emphasizing the importance of diverse strategies, including engineering solutions like seawalls and nature-based approaches like restoring mangroves. Additionally, it underscores how demographic changes, such as population decline in vulnerable areas, can naturally mitigate exposure to flooding risks. By identifying the most vulnerable areas and potential economic impacts, the study supports the development of targeted and equitable adaptation policies, promoting resilient and sustainable coastal development.
1 Introduction Changes in river flow pattern pose a severe and enduring threat to ecological sustainability (Petts, 2009 ). In recent decades, rivers globally have experienced dramatic flow regime shifts, leading to significant ecosystem degradation (Döll and Zhang, 2010; Gierszewski et al., 2020; Nilsson et al., 2005; Puig et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Dam construction, climate change, and land-use change are primary drivers altering flow regime (Cui et al., 2020; Dosdogru et al., 2020; Gebremicael et al., 2019; López-Ballesteros et al., 2020 ). Currently, dams affect 60 % of the world's rivers (Richter and Thomas, 2007 ), projected to reach 70 % by 2025 (Chen et al., 2016 ). Climate and land-use changes also significantly contribute to flow regime shifts (Ashraf et al., 2016; Baloch et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2011; Papadaki et al., 2016; Zhang and Wei, 2021 ). Over the past few decades, the global climate and land-use have changed dramatically (Diffenbaugh et al., 2015; Dosdogru et al., 2020 ; Naomi and Oreskes, 2004 ; Rosenzweig et al., 2008 ; Li et al., 2023 ). Recent research on dam construction, climate change, and land-use change shows significant impacts on river flow globally (Dai et al., 2010; Hirabayashi et al., 2013; Lutz et al., 2014, Peterson et al., 2002 ; Yin et al., 2023a ; Yin et al., 2023b ). Climate change exacerbates flood risks (Hirabayashi et al., 2013; Lutz et al., 2014, Peterson et al., 2002 ). Furthermore, the combined influence of climate change and human activities leads to more complex runoff patterns (Yin et al., 2023a ; Yin et al., 2023b ). In China, research on the impacts of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on river flow is also increasing (Li et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). These studies show significant impacts on runoff from these factors in different regions of China (Li et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). Therefore, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of flow regime changes for sustainable development and river protection, the following points are critical: 1. changes in the overall hydrological regime should be understood, and 2. changes in hydrological regime caused by dam construction, climate change, and land-use change should be separated. To date, more than 170 hydrological indicators have been developed and introduced to describe the different aspects of river regime (Gao et al., 2009; Jovanovic et al., 2016; Olden and Poff, 2003; Richter et al., 1996 ). Among these indicators, the Indicators of Hydrological Alteration (IHA) reflects the flow regime through five characteristics: magnitude, frequency, duration, timing, and rate of change (Richter et al., 1998; Richter et al., 1997 ), and are the most robust and widely used indicators (Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Richter and Thomas, 2007 ). Initially, IHA was used to evaluate hydrological impacts of dam construction by comparing prior-impact and post-impact periods (Gao et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017 ). This approach requires fewer data and is easier to implement. However, this method overlooks the impact of climate change and land-use change, attributing flow-regime changes solely to dam construction (Baloch et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2020; Dosdogru et al., 2020 ). Recent studies have explored changes in flow regime by considering different factors (Baloch et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2020; Dosdogru et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2019 ). Cui et al. (2020)  found that climate change primarily drives flow regime changes in the upper Yellow River. However, their method for quantifying these impacts is not suitable for assessing the timing of extreme water conditions. For example, if the timing of the annual maximum flow shifts from the 365th day to the 1st day, their method would interpret this as a 364-day advance, which is clearly unreasonable. Additionally, this study overlooks the impacts of land use changes on flow regime. Dosdogru et al. (2020)  observed significant effects from climate and land-use changes on flow regimes in Alabama, USA, but did not consider dam impacts. Tian et al. (2019)  noted high impacts from dam construction and land-use changes on the Wuding River Basin, yet ignored climate change. Overall, current methods inadequately quantify annual extreme water conditions. Additionally, previous studies typically focused on two factors at a time—climate change, land use, or dam construction, resulting in less comprehensive attribution analysis. The Ganjiang River, the largest river in the Lake Poyang basin and one of the seven major tributaries of the Yangtze River (Hu et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2015 ), has experienced significant changes in its runoff process over the past few decades due to reservoir construction, climate change, and land-use change (Guo et al., 2006; Ye et al., 2013 ). Huang et al. (2019)  observed significant flow regime changes due to dam construction, but did not consider the impacts of climate and land-use changes, which are also crucial (Baloch et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2020; Dosdogru et al., 2020 ). The study objective is to address the issue that past methods for quantifying the impact of different factors on flow regime is not suitable for quantifying the changes in the timing of annual water conditions. We have improved the formula to evaluate the timing of annual water conditions. Additionally, past studies often only quantified the impact of two factors of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change, on flow regime, resulting in an insufficiently comprehensive attribution analysis. To address these limitations, we propose a new framework to comprehensively quantify the impact of dam construction, climate change, and land use changes on flow regime, using the Ganjiang River Basin as a case study. This approach aims to provide more accurate and comprehensive quantification of the changes in flow regime caused by different factors, thereby supporting the formulation of sound ecological restoration policies for rivers and serving as a reference for flow regime evaluations for similar rivers worldwide.  2 Methodology 2.1 Framework for quantifying the impacts of climate change and human activities on flow regime Climate and land-use changes can significantly affect natural flows (Trenberth et al., 2003 ; Eum and Simonovic, 2012 ; Baloch et al., 2015 ). For instance, rising temperatures accelerates the water cycle and increase the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events, thereby altering the average runoff and intensifying extreme hydrological events (Trenberth et al., 2003 ; Eum and Simonovic, 2012 ). Afforestation can increase vegetation cover and evapotranspiration in a basin, thereby altering the hydrological regime (Baloch et al., 2015 ). In the past, changes in the flow regime were primarily attributed to dam construction (Gao et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017 ), leading to evaluation results to deviate significantly from the actual results.
