To address this issue, we propose a comprehensive framework for assessing basin flow regimes, separating the impacts of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change (see  Fig. 1 ). Long-term daily runoff data were prepared, and the abrupt points of the runoff sequence were identified. The period before the abrupt runoff point was regarded as the prior-impact period, while the period after the abrupt runoff point was regarded as the post-impact period. The abrupt time can be: the time of dam construction, a year when land use has changed significantly, or an abrupt point of the runoff sequence detected by the diagnostic technology, which would be considered the impact year. To show the entire process of the framework application, this study used a sliding t-test to judge abrupt points. The hydrological model reconstructed the runoff sequence unaffected by the dams after the impact period for comparison with the regulated runoff of the dam. In this study, the soil and water assessment tool (SWAT) model is used to simulate the scenario not affected by the dam. The SWAT model of the research basin was constructed using land-use, meteorological, and DEM data from the prior-impact period, with observed runoff data used for parameter calibration and validation. To reconstruct the runoff sequence affected only by climate change during the post-impact period, we input the meteorological data from this period while keeping other data and parameters unchanged. The model output was a runoff series affected only by climate change. To reconstruct the runoff sequence affected by both climate and land-use changes in the post-impact period, we input meteorological data and land-use data from this period, keeping other data and parameters unchanged. In this case, the model output was a runoff series affected by both climate and land-use changes. To assess the flow regime changes caused by dam construction, climate change, and land-use change, we used the IHA to describe flow regime changes and improved the standard IHA evaluation method to objectively reflect the change in the timing of annual extreme water conditions. The difference in the observed runoff between the prior- and post-impact periods was considered to include the overall impact of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change. The difference between the observed runoff in the prior-impact period and that affected only by climate change in the post-impact period reflected the impact of climate change alone (Step 3). The difference between the observed runoff in the prior-impact period and the runoff affected by climate change and land-use change in the post-impact period represented the combined impact of climate change and land-use change (Step 4). Thus, the impacts of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on the flow regime could be separated. Finally, the range of variability approach (RVA) was used to evaluate the overall impact of these different factors on the flow regime of the basin.  2.2 Sliding t-test A sliding t-test, as described in the literature (Guo et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2016 ), was used to identify abrupt change points in the runoff sequence. The sliding t-test was set to be a reference point in time series “x” with a sample size “n.” The two subsequences before and after the reference point were defined as x  1     and x  2    .(1) t = x  ̅   1   − x  ̅   2    s ∙ 1  n  1     − 1  n  2             where(2) s = n  1   s  1  2   + n  2   s  2  2    n  1   + n  2   − 2         n  1     and n  2     are the sample sizes of x  1     and x  2     respectively. Usually, n  1    =n  2    ; x  ̅   1     and x  ̅   2     are the averages of x  1     and x  2    , respectively, and s  1  2     and s  2  2     are the variances of x  1     and x  1    , respectively. If | t  i   | <  t  α     , there is no significant difference between the two subsequences. Otherwise, an abrupt change occurs at the reference point. To ensure the reliability of the results, each station adopted n  1    =n  2    =6a, n  1    =n  2    =7a, and n  1    =n  2    =8a for judgment.  2.3 SWAT model The SWAT model is a distributed physics-based hydrological model developed by the USDA Agricultural Research Service (Arnold et al., 1998 ). This model has been used worldwide to simulate long-term runoff and assess the impacts of climate change and human activity on hydrological processes (Krysanova and Srinivasan, 2015 ). In the SWAT model, a watershed is divided into multiple sub-watersheds, which are further divided into smaller spatial units called hydrological response units (HRU). Each HRU is defined by a unique combination of land use, soil, and slope ranges (Arnold et al., 2012 ). The SWAT model uses a modification of the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) curve number method to estimate the surface runoff. A detailed description of the hydrological components is provided by Arnold et al. (2012) . Before model calibration and validation, a sensitivity analysis of parameters is necessary. In this study, the Sequential Uncertainty Fitting (SUFI-2) algorithm within the Soil and Water Assessment Tool Calibration and Uncertainty Program (SWAT-CUP) (Abbaspour, 2015 ) was used for sensitivity analysis, calibration, and validation. The model parameters were selected based on a literature review, initial sensitivity analysis, conditions of the study area, and their known effects on hydrological processes (Luo et al., 2008 ).  Table 1  shows the hydrological parameters considered in the sensitivity analysis and their ranges. Following the recommendations of Abbaspour (2015)  in the SWAT user guide, default ranges were set for 12 parameters, and the t-stat was monitored to rank the parameters according to their sensitivity. Parameter calibration and validation are necessary to improve the accuracy of the SWAT model simulation (Arnold et al., 2012 ). We selected a section of the runoff sequence from the 1971–1980 prior impact period for parameter calibration and used another part of the runoff sequence from the 1981–1990 prior impact period to validate the model simulation. We then used the three statistical evaluation indicators recommended by Moriasi et al. (2015)  to evaluate the performance of the SWAT model during calibration and verification. These indices included the coefficients of determination (R2 ) (Eq. (3) ), percentage bias (PBIAS) (Eq. (4) ), and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) (Eq. R² value range of R²   is from 0 to 1, with 1 being the best. The PBIAS represents the mass balance error as a percentage, with 0 is the ideal value. The range of NSE is from -∞ to 1, and 1 is the best value. Latif et al. (2010) proposed that when NSE ≥ 0.7 and PBIAS ≤ 25 %, the simulation performance is good.  2.4 Flow-regime indicators In this study, we evaluated the impacts of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on the flow regime using the IHA proposed by Richter et al. (1996) . We divided the IHA into 5 categories and 33 indicators ( Table 2 ) according to the magnitude of monthly flow, annual duration, extreme water conditions, timing of extreme water conditions, high/low pulses, and changes in water conditions. Since there was no zero-runoff time in the Ganjiang River Basin, 32 indicators were used in this study. Previous studies (Cui et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2017 ) have used the deviation value and deviation degree of the IHA to evaluate the impact of human activities or climate change on the IHA. In our study, the deviation value for the IHA was calculated using the following equation:(6) M  c   = M  e   − M  0       where M  0     and M  e     are the median values of a given IHA for the pre- and post-impact periods, respectively, and M  c     is the deviation. The degree of deviation is calculated as follows:(7) P  i   = M  c    M  o     × 100 %      A positive P  i     indicates an increased median value in the post-impact period, whereas a negative P  i     suggests a decreased median value in the post-impact period. The standard IHA deviation calculation method increases the deviation value of the timing of the extreme water conditions. For example, if the timing of the minimum flow in the prior-impact period was 1 and the timing of the minimum flow in the post-impact period was 365. The deviation value calculated by the standard method is 364; however, it should be −1 because it is 1 day ahead of schedule. At the same time, the standard calculation formula for deviation degree leads to an inconsistency in evaluation standards for the timing of extreme water conditions. For instance, if the timing of the minimum flow in the post-impact period is delayed by 1 day compared with that in the prior-impact period, the deviation degree is 100 % if the timing of the minimum flow is the 1st day in the prior-impact period, and 1 % if it is the 100th day. This discrepancy has no positive significance for evaluating the change in the hydrological situation. To address these issues, we improved the calculation formula for the deviation value and degree of deviation in the timing of extreme water conditions. Because there are two types of changes, increases and decreases, the maximum deviation value was 182 days. The deviation formula for the improved timing of extreme water conditions is as follows:(8) M  c  ′   = M  e   − M  0   ,  M  e   − M  0      < 183   − M  e   − M  0    M  e   − M  0        × 365 − M  e   − M  0         ,  M  e   − M  0      ≥ 183           where M  c  ′     is the deviation value of the timing of the extreme water condition. M  e   − M  0        is the absolute value of M  e     and M  0    . The timing of extreme water conditions mainly determines the degree of stress on plants in the dry season and affects the spawning of fish. The spawning period of the four major fish species in the Ganjiang River is from April to July. At the same time, the weather in the Ganjiang River Basin has four distinct seasons. Therefore, we believe that the timing of extreme water conditions changes over 90 days, and the degree of deviation is 100%. This study suggests that the denominator in the formula calculating the timing deviation of extreme water conditions from the median value should be adjusted to 90. The formula for the deviation degree is as follows:(9) P  i  ′   = M  c  ′    90   × 100 %     where P  i  ′     is the degree of deviation in the timing of extreme water condition. A positive P  i  ′     indicates an increased median value in the post-impact period compared to the prior-impact period, whereas a negative P  i  ′     suggests a decreased median value in the post-impact period compared to the prior-impact period. To quantify the degree of hydrological alteration, Richter et al. (1997)  proposed the Range of Variability Approach (RVA) based on IHA metrics. For each indicator, we calculated the degree of hydrological alteration in a flow regime according to the following equation:(10) DHA  i   = N  o   − N  e    N  e     × 100 %     where N  o     is the observed number of post-impact years for the indicator value falling within the RVA category boundaries, which were the median plus or minus the 17th percentile based on prior-impact data, as suggested by Richter et al. (1998) . N  e     is the expected number of post-impact years for the indicator value falling within the RVA target range, and can be estimated r × N  T     (where r is the percentage of prior-impact period years for which the value of an indicator falls within the RVA target range, and N  T     is the total number of post-impact period years). The RVA generally assumes that the natural flow series of a certain flow regime is an ideal condition. If an environmental flow scheme reaches the preset target range at the same frequency as the natural flow, the flow regime is considered healthy. Richter et al. (1998)  suggested that there would be little or no alteration if DHA  i     < 33 %, moderate alteration if DHA  i     < 67 %, and high alteration if DHA  i      > 67 %. Furthermore, the following formula was used to calculate the overall alteration of the 32 indicators:(11) O D HA = ∑ i = 1  32   D HA  i  2     32         where O D HA    is the overall degree of hydrological alteration. When O D HA    was > 33 %, it was considered a moderate alteration, and when O D HA    was > 67 %, it was considered a high alteration.   3 Application of the framework 3.1 Study area The study area is the Ganjiang River Basin (113° 46′–116° 28′ E to 24° 29′–29° 50′ N). The Ganjiang River has a total length of 766 km, and its drainage basin covers an area of approximately 83500 km2 , accounting for 51 % of the land area of Jiangxi Province in Central China. The basin’s terrain is undulating, featuring a stepped topography from south to north, with an altitude range from −6–2103 m ( Fig. 2 ). The average elevation is approximately 112 m above mean sea level. The mean annual air temperature is approximately 17.8 ℃, with the highest and lowest temperatures being 39.5 ℃ and −5.8 ℃, respectively. The average annual precipitation of the basin is 1580 mm, with an uneven distribution throughout the year. Precipitation during the flood season (April–September) accounts for 78.6 % of the annual total. The furthest downstream hydrological station in the Ganjiang River Basin is Waizhou (Fig. 2 ), with an average annual runoff of 68.6 billion m3 . Runoff showed significant seasonal variations. Due to the substantial rainfall from April to September, the main flow occurred during this period. The basin is rich in vegetation, predominantly evergreen broadleaved forests. The Ganjiang River Basin supports 118 species of fish and 20 types of benthos and includes 12 spawning grounds for four species of domestic fish. In the 1980s and 1990s, numerous reservoirs were constructed in the middle and upper reaches of the river. The largest, Wan'an Reservoir, was built in 1990 with a capacity of 2.214 billion m3 . It is located in the upper reaches, 16 km above Dongbei hydrological station (Fig. 1 ). Previous studies have shown that the construction and operation of Wan'an Reservoir have a significant impact on the ecological environment of the Ganjiang River Basin (Huang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, this research focuses on the impact of Wan'an Reservoir on the downstream flow regime.  3.2 Study data The data used in this study included a digital elevation model, DEM, soil data, land-use data, meteorological data, and runoff data from the Ganjiang River Basin. Further details are provided in Table 2 . The information of meteorological stations is presented in the Table S1 .   4 Results 4.1 Detection of abrupt change point in the runoff series  Fig. 3  presents the results of the sliding t-test for different sections of the Ganjiang River Basin. The abrupt change time of different subsequence lengths (n  1    =n  1    =6,7,8) of the Dongbei, Xiajiang, and Waizhou stations was identified as 1991 and reached a significance level of 0.01. Based on this abrupt change point, the runoff time series was divided into two periods: the prior-impact period from 1971 to 1990 and the post-impact period from 1991 to 2013. Consequently, land use data from 1980 serves as the input data for the prior-impact period, while land use data from 2010 is used for the post-impact period.  Table 3   4.2 SWAT model performance in simulating runoff We adopted a method of gradually adjusting parameters from upstream to downstream, and the optimal parameters for each hydrological station are shown in  Table 4 . The observed and simulated daily runoff values at the Dongbei station, Xiajiang station, and Waizhou during periods 1971–1980 and 1981–1990 are shown in  Fig. 4 . The R ²    values of the three stations during both the calibration and validation periods were greater than 0.85, the NSE   coefficients for these periods were greater than 0.85, and the PBIAS   values were less than 9 %. Overall, the simulation performance for the three stations during the calibration and validation periods met high standards, and the daily runoff changes at these stations were effectively captured.  4.3 Dam construction, climate change, and land-use change effects on flow regime The observed runoff from 1971 to 1990 was taken as the baseline (natural runoff) since the sudden change in runoff occurred in the Ganjiang River Basin in 1991, coinciding with the construction of a dam. Factors such as dam construction, climate change, and land-use change have influenced the observed runoff from 1991 to 2013. To simulate runoff under the combined impacts of climate change and land-use change, the SWAT model was employed using observed meteorological data from 1991 to 2013 and land-use data from 2010. Runoff solely impacted by climate change was simulated using observed meteorological data from 1991 to 2013 and land-use data from 1980. The IHA method was then applied to assess the influence of different factors on the flow regime of typical sections in the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the Ganjiang River Basin. The results are presented below. 4.3.1 Typical upstream section The monthly runoff at Dongbei station, a typical upstream section of the Ganjiang River Basin, significantly decreased in April and May by 255 m3 /s and 405 m3/s, respectively (Table S2 ). A slight decrease observed in November, while from July to September, runoff increased substantially, ranging from 106 m3 /s to 361.5 m3 /s. other months showed slight increase, with the peak flow month shifting from May to June, while the minimum flow month shifting from January to May (Table S2 ,  Fig. 5 ). These monthly runoff changes were primarily influenced by dam construction and climate change. In April, May, July, and August, dam construction and climate change caused changes in the same direction, leading to significant changes in the total flow regime. However, in other months, dam construction and climate change had opposing effects. Climate change reduced the monthly runoff by 25.4 m3 /s to 197.4 m3 /s from September to December, while the dam construction increased the monthly runoff by 72.7 m3 /s to 170.4 m3 /s (Table S2 , Fig. 5 ). When considering the magnitude and duration of annual extreme water conditions, all indicators showed an upward trend, ranging from 2.5 % to 40 %, with the 30-day minimum increased the most at 40.5 %. The magnitude of the minimum flow indicators were primarily influenced by dam construction and climate change. Climate change caused downward trends in each minimum flow indicator, ranging from 28.5 % to 62.9 %. In contrast, dam construction and land-use changes led to an increase in these indicators, with land use contributing to an increase of up to 1.2 %. Dam construction was the dominant factor in the increase in each minimum flow indicator at the Dongbei station, causing increases from 43.6 % to 75.9 %. Climate change was the primary factor in the increase in the maximum flow indicators, with increases ranging from 4.3 % to 31.1 %. Land-use change and dam construction mitigated the increase in each maximum flow indicator. For example, land use change reduced the 1-, 3-, and 7-day maximum by 1.8–4.2 %, with minimal impact on the maximum flow at the 30- and 90-day maximums. Dam construction reduced the 7- and 30-day maximum by 13.7 % and 5.2 %, respectively. While, other maximum flow indicators were minimally affected, and the base flow remained unchanged, mainly because the base flow reduction caused by climate change and the base flow increase caused by dam construction were comparable (Table S2 ). The date of minimum flow at Dongbei station was advanced from the 361th day to the 348th day, primarily due to the 18 days advance of the date of minimum caused by dam construction and the 5 days delay of the date of minimum flow caused by climate change. The date of maximum was postponed from the 135.5th day to the 167th day, mainly due to the postponement of the date of maximum by 27.5 days due to climate change and by 4 days due to dam construction (Table S2 ). The frequency and duration of the high and low pulses at Dongbei Station changed significantly, with counts of high and low pulses increased by 3 and 9.5 times, respectively, corresponding to increases of 30 % and 172.7 %. The duration of high and low pulses decreased by 2 days and 5 days, respectively, corresponding to reductions of 40 % and 62.5 %. Dam construction increased the count of high and low pulses by 4 times and 11 times, respectively, and reduced the duration of high and low pulses by 5.5 days and 12 days, respectively. Climate change had the opposite effect, offsetting the impacts of dam construction on the counts of high and low pulse indicators. Land-use change had minimal impact on high and low pulse indicators, increasing them by 0.5 and 1.5 days, respectively (Table S2 ). The rise rate, fall rate, and number of reversals at the Dongbei station increased from 69.5 % to 145.8 %. Dam construction and climate change were the primary contributors to these increases. Climate change and dam construction contributed 64.4 % and 20.8 %, respectively, to the changes in runoff. Land use change mitigated the change in the rise rate, while dam construction increased the fall rate and number of reversals by 177.6 % and 104.1 %, respectively. Climate change offset the impact of certain dam construction on the fall rate and the number of reversals, and land use change had minor effects on these metrics, with changes of −1.2 % and −2.1 %, respectively (Table S2 ). The improved deviation value formula indicated a delay of five days in the date of the minimum flow due to climate change, while the standard formula showed an advancement of 360 days. Additionally, the improved formula showed that dam construction advances the minimum flow by 18 days, while the standard formula indicates a delay of 347 days (Table S2 ). Among the 32 IHA indicators, dam construction and climate change caused opposite changes in runoff effects in 28 indicators, with the dam construction aligning with the total flow regime change direction for 27 indicators. While both dam construction and climate change were the main factors affecting flow regime change at Dongbei station, dam construction was the primary factor affecting flow regime change direction (Fig. 5 ).  4.3.2 Typical middle section The monthly runoff at Xiajiang station in the middle reaches of the Ganjiang River Basin declined by 478 m3 /s and 455 m3 /s in April and May, respectively. In November, the runoff marginally decreased. A significant increase occurred from February to March and from July to September, with an increased range of 132.7 m3 /s to 820 m3 /s, and a slight increase occurred in other months; thus, the month of peak discharge shifted from May to June. Dam construction and climate change were primarily responsible for the change in monthly runoff. From April to September, both dam construction and climate change caused further altered the total flow regime significantly. From October to January of the following year, climate change reduced the monthly runoff by 105 m3 /s to 142.1 m3 /s, while dam construction increased it by 143.5 m3 /s to 213.2 m3 /s (Table S3 , Fig. 5 ). All the indicators for the magnitude and duration of the annual extreme water condition, except for the 30-day maximum, showed an upward trend, ranging from 2 % to 46.2 %; among these, the 3-, 7-, and 30-day minimum increased by 39.6–46.2 %. Minimum flow indicators were mainly affected by dam construction and climate change. Climate change caused each minimum flow indicator to decline from 9.9 % to 52.2 %. Dam construction and land-use changes caused the minimum flow indicator to increase, with land use change caused minimum flow indicators to increase by less than 1.3 %. Dam construction was the most important factor for each minimum flow indicator at Xiajiang station, increasing them from 32.6 % to 90 % due to dam construction. Climate change caused the 30-day maximum flow to decrease, while dam construction caused a slight increase in the 30-day maximum flow, resulting in minimal overall change. Climate change was the dominant factor for the increase in other maximum flow indicators, causing them to rise by 0.9–23.7 %. Dam construction and climate change had generally the same impacts on the maximum flow indicators, except for the 30-day maximum; however, the impact of dam construction was less than that of climate change. Land-use change reduced each maximum flow indicator by 0.1–2 %, with the change in basic flow being relatively small, primarily due to the decrease in basic flow caused by climate change and the increase caused by dam construction (Table S3 ). Climate change and dam construction advanced the minimum flow date at Xiajiang station from the 3rd day to the 357th day of the previous year. Additionally, the maximum flow date was delayed by 142.5 days to 167 days, mainly due to climate change and dam construction, which caused delays of 27.5 days and 4 days, respectively (Table S3 ). The low pulse indicators at Xiajiang station changed significantly; the low pulse count increased 3 times, and the low pulse duration decreased by 7.5 days, with deviation rates of 60 % and −62.5 %. These changes were mainly affected by dam construction, with deviation rates of 80 % and 70.8 % for the low pulse count and duration changes, respectively. The high pulse count increased by a factor of 1.5, and the duration was reduced by 0.8 days, with the deviation rates of 17.6 % and −13 %, respectively. Dam construction was the main factor affecting the frequency and duration of the high pulse and low pulse changes. Since climate change had the opposite effect on the high pulse indicators and had a greater impact on it, the impact on the high pulse count and duration changed by 17.6 % and 47.8 %, respectively, resulting in minor change in the high pulse indicators (Table S3 ). The rising rate at Xiajiang station changed slightly, with a deviation rate of only 2.2 %, mainly due to the opposite impacts of dam construction and climate change. The fall rate and the number of reversals at Xiajiang station are both increasing, with deviation rates of 98 % and 54.6 %, respectively, and the deviation rate of the decrease rate and the number of reversals caused by dam construction were 62.9 % and 66.3 %, respectively (Table S3 ). The date of the minimum flow calculated by the improved formula was advanced by 11 days with a deviation rate of −12.2 %, while that calculated by the standard formula was delayed by 354 days with a deviation rate of 1180 %. The minimum date affected by climate change was advanced by two days with a deviation rate of −2.2 % using the improved deviation value formula, while the standard formula delays the date by 363 days with a deviation rate of 12,100 %. Since the minimum date of the prior-impact period is the 3rd day, the standard formula calculates a deviation rate of −300 % for the minimum date, advancing it by nine days, while the improved formula calculates a deviation rate of 2.8 % for the minimum date (Table S3 ). The results for the improved formula are more reasonable. Of the 32 IHA indicators, 21 changed in opposite directions due to dam construction and climate change, and 25 changed direction in a flow regime consistent with that caused by dam construction. Climate change and dam construction were the main factors affecting the flow regime changes at Xiajiang station. Dam construction, in particular, influenced the direction of the flow regime changes at the Xiajiang station (Fig. 5 ).  4.3.3 Typical downstream section The monthly runoff at Waizhou station downstream of the Ganjiang River Basin experienced significant decreased from April to May, with reductions of 255 m3 /s and 405 m3 /s, respectively, and slight decreased in January and November. In contrast, from February to March and from June to September, runoff increase significantly, ranging from 215 m3 /s to 800 m3 /s, with a slight increase in other months. Consequently, the peak discharge month shifted from May to June. These changes were primarily influenced by dam construction and climate change. The decreased runoff from April to May and increased runoff from June to September were mainly due to climate change, which reduced runoff from April to May by 159 m3 /s–202 m3 /s and increased runoff from June to September by 489 m3 /s to 1216 m3 /s. Dam construction caused opposite effects to those of climate change. This offset a few of the differences caused by climate change from April, May, and June to September (Table S4 , Fig. 5 ). The magnitude and duration of annual extreme water condition indicators showed an upward trend, ranging from 2.2 % to 34.7 %. The 30-day minimum flow increased by 34.7 %. The rise in minimum flow indicators was mainly due to dam construction and land-use change. Climate change caused the minimum flow indicators to decline, offsetting the increase caused by dam construction and land use. This is also the reason for the rise in the maximum flow indicators, with climate change contributing to an 8.7–20.1 % increase. The decrease in basic flow caused by climate change was nearly balanced by the increase due to dam construction, resulting in only minor change in basic flow (Table S4 ). The minimum flow date at Waizhou station was advanced from the 4.5th day to the 1st day, mainly due to dam construction, which advanced the minimum flow date by 45 days, while climate change and land-use change advanced it by 20.5 days and 21 days, respectively. The maximum date was delayed from the 145th day to the 169th day, mainly due to climate change and dam construction, which delayed it by 22.2 days and 10 days, respectively (Table S4 ). The frequency and duration of high and low pulse indicators of the Waizhou station changed slightly, ranging from 0 % to 20 %, mainly because dam construction and climate change offset each other (Table S4 ). The opposing effects of dam construction and climate change primarily caused slight changes in the rising rate and reversal times of the Waizhou station, with deviation rates of 1.1 % and 4.3 %, respectively. However, the rise and fall rates were decreased by 76.1 % and 39.8 %, respectively, mainly due to the impacts of reservoir construction. The fall rate at Waizhou station showed an increasing trend, with a deviation rate of 42.9 %, primarily due to climate change, which contributed 38.6 % (Table S4 ). The minimum flow date at the prior-impact period was the 3rd day. The deviation rates of the minimum flow date calculated by the standard deviation rate formula for climate change, land use, and dam construction were 277.8 %, 288.9 %, and −311.1 %, respectively. However, the results calculated by the improved formula were 22.8 %, 23.3 %, and −50 %, respectively (Table S4 ). Dam construction and climate change were the main factors causing 22 of the 32 IHA indicators to change to the opposite direction, while 21 indicators changed in the direction of the total flow regime, which is consistent with the shift caused by climate change. Thus, dam construction and climate change were the primary factors affecting the flow regime change at Waizhou station, with climate change significantly influencing the direction of these changes (Fig. 5 ).   4.4 Hydrological alteration evaluation in Ganjiang River Basin using RVA We utilized the RVA method to evaluate the degree of hydrological alteration at typical sections of the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the Ganjiang River Basin. These sections were influenced by three different scenarios: 1) dam construction, climate change, and land-use change simultaneously; 2) climate change and land-use change simultaneously; and 3) climate change alone. In the typical upstream section of the Ganjiang River Basin, at Dongbei station, 19 indicators demonstrated more than moderate levels of alteration due to the combined effects of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change. Among these, 7 indicators, including average flow in May, 7-day minimum, low-pulse count and duration, high pulse count, fall rate, and number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold ( Fig. 6 ). A total of 16 indicators combined affected by land use and climate change were altered beyond moderate levels, with 8 indicators, including average flow in February and July, 1-, 3-, 7-, and 30-day minimum flows, base flow, and the number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold. When the station was affected by climate change alone, the number of indicators showing moderate and high levels of alteration was the same as when the station was combined affected by climate change and land-use change (Fig. 6 ). In the typical middle section of the Ganjiang River Basin, at Xiajiang station, 19 indicators showed more than moderate alteration when combined affected by dam construction, climate change, and land use. Among these, 5 indicators, including the average flow in May and November, the date of minimum flow, and the number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold (Fig. 6 ). Under the combined impact of climate change and land-use change, 18 indicators were altered above moderate levels, among which 6 indicators, including the average flow of January, 1-, 3-, and 7-day minimum flows, base flow, and the number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold (Fig. 6 ). When affected by climate change alone, 16 indicators showed more than moderate alteration. Among these, 6 indicators, including the 1-, 3-, and 7-day minimum flows, base flow, and the number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold (Fig. 6 ). In the typical lower section of the Ganjiang River Basin, at Waizhou station, 15 indicators changed more than moderately due to the combined effects of dam construction, climate change, and land use, with the 7-day maximum flow exceeded the high-level alteration threshold (Fig. 6 ). When combined affected by climate change and land-use change, a total of 16 indicators were altered more than moderately, among which 6 indicators, including average flow in July and September, 1-, 3-, date of minimum flow, rise rate, fall rate, and number of reversals, exceeded the high-level alteration threshold (Fig. 6 ). Under the influence of climate change alone, 16 indicators were altered more than moderately. Of these, 3 indicators, including the average flow in July, rising rate, and number of reversals, exceeded the high-level threshold (Fig. 6 ).  4.5 Overall assessment of hydrological alteration at different sections of Ganjiang River Basin  Fig. 7  presents a comparison of how different factors affect the total degree of hydrological alteration in various sections of the Ganjiang River Basin. Overall, the degree of hydrological alteration in the three sections of the Ganjiang River Basin was moderate. Specifically, when combined affected by dam construction, climate change, and land use, the overall degree of hydrological alteration was 53.1 % at Dongbei station, 46 % at Xiajiang station, and 36.6 % at Waizhou station. This indicates a gradual decline in the overall degree of hydrological alteration from upstream to downstream. When analyzing the impact of climate change alone, the overall degrees of hydrological alteration at the Dongbei, Xiajiang, and Waizhou stations were 48.2 %, 46.5 %, and 46.2 %, respectively. Although there was a slight decrease in alteration from upstream to downstream, the range of change was minimal. The combined effects of climate change and land-use change resulted in similar the overall degree of hydrological alteration at the three stations, with values ranging from 47.5 % to 48.2 %.   5 Discussion 5.1 Advantages of the new framework for river-regime impact assessment This sub-section summarizes the advantages of our novel framework, which, for the first time, attempts to separate the flow regime changes caused by dam construction, climate change, and land-use change. The standard approach for evaluating the impact of dams on the flow regime quantifies the relative changes in the observed flow regime metrics between the prior- and post-dam construction periods. This traditional method requires less data and is easier to execute. However, it does not consider the impact of climate change and land-use change, instead attributing the flow regime changes solely to dam construction (Cui et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2017 ). Recently, scholars have proposed frameworks for separate effects of dam construction from those of climate change effects (Cui et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2018 ). However, these frameworks do not fully consider all influencing factors. In this study, we demonstrated that dam construction and climate change are the main factors affecting hydrological regime change in the Ganjiang River Basin, with land-use change either intensifying or mitigating the impacts of climate change and dam construction on a few indicators. Therefore, to accurately assess the impact of dam construction on flow regime, the potential impacts of climate change and land-use change should be considered. Additionally, our study improved the calculation formula for the deviation value and deviation degree of the timing of extreme water condition indicators. The standard formula for evaluating IHA indicators (Cui et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2017 ) cannot compare the value and degree of deviation for the timing of extreme water condition indicators with other indicators in one dimension due to defects in the calculation logic. In contrast, our study compared the deviation value and degree of deviation of the timing of extreme water condition indicators in the Ganjiang River Basin calculated using improved and standard formulas. For instance, the improved formula delays the minimum date impacted by climate change for Dongbei station by 5 days, while the standard formula advances it by 360 days. Similarly, the improved formula advances the minimum date for dam construction impact by 18 days, whereas the standard formula calculates a delay of 347 days (Table S2 ). The improved formula advances the minimum date at Xiajiang station by 11 days, with a deviation rate of −12.2 %, while the standard formula estimates a delay of 354 days, with a deviation rate of 11800 %. The improved formula calculates that the minimum date affected by climate change occurs 2 days in advance, with a deviation rate of −2.2 %, whereas the standard formula calculates a delay of 363 days, with deviation rate of 12100 % (Table S3 ). The change ranges of the minimum date at Waizhou station due to climate change, land use, and dam construction calculated by the standard formula are 277.8 %, 288.9 %, and −311.1 %, respectively. In contrast, the improved formula yields 22.8 %, 23.3 %, and −50 %, respectively (Table S4 ). We can see that the actual minimum date at the Xiajiang station only advanced from the 3rd day to the 357th day of the previous year, an advance of only 11 days. The standard calculation formula delays the deviation value by 354 d, resulting in a deviation degree of 11800 %. Clearly, the improved formula is more accurate and useful for calculating the value and degree of deviation of the timing of the extreme water condition indicators.  5.2 Impact of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on flow regime The study results show that the hydrological regime of the Ganjiang River Basin is primarily affected by dam and reservoir construction. In the upper and middle reaches, the changes in the direction of the hydrological regime was dominated affected by dam construction, whereas in the lower reaches, the changes in the direction of the hydrological regime was dominated affected by climate change (Tables S2–S4 , and Fig. 5 ). Dam construction has significantly increased the monthly flow and minimum flow indicators in different sections of the Ganjiang River Basin in the dry season, while slightly reduced the maximum flow indicators (Tables S2–S4 , and Fig. 5 ), and decreased the pulse duration (Fig. 5 ). The regulatory effect of dams on runoff tends to make the flow process more uniform (Huang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017; Mittal et al., 2014; Vega-Jácome et al., 2018 ). Climate change reduces the minimum flow indicators and increases the maximum flow indicators in different sections of the Ganjiang River Basin. Additionally, climate change leads to an increase in the number and duration of flow pulses (Fig. 5 ), and causes the time distribution of runoff to become more concentrated (Lin et al., 2017; Ye et al., 2013 ). In general, land-use change has had relatively minor impact on the hydrological regime of the Ganjiang River Basin. It has slightly increased the minimum flow indicators and slightly reduced the maximum flow indicators (Fig. 5 ), possibly due to increased vegetation cover in the Ganjiang River Basin made the flow process more uniform (Huang et al., 2019 ). In summary, dam construction, climate change, and land-use change have significantly altered the hydrological regime of the Ganjiang River Basin. The impact of dams on the hydrological regime gradually decreases from upstream to downstream (Fig. 7 ), which is consistent with previous research findings (Lin et al., 2017 ). The changes induced by climate change and land-use change on the hydrological regime were similar across different sections of the basin (Fig. 7 ). Notably, dam construction and climate change had opposite effects on 77 % of all indicators (Fig. 5 ). We propose that well-planned dam operations may be an effective way to cope with climate change in the future. This conclusion contrasts with previous studies (Huang et al., 2019; Marak et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2015 ), which predominantly highlighted the adverse effects of dam construction on river hydrological conditions.   6 Conclusion This study proposes a novel framework to quantify the impact of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on hydrological regime, and applied it to the Ganjiang River Basin. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: We have improved the formula for calculating the timing of extreme water condition indicators. The new formula can avoids abnormal results and proves to be more reasonable than the traditional one. The proposed framework integrates the runoff abrupt-change-point judgment method, the SWAT model for reconstructing river flow under different scenarios, and the IHA and RVA methods. This integration can easily quantify the impacts of dam construction, climate change, and land-use change on the flow regime. This study observed significant changes in the hydrological regime of the Ganjiang River Basin, primarily driven by dam construction and climate change. Dam construction led to a notable increase in dry-season flow and minimum flow indicators across different river sections, while reducing maximum flow indicators. In contrast, climate change caused a decrease in minimum flow indicators and an increase in maximum flow indicators, as well as an increase in the count and duration of flow pulses. Interestingly, dam construction and climate change had offsetting effects in 77 % of the indicators. In the global context of climate change, this study suggests that intelligent dam operation could effectively mitigate the impact of climate change on river flow regime.
1 Introduction Terrestrial evapotranspiration (ET a ) is a key step in the transfer of water from the surface to the atmosphere during the hydrological cycle and plays a key role in the redistribution of water, carbon and energy (Melo et al., 2021 ). Accurate estimates of ET a  play an important role in agricultural drought prediction, water resource management and hydroclimate prediction (Vinukollu et al., 2011; Crago et al., 2016; Aminzadeh, 2017 ). Due to the complexity of evapotranspiration processes and the heterogeneity of influencing factors, it is still a challenge to accurately estimate ET a  at the global land surface scale (Mu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2018 ). ET a  is controlled by a variety of factors, such as climatic factors (such as precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, wind, and relative humidity), land surface factors (such as soil moisture, topography, and vegetation type), and human activities (such as human-induced land use/cover change, dam construction, and agricultural irrigation). These control factors interact with each other and vary greatly in space and time, which makes ET a  estimation at the global land surface scale very complicated (Bai et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018 ). An increasing number of global terrestrial evapotranspiration products based on remote sensing satellites combined with evapotranspiration models have been developed. These products include the ET_PT-JPL series, ET_ALEXI series evapotranspiration products (Zhang et al., 2010 ), Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) products, EB-ET evapotranspiration products, GLASS-ET evapotranspiration products, ET-Monitor and ET-Watch series products (Zheng et al., 2022a, 2022b ), Penman-Monteith-Leuning Model Version 2 (PML-V2) evapotranspiration products (Zhang et al., 2019 ), LSAF-series evapotranspiration products and Breathing Earth System Simulator evapotranspiration (BESS-ET) products (Jiang et al., 2020 ). However, due to differences in data sources, model structures and parameterization schemes, there are large differences in uncertainty among ET a  models (Aryalekshmi et al., 2021 ). Liu et al. (2023)  evaluated 10 kinds of global monthly scale ET a  products and concluded that the performance of products at the catchment scale is usually better than that at the site scale. Bai and Liu (2018)  analyzed the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) version 3.2 products, Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) version 2.0 catchment Land Surface Model (CLSM) dataset and Numerical Terradynamic Simulation in China Group (NTSG) datasets, compared them against each other and concluded that the annual ET a  time series based on the water balance in most basins could not be reasonably reproduced. Satellite data have the advantage of ground-scale uniformity, and when combined with traditional radiation-related and meteorological variable observations, can optimize data to address accuracy issues (Khan et al., 2018 ). To obtain spatially complete and relatively accurate gridded datasets, data assimilation systems such as the ERA5 (ERA5-Land Hourly - ECMWF Climate Reanalysis) and MERRA (MERRA-2 M2T1NXLND: Land Surface Diagnostics V5.12.4) reanalysis datasets have been developed. These systems integrate and optimize various sources and types of observations from satellite retrieval products (Rienecker et al., 2011 ). However, due to limitations in modeling and analytical techniques, uncertainties remain in reanalysis products, which can introduce propagation errors in the simulation of ET a . The diversity of input remote sensing datasets and algorithms for ET a  estimation is a major factor contributing to the uncertainties in modeled ET a  estimates (Mu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2018; Vinukollu et al., 2011 ). Additionally, differences in model mechanisms and parameterization also significantly contribute to these uncertainties (Gavilan et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2007 ). Model mechanisms primarily involve the fundamental equations on which the models are based, component partitioning methods, and physical constraints. Key parameters, such as the empirical coefficient (α) in PT-type models, surface resistance (r s ) in PM-type models, and surface roughness height (Z oh ) in energy balance models, as well as meteorological inputs, have been focal points of discussion (Shuttleworth and Calder, 1979; Yao et al., 2013; Paul et al., 2014 ). Beyond data input and model calculations, uncertainties in ET a  estimation also arise during model calibration and validation. As a result, substantial research on remote sensing-based ET a  focuses on ground validation experiments (Guo et al., 2022 ; Salazar-Martinez et al., 2022). The existing standards for calibrating and validating remote sensing ET a  products typically rely on observation data from flux towers. Other studies have also verified the uncertainty and accuracy of different ET a  products (Chen et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Salazar-Martinez et al., 2022). Since 1984, when the International Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) established the Working Group on Calibration and Uncertainty Testing, the development of ground verification tests has received attention from the international remote sensing community. In 1992, LandFlux-EVAL was launched as part of the Global Energy and Water Cycle Project, and in 2009, the European Space Agency introduced WACMOS-ET (the Water Cycle Multimission Observation Strategy for Evapotranspiration). Other researchers have systematically tested and evaluated the uncertainty of a variety of surface evapotranspiration remote sensing models and products at the global scale (Jiménez et al., 2018 ). Moreover, many other large-scale ground uncertainty verification tests have been carried out. For example, the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) project in the United States improved the monitoring accuracy of soil moisture by combining ground sensor data and satellite remote sensing data (Entekhabi et al., 2010). In Europe, the FLUXNET network provides critical atmospheric and ecosystem exchange data for validating satellite data, with extensive ground-based site coverage (McCabe et al., 2015; Miralles et al., 2016 ). The global actual evapotranspiration ET a  mainly consists of vegetation transpiration (T ), soil evaporation (E s ), vegetation canopy trapping loss (E i ) and other components (sublimation of open water and ice and snow) (E o ) (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012 ). The quantification of different evapotranspiration components in the global water cycle has attracted increasing attention (Maxwell and Condon, 2016; Wei et al., 2017 ). However, there are significant differences in the results obtained by various methods, and there is no consensus on the best method. Therefore, it is particularly necessary to investigate the differences in the components of different products because of the uncertainty of land evapotranspiration.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Calculation of land surface evapotranspiration products and components (1) ERA5-Land (ERA5-Land Hourly - ECMWF Climate Reanalysis) was created by rerunning the land portion of the ECMWF ERA5 climate reanalysis. (3) MERRA-2 (MERRA-2 M2T1NXLND: Land Surface Diagnostics V5.12.4) is a long-time-series reanalysis dataset that includes various meteorological variables, such as net radiation, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and turbulent evapotranspiration. Notably, the MERRA-2 data cover the whole world, with a spatial resolution of 0.5°×0.625° and a temporal resolution of 1 hour. The surface model used in MERRA-2 is the catchment surface model (Koster et al., 2000 ), where land evaporation is calculated as part of the surface energy balance. (4) The PML_V2 (PML_V2 0.1.7: Coupled Evapotranspiration and Gross Primary Product (GPP)) dataset is based on the Penman Monteith-Leuning (PML) model coupled with the GPP process according to the stomatal conductivity theory. Considering the mutual restrictions and limitations of GPP and ET a , the accuracy of evapotranspiration estimates in the PML_V2 dataset has been greatly improved compared with that of the estimates of previous models. In each cell grid, daily ET a  is the sum of E s , E t , E i  and E o , and the PML model estimates soil evaporation E s  and vegetation transpiration E t  according to the following methods (Leuning et al., 2008 ):(16) E  t   = ε A  c   + ρ C  p    / γ     D  a   D  a    ε + 1 + G  a    / G  c            (17) E  s   = f  ε   A  s    ε + 1        Where, ε  = s /γ , γ  is the psychological constant, s  = de */dT  is the slope of the temperature-dependent saturated water vapor pressure curve; ρ  is the density of air, C p  is the specific heat capacity of air under constant pressure; D a =e *(T a )-e a  is the water vapor pressure difference (humidity difference) of the air, where e*(T a ) is the saturated water vapor pressure at the air temperature, e a  is the actual water vapor pressure; G a  is aerodynamic conductivity; G c  is the crown transpiration conductivity; f  is the fraction from P  to equilibrium soil evaporation εAs /(1+ε ), estimated from the accumulated precipitation of the previous month. A  is the available energy absorbed by the surface (net absorbed radiation minus soil heat flux), which is divided into canopy absorption (A c ) and soil absorption (A s ) using leaf area index (LAI). E i  is modeled using an adapted version of the widely adopted Gash rainfall interception model and assumes that the ratio of moist canopy evaporation rate to rainfall rate is constant between heavy storms. The ET a  estimated in the land grid cell is aggregated from the ET a  estimated for each land cover type in the grid cell.   2.2 Flux site dataset Long-term stable flux site observations can be directly used to constrain near-surface carbon, water and energy cycles. The FLUXNET integrated network (http://fluxnet.fluxdata.org/ ) includes multiple shared-data flux sites. Land air interactions can be compared among different ecosystems and different climate conditions worldwide and can be used to assess the accuracy of model simulations and remote sensing inversion results (Zhang et al., 2010 ). The latest FLUXNET dataset is the FLUXNET2015 dataset, which includes annual data from 212 flux sites ( Fig. 1 ) that record carbon, water and heat fluxes in detail over time. The IGBP land cover classification system is used for the dataset, and the flux sites included the following 13 types of sites: evergreen coniferous forest (ENF), evergreen broadleaved forest (EBF), deciduous coniferous forest (DNF), deciduous broadleaved forest (DBF), mixed forest (MF), closed shrub forest (CSH), sparse shrub forest (OSH), forested grassland (WSA), savanna (SAV), grassland (GRA), permanent wetland (WET), croplands (CRO) and snow and ice (SNO). Through site data quality control, it was concluded that there was only 1 DNF-type flux site and 1 SNO-type flux site; additionally, the percentages of hourly and daily data gaps were greater than 50 % for SNO sites and 60.95 % for DNF sites ( Table 2 ). Therefore, only the remaining 11 site types were considered for verification in this study.  2.3 Watershed water balance data Pan et al., (2012)  was based on multisource data, such as in situ observations, satellite remote sensing inversion results, model simulation data and meteorological reanalysis data. A global water balance dataset was obtained by using a data assimilation method, and the errors of each data source were weighted. The dataset contained information for 32 large catchments with catchment areas greater than 2×105  km2  and multiyear monthly catchment water balance data covering the period from 1986 to 2006. In this study, 28 basins were selected for verification ( Fig. 2 ).  2.4 Model evaluation The accurate calculation of actual evapotranspiration is a key part of water consumption estimation. Therefore, remote sensing evapotranspiration model verification is used to assess the accuracy of calculated results. This study employs the Kling-Gupta efficiency coefficient (KGE) as a comprehensive metric to evaluate evapotranspiration models. The KGE measures the Euclidean distance from a point to the optimal point and combines three metrics: the correlation coefficient (CC), bias ratio (BR), and relative variability (RV). It yields a composite index within the range (-∞, 1).(18) KGE = 1 − CC − 1    2   + BR − 1    2   + RV − 1    2          (19) cov X , Y    = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   x  i   − x  ̅     y  i   − y  ̅          (19) std = 1  n   ∑ i = 1  n   x  i   − x  ̅     2           (21) CC = cov X , Y     std ( X ) × std ( Y )        (22) BR = x  ̅   y  ̅         (23) RV = std ( x ) / x  ̅   std ( y ) / y  ̅         Where x  and y  represent the modeled and observed values, respectively. Cov (X,Y ) denotes the covariance, std  indicates the standard deviation, subscript i  denotes the i th data pair, n  represents the total number of data pairs during the study period, and x  ̅    and y  ̅    represent the means of the modeled and observed values, respectively.   3 Results 3.1 Uncertainty in the land evapotranspiration model results  Fig. 3 a presents the spatial distribution of the KGE metric for the validation of 212 stations using ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA, and PML terrestrial evapotranspiration products. The ERA5 product and the MERRA product have 108 and 144 stations, respectively, with KGE > 0, primarily distributed in North America. The GLDAS and PML products have 186 and 187 stations, respectively, with KGE < 0, indicating relatively poor reliability in station validation. In comparison, the ERA5 and MERRA products are significantly superior to the GLDAS and PML products. Through a comparative analysis of 11 different vegetation types (Fig. 3 b), it is concluded that the MERRA product performs better than other ET a  products across various vegetation types. Except for the evergreen broadleaf forests (EBF), which show poor simulation performance and accuracy, the MERRA product demonstrates good simulation results for the other vegetation types, with median KGE values all greater than 0. The main reasons for this are that evergreen broadleaf forests are primarily distributed in tropical regions, which are characterized by complex ecosystems with abundant rainfall, high vertical diversity of vegetation, dense canopy layers, high understory vegetation coverage, and a hot and humid climate. These factors result in lower model accuracy for evapotranspiration simulation and larger errors. Through the comparison of monthly ET a  values from the ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA, and PML products from 2001 to 2017 (Fig. 3 c), it is found that the monthly ET a  values of the GLDAS product are significantly higher than those of the other products, indicating an overestimation. Using watershed water balance validation (Fig. 3 d), it is found that the ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA, and PML terrestrial evapotranspiration products perform poorly in the Amazon, Indus, Murray–Darling, Nile, and Northern Dvina basins, with KGE < 0. The Northern Dvina basin exhibits the worst simulation performance, with KGE values ranging from −11.25 to −21.53. The watershed water balance KGE of the PML product is overall superior to that of the ERA5, GLDAS, and MERRA products, with 23 basins having KGE values greater than 0. Moreover, the watershed water balance validation results for the ERA5 and MERRA products are similar. Through comprehensive analysis of Figures 3ad, it is concluded that watershed-scale data reduces the impact of local anomalies on simulation results, making watershed data validation overall superior to station validation.  3.2 Comparison of evapotranspiration components on land The actual evapotranspiration from land at the global scale encompasses vegetation transpiration (T ), soil evaporation (E s ), vegetation canopy interception loss (E i ) and other components (open water and ice and snow sublimation) (E o ). The ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA, and PML evapotranspiration products all exhibit similar global spatial patterns, but there are differences among the different products in different regions ( Fig. 4 ). The vegetation transpiration of the ERA5 products significantly different from that of the other products (Fig. 4 ). According to the spatial distributions of ERA5-T and ERA5-ES and the ranges of estimated values, there are large errors in the estimation of T  and E s  by the ERA5 algorithm, which overestimates E s  in the rainforest areas near the equator and underestimates T  in land areas (Fig. 4 ). As shown in  Table 3  and Fig. 4 , the PML products encompass the importance of water evaporation and ice sublimation, E o . According to the spatial distribution map of the annual mean value of PML-E o  from 2001 to 2017, the boundaries of ocean and land are unclear (leading to the misclassification of marine evapotranspiration and land evapotranspiration). The presence of a distinct high-value region (E o  peaks as high as 3803 mm/yr) at the land boundary (Fig. 4 ) leads to the overestimation of the proportion of E o  in land evapotranspiration. The GLDAS and MERRA products, on the other hand, include the sublimation from ice and snow but do not capture the evapotranspiration from land and open water bodies (such as lakes, reservoirs, channels, and rivers); this results in a low spatial distribution range of the annual mean values of the GLDAS and MERRA product E o , ranging from −74–323 mm/yr and −3–270 mm/yr, respectively. The spatial distribution of the four ET a  products showed local differences (Fig. 4 ), and the proportion of ET a  segmentation significantly differed (Table 3 ). The land evapotranspiration segmentation results of the ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA and PML products are mainly dominated by E o  and E s  values. The E o /ET a  value of the PML product reached 62.25 % (±4.0 %), followed by 47.70 % (±1.24 %) for ERA5. The E s /ET a  value of the MERRA product was as high as 84.31 % (±1.39 %), while that of the ERA5, GLDAS and PML products exhibited little difference, and the overall range was between 27.84 % (±4.47 %) and 31.46 % (±1.13 %). Canopy precipitation interception (E i ) was the third largest component of total evapotranspiration, accounting for a small proportion of E i /ET a , ranging from 4.07 % (±0.38 %) to 19.69 % (±4.76 %). The vegetation transpiration ratio T /ET a  was the lowest, ranging from 2.68 % (±0.48 %) to 12.71 % (±4.42 %). This conclusion contradicts the conclusions of several other scholars (Mianabadi et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019 ); therefore, based on the distribution of historical evapotranspiration, the causes for these differences are analyzed.  3.3 Component differences among vegetation types The transpiration (T ) estimates for CRO***, DBF***, EBF***, ENF***, GRA***, MF*** and SAV*** by the ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA and PML products were significantly different (P<0.001) (Fig. 6 ). The transpiration (T ) estimates for the OSH**, WET** and WSA** vegetation types were significantly different (P<0.01) ( Fig. 5 ). The soil evaporation (E s ) estimates for the CRO***, DBF***, EBF***, ENF***, GRA***, MF*** and WET*** vegetation types were significantly different (P<0.001) ( Fig. 6 ). The estimates of canopy interception loss (E i ) for CRO***, DBF***, ENF***, GRA***, MF***, OSH*** and WET*** were significantly different (P<0.001). The estimations of canopy interception loss (E i ) for the EBF**, SAV** and WSA** vegetation types were significantly different (P<0.01) ( Fig. 7 ). For the four ET a  products (ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA and PML products) used to estimate evapotranspiration, most of the values of vegetation transpiration (T ), soil evaporation (E s ) and vegetation canopy trapping loss (E i ) were significantly different at P<0.001, with a few differing at P<0.01. This finding suggests that the differences in the calculations of individual evapotranspiration components have an important influence on the uncertainty of ET a  estimates.   4 Discuss 4.1 Proportion of evapotranspiration on land In this study, the distribution of historical evapotranspiration was based on 4 sources of information, namely, the results of remote sensing evapotranspiration models, isotopes, the results of climate models and in situ observations ( Fig. 8 ), with a total of 17 historical records. Schlesinger and Jasechko (2014)  quantified T /ET a  by using vorticity covariance, flow measurements, and isotopic methods, with a value of 61 %±15 %. Liu et al. (2022)  obtained values of 57 %±14 % through in situ observations. Lian et al. (2018)  proposed a T /ET a  value of 62 %±6 % based on the CMIP5 climate model. Lawrence et al., (2007)  suggested that the T /ET a  value based on the CLM4SP climate model was 48 %. Wei et al. (2017)  proposed a T /ET a  value of 43 %±12 % based on the CMIP5 climate model. Fatichi, Pappas (2017)  obtained a T /ET a  value of 70 %±9 % based on the T&C climate model. The values of T /ET a  calculated by different climate models vary greatly. Good et al. (2015)  combined two large-scale flux allocation methods to quantify the ET a  component, and T /ET a  was 64 %±13 %. Coenders-Gerrits et al. (2014)  reported that the most conservative T /ET a  they calculated was 58 %±33 %. Jasechko et al. (2013)  considered the significant isotopic effects of T  and E  and showed that T  is by far the largest water flux from land, accounting for 86 %±7 % of land-based ET a . Based on remote sensing evapotranspiration models, T /ET a  ranges from 24 % to 80 % (Mianabadi et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019 ); the minimum value was derived from Miralles et al.’s (2016) calculations based on the PM-MOD model and highly differed from the T /ET a  values of other models. The scope of global T /ET a  varies greatly among various studies, but some scholars believe that ET a   is dominated by T  in the terrestrial hydrological cycle (T /ET a  >50 %) (Zhang et al., 2016 ).  4.2 Transpiration proportion for each vegetation type According to the statistics regarding the evapotranspiration ratio (T /ET a ) for historical vegetation ( Table 4 ), the T /ET a  value of forest ecosystems (ENF, EBF, DBF and MF) ranges from 0.31 to 0.88, and that of shrub ecosystems (WSA and SAV) ranges from 0.32 to 0.80. Moreover, T /ET a  ranges from 0.43 to 0.84 for tropical grassland ecosystems (WSA and SAV), 0.33–0.87 for grassland ecosystems (GRA), and 0.44–0.85 for cropland ecosystems (CRO). Most studies of evapotranspiration distributions have focused on vegetation transpiration, but few studies have focused on soil evaporation and canopy rainfall interception. The volume of canopy rainfall interception can reach approximately 20 % of total rainfall, mainly in forest ecosystems with large canopy widths (Chen et al., 2022 ). Soil evaporation occurs mainly in arid and semiarid ecosystems with low vegetation cover, such as scrub ecosystems (OSH and CSH). Due to the particularity of wetland ecosystems, there have been few studies of the wetland T /ET a .  4.3 Comparison of differences between different evaporation products Different data sources directly impact the accuracy and spatial resolution of ET a  products. For instance, ERA5 (ECMWF Reanalysis 5), developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, utilizes global atmospheric and surface observational data, providing high temporal and spatial resolution. On the other hand, MERRA (Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications) from Yale University and GLDAS (Global Land Data Assimilation System) integrate different observations and models, resulting in varying resolutions and data processing methods (Zhao et al., 2013 ). The physical parameterization and settings of models also vary among different ET a  products (Gavilan et al., 2007; Guo et al., 2007 ). The handling of factors such as soil moisture, land surface temperature, and vegetation type in models can lead to differences in evaporation estimates (Jiang et al., 2020 ). For instance, products like FLUXCOM, ETMonitor, and GLEAM may emphasize dynamic changes in soil moisture, whereas energy balance-focused products such as BESS and SEBS prioritize the influence of land surface temperature on evaporation (Srivastava et al., 2013; Miralles et al., 2015; Su, 2002; 2022a, 2022b ). The choice of data assimilation methods and time periods also influences the accuracy and reliability of ET a  products. Reanalysis products like ERA5 and MERRA typically include processes for assimilating observational data to enhance temporal and spatial consistency and accuracy (Fig. 3 ). However, ERA5 may exhibit larger errors compared to MERRA due to overestimation of solar radiation and complexities in vegetation canopy (Zhao et al., 2013 ). GLDAS, on the other hand, derives results by comparing and correcting model simulations with multiple observational datasets. The applicability of different ET products varies across regions and climate conditions (Miralles et al., 2016; Vinukollu et al., 2011; Crago et al., 2016 ), with some products showing superior performance in specific regions or seasons while underperforming in others (Miralles et al., 2015; Vinukollu et al., 2011 ). These differences depend on the product's development goals, availability of data sources, and the configuration of model parameters.   5 Conclusion The uncertainty and inconsistency of land evapotranspiration products must be addressed to improve the accuracy of subsequent modeling. We validated the ERA5, GLDAS, MERRA, and PML evapotranspiration products at 212 sites and 28 large river basins worldwide from 2001 to 2017 and assessed the uncertainty of evapotranspiration components used to estimate terrestrial evapotranspiration for different vegetation ecosystems. At the site scale, the ERA5 and MERRA products significantly outperform the GLDAS and PML products, with the GLDAS and PML products showing relatively poor reliability in site validation. The MERRA product demonstrates superior performance across 11 different vegetation types compared to other ET a  products. However, the evergreen broadleaf forests (EBF) exhibit poor model simulation performance and accuracy due to their complex ecosystems, abundant rainfall, and high vertical diversity of vegetation. From 2001–2017, the monthly ET a  values of the GLDAS product are significantly higher than those of the ERA5, MERRA, and PML products, indicating a certain degree of overestimation. At the watershed scale, the PML product's KGE is overall superior to those of the ERA5, GLDAS, and MERRA products. Due to the reduction of the impact of local anomalies on simulation results, watershed-scale data validation is overall superior to site-scale validation. The accuracy of evapotranspiration components used to simulate ET a  on land highly varied. There were large errors in the estimates of plant transpiration T  and soil evaporation E s  in the ERA5 product, with E s  overestimated in rainforest areas near the equator and T  underestimated in land areas. PML products emphasize the importance of water evaporation and ice sublimation (E o ). The difference in evapotranspiration components is significant among different vegetation types. The difference in evapotranspiration components has a considerable impact on the uncertainty of the final terrestrial evapotranspiration ET a , and for DBF***, EBF***, ENF***, MF***, GRA*** and CRO***, the four ET a  products display significant differences at the P<0.001 level.
