1 Introduction Understanding the global carbon balance and investigating carbon sources, sinks, reservoirs, cycling processes, and mechanisms within various ecosystems are crucial issues in global change and regional sustainable development research. This is also a core focus of several large-scale international collaborative scientific research programs. Among these, the carbon cycle in terrestrial ecosystems represents the most complex and human-influenced component of the global carbon cycle. Inland water bodies, including lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, and wetlands, play a significant role in carbon sequestration, transport, and mineralization. It is imperative to incorporate inland water bodies into the traditional carbon cycle for appropriate carbon dioxide management and climate change mitigation. Despite covering only 1 % of the Earth's surface, inland water bodies contribute significantly to the global carbon cycle compared to terrestrial and marine ecosystems, holding substantial scientific research value (Battin et al., 2009 ) Globally, rivers transport 0.3–0.6 Pg C to the oceans annually. Over 75 % of the carbon exported by rivers connected to the United States is in the form of inorganic carbon (Stets et al., 2014 ). Streams, rivers, lakes, and other inland water bodies are crucial factors in the coupled biogeochemical cycles between land, atmosphere, and oceans. The carbon emitted into the oceans through processes such as soil respiration, leaching, chemical weathering, and physical erosion represents only a small fraction of the carbon entering inland water bodies, with the majority returning to the atmosphere in the form of CO2  or being buried in reservoirs, lakes, floodplains, and other wetland sediments (Aufdenkampe et al., 2011 ). Lakes and reservoirs act as sentinels, integrators, and regulators of climate change, playing a critical role in the global carbon cycle by managing terrestrial, atmospheric, and aquatic carbon. Many lakes contain concentrations of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases higher than atmospheric balance and serve as primary conduits for the transfer of terrestrial carbon to the atmosphere (Williamson et al., 2009 ). Lakes play a significant role in the global carbon cycle and make substantial contributions to the dynamics of greenhouse gases and resulting climate change (Zwart et al., 2019 ).   Irrigation and drainage canals are hotspot areas for greenhouse gas emissions, playing a significant role in anthropogenic carbon emissions (Peacock et al., 2021 ). China boasts the world's largest irrigation and drainage network and is currently the largest consumer of chemical fertilizers (Guo et al., 2022 ). Overuse of chemical fertilizers has led to widespread pollution in drainage and irrigation canals, and the resulting carbon emissions and their biogeochemical processes remain largely understudied. A recent study conducted in the North China Plain revealed that the fluxes of CO2  and CH4  in agricultural ditches are 5 times and 12 times higher than those in rivers connected to the ditch system, respectively (Wu et al., 2023 ).  The Hetao Irrigation Area in Inner Mongolia is a large-scale irrigation zone located in the upstream of the Yellow River, classified as a world-class irrigation and drainage project with an irrigation area of approximately 733300 km2 . The Hetao Irrigation Area has established a well-coordinated seven-level irrigation and drainage system. From early May to late June, early September to mid-September, and early October to early November every year, the Sanshenggong Water Conservancy Hub introduces water from the Yellow River into the irrigation area for irrigation. The main drainage channel in the south of the Hetao Irrigation Area is the main water supply line for the irrigation area. The channel head is located on the north bank of the Sanshenggong Yellow River Water Conservancy Hub, and all branch channels draw water from the main drainage channel. There are 12 main drainage ditches in the irrigation area, of which nine ditches drain into the main drainage ditch, two ditches directly discharge into Ulansuhai Lake, and the last ditch is located downstream of the sluice gate in the south of Ulansuhai Lake (Wu, 2017 ). Simultaneously, the topography of the Hetao Irrigation Area slopes from southwest to northeast, with UlanSuhai Lake located in the lowest region of the irrigation area. Approximately 80 % of the drainage input into UlanSuhai Lake originates from the primary irrigation and drainage systems in the northern part of the area, making it a critical terrestrial water sink in the regionhan (Yue, 2021 ). The irrigation and drainage system of the Hetao Irrigation Area serves as the main link connecting the irrigation area and UlanSuhai Lake. It transports both suspended and dissolved substances, and the migration and transformation of these substances are crucial components of carbon balance, sediment balance, and nutrient balance (Wafar et al., 1989; Caddy and Bakun, 1994; Meybeck, 2003 ) DOC and DIC collectively constitute the primary carbon reservoirs in inland water bodies, interacting with atmospheric, terrestrial, and marine carbon. They engage in intense material cycling and energy exchange within terrestrial-aquatic ecosystems (Xu and Xu, 2018 ). Currently, there is limited research on the lateral outputs of carbon into inland water bodies and their metabolism and escape within aquatic continua, particularly in arid regions (Dubois et al., 2010; Bouwman et al., 2013; Iwata et al., 2013; Lottig et al., 2013; Powers et al., 2014; Yang, 2020 ). Based on VOS viewer visualization, an analysis of the major research hotspots in the Hetao Irrigation Area of Inner Mongolia and UlanSuhai Lake over the past four decades was conducted. The visualization analysis reveals that research hotspots in the Hetao Irrigation Area of Inner Mongolia and UlanSuhai Lake mainly focus on "salinization" and "eutrophication," with relatively less emphasis on carbon studies. From a spatial perspective, the Hetao Irrigation Area and UlanSuhai Lake are typically studied as independent entities, leading to a limited understanding of the continuum of agricultural drainage in the Hetao Irrigation Area to UlanSuhai Lake. In the future, the agricultural drainage-lake continuum in the Hetao Irrigation Area of Inner Mongolia is expected to be a hotspot for research in arid regions. This study focuses on the Agricultural Drainage-UlanSuhai Lake continuum in the Hetao Irrigation Area of Inner Mongolia. The research analyzes the concentration levels and distribution characteristics of DOC and DIC in different water bodies within the continuum. Utilizing stable carbon isotope techniques, the study explores the potential sources of DOC and DIC. Based on the variation characteristics of carbon dioxide partial pressure (PCO2 ) at the water-air interface, the migration and transformation processes of DOC and DIC in the continuum were clarified. The impacts of soil salinization in irrigation areas, farmland drainage, and the Yellow River irrigation water on the dissolved carbon in the continuum were revealed. This investigation not only provides data support for understanding carbon sources, sinks, and cycling in the river-lake continuum in arid regions and contributes to global carbon budgeting in arid areas but also holds significant importance for addressing issues related to watershed salinization, eutrophication, and protecting the water environment of the Yellow River.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The research was conducted in the Hetao Irrigation Area of Inner Mongolia, which falls under an arid to semi-arid climate. With an irrigation area of 8.6154 million mu (approximately 5743.6 square kilometers), it stands as the largest self-flowing Yellow River irrigation region in China. Additionally, it serves as a crucial barrier preventing the connection between the UlanBuh Desert and the Kubuqi Desert, playing a vital role in the national ecological security strategy known as the "Northern Sand Defense Belt. "The Hetao Irrigation Area is integral to maintaining regional system balance and regulating watershed carbon balance. It is a key component of the national ecological security strategy, contributing to the prevention of desertification and sandstorms. The average annual water volume entering UlanSuhai Lake through the irrigation and drainage system exceeds 5×108  m3 . After impounding in UlanSuhai Lake, the water is discharged into the Yellow River through the drainage canal (Cao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020 ). This region represents a typical cold and arid river-lake continuum ( Fig. 1 ).  2.2 Sample collection Sampling was conducted during the spring irrigation period (May) and the autumn irrigation period (October) in 2023. Instantaneous water samples were collected from the surface layer, up to 20 cm below the water surface. Sampling points were established at specific locations, including the Eighth Drainage Channel (C1)，Ninth Drainage Channel (C2)，and Tenth Drainage Channel(C3)；Main Drainage Channel (C4)，Tongji Channel (C5)，Changji Channel (C6)，Tabu Channel (C7)，and Main drainage Channel(C8). In Ulansuhai Lake, sampling points were designated in the Northeast Region(W1)，Access Lake Region(W2)，Wester Lake Region(W3)，Aquaculture Region(W4)，and Drainage Region(W5) ( Fig. 2 ). Water samples were preserved in high-density polyethylene containers. On-site, a 0.2 % saturated HgCl2  solution was added to the water samples, and the samples were sealed, refrigerated, and transported back to the laboratory. Analysis was completed within two weeks. Portable water quality analyzers (PONSEL, ODEON, France) were used for on-site measurements of water parameters such as temperature (TW ), pH, electrical conductivity (EC), salinity (SA), and dissolved oxygen (DO).  2.3 Chemical analysis 2.3.1 TN, TP and HCO3 −  concentration analysis Total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) concentrations were measured using a continuous flow analyzer ，(Alliance, Futura, France). Bicarbonate (HCO3 - ) concentration was determined using the dual indicator titration method.  2.3.2 DOC, DIC and PCO2  analysis For DOC and DIC, water samples were filtered through a 0.45μm quartz membrane (ignited at 450 ℃ for 4 hours in a muffle furnace) and stored in a refrigerator at −4 ℃. Two portions of the filtered water sample were taken: one portion was acidified with phosphoric acid to a pH of around 2, followed by ultrasonic oscillation for 5 minutes; the other portion was ultrasonicated directly for 5 minutes. DOC and DIC concentrations in the samples were determined using a total organic carbon analyzer (TOC Torch, TELEDYNE TEKMAR, USA). The analysis accuracy is less than or equal to 1.5 % RSD±15ppb. Using the equation established by Cai and Wang (1998)  based on measured pH and DIC data, the PCO2  in the irrigation and drainage system and lake water bodies was estimated：(1) P  CO 2   = CO  2      K  H     = C  T   H    2    H    2   + H    2   K  1   + K  1   K  2      K  H         where CT  is the DIC concentration, [H]=10−pH , KH  is the solubility constant, and K1  and K2  are the dissociation constants of carbonic acid (Xu and Xu, 2018 ). For DOC samples, 15 mL of water sample was placed in a 40 mL glass sample bottle (rinsed three times with ultrapure water, ignited at 450 ℃ for 6 hours in a muffle furnace to remove organic carbon). Hydrochloric acid (6 mol/L) was added, adjusting the pH to around 2, followed by ultrasonic oscillation for 15 minutes. The sample was left for 3 days to remove inorganic carbon. The δ13 CDOC  in the samples were determined using a total organic carbon analyzer-stable isotope mass spectrometry system. For DIC samples, 12 mL of water sample was placed in a headspace bottle, the bottle cap was tightened, and the headspace gas above the sample was replaced with high-purity helium using a Gasbench inflation needle. An airtight syringe was used to inject 0.1–0.2 mL of anhydrous H3 PO4  into the headspace bottle. The headspace bottle was heated at 70 ℃ in a metal bath for 1 hour to allow the carbonate to react fully with H3 PO4 . After cooling, the δ13 CDIC  were tested. (δ13 CDIC  and δ13 CDIC  are expressed relative to the international standard Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (V-PDB), δ).   2.4 Carbon isotope mixing model According to the carbon isotope mixing model(Zhou, 2020 ), the contribution ratios of different sources to dissolved carbon in the continuum were calculated as follows:(9) δ  SA   = f  A   × δ  A   + f  B   × δ  B       (10) f  A   + f  B   = 1     where f  A    andf  B    represent the respective contribution percentages of different end-elements, and δ  S A     reflects the sample's carbon isotope composition. SPSS 27 software was used for data standardization (Z-score normalization), correlation analysis, and regression analysis. Prior to correlation analysis, normality verification was conducted for the data. Geographic information data used in this study were obtained from the National Geographic Information Resource Catalog Service System (https://www.webmap.cn ) and the Geographic Spatial Data Cloud (https://www.gscloud.cn ).   3 Results 3.1 Hydrochemical changes in the agricultural drainage-lake continuum  Fig. 3  illustrates the variations in TW , pH, EC, SA, DO, HCO3 - , TN and TP concentrations in the agricultural drainage-lake continuum. The hydro-environmental characteristics of the continuum are evident. TW  ranges from 10.89℃ to 24.55℃. The pH values of the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System range from 7.51 to 8.55, while the pH values of the lake range from 8.12 to 8.94, with average values of 8.00 and 8.56 respectively, indicating an overall weakly alkaline condition. The EC of agricultural drainage ranged from 20.24μS/cm to 9920μS/cm, while that of the lake ranged from 2154μS/cm to 5274μS/cm, with average values of 3215μS/cm and 3462μS/cm, respectively. Both DOC and DIC increase simultaneously as EC increases ( Fig. 4 c). The SA of the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System ranges from 0.45 g/kg to 7.29 g/kg, while the lake's SA ranges from 1.15 g/kg to 2.68 g/kg. The average values are 2.67 g/kg and 1.82 g/kg respectively, with the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System having a higher SA than the lake. DO is an important indicator of water self-purification capacity. The DO in Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System ranged from 7.20 mg/L to 8.75 mg/L, while that in the lake ranged from 7.50 mg/L to 9.81 mg/L, with average values of 7.64 mg/L and 8.55 mg/L, respectively. DO decreased with TW  (R2 =0.36, P<0.05) and was negatively correlated with TN (R2 =0.28, P<0.05) (Figs. 4 a, 4 b). The HCO3 -  concentration ranges from 172.81 mg/L to 821.89 mg/L, with average values of 441.94 mg/L for the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System and 422.46 mg/L for the lake. The Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System has a higher HCO3 -  concentration than the lake. HCO3 -  was significantly positively correlated with SA (R2 =0.70, P<0.01) (Fig. 4 e).  3.2 Temporal and spatial variations of TN and TP TN concentrations in agricultural irrigation and drainage system range from 0.01 mg/L to 3.64 mg/L, while in lakes, it ranges from 0.01 mg/L to 0.99 mg/L, with average values of 1.65 mg/L and 0.32 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 3 ). TP concentrations in agricultural irrigation and drainage system range from 0.002 mg/L to 0.091 mg/L, while in lakes, it ranges from 0.002 mg/L to 0.020 mg/L, with average values of 0.031 mg/L and 0.010 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 3 ). The spatial variation of TN and TP concentrations is significant, with the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System having much higher concentrations than the lake. The TN and TP content in the lake gradually decreases from north to south ( Figs. 5 a, 5 b). Due to the extensive use of nitrogen and phosphorus-containing chemical fertilizers and pesticides in the irrigation area, as well as the discharge of aquaculture wastewater, the Yellow River irrigation water carries a large amount of nutrients such as N and P after passing through the irrigation area. These nutrients are then transported into the lake through the Agricultural Drainage System. Once entering Ulansuhai Lake, the content of nutrients in the lake water gradually decreases from north to south due to evaporation, consumption by primary productivity, and other factors.  3.3 The spatiotemporal variation of DOC and DIC During the spring irrigation period, the DOC concentration in the agricultural irrigation and drainage system ranged from 2.09 mg/L to 26.93 mg/L, with an average of 13.06 mg/L. The farmland drainage water had a higher DOC concentration than the Yellow River irrigation water. The concentration was the highest in tenth drainage channel and the lowest in Tabu channel. The DOC concentration in the lake ranged from 17.02 mg/L to 20.52 mg/L, with an average of 18.64 mg/L. The farmland drainage water had a higher DOC concentration than the lake and the Yellow River irrigation water. The concentration was the highest in the northeast region and the lowest in the Access Lake Region ( Fig. 6 a). DIC concentration in the Agricultural Irrigation and Drainage System ranged from 41.17 mg/L to 121.14 mg/L, with an average of 78.09 mg/L. The farmland drainage water had a higher DIC concentration than the Yellow River irrigation water. The concentration was the highest in ninth drainage channel and the lowest in Tongji channel. The DIC concentration in the lake ranged from 59.22 mg/L to 81.63 mg/L, with an average of 71.83 mg/L. The concentration was the highest in the access lake region and the lowest in the aquaculture region (Fig. 6 b). During the autumn irrigation period, the DOC concentration of the agricultural irrigation and drainage system ranged from 9.19 mg/L to 27.74 mg/L, with an average of 16.16 mg/L. The farmland drainage water exceeded the Yellow River irrigation water. The concentration of the Ninth drainage channel was the highest, while the Changji channel concentration was the lowest. The DOC concentration of the lakes ranged from 14.58 mg/L to 23.27 mg/L, with an average of 18.99 mg/L. The concentration in the access lake region was the highest, while the concentration in the drainage region was the lowest ( Fig. 7 a). The DIC concentration of the agricultural irrigation and drainage system ranged from 33.50 mg/L to 122.37 mg/L, with an average of 80.60 mg/L. The farmland drainage water exceeded the Yellow River irrigation water. The concentration of the Tenth drainage channel was the highest, while the concentration of the main channel was the lowest. The DIC concentration of the lakes ranged from 44.23 mg/L to 64.41 mg/L, with an average of 51.85 mg/L. The concentration in the drainage region was the highest, while the concentration in the northeast region was the lowest (Fig. 7 b). In the agricultural irrigation and drainage system-lake continuum, the DIC level is significantly higher than that of DOC ( Fig. 8 ). Specifically, the DOC and DIC concentration levels of Ulansuhai Lake (18.82 mg/L and 61.84 mg/L respectively) are remarkably higher than those of freshwater lakes (5.80 mg/L and 29.38 mg/L respectively) (Fig. 8 ). This river basin is located on the eastern wing of the Loess Plateau, where the loess is rich in carbonates. Being aeolian deposits, the soil is loose and the terrain is fragmented, resulting in intense mechanical erosion and chemical weathering. The Yellow River irrigation water migrates through the irrigation and drainage system in the continuum, dissolving soil CO2 , and ultimately distributing it in the water body in the form of HCO3 -  (Xu et al., 2022 ).  3.4 The spatiotemporal variation of PCO2  The range of PCO2  in the Yellow River irrigation water varied between 681.01μatm and 2365.00 μatm, while the PCO2  in farmland drainage water ranged from 659.56μatm to 2597.88 μatm. The PCO2  in the lakes ranged from 162.42μatm to 1939.79 μatm, with average values of 1248.84μatm, 1824.26μatm, and 922.78μatm respectively. The PCO2  levels followed the order of farmland drainage > Yellow River irrigation water > lakes. During the autumn irrigation period, the PCO2  levels in the Yellow River irrigation water and farmland drainage water were higher than during the spring irrigation period, and both periods were significantly higher than the average atmospheric level. In the Ulansuhai Lake area, the PCO2  level during the spring irrigation period was higher than during the autumn irrigation period, and unsaturated samples mainly occurred during the autumn irrigation period ( Fig. 9 ).  3.5 Analysis of influencing factors on DOC and DIC DOC is significantly positively correlated with SA (R2 =0.48, P<0.001) ( Fig. 10 a) and significantly positively correlated with HCO3 -  (R2 =0.30, P<0.05) (Fig. 10 b). Additionally, DOC exhibits a negative correlation with TN and TP (Fig. 4 b). Regression analysis indicates that SA, HCO3 - , TN, and TP collectively account for 86 % of the variability in DOC (R2 =0.86, P<0.05). The relationship analysis between DOC and DIC reveals a significant positive correlation (R2 =0.75, P<0.001) (Fig. 4 d), with DOC concentrations generally lower than DIC concentrations. DIC is significantly positively correlated with SA (R2 =0.60, P<0.05) (Fig. 10 c) and significantly positively correlated with HCO3 -  (R2 =0.65, P<0.05) (Fig. 10 d). Furthermore, DIC shows a negative correlation with pH and TP (Fig. 4 b). Regression analysis indicates that pH, SA, TP, and HCO3 -  are key factors controlling DIC, collectively explaining 93 % of the variability (R2 =0.93, P<0.01).  3.6 Characteristics of the continuum DOC and δ13 CDOC  The δ13 CDOC  variation range in the Yellow River irrigation water is from −28.93 ‰ to −26.12 ‰, while the δ13 CDOC  in farmland drainage water ranges from −27.66 ‰ to −26.70 ‰. In the lakes, the δ13 CDOC  variation range is from −27.68 ‰ to −25.11 ‰. The average values are −27.04 ‰, −26.88 ‰, and −26.81 ‰ respectively. The C/N ratios in the Yellow River irrigation water of the continuum range from 1.10 to 22.27, while the C/N ratios in farmland drainage water range from 5.17 to 83.62. In the lakes, the C/N ratios range from 18.32 to 192.97, with average values of 9.20, 33.41, and 88.39 respectively ( Fig. 11 ). If δ13 CDOC  is used alone for tracing, there might be overlapping issues with sources and processes (Chen et al., 2021 ). Therefore, we combined δ13 CDOC  and C/N values for a more accurate understanding of the potential sources and transformation of DOC in the agricultural drainage-lake continuum. As can be seen from  Fig. 12 , the δ13 CDOC  of farmland drainage are within the range of C3 plants (-32 ‰ to −22 ‰) and planktonic plants (-30 ‰ to −20 ‰), with a mean C/N ratio of 33.41. Taking terrestrial C3 plants as endmember A (-27.00 ‰) and planktonic plants as endmember B (-25.00 ‰). The δ13 CDOC  of the lake are between the range of farmland drainage (-27 ‰ to −26 ‰) and macrophyte (-30 ‰ to −16 ‰), with a mean C/N ratio of 88.39. Using farmland drainage as endmember A (-26.88 ‰) and macrophyte plants as endmember B (-23.00 ‰). Based on the isotopic mixing model, Eq. (9)- Eq . (10), the main sources of DOC in farmland drainage are C3 plants and planktonic plants, contributing 94.24 % and 5.76 % respectively. The main sources of DOC in the lake are farmland drainage and aquatic plants, contributing 98.19 % and 1.81 % respectively.  3.7 Characteristics of the continuum DIC and δ13 CDIC  The variation range of δ13 CDIC  in the Yellow River irrigation water is from −12.54 ‰ to −6.69 ‰, while the δ13 CDIC  in farmland drainage water ranges from −11.79 ‰ to −5.69 ‰. In the lakes, the δ13 CDIC  variation range is from −11.29 ‰ to −1.79 ‰, with average values of −10.39 ‰, −7.90 ‰, and −7.28 ‰ respectively (Fig. 11 ). The concentration of DIC does not change much, but isotopes exchange with soil or atmospheric CO2  (Zhong et al., 2024 ). The δ13 CDIC  values in farmland drainage lie within the theoretical range between the equilibrium dissolution process of carbonates with soil CO₂, ranging from −12.47 ‰ to 5.83 ‰, and the interval of irrigation water from the Yellow River, ranging from −12.54 ‰ to −6.69 ‰. The equilibrium dissolution process of carbonates with soil CO₂ is considered as endmember A (-3.33 ‰), while the irrigation water from the Yellow River serves as endmember B (-10.39 ‰). The δ13 CDIC  of the lakes are between the range of farmland drainage (-11.79 ‰ to −5.69 ‰) and atmospheric exchange (-6.82 ‰ to 1.14 ‰), with farmland drainage as endmember A (-7.90 ‰) and atmospheric exchange as endmember B (1.01 ‰) ( Fig. 13 ). Based on the isotopic mixing model, Eq. (9)- Eq . (10), the main sources of DIC in farmland drainage are soil CO2  dissolution - carbonate weathering and the Yellow River irrigation water, contributing 35.27 % and 64.73 % respectively. The main sources of DIC in the lakes are farmland drainage and atmospheric exchange, contributing 93.10 % and 6.90 % respectively.   4 Discussion 4.1 Impact of salinization in irrigation areas on dissolved carbon DOC, DIC is typically a major carbon pool in freshwater systems. DOC serves as the foundation for the heterotrophic microbial life in ecosystems and is a highly dynamic indicator in carbon cycling. It can influence the migration and transformation of elements in water through its coupling with DIC and other nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, silicon, etc.) (Chen et al., 2020 ). DO decreases with the decrease in TN(P<0.05) (Fig. 4 b), and in small and shallow rivers and lakes, higher TN, TP, and TOC contents are associated with lower O2  levels (Kortelainen et al., 2006 ). Nutrients (such as N and P) are one of the key driving factors regulating the metabolic production of CO2  and CH4  in aquatic ecosystems (Yang et al., 2024 ). DIC exhibits different relationships with TN and TP, exhibiting a negative correlation with TP while showing less significant correlation with TN (Fig. 4 b). An increase in nitrogen and phosphorus loading stimulates aquatic photosynthesis, leading to a decrease in PCO2  (Li et al., 2013 ). The introduction of exogenous salts caused by human activities in irrigated areas has a dual effect on dissolved carbon in water bodies. Saline and organic-rich farmland drainage can alleviate the growth limitations of aquatic plants (especially planktonic algae) due to N and P, resulting in a decrease in DIC concentration and PCO2  (Li, 2022 ). The pH value is closely related to the chemical forms of DIC and the distribution of δ13 C among these different forms. δ13 CDIC  corrects the influence of pH on DIC species through its unique δ13 C value. At the same time, changes in the chemical composition of DIC can lead to a positive correlation between pH and δ13 CDIC . As the main carbon source, CO2  is fixed during primary production, resulting in a synchronous increase in pH and δ13 CDIC . (Gu et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2021 ). In river and lake systems, DIC is the sum of HCO3 - , H2 CO3 , CO3 ²⁻, and CO2aq , and the balance between these components depends on temperature and pH value. In this study, the pH values within the watershed ranged from 7.51 to 8.94, and HCO3 -  was the dominant reservoir of DIC, considered to be equivalent to alkalinity (accounting for more than 99 % of the total alkalinity). The distillation factor of CO2 (g)-HCO3 - (aq) decreases with the increase of temperature, and dissolved CO2  escapes from the water surface in the form of bubbles when the water temperature is higher (Zhong et al., 2023 ). In mildly alkaline water bodies with higher pH values, more carbonate dissolves, and as the concentration of alkaline ion HCO3 -  increases, the equilibrium of carbonate ionization shifts to the left, resulting in an increase in CO2  concentration and subsequently an increase in PCO2 . Additionally, higher salinity can promote carbon exchange with the atmosphere (Lu et al., 2022 ). Lakes located in agricultural catchments with high nutrient salts emit more CO2  than oligotrophic lakes (Liao et al., 2024 ). The Hetao irrigation area suffers from severe salinization, annually introducing an average of 5 billion m3  of water from the Yellow River and discharging approximately 2.26 million tons of salt annually, while discharging about 1.2 million tons of salt into the Ulansuhai Lake, resulting in a salt accumulation trend throughout the irrigation area (Lü and Pei., 2014 ). If using EC > 1000 μs/cm as a criterion to assess the degree of salinization of different water bodies in the continuum, it can be determined that the water bodies in this continuum belong to brackish water. On one hand, with the increase of exogenous salts and organic matter, biological metabolism and organic matter degradation are promoted, increasing the demand for CO2  in the water, leading to an increase in pH, which promotes the carbonate precipitation process and DIC evaporation process in the water, potentially resulting in the escape of CO2  (Ye et al., 2015 ). Existing studies have shown that the hydrochemical types of the Yellow River - Hetao irrigation area - Ulansuhai Lake continuous system are represented by SO4 2- •Cl-  - Ca2+ •Mg2+ , HCO3 -  • Ca2+  • Mg2+  and Cl- -Na+  types (Yue, 2021 ). Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, and HCO3 ⁻ can generate CO2  and promote its emission. On the other hand, the irrigation water diverted from the Yellow River and the drainage water from farmland contain a large amount of organic matter. The increase in these organic matters directly provides a carbon source for water bodies through mineralization or decomposition processes, thereby promoting CO2  emission. In Taihu Lake, a eutrophic lake in eastern China, the peak PCO2  values appear in eutrophic zones and show strong sensitivity to anthropogenic nutrient inputs (Xiao et al., 2020 ). DIC is closely related to PCO2 , and PCO2  can affect the diffusion direction of CO2  at the water-air interface. In this watershed, 85 % of the PCO2  values are higher than the atmospheric PCO2  values, and unsaturated values mainly occur in the lake water during the autumn irrigation period (Fig. 9 ). During the process of CO2  release from water to the atmosphere, isotopic fractionation occurs, resulting in the enrichment of 13 C in residual DIC, leading to a positive shift in δ13 CDIC  (Zhong et al., 2023 ). DOC and DIC have a significant positive correlation with SA (Figs. 4 c, 10 a, 10 c), indicating that soil salinization in the irrigation area and industrial and agricultural activities affect the concentration levels of dissolved carbon through the irrigation and drainage system. The higher the DIC content, the more OC is produced by the water system. While DIC is converted into OC, "old" OC is released, and photosynthesis using DIC as a carbon source produces more "new" OC (Fukushima et al., 1996 ). Furthermore, biological metabolites can also lead to an increase in DOC content (Wetzel, 1992; Kortelainen et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2020 ). Abiotic degradation of organic matter allows DIC and DOC in the sediment to diffuse into the overlying water (Sobek et al., 2005 ) through analyzing a global-scale database of 4902 lakes, they found that temperature can only affect a small portion of the variation in lake PCO2 , while DOC concentration is an important regulator of CO2  partial pressure in lakes worldwide. Soil salinization and agricultural activities in the irrigation area increase the input of exogenous salts, leading to an elevation in DOC and DIC content with increasing salt concentration. Both concentrations increase simultaneously.  4.2 Analysis of dissolved carbon sources Due to isotope fractionation during various natural or anthropogenic processes, carbon isotopes distribute in different proportions among various substances. The distinct isotopic characteristics of different material sources, resulting from varying fractionation coefficients among different sources in ecosystems, are exploited for source tracing studies (Cao et al., 2018 ). δ13 C between different basins may be related to basin lithology, land use, vegetation types, and anthropogenic factors, leading to differences in carbon sources (Cao et al., 2018 ). The Hetao irrigation area has now formed a seven-level irrigation and drainage engineering system with complete irrigation and drainage facilities. From early May to late June, early September to mid-September, and early October to early November each year, the Yellow River water is introduced into the irrigation area through the irrigation and drainage system for irrigation. Therefore, during typical periods (spring and autumn irrigation periods), we use stable carbon isotope technology to analyze the sources of DOC and DIC in farmland drainage and Ulansuhai Lake in the watershed. Organic carbon (OC) can be categorized into three sources: in-situ production from planktonic algae, allochthonous sources from terrestrial organic matter, and anthropogenic sources from agricultural and industrial activities (Chen et al., 2021 ). The δ13 CDOC  and C/N ratios in the continuum resemble those of drainage water and terrestrial C3 plants. The dominant crops in the region include corn, wheat, soybeans, potatoes, and sunflowers (Bao et al., 2023 ). This indicates that the types of crops (C3 C4 plants) in the basin and agricultural drainage significantly impact the sources of dissolved carbon, with the Yellow River supplying water likely being an important source of C3 plant particles. Terrestrial organic matter is rich in fiber but has a low protein content, with C/N ratios ranging from 12 to 400. In contrast, algae and planktonic organisms, with higher protein and lower fiber content, have C/N ratios below 10, showing little variation. C/N ratios equal to or greater than 10 suggest exogenous sources dominate, while ratios below 10 suggest endogenous sources prevail (Zhao et al., 2022 ). The C/N ratios in the agricultural drainage are generally below 12, while those in the lake range between 12 and 400 (Fig. 11 ), reflecting a mixture of endogenous and exogenous sources for DOC. Sources of inorganic carbon (IC) mainly include surface runoff, water-air exchange, mineralization and decomposition of soil organic matter, and decomposition of sedimentary carbonates (Campeau et al., 2017 ). The PCO2  in farmland drainage is far higher than that in the atmosphere (Fig. 9 ), and the dissolved CO2  in the water body is in a state of effusion. Therefore, the contribution of water-air exchange to the DIC in farmland drainage can be ignored. In Ulansuhai Lake, the PCO2  is 80 % higher than the atmospheric level, and unsaturated PCO2  mainly appears in the northern part of the lake during the autumn irrigation period (Fig. 9 ). During the water-air exchange process, when atmospheric CO2  establishes equilibrium with DIC in water, the carbon isotope fractionation between atmospheric CO2  and different forms of DIC is a function of temperature (Zhang et al., 1995; Lei et al., 2012 ). The isotopic value of atmospheric CO2  is −8.1 ‰, and the water temperature of Ulansuhai Lake during the autumn irrigation period ranges from 10.89℃ to 12.41℃. Based on Eq. (11)- Eq . (13), the carbon isotope fractionation coefficients between H2 CO3 , HCO3 - ), CO3 2-  and atmospheric CO2  can be calculated to be between −1.37 ‰ to −1.36 ‰, 9.03 ‰ to 9.24 ‰, and 6.57 ‰ to 6.65 ‰, respectively. The value of δ13 CDIC  in water bodies under equilibrium conditions depends on the proportion of different forms of DIC. The pH of Ulansuhai Lake ranges from 8.12 to 8.94, and DIC is primarily composed of HCO3 - . Therefore, under water-air equilibrium conditions, the δ13 CDIC  value of Ulansuhai Lake is approximately 1.08 ‰.(11) ε  aq − g   = − 0.0049 ± 0.003    × T ℃    − 1.31 ± 0.06        (12) ε  H CO  3  −   − g   = − 0.141 ± 0.003    × T ℃    + 10.78 ± 0.05        (13) ε  CO  3  2 −   − g   = − 0.052 ± 0.03    × T ℃    + 7.22 ± 0.46         Fractionation occurs when soil CO2  dissolves into water, and this fractionation is influenced by pH and temperature. When the pH value is below 6, the main form of DIC is dissolved free CO2 . When the pH value reaches 7, HCO3 -  dominates. The extreme degree of carbon isotope enrichment between soil DIC and soil CO2  is approximately: −1 ‰ in water where CO2  dominates, and +10 ‰ in water where HCO3 -  dominates (Wachniew, 2006 ). The δ13 C value of residual CO2  from soil organic matter degradation in this watershed ranges from −11.469 ‰ to −4.187 ‰ (Wang, 2020 ). Therefore, the potential range of δ13 CDIC  in equilibrium with soil CO2  is from −12.469 ‰ to 5.813 ‰. In an open system, the isotopic composition of DIC during the equilibrium dissolution process between carbonates and soil CO₂ is controlled by the δ13 C of soil CO₂. In a closed system, however, the HCO₃⁻ produced by the dissolution of carbonate rocks by H₂CO₃ originates from two sources: half from the carbonate rocks and the other half from soil CO₂. Since the δ13 C value of the carbonate rocks is approximately 0 ‰, the range of δ13 CDIC  falls between −6.23 ‰ and 2.91 ‰. The HCO3 -  produced by the weathering of silicate rocks dissolved by H2 CO3  all comes from soil CO2 , and thus the δ13 CDIC  value ranges approximately between −12.469 ‰ and 5.813 ‰. HCO3 -  generated by the participation of exogenous acids (such as sulfuric acid and nitric acid) in rock weathering all comes from carbonate minerals, with a δ13 CDIC  value of approximately 0 ‰ (Li et al., 2020 ). Photosynthesis controls the fractionation of isotopes to a certain extent. During the photosynthetic process, "12 C" is preferentially utilized, resulting in the formation of a DIC pool rich in 13 C, which leads to a positive δ13 CDIC  in that region (Li et al., et al. 2020 ; Zhong et al., 2021 ). In addition, intense CO2  degassing can lead to higher δ13 CDIC  values (Zhong et al., 2023 ).  4.3 Carbon migration in the agricultural drainage-lake continuum Presently, numerous studies have utilized in-situ observations, laboratory analyses, carbon isotope tracing, and remote sensing (Cai et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2015; Ran et al., 2015 ) to conduct extensive research in regions such as the Yangtze River basin (Bao et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015 ), the Pearl River basin (Wei et al., 2003 ), and the Yellow River basin (Yao et al., 2015 ). These studies have analyzed the laws and spatiotemporal variations of carbon transport within waterborne continuous systems from a basin-wide perspective (Battle et al., 2000; McKee et al., 2004; Galy et al., 2007; Regnier et al., 2013 ). The Drainage-UlanSuhai Lake continuum in the Inner Mongolia Hetao Irrigation Area connects rivers and lakes, facilitating continuous material exchange between water and sediment interfaces. This continuum serves as a vital regional "source-sink" transformation site for carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other biogenic materials. Describing the carbon cycle in this continuum using the traditional "river conduit model" would overlook anthropogenic factors and the continuum's role. The irrigation and drainage systems in the area are rich in organic matter, resulting in an active carbon cycle. Carbon processes are interconnected through thin layers in the drainage-lake continuum. Carbon originates from the loess on the Loess Plateau, converges in the irrigation and drainage systems through the Irrigation water diverted from the Yellow Rive diversion, and migrates through the continuum to UlanSuhai Lake. Some carbon is buried in the irrigation channels, some undergoes vertical exchange with the atmosphere, and some enters UlanSuhai Lake, continually fixed and released in various forms within the lake. The remaining carbon returns to the Yellow River through drainage channels and completes the cycle. The carbon migration in the Drainage-UlanSuhai Lake continuum in the Inner Mongolia Hetao Irrigation Area comprises two short-distance carbon cycles (carbon from Irrigation water diverted from the Yellow Rive diversion to the irrigation and drainage systems and carbon from the irrigation and drainage systems to UlanSuhai Lake) forming a long-distance carbon cycle (carbon starting from the Loess Plateau, passing through the irrigation and drainage systems to UlanSuhai Lake, and ultimately returning to the Yellow River) ( Fig. 14 ).   5 Conclusion In typical periods, the concentration of DOC in the irrigation and drainage system-Ulansuhai Lake continuum is lower than DIC, and the concentrations of both increase simultaneously with the increase in salinity. The DOC reservoir is mainly controlled by terrestrial C3 plants and hydrological connectivity induced by farmland drainage, and the irrigation water from the Yellow River may also be an important source of C3 plant particles. For the DIC reservoir, the equilibrium dissolution process between carbonates and soil CO₂ is the essential process that affects the DIC concentration level and source in the drainage water, while metabolism and water-air interface carbon exchange jointly control the dynamics of DIC in the lake. Soil salinization and crop types in the irrigation area have significant impacts on the dissolved carbon reservoir. The irrigation and drainage system-Ulansuhai continuum is not a neutral "passive pipeline" but rather an "active site" for carbon migration and transformation. It serves as an active reactor, transporting and transforming both natural and anthropogenic carbon. If we attempt to describe the carbon cycle of this continuum using the traditional "river pipeline model," we would overlook the impact of human factors and the role of the continuum itself. Moreover, due to the limitations of local agricultural irrigation measures, our reliance on stable carbon isotope values during typical irrigation periods to determine carbon sources may overlook the influence of agricultural activities and seasonal changes on carbon sources. Agricultural irrigation and drainage channels are hotspot areas for greenhouse gas emissions, and their carbon escape and biogeochemical processes have largely remained insufficiently studied. It is necessary to quantify these carbon fluxes and consider them in the global carbon budget. Therefore, there is a need to better understand the potential mechanisms of dissolved CO2  and CH4  concentrations and their emissions within the continuum, further clarifying the link between aquatic carbon emissions and terrestrial metabolic processes. Besides considering eutrophication, biomass changes, and basic physicochemical factors, it is also essential to pay attention to the impacts of salinity, land use, and watershed hydrology on the carbon cycle in this watershed. Moreover, the fundamental key to maintaining the healthy development of aquatic ecosystems in Ulansuhai and the Yellow River Basin lies in the management of soil salinization in the irrigated areas.
1 Introduction Water resources are of utmost importance to food security and livelihoods in Afghanistan. Given the substantial variations in Afghanistan’s climate and landscape, the distribution of water availability is uneven throughout the country. Consequently, Afghanistan frequently encounters challenges coming from both ends of the spectrum: water scarcity, leading to drought conditions, and water excess, resulting in floods (Akhtar and Shah, 2020; Beekma and Fiddes, 2011; Habib, 2014; Qutbudin et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, Afghanistan is anticipated to face significant repercussions from climate change, with a global ranking as the 4th most vulnerable country to the impacts of climate change (European Commission. Joint Research Centre, 2023 ). More than ninety percent of the water resources in Afghanistan are allocated for agricultural purposes, a sector that not only contributes 33 % to the country’s gross domestic product but also employs 46 % of the national labor force. While the agriculture sector serves as the backbone of the country, it faces severe challenges in terms of water availability, largely driven by the impacts of climate change (Akhtar et al., 2022a ). The projected shift in weather patterns, from typical snowfall in November–February to rainfall in the summer monsoon season (Akhtar et al., 2022a ), can cause more occurrences of flash floods and less water availability during the early growing season. This shift could have detrimental effects on the agricultural sector. Additionally, Afghanistan heavily depends on snowmelt from the Hindu Kush mountains for around 80 % of its water supply. Climate change-induced alterations in the precipitation and temperature patterns significantly affect the snowmelt dynamics, and eventually exacerbate water scarcity and food insecurity in the region (Aawar and Khare, 2020; Azizi and Asaoka, 2020; Jawid and Khadjavi, 2019 ). Apart from being among the most vulnerable countries to climate change, water resource management and hydrological research in Afghanistan also face several pressing challenges. Firstly, the scarcity of environmental and use observations and inconsistency (i.e., ground measurements are not easily accessible) in Afghanistan makes it difficult to evaluate remote sensing applications and validate hydrological modeling in the region (Akbari and Torabi Haghighi, 2022; Dost et al., 2023 ). Secondly, ineffective and/or lack of a proper groundwater management framework has led to groundwater overexploitation in the region (Hayat and Baba, 2017 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Noori and Singh, 2021 ; Zaryab et al., 2023 ). Both of these issues are further worsened by the regional political turmoil and the institutional incapacity under the current regime (Přívara and Přívarová, 2019; Price, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2023 ). Additionally, due to the transboundary nature of the region, water challenges in Afghanistan extend beyond its 40 million residents and are poised to exacerbate existing water conflicts among Central Asian countries (Aryal et al., 2023; Tran et al., 2023b; Do et al., 2024; Atef et al., 2019; Price, 2019; Weinthal et al., 2014 ). Hence, it is critical to comprehend and monitor the dynamics of land water storage and availability for effective regional food security and water resource management. Terrestrial water storage (TWS) refers to the total amount of water present within the Earth’s landmass. This includes water stored in the soil, groundwater, snowpack, and glaciers, and surface water bodies (e.g., lakes, rivers, and reservoirs). Due to the high spatiotemporal variations of water storage, it is difficult to measure and analyze regional water storage using point-scale measurements (Frappart et al., 2013; Swenson et al., 2006 ). Additionally, the lack of long-term in-situ data and the associated operational costs pose challenges in assessing the comprehensive variations in water availability (Tapas et al., 2024, Nguyen et al., 2024 ), particularly in developing or geopolitically ungauged basins (Du et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023, 2024 ). Therefore, TWS change has been obtained through the space-borne observations of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE). The GRACE mission, launched in March 2002, involved a set of twin satellites, GRACE-1 and GRACE-2, which worked in tandem to measure variations in Earth’s gravity field that can infer the changes in terrestrial water storage (Tapley et al., 2004; Wahr et al., 2004 ). TWS observations from the GRACE mission (2002–2017) and its successor — GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) (2018–present) have been used in various hydrological problems, including drought (Nie et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2017 ), flood (Long et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2021 ), and groundwater monitoring (Chen et al., 2016; Frappart and Ramillien, 2018 ). Two common data forms of GRACE products are the spherical harmonic coefficients (SHC) and the mass concentration blocks (mascons) solutions. SHC data are processed by applying global spherical harmonics basis functions (Wahr, 1981; Wouters and Schrama, 2007 ). On the other hand, the mascon product parameterizes the observed gravity field into blocks of small, pre-defined regional mass concentrations (Watkins et al., 2015 ). Between the two approaches, mascon products are preferred for regional studies as they have a better representation of small-scale mass changes (Luthcke et al., 2013; Save et al., 2016 ). GRACE mascon products are available at three different centers: the University of Texas at Austin Center for Space Research (CSR), NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). TWS changes from GRACE are also used for data assimilation into land surface models (LSMs) to address the limitations of both the satellite-based and modeling approaches. For GRACE-based TWS, the main limitations lie in the coarse spatial resolution (approximately 150,000 km2  at mid-altitude), low temporal sampling (monthly), and inability to separate the vertical water storage components (Andrew et al., 2017 ). On the other hand, land surface modeling can produce individual water components with high spatiotemporal resolution depending on forcing input (Lawrence and Chase, 2007; Rodell et al., 2004 ). However, LSM by itself primarily focuses on simulating natural processes related to land-atmosphere interactions (i.e., climate-driven water storage change). Human-driven water storage changes (e.g., reservoir operation, and groundwater pumping) are often influenced by complex human activities and engineering interventions that may not be adequately represented in traditional land surface models (Fisher and Koven, 2020; Gädeke et al., 2020 ). Therefore, it is common practice to assimilate GRACE data into LSMs to improve the monitoring of how climate and anthropogenic changes affect global and regional TWS and its vertical components (Fisher and Koven, 2020; Girotto et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2012 ; Nie et al., 2019 ; Pokhrel et al., 2016 ). The latest version of the well-known Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS-2.2) from NASA Land Information System (LIS), which allows large-scale data assimilation of various remote sensing data into LSMs, has assimilated GRACE satellite observations to improve its simulation of terrestrial water storage and groundwater estimation (Rodell et al., 2004 ). For Afghanistan and Central Asia in particular, another instance of the NASA LIS platform named Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System – Central Asia (FLDAS-CA) was created to address the specific issues in the region (McNally et al., 2022 ). Since groundwater depletion has been a major concern for the region due to the heavy reliance on groundwater extraction for agricultural purposes (Akhtar et al., 2022b; Hayat and Baba, 2017; Mack et al., 2013 ), assimilation of GRACE TWS observation into FLDAS-CA can further improve groundwater monitoring and water resource management in Afghanistan and Central Asia. Three GRACE mascon solutions from three different processing centers have different processing variants, constraints, and block sizes. Several studies have evaluated the global variations and differences in long-term trends among the mascon products (Leńczuk et al., 2020; Scanlon et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, while there were studies on the spatiotemporal variations of GRACE SHC products during its first mission (Salehie et al., 2022; Sediqi et al., 2019 ) in Afghanistan, there are limited evaluations of the GRACE mascon products for both GRACE and GRACE-FO periods in the country and Central Asia in general. Additionally, since FLDAS-CA is generally new, a thorough search of the relevant literature shows no study that compares GRACE observations and FLDAS-CA TWS simulations. In this study, we evaluate the variations in TWS anomalies and their long-term trends in Afghanistan using three GRACE mascons products and FLDAS-CA for both the GRACE (2003–2016) and GRACE-FO period (2018–2022). Additionally, groundwater storage change is also estimated using TWSA from both GRACE observation and FLDAS-CA simulations to evaluate the status of groundwater in Afghanistan. We aim to address three specific research questions: (1) How has terrestrial water storage changed from 2003 to 2022 in Afghanistan and its five major river basins? (2) What are the differences in TWSA long-term trends among three GRACE mascon products and between GRACE observations and FLDAS-CA simulations? and (3) How has human-induced groundwater storage changed during the study period? The findings of this study can provide valuable insights for policymakers and local governments regarding the status of water availability in Afghanistan. Additionally, we want to highlight the importance of GRACE assimilation into land surface modeling by highlighting the difference between TWS observation and simulation.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Afghanistan, located in southern-central Asia, is a landlocked mountainous country. Approximately 75 % of the country is dominated by towering mountains, creating a complex and undulating terrain that defines its hydro-climatological character. Afghanistan’s diverse topography, ranging from lowlands to high mountain peaks, contributes to different climate patterns across the country (Sediqi et al., 2019 ). The climate regime varies with continental climate in the central and northeastern regions, arid climate in the southern and southwestern area, semi-arid climate in the northern plains and central highlands, and distinct mountain climate in the Hindu Kush and Pamir ranges (Shokory et al., 2023 ). Approximately 75 % of the mean annual precipitation occurs between November and April ( Fig. 1 c), with a predominant amount in the form of snow in the Hindu Kush and Pamir mountain ranges (Oki and Kanae, 2006 ). As one moves towards the arid and dry western and southwestern regions, there is a noticeable decrease in precipitation ( Fig. 2 a). Similarly, temperature follows the same pattern with lower temperatures in the northeastern highlands and warmer temperatures in the south and southwestern regions (Fig. 2 b). Water flows divide Afghanistan into five river basins including Amu Darya, Northern, Kabul (Indus), Harirod-Murghab, and Helmand River basins (Fig. 2 c). The largest river basin in Afghanistan is the Helmand River basin (approximately 262,341 km2 ). While it only holds approximately 11 % of Afghanistan’s water storage capacity, nearly one-third of the Afghan population and agricultural land is located in the Helmand River basin (Nazari et al., 2023 ). The second-largest river basin — Amu Darya (approximately 90,692 km2 ), which is part of the longest international river in Central Asia, mostly consists of mountainous areas with snow cover and glacier-fed rivers. As 80 % of Afghanistan’s water resources originate from snow and glacier melt from the Hindu Kush mountains, the Amu Darya basins play an important role in capturing a substantial portion of the country’s water availability (Salehie et al., 2022 ). The third-largest river basin is the Harirod-Murghab river basin (approximately 77,604 km2 ). Since most of the water resources of the Harirod-Murghab river basin originate in Afghanistan and are predominantly used downstream in other countries (i.e., Turkmenistan and Iran), water conflict is a critical problem due to the uneven distribution of water resources in the region (Nagheeby and Warner, 2018 ). Another important river basin is the Kabul River basin (approximately 76,908 km2 ) which includes the capital city Kabul and its surrounding urban area and holds around two-thirds of the forest area in Afghanistan (Nabizada et al., 2023 ). Lastly, the smallest river basin — Northern river basin (approximately 70,901 km2 ) covers up to 40 % of the rain-fed agricultural area in Afghanistan.  2.2 Data 2.2.1 GRACE and GRACE-FO data Terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) were obtained from GRACE and GRACE-FO observations. TWSA indicates the change to total water storage in response to any imbalance between the main water flux. TWS can be expressed as the summation of all potential water reservoir components:(1) TWS = GWS + SWS + SMS + SWE + CWS       where GWS is groundwater storage, SWS is surface water storage, SMS is soil moisture storage, SWE is snow water equivalent, and CWS is canopy water storage. We used three GRACE and GRACE-FO Mascon solutions from three different processing centers: the University of Texas at Austin Center for Space Research (CSR) (Save et al., 2016 ), NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) (NASA/JPL, 2019 ), and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) (Loomis et al., 2019 ). The three solutions provide monthly time series of global mass anomaly grids computed from GRACE (from April 2002 to June 2017) and GRACE-FO (from June 2018 to present). The three mascon solutions (RL06 v02) were downloaded from https://www2.csr.utexas.edu/grace/  (CSR), https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/data/get-data/jpl_global_mascon/  (JPL), and https://earth.gsfc.nasa.gov/geo/data/grace-mascon  (GSFC). The water storage anomalies from the three products are given in equivalent water thickness units (cm). JPL and GSFC mascon products were gridded at 0.5° (approximately 55 km) and CSR mascons were provided at 0.25° (approximately 27 km) resolution. The three mascon products also have fundamental processing differences, with the two most important distinctions being the shape of the grid cells and the constraint approach. The size and shape of the grid cell have major implications on the parameterization of the gravity field into each mass concentration block. CSR mascon parameterizes the gravity field into a geodesic equal area grid with hexagonal tiles of approximately 120 km at the equator (Save et al., 2016 ). Similarly, GSFC mascon defines the mascon grid as an approximately 110 km square cell with an equal area (Loomis et al., 2019 ). On the other hand, the JPL mascon uses a 3° × 3° (approximately 330 km at the equator) spherical cap cell, resulting in only 10 % of the number of grid cells used by CSR and GSFC (Watkins et al., 2015 ). Among the three mascon solutions, the JPL mascon product retains the approximate native resolution of GRACE (approximately 300 km), while CSR and GSFC mascons oversample the gravity field observations to increase spatial resolution at higher latitudes where more ground tracks exist (Scanlon et al., 2016 ). Each processing center applies distinct constraints to mitigate noise: CSR relies solely on GRACE data, JPL mascons utilize both GRACE observations and a terrestrial/ocean hydrological model, while GSFC employs an adaptive decomposition filter with anisotropic constraints (Leńczuk et al., 2020 ).  2.2.2 Land Data Assimilation System (LDAS) data Terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) from the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System – Central Asia (FLDAS-CA) (McNally et al., 2022 ) were also acquired for comparison with observations from GRACE. FLDAS-CA model provides near real-time daily output at 0.01° spatial resolution over the Central Asia region. The model is developed using the NASA Land Information System (LIS) (https://lis.gsfc.nasa.gov/ ) which leverages the well-established physics of land surface modeling with data assimilation techniques to simulate land surface conditions and fluxes by incorporating both satellite and ground-based observations (Kumar et al., 2008; Mohr et al., 2013 ). While the FLDAS global data stream, FLDAS-CA, and the well-known GLDAS are all instances of LIS, they have several variations (e.g., meteorological inputs, spatial resolution, and data latency) and serve different purposes. More information about forcing input and ancillary data used in FLDAS-CA can be found in McNally et al. (2022) . We chose the latest FLDAS2 Central Asia simulation (FLDAS_NOAHMP001_G_CA_D) (Slinski and Sarmiento, 2023 ). Compared to the previous version, FLDAS2 uses the upgraded Noah-MP 4.0.1 land surface model (LSM) (Niu et al., 2011 ) and includes terrestrial water storage (TWS) as one of the outputs. The aggregated TWS from Noah-MP is calculated as the summation of(2) TWS Noah − MP   = SMS + SWE + CWS + GWS       where SMS is the soil moisture storage (sum of soil moisture in all layers), SWE is the snow water equivalent, CWS is the plant canopy surface water, and GWS is the groundwater storage. GWS in NOAH-MP model represents the unconfined aquifer water storage depending on Darcy’s law recharge rate and discharge rate as a function of water table depth (Chang et al., 2020 ). Additionally, to highlight the importance of data assimilation of GRACE, we also obtained TWS from the Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2.2 (GLDAS-2.2) (Li et al., 2020 ). The model uses Catchment Land Surface Model F2.5 (Koster et al., 2000 ) with Data Assimilation for the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE-DA) from February 2003 to present. Compared to FLDAS-CA, GLDAS-2.2 simulations are much coarser (0.25°); therefore, our comparison only considered the TWSA average over Afghanistan to minimize the impact of resolution mismatch among GRACE observations, FLDAS-CA, and GLDAS-2.2. Similar to previous studies (Syed et al., 2008; Yang and Chen, 2015 ), we assume that the average estimate of TWS around the 15th day can represent the monthly water storage. As TWS from FLDAS-CA and GLDAS-2.2 is provided at a daily timestep, monthly TWS was estimated as the average of TWS from five days before to five days after the 15th day of each month. In addition, following GRACE products’ procedure, the monthly TWSA from FLDAS-CA was calculated by subtracting the average TWS between the 2004 and 2009 period from the monthly TWS. Monthly TWSA from two LDAS models were resampled to the same 0.5° spatial resolution of GRACE mascon products for consistent comparison between the two approaches. Additionally, we used monthly hydrological flux anomalies from the FLDAS global run for lag time correlation analysis with monthly TWSA from GRACE mascon products and FLDAS-CA. Since the FLDAS global anomaly data stream (FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_MA) provides readily monthly hydrological flux anomalies and to save computational power and data volume, we obtained the coarser total precipitation, runoff, soil moisture, evapotranspiration anomalies from FLDAS global dataset (NASA GSFC Hydrological Sciences Laboratory (HSL), 2018 ) instead of from FLDAS-CA data stream. While it is noted that the global FLDAS and the regional FLDAS-CA data stream have different configurations and uncertainties (e.g., meteorological forcing, models, spatial resolution), these differences should be minimal for this analysis. For instance, precipitation, which is a critical input to LSM, are different between the global data stream (i.e., 10 km Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS) (Funk et al., 2015 )) and Central Asia data stream (i.e., 1 km Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) precipitation (Derber et al., 1991 )). However, the monthly spatial average Spearmen rank correlation between two precipitation inputs over Central Asia are 0.92 (McNally et al., 2022 ), indicating that outputs from two data stream are well correlated. Additionally, since the hydrological anomalies are averaged over the entire country or major river basin and compared on a monthly scale, monthly anomalies from two data streams should have minimal impacts on this analysis and either the global FLDAS or FLDAS-CA could be used as a representation of LSM.  Table 1  summarizes the flux anomalies used in this study. Because the FLDAS anomaly global data stream only contains rainfall flux, we derived total precipitation anomalies from rainfall and snowfall flux from the FLDAS global data stream as snowfall is critical for Afghanistan (McNally et al., 2017 ). Additionally, soil moisture flux anomaly was calculated as the sum of all four soil moisture layers in FLDAS. To quantify the correlation and evaluate the possible lag time, we calculated the lagged correlation coefficient between monthly TWSA and monthly precipitation (P), runoff (Q), soil moisture (SM), and evapotranspiration (ET) anomalies that were obtained from the FLDAS global data stream. From a lag time of 5 months backward to 5 months forward, the lag month with the highest correlation coefficient is chosen as the lag between TWSA and hydrological fluxes.    3 Methods 3.1 Time series decomposition and trend estimation To better understand the long-term TWSA trend and its variations from GRACE and LSM in Afghanistan, we applied time series decomposition to all monthly TWSA data from three GRACE products from FLDAS-CA. We used the Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL), which decomposes a time series (Stotal ) into its fundamental components—Seasonal (SSeasonal ), Trend or Long-term (STrend ), and Residual (SRes ) (Cleveland et al., 1990 ):(3) S total  = S Trend  + S Seasonal  + S Res  .        The STL algorithm has two loops. The inner loop is responsible for iteratively smoothing the time series to extract the seasonal and trend components and the outer loop is responsible for minimizing the effects of outliers and anomalies in the time series. Both loops use Locally Weighted Scatterplot Smoothing (LOESS) for smoothing and the weights of LOESS are updated iteratively until a stable estimate of the seasonal and trend components is achieved. The method, with its robustness and flexibility, was used in numerous economic and environmental analyses in general (Aslam et al., 2020; Dufresne et al., 2013; Verbesselt et al., 2010 ). It is also common practice for TWS studies in particular to apply STL to de-seasonalize GRACE time series and isolate the long-term trend variations that give insights on water storage compartments such as groundwater, soil moisture, or snow mass (Frappart et al., 2013; Humphrey et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Scanlon et al., 2019 ). We then applied the Mann-Kendall (M-K) test (Mann, 1945 ) and Theil–Sen’s Slope estimation (Sen, 1968 ) on the Long-term component (STrend ) of each TWSA time series to quantify the variations between GRACE products and FLDAS-CA. Since there is a substantial gap between GRACE missions, the data from two study periods GRACE (2003–2016) and GRACE-FO (2019–2022) was separated before going through the time series and trend analysis process. Besides the gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO missions, missing values in the GRACE TWSA data were filled by interpolation.  3.2 Human- Induced groundwater storage estimation Compared to components in TWS from GRACE observations, Noah-MP LSM does not consider surface water storage (SWS) (Eq. (2) ) and has limited capacity in modeling the impacts of anthropogenic processes (e.g., irrigation, crop management, groundwater pumping) on groundwater storage (GWS) (He et al., 2023 ). Therefore, groundwater storage change (i.e., groundwater recharge and extraction) are often estimated using GRACE TWSA observations and water components from LSM (Chen et al., 2019 ; B. Liu et al., 2021 ; Nazari et al., 2023 ; Tangdamrongsub et al., 2018 ). Since SWS change is negligible compared to groundwater storage change for a dry and semi-arid environment like Afghanistan (Akhtar et al., 2022b ), we assumed that climate induced GWS changes (i.e., from rainfall and recharge) are represented similarly in GWS component from GRACE and Noah-MP; hence, anthropogenic changes to GWS (i.e., groundwater pumping) can be estimated as the differences between TWS from two approaches. Hence, we estimated the human-induced (i.e., groundwater pumping and extraction) GWS change GWSC  H − I     as:(4) GWSC H − I   = TWSA GRACE  ¯  − TWSA FLDAS − CA         where TWSA  FLDAS − CA     is TWSA from FLDAS-CA and TWSA  GRACE    ̅    is the TWSA ensemble average from three GRACE Mascon products. We assumed the TWSA differences between LSM and GRACE are entirely attributed to changes in groundwater storage and surface water storage changes are negligible. This assumption can be applied to Afghanistan since water usage in the region heavily relies on groundwater extraction. This assumption, however, would not hold for regions with substantial dams and reservoirs in operation and significant changes in lakes and rivers’ water storage (Yao et al., 2019 ). Additionally, the inherent difference in range and spatial resolution between GRACE observation and FLDAS-CA modeling is also another substantial uncertainty for this estimation.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 GRACE TWSA temporal variability in Afghanistan  Fig. 3  shows the comparison of the terrestrial water storage anomalies in Afghanistan from the three GRACE mascon solutions. We divided our study period into two periods GRACE (2003–2016) and GRACE-FO (2019–2022) based on the instrument’s operational period. Due to the substantial gap between the two GRACE missions, we excluded the 2017–2018 period from this analysis. Generally, all three GRACE mascon products agree very well and are highly correlated (Correlation coefficient (CC) > 0.9 among all three products in Table S1 ). Among the three products, the CSR solution has a slightly higher range of TWSA, especially at the negative peaks during the 2019–2022 period. During the 2003–2016 period, three products CSR, JPL, and GSFC TWSA observations range between − 11 cm to 13 cm, − 12 cm to 12 cm, and − 11 cm to 12 cm respectively. On the other hand, the ranges for these products during the 2019–2022 periods are − 20 cm to 4 cm, − 18 cm to 3 cm, and − 17 cm to 3 cm, respectively. In terms of inter-annual variation, GRACE TWSA in Afghanistan was relatively stable from 2003 to 2007 with a slight increasing trend. However, starting from 2008 and especially during the 2019–2022 period, the range of TWSA trended towards increasingly negative values, indicative of a significant reduction in total water storage within Afghanistan (Fig. 3 a). Specifically, during the 2003–2007 period, the average year-sum TWSA of three GRACE mascon products, JPL, CSR, and GSFC, was 2, 8, and 5 cm, respectively. On the other hand, the average annual TWSA declined to the range of approximately − 18 to − 22 cm and approximately − 104 to − 106 cm during the 2008–2016 and the 2019–2022 periods, respectively. In particular, the downward trend of TWSA was the most prominent during 2021 and 2022, which shows unprecedented loss of TWS during the months of autumn (September until November) in these years. During the autumn of the 2021–2022 period, water storage ranges from − 51 to − 43 cm, while for the rest of the years in our study period, it ranges from − 19 to − 17 cm among the three mascon products. The negative shift of TWSA is also indicated by the substantial difference between 2003 and 2016 and 2019–2022 intra-annual TWSA curve in Fig. 3 b. The significant negative shift of TWSA and its differences in the range between the two periods suggest that groundwater extraction has strong and potentially long-lasting effects on the country’s water storage and availability.  4.2 Seasonal variability of TWSA in Afghanistan Consistent seasonal patterns are observed in all three products with increasing water storage from January to May and decreasing water storage from June to November (Fig. 3 ). In both periods, the TWS reached its highest point in April (approximately 4 cm of TWSA average among three GRACE products) and lowest levels around October-November (approximately − 9 cm of TWSA average). The increase in TWS (positive TWSA trend) is due to snowmelt and increasing precipitation during these months of spring (March – May) and winter (December – February) (Sediqi et al., 2019 ). This is also indicated by the monthly total precipitation (Fig. 1 c) as precipitation occurs mostly during these months. On the other hand, the downward and negative trend in TWSA during the summer (June – August) and especially autumn (September – November) indicates a gradual decrease in water storage. As 80 % of water availability in Afghanistan comes from snowmelt, and there are very low levels of precipitation from June to October in most of the river basins (except the Kabul river basin which lies within the monsoon reason), farmers heavily rely on groundwater extractions for agriculture purposes during these months. Therefore, groundwater depletion is among the top factors impacting water availability and management in Afghanistan (Hayat and Baba, 2017; Rasouli, 2021 ). Additionally, while the TWSA intra-annual variation curves were nearly identical (CC = 0.99) for three mascon products during the 2003–2016 period, more differences among the products could be observed for the 2019–2022 period (Fig. 3 b). Most notably, TWSA from the CSR product has a much larger negative peak in magnitude in October than the other two products (-16 cm for CSR versus − 14 cm for other two products). Additionally, while all three products’ TWSA still peak in April during the 2019–2022 period, the peak is less substantial than during the 2003–2016 period. Instead, CSR and GSFC products show a higher magnitude of positive TWSA (bigger increase in TWS) during the earlier months of February and March. This shift of seasonal increase in TWS to earlier months could be the result of climate change that causes snowmelt to occur earlier and hence affects the hydrological regime of the country (Akhtar et al., 2022a ).  4.3 GRACE TWSA long-term trends and spatial variability While the three products have similar average temporal variability and trends across the study region, more distinctions could be observed from trend comparison on a pixel-scale and basin-scale. To better comprehend the long-term trend of water availability, we applied STL decomposition to all TWSA time series and then obtained the estimated slope of trend from applications of the M-K test and Theil–Sen’s Slope estimation on the TWSA long-term trend component time series.  Fig. 4  shows the results of STL for GRACE TWSA data from JPL during the original instrument’s mission. During both periods, significant (p-value  < 0.05 for the M-K test) and negative trends were observed for all three GRACE products. From 2003 to 2007, positive TWSA values could be observed in the long-term trend component (approximately 4 mm/year average among GRACE mascon products), indicating a non-seasonal increase in water storage in the country. However, starting from 2008, substantial declines in TWS (TWSA becomes more negative) are clearly evident from all three observations of GRACE. Additionally, this decreasing trend of water storage and differences in the rate of change among the three products were further exacerbated during the 2019–2022 period. On a pixel-scale,  Fig. 5  describes the spatial patterns of TWSA trends for three products in the 2003–2016 (GRACE) and 2019–2022 (GRACE-FO) periods. It is noted that CSR mascon data were resampled to the same spatial resolution as that of JPL and GSFC mascon products (0.5°). For the 2003–2016 period, significant water storage loss could be observed in the northeast region (Amu Darya basin) (ranging from − 16 to − 2 mm/year among three products) and the west and southwest regions (left side of Harirod-Murghab and lower left side of Helmand region) (ranging from − 19 to − 0.3 mm/year). We observed the most differences between the three mascon trend maps in the central area of Afghanistan. In this area, mostly non-significant trends (p-value  < 0.05 for M-K test) were observed from the JPL mascon product, significant but slightly decreasing trends were found in the CSR mascon products, and mostly positive slope of trends were observed from the GSFC mascon products. The exacerbation of TWSA’s negative shift during the 2019–2022 period was shown as the GRACE-FO slope of trend maps ranged from − 64 to 5 mm/year compared to the GRACE period’s (-19 to 6 mm/year). Similar to the 2003–2016 period, the northeast region exhibited a notable decrease in TWS across all three products. The trend slopes, ranked from highest to lowest, were observed in CSR, JPL, and GSFC mascons, respectively.  Table 2  and  Fig. 6  show the basin-averaged deseasonalized TWSA long-term trend component and Sen’s slope trend of five major river basins in Afghanistan. During the 2003–2016 period, similar observations and signs of long-term trends from all three products were obtained for the three basins Amu Darya, Helmand, and Harirod-Murghab (Figs. 6 b, 6 e, and 6 f). Specifically, all products agreed on the rate of TWSA decrease in Helmand basin (-4.8 mm/year) while JPL mascon produced a slightly smaller slope in Harirod-Murghab basin (-3.6 mm/year versus − 4.8 mm/year) and GSFC mascon overestimated the water storage decreasing rate compared to the other two products in Amu Darya basin (-7.2 mm/year versus − 4.8 mm/year). However, we found substantial disagreement in long-term trends among CSR, JPL, and GSFC GRACE mascon products in the Kabul and Northern basins (Figs. 6 c and 6 d). For the Kabul basin, JPL and GSFC solutions indicated a positive trend of 1.2 mm/year while CSR GRACE mascon product showed a negative trend of − 1.2 mm/year. On the other hand, the TWSA long-term component from JPL and CSR mascon had a negative trend of − 1.2 and − 2.4 mm/year respectively, while the GSFC product indicated a positive trend of 1.2 mm/year. Though contradicting long-term trends were obtained for the Kabul and Northern basins, the slope of change in these basins was much less substantial than in the other three basins of Afghanistan. During the 2019–2022 period, trends of substantial water storage loss could be detected across all basins in Afghanistan. The most significant negative trend was observed in the Amu Darya basin by approximately − 31.2 to − 43.2 mm/year while the least was in Helmand by approximately − 14.4 to − 30 mm/year from three different products. In general, the long-term TWSA trend observed in the GSFC mascon product exhibited a significantly smaller slope of negative trend compared to the trends observed in the other two products. In contrast, the mascons from JPL and CSR showed a considerably higher rate of decrease in various basins. A significantly higher rate of changes could be observed for JPL mascons in the Kabul (approximately 50 % increase for JPL versus the other) and Northern basins (approximately 71 % increase) and for CSR mascons in the Harirod-Murghab (approximately 31.58 % increase for CSR versus the other) and Helmand basins (approximately 67 % increase).  4.4 Comparison between GRACE and FLDAS-Central Asia Generally, the patterns of TWSA simulations from FLDAS-CA match with that of GRACE products. However, there exists a substantial difference between FLDAS-CA and GRACE observations (CC of FLDAS-CA and GRACE products is approximately 0.76 from Supplementary Table A1 ). Up to 2008, TWSA from FLDAS-CA and GRACE products in Afghanistan are closely aligned. As a result of FLDAS-CA and Noah-MP’s lack of account for surface water and human impacts such as groundwater pumping, the gap between the two approaches started to widen as groundwater extraction proliferated (Fig. S1 ) after 2008. However, the differences between FLDAS-CA and GRACE products were not uniform across all basins in the country, with more agreement between TWSA modeling and observations in the Amu Darya and Northern basins (CC ranging from 0.85 to 0.94) and substantial differences in the three remaining basins (CC ranging from 0.33 to 0.8) (Table S2 ). Fig. 6  (black line) and Table 2  show the long-term components and trends of TWSA from FLDAS-Central Asia (FLDAS-CA) in Afghanistan and its five major river basins.
