During the 2003–2016 period, FLDAS-CA projected a non-significant rate of change for Afghanistan as a whole, slightly increasing the trend of water storage for four river basins Kabul, Northern, Harirod-Murghab, and Helmand at a rate of ∼ 1.2–3.6 mm/year, and an exception of negative TWSA trend in Amu Darya (-7.2 mm/year). During the 2019–2022 period, significant negative trends could be seen across the country similar to that of the mascon products but at a much lesser degree ranging from − 12 mm/year in Helmand to − 22.8 mm/year in Kabul (Indus). A high correlation between both FLDAS-CA and GRACE mascon TWSA and precipitation could be observed as high precipitation years in 2005–2007, 2009–2010, and 2019–2020 periods (Fig. 1 a) associated with evident positive water storage and low precipitation periods in the 2011–2016 and 2021–2022 correlated with negative trend of TWSA. During the 2019–2022 period, the country went through a wet period during 2019–2020 followed by an extremely dry period during 2021–2022. The large shift in precipitation hence led to a bigger slope of negative trend in the 2019–2022 period for both FLDAS-CA and three GRACE products. However, though both approaches estimated climate-induced changes in water storage, only GRACE observations could measure human-induced changes and hence contained noticeable differences compared to FLDAS-CA.  Fig. 7  shows the spatial map of FLDAS-CA long-term component slope of trends in two study periods. It is noted that in Fig. 7 , FLDAS-CA data (0.01° of original spatial resolution) was resampled to match GRACE mascon observations’ resolution (0.5°) for better comparison. Compared to GRACE observations, a higher range of slope (approximately − 47 to 28 mm/year for the 2003–2016 period and approximately − 118 to 35 mm/year for the 2019–2022 period) could be observed in the FLDAS-CA TWSA long-term trend. Additionally, as GRACE TWSA was parameterized from observations with low resolution (original resolution of GRACE mission is approximately 300 km) into pre-determined mascon grids, the results are more centralized into certain areas. On the other hand, TWSA and its long-term trend from FLDAS-CA are more scattered across the country, resulting in a high spread of negative and positive trends. This is due to FLDAS-CA’s finer original resolution and the fact that water storage simulation from LSM is heavily impacted by meteorological forcing (e.g., precipitation and temperature) which has high spatial variabilities. The majority of long-term water storage decrease from FLDAS-CA was located at the high mountain area in Amu Darya basin for both periods, which explains the exceptionally high negative slope of trend in Amu Darya basin in Afghanistan for FLDAS-CA. For the 2003–2016 period specifically, we also observe a positive TWSA trend scattering across the country with the upper Kabul basin exhibiting the most notable gain in water storage. Conversely, during the 2019–2022 period, negative trends in TWSA prevailed throughout the country, except for the rightmost area in the Amu Darya basin, where prominent positive trends were observed.  4.5 Correlation between TWSA and hydrological flux anomalies Annual total precipitation was established to have a high correlation with TWSA from both FLDAS-CA and GRACE observations. We extend this analysis to other hydrologic fluxes anomalies. Since GRACE mascon products have a very high correlation to each other (Table S1 ), we only use the average of all three mascon products (Ensemble-Mascons) for the analysis.  Table 3  shows the highest correlation coefficient and corresponding lag time (months) for TWSA versus other hydrological anomalies. Precipitation generally has the strongest correlation with both TWSA products among the hydrologic anomalies(ranging from 0.47 to 0.75 for GRACE mascons and from 0.69 to 0.79 for FLDAS-CA). For P anomalies, a one-month time lag was obtained for most of the river basins, with the exceptions of Amu Darya, Northern, and Helmand basins with a two-month lag for GRACE mascons. This implies that a peak in rainfall and snowfall rate will result in a TWSA peak one or two months later depending on the basin. For the Harirod-Murghab and Helmand river basins, the dominant arid climate and low precipitation can be the reason for the slightly lower correlation of P anomalies to GRACE TWSA. The lag time between precipitation and GRACE TWSA can also be seen from the TWSA monthly average curve (Fig. 3 b) as precipitation in Afghanistan tends to peak in February-March (Fig. 1 c) while TWSA peaks one month later in April. Similarly, the largest decrease in TWSA is observed around October-November, which is approximately one month after the driest period of the year in September. In past studies, a lag time of four months was observed between precipitation and groundwater storage in Afghanistan (Akhtar et al., 2022b ). This is due to the snow melting and infiltration into the aquifer which increases the lag time. Other components in TWS, on the other hand, e.g., canopy water, soil moisture storage, and surface water storage, respond to changes in precipitation faster than that of groundwater storage. For Q, SM, and ET anomalies, there was no time lag between the hydrologic anomalies and TWSA, with the exception of one-month time lag between GRACE TWSA and Q in the Helmand river basin. Generally, TWSA from FLDAS-CA has a higher correlation with these hydrologic anomalies than from GRACE mascons. For FLDAS-CA specifically, SM anomalies generally have a higher correlation with TWSA than Q and ET, especially in Kabul and Harirod-Murghab basins. For mascons TWSA, a weak correlation (CC < 0.4) was observed across the nation for all Q, SM, and ET anomalies. Similar to P anomalies, correlations of other hydrologic anomalies were particularly low for Harirod-Murghab and Helmand river basins.  4.6 Human-induced groundwater storage change based on GRACE and FLDAS-Central Asia TWSA  Fig. 8  shows the annual human-induced groundwater storage changes (4)  in five major river basins in Afghanistan using FLDAS-CA and GRACE mascons data. Drastic groundwater depletion occurred across the country. Similar to the long-term trend, significant decreases in groundwater storage were observed starting from 2008 and worsening during the GRACE-FO period (2019–2022). For Amu Darya, Kabul, and Northern river basins, after the significant decline in groundwater storage in 2008–2009, groundwater storage started to trend upward, suggesting groundwater recharge rate taking place higher than the groundwater pumping rate during this period. However, for the Harirod-Murghab and Helmand basins, no significant positive groundwater storage change occurred, and human-induced groundwater depletion has been decreasing in a gradual fashion. Significant depletion of groundwater storage in Afghanistan was observed again after 2017–2018, which resulted in a substantial break between the 2003–2016 and 2019–2022 periods. Throughout the GRACE-FO period, we witnessed an extended period of depletion, with the most severe conditions occurring in 2021–2022. During the 2019–2022 period, the Helmand River Basin experienced the most severe groundwater depletion, reaching up to 121 cm of year-sum TWS decrease, while the Northern River Basin was the least impacted, with depletion levels of around 42 cm.  Fig. 9  shows the average annual ground storage change (cm) during the 2003–2007 and the 2008–2022 periods. Due to the gap between the GRACE and GRACE-FO missions, GWSA in the 2017–2018 period was not accounted for in the 2008–2022 period. As TWSA from GRACE and FLDAS-CA had very good agreements during the 2003–2007 period (CC > 0.96), there was negligible change in human-induced groundwater storage that could be observed during this period (Fig. 9 a). During the 2008–2022 period, negative human-induced groundwater storage changes were prevalent across the nation. The highest rates of groundwater depletion were found in the northeast region of the Kabul river basin and across the Harirod-Murghab and Helmand basins. While there is some significant positive groundwater storage change in the southern region of the Amu Darya river basin, this does not necessarily imply groundwater recharge. Indeed, in this area, both FLDAS-CA and three GRACE products showed a significant negative trend of TWSA (Figs. 5 and 7 ); however, as the slope of trends in FLDAS-CA is higher than that of GRACE, GWSC in this area is estimated to be positive, not because of actual positive groundwater storage change. Additionally, uncertainties in this area for GRACE observations can exist due to leakage from outside of the region and glacier melt in the upstream of Amu Darya basin and Hindu Kush mountain.  4.7 Impacts of GRACE Data Assimilation (GRACE DA) Compared to FLDAS-CA, GLDAS-2.2 assimilates GRACE mascon observations to improve groundwater and terrestrial water storage simulation of LSM (Li et al., 2019 ).  Fig. 10  shows the TWSA monthly average across Afghanistan. With GRACE DA, TWSA is much closer and has better correlation to GRACE observations (CC with FLDAS-CA TWSA and GRACE ensemble means is 0.77 while CC with GLDAS-2.2 TWSA and GRACE ensemble means is 0.94). As shown earlier, the gap between FLDAS-CA and GRACE mascons started to widen since 2008. Throughout the study period, GRACE DA significantly reduces the TWS overestimation but still cannot simulate the lowest points in TWSA during October-November. Generally, GRACE DA had significant impacts on the magnitude of TWS by correcting groundwater storage component of LSM with GRACE observations (Li et al., 2019 ); however, the trends and patterns of LSM TWSA remained relatively unchanged. The remaining differences between GLDAS-2.2 and GRACE observations could be the results of other factors including the underlying uncertainties of both approaches (e.g., hydrological forcing uncertainty for LSM and signal leakage for GRACE observations) and mismatching spatial resolution.  4.8 Discussion 4.8.1 Comparison of GRACE mascon products and FLDAS-CA TWSA Generally, the three mascon products have similar patterns and very high correlation coefficients during both the GRACE (2003–2016) and GRACE-FO (2019–2022) periods. However, significant differences among different mascon products can be observed when we decompose the TWSA time series and evaluate the long-term trends. More agreement in the magnitude and direction of trends among mascon products were found in the relatively bigger river basins while contradicting trends were found for the two smaller river basins Northern and Kabul (Section 4.2 ). This finding aligns with previous studies that have observed a significant increase in the difference in long-term trends among GRACE products, particularly as the size of the basin decreases (Scanlon et al., 2016 ). Additionally, while other studies had found that the magnitude of a long-term trend of JPL mascon was consistently higher than that of other mascons and SHC products (Jing et al., 2020; Leńczuk et al., 2020; Scanlon et al., 2016 ), we observed a higher magnitude of trend from CSR mascon product for the majority of river basins in Afghanistan. The long-term trend of the GSFC mascon was consistently more positive compared to the other two products, resulting in lower-magnitude negative trends. The discrepancies among the three mascon products are largely due to the differences in processing approaches of the three centers (e.g., constraint, mascons size, and shape). Additionally, since the actual resolution of GRACE mascons is coarse, uncertainties from signal leakage and glacier melt impact from upstream of Afghanistan could also affect the TWSA result of three mascon products (Humphrey et al., 2023; Jing et al., 2020 ). FLDAS-CA and GRACE mascons TWSA initially exhibited strong agreement, but they began to diverge more and more since 2008 (Fig. 6 ). While the long-term trend components of the two approaches have similar patterns, we observed a substantial increase in the gap between FLDAS-CA and GRACE mascons TWSA in 2008–209 and 2017–2018 periods. These periods coincided with severe droughts that happened in Afghanistan (Rousta et al., 2020 ). Indeed, the drought in 2018 was regarded as the most severe period of drought that Afghanistan has experienced in the past two decades. Although we did not incorporate GRACE observations for 2017 and 2018 due to the gap between the GRACE and GRACE-FO missions, we observed a significant decrease in TWSA during the transition from the GRACE to GRACE-FO period. Consequently, a substantial disparity also emerged between FLDAS-CA and GRACE observations. During these drought periods, since groundwater is Afghanistan’s main water supply and there is limited groundwater management in the nation (Hayat and Baba, 2017; Mack et al., 2013; Rasouli, 2021 ), overexploitation of groundwater extraction led to a serious decrease in TWS (Fig. 8 ). Since FLDAS-CA and Noah-MP LSM are not able to simulate complex anthropogenic impacts to groundwater, the model could not capture the full extent of water storage decrease in Afghanistan. For both FLDAS-CA and GRACE observations, TWSA has the highest correlation to total precipitation anomalies (rainfall and snowfall rate) with a lag time of 1–2 months. Since the majority of water in Afghanistan comes from snow and glacier melt, it takes time for water in precipitation form to travel vertically and horizontally before infiltrating down into groundwaters, and hence the lag time (Andrew et al., 2017; Jing et al., 2020 ). Additionally, given the weak correlation of GRACE observations with other hydrologic anomalies (runoff, soil moisture, evapotranspiration), the main drivers of water storage in Afghanistan are precipitation and groundwater depletion/recharge.  4.8.2 Implications on water availability in Afghanistan We estimated the human-induced groundwater storage change (i.e., groundwater pumping and extraction) in Afghanistan using TWSA from GRACE observations and FLDAS-CA. The GRACE-LSM combination approach has its limitations (e.g., uncertainties and signal leakage in GRACE observations and confined aquifer measurement) (Castellazzi et al., 2016 ). Nevertheless, this approach has been employed in numerous groundwater studies in Afghanistan and has yielded satisfactory results when compared with in-situ groundwater data (Akhtar et al., 2022b; Daqiq et al., 2023; Nazari et al., 2023; Tariq et al., 2023 ). Up to 2008, the rate of groundwater recharge was higher than usage due to the limitations in well-drilling techniques (roughly 10 billion m3  recharge and 2.8 billion m3  usage) (Rout, 2008 ). However, with improvements in confined aquifer drilling but lack of water resources management combined with climate change and population growth (Rasouli, 2021 ), groundwater has become a pressing issue in Afghanistan (Noori and Singh, 2021; Zaryab et al., 2023 ). Though there were signs of recharge for basins such as Amu Darya, Kabul, and Northern river basins, drastic groundwater depletion was observed following each severe drought (e.g., 2008 and 2018) (Fig. 8 ). For river basins with arid climates and high percentages of irrigated agriculture such as Helmand and Harirod-Murghab (Fig. 2 d), there has been a steady decrease in groundwater storage, suggesting an overexploitation of groundwater (usage exceeds recharge). The results from our study also highlight an ongoing issue in Afghanistan at the moment. During the 2019–2022 period, Afghanistan experienced a significant trend of negative TWSA from both GRACE mascons observations and FLDAS-CA. This is due to an ongoing drought in Afghanistan that started in 2021 (OCHA, 2023; Tayfur and Alami, 2022; Xu and Greenfield, 2023 ). The severity of the drought is exemplified by the notably low total precipitation amounts in 2021 and 2022 (Fig. 1 a). Hence, we observed a negative trend of large magnitude in TWSA from both FLDAS-CA and across Afghanistan. Furthermore, considering that the negative trend in GRACE observations (climate- and human-induced) is greater than that in FLDAS-CA (climate-induced), and based on the estimation of groundwater storage change, it is likely that groundwater depletion has worsened at an alarming rate in the past few years. Additionally, water scarcity and groundwater issues are projected to exacerbate in the future under the effects of climate change since changes in temperature and precipitation have a major impact on snowfall rate and timing. Under the representative concentration pathways (RCPs) 4.5 and 8.5, projections indicate a shift in precipitation and streamflow from snowmelt to earlier months in the near future (Akhtar et al., 2022a ). This shift has the potential to result in reduced water availability during the summer and autumn, precisely when TWS is expected to decrease the most due to low rainfall. Additionally, snow cover area and river flows in Afghanistan are also projected to decrease, resulting in diminished water reaching downstream areas in the late 21st century (Azizi and Asaoka, 2020 ).    5 Conclusion Water scarcity and groundwater depletion have been pressing issues in Afghanistan. In this study, we evaluate the variations in terrestrial water storage anomalies from three GRACE mascon products from CSR, JPL, and GSFC, and from the FLDAS-Central Asia model. While the three mascon products have similar patterns and have strong correlations among them, there are substantial discrepancies in the long-term trends of TWSA from the three mascon products. Among the three products, CSR and JPL mascons typically exhibited a more negative trend in TWSA depending on the river basin, while GSFC mascons typically showed a more positive trend in TWSA. The differences in the GRACE mascons products are mainly from the differences in processing approach and mascon’s shape and size of each center. On the other hand, as groundwater storage, which has a major contribution to water storage in Afghanistan, is not simulated in the FLDAS-CA and Noah-MP land surface model, we observed a significant variation between FLDAS-CA and GRACE observations’ TWSA. The gap between the two approaches expanded after each severe drought event (e.g., 2008 and 2018) when substantial groundwater extraction occurred. Particularly, during the 2019–2022 period, while both FLDAS-CA and GRACE showed negative trends of TWSA across five basins, GRACE mascons suggested a much more drastic rate of water storage loss due to the addition of human-induced impacts (approximately − 10.8 to − 22.8 mm/year for FLDAS-CA and − 14.4 to − 43.2 mm/year for GRACE mascons). Additionally, due to the high resolution of forcing input compared to the GRACE original resolution, TWSA trends in FLDAS-CA are much more scattered and have higher spatial variability compared to the more centralized results of GRACE mascons. TWSA from both approaches has a strong correlation with precipitation with a time lag of 1–2 months. Nevertheless, we observed a relatively weak correlation between GRACE TWSA and runoff, evapotranspiration, and soil moisture anomalies. This suggests that groundwater storage is indeed the primary driver of water storage change in Afghanistan. Due to the inherent spatial resolution discrepancies between GRACE observations and FLDAS-CA, some uncertainties (e.g., signal leakage in GRACE observations) can affect the results of our comparison. Additionally, while applications of coupled GRACE and land surface modeling for groundwater storage estimations are useful and have been validated in the region, the method suffers in confined aquifer and the inherently coarse spatial resolution of GRACE observations (Castellazzi et al., 2016 ). In the future, we plan to incorporate interferometry synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) techniques to complement the estimation and monitoring of groundwater storage. Further expansion of the analysis to Central Asia is also beneficial due to the vital information TWSA can give to the region (Hu et al., 2021 ). With the ongoing prolonged drought period in Afghanistan, coupled with the potential effects of climate change on water availability across the nation, accurate monitoring of water storage—especially human-induced impacts such as groundwater overexploitation—has become increasingly crucial and will continue to be so in the future. Furthermore, given the transboundary nature of Central Asia and the fact that many other countries in the region also experience groundwater issues (Hu et al., 2022 ; C. Liu et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2020 ), the assimilation of GRACE observations into FLDAS-CA will significantly enhance the model’s capacity for monitoring groundwater and water availability. This new capability will undoubtedly have a positive impact and serve as a valuable tool for decision-makers and local stakeholders in preparing and mitigating the impacts of drought as well as assessing the effects of climate change on groundwater and water storage. 1 Introduction Warming climate has been believed to accelerate the global- and continental-scale hydrological cycle (Alan et al., 2003 ). It can alter prime hydrological components, such as precipitation (Zhang et al., 2013a ). Alifu et al. (2022)  indicated that human-induced climate change has enhanced flooding more prominently in recent years, but because of limited evidence, the latest 6th Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Assessment Report expressed low confidence in changes in past floods at the global scale due to human-induced climate change (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021 ). The complexity of runoff generation and the streamfow process complicates the assessment of historical impact of human-induced climate change on river flooding (Alifu et al., 2022 ). The mechanisms and extent to which climate change influence flood occurrences still remain unresolved(Zhang et al., 2022c ). Furthermore, Because the frequency of large floods increased substantially during the twentieth century (Milly et al., 2002 ), and potential losses caused by floods have aroused pervasive concerns in recent years (Zhang et al., 2015; Hirabayashi et al., 2021 ), another question is: what is the linkage between flood risk and socioeconomic activities? Yellow River, the second longest river in China, long regarded as China’s mother river and the cradle of Chinese civilization (Zhang et al., 2022b ), has been known by frequent floods and droughts (Yang et al., 2008 ) and water shortages (Zhang et al., 2017 ). The Yellow River basin (YRB) is home to about 12 % of China's population (Zhao et al., 2019 ). In September 2019, the ecological conservation and high-quality development of the YRB was declared as a major national strategy, arousing widespread concerns about the sustainability of the ecological environment and human settlement across the basin. Due to the devastating impacts of floods on the eco-system and human society, flood losses and risk have aroused a great deal of concern (Lan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020 ). Floods are subject to high occurrence frequency due to summer monsoon climate, complex topographical features and ecological environment (He et al., 2008 ). The past 4000 years witnessed more than 1000 floods across the YRB (Chen et al., 2012 ) and large floods in recent decades (Webber et al., 2008 ). The 1964–2003 period observed more than 28 flood hazards across the middle YRB to the lower Wei River (He et al., 2008; State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters (SFCDRH), 1992 ). In 2005, about 4 billion hectares of drainage area of the YRB as well as the Wei River basin were afflicted by floods (China National Bureau of Statistics (CNBS), 2006 ). In 2017, 22 counties in the Shaanxi province were heavily influenced by flood hazards, and 456,000 people were affected (China Meteorological Administration (CMA), 2017 ). Therefore, the Outline of the Yellow River Basin Ecological Protection and High-quality Development Plan presented by the State Council of China in 2021 claimed that flood still remained the biggest threat to the YRB (The State Council of China (SCC), 2021 ). However, the spatiotemporal evolution of flood magnitude, flood risk and relevant drivers within the YRB are still inadequately understood, which significantly limits the mitigation of flood hazards and sustainable socioeconomic development. Global warming influents flood frequency and flood magnitude in most regions of the world (Alfieri et al., 2015, 2017; He et al., 2022 ). Meanwhile, population growth and socio-economic activities closer to floodplains have increased river flood-induced losses (Kundzewicz et al., 2014 ). However, the main factors affecting flood risk in the YRB are still less than clear, and studies on flood inundation in the YRB have focused mainly on specific floods or floods along certain river reaches (Zhang et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2019 ). Few reports are available addressing flood characteristics of the whole YRB from the perspective of flood inundation and flood risk assessment considering the exposure of disaster-bearing bodies. Therefore, the objectives of this study were to: (1) identify flood-susceptible regions within the YRB; (2) quantify spatial changes of flooding areas as well as flood magnitude; (3) evaluate flood risks for different return periods of flood magnitude events; and (4) explore the relationship between precipitation and flood magnitude as well as driving factors of flood risk.  2 Data The details of dataset have been listed in  Table 1 . Two sets of runoff data are used in this study: (1) daily discharge datasets of Huangheyuan, Tanglaiqv, Wushan, and Minhe hydrological stations ( Fig. 1 ) in the YRB covering the 1978–1997 period (Fekete et al., 2002 ); and (2) daily 0.25°×0.25° hydrologically based land surface flux datasets for conterminous China, 1961–2017 (VIC-CN05.1) (Miao and Wang, 2020a ). Comparatively, the generation of the latter aforementioned datasets is based on a new model version VIC 4.2.d and ground observation data like meteorological forcing dataset and soil simulation parameters of 2474 meteorological stations in China, which are appropriate for hydrological modelling and analysis for China’s river basins (Miao and Wang, 2020b ). In addition, the land use and land cover (LUCC) dataset of China (1980–2015) (Chinese Academy of Sciences Resource and Environmental Science Data Center, (CASRES) 2019 ) covering the periods of 1980, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015 has been used, wherein landsat TM/ETM remote sensing images of each period are used as the main data source with spatial resolution of 1 km. The 1 km grid dataset of China's population spatial distribution (Xu, 2017 ) in 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015 is obtained. Moreover, the daily precipitation data covering the 1978–2015 period is from the dataset of CN05.1.  3 Methods The procedure for analysis is shown as  Fig. 2  and specific methods are also described here. 3.1 VIC-Cama model The Variable Infiltration Capacity hydrological model (VIC) is a grid-based semi-distributed hydrological model (Liang et al., 1994, 1996; Miao and Wang, 2020b ) involving hydrological balance principles, variables such as precipitation, temperature, vegetation cover type and energy balance between land and atmosphere (Dahri et al., 2021, Yan et al., 2020b ). The Cama-flood model is a distributed global river confluence model that calculates river discharge and flood inundated area at each grid (Yamazaki et al., 2011, 2013 ). The model uses a 1 min resolution river topography maps as flow maps and river networks. Besides, the 3-arc-second DEM (MERIT DEM) was used as elevation input. The FLOW upscaling algorithm was used to draw topographic parameters, based on the above-mentioned river network and DEM (Yamazaki et al., 2011, 2012; Zhao et al., 2017 ). The Cama-flood model calculated flow velocity and discharge according to the local inertia equation (Bates et al., 2010 ). For each catchment unit, the flow input of the upstream unit, the flow output of the downstream unit and the local runoff input are considered using the mass conservation equation to update the water storage in the unit catchment area (Yamazaki et al., 2014 ). Here, we input 0.25° runoff raster data (VIC-CN05.1) generated by the VIC model into Cama-Flood model to construct the VIC-Cama coupled model, and extracted river discharge and flood inundated range with 1 min resolution (about 2 km) by setting the resolution of river network.  3.2 Model verification 3.2.1 Confluence grid position correction In the rasterization calculation procedure, the confluence grid which should correspond to the location of the hydrological station may be spatially shifted (Shin et al., 2019; Hanazaki et al., 2022 ). In order to determine the correct grid corresponding to the latitude and longitude of the hydrological station, it is necessary to calibrate the grid position. The position correction of the confluence grid was mainly calculated based on the flow map generated by the Cama-Flood model. First, we constructed a target circle as location area, whose center was set to be the longitude and latitude of the hydrological station, and the radius was 6 min. For each location grid, we obtained the confluence range of each location grid by tracing progressively back to its upstream grid, until we no longer found any upstream grid that flowed into the location grid. Then, the confluence range was loaded into ArcGIS and the positioning grid whose confluence range was consistent with the confluence area of the hydrological station provided by GRDC was identified. The positioning grid was finally determined to be the correctly-positioned confluence grid.  3.2.2 Verification indicators The quality of the simulation results were evaluated using three statistical indicators: Pearson correlation coefficient (R) is used to measure the correlation between two variables. R is between −1 and 1. The absolute value of the index R approaches 1, the higher the correlation between the two variables; a value greater than 0 indicates a positive correlation, while a value less than 0 indicates a negative correlation. R = 0 means no relations between two variables (Pearson, 1896 ):(1) R = ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   ) ( S  i   − S ¯   )   ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   )  2  ∑ i = 1  n  ( S  i   − S ¯   )  2             Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency coefficient (NSE) is a normalized statistical method used to determine the relative magnitude of residual variance compared with the variance of the observed data. It is a common indicator to verify the simulation results of the model. The closer the NSE is to 1, the more reliable the model is (Nash andSutcliffe, 1970; Miao et al., 2022 ):(2) N S E = 1 − ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − S  i   )  2    ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − O ¯   )  2          Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is used to measure the distribution of residuals, indicating the degree of data concentration near the best-fit line. The smaller the RMSE, the closer the simulation results are to the observed data (Koohi et al., 2022 ):(3) R M S E = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  ( O  i   − S  i   )  2          In Eqs. (1) - (3) , O  i     and O ¯     are, respectively, the observation series provided by the hydrological station and the mean value of observations, S  i     and S ¯     are, respectively, the model simulation series and the mean simulated values.   3.3 Flood behavior metrics Three metrics were constructed to characterize the flood process, namely, annual maximum flooded area (MFA), average flooded days (AFD), and average flooded area (AFA). MFA shows the extreme flooded condition, and specifically refers to the flood magnitude. AFD denotes the average accumulated flooded duration of each grid cell in the flooded area. AFA shows the average daily flooded area annually. The flood behavior metrics were used to evaluate changes in the flooded area and flooded magnitude from 1978 to 2015:(4) M F A  S  max  = ∑ j = 1  n  S max  i j        (5) A F D  D = ∑ j = 1  k  d ¯    i j     / k     (6) A F A  S m e a n = ∑ j = 1  n  S  i j     / d  i         where i  represents the i th year, j  represents the j th grid cell (j  = 1, …, n), k  denotes the number of grids in the floodplain; S max  represents the maximum flooded area (km2 ); S mean  denotes the average daily flooded area (km2 ) of a year; S  represents the flooded area (km2 ); D  represents the annual average flooded days; d ¯     represents the flooded days of grid; and d  represents the total days of the year.  3.4 Precipitation indices Precipitation indices were derived from extreme precipitation measures (http://etccdi.pacificclimate.org/list_27_indices.shtml ) and tailored to signal both intense precipitation occurrences and extended humid periods by employing varying thresholds. Generally, two categories (Croitoru et al., 2016 ) can be involved, i.e. precipitation intensity and the number of precipitation days. We traversed different thresholds for different categories of precipitation indicators, and conducted correlation analysis between precipitation indicators defined by thresholds and MFA to select the index with the highest correlation to determine the precipitation threshold that dominated flood magnitude changes over the YRB ( Table 2 ).  3.5 Flood risk assessment Flood risk is defined as the likelihood of alterations of community function caused by flood events and social conditions (Carrão et al., 2016; IPCC, 2012 ), and is considered as a combination of flood magnitude and exposure of property and entities, which are also called as disaster-bearing bodies (Hirabayashi et al., 2013 ). In this study, flood risk was expressed as the product of flood inundation ratio and the Total Amount of Disaster-bearing bodies (TADO) of each grid. To explore the dynamic changes of flood risk and the factors affecting flood risk (Hartmann and Spit, 2015; Roos et al., 2017 ), we quantified the exposure of four types of disaster-bearing bodies (e.g. population, cropland, forest and grass, and settlements) to floods from 1978 to 2015 by overlaying the flood magnitude and TADO layers of each year, as well as flood risk for different return periods using TADO in 2015. In addition, an Exposure Rate index (ER) was defined to evaluate the impact of flood magnitude on flood risk.(7) E R = E / T A D O      where E represents the exposure of disaster-bearing bodies in the flooded area, that is, the number of disaster-bearing bodies exposed to the floodplains; TADO represents the total amount of disaster-bearing bodies in the floodplains.   4 Results 4.1 Model verification To verify the performance of VIC-Cama model, we compared observed discharge series at Huangheyuan, Tanglaiqu, Wushan, and Minhe stations with modeled discharge series.  Fig. 3  a1 - a4 shows the simulated streamflow series at each of the aforementioned hydrological stations. It can be found from Fig. 3  a1-a4 that the simulated streamflow by the VIC-Cama model well captured the changing patterns of observed streamflow changes. The Huangheyuan station (a1) is near to the headwater region of the YRB. The simulated streamflow at the Huangheyuan station significantly underestimated streamflow changes when compared to the observed streamflow changes. There are several reasons to explain the underestimation: (1) because of the low discharge at the Huangheyuan station, small deviations can led to significant uncertainty; (2) although the VIC model considers frozen soil process and snow interception, it still causes great uncertainty in the simulated streamflow changes over the alpine region due to the complexity of streamflow generation conditions in the mountainous areas of western China (Figure. S6 ), which may introduce substantial uncertainty from ice-melt-induced flood identification (Zhang et al., 2013b; MiaoandWang, 2020b ); (3) errors of some input data like precipitation may be another factor causing the underestimation of observed streamflow changes. For simulated streamflow changes at the Wushan (Fig. 3  a3) and Minhe (Fig. 3  a4) hydrological stations, human activities and changes in underlying surface conditions such as vegetation cover shifts are the main factors behind the biased simulated streamflow changes (Yan et al., 2020a; Ni et al., 2022 ). The correlation coefficient (R) between simulated and observed flood discharges at these four stations during 1978–1997 was equal to /higher than 0.70, RMSE between 0.6 and 0.78, and NSE were satisfactory at the Minhe station (NSE=0.65). NSE was between 0.4 and 0.48 at other stations, which could be attributed to the uncertainty mentioned above. In general, the model performance was acceptable, and VIC-CN05.1 had a relatively more satisfactory performance (Miao and Wang, 2020b ). Therefore, this dataset was used for flood monitoring and simulation in this study.  4.2 Identification of flood-susceptible areas The flood-susceptible areas over the YRB were identified, based on the inundated extent simulated by the VIC-Cama model. In order to distinguish flood inundation from the fluvial water volume in river channels, we set criteria for the identification of flood-susceptible areas: (1) the number of cumulative flooding days of each grid should be less than a season per year (Zhou, 2022 ); (2) the flooding area of a single grid should be greater than 0.5 km2 . In this way, the flooding extent was retained. In the latter rule, the threshold value of flooding area was an empirical value determined by comparing the distribution of river network after multiple debugging.  Fig. 4  depicts the typical flood-prone areas labeled as A-E. Region A is the Ningxia reach of the YRB. According to flood records, five catastrophic floods have occurred in this region since 1940 (Yuan et al., 2021 ), and this region is still frequently-affected by small- and medium-scale floods, resulting in river bank flooding (Tian et al., 2019 ). Heavy rains and ice floods in the upper YRB cause floods and pose a threat to the construction of the local ecological landscape corridor and the life and property safety of residents on both sides of the strait. For example, abundant precipitation in the upper YRB and heavy rains across various tributaries of the YRB in 2018 led to multiple flood peaks in the Ningxia reach of the YRB (Gao et al., 2020 ). In addition, due to streamflow from low to high latitude and topographic features, the Ningmeng River reach of the YRB was dominated by high frequency of ice-jam floods (Fu et al., 2014 ). Region B belongs to the Daheihe River basin, which is a tributary of the northeast corner of the middle YRB and one of the most important river corridors in the Hetao plain (Huang and Zhang, 2018 ). Most areas of this region are steep mountainous with dry climate in winter and spring, and precipitation is mainly concentrated in summer being characterized by short duration rainstorms. Therefore, when heavy precipitation occurs, it is easy to form sudden mountain torrents with steep rise and fall of flood peaks (Han et al., 2012 ). Region C is located in the middle Fenhe River, which is a first-grade tributary of the YRB. Meanwhile, middle reaches of the Fenhe River are prone frequent flooding. From 1954–1996, five large-scale floods occurred (Guo, 2019 ) and the main driving factors were precipitation and topography. Besides, the distribution of precipitation in the middle Fenhe River is especially uneven both in space and time, which is concentrated in June to September, and is prone to heavy rainfall. In terms of topography, due to the inflow of many tributaries in this region, it is easy to cause a sudden increase in streamflow at the main stream. Owing to severe soil erosion, substantial sediment is carried into the Taiyuan Basin within the middle Fenhe River. The steep slopes contribute to significant sediment deposition, exacerbating flood risks (Wu, 2015 ). Region D is located in the lower Weihe River, which is the largest tributary of the YRB. Floods are characterized by sharp rise and fall and large sediment concentration (Wang et al., 2003 ). Moreover, the population and social wealth on both sides of the straits are concentrated, which has caused a large amount of social and economic losses given occurrence of the severe flood disasters from 1898 to 2003 (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Region E is located in the Sanmenxia to Jindihe River reach of the lower YRB. The upper YRB flows through the Loess Plateau, where soil and water loss are serious. As for sediment in the lower YRB, sediment load is constantly deposited and raises the riverbed and hence the ‘Suspended River’ (Xu et al., 2022 ). In this case, extreme precipitation is more likely to cause river flooding. The lower YRB is also subjected to stronger human activities, such as dam construction and other hydraulic infrastructure to reduce flood risk (Chen, 2019 ). As can be seen from Fig. 4 , a large area of off-channel inundation occurs in region E, which can be attributed to higher-than-ground riverbed in the downstream region, resulting in fewer tributaries converging into the main channel. When there occurs a rainstorm, overbank flooding can occur with high probability (Liu, 2012; Zhang et al., 2021 ). For example, in July 2021, the Henan province was hit by the once-in-a-thousand year rainstorm and flood (Guo et al., 2022 ) and the flood flow discharged into the Yellow Sea via the Huai River basin. However, due to the excessive short-term precipitation and the inability to discharge the flood waters in time, serious urban waterlogging and huge loss of life and property resulted.  4.3 Changes of flood behavior and determination of precipitation threshold To investigate climatic impacts on flood inundation across the YRB, we evaluated flood behavior metrics for inundation changes of floodplains over the YRB ( Fig. 5 ). During 1978–2015, from the perspective of the whole YRB (Fig. 5  (YR1) - (YR3)), changes of the three indices of MFA, AFD and AFA showed a weak trend, and the MFA, AFD and AFA showed an increasing trend at 3.247 km2 /year, 0.09 days/year and 0.764 km2 / year, respectively. Besides, the tendency of YRB and each region didn’t pass the 95 % confidence test. They showed that from the perspective of flood inundation of long time series, flood characteristics of the YRB did not change greatly due to climatic changes. Similar conclusions were obtained from the inundation characteristics of every 10 years in the YRB and the floodplains from 1978 to 2015 (Figure. S3  - Figure. S5 ). Wang et al. (2013)  indicated that changes in heavy precipitation over the YRB exhibited only a weak trend from 1959 to 2008, which was consistent with the stability of inundation characteristics. Specifically, for the five identified floodplains, MFA represents the extreme value of flood inundation, which can most directly reflect the annual flood magnitude of the region. The MFA in regions A and B shows a decreasing trend, and the decreasing rate is 1.657 km2 /year and 1.356 km2 /year, respectively. However, the MFA in regions C, D, and E increases at a rate of 0.342 km2 /year, 0.618 km2 /year and 5.165 km2 /year, respectively, but compared with the amount of MFA of each floodplain, the range is inconspicuous. AFD and AFA is averaged in the spatial and temporal domains on behalf of the annual floods in the average state (Wang et al., 2022 ) which in regions A and D shows a decreasing tendency, while region B, C, and E present a slightly increasing trend. At present, there is still a controversy about the change of flood under the influence of climate change (Aich et al., 2016; Chegwidden et al., 2020 ), but more and more studies have found that the impact of climate change on the flood magnitude in many regions is not as great as people thought (Abass et al., 2022 ). Our research results on YRB can serve as a supplement to this point. Precipitation anomaly is the direct factor leading to floods, but extreme precipitation is not necessarily the critical driving factor of floods (Wasko and Nathan, 2019 ). In order to explore the relationship between precipitation and floods in YRB, we evaluated the precipitation threshold leading to the change of flood magnitude based on five precipitation indicators ( Table 3 ). Results showed that the long-term accumulated precipitation with medium and high intensity had a higher correlation with flood magnitude and a greater impact on flood magnitude. Specifically, the correlation coefficient between annual total precipitation (PRCPTOT) and flood magnitude reached 0.757. When the threshold value of RXmm was 5.2 mm, the correlation coefficient between the index and flood magnitude was 0.751. When the percentage threshold of RXpTOT was 51 %, the correlation coefficient was the highest and reached up to 0.774. RxXdays represented the cumulative precipitation in consecutive days, and when the threshold was 144 days, the correlation reached the maximum value of 0.833. The threshold values of each index indicated that for YRB, the cumulative high precipitation in a long period of time was the dominant factor for the change of flood magnitude in the basin.  4.4 Flood risk assessment The Gumbel distribution was used to fit the daily inundated area to calculate the flood magnitude for different return periods (He et al., 2022; Lim et al., 2018 ), and combined with the distribution of disaster-bearing bodies to assess the flood risk ( Table 4 ). Results showed that under the distribution pattern of disaster-bearing bodies in 2015, when YRB suffers from 50-year-return flood magnitude, the corresponding exposure would be 1.47, 1.59, 1.0 and 1.60 times of Ep , Ec , Efg  and Es  from 1978 to 2015, respectively, and for the 100-year-return flood magnitude, they would turn into 1.65, 1.80, 1.12 and 1.80 times of the corresponding exposure from 1978 to 2015, respectively. When YRB suffered from 500-year-return flood magnitude, Ep , Ec , Efg  and Es  reached 2.09, 2.27, 1.38, and 2.27 times of the corresponding exposure from 1978 to 2015., while under the scenario of a 1000-year-return flood magnitude, Ep , Ec  and Efg  would be 2.27, 2.47, 1.50 and 2.47 times of the exposure from 1978 to 2015, respectively. The spatial distribution of maximum inundated extent for different return periods is shown in Figure.S7. The double increase of exposure caused by extreme floods indicated that under the distribution of disaster-bearing bodies in 2015, YRB still faced high risks when encountering extreme flood events, among which the risk of forest and grassland increased slightly, while the risk of cropland and settlements increased significantly. Therefore, strengthening the flood control and disaster reduction capacity of YRB and reducing flood risk in the basin are of great significance for social and economic development.  4.5 Identification of driving factors of flood risk By analyzing the changes of TADO from 1978 to 2015 ( Table5 ), we found that the population in the floodplain of YRB had increased by 889,100 people, and the area of settlements had increased significantly by 353 km2 , while the TADO of cropland and forest and grassland had decreased by 98 km2  and 118 km2 , respectively (Figure.S1-Figure.S2). The exposure of disaster bearing bodies in region A, B, and C decreased, but increased in the D and E regions, which may be mainly related to the change of MFA. In general, the extent of human activities has gradually concentrated in floodplains over the past 38 years, and as the extent of inundation increases, it is subject to increasing flood risk. The evolution of flood risk mainly involves two factors, one of which is the variation of environment caused by natural climate change, the other is the variation of spatial distribution of disaster-bearing bodies caused by social and economic development (Elmer et al., 2012; Di Baldassarre et al., 2013; 2015 ). Zischg et al. (2018)  referred to the concept of separating the driving factors of flood risk to identify the critical flood risk drivers and thus to discover where society needs to exert influence to effectively reduce flood risk. In this section, we draw on this idea to identify the driving factors of flood risk in YRB and various floodplains ( Fig. 6 ). Since the materials of disaster-bearing bodies are not continuous in temporal aspects, the data of TADO in floodplains was interpolated in time series by taking the nearest neighbor data. As can be seen from the figure, the variation characteristics of exposure and ER of the four types of disaster-bearing bodies were consistent with the change of flood magnitude, which was particularly evident in the population exposure. This was mainly owing to densely distributed population in YRB. However, the variation trend of ER of cropland, forest and grassland and settlements was different from that of flood magnitude due to the disturbance of spatial distribution of disaster bearing bodies. In order to quantitatively evaluate the interaction between flood magnitude and the spatial distribution of disaster-bearing bodies on flood risk, we calculated the correlation between the exposure and MIA and TADO in floodplains ( Fig. 7 ). Generally speaking, when the correlation coefficient reaches 0.7, it indicates a strong correlation. Therefore, the factor whose correlation coefficient exceeded 0.7 or was higher than that of the other factor was taken as the driving factor of flood risk in each region. Results showed that the population exposure in YRB and all floodplains was dominated by flood magnitude (0.80≤CorE-MIA ≤0.98), which was consistent with the analysis results in Fig. 6 . While the exposure of cropland was mainly affected by the spatial distribution of disaster-bearing bodies (0.83≤ CorE-TADO  ≤0.9998), according to Fig. 6 , the TADO of cropland in each floodplain was positively low during 1990–2010, which greatly limited the impact of flood magnitude on the exposure, thus being the driving factor of flood risk on cropland. Except for YRB and C region (0.83≤ CorE-TADO  ≤0.86), the exposure of forest and grassland in other floodplains was mainly affected by flood magnitude (0.62≤ CorE-MIA  ≤0.92). The driving factor of settlement exposure in YRB and B region was flood magnitude (0.64≤ CorE-MIA  ≤0.89), while in the A, C, D, and E regions it was the distribution of disaster bearing bodies (0.88≤ CorE-TADO  ≤0.9939). It was noted that the ER of YRB had been reaching up to 48.1 %, within the five floodplains it was up to 69.3 %, which showed that a significant percentage of disaster-bearing bodies was still in the high risk of flooding; overall, the distribution of disaster bearing bodies and flood magnitude played different roles in each region for different disaster-bearing bodies, of which MIA was the driving factor of flood risk for population, while for cropland it was TADO.   5 Discussion 5.1 Natural flow patterns In the 1990s, the concept of "natural flow pattern" was gradually developed in the field of ecology (Poff et al., 1997 ), which refers to the hydrological characteristics of rivers in the natural state, not affected by human activities, namely natural flow. In recent years, it has also been more and more widely used in the hydrological field. In practice, natural flow has usually been reconstructed to interpret climate information in hydrometeorology (Miao et al., 2022 ). For example, Assani et al. (2006)  identified the impacts of climate, topography and other environmental factors on the spatial variation of streamflow based on natural flow volume. In addition, Lajoie et al. (2007)  assessed changes in river hydrological characteristics caused by dams by comparing the differences between natural and reservoir flows. Shiau and Wu (2009)  deduced streamflow information in unmeasured areas based on natural flow. "Natural flow patterns" have also been frequently used in flood studies (Mazouz et al., 2013; Blythe and Schmidt, 2018 ), and are of great significance for assessing natural perturbations of flood events. In this study, we discuss the characteristics of flood evolution and flood risk under the influence of climate factors, that’s why we used natural flow for flood risk evaluation while the impact of human activities on water resources and flood was not considered. Thus, flood risk may be overestimated to some extent compared with that under the impact of human activities. Meanwhile, the discharge series of four hydrological stations across the YRB had been selected for model verification. These hydrological stations are mainly located in the upper and middle YRB, where hydrological characteristics are less affected by human activities (Mateo et al., 2014; Miao et al., 2022 ), which is more suitable for verification of the effects of simulated natural flow.  5.2 Influence of precipitation on flood magnitude In the context of climate change, changes in extreme precipitation are widely discussed and are often linked to flood events (Prein et al., 2017 ). However, correlation analysis of several extreme precipitation indices and flood magnitude in the YRB shows very low correlation between both intensity and duration of extreme precipitation and flood magnitude, implying that extreme precipitation events are somehow not tightly associated with occurrences of floods. On the contrary, the long-term accumulated precipitation with medium and high intensity had a higher correlation with flood intensity, which had a stronger influence on flood magnitude over the YRB. Nanditha and Mishra (2022)  and Ivancic and Shaw (2015) , respectively, analyzed the peak discharge of 390 river basins in the Indus River basin and the mainland United States and had similar findings, i.e. heavy precipitation does not necessarily lead to high discharge, and multi-day precipitation may contribute more to peak discharge. By means of hydrological model simulation, we further analyzed the relationship between extreme precipitation and peak discharge, which further confirmed that extreme precipitation was not the main driving factor of flood magnitude in the YRB. Sharma et al. (2018)  discussed the reasons behind this phenomenon and believed that the conditions of the catchment itself had great impacts, such as the influence of soil moisture in the catchment. According to this theory, for floods over the YRB, due to dry climate condition, soil moisture content is generally low (Li et al., 2016 ), and the long-term accumulated precipitation with medium and high intensity increases soil moisture due to infiltration. The combination of high soil moisture and heavy rain events dominates the flood magnitude change in the YRB. Besides, we give the threshold values of precipitation duration and intensity. This theory can partly explain the impact of precipitation on flood magnitude in the YRB. However, we noticed that the correlations between precipitation indices and flood magnitude was about 75–83 %, which means uncertainties exists, for example, extreme precipitation may have a greater impact in some small areas considering the runoff generation from excessive rain. In addition, changes in evapotranspiration caused by rising temperatures will also have an impact on soil moisture. In summary, flood magnitude is comprehensively affected by many natural factors. Although precipitation is the most intuitive and concerned factor among them (Nanditha and Mishra., 2022 ), it is still necessary to collect more evidence for further analysis in order to further explore the potential driving factors of flood magnitude.  5.3 Critical driving factors of flood risk Compared with 1978, Ep  and Es  in the YRB in 2015 had increased by 213,700 people and 34.54 km2 , respectively, which means that the flood risk increased significantly, and this conclusion is consistent with the results of global flood risk assessment (Kundzewicz et al., 2014 ). The MFA of YRB increased at an annual rate of 3.247 km2 , showing a relatively stable inter-annual variation trend, and the flood risk of the YRB was mainly affected by the spatial distribution of disaster-bearing bodies. Flood risk is mainly affected by two types of factors (Kundzewicz et al., 2005 ): (1) the change of disaster magnitude. Due to warming climate, atmospheric water holding capacity and precipitation, which are widely considered as the import factors that affect flood magnitude, are expected to increase. In addition, the duration and intensity of precipitation will increase (Trenberth, 2011 ), thus promoting the occurrence of more frequent flood events. However, the SREX report (Bates et al., 2008 ) pointed out that there is no observational evidence of climate-driven changes in the magnitude and frequency of river flooding globally over the past few decades. As a result, the impact of human activities on flood risk has received increasing attention (Mohanty and Simonovic, 2021 ). (2) Besides, the uncertainty of future flood risk under the influence of human activities is also greatly increased (McDermott, 2022 ), which also brings additional challenges to flood control and disaster reduction work in the YRB. The flood response paradigm also needs to shift from post-disaster response and flood control to flood risk management, thus minimizing the risk of flood damage (Klijn and Koppenjan, 2012; Hartmann and Spit, 2015; Carleton and Solomon, 2016 ). The significance of our study on flood characteristics and flood risk in the YRB is to identify the driving factors of flood risk in the YRB, and to emphasize the importance of reducing TADO in the floodplains through reasonable planning and other measures to reduce flood risk over the YRB.   6 Conclusions By coupling the runoff data simulated by VIC with the Cama-flood model, this paper identified typical floodplains across the YRB from the perspective of flood inundation, and explored the influence of different factors on flood risk by separating influencing factors, so as to evaluate the transformation and development of flood risk in the basin. We analyzed variations in flood magnitude, critical driving factors and risk evolution under the influence of natural factors, thus established a preliminary understanding of flood characteristics in the basin. Results showed that according to the simulated maximum flood inundation extent from 1978 to 2015, five typical flood areas were identified over the YRB, which are Ningxia reach (region A), Daheihe River Basin (region B), middle reaches of Fenhe River basin (region C), the lower reaches of Weihe River (region D) and the Sanmenxia to Jindi River reach (region E). This study evaluated the flood characteristics and flood risk of the basin, based on five typical floodplains. For the flood risk of the basin, Ep  and Es  increased by 213,700 people and 34.54 km2  respectively, while Ec  and Efg  significantly decreased during 1978–2015. From 50-year-return to 1000-year-return flood magnitude, Ep , Ec , Efg  and Es  were 1.47–2.27 times, 1.59–2.47 times, 1–1.5 times, and 1.6–2.47 times of the maximum exposure of 1978–2015, respectively. Flood risk is mainly affected by two factors of flood magnitude and distribution of disaster-bearing bodies; on the one hand, in view of the flood magnitude, there have not been significant changes. Besides, further analysis helps find stronger correlation between long-term accumulated precipitation with medium and high intensity and flood magnitude, which indicates the importance of soil water content and other environmental factors to flood events. When the threshold of annual cumulative precipitation days was 144 days, the correlation was the highest and reached 0.833. On the other hand, based on the analysis of the distribution of disaster-bearing bodies, it was found that human activities were constantly aggregating in floodplains during 1978–2015, which may cause higher flood risk. The TADO of population and settlements in the YRB increased by 889,100 people and 353 km2 , respectively, from 1978–2015, while the TADO of cropland and forest and grassland decreases. In order to evaluate the impact of flood magnitude and disaster-bearing bodies’ distribution on flood risk, the ER index was defined and analyzed. It was found that the ER of various disaster-bearing bodies in YRB had reached to 48.1 %, and the ER in the five floodplains had reached 69.3 %, indicating that a considerable proportion of disaster-bearing bodies were still facing high flood risk. In addition, flood risk to population and settlements in YRB were dominated by flood magnitude.
