1 Introduction The Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP), known as the “Asian Water Tower”, holds huge permafrost and glaciers and thus serves pivotal functions in downstream water availability to more than 1.4 billion people (Immerzeel et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2021 ). Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key determinant in linking water balance and energy budget (Baldocchi et al., 2021; Chapin et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2021 ) and consumes about half of the precipitation and net radiation over the entire QTP (Han et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024 ). The water budget (generally defined as precipitation minus ET, P−ET) reflects surface water provision ability and is directly determined by both precipitation and ET (Cui et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Despite such importance, the substantial uncertainties in long-term patterns of ground ET and P−ET on the QTP still exist relative to climatic variables (such as temperature, rainfall, and radiation), likely owing to the limited availability of field measurements and consequently inadequate understanding of intricate ecohydrological processes (Ma, Zhang, Szilagyi et al., 2015 ; Wang S et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023 ). For example, the increasing trends from 1982 to 2018 (Ma, Zhang, 2022a; Yuan et al., 2024 ) and decreasing trends from 2000 to 2010 (Song et al., 2017 ) of ET derived from different process-based models have been reported across the QTP. P−ET has been affected by the current unprecedented warming climate (Song et al., 2017 ), which resulted in endorheic lake level expansions (Biskop et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016 ) or undetectable river discharges (Cao et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009 ) of the QTP. Therefore, there are still significant uncertainties regarding the long-term variations of ET and P−ET, which urgently need to be addressed to clarify the changing patterns of the water cycle and ecohydrological processes of the QTP. The Penman-Monteith paradigm discloses that ET is comprehensively regulated by atmospheric evaporative demand, surface moisture supply, water vapor transfer resistance, and thermal conditions (Baldocchi et al., 2021, 2022; Ma, Zhang, Szilagyi et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2002 ). Over the last decades, numerous efforts have been made to explore the ET’s variability of alpine grasslands across seasons and types, but the environmental determinants and their relative contributions vary greatly. For instance, studies argued that ET’s variability was mainly controlled by either surface water supply, including soil moisture content (Ma, 2023; McFadden et al., 2003; Song et al., 2017 ) and precipitation input (Ma, Zhang, 2022a ), or energy availability (Chang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018 ), or bulk canopy resistance (Li, Wang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023 ). Regarding the role of vegetation, alpine plants generally adopt stress-tolerant strategies and are characterized by slow growth rate and prostrate stature (Ma, Zhang, Guo et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018 ), which substantially contributed to low plant transpiration and soil evaporation caused by the shielding of solar radiation (Wang et al., 2012 ), and consequently resulted in high water provision capacity (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). Other studies, however, suggested that vegetation growth exerted limited influences on ET’s variability (Ma, Zhang, 2022b ) and just played a proxy in partitioning ET into more plant transpiration than soil evaporation in alpine meadows (Cao et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018 ). These aforementioned inconsistent findings are usually derived from manifest variables’ correlation-like analysis of the short-term (< 10 years) studies, which makes our understanding of how ET responds to climate change still inadequate in alpine grasslands (Zheng et al., 2024, 2023 ). P−ET and topsoil water storage change (∆SWS) collectively modulate the regional atmospheric moisture circulations and surface water availability (Chapin et al., 2011; Pellet et al., 2020 ) and are regulated by complex soil moisture-atmosphere feedbacks (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2021 ). The warm-season precipitation generally converged to ET (Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022 ) and regulated the variations of P−ET in alpine grasslands (Li, Zhang et al., 2021 ). The water provision ability of alpine grasslands is thus possibly determined by the cold-season P−ET, which has increased in the western arid regions from 2000 to 2010 (Song et al., 2017 ) or remained stable (decreased) in the eastern semi-arid (humid) regions from 1982 to 2016 (Ma, Zhang, 2022a ), indicating an unexpected “dry get wetter, wet get drier” trend on the QTP (Allan et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021 ). ∆SWS represents the potential response of the water cycle to environmental perturbations whereas popular satellite-derived studies are less validated by long-term ground observations (Pellet et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Given the limited availability of multiyear ground-based observations, quantifying the long-term variations of ET, P−ET, and ∆SWS, as well as the relative contributions of environmental determinants remain largely unquantified, which poses challenges in the accurate assessments and projections of water provision of alpine grasslands (Pellet et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2024 ). Albeit covering ∼5% of the QTP area, alpine shrublands are generally located between uphill snowpack mountains and downhill alpine meadows and consequently play disproportional roles in regional water balance and ecosystem functioning (Li et al., 2019 ). Previous studies showed that the variations of the warm-season ET and P−ET in alpine shrublands were controlled by net radiation and precipitation, respectively (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019 ). Nonetheless, the full understanding of water balance is limited by the absence of knowledge from the cold season (Wang et al., 2021 ), when valid measurements are generally insufficient due to the harsh climates and system malfunctions. This question is particularly important for the QTP that have been experiencing rapid winter warming and significant water-related changes, such as permafrost and glacier degradation (Wang et al., 2021 ), water phase transformation from solid water and liquid or gaseous one (Ma, Zhang, 2022a; Yuan et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024 ), and vegetation degradation and restoration (Shen et al., 2015 ). Here we investigated the long-term (2003−2021) year-round flux measurements using eddy covariance techniques in an alpine shrubland on the northeastern QTP to address the two key issues: 1) quantifying the intra- and inter-annual variations of ET, P−ET, and ∆SWS; and 2) clarifying the relative contributions of environmental controls and underlying ecohydrological processes. We hypothesized that ET variability would be controlled by available energy and this alpine shrubland would not have a considerable water provision capacity, since the warm-season precipitation was almost evapotranspired to the atmosphere and the cold-season received limited precipitation around the study areas (Chang et al., 2022; Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Our findings would hopefully provide full assessments of the water balance and improve the projections of water conservation capacity in high-altitude alpine grasslands.  2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Study site The study site (N37°40', E101°20', 3400 m) is about 10 km north of Haibei National Field Research Station for Alpine grassland (Haibei Station,  Fig. 1 ), which lies on the northeastern QTP and is a member of China Flux Observation and Research Network (ChinaFLUX). The site is 3 km south from the foot of Lenglongling, which runs from north-west to south-east. The climate is plateau continental, with a cold-dry non-growing season from November to April and a warm-wet growing season from May to October. The mean annual air temperature (T a ) is –1.1°C, with the maximum and minimal monthly T a  averages 9.9°C in July and –13.1°C in January, respectively. The annual precipitation averages 460.0 mm, with ∼80% recorded as rainfall during the growing season (Li, Zhang et al., 2021 ). The shallow groundwater and permafrost in the study region are ∼4.0 m and ∼6.0 m belowground, respectively (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The vegetation is dominated by overstory deciduous shrubs (Potentilla fruticosa ) and understory herbages, including Kobresia humilis , Polygonum viviparum , Stipa aliena , Poa orinosa , Helictotrichon tibeticum , Elymus nutans , Aster flaccidus , Polygonum viviparum , and Leontopodium nanum . The canopy height and vegetation coverage of the shrub and grass layers are ∼50 cm and ∼60%, and ∼20 cm and ∼80%, respectively. The peak green leaf area index and aboveground herbaceous phytomass are ∼2.5 m2  m-2  in mid-July and ∼310 g m-2  in end-August, respectively. The shrubland is used as a winter pasture and grazed moderately (3.75 sheep·ha−1 ) by yaks and Tibetan sheep from end-October to mid-May (Li et al., 2016 ). The soil is a sandy loam. The surface (0-10 cm) soil constitutes 59.8% loam, 34.3% sand, and 5.9% clay. The surface soil bulk density and organic matter content are ∼0.60 g cm-3  and ∼120.0 g kg-1 , respectively. The saturated capacity and permanent wilting point of surface soil are 178.2 and 19.1 mm, respectively (Li et al., 2019 ).  2.2 Flux measurements, data processing, and quality control Since August 2002, ET has been continuously measured by an eddy covariance system, which comprised a 3-D ultrasonic anemometer (CAST3, Campbell Scientific, USA) and an open-path infrared gas analyzer (Li7500, Li-Cor, USA), mounted at a height of 2.5 m aboveground. The terrains of the flux tower were rather flat and homogenous, with areas of ∼10 km2  (Fig. 1  and S1). The 2-D footprint analysis (Kljun et al., 2015 ) using the daytime valid data of 2021 showed that the cumulative 90% fluxes occurred within a radius of ∼100 m of the flux tower (Fig. 1 ). The raw data frequency of 3-D wind speed, virtual temperature, and the density of CO2  and water vapor was uniform 10 Hz. The micro-climate has been simultaneously observed by an adjacent (< 5.0 m) auto weather station since August 2002. These variables were mainly composed of 1.5 m air temperature and water vapor pressure (HMP45C, Vaisala, Finland), 1.5 m wind speed and direction (034 A and 014 A, RM-Young, USA), 1.5 m four-component radiation (CNR-4, Kipp&Zonen, Netherlands) and photosynthetically photon flux density (LI-190SB, Li-Cor, USA), 0.5 m precipitation (52202, RM-Young, USA), −0.05 m (a negative value means belowground) soil heat fluxes (HFT-3, Campbell Scientific, USA), −0.05 m soil temperature (105 T, Campbell Scientific, USA), and −0.10 m and −0.20 m volumetric soil water content (CS616, Campbell Scientific, USA). The auto weather station was synchronized with the eddy covariance system and measured at 30-minute intervals. Because a tilting bucket precipitation gauge cannot accurately monitor snow and hail or system malfunctions, monthly precipitation data were interpolated using a linear regression derived from measurements of the shrubland and Haibei Station if necessary (mostly missing or a few data exceeded the 99% prediction intervals of the fitted linear regression). Precipitation of Haibei Station was observed manually two times (8:00 and 20:00, Beijing Standard Time) each day according to the conventional meteorological observation specifications. The flux tower and auto weather station were enclosed by a 50 m × 50 m wire fence to insulate sheep and yaks. Satellite-derived normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) was used to capture the temporal variations of plant growth and then to quantify the importance of vegetation growth to water balance. The 16-day NDVI was centered on the flux tower at a spatial resolution of 250 m and was generated by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center (ORNL DAAC, http://daac.ornl.gov/MODIS/modis.html ). Only the growing season NDVI (> 0.15) was used for analyses, since alpine plants are dormant during the non-growing season. The abnormal values in NDVI serials probably caused by high cloud coverage were discarded and temporally interpolated (Li et al., 2023 ). The 30-minute ET was recomputed from raw frequency data by EddyPro 7.0.4 (Li-Cor, USA). The main procedures included spike removal, 2-D coordinate rotation, time-lag compensation, Webb-Pearman-Leuning air density correction, low- and high-frequency spectral correction, and quality check. We discarded the poorest quality observations flagged “2” (Foken et al., 2005 ) and kept the others. The latent heat flux dataset was filtered to remove outliers (<−100 W m-2  or >500 W m-2 ) and screened with night-time friction velocity threshold (< 0.15 m s-1 ) because of sensor malfunctions or low turbulence (Li et al., 2023 ). The annual valid data proportion averaged ∼50% (Table S1 ), which was comparable to the results of ChinaFLUX (Zhang et al., 2020 ). ET data gaps mainly occurred during the non-growing season and the nighttime and were gap-filled by the boosted regression trees model (BRT), which is a supervised machine learning logarithm and outperforms other conventional gap-filling techniques (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ). Given that the ET of alpine grasslands was driven by different environmental controls during the growing season and non-growing season (Zhang et al., 2018 ), BRTs of these two seasons were separately trained by the valid data of ET and key environmental controls, including T a , water vapor pressure, solar radiation, wind speed, soil temperature, and soil water content. The fitted BRTs, combined with environmental controls corresponding to ET gaps, were used to fill those gaps (Li et al., 2023 ). The annual energy balance ratio during the growing season averaged 0.78 (Fig. S2 ). The energy imbalance resulted probably from the underestimation (∼10%) of soil heat flux in cold regions (McFadden et al., 2003; Xin et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Besides, our earlier studies (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018 ) suggested that the actual ET in midsummer could sometimes exceed the reference ET estimated by FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation on a hypothetical well-watered grass (Allen et al., 1998 ). Therefore, the ET of the shrubland should not be underestimated and energy balance residual correction on ET was not performed. The midday (9:00−17:00) aerodynamic resistance (r a ) and bulk canopy resistance (r s ) were calculated by the following equation from earlier studies (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018 ), respectively.(1) r  a   = W  s    u  *  2     + 6.2 W  s    − 0.67       (2) r  s   = ρ C  p   ( VPD )   λ ( LET )    + ( β Δ γ  − 1 ) r  a       where W s  is the wind speed (m s-1 ), u *  is the friction velocity (m s-1 ), ρ is the air density (kg m-3 ), C p  is the specific heat of air at constant pressure (1013 J kg-1  K-1 ), γ is the psychrometric constant (kPa K-1 ), Δ is the slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve at air temperature (kPa K-1 , 2503 e  17.27 T  a   / ( T  a   + 237.3 )    ( T  a   + 237.3 )  2      ), VPD is the saturated vapor pressure deficit (kPa), β is the Bowen ratio (H/LET, in which H is the sensible heat flux, LET is the latent heat flux). ET, P−ET, NDVI, r a , r s , and other environmental variables were aggregated or averaged into a monthly and annual scale for further analysis. The terrain surface water balance is generally determined by three major components: water input (precipitation and drainage from uphill mountains Di ), water loss (ET, surface runoff Dr , deep soil seepage Ds ), and soil water storage change ΔSWS (Chapin et al., 2011 ). Therefore, P−ET equals the sum of ΔSWS and discharge D. All items (Dr , Ds , and Di ) of D are not readily observed and can be estimated in our study according to Eq. (3) .(3) P − ET = Δ SWS + D      Monthly ΔSWS was simply calculated by the difference in SWS (the product of averaged SWC at 20 cm and 0−20 cm soil depth) of two adjacent months (Zhang et al., 2019 ). It should be noted that SWS just comprised liquid soil moisture because soil ice content can’t be observed by our instruments so far.  2.3 Statistical analysis BRT has a high tolerance for collinearity and non-normal distribution of predicted factors (Elith et al., 2008 ), and was further used to quantify the relative contributions of environmental factors to the variations in monthly ET. The key factors mainly included T a , the slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve with respect to T a  (△), saturated vapor pressure deficit (VPD), precipitation, wind speed (W s ), net radiation (R n ), 5 cm soil temperature (T s ), 10 cm soil water content (SWC), r a , r s , NDVI, and a categorical variable (Stage: GS for the growing season and NGS for the non-growing season). BRTs were conducted by the “Dismo” package (Elith et al., 2008 ). Piecewise structural equation model (SEM), which can partition the causal relationships of variables and separate the direct and indirect effects on predictors (Lefcheck, 2016 ), was conducted to explore the potential pathways of composite or observed variables on the monthly and yearly variations of ET, respectively, because of the different size of data volume. Those abovementioned manifest variables were divided into four composite variables, namely atmospheric evaporative demand (R n  and VPD), surface moisture supply (SWC, precipitation, and NDVI), water vapor transfer resistance (r a  and r s ), and thermal conditions (T a , T s , and △). SEM was separately solved by local estimation and was judged by alternative Shipley’s test of d-separation (Fisher’s C), Akaike’s and Bayesian Information Criterion (AIC and BIC), and P  value. The goodness-of-fit of the SEM was evaluated by a χ2  test comparing the estimated to the observed covariance matrices. SEMs were conducted by the “piecewiseSEM” package (Lefcheck, 2016 ). The difference in sensitivity (slope of linear regression) of ET (P−ET) with key controls between the vegetation growth stage (growing season and non-growing season) was estimated by marginal means of linear trends. The categorical stage was also introduced in linear models. It was performed by the “emmeans” package (Lenth, 2020; Lenth, 2020; Lenth, 2020; Lenth, 2020 ) The abovementioned statistical analysis, correlation, and linear (non-linear) regression, were conducted in R 4.0.2 (R Development Core Team, 2006 ).   3 Results 3.1 Inter-annual variations of environmental variables Annual T a  and precipitation were −1.1 ± 0.4°C (Mean ± S.D., the same as below) and 459.1 ± 58.4 mm, respectively. T a  increased significantly at a rate of 0.40°C decade-1  while precipitation decreased little (P  > 0.05,  Fig. 2 a, c). It should be noted that T a  increased significantly (R 2   = 0.17, P  < 0.01) and precipitation decreased marginally (R 2   = 0.13, P  = 0.07) only during the growing season (Fig. S3 ). Annual VPD was 0.22 ± 0.02 kPa and fluctuated little (P  < 0.05, Fig. 2 b). Annual R n  and SWC averaged 99.3 ± 9.3 W m-2  and 0.22 ± 0.02 m3  m-3 , respectively, both increased significantly (Fig. 2 d, e). Only the non-growing season R n  (R 2   = 0.22, P  < 0.05) and the growing season SWC (R 2   = 0.64, P  < 0.001) increased significantly (Fig. S3 ). Annual growing season NDVI was 0.41 ± 0.02 and significantly increased by 0.025 decade-1  (Fig. 2 f).  3.2 Monthly and yearly ET Monthly ET averaged 41.7 ± 31.9 mm and exhibited a unimodal season pattern with a peak (96.7 ± 26.4 mm) occurring in July ( Fig. 3 ). The BRT analysis on monthly ET of the whole season showed that the slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve with respect to T a  (Δ) alone accounted for 37.6% of variations in monthly ET ( Fig. 4 ). T s  and r s  had a secondary effect, with ∼20% of relative contributions (Fig. 4 ). The SEM analysis from composite variables consistently confirmed that thermal conditions, comprising T a , T s , and Δ, exerted predominant effects on the variations of monthly ET ( Fig. 5 a). The total effects of thermal conditions were 0.94, including its indirect effects through atmospheric evaporative demand (0.86 × 0.18) and water vapor transfer resistance (−0.24 × −0.24). It was worth noting that BRT and SEM analyses accordantly suggested that NDVI did not substantially affect growing season ET variability (Figs. S4 and S5 ). Annual ET ranged from 427.8 mm in 2018 to 679.6 mm in 2016 and averaged 512.2 ± 68.4 mm, with a mean value of 406.1 ± 54.1 mm in the growing season and 106.1 ± 17.5 mm in the non-growing season ( Fig. 6 a). Neither did they show significant temporal trends nor did they relate to precipitation (P  > 0.05, Fig. 6 a), supported by a phenomenon that higher annual ET coincided with lower annual precipitation (Fig. 2 ). Correlation analysis showed that ET was significantly related to r s  negatively and R n  positively (Fig. S6 ). The SEM analysis further revealed that the inter-annual variations in ET were controlled directly by r s  and indirectly by R n  (Fig. 5 b). The relationships of annual ET with r s  and R n  could be depicted by a one-phase exponential decay curve and a positive linear equation, respectively ( Fig. 7 ).  3.3 Monthly and yearly P−ET and ΔSWS Monthly P−ET cumulated to −4.4 ± 21.8 mm over the whole season, and averaged 18.3 ± 26.3 mm in August (16.2 ± 55.0 mm) and September (20.3 ± 60.5 mm) while stayed negative (−8.2 ± 17.6 mm) during the other months (Fig. 3 ). Monthly P−ET was significantly related to ET (R 2  = 0.25,  Fig. 8 ) more than precipitation (R 2  = 0.05, P  = 0.01, Fig. S7a ) during the non-growing season while to precipitation (R 2  = 0.47, Fig. 8 ) more than ET (R 2  = 0.05, P  = 0.01, Fig. S7b ) during the growing season. Across the whole season, the variations in monthly P−ET were determined by monthly precipitation, rather than monthly ET (R 2  < 0.01, P  < 0.05), providing that the growing season ET accounted for 97.1% of the whole season ET (Fig. S8 ). Monthly ΔSWS showed an “M” seasonal pattern, with a first peak (28.8 ± 11.2 mm) in May and a second peak (3.0 ± 2.7 mm) in September (Fig. 3 ). Partial correlation analysis showed that the variations of monthly ΔSWS were much more regulated by ET (r  = −0.19, P  < 0.05), rather than by precipitation (r  = −0.036, P  > 0.05) during the growing season. During the non-growing season, ΔSWS was collectively determined by ET (r  = 0.53, P  < 0.001) and precipitation (r  = 0.36, P  < 0.001). Annual P−ET averaged −53.2 ± 95.4 mm, being −1.5 ± 88.5 mm in the growing season and −51.6 ± 21.0 mm in the non-growing season. The variations of annual P−ET were jointly determined by precipitation and ET, regardless of vegetation growth stages ( Fig. 9 ). Moreover, the sensitivity (the absolute value of the slope from linear regression) of P−ET with precipitation and ET was similar (P  > 0.05, Fig. S9 ). Although the slope of P−ET with precipitation seemed to be lower than that of ET during the non-growing season (Fig. 9 ), the difference was insignificant (P  > 0.05, Fig. S10 ). Annual ΔSWS was almost zero (0.4 ± 3.8 mm, Fig. 3 ) and averaged 16.1 ± 9.0 mm in the growing season and −15.7 ± 9.8 mm in the non-growing season. ΔSWS increased marginally significantly (P  = 0.06, Fig. 6 c) only during the growing season. Annual ΔSWS was significantly related to ET negatively (r  = −0.59, P  < 0.01) in the growing season while to ET positively (r  = 0.62, P  < 0.01) during the non-growing season (Fig. S11 ). The sensitivity of ΔSWS with ET of the non-growing season was significantly higher than that of the growing season (P  < 0.001, Fig. S11 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Determinants of intra-annual variations in ET Effortful studies have summarized that ET was jointly regulated by biotic variables (photosynthesis type, vegetation form, and growth status) and abiotic factors (moisture status, energy supply, and aerodynamic condition) in alpine regions (Chang et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2021; McFadden et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2023 ). BRT and SEM analyses consistently showed that thermal conditions, more than other environmental factors, determined the intra-annual variations of ET in the alpine shrubland (Figs. 4 and 5 ). This finding aligned with the classic water-energy hypothesis (Budyko, 1974 ) and recent reports that T a  dominated ET’s variability in the eastern QTP where moisture supply was ample (Li et al., 2023; Ma, 2023; Ma, Zhang, 2022a; Yuan et al., 2024 ). However, the predominance of thermal conditions was somewhat different from the reports that the key driver of radiation energy availability in nearby alpine meadows (Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2024 ) albeit thermal status partly reflected the amount of radiation energy (Chapin et al., 2011; Körner, 2003 ). This difference could probably be attributed to the fact that alpine regions are generally constrained by thermal conditions and receive comparable net radiation energy relative to lowlands (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018 ). On the one hand, high thermal conditions meant the increased atmospheric moisture holding capacity (Allan et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021 ) and atmospheric evaporative demands (Fig. 5 a), which substantially simulated plant transpiration and soil evaporation under sufficient water availability (Baldocchi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2024 ). This was especially the case for the deep-rooted shrubs, which have more access to deep soil moisture reserves (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Ma, 2023 ). Such an explanation could be supported by the first-class importance of Δ on the variations of monthly ET (Figs. 4 and 5 ). On the other hand, thermal conditions were closely related to the kinetics of water molecules. The high temperature could favor liquid water vaporization and solid water melting and sublimation (Or et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024 ). It was partly supported by that ET was to some extent limited by moisture availability because of frozen topsoil (Chang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018 ) during the non-growing season (ET = 78.76SWC + 0.47precipitation + 3.04, R 2  = 0.68, P  < 0.001; Fig. S5b ). In addition, because of a relatively lower vapor pressure deficit, thermal conditions were found to be positively correlated to alpine plant stomatal conductance and vegetation transpiration (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2024 ), which accounted for ∼70% of ET in this alpine shrubland (Hu et al., 2009 ). The vegetation growth status, indicated by a stage categorical variable, played a negligible role in the variations of monthly ET (Fig. 4 , S4, and S5), which partly supported a proxy function that vegetation growth just partitioned ET into more transpiration than evaporation in alpine grasslands (Cao et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018 ). It potentially was a mechanism consequence of an equivalent water vapor transfer resistance from vegetation and topsoil. The optimal stomatal resistance among dominant alpine plants fluctuated little and approximately converged at 200 s m-1  (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023 ), which was comparable with the mean value (∼220 s m-1 ) of topsoil water vapor transfer resistance during the growing season (Hu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Such similar resistance of vegetation and topsoil indicated that the increased plant transpiration induced by vegetation growth could fully compensate for the decreased soil evaporation caused by the shading effects of solar radiation (Ma et al., 2021; Ma, Zhang, 2022b; Wang et al., 2012 ), and vice versa. Therefore, vegetation growth didn’t directly drive the temporal variations of ET in the alpine shrubland. However, this finding could not exclude the substantial effects on ET from plant community shifts caused by grassland degradation or ecological rehabilitation (Shen et al., 2015 ; Wang J et al., 2023). Future pairwise comparisons are urgently needed to detect how vegetation transformation affects ET in alpine grasslands, given that large-scale ecological restoration programs have been campaigning for the last decades over the QTP.  4.2 Determinants of inter-annual variations in ET Annual ET averaged 510 mm, which was consistent with the short-term studies of the same site (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2023 ) and was lower than ET (∼600 mm) of low-altitude (< 3200 m) alpine meadows while was higher than ET (∼350 mm) of high-altitude (> 4500 m) alpine grasslands on the QTP (Chang et al., 2022; Ma, Zhang, Guo et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018 ). The inter-annual variations of ET were indirectly controlled by R n  through bulk canopy resistance r s   (Fig. 5 b) and decoupled with precipitation in the shrubland, which agreed with the finding derived from the energy-limited ecosystems (Baldocchi et al., 2021 ; Wang S et al., 2023). Generally, r s   integrated the effects of soil vapor transfer resistance and vegetation stomatal resistance (Ma, 2023; Ma, Zhang, Guo et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2002 ), which were assumed to negatively scale with soil water content and leaf area at a given site (Baldocchi et al., 2021, 2022; Hu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Not NDVI (P  > 0.50) but SWC was significantly related to r s  (Fig. S12 , P  < 0.001). It might result from a certain coverage of overlying nonvascular mosses on the soil surface (Li et al., 2019 ), whose resistance exponentially increased when tissue water decreased and thus canceled the negative effects of vascular plant growth on vegetation stomatal resistance. This speculation might explain the vanishing effects on annual ET variability of thermal conditions, which little affected the long-term water conductance of nonvascular mosses (McFadden et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2022 ). The significantly negative effects of annual R n  on annual r s  (Figs. 5 and 7 ), together with an increased SWC (Fig. 2 ) while a relatively stable ΔSWS (Fig. 6 ), consistently manifested the energy-limited feature of annual ET in the alpine shrubland (Li, Zhang et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024 ). Because annual R n  increased significantly only during the non-growing season (Fig. S3 ) when ET was to some extent water-limited (Fig. S5b ), the increased R n  could not stimulate annual ET substantially (Fig. 6 ). The insignificant temporal trend of annual ET was linked with the stable r s  (Fig. 7  and S12) and resisted to current chronic climatic variability. This finding indicated that the shrubland had a biological-regulatory ability in ET variability, likely because of the co-existence of woody and non-woody plant species and nonvascular mosses and the consequent tradeoff between transpiration and evaporation (Wang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2024, 2023 ).  4.3 The intra- and inter-annual variations of P−ET and ΔSWS The season patterns of P−ET and ΔSWS reflected terrestrial water mass variations and could be ascribed to ET, precipitation, and additional water sources (Baldocchi et al., 2021; Pellet et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The negative P−ET and ΔSWS of the non-growing season (Fig. 3 ) were consistent with high winter ET/P ratio (∼3.5) and net water loss in alpine grasslands (Chang et al., 2022 ; Wang S et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023 ). The dominant roles of ET in variation of P−ET (Fig. 8 ) and ΔSWS (Fig. S11 ) during the non-growing season likely resulted from tight relations between water supply (precipitation and soil water content) and ET (Fig. S5b ), when moisture availability was substantially constrained by frozen soil (Wang S et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019 ) and limited precipitation input (Wang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018, 2023 ). In May, thawing soil moisture was retained in the top layer because of increased temperature and frozen subsoil (Yuan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2019 ), together with a lower ET, which explained the first peak of ΔSWS (Fig. 3 ). During August and September, the shrubland shifted from a water sink to a water source, which was consistent with increased river discharges (Cao et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009 ) and consequent endorheic lake expansions (Biskop et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2011 ) in autumn on the QTP. However, the second small peak of ΔSWS in September possibly resulted from not only extra P−ET but also the lateral flows of melting uphill snowpacks and glaciers (Wang et al., 2022 ). This hypothesis was partly supported by an insignificant pathway of ET with water supply (SWC and precipitation) during the growing season (Fig. S5a ). Besides, the positive (∼17.2 mm, Fig. 3 ) net discharge (P − ET − ΔSWS) also indicated the lateral flow supply albeit ET (∼406.1 mm) almost depleted the homochronous precipitation (∼404.5 mm). In addition, a recent study using a stable isotope technique found that the surrounding uphill thawing permafrost was another important moisture source for ET (Xiao et al., 2020 ). Future research is needed to clarify the effect of lateral flow and deep soil moisture on water balance, although it would be a major challenge because these water transports have not been non-destructively measured so far (Pellet et al., 2020 ). Given that the ET loss of near alpine meadows was more than its precipitation input (Chang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018 ) and ΔSWS tended to be conservative (Fig. 3 ), neither P−ET nor ΔSWS was not an appropriate indicator for water availability of alpine grasslands (Ma, Zhang, 2022a ). The variability in components of water balance suggested the response of the water cycle to climate change (Baldocchi et al., 2021; Pellet et al., 2020 ). Although annual T a , R n , SWC, and NDVI increased significantly (Fig. 2  and S3), none of P, ET, P−ET, and ΔSWS changed significantly (Fig. 6 ), which agreed with results that the water cycle was relatively stable (Zheng et al., 2023 ) and slightly connected with vegetation coverage (Li et al., 2023 ) in semi-arid shrublands. However, the continuous water deficit, together with a higher sensitivity of ΔSWS with ET during the non-growing season (Fig. S11 ), might lead to a direr region, when extra water supplies (i.e., melting of snowpack and glaciers, thawing of permafrost) would be depleted under the context of unprecedented warming on the QTP (Wang et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024 ). Besides, the water deficit of the non-growing season could consume the deep soil water reservoir, which was uplifted by soil freezing in winter (Zhang et al., 2019 ) but couldn’t be observed by our instruments. This might accelerate the ecosystem water loss and need to be quantified in the future. The negative annual P−ET underscored that the alpine shrubland played a function of water retention rather than water provision, by transforming rapid and intermittent precipitation into a slow and continuous ET (Chang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023 ). The inter-annual variations of P−ET were both determined by precipitation and ET and the sensitivities appeared to be homogenous (Fig. 9 , S9, and S10), suggesting the simultaneous increasing ET and precipitation would not directly impact P−ET (Li, Zhang et al., 2021 ), which supported a non-significant temporal trend in P−ET on the QTP over the last 35 years albeit both of them increased (Ma, Zhang, 2022a ). The equivalent contribution of ET and P on P−ET variability possibly stemmed from the dominance of precipitation under wetter conditions during the warm seasons (Li, Zhang et al., 2021 ) could cancel the dominance of ET under drier conditions during the cold seasons (Zhang et al., 2023 ).   5 Conclusion This study investigated long-term year-round measurements of ET, water budget, and soil water storage change by eddy covariance techniques in an alpine shrubland on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. The variations of monthly ET were determined by thermal conditions, especially the slope of the saturated vapor pressure curve with respect to air temperature. The shrubland was a water sink and monthly P−ET was dominated by ET during the non-growing season, and behaved as a water source and monthly P−ET was controlled by precipitation during the growing season. Annual ET was regulated directly by bulk canopy resistance and indirectly by net radiation. Annual P−ET variability was significantly controlled both by precipitation and ET, with a similar but opposite sensitivity. Our findings revealed the energy-limited feature of ET loss and a water retention function to catchments of the alpine shrubland. All authors critically collaborated in the interpretation of the results and the writing of the paper and gave final approval for publication.
1 Introduction In response to modern socioeconomic development and increased human activities, the vast water energy resources found in rivers and lakes require urgent exploitation. Consequently, an array of hydraulic structures such as reservoirs, sluice gates, and canals has emerged. These structures significantly influence rivers and lakes, altering not only the hydrodynamic characteristics of the water bodies but also their water quality, environmental conditions, and water exchange capacity. Structures drastically modify the hydrodynamic parameters, including the water level, flow rate, and velocity, by obstructing, withdrawing, and draining water. Concurrently, changes in flow pattern may induce eutrophication and algal blooms due to alterations in components such as microorganisms and nutrients, leading to water quality degradation (Defu et al., 2016). Several studies have suggested that there is a substantial correlation between the water exchange rate and water quality, as well as environmental conditions (Pan et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2021; Yerubandi et al., 2016; You and Zhang, 2018 ). The faster the water circulation is, the better the water quality is. For example, in certain lakes and bays where water stagnation occurs, nutrients tend to accumulate, exacerbating regional water environmental crises and eutrophication risks. Therefore, water exchange is a vital factor to understand the environmental quality of large-scale shallow lakes. There are several indicators that illustrate water exchange rates, including flushing time, residence time, and water age. The residence time is usually defined as the time it takes for a water parcel to leave the domain of interest (Delhez et al.,2004 ). The flushing time refers to the time a water body spends from its entrance into the study area to its departure. Water age, a concept proposed and refined by Bert et al. (1973)  and Delhez et al. (1999) , which is defined as the time that has elapsed since a water parcel under consideration left the region in which its age is prescribed as zero. When a body of water at a location has different sources, the water age at that location from different starting points to flow to the time of the weighted average of the amount of water from different sources. Indicators such as the flushing time can provide the water exchange rate of an entire lake or river section, however, they lack the precision to describe localized sections of a water body. Conversely, water age can be used to derive both the macro exchange rate for the entire water body and to depict the spatial variation of water exchange rate of study area, allowing for the quantification of the water renewal cycle and pollutant migration. It is a common timescale index utilized for describing water exchange and providing a new method for studies of water exchange. Numerous scholars worldwide have conducted extensive research on water exchange in lakes and rivers. For example, Huang et al. (2022)  and Qi et al. (2016)  developed water age models for Poyang Lake to explore its spatial and temporal characteristics, and they concluded that the factors influencing water age in Poyang Lake are primarily the upstream water inflow and the outlet level. Zhang et al. (2016)  established a hydrodynamic water quality model for Dianchi Lake and found that the diversion project reduced the lake's renewal time and reduced its TP with minimal effects on the TN and Chla contents. Liu et al. (2012)  calculated the water age of the Bohai Sea which from Yellow River, and suggested that tidal forcing plays the most dominant role in controlling the water age in the Bohai Sea. Liu et al. (2021)  established a water age model for Bosten Lake in Xinjiang to evaluate improvement measures for water body exchange, providing local government guidance on gate operations and farmland irrigation. Similarly, Liu et al. (2020)  established a water age model for Taihu Lake and found that the wind field can significantly change water age of large shallow lakes, and the flow and initial water level also affect water age. Ren et al. (2014)  and Zhang et al. (2021)  developed a hydrodynamic-water age model for the Pearl River Estuary. They concluded that water age of the upper layer is less than that of the lower layer, and tidal action affects water age at lower flow rates. They also quantitatively analyzed the effects of sensitive parameters such as the seasons, wind field, and surge on water age. Elías Pinilla et al. (2020)  explored the role of wind in the transport and vertical exchange of water bodies in the Patagonian fjord. Dongting Lake, located in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River Basin on the southern bank of the Jingjiang River (the middle section of the Yangtze River), the water is diverted from and flow into the Yangtze River. It is China's second-largest freshwater lake and also the first large-scale lake downstream of the TGD on the Yangtze River. Given its vast storage capacity, Dongting Lake serves as a crucial reservoir in the Yangtze River Basin, repeatedly alleviating flooding along the Yangtze River. In recent years, the interaction between the rivers and lakes has become increasingly complex, especially after the operation of the TGD, which significantly altered the hydrological conditions of the middle-lower reaches of the Yangtze River and Dongting Lake. As a result, this topic has received growing attention. For example, after the operation of the TGD, the water level at the Zhicheng station was found to be lower under the same flow rate (Li et al., 2016). Sediment scouring also modified the Jingjiang Three Outlet (JTO) system's topography, leading to a rise in the JTO’s water level. Zhang et al. (2019)  explored the hydrological status and lake level of the Dongting Lake Basin after operation of the TGD and concluded that the dam decreased the JTO diversions during the dry season and impaired the lake's storage capacity. Dai et al. (2017)  discovered that there was a reduction in JTO diversions from the Jingjiang River in September and October of each year prior to the TGD becoming operational, while the outflow of Chenglingji increased. However, the total water resources in the lake decreased, with an increase noted in May and June. Jiang et al. (2010) determined that the sand transport decreased and the scouring volume changed in the early stage of the operation of the TGD, and the decreased in the diversion and sand distribution at the JTO were basically consistent with the previous conclusions. In-depth studies have also been conducted on the primary water quality characterization indices of the lake. Geng et al. (2021)  examined pollution levels in each region of Dongting Lake during different years, explored the principal factors affecting water pollution based on the location, and proposed an evolutionary trend for the lake's water quality. Tang et al. (2022)  studied the changes in the fluxes and characteristics of metals such as cadmium and copper following the operation of the TGD. Tian et al. (2021)  explored the phosphorus transport pattern in Dongting Lake under the new water and sand conditions after the operation of the TGD. Lai et al. (2017) investigated the role of the TGD in resisting flooding events in Dongting Lake and provided reasonable suggestions. Zhang et al. (2023)  modeled and calculated the habitat suitability of waterbird in Dongting Lake, the results can be used as guidance for prioritizing certain management actions for waterbird conservation. Previous research on Dongting Lake has primarily concentrated on its hydrodynamic characteristics and water quality, such as the runoff, sand content, wetlands, flux of TP and TN. However, studies addressing the water exchange cycle of Dongting Lake are quite limited, particularly those considering the impact of the TGD on the lake's water exchange cycle following the operation of the TGD. As a result, research in this area is both urgently needed and highly significant. This paper seeks to address this gap by establishing a hydrodynamic-water age model to simulate water age of the lake under various conditions, both before and after the operation of the TGD. This model enables us to investigate the spatiotemporal distribution of the lake's water age and how the TGD has impacted the water exchange within the lake. This study provides certain ideas for the management and protection of Dongting Lake and the next development and utilization of the lake.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Dongting Lake (28°30'-30°20' N, 111°50'-113°05' E) is situated on the southern part of the Jingjiang River in the Yangtze River Basin, and on the border between Hunan and Hubei provinces. As depicted in  Fig. 1 , it is the first and largest interconnected river-lake systems on the mainstream of the Yangtze River. Dongting Lake serves as a critical storage lake in the Yangtze River Basin, with a total volume of 22 billion m³ and an average annual inflow of 301.8 billion m³. During the flood season, the lake's surface area is about 2600 km², and it decreases to about 645 km² during the dry season, showcasing the characteristics of a lake in the rainy season and a river in the dry season. The area of Dongting Lake shows a trend of first decreasing and then increasing (Xu et al., 2018 ). When the water level at Chenglingji reaches the warning level of 33 m, the lake's water storage capacity can reach up to 167 billion m³, with an average annual runoff of 312.6 billion m³. The lake consists of three regions - East Dongting Lake, South Dongting Lake, and West Dongting Lake, and receives discharge from four major tributaries (Xiangjiang River, Zijiang River, Yuanshui River, and Lishui River). The water from the Yangtze River mainly enters the Dongting Lake through three outlets located in the northwest catchment, including the Songzi, Taiping, and Ouchi Rivers, and discharges into the Yangtze River from Chenglingji, the only outlet of Dongting Lake. It is the inflow and outflow at JTO and Chenglingji that gives Dongting Lake its unique capacity to absorb and regulate the Yangtze River. The construction and operation of the TGD provided important protection for the safety of the rivers and lakes in the middle-lower reaches of the Yangtze River, particularly in the Dongting Lake Basin, and safety life of the people. In addition, the clear water discharge after the operation of the dam has disrupted the sediment balance between the mainstream of the Yangtze River and the downstream lakes, altering the water exchange relationship of the water bodies between rivers and lakes. The Yangtze River, the world's third largest river, is rich in hydro-energy resources, leading to the creation of major projects such as the TGD. The TGD, located in the Xiling Gorge section of the mainstream of the Yangtze River, is one of the world's largest water conservancy projects and has flood control, power generation, navigation, and water resource utilization functions. The Three Gorges Reservoir stretches from Jiangjin, Chongqing to Sandouping, Yichang, spanning approximately 660 km. At the normal water level of 175 m, the total storage capacity is 39.3 billion m³, with a surface area of 1084 km². After the impoundment of the Three Gorges Reservoir, in combination with the joint scheduling of upstream and downstream reservoirs such as the Xiluodu and Gezhouba reservoirs, it plays a role in peak cutting and valley filling for the mainstream of the Yangtze River. This reduces the pressure of flood control and drought resistance in the middle-lower reaches and provides significant benefits for navigation, power generation, and water resource utilization. However, the establishment of the TGD has sparked many controversies. The dam has blocked the mainstream of the Yangtze River, impacting its connectivity upstream and middle reaches (Tian et al., 2021 ). The dam's sediment retention and subsequent clear water discharge have caused river scouring, affecting the tributary's diversion and thereby impacting the hydrological situation in the Dongting Lake (Lai and Wang, 2017 ).  2.2 Model description The environmental fluid dynamics code (EFDC) was initially developed by John Hamrick at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science in the United States. It is an open-source hydrodynamic model, integrates various modules, including hydrodynamics, water quality, dye transport, and sediment transport modules. Subsequently, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency financed its further development. The EFDC model has been extensively applied in simulations of the hydrodynamics and aquatic environments (Hu et al.,2015; Geng et al.,2021; Zheng et al.,2021 ) of diverse one-, two-, and three-dimensional flow fields, including lakes (Chen et al.,2020 ), reservoirs (Tang et al.,2017, Wu et al.,2017 ), bays (Kiaghadi et al.,2018 ), wetlands (Chen et al.,2017 ), and estuaries (Zhou et al.,2014 ). The EFDC hydrodynamic model is based on three foundational assumptions: the Boussinesq assumption, the hydrostatic pressure approximate assumption, and the nearly three-dimensional approximate assumption. The model's theoretical foundation lies in the conservation laws of the fluid mass, momentum, and energy. The governing equations under these three major assumptions include the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion and other modules that handle parameters such as the salinity, temperature, and dye concentration. Specifically, water age module operates based on the following equations:(1) ∂ c t , x  →      / ∂ t   + ∇ u ∙ c t , x  →        − K ∇ c t , x  →        = 0    (2) ∂ α t , x  →      / ∂ t   + ∇ u ∙ α t , x  →        − K ∇ α t , x  →        = c t , x  →        where c   is the tracer concentration (mg/L), α   is the initial setting value of water age (d), u   is the flow velocity (m/s), K   is the diffusion tensor, t   is time (s), and x   is the coordinate. The conservative tracer represents, in our case, the fraction of river or ocean water and varies between 0 and 1. The age concentration provides a measure of the age of the water parcel, entering with a value of 0 from the sources and increasing its concentration proportionally with advancing time in the model. In this study, we used the EFDC model to establish a two-dimensional hydrodynamic-water age model for the Dongting Lake Basin. The simulation scope spans the Yangtze River from Zhicheng to Luoshan, the western, southern, and eastern of Dongting Lake (inclusive of the JTO water systems), and the Xiangjiang, Zijiang, Yuanshui, and Lishui rivers, extending from the four control hydrology stations on these rivers to the lake. The flow and water level in Dongting Lake exhibited significant inter-annual variations. The flood season in Dongting Lake spans from April to the end of September, and the dry season extends from October to the end of March. In this study, the simulations were conducted over the hydrological year for the study area, i.e., the simulations were run from April 1st to March 31st the next year. The lake region and river channels within the simulation scope were represented as two-dimensional structured grids, consisting of a total of 273,428 cells and covering an area of 4537.10 km2 . The average grid width is 132.57 m in the x-direction and 107.9 m in the y-direction. Given the absence of pronounced thermal stratification in the longitudinal direction and the necessity to save computational time, a standard σ-grid was employed without stratification. The topographical data were derived from a survey conducted in 2011. The inlet boundary of the hydrodynamic model is in six places: Xiangjiang River, Zishui River, Yuanjiang River, Lishui River and the Yangtze River, and the hydrodynamic conditions are actual flow data. The outlet boundary is set by the water level data at Luoshan station on the Yangtze River. The average temperature, rainfall, evaporation, and wind data over many years are used. Calibration and validation are carried out using measured water level data from the Xiangyin, Yingtian, Lujiao, and Chenglingji hydrological stations. The initial timepoint for water age simulation coincides with the five inlet boundaries of the hydrodynamic model, and all of water ages within the entire model are initially set to zero. The water age at the flow boundaries is also set to zero. As the simulation commences, water age begins to be computed, and it evolves over time and with the movement of the water. Water age at each location represents the time it takes for the water to travel from the flow inlet of the model to that location. Notably, unlike other hydrodynamic indices, water age is challenging to monitor and calibrate. However, conceptually, it can be argued that if the hydrodynamic model is accurate, the simulation of water age should also be accurate. Therefore, it is sufficient to conduct calibration and validation of the hydrodynamic model alone. The calibration and validation of the hydrodynamic model parameters are mainly roughness, were conducted over the span of a year, from April 1, 2010 to March 31, 2011, while the validation period extended from April 1, 2011 to March 31, 2012. The roughness values ranged from 0.02 to 0.055. The main floodway had small roughness values, and the shoal had large roughness values. The model validation was carried out by comparing the simulated water level data with the measured water level data from the hydrological stations within the model's scope. In this study, the water level data from Xiangyin, Yingtian, Lujiao, and Chenglingji stations were selected. A comparison of the measured and simulated water level data is presented in  Fig. 2 . The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) were utilized to assess the model's error magnitude. Upon computation, the NSE and RMSE of the measured and simulated water levels at the four stations are presented in  Table 1 . The evaluation indices are within the acceptable range, indicating that the model can simulate the hydrodynamic conditions of the specified range with a high accuracy.  2.4 Scenarios setting The multi-year average hydrological conditions better reflect the average state of the lake. Furthermore, to study the distribution of water age in the lake and the impact of the mainstream of the Yangtze River on water age in the lake, scenario 1–4, specifically the flow boundaries of the four rivers utilize the average daily flow data from 1985 to 2020. This approach mitigates the influences of these four rivers on the lake. scenario 5–7 are modelled using constant flow, the inlet boundaries of four rivers used the average flow during the flood season. The inlet average daily flow and outlet water levels before and after the operation of the TGD are considered in the model. The specific settings are detailed below. The diversion of JTO, flow pattern and outlet water level are considered as crucial factors affecting water age in Dongting Lake. In  Table 2 , Scenario 1 and 2, both the inlet and outlet boundaries of the mainstream of the Yangtze River used the flow and water level before and after the operation of the TGD. A comparison is made to evaluate the difference in water age distribution within the operation of the TGD. In Scenario 3, the inlet of the mainstream of the Yangtze River used the average daily before the operation of the TGD, while the outlet maintains the average daily water level after the operation of the reservoir. This setup, comparison with Scenario 2, allows for analysis the impact of the inflow from the diversion of JTO on water age in the lake. In Scenario 4, the mainstream of the Yangtze River adopts the total flow after the operation of the TGD, and the flow pattern was distributed according to the flow pattern before the operation of the TGD. The outlet water level was set at the average daily flow after the operation of the TGD. This scenario allows for comparison of the impact of the flow pattern on the lake's water age with Scenario 2. Scenarios 5, 6, and 7 included the varying flow frequencies during floods of the upper Yangtze River, corresponding to 10 %, 5 %, and 2 % floods, respectively. The downstream also set different water level that corresponded different frequencies, enabling the exploration of the influence of the outlet water level on the lake's water age based on comparisons of the different scenarios. The specific details are presented in Table 2 .   3 Results 3.1 Spatiotemporal distribution of water age in Dongting Lake The distribution of water age in the Dongting Lake exhibited distinct seasonal characteristics. To more intuitively represent the status of water age distribution in different periods after the operation of the TGD, we averaged the simulation results from Scenario 2 in spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These results are depicted in  Fig. 3 . Overall, water age in the lake exhibited a trend of high in autumn and winter and low in spring and summer. The highest water age is observed at point 8 on the southwest side of East Dongting during autumn. The lowest water age occurs at the exits of the various rivers entering the lake. The three parts of lakes showed noticeable regional differences in water age due to variations in the topography and the different water systems each region accommodates. The range of water age across the different seasons in these three areas is shown in  Fig. 4 . In autumn and winter, the Dongting Lake is primarily inundated only in the floodway and lower-lying terrains. The northern part of the West Dongting Lake and the central and western parts of the South Dongting Lake have higher terrains, and their hydraulic connections within the main floodway are weaker. The highest water ages in these areas are 58 days and 55.2 days during autumn, and 163 days and 98 days during autumn, respectively. In the floodway on the south side of both West and South Dongting Lakes, the confluence of the Xiangjiang River, Zijiang River, and Yuanjiang River occurs. Given the low-lying terrain of these river channels, water age remains relatively low. In contrast, the western side of the East Dongting Lake, which is located farther from the floodway, the higher the elevation is, the greater water age is. The east branch of the Ouchi River flows into the middle of East Dongting Lake and then eastwards into the main floodway. The Ouchi River receives water diverted from the mainstream of the Yangtze River, resulting in low water age. Thus, from the river's exit eastwards to the main floodway of East Dongting Lake with low water age. However, water age on the western side of the East Dongting Lake is generally higher, the outflow of east branch of the Ouchi River effectively splits the area into northern and southern sections. However, due to the inability to exchange water on the west side of East Dongting Lake, water age of the East Dongting River remains relatively high. The primary water exchange mechanism in the East Dongting Lake during autumn and winter is flooding to the continental beach when the water level in the floodway rises. This process results in a generally high water age in the East Dongting Lake during these seasons, with a maximum of 70 days in autumn and 178 days in autumn. In spring and summer, the flow from the four rivers and from the Yangtze River progressively increases. As a result, the water level of the lake rises, and the shoal is incrementally inundated. This leads to a significant increase in the water surface area of the lake throughout these seasons and accelerates the water exchange rate. Even though the West and South Dongting Lakes have relatively high terrains, including shoals, the increase in the water flow and the rise in the lake water level during spring and summer facilitate the flooding of these areas, thereby enhancing the water exchange process and potentially affecting water age. Our analysis revealed that, the confluence of the rivers and the perennially flowing watercourses along the northern and southern peripheries of these beaches notably influences them. The close of these shoals to the floodway further augment the swift water exchange within these locales. Therefore, water age remains relatively low, typically within 60 days during spring and 50 days during summer. These findings underscore the profound impacts of the seasonal river flow fluctuations and lake water levels on the water distribution and turnover within the Dongting Lake. However, the East Dongting Lake presents a unique facet within the Dongting Lake system. Contrary to the West and South Dongting Lake regions, East Dongting Lake lacks the convergence of large-scale rivers. Its primary water influx emanates from South Dongting Lake. Despite the surge in water levels during the flood season, the most of the East Dongting Lake exhibits robust water exchange, particularly around the shoal. This is likely due to the water influx of the floodway. Nevertheless, the vicinity of the embankments of the western part of the lake, which is lacking direct water input from the floodway, faces water exchange constraints. This results in less efficient water mixing in this part of East Dongting Lake, leading to higher water age, reflecting the slower turnover and exchange rates relative to other regions. The multifaceted hydrological attributes of the East Dongting Lake contribute to the considerable variations in water age distribution, particularly around the western embankments and bays. Water age varies extensively, from a minimum of 7 days to a maximum of 90 days in spring, and from 5.2 days to as long as 130 days in summer.  3.2 Intra-annual distribution of water age at Chenglingji and other locations The previous sections have described the overall spatial distribution of water age in the lake region during the different seasons. To delve further into the distribution of the observable water age in the lake region, it is necessary to select a few representative points: the vicinity of Xiaohezui (point 1) near the junction of West and South Dongting Lakes, the Xiangjiang River estuary (point 2) in South Dongting, Lujiao (point 3) on the eastern side of East Dongting Lake, and the Chenglingji lake outlet (point 4). The annual distribution of water age at these points under Scenario 2 is depicted in  Fig. 5 . Point 1 is located at the junction of West and South Dongting Lakes, and it receives incoming water from the Yuanjiang River, Lishui River, and a large portion of the JTO. Water age distribution at this location is primarily affected by the incoming flow from these water systems. Water age increases continuously from 3.5 days at the beginning of July to 13.8 days at the beginning of January. Then, it gradually decreases and returns to the low point by the end of June. Point 2 is situated at the intersection of the Xiangjiang River outlet and the southern side of South Dongting Lake, where the water system is complex and the terrain is undulating. Water age at this location is simultaneously influenced by the outflow of the Xiangjiang River and the overall water level of South Dongting Lake. From April to mid-June, it remains stable for 3–4 days, whereupon it increases to approximately 9 days within the following month, fluctuating from 6 to 11.8 days until December. Finally, it slowly decreases back to approximately 3 days from January to April. Point 3 is located in the floodway on the eastern side of East Dongting Lake, where water age is influenced by both the incoming water from upstream and the amount of water from the Yangtze River. From April to June, it fluctuates between 7 and 9 days, and then, it rapidly increases to 13 days from July to August. Over the next four months, it slowly increases to approximately 17 days. It reaches the highest level in early January, and finally, it gradually decreases back to a low point of approximately 8 days from January to April. Point 4 is located at the outlet of the Dongting Lake region and is an important channel linking the Dongting Lake region with the mainstream of the Yangtze River. Water age at Chenglingji can reflect the overall situation of the lake region's water age. In this region, water age remains low from April to June (8–10 days), begins to increase in July, and reaches a high level of 14–17 days in August. Then, it starts to decrease in early January and reaches a low point at the end of March. According to the definition of water age, its magnitude is closely related to the flow rate, flow speed, and other hydrodynamic conditions of the lake.  Fig. 6  shows the annual daily average flow of the four rivers into Dongting Lake and the mainstream of the Yangtze River. It can be seen that the flow of the four rivers starts to decrease sharply in July, and the flow in August is only half of that in July. In addition, the flow of the mainstream of the Yangtze River is maintained around its annual maximum, and the water level of the Yangtze River remains high, causing the outflow of the lake water to be impeded. Therefore, the sharp increases in water age at Chenglingji in July is due to the sharp decreases in the flow of the four rivers during this period. However, in February and March, only the main floodway in the lake region contains water, the flows of the Zishui River and Lishui River tends to stabilize, the mainstream flow of the Yangtze River gradually increases, and the flows of the Xiangjiang and Yuanjiang rivers start to significantly increase as they enter the flood season. During this time, water age at Chenglingji gradually decreases to the flood season level.  3.3 Water age distribution before and after the TGD operation Following the operation of the TGD, it primarily impacted the hydrodynamic conditions of the lake region through change in flow in different scenarios and the blocking effect at the Chenglingji outlet, which subsequently influenced water age within the lake region. In this paper, we also discuss the magnitude of this impact from the perspective of the four seasons.  Fig. 7  illustrates the difference in water ages under Scenarios 1 and 2, the difference in water age at a given location is calculated by subtracting the water age at that location under scenario 2 from the water age under scenario 1. A positive and larger value for a region indicates an increase in the age of the water in that region, and a negative and smaller value indicates a decrease in the age of the water in that region. The results presented in Fig. 7  show that under both scenarios1 and 2, the improvement in water age in most areas such as the main floodway and perennial water regions is rather mild. Some shoals and areas with large water level fluctuations are substantial impacted by the TGD, leading to substantial changes in water age. The changes in water age are more obvious in autumn, increasing by 60–80 days within a wide range in the shoal areas near the West and South Dongting lakes. However, water age at the western branch of the Xiangjiang River on the southern side of point 7 exhibits significant improvement, decreasing by approximately 150 days. Some improvement also occurs at point 8 and in the central shoals of East Dongting Lake, with a decrease in water age of nearly 170 days. During the spring, only the areas near point 6 in South Dongting Lake, on the western bank near point 8 and northwest side in East Dongting Lake exhibit noticeable improvement, with decreases in water age of approximately 11 days, 95 days, and 85 days, respectively. In summer, when the lake's surface is greatest, there is almost no difference in water age under the two scenarios in the main floodway, including the southern sides of West and South Dongting lakes and the eastern side of East Dongting Lake. However, as the distance from the main floodway increases, water age in the lake's shoals gradually increases. On the eastern side of East Dongting Lake, under Scenario 2, water age increases by approximately 16 days compared to that under Scenario 1. In autumn, water age increases in the shoals at point 5. Due to the complex water system at point 6, which results in turbulent flow, water age increases by approximately 24 days near the floodway, while it decreases by approximately 100 days in the areas farther away from the floodway. In addition, in most of the areas in East Dongting Lake and on the southern side of point 6, water age improves by 20–60 days, and is still on a downward trend. The water age at some locations in autumn and winter increased after the operation of TGD, which was due to the reduction in discharge flow from the TGD during this period. Although the water age has increased, it has had minimal impact on the overall water quality and water environment of the lake. The differences in water age under Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 at points 1, 2, 3, and 4 are mainly manifested in autumn and winter, and water age is lower under Scenario 2 than under Scenario 1. The specific situation is shown in  Fig. 8 . At point 1, from late August to November, water age is approximately 0.4 days less under Scenario 2 than under Scenario 1. The maximum difference occurs on early October (1.2 days). However, from early January to late March, water age is greater under Scenario 2 than Scenario 1, with the maximum difference of 1 day occurring on January 14th. There is no obvious difference in water age between the two scenarios during the rest of the year. At point 2, from mid-July to mid-November, water age under Scenario 2 is an average of 0.99 days less than that under Scenario 1, with a maximum difference of 2.1 days. There is no significant difference in water age between the two scenarios at other times. Point 3 is located on the east side of East Dongting Lake. From July to December, water age under Scenario 2 is an average of 0.48 day less than that under Scenario 1 with a maximum difference of 1.2 days. In March, water age under Scenario 2 is approximately 1.2 days greater than that under Scenario 1. There is no significant difference during the other periods. Near point 4, water age begins to rise from a low level in early July, and it reaches a high level from September to December. During this period, water age under Scenario 2 is 1–1.8 days less than that under Scenario 1, with the maximum difference of 2.1 days.  3.4 Factors influencing water age in the Dongting lake The operation of the TGD affected various hydrodynamic indicators of the Yangtze River mainstream, such as the diversion of JTO, water level, flow patterns, precipitation, wind fields, and thus affected the water age distribution pattern of the Dongting Lake. Therefore, in this section, we analyzed the impact of the operation of the TGD on water age in the lake from three aspects: the diversion at the JTO, the outlet water level, and the flow patterns. 3.4.1 Impact of the JTO diversion on water age in the lake The operation of TGD on the mainstream of the Yangtze River has a significant impact on the diversion of the JTO. The total amount of water diverted at the JTO before and after the operation of the TGD is shown in  Fig. 9 . It can be seen that from the end of June to the beginning of November, the water flow at the JTO significantly decreases, with the largest decrease occurring around the beginning of July, reaching a difference of approximately 3000 m3 /s. The impact is not conspicuous from November to June. The impact of the JTO diversion on water age in the lake mainly occurs in the West and South Dongting Lakes from June to November. Taking early July as an example, the outflows from the Lishui River, Songzi River, and Hudu River travel south and enter West Dongting Lake, where they merge with the outflow from the Yuanjiang River. At the confluence, a water age convergence line appears. The southern side is the outflow from the Yuan River, and the northern side is the outflow from the Songzi -Lishui River area. At the convergence line, due to the mixing and bracing effects, water age in some areas is larger. Before the TGD was built, the maximum was 8.3 days; and after it was built, the maximum was 24.8 days. Near the northwest side of point 6, an embankment in the South Dongting Lake, water age was 103 days after the TGD was built, while before it was built, water age in this area was similar to that in the surrounding areas, it was about 5 days. The impact of the JTO diversion on other areas is not conspicuous. In the dry season, among the JTO, almost only the Songzi River does not dry up. Since the operation of the TGD, the dry season flow has been increased through regulation. In the shoal areas of West and South Dongting lakes, where the water depth is less than 2 m, the exchange at the main channel is very slow, and water age often reaches 80–100 days. However, with the change in the JTO diversion, water age in the shoal can be improved by an average of nearly 18 days, reaching approximately 30 days, greatly increasing the rate of water circulation and improving the water exchange ability. No significant change in water age was observed within the main channel.  3.4.2 Impact of outlet water level on water age in lake Under Scenarios 4, 5, and 6, different downstream outlet water levels are set under different flow frequencies in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. The flow of the four rivers is set to a constant value, i.e., the average flow during the flood season. The simulation duration is one month, and after a month of simulation, the distribution of water age in the lake tends to stabilize. The results for day 30 are exported for analysis, and the average water age of three parts of the lake are shown in  Table 3 . Under the condition of the same flood frequency in Zhicheng, the higher the frequency of the floods in Luoshan is (i.e., the higher the water level at Luoshan station is), the higher water age in the lake is. The increase in water age at Luoshan under adjacent frequencies is 2–4 %. Water age changes more significantly in the East Dongting Lake than in the West and South Dongting lakes under adjacent frequencies at Luoshan, with an increase of 0.4 days (about 3 %). However, under the condition of Luoshan encountering a 5 % frequency flood, when the flow at Zhicheng are 10 %, 5 %, 2 % frequencies, water age decreases in various parts of the lake, with a reduction of 1–6.8 %.  3.4.3 Impact of flow pattern on water age in the lake Since the operation of the TGD and other projects, the annual distribution of the flow in the Yangtze River has changed. Scenarios 2 and 4 represent the impact of the flow pattern at Zhicheng station of the Yangtze River on water age in the lake. The simulation results can be used to determine water age in the lake under the conditions of the same total daily flow of the Zhicheng station throughout the year but under different flow patterns, thus revealing the impact of the flow patterns on water age. The average water age in each region and season under the two scenarios is shown in  Fig. 10 . From the comparison of the two scenarios, it can be concluded that the change in the flow pattern of the Yangtze River has a more noticeable impact on the East Dongting Lake through the effect of the outflow at Chenglingji, and it mainly affects the West Dongting Lake in autumn and winter through the JTO diversion. However, the impact on the South Dongting Lake is relatively weak. Therefore, it can be seen that the impact of the flow pattern of the Yangtze River on water age in the lake is simultaneously generated by the JTO diversion and the outflow at Chenglingji. In the East Dongting Lake, the region mainly affected by the flow pattern are the main flood channel in the southeast and the shoal between point 8 and the main flood channel. Under Scenario 2, the flow rate during the flood season decreases due to the regulation of the TGD, coupled with sediment deposition and winding in the Jingjiang area. This leads to a rise in the water level at the outflow channel of Chenglingji station, slowing the outflow of the water in the lake and leading to an increase in water age at Chenglingji, which in turn affects water age in the main flood channel in the East Dongting Lake. In contrast, in the beach areas on the south side of East Dongting Lake, the rise in the water level due to blocking of outflow from the flood channel accelerates the exchange rate of the water bodies in the flood channel and beach areas, and hence, water age is lower than that under Scenario 3. Point 8 is located quite far away from the main flood channel, making it difficult for the water bodies to circulate, so water age is relatively high under both scenarios. In the West Dongting Lake, the flow rate at Lishui is relatively stable, while the JTO area is significantly affected by the mainstream of the Yangtze River during the flood and dry seasons, especially after the operation of the TGD. The TGD has significantly changed the diversion situation and hydrological conditions in the JTO area, especially in the dry season when the JTO is almost completely cut off, increasing the diversion of the JTO and the West Dongting Lake. Therefore, changes in the flow pattern can also improve the problem of the poor water exchange in the shoal of the West Dongting Lake during the dry season. The difference in water age under these two scenarios in the East Dongting Lake is 0.9–1.5 days, with a reduction of 4.7–8.9 %. In the South Dongting Lake, the maximum difference under the two scenarios is 0.7 days, corresponding to 8.6. In the West Dongting Lake, the difference under the two scenarios during the dry season is 1–2.1 days, with the maximum reduction of approximately 12 %.    4 Discussion 4.1 Cause analysis of water age in the lake The findings of this study suggested that in the river and river network, the greater the flow is, the younger water age is. The reason is that there is a stable slope within the river, a single direction of water flow, and no situation where the water bodies remain in one place for a long time. Conversely, in the lake region, the main flood channel is similar to a river with a deeper riverbed, low roughness, high water flow speed, and a younger water age. Do the flat terrain and higher bottom roughness, the alluvial plain areas contain water bodies that remain for extended periods of time, which makes it difficult for the water in these areas to exchange with the faster water flow in the flood channel, resulting in a greater water age in the alluvial areas. At the junctions of rivers and lakes, such as the Xiangjiang Estuary, Zijiang Estuary, and Chenglingji, water age is mainly influenced by factors such as the flow rate and the backwater effect at the outlets of the rivers and lakes. According to the characteristics of large shallow lakes, the spatial distribution of water age in Dongting Lake is similar to that of Poyang Lake (Huang et al., 2022 ), Taihu Lake (Li et al., 2013 ) and Bosten Lake (Liu et al., 2021 ).
