Since, the resolution value is arbitrary for the sphere packing sample, without any loss of generality, in our analysis we use relative units for all the values which directly depend on resolution.  3.2 Subcubes selection To analyze both deterministic and statistical REVs, one should make the proper selection of subcubes from analyzed 3D sample images. We select a set of growing subcubes SCk  (i ) from the center and all the corners of the sample, as it is shown in Fig. 4  . We take subcube linear size Li   = L 0  + i ΔL , increment step ΔL  = 50 voxels, and L 0 = 50 voxels for all samples considered. The reliable sREV analysis is possible only if subcubes do not overlap or their overlap is limited. Therefore, we introduce the L sREV  parameter. For Li   ≤ L sREV , we cut from the considered sample all 9 subcubes SCk  (i ) with k  = 0,1,.,9. For Li  > L sREV , only the center subcubes SC0 (i ) are cut. We take L sREV  = 300 for CER and S1 samples (due to their smaller dimensions in voxels) and L sREV  = 600 for other four samples. For the estimation of sREV size for scalar metric S , we first calculate its values S ik   for the subcubes SCk  (i ), and then obtain mean value ⟨Si  ⟩, standard deviation σ i   and, finally, utilize Eq. (5) . For the estimation of dREV size, Eqs. (1) –(4)  are used instead. For Li   ≤ L sREV , we take Si  , equal to the value ⟨S i ⟩, calculated for sREV analysis, and for Li  > L sREV , Si   = Si  0 . It is obvious that for Li   ≤ L sREV  one can perform both sREV and dREV analysis, and for Li  > L sREV  only dREV analysis is possible. For the estimation of sREV size for vector metric V  , using proposed Eqs. (8) –(11) , we calculate distances between modified vector V  *( i  + 1)0  obtained for the subcube SC0 (i +1) and vectors V  ik   obtained for the subcubes SCk  (i ). Then mean value of this distance and its standard deviation are calculated, and Eqs. (8) –(11)  are used. Indeed, one can calculate the distances between all possible pairs of vectors at cut steps i  and i +1 to have more statistics and obtain more correct values of mean and standard deviation. However, we found that for considered samples the difference with results obtained with our selection scheme is small, which leads to the same sREV size values. For the estimation of dREV size, mean value of distance obtained for sREV analysis, as presented above, is substituted into Eq. (7)  for Li   ≤ L sREV . For Li  > L sREV , distance ||V  i 0  - V  *( i  + 1)0 || is substituted into Eq. (7) . The precise values of dREV and sREV sizes calculated using Eqs. (1) –(5)  and Eqs (7) –(11)  depend on threshold parameters ε 1   and ε 2  . In our study we consider two values of these parameters, 0.1 and 0.2, which have been used in previous papers on REV analysis (e.g., Zhang et al., 2000 ; Li et al., 2009 ; Constanza-Robinson et al., 2011 ; Borges et al., 2018 ; Koestel et al., 2020 ).   4 Metrics In this section, we describe the metrics for which we perform REV analysis and the methods to calculate them and vectorize non-scalar ones. 4.1 Porosity Subcube porosity is easily calculated by counting the number of pore voxels with subsequent normalization over the total number of voxels in the considered volume.  4.2 Permeability In order to compute permeability K , we solve Stokes's equation within 3D pore geometries using the FDMSS solver with 4-th order spatial accuracy scheme (Gerke et al., 2018 ). Three flow directions, along X, Y and Z axes are considered, so we obtain the components of permeability tensor Kx , Ky   and Kz   for each subcube sample. The flow of the fluid is generally described by the Navier-Stokes equation (Landau and Lifshitz, 1987 ):(12) { ∂ v  ∂ t   + ( v Δ   )  v − μ ρ  Δ   v + ∇ p  ρ  = 0    div  v  = 0            where v   = (vx ,vy ,vz  ) is velocity field, µ  is fluid viscosity, ρ  is fluid density, and p  is pressure field. In case of small Reynolds numbers R e = ρ v l  μ  ≪ 1    (l  denotes characteristic linear size) we can neglect inertial terms and describe so-called creeping stationary flow with the Stokes equation:(13) { μ Δ   v − ∇ p = 0    div  v  = 0             This equation is still expensive to solve. To tackle the problem with minimal computational resources we utilize a technique from 60s to add artificial compressibility and the time step. This way we can use very cheap explicit numerical scheme and iterate till stationarity of Eq. (13)  is achieved. So, in practice we solve the following system:(14) { ρ ∂ v  ∂ t   + μ Δ   v + ∇ p = 0  in  Ω      div  v  = 0    v ( x , t )  = 0  on  ∂ Ω      v ( x , 0 )  = 0            where Ω is the pore space, ∂Ω is its internal boundary and x  is the Cartesian coordinate within the modelling domain. In order to numerically solve Eq. (14)  on the staggered grid with pressures within voxels and velocities on their faces, we need pressure boundary conditions). One face of the cubical domain serves as an inlet and the face opposing it serves as the outlet. A pressure gradient is imposed between inlet and outlet to induce the flow. All four other faces of the cube parallel to the pressure gradient are treated as closed walls, thus simulating the permeameter laboratory measurement technique. The pressure gradient ∇p =1 Pa/m was used in all cases (note however that its value is not important to solving the Stokes flow problem, as velocity field will scale proportionally to applied pressure gradient). Zero velocity (or no-slip) boundary condition is used on the pore walls in all simulations (internal boundaries). After Stokes equation is solved numerically (for pressure and velocity fields) permeability is computed according to the Darcy law:(15) K = η L Q  Δ  p S   = η L 〈 v 〉 φ  Δ  p       where K  — is permeability, η — dynamic viscosity, L  — a distance between which pressure drop Δp  = pinlet   − poutlet   is applied, Q  — flow rate through cross-sectional area S , 〈v 〉 — average flow velocity within connected porosity, φ  — porosity (effective, because non-connected porosity does not facilitate flow) of the 3D image. The quality of the solution was ensured by reaching < 0.01 accuracy criterion based on imbalance of both continuity and motion parts of the Stokes equation.  4.3 Euler density We obtain Euler density χ n   by the normalization of Euler number χ  over the subcube volume (total number of voxels). The metric χ  represents the topological properties of considered voxel domain and can be calculated counting the domain elements as (Vogel et. al, 2010 ):(16) χ  =  N v e r    −  N e   +  N f   −  N v o l   ,     where Nver , Ne , Nf   and Nvol   — are the numbers of vertices, edges (unit lines connecting neighbor vertices), faces (unit squares formed by faces) and volumes (unit cubes formed by faces). If all vertices of an element belong to the voxel domain of interest, it contributes 1 to the corresponding element number N . One can also use the approximate expression for Euler number (Vogel et. al, 2001 ) using the characteristics of pore-network model (PNM), extracted from 3D image (see next subsection):(17) χ  ′    ≈  N p   −  N t  ,     where N p   and N t   are pore and throat numbers given by PNM.  4.4 Pore-network statistics Pore-network models (PNM) divide the void space of the 3D image into pores representing wider regions that are connected through narrower restrictions called throats. This representation is very suitable for the further single and multi-phase flow simulation, as empirical equations derived for pores and throats of a simple geometry can be used, or the results of the direct simulations can be implemented with the help of machine learning (Miao et al., 2017 ; Rabbani et al., 2019 ; Tembely et al., 2021 ). In this paper, we use PNM extraction algorithm (Delgado-Friedrichs et al., 2014 ; Zubov et al., 2022 ) based on discrete Morse theory (Forman, 1998 ) and persistent homology (Edelsbrunner et al., 2000 ). We map voxel structure of considered 3D image to a cubical complex (Kovalevsky, 1989 ), then construct gradient vector field for this complex using signed Euclidian distance transform (EDT) (Meijster et al., 2002 ) as the discrete Morse function and the algorithm ProcessLowerStar (Robins et al., 2011 ). Afterwards we transform the constructed vector field during the simplification process according to the fixed persistent limit (Delgado-Friedrichs et al., 2014 ), the free parameter of the model. We take its value equal to 1 for all samples and subsamples considered in our work. Simplification, based on the persistent homology, is the procedure of extreme importance, since missing this step leads to unrealistically large number of pores and throats. We perform the pore segmentation with the seeds corresponding to critical 0-cells (minima) of the vector field transformed after simplification, see Delgado-Friedrichs et al. (2014)  and Zubov et al. (2022)  for the details. Throats are treated as the watersheds between the found pore segments. We compute the characteristics of PNM for all samples and subsamples using in-house C++ code (Zubov et al., 2022 ). The statistics of the extracted PNM (distributions of pore R p   and throat Rt   radii and connectivity (also called coordination number) c  distribution) are presented for CER sample in Fig. 5  , as the example. We also present ball-and-stick diagram of pore network extracted for CER sample in this figure. We obtain and vectorize such diagrams for all subcubes considered in REV analysis with the same bin size s , which is the input parameter. The vectorization and modification of PNM distribution D PNM  (Rp , Rt   or c ) are carried out as the following: for the vector V  i  , we take range of vectorization as r (i ) = (0, D PNMmax ), and number of bins N bins (i) = D PNMmax  /s . After modification procedure, for vector V  *( i  + 1) , we have r (i +1) = r (i ) and N bins (i +1) = N bins (i ). Then we apply Eq. (6)  to calculate distance between two vectors.  4.5 Correlation functions Using in-house code in Julia language released as an open-source library CorrelationFunctions.jl (https://github.com/fatimp/CorrelationFunctions.jl ; Postnicov et al., 2024 ), we compute correlation functions (CF) for studied samples and their subcube cuts. In all of the cases, we take four types of volume-averaged CFs: two-point probability function S 2 (r  ) (Debye et al., 1957 ), lineal function L 2 (r  ) (Lu and Torquato, 1992 ), cluster function C 2 (r  ) (Torquato et al., 1988 ) and surface-surface function SS 2 (r  ) or F ss   (Ma and Torquato, 2018 ; Samarin et al., 2023 ). All these directional correlation functions (Jiao and Chawla, 2014 ; Gerke et al., 2014 ) are computed along three major orthogonal directions x, y  and z  exclusively for the pore phase. Each correlation function measures a probability of some event for a given length r  . Specifically, S 2  measures the probability that both ends of the r   line segment lie within pore phase, L 2  — the probability that the whole segment lies within the pore space, C 2  — that both ends of the segment lie within the same pore cluster, and SS 2  — that both ends fall into a pore-solid interface. The length r   was chosen to vary from 0 to a half of total linear size (in voxels) of the studied sample. Any additional details on different CFs can be found in comprehensive Torquato's book (Torquato, 2002b ). It is important to clarify the relationships between classical porous media parameters and correlation functions:a) Porosity is the zeroth moment of all but SS 2  function, i.e., S 2 (0), L 2 (0) and C 2 (0) all provide porosity value (or zeroth Minkowski functional);  b) Surface area. Both SS 2 (0) and S 2  contain full information on pore surface area (or first Minkowski functional), using S 2  it can be computed as a derivative at point S 2 (0) (Debye et al., 1957 );  c) Connectivity. The connectivity of the pore space is represented by C 2  (Torquato et al., 1988 ) and existing measures of percolation-like connectivity (e.g., Renard and Allard, 2013 ; Koestel et al., 2020 ) can be seen as equivalents of the cluster function;  d) Pore-size distribution. Pore-size distribution is described by lineal L 2  function, which measures the probability of the pore space to contain directional line segments of a given length r  ;  e) Additional Minkowski functionals describing pore curvature and Euler characteristic can be also extracted from the surface correlation functions (Ma and Torquato, 2020 ).    The set of correlation functions used in this study fully covers all conventional measures. While the exact correlation functions set to fully describe any given pore structure is still open question (Karsanina et al., 2015 ), Jiao et al. (2009)  provided some significant evidence that the set of CFs presented above should be enough to provide necessary information content. The exact methodology and equations to compute correlation functions as was performed in this study are extensively provided in Postnicov et al. (2023)  for surface-surface function, and in Postnicov et al. (2024)  for lineal, cluster and two-point probability functions. To make correlation functions independent of porosity value, we normalize all CFs by the porosity value as done for autocovariance function (Jiao et al., 2007 ):(18) S 2 n o r m   ( r )  = S 2  ( r )  − φ  φ ( 1 − φ  )        where φ is porosity. The same form of Eq. (17)  was utilized to normalize C 2  cluster function as for the majority of our samples the connectivity of the pore space was relatively high. In case the pore space originates from a single cluster S 2  and C 2  are the same which justifies this normalization choice. To normalize lineal function, we simply divide all L 2  values by L 2 (0), as for all CFs but surface-surface, the zeroth moment of the function computed for pore phase is CF(r  =0) = φ. For subcube with linear size Li  , correlation function, computed along one of three major orthogonal directions x, y  and z  for each distance value from 0 to Li  /2 is stacked to the single vector of size Li  /2. Vectorized S 2 , C 2 , L 2  and SS 2  correlation functions for CER sample are presented in Fig. 6  , as the example. We take bin size equal to the linear size of one voxel. Then for the vector V  i  , range of vectorization r (i ) = (0, Li  /2), and number of bins N bins (i ) = Li  /2. After modification procedure, for vector V  *( i  + 1) , we have r (i +1) = r (i ) and N bins (i +1) = N bins (i ). Then we apply Eq. (6)  to calculate distance between two vectors.  4.6 Persistence diagrams Persistence diagram is 2D visualization of persistent homology analysis applied to some 3D domain X  which obtains topological characteristics ck   (k  = 0,1,2). Here, c 0  is the connected component, c 1  is the ring structure, and c 2  is the cavity structure. The idea of persistent homology is based on the concept of filtration (Edelsbrunner et al., 2000 ). Let f  be a scalar function defined on X . Then a filtration of X  is the sequence of such subdomains Xa  , as for all points x  ∈ Xa , f (x ) ≤ a . If a topological characteristic ck   appears in a filtration subdomain Xb   and disappears in a filtration subdomain Xd  , then the pair (b, d ) corresponds to a birth-death cycle of ck   and is called a persistent pair. The total set of persistent pairs located in 2D coordinate plane form a persistence diagram PDk  . PD0  represents the births and deaths of connected components, PD1  — the births and deaths of 1-cycles (rings), and PD2  — the births and deaths of 2-cycles (cavities). The examples of PD construction for simple topological objects are presented in Fig. 9  from the survey of Chazal and Michel (2021) . PDs provide the scales of topological features and clarify the geometric relationships among them. Besides there is a connection between PDs and pore-network characteristics. For example, PD0  points (b  < 0, d  < 0) correspond to connected pores, PD0  points (b  < 0, d  > 0) correspond to isolated pores, PD1  points (b  < 0, d  > 0) correspond to pores with the ring structure and PD2  points (b  < 0, d  > 0) correspond to pores with the cavity structure (see Fig. 3  in Robins et al. (2016) . We should also mention the recent progress in using PD analysis to describe the physical properties of different heterogeneous media (Ichinomiya et al., 2017 ; Kimura et al., 2018 ; Jiang et al., 2018 ). In this study, we find the persistent pairs for 3D binary images using C++ library Diamorse (https://github.com/AppliedMathematicsANU/diamorse ). We take signed Euclidean distance transform (EDT) (Meijster et al., 2002 ) as the filtration argument a . We use the algorithm proposed by Chen and Kerber (2011)  to extract persistent pairs from the set of critical cells obtained for a cubical complex which maps an initial binary image. The found set of birth-death pairs can be visualized by persistence diagrams, the example of PDs constructed for CER sample is presented in Fig. 7  . There are two approaches to the comparison of persistence diagrams. In the first one, the direct comparison, the distance metric is computed directly using birth-death points locations at the diagrams being compared. The second approach requires initial vectorization of PDs, then one can compare the formed vectors using some distance norm or another metric. While in direct comparison of PDs all information about relative positions of PD points is preserved, grouping PD points in bins during vectorization procedure leads to information loss. Besides for all direct comparison metrics are proved to be stable to the small perturbations. In spite of such benefits, there is one disadvantage of direct comparison methods: they are time expensive, so can be barely used for PDs of large size or for large datasets of PDs. On the other hand, vectorization methods are usually faster, which provides their popularity in machine and deep learning applications. In this study we consider one direct compassion metric, sliced Wasserstein distance normalized over the total number of points in compared PDs and the following vectorization methods: simple binning, persistence image, landscape and silhouette. We take Euclidean distance as a comparison metric for the vectors extracted from PDs using these methods. In addition, we also consider MSSIM metric in simple binning method. One can find the short overview of PD comparison methodology in the Supplementary Materials. Vectorization of a persistence diagram D  consists of some initial transform T (D ), binning by two-dimensional grid being overlaid on transformed PD and assignment of some value to each bin, resulting in 2D histogram. Then we reshape this histogram into 1D vector with column-major order. While constructing 2D histogram in XY-plane for the considered PD, we set its range from minimal to maximal value at each axis, and, for simplicity, take equal numbers of bins for both axes Nx   = Ny   = N . Thus, for vector V  i  , we fix range of vectorization rxy  (i ) and number of bins N bins (i ) = N (i )× N (i ). After modification procedure, for vector V  *( i  + 1) , we have rxy  (i  + 1) = rxy  (i) and N bins( i  + 1)  = N bins (i ). We use GUDHI software (https://gudhi.inria.fr/ ) for the calculations of sliced Wasserstein distance, and for persistence image, landscape and silhouette methods of PD vectorization. We used in-house Python code to vectorize PD with simple binning and SSIM-based approach.   5 Results Let us first shortly remind the pipeline of our survey study. According to the methodology described in Section 3.2 , we cut subcubes from 6 binary images, presented in Section 3.1 . Then we calculate scalar and vector metrics described in Section 4  for each subcube and estimate sREV and dREV sizes for each considered sample, as described in Section 2 . For vector metric V   initially calculated raw metric data (1D histograms for PNM statistics, discrete functions for CF metrics and 2D scatter plots for PDs) should be preliminary converted to 1D vectors before dREV and sREV sizes estimation. We call such a procedure ‘vectorization’. The described pipeline is schematically shown in Fig. 8  . To clarify the sensitivity of estimated dREV sizes to the choice of specific formula from Eqs. (1) –(4) , we compare the results obtained using each formula within porosity and permeability dREV analysis. For Euler density, only the results obtained using Eq. (1)  are shown in this paper. We use Eq. (7)  to calculate vector metrics dREV size. As for sREV analysis, we apply Eq. (5) and Eqs. (8) –(11)  for scalar and vector metrics sREV size estimation, respectively. For PD vectorized with simple binning method we also take MSSIM metric besides Euclidean distance for vector comparison (see Section 1.1 in Supplementary Materials). For direct comparison of PDs using sliced Wasserstein distance, we substitute this metric value in Eq. (8) . All results according to this scheme are presented in this section, together with our interpretation. 5.1 Scalar metrics The dependencies of subcube with size L  for porosities and permeabilities are presented in Figs. 9–10   . Standard deviations of calculated values are shown with errorbars. By a visual assessment, one can conclude that these calculated characteristics with the increment of L  start to satisfy dREV and sREV criteria: the difference between both mean values and variations obtained for subcubes of fixed size decrease. One can find the same dependences of absolute values (for other considered scalar metrics) and distances between subcubes (for other considered vector metrics) on subcube size in Supplementary Materials (Figs. S3-S14). In addition to visual inspection, for REV size estimation we now utilize more precise mathematical models based on Eqs. (1) –(5) . Within dREV and SREV analysis we calculated the dependences of δ1  and σ norm   on linear size of subcube and compare them with threshold values, as it is shown in Fig. 11  . The rightmost crossing of function δ1 (L ) and σ norm  (L ) with the threshold horizontal line give us the estimation of dREV and sREV sizes, respectively. The estimated porosity and permeability dREV and sREV sizes are presented in Figs. 12-13   . The analysis of Figs. 11-13  and led us to several immediate conclusions. The choice of specific formula from Eqs. (1) –(4)  can have an influence on the estimated dREV size. Though for porosity dREV analysis, we obtain the close dREV size values using different formulas, situation is quite different for permeability dREV analysis. As one can see from Figs. 12-13 , the variation of dREV sizes while using different formulas can be significant. For example, for S3 sample and 10% threshold this value varies from 300 to 700. Using Eq. (2)  or Eq. (4)  for the calculations of dREV sizes ensures the strictest condition for the representativity. For a given sample, dREV size calculated for porosity is always smaller than one calculated for permeability, this our conclusion coincides with the results of previous studies (Zhang et al., 2000 ; Mostaghimi et al., 2013 ). Application of sREV analysis leads to larger REV sizes than in the case of dREV analysis for both characteristics using the same thresholds, which has also been mentioned previously (Zhang et al., 2000 ). Note, that dREV sizes for porosities calculated for different samples are quite small and close to each other, whereas for sREV sizes divergence between different samples becomes remarkable. This can indicate a larger sensitivity of sREV analysis to the difference between samples as compared to dREV analysis. For any metric, one can sort the considered samples both by their REV sizes and visual assessment of the curves δ1 (L ) and σ norm  (L ) in ascending order. From the analysis of Figs. 11-13 , we can conclude that such sorted sequence of samples is the same for dREV and sREV analysis of permeability: from the most representative CER sample to the least representative CAR sample. The same sequence is observed for porosity sREV analysis. As for porosity dREV analysis, such kind of sorting is difficult as the curves δ1 (L ) for several samples are strongly intersecting and very close to each other (see upper part of Fig. 11 ). Possibility to reproduce this sorted sequence of samples in another medium descriptor REV analysis can be treated as a factor of descriptor's quality in the sense of describing porous medium flow properties, therefore we summarized the found sorted sequences for all the metrics considered in this study. The obtained results are presented in Table. 2  . For the calculations of Euler densities we use both Eq. (17)  and approximate Eq. (17) . The magnitude of difference between χ n   and χ' n   in a plateau regime is mainly determined by complex topological structures (porous ring and cavity structures, junctions). The contribution of such structures is not taken into account in Eq. (17)  and positively affects the observed χ n   — χ' n   value (Zubov et. al, 2022 ). Similar to other metrics, for Euler density dREV and sREV analysis we calculated values δ1 , using Eq. (1) , and σ norm  , using Eq. (5)  for subcubes of different sizes. The results are presented in Table 2 . A very large divergence from permeability REV results is observed for SPH sample, calculated using precise Euler density, and for S2 and S3 samples, calculated using approximate Euler density. Note, that for these samples χ n   and (or) χ' n   values are closest to zero (see Fig. S3). This leads to the decrease of denominators in Eqs. (1)  and (5) , and corresponding increase of values δ1  and σ norm  . Thus, we conclude, that Euler density REV analysis provides doubtful REV size estimations in the case, when the analyzed characteristics are close to zero. For other cases, when χ n   or χ' n   are far from zero, Euler density dREV and sREV sizes can be larger, smaller or equal to permeability dREV sizes, one cannot observe strongly-pronounced trend here.  5.2 Sliced Wasserstein distance The results of sliced Wasserstein distance REV analysis are also presented in Table 2 . We observe no correlation with the value of sliced Wasserstein distance and permeability dREV size, calculated using Eqs. (1) –(4) . For example, for the most representative in porosity and permeability CER sample, sliced Wasserstein plateau distances are larger than for the most non-representative in permeability CAR sample. Note, that direct application Eqs. (1) –(4)  to sliced Wasserstein distance is not possible, as this metric is defined to be only relative. No absolute value of this distance for one PD (which contributes to denominators in Eqs. (1) –(4)  has sense. As for sREV analysis, though sliced Wasserstein distance sREV sizes do not exactly coincide with porosity and permeability ones, the relationship between different samples is very similar (see Table 2 ). The sorted sequence of samples for porosity and permeability is reproduced for sliced Wasserstein distance metric with only one exception: the exchange of SPH and S1 samples positions.  5.3 Vector metrics In this subsection we present the results of REV analysis for vector metrics. The results are presented in Table 2 . Normalization of distances between vectors is carried out, as in Eq. (7) . Standard deviations are presented by errorbars. For PNM-based and PD-based metrics number of bins is input parameters of calculations. It is obvious, that two small or two large numbers of bins are not suitable in our study. Fortunately, for each metric there is the interval of N bins , in which the obtained results are stable against small deviations of N bins  values. For each metric, we found and fixed such intervals in our calculations. As for CF-based metric, N bins  is not a parameter, its value is always equal to the half of subcube linear size. We found that for all considered metrics distance between vectors decreases with the growth of subcube size. This confirms their applicability to dREV analysis. For PNM-based metrics, taking vectorized pore sizes, throat sizes and connectivity distributions leads to close values of distances between vectors in plateau regime for all samples considered. Close distance values are also obtained at plateaus for X, Y and Z components of CFs in the most cases, this indicates to space isotropy of samples. For PD-based metrics, the distances between corresponding vectors are the largest for PD2 . This means that topology effects of solid phase (which is mainly contributes in PD2) become representative at larger sizes than ones of pore phase. The results of vector metrics sREV analysis strongly depend on a method of sREV size calculation. We can demonstrate this taking vectorized PNM statistics as the example. The dependences of values σ norm  , calculated using Eq. (8) , on subcube size are presented in Fig. 14  . These dependences do not show any pronounced decreasing trend, therefore sREV size estimation becomes problematic. We can explain the observed behaviour of σ norm   values by close to zero denominators in Eq. (8)  at subcube sizes larger than dREV size. We have already discussed this in Section 2.2 . The dependences σ (L ), calculated using Eq. (10)  are presented in Fig. 15  . As we take two values of dREV ε1  and sREV ε2  thresholds equal to 0.1 and 0.2, we take threshold values ε3  equal to the minimum and maximum of ε1 ε2  product. As one can see from Fig. 15 , the decreasing of σ  values with the growth of subcube size is observed now, and we can calculate sREV size, using Eq. (10) . The dependences σ1 (L ), calculated using Eq. (11)  with two different values ε1  =  0.1 and ε1  = 0.2, are presented in Fig. 16  . One can argue that dependence of sREV size on the choice of dREV threshold value ε1  is quite strong. We believe, that taking ε1  =  0.1 is more realistic, because taking ε1  =  0.2, we obtain rather small sREV sizes for CAR and S2 samples which are the least representative in porosity and permeability (see Fig. 11 ). Therefore, in Table 2  we show the results of vector metrics sREV analysis using Eq. (11)  and ε1  =  0.1 (see Figs. S15-S23 in Supplementary Materials). The results obtained with Eqs. (8) and (10)  are also available in Supplementary Materials, see Figs. S24-S37. The main conclusion one can make from the analysis of results presented in Table 2 , that except for PD-based metric with MSSIM vectorization method, for other vector metrics sREV size is larger than dREV size. As this is also valid for considered scalar metrics, we can claim that deviations of medium properties in subcubes cut from different places of a sample usually has more influence to representativity than average deviations depending on subcube size. The dREV analysis of PNM-based metrics similar to porosity and permeability dREV analysis separates the least representative samples CAR, S2 and S3 from the most representative CER, S1 and SPH for pore and throat size distributions. For connectivity distribution, all the samples except for SPH have close values of dREV sizes, for 10% threshold they vary in the interval 300–350. According to sREV analysis of PNM-based metrics, the least representative samples CAR, S2 and S3 are also prominent, though the sequence of samples ranged by sREV sizes differs from one for porosity and permeability. For PNM-based metrics sREV analysis, not CAR but S3 sample is the least representative, and not CER but SPH sample is the most representative. dREV analysis of S 2 , C 2  and L 2  metrics shows a strong correlation with porosity and permeability dREV analysis. The only one exception from permeability sequence is observed, the exchange of SPH and S1 samples positions. For SS 2  metric, correlation with porosity and permeability dREV analysis is very weak. Note, also that L 2  and SS 2  dREV sizes are smaller than ones for S 2  and C 2  metrics. As for CF sREV analysis, the permeability sorted sequence of samples is reproduced for S3, S2 and CAR set, but not for CER, S1 and SPH set. It is possible and likely useful in the future to merge all CFs into a single metric (Gerke and Karsanina, 2015 ). As for PD REV analysis, for all considered methods of vectorizations the results of PD2  REV analysis have a weaker correlation with ones for porosity and permeability than the results of PD1  and PD0  REV analysis. It seems to be natural, as intrinsic solid phase structure, mainly described by PD2 , does not affect medium flow properties. According to PD dREV and sREV analysis results obtained using simple binning method and Euclidean distance metric, less representative samples S3, S2 and CAR samples are separated from more representative CER, S1 and SPH, as for porosity and permeability. Though the order of samples in sorted sequence for PDs vectorized using this method does not coincide with permeability one. As for MSSIM metric, the correlation with permeability and porosity REV analysis results is weaker than for Euclidian distance. The sequence of samples sorted by porosity and permeability REV sizes is well reproduced for PD1  and PD0  persistence image REV analysis, there are a few differences in this sequence. As for binning vectorization method and Euclidian distance metric, PD1  and PD0  REV (both dREV and sREV) sizes are close, for persistence method vectorization method PD1  dREV and sREV sizes are larger than PD0  ones. Functions δ1 (L ) calculated for PDs vectorized with landscape method have oscillating structure even for very large cut sizes, though the mean decreasing trend is observed (see Fig. S22). Silhouette vectorization method, which develops landscape method by introduction of weight function shows its advantage over its predecessor: the oscillations vanish (see Fig. S23). More representative CER, SPH and S1 are separated from less representative CAR, S2 and S3 samples in PD0  and PD1  vectorized using landscape method REV analysis and PD1  vectorized using silhouette method REV analysis. As for other PDs, this correlation is weaker, for example SPH sample is found to be the least representative in PD0  dREV analysis with landscape vectorization method. Note, also that using landscape and silhouette vectorization methods lead to the largest sREV sizes among all considered PD vectorization methods.  5.4 Perfomance According to our pipeline (see Fig. 8 ), the total algorithm can be separated in several parts: data generation, which includes subcubes selection and metric calculation for each subcube, data vectorization (for vector metrics only) and data analysis, which results in REV sizes estimation. Therefore, the total computing time t  = t gen   + t an   for scalar metrics, and t  = tgen   + tvec   + tan   for vector metrics. Here, tgen, tvec and tan are times of data generation, vectorization and analysis, respectively. These times are presented in Tables 3-6      for all the metrics considered in present survey. The test computations to obtain time values were carried out using computer station with a double Intel Xeon Gold 6248R CPU. For the generation of permeability, PNM statistics and PDs, we used parallel codes run at 48 threads. The other metrics were calculated using non-parallel codes. As one can conclude from the analysis of Tables 3-6 , the values of t gen   mainly contribute into the total computing times for all the metrics considered. Note, that except for porosity, for which calculation is trivial, we use the external software to generate metric data. One can reduce data generation time using codes with better performance than used in our study. Another possibility is the parallel metric data generation for different subcubes. Permeability computations with FDMSS are the most time consuming within our pipeline; our recent solution based on multi-grid and GPU technology can solve this problem within tens of seconds (Evstigneev et al., 2023 ), but multi-GPU version for large cubes as in this study is still under development.   6 General discussion, interpretations, and outlook If we visually examine REV behavior for porosity (Fig. 9 ) and permeability (Fig. 10 ), it is clear that for some samples, notably CAR and S3, the behavior is quite different for these properties; moreover, they provide different REV sizes for φ  and K  (see Figs. 11-13  and Table 2 ). This result is not surprising and was reported before, however, it is important to understand why this happens. The reason is in different ability of permeability and porosity to characterize the pore structure that governs these two physical properties of a porous sample. We shall refer to this ability of some property to describe another property it depends on as to information content. To further elucidate potential porosity vs. permeability behavior and their relation to information content, let us consider a simple example of two subcubes of the same linear size L , presented in Fig. 17  . In the first one the pore space is formed out of a tube with square cross section, and in the second — from two parallel tubes of similar shape. If the sizes of these squares satisfy the condition b 2  = b 1 2  + b 2 2 , for both subcubes the porosity is equal to b 2 /L 2  and permeability is equal to 0.422b 2 /L 2 . In other words, both porosity and permeability (computed along tube major direction) do not “feel” the difference between two subcubes. But capillary pressure curve for two-phase flow (say, drainage for simplicity) through these subcubes would feel the difference (obviously, capillary entry pressures for Fig. 17 a and b are different). In this context, two-phase flow properties add critical information content in addition to φ  and K  as related to two considered pore geometries. Inability to achieve REV is usually explained due to two factors: insufficiently small volume (e.g., the fluctuations around volumes smaller or around the characteristic pore size), and heterogeneity on larger volumes. The problem in this interpretation is a lack of quantitative explanation. We argue that the universal explanation (for both cases) is the non-stationarity of the pore structure within the considered samples — pore geometry is essentially different within subvolumes. For example, the porosity value can be similar, but the orientation of pores could lead to variations in permeability. Local inhomogeneities can lead to a more complex situation when while subcubes are very different, their ensemble properties still show dREV behavior — Gerke and Karsanina (2021)  observed non-unique porosity/permeability dREVs within the same 3D image. They concluded, that dREV is necessary, but insufficient condition for representativity and stationarity of the pore structure is necessary as a stricter condition. But what is stationarity of the structure? Considering the 3D image to be a binary representation of the solid and pore phases, we can cite Torquato's definition (Torquato, 2002 ): "the media is statistically homogeneous if the joint probability distributions describing the stochastic process are translationally invariant, i.e., invariant under a translation (shift) of the space origin". As fitting a stochastic model (for example, Gaussian random field or other model) to describe porous media structure at hand is hardly possible in majority of cases (e.g., Cherkasov et al., 2021 ), the remaining option in quantifying stationarity lies with intercomparison of differences between image subregions under translation with the help of high-information content metric (Karsanina and Gerke, 2023 ). In this context, sREV analysis actually performs such an intercomparison, but only partially. It may seem that sREV is superior to dREV or even makes the latter obsolete. However, under the condition that of stationary 3D image, sREV and dREV will produce similar results. The only difference is that for metrics with low information content (such as porosity and even permeability) sREV is more sensitive to local inhomogeneities due to deviations analysis, something dREV overlooks by averaging the results. Purely stationary structures, especially for geological media or soils, are close to impossible to encounter in nature. Examples of stationary structures include periodic unit cells (Gerke et al., 2014 ; Rozman and Utz, 2002 ), some simple crystals (Gommes et al., 2012a ) and images produced by stationary processes with resolutions close to infinity (Lantuejoul, 1991 ). Thus, majority of experimental 3D images of porous media with limited resolution and size can be only weakly stationary and physically meaningful criterion for such stationarity can be established based on image analysis alone (Lavrukhin et al., 2023 ). Information content is an important factor to consider, as both sREV and dREV analysis are meaningless according to porosity and permeability as separate metrics — according to them all considered samples are REVs (Figs. 12-13 ). Thus, proposed vector metrics with much higher information content are essential for establishing representativity. Notably, correlation functions with the help of stochastic reconstructions potentially allow to establish their information content for a structure in question, however all existing methods are limited to S 2  correlation function (Gommes et al., 2012a , b ). Using similar approach based on energy landscape search one can assess information content for any metric or descriptor, but it may be too computationally expensive for majority of such metrics. Computational expenses are due to the need to establish all possible structural configurations and their properties, but analytical options now seem to be a promising solution (Cherkasov et al., 2023 ). Vector metrics based on PD, CFs and PNM arguably have the largest information content as they show the highest sensitivity to heterogeneities within our sample collection both for dREV and sREV analysis. The PD-based metrics describe the topology of pore space and were shown to correlate with major physical properties (Robins et. al, 2016 ; Obayashi et al., 2018 ; Moon et. al., 2019 ; Thakur et. al, 2021 ; Fedotov et. al, 2021 ). Correlation functions possess mainly morphological and connectivity information, that combined may possess some minor topological information too, but below that of PD. The PNM-based metrics combine both geometry and topology and, thus, we expect them to add little content to PD ∪ CFs set. On the other hand, PNM metrics can be useful in REV analysis of pore-networks extracted from 3D images (e.g., Jiang et al., 2007 ; Rabbani et al., 2014 ; Gostick, 2017 ; Gerke et al., 2020 ; Zubov et al., 2022 ). Considering that pore-network models can be the object of stochastic reconstructions (Jiang et al., 2012 ; Park et al., 2020 ), it is also possible to establish information content for PNM-based metrics. Note that correlation functions (or any other metric with quantifiable information content for that matter) could be effectively joined into a single descriptor (Gerke and Karsanina, 2015 ), but establishing information content for each CF first could improve this procedure and help in removing redundant computations. Based on the analysis of dREV and sREV curves for all vector metrics (Table 2 ) we speculate that a union of PD and CFs likely has the largest information content among studied metrics. This can be useful not only for REV evaluation, but for choosing features for machine learning properties predictions or input data for stochastic reconstructions (which, by the way, require representativity analysis of the 3D images used to extract the features during training or reconstruction). It is also an open question if calculation of all considered metrics for both pore and solid phases will significantly improve the information content of the descriptors set, balanced by increased computation burden. It is important to highlight that precise values of vector metrics to establish REV sizes depend on chosen thresholds. Whether these thresholds should be equal to ε used for scalar metrics is an open question. The values of ε1  and ε2  are purely arbitrary — studies that proposed these thresholds (Zhang et al., 2000 ; Li et al., 2009 ; Constanza-Robinson et al., 2011 ; Rozenbaum and du Roscoat, 2014 ; Borges et al., 2018 ; Koestel et.al, 2020 ) never proved the validity of these choices. Besides, sREV size depends on the methodology used for calculations as we discuss above. However, we can compare porosity and permeability dREV and sREV sizes with vector metrics ones using the same thresholds — in most cases considered vector metrics dREV sizes are located between porosity and permeability ones. As for vector metrics, sREV sizes are always larger than for porosity, but can be both larger or smaller than permeability sREVs for different samples and descriptors. However, considering that both sREV and dREV analysis in subcubes assume ergodicity, REV sizes larger than half of the 3D image are highly unreliable. The reason for this is that for smaller subcubes, even if ergodicity does not hold, the averaged metric based on its information content still may show differences to other subcubes. On the other hand, depending on the heterogeneities sizes, larger subcubes provide “over-averaged” values that fail to feel the inhomogeneities — this results in incorrect REV evaluation. Considering the lack of ergodicity in large subcubes, we argue that REV sizes based on vector metrics are actually larger than for scalar ones. Based on recent research and current findings we can now formulate REV definition for real materials as the following: “REV is a volume with lower and upper limit that has (weakly) stationary structure for the field of interest that allows for its homogenization”. Size limits are necessary, as smallest volume is needed to establish statistically homogeneous structure (Lantuejoul, 1991 ). The upper limit on volume indicates the largest volume that can be described by the smallest volume. This latter part is optional, as in classical theory this volume is infinite. Yet, real structures, especially geological material and soils, are heterogenous if sampled with large enough measuring window. The weak stationarity (Lavrukhin et al., 2023 ) of the field of interest refers to homogeneity of the property within the sample. For example, if one looks for permeability REV, then flow velocity field has to be analyzed for stationarity. As real structures are never strictly stationary, we look for weak stationarity instead. Finally, homogenization should be possible on a given volume, as there is a gap between classical homogenization and its application to pore-scale modelling results. If we consider classical works and take a permeability as an example (Whitaker, 1986 ), homogenization can be performed only on periodic domains. Real samples obviously never have periodic pore geometry. Such periodization is needed to obtain symmetric permeability tensor as required by Darcy equation. For example, if one applies pressure boundary conditions while solving Stokes equation, the resulting permeability tensor is non-symmetric (Manwart et al., 2002 ; Gerke et al., 2019 ). There is a gap between REV definition and homogenization that is usually closed by forced symmetry, e.g., by averaging non-diagonal values (Guibert et al., 2016 ). There are other problems with homogenization. All physical properties we have considered in this work are steady-state, e.g., porosity, interfacial area, and permeability. The latter, as many other properties such as thermal, electrical conductivity or diffusion coefficient (see Table 1.1 in Torquato (2002)  for a full list of such physical properties) a defined by a simple linear relationship between gradient/intensity field and a flux field, e.g., pressure field and flow velocity in Darcy law to obtain permeability. For porous media, multi-phase flow properties such as relative permeabilities or capillary/water retention curves are of special interest (to parameterize continuum-scale models based on multi-phase Darcy equation). The problem with, say, two-phase flow properties is that they are not defined by a simple linear relationship between gradient/intensity field and a flux field. For example, two-phase flow will be governed by wettability pattern (we can immediately expect that stationary wettability spatial distribution is needed to obtain REV), capillary number, boundary conditions (pressure of flux) and all other parameters affecting two-phase flow regime (Lenormand et al., 1988 ). Depending on the flow regime, two-phase flow can exhibit temporal fluctuations in addition to spatial ones (Armstrong et al., 2014 ; Rücker et al., 2021 ; McClure et al., 2022 ). Moreover, there is still a discussion to what extent such dynamics is important for creeping flow that can be effectively described using quasi-static models (Blunt, 2017 ; Bultreys et al., 2018 ). In other words, multi-phase properties cannot be established from pore geometry alone. While classical homogenization theory claims it can describe multi-phase flow (Cushman,1984 ; Baveye and Sposito, 1984 ; Wood, 2009 ; Davit et al., 2013 ), it's ability in doing so are very limited. The latter fact is stressed that obtaining of relative permeabilities for two-phase flow based on pore-scale simulations is still an active area of research (Raeini et al., 2014 ; Li et al., 2019 ; Pereira, 2019 ; Santos et al., 2022 ; Alpak and Saxena, 2023 ; Balashov et al., 2024 ). We previously mentioned that weak stationarity of the field of interest is required to obtain REV for a given property. Weakly stationary pore structure will result in stationary gradient/intensity field and a flux field for these properties. If we take permeability, electrical conductivity and diffusion coefficient as an example, the flow of fluid, electricity and molecular species within the same pore will be very different. This justifies a very well-known fact that REV is different for different properties. For the same reasons, it is very likely that REV for two-phase flow is larger than for single phase. However, relative permeabilities are usually expressed as a fraction of absolute permeability. While this is not a problem for infinite domain sizes usually used in classical homogenization approaches, for real applications this may pose problems if upper and lower bounds on REV sizes do not coincide. For this reason, it may be useful to establish a universal REV purely based on the 3D image analysis. Such a REV will work for all major physical properties defined by 3D geometry — porosity, permeability, thermal and electrical conductivity, diffusion, and dispersion tensors and many more (but not multi-phase flow as will discussed shortly). Separate analysis for each physical property can be computationally expensive; whilst extraction of structural metrics from 3D can be very fast, especially using modern GPU hardware (e.g., Postnicov et al., 2024 ). Finally, finding a universal solution is always appealing from fundamental point of view. At the moment we do not understand how the size and degree of inhomogeneity affect each property, and, thus, unable to choose the threshold between insignificant and large disturbances introduced by such heterogeneities (e.g., to flow velocity fields, two-phase flow, etc.). The simplest solution could be to choose the maximum REV size for all physical properties, but validity of such a universal REV requires more research. The final problem with homogenization, and with REV for this matter, that we want to discuss is absence of REV for heterogeneous samples. Image analysis by Lavrukhin et al. (2023)  suggest that numerous samples of real porous media, especially carbonates and soils, may possess no REV at all. Again, while classical homogenization theory provides some solutions for such cases as well (Cushman, 1984 ; Wood, 2009 ; Davit et al., 2013 ), they can address only simple cases that obey some simple (e.g., linear) trend. How to rigorously upscale physical properties, especially unsteady-state properties such as multi-phase ones, in case REV is not found is currently unresolved issue. The problem could be attacked by pore-scale simulations on large volumes and comparison against different upscaling schemes using continuum-scale model. Here we come back to the earlier question – do we really need REV after all? The answer is yes, at least for now. This is simply because the usage of REV simplifies homogenization of large enough homogeneous regions within the studied heterogeneous material. If REV cannot be established, other homogenization and upscaling techniques should be used. This may mean that generalized homogenization theory for nonstationary fields yet to be developed indeed may make REV concept obsolete. However, we still have a long way to go before such general theory can be established. Regardless of this, REV analysis is under the hood is exactly the same as stationarity analysis that will be necessary for application of such a unified theory (Gerke and Karsanina, 2021 ; Lavrukhin et al., 2023 ). In Fig. 18   we present an example of sandstone structure classification into two zones by analyzing structural descriptors within subregions and by clustering patches according to distances between them in terms of such descriptors. Some immediate problems with classical homogenization are obvious, for example, if the homogeneous zone is not large enough – this makes it impossible to simply substitute each classified computational cell with a single physical property as usually done in Darcy scale simulations (Durlofsky, 1991 ; Azizmohammadi and Matthäi, 2017 ; Sedaghat and Azizmohammadi, 2019 ). REV analysis is ultimately the same procedure where we explore some metric and compare it within windows of different sizes to observe plateau in value (dREV) or its standard deviation (sREV). In this paper we developed exactly this type of methodology based on PD ∪ CFs high information content set, that combined with spatial field analysis as introduced by Lavrukhin et al. (2023)  will be useful to classify the samples into REV and non-REV volumes. This discussion highlights the importance of the proposed technique not only to pore-scale images and processes, but for upscaling and continuum-scale modelling frameworks. Future improvements and directions of research to establish universal REV analysis may include:1) Combination of REV (deterministic and especially statistical) analysis with the 3D image stationarity analysis may uncover numerous additional aspects of representativity not currently understood, for example, the relationship between the size and magnitude of an inhomogeneity to perturbation of the sample's physical properties. Artificial 3D geometries with controlled degree of non-stationarity can also be useful in this regard (Karsanina and Gerke, 2023 ). This research direction may also help in establishing physically meaningful thresholds ε. Current study provide a solid foundation for merging of these two previously separate types of analysis into a single pipeline.  2) Implementation of automatic choice of parameters for vector metrics — recall that binning was performed by hand. It may be possible to establish bins by morphological analysis of the image, e.g., with the help of correlation functions.  3) Development of the REV analysis for multi-phase systems or multi-scale structures (Nordahl and Ringrose, 2008 ; Gerke et al., 2015a ; Karsanina et al., 2018 ; Wu et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) in the form of 3D images, and for (hierarchical) pore-network representations (Jiang et al., 2012 , 2013 ; Park et al., 2020 ) of the sample structure.  4) Information content evaluation for different metrics, not limited to correlation functions (Gommes et al., 2012a , 2012b ), that may even include assessment of information content for major physical properties based on stochastic reconstructions (Różański et al., 2023 ) and energy landscape exploration.  5) Addition of other major physical properties into REV analysis, including two-phase flow properties that will require massive research. In this study we limited our scope to permeability due to high-computational demand of two-phase simulations, uncertainty in spatial wettability properties for our samples and other considerations already discussed above.  6) Consideration of tensorial rather than scalar physical properties, something needed for majority of natural anisotropic materials (Guibert et al., 2016 ; Gerke et al., 2019 ; Thovert and Mourzenko, 2020 ; Scandelli et al., 2022 ; Lesueur et al., 2022 ).    Such studies are critical in numerous areas related to properties evaluation, as representability needs to be established for homogenization, machine learning (training on nonrepresentative samples can hamper prediction accuracy), stochastic reconstructions, and numerous other applications.  7 Summary and conclusions In present paper we introduced a method to perform vector metrics REV analysis and estimate corresponding REV sizes for porous domains. While applied to establish REV, the same pipeline can be combined with image analysis to divide sample into REV and non-REV portions. This builds foundation for a general upscaling technique that considers both stationary (and potentially REV) and non-stationary volumes within the studied material and, thus, may make REV concept obsolete. Based on recent research we have redefined classical REV to include stationarity condition and lower and upper limits on REV volume. We proposed to substitute difference between absolute values, used in scalar metrics REV analysis, by Euclidian distances between vectors. We can construct these vectors from descriptors defined at subcubes cut from the studied domain. It is possible to use both dREV and sREV criteria for vector metrics, similar to scalar metrics. If the compared vectors have different dimensions, one should apply the modification procedure before the calculation of distance. We considered different descriptors to obtain vector metrics for porous media: based on correlation functions (S 2 , C 2 , L 2  and SS 2 ), pore-network model statistics (pore and throat sizes and connectivity) and persistence diagrams. For PDs, we compare the results of REV analysis obtained using different techniques of vectorization and using scalar metric, sliced Wasserstein distance. We took six samples of porous media to test our methodology and considered vector metrics. First, we estimated their porosity and permeability REV sizes and make ascending sorting of results: from CER with the lowest dREV and sREV sizes to CAR with the highest one. Note, that for porosity and permeability REV sizes the found order of samples is the same. Besides we observed the same order for scalar sliced Wasserstein method. We also studied the dependence of dREV sizes on different mathematical interpretations of dREV, given by Eqs. (1) –(4)  and performed Euler density REV analysis. We found that Euler density REV size estimation for samples with Euler numbers close to zero lead to the doubtful results. Then for the same samples we performed vector metrics REV analysis. We calculated dREV sizes using Eq. (7)  and found that it is problematic to estimate sREV size using Eq. (8)  as its denominator are close to zero at subcube sizes larger than dREV sizes. It is better to use Eqs. (10)  or (11)  in sREV analysis. For the most of considered vector metrics, we observed a correlation of dREV and sREV analysis results with ones obtained for porosity and permeability. More representative samples CER, SPH and S1 are separated from less representative S2, S3, CAR in most cases. We can highlight S 2 , C 2  and L 2  CF metrics and PD0  and PD1  vectorized using persistence image methods to have the strongest correlation with porosity and permeability REV analysis results. Direct PD comparison metric sliced Wasserstein distance also strongly correlates with porosity and permeability in the sense of REV analysis. dREV sizes of the most of considered vector metrics are located between porosity and permeability ones. Their sREV sizes are larger than porosity ones and can be larger or smaller than permeability ones. For all considered scalar and vector metrics expect for PD-based metric MSSIM sREV sizes are larger than dREV sizes. This emphasizes the importance of sREV analysis, it is necessary to perform it solving any problem in which representativity is of large significance. Physical properties are tied to gradient/intensity field and a flux field related to material's inner structure, and, thus, one needs to search for REV within the (field's) structure to obtain a universal solution. Different properties/metrics possess different amount of information content about the structure at hand. Low information content metrics are incapable to elucidate such universal REV, likely to overlook potential inhomogeneities, and result in small REV volumes for such metrics, whilst other characteristics may have much larger or no REV at all. Different properties such as porosity or permeability possess different information content and, thus, usually have different REVs within the same structure. For practical applications of classical REV notion, sREV is better to use for low content metrics, as dREV is completely unable to describe ihomogeneities for such metrics. The size of the maximum subcube to analyze REV should be smaller than the size of the 3D image. The sREV is an overall better approach, as it incorporates stationarity analysis into REV analysis, and stationarity is a necessary condition for REV to exist (sREV and dREV produce the same results under stationarity condition). High information content metrics, namely correlation functions combined with persistent diagrams, seem to be enough to establish universal REV, that should be verified by evaluation and intercomparison of REVs for all major physical properties. The REV analysis based on vector metrics as presented in this paper may serve as a universal structure comparison technique and may be useful in developing advanced methods to divide structures/fields into stationary and nonstationary zones and universal upscaling techniques. We believe it will be useful for application of numerical techniques to composites, biological tissues, granular matter, food engineering, building materials and in other numerous areas.
1 Introduction Nonlinear or threshold behaviors are commonly observed due to alteration of the internal states or discontinuous boundary conditions in hydrological systems (Detty and McGuire, 2010a; McGuire and McDonnell, 2010; Zehe and Sivapalan, 2009 ). The nonlinear behaviors can occur across different climate zones, spatial scales, and geomorphic conditions (Ali et al., 2015; Saffarpour et al., 2016; Zehe et al., 2007 ). Previous studies identified different types and values of thresholds for runoff processes, including rainfall depth (Lehmann et al., 2007; Tromp‐van Meerveld and McDonnell, 2006 ), water table height (Detty and McGuire, 2010b ), soil water content (Penna et al., 2011 ), and a sum of soil water content and rainfall depth (Saffarpour et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022b ). Below the threshold, little to no stormflow/quick flow (QF) was generated, whereas a significant increase in stormflow was recorded once the threshold was exceeded. The threshold response is typically attributed to the hydrological connectivity of the flow network, which is activated by subsurface matrix flow, preferential flow, and soil pipe flow (Uchida et al., 2005 ). The threshold theory has advanced the interpretation of factors controlling runoff generation and the analysis of underlying mechanisms regulating different stages of runoff, enhancing the process understanding of water movement across different spatial scales. While, studies have revealed considerable variability of QF amounts during the above threshold phase (Buttle et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2021 ), hindering the accurate prediction and assessment of QF amounts during rainfall and limiting our insight into the hierarchical processes where the output from one process serves as input for another. Recently proposed multiple-phase threshold behaviors could well characterize the initial QF activation and the transition from slow to fast response of QF (Saffarpour et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2020 ), but the changes in threshold values due to continuous evolution in hillslope or catchment characteristics, such as soil thickness, vegetation cover, and soil properties, have received limited attention (Ali et al., 2015; Camporese et al., 2019; Camporese et al., 2014 ). This constrains a comprehensive understanding of the evolving hydrological behaviors associated with thresholds and limits deep insights into the dominant runoff mechanism. Soil thickness and its spatial variation determine the geomorphology of hillslopes or catchments and associated water storage capacity, consequently impacting hydraulic gradient, water movement, and flow paths, thereby governing the runoff processes (Liu et al., 2013; Patton et al., 2018 ). Buttle et al. (2004)  found a linear relationship between runoff and rainfall in thin soils, whereas thick soils exhibited a nonlinear behavior; Hopp and McDonnell (2009)  argued that changes in soil thickness did not significantly affect subsurface runoff coefficients, despite their considerable impact on the degree and timing of hydrological connectivity. Zhang et al. (2022)  found that surface and subsurface runoff contributions differed significantly between the shallow-soil plot and the deep-soil plot in the karst region. These findings consistently highlight the important and complex role of soil thickness in runoff processes, as variations in soil thickness not only change water storage but also divert flow paths within hydrological systems. This may potentially result in divergent runoff mechanisms even in areas with similar soil characteristics. However, many studies have treated soil as a uniform buffer without considering soil thickness-induced changes in preferential flow paths and associated characteristics (e.g., the continuity and connectivity). This is crucial given the dominant role that preferential flow plays in runoff processes both below and above the threshold phase in forests (Alaoui et al., 2011; Nanda and Safeeq, 2023 ). In humid forests, tree roots and faunal activities are confined to relatively shallow soil layers, known as the root zone (Fan et al., 2017; Nespoulous et al., 2019 ). Below the root zone, there is a variable depth of mineral soil overlaying the bedrock, resulting from landscape evolution or geomorphic conditions (Hartmann et al., 2020; Laine-Kaulio et al., 2015 ). Numerous studies have found that soil water storage capacity is influenced by vegetation roots through the reconstruction of soil pores, and by soil thickness through the augmentation of pore space (Buttle et al., 2019 ). Additionally, root–branching networks, animal burrowing networks, and cracks promote preferential flow paths, facilitating the movement of water from the soil surface into subsurface (Lin, 2010; Nimmo, 2021 ). For instance, a study conducted on three neighboring hillslopes with intensive wells for measuring water table fluctuations found that the lower percentage of well activation at the grassland was due to a higher storage capacity caused by thicker soil, whereas the similar percentage of well activation between the coniferous and mixed forests was attributed to preferential flow paths (Bachmair et al., 2012 ). Moreover, soil thickness also influences the connectivity of preferential flow paths due to soil layering and loss of roots, which in turn affects the timing and quantity of QF, significantly impacting the relationship between rainfall and QF (Scaife et al., 2020 ). Meanwhile, limited knowledge exists regarding the extent to which an increase in soil thickness affects the connectivity of flow paths within forest types in combination with the threshold behaviors. Particularly, conducting such studies in the field is challenging due to the complex interactions among the atmosphere, vegetation, and geomorphology on water retention and release within hydrological systems (Alaoui et al., 2011; Wang and Chen, 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ), which make it difficult to provide an effective platform for investigating physical processes under controlled conditions. Early studies have demonstrated that nuances of the surface and subsurface topography of hillslopes or catchments, even under similar climatic, pedologic, and geologic conditions, can lead to a wide variability in relevant processes and contrasting runoff mechanisms (Bachmair and Weiler, 2012; Jarecke et al., 2021 ). As a result, quantifying how studied field characteristics might explain differences in the threshold values becomes challenging, which in turn restricts our understanding, development, and application of rainfall-runoff models at various scales (Lehmann et al., 2007; Scaife and Band, 2017; Zehe and Sivapalan, 2009 ). Controlled experiments have the advantage of isolating irrelevant variables that might influence the results, thus clarifying the observed behavior (Volkmann et al., 2017 ). Additionally, intercomparison is a key approach for developing a holistic picture of the factors driving hydrological system responses (Bachmair et al., 2012; Hazenberg et al., 2016 ). In this study, we applied controlled experiments to explore the nonlinear behavior of QF under varying soil thickness in response to precipitation input in two contrasting humid forests. The main objectives of this work were to: (1) identify the variables related to the threshold behavior of the QF process in humid forests, (2) explore the roles of soil thickness and forest type on threshold behavior, and (3) gain insight into the dominant runoff mechanism(s) in humid mountainous forests.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site and artificial physical models This study focuses on two typical forest types in Mountain Gongga: coniferous and broadleaf forests. The forests are distributed along the elevation gradient of Mountain Gongga due to the dramatic rise in elevation over a short horizontal distance. Soil and vegetation surveys were conducted at 2280 m a.s.l. for the broadleaf forest and at 3020 m a.s.l. for the coniferous forest. The dominant species in the coniferous forest are Abies fabri  and Picea brachytyla , whereas Lithocarpus cleistocarpus  and Cercidiphyllum japonicum  dominate in the broadleaf forest. The monsoon climate in this area is characterized by distinct wet (May–October) and dry (November–April) seasons, with 80 % of the total precipitation occurring during the wet seasons (Hu et al., 2018 ). Previous work has indicated that 50 cm is a critical depth (Figure S1 ), below which plant roots almost disappear, except for anchoring taproots in both forest types. This is attributed to the humid climate, which consistently provides abundant moisture to the topsoil, eliminating the need for roots to grow deeper (Fan et al., 2017 ). The root zone has a higher soil organic content and saturated hydraulic conductivity (K s ) than the underlying mineral soil. The K s  decreases exponentially with depth, and we also find a higher saturated soil water content and residual soil water content of the root zone compared with the mineral soil (Wang et al., 2022a ). Soil water retention curves (SWRCs) were determined by multistep-outflow experiments on undisturbed soil columns, where soil water content was measured at specific soil water potentials through Pressure Plate Extractor (Soil Moisture Equipment Corp. USA). The soil parameters related to the SWRCs were then modeled with a van Genuchten–Mualem model using the measured relationship between soil water content and soil water potential (Van Genuchten, 1980 ; Van Genuchten et al., 1991 ). Finally, we averaged the modeled soil parameters from replicates of the soil columns to obtain the effective soil parameters (Table 1  ). Additionally, more information on soil texture, root biomass, and rock fragment content can be found in our previous work (Wang et al., 2022a ). To allow hydrological systems under controlled conditions, we constructed three artificial physical models (PMs) for each forest. The PMs were composed of concrete boxes, each with an identical projected length of 3 m and a width of 1 m, set at a fixed inclination of 30° (Fig. 1  a), and waterproof material was applied to the inside of the boxes to prevent leakage. Soils were moved to PMs in two ways: the root zone was cut into blocks and transported to PMs using 50 × 50 × 50 cm steel cubes with minimal disturbance; the poorly structured mineral soil (below 50 cm) was carefully collected and refilled into the concrete boxes at 10–20 cm intervals through manual dispersal and packing. A drainage layer (∼3 cm) composed of gravel was placed on top of the concrete bed to facilitate water drainage (Fig. 1 b). The PMs were situated at an open site near the Mountain Gongga Observation Station (∼3000 m a.s.l). The refilling process was completed by the end of September 2019, resulting in three distinct PMs representing the root zone (PM-0.5), the root zone capping thin mineral soil (PM-1), and thick mineral soil (PM-2), respectively.  2.2 Hydrometric observations Rainfall input was recorded using three tipping buckets near the open site. Soil water potential was monitored by T4e probes (UMS GmbH, Germany) deployed at depths of 10, 20, and 50 cm in the PM-0.5; 10, 50, and 100 cm in the PM-1; and 10, 50, 100, and 200 cm in the PM-2. The probes at 200 cm encountered severe damage in the middle of the monitoring period, so subsequent data were substituted with monitoring data from 100 cm, where the soil water potential was synchronized and similar according to previous observation. To drain potential outflows, a trench was positioned at the soil surface to collect surface runoff. Stainless-steel plates were placed at a depth of 20 cm in PM-0.5 and at a depth of 50 cm in both PM-1 and PM-2 to collect interflow. Subsurface flow along the concrete bed was drained through a hole in the lower part of the concrete box. All outflows were connected to tipping buckets via pipes for volume determination (Fig. 2  b). Notably, no surface runoff or interflow was generated in any of the PMs due to the high K s  and abundant preferential flow paths. This finding agrees with field studies demonstrating that interflow was only detected at depths below 300 cm in both forests (Figure S2 ). The tipping buckets and probes were connected to a data logger (CR1000, Campbell Scientific Inc, USA) via multiplexers to record the monitoring data at 15-min intervals. Before further analysis, the entire data set underwent screening. Early monitoring data collected before May 2020—eight months after the refilling process—was discarded to avoid the influence of soil disturbance. Soil water potential and outflow measurements taken at temperatures below 0 ℃ were excluded due to unreliable readings from frozen soils. Abnormally large oscillations between subsequent measurements during a rainfall event were visually checked and removed. Additionally, data with asynchronous rainfall-runoff relationships, equipment failures, or battery issues were also excluded.  2.3 Graphical hydrograph separation We defined rainfall events based on a specific time interval without rainfall, which was set at 12 h. Delineated rainfall events with a total rainfall amount of less than 1 mm were excluded. To calculate QF, we subtracted the base flow, which was assumed to be equal to the initial discharge, from the total outflow (i.e., subsurface flow in this study). The end of the event was defined either when the discharge in the falling limb of the hydrograph equaled the initial discharge or by the onset of the next event if the discharge in the falling limb was not met. The initial discharge of an event hydrograph was defined as the discharge immediately before the first pulse of rainfall (Haga et al., 2005 ). Thus QF (mm) was calculated as follows:QF = ∑ t = T i   t = T e    ( Q t   - Q i  ) / ( 1000 × A )        Here, QF represents the event quick flow (mm), Qt  (ml) denotes the subsurface flow during the t th  period, and Qi  denotes the initial discharge of the subsurface flow, Ti  and Te  are the initial and end time of the event subsurface flow, and A (m2 ) is the projection area of the PM. To characterize antecedent soil water storage, we used and calculated the depth equivalent antecedent soil wetness (ASW) by the following equation for different PMs:ASW = ( θ 10  × 15 + θ 20  × 15 )  × ( 1 - R F 1  )  + θ 50  × 20 × ( 1 - R  F 2  ) (PM - 0.5)     A S W = ( θ 10  × 30 + θ 50  × 30 )  × ( 1 - R F 1  )  + θ 100  × 40 × ( 1 - R  F 2  ) (PM - 1)     A S W = ( θ 10  × 30 + θ 50  × 30 )  × ( 1 - R F 1  ) + ( θ 100  × 60 + θ 200  × 80 )  × (  1 - R F 2  ) (PM - 2)           Here, θ i  denotes the soil water content (SWC) measured at i th soil depth, and SWC was converted using SWRCs with measured soil water potential. RF1  and RF2  denote the mean rock fragment contents in different soil layers and were set at 7.5% and 12% in the coniferous forest, 6.5% and 15% in the broadleaf forest according to our previous work.  2.4 Approach for thresholds detection To detect thresholds associated with QF, we aimed to define two types: generation and rising thresholds. The generation threshold represents the point at which a measurable output (i.e., subsurface flow in this study) occurs in 99 % of rainfall events. The rising threshold reflects a significant increase in QF above this threshold. To determine the thresholds, we used the piecewise regression analysis to calculate the threshold values (i.e., breakpoints) and derive linear slope parameters above and below the rising threshold. This approach benefits our understanding of the shift between slow and rapid QF. Piecewise regression analysis was carried out using the “segmented” package in R software, where breakpoints were automatically estimated based on the top-down approach and maximum likelihood approach (Muggeo, 2003 ).   3 Results 3.1 Rainfall–QF relationships The total precipitation during the monitoring period (May 6th to November 6th) was 1684 mm, with a total of 60 rainfall events. Event precipitation (P) ranged from 1.60 to 128.00 mm, with an average of 28.46 mm and a mean rainfall intensity of 0.69 mm/hour, and 75 % of events had a total precipitation exceeding 4.5 mm. After data screening for PM-0.5, PM-1, and PM-2, the number of events with detected QF was 45, 30, and 27 in the coniferous forest, and 38, 30, and 18 in the broadleaf forest, respectively (Fig. 2 ). The mean QF in the coniferous and broadleaf forests was 21.06 mm vs. 22.65 mm for PM-0.5, 20.62 mm vs. 26.28 mm for PM-1, and 17.74 mm vs. 20.62 mm for PM-2, respectively. QF was strongly correlated with P across all PMs (R 2  > 0.77, p  < 0.0001), and linear fitting was applied to derive the slope parameters to present the QF yield capacity. However, QF exhibited no evident correlation with rainfall intensity (Pi ), particularly displaying a high variability pattern when Pi  exceeded 1 mm/hour. The slope parameters for PM-0.5 and PM-1 in the broadleaf forest were higher than that in the coniferous forest, whereas the opposite trend was found for PM-2 (Figs. 3 and 4   ). The mean event quick flow coefficient (QF/P) in the coniferous and broadleaf forests was 0.46 vs. 0.49 for PM–0.5, 0.41 vs. 0.46 for PM–1, and 0.28 vs. 0.23 for PM–2, respectively.
