In each forest, there was no significant difference in QF/P between PM-0.5 and PM-1 (p  > 0.35), while a significant difference was found when compared with PM-2 (p  < 0.001). Additionally, there was an exponential relationship between QF/P and P across all PMs in both forests (Fig. 5  c, f, i and Fig. 6  c, f, i).  3.2 Threshold behaviors of QF The threshold of rainfall depth for QF generation was not clearly defined across PMs, as both the presence and absence of QF were recorded within an extensive range of rainfall depth, especially in PMs with mineral soil (Figs. 3 and 4 ). The depth equivalent ASW revealed a distinct difference between forest types (p  < 0.01). In the coniferous forest, the mean ASW values were 132.78 ± 6.52 mm (standard deviation) for PM-0.5, 229.77 ± 10.22 mm for PM-1, and 395.68 ± 22.88 mm for PM-2. In the broadleaf forest, the mean ASW values were 102.28 ± 2.83 mm for PM-0.5, 189.64 ± 6.02 mm for PM-1, and 330.29 ± 21.83 mm for PM-2, respectively. Nevertheless, there was no evident relationship between QF and ASW, nor was a threshold response detected (Fig. 5 a–c and 6a–c). Instead, the relationship between QF and ASW was highly variable across all PMs in both forests. Meanwhile, when the ASW was combined with the precipitation, a distinct three-phase relationship was observed with QF across all PMs (Fig. 5 d–f and 6d–f). The three-phase QF process was divided by the breakpoints of generation and rising thresholds (Figs. 5 and 6 ; Table 2  ). Between the generation and rising thresholds, the mean QF in the coniferous and broadleaf forests were 1.32 mm vs. 19.20 mm, 3.77 mm vs. 3.45 mm, and 6.55 mm vs. 7.92 mm for PM-0.5, PM-1, and PM-2, respectively; and the mean QF/P in the coniferous and broadleaf forests were 0.18 vs. 0.52, 0.26 vs. 0.20, and 0.17 vs. 0.18 for PM-0.5, PM-1, and PM-2, respectively. Above the rising threshold, the mean QF values in the coniferous and broadleaf forests were 28.05 mm vs. 71.6 mm for PM-0.5, 27.58 mm vs. 28.78 mm for PM-1, and 27.19 mm vs. 29.46 mm for PM-2, respectively; and QF/P was 0.53 vs. 0.83 for PM-0.5, 0.47 vs. 0.48 for PM-1, and 0.32 vs. 0.38 for PM-2 in the coniferous forest and broadleaf forests, respectively. Higher slope parameters were observed above the rising threshold phase in the broadleaf forest compared to the coniferous forest across all PMs. Specifically, the slope parameters were 0.83 vs. 1.27 for PM-0.5, 0.77 vs. 0.83 for PM-1, and 0.73 vs. 0.78 for PM-2 in the coniferous and broadleaf forests, respectively. However, the slope parameters between the generation and rising thresholds were extremely low for all PMs in both forest types, except for the PM-0.5 in the broadleaf forest, which had a slope parameter of 0.68. Notably, the slope parameters above the rising threshold decreased and underwent a narrower change as the thickness of mineral soil increased.  3.3 Soil water content and QF SWC at rainfall onset was defined as the SWC at the last monitoring time before the rainfall event, and SWC at the generation and rising thresholds was estimated by the SWC at the time when the ASW+P reached the specific threshold values during the rainfall event. When comparing the SWC under different conditions, we applied a stringent significance level (p  < 0.01) because all measurements were converted from soil water potential. The results showed that significant differences were observed among the SWC at different QF conditions (p  < 0.001), except at a depth of 100 cm (Fig. 7  ). This may indicate a threshold value of SWC in the root zone for QF generation and a shift to rapid QF. Besides, a comparison between forest types revealed that less water input was required to generate QF in the coniferous forest (Fig. 7 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Role of forest types in threshold values and QF amount Hydrological monitoring of QF revealed distinct differences in hydrological responses between the coniferous and broadleaf forests in terms of threshold values for QF generation and a shift to rapid QF (Table 2 ). To elucidate the differences between forest types, we compared the results of PM-0.5, which reflected the influence of hydrological processes from the vegetation and its root system. Firstly, a significantly lower threshold value of ASW+P for QF generation was identified in the broadleaf forest. Due to the presence of abundant preferential flow, subsurface flow can occur with a small amount of rainfall, resulting in a small proportion of rainfall compared to the depth equivalent ASW (P/ASW). This leads to the generation threshold being primarily determined by the ASW, which was higher in the coniferous forest than in the broadleaf forest (Fig. 7 ). Secondly, the discrepancy between ASW+P at the generation threshold and the mean ASW in the broadleaf forest (9.44 mm) was greater than that in the coniferous forest (5.31 mm), indicating that a higher amount of rainfall was required to initiate subsurface flow in the broadleaf forest. This was attributed to the greater soil water deficit resulting from stronger water uptake by plants in the broadleaf forest. This aligned with the observed higher variability of soil water potential (Wang et al., 2023 ) and the measured higher evapotranspiration by the eddy covariance system (Hu et al., 2018 ) in the broadleaf forest compared to the coniferous forest. Additionally, the litter layer in the broadleaf forest exhibited a larger interception capacity compared to the coniferous forest due to the additional interception from bowl-shaped depressions of fallen leaves that facilitated the lateral spreading of rainfall (Du et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2004). The coniferous forest exhibited a fast QF generation, whereas the broadleaf forest had a higher QF yield capacity, as indicated by the slope parameters (Figs. 3-6 ). Below the rising threshold, the slope parameter (m1  = 0.68) in the broadleaf forest was much higher than that of the coniferous forest, indicating the establishment of vertical connectivity of flow paths in the broadleaf forest. However, the coniferous forest showed unpredictable QF below the rising threshold phase. Above the rising threshold, the slope parameter > 1 was observed in the broadleaf forest. This finding aligns with an obtained slope parameter of 2.36 in a deciduous forest, where the fast QF was attributed to the connectivity of more preferential flow paths and the contribution of more soil water (Buttle et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021 ). This is also consistent with a comparative study showing that the coniferous (spruce) forest had the least size of preferential flow paths and the lowest number of earthworms compared to the broadleaf (oak and alder) forest (Jačka et al., 2021 ). Therefore, a greater number of preferential flow paths in the broadleaf forest can drive and accumulate more rainwater in deep soils within the same amount of time, leading to an increase in outflow amount.  4.2 Role of soil thickness on nonlinear behaviors The nonlinear hydrological behaviors, resembling a hockey stick shape, were consistent across PMs, indicating that the underlying mechanism of the storage-discharge relationship—reflecting the retention and release of event water—remained unchanged (Kirchner, 2009; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, an increase in the mineral soil thickness would primarily affect the slope and intercept of the nonlinear relationship between QF and ASW+P (Ali et al., 2013; Kirchner, 2009 ). Notably, there was no significant difference in the QF/P between PM-0.5 and PM-1, which aligns with findings from a virtual experiment conducted on the Panola experimental hillslope. This experiment examined the impact of varying soil thickness, with a medium value of 120 cm, on flow metrics, and found that runoff coefficients were not greatly affected (Hopp and McDonnell, 2009 ). Two reasons may explain the phenomenon. On the one hand, a modest increase in mineral soil thickness caused a limited expansion of soil water storage deficit compared to the high event rainfall input; on the other hand, the long-range vertical connectivity (i.e., continuity) of preferential flow paths within the studied depth was relatively complete and contributed significantly to the QF amounts (Figure S3 ). This is line with the previous dye tracer experiments, which showed that rock fragments in the coarse-textured mineral soil resulted in continuous preferential flow paths to a depth of 110 cm and 95 cm in the coniferous forest and broadleaf forest, respectively (Wang et al., 2022a ). As the thickness of mineral soil increased further, the long-range connectivity of preferential flow paths was lost due to the lack of biotic activities and the presence of soil layering. The water exchange between the preferential flow paths (e.g., macropores) and soil matrix became more pronounced, resulting in enhanced lateral water distribution and increased water retention within the soil (Nimmo, 2021 ). This result was supported by a study involving column experiments and numerical simulations, which showed that dead-end macropores reduced the flux into the main preferential flow paths and increased the lateral water transfer throughout the entire soil profile (Urbina et al., 2019 ). Consequently, there was a decrease in both QF/P and QF in the PM-2 compared to the other PMs. Meanwhile, the more stable SWC content in the deeper mineral soil resulted in a limited expansion of the soil water storage deficit, contributing to the narrower decrease in the slopes above the rising threshold phase.  4.3 Runoff mechanisms in humid forests The SWC consistently remained below saturation under various threshold conditions, with hardly observed soil saturation during the monitoring period (Figure S4 ). This indicated a dominant role of unsaturated/preferential flow in runoff processes in the studied area. When the rainfall fell on the ground, it was retained by the soil matrix and replenished the soil water storage deficit during the first phase of the nonlinear behavior, making runoff unlikely to happen. Subsequent rainfall continuously recharged soil water, creating connectivity among segmented preferential flow paths within part of the hydrological system. However, this connectivity was unstable and disordered, leading to an unpredicted QF during the second phase. This phase was consistent with observations from the humid Lang Lang River Catchment in Australia, where runoff was even produced below the generation threshold value due to fast subsurface preferential flow paths (Saffarpour et al., 2016 ). As more rainfall entered the hydrological system, the degree of soil wetness progressively increased and a large preferential flow system was achieved through the self-organization processes of preferential flow paths. Consequently, rapid QF was generated and mainly controlled by rainfall (James and Roulet, 2007; Nieber and Sidle, 2010; Sidle et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the SWC at the rising threshold indicated a connected flow path for rapid QF. In this study, the SWC at 100 cm showed no significant difference (p  > 0.12) among different hydrological phases. The mean SWC of 41 % in the coniferous forest and 44 % in the broadleaf forest at 50 cm was regarded as the threshold value of SWC for the connectivity of flow paths and the initiation of rapid QF (Fig. 7 ). The threshold value of SWC is similar to the 45 % found in Alpine grassland (Penna et al., 2011 ) and falls within the range of 41 %–46 % observed in the Tarrawarra catchment (Western and Grayson, 1998 ). However, it is higher than the 23 % recorded in a mature beech-maple forest (James and Roulet, 2007 ) and the 26 % found in a pine–oak forest (Farrick and Branfireun, 2014 ). Previous studies also found SWC threshold in near surface soil (James and Roulet, 2007; Penna et al., 2011 ) or the deeper soil (Farrick and Branfireun, 2014 ). These differences likely reflect the variability in the soil properties, which depend on drainable porosity (calculated by subtracting the SWC at field capacity from the total porosity) to determine how much mobile soil water is available for drainage (Farrick and Branfireun, 2014; Scaife and Band, 2017 ), as well as by local climate, which influences the general status of SWC. Drainable porosity often decreases quickly with depth owing to the change in bulk density or soil texture, and a decrease in drainable porosity allows little water input to generate a measurable output (Weiler and McDonnell, 2004 ). As previously revealed by Farrick and Branfireun (2014)  in a tropical dry forest, they found that when the SWC at the shallow soil layers (10, 30, and 50 cm) reached field capacity, excess rainwater can readily drain from shallow layers through the profile until the SWC at the deeper layer (100 cm) also attained field capacity. Once the unsaturated storage within the profile (0–100 cm) was met, the drainable water flowed laterally downslope and generated streamflow. In our study, a sharp increase in soil bulk density below 50 cm (Wang et al., 2022a ), together with the temporarily stable high SWC (i.e., soil water potential) of the mineral soil (Wang et al., 2023 ) resulting from the humid climate, led to a high leaching potential (Table 1 ; Figure S4 ). Therefore, the SWC threshold of this study was identified at a shallow depth, where little rainfall is sufficient to drive the soil profile to a drainable/wet state. Under this condition, flow paths are organized into a larger flow network, facilitating rapid QF. Moreover, the slope parameters above the rising threshold decreased as the mineral soil thickness increased, and the difference in these slope parameters went narrower. This occurs because SWC tends to be more stable in deeper soil layers due to reduced influence from evapotranspiration, leading to a limited expansion of the soil water storage deficit.  4.4 Implications and future prospects The absence of a unifying theory to connect or compare disparate process descriptions, coupled with the inherent uniqueness of study places, has spurred the development of increasing parameterized models aimed at representing diverse landscapes (Ali et al., 2013; Kirchner, 2006; Ross et al., 2021 ). However, the heterogeneity of landscape properties, as well as the limited transferability of findings from individual studies will persist and may even be exacerbated with enhanced observation capabilities and landscape changes over time. This has motivated a shift towards emergent properties, properties that cannot be predicted from the individual components but instead represent the interactions and feedbacks between the components in a complex system (McDonnell et al., 2007 ). Thresholds in runoff processes have been identified as an emergent property, reflecting that we can attain a rather good understanding of how a hydrological system works while being entirely ignorant of water particle physics. This will enhance the classification of runoff responses according to threshold theory, facilitating a better understanding of how runoff behaves under a wide variety of landscape and climate. Consequently, this will benefit the development of algorithms that embrace simplicity and applicability for predictive models, mitigating the issues of equifinality and our current reliance on overly calibrated models. Threshold behaviors are dynamic in the context of long-term soil evolution, forest transformation, and climate change (Mekonnen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024 ). The long-term nonequilibrium state between soil production and loss leads to changes in the spatial distribution of soil thickness, which is further exacerbated by climate change. Similarly, the forest transformation between deciduous and evergreen vegetation due to rising temperatures is also influenced by global climate change. Additionally, short-term strong disturbances, such as intensified floods, debris flow, and wildfire can impact the soil thickness and vegetation cover in a short time. These factors reflect the ubiquitous and dynamic changes of below-ground landscape elements. However, above-ground factors such as rainfall intensity and hydrological abstractions caused by evapotranspiration should also be taken into consideration. Rainfall intensity thresholds, which are typically related to saturation excess flow and infiltration excess overland flow (Ali et al., 2015 ), received less attention compared to storage thresholds (Ross et al., 2021 ). Runoff mechanisms in natural or disturbed areas with limited infiltration capacity are heavily influenced by rainfall intensity. This influence has intensified due to the increased intra-event variability of rainfall intensity under global climate change (Labonté-Raymond et al., 2020 ), potentially leading to conversion of runoff mechanisms during a single rainfall event. In addition, the intensified seasonal variability of plant water uptake under global climate change can significantly alter soil water storage deficit and impact the threshold behaviors, leading to nonstationary threshold values. Hence, to adequately characterize hydrological responses of systems across various landscapes and climates, it is imperative to consider multiple highly variable and threshold-mediated processes in future studies.   5 Conclusion Event-based analysis of the rainfall-quick flow relationship, varying by soil thickness and forest types, was conducted through controlled experiments to demonstrate how changes in water storage capacity and flow paths connectivity caused a threshold relationship between rainfall and hillslope quick flow. The results revealed that the nonlinear QF processes were related to the sum of antecedent soil wetness and rainfall amount in both coniferous and broadleaf forests. Forest types showed different litter interception capacity and plant water uptake, directly altering the soil water deficit and determining the rainfall amount for QF generation. While soil thickness expansion increased the soil water deficit and disturbed the flow paths connectivity, altering QF amount in response to rainfall events. A three-phase threshold behavior with a hockey stick shape and two breakpoints—the generation and rising thresholds—was identified under varying soil thickness and forest types, indicating a consistent storage-discharge relationship in humid forests. For QF generation, the broadleaf forest required more rainfall due to higher litter interception and soil water deficit. Above the rising threshold, a linear relationship between QF and the sum of ASW and rainfall amount were observed, attributed to the establishment of preferential flow paths network, with the broadleaf forest showing higher increase in QF than the coniferous forest. Preferential flow paths are well-connected in the shallow root zone and extend to the shallow mineral soil due to the coarse-textured and stony soil in both forests. A thick mineral soil would disrupt flow path connectivity, enhancing the lateral diversion of rainwater and water retention within the soil, leading to a significant decrease in both the quantity and coefficient of QF in forests. This study highlighted the influence of soil thickness and forest types on threshold-based QF in humid mountainous areas and emphasized the need to shift the focus to factors controlling preferential flow and its connectivity, which have significant consequences for soil hydrology and threshold behaviors.
1 Introduction Drought is a controversial topic in the context of climate change, with one view suggesting that droughts are increasing in intensity and frequency (e.g., Dai, 2012; Yuan et al., 2023 ); while another suggesting that global droughts are changing little (e.g. , Sheffield et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2020 ). However, drought events, as intermittent disturbances, have a substantial impact on water cycle processes (e.g., Yang et al., 2018; Peterson et al., 2021 ). Multi-year droughts can alter the precipitation-streamflow (P -Q ) relationship and even cross a threshold / move beyond the normal envelope of stationarity of a given catchment, consequently resulting in prolonged hydrological drought (e.g. , Peterson et al., 2021; Fowler et al., 2022; Goswami et al., 2022; Gardiya Weligamage, et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023 ). A sustained climate shift can trigger changes in catchment behaviour and is important for understanding how to predict future hydrologic conditions (Liu et al., 2023a; Saft et al., 2015 ). For example, changes in terrestrial evapotranspiration (ET ), the process of liquid water transport from the land surface to the atmosphere involving numerous complex biophysical processes, can be triggered by drought, affecting Q , soil moisture (Sm  ), and groundwater (Peterson et al., 2021; Saft et al., 2016 ), inducing evaporative cooling (e.g., Shen et al., 2015 ). Terrestrial ET  processes is comprised of three main components being: (i ) evaporation from soil; (ii ) transpiration from the plant canopy; and (iii ) evaporation of P  intercepted by vegetation canopy (Katul et al., 2012 ; Zhang et al., 2019 ). As ET  processes involve the available water and energy, multi-year P  deficits will trigger alterations in the linkages among climate, soil, and vegetation (Berry et al., 2005 ) and will mechanistically induce uncertainties in ET  explanations. The five possible mechanisms of multi-year drought impacts on ET  are (Fig. 1  ): (i ) Multi-year P  deficits decrease the amount of available water and induce reductions in ET  (denoted as mechanism 1, and abbreviated as Mec1) (e.g. , Orth & Destouni, 2018 ). Orth & Destouni (2018)  noted that drought-induced P  deficits through Sm   reductions impact ET  and Q , resulting in stronger and faster reductions in Q  than in ET  across Europe. (ii ) P  deficits generally increase evaporative demand, which is associated with reduced cloudiness and increased surface radiation, higher temperatures, and even heatwave events, which can reduce ET  (denoted as Mec2) (if water is not limiting; Miralles et al., 2019; Saft et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2022 ). Drought triggers stronger land–atmosphere feedback, compound drought–heatwave events have drawn increased amounts of attention (Yin et al., 2023 ). (iii ) Increases in vapour pressure deficit (VPD), induced by multi-year drought, will reduce the stomatal conductance of vegetation through stomatal closure and result in decreased ET  (denoted as Mec3) (e.g. , Leuning, 1990; Mott, 2007; Medlyn et al., 2017; Miralles et al., 2019; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2019 ). (iv ) The partitioning of P  indicates that surface soils and vegetation will intercept large portions of P  to maintain ET  (Liu et al., 2023b ), suggesting that ET  may not increase or decrease in proportion to P  (denoted as Mec4) (Avanzi et al., 2020 ). For example, measurements of ET  revealed that ET  can be sustained during multi-year droughts where and when vegetation can access groundwater and/or deeper soil moisture stores (Rungee et al., 2018 ). However, evidence has shown that multi-year droughts can result in a greater than expected decreases in Q  (e.g., Saft et al., 2015; Konapala & Mishra, 2020; Peterson et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b ), implying that more P  is used to replenish the catchment wetness (defined as P  minus surface Q ) (e.g., Horton, 1933; Troch et al., 2009; Abeshu & Li, 2021; Peterson et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b ). Finally, (v ) antecedent catchment storage (i.e., soil moisture and groundwater) which vary spatio-temporally within a catchment affects the amount of water that is available for drought-period ET  (denoted as Mec5) (Saft et al., 2016; Rungee et al., 2018 ). For examples: (i ) towards the start of a multi-year drought high levels of soil moisture storage can decouple ET  from P  thereby allowing vegetation to withstand periods of mild to moderate drought (Maurer et al., 2022 ); and (ii ) the seasonal groundwater recharge cycle is sustained, suppressed, or absent during periods of low rainfall, resulting in hydrological droughts that are shorter, longer or similar in duration to meteorological droughts (Apurv et al., 2017 ). Mechanisms Mec1 and Mec2, which represent the available water and energy, respectively, produced opposite ET  trends to drought impact. As expected, the ET  trends become more ambiguous when the vegetation response (Mec3), P  partition (Mec4), and antecedent catchment storage (Mec5) are involved. For example, enhanced ET  anomalies have been reported during multi-year droughts across both water- and energy-limited regions, with the mechanistic explanation being that deeper root depths may provide access to deeper water storage and sustained evaporation during multi-year drought periods (Massari et al., 2022 ). All these factors raise a series of questions: (a) at the catchment-level can we predict if ET  increases or decreases during a multi-year drought? (b) do alterations in ET  remain consistent across different climate regimes affected by multi-year P  deficits? and (c) do the underlying mechanisms of the ET  changes remain temporally consistent or do they have their own operating patterns in water-limited and energy-limited regions? Therefore, our objectives are: (i ) to explore how ET  responds to multi-year droughts across water-limited and energy-limited regions; (ii ) to clarify how droughts trigger changes in ET ; and (iii ) to examine the impact of droughts on ET  through attribute analysis by considering different climate regimes across global catchments. To elucidate the above scientific issues, multi-year droughts were detected in the 1069 catchments, and multiple linear regressions were used to identify the causes of changes in ET  with other ecohydrological variables (Section 2.2  Methods section). Then, in the results section, (i ) the changes in ET  caused by drought, (ii ) the ecohydrological responses induced by multi-year drought, and (iii ) the influences of water, energy and LAI on the changes in ET  (Section 3  Results section) aimed to answer our research objectives. The discussion section (Section 4 ) provided a detailed discussion of the results, and also presented uncertainties for the ET  response to drought, including “method and data. In Section 5 , conclusions are drawn.  2 Data description and method 2.1 Data description Precipitation : The monthly P  data were obtained from Beck et al. (2019) , who developed Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble P  (MSWEP) values at a 3 h temporal resolution and 0.1° spatial resolution from 1981 to 2011. Evapotranspiration : Robust ensemble averaged gridded ET  data were used to determine ET  (ETe  ). The database used includes actual monthly ET  data that were obtained from three datasets, including: (i ) Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM v3.6a, 0.25°) (https://www.gleam.eu ; Martens et al., 2017 ); (ii ) Global Land Data Assimilation System-NOAH (GLDAS-NOAH, 0.25°) (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov ; Rodell et al., 2004 ); and (iii ) Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS, 0.05°) dataset (https://glass.umd.edu ; Yao et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2014 ). Potential evapotranspiration (Ep  ): Monthly Ep   data from 1981 to 2011 were obtained from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU), calculated using Penman-Monteith formula (Allen et al., 1998 ), at a spatial resolution of 0.5° (https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/hrg ; Harris et al., 2020 ). Air temperature and dew point temperature : Monthly air temperature (Ta  ) and dew point temperature (Tdew  ) data were obtained from ERA5-Land monthly average data at a spatial resolution of 0.1° (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/home ; Muñoz Sabater et al., 2019 ). The vapour pressure deficit (VPD) was calculated from Ta   and Tdew   (Allen et al., 1998 ):(1) V P  sat   = 0.6108 e x p 17.27 T a   237.3 + T a             (2) V P  act   = 0.6108 e x p 17.27 T dew    237.3 + T dew              (3) V P D = V P  sat   - V P  act   .     where Ta   is the air temperature in o C, Tdew   is the dew point temperature in o C, VPsat   is the saturated vapour pressure (kPa), VPact   is the actual vapour pressure (kPa), and VPD is the vapour pressure deficit (kPa). Streamflow:  Monthly Q  data from 1069 out of the 30,959 selected catchments were collected from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata (GSIM) archive (Do et al., 2018 ). The GSIM data sources consisted of 11 databases worldwide, details of which can be found in Do et al. (2018) . The following criteria were then applied to the selected subset of available catchments: (i ) the catchment area must be between 10 km2  and 100,000 km2  to decrease channel routing effects (van Dijk et al., 2013 ); (ii ) the urban area must be < 2 %, as determined from the GlobCover map (v 2) (Bontemps et al., 2011 ); (iii ) the irrigated areas, if irrigated land is present, must cover < 3 % of the total catchment area, based on the Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA) (https://www.iwmigiam.org ; Siebert et al., 2005); and (iv ) the dam or reservoir capacities must be < 2 % of the annual Q  based on the Global Reservoir and Dam (GRanD) database (v 1.1) (Lehner et al., 2011 ). Considering the available Q  data, the study period (1981–2011, i.e., 31 years) strikes a balance between data availability and data length. Catchments with a fractional data loss > 10 % were excluded to ensure data continuity and integrity. These filters narrowed the total number of available catchments to 1069. Finally, out of 1069 catchments, only 448 catchments were used as they had multi-year drought with 471 drought events; defined in Section 2.2  (below) (Fig. 2  ). Soil moisture : Gridded soil data between 1981 and 2011 were deduced from volumetric soil water data obtained from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Integrated Forecasting System Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) (at a depth of 100 cm). The data were accessed from the ERA5-Land monthly averaged data at a spatial resolution of 0.1° (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/home ; Muñoz Sabater et al., 2019 ). Vegetation:  Satellite-derived vegetation activity data expressed as Leaf Area Index (LAI) data that was obtained from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) Global Agricultural Monitoring System (GIMMS) LAI3g at a 0.25° spatial resolution from 1981 to 2011 at a monthly scale (Mao & Yan, 2019 ).  2.2 Methods (1) Multi-year drought . Many indices have been proposed to quantify drought incidence, namely, the standardized P  index (SPI), standardized Sm   index (SSI), and standardized runoff index (SRI) (Satoh et al., 2021 ). Although the SPI, SSI and SRI are assessed using the same approach and consistent processes, additional uncertainties may still arise due to the different probability distribution functions used to fit the data when calculating these three drought indices (Yang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2023b ). Herein the method described by Saft et al. (2015)  was used to detect multi-year droughts (for ≥ 7 years). Firstly, annual P  anomaly data are calculated relative to annual mean data (i.e., 1981–2011; 31-years), and secondly the anomaly series is divided by the long-term mean annual P  value which is expressed as percentage and thirdly this is smoothed using a 3-year moving window (Saft et al., 2015 ) an example is shown in Fig. 3  . The multi-year droughts were identified in the following manner (Saft et al., 2015 ): (i ) length ≥ 7 years and (ii ) mean dry period anomaly < -5% (see Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, (iii ) for the case of one year with a positive anomaly > 15 % of the mean, the end year is set to the year preceding that year; alternatively, (iv ) if the last two years have slightly positive anomalies (but each < 15 % of the mean), the end year is set to the first year of the positive anomaly. The onset of drought was also defined to occur at the beginning of the initial 3-year negative anomaly period. To eliminate the uncertainty surrounding the P  anomaly threshold, sensitivity tests were carried out to examine the impact of varying magnitude of the P  anomaly and the number of drought events. The P  anomaly threshold, defined as −5%, was identified as the optimal point at which to test the drought event. (2) Attribution of ET  changes . Multiple linear regression was used to identify the causes of the changes in ET  with other ecohydrological variables (e.g. , LAI, P , and Ep  ) (e.g., Zeng et al., 2018; Forzieri et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023 ). The sensitivities of ET  to the changes in P , E p  and LAI were computed at the annual scale for both drought and non-drought periods. These values were expressed as the partial derivatives that resulted from multiple linear regressions, relating the interannual differences in ET  to the interannual differences in the annual cumulative average P  and Ep  , and annually averaged LAI.(4) Δ E T = ∂ E T  ∂ P   Δ P + ∂ E T  ∂ E  p   Δ E p  + ∂ E T  ∂ L A I   Δ L A I + ε     where ∂ E T  ∂ P     , ∂ E T  ∂ E  p      and ∂ E T  ∂ L A I      are the sensitivities of ET  to the changes in P , Ep   and LAI, respectively. ε  is the residual and represents the impact of other factors. Then, the trends in ET  that are induced by the trends in P , Ep  , and LAI are quantified by adding the outputs obtained by multiplying the three sensitivities with the trends in P , Ep  , and LAI, respectively. (3) The ecohydrological responses induced by multi-year droughts . The ecohydrological responses induced by multi-year droughts were investigated by comparing the Sm  , LAI, VPD, and Ta   values between the drought and non-drought periods. Following previous research (e.g., Berdugo et al., 2020 ), linear regressions were bootstrapped at both sides of each threshold for each variable to test whether the thresholds significantly affected the slopes. The slopes before and after the thresholds were subsequently extracted and were compared with each other using the Mann–Whitney U  test at the 0.01 confidence level.   3 Results 3.1 The shifts in ET  caused by drought Multi-year droughts reduced ET  and Q  and induced shifts in the P  partition (Fig. 4  ). However, multi-year droughts did not alter the asymmetrical P  partitioning in water-limited or energy-limited regions. In other words, more P  was partitioned into ET  in water-limited regions, while the opposite effect occurred in energy-limited regions. Compared with the non-drought period, the P  tended to maintain ET  in both water-limited and energy-limited regions and resulted in a lower (P -Q ) than ETe  , suggesting reductions in watershed water storage (including Sm   and groundwater) during the multi-year drought periods. P  deficits triggered larger reductions in ET  (13.84 %, ΔETe   /ΔP ) and Q  (39.30 %, ΔQ /ΔP ) in the water-limited regions than in the energy-limited regions, with 8.74 % (ΔETe   /ΔP ) and 35.82 % (ΔQ /ΔP ), respectively. Both the drought strengths and specific climate regimes can increase ecological responses (e.g., ETe   and LAI) (Fig. 5  ). ET  (herein represented as ETe  ) exhibited an asymmetrical hydrological effect with increasing drought strength. ET  tends to decrease in drier climate regimes but generally increases with increasing drought strength in wetter climate regimes (near the water and energy boundary). It is noteworthy that the ET  anomaly demonstrated a more rapid decrease in the presence of a P  deficit, while exhibiting a pattern of initial increase, followed by a decrease, and then an increase again with increasing drought strength at 0.18P /Ep  . The P  deficit, which ranged from −800 to −1350 mm, represented an intriguing threshold through which to elucidate the P -ET  compound relationship. The response of the LAI to drought (Fig. 5 b) suggested that vegetation tends to maintain greenness during periods of lower drought strength (i.e ., when P  deficit ranges between −150 to −750 mm/year) in drier climate regimes (i.e., when P /Ep   ranged from 0.16 to 0.25) and higher drought strength (i.e ., when P  deficit ranges between −1800 to −2100 mm/year) in wetter climate (i.e., when P /Ep ranged from 0.75 to 1.2) regimes. In drier regions (i.e ., P /Ep   is around 0.25) where there is a P  deficit, vegetation can enhance the LAI, resulting in elevated ET  (As shown in the supplementary Fig. 1 ). As drought persists and strength increases, ET  decreases with LAI decreasing. However, in wetter regions (i.e., P /Ep   > 1), LAI of vegetation declined more rapidly by drought stress, resulting in an ET  decrease, and interestingly, as the intensity of drought increased further, ET  correlated with increase in LAI. The reduction in the ET  anomaly induced by the P  deficit in arid regions (0.18P /Ep  ) indicated that the P  deficit increased the air temperature (as shown in Fig. 5 c).  3.2 The ecohydrological responses induced by multi-year drought Generally, multi-year droughts caused decreases in Sm   and LAI and resulted in increases in VPD. For example, significant differences were found between drought and non-drought periods in global catchments with value of 0.30 and 0.31 for Sm  , 0.81 and 0.83 for LAI, and 0.66 and 0.63 for VPD, respectively. However, greater decreases in Sm   were observed at higher (P -Q )/P  ratios [e.g. , (P -Q )/P >0.6] and near water-limited lines [(P -Q )/P =1, indicating 100 % of P  becomes ET ], suggesting that greater decreases in catchment storage occurred in catchments with higher ET  during multi-year droughts and that catchments with lower ET  were not the same (Fig. 6  a). The decreased LAIs induced by multi-year droughts presented complex response patterns with no obvious trend along increasing of (P -Q )/P , indicating complex regulatory mechanisms of vegetation across water- and energy-limited regions (Fig. 6 b). Interestingly, multi-year droughts caused significant increases in VPD when the (P -Q )/P  ratios reached a critical threshold [e.g. , (P -Q )/P >0.2], while the VPD exhibited insignificant changes in wetter catchments (energy-limited regions, Ep  /P <1) (Fig. 6 c). Interestingly, the observed ecohydrological variables exhibited consistent (P -Q )/P  shifts (∼0.50) (Fig. 7  ). Sm  , VPD and Ta   exhibited opposite trends, i.e., sharp reductions in Sm   and sharp increases in VPD and Ta   before and after the thresholds. Vegetation typically reduces its leaf area to adapt to dry conditions, while the differences in the LAI between the drought and non-drought periods exhibited insignificant differences (p  = 0.06) before and after the (P -Q )/P  threshold (Fig. 7 c).  3.3 The influences of water, energy, and LAI on the changes in ET  Generally, the multi-year P  deficits induced the ET  decrease, with ET  mainly being controlled by the available water (P ) in both the water-limited and energy-limited catchments, followed by Ep   and LAI (Fig. 8  a, b). The controlling factors for ET  in the energy-limited catchments were consistent with those in the water-limited catchments during non-drought periods. Unexpectedly, the available energy (labelled Ep  ) is not a primary factor that affects ET , and the LAI and P  play greater roles than energy in energy-limited regions during non-drought periods. Furthermore, the contributions of P  and Ep   to ET  in energy-limited regions were greater than those in water-limited regions, suggesting that the LAI had smaller effects on ET  in these regions. Induced by multi-year droughts, the contributions of P  and Ep   to ET  increased, while the effects of the LAI weakened in energy-limited regions. Asymmetric effects that were induced by multi-year P  deficits were found in the contributions of Ep  ; that is, the contributions of Ep   increased in energy-limited regions and decreased in water-limited regions. Unexpectedly, the effects of δP  and δLAI on the ET  changes were weakened, while δEp   contributed more to δET  during the multi-year drought (Fig. 8 c, d). In particular, associated with a prolonged P  deficit, δEp   contributed 40 % and 60 % of the changes in ET  in the water-limited and energy-limited regions, respectively.   4 Discussion Generally, multi-year P  deficits induce shifts in P  partitioning (e.g.,  reductions in ET  and Q ) (validated by Saft et al., 2016 ), while asymmetric P  partitioning increases between water-limited and energy-limited regions (as shown in Fig. 4 ). This suggests that the decreases in available water (underlying mechanism: Mec1) that are induced by prolonged P  deficits affect hydrological behaviour, while asymmetric P  partitioning reflects the complex interaction between water- and energy-limited regions induced by the catchment characteristics and vegetation responses (Liu et al., 2023b ) (underlying mechanism: Mec1-Mec4). For example, exacerbations of the Q  deficit during droughts are a common feature in all climates and are driven by evaporation enhancements (Massari et al., 2022 ), suggesting that catchment may have multiple steady states (e.g. , Peterson et al., 2021 ). Our results further confirmed that catchment water storage (including groundwater and antecedent soil water content) plays a vital role in driving the shifts in P  partitioning during multi-year droughts (mainly explained by the mechanism Mec1), which can induce the different response in water- and energy-limited regions. According to the conceptual model of drought propagation provided by Liu et al. (2023b) , the threshold switching characteristics during drought propagation control P  partitioning, indicating that ET  tends to be maintained even in drier regions (e.g.,  reflected by higher ET  proportions in water-limited regions, ETe  , reaching up to 74 % of P ) (Fig. 4 a). Assuming that ETe   and (P -Q ) are independent, the evidence provided by the differences between δETe   and δ(P -Q ) indicates that catchments tended to be drier in both water-limited [δETe  , −21 mm and δ(P -Q ), −93 mm] and energy-limited [δETe  , −15 mm; δ(P -Q ), −110 mm] regions (Fig. 4 ). Deficits in catchment water storage tend to increase to maintain ET  during drought periods (Zhou et al., 2022 ) and induce low-Q  states in catchments (Peterson et al., 2021 ). Regulated by the catchment water storage capacity, the partitioning of P  to Q  is minor until the subsurface is fully saturated, at which point Q  increases markedly (Bales et al., 2018 ). Undoubtedly, severe droughts usually decrease vegetation activity and even cause tree mortality (Li et al., 2019 ), even in humid regions, such as the tropical Amazon (Brando et al., 2014 ) (incorporating the two underlying mechanisms denoted Mec1 and Mec5 (see Fig. 1 )). However, Fig. 6  provides evidence that vegetation can maintain higher LAIs at lower drought strengths in drier climate regions and higher drought strengths in wetter climate regions (validated by Peterson et al., 2021 ). The regulating mechanism of available water (e.g. , soil moisture) on ET  (Underlying Mec5) can be validated by the drought threshold impacting vegetation and the critical role of soil moisture in influencing the recovery time of ecosystems from drought (e.g. , Sun et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, the drought-induced increases in ET  and LAI in wetter regions can be explained by the fact that droughts are characterized not only by reduced water availability but also by increased radiation and hence energy availability (Orth and Destouni, 2018; Luo et al., 2020 ). In wetter environments, vegetation growth is generally not limited by water but by other resources (e.g. , radiation and nutrients) (Nemani et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2015 ; Jiao et al., 2021 ), causing a less sensitive response of long-term catchment hydrological partitioning to vegetation change in these areas (Luo et al., 2020 ). This results in a decoupling of ET  from the soil moisture decreases (Li et al., 2023a ). As noted by Stampfli et al. (2018) , the reduced availability of Sm   caused by P  deficits leads to longer and more severe intermittent drought stress, which has the potential to broadly alter both ecosystem structures and functions. The responses of vegetation to drought in drier and wetter regions induced opposite trends (e.g., ET  increased with increasing LAI during low drought strength, and then ET  decreased with decreasing LAI in drier regions, while opposite trends were found in wetter regions) (Fig. 5 ), suggesting that the response mechanisms of vegetation to drought differ according to aridity by regulating physiological processes (i.e., photosynthesis, respiration, and transpiration) (e.g., Denissen et al., 2022; Knauer et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2023; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2013 ). For example, drought-induced reductions in vegetation function are largely driven by the downregulation of vegetation physiology such as stomatal conductance and light use efficiency, with the strongest down-regulation in water-limited regions (Li et al., 2023b ). The findings of Liu et al. (2023)  suggest that vegetation responses, such as a reduction in effective rooting depth, tend to offset the increase in watershed characteristic parameters (n ) resulting from a reduction in storm depth and an increase in aridity index under the Budyko framework during a multi-year drought. Generally, arid ecosystems respond to water availability in a highly plastic way, as plant species adapt to water shortages through physiological, anatomical, and functional strategies that reduce water losses, respiration costs, photosynthetic activities, and growth rates (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2013 ). In arid regions, the lack of available water leads to a surplus of net radiation, which in turn controls the ET  while Q  may remain largely unchanged because precipitation deficits are typically low and ET  decreases buffer the reduction in Q  (e.g. , Li et al., 2023a ). This reduction in the ET  anomaly indicates a reduction in latent heat, which inevitably induces an increase in sensible heat (Ta  ) (as showed in Fig. 5 c). Given that the stronger land–atmosphere feedbacks could be induced by drought and atmospheric warming, the combined drought-heatwave events have led to extreme temperatures due to drier land surfaces during heatwaves, which increase surface temperatures (Yuan et al., 2023 ). The hypothesis, tested by the optimal stomatal conductance model, shows that the available soil water combined with Ta   will trigger changes in stomatal conductance, which in turn affect ET  (Lin et al., 2015 ): in water-limited regions, a greater single slope parameter, g1  , is induced by increased Ta   and soil water drought. Lower g1   values are induced by decreases inTa   and soil water drought in energy-limited regions (as shown in Fig. 5  of Lin et al. (2015) ). Overall, the ET  shifts reflect the ecosystem responses and water availabilities that are induced by drought strengths and climate regimes, especially the increases in ET  that are caused by increases in the LAI in wetter regions (Fig. 5 ), which can be explained by the increases in Sm   during multi-year drought periods even when compared to those in non-drought periods in water-limited regions (Fig. 6 a) (Underlying mechanism: Mec5). Increased VPD levels during drought periods indicate atmospheric demand and increased ET  or plant response (stomatal closure), decreases in ET  (Massmann et al., 2019 ) (Underlying mechanism: Mec2). ET  decreased with increased VPD, and Ta   increased in the water-limited regions, while there were VPD increases and Ta   decreases in energy-limited regions (Fig. 6 ), suggesting that the mechanism controlling ET  should vary with drought strength and climate regime. As shown by Orth et al. (2018), the responses of ET  to droughts of different strengths are strongly dependent on the location-specific long-term dryness index, with ET  reductions occurring only in dry climates and even with ET  increases occurring in wet climates (mechanistic explanation by Mec1, Mec3 and Mec5). Interestingly, the mean annual (P -Q )/P  ratio (≈0.50) acts as a key threshold for controlling the ecohydrological responses (e.g., Sm  , LAI, VPD, and Ta  ) (as shown in Fig. 7 ), suggesting that wetter catchments [(P -Q )/P ≤0.50] can maintain their steady states even when influenced by multi-year droughts, while drier catchments [(P -Q )/P >0.50] could easily transition from one state to another. It is hypothesized that the water available from catchment water storage and [(P -Q )/P ≤0.5] plays a vital role in balancing the catchment ecohydrological states and acts as a two-stage controlled mechanism that drives E  (Underlying mechanism: Mec1 and Mec5). The interactions between the available water (P ), energy (Ep  ) and vegetation (LAI) control the P  partitioning. As shown in Fig. 8 , the P  deficit induced an increase in the magnitude of attribution in both the water- and energy-limited regions, which is consistent with the theoretical deviations associated with the Budyko framework (e.g., Zhang et al., 2001; Donohue et al., 2012 ). Unexpectedly, the magnitude of the vegetation contribution to ET  during the multi-year drought decreased to half of the normal value (0.18/0.40 *100 ≈ 45 %), suggesting that the vegetation response should be explained by the mechanisms of ET  changes, e.g.,  vegetation phenologies (Ma et al., 2015 ), species compositions, root depths, and vegetation cover densities (e.g., Mueller et al., 2005 ; Saft et al., 2015 ). For example,  vegetation tends to develop deep roots to satisfy its water demand as the groundwater amounts decline during multi-year droughts, which can also be deduced from the rooting depth theoretical model developed by Guswa (2008) that uses the carbon cost–benefit model. Furthermore, the Horton index [defined as the ratio of watershed ET  to wetness (P  minus surface Q ; Horton, 1933; Peterson et al., 2021 ] tends to increase during multi-year droughts (Peterson et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b ). This suggests that increases in catchment water storage capacities are accompanied by decreases in groundwater levels and soil water storage (Liu et al., 2023b ). In this case, a greater proportion of P  is used to refill the subsurface storage (Sm   and groundwater) and then maintain the ET  demand, leading to increased levels of P  contributions to ET  even in energy-limited regions (as shown in Fig. 8 a) (underlying mechanism: Mec4); this phenomenon has also been validated by other studies (e.g., Orth & Destouni, 2018; Wu et al., 2021 ). Unexpectedly, enhanced ET  levels were found during multi-year droughts compared to those during the remaining years, explained by the fact that greater rooting depths may provide access to deeper storage during water stress, thus sustaining evaporation even during dry periods (Massari et al., 2022 ). The hypothesis that ET  priority is derived from the mechanisms in which the threshold switching characteristics are combined with the traditional bucket water model (Liu et al., 2023b ) induces greater ET  ratios (e.g., Peterson et al., 2021 ). Generally, the underlying mechanisms of the ET  responses can be explained by the available water, available energy, and vegetation response (underlying mechanisms: Mec1, Mec2, and Mec3), which are regulated by the antecedent catchment water storage (including soil moisture and groundwater) and P  partitioning (regulatory mechanism: Mec4 and Mec5). According to the Budyko hypothesis (Budyko, 1948, 1974 ), the available water and energy and vegetation characteristics control the ET  processes (Zhang et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Drought strengths and climate regimes control the key mechanisms that regulate the response of ET  to drought (as shown in Fig. 5 ). However, uncertainties in terms of the ET  response include, but are not limited to: (i ) Enhanced Ta   dramatically affected vegetation phenology (e.g., Fu et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016 ) and inevitably induced a shift in P  partitioning (e.g., Geng et al., 2020 ), which should hardly separate its effects from the impact of drought; (ii ) vegetation greening, increasing CO2  fertilization, nitrogen deposition, climate change, and land cover change (e.g., Zhu et al., 2016; Piao et al., 2019; Gampe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024 ) have promoted a multi-decadal increase in global ET  since the 1980 s (e.g. , Zhang et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023 ); (iii ) increased water use efficiency may be induced by rising CO2  concentrations and subsequently lead to increased LAI values, which are negatively influenced by increased vapour pressure deficits (Cheng et al., 2017 ); (iv ) changes in the cryosphere, including the degradation of frozen soil, snowmelt, and glacial melting under a climate warming background, may also weaken or even mask the effects of multi-year droughts (e.g. , Wang et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2022 ). For example, the rising temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau (including the upper regions of the YRB) exhibit intensified melting, driven glacial retreat and degradation of frozen soil and have accelerated the regional water cycle (Wang et al., 2021 ). (v ) Due to the above selection criteria for catchments and drought events (mentioned in Section 2.1 ), only 448 (out of 30959) catchments were used to assess global ET  changes. The remaining 448 catchments exhibited a significantly uneven spatial distribution, with the majority of catchments in Africa and Asia being excluded. Furthermore, the catchment area are defined between 10 and 100, 000 km2  to decrease channel routing effects and reduce the non-consistency in precipitation patterns influence. Both of uneven spatial distribution and catchment size will bring uncertainties in describing the drought impact on ET  across global scale under the Budyko framework. As previously highlighted by Kampf et al. (2020) , the inherent uncertainties in the status of catchments resulting from climate change and anthropogenic activities will inevitably lead to a steady-state deviation within the Budyko framework. Considering the drying role of P  (Berghuijs et al., 2017 ), drought events were identified as multi-year P  deficit, and study period was stratified into a drought period and a non-drought period (Saft et al., 2015 ). However, this inevitably introduces uncertainties in catchment properties response. In fact, intra-annual climate variability (e.g. , P  seasonality, timing, intensity and form) can bias the attribution of catchment properties (Berghuijs and Woods, 2016 ). Uncertainties could be caused by adaptations of vegetation to climate change resulting from multi-year droughts and anthropogenic activities (e.g. , irrigation and revegetation activities), which inevitably trigger ET  alteration and require further research.  5 Conclusion Multi-year drought has induced shifts in P  partitioning across different climate regimes. Interestingly, the ET  responses to multi-year droughts, involving complex interactions between climate, soil and vegetation, still remain uncertain. In this study, the ET  responses to multi-year droughts in different climate regimes were investigated, and ET  changes were also attributed. (i ) Generally, multi-year droughts induced ET  reductions in both water- and energy-limited regions. However, asymmetric hydrological effects were found in water- and energy-limited regions, suggesting that the underlying mechanisms of the ET  responses varied across different climate regimes. (ii ) As expected, multi-year P  deficits were accompanied by significant Sm   decreases and LAI decreases across different climate regimes, while the inconsistent responses of VPD and Ta   (especially the opposite trends in Ta   and significant increases in water-limited regions, while insignificant decreasing trends in energy-limited regions) indicated that multi-year droughts may induce alterations in energy partitioning. Interestingly, the threshold, (P -Q )/P  (∼0.50), provides robust evidence that catchment wetness acts as a key indicator of catchment resilience, implying that catchments with higher wetness [(P -Q )/P >0.50] are better able to cope with the impacts of multi-year droughts. In addition, (iii ) the available water (P ) provided a greater magnitude of attribution of ET  in water-limited regions, followed by Ep   and LAI. Unexpected, multi-year droughts dramatically alter the controlled variables in energy-limited regions; vegetation contributes more strongly to normal situations, while the available water (P ) plays a decisive role in the ET  responses. The custom MATLAB (R2019b) code written to read and analyse data and generate figures is fully available on request from the corresponding author.
