In reaching Eq. (12) , we have assumed that the evaporative surface is saturated, i.e. e s  = e  s  ∗     , and ET estimated from the two approaches are the same, i.e. E T e  = ET  a    , and therefore they can be combined in a physically consistent manner (Fig. 1  ). However, these two assumptions cannot be satisfied at the same time for estimating the PET under dry conditions where the evaporative surface is no longer saturated (Fig. 1  and Section 3 ).   3 Problems related to estimating the PET under dry conditions 3.1 Violation of assumptions underlying the Penman equation Under dry (unsaturated) conditions, the Penman equation, i.e., Eq. (12) , has been extrapolated to estimate the PET over land by assuming that the evaporative surface is saturated.(13) λ P E T = Δ R n  + ρ c p  e a  ∗   - e a     r a    Δ + γ       As the values of meteorological variables, T a   , e a    and r a    that would have adjusted if the surface became saturated are unknown, observations corresponding to the dry surfaces have been used to estimate the PET over land (Greve et al., 2019; Milly and Dunne, 2017, 2016; Yang et al., 2019 ). This directly violates the first assumption of a saturated surface for the Penman equation. A higher ET that occurs over a wet surface would increase air humidity and reduce air temperature due to enhanced evaporative cooling, resulting in a lower vapor pressure deficit (e a  ∗   - e a    ). Due to the strong feedback of soil moisture on atmospheric conditions (Zhou et al., 2021, 2022 ), e.g., air temperature and humidity, the Penman equation would overestimate the PET under dry conditions. It has been argued that air temperature and humidity and other aerodynamic conditions over a dry surface would determine the evaporative demand of the atmosphere as measured by evaporation pans (Donohue et al., 2010 ). As the saturated surface is too small to affect the surrounding dry environment, the observed ET from an evaporation pan is more appropriately called the “apparent” evaporative demand, which is greater than the actual evaporative demand represented by the PET that would occur had the moisture not been limiting over the whole area (Brutsaert, 2015 ). The large amount of ET from a well-watered surface would increase the atmospheric moisture content and reduce the apparent evaporative demand driven by temperature, humidity, and aerodynamic conditions to the level of actual evaporative demand (PET) constrained by the net radiation (Yang and Roderick, 2019 ). The difference between energy and aerodynamic controls on the PET over a dry surface therefore violates the second assumption of the Penman equation that PET derived from the surface energy balance and that from the aerodynamic heat transfer are identical and hence can be combined in a physically consistent manner for a coupled land–atmosphere system. To examine this, the energy balance approach and the aerodynamic approach are used to estimate the PET, respectively, based on observed variables (i.e., R n   , e a   , T a    and T s   ) for a dry surface and the assumption that the evaporative surface is saturated (e s  = e  s  ∗      and β = β w    ). This is analogous to a small evaporation pan which has no practical impact on meteorological observations of its surrounding environment, and its temperature is assumed to be the same as that of the dry surface (T s   ), sustained by heat transferred from the surrounding environment. Similar to the estimation of E T e     in Eq. (2)  and E T a     in Eq. (3) , an energy-based PET (PE T e    ) and an aerodynamics-based PET (PE T a    ) can be estimated, respectively, and the only difference is that the evaporative surface is assumed to be saturated.(14) λ P E T e  = R n  1 + β w        (15) λ P E T a  = ρ c p  e s  ∗   - e a     γ r a        Noting that Eq. (15)  above can be rewritten as:(16) λ P E T a  = ρ c p  T s  - T a     r a   ∙ e s  ∗   - e a   γ T s  - T a          or from Eqs. (4) and (6) :(17) λ P E T a  = H β w       Comparing λ P E T e     from Eq. (14)  and λ P E T a     from Eq. (17) , and replacing R n  H    with 1 + β  β    from Eq. (2) , we have(18) PE T e   PE T a    = 1 + 1 β   1 + 1 β w         Eq. (18)  indicates that the second assumption of the Penman equation can be satisfied only when β = β w     and PE T e  = P E T a     under wet conditions. As partitioning of the net radiation shifts towards the sensible heat instead of latent heat, we have β > β w     and PE T e  < P E T a    , indicating that PE T e     and PE T a     are no longer the same under dry conditions, as the underlying assumption of a saturated surface and coupled atmospheric dry condition cannot both be valid at the same time. PE T e     measures the maximum ET that could occur for the same amount of net radiation when the evaporative surface is saturated, which represents the energy constraint on ET and is consistent with the definition of the PET. On the other hand, PE T a     depends on air temperature, humidity, and other aerodynamic constraints for ET, and would exceed PE T e    , i.e., energy constraint of the net radiation, due to energy transferred from the surrounding dry environment. This is similar to the ET from a small evaporation pan, or the apparent PET in a dry environment (Kahler and Brutsaert, 2006 ). However, PE T a     can never materialize over a large area where energy supply is limited, as a higher ET that occurs on a wetter surface would lead to a cooler and more humid atmosphere and reduce the PE T a     to the level of PE T e     given the surface energy constraint. PE T e     and PE T a    , representing the evaporative demand over wet and dry surfaces, respectively, are essentially associated with different climate conditions. Therefore, the Penman equation should not be directly extrapolated to evaluate the PET for hypothetical wet surfaces under dry conditions. Given the surface energy constraint and aerodynamic heat transfer under the prevailing atmospheric conditions, PE T e     equals the aerodynamics-based PE T a     only when the land surface is well supplied with water and fully coupled with the atmosphere. This indicates that PE T e     can be used as a good estimator of the PET over land, but PE T a     or the combination of the two, i.e., the Penman equation, would lead to an overestimation of the PET under dry conditions. Similarly, it can be shown that PE T a  > P E T e     for vegetated areas when water supply is limited, and the Penman-Monteith equation (Monteith, 1965 ) would also overestimate the PET in a dry environment (see Appendix A ). Such overestimation has been reported previously, as the PET estimated from the Penman and Penman-Monteith equations far exceeds that constrained by the net radiation and based on energy-based equations of PET, particularly in dry regions (Milly and Dunne, 2017, 2016 ).  3.2 Modification of the Penman equation under dry conditions Fig. 1  shows that the Penman equation can be modified to account for the difference between PE T e     and PE T a     under dry conditions. PE T a     equals PE T e     when the land surface is well supplied with water and coupled with the atmospheric conditions, and would exceed PE T e     due to apparent increases in the evaporative demand driven by reduced air humidity and increased air temperature when the land surface dries up. The ratio of PE T e     over PE T a    , i.e., Eq. (18) , indicates the difference in the evaporative demand over wet and dry surfaces. Let k = 1 + 1 β   1 + 1 β w       , kPE T a     equals PE T e     and represents the aerodynamics-based PET under wet conditions. The Penman equation can therefore be modified to estimate the PET    or PE T e     equivalently (Fig. 1 ).(19) λ P E T = Δ R n  + k ρ c p  e a  ∗   - e a     r a    Δ + γ       PE T a     can be estimated as(20) λ P E T a  = Δ R n  / k + ρ c p  e a  ∗   - e a     r a    Δ + γ       Under wet conditions with β = β w     and k = 1   , Eq. (19)  is reduced to the Penman equation (Eq. (13) ) to estimate the PET (i.e., PET = P E T e  = P E T a    ). Under dry conditions with β > β w     and k < 1   , the direct application of the Penman equation would overestimate the PET or PE T e     and underestimate the apparent PET or PE T a    . This is because the Penman equation overestimates the aerodynamic control on ET for a hypothetical wet surface and underestimates the energy supply to a small saturated surface, i.e., R n  / k   , without considering energy transferred from the surrounding dry environment. This indicates that the Penman equation should not be directly used to estimate the PET or the apparent PET over land.   4 Estimation of PET based on the energy balance approach While Eq. (19)  above resolves the problem related to the Penman equation, its practical application requires an estimate of the parameter k  . Given that PE T e     can be used as a good estimator of the PET, consistent with the modified Penman equation (Eq. (19) ), and surface temperature (T s   ) is now widely available in remote sensing and reanalysis products and climate model simulations, it is appropriate to use the energy balance approach in Eq. (14)  directly with the net radiation and the wet Bowen ratio (β w   ) to estimate the PET for practical applications. However, it warrants further investigation to determine whether β w    evaluated with Eq. (6)  and observations can indeed represent the Bowen ratio when the surface becomes saturated. 4.1 Estimation of the wet Bowen ratio Let T s 1     be the surface temperature and e s 1  ∗     the corresponding saturation vapor pressure, T a 1     and e a 1     the air temperature and vapor pressure, when the atmosphere has adjusted to the saturated surface. The wet Bowen ratio for the saturated surface, β w 1    , can be expressed as(21) β w 1   = γ T s 1   - T a 1      e s 1  ∗   - e a 1          or(22) β w 1   = γ Δ + e a 1  ∗   - e a 1    T s 1   - T a 1           While the wet surface temperature (T s 1    ) can be estimated based on observations (Monteith, 1981; Szilagyi and Jozsa, 2008 ), the air temperature and humidity when the surface becomes saturated are unknown. Therefore, it is impossible to determine the wet Bowen ratio, hence the PET, with certainty in a dry environment. A good estimator of the wet Bowen ratio ought to be similar to β w 1     without systematic bias. Many previous studies used the wet surface temperature (T s 1    ) along with observed air temperature and humidity to estimate the wet Bowen ratio, termed as β w 2     (Szilagyi and Jozsa, 2008; Crago and Qualls, 2018; Tu and Yang, 2022 ).(23) β w 2   = γ Δ + e a  ∗   - e a   T s 1   - T a          When the surface becomes saturated, the surface and air temperatures reduce rapidly, i.e., T s 1   < T s     and T a 1   < T a    , due to evaporative cooling. Reduced air temperature and increased water vapor in the air would also lead to reduced vapor pressure deficit, i.e., e a 1  ∗   - e a 1   < e a  ∗   - e a    , and we have β w 2   < β w 1     . This indicates that considering the surface cooling alone, β w 2     would systematically underestimate the wet Bowen ratio, i.e., β w 1    , when the surface becomes saturated. However, it remains unclear whether β w    is larger or smaller than β w 1    , as we have a situation where e a 1  ∗   - e a 1   < e a  ∗   - e a     and T s 1   - T a 1   < T s  - T a    . The latter is expected from the lower sensible heat, which is proportional to the temperature difference between the evaporative surface and the air, under wetter conditions. To address this source of uncertainty in the estimated wet Bowen ratio using Eq. (6) , it is crucial to assess how β w    varies with coupled changes in the temperature and humidity between the land surface and the atmosphere, and how sensitive β w    is to the level of surface moisture content.  4.2 Variations in the wet Bowen ratio under wet and dry conditions As the Bowen ratio is unknown for the land surface when saturated, we can use β w    values for the ocean to assess the potential variations in β w    under wet and hypothetical dry conditions. β w    can be directly estimated from Eq. (6)  and compared with the Bowen ratio (β  ) for the ocean. To illustrate how β w    would change with the surface moisture content, let’s consider an ocean grid cell at the state space (T s   , e s  ∗    , T a   , e a   ) (see blue points in Fig. 2  a). For a constant amount of net radiation and minimal advection, an isobaric and adiabatic process with changes in surface moisture content indicates that the moist enthalpy or equivalent temperature remains constant for the air and at the surface, i.e., the air and surface are isenthalpic (Crago and Qualls, 2021 ). While coupled variations in temperature and humidity may lead to variations in β w    under dry conditions, air and surface temperatures can be determined as T a  + e a  / γ    and T s  + e s  ∗   / γ   , respectively, when both air and surface humidities reach zero under the driest conditions. Therefore, β w    can be computed for such driest conditions (β w , d    ) and compared with that (i.e., Eq. (6) ) under wet conditions.(24) β w , d   = γ T s  + e s  ∗   / γ ) -  ( T  a  + e a  / γ      e s , d  ∗        where e s , d  ∗     refers to the saturation vapor pressure at surface temperature of T s  + e s  ∗   / γ    under the driest conditions. In addition to β w   , we also assess variations in the Bowen ratio as an empirical equation of γ / Δ    based on ocean observations (β o   ) (Yang and Roderick, 2019 ) and inferred from the widely used Priestley-Taylor equation (β pt    ) (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ), which has been widely used to estimate the PET under wet conditions:(25) β o  = 0.24 γ / Δ     (26) β pt   = 0.79 γ / Δ - 0.21     where Δ   is expressed as a function of surface and air temperatures (see Eq. (8) ), indicating that both β o    and β pt     are sensitive to temperature changes induced by surface moisture changes. To compare changes in the three Bowen ratios under wet and dry conditions, their sensitivities to temperature changes (reflective of surface moisture changes given the constraint of moist enthalpy) are calculated, i.e., the ratio of differences in the Bowen ratios over the difference in the mean of surface and air temperatures between wet and hypothetical driest conditions. In addition, the sensitivity of β w    to γ / Δ    is tested.(27) β w  = α γ / Δ , α ∈ ( 0 , 1  )      The sensitivity coefficient (α  ) may vary with air temperature and humidity, with α → 1    when the air is nearly saturated, corresponding to the equilibrium evaporation, and α → 0    when air temperature is close to surface temperature (sensible heat is close to 0 and β → 0   ).   5 Data analyses 5.1 ERA5 dataset The ERA5 global reanalysis dataset, i.e., the fifth generation reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), was used for data analysis. The ERA5 reanalysis has assimilated a large number of observations into models to produce high-resolution and high-quality reanalysis of the atmosphere, ocean, and land surface processes (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). Moreover, the ocean–land–atmosphere system is fully coupled in ERA5, which allows us to test whether different PET equations can be used to estimate the ET over the ocean (i.e., saturated conditions) accurately and whether the Bowen ratios and PETs are sensitive to surface moisture content and associated temperature changes by considering coupled changes in temperature and humidity between the ocean/land surface and the atmosphere. Monthly outputs of surface latent and sensible heat fluxes, air and dew point temperature at 2 m, surface (skin) temperature, and surface pressure at the spatial resolution of 1° × 1° for the period 1940–2022 were downloaded from the most recent ERA5 reanalysis. The net radiation minus ground heat flux (R n   ) was calculated as the sum of sensible and latent heat fluxes. Monthly outputs from ocean grid cells in ERA5 were used to assess the variation in β w    under wet and dry conditions. To reduce uncertainties caused by sea ice, grid cells/months when the monthly mean air or surface temperature is lower than 0 °C were excluded. In addition, grid cells/months when the Bowen ratio is less than zero or larger than γ / Δ   , as suggested by the two boundary conditions in Eq. (27) , were not used for data analysis. β w    in Eq. (6) , β o    in Eq. (25) , β pt     in Eq. (26) , and corresponding PE T e    , PE T o    , and PE T pt     , respectively, were estimated for ocean grid cells under both wet and hypothetical driest conditions. As the surface temperature can be lower than air temperature at night for many land grid cells, this would induce large uncertainties in the estimated β w    at the monthly scale. Under normal conditions, β w    is expected to be larger than that over the ocean (β o   ) (Tu et al., 2022 ), and β w    is smaller than β   as the land surface is not always saturated. These two boundary conditions, β w  ≥ β o     and β w  ≤ β   , were therefore applied in sequence to reduce the uncertainty in the estimation of β w    over land.  5.2 Variations in the wet Bowen ratio under wet and dry conditions Fig. 2 b, c shows changes in the three Bowen ratios and related PETs with the increase in the mean temperature from the wet to the hypothetical driest conditions for an ocean grid cell. As changes in air temperature and humidity in response to surface moisture changes between the wet and driest conditions are in fact unknown, the pink lines show just one possible pathway of changes in β w    and PE T e     when surface and air temperatures change in proportion from the wet to the driest states. It is worth noting that possible pathways between the wet and driest conditions are countless due to coupled changes in temperature and humidity of the air and at the surface, and β w    and PE T e     are determinate only for the wet and driest conditions (see Section 4.2 ). The estimated β w    is close to β   and PE T e     is close to ET under wet condition for the ocean grid cell, and the differences in β w    and PE T e     between the wet and driest conditions are relatively small. In comparison, β o    and β pt     as a function of γ / Δ    show larger departures from β   for the ocean grid cell. As the reduction in surface moisture content increases surface and air temperatures, β o    and β pt     decrease by a larger amount than β w    from wet to dry conditions. Over all assessed ocean grid cells, the sensitivity coefficient (α  ) of β w    to γ / Δ   , varies around 0.24 using ocean observations, i.e., β o   , for the wet and hypothetical driest conditions (Fig. 3  a–c). However, β pt     is greatly different from β w    and β o    for both wet and dry conditions (Fig. 3 a, b). Under wet conditions, the mean biases in β w    (−0.0016) and PE T e     (0.0025 mm/d) are the smallest among all three Bowen ratios and PETs over ocean grid cells (Fig. 3 d, e). Using β o    and β pt     would increase the bias in the estimated Bowen ratio (0.0040 and 0.1009) and PET (0.0362 and −0.0862 mm/d) under wet conditions (Fig. 3 d, e). In addition, the uncertainty range using PE T e    , i.e., −0.05 to 0.08 mm/d over 90 % of grid cells, is much smaller than that using PE T o     (−0.21 to 0.36 mm/d) and PE T pt      (−0.52 to 0.36 mm/d). This indicates that β w    and PE T e     are better estimators of the Bowen ratio and the PET under wet conditions. The small biases in β w    and PE T e     caused by nonlinear changes in temperature and humidity within a month could be reduced using data at finer scales, such as the original hourly outputs in ERA5. The variation in β w    and hence PE T e     are also the smallest among the three Bowen ratios and PETs between wet and dry conditions (Fig. 3 f, g). Consistent with the analysis in Section 4.1 , β w    may become higher or lower under dry conditions compared to the wet condition. The sensitivity of β w    to temperature increases caused by reductions in surface moisture content is only −0.0032 per °C on average, resulting in a mean sensitivity of 0.0098 mm/d/°C for PE T e    . As β o    and β pt     strongly depend on temperature, they become lower when temperature increases under dry conditions, and their mean sensitivities to temperature are as large as −0.0042 and −0.0139 per °C, respectively. Overall, β w    shows the smallest bias in the estimated Bowen ratio over the ocean, and the lowest variations between wet and dry conditions. This indicates that β w    and hence PE T e     can be used to estimate the Bowen ratio and ET over the ocean, and are also good estimators of the wet Bowen ratio and the PET under dry conditions over land.  5.3 Estimation of the wet Bowen ratio and PET over land Fig. 4   shows the estimated mean β w    and PE T e     for the period of 1940–2022. The spatial pattern of PE T e     largely resembles that of the surface net radiation, with a spatial correlation coefficient of 0.99 over all grid cells, and shows higher values in lower-latitude regions where the Earth’s surface receives and absorbs more solar radiation (Fig. 4 a, b). As the albedo is higher over land, the net radiation and hence PE T e     are generally lower over land than over the ocean. However, β w    is similar over land and surrounding oceans in low- and mid-latitude regions. In particular, β w    shows small differences between mid-latitude deserts and surrounding oceans, which again demonstrates that β w    is not very sensitive to surface moisture content, and the estimated β w    can well approximate the Bowen ratio over land when saturated (Fig. 4 c). It is noted that β w    is lower over high-latitude land areas compared to the surrounding oceans. This is because high-latitude land areas are covered by snow/ice in autumn, winter, and spring. It is possible that both β w    and the actual Bowen ratio are low and even negative (e.g., sensible heat is negative) during snow- and ice-covered periods. Over the past 83 years, PE T e     increased over most land areas, with a mean trend of 0.42 mm per year for the annual PE T e     over the global land area (excluding Greenland and Antarctica) in ERA5 (Fig. 4 d, g). The long-term increase in PE T e     is mostly attributed to increases in the net radiation over the same period (0.39 mm per year for R n  / λ   , Fig. 4 e, g), but also induced by warming-driven slight reductions in β w    (−7.6 × 10−5  per year, Fig. 4 f, h). In addition, the long-term trends in PE T e     and the net radiation are largely consistent over land, with a spatial correlation coefficient of 0.92 (Fig. 4 d, e). The large consistency in the global patterns and long-term trends of PE T e     and the net radiation suggest that PE T e     can represent the energy limitation for ET, i.e., the maximum ET constrained by the net radiation and regulated by land–atmosphere processes. In comparison, β o    and β pt     are higher than β w   , resulting in lower values of PE T o     and PE T pt      compared to PE T e     during the study period (Fig. 4 g, h). Moreover, the long-term trend of PE T pt      (0.48 mm per year) is higher than that of PE T e    , due to more rapid declines in β pt     (−1.6 × 10−4  per year) compared to β w    as the climate warms in recent decades (Fig. 4 g, h). Thus, PE T pt      may overestimate the rate of increase in the PET over time in a warming world.  5.4 Uncertainty analysis A common caveat of adopting the PE T e     equation, as well as many other PET equations, is that they do not account for potential changes in the net radiation under dry and wet conditions. When a dry surface becomes saturated, the net radiation may increase or decrease (see Fig. 5   for a comparison of the net radiation between dry and wet years), due to concurrent changes in surface albedo, cloud cover, surface and air temperatures, and other factors. For instance, increased cloud shading reduces the downward shortwave radiation, while reduced surface temperature leads to a reduction in the upward longwave radiation (Teuling et al., 2010; Tu and Yang, 2022 ). As various factors affect the net radiation in different directions, the net radiation for a hypothetical wet surface is essentially indeterminate and the observed net radiation is commonly used to represent the energy constraint for the PET. Additionally, the potential variation in the net radiation is not the primary reason for the systematic overestimation of the PET in a dry environment (Greve et al., 2019; Milly and Dunne, 2017, 2016 ). While the estimated β w    using observed variables in a dry environment is a good estimator of the Bowen ratio when the surface becomes saturated, potential changes in β w    under dry and wet conditions may affect the accuracy of PE T e    . To test this, the sensitivity of PE T e     to potential errors in β w    is derived from Eq. (14) .(28) dPE T e   PE T e    = - β w  1 + β w    d β w   β w       The estimated β w    is less than 0.25 over more than 90 % of the land area, and the global annual mean β w    is around 0.10 during 1940–2022 (Fig. 4 ). Based on the range of 0–0.25 for β w   , a 10 % error in β w    would lead to a relative error of only 0–2 % in PE T e    , which indicates that PE T e     would not be greatly influenced by the potential errors in the estimated β w   .   6 Conclusions This study has identified the fundamental problem related to the Penman equation for estimating the PET over land, and solved this problem based on the energy balance approach with the net radiation and the wet Bowen ratio (β w   ). While the original Penman equation can be used to estimate ET over wet regions, direct application of the Penman equation for estimating the PET over dry regions cannot meet the underlying assumption of a saturated evaporative surface and at the same time coupled radiative and aerodynamic processes as required by the Penman equation. In practice, the energy-based PE T e     equals the aerodynamics-based PE T a     and can be combined to estimate the PET under wet conditions. However, PE T a     begins to exceed PE T e     due to increases in the air temperature and reductions in humidity under dry conditions, and PE T a     or a combination of PE T e     and PE T a     in the Penman equation would therefore overestimate the PET systematically. PE T e    , i.e., the maximum ET that would occur when the net radiation remains the same but water supply at the evaporative surface is unlimited, represents the energy constraint on ET and can be used to estimate the PET over land. First, PE T e     can accurately estimate the ET with the net radiation and β w    under wet conditions. Second, β w    and PE T e     are not sensitive to changes in surface moisture content and associated temperature changes, thus estimated β w    and PE T e     under dry (unsaturated) conditions can be used to approximate the Bowen ratio and ET accurately when the surface becomes saturated. This indicates that the PET can be estimated based on observations, even if the meteorological conditions that would adjust to the condition of a wet surface are unknown. These two distinct advantages of PE T e     make it a good estimator of the ET over wet surfaces (e.g., oceans, lakes, and reservoirs) and the PET over land. By comparing the PE T e     with other energy-based equations for PET estimation, the widely used Priestley-Taylor equation (PE T pt     ) and the empirical equation based on ocean observations (PE T o    ) show much larger biases than using PE T e     when compared to monthly ET over the ocean and PE T pt      and PE T o     are more sensitive than PE T e     to surface moisture and temperature changes. Therefore, using meteorological data in a dry environment would lead to larger uncertainties in the estimated PET using PE T pt      and PE T o    . While β w    is estimated using meteorological data under dry conditions, the fact that β w    is fairly constant due to coupled changes in temperature and humidity of the air and at the land surface makes β w    a better estimator of the Bowen ratio when the surface becomes saturated. This has solved the problem related to PET estimation based on observations under both wet and dry conditions. Given the importance of the PET in meteorological, hydrological, ecological and agricultural research, our new approach would have important implications for accurate estimation of the PET and its practical applications.
1 Introduction Climate change is currently one of the most important global problems, disturbing the societal socio-economic, and environmental situations (Fulco et al, 2007). The impact of climate change becomes more visible in water resources, affecting the distribution and allocation in spatial and temporal aspects globally, making water scarcity a very serious global problem (Sun et al., 2008 ). The larger responsible driving factors for the change in climate at global and regional levels are anthropogenic activities, resulting in the emission of Greenhouse Gases (GHGs) (Henderson & Reinert, 2016 ). The future climate change is projected based on the possible continuing greenhouse gas emissions, land use change, and air pollutant emissions in the 21st century (IPCC, 2014 ). Evapotranspiration (ET) is one of the important components of the hydrological cycle which can potentially be altered by climate change. The term represents the combination of the two words evaporation and transpiration. The former implies the process by which water is moving directly from the land surface (soil, water bodies, and canopies) to the air, whereas the latter refers to the movement of water from the soil, through roots and vegetation bodies, on leaves, and then into the air. Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) is the maximum amount of water that can be lost by evapotranspiration if sufficient water is available, influenced by temperature, humidity, sunlight, and wind (Allen et al., 1998 ). The assessment of the PET or reference evapotranspiration (ETo) is very important for various hydro-climatic applications including designing and management of irrigation projects, water balance studies, and assessment of droughts and aridity index classification (Wang & Dickinson, 2012 ) (McMahon et al., 2013 ) (Weiß & Menzel, 2008 ). In recent years, it is well verified that climate change has become a major driving factor for the loss of water through evapotranspiration (Qu & Zhuang, 2019 ) (G. G. Haile & Tang, 2020 ) and increasing aridity on regional and global scales. Aridity is a climatic phenomenon that refers to the long-term persisting climatic condition over a region (Agnew, 1991 ), expressed in terms of the Aridity Index which is defined by the ratio of total annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration (Huang et al., 2016 ). Even though the changes in temperature and precipitation are considered as the two main indicators of climate change, AI is more important to understand the change in climate in terms of the bioclimatic condition (Moral et al., 2017 ). Due to the consistent rising temperature and declining water availability, it is indicated that aridity will increase over the 21st century in different parts of the world (Marvel et al., 2019 ) (Park et al., 2018 ) (Lin et al., 2018 ) (Fu et al., 2016 ) (Dai, 2013 ). Thus, it significantly alters the natural and human systems (Corlett, 2020 ), and once the aridity or dryness of a particular region increases beyond a certain level, it will be very tough to restore it (Adnan & Haider, 2012 ). Though it is well known that climate change is significantly affecting global water availability (IPCC, 2022a ), regionally, the distinct impacts of climate change on evapotranspiration should be quantified and projected to assess the dynamics of moisture availability. This consideration will enhance our understanding of its impact on water resources and ecosystem services in general (Allen et al., 2011 ) in large river basins and small-scale catchments. Numerous researches have revealed that climate change has been affecting the evapotranspiration condition of river basins in tropical regions. For instance, the rate of change in evapotranspiration is expected to rise by up to 4.8 % in the Tapajós Basin in the Brazilian Amazon (Farinosi et al., 2019 ), 12.7 % in the Subarnarekha basin in tropical India under RCP 8.5 scenario. In the Ethiopian context, the availability of water is projected to be prominently altered by climate change through the loss of much water by the evapotranspiration process in the upper Blue Nile basin (A. T. Haile et al., 2017 ) (Taye et al., 2018 ), Tekeze basin (Gebremeskel & Kebede, 2018 ), and Gilgel Gibe basin (Alemayehu et al., 2023 ). Most importantly, the rate of change in PET and rainfall under the change in climate in the upper Blue Nile basin is well studied and the overall results showed that there is a consistent increment of PET in various watersheds, whereas, the rate of change in rainfall is highly fluctuating in temporal and spatial patterns under different emission scenarios (G. G. Chakilu et al., 2020 ) (Worqlul et al., 2018 ) (Kim & Kaluarachchi, 2009 ) (G. G. Chakilu et al., 2023 ). According to (Mengistu et al., 2021 ), PET is expected to increase up to 27 % by the end of the 21st century under the RCP 8.5 scenario, whereas, rainfall is likely to decline up to 19 % under the same scenario in the upper Blue Nile basin. On the other hand, a study by (G. G. Chakilu et al., 2022a ) indicated that the rate of change in rainfall is projected to rise up to 27 % in the rainy season and decrease up to 19 % in the dry season at the end of 21st century in the same basin and under the same emission scenario. Similarly, (Bekele et al., 2021 ) reported that rainfall is expected to decline by up to 21 %, and rise in PET by up to 7 % in the mid-21st century under the RCP 8.5 scenario. The result of all the above studies clearly showed the consistent rise of PET due to increasing temperature, and seasonal fluctuation of rainfall with a decline in the dry season. Most of these results are used to evaluate the impact of climate change on stream flow of watersheds in the Upper Blue Nile basin. However, the consequent impact of the consistent and long-term increase of PET on the declining land moisture availability, or level of seasonal aridity in the entire area of watersheds especially in the dry season, has not been investigated in the basin. Thus, the objectives of this study are: 1) to assess the rate of change in precipitation (rainfall); 2) to evaluate the rate of change in potential evapotranspiration; and 3) to calculate the level of seasonal aridity or dryness in terms of Aridity Index (AI) in the headwater catchments of the Upper Blue Nile basin. For this investigation, the study focused on using the RCP8.5 scenario because the projected temperature and the subsequent PET in global and regional contexts are rising prominently under this scenario compared to other RCPs. Hence, it is always good to consider the worst-case scenario in the investigation for planning watershed development and management practices and applying different climate change adaptation and resilience mechanisms in the basin. However, the authors suggested that researchers should consider the Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP5-8.5) in CMIP6 climate models in similar future studies because the degree of increase in temperature and PET under this pathway is higher than RCP8.5.  2 Methods and materials 2.1 Study area description This study was conducted in the headwater catchments of the upper Blue Nile basin, Ethiopia namely: Megech, Gilgel Abay, Ribb, and Gumara watersheds (Fig. 1  ). The investigated watersheds are the sub-watersheds of the Lake Tana sub-basin which is the head and major source of the Blue Nile basin, geographically located between 10.95° and 12.78° N and 36.89° and 38.25° E. More than 93 % of water of the Lake Tana which is the largest lake in Ethiopia is collected from these four watersheds (Setegn, 2010 ). The general geophysical characteristics of the watersheds are presented in Table 1  .  2.2 Hydro-climate data processing Climate variables that are mainly used in this study are rainfall, maximum temperature (Tmax ), and minimum temperature (Tmin ). These climate variables with different spanning periods were obtained from Ethiopia's National Meteorological Agency (NMA). Even though, there are more stations in the region, only 14 meteorological stations were considered in the investigated watersheds because of lack of sufficient years of data (Table 2  ). Due to this, some of the stations were commonly used for two adjacent watersheds in the simulation process. Stations which are having a better spanning period of observed data were used for the bias correction process of projected climate variables and evaluation of the efficiency of investigated climate models. The missing values of climate variables were replaced by the average values of data of the nearest weather stations on the corresponding date (Te Chow et al., 1988 ) for bias correction purposes. However, for the period, used for the SWAT model were replaced by the model itself. Six climate models including CSIRO-Mk3-6–0, HadGEM2-ES, EC-EARTH, CanESM2, NORESM1-M, and CNRM-CM5 were used in climate data projection under the Coupled Model Inter-comparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) (Table 3  ). Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) was used as a data source, accessed at https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/projects/esgf-llnl/  website. Except for HadGEM2-ES, the other five climate models were selected based on their Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity (ECS) values which are within the recommended range value (1.5 to 4.5 °C) in CMIP5 (Meehl et al., 2020 ) (Wyser et al., 2020 ), whereas HadGEM2-ES was selected because of its good performance in the projection of surface temperature and precipitation in other previous studies (Kattsov et al., 2013 ) (Bhattacharjee & Zaitchik, 2015 ). The raw observed streamflow data of watersheds was obtained from the MoWE and processed before being used in the SWAT model simulation.  2.3 Geophysical data collection and processing The geophysical data such as soil, land use/cover, and slope were required to define and analyze of Hydrological Response Unit (HRU) in the simulation process of streamflow in the SWAT model. Soil data was obtained from the global digital soil map (FAO-UNESCO, 2007 ) with a 1:5000000 scale, whereas the land use was taken from Ethiopian MoWE. The slope of watersheds was generated from SRTM Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data with 30 m*30 m resolution, accessed from the United States Geological Survey (USGS). These geospatial data were processed using ArcGIS10.4 software based on the compatibility of the SWAT model.  2.4 Correction of errors in climate model outputs The projected future climate data were corrected using the historical 30 years (1971–2000) of observed and model output data of climate variables. Mostly, the biases between the projected and observed climate data are created because of the spatial resolution factors of climate models and topographical differences. Therefore, minimizing the great variation and maintaining the consistency and reliability of the future projected time series data is highly important for climate change analysis and impact studies. For this purpose, various statistical methods are being applied especially in future rainfall and temperature projections in various climate studies. In this study, the power transformation method was used for the correction of errors in rainfall climate model outputs, whereas both the Tmax  and Tmin  model outputs were corrected by the variance scaling method using CMhyd software (Rathjens et al., 2016 ). These two bias correction methods are selected based on the level of consistency of results in frequency-based statistics in previous studies (Teutschbein & Seibert, 2012 ) (Fang et al., 2015 ). Therefore, the amount of rainfall R in each day is transformed into a corrected R* by using Equation (1)  as follows:(1) R  ∗   = aR  b      The value of “a” and “b” are determined iteratively. Even though there are many PET estimation methods, the SWAT model supports only three methods. In the temperature-based method, only the Hargreaves method is used, whereas in the energy balance method, Penman-Monteith and Priestley Tylor estimation methods are supported in the SWAT model. Therefore, for this study, Penman-Monteith which is commonly used in the energy balance method was used in this study, whereas, in the temperature–based method, Hargreaves method was used in the PET simulation process. The result of these two methods was compared based on their performance in the simulation of stream flow by the SWAT model, and the best-fit method was selected and used in change analysis in PET and aridity index. Even though the applicability of CFSR climate data for hydrological models has already been verified, it has some uncertainty and errors compared to the ground-based data. Therefore, in this study, the verification is done by evaluating the performance in the simulation of streamflow of watersheds. In the validation process, the SWAT model considers PET as one of the important water balance components, and if the simulated streamflow is consistent with the measured flow, it is assumed that the estimated PET is also consistent with reality. Thus, in this study, the main purpose of using the SWAT model is to associate the estimated PET with the simulated streamflow of watersheds. The SWAT model uses a water balance algorithm in the simulation process using equation (10)  (Neitsch et al., 2002 ).(10) SW  t  = S W  0  + ∑ i = 1  t  R day   - Q surf   - E a  - W sweep   - Q gw      i      Where SWt  = the final soil water content (mm), Qsurf  = the amount of surface runoff (mm), i = time step (day), t = is time (days), SWo  = the initial soil water content (mm), Rday  = the amount of precipitation (mm), Wseep  = the amount of water entering the vadose zone from the soil profile (mm), Ea  = the amount of evapotranspiration (mm), and Qgw  = the amount of groundwater flow (mm).  2.7 Calibration and validation of the SWAT model The simulated flow, obtained by the default parameters and values of parameters was compared with the measured one, and a great difference was observed. To minimize this deviation, the sensitive SWAT model parameters were selected and calibrated using SWAT-CUP (SWAT-Calibration and Uncertainty Programs) version 12 software. The model was calibrated by seven years (1995–2001) of climate data in the four watersheds and the efficiency of the model was evaluated. The maximum efficiency of the model was observed after 2000 iterations through automatic calibration and by manual adjustment of parameter values. Once the maximum efficiency of the model and the optimum values of parameters were obtained, the consistency was also verified by four years (2002–2005) of climate data. Since the purpose of the study is to investigate climate change impacts, the same geophysical inputs of the SWAT model are used in the calibration and validation process. The efficiency of the SWAT model in default simulation, calibration, and validation was evaluated by using two statistical variables including Nash–Sutcliffe (NS), and Relative Volume Error (RVE), computed by equation (11)  and equation (12) , respectively.(11) NS = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  Q s i m i       - Q o b s i         2   ∑ i = 1  n  Q s i m i       -  Q  ¯   obs      2        Where Qobs  is the daily observed streamflow and Qsim  also represents the daily simulated streamflow, n = the number of days. The value of NS ranges between ─∞ and 1; 1 indicates the best performance of the model (Nash & Sutcliffe, 1970 ).(12) RVE = ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s i       - Q s i m i          ∑ i = 1  n  Q o b s i        ∗ 100 %     The optimal value of RVE is 0, whereas, the positive and negative values indicated underestimation and overestimation of the model, respectively (Gupta et al., 1999 ).  2.8 Estimation of aridity Index (AI) AI is the level of dryness of a certain region, expressed numerically. It is an index that indicates the availability of moisture in the soil, defined as the ratio between mean annual precipitation (P) and mean annual PET (UNEP, 1993 ).(13) AI = P PET       Even though AI is usually estimated based on the mean annual precipitation and PET, this study evaluated it based on the seasonal variability of precipitation and PET to assess the seasonal aridity condition of the region. Therefore, first, the change in precipitation and PET were evaluated in the mean monthly time scale, and the aridity index was also estimated accordingly.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Evaluation of the performance of climate models The performance of each model has been evaluated by comparing the simulated data with the corresponding station-observed data. The errors of climate models in the simulation of Tmax , Tmin , and rainfall are analyzed in terms of monthly time scale. Compared to the other climate models, the CanESM2 was the least efficient in the projection of all climate variables. All climate models have better efficiency in the simulation of Tmin  than Tmax . The highest average monthly errors of climate models in the simulation of historical rainfall, Tmax , and Tmin  ranged from ± 0.85 % to ± 1.17 %, 0.12 °C to 0.19 °C, and 0.08 °C to 0.14 °C, respectively (Fig. 2  ). All the highest variations in the three climate variables are observed in the CanESM2, whereas the lowest errors in the projection of both rainfall and Tmin  are detected by the CSIRO-Mk3-6–0 and in Tmax , it is under NORESM1-M model. These errors in all climate variables under all climate models are evaluated after the bias correction process is completed. Therefore, these errors could be considered as one of the causes for uncertainties observed in the simulation of PET and have an impact on the overall efficiency of the SWAT model Fig. 3.  .  3.2 SWAT model efficiency SWAT model was more efficient in simulating stream flow using the Hargreaves PET estimation method than the Penman-Monteith (PM) method in all watersheds, which is consistent with other comparison studies (Earls & Dixon, 2008 ) (Oudin et al., 2005 ) (Almorox et al., 2015 ). In both PET estimation methods, the best fit was observed in the Gilgel Abay watershed compared to the others in calibration and verification processes interms of NS (HR=0.86, PM=0.79). In the Megech watershed, although the performance of the model is improved by calibration, it is still weak compared to the other watersheds. Statistically, the performance of the model (NS) using the HR PET estimation method was 0.51 and 0.54 in the calibration and verification process, respectively, whereas in the PM method, the model performance in terms of NS was 0.47 and 0.56 in the calibration and verification process, respectively. The efficiency of the SWAT model in terms of RVE was also evaluated and the result showed that PET estimation using the HR method was more appropriate than PM in almost all watersheds, except in the model validation period of the Megech watershed (HR=–6.62 % and PM=–4.6 %). The negative values of RVE in the default simulation, calibration, and validation process indicated that there is an overestimation of streamflow (Table 4  ). The optimal values of sensitive parameters obtained by the calibration process were tested again by independent climate data for verification purposes, and it was found that the performance of the model was consistent in the validation process as well. The rank of the sensitivity of parameters was evaluated based on the t -test and p-values. A parameter with the highest t -test value regardless of its sign, and the lowest p-value has the highest degree of sensitivity (Table 5  ). The model was more efficient in the PM method than HR in capturing the peak flows in almost all watersheds, though there were overestimations in some calibration and verification years, especially in the Megech watershed. On the other hand, the HR method is more consistent in the low flow of watersheds.  3.3 Change in rainfall The ensemble mean values of rainfall data obtained from the six climate models were taken as input for the SWAT model and the mean value in each watershed was computed by the Thiessen polygon method. The change in rainfall in an annual time scale of all periods is evaluated compared to the baseline period (1971–2000). The change in rainfall in all watersheds and all periods ranges from 2.59 % to 4.87 %. The highest change is expected in the last thirty period of this century (2071–2100) in the Gumara watershed. Since the watersheds shared common meteorology stations the change in rainfall in the three periods showed the same pattern except for Megech watershed which showed a little decrement between the second (2041–2070) and the last period (2071–2100). Therefore, it is possible to conclude that in all periods, the mean annual rainfall showed an increasing trend in almost all watersheds (Fig. 4  ). In the study area, rainfall is common in the summer season (June – September), in the other seasons especially in the winter season, the area is dry. Therefore, the study was also committed to revealing the variability of changes seasonally in terms of monthly time scale. In all watersheds, the change in rainfall is showing an increasing trend in the summer and post–summer (autumn) seasons. Whereas, in the winter and spring seasons in almost all watersheds and periods, rainfall is expected to decrease compared to the baseline period. The change is more prominent in November in the Gumara, Ribb, and Megech watersheds; while in the Gilgel Abay watershed, it is higher in October. The highest increasing values of the change in the Gumara, Megech, Ribb, and Gilgel Abay watersheds are 19.69 % (November), 18.56 % (November), 16.09 % (November), and 14.80 % (October) in the 2041–2070, 2041–2070, 2071–2100, and 2071–2100 periods, respectively. The highest decreasing values of the change in Gilgel Abay, Megech, and Gumara watersheds are expected to be observed in March, and the values of changes are 7.74 %, 5.66 %, and 5.53 %, respectively in 2071–2100, but in the Ribb watershed, it is likely to be observed in June, and the magnitude of the change is 4.63 % in 2041–2070 (Fig. 5  ).  3.4 Change in potential evapotranspiration (PET) of watersheds The Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) of all watersheds was computed by the Penman-Monteith and Hargreaves method in the calibration and verification process of the SWAT model, and the result was compared based on selecting the best fit in streamflow simulation. The change in PET ranges from 5.99% to 16.66% in all watersheds and periods. The change is showing an increasing pattern in all watersheds and in the three time periods, more prominently it showed a significant increment in 2071–2100. In general, the results of this study revealed that the highest change in annual average PET in Megech, Gilgel Abay, Ribb, and Gumara watersheds are 16.66%, 15.53%, 14.68%, and 13.46%, respectively, which is going to be observed in 2071–2100 (Fig. 6  ). Like the change in rainfall, the change in PET in the four watersheds and three time periods is also evaluated regarding seasonal variability. As far as PET is computed using the temperature-based (Hargreaves) method, the change is highly based on temperature change, and the pattern of PET change in all watersheds is almost the same due to the watersheds shared common meteorological station in the SWAT model. In Megech and Gilgel Abay watersheds, the highest change in PET is expected to be observed in September and April, respectively, whereas in Gumara and Ribb watersheds, the highest change is more likely observed in March. The highest values of changes in the Megech, Gilgel Abay, Ribb, and Gumara watersheds are 21.17 %, 19.29 %, 19.26 %, and 17.51 %, respectively (Fig. 7  ). Unlike rainfall, the change in PET in all watersheds, all months, and the three time periods showed an increasing pattern; all values of changes are above zero. Comparatively, the change is more significant in 2071–2100 than in the other periods.  3.5 Change in aridity Index As shown in sections 2.3 and 2.4 , rainfall and PET in the study area showed considerable changes in all watersheds and all periods. Thus, as far as those two important climate variables determine the Aridity Index, the change in Aridity in the four watersheds has also shown an increasing pattern in the coming eight decades of this century. Annually, the change in the Aridity Index is expected to increase within the range of 0.006 to 0.061 in all watersheds and periods. The highest change is forecasted in the 2071–2100 time period in the Megech watershed, while the lowest change is in 2011–2040 in the Gilgel Abay watershed. The negative values of changes in (Fig. 8  ) indicated that the change in AI is increasing in the region due to the change in temperature and the consequent result of increasing loss of moisture by evapotranspiration. Not only compared to the baseline period, changes between three consecutive periods have shown considerable variability in all watersheds. Even though by definition Aridity Index is the ratio of annual rainfall and PET, this study intends to evaluate the expected seasonal aridity of the watersheds on a monthly time scale. The dynamics of change in the Aridity Index on a monthly time scale showed increasing and decreasing patterns in all periods and watersheds. The severity of aridity shows a significant increment in the winter season considering the three time periods. Like, the change in PET, the change in AI is more prominent in the last thirty years of this century (2071–2100). In the summer season, the study showed that the area is expected to be wetter than the baseline period. Thus, it indicated that the change in the availability of moisture (rainfall amount) is higher than the loss of moisture because of evapotranspiration in the region. The highest seasonal changes in AI during the winter season in Ribb, Gumara, Gilgel Abay, and Megech watersheds are –0.301 (March), –0.299 (March), –0.285 (April), and –0.273 (April), respectively. On the contrary, during the summer season, the highest changes in the watersheds are observed in August except in the Megech watershed which is observed in July, and the values of changes are 0.263, 0.258, 0.238, and 0.211, respectively (Fig. 9  ). The negative and positive values of changes in these different seasons indicated that the aridity is increasing and decreasing, respectively.   4 Discussion The change in rainfall in the Lake Tana sub-basin of the Blue Nile basin does not show a consistent pattern in terms of inter-annual and annual changes. The seasonal fluctuation of the change in rainfall in the region has also been indicated by other similar previous studies (Kim et al., 2008 ) (Elshamy et al., 2009 ) (Takele et al., 2022 ). The increasing rate of change in precipitation in the wet season and decrease in the dry season has directly been causing flooding and drought problems. In general, the change in precipitation could lead to significant and varied shifts in phenology (Huxman et al., 2004 ) (Cleland et al., 2007 ), reservoir management (Chaves et al., 2023 ) (Yasarer & Sturm, 2016 ), and ecosystem services (Parmesan et al., 2022 ). The change in temperature and its impact on the potential evapotranspiration in the upper Blue Nile basin has also been revealed by many other studies including (G. G. Chakilu et al., 2022b ) (Ayele et al., 2016 ) (G. G. Chakilu et al., 2020 ) and (A. T. Haile et al., 2017 ), in which the overall results indicated that the rising of atmospheric temperature could significantly cause the increasing of potential evapotranspiration in 21st century under the high emission scenario. For instance, temperature is expected to rise by 4 °C and the rate of change of rainfall shows a decline of 15 % in the dry season and a rise of 15 % in the wet season under RCP 8.5 over the long-term time windows. Similarly, the study conducted by (Takele et al., 2022 ) showed a temperature rise, and the annual evapotranspiration increased by about 10.4 % in the basin. In the same region, but out of the basin, a comparable trend of rising temperature and the consequent increase of PET is also expected to be observed at the end of this century. For instance, it is projected to increase up to 49.42 % in the Wabe Shebele basin (Gurara et al., 2021 ) and 22.66 % in the Gilgel Gibe basin (Alemayehu et al., 2023 ) under the same emission scenario. As PET increases, more water is evaporated from the soil surface and transpired by vegetation, which can lead to increase water demand from natural ecosystems, agriculture, and human settlements. If the increase in PET exceeds the available water supply, leading to water stress, faster soil moisture depletion and affects plant growth, reduced streamflow, and decreased water availability for irrigation, drinking water, and industrial use (Goyal, 2004 ) (Maracchi et al., 2005 ). Even though the investigated study area does not have an aridity problem on an annual basis, the area is going to be highly vulnerable in the dry season due to the sharp rise in temperature and ET. Because the dimensionless values of the Aridity Indexes were estimated using the ratio of rainfall and PET (UNEP, 1993 ), the increasing change in AI indicated that the water availability of the watersheds is likely to improve in the region; whereas the decrease in AI implied that the availability of water in the catchments is expected to deplete and leading to water stress in the region. Therefore, the result clearly showed that the dryness of the region is likely to increase in the dry season because of the consistent rise in temperature. The headwater catchments of the Upper Blue Nile basin are highly degraded due to the expansion of agriculture and the distraction of forest resources (Chakilu & Moges, 2017 ). Therefore, to minimize the vulnerability of catchments to climate change impacts and, most importantly to minimize the seasonal dryness of the area, it is highly recommended to use different climate change adaptation mechanisms including adopting suitable physical and biological water conservation techniques (Mena, 2018 ) to enhance the amount of water stored in the subsurface and joining the groundwater in the rainy season.  5 Conclusion • This study revealed that the change in climate under the high emission (RCP 8.5) scenario has considerably affected the evapotranspiration nature of watersheds in the headwater catchments of the upper Blue Nile basin and consequently, the aridity is expected to increase, especially in the dry season.  • The inter-annual rate of changes in rainfall showed considerable decreasing and increasing patterns in the dry and wet seasons, respectively, whereas the annual average rate of change is not likely to be significant in all watersheds.  • The projected rise in temperature is going to be directly affecting the water resources of watersheds in a way that escalates the evaporation of moisture from the soil, and transpiration from plants.  • The projected change in PET in the four watersheds is anticipated to increase consistently in both seasonal and annual time scales in all periods with a prominent rise in the 2071–2100 under the ensemble mean of all climate models.  • This study has also evaluated how much the ratio of rainfall and PET, i.e., Aridity Index (AI)) in all catchments is expected to change in the three consecutive periods. Due to the fluctuation of the change in rainfall, the change in AI does not show significant dynamics on an annual average basis, unlike PET. Seasonally, the variability of changes in AI is high between dry and wet seasons. In the dry season, due to an increment in temperature, and decreasing in rainfall, the change in aridity shows a significant increasing pattern, whereas in the wet season, even though there is an increment of PET, an increment of moisture availability because of rainfall is much higher than the loss of moisture by PET, aridity is decreasing.  • Generally, the result indicated that in the dry season, the region is likely to be drier, and in wet seasons it is predicted to be wetter in all watersheds and the three time periods especially in the 2071–2100.  • The overall results of the study give important indications on the potential impacts of climate change on the overall health of ecosystems in the headwater catchments of the upper Blue Nile basin and the consequent effects on natural and human systems due to the declining water availability in the lower catchment communities including in Egypt and Sudan.
