S.S. and T.Z. followed up on the whole work, and K.P. also contributed his role in an edition of the paper.
1 Introduction Water, wastewater, and stormwater systems (WWSSs) are essential infrastructure for public health and the economy. Implementing, operating, and maintaining such systems requires large allocation of resources, particularly during the implementation phase, which requires substantial capital investment. During operation, several on-going challenges are faced by water utilities to maximise WWSS lifetime and efficiency, such as rapid detection and response to system failures, and proactively adapting operations to changes in water availability, demand, and environmental conditions (He et al., 2021; Howard et al., 2016; Mandel et al., 2015 ). These challenges are difficult to be managed because WWSSs cover large areas, with most of their infrastructure being difficult to access for inspection. The increasing demand for water and generation of wastewater, due to population growth combined with a more erratic and reduced availability of water due to climate change, further adds complexities and uncertainties to WWSS management (Dandy et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2020 ), potentially leading to urban water scarcity (Howard et al., 2016 ). Urban water scarcity currently affects one third of the urban population and is expected to affect nearly half of the global urban population by 2050 (He et al., 2021 ). Water scarcity was identified as a priority challenge during the recent COP26, highlighting an urgency for the water sector to establish new business models using digital technologies and information management (Dwivedi et al., 2022; Zarza, 2022 ). However, water utilities often adopt a reactive approach and tend to maintain business as usual, due to a lack of capacity for innovation (Boyle et al., 2022; Kiparsky et al., 2016 ). Advancements in sensor and communication technologies are paving the way for WWSS digitalisation, which is also referred to as smart water, wastewater, and stormwater systems (SWWSSs). SWWSSs comprise both physical and cyber infrastructure. The physical component refers to the deployed hardware (e.g., power supply, sensors, and communication systems) to collect and transfer data, while the cyber component includes the software (e.g., data platforms, cybersecurity barriers, and numerical and statistical models) used to securely manage and support data-informed decision-making. Several devices, including accelerometers, ultrasonic, acoustic, optical fibre, piezoelectric, and fluorescence sensors enable real-time monitoring of pressure, water level, flow, material condition, and various water quality parameters (Bharani Baanu and Jinesh Babu, 2021; Boyle et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2021; Ibrahim et al., 2021; Jena and Gupta, 2021; Tariq et al., 2021 ). Digital solutions, including machine learning and numerical models, use the abundance of data from the newer generation of monitoring devices to develop decision-support tools for a number of challenges faced by water utilities, such as water consumption metering and billing (Rahim et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021 ), rapid and proactive detection of leaks and blockages in water distribution and sewerage networks (Abdulshaheed et al., 2017; Fan et al., 2022; Rosin et al., 2022; Tscheikner-Gratl et al., 2020 ), adaptation of operations to cope with changes in water quality and demand (Bertone et al., 2023; Gurung et al., 2016; Kara et al., 2016 ), and integrated management of water resources and assets (Yuan et al., 2019 ). Apart from the detection of traditional water quality variables such as nutrient loads (Alkandari et al., 2012 ) or contamination (Saab et al., 2018 ), near real-time detection of chemical substances in wastewater has helped to identify and locate the types of illicit drugs used in different areas of cities (Bade et al., 2018 ), which can be used to inform drug control (Li et al., 2019 ). It is argued, thus, that SWWSS can optimise water utility operations and foster an internal cultural change from reactive to proactive (Boyle et al., 2022 ), requiring collaborations between government institutions, research centres, and the private sector (Mounce, 2020; Rousso et al., 2023 ). A robust research effort is currently being made to advance the understanding and technology used to monitor and manage SWWSSs. While a vast literature on this topic exists, most publications are not interdisciplinary and have a narrow, specialist focus. This decreases the value of the research to practitioners and water managers, who are often overwhelmed with the increasing number of “revolutionary smart technologies” that lack proper field validation or clear cost-benefit analysis (Beal and Flynn, 2015; Gupta et al., 2020; Kulkarni and Farnham, 2016 ). A recent survey involving 64 water utilities from 28 countries revealed that digital technology adoption by water utilities is primarily driven by economic benefits, followed by government regulation and hydroclimatic factors (Daniel et al., 2023 ). Limited communication between practitioners and researchers hinders the development of a targeted research agenda comprising the most pressing demands to implement and operate SWWSSs. An industry-led report, after interviewing over 50 water utilities executives globally, also identified that interdisciplinary efforts, including research, are needed to accelerate digital technology adoption by the public and private water sector (Sarni et al., 2019 ). Frameworks have recently been proposed to foster digital technologies adoption in the water sector through leadership, regulations, and policies (e.g., Grievson et al., 2022; WSAA, 2022 ). However, the implementation and operation of SWWSSs, both at technical and organisational level, is still a major challenge worldwide. The challenges associated with digital transformation in the water sector can vary across regions globally and depend on factors such as utility size and ownership, requiring a case-by-case analysis (Rousso et al., 2023 ). For instance, public water utilities in low- and middle-income countries are likely to face additional challenges compared to those in high-income countries (Amankwaa et al., 2024 ). Nevertheless, successful case studies illustrating the implementation of digital transformations at the utility level can serve as benchmarks for researchers and practitioners seeking to accelerate digital transformation within their respective contexts. In this context, this paper aims to bridge the gaps between research and practitioners interested in using digital technologies to better manage WWSS by establishing a framework illustrated by real-world case studies in the Australian context. This paper is part of the special issue Current state and future directions in addressing hydrological grand challenges: an Australian perspective.  The paper starts with an overview of SWWSS in Australia, a country leading academia-industry joint research and implementation of SWWSS to face unprecedent droughts and flooding events. Then, the framework, including a continuous improvement process and a targeted research agenda, is presented. Subsequently, a detailed showcase of four selected case studies is made to illustrate key aspects of the proposed framework. Lastly, a critical discussion is provided, encompassing key challenges, opportunities, drivers, and future directions related to SWWSS.  2 Overview of smart water and wastewater systems in Australia Australia, renowned by its predominantly arid landscape and concentrated population along its coastline, is particularly susceptible to the adverse impacts of climate change (Jones and Pittock, 2002 ). Climate change has the potential to exacerbate the effects of various climate-driven hazards that have historically afflicted Australia. Prolonged droughts, exemplified by the Millennium Drought (Van Dijk et al., 2013 ), intense wet weather events, leading to recurrent floods along the East and South Coast (Simonovic et al., 2021 ), and extended dry periods, leading to bushfires (notably the 2019–20 Australian bushfire crisis) (Kemter et al., 2021 ), have collectively reduced both the quantity and quality of water resources in Australia over recent decades (Hughes, 2003; Head et al., 2013 ). Confronting these diverse climate hazards, amidst the natural water scarcity in Australia, has compelled water utilities to explore and implement innovative strategies to ensure the continuity of water services (Rousso et al., 2023 ). In doing so, Australian water utilities have emerged as pioneers in the adoption of digital solutions to enhance the management of WWSS, thus assuming a leadership role on the global stage (Weinstein Bloome and de Guzman, 2017 ). Australian water utilities are early adopters of customer digital water metering and many successful trials have been reported, both in metropolitan and regional areas, including from independent industry reports (Turner et al., 2010 ), water utility reports (SA Water, 2018, 2020; Sydney Water, 2020; TasWater, 2015 ), industry conferences (Collins et al., 2016; Nitschke and Clutterbuck, 2022; Roberts et al., 2019 ), and technology providers such as Taggle and Intron. Digital metering can add value to water business models by increasing customer satisfaction due to improved access and control of individual consumer water information (Boyle et al., 2013; Monks et al., 2019 ). In addition, digital water metering enables rapid detection of abnormal water consumption (Rahim et al., 2020; Stewart et al., 2018 ), and discretisation of water end uses to some extent (Mazzoni et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2018 ), which can contribute to water sustainability both by waste reduction and behaviour change (Anda et al., 2013; Monks et al., 2021 ). For example, a case study documents the 38-storey Miramar residential complex in Sydney’s central business district (CBD), which has many of its 500-odd apartments unoccupied for long periods (SBS News, 2019 ). The building manager required a means of equitable billing that provides an economic benefit to frugal tenants. Both cold and hot water services for each apartment were digitally metered with hourly frequencies. This enabled the building manager to identify water uses to each apartment and to act rapidly in case of any detected water leaks within the household, which resulted in a reduction in daily usage from 400 to 100 kilolitres (SBS News, 2019 ). Leaks in water distribution pipelines, often exceeding 50 % of the total water supplied, serve as the primary source of non-revenue water for water utilities (Gupta and Kulat, 2018; Lee and Schwab, 2005 ), besides constituting an environmental burden. Traditional methods for leak detection in water distribution networks are reactive and often slow to detect incidents (Al-washali et al., 2016 ). Rapid detection and repair of leaks using the newer generation of monitoring devices not only reduces water losses, resulting in positive economic and environmental impacts, but also decreases health risk due to potential contaminant infiltration in distribution pipelines (Fontanazza et al., 2015 ). Novel methods for leakage detection through continuous in-network monitoring using high-frequency sensors have been developed in Australia, using either pressure or acoustic sensors (Gong et al., 2021; Simpson et al., 2021; Stephens et al., 2022a, Stephens et al., 2022b ). There are several methods to detect leaks, varying in data requirements (e.g., pressure, and/or acoustic data) (Gong et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2020 ) and capabilities (e.g., leak type, stage, and localisation precision) (Rousso et al., 2023 ). Pressure-based leak detection lacks precision in pinpointing leakage location or in detecting leakages in early stages (i.e., developing cracks or corrosion). However, collecting continuous pressure data from water distribution networks using these techniques enables other applications, such as water demand modelling (Niknam et al., 2022 ) and optimisation of operations (Mala-Jetmarova et al., 2017 ). Pioneering methods for precise and early detection of leaks using acoustic data have been developed and validated in Australia and are operational in the Adelaide CBD water network (Gong et al., 2020; Stephens et al., 2018; Stephens et al., 2020a; Stephens et al., 2022c; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The ability to detect early cracks in pipelines allows not only leak detection but proactive pipeline repair, reducing water loss, water supply interruption time, and customer disruption. These potential significant economic benefits have motivated other Australian water utilities to expand the collection of acoustic data within their distribution networks, with a recent major rollout occurring in several Sydney suburbs (Bykerk and Miro, 2022; Nikoloska et al., 2020 ). It is worth highlighting that the early detection of pipe breaks and water leakages in water distribution networks is a subject of extensive research globally and not limited to Australia. A notable initiative in this area is the BattLeDIM (Vrachimis et al., 2022 ), which aims to foster the development of optimised methods for detecting and localizing leakage events through the utilization of flow and pressure sensors. This initiative resulted in top-ranked algorithms that leverage both numerical (e.g., Steffelbauer et al., 2022 ) and statistical (e.g., Daniel et al., 2022 ) models. Managing sewage systems is another substantial challenge faced by water utilities. While sewerage systems are designed to safely convey raw wastewater to treatment facilities, they often have decreased capacity due to blockages (e.g., accumulation of sediments or other non-degradable materials) or pipeline defects (e.g., joint failure), potentially resulting in overflows, environment pollution, public health hazards, and economic losses (e.g., fines, tourism loss) (De Silva et al., 2011 ). The prevalent management strategy among water utilities is either reactive, i.e., operate sewers until they block and then determine a course of action (De Silva et al., 2011; Tscheikner-Gratl et al., 2020 ), or preventative, i.e., regular schedule of maintenance activities to clean and inspect selected regions of the sewer system. Innovative solutions based on artificial intelligence have been proposed and trialled in Australia aiming to proactively manage sewers. These solutions include automated image assessment of closed-circuit television images of sewer pipes (Gokal et al., 2020; Stephens et al., 2020b ), early detection of choke events using ultrasonic water level sensors in manholes (Do et al., 2023 ); detection of pipe defects through acoustic signal analysis (Romanova et al., 2013 ); and, risk-based analysis of choke occurrence based on historical datasets (Cameron et al., 2017; Khadka et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ). Facing severe urban water scarcity (e.g., Millennium Drought) fostered Australian water utilities’ investment in using non-conventional water sources, such as recycled water and rainfall, making Australia a reference for other locations also under water stress (e.g., California, United States; Weinstein Bloome and de Guzman, 2017 ). The Water Smart program (2004–2012) was a major funding initiative in Australia, with a total funding of $1.48 billion and overall costs amounting to $4.96 billion (GHD, 2012 ). This program incentivised the development and adoption of smart technologies and practices, with 48 % of the investment directed toward water recycling projects (Radcliffe, 2015; Radcliffe and Page, 2020 ). By the end of the Millennium Drought, the greater Melbourne area was reusing 23 % of sewage inflows, mainly for agricultural purposes (Low et al., 2015 ). However, with the end of the Millennium Drought, recycled water uses in agriculture quickly declined due to higher availability of freshwater sourced water and uncertainties regarding recycled water impact in crops and soils (Barker et al., 2011 ). In contrast, the use of recycled water in urban settings (e.g., toilet flushing and outdoor uses) continued to increase after the Millennium Drought (Low et al., 2015 ). Rainwater tanks storing rainwater collected from household roofs were also strongly adopted in Australia during the Millennium Drought, with an increase from 16.7 % to 29.6 % (Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2007 ). The adoption was largely facilitated by government rebates (Australian National Water Commission and Marsden Jacob Associates, 2007 ). One of the key limitations for the success of rainwater tanks is their intrinsic decentralised nature, which complicates management and operation (e.g., Rousso et al., 2024 ). The development of automated systems, integrating weather forecasting, rainwater tank monitoring and water quality control, already implemented in Australia (Cooperative Research Centre for Water Sensitive Cities, 2017; Mishra et al., 2020 ) are promising alternatives to use rainwater as a reliable source of water besides mitigating peak flows in stormwater systems (Taji et al., 2021 ). The challenges of water scarcity, likely to be further exacerbated by climate change, have significantly impacted Australia's water resources, prompting water utilities to develop innovative strategies to ensure continuity of services. The adoption of digital solutions has emerged as crucial for enhanced management of water systems. Insights from the digitalisation efforts of Australian water utilities can inform the adoption of essential practices when pursuing digital transformation to improve business models, foster water sustainability, and promote environmental conservation.  3 Digital water utility transformation strategy and associated research opportunities Drawing from insights gained from documented experiences of Australian water utilities in implementing digital technologies, essential steps have been identified for ensuring the success and sustainability of such initiatives. First, it is essential to acknowledge that integrating digital technologies into water utilities' operations is an ongoing process, requiring targeted actions across five interconnected steps (Fig. 1  ). Additionally, for each step, priority areas of research were identified (Fig. 2  ). The five steps illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2  are elaborated as follows:• Step 1: The identification of which practices should be prioritised is the first step for a water utility digital transformation (Fig. 1 , step 1). This prioritisation must take into consideration the circumstances of the water utility operations and which areas lack internal understanding and control, being thus a water utility specific process (Kulkarni and Farnham, 2016 ). The decision of which area to “smarten up” must also consider the water utility current capacity (e.g., skilled personnel, budget allocation), in-place institutional processes (e.g., operating standards), existing government policies (e.g., incentives and penalties), and stakeholders’ interests (e.g., community acceptance of a specific solution) (Wu et al., 2016 ). The lack of common operating standards across water utilities is a barrier for transferring practices between organisations (Zhu et al., 2018 ). Generalisable tools supporting the mapping of a water utility status, capacity and needs, as well as indicators to rank priority areas to invest on considering cost-benefit uncertainties would facilitate wide water utilities digital transformation and should be the focus of future research (Fig. 2 ).  • Step 2: Once a specific area is defined as priority, it is crucial for the water utility to appropriately select and deploy devices able to collect the data required to develop and maintain decision-support tools (Fig. 1 , step 2). Despite the considerable number of devices already available at commercial level, water utilities are still unsure of their cost-benefit and maintenance requirements (Beal and Flynn, 2015; Daniel et al., 2023; IWN, 2022; Kiparsky et al., 2016 ). Besides the high cost to acquire such devices, maintaining them in the field require skills not usually present in water utilities. Reliability issues in communication services and battery life regarding sensors operation (e.g., sampling frequency) are barriers for deployment and operation of such devices. The development of more cost-effective and robust devices (e.g., more energy efficient, resistant to harsh conditions such as in sewers) should be the focus of future research (Fig. 2 ). At the same time, given the limited number of devices able to be maintained by a water utility, research on optimal sensor placement can significantly enable water utilities to develop and maintain decision-support tools using a reduced number of devices, topic that has been receiving increased attention by researchers (e.g., Adedoja et al., 2018; Romano, 2021 ).  • Step 3: The transition to the digital era where data is abundant requires business adaptation and incorporation of new skills into the workforce. The water sector is currently facing this transition and data management systems must cope with big data from multiple sources (e.g., high-frequency sensors, satellite imagery, field campaigns) comprising both qualitative (e.g., customer feedback) and quantitative (e.g., nutrient concentration, pressure) data. Integrating such data into existing systems is another challenge currently faced by water utilities, and a critical step in the digital transformation process (Fig. 1 , step 3). Importantly, integrated data platforms must consider final users (i.e., operators, customers) needs, meaning that the development of data platforms should be participatory to ensure their efficacy. While abundant data enables the development of advanced decision support systems, it also increases the risk of sensitive data leaks and terrorist attacks (Hassanzadeh et al., 2020; Tuptuk et al., 2021 ), both identified as crucial concerns by stakeholders in the water sector (Shapira et al., 2021 ). Therefore, it is essential that updated cybersecurity systems are in place and that cybersecurity awareness and training are perpetuated in water utilities (Bello et al., 2022; Hassanzadeh et al., 2020 ). Concerns regarding ownership and privacy of consumer water consumption data have also been highlighted in the context of water digital systems (Zipper et al., 2019 ). Preliminary efforts to address this challenge have been proposed; however, they lack comprehensive economic analysis and feasibility assessment for real-life implementation (Salomons et al., 2020 ).  • Step 4: Transforming data into valuable information for water management is the evident goal of implementing SWWSSs (Fig. 1 , step 4). However, water utilities often struggle to make this transformation due to the lack of internal capacity and are left with stranded data (Mounce, 2020 ). Traditionally, investments in assets are prioritised and easier to be justified than investments in resources to maintain and intelligently use data. Collaborations with research centres can provide discipline expertise to add value to the collected data when the water utility lacks internal capacity to develop customised decision-support tools. While several applications have been developed for various water management challenges, most applications lack generality (i.e., are site-specific) and have assumptions that oversimplify field conditions, limiting their practicality (Rousso et al., 2023 ). The lack of standardisation while reporting results from decision support tools (e.g., site characterisation, economic and savings, costs, uncertainties) is another barrier for transferring good practices among water utilities (Rousso et al., 2023 ). Applications also typically focus on answering a specific demand (e.g., leak location, chemical dosage in water treatment plant, water demand prediction) and lack integration among the multiple aspects of water management. Tools to support dynamic operation of water assets to save both energy and water, and solutions that increase the value of deployed monitoring devices are research areas of particular interest because they would result in short-term economic savings and act as direct enablers and accelerators for water utilities’ digital transformation (Fig. 2 ).  • Step 5: Besides responding to specific operational demands (e.g., early detection of water distribution mains failure, optimisation of pump operation), data-informed decision-support systems can support water utility’s strategic planning and operations. For that to be fully realised, the structure and roles within water utilities should be re-engineered considering not only the insights that can be derived from SWWSs but also the requirements and challenges to maintain and operate them (Fig. 1 , step 5). For example, quantifying distinct water demands throughout the day by various consumers can provide insights that could inform tariff systems akin to those employed in the energy sector, taking into consideration the costs associated with digital metering (such as operation, repair, and expansion), ultimately resulting in an integrated, data-informed pricing framework. Additionally, integrated digital solutions can facilitate urban planning and operations of city-level systems. This integration ultimately requires that all water utility stakeholders (i.e., from operational to executive board) are familiarised and trust the digital technologies in place, which is another endeavour by itself (e.g., Kosovac, 2016 ). In this sense, training using digital solutions (e.g., augmented reality, Muthalif et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023 ; serious gaming, Predescu et al., 2021 ) can foster a culture shift within the water utility, as seen in other industries (e.g., Paiola et al., 2021 ).    While all aspects of the framework are pertinent and merit consideration during the transition to digital technologies, their significance may vary based on the context of each water utility. Acknowledging this limitation, is it still argued that sharing insights from entities with similar objectives and structures can be of value for accelerating the digital transformation of water utilities.  4 Australian case studies on selected applications This section offers an in-depth examination of four Australian case studies that demonstrate the successful implementation of digital solutions in water utility operations. It is important to highlight that the implementation of digital technologies in water utilities is a multifaceted process that requires interdisciplinary expertise and resources. The need and requirements can vary depending on the specific application of the decision-support system and the water utility context. Therefore, a case-by-case analysis is required. The case studies were selected to cover different aspects of water utilities operations, including water supply and metering, and sewerage and stormwater management. They also serve as examples to highlight key framework steps that enabled their successful implementation and operation. The case studies include 1) a mixed-method approach to identify, quantify and model digital metering and smart water savings for several water utilities (Australia wide and international), 2) the development of an early warning system for pipe breaks in water distribution networks (Adelaide, Australia), 3) the development of a spill early warning system for sewerage systems (Adelaide, Australia), and 4) a case study demonstrating a smart integrated water management and reuse system (Melbourne, Australia). 4.1 Digital meters and smart water savings Smart metering has been one of the early digital solutions adopted by water utilities. Despite numerous trials in Australia, there is no consensus among researchers and practitioners regarding the expected benefits and challenges associated with implementing digital water metering. This case study developed a framework to identify the anticipated benefits, challenges, and technical and organisational requirements that each water utility is likely to encounter when implementing smart metering. Such an understanding is essential for the development of business cases and the consolidation of this practice. A participatory and qualitative approach, encompassing a literature review and interviews of 52 industry experts set out to catalogue the benefits of digital water metering (Monks et al., 2019 ). Besides identifying various aspects in which either the water utility or customers could be benefited from the use of digital water meters, the qualitative approach supports longed for methodologies to quantify the cost-benefit of implementing such devices. The taxonomy revealed 57 benefits for the water utility and 40 for the customer, with 22 benefits being advantageous for both parties. The need for organisational changes to achieve the benefits was recognised in eight broad areas of change: 1) automate meter reading using advanced meter infrastructure; 2) improve demand and revenue forecasting through advanced data analytics; 3) establish leak alerting; 4) establish a detailed customer data portal for single and complex properties; 5) offer monthly billing; 6) establish detailed water balancing of permanent and temporary DMAs; 7) establish a capability for meter/metering/end‐use data analytics; and, 8) increase knowledge of customers and assets. Based on the identified benefits taxonomy, a method for quantifying the water utility’s benefits was developed (Monks et al., 2020a ). Business benefits were classified as either water savings, or charges and operational costs. The potential savings between these two groups were distinctly different, allowing the generation of individual risk-based outcomes, which could then be aggregated from each benefit. Because the success of digital metering also depends on user acceptance, customers were surveyed. A series of hypothetical scenarios related to each of the customer benefits were put to 178 customers from Australian water utilities and their responses scored on a 0 to 10 scale (Monks et al., 2020b ). Compared to the baseline scenario established within the survey, it was identified that digital metering practices resulted in a considerable uplift in customers’ sentiment (Monks et al., 2020b ). These findings were incorporated into a modelling tool, the Digital Water Metering 360 (DWM360) (Monks et al., 2020c ). DWM360 facilitates the customization of scenario simulations, enabling users to adjust the inclusion and extent of benefits and enabling changes. This allows for tailored assessments of their impact on organizational performance and customer satisfaction, which can be aligned with the water utility specific circumstances, or level of confidence in the expected savings. The model was implemented for an undisclosed Australian water utility, and the benefits were analysed considering the three sustainability pillars perspectives: environmental, economic development and social equity (Monks et al., 2020c ). The simulations results revealed an additional 13 % savings for a single year and an average annual savings of 7 % over the 25-year simulated period when considering the rollout duration and customer growth projections.  4.2 Pipe break early warning system for water distribution networks Minimising service interruptions is critical for water utilities to maintain public trust and water supply effectiveness. This case study presents an innovative early warning system for pipe leaks and breaks using digital solutions. South Australian Water Corporation (SA Water) is responsible for providing water and wastewater services to over 1.6 million Australians, including the capital city of Adelaide in South Australia. In 2017, SA Water launched a smart acoustic water network project to improve the management and response to water main leaks and breaks across a 125 km water piping network in the Adelaide CBD. As of June 2019, the network has enabled SA Water to proactively detect approximately half of all water main breaks, leading to a significant reduction in water loss, water service interruptions, and commuter delays (SA Water, 2019 ). The Adelaide’s smart acoustic water network consists of 305 permanent acoustic accelerometer loggers, installed mostly on cast iron pipes of 80–250 mm in diameter and at the regions with higher risk of asset failures and economic loss (Stephens et al., 2020a ). The acoustic loggers record single daily noise levels at 5-minute intervals during the early morning hours when environmental noise is minimal, and at 30-minute intervals at other times of the day. In addition, a 10-second acoustic wave file is recorded at 2:05 am by each logger. Data is then transmitted and stored daily in a cloud server, following sharing between vendors and SA Water, mostly for data visualization and generic reporting. To enhance the value of this daily acoustic data, SA Water partnered with researchers from The University of Adelaide to address a capacity gap within their organisation. The first studies in Adelaide’s smart acoustic water network found that the cross-correlation method, a common leak localisation technique, only worked within a considerable limited range (Zhang et al. 2022 ). This was either because of lacking direct hydraulic connectivity or plastic (PVC160 or HDPE) pipe segments and numerous junctions that reduced the acoustic transmission. Following studies, therefore, focused on analysing signals from individual sensors for leak or break detections while considering their surrounding environment. Regarding the magnitude of noise, Zhang et al. (2020)  developed a method for detecting an abrupt change in the minimum daily noise. By combining three statistical tools, the Kalman filter, cumulative sum, and median interquartile range analysis, the joint-method was able to accurately identify pipe cracks or bursts. Several subsequential collaborative studies were carried out to develop advanced algorithms for proactive leak detection using time–frequency features of acoustic signals. Zhang et al. (2022)  developed a SVM using 12 different acoustic features from both time and frequency domains to classify the noise as either a leak or a non-leak. Zhang et al. (2023)  proposed a CNN algorithm to distinguish signals as either actual leaks, background (e.g., electrical noise, flow inducing noise), intermittent (e.g., traffic, water meter noise) or persistent (e.g., building pump, air conditions) signals (Fig. 3  ). Expanding on this, Stephens et al. (2022c)  utilized a rate-of-change statistical method to distinguish incipient and evolving circumferential and longitudinal cracks based om change in acoustic energy across frequency bands over weekly and monthly periods.  4.3 Spill early warning system for sewerage systems Eliminating or minimising wastewater overflows is a key challenge for sewerage management. Overflows can occur at any point within the sewers network due to obstructions such as tree roots, fat, oil, and grease build-up or foreign objects. Depending on the severity of the blockage, the hydraulic capacity of the gravity main may be hindered to a point where it cannot handle the hydraulic discharge, leading to sewage overflow to the environment. Proactively identifying and removing these obstructions can be costly for water utilities, and there are potential additional penalties associated with environmental hazards, public health, social, and economic impacts. In 2017, SA Water initiated the Smart Sewer project, conducting trials in a smaller reticulation network (Stonyfell sewer catchment) in South Australia. The project aimed to implement widespread monitoring for early detection of choke events, facilitating proactive maintenance scheduling, and preventing overflows. A total of 82 Pulsar dBi6 ultrasonic level sensors were installed in manholes, covering around 48 % of the entire Stonyfell network. These sensors were linked to communications modules, transmitting data wirelessly. The sensors measure water depth at 5-minute intervals, automatically transmitting the data to an analytics platform and to an alarm dashboard (Dix et al., 2021 ). The system then connects with operational processes to carry out necessary interventions. Several research studies were undertaken to evaluate the effectiveness and to improve the performance of the smart sewer project, including 1) optimizing sensor types and placement locations, considering basic switch sensors for cost-effectiveness or more precise but more expensive ultrasonic sensors) and their placement locations (unpublished data), 2) analysing changes in flow and depth patterns relevant to wastewater main chokes and overflows (Stephens et al., 2020b ), and 3) developing techniques for proactive choke detections (Do et al., 2023 ). Stephens et al. (2020b)  developed an ANN model with input depth measurements aggregated at 10-minute intervals, over seven days a week, to enable the prediction of the normal (no choke) depth at future time intervals on any day. These trained patterns are then used with a wastewater hydraulic model, and a virtual modelling approach to reduce measurement sensor densities. Do et al. (2023)  analysed the wastewater level in sewer manholes to discern and characterise hydraulic patterns before, during, and after sewer blockages. Growing blockage was linked to wastewater recurring holding-releasing processes, with distinctive hydraulic features. Based on these features, a continuous data scanning methodology to find time periods containing irregularly high-water levels for early detection of choke events was developed (as exemplified in Fig. 4  ), enabling time-sensitive management of sewer overflows.  4.4 Smart rainfall water reuse and flooding mitigation Like numerous major cities worldwide, the city of Melbourne, in Australia, is vulnerable to major water resource shortages (Cran et al., 2022 ), anticipated to occurs as early as 2028 due to climate change intensification (Melbourne Water, 2017 ). South East Water, a utility servicing water, sewerage, and recycled water in Melbourne's southeast region, has created and operationalised a smart system for rainwater reuse and flood control, known as the Aquarevo system. The system allows rainwater reuse for hot water services, decentralised alternative water treatment, and pre-emptive rainwater tank storage management. This initiative was tested in a residential development situated in Lyndhurst, Melbourne. The Aquarevo system includes two key sub-systems: the rainwater-to-hot water supply system, and a prediction and automated management system of the stored rainwater. 4.4.1 Rainwater-to-hot water supply system The rainwater-to-hot water supply system aims to reduce mains drinking water consumption, typically supplied for household hot water services. Following a review of treatment technologies for rainwater and stormwater reuse (Feng et al., 2022 ), the designed system comprised a rainwater roof collection system (gutter guard, first flush water diverter, downpipe), a 2000L rainwater storage tank, a 5 μm polyester spun cartridge filter, a ultraviolet (UV) disinfection unit, and a heat pump hot water system (Fig. 5  ). The system's treatment performance was validated through a systematic and challenging laboratory test, including a quantitative microbial risk assessment to establish the optimal water quality ranges for field operating conditions This assessment determined parameters such as required influent water turbidity, UV dosage, thermal treatment temperature set points, and contact time (Schang et al., 2021 ). Combined with other water saving measures, it is expected a reduction of 70 % of mains drinking water use for each residential property at Aquarevo (South East Water, n.d ). The processes within the rainwater-to-hot water supply system are automated using a sophisticated controller, allowing for remote monitoring and control. The initial 20L of rainwater received is directed to the stormwater drain to flush out small contaminants like leaves and dust, preventing them from entering the rainwater tank. Subsequently, the collected rainwater is diverted into the tank. When any hot water tap is turned on, rainwater is pumped from the tank to the hydraulic changeover device using a submersible pump. This device determines whether the household's hot water service will be supplied by mains drinking water or rainwater based on the water level sensor reading within the rainwater tank. The rainwater-to-hot water supply system also regulates the water quality of the rainwater. Rainwater treatment starts with a cartridge filter to eliminate small contaminants. Subsequently, it undergoes UV disinfection and a thermal process, ensuring compliance with the water quality standards for hot water services. To ensure effective UV disinfection, the system incorporates various alarms, such as for UV intensity, UV power loss, and UV lamp failure, which are established and monitored through the same controller for rainwater pumping. For the thermal treatment process, multiple temperature sensors are also installed to control the water treatment and supply to end uses in real-time, adjusting the treatment temperature and duration as needed. The controller plays a crucial role in automating the management of health risks associated with rainwater reuse, featuring 16 alarms and 2 alerts. For instance, if the system fails to meet treatment requirements (e.g., lower UV intensity, reduced thermal treatment temperature), an alarm is triggered, switching supply to the backup drinking water mains.  4.4.2 Prediction of stored rainwater and automated management With rapid urbanisation, large areas of natural ground are replaced with impervious surfaces, leading to urban flooding risks (Meng et al., 2022 ). Rainwater tanks can act as buffer systems, storing excessive runoff and mitigating sudden increases of water inflow into the stormwater network and waterways, which results in environmental, water quality, and safety benefits. However, rainwater tanks cannot function properly as flooding buffer systems if there is no advanced control of the rainwater tank water volume (i.e., if the rainwater tank overflows during heavy rainfall events, it does not mitigate the peak flow). The project has developed patented technology that proactively discharges rainwater from the rainwater tank under certain conditions, reducing rainwater tank overflow and flooding risks. The communication system monitors different parameters of the system in real-time, providing near real-time monitoring over storage volume, besides flexible remote control via mobile application (Fig. 6  ). Combined with weather prediction (e.g., upcoming rainfall event) and other system characteristics (e.g., rainwater tank location, roof catchment surface area, tank size), the system calculates the required storage volume for the incoming rainfall event. Depending on the existing water volume in the rainwater tank, the system can proactively release water from the rainwater tank prior to the rainfall event, creating a buffer for the peak flow and decreasing flooding risk. If the rainwater is discharged into the waterways directly, a variable valve and a stream flow algorithm are used to ensure minimum impacts on the waterways. The successful implementation in Lyndhurst (VIC, Australia) can serve as a benchmark to the system’s expansion to other locations.   4.5 Implications and key elements of success of the selected case studies Each case study covers different aspects of operations from water utilities. Their success was achieved through innovation and integration with each water utility context, providing benefits for the water utility, customers, and the environment. Each application also had challenges to be overcome and identified future research needs, summarised in Table 1  . The advantages of automated water metering infrastructure extend beyond mere cost savings from manual data collection and misreads, encompassing water conservation through early leak detection and consumers’ behaviour change. Its successful implementation hinges on understanding a water utility’s unique context. The benefits have been shown to permeate throughout the business. Modelling of the uplift in customer satisfaction has confirmed results of an earlier unpublished multi-year report. While digital metering benefits have been well-documented, realizing them necessitates adapting existing processes to accommodate the large influx of data, and leveraging it to achieve operational efficiencies, enhance customer service, and refine planning strategies. Many benefits rely on employing artificial intelligence methods, to analyse meter readings and other pertinent data. Both realms of digital metering and artificial intelligence methods have reached a level of maturity and are increasingly being applied in the water sector, being now considered integral tools for progressive companies (Cominola et al., 2020 ). However, building compelling business cases for digital metering adoption remains a significant challenge for many water utilities. Uncertainties regarding device management support, integration with existing processes, consumer engagement, privacy concerns, and achieving positive economic returns contribute to this challenge. Research efforts should prioritise the development of generalisable tools for assessing a water utility's status, capacity, and needs, alongside establishing indicators to prioritize investment areas considering cost-benefit uncertainties. Addressing these aspects would facilitate widespread digital transformation among water utilities and should be the focal point of future research on the topic. The case study on the pipe breaks early warning system for water distribution networks addressed limitations in sensor technology by employing smart data techniques, such as utilizing dual sensors and filtering techniques to mitigate air-borne noise, thereby enhancing accuracy in leak detection, and enabling the classification between different types of leaks and pipe breaks (Zeng et al., 2022 ). Given the significant investment in the smart sensing system, utilising historical data to pinpoint high-probability failure areas was essential for efficient logger deployment. Ensuring consistent sensors’ communication and data transmission were also important challenges. Critical considerations include recording data during periods of minimal environmental noise to minimize false alarms and establishing structured data platforms for easy access to clean, organized, and interpretable data. The success of the presented case study hinges on the ability of the water utility to prioritise, invest (in both infrastructure and internal capacity), and support the development of tailored decision-support tools. The concept of a “smart network” presents a pioneering endeavour in water utilities, opening new research avenues. Despite the increasing availability of big data, applying data-driven and machine learning approaches to practice presents hurdles, such as scaling AI-based solutions to diverse water distribution networks and integrating them with existing and often unique infrastructure (e.g., in-house IT systems). Seamless real-time data processing is crucial for integration of systems into operations and decision-making, and water utility’s in-house capacity is essential to ensure that. The case study on spill early warning system for sewerage systems exemplified the potential benefits and challenges of using the internet of things technology to wastewater. Though the research indicated the effectiveness and value of the system, its practical implementation and operation faces challenges, as it is difficult to justify its cost-benefit at technology’s current state. The capital and maintenance costs of the internet of things technology are relatively high compared to both reactive approaches, such as cleaning on-demand based on incidents reported by customers, or experience-guided preventative approaches, such as a regular clean-up schedule. Therefore, the deployment of smart sewer systems should be strategically targeted at critical areas where overspills could have severe consequences and investment is justified. Moreover, there is a mismatch between the extensive data collected by sensors and the level of sophistication in the current analytical approaches, creating the need for more advanced statistical and hydraulic techniques to fully exploit these datasets (Gong et al., 2024 ). Engaging in partnerships with research institutions, as done in this case study and essential for its success, can offer specialized expertise, enhancing the value of the data collected, particularly when water utilities lack the internal resources to develop bespoke decision-support tools. The smart rainfall water reuse case study showcases a large-scale implementation of innovative technologies supporting integrated water management, including alternative water sourcing and localized flood control, requiring significant resources, cross-organizational coordination, and adaptive planning. Strategic inclusion of alternative water sources in future water supply scenario planning, early engagement with policymakers and regulators, community consultation, and thorough risk assessment were essential components for the consolidation of the project. Providing comprehensive training and support to operators and early adopters has been shown crucial for the ongoing success of the system. The resulting patented technology, despite relying on rainfall which deviates from traditional practices of most water utilities, gained acceptance from the water utility board, regulators, and the community, serving as a benchmark for future expansions. While smart water management utilising rainfall remains relatively novel and faces challenges such as social acceptance, and high capital investment and maintenance requirements, further research should prioritise addressing these uncertainties and specifying scenarios in which this technology is suitable. Given the pioneering nature of the smart rainfall water reuse system, engaging policymakers, regulators, local communities, and other stakeholders is vital to understanding their needs and ensuring its successful adoption and implementation.   5 Challenges, barriers, drivers, and enablers for water utility digital transformation The digital transformation of water utilities is an irreversible journey that nearly all, if not every, water utility will need to face. As depicted in Fig. 1 , the digital transformation is a continuous process that takes time and effort to be sustained, as observed in many other industries (Bughin et al., 2017 ). Drawing from the wealth of Australian published case studies, key challenges, barriers, drivers, and enablers have been identified. It is important to acknowledge the limitations and risks of drawing conclusions relying solely on reported case studies, particularly those primarily funded by the industry. Such reliance may introduce potential biases, including selection bias (resulting in limited representativeness of reality), confirmation bias (reinforcing preconceived notions), reporting bias (underreporting of unsuccessful trials and projects), and response bias (participants' perceptions influenced by social norms), potentially leading to discrepant conclusions and unexpected real-world outcomes. Additionally, imbalances in funding for technology assessment and development compared to risk assessment can introduce bias. The quality of evidence is also a limitation, as the lack of abundant and standardized data, such as controlled randomized trials, hampers the execution of quantitative reviews and meta -analyses, which are widely regarded as the gold standard for quality of evidence (e.g., PRISMA, Liberati et al., 2020 ). Pursuing the digital transformation in water utilities incurs in a multitude of challenges, encompassing cybersecurity concerns, sustainability considerations, and the need for generalisable and adaptable applications. Cybersecurity emerges as a paramount challenge, given the vulnerability of digital systems to cyber threats and attacks, requiring robust measures to safeguard sensitive data and infrastructure (Bello et al., 2022; Hassanzadeh et al., 2020 ). Moreover, ensuring the economic and operational sustainability of digital systems poses a significant challenge, as water utilities must navigate the complexities of financing, maintenance, and long-term viability (Beal and Flynn, 2015; Daniel et al., 2023 ). Sustainability considerations extend beyond economic aspects to encompass environmental and social dimensions, requiring strategies to minimize resource consumption, mitigate environmental impacts, and ensure equitable access to water services (Dwivedi et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, addressing the cultural shift and evolving business models within water utilities presents a considerable challenge, as stakeholders must adapt to new technologies, workflows, and decision-making processes to realize the full benefits of digital transformation (Boyle et al., 2022; Kosovac, 2016 ). Barriers hinder the progress of digital transformation in water utilities. The lack of internal capacity to develop, operate, and integrate smart applications emerges as a significant barrier, as water utilities may lack the necessary expertise, resources, or organisational structures to effectively leverage digital technologies (Mounce, 2020 ). Moreover, the risk-averse culture prevalent within the industry when facing innovation often results in stakeholders resisting to adopt new technologies or processes due to concerns about reliability, compatibility, or potential disruptions to existing operations (Kane et al., 2019; Warner and Wäger, 2019 ). The absence of operational standards among water utilities impedes benchmarking and knowledge-sharing initiatives, hindering collaboration and collective learning efforts (Rousso et al., 2023 ). The lack of competing markets and lock-in to existing infrastructure are other detrimental barriers for water utilities digital transformation, which altogether are slowing down water utilities digital transformation compared to other industries (Boyle et al., 2022 ). The digital transformation of water utilities is primarily driven by economic benefits, government regulation, and the imperatives posed by uncertainties and challenges related to water scarcity, population growth, and climate change. Economic benefits are key for short-term uptake and long-term sustainability, as water utilities seek to achieve significant cost savings and efficiency gains through the adoption of digital technologies (Beal and Flynn, 2015; Daniel et al., 2023 ). By optimising operations, reducing water losses, and improving asset management, digital transformation is expected to enhance the sustainability of water utilities. Government regulation, policies, and incentives can further accelerate the adoption of digital technologies, as authorities increasingly mandate or incentivize the implementation of innovative solutions to address pressing water management challenges (Low et al., 2015 ). Moreover, uncertainties and challenges associated with water scarcity, population growth, and climate change can drive water utilities adoption of digital transformation to enhance water resource management, resilience, and adaptability (Dwivedi et al., 2022; Zarza, 2022 ). Enablers of digital transformation in water utilities encompass a suite of strategic initiatives and research endeavours aimed at facilitating the adoption and integration of digital technologies. Key enablers include the development of comprehensive frameworks to map water utilities' capacity and needs, enabling strategic decision-making and resource allocation. Advancements in sensor hardware, such as improvements in longevity, battery life, and reduced costs, are key enablers that enhance cost-benefit and uptake of digital monitoring systems. Integration of big, multi-sourced data and robust cybersecurity measures are other critical enablers, ensuring the seamless collection, storage, and analysis of data while safeguarding against cyber threats and breaches. Increasing the generality of smart data applications for various field conditions reduces the need for customization, streamlining water utilities’ uptake and implementation of technologies, and promoting their scalability. Moreover, data-informed proactive asset management and water pricing strategies can enable water utilities to optimise resource allocation, enhance system efficiency, and incentivise conservation efforts. As water utilities navigate persisting uncertainties and the demand for technological advancements, research plays a pivotal role in translating knowledge into actionable technologies, practices, and policies that enable digital transformation.  6 Conclusions This study provides a targeted research agenda and a continuous improvement process to support water utilities uptake of digital technologies and smart data analytics, which is argued to improve their proactivity to future challenges such as extreme weather events, population growth and ageing assets. Based on best practices and the current state-of-art of SWWSS, a critical discussion of challenges, barriers, drivers, and enablers for water utilities digital transformation was provided. Four case studies encompassing automated water consumption metering, early detection of water mains breaks, early detection of sewerage spills, and smart rainfall reuse and flood mitigation were presented to exemplify the potential benefits of SWWSS. This study complements existing frameworks on developing digital solutions by integrating challenges at utility level (e.g., implementation and integration with operation) and the forefront of research (e.g., generality of applications, improved and cheaper hardware). The digital transformation of water utilities should undergo a structured and planned process, comprising five interconnected phases: identification of priority areas for investment, choice of devices for data collection, appropriate management of collected data, seamless use of data in decision support tools, and integration of data-informed processes into strategic planning and operation. In each step of this continuous process additional research is required to further consolidate SWWSS and support wide water utilities’ digital transformation. Key research areas include: 1) frameworks to map water utilities status (i.e., capacity and needs), and rank priority areas of investment; 2) improvements in sensors hardware (e.g., energy efficiency, precision) and cost-benefit (e.g., optimal sensor location in networks); 3) integration of big, multi-source of data and cybersecurity; 4) increase in generality of smart data applications to match field conditions, and integration of multiple aspects of water management (e.g., water-energy nexus); and 5) data-informed proactive asset management and frameworks for water pricing. Key barriers for water utilities digital transformation are 1) a lack of internal capacity, 2) a risk conservative culture when facing innovation, and 3) a lack of operation standards among water utilities to foster benchmarking. Because of that, it is crucial that water utilities actively engage in the digital transformation process by collaborating with research centres and the private sector while simultaneously increasing in-house capacity through investments in skilled personnel and training.
1 Introduction Controlling soil erosion phenomena caused by rainfall and runoff is one of the most significant challenges in the management of sloping hillslopes, particularly if there is no vegetation. Interrill and rill erosion are the principal processes occurring when sloping hillslopes are not appropriately shielded from rainfall and runoff. Erosion phenomena, roughness and hydrodynamic properties interact with each other. Overland flows can be recognized for their shallow water depths and limited bed shear stresses (Abrahams et al., 1994; Toy et al., 2002 ). According to Emmett (1970) , the overland flow regime on hillslopes tend to vary from laminar at the hilltop to fully turbulent at some distance down the slope. Moreover, they have different flow regimes (i.e., from laminar to turbulent) (Cen et al., 2022 ) and hydraulic resistance characteristics in dependence of roughness characterizing the surface on which they move (i.e., bare soil, gravel, vegetated soil, etc.) (Ma et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024 ). For smooth beds, some Authors (Yoon and Wenzel, 1971; Shen and Li, 1973 ) pointed out the influence of rainfall intensity on overland flow resistance for Reynolds number Re  values less than 2000. For a rough bed made of glued sand grains, Katz et al. (1995)  observed that flow resistance is influenced by raindrop impact and channel-bed roughness. Nearing et al. (2017)  found an increasing relationship between slope and surface roughness, which counterbalances the expected increase in flow velocity on steeper slopes. This condition, called “slope velocity equilibrium”, is consequently due to the reciprocal influence between overland flow and soil surface morphology and is comparable with the feedback mechanism stated by Govers (1992)  (Di Stefano et al., 2021; 2022a ) for rill flows. Considering this hypothesis and the fact that slope and rainfall intensity affect the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor f , hydraulic equations like Manning and Darcy–Weisbach, are difficult to apply modeling runoff at hillslope scale. Polyakov et al. (2018)  reported the experiments performed at the Southwest Watershed Research Center for overland flows with rainfall simulation at the plot scale and with the presence of vegetation. These data were analyzed by Nicosia et al. (2020a) , who presented a theoretical overland flow resistance law and found negligible effects of roughness on flow friction due to the laminar flow regime characterizing the experimental measurements. Ferro and Nicosia (2020)  tested a flow resistance law by the measurements reported in Sun et al. (2020)  for tilled surfaces, characterized by different roughness conditions. The experimental measurements were used to determine the effect of the starting roughness and evaluate how the friction factor is affected by the temporal evolution of roughness. Their results highlighted that the starting roughness was influenced by the applied tillage method, and the flow resistance diminished during the experiment due to the flow modeling action. In fact, at the beginning of the experiments, both grain resistance and tillage-induced surface roughness constituted the total flow resistance, while, at the end of the experiments, the flow modeling action had reduced the surface roughness due to tillage and, consequently, its resistance. Nicosia et al. (2020a; 2020b; 2020c)  presented a theoretical overland flow resistance law, which is summarized below and in the Appendix A . Even if the vegetation types were different, similar values of a  coefficient were obtained, and this outcome was justified by the circumstance that the investigated flows were characterized by a laminar flow regime which determines negligible effects of roughness on flow resistance. Nevertheless, the results also highlighted that the best approach to estimate f  is using a specific coefficient a  for each vegetation type. As suggested by Ferro and Nicosia (2020) , the relationship between morphological surface roughness and hydraulic resistance can be a significant tool for fully understanding erosion phenomena and predicting some important variables, such as flow velocity. A significant issue in predicting overland flow is establishing the resistance coefficient for different surfaces (Kowobari et al., 1972 ). For this reason, in this study, a theoretical flow resistance law (Eq. (6) ) (Ferro, 2017, 2018, 2019; Ferro and Porto, 2018 ) was used for the measurements by Hinsberger et al. (2022) , performed for transitional and turbulent overland flows with different roughness conditions. The available data were used for (i) testing the accuracy of the approach to estimate f ; (ii) studying the effect of different roughness conditions on flow resistance; and (iii) establishing a relationship between the a , b , and c  coefficients and Manning’s n  values, corresponding to the roughness of the investigated surfaces.  2 Database by Hinsberger et al. (2022)  In this investigation, the measurements performed by Hinsberger et al. (2022)  were used (Hinsberger et al., (2021)  [dataset] https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.17142440.v1 ). These measurements were carried out in a sloping (slope s  varying from 1 to 40 %) rectangular flume, 0.5 m wide, 4 m long, and 0.35 m deep, with a coated plywood bottom and aluminum walls. During the experiments, the entire flume bed was covered with an inset. In particular, six different roughness conditions (aluminum, artificial grass, wheat, cement-based coating, asphaltic emulsion, and exposed aggregate concrete) were investigated. The flow discharge was measured by a magnetic-inductive flow meter, while water depth values were measured by a point gauge located in the flume axis to prevent disturbance due to the inlet and outlet areas. For the “wheat” runs, as the culms exceeded the flume walls, they were slightly bent at the top to measure the water depths. The two roughness conditions that investigate vegetation effects on flow behavior represent fully-submerged (artificial grass) and partially-submerged (wheat) vegetation. A total of 730 data were collected. In Table 1  ,  the ranges of slope, flow Froude number, and Reynolds number are listed. The investigated flows are always turbulent (7061 ≤ Re  ≤ 111258) and both sub-critical and supercritical (0.27 ≤ F  ≤ 6.86). The available data were divided into six datasets, distinguished by the examined roughness condition. Then, each dataset was divided into two sub-datasets for calibrating and testing the theoretically-based flow resistance law. The division was made including measurements covering the whole experimental ranges for both the calibrating and testing sub-datasets.  3 Results Fig. 1   clearly shows the trend of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor values, f=(8gRs)/V 2 , related to the roughness condition. Notwithstanding the differences in terms of f  highlighted by Fig. 1 , the theoretical approach guarantees a reliable estimate of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor also not considering the variability of the roughness condition, i.e., using the unique mean value of a  = 0.3613 and fixing the b  and c  coefficients to 1.05 and 0.562, respectively. However, the best estimate of f  is obtained when the roughness condition is considered calibrating Eq. (9)  for the whole dataset for each roughness condition. (9) , whose a , b , and c  coefficients were estimated by the calibrating sub-dataset (Table 1 ) , is positively tested by the independent testing sub-dataset and the obtained flow resistance law (Eq. (12) ) allows a reliable estimate of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor. The agreement between the measured f  values and those calculated by Eq. (12)  is characterized by errors in the estimate (Table 1 )  that, for 91–100 % of the cases, are ≤± 5 %. For the artificial turf condition, if the whole database is considered for estimating the a , b , and c  coefficients (Table 2 ), the agreement between the measured f  values and those calculated by Eq. (12)  is characterized by estimate errors (Table 2 )  that for 89.8–100 % of the cases are ≤± 5 %. The percentage of data falling into the error bands of ±5 % (Table 2 ) is not related to the investigated roughness condition, confirming that the theoretical flow resistance equation is able to give an accurate estimate of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor for different roughness and hydraulic conditions (Di Stefano et al., 2022b; Ferro, 2017; 2018; 2019; Nicosia et al., 2021 ). Considering, as obtained in previous investigations (Nicosia and Ferro, 2023 ), that the exponents b  (1.05) of the Froude number and c  (0.562) of slope can be assumed independent of the investigated roughness condition, the effect of roughness was explained exclusively by the a  coefficient (Table 3 ). The good agreement (Fig. 8 ) between the measured friction factor values and the ones, f , calculated by Eq. (12) , with b  = 1.05, c  = 0.562 and the corresponding a  values listed in Table 3 , confirms the reliability of the hypothesis to use a  as the single coefficient affected by the roughness condition. The agreement between the measured f  values and those calculated by Eq. (12) , with b  = 1.05, c  = 0.562 and the corresponding a  values listed in Table 3 , is characterized by estimate errors (Table 3 )  that for 70.4–100 % of the cases are less than or equal to ±5 %. Since the values of a  listed in Table 3  are included in a narrow range, the hypothesis to use an average value of a  coefficient (0.3613) independent of the roughness condition was also tested. This theoretical approach (Eq. (12) ) with a  = 0.3613, b  = 1.05, and c  = 0.562) guarantees a good estimate of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor even if the flow resistance tends to be underestimated for the vegetated conditions (wheat, artificial turf) (Fig. 10 ). The relationships between the a , b , and c  coefficients (Table 2 ) and Manning’s n  values, corresponding to the investigated surfaces and their roughness, (Fig. 11 ) pointed out that a different effect of the Manning’s n  on the considered coefficient can be observed. In particular, the comparison among Eqs. (13) , (14), and (15) highlighted that a  is the most affected by roughness conditions as the exponent of Manning’s assumes the highest value. In conclusion, the applied theoretical approach can give an accurate estimate of the Darcy–Weisbach friction factor and account for the surface roughness. The obtained results can help in modeling overland flow defining the resistance coefficient for variable roughness, especially the vegetated ones.  5 Conclusions Laboratory measurements, performed by Hinsberger et al. (2022)  in a flume characterized by six roughness conditions (aluminum, artificial grass, wheat, cement-based coating, asphaltic emulsion, and exposed aggregate concrete), were utilized to verify the reliability of a theoretical flow resistance equation suggested by Ferro (2019)  and already calibrated for vegetated channels and gravel-bed rivers. This equation was calibrated by the analysis of the relationship between Γ, F , and s  of the six data sets. Considering, as obtained in previous investigations, that the exponents b  (1.05) of the Froude number and c  (0.562) of slope can be assumed independent of the investigated roughness condition, the hypothesis of explaining the effect of roughness exclusively by the a  coefficient was also tested. The good agreement between the measured friction factor values and the ones calculated by Eq. (12) , with b  = 1.05, c  = 0.562 and the corresponding a  values listed in Table 3 , confirmed the reliability of the hypothesis to use a  as the single coefficient affected by the roughness condition.
1 Introduction With the continuous increase of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions globally, climate change has become a key factor affecting environmental security and sustainable development in all countries. Precipitation, as a vital component of the hydrological cycle, is highly sensitive to climate change (Pfahl et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023a ). China, a major food-producing nation with a substantial population, possesses the third-largest land area in the world, encompassing five different climate zones. The complexity and variability of its climate, together with its vast land coverage, make China’s precipitation patterns significant standing in global climate change research (Jiang et al., 2023 ). As global climate change intensifies, there has been a marked increase in interest and demand for accurate and detailed research on the spatiotemporal patterns of precipitation in China (Gu et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2023; Liang & Zhang, 2021 ; Q. Zhang et al., 2018 ). Extensive studies have uncovered the intricacies and variability of China’s precipitation patterns, which exhibit differing trends in response to environmental changes and carbon emissions (Guo et al., 2020a; Yun et al., 2020 ). Most existing research has mainly attempted to unveil the spatiotemporal distribution of precipitation on monthly or seasonal scales (Le et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Yun et al., 2020 ; R. Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023b ). For instance, recent study has indicated a scattered decreasing trend in spring precipitation and a uniform increasing trend in summer precipitation in the Yangtze River Plain, while an upward uniform trend in both frequency and intensity of precipitation is observed in the northwest region of China (Guo et al., 2020b ). Fu et al. (2023) , through analyzing daily precipitation data from nearly 800 stations in China, statistically examined the trends of the Annual Precipitation Concentration Index and the Seasonal Precipitation Concentration Index. They found that the precipitation concentration in southeastern China is higher than in the northwest, with strong regional variability. With global warming, drought-flood events are increasing persistently, and significant wetting trends have appeared in the northwestern regions of China. Konapala et al. (2020)  has noted that the apportionment entropy (AE) of China’s seasonal precipitation is at a moderate to low level, exposing the variability in seasonal precipitation patterns and the sensitivity of water availability. Chen (2020)  's study also shows that the intra-seasonal distribution of precipitation in solar terms of frequency and amount in eastern China has become significantly more uneven over the past nearly 50 years. For a country like China, with its varied geographical environments and complex climate types, research based on the seasonal scale does not fully meet the urgent need for precise precipitation patterns. We believe that to finely differentiate the precipitation patterns within different temporal units, it is necessary to upgrade the research beyond the seasonal and even monthly time scales. Hailed by the international meteorological community as the “fifth great invention of China,” the Twenty-Four Solar Terms (TFST) are a distinctive creation from ancient China. The TFST are divided according to the position of the sun on the ecliptic. It is a time system established by ancient Chinese agricultural society based on the annual cycle of the solar year, used to guide agricultural production. The solar year lasts about 365 days, and ancient Chinese astronomers divided the Earth’s orbit into 24 equal parts, corresponding to the 24 solar terms. The application of TFST in climate classification is essentially similar to seasons, except that seasons span three months while each TFST lasts about 15 days. For more detailed definitions and calculation methods of TFST, refer to Section 2.1 . Expressions like “The nurturing rain knows its time, arriving quietly with the spring’s sweet chime.” from poetry, and the Chinese proverb “The rain at XiaoShu starts to pour, ox toil in forty-five days no more.” exquisitely illustrate the ancient Chinese’s meticulous depiction and understanding of the distinct climatic nuances associated with each solar term. Despite the dimming of practices governed by the solar terms with today’s fast-paced lifestyle, as a crucial part of Chinese culture, their related knowledge and patterns endure steadfastly in the hearts of Chinese people. Unfortunately, despite TFST being an important calendar passed down by Chinese people to this day, it has lacked necessary attention in the study of precipitation patterns. Existing research on climate change in China, especially on extreme precipitation, has not considered or studied from the perspective of the traditional Chinese TFST. Furthermore, no one has statistically analyzed the authenticity and feasibility of TFST. We propose that using these solar terms as a temporal scale to analyze precipitation patterns may not only align more closely with the actual rhythms and experiences of the Chinese but could also enhance the temporal precision, thus providing a more contextually relevant viewpoint and framework for study. The core of this research involves leveraging the temporal scaffolding of the TFST to unveil new perspectives and methodologies for investigating precipitation patterns in China. Here, we attempt to corroborate the macroscopic representations of typical solar terms against the precipitation trends statistically, drawing from historical and future daily precipitation data based the CMIP6 future scenario models’ GCMs and CHM observation dataset. Moreover, this study integrates historical observational data with model simulation data under various future carbon emission scenarios, to conduct an in-depth exploration of the patterns and future trends of regular and extreme precipitation in China. The aim of this research is to achieve a seamless integration of modern meteorological and hydrological studies with traditional culture, using the Chinese TFST calendrical system. This work intends to provide a deeper understanding of the cyclical nature of extreme precipitation, offering a fresh perspective and theoretical support for the precise forecasting, early warning, and prevention of extreme rainfall patterns in the future. Within this research framework, we believe that we can carve out a new path that melds meteorological science with cultural heritage, bringing innovative thinking and practical solutions to the field of precipitation pattern research. This study focuses on addressing the following innovative questions: (1). For the solar terms in TFST which related to regular precipitation, does the inherent regularity summarized for Chinese precipitation hold statistically? (2). Regarding extreme precipitation in China, both past and future, does TFST exhibit significant spatiotemporal statistical patterns? Can we map the spatiotemporal distribution of extreme precipitation dominated by each solar term based on these patterns? (3). Under different carbon emission scenarios, what are the future trends in the frequency of extreme precipitation during the most dangerous solar terms in China?  2 Method 2.1 The definition and calculation framework of the TFST The Twenty-Four Solar terms (TFST) is a distinct invention of ancient China, devised by the country’s laboring populace to facilitate the mastering of agricultural activities. Widely circulated and applied among the general public, the TFST are a product of ancient agrarian civilization. On November 30, 2016, the TFST were officially inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Each solar term spans approximately 15 days, and the currently observed TFST are determined by the position of the sun along the ecliptic path: dividing the sun’s annual orbit into twenty-four equal sections, with each 15-degree segment representing one solar term, starting with LiChun and ending with DaHan (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). For example, during ChunFen, the sun reaches 0° on the ecliptic longitude; during XiaZhi, it reaches 90°; during QiuFen, it reaches 180°; and during DongZhi, it reaches 270°. The other solar terms are evenly distributed between these four main solar terms.
