In the actual application code of this study, we directly calculated the start and end times of each solar term for each year up to 2100 using formulas. Based on the annual movement of the sun, we can calculate the Gregorian calendar start dates for each solar term using the following formula:(1) D ST  m _ y r   = ( N m _ y r 2   × D + C ST  cent   )  - L m _ y r 2        Where, the D ST  m _ y r      represents the starting day of the ST  solar term in the year m_yr ; the N m _ y r 2      represents the last two digits of the year m_yr ; D  is the fractional part of the mean tropical year, approximately equal to 0.2422; C ST  cent      represents the fixed century value for the ST  solar term at the beginning of that century, for instance, the DongZhi in the 21st century has a C ST  cent      value of 21.94, while in the 20th century it was 22.6. L m _ y r 2      represents the number of leap years that have passed in the given century prior to the year m_yr . For example, the method to calculate the date when the YuShui solar term occurs in the year 2008 would be as follows:(2) D YuShui  2008  = ( N 2008  × D + C YuShui  21  )  - L YuShui   = ( 08 × 0.2422 + 18.73 )  - ( 8 - 1 )  / 4 ≈ 19      Therefore, in the year 2008, the start date of the YuShui solar term falls on February 19th. By similar calculations, we can determine that the JingZhe solar term of the same year begins on March 5th, which means YuShui ends on March 4th. Detailed values for the 20th and 21st centuries, as well as the specifics on calculating the start dates of all TFST, are presented in the Supplementary Material  (Supplementary Table 1 ). Through thousands of years of observation, ancient people recognized that atmospheric processes tend to undergo dramatic changes around the dates of the solar terms. These changes not only precipitate meteorological disasters but also have a triggering effect on geological disasters, particularly intense earthquakes. For millennia, people have been utilizing the objective laws of the interactions among celestial bodies, meteorological phenomena, and phenology to guide their economic activities and protect themselves against natural disasters. With the ongoing global climate change, regional precipitation patterns have also shifted, leading to significant temporal unevenness in the distribution of rainfall throughout the year.  2.2 Identification for conventional and extreme precipitation In this study, to verify the accuracy of solar terms, we first investigated the Difference Index of Effective Precipitation Days within 30 days (DIEP D 30 d  ST     ) before and after the YuShui and GuYu solar terms, along with the Difference in Precipitation within the same period (D P 30 d  ST     ). The formula is as follows:(3) DIEP D 30 d  ST   = EP D a f t _ 30 d  ST   - E P D b e f _ 30 d  ST    EP D b e f _ 30 d  ST   + 1 e - 9      D P 30 d  ST   = P a f t _ 30 d  ST   - P b e f _ 30 d  ST           where, EP D a f t _ 30 d  ST      and EP D b e f _ 30 d  ST      represent the number of effective precipitation days after and before the solar term, respectively (days with precipitation exceeding 0.5 mm are considered effective). Meanwhile, P a f t _ 30 d  ST      and P b e f _ 30 d  ST      represent the cumulative precipitation after and before the solar term over the corresponding 30-day intervals. Furthermore, to observe the spatial distribution of precipitation aridity and wetness across different solar terms in China, we introduced the Standard Precipitation Index based on the TFST, SP I ST     . We performed gamma distribution fitting on the continuous time series of aggregated precipitation for each solar term (approximately 15 days) from 2015 to 2100, deriving the corresponding cumulative probability functions, and then transforming the cumulative probability values into the z-scores of the standard normal distribution (Liu et al., 2021a ). When an area’s SP I ST      is greater than 0, it historically implies abundant precipitation during that solar term in the region; a value less than 0 indicates dryness. To explore patterns and predictability of extreme precipitation during different solar terms, we first identified the 95th percentile, R 95 P     , and 99th percentile, R 99 P     , of daily precipitation in China during the stable climate period (1981–2010). We then calculated the frequency at which each of the TFST surpassed these percentiles, under various modeled future scenarios. Subsequently, we statistically analyzed pixel by pixel to determine which solar term most frequently experienced extreme precipitation. This resulted in the distribution of extreme precipitation frequency for China, F R 95 P  ST      and F R 99 P  ST     , which helps ascertain which solar term historically and in projected futures has the highest probability of experiencing extreme rainfall. The same methodology was also applied in detecting more severe precipitation events: Event-Based Extreme Precipitation (EEP)(Wu et al., 2018 ) across China: Time distribution patterns, trends, and return levels. Extending the foundational definition of EEP rainfall events, we adapted EEP3 and EEP6 events for the TFST. An EEP3 event is defined as an occurrence within a solar term period where at least one day’s rainfall exceeds the R 95 P      threshold during a sequence of at least three consecutive effective precipitation days. An EEP6 event, within the same solar term period, is categorized when at least two days surpass the R 99 P      threshold within a sequence of at least six consecutive effective precipitation days. Clearly, EEP events are based on more extreme circumstances derived from daily rainfall percentiles, and EEP6 events signify highly extreme rainfall conditions that carry significant flood risks. Lastly, we compiled the frequencies of extreme rainfall events every five years from historical records to future model projections for China, to observe the spatiotemporal evolution of extreme rainfall frequencies during specific solar terms.  2.3 Data processing Here, we selected five climate models from CMIP6, that have shown satisfactory application results in China (Xu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021b ) (Supplementary Table 2 ). We analyzed the precipitation forecast data for the years 2015 to 2100 under four different future emission scenarios. We adopted four integrated future scenario models that take into account both Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs): SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5. SSP1-2.6 signifies a synthesis of low social vulnerability, low mitigation pressure, and low radiative forcing. SSP2-4.5 represents a combination of medium social vulnerability and medium radiative forcing. SSP3-7.0 combines high social vulnerability with relatively high anthropogenic radiative forcing, and SSP5-8.5 is an updated scenario from CMIP5′s RCP8.5 in CMIP6, delineating the only shared socioeconomic pathway that could result in reaching an anthropogenic radiative forcing of 8.5 W/m2  by the year 2100. To reduce the prediction bias of individual models, we employed a multi-model ensemble average for preprocessing. We also utilized a comprehensive simulated daily precipitation dataset, CHM-PRE (Han et al., 2023; Han Jingya, 2023 ), constructed from observations at 2839 stations within and surrounding China since 1961, to validate the original CMIP6 precipitation data. The CHM dataset boasts a resolution of 0.1°×0.1°, whereas the CMIP6 dataset’s resolution has been homogenized to 0.25°×0.25° using bilinear interpolation, and quantile mapping (Xue et al., 2022 ) was then used to calibrate the precipitation data.   3 Result 3.1 Significant variations in conventional precipitation indicators around typical solar terms In the ancient system of TFST, two solar terms are directly associated with precipitation: YuShui and GuYu. Chinese folklore says YuShui signifies the arrival of the spring breeze, the melting of ice and snow, increased humidity in the air, and a rise in rainfall, thus the solar term is named after this water increase. Meanwhile, GuYu, which translates to “the rain that nurtures the grain” marks a period of significant rainfall increase, crucial for the newly planted seedlings in the fields that require ample and timely rain for robust growth. As an age-old summary of the Chinese farmers’ understanding of precipitation patterns, the primary aim of this study is to verify the correctness of these assertions regarding these two solar terms, and whether there is direct scientific evidence supporting them. Looking back over the past 40 years, we have discovered, as expected, significant differences in cumulative rainfall and the number of effective rain days during the 30 days before and after these two solar terms. Both historical datasets, whether based on the mean value of five models from CMIP6 (referred to as 5MM) or CHM data regarding historical observations, support the Chinese sayings about these two solar terms. According to the statistical results presented in Fig. 3 , CHM datasets exhibit a mean increase of approximately + 8.7 mm in the precipitation 30 days before and after the GuYu term over the past 40 years, with the maximum difference reaching about + 236.9 mm. For YuShui, these values are + 3.4 mm and + 105.6 mm, respectively. Furthermore, future precipitation appears to follow this pattern. Comparing the first and second rows of Fig. 1  , the deeper blue of the first row indicates that in all four future scenario models, the difference in precipitation after GuYu calculated by 5MM is greater than after YuShui. In the SSP3-7.0 future scenario model, the average change in precipitation 30 days before and after GuYu reached a peak of about + 26.4 mm. For all four future scenarios, the mean differences for GuYu exceed + 23.5 mm, in descending order: SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5, SSP2-4.5, SSP1-2.6. The ancient Chinese concluded that the GuYu heralds a period of increasing rainfall abundance, while YuShui indicates that rain is about to begin. By analyzing the Difference Index of Effective Precipitation Days before and after each solar term over a 30-day span (referred to as DIEPD30d), we found both past and future data support this view. The extensive areas of green in the third row of Fig. 2   show that the DIEPD30d is positive across nearly all of China, as reflected in both the 5MM calculations and CHM observation data. Intriguingly, the differing shades of green for the two solar terms reveal that despite both being associated with increased rainfall, YuShui has a higher DIEPD30d value than GuYu, which affirms the saying that YuShui marks the commencement of rainfall. According to statistics in Fig. 3  , over the past 40 years, the average DIEPD30d following YuShui in China is + 0.126, with a maximum of + 0.319; for GuYu, these values are + 0.087 and + 0.261, respectively. In solar terms of future scenarios derived from 5MM calculations, average DIEPD30d values obtained for YuShui are as follows: +0.123 (SSP1-2.6), +0.131 (SSP2-4.5), +0.119 (SSP3-7.0), and + 0.121 (SSP5-8.5). As such, differences in the number of effective precipitation days under different future scenarios seem negligible. In summary, the statistical results suggest that the narratives about increased rainfall related to the two quintessential precipitation solar terms YuShui and GuYu from the TFST are indeed reliable. Moreover, their interpretations regarding trends in both “accumulated precipitation” and “number of effective precipitation days”, two highly correlated indicators, are supported by the statistical findings.  3.2 Patterns in past and future extreme precipitation across China’s TFST Under the context of global warming, the frequency of extreme precipitation events is expected to change significantly (Sun et al., 2018 ), and the spatial heterogeneity of changes in extreme precipitation intensity around the world was pronounced during the 20th century, with an increasing trend in both frequency and intensity of such events in the Asian region (Madakumbura et al., 2021 ; W. Zhang & Zhou, 2020 ). Since the ancient Chinese solar terms, which summarize precipitation patterns, have been deemed reliable to a certain extent, it raises the question: Are there specific patterns for extreme precipitation as well? Here, we focused on the spatiotemporal distribution of four types of extreme precipitation event indices across different solar terms. Fig. 4  (i) − (l) display the prevailing conditions of extreme rainfall frequency across China during the various solar terms over the past 40 years, as simulated by the 5MM model and observed by the CHM dataset. The solar term associated with each grid point represents the term during which extreme rainfall occurred most frequently in that region over the aforementioned period. Fig. 5  (a) − (d) present the latitudinal and longitudinal statistics of solar term dominance in extreme rainfall events. Results from both methods of analysis indicate that the XiaoShu and DaShu solar terms govern most of the extreme precipitation events across the majority of China. In the CHM dataset’s observational statistics of daily rainfall over the past 40 years, 79.4 % of the territory, dominated by the XiaZhi (15.1 %), XiaoShu (30.9 %), and DaShu (33.4 %), experienced extreme precipitation events as classified by R95p (Fig. 4 (k)). For R99p extreme precipitation events (Fig. 4 (l)), this figure is 70.6 % with the XiaZhi, XiaoShu, and DaShu accounting for 13.2 %, 23.6 %, and 33.8 %, respectively. At the same time, the 5MM model simulations support CHM’s observation that XiaoShu and DaShu predominantly influence the basic extreme rainfall events (R95p, R99p) in China but present a more balanced simulation outcome for other solar terms. According to Fig. 4 (i), in the 5MM simulations, XiaoShu (20.1 %) and DaShu (32.5 %) still lead in extreme precipitation events across 52.6 % areas of China, with solar terms such as the LiXia (9.2 %), XiaoMan (9.1 %), MangZhong (7.3 %), and XiaZhi (7.0 %) each dominating a comparably sized area of R95p extreme rainfall events. The spatiotemporal concentration of high-frequency extreme precipitation in China is generally consistent with the observational results of Nie et al. (2023) , L. Wang et al. (2021) , and , Zhang et al. (2023c) . The latitude-longitude statistics shown in Fig. 5 (a), along with data from Fig. 4 (k), imply that regions dominated by XiaoShu in R95p extreme rainfall events are mainly concentrated in a broad swath of China spanning from about 30.9°N to 46.7°N and 84.8°E to 101.6°E, and from 115.8°E to 124.1°E. Meanwhile, areas dominated by DaShu are chiefly found from about 33.7°N to 43.2°N latitude, and from 78.8°E to 88.8°E, and 99.1°E to 129.3°E longitude. When tied in with the strip distribution shown on the map, the regions dominated by XiaoShu and DaShu come close to approximating the boundaries of the 200 mm and 800 mm isohyet lines in China. The overall territory stretches from the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in the west to the Songhua River Basin in the east, encompassing large portions of the upper Yangtze River Basin and the Yellow River Basin. With China’s major independent river basins in mind, Fig. 6   shows that over the past 40 years, seven major basins experienced the most frequent occurrences of R95p and R99p extreme rainfall events during XiaoShu or DaShu. Specifically, within the Yellow River Basin, there were a total of 175 extreme precipitation events exceeding R95p during DaShu, accounting for 15.0 % of all occurrences. The Hai River Basin recorded the highest number, with 248 such events during DaShu (22.0 %). In contrast, the R95p extreme precipitation events in the basins of Southeast China and the Pearl River Basin were most commonly recorded during MangZhong, with 171 and 179 occurrences, respectively, and R99p events were most frequent during the XiaZhi, with 32 and 39 occurrences. Even though basin-wide averages suggest the Yangtze River Basin experienced the highest frequency of R95p and R99p events during the XiaZhi, with 212 and 54 occurrences respectively, Fig. 4  indicates that the most frequent solar terms for extreme precipitation vary from the lower to upper reaches of the Yangtze River Basin due to its spanning multiple climate zones in China. The color discrepancies depicted in the map broadly indicate that within the Yangtze River Basin, the solar terms corresponding to the highest frequency of extreme rainfall are consistent with a spatiotemporal shift from the downstream regions in the spring to the upstream regions in the summer. According to “A Collective Interpretation of the Seventy-two Phenological solar terms” by the Yuan Dynasty literary figure Wu Cheng, “intense heat, frequent thunderstorms and typhoons, and abundant rainfall” are the main characteristics of the XiaoShu and DaShu solar terms, with agricultural activities focused mainly on “urgent harvesting and planting, and combating droughts and floods.” From this, it is evident that the risks of flooding due to extreme rainfall, as well as compound events such as drought-heatwaves and flood-heatwaves during these solar terms, have long been recognized by the Chinese people as hazards to be guarded against. According to Fig. 4 (a) to (h), the 5MM model’s simulations of future scenarios indicate that the high frequency of extreme rainfall during the DaShu and XiaoShu periods is unlikely to change. Moreover, there are no significant differences in the distribution of extreme rainfall events among the four different scenarios considered. EEP3 and EEP6 represent more extreme rainfall conditions than those defined by R95p and R99p (definitions detailed in the method section), emphasizing the high risk associated with the XiaoShu and DaShu solar terms. Fig. 7  (k) and (l) show that EEP3 and EEP6 extreme rainfall events are still most frequent during these two solar terms. Specifically, 77.3 % of China’s area is dominated by XiaZhi (19.8 %), XiaoShu (29.7 %), and DaShu (27.8 %) in solar terms of the timing of EEP3 events. From Fig. 7 (a) to (d), it is noted that all four future scenario simulations agree that different solar terms dominate extreme rainfall events in the upper and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin. Under SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios, XiaoMan was the solar term with the most frequent occurrence of EEP3 events in the downstream Yangtze, while under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, MangZhong was most frequent, and SSP3-7.0 indicated both XiaoMan and MangZhong were dominant. Similarly, 50.7 % of China’s area is dominated by XiaZhi (13.5 %), XiaoShu (16.1 %), and DaShu (21.1 %) in solar terms of the timing of EEP6 events. Given that over 15.1 % of China’s region has never experienced EEP6 events, the statistics highlight the need for precaution against extreme rainfall during these solar terms. Comparing the blank areas in the northwestern river basins depicted in Fig. 7 (j) and 7(l), it becomes apparent that the 5MM model’s historical simulation for the same period concurs with the known historical record: no significant EEP6 extreme rainfall events have occurred in China’s northwest over the past 40 years. However, the depictions in Fig. 7 (e) through 7(h) suggest that these regions may face the risk of such extreme rainfall in the future, with a temporal concentration during the MangZhong and XiaZhi solar terms. In regions historically spared from events like EEP6, there’s a natural inclination to diminish the perceived risk awareness of extreme rainfall disasters. Nonetheless, we must not ignore the potential threats climate change may pose.  3.3 Trends in future extreme precipitation frequency during perilous solar terms Upon summarizing the spatiotemporal distribution of extreme precipitation, we have come to realize that XiaoShu and DaShu are the solar terms most frequently associated with extreme rainfall across China. The reality of global warming has heightened concerns about the future risk of extreme precipitation and the compounded threat of humid heat (Raghavendra et al., 2019; You & Wang, 2021 ). As the two solar terms with the highest frequency of extreme rainfall during the year, their future risk of extreme precipitation events seems to be more severe than anticipated, showing a notable increasing trend. Figs. 7 and 8   present the results of our Mann-Kendall trend statistical analysis on the frequency of extreme rainfall events during XiaoShu and DaShu under different future scenario models. Overall, both solar terms exhibit an increasing trend in the frequency of extreme rainfall, with XiaoShu displaying a more significant trend than DaShu. Looking at the frequency of R95p extreme precipitation events, for XiaoShu under three different future scenarios, the areas in China with MK-Z values greater than + 1.65 exceed 20 %, namely SSP5-8.5 (33.2 %), SSP3-7.0 (25.1 %), and SSP2-4.5 (21.8 %). Similarly, the proportions of areas with MK-Z growth trends reaching the 95 % significance level are 21.6 %, 16.6 %, and 15.9 %, respectively. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, characterized by lower societal vulnerability, lower mitigation pressure, and lower radiative forcing, the increasing trend in the frequency of R95p extreme precipitation for XiaoShu across China is relatively moderate, with the proportions of areas with MK-Z values greater than + 1.65 and + 1.96 at 11.9 % and 6.5 %, respectively. Future R95p extreme precipitation frequency results for the DaShu solar term (Fig. 9  ) show a non-significant increasing trend across China, with MK-Z values for all four future scenarios ranging between 0 and + 0.9. The proportion of areas in China with a trend significance level over 90 % exceeds 23 % only under the SSP5-8.5 scenario; the other scenarios present 18.0 % (SSP1-2.6), 10.1 % (SSP3-7.0), and 9.4 % (SSP2-4.5). More extreme precipitation inevitably brings higher risks (Lima et al., 2021; Wasko et al., 2021 ). The increasing trends in the frequency of future R99p extreme rainfall events are more troubling than estimated. Within the half-month period of XiaoShu and DaShu, under scenarios of “Regional Rivalry” and “Fossil-Fueled Development”, over 20 % of areas in China demonstrate a significant increase in the frequency of R99p extreme precipitation events. Remarkably, for XiaoShu under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, the proportion of areas within this category reaches an alarming 34.3 %, and the increasing trend is particularly pronounced in the Qinghai-Tibet region, as can be easily seen from Fig. 8 (h). For DaShu, the proportions of areas in China showing a 90 % level significant increase in R99p extreme precipitation frequency under SSP5-8.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP2-4.5, SSP1-2.6 scenarios are 26.1 %, 22.0 %, 6.2 %, and 7.7 %, respectively, with China’s average MK-Z value being the smallest at 0.31 under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. Observing the spatial distribution in Fig. 8 (l) and (p), we note that under “Fossil-Fueled Development”, the future increasing trend of R95p and R99p extreme precipitation frequency during DaShu is more significant in the southwestern river basin regions of China, while there is a less significant decreasing trend in the northwestern areas, particularly in the northern part of Xinjiang province. Although the trends for the decrease in extreme precipitation frequency covering about 16 % of China’s territory have not passed the 90 % significance test, these areas’ future risks of extreme precipitation events are at least not as concerning as other regions.   4 Discussion 4.1 Objective appraisal of the historical role of the TFST Through statistical analysis of historical data, we have confirmed a positive correlation between the YuShui and GuYu solar terms and the increase in spring precipitation. Furthermore, by comparing the changes in different conventional precipitation indicators, we have successfully validated the objective rationality behind the precise descriptions of precipitation characteristics during the solar terms in ancient China, providing modern scientific support for the climatic markers within the TSFT. Additionally, by examining the past 40 years’ Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) results from the 5MM model simulations (SF 2. of the Supplementary Material s), we observed that the spatial distribution of SPI across the TFST generally conforms to the pattern described by the Heihe-Tengchong Line (Hu Line) (Liu et al., 2021a; Liu et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022 ). That is, regions northwest of the Hu Line exhibit SPI values lower than 0, indicating insufficient precipitation over long time series, while regions southeast of the line have SPI values greater than 0, signifying abundant rainfall and a humid climate. Different future scenario models suggest that these two typical precipitation-laden solar terms will continue to exhibit the trends that past statistical results have shown. Although there are discrepancies in specific values across different future scenarios, the differences are not significant when viewed from the statistical mean results (Fig. 3 .). This demonstrates that the TFST calendar, formed through long-term observations by the Chinese civilization, can still guide agricultural activities in China based on macro predictions of precipitation centuries later. It is worth noting that TFST, like seasons, is a time system used to distinguish climate characteristics, but there are certain differences between the two. Seasons are divided based on the Earth’s annual climatic changes caused by its orbit around the sun and the tilt of its axis, while TFST is an ancient Chinese time system divided according to the sun’s position on the ecliptic. Generally speaking, seasons are a more universal and macroscopic method of time division, emphasizing general climatic characteristics, whereas TFST is a more detailed time division with specific cultural significance. Moreover, the concept of seasons is universal and applicable to most regions of the world. TFST is primarily based on China’s geographical location and climatic characteristics; although it can also be applied to other regions in East Asia, it may be less accurate or applicable in other geographical locations.  4.2 The correlation between TFST and extreme precipitation We have reviewed the spatial distribution of extreme precipitation events during the solar terms over the past 40 years in China. Our investigation indicates that the highest frequency of extreme rainfall events occurs during specific solar terms: XiaoShu and DaShu. In-depth analysis of this finding suggests that exploring the temporal mechanisms involved could aid in improving forecasts of precipitation seasonality and extreme events in our country. Moreover, this continuity can further prompt us to rethink whether our traditional solar terms could serve as an effective agricultural production and natural disaster management clock, thus optimizing agricultural strategies and disaster response measures through a combination of traditional knowledge and modern science. Our geographical statistical data on the historical frequency of extreme precipitation events in China reveal a clear latitude and longitude inclination, possibly linked to atmospheric circulation patterns, topography, and dynamics associated with geographic location. Combining these statistical results with geospatial distribution, we find that the upper and lower boundary lines of areas dominated by extreme precipitations during the solar terms of XiaoShu and DaShu somewhat approximate the China’s 200 mm and 800 mm isohyetal lines, respectively. In most regions along China’s southeastern coast, such as the Pearl River Basin and the Southeast River Basin, extreme precipitation events occur one to two solar terms earlier than in inland areas. The spatial distribution of the solar terms with the highest frequencies of extreme precipitation in China, from southeast to northwest, also presents a significant characteristic of first increasing and then decreasing over time. This pattern may be closely linked with the activities of the monsoon belt under the influence of atmospheric circulation, the transport of summer water vapor from southeast to northwest (G. Wang et al., 2020 ), the unique climatic effects of the Tibetan Plateau, and the distinctive continental and maritime distribution in East Asia. In the future, we will continue to delve into this direction to provide new perspectives for comprehensively understanding future precipitation patterns’ variability and to improve regional greenhouse gas reduction and climate adaptation strategies associated with geographic features. For more extreme precipitation events EEP, our statistical results also consider the spatial variability in China’s northwest region. In areas where events as extreme as EEP6 have historically never occurred, people instinctively downplay the risk awareness of extreme precipitation disasters; however, we should not overlook the potential threat of climate change. GCMs predict that even historically drier regions of the northwest may face entirely different climate scenarios under certain situations. This means that weather events that were previously rare in the past could become common and intense in the future. Therefore, rather than focusing solely on traditionally rainy areas, we should strengthen monitoring and disaster prevention measures in all potential risk areas nationwide. To adapt to the extreme climate conditions that may arise in the future, policymakers and relevant institutions must optimize emergency response processes and enhance the resilience of infrastructures, especially in areas such as agricultural production, water resources management, and urban planning. Concurrently, China’s public education and outreach activities should also pay greater attention to the impact between climate change and the solar terms, improving the public’s adaptability to extreme weather and awareness for self-protection.  4.3 Impact of varied scenarios on future extreme precipitation during perilous solar terms Although no researchers have previously considered China’s extreme rainfall from the perspective of the TFST’ timing, there has been growing concern about the increase of extreme precipitation in China with rising carbon emissions (Madakumbura et al., 2021; Pfahl et al., 2017; Wasko et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023d ). Against this backdrop, our study has deliberately adopted a new angle by focusing on the analysis of XiaoShu and DaShu − two solar terms that have been verified as critical periods of extreme rainfall risk − to discuss how the frequency of future extreme precipitation events may change with different carbon emission scenarios. This approach not only transcends traditional seasonal analysis in the temporal scale but also provides unique insights into the understanding of the solar term phenomenon closely associated with traditional agricultural culture. We believe that these two solar terms, DaShu and XiaoShu, are the periods with the highest frequency of extreme precipitation in China for at least the following three reasons: First, during DaShu and XiaoShu, the East Asian monsoon is active (mid-July to early August each year). Second, temperatures typically reach their annual peak during this time, leading to more frequent and intense thermal convection activities. Third, evaporation is particularly significant during DaShu and XiaoShu, and the high temperatures combined with high humidity during this period tend to create an unstable atmospheric condition, which easily triggers severe convective weather, resulting in frequent extreme precipitation events. The studies by Cong et al. (2024)  and Lu et al. (2014)  on the circulation patterns and moisture transport mechanisms of extreme summer precipitation in China have deepened our understanding of these two solar terms. From our statistical results, it is evident that all carbon emission scenarios predict an overall increasing trend in the frequency of extreme precipitation in China’s future, with the trend being most pronounced under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. Under this scenario, global greenhouse gas emissions are expected to continue without restraint, leading to intensified climate warming and thus increasing the probability of extreme precipitation events. Specifically, during the periods of XiaoShu and DaShu, about 30 % of areas in China show a significant increase in the frequency of R95p and R99p extreme rainfall, with confidence levels exceeding 90 %. These two solar terms are critical growth stages for agriculture in most regions of China, and the increasing extreme precipitation trend could significantly negatively affect crop production cycles, leading to reductions in agricultural yield and quality, thus threatening food security and agricultural sustainability. Additionally, our calculations suggest more significant increases in extreme rainfall frequency in the Tibetan region than previously anticipated under this future scenario. As the “Water Tower of Asia”, the Tibetan region plays an immeasurable role in the stability of the climate system, water resource supply, biodiversity conservation, and more for China and all of Asia (Immerzeel et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2022 ). Increased risks of extreme events could lead to more frequent natural disasters like floods, causing unpredictable impacts on the socio-economy and residents’ lives. In contrast, the least significant increase in the frequency of extreme precipitation in China is under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, which assumes that global measures will be taken to limit greenhouse gas emissions, keeping the global warming level below 1.5℃ by the end of this century. A milder trend in this scenario suggests that more aggressive emission reduction actions could effectively lower the frequency of extreme precipitation events in the future, somewhat supporting China’s “sustainable development strategy”. Furthermore, the distribution of extreme precipitation MK trends across different future scenarios also displays spatial heterogeneity. Regions showing a decreasing trend in the SSP1-2.6 scenario are concentrated around the lower reaches of the Yellow River, the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, and most of the Pearl River Basin. Under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, this decreasing trend is focused on the middle reaches of the Yellow River, the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, and parts of the northwest basins, while the Pearl River Basin shows an increasing trend. However, even under the lowest carbon emission scenarios, the frequency of extreme precipitation events during XiaoShu and DaShu is still likely to increase as a whole. This requires policymakers to take preemptive measures in water resource management and flood control strategies, to adapt flexibly according to the actual carbon emission scenario, and to employ more appropriate agricultural management methods and disaster prevention and reduction preparations to mitigate the potential impacts of extreme events.   5 Limitations and Prosepects The main source of uncertainty in this study stems from the bias in data sets. The CHM dataset, serving as the primary reference for historical precipitation data, utilized daily rainfall observations from over 2800 rain gauge stations across and around China (Han et al., 2023 ). Despite an increase in the number of stations compared to previous studies, the CHM data set suffers from an uneven distribution of station density, particularly in regions such as Tibet and Xinjiang, which may lead to data-related uncertainties. Predicting future patterns of extreme precipitation is further complicated by uncertainties in the trends revealed by different scenario models, a persistent challenge within climate science research (Lopez-Cantu et al., 2020 ). Zhu et al. (2021a)  and Zhu et al. (2021b)  evaluated the Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for Global precipitation measurement (IMERG) over mainland China, indicating that IMERG could capture precipitation patterns across the region with general overestimations both spatially and temporally. However, IMERG significantly underestimated precipitation in the southwestern region of the Tibet Plateau during the cold season. Although we attempted to minimize errors from individual simulations by utilizing multi-model ensemble averages when forecasting future rainfall, the process of resampling different GCMs from varying resolutions to a common one and then taking ensemble averages inevitably introduces some degree of uncertainty to data quality (Fig. S3  in the Supplementary Material s). Nevertheless, our results indicate that despite uncertainties in climate response, all scenario models consistently suggest an overall increase in the frequency of extreme rainfall events during the solar terms of XiaoShu and DaShu. This implies that even with inherent uncertainties, the scientific perspectives provided by this research are credible and relevant for future climate predictions and response strategies. As global average temperatures climb, the relationship between warming and extreme rainfall becomes more pronounced. High-temperature events have been proven to facilitate the occurrence of extreme rainfall to some extent by enhancing atmospheric updraft and moisture cycle (G. Wang et al., 2020 ). Our findings also highlight the high risk of extreme precipitation during the critical hot and humid solar terms of XiaoShu and DaShu in China, surpassing other periods. However, our analysis also emphasizes that under climate change, this relationship does not follow a linear pattern but is influenced by complex atmospheric fluctuations and geographic factors. Particularly for a country like China with large geographical complexity, varying terrains—from plateaus and river valleys to vast farmlands—impart specific regional differences to extreme precipitation events. Notably, in the northwestern regions of China, a decreasing trend in the frequency of extreme precipitation during DaShu is observed under future scenarios SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5. Although this decreasing tendency is not significant, when contrasted with the notably increasing trends in other regions, it could potentially lower the vigilance against extreme rainfall. Yet, in our statistics for more extreme EEP6 precipitation events, large parts of the northwest had not experienced EEP6 events in the past 40 years, while such events were recorded in projections for the next 80 years, suggesting a subjective contradiction with the overall non-significant decreasing trend. Without knowing whether this discrepancy is due to uncertainties in our predictions or other causes, referencing recent extreme precipitation events in arid areas like the UAE (Wehbe et al., 2019 ) demonstrates that regions with long-term rainfall deficits are not immune to extreme flooding risks. In conclusion, our research emphasizes that future changes in the frequency of extreme precipitation must be considered in conjunction with the impacts of global temperature rise and local geographic features. Decision-makers should not underestimate extreme precipitation risks at any temporal angle in any geographic region. Investigating from the perspective of the TFST can yield a more nuanced temporal understanding than previous seasonal precipitation studies, offering targeted insights. As the impact of climate change becomes increasingly apparent, future research needs to delve deeper into the complex relationship between global warming and extreme precipitation, focusing especially on regional differences and the occurrence of extreme events in specific periods. In this realm, the TFST serve as an innovative temporal scale for research, capturing weather pattern changes closely related to agricultural practices, thus enhancing our understanding and prediction of potential impacts on agricultural production and socio-economic activities. Future studies could build upon this to explore and forecast hydro-meteorological events associated with different solar terms, such as extreme cold snaps during DaXue and XiaoXue, or compound drought-heatwave-flood events during DaShu and XiaoShu. The innovative significance of the TFST analytical approach lies in merging traditional culture with modern scientific research and bringing new perspectives to seasonal and regional climate impact studies, bolstering adaptation to future climate change. To contend with and mitigate these complex climate risks, future efforts should also focus on developing more effective adaptation strategies, including smart agricultural technologies, the reinforcement of infrastructural climate resilience, and the improvement of emergency response plans. The study of the TFST will guide us in taking timely and appropriate actions to mitigate the risks and damages from potentially exacerbated extreme weather events in the future.  6 Conclusion This study leverages the traditional Chinese calendar system of the TFST to delve into the patterns and trends of both regular and extreme precipitation in China, and finally derives the following conclusions: (1) As nicknames directly related to regular precipitation, GuYu and YuShui in most parts of China show a significant increase in cumulative precipitation and the number of effective rainfall days within 30 days before and after these two solar terms. Statistical results indicate that over the past 40 years, the average difference in cumulative precipitation within 30 days before and after GuYu and YuShui is approximately + 8.7 mm and + 3.4 mm, respectively, with maximum differences of + 236.9 mm and + 105.6 mm. YuShui shows a more pronounced difference in solar terms of the number of effective rainfall days compared to GuYu, while GuYu exhibits more variability in accumulated rainfall. Synthesizing the results, we can confirm a positive correlation between these two solar terms and the increase in spring rainfall, echoing ancient China’s macroscopic descriptions and affirming their objective rationale in characterizing precipitation patterns through natural observation. (2) Over the past 40 years, XiaoShu and DaShu consistently present the highest frequency of extreme precipitation events in China, a pattern set to persist in future scenarios across four different models. Despite these two solar terms being nicknames for describing extreme heat, their proverbs and ancient poems clearly indicate the risk of extreme precipitation during this period. According to our spatiotemporal distribution map of solar terms dominating extreme precipitation (Fig. 4 ), a total of 79.4 % of China’s R95p extreme precipitation events are dominated by the summer solstice (15.1 %), XiaoShu (30.9 %), and DaShu (33.4 %). Geographical statistical data of historical extreme precipitation events revealed distinct trends in latitude and longitude (Fig. 5 ), with regions dominated by XiaoShu and DaShu extreme precipitation approximate with China’s 200 mm and 800 mm isohyet lines, respectively. Moreover, the southeastern coastal regions of China, represented by the Pearl River Basin and the Southeast River Basin, experience extreme precipitation events one to two solar terms earlier than inland areas. The spatial distribution of China’s extreme precipitation patterns shows a significant trend of first increasing and then decreasing from southeast to northwest along the temporal scale. (3) GCMs average simulations based on CMIP6 indicate that under four different future economic pathways, over 55.2 % of China’s regions will experience a concentration of extreme precipitation events during XiaoShu and DaShu. These events are especially prevalent in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, averaging over ten extreme precipitation events exceeding the 95th percentile every five years, with an increasing risk trend over time that has passed the 95 % significance threshold according to the Mann-Kendall trend test. (4) As the solar terms previously experiencing the most extreme precipitation in China, DaShu and XiaoShu will continue to show an overall increasing trend in the frequency of future extreme precipitation across all carbon emission scenarios. The scenario SSP5-8.5 suggests a particularly pronounced increase, with around 30 % of China’s areas showing significant trends in R95p and R99p extreme precipitation frequencies surpassing 90 % significance. In contrast, the SSP1-2.6 scenario illustrates the least significant trend of increasing extreme precipitation in China. Additionally, the spatial distribution of the Mann-Kendall trend for extreme precipitation under different future scenarios indicates spatial heterogeneity. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, regions with decreasing trends are concentrated in the lower Yellow River Basin, mid-lower Yangtze River Basin, and the larger Pearl River Basin. Conversely, under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, this decreasing trend centers on the middle reaches of the Yellow River Basin, the middle Yangtze River Basin, and small parts of the northwestern river basins, whereas the Pearl River Basin shows an increasing trend. By integrating China’s TFST timetable with modern hydro-meteorological research, this study forges an organic union between traditional culture and present-day science. Our results not only statistically validate the acute observational skills of ancient Chinese societies but also provide critical guidance for formulating targeted, timelier flood control and dispatch strategies. This includes the regular assessment of flood risks and the construction of immediate flood warning systems. In summary, our research offers new insights for disaster prevention and disaster management in China and other monsoon-affected countries, providing innovative perspectives and a solid theoretical foundation for managing extreme weather events brought about by global climate change.
1 Introduction The Mediterranean region is prone to marked precipitation and climate seasonality (Lulla, 1987; Vicente-Serrano, 2006; Quintana Seguí et al., 2010 ). In these regions, the majority of humid areas are located in the mountains, while lowlands and coastal regions are dominated by human activities and urban areas. Therefore, coastal socio-economic activities and ecosystems heavily rely on water from these mountainous headwaters, which are increasingly under threat from agricultural development, population growth, and climate change. These factors are already impacting the water cycle and are expected to intensify (Leduc et al., 2017 ). In the Mediterranean domain, these shifts affect continental water sources, where global warming has caused a decrease in streamflow (−0.13 to −0.25 l/s.km2 .year) for the Ebro and Sava watersheds (Lutz et al., 2016 ). Annual rainfall generally remains steady, but some areas experience notable decreases, with distinctively long-term distribution (e.g., a 4 % reduction in rainfall per 1 °C global temperature increase) (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), 2023 ). Future projections indicate more frequent and severe droughts, reduced streamflow, and precipitation in central and southern Mediterranean regions (Moutahir et al., 2017; Cramer et al., 2018 ). Considering this mountainous context, marked variability in rainfall and climate and future projections, baseflow plays, and will play, a growing important role in water management, withdrawals, river flow, and ecological continuity, particularly during dry periods and droughts (Singh et al., 2019 ). It is therefore an important component of hydrographs and streamflow that needs to be better characterized over time and space, as its definition may vary depending on the applied framework. It can be viewed as a reflection of watershed processes, representing the combined contribution, along with other components, to streamflow (typically surface runoff and baseflow). Baseflow is often considered to originate from deep groundwater and delayed subsurface sources, such as shallow underground storage (Hall, 1968; Smakhtin, 2001; Tallaksen, 1995 ). Baseflow has been studied in various hydroclimatic contexts worldwide, including the Mediterranean region. Notably, research has covered lowlands (Lu et al., 2022 ), agricultural areas (Kronholm and Capel, 2015 ), continental mountains (Miller et al., 2015 ), arid and semi-arid regions (Rimmer and Hartmann, 2014; Shao et al., 2020 ), and watersheds of various sizes (Lott and Stewart, 2016; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Its relative contribution to streamflow varies widely, influenced by the studied area and context. For instance, in arid to semi-arid watersheds in China’s Yellow River basin (2,799 to 10,653 km2, 2.58 to 19.4 % average slope, mostly loess hilly landform landscape), mean annual baseflow contributions range from 35.4 to 50.2 % (Hu et al., 2021 ). In the state of Michigan (warm summer humid continental climate − USA), covering the period from 1967 to 2011, 17 watersheds exhibited a mean annual baseflow contribution of 71 % (Zhang et al., 2013b ). In temperate and Mediterranean environments, higher baseflow contributions have been observed. For example, Lu et al. (2022)  found that over 30 years, three temperate lowland watersheds (ranging from 95 to 893 km2 , mainly sandy and loamy) displayed baseflow relative contributions ranging between 70 % and 84 %. A small wet Mediterranean watershed in Italy (3 km2 , made of sandstone) displayed seasonal variability, with values ranging from 90 % in dry conditions to 40 % in wet, rainy conditions (Longobardi et al., 2016 ). Finally, watersheds in the upper Manavgat River in the Taurus Mountains (karstic Mediterranean environment) showed a mean annual baseflow contribution of 73 % to 88 % (Eris and Wittenberg, 2015 ). Nevertheless, a scientific gap persists as no studies have yet explored the baseflow component in a mountainous Mediterranean environment with hard-rock aquifers and mostly perennial streams. Further evidence is required in this region, taking into account the specific context and resulting water management issues. However characterizing baseflow on a watershed scale across space and time is a challenge due to the difficulties of direct measurement (Cheng et al., 2022 ). To address this requirement, several methods classified into two main branches have been developed (Hu et al., 2021 ). The first category, known as tracer-based methods, utilizes natural environmental tracers, including geochemical and isotopic tools. The End-Member Mixing Analysis 'EMMA' (Christophersen et al., 1990 ) is a widely employed approach, assuming that the tracers defining end-members remain conservative and stable over time (Barthold et al., 2011; Delsman et al., 2013 ). The second category encompasses more empirical and analytical techniques, namely the non tracer-based methods, such as digital filters, and are intended for different purposes. Some may focus on the scale of rainy events, while others aim to compute baseflow responses from long continuous streamflow time series (Mei and Anagnostou, 2015 ). Tracer-based tools are more effective because they take into account chemical and physical processes and components such as baseflow at the watershed scale, but they can be costlier, challenging, and time-consuming to implement (Stewart et al., 2007; Mei and Anagnostou, 2015; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Non tracer-based methods, relying on empirical information, are more dependent on parameterization and user assumptions, but their outputs can be easily automated and reproduced using only streamflow data as input to derive baseflow contribution (Gonzales et al., 2009; Mei and Anagnostou, 2015 ). Eckhardt (2005)  suggested combining the two approaches to overcome the limitations of the two methods by calibrating non tracer-based methods with isotopic and geochemical data for long-term baseflow analysis. The present article therefore aims to characterize the baseflow component in a mountainous Mediterranean context with hard-rock aquifers under climate change conditions, by enhancing the understanding of baseflow mechanisms and patterns using innovative methodology. The innovation in the methodology comes from the tools employed to do this, i.e. the use of the first calibrated and validated non tracer-based methods in a Mediterranean area presenting hard-rock aquifers. The calibration and validation processes and the investigation focuses on two Corsican watersheds, the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu, as application models. These watersheds share common hydroclimatic, hydrogeological, and morphometric characteristics with other hard-rock aquifers in the Mediterranean mountains, making Corsica an ideal location for this research and allowing for the study of baseflow in this specific context (Erostate et al., 2019; Juhlke et al., 2021; Nlend et al., 2023; Santoni et al., 2016 ). The innovative method involving the first calibration of non tracer-based methods (empirical filtering and analytical digital filtering methods) was performed with natural tracer data (end-member mixing models) from prior work (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ), undertaken for the specific mountainous Mediterranean context. This calibration procedure of non tracer-based methods was conducted on the Tavignanu watershed. A protocol to assess then the performance and uncertainty of these calibrated non tracer-based methods is employed on the Fiumaltu watershed to validate and select the most suitable method for this specific context. To address the scientific gap regarding baseflow in such regions, functional analysis and temporal (seasonal, and interannual) characterization of baseflow is achieved using the selected and validated non tracer-based method, the two-parameter analytical recursive digital filter (TPDF) by Eckhardt (2005) . The seasonal and interannual distribution of the baseflow index (BFI), which is the ratio of baseflow to total streamflow, is examined as an indicator of deep groundwater and delayed subsurface flow contributions sustaining streamflow. The study also explores baseflow behaviour, mechanisms, and patterns, its origin, its relation with rainfall, and BFI distribution during a specific drought year, a phenomenon that is expected to become more frequent in the region, based on climate projections (Calvache et al., 2020; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), 2022; Tramblay et al., 2020 ).  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study sites 2.1.1 Location of study sites and morphometric characteristics This study was conducted on the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu watersheds on the island of Corsica, France, situated in the western part of the Mediterranean basin (Fig. 1   − a). The Tavignanu watershed covers a total area of 795.74 km2 , with a rounded shape (Gravelius index of 1.28), and a well-developed hydrographic network. The main stream is 88.7 km long, with 76 listed tributaries and a Strahler number of 5. The slope distribution follows the shift of the main geological features, decreasing from the steep mountain tops towards the watershed outlet with an average gradient of 23.7°. The Fiumaltu watershed has a total area of 126.67 km2  and exhibits a more tapered shape, indicated by a Gravelius index of 1.52. Although the Fiumaltu River is smaller than the Tavignanu (30.9 km), it collects 34 tributaries along its flow path, also having a Strahler number of 5. The average slope index (24.8°) and slope distribution are relatively similar. Refer to Fig. 1  − b for watershed locations and elevations, and Fig. 1  – c for a representation of the hydrographic network.  2.1.2 Hydroclimatic, hydrological context and land use The coastal regions of both watersheds exhibit a hot summer csa climate, mid-mountain areas a hot summer csb climate, and higher altitudes a subarctic dfc climate (Köppen and Geiger, 1930 ). This Mediterranean hydroclimatic context implies significant interseasonal and interannual temperature and precipitation variations (Bonaccorso et al., 2003; Vicente-Serrano, 2006 ). Precipitation distribution follows the northern Mediterranean climate pattern, with the lowest amounts in hot, dry summers and the highest in wet, mild months. Notably, higher altitude mountains are wetter, while coastal plains are drier and warmer. The mountainous landscape, particularly in the Tavignanu watershed where snowfall occurs, contributes to a torrential river regime due to seasonality, intense rainfall, and steep topography. Both streams exhibit perennial characteristics and follow a northern Mediterranean pattern where low flows align with hot, dry summers, and high flows occur during cold, mild winters. For the future, models predict that global change will further impact hydroclimatic conditions in the western Mediterranean with more extreme weather. Reduced precipitation (10–30 % during the dry season) and temperature increases (1 to 3.1 °C) are expected by the end of the 21st century (Cramer et al., 2018; Seker and Gumus, 2022 ). This could result in further impacts on water resources, affecting their sustainability, quantity, quality, and use and management (Cao et al., 2022 ). River flow is expected to decrease by 10 % to 50 % by the end of the 21st century as well. Furthermore, longer droughts and shorter aquifer recharge periods are also anticipated (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change IPCC, 2022 ). Both watersheds have been monitored daily at stations since April 1960, with a data gap in the 90 s, for continuous water levels and computed discharge data. Mean daily discharge data are directly accessible from the French Hydroportail database (https://hydro.eaufrance.fr/ ) and have been used from 1997 to 2019 for the Fiumaltu at the Acitaja Bridge, and until 2021 for the Tavignanu watershed at the Faiu Bridge. The average monthly discharges for this period (1997–2019/2021) are 11.1 m3 /s for the Tavignanu and 1.37 m3 /s for the Fiumaltu (see Fig. 1  – c for location of monitoring stations). The mean annual precipitation amount in the Tavignanu (1997–2021) is approximately 974 mm, while in the Fiumaltu (1997–2019) it is about 1116 mm. The average monthly temperature recorded during the period of 1997–2019 is 13.1 °C for the Fiumaltu and 11.9 °C during the period of 1997–2021 for the Tavignanu. The average monthly potential evapotranspiration is 45.4 mm for the Fiumaltu during the period of 1997–2019 and 43.1 mm for Tavignanu during the period of 1997–2021. Please refer to Table 1   for a summary of the hydroclimatic settings of the study sites over the period 1997–2021. The averages were computed aggregating data of weather stations (located upstream of each monitoring station) from the French national weather service, Meteo France (https://meteofrance.com/ ) (two stations each in Corti and Vivariu, and one in Venacu for the Tavignanu, and La Porta, Quercitellu, and Scata for Fiumaltu, see Fig. 1  − b,c). See Fig. 2   for discharge and precipitation data patterns over 1997–2019/2021 for both watersheds (a) and the study period for the Tavignanu at the Faiu Bridge (b) and the Fiumaltu at the Acitaja Bridge (c). The Tavignanu watershed features diverse land uses, with forests covering most of the area (87.85 %), agriculture (11.3 %) near the river mouth and coastal plain, and limited urban areas (0.85 %). Corti is the largest town in the watershed with 7549 inhabitants. In the Fiumaltu watershed, higher-altitude areas are predominantly forested (93.1 %). Urban areas (0.8 %) consist of small villages near agricultural fields (6.1 %), primarily located in the lower-altitude areas close to the coastal plain. Folelli, with 3355 inhabitants, is the largest town in the watershed.  2.1.3 Geological and hydrogeological background The Fiumaltu watershed, ranging from 50 to 800 m.a.s.l, exhibits dominant metamorphic geological features, including serpentinites, black quartz schists, marmoreal limestones, and quartzites in the headwatershed, followed by alternating carbonate–silicate schists (Guieu and Mathely, 1994; Rossi and Rouire, 1994; Genevier et al., 2013a ). Toward the river mouth, recent Tertiary sedimentary rocks (succession of marls, sands, sandy marls, conglomerates with rhyolite pebbles) and Quaternary formations (post-glacial alluvium), are present (Guieu and Mathely, 1994 ). The capacity of hard-rock aquifers in metamorphic units is heterogeneous but remains significant. Groundwater can circulate in the deep (50 to 100 m below the surface) weathered surface layer and the network of faults and fractures (the permeable stratiform layer, the ‘SFL’). Shallower groundwater, percolating towards the deeper SFL, may also come from the unconsolidated subsurface (0 to 50 m below the surface) part of the hard-rock aquifers, the saprolites or alterites layer, which is less transmissive but more capacitive (Wyns et al., 1999; Lachassagne et al., 2021 ). In addition, numerous ferruginous springs with high mineralization are found near the river (Genevier et al., 2013b; Dupuy et al., 2021 ). Upstream to downstream, the Tavignanu watershed presents three main geological features: high mountains (over 800 m.a.s.l) of igneous origin composed mainly of monzogranites and granodiorites, mid-mountain areas (50 to 800 m.a.s.l) resting on a metamorphic ophiolitic base of carbonate–silicate schists, and a coastal plain with Tertiary sedimentary rocks (marls, sands, sandy marls and conglomerates) covered by Quaternary post-glacial alluvial deposits (Rossi and Rouire, 1994 ). The whole watershed has heterogeneous but significant aquifer hydrodynamic properties as well. In the same way, groundwater in igneous features can flow through the most superficial alteration profiles (the subsurface component or end-member, represented by the alterites) or much deeper into the weathered bedrock through the network of pre-existing well-connected fractures and joints (the deep groundwater component or end-member – the SFL) (Frissant et al., 2010; Lachassagne et al., 2021 ). Refer to Fig. 1  − c for simplified geological maps.   2.2 Data collection and analysis Field surveys and stream water samples were collected monthly at both monitoring stations (Acitaja Bridge and Faiu Bridge for Fiumaltu and Tavignanu rivers, respectively) from September 2017 to September 2019 for in situ measurements, stable isotopes, and major ion analyses. On-site measurements, including electrical conductivity ‘EC’, dissolved oxygen, pH, and temperature, were taken using a WTW 3310 multi-parameter and a WTW 3310 IDS oximeter (WTW GmbH, Weilheim, Germany). Bicarbonate (HCO3 – ) concentrations were determined through on-site volumetric titration (HACH Company, Loveland, USA). Samples for stable water isotope analysis (δ18 O and δ2 H) were collected in 20 ml amber glass bottles to eliminate the presence of air space. Analyses were conducted using a DLT-100 liquid–water stable isotope analyzer (Los Gatos Research, San Jose, USA) following the International Atomic Energy Agency analytical procedure (IAEA, 2007 ). Water samples for the analysis of major dissolved ions (Na+ , K+ , Mg2+ , Cl- , NO3 –  and SO4 2- ) were filtered through 0.45 μm nitrocellulose membranes and collected in two 50 mL polyethylene bottles, one of which was acidified for cation analysis using ultrapure HNO3 . Major ion concentrations were determined using a Dionex ICS 1100 ion chromatograph (Thermo Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). The analysis of major dissolved ions and stable isotopes in water was conducted at the Hydrogeology Department (CNRS UMR 6134 SPE, University of Corsica, France). The field surveys, specific monthly rainfall data during the study period on the Tavignanu from September 2017 to September 2019, and all the tracer datasets detailed above come from (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ).  2.3 Baseflow separation tools 2.3.1 Non tracer-based methods, recession analysis, and BFImax  estimation Non tracer-based methods, including empirical to analytical filtering and digital filter methods, are easy to use for baseflow analysis because requiring only streamflow data as input. The results can also be easily replicated and involve few hypotheses (Mei and Anagnostou, 2015 ). The filter methods include local minimum, sliding, and fixed interval (Pettyjohn and Henning, 1979 ). These filter methods automatically compute baseflow by connecting low points within specific intervals on the streamflow hydrograph. The width of the interval is empirically determined following:(1) N = A 0 . 2      Where N is the number of days after runoff cessation, the interval width can be calibrated to the nearest number between 3 and 11, equal to 2 N, and A is the watershed area in km2 . Digital filters derived from signal analysis (Nathan and McMahon, 1990 ) improve previous filtering methods by introducing the linear relation between storage and discharge (Yang et al., 2021 ). One-parameter filters usually used comprise but are not limited to (Lyne and Hollick, 1979 ), (Chapman, 1991 ), (Chapman and Maxwell, 1996 ). Eckhardt, (2005) , proposed a new digital filter with an additional parameter, to better constrain geological and hydrogeological features of watersheds (Raffensperger et al., 2017; Eckhardt, 2023 ). Eckhardt (2005)  also notes that all one-parameter filters are special cases of the Two-Parameter digital filter ‘TPDF’. Baseflow using the TPDF is computed as follows:(2) b t  = 1 - B F I m a x     × α × b t - 1    + ( 1 - α )  × B F I m a x   × Q t   1 - α × B F I m a x         Where b t    is the baseflow discharge in m3 /s at any time t, α is the first filter parameter, ranging from 0 to 1, and BFI  max     is the second parameter, ranging from 0 to 1 and representing the maximum baseflow index that can be computed (BFImax  value of 1 would indicate 100 % baseflow contribution so that the storage and infiltration capacity of aquifers is high e.i.). Both digital filter parameters can be estimated through a recession analysis for α and various approaches for BFImax . The filter parameter α is usually associated with the recession constant K, found as the slope of an individual recession curve in a semi-logarithmic hydrograph representation (Kissel and Schmalz, 2020 ). The TPDF also needs the BFImax  parameter, which is not directly measurable (Eckhardt, 2005; Longobardi et al., 2016 ). To address this, a backward filter for BFImax estimation was proposed (Collischonn and Fan, 2013 ). Gonzales et al. (2009)  used tracer data, and Rimmer and Hartmann (2014)  proposed an algorithm minimizing the root-mean-square value of BFImax . The backward filter also assumes a linear relationship between groundwater discharge and storage over long recession periods:(3) b ( t - 1 )   = b t  α     Where b t    is the baseflow discharge (m3 /s) at any time t. Equation (5)  acts as a backward filter, stopping when baseflow is greater than streamflow. As the BFI represents the long-term baseflow to streamflow ratio, BFImax  can be estimated as:(4) B F I  m a x   = ∑ t = 1  n  b t   ∑ t = 1  n  Q t       In this study, the Sephydro online application (Danielescu et al., 2018 ) was used for daily baseflow separation applying several non tracer-based methods. The application includes the aforementioned filtering methods (Pettyjohn and Henning, 1979 ) and one to multi-parameter recursive digital filters (Lyne and Hollick, 1979; Chapman, 1991; Chapman and Maxwell, 1996; Eckhardt, 2005 ) using time series of daily streamflow data as the only input. The N parameter for the filtering methods was calibrated to the nearest number between 3 and 11 by trial and error. K for the digital filters was estimated through recession analysis, following the linear reservoir hypothesis (Boussinesq, 1877; Maillet, 1905; Horton, 1933; Thomas et al., 2015 ), implying that streamflow in dry conditions and recession periods is composed solely of baseflow and decreases exponentially:(5) Q t  = Q 0  × e a t       where Q t    is the streamflow discharge in m3 /s at any time t, Q 0    is the initial discharge when the recession begins ,  a     is a negative constant and the expression e  a      is generally replaced by the recession constant K or the first filter parameter α  :(6) Q t  =  Q 0  × K t   o r  Q t  =  Q 0  × α t     Master Recession Curves ‘MRC’ (Nathan and McMahon, 1990 ) were constructed to characterize the overall baseflow response, encompassing all individual recession segments from June to September 1996–2021, in the Tavignanu watershed. The matching strip and correlation methods (Langbein, 1938 ) were utilized to build MRC, determining K and the filter parameter α (Rimmer and Hartmann, 2014; Saraiva Okello et al., 2018; Kissel and Schmalz, 2020; Neira, 2021 ). The matching strip method was used on the R.C. software (Gregor and Malík, 2012 ), while the correlation method employed Excel spreadsheets. The USGS GWtoolbox’s RECESS tool (Rutledge and Mesko, 1996 ) was used to create an MRC and also included a module for estimating K through the correlation method. In this study, the BFImax  parameter was estimated by the backward filter within the GWtoolbox and tracer data. The backward filter, started at the end of summer 2019 (09/29), worked backward for two full years (09/29/2017) on the Tavignanu watershed, assuming a linear relationship between groundwater discharge and storage over long recession periods.  2.3.2 Tracer-based methods This study tested hypotheses to determine the best reference tracer baseflow for calibration, considering different behaviours (Fig. 2  – b). Tracer data were retained to define the reference tracer baseflow for calibration because they are more reliable and objective, and can accurately describe hydrogeological processes and components, such as baseflow contribution, due to their field-based nature (Mei and Anagnostou, 2015; Zhang et al., 2017 ). This included using baseflow derived from the two-component Conductivity Mass Balance ‘CMB’ using EC as a tracer (Zhang et al., 2013a ). The three-component EMMA (Christophersen et al., 1990 ) was also considered, with baseflow identified as the contribution of deep groundwater from the SFL only or deep groundwater plus delayed subsurface flow from the alterites layer (Fig. 2  – b). Both CMB and EMMA are used to define the relative contribution of different components to streamflow over time (Barthold et al., 2011 ), differing only in their mathematical definition. The three-component EMMA’s overdetermined set of equations was solved analytically using a least-squares procedure with an automated Excel spreadsheet:(7) Q s  1   C s a    C s b      1  1  1   C 1 a   C 2 a   C 3 a    C 1 b   C 2 b   C 3 b      - 1   = Q 1    Q 2    Q 3         Where Q s    represents streamflow discharge (m3 /s), Q 1   ,Q 2 ,     and Q 3    are discharge of contributing end-members and C represents environmental natural tracer concentration associated with end-members 1, 2, and 3. Superscripts (a, b, c) refer to natural tracers and subscripts (1, 2, 3) to the selected end-members. The CMB mass balance equation was solved using an Excel spreadsheet as follows (example for Q1 ):(8) Q 1  = Q s  × C s  - C 2    C 1  - C 2        Where Q s    is streamflow, Q 1    and Q 2    the discharge of the two contributing components, and C is the concentration of the associated natural tracer. EMMA was applied to define contributions of deep groundwater from the SFL, delayed subsurface flow from the alterites layer, and surface runoff in the two watersheds from September 2017 to September 2019 during each field survey (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ). End-members concentrations were estimated graphically using EC, Li+ , Ca2+ /Mg2+  ratio for the Tavignanu and EC, Mg2+ , K+  for the Fiumaltu watershed. Tracer choices reflect geological differences between the watersheds (Hofer et al., 1997 ). Additionally, CMB was applied in the Tavignanu watershed, considering two end-members: surface runoff and baseflow (no distinction between more superficial and deeper aquifer contributions). Baseflow concentration was set at the maximum observed EC (234 µS/cm), assuming rivers are solely baseflow during low-flow periods. Surface runoff was set at the lowest observed value (90 µS/cm), corresponding to wet periods (Stewart et al., 2007; Pellerin et al., 2008; Lott and Stewart, 2016; Zhang et al., 2017 ).  2.3.3 Calibration procedure of non tracer-based methods The calibration process was focused on the Tavignanu watershed, using 25 monthly data points from the tracer dataset during the study period (09/2017–09/2019). Following calibration procedures carried out in diverse hydroclimatic contexts (Lott and Stewart, 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Saraiva Okello et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2020 ), further steps were taken to enhance the match between computed baseflow from non tracer-based methods and tracer data. Firstly, a visual inspection assessed the consistency of computed baseflow curves and their proximity with tracer data on the hydrograph. Secondly, statistical indices used for hydrological model calibration and validation performance were selected for their robustness under various global hydroclimatic conditions (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). These indices include the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency ‘NSE,’ Absolute Percent Bias ‘PBIAS,’ RMSE-observation standard deviation ratio ‘RSR,’ and coefficient of determination ‘R².’ Table 2  , modified from (Moriasi et al., 2007; Carlos Mendoza et al., 2021 ), summarizes the general performance and function of these statistical evaluation indices for a monthly time step. Finally, emphasis was placed on computed baseflow statistics including the BFI and b > Q ratio. The b > Q ratio is an indicator of digital filter performance showing how often computed baseflow is greater than streamflow (Danielescu et al., 2018 ). The calibration was focused on the Tavignanu watershed, using 25 monthly data points from the tracer dataset during the study period (09/2017–09/2019).  2.3.4 Validation procedure of non tracer-based methods Validation was carried out in the Fiumaltu watershed for the same study period, using 25 more monthly tracer data points to establish validated and approved non tracer-based methods for mountainous Mediterranean watersheds. The validation procedure follows the same protocol described in section 2.4 involving a visual inspection of computed baseflow hydrographs, performance assessment using statistical indices, and examination of baseflow statistics from calibrated non tracer-based methods. This fulfils the requirement for at least two years of complete tracer data for mass balance and mixing model procedures (Hooper, 2003 ), with two hydrological years used for calibration and validation. Furthermore, performance improves with higher time steps and discrete monthly tracer data are adequate for the calibration and validation of non-tracer-based methods (Moriasi et al., 2007; Saraiva Okello et al., 2018 ). The final validation and approval of the model also considers the uncertainties encountered at the different stages of the method. These include the uncertainty linked to the definition of the reference tracer baseflow, which is used to calibrate and validate the non tracer-based method, and the uncertainties associated with the output of calibrated and validated non tracer-based methods, notably, the computed baseflow and BFI over long periods. In tracer-based methods, uncertainties in mixing fractions are linked to analytical precision and to the tracers themselves (identification of end-members, variations in their concentration, and non-conservative tracers) (Beven and Binley, 1992; Barthold et al., 2011 ). In non tracer-based methods, uncertainties in computed baseflow and BFI are related to the input streamflow data such as inaccuracies in flood stage, discharge measurement, and rating curve extrapolation, (Lang et al., 2006 ) and to the selection of parameters (N, α and BFImax ) (Eckhardt, 2012 ). In this study, both uncertainties have been taken into account by the general uncertainty propagation technique following (Genereux, 1998 ):(9) W y  = ∂ y  d x 1    × W x 1     2  + ∂ y  d x 2    × W x 2     2  + ⋯ + ∂ y  d x n    × W x n     2      Subscript y is a measured parameter which is a function of several measurands (subscripts xn ), ∂ y  d x n      are the partial derivatives of y with respect to each measurand xn  and W represents the absolute uncertainty related to y and xn . It was used by (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ) to constrain the propagation of uncertainty in each mixing fraction (contributing end-members) in the three-component EMMA model, and in the present study to define the propagated uncertainty in computed BFI by calibrated and validated non tracer-based methods. Subsequent general propagated uncertainties are given for the t statistics for the 70 % confidence interval. A workflow diagram is presented in Fig. 3   to summarize the materials, methods, and steps utilized for calibrating and validating non-tracer-based methods with tracer-based methods in a mountainous Mediterranean context.    3 Results & discussion 3.1 Selection of the reference tracer baseflow Before calibration, it was important to first assess non tracer-based methods performance in a Mediterranean mountainous context and then, to select the best reference tracer baseflow, as they behave differently based on the method used (Fig. 2  − b). Twenty-five tests of non tracer-based methods were conducted by randomly adjusting parameters (N, α, BFImax ), with due consideration of the values recommended in the literature in light of the characteristics of the study sites (Pettyjohn and Henning, 1979; Lyne and Hollick, 1979; Chapman, 1991; Chapman and Maxwell, 1996; Eckhardt, 2005 ). The performance overview of these tests, following the procedure in section 2.4, revealed consistently poor results, emphasizing the necessity for calibration in a Mediterranean mountainous context. As described in section 2.3, a three-component EMMA derived contributions from the SFL (deep groundwater component), the alterites layer (subsurface flow), and surface runoff in the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu watersheds (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ). A two-component CMB was also performed based on the assumptions mentioned earlier. To select the most efficient reference tracer baseflow for calibration and validation, a performance comparison of all tracer-based with non tracer-based methods was carried out. Although all non tracer-based methods performed poorly (except for Chapman and Chapman and Maxwell digital filters), the best performance was obtained when defining baseflow as contributions from deep groundwater combined with delayed subsurface flow in the three-component EMMA. The results of these tests demonstrated the necessity to calibrate and validate the non tracer-based methods for this Mediterranean context with hard-rock aquifers. Furthermore, the three-component EMMA was selected as the reference tracer baseflow for calibration and validation as it demonstrated the best performance with all non-tracer-based methods in the initial testing. In addition, the aforementioned tests permitted the preliminary selection of value intervals for the parameters N, α and BFImax of the non tracer-based methods for subsequent calibration and validation processes. This was defined based on the most optimal performance observed during the twenty-five random tests. The table in Supplementary Material S1  provides a test example with N=3, α = 0.4, BFImax = 0.25, and the best performance is observed between the Lyne and Hollick filter and the three component EMMA.
