This model was then selected as the reference tracer baseflow.  3.2 Calibration of non tracer-based methods for mountainous Mediterranean use 3.2.1 Estimation of α parameter – recession analysis The R.C. software and RECESS tool automatically select recession curves by specifying the analysis period and minimum flow duration. For this study (period June to September 1996–2021 on the Tavignanu watershed), continuous streamflow decrease during dry conditions in the Mediterranean context (Neira, 2021 ) was assumed. Manual inspection of the recession curves on a semi-logarithmic graph has led to the selection of 24 linear-shaped curves following the linear reservoir assumption for all recession analyses and MRC construction. The α values obtained are 0.9425 (Excel spreadsheets) and 0.979 (RECESS tool) for the correlation method, 0.981 for the matching strip method (R.C. software) and 0.989 for the MRC constructed using the RECESS tool. An overall average α of 0.973 and a high mean α (considering only the highest values) of 0.983 were calculated. Fig. 4   a, b and c illustrates K and α values obtained depending on the method. The resulting MRC from the RECESS tool appears curved, but linear portions can be identified, consistent with findings by Kissel and Schmalz (2020) . Typical K values for surface runoff (0.2–0.8), interflow (0.7–0.94) and baseflow (0.93–0.995) agree with the α values obtained (Tallaksen, 1995 ) and the preselected values intervals for this parameter that were identified previously. Calibration tests can now be carried out to optimize performance with different α values for one-parameter digital filters (Chapman, Chapman and Maxwell, Lyne and Hollick). The TPDF also requires prior estimation of the BFImax parameter before calibration tests.  3.2.2 Estimation of BFImax  parameter A range of BFImax  values on the Tavignanu watershed were estimated using the previous α values. The Excel spreadsheet and the RECESS tool correlation method estimated BFImax  at 0.76 and 0.42, respectively. The matching strip method provided an estimated BFImax of 0.39, while the MRC constructed using the RECESS tool yielded 0.28. The overall mean α resulted in a BFImax  value of 0.53, and the high mean α was 0.37 for BFImax . Fig. 4 -d) illustrates the estimated BFImax  value using the backward filter with α derived from the correlation method (0.9423). Despite initial assumptions (Neira, 2021 ) of higher BFImax  values during dry conditions in Mediterranean regions (see Fig. 4 -a), the obtained BFImax  values appear lower, potentially influenced by estimating its value over the entire year and not just during dry conditions. Consequently, and following the recommendations of Eckhardt (2005) , a BFImax  parameter was also estimated using tracer data. It was set at the highest tracer BFI observed during the study period in the Tavignanu (0.91 for October 2017) and Fiumaltu (0.81 for October 2017). Calibration tests can now be conducted using different combinations of previously estimated α for the one-parameter digital filters and BFImax  for the TPDF. The N parameter can be calibrated manually by trial and error for the filtering methods.  3.2.3 Calibration of non tracer-based methods with natural tracers The calibration process for filtering methods (local minimum, fixed, and sliding interval) involves manual adjustments to the N parameter (number of days after which runoff has ceased), by trial and error and taking into account the pre-selected value intervals of the N parameter. Optimal N values were found as 5 for the sliding interval and 7 for both the local minimum and fixed interval methods. Notably, the local minimum method gave the best performance with a superior RSR of 0.39, a PBIAS of 7.08, and an NSE of 0.84. These results suggest the calibrated local minimum is the most suitable filtering method for the mountainous Mediterranean conditions. The performance before and after calibration is comparable, with all indicators ranking very well, except absolute PBIAS, which improved from good (12.05) to very good (7.08) after calibration. Values during periods of high-flows are less constrained due to imperfect matching with tracer data during peak flows. However, the calibrated local minimum method exhibited improved fit during the low-flow conditions. See Table in Supplementary Material S2  for before-after calibration comparison. Among digital filters, the TPDF was chosen because of its better performance and broader physical basis, with the addition of the BFImax  parameter (Raffensperger et al., 2017; Eckhardt, 2023 ). Several tests were conducted to determine the optimal performance using different combinations of calibrated α and BFImax . The results consistently showed improved good to excellent performance for the TPDF for most combinations, except for R2 . It has been observed here that the BFImax  parameter had a greater impact on the computed baseflow data compared to the α parameter. The optimal combination of calibrated α and BFImax  parameters for the TPDF was determined to be α = 0.979 and BFImax = 0.81. While this choice slightly reduces the overall performance of the Tavignanu watershed, it remains highly acceptable (RSR=0.54, absolute PBIAS=3.38, NSE=0.71, R2  = 0.71). See Table in Supplementary Material S2  for before-after TPDF performance comparison. In addition, the b > Q index, below 30 % for a dataset of 886 points, indicates a good performance as well. Table 3   shows the performance evaluation using the statistical indices for both calibration and validation. Visual inspection of computed baseflow after calibration showed improved congruence during both high and low-flow periods (Fig. 5  -a). Consequently, the chosen parameter set (α = 0.979, BFImax = 0.81) appears well-suited for the hydroclimatic context of the study. However, to validate their applicability, further testing is recommended in another Mediterranean mountainous watershed (Fiumaltu River). While the two calibrated methods, local minimum and TPDF, exhibit comparable overall performance (see Table in Supplementary Material S2 ), the baseflow curves of the TPDF display better congruence during both low and high-flow conditions. As the local minimum method may present non-significant behaviour, such as plateaus (Raffensperger et al., 2017 ), the calibrated TPDF was then selected among all non-tracer-based methods for the validation phase in the Fiumaltu watershed.   3.3 Validation of calibrated TPDF and frameworks for mountainous Mediterranean area use The calibrated α parameters (0.979) and BFImax  (0.81) for TPDF were applied in the Fiumaltu watershed for validation. Visual inspection reveals proximity of computed baseflow data with tracers during low-flows. Computed data are slightly underestimated in recession periods but match tracers closely in peak flows (Fig. 5 -b). Performance is excellent for R2 , good for RSR and NSE, but poor for PBIAS. The b > Q index is very good with a value of 18.48 % for 947 data points. PBIAS is the only indicator whose performance is poor. Moriasi et al. (2007)  suggest that lower performance during validation may occur due to previously fixed input parameters (N, α, BFImax ). In addition, the calibration conditions and assumptions may differ from validation. Despite both watersheds being mountainous and Mediterranean with hard-rock aquifers, environmental variations may contribute to performance differences. Overall, validation suggests good model performance. The validated TPDF can directly compute baseflow discharge values from streamflow data alone, but caution is warranted due to its underlying assumptions. Specifically, it assumes a linear relationship between discharge and storage, which may not be true in scenarios involving significant groundwater storage variations, such as seasonal or interannual fluctuations, and aquifer properties regarding storage levels (Aksoy et al., 2009; Hall, 1968 ). Moreover, uncertainties associated with the TPDF are carefully considered. This acknowledges the propagated uncertainties within each mixing fraction of the three-component EMMA model, which serves as a reference tracer for baseflow and is considered acceptable (Mattei et al., 2021; 2024 ). The propagated uncertainties in computed baseflow and BFI in the validated TPDF are handled similarly. Refer to Supplementary Materials S3 and S4  for a comprehensive overview of general uncertainties related to mixing fractions, computed baseflow and BFI, associated partial derivatives, and detailed results tables for both the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu watersheds. The now approved TPDF can be applied over extended streamflow recording periods to conduct functional analysis and characterize baseflow patterns in mountainous Mediterranean watersheds where geochemical or isotopic data is lacking. The Mediterranean context exhibits a pronounced seasonality in rainfall and streamflow, influenced by high altitude gradients and a subarctic subclimate (Köppen and Geiger, 1930 ). The approved TPDF is applicable to Mediterranean watersheds with diverse geological features but similar hydrogeological properties such as hard-rock aquifers, morphometric characteristics with a well-developed hydrographic network, and size.  3.4 Long seasonal and interannual behaviour of baseflow in mountainous Mediterranean watersheds highlighted by the distribution of the BFI Baseflow separation using the previously approved TPDF was conducted for both watersheds from 1997 to 2019 for Fiumaltu and from 1997 to 2021 for Tavignanu. A more detailed examination focused on the BFI, specifically its long seasonal and interannual distribution at both sites and its correlation with recorded rainfall amounts. Additionally, consideration of extreme rainfall deficit periods between 2017 and 2019 aimed to observe the potential impact of droughts on the very short-term (monthly time step) distribution of BFI, as these conditions are predicted to recur. The geochemical composition of streamflow during the 2017–2019 period in the Fiumaltu watershed was considered to identify and confirm the terrigenous origin of BFI and baseflow, providing a basis for correlation of discussions. 3.4.1 Relationship between the BFI and rainfall in a climate change context The potential impact of climate change on baseflow responses over time was examined throughout the study sites. With the predicted reduction of streamflow and precipitation, an increase in the relative proportion of baseflow is expected for rivers under gaining conditions. However, the Mann-Kendal test (Yue and Wang, 2004 ) used here revealed no significant interannual trend in BFI distribution for the study watersheds from 1997 to 2019/2021. While the limited number of study years might contribute to this result, similar research has demonstrated the resilience of groundwater in northern Mediterranean regions to short-to-medium-term climate variability. Indeed, groundwater that may have a long residence time in aquifers, appears less sensitive to hydroclimatic hazards like rainfall variation and severe drought in Mediterranean regions. This resilience suggests that groundwater can function as a buffer against short-to-medium-term climate variability and change (Cramer et al., 2018; Fader et al., 2020 ). This highlights the importance of groundwater in sustaining streamflow, fluvial ecological continuity, and ensuring a reliable water supply, particularly during low-flow periods (Gao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2021 ). While the short-to-medium-term BFI displays no visible trend, hydroclimatic conditions, and precipitation distribution significantly influence the BFI at a smaller monthly scale. Monthly BFI and rainfall amounts (January 1997 to December 2020) were plotted for the Fiumaltu and the Tavignanu watersheds. Fig. 6   (a-b) shows a decreasing linear correlation between BFI and precipitation in the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu watersheds with satisfactory and good correlation coefficients (R2  values at 0.5242 and 0.6787, respectively). The highest R2  values were observed with a 0-month lag between precipitation and BFI, aligning with geological and morphometric settings (steep slopes) of the watersheds where the majority of runoff reaches rivers during rainfall and flood events. Consequently, lower precipitation corresponds to higher BFI values, and vice versa, as confirmed by Contingency Tables 4 and 5   . The tables highlight the correlation between the lowest precipitation classes in both watersheds and the highest BFI classes, and conversely. In situations where precipitation minimally affects streamflow, rivers continue to flow, indicating a larger relative contribution from deep groundwater and delayed subsurface reservoirs (high BFI). Conversely, heavy rainfall tends to reduce the proportion of deep groundwater and delayed subsurface flow by mixing, consequently impacting baseflow and BFI.  3.4.2 Interannual distribution of the BFI Close attention was devoted to the analysis of the interannual distribution of the BFI. Deep groundwater and delayed subsurface flow significantly contributed to both watersheds over the nearly 25-year study, resulting in an average BFI of 73 % (0.73 ± 0.04) for the Tavignanu and 77 % (0.77 ± 0.01) for the Fiumaltu, indicating that both watersheds are dependent on these resources (see Fig. 7  -a). Despite differences in morphometric and geological features, findings align with those of temperate lowland watersheds (with 70–84 % baseflow contribution over 30 years) (Lu et al., 2022 ) and Mediterranean watersheds (73 to 88 % mean baseflow contribution). This indicates a higher significance of groundwater and delayed subsurface flow in sustaining river flow in these temperate and Mediterranean environments. Differences are found in studies in semi-arid and humid climates, reporting notably lower BFI values (Hu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013b ), thus suggesting a higher relative contribution of groundwater in subsurface flow in the Mediterranean context compared to humid and arid to semi-arid regions. Segura et al. (2019)  provide detailed insights into the factors impacting baseflow contribution and the BFI in a mountainous watershed during both a typical hydrological year and a drought year, including hydroclimatic conditions, precipitation distribution, geological features, morphometrics, and land use. At the watershed scale, hydroclimatic conditions, encompassing temperature, rainfall patterns, and spatial distribution, play an important role in controlling baseflow (Qin et al., 2017; Segura et al., 2019 ). Geomorphological and geological features such as aquifer permeability and porosity significantly influence baseflow dynamics, particularly in drought years, as they control groundwater infiltration, storage, discharge, and transit times (Longobardi and Villani, 2023; Pfister et al., 2017 ). Additionally, morphometric characteristics, including watershed area, topography, and slope distribution, contribute to the behaviour of baseflow (Zimmer and Gannon, 2018 ). In this study, the observed differences or similarities between present results and those of other studies can be explained by these factors influencing the higher or lower relative contribution of baseflow (refer to Fig. 7 -a and Table in the Supplementary Materials S5 and S6  for detailed BFI values).  3.4.3 Seasonal distribution of BFI The BFI distribution from 1997–2019/2021 displays a strong seasonality, aligning with local hydroclimatic patterns in rainfall and streamflow. Peak baseflow contributions in the Tavignanu occur between May and August, while those in Fiumaltu are between April and August (Fig. 7 -b). Sustaining river flow in dry conditions relies on deep groundwater and delayed subsurface flow, contributing up to 89 % for Tavignanu and 90 % for Fiumaltu. The lowest contributions are observed from September to December for Tavignanu and October to November for Fiumaltu. Even in the wettest months, baseflow remains significant, representing 54 % (0.54 ± 0.01) for Tavignanu and 60 % (0.60 ± 0.04) for Fiumaltu (Fig. 7 -b). These results align with findings in Mediterranean dry conditions but exceed expectations in wet periods. Longobardi et al. (2016)  similarly observed strong seasonality in a small sandstone watershed in Italy with up to 90 % groundwater contribution in dry conditions and 40 % during wet months. It is important to recall the initial assumptions of this paper, defining baseflow by two components: deep groundwater from the SFL and delayed subsurface flow from the alterites layer. This definition helps to understand high values during wet conditions compared to Longobardi et al (2016) . Seasonal BFI distribution slightly varies between the Tavignanu and Fiumaltu watersheds, particularly in spring and autumn. While the two watersheds share some hydroclimatic similarities, their geological and morphometric characteristics differ. As hard-rock aquifers share similar hydrogeological properties, the BFI distribution contrast is primarily due to morphometric differences (variations in shape, area, and draining surface). Assumptions about the baseflow definition, including groundwater and delayed subsurface contribution, also contribute to these differences. Depending on the season and precipitation history, one component (deep SFL or subsurface alterites layer) can dominate over the other.  3.4.4 Influence of droughts on the BFI distribution and correlation with its origin Furthermore, mirroring the findings in the relationship between the BFI and rainfall section, severe droughts linked to precipitation significantly impact monthly BFI. Analysing the BFI distribution in 2017, a notably dry year, revealed a considerable rainfall deficit reported by local authorities across most of the island from March to November (DREAL Corse, 2018 ). The average rainfall during this period was 21.9 mm for Tavignanu and 24.4 mm for Fiumaltu, clearly lower than the average monthly rainfall from 1997 to 2019/2021 (80.9 mm for Tavignanu and 90.9 mm for Fiumaltu). A decline in both Tavignanu and Fiumaltu discharge was observed, averaging 4.15 m3 /s and 0.64 m3 /s, respectively, during the drought period. This is lower than the respective average monthly discharge of 11.1 m3 /s for Tavignanu (1997–2021) and 1.37 m3 /s for Fiumaltu (1997–2019), yet rivers continue to flow. Notably, baseflow exhibited a direct response during severe drought at the monthly time-step, particularly from March to November, where both watersheds displayed a higher BFI, approaching the average maximum BFI values (refer to Fig. 7 -c). Additionally, in the 2017–2019 study period, the geochemical composition of streamflow was examined to establish a correlation with the assumed deep and subsurface origin of baseflow and BFI. Monthly chemical data points from the previously described dataset were used to investigate the relationship between ions in streamflow, resulting from precipitation or long-term water–rock interactions. To prevent any interpretational bias, the natural tracers previously employed in the mixing models were removed. For this purpose, the local rainfall line ratio was employed to compare various cations to chloride (Cl- ) in the Fiumaltu watershed. Cl-  serves as a conservative tracer for marine and precipitation components (Appelo and Postma, 2005 ) and has not been used as a natural tracer in mixing models previously. The Cl-  vs Na+  binary diagram for the Fiumaltu watershed reveals a very good R2  of 0.9075, indicating the best and most significant linear correlation. Therefore, only this combination is illustrated in Fig. 8  . Much of the chemical streamflow data, situated below the local ratio line, exhibits Na+  enrichment, suggesting a terrigenous origin. Conversely, a small portion aligns near the rainfall ratio line, indicating that Na+  in this group originates from precipitation, similarly to Cl- . Monthly BFI values computed for the Fiumaltu over 2017–2019 were added to the diagram as a third dimension to identify their origin, whether from precipitation or water–rock interactions. BFI was classified into three categories: low (BFI<0.5), medium (0.5 to 0.75), and high (BFI>0.75). Data points with small and medium BFI contributions gather around the local rainfall line, aligning with the earlier findings in this section and the relationship between the BFI and rainfall section. Low BFI values are expected when rainfall proportion in streamflow is higher, leading to increased mixing between groundwater and surface runoff. The area showing Na+  ion enrichment, indicating a distinct origin from precipitation, predominantly exhibits high BFI values. This enrichment reflects a terrigenous origin, signifying the influence of long water–rock interactions within the deeper SFL and unconsolidated alterites layers in the hard-rock aquifers, consistent with the geochemical background of hard-rock aquifers in the Fiumaltu. As seen in section 2.1, the geological features of the Fiumaltu watershed are primarily composed of alternating carbonate–silicate schists. While sodium is not the dominant element in schists, it can be present in specific minerals like feldspars and micas. Feldspars, as sodium plagioclases, may contain sodium, and the structure of mica (e.g., muscovite) may also have Na+  cations (Marshall, 1962; Helmke and Sparks, 2018 ). This suggests that during high BFI values, baseflow originates almost exclusively from deep groundwater in the SFL and delayed subsurface flow in the alterites layer. This confirms that high BFI in streamflow is predominantly influenced by groundwater and delayed subsurface flow. This is of great importance, especially considering climatic models projecting more pronounced droughts, reduced precipitation, and lower future streamflow in the Mediterranean basin (Noto et al., 2022 ). Groundwater and subsurface flow will increasingly play a fundamental role in sustaining river flow, ecological continuity of the ecosystem, and related socio-economic activities. This highlights the need for improved characterization of the baseflow component across various watersheds and climate classes, emphasizing the importance of constraining parameters influencing baseflow for sustainable resource management.    4 Conclusion This paper introduces the first calibrated and validated digital filter with natural tracers for baseflow separation in two mountainous Mediterranean watersheds with hard-rock aquifers. Calibrating and validating the TPDF with monthly tracer data for the specific context has enabled the analysis of baseflow over an extended period, filling a significant knowledge gap in this region. Further examinations of the seasonal, interannual, and dry-year distributions of Baseflow Index (BFI), which indicates the contribution of deep groundwater and delayed subsurface flow to streamflow, were carried out. This was correlated with precipitation and the terrigenous origin of the BFI and baseflow. The findings show that BFI in mountainous Mediterranean areas follows a seasonal pattern, with the highest contributions (88–90 %) during dry conditions, confirming initial assumption. Even during the wettest months, baseflow significantly contributes to streamflow, with a high contribution of 54 % in the Tavignanu and 60 % in the Fiumaltu. Precipitation exerts a short-term influence on BFI, with the highest BFIs observed during the lowest precipitation amounts over 25 years. However, no specific trend was observed in the BFI distribution over the short-to-medium term (1997–2021 for the Tavignanu and 1997–2019 for the Fiumaltu). The average interannual contribution was also notably high, at 73 % for the Tavignanu and 77 % for the Fiumaltu, indicating reliance of river on baseflow and groundwater in the short-to-medium term. This demonstrate that groundwater can buffer hydroclimatic hazards, thereby improving its resilience. During severe droughts, BFI values well above the 25-year averages, confirming the terrigenous origin of BFI from prolonged water–rock interactions in hard-rock aquifers. Meaning, the deep groundwater component from the SFL, and the delayed subsurface flow component from the more superficial unconsolidated layer (alterites). In the context of climate change, with prediction of increased drought, reduced rainfall, and lower runoff in the Mediterranean basin, the utilisation of the calibrated digital filter is significant to provide valuable insights into behavior of mountainous Mediterranean watersheds. This made possible to show the increasingly important role of groundwater and delayed subsurface flow in sustaining rivers, ecosystems, and the human activities in this context. In response, this is of significant importance for stakeholders to better adapt and differentiated their water resource plans for this specific and sensitive region.
1 Introduction Accurate hydrologic simulations are essential for managing water resources, predicting future water availability, and anticipating extreme events. For understanding the impacts of climate change and water resource availability, estimation of terrestrial water storage (TWS) components (e.g., soil moisture, groundwater storage, snow, surface water) is essential for understanding the impacts of climate change and water resource availability (Hirschi et al., 2007; Soltani et al., 2021 ). Soil moisture or water saturation refers to the level of water content in unsaturated soil, where a value of 1 indicates fully saturated soil and a value of 0 signifies completely dry soil. Groundwater storage, on the other hand, pertains to the volume of water held within an aquifer, which is the saturated zone of the subsurface. Each TWS component has a particular impact on the climate as a whole and it is also an important climate change driver (Bierkens and Van den Hurk, 2007; Green et al., 2011 ). For instance, a major source of atmospheric humidity is supplied by soil moisture, and it is therefore a strong contributor to the climate system (Seneviratne et al., 2010 ). In order to obtain accurate seasonal forecasts, soil moisture should be accurately predicted (Koster et al., 2010; Van den Hurk et al., 2012 ). Groundwater storage variations (ΔGWS) should be determined accurately to be able to assess water resources in a reliable fashion, especially for dry climates with large abstractions of groundwater and significant temporal and spatial of climate variability (Soltani et al., 2022a ). Despite the importance of having reliable estimates of TWS, knowledge of spatial and temporal variations in TWS and its components is generally lacking. This is particularly true at large scales, or in less-developed countries where there is, in general, an absence of global monitoring systems (Soltani et al., 2020 ). Ground-based measurements, while very accurate, only provide point-wise estimates (Dorigao et al., 2011; Soltani et al., 2020 ). This is where hydrological models stand out as a solution to fill this gap at high spatiotemporal resolutions (e.g., Döll et al., 2003; Van Dijk and Warren, 2010 ). As a result, hydrological models are essential tools for sustainable management of water resources (Yu et al., 2015 ). However, absence of reliable data often means that the modeling process is challenged and this is further compounded by errors in modeling and model parameter uncertainties (Van Dijk et al., 2011; Vrugt et al., 2013 ). As a result, simulation results can be unreliable. Subsequently, models can be made more trustworthy by data assimilation (DA) (Bertino et al., 2003 ). For this purpose, additional information is supplied by means of new datasets which can constrain the estimators of model’s states to more meaningful values (Bertino et al., 2003; Hoteit et al., 2012 ). Assimilation of satellite data has applications in various fields such as magnetospheric (Garner et al., 1999 ), ocean (Bennett, 2005; Lahoz et al., 2006 ) and atmosphere (Schunk et al., 2004; Altaf et al., 2014 ) studies. It is also predominantly used in hydrological models where the accuracy of flux and/or storage components needs to be enhanced (e.g., Dillon et al., 2016; Khaki et al., 2018a; Khaki et al., 2018b ). TWS variations (ΔTWS) can be derived from gravity measurements by the Gravity Recovery And Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite mission (Tapley et al., 2004 ) and have been used in data assimilation studies and discussed widely in the literature (Soltani et al., 2021 ). Soltani et al. (2021)  provided an in-depth review of the recent studies on incorporating GRACE TWS data into hydrological models, highlighting their limitations, problems, and progress. They also presented an overview of the advantages and limitations of various data assimilation techniques, with a focus on the capacity of sequential methods for hydrological applications. Various filtering techniques, such as variational methods and sequential filtering, have been proposed and developed across different fields to achieve DA objectives. While variational methods are more prevalent in atmospheric and oceanic sciences, sequential methods are widely used in hydrological applications due to their reasonable computational requirements (Soltani et al., 2021 ). In recent decades, there has been significant attention on GRACE DA, particularly for improving deep storage components like groundwater levels (Tangdamrongsub et al., 2015; Zaitchik et al., 2008; Soltani et al., 2021 ). While the benefits of GRACE DA are evident in deep storage, its effectiveness in enhancing surface soil moisture remains a challenge (Li et al., 2012; Tangdamrongsub et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2017 ). The goal of multivariate DA is to combine the strengths of SM DA and GRACE DA to simultaneously improve soil moisture and groundwater level estimates. Recent studies showed that the accuracy of surface and deep storage components could be improved by assimilating GRACE and soil moisture data (Tian et al., 2017; Tangdamrongsub et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, and used multivariate DA to increase the skills of model state estimations and climate assessment indicators utilizing several satellite soil moisture and snow products (Jasinski et al., 2019 ). Based on these results, multivariate assimilation of GRACE and satellite soil moisture data (e.g., SMOS (Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity)) is projected to improve soil moisture and groundwater estimates (Kumar et al., 2019 ). This study develops a multivariate DA with GRACE and SMOS data to improve the accuracy of regional soil moisture and groundwater level estimates. The main research objective is to investigate the performance of multivariate DA in simultaneously improving soil moisture and groundwater level estimates. Different DA schemes are developed to incorporate different observations into the DA system simultaneously. Three different DA scenarios subject to three different observation cases (SM-only, GRACE-only, and both) are evaluated by using a novel probabilistic framework. The hydrological model used in this study is the fully coupled surface–subsurface hydrological model ParFlow-CLM (PARallel FLOW- Community Land Model), known for simulating the intricate interactions between land surface and subsurface hydrology effectively. This specialized model is particularly tailored to accurately represent the dynamics of water and energy fluxes at high spatial resolutions across extensive geographical areas (Sulis et al., 2017 ). ParFlow is a grid-based parallel integrated two-way coupled hydrologic modeling technique through which the surface and subsurface flow is simulated simultaneously in 3D. The ParFlow model can be used for various surface and groundwater problems over large and small basins (Ferguson and Maxwell, 2012 ). It does not include surface processes such as evaporation. Therefore, to generate more realistic outputs, ParFlow is often coupled with a land surface model, in particular, CLM (Kollet and Maxwell, 2008 ). The coupled ParFlow-CLM model combines high-resolution simulations, complex terrain representation, vegetation dynamics, climate change and land use studies, water resources management, and flood and drought analysis. ParFlow has been used to study different surface and groundwater problems in large domains (Ferguson and Maxwell, 2012 ), small basins (Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ), and even subsurface–surface (Soltani et al., 2022b ) and atmospheric (Shrestha et al., 2014 ) coupling.  2 Case study description The case study area encompasses portions of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman basin, notably including several significant sub-basins in the western and southwestern regions of Iran. This area incorporates the Karun, Jarahi, and Karkheh sub-basins, and collectively covers a substantial expanse of 158,000 km2 . This territory constitutes approximately ten percent of Iran's total land area. This case study is bounded by [29°N 35° N] and [46° E and 53° E], in the west of Iran and important cities such as Ahvaz, Khorramshahr, Shahr-e Kord, Kermanshah and Yasuj are in this region (Fig. 1  ). In the mountainous regions, the elevation ranges from over 4,000 m to sea level at the Persian Gulf coast (Fig. 1 ). Precipitation varies seasonally and geographically owing to the passage of mid-latitude storms that originate in the Mediterranean Sea region and the effects of the complicated topography (Kiany et al., 2020 ) The study area's mean annual precipitation ranges from 100 mm in the plains in the southwest to > 900 mm in some of the eastern mountainous regions (Raziei et al., 2012 ) and the average temperature in the summer and winter are 48° and 4 °C. Deserts in this zone have an area of 1.3 × 104  km2 , which is equal to eight percent of the basin’s area, which are predominantly located in the south and southwest arid and hyper-arid climatic zones (Ardebili and Khademalrasoulb, 2018 ). The important rivers that run through this basin are Jarahi, Karkheh, Karun, Zohreh and Dez, supplying 34 × 109  m3  of water annually, which is about 33 % contribution of the total water resources of the entire country. 83 % contribution of the water consumption in Zohreh-Jarahi, 88 % in Karun and 89 % in Karkheh were by agricultural use (Rahmani, 2021 ). This basin is a hub for agriculture, with 26.2 % dedicated to crops such as rice, wheat, barley, cotton, corn, sugarcane, and various summer crops, and 12 % dedicated to tree cultivation. These crops thrive on the fertile plains of the southwest, nourished by the water from the five major rivers (Ardebili and Khademalrasoulb, 2018 ).  3 Methodology and data 3.1 Model description The ParFlow-CLM model comprises two essential components. First, the ParFlow model solves the Richards equation, a governing equation for water flow through 3-D variably saturated porous media (Ashby and Falgout, 1996; Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ). The Richards equation takes into account critical factors such as soil properties, and topography, allowing the simulation of subsurface water movement. The ParFlow model utilizes a finite difference approach and parallel computing techniques to efficiently handle the complex computations involved in modeling these intricate processes (Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ). Second component, CLM (Oleson et al., 2004, 2008 ) focuses on representing land surface processes. It consists of modules dedicated to surface energy balance, vegetation dynamics, biogeochemistry, and snow accumulation and melt. These modules interact with the ParFlow subsurface component through flux exchanges, enabling processes such as water infiltration from the surface to the subsurface, evapotranspiration from vegetation, and heat transfer between the land surface and subsurface to be effectively simulated and integrated into the model (Soltani, 2022 ). In the sequential information exchange procedure, ParFlow sends the updated relative saturation (Sw  ) and pressure head (ψ ) for the top 10 layers to CLM. In turn, CLM sends the depth differentiated source and sink terms for soil moisture [top soil moisture flux (qrain), soil evapotranspiration (qe)] for the top 10 soil layers to ParFlow (Shrestha et al., 2014 ). For more details on the numerical aspects and other features of the model, refer to Kollet and Maxwell (2006) . Additionally, the model's structure and configuration are visually represented in Fig. 2  . The critical soil hydraulic properties, such as water retention and hydraulic conductivity curves, are described using Mualem-van Genuchten functions (Van Genuchten, 1980 ), with their parameters estimated through the application of pedotransfer functions. Notably, leveraging physics-based Integrated Hydrological Models (IHMs) offers a significant advantage over lumped hydrological models. IHMs deliver robust results without requiring extensive calibration steps (Soltani, 2022 ). The Van Genuchten relationships are utilized to define the relative saturation and permeability functions as follows:(1) S w  ( ψ  p  )  = s sat   - s res    ( 1 + ( α ψ  p  )  n  )  ( 1 - 1 / n )    + s  res       (2) K r  ( ψ  p  )  = ( 1 - ( α ψ  p  )  n - 1   ( 1 + ( α ψ  p  )  n  )  - m )   )  2  ( 1 + ( α ψ  p  )  n  )   m  2       where m  = 1−1/n ssat  [–] is the relative saturated water content, sres  [–] is the relative residual saturation, ψ  is the pressure head, α   [L-1 ] and n [–] are soil parameters.  3.2 Water balance ParFlow can perform water balance calculations for the Richards' equation, overland flow, and CLM capabilities. There are two types of water balance storage: subsurface and surface, as well as two types of flux calculations: overland flow and evapotranspiration. The storage components are measured in units [L3 ], whereas the fluxes can be instantaneous and measured in units [L3 T−1 ] or cumulative over an output interval and measured in units [L3 ]. The water balance has the following form (Maxwell et al., 2016 ):(3) Δ [ V o l surface   + V o l subsurface   ]  Δ t   = Q overland   + Q evapotranspiration   + Q source / sin k       where Volsubsurface  is the subsurface storage [L3 ], Volsurface  is the surface storage [L3 ], Qoverland  is the overland flux [L3 T −1 ], Qevapotranspiration  is the evapotranspiration flux passed from CLM [L3 T −1 ], and Qsourc/esink  are any other source or sink fluxes specified in the simulation [L3 T −1 ]. Only the external fluxes passed from CLM are included in Qevapotranspiration , which needs to be recorded as a variable in ParFlow. It is important to note that these volume and flux quantities, like any other quantity in ParFlow, are computed spatially across the entire domain and returned as array values. The subsurface water is the summation of soil moisture and groundwater storage. It is represented by the subsurface equivalent water thickness which is computed for all active cells in the domain, as follows (the outcomes represent as an array of balances by domain) (Maxwell et al., 2016 ):(4) H subsurface   = ∑ Ω  [ S w  ( ψ p  )  × S s  × ψ p  + S w  ( ψ p  )  × ψ p  ]      Here, H subsurface  [L] is equivalent water thickness in subsurface and Ss  [-] is the specific storage. The surface equivalent water thickness (Hsurface )is determined using the continuity equation over the top surface boundary cells in the domain Γ,as obtained by the mask. This is done on a cell-by-cell basis (resulting in an array of balances across the domain) like follows (Maxwell et al., 2016 ):(5) H surface   = ∑ Γ  ψ p      The summation of surface equivalent water thickness and subsurface equivalent water thickness results in TWS derived by GRACE.  3.3 Data 3.3.1 Land surface data and atmospheric forcing The land surface input data include topography, land cover, soil characteristics, and physiological parameters of the canopy which are static variables. Global Multiresolution Terrain Elevation Data 2010 (Danielson and Gesch, 2011 ) was used as Digital Elevation Model (DEM) which has a resolution of 1 km (see Fig. 1 ). The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite land-use classification (Friedl et al., 2002 ) was also used, where it was converted to Plant Functional Types (PFT). In order to include the soil characteristics, the percentage of soil and clay were obtained using FAO/UNESCO Digital Soil Map of the World (Batjes, 1997 ) which has numerous soil classes consisting of 19 classes, which was based on Schaap and Leij (1998) ’s pedotransfer functions. For the Manning’s coefficient, the values which has been proposed based on relationship between landcover type and roughness is used (Asante et al., 2008 ). The atmospheric forcing of the coupled ParFlow model with CLM including barometric pressure, wind speed, precipitation, specific humidity, downward shortwave and longwave radiations and air temperature near the surface is provided from GLDAS-Noah Land Surface Model L4 V2.1 data (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GLDAS_NOAH025_3H_2.1 ). This has a spatial resolution of 0.25° and temporal resolution of 3-hourly (due to the temporal resolution of the GLDAS data), and the data used covers the time period of 2015–2020. All model inputs given in Table 1  , were re-projected to have an equal cell size of 0.25° resolution. In this study, the model was employed for a total thickness of 300 m over 100 model layers (nz= 100) with different thickness. The model was implemented with a horizontal resolution of 0.25°. This grid comprises 28 cells in the x-direction (nx = 28) and 24 cells in the y-direction (ny = 24) (see Fig. 3  ).  3.3.2 GRACE TWS The GRACE data release 05 (RL05) was supplied by the University of Texas at Austin's Center for Space Research (CSR) (Bettadpur, 2012 ). This release includes the monthly spherical harmonic coefficients (SHC) complete up to degree and order 96. The GRACE-derived TWS, as well as its uncertainty over the case study, are calculated as follows: First, the Swenson et al. (2008)  degree 1 coefficients (SHC) are restored, and the C20 term is replaced by the value derived from the satellite laser range (Cheng and Tapley, 2004 ). Second, the mean covering the period from March 2015 to June 2017 is calculated and subtracted from the monthly product to produce the SHC variations, then restriping (Swenson and Wahr, 2006 ) and 300-km radius Gaussian smoothing filters are applied to the SHC variations to reduce the high-frequency noise. Third, following the method outlined by Wahr et al. (1998) , the TWS variation (TWS) is computed from the filtered SHC variations. Finally, a signal restoration algorithm (e.g., Chen et al., 2014 ) is used to the computed TWS. The strategy iteratively searches for the true TWS using a forward model built entirely from GRACE data. To be consistent with the model estimate, the ParFlow-CLM estimates of TWS temporal mean value (March 2015–June 2017) is added to the GRACE-derived TWS to produce the absolute TWS prior to the assimilation procedure (Zaitchik et al., 2008 ).  3.3.3 SMOS and SMAP soil moisture datasets This research relies on daily satellite soil moisture retrievals from the Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity mission (SMOS, Kerr et al., 2012 ). The SMOS missions consist in a L-Band (1.4 Ghz) interferometric radiometer that is sensible to surface soil moisture and vegetation optical thickness over continental surfaces. The level 3 gridded product (Al Bitar et al., 2017 ) provided by the Centre Aval de Traitement des Données SMOS (CATDS, https://www.catds.fr ) and run by the French Research Institute for Exploitation of the Sea for the Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales (CNES) is used to collect SMOS data (IFREMER). On the Equal-Area Scalable Earth (EASE; Brodzik et al., 2012 ) grid, data are accessible from January 2010 to present, with a spatial resolution of 25 km in m3 /m3 . SMOS data with a daily temporal resolution are spatially rescaled from 25 km × 25 km to 0.25◦ ×0.25◦  resolution using the nearest neighbor interpolation to match ParFlow-CLM. The data is filtered for Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) using the RFI probability flag. Jamei et al. (2020)  have evaluated the accuracy of soil moisture derived by SMOS (SMSMOS ) products over the Southwest and West regions of Iran for the time period of 2012–2015. The research results demonstrate that SMSMOS  model exhibits a high level of accuracy and agreement when compared to in-situ measurements. These findings substantiate the efficacy of utilizing remotely sensed data for estimating soil moisture, highlighting the potential of SMSMOS  as a reliable tool in such applications. The Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP, Entekhabi et al., 2010 ) mission consists of a L-Band radiometer at 1.4 Ghz with a mesh grid antenna (the radar component was only active during the first 3 months of the mission). The National Snow and Ice Data Center Distributed Active Archive Center (NSIDC DAAC, https://nsidc.org/data/smap ) supplied a grid product (SPL3SMP). The volumetric soil moisture obtained by the SMAP level 3 (version 4) passive microwave radiometer, available from 2015 to the present, is included in this package. To match the observations with the model grid space, the data for both SMOS and SMAP are resampled to a 0.25◦ resolution in m3 /m3 . When more than one SM retrieval is available on a given day, the daily average is employed to assure model time step consistency. A drawback of our research is the comparison of model results assimilated with Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) data against other remote sensing observations, specifically from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission, instead of using in-situ data. While both SMOS and SMAP provide valuable soil moisture information, they operate with different sensing technologies and retrieval algorithms, leading to potential discrepancies in the observed values. This methodological disparity can introduce biases and affect the accuracy of our model comparisons. Furthermore, the absence of in-situ data, which typically offers more precise and localized measurements, may limit the validation and robustness of our findings. By highlighting these considerations upfront, we aim to provide a clearer context for the interpretation of our results and underscore the necessity for caution when drawing conclusions based on these inter-comparisons.  3.3.4 Groundwater data In-situ groundwater level data obtained from the Iran Water Resources Management Company (IWRMC) for observation wells distributed across the case study area (http://www.wrm.ir ) is utilized. The size of each aquifer plays a crucial role in converting volumetric groundwater change values provided by IWRMC to equivalent water height. This conversion process is instrumental in ensuring a meaningful comparison. The results are then evaluated using an area-averaged time series of groundwater changes for each aquifer. Specifically, the modified in-situ groundwater time series, adjusted according to changes in well characteristics, seasonal variations, or calibration factors to address any biases or inaccuracies inherent in the initial measurements, are compared to the aquifer's average assimilation findings individually. This comparison provides insights into the effectiveness of the adjustments made to the in-situ groundwater time series in aligning it with the aquifer's average assimilation findings.   3.4 Data assimilation framework 3.4.1 EnKF The Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) is widely used in the previous papers due to its flexibility and simplicity of use in land surface models (e.g., Draper et al., 2012; Crow and Wood, 2003 ). Model state ensembles are created for estimating error covariance matrix of the state variable. This allows optimal merging of observations and model prediction. EnKF involves the computation of the updated state ensemble X t +    at time step t for the model-estimated state variable Xt   which encompasses the saturation degree of all grids for each ensemble member i. It is worth noting that the Van Genuchten relationships define the correlation between the degree of saturation and pressure head. Data Assimilation Framework requires filter algorithm parameters, observation files, and instructions for building an ensemble of model runs as input (Fig. 4  ). TWS/or SM data, it’s error information was derived using GRACE level 2/or SMOS data, and generated ensembles of input data were obtained during pre-processing. Post-processing involves evaluating ParFlow-CLM output against independent data sets. We evaluated the results of simulations by a cross-validation with SMAP data and in-situ groundwater measurements as shown in Fig. 4 .  3.4.2 ParFlow-CLM-DA experimental design The assimilation tests were carried out from March 2015 to March 2020. To acquire equilibrium initial state variables, a ten-year spin up was undertaken by simulating the input data of 2015 ten times. We used ParFlow-CLM for a case study of Iran with a spatial resolution of 0.25° in this work. The model was run with a 3-hour time step (due to the temporal resolution of the GLDAS data) and a 5-day time window for soil moisture updates. Because assimilation observations have various temporal resolutions, such as monthly GRACE TWS and daily soil moisture measurements, soil moisture observation is temporally rescaled into a 5-day resolution for data assimilation and GRACE TWS data is assimilated into the model in a monthly time scale. In this study, we assumed a spatially uniform observational error of 0.04 m3 /m3  for SMOS (Colliander et al., 2017; Lievens et al., 2017 ) and a diagonal error covariance matrix for GRACE TWS data in the ParFlow-CLM-DA setup. Both atmospheric forcing and soil properties affect the results of a land surface model. Precipitation and soil texture (%sand and %clay) were perturbed in this study to account for uncertainty in atmospheric forcing and soil texture. Precipitation received multiplicative perturbations that were log-normally distributed, geographically homogeneous, and temporally uncorrelated (Naz et al., 2019 ). The applied perturbation factors for precipitation had a mean and standard deviation of 1.0 and 0.10, respectively (Naz et al., 2019 ). A random noise with a standard deviation of 10 % was used to perturb the sand and clay content (Naz et al., 2019 ). The sand and clay content added up to 100 %, in order to ensure the physical meaning of the soil parameters. The sand and clay percentage have a direct impact on the computation of the soil pedotransfer functions that links the hydraulic pressure in the soil to the water content of the soil. In the simulation/assimilation experiment, the initial ensemble size for precipitation and soil texture was set to 36 to update the soil moisture of the top soil layer (0–15 cm) and pressure head. The main experiment consists of four ParFlow-CLM-DA simulations: (a) SMOS data assimilation, (b) GRACE TWS data assimilation and (c) combined SMOS and GRACE data assimilation, and (d) ensemble open-loop simulation (no data assimilation) (Fig. 5  ).   3.5 Evaluation 3.5.1 Deterministic assessment To assess model performance in simulating hydrological variables, we use absolute error, bias (BIAS), the correlation coefficient (R) and a probabilistic reliability assessment. The SMAP data is used for validation which shows that the application of data assimilation reduces misfits between the results and SMAP data compared to the open loop. The validation is carried out in terms of correlation and absolute error, with the estimated values presented in Fig. 7   and Fig. 8  , respectively. With an averaged correlation value of 0.67, ParFlow-CLM performs well in the estimate of the SM 0−15cm  and gives good agreement with SMAP data at all sites (see ensemble open loop in Fig. 7 ). The SMOS assimilation also minimizes erroneous peaks of the SM 0−15cm  estimate, such as in November 2018 (Fig. 6 ) and May 2018 (Fig. 6 ), resulting in greater agreement with the SMAP data. Clearly, the SMOS data should be considered in the DA process in order to retain the accuracy (in terms of agreement with the SMAP data) of the SM 0−15cm  estimate in the case study. The SM DA and multivariate DA increase the correlation value by 0.17 and 0.22, respectively (from 0.67 to 0.84 and 0.89). Since satellite SM observation is employed in the SM DA and multivariate DA, an improved outcome is expected. The GRACE DA, on the other hand, appears to have a negative impact on the SM 0−15cm  estimate (see, Fig. 7  and Fig. 8 ). The GRACE DA reduces the correlation by 0.08 when compared to the ensemble open loop. Poor performance is owing to sensitivity of GRACE data to the signal associated with the top soil component. The results of multivariate DA utilizing SMOS and GRACE data between March 2015 and June 2017 are compared to SMAP data (Fig. 6 ). The daily SM 0−15cm  estimations of SMOS assimilation clearly show a greater agreement with SMAP data (comparing to the ensemble open loop) (see, Fig. 7  and Fig. 8 ). The hydrological model did not benefit from the limited improvement in the hydrological model's estimation of surface soil moisture with GRACE assimilation can be attributed to GRACE's coarse spatial and temporal resolution. Additionally, the GRACE signal is not sufficiently sensitive to surface soil moisture variations, as it is more adept at capturing large-scale changes in terrestrial water storage. These factors hinder the model's ability to benefit from GRACE data for precise surface soil moisture predictions. However, it should be mentioned that even though soil moisture data assimilation improves the estimates for the top soil moisture, the accuracy for the whole water column may not necessarily increase.  4.1.2 TWS variations The basin-averaged time series of TWS variations from ParFlow-CLM before and after assimilating three different DA strategies is shown in Fig. 9  . It shows larger amplitude of TWS variations for the data assimilation results compared to open-loop results. Also, Fig. 10  , shows the correlation with respect to GRACE observations. Assimilating SM not only has the least impact on the TWS variations but also results in a negative impact on improving TWS estimates. The SM DA, reduces the averaged correlation value by ∼ 0.07 (Fig. 10 ). As a result, our findings show a lower level of agreement between the state estimate and the GRACE observation. SM assimilation appears to create a stimulatory effect that reduces the quality of TWS predictions. In the GRACE DA, the improvement is applied to the entire water column, leading to an improved agreement between the TWS variation estimate and the GRACE observation. The averaged correlation value increase by 0.20 compared to open-loop results (Fig. 10 ). GRACE DA appears to be more useful for improving TWS estimations than SM DA, but it may be of reduced benefit for the estimation of the other components (see, Fig. 7  and Fig. 8 ). The idea of incorporating the SMOS and GRACE observations into the model at the same time is motivated by the underlying strengths of each individually. Fig. 9  also shows the multivariate DA results using SMOS and GRACE data between March 2015 and June 2017 when compared with GRACE data. TWS estimations derived joint clearly demonstrate better agreement with GRACE data (comparing to the ensemble open loop and GRACE DA). When compared to open-loop results, the averaged correlation coefficient increases by 0.22 (Fig. 10 ). The SM 0 - 15cm  and TWS variations components of the multivariate DA are modified toward the SMAP and GRACE observations, yielding final state estimates that agree with both observations. TWS variations predicted with multivariate DA agree with GRACE observations by 0.2 in cross-correlation (Fig. 10 ) while, at the same time, the SM 0 - 15cm  estimate has a better correlation with SMAP data by 0.17. (See Fig. 7 ). TWS correlation increased by more than a factor of 1.3 using the GRACE DA and multivariate DA (Fig. 10 ). The SM DA, cannot provide a reliable TWS estimate, as evidenced by the correlation, which is less than the GRACE DA and multivariate DA (Fig. 10 ).  4.1.3 Groundwater level variations Fig. 11   depicts the time series of monthly averaged groundwater (GW) level variations over the case study for the time period of 2015–2017. In-situ groundwater measurements are used to validate assimilation results of the different DA strategies. The average correlation coefficients and their absolute error in in-situ groundwater measurements are shown in Fig. 12   and Fig. 13  , respectively. The application of the SM DA results in inaccurate groundwater level estimates in Fig. 12 , with a considerable difference between the GW estimate and in-situ groundwater measurements. When compared to the ensemble open- loop estimate, the assimilation of GRACE data (in both GRACE DA and multivariate DA) boosts the correlation and reduces absolute error between the GW estimate and in-situ groundwater level changes by a factor of more than two (see, Fig. 12  and Fig. 13 ). As a result, it is found that GRACE is more sensitive to the signal from the groundwater storage than the shallow storage component (similar to Tangdamrongsub et al. (2020) ’s findings). When compared to assimilating GRACE-only, assimilating both GRACE and SMOS observations performs better in the GW level variations estimate and delivers a 0.07 greater average correlation which is not a significant improvement (Fig. 12 ). The GRACE DA updates GW level variations in the multivariate DA after the SM DA is applied. The use of the SM DA (in the multivariate DA) reduces the uncertainty of the state estimate, which increases the contribution of GRACE data in the GRACE DA. Groundwater trends are generally negative over the entire time period (2015 – 2017). Again, it can be concluded that without using assimilation, these correct negative trends are not captured. Khaki et al. (2018b)  integrated GRACE Total Water Storage (TWS) data into the World-Wide Water Resources Assessment (W3RA) model, enabling a detailed examination of various water budget components, including groundwater, soil moisture, and surface water storage, across Iran's six major drainage divisions from 2002 to 2012. Their study revealed that assimilating GRACE TWS data significantly enhances the W3RA model's performance, offering improved insights into water availability in diverse locations. Particularly, the assimilation corrects for open-loop simulation variations, a crucial aspect for accurate groundwater level estimation. Our study, utilizing the ParFlow-CLM model, corroborates these findings, further supporting the efficacy of GRACE TWS data assimilation in improving water resource assessments“. Khaki and Awange (2019)  used the Ensemble Square-Root Filter (EnSRF) to integrate multi-mission satellite datasets such as TWS from the GRACE satellite mission and soil moisture products from the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer-Earth Observing System (AMSR-E) and SMOS into the W3RA model for estimating groundwater and soil moisture over South America. The use of joint data assimilation improves W3RA estimations when compared to groundwater in-situ measurements which is in a good agreement with our results. This effect was clearly seen for TWS estimations and, more critically, groundwater simulations, highlighting the potential for assimilating remotely sensed products to improve the W3RA hydrological model's reliability.   4.2 DA impacts on temporally averaged state variables Fig. 14   shows temporally averaged SM 0 - 15cm  variation from the ParFlow-CLM experiments derived ensemble open loop and different DA strategies (SM DA, GRACE DA, and joint DA) and the SMAP data over the time period of 2015–2017. Fig. 15   evaluates the performance of the DA in terms of BIAS error against the SMAP data to investigate the impact of different DA strategies on the SM 0 - 15cm  estimates. In comparison to the ensemble open loop, the SM DA and multivariate DA provide smaller BIAS error values (Fig. 15 ). This is to be expected, given that the SMOS data are incorporated into the state estimate via the SM DA and multivariate DA applications. The Kalman gain tries to statistically enhance the fit between the SM 0 - 15cm  estimates and the SMAP observation, resulting in better agreement (the maximum BIAS changes from 17.71 to 8.48). GRACE DA, on the other hand, increases the BIAS error. The increase is most likely caused by low sensitivity of GRACE observations to top soil moisture. The top soil component is largely influenced by high-frequency meteorological forcing, but GRACE can only measure monthly basin-averaged TWS changes, which are dominated by deep-water storage component with low-frequency variability. GRACE data, with its coarse spatial and temporal resolution, faces challenges in accurately simulating the high spatiotemporal variability of water storage in the top soil layer. The satellite's measurements, covering large areas with intervals of several weeks to months, are insufficient for capturing the rapid and localized changes in the shallow top soil layer. As a result, GRACE alone may not provide the level of detail needed for precise modeling of water dynamics in this specific layer, highlighting the importance of complementing GRACE data with other sources or advanced modeling techniques. The BIAS error (ensemble spread) of the SM 0 - 15cm  estimate is reduced in all DA strategies (Fig. 15 ). The SM DA and multivariate DA reduce uncertainty when compared to the ensemble open loop, while the GRACE DA reduces uncertainty. Importantly, the SM DA and multivariate DA applications result in less uncertainty than the allocated SMAP uncertainty estimate. Fig. 16   evaluates the performance of the DA in terms of absolute error against the in-situ groundwater level measurements data to investigate the impact of different DA strategies on the groundwater variation estimates. As shown in Fig. 16 , the BIAS inaccuracy indicates bigger differences from north to south and the biggest BIAS error is evident in the southwest of the basin. A similar pattern is seen in all DA scenarios. The BIAS inaccuracy in Fig. 16  clearly demonstrates the effect of DA. In SM DA, the biggest uncertainty is seen compared to other DA scenarios and ensemble open loop estimate, particularly in the central part of the basin. In GRACE DA and joint DA, the uncertainty decreases, and the lowest uncertainty is seen in the central part of the basin and this extends north and west when joint DA is employed. Tangdamrongsub et al. (2020)  assimilated multi-mission remote sensing observations, including soil moisture information from SMOS and SMAP missions, as well as TWS information from GRACE, into the Community Atmosphere and Biosphere Land Exchange (CABLE) land surface model over the Goulburn River basin in Australia to enhance model performance. The validation of data assimilation was conducted using in-situ soil moisture and groundwater level data. The study revealed that SMOS assimilation improves topsoil moisture but degrades groundwater level estimates. Conversely, GRACE assimilation enhances only the groundwater component.  4.3 Evaluating uncertainty in the DA strategies The failure probability of LSF (refer to Eq.15) is investigated as a criterion to assess model reliability using a novel application of the First Order Reliability Method (FORM). Specifying r smaller than 0.2 (see Section 3.4.2 ), can be used as a criterion to assess the reliability of model's results. To achieve this, the FORM calculates the failure probability (Pf ) of the model's closure results. The results of the FORM implementation in Table 2   show that failure probability of multivariate data assimilation has the lowest value, and the best solution was found to be multivariate data assimilation using both GRACE and SMOS data for improving soil moisture, TWS and groundwater estimates. Pf  of groundwater estimate using SM DA is larger than all DA strategies, and Pf  of groundwater estimate using GRACE DA and multivariate DA is lower than all DA strategies. Pf  of TWS estimates using GRACE DA is lower than all DA strategies, and Pf  of TWS estimates using SM DA is larger than all DA strategies. Pf  of soil moisture estimate using SM DA is lower than all DA strategies, and Pf  of soil moisture estimate using GRACE DA is larger than all DA strategies which indicates that the performance of DA mainly depends on the type of observations, the prediction variable of interest that are assimilate and the prediction variable of interest. Each DA strategy exhibits an acceptable Pf  value; however, if one choice is to be made, the joint DA approach appears more promising. It has the potential to enhance both soil moisture and groundwater estimates. It is essential to note that the significance of this finding may vary depending on the chosen hydrological model under consideration and the states incorporated in the Ensemble Kalman filter.   5 Summary and conclusion In this pioneering study, a novel approach emerges as both soil moisture from SMOS and total water storage (TWS) data from GRACE are concurrently assimilated into the coupled ParFlow-CLM hydrology model. Significantly, this marks the first-time integration of data assimilation (DA) techniques into the ParFlow-CLM model, a physically based model renowned for its capability to capture intricate interactions between surface and subsurface water dynamics. The intricacies of the interaction between subsurface and surface water are adeptly addressed through the utilization of the coupled surface–subsurface ParFlow-CLM model. This model, renowned for its physical realism, proves instrumental in simulating the complex processes occurring at the interface between the deeper subsurface and the surface. Three innovative data assimilation strategies are deployed to assimilate either one or both of GRACE and SMOS satellite products for basins in Iran. The assimilation method demonstrates proficiency in estimating soil moisture, particularly for the top 15 cm of the soil, when appropriate observations are incorporated. Strikingly, the assimilation of GRACE data significantly improves estimates of groundwater level variation, emphasizing its unique contribution. The novel aspect of this work lies in the revelation that assimilating both GRACE and SMOS data results in more accurate soil moisture estimates. Notably, single observation assimilation proves crucial for achieving the highest accuracy. This underscores the importance of incorporating SMOS data for enhancing soil moisture assimilation and elevating its precision, resulting in a substantial increase in correlation coefficient with SMAP data. In contrast to previous findings, the hydrological model in this study does not derive significant benefits from GRACE assimilation for estimating surface soil moisture values. The study acknowledges the well-documented uncertainties associated with total water storage, yet highlights the marginal impact of GRACE assimilation on reducing soil moisture uncertainty, cautioning against potential misattributions of deep groundwater to shallow groundwater. The breakthrough solution identified in this study is the application of multivariate data assimilation for both GRACE and SMOS data. This innovative approach adjusts high and low frequency values through soil moisture and GRACE assimilation, respectively. Consequently, the correlation coefficients for the top 15 cm of soil moisture and changes in groundwater level experience substantial increases with SMAP data and in-situ measurements. While multivariate data assimilation exhibits slightly lower performance compared to single assimilations for their respective target zones, it represents a significant advancement in improving soil moisture estimates. Importantly, the study underscores the utility of comparing model results with SMAP data to assess the model's ability to replicate key aspects of satellite observations, emphasizing the reliance on remotely sensed data in regions lacking in-situ measurements. The study's novelty is further accentuated by the integration of data assimilation into the ParFlow-CLM model, a milestone that expands the model's capabilities and enhances its utility in capturing the complexity of surface–subsurface interactions. Additionally, the proposed generalization of multivariate data assimilation to various data sources represents a groundbreaking step towards a more comprehensive and adaptable hydrological modeling framework. To ensure the robustness of the assimilation process, the study highlights the need for future investigations to conduct a cross-correlation analysis of SMOS errors, shedding light on their patterns and quantifying their impact on the assimilation processes. Additionally, despite the original resolution of GRACE exceeding 100 km, the research demonstrates its capacity to enhance groundwater level estimation accuracy for Iran at a 0.25° resolution, presenting a noteworthy advancement in spatial resolution for groundwater studies. We encourage future studies to utilize finer resolution data if available. This will likely enhance the precision of the simulations and address some of the drawbacks identified in our research. If higher-resolution atmospheric and surface datasets become accessible, we recommend repeating the simulations to potentially achieve more detailed and accurate results. In addition to the points mentioned, it's important to note that the validation results of our ParFlow-CLM simulations should also be compared with those obtained from other data assimilation techniques. While our study focused on a specific approach, other techniques such as Particle Filter (PF), or variational methods could potentially offer different strengths and weaknesses in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. These methods incorporate observational data in varied ways, which might enhance the simulation of surface soil moisture and other hydrological variables. Conducting comparative studies with these alternative techniques would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relative performance and reliability of our results. This comparison could highlight the advantages of using a fully coupled model like ParFlow-CLM versus simpler or different data assimilation methods, offering valuable insights for future research and practical applications in hydrological modeling.
1 Introduction Approximately 70 % of freshwater resources are consumed by agriculture (Steduto et al., 2012 ). The rate of water uptake by crop roots plays a pivotal role in determining water availability in the root zone and influences the water balance within agricultural ecosystems. Gaining a deeper understanding of the root water uptake (RWU) rate is crucial for comprehending the functionality of root systems, the dynamics of nutrient uptake, and the overall health and resilience of crop communities (Wang and Smith, 2004 ). Accurately quantifying and mapping the spatio-temporal characteristics of RWU at a regional scale can offer valuable insights into the water requirements of various crops (Faria et al., 2010 ). This information can enable the optimization of irrigation strategies and facilitate the assessment of the impact of water stress on crop productivity (Green et al., 2006 ). Furthermore, this knowledge can assist in identifying areas with high water demand, prioritizing water allocation, and ensuring the optimal use of limited water resources, especially in regions prone to drought or where water is scarce (Fernández García et al., 2020 ). However, obtaining regional-scale RWU still presents several significant challenges. Current RWU measurement techniques, including lysimeters, stable isotope tracing, and sap flow sensors, often involve invasive and localized procedures. Conducting large-scale RWU measurements to capture RWU spatial and temporal variability can be time-consuming and labor-intensive, demanding extensive fieldwork, data collection, and analysis (Oerter and Bowen, 2017 ). These methods also find it challenging to fully capture the intricacy of root-soil interactions and the impact of environmental conditions on RWU. Moreover, developing models and methodologies that can scale up and generalize RWU from localized measurements to a regional scale is a complex task (Kumar et al., 2015 ). It requires a comprehensive understanding of the underlying processes and interactions. The scaling-up process necessitates the integration of relevant data affecting RWU from various sources, such as soil properties, water contents, root distributions and densities, and climatic conditions (Molz and Remson, 1971; Luo et al., 2003 ). However, this can be difficult due to issues related to data availability, resolution, quality, and compatibility. Therefore, developing non-invasive and high-resolution techniques and reasonable scaling-up methods is crucial for accurately obtaining regional-scale RWU. Soil water flow models embedded with RWU functions, such as Hydrus and SWAP, are the most commonly used tools for the non-invasive evaluation of RWU (de Willigen et al., 2012; Camargo and Kemanian, 2016; Sharmiladevi and Ravikumar, 2021; Dong et al., 2023 ). These well-developed models, combined with field-measured data, including leaf area indices, root depths, and growing periods, have been effectively applied to calculate the point-scale RWU of maize, rice, and wheat (Hou et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2017; Hatiye et al., 2018 ), among other crops. However, obtaining measured crop growth data is also quite difficult and labor-intensive. Therefore, when only limited measured crop growth data are available, crop growth models, such as APSIM, DSSAT, and AquaCrop, are utilized to provide necessary crop growth data (Jones et al., 2003; Keating et al., 2003; Steduto et al., 2009 ). For example, Kanda et al. (2021)  obtained cowpea growth parameters using the AquaCrop model, which were then used in the Hydrus-2D model to simulate RWU under different irrigation management. Similarly, Shelia et al. (2018 ) coupled the DSSAT and Hydrus-1D models to obtain soybean and peanut growth parameters to calculate RWU. Wang et al. (2021 ) applied the APSIM model to get maize growth parameters for the Hydrus-1D model to estimate RWU. These multiple applications indicate that a non-destructive and labor-saving acquisition of point-scale RWU can be achieved. IDW (inverse distance weighted) and kriging interpolations are the most popular methods to aggregate point-scale data to a regional scale (Belkhiri et al., 2020; Yanto et al., 2022; Bel-Lahbib et al., 2023 ). These methods rely on the principle of similarity, using a semivariance function (semivariograms) and known point data to interpolate unknown point data in space (Li and Heap, 2011 ). However, these methods require a sufficient number of known data points to ensure the accuracy of interpolation results (Zhu et al., 2018 ). Moreover, the spatial differences in soil and climate characteristics at the regional scale could result in significant interpolation errors in methods that rely solely on the principle of similarity. Fortunately, the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform provides an online platform for manipulating a large amount of global-scale geospatial data (Gorelick et al., 2017 ). This platform can conveniently store petabytes of data, including climate data and soil properties at regional and global scales (Amani et al., 2020 ). With the GEE platform's powerful geographic and meteorological information acquisition capabilities, accurate regional-scale maps, such as the national-scale cropland map, the high-resolution soil attributes map, and the regional soil water content map, can be obtained (Htitiou et al., 2021; Poppiel et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022 ). However, no quantitative study has used the GEE platform to get regional-scale RWU maps. The objective of this study is to develop a robust approach that integrates the GEE platform, mathematical models, and machine learning algorithms to generate high-precision regional-scale RWU maps. Two mathematical models, Hydrus-1D and AquaCrop, are first utilized to calculate RWU for each point. Soil characteristics and geographical and meteorological covariates extracted from the GEE platform corresponding to these points are then used to train a machine-learning model using the CatBoost algorithm to estimate regional-scale maize RWU.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The primary rain-fed maize-producing area in Northeast China (31°23′04″–53°33′39″ N, 97°10′18″–134°46′32″ E) is considered to validate the effectiveness of our developed approach (Fig. 1  ). This region encompasses Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Hebei, Henan, Shandong, Shanxi, Beijing, Tianjin, and Shaanxi provinces, as derived from China maize phenological dataset from 2000 to 2019 (Luo et al., 2020 ). According to the National Bureau of Statistics of China, the 2022 maize production in this area exceeded 2.2 billion tons, accounting for over 80 % of the country's total maize production. We selected 122 meteorological stations to collect measured meteorological data across the study area. These stations were evenly distributed in the study area to ensure their representativeness (Fig. 1 ).  2.2 The integrated approach We developed a novel integrated approach that combines the GEE platform, mathematical models, and machine learning algorithms to estimate regional-scale actual RWU. The flowchart illustrating this approach is presented in Fig. 2  . Initially, we selected 122 representative meteorological stations, and their corresponding longitude and latitude coordinates were uploaded to the GEE platform to extract essential parameters, including soil properties, leaf area index, and growth period. These parameters, along with meteorological data from 122 agricultural meteorological stations, were applied to calculate point-scale RWU using the Hydrus-1D and AquaCrop models. Since Hydrus-1D can accurately simulate soil moisture movement based on detailed hydraulic parameter information in each layer of soil, and the AquaCrop model can accurately simulate the crop growth process with fewer parameters, the coupled model uses Hydrus-1D Provide detailed multi-layer soil hydraulic parameters for AquaCrop, and use the crop parameters provided by AquaCrop to import into Hydrus-1D to calculate point-scale RWU, along with 31 covariates extracted from the GEE platform, were employed in conjunction with the CatBoost algorithm to develop a machine-learning model for estimating regional-scale RWU.  2.3 Calculation of point-scale RWU Several variables and parameters, such as precipitation (Prec), reference evapotranspiration (ET 0 ), LAI , and rooting depth, need to be input as time-variable boundary conditions into Hydrus-1D to calculate daily point-scale RWU (for years 2015–2019) for the 122 agricultural meteorological stations (Simunek et al., 2005; Šimůnek et al., 2016 ). The root growth of maize is characterized in Hydrus-1D using a root distribution function (Hoffman and Van Genuchten, 1983 ). Daily precipitation data can be obtained from the agricultural meteorological stations, while daily ET 0  can be estimated using the Penman-Monteith equation (Allen et al., 1998 ). The LAI  values and root depths used as input in Hydrus-1D were obtained from the AquaCrop-OSpy model (Kanda et al., 2018 ). The depth of each soil profile was set to 250 cm, and the boundary conditions (BC) were assigned to an atmospheric BC at the soil surface and a free drainage BC at the lower boundary. In addition, the maize in the study area was assumed to be rain-fed, and no artificial irrigation was carried out.
