The sand content, clay content, soil bulk density, and field capacity were extracted from the GEE platform to estimate soil hydraulic parameters using the Rosetta module (Schaap et al., 2001 ) of Hydrus-1D. These parameters are then used in the van Genuchten-Mualem (1980)  equations to describe water retention and soil hydraulic conductivity functions. The van Genuchten-Mualem equations are described as follows:(1) θ h   = θ r  + θ s  - θ r     1 + α h    n     m   ,   h < 0    θ s  ,    h ⩾ 0            (2) K h   = K s  S e l  1 - 1 - S e 1 / m      m     2      (3) S e  = θ s  - θ r     θ - θ r          where θs   and θr   are the saturated water content (cm3  cm−3 ) and the residual water content (cm3  cm−3 ), respectively, Ks   is the saturated hydraulic conductivity (cm day−1 ), Se   is the effective saturation water content. α , m , and n  are empirical parameters, which can be obtained through the Rosetta module, and l  is a tortuosity parameter in the conductivity function, usually assumed to be equal to 0.5. RWU is accounted for in the Richards equation (1931)  by the sink term S (z ,t ), which represents the amount of water removed from a unit of soil volume per unit of time due to RWU. The Richards equation and required initial conditions can be described as follows:(4) ∂ θ  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ z   [ K ( h )  ( ∂ h  ∂ z   - 1 )  ]  - S    h ( z , 0 )  = h 0  ( z )            where θ  is the volumetric water content (cm3  cm−3 ), z  is the vertical space coordinate (cm), K (h ) is unsaturated hydraulic conductivity function (cm day−1 ), h  is the soil water pressure head (cm), h 0 (z ) is the initial soil water pressure head (cm), t  is time (day), and S  is a general sink-source term accounting for RWU (cm3  day−1 ) described as follows:(5) S = A ( h )  B ( z )  T p      (6) T p  = E T o  ( 1 - exp ( - k L A I )  )      (7) A h   = h - h 1   h 2  - h 3    ,   h 1  > h > h 2     1   h 3  > h > h 2     h - h 4   h 3  - h 4    ,    h 3  > h > h 4     0 ,    h > h 1   o r  h < h 4             (8) B z   = 1.66667  L R   ,   z > L - 0.2 L R     2.08333  L R   ,    L - L R  > z > L - 0.2 L R     0 ,    z ⩽ L - L R             where A (h ) and B (z ) are the water stress response function (Feddes, 1980 ) and root growth function (Hoffman and Van Genuchten, 1983 ), respectively, and Tp   is the potential transpiration rate (cm day−1 ), which can be calculated using reference evapotranspiration (ET 0 ), the extinction coefficient k  (usually considered with a value of 0.4 for maize), and LAI  obtained using the Aquacrop crop growth module (Belmans et al., 1983; Liu and Xie, 1998 ). In the stress response function A (h ), h 1  and h 4  are anaerobiosis and wilting point pressure heads, respectively, and h 2  and h 3  are the pressure heads defining the optimal moisture range for RWU. In this study, these parameters are extracted from the Hydrus-1D database (Wesseling et al., 1991 ). Finally, in the root growth function B (z ), L  is the vertical coordinate of the soil surface (cm), and LR   is the root depth (cm). Note that the actual transpiration rate is obtained by integrating the actual root water uptake rate S  across the root zone. This study uses the term point-scale RWU to represent the actual transpiration rate (de Melo and de Jong van Lier, 2021 ). The root depth and LAI  are estimated using the AquaCrop crop growth module (Kelly and Foster, 2021 ). Aquacrop uses the canopy cover (CC ) to describe the leaf development process instead of LAI . The LAI values are thus obtained in the subsequent step using the adjusted empirical relationship for maize (Hsiao et al., 2009 ).(9) CC = 1.005 × [ 1 - exp ( - 0.6 L A I )  ]  1.2        The procedure for obtaining LAI  and root depth values is described as follows:1) Set the meteorological parameters, including daily minimum temperature, maximum temperature, precipitation, and reference evapotranspiration.  2) Set soil parameters, including sand, silt, and clay content required to determine soil texture type, and field capacity (obtained from the GEE platform), and soil hydraulic conductivity (obtained from the Rosetta module of Hydrus-1D).  3) Obtain phenology information on maize from the GEE platform for each point.  4) Define the initial soil water conditions equal to field capacity.  5) Perform simulations from 2015 to 2019, saving crop growth files locally to extract daily values of LAI  and root depth data.    After using Hydrus-1D and Aquacrop to carry out RWU simulations for the selected 122 stations, the RWU values, longitude, and latitude of each point from 2015 to 2019 were included in the shp files and imported into ArcMap (v. 10.8). Then, the hot and cold spot analysis was performed to determine the spatial distribution characteristics of high and low RWU values (Songchitruksa and Zeng, 2010 ).  2.4 Scaling up point-scale RWU to regional RWU The CatBoost algorithm, based on the gradient boosting over decision trees approach, supports both numerical and categorical features (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018 ). More specifically, most algorithms based on the gradient-boosting decision tree (GBDT) method generate a base learner in each iteration, and as the number of iterations increases, the next base learner is trained on the gradient of the previous learner, but at each iteration the data points and target values used in this iteration are the same as those used in building the model, which will undoubtedly lead to a deviation between the estimated gradient and the true gradient. CatBoost advances the ordered-boosting method to separately sample each step in the boosting process, thereby avoiding gradient offsets in the estimation process, therefore, CatBoost has superior quality compared to other GBDT algorithm (Dorogush et al., 2018; Prokhorenkova et al., 2018 ). In this study, we utilized this algorithm to construct a machine-learning model using information about simulated RWU and 31 local covariates at 122 locations over five years (2015 to 2019). The 31 covariates were extracted from the GEE platform to train and test the CatBoost algorithm, thereby developing machine learning models for upscaling RWU. The procedure for upscaling is as follows (Gavrilidis et al., 2022 ):1) The 31 covariate parameters for each simulation point are cyclically extracted using the GEE platform and saved locally using Google Drive.  2) The calculated point-scale RWU values and the covariates extracted by the GEE platform are combined for data aggregation.  3) The point-scale RWU values are used as the label for the CatBoost model. The 31 covariates extracted from GEE are utilized as features to construct the CatBoost model. The TPE (Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator) optimization is employed to select hyperparameters, optimizing the number of iterations, tree depth, and learning rate (Bentéjac et al., 2021 ).  4) A sliding time window is used to divide the aggregated data into training and test sets. This ensures that each year's data can be utilized as training samples, allowing for a comprehensive exploration of the correlation between the data.  5) The TPE-optimized hyperparameters are passed into the CatBoost model to construct the regional RWU estimation model. This model serves as the basis for subsequent spatial mapping.    The CatBoost machine learning model was developed in a training environment consisting of a graphics workstation with the following specifications: CPU: Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-12900H CPU @ 3.00 GHz, GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX A2000, and RAM: 64 GB. The model training was performed using the Anaconda platform as the base platform, JupyterLab as the code integration development tool, and the underlying Python version is 3.8. After establishing the model, the feature importance analysis and the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis were used to elucidate the contribution rate of 31 covariates involved in the modeling to the model output. In the CatBoost algorithm, three methods for calculating feature importance scores are provided: Prediction Values Change, Loss Function Change, and Internal Feature Importances. For this study, the Prediction Values Change method is employed to calculate feature importance scores. This approach assesses the impact of alterations in the values of each feature involved in the modeling on the model prediction results, thereby providing a ranking of feature importance scores. Although not as precise as the other two methods, it significantly reduces computation time and yields faster score rankings. Conversely, the SHAP method not only provides feature importance rankings but also elucidates the impact（whether positive or negative）of each feature value change on the model prediction results. While SHAP method offering more accurate results, this method requires more time-intensive calculations. Therefore, to swiftly obtain feature importance ranking and interpretable results regarding feature ranking, the aforementioned methods have been chosen for this study. The principles and procedures of these two analysis methods have been described in the previously published studies (Slack et al., 2020; Zien et al., 2009 ).  2.5 Generation of regional RWU maps ArcGIS (10.8) was used in this study to generate regional RWU maps. Since the developed RWU estimation model only requires the extraction of covariates from corresponding points to complete the estimation process, the methods can be described as follows:1) The cultivated land within the study area is rasterized with a resolution of 500 m, and the central point of each raster cell is extracted as the covariate extraction point.  2) The latitude and longitude of points are uploaded to the GEE platform, and the covariate parameters required for modeling are extracted.  3) The extracted covariate parameters are aggregated, and the regional RWU estimation model is run to obtain RWU at each point for years from 2015 to 2019.  4) The points containing RWU estimates are imported into ArcGIS for point-to-raster mapping.     2.6 Data acquisition The covariate parameters used in the modeling are extracted from the GEE platform, including soil parameters, meteorological data, elevation data, and soil moisture data. After uploading the locations of 122 meteorological stations in the shape file format to the GEE platform, values of the dataset from 2015 to 2019 are extracted in a loop and exported to the local drive via Google Drive for machine-learning modeling purposes (Tamiminia et al., 2020 ). The covariate data obtained in this study are described as follows:1) Soil parameters dataset: The data is obtained from the OpenLandMap dataset, including the surface soil’s and root zone’s clay content (denoted as SurfaceClay and RootzoneClay, respectively), sand content (SurfaceSand and RootzoneSand), field capacity (SurfaceFC and RootzoneFC), and soil bulk density (SurfaceBD and RootzoneBD) (Hengl, 2018a–c; Hengl and Gupta, 2019 ). Each parameter is obtained for 6 standard depths (0, 10, 30, 60, 100, and 200 cm) at a resolution of 250 m. The variables differ only in terms of depth. To prevent mutual interference between variables, the soil parameters for the 0 cm depth represent surface parameters. The remaining depths are averaged and used as rootzone parameters, serving as covariates for modeling.  2) Altitude dataset: The data is obtained from the SRTM Digital Elevation Data, Version 4, providing elevation at a resolution of 90 m (Jarvis et al., 2008 ). When extracting altitude data for each point, the latitude and longitude information of the point is also extracted to supplement the geographic location factor in the covariate.  3) Daily climate dataset: The data is obtained from ERA5 Daily Aggregates-Latest Climate Reanalysis produced by the ECMWF/Copernicus Climate Change Service dataset (Service (C3S), 2017 ). It includes various variables such as mean 2-m air temperature (TempMean), max 2-m air temperature (TempMax), min 2-m air temperature (TempMin), 2-m dewpoint temperature (TempDew), total precipitation (TotalPrec), mean sea level pressure (Prs), surface pressure (SurPrs), 10 m u-component of wind (Wind10U), and 10 m v-component of wind (Wind10V).  4) Soil moisture dataset: The data is obtained from the SPL4SMGP.007 SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9-km Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture dataset (Model, n.d. ). It includes various variables such as top layer soil moisture (SurfaceSM), mean land surface temperature (SurfaceTemp), root zone soil moisture (RootzoneSM), evapotranspiration (ET), overland runoff (Runoff), baseflow, soil water infiltration rate (Infiltration), net downward shortwave flux over land (Shortwave), net downward longwave flux over land (Longwave), vegetation greenness fraction (Greenness), and vegetation leaf area index (LAI). Since the time resolution of this data set is 3 h, the data is aggregated by summing and averaging over a day to match the daily scale data used for modeling.    Covariates are extracted from the above-discussed datasets to provide data support for machine learning models. The statistics of point-scale RWU values and covariates are presented in Table 1  .  2.7 Error analysis The mean absolute error (MAE ) and the root mean squared error (RMSE ) are used for error analysis. Their calculation formulas are described as follows:(10) MAE = 1 m  ∑ i = 1  m  ( y i  - z i  )        (11) RMSE = 1 m  ∑ i = 1  m  ( y i  - z i  )  2        where m  is the number of data points, and yi   and zi   refer to the i -th calculated and predicted values, respectively.   3 Results 3.1 Point-scale RWU Point-scale maize RWU at 122 meteorological stations from 2015 to 2019 were calculated using the Hydrus-1D and AquaCrop models. The spatial clustering patterns of point-scale RWU with high or low values were investigated using a hot and cold spot analysis. The hot and cold spot analysis results reflect the strength and distribution characteristics of the RWU capacity. The results revealed an apparent clustering pattern of point-scale RWU values. Hot spot clusters, indicating higher RWU values, were found in mid to high-latitude areas such as Heilongjiang, Jilin, Inner Mongolia, Shanxi, and Hebei provinces. On the other hand, cold spot clusters, representing lower RWU values, were observed in low-latitude areas, including Hebei, Shandong, and Henan provinces (Fig. 3  ). We determined that these differences in RWU values in the hot and cold spot locations were influenced by latitude. Furthermore, the water uptake capability of maize in higher latitude locations was stronger. Fig. 4   shows the cumulative annual RWU during 2015–2019 averaged for all hot-spot and cold-spot locations, further highlighting their differences. Specifically, the initial time for RWU in the high-latitude locations (hot spots) was earlier than in the low-latitude locations (cold spots), with an average of 26 days earlier. The time series of the simulated daily RWU values during 2015–2019 for all hot-spot and cold-spot locations also aligns with this trend (Fig. S1 ). Additionally, from 2015 to 2019, the average annual cumulative RWU values in hot-spot and cold-spot locations showed an increasing gap. The gap for the average annual cumulative RWU values from 2015 to 2016 is 0.08–0.26 cm/year, while from 2017 to 2019, it is 2.42–5.22 cm/year. Considering the current global warming scenario, this may be related to the variations in maize potential RWU response to a temperature increase across different latitudes. The potential mechanism is examined in detail in the discussion section.  3.2 Regional-scale RWU The CatBoost machine learning algorithms were used to successfully develop a regional estimation model for maize RWU using RWU values calculated at 122 locations and 31 spatial covariates obtained from GEE. A hyperparameters optimization procedure was performed to ensure the accuracy of the developed model. The results demonstrated that the optimal hyperparameters, compared to the default hyperparameters, significantly enhanced the estimation accuracy of RWU values (Table S1 ). Furthermore, the optimized hyperparameters determined the developed model's most suitable number of iterations (243), tree depth (9), and learning rate (0.6874), which are all the CatBoost machine learning algorithm parameters. Moreover, we assessed the significance of various covariates for model accuracy. Feature importance scores of 31 covariates were analyzed to determine the variables (with higher scores) with a higher impact on changes in the output value of the model. Meteorological data (specifically TempDew and TempMax), spatial location information (i.e., Latitude), and surface soil moisture (i.e., SurfaceSM) were determined to be the primary covariate factors influencing regional RWU estimation (Fig. 5  ). To further elucidate the contribution rate of each covariate factor to the model output, we conducted the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis, which evaluates the impact of covariates in each sample by calculating the marginal contribution to the model output. The SHAP results are generally consistent with the covariates importance analysis results, highlighting that TempDew, TempMax, and Latitude significantly impact the RWU predictions (Fig. 6  ). Furthermore, their contributions to estimating regional RWU values are similar, meaning that higher values of these covariate factors result in larger RWU values. By utilizing the developed regional estimation model, we could compute the regional RWU, with their average values depicted in Fig. 7  . The annual variation patterns of RWU align with the growth pattern of maize. The predicted values (calculated by the developed machine-learning model) and measured values (calculated by Hydrus-1D and AquaCrop) exhibit a significant positive correlation at a 99 % confidence level (p  < 0.01), indicating excellent accuracy of the model in estimating RWU values (Fig. 7 ). The average mean absolute error (MAE ) and root mean squared error (RMSE ) for RWU are 0.0299 and 0.0398 cm d−1 , respectively. The interannual average MAE  and RMSE  values varied from 0.0262 to 0.0334 and 0.0346–0.0456 cm d−1 , respectively, which exhibited a consistent amplitude without significant fluctuations (Fig. S2 ). This suggests that estimated RWU values remain relatively stable over time. Regarding the spatial error, the range of MAE  and RMSE  values for RWU varied from 0.0286 to 0.0533 and 0.0558–0.0781 cm d−1 , respectively (Fig. S3 ). The developed model demonstrates good performance in terms of spatial estimations, with minimal differences in MAEs  between different provinces.  3.3 Regional RWU maps Using the developed regional RWU estimation model, we generated high-precision (500 m × 500 m) regional RWU maps from 2015 to 2019 (Fig. 8  ). Specifically, we focused on displaying the RWU values from May to September of each year (i.e., the main growth period for maize during each year), providing a detailed depiction of the monthly variation pattern of RWU. Overall, RWU shows similar trends during different months of different years between 2015 and 2019. These maps exhibit an increasing trend in RWU in early summer, reaching its peak in July, followed by a decrease over time. Although the overall trend of RWU in different years is similar, there are still differences in their spatial distribution characteristics. Due to extreme climate phenomena occurring in certain locations in specific years, the RWU values in these locations have shown significant differences compared to other locations. Except for climate conditions, these differences in RWU also signify the influence of diverse soil and management conditions on maize water uptake. The generated regional RWU maps provide comprehensive insights into root water uptake at the regional scale, offering valuable information for understanding the dynamics of crop water uptake and soil water scarcity. Some specific application cases of these maps were analyzed in the discussion section.   4 Discussion 4.1 Key covariates affecting regional RWU estimation We collected a large amount of data to perform an importance ranking analysis (Fig. 5 ) and the SHAP analysis (Fig. 6 ) for assessing the impacts of 31 covariate factors on the accuracy of estimating regional RWU (Lipovetsky and Conklin, 2001; Slack et al., 2020 ). These numerous data are repeatedly used to train the CatBoost machine learning algorithms to achieve optimal accuracy, thereby identifying key influencing factors for regional-scale RWU. This is the first evidence put forward to discern the critical factors impacting regional-scale RWU. The top four covariates identified in this study in both analyses, i.e ., TempDew, SurfaceSM, TempMax, and Latitude, are considered the key influencers. These findings partially challenge the previous understanding of various factors influencing point-scale RWU in field or pot experiments. Previously, numerous reports on point-scale RWU suggested that soil hydraulic characteristics and soil moisture were the primary factors affecting RWU (Puig-Sirera et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022 ). While we tend to agree with this view concerning point-scale RWU, we believe that comprehending RWU at different scales (point-scale and regional-scale) may yield different conclusions. We cannot find similar comparative studies since this is the first study estimating daily RWU at a regional scale. Crop transpiration, a result of RWU, is indicative of the RWU pattern, and most models dealing with RWU and transpiration consider the two to be numerically equivalent (de Melo and de Jong van Lier, 2021; Aston and Lawlor, 1979 ). Herein, to make a comparison, we have examined many quantitative studies on crop transpiration at a regional scale, which indicate that atmospheric moisture, pressure, temperature, and precipitation are key factors affecting crop transpiration at a regional scale (Christensen et al., 2008; Kropp et al., 2017; Kukal and Irmak, 2023; Peng et al., 2011 ). These factors that affect regional-scale transpiration have important reference significance for our understanding of regional-scale RWU. This study identifies TempDew as the most influential covariate factor for estimating regional-scale RWU. TempDew, denoting dew point temperature, represents the temperature to which the air must be cooled (at constant pressure) to reach a relative humidity (RH ) of 100 % (Wood, 1970 ). At this point, the air can no longer hold water in its gas form, leading to the condensation of water vapor into liquid form, such as fog or precipitation. A higher dew point indicates more moisture in the air, resulting in a more humid environment (Zounemat-Kermani, 2012 ). Therefore, TempDew strongly correlates with atmospheric humidity, pressure, and precipitation events, enabling tracking changes in the atmospheric moisture holding capacity (Wasko et al., 2018; Pumo and Noto, 2021 ). This is consistent with the aforementioned factors affecting regional-scale transpiration. On the other hand, latitude is a key covariate factor for estimating regional-scale RWU. The hot and cold spot analysis results discussed above support the significance of latitude for regional-scale RWU. RWU exhibits distinct latitude-dependent patterns, with higher RWU clusters predominantly located in mid and high-latitude areas, while lower RWU clusters are observed in low-latitude areas. In this study, the significant difference in latitude, approximately 22° between the northern and southern ends of the study area, results in an uneven distribution of water and heat resources, affecting the phenology and RWU of maize (Muchow, 1989a, 1989b ). Similar studies have also demonstrated that latitude plays a significant role in the developmental stages of maize, consequently impacting its RWU (Liu et al., 2013 ). This conclusion also differs from previous studies, which generally suggested that crop growth (the capability of RWU) in high-latitude and low-latitude areas is lower compared to middle-latitude areas (Afuakwa et al., 1984; Baloch et al., 2021 ). Higher RWU observed in high-latitude areas may be attributed to the current global warming. Global warming has intensified the already hot conditions in low-latitude areas, making them even hotter and drier (Peltonen-Sainio et al., 2016 ). Excessive heat can reduce crop yields by lowering RWU due to unfavorable climatic conditions (Meng et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2012 ). Conversely, high-latitude areas have experienced warming, and a warmer climate can enhance crop yields by promoting RWU. The report released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has shown that the period from 2015 to 2019 was the hottest five-year period, and greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere also rose to record levels (Siegmund et al., 2020 ). This high-intensity warming may reverse the original trend of higher RWU at low latitudes and lower RWU at high latitudes, increasing RWU at high-latitude locations (i.e., at hot spots).  4.2 High-precision regional RWU maps and their application The approach proposed in this manuscript enables the generation of daily spatial distribution maps of maize RWU at a resolution of 500 m or higher. However, our investigation revealed that published articles only report calculated point-scale RWU (Kanda et al., 2021; Shelia et al., 2018; Sulis et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021 ), and no similar studies or commercial products are available. Consequently, high-precision regional RWU maps have not yet been reported. The developed approach can directly produce RWU at a regional scale, which intuitively reflects whether crops are in a state of water scarcity on a spatial scale. We found that most of the key factors affecting regional-scale RWU are meteorological factors. Therefore, to verify the accuracy of the generated RWU maps, we chose the precipitation and evapotranspiration-driven indicator, the so-called standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI), for comparison. The SPEI index has a wide range of applications to reflect regional drought conditions (Beguería et al., 2014; Stagge et al., 2015 ). We selected the generated RWU maps for July 2015, 2017, and 2019 for comparison, showing a relatively consistent spatial distribution pattern for both variables, with lower values in the north and higher values in the south (Fig. 9  ). However, the SPEI index has a spatial resolution of 55660 m and a monthly cadence, while our product has the advantage of having a spatial resolution of 500 m and can be obtained at a daily scale. Our product can achieve a more accurate and real-time reflection of regional drought conditions. The generated RWU maps can be used to recognize and validate extreme meteorological events. For example, the published report demonstrated that the precipitation in the Liaoning province decreased by 78.7 % in July 2015, which caused a significant reduction in soil moisture (Liao et al., 2016 ). This event can be reflected in lower RWU values in July 2015 in our generated regional-scale RWU map (Fig. 8 ). Similarly, another previous report showed that precipitation in western northeast China and western Inner Mongolia decreased by 30–80 % from April to late July 2017, and the temperature increased by 1–2 °C (Feng et al., 2018 ). This decreased RWU is also reflected in the generated regional-scale RWU map (Fig. 8 ). Furthermore, we have recognized an extreme meteorological event (e.g., lower RWU values) in the western part of the Shandong province in July 2019 (Fig. 8 ). Our investigation revealed that this can be attributed to an intense heatwave that lasted for a month, which was the most severe event in this area since 1961 (Zeng et al., 2020 ). According to the covariate importance ranking discussed above, TempDew is the most important indicator for estimating regional root water uptake and is closely correlated with atmospheric temperature and precipitation events (Bui et al., 2019 ). SurfaceSM and TempMax emerge as the second and third most significant factors in regional-scale RWU calculations, following TempDew. The validation of these real-world cases demonstrated that the main identified factors (e.g., TempDew, SurfaceSM, and TempMax) greatly impact estimated regional-scale RWU. Our newly developed approach, combined with future climate change scenarios, can also predict future regional-scale RWU and drought degrees. This is of great significance for guiding the optimization of regional agricultural water resource management.   5 Conclusion We propose a novel approach integrating the GEE platform, mathematical models, and machine learning algorithms to calculate regional RWU. Mathematical models, which consider the complexity of root-soil-climate interactions, are utilized to accurately calculate RWU at the point scale, offering a non-invasive, time-efficient, and labor-saving method. By harnessing the capabilities of the GEE platform for extracting and fusing multi-source data and incorporating machine learning algorithms to use the amassed data for training, we achieve a reasonable upscaling of RWU from the point scale to the regional scale. TempDew, SurfaceSM, TempMax, and Latitude were identified as critical factors influencing regional RWU. The developed model for estimating regional RWU has been validated to have high accuracy, enabling the generation of high-precision (500 m × 500 m) regional RWU maps for 2015 to 2019. These findings will facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of root water uptake patterns and their variability across different spatial and temporal scales, significantly contributing to optimizing water resource management strategies.
1 Introduction As the physical habitat of in-stream biota, the in-stream habitat is comprised of the channel's physical structure as well as the spatial and temporal dynamics of the flow regime (Maddock 1999 ). Various in-stream and topographic variables affect habitat structure, including bed slope and deformation, near-bed velocity, and flow circulations (Pedersen et al. 2004 ). Sustaining biodiversity is essential to the health of our environment and to the quality of human life. For our survival, we are dependent on a variety of aquatic plants, organisms, and their ecological processes. Aquatic biodiversity depends on some factors including a) chemical variables of water quality including factors such as pH, dissolved oxygen, nutrient levels, and pollutants, b) water temperature, c) the structure and complexity of aquatic habitats, such as the presence of rocks, vegetation, or other physical features, d) availability of foods, e) the connectivity of aquatic habitats to other ecosystems, such as wetlands, rivers, or oceans and f) hydrodynamics of flow including velocity and discharge (J. Morin and McGrady‐Steed, 2004; Irfan and Alatawi, 2019; Protasov, et al., 2019 ). In this direction, the current research, in terms of eco-hydraulic, aims to investigate the hydrodynamic features of flow that affect aquatic organisms. Previous literature studies (Crowder and Diplas 2000, 2002; Gualtieri et al., 2017 , 2020) indicated that the hydraulic complexity parameters, M1  and M2 , provide a description of the magnitude of drag forces applied by aquatic organisms when they move between two locations. The first parameter, M1 , represents the spatial alteration in the flow's kinetic energy. This parameter is defined as a quantitative measure of the extent of power exerted in the process of transitioning from one specific location to another. The second parameter, referred to as M2 , functions as a gauge to determine the additional amount of energy an organism is required to expend when it moves from a region with a lower velocity to one with a higher velocity magnitude. The third parameter, M3,  provides information about circulation zones in the flow which could be potential feeding places for aquatic organisms such as fishes. Overall, with these three parameters, M1 , M2 , and M3 , it becomes possible to assess the hydraulic conditions that are conducive to the existence of an aquatic habitat. Aquatic habitat is extremely dependent upon the spatial heterogeneity and variability of flow characteristics, i.e. water depth and flow velocity. As an example, some researchers (Fausch and White 1981; Rempel et al. 1999 ) showed that flow patterns, eddies, transverse flows, velocity gradients, and thus turbulent kinetic energy, and other complex hydraulic characteristics can predict salmonid density (Smith et al. 2006 ). The natural streams were modeled using commercial packages such as River2D, which is a two-dimensional, depth-averaged hydrodynamic model (Blackburn and Steffler, 2002; Clark et al. 2008 ). Tritico and Hotchkiss (2005)  proved that natural boulders create vertical vortex structures downstream of gravel-bed streams based on spatial variations in bed roughness. Vertical vortices create areas of high and low pressure within the water column which can impact aquatic organisms and river ecology by creating flow circulation zones. This impact can be quite complex and can vary depending on several factors, including the size and strength of the vortex, the geometry of the river channel, and the local topography. As an example, Blettler et al. (2016)  verified that the macroinvertebrate diversity increased strongly downstream of the Bermejo and Paraguay River junction. Gualtieri et al. (2017 , 2020) investigated the hydraulic complexity parameters through the junction of Negro and Solimões rivers on the Amazon River in Brazil and determined that helical cells forming at the confluence directly affect the flow rotation strength. Yuan et al. (2023)  investigated M2  distribution, water quality and fish density at the confluence between the Yangtze River and the Poyang Lake and found that large values of M2  were observed where the kinetic energy was relatively low, such as in the stagnation zone near the apex of the confluence, as well as along the river banks. Nepf et al. (2022)  reported a review of some research works on the influence of hydraulic conditions on habitat selection and migration of fish and macroinvertebrates. They reported how habitat selection and swimming patterns are induced by velocity, turbulence, and bed shear stress. Golpira et al. (2022)  experimentally investigated the effect of rock-ramp boulder placement with varying boulder concentration and flow rate on habitat hydraulic complexity metrics, including the kinetic energy gradient and modified recirculation metrics. They found that boulder placement with the highest boulder concentration resulted in the greatest habitat hydraulic complexity. Bahmanpouri et al. (2023)  analyzed the hydraulic complexity parameters M1  and M2  based on laboratory and field data to investigate the drag forces applied by aquatic organisms. The present study, as continuation of Bahmanpouri et al.’ (2023)  work, aims to investigate the three hydraulic complexity parameters (M1 , M2 , and M3 ) in more detail. These parameters are of particular importance to determining the diversity of aquatic organisms based on analysing the kinetic energy and vorticities at the potential habitat zones. In the pursuit of this endeavour, it is imperative to consider both laboratory-based and field-based measurements, as they provide valuable insights into the development and validation of spatial metrics that are of essential importance in the realm of various stream conditions. The current research endeavours to establish a correlation between energy gradients, vorticity, and flow complexity, all of which play a crucial role in the comprehensive study of aquatic organisms within the context of eco-hydraulics. This study encompasses fishes belonging to diverse species and encompassing different stages of their life cycle. Thus, in the present research, data from both laboratory flume and the field, collected at a gauged section along the Tiber River, in central Italy, under different flow conditions are used. In particular, the analysis of laboratory data has allowed us to isolate the effects of the bed deformation and turbulence structures periodicity, which strongly influence the aquatic habitat, on stream parameters evaluation. Different cross-sections within each of the flow patterns of interest are calculated and scrutinized to examine the considered metrics. The paper is organized as follows: the first Section introduces the laboratory setup and field site, while the second Section describes the theory behind the hydraulic complexity parameters. In Section 3 , the results from both laboratory and field data are presented. The paper is ended with the conclusion in Section 4 .  2 Spatial metrics for river flow complexity: Theoretical background The velocity gradient is a prominent component in a spatially varying flow pattern. It is worth noting that velocity gradients exist near banks, boulders, and other obstructions and are potentially applicable parameters for quantifying and distinguishing between flows having similar depth and velocity values but influenced by different spatially varying flow patterns (Fig. 1  ). Two parameters that address local velocity gradients are defined as potential habitat metrics and they are inferred as (Crowder and Diplas 2000, 2002; Gualtieri et al., 2017 ; 2020):(1) M 1  = ∂ ∂ s   V  2  2  = V ∂ V  ∂ s   ≅ V ave   V 2  - V 1   Δ s       (2) M 2  = ∂ ∂ s   V  2  2   V  2  2   ≅ 1 2  V 2  2  - V 1  2   Δ s       V min  2  2   = 2 V ave   V 2  - V 1   Δ s    V min  2       where V  is the velocity and V 1  and V2   are magnitudes of velocity between the two consecutive velocity points 1 and 2, whose distance is Δ s    , V ave  is the average of V 1  and V2  ; V min  is the minimum value of V 1  and V2.   The distance Δ s     can be defined in the transverse direction as Δ y     (for the present work Δ y     = 0.07 and 1.0 m for the laboratory and field data, respectively). The first parameter M1  represents the spatial change in a flow’s specific kinetic energy (i.e. per unit mass and unit length [J/Kgm]). The second parameter M2  scales the spatial change in the kinetic energy of the flow at the point having the lower velocity magnitude. Thus, to distinguish between flows with similar water depth and velocity values but different velocity gradients surrounding them, the parameters M1  and M2  allow the evaluation of a flow's velocity gradient and its scaled specific kinetic energy, respectively. In other words, based on Crowder and Diplas (2000) , the first parameter (M1 ) is proportional to drag force on an organism and it is a measure of the amount of power expended in moving from one location to another. The second parameter (M2 ) represents how much more energy an organism such as fish must expend if it moves from the lower velocity to the higher velocity location. The concept of hydraulic complexity parameters considering the aquatic organisms is highlighted in Fig. 2  . For the first parameter, kinetic energy per unit mass (V  2  2  )     multiplied by a drag coefficient and a frontal area provides the drag force acting on a specific object or organism such as fish (Munson et al., 1990 ). Hayes and Jowett (1994)  and Fausch and White (1981)  presented some data to estimate the minimum and maximum possible values of 2 V ave   × ( V  2  - V 1     / Δ s | /  V min  2     that existed at the location of an aquatic organism such as fish. Further, they reported a range of focal point velocity values (V min ), “velocity shears” and “velocity differences” that existed at fish locations. The third parameter M3  highlights the weighted average of flow rotation in the transversal vertical or horizontal plane, known as ‘‘modified circulation”. This parameter is a scale of the strength and frequency of eddies and is defined, in the vertical plane, as (Gualtieri et al. 2020 ):(3) M 3  = ∫ ∫ ξ    Δ A  s   ¯    A TOT    = ∑ ( Δ w  Δ y   - Δ v  Δ z       ∑ Δ y  × Δ z    × Δ y  × Δ z      where Δ w ,   Δ v    and Δ u    are the variations of velocity in the vertical, transverse and streamwise directions, respectively. Fig. 2  depicts the meshing diagram of M3 , which can be calculated in both vertical and horizontal planes, respectively. The M3  parameter represents the flow circulation within an area, which is important for evaluating the environmental impact of turbulence structures. According to the data by Shields and Rigby (2005) , the approximate range of observed magnitudes in the field for the three selected parameters M1 , M2  and M3  is 0–0.2 J.kg −1 .m−1 , 0.9–1.3 m−1 , 0.2–1 s−1 , respectively. For the present work, the aforementioned parameters are investigated in dimensionless form, i.e. M1 * = (M1 -Mmin )/ (Mmax -Mmin ), M2 * = (M2 -Mmin )/ (Mmax -Mmin ), and M3 * = (M3 -Mmin )/ (Mmax -Mmin ). By employing these dimensionless representations, the collected data can be more effectively compared and analyzed, without losing their meaning.  3 Experimental- and field-scale studies and dataset 3.1 Laboratory-scale data The laboratory data were collected at the hydraulic laboratory of the University of Palermo (Italy) in research (Termini and Sammartano, 2008; Termini, 2015 ) aimed to evaluate the flow velocity field and the evolution of turbulent flow structures in a straight flume (see Fig. 3  ). The channel was of width B=40 cm with fixed banks and bed of quartz sand (D50   = median sediment diameter = 0.65 mm). For the purposes of the present work, two runs with flow discharge of 0.013 m3 /s (see also in Termini, 2015 ) are considered for the analysis: the “Smooth Banks” (“SB”) run, characterized by flat and rigid bed (i.e. the so-called pre-deformed-bed configuration), and the “Deformed Banks” (“DB”) run, which is a mobile-bed run with the same hydraulic conditions as the SB run. The run time was based on the reaching the equilibrium deformed-bed configuration. During the SB run, the 3D instantaneous flow velocity components were measured in 14 points along 5 verticals of 17 measurement cross-sections (sections A÷S in Fig. 3 a). At the end of the DB run, the bed was found covered by alternating regions of scour-holes/deposit-fronts, as for example Fig. 3 b shows in the channel reach between sections D and H. In the present work, the analysis is restricted to the channel reach D÷H where the alternating scour-deposit regions were clearly distinguishable. The examined sections D÷H were reciprocally distant of 20 cm so that the channel reach was 80 cm long. As Fig. 3 b shows, in section D a scour hole is found on the right side of the cross section and a front of deposit formed on the left side. In section E, a new scour hole starts on the right and the left sides. In section F, the bed configuration is similar to that observed in section D. In sections G and H, a front of deposit is found in the central part of the cross-section and two scour holes formed in the left and right sides of the cross-section, almost symmetrically with respect to the channel axis (more details can be found in Termini and Sammartano, 2008; Termini, 2015 ).  3.2 Field-scale case studies 3.2.1 Upper Tiber River (central Italy) The Upper Tiber River basin is bounded downstream by the hydrometric section of Ponte Nuovo, with a length of about 120 km from the springs and a drainage area equal to 4145 km2  (Fig. 4  ). In this work, the streamwise flow velocity measurement were carried out using an ADCP (acoustic Doppler current profiler) at Ponte Nuovo gauged section. Specifically, a total of three flow measurements were made under different hydraulic conditions, classified as low, medium, and high in Table 1  .    4 Results and discussion 4.1 Laboratory-scale case The dimensionless parameters M1 *, M2 *, and M3 * are first estimated by using the data collected in sections D÷H of the laboratory channel during the SB run. In a previous work (Bahmanpouri et al., 2023 ), the analysis of the gradient of the streamwise velocity in sections D and E allowed us to verify that M1  and M2  adequately indicate the spatial variation of the kinetic energy due to the alternating high/low velocity pattern in the streamwise direction. In the present work, all the parameters M1 *, M2 *, and M3 * are analyzed in sections D÷H. As Fig. 4  shows, while in section D higher values of flow velocity are found on the right side of the cross-section with peak values at Y/B=0.32, in section E higher values of flow velocity occur almost symmetrically to the channel axis at a relative distance Y/B=0.32 from the banks. In section F, the distribution of flow velocity is similar to that observed in section D but with lower peak values. In section G, and then especially in section H, the higher values of flow velocity are found almost symmetrically to the channel axis at a relative distance of 0.32 from the banks. In the last two sections, the velocity values are lower than those obtained in sections D÷F. According to findings obtained by Termini (2015)  (see also in Termini and Sammartano, 2008 ), by comparing the distributions of flow velocity shown in Fig. 5   with the bed deformation obtained at the end of the DB run (see Fig. 3 b), it is clear that the higher values of flow velocity occur in the correspondence of the scour holes obtained in the deformed-bed condition. Termini (2015)  demonstrated that the deformed-bed configuration is strongly related to the formation of alternating regions of high/low flow velocity in the pre-deformed configuration. Figs. 6 and 7    report the distributions of the parameters M1 * and M2 * estimated in sections D÷H. Fig. 6  indicates that in section D, a high spatial velocity gradient (M1 *) occurs on the right side of the cross-section, reaching its peak value at a relative distance around of 0.3 from the bank. In section E, higher values of M1 * are found both close to the bed at the right bank and close to the free surface on the left side of the cross section, while in section F, the peak values are observed on the right side of the cross section. Then, in section G, the parameter M1 * assumes values lower than in the previous sections with higher values close to the bed in both sides of the cross-section. These areas of high values of M1 * are then extended towards the free surface in section H. Fig. 6  shows the distribution of M2 * in sections D÷H. The higher values of M2 * are found on the right side of section D with a peak value close to the bed. Passing from section D to section F higher values of M2 * are found close to the right bank and including an area gradually smaller. In section G, two small areas with high values of M2 * are observed close to the banks. These areas of high values of M2 * are expanded in the whole water depth in section H. The distribution of the parameter M3 * in sections D÷H is reported in Fig. 8  . Alternated zones characterized by high/low vorticity values are found. In particular, section D shows high values of M3 * close to the bed and in the central part (i.e. in the range 0.35 < Y/B<0.65) where the bed profile changes. This behaviour is also observed in section E, where higher values of M3 * are especially observed moving from the right side towards the left side of the cross-section. In section F, small zones of high circulation can be observed especially at the bed close to both banks and peak values can be also observed near the free surface. In sections G and H, the zones of high circulation close to the bed tend to expand towards the free surface, almost symmetrically to the channel axis. To examine the relationship between the observed patterns of the parameters M1 * and M2 * and the alternating high/low velocity pattern along the analyzed channel reach, Fig. 9   illustrates the horizontal distribution of the depth-averaged velocity V in the reach D÷H. As Fig. 9  shows, a high peak of flow velocity occurs near the right bank of sections D and F while lower peak values occur almost symmetrically to the channel axis in sections E and G. In section H such a behavior is maintained although it is less evident and with velocity values lower than those obtained in the upstream sections. Fig. 10   reports the depth-averaged velocity, V, normalized by the mean velocity Um (with Um = Q/A), and the depth-averaged values of parameters M1 *, M2 * and M3 * in sections D÷H. This figure illustrates that in section D, M1 * decreases passing from the right bank to the left bank. The parameter M2 * assumes high values for relative distances from the right bank ranging from Y/B=0.25 and Y/B=0.6, where the aquatic organism should spend the higher energy. The flow circulation, given by the parameter M3 *, assumes an increasing trend passing from Y/B=0.25 cm to Y/B=0.4 and then it decreases assuming a low value at Y/B=0.6, then it increases again. In section E, the depth-averaged value of M1 * has a decreasing trend on the right side of the cross-section assuming the lowest value at Y/B=0.4, then it increases until it peaks around Y/B=0.60. The depth-averaged of M2 * has a similar trend but it assumes high values in the range 0.25 < Y/B<0.4. The depth-averaged value of M3 * decreases from the right bank to the transversal abscissa Y/B=0.55; then it increases assuming a high value at Y/B=0.65. In section F, while M1 * and M2 * are like in section D, M3 * decreases on the left side of the cross-section more largely than in section D. In section G, the values of M1 * in the right side of the cross-section are lower than those observed in section F assuming the lowest value at Y/B=0.4 then, it slightly increases. The values of M2 * assume a behaviour similar to M1 *. M3 * decreases from the right bank to the channel axis where it reaches a minimum value; then it increases again. Lastly, in section H, both M1 * and M2 * have higher values in the range at 0.25 < Y/B<0.4, then they decrease assuming the lower value at Y/B=0.55 cm and then they increase again. Additionally, the magnitude of M3 * decreases with increasing the distance from the right bank.  4.2 Field-scale case results Fig. 11   highlights the cross-sectional distribution of the velocity at Ponte Nuovo site, along the Tiber River, under high, moderate and low flow conditions, carried out by the ADCP. The investigated cross-section exhibited larger velocity magnitudes towards the center during high and moderate flow conditions, and towards the right half during low flow conditions. With an increase in discharge, a velocity dip (the maximum velocity below the water surface) is formed which is particularly notable in high-flow conditions (see Fig. 11 a). Formation of the velocity dip can be induced by various parameters, however, for the present cross-section, the aspect ratio appears to be the dominant one (Moramarco et al., 2017; Kundu and Ghoshal, 2019; Termini and Moramarco, 2020; Bahmanpouri et al., 2022a,b ). Fig. 12   shows the cross-sectional distribution of parameter M1 *. For comparisons with literature, at the Ponte Nuovo section, three different scales of 0.0–0.5 J/Kg∙m, 0.0–0.1 J/Kg∙m and 0.0–0.04 J/Kg∙m are observed under high, moderate and low flow conditions, respectively, for M1 . Notably, for all flow conditions, the larger magnitudes of parameter M1  are associated with the larger changes of velocity magnitude in the transverse direction. Accordingly, by moving from a low-velocity region to a high-velocity region, larger magnitudes of drag force are applied to aquatic organisms. Gualtieri et al. (2017)  reported the average magnitude of 0.01 < M1  (J/Kg.m) < 0.07 between Rio Negro and Rio Solimões in the Amazon River Basin with the 0.5 < Δ y     (m) < 2.0. The kinetic energy in these flow structures can be spent by swimming fish (Videler et al. 1999; Enders et al. 2003 ). Fig. 13   highlights the cross-sectional distribution of parameter M2 * for Ponte Nuovo site. Based on parameter M2 *, the amount of energy required for an organism to travel from a low-velocity to a high-velocity location is represented by the kinetic energy at the region with the lower velocity magnitude. Larger magnitudes of M2 * for example at the left side of the channel for different flow conditions induced by larger changes of velocity at these zones and are induced by bed shape and bank effect. For comparisons with the literature, the minimum, average and maximum magnitudes of M2  are equal to 0.05, 0.29, and 1.15 (1/m) under high flow, 0.04, 0.14, and 0.85 (1/m) for moderate flow, and 0.04, 0.13, and 0.75 (1/m) under low flow condition, respectively. Gualtieri et al. (2017)  documented the average magnitude of 0.09 < M2  (1/m) < 0.37 at the confluence between Rio Negro and Rio Solimoes in the Amazon River Basin. Other researchers calculated the minimum and maximum magnitudes of M2  as 0.08 and 0.34 (1/m) (Fausch and White, 1981 ), 3.1 and 40.7(1/m) (Hayes and Jowett, 1994 ) and 0.002 and 97.3 (1/m) (Crowder and Diplas, 2000 ). The value of M2  is influenced by the characteristics of the river, including its discharge and shape, which affect the flow velocity. In case of decreasing the flow discharge such as during dry seasons or existing obstacles that cause drag like rough surfaces or bedforms, the M2  metric would increase because the velocity in the denominator decreases. Fig. 14   shows the cross-sectional distribution of the parameter M3 * at Ponte Nuovo station based on available observational data. Their magnitudes are similar to those by Gualtieri et al. (2020)  for the low-flow condition through the Amazon River. Larger magnitudes of parameter M3 * are observed at the whole channel for the high flow conditions, and at the sides for low and moderate flow conditions, indicating larger rates of flow circulations in these areas. This could be due to the bed profile shape observed in the Ponte Nuovo cross-section that can result in the formation of secondary currents and flow circulations. The distribution of the depth-averaged values of M1 *, M2 * and M3 * and the velocity ratio is illustrated in Fig. 15   for all flow conditions. The parameter M1 * is associated with the change in velocity, such that higher values of M1 * corresponded to higher flow velocity gradients. The magnitude of the parameter M1 * is observed to be highest at the center of the channel for all flow conditions, with a maximum value of 0.5. Furthermore, the parameter M2 * exhibited larger magnitudes on the sides of the channel for moderate flow condition and on the right side for low and high flow conditions. In high-flow conditions, the magnitudes are particularly prominent. Parameter M3 * remained nearly constant across the transverse direction in the high-flow condition. However, it is larger on the channel sides under low and medium flow conditions. It is important to note that these parameters are normalized with respect to Um  (mean velocity). For instance, in the high-flow condition, the magnitude of Um  (1.09 m/s) is greater compared to that of medium and low flow conditions (0.55 m/s and 0.34 m/s, respectively).   5 Discussion The results obtained both from laboratory and field data highlight that the parameters M1  and M2  are strongly related to the formation of high/low velocity areas, and to the consequent accelerated-decelerated zones. By using laboratory data, high values of M2  are found in the zones where scour holes form. The variation of the parameters, especially M2 , is linked to the kinetic energy of the flow. This is especially important, as an example, in locally accelerated stream-wise velocity around obstructions, such as piers, which thus provide favorable migration corridors for fishes determining mean velocities that are greater than average reach velocities with low relative turbulence (Tritico and Hotchkiss 2005 ). The lowest achievable value of M2  for each zone would occur if the mildest velocity gradient surrounded the location of an aquatic organism. Conversely, the highest attainable value would be reached when the steepest change in velocity is found at the location. Shields et al. (1995)  based on the placement of spur dikes, which create vortices, substantially increased fish biomass in river flow. Their results reasoned that before attempting to restore the physical habitat, it is important to ensure that the water quality in terms of suspended particles is good enough to sustain aquatic life. The range of above parameters suggest the same flow patterns that may indicate suitable habitats for the organisms such as fishes. Based on previous research works (e.g. Gualtieri et al., 2017 , 2019), the difference in parameters values could be both because of different directions and distances between the velocity magnitudes. Furthermore, the varying flow kinematic conditions made it challenging to make a comprehensive comparison. Kozarek et al. (2010)  based on field data on Staunton River, Canada, reported that, although velocity or depth characteristics are insufficient to explain fish (brook trout) habitat preferences in the complex flows created by boulders and other flow obstructions, brook trout density generally increased as the flow complexity increased. The finding was in agree with the anticipated behavior of piscivorous species, which tend to exhibit a preference for positions in close proximity to regions characterized by high gradients. Such a strategic placement allows these species to conserve energy in slow-flowing areas while still benefiting from access to fast-moving currents for prey acquisition (Nestler et al., 2012; Liao, 2007; Booker et al., 2004 ). In the case of field observations, it was found that freshwater dolphins in the confluence of the Negro and Solimões Rivers actively avoided areas with high M2  values (Gualtieri et al., 2017 , 2020). Vorticity is a potentially useful metric for calculating spatial flow patterns for biological purposes (Crowder and Diplas 2002 ). The parameter M3  based on velocity components indicate the strength of rotation in the flow domain that can be applied to identify preferred spawning grounds for fish (Yang et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The laboratory data show that M3  higher values of circulation are found close to the front deposit and in the scour holes, i.e. especially where the bed profile changes. Thus, the obtained results suggest that the animal should spend more energy where the erosion process on the bed develops until the formation of the scour hole. Larger magnitudes of parameter M3  are also observed, under high and moderate flow conditions, close to the banks due to the deformed bed profile observed in the Ponte Nuovo cross-section, resulting in the formation of secondary currents and flow circulations. These findings confirm the observations reported by previous researchers. Bedulli et al., (1990)  reported that the total density of aquatic organisms such as zoobenthos decreased during the low flow condition in the summer months with respect to the preceding years. However, in samples collected in the late spring, Ferrari and Rossetti (1990)  observed a notable increase in the numerical importance of aquatic organisms such as phytal copepods and gastropod larvae. Some researchers defined a synthetic parameter, the mean individual size (B/A), i.e. the ratio between total biomass (B) and total abundance (A) of organisms to describe the disturbance effects on the community. Such a ratio tends to diminish progressively along a gradient of increasing organic enrichment of sediment (Pearson and Rosenberg, 1978; Weston, 1990, Ceccherelli et al. 1994 ). Therefore, it is thought that the zones with high vorticities are potential zones for deposited sediment particles. Consequently, these zones can be considered as potential zones for feeding aquatic organisms. Table 2   compares the minimum, average, and maximum magnitudes of hydraulic complexity parameters for the present research and the available data from the literature. In terms of the cross-sectional distribution of hydraulic complexity parameters, generally, M1  has an inverse relationship with M2  and M3  so that large magnitudes of M1  are observed at the center of the cross-section while large magnitudes of M2  and M3  are seen bear the banks. In terms of depth-averaged distribution of hydraulic complexity parameters, overall, all parameters have the same trend of changing the magnitude in the transverse direction. It means a change in kinetic energy of flow in transverse direction may result in the formation of circulations in flow. Vortices generated by the movement of a fish’s fins play a part in determining a fish’s maneuverability (Bandyopadhyay et al. 2000 ). Piscivorous predators and copepods can detect the presence of prey through the vortex structures left behind by fish and other organisms as they swim (Hanke et al. 2000 ). Way et al. (1995)  found that grooved blocks used to line parts of the Mississippi River created small eddies that allow macroinvertebrates to build feeding structures that are sheltered from high-velocity flows but remained in contact with faster feeding flows. Herein, larger circulations are observed at the bank sides or bottom of the cross-section due to larger vertical-averaged velocity differences. Crowder and Diplas (2002)  reported relatively high vorticities along the channel banks. Such observations suggest that aquatic organisms use vortices and other complex flows in different manners and at different scales.  6 Conclusions Flow patterns, such as changes in velocity, recirculation zones, and flows perpendicular to the main current, are usually caused by the presence of mesoscale topographical features. These flow patterns have a significant impact on stream ecology. The hydraulic complexity metrics known as M1 , M2 , and M3  are investigated for the velocity dataset collected at the laboratory as well as Ponte Nuovo gauged site, along the Tiber River in Italy. In this direction, the velocity components measured in selected cross-sections are used. In terms of ecological function, these parameters are of particular significance for analysing habitat metrics in 3D space. The M1  and M2  parameters provides an estimation of the kinetic energy spent by organisms in the flow to move. Flow circulation is highlighted by the M3  parameter, indicating that the areas with flow circulation are not considered as the primary habitats for aquatic organisms. However, these areas could serve as potential feeding grounds for aquatic organisms. Based on the laboratory data, the results demonstrate that the parameters, particularly M3 , effectively characterized the variation in flow velocity and the impact resulting from the development of turbulent structures and flow circulation within each cross-section. These parameters are strongly correlated with the formation of scour holes and deposit fronts. The obtained patterns of the stream parameters suggest that the animal should spend more energy where the erosion process develops on the bed until the formation of the scour hole. In these areas, flow circulation assumes also high values influencing the animal’s activities. The application of field data indicates that larger magnitudes of M3  are observed at different parts of the cross-section, especially near banks, depending on flow type allowing the detection of larger flow circulations zones. Overall, parameter M1  has an inverse direction with the parameters M2  and M3  as larger magnitudes of M1  are observed at the centre of cross-section while large magnitudes of M2  and M3  are seen near the banks. Generally, the results highlight the possibility to detect potential locations for a larger density of aquatic organisms. Overall, the findings suggest that the hydraulic complexity parameters might add some insights into the habitat heterogeneity as well as evaluate ecological and biological patterns in rivers with remarkable flood rates such as Tiber River. Finally, as a suggestion for future research, measuring velocity gradients using a mesh size (length scale) comparable to the size of aquatic organisms such as fishes would be of particular importance since they sense the velocity gradient over a distance proportional to their body size.
1 Introduction Aquifer pumping is a valuable technique for characterizing the hydraulic properties of aquifers, such as hydraulic conductivity and specific storage. During a pumping test, water is extracted from a well while temporal drawdown data are measured at observation wells. These hydraulic parameters can be determined using either an analytical drawdown solution coupled with an optimization method or a type-curve method for analyzing the measured data. Numerous studies have developed mathematical models for drawdown induced by pumping in confined aquifers (Theis, 1935; Hantush et al., 1964; Papadopulos and Cooper, 1967; Yeh and Chang, 2013; Lin et al., 2016 ). During well development, a skin zone may form near the well due to drilling and/or development activities. A positive skin (also called a low-permeability skin) usually results from damage caused by well drilling and incomplete development, creating a zone adjacent to the wellbore with lower hydraulic conductivity than the undisturbed formation (Houben, 2015; Houben et al., 2023 ). Conversely, a negative skin (or high-permeability skin) is a zone around a well with higher hydraulic conductivity than the surrounding formation (Yeh et al., 2008; Valois et al., 2024 ). Houben et al. (2022)  mentioned that this occurs when well development processes remove fine-grained particles during lateral insertion or subsequent operations because the removal of these fines enhances hydraulic conductivity near the well. Wellbore skin is commonly introduced to account for the skin zone’s influence on drawdown. The skin thickness may range from a few millimeters to several meters (Novakowski, 1989; Houben et al., 2023 ). The literature offers various approaches for developing solutions that consider the skin effect (Hurst, 1953; Van Everdingen, 1953; Hawkins, 1956; Agarwal et al., 1970; Sandal et al., 1978; Moench and Hsieh, 1985a; Novakowski, 1989; Moench, 1997; Cassiani et al., 1999 ). Two main types of approaches incorporate the skin effect on drawdown: the two-zone approach and the skin-factor approach. The two-zone approach assumes the skin zone is independent of the aquifer formation zone, with distinct physical properties and different initial and boundary conditions. These zones are connected using continuity conditions (Barker and Herbert, 1982; Moench and Hsieh, 1985a; Butler and McElwee, 1990; Novakowski, 1989; Yang and Gates, 1997; Yang and Yeh, 2005, 2007; Barua and Bora, 2010; Tsai and Yeh, 2012; Lin et al., 2016 ). On the other hand, the skin-factor describes a single flow model for the aquifer with a skin-factor condition as an inner boundary condition at the well. This model introduces a dimensionless parameter called the skin factor to reflect the head loss caused bythe skin zone (Van Everdingen, 1953; Hawkins, 1956; Moench, 1997; Moench and Hsieh, 1985b; Cassiani et al., 1999; Chen and Chang, 2003, 2006; Lin et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2022; Lin and Yeh, 2022; Mahdavi et al., 2024 ). Essentially, the two-zone model and the skin-factor model can be viewed as distributed-parameter and lumped-parameter models, respectively. In practice, the skin-factor model is more commonly applied to field tests due to its relative simplicity. The fewer parameters required by the skin-factor model help reduce uncertainties associated with parameter estimation in the model. The commonly used skin-factor approach is based on the assumption of positive skin, as evidenced by the head loss term in the head continuity equation (Moench, 1997 ). This positive-skin-factor (PSF) approach assumes discontinuous hydraulic heads between the wellbore and aquifer, while maintaining continuous fluxes through the skin zone. In the PSF approach, head loss is proportional to the wellbore flux and governed by a dimensionless skin factor (Van Everdingen, 1953; Hurst, 1953 ). However, the PSF approach is only effective when the skin zone permeability is sufficiently low. For negative skin, the assumption of head discontinuity is invalid due to the expectation of continuity. Applying the PSF approach to negative skin scenarios results in a physically impossible situation where the wellbore head exceeds the aquifer head, yet flow continues towards the pumping well. To address this issue, Brons and Miller (1961)  proposed the concept of an effective radius to account for the skin effect, suggesting that the skin effect diminishes as the effective radius increases. However, this empirical approach does not fundamentally resolve the PSF approach’s limitations in accurately representing flow behavior associated with negative skin. The mathematical techniques applied in well hydraulics are closely related to those employed in heat conduction, due to the similar physical principles and mathematical frameworks governing both phenomena. For instance, the foundational (Theis, 1935 ) solution was developed based on the analogies between radial groundwater flow and radial heat flow (Freeze, 1990; Kurylyk and Irvine, 2019 ). Consequently, methodologies used in the study of heat conduction can be effectively adapted for applications in well hydraulics. In the field of thermal conduction, Lin and Chen (2023)  focused on designing a thermal invisibility cloak that accounts for the effects of imperfect interfaces within a three-zone radial composite material. Their study considered the presence of low-conductivity and/or high-conductivity materials at the interface (in the middle zone). Their work demonstrates that the mathematical model of the middle zone can be simplified to interface conditions representing low- and/or high-conductivity type interfaces through an asymptotic approach using Taylor’s expansion, effectively characterizing the impact of imperfections across the interface. They found that the low-conductivity type interface describes the extra temperature drop at the imperfect contact with continuous heat flux, whereas the high-conductivity type interface maintains temperature continuity while allowing for heat flux discontinuity due to the presence of the high thermal gradient. We notice that the low-conductivity interface condition is analogous to the classical positive-skin-factor (PSF) approach in well hydraulics; namely, the PSF condition describes additional head loss at the wellbore surface due to the wellbore skin resistance with continuous water flux condition. Although the high-conductivity case resembles the negative-skin-factor (NSF) approach, it lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework. Ideally, this framework would account for the continuity of the hydraulic head while addressing the potential discontinuity in water flux. Inspired by this approach, we propose that the NSF approach in well hydraulics could be derived in a similar manner. In this study, we revisit the skin factor theory and derive a new skin-factor approach based on modifying two-zone model, building upon the approach presented by Lin and Chen (2023) . This two-zone model provides a general framework describing the flow interaction among the wellbore skin, aquifer formation, and wellbore. We derive the new NSF approach using a Taylor expansion of the two-zone model. We then incorporate the NSF approach into a groundwater flow model to describe drawdown distribution induced by constant-rate pumping in a partially penetrating well within a confined aquifer. The model solution is obtained using Laplace and finite cos-Fourier transform techniques, with the large-time solution derived through asymptotic expansion in the Laplace domain. We compare our solution to the classical PSF solution and large-time solution. We explore the effects of PSF and NSF approaches on pump-induced drawdown to understand their influence on the aquifer system’s hydraulic behavior under varying skin factor values. Moreover, we compare the proposed NSF model to the existing two-zone model. A sensitivity analysis is conducted to investigate the impact of various aquifer and wellbore parameters. Finally, we discuss the implications of this newly developed skin-factor model for groundwater management and well hydraulic modeling.  2 Methods 2.1 Groundwater flow model Fig. 1  presents a schematic representation of the conceptual model illustrating the aquifer drawdown distribution s ( r , z , t )     [L] induced by a partially penetrating well in confined aquifers with a uniform thickness of b   [L]. The variable r   [L] represents the radial distance from the center of the pumping well, z   [L] denotes the depth, and t   [T] represents the operating time. The pumping well has a radius of r  w     [L] and operates at a constant pumping rate Q   [L 3    T−1 ]. The screen of the well is installed from d   to l   [L]. The aquifer exhibits anisotropic hydraulic conductivities, denoted as K  r     and K  z     [LT−1 ] in the radial (r  ) and vertical (z  ) directions, respectively. The water extracted by the well is assumed to be instantaneously sourced from the specific storage S  s     [L−1 ] of the aquifer.  By integrating Darcy’s Law with the continuity equation, the governing equation for drawdown response can be expressed in cylindrical coordinates as (Bear, 2012 ) (1) S  s   ∂ s  ∂ t   = K  r   1  r   ∂  ∂ r   r ∂ s  ∂ r     + K  z   ∂  2   s  ∂ z  2     , ( r , z )  ∈ [ r  w   , ∞ )  × [ 0 , b ]       The associated initial condition and infinite-distance boundary condition can be respectively expressed as (2) s = 0 , t = 0     and (3) lim  r → ∞   s = 0      The aquifer is bounded by two impermeable layers, so no-flux conditions are applied to the top and bottom of the aquifer: (4) ∂ s  ∂ z   = 0 , z = 0 , b       2.2 Development of skin-factor approach for negative skin Consider a skin zone surrounding the wellbore with a uniform thickness of r  s     (Fig. 2 a). The drawdowns in the wellbore and skin zone are denoted as s  w     and s  s k i n    , respectively. Two interfaces are present: one between s  w     and s  s k i n    , and another between s  s k i n     and the drawdown in the aquifer (s  ). These interfaces are subject to continuity in both drawdown and flux.  The continuity equation, expressed in terms of Darcy fluxes within the skin zone, is given as follows (Chiu et al., 2007 ): (5) S  s , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   = − 1  r   ∂  ∂ r   r q  r , s k i n     − ∂  ∂ z   ( q  z , s k i n   )  ,  ( r , z )  ∈ [ r  w   , r  s   ]  × [ 0 , b ]  ,     where S  s , s k i n     is the specific storage of the skin zone [L−1 ], and q  r , s k i n     and q  z , s k i n     are the water fluxes in the skin zone [LT−1 ] in the r   and z   directions, respectively. Since r  s     is relatively small compared to the overall aquifer system (Fig. 2 b), the flux in the aquifer near the skin zone surface (q  r    ) [LT−1 ] can be approximated using a first-order Taylor series expansion: (6) q  r   ( r  w   + r  s  +   )  = q  r , w   ( r  w   + r  s  −   )  ≈ q  r , w   ( r  w   )  + r  s   ∂ q  r , w   ( r  w   )   ∂ r   + O ( r  s  2   )  ,     yielding: (7) q  r   − q  r , w    r  s     = ∂ q  r , w    ∂ r   .     where q  r , w     is the flux at the wellbore surface [LT−1 ]. At the surface of the skin zone, the first term on the right side of Eq. (5)  can be rewritten as: (8) 1  r  w   + r  s     ∂  ∂ r   ( r  w   + r  s   )  q  r , s k i n     = ∂ q  r , s k i n    ∂ r   .      By letting q  r   ≈ q  r , s k i n      and applying Eq. (7) , Eq. (5)  can be rewritten as: (9a) S  s , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   = − q  r   − q  r , w    r  s     − ∂ q  z , s k i n    ∂ z   ,     or: (9b) r  s   S  s , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   = q  r , w   − q  r   − r  s   ∂ q  z , s k i n    ∂ z   .      Note that the final term on the right side of Eq. (9b)  results from the surface Laplacian operator. Based on Darcy’s Law, the fluxes q  r , w    , q  r    , and q  z , s k i n     can be expressed as: (10a) q  r , w   = − K  w   ∂ s  w    ∂ r   ,     (10b) q  r   = − K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   ,     and (10c) q  z , s k i n   = − K  z , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ z   ,      where K  w     is the hydraulic conductivity of the wellbore [LT−1 ] and K  z , s k i n     is the hydraulic conductivity of the skin zone in z   direction [LT−1 ]. Substituting Eqs. (10a) and (10b)  into Eq. (9b)  yields: (11) r  s   S  s , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   = − K  w   ∂ s  w    ∂ r   + K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   + r  s   K  z , s k i n   ∂  2   s  s k i n    ∂ z  2     .      Finally, we obtain the following expression for the wellbore flux: (12) K  w   ∂ s  w    ∂ r   = K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   + r  s   K  z , s k i n   ∂  2   s  s k i n    ∂ z  2     − r  s   S  s , s k i n   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   ,     or (13) K  w   ∂ s  w    ∂ r   = K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   + S  f   ∂  2   s  s k i n    ∂ z  2     − C  g   ∂ s  s k i n    ∂ t   ,     where S  f     [L 2    T−1 ] is the skin factor for negative skin, defined as K  r , s k i n   r  s     , and C  g     [-] is a factor defined as S  s , s k i n   r  s     . This result corresponds with studies on high-conductivity interface conditions (Lipton and Vernescu, 1996; Lipton, 1997; Miloh and Benveniste, 1999; Lin and Chen, 2023 ), with the parameters adapted for common groundwater literature. Previous research has shown that this condition produces results closely aligned with the two-zone model when r  s   / r  w   < 0 . 01    (Chen and Lin, 2022b,a ). Eq. (13)  implies that the water flux in the wellbore depends on the water flux through the aquifer, diffusion within the skin zone along the wellbore surface, and water storage in the skin zone. Given that the wellbore drawdown is spatially averaged and independent of distance, the left-hand term of Eq. (13)  can be disregarded (i.e., ∂ s  w   / ∂ r = 0    at r = r  w     ). In typical aquifer setups, the factor C  g     can also be neglected (i.e., storage in the skin layer is very small), as both S  s , s k i n     and r  s     are small, rendering its effects negligible (i.e., C  g   = 0   ). This leads to: (14) K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   = − S  f   ∂  2   s  s k i n    ∂ z  2     ,  r = r  w   .      Assuming continuity of drawdown between the skin zone and aquifer formation (i.e., s  s k i n   = s    at r = r  w     ), the equation can be reformulated as: (15) K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   = − S  f   ∂  2   s  ∂ z  2     ,  r = r  w   .      This equation establishes a new skin-factor approach for the negative skin, i.e., NSF approach. To incorporate the flux due to pumping and the effects of wellbore storage (Papadopulos and Cooper, 1967 ), Eq. (15)  is modified to: (16) 2 π r  w   ( l − d )  K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   = − Q + π r  w  2   ∂ s  w    ∂ t   − 2 π r  w   ( l − d )  S  f   ∂  2   s  ∂ z  2     ,  r = r  w   .      The continuity condition for drawdown between the wellbore and aquifer is required, i.e., s = s  w      at r = r  w     . The inner boundary condition incorporating the new skin factor, expressed in terms of s  , can be written as: (17) 2 π r  w   ( l − d )  K  r   ∂ s  ∂ r   = − Q + π r  w  2   ∂ s  ∂ t   − 2 π r  w   ( l − d )  S  f   ∂  2   s  ∂ z  2     ,  r = r  w   .      Another condition is required to ensure drawdown continuity: (18) 1  l − d   ∫  z = d  z = l   s  d z = s  w   ,  r = r  w   .     Eqs. (17) and (18)  ensure continuity of drawdown at the wellbore surface while maintaining a discontinuity in water flux. In highly permeable media, the permeability is extremely high, leading to very high flow velocities. However, when fluid flows from the aquifer medium into the highly permeable medium, the sudden increase in permeability causes a sharp rise in flow velocity.
