If the skin layer is very thin, this can result in an apparent discontinuity in flow behavior at the macroscopic level.  2.3 Comparing to skin-factor approach for positive skin In the existing PSF approaches, the effect of the skin zone is incorporated into a dimensionless factor α   [-], which is derived based on a very thin skin zone around the wellbore. The skin factor condition at the well surface (r = r  w     ) can be expressed as (Moench, 1997 ) (19) 1  l − d   ∫  z = d  z = l   s d z − r α ∂ s  ∂ r   = s  w   , r = r  w       The skin factor α   is proportional to the ratio of skin permeability and skin thickness, i.e., α ∝ r  s   / K  r , s k i n     . This approach implies that the well drawdown is the sum of the aquifer drawdown and a head loss (proportional to the wellbore flux) due to the well skin. Therefore, it will result in discontinuous drawdown drop at the wellbore surface. In addition, this boundary condition is limited to the positive skin case.  2.4 Dimensionless equations and solutions Dimensionless parameters and variables are defined as follows: s  D   = 4 π K  r   b s / Q    (dimensionless drawdown); t  D   = K  r   t / r  w  2   S  s      (dimensionless time); r  D   = r / r  w      (dimensionless radial distance); z  D   = z / b    (dimensionless vertical distance); d  D   = d / b    (dimensionless depth to top of well screen); l  D   = l / b    (dimensionless depth to bottom of well screen); C  D   = 1 / 2 S  s   b    (dimensionless wellbore storage coefficient); κ = r  w  2   K  z   / b  2   K  r      (anisotropy ratio); and β = S  f   r  w   / b  2   K  r      (dimensionless skin factor for negative skin). Finally, the time-domain solution can be obtained using a numerical Laplace inversion scheme. Many studies have shown that the Stehfest (1970)  method works well for diffusion problems like groundwater flow (e.g., Hassanzadeh and Pooladi-Darvish, 2007 ). Therefore, the Stehfest method is employed here to invert Laplace solutions to time-domain solutions due to its straightforward implementation and accuracy. This method contains an integer parameter representing the optimal number of summation terms, which must be an even integer. Previous studies have determined that this value typically ranges from 8 to 24 (Wang and Zhan, 2015, 2017 ). In this study, a value of 10 is adopted because it provides sufficient accuracy for our solution while maintaining reasonable computation time  2.5 Large-time solutions The asymptotic solution for s  D     at large times (t  D   → ∞   ) can be derived by considering the limiting behavior of certain functions. As p → 0   , the approximation p   K  1   ( p   )  ≈ 1    holds true, and K  0   ( p   r  D   )     approximates − ln ( p   r  D   / 2 )  − γ   , where γ   is the Euler–Mascheroni constant, approximately 0.577216. As indicated in the equation, the large-time solution includes a logarithmic approximation of the (Theis, 1935 ) solution (Chen and Chang, 2006 ), along with a component related to the partial penetration effect (Hantush, 1961 ).  2.6 Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis is a powerful tool to evaluate the effects of various parameters on model output. The normalized sensitivity coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of the model-dependent variable with respect to a specific parameter (Kabala, 2001; Dell’Oca et al., 2020; Knabe et al., 2021 ): (28) X  k   = P  k   ∂ s  D   ( P  k   )   ∂ P  k         where X  k     indicates the sensitivity of s  D     to the k  th input parameter P  k    . Eq. (28)  may be approximated by a finite-difference formula as suggested by Liou and Yeh (1997) : (29) X  k   ≈ P  k   s  D   ( P  k   + Δ P  k   )  − s  D   ( P  k   )   Δ P  k         where Δ P  k      is chosen as 1 0  − 3   P  k     . Borgonovo and Apostolakis (2001)  introduced a measure of sensitivity analysis known as the differential importance measure, which is widely applied in the area of risk management for decision making (Borgonovo et al., 2003; Vinod et al., 2003; Marseguerra and Zio, 2004 ). This measure is defined as: (30) D I M  k   = P  k   ∂ s  D   ( P  k   )   ∂ P  k      ∑  j = 1  N   P  j   ∂ s  D   ( P  j   )   ∂ P  j           where D I M  k      is the differential importance measure of parameter P  k     and N   is the total number of model parameters. According to Eq. (28) , Eq. (30)  can be rewritten as: (31) D I M  k   = X  k    ∑  j = 1  N   X  j         Since X  k     may be negative, the absolute value is taken for X  k     and Eq. (32)  is then expressed as (Lin and Yeh, 2020 ): (32) D I M  k   = | X  k   |   ∑  j = 1  N   | X  j   |         Eq. (32)  is used in the NSF model (Eq. (25) ) to assess the effects of C  D    , κ  , l  D    , and α   and in the PSF model to evaluate C  D    , κ  , l  D    , and β  .   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Comparing to large-time solution In this section, the default values of the parameters to evaluate the dimensionless drawdown value are listed in Table 1 .   In the large-time solution (Eq. (26) ), the wellbore storage effect is negligible (C  D   = 0   ) because it primarily influences aquifer flow in the early stages. Consequently, the effect of wellbore storage on aquifer drawdown can be considered negligible. Fig. 3  illustrates temporal drawdown curves predicted by (a) the proposed NSF solution (Eq. (25) ) and (b) the large-time solution (Eq. (26) ) across different β   values at r  D   = 1    and z  D   = 0 . 5   . The large-time solution in the figure shows straight lines because it neglects wellbore storage effects. This result is consistent with the pattern predicted by Theis (1935)  solution. Furthermore, the drawdown curves predicted by both solutions align well across different β   values when t  D   > 1 0  6     , or when t > S  s   r  w  2   / K  r   × 1 0  6   ≈ 2 , 500    s (41.6 min) in our case. This suggests that the wellbore storage effect can be omitted for t  D   > 1 0  6     . The long-term alignment of these curves confirms the robust formulation of the large-time solution, making it a reliable alternative for assessing the late-time behavior of the NSF solution. The drawdown curves predicted by the large-time solution suggest that the dimensionless drawdown s  D     can be expressed as: (33) s  D   = m log t  D   + c     where m   is the slope and c   is the intercept. Using a least-squares fitting method, the slope m   is found to be 1, while the intercept c   varies with the value of β  . Applying a saturating growth model to find the relationship between c   and β  , it is approximated as: (34) c ≈ − 4 . 1 + 4 . 65 ( 1 − e  74 . 7 β   )      Thus, the relationship between s  D     and t  D     in this specific case can be expressed as: (35) s  D   = log t  D   − 4 . 1 + 4 . 65 ( 1 − e  74 . 7 β   )      As observed in Eq. (35) , when β   is very small, drawdown changes rapidly. However, as β   continues to increase, the change gradually slows down and approaches a stable value.  3.2 Comparing the skin-factor models for positive and negative skins Fig. 4  illustrates the temporal drawdown distributions predicted by the NSF model and the PSF model with varying corresponding skin factors β   and α  , measured at (r  D   , z  D     ) =   (1, 0.5). As indicated in the figure, increases in α   and β   result in higher drawdown values due to increased head loss in the skin zone. However, the drawdown curves influenced by changes in α   and β   exhibit different patterns. For instance, α   primarily affects the drawdown curves at early times; conversely, β   significantly impacts drawdown throughout the entire period. This difference may be attributed to the fact that α   operates in conjunction with wellbore storage, primarily influencing the drawdown response in early times. In contrast, the new factor β   depends on the vertical diffusion near the wellbore, which is not time-dependent, allowing it to continuously affect the flow system.  Fig. 5  presents the fluxes due to the skin factors α   and β   along the screen portion of the well (z  D   ∈ [ d  D   , l  D   ]    ). The flux attributed to β  , denoted by q  β    , is defined as β ∂  2   s  D   / ∂ z  D  2      at r  D   = 1   , while the flux due to α  , denoted by q  α    , is defined by α ∂ s  D   / ∂ r  D      at r  D   = 1   . The figure reveals that increases in both α   and β   lead to higher skin-induced fluxes. The spatial distribution of q  α     displays a uniform distribution with depth; however, the spatial distribution of q  β     exhibits an increasing trend and slopes with depth. This suggests that the skin portion in the casing section of the pumping well may also exert effects on the skin-induced flux, namely, the head loss caused by the high-permeability skin can be amplified near the casing portion.    3.3 Comparing to two-zone solution The two-zone model for considering the wellbore skin effect on aquifer drawdown induced by constant-rate pumping is applied for comparison to the proposed model. Pasandi et al. (2008)  proposed a semi-analytical solution of the two-zone model for unconfined flow using (Moench, 1997 ) free-surface approach. For comparison, the specific yield in Pasandi et al. (2008)  model is assumed to be zero, reducing their model to confined flow. To ensure comparability, the dimensionless parameters defined in Section 2.4  are imposed on the two-zone model. Additionally, the ratio of hydraulic conductivities of the wellbore skin and the aquifer is set to 10 (Yeh and Yang, 2006 ), and the skin zone thickness is assumed to be 0.001 m (Novakowski, 1989; Houben et al., 2023 ). For simplicity, the effect of wellbore storage is neglected (i.e., C  D   = 0   ). To verify the assumption used in the NSF model, the drawdown curves predicted by Eq. (25)  are compared to the two-zone solution modified from (Pasandi et al., 2008 ) (Fig. 6 ). As shown in Fig. 6 , the temporal drawdown curves predicted by both solutions match very well.    3.4 Findings from sensitivity analysis In the sensitivity analysis, four parameters are considered: C  D    , κ  , l  D    , and α   or β   for different models. The value of d  D     is fixed at zero, and thus, l  D     represents the well penetration ratio. Fig. 7  displays the temporal distribution curves of the DIM for (a) the NSF model and (b) the PSF model, observed at (r  D   , z  D     ) =   (1, 0.5). Fig. 7 (a) reveals that the effect of changes in C  D     is most pronounced during early times, while the impact of changes in κ   is negligible. The effects of l  D     and β   become significant at intermediate and later times, with the influence of β   slightly surpassing that of l  D    . Conversely, Fig. 7 (b) indicates that changes in C  D     and l  D     are most significant during early and late times, respectively. κ   exhibits some effects at late times but these are minor. The skin factor α   affects the early time, with a peak around t  D   = 1 0  6     . As indicated in Section 3.1 , t  D   = 1 0  6      is the time when the wellbore storage effect becomes negligible. Beyond this time, the DIM curves for C  D     and α   merge due to both effects being encompassed in the wellbore drawdown term. It is noteworthy that results clearly demonstrate that when considering a high-permeability skin zone, its impact on late-time drawdown is significant and cannot be ignored. This is because water flow in the skin layer, facilitated by a higher hydraulic conductivity, leads to vertical water flow distributing within the skin zone region. In contrast, the existing PSF model exhibits skin zone effects only during a brief initial period. As the pumping duration extends, these effects can be disregarded since the groundwater flow is dominated by the aquifer flow.     4 Conclusions This study introduces a new skin-factor approach to describe the negative skin, addressing limitations of past models derived based on positive skin assumption. The new skin factor and associated condition diverge from the traditional reliance on discontinuous drawdown between the wellbore and the aquifer. Instead, the proposed skin-factor approach depends solely on the discontinuous flux at the interface between the wellbore and the aquifer, enhancing the model’s realism. The newly developed skin-factor approach has been integrated into a groundwater flow model to describe pump-induced drawdown distribution in a confined aquifer. Utilizing the solution to this model through drawdown prediction and sensitivity analysis, it was found that the new skin factor predominantly influences the system at intermediate and late times, whereas the existing skin factor impacts the system primarily at early times due to its combined effect with the wellbore storage effect. Additionally, the existing skin factor does not account for the water redistribution effects in the skin zone, which may have a prolonged impact on the drawdown response. The proposed NSF approach offers a robust alternative for developing groundwater flow models in well hydraulic modeling, particularly in areas with high skin zone permeability. This method is versatile, applicable not only to constant-rate pumping tests but also to constant-drawdown tests and slug tests through boundary condition adjustments, enhancing its utility in hydrogeological investigations. A key limitation of this study is the lack of field data for analysis, which prevents direct demonstration of the approach’s application to real-world pumping tests. However, the method holds potential for estimating aquifer parameters at field sites during such tests. This can be achieved by combining Eq. (25)  with optimization techniques to analyze drawdown data when available. Future research incorporating field data would be valuable to validate and refine the approach under real-world conditions.
1 Introduction Meandering rivers are characterized by sinuous and winding courses (Fig. 1  a) that constitute one of the most common planforms of rivers in the downstream alluvial plain (Li et al., 2017; da Silva and Ebrahimi, 2017; Nyberg et al., 2023 ). Over time, the imbalances of the sediment transport necessitate the ongoing evolution for the floodplain’s topography that consequently influences the overall geomorphic and ecological dynamics of the region (Constantine, 2014; Xia et al, 2022; Gao and Li, 2024 ). Anthropogenic activities (including large-scale damming—most notably the recent construction of the Three Gorges Dam on the Middle Yangtze River—along with pollution and sediment mining) and extreme climate events (such as typhoon and heavy rainfall) significantly challenges the ecological and fluvial integrity of meandering rivers that ultimately threaten the life of livings and societal developments (Stark, 2010; Best, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2024 ). Understanding the dynamic processes underlying within the meandering flows is critical for managing and mitigating these impacts on the river systems, and in a border view, the environmental health of the region. Major dynamic processes of meandering streams include the radial cross-circulatory motion and convective redistribution of the longitudinal flow. Firstly, cross-circulatory flow ((ur  )C  ) results from imbalances between the transverse pressure gradient force and centrifugal force. Such rotating flow facilitates the transfer of mass and momentum that constitute a significant aspect of meandering flow dynamics (Marion and Zaramella, 2006; Blanckaert, 2010 ). On the other hand, the downstream variation of curvature in meandering streams causes the convective redistribution of the longitudinal flow, manifesting periodic alternation of the velocity core from the upstream inner bank to downstream outer bank (da Silva et al., 2006; Pan et al., 2022 ). The redistribution of the longitudinal velocity arises the laterally oscillating flow ((ur  )O  ) (considering the conservation of mass). Graphical illustration for the prominent location and the structure of the two radial flow components are shown in Fig. 1 b, in which the total radial flow can be expressed as:(1) u r  = u r     O  + u r     C      Following Blanckaert (2010) , in Eq. (1) , (ur  )O   can be regarded as the depth-averaged translatory motion while (ur  )C   is the local deviation due to cross-circulatory motion. Fundamental works regarding cross-circulatory flows was established as early as the 1960s by Rozovskii (1961) . On the basis of the equation of motions, Chang (1984a, b)  presented a comprehensive model that provides a general expression for the development of the cross-circulation velocities in bend flows. Yalin and da Silva (2001)  showed that:(2) u r     C  u av    = a c 2  sin 2 π l c  / L     h R a        where (ur  )C   is the cross-circulatory velocity, uav   is the longitudinal mean velocity, α is an empirical coefficient, c  is the dimensionless Chézy resistant coefficient, lc   is the longitudinal coordinate along the channel centerline, L  is the meander length Ra   is the radius at the apex section. At significant flow depth (B /h  = 2 to 5), the flow dynamics become more complex when the destabilizing effects of centrifugal forces overcomes the counter effects of fluid viscosity. The phenomenon, known as the Taylor-Görtler instability, leads to the formation of several coherent vortices along the outer bank (Blanckaert and de Vriend, 2004; Blanckaert, 2010; Li and Zhang, 2022 ). It is known that the property of the outer bank cell is primarily determined by the Dean number De  = Re ∙(h /Ra  ) (Blanckaert and de Vriend, 2004 ), other factors such as turbulent anisotropy, channel roughness are also reported to have notable influences (Demueren and Rodi, 1986; Stoesser et al., 2010; van Balen et al. 2010a,b ). Conversely, the significance for the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity has been long devalued (da Silva and Ebrahimi 2017 ). This is mainly because, starting from the early studies (also true for some of the nowadays works), flume experiments were carried out in channels formed by adjacent bend segments of constant curvature that lacks downstream variation (see. e.g., Chang, 1948a, b). Also, the resulted discontinuity at the channel intersects deviates significantly from continuous natural meandering streams (Yalin 1992 ). Given the content of the present study, sine-generated function is more suitable for mildly to moderately curved meanders (Duan and Julien, 2010; Chen and Tang, 2012; da Silva and Ebrahimi, 2017 ):θ = θ 0  · c o s ( 2 π l c  / L )       where, θ0  is the initial deflection angle, and θ is the deflection angle at any lc  . Despite recent recognition of the sine-generated channel in meandering flow researches (da Silva et al., 2006; Termini, 2009; Binns and da Silva, 2011, 2015; Xu and Bai, 2013; Li et al., 2021  among many others), several aspects of the flow dynamics remain elusive. More studies emphasize the sole role of cross-circulatory flow in shaping the fluvial process of meandering rivers (e.g., Bridge and Jarvis, 1982; Wormleaton et al., 2005; Constantinescu et al., 2011; Li et al., 2018 ), leaving some unexplainable laboratory and field observations (da Silva and El-Tahawy, 2008; Li et al., 2023 ). On the other hand, work from da Silva et al. (2006)  (see also da Silva and EI-Tahawy, 2008; Li et al., 2021 ) highlights the significance of convective redistribution of longitudinal velocity. In the present work, morphological impacts of cross-circulatory flow and convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity are elucidated. Series of numerical simulations in 70°  meandering channels are performed under varying flow depth h , facilitating the ratio of B /h  (=4.6 to 100) characterizing a board range of situations, from laboratory flume experiment to natural streams. The flow structures at the ‘classical’ pattern of cross-circulatory motion are validated and examined. The shift of significance for the two dynamics entities (cross-circulatory flow and convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity) are highlighted by two types of bed deformation patterns. Their specific relation with the flow conditions and are presented. The flow and sediment dynamics at the outer bank cell are also briefly discussed.  2 Methodology Before proceeding further, it should be noted that, the present work deal with the situation at the early stages of the fluvial processes of the meandering streams. The flow width B  is constant, and the meander wavelength ΛM  =2πB  (Yalin, 1992 ). The streams convey a constant flow rate Q  with sub-critical and quasi-uniform flows. Numerical model for the present study is based on the work by Cheng (2022)  that has been verified by experiments by da Silva et al. (2006) . Further validation of the simulated flows is facilitated by laboratory experiments of Sagnak (2023) . In the following, an overview of the numerical model is introduced, followed by a summary of the laboratory results and their comparison with the numerical simulations. 2.1 Numerical model The open-source computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software package OpenFOAM are used to develop the numerical model, in which the Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes equations and continuity equations for incompressible fluids are solved using Finite Volume Method (Kim, 2020; Yan et al., 2020 ). The Reynolds stresses are modeled by the Boussinesq approximation. The standard k -ε  model is utilized to close the turbulence equations. Further description for the computational process of the OpenFOAM involving the controlling equations and specific values of the related coefficients are included in Text 1 of Supplementary Material . The specific case of simulation for the flow having h  = 6.5 cm is exemplified in Fig. 2  , in which the computational domain for each run spans a full meander length with the upstream and downstream ends coinciding with apex sections (Fig. 2 ). The periodic boundary conditions are imposed on these two sections to simulate the fully developed flows. The walls are treated non-slip hydraulically smooth boundaries, while invoking the law of the wall to calculate the turbulent viscosity (νt  ). The rigid-lid approximation is used to model the free surface. The flow is driven by a pressure difference Δp  that is imposed between the two end sections. This replaces the longitudinal mean pressure gradient slope S  (= (Δp /γ)/L ). In the present study, a total of 10 runs are performed. The flow depth h  is increased from 0.8 cm to 17.4 cm under constant channel width B  (=0.8 m) (B /h  = 4.8–100). A summary for parameters used in the simulations is presented in Table 1  . Here, uav   is the channel averaged flow velocity (=Q /(Bh )); v*   is the shear velocity (= (gSh )1/2 ); F  is the Froude number (=uav  /(gh )1/2 ). The computational meshes were generated using the BlockMesh utility supplied within OpenFOAM. All meshes had a resolution of 512 cells in the longitudinal direction and 48 cells in the radial direction (Fig. 2 ). In the vertical direction, the number of cells was increased from 4 to 24 as the flow depth h  increased from 0.8 cm to 17.4 cm. The total number of cells for each case is presented in Table S1 . The computed results are transferred from the Cartesian coordinates (ux  , uy  ) to channel fitted coordinate (ul  , ur  ) by the Jacobian transformation matrix:(4) u  l     u  r        = cos θ  sin θ   - sin θ  cos θ      · u  x     u  y             2.2 Laboratory experiments and comparison with simulated results The experiment by Sagnak (2023)  was carried out in sine-generated channel having θ 0  = 70°  with constant flow width B  (=0.8 m) and meander wavelength ΛM   (=2πB ). The flume consists of two complete meandering cycles, starting and ending at apex sections. The side walls and channel bottom (horizontal) are made of high-density polyethylene (hydraulically smooth). During experiment, the flow rate Q  was kept constant throughout the duration of the run (steady flow). The mean surface slope S (=1/1000) was determined from the measurements of the free surface elevation along the channel centerline. The average flow depth at the apex cross-section was designated as the representative depth h  (=6.5 cm). The related flow parameters are summarized in Table 2  . Here, R  is Reynolds number (=uav h / ν, where ν is the flow kinematic viscosity). During the experiment, the longitudinal and radial velocities (ul  , ur  ) were measured along a full meander length. The measurement region spans from upstream to downstream apexes and is subdivided into 9 equally spaced cross-sections (Δlc   /L  = 1/8). Along each cross-section, vertical measurements were taken at every 10 cm (Δη = 1/8), starting from 5 cm from the inner bank wall. Comparisons between the simulated and measured longitudinal velocities ul   are facilitated in Fig. S1 . The computed flows (h  = 6.5 cm) are that in the center loop (ξ  = lc   /L  = 0–1/2) and delineated by the solid lines. Laboratory measurements (symbols) from two consecutive loops (ξ  = 0–1/2, 1/2–1) are superimposed using the mirror periodicity of the flow. For the longitudinal velocity, the computed and measured flows show remarkable agreement (Fig. S1 ). In addition, the plan distributions for the simulated longitudinal velocity ul   /uav   and its downstream gradient ∂ul   /∂l  are illustrated in Fig. S2 . Comparisons between the computed and measured radial flow velocities are provided in Fig. 3  . The related scatter plot of the relative discrepancy (RD  =((ur  )Meas - (ur  )Pred )/(0.3uav  ) and the corresponding occurrence frequency plot are shown in Figs. S3  a, b. Here, the denominator (0.3uav  ) is used as a benchmark that approximates the maximum simulated radial velocity (occurring towards the right lower ends of the cross-section ξc   = 1/4 in Fig. 3 ). As shown in Fig. 3 , the computed radial velocities align well with their measured counterparts, despite a systematic deviation occurring at the cross-section ξc   = 1/8. This results from the inverse of the rotating direction for the cross-circulatory cell, making precise simulation challenging for the present model. Such systematic deviation is also clear in the scatter plot of the RD  (Fig. S3 a at ξc   = 1/8) where the mean value deviate from 0. In general, 90 % of the simulated data fall within the range where the absolute value of the RD  is less than 0.2 (Fig. S3 b). The RMS of RD  is 0.15.   3 Results: Flow and sediment dynamics at the classical pattern of cross-circulatory motion Variations of the radial flow structure at increasing flow depth h  are illustrated in Fig. S4  for all simulated flows. As long as B /h  > 9, the flow characterizes a dominant cross-circulatory cell that strengthens with the increasing flow depth h  (‘classical’ pattern). However, for flows having B /h  ≤ 9, the Taylor-Görtler instability triggers an additional vortex along the outer bank (known as the outer bank cell) that evolves in counter direction to the primary cell and significantly change the overall flow structure. As evidenced by numerous studies (see section ‘Introduction’), the presence of the outer bank cell is not a model artifact; however, the accuracy of the simulation regarding the outer bank cell remains unclear as validation is only conducted against the flow exhibiting one dominant cell. Therefore, the primary focus of the present study is directed to the flow and morphodynamics regarding the classical cross-circulatory pattern. The outer bank cell simulations are nonetheless valuable, considered as an extrapolation of the present study, and presented in the ‘Discussion’ section. Note, because the simulated convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity shows significant consistency, its variation regarding different flow depth is not presented here. 3.1 Properties of the radial flow Fig. 4   exemplifies the radial structure of the meandering flow having h  = 6.5 cm (B /h  = 12), where a classical cross-circulatory pattern is shown. The figure insets on the right show the vector plots of ur   /uav   that highlight the moments when the cross-circulatory intensity is either near zero (ξc   = 1/16, indicated by zero near bed radial velocity) or at its maximum (ξc   = 5/16). Specifically, at the loop entrance, residual motion from the previous loop manifests as laterally oscillating flow in the upper cross-section and weak cross-circulatory flow near bed. Under reversing effects of the loop curvature, the residual motion dissipates while a new cross-circulatory cell emerges along the inner bank of the channel at ξc   = 3/16. The cross-circulatory cell rotates in the counterclockwise direction while arising significant negative near-bed radial velocity. The intensity of such rotating cell peaks just after the apex (ξc   = 5/16), still positioning towards the inner site of the channel. Proceeding further, the cross-circulatory cell subsides, making way to the dominant laterally oscillating motion at the loop exit. Empirical parameterization for the vertical distributions of the cross-circulatory and laterally oscillating velocities on the basis of the simulated data are served as a byproduct of the present work and provided in Supplementary Material  Text 2 and Fig. S4 . More importantly, intensities of the laterally oscillating are represented by the vertically averaged radial velocity along the channel centerline,u  ¯   r  / u av     ; while the cross-circulatory flow intensity are represented by the near bed radial velocity along the center of the cross-circulatory cell, (ur  )0  /uav  . Longitudinal distributions for u  ¯   r  / u av      and (ur  )0  /uav   are shown in Fig. 5  a under varying B /h  ratio. As is shown, both the two radial flow components exhibit sinusoidal variations with their wavelength coinciding with the meander length (L ). Particularly, laterally oscillating velocities (Fig. 5 a left) peak near crossovers (ξc   = 0, 1/2), while cross-circulatory velocities (Fig. 5 a right) exhibit a phase lag of 1/4 period that maximize near the apex (ξc   = 1/4). To illustrate the overall tendency, maxima of the velocities in Fig. 5 a are plotted in Fig. 5 b against varying B /h  ratio. For the laterally oscillating flow (Fig. 5 b left), the maximum intensities form a plateau ofu  ¯   r  / u av      = 0.11 as B /h  increases from 10 to 30, thereafter, increments of B /h  from 30 causes notable decrease. On the other hand, the maximum intensities of the cross-circulatory flow (Fig. 5 b right) exhibit a power decrease with increasing B /h , adhering to the analytical formulation proposed by Yalin and da Silva (2001)  (Eq. (2)  by identifying c  = 12.4 and α  = 0.028). The cross-circulatory intensity at B /h  = 100 is 10 times smaller than that at B /h  = 10.  3.2 Fluvial dynamics As noted by Binns and da Silva (2009), the patterns of erosion–deposition at the beginning of a meandering bed deformation experiment closely mirrors that at the end (equilibrium). Thus, the normalized bed deformation rates (∂zb  /∂t )/v *  at the early stages of bed deformation (plain bed) can be used to elucidate fluvial dynamics of meandering rivers. Consider now the sediment continuity equation in the channel fitted coordinate:(5) ( 1 - p )  ∂ z b   ∂ t   = - ( ∂ ( q  s  )  l   ∂ l   + ∂ ( q  s  )  r   ∂ r   + ( q  s  )  r  r  )       here, p  is the porosity of bed material (taken as 0.35 for the present case), zb   is the bed elevation, t  is time, qs    is the volumetric sediment transport rate vector, the sub-scripts l  and r  denoting the sub-components in l  and r  directions, respectively. For the sake of simplicity, only the bedload is considered (qs    = qsb   ). Invoking Mayer-Peter equation:(6) q sb   = β U  0   ( τ - τ cr   )  / γ s       where, U 0   is the flow velocity vector at the bed, β  (=0.4) is an empirical coefficient, τ  is the scalar form of bed shear stress, τcr   is the critical bed shear stress at the initiation of sediment transport, and γ s   is the specific submerged weight of sediment. The longitudinal and radial components of bed-load vector can be written as:(7) ( q sb   )  l  = u l  u l 2  + u r 2     β ( τ - τ cr   )  / γ s  , and   ( q sb   )  r  = u r  u l 2  + u r 2     β ( τ - τ cr   )  / γ s       The right-hand side of Eq. (5)  consists of three terms. Associating with Eq. (7) , it is clear that the first term ∂(qs  )l  /∂l  results from the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity, the second term ∂(qs  )r  /∂r  is due to lateral variation of the cross-circulatory velocity, and the last term (qs  )/r  originates from the centrifugal acceleration of the curved flow. Thus, denoting the (normalized) terms resulting from longitudinal and radial variations of the meandering flow as D I  (= (∂(qsb  )l  /∂l )/v * ) and D II  (= (∂(qsb  )r  /∂r  + (qsb  )r  /r )/v * ), respectively. The plan distributions of D I  and D II  for the flow having h  = 6.5 cm are presented in Fig. 6   to further elucidate the role of the two aforementioned dynamics processes in driving the meandering fluvial processes. The plan distribution of D I  (Fig. 6 a) mirrors the convective pattern of the longitudinal velocity ul   (Fig. S2 a). The resulted erosion and deposition zones (as implied by negative and positives zones of D I ) are found longitudinally adjacent along the inner bank apex while alternating along the two riverbanks. On the other hand, the plan distribution of D II  (as facilitated by cross-circulatory motions, Fig. 6 b) consists laterally adjacent erosion–deposition zones along the inner bank apex. It is important to note that the longitudinally adjacent erosion–deposition zones of D I  prompt downstream migration of the meander loop, while laterally adjacent zones of D II  lead to lateral expansions of the loop. These fluvial implications are illustrated in the Fig. 6 , where the dashed lines mark the anticipated location of the new bank (at the intersection at zero erosion–deposition). To further illustrate the morphodynamic implications at different scales, the overall normalized bed deformation rate (i.e., D  (=(∂zb  /∂t )/v * ) = D I +D II ) for the flows having B /h  = 100 and 12.3 are illustrated in Fig. 7  . Additionally, the computed sediment trajectories (for the sake of simplicity, the sediment are assumed to moves alone with the near bed water flow and the collision between the sediment grains are ignored) are super-imposed in Fig. 7 . The near bed radial velocities along depicted in Fig. S6 . Firstly, the flow with B /h  = 100 characterizes the typical large-scale nature rivers. The near bed radial velocities are negligible (Fig. S6 a). The sediment trajectories are found aligning with the meander path, exhibiting no cross-stream movement (Fig. 7 a). Thus, sediment eroded from upstream is deposited immediately downstream along the same side with the resulting bed deformation conforming to the D I  pattern of erosion and deposition. The location of maximum deposition occurs just after the apex (at ξ c   = 5/16). The flow with B /h  = 12 represents small scale natural streams or streams of the flume experiments. Significant negative near bed velocities occur due to cross-circulatory flow (Fig. S6 b). Notably, the sediment trajectories are thus deflected to the downstream of inner bank apex, coinciding with the location of prominent deposition (Fig. 7 b). In terms of the erosion–deposition pattern, the two types of deformation, D I  and D II , are superimposed (Fig. 7 b). As evident by the sediment trajectory, the deposited sediment along the inner bank consists of the sediment eroded from the same bank upstream and from the central channel (as indicated by the white arrow), accentuating the combined influence from both longitudinal and radial flows. It should be noted that even under strengthened cross-circulatory flow, the sediment motivated from the outer bank is not deposited directly into inner bank but diverted downstream. This agrees with the laboratory findings by Li et al. (2021)  where only very small amount of sediment was found to be transported from one side of the channel to another even at significant flow depth. The distinct bed deformation patterns of the aforementioned two flows under different B /h  ratio indicates a shift of significance in the driving forces of the fluvial process in a meandering river. Thus, the individual contributors, D I  and D II  (remembering the two implies contributions from the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity and the cross-circulatory velocity, respectively), to the overall bed deformation are quantified by integrating their negative parts of Eq. (7)  over the entire loop. The volume averaged values, <D I >and <D II > (here ‘< >’ denotes volume average), along with their relative contributions, are illustrated in Fig. 8   with B /h  ranging from 10 − 100. Before proceeding further, consider a straight uniform flow under similar hydraulic conditions (B , h , S ) to that in a meandering flow. The uniform sediment fluxes (i.e. ∇qsb    = 0) cause 0 net bed deformation (i.e., <D > = 0). Therefore, the non-zero values of <D I >and <D II > within meandering flows are the result of deviatoric properties of the flows. Particular in Fig. 8 a, the bed deformation pattern as driven by the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity, i.e. <D I >, exhibits similar tendency as the laterally oscillating velocity shown in Fig. 5 b left. Specifically, <D I >increases from near 0 to 0.060 as B /h  decreases from 100 to 20, then forming a plateau of 0.065 at further decrement of B /h.  That driven by the cross-circulatory velocity, i.e. <D II >, show continuous increase from near 0 to 0.060 as B /h  decreases from 100 to 10, also conforming to that of Fig. 5 b right for the cross-circulatory flow intensity. Regarding the relative contribution to the overall bed deformation (Fig. 8 b), <D I > predominates the total bed deformation. Even at the highest cross-circulatory intensity (B /h  = 10), <D I > still accounts for 53% of the total bed deformation. At the B /h  of 100,  <D I > approaches nearly 100%, as cross-circulatory velocity almost dissolves (Fig. 5 b right). This predominance of the bed deformation <D I >is in alignment with previous findings (da Silva and EI-Tahawy, 2008; Chen and Tang, 2012; Xu and Bai, 2013 ; and Li et al., 2021 ) where the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity is identified as the key factor that drives the fluvial process in meandering rivers, especially at significant B /h  ratio.   4 Discussion 4.1 Dynamics at the presence of the outer bank cell As Fig. S4  shows, the outer bank cell emerges firstly in the flow having h  = 8.9 cm (B /h  = 9) and intensifies at the increasing flow depth (decreasing B /h ). Key dynamic features for a typical outer bank cell flow are exemplified in Fig. 9   under h  = 13.7 cm (B /h  = 5.8). This includes the radial flow structural (Fig. 9 a), and the normalized bed deformation rate with sediment trajectory (Fig. 9 b). As shown in Fig. 9 a, the outer bank cell firstly arises from the left corner of the loop entrance. Intensifying downstream, such cell occupies much of the channel’s left side with the maximum intensity occurring at ξb   = 3/16. After the maximum, the outer bank cell rapidly dissipates and disappears at ξc   = 3/8. Along the same region (outer bank side of ξc   = 0–3/8), the local near bed radial velocities exhibit positive value, contrasting to those along the inner bank. The sediment trajectory is thus diverted outwards, resulting in an outer bank deposition zone extending from the upstream cross-over to the downstream of apex (Fig. 9 b). The discovered outer bank deposition zone of the present work aligns with the positive effect of the outer bank cell at preventing the outer bank erosion (Thorne, 1982; Li and Zhang, 2022 ). Nonetheless, the flow and bed deformation pattern along the inner bank are the same as that for flows dominated by one cross-circulatory cell (Fig. 7 b), in which longitudinally (D I ) and laterally (D II ) adjacent erosion–deposition zones are superimposed near inner bank apex. As is shown in Fig. 9 a, the growth of the primary cell is not as prominent under the impeding effect of the outer bank cell. The impeding effect of the outer bank cell is further highlighted in Fig. 10  a by extending the plot of central cell intensity in Fig. 5 b right to include data for flows having B /h  ≤ 9 (that exhibits the outer bank cell). As is shown, discrepancies between the simulated data and the analytical formulation by Yalin and da Silva (2001)  (Eq. (1) ) emerge at the occurrence of the outer bank cell (B /h =  9) and rapidly enlarge at the decrement of B /h . Notably at B /h  = 5.8, Eq. (1)  over-predicts the cross-circulatory intensity by 1.9 times. This necessitates the need to modify the original equation to account for the effect of the outer bank cell:(8) ( u r  )  C  u av    = ( 1 - e - 0.009 ( B / h )  2.5     )  · ( α c 2  B / R a  sin ( 2 π l c  / L )  h B  )      Graphical representation of Eq. (10) is delineated in Fig. 10 a by the dotted line.   The impact of the outer bank cell to the overall bed deformation are depicted in Fig. 10 b, c by extending Fig. 9 a, b to include flows having B /h  ≤ 9. In Fig. 10 b, increases in both <D I >and <D II >are observed at initial decrement of B /h , noting the effect of the outer bank cell. However, because the overall cross-circulatory intensity diminishes at further decrement of B /h  (Fig. 10 a), both data of <D I >and <D I >revert back to the original patterns. The relative ratio of <D I >and <D II >are consistent to the original tendency even at the present of the outer bank cell (Fig. 10 c).  4.2 Limitation and practical significance of the present study Limitation of the present study stems from the fact that it considers only the morphodynamics at the early stages of the bed deformation (plain bed). In the other works (see particularly Blanckaert, 2010; Chen and Tang, 2012; Pan et al., 2022 ), the deformed bed can further deflect the longitudinal velocity towards the outer bank while arising the laterally topography-driven flow. Therefore, further erosion of the outer bank should occur after the initial growth of the inner bank deposition bar (as shown by experiments of Binns and da Silva, 2011 ). Also, the cross-circulatory flow should strengthen within the deep pool that associates with higher width-to-depth ratio. According to Blanckaert (2010) , effects of the topography-driven flow and the cross-circulatory flow can reach the same order of magnitude within the deep scouring pool. Overall, the width-to-depth ratio should also have a significant role, as the bed deformation amplitude are also scaled with the flow depth and thus the width-to-depth ratio. Regarding the practical significance, the present work accentuates a shift of significance in the driving forces of the bed deformation process regarding different width-to-depth ratios. In particular, the increase of the flow depth (and thus the decrease of the width-to-depth ratio) critically enhances the non-equilibrium transport of sediment that can eventually leads to active fluvial evolution of meandering rivers. Under the background of climate changing and human activity intensifying, the increase in the variability and non-uniformity of precipitation and runoff lead to extreme water and sediment transport events. According to the present study, this eventually necessitates more vibrant and complex morphological dynamics of the meandering rivers. Recommendations include reinforcing the banks with riparian vegetation, managing sediment through controlled dam releases and dredging, and using structures like groynes to influence flow patterns. These measures shou collectively enhance river resilience and sustainability in the face of anthropogenic and climatic stresses.   5 Conclusions Series of numerical simulations are performed in 70°  sine-generate channels to elucidate the dynamic process driving the fluvial evolution of meandering streams. The flow depth h  is varied from 0.8 cm to 17.4 cm, facilitating the ratio of B /h  (=4.6 to 100) characterizing a board range from laboratory flume experiment to natural streams. During simulations, flows having B /h  > 9 characterize a classical cross-circulatory motion pattern with a single rotating cell. However, as B /h  decrease to ≤ 9, the Taylor-Görtler instability triggers the formation of additional vortices along the outer bank, known as the outer bank cell. Longitudinally, both the laterally oscillating and cross-circulatory velocities exhibit sinusoidal variations with the period coinciding with the meander length L . The laterally oscillating flow intensity stabilizes at a plateau as B /h  increases from 10 to 30, while the cross-circulatory flow intensity shows a power decay, aligning with the analytical expression by Yalin and da Silva (2001) . Bed deformation rates at the initial plain bed are computed using the sediment continuity equation. Two patterns of bed deformation, that respectively associates longitudinal and radial variations of the flow velocities, are distinguished and named as D I  and D II . D I  of bed deformation arises from the convective redistribution of the longitudinal velocity and characterizes the longitudinally adjacent erosion and deposition zones along the inner bank apex. That due to the cross-circulatory velocity (D II ) manifests radially adjacent zones. D I  and D II  facilitate downstream migration and lateral expansions of the meander loop, respectively. For flows having significant B /h  ratio (e.g., B /h  = 100), D I  dominates where sediment trajectories are almost parallel to the meander path. At the decrement of B /h , both patterns intensify while occurring in conjunction with each other. The sediment trajectories are diverted into the downstream of the inner bank apex, coinciding with the deposition region. Overall, decrement of B /h  ratio (from 100 onward) accentuates a shift of significance in the driving forces of the bed deformation processes while critically enhances the non-equilibrium transport of sediment that can eventually leads to active fluvial evolution of meandering rivers. For flows having B /h  ≤ 9, the outer bank cell arises from the left corner of the loop entrance and intensifies along the first half of the loop. The outer bank cell arises locally positive near-bed radial velocities, and thus leads to the formation of a deposition region along the outer bank. The outer bank cell also impedes the growth of the primary cell, causing the intensity of the latter significantly deviates from the analytical formulation by Yalin and da Silva (2001) . Limitation of the present work stems from the fact that it considers only the dynamics at the early stages of bed deformation, where the emergence of the topography-driven flow can significantly influence both the longitudinal and radial flow structures and thus the sediment transport patterns. The shift in morphological patterns under varying B /h  ratios, as revealed by the present work, has significant implications nowadays given the increasing variability and non-uniformity of precipitation and runoff due to anthropogenic pressures and extreme climate events.
1 Introduction As river water availability and quality are globally changing due to climate change and population increase (UNEP, 2016; UNEP-DHI, 2016 ), long-term river monitoring programs play a pivotal role in river basin management strategies worldwide. River monitoring projects are therefore ongoing in many river basins around the world to understand long-term trends to mitigate future challenges in river management practices. For instance, a comprehensive time-series dataset of suspended solids, major ions and nutrients can be found at the United Nations Environment Program's Global Environmental Monitoring System (GEMS/GLORI) database (Meybeck and Ragu, 1997 ) and from the International Program on Land–Ocean Interactions in the Coastal Zone (LOICZ) (Smith et al., 2003; Milliman et al., 1995; Harris, 2001 ). Long-term river monitoring datasets revealed that 80 % of river basins worldwide have water quality issues primarily by nutrient over-enrichment (e.g., Rhine and Danube) or by pathogens (Ganga, Brahmaputra, Indus, Amazon, Nile, Congo, Yenisei, Niger, Amur, Salween, and Mekong rivers) (UNEP, 2016; UNEP-DHI, 2016; Best, 2019 ). Vorosmarty et al. (2000)  and Oki and Kanae (2006)  both calculated higher water scarcity indexes in the Western United States, Northern Africa, South Asia and the Middle East regions, and that populations living in the areas of high-water stress and relative water demand would increase with the climate change, particularly the Colorado, Nile, Mekong, and Ganga-Brahmaputra River Basins. A common conclusion in most of the long-term monitoring studies is that there is significant human-driven water stress in river ecosystems (Best, 2019 ). Amongst the river basins around the world, the rivers in the Indian sub-continent have perhaps the most substantial societal impact. On the Indian subcontinent, the river Ganga has received special attention as it provides water and food security to half a billion people. As a result, the river Ganga and its tributaries are rigorously monitored by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and Central Water Commission (CWC), Government of India. However, detailed analysis of these long-term ground observation data is largely missing but critical to understanding how human-driven water stress in the Ganga River has evolved over time. For example, utilizing long-term concentration–discharge (C–Q) relationships is crucial for assessing water quality gradients and trends, as well as for devising effective water management strategies (Bowes et al., 2014 ). Similarly, as the water chemistry at a river monitoring station changes based on the flow path of water across the catchment, effectively acting as a 'fingerprint' of the transport, mixing, and reaction processes happening in the catchment (Knapp et al., 2020 ), analyzing how stream water chemistry responds to changes in discharge offers insights into how catchments manage the storage and release of water and solutes. Further, the C–Q relationships derived from long-term datasets are particularly effective for understanding the typical behaviour of a river catchment (Clow and Drever, 1996; Godsey et al., 2009; Godsey and Kirchner, 2014 ) and can act as indicators of hydrologic and biogeochemical processes. Here, we present the long-term river chemistry trends in the Ramganga River—a significant left-bank tributary (Bowes et al., 2020; Gurjar and Tare, 2019a,b; Sen et al., 2023; Sharmila and Arockiarani, 2016 ) of river Ganga—between 1981 and 2020. As previous studies in the Ramganga basin have primarily focused on shorter time scales, typically spanning 1–3 years, the impact of human activities on river water quality is underexplored despite the availability of time-series datasets and river Ramganga being regarded as one of the most polluted tributaries of the river Ganga. As a result. The objective of the study is to better understand how the water chemistry of the Ramganga River evolved over nearly last 40 years, capturing the controls of geological, hydrological and anthropogenic factors on long-term water quality trend. To do so, we present the detailed geochemical and geostatistical analysis of dissolved major ions (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , HCO3 – , F– , Cl− , SO4 2− ), dissolved silica (SiO2 ) and nutrients (NO3 – , PO4 3− ) spanning from 1981 to 2020 at three CWC monitoring stations in the Ramganga basin. This analysis is critically important to understand how the catchment responded to various external forcings at multi-decadal scales (Lamontagne et al., 2000; Likens et al., 1998; Pastor et al., 2003; Thompson et al., 2011; Valett et al., 2008 ) having significant implications for river basin management.  2 Study area and methods 2.1 Site description The Ramganga River, a major left-bank tributary of the Ganga River that emerges from the Kumaon Himalayas in India, travels through the Western Himalayas and the Ganga plains until its confluence with the Ganga River 10 km north of Kannauj (27.05° N, 79.91° E), Uttar Pradesh. The areal extent of the Ramganga catchment is ∼22,663 km2  (see Fig. 1  ) and covers parts of two Indian states, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh. The river is classified as a foothills-fed river (Sinha et al., 2005 ) and the basin receives water mostly in the rainy season from the southwest monsoon and, in the headwater reaches, by a minor quantity of snowfall during the winter season (Asthana et al., 2015 ). The northern part of the watershed consists of mountains with an elevation of more than 3000 m a.s.l., while the southern part consists of plains with an elevation of just around 120 m a.s.l. Forest and grassland predominate in the northern part of the watershed, while agricultural activities are more prevalent in the lowlands, attributable to topographic differences (Fig. 1 ). The river basin's geography plays a significant role in shaping its hydroclimatic diversity. According to data collected from 1969 to 2013, the maximum temperature in the catchment varies between 18 °C in January to 36 °C in May–June, whereas the minimum temperature ranges between 6 °C in January to 23 °C in July. From 1969 to 2013, there was an average of 85 wet days per year, with an annual rainfall of 1009 mm.  2.2 Data source The CWC and CPCB have monitored the Ramganga river for vital river water quality parameters namely temperature, pH, conductivity, alkalinity, total dissolved solids (TDS), total suspended solids (TSS), dissolved oxygen (DO), chemical oxygen demand (COD), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), total coliforms (TC), various nitrogen forms, trace elements, and major ions for last several decades (CPCB, 2011, 2014 ; Gurjar and Tare, 2019a,b; Khan et al., 2020, 2017, 2016; Pathak et al., 2018; Sarah et al., 2019; Sen et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2003; Tare et al., 2003 ). Water discharge, dissolved ions, silica and other physicochemical parameters for the period 1981–2020, sampled at monthly intervals, are taken from the CWC at 3-gauge stations, namely Moradabad (28.82° N, 78.80° E), Bareilly (28.30° N, 79.37° E), and Dabri (27.49° N, 79.37° E). The first two stations are in the middle part of the basin close to two major industrial cities and the third one is the most downstream station just before the confluence of the Ramganga with the Ganga River. These are the only gauge stations that have been monitored continuously by CWC since the 1980s and have been selected strategically in this study to assess the impact of industrial and population hotspots on the Ramganga River. The dataset has been categorized into winter, pre-monsoon, monsoon, and post-monsoon based on the classification provided by the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD, 2017 ). Seasonal variations in discharge, temperature, pH, TDS, electrical conductivity, and major ions have been analyzed to assess the seasonal trends in the dataset.  2.3 Chemometric assessment of physicochemical parameters Univariate analysis was conducted on the physicochemical parameters to assess the minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation in the dataset. To compare the physicochemical parameters across various sampling sites during different monsoon seasons, the datasets were subjected to bivariate analyses, which included Pearson’s correlation analysis and one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) at a significance level of p ≤ 0.05. Furthermore, a post hoc Tukey’s test was used to conduct pairwise comparisons of the various sampling sites. Welch tests and Brown‐Forsythe tests were used to assess the robustness of the ANOVA results. Significant outliers were identified using Grubb’s test and removed before performing any statistical analysis. All the statistical analyses were done using R software.  2.4 Solute concentration–stream discharge (C–Q) analysis All C–Q relationships were calculated on the logarithmic axes across multi-annual, annual, and seasonal timescales using the power law equation: C = aQb  (Godsey et al., 2009, 2019 ), where C and Q denote the solute concentration and discharge, respectively, and a and b are the constants obtained from the best fit of the power law curve. The coefficient of determination (R2 ) shows the strength of the C–Q relation being measured. A student’s t -test was performed to assess whether the best-fit slope was significant (p < 0.05) for the analyzed C–Q relationships. The slope (b-coefficient) of the curve determines the behaviour of the solutes in a C–Q analysis. C–Q patterns are considered to be chemostatic if −0.1 ≤ b ≤ 0.1, which means solute concentration varies slightly with considerable changes in stream discharge. The patterns are said to be chemodynamic if b ≤ −0.1 or b ≥ 0.1, which can further be explained as dilution (b ≤ −0.1) and flushing or mobilization (b ≥ 0.1) (Zimmer et al., 2019, Porter et al., 2022 ). For multi-annual and annual timescales, another parameter, CVC /CVQ , was also calculated, which denotes the coefficient of variation of solute concentration to stream flow and can be calculated using the equation given by Thompson et al. (2011) :(1) C V C   C V Q    = μ Q  μ C   σ C  σ Q       where μ and σ indicate the mean and standard deviation, respectively. In addition to the b-coefficient, CVC /CVQ  value can also be used to distinguish between the chemostatic vs chemodynamic behavior of solutes in a stream where CVC /CVQ  < 0.5 indicates a chemostatic behavior and CVC /CVQ  > 0.5 indicates a chemodynamic behaviour (Musolff et al., 2015; Rose et al., 2018; Thompson et al., 2011 ). However, unlike the b-coefficient, CVC /CVQ  values alone cannot distinguish whether the chemodynamic behaviour indicates a flushing or dilution pattern of the solute. To understand the seasonal patterns of C–Q relationships, we divided each calendar year into four seasons: winter (Jan–Feb), pre-monsoon (Mar–May), monsoon (Jun–Sep), and post-monsoon (Oct–Dec). Since we have monthly sampled data, we were unable to establish a seasonal C–Q relationship for individual calendar years. To overcome this issue, we pooled the data available for all calendar years seasonally and then plotted them against the seasonal discharge data. The seasonal C–Q patterns of various solutes give a general idea of how solute behavior changes seasonally, and which season dominates the behavior of various solutes on longer timescales.  2.5 Trend analysis The primary objective of trend analysis is to determine whether the dataset exhibits an upward, downward, or stable pattern over time. Detecting trends can be a complex task due to the inherent characteristics of the data. Furthermore, various statistical parameters such as mean, median, variance, autocorrelation, skewness, and other aspects of data, including meteorological, hydrological, and climatological data, exhibit time-dependent variability, as observed in reports from the IPCC. This variability can manifest as seasonal patterns, consistent trends, sudden jumps, or other established variations. To elaborate, these characteristics encompass the possible presence of seasonality, skewness, serial correlation, non-normal data, “less-than” (censored) values, outliers, and missing values (Helsel and Hirsch, 1992; Hirsch et al., 1991; Hirsch and Slack, 1984 ). Consequently, various assumptions have been devised to address these potential issues when applying trend analysis methods. One such challenge is the presence of positive autocorrelation, which can lead to an increased likelihood of incorrectly detecting a significant trend beyond what is indicated by the significance level (von Storch, 1999; Zhang et al., 2004 ). Many researchers commonly employ both parametric (distribution-dependent) and non-parametric (distribution-free) analysis methods for conducting trend analyses. These methods have been adapted to analyze different types of data, including annual, monthly, and seasonal time series, in various applications. For cases where the trend can be assumed to be monotonic and normally distributed, with no apparent seasonality or other cyclic patterns present in the data, the Mann–Kendall test was a suitable choice. In this study, therefore Mann–Kendall method was employed at two-tailed confidence levels of 95 %. 2.5.1 Mann–Kendall trend test The MK test is a commonly employed non-parametric analysis tool for assessing the presence of statistically significant trends in hydro-meteorological data (Kendall and Gibbons, 1990; Mann, 1945 ). In this test, it examines the hypothesis 'H0 : no trend' (null hypothesis) to determine if a trend exists within a time series, following the approach outlined by (Yenigün et al., 2008 ). The S statistics of the Mann–Kendall test is calculated using the following equations:(2) sgn x j  - x i      =  1 ;   If   x j  > x i     0 ;    If   x j  = x i     - 1 ;    If   x j  < x i              (3) S = ∑ i = 1  n - 1   ∑ j = i + 1  n  s g n x j  - x i         where xi   and xj   represent data values at times i  and j , with 'n'  denoting the size of the dataset, the sign of 'S' is indicative of the trend direction. A positive 'S'  implies an upward trend, while a negative 'S'  suggests a downward trend. This expression is applied as an assumption when dealing with datasets of length 'n' greater than 10, and the data is reasonably close to a normal distribution, characterized by a variance (σ2  = 1) and a mean (μ = 0) value.(4) var S    = n n - 1     2 n + 5     ∑ i = 1  m  t i  t i  - 1     2 t i  + 5         / 18      (5) Z = S - 1  var S        S > 0    0   S = 0    S + 1  var S         S < 0             In Eq. (4) , 'm'  is the count of tied groups, and the summation symbol (∑) signifies the summation across all these tied groups. 'ti '  represents the number of data values within the mth group. If no tied groups are present, you can safely omit this summation step. Once the variance of the time series data has been computed using Eq. (4) , the subsequent step involves calculating the standard Z value, as outlined in Eq. (5) . The standard Z  value obtained is then compared to the standard normal distribution table, considering two-tailed confidence levels, specifically α levels of 10 %, 5 %, and 1 %. When the calculated Z  value exceeds the range of |Z| > |Z1−α/2 | , the null hypothesis (H0 ) is rejected. This implies that the trend is statistically significant. Conversely, if the calculated Z  value falls within the range, the null hypothesis (H0 ) is accepted, signifying that the trend is not statistically significant, and the time series does not exhibit a distinct trend (considered as a trendless time series).  2.5.2 Assessment of constituent flux To estimate constituent flux, a modelling approach is needed due to the disparity in temporal resolution between daily-collected discharge data and monthly-sampled concentration measurements. Assessment of constituent flux for individual years was made using the rloadest  package in R (Runkel et al., 2004 ). The daily discharge and flux measurements were then summed up for each year to create an annual time series. The rloadest  package employs time series data of concentration and discharge to formulate a regression model, selected from a set of predefined multiple regression models using Akaike's information criterion. In this study, we adopted adjusted maximum likelihood estimation (AMLE) values due to the normal distribution of model residuals. The model results include regression statistics such as the standard error, the standard error for predicting fluxes, the R2  from the AMLE, residuals, and the serial correlation of those residuals; and the bias diagnostics including the bias percentage (Bp %), partial load ratio (PLR), and the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency Index (E). These outputs serve the purpose of assessing the goodness of fit of the model and ensuring that the residuals adhere to established guidelines for a normal distribution (Dornblaser and Striegl, 2009). To assess the significance of annual trends over time, we used a Mann–Kendall test. In this analysis, the slopes of the trends were computed using the Theil–Sen method. The trend analyses and slope calculations were performed using the “trend” package in the R programming language (Pohlert, 2020 ).  2.5.3 Assessment of trends in concentration To analyze concentration trends considering seasonal variations that could potentially skew the trend identification, we employed a Seasonal Kendall test. This method addresses seasonality by individually calculating the Mann–Kendall statistic for each of the p  seasons and subsequently aggregating these season-specific test statistics (Sp )  to establish an overall seasonal Kendall statistic (S′) :(6) S ′  = ∑ i = 1  p  Sp      We employed a modified version of the original Seasonal Kendall test to address the serial dependence in the dataset by utilizing an autoregressive moving average (1:1) method (Hirsch and Slack, 1984 ). Further, we assessed the magnitude of the trends using the Seasonal Sen Slope estimator following the Theil-Sen approach. The robustness of using Sen’s slope lies in its resistance against the presence of outliers (Achite et al., 2021 ).    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Stream chemistry A descriptive analysis of the physicochemical parameters (pH and TDS) and the hydrochemistry of major ions of the Ramganga River is given in Table 1  . The pH value in the basin ranges from 5.8 to 9, with an average pH of 7.97 ± 0.1 (1 S.D., n = 1194), suggesting that water in the basin remains slightly alkaline. The ionic concentration (Σanions + Σcations) varies from 3392 µeq/L to 3650 µeq/l, way above the global average of 1200 µeq/L (Meybeck, 2003 ). The total dissolved solids (TDS) value in the basin varies from 123–1170 mg/L, with an average value of 338 ± 13.2 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248). At all three sites, Ca2+  remains the major cation and its concentration ranges from 14 to 72 mg/L with an average value of 36 ± 2 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248). The next major cations in the samples are Mg2+ , Na+ , and K+  with an average value of 27 ± 2 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248), 20 ± 2 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1246), and 6.7 ± 0.7 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248), respectively. The anion load In the river is dominated by HCO3 –  which ranges from 73 to 510 mg/L with an average concentration of 257 ± 13 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248). SO4 2 -   is the second dominant anion in the basin with a concentration ranging from 6-78 mg/L and an average value of 28 ± 3 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248). The anion abundance in the basin is in order of HCO3 –  > SO4 2 -   > Cl−  > NO3 –  > F−  > PO4 3− . The dissolved silica concentration in the basin varies from 4 to 16 mg/L (average 8.5 ± 0.3 mg/L, 1 S.D., n = 1088). This value is found to be similar to the global average of 8.7 mg/L (Meybeck, 2003 ), and other major rivers such as Amazon (3.6–9.6 mg/L; Gaillardet et al., 1997 ) and Congo (8.41–12.62 mg/L; Dupré et al., 1996 ). The box plots of the monthly solute concentrations at the three monitoring stations (Fig. S1 ) illustrate the spatiotemporal variation in concentrations of various solutes in the river water. Ca2+ , Mg2+ , F− , and SiO2  exhibit relatively stable concentrations with minor fluctuations throughout the year at all the monitoring sites and they do not show significant variability during monsoon months (Fig. S1 ). This may indicate a strong geological control on the sources and concentrations of these solutes. Solutes such as Na+ , Cl− , and NO3 –  exhibit noticeable increases in variability and concentration during the monsoon months, suggesting a strong response to increase in river discharge and runoff. HCO3 – , K+ , and SO4 2−  show minor fluctuation throughout the year with a slight increase in variability and concentrations during the monsoon months, indicating a minor but important response to seasonal changes. PO4 3−  concentrations remain very low throughout the year, showing sporadic variability, particularly during the monsoon season which may indicate the localized sources or specific pollution incidents affecting its levels in the river water. The time series plot of all the solutes is provided in the supplementary section (Fig. S2 ). The one-way ANOVA analysis performed on the dataset suggests that there exists a significant yet non-systematic spatial variability for most of the major ions i.e., the concentration of the ions does not necessarily follow an increasing/decreasing pattern as we go downstream from source to sink. Also, most of the major ions except NO3 –  exhibit significant seasonal variability for all the monitoring sites. Pearson’s correlation analysis of all the major ions, except NO3 –  and PO4 3− , exhibit significant moderate to weak positive correlations among themselves (Fig. 2  ). At Moradabad, NO3 –  exhibits moderate to weak negative correlation with all the other major ions, except Mg2+ , with which it shows a weak positive correlation, whereas, at Bareilly and Dabri, NO3 –  exhibits weak to moderate positive correlations with other major ions. Similarly, PO4 3−  shows a weak-moderate positive correlation with other major ions at Moradabad, whereas at Bareilly and Dabri, it is negatively correlated with other major ions.  3.2 Concentration–discharge relationships 3.2.1 Decadal C–Q analysis All solutes, except NO3 – , show significant (p < 0.001) multi-annual C–Q relationships for the water years 1981–2020 for the three analyzed CWC monitoring stations at River Ramganga. The slope value (b coefficient) of the major solutes such as Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , HCO3 – , and SiO2  ranges from −0.10 to −0.20, and the R2  values of these solutes vary from 0.1 to 0.45. Other solutes like Cl− , F− , and SO4 2 -  also show negative slope values ranging from −0.10 to −0.19, and their R2  value varies from 0.13 to 0.26. Solutes such as NO3 −  and PO4 3 -  have a slope value between 0.025 and −0.32, and their R2  values vary between 0.001 and 0.24 (Fig. 3  a–c). NO3 –  is the only solute that shows a chemostatic behaviour (−0.1 < b < 0.1) at all the monitoring sites. In general, the concentration of all the solutes except NO3 –  decreases as the flow increases suggesting the dominant chemodynamic (dilution) behaviour of these solutes on decadal timescales. The CVC /CVQ  values of the major geogenic solutes vary between 0.07 and 0.27. For Cl− , F− , and SO4 2− , the CVC /CVQ  values range from 0.16 to 0.28. NO3 −  and PO4 3 -  have the highest CVC /CVQ  values ranging between 0.39 and 0.54. We have plotted the C–Q behaviour of the solutes on the slope (b) vs CVC /CVQ  space (Fig. S3 ) following Cartwright (2020) which further confirms the observed chemodynamic/chemostatic trends of the analyzed solutes on the multidecadal timescale.  3.2.2 Annual C–Q relationships All the measured solutes show significant (p < 0.05) C–Q relationships on the annual scale throughout the water years with available data (Fig. 4   a-c). The R2  values of the solutes were greater than or close to 0.5 for most of the calendar years, notably for the geogenic solutes such as Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , HCO3 – , F− , Cl− , and SiO2  (Fig. S4 ). Annual C–Q relationships for geogenic solutes and nutrients such as PO4 3 -  and NO3 −  were observed to be insignificant for multiple years spanning from 1 to 5 years (Fig. 4 a–c). The slope values (b-coefficients) of all the geogenic solutes are negative for almost all the years and less than −0.1 for most of the water years. The b-coefficients for the nutrients (PO4 3 - , SO4 2 - , and NO3 - ) were mostly negative and less than −0.1. Although a few positive b-coefficient values were also exhibited by the nutrients, they were mostly insignificant (p > 0.05) (Fig. 4 a–c). In general, all the analyzed solutes show a chemodynamic (dilution) behavior on annual timescales. The mean CVC /CVQ  values of the solutes range from 0.14 to 0.29, and their SDs varied from 0.04 to 0.26. The CVC /CVQ  values for individual years were typically below 0.5 for most of the solutes. Similar to the multidecadal C–Q pattern the combination of b and CVC /CVQ  values on an annual timescale (not shown) indicates the predominance of chemodynamic (dilution) behavior for most of the calendar years.  3.2.3 Seasonal C–Q relationships On the seasonal timescale, the C–Q patterns for four seasons (winter, pre-monsoon, monsoon, and post-monsoon) for the pooled seasonal data showed complex behavior of geogenic as well as anthropogenic solutes (Fig. 5  ). Although the R2  values of the pooled seasonal data are very poor due to high intra-seasonal variability in observed discharge and solute concentration, it gives a general understanding of the seasonal behaviour of the solutes. The predominantly geogenic solutes such as Ca2 + , K+ , HCO3 – , Cl–  and SiO2  remained chemostatic in the winter and pre-monsoon seasons and became chemodynamic (dilution) during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons at all the three monitored CWC stations. Solutes such as Mg2 + , Na+ , F− , PO4 3− , and SO4 2−  showed chemodynamic (dilution) behaviour for all the four seasons. NO3 –  is the only solute that shows very distinct behaviour at all the sites. NO3 –  showed a strong flushing behaviour (b > 0.1) at Moradabad for the winter, pre-monsoon, and post-monsoon periods and remained chemostatic during the monsoon period. At Bareilly and Dabri, NO3 –  exhibited dilution behaviour for winter and post-monsoon seasons and remained chemostatic for the pre-monsoon and monsoon seasons. The variation in the major ion concentrations with discharge on multi-decadal and annual timescales (Fig. 3, 4a-c ) eliminates the possibility of a simple dilution scenario resulting from constant baseflow input provided by substantial recent precipitation or surface runoff during periods of high discharge (Cartwright, 2020 ). In general, the changes in solute concentrations with discharge are best explained by the mobilization of moderately saline soil water or shallow groundwater as the catchments become wetter, potentially amplified by increased inputs of baseflow stimulated by hydraulic loading (Cartwright, 2020 ). The fact that Cl− , a solute predominantly derived from the evapotranspiration of precipitation in catchments devoid of halite beds, exhibits similar behaviour to other solutes indicates that variations in silicate weathering alone are not a major process controlling river chemistry. Despite the lithological diversity in the Ramganga catchment, most of the solutes show a dilution behaviour with increasing discharge on longer timescales, i.e., multi-decadal and interannual timescales. At seasonal timescales, the C–Q patterns during the low flow period (i.e., winter and pre-monsoon) are primarily shaped by the inputs from the deeper groundwater and, to a lesser extent, by shallow riparian aquifers. In contrast, during the monsoon and post-monsoon periods, the river is sustained by a mixture of precipitation input, groundwater, overland flow, and prolonged drainage from the shallow riparian zone aquifers, all of which exert a strong control on shaping the C–Q pattern during these periods. Moatar et al. (2017)  suggested that biogeochemical processes might affect C–Q responses at low flows, but during high flows, hydrology takes on the dominant role. For example, even though C–Q relationships of NO3 –  are frequently documented as chemostatic or negative in the literature (Alvarez-Cobelas et al., 2008; Dupas et al., 2016 ), our data shows a strong flushing behaviour of NO3 –  for low flow seasons at Moradabad. This phenomenon could be attributed to local transport limitation (i.e., the mobilization of isolated NO3 –  sources with increasing flow) or a reduction in the relative significance of biogeochemical processes that mediate NO3 –  delivery (e.g., denitrification and/or assimilation). The PO4 3−  usually exhibits episodic C–Q patterns in small basins (<200 km2 , Thompson et al., 2011 ) but remains chemostatic in large basins (Basu et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2011 ). The difference between C–Q patterns of NO3 –  and PO4 3−  in our study could be attributed to the different biogeochemistry of these solutes (Basu et al., 2011 ). In streams, nitrogen is predominantly transported as dissolved nitrate, whereas phosphorus is transported in both the dissolved and sorbed phases (sediment-bound PO4 3− ). While recognizing that the physical characteristics of an element play a significant role in its sourcing and distribution within a riverine system is not a new concept (Basu et al., 2010; Musolff et al., 2015 ), it is crucial to understand that elemental properties create a foundational C–Q template within catchments. This template is subsequently influenced by the prevalence of biological activity during low flows and the dynamic interaction of various catchment factors, including land use, topography, and hydrology, during high flows (Moatar et al., 2017 ). Liu et al. (2022)  suggested that among all catchment factors, catchment topography characteristics (e.g. slope, elevation, and maximum flow path length) exert the dominant control on the export patterns of solutes in a river catchment.   3.3 Long-term trends in major ion chemistry in the Ramganga River Historical records of major ion chemistry for the Ramganga River span nearly forty years, allowing us to analyze the long-term trend analysis of the major ions. The statistical results obtained from the modified Mann-Kendall test are given in supplementary tables (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 ). The trend analysis suggests that individual ions follow a similar trend throughout all the monitoring sites. The long-term variations in the major ions indicate a slight increase in the annual concentration of Ca2+ , K+ , F− , Cl− , and SiO2 , while other ions such as Mg2+ , HCO3 – , Na+ , and PO4 3− show a slightly decreasing trend. No statistically significant trend is observed for Cl−  and PO4 3−  apparently exhibit no change in concentration (slope ̴0) at Moradabad. The NO3 –  is the only solute that shows a strong positive trend in the concentration at all the monitoring sites (Fig. 6  ). The multi-year trend in the annual discharge in the basin suggests that the annual discharge over the monitoring period does not show a significant trend (Fig. 7  ). Over the monitoring periods of forty years (1981–2020), the annual fluxes of most of the major ions, except HCO3 –  and Mg2+ , significantly increase downstream, whereas annual fluxes of HCO3 –  and Mg2+  decrease downstream, though the trend is statistically insignificant (p > 0.05) at all the monitoring sites (Fig. 8  ). At Moradabad, only NO3 –  shows a significant trend of 2646 ton/year and trends in annual fluxes of all other major ions were statistically insignificant. At Bareilly, annual fluxes of major ions such as Ca2+ , K+ , F− , Cl− , SiO2 , NO3 – , PO4 3−  show a significant increasing trend. Among all the dissolved major ions, NO3–  exhibits the highest trend in annual flux followed by Ca2+ , Cl− , K+ , SiO2 , F− , and PO4 3− . At Dabri, only four major ions namely K+ , Cl− , NO3 – , and PO4 3−  demonstrate a statistically significant increasing trend in annual fluxes, with NO3 –  exhibiting the most prominent trend of 11,145 tons/year. Using a multi-decadal record of water chemistry at three different gauge stations along the Ramganga River, we were able to calculate the multiyear trend in the annual fluxes of major ions.
