We found out that the change in annual fluxes of Cl− , K+ , and SO4 2−  increases downstream drastically over the monitoring period, a result that is expected from rapid population growth, intensified agriculture, and industrialization in the basin. Also, NO3 – , and PO4 3−  show a significant increasing trend downstream resulting from the intensified agricultural activity over the monitoring period in the Ramganga basin.  3.4 Process controlling the major solute load in the river The mechanisms governing the hydrogeochemistry of river water can be deduced from the three end members in Gibbs schematic diagram: (1) End-member 1 – located in the lower right corner and has low TDS, usually <10 mg/l with high ratios of cations [(Na+ +K+ )/(Na+ +K+ +Ca2+ )] and anions (Cl− /Cl− +HCO3 – ), ranging from 0.5 to 1, indicating the dominance of precipitation; (2) End-member 2 – located in the middle of the left side and has moderate TDS values (70–300 mg/l) and low ratios of cations and anions (<0.5), reflecting the dominant control of rock weathering; and (3) End-member 3 – located in the upper right corner and has high TDS values (>300 mg/L) as well as high cations and anions ratios (0.5–1), demonstrating the dominant dissolution of evaporitic deposits (Gibbs, 1970; Jiang et al., 2015; Stallard and Edmond, 1987 ). The samples collected from the Ramganga River monitoring sites have moderate TDS and low cations and anions ratios. The TDS value of the Ramganga River varies from 123.5 to 1170 mg/L with an average value of 338 ± 13.24 mg/L. The cations and anions ratios vary from 0.08 to 0.35 and 0.03 to 0.31, respectively, with their average values of 0.19 ± 0.05 (1 S.D., n = 1246) and 0.14 ± 0.04 (1 S.D., n = 1246), respectively. The locations of the samples from the Ramganga River in the Gibbs diagram illustrate the predominance of geogenic factors at all three monitoring sites (Fig. 8 ). The findings of the Gibbs plot of this study are in good agreement with other Himalayan rivers, such as the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and the Indus, draining similar climatic and lithological environments (Pant et al., 2018 ).  3.5 Sources of major solutes and their ionic relationships in the Ramganga River The chemical composition of surface water is predominantly controlled by the source rock as water–rock interaction is the primary factor influencing the river’s chemistry. The ions generated through the weathering processes of various rocks exhibit variations. The impact of weathering dissolution in evaporative, carbonate, and silicate rocks on the chemical composition of water can be qualitatively assessed through Na normalization (Jiang et al., 2015 ). Na-normalized molar ratios (Ca2+ /Na+  vs. Mg2+ /Na+  and Ca2+ /Na+  vs. HCO3 – /Na+ ) of Ramganga River with the potential geogenic “end-members,” which help distinguish the interaction of surface water with carbonates, silicates and evaporite deposits (Gaillardet et al., 1999 ). The overall correlations between the molar ratios of Ca2+ /Na+  versus Mg2+ /Na+  and Ca2+ /Na+  versus HCO3 – /Na+  are 0.511 and 0.629 (n = 1240), respectively. Molar ratios of the Ramganga River lie close to the silicates field along the silicates-carbonates mixing line ( Fig. S5 a, b) , indicating a strong influence of the silicate lithology on its chemistry. The geology of the basin suggests that Ca2+  and Mg2+  is predominantly derived from the Lesser Himalayan carbonate formations, whereas Na+  and K+  are primarily originated from the felsic rocks in the basin (Khan et al., 2022 ). To understand the hydrogeochemical evolution of the surface water in the Ramganga basin, major cations and anions were plotted on the Piper trilinear diagram (Fig. S6 ) along with the end-member composition of the general rock types based on their average ionic compositions (Spence and Telmer, 2005 ). The Ramganga River waters are well explained by the weathering of silicate and carbonate rocks by H2 CO3  acid and, to a lesser extent, carbonate, and silicate weathering by sulfuric acid (Fig. S3 ). Although the individual contributions from weathering of basaltic versus granitic compositions cannot be distinguished in the presence of carbonates; but the Ramganga waters plot much closer to the end-member composition for weathering of mafic rocks by carbonic acid than that of felsic rocks by sulfuric acid. Also, mafic rocks are susceptible to weather more rapidly than their felsic counterparts, making it logical to assume that the dissolution of mafic rocks rather than felsic, is the predominant silicate weathering process in the Ramganga basin. Dissolved ionic species and their inter-relationships can unfold the origin of the solutes and the processes governing their observed geochemical composition in the river water. Statistical analyses revealed significant positive correlations among a few pairs of parameters (Fig. S7 ). The potential origin of Na+  and K+  concentrations in surface waters include atmospheric precipitation, the dissolution of halite (rock salt), and the weathering of silicate minerals containing Na+ . If halite dissolution controls the Na+  concentration, the Na+ /Cl−  molar ratio remains ̴1, whereas Na+ /Cl−  > 1 typically denotes that Na+  gets released from silicate weathering or the presence of Na-bearing salts (Meybeck, 1987 ). In this study, the molar ratio of Na+ /Cl−  ranges from 0.169 to 8.28, with an average value of 1.43. Meanwhile, most of the samples on the (Na+ +K+ ) versus Cl−  plots lie above the equiline (Fig. S7 a), suggesting the dominance of the Na- and K-aluminosilicate weathering and other anthropogenic sources in the basin rather than Cl− -evaporite weathering. Atmospheric dust and marine aerosol can also significantly contribute to the Na+  and Cl−  budget of the river water (Galy and France-Lanord, 1999 ). However, the average Na+ /Cl−  ratio in the Ramganga basin is 1.43, which is different from the seawater Na+ /Cl−  composition (Gaillardet et al., 1999 ). Furthermore, being distant from the ocean, the contribution from marine aerosols remains negligible. The origin of Ca2+  and Mg2+  in the surface waters can be determined from (Ca2+  + Mg2+ )/HCO3 –  ratio. If the samples lie above the equiline, it suggests that the excess Ca2+  and Mg2+  can be attributed to sulfates. The 1:1 equiline represents the dissolution of carbonates playing a pivotal role in generating the Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and HCO3 –  signatures in the surface waters. Samples lying below the equiline indicate the dominance of carbonic acid-mediated silicate weathering governing the HCO3 –  composition in the surface waters. Most of the samples of the Ramganga River lie below the 1:1 equiline (Fig. S7 b), suggesting the dominant role of Na- and K-aluminosilicates weathering in generating the excess HCO3 –  (Zhang et al., 2007 ). The (Ca2+  + Mg2+ ) concentrations of the samples lie far above the equiline on the (Ca2+  + Mg2+ ) versus SO4 2−  plot (Fig. S7 c) indicating that (Ca2+ +Mg2+ ) is derived from other important sources either from carbonate or silicate weathering rather than evaporites in the basin. The SO4 2−  in the surface waters can be derived from various sources such as dissolution of sulfate evaporites, sulfide minerals oxidation, organic S, and anthropogenic inputs (Lang et al., 2006 ). The poor correlation (R2  > 0.02) shown by Cl−  and SO4 2−  (Fig. S7 d) indicates that SO4 2−  is dominantly controlled by sulfide evaporite weathering and atmospheric deposition in the basin (Khan et al., 2022 ). Pyrite and gypsum deposits present in the Lesser Himalayan lithologies can be the probable source of SO4 2−  in the Ramganga River (Chakrapani and Vezier, 2006; Chakrapani et al., 2009; Dalai et al., 2002 ).  3.6 Industrial, agricultural, and domestic pollution in the river Anthropogenic activities such as atmospheric acid deposition, municipal and industrial effluents, excess use of agricultural fertilizers, and other pollution sources impact the hydrogeochemistry of surface waters (Chetelat et al., 2008 ). While industrial effluents and acid deposition primarily affect the SO4 2−  and NO3 –  in the surface runoff, domestic sewage draining into the river system impacts the Na+ , Cl− , and NO3 –  budget of the riverine ecosystem. The use of potassium and nitrogen fertilizer in agricultural practices leads to non-point source pollution and subsequently impacts K+  and NO3 −  concentrations in the receiving waters (Chetelat et al., 2008; Wu and Chen, 2013 ). The Ramganga basin is subjected to extensive agricultural practices and a few industrial hotspots, contributing significantly to the anthropogenic pollution in the river. The SO4 2−  and NO3 –  concentrations in the basin range from 6.2 to 78.2 mg/L and 0.33 to 30.7 mg/L with an average value of 9.12 ± 0.39 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 395) and 27.8 ± 3.17 mg/L (1 S.D., n = 1248) mg/L, respectively. The Ca2+ - and Na+ -normalized NO3 –  and SO4 2−  molar ratios are generally used to understand the relative role of industrial and anthropogenic pollution in water bodies. In the Ramganga River, there is no correlation observed between the NO3 – /Ca2+  versus SO4 2− /Ca2+  and NO3 – /Na+  versus SO4 2− /Na+  plots (Fig. S8 a, b), suggesting that there exist different sources contributing to the observed NO3 –  and SO4 2−  concentrations in the basin. Correlation between the NO3 – /Cl−  molar ratios with Cl−  concentrations (micromolar) gives additional insight into the source of nitrates in the basin (Liu et al., 2006; Torres-Martínez et al., 2021; Widory et al., 2005; Zeng and Wu, 2015 ). Chemical fertilizers generally show high NO3 –  over Cl−  concentrations whereas domestic sewage waste and manure have High Cl−  concentrations with low NO3 – /Cl−  ratios (Guo et al., 2020; Han and Xu, 2022; Liu et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2015; Torres-Martínez et al., 2021; Widory et al., 2005; Zeng and Wu, 2015 ). The Cl−  concentration in the diagram needs to be corrected for Cl−  contributions from halite. As the source rocks in the Ramganga basin are devoid of any halite beds, the contribution of Cl−  from halite can be considered negligible. The NO3 – /Cl−  vs Cl−  plot (Fig. 9  ) suggests that three major sources, i.e., agricultural input, soil nitrogen input and sewage input, are primarily responsible for the NO3 –  pollution in the Ramganga basin.  3.7 Fluxes to the Ganga River Using major element chemistry and water discharge data obtained at Dabri station, we computed the fluxes of major dissolved solutes from the Ramganga River to the Ganga River. Dabri station was chosen due to its location as the most downstream station before the Ramganga–Ganga confluence. Supplementary Table S2  provides a comprehensive overview of the model’s performance for the analyzed solutes. Except for PO4 3− , SO4 2− , and NO3 – , most of the solutes show high model efficiency (E) and low bias percentage (Bp), suggesting reliable flux estimates. PO4 3− and SO4 2−  show a slightly higher bias (positive Bp), indicating overestimation of their relative fluxes, while NO3 –  shows a moderate model efficiency (E = 0.56), suggesting that the model did not capture the NO3 –  flux very well. Supplementary Figure S9  shows the mean daily flux of the solutes calculated for the individual calendar year and their associated uncertainties. The uncertainties associated with the mean daily flux estimation for individual calendar years were low for most of the solutes (typically < 5 %, Fig. S9 ), except for NO3 –  and PO4 3− ,  for which the uncertainties were comparatively high (>5%, Fig. S9 ). Between 1990 and 2020, the Ramganga River transported an average of approximately 2.57 million ton/year of Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) to the Ganga River (Supplementary Table S4 ). The dissolved flux is predominantly controlled by HCO3 −  and Ca2+  ions, accounting for 70 % of the total dissolved flux of the Ramganga River (Supplementary Table S4 ). Overall, the Ramganga river constitutes only a small amount (3.29 %) of total dissolved flux of the Ganga River. Nutrients, such as NO3 – , PO4 3− , and SiO2  concentration in the Ramganga River varied from 0.33 to 30.7, 0.01 to 0.53 and 2 to 16.4 mg/L, respectively. The NO3 – , PO4 3− , and SiO2  yield for the Ramganga River is 3.64, 0.027 and 2.25 ton/km2 /year, respectively (Supplementary Table S5 ). The Ramganga River exhibits a greater nutrient yield in comparison to other rivers in India. (Supplementary Table S5 ). The total dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN, i.e., the total dissolved ammonium + nitrate + nitrite) content of the Ramganga River is found to be very high. Netravati is the only Indian river that has a DIN yield similar to the Ramganga River DIN yield. It is also noteworthy that the DIN yield for the Ramganga River (3.64 ton/km2 /year, Supplementary Table S5 ) is much higher than the major world rivers including Amazon (0.797 ton/km2 /year), Mississippi (1.302 ton/km2 /year), Yangtze (1.736 ton/km2 /year), and Trinity (1.178 ton/km2 /year) and Arctic rivers such as Yukon (0.085 ton/km2 /year), Mackenzie (0.02 ton/km2 /year), Ob (0.47 ton/km2 /year), and Yenisei (0.38 ton/km2 /year) (Holmes et al. 2000 ; Guo et al., 2004 ). In contrast, the phosphate yield of the Ramganga River is less than or in some cases comparable to major Indian rivers. Also, the phosphate yield for the Ramganga River is less than major world rivers such as the Amazon (0.066 ton/km2 /year), Mississippi (0.133 ton/km2 /year) Trinity (0.084 ton/km2 /year), and the Ganges (0.04 ton/km2 /year) (Supplementary Table S5 ). It is important to highlight that comparing these aspects with those of other river systems worldwide may present challenges due to the unique nature of agricultural management practices, cropping intensities, policies related to effluent discharge, waste management, socio-economic conditions across the basin, and cultivation patterns in the Indo-Gangetic flood plains. The rain-fed south Indian rivers contribute (0.12 ± 0.03) × 106  tons/year of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and (0.08 ± 0.02) × 106  tons/year of phosphate during the monsoon season annually to the Bay of Bengal (Krishna et al., 2016 ). On the contrary, rivers in northern India, which are fed by glaciers, showcase elevated concentrations of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) owing to their extensive catchment area and greater volume of discharge. Additionally, the use of fertilizers in northern India, totalling approximately 18 × 106  tons/year, surpasses that in southern India by roughly five-fold (3.5 × 106  tons/year, Seitzinger et al., 2010 ). Glacial-fed rivers originating from the Indian subcontinent, except for the Irrawaddy and Salween rivers, are estimated to export (1.62 ± 0.40) × 106  ton/year of nitrate, (0.27 ± 0.06) × 106  ton/year of phosphate, and (3.58 ± 0.89) × 106  ton/year of silicate fluxes to the northern Indian Ocean (Krishna et al., 2016 ). Our calculations reveal that the Ramganga River contributes ̴ 98,164 tons/year of DIN and ̴708 tons/year of phosphate to the Ganges River (Supplementary Table S5 ). These values account for 12.3 % and 1.66 % of the total DIN and phosphate fluxes, respectively, to the Bay of Bengal (Supplementary Table S5 ).   4 Limitation of the work and future scope The major limitation of this study is the unavailability of high-frequency measurements of the geochemical data, which inherently mask short-term variations in Concentration–Discharge (C–Q) dynamics. During these intervals, factors such as hydrology, biological activity, and the prior distribution of solute sources are likely to exert a more significant influence, as suggested by various studies of hysteresis at the event scale (Chanat et al., 2002; Evans and Davies, 1998; Hornberger et al., 2001; Strohmeier et al., 2013 ). It is also important to note that the long-term groundwater and soil water geochemical data for the Ramganga basin is rarely available, which could really have helped us in developing a diagnostic tool of mixing models (DTMM) and end-member mixing analysis (EMMA) to understand the different sources of solutes and flow path routing in the Ramganga basin (Kendall et al., 1999; Ohte et al., 2004; Porter et al., 2022; Sebestyen et al., 2008 ). Further, the unavailability of carbon, oxygen, and sulfur isotopic data in the Ramganga Basin limits our understanding of biogeochemical cycles and water–rock interactions. The unavailability of isotopic data limits accurate assessments of contributions from different industrial and anthropogenic sources. Without this crucial information, comprehensive insights into ecological processes, sediment provenance, and potential pollution sources remain elusive, impeding effective watershed management strategies.  5 Conclusions The dataset utilized in this study comprises monthly monitored data from 3 stations spanning nearly 40 years. This extensive data set enabled us to investigate the spatial distribution, long-term trends, and the underlying mechanisms of the major-element chemistry of the Ramganga River. The significance of this high sampling density, frequency, and duration becomes apparent due to the lithological and climatological heterogeneity within the river basin. The long-term data provides important insights into the solute behaviour, trends in concentration and annual fluxes of the solutes, dominant weathering processes, and anthropogenic pollution in the basin. The long-term data of the major ion chemistry of the Ramganga River indicates that:• The relative dominance of silicate weathering over carbonate weathering in generating the observed solute concentrations in the basin.  • Most of the solutes in the Ramganga basin show a dilution pattern on multi-decadal and inter-annual timescales.  • Solute behaviour becomes quite complex at seasonal timescales, where relative dominance of biogeochemical properties, landscape dynamics and hydrology play a key role in the source and transportation of these solutes.  • The long-term trend in the geogenic solute concentrations at multiple monitoring sites indicates a statistically significant (p < 0.05) increase in the concentration in the basin over the recent decades.  • The changes in annual fluxes of most of the geogenic solutes except Mg2+  and HCO3 – , increase significantly downstream.  • The increasing trend in annual fluxes of NO3– , PO4 3− , and SO4 −  downstream indicates the manifold increase in the influence of anthropogenic activity in the basin.  • NO3− and SO4 −  pollution in the basin predominantly originates from various sources of industrial effluents, agriculture activities, domestic sewage, and manure input. 1 Introduction Water levels are constantly changing due a variety of stresses such as barometric pressure, Earth and ocean tides, surface water levels, precipitation, pumping and injection, loading and unloading, earthquakes to name a few. Not only do they respond to nearby stress changes but they can respond to changes originating thousands of miles away, which travel through different volumes of the subsurface. These water level fluctuations may be small (sub-millimeter) or large (meters) and be short (sub-second) or long-lived (days to years). Historical and present technical limitations lead to many of these changes going unnoticed or unrecognized due to inadequate monitoring frequency and insufficient equipment precision. As monitoring technology continues to improve, new analysis methods will be necessary to better interpret the multitude of water level responses. To evaluate what can be gained by using higher frequency measurements, water pressures were collected every second for multiple months at a fractured sandstone site. Using natural stress changes caused by barometric pressure, ambient water pressure responses are probed at a temporal scale not commonly examined. The barometric response is important for three primary reasons: barometric responses are present in water levels across the Earth (data is widely available); the response is related to subsurface parameters and character (information rich, i.e. hydrogeologic insights); and the removal of the barometric response can reveal previously obscured signals (improved data quality via noise reduction). In this paper we define high frequency as a sampling interval that is less than one minute, which contrasts with common sampling intervals for ambient monitoring of 5 min or greater. The collection of high frequency data for long periods of time (months to years) requires equipment with suitable memory and power so that they that can operate for months at a time with minimal intervention. In addition, a clear motivation for collecting the high frequency data is necessary and we hope this paper encourages the collection of higher frequency data to improve subsurface characterization and parameterization. Historically the technological limitations and associated costs likely contributed to lower data collection frequencies, however, many of the technical limitations are being addressed with inexpensive memory and low power consumption devices. In addition, following data collection, new methods may be required to be able to evaluate the larger data sets. The goal of this paper is to introduce a time domain method that can be used to characterize water level responses and encourage others to collect high frequency data to advance scientific understanding. First, methods are applied to a synthetic example with known properties, followed by examples with field data from a sandstone site. While this paper focuses on the barometric response, the methods can also be applied to other responses such as river stage, pumping, precipitation and others. The relationship between water levels (or water pressures) and barometric pressure is often conceptualized with a single value − the barometric efficiency (Acworth et al., 2016; Clark, 1967; Davis and Rasmussen, 1993; Gonthier, 2007; Jacob, 1940; Smith et al., 2013; Turnadge et al., 2019 ). This relationship assumes a confined aquifer with an instantaneous response to changes in barometric loading. While many methods exist to estimate barometric efficiency, there is a key deficiency of single value (BE) methods that goes beyond their ability to handle noise (non-barometrically induced changes) in the data set; they assume a lag free or frequency independent response. To have an instantaneous response, the formation must respond (deform) instantly and the monitoring well must represent the formation pressure without any time lag. In practice, there is often a finite amount of time required for a signal to propagate through the subsurface and generate changes at the monitoring well (Hvorslev, 1951 ). These changes may occur rapidly (seconds) or slowly (days) depending on the source of the stress, the well design and geologic properties. Characterizing delayed or lagged responses can be difficult due to equipment limitations, the signal to noise ratio, interfering signals, and inadequate monitoring where the monitoring frequency is too low or the associated input signals (barometric pressure, precipitation, etc.) are collected too far away from the monitoring well. The limitation of using a single barometric efficiency can be overcome by describing the barometric response with a time lag or frequency dependence. Barometric response functions were introduced to solve this problem and expand the notion of barometric efficiency to semi-confined and unconfined systems (Odling et al., 2015; Rasmussen and Crawford, 1997; Rasmussen and Mote, 2007; Rojstaczer, 1988; Toll and Rasmussen, 2007 ). These methods provide additional information over the traditional barometric efficiency that can provide diagnostic information about the subsurface. For example, Rojstaczer (1988)  describes four imbalances that occur after a barometric pressure change for a semi-confined aquifer: (1) Vertical air flow in the vadose zone to the water table (vadose response); (2) vertical groundwater flow between the water table and the confining layer; (3) vertical groundwater flow between the aquifer and confining layer; and (4) Lateral groundwater flow between the formation and well (well-bore storage). While the pressure imbalances are established instantly, the lagged (or frequency dependent) response propagates through different volumes of the subsurface and occurs over multiple time scales. A single value is unable to describe these changes and the timing and magnitude of the response is related to subsurface and well properties. The first (1) imbalance will be related to the thickness and pneumatic diffusivity of the vadose zone (Furbish, 1991; Kuang et al., 2013; Rojstaczer, 1988; Weeks, 1979; Yang and Shibata, 2020 ), imbalances (2) and (3) are influenced by the vertical hydraulic diffusivity of the aquifer(s) and confining layer (Butler et al., 2011; Ritzi et al., 1991; Rojstaczer, 1988 ), and imbalance (4) is related to the well geometry and formation transmissivity (Hvorslev, 1951; Rojstaczer, 1988 ) (Fig. 1  ). In theory, the parameters associated with these responses should be obtainable by fitting the appropriate model to the barometric response function, but in practice this continues to be a difficult task. Hussein et al. (2013)  presented a series of theoretical barometric response functions in the frequency domain to demonstrate the sensitivity of the barometric response to different aquifer, confining layer, and vadose zone properties. These values are calculated for multiple scenarios and the responses vary over eight orders of magnitude in the frequency domain (10,000 to 0.0001 cycles per day), however, the typical empirically determined barometric response in the literature covers less than two orders of magnitude (15 min to one day time lag or 0.02 to 2 cycles per day). Lai et al. (2013)  presented coherent barometric responses up to 30 cycles per day and this frequency remains uncommon. Researchers have long known about the importance of frequency dependent responses but four primary reasons for the lack of field examples are: (1) technical limitatations of monitoring devices (2) water levels are rarely collected at high frequency; (3) the increased computational effort required for larger data sets; and (4) increased cost of monitoring. This paper introduces the R hydrorecipes  package, which provides methods to better understand hydraulic responses (Kennel and Parker, 2024 ). R is a programming language with statistical roots and a growing user community (R Core Team, 2024 ). The hydrorecipes  package was heavily influenced by the recipes  package, a popular framework for pre-processing and feature engineering (Kuhn and Wickham, 2022 ). The goal of the package is to provide tools that can be efficiently applied to moderately large data sets (millions of observations). For this study, the monitoring frequency for barometric and water pressure was selected to be every second to characterize a larger portion of the barometric response than previously explored. The hydrorecipes  package handles increasing computational demands by modifying the lagging method of Rasmussen and Crawford (1997)  to use distributed lag models that can efficiently scale to much larger data sets. Distributed lag models are common in econometrics and are ideally suited to smoothly varying responses (Almon, 1965; Gasparrini, 2011; Haugh and Box, 1977 ). The method is first tested on a synthetic data set and then applied to high frequency data collected every second from conventional monitoring wells at a mountainous, semi-arid, fractured sandstone site. With the higher frequency data, the ability to estimate subsurface properties is improved by increasing the ability to fit models to a larger range of time lags or frequencies and thus evaluate rapid responses that correspond to higher diffusivity systems.  2 Background and methods 2.1 Barometric efficiency Water level changes due to barometric pressure fluctuations are commonly described by a single value, the barometric (or loading) efficiency (Acworth et al., 2016; Clark, 1967; Gonthier, 2007; Hendry et al., 2018; Jacob, 1940; Rau et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2013 ). Single value methods work best on confined systems with minimal well-bore storage; however, in practice they are often applied to more complicated scenarios having lagged or frequency dependent responses. The barometric/loading efficiency can be estimated in multiple ways and is being used for the estimation of specific storage, therefore, representative and accurate values are necessary (McMillan et al., 2020; Rau et al., 2022; Turnadge et al., 2019 ). A goal of many of these methods is to isolate the water level changes that result solely from barometric pressure changes. This may involve the inclusion of secondary variables like Earth tides or trend removal using first differences. The barometric efficiency (BE) relates a portion of a barometric pressure change to a water level change and can be described with the following equation:(1) BE = - Δ W L  Δ P baro         where Δ W L    is the change in water level, and Δ P baro      is a change in barometric pressure. The related property called the loading efficiency (LE) is defined as the change in absolute pressure as a fraction of the barometric pressure change and is related to the barometric efficiency by the equation:(2) LE = 1 - B E     For confined aquifers the barometric efficiency can also be related to the specific storage (S s   ) modified from Jacob (1940)  equation 43:(3) S s  = ρ w  g θ E  C w   BE       where S s    is the specific storage, ρ w    is the density of water, θ E    is the effective porosity of the formation, and C w    is the compressibility of water. The density of water and the compressibility of water are often assumed, leaving the effective porosity and barometric efficiency to be estimated.  2.2 Barometric response functions While these definitions may work for the ideal confined well with minimal well-bore storage, many wells in complex geologic environments do not behave in an ideal manner. In these cases, a single value is limited, does not provide the context necessary for interpretation, and can be misleading. To interpret results a more complete analysis of the time or frequency dependent response is necessary. One method to examine the time dependent response was introduced by Munk and Cartwright (1966)  and was later applied to barometric pressure responses in groundwater (Butler et al., 2011; Furbish, 1991; Rasmussen and Crawford, 1997; Spane, 2002; Weeks, 1979 ). This method calculates an impulse response using regression deconvolution and has been implemented in the freely available BETCO, KGS programs, and the https://groundwater.app  which use equally spaced (regular) lags (Bohling et al., 2011; Toll and Rasmussen, 2007 ). The equation for regularly spaced lags from Rasmussen and Crawford (1997)  can be written as:(4) P wl - b   t   = ∑ i = 0  n  β i  P b  t - i       where P wl - b     is the component of water pressure due to barometric pressure, P b    is the barometric pressure, n   is the maximum lag of the model, i   is the time lag, and t   is the time and β i    are the regression coefficients to be determined. To minimize the effect of background trends and noise in the data, this formula is often written in terms of first differences:(5) Δ P wl - b   t   = ∑ i = 0  n  β i  Δ P b  t - i       where Δ P wl - b      is the change in water pressure due to barometric pressure, Δ P b     is the change in barometric pressure occurring over some time period, typically the monitoring frequency but it could also be an integer multiple of the monitoring frequency. While these methods work well with data sets with tens to hundreds of lag terms (β i   ) and thousands of observations, they can suffer from multicollinearity and become computationally inefficient for thousands of lags and millions of observations which is the case for high frequency data. Multicollinearity arises when regressors are highly correlated and lagged regressors will likely be correlated particularly when sampling frequency is high. In many instances the the effect of multicollinearity can be safely ignored, but it results in elevated standard errors for the coefficients. Two alternative methods for doing regression deconvolution that can scale to larger data sets and minimize multicollinearity are proposed. The first method uses the non-difference version of the regression deconvolution equation but determines β i    at irregularly spaced lags:(6) P wl - b   t   = ∑ k = 1  m  β i k     P b  t - i k         where m   is number of lagged terms in the model, and k   is the lag term number. The implementation of the method should have many lag terms where the response is expected to change most rapidly (typically early lag times) and fewer lag terms when the response is slowly varying (late lag times) and in practice logarithmically spaced lags are often suitable. In some ways this could be thought of as a manual form of lasso regression (L2 penalty) where terms that do not provide much additional information are manually zeroed out (excluded from the model) (Tibshirani, 1996 ). The number of regressors can often be decreased from many thousands to hundreds but the model may still suffer from multicollinearity and not be applicable to data sets with millions of observations. Distributed lag models provide additional efficiency for these larger data sets (Almon, 1965; Gasparrini, 2011; Haugh and Box, 1977 ):(7) P wl - b   = ∑ j = 1  m  β j  s j  x       where j   is the basis function index, s j    is the j  th     basis variable determined by convolving P b    and the j  th     basis function. The basis functions can be determined in a variety of ways but B-splines are popular, quick to generate, piecewise continuous, and the derivaties are commonly continuous and therefore suitable for modeling a variety of responses (Wang and Yan, 2024, 2021 ). The convolution can be done in the time or frequency domain and for regularly spaced data the frequency domain convolution will typically be more computationally efficient. To further elaborate on this method, suppose we want to model 30 days of data collected every second (n = 86400 * 30 = 2592000 measurements) with up to 4 days of lags (m = 86400 * 4 + 1 = 345601 lags). The standard approach would require a regressor term for each one of these lags and the generated matrix would end up being (n x m = 2592000 x 345601). The distributed lag method aims to reduce this and starts by selecting a basis function generator (e.g. B-splines) and the number or locations of knots (e.g. at 0, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 345,600 lag time and j = 8 for this set), which are the points where the piecewise polynomial functions meet and curvature can vary. By spacing knots closer together at early lag times, we attempt to better capture the response where it is changing most rapidly. An m   (number of lags) x j   (number of basis functions) matrix is then created by specifying the lag vector (0 to 345600), the knots, and other arguments to the B-spline generator (e.g. intercept, degree). Each column of this matrix is then convolved with the 30 days of barometric pressure data and results in an n   x j   (2592000 x 8) matrix of regressors. So instead of having a 2592000 x 345601 matrix, we end up with a 2592000 x 8 matrix. This technique decreases the number of regressors (or columns of the regression matrix) by assuming the barometric response function is smoothly variable in time so a set of curves can describe the response. Knots define regions of the response where polynomial parameters in the regression vary (i.e. changes in response curvature). For barometric response functions we suggest logarithmic spacing for the lags and knots in the irregular spaced and distributed lag models respectively. Distributed lag models further decrease the required number of regressors and are less influenced by multicollinearity.  2.3 Building and fitting the regression deconvolution model In the section above we describe how the regression terms are created for the different lagging methods. While barometric pressure responses are commonly found in water pressure or water level data sets, they are not the only stressor of importance. Therefore, the regression model needs to include multiple stresses and terms in addition to the barometric response. To do this, a matrix of regressors is generated which is based on the data sets that contribute to water pressure responses. For example, this may include Earth tides, pumping, precipitation, ocean levels, or other signals. In some cases the appropriate auxiliary data is absent and a regression spline can be helpful to capture background trends not related to barometric pressure or the desired signals to analyze. For example if we have a water pressure dataset that contains a barometric response and a background trend the regression equation in matrix form could be written as:(8) P 1  wl     P 2  wl      ⋮    P n  wl          n × 1   = s 1  1   s 1  2   ⋯  s 1  j   t 1  1   t 1  2   ⋯  t 1  k    s 2  1    s 2  2   ⋯  s 2  j   t 2  1   t 2  2   ⋯  t 2  k    ⋮   ⋮  ⋮  ⋮  ⋮  ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   s n  1    s n  2   ⋯  s n  j   t n  1   t n  2   ⋯  t n  k        n × m   β s  1     β s  2      ⋮    β s  j      β t  1      β t  2      ⋮    β t  k          m × 1       where P 1 : n  wl     are the water pressure observations, s 1 : n  1 : j     are the distributed lag terms for barometric pressure, t 1 : n  1 : k     are the regression spline terms for the background trend, and β s  1 : j      and β t  1 : k      are the coefficients to be determined by the regression for the barometric pressure and background trend respectively. Additional regressors, such as Earth tides can be added to the model in similar manner and allow all coefficients to be solved simultaneously. In this format, the equation can be solved in a number of ways, with least squares regression being one of the most common. However, as in the case with the traditional regularly spaced lagged models of Rasmussen and Mote (2007) , it is also possible to use generalized linear models with different regularization constraints that can reduce the problems of overfitting. Once the regression equation is solved and the coefficients determined, these coefficients can be multiplied by the regressor columns to determine the contribution for each regressor group (i.e. barometric pressure and background trend components) or used for prediction. Similar to regression with regularly spaced lags, the standard error of the coefficients and coefficient confidence intervals can be determined and used to evaluate the precision of each individual coefficient in the model and whether each coefficient is statistically significant.  2.4 Synthetic responses Determining the barometric response from field data is error prone due to the presence of confounding signals, non-linearities, violation of model assumptions, noise, and error in collected data sets. Many studies have estimated barometric responses using field data where the true solution is unknown; however, method comparison using synthetic data with a known solution can provide increased clarity. Synthetic water pressures were generated by convolving loading response kernels (i.e. the response as a function of time or frequency) with field measured barometric pressure data (Fig. 2  ). Four scenarios were tested: (1) Confined response; (2) Vadose response; (3) Well-bore storage response; and (4) a combined vadose and well-bore storage model. The confined response kernel is a single loading value equal to 0.38 and leads to a water level that is a scaling of the barometric pressure. The vadose kernel used in the vadose response was calculated using the 1-D air flow model of Weeks (1979)  considering a unit change in barometric pressure calculated for multiple times:(9) Δ P wl   t   = 1 - 4 π  ∑ m = 1 , 3 , 5 , ⋯  ∞  - 1    m - 1   2   1 m  e x p - m  2  π  2  D air   t  4 L  2            where Δ P wl   t      is change in water pressure at time (t), L is the thickness of the vadose zone, Dair  is the pneumatic diffusivity of the vadose zone. The infinite sum is truncated when the absolute value of an additional term is less than 1 × 10  - 16      of the starting value. The response function begins at zero and increases to the loading efficiency set to unity and having the following vadose zone parameters: a pneumatic diffusivity of 0.1 m2 /s and vadose zone thickness equal to 40 m. The late time values do not represent formation compressibility but the unattenuated air pressure transmission through the vadose zone. The well-bore storage kernel was calculated by numerically inverting the Laplace solution of Cooper et al. (1967) :(10) Δ P wl   t   = r s  S K 0  r w  q    T q r s  q K 0  r s  q   + 2 α K 0  r s  q           where(11) q = pS  T       and(12) α = r s  2  S  r w  2       where rs  and rw  are the screen and well radii, S is the storativity, T is the transmissivity, K0  is the modified Bessel function of the second kind and order 0, and p is the Laplace transform variable. The following well and aquifer parameters are used in the Cooper et al. (1967)  model to generate the response kernel: radius of the well and screen equal to 0.10 m, aquifer storativity equal to 1 × 10  - 5      m/m, transmissivity equal to 5 × 10  - 4      m2 /s. The combined response kernel contains the vadose air flow and the well-bore storage models and is stylistically similar to response functions calculated for field data with both short (seconds to minutes) and long (hours to days) duration components. The synthetic water pressures and the associated response functions in the time and frequency domains are presented in Fig. 2 .  2.5 Field application Barometric pressure and well water pressures were collected from a fractured rock study site located near Simi, California with monitoring wells completed in the Upper Cretaceous Chatsworth formation consisting of a turbidite sequence of sandstones and interbedded siltstones and shales (Cilona et al., 2016; Colburn et al., 1981; Link et al., 1984 ). During the analysis period between 2016–08-18 and 2016–10-13, barometric loading, Earth tides, earthquakes, and a recession following precipitation were the dominant signals present in water levels. The monitoring wells were open to the atmosphere and instrumented with a RBRsoloD pressure transducer (non-vented) reporting a sub-millimeter precision (0.0002 decibar which is ∼ 0.0002 m freshwater) (https://rbr-global.com/products/compact-loggers/rbrsolo-d ). All pressures in decibar were converted to an equivalent pressure head using 1.02 m freshwater per decibar. Transducers were set to record pressure every second and typically placed ten meters below the well water level. Table 1   presents the well construction details for the monitoring wells in this paper. Barometric pressure was measured in RD-130 using a transducer located approximately five meters below top of casing (above the well water level) to avoid large fluctuations in temperature. This well also contained a pressure transducer in the water column and was used to evaluate the distributed lag model and calculate transmissivity and vadose zone pneumatic diffusivity. Responses from two well pairs (C-03, RD-45B and RD-77, RD-121) each separated by approximately one hundred meters are compared to examine spatial variability and similarity of the barometric response (Fig. 3  ).  2.6 Barometric pressure Barometric pressure is often assumed to be spatially constant at the field site scale. To assess this assumption, two weeks of barometric pressure data from four sensors located in three wells are compared by calculating the time domain response functions. Two transducers were placed in the air column of RD-130 at depths of ∼ 5 m bgs (shallow), and 35 m bgs (deep), and the other transducers were located in the air columns of wells RD-08 (∼5 m bgs) and RD-10 (∼5 m bgs) which are separated from RD-130 by 3000 m and 700 m respectively.  2.7 Data processing A 56 day period between 2016–08-18 and 2016–10-13 was chosen for analysis as precipitation events, sampling, and earthquakes responses (based on United States Geological (USGS) Earthquakes Hazards Program catalog (Survey, 2019 )) were expected to be minimal during that time period (Fig. 4  ). The selected period minimized the presence of water level perturbations but is long enough to separate the primary Earth tide components. For this study we focus on pressure changes, and the mean is removed from each data set to improve the visual comparison of values. No other data processing was performed before the application of the regression models.  2.8 Response calculation The following methods were applied to calculate the static loading efficiency for the synthetic data sets: (1) Ordinary least squares (lag free model of barometric and water pressure); (2) Clark (1967)  method using differences calculated between observations spaced 1 h and 1 day apart; (3) and the Acworth et al. (2016)  method with zero Earth tide component (amplitude ratio for 2 cycles per day). To demonstrate the computational efficiency and accuracy of the distributed lag method relative to regular and irregular spaced regression deconvolution models, we tested the three techniques on a 2.5 day noise free synthetic data set that combined vadose and well-bore storage models (Fig. 2 ). The distributed lag and static loading efficiency methods are applied to the field data from RD-130 (Fig. 4 ). Prior to the static loading efficiency calculations, the barometric and water pressures were linearly detrended. The Acworth et al. (2016)  method included the Earth tide component determined using the earthtide  package which is an R port of Eterna 3.4 (Kennel and Parker, 2019; Wenzel, 1998 ). For the time domain distributed lag model, Earth tides were included as wave groups including satellite tidal constituents and not single frequencies (harmonic least squares) (Foreman and Henry, 1989 ). For the frequency domain response function the complete Hartmann and Wenzel (1995)  catalog was used to generate the volumetric strain due to Earth tides (Fig. 4 ). All examples are presented in terms of loading responses, i.e., absolute pressure heads. The response function methods are also calculated with the following levels of subsetting to explore how downsampling can affect the results: 60, 900, 3600, 7200 s. Following the application to RD-130 we apply the distributed lag model to two unconfined wells (RD-77, RD-121) and two semi-confined wells (C-03, RD-45B) (Fig. 3 ). Four regressor groups were simultaneously fit to the data in the distributed lag model: global intercept, barometric/loading response, Earth tide response, and the background trend. The global intercept accounts for the different mean values between the water level and barometric measurements. The barometric/loading response is calculated using the distributed lag model presented above. Earth tides (volumetric strain) are calculated in the regression model using harmonic analysis of wave groups simulated with the R earthtide  package (Kennel and Parker, 2019 ) and compared to theoretical equilibrium amplitude ratios (Hartmann and Wenzel, 1995 ). The close coupling of the hydrorecipes  and earthtide  packages simplifies the method to obtain amplitude and phase information from water level data sets at multiple frequencies. This is an extension of the Rasmussen and Mote (2007)  method to use wave groups instead of specified frequencies which allows for the inclusion constituents with nearby frequencies (e.g. K 1   , P 1    and K 2   , S 2   ) in the regression as is commonly done in oceanography (Foreman et al., 2009; Tamura et al., 2007; Wenzel, 1998 ). The number of wave groups is typically chosen based on the equipment precision and the time span of the input data sets that is directly related to resolving different frequency components (Foreman et al., 2009; Tamura et al., 2007 ). The trend is calculated using natural cubic splines with 27 degrees of freedom. Barometric pressure, water pressure, and synthetic Earth tides are presented in Fig. 4 .  2.9 Parameter estimation Parameters were estimated by fitting a combined vadose zone (Weeks, 1979 ) and well-bore storage model (Cooper et al., 1967 ) to the distributed lag response in RD-130. The model was scaled using the loading efficiency and an offset term to account for attenuation in the vadose zone. The storativity of the aquifer was fixed at 5.0 × 10  - 6      m/m and the model fit the following: the vadose zone thickness, the air diffusivity of the vadose zone, the transmissivity of the aquifer, the loading efficiency, and the attenuation term. The parameters were fit using non-linear least squares with the Gauss-Newton algorithm (Hastie, 2017 ). The first thirty seconds of the response were excluded in the model fit as it is not likely representative of the formation response (low signal to noise).   3 Results 3.1 Static response for synthetic data Table 2   and Fig. 2  compare the results of the static methods applied to the synthetic data representing confined, unconfined and well-bore storage scenarios. For the confined example with no well-bore storage, all methods successfully reproduce the loading efficiency value; however, for well-aquifer combinations with lagged or frequency dependent responses as presented in Fig. 2 , the estimated barometric or loading efficiency requires additional context to interpret. The response time of a system is often not known a priori, and a single value provides minimal context about the time dependent nature of a response. It is important to note that these are based on noise free data with no external signals and highlights a key deficiency of single valued methods when applied outside their intended use. This is particularly evident in methods that rely on calculating differences between measurements such as Clark’s method or have a frequency dependence such as the Acworth method which is typically focused on 1 or 2 (diurnal and semi-diurnal) cycles per day. The performance of a method is linked to the underground and monitoring setup and we have applied these methods outside of their intended use, but unfortunately this is commonly done in practice, and a single value provides limited information to assess the applicability of the method.  3.2 Time domain methods on synthetic data set Using the combined well-bore storage and vadose zone synthetic response, regular, irregular and distributed lag models were compared. The computational requirements and model fit to the known solution are presented in Table 3  . All methods used the base R lm  function to solve the multiple linear regression problem in R (R Core Team, 2024 ), however, alternative methods can be used to solve the system of equations. The regular lag model was calculated by decimating the full 1 s data set into 15 s, 10 min, and 1 h subsets. The regular lag model quickly reached computational limits both in execution time and memory even when applied to a short time period (∼1.5 days). One day is lost from the original 2.5 days because the maximum time lag used was one day. Calculating the response function for the full 1 s data set either requires changing the method, the solver, or having a powerful computer and patience. For the irregular lag model, the full 1 s data set could be used, and the number of logarithmically spaced lags was varied between 20 and 400 terms. The one hundred term model visually matches the synthetic response. For data sets of (millions of observations) the method may be hardware limited due to the large number of terms and observations. The distributed lag model with the full 1 s data set used 15 to 25 logarithmically spaced knots. This method outperformed the regular and irregular lag methods in computation time, memory consumption and accuracy. If the input (barometric pressure) is measured at a higher rate than the output (water pressure) it is possible to generate the lagged regressors using the higher frequency inputs at each output time. This approach can also be accomplished by subsetting the output data set during the lagging process to further reduce the size of the regression model while still resolving the early time response. Generally, we suggest collecting the inputs and outputs at the same frequency, however, collecting the inputs (precipitation, surface water levels, pumping rates, barometric pressure, etc.) at a higher frequency than water pressure can be an efficient use of time and computational resources.   4 Field application 4.1 Spatially variable barometric pressure Understanding the barometric pressure input is necessary for the interpretation of water level responses. The distributed lag response between barometric pressure measurements at different locations is presented in Fig. 5  . The results suggest that barometric pressure should be monitored as close to the monitoring well as possible if high frequency monitoring is being used. At this site, the precision of the transducer and the spatially variable barometric pressure affects the early time (up to a few minutes) response, which may manifest as an artificial time lag or a decrease in gain or phase shift for frequency responses (Figure: 5). For the two transducers deployed in the same air column of RD-130 the cumulative response is greater than 90 % of the impulse after ten seconds. However, for the locations 700 m (RD-10) and 3000 m (RD-08) away from RD-130, the spatial variability of barometric pressure manifests as a delayed response in the time domain, and a decrease in coherence in the frequency domain at around 100 cycles per day. These differences may be due to both the deployment method in the borehole, differing borehole completions, transducer manufacturing variability (clock drift, sensor sensitivity), the spatial variability of barometric pressure and potentially other factors. At this field site the barometric pressure is temporally variable due to seasonal winds and surface heating that may differentially affect the monitoring locations on site.  4.2 Barometric responses (RD-130) In contrast to the noise free synthetic data sets, field data sets are inherently noisy. To mitigate noise from external signals the analysis time period was selected so that pumping, precipitation and earthquakes effects were minimal. The predominant signals in the water pressure data result from barometric pressure changes (distributed lag), Earth tides (harmonic wave groups) and declining water levels following antecedent precipitation (natural cubic spline). All these signals were included in the loading response function regression model. Loading response functions due to barometric pressure are presented in Fig. 6  . There are three regions defined by the responses: low signal to noise; well-bore storage; and vadose air flow (Fig. 6 ). The duration of these regions are dependent on the monitoring well design, monitoring equipment, and subsurface properties. For this data set the first 10 s of lag time of the response is characterized by low signal to noise and is due to a variety of factors, including, the transducer precision, temporal drift of transducers, borehole air flow, time required for aquifer deformation, and potentially non-linearity of the response due to changing borehole and formation conditions. The monitoring frequency has a direct impact on the resulting response functions and for this well a monitoring frequency of 60 s is too coarse to estimate the well-bore storage response that is related to the formation transmissivity and well geometry (Fig. 6 ). In addition, the vadose response, used to estimate the pneumatic diffusivity of the vadose zone, is not clearly resolved with a monitoring frequency greater than 900 s. The static loading efficiency values presented in Fig. 6  are 0.47 (Clark 1 h), 0.61 (Acworth 2 cpd), 0.85 (Clark 1 day) and 0.83 (least squares). We present this not to advocate one method over another or to suggest the values are in error, but to highlight the importance of context when interpreting a single valued response. The appropriate context to understand these differences is available via the response functions. Four visual checks were made to evaluate the quality of the barometric/loading response functions using the distributed lag method (Fig. 6 ). First, it is assumed that the barometric/loading response function should be smoothly varying and jagged or large oscillations in the response suggest the presence of unaccounted for noise or trends in the data, potential error in the analysis, or a more complex barometric/loading response than commonly predicted. Second, the frequency response function method and the distributed lag methods should give similar results. Third, Earth tide amplitude ratios determined using harmonic analysis should be similar to theoretical amplitude ratios. Finally, residuals should have a random pattern centered on zero and should not be much larger than transducer precision. A closer examination of items 3 and 4 is presented below.  4.3 Signal decomposition Fig. 7   presents the input data sets and the signal decomposition obtained from the distributed lag model (barometric pressure component, Earth tide component, and spline component). Absolute residuals from the model fit are generally near the transducer resolution of ∼ 0.02 cm water. Remaining structure (time periods of large residuals or biased positive/negative) in the residuals is likely the result of seismicity, temporal offsets between transducers (clock drift), air flow between vadose zone and borehole, and other stresses or physical changes not accounted for in the model. Earth tides are measurable but have amplitudes less than 0.05 cm freshwater and have ratios consistent with the theoretical ratios from the Hartmann and Wenzel (1995)  catalog (Fig. 7 ). Even though these amplitudes are near the instrument precision the relative amplitudes of tidal constituents match theory. This suggests that the majority of the barometric pressure component was effectively removed (i.e. the removal of the barometric pressure component allowed the Earth tide component to be quantified). If existing barometric signal was present the relative magnitudes of the Earth tide components would likely differ from theory particularly at the S2  and K1  frequencies. The diurnal (nominally one cycle per day) differences from the theoretical tides may result from local variability of tidal signals, ocean loading, the presence of additional diurnal forcings not accounted for in the model such as evapotranspiration, or the incomplete removal of the barometric signal due to non-linearities of the response.  4.4 Spatially variable barometric responses Barometric responses from an unconfined well pair (RD-77 and RD-121) and a semi-confined well pair (RD-45B and C-03) are compared to examine spatial variability (Figs. 8 and 9   ). At this site it is expected that the timing of the lagged response is related to investigation scale: early time corresponds to local properties; and late time corresponds to larger scale properties (>100 m). The responses for the well pairs support this expectation as each well in the well pair has a unique early response, however, at late time they collapse to the same values suggesting the same controlling features or mechanisms. Conceptually this is consistent with the early time response being related to well-bore storage, a response dependent on the local formation transmissivity (or well skin) and borehole geometry. At this site, the late time response will be governed by different components of the subsurface for the unconfined and semi-confined wells. Specifically, the unconfined wells are more sensitive to vadose zone properties (water saturation, pneumatic diffusivity) and the semi-confined wells will be more sensitive to confining layer properties (vertical diffusivity). The unconfined and semi-confined responses can be interpreted to better understand the continuity of subsurface properties (Fig. 8 ). The water level elevation for the unconfined wells (RD-77 and RD-121) is roughly the same, however, the vadose zone is 13 m thicker at RD-121 than RD-77. Assuming vertical air flow and the same pneumatic diffusivity, the thicker vadose zone would lead to a delayed response at RD-121 relative to RD-77. The two responses converge after ∼12 h (0.5 cycles per day) and are attenuated by a similar magnitude (Fig. 8 ). The value of the response at 1.5 days for both wells is 0.68 suggesting a similar mechanism is governing the value. We expect that this late time value is primarily due to capillary fringe attenuation highlighted by Evans et al. (1991) , which could be considered similar between the monitoring wells. The semi-confined response is indistinguishable after time lags of 1 h (∼7 cycles per day). This suggests that the semi-confining layer has continuity and similar properties in the vicinity of the monitoring wells. Cumulative responses for each well are based on independent water level data and the close similarity at late time provides additional confidence in the results. Fig. 9  displays the responses from the five water pressure data sets. After barometric pressure, Earth tide and background trend components are removed from the water pressure data, small seismic events are clearly visible in the residuals from the model fit (RD-45B in particular). The general lack of structure in the residuals, which are near instrument precision, further supports the quality of the regression deconvolution method with distributed lags and harmonic Earth tide constituents.  4.5 Parameter estimation Following the determination of a response function, an interpretive model can be fit to estimate subsurface properties. The combined Weeks (1979)  and Cooper et al. (1967)  model was applied to the time domain response function for RD-130. The model fit for RD-130 is presented in Fig. 10  . The first 30 s of response were excluded as it is characterized by a low signal to noise ratio. While the fit is far from perfect using this model applied to a fractured, folded and faulted system, the result suggests that given high frequency data it is possible to extend the range of transmissivity estimates from barometric/loading responses to greater than ∼ 1 × 10  - 4     m2 /s as was noted as a practical limitation in Spane (2002) . Without the high frequency barometric data set it would not have been possible to estimate the transmissivity from the water level response as the system responds too rapidly relative to the observation frequency. Unfortunately, there is no independent transmissivity measurement for RD-130 so the validity of this estimate remains uncertain. The result of 5 × 10  - 4      m2 /s lies in the upper range of transmissivities presented in Allègre et al. (2016)  for the site. The value of air diffusivity of 0.2 m2 /s is in the range presented by Spane (2002) . The relatively simple model is unable to perfectly represent the empirically derived response and demonstrates the need for further work to characterize the complexity imparted by these fractured and faulted systems. This complexity may be the result of multiple pathways of pressure migration through the vadose zone (fractures vs. faults vs. matrix) and spatial variability of hydraulic conductivity and storativity.  4.6 Summary and conclusions This paper presents an improved method of determining the water level response following a series of barometric pressure changes in the presence of Earth tides and background trends at high frequency (i.e. 1 s data) now technologically practical. The distributed lag method scales to data sets with millions of observations and long maximum lag times (multiple days). Given the appropriate monitoring strategy, water and barometric pressures coherence values of ∼ 0.8 at one thousand cycles per day were obtained, an extension of two orders of magnitude from currently presented examples. This effectively allows for the quantitation of formation responses that occur rapidly and has a direct influence on the increasing range of hydraulic diffusivities and therefore, higher transmissivities can be estimated. Multiple components of the hydrogeologic system are characterized from a single barometric/loading response function as the barometric pressure changes result in stress changes that travel through different portions of the subsurface and at different rates. Site specific conditions determine response times and at this site the early time response is governed by local well conditions and the late time is related to larger scale characteristics such as vadose zone conditions and confining layer properties. The single valued barometric efficiency was shown to be ill-suited to evaluating these types of lagged responses. The typical frequency for ambient monitoring of water levels in hydrogeologic and geotechnical investigations is a few minutes to hours, and the choice is based on historical practice, instrument specifications, signal to noise ratio, power consumption, data storage and processing capabilities. In practice, the monitoring frequency is rarely selected based on the formation and well properties. Hendry et al. (2018)  suggest that intervals less than thirty minutes may be useful and shorter measurement intervals are better. Fortunately, the ability to record water pressure changes at high frequency and precision is possible with little additional effort. Combined with increasing computational capabilities and software advancements, data sets with millions of observations can be analyzed on a mid-range laptop. This paper focused on barometric responses; however, the distributed lag method is applicable to other signals such as variable rate pumping, surface water levels, and precipitation. All methods mentioned in this paper have been implemented in the actively developed open source R  software package hydrorecipes  creating a consistent framework for the analysis of groundwater level/pressure responses to barometric pressure (and other) signals.
1 Introduction Urbanization attracts people to live in urban areas, leading to the expansion of impervious surfaces such as pavements and roofs. These impervious surfaces prevent rainfall from infiltrating into the soil, resulting in increased stormwater runoff volumes and significant environmental impacts including the degradation of natural ecosystems and higher pollution loads conveyed to receiving water bodies (Weiss et al., 2020 ). Evaluating the impacts of urbanization on stormwater runoff quantity and quality is complex due to the proliferation of impervious surfaces and the diversification of land use types (Hester & Bauman, 2013 ). To address these challenges, multiple hydrological and hydraulic models have been developed. These models require an accurate determination of runoff volume and its origin, which is also essential for selecting appropriate stormwater control measures (SCMs) and optimizing their design and placement in urban catchments (Epps and Hathaway, 2019 ). The primary lumped metric to measure imperviousness in urban catchments is the total impervious area (TIA), presented as a fraction or percentage based on the ratio of total impervious surfaces over the catchment area (Ariano & Oswald, 2022 ). TIA can be estimated via field surveys or map measurements. Field surveys are time- and labor-intensive, especially for large watersheds. TIA estimation using map measurements can be performed using remote sensing (Prisloe et al., 2000; Flanagan & Civco, 2001 ), but is sensitive to the imagery resolution. Generally, urban imagery data available in low resolution (e.g., National Land Cover Database or NLCD that is based on Landsat satellite with 30 m resolution) are classified based on broad land cover (LC) categories (e.g., water, developed, barren, forest, shrubland, herbaceous, planted/cultivated and wetlands in NLCD); as resolution increases, the classifications are inclined toward more detailed LC where impervious and pervious surface types are distinct (e.g., roofs, roads, parks, trees). Using TIA in rainfall-runoff modelling causes runoff overestimation since not all the generated runoff from TIA flows into storm sewer systems (Alley & Veenhuis, 1983; Boyd et al., 1993; Booth & Jackson, 1997 ). This overestimation results in an inaccurate estimation of non-point source pollution loads and overdesigned SCMs (Hatt et al., 2004; Walsh et al., 2005 ). Hence, other imperviousness parameters, including the directly connected impervious area (DCIA) and the effective impervious area (EIA), have been developed to identify the impervious surfaces that contribute to runoff. DCIA is the portion of TIA that is directly connected to the storm sewer system via impervious pathways (Boyd et al., 1993; Lee and Heaney, 2003; Shuster et al., 2005; Roy & Shuster, 2009 ). EIA represents the portion of TIA that is hydraulically connected to the drainage system (Boyd et al., 1993; 1994; Ebrahimian et al., 2016a; b ). DCIA is defined based on the connectedness of impervious areas to the drainage system through impervious pathways with no considerations of water losses along the flow path (Lee and Heaney, 2003; Han and Burian, 2009; Ebrahimian et al., 2016b ). In contrast, EIA incorporates the assessment of losses along the flow paths of runoff over the impervious surfaces. These losses can be due to infiltration through cracks on pavements, depression storage on impervious surfaces, and vegetative interception. There are also other factors such as unconnected rooftops to storm sewers (disconnected downspouts) and maintenance issues such as blockage of gutters and clogging in inlets which cause DCIA to be different than EIA. Hence, EIA is often more accurate than DCIA in urban hydrologic modeling and predicting runoff volume from urban catchments (Ebrahimian et al., 2016b ). While EIA and DCIA are different indicators of urban imperviousness, they have been used interchangeably in urban hydrology literature, leading to confusions. EIA is a better predictor than TIA for pollution loads from stormwater runoff as it is the contributing area to runoff during small storm events that are primary sources of non-point source pollution (Lee and Heaney, 2003; Epps and Hathaway, 2021 ). There are also studies indicating the suitability of EIA for predictive models in receiving water bodies ecosystem studies (Walsh et al., 2005; Wenger et al., 2008; Baruch et al., 2018 ). EIA fraction (fEIA ), defined as EIA divided by total watershed area, can be determined by rainfall-runoff data analysis, not by map measurements (Boyd et al., 1993; 1994; Ebrahimian et al., 2016a; b ). The fEIA  determination method (Ebrahimian et al., 2016a ) is applicable only in gauged watersheds (where observed rainfall and runoff data are available) but there have been attempts for estimating fEIA  in ungauged urban watersheds. Ebrahimian et al. (2018)  presented a semi-empirical method for fEIA  estimation in ungauged watersheds based on the asymptotic curve number (Hawkins, 1993 ) using LC (fTIA ) and soil characteristics (soil saturated hydraulic conductivity or hydrologic soil group).While this fEIA  estimation method has been found suitable in other studies (e.g., in the Yamuna River watershed by Balha et al., 2023 ), caution should be taken when the derived empirical relationships are applied to areas other than those used for the development of the method (e.g., check fEIA  values against fDCIA ). Additionally, this method determines EIA fraction only, not the spatial distribution of EIA in the watershed. Epps and Hathaway (2018)  defined an impervious runoff connectivity parameter to assess the connectivity of each impervious surface point based on runoff attenuation while traversing pervious surfaces and used it as a proxy for fEIA . However, application of this method is still limited to gauged watersheds and demands high-resolution spatial data. Sytsma et al. (2020)  developed a conceptual model for the connectivity of impervious surfaces, applied it to an idealized catchment under various geometric configurations, rainfall, soil moisture, and soil texture scenarios, and used the results to train a predictive regression tree that enables estimation of hydrologically connected impervious areas in an urban catchment. Lack of soil-related and rooftop connectivity data are some of the challenges of this method. Overall, the existing EIA methods lack the capability of determining the spatial distribution of EIA in ungauged urban watersheds. An accurate DCIA distribution can be used to partially address this issue, indicating the need for further research to improve DCIA distribution. This includes assessing the impacts of spatial data resolution and availability, which is the central focus of this paper. DCIA can be determined by field investigations (e.g., Sahoo & Sreeja, 2016 ), empirical methods (e.g., Alley & Veenhuis, 1983; Sutherland, 1995 ), or geospatial analyses (Han & Burian, 2009 ). Determining the spatial distribution of DCIA (i.e., DCIA delineation) through field surveys is inherently time- and labor-intensive, and not practical for large drainage areas (Alley & Veenhuis, 1983; Han & Burian, 2009; Roy & Shuster, 2009 ). Empirical equations relating DCIA to TIA lack generalizability (may provide inaccurate results in watersheds beyond those that were used for the development of the empirical equation) and exhibit sensitivity to the scale of study (e.g., parcel- vs. watershed-scale) (Roy & Shuster, 2009; Sahoo & Sreeja, 2016 ; Sohn et al., 2017 ; Ariano & Oswald, 2022 ). Additionally, these equations cannot be used for DCIA delineation. Conversely, DCIA delineation can be determined through the geospatial analysis method proposed by Han and Burian (2009) . This method is applicable to any ungauged watershed but requires multiple spatial data inputs (including land cover, slope, and the location of runoff collection system) and cannot determine the connectivity of rooftops (that could comprise a substantial portion of urban watersheds). Evaluating rooftop connectivity is complicated and demands substantial efforts (e.g., field investigations, evaluating building ages and corresponding codes, local ordinances, landowner retrofit). Despite the extensive literature confirming this issue (Han and Burian, 2009; Sahoo and Sreeja, 2016; Sytsma et al., 2020 ), a generally applicable methodology is still lacking. Achieving accurate estimates of DCIA necessitates a comprehensive consideration of often overlooked data availability and resolution challenges. Addressing these issues is pivotal for enhancing DCIA estimation methodologies. The importance of high-resolution LC, digital elevation model (DEM), and drainage system data for accurate DCIA determination is evident, yet preparing such data presents practical constraints and feasibility issues. This research explores the challenges posed by data availability and resolution in spatial determination of DCIA and emphasizes the importance of addressing these issues for robust DCIA determination methodologies. The main objective of this research is to investigate the effects of data availability and resolution on the values and spatial distribution of TIA and DCIA in urban catchments. TIA and DCIA values and their spatial distributions are determined for nine urban catchments within the Capitol Region Watershed District, Minnesota, under different scenarios, including various spatial data types, sources, and resolutions. The results are also compared to the EIA values from rainfall-runoff analyses. The research develops comprehensive insights into the spatial determination of DCIA in ungauged catchments and provides practical guidance to researchers and practitioners working in the areas of urban hydrology and stormwater management. The findings of this study have profound implications for the use of appropriate metrics of impervious cover in urban hydrologic models and the optimal placement and design of SCMs in urban catchments.  2 Study area Nine urban catchments, ranging from 15.9 ha to 2034 ha, located in the Capitol Region Watershed District (CRWD) in the upper Mississippi River basin, Minnesota, USA, were selected as the study areas (Fig. 1   and Table 1  ). The selection of catchments was because of the availability of local monitoring programs for high temporal-resolution rainfall-runoff data and fine spatialresolution geospatial data (land cover and DEM) as well as the variety of size and land use that enable a comprehensive examination of TIA, DCIA, EIA, and their relationships. The study catchments are all located in a highly urbanized part of the watershed that includes primarily the city of Saint Paul and parts of surrounding cities (Table 1 ). All the catchments contain residential, commercial, and industrial land uses, while single-family residential is dominant. Notably, the Sarita catchment includes allocated zones for institutional/ recreational activities, like the Minnesota State Fairgrounds, and agricultural uses. The Saint Anthony Park (SAP) catchment is home to the Saint Paul Campus of the University of Minnesota and Sarita is a sub-catchment of this catchment.  3 Methodology In the following sections, methods for determining imperviousness metrics (TIA, DCIA, and EIA) using a combination of various data types and resolutions in eight scenarios are explained. All the spatial data analyses were conducted using the existing toolsets in ArcGIS Pro (version 3.2, Esri Inc.). 3.1 Data types and resolution Description and sources of the utilized data in this research are presented in Table 2  . Land cover data with two different resolutions and from two different sources (nationally and locally available) were employed to assess the impacts of data resolution and availability on the spatial characteristics of impervious areas contributing to runoff. Since high-resolution LC data may not be available for urban catchments, the suitability of nationally and readily available, but low-resolution (30-m) LC data from NLCD was investigated. Two NLCD products with 30-m resolution were downloaded: “Land Cover” and “Urban Imperviousness” (NLCD, 2019 ). The “Land Cover” data is a raster file with eight classes: 1) water, 2) developed, 3) barren, 4) forest, 5) shrubland, 6) herbaceous, 7) planted/cultivated, and 8) wetlands. “Urban Imperviousness” is a raster file with hundred classes ranging from 0 to 100 %. The 60-cm resolution locally available LC data, prepared by the Department of Forest Resources at the University of Minnesota (UMN) using high-resolution multi-spectral satellite imagery and LiDAR data, has seven classes: 1) tree canopy, 2) grass and shrubs, 3) bare soil, 4) water, 5) rooftop, 6) street, and 7) other impervious areas. The DEM data with 30-m and 1-m resolution were obtained from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) website and Minnesota’s Ramsey County data hub, respectively. In this study, the high-resolution LC data was reclassified to six cover types: 1) tree canopy, 2) grass and shrubs, 3) bare soil, 4) water, 5) rooftop, and 6) pavement (that combines street and other impervious areas from original classification into this category) and later, resampled to 1-m resolution to be compatible with the 1-m DEM. The catch basin data (inlet points) for each catchment were acquired from the respective cities. Road and alley data, generated by UMN as byproducts of the 60-cm resolution LC data, were also collected.
