In urban areas, roads and alleys may serve as a pathway for channeling stormwater runoff toward catch basin points. This fact was leveraged to develop an alternative runoff collection network in this research. The obtained data were utilized to create the runoff collection raster layer via “Polygon to Raster” and “Map Algebra, con” Tools.  3.2 TIA TIA is the total impervious area of a catchment and is determined by adding up all the impervious surfaces like parking lots, streets, driveways, sidewalks, and rooftops. The TIA fraction (fTIA ) is obtained by dividing TIA by the total drainage area of the catchment. The availability of LC datasets with high spatial resolution from state or regional organizations (developed based on aerial photography, satellite imagery, and GIS) facilitates TIA delineations. However, it is crucial to ensure that LC data accurately reflect impervious surfaces. This accuracy can be compromised by factors such as the shades of tree canopy over impervious surfaces (Cablk and Minor, 2003 ). During aerial photography or satellite imagery, tree canopies can cover the entire or a portion of impervious surfaces (Schmidt & Barron, 2020 ; Langenkamp & Rienow, 2023 ) and cause the LC data to be formed with less impervious surfaces, resulting in TIA underestimation. Since the high-resolution LC data in this study contained tree canopy, a land cover modification (unshading), based on Ebrahimian (2015) , was conducted as a preprocessing step before the determination of imperviousness metrics. This process requires the availability of the unshaded impervious elements (e.g., rooftops, roads, and sidewalks) in vector formats. The latter data was accessed from a local source (impervious LC, refer to Section 3.1  for details) and utilized in this study. In the absence of local or regional data, alternative national sources (e.g., Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing system or TIGER, Unites States Census Bureau) can be considered. The modification process involved separating various impervious elements, converting into raster files, and assigning unique values to each LC type that differed from those in the original LC raster file. These raster files were then overlaid onto the original LC and the resulting raster file from the overlay was updated by reclassifying pixels. All the pixels retaining values from the original LC remained unchanged but the new values assigned during the vector-to-raster conversion were adjusted to match the corresponding impervious surface types in the original LC. The modified LC data were used in fTIA  estimation, and the results were compared with those obtained from the original LC data. Estimating TIA form NLCD “Land Cover” data is not possible unless assumptions made for the percent imperviousness of developed areas (e.g., 80% for highly developed areas and 50% for medium developed areas). However, the “Urban Imperviousness” data from NLCD can be utilized to estimate the TIA in urban catchments using Equation (1)  (Sultana et al., 2020 ).(1) TIA = A P  × ∑ i = 1  n  IP  i  × N i   100      where IP  i    , N i    , and A P     represent the imperviousness percentage (pixel value), number of pixels with the same percentage, and pixel area (here, 30 m x 30 m), respectively.  3.3 DCIA Inspired by Han and Burian (2009) , DCIA distribution in urban catchments was determined by following runoff from impervious surfaces and determining whether it will end up in the runoff collection system (e.g., storm sewer inlets). The DCIA determination procedure (modified from Janke et al., 2011 ) was performed via a Python script under ArcGIS Pro environment (Jupyter Notebook) by the combination of Python libraries and ArcPy. The code uses four input raster layers, i.e., LC, DEM, flow direction, and runoff collection system, with the same pixel size (Table 2 ). These raster files were converted to NumPy arrays (Walt et al., 2011 ) to enable a cell-by-cell navigation. The code tracked the flow originating from impervious surfaces in the LC layer based on flow direction from each cell to its steepest downslope neighbor (D8 flow method) and checked whether the flow ultimately discharges into the inlet point in the runoff collection layer. If the flow ended in a pixel representing rooftops in the LC layer, an alternative pathway toward another neighborhood cell with the steepest slope would be chosen using the DEM layer and the slope between the center cell and neighborhood cells. If the flow ended in an inlet point, the original cell where the runoff originated would be considered as DCIA; otherwise, the original cell would not be DCIA (Fig. 2  ). A detailed explanation of the DCIA delineation procedure can be found in Supplementary Information . To calculate the fraction of DCIA (fDCIA ),  sum of all the identified DCIAs was divided by the catchment total area.  3.4 EIA EIA is the impervious area in a catchment that is hydraulically connected to the sewer system (i.e., the runoff generated from this area travels on impervious surfaces and reaches the sewer system with no volume loss). Unlike DCIA, EIA determination in a catchment is based on the analysis of rainfall events and corresponding runoff. The EIA fraction (fEIA ) is the ratio of EIA over the total area of the catchment. This fraction can be calculated for gauged catchments (where observed rainfall-runoff data is available) based on the theory discussed in Ebrahimian et al. (2016a)  indicating a linear relationship between runoff depth and rainfall depth in an urban catchment when runoff is only from impervious areas. Ebrahimian et al. (2016a; b)  propose using a successive weighted least square (WLS) method where the rainfall-runoff events are classified as either EIA events (generating runoff from impervious surfaces only) or combined events (generating runoff from both impervious and pervious surfaces) based on Equation (2) .(2) y j  = EIA  e v e n t   f  ε j  ⩽ δ c     Combined  e v e n t    if  ε j  > δ c              j = 1 ,  … ,  n         where y j     is the jth  event in the runoff depth vector, ε j     is random error for the jth  event, and δ c     is the EIA criterion as presented in Eq. (3) .(3) δ c  = m a x 2 S E , 1 m m        where SE is the standard error. After plotting runoff depth vs rainfall depth for all the observed events and fitting a straight line to data using WLS regression, the combined events will be removed and another WLS regression line will be fitted to the remaining data. The procedure of omitting the combined events will continue until all the remaining data are classified as EIA events. At this step, the slope of the WLS regression line fitted to the EIA events equals fEIA .  3.5 Scenarios DCIA delineation using high-resolution LC (60 cm) was implemented under eight scenarios, including the combination of two different LCs (original and unshaded LC), rooftop connectivity to the storm sewers (0% and 100% connected rooftops) and stormwater runoff collection system type (inlets and roads) (Fig. 3   and Table 3  ). High-resolution LC cannot provide information about the connectivity of rooftops to storm sewer systems, creating issues in estimating impervious surfaces contributing to runoff, especially in highly urban areas where rooftops comprise a substantial portion of the catchment areas. Hence, the rooftop connectivity issue requires additional considerations. Two extreme conditions were examined in this study to evaluate rooftop connectivity impact on DCIA estimation: 1) None of the rooftops are connected to the storm sewer system (scenarios 1,2,5, and 6) and 2) all rooftops are connected (scenarios 3, 4, 7, and 8). Given the 30-meter resolution of the LC data from NLCD, the study explored an alternative approach by considering entire roads and streets as recipients of stormwater runoff instead of catch basin inlet points. This approach involved substituting the catch basin point data with roads and street data in the developed script, enabling an evaluation of how this modification affects the delineation of DCIA in urban catchments. The obtained DCIA delineations were used to determine fDCIA  in each scenario. The fEIA  values for all the study catchments were taken from Ebrahimian et al. (2016b)  and compared with their corresponding fDCIA  and fTIA  values.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 TIA A breakdown of the percentages for each LC class using the original and modified LC data for all the catchments is shown in Fig. 4  . A similar chart using the original LC data is presented as Figure S1  in Supplementary Information . TIA estimation was carried out using the original and modified 60-cm LC (see an example in Fig. 5  ). The changes in each LC type as the result of LC modification (unshading) for all the study catchments are presented in Table S1  (Supplementary Information ). The fTIA  values using the modified LC were higher than those obtained with the original LC, with the average and median fTIA  increasing by 22.0% and 16.8%, respectively, and the range shifting from 0.33–0.49 to 0.37–0.61 (Fig. 6  ). The suitability of urban imperviousness data from NLCD for determining TIA fraction (fTIA ) was investigated by comparing fTIA  from the high-resolution (60 cm) LC (both the original and modified data) and the low resolution (30 m) urban imperviousness data (Fig. 7  ). The fTIA  values from the modified high-resolution LC were found to be close to those from the low-resolution urban imperviousness data for all the catchments except Sarita (0.367 and 0.446, respectively). This can be explained by the lack of street/pavement data located between the farms in the high-resolution LC data of Sarita. A statistical analysis of fTIA  values at watershed scale showed that fTIA  values from the readily available, low-resolution NLCD imperviousness data and the modified high-resolution LC data were not significantly different (mean and standard deviation of 0.53 and 0.07, respectively, using NLCD imperviousness, and 0.50 and 0.07, respectively, using the modified high-resolution LC). Therefore, it was concluded that the readily available NLCD urban imperviousness data can be used to determine comparable fTIA  values to those from modified high-resolution LC data, when the latter data is not available. Further studies are needed to evaluate the applicability of this conclusion to other urban catchments.  4.2 DCIA DCIA fraction and spatial distribution were determined for various scenarios in Table 3 . The fDCIA  in each scenario was compared with corresponding fTIA  and fEIA  values. The fEIA  values for all the study catchments were taken from Ebrahimian et al. (2016a) . 4.2.1 DCIA delineation using NLCD products The delineation of DCIA using LC data from NLCD (readily available, 30-m resolution) proved unfeasible due to the challenge of tracking flow between cells on the LC map in which impervious cells and types were not classified. This resolution and classification did not offer the necessary information to discern specific details about the LC type, specifically whether it was impervious. Furthermore, creating a raster file with the 30-m pixel size would cause the loss of some catch basin inlet points data. Using the entire roads/streets (instead of catch basins inlet points) as the alternative runoff collection system to address the loss of inlet points did not yield viable results.  4.2.2 DCIA delineation using high-resolution LC data For the nine study catchments, DCIA was delineated using the 60-cm LC data and 1-m DEM considering various scenarios to evaluate possible enhancement and their effects on the final results. Corresponding fEIA  values were used as a reference to assess fDCIA  results in each scenario. 4.2.2.1 DCIA delineation using original LC The distribution of DCIA for all the catchments using the original LC data and inlets as collection layer can be found in Fig. S2  (Supplementary Information ). fDCIA  values for all the scenarios where original LC was utilized for DCIA distribution (scenarios 1 to 4) are presented in Table 4  . Shades of tree canopies on the paved areas (e.g., streets and alleys) influence flow-tracking for determining DCIA. When running the DCIA script, tracking the runoff flow would automatically stop when reaching a pixel defined as tree canopy, and the original cell from which the flow was generated would be considered a non-connected impervious area, deteriorating the accuracy of DCIA delineation and underestimating the fDCIA  values.  4.2.2.2 DCIA delineation using modified LC As discussed in the previous section, shades of tree canopies on impervious surfaces cause underestimation of DCIA (Schmidt & Barron, 2020 ). To address this issue, LC data was modified (scenarios 5 to 8) through the unshading procedure explained in section 3.2 . Subsequently, executing the DCIA script using the modified LC increased the number of directly connected cells (DCIA), more accurately representing the actual condition of catchments. Fig. 8   illustrates the distribution of DCIA utilizing the modified LC approach, with inlets as collection layer. Table 4  provides the fDCIA  values for scenarios 5 to 8, where the modified LC was employed for DCIA determination. The efficacy of LC modification could be further improved if the LC dataset encompasses a wider range of impervious LC classes such as sidewalks.  4.2.2.3 DCIA delineation under assumptions of rooftop connectivity and runoff collection system To evaluate the effects of rooftop connectivity, DCIA fraction values for all the study catchments considering both non-connected and fully connected rooftops were plotted against corresponding EIA fraction values in Fig. 9  . The a and b plots in Fig. 9  present fDCIA  values from the original and modified LC data, respectively. The results of the modified LC (Fig. 9 -b) showed that fEIA  values were smaller than corresponding fDCIA  values with the assumption of all connected rooftops (scenario 7). Fig. 9 -b also showed that the fEIA  values were greater than corresponding fDCIA  values with the assumption of non-connected rooftops (scenario 5) (i.e., fEIA  falls between the fDCIA  for non-connected and connected rooftops) except for three catchments, AHUG, Como 3 and Sarita, where the fDCIA  values based on the non-connected scenario yielded higher values than fEIA . After closer inspection of these three catchments, it can be discerned that in two of them (Como3 and Sarita) the rooftops comprise less than 30% of TIA, meaning that rooftops did not have a dominant role in impervious areas evaluations compared to other impervious surfaces. This observation also indicated that some undetected sources of runoff volume loss in the flow path toward the sewer system may have been ignored during DCIA determination in these three catchments. These loss sources may include the existence of large cracks/potholes on pavements or natural/man-made stormwater control practices that disconnect impervious areas from the sewer system. In contrast with Fig. 9 -b, it is hard to find a constant pattern in Fig. 9 -a. In Fig. 9 -a, it was observed that the fDCIA  values were higher in connected rooftop scenario (scenario 3) compared to non-connected scenario (scenario 1), as expected. The presence of three catchments, EK, PC, and TBO, with fDCIA  values lower than fEIA  could be attributed to the shading effect of tree canopies. In these catchments more than 60% of TIA are impervious surfaces other than rooftops (roads, alleys, and other paved surfaces), causing a notable fDCIA  underestimation because of shaded impervious surfaces that cannot be counteracted by considering a fully connected rooftop scenario. In comparing fDCIA  results derived from original and modified LC raster files with fEIA  (Fig. 9  and Table 4 ), it was observed that fDCIA  estimation using modified LC data (scenarios 5 and 7) demonstrated reasonable deviations from fEIA  for most catchments while it is hard to understand and explain the relationship between fEIA  and fDCIA  using original LC data. Therefore, the use of modified LC raster data is recommended as the preferred input dataset for accurate DCIA estimation in ungauged catchments. Another input data that plays an essential role in DCIA delineation is catch basin inlet data whose accuracy can enhance the DCIA delineation results. Vector files including the location of inlet points in the study catchments were acquired from the cities where they were located in. However, discrepancies in the placement of inlet points were evident in the vector files, as some inlet points were identified within tree canopy or grass pixels, while upon verification via Google Street View, their actual locations were curbside. This discrepancy may be attributed to factors related to data gathering, imagery resolution, and vector file preparation. This issue was partially addressed by the LC modification through unshading the impervious areas. Another challenge regarding catch basin inlet data was acquiring data from relative authorities. This information is not always open to the public and available on local, regional, or state data platforms; plus, it is often unattainable from private landowners. In this study, catch basin data were acquired through direct communication with the stormwater division of each respective city. However, the catch basin data of the SAP and Sarita catchments (mostly including the University of Minnesota and the Minnesota State Fairground) were absent from the datasets of both the Cities of Saint Paul and Falcon Heights (refer to Table 1 ). The catch basin data for the University of Minnesota was obtained from UMN but the Minnesota State Fairground data was unattainable, leading to its exclusion from the DCIA delineation in Sarita Catchment. The challenges in obtaining catch basin inlet data, combined with the concerns about their accuracy, motivated us to proceed with the DCIA delineation process without explicit consideration of inlet points. Instead, the (readily available) roads and alleys data were considered as a proxy for the inlet points data and integrated into the DCIA script as the runoff collection data (scenarios 2,4,6 and 8). The DCIA delineation process was then performed using both original and modified LC data. The cells representing streets and alleys in the LC layer, from where runoff originated, were considered as part of the DCIA, unless their runoff was directed towards a grass/tree canopy pixel. The same criteria applied to the other impervious cells whose runoff found a path to a street or alley pixel. Fig. 9  presents a comparison between EIA and DCIA fraction values obtained based on catch basin inlets versus roads as runoff collection data and using the original (Fig. 9 -a) and modified LC (Fig. 9 -b) for all the study catchments. Examining Fig. 9 -a, it was evident that across all catchments, except PC and GCP, differences between scenarios under unconnected rooftops were close to those under connected rooftops. In the PC catchment, while the difference between scenarios 1 and 2 (inlet and roads as collection layers, respectively) under unconnected rooftops was 12%, this difference significantly rised to 69% under connected rooftops when comparing scenarios 3 and 4. The range of differences for catchment GCP was notably broader (72%). Given the variations in fDCIA  results using inlet and roads as runoff collection data (−0.77% to 72%), using roads network as the collection layer with unmodified LC is not advisable. The DCIA values based on roads data were found to be close to those based on catch basin inlet data in all the study catchments when using modified LC, Fig. 9 -b (the difference in DCIA values was not significant at 5 % level). The findings indicate that the DCIA delineation process can be adequately employed in catchments lacking catch basin inlet data by using road networks as a substitute for inlet data (Fig. 9 -b). Nonetheless, it is imperative to conduct a more in-depth analysis for a comprehensive understanding of the spatial distribution of DCIA under this assumption, especially when there is a substantial difference in fDCIA , as observed in GCP where it surpasses the fDCIA  values obtained using inlets as the runoff collection system (Fig. 9 -b). In this catchment, the flow direction in the majority of alleys did not lead toward inlet points. The utilization of roads as the collection system compelled these alleys to be identified as DCIAs, resulting in noticeably elevated fDCIA  values. In general, the derived fDCIA  values using roads and alleys as the runoff collection system, when utilizing modified LC, aligned with, and in some instances, surpassed those derived using inlet points. This augmentation stemmed from the identification of designated cells as inlets within the runoff collection data. With the transition to the new runoff collection data, the number of cells classified as inlet cells expanded from a limited number of specific points (inlets) to strips of roads and alleys. This discrepancy may be negligible depending on the project's scale and sensitivity. A Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to compare the fEIA  and fDCIA  values. The results (Table 5  ) revealed that using the modified LC data (scenarios 5 to 8) generally increased the correlation coefficients (the range shifting from 0.49–0.88 to 0.77–0.87). Among the scenarios using modified LC data, those assuming zero percent rooftop connectivity (scenarios 5 and 6) showed a higher correlation compared to those with fully connected rooftops (scenarios 7 and 8). Moreover, using roads as collection systems further enhanced the correlation (scenarios 6 and 8 compared with scenarios 5 and 7). Scenario 3, which is based on original LC, fully connected rooftops, and inlet points as runoff collection systems, presented the lowest correlation between fDCIA  and fEIA  (0.49). However, scenario 2, which also uses original LC but with zero percent rooftop connectivity and roads as runoff collection system, demonstrated the highest correlation (0.88) similar to that in scenario 6 (0.87), which uses modified LC under the same assumptions for rooftops and roads. This suggests an inclination toward the zero rooftop connectivity assumption and using roads as runoff collection systems when determining fDCIA  in ungauged urban catchments with inadequate or inaccurate information on rooftop connectivity and inlets.    4.3 EIA 4.3.1 fEIA  and fDCIA  comparison A comparison of fDCIA  using modified LC and corresponding fEIA  values revealed that when considering fully unconnected and connected rooftops, EIA was 1.34 and 0.65 of DCIA, respectively, on average for all the study catchments (Fig. 10  ). These results, when compared to those from the literature (0.75 in Melanen and Laukkanen, 1980 , 0.85 in Boyd et al., 1993 , and 0.77 in Ebrahimian et al., 2016a ), highlighted the significance of rooftop connectivity considerations. DCIA values in Boyd et al. (1993)  were obtained via map measurement and photographs for their study watersheds where the rooftops were mostly connected to the sewer system. Ebrahimian et al. (2016a)  calculated EIA fractions for the same watersheds as Boyd et al. (1993)  and compared them with the DCIA fraction values reported by Boyd et al. (1993) . Under the fully connected scenario of the current study, the ratio of EIA over DCIA (0.65), while in agreement, is smaller than those from previous studies which can be explained by the different EIA determination methods and existence of some unconnected rooftops in Boyd watersheds that reduces DCIA and increases the ratio of EIA/DCIA. Inaccuracies of impervious cover data (e.g., existence of tree canopy shading) are not discussed in Boyd et al. (1993)  but this could have been another reason for reduced DCIA and increased EIA/DCIA values. Through an interpolation between the coefficients in Fig. 10 -a and Fig. 10 -b, 49.63% rooftop connectivity is required to have fEIA =fDCIA . To further evaluate rooftop connectivity in the study catchments and its effects on the differences between EIA and DCIA, the fraction of connected rooftops which leads to DCIA=EIA was calculated in each study catchment using Equation 4. Calculations were performed using unshaded LC for both cases of inlets and roads as runoff collection system (results in Table 6  ).(4) f EIA   = f DCIA  0   + ( α × f rooftop   )      where  f D C I A  0      is DCIA fraction with zero percent rooftop connectivity, α    is the fraction of connected rooftops in a catchment, and f r o o f t o p      is the fraction of rooftops (ratio of all rooftops area divided by total area of the catchment). The results did not show a notable correlation between α    and the catchment size (total catchment area- At ) or land use. Sarita and Como3 have the lowest frooftop  values among the study catchments (0.107 and 0.111, respectively). Therefore, the negative α    values in these catchments are most likely an indication of zero rooftop connectivity and some other runoff losses from DCIA that caused fEIA  to be smaller that f DCIA  0     . The lower value of fEIA  than f DCIA  0      in AHUG (negative α )    is, however, attributed to the existence of SCMs and the reduced runoff volumes associated with them. Putting AHUG aside and considering a zero rooftop connectivity (α = 0   ) for Como 3 and Sarita, the average and median values of α    for the study catchments were 0.374 and 0.401, respectively, considering inlets, and 0.306 and 0.239, respectively, considering roads as runoff collection system. The α values considering inlets and roads are close in all the catchments except GCP (0.514 for inlets vs 0.086 for roads). After checking the roads and inlets data and comparing them with Google Street View, inlets were not found in some of the roads and almost any of the alleys in GCP, explaining the higher f DCIA  0      and lower α values in GCP. While the α values need to be further investigated in other urban catchments, the results of this study indicate an inclination toward the unconnected rooftops assumption for achieving comparable DCIA and EIA values. This has implications in urban hydrologic modeling, especially in ungauged catchments, as most models (e.g., SWMM) require directly or hydraulically connected impervious areas as an input parameter. In the absence of catchment-scale information about rooftop connectivity, f DCIA  0   + ( α × f rooftop   )     with an α    = 0 to 0.4 can be used as an estimate for the directly or hydraulically connected impervious areas in modeling and calculations. Comparing fEIA  and fDCIA  can also deliver additional insights about urban catchments. Similar or close values of fEIA  and fDCIA  in an urban catchment suggest minimal water loss on the runoff impervious pathway to the sewer system. This implies well-maintained pavements without substantial cracks and potholes, insignificant water retention on the impervious surface (through SCMs or vegetative interception), unclogged inlets and gutters, and adequate hydraulic capture efficiency of inlets (appropriate design and construction). The results indicated that in most cases fEIA  is greater than fDCIA  with unconnected rooftops and smaller than fDCIA  with fully connected rooftops. Conversely, a smaller fEIA  than fDCIA  under the zero percent rooftop connectivity assumption indicates runoff volume losses throughout the flow path toward the sewer system. These losses could result from the aforementioned items or the presence of SCMs that disconnect parts of the catchment from the segment of the sewer system connected to the catchment’s main outlet where the observed data is collected.  4.3.2 fEIA  and fTIA  comparison Empirical equations with the same format (power function) as Sutherland (1995)  were developed for these nine catchments to explore relationship between fEIA  and fTIA  estimated based on NLCD data and modified high-resolution LC (Eq. (5) and (6), respectively). However, these equations are based on the conditions in the nine study catchments in Minnesota and may not be applicable in other areas.(5) f  TIA    based  on  NLCD :  f  EIA   = 2.06  f  TIA     3.84       (6) f  TIA    based  on  modified  LC :  f  EIA   = 1.99  f  TIA     3.36          4.4 fDCIA  and fTIA  comparison The pairwise comparison of DCIA and TIA fractions was made for each catchment using original and modified LC, considering two conditions of rooftop connectivity (Fig. 11  ). Fig. 11  revealed how TIA overestimated the imperviousness of catchments for rainfal-runoff analysis even when all rooftops were considered connected to the sewer system during DCIA delineation (scenarios 3 and 5). Therefore, it is not advisable to estimate the runoff volume solely based on TIA if fine-resolution LC and DEM data are available. Comparing Fig. 11 -a and -b illustrated that the LC modification led to shifting values to the right and up on the plot, demonstrating a rise in the estimation of TIA and DCIA. Similar to Equations 5 and 6, empirical equations (Equations (7)–(10)) were developed for fDCIA  as a function of fTIA  using modified LC for TIA and DCIA delineations. The methods were applied to nine urban catchments, with a size range of 16–2035 ha and a variety of land uses, in Capitol Region Watershed District (Saint Paul, MN). Effects of LC modification through removing tree canopy shades over impervious surfaces (unshading) on TIA was investigated. A comprehensive approach for determining DCIA was utilized to assess the impacts of the spatial resolution and availability of input data (LC, DEM, and runoff collection system) in DCIA delineation. The DCIA delineation method employed a systematic flow tracking algorithm, accounting for various scenarios, including LC modification (unshading), rooftop connectivity to storm sewers, runoff collection system type, and resolution of LC data. The results were compared with the corresponding EIA fraction values from the previous studies by Ebrahimian et al. (2016a, b) . The choice of input data is critical for accurate DCIA delineations. High-resolution LC data, classified as 1) tree canopy, 2) grass and shrubs, 3) bare soil, 4) water, 5) rooftop, 6) road/alley, and 7) other impervious areas (e.g., parking lots), was found to be preferable over NLCD, especially when the LC modification was applied to remove shading by tree canopies. This “unshading” resulted in a TIA increase from 5.8% to 30% (22% on average) in the study catchments, demonstrating the importance of tree canopies as a major source of TIA inaccuracy in urban areas with high tree canopy coverage. The LC modification also led to more comparable DCIA values to EIA. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of catch basin inlet data availability, accessibility, and reliability for DCIA delineations. These data are often unavailable to the public and their verification or location adjustment demands high-resolution spatial data or site visits which are both challenging (time- and labor-intensive). Instead, the use of roads as a proxy for runoff collection data was found appropriate when modified LC is employed, enabling DCIA delineation without catch basin inlet data. The assumption of zero rooftop connectivity to storm sewers provided closer fDCIA  results to fEIA,  compared with that of 100% rooftop connectivity. This has implications in urban hydrologic modeling, especially in ungauged catchments, as most rainfall-runoff models (e.g., EPA SWMM) require directly or hydraulically connected impervious areas as an input parameter. Further research is needed to investigate the applicability of this conclusion to other urban catchments. Other conclusions of the research are as follows. High resolution and reliable spatial data (e.g., LC, roads, and inlets) are critical for DCIA estimation that can be used as a proxy for EIA in ungauged catchments. This indicates the need for the development of such data by relevant management organizations. NLCD urban imperviousness data can be used as a proxy for high-resolution LC data when eatimating fTIA  in the absence of high-resolution LC data. Given the nationwide availability and regular updates of NLCD, this finding presents a highly practical solution for practitioners and researchers working on urban watersheds. In addition to the importance of this study in urban hydrology and rainfall-runoff modeling, the outlined procedure for DCIA delineation also holds substantial promise for siting SCMs or green stormwater infrastructure to disconnect urban impervious surfaces. Moreover, the improved estimation of fDCIA  serves to optimize stormwater infrastructure design, presenting an integral step toward ensuring effective urban water management and sustainable development. The findings of this study can also be reflected in stormwater utility fees, which mostly depend on the total amount (or percentage) of impervious areas (i.e., TIA) in various calculation methods (Kea et al., 2016 ). Accurate quantification of the impervious surfaces that generate runoff (e.g., using DCIA instead of TIA) can decrease the stormwater utility fees, demonstrating the implications of this study in improving social equity, especially in low-income communities. Further studies can be performed regarding the social benefits of impervious cover characterization for vulnerable minority groups and underserved communities.
1 Introduction The soil–water retention curve (SWRC) is considered a fundamental constitutive relationship in unsaturated soil mechanics, hydrology and agriculture science. It describes the energy equilibrium conditions between soil moisture and its prevailing matrix suction, sharing of theoretical importance and practical significance to strength, deformation, permeability and diffusivity problems in unsaturated zones. Historically, SWRC was regarded as characteristic for a given soil, but past studies revealed various influencing factors, e.g., mineralogy, soil fabric, pore water chemistry, temperature, etc. Nonetheless, unique relations between suction and gravimetric water content were extensively reported in the high suction range for clays (Baker and Frydman 2009 ). In essence, two distinct physical–chemical mechanisms (i.e., adsorption and capillarity) jointly control the soil–water retention (SWR), and the relative importance of adsorption grows with increasing ratio of clay mineral, especially montmorillonite (MMT) (Zhang and Lu, 2018 ). Because experimental measurement is usually laborious and time-consuming, continuous description of SWR is of great significance, and three popular conceptions are available for SWRC simulation, i.e., i) Type I – to consider only capillarity based on the classical bundle of cylindrical capillaries (BBC), ii) Type II – to consider the fabric evolution, and iii) Type III – to consider both capillarity and adsorption. The BBC-based approaches, e.g., Brooks-Corey (abbreviated as BC; Brooks and Corey, 1964 ), van Genuchten (abbreviated as VG; van Genuchten, 1980 ) and Fredlund-Xing (abbreviated as FX; Fredlund and Xing, 1994 ) models, are the prevailing and well justified for sandy and silty soils. However, they usually fail to capture the dry end of SWRC and the physical meaning of residual moisture is vague, indicating an inappropriate representation of SWR by non-capillary forces. Type II models were developed to account for clay fabric, mainly relying on sufficient microscale information (e.g., using mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) technique). For instance, Romero et al. (2011)  and De la Morena et al. (2021)  considered the void ratio dependency at low suctions where capillarity dominated. However, the boundary between micropores and macropores varied with clay type, and phenomenological approach was also used to determine certain material-specific parameters, which neglects SWR mechanism and limits practical implication. To capture the realistic conditions, Or and Tuller (1999)  first proposed a theorical model in which contributions of adsorption and capillarity were separated, but it was mathematically complicated and difficult for practical implication. Khlosi et al. (2006)  adopted the linear relation of SWRC on a semi-log plot at low water content (Campbell and Shiozawa 1992 ) to replace the residual moisture concept in the four-parameter Kosugi (1999)  model. Revil and Lu (2013)  (abbreviated as RL) proposed a unified model combining the cation exchangeable capacity (CEC)-normalized Freundlich isotherm (Duong, 1998 ) and the VG model, which was later extended to a generalized form by simplifying the adsorption part in Lu (2016)  (abbreviated as Lu) model. Zhou et al. (2016)  proposed a new water retention model for unsaturated soils, which takes into account the capillary condensation of adsorbed water. Compared with segmented models proposed by Du (2020)  and Chen et al. (2021) , continuous models are more attractive, because the discontinuity at special nodes of the former would limit the model adaptability (Gao et al., 2024 ). Due to better consideration of adsorption, Type III models usually predict very well in a variety of soils, but additional parameters were unavoidably introduced, which may cause unexpected difficulty in parameter estimation. Despite providing satisfactory results, most SWRC models proposed up to now are not particularly suited and verified for high active clays, e.g., bentonite. On the one hand, bentonite usually exhibits strong adsorption potential due to its high specific surface area (SSA) and CEC, which were rarely addressed. Abed and Solowski (2021)  developed a SWRC model for bentonite based on mineralogy and MIP tests, with assumptions of homogenous and simultaneous hydration of interlayer and interparticle pores. However, this is a vast simplification, because the bentonite hydration is heterogeneous in nature and its sequence depends upon exchangeable cation (Salles et al., 2007, 2013 ). Pure phenomenological methods are still often used to describe water adsorption in clays in the high suction range, thus the generality of corresponding model prediction will be largely restricted (Li et al., 2024 ). On the other hand, current precise models considering both capillarity and adsorption are mathematically complex, with many parameters being inevitably introduced. This could lead to heavy calibration procedures that require enough material-specific information, and strong demand for sufficient data for parameter estimation. Otherwise, the curve fitting may encounter convergence problem, and the estimated parameter may lose its physical meaning to some extent. However, due to difficulty and long duration in experiment on bentonite (Villar, 2007 ), existing SWR data are mostly located at high suctions upon wetting. It means that, not only predicting SWRC efficiently through a limited number of data, but also performing concise modelling easy to utilize for parameter estimation and practical implication, are well worth pursuing. The aim of the present work is thereby threefold: i) to emphasize the homogenous vs heterogenous nature of bentonite hydration and possible influence on SWR; (ii) to propose a SWRC model with simple mathematical form that explicitly considers adsorption and capillarity, and develop simple approach for parametric estimation; and iii) to validate the generality of proposed model for accurately representing experimental data of various bentonite materials, and examine its applicability to the full suction range.  2 Mechanism for bentonite hydration and soil–water retention As the major mineral constitute of bentonite, MMT belongs to the smectite group of 2:1 phyllosilicate. From a multiscale view, a dense assembly of unit layers with strong orientation correlations is usually referred as a particle, and an assembly of particles with mechanical cohesion may be defined as an aggregate. Due to isomorphic substitutions, the layer bears a permanent negative charge normally compensated by exchangeable cations (e.g., Li+ , Na+ , Ca2+  and Mg2+ ) located primarily in interlayer space (Salles et al., 2007; 2013 ). Over a wide relative humidity (RH ) range, the ions (located mainly in interlayer space) and the charged surfaces can strongly interact with polar water molecules and easily undergo hydration. In general, adsorption occurs at high suction due to mainly cation hydration and surface hydration, and the adsorptive water is discernible around surface of soil elementary units and exists in smaller pores. Clearly, a water molecule in bulk water is in a different energy state from that near an ion. In contrast, the capillarity originates due to the presence of curved air–water interface in soil pores, and the capillary water resides in bigger pores between aggregates/grains and has similar physicochemical properties to bulk water (Dueck, 2004; Navarro et al., 2015; Zhang and Lu, 2018 ). Considered that capillary phenomenon in soil has been extensively analyzed in detail in literatures, only the adsorption phenomenon in MMT is discussed below. The determining force of such hydration process in smectites is strongly dependent on the nature of interlayer cations, but the modification of clay layers as a function of interlayer cation has also to be concerned (Salles et al., 2007, 2013 ). For Ca- and Mg-MMT, the cation hydration occurs preferentially at low RH , accompanied with weak destruction of particles and delayed mesopore hydration. For Li- and Na-MMT, before mesopore filling at high RH , external surface hydration occurs at very low RH , after which the interlayer hydration proceeds and strong destruction of particles happens. In other words, the hydration process of smectite does not simply corresponds to a successive adsorption of water molecule layers, due to the competing effects of cation hydration, surface hydration and structural modification. Many previous studies have focused on the homogeneous vs. heterogeneous natures of hydration state in smectite as a function of RH , and X-ray diffraction (XRD) profile modelling allowed for quantitative insights into the nature, composition and amount of different layer types which coexist in the smectite structure (Holmboe et al., 2012 ). Also, Laird (1999)  suggested that instead of uniform film, the water molecules were clustered around cation/charge sites. Therefore, these probably imply that neither ideas of homogenous hydration and uniform layer (in flat surface) nor absolute priority in interlayer hydration is realistic. It is no wonder that the applicability of SWRC modelling based on homogenous hydration is limited to a certain type of bentonite (Abed and Solowski, 2021 ), but the concept of uniform layer may be still conducive for qualitative analysis and approximate estimation in a sense. It is thus suspected that description of MMT hydration in nanoscale may be more reasonable from thermodynamics or using the concept of micropore filling, which will be discussed below.  3 Model development 3.1 Background on SWRC modelling In thermodynamic equilibrium, considering the coexistence of the bulk water and a wetting film, Philip (1977)  developed a quantitative unitary approach to capillary condensation (s c ) and adsorption (s a ) in porous media, i.e., the augmented Young-Laplace equation,(1) s = s c  + s a  = 2 γ  r m   + - R g  T ln R H  v w       where s  is matric suction (kPa), γ  = 72 mJ∙m−2  is the surface tension of air–water interface at T =298.15 K, T  is the absolute temperature (Kelvin), r m  is Kelvin's radius, Rg   = 8.3145 J∙K−1 ·mol−1  is the universal gas constant, RH  is the relative humidity and v w  = 18.04 cm3 ∙mol−1  is the molar volume of water. Eq. (1) implies that there is a critical thickness of water film h c  in statistical average, which is typically quite small (∼3–72 Å) and is dependent on the crystallochemical features of minerals (van Honschoten et al., 2010; Osipov, 2012 ). In other words, water films with a thickness < h c  are metastable, indicating the dominant role of adsorption forces, thus s  is approximately equal to s a  at low RH . While water films with a thickness > h c  are stable, indicating negligible adsorption forces, thus s  is equal to s c  at very high RH  (Philip, 1977 ). As for how to embody the SWR mechanism, there is an objective necessity to account for the adsorption and capillarity separately, depending on the levels of matric suction. To this regard, the gravimetric water content retained in soils is clearly defined with explicit inclusion of both adsorptive (w a ) and capillary waters (w c ),(2) w = w c  + w a       Due to intrinsic complexity in pore and surface, practical solids rarely conform to the fundamentals of pure component adsorption equilibria, because the basic assumptions made in the kinetic approach and thermodynamic equation are not readily satisfied (Duong, 1998 ). To this end, semi-empirical approaches are generally favored for practicality, but most are still far from the full coverage of RH . For instance, the Brunauer-Emmet-Teller (BET) theory is commonly used to describe the multilayer adsorption on soil particle, but it did not predict a finite amount of bound water at very high RH  (Woodruff and Revil, 2011 ) and its application range is still considerably limited in expansive clays even after improvement (Luo and Lu, 2021 ). The Freundlich model that reaches a clear limit at low suction was thus adopted by Revil and Lu (2013)  to describe the adsorptive water retention (w aRL ), expressed by incorporating a form of the kelvin equation as follows:(3) w aRL  ( s )  = w mac  ( R H )  1 /  M   = w mac  [ exp ( - v m  s  R g  T   )  ]  1 /  M       where M  is the adsorption strength and w mac  means the maximum adsorption capacity of water. Eq. (3) was later improved by Lu (2016)  to satisfy thermodynamic equilibrium, and the characteristics of the power function for adsorption were preserved. The new equation for estimating adsorptive water content (w aLu ) is thus given below:(4) w a Lu   ( s )  = w mac  { 1 - [ exp ( s - s max   s  )  ]  j  }      where s max  means the highest suction corresponding to zero water content, and j  also denotes the adsorption strength. Obviously, hydration beyond a certain range will inevitably result in water filling of mesopores and macropores through capillary condensation. As already discussed in detail by Duong (1998)  and Fredlund and Xing (1994) , the capillary water retention can be quantitatively characterized based on pore size distribution (PSD) and by applying the Young-Laplace equation. Besides, once the PSD of a soil is known, the SWRC can be uniquely determined, revealing subjective choice on PSD function. In practice, an equation for capillarity with simpler mathematical form is generally more popular and can also simply further application, please see Section 3.2 . For instance, the VG model was frequently utilized to quantify capillarity (Romero et al., 2011; Revil and Lu, 2013; Lu, 2016; Dieudonne et al., 2017; Du, 2020; Abed and Solowski, 2021; Dong et al., 2023 ), maybe for its simplicity in mathematical form. If single equation is used to model SWRC of clays, the features of wide suction range and ''long tail'' could make the mathematical expression very complicated, e.g., FX model. When the adsorption and capillarity are separately considered, adsorptive and capillary components should be mainly existed in different suction ranges, while the ''long tail'' can be included within adsorptive component. It is also interesting to note that, when the adsorption and capillarity are separately considered, the SWRC is recently more inclined to be expressed in terms of gravimetric water content (w ), instead of volumetric water content (θ ) or saturation degree (S r ) (e.g., Revil and Lu, 2013; Lu, 2016 ). One possible reason is that only minerology and chemical composition are unique for a given soil, whereas different soils may possess similar PSD, thereby exhibiting similar capillary water retention. Another issue is that compared with non- or low-expansive soils, the compactness and PSD of bentonite are not constant but significantly evolve with suction, which causes difficulty in separately defining the real-time distribution of adsorptive and capillary pores and in turn θ  and S r .  3.2 Proposed approach to model SWRC of bentonite Based on the early potential theory (Polanyi, 1932 ), Dubinin and his co-workers developed the concept of micropore filling mainly for active carbons with molecular pores (Dubinin and Astakhov, 1971; Duong, 1998 ), and corresponding theorical basis was given in Chen and Yang (1994) . Dubinin's concept received little attention in characterizing clay adsorption, but several works preliminarily proved its capability of describing water vapor adsorption on bentonites (Kraehenbuehl et al., 1987; Fernández and Rivas,2005; Dieudonne et al., 2017 ). In this work, the D-A model (Dubinin and Astakhov, 1971 ), i.e., a more generalized version of Dubinin's isotherm, is adopted to describe the water adsorption behavior of micropores:(5) W = W 0  exp [ - ( - R g  T ln R H  E  )  c  ]      where W  and W 0  are the filling and entire volume of micropores, respectively. E  is the characteristic adsorption energy (kJ∙mol−1 ) and c  represents the surface heterogeneity. Substituting Eq. (1) into Eq. (5) yields(6) W = W 0  exp [ - ( s E /  v w    )  c  ]       Since the density of adsorptive water varies with suction or water content, Eq. (6) cannot be directly used to estimate the adsorptive water mass. In terms of gravimetric water content vs. suction, Eq. (6) can be thus rewritten to describe the adsorption component (i.e., adsorptive water retention curve, AWRC):(7) w a  ( s )  = w mac  A ( s )  = w mac  exp [ - ( s b a   )  c a   ]      where b a  = E /  v w      (positive) denotes the characteristic adsorption suction (kPa) and c a  (positive) depicts the adsorption strength. Considering that as cumulative density function (CDF), A (s ) shows the same mathematical form with the inverse Weibull distribution function, i.e., reliability function, thus A (s ) should enable it to characterize the stability of water films around surface. To quantify the capillary component (i.e., capillary water retention curve, CWRC), let us consider a porous soil having a capillary pore volume distribution f (r ) (ml∙g−1 ), where f (r )dr  is the volume of capillary pores that have radii ranging between r  and r  + dr . When the cylindrical pores with radius r  ≤ R  are filled with water, the filling capillary pore volume V (R ) and capillary water content w c  can be correspondingly given as,(8) w c  ( r )  = ρ w  V ( R )  = ρ w  ∫ 0  R  f ( r ) d r      where ρ w  is the density of water taken as common value of 1.00 g∙cm−3  and f (r ) is the capillary pore volume distribution (ml∙g−1 ). Strictly speaking, there should be a lower limit of pore range in which the capillary condensation starts. Recently, the macroscopic Kelvin equation was experimentally verified to predict capillary condensation under atomic-scale confinement, i.e., down to less than 4 Å in height and can accommodate just a monolayer of water (Yang et al., 2020 ), approximately corresponding to s  = 252 MPa at T =294 ± 1 K. Considered that assuming a singly censored pore range may cause difficulty in mathematical analysis, the lower limit in Eq. (8) was thus chosen as zero for simplicity. By applying the Young-Laplace equation in soils with cylindrical pores, Fredlund and Xing (1994)  further suggested a general form to approximate SWRC, which can be expressed as:(9) w c  ( s )  = ρ w  V s  ∫ s  ∞  f ( s ) d s  = w mcc   ∫ s  ∞  f ( s ) d s      where Vs   is the filling capillary pore volume at s , f (s ) is the capillary pore volume distribution as a function of s , and w mcc  is the maximum capillary capacity. Eq. (9) is supposed to generally exhibit a nonsymmetrical S-shaped curve (Fredlund and Xing, 1994 ), thus it is meaningful to choose an optimum function of f (s ) with limited parameters but adequate flexibility. Bayat et al. (2015)  performed a comprehensive review to evaluate the ability of abundant different mathematical models in fitting the particle size distribution over a wide range of soils textures, and results showed that the statistical Weibull-type distributions represented high fitting accuracy, adequate flexibility and simplicity. Given the intrinsic relation between particle and PSDs, the density function (DF) of two-parameter Weibull distribution function is suggested to describe f (s ),(10) f ( s )  = c c  b c   ( s b c   )  c c  - 1   exp [ - ( s b c   )  c c   ]      where b c  (positive) denotes the characteristic capillary suction related to the dominant capillary pore size and c c  (positive) describes the uniformity of capillary pores. Integrating Eq. (9) using Eq. (10) gives the following relationship between capillary water content and suction,(11) w c  ( s )  = w mcc  exp [ - ( s b c   )  c c   ]       Consequently, the gravimetric water content retained in soils at any suction is the sum of capillary and adsorptive water contents, expressed in the form of twofold model (cumulative distribution function, CDF) as follows:(12) w ( S lg  )  = w a  ( S lg  )  + w c  ( S lg  )  = w mcc  exp [ - ( S lg  b c   )  c c   ]  + w mac  exp [ - ( S lg  b a   )  c a   ]      where S lg  (dimensionless) is the common logarithm of s  in kPa, i.e., S lg  = lg s   . Eq. (12) completely defines the proposed SWRC model with a total of 5 physical parameters: 2 for capillary water, i.e., b c  (characteristic capillary suction) and c c  (uniformity of capillary pores), and 3 for adsorptive water, i.e., w mac  (maximum adsorption capacity), b a  (characteristic adsorptive suction) and c a  (adsorption strength). It allows for easy and full decomposition between adsorptive and capillary components, consistent with current understanding of SWR controlled by different mechanisms. It is assumed that the saturation state is achieved at S lg  = 0 (i.e., s  = 1 kPa). Since adsorptive water is held in nanoscale pores, c a  may also depict the uniformity of adsorptive pores to some extent. Comparing the pore size that relates to adsorption and capillarity, there should always exist the relationship: b c  < b a .   4 Parametric analysis and comparison with existing SWRC models 4.1 Parametric analysis Obviously, Eq. (12) exhibits quite similar mathematical form with the reliability function of a twofold Weibull distribution. Parametric analysis and estimation of Eq. (12) can be thus referred to Rinne (2009)  and Jiang and Murthy (1995) , but only special case is discussed herein, i.e., 0 < b c  < b a . Differentiating Eq. (12) leads to a density function (DF),(13) w ′  ( S lg  )  = w c ′  ( S lg  )  + w a ′  ( S lg  )     = w mcc  c c  b c   ( S lg  b c   )  c c  - 1   exp [ - ( S lg  b c   )  c c   ]  + w mac  c a  b a   ( S lg  b a   )  c a  - 1   exp [ - ( S lg  b a   )  c a   ]           Taking only the adsorption part as an example, Fig. 1   shows the influence of parameters b a  and c a  on graphical representation. Enlarging b a  reduces the density and widens the abscissa range, implying that the adsorption process mainly occurs over a wider suction range. There exists a characteristic point (b a , w mac /e) (e is the natural constant). Enlarging c a  changes the form of DF graph and shortens the abscissa range, implying a strong adsorption process. Fig. 2   shows the illustration of proposed model with changeable capillary part while constant adsorption part. The proposed model can display both unimodal (when b c  and b a  are close in values) and bimodal SWRCs by different parameter combinations. Since the dominant pore sizes in nano and meso/macro scales deviate significantly in general, parameters b c  and b a  should also deviate sufficiently. In this circumstance, parameters b c  and b a  may be also regarded approximately as inflection points, and another characteristic point (b c , w mac  + w mcc /e) could also exist. From the statistical point of view, b c  and b a  are scale parameters in graphical representation of Eq. (12), while c c  and c a  are form/shape parameters (Rinne, 2009 ).  4.2 Parametric estimation In the literature, least squares method was frequently used for linear and non-linear curve fittings to determine parameters in SWRC models, via computer analysis. However, such estimation procedures do not always operate perfectly and yield useful information, e.g., issues about convergence and parameter rationality. Among 5 parameters in proposed SWRC model, w mac  deserves special consideration to avoid unreasonable fitting, since either component in Eq. (12) is probably able to achieve best fitting under unimodal conditions. However, to the author's knowledge, there is so far no general consensus among researchers about the maximum adsorptive water content in clays. For nearly a century, the Weibull distribution has attracted the attention of statisticians working on theory and methods as well as in various fields of applied statistics, e.g., economics, hydrology and engineering science, and corresponding experience is referred herein to provide reasonable and efficient parameter estimation (Rinne, 2009 ). Note that, Jiang and Murthy (1995)  have presented a graphical approach to decide on the appropriateness of a twofold Weibull distribution to model monitored data. Based on this procedure, it is thus entirely possible to estimate all 5 parameters in Eq. (12) if the sample size was large enough. However, the SWR data was generally uncomplete over the full suction range, thus it is advised to firstly focus on estimation of w mac . First, a graph is plotted in terms of y = ln - ln w ( S lg  )  /  w sat             and x = ln S lg    , and a L -named smooth curve is fitted. Then, the asymptotes of L -curve are draw, generating straight lines as x  → ∞. At last, a point I  can be defined as the intersection of the horizontal asymptote for large x  with L -curve, and the approximation y I  = ln - ln w mac  /  w sat             is used to obtain w mac . An example was performed on GMZ01 bentonite with void ratio (e ) of 0.785, as shown in Fig. 3  . For further details of the approximation procedure, please see Jiang and Murthy (1995) . After w mac  is estimated by the graphical method, the remaining parameters are determined using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm for non-linear curve fitting. Lower and upper bounds are applied to parameters b c  (0–4), b a  (4–6), c c  and c a  (1–50) to aid the optimization process during curve fitting. It should be noted that, when SWR test was conducted under constant-volume condition or up to near full saturation, w mcc  can be directly deduced from the difference between w sat  and w mac . Otherwise, w mcc  cannot be obtained since it is hard to estimate w sat  under free expansion condition, thus the value of w sat  was assigned to be 200 % for curve-fitting purpose in this case.  4.3 Comparison with existing SWRC models Lu (2016)  indicated that compared with traditional VG and FX models, both RL and Lu models predicted test data more closely and were capable of decomposing the SWRC. In the following section, the proposed model will be compared with RL and Lu models to demonstrate its superiority. As mentioned above, based on the adsorption isotherm and capillarity model, both Revil and Lu (2013)  and Lu (2016)  respectively gave hybrid equations for SWRC simulation as follow:(13) w = w aRL  + w sat  - w aRL   1 + ( α s )  n      1 - 1 / n    ,  RL model      (14) w = w aLu  + 1 2  1  -   erf 2   s - s c   s c           w sat  - w aLu   1 + ( α s )  n      1 - 1 / n    ,  Lu model      where on the right-hand sides of Eqs. (13) and (14), the first terms are adsorptive components mentioned above, while the second terms comprise the VG model. 1/α  is the capillary air-entry suction, n  is the pore size exponent, erf() is the error function and s c  is the mean cavitation suction.   5 Model assessment The model performance will be assessed in three aspects: i) fitness to model SWR data for various bentonite materials, ii) capability to separate contributions of adsorption and capillarity, and iii) comparison with other hybrid SWRC models (i.e., Revil and Lu, 2013; Lu, 2016 ). 5.1 SWR dataset SWR data of various bentonite materials from the literature, mainly in the context of nuclear waste disposal and landfill, are employed to assess the performance of proposed model. Corresponding basic properties and test descriptions are summarized in Table 1  , please refer to original references for more detailed information. As for GCL product, the MMT content is 50–55 % for bentonite cores in GCL2 (Beddoe et al., 2011 ), and 82 % in GCL5 (Lau et al., 2022 ). Besides, only SWR data reported at s  ≥ 1 kPa were utilized here, disregarding the impact of geotextile on SWRC. In addition, as expected to exhibit bimodal characteristics, SWR data of various sand-bentonite mixtures with Wyoming bentonite content ranging from 20 % to 100 % were also adopted here. Note that, there assumed a zero point at s  = 106  kPa for reasonable parameter estimation, since there lack data points at s  > 105  kPa in some cases. All SWR data were obtained from the wetting path, disregarding the effects of hydraulic hysteresis and volume change along the SWRC in the present work.  5.2 Model performance The best-fit parameters and corresponding coefficients of determination R 2  for all bentonites and sand-bentonite mixtures are listed in Table 2  . Clearly, the proposed SWRC model is capable of perfectly simulating the SWR data for all cases, as evidenced by the extremely high R 2  (all greater than 0.98) with no except. For sand-bentonite mixtures, the estimated w mac  using the graphical method increases with increasing bentonite content. For pure bentonites, the estimated w mac  ranges from 14.2 % for Kunigel-V1 bentonite with almost the lowest MMT content (48 %) and total SSA (∼389 m2 /g) as well as up to 26.4 % for FEBEX bentonite with the highest MMT content (>90 %) and total SSA (725 m2 /g). Such phenomenon that w mac  increases with the MMT content or total SSA is generally in line with traditional cognition, indicating the feasibility of the graphical method for estimating w mac . Another important point is that, for each bentonite (i.e., GMZ01, GMZ07, MX-80, Wyominga  and FEBEX) wetted under constant volume condition, w mac  generally slightly increases with decreasing initial void ratio. This indicates that the value of w mac  could be not necessarily unique for a given bentonite, implying that volume restriction can have some certain impact. Interestingly, parameter b a  for all bentonite materials is distributed within a limited range (i.e., 4.72–5.38), but it generally exhibits minor change with varying void ratio for the same bentonite. Besides, the distribution range of c a  is relatively larger but still limited (i.e., 7.76–16.55), and c a  seems to be greater for the same bentonite with lower initial void ratio. In a sense, this probably suggests that b a  is nearly independent of initial void ratio, while increasing compaction could cause pore contraction and homogenization in nanoscale, as confirmed by greater c a . It also means that bentonite with high MMT content is inclined to show unique but broadly similar adsorption process, thus parameters b a  and c a  could be easily estimated. Likewise, both parameters b c  and c c  for capillarity appear to increase with decreasing initial void ratio, but manifest relatively much larger variation. In other words, it implies that for denser bentonite, the dominant pore size and corresponding peak intensity of capillary pores are expected to be basically smaller. This generally coincides with MIP results and traditional ideas that with increasing compaction, the bentonite specimens tend to exhibit smaller pores between aggregates, with obvious reduction in peak intensity and inapparent decrease of dominant pore size (Dieudonne et al., 2017 ). Besides, in most cases, b c  is also distributed within a narrow range (i.e., 3.42–4.00) for bentonites and sand-bentonite mixtures under constant volume condition, which also allows for easy estimation of b c . Fig. 4   first shows the comparison of model fitting with test data of total, adsorptive and capillary water contents in Wyominga  bentonite. Corresponding test data was obtained by NMR technique and reported in detail in Liang et al. (2023) . As shown, the proposed model performs well for simulating the total water content (R 2  ≥ 0.98) and produces fitting curves close to each other at S lg  ≥ 4.3. Similarly, the decomposed fitting curves of adsorptive and capillary water contents also generally match well with the test data, showing the existence of adsorptive water over the full suction range and the onset of capillarity at approximately S lg  = 4.3 except for the powder. Admittedly, there exists some deviation between fitting curves and test data in Fig. 4 (b). However, such discrepancy is still limited and foreseeable, because it occurs due to the lack of test data at lower suctions that caused underestimation in w mac  and in turn overestimation of capillary water content. Given the dependence of w mac  on initial void ratio as mentioned, it is no wonder that the fitness to simulate SWRC is better for Wyominga  bentonite with lower initial void ratio (e.g., e i  = 0.588). To this end, the proposed model is probably the first to be directly validated with experimental results, confirming its capability to accurately separate total water content into adsorptive and capillary components. Fig. 5   illustrates the performance of proposed model for different bentonites (i.e., GMZ01, GMZ07, MX-80 and FEBEX) under constant volume condition. For S lg  ≥ 4.2, the proposed model predicts the SWR data very closely and the fitting curves agree with each other for all bentonites with varying initial void ratio. It is also observed that at S lg  < 3.6, adsorptive water varies little and capillary water is thus responsible for any changes in total water content. This feature indicates that enough test data existed at S lg  < 3.6 should be thus a strong promise for reasonable estimation of w mac . The capillary onset varies with bentonite type, i.e., S lg  = 4.2 for GMZ01, S lg  = 4.9 for GMZ07, S lg  = 5.0 for MX-80 and S lg  = 4.2 for FEBEX, and such discrepancy should be largely caused by the difference in the soil particle size and ability to retain water by adsorption (Luo and Lu, 2021 ). Under constant volume condition, the initial void ratio can impose a significant effect on the capillary water retention behavior (i.e., w mcc  and variation rate). Fig. 6   shows the fitting results for various sand-Wyoming bentonite mixtures over a wide suction range under constant volume condition. As shown, the fitting curves match well with the test data as bentonite content varies from 20 % to 100 %, indicating that the proposed model can also work well with the sand-bentonite mixtures. Compared with pure Wyoming bentonite, the sand-bentonite mixture with a higher sand content is expected to exhibit more noticeable bimodal SWRC. This reveal that the proposed model may work with low active clays generally exhibiting bimodal PSDs and SWRCs, but it still needs further verification. Fig. 7   presents the fitted SWR results for bentonite powders (FEBEX, Wyomingb  and Kunigel-V1) under free expansion condition. Obviously, compared with that under constant volume condition, the capillary water develops dramatically since intrinsic swelling potential can be transformed into volume expansion that widens the capillary pores and enhances the capillary ability to retain water. This subtle yet noticeable transition from adsorptive regime to capillary regime can be observed for S lg  < 4. It seems that this phenomenon is less evident in Ca-bentonite (i.e., FEBEX), since particle breakage upon hydration is more limited in Ca-bentonite, compared with Na-bentonite (Salles et al., 2007, 2013 ). Fig. 8   highlights the model performance over the full suction range, by examining SWR data of bentonite cores in GCL2 and GCL5. For total water content, the predicted curves agree well with test data both at high and low suction ranges. The development pattern for capillary water in bentonite core in GCL5 is quite different from that in GCL2, showing a sharp slope after the capillary onset. This can be attributed to the discrepancy in both the soil particle size and CEC as mentioned. Based on the fitting results in Figs. 4-8 , it is found that the transition process form adsorption to capillarity on the SWRCs of bentonites does not occur suddenly at one specific suction point but takes place gradually within a certain suction range. Adsorption will continue after the capillary onset until it reaches the ultimate state, giving a certain upper bound defined by the completion of adsorption (w mac ). It is also interesting to note that, the value of total water content at S lg  approaching 4.0 (i.e., s  ≈ 10 MPa) is approximately equal to that of w mac , which was also basically in accordance with existing experimental evidences that the free water was almost ignorable at s  > 14 MPa, implying invalidity of most semi-empirical methods for adsorption. For instance, Salles et al. (2008)  observed no free water in Na-MMT via thermoporometry at s  > 14 MPa, and negligible capillary water was measured via nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) in Ningming expansive clay (Ma et al., 2020 ) and sodium MX-80 bentonite (Liang et al., 2023 ) at s  > 22 MPa.  5.3 Comparison with other hybrid SWRC models Fig. 9   presents the comparison between the proposed, RL and Lu models for the SWRC simulation in two cases (i.e., wetted under constant volume and free expansion conditions). To emphasize the rationality of the suggested graphical method, the parameter estimation for proposed model was also performed by pure curve fitting. As shown in Fig. 9 , these four approaches generally fit the test data well over a wide suction range. However, for the suction approaching 106  kPa, the RL model exhibits some overestimation in Fig. 9 (a), while not in Fig. 9 (b). By the proposed model with and without graphical method, RL and Lu models, the estimated values of w mac  are 23.6 %, 60.2 %, 30.23 %, and 36.8 % for bentonite core in GCL5, and 16.2 %, 8.9 %, 9.6 %, and 12.2 % for GMZ07 bentonite with e i  = 0.80. It is suspected that without determining w mac  in advance, the model fitting appears to be totally decided by the curve features, which could be sensitive to the abnormal data points in the transition suction range and the amount of data points. In other words, it is suggested to estimate w mac  based on available knowledge as possible, otherwise the estimated w mac  by complete curve-fitting may actually loose its physical meaning. Nevertheless, it should be noted that fitting by the proposed model with graphical method can be completed within dozens iteration times in general, but fitting by RL and Lu models is comparatively difficult, showing worse convergence efficiency (i.e., dozens to thousands iteration times) and stability. This phenomenon could be attributed to the difference in formula structure and strategy for the parameter estimation. Although assumptions were more or less made in RL and Lu models (Revil and Lu, 2013; Lu, 2016 ) for convenience of curve-fitting, the value and distribution range of model parameters generally varied significantly. It is thus difficult to select appropriate estimate of the desired parameters of initial guess, thereby making the iterative curve-fitting algorithm too hard to work. Importantly, the expression of w sat -w a (s ) in RL and Lu models differs from the proposed one (i.e., w sat -w mac ) in that it allows completely decoupling the adsorptive component of retained water content from the capillary part. This decoupling feature is not only supposed to provide better iteration efficiency, but also conducive and easy for further inclusion of void ratio effect on SWRC in a consistent way with how volume change affects the PSD. Besides, this strategy also results in a concise model form (i.e., Eq. 12) and more reasonable parameter estimation. These probably ensure easy and efficient application in practice. Consequentially, the advantage of the proposed model in this study is three-fold: i) simple and continuous mathematical form easy for application, ii) full decoupling between adsorptive and capillary water retentions, and iii) efficient and reasonable parameter estimation, as well as less need of test data.   6 Discussion and limitations The high active clays, especially for bentonite, have been used as barrier materials in geotechnical engineering, e.g., nuclear waste disposal and landfill. As crucial factors affecting the engineering performance, hydraulic properties of bentonite are critical that deserve special considerations. The proposed SWRC model was validated on bentonites and sand-bentonite mixtures for certain purpose, but it should be also applicable for other soils exhibiting especially bimodal characteristics according to the concept of pore filling. However, in practical engineering, bentonite could be subjected to wetting and drying, resulting in volume change and hydraulic hysteresis, which were not considered in present work. Besides, the graphical method for determining the maximum adsorption capacity enables it to avoid unreasonable parameter estimation via the curve fitting, but it may be sensitive to data integrity and somewhat subjective. Since two distinct physical–chemical mechanisms controls the soil–water retention, the adsorptive and capillary water should contribute differently to the hydro-mechanical behavior of unsaturated soils. The role of capillary water on the shear strength has been well highlighted in Zhou et al. (2016) , and capillarity has been also well included in complex constitutive modelling of unsaturated soils by Zhou et al. (2018) . Comparatively, how to embody the role of adsorption in modelling the hydro-mechanical behaviors of unsaturated soils still faces many difficulties and challenges, especially when the adsorption takes the dominant role, partly due to the complex nature of adsorptive water. Nevertheless, because of its concise mathematical form and the full decoupling between capillarity and adsorption, the proposed model may provide a new perspective to study the hydro-mechanical behaviors of unsaturated soils, but great efforts are still needed in further works.  7 Conclusions Based on this work, the following conclusions have been reached.(i) A novel twofold model based on the concepts of pore filling and capillary phenomenon was proposed to continuously simulate soil–water retention behavior of bentonites in wetting path, and a graphical method was suggested to determine the maximum adsorptive capacity to avoid irrational parameter estimation. The proposed model predicted test data of bentonites and sand-bentonite mixtures quite closely with high R 2  (≥0.98) over the full suction range. Its ability to explicitly separating adsorptive and capillary water retentions was also well confirmed by comparisons with experimental results.  (ii) In the proposed model, the adsorption parameters were distributed within a narrow range, i.e., 4.72–5.38 for characteristic adsorptive suction and 7.76–16.55 for adsorption strength. The distribution range of characteristic capillary suction was also limited for bentonite materials wetted under constant volume condition (3.42–3.99). The value of maximum adsorptive water content can be approximately equal to that of total water content for suction approaching 10 MPa. These provide special support for bentonite application in the context of nuclear waste disposal and landfill.  (iii) Comparison with other hybrid models indicates that the advantages of the proposed model are simple mathematical form, full decoupling between adsorptive and capillary water, and efficient and reasonable parameter estimation. It provides a new insight into the hydraulic property of unsaturated soils.
1 Introduction Rainfall-runoff models play a significant role in characterizing hydrologic responses and simulating flow in catchments worldwide (Ji et al., 2023 ). Among alternate model types, conceptual models are widely utilized due to their lower model complexity and fewer data requirements (Buzacott et al., 2019 ). Earlier conceptual models overlooked the spatial variability of hydrologic variables, including that of soil moisture (Sivapalan et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2007 ). Not until the 1980s was spatial variability of soil moisture formally addressed through the empirical distribution developed in the Xinanjiang (XAJ) model (Zhao et al., 1980; Zhao, 1992 ), enabling the model to simulate partial saturation during hydrological processes (Blyth et al., 2004 ). The most ingenious part of the soil moisture module in the XAJ model was its use of an empirical formulation to circumvent the need for specific tension water storage capacity (TWC) information at each spatial location, a challenging task given the limited availability of in-situ hydrologic data (Wolock & McCabe, 1995 ; Kavetski et al., 2003 ). This empirical distribution has been widely employed and regarded as a cornerstone in several hydrologic models, including the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model (Liang et al., 1994 ), ARNO model (Todini, 1996 ), HYdrologic MODel (HYMOD) (Boyle et al., 2000; Boyle, 2001; Wagener et al., 2001 ) and Probability Distributed Model (PDM) (Moore, 2007 ). The use of TWC distribution enables the estimation of catchment contributing areas and ensuing runoff (Guo et al., 2016 ). However, this empirical, non-positional distribution assumes that the TWC distribution follows a parabolic function, lacking physical foundations and leading to an inability to effectively redistribute hydrologic components, such as local soil moisture and contributing area, back to the real catchment (Todini, 1996; Xiong & Guo, 2004 ). Given the significance of TWC in runoff partitioning (Crave & Gascuel-odoux, 1997; Tombul, 2007; Eluwa et al., 2023 ), it is imperative to revisit the empirical distribution. The topographic wetness index (TWI) is a popular alternative for bridging local topographic information and hydrologic responses and serves as the basis for this research (Woods et al., 1997; Hjerdt et al., 2004; Sörensen et al., 2006; Zhang & Liu, 2022 ). Described as ln(a /tanb ), where a  represents the local upslope contributing area draining through a certain point per unit contour length and tanb  represents the local slope (Beven & Kirkby, 1979 ), the TWI logic in TOPMODEL parallels the TWC logic in the XAJ model (Franchini et al., 1996 ). Sivapalan et al. (1997)  suggested that the empirical TWC distribution can be substituted by the cumulative distribution of a scaled bucket in the transformation form of TWI. Blyth et al. (2004)  mapped the non-positional distribution of TWC in the XAJ model onto the terrain based on TWI information alone. Tong et al. (2018)  developed a logarithmic Weibull relationship between the TWC and TWI to derive the spatial distribution. Collectively, these studies have sought to utilize TWI information to improve the empirical TWC distribution in conventional rainfall-runoff models. However, the majority of these studies focused exclusively on the TWI in the form of ln(a /tanb ) (Hjerdt et al., 2004 ).
