It is important to note that the original TWI was modulated based on the assumptions in TOPMODEL, with one of the key assumptions being that the transmissivity profile follows an exponential function of water storage deficit (Rupp & Woods, 2008; Beven, 2012 ). Ambroise et al. (1996)  discovered that this pattern is not universally applicable, as evidenced by their study of the recession curve in a French catchment. A generalized power transmissivity function was developed, encompassing exponential, parabolic, and linear functions as special cases (or subsets) (Duan & Miller, 1997; Iorgulescu & Musy, 1997 ). Under this condition, the original TWI can be transformed into the a t a n b      α     formulation, where α    represents an exponent parameter. This new form of the topographic wetness index is denoted as the generalized topographic wetness index (GTWI) in the subsequent discussion. However, there is a scarcity of studies that have tested the GTWI in real catchments, let alone integrated it into conceptual rainfall-runoff models (Sun et al., 2014 ). The primary aim of this study is to revisit the empirical TWC distribution in traditional conceptual rainfall-runoff models to enhance the performance of streamflow simulations and gain insights into spatial variations during hydrological events. To achieve this, four conceptual rainfall-runoff models with two empirically-based and two topography-based TWC distributions are proposed and investigated. The four models are applied to 460 Australian catchments to assess the influence of TWC distribution on daily streamflow simulations. HYMOD, a lumped conceptual rainfall-runoff model featuring the embedded TWC distribution of the XAJ model, is selected for the water balance simulation due to its simple structure and few parameters, allowing focus on the distribution function without interference from the complexity of the model structures used. Other conceptual rainfall-runoff models with embedded XAJ tension water storage capacity distribution can serve as benchmark models, including the modified form HYMOD2 (Roy et al., 2017; Mai et al., 2021 ) or PDM (Moore, 2007 ). However, to maintain focus on the alternate soil moisture representations, use is made of the simpler model architecture HYMOD offers in the remainder of this study.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area This study is performed on 460 catchments across Australia. The catchments are part of the Australian Hydrologic Reference Stations (HRS), which currently encompass 467 gauging stations with high-quality streamflow records (Jaffrés et al., 2021 ). All the stations are selected as unregulated and unimpaired with minimal anthropogenic effect, representing all hydro-climatic regions across Australia (Kim & Sharma, 2019 ). Out of the 467 catchments, 460 catchments with complete daily streamflow spanning 2005–2014 (10 years) are used in this study. Locations of the 460 streamflow gauging stations and catchment polygons are presented in Fig. 1  . Throughout the study period, the potential impact of human activities or climate change is assumed to be negligible.  2.2 Data Daily precipitation (P), potential evapotranspiration (PET), and streamflow (Q) covering 2005–2014 are collected for model calibration and validation. Streamflow observations are available from the HRS. Daily gridded precipitation, provided by the Australian Water Availability Project (AWAP), is available at a 0.05° resolution (approximately 5 ×    5 km) (Ajami et al., 2017; Raupach et al., 2009, 2012 ). Daily gridded potential evapotranspiration (PET) at 0.05° resolution is sourced from the Australian Water Resource Assessment Landscape (AWRA_L) (Frost et al., 2016 ). The topographic index is derived from the GEODATA 9-second digital elevation model (DEM), covering the entirety of Australia (Hutchinson et al., 2008 ). The R package “topmodel” offers a convenient method for estimating the TWI when provided with DEM information (Slater et al., 2019; Buytaert, 2022 ).  2.3 Multi-curve of tension water storage capacity distribution Fig. 2   presents the conceptual illustration of tension water storage capacity (TWC) and tension water storage (TWS). Suppose a catchment consists of numerous grids, each characterized by a TWC. The TWC represents the maximum amount of tension water stored in local soil (Lei et al., 2023 ). It is fixed for a certain pixel but varies for all the grids spatially distributed within a catchment. The TWS is the water stored in one pixel, it changes with time and satisfies TWS≤TWC. They are typically expressed as a depth in millimeters. Due to the complexity of spatial patterns of soil types, soil properties, and topography, the TWC and TWS within a catchment are expected to be highly variable in space (Merz & Plate, 1997; Gómez-Plaza et al., 2001 ). However, sparse ground-based observations make specifying spatial variability of soil moisture-related items difficult (Dobriyal et al., 2012 ). 2.3.1 Curve 1: Empirically-based parabolic distribution The empirical parabolic distribution in the Xinanjiang model has been taken as the most readily used method to describe the spatial variability of TWC, allowing some areas to be saturated while others remain unsaturated (Blyth et al., 2004 ). The Xinanjiang distribution is a cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the TWC, it gives the spatial variations while not knowing the specific positional information of TWC. This distribution is described as Curve 1 in this study (Fig. 3  a1).(1) F C    = 1 - 1 - C C max       β  , 0 ≤ C ≤ C max       where C    is a local TWC, C max      is the maximum TWC within a catchment, F C       represents the CDF of spatially distributed TWC, the distribution also offers insights into contributing area, representing the proportion of areas between runoff generation regions and catchment areas, and β  (β  ≥ 0) is a parameter describing the degree of spatial variability of TWC. A smaller value of β  indicates a more uniform distribution, β =  0 implies all TWCs are spatially distributed uniformly.  2.3.2 Curve 2: Empirically-based linear distribution For comparison, a special case of Curve 1 but with a fixed parameter β  is proposed. Curve 2 is displayed as an empirical linear distribution when parameter β  equals 1 (Fig. 3 a2). The distribution is:(2) F C    = C C max    , 0 ≤ C ≤ C max         2.3.3 Curve 3: TWI-based distribution Several studies have revealed that the topographic wetness index (TWI) explains the spatial variability of soil moisture (Bárdossy & Lehmann, 1998; Kim & Kim, 2007; Raduła et al., 2018 ). The TWI is defined as (Beven & Kirkby, 1979 ):(3) TWI = ln a t a n b          where a  is the local upslope contributing area draining through a specific point per unit contour length and tanb  represents the local slope. Locations sharing the same TWI value are assumed to exhibit a similar hydrologic response (Wolock & McCabe, 1995 ). For a given catchment, points with higher TWI values are considered to be more susceptible to saturation and subsequent runoff generation compared to those with lower TWI values (Lyon et al., 2004 ). The TWI is underpinned by three fundamental assumptions (Beven, 1997, 2012 ): (1) there is a saturated zone whose dynamics can be approximated by a steady rate over an upslope contributing area (a   ); (2) local surface slope (tanb ) can be used for approximating the hydraulic gradient; and (3) an exponential function is adopted to describe the downslope transmissivity profile with depth. Based on these assumptions, the relationship between the TWI and soil moisture deficit can be described as follows (Beven, 2012 ):(4) D = D  ¯   + m 0  λ - T W I        where D    represents a local soil moisture deficit expressed as a water depth, m 0     is a parameter controlling the rate of decline of transmissivity, D  ¯      denotes the catchment-average mean soil moisture deficit, and λ    represents the catchment-average TWI. Considering the related logic between capacity and deficit, the above equation can be transformed into:(5) C = C  ¯   + m λ - T W I        where C  ¯      is the catchment-average TWC, and m  is a parameter relating to catchment attributes such as field capacity and wilting coefficient (Duan et al., 2001; Koren et al., 2003 ). For a specific catchment, points with lower capacities are more prone to saturation and subsequent runoff generation, contrary to the logic implied by TWI. Consequently, the following limits are imposed:(6) C max   = C  ¯   + m λ - TWI  min          (7) C min   = C  ¯   + m λ - TWI  max          where C max      and C min      are the maximum and minimum TWC within a catchment respectively; TWI  max      and TWI  min      are the maximum and minimum topographic wetness index within the catchment respectively. The scaled TWC (STWC) is subsequently derived to eliminate the parameters C  ¯      and m   , using the min–max normalization method (Al Shalabi et al., 2006; Liu, 2011 ):(8) STWC = C - C min    C max   - C min     = TWI  max   - T W I  TWI  max   - TWI  min          After scaling, the STWC ranges between 0 and 1 and is solely dependent on the TWI, aligning with the scaled bucket size developed by Sivapalan et al. (1997) . To obtain the unscaled values, the scaled ones should be multiplied by k = m TWI  max   - TWI  min        , under the assumption that the minimum capacity across a catchment is zero. The CDF of STWC (F (STWC )) is taken as the distribution of Curve 3 (Fig. 3 a3).  2.3.4 Curve 4: GTWI-based distribution A generalized power function was developed to modify the limitation of the exponential transmissivity assumption in TWI (Duan & Miller, 1997; Iorgulescu & Musy, 1997 ), leading to the generalized TWI form (GTWI). The GTWI is expressed as a t a n b      α    . Denoting TI    as a t a n b       , the GTWI equals TI  α     to highlight the parameter α   . The introduction of GTWI brings about changes in the relationship between the topographic index and soil moisture deficit (Duan & Miller, 1997; Iorgulescu & Musy, 1997 ):(9) D = m 0  α  - TI  α  λ  ′   m 0  α  - D  ¯          where α    is an exponent parameter of the GTWI, α ≠ 0   , but α    can be negative and acts as being more extreme than the exponential case (Rupp & Woods, 2008 ). λ  ′     represents the catchment-average GTWI. Similar to the traditional TWI logic, the TWC for the GTWI can be described as:(10) C = m α  - TI  α  λ  ′   m α  - C  ¯      , α ≠ 0      Following the application of the min–max normalization method to eliminate parameters C  ¯      and m   , the scaled TWC for the GTWI can be developed (further details of this derivation can be found in the Supplemental file ):(11) STWC = C - C min    C max   - C min     = ( T I  max   )   α  - ( T I )  α   ( T I  max   )   α  - ( T I  min   )   α    , α ≠ 0     where TI  max      and TI  min      are the maximum and minimum a t a n b        values within a catchment, respectively. In this case, the STWC ranges between 0 and 1 and is dependent on the GTWI. To obtain the unscaled values, the scaled ones should be multiplied by k  ′  = [ m α  ∗ TI  max    α  - TI  min    α     ]    / [ λ  ′  + STWC  ¯   TI  max    α  - TI  min    α     ]    , STWC  ¯      represents the catchment-average STWC. The CDF of SWTC based on the GTWI is taken as the distribution of Curve 4 (Fig. 3 a4).   2.4 Conceptual rainfall-runoff models The lumped conceptual rainfall-runoff model HYMOD is selected as a benchmark model due to its flexible structure and few parameters (Boyle, 2001; Wagener et al., 2001 ). HYMOD primarily comprises two components: runoff generation and runoff routing (Fig. 3 a1 & 3b). The runoff generation is based on the saturation excess mechanism using Curve 1, which means the runoff will not be generated until the TWS reaches TWC (Lei et al., 2023 ). Model inputs are daily precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PET), and model output is daily streamflow. Actual evapotranspiration (E) is an intermedial variable and is modeled as a function of PET and available soil water. When sufficient water (i.e., P and TWS) is available, E equals potential evapotranspiration, otherwise, it equals the available amount of water (Wagener et al., 2001 ). The runoff routing consists of two sets of linear reservoirs: three reservoirs in serial for quick flow (or surface flow) and a single reservoir for slow flow (or baseflow). The quick flow is routed through the three reservoirs to rivers with a common routing rate Kq , while the slow flow is routed through the ground with another routing rate Ks . The two types of flow together constitute the total streamflow at the outlet of a catchment (Boyle, 2001 ). Based on the model framework of HYMOD, four TWC curves (i.e., Curve 1, Curve 2, Curve 3, and Curve 4) are coupled with the runoff routing part of HYMOD respectively to build four models. The four models are all conceptual rainfall-runoff models and are described as HYMOD, Linear-HYMOD (LHYMOD), Topography-based HYMOD (THYMOD), and Generalized topography-based HYMOD (GTHYMOD) based on their respective TWC curve characteristics. Fig. 3  presents the overall model structure for the four models, while only one curve is selected in the runoff generation part for each model. Topographic attributes will be introduced as an additional model input for the THYMOD and GTHYMOD. The description and initial ranges of the model parameters (Sun et al., 2010, 2012 ) are presented in Table 1  . While the number of quick flow reservoirs can be a calibrated parameter, for consistency with the early versions of HYMOD (Wagener et al., 2001 ) and to reduce the computational complexity of the large-sample study, this parameter is set to a fixed value (3) and is not listed in Table 1 . Curve 2 and Curve 3 can be perceived as special cases of Curve 1 and Curve 4 respectively when parameter β  equals 1 and parameter α  approaches 0. Therefore, HYMOD and GTHYMOD encompass 5 parameters, while LHYMOD and THYMOD involve 4 parameters.  2.5 Model setup and evaluation Finally, the four conceptual rainfall-runoff models are implemented over the 460 Australian catchments from 2005 to 2014 to check the impacts of TWC distributions on streamflow performance. In order to maximize the utilization of the entire 10-year dataset, 2-fold cross-validation is applied (Friedman et al., 2001; Singh & Panda, 2011; Tegegne et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2020; Zahmatkesh et al., 2021 ). The entire dataset is divided into two equal-sized subsamples, with one subsample retained as the validation data and the remaining subsample utilized for calibration (Raju et al., 2018 ). This process is iterated to ensure that each subsample is employed once as the validation data (Jiang & Chen, 2016; Zahmatkesh et al., 2021 ). In this context, the 10 years of data are partitioned into two halves. When the first half of the data is used for model calibration, the remaining half will be used for validation, and vice versa. The overall calibration (validation) for a given catchment comprises the combination of the first and second calibration (validation) sets, respectively. The Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) method (Bonyadi & Michalewicz, 2017; Bruno & Victor, 2019 ) is employed to calibrate the model parameters by maximizing the KGE (Gupta et al., 2009 ), which has gained widespread adoption for model calibration and evaluation (Knoben et al., 2019 ). The KGE incorporates three key simulation metrics: correlation, variability, and bias, and is defined as follows:(12) KGE = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( s - 1 )  2  + ( e - 1 )  2        where r  is the Pearson correlation coefficient between simulations and observations, s  is a measure of variability calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation of simulations to that of observations, and e  is the bias error calculated as the ratio of the means of simulations to observations. The closer each component of the KGE is to 1, the more accurate the model simulation. A KGE value of 1 indicates a perfect match between simulations and observations (Knoben et al., 2019 ). Model performance is considered satisfactory or good if KGE≥0.50 (high KGE), and unsatisfactory or poor if KGE<0.50 (low KGE) (Cislaghi et al., 2020; Lilhare et al., 2020 ). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test (Smirnov, 1939; Kolmogorov & Bharucha-Reid, 2018 ), a robust non-parametric method, is employed in this study to evaluate potential differences in the streamflow performance of the four models. The KS test serves to determine whether the differences among the model performance are statistically meaningful. The null hypothesis presumes no significant difference exists between the distributions. A significance level of 0.05 is stipulated for the p-value. If this p-value is found to be less than 0.05, the null hypothesis will be rejected and a significant difference exists. Conversely, if the p-value is equal to or greater than 0.05, we cannot confidently reject the null hypothesis.   3 Results 3.1 Conceptual rainfall-runoff model performance To illustrate how different TWC distribution curves affect the streamflow calibration and validation across the 460 study catchments, the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of the KGE and its three components are presented in Fig. 4  . Starting with the model performance in the calibration period in Fig. 4 a, all four conceptual rainfall-runoff models perform differently where LHYMOD performs worst and GTHYMOD performs best. However, in the validation period (Fig. 4 a), THYMOD and GTHYMOD perform equally well while LHYMOD remains the worst. The comparisons show the sensitivity effects of the TWC distribution on model performance, especially for the empirically based ones. The KS Test is applied to test whether the CDFs statistically differ from each other. The results for the comparison between HYMOD, THYMOD, and GTHYMOD are presented in Table 2  . The LHYMOD is removed in this comparison because it performs worst whenever in the calibration or validation period. The results show that in the calibration period, the KGE of HYMOD and THYMOD does not have significant differences, but GTHYMOD improves a lot. While in the validation period, THYMOD and GTHYMOD perform similarly but see the KS statistics, GTHYMOD is significantly superior to HYMOD with a larger statistic value than THYMOD. The CDFs of the decomposed KGE components during the validation period are presented in Fig. 4 b-d. The three models, i.e., HYMOD, THYMOD, and GTHYMOD, show a similar Pearson correlation CDF shown in Fig. 4 b, which are all superior to that of LHYMOD. Among the correlation performances, GTHYMOD presents its superiority. The larger differences between the four models are visible in the variability and bias error (Fig. 4 c & 4d), especially for HYMOD and LHYMOD. The orange shades are presented in this figure for better visualization as the variability and bias error components reach 1 representing good performance. The figure illustrates that THYMOD and GTHYMOD perform similarly in the validation period where GTHYMOD presents a better performance for the correlation component of KGE, the superiority of GTHYMOD in the calibration period is also seen. Worse performance of LHYMOD in any evaluation metrics is obtained. Considering that the assumption within the TWI of Curve 3 may not universally apply compared to the more generalized assumption in Curve 4 of GTHYMOD, it is clear that GTHYMOD is considered the superior model for subsequent analysis.  3.2 Spatial analysis of validation period results The CDFs do not provide spatial information at a catchment scale. To gain insight into the spatial distribution of the KGE values across Australia, Fig. 5   presents the KGE values of the 460 study catchments derived from the four models during the validation period. A histogram of high KGE and low KGE catchment numbers among the 460 catchments for each model case is also included in this figure. As illustrated in Fig. 5 , catchments located near the eastern coast of Australia tend to present higher KGE whenever which model is used, including LHYMOD. These catchments are located in Queensland, New South Wales, and Tasmania. While the KGE in most of the Victoria catchments are larger than 0.4 (LHYMOD excluded), they are relatively worse than the aforementioned regions. Catchments near the western coast of Australia tend to have lower KGE performance, most of them located in Western Australia and South Australia. As analyzed in Section 3.1 , HYMOD performs better among the empirically-based models, while GTHYMOD performs better in the topography-based models. Differences between the two models are then compared in Fig. 5 a and Fig. 5 d. An improvement of the KGE is seen in the southwest of Western Australia, northwest of the Northern Territory, and north Queensland when GTHYMOD is used. Compared to the HYMOD model, where 66.7% of catchments are identified within high KGE performance, the GTHYMOD demonstrated an 8.1% increase, resulting in 74.8% of catchments being situated within high KGE performance.  3.3 Study of tension water storage capacity distribution curves 3.3.1 Parameters within curves Four conceptual rainfall-runoff models are introduced, each with its unique tension water storage capacity distribution. Among these, Curve 2 is a special case of Curve 1, and likewise, Curve 3 can be seen as a special case of Curve 4. Therefore, Curves 1 and 4 are compared against their individually calibrated parameters. Fig. 6   shows the spatial distribution of the parameter β  in Curve 1 and the parameter α  in Curve 4. In Fig. 6 a, it can be seen that the majority (77.6%) of parameter β  is less than 0.50, some high values are mainly located in northeast Queensland and west Tasmania. In Fig. 6 b, the parameter α  is equally distributed into positive (48.7%) and negative (51.3%) values. Most negative α  locates in Western Australia, Northern Territory, southeast Victoria, and west Tasmania, while positive α  concentrates on Queensland and New South Wales. Fig. 7   gives us an insight into how the curves vary with the parameters. The probability density functions (PDFs) of Curves 1 and 4 with various parameter values are presented. The scaled TWC (min–max normalization method) is used for visualization purposes. In Curve 1, the PDF is only based on parameter β  when the capacities are normalized, it applies to all kinds of catchments. In Curve 4, the PDF is related to parameter α  as well as local topographic information, Fig. 7 b gives an example (ID: 312061) of the capacity variations with the parameter. Different catchments may have different PDFs but the shape of the distribution remains similar. As depicted in Fig. 7 a, the PDF peak of Curve 1 occurs solely at its minimal capacity (when β > 1   ) or maximum capacity (when 0 < β < 1   ), consistent with the findings of Wang (2018) . This extreme condition indicates that the minimal or maximum capacity is assigned to the largest proportion. However, in Fig. 7 b, the PDF of Curve 4 exhibits an unimodal function, demonstrating flexibility in capturing various catchment states. This flexibility enables Curve 4 to accommodate the diversity of capacities within a catchment, potentially enhancing the overall performance of GTHYMOD. That elucidates why GTHYMOD demonstrates superior overall performance across 460 catchments with diverse hydrometeorological characteristics.  3.3.2 Spatial variability in individual catchments As a sample of the spatial distribution ability description of Curve 4, Figs. 8 & 9    illustrate the spatial distribution of the TWC and contributing area in two catchments. The catchments are sampled based on streamflow performance to avoid presentation bias. The catchments with all KGEs from the four models larger than 0.50 are categorized into good catchments, and vice will be concluded into poor catchments. The first catchment, Hellyer River at Guilford Junction station (Catchment HR, ID: 312061), covers an area of 100.8 km2 , with an annual average precipitation of 2089 mm and potential evapotranspiration of 1084 mm, categorizing the HR catchment as a humid, good catchment. The second catchment, CoCreekburn River at Mulla Crossing station (Catchment CR, ID: 419016), spans an area of 896.6 km2 , with an annual average precipitation of 780 mm and potential evapotranspiration of 1669 mm, placing the CR catchment as a semi-arid, poor catchment. One of the primary advantages of Curve 4 over Curve 1 is its capability to map key hydrologic components, such as TWC and contributing area, onto the terrain. Fig. 8  illustrates the spatial distribution of the digital elevation model (DEM) and scaled TWC estimated by GTHYMOD for the two individual catchments. After normalization, the scaled TWC ranges from 0 to 1 within each catchment. As depicted in Fig. 8 a & c, Catchment HR predominantly features smaller scaled capacities. These small-capacity grids tend to be situated near riparian regions, whereas grids with larger capacities are prevalent in high-elevation sites. However, for Catchment CR in Fig. 8 b & d, the majority of the catchment is characterized by larger scaled capacities. Similar to Catchment HR, grids with smaller capacities concentrate on riparian regions while those with larger capacities are consistent with high elevation. Note that the capacities discussed herein are relative to each individual catchment due to being scaled. Ordinarily, humid catchments present larger capacities compared to arid ones. The capacities accompanying smaller scaled values in Fig. 8 c might exceed those linked with larger scaled values in Fig. 8 d. Given the limited global temporal and spatial coverage of ground measurements of soil moisture (Ray et al., 2017 ), satellite surface soil moisture is employed to evaluate the reasonableness of Curve 4 in GTHYMOD. In this study, the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative (CCI) soil moisture product is utilized for the two study catchments due to its long time series data, which covers the study period. The ESA CCI product offers direct sensing of soil moisture in the top 2–5 cm of a soil column since 1978, with a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° and a temporal resolution of 1 day. While the coarse spatial resolution and differing interpretation of soil water render the product unsuitable for spatial validation or multi-objective parameter estimation for GTHYMOD, it aids in evaluating the TWC distribution to some extent by calculating the temporal correlation of satellite soil moisture and GTHYMOD simulated TWS. The correlation coefficients between ESA CCI soil moisture and model simulations for the HR catchment and CR catchment are 0.50 and 0.44, respectively, providing a quantitative assessment of the reasonableness of the spatial distribution of Curve 4 (Alexandridis et al., 2016 ). Simultaneously, the spatial distribution of the contributing area undergoes temporal variations during hydrological events. Fig. 9  showcases four-time points representing different levels of the contributing area, illustrating the spatial and temporal variations of the contributing area in Catchment HR and CR. Given that a small TWC within a lumped catchment indicates a higher likelihood of runoff generation, grids near the rivers tend to generate runoff first, a phenomenon corroborated in Fig. 9 . The area of these saturated sites gradually expands to the entire catchment in response to precipitation (Yao et al., 2012 ).    4 Discussion 4.1 Relation between KGE and catchment attributes In this section, it is investigated if the GTHYMOD model performance (validation period) varies based on the catchment attributes such as catchment area and humidity. 4.1.1 Catchment area Fig. 10   shows the association of model performance with catchment areas across the 460 catchments. Panel (a) sheds light on this relationship by presenting a vivid scatter plot correlating the KGE with catchment area (log base 10). Of these catchments, 63.3% of the catchment area falls within the range of 2 to 3, and 83.3% of that situated between 2 and 4. Panel (b) provides the counted numbers of high KGE and low KGE catchments in each area category. As illustrated in Fig. 10 b, the high KGE catchments dominate in numbers, regardless of variances in the size of the catchment area. To be specific, when the catchment area ranges from 2 to 3, 48.5% of all studied catchments (460 in total) are identified to have high KGE performance while 14.8% display low KGE performance. Extending the area range to 2 to 4, the proportion of high KGE performing catchments increases to 61.7%, whereas the low KGE performers constitute 21.5%. The discussion indicates that the catchment area and streamflow performance do not appear to have a significant correlation, the model efficiency is maintained across various catchment sizes.  4.1.2 Catchment humidity As presented in Section 3.2 , catchments near the eastern coast of Australia are observed to yield high KGE performance while those residing along the western coastline own a markedly lower KGE performance. Fig. 11   presents an insight into the spatial distribution of catchment humidity to investigate whether the model performance relates to catchment humidity. Catchment humidity is quantified through the humidity index (HI), a metric that represents the ratio of the annual average precipitation to the annual average potential evapotranspiration (P / PET) (Goeking & Tarboton, 2022 ). The 460 catchments are categorized into humid (HI≥0.65), semi-humid (0.50 ≤ HI<0.65), semi-arid (0.20 ≤ HI<0.50), and arid regions (HI<0.20). As presented in Fig. 11 , the HI for catchments in Western Australia is smaller compared to those along the eastern coastline of Australia. The Pearson correlation coefficient is calculated between the KGE and HI, and a statistically significant positive correlation (0.37, p < 0.01) is obtained. Further investigation of the implications of catchment humidity on KGE performance is presented in Fig. 12  . In Fig. 12 a, the KGEs during the validation period under GTHYMOD for the 460 catchments are plotted with the HI. In line with the analysis in Fig. 11 , an evident positive correlation can be seen in Fig. 12 a. Therefore, in Fig. 12 b, the proportion of catchments exhibiting high and low KGE streamflow performance within each defined category, namely humid, semi-humid, semi-arid, and arid regions, is quantified. Over 90%, 70%, and 60% of catchments in the humid, semi-humid, and semi-arid regions respectively exhibit high KGE performance. It is observed that as the HI increases, so does the percentage of catchments with high KGE performance. On the contrary, catchments indicated by a smaller HI are more likely to exhibit a low KGE model performance.   4.2 Relation between TWC and topography attribute In Section 3.3.2 , the potential relationships between the TWC and elevation are explored in two individual catchments but lack a statistically large sample analysis. Fig. 13   shows the Pearson correlation coefficient of grid-based elevation and TWC in each of the 460 catchments. As depicted in Fig. 13 a, the correlation between the TWC and elevation is significant (p < 0.05) for most of catchments (three catchments labeled in red excluded). Further, a visual representation of the correlation coefficients' distribution is manifested in the form of a histogram, as shown in Fig. 13 b. The majority of correlation coefficients have concentrated within 0.2 to 0.6. Out of the 460 catchments, a robust correlation characterized by a coefficient greater than 0.40 is observed in 38.9% of the catchments under study. It suggests that a considerable proportion of catchments manifests a significant interplay between TWC and elevation.  4.3 Applicability of the models The benchmark model HYMOD, whose runoff is generated based on Curve 1, has been successfully applied to catchments worldwide with diverse hydrometeorological characteristics (Kollat et al., 2012; Bastola & Murphy, 2013; Naseem et al., 2015; Thiboult et al., 2016; Tajiki et al., 2020; Mai et al., 2021; Yoosefdoost et al., 2022 ). However, the relationship between model runoff generation mechanisms and catchment attributes is usually overlooked. The saturation-excess (runoff is generated when the TWC is saturated) (Dunne & Black, 1970; Dunne, 1978 ) and infiltration-excess (runoff is generated when rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration rate) (Horton, 1933 ) are two widely used runoff generation mechanisms (Yang et al., 2015 ). In this study, all the four models are based on the saturation-excess runoff generation mechanism. This categorization results in some catchments aligning more closely with the mechanism than others (Euser et al., 2013 ), leading to high KGE and low KGE model performance. Previous studies have indicated that saturation-excess runoff dominates in wet conditions, while infiltration-excess runoff dominates in relatively dry conditions (Latron & Gallart, 2008; Huang et al., 2016; Hoang et al., 2017; Huo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022 ). That explains why models perform well in the humid, semi-humid, and semi-arid regions, while exhibiting generally poorer performance in the arid regions.  4.4 Limitations and outlook The parameters within the models including HYMOD, LHYMOD, THYMOD, and GTHYMOD are all individually calibrated to maximize the objective function — KGE of streamflow in this study. Consequently, there may be a parameter compensation effect to some degree (i.e., differences in hydrograph may be compensated by adjusting parameters in different models), leading to similar streamflow simulations under different TWC distributions, similar findings have also been revealed in previous studies (Wolock & McCabe, 1995 ; Franchini et al., 1996; Gong et al., 2011 ). The impact of parameter fluctuations on model output has not been investigated in this work. Parameter sensitivity analysis could be used in our future work to provide further insight and improvement. This approach stands to differentiate the effects resulting from model setup from those originating in parameter calibration. The four models applied in this study are lumped and calibrated individually across various Australian catchments. Each catchment is treated as an isolated unit, assuming no water exchange between them, an approach that might overlook the potential hydrological connectivity among different catchments. Furthermore, within a particular catchment, the connectivity is deemed negligible and hence not accounted for in the results. The unsatisfactory result in the arid and semi-arid catchments (Fig. 12 ) suggests that a hydrological model with a single runoff generation mechanism has limitations in representing runoff in all types of catchments. Therefore, our future work will involve incorporating both saturation-excess and infiltration-excess runoff in the models, and acknowledging the potential for connectivity between catchments to enhance the streamflow performance.   5 Conclusions This study revisits the empirical tension water storage capacity distribution widely used in conventional conceptual rainfall-runoff models and introduces three other alternative distributions for comparison. Four conceptual rainfall-runoff models, involving the HYMOD, LHYMOD, THYMOD, and GTHYMOD, are employed in 460 Australian catchments to investigate the impact of the TWC distribution on daily streamflow performance. The major findings of this study are as follows:(1) Changes in the TWC distribution would remarkably affect the streamflow performance, where GTHYMOD performs best and LHYMOD tends to produce less satisfactory results on the whole. Spatial analysis reveals that the catchments situated near Australia’s eastern coast generally exhibit higher KGE whereas those near the western coast are associated with lower KGE performance. Furthermore, 74.8% of catchments are identified with high KGE in GTHYMOD compared to 66.7% in HYMOD during the validation period. Notable improvements in GTHYMOD are observed in the southwest of Western Australia, northwest of the Northern Territory, and north Queensland.  (2) Comparing the empirical Curve 1 with topographic Curve 4 reveals the latter’s ability in GTHYMOD model to flexibly capture the distribution of catchment capacities without succumbing to extreme minimum or maximum conditions, enhancing its adaptability across a range of catchments. Moreover, GTHYMOD presents the ability to redistribute the spatial variation of key hydrological elements, including the TWC and contributing area, into the real world. The results suggest that the GTWI-based TWC distribution presents a potential alternative to the currently used empirical distribution in traditional conceptual rainfall-runoff models.  (3) A statistically significant positive correlation between the KGE performance and catchment humidity is discerned. High KGE performance is noted in over 90% of catchments in humid regions, 70% in semi-humid regions, and 60% in semi-arid regions respectively. Meanwhile, a significant relationship between the TWC and elevation is discovered, and a robust correlation with a coefficient exceeding 0.40 is observed in 38.9% of the catchments under study.
1 Introduction To cope with global climate change, China has explicitly set the goal of “carbon peaking by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060”. This commitment aims to upgrade the capability of green development by promoting the construction of a modern energy system (Liu et al., 2022 ). In response to the need for renewable energy sources in the transformation of the sustainable energy system, China has explicitly outlined the actions of promoting the substitution of renewable energy in the “14th Five-Year Plan”. One of these actions is actively implementing the construction of major hydropower bases, such as those located in the lower Yarlung Zangbo River, the middle and upper Jinsha River, and the middle Yalong River (National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), 2021; Mallapaty, 2020 ). These basins are concentrated in the southwestern region of China, where there are mostly high mountains and deep canyons with abundant precipitation. In addition, many rivers in this region twist and turn, creating numerous river bends with great drops. For example, at the large bend of the Yarlung Zangbo River, there is a significant 2400 m drop over a distance of 35 km, and the hydraulic energy reserves in this area are estimated to be nearly three times that of the Three Gorges Reservoir (Yang et al., 2019 ). At the Jinping bend of the Yalong River mainstream, a drop of 310 m is amassed over a distance of only 16 km (Wu and Wang, 2011 ). Furthermore, at the Tianshengqiao bend of the Nanpan River, a significant decrease of 180 m is generated within a relatively short distance of 10 km (Zhang and Chen, 2016 ). As shown in Fig. 1  , the topographic and geomorphologic conditions of these areas can be strategically leveraged to build diversion tunnels for efficient water redirection and electricity generation, which can not only effectively concentrate the substantial drops in river bends, but also reduce the need for the construction of large reservoirs, thereby achieving the dual benefit of economic viability and environmental conservation. However, in some river bend areas, where the ultrahigh hydraulic head significantly exceeds the typical range for conventional hydroelectric plants, direct utilization of this immense hydraulic potential for power generation has become exceedingly challenging. In such cases, one viable solution is to arrange a series of interconnected multistage hydropower stations end-to-end, thereby gradually harnessing the concentrated high hydraulic head and abundant streamflow. Fig. 2   shows a schematic diagram of CSDHP. The CSDHP system includes multiple tunnels and multiple units, and complex hydraulic and electric couplings exist, which makes the short-term coordinated scheduling of the CSDHP system extremely complicated compared with that of conventional diversion type hydropower plants. On the one hand, limited by topographic conditions, environmental limitations, and economic factors, only small regulating reservoirs with poor storage can be constructed between hydropower plants of CSDHP, which serve primarily for emergency regulation in the case of operational disruptions, so the turbine discharge of upstream and downstream hydropower plants needs to be strictly matched during normal operations. On the other hand, there are numerous complexities of the CSDHP system, such as multiple units sharing one diversion tunnel, different numbers of units sharing the same diversion tunnel in different hydropower plants, and different types of units in different hydropower plants, which leads to serious hydraulic interconnections between units, and further increases the complexity of the problem. With the vigorous development of hydropower in Southwest China, an increasing of CSDHP systems will be placed into operation in the future, and the coordinated scheduling and safe operation of the system will face great challenges (Guo and Zhu, 2018 ). Therefore, it is essential to study the accurate modeling and rapid solving of the short-term load distribution problem of CSDHP systems under complex conditions, which is important for the development and the efficient and safe operation of hydropower in water-rich regions of Southwest China. The short-term scheduling of hydropower plants typically aims to determine the optimal generation outputs, water storage, and flow rates of each plant and to achieve specific objectives such as minimum water consumption, maximum generation, and water management regulations under the corresponding hydraulic and electrical constraints. In recent years, many scholars have conducted in-depth research on the short-term scheduling of hydropower plants. The scheduling objectives include power generation maximization (Avesani et al., 2022 ), water consumption minimization (Liao et al., 2023 ), and system peak shaving (Cheng et al., 2018; Su et al., 2022 ). The power generation maximization model formulates the optimal scheduling plan based on the inflow forecast, so that the system can operate at high efficiency and achieve the highest power generation; the water consumption minimization model determines the output process of plants according to the issued power generation plan or load forecast results of the system, and minimizes water consumption while meeting power demand, thereby improving system economy; and the peak shaving model aims to reduce the fluctuation of residual load by taking full advantage of hydropower flexibility, to avoid frequent adjustments of thermal output and ensure a clean and efficient power system. In addition, some scholars are committed to achieving more precise descriptions of the model by considering corresponding constraints. Su et al. (2020 ) constructed a day-ahead scheduling model to maximize the power generation profit, which considered the head-dependent irregular forbidden zones of units and other hydraulic couplings between cascade hydropower plants. Lei et al. (2022 ) introduced the concept of equal reservoir full storage rate to guide the load distribution of cascade hydropower plants, to achieve synchronous peak shaving and the goal of fairness. Belsnes et al. (2016 ) considered the uncertainty of price and inflow in the future, established a short-term stochastic scheduling model, and transformed it into a linear form for the solution. Daadaa et al. (2021 ) considered the energy losses caused by unit start-ups in the unit commitment problem, and limited the maximum number of unit start-up times. Shen et al. (2014 ) proposed a mutative scale scheduling method for large-scale hydropower plants to address complex temporal coupling constraints such as output ramping constraints, and achieved efficient solutions. However, the aforementioned studies have primarily concentrated on the scheduling of reservoir-type cascade hydropower plants, and the complex situation of CSDHP studied in this paper has been infrequently addressed. At present, overall research on diversion-type hydropower plants is limited to the problems of single hydropower plant. For example, Liao et al. (2021 ) proposed a short-term scheduling model to solve the problem of two units sharing one tunnel in the Tianshengqiao-II hydropower plant. In this model, the water consumption requirements for start-ups and shut-downs of units as well as crossing the forbidden zones were considered in detail, which effectively reduced the water consumption of the plant. Zhao et al. (2019) and Liao et al. (2019 ) proposed a two-stage optimization model to study the same problem, where the optimal unit commitment is determined in the first stage, and then the load distribution is achieved under the goal of minimum water consumption in the second stage. Some scholars have studied the problem of multiple units sharing one tunnel in cascade hydropower plants. For example, Skjelbred et al. (2020 ) studied the accurate modeling and linearization method of the hydropower production function of units based on the short-term scheduling problem of a hydropower system in Norway. Among them, three units with different characteristics of the Vinje hydropower plant share one main tunnel, and four units with the same characteristics of the downstream Tokke hydropower plant share two penstocks and one main tunnel. However, there is a reservoir between the above two diversion-type hydropower plants, which can be used to regulate the water flow, so that the two plants operate independently, and there are no complex conditions, such as strict matching of turbine discharge in this paper. Therefore, the conditions are not suitable for the coordinated optimal scheduling of complex CSDHP systems, which is the focus of this paper. The main challenges of the scheduling problem for the CSDHP system in this paper are the complex characteristics posed by diversion-type hydropower plants operating in series. On the one hand, there is only a large reservoir present in the first plant within the CSDHP system, and the remaining plants are equipped with only regulation pools that have limited storage capacity and serve primarily as emergency backups. Therefore, the operation of the CSDHP system requires meticulous synchronization of turbine flow between the upstream and downstream hydropower plants to ensure operational security. On the other hand, the complexity is compounded by the constraints in which multiple units share a common tunnel, thereby introducing numerous hydraulic and electrical constraints. How to cater for these special operational demands and facilitate the actual scheduling management are the major concerns that need to be considered in detail. Based on the aforementioned background, this paper targets the intricate short-term scheduling problem of the CSDHP system by proposing a load distribution model that accounts for the strict matching of the turbine flow and multiple units sharing a common tunnel. This allows for precise modeling and efficient resolution, ultimately ensuring safe and cost-effective CSDHP operation. First, a simplified method based on unit groups is proposed to divide the units sharing the serial diversion tunnels into a unit group according to the structure of the CSDHP system. Second, the flow matching of the plants is transformed into flow matching within each unit group. Third, to minimize total water consumption, a load distribution model is constructed by comprehensively considering complex hydraulic and electric couplings such as water head loss from long-distance water diversion, water consumption during unit start-ups and shut-downs, unit forbidden zone avoidance, and strict matching of the turbine flow. Then the model is transformed into a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) format using linearization techniques, and the problem complexity is further addressed by employing an iterative approach. This reduces the model’s dimensionality through the fixed gross water head principle for each unit, augmenting the accuracy of the optimal solution through successive approximation. Finally, the effectiveness and practicability of the proposed model are verified through a CSDHP system in the southwest region of China. The contributions of this paper are as follows:(1) Constructing a novel short-term load distribution model for the CSDHP system, which considers complex hydraulic and electric couplings such as the strict matching of the turbine flow and multiple units sharing a common tunnel.  (2) A simplified method based on unit groups is proposed, in which the upstream and downstream corresponding diversion tunnels are regarded to be connected in series, and multiple units sharing the serial diversion tunnels are classified into a unit group.  (3) The model is applied to CSDHP in Southwest China to verify its performance. The results demonstrate that the model can effectively achieve the load distribution of CSDHP system and can significantly reduce water consumption compared to traditional methods, proving to be invaluable in aiding the day-ahead scheduling of CSDHP.    The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2  delineates the intricacies of the proposed model. Section 3  presents the reformulation of the model into a mixed integer linear form and describes the implementation of an iterative technique to enhance computational efficiency. The performance of the model in real case studies is elucidated in Section 4 . Finally, Section 5  presents the conclusions of the study.  2 Short-term load distribution model of the CSDHP system 2.1 Grouping of units in the CSDHP system According to the structure of the CSDHP system in Fig. 2 , there are only regulation pools between upstream and downstream plants, which have limited storage capacity and serve primarily as emergency backups. Therefore, the discharge of upstream and downstream hydropower plants needs to be strictly matched during operation. However, there are numerous complex constraints and high-dimensional nonlinear variables in the problem, thus imposing great difficulties on the solution of the model if all the units are modeled independently. In this regard, this paper innovatively proposes a simplified method based on unit groups, in which the corresponding upstream and downstream diversion tunnels are regarded to be connected in series, and multiple units sharing the serial diversion tunnels are classified into a unit group, as shown in Fig. 2 . Therefore, the flow matching and synchronized regulation of all hydropower plants can be realized by ensuring flow matching within each unit group, which greatly reduces the size of the problem, and the unit control is simpler and aligns more closely with the actual operation control requirements of the hydropower station. Each unit of the CSDHP system can then be indexed according to the plant and unit group to which it belongs, where t   and T   denote the time period index and the total number of time periods, respectively; m   and M   denote the hydropower plant index and the total number of cascade plants, respectively; i   and I   denote the unit group index and the total number of unit groups, respectively; and j   and J i , m     denote the unit index and the total number of units corresponding to hydropower plant m   within the i  -th unit group.  2.2 Objective The overall power output curve of a cascade hydropower plant in actual operation is arranged by the grid company, so the main task of the short-term load distribution of the CSDHP system is to distribute the system load demand to each unit, and to ensure the minimum water consumption of the plants within various constraints, to obtain the on–off strategy of the units and the scheduling plan of the units.
