According to the theory of unsteady flow in pressurized pipeline, the propagation speed of water hammer in diversion tunnel is relatively fast; therefore, for short-term operation with a time step of 1 h, the transmission time (<10 s) can be ignored in this study, and it can be simplified to consider that the flow in long diversion tunnels of a unit group is equal everywhere. The flow in a diversion tunnel includes the water consumption for start-ups and shut-downs of units, the water consumption for crossing the forbidden zones, and the water consumption for power generation, which can be expressed as:(25) q i , t  tunl  = ∑ j = 1  J i , m    q i , m , j , t   + γ i , m , j , t  on  · W i , m , j  on  + γ i , m , j , t  off  · W i , m , j  off  + o i , m , j , t  cross  · W i , m , j  cross    3600 · Δ t     ; i ∈ 1 , I   , m ∈ 1 , M   , t ∈ 1 , T      where W i , m , j  on    , W i , m , j  off    , and W i , m , j  cross     are the water consumption for start-ups, shut-downs, and crossing the forbidden zones of unit #i  -m  -j  , respectively. If the unit is turned on, shutdown, or crosses the forbidden zones during the period, the corresponding 0-1 variables are taken as 1, and vice versa, then the total flow through the unit can be obtained. This constraint ensures that the tunnels within a unit group have equal flow at all sections and in all periods, and is refined to consider the different water consumption of the units. In this study, the pressurized pipes are very long, and bear a large water head, thus generating a strong water hammer pressure that can significantly impact safety; hence, the change rate of the flow in the pipes needs to be limited:(26) q i , t + 1  tunl   - q i , t  tunl     ≤ Δ q  ¯   i  tunl   ; i ∈ 1 , I   , t ∈ 1 , T - 1       where Δ q  ¯   i  tunl      is the maximum flow fluctuation of the i  -th diversion tunnel between two periods.    3 Model solution method The proposed model represents a challenging high-dimensional and nonlinear optimization problem. Intrinsically, the model features an extensive array of nonlinear constraints that augment its complexity. Therefore, an appropriate method is required to mitigate the computational complexity involved. 3.1 Model linearization The production function of the hydropower unit is a two-dimensional nonlinear relationship that relates the output to both the net water head and turbine discharge. Linearizing these functions is a commonly used method, that has been widely applied in the field of hydropower scheduling. At present, mixed integer linear programming (MILP) modeling methods, which discretize a two-dimensional surface into meshed form and introduce 0-1 variables for modeling, such as the multiple choice method (MC) (Garcia-Gonzalez and Castro, 2001; Tong et al., 2013 ), special ordered sets of type 2 method (SOS2) (Zhao et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2017 ), logarithmic method (Vielma et al., 2010; Brito et al., 2020 ), and triangle method (Babayev, 1997; Li et al., 2014 ) are mature methods for addressing this nonlinear function. However, the short-term scheduling model of the CSDHP system developed in this research encounters challenges arising from an extensive array of units with complex hydraulic couplings, coupled with an increased number of 0-1 variables introduced when employing the traditional MILP modeling method, which retains considerable complexity even after linearization. To reduce the number of nonlinear variables in the model and enhance the solution efficiency, this study introduces a linear approximation model that circumvents the introduction of 0-1 variables by leveraging the parallelogram method proposed by Guisandez and Ignacio Perez-Diaz (2021) ). In the parallelogram method, the turbine discharge Q and the net water head H are gridded, where each grid is a parallelogram (not required to be orthogonal), and the original surface is sampled according to the grid vertices. However, the feasible domain of Q-H obtained by this method is not a rectangle, but a parallelogram in which the maximum and minimum turbine discharge increase accordingly with increasing net water head, which is different from the characteristics of the unit in this paper, so the grids are set to be rectangles that are orthogonal to each other. Then, we linearize constraint (24) :(27) h i , m , j , t   ≥ H i , m , j  0  + ∑ u = 1  U  h i , m , j , t , u  aux       (28) h i , m , j , t , u  aux   ≤ γ i , m , j , t   · H i , m , j  1  - H i , m , j  0    ; u = 1    h i , m , j , t , u  aux   ≤ h i , m , j , t , u - 1  aux   ; u > 1           (29) q i , m , j , t   = γ i , m , j , t   · Q i , m , j  0  + ∑ v = 1  V  q i , m , j , t , 1 , v  aux       (30) q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux   ≤ γ i , m , j , t   · Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1     ; u = 1    q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux   ≤ h i , m , j , t , u - 1  aux   · Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1     / H i , m , j  u - 1   - H i , m , j  u - 2     ; u > 1           (31) q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux   ≤ q i , m , j , t , u - 1 , v  aux   ; u > 1     (32) P i , m , j , t   = γ i , m , j , t   · P i , m , j  0 , 0   + ∑ v = 1  V  q i , m , j , t , 1 , v  aux   · P i , m , j  0 , v   - P i , m , j  0 , v - 1    Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1       + ∑ u = 2  U  q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux   · P i , m , j  u - 1 , v   - P i , m , j  u - 1 , v - 1    Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1     - P i , m , j  u - 2 , v   - P i , m , j  u - 2 , v - 1    Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1         + ∑ u = 2  U  q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux   · P i , m , j  u - 1 , v   - P i , m , j  u - 1 , v - 1    Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1     - P i , m , j  u - 2 , v   - P i , m , j  u - 2 , v - 1    Q i , m , j  v  - Q i , m , j  v - 1         + ∑ u = 1  U  h i , m , j , t , u  aux   P i , m , j  u , 0   - P i , m , j  u - 1 , 0      / H i , m , j  u  - H i , m , j  u - 1         where U   and V   are the number of discrete segments of the net water head and turbine discharge, respectively. Q i , m , j  v   , H i , m , j  u    and P i , m , j  u , v     are the Q-H grid point coordinates and the corresponding output value of the hydropower production function of unit #i  -m  -j  , respectively. h i , m , j , t , u  aux     and q i , m , j , t , u , v  aux     are the net water head auxiliary variable (U   dimension) and the turbine discharge auxiliary variable (U × V    dimension), respectively. A schematic of the linearization is shown in Fig. 4   below. This method requires that the hydropower production function be concave, i.e., the increase in output slows down as the turbine discharge increases, because there is an implicit condition in the method that requires the unit to prioritize the utilization of the more efficient portion of the unit, thus preventing the auxiliary variables from taking arbitrary values. Since water consumption is guaranteed to be minimized in the objective function, ensuring that the hydropower production function is concave will satisfy this condition naturally. Similar to the aforementioned two-dimensional linearization method, MILP modeling of a one-dimensional curve is a mature method. The one-dimensional relationships (23)  are linearized using the multiple choice method (Tong et al., 2013 ), and the specific process of the method is note described in detail.  3.2 Iterative method According to constraint (22) , the net water head of the unit is obtained by subtracting the head loss in the diversion tunnel from the gross water head, which is determined by the average forebay water level and the tailwater level during the period. By assuming a constant gross water head, the two accompanying nonlinear constraints, specifically the relationship between the forebay water level and reservoir storage and the relationship between the tailwater level and the total discharge, can be obviated, hence significantly mitigating the model complexity. However, the generating units within CSDHP are acutely sensitive to changes in the water head, and their power generation output is substantially influenced by fluctuations in the net water head. Disregarding this factor would lead to considerable errors in short-term scheduling, which cannot meet the increasing demand for accuracy in scheduling. Therefore, to reconcile the need for both model simplification and accuracy, this paper introduces an iterative approach that enhances the accuracy of the model through successive refinements, thereby progressively diminishing scheduling errors. The water head-based iterative method first fixes the gross head of each unit, and then solves the scheduling problem, and the gross head in the result is used as the initial value for the next iteration, which is repeated until the accuracy requirement is met. The solution process is shown in Fig. 5  . This method has been widely applied in hydropower scheduling problems (Liao et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020 ), and the specific steps are shown below.(1) Estimate the turbine discharge according to the average output scheduling model (equal discharge for each unit belonging to the same unit group and same hydropower station), so that the gross head h i , m , t  gross     is calculated as an initial value;  (2) Establish an MILP model in which constraint (22)  is transformed into constraint (33)  and constraint (6)  and constraint (7)  are eliminated. Then, the MILP solver is invoked to solve the model;   (33) h i , m , j , t   = h i , m , t  gross   - h i , m , t  loss       (3) Based on the actual operation process in the above result, the gross head of each unit is obtained and updated as a known parameter for the next calculation;  (4) Repeat steps (2) to (3) until gross water head error reaches the requirement.    By the iterative method, two nonlinear constraints are eliminated, the number of 0-1 variables and constraints are greatly reduced, and the efficiency of the MILP model can be enhanced.   4 Case study China's southwest region has many high mountains and deep valleys, and some rivers have large drops and turns, which are very suitable for the construction of long diversion tunnels to amass and utilize the natural drop of the river for power generation. With the continuous improvement of hydropower development technology in China, the country has also begun to gradually develop hydropower projects with higher engineering technical requirements. In the southwestern regions of China, some areas with significant drops and turns in river terrains are being increasingly planned and exploited as CSDHP, which aim to effectively utilize the available high water heads. The unique flow-matching mechanisms of these cascade hydropower plants pose significant challenges in the optimization of large-scale unit operational scheduling, which necessitates in-depth research. This paper examines a case study of a planned hydropower system in Southwest China to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model. The structure of the system is shown in Fig. 6  , the parameters of each unit are shown in Table 1  , and the boundary conditions of the case study are shown in Table 2  . The CSDHP system exhibited obvious differences between the flood and dry seasons. Therefore, this paper considers the typical days of the two seasons to analyze the effectiveness of the model. The system load demand on a typical day during the flood and dry seasons is shown in Fig. 7  , and the natural inflow and load data used in the case studies are provided in the Supplement Table S1 . To compare and analyze the effect of the model in this paper, the average output scheduling model and the traditional one-tunnel-multiple-units model are introduced, and the differences between each model are shown in Table 3  . Among them, the average output scheduling model first determines the on–off combination according to the minimum and maximum turbine discharge of the units and their rated capacity, then runs each unit in the on-state at equal turbine discharge, and finally determines the operation process of each unit according to the load demand; the traditional one-tunnel-multiple-units model does not consider the strict matching of the turbine discharge of the serial diversion tunnels. Moreover, the previously constructed linearized model is modeled using Pyomo in Python and solved by Gurobi 10.0. The solution procedure is shown in Fig. 5 , in which the termination criterion of the iteration is set to an error of less than 0.001, and in each iteration the procedure is interrupted when the gap reaches 0.001. All programs were developed and implemented on a personal computer equipped with an Intel Core i7-7700HQ CPU @2.80 GHz and 16.0 GB of RAM. 4.1 Flood season During the flood season, the hydropower system experiences a significant increase in inflow, and with a higher load demand, which typically manifests as a pronounced single-peak pattern, as shown in Fig. 7 . Additionally, to comply with flood control mandates, it is crucial to maintain the reservoir’s water level below the designated flood control limit. Consequently, reservoir water levels during the flood season are usually lower than those during the dry season, which in turn reduces the hydraulic head at the first stations of the CSDHP. By solving the model for a typical day during the flood season, the flow of each diversion tunnel and the net water head of each unit are obtained as shown in Fig. 8  . This model takes into account the turbine discharge matching constraints so that the tunnels within each serial unit group have equal flows (i.e., Tunnel 1-1 is equal to Tunnel 1-2, and Tunnel 2-1 is equal to Tunnel 2-2). During the peak load periods, the flow in the tunnels is higher, and the turbine discharge of the units is close to their maximum capacity. In terms of the unit net water head, the head loss of multiple units sharing a long, pressurized diversion tunnel is greatly affected by the flow, which can reach 10 ∼ 12 m during the flood season, resulting in drastic fluctuations in the net water head of the units. In Fig. 8 (b), the diversion tunnels corresponding to upstream hydropower Plant A have a smaller drop and therefore a lower net water head (as shown by the solid line in the figure for Tunnel 1-1 and Tunnel 2-1), while the diversion tunnels corresponding to downstream hydropower Plant B have a larger drop and therefore a higher net water head with a greater fluctuation (as shown by the dashed line in the figure for Tunnel 1-2 and Tunnel 2-2). Since the flows of the serial tunnels are matched and the head loss is related to the flow, the net water head fluctuations of the serial tunnels share a similar trend, but the magnitude varies considerably depending on the concentrated drop as well as the tunnel parameters. The results of the load distribution for each unit are shown in Fig. 9  . The load is notably higher from 8:00 to 21:00, during which all units operate at high output levels. For the units of hydropower plant A (#1-1-1, #1-1-2, #2-1-1, #2-1-2), which has an upstream reservoir, the water level is kept low in the reservoir to ensure safe operation during the flood season. This results in the turbine discharge reaching the maximum capacity of the unit before the power output attains the rated capacity. Conversely, the units of hydropower plant B (#1-2-1, #1-2-2, #1-2-3, #2-2-1, #2-2-2, #2-2-3) benefit from an upstream regulation pool, and due to the strict matching constraint of the flow in the serial diversion tunnels, the water level of the regulating pool remains relatively stable, and the downstream tailwater fluctuation is small (see detail in Supplementary Table S2 ). This enables the units to consistently operate at a high net water head, allowing the units to approach their rated capacity. As shown in Fig. 9 , the operation strategy for the proposed model aims to maintain the power output on the stable side of the forbidden zone to avoid falling into the forbidden zone. Moreover, due to the minimum turbine discharge limit and the higher water consumption rate at lower outputs, units are shut down under low load conditions to meet economic operation requirements, with the remaining load being distributed among the operational units. In contrast, the average output model makes the working units share the same power output task, making the output of each unit quite low during low-load hours and thus far from the high-efficiency zone. In addition, since the average output model cannot consider the forbidden zone constraints, the units frequently fall into the forbidden zone during operation, which is seriously detrimental to the safe operation of the hydropower plant. Similarly, the one-tunnel-multiple-units model traverses the forbidden zone more frequently compared to the proposed model as the former does not consider the turbine discharge matching constraints. According to these constraints, the downstream flow in one tunnel includes the water consumption for start-ups and shut-downs, the water consumption for crossing the forbidden zones, and the water consumption for power generation of the upstream units, therefore, if the turbine discharge matching constraints are ignored, the water consumption caused by the upstream units crossing the forbidden zones will not be related to the downstream. Since the model penalizes the unit for crossing the forbidden zones by considering the relevant water consumption, the lack of turbine discharge matching constraints will lead to more times of crossing forbidden zones. In Table 4  , the number of times forbidden zones are crossed is presented. The data indicate that by considering the water consumption of crossing the forbidden zones and the flow matching, the number of times that the unit traverses the forbidden zone decreases from 28 and 30 to 15, which constitutes a 46.4 % and 50.0 % reduction, respectively. This substantial decrease indicates that the proposed model can lead to significant decreases in the wear experienced by the units and the water consumption, thereby achieving augmented economic benefits. Table 5   presents a comparison of the results from different models. The water consumption of the proposed model is the lowest, a decrease of by 1.8 % and 0.2 % compared to that of the average output scheduling model and the traditional one-hole-multiple-units model, respectively. This difference in water consumption of the former is attributed to the varying number of units activated at different times across different models, as detailed in Section 4.3 ; and the latter is mainly due to the different times that the units crossing the forbidden zones, as shown in Table 4 , the upstream units (#1-1-1, #1-1-2, #2-1-1, #2-1-2) of the one-tunnel-multiple-units model traverse the forbidden zones more frequently as it does not consider the turbine discharge matching constraints, resulting in higher water consumption.  4.2 Dry season On a typical day in the dry season, the load demand exhibits a double-peak pattern. During the dry season, characterized by reduced inflow, hydropower plants experience a decrease in power generation and are primarily used for peak shaving due to their inherent regulation flexibility. The case of a typical day during the dry season is solved, and the flow of each diversion tunnel and the net water head of each unit are shown in Fig. 10  . As demonstrated, during periods of low demand, only one unit group operates, maintaining high operational efficiency and avoiding the need to activate other units that would run inefficiently at lower turbine discharges. This strategy minimizes water consumption across the system. As the load demand increases, another unit group is activated to collaboratively satisfy the escalating system load requirements. The load distribution results for each model on the typical day in the dry season are depicted in Fig. 11  . During these periods, the contribution of hydropower to peak shaving is more critical, and the unit output fluctuates more frequently to leverage the flexibility of hydropower. As shown in Table 6  , the power fluctuations caused by hydropower peak shaving during the dry season greatly increase the number of times that the units cross the forbidden zone compared those during the flood season. In addition, the number of times that the units traverse the forbidden zone in the proposed model decreases by 35.1 % and 52.0 %, respectively, compared to the other two models. In contrast to the flood season case, the reservoir’s operational strategy maintains higher water levels in the dry season, facilitating high water head and enabling units to reach the rated capacity. As shown in Table 7  , when comparing the proposed model’s performance to that of the average output scheduling model and the traditional one-tunnel-multiple-units model, the water consumption is reduced by 6.1 % and 0.7 %, respectively.  4.3 Comparison of the results Based on the case study, the water consumption of the proposed model is reduced by 1.8 % and 0.2 % compared to that of the average output scheduling model and the traditional one-tunnel-multiple-units model during the flood season and by 6.1 % and 0.7 %, respectively, during the dry season. There appears to be a focus on conserving more water during the dry season. The discharge process and the on/off status of the units of each model are shown in Figs. 12   and 13  . As we can observe from the comparison of the results in Figs. 12 (a) and 13 (a), the average output model requires larger water consumption during the low load hours. This is because the average output model first determines the on/off combination of the units according to their minimum turbine discharge, maximum turbine discharge, rated capacity and load demand, which must ensure that the load demand can be met under any complex circumstances and leaves a large redundancy, resulting in more working units in operation, as shown in Figs. 12 (b) and 13 (b). Therefore, the turbine discharge for each unit is smaller, resulting in a lower output efficiency. The other two models are optimal scheduling models, which can keep the units in the high-efficiency zone as much as possible, so there is a large difference in water consumption during low load hours. During peak load hours, the output of the system is high, and all the units are operated in the three models, so their output efficiencies are relatively close. In summary, by solving the optimization problem, the model proposed in this paper ensures the optimal combination of working units, which can manifest greater advantages and achieve greater economic benefits during low-load periods. Compared with the flood season, the peak load period is shorter and the low load period is longer in the dry season, so the proposed model conserves more water during the dry season. Furthermore, the water consumption rate of the proposed model on the typical day during the dry season is 1.345 m3 /kW·h, while it is 1.450 m3 /kW·h on the typical day during the flood season, a difference of 7.2 %. This is because the forebay water level is controlled at a low state during the flood season for safety, resulting in a lower water head, as shown in Figs. 8 and 10 . Therefore, the efficient use of a higher water head in the dry season translates to a lower water consumption rate than that in the flood season.   5 Conclusion With the ongoing planning and development of China’s CSDHP systems, these facilities present complex hydraulic and electrical challenges for hydropower operation and power grid dispatching management. In anticipation of the scheduling requirements of large-scale CSDHP, this paper addresses the short-term scheduling problem by establishing a comprehensive load distribution model. This model considers the coordination of turbine discharge between diversion tunnels and the intricate constraints of multiple units sharing one tunnel. To diminish the computational complexity, this paper effectively transforms the model into an MILP form using a linearization approach and verifies its practicability and effectiveness through case studies. From these studies, the following conclusions can be drawn:(1) The proposed model aims at achieving efficient load distribution among units while minimizing water consumption, and takes into account both the turbine discharge matching constraints of serial diversion tunnels and the complex constraints of multiple units sharing one tunnel. It precisely delineates the engineering complexities of CSDHP and quantifies the head loss of diversion tunnels, the water consumption of the units' start-ups and shut-downs, the forbidden zones, and the water consumption of crossing the forbidden zones, thereby achieving a more effective reduction in system water consumption.  (2) By employing a two-dimensional linearization technique and an iterative approach that bypasses the need for a large number of binary variables, the model considerably decreases the number of nonlinear variables and model complexity. This approach allows the model to handle the complex scheduling problems in this paper.  (3) The efficiency of the proposed model is verified through case studies of a CSDHP system. By linearizing the model to an MILP form and employing iterative computation, the previously challenging large-scale nonlinear problem is solved both efficiently and accurately. On typical days during the flood and dry seasons, the model achieves water savings of 1.8 % and 6.1 %, respectively, compared with the average output scheduling model, which effectively improves the economy of the system.
1 Introduction The state of plant water is a balance between soil water supply and atmospheric water demand (Donnellan et al., 2018 ). Studies show that radial water dynamics between stem water storage tissue and xylem vessel determine stem shape such as stem volume and diameter (Vandegehuchte et al., 2014 ). Thus, changes in stem diameter are often used to determine the state of plant water (Lee et al., 1998 ). Additionally, micro-change in stem diameter is not only affected by change in the plant water state, but also by the process of xylem vessel formation. While the reverse expansion or shrinkage of stem volume is caused by plant water budget balance, the division and elongation of cambium cells can lead to irreversible xylem vessel growth (Deslauriers et al., 2003; Downes et al., 1999 ). The prerequisite for the irreversible growth in stem diameter is sufficient radial water transport intensity. As cell expansion pressure exceeds a specific threshold, cell expansion occurs that in turn causes carbohydrate to enter the cell structure (Vandegehuchte et al., 2014 ). This suggests that both biophysical hydraulic and carbon-related processes affect the radial transport between xylem and storage tissues, which further impact the stem diameter growth (Zweifel et al., 2006; Zweifel et al., 2021 ). Thus, studies on trunk diameter growth could explain the complex reciprocal feedback among plant carbon balance, water state and external environmental conditions. These are important elements of the response of plants to drought stress and the basis for water management strategies such as irrigation (Vandegehuchte et al., 2014 ). Moreover, fruit trees with vigorous secondary growth have competitive advantage for light, water and nutrients. Thick branches provide sufficient space for adequate canopy development conducive for the accumulation of leaf and fruit biomass to support heavy loads of fruits and high yields (Plavcová et al., 2022; Poorter et al., 2012 ). Thus, the study of trunk diameter growth is always important in agricultural research. Studies show that in addition to plant physiological factors, trunk diameter growth is affected by external environmental conditions, particularly water. In areas with well-defined dry and wet seasons, the trunk diameter growth rate in the wet season is generally higher than that in the dry season (Santini et al., 2013 ). However, in perennially humid areas, seasonal variations in the growth rate of trunk diameter are not obvious (Krauss et al., 2007 ). In the diameter growth study on Prosopis glandulosa  in Rio Grande River in Texas, USA, Miller et al. (2001)  noted significant positive correlation between trunk diameter growth and annual precipitation for dry years and a poor one for wet years. In arid areas, long-term droughts negatively affect diameter growth of Populus tremuloides  (Chen et al., 2017 ). Studies also show that drought reduces Gross Primary Production (GPP). For example, in Southwest United States, compared with the average value for 2015–2019, GPP was much lower in 2020, a year which experienced a severe hot drought (Dannenberg et al., 2022 ). Thus, the effect of water on trunk diameter growth is more obvious in arid areas. Zweifel et al. (2006)  found that diameter growth of beech  depends strongly on water conditions in the alpine valley ecosystem in Switzerland, where drought is a major climatic feature. In a study on fur oak , sphagnum pine , and fir  in two arid areas in Central Wallis, Switzerland, Ma et al. (2021)  observed that rainfall is both the direct and indirect factor that affects tree diameter growth. Studies by Liang et al. (2006)  in northeastern Tibetan Plateau and Wang et al. (2016)  in Qilian Mountains show that trunk diameter growth of Sabina chinensis  and Picea crassifolia  was significantly correlated positively with daily rainfall and relative humidity. Liu et al. (2021)  noted steady expansion in trunk diameter under continuous rainfall. Trunk diameter was maximum under saturated soil water condition, suggesting that the magnitude and duration of rainfall affect change in the trunk diameter of Castanopsis hystrix . The fact that rainfall supports rapid and sharp increase in trunk diameter (Robert et al., 2014; Santini et al., 2014; Steppe et al., 2018 ) underscores its role in trunk diameter growth. Rainfall is generally beneficial for root water uptake as it replenishes soil water content, thereby improving soil conditions such as desalinization. In addition, rainfall is conducive for rapid growth of trunk diameter by increasing air humidity and reducing temperature (Robert et al., 2014; Santini et al., 2014; Reef and Lovelock., 2015 ). Steppe et al. (2018)  found that mangrove trees can absorb rainwater through leaves and thereby regulate the tree water balance and substantially increase trunk diameter. Generally, the impact of rainfall on trunk diameter growth varies significantly among different tree species, environment conditions and management practices (Köcher et al., 2012 ). However, the vegetation type and growth environment in relevant studies are still not diverse enough. Most studies focused on precipitation effects on trunk growth of natural tree species, while rainfall effects on trunk growth of fruit tree species remain largely unclear. Moreover, the impact of rainfall on the growth of trunk diameter is still largely descriptive. Although rainfall is a key driver of trunk diameter growth (with some rainfall events causing dramatic expansion of trunk diameter), data on rainfall threshold with such dramatic expansion is lacking. All of these confirm that there are still many unknowns in the underlying causes of trunk diameter growth and the related impacts of rainfall. Thus, this study explored the impact of rainfall on the growth of trunk diameter of orange trees, a typical economic plant in the dry-hot valleys of Southwest China. Here, seasonal drought is not only severe, but also accompanied by high temperatures and repeated droughts. The specific climatic conditions in the region include abundant light and pronounced contrasts in water and heat conditions. Water is a key limiting factor for fruit tree plantation in the region. There are three typical seasons in the region. Most of the rain falls in the rainy season (June-October), but there are still some intermittently short-period droughts between rainfall events because of the high air temperature. While there is less rainfall in the dry season (November-February of the following year) with relatively low air temperature. In the dry-hot season (March-May), the rainfall is quite limited (with no rains in some years during this period) and air temperature rises rapidly. As a result, droughts are more frequent and last longer during the dry season and the dry-hot season. Therefore, the region mainly faces drought problems in the dry season but facing drought and hot compound problem in the dry-hot season. In this study, the growth characteristics of orange tree trunks and its relationship with dry-wet conditions were analyzed. The following questions were addressed in this study: i) How much does rainfall contribute to diameter growth? In what aspects? ii) Why do some rainfall events cause common diameter expansion but some cause dramatic diameter expansion? What are the rainfall event characteristics that caused each of the two different diameter growth types? iii) Which environmental factors affect the driving force of rainfall on the diameter growth?  2 Method and materials 2.1 Study site As a typical economic plantation which covers a large area of the dry-hot valley region in Southwest China, orange orchard was selected for research in this study. The variety of orange is Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck , an evergreen perennial tree species. The orchard is in Xinping County in Yuxi City at 24°03′N, 101°35′E (Fig. 1  ), Yunnan Province, Southwest China. It belongs to the dry-hot valley region of Yuanjiang River with a subtropical monsoon climate. Based on observations at the Yuanjiang Savanna Ecosystem Research Station (Chinese Academy of Sciences) from 2012 until 2017, mean annual temperature in the region is 24.7 °C; with maximum daily temperature of 43.7 °C (including high temperatures above 35 °C for more than 100 days) and minimum daily temperature of 3.6 °C. During the 2012–2017 period, average annual rainfall is 732.8 mm (77.9 % of which occurred in the May-October rainy season), the annual average sunshine hours and potential evaporation are 2350 hr and 1750 mm, respectively. The typical soil texture is silty loam [clay = 11 %, silt = 54 %, sand = 35 % — Soil Survey Division Staff (1993) ], with pH of 6.1. According to FAO classification, the soil type is Acrisols. During the 2020–2022 trial period, appropriate drip irrigation (based on the degree of drought) was applied at the end of the dry season or during the dry-hot season. The other fraction of the year was rain-fed. Specifically, the orchard was irrigated three times each year in the following way: 25 mm on 27 January 2021, 25 mm on 11 February 2021, 30 mm on 25 February 2021, 25 mm on 19 February 2022, 25 mm on 11 March 2022 and 25 mm on 2 April 2022.  2.2 Measurement of environmental factors A meteorological station was installed (AG1000, Campbell Scientific Inc. USA) to measure meteorological data such as air temperature (Ta, °C), total solar radiation (Rs , MJ m−2  d-1 ), relative humidity (RH, %) and wind speed (Ws , m s-1 ) during the 2-year period from May 2020 to May 2022. Rainfall was recorded using a tipping bucket rain gauge. Vapor pressure deficit (VPD, kPa) was calculated from measured air temperature and relative humidity following (Nauš et al., 1999 ) as:(1) VPD = 0.6108 × e 17.27 × T a   T a  + 237.3   × 1 - RH  100           where VPD  is vapor pressure deficit (kPa); Ta   is air temperature (℃); RH  is relative humidity (%). The set of TDR (CS650, Campbell Scientific Inc., USA) soil water and heat monitoring systems was buried at four randomly selected sites in the orange orchard (at 20 cm depth interval) to monitor volumetric soil water content (VWC, %) in the 0–1 m soil layer. The measured volumetric soil water content data were calibrated using the thermo-gravimetric method (Yan et al., 2020 ). A leaf wetness sensor (PHYTOS31, METER Group Inc. USA) was used to record the fruit tree leaf wetness. Specifically, the tree canopy was divided into three layers – top layer (upper 1/3 canopy space), medium layer (middle 1/3 canopy space) and bottom layer (lower 1/3 canopy space). Six sensors were randomly installed in each tree canopy layer for a total of 18 sensors (Fig. 2  ). Based on the recommended instrument threshold of 460, the leaf is moist state if the threshold value is exceeded. Otherwise, the leaf is in the dry state. The cumulative time for which the threshold value exceeds 460 under each rainfall event was used to determine the corresponding leaf wetness time for the rainfall event. A CR1000X data collector was used to collect meteorological and leaf surface humidity data every 15 min.  2.3 Tree physiology measurements Five and seven representative orange trees were randomly selected in the orange orchard for trunk diameter and trunk sap flow monitoring, respectively (Fig. 2 ). The average dimensions of the selected 12 trees were as follows: tree trunk diameter was 7.48 ± 0.34 cm, tree height of 2.86 ± 0.28 m, and canopy width was 2.74 ± 0.31 m. Thermal diffusion probes (TDP — SF-G, Ecomatik GmbH, Germany), were used to measure sap flow in the orange tree trunks. To reduce damage to the tree, only one group of probes (probe length of 2 cm) was installed on each tree. The probe was uniformly installed at a height of 50 cm from the ground surface on the side of the trunk facing north and wrapped in aluminum foil to minimize the impact of environmental heat (Kume et al., 2008 ). A CR1000X data collector was used to record the data every 15 min. Based on the measured temperature difference between two heating probes, liquid flux density (Js) and liquid flux (SF) of sapwood in the tree trunk were calculated (Granier et al., 1987 ):(3) J s  = 119 Δ T m  - Δ T  Δ T     1.231       where J s    is sap flux density (g m−2  s−1 ); Δ T    is temperature difference between heated and unheated probe; and Δ T m     is temperature difference at zero sap flow.(4) SF = K × J s  × A s      (5) A s  = 7.044 D B H - 15.809  R 2  = 0.98     where SF    is sap flow (mm h−1 ); K   is unit conversion coefficient of 36 × 24 / 1000 ≈ 0.00864   ; and A s    is sapwood area (cm2 ), calculated based on the relationship between sapwood area and tree diameter (DBH, cm). The instrument was installed at 20 cm from the ground surface and the data recorded every 15 min using the U30 a data collector — U30, Onset Computer Corporation, USA. Daily trunk diameter increase (DI, mm) was obtained by subtracting the maximum diameter value between two consecutive days as (Bouriaud et al., 2005 ):(6) DI = MXS D af   - M X S D be          where MXSD be  is the maximum diameter on the previous day (mm) and MXSD af  is the maximum diameter on the next day (mm). In this study, trunk diameter changes were classified into the following four types based on DI value — dramatic expansion (DI>0 and DI exceeding common positive DI range), common expansion (DI>0 and DI within common positive DI range), dramatic shrinkage (DI<0 and DI exceeding common negative DI range), and common shrinkage (DI<0 and DI within the common negative DI range). Since rainfall events often last for several days, two diameter growth indexes were used in this study — cumulative DI (sum of DI for every day during a rainfall event) and average DI (average DI for every day of rainfall event). The monitoring times of the tree physiological and environmental indicators were in sync for the entire 2020–2022 period.  2.4 Statistical analysis Origin 2021 software (Origin Lab Corporation, Northampton, Massachusetts, USA) and SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York, USA) were used for drawings and descriptive statistical analyses. Pearson correlation analysis was used to determine the relation between trunk growth-related indicators and environmental factors. The non-parametric test of relevant samples (paired samples) was used to determine any significant differences in the growth rates of trunk diameter among the different growth stages.   3 Results 3.1 Meteorological factors and trunk diameter growth The dynamics of meteorological factors (Fig. 3  ) show that for the 2-year study period, monthly average temperature was highest in May (32 °C), with a monthly maximum of 47 °C. The minimum average monthly temperature was in January (15 °C), with a minimum monthly value of 5 °C. The difference between the maximum and minimum temperature in a year was 42 °C. Rs, ET0 and VPD were similar in trend to air temperature. The minimum values were in January (8.8 MJ m-2  d-1 , 1.9 mm d-1 , and 0.9 kPa respectively), which gradually increased to the maximum values in May (16.8 MJ m-2  d-1 , 5.5 mm d-1  and 3.5 kPa respectively). The high values persisted until September, followed by a rapid drop in trend, hitting minimum values in January the next year. The total rainfall for the two years was 1736 mm, with the total number of rainfall days of 190. The proportion of rainfall from June to October was 83 % in 2021 and 75 % 2022. It showed that rainfall mainly occurred during the June-October period, with a trend of change in soil water content consistent with that in rainfall. For the 2-year study period, the trunk growth of orange trees was divided into three stages (Fig. 4  ). There was the semi-dormancy stage (from mid-November to end of March the next year), rapid growth stage (from early April to mid-May), and stable growth stage (from late May to early November). The trunk diameter of orange trees showed an overall gradual growth trend. At the semi-dormancy growth stage, trunk diameter essentially did not change. This stage coincided with the dry-hot season, when temperature and radiation increased rapidly with little rain. At the rapid growth stage, trunk diameter grew rapidly. This stage coincided with the dry-hot season; during which period temperature and radiation increased rapidly with little rain. At this stage, irrigation supplemented soil water due to low rainfall. Subsequently, the trunk diameter entered a stable growth stage; during which trunk growth rate was faster, rainfall higher and corresponding with the rainy season. The total growth of trunk diameter was 7.44 mm and the average growth rate was 0.01 mm d-1 . The respective growths during the semi-dormancy growth, rapid growth and stable growth stages were 0.36, 2.02 and 5.06 mm; with corresponding growth rates of 0.0014, 0.018 and 0.014 mm d-1  (Fig. 5  a). The stable growth stage had the longest duration and most of the growth, accounting for 68 % of the total trunk diameter growth. The rapid growth stage had the fastest growth rate and the shortest duration, accounting for 27 % of the total trunk diameter growth. The lowest trunk diameter growth and growth rate were in the semi-dormancy growth stage. While the number of rainy days accounted for only 25.6 % of the study period, it contributed 66 % to the total trunk diameter growth. The number of rainy days in the stable growth stage accounted for only 36.4 %, but contributed some 85 % to the diameter growth. Except for the rapid growth stage, rainy days accounted for more than half of the growth in the other two growth stages (Fig. 5 b). The rapid growth stage corresponded with the dry-hot season, during which period the number of rainfall days was only 12.8 %, with little rainfall amount (less than 5 mm, Table 1  ). Under this condition, rainfall contribution to trunk diameter growth was relatively small.  3.2 Diameter change under various weather conditions As the stable growth stage was longest with the fastest radial trunk growth, it was the largest contributor to total trunk diameter growth of the orange trees. From detailed analysis of the changes in diameter growth at the stable growth stage in 2020 (Fig. 6  a) and 2021 (Fig. 6 b), it was clear that tree trunk diameter dramatically increased during this stage. The growth rate was 20 times more than that of common growth. Dramatic trunk diameter expansion was often driven by heavy rainfall events, suggesting a strong link between dramatic trunk diameter expansion and rainfall. However, not all rainfall events resulted in a sudden increase in diameter. For example, the rains on 27 July 2020 and 25 August 2020 did not lead to any sudden increase in trunk diameter — the point of the yellow arrow in Fig. 6 a. To determine the effect of rainfall on trunk diameter growth, a frequency analysis of the daily diameter growth (DI) was done for the 2-year study period. It showed that DI followed a normal distribution curve (Fig. 7  a). Trunk shrinkage (DI<0) occurred for 43 % and expansion (DI>0) 57 % of the study period. The frequency of change in trunk diameter was high for common expansion/shrinkage and low for dramatic expansion/shrinkage. Daily change in trunk diameter was grouped into two categories — common (5 % cumulative frequency) and dramatic (95 % cumulative frequency). Also, four groups of diameter changes were observed — common diameter expansion (0 <DI<0.048 mm), dramatic diameter expansion (DI>0.048 mm), common diameter shrinkage (−0.016 mm< DI<0) and dramatic diameter shrinkage (DI< −0.016 mm). The analysis showed that 82 % of the total dramatic trunk diameter expansion occurred under rainy days. There was no dramatic diameter expansion at the semi-dormancy growth stage. For rapid growth stage, 40 % of the dramatic diameter expansion occurred during rainy days. It was as high as 91 % for the stable growth stage (Fig. 7 b). This suggested that rainfall was the main driver of dramatic expansion in diameter during the stable growth stage. However, not all rainy days led to dramatic diameter expansion, common expansion also occurred on some rainy days (Fig. 7 c). Under certain conditions, rainfall events triggered dramatic diameter expansion for the trunk of orange trees. Overall, 52 % of the growth on rainy days was considered dramatic expansion (Fig. 8  a); slightly higher than that for common expansion. Generally, the trunk diameter shrinkage of orange trees occurred on rainless days, especially for dramatic shrinkage. No dramatic trunk diameter shrinkage occurred on rainy days for the 2020–2022 study period (Fig. 7 d). Although a small amount of common trunk diameter shrinkage occurred on rainy days, that proportion was as low as 2 % overall (2 % for the semi-dormancy growth stage, 15 % for the rapid growth stage and 0 % for the stable growth stage, Fig. 7 e). On the whole, there were 190 days of rain during the study period. Of this, tree trunk diameter shrinkage occurred for only 10 days (8 days in semi-dormancy growth stage and 2 days in rapid growth stage). The rainfall amount for the 10 days was even less than 3 mm, with duration shorter than 30 min, which corresponds with very slight rain. And among the 10 days, there were 2 days had similar circumstance that the rainfall amount was much less than the day just before it (e.g., 1.3 mm vs 15 mm), leading to relative lower maximum diameter value than the previous day, therefore DI value was negative. So, rainfall was conducive to promoting dramatic expansion and inhibited shrinkage of trunk diameter. For the study period, trunk diameter growth in rainy days was 4.92 mm (66 % of the total growth); with dramatic expansion accounting for 46 % of that total growth (Fig. 9  a). For the stable stage, trunk diameter growth was 85 % and dramatic expansion 62 % (Fig. 9 b). These were significantly lower for the semi-dormancy growth and rapid growth stages (Fig. 9 c, d). This was because the two stages coincided respectively with the dry season and the dry-hot period with limited rain days and rainfall amount in the region.  3.3 Daily characteristics of diameter micro-variation in relation to precipitation To further explore the response of trunk diameter dramatic growth to rainfall, changes in trunk diameter, rainfall, leaf wetting time, and trunk sap flow were compared for typical rainfall events (Fig. 10  ). For rainless days, trunk sap flow was lowest at night. It gradually increased in the morning, peaked at noon and dropped thereafter. The diurnal dynamics of trunk diameter showed a reverse trend. As sap flow gradually increased in the morning, trunk diameter shrunk. It continued to contract till lowest value at noon. It then expanded till night, reaching the highest value in the morning of the next day. Peak sap flow corresponded with smallest diameter growth. With rainfall, however, both sap flow and diameter change were altered to varying degrees. Under rainfall event of long duration, sap flow steadily dropped and with smaller amplitude of fluctuation throughout the day (Fig. 10 a). For small and short daytime rainfall events, the daily dynamics of sap flow did not change (Fig. 10 b). With regards to rainfall event occurred during night, it changed the maximum sap flow value in the next day but had little effect on the overall intraday fluctuation trend (Fig. 10 c). In contrast, diurnal dynamics of trunk diameter was more sensitive to rainfall. The diurnal shrinkage/expansion cycle of trunk diameter was broken by rainfall. Further analysis showed that canopy leaf wetness directly affected trunk diameter shrinkage. Single rainfall resulted in rapid wetting of the leaf surface, with the leaves remaining wet for a while even after the rainfall stopped. With gradual evaporation of leaf surface water, leaf humidity also gradually dropped until it dried out. With multiple rainfall events over wet leaves (due to previous rainfall), leaves remained wet for a long time. After comparing the three different types of rainfall events, it was found that if the leaves were wet during the period of trunk expansion, the expansion of trunk diameter intensified. If the leaves were wet during the period of gradual trunk shrinkage, the trunk diameter continued to expand but with a slower speed. If the leaves were wet during the period of strong trunk shrinkage, there would be no obvious shrinkage or expansion of the trunk diameter (Fig. 10 ). Overall, the diurnal dynamic changes in trunk sap flow and diameter showed upward and downward trends. The higher the peak sap flow, the higher the trunk diameter shrinkage and the lower the trunk diameter expansion. Contrarily, the lower the peak sap flow the lower the trunk diameter shrinkage and the higher the trunk diameter expansion (Fig. 10 d). Comparison of the three rainfall event categories suggested that concentrated short-durational heavy rainfall events induced a quick and sharp expansion of tree trunk diameter (Fig. 10 c). Under heavy rainfall events with a medium duration, trunk diameter expansion was mainly at the initial period of the rain, with the expansion gradually dropping with time (Fig. 10 a). For multiple, dispersed and short-to-medium duration rainfall events over a number of days, trunk diameter expansion due to each rainfall event was small, but the cumulative expansion was obviously large (Fig. 10 b).  3.4 Environmental control on trunk diameter expansion on rainy days The above analysis shows that dramatic tree trunk diameter expansion occurred during rainfall events, but the degree of expansion varied among different rainfall events. Rainfall characteristics affected cumulative DI during rainfall events and hardly had any effect on average daily DI (Table 2  ). The correlation between cumulative DI and rainfall duration (RD) or leaf wetting duration (LWD) was significant at p  < 0.01. The correlation between cumulative DI and rainfall amount (RA) was lower significantly, while between cumulative DI and rainfall intensity was insignificant at p  > 0.05 (Table 2 ). Regression analysis showed significant quadratic correlation across cumulative DI and LWD, RD and RA. The correlation was stronger for dramatic than for common tree trunk diameter expansion (Fig. 11  a, b, c). Among the three indicators, the effects of rainfall time on dramatic diameter expansion were stronger than that of the rainfall amount. Although there was a clear linear correlation between LWD and RD (R 2  = 0.90; Fig. 11 d), leaf wetting duration more directly influenced cumulative trunk expansion than rainfall duration. The impact of the other environmental factors on dramatic trunk diameter expansion for rainfall periods was small and insignificant (Table 3  ). However, most of the other environmental factors had significant impacts on common tree trunk diameter expansion under rainfall events. Temperature, volumetric soil water content and ET0  were all significantly correlated with mean daily DI (common), but not with cumulative DI (common, Table 3 ).  3.5 Environmental control on trunk diameter shrinkage on rainless days With no rains, radial variations in trunk diameter included dramatic and common shrinkage, and the shrinkage amount varied with environmental conditions. While DI was significantly negatively correlated with average air temperature, minimum air temperature and wind speed under dramatic shrinkage, it was significantly positively correlation with volumetric soil water content. The results were similar for common shrinkage too, but more environmental factors were significantly correlated with DI (Table 4  ). After grading minimum air temperature, wind speed and volumetric soil water content into subsequent groups, it became clear that higher air temperature and wind speed corresponded with higher trunk diameter shrinkage. Also, higher volumetric soil water content was in sync with lower trunk diameter shrinkage (Fig. 12  ). These trends were consistent with the ones from the correlation analysis.   4 Discussion In this study, the relationship between orange tree trunk diameter (an evergreen citrus species) and environmental factors in the dry-hot river valley region of Southwest China was explored. Particular attention was pay on rainfall event effects analysis. The data presented seasonal variations in trunk diameter growth (Fig. 5 a). Although orange trees had green canopy at the semi-dormancy stage (November to March), new branches did not develop at this stage. The rate of growth of trunk diameter was very slow (0.0014 mm d-1 ). The stage coincided with the dry season, during which rainfall was low with moderate temperature (intra-day maximum temperature not exceeding 26 °C). At the rapid growth stage, trunk diameter growth was rapid (with an average growth rate of 0.018 mm d-1 ). This stage coincided with the dry-hot season, during which period the temperature was high, solar radiation strong and rainfall about zero. To, however, prevent the fruit trees from dying out at the stage, irrigation was done. This maintained the soil water content above 15 %, close to that for the rainy season (Fig. 3 ). Therefore, it was inferred that one of the important reasons why trunk diameter could maintain high-speed growth during this period was that irrigation improved the soil water condition above a certain threshold, which ensured the precondition for diameter quick growth. The other possible drivers of the rapid growth included the orange plant growth rhythm and phenological process. For many plants, biomass accumulation enhances rapid growth at the early stage, gradually followed by stable growth (Furze et al., 2018; Cuny et al., 2015; Koester et al., 2014 ). In this study, the rapid diameter growth stage coincided well with the vegetative growth dominant period. Furthermore, the late phase of the stable diameter growth stage roughly coincided with the reproductive growth competition phase. Thus, plant inherent growth patterns might be the reason for the differences in the two growth stages. The stable growth stage was characterized by high rate of growth of trunk diameter (0.014 mm d-1 ). This stage roughly coincided with the rainy season, with high temperature, strong solar radiation and with rainfall higher than in the other periods. Even without irrigation, there was high soil water condition (Fig. 3 ). The growth rate of orange tree’s trunk diameter was fast under good soil water conditions. This was evident in the positive correlation between cumulative DI and volumetric soil water content (Table 3 ). In a study in arid western Australia, it was noted that the growth rate of tree trunk diameter was significantly higher in wet than in dry years (Santini et al., 2013 ). In the Piracão River region (in the southern part of Southeast Brazil) and in the coastal area of Kenya where rainfall distribution is bimodal, the growth rate of tree trunk diameter decreases during dry season (Estrada et al., 2008; Verheyden et al., 2004 ). It was noted that although orange tree’s trunk diameter growth was fastest during the rapid growth stage, that stage lasted for only about three weeks. Thus, the cumulative growth at the stage accounted for only 27 % of the total growth. In comparison, nearly 70 % of the growth occurred during the stable growth stage; driven by fast growth rate and long duration (six months). This suggested that orange tree’s trunk diameter growth in the dry-hot valley study area occurred mainly during the rainy season. Krauss et al. (2006)  noted that 75–90 % of mangrove tree trunk diameter growth in subtropical region of southern Florida occurs in the wet season. It suggested that rainfall was crucial for trunk diameter growth. Specifically, although only 25.6 % of the study period was rainy, the corresponding contribution to trunk diameter growth was 66 % of the total growth. For the stable growth stage (which was in the rainy season), only 36.4 % of the rainy days accounted for up to 85 % of the trunk diameter growth (Fig. 9 ). Almost all negative trunk diameter growth occurred under rainless conditions (Fig. 9 ). This showed that rainfall was critical for orange tree’s trunk diameter growth in the dry-hot valley study area. Further analysis showed that common expansion accounted for approximately 50 % of the growth during the rainy season and the other 50 % explained by dramatic expansion (Fig. 8 ). The possible reason for trunk diameter growth (normal or otherwise) was the increase in soil water content due to the rains. This in turn enhanced not only root water uptake, but also reduced water potential of the xylem vessel (Steppe et al., 2006, 2015 ). The factor induced radial water flow through the cambium cells, resulting in the expansion of cambium cells and the differentiation derivatives, and enhancing cell division, expansion and enlargement (Köcher et al., 2012 ). This was the main factor driving daily trunk diameter growth in the study area (Deslauriers et al., 2003 ). Humid conditions (with high RH and lower VPD) during the rains also support tree trunk diameter growth due to low transpiration rate. This condition lowers the risk of stomatal closure under dry-hot conditions, allowing better photosynthesis and trunk growth (Woodruff et al., 2009; Thomas, 2014 ). While the above explanation supports tree trunk diameter expansion, it hardly explains dramatic expansion under rainy days. There was growth for every rainy day, but dramatic trunk expansion was not on all rainy days. There was significant correlation between environmental factors (such as VWC, RH, VPD, ET0 , etc.) and trunk diameter growth for common expansion on rainy days, but not for dramatic expansion. It then suggested that high rainfall and relative humidity (and enhanced soil water content) were not the main drivers of dramatic trunk diameter expansion (Steppe et al., 2018; Robert et al., 2014 ). For example, in a study by Robert et al. (2014) , there was no matching correlation between increasing soil water content and decreasing salinity (from flooding) and dramatic increase in trunk diameter. There was a strong correlation between dramatic expansion of trunk diameter and wet leaf duration from rainfall. Irrespective of high-intensity and long-duration (Fig. 10 a), low-intensity and long-duration (Fig. 10 b), and high-intensity and medium-duration (Fig. 10 c) rainfall, there was continuous increase in trunk diameter so long leaf wetting continued. Wetting of leaves by rain breaks intra-day cycle of trunk diameter expansion and shrinkage, maintaining continuous diameter growth all day long, or keeping stable high values without shrinkage. Furthermore, the degree of dramatic expansion driven by rainfall varied with rainfall event. There was significant positive correlation between cumulative DI and leaf wetting duration (Table 2 , Fig. 11 a). This relationship was stronger and more direct than that between cumulative DI and rainfall amount and duration. It indicated that the moist state of leaves was the driver of dramatic trunk diameter expansion during rainfall. Two main reasons were suggested for the dramatic trunk diameter expansion on rainy days. One reason was that rainfall kept tree canopy moist for a period of time (Steppe et al., 2018 ), leaves supplemented plant water uptake by direct absorption of rainwater and transportation to the branches, stems and roots of trees. Tree trunk xylem vessel water was supplemented and the accumulated swelling pressure triggered trunk diameter growth. Irreversible radial growth occurred when the swelling pressure exceeded a certain threshold. Such was observed as leaf water absorption occurred concurrently with leaf wetting. Studies show that leaf water uptake is critical for tree growth (McHugh et al., 2015; Rosado et al., 2018 ). Absorbed water from leaf surfaces offsets water loss due to transpiration (Yang et al., 2010 ). The reduces the negative effects of drought and maintains normal physiological processes in plants (Schreel and Steppe, 2020 ). Studies show that water film (from dew, fog and rain) on leaf surfaces is absorbed to supplement plant water. In tropical mountain forests (Eller et al., 2013; Goldsmith et al., 2013 ), coastal mangrove forests (Hayes et al., 2020 ), succulent plants and arid shrubs (Martin et al., 2000; Cavallaro et al., 2020 ), plants absorb dew, fog and rainfall to supplement water and promote growth through hydrophilic cuticles (Eller et al., 2013; Oliveira et al., 2014; Zimmermann et al., 2004 ), stomata (Burkhardt et al., 2012 ), leaf trichrome (Schreel et al., 2020 ) and other ways (Lehmann et al., 2018 ). Under climate change with decreasing global rainfall and more frequent extreme weather conditions, leaf water uptake is critical for overall water replenishment, nutrient metabolism, drought mitigation, growth, development and adaptation of plants (Boucher et al., 1995; Simonin et al., 2009 ). Another possibility for the dramatic expansion of tree trunk diameter on rainy days is that rainfall makes canopy leaves wet and evaporation of rainwater on the leaves uses energy. In this case, it suggests that water vapor exchange is more a critical driver of evaporation of rainwater on canopy leaf surface than canopy transpiration (Bosveld and Bouten, 2003 ). Thus, transpiration intensity of trees was weak under moist canopy conditions (Kume et al., 2006 ; Wang et al., 2020), enhancing tree water preservation. This was conducive for radial water flow in plant tissues which promoted diameter expansion (Deslauriers et al., 2003 ). In this study, rainfall significantly reduced intra-day sap flow, lowered transpiration intensity associated with small trunk shrinkage and higher trunk expansion (Fig. 10 ). Furthermore, canopy wetting duration determined the extent of transpiration. The clear relationship between trunk sap flow and trunk diameter change indicated that intercepted rainwater evaporation inhibited leaf transpiration and then triggered rapid trunk diameter growth. The visible correlation between leaf wetting and rainfall duration (Fig. 11 d) showed that the duration of rainfall was a more important factor than the amount of rainfall for dramatic trunk diameter expansion (Steppe et al., 2018 ). Although high-intensity and short-duration rainfall event yielded a high amount of rainfall, it, however, failed to produce dramatic increase in trunk diameter (see yellow arrow in Fig. 6  for details). Overall, about 50 % of the trunk diameter growth during rainy days was due to dramatic expansion and the other 50 % due to common expansion. This implied that not all rainfall events resulted in dramatic expansion of trunk diameter and that some rainfall events only supported common growth in trunk diameter. This was so for several reasons, among which was rainfall duration. For short intensity rains, leaves were wet for a short period of time and the amount of water absorbed was not enough to trigger significant diameter growth. The second factor was the timing of rainfall, which affected leaf water uptake efficiency — highest in the morning than any other time of the day (Berry et al., 2014 ). Post-midday rains dry rapidly in hot weather conditions, resulting in short leaf wetting time (Kume et al., 2006 ) that limits leaf water uptake. Therefore, the time of rainfall and the corresponding climatic conditions could variously impact trunk diameter growth. Putting together the 190 rainfall events in the period of study, it was found that rainfall events that lasted for over 7.00 hr (66 events in total) had high probability (82 %) of inducing dramatic growth in tree trunk diameter. The orange tree trunk diameter also increased dramatically under rainless conditions (Fig. 8 ). Specifically, 12 % of the total growth under rainless conditions was dramatic expansion. In the 2-year study, there was a total of 10 dramatic increase in trunk diameter under rainless conditions. This occurred on the next days after rainfall, accompanied by long dew condensation. In this study, leaf surface humidity sensor was also used to determine dew duration. The aftereffect of rainwater on trunk growth lasted longer under high air humidity and long dew fall duration on the days after rainfall. There was no dramatic increase in tree trunk diameter for almost all the other days with dew. This showed that the small amount of dew in the dry-hot valley was generally not enough to cause dramatic growth in tree trunk diameter (Steppe et al., 2018 ). Note that the increase in soil water content and decrease in evapotranspiration due to rainfall not directly result in dramatic expansion of the trunk diameter of orange trees in the study area. However, the effect of these factors on common expansion of tree trunk diameter was evident (Table 3 ). Moreover, environmental factors such as soil water content, temperature, radiation and wind speed negatively affected trunk diameter growth under rainless conditions (Table 4 ). Sufficient soil water content and low evapotranspiration conditions coincided with light droughts, under which little negative trunk diameter growth was noted. The results suggested that orange tree trunk diameter growth due to rainfall was complex and driven by factors that are usually overlooked in popular studies. This therefore requires much wider research for a full understanding of this aspect of plant growth and development.  5 Conclusions Rainfall is critical for the growth of trunk diameter of orange trees in dry-hot valleys of Yuanjiang River. There were both positive and negative growths in tree trunk diameter under rainless conditions. For rainy days, however, trunk diameter growth was only positive. Rainfall induced dramatic expansion in the trunk diameter of orange trees, quite different from common expansion. There was a strong correlation between dramatic trunk diameter expansion and canopy leaf wetting time. Moreover, increased soil water content and dropped dry air after rainfall enhanced tree trunk diameter growth. Positive common expansion was promoted and negative trunk diameter growth was reduced for the days after rainfall. Rainfall significantly enhanced secondary growth of orange trees. There was the need for a comprehensive assessment of the effects of rainfall on tree growth under rainfed conditions in the face of the worsening climate change. For irrigated conditions, it was necessary to consider potential positive effects on tree growth from wet canopy and foliar water uptake. For example, it is not clear whether sprinkler irrigation (which could wet the canopy) is better than other irrigation methods in this case. Given the complex interaction effect of environmental and human factors on secondary tree growth, there is a need for further research on quantitative assessments of environmental controls on trunk diameter growth. Furthermore, studies are needed on various plant species and varieties for the full understanding of the regulation effect of precipitation and drought on tree trunk diameter growth.
1 Introduction The Chinese Loess Plateau (CLP) is situated in arid and semi-arid regions, characterized by its distinct abundance of gullies, a fragmented landscape, and a widespread distribution of loess, becoming a typical ecologically fragile area (Fu et al., 2017 ). Following long-term revegetation, considerable changes in the pattern of rainfall infiltration on the CLP have been observed (Feng et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021; Mu et al., 2019 ). While existing studies on the CLP primarily focus on rainfall infiltration patterns during the growing season (Jin et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015 ), partly due to the challenges of field monitoring in non-growing seasons (also cold seasons on the CLP), the infiltration patterns during the non-growing season remain relatively underexplored. As a result, omitting the non-growing season leads to an incomplete understanding of rainfall infiltration pattern on the CLP. Rainfall attributes and vegetation conditions are widely recognized as key factors influencing the infiltration process, which show substantial disparities between growing and non-growing seasons (Cheng et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017 ). During the growing season, vigorous vegetation growth contributes to strong redistribution of the gross rainfall (Yuan et al., 2022 ), and root proliferation serves to enhance the infiltration rate and wetting depth, further redistributing rainfall in the subsurface (Li, 2011; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Nonetheless, substantial evapotranspiration (ET) in the growing season intensifies soil moisture scarcity, leading to soil desiccation and dry initial soil condition that can, in turn, influence the infiltration processes, such as the frequency of preferential flow after rainfall (Chen et al., 2010; Guo and Lin, 2018; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Conversely, during the non-growing season, plant transpiration and soil evaporation typically diminishes, allowing for effective soil moisture replenishment via precipitation or groundwater recharge. This process can help offset the substantial depletion of soil moisture experienced during the growing season due to ET and facilitate the greenup of vegetation in the coming growing season (Feng et al., 2017; Jian et al., 2014 ). In addition, the factors controlling soil moisture variability and infiltration process appear to fluctuate seasonally (Zhu and Lin, 2011 ). Given these observed differences, additional research is required to discern whether variations exist in soil moisture dynamics between the growing and non-growing seasons, and how the primary factors influencing rainfall infiltration on the CLP may change accordingly. Long-term vegetation restoration on the CLP can further enhance the seasonal difference in rainfall infiltration patterns between the growing and non-growing seasons. Because the enhanced land–atmosphere interactions induced by vegetation restoration drive increased precipitation and evapotranspiration, greatly accelerating the local water cycle on the CLP (Bai et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022 ). In addition, vegetation restoration profoundly modified soil texture and structure. It reduced soil moisture and bulk density, while enhancing total porosity, macroporosity, and soil organic matter levels (Kalhoro et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023 ). Particularly, the introduced forest and shrub species have developed extensive root systems that facilitate preferential flow through macropores and root channels (Gao et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2023 ), which considerably alters the infiltration process. Natural vegetation restoration and tree planting are important measures of vegetation rehabilitation on the CLP. After long-term revegetation, catchments with tree planting measure often exhibit a forest landscape with dense forest cover and abundant undergrowth shrubs and grasses; whereas, catchments undergoing natural vegetation restoration typically show a grassland landscape (Jin et al., 2020 ). Therefore, based on existing research results, we hypothesize that the difference in rainfall infiltration patterns between the growing and non-growing seasons would be more noticeble in forestland catchments compared to grassland catchments, as the forestland catchments foster more extensive root systems and show stronger seasonal vegetation dynamics. This study built on previous research on the CLP by (Jin et al., 2018 ), which analyzed the 30-min interval soil moisture response to 15 rainfall events in a grassland catchment and a forestland catchment over the growing season of 2016. They adequately quantified soil moisture response to rainfall (i.e., wetting depth, wetting front velocity, soil moisture increase) after long-term revegetation. From the analysis of 15 rainfall events, (Jin et al., 2018 ) found that vegetation, topography, and rainfall attributes together determined rainfall infiltration and soil moisture replenishment. However, (Jin et al., 2018 ) focused only on soil moisture dynamics in one growing season and did not quantify preferential flow occurrence during infiltration. Therefore, addressing these research gaps is essential for a comprehensive grasp of soil moisture dynamics and infiltration mechanisms, particularly across multiple seasons and under diverse environmental conditions. Our study extended the analysis of (Jin et al., 2018 ) to three growing seasons and three non-growing seasons (May 2016-December 2018) by investigating soil moisture dynamics at 10-minute intervals across five soil depths, extending down to a depth of 1 m in paired headwater catchments. The paired catchments include a grassland catchment after natural vegetation restoration and a forestland catchment after tree planting. Leveraging this relatively long-term, high-frequency soil moisture dataset, the goal of this study is to: (1) analyze the dynamic responses of soil moisture to rainfall input during the growing and non-growing seasons on the greening CLP, (2) identify seasonal shifts in key factors that regulate rainfall infiltration into loess hillslopes, and (3) augment our understanding of rainfall infiltration mechanisms on the CLP after different long-term revegetation measures. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of seasonal variations in rainfall infiltration after revegetation, thus contributing valuable insights towards effective soil and water management strategies on the CLP.  2 Study sites This study was performed in the Nanxiaohegou watershed (35° 42′ N, 107° 33′ E, area 36.3 km2 , elevation 1,050 ∼ 1,423 m asl.) on the CLP, near the city of Qingyang, Gansu Province (Fig. 1  a). The study area is characterized by a semi-arid inland climate, with an average annual temperature of 9.3 °C and precipitation of 556.5 mm. Over 80 % of the annual precipitation is concentrated from May to October (Jin et al., 2018 ). The Nanxiaohegou watershed presents a distinctive landscape, featuring an alternation between loess tablelands and gullies, which is the typical CLP tableland landscape. The local loess soil was primarily derived from the Quaternary sediments and extends to an average depth of around 250 m, with the texture of silty loam. A pair of catchments, located on the south side of the third-level tributary of the Yellow River, Nanxiaohe, with a separation of about 140 m and similar terrain, including river length, average gradient, and river density, were selected for this study. Both catchments have been undergoing ecological management since 1954, with the grassland catchment (1.15 km2 ) having undergone natural regrowth of native grass species since 1954, and the forestland catchment (0.87 km2 ) planted with trees from 1954 to 1958. After 60 years of vegetation restoration, the two catchments have formed completely different landscapes (Fig. 1 c, d). These catchments are mainly composed of tableland, uphill slope, and downhill gully (Fig. 1 b). The tableland is a flat area (<5°) on the mountain ridge, managed for agricultural cultivation without vegetation restoration, primarily growing winter wheat and summer corn. The steep downhill gully (>25°) has higher vegetation coverage, especially the downhill gully of the forestland catchment, which is covered by dense undergrowth and a higher distribution density of trees. The gently sloping uphill (10°∼20°) connects the uphill tableland and the downhill gulley, accounting for 25 % of the total study area. In the grassland catchment (Fig. 1 c), the dominant grass species are Agropyron cristatum , Bothriochloa ischaemum , Arundinella hirta , Artemisia argyi , and Echinochloa crusgalli . The uphill slope was planted with a number of shrubs, prominently featuring Ziziphus jujuba , and displays a vegetation coverage of approximately 60 %, primarily consisting of A. cristatum , B. ischaemum , and Z. jujuba . Whereas, the downhill gully exhibits a higher vegetation coverage of about 65 %, with A. cristatum , B. ischaemum , A. hirta , and A. argyi  as the dominant species. Most of the grassroots were distributed in the surface soil layer (0 ∼ 20 cm), and the soil organic carbon content at the depth of 0 ∼ 100 cm was 5.22 g/kg. In the forestland catchment (Fig. 1 d), the dominant tree species planted were Robinia pseudoacacia , Armeniaca sibirica , Pinus tabulaeformis , Salix matsudana,  and Platycladus orientalis . The downhill gully is characterized by a lush undergrowth of shrubs, such as Rubus palmatus , Rubus parvifolius , Ampelopsis aconitifolia,  and Rhamnus leptophylla . The uphill slope exhibits approximately 50 % vegetation coverage, with a sparse understory primarily made up of A. cristatum . Meanwhile, the downhill gully features a dense vegetation coverage of over 90 %, mainly made up of R. pseudoacacia  and various understory vegetation species. The root systems of trees and shrubs were several meters deep, and the soil organic carbon content was 3.84 g/kg at 0–100 cm depth. During the growing season, grasses, shrubs and trees experience rapid growth marked by proliferation of leaves and stems. In contrast, the non-growing season sees a sharp decline in vegetation growth rates, and their above-ground parts often wilt. Nevertheless, their root systems remain viable, facilitating regrowth when the next growing season arrives.  3 Data and methods 3.1 Vegetation index and meteorological factors To distinguish differences in vegetation conditions and meteorological factors between growing and non-growing seasons, we compared NDVI, LAI, evapotranspiration, air temperature, and rainfall amount from January 2016 to December 2018, respectively. The NDVI and LAI data was from the GEE platform through the Landsat 8 OL1 satellite with a resolution of 30 m. Monthly-scale NDVI and LAI was calculated by combining and averaging multiple Landsat 8 OLI images for each month, accompanied by the application of a Savitzky-Golay filter to facilitate data smoothing (Chen et al., 2004 ). Moreover, we calculated monthly reference evapotranspiration (ET0 ) among the study sites to further elucidate the differences in soil moisture consumption between the growing season and the non-growing season.
