This dataset was derived through the Penman-Monteith equation in the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) AquaCrop model:(1) E T 0  = 0.408 Δ R n  - G     + γ 400 T + 273   e s  - e a       Δ + γ 1 + 0.34 u 2            where E T 0     is reference evapotranspiration (mm day−1 ), R n     is net radiation at the surface (MJ m−2  day−1 ), G is ground heat flux density (MJ m−2  day−1 ), T is the mean daily air temperature at 2 m height (°C), u 2     is the wind speed at 2 m height (m s−1 ), e s     is the saturation vapor pressure (kPa), e a     is the actual vapor pressure (kPa), Δ    is the slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve (kPa °C−1 ) and γ    is the psychrometric constant (kPa °C). An automatic weather station was set up in a cleared area near the grassland uphill slope site. Rainfall was recorded every 10 min (Fig. S1 e) by a tipping bucket rain gauge (0.2 mm/tip; Jiangsu Naiwch Corporation Inc., China). It should be noted that the installed equipment only took measurements of liquid precipitation and did not measure snowfall amount. Air temperature was recorded every 10 min by an external sensor (±0.25 °C from −40 to 0 °C; ±0.2 °C from 0 to 70 °C; Hobo Prov2 U23-001A). Considering factors such as the growth of vegetation and meteorological conditions (Fig. S2  ), the growing season was designated from May 1st to October 30th each year, and the remaining days of the year are considered the non-growing season.  3.2 Rainfall event delineation We used a heuristic event separation method to delineate the continuous rainfall time series into individual rainfall events. This method relied on two thresholds: the minimum period without rain (T  p     ) and the minimum rainfall amount (T a    ). A new rainfall event starts when T  p      is exceeded and the subsequent rainfall amount is above T a    . Conversely, the rainfall event ends when the previous rainfall amount is below T a     and T  p      has passed (Wiekenkamp et al., 2016 ). The selection of a threshold plays a crucial role in the characteristics of the delineated rain events (Fig. S3  ). Balancing the number of rainfall events, the mean total rainfall, and the event duration, as well as exceeding the instrument noise threshold, we defined T a   as 0.4 mm and Tp   as 96 h (4 days), referring to our previous study (Jin et al., 2018 ).  3.3 Rainfall infiltration monitoring and analysis Rainfall infiltration patterns were compared (by measuring lag time, accumulated rainfall amount, maximum change in soil moisture, wetting depth, wetting-front velocity, and preferential flow occurrence) and associated controlling factors between the growing and non-growing seasons. 3.3.1 Soil moisture monitoring Soil moisture monitoring sites were established in the downhill gully and uphill slope of each catchment. The local slope gradients are ∼ 20°, ∼35°, ∼20°, and ∼ 45° at the grassland uphill slope site, grassland downhill gully site, forestland uphill slope site, and forestland downhill gully site, respectively. At each site, a vertical array of soil moisture probes (EC-5 probes with a precision of ± 0.1 vol%; The METER Group, Inc., Pullman, Washington) was installed in the upslope facing direction of a soil pit at five depths (10, 20, 40, 60, and 100-cm depth). Soil moisture was recorded every 10 min and stored in the EM50 dataloggers. The monitoring soil profiles were relatively homogenous and very similar across the four sites without discernible soil layering structures below the surface organic layer (∼10 cm thick). The 10-min soil moisture data from May 2016 to December 2018 were used for exploring soil moisture behavior in response to rainfall (Fig. S1  a-d ).  3.3.2 Soil moisture response to the rainfall Soil moisture readings at the surface soil layer (∼20 cm depth) are sensitive to diurnal soil temperature fluctuations, potentially leading to a rise in soil moisture content by 0.1 vol% every 10 min during daylight (Chanzy et al., 2012; Verhoef et al., 2006 ). Deeper layers experience less variation in diurnal soil temperature. To accurately pinpoint the soil moisture response to rainfall, we establish specific criteria. For shallower probes (10 and 20 cm depth), we identify the initiation of the soil moisture response to rainfall infiltration as the first documented increase in soil moisture by ≥ 0.4 vol% within a 10-minute interval. For deeper probes (40, 60, and 100 cm depth), we define the start of the soil moisture response to rainfall infiltration if the accumulated soil moisture increment was > 0.2 vol% compared to initial conditions present at the onset of a rainfall event, thereby surpassing the possible instrument's noise (i.e., 0.1 vol% for EC-5 soil moisture probe; Rosenbaum et al., 2010 ). Moreover, we define several variables to measure the magnitude of soil moisture response to rainfall and thus quantitatively describe the infiltration process. Specifically, the maximum increase in soil moisture represents the greatest increase in soil moisture due to infiltration in a rainfall event. Wetting depth (WD) is denoted as the depth of the deepest soil moisture probe that detected a soil moisture response to rainfall infiltration. The lag time refers to the time difference between the start of a rainfall event and the start of soil moisture response. The accumulated rainfall amounts indicate the total rainfall amounts during the lag time, which is considered the threshold rainfall amount required to trigger soil moisture response. The wetting front velocity (Vwf ) is calculated as the ratio of the soil moisture penetration distance to the time of infiltration. By comparing these variables between the growing and non-growing seasons, we can gain a clearer understanding of the seasonal variations in rainfall infiltration patterns into loess hillslopes on the CLP. Finally, we categorize the infiltration behavior by the sequence of response times at different soil depths. Preferential flow (PF) has been characterized by two main expressions: (i) a non-sequential response to rainfall, with deeper soil moisture probes responding quicker compared to shallower probes, and (ii) a high velocity through the soil profile, resulting in a sequential response with minimal differences in lag time (Graham and Lin, 2011 ). Taking these criteria into account, this study divided the soil moisture response to infiltration into the following three categories of subsurface flow:1. Preferential flow  was identified by a non-sequential order of response times among the five probe depths. Also, PF was defined by a sequential response with depth at a velocity surpassing a specific threshold, i.e., typically the saturated soil hydraulic conductivity (Ks  ). Given the corresponding measurements by (Guo et al., 2018 ), the velocity threshold was set to 10.0 cm/h for the grassland catchment and 20.0 cm/h for the forestland catchment.  2. Sequential flow  was designated to the sequential response of probes in order of depth and with the wetting front velocity lower than the velocity threshold.  3. No response  was identified by a soil moisture sequence in which none of the probes in a monitoring soil profile recorded soil moisture response to infiltration.    Preferential flow frequency was calculated as the ratio of the number of rainfall events with PF occurring to the number of total rainfall events.(2) P F %    = Preferential  f l o w  e v e n t s  All  r a i n f a l l  e v e n t s         3.3.3 Soil water storage Soil water storage for the surface 100-cm soils was compared between the growing and non-growing seasons among the study sites, with the calculation based on the following equation:(3) SWS = ∑ z = 1  5  θ z  d z          where SWS  is the soil water storage, θ z     is the volumetric soil water content measured at the zth  -depth interval (i.e., 10, 20, 40, 60, and 100 cm depth), and d z     is the thickness of each depth interval (i.e., 0–10, 10–20, 20–40, 40–60, and 60–100 cm depth). In addition, we compared the average soil moisture profile of the growing and non-growing seasons across the four monitoring sites to reveal seasonal differences in the vertical distribution of soil moisture.   3.4 Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) modeling Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) were carried out to rank the relative influence of landscape and rainfall characteristics on soil moisture response (WD, Vwf  and PF) during the growing and non-growing seasons, respectively. The MARS model is a nonparametric regression method that divides the dataset into segments (i.e., spline) and models them individually, resulting in piecewise curves called basis functions. The basic functions (BFs) allow flexibility in simulating thresholds as well as interactions between variables and combining them (Zhang and Goh, 2016 ), as shown in the following equation:(4) f x    = α + ∑ p = 1  k  α k  B F x        where f x       is a linear combination of BFs, α    and α k     are coefficients, and k  is the number of segments. We conducted variable importance analysis using the MARS model, primarily based on N subsets     and residual sum of squares (RSS). N subsets     is defined as the number of times a variable was used in modeling BFs, while the RSS is a parameter that tracks model error derived from observed and predicted responses (Singh et al., 2021 ). It can be interpreted as the higher the N subsets     value, the greater the decreases in RSS, indicating the more important the variable. The MARS model was performed using the “Earth” package in R (RStudioTeam, 2016 ).  3.5 Statistics Descriptive statistics (mean, median, and standard error (SE)) were computed for response metrics (lag time, accumulated rainfall amount, maximum change in soil moisture and Vwf ). Mann-Whitney U  test was used to compare the difference in environmental factors (Duration, total amount, peak intensity and average intensity) between the growing and non-growing seasons. The level of Significance was assumed to be α    = 0.001. In this study, statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 27.0 (SPSS Inc., USA).   4 Results 4.1 Seasonal variations of environmental factors and rainfall events delineation The NDVI, LAI, mean air temperature, and average rainfall from 2016 to 2018 revealed distinct seasonal patterns and generally exhibited similar trends (Fig. 2  and S2). The NDVI and LAI time series reflected the growth curve of vegetation (Fig. 2  a). Between May and October, the NDVI values consistently remained high (>0.3), reaching their peak from June to August with an average of 0.585 (Fig. 2 b). Conversely, from September to February, the NDVI values showed a noticeable decline. The NDVI values from December to March dropped below 0.15, indicating possible plant mortality or dormancy. The annual LAI trends mirrored those of NDVI, showing a clear seasonal pattern (Fig. 2 a and S2). Between May and October, the LAI for both forestland and grassland remained high, with forestland LAI peaking in August 2016 at 9.57 and grassland LAI reaching 8.486. In contrast, from November to April, the LAI values were significantly lower, with forestland LAI dropping to 3.479 and grassland LAI reaching 1.415. Throughout the study period, forestland LAI consistently exceeded grassland LAI, indicating higher leaf density and canopy coverage in forestland. The 61 rainfall events that we identified are generally representative of the wide range of rainfall characteristics experienced in the Nanxiaohegou watershed (Table 1  ). Over the study period from May 2016 to December 2018, the catchment received a total of 1489.3 mm of rainfall, averaging 558.5 mm year−1 . Excluding periods with no rain, the median rainfall for a rainfall event was found to be 9.6 mm. The 61 identified rainfall events were distributed over three growing seasons (43 events) and two and a half non-growing seasons (18 events). It is worth noting that the total rainfall amount during the growing season accounted for 89.0 % of the annual rainfall recorded during the study period, amounting to 1325.2 mm. Statistical significant differences (p < 0.05) were detected in the duration, total amount, and peak intensity between the growing and non-growing seasons (Fig. 3  ). Average intensity showed no significant difference (p > 0.05) between the growing and non-growing seasons, with the non-growing season having a lower median of average intensity. These findings suggest a distinct seasonal pattern in the characteristics of rainfall.  4.2 Rainfall infiltration comparison between growing and non-growing seasons 4.2.1 Initiation of soil moisture in response to rainfall To evaluate the susceptibility of soil to rainfall infiltration, comparisons were made between the growing and non-growing seasons in terms of the lag time, accumulated rainfall amount, and the maximum change in soil moisture from the start of the rainfall event until the earliest soil moisture response in soil profiles (Fig. 4   and Table 2  ). During the non-growing season, the lag time is significantly longer compared to the growing season (p < 0.001). Specifically, the average lag time for the growing season was 23.34 h across four sites, whereas during the non-growing season, it averaged 56.84 h (Fig. 4 a and Table 2 ). The largest discrepancy in lag time between the seasons was observed at the grassland upslope site, with a mean difference of 56.04 h. The highest variation in lag time was seen at the forestland downslope site, likely due to vegetation cover and topography (SE=78.58 in the growing season and SE=85.69 in the non-growing season). During the growing season, the accumulated rainfall amount required to elicit soil moisture response was significantly greater than in the non-growing season, with a mean value of 50.41 mm compared to 10.28 mm, indicating a clear seasonal impact (p < 0.001). Despite this, the rainfall thresholds required to trigger soil moisture response (indicated by the green dashed line in Fig. 4 b) were similar across the seasons. This is likely due to enhanced canopy interception, particularly at the forest downslope site, which requires a higher rainfall amount of 5.8 mm to trigger a response. In contrast, the other three sites only require approximately 3.2–3.4 mm of rainfall to initiate soil moisture changes (Fig. 4 b and Table 2 ). During the growing season, the average maximum increase in soil moisture is 2.5 % cm3 /cm3 , which is significantly higher than that observed during the non-growing season, i.e., 0.5 % cm3 /cm3  (Fig. 4 c and Table 2 ). This demonstrates that the rainfall during the non-growing season is not able to effectively replenish soil moisture.  4.2.2 Wetting depth There is a significant difference in the WD of soil moisture after rainfall between the growing and non-growing seasons (Fig. 5  ). During the growing season, rainfall events exhibit higher peak intensity and greater rainfall amounts, which easily trigger soil moisture response and increase the depth of rainwater infiltration (Fig. 5 e). This leads to more soil moisture response events during the growing season, particularly in the deep soil layers (40–100 cm). In the forestland catchment, this difference in WD is more pronounced, possibly due to the significant changes in the growth status, water uptake, and evaporation of forest vegetation during the two seasons. The WD after 61 rainfall events varied with depth and landscape positions across the compared catchments (Fig. 5 ). The response percentage is greatest at shallow depths (10–20 cm) and downslope positions. Compared to the grassland catchment, the forestland catchment (Fig. 5 c, d) demonstrates a higher response in the deep soil layers (40–60 cm). In particular, the downhill gully site at the forest catchment hinders the downward transport of rainwater to 40 and 60 cm depth. Additionally, the lower the antecedent moisture conditions (AMC), the deeper the WD (Fig. 5 a-d). When the initial moisture content is lower, it indicates that the soil has a greater capacity to absorb and retain moisture from rainfall, enabling the moisture to penetrate deeper into the soil profile. In contrast, when the AMC is high, the soil already contains a significant amount of moisture, limiting its ability to absorb additional rainwater.  4.2.3 Wetting front velocity Compared to the non-growing season, the mean wetting front velocity (Vwf ) during the growing season was significantly higher, reaching 34.6 mm/h (Table 2 ). Additionally, during rainfall events with greater precipitation and higher peak intensity, mean Vwf  further increased (Fig. 6  e). Throughout the growing season, there was a wide range of variation in Vwf  (Fig. 6  and Table 2 ). This demonstrates that the soil moisture movement is highly active during the growing season, with both matrix flow and PF playing vital roles in water transportation. In addition, there is a negative correlation between Vwf  and AMC. (Fig. 6 a-d). This indicates that when the soil moisture content is lower, the hydraulic conductivity of the soil increases, leading to a higher infiltration rate of moisture into the soil. Whether it was during the growing season or the non-growing season, the mean Vwf  on forestland uphill was higher than that on grassland uphill (Fig. 6  and Table 2 ). This is due to the well-developed root systems of trees and shrubs in forestland, as well as the looser soil structure and larger pore spaces, resulting in better soil permeability. In contrast, the soil in grasslands could be denser with smaller pore spaces, leading to poorer soil permeability. On the downhill slope in forestland, the mean Vwf  was lower than that in the grassland downhill slope. This is because forestland downhill had high vegetation coverage, which intercepted rainfall during the growing season and slowed down the infiltration of soil moisture. However, due to the active development of root systems, Vwf  in forestland downhill was only slightly lower than that in grassland. During the non-growing season, trees in forestland downhill enter a dormant or leaf-fall state, and root activity decreases. The soil surface can accumulate thick layers of dead leaves and plant residue, hindering water infiltration and significantly reducing the speed of soil moisture penetration.  4.2.4 Frequency of preferential flow The frequency of PF varied with season, vegetation, slope, and depth (Fig. 7  ). In the monitoring area, the average frequency of PF was 14.74 %, with a higher occurrence during the growing season (19.77 %) compared to the non-growing season (9.72 %). During the growing season, rainfall events with high precipitation and peak rainfall intensity corresponded to frequent occurrences of PF (indicated by green dashed lines). In the growing season, the average frequency of PF in forested areas was 23.26 %, which was higher than that in grassland areas (16.28 %), indicating that the root channels formed by trees and shrubs accelerated the PF process. During the non-growing season, the frequency of PF on uphill grasslands was the lowest, likely due to reduced root activity and topographic constraints in the area. Throughout the year, PF in grassland catchment frequently occurred at depths of 40 cm and 60 cm, while in forestland catchment, PF frequently occurred at depths of 40 cm and 100 cm. Particularly during the growing season, frequent occurrences of PF were estimated in the Grassland upslope (40 cm), Forestland upslope (40, 100 cm), and Forestland downslope (40 cm) areas (>5 times). In addition, there is a negative correlation between AMC and the occurrence of PF, which is similar to other response characteristics.  4.2.5 The MARS models and relative influences of soil moisture response The MARS models explained 61.55 % of the variability in observed WD during the growing season, followed by 48.41 % of variability in observed Vwf , and 36.93 % of variability in observed PF. During the non-growing season, it explained 66.81 % of the observed WD variability, followed by 44.24 % for Vwf  variability, and 36.63 % for PF variability (Tab. S1  ). Additionally, the models illustrated the relationships between various explanatory variables and the response variables WD, Vwf , and PF (Fig. 8  ). In the growing season (Fig. 8 a), WD showed strong associations with rainfall amounts (RA), peak intensity (PI), vegetation type (VT) and antecedent moisture conditions (AMC). Vwf  was influenced mainly by PI, RA and AMC, while PF was primarily linked to RA, AMC and soil depth (SD). In the non-growing season (Fig. 8 b), AMC was no longer a significant explanatory variable. WD was still predominantly influenced by RA and PI, Vwf  showed a significant association only with RA, and PF was mainly explained by PI, RA, and SD. Overall, rainfall variables (RA and PI) played a crucial role in the rainfall infiltration process during both growing and non-growing seasons. However, environmental variables like AMC and VT exhibited differences between growing and non-growing seasons.   4.3 Seasonal difference in soil water storage The variation in soil water storage between the growing and non-growing seasons is not substantial among the monitoring sites (Fig. 9  ). However, the soil water storage tends to be higher during the growing season compared to the non-growing season. During the growing season, even though there is increased plant growth and evaporation (Fig. S4  ), the larger amount and higher intensity of rainfall contribute to replenishing soil moisture and facilitating water infiltration. The dense root systems of plants penetrate deep into the soil, enabling efficient absorption and storage of water, thereby leading to relatively higher soil water storage. During the non-growing season, plant growth activities weaken or cease, and vegetation cover diminishes, resulting in reduced water evaporation and plant water needs. Nevertheless, due to lower rainfall, soil water storage is relatively lower. Compared to grassland catchment, forestland catchment displayed more pronounced variations in soil moisture at different depths throughout the growing and non-growing seasons. The root zone of the grass species is less than 20 cm depth, which has a limited impact on the deeper soil moisture (Fig. 9 a, b). In contrast, the soil moisture at a depth of 100 cm is significantly reduced in forestland catchment during the growing season compared to the non-growing season (Fig. 9 c, d). This decline can be attributed to insufficient replenishment of deep soil moisture from rainfall (Fig. 4 c) and the potential for heightened utilization of deep soil moisture by plant roots during the growing season.   5 Discussion 5.1 Seasonal difference in rainfall infiltration patterns The CLP is located within a continental monsoon climate zone, subject to distinct rainy seasons influenced by the annual summer and winter monsoons. The rainy season on the CLP principally spans May to October (Wan et al., 2014 ), coinciding with the typical growing season of the vegetation (Fig. 2 ). Vegetation acquired and retained soil moisture resources more quickly and efficiently over the growing season, resulting in higher infiltration efficiency (Chen et al., 2020; He et al., 2012 ). Therefore, during the growing season, the lag time in the soil moisture response to rainfall was short (23.34 h) and soil moisture rose significantly (Fig. 4 ) . Soil moisture was more inclined to infiltrate into the soil to 60–100 cm depth, and PF occurred more actively at 40–100 cm depth (Figs. 5 and 7 ). Heavy rainfall events result in a deeper soil moisture WD, a more rapid Vwf , and an increased frequency of PF occurrence (Figs. 5-7 ). Despite vegetation consuming more water during the growing season, soil water storage is simultaneously augmented (Fig. 9 ), which aligned with the findings of (Wang et al., 2012 ). In contrast, the non-growing season is characterized by less rainfall and lower rainfall intensity (Fig. 3 ), which makes it less likely to trigger soil moisture response events (only 4 out of 18 rainfall events). Although the Vwf  is limited, WD can reach 40–100 cm depth at some sites (Figs. 5 and 6 ). PF also occurs at deeper depths (40–100 cm) during the non-growing season (Fig. 7 ). At 100 cm depth, soil water storage was slightly higher in the non-growing season than in the growing season (Fig. 9 ). This may be related to the replenishment of deep soil water deficiency caused by high ET during the growing seasons through rainfall during the non-growing seasons (Jian et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2021 ). Overall, the rainfall occurring during the non-growing season appears restricted in terms of its capacity to infiltrate into the hillslopes and replenish soil moisture. This pattern considerably departs from the infiltration behaviors observed during the growing season. In the forestland catchment, WD, Vwf , and PF differed by 11 cm, 13.77 cm/h, and 12.14 % between the growing and non-growing seasons, respectively. On the other hand, in the grassland catchment, the difference in WD, Vwf , and PF was 5 cm, 8.93 cm/h, and 7.95 %, respectively (Figs. 5-7 ). Therefore, the difference in soil moisture infiltration between the growing season and non-growing seasons in forestland catchment is greater. Moreover, forestland catchment exhibited significant differences in soil water storage across various depths, whereas grassland catchment generally showed consistent soil water storage at different depths (Fig. 9 ). Based on the results, we found that rainfall infiltration patterns in forestland catchment differed more between growing and non-growing seasons than in grassland catchment, which confirms the hypothesis proposed above.  5.2 Controlling factors of rainfall infiltration in different seasons Rainfall infiltration is contingent upon a range of factors, and the significant differences in the controlling factors between the growing and non-growing seasons lead to variations in seasonal rainfall infiltration patterns. According to the results of the MARS model (Fig. 8  and Tab. S1  ), irrespective of the season, the total amount and peak intensity of rainfall serve as principal factors that catalyze changes in soil moisture, with an average importance exceeding 70 %. Rainfall with a high peak intensity and amount expedites water penetration into the soil substrate (Figs. 5-7 ), which was similar to the results of (He et al., 2020 ). During the growing season, AMC plays a particularly essential role in the rainfall infiltration process (WD, Vwf , and PF). As AMC decreases, the hydraulic gradient increases (Hardie et al., 2011 ), inducing an acceleration of soil moisture movement within the soil and an increase in PF (Figs. 6 and 7 ). In particular, AMC has the most significant effect on PF with a high importance value of 87.8 % (Fig. 8 a). Under dry conditions, the soil cracks or the water repellence factor are more favorable for PF to occur (Tang et al., 2020 ). (Hardie et al., 2013 ) also found that the occurrence of PF was related to AMC. In addition, (Wiekenkamp et al., 2016 ) revealed a strong negative relationship between AMC and PF occurrence with a high rainfall amount. This is similar to the result of our study, the negative correlation between AMC and PF was evident in high rainfall events such as P28, P29 (Fig. 7  and Table 1 ). This further explains that the insignificant relationship between PF and AMC during the non-growing season may be due to the little rainfall amount (Fig. 7 ). Moreover, the vegetation type exerts a significant impact on the WD during the growing season (Fig. 8 a). Different vegetation types play different roles in redistributing rainfall, partitioning, and storing, thereby producing differences in rainfall infiltration patterns (Spencer and van Meerveld, 2016 ). In the grassland catchment, the maximum WD observed after rainfall events escalates up to 60 cm; whereas, in the forestland catchment, WD reaching 100 cm occurs approximately five times (Fig. 5 ). Grassland has limited ability to redistribute rainfall, while forestland exhibits a contrasting phenomenon. Rainfall is spatially concentrated by tree stems via stemflow in forestland catchment (Levia and Germer, 2015 ). It gathers limited rainwater resources into the soil layer where the tree root system is concentrated, allowing further infiltration into deeper soil layers. Additionally, different plant species have distinct root structures and water requirements, which influence the rainwater transport along roots (Gao et al., 2018 ). The root depth of grass (e.g., A. cristatum , B. ischaemum ) in this area is usually within 20 cm, limiting deep infiltration of soil moisture. Deep-rooted plants, such as trees (e.g., R. pseudoacacia or P. tabuliformis ) and shrubs (e.g., R. palmatus ), have developed extensive root systems, which can produce more macropores and increase soil permeability and easily transported along coarse roots to the deeper layers (Alaoui et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2017 ). However, during the non-growing season, plants exhibit a relatively low ability to absorb and utilize soil moisture, resulting in less pronounced differences in WD. During the non-growing season from November to March, there is a cycle of snow cover accumulation and ablation processes in the CLP (Jin et al., 2015 ). However, due to limitation of the equipment adopted in this study, the infiltration process after snowfall melting was not considered. This may have affected soil moisture transport and replenished soil water storage during the non-growing season (Pan et al., 2022; Wallace and Minder, 2021 ), necessitating further research to monitor snowfall and infiltration mechanisms after snow melting.  5.3 Effects of revegetation on the rainfall infiltration processes in the CLP Multiple studies have underscored the significant impact of long-term revegetation projects in headwater catchments on the CLP (Chen et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The restoration of natural grassland and afforestation represent two critical vegetation restoration patterns in this region. Our study revealed that the WD in a forestland catchment following rainfall during the growing season was deeper than that in a grassland catchment, and there was more variability in soil water storage during both the growing and non-growing seasons (Figs. 5 and 9 ). This indicates that the forestland catchment might possess superior infiltration capacity to that of the grassland catchment. However, with a marked increase in forest coverage, hydrological effects such as enhanced vegetation interception, an increase in catchment evaporation, and alteration in soil moisture response mechanisms to rainfall have taken place (Feng et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2012 ; Liu and Shao, 2016 ). Remarkably, the downhill site in the forestland catchment displayed over 90 % vegetation cover, which is markedly greater than the coverage (only 50 %) on the uphill site (Fig. 1 d). This leads to the longest response time of soil moisture to rainfall infiltration at the forestland downslope site (57.66 h), with the highest rainfall threshold required (5.8 mm), and restrictions on WD and Vwf  compared to the forestland upslope site (Figs. 4-6 ). (Pierret et al., 2016 ) also considered that deep-rooted species such as forest trees utilize not only precipitation in shallow soils but also deep soil moisture that has accumulated over the long term. Therefore, the continued expansion of revegetation can potentially limit the efficiency of rainfall infiltration (Li et al., 2021 ). The strong association between vegetation planting patterns, topography, and rainfall infiltration is clear (Chen et al., 2018; He et al., 2020 ). Both during the growing season and the non-growing season, the slope impacts the WD (Fig. 8 ). In the grassland catchment, the downhill slope site exhibited deeper WD and quicker Vwf  than the uphill slope site (Figs. 4-5 ). Soil water storage also shows variance among the four sites, gradually decreasing from the grassland downhill gully site to the forestland uphill slope site, followed by the grassland uphill slope site, and finally the forestland downhill gully site (Fig. 9 ). The tendency for higher rainfall infiltration into deeper soil layers with a smaller cumulative rainfall needed to replenish soil moisture (Figs. 6 and 7 ), combined with limited water consumption by vegetation in deeper soil layers (Fig. 1 c and 11b), and the pooling of water in depressions caused by terrain, along with reduced solar radiation in gullies (Fig. 1 c), collectively result in higher soil water storage in the grassland downhill gully site (Zhu et al., 2020 ). In the future, it would be beneficial to establish replicable points within each landform-vegetation unit to further enhance our understanding of rainfall infiltration and the associated hydrological processes on the CLP. Moreover, the noted distinctions between the growing and non-growing seasons (Figs. 4-9 ) suggest that future ecological restoration initiatives on the CLP can prioritize tree planting early in the growing season, when conditions for soil moisture infiltration and storage are more favorable. Additionally, choosing tree species that can withstand seasonal fluctuations in soil moisture is vital (Wang et al., 2021 ). Employing strategies that mix vegetation, such as combining forestland and grassland catchments, could aid in maintaining balanced soil moisture dynamics year-round.   6 Conclusions In this study, we conducted detailed monitoring soil moisture at the 10-min interval across five depths (10, 20, 40, 60, and 100 cm) within both forestland and adjacent grassland catchments on the CLP, spanning from May 2016 to December 2018. During the study period, a total of 61 rainfall events were delineated, consisting of 43 in the growing season (May to October) and 18 in the non-growing season (November to April). Our findings reveal considerable seasonal variations in rainfall attributes, NDVI, and meteorological factors, alongside distinct infiltration patterns and their determinants across seasons. Despite requiring similar rainfall thresholds (3.2–5.8 mm) to trigger a soil moisture response in both seasons, the non-growing season had a longer lag time (56.84 h). The growing season was characterized by a notable increase in soil moisture (up to 35.7 % cm3 cm−3 ) is found, a deeper WD (often extending to 40–100 cm depth), faster Vwf  (17.44 mm/h), and a higher frequency of PF (19.77 %). In contrast, the non-growing season saw modest changes in soil moisture (only up to 6.4 % cm3 cm−3 ), with a shallower WD (often restrained at depths of 10–40 cm), slower Vwf  (6.24 mm/h), and reduced PF frequency (9.72 %). These observations underline a more efficient rainfall infiltration during the growing season, which, coupled with increased soil water storage, occurs despite elevated evapotranspiration rates. Moreover, the application of the MARS model highlighted the crucial role of rainfall amount and peak intensity in influencing rainfall infiltration across both seasons. During the growing season, additional factors such as AMC and vegetation type further affected WD, Vwf , and PF frequency. Overall, this study offers vital insights into the infiltration processes of hillslope environments following long-term revegetation on the CLP and provides a robust scientific foundation for optimizing soil and water management in the region.
1 Introduction Floods pose a significant threat to human lives, properties, and socioeconomic well-being, causing substantial damage to infrastructure and agricultural production (Kao et al., 2021; Mahdizadeh and Perez, 2023 ). In flood prevention, accurate flood forecasting is a crucial non-engineering measure, essential to operational flood prevention platforms and systems. Physically-based hydrological models, such as the soil and water assessment tool model (Tan et al., 2021 ), the hydrologiska fyrans vattenbalans model (Lindström et al., 1997 ), the tank model (Lee and Singh, 1999 ), and the Xinanjiang (XAJ) model (Zhao, 1992 ), serve as foundational tools in operational flood forecasting due to their interpretability and reliability (Imhoff et al., 2021 ). However, the application of these models is challenged by various sources of uncertainty, primarily encompassing model inputs, parameters, model structure, and initial conditions (Liang et al., 2021 ). To reduce flood forecast uncertainty, a feasible approach is to update hydrological model states. Reducing the compounded errors caused by uncertainties in state estimates is a significant advantage. Notably, these uncertainties exert a primary influence on forecast accuracy, particularly during the initial forecasting stage (Lee et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2020 ). The Kalman filter is a time-domain filtering approach for the state-space model, offering explicit solutions for unbiased estimation of state variables (Kalman, 1960; Vetra-Carvalho et al., 2018 ). Due to its efficacy in reducing state estimate errors, The Kalman filter has shown potential to improve the forecasting performance of hydrological models (Khaki et al., 2019 ). However, it follows a linearized assumption that cannot be readily applied to most hydrological models (Shen et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023 ). Nonlinear extensions of the Kalman filter are gaining more popularity and applicability in the hydrologic community. The most commonly used nonlinear extension is the ensemble Kalman filter (Evensen, 1994; Clark et al., 2008; Kivi et al., 2022 ). The ensemble Kalman filter can estimate nonlinear system states through a Monte Carlo-based sampling method (Zhang et al., 2020 ). Nonetheless, the primary challenge facing the ensemble Kalman filter to ensure estimation accuracy is its reliance on a substantial number of samples, with computational efficiency and stability as the main concerns (Rakovec et al., 2015; Vetra-Carvalho et al., 2018 ). Hydrological models often involve a large number of state variables and parameters, leading to a high dimensional state space. Such intricate presents significant computational challenges to the ensemble Kalman filter. The unscented Kalman filter (UKF) is an alternative nonlinear filtering technique that follows more relaxed prior assumptions than the ensemble Kalman filter (Julier et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2020 ). The unscented transformation, a fundamental concept in the UKF, involves the creation of a set of sigma points with fixed weights to convert prior state estimates into current ones (Liu et al., 2012 ). Renowned for its efficient sampling strategy and stable filtering performance, the UKF has garnered interest in filtering high-order, nonlinear coupled systems in various scientific and engineering domains (Jiang et al., 2019 ). Within the realm of hydrological research, Yang (2021)  applied the UKF to regional frequency modelling, demonstrating its superior estimate performance over other filtering approaches in extreme non-stationary conditions. Zhou et al. (2020)  proposed a UKF-based probabilistic flood forecasting model, highlighting its efficacy in enhancing the reliability of flood forecasts. Sun et al. (2020)  emphasized the UKF's potential to improve hydrological models’ predictive accuracy, outperforming the ensemble Kalman filter in terms of both computational efficiency and effectiveness. Although the UKF has shown significant potential to optimize the predictive capability of hydrological models, it has received less attention and implementation than the ensemble Kalman filter. Similar to other Kalman filtering techniques, the performance of UKF relies on precise noise statistics estimation (Pathiraja et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2023 ). The noise statistics consist of the system noise and measurement noise, which can be viewed as aggregative indicators encompassing uncertainties in input, model structure, parameters, observations, etc.  According to the fundamental assumptions of Kalman filtering theory, the filter can achieve optimal state estimates only if the noise follows a Gaussian distribution and the statistical values are known (Kalman, 1960; Julier et al., 2000 ). However, these assumptions may not hold true in practice, as noise prior statistics are often unknown and may change over time. This challenge is particularly pronounced in nonlinear hydrological models, where accurately specifying noise characteristics can be especially difficult due to the inherent variability and uncertainty in hydrological processes. The classical UKF lacks adaptability to complex time-varying noise. When noise statistics are unknown or change over time, a high risk of reduced filtering accuracy or even divergence would appear in the implementation of the classical UKF. To estimate noise statistics, several adaptive methods and online methods have been proposed for quantifying these uncertainties. The adaptive approaches adjust the noise statistics by utilizing information in prediction residuals and observations. However, their reliability would be unwarrantable since unobservable state variables may cause additional uncertainty and bias (Yang, 2021 ). Another approach is to estimate noise statistics online, mainly implemented by Bayesian error analysis and Mont Carlo simulation (Teweldebrhan et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2022 ). Due to diverse sources of uncertainty and their sophisticated interrelationship, online methods may introduce unsuitable prior assumptions of the noise distribution, let alone necessitate rather intricate algorithms for a posteriori estimate. To all intents and purposes, the lack of prior knowledge in recognizing and estimating uncertainty poses formidable obstacles to the practical application of UKF. As a possible solution to address this issue, deep neural networks have demonstrated a significant advantage by extracting implicit features from nonlinear systems, independent of domain-specific knowledge (Lin et al., 2020; Mo et al., 2022 ). In the realm of hydrological research, the recurrent neural networks, especially the long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks proposed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) , have been widely used to model dynamical systems like rainfall-runoff process. The LSTM models overcome the technical bottleneck of vanishing or exploding gradients in traditional recurrent neural networks, and can simulate both static and dynamic dependencies over short and long periods (Gao et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2023 ). Many studies have highlighted the LSTM's unique advantage in capturing hidden features and dynamic patterns over other deep neural networks (Cui et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023 ). It can be noticed that LSTM have been successfully applied to correct the predictive errors of physically-based flood forecasting models. Khatun et al. (2023)  developed a framework, with their findings demonstrating LSTM's effectiveness as a robust error prediction model. This framework significantly improved the flood forecasting accuracy of MIKE11 within a 1 to 5-day lead time. Moreover, some prior studies have investigated the fusion of deep neural networks with Kalman filter-based models, demonstrating their potential to improve filtering accuracy (McMillan et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023 ). Nonetheless, these approaches follow the weak-coupling framework, where the deep neural networks and filters operate independently, leaving the challenge of noise estimation unresolved within the filtering process. To address the technical limitations of UKF, an alternative approach is proposed— a deep fusion between LSTM and UKF, leveraging the strengths of LSTM to tackle the challenging noise estimation problem. The computational process of UKF shows that the effect of noise statistical moments on the posteriori state estimation is mediated through the recursive computation of the Kalman Gain. Given the LSTM's inherent memory and non-linear mapping abilities, it is well-suited to serve as an internal memory element for tracking the Kalman Gain. By embedding the LSTM as a sub-module within the UKF filtering process, this fusion approach can capture and implicitly estimate noise-related information. It presents a promising solution to overcome the inherent challenges of the UKF, which contributes to enhancing the accuracy and robustness of hydrological model updates. The innovative aspect of this study lies in fusing the LSTM neural networks into UKF (LSTM-UKF) to overcome the intricate noise estimation challenges faced by the Kalman filter during hydrological model updates. The primary objective is to mitigate cumulative state estimation errors in hydrological models, consequently enhancing the accuracy and reliability of flood forecasts. Through case studies conducted in the Jianxi and Tianyi basins in China, the performance of the proposed LSTM-UKF against the conventional UKF was compared. Both filters are applied to update the XAJ hydrological model, particularly suited for modelling rainfall-runoff processes in semi-humid and humid regions. The study comprehensively evaluates the filters' effectiveness in improving multi-step-ahead flood forecasts. 1.1 Methodology This study proposes an LSTM-UKF approach to improve flood forecasts for physically-based hydrological models. The LSTM-UKF can update and correct model states without requiring accurate noise estimation, making it more adaptive than the UKF. The study assesses its performance in enhancing the XAJ model, comparing it with the UKF. Fig. 1   illustrates the architectures of these models: Fig. 1 a visualizes the state transfer process of the XAJ model, Fig. 1 b depicts the computational framework of the UKF, and Fig. 1 c presents the structure of the LSTM-UKF. The following is a brief introduction to the models used in this study.  1.2 The Xinanjiang (XAJ) model This study uses the XAJ model as the physically based flood forecasting model, which has widespread application in humid and semi-humid regions of China (Zhao, 1992; Zhang et al., 2021 ). The conceptual diagram of runoff calculation process of the XAJ model is shown in Fig. 1 a. The XAJ model consists of four modules: a three-layer evapotranspiration module (with a three-layer soil structure), a runoff generation module, a runoff separation module, and a runoff routing module as described by Gong et al. (2021) . The evapotranspiration module calculates soil evaporation based on potential evaporation. Runoff generation occurs when the storage reaches its maximum capacity, and this capacity is distributed across the basin. The runoff production is then separated into three components: interflow, surface, and groundwater, based on Horton's concept of infiltration. Finally, the runoff is routed to the outflow using a lag and route technique. The XAJ model can be described as a state-space model (Sun et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023 ), denoted explicitly by equation (2.1) .(2.1) X t  = F X t - 1     + w t - 1   , w t - 1    N 0 , Ω t - 1        Q t  = H X t    + v t  , v t   N 0 , Ψ t              where X t  ∈ R  m     symbolizes the m  -dimensional state vector of the system; Q ∈ R  n     symbolizes the n  -dimensional observation variable; F ·    is the nonlinear state transition equation, reflecting dynamic evolutions of model states; H ·    is the measurement equation, denoting the relationships between system states and observations; w t    and v t    are independent random variables, respective representing system noise and measurement noise; Ω t - 1     and Ψ t    are noise covariance matrices. Specifically, the sub-modules, state variables, and parameters of the XAJ model are presented in Table 1  . For time step t  , the model input consists of basin-averaged precipitation P t    and potential evaporation E M  t   . The output is the basin outflow Q t   . The computational process of model states can be summarized as a nonlinear state transfer equation F ·    comprising four sub-functions. In the evapotranspiration function f 1  ·   , the evapotranspiration from different soil layers is calculated firstly for calculating the variation of total tension water storage. Then, the variation is allocated to different layers’ soil moisture states (W U  t   , W L  t   , W D  t   ). The runoff generation function f 2  ·    aims to estimate free water storage S t    and compute the generated runoff and overland flow (in impervious area, considered as part of the surface runoff). The generated runoff is determined by soil moisture states and tension water capacity based on the saturation excess runoff generation mechanism in the XAJ model. The runoff separation function f 3  ·    is responsible for separating the runoff into surface flow Q S  t   , interflow Q I  t   , and groundwater flow Q G  t   . Subsequently, the runoff variables are updated by the runoff routing function f 4  ·   , representing the concentration process. The measurement function H ·    is a summation of three updated runoff variables, corresponding to the outflow Q t   . Additionally, the system noise w t - 1     and measurement noise v t    represent uncertainties in state estimation and observation, respectively. Due to the intricate nature and uncertainties in the hydrological system, the system noise is a summation of uncertainties in model input, model structure, model parameters, and initial states (Hu et al., 2019 ). Besides, the measurement noise primarily arises from uncertainty in discharge measurements (Gong et al., 2023 ).  1.3 Unscented Kalman filter (UKF) The UKF is a nonlinear Kalman filtering technique, that offers the benefits of superior filtering accuracy and dependable convergence for real-time state estimation of a nonlinear system (Cui, Hong, and Layne, 2005 ). The heart of UKF is the unscented transformation, a sampling technique that generates a symmetric set of sigma points with deterministic weights to estimate state probability density (Julier et al., 2000 ). With respect to Taylor series expansion, the approximations provided by UKF are capable of achieving at least second-order accuracy when dealing with any nonlinear functions (The approximation is capable of achieving a minimum of third-order accuracy when dealing with Gaussian distribution.). As depicted in Fig. 1 b, the state updating process for the XAJ model can be described as follows. Step I:  sigma point sampling.  For time step t  , a set of sigma points, denoted as X ^  t - 1  i    , i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , 2 m + 1   , was sampled for initial states estimation. Each sigma point represents a combination of state variables obtained from their prior distribution. Specifically,(2.2) X ^  t - 1  i    = X ^  t - 1   , i = 1    X ^  t - 1   + m + λ   Σ t - 1       i  , i = 2 , 3  ⋯ , m + 1    X ^  t - 1   - m + λ   Σ t - 1       i  , i = m + 2 , ⋯ , 2 m + 1            where m   is the number of state variables, m = 7    in this study. X ^  t - 1     and Σ t - 1     represent the mean and covariance at the previous time step t - 1   , respectively. The parameter λ is defined as λ = α  2  m + κ   - m   , where α   controls the distribution of sigma points around the mean during sampling, and κ   is a secondary scaling factor. According to Julier et al. (2000) , κ = 3 - m    and 10  - 4   < α ≤ 1    are recommended. Next, the weights W i  m    and W i  c    of each sigma point are calculated by:(2.3) W i  m  = λ m + λ   , i = 1    1 2 m + λ     , i = 2 , ⋯ , 2 m + 1            (2.4) W i  c  = λ m + λ   + 1 - α  2  + β , i = 1    1 2 m + λ     , i = 2 , ⋯ , 2 m + 1            where β   is used to introduce high statistical information for states variable. If the state variables are approximated as Gaussian distributions, the appropriate value of β   is set to 2. Step II:  Prediction. The initial states of each sigma point are propagated to X ^  t | t - 1  i      by using transfer function F Â ·     , and their predictions Q ^  t | t - 1  ( i )     are calculated through measurement function H Â ·     .(2.5) X ^  t | t - 1  i    = F X ^  t - 1  i          (2.6) Q ^  t | t - 1  i    = H X ^  t | t - 1  i           Using the unscented transformation, statistical moments of the current prior states can be computed by using the weighted points and pre-defined process noise covariance Ω t - 1    . For state updating, the Kalman Gain K t    and the residual Δ Q  t    are computed by using the second-order moments and observation Q t   (2.12) K t  = Σ x q , t   Σ q q , t    - 1       (2.13) Δ Q  t  = Q t  - Q ^  t | t - 1        Therefore, the posterior estimates of the updated states can be computed, of which the mean X ^  t    and covariance Σ t    are calculated as:(2.14) X ^  t  = X ^  t | t - 1   + K t  Δ Q  t      (2.15) Σ t  = Σ t | t - 1   - K t  Σ q q , t   K t  T       As in other Kalman filtering techniques, improperly specified noise statistics can significantly reduce accuracy or even divergence in filtering. Therefore, accurate noise estimation is essential for UKF to update model states. Researchers have used either empirical or statistical methods for the a-posterior error estimation by assuming prior noise distribution (Fan et al., 2022 ). However, those prior assumptions may not align with the authentic conditions, and the complexity of the proposed methods for a-posteriori estimation can present practical challenges. The noise statistics are relevant to syntheses of various forecasting uncertainties, which inherently exhibit non-stationary and non-linear properties. To surmount the bottleneck in UKF caused by a lack of prior knowledge regarding these uncertainties, the LSTM model emerges as a potential solution. Leveraging its superior data mining ability, the LSTM can extract implicit noise-related information that helps to improve the estimation accuracy.  1.4 Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network The LSTM neural networks are widely utilized for modelling complex and time-varying systems, as they can capture the hidden dependencies of variables in both long-term (static) and short-term (dynamic) ways (Cui et al. , 2021). An LSTM unit contains a memory cell (core cell) and three gate cells, where the memory cell's state information can be stored and updated by these gates for extracting the temporal dependencies of sequences. From the computational process of UKF, it can be inferred that the influence of noise statistical moments on a-posteriori state estimation is basically through the Kalman Gain. Therefore, the LSTM units are used to estimate the Kalman Gain adaptively by extracting and memorizing noise-related information. The principle of the LSTM unit is as follows.(1) Concatenate the memory vector (H t - 1    ) at the preceding time step and the input vector (S t   ) at present step, to form a combined input (I t   ) for the LSTM unit.   (2.16) I t  = H t - 1   + S t      where S t    is a concatenation of vectors, which encapsulate the uncertainty of evolutional information.(2) Compute the memory cell’s output vector.   (2.17) Y t  = f c  W c  · I t  + b c        where Y t    and f c    denote the output vector and the Tanh activation function of the memory cell, respectively. W c    and b c    denote the weight matrix and the bias vector of the memory cell, respectively.(3) Compute gates output vectors   (2.18) G i  = f g  W i  · I t  + b i        (2.19) G f  = f g  W f  · I t  + b f        (2.20) G o  = f g  W o  · I t  + b o        where G i   , G f   , and G o    denote the output vectors of each gate, respectively. ( W i  , W f  , W o  )    and ( b i  , b f  , b o  )    denote the weight matrices and the bias vectors of each gate, respectively. f g    denotes the Sigmoid activation function applied to these gates, where the output values lie in the interval of [0, 1].(4) Update long-term memory unit’s state vector.   (2.21) Y t  ′  = G i  · Y t     C t  ′  = G f  · C t - 1   #    C t  = Y t  ′  + C t  ′          where Y t  ′    denotes the original output of the LSTM. C t  ′    denotes the corrected state vector of the preceding time step's memory cell state C t - 1     through the forget gate output value G f   . C t    denotes the updated state vector of the long-term memory cell, to be reused in the subsequent iterations.(5) Compute the output vector H t   , which encapsulates high-dimensional noise-related information. This vector would be transformed into the Kalman Gain by a nonlinear mapping layer.   (2.22) H t  = f c  C t    · G o        1.5 A fusion of long short-term memory neural network and unscented Kalman filter (LSTM-UKF) The LSTM-UKF is proposed to overcome the UKF bottleneck in updating the hydrological model. The computational process of the proposed LSTM-UKF, illustrated in Fig. 1 c, is akin to that of the UKF. It involves the sigma point sampling, prediction, and update steps (with a Kalman Gain estimation module). The Kalman Gain estimation module is composed of an LSTM unit and two fully connected neural networks, to eliminate the over-reliance on noise statistics when calculating the Kalman Gain. For time step t ∈ T   , the state updating process is as follows.Step I:  Sigma point sampling. A group of sigma points are generated with definite weights under the sampling strategy, the same as that of UKF (refer to the description in Sect.2.2).  Step II:  Predicting. The prediction step is similar to that of UKF. Firstly, the propagated state estimations and predictions of every sigma point are calculated by equation (2.5)  and equation (2.8) . Then, the first-order statistical moments of the current prior state estimation X ^  t | t - 1     and prediction Q ^  t | t - 1    , and their cross-covariance Σ x q , t    , are computed by the unscented transformation. The LSTM-UKF does not rely on any prior knowledge of noise distribution, so there is no need to calculate the noise-related statistical moments (Σ t | t - 1     and Σ q q , t    ).  Step III:  Kalman Gain estimation. As shown in Fig. 1 c, the LSTM block, comprising an LSTM unit and two fully connected layers, is responsible for estimating the Kalman Gain. The input vector to this block is a combination of observation difference Δ Q ^   t    and state update difference Δ X ^   t    (Δ X ^   t  = X ^  t - 1   - X ^  t | t - 1     ), with a dimension of n  2  + m   , as the variations in both data sources implicitly contain noise information. The input vector would be transformed into a high-dimensional vector by the first fully connected layer, and then fed into the LSTM unit. After that, the noise information required for Kalman Gain estimation would be memorized and tracked implicitly by the LSTM unit. Subsequently, another fully connected layer nonlinearly maps the output vector H t    into an m × n   -dimensional vector, corresponding to the Kalman Gain K t    used for state update.  Step IV:  State updating. With the critical coefficient K t    in hand, the posterior mean X ^  t    can be computed through the equation (2.14) . However, since the prediction covariance Σ q q , t     is unknown, the posterior covariance Σ t    cannot be computed directly using equation (2.15) . It is worth noting that Σ x q , t     is irrelevant to noise statistics, and thus is computable. Therefore, following the assumption that X ^  t    serves as an asymptotically optimal approximation of X t   , Σ t    can be calculated by substituting equation (2.12)  into equation (2.15) , as detailed below.   (2.23) Σ t  = Σ t | t - 1   - K t  Σ q q , t   K t T  = C o v X t  , X ^  t | t - 1     - K t  Σ q q , t   K t T  = C o v X ^  t  , X ^  t | t - 1     - Σ x q , t   K t T       1.6 Training process of the LSTM-UKF The training process of the LSTM-UKF model includes data pre-processing, model parameter initialization, optimization algorithm configuration, and computation termination. Since the actual state observations are not practically available, defining a loss function based on the difference between state estimates and observations is not feasible. To address this issue, we devised an unsupervised training strategy, broadening the applicability of LSTM-UKF under various conditions. The training process is described as follows:Step I : Data pre-processing. To create datasets for model training and testing, the precipitation, evaporation, and streamflow observations collected from the basin meteorological and hydrological gauge stations are pre-processed. To segment the time series data, a time sliding window is used. The time window has a length of N   that contains trajectories of the observations over N   consecutive time steps. It's worth noting that the rainfall, runoff, and evaporation data are not normalized, as they serve as inputs to the physically-based model. The processed dataset is described as follows:   (2.24) D = P i  , E i  , Q i       i = 1  T - N      where T   is the number of total time steps. P i  , E i  ,    and Q i    denote the observation vectors of basin-averaged rainfall, evaporation, and outlet streamflow/ inflow with a length of N   within the i  -th window.Step II : Model parameter initialization. The parameter initialization of the LSTM block and UKF part are included in this step. Since it does not require presetting noise statistical moments, the initial states are the only parameters that need to be initialized for the UKF part. Therefore, continuous simulation is conducted on the XAJ model, from which the mean X ^  t    and covariances Σ t    of the initial states are generated, t = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , T   . This step enables effective preconditioning of the model, allowing the state variables at different time points to more accurately reflect the actual conditions. As a result, it reduces the uncertainty associated with the initial parameter settings. Regarding the LSTM block, the Xavier method (Ghatak, 2019 ) is utilized to initialize all trainable parameters, including W i   , W f   , W o   . It is known that the initial parameter settings are important to neural networks, since inappropriate initialization can lead to slow convergence or failure to converge, as the optimizer may struggle with poor starting points. For example, very large or very small initial weights can cause gradients to explode or vanish. The Xavier method considers the amounts of input and output neurons to equalize the variance between the input and output of each layer, thus ensuring model stability in both forward and backward propagation (Cui et al., 2022 ). While the bias terms, such as b i   , b f   , b o   , et al. , are initialized by sampling from the standard Gaussian distribution N  ( 0 , 1 )   .  Step III: Optimization algorithm configuration. The Adam optimization algorithm is used for parameter optimization (Sayed, 2014 ). Compared to other optimization algorithms like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Momentum, and Root Mean Square Propagation (RMSprop), the Adam algorithm offers adaptive learning rate adjustment, accelerates convergence, and effectively manages sparse gradients (Duchi et al., 2011; Kingma and Ba, 2015; Tieleman and Hinton, 2012 ). These characteristics make hyperparameter tuning simpler to reduce overall complexity. The Adam algorithm adjusts the learning rate based on gradient estimates to ensure stable and effective model updates during training. The hyperparameters include the maximum number of iterations I m a x    , which should be set properly to prevent both overfitting and underfitting; adjustment coefficients (b e t a  1    and b e t a  2   ), which control the convergence speed and model accuracy; epsilon, which influences the numerical stability in model training; initial learning rate (l r   ), which constrains the adjustment rate to model parameters with respect to the gradient of the loss function. The grid search method is used to tuning the hyperparameters (Moradi et al., 2023 ). The grid search method provides a thorough examination of the specified hyperparameter space by evaluating every possible combination. This ensures that all defined values are considered, which can help in finding the optimal configuration. In this study, the hyperparameter values are set as follows: I m a x     = 500, b e t a  1    = 0.90, b e t a  2    = 0.995, epsilon = 10  - 8    , and l r    = 0.001.  Step IV: Unsupervised training. Considering the observations of the XAJ model state variables are unavailable, an unsupervised training approach is introduced in this study. In this approach, the LSTM-UKF is adapted in an unsupervised manner by training it to minimize the L   2-norm residual, denoted as ‖  Δ Q  t  ‖   2   , between the streamflow predictions and observations. Based on equations (2.5) (2.8) (2.13), and (2.14), and applying the derivative chain rule, it can be demonstrated that ‖  Δ Q  t  ‖   2    allows for the gradient computation concerning trainable parameters of the LSTM block, which outputs the learned Kalman Gain. Indeed,   ∂ ‖ Δ Q  t  ‖  2   ∂ K t - 1     = 2 · Δ Q  t  ∂ Δ Q  t   ∂ Q ^  t | t - 1     · ∂ Q ^  t | t - 1    ∂ X ^  t | t - 1     · ∂ X ^  t | t - 1    ∂ X ^  t - 1     · ∂ X ^  t - 1    ∂ K t - 1        (2.25) = 2 · Q t  - H F X ^  t - 1        · ∂ Q ^  t | t - 1    ∂ X ^  t | t - 1     · ∂ X ^  t | t - 1    ∂ X ^  t - 1     · ∂ X ^  t - 1    ∂ K t - 1     = 2 · Q t  - H F X ^  t | t - 1   + K t  Δ Q  t        · θ · Δ Q  t - 1       where θ   represents the gradient of the state transfer functions regarding the state variables, which are differentiable in the XAJ model. It should be noted that the gradient computation pertains to Δ Q  t    concerning K t - 1    . This is because, within the framework of LSTM-UKF (as well as the UKF), Δ Q  t    depends on the accuracy of X ^  t | t - 1    , which represents the transformed states of X ^  t - 1     updated by K t - 1    . On this premise, the loss function can be expressed as the equation (2.27). Consequently, the model output is computed through forward propagation, and the loss function is calculated accordingly. Then, the gradients of the loss function concerning each trainable parameter are obtained through backpropagation.
