The training process is terminated by using a predetermined criterion for cessation. Specifically, if the iterations reach the maximal value (I m a x    ) or if the loss function value keeps a constant for 50 consecutive iterations, the training process is halted. Once the computation is terminated, the hyperparameters and the model's trainable parameters are stored for further analysis or future use.      2 Case study and materials 2.1 Study areas and materials To validate the applicability of the LSTM-UKF, two basins with distinct underlying surface characteristics, including the predominantly mountainous Tianyi basin and the plains-and-hills-dominated Jianxi basin, are selected to conduct the case studies. 2.1.1 Tianyi basin The Tianyi Basin is situated southeast of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau in China with a vast drainage area of 50,139 km2 , exhibiting a northwest high to southeast low terrain. This basin falls within a subtropical monsoon climate zone, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The upper reaches of the Tianyi Basin have extensive limestone distribution, constituting more than half of the area and representing a typical karst region to facilitate the formation of subterranean runoff. Fig. 2  (b) displays the hydro-meteorological gauge stations of the Tianyi basin, along with their location. The 3-hour data series were collected during the rainy season (April 1st to August 31st) from 2009 to 2020. The series included the rainfall and evaporation data from 64 gauge, and the inflow data of Tianyi reservoir.  2.1.2 Jianxi basin The Jianxi basin is in Fujian Province, China, and covers 14,787 km2  of drainage. The region is predominantly influenced by subtropical monsoons from the Southwest Indian and Southeast Pacific oceans, resulting in a humid and rainy climate. The annual rainfall of the basin falls between 1800 mm and 2200 mm, with most rainfalls occurring between March and September. The Jianxi basin mainly comprises hills and plains, with well-developed water systems and high vegetation coverage. Fig. 2 (c) provides an illustrative map of the basin. There are 16 rainfall gauge stations and three evaporation gauge stations located upstream. The 3-hourly streamflow, rainfall, and evaporation data observed during the flood season from 2005 to 2019 (April 1st to August 31st) was collected from these gauge stations. In addition, we collected rainfall, evaporation, and runoff observational data during a flood event in the Jianxi basin from May 21 to May 28, 2023. Moreover, we obtained precipitation forecast data for the corresponding period from the Global/Regional Assimilation and Prediction System (GRAPES) model (Xia et al., 2024 ). The precipitation forecasts provide a maximum 24-hour lead time, with a spatial resolution of 10 × 10 km and a temporal resolution of 1 h. Since the time intervals for rainfall, evaporation, and streamflow data were 3 h, the GRAPES data was aggregated in 3-hour increments to ensure consistency.  2.1.3 Data preparation The basin-averaged precipitation and evaporation were calculated using the Thiessen polygon approach, based on data collected from the Tianyi and Jianxi basins. The data was then separated into the training and testing datasets. For the Tianyi basin, the model was trained using the data collected from 2009 to 2018 (training stage) and validated using the data from 2019 to 2020 (testing stage). In the Tianyi basin, the maximum peak flow is 5,836 m3 /s in the training stage and 3,947 m3 /s in the testing stage. Similarly, for the Jianxi basin, the training dataset comprised data collected between 2005 and 2017, and the testing dataset covered the period between 2018 and 2019. The maximum peak flow in the Jianxi basin is 17,456 m3 /s in the training stage and 10,745 m3 /s in the testing stage. During the training stage, the model parameters were adjusted, and the model's performance was evaluated during the testing stage. The observed rainfall, evaporation, and runoff data for the flood event in the Jianxi basin in 2023, along with the GRAPES precipitation forecast data, were used to assess the effect of precipitation forecasts on the forecasting performance of our proposed model.   2.2 Model construction To compare the performance of LSTM-UKF and UKF in improving the hydrological model flood forecasts, both filters were constructed to update the XAJ model states. The parameterization schemes for these respective models are detailed as follows:(1) UKF. The required parameters include the system noise covariance Ω t - 1    , measurement noise covariance Ψ t   , and sampling parameters (κ  , α  , and β  ). Due to the unknown prior information, all the noise statistics are assumed to be time-invariant and determined through an empirical trial-and-error procedure. The values of the measurement noise are set to 0.1 and 10 for the Jianxi band Tianyi basins, respectively. The system-noise covariance is configured as Ψ = d i a g [ 1 , 1  , 1 , 0.1 , 30 , 15 , 15  ]    for the Jianxi basin and Ψ = d i a g [ 1 , 1 , 1 , 0.1 , 50 , 30 , 30 ]    for the Tianyi basin, corresponding to the state variables (WU, WL, WD, S, QS, QI, and QG). Regarding the sampling parameters, to avoid covariance matrices of non-semi-positive definite, κ   and α   are set to 1 and 0.99, respectively. Additionally, β is set to 3 to introduce more high-order information.  (2) LSTM-UKF. Since the sampling parameters are consistent with the UKF, the primary focus is configuring the LSTM block's hyperparameters. As shown in Fig. 1 c, the LSTM block consists of two fully connected layers (an input layer and an output layer), and a LSTM unit with two hidden layers. The number of hidden layers in LSTM unit is determined by using the trial-and-error approach. The input layer has 8 neurons aligning with the dimension of the input vector (n  2  + m   ), along with 24 neurons for mapping the vector into a high-dimensional feature space. The LSTM unit comprises 24 neurons to process the mapped vector and generate the hidden-state vector. The number of neurons in LSTM unit is the joint dimensionality of the input vector (n  2  + m   ), and the eigenvectors of states covariance ( m )   , measurement covariance ( n )    and noise covariances ( m + n )   , for tracking the variation of second-order moments. The output layer comprises 24 neurons to receive the hidden-state vector and 7 to output the Kalman Gain vector. Moreover, the data pre-processing, loss function, optimizer selection for model training is described in Sec.2.1.  (3) XAJ model. The SCE-UA method (Duan et al., 1992 ) was used for model calibration, entailing the optimization of 15 parameters. The objective was set to maximize the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE). Continuous sequences in the training datasets were used for model calibration, including basin-averaged rainfall, evaporation, and basin outlet streamflow. Meanwhile, the test datasets were used to evaluate the predictive performance of the XAJ model.    The LSTM-UKF and UKF models adopt the “update-forecast” procedure to improve multi-step-ahead flood forecasts, as shown in Fig. 3  . In the update step, both the LSTM-UKF and UKF correct the state estimations by assimilating streamflow observations. Given that the maximum concentration time is not more than 21 h in the Jianxi basin (Cui et al., 2022 ), and it is about 18 h in the Tianyi basin, according to the survey by its hydrological bureau. Moreover, sufficient time is essential to ensure filter convergence in the update step. The time windows for the update step are determined through tuning on the training dataset. For the Jianxi basin, the time window is 48 h (t- 16 ∼ t- 1), and for the Tianyi basin, it is 36 h (t- 12 ∼ t- 1). In the forecast step, the updated states serve as the initial conditions of the XAJ model to generate multi-step flood forecasts (without precipitation forecast input). Therefore, the forecasting horizons for Jianxi and Tianyi basins are set to be 21 h (t + 1 ∼ t + 7) and 18 h (t + 1 ∼ t + 6), respectively, covering their maximum concentration time.  2.3 Evaluation metrics Forecasting performance was assessed using three metrics: the RMSE, MAE, and NSE (Ritter and Muñoz-Carpena, 2013 ). The RMSE and MAE are used to assess the accuracy of point forecasts, and the NSE is used to evaluate the fitting goodness of the flooding process. Additionally, the Standard Deviation of Prediction Residual (SDPR) is utilized to evaluate the stability of filters. When the filter provides stable estimations, the corresponding SDPR value tends to be smaller as prediction residuals converge to zero. Conversely, if the filter diverges, the SDPR value becomes more extensive. To evaluate the model performance in predicting flood characteristics, two metrics, the Percentage error in peak flow (PEPF) and the Time shift in peak flow (TSPF) are used in this study. The metrics are described in detail as follows.(3.1) N S E = 1 - ∑ 1  T  Q t  - Q ^  t     2   ∑ 1  T  Q t  - Q  ¯      2    , N S E ≤ 1     (3.2) R M S E = ∑ 1  T  ( Q t  - Q ^  t  )  2   T       (3.3) M A E = ∑ 1  T  Q t  - Q ^  t     T      (3.4) S D P R = ∑ 1  T  Δ Q  t  - Δ Q  ¯      2   T       (3.5) P E P F = Q p e a k   - Q ^  p e a k    Q p e a k    × 100     (3.6) T S P F = T ^  p e a k   - T  p e a k       where T   is the number of time steps. Q  ¯     is the mean value of the observed sequence. Δ Q  ¯      is the mean value of the prediction residuals. T p e a k     and T ^  p e a k     represent the observed and predicted peak discharge time, respectively. Q p e a k     and Q ^  p e a k     represent the observed and predicted peak values, respectively.   3 Results This study aims to explore and evaluate the proposed LSTM-UKF to update hydrological models and its potential to improve flood forecasting. The experimental results and comprehensive analysis are presented below. 3.1 Evaluation of the model performance In consideration of the inherent stochastic nature of artificial neural networks, the model weights and biases of LSTM-UKF were initialized using random seeds. The model underwent 20 rounds of training, and its performance was subsequently assessed using test datasets. To maintain clarity, references to “LSTM-UKF” and “UKF” pertain to the state-updated results of these respective methods, while “XAJ” denotes non-updated results. The NSE, RMSE, and MAE metrics were utilized to evaluate the forecasting accuracy of the models. Table 2   lists the evaluation metrics of the Jianxi and Tianyi basins' single-step forecasts for the LSTM-UKF, UKF, and XAJ models. During both the training and testing stages, the LSTM-UKF outperforms other models, indicating a noteworthy enhancement in predictive accuracy compared to the XAJ model. Median values from 20-round results for the Jianxi and Tianyi basins reveal averaged enhancements of 9.8 %, 48.8 %, and 65.8 % for NSE, MAE, and RMSE, respectively, during the training stage, and 9.5 %, 36.4 %, and 57.9 % during the testing stage. Compared with the UKF, the averaged improvements for those metrics are 2.3 %, 29.4 %, and 22.8 %, respectively, during the training stage and 5.4 %, 13.0 %, and 12.2 % during the testing stage. Beyond improved forecast accuracy, the LSTM-UKF demonstrates strong generalization ability. The training and testing results reveal minimal variations in each metrics, highlighting the LSTM-UKF's effectiveness in mitigating accumulated estimation errors for hydrological model states. To identify the optimal LSTM-UKF model for further evaluation, a composite score was computed by assigning equal weights to the metrics, facilitating the ranking of multi-round results. The highest-scored model was selected, and its state estimation stability was compared with the UKF. The SDPR metric was used to assess and compare the filtering convergence and stability of the LSTM-UKF and UKF models. Fig. 4   presents violin plots depicting the distribution of the SDPR values for both LSTM-UKF and UKF across different basins and stages. The central part of the violin plot presents the kernel density estimation of the SDPR, illustrating its density across different prediction residuals. The curves on either side of the central kernel density display the SDPR distribution. Observing the SDPR distributions, it is evident that LSTM-UKF exhibits more concentrated and horizontally aligned distributions compared to the UKF. This outcome signifies a narrower dispersion of prediction biases, maintaining them at a consistently lower level of variability. Examining the outliers for both models, the LSTM-UKF has a significantly smaller outlier range than the UKF. In both the training and testing stages, the maximal SDPR metric decreased by 27.7 % and 21.1 %, respectively, in the Jianxi basin and by 68.4 % and 52.8 %, respectively, in the Tianyi basin, compared to the UKF. This suggests that the LSTM-UKF presents better filtering convergence and stability, as evidenced by its reduced likelihood of extreme prediction biases, which are significantly lower compared to the UKF model. The key distinction between LSTM-UKF and UKF is that the LSTM-UKF can adaptively learn and update noise information, enabling it to dynamically track changes in real-time conditions. In contrast, the UKF relies on fixed initial parameters, which may not adequately capture the dynamic variability in system and measurement noises.  3.2 Evaluation of the model reliability To further evaluate model reliability, comparisons are conducted for multi-step flood forecasts of each model using the test dataset and two extreme flood events. Fig. 5   presents the evaluation metrics (NSE, RMSE, and MAE) for multi-step flood forecasts during the testing stage for the LSTM-UKF, UKF, and XAJ models in two basins. The LSTM-UKF presents a significant improvement in flood forecasting performance compared to the XAJ model. Taking the results in the Tianyi basin as an example, the improvement range in the NSE varies from 4.5 % to 10.1 %, the RMSE metric shows a decrease ranging from 56.7 % to 74.6 %, and the MAE metric exhibits a decrease ranging from 41.3 % to 46.9 %. Although those two filters outperform the XAJ model, the LSTM-UKF shows superior improvements compared to UKF at each horizon and basin. Concerning the Jianxi basin, the LSTM-UKF shows an average improvement of 9.1 %, 18.7 %, and 22.6 % for the NSE, RMSE, and MAE, respectively. As for the Tianyi basin, the averaged improvements for those metrics are 4.3 %, 15.5 %, and 17.8 %, respectively. It is noticeable that the forecasting accuracy drops with longer horizons, but the decline of the NSE metric is less obvious for LSTM-UKF. The NSE metric of LSTM-UKF reduces by 12.5 % for the Jianxi basin and 35.4 % for the Tianyi basin as the horizon extends from t + 1 to t + 7. Similarly, the NSE metric of UKF decreases by 13.9 % and 36.4 %, respectively, for the same basins. In multi-step-ahead flood forecasting, the hydrological model states cannot be updated during the forecasting step due to the unavailability of future streamflow information. Therefore, the accuracy of the model’s initial state is crucial for maintaining forecast precision as the forecasting horizon extends. The LSTM-UKF provides more accurate state corrections, so it is likely to achieve better forecasting accuracy over longer forecast horizons. Figs. 6 and 7    present the scatter plots and kernel density distribution curves of model multi-step flood forecasts for the Jianxi and Tianyi basins, respectively. It can be observed that the scatter plots for all three models show a close alignment between the regression lines and the 45-degree line at the early horizons. As the forecast horizon extends, the dispersions of scatter points increase, and the deviations between the regression and 45-degree lines expand gradually. In comparison to the UKF and XAJ models, the LSTM-UKF demonstrates a notably smaller dispersion range and less deviation from the 45-degree line, as shown in the scatter plots. Given the critical importance of accurate forecasts for high-flow conditions (more than 8000 m3 /s for Jianxi basin and 3000 m3 /s for Tianyi basin) in flood forecasting, it is worth mentioning that the forecast points for the LSTM-UKF exhibit less deviation from the 45-degree line compared to the UKF and XAJ models, particularly in high-flow conditions. These results indicate that the LSTM-UKF has an advantage in improving high-flow forecasting accuracy when the forecast horizon extends. During high-flow conditions, the model is frequently subjected to external disturbances such as intense rainfall and rapid increases in streamflow, which challenge the performance of the filtering methods. In contrast to the static nature of the UKF, the LSTM-UKF can dynamically adjust the filter state by continuously learning noise information in real-time. Such capability enables it to better capture the complexities of changing conditions and provides more accurate high-flow forecasts. To assess the reliability of LSTM-UKF, two flood events were selected from the testing datasets: flood event (a) in the Jianxi basin with a peak flow of 9,843 m3 /s, and flood event (b) in the Tianyi basin with a peak flow of 3,030 m3 /s. The highest peak flows of Jianxi basin and Tianyi basin in the testing dataset are 10,745 m3 /s and 3,947 m3 /s, respectively. The selected flood events have peak flows close to the highest recorded values in their respective basins, making them representative. The evaluation metrics are shown in Table 3   and Table 4  . The result indicates that the LSTM-UKF consistently exhibits higher forecasting accuracy improvement rates than the UKF. As shown in Table 3 , the average improvements of NSE, RMSE, and MAE are 5.1 %, 22.9 %, and 30.1 %, respectively, for flood event (a), and 5.7 %, 18.0 %, and 20.5 % for flood event (b). In Table 4 , the average improvements of PEPF are 36.1 % and 45.8 % for flood event (a) and flood event (b), respectively. For the TSPF metrics, the LSTMUKF has better accuracy in peak time than UKF and XAJ in each horizon by and large. Fig. 8   illustrates the observed and forecasted flood hydrographs. It is evident that although the maximum forecast horizons do not exceed the concentration and confluence time for basins, the forecasting performance of the XAJ model significantly worsened as the forecast period extended. This deterioration is particularly evident during the flow rising stage, where the XAJ model underestimated actual processes. This may be attributed to the fact that the XAJ model, as a typical rainfall-runoff model, cannot utilize real-time flow information, leading to the accumulation of various composite errors in the early stages. With the model states updated by LSTM-UKF and UKF, the predicted hydrographs closely match the actual flood processes. Additionally, while the UKF presented reasonably well-fitted hydrographs during the rising and receding process, its performance in the high-flow stage was inferior to the LSTM-UKF. Considering that the performance of all three models was equally affected by the lack of precipitation forecast information, it is evident that LSTM-UKF exhibits relatively smaller peak discharge errors and time lags compared to other models. Overall, these results demonstrate the LSTM-UKF’s reliability in improving the multi-step flood forecasts for extreme flood events. The results above indicate that the absence of rainfall information during the forecasting stage will inevitably introduce significant uncertainty into the model predictions and further impact the effectiveness of LSTM-UKF. This study further investigates the effect of LSTM-UKF on improving predictive performance of hydrological models with forecast precipitation input, focusing on a significant flood event that occurred in the Jianxi basin from May 21, 2023, to May 28, 2023. Specifically, we employed the Update-Forecast framework as illustrated in Fig. 3  to conduct multi-step flood forecasting from t + 1 to t + 7. The observed streamflow, rainfall, and evaporation data was used during the update step, while rainfall forecast data provided by GRAPES model and average evaporation were utilized for the forecast step. The forecasting performance of three models are compared in two scenarios, (a) Without precipitation forecasts and (b) With precipitation forecasts (a) without precipitation forecasts and (b) with input precipitation forecasts. The evaluation metrics are presented in Tables 5 and 6   . Fig. 9   illustrates the observed and forecasted flood hydrographs for these models in two scenarios. From Tables 5 and 6 , it can be observed that in scenario (a), the evaluation metrics show a progressively larger decline as the forecasting horizon extends. However, when precipitation forecast data is used in scenario (b), the decrease in metrics is less pronounced. It is also noted that the improvement in predictive performance varies among the three models with rainfall forecast information. Compared to the results without rainfall input, the LSTM-UKF model shows an improvement of 13 % in NSE, 38 % in RMSE, and 31 % in MAE when utilizing rainfall forecast information. The UKF model exhibits an improvement of 10 % in NSE, 21 % in RMSE, and 19 % in MAE, while the improvement of XAJ model is 4 % in NSE, 31 % in RMSE, and 8 % in MAE. Additionally, the improvement in model predictive capability regarding peak discharge and peak timing is also evident by using precipitation forecast data as input. From Fig. 9 , we can observe that the precipitation input plays a significant role in reducing the peak flow prediction errors and alleviating time lag issues for these models. These findings underscore the pivotal role of rainfall forecast information in bolstering the LSTM-UKF model's capacity to enhance hydrological model forecasts, extends its advantages.  3.3 Assessment of the effect of state updating on forecasting performance Fig. 10   illustrates the trajectories of model states and prediction residuals during the initial state update step, highlighting a flood rising process in the Jianxi basin during the testing stage. This scrutiny aims to evaluate the impact of state updating on forecasting improvements. It can be observed that both the lower and deep soil moisture states (W L  t    and W D  t   ) have already reached saturation in the XAJ model. As the observed flow at the basin outlet increased rapidly from approximately 350 m3 /s to 2470 m3 /s (Fig. 10 (a)), the fluxes of surface runoff (Q S  t   ), interflow (Q I  t   ), and baseflow (Q G  t   ) were all at low-level amounts, which indicates that the initial state estimation error led to an underestimate of the actual conditions (Fig. 10 (b)). Both the LSTM-UKF and UKF effectively corrected these inaccurate state estimates, encompassing upper soil moisture state (W U  t   ), free water state (S t   ), and three runoff fluxes (Fig. 10 (b)). These corrections enhanced the runoff generation capacity of the XAJ model, bringing forecasts closer to actual values. Moreover, it is clear that under the conditions of a rapid shift in system state, i.e., the sudden rainfall occurrence or rapid streamflow fluctuations, both filters present increased prediction residuals Δ Q   , but the LSTM-UKF displayed significantly smaller variation of Δ Q    and faster convergence compared to the UKF. These results imply the superior adaptability and robustness of the LSTM-UKF in updating the hydrological model states, positioning it as a key contributor to improved flood forecast accuracy.   4 Discussion Accurate noise estimation poses a critical challenge in updating hydrological model states using the UKF, particularly when faced with the complex uncertainties inherent in flood forecasting. To surmount this obstacle, our study introduces a novel approach – the deep fusion of long short-term memory neural network and unscented Kalman filter (LSTM-UKF). This methodology enables adaptive updates to hydrological model states without explicit noise estimation. The performance and reliability of LSTM-UKF are compared to the UKF, and their abilities to improve the multi-step-ahead flood forecast are evaluated using the XAJ hydrological model. The UKF is a nonlinear filtering technique grounded in Kalman filtering theory, which is suitable for updating nonlinear hydrological models (Sun et al., 2020 ). However, the reliance on noise estimation becomes apparent in the prediction residual trajectories (Fig. 10 ), where significant disturbances, such as heavy rainfall inputs and rapid streamflow fluctuations, challenge the stability and accuracy of the UKF. The dynamic and time-variant nature of noise statistics, exacerbated by various uncertainties, complicates the estimation process. In contrast, the LSTM-UKF excels in adaptively updating model states by learning noise-related information during the estimation of the Kalman Gain. This unique advantage enables prompt perception and tracking of noise variation characteristics, leading to more accurate state estimation and a significant enhancement of multi-step flood forecasts. The results depicted in Fig. 10  underscore the superior performance of the LSTM-UKF, demonstrating more accurate and robust estimations compared to the UKF when confronted with system disturbances. Moreover, the LSTM-UKF improves the forecasts and exhibits smaller accuracy declines for non-stationary flood events, highlighting its reliability. Consequently, the LSTM-UKF proves effective in updating model states, rectifying estimation errors, and improving the multi-step-ahead flood forecasts for hydrological models. While the LSTM-UKF demonstrates its superior performance in enhancing the forecasting skill of the XAJ model, peak underestimation and time lags (Figs. 8 and 9 (a)) in the forecast results can also be observed. We attribute these issues to two main reasons. Firstly, the LSTM-UKF relies on streamflow observations to update the hydrological model states. Therefore, the hydrological model states cannot be updated during the forecasting stage, since future streamflow information is unavailable. Secondly, we seek to investigate the performance of LSTM-UKF in situations where the predictive performance of hydrological model deteriorates. Hence, the precipitation forecast was not used as input in the forecasting stage, which is important to the forecast accuracy of hydrological models. However, despite facing these challenges, LSTM-UKF still plays a significant role in improving the forecast accuracy of hydrological models and maintains its advantageous position over UKF. The implications of this study extend beyond practical considerations, offering valuable insights into the potential of integrating deep neural networks into nonlinear Kalman filtering for improved hydrological model forecasts. Our research provides solutions to address challenges in UKF applications and contributes to the advantageous integration of data-driven and physically-based models. It sets a direction for future research, emphasizing the synergy between deep learning and traditional modelling approaches in the domain of hydrological forecasting.  5 Conclusion Accurate state estimation plays a pivotal role in enhancing flood forecasting capabilities of physically-based hydrological models. Leveraging the strengths of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network in extracting intricate features from observational data, this study introduced a fusion of LSTM and the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) – LSTM-UKF – to adaptively update hydrological model states, particularly in scenarios lacking precise noise statistics. The proposed LSTM-UKF effectively improves the forecasting skill of the XAJ model, and presents superior adaptability and robustness compared to the UKF. The findings are summarized as follows.(i) The LSTM-UKF effectively updates hydrological model states without requiring precise noise statistics, reducing accumulated errors in state estimations. Across the Jianxi and Tianyi basins, the LSTM-UKF enhances the forecasting accuracy of the XAJ model, demonstrating notable improvements in flood forecasting and consistently stable performance compared to the UKF.  (ii) In assessments involving high-flow and non-stationary flood events, both the XAJ model and UKF show significant decreases in accuracy as the forecast horizon extends. In contrast, the LSTM-UKF consistently achieves accurate predictions for high-flow conditions over extended forecasting horizons, showcasing its reliability and superiority in improving multi-step flood forecasting.  (iii) The LSTM-UKF overcomes the bottleneck faced by Kalman filtering methods, which relies on prior knowledge of noise statistics for model state estimation. By fusing LSTM and UKF, the LSTM-UKF can adaptively estimate the noise-related Kalman Gain from data, providing accurate state estimate without requiring prior noise knowledge. This practical framework effectively mitigates error accumulation in model states, enhancing the accuracy, stability, and reliability of multi-step flood forecasting.    While this study primarily utilizes streamflow data for updating hydrological model states, it is essential to recognize that factors such as model structure, parameters, and meteorological inputs collectively contribute to state estimation uncertainty. Accounting for these uncertainties is a critical consideration for future research. Additionally, incorporating comprehensive observational data, including information on vegetation cover, land use, soil moisture, among others, holds promise for further enhancing the predictive performance of hydrological models. Future research endeavours could explore additional error correction methods and leverage richer data resources for continuous improvement in hydrological model accuracy and reliability.
1 Introduction Total Dissolved Gas (TDG), simply defined as the quantity of dissolved air in a river water system (i.e., N2 , O2  and CO2 ), serves as one of the most critical components of ecological indicators and assessment of water quality downstream of high dam reservoirs (Yuan et al. 2023 ). Constructing and maintaining high dams are vital for hydropower and electricity generation, yet their negative impact on the ecosystem is prominent. During spill season, excess water flows into a dam reservoir to maximize electricity at hydropower stations. This excess water diverted through numerous structures such as open channel spillways, diversion tunnels, and low-level sluice gates to route flow past dams. Waterfall resulting from these structures, especially open channel spillways, dives into the tailwater pool of dams, where the bubbles of atmospheric gases slowly dissolve into solution with the water (i.e. frothy white plume of flow). Under normal conditions, when water has an equilibrium in terms of dissolved gas, it is called saturation level. However, due to the above-mentioned reasons, the water in a river system can become supersaturated. These gases cannot dissipate to restore normal condition (i.e. equilibrium) after traveling even hundreds of kilometers downstream of the spillway, thus, supersaturation TDG poses significant risks to aquatic ecosystems, especially for fish such as salmon and steelhead (Pleizier et al., 2020; Zhang et al. 2024 ), as well as damaging the broader eco-environment. Direct mortality in aquatic organisms is one of the most common negative impacts of gas bubble disease (Ebel, 1969; Beiningen and Ebel, 1970; Dawley and Ebel, 1975 ). For instance, Feng et al. (2018)  stated that according to Yangtze River Fisheries Research Insitute Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences (2014) , during the summer of 2014, 100,000 kg of fish died in China resulting from TDG supersaturations. Recently, TDG supersaturation has emerged as a very serious environmental issue in several key river systems worldwide such as the Columbia River in the United States and Canada (Li et al., 2009 ), the Vetlefjordselva River and the Otra River in Norway (Pulg et al., 2016; Lennox et al., 2022; Stenberg et al., 2022 ), and the Pearl River and the Yangtze River system in China (Wang et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2019 ). The United States of America Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) has established regulations to cap TDG concentrations at 115 % saturation to mitigate harm to aquatic life (USEPA, 2020 ). However, measurements downstream from high dams frequently exceed this limit, with levels reaching upwards of 180 % (Pulg et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019 ). Quantifying TDG values and developing a highly accurate predictive model for TDG can safeguard the downstream ecosystem. Globally, information and data about TDG are limited and sparse and predominantly available only from selected locations in the USA and China. Most of the extant research has centered on how TDG supersaturation is generated downstream of a dam or strategies for its mitigation; however, literature on predicting TDG is limited (Ma et al. 2019 ). Therefore, finding an alternative model/approach/method for TDG prediction is highly recommended, offering a beneficial and cost-effective tool for water quality management. Numerical and mechanical models have been developed as crucial and effective methods for TDG prediction, thereby enhancing our understanding of its formation and dissipation processes. These models include the 1-D unsteady TDG model (Ma et al. 2016 ), the 2-D depth-averaged model for TDG dissipation (Shen et al., 2016 ), mass transfer for modeling TDG using water depth (Li et al. 2009 ), the numerical 2-DTDG model (Feng et al. 2013 ), and the two-phase flow model (Wang et al. 2019 ). Although these models have been successfully developed and applied, their application and implementation encounter significant challenges. These include the requirement for extensive data for calibration, the time-consuming and laborious calibration process, limited applicability beyond the calibrated site, and restricted datasets (Witt et al. 2017 ). Recently, the application of machine learning models in hydrology and water science has surged, attributed to their user-friendliness, simplicity in set-up and model development, minimal input data requirement, efficient calibration process, and their capability to produce robust and credible outcomes. Notable machine learning-based models employed for TDG prediction include the Generalized Regression neural network (GRNN) (Heddam, 2017a ), Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLPNN) (Han and Han, 2019a ), least squares support vector machine (LSSVM) (Keshtegar et al., 2019a ), kriging interpolation method (KIM) and response surface method (RSM) (Heddam et al., 2020 ), Support Vector Regression (SVR) (Alomar et al. 2020 ), the dynamic evolving neural-fuzzy inference system (DENFIS) (Heddam and Kisi, 2020 ), Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) optimized by genetic algorithms (Wang et al., 2022 ), and parallel chaos search based incremental extreme learning machine (PC-ELM) (Heddam, 2023 ). Heddam (2016)  developed and applied a generalized regression neural network (GRNN) algorithm for predicting total dissolved gas. They compared their results with the multiple linear regression (MLR) model. Their findings revealed that the GRNN model outperforms MLR. Heddam et al. (2019)  proposed two new models, the kriging interpolation method (KIM) and response surface method (RSM), for TDG prediction. Subsequently, the results were evaluated against the standard feedforward neural networks (FFNN) model. The finding indicated that the KIM model has a higher performance than RSM and FFNN models at three dams, while FFNN is the best at the fourth case. Keshtegar et al. (2019b)  developed a high-order ordinary response surface method (H-RSM) for TDG prediction, comparing it with several benchmark models, including least squares support vector machine (LSSVM), M5 model tree (M5Tree), and multivariate adaptive regression spline (MARS) models. They concluded that the H-RSM model with four input variables, achieved the best accuracy across all stations. Wang et al. (2022)  investigated the prediction accuracy of ELM, SVR, ELM-Genetic Algorithm (GA) and SVR-GA for TDG prediction at two stations: Dagangshan hydropower station of Dadu River and Xiluodu hydropower station of Jinsha river in China. Their analysis showed that all models performed reasonably well, with relative errors typically under 5 %. However, SVR-GA model demonstrated superior performance. Heddam et al. (2024)  developed six standalone models, including multilayer perceptron neural network (MLP), Gaussian process regression (GPR), random forest regression (RFR), random vector functional link (RVFL), adaptive boosting (AB), and Bootstrap aggregating (Bagging) for TDG prediction at four stations in the USA. They further enhanced these models by integrating empirical mode decomposition (EMD), variational mode decomposition (VMD), and the empirical wavelet transform (EWT) preprocessing signal decomposition algorithms with the above-mentioned machine learning models. Their findings revealed that the Bagging model has a higher performance than the other five models. However, the extracted IMFs and MRA components using the EMD, VMD, and EWT notably improved the performance of the hybrid models. Although a variety of models have been successfully applied across different areas of hydrology and water science such as RFR, random tree, M5 Prime, Gaussian process, adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), or deep learning models, research regarding TDG prediction is rare and is in its nascent stage. These models have proven effective in various fields such as the prediction of flood (Nevo et al. 2023; Tang et al. 2023 ), landslide (Wang et al. 2021 ), groundwater (Pourghasemi, 2020 ), land subsidence (Azarakhsh et al., 2022 ), scour depth (Khosravi et al., 2021 ), and evaporation (Abed et al. 2022 ). The literature review showed that integrating two models can improve the modeling performance, and this integration can be through metaheuristic algorithms such as cultural, bees, and invasive weed optimization algorithms. Additionally, this hybridization can be implemented by combining two algorithms, with one serving as a base learner and the other one as a classifier, leading to higher performance (Bui et al. 2021 ). Kargar et al. (2021)  implemented the weighted instances handler wrapper (WIHW) and rotation forest (ROF) algorithm combined with reduced error pruning tree (REPT), RFR and random tree (RT) for sediment transport modeling. They stated that all models provide reasonable accuracy while WIHW provides higher performance. However, selecting the most optimal and efficient models remains a significant challenge. In addition, in all literature reviews, the dataset for each considered station is typically divided into two or three parts for modeling, testing, and validation. It means that the testing and validation subsets are from the same station and generally exhibit similar trends, ranges, and characteristics, which casts uncertainty on the generalization power of the previously used modeling framework. In contrast, our study introduces a new framework aimed at exploring and enhancing the generalization power of these models. In the current study, a model was developed and tested using data from one station, while its generalization power was assessed by feeding the entire dataset from another station for the first time. Consequently, the developed model can predict TDG from any part of the USA with similar conditions with reasonable and acceptable results. In the present study, a rule-based M5-Rule algorithm is performed due to its simplicity and cost-efficiency and not very resource-intensive to develop since it does not require extensive data collection and cleaning. The novelty and aim of the current study are outlined as follows: (1) developing several new ensemble-based models for TDG prediction, including Iterative absolute error regression (IAER-M5-Rule), Disjoint Aggregating (DA-M5-Rule), Random Subspace (RS-M5-Rule), Weighted Instance Handler Wrapper (WIHW-M5-Rule) for the first time, and comparing the results with the SVR model as a benchmark, (2) applying a new feature selection technique, namely Bidirectional Best-First technique (BBF), for the first time to optimally select the best input scenario from effective variables including water temperature (Tw in °C), barometric pressure (BP in mmHg), Spill from Dam (SD in kcfs), sensor depth (H in ft) and discharge (Q  in kcfs), (3) testing the model’s predictive power using data from the same station on which the model is developed based on (70 % for modeling and 30 % for testing), and finally, (4) validating the model’s predicting ability using data from a new station to assess its generalization capabilities, by feeding the data of new station (USGS 12462600) to the developed model from the other station (USGS 12453700).  2 Study area and data In this study, two United States Geological Survey (USGS) stations were considered for modeling performance and evaluation (Fig. 1  ). Data includes hourly Tw, BP, SD, H, Q, and TDG starting from 1/1/2020 to 13/6/2022 (each 21,371 row) were downloaded directly from the USGS website https://or.water.usgs.gov/cgi-bin/grapher/table_setup.pl . These two stations are: (1) USGS 12453700: Columbia River at Rocky reach Dam, WA (Latitude 48°31′28″, and Longitude 119°18′04″ NAD27) and (2) USGS 12462600: Columbia River below Rock Island Dam, WA (Latitude 47°19′57″, and Longitude 120°04′48″ NAD27). All data except TDG are considered as a potential input variable while TDG is considered as an output variable. Next, the dataset from USGS 12453700 station was split into two main groups in a 70:30 ratio, which means 70 % of the dataset is applied for model development (i.e. training dataset), while the rest of 30 % is used for model evaluation (testing dataset). For the other station (USGS 12462600), the entire dataset was utilized as a validation dataset. This means that when models are developed and tested with station USGS 12453700, the entire dataset from station USGS 12462600 is fed as validation data to explore the models’ generalization power. In the current study, for the first time, the prediction capability of the developed models is investigated through data from a new station, allowing for their potential utilization worldwide. Table 1   and Fig. 2  a-b show a brief descriptive statistics and correlation matrix for all datasets across both stations. The methodology of this study is outlined in Fig. 3  , including several key steps such as data collection, data splitting to training and testing, feature selection, model development, enhancement through hybridization, hyperparameter tuning, testing, validation and finally comparing them with benchmark model. Additionally, the generalization power of the models is compared using data from an additional station.  3 Method 3.1 Feature selection technique In the current study, one of the most novel and practical methods called the bidirectional best first (BBF) feature selection (FS) technique was applied to determine the most effective input scenario. BBF algorithms explore the space of attribute subsets through a greedy hill-climbing approach augmented with backtracking facility and bidirectional direction to identify the most relevant subset of features from the given dataset. Classified as heuristic search algorithms, BBF techniques are known for their time-consuming nature, making them more suitable for application with small datasets, like our current study (Yongjie and Zhao, 2018). However, BBF stands out as the only algorithm that starts with 0 field, making its results more practical for selecting the most efficient features of the dataset. The workflow of the BBF technique can be summarized in the following steps:1. Initialization: It may start with the empty set of features and search forward or start with the full set of features and search backward. In the current study, we applied the forward method.  2. Evaluation: It determines the importance of each feature using predefined error criteria (i.e. see step 4).  3. Search: BBF sequentially adds features to the set of selected features and ‘’Best-First’’ technique starts working to select the feature that provides the first improvement in the modeling performance.  4. Termination: BBF continues the processing until the stopping criteria (i.e. fixed number of features, or specific level of performance) is reached. In the current study, specify the number of consecutive non-improving nodes to allow before terminating the search was performed. This step is called ‘SearchTermination’.  5. Output: Determines the optimal number of features.     3.2 Model description Fig. 4   is presented to illustrate the methodological framework of the ensemble-based models. All these models were implemented using WEKA 3.9 software. 3.2.1 Iterative absolute error regression (IAER) IAER is a type of regression-based machine learning approach particularly useful when dealing with datasets containing outliers or skewed distributions. This algorithm minimizes the sum of absolute error (AE) using a base learner to predict the optimum regression coefficient (RC) that minimizes the weights square error. The methodological framework of the IAER can be summarized in 4 main steps including initialization, iterative refinement, convergence, and a final prediction that each step described as in detail: (1) step1: this algorithm starts with the initial/default value of the RC through standard regression technique (SRT), (2) step 2: IAER minimizes the sum of AE between measured and predicted values using a base-learner to predict the optimum RC, (3) step 3: Convergence can be identified using predicted RC or AE between iteration that locates below the predefined threshold, therefore, this algorithm will continue to perform until reaching the convergence criteria, (4) step 4: at the last phase, the CR is determined when the convergence is obtained. This RC shows the best-fit-line that is able to minimize the AE. For more detailed information about this algorithm, refer to Schlossmacher (1973) .  3.2.2 Disjoint aggregation (DA) DA, dagging or bagging with disjoint samples is a type of ensemble-based classifier technique first introduced by Ting and Witten (1997a) . The DA algorithm develops a number of disjoint subsets, dividing the data into different groups. Each separated group is assigned a different copy from the main classifier to analyze and predict the target variable. Predictions are made by majority voting, since all the generated base classifiers are put into the regression task meta -classifier. The methodological framework of the DA algorithm can be summarized into 4 main steps including data splitting, base model training, prediction aggregation, and output phases, each described as follows:1. Step 1: In the first step, the entire dataset is split into several equal-sized disjoint subsets without replacement (i.e. number of folds ). Then, a machine learning-based model (i.e. M5-Rule model in the current study) is applied to each disjoint subset to train them using separate base models.  2. Step 2: Multiple instance base learner methods (i.e. in the current study we used the M5-Rule-based model) are developed separately using these disjoint subsets of the training dataset.  3. Step 3: After developing models using each based learner from the previous stage, predictions for each base-learner are made during testing phase.  4. Step 4: The predictions are aggregated to calculate the final prediction for each instance by averaging the predictions from all the base learners using regression techniques (Anyfantis et al. 2007 ).    For detailed description and information about the DA algorithm, please see Ting and Witten (1997b) .  3.2.3 Random subspace (RS) The RS model is among the powerful ensemble-based machine learning that has an ability for both classification and regression-based prediction issues. The RS algorithm was first developed by Ho (1998)  as a classical integrated algorithm. RS has some similarity with Bagging algorithm, but one of the main differences between these two approaches is the random selection of training (Mielniczuk and Teisseyre, 2014 ). The structure of RS for predicting the final prediction can be presented in five main steps: (1) base model creation: similarly, the RS algorithm constructs multiple base models but trains them via randomly selected subsets of features (as stated Bagging use the entire dataset for sampling), (2) feature subspace selection: before base-learner development, a subset of features can be randomly selected either in a fixed size or fraction of the total features as well as with or without of replacement, (3) base model training: after determining feature subspace, a base model (i.e. here M5-Rule model) is developed using training data of the selected feature subsets, and (4) ensemble construction and prediction: finally, ensemble based technique is applied to the final prediction by combining and aggregating all predictions of each selected feature subspace (Zhang and Jia, 2007 ). For detailed description and information about the RS algorithm, please see Ho (1998) .  3.2.4 Weighted instance Handler Wrapper (WIHW) WIHW is a type of wrapper approach that is able to justify the learning algorithm to handle imbalanced datasets by allocating different weights to instances. The WIHW algorithm predicts the final prediction through 4 main steps as follows:1- Instance weighting: By assigning weights to instances, the learning algorithm can effectively handle imbalanced datasets. Instances of minority classes receive higher weights compared to majority classes (less frequent classes have a higher weights).  2- Learning algorithm modification: In this section, the underlying learning method is justified and implemented to involve the instance weights throughout the model developing phase.  3- Training: Weighted instance has been applied to justify the training algorithms. Throughout the training process, the algorithms dynamically tune its parameters to reduce a modified from of the loss function, where the impact of every data point on the overall loss is adjusted according to its allocated weights.  4- Prediction: Following the training step, the developed model gains the capability to provide predictions for novel instances by factoring in their class probabilities. The incorporation of weighted training enables the model to effectively address imbalanced datasets, thereby enhancing its ability to offer precise predictions, particularly from minority classes.     3.2.5 M5-Rule The M5-Rule based machine learning algorithm provides a decision list for regression issues through separate-and-conquer. In each iteration, it constructs a model tree using M5 and makes the “best” leaf into a rule. The M5-Rule algorithm is a developed version of M5 proposed by Quinlan (1992) . This algorithm integrates the decision tree-based models with simple linear regression to generate hybrid-based models capable of enhancing the model’s prediction accuracy. The methodological working framework of M5-Rule-based models can be summarized into six primary steps: (1) hybrid method: integrates the decision tree-based models with simple linear regression to generate the hybrid based models, (2) rule based model: In this section a set of rules, including if-then statements, is generated using both decision tree arrangement and linear regression models linked with individual leaf nodes, (3) continuous and categorical variables: one of the advantages of the M5-Rule base models is that it can handle both continuous and categorical variables as a mixture (data type), making it practical and powerful for a wide range of data, (4) pruning and model complexity: The M5-Rule model implements a pruning approach to avoid overfitting and enhance the model’s generalization power, (5) handling missing value: one of the main aspects that make M5-Rule algorithm robust is its ability to handle missing values, making it flexible and powerful for real-world scenarios where data is scarce, (6) interpretability: due to its rule-based nature, this algorithm allows for interpretable reasoning behind the model’s predictions. For detailed description and information about the M5-Rule algorithm please see Holmes and Hall (1999), Quinlan (1992) , and Wang, and Witten (1997) .  3.2.6 Support vector regression (SVR) SVR is a powerful supervised machine learning algorithm commonly used for regression problems. As the SVR algorithm is used frequently, only a brief description will be provided here. This model methodology can be summarized as:1. Objective: it focuses on fitting a tune around the data point instead of finding the best-fitting line  2. Margin: The SVR model aims to maximize the differences between the hyperplane and the closest data-point (margin) while ensuring that it does not exceed the predefined threshold  3. Kernel trick: The SVR algorithm applies the kernel trick that enables it to covertly transform input data into a high dimensional feature space, and this empowers it to grasp intricate non-linear connections between input and output variables.  4. Support vector: The support vector or subset of training data has an impact on building the regression function.  5. Regularization: Regularization parameters such as C (penalty parameter) and ε (epsilon) should be optimized to control the trade-off between minimizing error and maximizing the margin.  6. Loss function: The SVR model applies the loss function that penalizes the error exceeding the margin, while disregarding errors within the margin.  7. Prediction: Finally, the predicted values are generated through the regression model built in steps 1 to 6.    The detailed information regarding the SVR model can be found in (Alade et al. 2019; Owolabi 2019; Hamed et al. 2020 ).   3.3 Model hyperparameter tuning Model hyperparameter tuning, which involves determining the optimum values for the model’s operator, significantly influences the predictive power of the modeling process. In the current study, manual search methods (trial and error approach) (Xia et al., 2017; Rehamnia et al., 2020 ) were employed to identify the most effective value. Initially, each model was implemented using default parameter values, followed by testing higher and lower values (i.e. relative to the default setting) to reach the optimum values. The optimal value was determined based on the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) error metric, with the value resulting in the lowest RMSE being selected as the optimum one.  3.4 Model evaluation and comparison In the current study, various qualitative and quantitative error-based approaches were implemented to evaluate the performance of newly developed models. Qualitative methods used in the present study are scatterplot, density distribution histogram, box normal plot of residuals and Taylor diagram. Quantitative-based error metrics include RMSE, Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency coefficient (NSE), Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE), coefficient of uncertainty with a 95 % confidence level (U95% ), Percent of BIAS (PBIAS) Relative Deviation (RD) and Willmott index of agreement (WI). The ideal model has the RMSE, PBIAS, RD and U95%  of 0, and NSE, KGE and WI of 1. The results indicate that SD emerges as the most influential variable for TDG prediction at both stations, whereas Tw ranks as the second most important variable at USGS 12453700, and Q holds the same position at USGS 12462600. The least effective variable at both stations is BP. According to the BBF technique, although Q  exhibits a high correlation with TDG, it does not significantly impact the results. Therefore, it was excluded from the modeling process, and only SD, Tw, BP, and H were retained as input variables.  4.2 Model performance 4.2.1 Testing stage (Station USGS 12453700) In the current stage, all developed models are evaluated using the testing dataset. Initially, a comparison is made through a scatterplot analysis between predicted and measured TDG values (Fig. 6  ). The results indicate that the ensemble-based DA-M5-Rule algorithm demonstrates superior predictive capability, as evidenced by the tighter clustering of data points around the bisector line compared to other models. In contrast, the SVR model exhibits poorer performance. Overall, the hybrid models developed in this study consistently outperform the SVR model. Fig. 7   and Table 2   present the relative percentage difference distribution (%) between measured and predicted values in terms of histogram-density function, as well as the relative deviation (RD) for all the developed models. The DA-M5-Rule exhibits narrower error ranges compared to the other models. Based on the achieved results, the DA-M5-Rule based model demonstrates superior performance with the least RD (0.20 %), followed by the IAER-M5-Rule (0.21 %), WIHW-M5-Rule (0.22 %), RS-M5-Rule (0.53 %) and SVR (0.78 %), respectively. The results reveal that in terms of RD, the DA-M5-Rule model has 5 %, 10 %, 165 % and 290 % less deviation compared to IAER-, WIHW-, RS-M5-Rule and the SVR models, respectively. Fig. 8   shows the normal box-plot illustrating the residuals or differences between measured and predicted values. According to the achieved results, the ensemble-based DA-M5-Rule algorithm exhibits the highest performance, characterized by the lowest median (0.027) and interquartile range (IQR) values (4.03), followed by IAER-M5-Rule (median = 0.046 and IQR=5.18), RS-M5-Rule (median = -2.17 and IQR=7.96), WIHW-M5-Rule (median = 2.29and IQR=8.21), and SVR (median = -2.30 and IQR=8.26), respectively. Fig. 9   illustrates the model performance evaluation during the testing set using a Taylor diagram. The results indicate that the DA-M5-Rule ensemble-based model outperforms the other models, followed by IAER-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule and SVR, respectively. The DA-M5-Rule model exhibits a correlation coefficient between 0.8 and 0.9, while IAER-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule, and WIHW-M5-Rule demonstrate a correlation between 0.70 and 0.80 and the SVR model correlates just slightly higher than 0.60. In terms of St.D., the IAER-M5-Rule and the WIHW-M5-Rule are closer to the measured value. All quantitative error metrics indicate that the DA-M5-Rule model exhibited the highest predictive power (Fig. 10   and Table 3  ), followed by IAER-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule and SVR. The coefficient of uncertainty with a 95 % confidence level reveals that the DA-M5-Rule has the lowest coefficient of uncertainty (11 %), followed by IAER-M5-Rule (12.16 %), WIHW-M5-Rule (12.17 %), RS-M5-Rule (12.23 %) and SVR with 15 % has the highest coefficient of uncertainty. Table 3  highlights that the DA-M5-Rule model surpasses IAER-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule, WIHW-M−Rule, and SVR models by 10.25 %, 15.25 %, 10.5 %, and 42.75 % in terms of RMSE, respectively. According to the PBIAS metric, all the developed models overestimated TDG values (i.e. negative PBIAS).  4.2.2 Validation stage (station: USGS 12462600) The primary difference between our research and previous studies lies in our methodology. In the literature review, researchers typically developed models and tested them using data from the same station, with split data for training and testing within that station. This approach limited the ability to assess the generalization power of the developed model on a global scale. Therefore, in this research, we determine our model’s generalization power by feeding the entire dataset from the second station to the developed model to explore its performance in other areas. In the current stage, all the developed models are evaluated using a validation dataset. Initially, all models are compared through a scatterplot between predicted and measured TDG (Fig. 11  ). Results reveal that, similar to the test stage, the DA-M5-Rule algorithm has the highest prediction power. This is evidenced by the cloud points being less dispersed and more closely aligned with the bisector line compared to other models. Conversely, the SVR model shows the weakest modeling prediction power. Generally, all developed ensemble-based models demonstrated higher performance than the SVR model. Fig. 12   and Table 4   depict the relative percentage difference distribution (%) between measured and predicted values in terms of histogram-density function, alongside the RD for all developed models during the validation phase. The findings show that the DA-M5-Rule based model has a higher performance with the least RD (1.73 %), followed by IAER-M5-Rule (1.87 %), WIHW-M5-Rule (1.88 %), SVR (1.89 %) and RS-M5-Rule (2.00 %) respectively. Moreover, the RD, DA-M5-Rule model demonstrates 8 %, 15.6 %, 8.67 % and 9.24 % less deviation compared to IAER-, WIHW-, RS-M5-Rule, and SVR models. Fig. 13   illustrates the normal box-plot depicting residuals between measured and predicted values. According to achieved results, the ensemble-based DA-M5-Rule algorithm demonstrates the highest performance with the lowest median (−1.52) and IQR values (4.27), followed by RS-M5-Rule (median = -1.60 and IQR=4.56), IAER-M5-Rule (median = -1.69 and IQR=4.47) = WIHW-M5-Rule (median = 1.69 and IQR=4.47), and SVR (median = -1.70 and IQR=4.50). Fig. 14   shows the model performance evaluation during the validation phase using a Taylor diagram. The results reveal that the DA-M5-Rule ensemble-based models outperform other models, followed by IAER-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule and SVR respectively. All developed models correlate close to 0.90, whereas SVR correlates approximately 0.85. In terms of St.D ., the RS-M5-Rule models are closer to the measured value compared to other models. Most of the quantitative error metrics indicate that the DA-M5-Rule model had the highest generalization power (Fig. 15   and Table 5  ), followed by RS-M5-Rule, IAER-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule, and SVR. The coefficient of uncertainty with a 95 % confidence level, shows that RS-M5-Rule with 10.90 % has the lowest coefficient of uncertainty, followed by DA-M5-Rule (11.08 %), IAER-M5-Rule (11.40 %), WIHW-M5-Rule (11.44 %) and SVR with 13.50 % has the highest coefficient of uncertainty. As depicted in Table 5 , the DA-M5-Rule model exhibits 2.13 %, 0.23 %, 3.5 % and 18.80 % higher performance than IAER-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rulle, WIHW-M−Rule and SVR models in terms of RMSE, respectively. The results of the PBIAS metric show that all developed models overestimated TDG as evidenced by negative values. Fig. 16   displays the time-series graph of predicted versus measured value for the ensemble-based DA-M5-Rule based models, illustrating the accuracy of predicted TDG during the validation phase. It demonstrates that the developed model accurately captures TDG trends and fluctuations within a reasonable and acceptable range. Additionally, the results highlight that TDS often exceeds the threshold (dashed black line), emphasizing the need for careful decision-making by environmentalists and decision-makers.    5 Discussion In the current research, a large dataset of TDG supersaturation was acquired from two different stations across the Columbia River system in the USA. For the first time, the generalization power of the developed models was properly and thoroughly investigated. We developed several new ensemble-based models using data from one station and assessed their efficiency using a testing set from the same station. Additionally, the entire dataset from the second station was fed to the developed models to explore their generalization power and efficiency when used in ungagged areas around the world. It should be noted that several factors significantly impact the modeling prediction power, such as determining the best input scenario, considering proper and sufficient input variables, modeling structure and hyperparameter tuning, sufficient length of data, data splitting ratio, data resolution and data quality. In the following sections, we will discuss each aspect in detail.1- Feature selection importance    The selection of accurate and flexible feature selection (FS) techniques leads to an efficient input scenario and ultimately higher modeling performance results. In the current study, the BBF technique was applied as the optimum FS approach. The BBF technique offers several advantages, including Efficiency, flexibility, scalability, feature importance ranking, reduced overfitting, interpretability, improved model generalization, feature engineering guidance, and computational complexity. This technique can guarantee the globally best subset without requiring exhaustive enumeration for any criterion (Xu et al. 1988). Our findings demonstrate the flexibility and efficiency of the BBF technique, as it consistently led to robust generalization power in TDG prediction. In addition, we considered a comprehensive set of input variables, all of which proved to be relevant and effective in TDG prediction. The model's generalization ability was rigorously tested through data from an additional station and yielded highly satisfactory results. Notably, the constructed input scenarios demonstrated appropriate consideration and construction. As the higher performance observed during the validation phase compared to the testing phase underscores the effectiveness of the correlation between inputs and outputs on modeling performance. Specifically, the slightly higher correlation observed at the second station (i.e., validation data) further validates the effectiveness of the input–output relationship.2- Models structure and hyperparameter tuning    In the present study, several new and advanced ensemble-based machine learning algorithms are developed. Previous research has consistently shown that hybridized models can achieve superior performance due to increased flexibility resulting from (1) better learning and training and (2) non-linearity structure (De’ath and Fabricius, 2000 ). It is worth noting that the model’s structure itself significantly impacts the output performance. Given that TDG exhibits a nonlinear structure and involves a complicated process, its prediction requires powerful, nonlinear, and flexible algorithms. In the current study, the ensemble-based DA-M5-Rule based algorithm demonstrated higher performance during the testing phase and exhibited higher generalization power during the validation phase. The main advantages of the DA algorithm include benefiting from resampling ensemble methods and the capability of combining a variety of classifiers using the same learning technique for the base classifier (i.e. here M5-Rule). Additionally, higher fault tolerance (FT) is considered another advantage of disjoint algorithms (i.e. DA) over non-disjoint models. Generally, DA algorithms offer versatile, practical, and powerful solutions due to their improved generalization, robustness, and scalability. The DA model enhances the model’s performance by combining predictions from multiple models (i.e. with a diverse subset of data) (Tama and Comuzzi, 2019 ). In addition, the DA algorithm can handle large datasets or high dimensional feature space by training-based models in parallel on different subsets of data. Robustness to outliers, insensitivity to distribution assumptions, non-parametric nature, convergence properties, and applicability are among the greatest advantages of IAER, making it one of the powerful algorithms in the present study.3- length of data, data splitting ratio, and data resolution    The length of the data, the data splitting ratio, and the data resolution stand out as the three most important factors affecting modeling performance. In the current study, utilizing an hourly dataset for modeling facilitated comprehensive training of each developed model due to the high-resolution and large time-series dataset available. In addition, the hourly dataset accurately presents the patterns, relationships between input and output, and the underlying physics governing the target variable properly. Whereas, monthly or yearly datasets would overlook this information, resulting in models being unable to detect the pattern properly. While there is no global consensus among researchers regarding the optimum data-splitting ratio that leads to higher performance, the 70:30 ratio is widely used for both spatial and time-series modeling worldwide (Chen et al., 2017; Kouadio et al., 2018; Samadianfard et al., 2019 ). Additionally, increasing the training set from 50 % to 75 % has been shown to enhance the prediction capability of models (Kisi et al., 2019 ).4- Comparing with previous studies.    The current study introduces novel models for TDG prediction, making direct comparisons with existing methodologies impossible. Additionally, the methodology applied in the present study is utilized for the first time, testing the generalization power of models by developing a model and testing it at one station and subsequently assessing its generalization power using the entire dataset from another station. Han and Han (2019b)  implemented the MLPNN algorithm to simulate TDG using several input variables, including Q, BP, Tw, SD, and water elevation (WL). Their results showed that the MLPNN was more accurate compared to the multiple linear regression (MLR) model. Alomar et al. (2020)  developed and compared the prediction performance of ELM and SVR models for predicting TDG one hour in advance (t + 1) through considering several input variables (i.e. Tw, BP, Q and H). Their results showed that the SVR is slightly more accurate than the ELM model. Wang et al. (2022)  implemented the SVR, ELM, genetic algorithm ELM (ELM-GA), and SVR −GA for TDG prediction. They found that the SVR-GA model was more accurate compared to the GA-ELM model. Our results reveal that the SVR has the lowest performance among all five developed models. It can be concluded from the entire literature review (here and introduction) that generally, our developed models are novel and possess high generalization power. Heddam (2017b)  compared the prediction capability of GRNN for TDG prediction at two stations in the USA. They finally reported that the NSE for the validation and testing phase at station 1 is between 0.07–0.52 and 0.06–0.54 respectively. The values for the second station are between 0.15–0.73 and 0.149–0.74. There is no common error metric for comparison, but their modeling performance is moderate. Additionally, Heddam and Kisi (2020)  applied several models including Dynamic Evolving Neural-Fuzzy Inference System (DENFIS), ANFIS and MLR for TDG prediction in the USA. Their results at one station were excellent (NSE=0.949), but at other stations, they were moderate to good (NSE=0.70). It indicates that (1) to explore the generalization power of models, they should be tested across more than 1 station and (2) each dataset and station has different complexities and processes, thus directly comparing different models across different stations is not meaningful. Instead, benchmark models (e.g., SVR in our study) offer a more appropriate basis for evaluation.5- Limitation and future work recommendation    In the current study, we investigated the model’s generalization power using data from one extra station. However, it would be preferable to test it using datasets from China or other available data sources (i.e. as stated in the literature, available data is scarce in USA and China). If the developed models based on the data from the USA yield promising results when validated using data from China, their applicability could extend to various regions worldwide. In addition, comparing our newly developed models with deep learning models and evaluating their performance would offer valuable insights.  6 Conclusion The current study proposes a novel methodology and new ensemble-based algorithms for predicting Total dissolved gas (TDG) supersaturation at USGS 12453700 and USGS 12462600 stations over the Columbia River, USA. Nowadays, machine learning techniques have emerged as promising predictive tools in all fields of study. To enhance performance by identifying optimal input combinations, we employ a novel Bidirectional best-first (BBF) algorithm for feature selection. In addition, the present research investigates the feasibility of newly proposed ensemble-based models, namely Iterative absolute error regression (IAER-M5-Rule), Disjoint Aggregating (DA-M5-Rule), Random Subspace (RS-M5-Rule), and Weighted Instance Handler Wrapper (WIHW-M5-Rule) applied for TDG prediction for the first time. Then, the results have been compared with the support vector regression (SVR) model as a benchmark. In the current research, each model is developed and evaluated through the same station, while its generalization power is evaluated through a second station (i.e. the entire data was fed to the developed models from the first station). The main findings of the current study can be summarized as (1) according to the bidirectional best first algorithm, a combination of water temperature, barometric pressure, spill from dam, and sensor height leads to an optimum input scenario, (2) results of the current study shows that spill from dam is the most effective variable in TDG prediction at both stations, whereas BP is the least effective variable, (3) according to the BBF technique, despite its high correlation with TDG, Q was found to have no significant impact on the results, leading to its removal from the modeling process, (4) the newly proposed DA-M5-Rule model exhibited the highest predictive power followed by IAER-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule, RS-M5-Rule and SVR during the testing stage, (5) for generalization stage, DA-M5-Rule model demonstrated the highest generalization power, followed by RS-M5-Rule, IAER-M5-Rule, WIHW-M5-Rule, and SVR. The results of developed models can be applied as a promising tool across the USA. Overall, the findings of the current study are significant for constructing an intelligent-based system to precisely predict TDG worldwide, particularly after evaluating its generalization power beyond the USA. It would be preferable to test our developed models using datasets from China or other available data sources, then, the models can be applied worldwide.  7 Data Data related to this study is available upon request. In addition, it is publicly available on the USGS website.
1 Introduction The runoff coefficient (Rc) was initially formulated by Sherman (1932)  in the early twentieth century. It represents the ratio of runoff to rainfall (Bedient et al., 2008; Burak et al., 2021 ) and is extensively employed in engineering practices (Chen et al., 2020 ). In hydrology, Rc serves as a diagnostic variable, playing a key role in describing runoff generation within a catchment (Merz et al., 2006 ), and which is well-known to be influenced at different scales by the ongoing global warming (Blöschl et al., 2019; Masseroni et al., 2021; Dari et al., 2023 ). Understanding the impact of climatic and human-induced changes on local hydrological processes is essential, emphasizing the significance of assessing Rc changes in river basins (Velpuri and Senay, 2013 ). The Rc displays substantial variability in both space and time due to various influencing factors (Norbiato et al., 2009; Merz and Blöschl, 2009 ; Penna et al., 2011 ). For example, Chen et al. (2020)  highlighted the crucial influence of groundwater levels on the temporal variability of the Rc. Merz and Blöschl (2009)  studied the variation of Rc across a broad range of Austrian basins and found that Rc are mainly influenced by climate indicators like mean annual precipitation and the long-term ratio of actual evaporation to precipitation, with minimal impact from land use, soil types, and geology in the studied catchments. Similarly, Massari et al. (2023)  investigated how basin pre-storm conditions influence the Rc across 284 European basins and 60,620 flood events. Strong correlations of Rc were observed with deep soil storages, pre-storm discharge, and snow water equivalent among different basins. Their findings emphasized accurate flood forecasting relies on understanding how pre-flood conditions relate to the Rc, to establish links for early-warning systems. Rahi et al. (2023)  used continuous wavelet coherence analysis (WCA) to investigate the impact of hydroclimatic variables, including temperature (T), precipitation (P), soil water storage (SWS), and Land Use Land Cover (LULC) changes, on the Rc. Their findings revealed that precipitation correlation with Rc remained moderately unstable. In contrast, weak correlations were observed with LULC changes, while a strong positive but lagged correlation with SWS (1 month) and a strong lagged (3–6 months) but negative correlation with T suggested the prevailing significance of hydroclimatic factors over LULC changes. The evolving challenges in complex hydrological issues like real-time flood and drought forecasting, as well as water resource management, underscore the need for precise modelling of the regional-scale rainfall-runoff process. Despite numerous proposed approaches and the development of various models over the past decades, a comprehensive solution remains hard to attain. This challenge is driven by the substantial temporal and spatial variability inherent in the rainfall-runoff system (Merz and Blöschl, 2009 ) and the limitations in the availability of suitable mathematical tools to fully capture the dynamics underlying this process. Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are widely used in hydrology due to their flexibility, transferability, and computational efficiency (Wu et al., 2009; Nourani et al., 2011; Shoaib et al., 2014 ). However, the limitation of more classical AI-based techniques such as Artificial neural networks (ANNs) lies in the absence of temporal information on model inputs, affecting their ability to capture the temporal reaction of runoff to meteorological data (Kratzert et al., 2018 ). Hydrological hysteresis, a time-dependent phenomenon (Gharari and Razavi, 2018 ), complicates rainfall-runoff simulations by retaining the historical impacts on present or future occurrences. With the evolution of computational hardware capabilities and algorithms during the past decades, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) as a class of recurrent neural networks (RNN) has become prominent. The LSTM outperforms the traditional models in simulating runoff, specifically in addressing time series data challenges in hydrology (Kratzert et al., 2018; Bergen et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2021 ). The LSTM model has exhibited considerable potential in addressing temporal issues by memorizing sequence, accounting for prolonged temporal relationships and multiple output variables (Xiang et al., 2020 ). LSTM’s key advantage lies in its capacity to capture and learn long-term dependencies between the input and output data within the network (Kratzert et al., 2018 ). Systems that show the presence of hysteresis or of which the evolution depends on past states are typically denoted as “path-dependent systems” or “systems with memory” (Hassani et al., 2014 ). However, hydrological hysteresis has not been extensively studied in the context of water circulation (Gharari and Razavi, 2018 ), some studies indicated that there might be a lagged response of runoff to meteorological variables, which can extend beyond 100 days (Chen and Kumar, 2002; Orth and Seneviratne, 2013 ).
