In this regard, a range of studies has explored the use of LSTM models in capturing temporal relationships in wind power and flow stream estimation using static look-back windows (Wang et al., 2020; Girihagama et al., 2022 ), while Li et al. (2021)  introduced dynamic time-delays to improve the prediction performance of industrial time series models. Standard RNNs face long-term dependence issues, such as gradient vanishing or exploding (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ). Despite efforts with variants like LSTM, gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), and bidirectional GRU (BiGRU), these models may struggle with highly nonlinear and noisy time series without proper preprocessing (Zhou et al., 2024 ). Nhita et al. (2016)  proposed to use the moving average as an effective data smoothing method, enhancing the modelling and forecasting capabilities when using neural networks. Another approach to attenuate noise involves decomposing the problem into smaller subproblems, reducing complexity, and distributing the noise effects across each subproblem for more effective mitigation (Sáez et al., 2014 ). Recent advances in hybrid machine learning models (MLMs) have utilized various time series decomposition techniques to improve the MLM performance, including discrete wavelet transform (DWT) (Mallat, 1989; Liu et al., 2014 ), maximal overlap DWT (MODWT) (Adamowski and Sun, 2010 ), wavelet packet transform (WPT) (Moosavi, et al., 2017 ), empirical mode decomposition (EMD) (Huang et al., 1996, Napolitano et al., 2011 ), and ensemble EMD (EEMD) (Wang et al., 2015 ) and variational mode decomposition (VMD) (Dragomiretskiy and Zosso, 2014 ). These methods decompose complex time series data into simpler sub-series for separate modelling, effectively capturing valuable information at different temporal scales (Gokhale and Khanduja, 2010 ). In addition, Adamowski and Sun (2010)  showed that combining an ANN with DWT improved the prediction of daily streamflow. Furthermore, Seo et al. (2017)  proposed VMD-based extreme learning machine (VMD-ELM) and VMD-based least squares support vector regression (VMD-LSSVR) models, which demonstrated higher accuracy for daily rainfall-runoff modelling compared to single and DWT-based MLMs. Finally, Guo et al. (2023)  found that hybrid models combining two-stage decomposition methods with LSTM, specifically WT with CEEMDAN, VMD, and LMD, outperformed traditional and standalone models in forecasting daily runoff over the Pearl River in China. The MODWT decomposes a signal in both time and frequency domains, similar to the DWT. However, unlike the DWT, the MODWT retains down-sampled values at each decomposition level and can be applied to signals of any length without the power-of-two restriction. According to Cornish et al. (2006) , the MODWT offers several advantages over the DWT. These advantages suggest that combining MODWT with soft computing models could be a more effective and efficient approach for river stage modelling (Seo et al., 2017 ). Despite extensive studies on Rc and its influencing factors, there remains a gap in modelling Rc at regional and global scales. This paper addresses this gap by utilizing LSTM to predict Rc, incorporating the decomposition method. The first configuration of undecomposed Rc has been considered to investigate the capability of the LSTM method in modelling noisy Rc. The second configuration is defined to mitigate noise effects in Rc modelling, using the MODWT method to decompose Rc into sub-components, thereby reducing noise impact and improving model accuracy.  2 Study area The analysis has been carried out using data from the Stah outlet of the Rur catchments, in Germany (see Fig. 1  ). It covers an area of 2,245 km2  predominantly situated in the North Rhine-Westphalia region and is part of the TERENO (TERrestrial ENvironmental Observatories) network in Germany (Zacharias et al., 2024 ). Small portions of the basin extend into Belgium (6.7 %, 157 km2 ) and the Netherlands (4.6 %, 108 km2 ) as well. The terrain elevation gradually decreases from south to north, ranging from 680 to 30 m above sea level. The annual precipitation ranges from 650 to 1200 mm/yr increasing from north to south of the catchment (Bogena et al., 2005a ). Fig. 1 b provides land cover features at 100 m resolution derived by the Corine Land Cover data set referring to the year 2018 (CLC 2018). Agricultural areas cover 49 % of the catchment, mainly concentrated in the lowland regions of the northern part, while urban areas cover approximately 17.7 % of the area, primarily concentrated in the same northern region. Natural areas are predominantly situated in the elevated regions of the catchment, accounting for 31.8 % of the entire Rur catchment area. Water bodies and peat bogs represent less than 1.5 % of the total area (Fig. 1 b). The upland region (southern part), characterized by low permeable rock strata and limited groundwater recharge, relies on reservoirs for managing water resources. The upper Rur catchment exhibits pronounced seasonality, displaying a fast runoff response following rainfall events (Rudi et al., 2010 ). In contrast, water management strongly regulates runoff in the lower Rur catchment (Bogena et al., 2005a ). The flatland region from the centre to the north, containing loose rock aquifers, features relatively high groundwater recharge rates (Bogena et al., 2005b ), which are subject to intensive groundwater withdrawal. The Rur is a typical low mountain river with a very unbalanced discharge behaviour (the ratio of discharge values can fluctuate between 1:1000 and 1:2000 in extreme cases of dry weather and flood discharge). To compensate for these strong fluctuations, as well as for drinking water and energy production, a networked water reservoir system with several dams was established in the first part of the 20th century in the upper reaches, with a maximum reservoir volume of around 300 million cubic meters.  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Data In this investigation, monthly runoff volumes recorded at the Stah outlet during the period 1961–2021 were used. The runoff height was subsequently computed by dividing the volume by the basin’s area. For the timeframe 1961–2021, historical P data were downloaded by the climatic data center service (CDC, https://opendata.dwd.de/climate_environment/CDC/ ), and information was gathered from 10 meteorological stations within the study area (see Fig. 1 a). Cumulative monthly values of P recorded by each rain gauge were collected for all considered years, and the Thiessen polygons method was applied to derive basin-averaged monthly P data. Then, Rc for the entire catchment was calculated as the ratio between runoff height and basin-averaged P. The average monthly T data at 2 m elevation, the cumulative monthly data of total evaporation (ET), and the average monthly data of volumetric soil water content (SWC) from 1961 to 2021 were acquired from the Copernicus ERA5-Land (European Reanalysis v5-Land) service (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ) with a spatial sampling of 9 km. To quantify SWS, the initial 4 layers of the product’s physical schematization were considered, encompassing a depth of up to 2.89 m, SWS represents the total amount of water that is stored in the soil profile. All the data were spatially averaged over the Rur basin prior to the analyses (Table 1  ). Overall, the choice to use in-situ rainfall data ensures that we leverage the high-resolution, long-term observational data available in the region, thus enhancing the reliability of our LSTM forecasts. This approach aligns with our study’s focus on combining LSTM modelling and wavelet decomposition to improve forecast accuracy in an anthropized basin covering 2,245 km2 . The primary focus of this study was to develop a technique to overcome the effects of noise while forecasting Rc. The proposed technique can be potentially implemented elsewhere, upon availability of adequate records to fit the train set. For larger scale Rc forecasts, combining AI-based model with wavelet technique using satellite data can even be applied, though this is beyond the scope of our current research.  3.2 LSTM modelling LSTM, a specialized form of RNN, overcomes the limitations of traditional ANNs in managing long-term dependencies through the integration of memory structures (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ). In this study, an LSTM structure has been defined to develop a hydrological model for predicting Rc. 3.2.1 LSTM design The basic model includes a cell state C for each time step, preserving crucial information for short- and long-term memory. Each cell receives the previous state of the target variable h t - 1      and one or more predictor variables x as input and returns the current state of the target variable h t     as the output. Fig. 2  a illustrates the core structure and algorithms of a modern LSTM model, updating six parameters in each time step through equations (1) to (6) :(1) f t  = σ ( W f  . h t - 1   , x t     + b f  )      (2) i t  = σ ( W i  . h t - 1   , x t     + b i  )      (3) c ∼  t  = t a n h ( W C  . h t - 1   , x t     + b C  )      (4) C t  = f t  × C t - 1   + i t  × c ∼  t      (5) o t  = σ ( W o  . h t - 1   , x t     + b o  )      (6) h t  = o t  × tanh ( C  t  )       The first parameter, f t    , is associated with the forget gate, determining the extent to which the previous cell state should be disregarded. This decision is made by a sigmoid function with a linear calculation involving the current input x t     and the previous state h t - 1     . The weights (W   ) and biases (b   ) in each LSTM cell vary in different steps for the linear equations. A lower f t     value (close to zero) prompts the sigmoid function to forget the previous cell state C t - 1      more. The second parameter, i t    , is linked to the input gate, deciding what new information is to be retained and added to the cell state. Calculated by a sigmoid function with a linear relation on x t     and h t - 1     , it influences the candidate values c ∼  t     for the new cell state, determined by a hyperbolic tangent (tanh) function. Subsequently, the cell state C t     is updated. Finally, the output parameter o t     is computed by a sigmoid function with a linear relation on x t     and h t - 1     . The output result at the current state, h t    , is the product of o t     and the tanh function value of the cell state C t    . In summary, f t    , i t    , c ∼  t    , C t    , o t    , and h t     are all vectors. Specifically, f t     and i t     range between 0 and 1, c ∼  t     ranges between −1 and 1, C t     can take any real value, o t     ranges between 0 and 1, and h t     ranges between −1 and 1. All these vectors allow the LSTM network to handle multiple units of data simultaneously, which enhances its ability to learn and model complex temporal patterns. In this study, we set our predictor variable x to contain states of T, P, SWS, and ET as Chen and Xu (2021)  demonstrate that the inclusion of more meteorological variables can improve LSTM performance. To frame our model, we employed the pre-existing LSTM layer components within the Keras (Chollet, 2021 ) framework in Python. In principle, each cell of the LSTM model only takes into account the previous state of the target variable, but not the previous states of the predictors. Therefore, any possible lagged relationship between the predictors and the outcome variable must be considered. In this regard, a new predictor variable is usually obtained from the original predictor variable, using a specific look-back window. In our analysis, we examined different look-back windows with values ranging from 1 to 6 months to obtain the best look-back window according to the trial-and-error concept. Shukla et al., (2023)  compared the runoff simulations and observed data for the calibration period (2000–2010) and the validation period (2011–2015) at the stations Monschau, Linnich, and Stah in the Rur catchment. They found the model performed best at Monschau, likely due to fewer anthropogenic interventions compared to the more urbanized and agricultural northern parts of the basin, where water use, channel diversions, and dams, which are not considered in the model, significantly affect stream flow. Considering the regulated runoff due to dam construction and water treatment in the northern part of the Rur catchment, the stochastic nature of rainfall data may lead to high variance and noisy Rc signals, complicating modelling efforts. Consequently, the Rc estimated in this work is influenced by those above-mentioned human activities. However, studies (e.g., Shukla et al., 2023 ) indicate that the Rur river’s discharge dynamics remain relatively natural, as less than 5 % of runoff is used for drinking water and efforts are made to maintain natural discharge conditions to protect the ecosystem. Therefore, the Rc values from this study should still approximate natural conditions, though precise quantification of the dam-regulating effect is beyond this study’s scope. To overcome the noise effects, we implemented two configurations: 1) we modelled the noisy signals of Rc without any preprocessing and 2) we first decomposed Rc signals using MODWT into low-frequency (A) and high-frequency (D) components (see Table 2  ) and then modelled each component separately and combined them at output level to reconstruct the original signal of Rc (see Fig. 2 c):(7) Rc = ( ∑ i = 1  m  D i  )  + A m      where m is the level of decomposition.  3.2.2 Model setting and parametrization In the model architecture, two LSTM layers are employed: the first layer consists of 512 neurons with a rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function and is configured to return sequences. The subsequent LSTM layer contains 256 neurons, also utilizing the ReLU activation function. Following the LSTM layers, a dense layer, with an activation function of ReLU, is added with a number of neurons equal to the target output’s shape. An epoch represents one complete pass through the entire training dataset, allowing the model to update its parameters to improve performance. To prevent overfitting, an early stopping indicator is implemented with a patience of 20 epochs, restoring the best weights based on monitoring the validation loss. The optimization process utilizes stochastic objective functions, based on adaptive estimates (Adam) developed by Kingma and Ba (2015) , a gradient descent-based algorithm, with an initial learning rate set to 0.0001, and it is adjusted by a factor of 0.001 when the loss on the validation set fails to decrease, thereby mitigating overfitting.  3.2.3 Evaluation metrics The model aims to minimise the fraction of unexplained variance, employing mean squared error (MSE) as the loss function. The choice of MSE aligns with the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), a widely-used performance evaluation method in hydrological modelling. NSE ranges from −∞ to 1, and the closer its value is to 1, the better the model performs (Arnold et al., 2012 ):(8) MSE = ∑ i = 1  n  ( Y i  - Y i  ^  )  2   n      (9) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  ( Y i  - Y i  ^  )  2   ∑ i = 1  n  ( Y i  - Y  ¯    )  2         Where Y i     is the observation at the time i   , Y i  ^     is the model result at time i   , Y  ¯      is the mean of all observations, and n    is the total number of observations. In alignment with Moriasi et al. (2015) , this study utilizes NSE to categorize results into unsatisfactory (NSE ≤ 0.5), satisfactory (0.5 < NSE ≤ 0.7), good (0.7 < NSE ≤ 0.8), and very good (NSE > 0.8), providing a concise evaluation of model accuracy and reliability. Root mean square error (RMSE) serves as an indicator of the standard deviation of the prediction error in a model. A smaller RMSE value indicates a smaller prediction error, signifying better performance of the model (Naabil et al., 2017 ). RMSE represents the errors between predicted values and actual values and is calculated as:(10) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  ( Y i  - Y i  ^  )  2         In the current study to verify the hydrological modelling of Rc, two metrics, NSE and RMSE, were used to evaluate the differences between Rc simulated in the train set (1961–2001), validation set (2001–2011) and test set (2011–2021) with observed Rc.  3.2.4 Model optimization The optimization of the LSTM model parameters was carried out differently for the main parameters and hyperparameters. The look-back window parameter, was tuned by testing and iteration to achieve the optimum output, while the hyperparameters are predefined settings that control the learning process (see Table 3  ) were optimised by Grid Search Cross-Validation (GridSearchCV), a Hyper-Parameters Optimization (HPO) technique used in machine learning (Goel et al., 2020 ; Bischl et al., 2023 ). Grid search is a systematic approach to parameter tuning in machine learning models, evaluating each combination of algorithm parameters specified in a grid. In this process, the key terms include the estimator, implementing the scikit-learn estimator interface, and representing the classifier to be trained. The parameter grid is a Python dictionary with parameter names and corresponding settings, testing all combinations to identify the optimal accuracy. Cross-validation is crucial in this context, determining the resampling strategy for evaluating models and mitigating bias. It involves randomly shuffling and splitting the dataset into k groups, using each as a test set while the others act as training data. This process provides more reliable results compared to a simple train-test split, as it ensures that each sample is present in the testing data once and used for training k-1 times (Ranjan et al., 2019 ). In this study, several key hyperparameters (see Table 3 ) have been optimized to achieve the best possible performance of our model. The remaining hyperparameters, which have been set to default or predetermined values based on empirical best practices, include the learning rate and early stopping (see section 3.2.2 ). This approach ensures a balanced between computational efficiency and model accuracy, allowing us to focus on the most impactful hyperparameters for our specific application.   3.3 Model configurations As previously explained, two different configurations have been defined to implement and compare the results of the proposed LSTM modelling approach: 1) Undecomposed Rc and 2) Decomposed Rc. 3.3.1 Undecomposed Rc In this approach, the undecomposed Rc has been modelled by the LSTM method considering a look-back window, which was set on the basis of the concept of “lag” derived by the WCA, a theory recently applied to hydrological studies (Rahmati et al., 2020; Rahi et al., 2023; Dari et al., 2024 ). Fan et al. (2020) , found that an improper window size can significantly impact model performance. Referring to Appendix A , we assessed the phase shift and lag between the benchmark signal (Rc) and P, SWS, T, and ET time series following Rahmati et al. (2020) , then different look-back windows evaluated by LSTM to find the optimum value.  3.3.2 Decomposed Rc In the second approach, the MODWT was used to decompose Rc using the Coif mother wavelet into its approximation (A) and details (D), depending on the decomposition level. The MODWT analyses signals into progressively finer octave bands. This multiresolution analysis enables to detect patterns that are not visible in the raw data. The level for MODWT computation (decomposition level) is indicated as a positive integer, not exceeding the floor of the log 2  N   , where N    represents the size of the input layer in the time dimension. In this study, with a time dimension of 720 months (starts from January 1961 to December 2020), the maximum level is set to 9. However, Srivastava et al. (2016)  argue that the level of decomposition can be recognized by visual inspection where the approximation coefficient and detail have visual similarity. Therefore in accordance to Srivastava et al. (2016)  plus inspection of the accuracy of the developed models, we decided to decompose Rc up to 3 levels. The MODWT partitions the energy of the signal across the various scales and scaling coefficients. The relative energy is defined as the proportion of energy in each component by level, relative to the total energy of decomposition level. The sum of relative energies in all components equals 1 (see Table 2 ). Then, the decomposed signals (one approximation and three details) were modelled separately applying the LSTM method with the same look-back window setting as defined in previous section. Finally, the modelled decomposed signals were combined with each other to reconstruct the Rc signal. By comparing the reconstructed and undecomposed Rc signals, we were able to evaluate the accuracy of the model at the output level, in addition to checking the accuracy of each individual model for each component.    4 Results and discussion The outcomes of this study reveal commendable stability in the monthly resolution performance of the LSTM model, showcasing its ability to reproduce the complex features of the Rc. Based on the WCA results (Appendix A ), a temporal lag of 1–6 months between Rc and the key input variables (i.e., P, SWS, T, and ET) has been identified. The temporal lag deduced by the WCA has been considered as a look-back window. After several trials considering entities of the look-back window within the range of 1–6 months, the optimal LSTM model performances have been found when employing a look-back window equal to 4 months. Such a value is a good trade-off between capturing relevant temporal dependencies and preventing overfitting (Fig. 4 ). In this study, GridSearchCV was employed to optimize hyperparameters (Listed in Table 3 ). The findings revealed that the most accurate results in forecasting both decomposed Rc and undecomposed Rc can be obtained by applying the optimized parameters as presented in Table 4  . In the following subsections, we will report the results obtained for each configuration. 4.1 Undecomposed Rc In Fig. 3  a results of training and validation loss (look-back window equal to 3 months) show that the model fails to predict undecomposed Rc accurately, and the result contains uncertainty and needs to be improved. The NSE for both the train and validation sets is equal to 0.51 and 0.49 respectively, indicating unsatisfactory match with observed Rc from 1961 to 2001 (Fig. 3 b). However, a noteworthy challenge arises in the test set, where the NSE drops to 0.05, indicating diminished accuracy and underscoring the imperative need for a targeted solution. Holman-Dodds et al., (1999)  found that the temporal sampling of precipitation can affect model calibration, where lower sampling frequencies may result in the underestimation of runoff. This is probably due to missing the possible lagged responses between precipitation and runoff, which probably is the case in our analysis, too. Therefore, we modelled the undecomposed Rc by the LSTM method applying a look-back window equal to 4 months. The results showed that the NSE of the train and validation set remained constant, while NSE of test set enhanced to the value of 0.15 (Fig. 3 d). Although using the look-back window equal to 4 improved the results, the results were still very poor. Patry et al. (1989)  and Gusev et al. (2017)  both highlight the role of uncertainty in hydrological models, particularly in the presence of noise. Onstad and Jamieson (1970)  further emphasize the importance of considering land use modifications in runoff modelling, which can be affected by noise. Gelfan et al. (2015)  extend this discussion to the analysis of hydrological extreme uncertainty, which is also influenced by noise. Therefore, upon a detailed examination of the Rc time series, the primary source of discrepancy was traced back to inherent noise associated with precipitation and runoff data. These noise elements introduced a level of unpredictability in the Rc values, leading to suboptimal model fitting during the training phase and subsequently reduced accuracy in forecasting.  4.2 Decomposed Rc The obtained results for this approach show that the detail component D1 contain varying amounts of noise (panels (e) of Fig. 4  ), whereas the noise (low frequency) from components D2, D3and A3 is extremely minimal and indistinguishable (see panels b-d of Fig. 4 ). In panel (a) of Fig. 5  , the training and validation loss profiles for the first level of decomposed Rc are depicted, which correspond to the highest frequency (0.25–0.5) component in the signal. The presence of high-frequency noises in runoff and precipitation can lead to overfitting in hydrological models. The overfitting of training data compromises the model’s suitability to be generalized, rendering its performance unreliable when applied to new measurements (Piotrowski and Napiorkowski, 2013 ). The result of this study indicates that the training set has been effectively simulated; however, the validation set exhibits signs of overfitting which is attributable to the presence of high-frequency noises in the D1. Examining panel (c) of Fig. 5  reveals NSE values for the train, validation, and test sets equal to 0.92, 0.81, and 0.71, respectively. Furthermore, RMSE values for the train, validation, and test sets are observed as 0.03, 0.03, and 0.05, respectively. Despite the expected presence of high-frequency noises in the D1, the LSTM model demonstrates a well-fitted behaviour, yielding significant simulation results across train, validation, and test data sets. Upon inspecting Fig. 5 b, it becomes apparent that the fitting for component D2 surpasses the D1. Notwithstanding this improvement, the overfitting of the validation set persists, albeit with noticeable advancements. The LSTM model’s enhanced fitting component D2 is reflected in the improved NSE values for the train, validation, and test sets, showing as 0.97, 0.80, and 0.81, respectively. This enhancement in the efficacy metrics underscores the model’s proficiency in capturing underlying patterns within the data. Concurrently, the RMSE values for the train, validation, and test sets are equal to 0.01, 0.02, and 0.03, respectively. Hence, the model has effectively mitigated the impact of high-frequency noises associated with D1 and D2, showcasing acceptable performance in simulating Rc dynamics across the train, validation, and test datasets. In Fig. 6  a, a notable improvement in modelling accuracy is evident for D3. The NSE values, reaching 0.99, 0.99, and 0.96 for the train, validation, and test sets respectively, underscore the robust performance of the model. Such high NSE values indicate the model’s ability to accurately capture the complexity of the data across train, validation, and test datasets. Furthermore, RMSE values equal to 0.005, 0.008, and 0.001 for the train, validation, and test sets, respectively, are found (refer to Fig. 6 c). The modelling of the component A3 using LSTM (refer to Fig. 6 b and d) has been implemented with high precision. The training and validation loss presented in Fig. 6 b reflects an outstanding simulation, resulting in NSE values of 0.99, 0.99, and 0.99 for the train, validation, and test sets, respectively. This model was expected to exhibit the most precise fitting among component D3 and A3. This anticipation arises from the fact that the approximation coefficient filters by a low-pass frequency, aligning with the characteristics of the mother tongue. The RMSE for the A3 consistently maintains a low value, reminding the behaviour of the D3, which exhibits the least uncertainty among all decomposed details. This stability underscores the robustness of the A3 in capturing underlying patterns with minimal errors, assuring its crucial role in achieving accurate and stable results within the broader context of the decomposition analysis. Inspecting the efficacy values shows that the LSTM could fit the train set, however, the efficacy does not show satisfactory accuracy value (Fig. 7  a). To overcome this challenge, Rc was decomposed to specific levels of 1 and 3, with particular emphasis on employing the LSTM model through the decomposed components of each level. Then reconstructed Rc was obtained from equation (7)  for both levels 1 and 3 of decomposition. The results show that NSE values of decomposed Rc at level 3 are enhanced significantly in comparison with undecomposed Rc, mainly regarding the test set which shows a value of 0.90 being much higher compared to the value of 0.15 for that of the test dataset of undecomposed signal. Additionally, the results of level 3 of decomposition remain almost constant compared to level 1 except for the test set where it improves. This enhancement may refer to decomposing the noise in two components (D1 and D2) which allows the LSTM to better fit the noise components. The LSTM model has been successfully implemented across different levels of decomposition, demonstrating very good accuracy. In contrast, the LSTM fails to fit the undecomposed Rc adequately, yielding less acceptable accuracy. This underscores the effectiveness of leveraging decomposition techniques in conjunction with the LSTM model for improved accuracy in modelling the Rc. This indicates the importance of considering the complex details captured at various decomposition levels. However, the findings show that the accuracy of the developed models remained nearly constant for levels beyond 3. The integration of ERA5 land service data with observed data in the LSTM model showcases remarkable resilience (Pelosi et al., 2020; Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ), as the model’s accuracy and simulation performance remain unaffected. This seamless combination underscores the robustness of the LSTM framework in accommodating diverse data sources, reaffirming its reliability in capturing the intricacies of hydrological dynamics. The methodology presented in this paper can indeed be extended to larger scales, though it is essential to consider several factors. One of the primary advantages of this approach is its reliance on widely available meteorological and hydrological data, which makes it feasible to apply in various regions, even if only small amount of high-resolution data is available. However, when scaling up to regional or global levels, challenges such as data heterogeneity, varying climatic conditions, and differing land-use patterns must be addressed. Moreover, in highly anthropized basins, where human activities significantly alter the hydrological cycle, additional factors such as water withdrawals, reservoir regulations, and land-use changes must be incorporated into the model. This necessitates more complex modelling frameworks that can account for these variables. Similarly, in regions with limited data availability, the accuracy of Rc predictions may be reduced. In such cases, employing satellite data and integrating multiple data sources can help improve model performance. Overall, while our model provides a robust framework for Rc estimation, careful consideration of local conditions and data quality is essential when applying it to different scales and contexts. Future work should focus on enhancing model adaptability and accuracy in diverse and data-limited environments. To better visualize the results of modelling Rc at level 3 of decomposition, 3 insets have been illustrated in Fig. B1 . These insets (Panels b-d of Fig. B1 ) refer to the windows among different sets to show more detailed information about the fitted sets. The results indicate a reduction in peak underestimation when combining the LSTM and decomposition method compared to the results of undecomposed Rc.   5 Conclusions This study introduces an innovative LSTM modelling approach for the prediction of Rc on the basis of key hydrometeorological variables, employing the Rur basin in Germany as a case study for the period 1961 to 2021. The findings reveal that the standard LSTM model performed inadequately when applied to undecomposed Rc, yielding unsatisfactory accuracy across training, validation, and test sets. However, although optimizing the look-back window to 4 months notably improved the modelling in comparison to other values (1–6 months lag), it was still a challenge to predict Rc with acceptable accuracy. Using the LSTM model in conjunction with Maximal overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform demonstrated effectiveness across various levels of decomposition. In our study we decomposed the Rc signal in three levels spanning frequency levels of 0–0.061 and 0.056–0.500 cycle/month for approximation and details, respectively. The NSE values of 0.97, 0.95, and 0.90 for the training, validation, and test sets at level 3 of decomposition, underscore the robust performance of this approach. Notably, the results showcase a very good accuracy of decomposition approach compared to undecomposed Rc. Additionally, we found an approximately 6 % enhancement in the NSE value of the test set when modelling at level 3 compared to level 1, while the NSE values for the training and validation sets remained constant. These findings suggest the potential application of this innovative technique through hydrological modelling to enhance the reliability of prediction in future studies.
1 Introduction Drought is one type of the most devastating natural disasters (Dai, 2013 ), causing an average annual economic damage of approximately 6–8 billion dollars worldwide (Yagci et al., 2013 ). Broadly, drought is classified into four primary categories: meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic drought (Wilhite and Glantz, 1985 ). Meteorological drought, which is characterised by the deficit in precipitation, behaves as a precursor for the remaining drought types (Dash et al., 2019; Sang et al., 2018 ). Agricultural drought, resulting from deficit in soil moisture and resulting in reduction in crop yield (Chatterjee et al., 2022; Leng and Hall, 2019 ), lowers the global crop yield in the range of 9-10 % and subsequently, accounts for more than 80 % of global drought-related impacts (Wu et al., 2022; Lesk et al., 2016 ). The official report from Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters reveals that agricultural drought annually impacted over 20 million ha cropland of China, accounting for about 10 % of the total Chinese cropland (Xu and Tang, 2021 ). An escalation in the frequency and severity of agricultural drought is anticipated due to the impacts of global warming (Kang and Eltahir, 2018; Piao et al., 2010; Zhai et al., 2016 ). The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which outline the transformative global agenda for 2030, address the pressing need to confront adverse agricultural drought conditions, eradicate hunger, ensure food security, and promote sustainable agricultural practices (UN, 2015; Wu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021; Mohammed et al., 2022 ). Given this context, the prevention of agricultural drought occurrence and mitigation of agricultural drought related impacts assume paramount importance in optimizing agricultural water management, safeguarding food security, and advancing the attainment of SDG objectives at both regional and global scales. Over the last decades, primary hydrometeorological variables (precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, groundwater storage, etc. ) and vegetation indices (leaf area index (LAI), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), etc. ) have been individually or collectively used to develop agricultural drought indices (Wu et al., 2021 ), and subsequently, describe the characteristics of agricultural drought severity, frequency, and duration (Wang et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020b; Yao et al., 2020 ). These agricultural drought indices have effectively explained climatic anomalies (Won et al., 2020 ), vegetation dynamics (Bian et al., 2023; Jiao et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020b ), and soil moisture regimes (Martínez-Fernández et al., 2016; Mishra et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2021 ) across varying spatiotemporal scales. Yet, most of these studies only considered water-related variables but did not include drought impact variables (Blauhut et al., 2015 ). They only reflected the moisture deficit conditions but failed to describe the potential negative consequences of drought which are acutely needed for agriculture management. For example, the crop yield reduction owing to the field-scale onset of agricultural drought phenomenon has been rarely discussed in these studies. As a result, the agricultural drought area extracted by certain thresholds of such drought indices may not be consistent with the actual distribution of agricultural drought impacted area. The outcomes may often be unreliable for developing effective formulation of prevention and mitigation policies in the context of early warning of agricultural drought. A recent study highlights the need to go beyond conventional drought monitoring toward impact-based drought assessment – i.e., linking climatic anomalies to expected drought impacts (AghaKouchak et al., 2023 ). The research gap is mainly due to the absence of reliable historical high-resolution datasets of agricultural drought that can be linked to potential impacts. In practice, the existing historical agricultural drought data are commonly reported by local administrative entities, and are confined to annual-scale and county- or provincial-scales for public (Xu and Tang, 2021 ). The relatively limited information provided by existing coarse agricultural drought databases poses significant challenges to efficient monitoring and timely warning of intricate agricultural drought events, particularly linking climatic information to local anthropogenic activities (AghaKouchak et al., 2021 ). Spanning an expansive area of 40 million hectares, the North China Plain (NCP) emerges as one of China's principal agricultural hubs. Within its bounds, it stands as one of the nation's key granaries, contributing over 50 % (33 %) of China's total wheat (maize) production (Jeong et al., 2014 ). However, the NCP with semi-arid climatic conditions encountered acute water shortage problems, especially continuous groundwater overexploitation during the last four decades (Chen et al., 2023 ). The conflict between high irrigation water demand and severe water shortage problem caused the NCP to become highly vulnerable to agricultural drought. Over the past two decades, more than 2 million ha/year of cropland in the NCP were subjected to severe agricultural drought disasters. The agricultural drought across the NCP is characterized by significant inter-annual variability, e.g., 3 million ha of cropland in the NCP were impacted by agricultural drought during winter and spring seasons of the year 2009, while the year 2020 experienced only 0.5 million ha of coverage (The Ministry of Water Resources of the People’s Republic of China, 2020 ). Certainly, cultivating the winter wheat and summer maize through rotational means in the NCP leads to high intra-annual variation of drought conditions. However, the official Chinese drought data source, i.e., the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters, can only provide one data record of historical agricultural drought area in each year for the two major provinces, i.e., Hebei and Shandong located in the NCP. Indeed, basing the assessment solely on a single historical drought record per year renders the investigation into drought impacts across distinct crop growing seasons within an extensive geographical expanse, especially in a finer field-scale spatial resolution framework, impractical. Consequently, an immediate imperative emerges to develop a novel approach for accurate agricultural drought areas identification in the NCP. Such an approach would play a pivotal role in facilitating meticulous crop and water management planning, and validating drought prediction model (AghaKouchak et al., 2022 ). However, deriving a methodology for generating high resolution agricultural drought area dataset given the limited observational data represents a formidable challenge. In the context of regional agricultural drought areas identification at high-resolution and continuous timescale, the observed hydro-meteorological and agricultural field datasets often prove essential but inadequate (Dash et al., 2021 ). In response, the utilization of a remote sensing-based indirect approach to extract essential crop physiological parameters has demonstrated notable efficiency. LAI can reflect the potential amount of photosynthesis and dry matter accumulation during the reproductive stage, suggesting that it has a good ability of monitoring crop growth and yield (Darvishzadeh et al., 2008; Liang et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2020 ). Leveraging the moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite-derived LAI product alongside historical observed drought data from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China, this study connects the agricultural drought indicator and provincial agricultural drought data, and employs these sources to construct the foundational inputs for its research. Addressing the aforementioned research gaps, this study is guided by the following specific objectives: i) to develop a LAI-based relative thresholds method for the identification of agricultural drought areas; ii) to determine the LAI thresholds specifically tailored for the NCP region, enabling the quantification of different degrees of agricultural drought; and iii) to generate a 500 m-resolution agricultural drought area dataset covering the NCP during 2006-2019, focusing on the two crop harvesting seasons of summer and autumn. The findings of this study hold the potential to function as a proactive tool for impact-based drought assessment and early warning in the face of impending agricultural drought predictions or scenarios.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The NCP constitutes the coordinate 32◦ 08′N to 40◦ 23′N and 112◦ 51′E to 122◦ 42′E, and is a typical alluvial plain with an average elevation of 73.5 m (Fig. 1  ). It partly covers 5 provinces (Hebei, Henan, Shandong, Jiangsu and Anhui) and 2 municipalities (Beijing and Tianjin) locations. Beijing and Tianjin locations have small croplands resulting in limited crop production (National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2020 ); hence, the two locations are excluded in the study. As shown in Fig. 1 , the primary land use types in the NCP include cropland, forest, grassland, water area, urban area, and unused area. Cropland accounts for about 87 % of the total land in the NCP (Wu et al., 2021 ), implying its significance for crop production and food safety in China. Considering the existing crop calendar of the NCP region, the crops can be categorized under two major heads, viz., summer-harvest crops and autumn-harvest crops. Winter wheat is the main summer-harvest crop, which is sown in October and harvested in the next summer. Autumn-harvest crops are usually sown in April and July and harvested in autumn, that include summer maize and a small percentage of spring maize, spring wheat, cotton and peanut, with the key phenological period lying between July to August (Li and Lei, 2021 ). The main phenological periods of both summer-harvest crops and autumn-harvest crops include sowing period, heading period, and harvest period. The detailed description about the followed crop calendar in the NCP region is shown in Table S1 .  2.2 Data Three different kinds of datasets, including historical agricultural drought information, crop area coverage, and LAI information were used in this study. The historical agricultural drought data encompassing the years 2006-2020 within the NCP region was sourced from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China. This valuable dataset is made available by the Ministry of Water Resources of the People's Republic of China. This particular dataset served as the foundational reference to create the 500-meter resolution agricultural drought areas dataset specific to the NCP. In the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China, the agricultural drought was characterized under three heads: drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area, which represent the sown area with ≥10%, ≥30%, and ≥80% crop losses due to agricultural drought, respectively. The three degrees of data will be analysed individually, and their corresponding historical agricultural drought areas will be extracted. The crop area data consisted of crop coverage information under two growing phases, i.e., summer-harvest crop area and autumn-harvest crop area. These datasets determined the boundary domain of the agricultural drought areas dataset generated in the present study. Summer-harvest crops are dominated by winter wheat, whose areas during the period 2006-2019 were obtained from the China Crop Area 1-km (Luo et al., 2020 ), as a reliable and widely used 1-km crop harvesting area dataset for three staple crops (wheat, maize and rice) in China. Considering the Zhangjiakou region (i.e., the northwest part of Hebei Province) prevalent with spring wheat cultivation, the region was excluded from analysis, and the residual winter wheat area was treated as the summer-harvest crop area in the NCP. Besides, summer maize and a small percentage of spring maize, spring wheat, cotton, and peanut are harvested in autumn growing season across the whole cropland region of the NCP (Table S1 ), and subsequently, treated as the autumn-harvest crop area of the NCP. LAI is an effective and critical vegetation indicator that is sensitive to the changes in crop yield, offering a reliable representation of crop health status. It has been widely used in assessing agricultural drought, predicting potential crop yields and detecting the feedback of crops to drought (Zhou et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Cao et al. 2024 ). Hence, it was applied in this study as a proxy to describe agricultural drought conditions in the NCP region. Among all the available satellite-based LAI products, the MODIS LAI time series data has proven to be more accurate and behaves as an excellent monitoring tool in assessing the drought phenomenon at regional scale (Yang et al., 2007 ). Thus, MODIS LAI product (MCD15A2) with a spatial resolution of 500 m at 8-day temporal resolution was used in this study. Considering the trajectory of satellite pass in the NCP region, the MODIS image tiles h26v04, h26v05, h27v04, and h27v05 were acquired to cover the study area. More details about the used data and sources of availability can be found in Table 1  . Furthermore, the winter wheat area data and land use data were resampled to 500 m-resolution and the analysis period was set to 2009-2020. The land use data for the NCP at a spatial scale of 1 km provided by the Resource and Environment Science and Data Centre Platform available at 5-years interval was adopted in this study (Table 1 ). Contemplating the available year of China Multi-time Land use and Land Cover Dataset, the land use data of the years 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020 were used for the drought area development for the period 2006-2007, 2008-2012, 2013-2017, and 2018-2020, respectively. Moreover, the summer-harvest crop area data in the year 2020 was kept the same as that for the year 2019, for maintaining the period consistency of all data sources.   3 Methodology To develop the agricultural drought area identification approach of LAI-based relative thresholds method within the NCP, the subsequent three pivotal considerations have been meticulously tackled: i) a reliable baseline scenario for LAI was chosen to quantify relative severity of agricultural drought, ii) suitable LAI thresholds were determined to classify different degrees of agricultural drought and identify agricultural drought impacted areas, and iii) the 500 m-resolution agricultural drought areas dataset spanning the entirety of NCP was generated by extracting the drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area for each harvest season during 2006-2019. 3.1 Choice of drought baseline A reliable drought baseline is essential to quantify the relative severity of agricultural drought over time. In practice, two types of drought baselines have been widely used in drought monitoring. The first involves utilizing the average agricultural drought condition within a specified time period as the baseline, while the second entails selecting the drought state of a specific year within the analysis period as the baseline for agricultural drought assessment. The former baseline definition yields an average agricultural drought degree, which inherently introduces a bias in the relative assessment of drought severity across different years. This consequently casts doubt on the accuracy of the resultant agricultural drought areas datasets. Thus, this study departed from this approach and instead designated the drought condition in the year 2020 as the baseline for relative agricultural drought degree evaluation throughout the 2006-2019 timeframe. The rationale behind this choice is rooted in the observation of the historical records from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China, where the agricultural drought areas of all three degrees were relative smaller in the year 2020, being close to a no-drought condition. Besides, previous studies of soil moisture, net primary productivity and crop yield also demonstrated that crops were all in good moisture condition in 2020, without being obviously damaged by agricultural droughts in the NCP (Li et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024 ). This particular year's conditions thus serve as an apt reference point for gauging relative agricultural drought during the specified period.  3.2 Determination of LAI thresholds After choosing the drought condition in year 2020 as the baseline, suitable LAI thresholds were subsequently determined to classify drought-covered area, drought-damaged area and crop failure area. Presently, there are two types of thresholds broadly utilized for agricultural drought classification: the absolute thresholds, typically assuming a uniform absolute threshold for the entire study area (Zhang, 2013 ), and the relative thresholds, to describe the relative degree of agricultural drought severity at specific location. However, assumption of a constant absolute LAI threshold in regional-scale analysis certainly ignores the spatial variability in the crop characteristics, owing to the inherent spatial heterogeneity of environmental factors. In contrast, it is more reasonable to evaluate the agricultural drought degrees upon relative thresholds by estimating the percentage of actual agricultural drought condition with respect to its own baseline magnitude, and further classifying the percentages to represent different agricultural drought degrees at specific location (Ma, 2020; Xu et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the dynamic type of LAI relative threshoding as discussed before was used in this study to extract the agricultural drought areas corresponding to different drought degrees in the NCP. Considering the drought-covered area as example, the specific steps for determing the LAI relative thresholds are detailed below:(1) Determine the boundaries of summer-harvest crop area and autumn-harvest crop area in the NCP, at a spatial resolution of 500 m ×500 m;  (2) Choose a precise phenological period of summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops, and calculate the average LAI during this phenological period of each year to generate the LAIs  and LAIa  time series, respectively for each grid location. The average LAI values in 2020 (LAIs2020 , LAIa2020 ) are calculated and taken as the baseline at each grid, respectively;  (3) Set the relative threshold T s    of summer-harvest crops as 1 %;  (4) Extract the grids with their LAIs  ≤ ( T  s   ×  L A I  s 2020   )     in each year, and take their sum to obtain the total area of the extracted grids, achieving yearly time series of the drought-covered area for summer-harvest crops (A s  )    ;  (5) Similarly, fix the relative threshold T a    of autumn-harvest crops as 1 %;  (6) Extract those grids with their LAIa  ≤ ( T a    ×  L A I  a 2020   )     in each year, and estimate the sum in each year to obtain the total area of the extracted grids, generating the yearly time series of the drought-covered area for autumn-harvest crops (A a  )    ;  (7) Denoting the historical drought-covered area as HA, obtain the estimated drought-covered area E A = A s  + A a  + H A  2020      (8) Subsequently, evaluate the consistency between HA and EA using R  and RMSE goodness-of-fit indices (Willmott and Matsuura, 2005; Entekhabi et al., 2010 ):   (1) R = ∑ ( E A - ∑ E A  n  )  ( H A - ∑ H A  n  )   ∑ E A - ∑ E A  n    2   ∑ ( H A - ∑ H A  n  )  2          (2) R M S E = 1 n  ∑ ( E A - H A )  2         where R  is the correlation coefficient and RMSE is the root-mean-square error, and n  represents the number of study years. A higher positive R  value and a lower RMSE value indicate a better consistency between the HA and EA, implying better predictive performance for the estimated drought-covered area;(9) Keep the threshold value T s    of summer-harvest crops constant, increase T a    from 1 % to 100 %, with an interval of 1 %, and iteratively repeat steps (6)-(8) to obtain all R  and RMSE results corresponding to Ts =1 %;  (10) Further, increase T s    from 1 % to 100 %, with an increment of 1 %, and repeat the steps (4)-(9) to obtain the R  and RMSE estimates corresponding to all 10000 combinations of T s    and T a    during the concerned phenological period;  (11) For other phenological periods (see Table S1 ), repeat the steps (2)-(10) to calculate all R  and RMSE values for all periods;  (12) Make a comprehensive comparison of R  and RMSE to find the best result, and the corresponding relative thresholds are determined as the most suitable thresholds of Ts * and Ta *, for extracting the drought-covered area of summer-harvest crops and autumn-harvest crops, respectively.    The above steps for determining LAI relative thresholds are also illustrated precisely in Fig. 2  . Besides, the LAI relative thresholds for extracting drought-damaged area and crop failure area can also be determined by using the above-described methodology.  3.3 Extraction of agricultural drought areas After proposing the methodology for determination of LAI relative thresholds in Fig. 2 , the applicability and robustness of the proposed approach are needed to be verified cross both spatial and temporal domain for the further agricultural drought areas extraction. The spatiotemporal verification of the proposed methodology is shown in Fig. 3  . To be specific, considering that the Shandong Province is the only province entirely located in the NCP (Fig. 1 ), the LAI data and historical agricultural drought areas dataset in Shandong Province for the period 2006-2013 (treated as the simulation period) were used to determine the LAI relative thresholds; and subsequently, the period 2014-2019 was treated as the validation period to check the relative agreement between the simulated and actual agricultural drought areas to verify the temporal applicability of the LAI relative thresholds. Furthermore, the determined LAI relative thresholds for the Shandong Province were adopted to handle the drought data for the period 2006-2019 in the Hebei Province, for validating the methodology performance at spatial domain. Lastly, considering the consistency in the meteorological condition, crop phenological calendar as well as crop growing dynamics in the NCP (Luo et al., 2020; Li and Lei, 2021 ), the determined LAI relative thresholds were used to extract the agricultural drought areas with three different degrees across the whole NCP. In addition, the historical drought records procured from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China were evaluated with respect to the newly generated drought areas dataset for justifying the robustness and reliability of the proposed approach across varying spatiotemporal domains.   4 Results 4.1 Determination of LAI thresholds in Shandong Province The evaluation of accuracy for the estimated agricultural drought areas pertaining to both summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops across diverse phenological periods within the NCP is shown in Fig. S1 . As envisaged from Fig. S1 , the agricultural drought areas estimated from the heading period exhibit relatively higher accuracy (with average R  above 0.46) than those from the harvest period (with average R  of about 0.21). These outcomes are in line with the findings from past studies, which reported that LAI at the heading stage showed the strongest correlation with crop yield among all periods (Huang et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2017 ). Moreover, the results from the heading stage with 32 days (DOY113-145) of summer-harvest crops and 24 days (DOY 201-225) of autumn-harvest crops indicate the best performance. Therefore, the average MODIS LAI information during the heading period of summer-harvest crops (DOY113-145) and autumn-harvest crops (DOY201-225) for the period 2006 to 2019 was selected for determining the LAI relative thresholds and generating the 500 m agricultural drought areas dataset in this study. Building upon the methodology explained in Fig. 2 , different LAI relative thresholds were established to compute the extent of drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area for both summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops. The degree of variability in the predictive performance of the drought area assessment as quantified in terms of R  and RMSE goodness of fit indices is illustrated in Fig. S2 , and the determined most suitable thresholds are presented in Table 2  . After following the proposed iterative procedure, the LAI relative thresholds for identifying drought-covered area were estimated to be 56 % and 45 % for summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops, respectively, with the highest LAI threshold was observed for drought-covered area followed by the drought-damaged area and the crop failure area. The decrease in the LAI relative thresholds along with the aggregating severity of agricultural drought implies the justification for the obtained thresholds (Table 2 ) (Chaturvedi et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2017 ). Further, the agricultural drought areas of Shandong Province during the simulation period of 2006-2013 were extracted by using the above thresholds, which revealed a good match between the estimated and historical agricultural drought areas (R  ranges from 0.69 to 0.83 and RMSE ranges from 50.3 to 215.61 thousand ha), depicting that the estimated areas can effectively reflect temporal variations of actual agricultural drought areas (Fig. 4  ). The estimated drought-covered area can not only accurately capture the peaks of the historical drought-covered area magnitudes in the year 2006, 2009, and 2011, and but also mimic the troughs occurred during the year 2008, 2010, and 2013. Moreover, the estimated drought-damaged area and crop failure area also agree well with historical drought-damaged area and crop failure area, with correlation coefficient estimates of 0.72 and 0.69, respectively. Among the three degrees, the estimated drought-covered area with the highest correlation coefficient (R =0.83) and low RMSE (215.61 thousand ha), outperforms the areas corresponding the other two degrees of agricultural drought, thereby depicting the difficulty in extracting the agricultural drought areas with severer degrees in the Shandong Providence. To further quantify and validate the LAI relative thresholds, temporal verification was performed using the available data of Shandong Province in the verification period of 2014-2020. Consequently, the derived LAI thresholds as presented in Table 2  were used to extract the agricultural drought areas, and subsequent performance evaluation. The reproduction of historical agricultural drought extent by the proposed methodology is illustrated in Fig. 4 . The proposed approach captured the drought-covered area and drought-damaged area with acceptable R  estimates of 0.71 and 0.57, respectively. However, the RMSE (400.12 thousand ha) of drought-covered area is not good enough, which is mainly caused by the discrepancies of historical record and simulation result in 2015. Besides, the representation of the crop failure area in the Shandong Province during the verification period is not promising as depicted from R  estimate of 0.12. The poor performance in representing the crop failure area by the proposed approach could be attributed to the lack of understanding in the translation of drought effects on the crop physiology. Further, poor accuracy in the historical crop failure area of Shandong Province, which pose a big difference with the Hebei Province (Fig. 5  ), could be resulting the lower R  and higher RMSE estimates.  4.2 Extraction of agricultural drought areas To ascertain the validity of the proposed approach across varying spatial-scales, the LAI relative thresholds presented in Table 2  were used to estimate the agricultural drought areas in the Hebei Province during the period 2006-2019. As envisaged from Fig. 5 , the estimated drought-covered area time series very well reproduces the actual drought-covered area (R =0.70 and RMSE=316.53 thousand ha). Unlike the Shandong province, the approach performed excellent in simulating the drought-damaged area and crop failure area in the Hebei Province with correlation coefficient and RMSE estimates ranging between 0.74 to 0.83 and 62.26 to 212.37 thousand ha. Further, the improved performance in the Hebei Province points towards the inconsistency in the observed data of the Shandong Province region arising poor simulation performance. A close insight at the temporal behaviour of the three-drought extent revealed a decreasing tendency of agricultural drought areas in Hebei Province over the last two decades, which could be resulting due to improved water management practices. Overall, both temporal and spatial verifications of the proposed agricultural drought quantification approach demonstrate high reliability and applicability of the determined thresholds in regional-scale applications. Finally, the verified thresholds in Table 2  were used to extract the drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area in the NCP (except Beijing and Tianjin) region during the period 2006-2019 (Figs. 6 and 7   ). The temporal variations in the agricultural drought areas for summer-harvest crops, autumn-harvest crops, and annual-scale in the NCP are presented in Fig. 8  . There exists significant difference in the derived agricultural drought areas across the NCP at both inter- and intra-annual (i.e., summer-harvest crops and autumn-harvest crops) scales. The agricultural drought areas pertaining to the summer-harvest crops are mainly confined to the south-east part of Hebei Province and north-west part of the Shandong Province, with substantial inter-annual variation during the period 2006-2011. However, the inter-annual variability reduced gradually during the period 2012-2019 as compared to the former period, attributed to the adoption of more effective water management practices during the concerned period to ensure healthy growth of summer-harvest crops (typical irrigated agriculture practice followed in the NCP) (Wu et al., 2020a, 2022 ). According to the Bulletin of Water Resources (The Ministry of Water Resources of the People’s Republic of China, 2006, 2020 ), the average amount of water used for agricultural irrigation in Hebei and Shandong provinces decreased from 25.4 billion m3 /acre in 2006 to 17 billion m3 /acre in 2020, while the irrigation water use efficiency of crop land raised from 0.57 to 0.65 correspondingly. Practically, the reorganization of irrigation schedule, improvement of soil fertility, as well as application of water-saving irrigation technologies such as drip irrigation and micro-sprinkling irrigation, significantly improved the water use efficiency in the NCP (Li et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018 ; Bai et al., 2020 ; Sun et al., 2021 ). Conversely, the agricultural drought areas of autumn-harvest crops, treated as rainfed crops, are mostly concentrated in the southern region of the NCP, exhibiting significant interannual variations (Fig. 7 ). Unlike the summer-harvest crops, the autumn-harvest crops just exhibit a slight decreasing trend in the agricultural drought areas owing to the little following of any crop-specific water management practices for rain-fed crops (Fig. 8 b). As envisaged from Figs. 6-7 , the NCP suffered severe agricultural droughts in the periods 2006 and 2009, resulting both summer-harvest crops and autumn-harvest crops to be damaged badly. According to the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China (2006 ), spring period (March to April) droughts were more prevalent in the northern winter wheat region due to lack of adequate precipitation, rising temperature, and frequent windy weather conditions, affecting the summer-harvest crops badly. Similar impacts on summer-harvest crops in the northern NCP can also be observed in the estimated agricultural drought area in 2006 (Fig. 6 ). Further, summer droughts occurred and developed under the influence of continuous high temperature and limited precipitation during June and July, 2006, tended to impact the autumn-harvest crops adversely, signifying the extent of drought propagation across the NCP region (Fig. 7 ). The cumulative winter precipitation in the central and southern part of the Hebei Province in 2008 was approximately 80 % less than the average annual precipitation (The Ministry of Water Resources of the People’s Republic of China, 2009 ), which resulted in the large area affected by drought throughout Hebei Province in 2009 (depicting in Fig. 6 ). As demonstrated by the spatiotemporal consistency between the estimated and actual historical drought information for the years 2006 and 2009, the developed drought areas extraction approach can effectively generate synthetic long-term drought information in need. Overall, the newly generated agricultural drought areas dataset has a high consistence with the spatiotemporal patterns of actual agricultural drought conditions in the NCP during the last two decades, and it can also very well replicate both intra-annual and inter-annual agricultural drought characteristics, demonstrating its true potential for accurate drought monitoring, forecasting, and early warning in the concerned region.   5 Discussion 5.1 Main contributions of this study Agricultural drought stands as a dominant natural hazard in the NCP (Wu et al., 2021 ), showing increasing frequency and severity over recent decades (Yu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2016 ). However, limitations posed by the coarser spatiotemporal resolution of accessible agricultural drought data archives impede the application of regional-scale agricultural drought simulation and monitoring studies. In this study, we adopted LAI as the agricultural drought indicator, and subsequently devised a methodology cantered around LAI relative thresholds. This approach enables us to establish critical thresholds that signify various levels of agricultural drought severity across the NCP. This method underpins the generation of a 500 m spatial resolution agricultural drought areas dataset spanning the years 2006 to 2019 over the NCP. This dataset encompasses key parameters such as drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area for both summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crop seasons. By analysing the newly generated dataset, we gain valuable insights into the spatial distribution and interconnectedness of areas affected by agricultural drought. This, in turn, provides us with a deeper understanding of the inter-annual fluctuations within crop growing seasons. The presented dataset can serve as a reliable data source supporting the impact-based agricultural drought researches in the NCP. The developed approach paves the way for refined object-oriented studies, allowing for more accurate drought monitoring at a finer spatiotemporal resolution. Moreover, the relative threshold-based methodology proposed herein holds a unique advantage in characterizing the relative extent of agricultural drought at specific locations, quantifying the deviation from baseline conditions. This robustness sets it apart from existing absolute threshold-based methods, which often struggle to accommodate the spatial discrepancies in crop characteristics arising from region-specific environmental condition. The implications of this study are broad-reaching, advocating for the widespread adoption of the relative threshold-based approach in global contexts. It offers an efficient means to identify and extract high-resolution agricultural drought areas information, thereby fostering a more universally applicable solution.  5.2 Assessment of inherent predictive uncertainties The uncertainties associated with this study primarily revolve around the utilized input data sources and the adopted methodology, which are expounded upon below. Input data uncertainties stem from both historical agricultural drought data and crop growth data specific to the relevant region. The historical agricultural drought areas data, drawn from the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China, effectively captures temporal fluctuations in agricultural drought. However, discrepancies present in the field-scale drought monitoring process could accumulate as the transition into a broader spatiotemporal context, such as the county-province-country drought-reporting system (Blauhut et al., 2015 ). As an illustration, the historical drought areas attributed to Shandong Province in 2015 tend to be overestimated in the historical records. This disparity raises concerns, particularly when examining the extracted LAI and NDVI values for both summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops during the heading period of 2015. These values bear similarity to those observed in 2014—a year of relatively moderate drought—yet they greatly exceed values from 2006—a year characterized by more severe drought conditions (Fig. S3-S4 ). This discrepancy challenges the credibility of the severe drought situation reported for 2015 in the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disasters in China. Moreover, other studies such as those conducted by Wan et al., 2022  and Wu et al., 2020a  do not classify 2015 as a year of severe drought, further underscoring the uncertainties inherent in the input data. While modest degrees of uncertainty are evident in some analysis years due to the adopted input data, the substantial spatial coherence observed between the estimated and historical agricultural drought areas over the entire analysis period from 2006 to 2020 validates the reliability of the study's outcomes. Given the absence of refined data pertaining to actual crop types, this study categorizes crops into summer-harvest and autumn-harvest varieties. With context of the predominance of single cropping systems and a consistent heading period within the NCP, any potential influence on the generated dataset is expected to be limited. Furthermore, the spatial agreement between the results presented in Figs. 6-7  and the records in the Bulletin of Flood and Drought Disaster underscores the applicability of the resulting agricultural drought areas dataset. While the land use/land cover (LULC) datasets with spatial resolutions of 10 m and 30 m are readily accessible, a thorough comparison of the total cropland areas covered by these publicly available datasets against the actual crop planting area statistics from the Shandong Statistical Yearbook (Shandong Provincial Bureau of Statistics, 2020 ) brings to light a pertinent finding. This analysis underscores that the 1 km LULC data adopted within this study exhibits a higher degree of consistency with the genuine statistics (Table S2 ). As a result of this observation, the 1 km-resolution data relating to the area of autumn-harvest crops was deliberately chosen, reinforcing the reliability and accuracy of the conclusions drawn from this study. Methodological uncertainties predominantly revolve around the choice of the drought indicator employed within the study. Specifically, LAI was chosen as the agricultural drought indicator. Given the practical imperative of agricultural prevention and mitigation, this study emphasizes the ultimate adverse effects of drought on agriculture, discernible through the total area experiencing varying degrees of crop yield reduction. This focus diverges from a comprehensive examination of the intricate physical processes associated with agricultural drought. While a myriad of comprehensive agricultural drought indicators encompassing hydrological variables, meteorological components, and vegetation attributes are commonplace in practical applications, vegetation drought indices were considered as the most direct driver for gauging actual crop growth conditions and, consequently, yield outcomes (Becker-Reshef et al., 2010; Bolton and Friedl, 2013 ). Among those vegetation indices, LAI stands out as a better vegetation index that is more sensitive to changes in crop yield (Zhou et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2024 ). Hence, this study utilized LAI as the proxy for agricultural drought, and subsequently, identified the agricultural drought areas based on this information over the NCP.   6 Conclusions Agricultural drought has inflicted significant crop production losses in the recent decades, and the frequency and severity of these events are projected to escalate in the foreseeable future. Nonetheless, the lack of reliable historical agricultural drought information at finer spatiotemporal resolution poses a challenge to formulating effective strategies for drought prevention and mitigation, particularly concerning impact-based drought monitoring and early warning systems. To address this key issue, this study introduced a LAI relative threshold-based approach. It established key thresholds to quantify different degrees of drought impact on both summer-harvest and autumn-harvest crops. Ultimately, this approach yielded a 500 m-resolution agricultural drought areas dataset for the entire NCP region, encompassing three distinct degrees of drought impact: drought-covered, drought-damaged, and crop failure areas. Notably, the determined LAI relative thresholds for drought-covered area, drought-damaged area, and crop failure area were found to be 56 %, 51 %, 34 % for summer-harvest crops and 45 %, 41 %, 28 % for autumn-harvest crops within the NCP, respectively. The accuracy assessment of the approach within the Hebei province demonstrated the dataset's reliability and applicability in representing drought-covered area (R=0.70 and RMSE=316.53 thousand ha), drought-damaged area (R=0.74 and RMSE=212.37 thousand ha) and crop failure area (R=0.83 and RMSE=62.26 thousand ha). Nevertheless, due to discrepancies in the historical drought datasets of Shandong Province, the predictive performance for crop failure representation exhibited limitations. In conclusion, the LAI-based relative thresholds method effectively serves as a methodological foundation for identifying drought-affected regions and gauging crop damage areas, thus fostering impact-based drought assessment, sustainable agriculture management, and food security promotion. Further validation and evaluation under varying topographic and climatic conditions are essential to establish its robustness for global applications. Upcoming research endeavours will continuously refine the spatiotemporal resolution of the generated data in relation to input data quality, comprehensive drought indicators, spatial variation of relative thresholds, and the underlying drought characteristics accordingly. This will offer a more detailed understanding of the potential applicability and transferability to other regions around the world. Data Availability Statement. The generated 500 m-resolution agricultural drought areas dataset is publicly available via https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8207700 (Shi et al., 2023 ).
1 Introduction Floods can cause casualties and loss of assets in the Canadian prairies (Pomeroy et al., 2016; Shook, 2015 ). Accurate estimation of flood quantiles is essential to mitigate flood damages by efficiently designing infrastructure and flood protection works. Flood frequency analysis (FFA) is the typical way to assess the risk of floods (Zaghloul et al., 2020b  and references therein). However, FFA encounters high levels of uncertainty at sites with limited historical records and is inapplicable at ungauged sites (Durocher et al., 2018 ). Regional FFA is known to enhance the accuracy of quantile estimation by using regional information from hydrologically similar sites, i.e., a pool of sites (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ). The hydrologic similarity among pooled sites is critical for accurate regional FFA (Lettenmaier et al., 1987; Requena et al., 2017 ). Castellarin et al., (2001)  illustrated the role of hydrologic similarity on the accuracy of regional quantiles. In past studies, different site-similarity measures, such as basin area, mean precipitation, flood seasonality, and flood regularity have been applied (Burn, 1997; Drissia et al., 2019; Zadeh & Burn, 2019 ). The validity of these measures to describe the hydrologic similarity could be questionable in some regions, even if combinations of these measures are hierarchically applied as suggested by Zadeh & Burn (2019) . An example of such a region is the Canadian prairies, where flat terrain and numerous land depressions exist (Shook et al., 2021; Shook & Pomeroy, 2011 ). The Canadian prairies extend across the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba and are considered semi-arid (Gray and Landine, 1988 ). The prairie hydrologic processes vary seasonally with rainfall, evapotranspiration, infiltration, and percolation to groundwater in Summer; and snowfall, snow sublimation, blown snow, snowmelt, and little infiltration into frozen soil in Winter (Dingman, 2015 ; Jw Pomeroy et al., 2005a ). This region is characterized by numerous land depressions, among other features, that cause a fill-and-spill process (Shaw et al., 2012 ), which affects the hydrologic generation of streamflow (Shook et al., 2021; Shook & Pomeroy, 2011 ). The average temperature ranges between - 15    and 30    degrees Celsius and occasionally drops below - 40    or exceeds 40    degrees Celsius, resulting in extreme wet or extreme dry events (Bonsal et al., 2013; Mahmood et al., 2017 ). The precipitation highly correlates to whether a flood or a drought occurs in the Canadian Prairies. The precipitation typically ranges between 300–400 mm per year (Pomeroy et al., 2005b ) with about one-third of this precipitation falling in winter as snow (Akinremi et al., 1998; Gray and Landine, 1988 ). The wind redistributes snow from exposed to sheltered areas and snow encounters sublimation that reduces the amounts of winter snowpack (Buttle et al., 2016; Pomeroy et al., 1993; Pomeroy & Gray, 1995 ). Considerable overland flows start in Spring when the snow melts over frozen soil. This spring thawing accounts for approximately 80 % of annual runoff (Gray et al., 1985; Gray and Landine, 1988 ) while the remaining proportion occurs in Summer and Fall. These cold region aspects coexist with the prairies’ land depressions, which result in high hydrologic complexity (Ahmed et al., 2020 ).
