Although the prairies’ land depressions significantly affect streamflow characteristics in prairie regions, none of the past site similarity measures consider it for regional FFA (D.H. Burn, 1997; Castellarin et al., 2001; Cunderlik & Burn, 2002; Papacharalampous et al., 2021; Stein et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2018 ). Therefore, there is a gap in evaluating site hydrologic similarity for pooling similar sites in prairie regions. Using the traditional site similarity measures without a proper representation of hydrologic similarity could mislead the pooling of sites and deteriorate the estimation accuracy of regional FFA (Lettenmaier et al., 1987 ). So, it is necessary to develop a new site similarity measure that considers similarity in depressional storage for accurate regional FFA. The concept of integrating hydrologic simulations with statistical inference was previously adopted (Salazar-Galán et al., 2021 ) using the TETIS hydrologic model (Francés et al., 2007 ). Salazar-Galán et al. (2021)  used a tri-variate probability distribution to describe the maximum streamflow, rainfall, and simulated soil moisture conditions generated from the TETIS model to support at-site flood frequency analysis. The present paper further explores the integration of hydrologic modeling with statistical analysis for regional FFA. Here, a new site similarity measure is introduced to account for a salient hydrologic factor in prairie regions. For a group of sites, a basin for each site is identified and the HYdrological model for Prairie Region (HYPR) (Ahmed et al., 2020 ) is employed. HYPR is a modified version of the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Seibert, 2005 ) that represents the states of depressional storage when land depressions exist, which makes it an optimum choice for prairie lands. The prairies exhibit an undulating topography characterized by flat slopes, interspersed with thousands of potholes and wetlands. Within this landscape, runoff is trapped in non-contributing areas, resulting in only a portion of the basin actively contributing to streamflow at the outlets. These basins undergo a hydrological transformation, where the nature of runoff differs from the streamflow. This transformation is driven by a fill-and-spill mechanism, causing the contributing area to dynamically expand and contract based on various factors, such as storm intensity and antecedent basin conditions. Despite being a lumped model, HYPR adeptly captures the overall daily scale of the contributing area in a non-spatially distributed manner (Ahmed et al., 2020 ). Accordingly, HYPR simulations are employed to describe the state of contributing areas. The average daily percentage of contributing areas at the time of annual maximum simulated streamflow is used to estimate a novel site similarity measure for pooling similar sites in regional FFA. Hereafter, the new site similarity measure will be referred to as Mean Fractional Contributing Areas ( M F C A )   . The M F C A    is used along with other site similarity measures for pooling groups of similar sites, and the index flood method (Hosking & Wallis, 1993; 1997 ) is applied to regionally quantify flood quantities using several probability distributions. This paper reveals the essential need to consider the state of land depressions for pooling hydrologically similar sites and conducting accurate regional FFA in prairie regions.  2 Methodology A new measure is introduced to account for contributing areas in representing hydrologic similarity for regional FFA. This measure was evaluated by pooling 109 sites in the Canadian prairies that are characterized by high levels of hydrologic heterogeneity. A drainage basin of each site was identified and simulated using the HYPR model (Section 2.2 ). The HYPR model estimated the dynamic contributing areas that are utilized to define the novel site similarity measure, M F C A   . Fig. 1   illustrates the proposed integration of the HYPR simulations into regional FFA. The M F C A    was illustrated and combined with different traditional site similarity measures in Section 2.3 . The combined site similarity measures were used to form groups of similar sites in Section 2.4 . These combinations were referred to as scenarios and were designed for comparative purposes to illustrate the advantage of considering the M F C A   . For each scenario, groups’ homogeneities were evaluated and regional quantiles were obtained using the index flood method (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ) and assessed using several error measures. 2.1 Study area and data The Canadian prairie region, about 1.78 million square kilometers in area, is the study area selected for testing the effectiveness of the proposed M F C A    for regional FFA. The meteorological data used in this investigation considered daily records of total precipitation and average temperature from the Daymet database (Thornton et al., 2017 ). The Daymet database provides these data from 1980 to 2018 with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km. Additionally, the daily average streamflow from 1909 to 2020 from the hydrometric database of Environment and Climate Change Canada was also considered (ECCC; version 1.0, http://collaboration.cmc.ec.gc.ca/cmc/hydrometrics/ ). The quality of the hydrometric data underwent meticulous scrutiny through visual inspection, encompassing records from unregulated sites devoid of hydraulic structures. Records with suspicious trends or abrupt changes were identified and excluded. After screening, 109 gauged sites across the Canadian prairies were considered, with record lengths ranging from 30 to 99 years. The drainage basins associated with the 109 selected sites (as outlets) were provided by the Water Survey of Canada (WSC; https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset ; Fig. 2  ). Their gross drainage areas were obtained from Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada at https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/063ee9b6-b3f2-45ab-9bed-d330880064d5 . The gridded meteorological data were transferred to the basin scale as a grid average from the grid cells spatially intersecting each basin.  2.2 Hydrological model for prairie region The HYdrological model for Prairie Region (HYPR) is a modified version of HBV that accounts for land depressions. Ahmed et al. (2020)  provided a schematic representation of HYPR demonstrating how it incorporates the storage and evaporation from land depressions using the Probability Distribution Model-based RunOFf generation (PDMROF) algorithm (Mekonnen et al., 2014 ). This study used HYPR to simulate the streamflow at the 109 prairie basins presented in Fig. 2 . The simulation was conducted on a daily timestep, and the time window of the simulation depended on the availability of hydrometric and meteorological data for each basin. The simulation periods across the different basins range from 31 years to 38 years in the period between 1980 and 2018. The first two years in any simulation period were set for spinning up the HYPR model to eliminate inaccuracy in initial conditions. This period for spinning up the HYPR model was tested and found suitable for basins that are similar to those under investigation (Ahmed et al., 2020 ). The simulation period after spinning the model was divided into two equal periods for calibration and validation, where the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) metric (Nash & Sutcliffe, 1970 ) was used as the objective function for model calibration. The inputs to HYPR are minimal, that is, the model requires daily records of precipitation and temperature besides simple physiographic information, such as basins’ gross area and latitude. These inputs were discussed in 2.1. The model simulates daily streamflow and provides information on its associated state variables, such as the daily percentage of contributing areas. Although the HYPR model is a lumped one, it has the potential to simulate internal hydrologic processes (Ahmed et al., 2020 ). It uses basin-average forcings, and thus, only its spatially lumped fractional contributing area across the basin are considered.  2.3 Similarity measures A basin’s gross drainage area, mean annual precipitation, flood seasonality, flood regularity, and the proposed M F C A    are the site similarity measures used in this study to represent the hydrological similarity among sites. This section demonstrates each similarity measure and identifies scenarios of using different combinations of them for regional FFA. 2.3.1 Basin area The basin’s drainage area is one of the oldest site similarity measures (Cunnane, 1988; O’Connell, 1868 ). Markedly, Burn et al. (1997)  stated clearly that physiographic measures, such as the drainage area might not suffice to represent the hydrologic response, especially in regions with complex hydrologic nature. So, it is necessary to consider the basin area in combination with other similarity measures to supplement the hydrologic representation of basins. For example, Ahn & Palmer (2016)  associated the drainage areas of 30 basins northeast of the United States and precipitation patterns with their mean annual floods and found the basin area as one of the most effective explanatory variables. Also, Chebana et al. (2014)  associated the drainage areas and meteorological variables with the floods of 151 basins South of Quebec and found the basin areas adequate to represent the scale of basins. Similarly, this study investigates the gross drainage area in combination with different similarity measures.  2.3.2 Mean precipitation Due to the close interrelation of precipitation and streamflow (Shook et al., 2015 ), the Mean Daily non-zero Precipitation of each year ( A M P )   , where A M P = ∑ P   / n i    , was used in literature where P   represents the daily non-zero precipitation and n i    is the number of days with non-zero precipitation in each year i  . The mean value of AMP (M A M P )    from a set of y   years with observations was considered as a site similarity measure for regional FFA (Zadeh & Burn, 2019 ). This similarity measure was also considered in this study and was estimated for each basin as(1) M A M P = ∑ i = 1  y  A M P  y      For example, a hypothetical basin with 3 years of observations, such that year-1 had 400 mm in 100 rainy days, year-2 had 440 mm in 110 rainy days, and year-3 had 320 mm in 80 rainy days, would have MAMP equal to 4 mm.  2.3.3 Flood seasonality and regularity Sites that share similarities in the timing and regularity of their floods could be considered potential candidates belonging to a common pooling group (Ouarda et al., 2006 ). The timing and regularity of floods were described using directional statistics following Burn (1997), Formetta et al. (2018) , and Zadeh & Burn (2019) . Flood seasonality and regularity were associated with flood dates to represent the mean date of floods and how often they occur around this date, respectively. The flood seasonality was estimated as the mean Julian date (M D   ) of annual peak flow, and the regularity (r  ¯    ) answers the question of how often these events occur around the M D   . The M D    was estimated in Julian dates and the r  ¯     ranges between 1 (high regularity) and 0 (low regularity), such that(2) M D  i  = 1 n  ∑ j = 1  n  d j  ,     (3) r  ¯   i  = 1 n  ∑ j = 1  n  cos θ j     2  + 1 n  ∑ j = 1  n  sin θ j     2    ,     (4) θ j  = d j    2 π  365      where M D  i    and r  ¯   i    are estimated for each basin i  ; d j    is the Julian date of an annual peak flow in year j  ; and θ j    is the angular conversion of d j   .  2.3.4 Mean fractional contributing area The M F C A   , introduced here, is a single numerical value estimated for each basin and represents the level at which land depressions affect the contributing and non-contributing areas at the time of simulated peak flows. By definition, land depressions cause a hysteretic effect on streamflow generation by holding substantial quantities of surface runoff (Shaw et al., 2012 ) and causing a fill-and-spill mechanism that leads to disconnected surface water that does not feed into the streamflow during periods of low snowmelt or rainfall (Hayashi et al., 2003 ). This hysteretic effect could mislead some of the traditional site similarity measures that rely on the gross drainage area, the quantity of precipitation, and the timing of peak streamflow events. This highlights the importance of the proposed MFCA similarity measure in accounting for the similarity in land depressions, which is responsible for such a hysteretic effect. Daily contributing areas are determined by the PDMROF algorithm (Mekonnen et al., 2014 ) that runs within the HYPR simulation to represent dynamic (one value per day) contributing areas as a percentage of the basin. These daily contributing areas are called the daily Fractional Contributing Areas (FCA). The MFCA is typically the mean percentage of these FCA that are observed on the days of annual maximum flows. The value of the MFCA could range from 0 (hypothetically, a basin full of land depressions with no contribution to streamflow) to 1 (fully contributing drainage area). The FCA at the times of annual maximum streamflows are averaged to estimate the M F C A   , such that(5) M F C A = 1 n  ∑ y = 1  n  F C A y  ,     where F C A y     is the fractional contributing area obtained from the HYPR simulation at the time of the annual maximum streamflow of year y  , and n   is the number of the simulated years minus the spin-up period.  2.3.5 Combinations of site similarity measures The basin area, mean precipitation, flood seasonality, flood regularity, and the mean fractional contributing area were considered as site similarity measures here. In addition to the MFCA similarity measure, the remaining metrics have been extensively documented in the literature. They are well-established and are known for their relevance to the hydrological processes that impact both the frequency and magnitude of floods (Salinas et al., 2014a,b , and references therein). For example, Zadeh & Burn (2019)  considered the mean annual precipitation, basin area, flood seasonality, and flood regularity using a super-region approach. This approach is a hierarchical application of similarity measures such that the similarity is defined in a multi-step clustering approach. Similarly, Durocher et al. (2018)  considered the Mahalanobis distance between basin descriptors (Cunderlik & Burn, 2006 ), mean annual precipitation, and the basin area using the Region of Influence approach. The five similarity measures of this analysis were evaluated separately and in combination. The number of combinations without repetition of n   objects placed in a set of size r   is estimated as C n  r  = n ! / r ! n - r   !   . So, the number of all possible combinations that can be generated by 5 similarity measures is C 5  1  + C 5  2  + C 5  3  + C 5  4  + C 5  5  = 31    combinations. The combinations were related to scenarios as characterized in Table 1   with reference letters referring to similarity measures. The letter “A” refers to the drainage area (Section 2.3.1), “B” refers to the MAMP (Section 2.3.2), “C” refers to the mean flood date (Section 2.3.3), “D” refers to the flood regularity (Section 2.3.3), and “E” refers to the MFCA (Section 2.3.4).   2.4 Grouping similar sites The process of grouping sites with hydrologic similarity, known as pooling, is an essential step for regional FFA (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ). Among several clustering algorithms that could pool similar sites, the Ward clustering algorithm (Ward, 1963 ) was adopted as recommended by Hosking & Wallis (1997)  to cluster the 109 sites. The clustering of sites could result in groups that are not perfectly homogeneous. Therefore, a measure of discordancy for each site was estimated and used to guarantee that sites are removed from their group if their L-moments are distinctly different from the group’s average L-moments. This procedure is detailed by Hosking & Wallis, (1997) . The number of clustered groups was based on two criteria. The first one is maintaining a minimum of 500 records within each group as recommended by Kjeldsen et al. (2008) . On average, there were 52 annual maximum flow records per site among the investigated 109 sites. With a rough calculation, a maximum of 10 groups should be allowed to maintain the first criterion. The second criterion is optimizing the groups’ hydrological homogeneity (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ). The hydrological homogeneity among each of the clustered groups was evaluated using the heterogeneity measure (H  ) proposed by Hosking & Wallis, (1997) , where lower values of H   indicate better homogeneous regions. The heterogeneity measure assesses the standardized value of the dispersion ( V )    of observations within a group using Monte Carlo simulations. The Monte Carlo simulations are designed to create 1000 theoretical replicants of the group and estimate the dispersion value for each trial. The mean and standard deviations of the 1000 dispersion values are μ V    and σ V    respectively (Equation (6) ). The three heterogeneity metrics of Hosking & Wallis, (1997) , H 1  , H 2  ,  a n d  H 3   , are adopted in this study and estimated in the same way as illustrated in Equation (6) . These three heterogeneity metrics are obtained using three distinct measures of dispersions that are V 1  , V 2  ,  a n d  V 3    (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ); Equations (7) , (8), and (9). This assessment only uses the observed annual maximum flows. All other variables such as the basin area and MFCA are not used in assessing the H metric because they were used in pooling the sites. Step 1 scales the observed annual maximum flow values of each site within the group. The scaling factor of each site is the mean value of its annual maximum flows. Step 2 measures the dispersion of observations, V 1   , using Equation (7) . This obtains the V   value in Equation (6) . Step 3 determines the argument inside Equation (7)  which is related to the L-moment ratios of the observed annual maximum flows. Step 4 obtains the remaining μ V    and σ V    of Equation (6)  to get H 1   . These two values are obtained using Monte Carlo simulations. Step 5 represents the Monte Carlo simulations where 1000 theoretical groups are created having similar characteristics as the group of interest, in terms of the number of sites within the group and the size of the sample of each site. Step 6 obtains 1000 V 1    values from the 1000 theoretical groups using the same steps as indicated in step 2 and step 3. Step 7 estimates the remaining μ V    and σ V    of Equation (6)  as the mean and standard deviation of the 1000 V 1    values that were obtained from the Monte Carlo simulations. By that, all the components of Equation (6)  are available to obtain the H 1    measure. Note that H 2    and H 3    are estimated in the same way as H 1    with the only difference of using V 2    and V 3    instead of V 1   .  2.5 At-site and regional quantile estimation Several distributions were used for describing at-site and regional annual maximum flow records. These distributions are characterized and commonly used in literature (Burr, 1942; Papalexiou, 2018; Papalexiou & Koutsoyiannis, 2016 ; Salinas et al., 2014a ; Villarini et al., 2011 ; Zaghloul et al., 2020b ). The selected candidates were the Burr Type-III (BrIII), the Burr Type-XII (BrXII), the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV), the Log-Normal Type-III (LN3), the Pearson Type-III (Pe3), and the Generalized Pareto (GPa) distributions. The fitting was conducted by minimizing the sum of squared errors such that the objective function is(13) θ = arg min  θ  log 10  ∑ i = 1  n  Q i  θ   - Q ^  i     2          where Q ^  i    is the observed quantile value of rank i   in an ordered sample of size n  ; Q i  θ      is the theoretical quantile function of the fitted distribution, see LMoFit functions (Zaghloul et al., 2020a ), and θ   is a vector of distribution parameters that were estimated using the “L-BFGS-B” minimization algorithm (Byrdt et al., 1995 ). The log function was added to the objective function to enhance the performance of the minimization algorithm. For at-site analysis, the probability distributions were fitted to the observed annual maximum flow values. However, for regional analysis, these distributions were fitted to the regionally blended sample using the index-flood method (IFM) (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ). The IFM assumes that all annual maximum flow values observed within a group of pooled sites are identically distributed apart from a scaling factor μ  . If site i   belongs to a group of N   sites. Then the quantile function of site i   is Q i  u     , 0 < u < 1   . This function was related to a regional dimensionless quantile function q u      called the “regional growth curve” such that(14) Q i  u   = μ i   q u       where μ i    is the scaling factor of site i   and is estimated as the mean value (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ) of the annual maximum flow of site i  . Therefore, the above-mentioned probability distributions were fitted to describe the regional growth curve, i.e., the dimensionless observations collected from the N   sites and scaled to represent the quantile function of each member site.  2.6 Evaluation of fitting Four error measures were used to compare the performance of fitting theoretical distributions to the annual maximum flow. These measures were the root mean square error (RMSE) applied to non-exceedance probabilities, and three other measures applied to quantiles (Papalexiou & Koutsoyiannis, 2016 ; Zaghloul et al., 2020b ), that is,(15) R M S E = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  u i  - u ^  i     2    ,     (16) E R  1  = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  Δ x  i  ,     (17) E R  2  = 1 m  ∑ i = n - m + 1  n  Δ x  i  ,     (18) E R  3  = m a x Δ x  1  , ⋯ , Δ x  n    ,     where i   represents the rank of records in an ascendingly ordered sample x ^  1  , ⋯ , x ^  n      with respective empirical non-exceedance probabilities u ^  1  , ⋯ , u ^  n     , estimated using the Weibull formula such that u ^  i  = i / n + 1     . Theoretically, the fitted distribution function obtained a theoretical non-exceedance probability u i    that corresponds to each x ^  i    to be used in Eq. (15) . The prior was applied to probabilities while the latter is less sensitive to outliers and was applied to flow quantities; E R  2    offers an insight on fitting the highest m   values (set to m = 10   ); and, E R  3    identifies the greatest absolute quantile error between predictions and observations.   3 Results and discussions 3.1 HYPR simulation Incorporating statistical inference with hydrologic simulations was implemented for regional FFA using the HYPR model. The results show that the performance of the HYPR model varies across the prairie basins. The NSE metric has a mean value of 0.48 and is normally distributed between 0.11 and 0.82 (Fig. 3  a). Spatially, Fig. 3 b shows that the model performance varies across the Canadian prairies, Burn & Whitfield (2018)  characterized the flow at a few prairie sites as nival, and a broader investigation revealed that annual maximum flows occur in the window of March to August in the Canadian prairies (Zaghloul et al., 2020b ). The wide window reflects the possibility of flows being nival, mixed, and pluvial, which illustrates the challenge of HYPR to simulate the hydrologic diversity that could occur within a basin. So, it is normal to observe the current variation in the model performance with low NSE at a few basins across the prairies. The poor performance is acknowledged at 14 % of the basins with N S E ≤ 0.3   . Yet, the overall performance of the model across the prairie basins is reasonable, considering the complexity of the Canadian prairies (Ahmed et al., 2020; Shaw et al., 2012; Shook et al., 2021 ). Like traditional site-similarity measures (Do et al., 2020 ), the effectiveness of the new site-similarity measure that relies on HYPR to capture hydrologic similarity could vary across different basins. However, the use of multiple site-similarity measures solves this issue. If one measure fails to fully capture the hydrologic similarity, the joint site-similarity measures could continue functioning to represent other hydrologic aspects (Zadeh & Burn, 2019 ) and capture the similarity. The results in the next sections demonstrate the advantages of incorporating HYPR simulations for regional FFA, even if some basins encounter a poor performance of the HYPR simulations.  3.2 Fractional contributing areas The relation between FCA and streamflow is presented to justify the association of FCA with streamflow. Two basins, 05AB005 Trout Creek Near Granum in Alberta, and 05AC030 Snake Creek Near Vulcan in Alberta, Fig. 4  , are used as examples to support the use of FCA as a measure for assessing the hydrologic similarity between sites for regional FFA. The two examples were chosen carefully to have a different presence of land depressions. One basin, 05AC030, has a flat topography with lots of land depressions depicting its poor connectivity and drainage (Fig. 4 ). On the contrary, the other basin, 05AB005, has steeper slopes which depicts better drainage and connectivity. This is meant to differentiate between the two cases and show the discrepancies in their hydrologic characteristics, described by the FCA. Basin 05AB005 is located about 120 km south of Calgary with its upstream portion in the Rocky Mountains with considerable slopes, while its downstream portion is in the prairies having mild slopes. The gross drainage area of 05AB005 is 441 km2  and the basin exhibits daily FCA values up to 0.85. Typically, the FCA values of this basin range from 0.08 to 0.85 (Fig. 5  ). There is a strong correlation, equal to 0.9, between the values of annual maximum flows and the FCA values of their corresponding days. The minimum FCA value is simultaneous with the minimum observed annual maximum flow on June 16, 2001, and the maximum FCA value is simultaneous with the maximum observed annual maximum flow on June 18, 2010 (Fig. 5 ). This justifies the high correlation as increasing the percentage of contributing areas typically means that a greater proportion of the basin is actively contributing to generate flow, which increases the flow magnitude and vice versa. The high correlation between the values of annual maximum flows and their corresponding FCA values affirms the descriptive ability of FCA in assessing the hydrologic similarity of flows in terms of the level of connectivity within basin 05AB005. A well-drained basin such as basin 05AB005 with few land depressions would encounter high values of FCA. On the contrary, a poorly drained basin such as 05AC030 with plenty of land depressions would have limited values for its FCA. Basin 05AC030 exemplifies the case when land depressions prevail. This basin is located about 100 km southeast of Calgary entirely in the prairies with mild slopes. The gross drainage area of 05AC030 is 350 km2  and the basin exhibits FCA values up to 0.21. The FCA values of this basin range from 0.02 to 0.21, Fig. 5 , which are lower than the values obtained for 05AB005. This affirms that the connectivity of 05AC030 is poor in comparison with that of 05AB005, which is physically related to the milder topography and presence of more land depressions in 05AC030. Similarly, a strong correlation, equal to 0.95, between the values of annual maximum flows and their corresponding FCA values confirms the strong relationship between the FCA and the flow of 05AC030. The minimum FCA value was found simultaneous with that of the annual maximum flow on February 20, 2004, and similarly for the maximum values of FCA and the maximum observed annual maximum flow on March 23, 1997. This high correlation affirms the ability of the FCA to describe the flow at 05AC030. Yet, the low values of the FCA represent the poor drainage ability of basin 05AC030 due to the presence of numerous land depressions impeding its surface flow. The results presented from the above examples suggest that the FCA could be useful in determining the hydrologic similarity between different basins, especially in aspect to the presence of land depressions which could add much value to pooling hydrological similar sites for regional FFA.  3.3 Similarity measures The marginal distributions of the site-similarity measures (Fig. 6  a to Fig. 6 e) vary, suggesting that each measure is unique, which is important to avoid redundancy in describing hydrologic similarity. For example, the drainage area in Fig. 6 a is positively skewed with a heavy tail that could negatively affect the clustering process and result in clusters with significantly different basin sizes. Considering combinations of site similarity measures (Stein et al., 2020; Zadeh & Burn, 2019 ) could provide a better representation of hydrologic similarity rather than depending on just one aspect. Here, the cross-correlation structure between the site similarity measures reveals the importance of the MFCA. Fig. 6 f shows that the MFCA has a low correlation with each of the other measures, ranging between 0.03 and 0.34. Since each site similarity measure could describe a hydrologic aspect of similarity, then a measure that is independent of the others is salient. For that reason, the MFCA is prominent. The result in this section suggests the use of a combination of site similarity measures for describing the hydrologic similarity between sites and highlights the importance of considering the MFCA. The choice of the right combination of site similarity measures is discussed in the next section.  3.4 Assessment of pooled groups The choice of the number of clusters and the effect of considering the MFCA on the homogeneity of pooled groups were investigated. For each scenario, the sites were pooled into different numbers of clusters ranging from 2 groups to 10 groups. The three heterogeneity measures of Hosking & Wallis (1993; 1997)  were estimated for each of the pooled groups. The different scenarios resulted in different groups, for which each heterogeneity measure was averaged. Therefore, each scenario had three values representing the groups’ average heterogeneity measures, Fig. 7  a, c, and e, respectively. The inverse relation between each of the heterogeneity measures and the number of clusters was observed due to the reduction in the dispersion of observations when the number of sites per group is reduced. Yet, it is a multi-objective task to balance the group’s size (keeping it as large as possible) while preserving the group’s homogeneity. The relationship between the mean groups’ heterogeneities and the number of clusters in Fig. 7  clearly illustrates the advantage of considering the MFCA regardless of the selected scenario for pooling any number of clusters. Better homogeneous groups were formulated using the same settings and pooling approach when the MFCA was employed. The slope of the curves in Fig. 7 a, c, and e affects the reliability of the regional FFA. A curve that starts with a steep slope and then gets flatter quicker indicates that a smaller number of clusters can obtain reasonable homogeneity. The smaller number of clusters with larger regional group sizes is preferable for reliable regional FFA (Hosking & Wallis, 1997 ). With MFCA, the curves tend to start with steep slopes and reach lower heterogeneity values compared to the other case. Due to the known variability that exists in the Canadian prairies (Stein et al., 2020 ), the number of sites within a group needs to be limited to preserve the group’s homogeneity by increasing the number of clusters. Yet, it is not recommended to increase it over 10 clusters to avoid losing the advantage of regionalization. Therefore, 10 clusters were used for the current application. Further, choosing the right combination of similarity measures impacts the homogeneity of the pooled groups. After clustering the sites into 10 groups using each of the pooling scenarios, the heterogeneity measures are compared in Fig. 7 b, d, and f. At first glance, the use of MFCA in combination with other measures proved to outperform the opposite condition. Yet, it is not recommended to use the MFCA as a single similarity measure (black dashed line in Fig. 7 ) although it could result in better homogeneous groups than most of the other scenarios lacking the MFCA. By comparing the different scenarios, Scenario 8 is the most desirable. It represents the case when the hydrologic similarity is described by the mean annual precipitation, the mean flood date, and the MFCA, see Section 2.3.5. Interestingly, Scenario 1, which only considers the drainage area and MFCA, is almost as good. Scenario 1 has the greatest enhancement after applying the MFCA. Yet, using the drainage area alone could be considered the most undesirable. Even though these results could be case-dependent, it is recommended to test the performance of all scenarios if this methodology is implemented in a different region.  3.5 Evaluation of quantile estimation The relation between the uncertainty in flood quantiles and return periods is known to be proportional. This relation is usually impacted by the size of the observed sample. The regional FFA increases the sample size by using a regional sample of observations from similar sites, but it relies on a fundamental assumption that the grouped sites are hydrologically similar. The validity of this assumption could significantly affect the uncertainty of regional FFA. Since the hydrologic similarity of grouped sites is described by site similarity measures, then it was essential to clarify the impact of using different site similarity measures on the estimated quantiles. The scenarios in Section 2.3.5 were used to represent the use of different site similarity measures and to test the effect of considering the MFCA. The regional quantiles, when the different pooling scenarios were applied, were compared with the observed at-site quantiles. The at-site fitted theoretical probability distribution was also considered. The comparison in Fig. 8   is obtained by fitting a theoretical probability distribution, Section 0, to the observations at one site. Next, a regional distribution is fitted for each of the tested scenarios and scaled to represent the site using its scaling factor. Therefore, Fig. 8  clarifies the effect of considering the MFCA as a site similarity measure and describes the effect of changing site similarity measures on regionally estimated quantiles. For example, the evaluation for site 05EA001: Sturgeon River Near Fort Saskatchewan which is located in Alberta is presented. This site was chosen as an example for its relatively long record of observations, 99 years, compared to the other sites in the Canadian prairies. The ribbons in Fig. 8  represent an ensemble of regionally fitted probability distributions. In comparison to the observed sample, black dots in Fig. 8 , the ensemble that considered the MFCA is narrower and better represents the observations than the ensemble that did not apply the MFCA. For the two cases, the ensemble width tends to get narrower for higher return periods which illustrates the non-uniform impact of using different site similarity measures for regional FFA. It is also observed that the ensemble that considers the MFCA competes with the at-site fitting in describing the observed sample and tends to better describe the sample for return periods greater than 2 years. For further comparison, Section 3.7 compares the accuracy of both regional and at-site estimated quantiles. This concludes the importance of choosing a set of site similarity measures that could potentially affect the accuracy of the estimated quantiles. The importance of considering the MFCA as a site similarity measure is also notable in this aspect.  3.6 Assessment of at-site and regional fitting The regional fitting is proven to be more accurate than the at-site fitting in this case study. Not only the medians of the error metrics were reduced, but also the interquartile ranges were lower and narrower (Fig. 9  ). The overall performance assessment shows a reduction in both the R M S E    and the E R  1    metrics, indicating that the regional FFA could provide more reliable estimates of probabilities and quantiles. Also, the regional FFA could describe the peak events with more accuracy as interpreted from E R  2    and E R  3    metrics, indicating that regional FFA could be more reliable for predicting streamflow quantiles of high return periods. Regional FFA aims to enhance the determination of quantiles beyond the range of observations while preserving the quality of describing the distribution within the observed range. The consideration of the MFCA in regional FFA proved its ability to preserve the distribution within the range of observations at the 109 sites (Fig. 10  ). Further it slightly enhanced the interquartile ranges of the four error measures (Fig. 10 ). This is caused by the reduced dispersion of regional observations that is achieved when the MFCA is considered. Beyond the range of observations, it is more reliable to predict quantiles from regions with less dispersed observations that are detected within groups of sites with better hydrologic similarity (Fig. 7 ).   4 Conclusions This study introduces a new site similarity measure, the Mean Fractional Contributing Area (MFCA) to account for the role of depressional storage in pooling hydrologically similar groups for regional flood frequency analysis. The MFCA was obtained using the hydrologic model HYPR, which was set to simulate the streamflow generation within the studied basins of the Canadian prairies. Sites were pooled into groups following different pooling scenarios with different combinations of similarity measures. The results illustrate the importance of considering the MFCA and suggest combining it with other site similarity measures. More specifically, the results show that.• The MFCA is salient for describing the hydrologic similarity in prairie regions.  • The MFCA enriches the reliability of regional flood frequency analysis by forming fewer clusters with larger samples.  • The MFCA could boost groups’ homogeneity compared to other scenarios lacking MFCA.  • The MFCA is most desirable to describe the hydrologic similarity in combination with the mean annual precipitation and the mean flood date.    The proposed MFCA has demonstrated significant improvements in the homogeneity of groups for regional flood frequency analysis. The hydrologic simulations that account for land depressions' effect on streamflow generation provide a better representation of hydrologic similarity, which is essential for accurate estimates of regional annual maximum flows. The comparison of the proposed measure with other traditional site similarity measures has shown that the pooling process's impact on the regionally estimated quantiles is highly susceptible to the choice of similarity measures. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the proposed measure when land depressions exist to capture this critical hydrologic aspect. This study's findings highlight the importance of developing and applying appropriate site similarity measures to enhance the accuracy of regional flood frequency analysis, which is crucial for effective flood management and risk assessment.
1 Introduction Human activity has shaped the hydrological cycle for generations. As far back as 1864, G.P. Marsh observed that human actions can both spark and halt hydrological change. Marsh observed that clearing forests for agriculture changes the patterns of soil drainage and affects local humidity levels. Similarly, he found that clearing fallen trees and other debris from waterways stops the formation of bogs and the lateral movement of streams (Marsh, 1965 ). Over time our understanding of the extent of human impacts on the hydrological cycle has increased. Land cover change alone impacts infiltration, groundwater recharge, surface water flow regimes, water quality, biodiversity, and water and energy budgets (Sehot et al., 1992; Sivapalan, 1996; Tong & Chen, 2002; Vahmani & Hogue, 2014; Vörösmarty et al., 2010; Wissmar et al., 2004 ). Further, these impacts span the sub-meter, watershed, and global scales (Bhaduri et al., 2000; Reyes et al., 2015; Vörösmarty et al., 2010 ). In recent decades, human impacts on Earth systems, including hydrological systems, have accelerated (Steffen et al., 2015 ) and most watersheds now have some degree of human impacts on hydrological responses (Bosmans et al., 2017; Haddeland et al., 2014 ). This increased human influence on hydrological responses intensifies the challenge of building process understanding and predicting hydrological variables of interest as human influence can amplify or dampen hydrological processes, introduce new processes, and restructure the system (Wagener et al., 2010 ). There is growing recognition of the need to account for human impacts in hydrological modeling. Researchers have integrated human impacts into watershed hydrological models to a range of degrees. For example, Zhang et al. (2020)  investigated the impact of a single human impact, the construction of check dams. In contrast, Zhou et al. (2018)  coupled the WEP-L distributed hydrological model (Jia et al., 2006 ) with a social water cycle model to simulate human impacted hydrology in the Haihe River Basin, an intensively developed watershed in China. Their social water cycle model included water withdrawals and use, wastewater discharge, irrigation, leakage, and drainage. A wide range of data sets were required to build and test this model including reservoir characteristics, reservoir storage time series, agricultural land area and crop types, irrigation patterns and water use data for agriculture, industry and domestic use, in addition to hydroclimatic data sets typically required for hydrological modeling. Wendt et al. (2021)  developed a stylized model which reduced data demands. They modified the lumped HBV model (Van Lanen et al., 2013 ) structure to incorporate regional water management activities during drought, using drought management plans to parameterize the model to a series of representative systems in the UK. In recent years, several large-scale hydrological models have been developed that incorporate water use, reservoir regulation and land cover change (Veldkamp et al., 2018; Wada et al., 2017 ). However, data availability remains a major hurdle to incorporating these interferences and to adding processes such as groundwater pumping and interbasin transfers in large scale hydrological models (Wada et al., 2017 ). Regardless of scale, the genre of models currently used to study human influence have tended to be bottom-up models within which the human impacts are prescribed with appropriate parameterizations, and then the observed flow records are used to calibrate and validate these models. The data challenges of integrating human impacts into hydrological models raise the question, which human impacts do we need to incorporate to represent observed streamflow patterns at different timescales? A particular challenge in the development of watershed models to study hydrologic change is the paucity of precise historical records of the nature and extent of human-induced land cover changes and other human interferences in the hydrologic cycle. In the absence of such records hydrologists are then forced to infer or reconstruct these changes, including human interferences, from available historical records of precipitation, streamflow and proxy variables such as population. To address this challenge, in this paper we present what we call a diagnostic approach  to modeling watersheds with human interferences. The purpose of taking this approach is to build understanding of the relative impact of various human impacted processes on streamflow patterns across time scales. Our approach is similar in spirit to Gupta et al. (2008)  as it likewise identifies the information contained in the data and determines how the model could be reconciled with the data but differs from Gupta et al.  in our application of the top-down approach. Our approach builds upon the top-down modeling method which incrementally develops a hydrological model of appropriate complexity while generating process understanding (Sivapalan et al., 2003 ). The top-down approach starts with an observed temporal pattern in the variable of interest at a chosen (time) scale, and then hypothesizes and investigates the steps or processes at a lower level that could have generated that pattern. This approach stands in contrast to the bottom-up approach which integrates small scale processes at a lower level to discover what patterns might emerge at the higher system level (Klemeš, 1983 ). The way that Sivapalan et al. (2003)  implemented it, the top-down approach involves incrementally adding complexity to hydrological models to generate understanding of which hydrological processes are required to generate specific streamflow patterns at different timescales. There have been several applications of the top-down approach to hydrologic modeling (Farmer et al., 2003; Jothityangkoon et al., 2001 ), which have helped to not only generate parsimonious models of watershed water balances but have also generated novel insights into process controls on observed hydrologic responses in different climate settings (Atkinson et al., 2002; Jothityangkoon & Sivapalan, 2009; Massmann, 2020 ). More complex modeling approaches have advantages in explaining a higher percentage of streamflow variation or achieving better predictive performance. However, the complexity introduced challenges to the attribution of model performance to specific processes or features. Therefore, we apply the top-down approach as our goal is to diagnose what human influenced hydrological processes are important across time scales in the context of a specific case study. In this paper, for the first time, we extend the top-down, diagnostic approach to modeling as a vehicle to interrogate observed historical precipitation-streamflow records in human impacted watersheds to make inferences about the historical, human-induced changes to the water balance and along the way also develop a parsimonious model of the changing hydrology. The goal is not to develop a universal model of human impacted catchments but introduce and test a transferable methodology to develop site-specific models based on data inference. By incrementally adding complexity in the way we model human impacts we test which processes are important in a particular catchment across timescales of interest to hydrologists: daily, monthly and annual. We demonstrate this approach in the watershed of the East Fork of the Upper Russian River in California, USA. Human activity has shaped the hydrology in the Upper Russian River for decades through well-documented water imports, allocation of rights to withdrawal surface water, irrigation and land cover change, making it an ideal test case for this modeling study. The availability of over seven decades of data presents a unique opportunity to examine the hydrological signatures of human development. The lessons learned from this modeling case study are however applicable to other human-impacted watersheds, both in terms of methodology and in terms of fundamental insights about the effects of human interferences in the hydrologic cycle. Further, the rich case history and long period of available data make this case ideal for developing an approach and setting the groundwork for future comparative studies.  2 Materials and methods Our primary goal in this study is to develop a minimalist model of the water balance response of the Upper Russian River watershed over the 1942–2013 period, a period over which there has been significant human interference in the watershed hydrologic cycle. Critically, we propose a mixed-methods approach to developing this model, synthesizing qualitative data from the case history with time series data to craft hypotheses of the model structure. The top-down modeling methodology in “pristine” catchments begins with descriptions of the hydroclimatic setting and assembling multi-year time series of hydroclimate data (e.g., precipitation, potential evaporation, and streamflow), as seen in the work of Jothityangkoon et al. (2001)  and Farmer et al. (2003) . Modeling of the water balance of human-impacted catchments requires, in addition to the hydroclimatic data, information on the history of human interferences that may have contributed to the changes in hydrology. Some of this information may be in the form of time series, while other information may only be qualitative, in the form of case narratives, which may have to be converted to quantitative information for modeling purposes. The putting together of a case narrative thus becomes part of the methodology of model development, which is what makes it a mixed-methods approach. The case study description, including the hydroclimatic setting and the case narrative is presented in section 2.1 . Then, given the availability of a “naturalized streamflow” record over the corresponding period, we carried out the model development in two phases. In the first phase, we use the top-down methodology to develop a model of “natural” hydrology prior to human interventions. In the second phase, we then extend the baseline model developed during the first phase to add features to account for the human interventions, again using the top-down methodology. It should be noted in passing that the “naturalized” streamflow record is a product of another hydrologic model. Therefore, the modeling of naturalized streamflow is simply an intermediate methodological step, a building block, on the way to a model of observed streamflow that reflects a combination of natural and human-influenced hydrological processes. This step was forced on us because historical data under pristine conditions was not available in this catchment, or in neighboring catchments. We further test all feasible combinations of hydrological and human impacts models to ensure that the use of naturalized streamflow has not biased the final model selection. Lastly, we demonstrate the use of the diagnostic approach in two applications: testing for structural change and selecting a model under a counterfactual scenario. 2.1 Case study description: Hydroclimate and human impact history The East Fork of the Upper Russian River is in the Northern California Coast Range in Mendocino County, CA with the headwaters located in Potter Valley (Fig. 1  ). The Northern California Coastal Range has a Mediterranean climate (Koppen-Geiger climate type Csb (Peel et al., 2007 )) characterized by warm dry summers and cool wet winters with approximately 80 % of the precipitation occurring between November and March (Flint et al., 2018 ). The region experiences Pacific storm systems, due to its proximity to the northeast Pacific (Sumargo et al., 2020 ). Precipitation and average annual temperature also vary between years as seen in Fig. 2  A–B. Streamflow patterns in the East Fork also show both the intra- and interannual variability seen in precipitation. The average annual streamflow in the East Fork is approximately 8.83 m3 /s (1167 mm/yr normalized by watershed area), with a peak annual inflow of 17.32 m3 /s (2287 mm/yr) in 1983 and a minimum annual inflow of 1.75 m3 /s (231 mm/yr) in 1977 (Fig. 2 C). Note that we use calendar years and not water years in this study as some data sets are only available on an annual basis by calendar year. This choice is justified because snow processes are not dominant in this watershed as the precipitation record shows only 19 total days of snow in the study period, resulting in no more than 2.4 % of precipitation in any water year. This is to be expected as prior studies have found that the snow line during winter storms is between 1000 m and 2000 m elevation and the highest elevation in the East Fork watershed is 1195 m, making the watershed below the snow line for most storms (Kim et al., 1998 ). Historic vegetation cover in the East Fork watershed included a mixture of hardwood, conifer, oak, and chaparral (Moidu et al., 2021 ). Currently predominant land covers include mixed forest, chaparral, orchards, hay fields, and vineyards (Potter Valley Irrigation District, 2022; USGS, 2016 ). This change in vegetation is hypothesized to alter monthly patterns in streamflow. Further a shift from natural to agricultural land cover is often accompanied by the construction of drainage systems which influence runoff timing. Ditch drainage systems with fast response times are dominant in Mendocino County. As our finest time scale is daily, we did not further consider the effects of drainage. The basin is underlain by the Franciscan Complex, which is dominated by sandstones, shales and conglomerates (Berkland and Ray, 1972 ). Alluvium deposits are also present, and these are characterized by a high silt and clay content, with pockets of sand and gravel (Cardwell, 1965 ). Throughout the Russian River basin, headwaters remain wetted throughout the year through baseflow contributions (Grantham, 2013 ), and in the East Fork a water transfer from the adjacent Eel River keeps flows elevated during the summer dry season. Groundwater levels at many wells show seasonal declines in the summer, although other locations show a seasonal increase due to irrigation in excess of crop water demands (Cardwell, 1965 ). Potter Valley annual groundwater withdrawal in 1954 was estimated to be on the order of 2.38 mm/yr (500 ac-feet/yr) (Cardwell, 1965 ). No more recent estimates are available at the watershed level, but the 2010 USGS estimate of Mendocino County groundwater withdrawals yields an estimate of 5.23 mm/yr normalized over the county area (Maupin et al., 2014 ). This leads us to hypothesize that groundwater pumping may influence the daily distribution of streamflow through its impact on baseflow and runoff generation. The East Fork watershed above the Calpella gauge is approximately 238.7 km2  (92.2 mi2 ) and ranges from 246 m to 1195 m above mean sea level. Lake Mendocino, formed by the Coyote Valley Dam, is located just downstream of the gauge. Lake Mendocino regulates streamflow from our study catchment including flow generated in the East Fork watershed and water diversions on the Eel River conveyed via the Potter Valley Project as a byproduct of hydropower generation. The Sonoma County Water Agency operates Lake Mendocino by collecting water for storage in the reservoir’s water-supply pools when water is available for collection, and by releasing stored water to supplement natural flows as necessary (Sonoma County Water Agency, 2015 ). Understanding streamflow patterns in the East Fork is critical to inform long term operation of this reservoir. The Potter Valley Project was initiated by the Eel River Power and Irrigation Company in 1900 and first generated power in 1908 (Potter Valley Irrigation District, 2022 ). Without upstream storage, however, the project could only generate hydropower at capacity during fall and spring; Scott Dam was constructed to store water and facilitate year-round power generation. Eel Valley residents protested the construction of Scott Dam due to concerns about damages to fish habitat and lost natural resource development opportunities locally (Langridge, 2002 ). In 1922, Pacific Gas & Electric Company (PG&E) acquired the system, Scott Dam was completed, and Lake Pillsbury Reservoir began to fill (Potter Valley Irrigation District, 2022 ). In addition to stabilizing hydropower production, Scott Dam also changed the seasonal pattern of streamflow in the East Fork, significantly increasing summer streamflow. Prior to the Potter Valley Project, the Potter Valley was dry farmed as there was little streamflow during summer months of peak crop water demand. Large scale irrigation began in 1922 and expanded in 1924 with the formation of the Potter Valley Irrigation District (Cardwell, 1965 ). In 1950, PG&E expanded the capacity of the Potter Valley Project transmission tunnel and entered into a contract with the Potter Valley Irrigation District to provide 1.4 m3 /s (50 ft3 /s) (State Water Resources Control Board Division of Water Rights, 1997 ). The water transferred into and withdrawn from the river is hypothesized to alter the annual water balance and therefore streamflow patterns across timescales. The original hydroelectric power plant license issued in 1922 expired in 1972; the renewal process triggered an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) which brought the decades old concerns about fish habitat back to the forefront (Langridge, 2002 ). Ultimately, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission recommended a reduction of the water transferred from the Eel River to the East Fork. This reduction can be seen in Fig. 2 D. Fig. 2 C illustrates the annual variation in streamflow observed at the Calpella gauge, normalized by watershed area (USGS, 2022 ). Fig. 2 C also illustrates the annual variation in naturalized or unimpaired streamflow, a model product developed by the USGS that approximates streamflow in absence of human activity (Flint et al., 2015 ). Flint and colleagues (2013)  developed the Basin Characterization Model, a gridded (270-m grid cell resolution) regional water-balance model developed for the state of California that partitions precipitation into evapotranspiration, infiltration, runoff and percolation. Applying the model Basin Characterization Model at a daily time step, Flint et al. (2015)  used undisturbed upland tributaries to calibrate the model for unimpaired flows in the Russian River. For model testing, they then used regression to estimate streamflow losses due to irrigation diversions and applied a conditioning method to reduce error in high and low flows and refine the calibration. Comparing the two streamflow time series gives us a window into the magnitude and patterns of human influence. From Fig. 2 C we see that the magnitude of observed streamflow is higher than naturalized flow and that a decreasing trend is present only for observed streamflow. The availability of well vetted naturalized streamflow makes this case ideal for modeling the impacts of human activity on hydrological processes. In this study, we examine the trajectory of the East Fork of the Upper Russian River from 1942 (the first full year when observed streamflow is available) through to 2013 (the latest when year naturalized streamflow is available). Variability in precipitation and temperature (Fig. 2 A and B, respectively) shape both observed and naturalized streamflow. Human actions such as water imports (Fig. 2 D, normalized by watershed area), expansion of agricultural and irrigated lands (Fig. 2 E), and water withdrawals affect only observed streamflow. Historical data on water withdrawals is not available for this case; alternatively, we use the record of surface water rights within the watershed to approximate the upper limit of water withdrawals (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022 ). Note that Fig. 2 F shows water rights normalized by watershed area to facilitate comparison across variables. The State Water Resources Control Board notes that while Riparian and pre-1914 water rights holders are required to file diversion and use statements, not all water users have, leading to data gaps (State Water Resources Control Board Division of Water Rights, 1997 ). In addition, Grantham and Viers (2014)  found that face-value water rights across California are approximately five times greater than surface water withdrawals. Therefore, we use the water rights record to approximate the maximum allowable withdrawal (irrespective of demand or physical availability of water). Water rights do not specify how water use can be distributed throughout the year. Here we assume that the usage of water rights follows the intra-annual distribution of losses (primarily due to agricultural water use) between the Capella gauge and Lake Mendocino (Sonoma County Water Agency, 2015 ). A full summary of data sources can be found in Table 1  .  2.2 Modeling “Natural” hydrology We first model the natural hydrology of the Upper Russian River using the top-down approach to identify the level of hydrological process detail that must be included to reproduce annual, monthly and daily streamflow patterns. Unfortunately, we do not have streamflow and meteorological records before intensive human activity in the watershed, nor do we have an appropriate adjacent catchment for a paired catchment analysis. Therefore, we use the naturalized streamflow described above as an approximation of streamflow patterns without human influence. While naturalized streamflow is a model product not observational data, it is well vetted and used by Federal agencies (Johnson et al., 2016 ) and the Sonoma County Water Authority (Sonoma Water, 2021 ). We use four versions of the hydrological model, developed in a series of papers by Jothityangkoon et al. (2001), Atkinson et al. (2002)  and Farmer et al. (2003) , starting with the simple Manabe bucket model (Manabe, 1969 ). More recently, these models have also been applied with minor changes by Bai et al. (2009)  and Massmann (2020) . Here, we apply the version of the models presented by Bai et al. (2009) . All four models apply continuous moisture accounting to the chosen bucket configuration, and estimate actual evapotranspiration and forms of runoff generation, as parameterized functions of soil moisture storage. Note that potential evapotranspiration is computed using the Hamon equation and adjusted to the watershed vegetation through the selection of kv  (Dingman, 2015 ). The models proceed from S1, the simplest, to S4, the most complex (Fig. 3  ). Model S1 tracks moisture in a single soil volume and employs just the saturation excess runoff mechanism and accounts for evaporation and transpiration separately. Model S2 adds subsurface flow as an additional runoff mechanism, which is controlled by soil moisture in excess of a field capacity threshold. Model S3 divides the soil profile into saturated and unsaturated zones and adapts the evaporation and transpiration to separately determine fluxes from both saturated and unsaturated soil components. Lastly, model S4 adds a groundwater storage recharged via percolation and runoff generated in the form of baseflow (Bai et al., 2009 ). Infiltration excess, triggered by rainfall intensities greater than the infiltration capacity, is episodic. Comparing precipitation frequency estimates (NOAA, 2017 ) with average surface saturated hydrologic conductivity across the watershed (USDA, 2019 ), the occurrence of infiltration excess with a duration of 10 min (26 mm/hr) would be a one-year return period event. Given the daily rainfall-runoff data, the rarity of infiltration excess in the catchment, and the challenge of diagnosing in daily data, we will only test the addition of this mechanism if model performance warrants further revisions. Snow processes are also not included in the model because of the limited snow fall as explained in Section 2.1 . The full set of equations for models S1 through S4 can be found in Bai et al. (2009)  and all variables and parameters are defined in the Appendix A  (Table A1 ). All models are implemented with a daily timestep and consider the East Fork watershed as a single control volume. Most model parameters are specified directly from the data. For example, soil depth (D) and texture were extracted from 30 m resolution Web Soil Survey data (USDA, 2019 ) and texture is used along with the relationship between texture and soil properties from Clapp and Hornberger (1978)  to specify the porosity (φ), field capacity (θfc ) and wilting point (θwp ). Reconstructed pre-settlement land cover data (Kelly et al., 2005; Kelly et al., 2008 ) with a minimum mapping unit of 0.16 km2  is used to specify the fraction of vegetation coverage (M). Spatial averages of soil and land cover parameters were used for the lumped model. For model S1 we have one calibration parameter, the interception coefficient (αi ). We add the recession coefficients for subsurface flow from saturated zone (αss ) for S2. S3 has the same two calibration parameters as S2. In model S4 we add a groundwater storage volume. We further add the recession coefficient for baseflow from deep storage (αbf ) and the deep recharge coefficient (kd ) for S4. The four models are fitted to the naturalized flow data in sequence. Model fit is compared using three hydrological signature plots, inter-annual streamflow variability, the monthly regime curve, and the flow duration curve, and two metrics, percent bias (Eq. (1) ) and Nash Sutcliff Efficiency (NSE, Eq. (2) ), computed for both real and log space streamflow (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). Log space metrics are used to reduce the influence of high flows on the metrics and assess model performance on average and low flows. The four metrics are used collectively to avoid a focus on matching one aspect of the hydrograph at the expense of other features (Boyle et al., 2000 ). Where metrics disagree, we select the model that balances performance across the metrics. Manual alternate year calibration is used to ensure that calibration and validation data sets both contain periods with minimal and present-day levels of human activity in the watershed (Garcia and Islam, 2019; Gowda et al., 2012 ).(1) PercentBias = 1 100  1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  Q i  sim   - 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  Q i  obs      = 1 100  Q sim    ¯   - Q obs    ¯          (2) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  Q i  obs   - Q i  sim      2   ∑ i = 1  N  Q i  obs   - Q obs    ¯      2           In Eq. However, we update the vegetation fraction (M) based on the 2016 National Land Cover Database (USGS, 2016 ). Then, once again, following the top-down modeling philosophy articulated by Jothityangkoon et al. (2001) , we begin by adding fluxes and processes that are hypothesized to affect the annual water balance. Then we sequentially proceed to processes hypothesized to streamflow patterns at the monthly and finally daily time scales. This approach is also guided by our research question and interest in identifying the requisite complexity for each timescale of interest. We begin with the natural hydrology model (S4) as a zero-order model of the human-impacted hydrology which we term H0. (Subsequent models are named from H1 to HN in order of increasing complexity.) While not expected to perform well in a watershed with intensive human impacts, it serves as baseline for performance comparison. We start the model development for human-impacted hydrology with processes hypothesized to influence annual streamflow pattern (our longest time scale) and proceed to add processes hypothesized to influence monthly and then daily streamflow patterns. From the case background and time series data (Fig. 2 ) presented in Section 2.1 , we know that there is a water transfer from the Eel River via the Potter Valley Project and a long history of water withdrawals, primarily for agricultural use. Both the transfer into the Russian River and direct withdrawals from the Russian River are likely to impact the annual water balance. However, as we have no record of withdrawals, we use water rights, a legal maximum of withdrawals, as an approximation. Therefore, our first version of the human-impacted hydrology, model H1, adds these two fluxes (Eq. As these are fluxes to and from the river, there is no change to the soil moisture accounting or actual evapotranspiration, and all other equations remain the same. After accounting for fluxes directly in and out of the river, we move to incorporate human activities affecting soil moisture dynamics, which are hypothesized to influence streamflow patterns on a monthly timescale for model H2.
