Equations of model S4H3 can be found in the Appendix A  along with variable and parameter definitions. All other model equations can be found in the Supplemental Material (S1–S4) .  2.4 Investigating structural change A challenge of hydrological modeling in human impacted watersheds is that over time, human actions may add new processes or amplify or diminish the influence of existing processes such that model structure needs to undergo changes. The iterative diagnostic method introduced above can be applied to portions of a time series to test for model structure change. Here we identify a sharp increase in water rights in 1980 (Fig. 2 E). This increase is presumably in response to a general increase in irrigated agriculture and follows shortly after the record lows in annual observed flow and water imports in 1977 (Fig. 2 A&D). We hypothesize that this could represent a significant change in the hydrologic system, which needs to be accommodated with a change in appropriate model structure between the pre and post 1980 periods. Specifically, we hypothesize that this change could alter the relative importance of groundwater pumping (if surface water use replaced groundwater use) or change the percent of time that all irrigation demands are met, both of which have the potential to impact the model structure. To assess this, we apply the diagnostic process described in Section 2.3  separately for each period and compare the selected conceptual models.  2.5 Counterfactual experiment Counterfactuals are hypothetical scenarios of what would have occurred under conditions that differ from the historical reality (Lewis, 1973; Müller & Levy, 2019 ). Counterfactual experiments with the model can illustrate how the system would have responded if different decisions were made but exogenous factors remain as observed in the historical record. This strategy was effectively used by Srinivasan (2015)  to generate key insights into human responses to droughts in the city of Chennai, India and by Penny et al. (2020)  to assess the effects of the Ganges water treaty on salinity levels in the Ganges Delta. Here we examine the case of agricultural and irrigation intensification by scaling the historical record of expansion of irrigated land such that it covers 80 % of the catchment by 2013 (the last year in the study period). This choice preserves but magnifies the existing trend and allows us to explore the hydrological impacts of an alternate development trajectory and the impact of model structure on streamflow simulation in that alternate past. Thus, the counterfactual experiment enables us to test the diagnostic approach under alternate conditions within a single case.   3 Results The results are described in four parts below: modeling natural hydrology, modeling human-impacted hydrology, investigating structural change and applying the diagnostic approach to a counterfactual scenario. 3.1 Natural hydrological model results Fig. 5   shows the hydrological signatures for naturalized streamflow and the four versions of simulated streamflow. Fig. 5 A illustrates the annual pattern in streamflow and shows that all four versions of the model capture most of the year-to-year variation in streamflow. Moving to monthly and seasonal patterns, we examine the regime curve in Fig. 5 B, which shows that model S1 tends to underestimate flows during the winter (high flow) months (December to February), while models S2 and S3 show a slight tendency to over-estimate flows during these same months. Model S4 shows the least bias during the winter months. In the spring (March through May) models S1 to S3 underestimate flows while model S4 is unbiased for March and April and biased high in May. The differences in the models are most stark at the daily timescale, as shown in the flow duration curve (Fig. 5 C). All models can replicate high flow days (flow exceeded on 10 % of days or less) but only model S4 captures the distribution of medium to low flows. The advantages of model S4 are also clear in the model performance metrics for both the calibration and validation periods shown in Table 2  . Note that the associated best fit parameters are shown in Table 3  . Specifically, only model S4 shows good performance during low flows, as evidenced by the log space NSE and log space percent bias. This finding shows that surface groundwater connectivity and baseflow contributions are key to replicating the distribution of streamflow at the daily timescale. Note in passing that in previous applications of the top-down approach (e.g., Farmer et al., 2003 , Atkinson et al., 2003), there was an opportunity to add further complexity to the model structure to more accurately reproduce daily streamflow in (especially) arid regions. However, we did not choose to do this here because of the good fits we already obtained with model S4. Previous work by Massman (2020) across the United States has shown that required model complexity is minimal for watersheds experiencing the Mediterranean climate, as in California.  3.2 Human modified hydrological model results Based on the results of modeling natural hydrology (Section 3.1), we use model S4 as a hydrological basis for adding human impacts on hydrological processes. Fig. 6   illustrates the hydrological signatures for observed streamflow and the four versions of simulated streamflow. Model S4H0 (equivalent to model S4) is biased low and cannot account for interannual variability as seen in Fig. 6 A. The addition of water transfer and water withdrawal fluxes in S4H1 improves the model as seen in the annual timeseries (Fig. 6 A) and addressed the negative bias in the previous model (Table 4  ). However, model S4H1 cannot replicate the summer and fall (June through October) observed low flow patterns (Fig. 6 B). Note that streamflow simulated with S4S1 remains higher than streamflow simulated with S4H0 even as rights and irrigation increase and the transfer declines. This is because not all rights can be met due to the temporal mismatch of crop water demand and available water. The addition of irrigation driven by crop water demand in S4H2 improves the model fit at the monthly and daily timescales (Fig. 6 B&C). The calibration log space NSE and percent bias improve to 0.82 (0.77 for validation) and 8.00 (6.94 for validation) respectively, clearly demonstrating that model S4H2 has an improved representation of low flow processes. Lastly, model S4H3 adds groundwater pumping when surface water rights cannot meet irrigation demand. There are negligible differences between models S4H2 and S4H3 in terms of hydrological signatures (Fig. 6 ) and metrics (Table 4 ). This indicates that representing groundwater pumping is not critical to matching streamflow patterns across timescales in the East Fork watershed. Note that each model version was calibrated manually and that the best fit parameters for each model versions can be found in Table 3 . As a model product, naturalized streamflow has embedded assumptions that could impact our understanding of hydrological processes presented in Section 4.1, and subsequently bias the selected model of human impacted hydrology in the East Fork watershed. To reduce the risk of such bias, we compared all feasible combinations of hydrological modules (S1-S4) and human impacts modules (H0-H3; Fig. 7  ). Note that groundwater pumping can only be represented if groundwater storage is included in the hydrological model, therefore, only hydrological module S4 is compatible with H3. This comparison shows that while any of the selected hydrological models performs well with average to high flows as evidenced by NSE and percent bias computed in real space (Fig. 7 A-B), only hydrological model S4 with human impact modules H2 or H3 can adequately represent low flows as evidenced by NSE and percent bias computed in log space (Fig. 7 C–D). The comparison confirms that model S4H2 remains the model choice that maximizes performance across all three timescales while minimizing model complexity.  3.3 Investigating structural change results While model S4H2 is a good fit for the full period, changes in water rights and irrigated area warrant investigation of structural changes over time. We apply the models for human-impacted hydrology developed above and, in this comparison, we applied the best fit parameters found in Section 4.2 and did not perform further calibration. Table 5   compares the model metrics for the period from 1942 through the end of 1979 (pre-1980) and the period from 1980 through 2013 (post-1980). Figs. S5 and S6  in the Supplemental Material  show the hydrological signatures for both periods. Consistent with the analysis of the full study period, models S4H0 and S4H1 do not replicate the patterns in the observed data for either pre-1980 or post-1980 periods as evidenced by low log space NSE and high log space NSE percent bias. Further, we find that in both pre- and post-1980 periods model S4H2 has improved model performance on all metrics and that introducing groundwater pumping in model S4H3 does not improve model performance. These results support the null hypothesis of no structural change in the catchment, indicating that we can proceed to apply a single model for the full period.  3.4 Counterfactual experiment The counterfactual experiment tested the diagnostic approach’s ability to detect the appropriate model structure under alternate conditions, specifically the case of agricultural and irrigation intensification. As no additional surface water is available, increased irrigation results in higher groundwater pumping. Fig. 8  , illustrates the differences in simulated streamflow between model structures S4H2 (irrigation but no pumping) and S4H3 (adds pumping). Compared to the historical case, there are visible differences in the simulated streamflow across annual, monthly and flow duration curve plots. Fig. 8 A shows that the differences between simulated streamflow from S4H2 and S4H3 grows over time which is consistent with the increase in groundwater pumping over the counterfactual period, which we attribute to reduced baseflow caused by groundwater drawdown. Fig. 8 C supports this interpretation as the flow duration curve shows that high and average simulated streamflow is similar across the two models while low flows are notably lower for S4H3 when groundwater pumping is incorporated. An additional computational experiment attributing streamflow change can be found in the Supplemental Material (S7) .   4 Discussion 4.1 Timescales and model complexity The diagnostic approach to modeling human-impacted hydrology in the Upper Russian River has both generated case specific insights and demonstrated the potential to build generalizable knowledge of human-impacted watersheds. In the case of the East Fork of the Upper Russian River, applying the diagnostic approach to modeling natural hydrology showed that a single bucket soil moisture module with surface runoff paired with an actual evapotranspiration module was able to capture year to year variability but not monthly or daily patterns. The addition of sub-surface runoff improved the model’s ability to represent monthly patterns but only with the addition of deep groundwater storage and baseflow can the model replicate the daily streamflow distribution. This is consistent with findings in other watersheds with similar climatic aridity (Atkinson et al., 2002 ). Applying this diagnostic approach to the observed human-impacted streamflow demonstrated that accounting for water imports and water rights is sufficient to replicate annual streamflow patterns. However, at monthly and daily timescales, modeling irrigation based on crop water demand and irrigation efficiency is critical to replicating observed streamflow patterns. Adding groundwater pumping provides marginal improvements to the model, indicating that pumping has not impacted baseflow significantly during the study period. This is likely due to the fact that pumping has had a minimal effect on aquifer levels in this case (California Department of Water Resources, 2021 ), as surface–groundwater connectivity is high in the Upper Russian River (Marquez et al., 2017 ). The counterfactual experiment reinforces this interpretation as it illustrates that higher levels of groundwater pumping in the same catchment would result in baseflow impacts. Collectively these findings tell us that in the East Fork watershed: 1) the annual water balance is dominated by precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, water imports and water withdrawals; 2) the monthly water balance is influenced by sub-surface runoff, crop water demand and irrigation efficiency; and 3) the daily water balance can only be explained by accounting for baseflow contributions. This is significant because different management applications emphasize different timescales. For example, water supply management typically requires an understanding of and an ability to predict monthly streamflow (U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, 2012; Wurbs, 2005 ). In contrast, riverine flood control operations require process understanding and predictions at the daily timescale (or shorter). Paired with this diagnostic approach, the water management application and its timescale can inform the information required to represent human impacted hydrology. Identifying the required complexity helps to decrease the data challenges of modeling human-impacts on watershed hydrology. More broadly, the diagnostic approach presented above provides the foundation for further research to identify patterns in both human and hydrological characteristics that influence the required model complexity and best fit model structure. In comparing nine pristine catchments Atkinson et al. (2002)  found that the aridity index of the catchment along with the timescale of interest determined the hydrological model complexity needed to replicate streamflow patterns. More recent work by Bai et al. (2009)  and Massmann (2020)  confirmed these findings. Analogously, future comparative modeling studies focused on human-impacted catchments may shed light on the characteristics that influence the dominant human-impacted hydrological processes and therefore the required model structure. While further comparative work is needed to develop and test robust hypotheses, from this single case we identify relationships between catchment characteristics and direct-human impacts that may influence the model structure and complexity needed. First, we hypothesize that the strength of the surface–groundwater connection in combination with the intensity of pumping impacts model complexity. Second, we hypothesize that a larger phase shift between PET and P increases the importance of irrigation in explaining streamflow seasonality. Future comparative work can refine and test these hypotheses as well as inform other hypotheses. Note that while naturalized streamflow is not frequently available, the top-down approach can be applied directly to observed streamflow as demonstrated in Fig. 7 . However, a key obstacle to applying this approach to many catchments is that many of the required data sets are not available in a consistent form across the U.S. (or other countries) or are only available aggregated by county, which does not correspond with watershed boundaries (Maupin et al., 2018 ). Initiatives to assemble spatially explicit databases such as the current effort to assemble a national database of water transfers within the U.S. (Dickson et al., 2020 ), would greatly facilitate such comparative analyses.  4.2 Diagnosing changes over time Watersheds, as with any natural system, change over time. However, human activity has accelerated the pace and expanded the scope of change, creating an additional challenge for hydrological modeling (Wagener et al., 2010 ). To address this challenge, in this paper we applied this diagnostic modeling approach to check for changes in the required model complexity over time. Based on a significant expansion in water rights in 1980, we separated the time series data into two periods, before and after this expansion. The diagnostic modeling approach identified the same best fit model, S4H2, for both time periods, consistent with the analysis of the full study period. This indicates that there were only quantitative and not qualitative process changes between these two periods. In contrast, the counter-factual experiment demonstrates a situation in which a model change would be needed. The experiment showed that if irrigated agriculture intensified in this watershed the magnitude of groundwater pumping could reach a level where accounting for the pumping in a hydrological model would be needed to accurately simulate streamflow. Beyond the case of the Upper Russian River, the approach can be applied to assess the need to adapt the model structure over time to account for human induced hydrological change.  4.3 Limitations and next steps The diagnostic approach and model developed in this study is intended to aid in diagnosis of the natural and human influenced hydrological processes that explain streamflow variability from the annual to the daily scale. Following this objective, the simplicity of the model and its iterative development is both intentional and supported by prior research (Bai et al., 2009; Farmer et al., 2003; Jothityangkoon & Sivapalan, 2009; Massmann, 2020 ). In focusing on the objective of diagnosis, the model has not been designed for prediction or decision support. However, the knowledge gained through the diagnostic analysis presented here could inform the development of improved prediction and decision support models for the East Fork watershed by targeting data collection and model refinement efforts to the most impactful variables and processes. The diagnostic capabilities of this model could also be improved through further data collection and model refinement. The model developed in this paper is lumped and a next step is to develop a semi-distributed version of the model that breaks the East Fork watershed into sub-catchments to better represent spatial heterogeneity in catchment properties, including land cover. Additional research could also target refinement of the representation of surface–groundwater connectivity in specific areas of the watershed and collecting additional data to assess the relationship.   5 Conclusions Human activity impacts hydrological responses in most watersheds globally. Hydrologists are increasingly called upon to isolate hydrologic impacts of past human actions and make predictions of future impacts under projected scenarios of human-induced changes. These human interferences and their hydrologic impacts are highly site specific, and continually evolve over time. Because of this, these impacts cannot be accounted for in most hydrological models in a generic manner. Indeed, incorporating all plausible human impacts in one model comes at a high data acquisition and modeling cost, raising the questions such as: in what way do the various human interferences impact hydrologic variability?, and, in which way should we incorporate these human impacts in hydrologic models, and at what level of detail? Given the diverse nature of human interferences, there is considerable merit to exploring this question using a data-based, top-down modeling approach. This paper represents an important first step in this direction. This paper is aimed at developing a parsimonious hydrologic model capable of representing observed streamflow variability at multiple timescales in a highly human-impacted catchment in California. To achieve this, we developed a diagnostic approach to modeling watersheds with human interference. This approach builds on the top-down hydrological modeling approach in which process complexity is incrementally added to identify which hydrological processes are important to replicate observed streamflow patterns in a particular location and at a specific timescale. Here we incrementally added processes through which humans modify hydrology in the sub-watershed of the East Fork of the Upper Russian River in California, USA, a watershed influenced by over a century of human activity. Applying this method, we found, for example, that incorporation of just water imports and water rights can replicate annual patterns sufficiently well. However, adding crop water demand and irrigation is required to replicate monthly and daily patterns. The incorporation of groundwater pumping does not change model performance and is not needed in this case. However, in a counterfactual experiment we find that if irrigation and groundwater pumping intensified the model would require pumping to replicate patterns. Further, we apply the model to test for structural changes in the best fit model over time and to test hypotheses of the drivers of a recent decline in streamflow. We find that no changes in model structure are warranted for the 1942 to 2013 study period. These insights into the human-impacted hydrological responses of the Upper Russian River serve to demonstrate the potential to build process understanding of human-impacted watersheds generally, and to identify both hydrological and human systems characteristics that can indicate the level of complexity and structure of model required. What this case demonstrates is that the diagnostic approach can be used to identify the minimum level of model complexity needed for the time scale of interest. This avoids unnecessary model complexity and parameterization, focusing data collection and parameterization efforts on highly influential human activities. Over time, this approach to modeling can be replicated in many human-impacted catchments in the region, and eventually in other more diverse regions globally. The insights so gained can then be used to develop generalized understanding of human impacts on hydrology, and more generic models for the prediction of the effects of human impacts on hydrologic variability.
1 Introduction Global plant assimilation of atmospheric CO2  through photosynthesis is accompanied by a loss of water vapor through the stomata on leaf surfaces (Berry et al., 2010 ), which regulate the diffusion of these two gases between the leaf and the atmosphere (Keenan et al., 2013 ). The carbon gain to water loss is generally referred to as vegetation water use efficiency (WUE ) (Keenan et al., 2013 ) and is one of the most important ecosystem functional properties shaping global water, energy and carbon cycles (Cheng et al., 2017 ). Increasing atmospheric CO2  concentration enhances terrestrial vegetation productivity through CO2  fertilization (Wang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022 ), which is the main driving factor of global vegetation growth (Piao et al., 2020 ). Simultaneously, plant stomatal conductance often declines as CO2  increases, limiting water loss from leaves to the atmosphere (i.e., reducing transpiration) (Kooperman et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2018; Skinner et al., 2018 ). Consequently, recent studies have suggested an increase of WUE  in response to atmospheric CO2  concentration during the past decades (van der Sleen et al., 2015; Adams et al., 2019 ), i.e., CO2 -driven gains in vegetation water use efficiency ( CO  2  - W U E = δ W U E  δ CO  2      , defined as the relative increase in WUE  in response to a 100-ppm increase in atmospheric CO2  concentration). For instance, Zhang et al., (2022)  suggested that the global WUE  increasing trend was largely a result of increasing CO2  (51 %), especially in most of tropical forests. Van Der Sleen et al., (2015)  observed a 30 – 35 % enhancement in the intrinsic water-use efficiency of the tropical trees as atmospheric CO2  concentrations increased. The observed CO2_ WUE  has increased terrestrial water availability by increasing continental scale runoff (Betts et al., 2007 ), extending the vegetation growing season (van der Sleen et al., 2015 ) and enhancing plant drought tolerance (Franks et al., 2013 ). Although CO2_ WUE  has important implications for ecosystem functioning, as well as feedbacks to the climate system (Cheng et al., 2017 ), the spatial patterns and temporal dynamics of future CO2_ WUE  remain uncertain across the globe (Cheng et al., 2017; Soh et al., 2019; Adams et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, due to the physiological limits of the capacity of vegetation to respond to additional CO2  (e.g., limited photosynthetic capacity), CO2_ WUE  may slow down or even become saturated (i.e., CO2_ WUE ≤0) (Adams et al., 2020 ), but whether CO2_ WUE  may altogether cease changing remains unknown. A key reason for the uncertainty is that many environmental factors, including vapor pressure deficit (VPD ), availability of nutrients and water, can affect the magnitude and trends of the plant physiological responses to CO2 , thereby complicating the temporal dynamics of global CO2_ WUE . A recent study reported that the rates of increase of WUE  with CO2  (i.e., CO2_ WUE ) have declined by half over the twentieth century based on 422 globally-distributed tree-ring isotope series (Adams et al., 2020 ). A CO2_ WUE  decline represents either an increase of terrestrial water loss, or a decrease of photosynthetic carbon uptake in response to increasing CO2 , or both simultaneously. If such declining trends prevail across the globe, the global land surface will witness a higher water cost for the land carbon sink, thereby potentially increasing the challenge of mitigating global warming and increasing the risk of worldwide water shortages, due to e.g. more frequent heatwave and drought events. To better understand the global cycles of carbon, water and energy, therefore, a comprehensive assessment of the temporal dynamics of global CO2_ WUE  is required. In this study, we estimate past (1982–2015) and future (2016–2100) spatial–temporal dynamics of global CO2_ WUE  through multiple regression. We detect the time and place of occurrence of the saturation point, where the gains in WUE  from increasing CO2  decrease to zero (i.e. CO2_ WUE ≤0). Exploring the driving mechanisms of the changes in CO2_ WUE  is fundamental to understand regional and global water and carbon cycles (Brümmer et al., 2012 ) and to predict future climate change (Cheng et al., 2017 ), but there are still large gaps in our understanding of these drivers. For this reason, observations and simulations of nitrogen (N ), phosphorus (P ), precipitation, soil water and VPD  are employed to identify the dominant driver of the global changes in CO2_ WUE  (See Method in Supplementary Text S1  and Data source in Supplementary Text S2 ). Hence, we present an integrated picture of the characteristics and drivers of past and future global CO2_ WUE , which may help improve ecosystem and water resources management for mitigation as well as adaption to global hydrological change.  2 Method for estimating global CO2_ WUE  and its temporal dynamics In this study, ecosystem WUE  (Equation (1)  is defined as ecosystem GPP  per unit of terrestrial water loss (i.e., ET ) (Keenan et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2017; Guerrieri et al., 2019 ). Based on annual WUE , atmospheric CO2  concentration (CO2  ), VPD  and maximum land surface air temperature data at each pixel, we used linear multiple regressions (Equation (2)  and Equation (3)  to estimate the spatial–temporal dynamics of global CO2_ WUE  with 15-year moving windows (i.e., the relative increase in WUE  in response to a 100-ppm increase in atmospheric CO2  concentration within the 15 years) for the period of 1982–2100. Equation (3)  provides additional interaction effects of CO2 and climate on vegetation dynamics. Several additional analyses were employed to test the robustness of the global CO2_ WUE  temporal dynamics:(a) Firstly, due to the large discrepancy of GPP between different datasets, observed global vegetation dynamics from the four datasets (AVHRR NIRv, AVHRR+MODIS NIRv, NIRv + SIF and GLASS-GPP datasets) were used to estimate the temporal dynamics of CO2_ WUE .  (b) Secondly, aside from the climate variables of CO2  concentration, VPD  and temperature, Equations (2) and (3)  do not take the other hydro-meteorological variables into consideration, which may prevent us from obtaining a more accurate estimate of CO2_ WUE . After adding the other climate variables of soil moisture, terrestrial water storage, radiation and atmospheric nitrogen deposition into Equations (2) and (3) , we checked the robustness of the original estimates of CO2_ WUE  that only consider CO2  concentration, VPD  and temperature in the equations.  (c) Thirdly, the multiple regression approach (Equations (2) and (3)  does not take into consideration the effects of land cover changes (i.e., deforestation, fires, irrigation, afforestation, etc.) on WUE . Therefore, after excluding the regions with substantial human activities (e.g., afforestation, deforestation, fires and agricultural activities), we checked whether the observed CO2_ WUE  decline still exists or whether it is merely an artefact of land cover changes (See Supplementary Text S3 ).  (d) Finally, various moving window lengths (from 10 to 20 years) were applied to test whether the observed CO2_ WUE  decline still exists, irrespective of the moving window length (see Supplementary Text S4 ).     3 Results 3.1 Temporal dynamics of the observed global CO2_ WUE  We use three satellite datasets that are proxies for gross primary productivity (GPP, i.e., AVHRR NIRv, AVHRR+MODIS NIRv and NIRv + SIF) (Wang et al., 2020 ), using linear multiple regression to isolate CO2_ WUE  from the total WUE  changes that are affected by various environmental factors (not merely CO2 ). The observed multi-year mean CO2_ WUE  indicates that increasing CO2  has enhanced WUE  (mean CO2_ WUE= 5.65 ± 1.14 % 100 ppm−1 ) across most of the global land surface (Fig. 1  a), especially in the northern high latitudes, which is consistent with recent field observations (Medlyn and De Kauwe, 2013; Holmes, 2014 ). By calculating the time series of CO2_ WUE , we find that all three data sets present a significant downward trend of global mean CO2_ WUE  during 1982–2015 (−1.38 ± 0.19 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1 , Fig. 1 b and c, p  < 0.01), implying weakening gains of WUE  with the increasing atmospheric CO2  over time. However, satellite-based estimates of GPP  are likely to underestimate the CO2  fertilization effects (and thereby possibly underestimate CO2_ WUE ) because they do not consider the direct effect of increasing CO2  on the light-use efficiency of C3 vegetation leaves, which cannot be observed from space (De Kauwe et al., 2016 ). To further assess the CO2_ WUE  decline, therefore, we used a long-term global GLASS-GPP dataset from Zheng et al., (2020)  that is developed based on the light use efficiency principle (i.e., accounting for the direct effects of CO2  on light use efficiency). This GLASS-GPP dataset has been shown to provide a reliable long-term estimate of global GPP (interannual variations in GPP in particular). The negative trend of CO2_ WUE  in most of the Earth’s land surface is also found when using the GLASS-GPP dataset (−1.32 ± 0.18 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1  on average, Fig. 1 e). The multiple regression Equation (2)  that is used to derive CO2_ WUE  represents WUE  as a linear combination of a limited number of drivers: CO2 , VPD  and temperature. However, Equation (2)  does not include interactions between the variables, nor does it include some of the other hypothesized controls on WUE  (e.g., soil water and radiation). Therefore, we also used a non-linear multiple regression (Equation (3)  that is more physically realistic and includes the interactions between variables, and again found a similar declining trend in CO2_ WUE  (−1.399 ± 1.537 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1 ). Further, after adding various environmental factors (including temperature, VPD , precipitation, soil moisture, terrestrial water storage, radiation, atmospheric nitrogen deposition, etc.), we still obtain very consistent estimates of the CO2_ WUE  decline (−1.30 – −1.54 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1 ). It should be noted that the multiple regression (Equations (2) and (3)  does not take the effects of land cover changes (LCCs, i.e., the regions with deforestation, fires, irrigation, afforestation, etc.) on WUE  into consideration. Therefore, it is important to assess whether the observed CO2_ WUE  decline might be an artefact of land cover changes. After excluding the regions with large LCCs (see details in Supplementary Text S3  and Supplementary Fig. 1 ), we still find a similar declining trend of CO2_ WUE  (−1.55 – −1.62 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1 ). This implies a weak effect of LCCs on the global land carbon sink and terrestrial water losses (Pokhrel et al., 2021 ). The estimation of CO2 _WUE  involves the use of VPD  data. Therefore, the source of VPD  data from different datasets can affect the calculation results of CO2 _WUE . To evaluate the magnitude of this impact, we calculated CO2 _WUE  based on five VPD  databases: HadCRUT4, ERA-Interim, MERRA, 20CRv2c, and CERA-20C, and conducted a comparative analysis. Our results suggest that, irrespective of the choice of VPD  data, the CO2 _WUE  time series still show a consistent and statistically significant downward trend across the multiple datasets. The variability in CO2 _WUE  values between the different VPD  sources is relatively small, only of 0.7–9 % (Supplementary Fig. 2 ).  3.2 Spatial patterns of the observed global CO2_ WUE  trends Geographical distributions of observed CO2_ WUE  trends (Fig. 1 d and Supplementary Fig. 4 ) reveal that the decline is widespread across most of the Earth’s land surface, especially in the northern high latitudes where VPD  increased the most. In contrast, 23.2 % of the global land surface witnessed an increase in CO2_ WUE  (e.g., the Great Green Wall at the southern border of the Sahara Desert, and Australia), which might be related to human activities that increased GPP rapidly (i.e., re-vegetation and agricultural activities) (Kojwang and Larwanou, 2015; Yao et al., 2017 ). When comparing climate zones (See Method in Supplementary Text S1 ), we find that humid regions experienced the largest decreases in CO2_ WUE  (Supplementary Fig. 6 ), while semi-arid regions experienced increases, on average. These differences indicate that limited water availability is not a key driver of the global CO2_ WUE  decline (i.e., areas with high water availability saw the largest CO2_ WUE  decline). Across different vegetation types (See Method in Supplementary Text S1 ), CO2_ WUE  weakened considerably for needleleaved evergreen and needleleaved deciduous trees (located in high northern latitudes), but far less for broadleaved evergreen trees (located in tropical areas). These phenological differences may be because vegetation in the northern high latitudes is affected by both indirect effects on leaf area index (i.e., CO2 -induced stimulation of carboxylation per unit leaf area) and direct effects on foliar physiology (i.e., increased carbon sequestration used for leaf area expansion), while vegetation in tropical areas experiences only a physiological effect, as the leaf area index in some tropical humid regions may be close to saturation (Wang et al., 2020 ). Special attention here is paid to the saturation point where the gains of WUE  from increasing atmospheric CO2  concentration cease (i.e., CO2_ WUE ≤0 % 100 ppm−1 ). All three observational datasets show that the global mean CO2_ WUE  crossed this saturation point in the 1990 s (Fig. 1 b) in 55.4 % of the land surface (Supplementary Fig. 7 ). Crossing of the saturation point is also supported by recent studies. Based on 422 tree-ring isotope series, Adams et al., (2020)  reported that the rates of WUE  increase with CO2  declined by half over the twentieth century, and that for angiosperms they have been close to zero since 1990 (basically reaching the saturation point) (Adams et al., 2020 ). The underlying mechanisms for this phenomenon may be due to the following reasons: As atmospheric CO2  concentrations continue to rise, the CO2 -driven enhancement of WUE  in plants will not continue indefinitely. Rather, WUE  will ultimately reach a saturation point due to the intrinsic physiological regulatory mechanisms of plants. This saturation effect occurs because the positive impact of rising CO2  on WUE  eventually levels off, with further CO2  increases failing to produce much additional WUE  improvement. Importantly, the CO2 -induced increase in WUE  is affected by multiple environmental factors, including VPD , water availability, and nutrient status. When these other limiting factors come into play, the positive effect of elevated CO2  on WUE  can be constrained, even as CO2  levels continue to increase. Of particular note is the substantial increase in global VPD  in recent years, driven by warming temperatures and declining relative humidity. VPD  amplification may be a key factor underlying the saturation of CO2 ′s positive impacts on WUE . Elevated VPD  can accelerate plant transpiration rates and water loss, while also limiting photosynthetic carbon uptake, thereby dampening CO2 -induced WUE  enhancements. When vegetation WUE  reaches a saturation point with further increases in atmospheric CO2  concentration, this could lead to a series of adverse eco-hydrological consequences for regional and global carbon, water, and energy cycles. The presence of this saturation point indicates that vegetation drought tolerance may weaken or stop increasing (i.e., water loss per unit of carbon sequestration) in contrast with the increasing drought tolerance found in previous studies (van der Sleen et al., 2015 ). After crossing this point, the role of vegetation in regional or global cycles of carbon, water and energy might be reversed. For instance, when WUE  decreases with increasing CO2  (i.e., CO2_ WUE ≤0% 100 ppm−1 ), either total evaporation increases or gross photosynthetic carbon uptake decreases, or both occur simultaneously, which may generate risks of water shortages especially in arid regions, and weaken the capacity of vegetation to act as a land carbon sink (Wang et al., 2020 ). Such changes could significantly impact global carbon cycle processes and potentially exacerbate the rise in atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations. Furthermore, alterations in vegetation WUE  can affect regional energy and water cycles, triggering feedbacks in regional climate. These climate feedbacks may further intensify the occurrence of local droughts, alter precipitation patterns, and increase the frequency and severity of extreme climate events.  3.3 Ability of models in reproducing and predicting the global CO2_ WUE  We employ simulations from the latest generation of Earth system models (CMIP6) to assess the spatial–temporal dynamics of simulated CO2_ WUE  during 1982–2015. The seven CMIP6 models all present a downward trend of CO2_ WUE  (−0.43 ± 0.057 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1 , Fig. 1 b and c) in most of the global land surface (>60 % of the total land area, Fig. 1 f and Supplementary Fig. 8 ). The CO2_ WUE  declines are also identified in the terrestrial carbon cycle of 13 TRENDY-v9 models [-0.244 ± 0.366 under the simulations of S2 (considering CO2  and climate, Supplementary Fig. 9 a) and −0.229 ± 0.360 under S3 (considering CO2 , climate and land use, Supplementary Fig. 9 b)] in 52.3–54.9 % of the Earth’s land surface. However, the current models strongly underestimate the global CO2_ WUE  decline, in comparison with the observed rate of −1.38 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1  over the same period. This underestimation might be due to the overestimated effects of CO2  fertilization on the land carbon sink (as reported by Wang et al., 2020 , Supplementary Table 2 ) and the underestimated growth rates of total evaporation by the models (Supplementary Table 3 ). The poor performance of ESMs in reproducing recent CO2_ WUE  dynamics is likely to prevent them from reliably predicting future climate changes, i.e., due to overestimated predictions of the land carbon sink or water availability. Based on the predictions from the CMIP6 models, we further examined the future trends of global CO2_ WUE  under the SSP370 and SSP585 emission scenarios during 2016–2100. All the models predict a decreasing trend of CO2_ WUE  in 91.4–92.2 % of the global land surface, at rates of −0.129 ± 0.011 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1  (SSP370) and −0.117 ± 0.007 % 100 ppm−1  yr−1  (SSP585) (Fig. 1 b and c, Supplementary Fig. 10 ). Such a large-scale and long-term decline in CO2_ WUE  indicates that in the future, the global land surface may experience either a higher risk of water shortage due to higher total evaporation or weakening capacity of the land carbon sink, or both simultaneously, thereby affecting future global cycles of water, carbon and energy.   4 Discussion 4.1 Key role of increasing VPD  in driving global CO2_ WUE  decline VPD  refers to the difference between the actual water vapor pressure in the air and the saturation vapor pressure at a given temperature. As atmospheric CO2  concentrations rise, this often leads to an increase in VPD  due to the associated warming and drying of the air. The VPD  increase may have large implications for the hydrological cycle and ecosystem functioning in terrestrial environments. First, higher VPD  will exacerbate land surface water loss through evaporation and plant transpiration. As the air becomes drier, it can draw more water from the soil and vegetation, enhancing both soil evaporation and leaf-level transpiration. This intensification of terrestrial water loss, particularly in water-limited regions, may exacerbate drought conditions and disrupt regional water budgets. Simulations and experiments both indicate that the increasing effect on ET  generally overwhelms the decreasing effect under the current climate conditions (Grossiord et al., 2020 ) (Fig. 2  d). For instance, field experiments have found that 40 % increases in VPD  can enhance transpiration by 29 % (Will et al., 2013 ). Secondly, the plant's stomatal closure response to elevated VPD  is a key mechanism underlying the observed decline in CO2 _WUE . As VPD  increases, plants tend to close their stomata more extensively to reduce water loss, but this also decreases the uptake of CO2  for photosynthesis. The imbalance between water loss and carbon assimilation results in a decline in water-use efficiency, i.e., more water lost per unit of carbon gained. Furthermore, different plant species and functional types may exhibit varying sensitivities to VPD -induced stomatal regulation, leading to differential responses and potentially driving changes in community composition and ecosystem structure. These shifts in vegetation dynamics can have cascading effects on regional and global biogeochemical cycles, as well as the provision of ecosystem services. All five observational datasets (i.e., HadCRUT4, ERA-interim, MERRA, 20CRv2c and CERA-20C) (Yuan et al., 2019 ) present a significant increasing trend in VPD  (p value < 0.001) during 1982–2015 (Fig. 2 a and Supplementary Fig. 11 , See Method in Supplementary Text S1 ) due to increases in the frequency of droughts (i.e., low actual atmospheric water vapor content) and warming climate (i.e., high saturated water vapor pressure) (Yuan et al., 2019 ), with an average estimated increase of 1.89 ± 0.51 % decade-1 . The seven CMIP6 models all predict that this increase should continue throughout the remainder of the 21st century (Fig. 2 a and Supplementary Fig. 12 ), with increases of 30–33.4 % during 2091–2100 relative to 1982–2015. As the driving force for atmospheric water demand, long-term and large-scale increases in VPD  over 85.5–99.9 % of the Earth’s land surface during 1982–2100 (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12 ) are expected to substantially enhance water losses from the land to the atmosphere (Huang et al., 2015 ), especially in the high northern latitudes where CO2_ WUE  decreased the most, thereby driving the CO2_ WUE  decline. Tight positive linear correlations between VPD  and ET  in the observations (r  = 0.78, p value  < 0.001, Supplementary Fig. 13 a) and also in the predictions (r  = 0.99, p value  < 0.001, Supplementary Figs. 13b–c ), further confirm a strong positive response of ET  to VPD  (i.e., a higher VPD  is normally associated with a higher water loss for carbon sequestration). Simultaneously, increasing VPD  tends to decrease the rate of CO2  diffusion into the leaf by driving stomatal closure (Fig. 2 d), which then decreases the rates of vegetation carbon sequestration, leading to even higher mortality (Sanginés de Cárcer et al., 2018; McDowell et al., 2020 ). Recent studies have indicated that increased VPD  is a primary factor in reducing the global land carbon sink (Yuan et al., 2019; Humphrey et al., 2021 ) and driving recent tree mortality events (Park Williams et al., 2013 ). For instance, simulated evidence has suggested that the global GPP  would decrease by 13.82–18.29 Pg C with a VPD  increase of 0.1 kPa (Yuan et al., 2019 ). Several tree-ring studies also reported that rising VPD  is an important limitation to tree growth at least for current climate conditions (Park Williams et al., 2013; Babst et al., 2019 ). In general, the increase in VPD , which tends to enhance ET and weaken the land carbon sink, plays a key role in driving the global CO2_ WUE  decline, which can also be seen by exploring Equation (4)  (See Method in Supplementary Text S1 ). Equation (4)  describes the coupling between carbon and water in vegetation, where A  and T  are the rate of CO2  assimilation and transpiration, respectively; and ca   and ci   are the ambient and inner leaf partial pressures of CO2  (hPa), respectively. The factor of 1.6 indicates the ratio of molecular diffusion coefficient for H2 O relative to that of CO2 . Decades of controlled experiments (Ainsworth and Rogers, 2007 ) have consistently shown that ci   is proportional to ca  , i.e., ci  /ca   is constant (Medlyn and De Kauwe, 2013 ). Thus, Equation (4)  indicates that increases in ca   will enhance WUE  (i.e. CO2_ WUE ), while increases in VPD  will weaken CO2_ WUE . Interestingly, the increasing rate of VPD  is normally slower than the increasing rate of ca  , i.e., the positive effects of ca   overwhelm the negative effects of VPD , driving the global land towards an increase in WUE ; but the increasing trends decelerate due to the suppression from VPD  (Yuan et a., 2019).(4) WUE = A T  = c a  - c i   1.6 · V P D   = c a  1.6 · V P D   ( 1 - c i  / c a   )      Attention should be paid to the period of 1997–2015 when the CO2_ WUE  experienced a temporary increase (Fig. 1 b), which might be partially caused by the slowdown of VPD  (increasing rates decreased by 53.8 % relative to 1982–1996 based on the HadCRUT4 dataset). To further examine whether changes in CO2_ WUE  can be linked with recent changes in VPD , we investigated the relationship between both factors. Results indicate that the observed global CO2_ WUE  is strongly negatively correlated with VPD  during 1982–2015 for all five datasets (r  = 0.89, p value  < 0.001, Fig. 2 b), i.e., high VPD  normally associates with a low CO2_ WUE . This negative correlation can be seen throughout 66.3 % of the global land surface (Fig. 2 c), implying that increasing VPD  is a strong driver of the global CO2_ WUE  decline. One distinct region is Australia, where CO2_ WUE  increases (Fig. 1 d) might be caused by the decrease in VPD  that relieved the physiological stress on plants. Historical simulated evidence presenting a strong negative relationship between CO2_ WUE  and VPD  for the CMIP6 models (r  = 0.88, p value  < 0.001, Supplementary Fig. 14 a) further indicates a strong constraint of increasing VPD  on the WUE  gains from CO2 . These tight correlations also exist in the mean predictions across CMIP6 models for the period of 2016–2100 (r  = 0.89–0.96, p value  < 0.001, Supplementary Figs. 14b and c ) covering 83.8–93.1 % of the Earth’s terrestrial areas (Supplementary Fig. 15 ). However, VPD  is not the only driver of changing CO2_ WUE , so we also examine the role of nutrient and water availability.  4.2 Effects of limited nutrient availability on the global CO2_ WUE  decline Several studies have suggested that increases in plant biomass in response to increasing CO2  are highly constrained by the insufficient N /P  supply (Reich et al., 2014; Campbell et al., 2017 ) which may limit leaf area and photosynthetic capacity (Reich and Hobbie, 2013 ), driving the CO2_ WUE  decline. However, current evidence indicates that global mean N  deposition presents an increasing trend (Fig. 3  a with a relative increase of 2.51 % decade-1 ) due to the emission of N  compounds from combustion processes (Galloway et al., 2008 ), and that P  deposition has no significant trend (Fig. 3 a and Supplementary Fig. 16 ). During 2016–2100, the twelve CMIP6 models all project substantial increases in soil N  across 77.7 % of the global land surface (1.75 ± 0.87 10-4  kg m−2  yr−1  under SSP370 and 1.37 ± 1.16 10-4  kg m−2  yr−1  under SSP585, Supplementary Fig. 17 ). These continuous increases in nutrients may enhance the rates of vegetation growth and thus carbon sequestration, thereby increasing CO2_ WUE  instead of driving a decrease in global CO2_ WUE . Negative and weak relationships between CO2_ WUE  and N /P  deposition are found at the global scale (Supplementary Fig. 18 ) and in most of the global land surface (r  < 0.4 in 84.2–88.1 % of the globe, Fig. 3 b and c), further emphasizing a relatively weak constraint of nutrient levels on global CO2_ WUE . Even in regions with a decreasing trend of N /P  deposition due to a combination of emission abatement policies and economic transformation (Schmitz et al., 2019 ) (e.g. Europe and Southeastern North America, Supplementary Fig. S16 ), high deposition levels that exceed nutrient‐saturated stage (a critical threshold of nutrient saturation, when nutrient availability exceeds microbial and plant demands) may still meet the demand of nutrients for vegetation growth (Supplementary Fig. S19 ), thereby contributing somewhat to the CO2_ WUE  decline. For instance, the N deposition level in Europe and Southeastern North America (Supplementary Fig. 19 ) already has exceeded the N ‐saturated stage (>800 mg m2  y-1 ), where N  availability exceeds microbial and plant demands (Fleischer et al., 2013 ). By contrast, the CO2_ WUE  decline might be related to limited nutrient availability in the high northern latitudes (low N  deposition levels and a decreasing trend), and tropical forests, i.e., Amazon and Central Africa (low P  deposition levels and a decreasing trend; Fig. 3 b and c). Although the decreasing nutrient availability in these regions may be driving the CO2_ WUE  decline by suppressing GPP,  field experiments have indicated that limited nutrient availability also tends to decrease ET (Zhong and Shangguan, 2014 ) (hence enhancing CO2_ WUE ), which may partly offset the negative effects from GPP . The mechanism is that the insufficient nutrient supply may be limiting further vegetation growth and root production, thereby preventing further soil water from being absorbed by the vegetation. Other nutrients such as potassium, calcium, and magnesium are also essential for vegetation growth. However, there is a lack of comprehensive and long-term observational data on potassium, calcium, and magnesium globally, making it difficult to analyze the impact of their changes on the reduction of CO2_WUE . While nutrients like potassium, calcium, and magnesium are essential for various physiological processes in vegetation, it is unlikely that their availability is the primary driver of the observed global decline in CO2 _WUE .  4.3 Effects of limited water availability on the global CO2_ WUE  decline The disproportionate change in carbon gain and water loss indicates that the response of WUE  to climate change was mainly determined by the acclimation of vegetation carbon, rather than water loss (Huang et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020 ). This indicates that reduced water availability controls the CO2_ WUE  decline mainly by affecting vegetation carbon sequestration. High water stress can decrease rates of photosynthesis, weaken vegetation carbon sequestration and even cause vegetation mortality (Phillips et al., 2009; Reich et al., 2014 ), thereby possibly driving the CO2_ WUE  decline. However, observations from 11 global precipitation data sets (Fig. 3 a and Supplementary Figs. 20a and b ) and simulations from 26 CMIP6 models (Supplementary Figs. 20c to f ) all indicate that global mean precipitation has increased during 1982–2015 (0.14 ± 0.09 % yr−1 ) and that this increase is expected to persist until 2100 (0.11 ± 0.002 % yr−1 ) in most of the Earth’s land surface, especially in the northern high latitudes where CO2_ WUE  decreased the most (see Supplementary Figs. 20d and f ). This continual increase in water supply may thus relieve water stress for vegetation growth, rather than drive the CO2_ WUE  decline. Based on the CFSR and ECV data sets, the slight increase in soil water since 1982 further confirms decreasing water stress for the land carbon sink (see Supplementary Fig. 21 ). Geographical distributions show that poor (p value > 0.05) or negative relationships between CO2_ WUE  and precipitation are found across most of the global land surface (r  < 0.4 in 76.9 % of the globe, Fig. 3 d). Therefore, the changes in water availability are unlikely to be driving the CO2_ WUE  decline in these regions, especially in humid regions (e.g., northern high latitudes and Amazon rainforest) where the land surface is becoming wetter than before (Greve et al., 2014; Donat et al., 2016 ). Attention should be paid to arid regions (e.g., southern regions of the Sahara Desert and Australia) where the land surface has become drier since 1982 and is also experiencing a decline in CO2_ WUE . Limited water availability tends to weaken photosynthesis and decrease rates of carbon sequestration (Wang et al., 2020 ), thereby possibly driving the CO2_ WUE  decline. However, several studies have argued that under water-deficit conditions, plants respond to droughts by partially closing their stomata to reduce water loss via transpiration (Hatfield and Dold, 2019 ). More importantly, the reduction of transpiration is greater than the reduction in carbon sequestration (both due to limited water availability) (Peters et al., 2018 ), thereby leading to an increase in CO2_ WUE . Thereby, although drought is not the dominant driver of the observed decline in CO2 _WUE , drought-induced impacts on plant physiology and function could indeed influence CO2 _WUE  by altering the availability of water and affecting stomatal conductance, which in turn can impact carbon assimilation rates.  4.4 Contribution of potential driving factors to the global CO2_ WUE  decline Using a sensitivity analysis (Jung et al., 2017; Chai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Humphrey et al., 2021 ), we isolated the contributions of potential driving factors (i.e., water availability, nutrient availability, VPD , temperature and net solar radiation, See Method in Supplementary Text S1 ) to the global CO2_ WUE  decline. Since VPD  is highly correlated with temperature and it might be difficult to estimate their respective contribution, we only calculated their total contributions (i.e., VPD  & Tas ) following the method from Humphrey et al., (2021) . Our sensitivity analysis indicates that the observed global CO2_ WUE  decline during 1982–2015 is primarily driven by VPD  & Tas  (74.6 %) across most of the global land surface (Fig. 4  a). By assuming that VPD  and temperature were independent from one another, we further estimated that the VPD  (contributing 42.3 %) contributed roughly the same as temperature (32.3 %) to the observed global CO2_ WUE  decline. However, such a result may substantially underestimate VPD ’s contribution, because partial effects of temperature on CO2_ WUE  are achieved through the VPD  and thus partial contributions of temperature should be attributed to VPD . Therefore, it can be assumed that VPD  indeed dominated the global CO2_ WUE  decline, and is supported by a recent study (Humphrey et al., 2021 ) which also found that VPD  has played a much larger role than temperature in the reduction of global carbon cycles. In contrast, limitations in nutrients and water availability have smaller contributions of 14.0 % and 6.7 %, respectively. Similar to the strong correlation between VPD  and temperature, we also need to analyze whether nutrients and water availability have such a significant correlation relationship, which could influence the calculation of their contribution rates. We found that the correlation between global-scale nutrient deposition and water availability is relatively weak. The global mean correlation coefficient between nitrogen deposition and precipitation is 0.25, and the global mean correlation coefficient between phosphorus deposition and precipitation is 0.22 (Supplementary Fig. 22 ). Therefore, the relationship between nutrients and water availability has a small impact on the calculation of their respective contributions to the global decline in CO2_ WUE . The net solar radiation plays an important role in plant physiological processes. For instance, the rate of increase in global land net solar radiation slowed from 2000 to 2014 (2,344 J m−2  yr−1 , Supplementary Fig. 23 ) compared to the earlier period of 1982–1999 (7,757 J m−2  yr−1 ). This deceleration in the net solar radiation trend during the global dimming period likely played a role in initiating and contributing to the declining trend observed in the CO2 _WUE  metric, especially since the year of 2000. Our analyses have quantified the contribution of net solar radiation to account for 7.7 %-9.1 % of the total declining CO2 _WUE  trend. The relatively small contribution of net solar radiation can likely be attributed to the observed significant increase in global land net solar radiation, which appears to have helped increase the positive effects of elevated CO2  on plant water use efficiency. This would have a tendency to increase plant water use efficiency, making it less plausible that changes in solar radiation were the main driver of the declining CO2 _WUE  trends. In contrast, the substantial increase in VPD  can counteract the positive effects of elevated atmospheric CO2  on plant water use efficiency, as plants may need to close their stomata more frequently to conserve water, thereby reducing CO2  uptake and photosynthesis rates. During 2016–2100, VPD  & Tas  continue to dominate the global CO2_ WUE  decline under both emission scenarios of SSP370 (66.0 %) and SSP585 (70.2 %) across most of the Earth’s land surface, especially in the northern high latitudes (Fig. 4 b and c). By contrast, nutrients availability, water availability and net solar radiation only contribute 10.0–10.3 %, 11.8–15.7 % and 7.7–8.3 %, respectively. Our sensitivity analysis further highlights the dominant role of increasing VPD  generated by warming temperatures in driving spatial–temporal dynamics of CO2_ WUE . This conclusion is consistent with recent studies, which also revealed that increasing VPD  is a primary driving factor both for the reduction of the global land carbon sink (Humphrey et al., 2021 ) and for increases in terrestrial water losses.   5 Implications and conclusions In summary, our analyses reveal a significant downward trend of CO2_ WUE  across most of the global land surface since 1982. Projections suggest this decrease will continue in the coming century. The projected decline implies weakening gains of WUE  in response to the increasing atmospheric CO2 , as well as increased societal dependence on future strategies to mitigate climate warming and water shortages (Wu et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, observed evidence from multiple datasets shows that the global CO2_ WUE  crossed a saturation point in the 1990 s at which gains of WUE  from increasing atmospheric CO2  concentration ceased (i.e., the water required to maintain carbon assimilation rates increased). Crossing this threshold indicates that either total evaporation has increased or gross photosynthetic carbon uptake has decreased, or both have occurred simultaneously, which may enhance risks of water shortages especially in arid regions, and weaken the capacity of the land carbon sink. It should be noted that mid-to-high latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere may become the focal point for future declines in CO2 _WUE . It is recommended to establish a robust regional monitoring network, strengthen data sharing and exchange, and closely track trends in CO2 _WUE  in these regions to support the development of targeted policy responses. Additionally, for these potential hotspot regions, future priority should be given to protecting their key ecosystems, including forests and wetlands, to enhance resilience to climate change and maintain the regional water-carbon balance. As the carbon sequestration capacity per unit of water consumption declines, more water resources will be required to achieve the same level of carbon absorption. This will increase pressure on water resources and exacerbate risks of water scarcity in water-stressed regions. These regions should be research priorities, optimizing future regional water resource management. Measures such as differentiated water use limits and improved irrigation technologies should be developed based on the characteristics of each region, to enhance water use efficiency and ensure sustainable regional water resource utilization. Increasing VPD  is identified as the dominant driving factor for the global CO2_ WUE  decline, by enhancing water losses from the land to the atmosphere through atmospheric water demand and weakening rates of vegetation carbon sequestration by causing stomatal closure. In contrast, the increasing availability of water and nutrients both display poor relationships with CO2_ WUE , and represent only secondary effects. These results highlight the key role of VPD  in driving CO2_ WUE , which is central to the global cycles of water, energy and carbon. Close attention should be paid to the CMIP6 models and the TRENDY-v9 models, as they still fail to adequately capture observed fluctuations in global CO2_ WUE . The substantial underestimation of the CO2_ WUE  decline by the models possibly originates from their limitations in adequately representing the constraints of VPD  on vegetation dynamics. Thereby, it is recommended to further strengthen research on the mechanisms driving CO2 _WUE  changes, particularly the impacts of VPD  variations and their effects on vegetation carbon sequestration. This will help improve the simulation capabilities of the next generation of climate-carbon cycle models, providing more reliable scientific evidence to support policy decisions. In addition to the multiple regression analysis approach for calculating CO2_ WUE , other potential analytical approaches include: 1). Field observations, setting up long-term monitoring plots under different environmental conditions to measure the responses of plants to changes in CO2  levels. 2). Experimental studies, conducting artificial CO2  enrichment experiments in controlled settings to quantify the impact of increased CO2  on the terrestrial carbon sink. 3). Model simulation, using process-based ecosystem models to simulate the CO2_ WUE , and calibrating and validating the models with observational data to provide important insights into the underlying mechanisms. 4). Machine learning, employing techniques like neural networks and random forests with multi-source observational data to explore the non-linear patterns of CO2 _WUE  changes. These alternative approaches could supplement the multiple regression analysis in future work to provide a comprehensive assessment of the CO2_ WUE .
1 Introduction Cyanobacterial blooms have become a serious environmental issue in freshwater lakes over the past few decades (Qin et al., 2015 ). With rapid urbanization and increased human activities, the discharge of pollutants, especially nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), into lakes has exacerbated severe eutrophication problems and accelerates the cyanobacterial blooms(Sun et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Under suitable hydro-meteorological conditions, cyanobacteria can proliferate rapidly, forming cyanobacterial blooms (Ranjbar et al., 2022 ). These blooms can lead to a significant deterioration in water quality, threatening aquatic life and even posing health risks to humans (Chen et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2016 ). The decomposition of cyanobacteria bloom biomass (CBB) by heterotrophic bacteria can consume oxygen, causing hypoxia or anaerobic conditions in the water column, and in severe cases black water phenomenon – the so called black blooms (Fan, 2015 ). The occurrence of black blooms will not only turn the water column black, but also release N, P, organic matter, odor, causing the water quality to deteriorate, seriously threatening the safety of drinking water and aquatic ecosystems (Cao et al., 2020 ). In May 2007, a severe black bloom event occurred near the intake of the Wuxi Gonghu Water Plant, leading to a drinking water crisis lasting several days (Wang et al., 2011 ). The occurrence of black blooms has drawn the attention of numerous scholars both domestically and internationally. Previous studies have shown that the formation of black blooms is related to cyanobacterial blooms outbreaks, aggregating and death under specific meteorological and hydrological conditions (Fan, 2015; Wang et al., 2011 ). In the past, researchers studied the meteorological and hydrological conditions during the black blooms over the past few years. Several consecutive days of relative high temperatures, low wind speeds, near-zero rainfall, and significant accumulation of CBB were important meteorological and hydrological conditions for the formation of black blooms (Duan et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016 ). On the contrary, heavy rainfall, sudden drop in temperature, and strong winds are the driving factors for the disappearance of black blooms (Zhang et al., 2016 ). However, the impact of hydrodynamic disturbances on the formation and disappearance of black blooms remains poorly understood. Microbial communities are important components of aquatic ecosystems, and different community compositions endow them with different functions (Trevathan-Tackett et al., 2021 ). Microorganisms participate in the biogeochemical cycles in sediments, including the cycles of elements such as C, Fe, S, N, and P, and play an important role in maintaining the stability of the ecosystem (Du et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2020; Zhuo et al., 2023 ). The decomposition of CBB by microbial communities also drives the formation of black blooms (Fan, 2015 ). Anaerobic bacteria decompose organic matter into small molecules, producing sulfur compounds, sulfur ions and H2 S, which make the water black and emit odors (Feng et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2016 ). The difference of hydrodynamic conditions can affect the assembly and function of microbial communities, leading to variations in organic matter degradation and energy transfer (Fang et al., 2017; Samson et al., 2019 ). Therefore, it can be expected that different hydrodynamic conditions would drive the occurrence of black blooms by influencing the composition and function of microbial communities. Sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) are a group of anaerobic microorganisms widely present in lake and river sediments that can reduce sulfate through dissimilatory processes (Pester, 2012; Rabus et al., 2015 ). Studies have found that SRB are commonly present in sediments of areas occur black blooms or black-odorous, and their abundance is positively correlated with the darkness of the algal blooms (Duval and Ludlam, 2001; Fan, 2015; Feng et al., 2014 ). Previous research has found that during the development of black blooms, SRB play specific roles in bacterial networks at different stages of the blooms, establishing various interactions with other microorganisms by altering their metabolic activity (Chen et al., 2022a; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Hydrodynamic disturbances can alter the microbial community composition by affecting the availability of resources and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the sediments, and can also impact the abundance of obligate anaerobic microorganisms such as SRB (Chen et al., 2022b; Huettel et al., 2014; Probandt et al., 2017 ). Therefore, it seems reasonable to assume hydrodynamic disturbances affect the metabolic activities of SRB and their interaction with other microorganisms at different stages of black blooms in sediments. Here, we studied the impact of hydrodynamic disturbance on the formation and disappearance of black blooms, as well as the impact on the composition of the microbial community and the transformation of the functions of SRB in sediments related to the formation of black blooms. From June to July 2022, in-situ research was conducted on the black bloom in the Fudu Port area of Zhushan Bay in Lake Taihu, and the change process of hydrodynamic disturbance intensity during the study period was simulated. By conducting physicochemical parameter analysis on water and sediment samples collected during the study period, as well as the sequencing of sediment 16S rRNA gene amplicons, the study aimed to investigate changes in water quality during the black bloom and alterations in the composition and functionality of microbial communities in the sediment. The objectives of this study were: (1) to investigate the relationship between hydrodynamic disturbance and the concentration of anaerobic substances in the black bloom, (2) to examine the driving role of disturbance on changes in microbial community composition and functional abundance during the occurrence of black bloom, and (3) to explore the processes driving the disturbance on the transformation of SRB bacterial activities and the interactions between SRB and other relevant bacteria.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Water and sediment sampling Lake Taihu is the third-largest freshwater lake in China, with an average depth of 1.9 m and a surface area of approximately 2338 square kilometers (Qin et al., 2007 ). Over the past few decades, Lake Taihu has experienced frequent issues with cyanobacterial blooms and occurrences of black blooms. On June 15, 2022, a large-scale accumulation of cyanobacterial blooms, appearing brown in color, was observed in the Fudu Port area of Zhushan Bay (31°25′N, 120°01′E). Sediment samples were collected from three locations using a gravity corer immediately after the observation. All samples were preserved with dry ice and promptly transported to the laboratory for analysis. On June 18, surface water samples were collected below the surface (50 cm depth) using an organic glass water sampler at three points: F1, F2, and F3, totaling 5 L per sampling point. A YSI water quality meter was used for in-site measurements of dissolved oxygen (DO), water temperature (WT), and pH. The water samples were sent to the laboratory for analysis, and all chemical analyses of water quality were completed within 24 h after sampling, including permanganate index (CODMn), chemical oxygen demand chromium (CODCr), ammonia nitrogen (NH4 + -N), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and phytoplankton biomass (PM). Subsequent surveys used the same methods for sample collection and analysis on June 18, 20, 21, 24, and July 8 and 12. Surface sediment samples were collected on June 15, 18, 21, 24, and July 8 and 12.  2.2 Chemical analytical methods WT, pH, and DO were measured in situ using a multifunctional water quality parameter meter. According to the technical specifications of the 'Methods for Monitoring and Analysis of Water and Wastewater', TN was determined using the alkaline potassium persulfate digestion ultraviolet spectrophotometric method, NH4 + -N was determined using the Nessler's reagent spectrophotometric method, and TP was determined using the molybdenum antimony anti-spectrophotometric method. PM was measured according to the technical specifications outlined in the 'Technical Regulations for the Monitoring of Phytoplankton in Inland Waters' (SL733-2016).  2.3 Hydrodynamic model The FVCOM model was employed in this study for the simulation and calculation of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) based on a three-dimensional hydrodynamic model. The FVCOM model discretizes the original Navier-Stokes (NS) equations using the finite volume method, employing an unstructured triangular mesh in the horizontal direction (Chen et al., 2006 ). The computational domain covered the entire region of Lake Taihu, with grid refinement near the shores and islands. The model was initialized from a cold start, and the wind field forcing data were derived from the land-enhanced reanalysis dataset of the Fifth Generation European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ERA5) (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2019 ). As the hydrodynamics in Lake Taihu are primarily driven by wind-induced currents, this study temporarily excluded the consideration of river boundary inputs. In-situ current speed data was measured by Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers (ADCP) at ZSH1 (31°24.146′E, 120°0.900′N) and ZSH2 (31°22.627′E, 120°1.422′N) from 30 September to 11 October.  2.4 DNA sequencing and statistical analysis Microbial DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A. Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-Tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.). The V3-V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified by PCR, using primers 341F 5′- CCTAYGGGRBGCASCAG-3′ and 806R 5′- GGACTACNNGGGTATCTAAT-3′. Amplicons were extracted from 2 % agarose gels and purified using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen Biosciences, Union City, CA, U.S.) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The purified PCR products were sequenced (2 * 250 bp) on an Illumina platform (Shanghai BIOZERON Bidtech. Co., Ltd.) according to the standard protocols. Illumina sequencing data was analyzed using QIIME 1.8.0 software (Caporaso et al., 2010 ). All the microbial community analyses were conducted with R software version 4.3.1 (Makowski et al., 2019 ), Gephi software version 0.10 (Bastian et al., 2009 ) and FAPROTAX software (Louca et al., 2016 ).   3 Results 3.1 Changes in water quality during black bloom Fig. 1   illustrates the changes in water quality indicators during the investigation of black blooms in 2022. WT ranged from 29.4 to 33.2 ℃, showing a significant decrease after June 21 and a rise to relatively high levels after July 8, with only minor differences among the three sampling points. The pH values reached the lowest on June 24, with sites F1, F2, and F3 being 6.94, 7.31, and 7.38, respectively. After July 8, there was a rapid increase in the pH of F2 and F3, reaching 9.4 and 9.24, respectively (Fig. 1 b). Similar to the trend in pH, DO reached their lowest on June 24. F2 and F3 showed a significant rebound in the later period, but F3 exhibited a peak value on June 21 (Fig. 1 c). Interestingly, during the investigation, there was a high consistency in the variation trends of CODMn, CODCr, NH4 + -N, TN, and TP values (Fig. 1 d, e, f, g, h). F1 exhibited higher peaks, occurring on June 24, while F2 and F3 tended to show a bimodal characteristic, appearing on June 20 and June 24, respectively. The PM at F1 was higher than at F2 and F3, reaching 1560 mg/L on June 24, while F2 and F3 were an order of magnitude smaller, reaching higher values on June 19th and 18th, at 346 and 380 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 1 i).  3.2 Validation of hydrodynamic model and turbulence analysis The hydrodynamic model was calibrated and validated using the measured vertically averaged current speed. The FVCOM model showed better simulation of current speed at the ZSH2 point, with average error (AE), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0164, 0.0186, and 0.0235 m/s, respectively (Fig. 2  ). For the ZSH1 point, these values were 0.0173, 0.0180, and 0.0223 m/s, respectively. From the simulation results, it appeared that the model tended to underestimate the current speed when wind speeds were relatively low and became more accurate when wind speeds were relatively higher. In summary, the simulated results of the model could be used to characterize the hydrodynamic conditions in the region of Zhushan Bay. Based on in-situ observations of the black bloom, we categorized its development into three stages, where ES represents the early stage, MS represents the middle stage, and LS represents the late stage or recovery stage. Fig. 3   presents our simulated results of the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), an index of hydrodynamic turbulence intensity, for these three stages. Through the Wilcox test, it was found that there was significant overall difference among the three stages (p < 0.05). In ES, the upper quartile, median, and lower quartiles of TKE values were 0.000028242, 0.000024014, and 0.000012523 m2 ⋅s−2 , respectively. In MS, they were 0.000072898, 0.000061788, and 0.000010488 m2 ⋅s−2 , and in LS, they were 0.000015665, 0.0000076078, and 0.0000043022 m2 ⋅s−2 , respectively. Among the three stages, the MS had the highest mean TKE value, which was 159.28 % higher than that of the ES. The LS had the lowest mean TKE value, decreasing by 73.81 % compared to MS and 32.10 % lower than ES. Although TKE showed no significant correlation with water quality indicators in the water column (p > 0.05), correlation coefficients indicated a certain degree of correlation between TKE and NH4 + -N, TN, and TP, with coefficients of 0.29, 0.24, and 0.26, respectively (Fig. S1 ).  3.3 Top 10 microbial abundances and spatiotemporal patterns of the microbial community A total of 5971 bacterial Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) were observed in sediment, encompassing 58 phylum-level and 897 genus-level taxonomic classifications. At the phylum level (Fig. 4  a), the highest abundance was observed in Proteobacteria  (50.62 %), followed by Firmicutes  (14.92 %), Bacteroidota  (7.86 %), Chloroflexi  (6.51 %), Acidobacteriota  (5.13 %), Desulfobacterota  (3.26 %), Actinobacteriota  (3.16 %), and Nitrospirota  (2.07 %). During the observation, Proteobacteria  dominated the bacterial community in the sediment. At the genus level (Fig. 4 b), Acinetobacter  was the most abundant bacteria (31.33 %), followed by family Steroidobacteraceae  (5.65 %), Exiguobacterium  (3.10 %), family Anaerolineaceae  (2.34 %), and family Sutterellaceae  (2.13 %). In order to identify microbial community differences under different turbulence levels, we employed alpha diversity analysis and principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). Significant differences were observed in alpha diversity analysis between ES and MS (Fig. 5  ), as well as between ES and LS (p < 0.05), however, no significant difference was found between MS and LS (p > 0.05). The results of the Simpson diversity index indicated that microbial community diversity was higher in ES, with a Simpson mean value of 0.9493. In MS, community diversity reached its lowest, with a Simpson mean value of 0.9861. By LS, there was some recovery in community diversity, and the Simpson mean value decreased to 0.9763. At different turbulence levels, microbial communities exhibited significant differences (Fig. 6  ) (ANOSIM, R = 0.477, p < 0.05), where PCoA 1 explained 35.28 % of the variation, and PCoA 2 explained 23.79 %.
