There is no significant difference in pH between Groups I and II during the wet, dry and normal seasons. The water temperatures and EC of Group I are significantly higher than those of Group II in all three seasons, and both Groups I and II have relatively high EC compared to other karst rivers in lower urbanized region. In WWTP effluents water temperature average of 21.50±0.72 °C (varied from 20.0 to 23.0 °C) and EC values are higher on average 729.50±109.95 μs/cm (varied from 629 to 1125 μs/cm). DO levels in the water of Group I are significantly lower than that in Group II during wet season, while DO in WWTP effluents average of 5.42±1.79 mg/L (varied from 0.33 to 7.41 mg/L). Moreover, Group I exhibits significantly higher levels of TN and TP in comparison to Group II, and the concentration of DOC in Group I is also significantly higher than in Group II during the dry season (Supplementary Table S2 ).  4.2 Composition of water chemistry The average concentrations of cations and anions in the river water generally follow the order of Ca2+  (92.83±21.69 mg L−1 ) > Mg2+  (17.10±6.45 mg L−1 ) > Na+  (16.97±9.76 mg L−1 ) > K+  (9.10±4.22 mg L−1 ), and HCO3 −  (195.81±44.57 mg L−1 ) > SO4 2−  (105.06±30.94 mg L−1 ) > NO3 −  (18.57±10.85 mg L−1 ) > Cl−  (16.94±11.61 mg L−1 ). Ca2+  and HCO3 −  as main ions in river water, accounting for approximately 69±3 % of the total cations and 58±3 % of the total anions, respectively, and the Piper diagram shows HCO3 − Ca as the dominant hydrochemical type in the Nanming River basin (Supplementary Fig. S1 ). On the whole, the concentration of major ions (except Cl− ) in the Nanming River basin decreased in the order of dry season > wet season > normal season due to the dilution effect. The concentrations of K+ , Na+ , Mg2+ , Cl− , and NO3 −  in Group I show significantly higher than those in Group II in the three seasons (Table 1 ). Interestingly, the concentrations of those ions are also relatively high in WWTP effluents (K+  average of 17.45±5.68 mg L−1 , Na+  average of 53.60±27.93 mg L−1 , Mg2+  average of 21.42±4.21 mg L−1 , Cl−  average of 55.80±26.23 mg L−1 , NO3 −  average of 24.90±9.86 mg L−1 ) (Supplementary Table S1 ), which reflects that the hydrochemical characteristic of Group I is influenced by WWTP effluents. In addition, the HCO3 −  concentration of Group I also characterized significantly higher than Group II during wet and normal seasons. Nevertheless, both Group I and Group II have higher ion concentrations when compared with karst rivers in lower urbanized region (Table 1 ). Fig. 2   shows the spatial variation in Ca2+ , HCO3 −  and δ13 CDIC  values in river water during the three seasons. In the wet season, high concentrations of Ca2+  and HCO3 −  are scattered in the eastern and western rivers. During the dry season, high concentrations of Ca2+  and HCO3 −  are mainly concentrated in the Nanming River, in addition, the eastern tributaries are also generally distributed with high concentrations of HCO3 − , such as the Toubao River. In the normal season, lower concentrations of Ca2+  and HCO3 −  are generally distributed across the rivers in the study area, except for a few high concentrations of Ca2+  and HCO3 −  distributed in the southern region. Furthermore, there is a significant response of the spatial variation of K+ , Na+ , and Cl−  concentrations to the discharge of WWTP effluents. The key manifestation is that the concentrations are low upstream of the Nanming River mainstream and gradually increase downstream upon receiving WWTP effluents, whereas the eastern tributaries consistently show low concentrations (Supplementary Fig. S2 ).  4.3 Isotopic signature of DIC The δ13 CDIC  values of river water exhibit a wide range, from −12.53 to −4.64 ‰, with an average of −9.18±1.46 ‰, which is obviously higher than that of the WWTP effluents (mean: −11.84±0.93 ‰) (Supplementary Table S1 ). During dry season, Group I exhibit significantly higher δ13 CDIC  values than Group I (Table 1 ). Seasonally, the δ13 CDIC  values range from −11.74 to −4.84 ‰ during the wet season, from −12.53 to −8.41 ‰ during the dry season, and from −11.92 to −4.64 ‰ during the normal season, the mean values of δ13 CDIC  decreased in the order of normal season (average of −7.95±1.40 ‰) > wet season (average of −9.45±1.05 ‰) > dry season (average of −10.10±0.95 ‰). Spatially (Fig. 2 ), the scale of variation in δ13 CDIC  is small for each river during the wet season, except for the higher δ13 CDIC  values distributed in the partial tributaries and the lower δ13 CDIC  values distributed in the eastern region. During the dry season, lower δ13 CDIC  values are frequently observed in the Toubao River and Dazhai River. The Nanming River and its tributaries in the west show relatively high δ13 CDIC  values than its tributaries in the east. In general, higher δ13 CDIC  values are dispersed in the study area during the normal season. In the Nanming River, its midstream has relatively low δ13 CDIC  values compared to the upstream and downstream.   5 Discussion 5.1 Dynamics of riverine p CO2  following reception of WWTP effluents To test our initial hypothesis − WWTP effluents discharge is one of the main factors contributing to increased p CO2  levels in streams in highly urbanized areas −, we illustrate a folded plot of the variation of p CO2  levels with river distance based on the Nanming River mainstream affected by WWTP effluents discharge (Fig. 3  ). The p CO2  level in the river water is generally higher than that of the atmospheric (420 µatm) during all three seasons, indicating that the Nanming River is CO2  source to the atmosphere (Fig. 3 ). Upstream of each WWTP effluents confluence, the p CO2  for three seasons is characterized by a gradual decrease with distance, this is likely related to the fact that the headwater usually has a faster flow rate, which favors the formation of turbulence (Billett and Harvey 2012; Wallin et al., 2011 ). Since stream p CO2  also responds to discharge, which tends to increase the gas transfer velocity via surface turbulence (Demars and Manson 2013; Dristi and Xu 2023 ). With the WWTP effluents entering the river, p CO2  exhibits pulsatile characteristics. During the wet season, the midstream has a relatively smaller change in p CO2  after receiving WWTP effluents, which may be due to high rainfall and large influx of tributaries (low p CO2 ) into the mainstem, while the size of the riverine CO2  pool will determine the CO2  concentration gradient at the water–air interface (Duvert et al., 2018 ). In contrast, during the dry and normal seasons, midstream p CO2  showed a clear increasing trend after receiving the WWTP effluents, and subsequently showed a clear decreasing trend. This may have been related to the construction of several dams in the mid- and downstream reaches for the purpose of urban flood control, as they can change the morphology and flow pattern of the river. This morphological change can strongly influence the runoff generation and flow turbulence, thereby affecting the aquatic boundary layer (which forms on surfaces immersed in moving fluids through the action of fluid viscosity, with boundary layer conditions being the most pervasive physical influence on the biology of many aquatic organisms), enhancing gas exchange at the water–gas interface (Marx et al., 2017 ), leading to more CO2  escaping into the atmosphere. The dry season of Supplementary Fig. S3  further demonstrates this fluctuation tendency, where the p CO2  of the river water showed a gradual decreasing trend as the distance (ΔL) from the WWTP outfalls increased, and the difference of the river water p CO2  (Δp CO2 ) diminish gradually. Conversely, the tendency of p CO2  fluctuation in wet and normal seasons may have been upset by heavy rainfall and active biological activity (section 5.3 ). Moreover, biological photosynthesis and respiration are also important factors affecting river p CO2  (Herath et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2007 ). WWTP effluents can indirectly influence river p CO2  fluctuation by enhancing photosynthesis and/or respiration. This is because the WWTP effluents discharge large amounts of nutrients and organic carbon into the river, and the increase of nutrients have been found to promote the growth of phytoplankton and increase photosynthesis (Zhang et al., 2023a, Zhang et al., 2023b ); on the other hand, the death of phytoplankton will increase organic carbon in the sediment and thus increase respiration (Upadhyay et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). Fig. 4   illustrate these processes, specifically, TP and TN both demonstrated a significant positive connection with p CO2  during the normal season and the dry season, respectively. In contrast, TN/TP was not significantly correlated with p CO2  during the wet season and DOC was not significantly correlated with p CO2  during the three seasons. This could be attributed to two main factors: On the one hand, high and fast river flows during wet season make nutrient concentrations low and retention times short, and the efficiency of aquatic plants in utilizing nutrients is greatly reduced (Zeng and Jiang 2016 ); On the other hand, the disproportionate inputs of p CO2  and DOC in WWTP effluents and the CO2  produced by respiration and consumed by photosynthesis may collectively determine that DOC was not significantly correlated with p CO2  (Wang et al., 2023 ). This therefore highlights the fact that in urban river reaches WWTP effluents discharge is an important factor causing a rise of riverine p CO2 .  5.2 Influence of WWTP effluents on rock weathering end-members discrimination The ion molar ratios of mineral dissolution products in different types of rocks are different and thus can be distinguished using the relevant ion ratio relationships (Jiang 2013 ). For instance, Gaillardet and others (1999) compiled global rivers HCO3 −  and Ca2+  and Mg2+  to Na+  concentration ratios, and compared the values with the silicate, carbonate, and evaporite end-members of weathering. We have expanded upon this by adding the WWTP effluents end-member and found that this is relatively similar to the end-member of the weathering of silicate rocks (Fig. 5  a and b). The river water samples of the three seasons mainly fall between the three end-members of weathering of carbonate rocks, weathering of silicate rocks and WWTP effluents, with Group I being nearer to the WWTP effluents and silicate rock weathering end-member compared to Group II. Nonetheless, this does not equate to the contribution of silicate weathering and WWTP effluents to riverine DIC is comparable. First of all, there are only a few clastic rocks distributed in part of the Nanming River Basin (Fig. 1 a), which are dominated by quartz and clay minerals, and the content of feldspar minerals is less than 1 % (Cao 2012 ). Secondly, the weathering rate of silicate minerals is much lower than that of carbonate minerals (Xiong et al., 2022 ). Moreover, in this study, the average Ca2+ /Na+  of the river water samples in the three seasons is 4.07±2.31, the average Mg2+ /Na+  is 1.17±0.65 and the average HCO3 − /Na+  is 5.53±2.92, all much greater than the Na normalized molar of the end-members of granitic silicate rocks ratio: 0.35±0.15 for Ca2+ /Na+ , 0.24±0.12 for Mg2+ /Na+ , and 2±1 for HCO3 − /Na+  (Gaillardet et al., 1999 ). These results indicate that silicate rock weathering has marginal influence on DIC in the Nanming River basin. Consequently, cautions should be paid while interpreting the end-members of rock weathering by the anion ratios of river water samples, especially these collected from city rivers. (Ⅰ) Natural conditions:(2) C a x  M g 1 - x      C O 3  + C O 2  + H 2  O → x C a 2 +   + 1 - x    M g 2 +   + 2 H C O 3 -      (3) CaA l 2  S i 2  O 8  + N a A l S i 3  O 8  + 2 C O 2  + 4 H 2  O → C a 2 +   + N a +  + 3 H C O 3 -  + 5 S i O 2  + 3 A l OH    3      (Ⅱ) Anthropogenic impact:(4) 3 ( C a x  M g 1 - x   ) C O 3  + H 2  S O 4  + H N O 3  → 3 x C a 2 +   + 3 1 - x   M g 2 +   + 3 H C O 3 -  + S O 4 2 -   + N O 3 -      In addition to being influenced by natural carbonic acid, the chemical weathering of carbonate rocks is generally affected by exogenous acid (sulfuric and nitric acids) discharged from human activities, such as processes of fossil fuel combustion, agricultural fertilization, etc. (Xie et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021 ). Meanwhile, the WWTP effluents also shows the relatively higher concentrations of nitrate and sulfate with lower pH (Supplementary Table S1 ), which may have had impact on the dissolution of carbonate. Under natural conditions, theoretical HCO3 − /(Ca2+ +Mg2+ ) for the weathering process of carbonatite (Eq. (2)  and silicate rocks (Eq. (3)  is 2:1 and 3:1, respectively. Under anthropogenic impact, the HCO3 − /(Ca2+ +Mg2+ ) for the weathering process of carbonate rocks (Eq. (4)  is theoretically 1:1. Fig. 5 c shows that most of the river water samples in the three seasons fall between the 1:1 line and 2:1 line, and away from the 3:1 line, which further indicates that the DIC is affected by carbonic acid and exogenous acid combined dissolving carbonate rocks. Part of the river water samples falls below the 1:1 line, indicating a characteristic high concentration of Ca2+  or Mg2+ , which may be related to the dissolution of evaporated salt minerals of sulfate (e.g., gypsum) (Lang et al., 2006 ). The K+ /HCO3 −  and Na+ /HCO3 −  values of carbonate rock weathering is low due to the almost complete absence of K+  and Na+  in carbonate rocks. According to Fig. 5 d, it is clear that carbonate rock weathering dominates rock weathering processes in the Nanming River basin, however, under influence of the WWTP effluents, the K+ /HCO3 −  and Na+ /HCO3 −  values of water samples in Group I are relatively higher than Group II.  5.3 Geochemical processes of DIC within urbanized karst river In all seasons, HCO3 −  concentrations and δ13 CDIC  in the Nanming River mainstream showed poor or no significant correlation (Fig. 4 ), which is mainly related to the presence of complex geochemical processes in the river system, including carbonate dissolution, degradation of organic matter, coupled photosynthesis/respiration cycles, and CO2  outgassing processes, etc. (Battin et al., 2023; Herath et al., 2022; Liu and Han 2020 ). Due to the difference in DIC behavior driven by different geochemical processes, changes in its dominant process during different hydrological seasons often mask the effects of other processes on HCO3 −  concentrations and δ13 CDIC  signals and result in high spatiotemporal variability (Marx et al., 2017 ). Therefore, a model relationship based on the evolutionary pattern of DIC concentration versus δ13 CDIC  was established, and a plot of DIC concentration and δ13 CDIC  was developed (Fig. 6  ) to better explain and discern the geochemical processes controlling DIC and δ13 CDIC  in karst river waters under the influence of WWTP effluents (Wang et al., 2019 ). The specific computation formula was described as follows:(5) Δ DIC  = D I C ( i )   - D I C ( 1 )      Δ [ δ 13  C D I C   ] = δ 13  C D I C ( i )   - δ 13  C D I C ( 1 )          where Δ[DIC] and Δ[δ13 CDIC ] represent the difference between the HCO3 −  concentration and δ13 CDIC  at any Nanming River mainstream water sampling site i and the HCO3 −  concentration and δ13 CDIC  at the corresponding hydrological season headwaters sampling site 1, respectively. HCO3 −  concentration and δ13 CDIC  at sampling site 1 were 3.22 mmol/L and −9.96 ‰ in wet season, 3.28 mmol/L and −9.25 ‰ in dry season, and 3.54 mmol/L and −8.50 ‰ in normal season. 5.3.1 Carbonate dissolution The river water samples during the wet season mainly fall in quadrant (a) (Fig. 6 ), suggesting that the carbonate dissolution path I dominates the signal changes of DIC and δ13 CDIC  in the river water. In urbanized karst rivers, besides WWTP effluents inputs, DIC in the raw river water is mainly derived from the dissolution of carbonate rocks (Samanta et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022 ). CO2(aq)  and exogenous acids control the dissolution of carbonate minerals (Eqs. (2) and (4) . Increased precipitation during the wet season would runoff soil CO2  and transport it into the river water (Zhang et al., 2019 ), accelerating the large-scale dissolution of carbonate minerals, which is suggested by the positive correlation between Ca2+  and HCO3 −  during the wet season (Fig. 4 ). Previous research has indicated that marine carbonates typically have a more positive δ13 C (Galy and France-Lanord 1999 ). Shang et al., 2015  reported a high δ13 C value for Late Permian to Early Triassic carbonate rocks in the Guiyang area, with an average of about 0.96 ‰. Thus, the more dissolution of carbonate rocks, the relative higher the δ13 CDIC  value could found in the river water, However, excessive soil CO2  inputs can also cause elevated pCO2  in river waters, resulting in a negative correlation between SI c values and p CO2 , which is also seen in our study (Fig. 4 ).  5.3.2 CO2  outgassing and biological primary production Globally, most rivers exhibit higher levels of p CO2  than the atmosphere, such as the Amazon (Borges et al., 2015 ), the Mississippi River (Reiman and Xu 2019 ), and the Yellow River (Ran et al., 2015 ). In this study, the Nanming River mainstream p CO2  values are essentially higher than the atmosphere (Fig. 3 ), and isotopic fractionation occurs during the release of CO2  from the river to the atmosphere (Halas et al., 1997; Schulte et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 1995 ), resulting in enrichment of 13 C in the residual DIC and a decrease in DIC concentration. In Fig. 6 , most of the river water samples from the normal season fall in quadrant (b), indicating that DIC and δ13 CDIC  are influenced by biological primary production (photosynthesis) in addition to CO2  outgassing. Prior studies have shown that photosynthesis increases with increasing water temperature (Atekwana and Krishnamurthy 1998; Peter et al., 2014 ), and Chlorophyceae  are often observed during the warm season (Gamier et al., 1995 ). Nanming River mainstream has abundant aquatic plants, with a total of 31 species of advanced aquatic plants, including Potamogeton , Ceratophyllum , Myriopyllum , and Alternanthera  (Qin et al., 2007 ), field investigations have revealed that the mainstem of the Nanming river is covered with 80 % submerged plants (Supplementary Fig. S4 ). Both the moderate water temperature (17 °C) and slow flow (12.1 m3 /s) during the normal season favored photosynthesis, with more CO2(aq)  being taken up by aquatic plants and preferentially taking up lighter 12 C, producing more dissolved oxygen in water body (Dubois et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Thus, strong photosynthesis of aquatic plants during the normal season results in a decrease of DIC concentrations and p CO2  in the river water and an increase of δ13 CDIC , DO, and pH values, along with calcium carbonate precipitates (SI c > 0) (Fig. 6  quadrant (c)). The correlation analysis during the normal season fully confirms this observation (Fig. 4 ), in addition Ca2+  and HCO3 −  also show a significant positive correlation during the normal season, highlighting the significant contribution of carbonate rock dissolution to riverine DIC. As for the lack of carbonate dissolution signals during the normal season in Fig. 6 , this is most likely due to the combination of CO2  outgassing and strong photosynthesis processes that obscure the signature of DIC and δ13 CDIC  variations induced by carbonate dissolution.  5.3.3 Degradation of organic matter and respiration In the dry season, the majority of our river water samples fall within quadrant (d) (Fig. 6 ), suggesting that organic matter degradation and respiration processes are the dominant factors affecting river water DIC and δ13 CDIC . The low amount of rainfall during the dry season in the study area leads to a relatively high proportion of WWTP effluents in the Nanming River mainstream. It is well known that wastewater treatment processes tend to convert large amounts of organic carbon (OC) into DIC (similar to the organic matter degradation process) and, thus, the effluents δ13 CDIC  value is closely related with the δ13 C value of the influent degradable OC (Liu et al., 2019 ). In a recent study, Lee et al., 2023  reported that OC δ13 C values in residential WWTP effluents had a narrow and negative range of −28 ‰ to –22 ‰. Consequently, wastewater treatment processes can cause effluents DIC concentrations to increase and δ13 CDIC  to become relatively more depleted similar to OC (Hullar et al., 1996; Li et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023b ). In fact, the Nanming River mainstream receives WWTP effluents throughout the year; but, the impact of the organic matter degradation process is inadequately presented in Fig. 6  during the wet and normal seasons, presumably because the strong response of carbonate dissolution during the wet season and photosynthesis during the normal season obscure the signal of organic matter degradation. Variations in biogeochemical process responses across hydrological seasons may be attributed to dynamic flow changes (Dinsmore et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2014 ). In this study, the average water temperature was 14.2 °C during the cold dry season, which led to a decrease in surface photosynthesis and a gradual domination of respiration (Atekwana and Krishnamurthy 1998; Wang et al., 2019 ). During respiration, aquatic organisms absorb more dissolved oxygen and preferentially release 12 C into the river (Doctor et al., 2008; Herath et al., 2022 ), consequently, this leads to an increase in DIC concentration and p CO2  in the river water, while δ13 CDIC , DO and pH values decrease, and calcium carbonate dissolves (SI c < 0). Fig. 4  demonstrates support for this statement, even though the negative correlation between CO2(aq) , p CO2 , and δ13 CDIC  is weak during the dry season. Additionally, quadrant (d) in Fig. 6  illustrates the process of carbonatite dissolution path II, which suggests that the generated DIC will further participate in the carbonatite dissolution within the watershed as H2 CO3  (Huang et al., 2022 ), and those DIC are derived from either WWTP effluents or respiration. However, the positive δ13 C value of carbonate rocks cause a slower decrease in δ13 CDIC  of carbonate dissolution path II with an increase in DIC concentration. Therefore, it can be inferred that both WWTP effluents and respiration significantly contribute to DIC in river water during the dry season, resulting in the δ13 CDIC  depletion in river water.   5.4 Contribution of WWTP effluents to riverine DIC In the light of the foregoing discussion, it becomes clear that karst rivers in highly urbanized areas are significantly impacted by the high DIC concentrations found in WWTP effluents. To quantify the contribution of DIC from WWTP effluents, an end-member mixing model was developed using the average Cl−  concentration of the raw river water (i.e., upstream river water sampling sites 1–5, which were not affected by WWTP effluents) and WWTP effluents in the Nanming River mainstream. Based on the Eq. (1) , the calculated percentage contribution of the WWTP effluents end-member to the river water are illustrated in Fig. 7  . Overall, in the wet, dry, and normal seasons, WWTP effluents contribute on average 16±10 %, 49±18 %, and 38±20 % of river water, respectively, it suggests that the dry season WWTP effluents proportion in river water is the highest and has the most influence on the river, which is consistent with the previous discussion. The hydrological station Guiyang (III) is located nearby sampling site 22 (Fig. 1 a), thus based on the corresponding seasonal river flow and the DIC concentration at sampling site 22, the riverine DIC flux can be estimated as shown in Table 2  . Furthermore, utilizing the percentage contribution of WWTP effluents to the river water and the average DIC concentration of WWTP effluents, the direct contribution of the WWTP effluents to the riverine DIC can be estimated as shown in Table 2 . In the wet, dry and normal seasons, the DIC flux from the WWTP effluents was 121.94±76.70 t/d, 117.65±43.70 t/d and 110.02±55.79 t/d, respectively, with a contribution of 21±13 %, 58±21 % and 66±33 % of the riverine DIC, respectively. These results further indicates that WWTP effluents should not be disregarded as a crucial contributor to the karst river DIC pool.  5.5 Challenges and uncertainties Wastewater treatment plants are one of the very important environmental protection facilities in urban development, but the amount of DIC in the discharged effluents has not been estimated. Here, we make first-hand estimates, which has implications for other rivers draining urbanized areas. In our study, the urban population covered by the sampled WWTPs amounts to 6.31 million, and the total treatment capacity is about 151.5 × 104  m3 /d (Supplementary Table S1 ). Based on the mean concentration of HCO3 −  and CO2(aq)  in the treated wastewater, the average contribution of DIC is 13.22 gC per person per day (or 4.93 kgC per person per year). Globally, the urban population has reached 4.52 billion in 2022, according to the statistical data from the world bank (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.URB.TOTL?end  = 2022&start = 1960&view = chart), assuming that all of the domestic wastewater were treated, therefore, it is estimated that worldwide WWTPs could discharge 21.81 Tg C/yr (1 Tg = 1012  g) as DIC. Since the treated wastewater is characterized by significantly low pH (Supplementary Table S1 ), the treated wastewater may release some CO2  at the initial discharge, based on the carbonate equilibrium. On the other hand, it could enhance the CO2  outgassing in receiving rivers, as a recent study found that p CO2  in the WWTP effluents receiving water increased 4-fold (Yoon et al., 2017 ). Hence, WWTP effluents may be underappreciated as sources of GHGs. For these reasons, this kind of “anthropogenic C” pulse emission of CO2  effect in river should be attention, because effluents water from wastewater treatment plants is often used as an important source of water for improving the water ecology of urban rivers (Xia et al., 2022; Zhu and Dou 2018 ). Uncertainties may exist in our DIC flux estimation from WWTPs. First of all, according to statistics, the global wastewater production is estimated at 359.4 × 109  m3 /yr, of which 63 % (225.6 × 109  m3 /yr) is collected and only 52 % (188.1 × 109  m3 /yr) is treated (Jones et al., 2021 ). There is little information with regard to DIC concentrations in untreated wastewater. Secondly, this study deals with a river that drains a karst landform with a relatively low sampling frequency. More field observations of other urban rivers and WWTP effluents are needed to obtain a global picture of the human-direct contribution of DIC from urbanized watersheds. Thirdly, some studies (Kim et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2013 ) have found that treated wastewaters can be an important input of dissolved organic matter in urbanized rivers, while the organic carbon discharge fluxes from WWTPs are not taken into account in our flux estimation. Finally, more filed observations are also needed to assess the CO2  emission fluxes during the initial treated-wastewater discharge.   6 Conclusions This study clarified the influence of wastewater treatment plant effluents on dissolved inorganic carbon in a river that drains intensively-urbanized karst areas. p CO2  levels in the river water near the WWTP outfalls show a clear trend of increasing during both the dry and normal seasons, which explains why recent studies have found increased CO2  concentrations in the river that drain urbanized areas. The ion molar concentration ratios observed for WWTP effluents and silicate rock weathering in the river are remarkably alike; Therefore, the relationship between WWTP effluents and silicate rock weathering contribution to riverine DIC needs to be cautiously judged when determining the rock weathering end-members of karst rivers in highly urbanized areas, in order to avoid overestimating the carbon sink capacity of rock weathering. Based on the evolutionary pattern model of DIC concentration versus δ13 CDIC , the study karst river is mainly influenced by carbonate dissolution during the wet season, organic matter degradation (WWTP effluents) and respiration during the dry season, and photosynthesis and CO2  outgassing during the normal season. Season to season variations in the geochemical processes they respond to are mostly caused by changes in river water temperature and flow. Meanwhile, based on Cl−  mass balance model, we estimate the following contribution of WWTP effluents to the river DIC pool: 21±13 % in the wet season, 58±21 % in the dry season, and 66±33 % in the normal season. Since wastewater treatment processes do not consume atmospheric or soil CO2 , but increase the DIC concentration in the water column, the DIC from WWTP effluents should be caution when estimate the carbonate rock weathering carbon sink budget by using Hydrogeochemistry method. These findings validate our initial hypothesis that WWTPs in highly urbanized environment play a significant role in the riverine DIC pool, which has important implications for predicting carbon source/sink fluxes in rivers as affected directly by humans.
1 Introduction Soil moisture (SM) is a key hydrologic variable in the land surface-atmosphere interaction processes (Blöschl et al., 2017; Seneviratne et al., 2006a ). It controls the exchange and distribution of water fluxes by dividing the precipitation into runoff and infiltration. Meanwhile, SM regulates the energy balance between the lower atmosphere and land by affecting sensible and latent heat exchange. Its importance spans across various domains, including agriculture (Gupta et al., 2020; Tong et al., 2020 ), hydrology (Allen et al., 2019 ), ecology (Liu et al., 2020 ), climate modelling (Williams et al., 2020 ), and water resource management (Grove, 2019; Ladanyi et al., 2021 ). The accurate estimation of SM is crucial for predicting extreme weather events (Forgotson et al., 2020 ), assessing drought and flood risks (Yuan et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2021 ), optimizing agricultural practices (Zhang et al., 2022 ), and understanding climate change impacts (Dadap et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2019 ). Currently, there are various techniques and methods for SM monitoring, such as in situ observations, remote sensing observations, land surface model simulations, and data assimilation (Li et al., 2022 ). In general, in situ observations provide the most accurate SM, but station deployment is labor-intensive, time-consuming and costly. Meanwhile, SM is highly spatial heterogeneous due to a large number of factors, such as soil texture and structure, topographic features, land cover patterns, and meteorological forcing (Brocca et al., 2007; Crow et al., 2012; Mohanty and Skaggs, 2001 ). Therefore, in situ SM observations have a poor spatial representation. For remote sensing observations, SM is mainly retrieved from satellite microwave radiometers directly based on the relationship between the electromagnetic radiation, soil dielectric, and water content (Ebrahimi-Khusfi et al., 2018; Mohanty et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2023 ). Microwave remote sensing observations are resistant to weather and night-time conditions owing to the penetrating capability of microwaves (Shangguan et al., 2023 ) and can obtain SM over large areas. However, compared to in situ observations, microwave remote sensing observations can only obtain SM from the top layer (typically ∼ 5 cm). In addition, satellite remote sensing cannot directly retrieve global seamless SM due to the limitation of the revisit period. Land surface models can simulate SM across multiple soil layers with seamless spatial distribution (Gu et al., 2019 ). However, the heterogeneity of spatial sub-grids, such as soil texture and land cover patterns (Yang et al., 2009 ), as well as the parameterization of the physical model result in large uncertainty in SM simulation. This is mainly due to the fact that the model is not a complete and perfect description of the physical process (Kumar et al., 2009 ). Reanalysis products are usually obtained by further fusing in situ observations, remote sensing data, and model simulations through data assimilation techniques (Chen et al., 2021 ). Compared to other products, reanalysis products can provide SM at deeper soil depth and for longer periods of time. However, reanalysis products are not necessarily more accurate than products prior to assimilating in situ data, for the reason that the assimilated meteorological variables (e.g., precipitation) may be biased (Balsamo et al., 2015 ). In general, there are pros and cons for the various SM data estimation methods. Hence, numerous studies have been conducted to compare the differences in the accuracy of various SM products based on in situ observations. For example, Vinodkumar and Dharssi (2019)  evaluated the application of a new SM product to wildfire prediction and management practices in Australia based on ground-based network observations using min–max matching, mean–variance matching and cumulative distribution function matching. Fang et al. (2020)  proposed a downscaling method for the Soil Moisture Active and Passive (SMAP) satellite based on the thermal inertia principle and used International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) data to evaluate downscaled products in the Continental United States. Additionally, Fan et al. (2022)  evaluated the accuracy of thirteen satellite- and model-based surface soil moisture (SSM) products and four root zone soil moisture (RZSM) products for cropland in Jiangsu Province, China, using in situ observations from 91 sites. Consequently, it is evident that in situ SM observations are primarily used to evaluate the accuracy of other SM products. However, evaluation based on in situ SM observations is still challenging due to inconsistencies in instrument type, calibration methods and reporting depths (Dorigo et al., 2015; Dorigo et al., 2013 ). To solve this problem, national SM observation networks are currently being established globally—for example, in the United States (Quiring et al., 2016 ) and in China (Shi et al., 2014 ), both of which provide a solid foundation for evaluating SM products over large areas. In previous studies, there are many evaluations on SM products of satellite remote sensing (Chen et al., 2017; Fang et al., 2020; Sathyanadh et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, SSM products have been evaluated more often since remote sensing data tend to provide only SSM (Zhang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Actually, SM can be briefly categorized into two aspects of data, namely, SSM and deep soil moisture (DSM). In the study of DSM, more attention is paid to RZSM, which refers to the soil water content at a depth of 0–100 cm. SSM is greatly influenced by rainfall infiltration and evapotranspiration, whereas water in deep soil layers is not sensitive to daily evapotranspiration and regular rainfall events (Cao et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2016 ). Moreover, SSM is a regular water source for vegetation growth, while DSM is essential for plant growth during the dry season, as it can be replenished by rainfall infiltration in the rainy season and can provide the necessary water for plant growth in the dry season (Jia and Shao, 2014; Yang et al., 2012 ). Hence, the evaluation of RZSM products is just as important as the evaluation of SSM products. In addition, most satellite products do not provide global seamless SM due to the revisit cycle of satellites. Consequently, a few studies have evaluated SM products that are globally seamless in time and space (Chen and Yuan, 2020 ). Against this background, this study was conducted to evaluate the global seamless SM products, including SSM and RZSM products. Different evaluation strategies may yield different results, which has not been fully considered in previous studies. While in situ observations may be the most accurate way to obtain SM, the use of in situ observations for satellite- or model-based SM evaluation does suffer from representativeness errors (Crow et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018 ). There is a scale mismatch between in situ observations, which are representative of only tens of square meters, and other products such as satellite- or model-based products, which have a spatial resolution of hundreds of square kilometers. Therefore, in addition to utilizing in situ SM observations for the evaluation, this study also utilized in situ precipitation observations for the evaluation in order to address the issue of spatial representativeness. This can largely mitigate the problem of poor spatial representation of in situ observations, as precipitation is not only a point event, but also a regional event. Meanwhile, we divided the stations based on precipitation to distinguish between drier and wetter stations and analyzed the performance of SM products under different precipitation conditions. In addition to this, we analyzed changes in SM induced by daily precipitation and compared the differences in these changes between in situ SM observations and SM products to assess the sensitivity of SM to precipitation. Consequently, this study further validates the accuracy of each SM product by comparing its sensitivity to precipitation, in an attempt to provide additional basis for agricultural water management. The remainder of this paper is organized in the following manner. Section 2  briefly introduces the SM products evaluated in this paper and the in situ observations used for the evaluation. Data preprocessing and evaluation methods are presented in Section 3 . Section 4  describes the results of the evaluation and the results are discussed and analyzed in section 5 . Finally, the main conclusions are provided in Section 6 .  2 Study area and materials 2.1 Study area China, which has a vast area of approximately 9.6 million square kilometers, is in eastern Asia and borders the west bank of the Pacific Ocean. China has a complex topography and an extremely diverse climate, which form a volatile environment of heat and humidity under the impact of the monsoon. The heat and moisture conditions in China are unevenly distributed under spatial and temporal scale. The overall terrain is gradually decreasing from the west to the east part of China, and the amount of annual precipitation decreases from the south-east coastal area to the north-west inland (Fig. 1  ), influenced by the climate of the continent and ocean. The precipitation in the study area shows seasonal characteristics, with more amount of precipitation concentrated in July and August, and less in December and January. Following the same seasonal characteristics as precipitation, SM also shows high and low values in the corresponding months.  2.2 Global soil moisture products The aim of this study was to evaluate the global seamless SM product, including SSM and RZSM products. Since remote sensing can only retrieve SSM, the SM products selected for this study were mainly derived from land surface model simulations and data assimilation. Based on this criterion and the popularity of different SM products, four SM products were selected for evaluation in this study. The details of these products are summarized in Table 1  . The Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission launched in January 2015 by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) used an L-band synthetic aperture radar instrument and an L-band radiometer to measure SM. SMAP provides direct sensing of SM in the top 5 cm of the soil column. However. several of the key applications targeted by SMAP require knowledge of RZSM in the top 1 m of the soil column. Hence, SMAP level 4 utilizes an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to merge SMAP observations with SM estimates from the NASA Catchment land surface model. The model interpolates and extrapolates SMAP observations in time and space, producing 3-hourly estimates of SM at a resolution of 9 km. There are two kinds of SMAP-L4 SM products and SPL4SMGP (version 7) was used in this study. ERA5 is the fifth generation European Center for Medium Weather Forecasting (ECMWF) reanalysis for the global climate and weather. ERA5-Land is an enhanced version of the ERA5. It utilizes ERA5 atmospheric forcing data for numerical modeling and correction with global observations to obtain higher resolution and more accurate land variable estimates. ERA5-Land provides hourly SM in four layers (i.e., 0–7 cm, 7–28 cm, 28–100 cm, 100–289 cm) at 0.1° resolution from 1950 to the present. The temporal and spatial resolutions of ERA5-Land make this dataset rather useful for all kinds of land surface applications such as flood or drought monitoring. The Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) is a global land surface data assimilation system developed by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP). The goal of the GLDAS is to generate optimal land surface states based on advanced land surface modeling and data assimilation techniques by ingesting satellite- and ground-based observational data products (Rodell et al., 2004 ). In this study, the GLDAS NOAH version 2.1 data was used, which is forced with a combination of the Noah Model 3.6 and observation data from the year 2000 to present. The Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) is a set of algorithms that separately estimate the different components of land evaporation. Additionally, GLEAM provides SSM and RZSM. Its SM is calculated using a multi-layer running water balance that describes the infiltration of observed precipitation through the vertical soil profile and microwave observations of SSM are assimilated into the soil profile (Gash, 1979 ). GLEAM V3.6a was evaluated in this study. It spans from 1980 to 2021 and provides daily SM at a resolution of 0.25°.  2.3 In situ observations The in situ SM observations from 2693 stations in mainland China for the period from 2019 to 2021 were collected from the automatic soil moisture observation (ASMO) system, which is provided by the China Meteorological Administration (CMA). This dataset has been widely used in the validation of SM products in China and in previous downscaling studies (Chen and Yuan, 2020; Fan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; Song et al., 2022 ). The ASMO sensors are developed based on the frequency domain reflection (FDR) method (Xue and Ye, 2013 ). At each station, the sensors automatically detect the hourly soil volumetric moisture content at depths of 0–10 cm, 10–20 cm, 20–30 cm, 30–40 cm, 40–50 cm, 50–60 cm, 70–80 cm, 90–100 cm. The soil relative humidity, soil weight moisture content, and available soil water storage can be calculated based on soil volumetric moisture content. The original in situ SM observations were arithmetically calculated to obtain daily averages in this study. In details, they were calculated from the arithmetic mean of observations taken 24 times from 21:00 of the previous day to 20:00 of the current day. The in situ precipitation observations were derived from 2421 meteorological stations (including 211 national benchmark meteorological stations, 631 national basic meteorological stations and 1579 regionally intensified stations) in mainland China. Daily data on evaporation, precipitation, ground temperature, air pressure, relative humidity, hours of sunshine, air temperature, and wind speed are available for each station. This study focused on applying ground temperature and precipitation data for quality control and accuracy validation. Daily ground temperature in the dataset was arithmetically calculated from the observation data recorded four times a day (2:00, 8:00, 14:00, and 20:00). Daily precipitation was the arithmetic sum of the two time periods (20:00 of the previous day to 8:00 of the current day, and 8:00 of the current day to 20:00 of the current day) recorded each day. The dataset has been quality controlled before use and the calculated interval of daily data in this dataset is consistent with that of in situ SM observations.   3 Methodology 3.1 Data pre-processing For a fair assessment, the following preprocessing was performed on all datasets for the same period (from 2019 to 2021). Since SM stations were not perfectly matched to precipitation stations, we retained 1311 stations based on station ID correspondence. Meanwhile, quality control procedures were used to select good-quality stations. First, according to the working range of the FDR sensor and the observation specification by CMA, in situ SM observations which are larger than 0.5 m  3  m  - 3      were excluded (Xue and Ye, 2013 ). Second, based on ground temperature and precipitation observations, spurious SM observations due to frost and anomalous increases in SM without precipitation were excluded. Third, each station was required to have at least 365 days of SSM records. After quality control, data from a total of 1141 stations were used to evaluate SSM accuracy in the next step. Simultaneously, the stations used to evaluate RZSM accuracy were also screened. On the basis of quality control for SSM data, stations with less than 365 days of complete data records at eight specific depths were eliminated. Finally, a total of 42 stations remained for accuracy validation of RZSM products. For the calculation of RZSM, the depth-weighted mean method (Fan et al., 2022 ) was adopted in this study. It is calculated as follows:(1) θ RZSM   = 2 θ 1  L 1  + θ 1  + θ 2     L 2  + θ 2  + θ 3     L 3  + ⋯ + θ i - 1   + θ i     L i   2 L 1  + L 2  + L 3  + ⋯ + L i                where θ RZSM      represents the RZSM, θ i     represents SM values at the i-th layer, and L i     represents the i-th layer depth, which includes eight specific depths (i.e., 0–10 cm, 10–20 cm, 20–30 cm, 30–40 cm, 40–50 cm, 50–60 cm, 60–80 cm, 80–100 cm). The RZSM was provided by SMAP-L4, GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM directly. ERA5-Land RZSM was calculated using a weighted average method by combining the SM at the first (0–7 cm), second (7–28 cm), and third (28–100 cm) layers (Martínez-Fernández et al., 2015 ). The temporal resolution of all evaluated products was not consistent. The daily average data of all evaluated products (except GLEAM) were arithmetically calculated based on the calculation interval of daily average data from SM stations. The product data were then obtained from the pixels corresponding to each station by following the nearest grid method (Al-Yaari et al., 2019 ). In addition, multiple in situ stations within a grid cell were considered independent stations and were compared separately, as each station can partially represent the grid cell truth values (Xu et al., 2021 ).  3.2 Evaluation methods The error characteristics of the SM products cannot be fully characterized by a single validation metric. In this study, four commonly used metrics—that is, the Pearson correlation coefficient (R), root mean square error (RMSE), unbiased RMSE (ubRMSE) and bias—were selected to evaluate the performance of the four products using in situ SM observations. R and ubRMSE were considered the main criteria because they are less affected by differences in depth between in situ observations and SM products (Yang et al., 2020 ). R can be used to assess the difference in time-varying trends of the SM products with respect to the in situ observations when it can pass the 0.05 significance test. Further, bias measures the dryness or wetness of the SM product with respect to the in situ observations. RMSE and ubRMSE are interpreted as standard deviations of random errors (Montzka et al., 2020 ). These metrics were calculated as the following equations:(2) R = ∑ i = 1  N  SM  e v a l u a t e d i      - SM  evaluated    ¯      SM  in - s i t u i      - SM  in - s i t u    ¯       ∑ i = 1  N  SM  e v a l u a t e d i      - SM  evaluated    ¯      2    ∑ i = 1  N  SM  in - s i t u i      - SM  in - s i t u    ¯      2              (3) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  N  SM  e v a l u a t e d i      - SM  in - s i t u i         2   N            (4) ubRMSE = ∑ i = 1  N  SM  e v a l u a t e d i      - SM  evaluated    ¯     - SM  in - s i t u i      - SM  in - s i t u    ¯          2  N            (5) Bias = ∑ i = 1  N  ( S M  e v a l u a t e d i      - SM  in - s i t u i      )   N           where the SM  evaluated      and SM  in - s i t u      represents the SM products and the in situ SM observations, respectively. N is the number of comparison SM data pairs. In order to analyze the results of stations under different climatic conditions, this study classified the station types based on the criteria for classifying arid and humid regions in China (Chen et al., 2020; Piao et al., 2010 ). In situ stations were categorized into the following four groups based on annual precipitation: humid region (precipitation ≥ 800 mm/yr), semi-humid region (400 mm/yr ≤ precipitation < 800 mm/yr), semi-arid region (200 mm/yr ≤ precipitation < 400 mm/yr), and arid region (precipitation < 200 mm/yr) (Li et al., 2023 ). Finally, 776 stations in the humid region, 290 stations in the semi-humid region, 33 stations in the semi-arid region, 42 stations in the arid were obtained. By dividing the different station conditions, we compared the performance of each SM product under different precipitation conditions. In addition, this study also utilized in situ precipitation observations to evaluate the sensitivity of SM products to precipitation. In situ precipitation observations are more spatially representative than in situ SM observations because precipitation tend to be a regional event. Meanwhile, at larger scales, almost all positive increments in the SM time series are caused by precipitation events, while positive increments in SM at small scales can be caused by a variety of mechanisms, including run-on, capillary rise, irrigation, and precipitation events (McColl et al., 2019). This may also partially mitigate the scale mismatch between in situ observations and coarse resolution SM products. For evaluation based on in situ precipitation observations, two methods are used in this study for validation. Due to the presence of evapotranspiration, it is not the case that SM increases when precipitation occurs. Therefore, the first method is to detect the minimum amount of precipitation needed for the increase in SM. We extracted the changes in SM when precipitation occurs. These changes in SM may be positive or negative because SM still decreases under the effect of evapotranspiration when precipitation is little. For each station, we extracted the amount of precipitation when the change in SM was negative, and then calculated the maximum and mean values of these precipitation separately. When the result of the SM product is closer to the result of the in situ observations, the product has a stronger ability to capture precipitation dynamics. In addition, the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (ρ   ) was used to evaluate all SM products in this study. Because precipitation does not conform to a normal distribution (Tuttle and Salvucci, 2014 ), the commonly used metrics for measuring the strength of the relationship between two variables are not applicable to precipitation and SM. However, it is an obvious fact that greater precipitation will lead to greater increases in SM. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient can reflect this fact to a certain extent and has no requirements for the distribution of variables. Therefore, we performed rank correlation calculations for the amount of daily precipitation and the change in SM caused by precipitation. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient is calculated as:(6) ρ = 1 - 6 ∑ i = 1  n  R i  - Q i     2   n n  2  - 1               where the R    represents the rank of the amount of daily precipitation at a specific station and the Q    represents the rank of SM change before and after precipitation at the station; n is the total number of precipitation days at the station from 2019 to 2021.   4 Results 4.1 Evaluation of surface soil moisture products 4.1.1 Evaluation under all-weather conditions The accuracy of the four SSM products was evaluated using all the post-quality control data from in situ stations. Fig. 2   displays the basic evaluation results of the four SSM products. The mean values of the SSM at each station and that of the corresponding pixels in the products were transformed into a scatter plot, which displays in Fig. 2 a. The four metrics (R, RMSE, ubRMSE, and Bias) presented in the plot are the median values of the metrics computed at each station. Overall, ERA5-Land can capture spatial variations of in situ SSM well, with the highest median R value (0.6530) among the four products. It was followed by SMAP-L4 with the median R value of 0.6236. Nevertheless, GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM had poor spatiotemporal correlation with the median R values of lower than 0.55. SMAP-L4 had the lowest RMSE (median RMSE=0.0831 m  3  m  - 3     ). In addition, GLDAS-Noah obtained lower median RMSE (0.0927 m  3  m  - 3     ) compared to ERA5-Land and GLEAM, which showed relatively higher median RMSE with the values of 0.1115 and 0.1268 m  3  m  - 3     , respectively. With regard to the ubRMSE, SMAP-L4 performed a little better than the other SSM products, with a value of 0.0537 m  3  m  - 3     , while the highest ubRMSE was obtained by ERA5-Land (median ubRMSE=0.0557 m  3  m  - 3     ). In terms of bias, SMAP-L4 also obviously had a better performance than the other three SSM products, with the lowest bias (median bias = -0.0006 m  3  m  - 3     ), followed by GLDAS-Noah (median bias = 0.0510 m  3  m  - 3     ). The frequency distribution of SSM for all SSM products as well as in situ SSM observations is depicted in Fig. 2 b. It is obvious that the SMAP-L4 had the best performance, with the other three SSM products showing noticeably wet bias compared to the in situ observations. GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM yielded higher variability of approximately 0.35 and 0.4 m  3  m  - 3     , respectively. Meanwhile, GLEAM yielded lower variability in the values ranging from 0 to 0.2 m  3  m  - 3     , while GLDAS-Noah yielded low variability of approximately 0.1 m  3  m  - 3     . ERA5-Land presented a wet bias in general, compared to the in situ observations. Fig. 3   depicts the general spatial distribution of the evaluation results for the four SSM products. SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land had higher R values than GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM in general, and the four SSM products performed poorly in Xinjiang, Sichuan, Chongqing, and Guizhou. GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM also performed poorly in Gansu Province, with R values less than 0.2. According to the spatial distribution of RMSE, SMAP-L4 and GLDAS-Noah performed better than ERA5-Land and GLEAM. SMAP-L4 performed poorly at several stations in Xinjiang and ERA5-Land had poor performance in Sichuan, Tibet, and parts of North China. In addition, GLEAM did not perform as well as the other three SSM products across the board. After eliminating the bias, the four SSM products performed similarly on the ubRMSE metrics. All four products showed poor accuracy in Sichuan, Guizhou, parts of central China, and Xinjiang, where calculated ubRMSE values were generally around 0.075 m  3  m  - 3     , while in other regions they were largely less than 0.05 m  3  m  - 3     . In terms of bias, all four SSM products showed dry bias in the Xinjiang, particularly SMAP-L4. Simultaneously, SMAP-L4 showed a dry bias in North China, although the bias scores of SMAP-L4 in North China were small. Meanwhile, ERA5-Land and GLDAS-Noah also showed low dry bias in North China and high wet bias in other regions. In contrast to other products, GLEAM showed a significant wet bias almost nationwide compared to the in situ SSM observations, particularly in Sichuan, Chongqing and North China. It can be noted that the evaluation results of all four SSM products have a few similarities in spatial distribution. All four products showed a poor performance in some regions, such as Sichuan, Chongqing and Xinjiang.  4.1.2 Evaluation under different precipitation conditions The evaluation results based on in situ SSM observations were classified according to different precipitation conditions. Fig. 4  a reveals the boxplot of R values calculated by four SSM products under different precipitation conditions. All SSM products, except GLEAM, had the highest median R values at humid stations, and all SSM products, except GLDAS-Noah, had the lowest median R values at semi-arid stations. At the arid stations, GLEAM had the highest median R values and GLDAS-Noah had the lowest median R values. For each product, the median R values at the semi-humid stations were always better than that at the semi-arid stations. Overall, SSM products had higher R values at wetter stations. Fig. 4 b presents the boxplots of RMSE scores calculated by four SSM products under different precipitation conditions. The four SSM products obtained the highest median RMSE at the semi-humid stations, which demonstrates that none of these products can estimate SSM under semi-humid conditions very well. At the arid stations, SMAP-L4 outperformed, while the other three SSM products all obtained the lowest median RMSE at the semi-arid stations. Fig. 4 c depicts the boxplots of ubRMSE calculated by four SSM products under different precipitation conditions. For all SSM products, the lowest median ubRMSE was obtained at the arid stations and the second lowest median ubRMSE was obtained at the humid stations. With regard to the semi-arid and semi-humid stations, SMAP-L4 and GLDAS-Noah had a lower median ubRMSE at the semi-arid stations than that at the semi-humid stations, while the opposite was true for ERA5-Land and GLEAM. However, all products had similar median ubRMSE at semi-arid stations and semi-humid stations. Fig. 4 d shows the boxplots of bias calculated by four SSM products under different precipitation conditions. The four SSM products had lower median bias at the semi-arid stations than other stations. Since SMAP-L4 had the best overall bias performance, a drier median bias was found for SMAP-L4 at the semi-arid stations compared to that at other stations. In contrast, due to the fact that the other three SSM products revealed a wet bias overall, their median bias at the semi-arid stations were instead better (close to zero) than that at the other types of stations. Meanwhile, all the evaluated SSM products obtained higher median bias at the semi-humid station than the overall level. Moreover, the median bias of all SSM products at arid and humid stations were close to the median bias for all stations. From the results of the in situ evaluation under different annual precipitation scenarios (Fig. 4 ), based on the main criteria R values and ubRMSE, all products except GLEAM obtained the highest median R values under humid conditions and all products obtained the lowest median ubRMSE under arid conditions. Meanwhile, all products obtained a lower median ubRMSE under humid conditions compared to semi-arid and semi-humid conditions. When we consider the RMSE and Bias metrics, the highest median RMSE was obtained for all the products under semi-humid conditions and all products except GLDAS-Noah obtained the highest median Bias values under semi-arid or semi-humid conditions. This indicates that SSM estimates are more sensitive to precipitation when precipitation is particularly high or low. On the other hand, this may also be due to the fact that the models are not particularly accurate in predicting precipitation, which leads to the transfer of inaccuracies in the simulation of precipitation to the simulation of SSM. In this study, we also categorized the in situ SSM observations into observations in the absence of precipitation and observations in the presence of precipitation. Fig. 5   presents the validation results for all SSM products under the precipitation, no-precipitation, and all-weather scenarios. The median R values for all four SSM products, except SMAP-L4, were higher under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the precipitation scenario. ERA5-Land still obtained a higher median R value under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the all-weather scenario. Moreover, SMAP-L4, ERA5-Land, and GLEAM obtained lower median RMSE under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the precipitation scenario, while the opposite was true for GLDAS-Noah. Although there was little difference between the results of GLDAS-Noah under the no-precipitation and precipitation scenarios. With regard to ubRMSE, all products obtained lower median ubRMSE under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the precipitation scenario and also showed better results under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the all-weather scenario. GLDAS-Noah obtained a higher bias under the no-precipitation scenario than that under the precipitation scenario, while the bias scores of the other three SSM products under the no-precipitation scenario were all closer to zero than that under the precipitation scenario. Meanwhile, the bias scores of ERA5-Land and GLEAM under the no-precipitation scenario were also closer to 0 than that under the all-weather scenario. In addition, SMAP-L4 revealed a dry bias under the no-precipitation scenario and a wet bias under the precipitation scenario, which demonstrates that SMAP-L4 overestimated the increase in SSM caused by precipitation. The above results reveal that the evaluation results using the in situ SSM observations without precipitation are better than those using the in situ SSM observations with precipitation in most cases. Validation accuracy tends to decrease when precipitation occurs, particularly for ERA5-Land and GLEAM. This implies that model-based SSM products need to improve precipitation accuracy and model structure between precipitation and SSM to improve SSM accuracy.  4.1.3 Evaluation based on in situ precipitation observations Based on the precipitation observations, we obtained two aspects of the evaluation results. Fig. 6  a-b presents the sensitivity of the increase in SSM to the magnitude of precipitation, and Fig. 6 c presents the sensitivity of the in situ SSM observations as well as the SSM products to precipitation for each station. From the former results, it can be seen that the in situ SSM observations are more sensitive than products to the increase in SSM caused by precipitation, regardless of calculating the maximum value or calculating the mean value, closely followed by SMAP-L4. GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM were less sensitive to the increase in SSM caused by precipitation. This may be related to the coarse resolution of GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM. With regard to the latter results, in situ SSM observations presented the best results overall compared to the other four SSM products. SMAP-L4 performed better than the other SSM products with a median ρ    of 0.4151, followed by ERA5-Land (median ρ    = 0.3732). GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM performed poorly, with the median ρ    of 0.2137 and 0.1893, respectively. From this result, it can be evident that the SSM of SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land are more sensitive to precipitation than those of GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM, which explains the superiority of SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land over GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM in the statistical validation based on the in situ SSM observations presented above.   4.2 Evaluation of root zone soil moisture products 4.2.1 Evaluation under all-weather conditions Similar to the SSM products, the scatter plots of the mean values of the in situ RZSM observations at each station and the mean values of the corresponding pixels in the product are presented in Fig. 7  a. SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land outperformed the other RZSM products, with higher R values of 0.6198 and 0.7165, respectively. Meanwhile, SMAP-L4 obtained the lowest median RMSE (0.0751 m  3  m  - 3     ) and bias (0.0303 m  3  m  - 3     ). The lowest median ubRMSE was obtained by ERA5-Land with the value of 0.0350 m  3  m  - 3     , which was closely followed by SMAP-L4 (median ubRMSE=0.0355 m  3  m  - 3     ). Nevertheless, the largest errors were obtained by GLDAS-Noah with the highest median RMSE (0.2184 m  3  m  - 3     ) and bias (0.2069 m  3  m  - 3     ). Fig. 7 b presents the frequency distribution of the four RZSM products and in situ RZSM observations. Compared to the frequency distribution of the in situ RZSM observations, GLDAS-Noah performed very poorly, with an even distribution in the range of 0–0.6 m  3  m  - 3     . The other three RZSM products revealed a wet bias compared to the in situ RZSM observations, with ERA5-Land and GLEAM being more concentrated around 0.41 m  3  m  - 3      and SMAP-L4 being more concentrated at 0.34 m  3  m  - 3     . Further, compared to the four SSM products, all four RZSM products had lower ubRMSE scores. Meanwhile, all four RZSM products obtained higher median R except GLEAM and lower median RMSE except GLDAS-Noah and ERA5-Land. With regard to bias scores, ERA5-Land and GLEAM had slightly lower median bias in RZSM evaluation than their median bias in SSM evaluation, whereas the opposite was true for GLDAS-Noah and SMAP-L4. Overall, SMAP-L4 performed well in both SSM and RZSM, while the GLDAS-Noah performed significantly worse in RZSM evaluation compared to that in SSM evaluation. Although there are only 42 stations used in the RZSM evaluation, the spatial distribution of the evaluation results is presented in Fig. 8  . The spatial distribution of these 42 stations revealed differences between the three main regions of the southeast coast, central, and northwest regions of China. The highest R value appeared in the southeast coastal and central regions of China, and the R values in the northwest region were generally lower than 0.5. With regard to RMSE and ubRMSE, SMAP-L4, ERA5-Land, and GLEAM did not show particularly significant spatial heterogeneity in space, which perhaps needs to be validated with more stations. GLDAS-Noah obtained higher RMSE at the lower latitude stations, with the value generally greater than 0.3 m  3  m  - 3     . In terms of bias, all four RZSM products showed a dry bias in the northwest and a wet bias in the southeast coast and in the central regions of China. SMAP-L4 had the lowest bias in the southeast, while GLDAS-Noah had the highest bias. In addition, SMAP-L4, ERA5-Land, and GLDAS-Noah also obtained a dry bias at several stations in North China. Combined with the characteristics of precipitation decreasing from the southeast coast to the northwest inland in China, this result suggests that all four RZSM products overestimate the RZSM in rainy areas and underestimate the RZSM in arid areas.  4.2.2 Evaluation under different precipitation conditions Similar to the SSM evaluation, in situ stations were categorized based on the occurrence or absence of precipitation and the evaluation results are depicted in Fig. 9  . Fig. 9 a illustrates the median R values calculated by each product under different precipitation conditions. For all of the four RZSM products, the R values under the no-precipitation scenario were higher than those under the all-weather scenario and the rainfall scenario, and the results under the precipitation scenario were still worse than those under the all-weather scenario. It can be noted that these RZSM products do not capture the RZSM temporal variation well under precipitation. Meanwhile, similar results of the four RZSM products in terms of ubRMSE were also found—that is, each product had the lowest ubRMSE under the no-precipitation scenario and the highest ubRMSE under the precipitation scenario. With regard to RMSE, SMAP-L4 and GLEAM had the lowest RMSE under the precipitation scenario, ERA5-Land and GLDAS-Noah had the lowest RMSE under the no-precipitation scenario. In terms of bias, the four RZSM products all obtained a wet bias regardless of the conditions. However, SMAP-L4 and GLEAM obtained a lower wet bias under the precipitation scenario and a higher wet bias under the no-precipitation scenario, while the opposite was true for ERA5-Land and GLDAS-Noah. Through the more critical metrics of R and ubRMSE, it is evident that the validation accuracy of the RZSM products under the no-precipitation scenario is always higher than that under the all-weather and precipitation scenarios. Meanwhile, the results of the bias revealed that SMAP-L4 and GLEAM underestimated the effect of precipitation on SM, while ERA5-Land and GLDAS-Noah overestimated the effect of precipitation on SM. This may be due to different model structures and parameterization in the land surface model, which results in different changes in its feedback to precipitation.  4.2.3 Evaluation based on in situ precipitation observations With regard to the sensitivity assessment for RZSM based on the in situ precipitation observations, Fig. 10   shows the sensitivity of the four RZSM products to precipitation. Compared to SSM, in situ RZSM observations and nearly all RZSM products require a higher magnitude of precipitation for the increase in RZSM. Meanwhile, in situ RZSM observations remained highly sensitive to the increase in SM caused by precipitation and the results of SMAP-L4 were proximate to in situ observations. GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM still performed poorly, limited by their coarse resolution. In terms of the Spearman rank correlation coefficient, the in situ RZSM observations outperformed the four RZSM products, with the highest ρ    (median ρ    = 0.5487). The lowest ρ    was obtained by GLDAS-Noah (median ρ    = 0.2691). The results of SMAP-L4, ERA5-Land, and GLEAM were similar, with SMAP-L4 (median ρ    = 0.4419) performing slightly better and GLEAM (median ρ    = 0.3717) performing slightly worse. Combining the results of SSM with those of RZSM, it can be seen that there is a certain consistency in the results. Furthermore, higher resolution products also performed better in the sensitivity of RZSM to precipitation.    5 Discussion Overall, the evaluation results revealed that SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land have better accuracy, while GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM have poorer accuracy. In terms of sensitivity to precipitation, SMAP-L4 still performed well. However, SMAP-L4 is not optimal according to every metric. There are many significant uncertainties in the dataset and methodology. Moreover, the results are also affected by scale effects, as the spatial resolution of the assessed datasets is not entirely uniform. Therefore, it is necessary to discuss these issues and compare the results with those of previous studies. 5.1 Different scales and emphasis of products The uncertainty of SM evaluation at point scale mainly arises from the scale mismatch between in situ SM observations and SM products. Due to the large spatial heterogeneity of SM (Luo et al., 2022 ), in situ observations for one station are only representative of SM in the tens or hundreds of square meters around it. However, the spatial resolution of global seamless SM products tends to be coarse, typically 0.1° or 0.25°. This scale mismatch reduces the representativeness of in situ observations—that is, the in situ observations do not represent the true values within the product pixels. Simultaneously, the spatial resolution between the SM products is also inconsistent, with spatial resolution of 0.1° for SMAP-L4 and ERA5-Land and 0.25° for GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM. Accordingly, the resolution of GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM is much coarser than that of ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4, which may be one of the reasons for their poorer evaluation results. To mitigate the effects of the scale mismatch problem, some scholars have averaged the observations from multiple stations within the same pixel and resampled products at different resolutions to achieve the same resolution prior to evaluation. However, due to the influence of scale effects, such pre-processing does not completely solve the problem and even introduce more errors (Ford and Quiring, 2019; Wu et al., 2016 ). To investigate this scale mismatch, Table 2   shows the accuracy of SSM and RZSM after ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 resampling to 0.25°, respectively. Therefore, all four products achieved the same resolution. It is evident from the results that the accuracy after resampling was slightly decreased compared to the accuracy of the initial resolution. However, the resampled ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 still performed better than GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM. Although precipitation is a regional event, the extent of each precipitation event is not uniform, so there is some uncertainty about the spatial representativeness of in situ precipitation. In particular, there are also differences in precipitation within the range of a single precipitation event. Therefore, we performed some analysis of the spatial representativeness of in situ precipitation. We evaluated the SM products after resampling using in situ precipitation observations as well. Fig. 11   illustrates the results of SM sensitivity to precipitation for SM products with original and resampling spatial resolution. Fig. 11 a-b shows the minimum amount of precipitation needed for the increase in SM. It can be seen that the results of resampled ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 were not significantly different from the original results. Therefore, the results of resampled ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 remained superior to GLDAS-Noah and GLEAM. As for the Spearman rank correlation coefficient, which is shown in Fig. 11 c, there was also little difference between the results of ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 before and after resampling. However, regardless of SSM or RZSM, the median ρ    calculated after resampling was always smaller than the median ρ    before resampling. Specifically, the median ρ    of SSM and RZSM for ERA5-Land before and after resampling decreased from 0.4151 and 0.4419 to 0.4135 and 0.4354, respectively. The median ρ    of SSM and RZSM for SMAP-L4 before and after resampling decreased from 0.3732 and 0.3793 to 0.3716 and 0.3740, respectively. Although both declines in ρ    are very small, the same trends of ERA5-Land and SMAP-L4 demonstrated that utilizing in situ precipitation for evaluation is more advantageous for high resolution SM products. In other words, the higher resolution SM products will perform better in terms of the sensitivity of SM to precipitation. In terms of the SM products themselves, retrieving global seamless SSM and RZSM requires the use of land surface models. However, each of the four products evaluated in this study have their own focus. Currently, SMAP is one of the most accurate SM satellites in the world (Beck et al., 2021 ). Based on its accurate SSM estimation, combined with land surface modeling, it also provides more accurate and seamless SSM and RZSM extrapolation. GLEAM focuses more on the different components of land evaporation rather than SM, although it also performs well in SM (Martens et al., 2017 ). ERA5-Land and GLDAS-Noah use land surface models and data assimilation techniques to obtain numerous surface variables. Owing to the direct satellite remote sensing by SMAP and the assimilation of SMAP L-band brightness temperatures in land surface modeling, the good accuracy of SMAP SSM directly impact the RZSM estimation. In addition, the more dominant error in SM estimation stems from its model simulation. During the model simulation process, the transmission of errors, parameterization of physical processes, and scale matching of various types of data (i.e., land cover, soil texture, and digital elevation) affect the accuracy of SM simulation. For a few complex physical processes, the model utilizes a parameterized scheme for their simplified substitution. Moreover, certain anthropogenic activities are not well incorporated into the model, such as irrigation, which can also lead to the increase in SM in the absence of precipitation. Generally, models are not perfect. Hence, the different emphasis of the SM products also makes a difference in their accuracy.  5.2 Uncertainty of evaluation using precipitation Further, precipitation forcing is one of the most important drivers of SM estimations (Xu et al., 2021 ). From the results of the rank correlation between SM changes and precipitation, all four products failed to capture daily precipitation dynamics very well. However, one uncertainty that must be note is that light precipitation may lead to greater increases in SM compared to heavy precipitation when precipitation continues for several days. This is because light precipitation on the first day may cause the SM to reach a state of near saturation and subsequent heavy precipitation has less impact on the SM. Therefore, there is some uncertainty in using rank correlation to assess the relationship between SM change and precipitation. In other words, the magnitude of already existing SM and SM memory have large effect on analysis using rank correlation coefficient between SM changes and precipitation. In simple terms, for the same magnitude of precipitation, the change in SM caused by precipitation is likely to be smaller when the already existing SM is greater. However, the SM memory is usually calculated by SM time series autocorrelation (Orth and Seneviratne, 2013; Ghannam et al., 2016 ), which is difficult to be included in the evaluation process of SM change through precipitation observations. In order to discuss the impact of this issue, we classified pre-existing SM conditions into five classes and calculated the rank correlation coefficient for each product under each class separately, and the results are shown in Fig. 12  . We found that the rank correlation coefficient of different products can be affected by the pre-existing SM. However, this effect does not change the results of the comparison of accuracy between products, with SMAP-L4 still presented the best performance. Therefore, we believe that this issue does not affect the results of evaluating different products based on the methodology in this paper. On the other hand, soil characteristics also have an impact on the calculation of the rank correlation coefficient between SM changes and precipitation. Therefore, according to the soil characteristics data of Shangguan and Dai (2019) , we distinguish the stations with different soil characteristics and analyze the rank correlation coefficient ρ    calculated for different soil characteristics, and the results are shown in Fig. 13  . The relations between ρ    and soil sand and clay fractions are relatively unclear. However, it can be seen that different soil characteristics do have an effect on the calculated rank correlation coefficients. Soil characteristics have no impact on the results of previous evaluations while we were comparing evaluation results between different products. This may be due to the fact that we are calculating each station individually in our evaluation, and the soil characteristics at each station can be considered almost invariant over the time series. Therefore, as with the issue of pre-existing SM mentioned above, different soil characteristics do not affect the judgement of accuracy comparisons between different products. For the evaluation of RZSM, the SM memory is also an uncertainty factor (Seneviratne et al., 2006b ). Fig. 14   shows the rank correlation between the increase in SM and precipitation under different lag time conditions at different depths. For SSM, the response to precipitation is fastest.
