This is in agreement with our modelling framework, in that multiple lagged regressors can be skilful predictors of drought metrics, however comparison with our results highlights how the stochastic nature of instantaneous meteorological variables limits systematic lags to shorter timescales. Multiple studies have proposed methods to forecast European drought characteristics using lagged response from hydrometeorological variables (including the NAO), with good forecasting performance (normalized performance measures (such as r2 ) > 0.5), but with limited lead times (typically less than 6 months) (e.g., Santos et al., (2014), Sutanto et al., 2020a; Svensson et al., 2015; Scaife et al., 2014; Kingston et al., 2015; Svensson and Hannaford 2019 ). Sutanto et al., (2020b)  highlights that longer drought forecast lead times can be achieved in systems with longer persistence times, demonstrated through a comparison between hydrological and meteorological drought forecasts. Our results align with this concept, showing that improved lead-times can also be found in atmosphere-drought linkages at multi-annual periodicities. Our results show that multi-year NAO behaviours have less predictive performance in flashier catchments, or for short-term flash droughts, potentially limiting their application in certain regions or to certain hazards (such as agricultural drought). Fast-responding catchments typically exhibit a high degree of noise in their hydrological behaviour, as they respond to fine-scale variability in meteorological drivers (Carr and Simpson, 2018 ), making drought forecasting in these regions challenging. For instance, MacKay et al., (2015) , found reduced model performance (Relative Operating Characteristics) of seasonal groundwater drought forecasts, using a process-based modelling approach, in quick-responding groundwater catchments when compared with forecasts from slower-responding hydrogeological catchments. Similarly, the UK Hydrological Outlook (a hybrid statistical and process-based hydrological framework used for hydrological extremes forecasting in the UK, Prudhomme et al., (2017)  found reduced forecasting performance in flashier catchments (such as Limestone or Oolite) with hindcast correlations of between r = 0.23 and 0.5 in streamflow, at a seasonal forecasting horizon. These correlation ranges are equivalent to an r2 of between 0.05 and 0.25. As such, despite their reduced performance in fast-responding catchments, semi-periodic NAO behaviours as predictors for hydrological drought may outperform some existing forecasting systems, with the additional benefit of longer forecast horizons. Another potential limitation is the reliance on a locally stationary relationship between NAO and groundwater semi-periodic behaviours. While the model does not require a stationary relationship at timescales greater than 15-years (as defined by the window length), stationarity is assumed within this timescale. The impact of this can be seen in the forecasted time series between 1980 and 1990 where model performance is reduced across most regions (particularly at longer forecast horizons), likely due to a step-change in the NAO-groundwater lag that occurred during this time for these semi-periodic behaviours (Rust et al., 2022 ). The impact of these local non-stationarities may be reduced by combining multi-year NAO behaviours with other explanatory variables in future applications. For instance. previous research has shown that the performance of drought forecasting systems can be improved by including multiple explanatory variables or regressors from disparate systems (e.g. Wunsch et al., 2018; Svensson et al., 2015; Li et al, 2019 ). Finally, if the methods used here were applied in a real-time forecasting system, it is recommended that sensitivities of the wavelet transform are understood further, such as the impact of edge-effect or wavenumber on forecasting capability. For instance, Quilty and Adamowski, (2018)  highlight the importance of accounting for edge-effects when using the wavelet transform in forecasting applications. While edge-effects were minimized in this study using full historical records (as previously discussed), corrections such as those proposed by Adamowski (2008)  may be required if the wavelet transform is applied to a real-time system. While there are limitations to the use of semi-periodic NAO behaviours as predictors for drought coverage, we show that the performance of these predictors may be better than existing dynamic seasonal drought forecasting systems while providing considerably longer forecast horizons. Most drought management plans in Europe require water authorities to define their drought management strategies every 5 or 6 years (Hervas-Gamez and Delgado-Ramos 2019; Rossi and Cancelliere, 2013; DEFRA, 2021 ). At present, dynamic hydrological forecasts are rarely used in these plans given their limited forecast horizons, instead favouring probabilistic approaches which do not given predictive information on water resource variability. Applying multi-annual periodicities in teleconnection systems to drought forecasting has the potential to transform current drought management practices by providing dynamic long-lead forecasts of drought-rich and drought-poor periods.   6 Conclusion This paper evaluated the predictive capability of multi-year semi-periodic behaviours in the NAO for forecasting groundwater drought coverage at multi-year timescales. We apply a data-driven modelling approach to forecast an 8-year and 16-year semi-periodic component of groundwater drought coverage series (for a range of drought characteristics) using matching behaviours from the NAOI. Forecasted composite semi-periodic components were then converted back into original feature space via a regression model. Through this method, we show that NAO semi-periodic behaviours can be effective predictors of the regional and national extent of droughts of a range of severity and duration, and that multi-year lags in atmosphere-hydrology systems (at specific frequencies) provide a novel way to forecast drought at multi-year lead times. Performance of semi-periodic NAO behaviours as predictors for hydrological drought were greatest in hydrogeological regions dominated by lower transmissivity and longer response times. Conversely, model performance was lower in flashier catchments, or for short-term droughts where short-term meteorological variability has a greater influence on hydrological behaviour. Previous studies have highlighted that non-stationarities between multi-year semi-periodic behaviours in the NAO and hydrological variables may preclude the use of these relationships in forecasting applications, however we show here that there is sufficient permanence within the strength of these behaviours to generate skilful drought forecasts. At present, long-range dynamic drought forecasts are not utilized in drought management strategies due to limited lead times in existing drought forecasting approaches. Our results show that teleconnection indices can be a skilful predictor of hydrological drought dynamics at multi-year timescales, opening new opportunities for long-lead groundwater drought forecasts to be integrated within existing drought management strategies in Europe. Given the importance of other teleconnection systems (such as El-Nino Southern Oscillation, or Indian Ocean Dipole) for driving hydrometeorological variability across multiple global regions, the methods established in this study have the potential for worldwide application. This could markedly enhance the global resilience to hydrological drought in a changing climate.
1 Introduction Evapotranspiration (ET) is at the core of terrestrial ecosystem water cycling and serves as a key process driving ecosystem changes (Wang et al., 2017 ). The strong mutual feedback between ET and ecosystems has made the response of ET to climate change a focal point in global ecosystem research (Fleischmann et al., 2023 ). ET is a complex process involving the atmosphere, soil, vegetation, and closely related to weather and climate (Deng et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023 ), playing a crucial role in ecosystem water-heat balance and water cycling (Wever et al., 2002 ). Some studies have shown that approximately 60 % of annual precipitation globally returns to the atmosphere in the form of ET (de Dios et al., 2015 ). This process indirectly influences surface temperature through responses to rainfall and latent heat flux, thereby playing a significant regulatory role in regional and global climate characteristics (Ainsworth & Rogers 2007; Li et al., 2007 ). Therefore, accurately determining ET is crucial for studying the mechanisms of eco-hydrological cycles in agricultural fields and guiding efficient irrigation practices. Since the 1980s, eddy covariance (EC) instrumentation has become fundamental in measuring exchanges of matter and energy between the surface of earth and the atmosphere due to its high temporal resolution and large area coverage (Baldocchi, 2020; Chu et al., 2021 ). Currently, several regional networks based on EC have been established, such as the Integrated Carbon Observation System (ICOS), AmeriFlux, the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON), AsiaFlux, ChinaFLUX, TERN OzFlux, and various sites within different biomes measuring energy exchange between land and atmosphere, they collectively sharing data from over 200 sites through the FLUXNET project (Jiang et al., 2022; Pastorello et al., 2020a,b ). However, issues such as instrument malfunctions, maintenance needs, and environmental constraints result in approximately 17 % to 50 % of the data being unusable annually (Vitale et al., 2020; Foken et al., 2004 ). These gaps significantly impact the analysis of evapotranspiration trends and modeling, increasing uncertainties in hydrological and meteorological studies (Falgeet al., 2001; Jung et al., 2019 ). Addressing these challenges by developing a robust, reliable gap-filling method for various scenarios has become crucial. Therefore, developing a highly applicable (not limited by the amount of missing data and not limited by regional, temporal, or site-specific observation data), robust (unaffected by outliers and random noise), and reliable (high precision) gap-filling method for different data missing scenarios has become an urgent issue that needs to be addressed. Robust gap-filling methods are vital for evapotranspiration (ET) as even slight inaccuracies can significantly impact studies of annual ET quantities, particularly under the influence of climate change on the water cycle (Kim et al., 2020 ; Qian et al., 2024 ). ET modeling is complex due to its sensitivity to a range of factors including radiation, air and soil temperatures, vegetation cover, wind speed, humidity, and topography, which vary across different locations and times (Chen et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2023 ). Unlike other ecosystem fluxes, such as methane, much of the daily variation in ET is influenced by geographic and seasonal factors (Wolf et al., 2023; Bellocchi et al., 2023 ), which challenges the consistency and geographical applicability of some gap-filling methods. Interannual ET variations, influenced by climatic factors and soil properties like precipitation, soil type, and land cover (Guo et al., 2023; Vremec et al., 2023 ), present additional complexities. Empirical regression-based methods and machine learning algorithms may not effectively capture non-stationary ET trends due to the slow-changing nature of these factors (Reichstein et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2018a,b ). Moreover, ET rates exhibit hysteresis in response to changes in environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, and solar radiation, complicating the understanding of precipitation and vegetation impacts on ET (Zheng et al., 2014 ). It remains unclear if current methods can adequately address this hysteresis effect (Reichstein et al., 2019 ). Due to the characteristics and driving factors of ET, selecting appropriate gap-filling methods for it poses certain challenges. While traditional methods like using temperature, humidity, and solar radiation can be effective, they aren't consistently reliable. Researchers have employed Marginal Distribution Sampling (MDS) algorithms to infer missing ET data using the distribution of environmental variables (Reichstein et al., 2005; Novick et al., 2009; Du et al., 2014; Pastorello et al., 2020a,b; Lucas-Moffat et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022 ). Despite its widespread use in hydrology, facilitated by robust software (Wutzler et al., 2018 ; Kim et al., 2020 ), MDS often fails to capture complex causality of ET with these variables. Recent studies have tried replacing MDS input variables with ones more directly linked to ET, like soil moisture, NDVI, and LAI (Chen et al., 2012; Peer et al., 2010; Zhao and Huang, 2015; Deventer et al., 2019 ). However, these adjustments may not fully overcome multifactorial dependencies of ET. Additionally, MDS struggles with long-term gaps over 15 days, where its accuracy significantly drops (Moffat et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2022 ). Other common interpolation techniques like Mean Diurnal Variation (MDV), Look-Up Table (LUT), and Linear and Non-Linear Regression (LR and NLR) face difficulties in capturing the nonlinear interactions between water, heat, carbon fluxes, and environmental factors (Falge et al., 2001; Desai et al., 2008; He et al., 2006 ). MDV introduces biases in extreme weather, while NLR fails to simulate high-frequency fluctuations of ET, resulting in data smoothing (Hui et al., 2004 ). LUT, which uses an index table to fill gaps, is affected by factors like the timing of the selection of table and environmental conditions (Falge et al., 2001 ). For instance, Zhao and Huang (2015)  investigated the issue of missing data in measurements of CO2, water, and energy fluxes between the biosphere and the atmosphere using eddy covariance (EC) systems. Their study evaluated three methods – Mean Diurnal Variation (MDV), Look-Up Table (LUT), and Non-Linear Regression (NLR). They found that an integrated approach using non-linear regression and look-up table methods could reduce errors in short vegetation scenarios, although the overall accuracy remained unsatisfactory. Boudhina et al. (2018)  assessed different data gap-filling methods in an agricultural hilly watershed in northeastern Tunisia and determined that REddyProc was the most suitable technique. This method performed well in handling the latent heat (LE) time series data from hilly croplands, but the filling accuracy became highly unstable as the proportion of gaps increased. In recent years, the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms to address missing ET data in time series flux data, such as gross primary productivity, ecosystem respiration, net ecosystem exchange, and transpiration, has gained traction. Machine learning offers an advantage over traditional gap-filling techniques as it can model nonlinear relationships between input and output variables without the need for pre-defined complex mathematical expressions, often outperforming conventional methods (Kang et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020 ). For example, Kim et al. (2019) compared the performance of MDS and three ML algorithms in methane gap filling using a combination of multiple auxiliary variables, with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) as input to address the multiple driver dependencies of FCH4 and reduce the internal complexity of the algorithm structure. Their results indicated that compared to traditional inputs, PCA improved gap-filling performance, with RF outperforming other techniques at all sites. Kang et al. (2019)  evaluated the applicability of Support Vector Machines (SVM) in filling long-duration gaps in various flux data, finding that using longer training datasets typically yielded better model performance, thus proposing a strategy for precise gap filling in long-interval flux data. Mahabbati et al. (2021)  compared three common flux missing value estimation algorithms and eight environmental driver-based machine learning algorithms. Their findings indicated that for gaps shorter than 30 days, the differences among the algorithms were not significant. However, for longer gaps, the Random Forest (RF) algorithm demonstrated the most consistent performance and was slightly superior to other algorithms. Yao et al. (2021)  filled CO2 flux gaps in semi-arid regions using Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Random Forest (RF), showing superior performance compared to K-nearest neighbors (KNN) and Support Vector Machines (SVM), particularly in filling gaps spanning several hours to days. For extremely long gaps of several months, a two-layer filling framework based on RF significantly enhanced model performance, especially for nighttime data. Zhu et al. (2022)  conducted experiments at 94 global FLUXNET2015 sites and proposed a new gap-filling method named Random Forest Robust (RFR). Utilizing three to ten driving variables, the RFR method effectively filled data gaps for CO2, latent heat, and sensible heat fluxes, improving the accuracy and stability of gap filling compared to traditional methods. Gao et al. (2023)  developed a novel framework combining machine learning and time series decomposition (TSD) to fill discontinuities in NEE data. Evaluating NEE data from 25 AmeriFlux sites, they discovered that a combination of Random Forest and moving averages performed better across various gap lengths, reducing data variability and the complexity of extracted low-frequency NEE data changes, with an R2  improvement of about 34 %. Vekuri et al. (2023)  employed eddy covariance, a key measurement technique, to quantify these carbon sinks and calibrate models but required data interpolation to determine the annual carbon balance of ecosystems. Through analyzing extensive global datasets, they found that the machine learning XGB method could correct the MDS method to significantly reduce biases in gap filling across the Northern Hemisphere. However, the accuracy of machine learning models in filling long-term data gaps declines significantly when the gaps exceed a certain threshold (Zhu et al., 2022 ). Deep Learning (DL), comprising a series of advanced Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), has seen substantial development since 2012 and has been demonstrated to be more effective than other machine learning (ML) techniques (LeCun et al., 2015; Shen, 2018; Mahabbati et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a,b ). For instance, Fine et al. (2022)  found that deep learning-based gap filling methods were more reliable than conventional techniques such as Marginal Distribution Sampling (MDS) in addressing data gaps in eddy covariance flux measurements. Specifically, these methods significantly reduced the normalized root mean square error (nRMSE) across the entire dataset and during missing periods by up to 13.5 % on a half-hourly time scale. Lucas-Moffat et al. (2022)  assessed the performance of these techniques using artificially created data gaps and filled real missing values in flux datasets of various gases. The results showed that four models, including ANN, were successfully applied to gaps in four different types of flux gases. This is because environmental factors such as air temperature, radiation, and relative humidity exhibit seasonality and time dependence. Therefore, ET gap filling can be viewed as a time series regression problem. While some ML models struggle with the time-dependent aspects of evapotranspiration, DL models excel in handling trends, seasonality, and learning time dependencies (Sharma et al., 2022 ). Unlike classical ANN commonly used in ET studies, other DL models adeptly learn complex hydrological patterns, manage multiple inputs, and use the spatial or temporal structures of data hierarchically (Papale and Valentini, 2003; Braswell et al., 2005; Fine et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2022 ). This capability allows DL models to incorporate various climatic parameters such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed, enhancing prediction accuracy and showing superior performance in ET gap filling at the point scale (Kumar et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021; Peppert et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a,b ). Due to the effective resolution of a large number of data, complex relationships of multivariables, and multi-step time series prediction tasks, deep learning (DL) models have successfully addressed various gap-filling tasks for different data types, such as NDVI (Liu et al., 2017a,b,c ), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) (Poggio et al., 2012 ), Precipitation (Kim and Ryu 2016 ), Methane flux (FCH4) (Kim et al., 2019), Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) (Moffat et al., 2007 ), Temperature (Lompar et al., 2019 ), and carbon dioxide (CO2) (Dragomir et al., 2012 ). For instance, Khan et al. (2021)  utilized satellite remote sensing technology in an environmental monitoring study at a specific site, employing two deep learning models and machine learning models to fill missing data for latent heat flux (LE) measurements obtained from an Eddy-covariance (EC) station. Time series analysis and Taylor diagrams indicated that an improved two-dimensional CNN was most capable of capturing the temporal trends of LE, and performed better when specific meteorological factors were removed during the training phase. Wang et al. (2022a,b)  addressed the issue of missing information in time series data from sensors on satellite platforms by proposing a deep learning-based method called the content-sequence-texture generation (CSTG) network, which was trained and tested using MODIS data from various regions, yielding favorable results in artificial experiments with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.016. Xie et al. (2021)  introduced a deep learning-based model, BiLSTM-I, which effectively filled gaps in semi-hourly temperature observations by incorporating low-frequency manually collected temperature data. Experimental results demonstrated that the BiLSTM-I model outperformed other methods, exhibiting excellent generalization capabilities and potential for application in other data-filling scenarios. Zhao et al. (2022)  combined machine learning methods with deep neural network (DNN) models to address data gaps in environmental footprint accounting. The results showed that the DNN model significantly improved filling performance, with the R2  value increasing from 0.6412 to 0.8726 for short-term gaps, and from 0.5271 to 0.7893 for long-term gaps. Research by ElSaadan et al. (2021)  proved that the ConvLSTM algorithm, which combines CNN and LSTM, was notably superior in filling soil moisture gaps, achieving an average regional correlation coefficient of 0.9. However, the majority of current research is predominantly confined to individual or a limited number of regional sites, leaving gaps in the global scope of evapotranspiration (ET) gap-filling. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models are widely used to address hydrological and ecological challenges in evapotranspiration (ET), showing improved outcomes (Li et al., 2023a,b; Danandeh Mehr et al., 2022 ). CNN excel at detecting spatial patterns in ET data, effectively identifying local patterns and integrating environmental variables for comprehensive analysis (Li et al., 2022; Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020a,b ). LSTM handle long-term data sequences well, preventing gradient issues and enhancing interpolation accuracy by maintaining historical context and predicting future values (Granata and Di Nunno 2021; Babaeian et al., 2022 ). A hybrid CNN-LSTM model offers superior performance in ET data gap filling, though its application in this area is still limited (Sainath et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2022 ). Currently, most studies set relatively short artificial gap ratios. For example, in the study by Zhu et al. (2022) , which employed machine learning techniques to fill gaps in eddy covariance data, the longest gap set was only one month, without verifying whether the method maintains high accuracy in longer time intervals. Furthermore, most studies only utilize environmental meteorological factors from observation stations as input variables (Kim et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2021; Mahabbati et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022; Fine et al., 2022 ), which reduces the applicability of current filling methods and imposes significant limitations in both time and space. In recent decades, to overcome the constraints of geographical location and time in ET research, researchers have developed global ET products with different spatiotemporal scales based on remote sensing, reanalysis data, land surface model estimates, and data assimilation methods. These include MOD16A2 (Mu et al., 2011a,b ), GLDAS (Rodell et al., 2004 ), GLEAM (Miralles et al., 2011 ), ERA5 (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ), REA (Lu et al., 2021 ), PMLv2 (Zhang et al., 2019 ), and EB-ET (Chen et al., 2021 ), among others. These products, which integrate various data types and undergo rigorous quality calibration, show high accuracy and are suitable for filling ET gaps across various timescales (Khan et al., 2018 ). They reduce model input demands and decrease sensitivity to errors from single data sources (Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, no effective attempts have yet been made to integrate these ET products with deep learning for gap filling. In summary, the main research content and contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:1) Development and evaluation of the CNN-LSTM model for filling ET gaps with different missing ratios: Based on observations from 241 flux towers, five gap ratios are set, assuming 5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 35 %, and 50 % missing proportions of flux tower data. This is done to evaluate and compare the filling performance of the target model CNN-LSTM and five comparative models (CNN, LSTM, RF, SVM, ELM) under different artificial gap scenarios. And in the 50 flux towers with high data time span and integrity, we continue to increase the gap ratio to explore the limit of gap filling.  2) Comparison of gap filling with and without ET product inputs: Two input combinations are evaluated—one using only environmental factors (maximum temperature, minimum temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, 10 m wind speed, precipitation, surface soil moisture from ERA5 reanalysis data, and NDVI from NOAA), and another combining these environmental factors with ET products (GLEAM, GLDAS, ERA5, REA).  3) Evaluation of the gap filling capabilities of the model under different latitudes, land cover types, and climate types: Assessing the impact of different latitudes, land cover types, and climate types on the gap filling performance of target model.     2 Data and materials 2.1 Study area and distribution of flux towers The eddy covariance method is a widely used technique for continuous measurement of energy fluxes, allowing for the continuous measurement of water and energy exchanges (Mu et al., 2011a,b ). The FLUXNET2015 dataset provides continuous measurements of carbon flux and energy flux on an hourly basis using the eddy covariance method (Ma et al., 2021 ). In this study, latent heat flux (LE) from 241 flux towers worldwide is synthesized into daily data (see specific geographical distribution in Fig. 1  ). The flux tower data can be accessed online at https://fluxnet.fluxdata.org/ . To investigate the influence of different latitudes on the gap filling performance of model, the study categorizes these sites into three latitude groups: high, medium, and low. Additionally, based on the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) classification system (Friedl et al., 2010 ), the sites are categorized into seven land cover types. Furthermore, according to the global 1-kilometer climate type distribution provided by Beck et al. (2018) , this study aggregates the flux towers containing 27 Köppen climate types into seven climate types. The specific number of types for different latitudes, climate types, and land cover types are summarized in Table 1  . Further explanation on climate types can be found in the Supplementary Table S1 .  2.2 Flux tower data FLUXNET2015 dataset has undergone quality control and preprocessing to enhance consistency and comparability among sites, as detailed by Pastorello et al. (2020a,b) . Two independent methods, namely marginal distribution sampling (suffix_F_MDS) and ERA-Interim (suffix_F_ERA), are used to fill missing data. Despite nearly 50 years of development, the eddy covariance method remains the most advanced and preferred technique for flux observations in current studies of land–atmosphere exchange (Stocker et al., 2018 ). However, this method often encounters challenges in achieving energy balance closure when analyzing fluxes. Practically all land–atmosphere exchange models are based on the fundamental principles of energy and mass balance. In ecosystem observations, when energy enters the ecosystem from above, R n     takes positive values; conversely, R n     takes negative values. The surface energy balance equation is expressed as:(1) R n  - G - S - Q = H + L E      In the equation, R n     represents net radiation; G    denotes soil heat flux; S    represents the heat storage in the canopy layer; Q    stands for the sum of additional energy terms; H    is sensible heat flux, and LE    represents latent heat flux. Since S    and Q    are usually negligible, (R n  - G   ) is referred to as the available energy, while (H + E   ) is termed as the turbulent energy. Thus, when the available energy equals the turbulent energy, it is called energy balance closure; otherwise, it is termed energy balance non-closure. However, the turbulent energy observed by the EC method often deviates by approximately 10 %–30 % from the available energy (Chen et al., 2018 ). To correct for the energy imbalance in eddy covariance flux observations, this study assumes that the half-hourly Bowen ratio (the ratio of sensible heat flux to latent heat flux) remains unchanged before and after correction, thereby compensating for the energy deficit using the difference between available energy and turbulent energy (Jung et al., 2010 ). This study utilizes flux tower data (LE) and selects sites with at least one year of valid data. Finally, the observation data of flux tower (FLUXNET ET) can be obtained by dividing the latent heat flux variable (LE) of the flux tower by the conversion factor λ (2.45 MJ/kg) (Qian et al., 2023 ). To evaluate the efficacy of various methods for filling data gaps, data quality control and screening were initially conducted at the selected 241 sites. We excluded any half-hour records that lacked essential meteorological variables such as wind speed, relative humidity, air temperature, and radiation. Furthermore, we excluded ET (LE) values that were not within the range of −100 W/m2  to 700 W/m2  (Jiang et al., 2022 ). After quality control, days at each site with complete half-hourly (N = 48) ET and meteorological measurement data were further selected. These half-hourly measurement data were then aggregated into daily data formats. Based on this, the distribution of ET gaps across the selected 241 flux towers was statistically analyzed, revealing significant variability in the gaps present. Fig. 2   illustrates the histogram of daily ET gap percentages (the ratio of days with missing ET data to total ET days) for the selected flux towers. It can be observed that nearly all flux towers experience ET gaps, with the majority (approximately 83 %) having gaps less than 50 %. However, a small fraction of sites have data gaps exceeding 70 %. And the distribution of these gaps is completely random and irregular, which may be missing for a single day or several consecutive days, likely attributed to field operations, instrument malfunctions, power outages, sensor failures, and downtime. These substantial gaps underscore the necessity and urgency of gap-filling efforts. Specific proportions of gap for each flux towers are provided in Table S2  in the Supplementary materials .  2.3 Input variables 2.3.1 ERA5 reanalysis meteorological data and NDVI Drawing upon previous research (Tramontana et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2019 ), this study selects meteorological variables from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset that are most closely associated with ET as input variables (see Table 2  ), thus overcoming geographical and temporal data limitations. These variables include maximum temperature (Tmax ), minimum temperature (Tmin ), relative humidity (RH), surface solar radiation (Rs ), 10-meter wind speed (WS), precipitation (Pre), and soil moisture content (SMC). The ERA5 data have an original spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25°. Additionally, daily Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data are obtained from the NOAA Climate Data Record (CDR) AVHRR product (Version 5) (Pedelty et al., 2007 ; Zhang, 2015 ), providing measurements of surface vegetation activity globally from 1981 to 2019 at a spatial resolution of 0.05°. The ERA5 and NDVI data can be accessed online from https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/  and https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/climate-data-records , respectively. Finally, since the ERA5 reanalysis meteorological data are part of a gridded dataset, there is a need to address the issue of matching these data with flux tower measurements. Consequently, this study employs the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) technique to interpolate meteorological data from four neighboring grid points to the flux tower locations. Inverse Distance Weighting is a deterministic interpolation technique that allocates weights based on distance. The underlying principle involves using a weighted moving average method, where weights are determined by the spatial distance between the interpolation point and the data points. This approach ensures that meteorological data are tailored to the specific sites of the flux towers, enhancing the accuracy and relevance of environmental data integration. The calculation formula can be found in the attachment (model). Our study also used the IDW method to interpolate the ET values of grid ET products into flux towers.  2.3.2 ET products The Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM, https://www.gleam.eu/ ) (Martens et al., 2017 ) is a remote sensing tool for simulating land evaporation and soil moisture. GLEAM breaks down evaporation into components like plant transpiration and interception loss, using remote sensing data and surface variables (Martens et al., 2017 ). It calculates evapotranspiration (ET) based on potential evaporation and soil water stress, suitable for use in hydrological models due to its low data requirements. The model uses a simplified Priestley-Taylor equation and accounts for different surface types (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ; Zhao and Huang, 2015 ). This study used GLEAMv3.8b version, which offers a 0.25° × 0.25° spatial resolution. The Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS, https://ldas.gsfc.nasa.gov/gldas/ ) (Rodell et al., 2004 ) is a sophisticated land simulation system that merges land and atmospheric data using advanced models and data assimilation techniques to simulate land surface conditions and fluxes globally. It offers global flux data at both coarse (0.25°) and fine (0.01°) resolutions, updating every three hours and monthly. For details, visit the NASA Hydrology Data and Information Services Center website. Our study used the CLSM (Community Land Model with Subgrid Parameterization) model data from GLDAS, focusing on land surface parameters from 1948 to 2014 with a resolution of 0.25°. The Reliability Ensemble Average Products (REA, https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/home ) (Lu et al., 2021 ) generate global daily evapotranspiration datasets using model-based data from ERA5, MERRA2, and GLDAS2-Noah. These products apply a coefficient of variation to identify highly consistent regions, utilizing a reliability ensemble averaging method (Lu et al., 2021 ). The datasets cover the period from 1980 to 2017 with a spatial resolution of 0.25°. Validation was performed using GLEAMv3.2a and flux tower data, showing accurate trends in evapotranspiration across various vegetation covers. The data, including elements like longitude, latitude, and time, are stored in NetCDF format for the years 1980 to 2017. ERA5 (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu ) (Wang et al., 2023 ), released by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in 2021, is a global dataset from the fifth generation reanalysis of ECMWF. It utilizes the 4D data assimilation technique and the land surface model of ECMWF. The dataset features 137 isobaric levels, a 0.01 hPa spacing, and includes temperature, humidity, wind speed, and surface pressure variables (Albergel et al., 2018). ERA5 shows marked improvements over the ERA Interim, especially in latent heat data, and spans from 1979 to 2021 with a resolution of 0.01°.   2.4 Input combination In order to explore the effect of ET products as inputs on the gap filling performance of the model, two input combinations are set up in this study: 1) without ET products as inputs (input combination M1), where the input variables include Tmax , Tmin , RH, Rs , WS, SMC, Pre, and NDVI; 2) with ET products as inputs (input combination M2), where the input variables include all the above environmental factors and the four ET products (GLEAM, GLDAS, REA, and ERA5).  2.5 Artificial gap scenarios To assess the sensitivity of different interpolation methods to the length of missing segments and ensure that these methods are not influenced by the number and distribution of data gaps, this study randomly generated missing segments at various proportions. Specifically, we introduced missing data at five different proportions (5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 35 %, and 50 %) based on the original data. This significantly enhances the adaptability of gap-filling methods. To improve data utilization and ensure the accuracy and stability of the computational results, each missing scenario was randomly repeated 30 times, and the computational results were averaged in the end. Additionally, in the 50 flux towers with high data time span and integrity, we will continue to increase the gap ratio to explore the limit of gap filling, and the specific information of 50 flux towers can be found in attachment Table S3 .   3 Methodology 3.1 Marginal distribution sampling (MDS) The Marginal Distribution Sampling (MDS) method combines the use of the MDV and LUT method (Reichstein et al., 2005 ). When observational data for temperature (Ta ), total radiation (Rg ), and saturated vapor pressure deficit (VPD) are available, within a specified time window (14 to 28 days before and after missing data), Ta , Rg , and VPD are interpolated with variation ranges constrained to 2.5 °C, 50 W m−2 , and 0.5 kPa, respectively (Mahabbati et al., 2021 ). When only Rg  data is available, the interpolation time window is narrowed to 14 days before and after. In cases where all meteorological observation elements are missing, the MDV method is used to interpolate missing data (Falge et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2020 ). If gaps persist, the time window is expanded, and the aforementioned steps are repeated until all missing data are interpolated (Zhu et al., 2022 ). This study evaluated the LE data filled by the MDS method (LE_F_MDS) in the Flux2015 dataset.  3.2 Random Forest (RF) RF is an ensemble algorithm proposed by Breiman (2001) . The basic procedure involves constructing multiple regression decision tree models by bootstrapping samples from the training set using the bootstrap sampling method. The final prediction of the random forest is obtained by averaging the predictions of all regression decision trees. More detailed information and hyper-parameters about RF can be found in the attachment.  3.3 Support Vector Machine (SVM) SVM is a supervised learning model used for classification and regression tasks. Its core idea is to find an optimal hyperplane in the feature space that maximizes the margin between data points of different classes. By utilizing kernel functions, SVM can handle nonlinear problems. It possesses the advantages of efficiency in high-dimensional spaces and strong generalization capability. However, SVM is sensitive to parameters and involves high computational complexity. More detailed information and hyper-parameters about SVM can be found in the attachment.  3.4 Extreme learning machine (ELM) ELM is a single-hidden-layer feedforward neural network algorithm (Vapnik, 1995 ). Its distinctive feature lies in the fact that during the training process, only the connection weights between the hidden layer and the output layer need to be randomly initialized. Subsequently, the output weights are directly computed through an analytical solution. This approach enables efficient and rapid training as well as excellent generalization capability. More detailed information and hyper-parameters about ELM can be found in the attachment.  3.5 Convolutional neural network (CNN) CNN is a type of deep learning model that is particularly well-suited for processing and recognizing image data. It automatically learns features of input variables through components such as convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers, achieving progressive extraction and transformation from raw feature variables to high-level abstract features. CNN has achieved significant success in tasks such as time series forecasting and multi-input regression. The Architecture of CNN model is shown in Fig. 3   and more detailed information and hyper-parameters about CNN can be found in the attachment.  3.6 Long short term memory (LSTM) LSTM is a special type of recurrent neural network (RNN) designed specifically for processing and predicting time series data. Compared to traditional RNN, LSTM exhibits stronger memory capabilities, enabling effective resolution of long-term dependency issues. Through gate mechanisms, LSTM can selectively remember or forget past information, making it perform excellently when dealing with long sequence data. It has been widely applied in tasks such as language modeling, text generation, and time series forecasting. The Architecture of LSTM model is shown in Fig. 4   and more detailed information and hyper-parameters about LSTM can be found in the attachment.  3.7 CNN-LSTM CNN-LSTM is a hybrid neural network that combines convolutional neural network layers and LSTM layers into a unified framework (Sainath et al., 2015 ). It has been demonstrated in the past that providing relevant characteristics of input variables further enhances the performance of model (Pascanu et al., 2013 ). CNN is widely known for its ability to extract relevant features from datasets. This hybrid algorithm has been applied to various time series estimation and prediction problems (Sharma et al., 2022 ), but has not been studied in the context of gap filling. In this study, the CNN-LSTM algorithm is employed to fill gaps in missing data, where the CNN layer extracts relevant features from meteorological variables, NDVI, and ET products, and identifies correlations between multivariate time series affecting the evapotranspiration process. Subsequently, the output of this layer is used as input to the LSTM layer (after several other layers such as pooling and flattening layers) to model temporal information for predicting the evapotranspiration value at the next time stamp. The network model is illustrated in Fig. 4 . Batch normalization (BN) is applied after each convolution operation to prevent overfitting. Dropout is used for random deletion after the second pooling operation, and adaptive moment estimation (Adam) is employed for adaptive learning rate, with an initial value of 0.001. The cross-entropy loss function is chosen as the objective function, and biases and weights are updated through backpropagation. The specific schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 5  . The selection of hyperparameters can significantly influence the learning speed and performance of a given model. Here are the main parameters and settings of the model in this paper: In the provided code, the CNN part comprises two convolutional layers. The first convolutional layer consists of 16 filters with a kernel size of [2, 1], and the second convolutional layer consists of 32 filters with the same kernel size of [2, 1]. ReLU activation functions are applied after each convolutional layer. The LSTM layer contains 4 hidden units, with the output mode set to 'last'. Subsequently, there is a fully connected layer with 1 output neuron, utilized for regression tasks. The input layer of the model accepts sequence inputs with data dimensions of [12, 1, 1] or [8, 1, 1]. The hyper-parameters about CNN-LSTM can be found in the attachment, and below is the roadmap for the implementation of this model (Fig. 6  ):  3.8 Permutation importance This paper employs the Permutation Importance (PI) method for feature selection. The essence of the Permutation Importance method is to assess the importance of a particular feature by permuting its values while keeping other variables unchanged, then utilizing the permuted data for prediction. Subsequently, the change in model accuracy before and after permutation is calculated to determine the importance of feature. If a feature significantly impacts the predictive model, permuting its values will lead to a notable change in model accuracy. Conversely, if there is little to no effect, it suggests that the feature has low importance for the model (Aldrich, 2020 ). The steps for using the PI method to identify important features are as follows:1) Train a model using all features.  2) Validate the performance of model on a validation set and compute the loss (loss_raw).  3) Randomly permute the data corresponding to one feature in the validation set and re-estimate the loss (loss_permuted).  4) Calculate the difference between the losses to obtain the importance score for feature: impr = (loss_permuted – loss_raw).  5) Repeat steps 3 and 4 for each feature to obtain the importance of each feature.  6) Select appropriate features based on the computed importance.  7) Train another model using the selected features and validate its performance on a test set.    The computation of feature importance in this method occurs after model training, eliminating the need for retraining other models, thus significantly saving time. Randomly permuting the data of a feature diminishes the performance of model on the test set since the permuted data lose their original meaning. The more crucial a feature is, the worse the estimation results will be after permutation. Features with minimal impact on estimation will result in relatively unchanged estimation performance even after permutation. Hence, the difference between estimation loss of the model with permuted data (loss_permuted) and the original loss (loss_raw) characterizes the importance of feature. Compared to other feature selection methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), the PI method has two advantages: it provides a numerical measure of each importance of feature, enabling researchers to intuitively understand which features are important and why; and once important features are identified, future estimations on new data can be directly performed using only those features, unlike methods like PCA, which require all features to be processed for dimensionality reduction before estimation.  3.9 Model training and statistical metrics In this study, initially, 241 flux tower data along with corresponding ERA5 meteorological variables, NDVI, and ET products are divided into retained and missing data sets, with missing proportions of 5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 35 %, and 50 %. A 5-fold cross-validation method is employed to train the model. The retained data of the 241 flux towers are randomly divided into 60 % training set, 20 % validation set, and 20 % test set at each station. The training set is used for training the imputation model, while the test set is used for evaluating the imputation model. Finally, the missing data sets are inputted into the trained model to predict the missing ET data. The imputation accuracy of different models in the missing data sets is evaluated by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient (R2 ), root mean square error (RMSE, mm/d), and percentage bias (PBias, %) between the predicted values and the true values. Here, R2  closer to 1 indicate a better fit between the estimated values and the true values. A smaller RMSE suggests less error between the estimated values and the true values. PBias closer to 0 indicates less deviation between the estimated values and the true values. When PBias is negative, it indicates underestimation, whereas when it is positive, it indicates overestimation.   4 Result 4.1 Overall gap-filling performance In general, the performance of the model filling decreases with the increase of gap ratio. Concerning model relevance (Fig. 7  a–b), when the gap ratio is 5 %, the R2  of most sites ranges between 0.9 and 0.95. However, as the gap ratio exceeds 20 %, the number of sites with significant decline in R2  increases. When the gap ratio reaches 50 %, R2  concentrates between 0.75 and 0.85. Specifically, sites in North America and Europe are predominant, with CNN-LSTM exhibiting higher R2  in the Northern Hemisphere. With increasing gap ratio, noticeable declines in R2  are observed in South America, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Compared to models without ET products as inputs, the addition of ET products significantly improves R2 , particularly concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere, notably in Northern Europe and Russia. However, some regions exhibit suboptimal accuracy, such as Central Africa and Central-Southern Asia. Furthermore, from the distribution of R2  mean values in the latitude direction (Fig. 7 c), it is evident that adding ET products as inputs can significantly enhance model relevance, with R2  performing well in high-latitude regions and showing significant fluctuations in mid and low latitudes. From the perspective of model bias (Fig. 8  a–b), when the gap ratio is below 10 %, the PBias of most site locations remains within 30 %. However, as the gap ratio reaches 20 %, the model bias exhibits significant fluctuations, and when the gap ratio reaches 50 %, both overestimation and underestimation biases can reach 80 %. Meanwhile, without ET products as inputs, the number of overestimated and underestimated sites is roughly equivalent. However, with the addition of ET products as inputs, there is a noticeable improvement in model performance, with only slight overestimation observed at most sites. This improvement is particularly evident in North America, Northern and Central Europe, Eastern Russia, most parts of Asia, and Australia. Lastly, from the distribution of PBias mean values in the latitude direction (Fig. 8 c), it is apparent that without ET products as inputs, the model bias exhibits significant fluctuations, predominantly showing underestimation. The addition of ET products as inputs can significantly reduce model bias, and similarly performs well in high-latitude regions.  4.2 Sensitivity of gap-filling to gap length 4.2.1 Estimation without ET products In the absence of ET products as model inputs, significant performance differences are observed among different methods across the five gap scenarios (Fig. 9  ). Overall, the hybrid CNN-LSTM model performs the best across all scenarios, followed closely by CNN and LSTM models. Based on the models' average performance, the ranking from best to worst among the six models is as follows: CNN-LSTM > CNN > LSTM > RF > SVM > ELM. As shown in Fig. 9 a, when the ET data gap ratio is 5 %, all models exhibit optimal performance, with most methods achieving a correlation coefficient (R2 ) above 0.8 between the filled ET and FLUXNET ET at most sites. The R2  values for CNN-LSTM are concentrated above 0.9, although some sites still have R2  values below 0.8. The average R2  values for CNN and LSTM are around 0.89, while the performance of the three machine learning models is noticeably lower than that of deep learning (with R2  values around 0.83), and more sites have R2  values below 0.6. As the data gap ratio increases, the filling performance of the models gradually decreases. The difference in R2  between gap ratios of 5 % and 10 % is relatively small, but when the gap exceeds 20 %, the model correlation significantly increases, and the estimation stability deteriorates further (with an increasing number of sites having R2  below 0.4). As shown in Fig. 9 c, when the gap ratio is below 20 %, the differences in RMSE between different methods for filling ET and FLUXNET ET are small. When the ET data gap ratio is 5 %, the RMSE values for all six models are concentrated within 1 mm/d (with the worst site not exceeding 3 mm/d), with CNN-LSTM having an RMSE below 2 mm/d for all sites. However, at gap ratios of 35 % and 50 %, the RMSE of the models increases significantly, and the errors at different sites are more dispersed. CNN-LSTM still maintains an RMSE below 1 mm/d for most sites, while the RMSE values of the other models are concentrated between 1 mm/d and 2 mm/d, with the highest approaching 5 mm/d. Finally, we also analyzed the overestimation and underestimation of different models (Fig. 9 b). The results indicate that when the data gap ratio is below 20 %, the estimation performance of all models is relatively stable, with PBias concentrated within −25 % to 25 %. Except for CNN-LSTM, which has a more balanced distribution of overestimation and underestimation sites, the other models generally exhibit slight underestimation, which becomes more pronounced as the data gap increases. In summary, when ET products are not included as inputs, the accuracy of the CNN-LSTM model decreases noticeably with an increase in the ET data gap ratio. When the gap ratio increases from 5 % to 50 %, the average R2  decreases from 0.916 to 0.784, representing a reduction of approximately 14 %. Similarly, the RMSE increases from 0.552 mm/d to 0.952 mm/d, indicating an average increase of approximately 72 %. Additionally, the phenomenon of underestimation intensifies as the data gap ratio increases.  4.2.2 Estimation with ET products As shown in Fig. 10  , the performance differences among different methods under the five categories of missing gaps are significantly reduced when ET products are included as inputs. Overall, the CNN-LSTM model continues to exhibit the best performance. As depicted in Fig. 10 a, when the ET data gap ratio is within 35 %, all models demonstrate relatively good performance. For most sites, the R2  between the filled ET and actual FLUXNET ET remains above 0.8. Specifically, CNN-LSTM achieves R2  values concentrated above 0.9. Even when the data gap ratio reaches 50 %, the model performance experiences a noticeable decrease but remains within an acceptable range. However, except for CNN-LSTM and CNN, approximately 1/4 of the sites show R2  values below 0.8 for the other models, while ELM exhibits over 60 % of sites with R2  values below 0.8. Moreover, the increase in the data gap ratio only affects the upper limit of the model estimation correlation, with minimal change in the lower limit. The lowest R2  values for all models under different data gap ratios remain around 0.6. As shown in Fig. 10 c, the differences in RMSE between different methods for filling ET and FLUXNET ET are relatively small under all five categories of data gap ratios, with the majority of site errors concentrated within 1 mm/d. When the ET data gap ratio exceeds 35 % and the errors at different sites become more dispersed, the RMSE of the models at some sites may exceed 3 mm/d. Lastly, as depicted in Fig. 10 b, the performance of CNN-LSTM remains relatively stable under all data gap ratios, with a balanced distribution of overestimation and underestimation sites. The PBias mainly concentrates within −25 % to 25 %, with the highest not exceeding 50 %. In contrast, the other models generally exhibit slight overestimation, which becomes more pronounced as the data gap ratio increases. Furthermore, compared to when ET products are not included as inputs, the addition of ET products as model inputs leads to a significant improvement in estimation performance (Fig. 11  ). For instance, in the case of CNN-LSTM, when the data gap ratio is 5 %, the difference in R2  and RMSE between with and without ET products as inputs is 0.035 and 0.161 mm/d, respectively. However, when the data gap ratio increases to 50 %, the difference in R2  and RMSE can reach 0.072 and 0.434 mm/d, respectively. As for the other models, in terms of R2 , the difference in model R2  with and without ET products as inputs ranges from 0.045 to 0.159 across different data gap ratios, while the difference in RMSE ranges from 0.265 mm/d to 0.947. The specific improvement in model performance after adding ET products as inputs under different data gap ratios can be observed in Fig. 11 . In summary, when ET products are included as inputs, the decrease in accuracy of CNN-LSTM due to an increase in the ET data gap ratio is significantly reduced. For instance, when the gap ratio increases from 5 % to 50 %, the average R2  decreases from 0.952 to 0.846, representing a reduction of approximately 11 %, while the average RMSE increases from 0.491 to 0.620, indicating an increase of approximately 26 %. Moreover, the phenomenon of underestimation is significantly mitigated. Additionally, compared to when ET products are not included as inputs, adding ET products as inputs on top of environmental factors can significantly improve the accuracy of gap filling models. On average, the R2  increases by 5 % to 15 %, the RMSE decreases by 15 % to 35 %, and the underestimation phenomenon is notably improved.  4.2.3 Limits of gap-filling models To further investigate the performance of model, we conducted an analysis of the filling limits of six gap-filling models and compared the filling limits with and without ET products as inputs. By gradually increasing the gap ratio to obtain the corresponding performance of the model, when the filling R2  falls below 0.4, we consider that the model has reached its gap-filling limit. In general, when the gap ratio exceeds 50 %, the filling performance of different methods will significantly decline. Among them, CNN-LSTM consistently outperforms other methods, while ELM exhibits the poorest performance. Specifically, when ET products are not used as inputs (Fig. 12  a–b), different methods can maintain R2  around 0.6 when the gap ratio reaches 60 %. However, as the gap ratio further increases, the R2  of all methods except CNN-LSTM shows a significant decline. ELM, SVM, and RF reach their filling limits when the gap ratio is below 70 %, while LSTM and CNN reach their limits slightly above 70 %. CNN-LSTM maintains R2  between 0.4 and 0.6 when the gap ratio is 70 %, and the correlation between CNN-LSTM filling and FLUXNET drops below 0.4 when the gap ratio reaches 80 %, reaching the filling limit. When ET products are used as inputs (Fig. 12 c–d), there is a significant improvement in filling performance. When the gap ratio reaches 65 %, CNN-LSTM can still maintain R2  around 0.8, while the other methods can maintain R2  around 0.75. As the gap ratio further increases, the filling performance of the five comparison models and methods will significantly decline, but R2  can still reach 0.5 at the gap ratio of 80 %, and the filling limit ultimately falls between 85 % (ELM) and 90 % (CNN). The R2  of CNN-LSTM remains concentrated between 0.4 and 0.6 when the gap ratio is 80 %, and eventually reaches the filling limit at around 93 % gap ratio. Furthermore, we divided the 241 flux tower sites into 7 categories based on the magnitude of the gap ratio to assess the data filled by the MDS method in the observation dataset, as detailed in Appendix Fig. 5 A. Overall, the performance of the MDS method at different gap ratios is lower than the aforementioned deep learning and machine learning methods. Specifically, at sites with the gap ratio below 10 %, the MDS method exhibits good filling performance, with an average R2  above 0.8. When the gap ratio exceeds 20 %, there is a noticeable initial decline in filling performance, with R2  decreasing to around 0.6. Between gap ratios of 50 % to 65 %, more than half of the sites reach the filling limit, with R2  dropping below 0.4. For all sites with a gap ratio exceeding 65 %, MDS reaches the filling limit, with an average R2  below 0.3. In summary, adding ET products as inputs can significantly improve the gap-filling limit of model, with an average improvement of 13 percentage points.   4.3 Specific performance of CNN-LSTM for ET gap filling 4.3.1 Performance at different latitudes regions Fig. 13   illustrates the performance of CNN-LSTM in filling ET under different gap scenarios and latitude regions, with corresponding R2  values displayed in the graph.
