The eddy covariance (EC) technique is a highly reliable way to measure ET in natural ecosystems. However, instrument issues and abnormal weather often cause data gaps averaging 20–60 %, complicating model training, validation, and ET research (Vitale et al., 2020 ). Gap filling in high-frequency EC time series is challenging due to variability and nonlinear interactions with atmospheric of ET, vegetation, and soil moisture factors. Various procedures have been proposed to fill the gaps in ET measurements from EC, but few methods simultaneously address the issues of temporal and spatial coverage while ensuring filling accuracy, with most methods limited to short gap filling at a few sites and poor spatiotemporal scalability (Jiang et al., 2022 ). This study proposes a deep learning-based gap-filling scheme using ET products and environmental factors from 241 global flux tower observations. Eight key factors are considered, including maximum and mean air temperature, solar radiation, NDVI, relative humidity, precipitation, and wind speed. To improve the performance of models in gap filling, ET products are used alongside environmental data. Though requiring a range of meteorological inputs, data can be easily obtained through ERA5 or other reanalysis sources, making this method broadly applicable without field measurement dependency or spatiotemporal limitations. 5.1 Physical meaning and importance of environmental factors and ET products to ET Evapotranspiration (ET) is a crucial process in the hydrological cycle that transfers moisture from land to the atmosphere and redistributes it back to the surface through precipitation and other forms, playing an essential role in maintaining the balance of water resources (Joo et al., 2017 ). It directly influences regional humidity, precipitation, and temperature, thereby having a decisive impact on climate and ecosystem balance (Bai and Liu, 2018 ). Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the physical meaning of ET is vital for gap filling, water resource management, and agricultural production. The hydrological cycle involves the continuous movement of water among the atmosphere, land, and oceans, forming the basis for the distribution of global water resources. As a critical component of the hydrological cycle, ET is the key process of water exchange between the atmosphere and land, moving significant amounts of moisture into the atmosphere through plants and soil surfaces (Li et al., 2018 ). ET mainly comprises evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation refers to the process by which water on surfaces, including bodies of water, soil, and plants, directly converts from liquid or solid to gaseous form, entering the atmosphere (Wu et al., 2020a,b ). This process is influenced by the physical properties of water and environmental factors. On the other hand, transpiration is the process through which plants absorb water from the soil via their roots and release it into the atmosphere by evaporating it through stomata in their leaves (Mu et al., 2007 ). Plants require substantial amounts of water for photosynthesis to keep their stomata open and maintain metabolism, while water also evaporates through transpiration (Yang et al., 2018 ). Stomatal opening and closing are influenced by various environmental factors and are closely linked to the physiological activities of plants. In extreme conditions like high temperatures or drought, plants may close their stomata to reduce water loss (Xie et al., 2024 ). 5.1.1 Importance of environmental factors Evapotranspiration (ET) is a crucial process in the hydrological cycle that transfers moisture from land to the atmosphere and redistributes it back to the surface through precipitation and other forms, playing an essential role in maintaining the balance of water resources (Joo et al., 2017). It directly influences regional humidity, precipitation, and temperature, thereby having a decisive impact on climate and ecosystem balance (Bai and Liu, 2018 ). Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the physical significance of ET is vital for gap filling, water resource management, and agricultural production. The hydrological cycle involves the continuous movement of water among the atmosphere, land, and oceans, forming the basis for the distribution of global water resources. As a critical component of the hydrological cycle, ET is the key process of water exchange between the atmosphere and land, moving significant amounts of moisture into the atmosphere through plants and soil surfaces (Li et al., 2018 ). ET mainly comprises evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation refers to the process by which water on surfaces, including bodies of water, soil, and plants, directly converts from liquid or solid to gaseous form, entering the atmosphere (Wu et al., 2020a,b ). This process is influenced by the physical properties of water and environmental factors. On the other hand, transpiration is the process through which plants absorb water from the soil via their roots and release it into the atmosphere by evaporating it through stomata in their leaves (Mu et al., 2007 ). Plants require substantial amounts of water for photosynthesis to keep their stomata open and maintain metabolism, while water also evaporates through transpiration (Yang et al., 2018 ). Stomatal opening and closing are influenced by various environmental factors and are closely linked to the physiological activities of plants. In extreme conditions like high temperatures or drought, plants may close their stomata to reduce water loss (Xie et al., 2024 ). The aforementioned environmental factors have a complex and intricate influence on the evapotranspiration (ET) process, determining the movement, distribution, and recycling of water in the hydrological cycle. Thus, this paper primarily focuses on several key factors affecting ET during gap filling. Temperature (Tmax  and Tmin ) is a crucial driver of ET, as rising temperatures provide sufficient energy for water molecules to break free from their liquid or solid states (Wu et al., 2020a,b ). In transpiration, higher temperatures cause plant stomata to open wider, leading to a higher transpiration rate that releases water while absorbing more carbon dioxide (Yu et al., 2023 ). However, under extreme heat, plants may close their stomata to reduce water loss (Qian et al., 2023 ). Solar radiation (Rs ) is the direct energy source for ET, directly influencing the temperature of soil, vegetation, and water bodies (Sabziparvar et al., 2013 ). It also drives plant photosynthesis, affecting stomatal behavior and transpiration rates. In densely vegetated regions, solar radiation is closely tied to photosynthesis, directly impacting stomatal conductance and transpiration rates. Reduced radiation during cloudy periods and nighttime also lowers evaporating rates (Blonquist Jr et al., 2010 ). Relative humidity (RH) directly affects the moisture gradient between the air and surface, representing the tendency of water to diffuse from high to low concentration areas, serving as a fundamental driver of ET. Lower humidity facilitates water entry into the atmosphere, while higher humidity inhibits this process (Xiao et al., 2020 ). In transpiration, water absorbed by plant roots is released into the air via leaf stomata, creating a moisture gradient from the plant interior to the atmosphere. However, significant humidity fluctuations can disrupt stomatal regulation, impacting transpiration rates. Wind speed (WS) exerts a dual effect on ET. On one hand, it accelerates evaporation and transpiration by disturbing the air boundary layer and removing humid air from leaf and soil surfaces, facilitating new evaporation. On the other hand, strong winds may cause extreme dryness, increasing evaporation and transpiration pressure on soil and plants, affecting plant growth (Fan and Thomas, 2013 ). Precipitation (Pre) significantly impacts ET as an important supplement to surface water. Ample precipitation moistens soil and aids plant transpiration, but excessive rainfall may cause saturation, suppressing evaporation. Conversely, during droughts with scarce rainfall, dry soil inhibits plant growth and reduces transpiration (Wu et al., 2020a,b ). The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is crucial in ET research for several reasons. First, as an indicator of vegetation growth status, NDVI indirectly reflects vegetation transpiration levels, influencing regional ET. Second, NDVI indicates vegetation coverage, and higher NDVI values generally signify more vegetation coverage, reducing soil moisture evaporation and influencing soil moisture loss, which impacts ET (Maselli et al., 2020 ). Additionally, vegetation can regulate climate factors such as surface temperature, humidity, and wind speed, affecting ET occurrence and intensity. In summary, meteorological variables significantly influence the ET process and determine water flow in the hydrological cycle, playing a crucial role in achieving high-precision gap filling.  5.1.2 Importance of ET products Our study findings indicate that the incorporation of ET products significantly enhances the ability of various models to fill ET at different gap ratios. This is because ET products, based on physical models and ecological principles, provide direct information on the water evaporation process. Using them as input variables enables models to access actual evapotranspiration data, offering detailed and specific features (Beck et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018a ). This helps models capture the relationship between evapotranspiration and meteorological conditions more accurately, as they account for interactions among soil, vegetation, and atmosphere (Huang et al., 2015a,b ). Additionally, ET products may improve model robustness by adapting to nonlinear or unusual changes in vegetation transpiration, directly involving actual ET measurements or estimates. Furthermore, these high-quality and precise datasets, derived from multiple observational and model sources, can significantly improve the quality of gap-filling results. Most ET products offer long-term ET estimates that span years or decades, allowing models to analyze trends and validate results over time, thus providing insights into ET evolution (Jia et al., 2022 ). With high temporal and spatial resolution, they supply detailed and accurate information crucial for gap-filling models like the hybrid CNN-LSTM model, which requires spatiotemporal data to capture ET dynamics (Xie et al., 2024 ). ET products also serve as benchmark datasets for evaluating model performance, enabling quick detection of filling biases and errors (Taia et al., 2023 ). Their cross-regional applicability enhances the versatility of CNN-LSTM model, ensuring reliable ET estimates across diverse regions and climatic conditions. Regional ET products, tailored to specific geographical, climatic, and ecological characteristics, also enhance model applicability (Xu et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2020 ). Lastly, models overly reliant on meteorological data may struggle to interpret them. ET products can help calibrate models, improving their understanding and utilization of meteorological data for ET gap filling (Kim et al., 2012 ; Liaqat and Choi, 2017 ). Since meteorological data alone may be insufficient to predict vegetation transpiration, ET products compensate by providing practical evapotranspiration data (He et al., 2023 ). Their use adds data diversity and robustness, leveraging remote sensing and meteorological observations to offer comprehensive information on surface features and climate conditions (Lu et al., 2022 ). Moreover, combining ET products with other environmental factors enhances surface and atmospheric knowledge, improving filling quality. In summary, using ET products offers multiple advantages for ET gap filling, including data quality, spatiotemporal resolution, benchmark datasets, data diversity, remote sensing supplements, and multi-source data integration. They enrich evapotranspiration information, improve model robustness, and enhance meteorological data sensitivity.   5.2 Importance of CNN-LSTM for ET gap filling To integrate the aforementioned environmental factors and ET products, selecting an appropriate model is crucial. This study employs a hybrid deep learning model, CNN-LSTM, as the imputation model. The findings indicate that this model significantly outperforms individual models (CNN, LSTM) and traditional machine learning models (RF, SVM, ELM) in filling gaps. First, the CNN-LSTM model effectively handles spatiotemporal data (LeCun et al., 2015; Schütt et al., 2017 ). Since environmental factors and ET products exhibit spatiotemporal variations, the CNN-LSTM model can capture these complex relationships, thus providing more accurate ET predictions (Jung et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2017a; Yuan et al., 2020 ). The CNN component extracts spatiotemporal features, while the LSTM component captures long-term dependencies in sequential data. This structure enhances the ability of model to comprehend temporal patterns and spatial correlations in input data (Koppa et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a,b ). Furthermore, the model efficiently utilizes ET products as input, improving prediction accuracy and stability. ET products, which reflect the spatiotemporal distribution of surface moisture, provide essential auxiliary information (Li et al., 2022; Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020a,b ). By integrating ET products with environmental factors as inputs, the CNN-LSTM model more comprehensively considers various factors influencing ET, making the imputation results more accurate and reliable. Secondly, the CNN-LSTM deep learning model excels at multi-source data fusion. ET gap-filling often requires considering information from various sources, such as meteorological data, surface features, and ET products. CNN-LSTM effectively integrates these heterogeneous datasets and learns their interrelationships, enhancing the performance of model (Sharma et al., 2022 ). This flexibility arises from the ability of model to handle multiple input channels simultaneously. Unlike traditional machine learning models, CNN-LSTM possesses automatic feature extraction capabilities (Dong et al., 2024 ). The CNN layer automatically learns features suited for ET products and environmental data without manual feature engineering (Wang et al., 2022a,b ). This adaptability enables the model to handle different data characteristics without relying on domain experts' prior knowledge (Li et al., 2022 ). Moreover, CNN-LSTM enables end-to-end learning, allowing the model to directly learn features relevant to the imputation task from the input data (Sharma et al., 2022 ). Therefore, CNN-LSTM demonstrates excellent capability in processing time series data. In contrast, traditional machine learning models often rely on manual feature selection and engineering, which can lead to information loss and decreased performance. End-to-end learning makes the CNN-LSTM model more robust, enabling it to better capture complex data relationships (Karbasi et al., 2022 ). Finally, deep learning models generally adapt well to large-scale data and complex patterns (Sharma et al., 2022; Koppa et al., 2022; Dong et al., 2024 ). This study used extensive, multi-year, multi-site meteorological and ET product data for training, which contain abundant information. CNN can effectively handle this data scale and complexity, better capturing the patterns and relationships (Xu et al., 2022 ). The high capacity and complexity of deep learning models improve imputation performance (Sharma et al., 2022 ). Thus, combining ET products with the CNN-LSTM model leverages automatic feature extraction capabilities of deep learning while utilizing its strengths in handling time series data and capturing spatial information. This provides an efficient and reliable method for ET gap-filling.  5.3 Uncertainty on gap filling Our results reveal significant errors and uncertainties still exist in certain sites, regions, land cover types, and climate types, influenced by various factors. Primarily, the EC measurement method itself significantly impacts the ET filling results. Despite utilizing 241 EC sites in this study, they fail to cover the entire continent or globe due to their sparse and uneven distribution, primarily concentrated in North America, Europe, and Asia, with sparse coverage in Africa, Australia, and South America. Moreover, the limited coverage of land cover and climate types means these point-scale observational data cannot reflect the overall situation (Yao et al., 2017b; Yao et al., 2015 ), greatly affecting both model training and the accuracy of ET products. Furthermore, inaccuracies and energy imbalances in flux tower observational data introduce uncertainties. Error rates in flux tower field measurements range from approximately 10 % to 30 % based on comparisons among multiple tower setups at the same location (Mu et al., 2011a,b ), which typically lead to about 5 % to 20 % errors (Foken, 2008 ). Although we corrected energy imbalances using the Bowen ratio correction method developed by previous researchers, these corrections also introduce certain errors (Scott, 2010 ). Another reason for uncertainty lies in the ET products themselves, primarily due to scale mismatch between ET products and observed values. The spatial footprint of flux tower observations is typically a few hundred meters, while the resolution range of the ET products involved in this study is 10 to 30 km (Barcza et al., 2009 ), thus introducing significant uncertainty in ET products due to spatial scale errors between ground measurements and satellite observations (Fisher et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2014 ). This uncertainty is particularly pronounced when flux tower measurements are used to assess ET products at the point scale, with scale effects uncertainty reaching up to 25 % (Li et al., 2009 ). The third factor contributing to the uncertainty of filling results is the varying impacts of different latitude regions, land cover types, and climate types on the model outcomes. Research findings indicate that sites in low latitude regions perform the worst, with CNN-LSTM showing predominantly underestimated values in most of these locations, likely due to the complex climatic conditions and diverse vegetation types in low latitude regions (Salazar-Martínez et al., 2022 ). Low latitude regions typically exhibit characteristics of high temperature and humidity, leading to higher rates of evapotranspiration. Seasonal precipitation and tropical cyclones, among other climatic features, may also influence the evapotranspiration patterns (Salazar-Martínez et al., 2022; Fuentes et al., 2024 ). Additionally, in low latitude regions, observational methods such as the eddy covariance technique may face certain limitations. For instance, in densely vegetated areas like tropical rainforests, observation equipment may be obstructed or interfered with by vegetation, leading to a decline in data quality, which could affect the training and filling effectiveness of models (Yang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023 ). Concerning land cover types, models exhibit poor performance in EBF (Evergreen Broadleaf Forest) and CRO (Cropland), this is consistent with recent work (Nemitz et al. 2018; Kim et al. 2020; Knox et al. 2019 ). Evergreen broadleaf forests possess complex vertical structures, including multiple layers such as canopy, understory, and ground vegetation, resulting in distinct vertical gradients in the utilization of light, water, and heat by vegetation (Liu et al., 2017a,b,c; Wu et al., 2020a,b; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the response of evergreen broadleaf forests to environmental changes may be more complex, including seasonal leaf shedding and regeneration, differences in water use among different plant functional types, making it relatively challenging to simulate and capture the processes of water evaporation and transpiration (Barraza et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017a,b,c ). The characteristics of vegetation in croplands vary with seasons and agricultural management activities, including the types of crops, growth stages, and the influence of management practices such as irrigation and fertilization (Liu et al., 2017a,b,c; Qian et al., 2023 ). Additionally, soil cover and crop root structures in agricultural fields significantly affect soil moisture evaporation and transpiration processes, making it difficult for models to accurately simulate these complex land use and vegetation dynamics (Zhao et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2022 ). Lastly, concerning climate types, models perform poorly in Arid and Polar regions. In Arid regions, water resources are extremely limited, leading to severe constraints on soil moisture and evapotranspiration processes. These water limitations result in lower rates of soil moisture evaporation and vegetation transpiration compared to other climate types, making the evapotranspiration process slower and discontinuous (Tabari et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016 ). Additionally, the topography in Arid regions often comprises arid desert or desert landscapes with poor soil fertility, sparse vegetation, and extremely low soil moisture content, leading to relatively slow soil moisture evaporation processes but influenced by intense sunlight and high temperatures (Zhang et al., 2020 ). As for Polar regions, the extreme climate conditions, with very low temperatures and prolonged snow and ice cover, result in complex soil freezing and moisture evaporation processes. Frozen soil restricts soil moisture evaporation and transpiration from already sparse vegetation, while snow and ice cover affect surface energy balance, making it difficult to accurately simulate evaporation and transpiration processes (Anderson et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013 ). Additionally, the topography in these regions mostly consists of glaciers, permafrost, and sea ice, with high degrees of soil freezing and complex soil moisture dynamics. Moreover, there are significant seasonal variations and polar day-night phenomena, where during polar nights, the surface is less affected by sunlight, whereas during polar days, continuous sunlight exposure leads to drastic changes in surface temperature and moisture evaporation processes. These seasonal and sunlight differences significantly impact the filling effectiveness of models (Mu et al., 2009 ). Furthermore, Arid and Polar regions typically have sparse populations, limited monitoring sites, and harsh geographical conditions, making maintenance of monitoring equipment difficult. This results in scarce and uneven quality observational data in these regions, affecting the reliability and sufficiency of model training data, thereby impacting the filling effectiveness of models (Vitale et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2022 ).  5.4 Limitation and prospects of this study Firstly, the padding performance of the target model CNN-LSTM and the comparison models decreases with increasing gap ratios. However, during the process of increasing the gap ratio, no site selection was conducted. For instance, some sites had gap ratios exceeding 80 % (see Fig. 2 ), yet these sites were still included in the computation for longer artificial gaps (35 %, 50 %). This may partially affect the computational results, as fewer training data would degrade the padding performance of the models. Future research could focus on setting more appropriate artificial gaps based on the gap ratios of different sites. Additionally, similar to other comparative studies such as Moffat et al. (2007)  and Zhu et al. (2022) , non-random gap occurrences like those resulting from regular maintenance plans or routine harvesting operations in agricultural systems were not considered in our study. Designing data gap probabilities based on the environmental and management challenges across all 94 sites would be highly challenging. Hence, we suggest that a key focus of future research could be on the gap filling performance of non-random gaps. Secondly, according to previous studies (Moffat et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022 ), EC-based flux tower observation data also exhibit numerous irregular gaps at half-hourly scales. Therefore, the applicability of our method at half-hourly scales remains to be validated. As nighttime gap filling performance still lags behind daytime performance in capturing the diurnal pattern of latent heat flux (LE) (R2  < 0.5 in many ecosystems) (Zhu et al., 2022 ), attributed to factors like lower frictional velocity at night and stable atmospheric conditions (Aubinet et al., 2012 ), and the proportion of rejected nighttime fluxes may reach up to 70 %. Nighttime gap filling poses a challenge as shortwave solar radiation (crucial for gap filling) diminishes (Reichstein et al., 2005 ). Finally, the deep learning models used in this study consume significant time and computational resources during model training and estimation, especially when applied to large datasets. Therefore, achieving simple model structures and fewer input data while maintaining high accuracy in filling results is a future research focus and challenge. For instance, the RF model is relatively easy to adjust, capable of rapid training even on large datasets, and requires minimal preprocessing, yet its filling accuracy is notably lower than that of the target model (Irvin et al., 2021 ). In contrast, MDS, tested as a simple and fast method compared to DL and ML methods, utilizes only three predictor variables. However, the performance of MDS falls even further below the best ML models, and Kim et al. (2020)  also found that MDS introduces statistical bias more frequently in annual sums compared to ML models.   6 Conclusion This study, based on 241 global flux tower sites, evaluated the filling capabilities of the target CNN-LSTM model and five comparative models (CNN, LSTM, RF, SVM, ELM) for different proportions of ET gaps using ET products, ERA5 meteorological factors, and NDVI as inputs. The comprehensive approach compared the gap filling performance of the models under five different data gap proportions (5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 35 %, and 50 %) with and without ET products as inputs. Furthermore, it assessed the influence of different latitudes, land cover types, and climate types on the target model. The research conclusions are as follows: Firstly, the target CNN-LSTM model performed well in filling daily ET gaps in EC measurements and outperformed other comparative models. Its accuracy decreased with increasing gap filling proportions but still maintained good performance. Even at a 50 % gap proportion, the majority of sites maintained R2  above 0.8, and RMSE remained within 0.8 mm/d. Secondly, compared to not using ET products as inputs, incorporating ET products significantly improved the filling performance of the model. The average increase in R2  ranged from 5 % to 15 %, and the average decrease in RMSE ranged from 15 % to 35 %, with a noticeable improvement in underestimation. Thirdly, the contribution of ET products to the model estimation was much greater than that of ERA5 meteorological factors and NDVI. Fourthly, as the gap proportion increased, the contribution of ET products also increased (from 58.0 % to 73.6 % for four ET products). Additionally, the addition of ET products can significantly increase the limit of model filling, from less than 80 % to 93 % for CNN-LSTM. Finally, different latitudes, land cover types, and climate types influence the model filling performance, with better performance observed in high-latitude regions, GRA, and Dry-Cold climates. In summary, the hybrid CNN-LSTM model performed the best among the tested gap filling models and was not dependent on site-specific measured data, nor was it limited by time and space. Therefore, it can serve as a good candidate for filling gaps in EC-based ET measurement data collected in regional and global flux networks, especially at sites with limited measured data, where the model still maintains high accuracy and stability.
1 Introduction Drought is one of the most widespread and severe natural disasters in the world, and there are few natural disasters that have global destructive effects like drought (Pourzand et al., 2022 ). With global climate change, the frequency, scope, and severity of global droughts are increasing (Zhang et al., 2015 ). Drought and water scarcity pose a growing threat to agricultural cultivation, industrial production, and residential life. Drought has become a norm that affects national production and life. Therefore, it is of great significance to grasp the frequency, intensity and scope of drought in time and accurately for agricultural production. Drought prediction is one of the key links to actively respond to climate change and establish an efficient disaster early warning system. At present, many scholars have widely used traditional regression models or data-driven models to predict drought (Mouatadid et al., 2018 ). The Differential Integral Moving Average Autoregressive Model (ARIMA) is widely used in some time series prediction because of its simple structure and easy construction and training (Ho et al., 1998 ). Yeh et al., (2019)  used seasonal ARIMA model to predict and analyze the drought index SPI in different time scales, and achieved good results. Later, this method was proved to be robust in the prediction of agricultural drought index (KumarMahto et al., 2019 ). However, it is difficult for statistical forecasting methods to accurately predict future droughts during sudden meteorological changes (Islam et al., 2021 ). Data-driven models based on computer technology, including machine learning model (ML), have been widely used in many fields, such as finance (Fernández et al., 2019 ), energy (Mosavi et al., 2019 ), environment (Tahmasebi et al., 2020 ) and meteorological forecast (Bochenek et al., 2022 ). Han et al. (2021)  used the data-driven model to optimize the simulation data to match the observation data. The results show that the data-driven model has good predictability and applicability in areas without observation systems. Some researchers pointed out some limiting factors in the internal parameter adjustment, human interaction and feature extraction of ML model. For example, the ANN model has the disadvantage of falling into a local minimum, and external optimization such as particle swarm optimization (PSO) may be needed (Mohamad et al., 2015 ). It is noteworthy that the machine learning model still has a very large expansion space and development prospect in the application of drought prediction and early warning (Hao et al., 2018 ). With the development of artificial intelligence, some deep learning models (DL) have gradually become the mainstream methods of time series prediction, such as recurrent neural network (RNNs), convolutional neural network (CNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM), which are widely used (Sundararajan et al., 2021; Ghimire et al., 2021 ). Maity et al. (2016)  found that ML model based on wavelet transform (WT) has higher accuracy and stability than single prediction model. Xu et al. (2020)  combined Complementary Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (CEEMD) and ARIMA, and the results showed that the CEEMD-ARIMA model is suitable for drought prediction. When a single prediction model is used to predict time series, due to the lack of data mining ability, it can not effectively extract the hidden information contained in the data, which may lead to under-fitting, insufficient prediction ability for non-stationary series and weak generalization ability (Zhou et al., 2020 ). Wen et al. (2019)  designed the mixed model CVEE-ELM by using the data-driven model, improved the stability and accuracy of the EMD(Empirical Mode Decomposition) method by using the Adaptive Noise Complete Set Empirical Mode Decomposition (CEEMDAN), and successfully predicted and improved the multi-scale runoff prediction accuracy by using the CVEE-ELM model. Abbasi et al. (2021)  used the combination of genetic algorithm (GA) and ARIMA to predict the drought sequence of SPEI in Urmia Lake Basin. The research shows that the prediction accuracy of GA-ARIMA model is directly related to the time scale of SPEI. Mi et al. (2022)  put forward a deep learning hybrid model (CLSTM) based on long-term and short-term memory neural networks to forecast the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index SPEI of China Meteorological Station. The results show that LSTM has higher time series forecasting ability than ARIMA. Do et al. (2018)  proposed applying Graph Attention Neural Network (GAT) to aggregate and extract spatiotemporal features from raw wind speed data. The extracted features were then placed into Gated Recursive Unit (GRU) and Time Convolutional Network (TCN) methods to establish a wind speed prediction model. Research has shown that seasonal wind speed trends can have a certain impact on prediction accuracy. Deep learning (DL) models have significant advantages over traditional statistical methods such as genetic algorithm GA, Bayesian fuzzy rule model BFRM, and ARIMA, especially various mutation models based on GRU or LSTM (Pierre et al., 2023 ). On the one hand, DL models based on digital driven models attach great importance to data and data volume, believing that the data itself contains key information to solve problems (Shen et al., 2019 ). On the other hand, DL models directly train (learn) data to induce, analyze, and summarize patterns. Therefore, DL models can quickly adapt to various data and problems, not limited to specific theories or models (Feizadeh et al., 2021 ). However, Gaur et al. (2021)  pointed out that most DL models are difficult to explain their internal working mechanisms, and the generated training models may be more like a “black box”, even if their generated output results appear reasonable, they are often difficult to explain and verify in terms of physical consistency (Irrgang et al., 2021 ). At present, most of the deep learning (DL) models are single models, lacking in-depth mining of the original drought index data characteristics (Mosavi et al., 2018 ). Therefore, this article proposes to use DEDI data to combine the signal decomposition estimation method VMD with the DL model CBiLSTM, which is good at mining the internal rules of the data, to establish a hybrid deep learning model VMD-CBiLSTM, predict and evaluate the drought situation in different regions of Shaanxi Province, analyze the contribution of different influencing factors to the model, and the results can provide new methods for data decomposition and deep learning model fusion, and provide new ideas for improving the accuracy of drought prediction.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area This research area includes Yulin, Jinghe, and Ankang in Shaanxi Province, China. It is located in the hinterland of China, between longitude 105°29′-111°15′E and latitude 31°42′-39°35′N, with a land area of approximately 2.058 × 105 km2, It accounts for 2.1 % of China's land area (as shown in Fig. 1  ). The Beishan and Qinling Mountains divide Shaanxi into three unique natural regions: the Shaanbei Plateau, the Guanzhong Plain, and the Shannan Mountains. Shaanxi belongs to a typical continental monsoon climate, with a north–south longitudinal length of over 800 km and multiple latitudes, resulting in significant differences in the north–south climate within its territory. The Loess Plateau in northern Shaanxi belongs to the arid and semi-arid region, while the Guanzhong Plain has a temperate semi-arid or semi humid climate, while the southern Shaanxi region mostly has a subtropical or warm humid climate.  2.2 Data source and preprocessing This study focuses on exploring the predictive performance of deep learning models on DEDI data, and the required data is shown in Table 1  . The meteorological data is on a daily scale, and the overall missing rate of the selected data is less than 5 %. For the convenience of subsequent research, the collected hourly meteorological data will be integrated into daily data, where the average values of temperature, sea level pressure, and wind speed will be taken, and cloud cover will be accumulated for calculation. For months with missing individual data (mainly temperature and precipitation data), linear interpolation is adopted. Temperature and precipitation have a relatively smooth trend in a short period of time. Linear interpolation can ensure the integrity of the data in the time series.  2.3 Research method 2.3.1 Calculation of DEDI DEDI is a new daily scale drought index constructed based on the difference between actual evapotranspiration (AET) and potential evapotranspiration (PET) in the high-resolution ERA5 reanalysis dataset of ECMWF (Zhang et al., 2022 ).The formula is as follows:(1)            D E D I  i  = D i  - D A V E    D S T U    , D i  = A E T  i  - P E T  i       In the formula, i   represents time, A E T  i    represents the actual evapotranspiration on day i   (in mm/d), P E T  i    represents the potential evapotranspiration on day i   (in mm/d), D i    represents the evapotranspiration deficit on day i  , that is, the difference between AET and PET, and D A V E     and D S T U     represent the average and standard deviation of the climate over the years, respectively. Zhang et al. (2022 ) standardized the difference between D i    and D A V E     using D S T U    , and the standardization of D S T U     can effectively maintain the shape of the data distribution and handle outliers in the data robustly (Buzzi et al., 2011 ). DEDI calculates PET by Penman-Monteith model, and considers the influence of ground factors such as soil moisture, vegetation coverage and wind speed on evaporation. This method is different from the standardized evapotranspiration deficit index (SEDI) developed by Kim et al., (2016)  and Vicente et al., (2018) . The latter adopts Budyko theory and probability distribution algorithm respectively, and DEDI can directly reflect the actual difference between actual evaporation and potential evaporation, instead of just focusing on individual actual evaporation or potential evaporation. This is helpful to further understand the water use efficiency and water resources utilization of the system (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The classification standards for dry and wet grades in DEDI (Zhang et al., 2022 ). are shown in Table 2  .  2.3.2 VMD-CBiLSTM model (1) VMD principle    Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) is an adaptive, completely non recursive modal variation and signal processing technique (Dragomiretskiy et al., 2013 ), which has a more solid theoretical foundation compared to Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD). VMD can effectively reduce the modal aliasing effects that traditional EMD tends to exhibit (Jiang et al., 2018 ). The main formula of VMD is as follows: Let f ( t )    be a time series, and describe the variational problem as using the central frequency to find K finite bandwidth modal functions u k  ( t )    , wherek   = 1, 2,…、k  , so as to minimize the sum of bandwidth estimates for each modality. The sum of all intrinsic mode components is equal to the original signal (t), which is defined as follows:(2) mi n { u k  }  , { ω k  }    ∑ k = 1  K  ‖ ∂ ( t )   [ ( δ ( t )  + j π t   ⊗ u k  ( t )  )  ]  e  - j ω k  t   ‖   2  2     s .  t . ∑ k = 1  K  u k  = f            In the formula, K   is the pre decomposed modal component, u k      and ω k      are the components and center frequency of the k-th mode after decomposition, f   is the original data sequence, δ ( t )    is the Dirac distribution function, ∂ ( t )    is the partial derivative at time t, and ⊗   is the convolution operation. Introduce a quadratic penalty factor and Lagrange multiplication operator to obtain the optimal solution for the above constraint variables, which is defined as follows:(3) L u k    , ω k    , λ   = α ∑ k = 1  K  ‖  ∂ Ä ±   δ ( t )  + j π t     u k  ( t )    e  - j ω t t   ‖   2  2  +    ‖ f ( t )  -  ∑ K  u k  ( t )    ‖   2  2  + < λ t   , f t   - ∑ u k  t   >          In the formula, α   is the penalty coefficient, λ   is the Lagrange multiplier, and <> is the inner product calculation of two vectors. Obtain a unconstrained model and use the alternating direction multiplier method to search for and iteratively calculate the optimal results for ω k   , u k    and λ  . And all components can be obtained from the frequency domain, which is defined as follows:(4)               u ^   k  n + 1   ( ω )  = f ^  ( ω )  + λ ^   n  ( ω )   2  - ∑ i ≠ k   u ^  i  n  ( ω )   1 + 2 α ω - ω k  n     2         In the formula, u ^  k  n + 1   ( ω )     can be regarded as the result of Wiener filtering the current residual f ^  ( ω )  - ∑ i ≠ k   u ^  i  n  ( ω )    , and n   is the iteration number. The algorithm re-estimates the center frequency according to each component and updates it according to the following formula.(5) ω k  n + 1   = ∫ 0  ∞  ω u ^  k  n  ( ω )     2  d ω  ∫ 0  ∞  u ^  k  n  ( ω )     2  d ω        The central frequencies ω k  n + 1     of these obtained modes can be calculated easily by using Formula (4), which indicates that the new central frequencies are placed at the center of gravity of their respective modal frequencies.(2) Construction of VMD-CBiLSTM model    As the underlying structure, CNN can well retain the topological structure of the original data and directly receive the one-dimensional (1D) tensor of the IMF without readjusting the rows and columns of input elements, and can make full use of the spatial characteristics of the IMF components. The formula of convolution process is as follows:(6) C j  = σ ∑ A i  ⊗ ω i  + b i         Where, A i    represents the input, σ is the activation function, Relu and ω i    are selected here to represent the weight matrix, b i    represents the offset matrix, and ⊗   represents the convolution operation. The upper structure of the hybrid deep learning model adopts BiLSTM to receive spatial features extracted from CNN. In the BiLSTM layer, the time series data will be processed and the predicted values of each IMF component will be obtained. The basic unit of BiLSTM is LSTM, and the model structure is shown in Fig. 2  . The basic neural unit LSTM formula is as follows:(7) f t  = σ W f  · h t - 1   , x t    + b f        (8) i t  = σ W i  · h t - 1   , x t    + b i        (9)            C ∼  t  = t a n h W c  · h t - 1   , x t    + b c        (10) C t  = f t  ⨂ C t - 1   + i t  ⨂ C ∼  t      (11) o t  = σ W o  h t - 1   , x t    + b o        (12) h t  = o t  ⨂ t a n h C t         In the formula, f t  ,  i t    a n d   o t     are respectively designed as input gates, forgetting gates and output gates to solve the problem of gradient disappearance; W f   , W i  ,  W c     and W o    are weight matrices; b f  ,  b i  ,  b c     and b o    are bias vectors; h t - 1     and h t    are the input of the previous unit and the output of this unit respectively; C ∼  t    is the candidate cell state passing through the input gate; C t - 1     and C t    are the cell states of the previous unit and this unit respectively; σ is the activation function, and the Relu function which is friendly to negative values is selected here; ⊗   represents for convolution operation. Due to the fact that information can only propagate from front to back in a unidirectional LSTM network, and for drought prediction, the current drought data is associated with both past and future drought data, the unidirectional LSTM network cannot effectively explore the relationships between drought data. The bidirectional LSTM neural network (BiLSTM) has bidirectional information flow, which can closely link the current state with the past and future states, and effectively handle the relationship between drought index data. This article first uses meteorological data provided by meteorological stations to perform VMD decomposition on the DEDI data of each meteorological station, obtaining 7 IMF components; By repeatedly comparing the combination forms of CNN and BiLSTM neural networks, analyzing the hyperparameter values of different combination forms, taking the average of these values to find the optimal set of model hyperparameters, and achieving the best effect in training the fusion model; Finally, the VMD processed data components are predicted using an optimized combination model, and the results of the 7 predicted components are stacked and combined to obtain the DEDI prediction results. At this point, the construction of the VMD-CBiLSTM model has been completed. The structure of the VMD-CBiLSTM model is shown in Fig. 3  .  2.3.3 Model evaluation indicators This article uses three indicators to comprehensively evaluate the predictive performance of the model, which are the coefficient of determination (R2 ), Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). The determining coefficient (R2 ) can be used to measure the fitting degree of the model to the actual data.The Mean absolute error (MAE) calculates the average of the mean absolute error between the predicted value and the real value, and the smaller the MAE value, the closer the predicted value of the model is to the real value. The root mean square error (RMSE) can directly reflect the absolute error between the predicted value and the true value, and give greater weight to the extreme value error, so it is sensitive to the fluctuation of the maximum or minimum value. The three indicators are calculated by the following formula respectively.(13) R  2  = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  y ^  i  - y  ¯      2   ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y  ¯      2        (14) MAE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y 0        (15) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y 0     2         In the formula, y i    is the predicted value at time i  ; y 0    is the measured value at time i  ; y  ¯     is the mean of the measured values (i   = 1,…, N); N is the number of samples.    3 Results and analysis 3.1 VMD decomposition In Fig. 4  , (a) and (b) are the time series of monthly precipitation and monthly scale DEDI at Yulin meteorological station from 1979 to 2020, respectively. It can be seen that the monthly precipitation values show significant instability, with DEDI values fluctuating significantly between positive and negative, which is not conducive to feature extraction in the prediction process. In order to further explore the inherent patterns of information and improve prediction ability, VMD processing was performed on the original meteorological station data in this study. In order to make the original data more suitable for the training and verification of the deep learning model, the VMD algorithm was used to perform multi-scale decomposition on the drought time series data of Yulin, Jinghe, and Ankang stations. The data subsequence after Yulin DEDI data decomposition is shown in Fig. 5  . In order to further illustrate the influence of VMD decomposition processing on the prediction accuracy of the model, this paper takes DEDI data in 2020 as an example for analysis. The time series prediction results of daily scale DEDI before and after VMD decomposition processing are shown in Fig. 6  . For the daily scale DEDI data after decomposition, the numerical value has a similar trend change with the predicted value, and the prediction accuracy is greatly improved, R2  is increased from 0.58 to 0.96.  3.2 VMD-CBiLSTM model prediction In the VMD-CBiLSTM model, 500 rounds of training and validation prediction work are first carried out, with each round of prediction performing decomposition, prediction, and reconstruction steps. Then, the VMD-CBiLSTM model is used to predict the DEDI data from 1979 to 2020. The prediction results without VMD decomposition are shown in Fig. 7  , with an overall accuracy of R2 、MAE and RMSE are 0.376, 0.603, and 0.795, respectively; The predicted results after VMD decomposition are shown in Fig. 8  , with an overall accuracy of R2 , MAE and RMSE are 0994, 0.060, and 0.075, respectively. It can be seen that the prediction accuracy has been greatly improved after VMD decomposition processing. The VMD-CBiLSTM model can better capture the trend of changes in the DEDI sequence. Therefore, under the condition of ensuring sufficient original information, the VMD-CBiLSTM prediction model has good predictive performance.  3.3 Comparative analysis of several combination prediction models In order to further verify the effectiveness of the VMD-CBiLSTM model in predicting data at different time scales, this paper takes the DEDI data in Yulin as an example, selects DEDI value series in time scales of 1 month, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months as data sources. Four prediction models, VMD-ARIMA, VMD-BiLSTM, VMD-LSTM, and VMD-CBiLSTM are selected for comparative analysis. Three evaluation indicators, MAE, RMSE, and R2 , are used to verify the accuracy and credibility of model predictions. Fig. 9   shows the DEDI prediction curve and scatter plot for Yulin's 1-month lead time at four monthly time scales: 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months. Through observation and analysis, it can be seen that all four models can obtain the trend of meteorological drought changes at different time scales, but the accuracy values have certain differences. Further combining the curve and scatter plots, it can be seen that compared with the other three models, the VMD-CiLSTM model has a better fitting effect between predicted values and true values, higher prediction accuracy, and the overall performance is the best. The VMD-LSTM and VMD-BiLSTM models perform second, while VMD-ARIMA can only roughly capture the trend of drought changes, with the worst prediction effect. Due to the worst prediction performance of the VMD-ARIMA prediction model, this article only compares and analyzes the predictive capabilities of the three prediction models: VMD-BiLSTM, VMD-LSTM, and VMD-CBiLSTM. Fig. 10   shows the variation curve of the loss value of the training set with the number of training iterations at four different monthly scales during the training of the three models. It can be seen that when the number of training reaches about 200, the loss value of the three models tends to be stable, among which VMD-CBiLSTM has the lowest loss value and the most stable performance, which shows that the training stage of this model can achieve the best learning results. According to Fig. 11  , the Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (ECDF) examined the predictive performance of the VMD-ARIMA, VMD-BiLSTM, VMD-LSTM, and VMD-CBiLSTM models in the data distribution space of Yulin meteorological station at the time scales of January, March, June, and December. By analyzing Fig. 11 , it can be seen that VMD-CBiLSTM shows excellent stability and good robustness compared with VMD-ARIMA. The error generated by the selected research site within 95 % percentile ranges from 0 to 0.35, which indicates that the VMD-CBiLSTM model has good stability.  3.4 Stability testing of predictive models Yulin, Jinghe and Ankang are located in different locations in Shaanxi Province. Yulin is located in arid and semi-arid temperature zone; Jinghe River is located in the plain with a semi-arid and semi-humid climate. Tables 3, 4, and 5     show the simulation accuracy of the prediction models for Yulin, Jinghe, and Ankang at four different monthly time scales. Ankang is located at the southernmost tip of Shaanxi, with the highest average annual rainfall, belonging to a humid climate zone. In order to further evaluate the applicability of the prediction model in different climatic environments, this paper selects DEDI data of one station in each city to test the stability of the model. Taking Yulin as an example, compared with VMD-ARIMA, the average values of the evaluation indexes MAE, RMSE and R2  of VMD-LSTM prediction model in the one-month lead period are increased by 0.505, 1.581 and 0.230 respectively. Compared with VMD-ARIMA, VMD-BiLSTM performed better, and the values of MAE, RMSE and R2  increased by 0.599, 1.691 and 0.282 respectively. Compared with VMD-ARIMA model, VMD-CBiLSTM performed best, and the average values of MAE, RMSE and R2  increased to 0.662, 1.767 and 0.308. This can be attributed to the VMD algorithm being able to reduce the highly volatile sequence anomalies; On this basis, the bidirectional long short-term neural network integrates convolutional operations for feature extraction, improving the adaptive learning ability and nonlinear mapping ability of the CBiLSTM prediction model, making the prediction results closer to the actual values. Taylor diagram can express the correlation between target prediction and DEDI value more intuitively (Taylor et al. 2001 ). As shown in Taylor chart of Fig. 12  , the predicted value of VMD-CBiLSTM model is the closest to the real value, and the average value of correlation coefficient R reaches 0.996. At the same time, the standard deviation of DEDI data predicted by VMD-CBiLSTM model is 5 % to 30 % lower than that predicted by VMD-LSTM, VMD-BiLSTM and VMD-ARIMA model. Each station shows similar prediction results under the same time scale: with the time scale gradually increasing, the prediction accuracy of the target model also increases.   4 Discussion In this paper, the meteorological data of three representative stations are selected as data sources to participate in the prediction of drought index, and the stability test is carried out, which further shows that DL model has good adaptability. Combining the universality of meteorological data characteristics (yang,et al., 2018 ) and the portability of DL algorithm (Shen, et al., 2019 ), we have reason to believe that the VMD-CBiLSTM hybrid model can be competent for drought prediction in arid or semi-arid areas. Although the accuracy of meteorological data of stations is often low (the spatial resolution is generally less than 10 km), and raster data can further improve the regional continuity of stations and enhance the spatial correlation (Das,et al., 2016 ), it has always been a research difficulty to realize drought prediction from station data to raster data by using DL (wang, et al., 2023 ). Among them, the biggest challenge of DL technology in grid drought prediction is the lack of high-quality data sets for training (Chantry, et al, 2021 ) and the limited ability to deal with massive data (Pfaff T, et al. 2020 ). Compared with DL model, the adaptability of ARIMA statistical model to non-stationary time series data needs to be improved (Shumway et al., 2017 ). The statistical model of ARIMA is usually completed by observing the autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial autocorrelation function (PACF), while the establishment of autoregressive (AR) model must be stationary (liu et al., 2016 ). Even if the DEDI data is decomposed by VMD, the non-stationarity of the data is reduced, but the trend of drought changes with seasons is still obvious, which reduces the forecasting ability of ARIMA to some extent. Therefore, we recommend to use deep learning model to predict drought. At present, the LSTM model has been used to predict the trend of meteorological drought, and good results have been achieved (Maity et al., 2021; Tyagi et al., 2022 ). The global optimization problem has always been one of the problems that ML and DL need to solve (Yurtkuran et al., 2015 ). In order to further improve the generalization fitting ability of LSTM model and reduce the over-fitting phenomenon, there are two main solutions at present. One is to optimize the parameters of the model. For example, Li et al. (2022)  combined with Grey Wolf Optimization Algorithm (GOW) and LSTM successfully predicted the monthly runoff series data, with r > 80 %. Secondly, the original time series data is decomposed into several sub-sequences by combining decomposition algorithm, and each sub-sequence is simulated by LSTM, and the results of each sub-sequence are aggregated into the final result. On the basis of considering these two schemes to improve the prediction accuracy, this paper combines CNN's local perception and weight sharing to improve the operation efficiency of the combined model, which can greatly save time and cost, and the experimental results are consistent with the conclusions of Jin et al. (2022) . In addition, combining multiple ML models to construct a mixed model is also an important method to improve the accuracy of drought prediction. For example, Park et al. (2020)  established a short-term (8-day) drought prediction model by combining ConvLSTM and RF methods, and confirmed that the short-term drought hybrid prediction model is effective for drought intensification or alleviation.In  this study, the performance of VMD-CBiLSTM in forecasting meteorological drought is far better than that of the model before signal decomposition. The main reason may be that VMD model is added. VMD model can decompose the drought index time series into multiple sub-sequences, which can not only remove redundant prominent variation data, but also reveal the potential multi-scale phenomenon implied in the time series. Huang et al. (2021)  pointed out the necessity of original data decomposition by evaluating the influence of EMD (empirical mode decomposition), EEMD (integrated empirical mode decomposition), CEEMDAN (complete integrated empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise), VMD, WD (wavelet packet decomposition) and WPD (wavelet packet decomposition) on the performance of neural networks, and showed that VMD's anti-noise performance and generalization performance were much higher than others. In this paper, VMD-CBiLSTM model is selected to test the short-term drought prediction performance under different drought conditions, and the accuracy change of VMD-CBiLSTM model and its applicability are analyzed. Due to the influence of geographical location and climatic conditions, Shaanxi Province is mainly characterized by warm winters and droughts. In this paper, DEDI time series data of three weather stations from November 1, 1998 to March 31, 1999 are selected for testing. Fig. 13  , Fig. 14   and Fig. 15   respectively show the forecast results of Yulin, Jinghe and Ankang meteorological stations under different lead time scales and the change of relative error between the forecast value and the original value, in which DEDI<-0.91 is above the middle drought level. By analyzing the changing trend of DEDI in these three areas, we can know that compared with the other two areas, the DEDI data in Yulin is the most obvious for drought events, and after drought accumulation, the drought degree reached the highest around February 1999. According to real historical events, in 1999, many places in Shaanxi Province suffered from extremely serious spring drought, of which Yulin in the north of Shaanxi Province was the most serious, with the temperature 1.8 ∼ 2℃ higher than normal and the precipitation 30 % ∼ 40 % lower than normal (Sha et al., 2002 ). The results show that DEDI data can reflect drought events well. Under different forecast lead times, the prediction accuracy of the model is different. Taking the data of Yulin weather station as an example, with the increase of forecast lead time, the forecasting ability of the model first becomes weak and then becomes strong, and the forecasting ability of the model is the weakest when the lead time is 30 days, and its r is only 0.882. This phenomenon is clearly reflected in the relative error distribution curve. At the same time, it can be seen from the experimental results that the degree of drought is a process of accumulation with time, and the occurrence period of severe drought events (−1.93 < DEDI<-1.27) can be well found between February and March on a large scale, such as a 90-day lead time. In addition, for the drought time series data of three weather stations, the short-term forecast is more sensitive to the drought intensity, which is consistent with our understanding of the drought change law (Xu et al., 2015 ). It can be seen that VMD-CBiLSTM model can achieve good results in predicting the evolution trend of drought, confirming the occurrence of drought events and evaluating the degree and intensity of drought. The geographical locations of the three weather stations are obviously different, and the drought conditions are different. The VMD-CBiLSTM model is selected to predict the drought data of the three weather stations, and all the results are consistent. It can be seen that the VMD-CBiLSTM model has certain applicability. For the evaluation of drought prediction models, prediction accuracy is a common evaluation indicator, while there is little discussion on how each feature variable in deep learning models affects model performance (Nohara et al., 2022 ). This article attempts to evaluate the impact of each meteorological feature on the VMD-CBiLSTM model using SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) values as an indicator. By weighting and summing up all possible permutations of the feature subset, the contribution value of each feature to the model prediction result is calculated. In Fig. 16  , the left graph shows the honeycomb diagram of the influence of each feature on the model output on the daily scale, and the right graph shows the average SHAP value contributed by the overall feature to the model. We can see the extent to which each feature variable has an influence on forecasting the drought time series, especially the wind speed and air temperature, and whether it is positive or negative, it has the strongest influence on the model prediction. Both wind speed and temperature have the greatest overall contribution to the predictive performance of the model, while the contribution of precipitation is average. However, this conclusion differs to some extent from the simulation results at a 3-month time scale. By analyzing Fig. 17  , it can be seen that due to the fact that the calculation of DEDI data relies more on the daily measured water evapotranspiration, meteorological factors such as precipitation and air pressure have a much lower impact on short-term evapotranspiration than wind speed and temperature. This may be one of the reasons why the daily scale drought index is more sensitive to drought events than the monthly scale drought index. In this paper, VMD-CBiLSTM model effectively combines VMD, CNN and two-way LSTM model, which provides a new forecasting method for drought prediction. Generally speaking, the performance of hybrid model in DL technology is better than that of single model, and hybrid model can overcome the weakness of single model. However, when using DL model, there are still limitations: the parameter optimization setting of DL model is dual, on the one hand, it can provide adjustment methods to improve the prediction ability, such as trial and error method, grid search and group-based training method (Syarif et al., 2016; Mokhtaret et al., 2021 ), on the other hand, these methods will be very time-consuming and occupy a lot of resources. In addition, although the VMD-CBiLSTM model proposed in this study only considers several common drought factors and is effective in drought prediction, more drought factors need to be considered in order to better understand the drought mechanism, such as atmospheric circulation, natural changes and human activities (Jehanzaib et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020 ). Due to the phenomenon of signal loss during the decomposition process using any decomposition technique, the performance of deep learning models is also not ideal when facing extreme data. Therefore, how to simulate real scenarios to the maximum extent while ensuring the integrity of raw data, and improve the generalization ability of prediction models by learning extreme events, is our future research direction.  5 Conclusion In this paper, a deep learning hybrid model VMD-CBiLSTM based on VMD decomposition is proposed for meteorological drought prediction, and its forecasting ability and adaptability are discussed. The main conclusions are as follows:(1) Through VMD decomposition, the prediction ability of CBiLSTM model has been greatly improved. VMD decomposition can further reduce the proportion of abnormal mutation values in drought index, and explore the details of drought trend of original signal. The R2  value of CBiLSTM model after VMD decomposition is 0.38 higher than that without decomposition.  (2) The accuracy and stability of VMD-CBiLSTM are better than those of VMD-LSTM, VMD-BiLSTM and VMD-ARIMA models during the training and verification in three weather stations. The average value of DEDI prediction accuracy R2  is increased by 0.076, 0.034 and 0.328 respectively, the average value of RMSE is decreased by 0.178, 0.094 and 1.373 respectively, and the average value of MAE is decreased by 0.145 respectively. The results show that VMD-CBiLSTM model has reliable prediction ability for non-stationary drought index time series, and the prediction accuracy of one month ahead, three months ahead, six months ahead and twelve months ahead is above 0.97, which can be effectively applied to drought event monitoring and prediction in arid and semi-arid areas. 1 Introduction The floating canopy of vegetation, which is widely observed in natural streams and wetlands, plays an important role in purifying water, removing pollutants and triggering sediment resuspension (e.g., Ai et al., 2020; Gui et al., 2023, 2024; Huai et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2022; Plew, 2011 ). Floating vegetation (e.g., Eichhornia crassipes ) includes leaves and flowers above the water surface and unanchored roots extending downward into the water. Floating vegetation exists widely in Asia, Africa, and North America (e.g., Bai et al., 2022; Rumjit et al., 2022; Simberloff, 2013 ). Under appropriate environmental and weather conditions, due to strong fecundity, floating vegetation can bloom in a short period, and its roots can connect and form a dense mat covering the entire water surface (e.g., Goeden and Andrés, 1999; Stohlgren et al., 2013; Van Driesche and Abell, 2008 ). For example, E. crassipes  invades a wide range of habitats downstream of the Yangtze River Delta, such as the Taihu Lake drainage basin, which alters local sediment resuspension and deposition (Huang et al., 2020 ). This study focused on the flow structure and sediment deposition below the floating canopy of model vegetation and real E. crassipes . Understanding the impact of floating vegetation on flow and deposition can provide guidance for restoring aquatic environments in rivers and wetlands. In an open channel, a floating canopy of vegetation deflects flow vertically from the canopy interior (H  > z  > hg  , in which the height of the free-flow region below the canopy hg   is defined as the distance from the channel bed (z  = 0) to the canopy bottom, Fig. 1  ) to the region below the canopy (hg   ≥ z  ≥ 0) over the entire flow adjustment distance (XD   > x  > 0). The flow adjustment distance, XD  , defined as the distance between the canopy leading edge (x  = 0) and the position at which the in-canopy velocity decreases to its minimum constant (Fig. 1 ), is a function of the canopy flow blockage (CD ahc  ) and the relative flow depth (h g /H ) (Gui et al., 2023 ):(1) X D  h c   = 2.8 + 3.4 1 C D  a h c    + 3.7 h g  H     2      where hc   is the canopy height, defined as the distance from the floating canopy bottom (z  = hg  ) to the water surface (z  = H ), CD   is the vegetation drag coefficient, a  is the frontal area per floating canopy volume, hg   is the height of the free-flow region below the canopy, and H  is the flow depth. With increasing flow adjustment distance, the depth-averaged in-canopy flow velocity (Uc  (x ) = ∫ h g   H  U x , z      d z   ) decreases due to vegetation drag, and the depth-averaged flow velocity below the canopy (Ub  (x ) = ∫ 0 h g   U x , z      d z   ) accelerates due to flow continuity. Beyond the flow adjustment distance (x  > XD  ), the flow within and below a floating canopy is fully developed, resulting in a constant depth-averaged flow velocity within (Ucf  ) and below (Ubf  ) the canopy in the streamwise direction (Gui et al. 2024 ). The in-canopy flow velocity is always lower than the below-canopy flow velocity, yielding a shear layer at the bottom of the floating canopy. If the shear strength is sufficiently strong, Kelvin–Helmholtz (KH) vortices begin to develop and may dominate the exchange of momentum and mass between in-canopy and below-canopy layers. The KH vortices penetrate upward through the canopy bottom into the canopy interior at a penetration distance, δe   (Fig. 1 ), which is inversely proportional to the vegetation drag (Gui et al., 2024 ). The penetration distance, δe  , is a function of vegetation density and is limited by the canopy height (hc  ) and the height of the free-flow region below the canopy (hg  ):(2) δ e  x    = min 0.13 ± 0.02    x C D  a   , h c  , h g           Based on the flow continuity and layer-averaged momentum equations, Gui et al. (3)–(5) ) has been confirmed to be a valid method for predicting the velocity evolution in a channel with a real E. crassipes  canopy (see details in Gui et al. 2024 ). The flexibility of floating vegetation roots has a negligible impact on the velocity evolution inside real E. crassipes  canopies (Gui et al., 2023  in Fig. 9 ). Given this fact, it is reasonable to use Eqs. (3)–(5)  to predict the velocity evolution inside the model and real E. crassipes  canopies. In a channel with a floating canopy, the flow velocity below the canopy is related to the near-bed turbulent kinetic energy (TKE ), which determines sediment deposition and resuspension. To examine the deposition pattern below a floating canopy, it is important to understand how the near-bed TKE  below the canopy varies in the streamwise direction. Previous studies have numerically and experimentally investigated the velocity evolution inside and below a floating canopy (e.g., Gui et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2017 ). The flow evolution within and below a floating canopy is highly dependent on the channel-average velocity, vegetation density and relative flow depth, which can be predicted by numerical and analytical models (e.g., Huai et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2023; Gui et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2021 ). For example, Eqs. (3)–(5)  were reported by Gui et al. (2023) . However, the relationship between flow velocity and near-bed TKE  has not been clarified in floating vegetation cases. In particular, there is no valid method for predicting the longitudinal evolution of near-bed TKE  below a floating canopy. One goal of this study was to understand how a floating canopy of vegetation impacts the evolution of near-bed TKE  over a wide range of flow and vegetation conditions and to propose a model for predicting the longitudinal distribution of the near-bed TKE  below a floating canopy. Another main goal of this study was to explore sediment deposition patterns below a floating canopy and predict the longitudinal distribution of deposition. Previous studies have confirmed that in vegetated channels, sediment resuspension and deposition are strongly related to the near-bed TKE , not the bed shear stress (e.g., Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2023; Shan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016, 2021 ). The near-bed TKE  is a combination of bed-generated turbulence, kt  (bed) , and vegetation-generated turbulence, kt  (veg)  (e.g., Liu et al., 2024; He et al., 2024 ). Compared to bare beds (no vegetation), diminished deposition was observed within the leading edge of a submerged (Zhang et al., 2020 ) or emergent canopy (Liu and Nepf, 2016 ) due to the enhanced near-bed TKE  associated with the presence of vegetation-generated turbulence (stem-scale eddies). Stem-scale eddies were present in flows with a stem Reynolds number Rec   (= U c ′  d / ν   , with the stem diameter d , and constricted velocity within the canopy, U c ′  = U c  ( x )  / ( 1 - 2 ϕ / π   )        , Etminan et al., 2017 ) greater than 120 (Liu and Nepf, 2016 ). In contrast, vegetation-generated turbulence was absent at Rec   < 120, so enhanced deposition was observed inside canopies due to diminished near-bed TKE  (Zong and Nepf, 2011; Liu and Nepf, 2016 ). For an emergent canopy of Phragmites australis , Liu et al. (2022)  proposed and validated a model to predict sediment deposition inside the canopy by using the near-bed TKE  and deposition probability. However, for a floating canopy, sediment deposition in the free-flow region below the canopy may not be affected by vegetation-generated turbulence. The previous method (e.g., Liu et al., 2022; Shan et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024 ) cannot be directly used for a floating canopy case. To our knowledge, the impact of floating vegetation on sediment deposition has not been investigated, so there is no valid model for determining the deposition distribution below a floating canopy. To address this research gap, this study clarified how channel-average velocity, vegetation density, and relative flow depth impact deposition distribution and proposed a model to predict deposition distribution below a floating canopy.  2 Theory This section introduces the theoretical model for predicting the near-bed TKE  and deposition. Section 2.1  introduces the method for predicting the longitudinal evolution of the near-bed TKE  below a floating canopy. Section 2.2  describes the method for predicting the deposition distribution below a floating canopy. 2.1 Predicting near-bed TKE  below a floating canopy The near-bed TKE  per fluid mass below a floating canopy primarily depends on bed-generated turbulence, which is related to bed shear stress. The bed shear stress is related to the near-bed turbulent kinetic energy, kt  (x ), i.e., τ b  x    = ω k t  x      , in which ω  (=0.2) is the scale constant (Soulsby and Dyer, 1981; Biron et al., 2004 ). In a channel with floating vegetation, due to the discontinuity of drag induced by the floating vegetation, the vertical profile of velocity no longer follows the logarithmic law. It is reasonable to use the depth-averaged velocity below the floating canopy to estimate the bed shear stress (i.e., τ b  x    = ρ C f  U b  x        2    ) rather than the depth-averaged velocity over the full water depth. The near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), at the x  position below the floating canopy is predicted by:(6) k t  x    = τ b  x     ω  = ρ C f  U b  x        2   ω       Note that kt  (x ) (= ∫ 0 H nb    k t  x , z     d z    ) is the depth-averaged TKE  in the near-bed region at the x  position, in which kt   (x , z ) is the lateral average turbulence over the horizontal distance across the channel at the x  position, which eliminates the lateral heterogeneity in turbulence but retains the vertical variation. The height of the near-bed region (Hnb  ) is assumed to be associated with the height of the bed boundary layer (δb  ) because the flow structure and velocity profile in the bed boundary layer are affected mainly by bed roughness. Across all the cases, δb   ranged between 1.8 and 5.5 cm, as estimated via the method of Gui et al. (2024) . Based on this, three different heights of the near-bed region (Hnb   = 2, 3.5 and 5 cm) were chosen. The difference between the near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), for three heights of the near-bed region was less than 8 % (Fig. S1  in the Supporting Information ), suggesting that it is reasonable to use the depth-averaged TKE  in the near-bed region with a height of Hnb   = 2 to represent the near-bed TKE , kt  (x ). Eq. (6)  suggests that a rougher bed surface (a greater Cf  ) and greater depth-averaged velocity below the canopy, Ub  (x ), can produce a stronger near-bed TKE , but Eq. (6)  ignores the contribution of the shear-generated turbulence that is associated with the vortices at the canopy bottom to the near-bed TKE  (see Section 5.1  for details). (2023) .  2.2 Predicting sediment deposition below a floating canopy A deposition probability model (Engelund and Fredsoe, 1976 ) was used to predict the rate of net deposition below a floating canopy. First, the rate of mass accumulation at the channel bed was defined as:(8) dDep  dt   = p w s  C     where Dep  is the total net deposition per bed area of suspended particles; p  is the probability of the particles reaching the bed and remaining deposited; w s     is the settling velocity of the particles; and C  is the suspended sediment concentration. The residence time below the floating canopies was 15 ∼ 30 s, estimated from canopy length and the fully developed depth-averaged velocity, Ubf  , below the canopy, which was shorter than the particle settling time (H /w s     = 625 ∼ 875 s). This finding suggested that the sediment supply was not restricted (i.e., κ  = L / U bf    H / w s       < 1, Sun et al. 2023 ) and that the concentration of suspended sediment remained approximately the same along the channel. It was reasonable to assume a constant sediment concentration, C , throughout the channel, both inside and outside the canopy. During the deposition experiment, the initial concentration, C 0 , decreased with time due to sediment deposition, but the concentration in the channel was spatially uniform at each moment.
