The flume had a flow straightener at the entrance to produce uniform velocities in the lateral direction. The flow depth was controlled by modifying the tailgate at the end of the flume and was measured upstream and downstream of the test section using rulers. To investigate the impact of the relative flow depth on sediment deposition, the flow depth was varied between 20 and 30 cm. The channel-average flow velocity (U 0 ) measured at the leading edge of the test section ranged from 11.5 to 24.5 cm/s, which was consistent with the favorable flow velocity (=5 to 25 cm/s) for E. crassipes  growth, as observed in Taihu Lake (=5 to 20 cm/s, Huang et al., 2020 ), Bribie Lake in Australia and the Kshipra River in Central India (=7 to 25 cm/s, Nichols et al., 2016; Billore and Sharma, 2009 ). The test section was located 3 m downstream from the flume entrance. Preliminary experiments confirmed that the flow had fully developed prior to entering the test section. The flow was turbulent, with Reynolds numbers ranging from 20,641 ∼ 35,000 (Re  = U 0 R /ν , in which ν  = 0.01 cm2 /s is the kinematic viscosity and R  is the hydraulic radius), and the flow was subcritical, with Froude numbers ranging from 0.07 ∼ 0.18 (Fr  = U 0 /g H     , where g  is the gravitational acceleration). 3.1 Model vegetation and real E. crassipes  Rigid cylinder arrays were used to mimic the floating canopies of vegetation at the water surface. The 1-cm-thick polyvinyl chloride (PVC) boards were fixed above the water surface, and cylinders were glued vertically onto PVC boards in a staggered arrangement. The cylinder diameter d  (= 0.8 cm) was chosen from the observed diameter range for 2- to 6-month-old E. crassipes  (d  = 0.1 to 1.5 cm, Downing-Kunz and Stacey, 2011, 2012; Zhao et al., 2012 ). The cylinder densities (n ) were 0.020 and 0.038 plants/cm2 , yielding frontal areas per canopy volume a  (= nd ) of 1.6 and 3.0 m-1 , respectively, which matched the observed range for E. crassipes  in the field (a  = 1.0 to 4.5 m-1 , Downing-Kunz and Stacey, 2011, 2012; Center and Spencer 1981 ). The floating canopies were 4 m long and 1 m wide and covered the full width of the flume, so the flow was adjusted only in the streamwise and vertical directions (Fig. 2 a and 2b). Two flow depths (H ) were considered for rigid cylinder arrays (Cases 1–7): H  = 20 and 28 cm. The floating canopy height (hc  ) varied between 4 and 14 cm, and the relative flow depth (hg  /H ) ranged from 0.3 to 0.8, which fell within the observed range (hg  /H  = 0.1 to 0.9) for E. crassipes  in natural rivers, streams, and ditches (e.g., Gui et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2016; Yamasaki et al., 2022 ). hg   was defined as the height of the free-flow region below a floating canopy, calculated by hg   = H  − hc  . The experimental parameters are summarized in Table 1  . The near-bed TKE , depth-averaged velocity below the canopy, Ub  (x ), and deposition distribution were measured in model canopies (Cases 1–6, Table 1 ), which were used to verify the proposed near-bed TKE  (Eq. (6) ) and deposition model (Eq. (10) ). Note that Case 7 was used to examine only the impact of shear-generated turbulence, kt  (shear) , on the near-bed TKE  evolution and deposition distribution (Section 5.1 ). E. crassipes  blooms and covers the entire water surface in natural environments in summer (see Fig. 1  in Gui et al., 2023 ). The leaves and flowers of E. crassipes  float at the water surface because the spongy chambers near the base of its bulbous petioles provide buoyancy (Fig. 3  a). Due to their strong reproductive capability, elongated stolons produce and connect the ramets distally (Fig. 3 c). In this study, mature E. crassipes  (approximately 3 ∼ 4 months old) were randomly distributed at the water surface of the flume to simulate a real floating canopy in the summertime. The frontal area per E. crassipes  canopy volume was a*  (=N*D , with the vegetation density, N* , and the total diameter of the root system of a single E. crassipes  plant, D ) and varied from 2.4 to 2.8 m-1 . In Cases A-C, the average root length of the E. crassipes  canopies ranged from hc   = 7 to 8.5 cm, respectively. The flexible roots were slightly reconfigured in response to flow deflection at the leading edge of the canopy (x  = 0), but most roots remained straight. Each canopy was 4 m long and covered the entire channel width (Fig. 3 b and 3c). The flow depth ranged between 21 and 30 cm, and the yielding channel-average velocity (U 0 ) ranged from 12.5 to 17 cm/s. We measured the deposition distribution below real E. crassipes  canopies (Cases A-C, Table 2  ) to verify the proposed deposition model (Eq. (10) ).  3.2 Velocity measurement The coordinates x , y  and z  represent the streamwise, lateral and vertical directions, respectively. Specifically, x   = 0 was the leading edge of the floating canopy, y  = 0 was the centerline of the flume and canopy, and z  = 0 indicated the channel bed surface. The velocity was measured for only the model canopy cases (Table 1 ). The streamwise (u ), lateral (v ) and vertical (w ) instantaneous velocities were recorded using a Nortek Vectrino profiler for 120 s at a frequency of 50 Hz. The raw velocity data with correlations less than 75 % and a signal-to-noise ratio smaller than 15 db were removed. The remaining data were despiked using the method of Goring and Nikora (2002) . The filtered instantaneous velocities were decomposed into time-average components (denoted U , V  and W ) and fluctuating components (denoted u  ′     , v  ′      and w  ′     ) via MATLAB. The turbulent kinematic energy, k , was defined as:(14) k = 1 2  ( u ′  2    ¯   + v ′  2    ¯   + w ′  2    ¯   )       To eliminate the influence of flow heterogeneity on the measurements in the lateral direction (y ), within the floating canopy, the velocity and TKE  were measured at y  = 0, -dy /8, and  dy /8 in a characteristic region at each x  position, where dy  is the lateral spacing between two adjacent neighboring cylinders and dx  (=5.4 cm) is the longitudinal spacing between two adjacent cylinders (Fig. 2 d). The mean of the three values in a characteristic region was defined as the horizontal-average velocity, U m  ( = 1 3  ∑ 1 3  u )    , and TKE , k t  ( = 1 3  ∑ 1 3  k )     at each z  position. The vertical profiles of Um   and kt   were measured along the centerline of the canopy at x  = 35, 95, 155, 195, 235, 275, 325, and 350 cm in Cases 1–5 and at x  = 30, 50, 70, 100, 130, 150, 170, 200, 250, 300, and 350 cm in Cases 6–7. Over the full water depth (z  = 0 to H ), the flow velocity, Um ,  and turbulent kinetic energy, kt ,  were measured with a resolution of 0.3 cm. At each x  position, the near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), was the average of the measured horizontal-average TKE , kt  , in the near-bed region of Hnb   = 2 cm (see details in Section 2.1  and Fig. S1 ). The mean near-bed TKE  (kt  (m) ) was the average of the measured near-bed TKE  below the entire floating canopy, k t ( m )   = ∑ i = 1  N  k t  ( x )   / N   , where N  represents the number of kt  (x ) measured below a floating canopy. The bed friction coefficient, Cf  , was determined using C f  = τ b  / ρ U 0 2       based on the method of Liu and Shan (2019) , in which τb   is the measured near-bed shear stress and U 0  is the measured channel-average velocity. PVC boards were placed on the entire channel, producing bed friction coefficients of C f  =    0.004 ± 0.001 (PVC boards with no holes, Cases 1–7) and Cf   = 0.006 ± 0.001 (PVC boards with holes, Cases A-C). The vegetation drag coefficient was estimated from C D  = 1 + 10 R ec  - 2 / 3      (White 1991 ). Across all cases, CD   = 1.0 ∼ 1.2; for simplicity, it is reasonable to use CD   = 1 in the following prediction. To quantitatively compare the differences between the predicted and measured values, the relative error (RE ) was computed as follows:(15) RE = 1 X  ¯       1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( X ( m )  - X ( p )  )  2        where X (m ) and X (p ) are the measured and predicted values, respectively, and X  ¯        is the mean of the measured values.  3.3 Sediment deposition Deposition experiments were performed to explore sediment deposition below a floating canopy. The deposition distribution was measured below both the model canopy (cylinder arrays) and the real E. crassipes  canopy. The suspended sediment was simulated by glass spheres with a mean diameter of ds   = 22 ± 3 μm. The settling velocity of the particle w s     was estimated as follows (Cheng 1997 ):(16) w s  d s   ν  = ( 25 + 1.2 d *  2    - 5 )  1.5       where d *     is the dimensionless particle size,(17) d *  = d s  ( ρ s  - ρ ) g  ρ ν 2       1 3       in which ρ s    (=2.65 g/cm3 ) is the particle density and g  is the gravitational acceleration.w s     = 0.03 cm/s for a particle with ds   = 22 ± 3 μm. The model particle was chosen to have a ratio of settling velocity to channel shear velocity w s  / u ∗   = 0.02 - 0.04   , which matched the observed range of that for suspended organic matter in fields, for which w s  u ∗    =    0.002 to 0.3 (Ortiz et al., 2013 ), where u ∗   = C f    U 0    . The dimensionless particle size d *     of 0.6 was within the range of 0.3 to 19, yielding Θ c  = 0.25 d ∗  - 0.6   tan 30 ° = 0.21    (Julien and Klaassen, 1995 ). The critical turbulence for resuspension, k t ( c )      (=3.7 cm2 /s2 ), was estimated by Eq. (13) . Deposition experiments were conducted separately from velocity measurements to avoid possible mutual impacts on the results. Clean glass slides (7.5 cm × 2.5 cm) were used to measure the net deposition. Before each sediment deposition experiment, the slides were weighed and placed in two rows along the centerline of the flume at target positions with no flow (Fig. 2 c). The interval between two neighboring x  positions was set to 20 cm for Cases 1–5 and 10 cm for Cases 6–7 and Cases A-C in the flow adjustment region (x  = 0 to XD  ) and to 25 cm in the fully developed region (x  = XD   to L ). Slides were also placed upstream of the floating canopy (x  = −150 cm) to measure the reference deposition for bare beds, denoted as Dep (0)  (Table 1 ). The pump rate was slowly increased to the desired channel-average velocity, after which the sediment particles were mixed with water in a large measuring cup. The slurry was gently poured into the downstream tank and immediately transported to the upstream tank by a recirculating pump. The particles and water were fully mixed within 5 min to achieve a uniform sediment concentration of C 0  = 100 g/cm3  in each case, as estimated from the added particle mass and water volume in the flume. The duration of the experiment was 4 h. After 4 h, the pump was slowly stopped to avoid generating waves, and the water was drained over 20 mins. To evaluate the deposition during the draining time, three additional weighed slides were gently placed on the channel bed to confirm that the draining period did not alter the deposition distribution. Next, the slides were dried in the flume for at least 12 h and then moved to an oven at 50 °C for 8 h to remove the remaining moisture. Finally, the dried slides were reweighed, and the net deposition at each position was the difference between the weight of each slide before and after the experiments. The glass slides were all weighed before and after the experiments using an electronic analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.0001 g. Each case had two replicates. At each x  position, the net deposition was the mean of the two replicates, and the standard deviation of the two replicates was also calculated. Because the smallest net deposition per glass slide (= 0.0008 g, Fig. 6 j to 6l) was greater than the balance accuracy and replicate experiments were considered, the deposition measurements were reliable. In each case, the spatial mean deposition, Dep (m)  (= ∑ i = 1  M  Dep ( x i  )  / M   ), was the average of the measured deposition below a floating canopy, where Dep (xi  ) indicated the net deposition at each measured position and M  represented the number of deposition measurements below a floating canopy. Case 1 included the condition of no resuspension (see Section 4.2 ), such that the spatial mean deposition at x  = 0 to 2 m in Case 1 was considered pure deposition, Dep ( p  = 1)  = 3.0 ± 0.2 mg/cm2 . Given that the initial concentration (C 0 ), settling velocity (w s    ), and experiment duration (t ) were the same in each case, it is reasonable to conclude that the pure deposition Dep ( p  = 1)  remains the same across all cases.   4 Experimental results 4.1 Depth-averaged velocity and near-bed TKE  below a floating canopy The near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), measured below the floating canopy increased linearly with increasing depth-averaged velocity below the canopy, Ub  (x ), and the bed friction coefficient, Cf   (Fig. 4  a), which is described by Eq. (6) . For a floating canopy, due to flow deflection, the in-canopy depth-averaged velocity decreased (H  > z  > hg  ), and the depth-averaged velocity, Ub  (x ), below the canopy increased (hg   ≥ z  ≥ 0) until the flow fully developed (x  = XD  ); thus, the near-bed TKE  increased from the leading edge of the canopy (x  = 0) to a maximum value beyond the flow adjustment distance (x  > XD  ) (Fig. 4 b–4d). In Fig. 4 b–d, the symbol color varies from light to dark with increasing x , indicating increasing measured depth-averaged velocities below the canopy, Ub  (x ). The channel-average velocity (U 0 , Fig. 4 b), vegetation density (canopy frontal area, a , Fig. 4 c) and relative flow depth (hg  /H , Fig. 4 d) had significant impacts on the evolution of Ub  (x ) below the canopy, which in turn affected the evolution of the near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), below the canopy. Specifically, for the same hg  /H  and a , a larger channel-average velocity U 0  provided a larger depth-averaged velocity below the canopy, such that the near-bed TKE  was also enhanced (Fig. 4 b). The mean near-bed TKE  (= 5.8 ± 1.5 cm2 /s2 ) in Case 7 (U 0  = 11.5 cm/s) was 57 % smaller than that in Case 6 (U 0  = 20 cm/s) with kt  (m)  = 13.6 ± 2.8 cm2 /s2 . For the same hg  /H  and U 0 , a larger near-bed TKE  was observed with a greater vegetation density a  (Fig. 4 c). This was because greater vegetation density produced a lower depth-averaged in-canopy velocity but a greater depth-averaged velocity Ub  (x ) below the canopy, which elevated the near-bed TKE . For the same a  and U 0 , a lower relative flow depth hg  /H  produced a greater Ub  (x ) and thus a larger near-bed TKE  below the canopy (Fig. 4 d). As Eq. (7)  contains the main factors, hg  /H , ϕ  (also a ) and U 0,  as discussed above, the velocity evolution Ub  (x ) predicted by Eq. (7)  agreed well with the measurements, with a relative error of RE  < 10 % across all cases (Cases 1–6, Fig. 5  ). The near-bed TKE  predicted by Eq. (6)  also agreed with the measurements, with a mean RE  = 14 % (Cases 1–6, Fig. 6  a–6f) and a maximum RE  = 18 % in Case 5.  4.2 Sediment deposition below a floating canopy Net deposition below floating canopies was dependent on both the velocity below the canopy (Ub  (x )) and the near-bed TKE . For low-velocity Case 1 (U 0  = 11.5 cm/s, a  = 1.6 m-1 , hg  /H  = 0.5 and H  = 28 cm), the sediment deposition was almost the same as that of the upstream reference, Dep (0) , at x  = 0 to 2 m (3.2 ± 0.2 mg/cm2 , denoted by a horizontal gray bar in Fig. 6 g) but was smaller than that of the reference at x  > 2 m. This finding was consistent with the measured near-bed TKE , which was smaller than or the same as the predicted critical TKE  (kt  ( c  )  = 3.7 cm2 /s2 , the horizontal dashed line in Fig. 6 a) at x  = 0 to 2 m but was slightly greater than the critical at x  > 2 m. For high-velocity cases (Fig. 6 h–6l), the net deposition in the flow adjustment distance, XD  , was smaller than the upstream reference, Dep (0) , and gradually decreased to the minimum value with increasing x  position. This is because the near-bed TKE  below the canopy exceeded the critical turbulence for resuspension, k t ( c )     , and gradually increased to the maximum value over the adjustment distance of XD   (Fig. 6 b–6f). Beyond the distance (x  > XD  ), both the velocity and near-bed TKE  below the canopy remained constant (i.e., the flow below the canopy was fully developed), so sediment deposition remained the same. If the channel-average velocity increases to a sufficiently large value, all deposition may be resuspended, and deposition may be very small. For example, the mean net deposition below the floating canopy in Case 5 (U 0  = 24.5 cm/s, H  = 20 cm, a  = 1.6 m-1 , hg  /H  = 0.3, Fig. 6 k) was only Dep (m)  = 0.1 mg/cm2  due to the highest near-bed TKE  across all the cases in this study (Fig. 6 e).  4.3 Model validation The experimental data from the model floating canopies of this study (Cases 1–6, U 0  = 11.5 ∼ 24.5 cm/s, a  = 1.6 and 3.0 m-1 , hg  /H  = 0.3 ∼ 0.8) were used to verify the proposed model. The longitudinal evolution of the near-bed TKE , predicted from Eq. (6) , and the critical for resuspension kt  ( c  ) , estimated from Eq. (13) , were inserted into Eqs. (10)–(12)  to predict the longitudinal distribution of net deposition. The predicted deposition, shown as red lines, agreed well with the measurements within uncertainty (Fig. 6 g–6l). This suggests that the deposition probability can be defined by the near-bed TKE  for floating canopy cases and confirms that this study provides a reasonable way to predict the deposition distribution. The deposition model (Eq. (10) ) was then verified using measurements of real floating E. crassipes  canopies (Cases A-C). At U 0  = 12.5 ∼ 17 cm/s, a  = 2.4 ∼ 2.8 m-1 , and hg  /H  = 0.67 ∼ 0.73 (Fig. 7  ), the predicted deposition agreed well with the measurements, indicating that the proposed model is also valid for predicting deposition in scenarios involving real E. crassipes  canopies.   5 Discussion 5.1 Shear-generated turbulence kt  (shear)  A floating canopy forms a shear layer at the interface of the canopy bottom due to the velocity difference between the in-canopy and below-canopy layers, such that shear-generated turbulence is produced and its intensity is related to the momentum exchange through the two layers. Herein, we consider the situation in which the vortices along the canopy bottom (i.e., shear structure) were sufficiently strong to impact the near-bed flow condition and thus contributed to the near-bed TKE . The canopy average shear production was defined as:(18) P shear    = 1 h g   ∫ 0 h g   - ρ u ′  w ′      ∂ u     ∂ z    d z     where - ρ u ′  w ′         is the Reynolds shear stress. We assumed that the shear production decreased linearly from the canopy bottom to the position at which the Reynolds shear stress was zero (- ρ u ′  w ′      = 0   ), i.e., z  = δb  . By modifying the calculation method of the canopy average shear production proposed by Zhang et al. (2020)  for a submerged canopy, the canopy average shear production can be estimated from (see the detailed derivation in the Supporting Information  ):(19) P shear  x       = 1.25 h g  - δ b  x         δ e  x    h g    C ∗ 3 / 2   U b  x    - U c  x        3      where δe  (x ) is estimated from Eq. (2)  and δb  (x ) is the height of the bed boundary layer, estimated by δ b  ( x )   h g   = 0.024 ± 0.004     F D  ( x )   τ  b  ( x )      , with the vegetation drag F D  ( x )  = ρ C D  a h c   2 ( 1 - ϕ )   U c  ( x )      2    . C*  is the shear parameter, and C* = 0.076 ± 0.025 for floating canopies. In the fully developed flow region, the TKE  budget is characterized by an equilibrium between wake-induced production and viscous dissipation (Raupach and Shaw, 1982; Zhang et al., 2020; Tanino and Nepf, 2008 ). Based on this assumption, we defined β*  as a scale factor from a bulk perspective that is less than 1 (Eq. (19) and (20) , the shear-generated turbulence, kt  (shear) (x ), is written as:(21) k t shear      x    = l t  β ∗  P shear  x            2 / 3   = 1.25 h g  - δ b  x         δ e  x    h g    C ∗ 3 / 2   U b  x    - U c  x        3  β ∗  h g      2 / 3        Finally, the near-bed TKE , kt  (x ), below a floating canopy is predicted by:(22) k t  x    = C f  ω  U b  x        2   ⏟  k t (bed)   x      + 1.25 h g  - δ b  x         δ e  x    h g    C ∗ 3 / 2   U b  x    - U c  x        3  β ∗  h g      2 / 3   ⏟  k t ( shear )   x           The scale factor, β* , was estimated from Eq. (22)  using the measured kt  (x ) and the depth-averaged velocity within (Uc  (x )) and below (Ub  (x )) the canopy. A greater β*  suggests that the K-H vortices below the floating roots more easily reach the channel bed. For a submerged canopy, Tseng and Tinoco (2020)  reported that the scale factor β * is related to the streamwise-averaged shear velocity (u ∗ c     ), time-averaged bulk velocity (u b    ), vegetation density (a ), and submergence ratio (hc  /H ), scaled with β ∗  ∼ u ∗ c   / u b    . For a floating canopy case, we would like to examine how β*  varies with channel-average velocity U 0 , vegetation density a , and relative flow depth hg  /H . Fig. 8   suggests that the impact of vegetation density and relative flow depth on β*  is negligible. More importantly, β * decreases with increasing channel-average velocity. The reason may be that the formation of K-H vortices primarily depends on the strength of the shear layer, which is associated with the channel-average velocity. A greater channel-average velocity may produce a stronger shear layer but may also restrict the K-H vortices from reaching the channel bed. Across all cases, β*  ranges between 0.02 and 0.14. The shear-generated turbulence below a floating canopy increases to a maximum in the fully developed flow region (x  > XD  ), which may increase the near-bed TKE . Fig. 9   shows the bed-generated turbulence, kt  (bed- f  ) , and shear-generated turbulence, kt  (shear- f  ) , over a wide range of vegetation densities (a  = 0.5 ∼ 4.5 m-1 ) and relative flow depths (hg  /H  = 0.3 ∼ 0.8). First, kt  (bed- f  )  and kt  (shear- f  )  exhibit two different trends (Fig. 9 a and 9b). For the same relative flow depth and channel-average velocity, increasing vegetation density enhances the depth-averaged velocity below the canopy, Ub  (x ), and the velocity gradient at the canopy bottom, increasing both kt  (bed- f  )  and kt  (shear- f  )  (Fig. 9 a and 9b). However, hg  /H  has different impacts on kt  (bed- f  )  and kt  (shear- f  ) . For the same vegetation density and channel-average velocity, increasing relative flow depth consistently reduces Ub  (x ) and thus kt  (bed- f  ) , but kt  (shear- f  )  increases as hg  /H  increases from 0.30 to 0.55 but decreases as hg  /H  further increases from 0.55 to 0.80. Next, we compared the ratio of the bed-generated turbulence to the shear-generated turbulence, kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  ) , across a wide range of relative flow depths, hg /H  (= 0.3 to 0.8, consistent with the values of this study, Table 1 ), and vegetation densities (= 0.5 to 4.5 m-1 ) at high (U 0  = 20 cm/s) and low flow velocities (U 0  = 11.5 cm/s). Cases 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 are marked in Fig. 9 c and d (parameters summarized in Table 1 ). The two plots show that kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  varied with both vegetation density and relative flow depth. The shear-generated turbulence must be included if the ratio of the bed-generated turbulence to the shear-generated turbulence is less than 3, i.e., kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  ≤ 3. For high-velocity cases (U 0  = 20 cm/s), kt(  bed- f)   was dominant because kt(  bed- f)  /kt  (shear- f  )  = 4.5 to 14.3 in Cases 2, 3, 4 and 6 (Fig. 9 c). For low-velocity cases (U 0  = 11.5 cm/s), Case 1 had a similar condition in which kt(  bed- f)   dominated the near-bed TKE  (kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  = 3.7, Fig. 9 d). For the highest velocity case (U 0  = 24.5 cm/s, data not shown in Fig. 9 ), the contribution of kt(  bed- f)   to the near-bed TKE  was much greater than that of k t(shear- f  ) , with a measured ratio of kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  = 18.7 in Case 5. The above analysis confirms that it is reasonable to ignore shear-generated turbulence in Cases 1 to 6. However, the shear-generated turbulence cannot be ignored in Case 7 because the bed-generated and shear-generated turbulences were comparable (kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  = 1.8, Fig. 9 d). As shown in Fig. 9 c and 9d, the proposed method can be used to determine whether the contribution of the shear-generated turbulence, kt  (shear -f  ) , to the near-bed TKE  can be ignored. If we consider the threshold as the ratio of kt  (bed- f  ) /kt  (shear- f  )  = 3, as shown in two plots, the threshold varies with the relative flow depth (hg  /H ), vegetation density (a ), and channel-average velocity (U 0 ). For example, across hg  /H  = 0.3 to 0.8, the threshold stands for the vegetation density of a  < 3.5 m-1  at U 0  = 20 cm/s, while it stands for a  < 1.5 m-1  at U 0  = 11.5 cm/s, which perfectly matches the measurements (circles in Fig. 9 c and 9d). This finding suggests that the proposed method provides a reasonable way to evaluate whether kt  (shear -f  )  can be ignored relative to kt  (bed- f  ) . In addition, for a deep relative flow depth (e.g., hg /H  = 0.8), kt(  bed- f)   and k t(shear- f  )  may be comparable at low velocities. The shear vortices may not contribute to the near-bed TKE  due to the large distance (e.g., hg   = 0.8H ) from the canopy bottom to the channel bed, particularly in the case with a deep flow depth H . Based on the predicted near-bed TKE  of Eqs. (6) and (22) , the difference between the predicted deposition is 15 % for the vegetation density of a  < 3.0 m-1  at U 0  = 11.5 cm/s, indicating that the shear-generated turbulence has a negligible contribution to deposition for a high relative flow depth and low-velocity case. However, the high relative flow depth and low-velocity scenario need further verification. To further examine the impact of shear-generated turbulence on the near-bed TKE  and deposition, Case 7 was taken as an example, in which the near-bed TKE  predicted from Eq. (6)  (only bed-generated turbulence) and Eq. (22)  (both bed-generated and shear-generated turbulences) and deposition distributions using the predicted near-bed TKE  of Eq. (6) and (22)  were compared. Fig. 10  a shows that Eq. (6)  underestimated the near-bed TKE  below the floating canopy, but Eq. (22)  agreed with the evolution of the near-bed TKE . This is because in Case 7, the near-bed TKE  consisted of both bed-generated and shear-generated turbulences, and the two components were comparable (Fig. 9 d). Therefore, the deposition distribution using the predicted near-bed TKE  of Eq. (6)  was overestimated, while that using the predicted near-bed TKE  of Eq. (22)  matched the measurements (Fig. 10 b). This suggests that the shear-generated turbulence may be ignored only if its contribution to the near-bed TKE  is very small.  5.2 Comparison of resuspension results below floating canopies In a channel with a floating canopy, the increase in the near-bed TKE  below the canopy drives the resuspension of the deposited particles. Herein, we considered a natural river filled with floating vegetation. The floating canopy was assumed to be sufficiently long (much longer than the flow adjustment distance XD  ), and most of the flow below the canopy was assumed to be fully developed. The proposed models (Eqs. (10) and (11) ) were used to quantitatively compare the impact of a floating canopy on resuspension under different channel velocities (U 0 ) and vegetation conditions (hg  /H  = 0.1 ∼ 0.9 and a  = 0.5 ∼ 4.5 m-1 ). The medium size of the suspended materials in the rivers was considered ds   = 22 μm. The bed friction coefficient was Cf   = 0.004, and the critical velocity for resuspension was Uc  (bare) = ω k t ( c )    ρ C f         = 13.5 cm/s. Three channel-average velocities, U 0 , were considered, representing the absence (U 0  = 5 cm/s and 11 cm/s) or presence (U 0  = 20 cm/s) of resuspension in the bare channel upstream of the floating canopy. The ratio of the bed-generated turbulence to the shear-generated turbulence, kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  ) , must be evaluated before using the proposed model. If kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  ≤ 3, the shear-generated turbulence must be considered, and sediment deposition below the floating canopy relative to that in the bare channel, Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare) , is estimated from the predicted near-bed TKE  (Eq. (22) , denoted as open diamonds in Fig. 11  ). If kt(  bed- f)  /k t(shear- f  )  > 3, the shear-generated turbulence can be ignored, and the predicted near-bed TKE  of Eq. (6)  is used to estimate Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare) . Fig. 11  shows that vegetation density (a ) and relative flow depth (hg  /H ) had a negligible influence on the deposition distribution if U 0  was sufficiently low. For very low-velocity conditions (U 0  = 5 cm/s, Fig. 11 a), the depth-averaged velocity (= 5.9 to 7.1 cm/s) below the canopy was also low, so resuspension was absent in the bare channel and below the canopy. The deposition in the bare channel, Dep (bare) , was the same as that below the canopy, Dep ( f  )  (both Dep  values were estimated from Eq. (10) ). As the vegetation density (a ) and channel-average velocity (U 0 ) increased, resuspension below the canopy started, and significant resuspension occurred at U 0  = 20 cm/s (Fig. 11 a). Under high-flow conditions, nearly 80 % of the deposition (Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare)  ≈ 0.2) was resuspended in water when a  > 2.5 m−1 . This comparison suggested that both the channel-average velocity and vegetation density impact resuspension below a floating canopy. The comprehensive effect of relative flow depth (hg  /H ) and channel-average velocity (U 0 ) on resuspension is clarified at a given vegetation density (a  = 2 m-1 ) (Fig. 11 b). The deposition distribution does not change (Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare)  = 1) in the very-low-velocity case (U 0  = 5 cm/s). As the channel-average velocity increased, resuspension below the canopy was observed (Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare)  < 1) and became significant with decreasing relative flow depth (hg  /H ) (Fig. 11 b). For the high-velocity case (U 0  = 20 cm/s), at hg  /H  = 0.2, approximately 93 % of the deposition was resuspended (Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare)  ≈ 0.07). Note that Dep ( f  ) /Dep (bare)  (≈ 0.11) at hg  /H  = 0.1 is larger than that (≈ 0.07) at hg  /H  = 0.2, suggesting a weaker resuspension at hg  /H  = 0.1. This is because the depth-averaged velocity below a floating canopy Ubf   (= 28.6 cm/s) at hg  /H  = 0.1 is smaller than Ubf   (= 29.9 cm/s) at hg  /H  = 0.2 due to a nonmonotonic trend between Ubf   and hg  /H  (Eq. (7) ). Given this fact, the near-bed TKE  at hg  /H  = 0.1 was smaller than that at hg  /H  = 0.2. Nevertheless, a small relative flow depth hg  /H  (e.g., 0.1 and 0.2) results in significant resuspension. This result confirms that the growing roots of floating vegetation can directly impact deposition below the vegetation. As the floating root length increases, the height of the free-flow region (hg  ) gradually decreases, yielding a shallower relative flow depth, hg  /H . A large amount of deposition below the vegetation becomes suspended sediment, resulting in diminished net deposition. In a channel with shallow flow, when floating canopies are used to remove nutrients and drive the deposition of small particles, elongating vegetation roots may cause resuspension of the deposited particles, which in turn releases pollutants present below the previously deposited material.  5.3 Model limitations Three limitations of this study should be clarified. First, the proposed method (Eq. (6) ) estimates the near-bed TKE , which considers only the bed-generated turbulence kt  (bed) . We reiterate that the channel-average velocity, vegetation density, and relative flow depth alter the velocity structure (also the shear layer) within and below the canopy and thus impact the shear-generated turbulence, kt  (shear) . We suggest that if kt  (bed) /kt  (shear)  > 3, the estimation of the near-bed TKE  can ignore kt  (shear)  (using Eq. (6) ). If kt  (bed) /kt  (shear)  ≤ 3, the estimation of the near-bed TKE  must consider both kt  (bed)  and kt  (shear)  (using Eq. (22) ). Second, this study focused on suspended sediment with a uniform particle size (ds   = 22 μm) in the laboratory experiments. Although ds   = 22 μm is a typical particle size in the field (e.g., Widdows et al., 2008 ), a uniform particle cannot simulate the complex mixing process among particles of different sizes. For the scenario with a wide distribution of particle sizes, the median particle size may not be a representative indicator for estimating deposition and resuspension below floating canopies. The model accuracy needs further verification. Finally, the greatest difference between the laboratory and field systems is the sediment supply. The proposed model exhibits good performance in scenarios with an unlimited sediment supply. If the channel-average velocity is sufficiently low, sediment supply may be limited in the case of a dense and long canopy. In particular, when the ratio of the advection time scale to the settling time scale is greater than or equal to 1, i.e., κ  = L / U bf      / H / w s         ≥ 1 (Sun et al., 2023 ). To fill the gap between laboratory studies and field studies, a model for a limited sediment supply needs further investigation.   6 Conclusions Laboratory experiments were performed to investigate the impacts of the channel-average velocity, vegetation density, and relative flow depth on the near-bed TKE  evolution and deposition distribution below a floating canopy. The near-bed TKE  was the dominant factor in sediment deposition and resuspension. Without resuspension, the net deposition was spatially uniform throughout the channel. As the channel-average velocity increased, the vegetation density increased and/or the relative flow depth decreased, and the near-bed TKE  increased and surpassed the critical value for resuspension. Relative to an upstream reference, net deposition below a canopy was reduced, and the deposition distribution changed due to a higher near-bed TKE . Models (Eqs. (6) and (10) ) for predicting the evolution of the near-bed TKE  and deposition distribution below a floating canopy were proposed and validated. The predicted near-bed TKE  and deposition were in agreement with measurements below model canopies and real E. crassipes  canopies.
1 Introduction Flood frequency analysis (FFA) is needed to estimate design flood magnitude and determine flood return period (Singh and Strupczewski, 2002; Guo et al., 2016 ). The basic presupposition of traditional FFA is that hydrologic data satisfies the stationarity assumption (Liang et al., 2011; Gilroy and McCuen, 2012; Salas et al., 2018 ). However, under the influence of global climate change and intense human activities, the fundamental assumption of stationarity is disrupted, and observed hydrologic data indicate non-stationary characteristics (Xie et al., 2018; Milly et al., 2008, 2015; Song et al., 2013; Sang et al., 2015, 2018; Yang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021 ). In this condition, the stationarity-based FFA results would be biased, increasing the risk of hydrologic engineering design, construction and operation (Xiong et al., 2018 ). For overcoming the impact of stationarity assumption, non-stationary flood frequency analysis (NFFA) methods have been developed, such as decomposition and synthesis-based methods (Xie et al., 2005), mixed distribution models (Singh and Sinclair, 1972; Alila and Mtiraoui, 2002; Cheng and Song, 2010 ), conditional probability distribution methods (Singh et al., 2005; Renard et al., 2006; Song et al., 2012; Bracken et al., 2018 ) and time-varying moments-based methods (Strupczewski et al., 2001a, 2001b, 2001c; Rigby and Stasinopoulos, 2005; Villarini et al., 2009a, 2009b, 2010, 2011; Anzolin et al., 2023 ). These methods have been applied widely (Sang et al., 2019 ). However, when applied to analyze annual maximum flood series (AMFS), as typical hydrologic extreme events, a common drawback of these NFFA methods is that they ignore the useful statistical information contained in daily flow observations (Xiong et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2022 ). Since annual maximum flood information is extracted from annual daily flow series (ADFS), statistical information contained in ADFS would be useful for doing NFFA. Following the extreme value theory, the norming constants method (NCM) had been developed for doing NFFA, aiming to incorporate non-stationarity information of ADFS to analyze AMFS (Xiong et al., 2015 ). The extreme value theory claims that the maximum of independent and identically distributed random variables, when properly centered and normalized, can only converge to one of three possible distributions, namely the Gumbel distribution, the Fréchet distribution or the Weibull distribution (Fisher and Tippett, 1928 ). It can also be said that the distribution of random variables, namely the parent distribution (PD), belongs to the maximum domain of attraction of the extreme value distribution (Embrechts et al., 1997 ). ADFS are generally considered to follow the Lognormal distribution (LN) or Gamma distribution (GA) (Fennessey and Vogel, 1990; Blum et al., 2017; Atieh et al., 2015; Gottschalk et al., 2013a, 2013b ), both of which belong to the maximum domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution (Λ  ). The relationship between the PD used to fit ADFS and the extreme distribution used to fit AMFS can be established by using the centering constant and the normalizing constant, jointly referred to as the norming constants. It is the basis of NCM for doing NFFA. Embrechts et al., (1997)  elaborated on how to calculate the norming constants and derived the norming constants of some typical distributions, such as Cauchy distribution, Beta distribution, Lognormal distribution, and others. Applications indicated the superiority of NCM compared to those methods for analyzing AMFS under the assumption of stationarity (Xiong et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2022 ). However, conventional NCM ignored one key point: the calculation of norming constants closely depends on the tail characteristics of the PD (i.e., high quantiles of ADFS concerned in this study). ADFS are complex time series and usually exhibit significant seasonal characteristics, implying that the high quantiles and low quantiles in ADFS follow different distributions (Cheng et al., 2012; Blum et al., 2017; Song et al., 2018 ). When applying conventional NCM, the method of probability weighted moments is used to fit all data points in ADFS, however, it does not fit the PD’s tail well due to the influence of low quantiles on high quantiles in ADFS, which would inevitably cause bias of norming constants in NCM and would result in biased NFFA results. The objective of this study therefore is to develop a new method for improving NFFA results. The basic idea of the developed method is to combine higher-order probability weighted moments (HPWM) with NCM, and the method is thus called HPWM-NCM. As probability weighted moments with higher orders depend more on higher quantiles of the variables (i.e., the tail of its distribution) (Wang, 1997a, 1997b, 1998 ), the parameters estimated by HPWM will better fit the tail of the distribution of ADFS, and the norming constants will be more accurately calculated. To be specific, the HPWM-NCM is to accurately describe the tail characteristics of the distribution of ADFS by concerning high quantiles more than low quantiles. In this manner, the norming constants can be more accurately calculated and then using NCM accurate NFFA results can be obtained. The paper is organized as follows. After Introduction, Section 2  derives HPWMs of the LN and GA distributions and elaborates how to calculate the norming constants from the two distributions; moreover, the specific steps of NFFA by using HPWM-NCM are also explained. In Section 3 , we verify the goodness-of-fit of HPWM-NCM for NFFA through Monte-Carlo experiments. In Section 4 , HPWM-NCM is applied to analyze the AMFS in the Rhine River basin, and is compared with conventional NCM and stationary FFA method (PWM) for further verification. Conclusions are given finally.  2 Development of HPWM-NCM 2.1 Higher-order probability weighted moments The probability weighted moment (PWM) β r    is defined as (Greenwood et al., 1979 ):(1) β r  = ∫ 0  1  x ( F )  F  r  d F     where x ( F )    is the inverse form of the distribution function F  , and r   is the order of the PWM. (21)  yields(22) lim  n → + ∞   P ( M ∼  n  e  μ + σ d n     ≤ 1 + σ c n  x + o ( c n  )  )  = Λ ( x )       Since c n  → 0    as n → + ∞   , it follows that(23) M ∼  n  - e  μ + σ d n     σ c n  e  μ + σ d n      → Λ      Thus, the norming constants of the Lognormal distribution can be derived from the norming constants of the standard normal distribution as:(24) d ∼  n  = e  μ + σ d n       c ∼  n  = σ c n  e  μ + σ d n               If F   is a Gamma distribution, its norming constants can be derived from parameters α   and β   as:(25) d n  = β  - 1   ( ln n + ( α - 1 )  lnln n - ln Γ ( α )  )     c n  = β  - 1              The detailed derivation of the norming constants for the standard normal distribution and the Gamma distribution can be found in (Embrechts et al., 1997 ). As ADFS may not always satisfy the independence assumption, the sample size n   should be a value less than 365 or 366 for each year (Tasker, 1983; Fennessey and Vogel, 1990; Gottschalk et al., 2013a ). We calibrate n   to obtain the effective sample size n  ∗     using the Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Xiong et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2022 ), which will replace n   in the calculation of the norming constants. After obtaining the norming constants, the NFFA can be conducted for each year based on the Gumbel distribution:(26) Λ ( z t  )  = exp ( - exp ( - z t  - d n  ∗   , t    c n  ∗   , t    )  )      where z t    is AMFS; d n  ∗   , t     and c n  ∗   , t     are the centering constant and normalizing constant, respectively, which are derived from the parameters (in Eq. (8)  for the LN and in Eq. (16)  for the GA) of ADFS for year t  . Following the main idea of NCM, it can be seen from Eq. (17)  that the tail characteristics of the PD (i.e., high quantiles of ADFS concerned in this study) have a significant impact on the calculation of the norming constants. When applying conventional NCM, the method of probability weighted moments is used to fit all data points in ADFS. However, it cannot fit the PD’s tail well, especially when the low quantiles have a significant impact on high quantiles. As a result, conventional NCM does not accurately estimate d n  ∗   , t     and c n  ∗   , t     in Eq. (26) , which influences the accuracy in analyzing AMFS.  2.3 Proposed HPWM-NCM In order to obtain accurate NFFA results based on NCM, the tail of the distribution of ADFS needs to be fitted well for accurately estimating norming constants. Previous studies showed that higher-order probability weighted moments (HPWM) had advantages in estimating high quantiles (i.e., tail of a distribution) over other methods (Wang, 1997a, 1997b, 1998 ). Following Eq. (1) , it is specifically known that higher order r   corresponds to larger probability weight F  r    for larger values (i.e., higher quantiles) of the variables. That is to say, HPWM can reduce the influence of the low quantiles on the high quantiles in ADFS, and thus improve the fitting results for the tail of the distribution of ADFS. Thereby, the combination of HPWM and NCM is expected to improve the estimation of norming constants, based on which NFFA results can be further improved. This is the basic idea of the proposed HPWM-NCM. The specific steps of NFFA by using the HPWM-NCM are explained as follows: (1) Extract annual maximum information from annual daily flow series (ADFS) to generate the annual maximum flood series (AMFS); (2) Apply the Mann-Kendall (MK) test to detect the trends of AMFS and its variance series. If significant trends are identified, NFFA needs to be conducted. (3) Considering that ADFS generally follow the LN or the GA distribution, they are selected as the PD for NFFA in this study; (4) Set order r = 1   , and apply HPWM to estimate the parameters of the LN and the GA using Eq. (8)  and Eq. (16) , respectively; (5) Assume the sample size n = 365    (less in theory) for each year and calculate the norming constants for the LN and the GA using Eq. (24) and (25) , respectively; (6) Decrease the value of n  , and repeat step (5) to obtain the norming constants for different n ,    until n = 50    as the minimum effective sample size set in this study; (7) Determine the effective sample size n  ∗     based on the Akaike information criterion as:(27) AI C n  = - 2 ln ( L ( n )  )  + 2 k    L ( n )  = ∏ t = 1  N  [ 1 c n , t    exp ( - z t  - d n , t    c n , t    - exp ( - z t  - d n , t    c n , t    )  )  ]            where l n ( L ( n ) )    is the logarithmic likelihood function of the Gumbel distribution; k   is the number of estimated parameters; and N   is the total number of years. The n   corresponding to the minimum value of AIC is determined as the effective sample size n  ∗    . The norming constants corresponding to n  ∗     are chosen as the effective norming constants; (8) Increase the order r   and repeat steps (4)-(7) to obtain the effective norming constants corresponding to different order r ,    until r = 10    set in this study; (9) Determine the best order r  ∗     and the suitable PD (LN or GA) for HPWM-NCM. Here, the difference (denoted as DET) between the empirical frequency and the theoretical probability of centile curves is analyzed to determine the best order and choose the suitable PD:(28) DET = ∑ i = 1  5  1 N  ∑ t = 1  N  I ( z t  , D u , r , P i  , t   )  - P i        where u   is the type of the PD; i   is the sequence number of the representative theoretical probability P i    (usually 5 %, 25 %, 50 %, 75 %, 95 %); D   is the design value; and I   is an indicative function with a value of 1 if z t  ≤ D u , r , P i  , t      or 0 if z t  > D u , r , P i  , t     . The r   and the PD corresponding to the minimum value of DET are determined as the best order r  ∗     and the most suitable PD, respectively. The norming constants related to r  ∗     and the selected PD are determined as the optimal norming constants for HPWM-NCM; (10) Conduct non-stationary annual maximum flood frequency analysis based on the Gumbel distribution and the optimal norming constants determined in the above step. To be specific, for a flood return period T  , the time-varying design flood value D t    can be obtained by:(29) D t  = d n  ∗   , r  ∗   , t   - c n  ∗   , r  ∗   , t   ln [ - ln ( 1 - 1 T  )  ]       Besides, for a design flood value D  , its time-varying flood return period T t    can be obtained by:(30) T t  = 1 1 - exp [ - exp ( - D - d n  ∗   , r  ∗   , t    c n  ∗   , r  ∗   , t    )  ]        The flowchart of NFFA by using the proposed HPWM-NCM is also shown in Fig. 2  .  2.4 Criteria for evaluation of different methods In this study, we will compare the proposed HPWM-NCM with the conventional NCM and stationary FFA method for illustrating the superiority of the former. The probability weighted moments (PWM) method can utilize dual information of sample value and rank; it has advantages compared to other stationary FFA methods (Greenwood et al., 1979; Kumar et al., 1994; Huang and Chen., 2011; Li et al., 2014 ) and thus it was used for comparison in this study. The performances of the three methods were evaluated from three aspects: overall fitting bias quantified by AIC, residuals’ correlation described by Filliben correlation coefficient F r   , and residuals’ maximum error described by Kolmogorov–Smirnov value D KS    . The former can serve as the selection criteria for the optimal method, and the other two can test the goodness-of-fit of selected method for hydrologic time series (Xiong et al., 2018 ). The three indexes are explained as follows. (1) The AIC is determined using Eq. (27) . A smaller AIC value means smaller overall fitting bias; (2) The Filliben correlation coefficient (Filliben, 1975 ) can be calculated as:(31) F r  = ∑ t = 1  N  ( R t  - R t   ¯   )  ( M t  - M t   ¯   )   ∑ t = 1  N  ( R t  - R t   ¯   )  2  ∑ t = 1  N  ( M t  - M t   ¯   )  2         where R t  = Φ  - 1   ( A s c ( Λ ( z t    d n , t   , c n , t   )  )  )     is the empirical normalized quantile residuals, and M t  = Φ  - 1   ( t - 0.375  N + 0.25   )     is the theoretical normalized quantile residuals (Xue and Chen, 2006 ), both of which are referred to as residuals subsequently; Asc    is the ascending function and Φ  - 1     is the inverse function of standard normal distribution. When F r    is bigger than the threshold value of 0.978 at the significance level of 5 %, the method passes the Filliben correlation coefficient test, and bigger F r    means the method’s residuals are closer to the standard normal distribution, indicating better performance. (3) The Kolmogorov–Smirnov (K-S) value (Chakravarti et al., 1967 ) can be calculated as:(32) D KS   = max  1 ≤ t ≤ N   A s c ( Λ ( z t    d n , t   , c n , t   )  )  - t N + 1          When D KS     is smaller than the threshold value of 1.36 / N     at the significance level of 5 %, the method passes the K-S test, and smaller D KS     means smaller residuals’ maximum error and thus better performance. In addition, the worm plot (Buuren and Fredriks, 2001 ), as a de-trended Quantile-Quantile (Q-Q) plot of residuals, was employed to intuitively reflect the difference between the empirical and theoretical residuals, and the centile curve plots were drawn to visually observe how the norming constants calculated by three methods captured the variability of AMFS.   3 Verification of HPWM-NCM by Monte-Carlo experiments Here, we designed Monte-Carlo (MC) experiments to verify the superiority of the proposed HPWM-NCM. Considering that ADFS generally follow the Lognormal (LN) or the Gamma (GA) distribution, the time-varying synthetic time series were generated following six parameter schemes, as shown in Table 1  , which represents different time-variant and time-invariant parameters for LN or GA. The sample sizes n   were set as 200, 300, 400, and the total number of years N   was set as 100. For each parameter scheme and sample size, the synthetic time series with the total length n ∗ N    were generated. Moreover, in order to simulate the non-stationary characteristics of observed ADFS, we multiplied all the values below the 50th percentile by a scaling factor δ = 0.5    to disrupt the identically distributed property of synthetic time series, for reflecting the influence of the low quantiles on the high quantiles. For each synthetic time series, we calculated its norming constants by using the proposed HPWM-NCM, conventional NCM, and PWM, respectively. We determined the best order r  ∗     by HPWM-NCM and calculated related indexes of AIC, F r   , and D KS    . Each MC experiment was repeated 1000 times to ensure the stability of results, and the statistical average values of r  ∗    , AIC, F r    and D KS     were calculated and denoted as r  ∗    ¯    , AIC  ¯    , F r   ¯     and D KS    ¯    . In addition, the passing rates of test of F r    and D KS     were also calculated as:(33) R F r  = 1 1000  ∑ i = 1  1000  J ( F r , i   , 0.978 )     R D KS   = 1 1000  ∑ i = 1  1000  I ( D KS , i   , 1.36  N   )            where J   is an indicative function with a value of 1 if F r , i   ≥ 0.978    or 0 if F r , i   < 0.978   ; I   is an indicative function with a value of 1 if D KS , i   ≤ 1.36 / N     or 0 if D KS , i   > 1.36 / N    . Fig. 3   shows the best order r  ∗    ¯     determined by HPWM-NCM under different parameter schemes and sample sizes. The r  ∗    ¯     increased along with the sample size n  , indicating that higher order was needed to calculate the norming constants for more complex time series, as bigger sample size means more influence of low quantiles on high quantiles due to the setting of scaling factor δ   in the MC experiments. Besides, all r  ∗    ¯     values were below 6, implying that the order r   used in HPWM-NCM for NFFA generally needn’t to be very high, which also supports the rationality of the threshold of r   set as 10 in Section 2.3 . Fig. 4   shows the values of AIC  ¯    , F r   ¯     and D KS    ¯     under different parameter schemes and sample sizes. It clearly demonstrates the superiority of the proposed HPWM-NCM regarding the overall fitting bias, residuals’ correlation and residuals’ maximum error. To be specific, results in Fig. 4 (a) show that the AIC  ¯     values (all schemes’ mean value was 955.58) of HPWM-NCM were lower than that (1021.33) of conventional NCM and much lower than that (1295.47) of PWM in all given parameter schemes and sample sizes, indicating the better performance of HPWM-NCM in overall fitting bias. For the F r   ¯       values in Fig. 4 (b), HPWM-NCM kept the highest for all schemes, with mean value of 0.9905, indicating that its residuals were the closest to standard normal distribution compared to the other two methods with mean values of 0.9861 and 0.9501, respectively. Especially, PWM’s F r   ¯     values were very low as it failed to capture the time-varying characteristics of the norming constants, which caused the poor correlation between its residuals and theoretical residuals. Fig. 4 (c) shows that the D KS    ¯     values (all schemes’ mean value was 0.1028) of HPWM-NCM were lower than those of conventional NCM and PWM (all schemes’ mean values were 0.1654 and 0.1279, respectively) in most cases, indicating that residuals’ maximum error of HPWM-NCM was the smallest. The passing rates of test of F r    and D KS     (i . e . ,  R F  r    and RD  KS   ,  r e s p e c t i v e l y   ) are shown in Fig. 5  . It clearly shows that the HPWM-NCM had higher passing rates in both the Filliben correlation coefficient test and K-S test compared to conventional NCM and PWM, which further illustrates the better goodness-of-fit of the proposed HPWM-NCM for analyzing non-stationary annual maximum flood series. Specifically, the passing rates of correlation coefficient test by HPWM-NCM were all above 85 % and the mean passing rate was 95.44 %, which was higher than conventional NCM with mean passing rate of 83.97 % and much higher than PWM with mean passing rate of 12.61 %. For the D KS    , HPWM-NCM still kept the highest passing rates with the mean value of 88.18 %, which was higher than 48.49 % and 53.29 % of conventional NCM and PWM, respectively. Detailed calculation results of r  ∗    ¯    , AIC  ¯    , F r   ¯     and D KS    ¯     and the passing rates of test of F r    and D KS     can be found in Tables S1 and S2 . Overall, it was found from the MC experiments that HPWM-NCM had improved conventional NCM’s performance in terms of overall fitting bias, residuals’ correlation, and residuals’ maximum error, and it was far superior to PWM. In order to further clarify the essence of improving the calculation of norming constants by HPWM-NCM compared to conventional NCM, the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) for all quantiles, low quantiles and high quantiles between the set design values and the calculated design values were calculated respectively. The MAPE were calculated as:(34) MAPE = 1 N ∗ m   ∑ t = 1  N  ∑ j   P   x t , j   - x ^  t , j    x t , j          where P   is the design frequency with P ≥ 0 %    (all quantiles), P ≤ 50 %    (low quantiles) and P ≥ 90 % , 95 % , 99 %    (high quantiles); m   is the number of the sample values involved in the t -th year’s calculation; x t , j     is the set design value, and x ^  t , j     is the calculated design value. Fig. 6   shows the statistical average values of MAPE for different quantiles under all parameter schemes and sample sizes by HPWM-NCM and conventional NCM. It was found that for all quantiles and low quantiles, HPWM-NCM was inferior to conventional NCM; while for high quantiles, the former was much superior. It should be noted here that the calculation of norming constants is closely related to the tail characteristics of the PD (Embrechts et al., 1997 ), namely, high quantiles of ADFS in this study. Thus, it is concluded that HPWM-NCM can more accurately describe the tail characteristics of the distribution of ADFS than conventional NCM, as the former can more concern high quantiles than low quantiles, and further improve the calculation results of the norming constants, which correctly supports the idea of the development of HPWM-NCM for NFFA.  4 Case study In practice, observed ADFS data are more complicated than synthetic data used in the above MC experiments. Here we used the observed ADFS data in the Rhine River basin to further verify the performance of the proposed HPWM-NCM for NFFA. The Rhine River basin has a typical temperate marine warm and humid climate, with abundant rainfall throughout the year. Global warming, urbanization, and agricultural intensification are changing the frequency and intensity of flood events in the basin (Pfister et al., 2004; Pinter et al., 2006; Ngo et al., 2023 ). The ADFS data observed at 62 hydrologic stations in the basin were collected from the Global Runoff Data Centre (https://www.bafg.de/GRDC ). The basic information of these stations can be found in Table S3 . We employed the annual maximum (AM) method to obtain AMFS from the ADFS data. The MK test was used to detect the non-stationarity in AMFS. Some studies have shown that the non-stationarity in the variance (the squares of the residuals for the time series) and higher moments of the time series may also affect non-stationary modelling (Villarini et al., 2009a, 2009b; Jiang and Xiong, 2012; Song et al., 2018 ). Thus, we consider the non-stationarity of both AMFS and its variance series. As a result, the AMFS data at 12 of the total 62 hydrologic stations were found with significant trends (see Fig. 7  ), and they were considered for NFFA. The norming constants of AMFS at the 12 hydrologic stations were calculated by the proposed HPWM-NCM, conventional NCM and PWM, respectively. The suitable PD and the best order r  ∗     by applying HPWM-NCM for NFFA were determined and related indexes were also calculated. Table 2   shows the selected PD, the best order r  ∗     and the AIC, F r   , D KS     values at the 12 hydrologic stations. It was found that the LN was chosen as the suitable PD at 10 of the total 12 stations, implying that the LN was more suitable for fitting ADFS than GA in the study area, which is consistent with previous research (Fennessey and Vogel, 1990; Xiong et al., 2015; Blum et al., 2017 ). The HPWM-NCM’s best order r  ∗     was lower than 6 at 9 of the total 12 stations, implying that the suitable order for HPWM-NCM doesn’t need very high, unless the low quantiles have significant impact on the high quantiles. The result here is similar to the result from the MC experiments. The AIC values of HPWM-NCM kept the lowest at all 12 stations, indicating that HPWM-NCM had the smallest overall fitting bias compared to the other two methods. The mean values and the passing rates of correlation coefficient test at all 12 stations by HPWM-NCM, conventional NCM, PWM were 0.9938, 0.9875, 0.9810 and 100.0 %, 91.7 %, 75 %, respectively, and those of K–S test were 0.0600, 0.1414, 0.0798 and 100.0 %, 58.3 %, 100.0 % respectively, which are basically consistent with the results of the MC experiments. It means that HPWM-NCM was superior to conventional NCM and PWM regarding to residuals’ correlation and residuals’ maximum error, and high passing rates of both correlation coefficient test and K-S test were achieved by HPWM-NCM rather than conventional NCM and PWM. Similar to the MC experiments, we also calculated the MAPE for different quantiles at the 12 hydrologic stations, to explain why HPWM-NCM improves the calculation results of the norming constants compared to conventional NCM. The results in Fig. S1  clearly indicate that for all quantiles and low quantiles, HPWM-NCM was not as good as NCM, but for high quantiles, HPWM-NCM had an advantage over conventional NCM, which once again validated our main idea in this study: HPWM-NCM can better fit the tail of the distribution of ADFS to improve the estimation of norming constants, by reducing the impact of low quantiles on high quantiles caused by ADFS’ own complexity. Fig. 8   shows the worm plots of residuals calculated by the three methods for intuitively illustrating the difference between the empirical and theoretical residuals, taking the BR, BG and K3 stations as examples. Note that other stations have similar results. If the worm point is within the confidence interval, the method passes the test, and the flatter the worm line, the closer the empirical residuals to the theoretical residuals, indicating better fitting of the method. It can be seen that all worm points for HPWM-NCM were within the confidence interval and the worm lines were very flat at three stations; while the other two methods failed to achieve it. Especially, the worm points from conventional NCM were completely outside the confidence interval at the K3 station, which means that empirical residuals were much higher than theoretical residuals due to poor fitting in high quantiles of the ADFS. By increasing the order of PWM, the impact of low quantiles on high quantiles becomes weak to better fit the tail of the distribution of ADFS, thereby improving the method’s performance for NFFA, which also explains the superiority of HPWM-NCM to conventional NCM. The centile curve plots are drawn to observe how the norming constants calculated by the three methods capture the variability of AMFS at the BR, BG and K3 stations, as shown in Fig. 9  . It shows that both HPWM-NCM and conventional NCM described the variability of AMFS and captured the increasing trends at the BR and BG stations and the decreasing trend at the K3 station, while PWM did not achieve it. Observed AMFS falling below each centile curve were counted and the corresponding empirical frequency was calculated. Table 3   shows the comparison between the theoretical probability and the empirical frequency at the three stations. If the difference of 5 % between the theoretical probability and the empirical frequency was set as the criterion, all the differences were within 5 % for HPWM-NCM, but except for the other two methods, which further demonstrates the reasonability and effectiveness of the proposed HPWM-NCM. Since the reliability of HPWM-NCM had been verified, non-stationary annual maximum flood frequency analysis was conducted. Taking the BR, BG and K3 stations as examples again, we calculated the flood magnitudes with once–in–a-century (1 %) return period (Fig. 10  ). The 1 % design flood magnitude estimated by HPWM-NCM changed from 1934.5 m3 /s (in 1893) to 7419.0 m3 /s (in 1999) at the BR station and from 546.1 m3 /s (in 1921) to 1901.1 m3 /s (in 2006) at the BG station, and there were significant upward trends at the two stations. But for the stationary method (PWM), the design flood magnitude was constant at 4431.7 m3 /s and 1303.3 m3 /s at the two stations, respectively. At the K3 station, the 1 % design flood magnitude estimated by HPWM-NCM changed from 492.8 m3 /s (in 1965) to 38.0 m3 /s (in 2014) and there was a downward trend, compared with the constant design value of 256.0 m3 /s from PWM. Overall, the proposed HPWM-NCM effectively captured the variability of design flood magnitude, which can provide reliable support for hydrologic engineering construction and flood control management.  5 Discussion Since the assertion “Stationarity is dead: Whither water management?” (Milly et al., 2008, 2015 ) was proposed, non-stationary flood frequency analysis has become a research hotspot for hydrology research. Our proposed HPWM-NCM integrated the advantages of HPWM in better fitting the tail of the distribution of ADFS, as well as the advantages of NCM in considering the statistical information contained in ADFS for better analyzing AMFS. Thus, it has solid mathematical foundation and clear statistical meaning, and the results of both MC experiments and observed streamflow data demonstrated the superiority of the proposed HPWM-NCM method. Here, some issues worth further research are discussed, based on the proposed HPWM-NCM. When using the proposed HPWM-NCM, the key to obtain reliable NFFA results is how to accurately extract the information of high quantiles from ADFS by HPWM. However, HPWM with excessively high order may cause the parameter estimation results to be sensitive to the outliers of ADFS’s high quantiles (Wang, 1997b; Song et al., 2018 ). Thus, it’s necessary to balance the effective extraction of flood information from ADFS and the sensitivity of parameter estimation results to sample outliers by determining a suitable order. In this study, it is a feasible and reasonable way to determine the best order by choosing the minimum value of DET, which can ensure the excellent performance of the proposed HPWM-NCM. In the future, more effective criteria for determining the order are encouraged to develop for ensuring accurate NFFA. The formulae used in this study for calculating the norming constants are classical ways, which is an effective pathway to do NFFA based on the extreme value theory. In fact, any constants that can converge the maximum of parent distribution to the extreme value distribution can be chosen as norming constants (Embrechts et al., 1997 ). Taking the standard normal distribution as an example, Mills’ ratio (Mills, 1926 ) and its upper and lower bounds (Gorden, 1941 ) can serve as the auxiliary function, and thus there are at least three kinds of norming constants in it (Xu et al., 2022 ). Different norming constants indicate different velocity of the approximation of the normalized maxima toward the extreme value distribution law (Hall, 1979; Gasull et al., 2015 ; Du and Chen, 2016 ; Huang et al., 2016 ). Thus, in the future research, it is interesting and meaningful to explore how to reduce the limit approximation error by choosing suitable norming constants. In addition, our proposed HPWM-NCM can effectively capture the variability characteristics of AMFS, and can more objectively and realistically reflect the evolution of extreme flood events in changing environment. In the future, the physical basis of the proposed method can be further considered by coupling meteorological factors and human activity indices. For instance, the multiple linear or nonlinear relationships can be established between the norming constants and annual precipitation, annual mean temperature, urbanization rate, reservoir index, etc. (Xiong et al., 2015, 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ), which will strengthen the proposed method’s physical basis. To this end, it should be pointed out that no matter stationary flood frequency analysis or non-stationary flood frequency analysis, our major aim is to obtain the design flood value corresponding to a certain return period. The proposed HPWM-NCM can provide more theoretical support for solving the problem of design flood calculation faced with a changing environment. In practice, we can also combine HPWM-NCM with other non-stationary flood design methods, such as the expected number of exceedances method (ENE, Cooley, 2013 )and the expected waiting time method (EWT, Salas et al., 2013, 2014; Cooley, 2013 ). In that context, the constant flood design value can be obtained and provide more meaningful reference for hydrologic engineering construction for improving the practicability and operability of the results.  6 Conclusions In this study, a method called HPWM-NCM was proposed by coupling higher-order probability weighted moments (HPWM) with the norming constants method (NCM) for improving non-stationary annual maximum flood frequency analysis. To be specific, the HPWM method was used to accurately estimate parameters of ADFS, and the NCM was used to obtain the norming constants of AMFS from parameters of ADFS and do NFFA. The proposed HPWM-NCM concerns high quantiles more than low quantiles, which better fit the tail of the distribution of ADFS, and obtain more accurate NFFA results. The results of Monte-Carlo (MC) experiments showed that HPWM-NCM improved conventional NCM’s performance in terms of overall fitting bias, residuals’ correlation, and residuals’ maximum error, and it was far superior to the typical stationary method (PWM). The proposed HPWM-NCM was further applied to analyze the AMFS at 12 hydrologic stations with significant trends in the Rhine River basin. Its advantage compared to conventional NCM and PWM was further verified. Low overall fitting bias and high passing rates of correlation coefficient test and K-S test were achieved by HPWM-NCM rather than conventional NCM and PWM. Overall, the advantages of the proposed HPWM-NCM for non-stationary annual maximum flood frequency analysis were confirmed comprehensively. Finally, it is pointed out that the proposed HPWM-NCM can not only be used for flood analysis, but also for analyzing other extreme events (such as extreme precipitation, extreme temperature), thus it has a wide potential application range. In the future, the HPWM-NCM is expected to be applied in other study areas with changing environments to deal with more challenges caused by extreme hydrometeorological events, and also to further verify its applicability and practicality.
1 Introduction Atmospheric aerosols, the liquid or solid particulate matter in the atmosphere, play an important role in the weather and climate at regional and global scales. The influence of atmospheric aerosols on precipitation patterns, especially on extreme rainfall events, is a critical area of study within atmospheric science. Aerosols affect not only the microphysical properties of clouds but also have broader implications for storms' scale and intensity. The direct effect of aerosols through scattering and absorbing solar radiations leads to decreases in wind speed, surface temperature and the height of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) while increasing relative humidity (RH) and atmospheric stability (Jacobson et al., 2007 ). The indirect effect of aerosols through serving as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) results in a reduction in cloud droplet size and a rise in cloud droplet number concentration (CDNC), precipitation, cloud coverage and lifetime of low-level clouds (Albrecht, 1989 ). The aerosol-cloud-precipitation-meteorology interaction and feedback have been observed in many field experiments by various satellites and surface networks (Ramanathan and Carmichael, 2008; Rosenfeld et al., 2007, 2008; Zanis, 2009; Levin and Brenguier, 2009 ). The assessment of aerosol impacts is challenging because these particles not only have large spatiotemporal variability and short lifetimes, but also have sizes that span several orders of magnitude and complex physical and chemical properties. The fine-mode particles with a diameter less or equal to 2.5 µm (PM2.5) are composed of various chemical compounds such as nitrate (NO3 ), ammonium (NH4 ), sulfate (SO4 ) and organic and black carbon (OC and BC). Sea salt aerosols (primarily composed of N a  +    and C l  -   ) and some species from soil dust are usually in coarse mode. Apart from primary aerosols (e.g., BC, OC, sea salt and dust) that are emitted directly into the atmosphere, a large part of the aerosol mass is secondary aerosols (e.g. NO3 , NH4 , SO4  and secondary organic aerosol (SOA)) that are formed by chemical reactions from its gaseous precursors such as NOx, NH3 and SO2. As noted by Lohmann and Feichter (2005)  and Chen et al. (2008) , the magnitude of the aerosol semi-direct and indirect effects is influenced by the particle size, number concentration and composition of the atmospheric aerosols that serve as CCN or ice nuclei (IN). Particles containing hygroscopic components like water-soluble ions (e.g., N a  +  ,  C l  -  ,  N O  3  -  ,  S O  4  2 -     ) readily act as CCN (Chen and Lamb, 1994 ). On the contrary, hydrophobic components such as elemental carbon must be wrapped by hygroscopic substances before they become CCN (Dusek et al., 2006 ). Furthermore, the transformation of primary aerosols into secondary aerosols also changes aerosol properties, which greatly impacts cloud-aerosol interactions and subsequent rainfall patterns. For example, SSA can react with various atmospheric compounds and form new aerosol types like sodium nitrate (NaNO3 ), sodium sulfate (Na2 SO4 ) and internal mixtures. This transformation process is known as the “ageing of sea spray aerosol”. Hung et al. (2016)  noted an increasing trend of NaNO3  absorbance at particle diameter ≥ 1 µm due to the reaction of nitric acid with SSA. In addition, Zieger et al. (2017)  demonstrate that the hygroscopic growth of inorganic sea salt is lower than pure sea salt particles. They also observed an increase in hygroscopic growth with decreasing particle size (for particle diameters < 0.15 µm) and this increase is independent of the particle generation method. According to previous studies, the hygroscopicity and optical properties of aged SSA depend on the changes in chemical composition, mixing state and particle size of SSA before and after ageing (Carrico et al., 2003; Randles et al., 2004; Bougiatioti et al., 2011; Schill et al., 2015; Rosati et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the aged aerosols often have distinctly different properties and will lead to unpredictable impacts on cloud droplets, cloud albedo and amount of rainfall. In addition to understanding aerosol properties, aerosol transport is critical to determining the impact of atmospheric emissions and improving meteorological models. Pollutants, bacteria and nutrients can be transported through the atmosphere over large distances across the globe (e.g., Lindqvist et al., 1991; Artaxo et al., 1994; Maki et al., 2019 ). Braun et al. (2020)  evaluated the influences of local and long-range transport of aerosol to the Philippines during monsoon seasons under various synoptic- and local-scale conditions. They found that the events affected by biomass burning transport had the highest level of water-soluble organic acids, while the events affected by long-range transport from continental East Asia showed high contributions of oxalate to the organic aerosol. Besides, the high-aerosol-loading events had smaller precipitation accumulation than low-aerosol events. Some other Asian studies also indicated that air pollution from China can impact regional weather systems and coupled with convective systems downstream through long-range transport, which intensifies mid-latitude storm tracks and further influence global circulation (Zhang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014 ). Chen et al. (2016)  demonstrated the atmospheric transport of SSA from the North Sea to central Europe in detail. They found the influences of SSA indirect effect on nitrate particles can extend to a broader region reaching as far as 400 km from the coast through the “aloft bridge” transport mechanism. Furthermore, previous UK studies suggested that some high pollution episodes are associated with easterly winds and a significant proportion of pollution originated from industrialised parts of continental Europe (King and Dorling, 1997; Stedman, 1998; Buchanan et al., 2002 ). Because of the large import of inorganic aerosol (OIN) components from mainland Europe, a substantial part of the UK, particularly the south and southeast, is close to or exceeds annual mean limit values (Vieno et al., 2014 ). Thus, when assessing the impact of aerosols on regional rainfall simulations, it is important to consider not only local aerosols but also externally transported aerosols, especially for some areas with low local anthropogenic emissions. The influence of aerosol direct and indirect effects has significant seasonal differentiation, which has been highlighted in many meteorological studies. Schultze and Rockel (2018)  found a distinct reduction of solar irradiance in long-term aerosol-including simulations over Europe and this reduction is strongest in summer. At the same time, cloud water and ice content decreased over central Europe in summer, reinforcing aerosol absorption and enhancing vertical warming. Another European aerosol study shows that the “Black Triangle” area had obvious changes in both total and light precipitation frequency for directions at which sulphate trends were largest. This trend was also most significant in the summer season (Stjern et al., 2011 ). In some cases, the seasonality of aerosol impacts is also linked to regional differentiation. According to Cheng et al. (2017) , the relationship between aerosol optical depth and cloud effective radius is dominated by the negative correlation over North China in winter and spring and entire China in summer, while the relationship between precipitation and cloud effective radius is dominated by the positive correlation over North China in summer and entire China in autumn. Jiang et al. (2015)  investigated the seasonality in anthropogenic aerosol distributions and their effects on clouds and precipitation in East Asia. They summarized that the climate response to anthropogenic aerosols is shown as a northward shift of reduced precipitation, resulting in spring drought in South China and summer drought in North China. In their study, the direct and indirect anthropogenic aerosol effects jointly contributed to spring drought and summer drought was mainly affected by the direct effect. Song et al. (2021)  reported a seasonal precipitation delay of 4 to 5 days during 1979–2019 over the northern tropical land and Sahel. Most of the delay was caused by decreased anthropogenic aerosols and increased greenhouse gases that produced more mister atmosphere and enhanced its lag in response to seasonal solar forcing. In particular, these seasonal delays were projected to amplify further in the future decades. While extensive research has been conducted on the broad-scale impacts of aerosols on global climate and long-term weather patterns, in-depth investigations into the variability of short-lived extreme rainfall events under different conditions remain deficient. Particularly, studies that evaluate the combined impacts of aerosols and seasonal factors on the accuracy of extreme event simulations are limited. Furthermore, a key focus of this study is to compare the performances of the numerical weather prediction (NWP) model with and without aerosol inputs. It tried to figure out whether simulations incorporating aerosol chemistry consistently outperform those based simply on meteorological inputs and under what circumstances this is the case. Given the significant increase in computational demands when including chemical inputs, it is important to understand whether these costs are worthwhile and where shortcomings remain. These knowledge gaps will be filled by conducting a comprehensive analysis of how aerosol properties (mainly particle size and chemical component), transport pathways, and seasonal variations influence the accuracy of WRF-Chem extreme rainfall simulations. In this study, 4-month simulations with aerosol direct and indirect effects and 4-month simulations without aerosol effects over the UK and Ireland were evaluated.
