These variables provide insights into the intensity of the fluctuations and their impact on the basin's water volume, respectively. The boxplot can convey the level, spread, and symmetry of a distribution of data values. The analysis reveals seasonal variations in the amplitude of diurnal fluctuation, with higher variability observed during the summer and autumn months (July to November) in contrast to spring and winter. In particular, the amplitude in August exhibits the most significant variability. The median amplitude consistently falls within the range of 0.5–1.0 L/s in all months, except for August, where it slightly surpasses this range. From December to June of the following year, the discharge at XEW remains relatively stable. In February, the influence of snow and ice melting contributes to slightly elevated flow, resulting in a notably lower mean relative amplitude of approximately 0.21. In contrast, during the other months, when discharge at XEW is lower, diurnal fluctuation constitutes a more significant proportion of the total flow, resulting in a mean relative amplitude exceeding 0.36. This indicates a potential bias of 0.36 in selecting inappropriate moments for discharge measurements as the mean daily discharge during this period. In other research, this varies widely from over 0.1 up to 0.5 (Constantz et al., 1994; Deutscher et al., 2016; Graham et al., 2013; Lundquist & Cayan, 2002 ), which is consistent with the values of our study. While the diurnal fluctuation characteristics of each basin correlate with climatic or geographic variations on interannual timescales, we do not find the presence of universal correlations that link characteristics of a basin to the diurnal cycle. With the onset of the rainy season in July, abundant precipitation leads to increased total flow, subsequently causing a reduction in the relative amplitude of diurnal fluctuations in discharge. A r     reaches its minimum in August and September, with a mean monthly A r     of around 0.1. Notably, this observation aligns with the findings from Lundquist and Cayan's study (Lundquist & Cayan, 2002 ) on streamflow diurnal fluctuations in the western US. They similarly noted a smaller A r     during July and September, while May exhibited higher A r    . However, it is crucial to note a distinction: in February, corresponding to the snowmelt period, the A r     is significantly larger than in May in their research, whereas in our study, the opposite holds true. This discrepancy arises from the fact that A r     is determined by both absolute amplitude and daily mean discharge (Eq. (2) , and the varying snowmelt processes in watersheds with different characteristics impact these two variables differently. To comprehensively understand the intra-annual variation in streamflow diurnal fluctuation characteristics, we analyzed 10-minute discharge data from all PFPs monitored at XEW between August 2014 and December 2023. Employing a 90-minute sliding window average to this dataset, we identify two distinct fluctuation patterns, in terms of the time of hydrograph peaks and troughs occurrence, during the PFP between the rainy and dry seasons (see Table 1  ). Fluctuations during the rainy season (June to September) are characterized by nighttime peaks and midday troughs, while fluctuations during the dry season (October to May) exhibit afternoon peaks and morning troughs. This distinction suggests that when high-frequency discharge monitoring is challenging, observation timing can be optimized based on the season to reduce bias due to fluctuations. In specific, discharge measurement at 4:00 or 16:00 is close to the daily mean value in rainy seasons, while measurement at 9:00 or 20:00 is close to the daily mean value in dry seasons. Furthermore, the varying fluctuation characteristics between rainy and dry seasons hint at the possibility of distinct driving mechanisms. Preliminary analysis of diurnal fluctuations in dry-season flows suggests that snowmelt may serve as the driving factor. However, the previous observations at XEW provide limited data on snow accumulation and snowmelt processes in dry seasons compared to rainy seasons with more systematic and comprehensive observations. Consequently, further analyses focus on the rainy seasons. We conducted an examination of discharge data from the years 2015, 2016 and 2020–2023, during which high-quality observation data was available for the rainy season, to analyze the annual variation of diurnal fluctuation characteristics. The results indicate that the streamflow fluctuation amplitude A    (as shown in Fig. 5  a) remains relatively consistent, averaging around 1 L/s, except for 2021 and 2023, which shows a significant increase. Since streamflow during PFP is primarily replenished by groundwater, higher discharge indicates elevated groundwater levels. Consequently, the fluctuation driving signal is more significant when the groundwater level is closer to the surface. Comparison between Fig. 5 a and b reveals a notable pattern: basically, a higher value of A r     is recorded in the year that concurrently experiences lower Q m    . This finding emphasizes the significant impact of discharge fluctuation, particularly in years with lower discharge. Notably, the distinct fluctuation pattern observed in 2023 is likely driven by the unique hydrological processes of the year, characterized by consistently low base flow conditions punctuated by a single, extreme storm (July 31) that generated significant runoff.  3.2 Driving mechanisms of diurnal fluctuations in rainy seasons We conducted a comprehensive analysis to explore the driving mechanisms behind streamflow diurnal fluctuations during the period of June 11–13, 2021. During this period, stream discharge exhibits typical streamflow fluctuations pattern during rainy seasons, with nighttime peaks and midday troughs. The analysis focuses on two soil moisture profiles and four groundwater observation boreholes at different locations. Specifically, GW2-3 and GW1-3 are located on the hillslope, while GW2-2 and GW3-1 are located in the riparian zone. Unlike soil volumetric water content (VWC), groundwater level (GWL) exhibits a significant decline during the recession period. This notable decline poses challenges in accurately identifying the diurnal GWL fluctuation pattern. Therefore, we detrend GWL fluctuations for further analysis. Soil moisture (Fig. 6  a and b) exhibits an overall decreasing trend throughout the study period for hillslopes, accompanied by daily-scale cyclic fluctuations. Conversely, soil moisture in riparian zones exhibits cyclic fluctuations at all depths and no significant decreasing trend at all depths, except for the 0 ∼ 10 cm layer. The periodicity of soil moisture fluctuations from 0 to 60 cm in both riparian zones and hillslopes is pronounced, characterized by daytime decrease and nighttime increase. Groundwater level (Fig. 6 c) fluctuates diurnally at all four locations, with relatively similar fluctuation amplitudes. However, the phases of GWL fluctuation vary among locations, with riparian zones (represented by GW2-2 and GW3-1) and hillslopes (represented by GW2-3 and GW1-3) exhibiting in-phase fluctuations, respectively. The fluctuations in the hillslope lag behind those in riparian zones, which aligns with VWC, by approximately 6–9 h. Previous studies have also reported that in areas lacking vegetation cover or with significant groundwater depths, diurnal signals may be absent, as observed in the GWL of hillslopes measured by Tsang et al. (2014) . Based on existing research findings, potential driving factors such as snow and ice melting rate, aquifer hydraulic conductivity, and evapotranspiration rate are considered to induce streamflow diurnal fluctuations at XEW. Observations from the highest meteorological station (1100 m above sea level) indicate the absence of snow during rainy seasons (June to September). Taking into account the trend, magnitude, and peak occurrence time of streamflow fluctuations during PFP, we hypothesize that the possible drivers of diurnal fluctuations during this rainy season period are diurnal fluctuations in evapotranspiration rate and aquifer hydraulic conductivity. As depicted in Fig. 6 d, both variables exhibit noticeable daily-scale periodicity. To quantitatively assess the relative contributions of evapotranspiration rate (E) and aquifer hydraulic conductivity (K) to dominant streamflow diurnal fluctuations, we developed a one-dimensional flow equation (Eq. (5) ) for GWL in the riparian zone along the hillslope-channel direction. The change in groundwater storage can be converted into a change in GWL by the specific yield (S y    ). The applicability of the S y     calculation of Eq. (7)  needs to be discussed beforehand. It is important to note that due to the low initial water content and significant infiltration capacity of the soil, no surface runoff occurred during rainfall event. Fast groundwater movement allows for the neglect of evapotranspiration. Therefore, Eq. (7)  is applicable for calculating S y    . We selected 2021 and 2023 as the simulation years because of the significantly different diurnal fluctuation patterns in 2021 and 2023 (Fig. 5 ). The simulation results regarding groundwater levels in the riparian zone reveal noteworthy insights. The model driven by measured K    and E    in Scenario 1 gives an impressive simulation of the GW3-1 fluctuations of June 11–13, 2021, with a Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) value of 0.945 (Fig. 7  a). This suggests that, during PFPs in rainy seasons, the diurnal fluctuations at XEW can be predominantly attributed to the diurnal variations in K    and E   . Scenario 2, which employs K m     in combination with E ( T )   , still manages to accurately capture the GWL fluctuation trend, with an NSE value of 0.865. In contrast, Scenario 3, driven by K ( T )    and E m    , falls short in effectively simulating the fluctuation trend of GWL (NSE = 80.313). This result strongly implies that, within the riparian zone of the XEW, evapotranspiration is the dominant factor influencing GWL fluctuations, while the contribution of aquifer hydraulic conductivity appears relatively insignificant. It is evident that the model's performance is generally less precise in GW2-2 (Fig. 7 b) when compared to GW3-1. Nevertheless, it is still evident that Scenario 3 fails to accurately reproduce the fluctuation trend in GWL. The simulation results for 2023 indicated suboptimal performance, particularly concerning the groundwater level recorded on the evening of June 13 at GW2-2. This discrepancy is likely attributed to the distinctive climate of 2023, marked by a particularly dry period with minimal rainfall (53 mm) between March 1 and June 10 (prior to the study period). These conditions introduce complexities in the water transport process, making it challenging to accurately capture it using the simplified one-dimensional model. Nevertheless, the overall results remained consistent with those observed in 2021, suggesting that evapotranspiration is the primary driving factor despite the anomalous climatic conditions. To better understand the amplitude of diurnal fluctuations at XEW, we conducted a comprehensive review of fluctuations primarily driven by evapotranspiration during rainy seasons (see Table 2  ). Runoff depth is utilized here to eliminate the effect of watershed size. The finding reveals a weak correlation between basin size and runoff depth fluctuation amplitude during PFPs within rainy seasons. In essence, smaller basins tend to exhibit larger fluctuations and a broader amplitude range. This phenomenon may be attributed to the typically more extended stream channels in larger basins, which leads to significant variations in the time required for streamflow fluctuation signals to propagate to gauging stations. Consequently, this phenomenon diminishes fluctuations to a certain extent. Additionally, it underscores the regulating role of groundwater reservoirs in large basins.  3.3 Propagation of fluctuation signal along hillslope-riparian-stream pathway The analysis in section 2.2  has identified the evapotranspiration rate as the primary driver of diurnal fluctuations in streamflow within XEW. However, it remains uncertain where these evapotranspiration rate fluctuations signals originate and how they propagate throughout the watershed. We aim to address this question through further analysis. Previous research has indicated the existence of a time lag between the occurrence of daily maximum evapotranspiration and minimum discharge. This lag is determined by the propagation time of fluctuating signals from the “contributing sources” to the “stream gauging station”. It typically ranges from 1 to 4 h (Bond et al., 2002; Deutscher et al., 2016; Gribovszki et al., 2008; Szilágyi et al., 2008 ), depending on watershed characteristics. Steep, narrow watersheds tend to exhibit relatively fast lateral flow with short lag times, while flat, vast watersheds induce slower flow with longer lag times (Troxell, 1936 ). In specific watersheds, one perspective posits that the timing of trough discharge remains relatively constant across seasons (Lundquist & Cayan, 2002 ). This stability arises from the proximity of the contributing sources within small watersheds to the stream gauging stations, resulting in minimal variations in transport time caused by changes in lateral flow velocities. Another perspective suggests that, as soil gradually dries out during recession periods, lateral flow transitions to slower pathways, resulting in increased lag times (Bond et al., 2002 ). This study employed cross-correlation analysis to investigate the time lag between the daily maximum evapotranspiration rate and minimum discharge during each PFP to aid explicate the propagation path of evapotranspiration fluctuation signals at XEW. The approach involves testing different time lags (t lag     ) ranging from 0 to 12 h and calculating the correlation coefficient (r   ) under each t lag      using Eq. (11) . The t lag      at which the correlation coefficient reaches its minimum value represents the time lag between daily maximum evapotranspiration rate and minimum discharge. The study focused on six 3-day PFPs at XEW during the rainy seasons of 2020 and 2021, specifically: August 27–29, September 7–9, September 25–27 of 2020, and June 11–13, August 20–22, September 21–23 of 2021. Fig. 8   illustrates the phase relationship between evapotranspiration rate and discharge during these periods. Notably, the analysis consistently finds a 0-hour time lag between the daily maximum evapotranspiration rate and minimum discharge for all six PFPs. This suggests two critical findings: 1) streamflow responds extremely rapidly to evapotranspiration, as evident in Fig. 6 c, and 2) this rapid response remains consistent over time. It implies that the primary area contributing to streamflow diurnal fluctuations is the riparian zone, which discharges the stream swiftly. On a spatial scale of 4.22 km2  within XEW, we conclude that the response time of streamflow to basin-wide groundwater is less than one day, ensuring no overlap of curves due to a time lag exceeding one periodicity (e.g., 25 h and 1 h). It is essential to highlight that in scenarios where evapotranspiration rate dominates the diurnal discharge fluctuation, previous research has suggested that groundwater and streamflow respond to evapotranspiration almost simultaneously and fluctuate in the same phase, see references (Chen, 2007; Gribovszki et al., 2008; Szilágyi et al., 2008 ). However, our study uncovers a different behavior. When the evapotranspiration rate reaches its daily peak, discharge reaches its minimum, while the groundwater levels decline continuously (Fig. 6 c and d). This divergence occurs because the diurnal cycle of evapotranspiration has distinct effects on streamflow and groundwater. Specifically, fluctuations in evapotranspiration directly impact discharge, whereas they influence the rate of change in groundwater level (storage). Consequently, this study concludes that groundwater and streamflow exhibit distinct response mechanisms to evapotranspiration rate changes. Their response patterns to evapotranspiration rate fluctuations cannot be deduced solely based on the shape of the groundwater hydrograph and their extreme points. When interpreting the fluctuations in soil moisture and groundwater level presented in Fig. 6  in the context of our earlier conclusions, we can illustrate the water transport process during PFPs in rainy seasons. During the daytime (Fig. 9  a), groundwater E RG      and soil water E RS      in the riparian zone, along with soil water in the hillslope E HS     , with higher hydraulic connectivity to vegetation roots (Harmon et al., 2020 ), directly contribute to evapotranspiration, leading to local water storage reduction in this zone. This, in turn, impacts groundwater discharge from the riparian zone to the channel, causing a continuous decrease in streamflow. Meanwhile, due to the deeper location of groundwater in the hillslope, there is a lag in the decline of groundwater levels in this area. During the nighttime (Fig. 9 b), when the evapotranspiration rate decreases to zero, groundwater from the hillslope replenishes the upper or adjacent soil water due to matrix potential, leading to a gradual recovery of soil moisture and groundwater level in the riparian zone and soil moisture in the hillslopes. The discharge increases and reaches its peak due to receiving additional recharge. Therefore, these fluctuations are determined by the relative magnitudes of point-scale hydraulic gradients induced by riparian vegetation uptake (upward) and hillslope-scale hydraulic gradients caused by gravity (downslope), which has been simulated by Szilágyi et al. (2008) . Importantly, when the depth of groundwater in the riparian zone is shallower, the streamflow fluctuation induced by evapotranspiration becomes more pronounced. Evapotranspiration-induced fluctuation signals are transmitted across the riparian zone, ultimately affecting the streamflow at XEW. Previous research indicates that diurnal fluctuations due to hydraulic conductivity or evapotranspiration are typically observed in small headwater basins outside of the melting seasons. We further propose that evapotranspiration can induce diurnal fluctuations in the streamflow of adjacent reaches, even in large-scale basins. The primary distinction among basins of varying scales lies in the transmit time required for the fluctuation signal to reach the streamflow gauge. In large basins with extensive channel networks, the transmit time can vary considerably, leading to the superposition of fluctuation signals with different phases and, consequently, the attenuation of streamflow fluctuations at the gauge station. In basins with sparse vegetation, temperature-induced changes in hydraulic conductivity may be the primary cause of diurnal fluctuations. Thus, vegetation cover in the riparian zone may be the critical factor determining the driving mechanism of these fluctuations.  3.4 Evapotranspiration measurement uncertainties The evapotranspiration rate in this study is determined using the EC method, which follows well-established standard procedures and provides relatively accurate estimates (Heusinger & Weber, 2017 ). A previous study by Tie et al. (2018) achieved ideal energy balance closures, indicating the EC method's applicability and reliability in XEW. Moreover, the study highlighted the method's robust capability to track evapotranspiration trends on both daily and hourly scales. In our simulation, the trend in evapotranspiration is more important than its absolute value due to the presence of model parameters. Therefore, we believe the existing data are sufficiently reliable to achieve our aim of identifying whether evapotranspiration or hydraulic conductivity is the dominant driving factor for diurnal fluctuations. Furthermore, Tie et al. (2018)  compared evapotranspiration based on EC systems at 15 m and 30 m heights and found excellent consistency between the results, suggesting that the distribution of different types of woodland in the XEW is relatively uniform. Thus, the EC method can provide evapotranspiration values representative of the entire watershed. This lays the foundation for the spatial scale comparability required for applying watershed-scale evapotranspiration to the riparian zone in subsequent research.   4 Conclusion This study focused on the Xitaizi Experimental Watershed, located in a semi-humid monsoon mountainous region in North China Plain. It aims to investigate diurnal fluctuations in discharge and shallow groundwater levels and identify their characteristics, driving mechanisms, and signal propagation along hillslope-riparian-stream pathway based on years of observation. The primary findings are as follows:1. Streamflow exhibits diurnal fluctuation during rainless periods throughout the year, with variations up to 36 % of the daily mean and distinct patterns in rainy (peak at night) and dry seasons (peak in the afternoon), offering valuable insights for discharge measurement in similar hydrogeological conditions to minimize bias attributable to fluctuations  2. In rainy seasons, the impact of discharge fluctuation is significant, particularly in years with lower mean discharge. Meanwhile, groundwater levels in the riparian zone and soil moisture content in both the riparian zone and hillslope decline during the day and recover at night. In contrast, the groundwater level in the hillslope fluctuates, lagging by 6 ∼ 9 h. These fluctuations are primarily attributed to evapotranspiration, while the impact of hydraulic conductivity fluctuation on a time scale of several days is insignificant to the flow process. As such, it is suggested that variables such as aquifer hydraulic conductivity and specific yield can be estimated using the relatively easy-to-observe variables  3. The constantly rapid response of discharge to evapotranspiration rates in rainy seasons of XEW is primarily contributed by the riparian zone. Fluctuations in groundwater levels in the riparian zone impact its contribution to streamflow and, in turn, lateral recharge from upslope areas. This finding reveals critical water transport pathways within the watershed during PFPs in rainy seasons
1 Introduction Due to geological processes and tectonic actions, bedrock fractures are ubiquitous in nature. Since permeability is much larger than the surrounding matrix, rock fractures (or fracture networks) are the main channels for the transport of substances (e.g., fluid, solute, and gas) (Xing et al., 2021a). Therefore, fluid flow in fractured media has become an important topic in hydrological groundwater and geophysics, with applications in geothermal resource extraction, nuclear waste treatment, the storage of CO2,  and oil or gas exploration (Berkowitz et al., 1994; Qian et al., 2015; Xing et al., 2021b ; Zou et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2023 ). However, the description of seepage in fracture networks has remained a challenge because of the heterogeneity and spatial–temporal variability of fracture media (Berkowitz et al., 2002). Flow behavior in fractured rock mass has been studied in depth using modeling techniques of discrete fracture networks (DFNs) (Miao et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018 ). Modeling flow and transport by DFN approach is known to be more accurate due to incorporation of the detailed fracture network structure over continuum-based methods (Karra et al., 2018 ). Significant advances have been made in DFN simulation capabilities in recent years, and the simulation of large explicit fracture networks containing detailed structures with high accuracy is now possible. However, capturing the flow and transport over such large scales remains computationally intractable. To reduce the burden, DFNs can always be decomposed into a combination of multiple single fracture sections and intersections regardless complexity. However, the flow characteristics obtained for a single fracture are not suitable for the case of fracture intersections, especially when considering flow nonlinearity (Xiong et al., 2020 ). Therefore, a thorough understanding of the fluid flow and distribution at fracture intersections is important to accurately predict fluid infiltration and contaminant transport in DFNs. Numerous laboratory experiments (Wilson & Witherspoon, 1976; Tian, 1986; Liu et al., 2016b ) and numerical simulations (Zou et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2023b ) have been conducted to investigate the flow behavior at the intersection from 2D (Li et al., 2016 ) or 3D (Zafarani & Detwiler, 2013; Li et al., 2024 ) perspectives. Two-inlet-two-outlet cross-fracture (Johnson & Brown, 2001; Karimzade et al., 2023 ) and one-inlet-two-outlet furcating-fracture (Fan et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023b ) have been the focus of past research. In those fractures, fluid flow converges and deflects at fracture intersections (Huang et al., 2019 ). Thus, the flow properties of surrounding fracture branches are dramatically affected by fracture intersections (Karimzade et al., 2023 ), like flow regime variability (the transition from linear to nonlinear flow) and flow redistribution (Liu et al., 2022 ). Studies on the flow behavior at intersections of cross-fracture have mainly focused on the local head loss, flow nonlinearity, and hydraulic characteristics (Li et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016a; Xiong et al., 2020 ). Unlike the regular single fracture, the geometry of the intersection is sharply varied, resulting in a non-negligible local head loss in addition to frictional head loss (Hu et al., 2005 ). Besides, the irregular geometry of the intersection also enhances the inertial effect causing the nonlinear flow (Kosakowski & Berkowitz, 1999 ). Moreover, the interplay between the hydraulic characteristics of flow and geometric characteristics of fracture induces an intriguing competition between viscous and inertial effects, which consequently affects flow behaviors in fracture intersection (Wood et al., 2005 ). This interplay causes the spatial and temporal flow characteristics to be remarkable modified by the fracture intersection, leading to flow redistribution. Once the distribution law of various intersections is quantified, a physically known model of large-scale fracture networks can be established (Yang et al., 2019 ). Philip (1988)  discussed the applicability of proportional routing at fracture junctions and established solutions for arbitrary discharge patterns through four-way coplanar junctions: exact solutions for Laplace flows (Hele-Shaw flows and Darcy flows (fractures filled with porous material)) and approximate solutions for Stokes flows. However, the effect of geometry at the intersection is not considered in the solution. Numerous published studies have demonstrated that flow distribution at intersections is significantly affected by hydraulic and geometric properties e.g., aperture, Reynolds number (Xiong et al., 2020 ), hydraulic gradient (Li et al., 2016 ), angle (Fan et al., 2019 ), and roughness (Li et al., 2022 ), etc. Parameters commonly used to describe flow redistribution in those studies can be broadly classified into two categories: (1) ε  = q1  /q2  , where q1   and q2   are the flow rates of the two outlets, and the meaning of ε  is the ratio of the two outlet flow rates (Fan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022 ); (2) Ra   = q1  /(q1   + q2  ), the meaning of Ra   is the ratio of the individual outlet flow rate to the total flow rate (Li et al., 2016 ; Liu et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2023a). Nevertheless, both ε  and Ra   have the following limitations: 1) they are valid only when the inlet flow rates are the same, 2) only reflect the results of the flow distribution at the outlet, and 3) cannot describe the process of the flow distribution at the intersection. Most of the previous work on fracture intersections has focused on the result of flow redistribution at the outlet. Much less attention has been paid to quantifying the dynamic partitioning of water at the intersection. Tian (1986)  found the phenomenon of deflection flow at the intersections in fracture with unequal aperture based on a cross-fracture model employing satisfies specific parameters (e.g., angle, aperture, and inlet/outlet head difference of inlet and outlet), which leading to certain limitations in the identification of deflection flow. Whether the conclusions apply to flows in fractures with different geometric and hydraulic characteristics, which are more common in underground rocks, is unclear. Therefore the traditional theory of deflection flow needs to be further develop. There is an urgent need to address the following issues: (1) Characterize the deflection flow and elucidate its mechanism; (2) Determine the impact factors of deflection flow and quantify the relationship between them; (3) Reveal the conditions that limit the occurrence of deflection flow. In this study, we focus on the deflection flow at the intersection of cross fractures and aim to answer the questions above. Based on solving NSE, the flow behavior at the intersection with varying hydraulic and geometric characteristics, is systematically investigated by numerical simulations. Previous experimental results were utilised to validate the numerical model. The results can provide new insights into the flow through a fracture intersection.The results from this study may provide new insights into the flow through a fracture intersection and contribute physical constraints on construction of flow models based on discrete fracture networks.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Theoretical background For isothermal, steady-state in-compressible Newtonian fluid in a single fracture, the governing equations are the Navier–Stokes equations (NSE) derived from Newton’s second law, which represent mass and momentum conservation, and the equations are expressed:(Neuville et al., 2013; Rong et al., 2020 )(1) ∇ P = μ ∇  2  u  - ρ u  ∙ ∇   u      (2) ∇ ∙ u  = 0      where ρ (kg/m3 ) is the fluid density, u  (m/s) is the velocity of flow, P (Pa) is the pressure, and μ  (Pa·s) is the viscosity coefficient. COMSOL had been proven to possess superior reliability in computational fluid dynamics and had been widely employed for groundwater simulations due to its visualization and high efficiency (Cardenas et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2015 ). 2D regular cross fractures rather than three-dimensional fractures were used as geometric inputs to numerical simulation for the following reasons: Firstly, an intrinsic assumption of the two-dimensional simplification was to ignore one of the principal widths (the in-plane width). Previous studies (Liu et al., 2016a ) have proven that when the width is more than 8 times the aperture, the width interference can be ignored. Since the length and width of the fracture were far greater than the aperture in this study, two-dimensional simplification was acceptable. Secondly, the 3D model is dimensionally closer to the natural cross fracture, but the modeling process is much more difficult and the solutions of 3D NSE requires significant computer resources. Many studies have shown that using 2D NSE to study fluid flow in cross fracture is reliable (Huang et al., 2023a, 2023b; Fan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Li et al., 2016 ). Moreover, the 2D physical model can be used as an ideal test case for the 3D model and provides theoretical support for further understanding of the mass transfer in complex flow fields (Lee et al., 2015 ). Finally, the aim of this study is to reexamine and extend the theory of deflection flow, where 2D models are able to intuitively reveal the mechanism of deflection flow, and not necessarily require a high degree of complexity for a cross fracture (for instance, the development of cubic law is based on a simple smooth parallel plate model). And the conclusions can be verified by more complex models in the future. Therefore, the regular 2D simplified cross fracture is sufficient for our purposes.  2.3 Simulation setup The Navier-Stokes equation was used as a governing equation to solve for the saturated flow in fractures. The meshes at the intersection were locally refined to properly represent the geometry until stable accurate results were obtained. The total number of meshes in each model was nearly 104 . When the normalized velocity and continuity residual ratios were less than 10−4 , steady-state solutions were considered to be converged. The laminar steady-state module was selected for water flow simulation. Nonslip boundary conditions were assigned to the fracture walls and wall movement is 0. Sequence type in grid settings was ‘Physical field control grid’, and grid size was set as ‘extremely refined’. ‘Solver configuration’ was set to ‘Steady-State Solver’ and ‘Algebraic Multigrid Solver (spf)’. ‘Inlet boundaries’ were set to ‘flow rate boundary conditions’ and ‘Outlet boundaries’ were considered ‘pressure boundary conditions’. The outlet flow boundaries were set at a pressure of 0 to conveniently control ΔP  and hydraulic gradient J . The models in this study were divided into three patterns as Fig. 1  shown:  (a) Pattern I: Only the angle φ  varied; (b) Pattern II: Only the inlet flow ratio n (=Q1 /Q2 ) varied; (c) Pattern III: Only the aperture ratio k (=b 2 /b 1 ) varied. The specific model parameter settings were shown in Table 1  .   3 Deflection flow at intersections 3.1 Definition of deflection flow Based on flow experiments in the cross-fracture model with planar wall, Tian (1986)  pointed out that in the cross fracture with unequal aperture, the fluid flow through the intersection can be divided into three streams respectively: (i) the stream from the narrow section across the intersection into the wide one, named α   flow; (ii) the stream from the wide section across the intersection into the narrow one, named β  flow; (iii) the stream from the wide section across the intersection into the wide section, maintain inertial flow direction. However, the definition of α , β  flow in this way contains certain limitations, i.e., it occurs in an unequal width fracture with equal pressure at the inlet. This limitation can cause inconvenience in the practical operation when the direction of deflection has to be recognized first. In order to be applicable to all cases in cross fractures, it is necessary to define α , β  flow in a generalized sense. Fig. 3    shows the generalized definition of deflection flow proposed in this study. The stream flow from section Ⅰ to section Ⅳ is called as α   flow; and the stream flow from section Ⅱ to section Ⅲ is called as β  flow (Fig. 3 (a) ). In the absence of deflection flow, there are only α , β  streams at the intersection (satisfies q α  = Q 1  = Q 4  and q β  = Q 2  = Q 3 ). When deflection flow occurs, there is a third flow in addition to the stream mentioned above, which does not deflect like α , β  stream when flowing across the intersection, but continues to flow in the inertial direction. Fig. 3 (b)  and Fig. 3 (c)  show the deflection flow in different directions.  3.2 Model validation The numerical simulation of the cross-fracture model adopted the geometrical parameters as follows: two single fractures intersecting at 45° formed a cross-fracture, the aperture, length and height of the single fracture was 2 mm, 151 mm and 42 mm respectively, and another fracture was 15 mm, 151 mm and 42 mm respectively. A certain pressure of water flows into the cross-fracture from two entrances respectively. To verify the validity of the numerical model, the simulated results were compared with experimental results from published laboratory studies (Tian, 1986 ). The numerical simulation adopted the same geometrical parameters as the experimental model. Fig. 2  shows the v-J  images of the simulated and experimental results, where vα _ S, vα  _E denote the experimental and simulated values of water velocity in the α -direction, and vβ  _E, vβ  _S show the experimental and simulated values of water velocity in the β -direction. As shown in Fig. 2 , the experimental data points vα  _E and vβ  _E fell evenly on both sides of the simulation curve, indicating a good agreement between numerical and experimental results. The hydraulic gradient in the experiment was small, thus the flow velocity and the hydraulic gradient were still linearly related, in accordance with Darcy's law (see enlarged view in Fig. 2 ). The Reynolds number range in the simulation was much larger, showing a flow nonlinearity when the flow velocity is higher. The Forchheimer equation could describe the phenomenon better. Fig. 3  shows the distribution of streamlines at progressively increasing Re . Given that the simulation model established in this study was reliable to simulate the flow in the cross fracture.  3.3 Mechanism analysis of deflection flow Energy loss occurs when the fluid flows in the cross fracture, which is manifested by the head loss. Generally, head loss includes frictional head loss and local head loss. Water flow in the fracture section due to the regular geometry, the head loss is mainly frictional head loss. When water flow enters the intersection, the local head loss is generated due to the variation of geometry (Hu et al., 2005 ). As the length of the intersection is usually small, the local head loss dominates compared to negligible frictional head losses. Since the intersection is where the deflection flow occurs, the local head loss becomes the key factor of the deflection flow effect. According to Equation 8  and Equation 14 , the frictional head loss per unit weight of fluid in the fracture section F1, F2 for α   flow can be derived as (b 1  = b 3 , b 2  = b 4  in this study)(20a) h f 1  α  = 12 μ  ρ g   ∙ L 1  b 1  3   ∙ Q 1  w      (20b) h f 2  α  = 12 μ  ρ g   ∙ L 4  b 4  3   ∙ Q 4  w       the frictional head loss per unit weight of fluid in the fracture section F1, F2 for β   flow can be derived as(21a) h f 1  β  = 12 μ  ρ g   ∙ L 2  b 2  3   ∙ Q 2  w      (21b) h f 2  β  = 12 μ  ρ g   ∙ L 3  b 3  3   ∙ Q 3  w       where h f 1  α   , h f 2  α    are the frictional head losses of α   flow in F1 and F2 sections before and after the intersection, respectively; h f 1  β   , h f 2  β    are the frictional head losses of β   flow in F1 and F2 sections before and after the intersection, respectively. The local head loss per unit weight of fluid in the α   and β   directions through the intersection is the difference between the total head loss and frictional head loss, according to Equation 11  and Equation 13  can be obtained as follows(22a) h l  α  + h f 1  α  + h f 2  α  = Δ H 4  1  + 1 2  ρ v 4  2  - v 1  2        (22b) h l  β  + h f 1  β  + h f 2  β  = Δ H 3  2  + 1 2  ρ v 3  2  - v 2  2         where h l  α   , h l  β    are the local head loss in α   and β   direction respectively, Δ H 4  1     is the measured head difference between inlet Ⅰ and outlet Ⅳ, Δ H 3  2     is the measured head difference between inlet Ⅱ and outlet Ⅲ; v 1  , v 2  , v 3  , v 4     are the flow velocity of each inlet and outlet respectively. The specimens used in this study satisfy the following conditions (Fig. 1 )(23a) e 1  = b  1   = b  3      (23b) e 2  = b  2   = b  4      (23c) L = L 1  = L 2  = L 3  = L 4      (23d) Q 1  + Q 2  = Q 3  + Q 4       Substituting Equations (20) , (21) , and (23)  into Equation (22) , the results are obtained as follows:(24a) h l  α  = J 4  1  ∙ 2 L - 12 μ L  ρ g w   ∙ Q 1  e 1  3   + Q 4  e 2  3         (24b) h l  β  = J 3  2  ∙ 2 L - 12 μ L  ρ g w   ∙ Q 2  e 2  3   + Q 3  e 1  3         Δ h l  = h l  α  - h l  β  = 2 L J 4  1  - J 3  2    + 12 μ  ρ g w   1 e 2  3   + 1 e 1  3     Q 3  - Q 1          (24c) = 2 L J 4  1  - J 3  2    + 12 μ  ρ g w   1 e 2  3   + 1 e 1  3     Q 2  - Q 4           Δ h l     is the total local resistance head loss per unit weight of fluid at the fracture intersection. When the head difference between the two outlets and the inlet is controlled to be the same, i.e. J 4  1  = J 3  2    , there is Δ h l  ∝ Q 3  - Q 1      . According to Equation 24c , when Δ h l  ≥ 0   , corresponding to q β  > q α    , the fluid per unit weight is subject to greater local resistance in the α   direction, and the flow is deflected in the β   direction; conversely, the flow is deflected in the α   direction; when Δ h l  = 0   , corresponding to q β  = q α    , the local resistance in the direction of α   and β   is the same, and the deflection flow does not occur. In the universal case, whenever the total local resistance head loss per unit weight of fluid exists (Δ h l     ≠ 0), it must lead to a difference between flow rate of the inlet and outlet in the same fracture section (Q 1  ≠ Q 3  or Q 2  ≠ Q 4 ), implying the presence of deflection flow. In other words, the unequal local resistance at the intersection is the fundamental reason for the occurrence of deflection flow. Combined with the simulation results, the mechanism of the deflection flow effect can be further elaborated. As Fig. 4   shown, when the fluid flows through an intersection in the cross fracture, the cross-section area is enlarged compared with the single fracture section, and the variation of the geometry shape leads to the difference in local resistance. The flow will be more difficult to flow in the direction of high resistance, such as the β   direction in Fig. 4 . This difference in resistance leads to an imbalance in energy distribution, which is intuitively reflected in the flow velocity field. It is clear that a region of low flow velocity exists in the outlet section near the lower wall (the dotted red part). The low-velocity zone acts as a barrier to significantly narrow the flow cross-section area, resulting in a decrease in the permeability of this flow channel, further exacerbating the difficulty of fluid at intersection flow into this outlet section. Therefore, the fluid tends towards another flow channel with less resistance, leading to the occurrence of deflection flow.  3.4 Characterization of deflection flow The deflection flow does not deflect to α  or β  direction as it passes through the intersection but keeps the flow original. In order to quantify the deflection flow, the parameter X  φ    is proposed, which represents the intensity of the deflection flow in the cross fracture with the intersection angle φ :(25) X  φ  = Q 4  - Q 3    - Q 1  - Q 2     Q 1  + Q 2         where X  φ    implies the ratio of the difference value between the difference of two outlet flow rates and the difference of the two inlet flow rates to the total flow rate. For the sake of discussion, it is artificially specified that Q1   ≥ Q2  . The positive and negative values of X  φ    reflect the direction and the absolute value reflects the magnitude of the deflection flow. 3.4.1 Magnitude of deflection flow Denote n = Q 1  / Q 2    , according to Equation 25 , the range of X  φ    can be determined as follows:X  φ    = Q 4  - Q 3    - Q 1  - Q 2     Q 1  + Q 2      ≤ - Q 3  - Q 1  - Q 2     Q 1  + Q 2          ⇒ Q 4  = 0   - Q 1  + Q 2    - Q 1  - Q 2     Q 1  + Q 2      = 2 Q 1   Q 1  + Q 2    = 2 1 + 1 n    < 2      thus, the range of X  φ    is - 2 < X  φ  < 2   . The hydraulic pressure at the intersection is noted as P0  (Fig. 1 ), according to Equation 4  and Equation 5  can be obtained as follows:(26) Q i  = g b 1  3   12 γ   p i  - p 0    L i   ( i = 1 , 2  , 3 , 4  )       Because of the conservation of mass, substituting Equation 26  into Equation 23d  leads to:(27) P 0  = ∑ i = 1  4  P i  b i  3   L i    ∑ i = 1  4  b i  3  L i          Because of Equation 23 , there is k = b 2  / b 1  = e 2  / e 1    , Denote k = e 2  / e 1    , substituting Equation 26  into Equation 25  leads to:(28) X  φ  = k  3  P 0  - P 4    - k  3  n - 1   P 2  - P 0    - P 0  - P 3     k  3  n + 1   P 2  - P 0           Equation 28  can also be written in the following form:(29) X  φ  = C 1  + 2  n + 1   - C 2  k  3  n + 1     - 1       Where(29a) C 1  = P 0  - P 4   P 2  - P 0    = J 4  0  J 0  2       (29b) C 2  = P 0  - P 3   P 2  - P 0    = J 3  0  J 0  2        J 3  0    are the hydraulic gradients between the intersection and outlet III, J 4  0    are hydraulic between the intersection and outlet IV, and J 0  2    are the hydraulic gradients between the inlet II and the intersection.  3.4.2 Direction of deflection flow The positive and negative signs of X  φ    reflect the direction of the deflection flow, as follows: (a) WhenX  φ    < 0, all the fluid in section II flows into section III, while parts of the fluid flow in section I flow to section IV, and the remaining replenishes section III, and the direction of deflection flow is F1 (Fig. 3 (a) ). (b) WhenX  φ    = 0, all the fluid flow in section I flow to section IV, and all the fluid in section II flow into section III, that is, Q 1  = Q 4    , Q 2  = Q 3    , the deflection flow does not occur (Fig. 3 (b) ). (c) WhenX  φ    > 0, all the fluid in section I flow into section IV, while parts of the fluid flow in section II flow to section III, and the remaining replenishes section IV, and the direction of deflection flow is F2 (Fig. 3 (b) ). It should be noted thatX  φ    < 0 is also divided into the following two cases: (1) Q 4  > Q 3    , when the deflection flow occurs but is not obvious. (2) Q 4  < Q 3    , when the deflection flow occurs dramatically and the stream in the fracture section Ⅰ flows into the fracture section Ⅲ at the intersection. Although the parameter deflection flow intensity X  φ    is also defined by the flow at the inlet and oulet (please see Equation 25 ), which is not much different from previous mixing ratios (Philip, J.R., 1988). Compared to the parameter ε  = q1  /q2   (Fan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022 ) and Ra   = q1  /(q1   + q2  ) (Li et al., 2016 ; Liu et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2023a) which is commonly used to describe the flow redistribution at intersections, the advantage of X  φ    is that it is effective even when the inlet flow rate is different. Moreover, X  φ    reflects both the result and the process of flow distribution. The derivation of equation substitution gives X  φ    controlled by the hydraulic parameter n  and the geometric parameter k  (please see Equation 29 ). The parameter X  φ    takes into account both geometric and hydraulic properties, which is not considered in previous parameters that characterize the flow distribution at intersections.    4 Impact factors of flow behavior at intersection According to Equation 29a , the deflection flow intensity X  φ    is affected by the intersection angle φ  , the inlet flow ratio n = Q 1  / Q 2       and the aperture ratio k = e 2  / e 1      . The effects of each factor are discussed as follows. 4.1 Effect of angle φ  The simulation of Pattern Ⅰ in Table 1  was carried out, and the results of varying X  φ    with φ   are obtained as shown in Fig. 5  . The results can be divided into three cases: (1) when n   = 1 and k   = 1, the deflection flow intensity X  φ    remains 0 with increasing intersection angle φ  , and the deflection flow does not occur; (2) whenn   ≠ 1, the deflection flow intensity X  φ    increases with the increasing φ  ; (3) whenk   ≠ 1, the deflection flow intensity X  φ    decreases with the increase of φ  . The effects of φ  on X  φ    is closely related to the value of n , k , but the coupling of multiple influences is beyond the scope of this study and requires further research in the future. In addition, the gradually increasing angle φ   has a significant effect on the flow regime. As shown in Fig. 6  , as the flow velocity increases, the inertial effect increases, and more energy is needed to overcome the pressure drop caused by the inertial force. As a result, the slope of the curve increases corresponds to an increasing nonlinearity, which can be well fitted by the Forchheimer equation (Equation 10 ). And as the intersection angle φ   increases, the coefficient b   in the Forchheimer equation gradually increases, and according to Equation 10b , the nonlinear coefficient β  ′    can be obtained to increase significantly. Numerous previous studies (Xing et al., 2021b; Zhou et al., 2019 ) have demonstrated that the development of vortices is the critical factor of nonlinearity in a single fracture. This conclusion is also applicable to cross fractures. As can be seen from Fig. 7  , the vortex in the low-velocity zone gradually develops as φ  increases. The developing low-velocity zone narrows the flow path, results in an increase in flow velocity and inertia effect, ultimately enhancing flow non-linearity. The area of the low-velocity zone is gradually increasing, narrows the flow channel, and leads to an increase in flow velocity and a more significant inertial effect, which eventually result in an enhanced flow nonlinearity.  4.2 Effect of the inlet flow ratio n  The simulation of Pattern Ⅱ in Table 1  was carried out, and the obtained results were shown in Fig. 8  . There is a clear interface between the streams from two inlets (shown by the black dashed line in Fig. 8 ). Whenn   = 1, the deflection flow does not occur and the interface coincides exactly with the geometric diagonal of the intersection (Fig. 8 (a) ). Subsequently, as n   increases, the separation interface between the two streams from different inlets keeps shifting downward, and the proportion and magnitude of deflection flow keep increasing, leading to an increase in X  φ   . As shown in Fig. 8 (f) , when n → ∞   , there is Q 1  ≫ Q 2    , the inflow from segment II is negligible. At the same time, the interface is close to the inflection of the intersection, the intersection is nearly close to the inflow of segment II though connected to each other, and the hydraulic characteristics in the two-inlet-two-outlet cross fracture are close to those in the one-inlet-two-outlet bifurcating fracture. In addition, the effect of inlet flow ratio n   on the flow regime is shown in Fig. 9  . Under the condition of geometric characteristics of the cross fracture remaining constant, all data points are distributed on the same curve regardless of the variation of the inlet flow ratio n  , indicating that the nonlinear coefficient β  ′    is independent of n  . The result obtained in this study also confirms that β  ′    is related to the geometric characteristics but not to the hydraulic characteristics (Rong et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020 ). Although n   does not affect the flow regime, it has a significant effect on the flow rate at the outlet. Fig. 10   shows the variation of X  φ    with n  . Intuitively, when n > 1   , X  φ  < 0   , representing the direction of deflection flow in the F1 direction. As n   increases, the magnitude of X  φ    keeps increasing, and the growth rate of X  φ    is large at the beginning, then the growth rate gradually decreases. Finally, the curve gradually becomes flat when X  φ    tends to −1. The simulation results are fitted and the fitted curve expressions are:(30) X  φ  = 2 n + 1    - 1      The correlation coefficient R  2    is 0.996. The asymptote of the simulation result is X  φ  = 1    according to Equation 30 . Moreover, Equation 30  also exactly matches the expression of Equation 29  at k = 1   , which indicates the reliability of the simulation results.  4.3 Effect of the aperture ratio k  The simulation of Pattern III in Table 1  was carried out. Whenk   = 1, the deflection flow does not occur and the interface coincides exactly with the geometric diagonal of the intersection (see Fig. 11  (a) ). With the increase of the aperture ratio k  , X  φ    gradually increases, the interface between the two streams from different inlets is constantly moving up, and the low-velocity zone near the lower wall of section III is significantly developed, constantly compressing the flow channel. When k   is very large, the low-velocity zone will completely block section III and finally lead to the inertial stream flow from section II to section III all flow into section Ⅳ. At this time, although section Ⅲ is still connected to the intersection, the crossover is actually completely closed to it, and all the water flows into section IV. The hydraulic characteristics in the two-inlet-two-outlet cross fracture are close to those in the two-inlet-one-outlet bifurcating fracture. The aperture ratio k   also has a significant effect on the nonlinearity. As shown in Fig. 12  , the coefficient b   in the Forchheimer equation gradually decreases as k   increases. According to β  ′  ∝ b    (Equation 10b ) the nonlinear coefficient β  ′    decreases and the nonlinearity gradually diminishes. This is exactly the opposite effect of φ  . Fig. 13   shows the variation of X  φ    with k  . Intuitively, when k > 1   , X  φ  > 0   , representing the direction of deflection flow in the F2 direction. Although the direction of deflection flow is opposite to that when n   increases, the trend is very close. As k   increases, the magnitude of X  φ    keeps increasing and then slows down. Finally, the curve gradually becomes flat when X  φ    tends to 1. The simulation results are fitted and the fitted curve expressions are:(31) X  φ  = 0.97 - 1  k  3   + 1        the correlation coefficient R  2    is 0.972 indicating a favorable fitting effect. The asymptote is obtained from Equation 31  as X  φ  = 0.97   . Moreover, Equation 31  also exactly matches the expression of Equation 29  at n = 1   , thus indicating the accuracy of the simulation results.   5 Discussion 5.1 Sensitivity analysis of impact factors The more sensitive impact factors could easily cancel out the deflection flow effects caused by these with less sensitivity, which can guide the prioritization of flow control in practical applications. The focus of this study is on the deflection flow at the intersection, a sensitivity analysis of the deflection flow intensity X  φ    due to n , k ,    and φ   was performed by the Morris method with X φ    as the target index. Morris methods based on calculating the elementary effects (EE) of each parameter have been proposed and widely used to identify parameter sensitivities in multi-parameters models (Yuan et al., 2016 ). The specific principles of the Morris method are shown in the Appendix 1 . In this study, a total of three types of parameter on the output resultant deflection flow intensity Xφ  . are discussed: (i) angle φ : the sample interval is (15, 150), the number of samples is 6, and the sample takes the value φ  = 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150; (ii) the inlet flow ratio n : the sample interval is (1, 100), the number of samples is 6, and the sample takes the values n  = 1, 3, 6, 10, 50, 100; (iii) the aperture ratio k : sample interval is (1,10), sample number is 6, sample value k  = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 (Sample values of intervals do not need to be equally spaced according to the principle of the Morris method) (Yuan et al., 2016 ). The results of the Morris analysis shown in Fig. 14   were obtained: μ k  > μ n  > μ φ    , and μ k  = 0.57 , μ n  = 0.4 , μ φ  = 0.03   . The results indicated that the deflection flow is most sensitive to the aperture difference, followed by the inlet flow rate, and the angle has the least effect. In a cross fracture, the effect of the angle φ  on the deflection flow is almost negligible compared to the inlet flow ratio n  and the aperture ratio k . In studies by others, the variation in the converted deflection flow intensity X  φ    was less than 5 % when the angle φ   of the cross fracture was increased from 60° to 120° (Liu et al., 2016b ). To the best of our knowledge, not only in a single cross fracture but even in a fracture network consisting of several cross fractures, the sensitivity of the fracture angle φ  on the flow characteristics was much less than the others (Jafari & Babadagli, 2009 ).  5.2 Conditions for no deflection flow occurs Increasing both n  and k  in cross fractures results in opposite directions of deflection flow: the former deflects the stream flow in the direction of high flow rate, i.e., F1 direction, while the latter deflects the stream flow in the direction of the wide segment, i.e., F2 direction. This also implies that there is a certain flow ratio n c    in the cross fracture with a specific aperture ratio, counteracting the deflection flow effect. The results of the variation of deflection flow intensity X  φ    with the increase of inlet flow ratio n   under different aperture ratios k   were obtained as shown in Fig. 15  . In the beginning, whenk   = 1, all the data exceptn   = 1 were under X  φ  = 0   . The horizontal coordinate where the curves composed of data intersect X  φ  = 0    was recorded as the critical flow ratio n c    at the corresponding k  , and n c    satisfy the following conditions: when n < n c    , deflection flow occurs in the direction of F2; when n = n c    , no deflection flow occurs; when n > n c    , deflection flow occurs in the direction of F1. As k   increases, the curves keep moving up, and the corresponding critical flow ratio n c    also keeps increasing (see Fig. 15 ). Since X  φ    < 2    and X  φ  - n    is a monotonic function, the image of X  φ    is an asymptotic curve, and the asymptote moves up above X  φ  = 0    when k   increases to a certain value. At this time, no matter how n   increases, there is always X  φ  ≠ 0   . The limiting aperture ratio k l    is recorded as the k   corresponding to the curve asymptote beingX  φ    = 0. Based on the sensitivity analysis above, the presence of k l    results from the sensitivity of X  φ    to the difference in aperture is greater than the difference in flow rate. Fig. 16   shows the relationship between k   and the critical flow ratio n c   . n c    is significantly linearly and positively correlated with k  , which can be described by n c  = c 1  k + c 2    , where c 1   , c 2    are regression coefficients and c 1  > 0   ; k  h a s  a  r a n g e :  1 ≤ k ≤ k  l    . In the case of study, c 1   , c 2    are 16.5, −21.4 respectively, and k l  = 7   . The correlation coefficient R  2  = 0.987   , indicating a favorable fit. However, it should be noted that the conclusion satisfies the initial value settings in this study, i.e., inlet flow rate Q 2  = 1 × 10-5  m3 /s, branch aperture e 1  = 2 mm and angle φ  = 45°. This result reflects the conditions and limitations of deflection flow under the combined effect of geometric and hydraulic characteristics. It is worth noting that similar conclusions have been obtained in unsaturated flows. Yang (2019) conducted an experimental study on the flow-splitting behavior at a T-shaped intersection and found that when the two fracture segments satisfy bh   < bv   (where bh  , bv   are the apertures of the two outlet branches, respectively, bh   is the aperture of the horizontal fracture section and bv   is the aperture of the vertical fracture segment, corresponding to kl   > 1 in this study), there exists a threshold flow rate Ch   (corresponding to nc   in this study), where Ch   is a threshold flow rate below which droplets almost completely imbibe into the horizontal fracture, resulting in η  → 1 (corresponding to Xφ   = 0 in this study). However, differences in the mechanisms of flow redistribution at intersections need to be noted. In unsaturated flows, viscous forces dominate, and droplet intrusion is a contest between capillary forces and gravity, whereas in saturated flows inertial forces are not negligible and the deflection flow is a competition between resistance forces in different flow directions.   6 Conclusions In this study, the identification and quantification of deflection flow in cross fractures were demonstrated, and the factors influencing the flow behavior at intersections were analyzed in detail. The main conclusions were summarized as follows:In a cross fracture, geometric irregularities result in differential local resistance of flow at intersection. The disturbed flow field tends to flow in the direction of less resistance, ultimately leading to the occurrence of deflection flow.  An increase of φ   or a decrease of k   leads to an increase in flow nonlinearity caused by the development of low-velocity zones in the fractures, but a varying n   does not affect the flow regime due to the constant nonlinear coefficient β' .  X  φ    is affected by the inlet flow ratio n  , the aperture ratio k   and the intersection angle φ  . The effect of φ   on X  φ    is closely related to n   and k  . The relationship between n  , k   with X  φ    in this study can be expressed as X  φ  = 2 n + 1    - 1    and X  φ  = 0.97 - 1  k  3   + 1      , respectively. The results of the sensitivity analysis of the three for X  φ    are: μ k  > μ n  > μ φ    .  Increasing either n   or k   intensifies the deflection flow effect, but the directions of the induced deflection flow are reversed. A critical flow ratio n c    was found below which the deflection flow occurs in the direction of F2 and vice versa in the F1 direction. When 1 ≤ k ≤ k  l    , the conditions for no deflection flow to occur are: n c  = c 1  k + c 2     (where c 1    and c 2    are constants and c 1  > 0   ).    The deflection flow at fracture intersections affects not only the effectiveness of infiltration to recharge the groundwater but also the transport of solutes. Flow dynamics at intersections is a key factor to be considered in fracture networks modelling. The further understanding of deflection flow at intersections of cross fractures obtained in this study may provide important practical insights and constraints for constructing reduced order flow and transport models (e.g., Formaggia et al., 2014; Karra et al., 2018 ) based on graph representation of DFNs. It should be noted that numerical studies tend to be highly simplified with respect to representations of natural system, and the fracture model applied in this study is two-dimensional cross-fractures with smooth-walled. However, the geometrical features of natural fractures can be more complex and more factors need to be taken into account, such as surface roughness, fracture fillers and 3D effects, etc. Furthermore, the specific initial values used in this study, the initial values may have some impact on the results. In the future, systematic studies are needed to investigate the coupling effect of multiple factors on the deflection flow in real fractures as well as the influence of initial values.
1 Introduction Unprecedented rainfall events have become more frequent in recent times than in the past, and it might become more common in the future because of global warming. Although there is no formal definition of unprecedented rainfall events, unprecedented events can share the same definition as extreme rainfall events—events with low probability of occurrence but very high magnitude. However, unlike extreme events, historical records might not provide sufficient evidence of unprecedented rainfall events. The major difference between extreme and unprecedented events is that the number of observed unprecedented events is much lesser compared to extreme events. As a result of lack of samples, the statistical modeling of unprecedented events is further challenging compared to extreme events. Rainfall related to Hurricane Harvey (2017) in the USA or the downpour in Kerala, India (2018), that resulted in devastating floods are only two examples of unprecedented events. Former studies have reported that extreme weather events became more common across the globe in the second half of the 20th century [Knapp et al., 2008, IPCC, 2021 (a), Kent et al., 2022 ]. Among meteorological variables, extreme rainfall and extreme temperature have shown an increased likelihood of occurrence due to their direct association with anthropogenic climate change, finally impacting water resources, agriculture, and human health [Pal et al., 2000, Groisman et al., 2001, Das Bhowmik et al., 2019, IPCC, 2021 (a) ]. Nevertheless, unprecedented rainfall events are on the rise across the globe, potentially resulting from increase in the global mean temperature [Emanuel, 2017, Papalexious and Montanari, 2019 ]. The Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change Assessment report 6 (IPCC AR6) noted that the increased frequency of unprecedented events should be projected as natural climate variability, primarily because of enhanced global warming [IPCC, 2021 (a) ]. As unprecedented events emerge as the new reality, they will certainly have far-reaching socioeconomic consequences, posing a serious threat to human life and civilization. In hydrological sciences, unprecedented rainfall events are considered a risk to existing hydrologic systems, given that they have been designed to withstand historically extreme conditions. Therefore, hydrologic resilience must be studied to mitigate the impacts of unprecedented weather conditions. Diffenbough et al. (2015) noted that unprecedented hot, warm, and dry extremes have been increasing substantially in North America because of anthropogenic activities. Furthermore, Gessner et al. (2021)  found that past record-breaking hot waves may be surpassed in the future even if global warming recedes. A similar finding is also reported by Satoh et al. (2022) , who identified a high likelihood of hydrological droughts regardless of the trend in greenhouse gas emissions. Earlier research has focused on analyzing the trend, magnitude, and risks associated with extreme weather events [Meehl et al., 2000; Krishnamurthy et al., 2009 ], and modeling/ simulation of extreme events [Wilson and Toumi 2005, Serinaldi et al., 2014, Cavanaugh et al., 2015, So et al., 2015, Nerantzaki et al., 2019, Papalexiou 2022 ]. Further, significant efforts have been made over the past years to analyze unprecedented extreme events and its drivers (for example, Keellings and Ayala, 2019, Smith et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019 ); however, only a few studies have been conducted to estimate the likelihood of rare rainfall events [Webber et al. (2019), Banfi et al., (2022) , Peleg et al., 2017, Moraga et al., 2022]. Stochastic Weather Generators (SWG) are common data generation tools that synthetically produce an intended length of weather data at a specific location while preserving the historical climatology [Wilks and Wilby, 1999; IPCC, 2019 ]. Multiple studies have investigated the efficiency of conventional SWGs in replicating observed extreme events [Semenov, 2008, Furer and Katz, 2008 ]. Semenov (2008)  tested the skill of LARS-WG and found that it reproduces temperature extremes with less accuracy compared to central tendencies. Sparks et al., (2018) noted that IMAGE, a multivariate and multi-site stochastic weather generator for European weather and climate, fails to simulate daily values that exceeds the observed at grid points. Nevertheless, the development of General Circulation Models (GCMs) has largely underscored the necessity of SWGs [Taylor et al., 2014 ]. However, several studies found that GCM have limited ability in modeling extreme rainfall events, while successfully projecting shift in the mean and variability of a meteorological variable [Kharin et al., 2007, Min et al., 2011, Mishra et al., 2014 ]. Considering these aspects, the current study pursues a straightforward objective of developing a stochastic rainfall generator to simulate unprecedented rainfall events. One of the major challenges in the statistical modeling of unprecedented events is that non-stationary distribution needs to be considered for sampling these events. Non-stationarity in extreme value distribution is typically achieved by allowing the generalized extreme value distribution parameters to be a function of either the time variable or the oceanic states (e.g., Mondal and Mujumdar, 2015 ). Webber et al. (2019)  considered a diffusion-based Monte Carlo to sample the extreme tail behavior of rare mesoscale weather events. Furthermore, Banfi et al. (2022)  compared three non–/semi-parametric methods for the extrapolation of extreme quantiles to find that none of the three approaches outperformed the others. Additionally, a few former studies considered statistical physics while relying on numerical models to generate rare events [Ragone et al., 2017, Bouchet et al., 2019 ]. Former studies related to AWE-GEN-2d, a stochastic weather generator, considered factor of change method to calibrate the generator for future simulations [Peleg et al., 2017, Moraga et al., 2022] which would yield the first-order non-stationarity in simulated rainfall. In addition, major challenge in the statistical modeling of unprecedented events is related to appropriate validation, since there may either be only few data or no available data for validation. Validation of an unprecedented event generator becomes even more challenging if samples are drawn from a non-stationary distribution. Considering these aspects, the current study primary objective of the study is to develop a stochastic daily rainfall generator to yield unprecedented events, whereas two secondary objectives are as follows.1. To estimate the revised return periods of Hurricane Harvey rainfall considering the rain generated by the proposed approach.  2. To employ an unorthodox validation technique by comparing current results to that of Emanuel (2017)  since a few or no observed unprecedented rainfall records is available for Southwest Texas, United States.    The current study follows a ‘serial’ type stochastic daily rainfall generator which first generates a sequence of wet and dry days and subsequently predicts rain for a wet day [Hutchinson and Bunting (1987) ]. The proposed approach divides the observed rainfall into several segments whose transition probability is modeled as a finite state Markov Model. While the number of wet days within a partition is modelled as a Poisson counting process, the probability distribution of the amount of daily rainfall is modelled through a heavy tailed distribution. The main methodological novelty of the current study is that it adopts a weighted resampling scheme to estimate the model parameters that assists to replicate the serial dependence properties of the rainfall data on unprecedented conditions in the simulation model. The key to generating unprecedented events within a daily rainfall sequence is controlling the weight function and the tail properties, which enable the generation of daily rainfall data from a much larger class of underlying probability distribution. During validation, the study allows non-stationarity in the means and standard deviations of the monthly and annual rainfall estimates according to expected changes in the mean rainfall in the future, as suggested by the IPCC AR6 [IPCC, 2021 (a) ]. Nevertheless, the study employs the proposed methodology to estimate return periods related to the rainfall associated with Hurricane Harvey (USA, 2017). Benchmark return periods related to Hurricane Harvey are obtained from a former study [Emanuel, 2017 ], based on which a subjective comparison is performed. In the next section, data and study area used in this study are discussed. The proposed methodology is discussed in section 3 . The results are presented in Section 4 , which is followed by a summary and discussion in Section 5 .  2 Data and study area The study obtained the observed gridded daily rainfall for the period 1970–1999 from the repository of the Bureau of Reclamation [Maurer et al., 2002, Reclamation, 2014 ] for model training. This data has a spatial resolution of (0.125°×0.125°). Initially, a total of forty grid points are identified either on or near eight rain gauge stations that recorded the Hurricane Harvey rain. The historical daily rainfall records for these forty grid points have been considered to increase sample space. However, multiple overlapping grid points are identified; hence, only twenty-six non-overlapping grid points are considered for further analysis. Further, Hurricane Harvey, hit coastal Texas on the night of 25 August 2017 as a Category 4 hurricane. Massive rainfall began from the night of August 25 and continued till August 30, 2017, resulting in widespread and devastating flooding. The National Weather Service (NWS), USA, released the daily and total rainfall estimates of August 25–31, 2027 for multiple stations located in Southeast Texas, wherein catastrophic flooding was recorded in the Friendswood, Santa Fe and League city areas [Blake and Zelinsky 2018 ]. The current study selects eight stations that recorded receiving the most rainfall (details in Table 1  ). To note, daily observations for seven days may not be available for several stations in the region, even though the total rainfall information might have been reported, since the NWS receives rainfall information from multiple sources (additional details can be found at https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/supplemental/harvey_rain.xlsx ). Nevertheless, the 7-day total rainfall records are available for all eight stations considered by the study. However, in the absence of daily records, the 7-day maximum and 7-day average are assumed to be same for four out of eight stations. Due to service disruptions, rainfall estimates in Table 1  might not present the ground reality related to the highest rainfall experienced in the Friendswood area. Although, considering these four stations could results in underestimation of return periods related to hurricane Harvey, these stations have been included since the average rainfall recorded by these stations are higher than other neighboring stations. Finally, the current study uses the 7-day average and 7-day maximum daily rainfall of the eight stations for further calculation. The location of the gauge stations and grid points are presented in Fig. 1  .  3 Methodology The study primarily considers an observed dataset on the rainfall over n  consecutive days, denoted by x = x 1  , x 2  , ⋯ , x n      . The observed rainfall varies within a continuous interval [0, R] , where 0  indicates a dry day and R  is the highest rainfall amount. In significantly different rainfall conditions than the observed dataset the rainfall may vary within a superset of the observed interval [0, R],  denoted by [0, R0 ],  where R0  > R.  Moreover, the rainfall distribution may also show significantly different tail properties than the observed rainfall data distribution in such extreme situations. The goal here is to devise a probabilistic model S(θ)  which represents the distributional properties of the observed rainfall data. Further, on suitably modifying the labelling parameters θ   and generating observations from the model S(θ),  unprecedented rainfall conditions can be generated along with regular rainfall observations. Towards this, the study perturbs the parameter θ   around its estimated value θ ^    such that the simulation model incorporates such broader possibilities of unprecedented rainfall conditions. 3.1 Overall model estimation framework The current subsection1 describes the overall methodology. Whereas subsections 3.1.1 to 3.3 details the chronological steps. If a new study attempts to replicate the current study, they should follow subsections 3.1.1 to 3.3. We describe the deployment of the proposed approach for southeast Texas in subsection 3.4. The rainfall amount and occurrence of wet days typically exhibit irregular high frequency variations, which are difficult to model. Hence, we first develop consecutive data segments of fixed length by grouping the daily rainfall data. Following which, two data aggregation processes are performed within the consecutive disjoint segments, namely, the average rainfall amount and wet days counts within segments. Average rainfall and wet days count for segments are found to be significantly smoother and hence they are more tractable by statistical models. The study proposes to model the wet days count in the consecutive segments by a Hidden Markov model-based approach. Further, the daily rainfall amount is modelled with a power law distribution. The model parameters are estimated by maximizing the data likelihood. Moreover, to incorporate the variation due to the observed serial dependence in the estimated model parameters, we employ block-resampling technique, widely used in bootstrap and resampling literature for dependent observations (for further details readers are encouraged to consult Kreiss and Lahiri, 2012 ). The bootstrapping is appropriately tuned to represent the unprecedented conditions in the estimated model S θ     . The method is described in the following subsections and a schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 2  . Additionally, a pseudo code related to the proposed method is presented as supplemental information . 3.1.1 Segments of daily data The daily data is grouped into several consecutive segments. Each segment is fixed at length of 5 days; hence, for observed daily data over n  consecutive days, the number of segments formed is m = [n/5] , the largest integer contained in n/5 . The segment length is varied over different simulations with the same training data to fix a segment length. The segment length should be such that major high frequency variations are negated in the segment processing, although the important low frequency variations of the original data distribution are retained in the segments. The periodogram analysis of the segment wise average rainfall shows a satisfactory retention of low frequency components at segment length of 5 days (results not presented). Further modeling has been done on the rainfall data processed at these segments level. The study computes the number of wet days in different segments in the data vectors C = c 1 ,   c 2  , ⋯ , c m       which is the key component for the model estimation. To note that each segment has a fixed length of five days, but the number of wet days within a segment may vary.  3.1.2 Modeling segment level rainfall data The average rainfall amounts over different consecutive segments are assumed to follow a finite state space Markov process of order one. The number of wet days count C   are assumed to be independently distributed conditioned on the rainfall states. The modeling framework falls within the paradigm of Hidden Markov Model (HMM) widely used to fit time series data which are characterized by an underlying process [Mor et al., 2021 ]. We assume the number of states of the HMM to be K,  given by the state space S = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , K     .  The HMM is characterized by three sets of multidimensional parameters: an initial distribution Q = q 1  , q 2  , ⋯ , q K      , a transition probability matrix P = p ij          and an emission probability matrix E = e c i   s t    , s t  ∈ S       . The initial distribution Q  decides how the rainfall amount varies over the different states when the process initiates to generate. The transition probability matrix decides how the rainfall amount transitions from one state to another and finally, the emission probability matrix controls the emitted rainfall count data conditioned on the underlying rainfall states.  3.1.3 Modelling wet days count The study assumes that the number of wet days, for the average rainfall state l , follows a Poisson count distribution with mean parameter λl . Hence, for the K  average rainfall states,  there are K  Poisson parameters, denoted by Λ = (λ1 , λ2 , …, λK ).
