To incorporate the data skewness for segments with lowest average rainfall, with predominant dry days within those segments, the study assumes the distribution of the number of wet days (denoted by r ) within such segments to be a zero-inflated Poisson distribution (zip). Without loss of generality, the first state of the HMM model is assumed to emit rainfall count having the zero-inflated Poisson distribution and rest of the states emit rainfall count following the traditional Poisson distribution. The probability mass function of the zero-inflated Poisson distribution (zip) is given by equation (1) .(1) P zip   r | π ,  λ 1    = π + 1 - π   exp - λ 1    i f r = 0 = 1 - π   λ 1  r  exp - λ 1     r !   i f r ∈ { 1 , 2  , ⋯ }      The zero inflated Poisson distribution assigns a fixed probability mass on the count 0 controlled by a zero-inflation parameter π  . The study varies the number of Markov states over a range and estimates the model parameters following maximum likelihood method (described next in Equation (2)  and records the Akaike information criterion (AIC). The AIC showed diminishing marginal change after K=5  which is the number of states the study choses to fix (results not shown). Since the Markov model parameters are unknown, they are estimated from the segment wise rainfall count training data C . A sample set of estimated parameter values are presented in the supplemental information  (SI Table 1 ). For the observed rainfall count data C = c 1 ,   c 2  , ⋯ , c m       with unknown sequence of states S = s 1 ,   s 2  , ⋯ , s m       we maximize the data likelihood function mentioned in equation (2) .L Q , P , Λ , π | C , S   = q s 1   ∏ i = 2  m  P ( s i  | s i - 1   )  ∏ i = 1  m  P ( c i  | s i  )      = q s 1   ∏ i = 2  m  p s i  , s i - 1     ∏ i = 1  m  e c i   ( s i  )      (2) = q s 1   ∏ i : s i  = 1   P zip   ( c i  | π , λ 1  )  ∏ j = 2  K  ∏ i : s i  = j   P poi   ( c i  | λ j  )  ∏ i = 2  m  p s i  , s i - 1         Here P zip     and P poi     are the probability mass functions of a Zero inflated and a traditional Poisson distribution respectively which specify the Emission probabilities conditioned on the K  states. The model parameters are estimated by the forward–backward Baum-Welch Algorithm [Baum, 1972 ], which is essentially an iterative Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm of the likelihood function.  3.1.4 Rainfall amount modelling The study proposes a mixture distribution: The observed empirical rainfall distribution and a power law distribution to convert the simulated segment level data back to the rainfall data at daily level. The study assumes the daily rainfall amount to follow the power law distribution beyond a threshold value [Clauset et al., 2009 ], presented in equation (3) .(3) f x  min  , α   x   = α - 1  x  min    x x  min       - α   ,  α > 1 , x  min   > 0     The parameter x  min   > 0    controls the value of the daily rainfall beyond which the power law behaviour is observed (referred as the tail threshold parameter) and the parameter α > 1    controls the tail thickness (referred as the tail thickness parameter). Further, below the threshold, the rainfall distribution continues to remain same as the observed empirical rainfall data distribution. All the model parameters are captured in the labelling parameter θ = ( Q , P , Λ , π , x  min   , α )   . The different model constructs and associated maximum likelihood estimation for a given daily rainfall data series is schematically shown in left side panel of Fig. 2  and referred as the estimation method.   3.2 Weighted resampling strategy for parameter estimation The raw observed daily rainfall data shows moderately smooth variation over consecutive days within a short range typically observed in case of nonzero serial correlation or other short-range dependences. The study employs a modified version of the Moving Block Bootstrap (MBB) technique (See Kreiss and Lahiri, 2012 ) to capture the short-range dependence in the estimation of θ. In the current sub-section, the study presents the resampling technique to create multiple replicates of the daily rainfall data. Following which, the study applies the estimation method on each of the replicates to obtain multiple resampled estimates of the parameters. The resampled estimates have been averaged to obtain the final bootstrapped model parameter estimate (θ Boot   ) .   ^    These steps are also described in right side panel of Fig. 2 . Instead of equal probability sampling of overlapping blocks, we propose resampling higher average rainfall blocks with greater probability. Hence, each replicate based on the sampled blocks is essentially a generated rainfall data with a controlled perturbation from the observed data depending on the choice of the probability weight function. The replication strategy guarantees specification of high rainfall states with greater probability and Power law of greater tail thickness in the resampled parameter estimates. The MBB resampling technique essentially involves the following steps-.i. The observed time series data of rainfall over n  consecutive days x = x 1  , x 2  , ⋯ , x n       are divided into several overlapping blocks, with a fixed block length h  and block separation of 1, denoted by B 1  , B 2  , ⋯ , B L     such that B 1  = x 1  , x 2  , ⋯ , x h    , B 2 =   x 2  , x 3  , ⋯ , x h + 1     , ⋯ , B L =   x n - h + 1   , x n - h + 2   , ⋯ , x n       with L = n - h + 1   . It is assumed that the overlapping blocks preserves the ordering and dependence structure of the neighborhood observations within the blocks.  ii. The average rainfall corresponding to the uth   block is given as μ u  .    We sample [ n h   ]  blocks from the collection of the blocks B 1  , B 2  , ⋯ , B L      with replacement with probability proportional to the weights w 1  , w 2  , ⋯ , w L      where w u  = exp - μ u  - a    2  b  2       . In the weight function, a  and b  represent the location and scale parameters, respectively. Selecting the weight function parameter, a = a0   will render high selection probability to the blocks having average rainfall in the neighborhood of a 0 . Additionally, parameter b  decides the size of the neighborhood and the rate at which the probability weight function tapers off as we move to either lower or higher average rainfall range. The values of a  and b  are decided based on a grid search (SI Table 1 ).  iii. Block resampling has been repeated to form the replicates as described in step (ii) for i = 1 , 2  , ⋯ N    times to form N  resampled replicates of the daily rainfall data given by R 1  , R 2  , ⋯ , R N     .  iv. The model parameters, θ ∗  1  , θ ∗  2  , ⋯ , θ ∗  N     , are estimated following the estimation method on each of the N  replicates. The final Moving block bootstrap estimated model parameters is given by θ Boot   ^  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1   N  θ i  ∗     .     3.3 Simulation strategy For a chosen value of the probability weight function specified by the weight parameters ( a , b )    and fixing the number of HMM states and MBB block length, the model parameters are estimated as θ Boot   ^  = Q Boot   , P Boot   , Λ Boot   , π Boot   , x Boot  min   , α Boot     .    The bootstrap estimated model parameters θ Boot   ^    specifies a baseline simulation model S ( θ Boot   ^  )    which can be subsequently perturbed to generate rainfall data with desired level of unprecedented rainfall events. Users can simulate the average wet days count and average rainfall states over consecutive segments of days from the estimated model S ( θ Boot   ^  )   . The segment level rainfall states and wet days count are simulated respectively as Markov states and Emissions of the HMM model component with labelling parameters Q Boot   , P Boot   , Λ Boot     .    The occurrence of dry days can be controlled by perturbing the zero inflation and wet days count parameters ( π Boot   , λ 1 , B o o t   )    within a chosen neighborhood. Finally, the power law tail parameters (x Boot  min   , α Boot     ) can be tuned to values other than the estimated ones to generate unprecedented rainfall instances with chosen extremities. A larger value of x Boot  min     and smaller values of α Boot     will generate extreme simulated rainfall observations along with regular rainfall instances. Towards this, the study introduced two multiplicative factors, tail thickness tuning and tail threshold tuning parameters, that increases the maximum likelihood estimates of the power law parameters. The study found that the proposed framework is extremely sensitive to power law tuning parameters (described later in the results section). In brief, controlling the probability function of the block resampling and tail properties of the heavy tailed rainfall distribution enables the generation of rainfall data over a much larger class of underlying probability distributions. In the current context, larger class of underlying probability distribution indicates that the simulated rainfall has the same probability distribution as the observed rainfall, but with higher statistical attributes; hence, introducing non-stationarity in simulated rainfall.  3.4 Deployment of the SRG The model is deployed over twenty-six grid points over Southeast Texas to generate daily rainfall records of thirty years. Observed daily rainfall data for twenty-six stations are considered to train the model. For each station, fifty realizations are generated. Results are presented in the next section that typically averages across grid points and realizations. To note that since the proposed SRG is one of the data generation approaches, a daily correspondence between the observed and the simulated has not been yielded. Hence, scaler performance measures such as root mean square error would not represent the model skill. The study estimates long term statistics between the observed and the simulated to evaluate model performance. In addition, magnitude of rain for different return periods are estimated following two probability distributions. The study assumes that simulated rainfall magnitude higher than the observed maximum rainfall for a station is an unprecedented event. Finally, using the observed and the simulated daily rain, the study estimates the return periods of Hurricane Harvey rainfall for eight rain gauge stations. The authors note that a traditional validation of the proposed approach is impossible since historical records of unprecedented events may not exist. To note that the objective of the current study is not to forecast unprecedented events but to estimate the likelihood of unprecedented events. Therefore, at the later part of the study, a validation of the proposed model has been performed by comparing the return period yielded by the current study to that of a former study of Emanuel (2017) . The current study estimates rainfall magnitudes correspond to 50, 100, 250, 500-year return periods. Towards this, the study fits two probability distributions: Extreme value distribution, type I and log-normal distribution.(4) f x   = 1 β  e  x - μ  β   e  - e  x - μ  β         where μ   and β   are scale and location parameters respectively. Additionally, if Z follows standard normal distribution, and X is defined as e  ( μ + σ Z )    , then Z would follow a log-normal distribution. To note, both distributions are widely used in hydrological frequency analysis. Further, to estimate the return period of Hurricane Harvey for a particular weather station, we follow two steps: 1) We fit type I Extreme value distribution to historical/ simulated rainfall data for five nearby grid points to the weather station, 2) Extract the return period of Hurricane Harvey rainfall for the weather station from the rainfall distributions related to five neighboring grid points. We found that it is possible that the return period of Hurricane Harvey rainfall with respect to historical rainfall distribution might fall beyond the estimated return period range; such cases are marked as unprecedented events.   4 Results The application of the proposed methodology is demonstrated in Fig. 3  . The objective of the current study is to present evidence that the proposed methodology can generate unprecedented rainfall events. To this end, the study applies the SRG on five grid points that surround Webstar weather station. First, thirty years of observed rainfall records are considered for model training. Finally, thirty years of rainfall data is generated for the five surrounding grid points. However, in Fig. 3 , simulation results related to only one grid point is presented. Simulations are carried out for tail tuning parameter values equal to 1.2 which should simulate more unprecedented events compared to the observed records (SI Fig. 1  presents similar histograms but for tuning parameter values equal to 1.8). Fig. 3  presents histograms related to four rainfall categories based on the rainfall magnitude from the observed and simulated daily rainfall values. The rightmost column represents the high-extreme rainfall category (>100 mm/day) whereas the leftmost columns represent the low-extreme rainfall category (<30 mm/day). The study identifies that the observed and simulated records of rainfall distribution in the moderate to low rainfall categories (<30 to 60mm/day < rain > 100mm/day) are similar. However, the simulated rainfall records exhibit the presence of very high extreme rainfall occurrences (for rain > 100 mm/day), which is absent from the observed records. Furthermore, there is no observed record of daily rainfall estimates exceeding 200 mm, whereas there are multiple occasions where the simulated daily rainfall exceeds 200 mm. A large difference between observed and simulated histograms for observed rainfall greater than 60 mm is expected as tail threshold and thickness tuning parameter values 1.2 would result in more unprecedented events which introduce a nonstationary in the simulated rainfall distribution. Empirical cumulative distributive functions for two tuning parameter combinations in simulating daily rainfall of four months are presented in the supplemental information  which also confirms that the proposed methodology has the potential to generate estimates for unprecedented rain events (SI Fig. 2 ). As mentioned in Section 3 , the proposed SRG is sensitive to two tuning parameters related to the power law—tail threshold and tail thickness. A wide range of unprecedented events embedded in a daily time series can be generated by skillfully changing the tail parameters. However, doing so requires further guidance on properly understanding the sensitivity of the tuning parameters in yielding the observed mean and the observed standard deviation in simulated rainfall. A non-stationarity in the mean and the standard deviation will be introduced in the simulated rainfall distribution if the observed mean and the observed standard deviation have not been preserved during simulation. Hence, to understand the changes in statistical moments with respect to changes in the tail tuning parameters, this study considers thirty-six pairs of tail tuning parameters to estimate the percentage change in six statistical moments (SI Table 2  for list of combinations). Tail tuning parameter values have been changed from 1 to 2, with an increment of 0.20. The study considers the following six common statistical attributes: mean of the daily rainfall, standard deviation of the daily rainfall, mean of the monthly/annual rainfall, standard deviation of the monthly/ annual rainfall, 25th percentile of the daily rainfall, and 99th percentile of the daily rainfall. The simulation can be conducted using either the daily observations for a particular month (mentioned later as monthly run) or the daily observations for all months (mentioned later as annual runs). The simulation that considers daily observations from a particular month would yield the seasonality in the data. To note, it is important to yield the monthly seasonality in the simulated rainfall if the simulated rainfall is further forced into a hydrologic model for flood simulations. Furthermore, the SRG is applied on twenty-six grid points, and the final performance is evaluated by averaging the metric of percentage change in the statistical attributes. The current analysis is summarized in Figs. 4 and 5   . Fig. 4  indicates the percentage change in the values related to the simulation based on daily observations for four months: January, April, August, and October. These four months belong to the four seasons of a year. The six rows in Fig. 4  denote the six statistical attributes. The study found that a smaller value of the tail tuning parameters results in higher change in the statistical attributes hence results in a non-stationarity in the simulated rainfall distribution. Furthermore, the means of daily rainfall and monthly rainfall are more sensitive to the tail thickness tuning parameter compared to the tail threshold tuning parameter. In addition, the standard deviations of daily rainfall and monthly rainfall are influenced primarily by the tail threshold tuning parameter. The study found that the percent change in standard deviation can be as high as 200 % as the tail threshold tuning parameter closer to 1. Tail threshold parameter is primarily associated with low rainfall threshold (equation (3) ); whereas the thickness parameter is associated with the extreme values of the rainfall distribution. Hence, it should be noted that tail thickness parameter does not exhibit substantial sensitivity in yielding the low flows (row 4 of Fig. 4 ). The tail thickness tuning parameter especially plays a critical role in generating extreme rainfall estimates (99th percentile of daily rainfall). The study performs a similar analysis that counts the average number of unprecedented events generated by the proposed approach with respect to the changing tail tuning parameters. The study found that the proposed approach is generating unprecedented events that is 0.6–1 % of the data length, i.e., thirty years (results presented as supplemental information , SI Fig. 3 ). Notably, the current figure does not consider the spatial variation in percent change across twenty-six grid points which can be found in the supplemental information  (SI Fig. 4 a and 4b). Overall, it is suggested that a smaller value of the tail tuning parameters generates unprecedented events while also yielding non-stationarity in the mean and the standard deviation, whereas higher values of the tail tuning parameters preserve the observed mean and standard deviation in the simulated rainfall. We found that both parameters behave similarly across months; but their sensitivity in yielding non-stationarity in observed statistical attributes do vary. For example, a smaller value of either of the parameter results in substantial non-stationarity in statistical attributes for any month of the year. However, the influence of a particular parameter on the statistical attribute is different from the other parameter. Similar conclusions can be drawn when rainfall is simulated using the observed daily rainfall from all months (Fig. 5 a to 5e). However, the percentage change values are higher for the current case compared to the monthly runs as the size of training set increases from monthly to annual runs, thus a higher number of extreme events (including unprecedented extremes) are generated during annual simulations as compared to monthly simulations. The previous analysis confirms the trade-off between the generation of unprecedented rainfall events and non-stationarity in statistical moments with respect to tail tuning parameters. Hence, the flexibility in selecting the tail tuning parameter rests with the user of the SRG. Although this study has considered thirty-six pairs of tail tuning parameters, any integer can be selected to execute the SRG since the tail tuning parameters are continuous variables. Therefore, an additional guideline might help the user to identify appropriate values of the tail parameters. For this purpose, the current study consults the Assessment Report 6 of the Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change (IPCC AR6). Changes in extreme rainfall is strongly associated with changes in the global mean temperature. Additionally, the annual maximum rainfall is likely to increase globally in response to increase in greenhouse gas concentrations. As per the IPCC-AR6, in Southeast Texas, global warming level of 1.5 °C, 2 °C, and 4 °C results in 10 %, 20 %, and 30 % increase in annual maximum daily precipitation, respectively compared to 1850–1900 (refer to Fig 11.16 Seneviratne et al., (2021) ). To note, the suggested increase in global warming is based on the results from multi-model ensemble under Shared Socio-economic Pathway (SSP), SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Multi-model outputs reaching the suggested levels from all scenarios were averaged to obtain the percent change in annual maximum daily precipitation; hence, the results do not represent a particular SSP [IPCC 2021 (b) ]. The previous analysis (Figs. 4 and 5 ) suggests that typically with lower tail tuning‘ parameter values the proposed approach will generate more unprecedented events while introducing non-stationary in the mean and in the standard deviation of the simulated rainfall. Hence, combining the major findings from the previous analysis and the IPCC-AR6 report, the current study suggests a comprehensive list of tail tuning parameters that would results in a various degree of non-stationarity (i.e., 10 %, 20 % and 30 %) in the annual mean rainfall that is expected in the Southeast Texas (Fig. 6  ). We infer from IPCC-AR6 that a 10 % (20 %) change in the annual mean rainfall is associated with a global warming level of 1.5 °C (2 °C). Further, from previous analysis the study found that tail tuning parameter values of 1.6 and 1.4 would results in a 10 % change in January maximum daily rainfall. Hence, combining the IPCC-AR6 and our previous analysis, the study relates that the tail tuning parameter values of 1.6 and 1.4 for January are associated with global warming level of 1.5 °C (Fig. 6 a). Similarly, the study suggests that the tail tuning parameter values of 2 and 1.2 for January are associated with global warming level of 2 °C (Fig. 6 b). The authors note that the current suggestions are primarily logical understanding but not based on mathematical reasoning. The objective of current suggestion is to provide a physical interpretation of the behaviors of tail parameter to the users so that the users can select the tail tuning parameters based on the suggestions. Nevertheless, the current study identifies that although the tail tuning parameter values do not change significantly for a given scenario, they change substantially between two scenarios, indicating the dominant role of scenario uncertainty in long-term climate projections (Hawkins and Sutton, 2011 ). The current study estimates the observed and simulated rainfall magnitudes for high to low frequency rainfall events (i.e., rainfall events of four different return periods) for twenty-six stations. Fig. 7   presents the tail tuning parameter values for three global warming levels-1.5 °C, 2 °C, and 4 °C (represented in three rows of the figure). Since the current analysis is performed by considering all data points, the tail tuning parameter results related to the annual run (Fig. 6 d) are considered. Rainfall estimates for a given return period are estimated by fitting two probability distributions — Extreme Value distribution Type-I and Log-normal distribution (represented as two columns) to the observed and simulated rainfall. Fig. 7  presents a comparison of the rainfall estimates for a given return period for three warming levels. The length of the boxes indicates spatial variance in the rainfall estimates across twenty-six stations. The results confirm that difference in the rainfall estimate for a given return period increases with increase in the global mean temperature. Similarly, spatial variance in the rainfall estimates also increases with increase in global warming. An additional calculation related to rainfall return period is conducted with both tail tuning parameter values equal to 2 which will result in limited to no unprecedented events in the generated data (presented in the supplemental information SI-Fig. 5 ). SI-Fig. 5  confirms that observed return periods almost match the return periods of simulated rainfall. Overall, the study found that if global warming persists, high frequency rainfall events will continue to increase in magnitude in the future, compared to the past. In the final analysis, the study estimates the return periods of Hurricane Harvey-like rainfall over eight weather stations in Southeast Texas. Return periods of 7-day maximum and 7-day average rainfall for each weather station are estimated. Furthermore, the lognormal probability distribution can be fitted either to the observed records or to the simulated rainfall over five surrounding grid points for each weather station. The proposed SRG is applied to simulate thirty years of rainfall with tail tuning parameters equal to 1.2, following the indication obtained from Fig. 6 d. Since the study simulates the daily rainfall for all days, tail tuning parameter values related to annual runs are considered. Furthermore, for each weather station, five return periods either for the observed records or for the simulated rainfall are obtained. Fig. 8   presents a comparison of the observed and simulated return period for eight weather stations—their return periods from five grid points are spatially averaged (spatial variance in estimated return period is presented in SI Table 3  and SI Fig. 6 ). For a given station, the numbers on the left and right respectively indicate the return period of simulated and observed rainfall. If the observed return period cannot be estimated due to lack of data, it is marked as “UP”. The analysis noted a substantial change in the return period from the observed to the simulated, indicating a higher risk of unprecedented rainfall events under global warning conditions. Overall, although incidents similar to Hurricane Harvey are found to be unprecedented in the past, they would not be a rare occurrence in the near future as the frequency of such events increase. The primary challenge of the proposed framework relates to the validation of the simulated unprecedented events. Since unprecedented events are either absent from historical records or limited in number, a direct comparison between observed and simulated unprecedented events is difficult. Hence, traditional model validation methods would not be appropriate in the present case. Since a direct validation of the simulated unprecedented events is impossible, the study compares the return period of Hurricane Harvey-like rainfall (from the simulated data) with the estimates from the study by Emmanuel (2017), who developed a numerical hurricane model to predict the future return period of the Texas storm under future greenhouse gas emission scenarios. Emmanuel’s study found that the revised return period of the Hurricane Harvey rainfall is around 16 years, which can be expected to increase further (5.5 years) by the end of the century. The current study as well as the one by Emmanuel (2017) exhibit similar order of magnitude of the return period of Hurricane Harvey-like rainfall. Hence, drawing on the above analysis, the authors conclude that the proposed SRG is reliable for estimating future return periods of unprecedented events.  5 Summary and discussion The current study proposed a statistical framework for generating daily rainfall values for unprecedented rainfall events. This framework follows a traditional stochastic weather generator approach—creating a sequence of dry-wet days, followed by generating the rainfall magnitudes on wet days. The advantage of the proposed framework lies in its ability to generate daily rainfall values, including for dry days, while also developing estimates for unprecedented events resulting from increase in the global temperature. The potential of the proposed framework in generating unprecedented events relies on the idea that its model parameters can be resampled to yield non-stationarity in rainfall distribution. Furthermore, the framework was applied on twenty-six grid points across Southeast Texas that experienced Hurricane Harvey. The current study estimated the revised return period of Hurricane Harvey based on the simulated rainfall in eight weather stations. Significant findings of the current study are as follows:1. The proposed framework can generate estimates for unprecedented rainfall that were previously absent from historical records  2. The proposed framework is sensitive to two power law tuning parameters—tail threshold and tail thickness tuning parameters  3. Typically, a lower value of the tuning parameters ensures the generation of more unprecedented events and vice versa  4. The presence of unprecedented events introduces non-stationarity in the long-term statistical attributes of historical rainfall records. This study considers the percentage change in the mean daily rainfall to tune the power law parameters.  5. Under global warming levels, extreme rainfall magnitudes corresponding to a given return period increases significantly. The magnitude further increases with changes in the warming levels  6. A Hurricane harvey-type rainfall is observed to be unprecedented for the eight weather stations studied in this research. The return period of Hurricane Harvey in the future also decreases substantially    The authors note three major limitations of the current framework, i.e., proposed model and the proposed validation 1. Absence of a traditional validation, 2. Selection model tail tuning parameters, and 3. Estimation observed serial dependence in simulated rainfall. The authors emphasize that a similar validation by comparison with former studies may not be possible if the SRG is applied on a different region, other than Southeast Texas, and for a different unprecedented storm event. In such a case, an external dependence of one of the model tuning parameters will be helpful in generating the unprecedented event estimates. In the current study, qualitative suggestions have been provided to select tail tuning parameters. However, since the proposed model is sensitive to power law parameters, these parameters can be associated with the signals of climate change, assuming a non-stationarity in the power law parameters. In this context, the simplest approach would be to regress the power law parameters, derived for different time windows, with external climate covariates. Alternatively, a hierarchical model that provides posterior information related to the power law parameters can be developed, which would yield the parametric uncertainties associated with the generation of unprecedented events. Additionally, the current study did not consider the persistence of daily rainfall as the wet days within a non-overlapping block can be distributed randomly. We found that although the proposed approach can yield the transition probability of rainfall states, the autocorrelation in daily rainfall may not be preserved (SI Figs. 7 and 8 ). Hence, there is a possibility that that the accumulation of simulated rainfall might be biased which eventually impacts the return periods estimated for 7-day maximum and 7-day average rainfall related to hurricane Harvey. Towards this, the study carried out two additional runs: one with tail tuning parameter values 1.2 that will generate unprecedented events and second run with tail parameter values 2 that will keep the rainfall distribution stationary (presented in supplemental information , SI Fig. 9 ). Results confirm that for a regular run the bias between observed and simulated is very small which increases for simulated with tail tuning parameter values of 1.2. The current study applied the proposed SRG over a small region, involving only a few weather stations and covering twenty-six grid points. The next step for this line of study would be to apply the SRG over a climate region that has witnessed unprecedented events in the recent past. Regional application of the proposed model should yield the spatial coherence in unprecedented rainfall events. Traditionally, Max Stable Process and spatial GEV models are known to incorporate the spatial dependence in extreme value modeling (Reich and Shaby 2012, Sampaio and Costa 2021 ). The authors are currently engaged in extending the proposed approach in yielding spatial dependency in unprecedented rainfall events. We note that regional application would require significant computational power, considering that the computation time for the current methodology in a high-performance computer cluster is between three to four hours for a single run. When this model is applied over a climate region or a watershed, the hydrological risk assessment can be conducted by forcing the simulated rainfall into a hydrologic model. Overall, the current study successfully demonstrates that unprecedented rainfall events can be successfully generated by following a statistical framework even when there is limited or no record of such events in the past.
1 Introduction Water resource shortage is an urgent problem facing most regions of the world, and large-scale inter-basin water transfer projects are built (Han et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021 ) is an effective means to solve the unequal distribution of water resources. Water transfer projects can transport water resources from water-rich areas to water-poor areas through built channels, pipelines, etc. When the terrain of water-scarce areas is higher, it is necessary to build pumping stations to achieve water extraction by stepping pumps. However, the cascade pumping station water supply canal system (WSCS) usually has the characteristics of long distance and large scale, and the cascade pumping station needs to consume a lot of energy during operation (Yan et al., 2022 ). Therefore, it is very important to improve the operation efficiency of pumping station and reduce the energy consumption of pumping station. Mathematical programming methods are widely used to solve the energy optimization scheduling problems of these systems. Wang et al. (2019)  established a mixed-integer linear programming model with constraints on water balance, conveyance capacity, and pipeline operation to minimize total conveyance and pump operation costs. Negishi & Ikegami (2021)  established an optimization model using mixed-integer linear programming and verified the reduction in operational costs through pumping scheduling simulations. Vieira et al. (2020)  presented a new linear relaxation of nonlinear integer programming formulation to optimize the operational cost of water distribution systems. Zhang et al. (2019)  used a functional analysis-based dynamic programming approach to reduce the number of pumping stations and optimize pump operation costs by formulating appropriate skip station strategies. Gong & Cheng (2018)  solved the minimum pumping energy consumption problem of cascade pumping station systems using dynamic programming. Zhuan & Xia (2013)  proposed an extended simplified dynamic programming algorithm to solve the optimal scheduling problem of multi-pump stations. With the development of intelligent optimization algorithms, single-objective optimization algorithms have been widely used to solve scheduling optimization problems. Luna et al. (2019)  and Wu et al. (2015)  used genetic algorithms for scheduling optimization, improving the energy efficiency of WSCSs. Yi & Wenhao (2023)  employed a successive approximation genetic algorithm to address problems such as mismatched pump heads and water levels in each time period during the solution process. Tang et al. (2014)  applied particle swarm optimization algorithms to solve optimal control problems considering pump switching and cumulative operating time. Abdelsalam & Gabbar (2021)  controlled pump on/off operations using the artificial electric field algorithm to minimize the energy cost and number of pump switches in the water network. However, single-objective optimization algorithms exhibit a clear tendency toward single benefits. Multi-objective optimization algorithms can balance the advantages of multiple objective benefits and have been proposed and used to enhance the overall efficiency of systems. Non-dominated sorting genetic algorithms (Chen et al., 2021; Gong & Zhu, 2022; Zhong et al., 2023 ) have been widely used to solve multi-objective optimization problems related to pump station energy, reducing both operational energy consumption and improving other benefits such as time and safety. M. Wang et al. (2022)  constructed a new framework for comparing multi-objective methods and tested it in a case study in China, validating its effectiveness in finding the best-performing optimization method. However, whether using single-objective algorithms or multi-objective algorithms, the range of applications under fixed parameter conditions is relatively limited. Adaptive algorithms can maintain high performance under multiple operating conditions by adjusting parameters, making them suitable for energy optimization of pumping station systems in more complex environments. Liu et al. (2019)  proposed an improved adaptive grey wolf algorithm to obtain more efficient and economical cascade pumping station scheduling schemes. Makaremi et al. (2017)  solved optimization problems with energy cost and pump switch numbers as objectives using an adaptive multi-objective genetic algorithm, and the actual optimization results showed a significant reduction in pump switch total numbers without significantly increasing energy costs. De O. Turci et al. (2020)  proposed two adaptive and one improved population-based natural pumping station scheduling optimization algorithms, achieving better performance than traditional methods. However, these studies mainly focus on improving method performance, with relatively few studies on simulation and modeling. Indeed, the selection of simulation and modeling methods is crucial for energy optimization of pumping station systems. Liu et al. (2019)  optimized the operation cost of pumping stations based on a steady flow simulation model considering time-of-use electricity prices, obtaining the optimal flow distribution throughout the day. However, steady flow models cannot effectively describe hydraulic processes under short-term adjustments (Yuan et al., 2021 ). Therefore, unsteady flow simulation models (Lei et al., 2019; Mallios et al., 2022 ) are gradually being used to optimize pumping station operation cost control strategies. Gong and Cheng (2018)  obtained the optimal head distribution and pump unit operation mode through numerical simulation of unsteady flow in channels. Yan et al. (2022)  constructed a multi-objective optimization model based on unsteady flows considering engineering water supply safety and pumping station operational economy, which achieved significant comprehensive benefits in the Miyun Reservoir cascade pumping station WSCS. However, due to the various uncertainties and disturbances in the water transmission process of WSCSs, and most of these studies are conducted offline, the predictive accuracy of simulation models for future pump station states is limited. Therefore, it is particularly important to propose a real-time scheduling method that can calculate online and provide timely feedback to correct system state adjustment prediction models. From the perspective of control theory (Bryson, 1996 ), simulation optimization methods can be divided into closed-loop control and open-loop control modes according to whether there is state correction. Closed-loop control (Galuppini et al., 2022; Salomons & Housh, 2020; Siddiqui et al., 2021 ) can achieve regular online calculations and feedback correction, making it considered effective in addressing uncertainty issues and beginning to be applied in the WSCSs of cascade pumping stations. Kong et al. (2023)  applied closed-loop control algorithms with unsteady flow models as simulation models, considering energy consumption and cost as two driving objectives, and applied them to the WSCS of the Yangtze-to-Huaihe Diversion Project cascade pumping station under uncertain conditions, achieving higher economic benefits and robustness than open-loop control methods. However, unsteady flow model construction is complex and difficult for control algorithm design, and has high computational costs. Kong et al. (2021)  used an integrator-delay (ID) model as a predictive model for closed-loop control of water level differences in the middle route canal pools under two disturbance conditions. The results show that this method can effectively shorten the control time. However, there is little research on applying the ID model to cascade pumping station WSCSs. In addition, the water supply plans of cascade pumping station WSCSs usually have a long time dimension. Previous studies often utilized single time-scale closed-loop scheduling models to solve such problems. However, if a single time-scale closed-loop scheduling model adopts a larger control step, it may lead to a decrease in prediction accuracy within the control step. Conversely, using more control steps may decrease the effectiveness of the first control step. Selecting appropriate control step sizes and numbers is necessary. However, this may result in mismatches between the control time domain and the duration of the pumping station water supply plan, leading to ineffective water supply guidance in the control time domain, thus limiting the scheduling benefits of the system. Therefore, this study adopts scheduling models with two different time scales of closed-loop control modes, establishing a multi-scale closed-loop (MCL) coupled real-time scheduling framework. The large-scale closed-loop scheduling model utilizes a storage balance model and hydraulic response relationships to formulate small-scale water supply plans based on rolling optimization of pumping station water supply plans. Meanwhile, the small-scale closed-loop scheduling model employs an ID model and hydraulic response relationships to formulate real-time scheduling strategies. Through the rolling optimization stage of closed-loop control, the system is updated and optimized in real-time to enhance the comprehensive benefits of WSCSs with longer time-scale scheduling demands under uncertain conditions. The main innovations of this study are as follows: Firstly, the establishment of a large-scale closed-loop scheduling model considering canal pool storage balance and hydraulic response relationships enhances the macroscopic guidance of water quantity scheduling. Secondly, the establishment of a small-scale closed-loop scheduling model based on canal pool ID models and hydraulic response relationships improves computational efficiency. Lastly, a hierarchical structure is utilized to construct and solve a MCL real-time scheduling model framework, enhancing water supply efficiency and economic performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2  introduces the proposed methodology, and Section 3  provides a detailed description of the case study and test results. Section 4  further analyzes the results, and Section 5  summarizes the conclusions.  2 Methodology 2.1 MCL coupled real-time scheduling framework This study employed a MCL coupled real-time scheduling framework and applied it to the WSCS of cascade pumping station. A flowchart of this methodology is illustrated in Fig. 1  . Both the large-scale scheduling model and small-scale scheduling model consist of internal prediction models and objective functions. However, they differ in their approaches. The large-scale scheduling model uses the canal pool storage balance model and the hydraulic response relationship to predict the upstream and downstream water levels, and the scheduling instructions of the small-scale scheduling model are obtained through closed-loop rolling optimization, while the small-scale scheduling model uses the ID model and the hydraulic response relationship to predict the upstream and downstream water levels, and the real-time scheduling instructions are obtained through closed-loop rolling optimization, which are executed in the virtual WSCS. The results are fed back, and the state, disturbance and control variables of the large-scale and small-scale models are updated respectively according to the time scale, and the rolling optimization is carried out continuously forward by time step.  2.2 Large-scale closed-loop scheduling We employed the principle of volume balance and hydraulic response relationship of canal pools to construct an large-scale water quantity scheduling model with the objective of providing mid-term water quantity scheduling services to plan and guide the real-time scheduling of WSCSs at the macroscopic level. 2.2.1 Large-scale internal prediction model The large scale adopts a storage balance model to predict the storage capacity of the canal pool. The formula is as follows:(1) S ( k + 1 )  = S ( k )  + Δ S ( k )  + Δ W u  ( k )  - Δ W d  ( k )  - Δ W o  ( k )      where S ( k )    is the storage volume for a step length of k   , Δ S ( k )    is the variation in storage volume for a step length of k   , Δ W u  ( k )     is the variation in upstream control water quantity for a step length of k   , Δ W d  ( k )     is the variation in downstream control water quantity for a step length of k   , and Δ W o  ( k )     is the variation in the diversion quantity for a step length of k   . The upstream water level of the canal pool is calculated using the water level-storage response relationship. The formula is as follows:(2) l u  ( k )  = μ S 2  ( k )  + ν S ( k )  + λ     where l u  ( k )     is the upstream water level for a step length of k   . The downstream water level of the canal pool was calculated using the downstream water level-upstream water level-flow response relationship. The formula is as follows:(3) l d  ( k )  = f ( l u  ( k )  , Q d  ( k )  )      where l d  ( k )     is the downstream water level for a step length of k    and Q d  ( k )     is the downstream control flow for a step length of k   .  2.2.2 Large-scale optimization objective function The objective function of the large-scale model is the weighted sum of the violation values of the water quantity tasks within the predicted time domain for the large scale, violation sum of the storage capacity limits for the canal pool, and violation sum of the upstream and downstream water levels for the canal pool. The formula is as follows:(4) minJ = α O 1  + β O 2  + ϕ O 3      where O 1     is the total violation value of the water quantity tasks within the large scale control time domain; O 2     is the total violation value of the canal pool storage capacity constraints within the large scale control time domain; O 3     is the violation value of the upstream and downstream water levels in the canal pool within the large scale prediction time domain; and α   , β   , and ϕ    are the respective weights of these three terms. The sum of the violation values of the water quantity tasks within the control time domain for the large scale is calculated as follows:(5) O 1  = ∑ i N  |  ∑ j = 1  m  W i  ( k + j | k )   - D i , m   |       where m    represents the control time domain, W i  ( k + j | k )     is the water supply of the i   −th pumping station at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step, D i , m      is the water demand of the i   −th pumping station within the control time domain, and N    is the total number of pumping stations. The sum of the violation values of the storage capacity limits for the canal pool within the control time domain for the large scale is calculated as follows:(6) O 2  = ∑ r C  ∑ j = 1  m  S r  ( k + j | k )  - S r , max   , ( S r  ( k + j | k )  > S r , max   )     |  S r  ( k + j | k )  - S r , min   | ,  ( S r  ( k + j | k )  < S r , min   )     0 , ( S r , min   ⩽ S r  ( k + j | k )  ⩽ S r , max   )              where S r  ( k + j | k )     is the storage capacity of the r   −th canal pool at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step, and S r , max      and S r , min      are the upper and lower limits, respectively, of the storage capacity of the r   −th canal pool. The formula for the violation values of the upstream and downstream water levels of the canal pool within the prediction time domain for the large scale is as follows:(7) O 3  = ∑ r C  ∑ j = 1  p  l u r  ( k + j | k )  - l u r , max   , ( l u r  ( k + j | k )  > l u r , max   )     | l  u r  ( k + j | k )  - l u r , min   | ,  ( l u r  ( k + j | k )  < l u r , min   )     0 , ( l u r , min   ⩽ l u r  ( k + j | k )  ⩽ l u r , max   )             + ∑ r C  ∑ j = 1  p  l d r  ( k + j | k )  - l d r , max   , ( l d r  ( k + j | k )  > l d r , max   )     | l  d r  ( k + j | k )  - l d r , min   | ,  ( l d r  ( k + j | k )  < l d r , min   )     0 , ( l d r , min   ⩽ l d r  ( k + j | k )  ⩽ l d r , max   )                  where p    is the prediction time domain; l d r  ( k + j | k )     and l d r  ( k + j | k )     are the upstream and downstream water levels, respectively, of the r   −th canal pool at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step; l u r , max      and l u r , min      are the upper and lower limits, respectively, of the upstream water level of the r   −th canal pool; l d r , max      and l d r , min      are the upper and lower limits, respectively, of the downstream water level of the r   −th canal pool; and C    is the total number of canal pools.   2.3 Small-scale closed-loop scheduling In this study, a small scale closed-loop scheduling model was constructed using an ID model and the hydraulic response relationship of canal pools. The objective was to provide short-term water quantity scheduling services and develop real-time scheduling measures that can cope with uncertainty disturbances in accordance with the water quantity scheduling tasks formulated by the large-scale scheduling model. 2.3.1 Small-scale internal prediction model In recent years, the ID model (Schuurmans et al., 1995 ) has been widely used as a simplified hydraulic model for open-channel hydraulic calculations (J. Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2019 ). The formula is as follows:(8) de ( t )  dt   = 1 As   [ q in   ( t - τ )  - q out   ( t )  - d ( t )  ]      where e ( t )    represents the change in the downstream water depth H d  ( t )     of the canal pool at time t    relative to the downstream water depth H d  ( 0 )     at the initial time, q in   ( t - τ )     represents the change in the inflow Q in   ( t - τ )     of the canal pool at time ( t - τ )    relative to the inflow Q in   ( 0 )     at the initial time, q out   ( t )     is the change in the outflow Q out   ( t )     from the canal pool at time t    compared to the initial outflow Q out   ( 0 )    , d ( t )    is the change in the offtake flow D ( t )    at time t    compared to the offtake flow at the initial time D ( 0 )    from the canal pool, and As    and τ    are the surface area of the backwater part and delay time, respectively. The incremental discrete form of the ID model used to predict the downstream water level in the small-scale model is as follows:(9) e ( k ′  + 1 )  = e ( k ′  )  + Δ e ( k ′  )  + T 2  A s   [ Δ q in   ( k ′  - k d  )  - Δ q out   ( k ′  )  - Δ q o  ( k ′  )  ]      where e ( k ′  + 1 )    and e ( k ′  )    are the downstream water level deviations of canal pools with time steps k ′  + 1    and k ′    , respectively; Δ e ( k ′  )    is the variation range of downstream water level deviations with time step k ′    ; T 2     is the calculation time step of the small scale ID model; k d  = τ / T 2     is the time delay in discrete time form; Δ q in   ( k ′  - k d  )     is the inflow variation of the canal pool with time step k ′     in the upstream region; Δ q out   ( k ′  )     is the outflow variation of the canal pool with time step k ′     in the downstream region; and Δ q o  ( k ′  )     is the diversion variation of the canal pool with time step k ′    . The upstream water level of the canal pool is predicted using the upstream water level, downstream water level, and downstream flow relationships. The formula is as follows:(10) l u ′  ( k ′  )  = f ( l d ′  ( k ′  )  , Q d ′  ( k ′  )  )      where l d ′  ( k ′  )     is the downstream water level of the canal pool with time step k ′     and l u ′  ( k ′  )     is the upstream water level of the canal pool with time step k ′    .  2.3.2 Small-scale optimization objective function Considering the varying importance of pump stations in terms of the completion of water-supply tasks, operational safety, and energy efficiency, the small-scale model aims to minimize the weighted sum of the total violation of the water-supply tasks of the pump station, the total violation of the upstream and downstream water levels in the canal pool, and the unit pumping energy consumption of the pump station within the prediction time domain. The objective function is defined as(11) minJ = a O a  + b O b  + c O c      where O a     is the total violation value of the supply tasks of the pumping stations within the small-scale control time domain; O b     is the total violation value of the upstream and downstream water levels in the canal pools within the small-scale prediction time domain; O c     is the total pumping energy consumption of the pumping stations within the small-scale control time domain; and a   , b   , and c    are the weights of the three factors, respectively. The formula for the total violation of water supply tasks for pump stations within the small-scale control time domain is as follows:(12) O a  = ∑ i N  |  ∑ j = 1  m ′   W i ′  ( k + j | k )  - D i , m ′   ′  |        where m ′     is the small-scale control time domain, W i ′  ( k + j | k )     is the pumping volume of the i   −th pumping station at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step, and D i , m ′   ′     is the water demand of the i   −th pumping station within the control time domain. The formula for calculating the total violation of the upstream and downstream water levels for a canal pool within the small-scale prediction time domain is as follows:(13) O b  = ∑ r C  ∑ t p ′   l u r ′  ( k + j | k )  - l u r , max  ′  , ( l u r ′  ( k + j | k )  > l u r , max  ′  )     | l  u r ′  ( k + j | k )  - l u r , min  ′  | ,  ( l u r ′  ( k + j | k )  < l u r , min  ′  )     0 , ( l u r , min  ′  ⩽ l u r ′  ( k + j | k )  ⩽ l u r , max  ′  )             + ∑ r C  ∑ t p ′   l d r ′  ( k + j | k )  - l d r , max  ′  , ( l d r ′  ( k + j | k )  > l d r , max  ′  )     | l  d r ′  ( k + j | k )  - l d r , min  ′  | ,  ( l d r ′  ( k + j | k )  < l d r , min  ′  )     0 , ( l d r , min  ′  ⩽ l d r ′  ( k + j | k )  ⩽ l d r , max  ′  )                  where p ′     is the small-scale prediction time domain; l u r ′  ( k + j | k )     and l d r ′  ( k + j | k )     are the upstream and downstream water levels, respectively, of the r   −th canal pool at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step; l u r , max  ′     and l u r , min  ′     are the upper and lower limits, respectively, of the upstream water level of the r   −th canal pool; and l d r , max  ′     and l d r , min  ′     are the upper and lower limits, respectively, of the downstream water level of the r   −th canal pool. The total unit pumping energy consumption of the pump stations within the small-scale control time domain is calculated as follows:(14) O c  = ∑ i N  ∑ j = 1  m ′   E i ′  ( k + j | k )     ∑ i N  ∑ j = 1  m ′   W i ′  ( k + j | k )          where E i ′     is the energy consumption of the i   −th pumping station at the k + j   −th step predicted at the k   −th step.   2.4 Optimization solution In this study, intelligent optimization algorithm is used to solve the multi-scale closed-loop coupled real-time scheduling model and develop real-time scheduling strategy. The approach begins by employing a differential evolution algorithm to solve the large scale water quantity scheduling model, execute medium-term water quantity scheduling plans within the large scale control time domain, and use them as predictions for the water quantity task within the water quantity scheduling model at a small scale. Next, the differential evolution algorithm was applied again to optimize and solve the small scale water quantity scheduling models. Then, the time step by step rolling optimization is carried out to obtain the optimal real-time scheduling strategy.   3 Case study 3.1 Study area In this section, we consider the Xuhong River WSCS in the Jiangsu segment of the Eastern Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project in China as an example. We experimentally evaluated the performance of MCL real-time water quantity optimization scheduling for cascade pumping station WSCS. A generalized map of the study area is shown in Fig. 2  . Hongze Lake is upstream along the Xuhong River, and water is pumped from Hongze Lake to Luoma Lake through the Sihong (SH), Suining (SN), and Pizhou (PZ) pumping stations. Both the Hongze and Luoma lakes serve as water level boundaries. The relationship coefficients of the water level and storage capacity, ID model parameters, and initial water diversion flow of the canal pools in the study area are listed in Table 1  . The initial conditions of the pumping stations in the study area are provided in Table 2  .  3.2 Research scenarios It is difficult to develop a model that can predict the state of the system with absolute accuracy because of various uncertainties in the real WSCS. In this study, the uncertainty related to the water diversion of the canal pool is used as the main source of uncertainty, making the prediction model unable to accurately predict the virtual model. On the basis of the initial water diversion flow, two small-scale scheduling simulation models of water diversion disturbance in Fig. 3   are used as virtual models of the real system to generate “real” state data, including water level and energy consumption of the cascade pumping station. A simplified internal prediction model which does not consider the water diversion disturbance but only uses the constant initial water diversion flow as the prediction model. In order to reflect the performance of the proposed method under different types of water diversion disturbance, the water diversion disturbance flow of a single time node is used as scenario S1, and the continuous water diversion disturbance flow is used as scenario S2.  3.3 Method settings To assess the disparities between existing studies and our research, we employed the single-scale closed-loop (CL) scheduling method and open-loop (OL) scheduling used in existing studies for comparison. The CL scheduling method utilized a small-scale closed-loop scheduling model for rolling optimization at each time step, while the OL scheduling method employed a small-scale predictive model for a single optimization. In the studied WSCS, the pump adjustment interval was set to 8 h, and the pumping plans for SH, SN, and PZ pumping station over three days were 1.550×107 m3 , 1.503×107 m3 , and 1.452×107 m3 , respectively, adhering to this pattern across all methods. In the proposed MCL scheduling method, the large-scale optimization horizon was set to 72 h, comprising 24 h small-scale water scheduling instructions with three prediction steps, while the small-scale optimization horizon was set to 24 h, including real-time pump control actions with three prediction steps. The control parameter settings for both large-scall and small-scale scheduling methods are presented in Table 3  . Additionally, through trial and error, for the large-scale optimization objective function, weight coefficients α   , β   , and ϕ    were set to 10, 0.00001, and 10, respectively; For the small-scale optimization objective function, a   , b   , and c    were set to 1, 10, and 1, respectively. In the CL scheduling method, only the small-scale closed-loop scheduling model was utilized, with control parameter settings as indicated in Table 3 . Unlike the MCL scheduling method, there was no large-scale closed-loop scheduling model providing small-scale water scheduling instructions. Instead, an averaging method was used to issue instructions, whereby each rolling optimization task executed water tasks amounting to 1/3 of the total water plan each time. In the OL scheduling method, apart from the optimization horizon being set to 72 h, other parameter settings were the same as those for the small-scale closed-loop scheduling model. Unlike closed-loop scheduling methods, it could not employ a rolling optimization strategy and required a complete control strategy to be formulated at the beginning of the 72 h period. We employed the differential evolution algorithm to solve the all of optimization problem and set the number of populations to 100, mutation factor to 0.4, crossover rate to 0.3, and number of iterations to 100.  3.4 Results 3.4.1 Accuracy verification of water level and energy consumption The three methods are respectively used in the water diversion disturbance scenarios S1 and S2. The absolute deviation of water level and the relative deviation of energy consumption of these methods are shown in Fig. 4   and Fig. 5  . In Fig. 4  and Fig. 5 , the deviation of water level and energy consumption of the closed-loop scheduling method CL and MCL is generally similar, in which the absolute deviation of water level is controlled within the range of −0.02 m ∼ 0.04 m, and the relative deviation of energy consumption is controlled within −1.33 % ∼ 0.79 %, which proves the high precision of the two closed-loop scheduling methods. However, the deviation between water level and energy consumption of OL method is relatively large, in which the absolute deviation of water level reaches 0.46 m and the relative deviation of energy consumption reaches −16.97 %, which may not meet the accuracy requirements of actual scheduling. In Fig. 4  (3) and (4), the absolute deviation of the water level before the pumping station by CL and MCL methods is exactly the same, because the two methods both use the small-scale ID model to predict the water level before the pumping station, while the virtual WSCS also uses the ID model as a linear prediction model. It will result in consistent deviation results for different pumping station control actions formulated by different methods under the same water distribution disturbance scenario. However, in Fig. 4  (1) and (2), the absolute deviation of the water level after the pumping station of CL and MCL methods is different to some extent, because both methods predict the upstream water level by using the small-scale relationship between upstream water level, downstream water level and downstream flow. This nonlinear relationship will directly lead to the prediction of the upstream water level with nonlinear change under the same flow. For the OL method, Fig. 4  (a) shows that in the case of water distribution disturbance at a single time point, the disturbance will persist and affect all periods after the disturbance occurs due to the absence of rolling optimization strategy. The absolute deviation of water level caused by this disturbance is approximately fixed, and the volatility is determined by the nonlinear prediction method of upstream water level. Fig. 4  (b) shows that under continuous water distribution disturbance, the water level deviation accumulates and increases with time. The two closed-loop scheduling methods CL and MCL can update the system status regularly and eliminate the past water level deviation due to their rolling optimization links, so that when they deal with the water distribution disturbance at a single time point, they can eliminate to zero in time at the beginning of the next control step after the deviation, and when dealing with continuous water distribution disturbance, they can eliminate to zero in time. It can constantly update the status and deviation at each control step, so that the absolute deviation of the water level is wavy and always controlled within the safe range. As for energy consumption, Fig. 5  shows that the relative deviation of energy consumption of the three methods shows a change process similar to the absolute deviation of water level. Since OL method has no rolling optimization link, it cannot update the system state regularly, resulting in energy consumption deviation showing persistence in single time node water distribution disturbance (scenario S1), and monotonically increasing in continuous water distribution disturbance (scenario S2). As the CL and MCL methods can optimize and update the system state on a rolling basis, the energy consumption deviation shows unimodal characteristics in the single time node water distribution disturbance (scenario S1), while it shows multi-modal characteristics in the continuous water distribution disturbance (scenario S2).  3.4.2 Results and analysis of water supply benefits The closed-loop scheduling methods CL and MCL with rolling optimization links both have the ability to cope with different water distribution disturbances. In order to further compare the water supply benefits of the two closed-loop scheduling methods, we conducted a simulation calculation on the implementation of the three day water supply plan of the cascade pumping station, and the results are shown in Fig. 6   and Fig. 7  . Fig. 6  shows that the relative deviation of water quantity plan execution of each pumping station using MCL method is generally low in the two water distribution disturbance scenarios, less than 0.4 % and 1.0 % respectively, which can better meet the water demand of the WSCS and provide better water supply benefits. The relative deviation of water quantity plan execution of pumping stations using CL method showed a large difference in the two water distribution disturbance scenarios. The relative deviation of water quantity plan execution of SH pumping station was the largest, which exceeded 6.0 % under both water distribution disturbance scenarios, while the relative deviation of water quantity plan execution of SN pumping station was the smallest, which was always lower than 0.3 % under the two water distribution disturbance scenarios. This is because the CL method has only one layer of small-scale closed-loop scheduling model, and lacks effective guidance of small-scale scheduling plan. The average method may not meet the multi-objective of high precision and high water supply efficiency at the same time. Fig. 7  shows that the MCL method, guided by the large-scale closed-loop scheduling model, enables the water quantity planning of each pumping station to be completed well, resulting in a significantly lower average relative deviation of the overall water quantity planning execution than the CL method, which is 3.4 % and 5.9 % lower under the two water distribution disturbance scenarios, respectively. Therefore, the proposed MCL method has big advantages in terms of water supply efficiency.  3.4.3 Results and analysis of economic benefits It is a basic condition to ensure the high accuracy of water level and energy consumption prediction for the real-time water scheduling of the WSCS of the cascade pumping station. In addition, it is not only necessary to ensure water supply but also to reduce costs and increase efficiency. In order to further evaluate the economy of the proposed method, we carried out a simulation calculation of the operation energy consumption of the cascade pumping station, and the results are shown in Fig. 8   and Fig. 9  . Fig. 8  shows that the unit energy consumption of each pumping station in the CL and MCL methods is relatively close in the two water diversion disturbance scenarios. Among them, the average unit energy consumption of SN pump station under the two methods is the closest, and the average deviation is only 0.5 kWh/104 m3 . The unit energy consumption of SH station is 3.8 kWh/104 m3  higher than that of CL method in MCL method, and the unit energy consumption of PZ pump station is 2.2 kWh/104 m3  lower than that of CL method in MCL method. As shown in Fig. 9 , the overall unit pumping energy consumption of cascade pumping station using CL and MCL methods shows a great difference in the two water distribution disturbance scenarios. The unit pumping energy consumption of MCL method is 1.7 kWh/104 m3  and 1.5 kWh/104 m3  lower than that of CL method respectively, indicating that MCL method has better economic benefits. Combined with Fig. 8 , it is not difficult to find that the economic benefit advantage of the proposed MCL method is mainly derived from the efficient optimization of Pizhou pumping Station. The overall optimization is achieved by abandoning the benefits of some low-energy SH pumping stations in exchange for the benefits of high-energy PZ pumping stations.    4 Discussion In the real-time scheduling of the WSCS, the rolling optimization strategy can update the state of the system regularly and formulate the real-time control action of the new state, and the error is constantly corrected. Therefore, the CL and MCL methods using rolling optimization strategy can effectively reduce the accumulation of errors and improve the accuracy and stability of water level and energy consumption prediction, no matter the water distribution disturbance at a single time point or the continuous water distribution disturbance. However, because OL method has no rolling optimization link, it cannot eliminate the prediction error caused by the disturbance in the optimization process, resulting in the deviation of water level and energy consumption in the single-point water distribution disturbance and continuous water distribution disturbance, respectively, showing persistence and growth. The MCL method can make use of the large-scale closed-loop scheduling model to develop small-scale scheduling instructions with smaller deviation of water execution and more energy saving, which has more guiding advantages than the scheduling instructions obtained by the average method, which directly leads to the performance difference between the small-scale closed-loop scheduling models of MCL and CL methods. The final real-time scheduling strategy inherits the macro-scheduling advantages of the large-scale closed-loop scheduling model, which makes the average relative deviation of water supply plan execution and the energy consumption of cascade pumping station by MCL method lower than that by CL method. The state update time of large-scale closed-loop scheduling model is slower than that of small-scale closed-loop scheduling model, but the coupling of large-scale and small-scale makes the rolling optimization process of scheduling change from a single time line evolution to a hierarchical step-by-step evolution, and the state update amount of the small-scale model at the same level will accumulate and transfer to the large-scale scheduling model. Therefore, the multi-scale coupled closed-loop scheduling model can effectively deal with the uncertainty of water distribution disturbance. In addition, the coupling of the multi-scale closed-loop scheduling model will increase the complexity of the model structure, but the complexity of the computation time is still within the acceptable range, because in the actual scheduling process, we only need to implement the control strategy of the first step. Therefore, when formulating the real-time control strategy of pumping station, it is only necessary to calculate the closed-loop scheduling model of different scales once. In this study, the calculation time of each control step of MCL method under two kinds of perturbations does not exceed 17 s. Therefore, this multi-scale hierarchical approach to uncertainty processing can be extended to solve the uncertainty problem of scheduling requirements with longer time dimensions. Through rational splitting of multi-level time scales, the optimal strategy of the maximum-scale closed-loop model can be gradually transferred to the minimum-scale closed-loop model with the gradual evolution of layer by layer, resulting in the overall optimal performance.  5 Conclusion In this paper, a real-time water quantity scheduling method for cascade pumping station WSCS based on MCL is established. The purpose is to make use of the advantages of multi-scale closed-loop dispatching and improve the water supply benefit and operation economic benefit of pumping station. The method has been tested on the Xuhong River WSCS in Jiangsu section of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project. The main findings of this study are as follows:1. The closed-loop control methods CL and MCL make the predicted water level deviation of the pumping station controlled within the range of −0.02 m ∼ 0.04 m, and the relative deviation of energy consumption controlled within the range of −1.33 % ∼ 0.79 %. These closed-loop control methods can update the state of the system periodically through rolling optimization, effectively reducing the accumulation of errors, no matter the water distribution disturbance at a single time point or continuous water distribution disturbance.  2. Under the two disturbances, MCL method reduces the average relative deviation of water supply plan execution of pumping station by 3.4 % and 5.9 % respectively compared with CL method, and the unit energy consumption of cascade pumping station operation by 1.7 kWh/104 m3  and 1.5 kWh/104 m3  respectively. The MCL scheduling model can make use of the large-scale closed-loop model to develop small-scale scheduling instructions with better comprehensive benefits, so that the small-scale closed-loop scheduling model inherits its macro-scheduling advantages and optimizes high-performance real-time scheduling actions.  3. MCL method can effectively deal with the uncertainty of water distribution disturbance through the accumulation and transmission of state update quantity of the large and small scale closed-loop model, and the complexity of calculation time of this multi-scale hierarchical treatment of uncertainty is within the acceptable range. Therefore, it can be generalized to solving scheduling demand uncertainty problems with longer time dimensions.
1 Introduction Shallow aquifers in the Bengal Basin’s Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) delta, stretching from West Bengal in India to Bangladesh, represent the most severe case of dissolved geogenic arsenic (As) contamination globally (Bhowmick et al., 2013; Chowdhury et al., 2000; DPHE/BGS, 2001; Fendorf et al., 2010; Nickson et al., 2000; Smedley and Kinniburgh, 2002; Smith et al., 2000 ). Despite decades of sustained efforts by governments, non-profit and inter-governmental organizations, and scientists to mitigate the As poisoning, the number of people (∼100 million people) exposed to toxic concentrations of groundwater-borne As (>10 µg/L) remains relatively unchanged in South Asia (Chakraborti et al., 2009; Chakraborty et al., 2015; Human Rights Watch, 2016; Smith et al., 2000 ). It is generally accepted that an important source of dissolved As in shallow aquifers in South and Southeast Asia is the microbially-mediated reductive dissolution of As-bearing Fe(III)-oxyhydroxide minerals (referred to herein as Fe(III)-oxides) (Fendorf et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2002; Islam et al., 2004; Mailloux et al., 2013; McArthur et al., 2001; Nickson et al., 2000; Polizzotto et al., 2008; Smedley and Kinniburgh, 2002; Stahl et al., 2016; van Geen et al., 2004 ). However, the process of advective transport of reactants, such as dissolved organic carbon (DOC), to sites of reaction with solid-phase minerals, such as Fe(III)-oxides, and the advective transport of their products through heterogeneous sedimentary layers produce a highly heterogeneous distribution of dissolved As concentrations (Aziz et al., 2008; Chakraborty et al., 2020, 2015; Kazmierczak et al., 2022; Mailloux et al., 2013; Polizzotto et al., 2008; Stahl et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2023 ). In the Bengal Basin, ancient fluvial processes control the stratigraphy of the alluvial aquifers whereas recent fluvial processes shape land-surface morphology along current riverbanks (Goodbred et al., 2003; Kuehl et al., 2005; Wilson and Goodbred, 2015 ). The spatial variability of dissolved As is influenced by the hydro-stratigraphic settings shaped by these ancient (Aziz et al., 2008; Kazmierczak et al., 2022; Postma et al., 2007; Weinman et al., 2008 ) and recent fluvial processes (Stahl et al., 2016; Stute et al., 2007; Wallis et al., 2020 ). In their detailed study of the 25 km2 -sub-district of Araihazar in central Bangladesh, Weinman et al. (2008)  reported that the dissolved As concentrations are largely influenced by the grain size, thickness, and distribution of fine-grained sediments overlying the buried sandy aquifers in Bangladesh. They demonstrated that the dissolved As concentrations were generally lower in areas where aquifer sands are exposed at or near the surface, but higher beneath or adjacent to thicker layers of find-grained deposits. Groundwater modeling (Desbarats et al., 2014; Mozumder et al., 2020 ) and tritium–helium age-dating (Stute et al., 2007 ) demonstrated orders of magnitude differences in travel times from ground surface to the depth of 20 to 30 m. This is the depth interval in which the highest dissolved As concentrations typically occur within shallow aquifers. Empirical studies in Araihazar found that shallow unconfined aquifers have average residence times of months to years, whereas clay or silt-capped aquifers typically have residence times of tens to hundreds of years (Aziz et al., 2008; Stute et al., 2007 ). Furthermore, shallow aquifers underlying floodplains which are annually inundated by river water have some of the highest As concentrations (Connolly et al., 2022 ). The physical or chemical processes that are initiated or prevented by certain types of surface lithology which impact As mobilization are still poorly understood. The aforementioned observed spatial associations between shallow aquifer As concentrations and find-capped aquifers, including annually flooded floodplains, could be explained by: i) kinetically limited buildup of As concentrations in porewaters interacting with the longer physical travel times through clay and silt layers; ii) a finite amount of easily mobilizable As on sediments which is rapidly flushed from sands, but flushed slowly from clays and silts (van Geen et al., 2008 ); iii) reductants diffusing from clay layers which release As from aquifer sands by reduction of Fe(III)-oxides (Mihajlov et al., 2020 ); or iv) freshly deposited riverine sediments with abundant and easily mobilizable DOC which acts as the reductant for Fe(III)-oxides (Polizzotto et al., 2008 ). These mechanisms may not operate exclusively. Arsenic may be released in some places by a kinetically-governed slow process, such as silicate weathering, equilibrium-governed desorption or competitive desorption by phosphate, or have fast kinetics that are limited only by the supply of reactants as is the case for pyrite weathering in mountainous regions with high rates of physical weathering (Bufe et al., 2021 ).
