In contrast, eutrophic taxa were sparse and cyanobacteria production was relatively low in Poyang Lake, indicating that free hydrological connectivity with the main channel may mitigate against eutrophication in these Yangtze floodplain lakes (Fig. 5 ). 4.1 Water level and UV radiation exposure The large and directly connected Poyang Lake (0 – 250) apparently experienced higher variability in UV exposure than the small and dammed Wanghu Lake (0 – 60) (Fig. 5 C), suggesting that underwater light availability in floodplain lakes was related to changes in water level (Sokal et al., 2010; Cantonati et al., 2014 ). Due to the scatter and absorption in the water column, underwater light intensity exponentially declines with water depth generally (Scheffer et al., 1997). Therefore, changes in water level play an important role in regulating the underwater light availability, leaving shallow littoral areas of the lake which are more sensitive to the change in water level particularly susceptible to UVR exposure (Cantonati et al., 2014 ). Poyang Lake is freely and directly connected with the Yangtze River, whereas Wanghu Lake is indirectly connected with the Yangtze River via a tributary. Poyang Lake experiences more intensive hydrological variation in the water surface area and water level than Wanghu Lake (Fig. 1 , Fig. S4 ). This can be reflected by the larger median grain size of the sediments in Poyang Lake (7.4 μm) than that in Wanghu Lake (3.3 μm) (Fig. S4 B), as coarser particles normally indicate strong hydrodynamic conditions (Chen et al., 2022b ). As shown by the satellite images, Poyang Lake experiences large seasonal variations in the water surface area (from < 1000 km2  in the non-flooding season to ∼ 4000 km2  in the flooding season) (Fig. 1 B) (Liu et al., 2019 ). The average intra-annual water level fluctuation is > 7.3 m in Poyang Lake (Liu et al., 2019 ), which is even larger than the maximum recorded water depth of Wanghu Lake (5.2 m) (Yi et al., 2006 ). This probably resulted in the more variable underwater light availability and exposure of littoral areas in Poyang Lake compared to Wanghu Lake. Therefore, our results reveal that exposure of aquatic biota to UV radiation is more variable in floodplain lakes with free hydrological connections to the main channel.  4.2 Damming and water clarity Local dam construction also appears to influence floodplain lake water clarity as recorded by increases in the UVR index in Wanghu Lake after the local dam was installed (Fig. 5 ). Suspended particles are of particular importance in influencing the attenuation of light in the water column (Scheffer et al., 1997). Waterbodies with high suspended particle concentrations are normally characterized by high turbidity and low light conditions, whereas waters with low suspended particles have low light attenuation and hence high light penetration deeper into the water column (Scheffer 1997; Swift et al., 2006 ). For floodplain lakes, the main channel is the primary source of suspended particles, especially in tropical and sub-tropical floodplain areas where the main channel has a high sediment load (Roberts et al., 2022 ). In natural and unmanaged northern floodplains, hydrologically-isolated lakes have clearer and better illuminated waters as lower suspended particle loads are transported into them (Squires and Lesack, 2003; Sokal et al., 2010 ). The Yangtze River ranks fourth in the world in terms of sediment loads, with an annual sediment load of ∼ 470 Mt in the middle reaches before the 1980 s (Wang et al., 2008 ). After the local dam construction which restricted the hydrological connection between Wanghu Lake and the Yangtze River, the suspended particle influx declined, increasing the light penetration. Therefore, the observation in Wanghu Lake seems to suggest that light conditions were improved by damming which impeded suspended sediment loads.  4.3 Dual effects of damming on the lake ecosystem Compared with the freely connected Poyang Lake which exhibited relatively small variations in the chironomid assemblages, there was an increase in the UVR index and macrophyte-related chironomid taxa after local dam construction in the 1960 s CE in Wanghu Lake, followed by a decrease in the UVR index and a shift to eutrophic chironomid taxa with nutrient enrichment since the late 1980 s (Fig. 4 ; Fig. 5 ). This suggests that local damming has a dual influence on ecosystem state changes (macrophytes and clear water versus algal-dominated and turbid) by regulating light and nutrients. The improvement of underwater clarity after local dam construction appears to have promoted the growth of aquatic macrophytes when nutrient loading was low. In Wanghu Lake, the proportion of macrophyte-related chironomids was at moderate or low levels before damming, suggesting that the freely connected lake provided a suitable habitat for macrophyte growth. The variable chironomid community composition in the large, hydrologically open Poyang Lake also supports the idea that macrophyte development in regularly-flooded lakes varies through time (Blindow et al., 1993; Beklioglu et al., 2006; McGowan et al., 2011 ). Therefore, it appears that water level fluctuations and disturbances from flooding result in intermediate levels of plant coverage over decadal timescales, and this is likely due to substantial seasonal or inter-annual variability (Burdis et al., 2020; Ersoy et al., 2020 ). After local dam construction in 1965 CE, there was a substantial increase in the abundance of macrophyte-related taxa in Wanghu Lake (e.g., E. tendens -type, E. albipennis -type, E. dissidens -type). This “post-damming macrophyte development” phenomenon has also been recognized in other Yangtze floodplain lakes with relatively low nutrient conditions (Futou Lake, TP: ∼0.04 mg L-1 ; Liangzi Lake, TP: ∼0.02 mg L-1 ) (Zeng et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019 ). The piecewise SEM revealed direct and indirect (via underwater availability) influence of hydrological modification on aquatic macrophytes in Wanghu Lake (Fig. 7 A). Therefore, it is possible that the stabilized hydrological condition and improvements in light conditions after local dam construction initiated the spread of macrophytes (Bilotta et al., 2008; Sokal et al., 2010 ) when anthropogenic nutrient loadings were low, as recorded by the concurrent increase in the UVR index in Wanghu Lake. Macrophytes play an important role in buffering shallow freshwater ecosystems against regime shifts into the turbid algae-dominated state (Scheffer et al., 1993 ). Therefore, it is reasonable to expect that Wanghu Lake would have remained in a macrophyte-dominated clear water state after local dam construction. However, several lines of evidence demonstrate that Wanghu Lake shifted into an algal dominated turbid state after the late 1980 s CE with the intensification of industrial activities in the catchment: 1) the dominant chironomids showed a quick turnover from macrophyte-related taxa to eutrophic taxa; 2) the concentration of cyanobacteria-derived canthaxanthin profoundly increased; 3) the UVR index sharply declined (Fig. 5 ). In contrast, macrophyte-related chironomid remained dominant and eutrophic chironomid taxa were sparse after the late 1980 s in the large, hydrologically open Poyang Lake, although canthaxanthin significantly increased and the UVR index decreased (Fig. 5 ). As revealed by the significantly higher rate of changes in the sedimentary proxies in Wanghu Lake than Poyang Lake after the 1980 s (Fig. 6 ), the contrasting response in the two lakes probably indicates that local dam construction accelerated ecosystem state changes into the algal dominated turbid states in floodplain lakes when nutrient conditions were high (Dong et al., 2016; Lopera-Congote et al., 2021 ), which has been reported in lakes of the tropical American floodplain, the Mississippi and the Murray floodplains (Bhattacharya et al., 2016; Kattel et al., 2016; Lopera-Congote et al., 2021 ). The results of the piecewise SEM indicate that local dam construction accelerated the transition from the macrophyte-dominated clear water state to the algal dominated turbid state primarily by amplifying the effects of nutrient enrichment but desensitizing the responses to hydrological variation in Wanghu Lake (Fig. 7 ). Water exchange is important in regulating nutrient retention in floodplain lakes (Vollenweider, 1976; Chen et al., 2016 ). Water flushing rates in floodplain lakes are fundamentally controlled by hydrological connectivity with the main channel (Junk et al., 1989 ). Dam construction prolongs the water retention time and reduces the water exchange ratio (Chen et al., 2016 ), promoting the retention and active recycling of nutrients between the benthic and pelagic areas in the lakes (Tockner et al., 1999; Hambright et al., 2004 ); whereas free hydrological connection with the main channel may alleviate eutrophication in floodplain lakes by diluting nutrient concentrations (Sokal et al., 2010 ). Compared with the hydrologically open Poyang Lake (∼30 days), the water retention times are significantly longer in lakes with local dams (∼190 days) in the Yangtze floodplain (Wang and Dou, 1998 ). Consistent with this, the accumulation of TP was significantly higher in Wanghu than Poyang Lake (Zeng et al., 2023b ). Therefore, our results support the idea that the installation of dams may accelerate the regime shifts from a clear water state to a turbid state by promoting nutrient retentions. It should be noted that industrial activities appeared to exert a direct negative influence on aquatic macrophytes in Wanghu Lake as revealed by the piecewise SEM (Fig. 7 ), probably via macrophyte harvesting for aquaculture as reported in other Yangtze floodplain lakes (Song et al., 2016 ). While remaining dominant, the abundance of macrophyte-related chironomid taxa declined in Poyang Lake after the TGD installation (ca. 2003 CE), while canthaxanthin exponentially increased during this period (Fig. 5 ), indicating initial signals of ecosystem deterioration. This is consistent with a previous study, which reported the gradual replacement of benthic and epiphytic diatoms by planktonic diatoms in Poyang Lake after the ca. 2000 s CE (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Apart from the influence of industrial nutrient influxes, the piecewise SEM suggests that the TGD was a major factor causing the initial ecosystem deterioration in Poyang Lake (Fig. 7 B), both directly by promoting the retention of cyanobacteria and indirectly via nutrient retentions as the water retention times were prolonged and the water exchange ratios were lower after the TGD installation (Tockner et al., 1999 ). Similar results have been reported in the second largest freshwater lake (Dongting Lake, area) in China which is also directly connected with the Yangtze River, where algal production and cyanobacteria significantly increased after the TGD installation (Chen et al., 2016 ).   5 Conclusions By using paleolimnological proxies, our study discloses that on decadal scales the UV radiation index of water clarity and ecosystem states of the Yangtze floodplain lakes are strongly influenced by local damming, effects of which are impossible to investigate by limnology in developing regions due to the lack of long-term monitoring data. The comparison of lakes with and without local damming in this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of regime shifts in the Yangtze floodplain lakes, indicating that local damming has dual effects on the aquatic stable state transition in Wanghu Lake (TP=0.22 mg L-1 ). This contrasts with previous studies of other Yangtze floodplain lakes which are characterized by low nutrient concentrations (e.g., Futou Lake and Liangzi Lake with relative low TP concentrations of ≤ 0.04 mg L-1 ), where damming can facilitate the macrophyte-dominated clear water state (Zeng et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Our study indicates that the influence of local damming on floodplain lake ecosystems is dependent on the nutrient conditions of the lake. Under low nutrient conditions, local damming appears to facilitate the macrophyte-dominated clear water state. With nutrient enrichment, damming can accelerate the shifts to the algal dominated turbid state. Therefore, it is necessary to remain free hydrological reconnection with the main channel to alleviate the symptom of eutrophication under the scenario of enhanced anthropogenic nutrient loadings in floodplain lakes. Moreover, considering the large water surface area and hydrological discrepancy at different parts of Poyang Lake, further comparison of multiple sediment cores collected from the central and littoral parts are worthy to directly investigate the influence of water level variation on the underwater light availability and ecosystem states of floodplain lakes and to deal with the potential spatial variability, while our sedimentary records provide a representative record of the major ecosystem changes in Poyang Lake.
1 Introduction Flooding is one of the most serious natural disasters in the world (Han et al., 2014; Leitão et al., 2018; Lyu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2023b ). In recent years, urban flooding has become more and more frequently influenced by extreme weather and rapid urbanization around the world (Chen et al., 2018; Kulp and Strauss, 2019; Kumbier et al., 2018; Moy de Vitry and Leitão, 2020; Shi et al., 2022 ). The damage and losses flood caused have been increasing. For example, Zhengzhou City suffered a flood disaster due to an extreme rainstorm on July 20, 2021, resulting in 380 casualties and direct economic losses of RMB 40.9 billion (Sun et al., 2023 ). The damage caused by flooding in coastal cities is more severe than inland cities because coastal cities have a more dense population and economic prosperity. In addition, the frequency of heavy rainfall and high tide levels that occur simultaneously are increasing during extreme weather such as typhoons (Ward et al., 2018 ). Flooding in coastal cities is often caused by the compound influence of several flood drivers such as intense rainfall and high tide levels (Bevacqua et al., 2024; Wahl et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2018 ). The tidal dikes in many coastal areas of China adhere to rigorous construction standards, yet urban flooding along the coast persists, primarily due to the jacking effects of high tides and limitations in the drainage network (Xu et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023a ). During extreme weather events such as typhoons, intense rainfall funnels into the river system via the drainage network. The river drainage is impeded by the high tides, resulting in a swift rise in water level, which in turn causes the river to overflow and flood. Concurrently, the inadequate drainage capacity of the pipe network due to the jacking effect of high levels of river exacerbates urban flooding. For instance, during the landfall of Typhoon “ Seagull ” in Hainan Province, China in 2014, inadequate drainage capacity of the Meishe River led to difficulty in draining accumulated water into the river, resulting in severe inland flooding (Hong et al., 2022 ). Consequently, investigating the interconnections among various flood drivers is crucial for addressing flooding in coastal urban areas. Currently, compound flooding in coastal cities has become a research hotspot (Ward et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2013 ). These researches focus on two main aspects. The one is to use statistical methods to calculate the dependence and return period of compound floods. The other is to apply numerical models to simulate the inundation of compound floods to develop flood prevention measures (Fang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022 ). Xu et al. (2014)  studied the joint probability of extreme precipitation and storm surge levels in a changing environment using the copula function. Jalili Pirani and Najafi. (2020)  analyzed the correlation trend of rainfall, runoff, and storm surge along the western Pacific coast, eastern Atlantic coast, and the Great Lakes region. It was found that the joint frequency of rain-runoff-storm surge is increasing. In addition, accurate simulation for flooding can be obtained by numerical models. Then the measures for flood control and drainage can be taken according to the location of flooding. For example, Lian et al. (2013)  input rainfall and tide levels as boundary conditions into HEC-RAS to simulate compound floods in Fuzhou City and installed drainage pumps at the flooding area to mitigate inundation. However, it is not scientific enough to formulate prevention and control strategies based solely on the location, depth, and other characteristics of floods without considering the real causes of floods. Recently, several studies have attempted to identify and quantify the main flood drivers in flooded areas and target the management of areas affected by different flood drivers. For example, Lian et al. (2017)  proposed a method for zoning for the key drivers leading to flooding based on a numerical simulation method. Bilskie and Hagen. (2018)  were the first to delineate the flood drivers by dividing hydrological, transitional, and tidal zones. Their effects on urban flooding were studied to better distinguish the main flood drivers for the arrangement of flood prevention measures in coastal cities. In addition, the hydraulic connections between sub-catchments and rivers are complex and tight. Therefore, it is necessary to effectively identify flood sources and quantify the contribution of different flood drivers to achieve optimal flood discharge. There are studies that have used the tracer method to visualize water flow paths and reveal the hydraulic connections between different elements in urban drainage systems (Qi et al., 2022a; Zhuang et al., 2023 ). For example, Qi et al. (2021)  studied the hydraulic connections between different sub-catchments in Haikou City through the tracer method coupled with a numerical model. Then the disaster prevention and mitigation strategies were proposed based on the results. However, although many studies have been conducted to analyze the zoning of flood drivers in coastal cities, there is still a lack of studies applying the tracer method to the zoning of floods in coastal cities. The tracer method can effectively track the flow paths of different flood drivers, which plays an important role in investigating the causes of coastal flooding and proposing regulatory measures. The purpose of this study is to investigate the impact of urban inland rivers on flooding in the coastal city. A zoning method was proposed for the main flood drivers of coastal urban flooding. The inundation areas affected by different flood drivers are divided based on the numerical simulation model coupled with the tracer method. Moreover, the water tracing method is employed to simulate the process of urban river flow during flooding disasters. Finally, the effects of urban river flow on compound floods driven by heavy rainfall and high tide levels were evaluated. The flow chart of this study is illustrated in Fig. 1  . The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2  describes the basic information of the study area and data for the urban flooding model. Section 3  introduces the methods employed in this study. The results of zoning and water tracing are analyzed in Section 4 . Finally, Section 5  makes a discussion and summarizes the conclusions.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area This study takes Haikou City, Hainan Province as a case study. The location of the study area is shown in Fig. 2  . Haikou is located at the northern edge of the low-latitude tropics and is bordered by the Qiongzhou Strait to the north, which is a typical tropical monsoon climate region. Haikou City is one of the cities in China that is frequently attacked by typhoons. The topography of the study area is flat. Due to the monsoon climate and the Qiongzhou Strait, the study area is highly susceptible to urban flooding. Concurrent high-water levels in inland rivers and elevated tides can impede the drainage capacity of urban stormwater systems during heavy precipitation events. This phenomenon results in a series of adverse consequences, including surface inundation, disruption of transportation networks, and damage to public infrastructure. For example, tropical cyclone Bebija made landfall in Haikou City in August 2018, causing widespread flooding across 25 roads in the city. This inundation resulted from the compound effects of river flooding and high tides, with some areas experiencing water depths of up to 1.1 m. The flooding significantly disrupted the traffic and transportation capacity of the city.  2.2 Data The inundation data of urban flooding is obtained by using a numerically simulated model. The basic data of the model mainly include rivers, pipe network, catchment wells, digital elevation model (DEM), buildings, rainfall, and tide level, in which the rivers, pipe network, catchment wells, DEM, and buildings were provided by the Haikou Municipal Water Bureau. The rainfall data and tide level data for calibrating the numerically simulated model (Fig. 3  ) were obtained from the Haikou rainfall gauge station and Haikou tide gauge station on 18 July 2014 when Typhoon Rammasun landed. The designed rainfall and tide levels for different return periods were obtained using the Pearson type-III distribution based on the measured data from 1974 to 2012. Then three cases were formed by combing the designed rainfall and tide level, as shown in Fig. 4  . The numerically simulated model was calculated under the three cases to identify areas affected by different flood drivers.   3 Methodology 3.1 Urban flooding model coupled with water tracer method The hydrologic and hydrodynamic model is a preventive solution to the lack of inundation data (Li et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2024 ). This study utilizes the one- and two-dimensional coupling model based on the personal computer stormwater management model (PCSWMM) for the simulation of urban flooding. PCSWMM, a software developed by Computational Hydraulics International (CHI), supports functions such as large and small drainage system design (Bibi et al., 2023 ), watershed simulation (Carvalho et al., 2019 ), low impact development (LID) (Jiang and McBean, 2021 ), water quality simulation (Abduljaleel et al., 2023 ), and integration of one-dimensional (1D) drainage network and two-dimensional (2D) surface inundation models (Yang et al., 2023 ). In this study, the flow transmission of the pipe network is simulated by the dynamic wave method, and the one- and two-dimensional model is connected through the bottom orifice. PCSWMM performs hydraulic simulations by solving the continuity equation (Eq.1) and the momentum conservation equation (Eq.2).(1) ∂ Q  ∂ L   + ∂ A  ∂ t   = 0     (2) ∂ Q  ∂ t   + ∂ Q 2  / A      ∂ L   + g A ∂ H  ∂ l   + g A S f  + g A h L  = 0     Where Q  is the flow of the pipe, L  is the distance along the pipe, A  is the cross-sectional area of the pipe, t  is the water flow time, g  is the gravity acceleration, H  is the water depth, hL   is the local energy loss per unit length in the pipe, and Sf   is the friction slope. Based on the construction of PCSWMM, this study intends to investigate the impact of urban inland rivers on coastal urban flooding by using the water tracer method. The water tracing method is in its infancy in the field of numerical simulation of urban flooding. A few scholars used the water tracing method to study the connection of water volume between catchments with the source tracer set in different drainage catchments (Ma et al., 2022 ). This study uses the same calculation module as the study of Ma et al., (2022) , yet the source tracer is set in the river to simulate the whole process of inland river flow in urban flooding and obtain the connection of hydraulic and water volume. This study applied PCSWMM to construct a simulation model of coastal urban floods integrating tracers. Because PCSWMM can realize tracer generation, inflow, and migration, and the types of tracers are not limited. The tracer transport in the pipe network and river channel takes a one-dimensional transport diffusion equation to calculate the changes in concentration. The transport diffusion equation is shown in Eq. (3) . The velocity of tracer transport is set to the same as the water flow. It is assumed that the tracer is uniformly mixed in the nodes and pipes.(3) ∂ c  ∂ t   = - ∂ ( u c )  ∂ x   + ∂ ∂ x   D ∂ c  dx       + r ( c )      Where c  is the concentration (M/L3 ); t  indicates time (T); u  denotes the longitudinal velocity (L/T); x  denotes the longitudinal distance; D  is the coefficient of diffusion (L2 /T); r(c)  indicates the function of response speed. When water flows out of the pipe network, the concentration of tracer mass is calculated by the mass balance equation. The model achieves coupled water and tracer simulation by incorporating the water balance equation with the balance equation of the tracer mass. The mass balance equation is shown in Eq. (4) .(4) d ρ s  S     d t   = ∑ l  I j  ρ l j   - ∑ k  O k  ρ o k       Where ρs   is the concentration of the tracer mass, mg/L; S  is the storage volume of node, pipe network and river, L; Lj  , Ok   is the discharge for j  inflow mode (e.g. side inlet) and k  outflow mode (e.g. side outflow), L/s; ρ L j      is the tracer mass concentration in the flow of j  inflow mode, mg/L; ρ O k      is the tracer mass concentration in the flow of k  outflow mode, mg/L. In order to study the connection of hydraulic and water volume between inland rivers and pipe networks, an urban flooding model with tracers was developed in this study. Qi et al. (2022b)  showed that simulation results for water quality from PCSWMM can be used to identify complex connections of water quantity between urban areas. The jacking effect of high tide is mainly concentrated at each outlet node of the drainage system. Therefore, this study intends to use the form of point source pollution to simulate the tidal movement with the tracer set in each outlet node. To keep the tracer concentration constant in the flow through the outfall, the nodal pollutant treatment function is enabled, and the tracer concentration of nodal tide is set to 1 mg/L as a constant function.  3.2 Zonation method for flood drivers The flood zoning for flood drivers is performed according to the inundation of the coastal city under different cases. The zonation method in this study is appropriately improved based on the research of Bilskie and Hagen. (2018) . This study divides the flooded area of the coastal city into the rainfall-affected area, the tidal-affected area, and the compound-influenced area, which are mainly infected by rainfall, tide level, and both, respectively. In other words, the flooded area incorporates the three types of areas, as shown in Eq.5.(5) A F  = A T  + A R  + A C      Where AF   is the total area where floods occur, AT   is the flooded area affected by tide level, AR   is the flooded area affected by rainfall, and AC   is the flooded area affected by the compound influence of rainfall and tide level. For any of the areas affected by different flood drivers, the calculated equation of its area is shown in Eq.6.(6) A = ∑ i = 1  n   a i      Where A  is the area affected by a certain flood driver, and ai   is the area of the i- th grid (the smallest computational cell in the two-dimensional flooding calculation). In this study, three cases are developed to delineate the influence area of rainfall and tide level. Given that both the flood protection standard for Haikou and the design standard for urban rivers are 50 years, a return period of 50 years was selected for the combined flooding scenario involving heavy rainfall and high tide events. Case 1: The boundary condition is rainfall with a 50-year return period and average tide level from 1974 to 2012. The purpose of this case is to investigate the impact of heavy rainfall on coastal urban flooding; Case 2: The boundary condition is rainfall with a 2-year return period and tide level with a 50-year return period. This case aims to probe the impact of high tide levels on coastal urban flooding; Case 3: The boundary condition is rainfall and tide level with the same return period of 50 years. This case aims to explore the compound influence of heavy rainfall and high tide levels on coastal urban flooding. The maximum inundation depths of grid i  under cases 1, 2, and 3 are hih  , his  and hip  , respectively. For the tidal-affected area, the tide level is the main flood driver, while there is little effect of rainfall. Therefore, the grid i  of tidal-affected area should meet the following conditions:(7) h ip    - h ih   ≥ α    h ip   - h is    < β             Where α  is the minimum value of the excess of the primary flood driver in the tidal-affected area, and β  is the maximum value of the excess of the secondary flood driver in the tidal-affected area. In the rainfall-affected area, heavy rainfall is the dominant flood driver, and the influence of tide could be neglected. Thus, the grid i  of the rainfall-affected area should satisfy the following conditions:(8) h ip   - h is   ≥ α    h ip   - h ih   < β              In the compound-influenced area, rainfall and tide level are both flood drivers that cannot be ignored, so the grid i  of the co-influence area should satisfy the following conditions:(9) h i p   - h i s   ≥ α    h i p   - h i h   ≥ α             The priority of the compound-influenced area in the regional division is greater than the rainfall-affected area and tidal-affected area. For example, if an area meets the conditions of both rainfall-affected area and compound-influenced area, the area will be regarded as the compound-influenced area.  3.3 Flood regulation measures based on inland rivers In this study, flood control measures based on inland rivers are proposed to regulate floods in zones of different flood drivers. In China, the water level of urban inland rivers is usually lowered before the onset of heavy rainfall to meet the urban drainage demand. Some researchers have studied specific measures for tidal-affected zones and rainfall-affected zones (Shen et al., 2019 ), but few studies have proposed regulation methods for urban inland rivers. Therefore, to fill the research gap, this study only considers the flood regulation methods of urban inland rivers. The river flow is used as the control condition, and the initial river flow is changed to regulate the urban flooding. Specifically, given rainfall and tide levels with the same return periods of 50 years as constant inputs, the urban flooding model based on PCSWMM is conducted under different inland river flows. As a result, the average inundation depth of rainfall-affected area and tidal-affected area are calculated. In practical applications, the influence of the rainfall-affected and the tidal-affected area by urban flooding can be minimized by controlling the inland river flow according to the results.   4 Results 4.1 Construction and calibration of the urban flooding model The developed numerical simulation model is shown in Fig. 5  . There are 4961 junctions, 4932 pipelines, and 53 sub-catchments in the model. The measured inundation data during Typhoon Rammasun in July 2014 was utilized for parameter validation of the model. The calibrated parameters of PCSWMM are shown in Table 1  . There are 5 observation points in Fig. 6   for measuring inundation depth during floods. Table 2   exhibits the error between the measured inundation depth and simulated inundation depth by PCSWMM. The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) coefficient is 0.86. It indicates the model constructed in this paper has a high reliability.  4.2 Flood zoning under the compound effects of heavy rainfall and high tide levels 4.2.1 Flood zoning results The calibrated PCSWMM model is used to run three cases to divide the study area into the rainfall-affected area, tidal-affected area, and compound-influenced area. Considering the physical interpretations of α  and β , along with the required simulation accuracy of PCSWMM for flood control applications in Haikou City, 0.01 m is chosen for both α  and β . In case 1, the model was run with the 50-year return period rainfall and the average tidal process from 1974 to 2012. The model results for this case are shown in Fig. 7  a. In case 2, the model was run with the 50-year return period tide level and 2-year return period rainfall. The model results for this case are shown in Fig. 7 b. Finally, in case 3, the model was run using both the 50-year return period rainfall and tidal process. The model results for this case are shown in Fig. 7 c. The flood zoning results were carried out by employing the zonation method for flood drivers, as shown in Fig. 7 d. The zoning analysis revealed that 26.06 % of the study area was inundated. This inundated area can be further subdivided based on the primary flood driver. Area tidally influenced comprised 3.48 % of the total inundated area. The compound-influenced area, affected by both rainfall and tide levels, accounted for 39.05 %. The largest portion (57.47 %) was the rainfall-affected area. Due to the rainfall-affected area being far from the ocean, flooding in this area is primarily attributed to inadequate drainage capacity for rainwater. The tidal-affected area closer to the coastline is more susceptible to flooding due to the jacking effects of high tides. The co-influenced zone typically occupies the interface between the rainfall-affected area and the tidal-affected area. Within these flood-prone areas, rainwater runoff is impeded by the capacity limitations of the pipe network and the river. Additionally, high tides can act as a backwater effect, further elevating water levels and exacerbating the severity of flooding events.  4.2.2 Comparative analysis of tide tracer results and zoning results This study constructed a tracer model of the tidal jacking effect based on the tracer method to calculate the zoning results. Tracer simulations were conducted for tides using the rainfall and tides with a return period of 50 years as model inputs. The tracer results and zoning results are presented in Fig. 8  . To analyze the spatial relationship between flooding points affected by tides (including both the tidal-affected zone and the compound-influenced zone) and the pipeline with tracer, a neighborhood search analysis was conducted. The analysis used the pipeline with tracer as the reference point and identified the flooding points affected by tides comprised 94 % of total flooding points within 10 m range. Furthermore, the density analysis module in ArcGIS was employed to calculate the correlation coefficient between the densities of flooded points and the pipeline with tracer, both represented as raster data sets within the same spatial extent. The resulting correlation coefficient is 0.84. It can be considered that the densities of flooded points and the pipeline with tracer are highly correlated. Thus, the reliability of the tracer model of tidal jacking and the zoning results for flood drivers are further verified.   4.3 Impact assessment of urban inland river 4.3.1 Impact of inland river on urban flooding Within the study area, inland rivers play a critical role in flood discharge. To assess the impact of inland river flow on flooded areas, this study adopts river discharge as the control variable. We sequentially increase the inland river flow while maintaining constant tide levels and rainfall conditions. The resulting simulations for two typical cases are presented in Fig. 9  . As the inland flow increased from 15 m3 /s to 25 m3 /s, the inundated area decreased by 3.71 %. This decrease in the inundated area occurred in the compound-influenced area and tidal-affected area, while the inundated area in the rainfall-affected area increased. The results indicate that an increase in inland river flow elevates the risk of flooding within the rainfall-affected area. In addition, the impact of the inland river on the tidal-affected area and the compound-influenced area is mainly because the water in the river restricts the process of tidal backflow. Furthermore, this study explored the effect of inland river flow on the flooded area based on the water tracer model. Rainfall and tide levels with the same return period of 50 years were selected as inputs to the model. The tracer simulation for the river was carried out under the inland river flow of 15 and 25 m3 /s, respectively. The maximum concentrations of tracer at the surface are shown in Fig. 10  . Analysis of tracer concentration results reveals that when the inland river flow rate is below 25 m3 /s, the urban inland river does not directly cause flooding within the tidal-affected area. Instead, it primarily exhibits hydraulic and water volume exchange between the inland river flow and water flows from other sources. This is because as the inland river flow increases, the flow entering the tidal-affected area also increases. This portion of the flow initially prevents the tide from backflow, thereby reducing the extent of flooding in the tidal-affected area. From the perspective of tracer concentration changes, a small amount of overflow occurs in the inland river due to the water level of the river rising rapidly under intensive rainstorms. As a result, the tracer migrates to both sides of the river along with the water flow. In addition, the range of tracer concentration grows as the inland river flow increases. This indicates that an enlargement in inland river flow augments the risk of inundation in the rainfall-affected area.  4.3.2 The connection of hydraulic and water volume between inland river and drainage networks To investigate the connection of hydraulic and water volume between inland rivers and pipe networks, this study established a comprehensive river flow simulation model based on the hydrological and hydrodynamic modules and the water quality module of PCSWMM. This model enables real-time tracking of water flow between rivers and pipe networks. Since the flow rate of inland rivers is relatively small, the initial tracer concentration in each river section was set to 10 mg/L to better study the flow characteristics of inland rivers. Once the tracer with identical concentrations was generated, it was allocated to the land use of each catchment. The tracer flow with the inland rivers will follow rivers going into adjacent pipelines if there is a hydraulic and water volume connection between the river and the pipeline network. The method for setting river tracers is shown in the Fig. 11  . The analysis demonstrates the significant influence of urban inland rivers on zoning results. A tracer model for inland river flow was employed to examine the hydraulic interaction between the river and the pipeline network. We maintain constant tide level and rainfall while simulating tracer movement of inland rivers under the river flow of 5, 15, 25, and 45 m3 /s. The simulation results are presented in Fig. 12  . As illustrated in Fig. 12 , the influence of river discharge on the drainage network expands gradually towards both banks with increasing river flow. When river discharge reaches 25 m3 /s, tracer concentration diffuses into the tidal-affected area, intensifying the impact of river discharge on the tidal-affected area and further hindering tidal jacking and backflow. When river discharge further increases to 45 m3 /s, the increase in flow significantly reduces the drainage capacity of the drainage network, leading to exacerbated flooding in the study area. As river discharge increases, the distribution range of river tracers gradually grows from 18.5 % to 28.0 % as shown in Fig. 13  . The accumulated tracer mass of the pipes within the areas is higher than in other areas. The results demonstrate that the drainage network in the areas of dense river networks exhibits frequent hydraulic exchange with river water. Moreover, the tracer range of pipes within the tidal-affected area and rainfall-affected area expands with the river discharge increases, but the growth in the tidal-affected area is more pronounced.   4.4 Flood regulation results of inland river flow in the study area Based on the compound flood zoning of heavy rainfall and high tide levels and the impact assessment of inland rivers, the catchment T with the largest tidal-affected area in the study area was selected as the typical tidal-affected area. The catchment H with a large rainfall-affected area and proximity to the rivers in the study area was selected as the typical rainfall-affected area. The locations of the two areas are shown in Fig. 14  a. Referring to the flood control planning of Haikou City, the inland river flows were set to 5, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 45 m3 /s, respectively. The average depth of inundation in the flooded area was used as the comparison index. The simulation results are shown in Fig. 14 b. With the increase in river flow, the average inundation depth of the tidal-affected area, represented by the study area T, initially decreases before rising again. This is primarily attributed to tidal jacking and backflow. Specifically, inland rivers with a flow rate of less than 25 m3 /s partially prevent seawater backflow, thereby reducing the average inundation depth of the study area T. However, rivers with a flow rate exceeding 25 m3 /s impede the normal drainage of study area T, leading to inundation in surrounding areas. The average inundation depth of the study area H increases with the rise in river flow. This is because the river serves as the primary drainage channel for the study area H, and its drainage capacity decreases with increasing river flow. In summary, coastal cities, when facing impending heavy rainfall, should control the flow of inland rivers within a certain range if tidal-affected areas constitute a significant proportion. Conversely, if rainfall-affected areas dominate, efforts should be made to minimize the flow of inland rivers.   5 Discussion and conclusion At present, few studies have explored the impact of inland river flows on floods in areas affected by different flood drivers. To fill this gap, a catchment area in Haikou City, Hainan Province, China is used as a case study, this paper uses the water tracer method based on the urban flood model to calculate the flood degree of each flood zone under different inland river flows. According to this, flood regulation measures based on urban inland rivers are proposed. The flood zones are determined by processing the flood simulation results under 3 cases, and then are verified with the zoning results based on the tide tracer approach. At last, the tracer method is used to study the impact of urban inland rivers on flooding and the connection of hydraulic and water volume between rivers and pipelines. The results indicate that the inundation area decreased by 3.71 % as the river flow increased from 15 to 25 m3 /s. In the process of river flow rising from 5 to 45 m3 /s, The average flooding depth in the rainfall-affected area climbs slowly from 0.53 m to 0.62 m; In the tidal-affected area, the average flooding depth drops from 0.52 m to 0.12 m when the inland river flow increases from 5 to 25 m3 /s, and rises from 0.12 m to 0.54 m when the inland river flow continues from 25 to 45 m3 /s; The percentage of pipelines grows from 18.5 % to 28.0 %. This study provides scientific support for flood prevention planning and flood control strategies based on urban inland rivers in coastal cities. This study conducted on the numerical simulation model based on PCSWMM. Due to the scarce of observed data, however, the methods of this study are not used in real world. With the development of measurement technology, the application of water tracing method on the effect of urban inland rivers on flooding will be studied in practical scenarios.
1 Introduction In terrestrial vegetated ecosystems, the growth, structure, and productivity of vegetation are strongly governed by access to water and nutrients (Fernández-Martínez et al., 2014; Gebauer and Ehleringer, 2000; Lebauer and Treseder, 2008; Ma et al., 2021 ). Incident gross rainfall is partitioned into interception loss (IL), throughfall (TF), and stemflow (SF) by passing through vegetation canopies, which greatly alters the hydrological and chemical fluxes between vegetation and soil (Levia and Germer, 2015; Llorens and Domingo, 2007; Parker, 1983; Yuan et al., 2022 ). These alterations affect water and nutrient balances at local, catchment, and regional scales (Oda et al., 2019; Wang and Wang, 2020; Zhu et al., 2019 ), highlighting their pivotal significance for the functioning and sustainability of vegetated ecosystems. Hydrologically, IL represents the portion of rainfall lost to vegetation systems (a global median of 21.8 %), directly evaporating back into the atmosphere during and after rainfall events (Lian et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2021 ). TF, constituting the major share of rainfall (a global median of 75.8 %), reaches the under-canopy soil by dripping from canopy as released throughfall (subdivided into canopy drip and splash throughfall) and/or by penetrating through the canopy as free throughfall (Dunkerley, 2000; Levia et al., 2017 ). SF, a highly localized point input, accounts for a smaller fraction of rainfall (a global median of 2.7 %), flowing down the trunks/stems (Levia and Frost, 2003; Zhang et al., 2021 ). However, SF assumes disproportionate significance due to its “double funneling” effect (Guo et al., 2020 ; Johnson and Lehmann, 2006 ; Li et al., 2013; Schwärzel et al., 2012 ). Chemically, solutes in TF and SF are greatly altered through canopy exchange processes (uptake or leaching) and the wash-off of dry deposition from vegetation canopy surfaces (Levia et al., 2011b; Neary and Gizyn, 1994; Parker, 1983; Ponette-González, 2021; Tonello et al., 2021 ). The extent of these alterations is associated with climatic conditions and airmass provenance, vegetation composition and physiological activity, and proximity to industrial sources, among others (Jochheim et al., 2022; Levia and Germer, 2015; Siegert et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2021 ). The pronounced differences between TF and SF, regarding their flowpaths and residence times along vegetative surfaces, result in notable distinctions in solute concentrations and mass fluxes of canopy leachates (Jiang et al., 2021; Levia et al., 2011a; Yuan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Recent synthesis studies and/or quantitative reviews have elucidated the hydrological patterns of rainfall partitioning components by vegetation and their potential drivers at regional or global scales (e.g., Llorens and Domingo 2007, Whitworth-Hulse et al., 2021, Yue et al., 2021, Zhang et al., 2021, 2023, Magliano et al., 2022 ). Moreover, numerous field studies have illustrated the chemical alteration of TF and/or SF by specific nutrient-ions for specific plant species/community at specific sites. Both chemical enrichment (which seems to be more common) and depletion were found for TF and SF in the literature. Despite these valuable insights, there are rather few macro-level quantitative syntheses and meta-analyses concerning the chemical alteration of rainfall as it traverses vegetative canopies. This gap leaves the scientific community inadequately informed about the general patterns and magnitudes of the chemical alterations of TF and SF. Conducting such an analysis would help to bridge this existing gap and enhance our understanding and estimation of the relevance of rainfall partitioning to nutrient budgets at regional or global scales. China, with its vast territory (∼9.6 million km2 ) and diverse ecosystems influenced by variable climatic conditions, has been the focus of numerous studies on rainfall partitioning (Supplementary Figure S1 ). A recent synthesis paper systematically quantified the hydrological fractions of rainfall partitioning by vegetation in China (Zhang et al., 2023 ). In terms of the chemical aspect, another dimension of rainfall partitioning by vegetation, a quantitative synthesis and meta-analysis of the existing studies in China would be critical for holistically assessing the nutrients balance of vegetated ecosystems within China. Here, we provide a comprehensive dataset of the chemistry of rainfall partitioning by vegetation in China, compiled from 131 papers (28 in English and 103 in Chinese) published between 1988 and 2023 (Supplementary Figure S1 ; Appendix S1). The dataset includes pH, TN (total nitrogen), TP (total phosphorus), and 12 other commonly reported nutrient-ions (K+ , Na+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Mn2+ , Zn2+ , Cu2+ , NH4 + , NO3 − , SO4 2− , Cl− , and PO4 3− ) in rainfall, TF, and SF, along with data of twelve potential drivers that are presumed to affect chemical properties during the rainfall partitioning process (Supplementary Data S1 ). The focus on these particular ions is necessary because they are important to plant metabolism (see Marschner, 1995 ). For example, K+  and NO3 −  are of importance to osmoregulation, whereas enzyme activation and protein synthesis utilize Mg2+ , Mn2+ , and Cu2+  (Marschner, 1995; Nagajyoti et al., 2010 ). Further, Ca2+  plays a role in signal transduction and cell wall stabilization, while Na+  is important for cell compartmentation (Marschner, 1995 ). We aimed to (1) investigate the general characteristics of rainfall partitioning in terms of chemical alteration in China; (2) determine whether and to what extent the chemical composition of rainwater is altered during rainfall partitioning into TF and SF; and (3) identify the key drivers and further elucidate their partial effects on the magnitude of chemical alteration in TF and SF. The study contributes a valuable dataset to global rainfall partitioning database, and provides a comprehensive and quantitative evaluation of chemical alterations in rainfall partitioning fluxes across China.  2 Methods 2.1 Data collection and compilation We conducted a thorough and systematic literature search, compiling peer-reviewed papers published before 2023 (inclusive) from Web of Science (WoS) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI; https://www.cnki.net/ ) using the following keyword combination (and their equivalents in Chinese): [(“stemflow” OR “stem flow” OR “throughfall” OR “rainfall interception” OR “rainfall partitioning” OR “precipitation interception” OR “precipitation partitioning” OR “rainfall redistribution” OR “precipitation redistribution”) AND (“China” OR “Chinese”)]. This search yielded a total of 1845 peer-reviewed papers (937 in WoS and 908 in CNKI), with 1629 unique records remaining after removal of duplicates (see Supplementary Figure S2  for the PRISMA diagram). Subsequently, each paper underwent scrutiny to assess whether the studies fulfilled the following criteria: (a) studies were exclusively conducted in China; (b) data were exclusively obtained from field experiments; (c) reporting the mean values (along with standard deviations and sample sizes) of pH, and/or TN, and/or TP, and/or at least one of the commonly reported ions (K+ , Na+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Mn2+ , Zn2+ , Cu2+ , NH4 + , NO3 − , SO4 2− , Cl− , and PO4 3− ) in rainfall and in at least one of TF or SF; (d) when multiple papers were published on the same plant species/community at the same study site, preference was given to the longest study. In total, we discerned 131 papers (28 in English and 103 in Chinese) that met our aforementioned criteria for data extraction (a list of the papers could be found in the Supplementary Appendix S1). These studies were published between 1988 and 2023 (Supplementary Figure S1 ) and were conducted across a total of 97 field sites (Fig. 1  ). The means, standard deviations (SD), and sample sizes (n ) were extracted from the main text, tables, and figures. Data extraction from figures employed GetData Graph Digitizer (version 2.26). In instances where studies reported standard error (SE) instead of SD, the SD was derived using the formula SE×n     . For TN, TP, and 12 nutrient-ions, the units of concentration were standardized to mg L−1 . Additionally, we extracted information pertaining to three climatic variables and eight vegetation metrics (Table 1  ) that are considered to affect the chemical attributes of rainfall partitioning into TF and SF (Levia and Germer, 2015; Ponette-González et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023 ), including mean annual precipitation (MAP, mm), mean annual temperature (MAT, ℃), wind speed (m/s), forest type (natural forests, plantations), stand height (m), stand density (individuals ha−1 ), diameter at breast height (cm), canopy density (%), leaf phenology (deciduous, evergreen, mixed), leaf type (broad, needle, mixed), and bark texture (smooth, rough, mixed). In cases where original articles omitted reporting MAP, MAT, and mean wind speed, the values were derived from the WorldClim database (Fick and Hijmans, 2017 ) using the location information (latitude and longitude) with a spatial resolution of ∼ 1 km2 . In instances where leaf type, leaf phenology, or bark texture could not be deduced from the original articles, this information was obtained from the “Chinese Virtual Herbarium” (https://www.cvh.ac.cn ) and “National Specimen Information Infrastructure” (http://www.nsii.org.cn ). Anthropogenic activities also influence the chemistry of TF and SF (e.g., Wood and Bormann, 1975; Rodrigo et al., 2003; Imamura et al., 2023 ). The Human Footprint (HFP) index (ranging 0–50) was selected as it reflects synthesized effect of multiple anthropogenic activities (built environments, population density, electric infrastructure, crop lands, pasture lands, roads, railways, and navigable waterways) (Venter et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2020; Mu et al., 2022 ). A higher HFP typically indicates more intense anthropogenic activities, and consequently, more anthropogenic sources. The HFP data was sourced from Mu et al. (2022)  based on the location information. The final dataset can be found in Supplementary Data S1 .  2.2 Data analysis We employed a meta-analysis to assess the chemical alterations as GR is partitioned into TF and SF, using Hedges’ g  as an estimate of the unbiased standardized mean difference (SMD) (Hedges and Vevea, 1998 ). Hedges’ g  is a useful effect size and has been widely used in ecological meta-analysis (Gu et al., 2023; Rossetti et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2020; Whitworth-Hulse et al., 2021; Závorka et al., 2018 ) because it statistically corrects for variance that may be introduced when sample sizes are small (Hedges, 1981 ). For each comparison, the SMD was calculated as (m1i – m2i)/spi, where m1i and m2i denote the mean pH or the mean concentrations of TN, TP and each nutrient-ion for TF and GR (or SF and GR), and spi is the pooled standard deviation of the two groups (Viechtbauer, 2010 ). A random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation was fitted via the R package “metafor” (Viechtbauer, 2010 ). Hedges’ g  effect sizes were considered significantly different from zero if their 95 % confidence intervals (CI) did not encompass zero (Borenstein et al., 2009 ). For pH, negative mean effect sizes indicate an acidification effect in TF (or SF) in comparison to GR, whereas positive values suggest the opposite. For TN, TP and nutrient-ions, positive mean effect sizes signify that chemical concentrations in TF (or SF) are significantly higher than in GR, exhibiting significant chemical enrichment after rainfall partitioning into TF (or SF), whereas negative values indicate chemical depletion. We assessed the possibility of publication bias by testing the significance of asymmetry of the funnel plots with Egger’s regression test (Egger et al., 1997 ). Egger’s regression test was significant (p  < 0.05) for pH and some ions, suggesting possible publication bias (Supplementary Table S1 ). We then calculated the Rosenthal’s fail-safe number to assess the robustness of our results (Rosenberg, 2005 ). For cases exhibiting possible publication bias, we found that the observed Rosenthal’s fail-safe numbers were considerably larger than 5 k  + 10 (k  is the number of studies) (Supplementary Table S1 ), indicating that results are robust regardless of publication bias. As such, we did not consider publication bias to be a concern for interpretation of the results. We also conducted a sensitivity test with leave-one-out analysis using the “leave1out ” function from “metafor” package, and found our findings are unlikely to be driven by a single influential study (Supplementary Figure S3 ). To quantify the modification of vegetation canopy on rainwater chemistry, we calculated the concentration-based enrichment ratio for TN, TP and each nutrient-ion by dividing the chemical concentration in TF (or SF) by that in GR (André et al., 2008 ). For the change in pH, we calculated the difference of pH value between TF (or SF) and GR. We then compared the differences in the change of pH and the enrichment ratios of TN, TP, and each nutrient-ion between TF and SF using a Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test due to data non-normality. Differences were considered statistically significant at p  < 0.05. We used boosted regression trees (BRT) to determine the relative influence and the partial effects of twelve predictor variables (Table 1 ) on the effect sizes of pH, TN, TP, and studied nutrient-ions (Mn2+ , Zn2+ , Cu2+ , and PO4 3−  were excluded due to limited observations) for TF and SF, respectively. BRT, an advanced statistical learning technique, sequentially fits numerous simple regression trees in a forward, stagewise manner before combining them into a final predictive model (Elith et al., 2008 ). Alongside its high predictive performance, BRT deals adeptly with different types of response and predictor variables and outcomes are unaffected by differing measurement scales among predictors, is robust to missing values and outliers in predictor variables, accommodates non-linear relationships, and automatically captures interaction effects between predictor variables (Elith et al., 2008 ). Given the diverse variable types and the presence of missing values within some predictor variables, the BRT approach is a logical choice for our analyses. BRT models were fitted using “gbm.step” function of the R package “dismo” (Hijmans et al., 2022 ), with ten-fold cross-validation (CV) applied to tune model parameters and assess model performance. Three meta-parameters require tuning in a BRT model: tree complexity (tc ; determines the number of interactions), learning rate (lr ; regulates the contribution of each new tree), and bag fraction (bf ; specifies the proportion of data to be randomly selected at each iteration) (Elith et al., 2008 ). We tested the following meta-parameter settings: tc  = 1–5, lr  = 0.05, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001 and 0.0005, bf  = 0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, and 0.80, resulting in 175 models for each response variable (the effect sizes of pH, TN, TP and nutrient-ions). We then selected the optimal settings (Supplementary Table S2 ) with the lowest CV deviance (squared error) while containing a minimum of 1000 trees to generate the final BRT models. Model performance was mainly assessed on the training data (deviance explained, %) and on predictions to test data (CV deviance explained, %) (Supplementary Table S3 ), enabling us to evaluate our ability to explain observed data and predict hold-out data, respectively (Buston and Elith, 2011 ). Relative influence (RI) scores of individual predictors were calculated based on the number of times a predictor is selected for splitting, weighted by the squared improvement to the model, and averaged across all trees (Elith et al., 2008 ). RI scores are scaled so that all predictors sum to 100 %, and predictors with a RI score above that expected by chance (100/number of predictors) are considered significant, with higher values indicating stronger influence (Elith et al., 2008; Jouffray et al., 2019; Muller et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Partial dependence plots (PDPs) were then provided to visualize the partial effect of these significant predictors on the effect sizes. The x -axis depicts the distribution of the data points, and the PDPs flatten in regions without change or where data are unavailable. For enhanced interpretation, the actual response plots were also smoothed using a smoothing spline. All statistical analyses were conducted within the R statistical framework (R Core Team, 2023 ), mainly using the following packages: “dismo” (Hijmans et al., 2022 ), “ggBRT” (Jouffray, 2022 ), “ggthemes” (Arnold, 2021 ), “metafor” (Viechtbauer, 2010 ), “patchwork” (Pedersen, 2022 ), “raster” (Hijmans, 2023 ), “rstatix” (Kassambara, 2021 ), and “tidyverse” (Wickham et al., 2019 ).   3 Results 3.1 Field studies of chemical alteration in rainfall partitioning by vegetation in China We identified a total of 97 study sites (spanning 19.5–53.4 °N and 87.2–130.7 °E), with data being scarce for the northwestern part of China (Fig. 1 a). These study sites exhibited a broad spectrum of MAP (110–3634 mm) and MAT (−5.3–25.5 ℃), with MAP mostly below 2000 mm (Fig. 1 b). The sites were predominantly designated as forests, with only three sites designated as shrubland (Fig. 1 a). According to the Whittaker biome classification, studies were mostly concentrated in temperate seasonal forests and tropical seasonal forests (Fig. 1 b). Five of the most studied genera included Pinus , Castanopsis , Cunninghamia , Quercus , and Betula . For Mn2+ , Zn2+ , Cu2+ , and PO4 3− , observations were relatively limited (n  < 30).  3.2 Chemical alterations as GR partitions into TF and SF The mean effect size (Hedges’ g ) of pH for SF (mean =  − 2.11; 95 % CI= − 2.74 to − 1.47) was significantly (p  < 0.001) lower than zero, suggesting the pronounced acidification effect as rainfall partitions into SF; whereas the effect size of pH for TF (mean =  − 0.05; 95 % CI= − 0.50 to 0.40) did not differ significantly (p  > 0.05) from zero, suggesting pH was similar between TF and rainfall (Fig. 2  ). Effect sizes of nearly all other studied chemical species were significantly higher than zero (p  < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001) for TF and SF, respectively. The exceptions showed that the effect size of Cu2+  did not differ significantly (p  > 0.05) from zero for both TF and SF, and of Zn2+  for TF, and that the effect size of Zn2+  was significantly lower (p  < 0.05) than zero for SF (Fig. 2 ). Noteworthy ions such as K+ , Mg2+ , SO4 2− , and Cl− , as well as TP demonstrated relatively higher effect sizes. The individual forest plots for pH, TN, TP, and each of studied nutrient-ions can be found in Supplementary Figures S4 and S5 . Significant differences were found in the changes of pH between TF and SF with GR as the baseline (p  < 0.0001; median: −0.13 for TF vs. − 0.70 for SF). Significant differences were also detected in the concentration-based enrichment ratio between TF and SF for TN (p  < 0.001; median: 1.4 vs. 2.3), TP (p  < 0.05; median: 1.9 vs. 2.8), K+  (p  < 0.0001; median: 4.0 vs. 8.1), Na+  (p  < 0.0001; median: 1.2 vs. 2.1), Ca2+  (p  < 0.01; median: 1.9 vs. 2.2), Mg2+  (p  < 0.0001; median: 2.6 vs. 4.3), Mn2+  (p  < 0.01; median: 3.2 vs. 6.2), NH4 +  (p  < 0.0001; median: 1.4 vs. 2.2), NO3 −  (p  < 0.01; median: 1.5 vs. 2.1), and SO4 2−  (p  < 0.0001; median: 2.0 vs. 3.2), respectively (Fig. 3  ). The differences, however, were not significant (p  > 0.05) between SF and TF for Zn2+  (median: 1.0 vs. 1.4), Cu2+  (median: 1.2 vs. 1.4), Cl−  (median: 2.4 vs. 2.7), and PO4 3−  (median: 1.8 vs. 1.2) (Fig. 3 ).  3.3 Effects of biotic and abiotic predictors on the chemical alteration of rainfall partitioning BRT models performed well in predicting the effect size of pH, TN, TP and nutrient-ions for TF (explained 34.8–99.8 % of the deviance for training data and 18.6–69.6 % for hold-out data using CV) and SF (explained 80.9–99.3 % of the deviance for training data and 39.2–85.0 % for hold-out data using CV), although relatively weak for that of K+  (35.1 % and 5.8 %) and Na+  (15.1 % and 1.3 %) for TF, and that of TN (45.5 % and 2.3 %) for SF (Supplementary Table S3 ). Fig. 4   shows the RI scores of individual predictors on the effect sizes of pH, TN, TP, and nutrient-ions for TF (Fig. 4 a) and SF (Fig. 4 b), respectively, and the PDPs for the significant predictors are shown for TF in Fig. 5   and for SF in Fig. 6  . In general, MAP, MAT, wind speed, and HFP emerged as significant predictors for all effect sizes (except occasionally for a few chemical species) with high RI scores (Fig. 4 ). PDPs revealed that MAP generally exerted a positive effect on the effect sizes, whereas MAT, wind speed, and HFP displayed varying trends (positive, negative, initially positive and subsequently negative, or initially negative and subsequently positive) depending on the response variables (Figs. 5 and 6 ). For example, regarding the effect sizes for TF (Fig. 5 ), HFP generally exhibited a positive effect on TN (19.2 %), NH4 +  (14.8 %), and NO3 −  (16.3 %), a negative effect on pH (13.4 %), TP (72.3 %), Na+  (34.2 %), and Cl−  (10.9 %), an initially positive and subsequently negative effect on Mg2+  (29.3 %), and an initially negative and subsequently positive effect on K+  (28.0 %) and SO4 2−  (19.2 %). For vegetation metrics, DBH exerted significant effects on the effect size of pH, TN, TP, and most nutrient-ions for TF (except for Na+ , Mg2+ , SO4 2− , and Cl− ) and SF (except for Na+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and SO4 2− ), with partial effects exhibiting divergence (positive or negative) depending on individual chemical species or nutrient-ions. For example, DBH generally had positive effects on the effect size of TN (33.5 %), and K+  (11.3 %) for TF, but negative effects on that of pH (10.0 %), TP (10.0 %), NH4 +  (15.5 %), and NO3 −  (16.4 %) for TF (Fig. 5 ). Stand height emerged as a significant predictor, with positive effects on the effect size of pH (13.6 %) for TF, and on the effect size of TP (19.3 %), Na+  (9.5 %), NH4 +  (9.2 %) and NO3 −  (22.4 %) for SF, but negative effects on the effect size of pH (24.3 %) for SF and of Ca2+  (9.9 %) and NO3 −  (8.7 %) for TF. Bark texture was significant for the effect size of Cl−  (9.3 % and 15.2 %) for both TF and SF, and of TN (14.0 %) and TP (16.3 %) for SF, with smooth bark exerting a greater impact on Cl−  and mixed bark textures exerting a greater impact on TN and TP. Forest type was only significant for the effect size of NO3 −  (10.4 %) for SF, with plantations exerting a more pronounced effect. Canopy density was only significant for the effect size of NH4 +  (16.7 %) for TF, exerting a positive effect. Leaf type, leaf phenology and stand density were not identified as significant drivers for all the effect sizes (Figs. 5 and 6 ).   4 Discussion We complied a comprehensive chemistry dataset pertaining to rainfall partitioning by vegetation in China, synthesizing information from 131 peer-reviewed papers (28 in English and 103 in Chinese) published hitherto (Fig. 1 ). This dataset stands as a valuable supplement to the global rainfall partitioning database, particular considering that four-fifths of these studies have been published in Chinese and are largely inaccessible to international readers. We noted that most of the aforementioned studies were conducted in forests, and data are scarce for the vast northwestern part of China where the land cover is dominated by grassland. As such, our dataset contributes significantly to the accurate and comprehensive estimation of nutrient budgets within forest ecosystems in China, while highlighting the pressing need for future studies in other vegetated ecosystems such as shrublands, croplands, and grasslands. Furthermore, we observed distinct attention given to certain ions, with pH, K+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , NO3 − , and NH4 +  being extensively studied, whereas Mn2+ , Zn2+ , Cu2+ , and PO4 3−  were least reported, and others (TN, TP, Na+ , SO4 2− , and Cl− ) fell into an intermediate category (Fig. 2 ). Our meta-analysis revealed that the mean effect size of pH was significantly (p  < 0.001) lower than zero for SF, but did not differ significantly (p  > 0.05) from zero for TF (Fig. 2 ), suggesting that acidification occurs in SF but not in TF as rainfall passes through the canopy (Fig. 7  ). In general, the acidification observed in SF can be attributed to two principal mechanisms: the input of H+  into SF through the dissolution of both organic and inorganic acids, and the ion exchange reaction (Fillion et al., 1998; Satake et al., 1996; Takenaka and Sasama, 2000 ). The latter process takes place between the protons of water-insoluble acidic groups, such as carboxyl groups (R-COOH) present in the bark, and the cations in initial stemflow or rainwater, and has been acknowledged as the more decisive contributor to the observed acidification phenomenon (Nakanishi et al., 2001; Takenaka and Sasama, 2000 ). The minimal alteration in pH values observed in TF may be attributed to its notably shorter contact time and insufficient interaction with canopy tissues, particularly the trunk bark, which limits the extent of acids input and ion exchange reaction, although canopy drip throughfall originating from foliar or structurally-mediated woody surface drip points has variable residence times in the canopy (Nanko et al., 2022 ). The repercussions of stemflow acidification may extend to the pH of the soil beneath the canopy affected by SF (Aboal et al., 2015; Corti et al., 2019; Falkengren-Grerup and Bjork, 1991 ). This, in the long run, may influence microenvironments, species composition, and density of soil microflora and fauna around tree trunks (Aboal et al., 2015; Scheu and Poser, 1996 ), potentially affecting other soil processes such as decomposition and predation beneath the canopy. For TN, TP, and the 12 studied nutrient-ions, we observed prevalent and significant chemical enrichment (p  < 0.05) in both TF and SF, with non-detectable exceptions for Cu2+  of both TF and SF and a significant depletion for Zn2+  of SF (Figs. 2 and 7 ). Dry deposition wash-off and canopy exchange (uptake or leaching) are considered to determine the chemical alteration in TF and SF (André et al., 2008; Fan and Wei, 2001; Levia et al., 2011b; Neary and Gizyn, 1994 ). Therefore, for most of the nutrient-ions examined, the prevalent enrichment implies that dry deposition wash-off and/or canopy leaching by rainwater play more substantial role than canopy uptake, leading to a substantial input of nutrients into the soil below vegetation canopies. Particularly noteworthy is the high enrichment observed for K+ , Cl− , Mg2+ , and TP in both TF and SF. A dominant source of chloride is sea spray, while phosphorus is not typically exuded directly from canopy as it is tightly cycled and a limiting element in unpolluted forests, with both behaving conservatively within the canopy (e.g., Ponette-González et al., 2010; Staelens et al., 2008; Teixeira et al., 2023 ). In fact, dissolved phosphorus levels were most often below detection limits in rainfall and TF in an experiment involving European beech saplings (Michalzik et al., 2016 ). Therefore, the higher enrichment of Cl−  in TF and SF is assumed to primarily originate from wash-off of dry deposition as well as canopy leaching, especially during emergence (Staelens et al., 2007; Siegert et al., 2017 ). Higher enrichment of TP in TF and SF is attributable to anthropogenic sources, likely linked to the proximity to industrial areas and intensive farming practices. The depletion of Zn2+  in SF may suggest that canopy uptake played a dominant role, possibly since Zn2+  is a plant micronutrient used for enzyme activation and protein synthesis (Brown et al., 1993 ). The heterogeneous flow of rainwater over space and time, generated by rainfall partitioning into TF and SF, inevitably influences the heterogeneity and availability of enriched nutrients in soils, resulting in biogeochemical “hot spots” and “hot moments” beneath vegetation canopies (McClain et al., 2003 ). This has been extensively reported to positively affect a wide array of ecosystem processes, such as productivity and nutrient cycling, across diverse ecosystems (e.g., Levia and Germer, 2015; McDowell et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2024 ). For areas experiencing increased loads of nutrient and pollutant deposition due to climate change and/or anthropogenic activities, this chemically enriched water entering the soils via TF and SF may represent an additional environmental stress to ecosystems, potentially leading to changes in species composition and regeneration, microbial activities, and stream water chemistry (e.g., Chen and Mulder, 2007; Chiwa et al., 2003; Ponette-González et al., 2010 ). Additionally, we found that SF was generally more chemically enriched than TF (Figs. 2 and 3 ). The larger chemical enrichment in SF than in TF is partly attributable to the generally longer flow path and residence time of SF than TF before SF was running down the tree trunk/stem (which can have greater leachability than foliage) and then channeled to the soils (Levia et al., 2011a ). Despite SF representing a smaller percentage of GR (median of 2.7 % with the interquartile range of 1.2–6.0 % in China) compared to TF (a median of 74.3 % with the interquartile range of 66.7–80.3 % in China) (Zhang et al., 2023 ), due to SF’s highly-localized point input manner and high funneling ratios per basal area or infiltration area (Carlyle-Moses et al., 2018; Levia and Germer, 2015; Metzger et al., 2021; Niu et al., 2023; Su et al., 2023 ), the nutrients delivered to the soil via SF could be disproportionately substantial compared to that in GR falling over the same area. Neglecting SF, as has conventionally been done, may introduce non-negligible bias in estimating nutrient budgets in vegetated ecosystems. Furthermore, these nutrients are predominantly dissolved, making them readily acquired by plant roots (Hofhansl et al., 2012; Parker, 1983 ). This availability helps to sustain vegetation growth and productivity in terrestrial ecosystems, which is especially important for nutrient-impoverished environments. In drylands, the enrichment of nutrients in SF may constitute a crucial biological mechanism contributing to the formation and evolution of the commonly observed “fertile islands” (Ridolfi et al., 2008; Whitford et al., 1997 ). Climatic conditions, vegetation metrics, and anthropogenic activities are typically considered to affect chemical alterations in TF and SF. Employing a machine learning method (BRT), we quantified the relative influence of twelve biotic (e.g., vegetation structure) and abiotic (e.g., climate) predictors (Fig. 4 ) and elucidated the partial effects of the most influential drivers on the magnitude of chemical alteration (i.e., effect sizes) in TF and SF (Figs. 5 and 6 ), and the BRT models exhibited a commendable explanatory power for most effect sizes (Supplementary Table S3 ). It is noteworthy that MAP, MAT, wind speed, and HFP emerged as significant predictors for most of the effect sizes, usually ranking among the top four drivers, while DBH, stand height, and bark texture were also frequently identified as significant predictors (Figs. 4 and 7 ). BRT models also demonstrated that non-linear relationships are prevalent between effect sizes and their significant drivers. For instance, MAP, MAT, wind speed, HFP, and DBH were identified as the significant drivers affecting the effect size of K+  for both TF (Fig. 5 d) and SF (Fig. 6 d), although the rankings of RI scores were somewhat different between TF and SF. PDPs show that MAP had a generally positive effect on the effect size of K+ ; MAT initially exerted a negative effect on the effect size of K+  for TF, whereas it started positively and turned negatively for SF; HFP initially showed a negative effect on the effect size of K+  for TF and then became positive, while it generally exhibited a positive stagewise effect on that for SF; Wind speed and DBH consistently exerted positive effects. The intricate mechanisms as exemplified above have rarely been explored, and our findings thus contribute valuable insights into the multifaceted relationships between biotic (e.g., vegetation structure) and abiotic (e.g., climate) predictors and the chemical alteration of rainfall partitioning in TF and SF (Fig. 7 ). From a forest management perspective, understanding these impacts is important for comprehensively evaluating forest health and developing effective strategies to mitigate the potential negative effects of chemical enrichment in rainfall partitioning within forest ecosystems. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that our aggregate analysis endeavored to capture macro-level signals and patterns of chemical alterations in rainfall partitioning by vegetation, which may sometimes differ from those obtained through detailed individual studies.  5 Conclusions We provide a comprehensive dataset pertaining to the chemistry aspects of rainfall partitioning by vegetation in China, compiled from 131 peer-reviewed papers published between 1988 and 2023. Our analysis discerned a pronounced acidification in SF but not in TF, and demonstrated a prevalent chemical enrichment in TN, TP, and 12 frequently reported nutrient-ions (except for Cu2+ ) in both TF and SF, with SF generally being more chemically enriched than TF. Employing BRT modeling, we identified the most influential predictors and delineated their non-linear effects on the magnitude of chemical alteration as rainfall partitions into TF and SF. Our findings can facilitate an accurate estimation of nutrient budgets in vegetated ecosystems, deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanisms regulating the chemical alterations of rainfall partitioning by vegetation throughout China, and assist in evaluating forest health and developing effective forest management strategies.
1 Introduction Rivers, integral to human existence, play a crucial role in the sustainability of river ecosystems and their management across the Earth's surface (Polvi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). Despite the pivotal role in the earth's dynamic water cycle, worldwide rivers are facing escalating threats, including increased erosion due to land use changes, sediment trapping by large-scale damming, pollution, and the cascading hydrological and sedimentological impacts of climate change (Jim, 2018; Luo et al., 2023 ). River flow and sediment variations in hourly scale are vital with the changing precipitation, temperatures, and antecedent natural disaster conditions (Langhorst et al., 2023 ). However, the understanding and measurement of these co-effects are hindered by the limitations of traditional geomorphic sampling methods with low resolution (daily or weekly durations at hydrological stations), e.g., the discontinuous deployment of sediment samplers (Kristin Bunte, 2007; Cook et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, fluvial observation is constrained by complex environments often featuring remoteness, harsh conditions, and vast geographic dimensions, especially during periods of floods and mobilized riverbeds in mountainous river regions (Tsai et al., 2012; Wyss et al., 2016; Misset et al., 2021; Dietze et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023 ).
