River flows and sediment transport variations, and their impacts, often remain largely unknown due to insufficient monitoring, hindering the understanding of ongoing changes and prediction of future variations in river conditions (Dethier et al., 2022 ). Particularly, the complexity of relationships, such as the feedback between climate and river flow, is undergoing amplification, particularly in the great rivers originating from the Asian Water Tower (AWT) which supplies water, food, and energy to approximately 3 billion people (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The state-of-the-art instrumentation is therefore needed for disentangling the complexities brought by the superposition of various factors in such challenging environments, e.g., the uneven uplift of the Himalayas, long-term climate change, and human activities. The Yarlung Tsangpo River, flowing from west to east across the southern part of the AWT region, is the longest river on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau and the upper reach of the Brahmaputra River, with the steepest gradient and the highest elevation in the world (Shi et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2023 ). Its midstream serves as a crucial center for human habitation in Tibet, encompassing major cities such as Lhasa and Shigatse. The flow and sediment variations across both temporal and spatial scales in the Yarlung Tsangpo River evidence the interaction among the river, hydroclimatic variables, and intricate geomorphologies (Knight and Harrison, 2009; Shi et al., 2018 ). The assessments of feedback between flow and sediment in this region are notably scarce. According to reports published by the local government, there are only seven hydrological stations along the Yarlung Tsangpo River. This equates to 0.40 stations per 10,000 km2 , significantly lower than the minimum station densities recommended by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO, 2008 ). Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a new automated monitoring system for flow and sediment in the harsh natural environment and under the extreme fluvial flow conditions that characterize the AWT region. Over the past century, numerous flow and sediment measurement instruments, based on various physical principles, have been developed for field monitoring. Most hydrological stations have been strategically positioned in locations with particularly good conditions along rivers to measure a wide range of parameters, including salinity, temperature, nitrate, pressure, oxygen, biomass, etc. (WMO, 2008 ). In addition, both the temporal and spatial resolutions of these measurements strongly depend on the frequency of manual measurements and the density of the monitoring network (Achterberg et al., 2019 ). Traditional measurements are limited due to their time-consuming nature, reliance on infrastructure, and manual measurements' low frequency and density. In small rivers or streams, most high-resolution sensors were indirectly installed to monitor variations in the river, such as seismometers installed near the river bed (Roth et al., 2016; Dietze et al., 2019; Dietze et al., 2022 ), the Swiss plate geophone (Rickenmann, 2018; Rickenmann, 2020 ), the hydrophone (Geay et al., 2020 ), open-source turbidity and depth sensors (Langhorst et al., 2023 ), etc. The massive development of monitoring technologies and techniques was more prevalent in smaller rivers or streams due to the smaller discharge and relatively lower cost of installation. In ocean observation, autonomous platforms, such as a variety of Lagrangian platforms (gliders, profiling, and Lagrangian floats, surface drifters), several vessels formed an observational array, etc., have already been instrumented in providing key data for several essential ocean variables, driven by decreasing costs and increasing scientific capabilities and reliability (Lindstrom et al., 2017; Whitt et al., 2020 ). However, no automatic water and sediment observation system worldwide can be used in strong hydrodynamic conditions of supersized mountain rivers. Several monitoring challenges in this condition need to be addressed: (1) the flow resistance of the system under strong hydrodynamic conditions; (2) the anti-rollover capability of the system when entering the river; (3) the anti-sand impact capability of sediment above the riverbed; (4) the ability to resist sliding on the riverbed. In this study, aiming at the co-variations of flow and sediment in this highly variable fluvial environment, a novel self-contained hydrodynamic observation platform system with ultra-high-resolution monitoring was developed for the first time and deployed in the middle reach of Yarlung Tsangpo River. Flow and sediment data spanning nearly two months, with ultra-high resolution, were collected and analyzed in terms of time and period. Subsequently, three flooding events with different flow and sediment behaviors during this period were discussed. Finally, the potential deployment and limitations of this novel system were explored, providing a new perspective on its practical application in the field of riverine monitoring.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Field site description The field site is situated in the middle section of the Yarlung Tsangpo River on the southwestern of the Tibetan Plateau (91.82°E, 29.26°N), which is encompassed by towering mountains and pristine glaciers on the northern incline of the Himalayas, with an averaged altitude of over 3500 m a.s.l, as depicted in Fig. 1  (a). The channel morphology in the vicinity of this location displays a predominantly straight configuration and the primary channel itself remains relatively stable during the dry season with the mean daily discharge of 970 m3 /s. The channel width at this field site is about 230 m and the average riverbed slope is about 0.14 %. The mean daily suspended sediment flux and suspended sediment concentration at the Yangcun hydrological station (e.g., this field site) are 551 kg/s and 0.22 kg/m3 , respectively (Shi et al., 2018 ). At the field site, the fluvial sands are distinguished by fine texture (106–183 μm average grain size), lower sorting degree (σ Φ : 0.87–1.09), and higher content of both very coarse silt (32–62 μm: 5.6 %–14.6 %) and finer silt/clay particles (<32 μm:1.6 %–6.8 %) (Liang et al., 2023 ). In recent years, during the flood season, the peak discharges ranged from 1500 to 6000 m3 /s (Han et al., 2023b ). Upstream of this field site, numerous bars and islands in braided river reach have emerged within expansive valleys spanning 3 to 10 km in width. Within these broad valleys, a substantial deposit of sediment rests, characterized by a remarkably thick layer measuring 400–800 m. This sediment accumulation primarily comprises gravel and sand, indicating a prolonged high sediment supply over an extended period. Within these broad valleys, there is a very thick layer of sediment storage characterized by a remarkably thick layer measuring 400–800 m consisting of gravel and sand (Lavé and Avouac, 2001; Wang et al., 2015 ). In the downstream gorge sections of the site, where the widths narrow down to a mere 0.1–0.2 km, Bedrock is exposed to the water flow at many places and big boulders of 1 m in size or larger overlap (Wang et al., 2015 ). It is worth mentioning that this site is strategically positioned at the pivotal juncture of the braided river in broad valley, which can serve as a highly representative vantage point to observe the natural variability in flow and sediment along the upper and middle sections of the Yarlung Tsangpo River, unaffected by the influence of damming.  2.2 A self-contained hydrodynamic observation platform system Self-contained subsea observation platforms, with pyramid-shaped frame structures, are predominantly well-suited for flow environments without a fixed direction. However, these pyramid-shaped observation systems are prone to water rollover when subjected to intense unidirectional flow, making them unsuitable in mountainous rivers (as illustrated by the field test failure of a pyramid-shaped self-contained subsea observation prototype in Figure S1 ). In the southwestern mountainous regions of China, a fish species called Euchiloglanis (Teleostei: Sisoridae) thrives in the gravel banks of rivers, subsisting primarily on a diet of aquatic insects and larvae (Zhou et al., 2011 ). The Euchiloglanis, of moderate size, boasts an elongated and flattened physique with a broad, flat head, a raised dorsum, a relatively flat abdomen, and a distinctly flattened posterior region (Fig. 1 b). Long-term natural selection has thoroughly shaped the appearance of this fish, making it well-adapted to the strong water dynamics of mountainous rivers. Inspired by the appearance and characteristics of Euchiloglanis, a new self-contained hydrodynamic observation platform was developed. The platform, featuring a wide and flat bottom, is divided into left, center, and right columns following the water flow (Fig. 1 c). The left and right columns, characterized by their sleek sides, raised back, and flat base, provide balance. Flattened side wings at the rear ensure that the 'head' of the device faces upstream when submerged, efficiently aligning itself with the downstream water flow. The observation compartment, situated in the middle column, elegantly houses various monitoring equipment, all aligned with the central axis, with the detailed system dimensions shown in Fig. 1 d and Fig. 2  . Furthermore, the platform is secured by movable anchors to withstand floods and shifting riverbeds. The heart of any observation platform system lies in its sensors. In this platform, measurement equipment is strategically arranged in the observation compartment from front to back based on the elevation of the device probes, including vertically upward-mounted Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers (Nortek Signature 1000, 16 Hz), the LISST-AOBS Super-Turbidity Sensor, the LISST-200X Submersible Particle Size Analyzer, and a vertically upward-mounted Vector current meter (Nortek ADV vector), to avoid interference with the water flow between the devices (Fig. 1 d). A schematic diagram of this platform system showing the relative positions of the measuring point/line of each device above the riverbed is illustrated in Fig. 3  . The main technical specifications of each device are summarized in the Table S1  in the Appendix. The ADCP operates according to a measurement plan that profiles a range from 0.2 m to 20 m with a cell size of 0.2 m. Its sampling scheme comprises an average interval of 600 s and a measurement duration of 10 min. The LISST-200X and LISST-AOBS follow a measurement strategy that involves averaging 32 measurements to create a single sample, with a sample interval of 1 s, 5 samples per burst, and a burst interval of 10 min. The ADV adheres to a measurement plan that includes a sampling rate of 64 Hz, a burst interval of 600 s, and 10 samplings per burst. Those instantaneous velocities with a lower signal–noise ratio lower than 15 dB and with a correlation coefficient lower limit of 70 % were removed to improve measurement data quality (Goring and Nikora, 2002 ). The remaining instantaneous velocities were decomposed into time-averaged and fluctuating components for evaluating the flow velocity and flow turbulence. Besides, the rear section of the system incorporates a floating ball recovery mechanism, to aid in the retrieval of the platform after completion of sampling. The measurement flow and sediment data included (1) flow velocity near the riverbed (V), (2) flow turbulence near the riverbed (TKE), (c) water depth (WD), (3) suspended sediment concentration (SSC), and (4) the median particle size of suspended sediment (D50 ). The devices installed on the platform are equipped with their own battery compartments, each housing lithium batteries of varying capacities. The lifespan of these batteries is intricately tied to the frequency of data sampling. The flow and sediment data gathered by the devices are stored on their respective local memory cards. After a specific interval, the platform system must be retrieved to the water surface for both the duplication of the accumulated data and recharging. All devices are meticulously programmed to gather data according to the aforementioned settings, ensuring a comprehensive measurement duration that can sustain a two-month research period.  2.3 Wavelet analysis Wavelet analysis has been widely used in the hydrological field for analyzing timeseries (Labat, 2005 ). It provides the power spectrum of timeseries in the time and frequency domain, which also avoids the limitations of Fourier transformation (Cheng et al., 2021 ). The Coherency between each two data series based on CWT presents their correlations in frequency scale, rather just the similarities in the variation of values (Smith et al., 1998 ). In order to capture the temporal position of periodic signals inside each data series, all measured variables were transformed from time scale into frequency-time domain under continuous wavelet transformation (CWT). The data was collected from 11:00 AM on May 11th, 2021, until 11:00 AM on July 2nd, 2021, except for the single-point vertical flow velocity distribution which covered the period from 11:00 AM on May 11th, 2021, to 2:40 AM on June 9th, 2021. Owing to severe natural conditions and restrictions imposed by local policies, the hydrological data of the Yarlung Tsangpo River measured by the hydrological station was severely limited. In this measured period, the daily average suspended sediment concentration (SSC) and daily unit width discharge per unit width (q) at Yangcun hydrological station have been obtained. The SSC at Yangcun hydrological station was obtained by averaging samples from multiple points across the cross-section using a horizontal integration method, and the discharge (q) was measured using an ADCP (SonTeK M9) mounted on an unmanned boat. The compariration results measured by the new system and the hydrological station were illustrated in Fig. 4  . The discharge per unit width measured by this new system was calculated by product of the Water Depth (WD) and flow velocity near the riverbed (V). It’s noted that the discharge measured by this new system only presented a single point in the river cross-section, which needs a conversion coefficient to gain the average unit width discharge across the cross-section measured by the hydrological station. However, this coefficient, related to the cross-sectional shape and the measurement location, only affected the magnitude, not the trend of variation. Fig. 4 (a) showed that when the coefficient in Yangcun hydrological station was set as 0.6, the measured difference was relatively small. The median value of data measured by the system was basically consistent with that from the hydrological station. However, the superiority of the system was reflected in the more significant daily average change in the unit-width discharge it measures, especially during the flooding period. The compararition of suspended sediment concentration (SSC) measured by the new system and the hydrological station was shown in Fig. 4 (b). It's clearly seen that the values measured by both were within the same order of magnitude and the fluctuations were quite significant. Before June 11th, the daily SSC measured by the hydrological station was generally higher than the near-bottom SSC measured by the new system. After June 11th, the increase in unit-width discharge during the flooding period resulted in a near-bottom SSC higher than the measured daily SSC.  4 Temporal-spectral analysis of flow and sediment with ultra-high-resolution 4.1 Temporal fluctuation The ultra-high-resolution data for Water Depth (WD) in Fig. 5  (a1) suggested that minimum depth during the night and dawn (darker markers of blue and red), with depths increasing through the morning, peaking at noon or afternoon (light markers of blue and red), and subsequently decreasing. The diurnal cyclical variation in WD could reach approximately 0.6 m due to varying contributions from the glacier melt of tributaries caused by diurnal temperature fluctuations, with the runoff peaking after noon owing to the lag between snow melt and peak runoff. Conversely, as temperatures drop in the evening, runoff diminishes, resulting in the shallowest water depths. Moreover, the daily average water depth consistently rose until May 22nd, then underwent a slight increment until June 11th, after which it diminished by 0.3 m, eventually rebounding on June 16th. Contrasting trends in WD and flow velocity near the riverbed (V) were vividly discernible through a Savitzky-Golay smoothing method with a one-day window phase, with the lowest values generally seen at noon and the highest values mostly observed at night, as evidenced by the alternating positions of the red and blue colors in Figure S2 . As depicted in Fig. 5 (b1), the daily variation in V was slightly larger than that of WD, with a marginally higher standard deviation of 0.0574 m/s for detrended velocity compared to 0.0544 m for detrended water depth. Until May 22nd, the daily average flow velocity marginally decreased, then it stabilized. However, on June 11th, the range of flow velocity variation increased from 0.6 m/s to 1.5 m/s. The peak value of flow turbulence near the riverbed (TKE) at the river bottom corresponded with the peak of the bottom flow velocity, as illustrated in Fig. 5 (c1). The daily average TKE marginally decreased by 0.01 m2 /s2  on May 22nd, then mildly increased to about 0.06 m2 /s2  until June 11th, after which it gradually declined until 0.03–0.04 m2 /s2 . The fluctuation range also expanded from 0.04 to 0.18 m2 /s2 , which essentially aligned with the trend of flow velocity. Additionally, the higher velocity zone larger than 1.0 m/s spread at a distance of 0.5–2.0 m from the riverbed and the range of this zone was greater before May 22nd than after, as illustrated in Figure S3 . The daily fluctuations in the bottom suspended sediment concentration (SSC), as shown in Fig. 5 (d1), vary by approximately one-third. However, the timing of the peak values seems to be irregular. Before May 18th, SSC increased from an average of 178 to 275 mg/l, and the WD during this period also correspondingly increased, suggesting that the gradual increase trend in discharge amplified the sediment carrying capacity of the flow. Subsequently, it slowly dipped to around 145 mg/l, abruptly jumping to 1162 mg/l at 6:20 on June 9th, then gradually decreased during the morning of June 9th, and returned to a level not much different from before by evening. From June 12th to July 3rd, SSC first dropped then rose, then dropped and rose again, with two peaks on June 19th (340 mg/l) and June 25th (337 mg/l). Meanwhile, after June 12th, the range of SSC fluctuations significantly diminished. The daily fluctuation trend of median suspended sediment size (D50 ) at the river bottom in Fig. 5 (e1) was similar to that of SSC, with the maximum values differing by about one-third, and the timing of the maximum values seems to be irregular. Before May 18th, as SSC rose, D50  dropped from 97 μm to 80 μm. It then slowly decreased to 16 μm at 11:00 on June 9th, when the SSC significantly surged. Subsequently, from June 15th to June 28th, it exhibited a sharp increase and substantial fluctuations, with four major peaks on June 17th (134 μm), June 20th (179 μm), June 23rd (186 μm), and June 26th (133 μm). After June 28th, it reverted to the D50  level that it was before June 15th.  4.2 Spectral variation The power spectrums fluctuation of flow and sediment variables at the river bottom amid the cross-section of the field site were depicted in Fig. 5 (a2)-(e2), correspondingly. In the short-period range (∼4 h), WD changed significantly about every half day, correlating with daily cycle troughs, suggesting stronger short-period fluctuations during low water levels. Between the 2 ∼ 8.5 h period range, significant changes mainly occurred on May 17th, June 7th, and June 27th, suggesting unique 2–8 h water depth periodic changes during this period. Just below 17 h in the period, WD showed notable 17-hour cyclical variations, appearing as a distinct peak in the global power spectrum. The V and TKE exhibited persistence post-June 11th in the short-period range, with uniform frequency distribution. The stronger periodicity of TKE and V were mainly observed after June 11th, suggesting high oscillations. The velocities of period at 17 and 136 h showed consistent prominence with periodic flow velocity variations of 17 h and 5.5 days from the global power spectrum analysis, while the TKE of greater than period at 34 h was observed from June 4th to June 18th with the energy primarily oscillates of a 1–2 day periods. Meanwhile, in the TKE global spectrum in Fig. 5 (c3), only the 17 h period segment slightly exceeded the confidence level, with energy variations of the original signal uniformly distributed across all periods. In the short-period range, The SSC mainly showed 0.5–2 h periodic fluctuations around May 17th, June 7th, and June 27th, while the D50  predominantly amassed before June 11th, implying a persistent short-period cyclical fluctuation in the D50  within this specific time–frequency domain. The SSC in the middle period (4 ∼ 68 h) was significant from June 4th to June 11th, corresponding to increases in suspended sediment concentration in the original sequence. The long-period part of SSC (68 h) was significant from May 28th to June 25th, both centered around June 7th, yet the long-period periodic signals of D50  were not captured. From a comprehensive spectral perspective in Fig. 5 (d3)-4(e3), SSC exhibited statistical significance solely at periods less than 17 h, whereas D50  demonstrated significance strictly within the longest period ranges.  4.3 Wavelet coherence Wavelet coherence was implemented to assess potential interactions among the hydrological signals. Pairwise coherences between sediment variables and flow variables were given in Fig. 6  (a1)-(c2), and coherences of internal variables were illustrated in Figure S4 . The global coherency of sediment variables versus flow variables in Figure S5 , at the scales of less than 136 h, differed gently. Here, we only considered the coherency pattern at the scales of less than 136 h owing to the length of sampling duration. In general, the highest coherency between those signals (>0.4 on average) was observed at the interval of fewer than 1 h and at 17 h, followed by a significant loss of coherency elsewhere (1 ∼ 8.5 h and 34 ∼ 136 h). It is worth noting that three significant regions with the highest coherency were identified within the 1 ∼ 8.5 h interval, centered around May 28th, June 7th, and 25th June, respectively. The phase difference of those flow and sediment variables was nearly negligible at short periods (<π/2 rad), and then slightly increased at around 17 h. The short-period signals (<8.5 h) displayed no discernible pattern in their significant regions, while a localized consistency in phase difference was evident in the long-period signals characterized by 17 h. This result suggested that a high correlation between those signals exists in short‐term scales (∼1 h), and the daily changes in sediment variables were less correlated with flow variables, except for the duration of flood events. In addition, the coherence of internal flow and sediment variables also demonstrated significance in the long-period region during the three flood periods, apart from the coherence in the short-period region.   5 Discussion 5.1 Different behaviors of flow and sediment in flood events Ultra-high-resolution flow and sediment over nearly two months revealed three significant hydrological fluctuations in the Yarlung Tsangpo River around May 17th, June 7th, and June 27th. Additionally, mean daily precipitations along the Yarlung Tsangpo River have been incorporated for the period spanning May 11 to July 2nd, including (a) Duoxong Tsangpo site (87.25°E, 29.45°N), (b) Upstream site (87.75°E, 29.25°N), (c) Nianchuhe site (89.25°E, 29.15°N), (d) Lhasa site (91.05°E, 29.65°N), and (e) Yangcun site (91.85°E, 29.25°N), as illustrated in Fig. 7   (Han et al., 2023a ). It is worth noting that the characteristics of flow and sediment during these three flood events induced by rainfall were different, corresponding to increased local rainfall along the catchment. The increase in water depth and velocity during the first flood was mainly induced by the variations of the Lhasa River composed of fine sediments. Riverbed sediment in the Lhasa River was mobilized partly and increased the supply of suspended sediment in the main river, leading to a slight increase of bottom SSC, but there was virtually no change in D50 . Owing to the subtle size difference between suspended sediment and movable riverbed sediment, the high-frequency exchange between bottom suspended sediment and movable riverbed sediment resulted in continuous periodic signals in the short-period range, while long-period signals were less noticeable. Therefore, the first flood event drove the changes in suspended sediment under the replenishment of riverbed sediment in a coarsening riverbed. The second flood, characterized by higher rainfall intensity in the Lhasa and Nianchu Rivers, led to a significant increase in water depth, triggering extensive riverbed sediment movement and a substantial rise in bottom SSC. Larger discharge from the Lhasa River enhanced the river's sediment-carrying capacity to trigger finer sub-surface bed sediment in the main river, resulting in an increase in bottom SSC and a decrease in the D50  of transported suspended sediment. Due to the reduction in exchange of bottom sediment, the periodicity of short-period signals of suspended sediment variables correspondingly weakened. Hence, the second flood exemplified changes in suspended sediment following large-scale riverbed sediment replenishment after riverbed coarsening disruption. The third flood event, triggered by sustained rainfall in Nianchu River, Duoxong Tsangpo, and upstream of the main river, showed increased water depth, broader velocity and turbulence variations, fluctuating SSC, and a steep rise in D50 . In these reaches, there were rich in solid detritus composed of larger particle sizes (Wang et al., 2015 ). Long-term rainfall can trigger natural hazards like landslides, debris flows, and flash floods within the catchment, causing excessive sediment influx to rivers. Increased detritus particles from natural hazards enhanced waterborne sediment size, leading to a sharp rise in the D50 . However, the SSC of the third flood was significantly lower than that of the second flood. Although there was an instantaneous excess sediment supply, the river was still in a state of unsaturated sediment transport due to low discharge (rainfall was less than that during the second flood). The increase in grading of the excess sediment supply resulted in the decrease of transported SSC, which was similar to the first flood. Nonetheless, the long-duration rainfall increased the randomness of the excess sediment supply occurrence in the catchment, resulting in the significant fluctuation of SSC. Additionally, the short-period signals of D50  in the third flood were persistent, while the short-period signals of flow velocity and turbulence were very pronounced, which was entirely different from the first and second floods.  5.2 Potential deployments and limitations This novel system represents the first known globally, specifically engineered for in-situ flow-sediment observations in large mountain rivers, characterized by high temporal resolution and comprehensive monitoring. It can be utilized for automated benthic observations, facilitating the collection of comprehensive data within a catchment area. By integrating more sensors onto the platform, it can monitor the translocation intensity of fluvial constituents. This comprehensive data collection and monitoring capability will inform the construction of more resilient bridges and dams, guide river navigation, and contribute to the preservation of aquatic habitats by monitoring sedimentation patterns. Besides, by employing a cableway across the river segment, this system can conduct comprehensive cross-sectional measurements of multiple substances in the river, reducing the need for repeated manual instrument changes of the traditional 'lead-line' measurement method to significantly enhance the efficiency of conventional hydrological monitoring. Indeed, it must be acknowledged that this hydrodynamic observation system still harbors several limitations that require further refinement from numerous practical applications. These include the challenging underwater attitude of the platform which can affect measurement accuracy, a tendency for the platform to become buried necessitating an increase in the contact area with the riverbed surface, and the lack of capabilities of real-time data transmission, among others. Additionally, numerical simulation methods could be employed to further optimize the arrangement of sensors, to minimize interference between instruments. More sensors could be installed on this platform through global cooperation (Jessica and Peter, 2023 ). For example, the impact signals (vibration signals, sound signals, photoelectric signals, etc.) caused by the movement of the bedload at the river bottom should also be effectively utilized to monitor the transport intensity of the bedload. What’s more, an enhanced array of sensors should be integrated into the platform as part of a global collaborative effort. For example, the impact signals (e.g., vibration signals, sound signals, photoelectric signals, etc.), generated by the interaction of the bedload movement with the device at the riverbed, provide valuable data for monitoring and quantifying the intensity of bedload transport in large riverine systems, resulting in more comprehensive and sophisticated insights from ultra-high-resolution data.   6 Conclusions This study focused on the challenges and advancements in monitoring the complex dynamics of mountain river systems. A novel, self-contained hydrodynamic observation platform, inspired by the Euchiloglanis fish, which thrives in the gravel banks of rivers, was developed first. This platform, equipped with state-of-the-art sensors, was successfully deployed in the middle reach of the Yarlung Tsangpo River in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau of the Asian Water Tower region, collecting ultra-high-resolution data on flow and sediment over nearly two months. The results showed that the median value of discharge per unit width measured and suspended sediment concentration by this system was consistent with the daily measurements from the Yangcun hydrological station. Besides, the system's superiority is highlighted by the more pronounced daily average changes it measures, particularly during the flood period. The data revealed significant minute-scaled hydrological fluctuations and a complex interplay of factors affecting the river's flow and sediment transport. Wavelet coherence was used to assess potential interactions among the hydrological signals, revealing the persistence and significance of short-period signals of flow and sediment variables and the coherence of long-period signals during three flood periods. Ultra-high-resolution data also identified different behaviors of flow and sediment during these flood events owing to the cooperative relation between riverbed sediment replenishment and instantaneous excess sediment supply, providing valuable insights into the river's response to environmental changes. The hydrodynamic observation platform held promise for future applications, including automated benthic observations and replacing traditional 'lead-line' measurement methods used in hydrological stations. However, the study acknowledged the limitations of underwater attitude, burying tendency, real-time data transmission capabilities, and so on, suggesting areas for further refinement, such as preventing sinking in sandy riverbeds and optimizing sensor arrangement. Overall, this study underscored the importance of innovative, ultra-high-resolution monitoring systems in understanding and managing the complex dynamics of river systems, particularly in the face of escalating environmental threats. These advancements were crucial for informed decision-making in river ecosystem management, infrastructure planning, and resource allocation, especially in challenging environments like mountain rivers.
1 Introduction Successful streamflow forecasting depends in key part upon the adequacy and skill of the representation of the rainfall-runoff relationship. Operational streamflow forecasting throughout the world, including as at the US National Weather Service (NWS), relies on multiple models of this process. Forecasting systems often rely on a centerpiece rainfall-runoff model, such as the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model (SacSMA) at the US NWS (Burnash, 1995 ). Many historical rainfall-runoff models have linearized and simplified known mechanisms for computational tractability, or miss some of the essential physics for how runoff is generated in certain circumstances: the structure of any single hydrological model limits the hydrograph behavior it can reproduce. For example, SacSMA baseflow is generated using a superposition of two linear reservoirs, but larger catchments for which streamflow forecasts are generated often exhibit more highly nonlinear behavior (Clark et al., 2009 ). Where system uncertainty is high, reliance on observed data and on historical analogs to operational events is a common method used to adjust calibrated forecasting models to unique local conditions. The basic concept of rainfall-runoff modeling can be expressed in terms of some filter acting on incoming precipitation and which generates the runoff response. The modeler then selects a representation of the filter process through which the rainfall signal becomes runoff. For example, Sac-SMA is the “filter” through which precipitation is passed in many operational NWS systems. However, where this algorithm is a representation of the physical runoff-generating process, it may be more or less representative of the true physical processes occurring in the catchment. Furthermore, if models were developed within one specific scientific paradigm, they may not be generalizable to all scenarios where different physical processes may be predominant. Our understanding of the physical mechanisms for how streamflow is generated at the catchment scale is still evolving, and hydrologic science has evolved considerably from the traditional linear, stationary, and static processes that historical rainfall-runoff models have utilized (Kirchner et al., 2023 ). An additional consideration for operational flood forecasting is the necessity for computational efficiency – a pressing need for a rapid delivery of information sometimes necessitates linearization and simplification for model tractability and efficiency. After a physically-based hydrologic model is selected, it is implicitly assumed that the essential nature of the physical system at hand is represented in the selected model. Observed data are used to calibrate the model; once the model is calibrated, the historical observed data are no longer used for prediction. However, model calibration presents challenges such as equifinality, where multiple parameter sets that represent different hydrologic functioning may each offer “optimum” solutions in calibration (Beven, 2006 ). Model calibration also suffers from an unclear relationship of conceptual parameters to actual physically measurable quantities. Finally, the selection of an objective function, and issues of what to optimize for (e.g., NSE, r2 , RMSE) may be highly influential in the final behavior of a model, and give undue weight to only certain parts of the hydrograph (e.g., calibrating to mean behavior rather than the extremes of interest to flood forecasting) (Gupta et al., 1999; Westerberg et al., 2011 ). Another essential operational consideration is the necessity for real-time rapid data assimilation. The physics-based models utilized currently are often unchanged by observed streamflow: streamflow is their output, deterministically simulated from observed inputs (such as precipitation/temperature/etc.). Divergences between observed and simulated streamflow may be due to input uncertainty, calibration issues, or problems with the inherent physical process representation. To align observed streamflow and simulated streamflow when they diverge, a hydrologic forecaster must alter the underlying model states of the physics-based model manually, such as soil moisture, to assimilate observed streamflow data “on the fly” and to force the model to reproduce observed streamflow behavior. This manual assimilation process is time-consuming, and includes considerable uncertainty as to which among many underlying model states to change in a given operational situation. Additionally, overfitting model states to a current event may lead to poor model performance in a future event. Automatic data assimilation is possible (Seo et al., 2003 ), but presents the same possibility to overfit to current events at the expense of future events, and can be computationally expensive especially when short-fuse operations require rapid forecasting response. Data-driven and AI models have received increased attention in hydrology (Nearing et al., 2021 ). These data-driven approaches offer distinct advantages in leveraging extensive networks of data collection and bringing them to bear on simulation and prediction. However, some AI approaches can be a “black box”, where practitioners are uncertain how the models are functioning and are difficult to interpret. To address issues of physically-based models, and to develop data-driven methods that are simple to interpret, computationally cheap, and yet have a rich foundation in theory, we present a data-driven modeling system the centerpiece of which is a k-Nearest-Neighbor (kNN) approach that is able to find most-similar historical hydrographs in the observed streamflow record, and apply historical observed hydrograph topology to forecast hydrographs. In its most basic form, the kNN approach is a predictive algorithm that quantifies the state of the current system, compares it to observed system states in some training period, chooses k  nearest neighbors in that state space upon which to base a forecast, and then evolves the current system state according to the state evolution of these nearest neighbors. The kNN approach was developed in the computer science literature as a data-driven and first generation artificial intelligence approach for forecasting, with the algorithm and concept with roots in the 1950s (Steinbach and Tan, 2009 ). The concepts of state embedding and nonlinear timeseries analysis, forming the physical basis for the method, were developed in the context of the study of nonlinear and chaotic dynamical systems (Farmer & Sidorowich, 1987; Takens, 1981; Bradley & Kantz, 2015 ). The kNN algorithm has been applied with its foundation in nonlinear dynamical systems and chaos theory both for hydrology (Galeati, 1990; Porporato & Ridolfi, 1997; Ruskeepää et al., 2023 ) and from wide-ranging systems such as disease dynamics, population ecology, and even the motion of a ball on a roulette wheel (Sugihara & May 1990; Bradley & Kantz, 2015 ). In the dynamical systems motivation of the kNN forecasting approach, the system for which prediction is desired is assumed to be a low-dimensional set of nonlinear differential equations. The response variable is embedded into the state space according to the methods set forth in Takens (1981) ; and, then some variant of kNN is often used to develop a short-term forecast. Essentially, the Takens Theorem shows that one can use the observations from a chaotic dynamical system to reconstruct that system’s state space through delay-coordinate embedding. In hydrology, kNN methods have been applied for hydrologic analog selection in addition to streamflow and stream temperature forecasting series (Caldwell et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020; Yates et al., 2003 ), and prediction of streamflow water yield in small catchments (Gharun et al., 2015 ). Other uses of the kNN method in hydrology include resampling and error analysis (e.g., adjusting a physics-based model; Sikorska-Senoner & Quilty, 2021 ), generating ensembles and possible probabilistic scenarios (Lall and Sharma, 1996; Sapin et al., 2017 ), and forecasting hydrological timeseries (Karlsson and Yakowitz, 1987 ; Galeati, 1990 ). Streamflow as a chaotic variable from a nonlinear dynamical system has been conceptually proposed and long debated in the literature (Sivakumar, 2000; Wang et al., 2005; Kędra, 2014 ). Although some support has been found for river discharges being represented as a low-dimensional deterministic chaotic system (e.g., Porporato & Ridolfi, 1996 ), other work has found support for a high-dimensional stochastic representation (Pasternack, 1999 ). Because catchments are “forced” systems, accounting for the forcings of the observed response is crucial. More recent work in hydrology has leveraged the simple dynamical system of the water balance in small catchments, using techniques from the study of dynamical systems to gain insights into hydrologically relevant fluxes (Kirchner, 2009; Li & Nieber, 2017 ). In this study, we explore the kNN for hydrological prediction at multiple different timescales (long-term, greater than 1 year; short-term 7-day forecasts), utilizing a novel way to weight the state space and neighbors using the catchment forcings. We also assess the data assimilation skill of the kNN method for streamflow forecasting and its performance in a flood-of-record (hence, outside of the training set), making a direct link to operational hydrology where data assimilation and updating forecasts are central to decision making. Finally, we report on 2 different probabilistic techniques − ensemble-based and postprocessing − and their skill in generating forecasts in the face of uncertainty. While the nonlinear dynamical systems and chaos tradition serves as the conceptual backdrop for model development of a kNN approach for streamflow forecasting, critically, the approach in this paper focuses on gaining data-driven forecasting skill rather than starting with a priori  considerations of theory. Instead, intuitive spatial reasoning about the reconstructed state space, and distances and trajectories therein, were used to build up a forecasting model.  2 Methods 2.1 General approach Our objective was to create a parsimonious forecasting system that incorporates streamflow drivers as a data-driven rainfall-runoff model on a kNN platform that provides both long-term model runs (>1 year) with no streamflow data assimilation as well as the ability to provide meaningful forecasts with assimilation of observed streamflow. To be useful, the forecasting system must provide accurate results in operationally relevant contexts and be computationally inexpensive, adaptable and scalable. We assume that the rainfall-runoff relationship can be represented as a system of nonlinear differential equations which evolve through time (i.e., a nonlinear dynamical system), which are unknown. While the number of variables needed to fully describe the evolution of the system through time are also unknown, we do know that one of the variables is streamflow, q  ; the amount of water flowing through a stream or channel at a specific time and location. Historical records of q    provide large, uniformly time sampled datasets that make ideal candidates for time series analysis techniques to model the behavior of the nonlinear dynamical system. In general, we follow the canonical kNN forecasting approach of Farmer and Sidorowich (1987)  to reconstruct an m-dimensional dynamical system, Q   , from the streamflow record. We then use the state-space, Q   , to forecast the streamflow.  2.2 Theory and model development The reconstruction of the state-space of a dynamical system, Q   , from the information in a single time series, q   , requires the selection of an embedding dimension m  and time-delay parameter τ d     (Takens, 1981 ).(1) q  = q ( t  1  ) ,  q ( t  2  ) , ⋯ , q ( t  N  )     = [ q 1  , q 2  , ⋯ , q N  ]      (2) Q  = Q  1    Q  2     ⋮    Q  N - m - 1    ∗ τ d            = q 1   q 1 + τ d     ⋯  q 1 + m - 1    ∗ τ d      q 2    q 2 + τ d     ⋯  q 2 + m - 1    ∗ τ d      ⋮   ⋮  ⋮  ⋮   q N - m - 1    ∗ τ d      q N - ( m - 2 )  ∗ τ d     ⋯  q N              Each row of Q   is a vector Q  i     that gives the coordinates of a point in the newly constructed m dimensional space. The N points in the streamflow time series q     become N - m - 1    ∗ τ d     points in the new, m dimensional system, Q  . Each vector Q  i     in the new system quantifies the shape  of a hydrograph that is comprised of ‘m’ streamflow observations. Furthermore, each hydrograph shape is evolving through time; this can be thought of as the trajectory of the system. For example, Q  1     evolves into Q  2    , and so on until the state Q  N - m - 1    ∗  τ d       is reached. For our implementation of the kNN algorithm, we selected an embedding dimension by considering the qualitative basin responsiveness to precipitation and how many subsequent timesteps may be required to encapsulate the “shape” of a hydrograph within a state space, and by testing the performance of several low-dimensional embedding dimensions between 2 and 15 dimensions. We constrained the time-delay parameter τ d     to τ d  = 1   . The kNN method can be visualized spatially. For example, Fig. 1   shows the construction of dynamic system with a dimensionality of m  = 3 days, and a time delay of τd  = 1 day. Each state Q  i    ,  in the system Q   , provides a m-point “hydrograph shape” that is comprised of sampled data from the original time series. Embedding the current state into the system requires knowing current and historical streamflow data. In this example with m = 3 and τd  = 1, the current state, Q  o    ,  is constructed from the current streamflow, q 0    , and the previous two days streamflow, q 0 - 1      and q 0 - 2     , (see Fig. 2  a). Once the current state is embedded, forecasting a future streamflow, q New     , requires evolving the current state of the system to a new state, Q  New   .    The desired forecast streamflow, q New     , is the newest component of Q  New     , (see Fig. 2 b). The first step in evolving the system is to search the space and calculate the distances between all historical states, Q  i  ,    the current state Q  0    . The k  nearest neighboring states are found according to some distance metric applied to the state space (Fig. 2 c). Next, the trajectories of the k nearest neighbors are applied as a weighted average according to distance or similarity to the current state, Q  0    , (Fig. 2 d), evolving it through the space to the new state, Q  New     , (Fig. 2 e). If sequential forecasts are needed, the forecast state Q  New      is reinitialized as Q  0    , and the process is repeated. In addition to embedding streamflow, we embedded precipitation and temperature within a state space to aid in the search and selection of the streamflow state space. With a time-delay of one, we used a precipitation embedding dimension that was often longer than the streamflow embedding dimension but remained relatively low dimensional (between 3 and 15 days). Further, we also weighted hydrograph selection by mean air temperature to select the best-suited hydrographs to form the basis for prediction. To weight precipitation and temperature, we calculated the Euclidean distance between the embedded t0  precipitation and temperature vectors, and all observed embedded precipitation and temperature vectors in the historical record, then centered-and-scaled precipitation and temperature distances by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The streamflow distance was also first calculated as a Euclidean distance, but then centered-and-scaled. The center-and-scaling transformed the distances to Mahalanobis distances, which are scale invariant and unitless, yet retain the correlation structure of the underlying data (Mehrotra & Sharma, 2006 ). Therefore, the streamflow, precipitation, and temperature distances were unitless, and able to be added together into a new distance metric (Fig. 3  ). The k  hydrographs that minimized this distance metric (dist  w     in Fig. 3 ) were then used to make the forecast. Once the k  hydrographs were selected, Gaussian kernel weighting (Bidanset and John, 2014 ) was used to weight the individual k  points in how much they relatively influenced the trajectory of the t 0     point, by creating a weighted regression version of the non-weighted regression outlined in Farmer and Sidorowich (1987) , with weights determined by the precipitation-distances. For the selection of k , Farmer and Sidorowich suggest using k > m + 1    (1987). Though testing the of different values of k suggests that in some cases, k = m + 1    gives the best results (See Model testing, section 2.3.1), a constant value for k  was used equal to 2 times the embedding dimension. This was done to ensure stability in the prediction when using different embedding dimensions.  2.3 Model testing To test our kNN technique we first looked at long-term behavior of two very different systems, one in the Appalachian Mountains, USA and the other in northern Minnesota, USA. We applied the model in three different scenarios. First, we investigated a long-term test period with no real data assimilation in a rainfall-dominated research catchment at the Coweeta Hydrologic Lab in North Carolina, USA. Next, we included a conceptual snowmelt model to drive the long-term simulation and studied boreal-temperate transition zone catchments in northern Minnesota, USA. The study area including a small (<10 ha) research reference catchment at the Marcell Experimental Forest and a large river basin (>19 k sq mi) with incomplete forcings information. And finally, we conducted a pseudo-operational forecasting test for a large river basin in northern Minnesota, USA with a focus on performance forecasting a flood-of-record on the Rainy River. The test involved reforecasting, data assimilation, and implementation of ensemble and postprocessing bias correction uncertainty-quantification schemes. We assessed model performance with the Nash-Sutcliffe Model Efficiency (NSE: Nash & Sutcliffe, 1970 ) and the Mean Absolute Percent Error (MAPE). To determine how well the model performs in flooding scenarios, we also assessed model performance for the high-flow regime where the observed streamflow was greater than the 95th percentile flow, using the NSE and MAPE. The locations used in this study are shown in Fig. 4  . 2.3.1 Testing long-term behavior in an Appalachian deciduous forest catchment First, the kNN approach was tested at a reference catchment at the Coweeta Hydrologic Laboratory, WS18 (Elliott et al., 2017 ). WS18 is 12.5 ha, with streamflow data collected since 1937. The meteorological data were from station RRG06, which is near the catchment. The Coweeta Hydrologic Lab is at the southern end of the Appalachian Mountain Chain and is forested with mixed deciduous species. Average precipitation is approximately 2000 mm/year almost entirely as rainfall, and the mean average temperature is 12.6 °C. The model training period was 1937–1999, and the testing period was 2005–2019. Although kNN is definitionally assimilating streamflow timeseries as the timeseries evolves, and chaotic dynamics should not be predictable over long time horizons, we only initialize the streamflow timeseries with the first m  observed streamflow values, then only simulated a long-term streamflow timeseries based on precipitation and temperature alone (i.e., with no observed streamflow data assimilation). Thus, the viability of treating the model as a traditional, non-assimilating, hydrologic model is tested in long-term validation metrics during the testing period with no additional assimilation. If the model performs well in this setting, this implies that the state space characterizes an intrinsic rainfall-runoff relationship, and the system is entirely “forced” by the drivers of precipitation and temperature.  2.3.2 Testing long-term behavior in northern MN boreal-temperate forest catchments The kNN approach was also tested at the S2 reference catchment of the Marcell Experimental Forest (9.2 ha) (Sebestyen et al., 2011 ). The Marcell Experimental Forest is in the boreal-temperate transition zone, and the catchments consist of a central (evergreen-forested) peatland and an upland rim of deciduous forest. The annual avg temp is 3.2 °C, and about 1/3 of the annual precipitation (average 784 mm) falls as snow. Streams completely freeze up during winter months, ∼ November through February. The annual maximum streamflow peak is often associated with snowmelt or rain-on-snow (McEachran et al., 2021 ), so a snow model was also needed to represent snowmelt dynamics. Snow cores are taken approximately every two weeks starting in February until the snowpack is gone, on both upland and peatland portions of catchments (Sebestyen et al., 2021 ). We brute-force calibrated a lumped, catchment-scale Snow-17 model to the catchment-scale aggregated snow observations using the sacsmaR package in R (Astagneau et al., 2021 ). To estimate the Snow-17 parameters, we randomly sampled the parameter space 56,010 times within the bounds defined by He et al. (2011)  and additionally bounded based on parameter constraints and physical interpretation of parameters in Anderson (2002). We accepted the parameterization that resulted in the highest NSE. This Snow-17 model had r2  = 0.37 and NSE=0.18. Simulated daily Rain And Melt (RAIM) timeseries from the model were used as the “precipitation” timeseries used to search the streamflow state space. The forcings-weighted kNN was also tested with a long-term simulation in a large catchment with incomplete forcings information, which is at a more operationally relevant spatial scale. The Rainy River of northern Minnesota and south-western Ontario begins where several Canadian Shield tributaries come together draining into Rainy Lake. The ∼ 19,200 mi2  catchment (at the USGS Gauge at Manitou Rapids, 05133500) begins in a forested shallow-bedrock Canadian Shield area, and drains eventually into Lake of the Woods, with western tributaries occupying glacial lake and beach ridge sediments with deep and expansive peatlands. Groundwater-surface water interaction is pervasive. Approximately 40 % of the catchment area is on the US side, with 60 % of the catchment area in Canada. However, historically the NWS has only operationally tracked precipitation and temperature data for the US side of the basin, as river forecast services were not officially codified in the region until 2023. Therefore, only 40 % of the catchment area is represented in the “operational” forcings. However, since the record 2022 flooding in the region, there has been an increase in demand for river forecast services, so significant model development work has been underway. Because of the unique northern hydrology of the region, and considerable uncertainty in input forcings, the basin serves as a test for the kNN performance in the face of uncertainty. We used the NWS Snow-17 modeled RAIM as precipitation forcings for the forcings-weighted kNN, aggregated to a daily timestep from the native six-hourly and spatially averaged across the US drainage area of the Rainy River basin (representing only ∼ 40 % of the total drainage area). Due to this uncertainty, and the increased demand for probabilistic forecast services, we also developed probabilistic techniques to create more robust forecasts that would be applicable in an operational setting. We used the time period 1950–1999 for training the kNN method; 2000–2013 for training a bias correction, and 2014–2019 for validation. The flood-of-record was in 2014 for the Rainy River at Manitou Falls gauge, so was included in the validation time period. We used a postprocessing approach with a linear bias correction, using Bayesian parameter estimation, to bias-correct the long term forecast for the Rainy River basin. Postprocessing is how the US National Weather Service currently accounts for “hydrological uncertainty” in streamflow forecasts stemming from the rainfall-runoff process (Brown et al., 2014 ). To postprocess the long-term simulation of streamflow, we fit a linear regression between the observed streamflow and the raw kNN streamflow forecast in the bias correction training period, then used those parameters to create a postprocessed simulation for the true testing period. Parameter estimation was conducted in a Bayesian framework using Jags (Plummer, 2003 ) through the R2Jags package (Su & Yajima, 2021 ), within R Version 4.2.0 (R Core Team, 2023 ). Thus, we could compare both the raw kNN to the bias-corrected kNN.  2.3.3 Testing pseudo-operational flood forecasting in a large river basin in northern MN Next, we conducted a continuous series of 7-day reforecasts throughout the testing period in the Rainy River Basin to test the performance of the assimilating kNN. This set of simulations were  assimilating, so made use of the observed data as it became available and reforecast a seven-day forecast on each day (initializing on that day’s observed mean streamflow). We generated a raw kNN forecast. We compared two methods for probabilistic forecasting based on the kNN approach: first, we used a postprocessing approach with a linear bias correction, using Bayesian parameter estimation. This linear bias correction is the same used when we developed long-term forecasts of the Rainy River basin in Section 2.3.2. Credible intervals for forecasts on each day of lead time were calculated by sampling across the posterior density (both parameter and error uncertainty) that was generated by the bias correction regression for each lead time. Secondly, we take advantage of the inherent nature of the kNN approach to generate ensemble forecasts by resampling the reconstructed state space and generating an ensemble of forecasts based on this resampling (Lall & Sharma, 1996; McInerney et al., 2021 ). We limit the uncertainty quantification to account for the uncertainty attributable to the rainfall-runoff response of the basin to precipitation, and not to the uncertainty in the meteorological drivers of precipitation and temperature, which we hold fixed. However, it should be noted again that the precipitation and temperature are those over the entire basin on the US side of the border, only representing 40 % of the overall basin area. We do not drive ensembles based on meteorological drivers because we are focusing on the rainfall-runoff performance of the kNN and on the uncertainty within that response. Therefore, we underestimate what the true “operational” uncertainty would be where weather drivers are uncertain. Furthermore, for each day’s forecast, we only accounted for one day’s worth of (observed) precipitation forecast. Beyond one day, we allowed snowmelt to be considered, but set additional precipitation to zero. Thus, each day’s forecast was only conditional on the water already accounted for in the catchment, plus one day’s precipitation forecast. This is done operationally in US NWS forecasts to hedge against large swings in precipitation forecasts and was chosen to mimic the setting of US NWS operations. To generate streamflow ensembles, instead of aggregating over the k nearest neighbors in the state space, at each forecast step, we sample 3*k nearest neighbors, then used weighted resampling with replacement to sample k neighbors used for calculating the state space trajectory of the current point. We weight the resampling by the distances within the state space so that the closest neighbors will have the greatest chance of being selected using Gaussian Kernel resampling. These k samples are then passed to the precipitation-weighted kNN algorithm just as in the non-ensemble outlined above. We generate 50 7-day forecasts for each t0 , and take the mean of these ensembles at each timestep as the “mean” forecast. To show the performance of the assimilating kNN, we present the NSE value and biases on Day 1, Day 3, and Day 7 after forecast issuance. We report the Day 1 skill also with respect to the “persistence” forecast of simply using the t0  observed streamflow as the t + 1 forecast, and assess relative skill compared to the persistence forecast using the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE; Ghimire & Krajewski, 2020 ). Finally, we provide an analysis of the 2014 flood of record to show the performance of the assimilating kNN, and compare/contrast the two uncertainty quantification methods (postprocessing and ensemble-based).    3 Data We utilized operational archived NWS operational forcings of mean areal precipitation (MAP) and mean areal temperature (MAT) for the Rainy River analyses. Precipitation estimates are based on gage analysis from 1950 to 2019 done internally at NCRFC according to the quality control methods of Anderson, 2002. The forcings data were originally derived at a 6-hour timestep, but were aggregated into daily values. Streamflow data were mean daily streamflow from the USGS for the Rainy River at Manitou Rapids (USGS 05133500; USGS, 2023 ). For experimental catchments, Coweeta data were available on the USFS Research Data Archive (Miniat, 2015, 2016, 2017 ), as were the MEF data (Verry et al., 2018; Sebestyen et al., 2020a; Sebestyen et al., 2020b; Sebestyen et al., 2021 ). All data are publicly available.  4 Results 4.1 Results for long-term behavior in an Appalachian deciduous forest catchment We found the optimal embedding dimension was m = 3 (Fig. 5  ). We used a streamflow embedding dimension of 3 days, with 7 days of precipitation plus one additional day of perfectly-known forecast precipitation (for a total of 8 dimensions), and 3 days of temperatures. We used observed precipitation as the future “forecast” to constrain our scope to hydrological model performance in the face of observed precipitation, rather than meteorological uncertainty. Our testing also supported our use of k = 2*m, as model skill was mostly invariant to the choice of k once it was high enough to support stability and convergence of the state space regression (Fig. 6  ). For the testing period, the model replicated the hydrograph “shape” of the Coweeta discharge well, exhibiting rises and recessions mimicking the observed hydrographs: observed and simulated hydrographs were highly correlated (Fig. 7  a, 7d). This was reflected in the NSE of 0.74, and the R2  value of 0.79. MAPE was 32 %. However, it was immediately apparent that a deterministic and periodic bias was present (Fig. 7 b). Thus, we did a post-hoc  spectral analysis on the model errors (Fleming et al., 2002 ) to determine the periodicity of the bias. The simulated WS18 streamflow errors had a dominant spectral magnitude at a period of 375 days, indicating an approximately annual bias in the model errors (Fig. 7 c). For the high flow regime (greater than the 95th percentile flows), the simulated and observed were still correlated (r2  = 0.50), but the overall model skill was poor (NSE=0.00). The MAPE was similar in the high flow regime compared to the overall timeseries (MAPE=31 %). 4.1.1 Results for long-term behavior in northern MN catchments For the MEF, we started by using the same embedding dimensions as the Coweeta (streamflow m  = 3, precipitation m  = 7 plus 1 day of forecast for a total of 8 days, and temperature = 3), but increased m  to m  = 5 because of some instability in the simulation for the testing period when m  = 3 that was visually apparent. For the testing period of 2000 through mid-2016 for the Marcell, the simulated streamflow had an r2  of 0.40, with an NSE of 0.40 (Fig. 8  ). MAPE (886 %) was not a reliable metric for model performance for the Marcell Experimental Forest: 44 % of even the nonzero streamflow was less than 0.1 mm/day, which means that even a very small error can be large in percent terms. Trends in model error were noisy with no clear periodicity; the spectrum was taken on the raw error, not the percentage error, because of how many days had flow = 0. The 5-highest magnitude periods in the spectrum were 128 days, 206 days, 182 days, 46 days, and 77 days. Thus, there is a multi-month yet sub-annual, seasonal-scale effect to the bias, but without the strongly periodic dominance of the Coweeta errors. Visual inspection of the hydrographs revealed that significant errors could be attributed to snowmelt-modeling errors: for example, simulated spring peaks would rise early and be offset to observed streamflow. Given the low performance of the Snow17 model for modeling observed snowpack (NSE=0.18), this is unsurprising. The streamflow model errors for the MEF do not only represent errors in the rainfall-runoff representation, but also errors in the snowpack modeling present within the training and  testing period (because the kNN method trains on the modeled snowmelt). For the high flow regime, the NSE was 0.06 and the r2  was 0.26; MAPE was 47 %. MAPE is illustrative for the high flow regime because very small flows that caused the MAPE to be high were filtered out of the calculation. For the Rainy River, we used a streamflow embedding dimension of 3, precipitation of 10 plus one forecast (but perfectly known) RAIM (total of 11), and temperature dimension of 3. We used the longer precipitation embedding dimension to reflect the larger basin and thus longer travel time for precipitation to influence runoff at the gage. The long-term simulation had a persistent low bias (−27 %), but replicated the hydrograph shape well (NSE=0.28). Utilizing a linear bias correction, the NSE went up to 0.50 (Fig. 9  ). The bias corrected and raw kNN long-term Rainy River forecasts had 32 % and 34 % MAPE, respectively. Despite better overall performance, the bias correction also generated a worse simulation in certain years; with a simple linear bias correction, complexities in the bias are not captured. For the long-term forecast, the kNN was not skillful for high flows (top 5 %) on the Rainy River, with an NSE of −2.3, bias of −37 %, and MAPE of 37 % for the high flow regime. In the spectrum of the percentage error for the raw kNN, when run for the full 2000–2019 time period (to capture potential low-frequency error trends), the primary periods in the percentage error are approximately at six months, two years, and four years, with the strongest trend at the 4-year time period.   4.2 Results for pseudo-operational flood forecasting in a large river basin in northern MN For the testing window, we assessed the NSE of the one-day lead time, three-day lead time, and 7-day lead time forecast, for both the raw kNN and a bias-corrected version with a simple linear regression with Bayesian parameter estimation (Table 1  ). The raw kNN and the bias-corrected version performed similarly in skill, but the bias-corrected version reduced the low-bias for the longer lead-times (3–7 days). In keeping with current operational procedures, the kNN simulation only included 1 day of forecast precipitation, so it is not surprising that it is biased low. For the high flow regime (greater than the 95-percentile observed flow), the streamflow forecasts maintained their skill in the Day 1 lead time (postprocessed NSE=0.96; raw NSE 0.96), had moderate performance at Day 3 (postprocessed NSE=0.72; raw NSE=0.69), and had no skill at Day 7 (NSE<0). The performance drop is likely related to the lack of precipitation information given to the model beyond Day 1. Compared to simply using the most recent observed streamflow as the forecast as a benchmark (the “persistence” forecast), the kNN and bias-corrected/postprocessed kNN had lower error (RMSE=1027 cfs for using the day 0 observed value for the day 1 forecast, while RMSE=939 cfs to 949 cfs on the bias corrected kNN and raw kNN, respectively). The skill improvement of kNN over the most recent observed streamflow is more apparent in the high (top 5 %) flow range: RMSE=2419 cfs for using the day 0 observed value for the day 1 forecast, while RMSE=1877 cfs to 1962 cfs on the bias corrected kNN and raw kNN, respectively). We assessed the operational forecast evolution generated by the bias-corrected and ensemble-based kNN model in the days leading to the record 2014 flood at Manitou Rapids, the mean daily flow of which was 75.6 kcfs on June 17. The second-highest peak was in 1950, at 71.3 kcfs (instantaneous). The kNN method retains its behavior for a flood-of-record (Fig. 10  ). Furthermore, the ensemble and postprocessing-based probabilistic approaches offer a similar performance. With 7 days of lead time, both methods give similar results showing a recession, because the precipitation driving the record flood was not yet within the precipitation forecast window. With 3 days of lead time, the flow forecast for the day of the record crest for the ensemble forecaster was 65.3 kcfs (−13.6 % error; 58.8–70.3 kcfs 95 % ensemble quantile). The postprocessed forecast with bias correction for the 3-day lead time was 69.7 kcfs (−10.4 % error; 65.3–74.2 kcfs 95 % credible interval). For the one-day lead time, the ensemble method forecast 71.3 kcfs (−5.7 % error; 66.9–75.0 kcfs), with a mean forecast value of 73.1 kcfs for the postprocessed forecast (−3.3 % error; 71.1–75.1 kcfs). In the one day lead time, the postprocessed/bias-corrected forecast had lower error for the mean forecast. Neither method captured the record flood within the 95-percentile bound. These were undersimulations for the flood of record, yet the forecasts retained generally high levels of skill and were able to extrapolate performance beyond what was available in the training set (which had the greatest mean daily streamflow of 71.3 kcfs). This indicates the method retains reliable behavior even for flows not documented in the training time period. In the one-day lead time forecast, the simulation showed a recession, while the hydrograph rose for one more day; the record flood ended up being a 99.4 % quantile event according to the posterior density derived from the bias correction (Fig. 11  ). Despite this, overall error with one day of lead time was low (between 3 % and 6 % low depending on uncertainty method).   5 Discussion 5.1 Overview The kNN forecasting approach successfully replicated the complex behavior of observed hydrographs, and represents a parsimonious model that did not require any formalized calibration and minimal parameterization. Particularly where snowmelt processes were not dominant (i.e., Coweeta), the rainfall-runoff relationship appeared to be adequately encoded within the reconstructed state space to produce high-skill simulations just based on precipitation and temperature data at the catchment scale (Fig. 7 ). However, where snowmelt processes drove the most significant annual flux of water, and the conceptual Snow-17 model was used to model catchment-available water for runoff, additional errors were introduced. Future efforts should focus on incorporating empirical measurements of snow-water to generate “runoff-available water” estimates with which to search the reconstructed streamflow state space. Finally, in a large basin with only a partial record of basin-scale precipitation (where precipitation for only ∼ 40 % of the catchment area was assumed to be representative of the entire basin), raw kNN replicated the hydrograph shape well, with further improvement due to bias correction. Bias-corrected forecasts were stable for a flood-of-record that occurred within the testing period, with a peak estimation error of −3.3 % for the flood-of-record, and the record streamflow being a 99.4-percentile event according to the probabilistic estimation from a bias correction.  5.2 Long-Term behavior The kNN approach simulated long-term streamflow at WS18 at the Coweeta Hydrologic Lab with high skill (NSE=0.73, r2  = 0.78), using only the precipitation and temperature forcings. However, an annual bias was apparent, with a periodicity in the errors of approximately one year. Thus, while the kNN approach does not attempt to model any physical processes, patterns in the error implicate additional physical variables that may be critical for the rainfall-runoff response. Oversimulation of the kNN approach tends to occur in the dormant season of the deciduous-forested WS18, while undersimulation occurs in the summer while trees are leafed-out. While specific methods of incorporating land cover variables were not accounted for, using these land cover and soil variables to search the reconstructed state space and select nearest neighbors would help account for the periodic model biases observed. Furthermore, Coweeta had the longest training record (1937–2000), also helping to explain the high performance. At the MEF, the S2 simulation was a little more than half as skillful as the Coweeta WS18 model (NSE=0.40 at MEF; NSE=0.73 at Coweeta) (Fig. 7 ). It was apparent based on visual inspection of the simulated versus observed hydrographs that in some years, large errors were introduced due to the timing of snowmelt, which was primarily influenced by the Snow-17 model simulated snowpack, which did not have high skill modeling the observed historical snowpack (NSE=0.18). The Rainy River case study indicated a pervasive low bias to the forecasting method for long-term simulations (Fig. 9 ). However, the hydrograph shape was preserved well. The linear bias correction increased the NSE even more, but it was clear that the bias correction did not perform reasonably in some years. This was perhaps due to periodicity in the bias, or heteroscedacity and nonlinearity in the errors. Because the hydrograph shape was simulated well, a more sophisticated bias correction routine has the potential to increase performance even more.  5.3 Forecasting The forcings-weighted kNN method had high performance for the 7-day forecasts, even when limited with only one day of precipitation forecast for each 7-day streamflow forecast, and limited with the “known” precipitation only representing that occurring on 40 % of the large basin area. The NSE of the 7-day forecasts varied between 0.99 on Day 1 after forecast issuance, to 0.81 on Day 7. For the top 5-percentile of observed streamflows, the Day 1 performance was still strong (NSE=0.96), but dropped off more rapidly than the overall record (Day 3 NSE between 0.69–0.72 depending on use of postprocessing). The NSE performance in days 1–3 on the Rainy River, and the Coweeta “no-assimilation” long-term run, is comparable with overall test period performance of several deep learning methods with data assimilation recently reported (Feng et al., 2020; Nearing et al., 2022). The NWS North Central River Forecast Center (NCRFC; responsible for flood forecasting in the region of the Rainy River and Marcell Experimental Forest) operational forecast streamflow models, the centerpiece of which is the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting Model (Burnash, 1995 ), has a median NSE in the Upper Midwest, USA region of 0.66 (0.50 to 0.75, Interquartile Range; NCRFC internal analysis). The NCRFC river model for the Rainy River at Manitou Rapids, forced by incomplete precipitation, has an NSE of 0.18; however, this river model is not currently in operational status due to data constraints and lack of adequate calibration. Thus, the assimilating kNN offers comparatively high performance for forecasting in the Rainy River, and more broadly in river forecasting given the high skill of the kNN within the first several days after forecast issuance. We tested multiple uncertainty quantification schemes: both the ensemble-based and postprocessing uncertainty sampling incorporated hydrologic uncertainty within the pseudo-operational forecasts (Fig. 10 , Fig. 11 ). Thus, the forecast for each day had uncertainty bounds for each forecast timestep in the future, with associated uncertainty that decreased through time (illustrated in Fig. 11 ). The flood-of-record was a 99.4 %-percentile in the one-day-lead-time forecast for its date of occurrence, and the mean of the posterior density of the day’s forecast was −3.3 % biased for that day (for the postprocessing method; −5.7 % for the ensemble method). The forecasts near the flood-of-record were physically plausible and reasonable forecasts, given the precipitation forecast window, indicating that the kNN method is relatively stable to extrapolation beyond the observed timeseries. This is likely because the relative trajectories  of the reconstructed state space points are applied to the current operational hydrograph to generate additional forecasts. Thus, if the k-nearest-neighbors are all lower in magnitude, but had an “increasing” shape through time, an increase would be applied to the current operational point in the state space. However, the flood of record forecast was still biased low; a low bias for flood peaks especially outside of the observed within the training period is a common problem for data-driven methods, including the kNN, despite some resiliency to this limitation being observed.  5.4 Future research The kNN method has demonstrated promise as an operational forecasting tool, even for a flood-of-record; further, the forcings-weighted state space has been shown to behave as a relatively high-performing rainfall-runoff model when fed only precipitation and temperature over a multi-year simulation (Fig. 7 ). The long-term simulations showed an indication of deterministic bias (Fig. 7 b, 7c), indicating that our forcings-weighted kNN approach does not account adequately for all physical streamflow generating mechanisms. Our approach is a simple, understandable algorithm, but lacks a robust treatment of the physics of the rainfall-runoff transform in its current pragmatic form. The framing and success of the method in this paper has focused on its use as a way to choose the k-“most-similar hydrographs” in the past, and base the forecast based on these analogs. However, given the success of the kNN method in replicating observed rainfall-runoff hydrographs, further exploration of the dynamical systems foundation of the method is warranted. The idea of low-dimensional chaotic behavior in river discharge timeseries has been explored in previous papers – many reviewed in (Sivakumar, 2000 ); however, true reconstruction of the underlying nonlinear dynamical system of equations that gives rise to the success of the method has not been attempted (Brunton et al., 2016; Ribera et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the search for chaotic dynamics in streamflow timeseries has focused in the literature on applying analyses directly on streamflow timeseries, without isolating the driving precipitation regime to just focus on the catchment transformation of its forcing precipitation as its own dynamical system (Porporato & Ridolfi, 1997 ). However, if the runoff-generation mechanism can exhibit low-dimensional chaotic behavior, it may be necessary to also control for precipitation.
