An analogy can be found in “driven oscillator” scenarios, where the driver-characteristics (such as frequency of the drive motor) are a constant that is known and given directly to the differential equations of motion for the response system – e.g., (Tran et al., 2013 ). We used a simple weighting scheme to search the reconstructed state space based on precipitation, temperature, and  streamflow distances to attempt to “isolate” the rainfall-runoff response dynamics, and find the proper region of the attractor to use for prediction. However, more sophisticated routines may be used, or more analytical methods for isolating the attractor corresponding specifically to the rainfall-runoff transform, may be derived. The underlying “equations-of-motion” for the rainfall-runoff transform could be said a priori  to consist of the water balance, such as in Kirchner, (2009) , and Li & Nieber, (2017) . We hypothesize the water balance and underlying system attractor would have similar dimensions. Additional work could possibly identify simple functional forms for system of low-dimensional differential equations that exbibit behavior in one of its dimensions akin to streamflow (Brunton et al., 2016 ). The system is in one respect definitionally high-dimensional stochastic, from the perspective of solving Newton’s Second Law for a continuum of control volumes throughout a catchment giving rise to statistical relations, such as in statistical mechanics or classical thermodynamics; however, recent literature has shown critical insights are possible using the low-dimensional water balance as a governing differential equation for catchment water flux behavior (Kirchner, 2009 ). Therefore, future work should focus on reconstructing “rainfall-runoff-like” equations based on insights from foundational considerations of the water balance in concert with kNN embedding assessment.   6 Conclusions As presented, the kNN method offers a simple, relatively efficient, and parsimonious framework for prediction. Although its performance offers evidence to explore the dynamical systems underpinning of the method further, its relative simplicity and robustness to an essential lack of calibration effort should be considered as a standalone forecasting tool that is able to simply make forecasts by identifying suitable historical analogs, independent of the ultimate foundations within the investigation of dynamical systems. Additional adaptation of the method could focus on optimizing embedding dimension and time lag parameters with respect to its dynamical systems underpinning, but could also simply focus on model performance for forecast generation alone. As with all data-driven methods, however, it is unclear how to generalize the method’s success within ungauged basins. This is another investigation that would be bolstered by identifying characteristics of “equations of motion” for the rainfall-runoff response, as these could help extrapolate behavior to never-before-observed regions on the rainfall-runoff attractor. As more “black box” deep learning models for streamflow forecasting are reported on in the literature, it is important to consider the degree of complexity needed for specific applications, and that simple methods such as the kNN may still offer robust performance: especially when paired with developments to these methods such as novel approaches for searching the state space. The forcings-weighted kNN method can be applied to other forced systems as well, beyond the catchment rainfall-runoff transform. Simple pendulum systems with variable interaction potential may be one way to test the robustness of the forcings-weighted kNN in a system where the equation of motion is well-known and chaotic (Tran et al., 2013 ). Other applications in earth and environmental systems where this method is well-suited are in disciplines where the object of study is closely coupled and responsive to highly variable external drivers, such as sea ice (Lv et al., 2008 ), nonlinear groundwater head (Peterson & Western, 2014 ), and broadly the modeling of Critical Zone processes that can be represented as nonlinear differential equations (Brantley et al., 2007 ). In summary, the kNN forecasting method, through searching the reconstructed state space according to hydrograph, precipitation, and temperature similarity using a very simple distance scheme and low dimensions (<15), provided both long-term and short-term forecasts that fit observed data moderately to quite well (long-term NSEs ranged from 0.28 to 0.73, whereas short-range NSEs ranged from 0.99 in day 1 to 0.78 in day 7). Accompanied by a bias correction to estimate uncertainty that included Bayesian parameter estimation, credible intervals were available for each forecast timestep through time that quantified hydrologic uncertainty in model predictions. The kNN ensemble method also produced uncertainty estimates similar to the postprocessing method during a flood-of-record, and was able to be calculated by virtue of the structure of the kNN approach. The method is parsimonious and conceptually simple when viewed as a sophisticated way to choose historical analogs with which to forecast with, but the method has a rich foundation in the dynamical systems literature that offers exciting avenues for future research in reconstructing “rainfall-runoff” equations of motion, allowing for investigation of essential low-dimensional relationships between driving and response variables at the catchment scale. The low-dimensional dynamical systems approach has been demonstrated using the water balance (Kirchner, 2009; Li & Nieber, 2017 ), so future research should bring into dialogue the dynamical systems traditions within catchment science and applied physics. Key Points: • Simple low dimensional state space reconstructions have significant forecasting skill, especially when paired with postprocessing  • New forecasting system conceptually simple, computationally cheap, and performs reasonably for a tested flood-of-record  • The success of the method shows that future efforts should concentrate on reconstituting analytical governing equations
1 Introduction Urban drainage systems are an essential part of urban infrastructure and play an important role in managing excess surface water and preventing urban flooding (Kaspersen et al., 2017; Yazdanfar and Sharma, 2015; Zhou et al., 2021 ). With the acceleration of urbanization, the number of artificial surfaces such as buildings and roads has increased, resulting in an increase in surface imperviousness, which in turn leads to an increase in peak discharge and runoff volume, and an acceleration of accumulation speed (Arnone et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Rahaman, 2021; Zhou et al., 2019 ). At the same time, the increasing number of extreme weather events under the influence of climate change has also led to more frequent urban flooding disasters (Krebs et al., 2014; Mahmoud and Gan, 2018 ), putting more pressure on urban drainage systems. Traditional urban drainage planning is typically performed manually by municipal designers based on a series of theoretical calculations and topological designs (Butler and Davies, 2010; Palumbo et al., 2014; Urich et al., 2010 ). This is a complex and time-consuming process, especially for large urban areas, because the design depends on a variety of factors such as land use distribution, subcatchment hydrological parameters, transportation network layout, and surface topography (Thorndahl et al., 2006; Yin et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Manual characterization of these factors is not only labor-intensive, but also inaccurate and error-prone (Mannina, 2018; Warsta et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2023 ). Given that such design processes need to be applied extensively and repeatedly for drainage network planning and/or system rehabilitation, there is an urgent need for more advanced and automated approaches to provide more reliable and efficient design solutions to better cope with the changes brought about by future extreme scenarios (Krebs et al., 2014; Warsta et al., 2017 ). The automatic generation of stormwater drainage systems depends on the accurate detection and feature extraction of urban land use type and distribution pattern. This can be achieved by efficient image recognition and segmentation methods. Threshold (Upadhyay and Chhabra, 2021 ) and clustering-based (Mittal et al., 2022 ) segmentation algorithms were easy to use and fast to compute, but sensitive to noise and image changes. Supervised learning methods based on feature extraction and classifiers, such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Liu et al., 2017 ) and Random Forest (RF) (Belgiu and Drăguţ, 2016 ), further improved detection accuracy, but relied on a large number of labeled data and had relatively poor generalization ability. The semantic and instance segmentation based on deep learning (DL) technology developed in recent years can efficiently process a large amount of data, and have shown high detection accuracy and strong generalization ability (Chen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022a ). Several scholars have employed deep learning methods with residual networks, skip connections, and guided filters to detect specific types of land use based on high-resolution remote sensing/satellite imagery (Chen et al., 2019; Mboga et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2018 ). In particular, the DeepLab-based algorithms have shown great potential for urban land use detection and segmentation (Akcay et al., 2022; Boonpook et al., 2023; Liu, 2023 ). How to automatically generate the topological structure of stormwater drainage based on the segmented land use pattern and regional terrain characteristics, and realize the design capacity estimation of the system is another research direction to be explored. The typical generation process includes layout planning according to land use distribution (especially road network), catchment subdivision with hydrological characterization, and structural design and capacity estimation (Hesarkazzazi et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2020 ). Previous studies have focused on how to optimize the structure and design parameters of existing drainage networks using traditional optimization algorithms and neural networks (Liang and Wang, 2020; Moeini and Afshar, 2017; Steele et al., 2016 ). Some researchers have attempted to automatically generate the partial structure of drainage systems, particularly the delineation and generation of subcatchments (Li et al., 2020; Warsta et al., 2017 ). A typical method was based on the Thiessen polygon approach (Guth and Klingel, 2012 ), which used geometric calculations to divide spatial areas according to the distribution of network nodes. However, this approach ignored the actual driving mechanism of surface water flow, so methods based on DEM and geohydrological analysis, such as the D8 algorithm, were subsequently proposed to delineate natural drainage watersheds (Freitas et al., 2016 ). Regarding the urban context, Jain et al. (2016)  proposed to delineate urban catchments based on street zoning. Therefore, a more reasonable approach is to first use actual urban streets and water bodies as boundaries, and then divide catchments and determine flow direction based on hydrological analysis (Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020 ). With the development of computer and mathematical modeling technology, the topology generation methods of the drainage system have become more intelligent and automatic. Haghighi (2013)  used a loop-by-loop cutting algorithm to cut the looped road network into a tree-like stormwater network. This method was only suitable for network design in flat areas, as surface elevation and slope were not considered. Kim et al. (2021)  developed a connectivity-informed deep convolutional generative adversarial network that can reproduce the drainage network from network samples without repeating lengthy modeling, but the generated drainage network could not explicitly show the spatial structure information. A number of studies have focused on the generation methods and performance comparisons of centralized and decentralized drainage systems. Eggimann et al. (2015)  proposed a method of shortest path finding and hierarchical-agglomerative clustering algorithms to determine the optimal concentration layout of the drainage network. Bakhshipour et al. (2019)  introduced a hanging garden algorithm to generate all possible drainage network layouts and explore different degrees of decentralization. Hesarkazzazi et al. (2022)  proposed a scheme to generate and optimize the (de)centralization layouts of urban drainage systems for both flat and steep terrains using a combinatorial graph theory-based multi-objective optimization framework. In summary, despite the achievements of previous studies, research on automated design of urban drainage systems is still relatively limited and associated with some shortcomings/limitations (see a summary of related studies in Appendix Table A1 ). Most of the previous work has focused on local/individual aspects of drainage design, such as recognition of drainage patterns, reproduction of drainage networks, prediction of maximum overflows and hydrographs. Currently, there is a lack of a general, practical and automated framework that can realize the whole set of urban drainage design processes. Our framework distinguishes itself by the use of deep learning for data generation and innovative algorithms for network design. The main contributions of the framework are summarized below:(1) The detection and segmentation of urban land use is improved by deep learning, using the promising DeepLabv3+ semantic segmentation algorithm that incorporates multiple data sources as prior knowledge. Our method considered more types of urban land use and achieved higher detection and segmentation accuracy in terms of land use categories and geometric features in complex urban environments compared to previous studies. This is of great significance for subsequent subcatchment division, hydrological characterization and topological generation. For example, Boonpook et al. (2023)  used semantic segmentation to classify land use into five rough categories, with most urban areas primarily identified as Urban or Miscellaneous. Jia et al. (2024)  proposed an improved convolution operation to improve semantic segmentation models for identifying six land use types, but their distinction between impervious surfaces and clutter remains vague.  (2) An automatic generation algorithm for urban drainage system is proposed, which can not only generate the network topology of the system, but also perform hydraulic calculation and evaluate the design capacity of the pipe network. Previous studies mainly applied their respective algorithms to optimize the layout and design capacity of existing urban drainage networks (Bakhshipour et al., 2019; Eggimann et al., 2015; Hesarkazzazi et al., 2022 ). Kim et al. (2021)  used DCGAN to automatically generate drainage networks, but their approach was mainly based on network replication of existing models and did not consider the calculation of pipeline capacity. In addition, this study further explored the effects of connection angle and constraint length on algorithm performance and design robustness.  (3) Most importantly, the key contribution of this study is the development of a comprehensive and automated framework for the entire urban drainage design process based on deep learning driven urban land use detection and innovative drainage network generation algorithms. Few previous studies have integrated land use segmentation, hydrological characterization, topology generation and pipeline capacity calculation into a fully automated framework. Although some studies have implemented topology generation, their initial data preparation and processing have been done manually (Chegini and Li, 2022 ; Döring and Neuweiler, 2019). The performance and applicability of the framework are verified through two urban case studies. The results showed promising implications for the automatic generation, planning and renovation of stormwater drainage systems.     2 Methodology Fig. 1   shows the main workflow of the methodology. The first module is the preparation and preprocessing of basic data and prior knowledge, which provides input, correction and supplementary information for the subsequent modules. The second module is a deep learning based semantic segmentation algorithm for urban land use detection, providing a detailed description of its type, location and geometric features. The third module implements automated division of subcatchments and related hydrological characterization. The fourth module realizes the automatic generation of drainage network topology and hydraulic estimation of design capacity based on the input from the above modules. 2.1 Prior knowledge processing In this study, several open-source datasets were used to prepare and process input data and prior knowledge (Table 1  ), which laid the foundation for the generality and applicability of the proposed methodology. Urban land use detection was performed based on high-resolution satellite maps obtained from Google Earth. We used the highest resolution available (i.e., 0.275 × 0.275 m) to ensure the accuracy of land use segmentation. Data on roads, water bodies and buildings were collected from Open Street Map (OSM) as prior knowledge to make detailed corrections and supplements to the segmented land use maps. Raster data of forests and green areas were obtained from Sun Yat-sen University (Shi et al., 2023 ). The surface elevation data were provided by the GDEMV3 30 M resolution digital elevation model (DEM) jointly published by NASA and METI and available in the Geospatial Data Cloud. Through a series of coordinate projections, geographic mapping, spatial and zonal processing, all land use data were integrated into a prior knowledge mask to provide corrective and supplementary information to the results generated by subsequent modules. As for the DL-based semantic segmentation model, two types of datasets were used as inputs, see Fig. 2  . First, the data for training and validation of the model came from the land cover dataset LoveDA (containing remote sensing images and corresponding label images) provided by Wuhan University (Wang et al., 2021 ). This dataset contains 5987 images of three cities in China, namely Nanjing, Changzhou and Wuhan. Each image has a resolution of 0.3 m and a sample size of 1024 × 1024 pixels. We selected the urban part of this dataset as the training and validation samples for the segmentation model. The urban land use is classified into eight main categories: background, buildings, roads, water, barren areas, agricultural lands, forests and no-data areas. The background category generally refers to paved areas, excluding roads and buildings. Our two case studies are not covered by LoveDA, but their urban layouts and characteristics are close to those of the three cities mentioned above. Once the model has been trained and validated, the inputs to the segmentation model are the high-resolution remote sensing images of the specific case studies, and the outputs are the corresponding segmented land use maps.  2.2 Deep learning-based segmentation of urban land use Fig. 3   shows the main workflow of land use type detection and segmentation. First, the network architecture of the deep learning-based semantic segmentation model was established, and the model training and performance validation were carried out based on the aforementioned segmentation dataset. Second, the remote sensing images of the study areas were fed into the trained model to generate and output the primary segmented land use map. Finally, the prior knowledge mask was used to correct and supplement the details of the segmented map, and a refined version of the land use map was obtained. In this study, the state-of-the-art DeepLabv3+ model was used to perform pixel-level segmentation of urban land use. As shown in Fig. 3 , the model contained two main structures: an encoder and a decoder. The encoder was used to extract spatial and semantic features from the input images and included a basic backbone network (i.e., a deep convolutional neural network, DCNN) and an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module. The DCNN network was used to extract data features from the input images. Through multi-layer convolution and pooling operations, DCNN gradually abstracted simple texture and edge features into complex object features. ASPP used a series of convolutional layers with different dilation rates to cluster image specifications and capture multi-scale information. This approach expanded the receptive field without adding extra computational burden, and enabled the network to access a wider range of contextual information. ASPP operated multiple convolutional layers in parallel, each with a different dilation rate, allowing it to simultaneously process and detect features at different scales in an image. Specifically, the ASPP module contained five layers of different sizes. The first four atrous convolution layers were used to expand the perceptual field of view and extract image features at different scales, and the last global average pooling layer was used to obtain the global features of the image. After concatenation, channel compression was achieved by a 1 × 1 convolution. In the decoder, a 1 × 1 convolution was used to process the low-level features from the DCNN to reduce the number of channels in the feature images. The low-level features were further concatenated with the high-level features from the ASPP structure. Due to the adoption of the pooling layer, the processed feature map had a smaller size (i.e., lower resolution) than the original image, so an upsampling technique was finally used to recover the lost information in the location boundary and spatial dimension of the feature maps. Finally, the output layer showed the detected land use type for each pixel in the segmented images. Note that in the model training, two types of data augmentation techniques, namely random reflection and random rotation, were implemented by using the ‘imageDataAugmenter ’ tool in Matlab2022a to increase the quality and quantity of the training dataset. After augmentation, 2082 and 462 images were used for training and validation of the model. ResNet-18 was used as the backbone model to achieve high accuracy and speed at the same time. The optimizer was Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum (SGDM) with a momentum parameter of 0.9. The initial learning rate, training epochs and mini-batch size were set to 0.001, 30 and 1, respectively. The experimental environment was Windows 10, and the hardware was Intel Core i5-10200H CPU and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 GPU (6 GB memory). Furthermore, this study employed three types of indicators (see Eqs. (1)–(3) ) to evaluate the performance of the segmentation model: (1) Pixel Accuracy (PA), is the proportion of correctly classified pixels to the total number of pixels; (2) Mean Pixel Accuracy (MPA), is the average PA of all predicted classes; (3) Intersection over Union (IoU), is the intersection and union of the predicted results and the ground truths for all classes.(1) PA = TP + T N  TP + T N + F P + F N       (2) MPA = 1 2  ( TP  TP + F P   + TN  FN + T N   )      (3) IoU = area ( A p  ∩ A r  )  area ( A p  ∪ A r  )       where, TP  is True Positive, indicating that the model prediction and the true value are both category 1. FP  is False Positive, referring to the case where the model prediction is category 1 while the true value is category 0. FN  is False Negative, indicating that the model prediction is category 0 while the true value is category 1. TN  is True Negative, meaning that both the model prediction and the true value are category 0. Ap  is the pixel area predicted by the model, and Ar  is the actual pixel area.  2.3 Subcatchment division and hydrological characterization In urban areas, drainage subcatchments are typically regionally subdivided along the road network. Fig. 4   shows a GIS-based processing workflow that automates the subcatchment division and associated hydrological characterization. Specifically, the road pixels detected by the refined segmentation model were first extracted and combined with the OSM data to generate a network description of road centerlines. Then, the entire case area was subdivided by the road network to obtain the boundary coordinates and shape descriptions of each subcatchment (Fig. 4 b). GIS tools such as spatial join and zonal statistics were further used to calculate the pixels/areas and proportions of different land use types in each subcatchment (Fig. 4 c). The comprehensive runoff coefficient (RC, which reflects the surface permeability) in Fig. 4 c-d was estimated for each subcatchment by the weighted mean method (R C = ∑ Ψ i  × F i   F    , where F i    is the number of pixels for each land use type in each subcatchment, Ψ i    is the runoff coefficient corresponding to the specific land use type, and F is the total number of pixels of the subcatchment). The runoff coefficient of each land use type was taken with reference to the values in the Code for Design of Outdoor Wastewater Engineering. In general, the higher the RC value, the weaker the ability of the subcatchment to intercept and attain the surface runoff, and the greater the pressure generated by rainfall on the stormwater drainage system, so the larger the conveyance capacity is required. In this study, the average RC of the entire region calculated based on the land use map segmented by DeepLabv3+ was 0.64, which is consistent with the required range (0.6–0.7) of the comprehensive runoff coefficient of urban built-up areas in the design code.  2.4 Automatic generation of network topology and design capacity The layout of stormwater drainage network generally follows the main direction of road network and surface elevation, so as to expand the range of gravity flow. Therefore, the basic logic of the automatic topology generation algorithm is to first determine the locations of manholes according to the road network structure, and then generate pipelines of different levels and flow directions according to the shortest path principle, segment connection judgment and hierarchy/level calculation based on the predefined outlet locations. The algorithm mainly consisted of seven steps, as shown in Fig. 5  . The first step was to import the basic data (outlets and road segments) from the previous modules to locate the drainage network. In this step, the coordinates and altitudes of the beginning and end nodes of all road segments and outlets were calculated based on the processed road centerlines and outlet points. Meanwhile, it was necessary to assign a corresponding ID number to each node and road segment to create an individual dataset for each type of information (Fig. 5 a). In the second step, each road segment was assigned to the nearest outlet according to the shortest path principle, and a road division dataset was created accordingly (Fig. 5 b). The third step was to determine the starting pipe, i.e. the initial main pipe connecting to the outlet. For each set of roads, starting with the outlets, the algorithm first found the roads connected to the outlets. This was done by iterating over the nodes of all road segments and searching for segments whose coordinates matched those of the outlets. The matching segments were assigned to the [starting pipe] set as initial pipes and removed from the [road] set. After the iteration was completed, all of the [starting pipe] were appended to the [main pipe] set (Fig. 5 c). The fourth step was to identify the remaining main pipes. First, by traversing each starting pipe and defining it as the current pipe segment, the algorithm found all road segments connected to the pipe. All road segments with less than the constraint length were selected as potential candidates, and the one with the smallest connection angle and less than the constraint angle was appended to the [main pipe] and set as the current pipe segment. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 5 d, the connection angle was the angle formed between the extension line of the current pipe (dashed purple line) and the subsequent connection roads (dashed yellow lines) (Fig. 5 d). The constraint angle and length were used to limit the maximum angle and pipeline length that could be formed, respectively. The algorithm continued to search for the main pipe until there was no eligible road segment, and the main pipe evaluation of the next starting pipe was started. The fifth step was to determine the initial flow direction of the pipelines. First, the flow direction of the main pipe was defined as the direction from the segment to the outlet. For the road segments that were not assigned to the main pipes, they were all classified as [branch road], and the flow direction was determined by the ground elevations of the nodes at both ends of the segment from high to low. Note that the flow direction defined in the algorithm was from the beginning point to the end point (Fig. 5 e). The sixth step was to determine the initial drainage network. Specifically, all main pipes were set as primary pipes, and those connected to and flowing towards the primary pipes were defined as secondary pipes, and so on. The above steps resulted in an initial drainage topology network with flow direction and hierarchy information (Fig. 5 f). The final step was to determine the final drainage network topology. After the previous steps, there were still some roads that could not be connected to the drainage network, which were then kept in [branch road] for processing. First, it was necessary to evaluate the roads in [branch road] to find those whose beginning point was connected to [level(1)], delete them in [branch road], reverse them and add them to [level(2)] (Fig. 5 g). After the aforementioned processing, parts of the roads in [branch road] could be linked to the reversed pipes and subsequently integrated into the network, and these roads were further added to the sets with the corresponding levels (Fig. 5 h). Next, the beginning point of the road connected to [level(2)] was found (Fig. 5 i), and so on until the final drainage network topology of the study area was established (Fig. 5 j). It should be noted that Fig. 5  only shows the main flow of the algorithm and does not list all the subdivision steps involved. For example, when determining the main pipes, specific operations such as determining the flow direction of each segment, estimating the pipe extension, calculating the connection angle and iterative evaluation were not shown in detail. This was because this type of information was a computational detail and did not affect the overall generation process, but the brief expression does not imply the simplicity of the algorithm. As shown in Fig. 6  , based on the generated topology network, the hydraulic calculation of pipe capacity was performed based on the data obtained from the land use segmentation and hydrological characterization modules. First, each subcatchment was assigned to the corresponding pipe section with the minimum starting elevation, and then the effective drainage area, the time of concentration in the pipeline, and the design flow of each pipe section were calculated in turn to estimate the design capacity of each pipe. So far, this completed the whole process of drainage topology generation and capacity estimation. Furthermore, the performance indicator, namely Critical Success Index (CSI), was used to evaluate whether the generated pipe network met the expectation, as shown in Eq. (4) .(4) CSI = Hit  Hit + M i s s + F a l s e h o o d s   × 100 %     where Hit  is the number of pipe segments that match the location of both the actual and generated pipe networks. Miss  is the number of pipe segments missing from the generated network compared to the actual network. Falsehoods  is the number of pipe segments that do not match the design specifications of the actual pipe network. In general, the higher the CSI value, the closer the automatically generated pipe network matches the actual pipe network.  2.5 Case study In order to verify the feasibility and applicability of the proposed methodology, this study took two Chinese cities as case studies, namely Lanzhou, located in the inland region of northwestern China, and Guangzhou, located in the coastal region of southern China. The satellite maps, road networks and DEMs of the two case studies are shown in Fig. 7  . The overall terrain of Lanzhou is relatively high and the surface topography slopes from southwest to northeast, with a flat plain in the central part. The DEM ranges from 1504 to 1951 m, and the average annual precipitation is approximately 327 mm. The selected area of Guangzhou has relatively flat terrain. Due to the subtropical monsoon wet climate, the average annual precipitation is between 1600 and 1900 mm. As can be seen from the satellite map, except for urban infrastructure and buildings, more green areas can be seen in Guangzhou due to the climate. Meanwhile, both areas have natural water systems, which are also the main locations of drainage outlets. It is worth noting that the two case studies present a complex and fragmented land use layout when viewed in detail. Many regions contained multiple types of land use and were associated with a large number of details. It was very difficult to detect and distinguish the different land uses by traditional manual methods, and the proposed deep learning model was necessary for accurate and efficient detection and segmentation. Meanwhile, it should be noted that the proposed framework was data friendly as the basic inputs were open source. This has greatly improved the applicability of the methodology in different regions, especially providing a valuable analysis tool for areas with limited data.   3 Results and discussion Fig. 8  a shows the training and validation accuracy and loss curves of the DeepLabv3+ model. It can be seen that all the curves converged stably after 15,000 iterations. Fig. 8 b shows the confusion matrix of land use detection, and it can be seen that the DeepLabv3+ achieved higher detection accuracy for water bodies, buildings and roads, while the segmentation performance of barren land and background could still be improved. The model tended to misclassify the two types of land use because barren land and background were very similar in color and texture. In addition, some areas of the satellite images were obscured by shadows, resulting in color and texture interference, which further increased the difficulty of detection and segmentation. Overall, except being identified as their own types, most land use types had a relatively high probability of being misclassified as background. Fig. 8 c summarizes the detection accuracy and IoU (i.e., segmentation accuracy) of each land use type. The IoU values of barren land and forest were the lowest, mainly because the characteristics of these two types were not obvious and their shapes were complex and changing. Thus, it was difficult for the area segmented by the model to fully match the actual shape. In contrast, water bodies and buildings had prominent geometric features and were the easiest types to locate and delineate. Fig. 9   shows a comparison of the samples of input images, OSM and forest data, predictions from DeepLabv3+ and refined segmentation maps from the two case studies. Visually, the deep learning model can predict the location and shape of most buildings and roads; however, due to the large detail, high complexity and various influencing factors of the satellite maps, the established model was not sensitive to the regions with many small surface objects and mixed edges, and the resulting boundaries were not clear and smooth enough. For the detection of forests, to be more precise, the urban green space, the localization and segmentation performance of the model was not satisfactory and the input of prior knowledge was necessary. Similarly, the detailed description of water bodies can be improved, especially in the case of multiple interwoven and adjacent land uses, which makes the identification of water bodies more challenging. On the other hand, the OSM and Forest datasets had high accuracy in describing the details of urban features. However, these two datasets did not cover all urban areas, and the information for many local regions was incomplete. For example, the labeling of buildings in the selected areas (dotted circles) in Fig. 9 b was sparse, and part of the forest in Fig. 9 c was not detected. In this case, it was necessary to supplement these existing datasets with the segmentation maps in Fig. 9 d. If only the existing datasets were used to describe land use, it was easy to generate drainage networks that did not meet the actual situation (Samani et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022b ). In addition, the OSM and forest datasets in the case study were mainly used to provide information on building and forest, while other types of land use such as background, barren and agriculture could not be detected at the same time. Therefore, it was necessary to use map segmentation to simultaneously detect and classify the main urban land use in the entire region, and further combine with the previous databases to improve the accuracy of the description (e.g., the edge of buildings, the extent of green space and water bodies). As shown in Fig. 9 e, the combination of DeepLabv3+ and the prior knowledge effectively improved the segmentation accuracy and the final detection output (i.e., the refined map) could accurately reflect the different types of urban land use. Fig. 10   summarizes the influence and optimization of the constraint connection angle and length on the CSI indicator. In general, the performance of the topology algorithm was robust as the obtained CSI values were relatively stable and acceptable under the varying conditions of the two types of parameters. The average CSI values of the first and second case studies were 0.65 and 0.83, respectively. The reason for the higher CSI value of the second case is that its terrain slope, water system and road structure were relatively simple, so the selection of connecting pipes was more intuitive. The results showed that the CSI reached the maximum value when the constraint connection angle was in the range of 50–60 degrees. As for the constraint length, the looser the constraint length, the higher the CSI value; however, on the whole this type of parameter had less influence on the CSI, so the optimization of this parameter can be less considered in the algorithm design. Table 2   shows the comparison between the generated topological feature data and the ground truth value under the optimal CSI index condition (i.e., the connection angle was 60 degrees and an unrestricted length of main pipes). It was shown that in both study areas, the generated network had a high degree of agreement with the expert judgment. Only 8 % and 21 % of the pipelines, respectively, did not match the expert design, indicating the satisfactory performance of the proposed methodology. Fig. 11   shows a visual comparison between the generated network topology and the ground truth under the optimal parameter conditions for the two case studies. In general, the higher the number of hits, the higher the quality of the model generation. Meanwhile, five local regions (boxes a-e) with larger generation errors were marked and it was noted that redundant pipes were more likely to occur in areas with a high density of road intersections and loops, as the algorithm tended to use all road segments to generate drainage networks. The presence of complex road networks made the selection of connecting pipes and the discarding of road segments more difficult. Fig. 12   shows the incorrectly generated pipelines in each of the five sample regions and the reasons behind them. However, in general, most of the generated pipelines were feasible, so the automatic approach can save a lot of time and resources compared to manual designs. The yellow transparent layer in Fig. 12  was the actual road network, which was used to verify and compare the accuracy of the topological structure of the drainage network. Fig. 12 a and b showed the first typical scene where the network topology was prone to errors, namely the overpass area. Due to the complexity of the road composition and structure, the algorithm was confused about which roads could be used to generate the drainage network, resulting in incorrect path selection. The second typical scene was the roads along the river banks (Fig. 12 c). In the process of road network extraction, due to the accuracy problem, the extracted routes were partially merged and partially separated, resulting in the generation of redundant or incorrect pipelines. Fig. 12 d shows a similar error scene, which was mainly caused by the small distance between adjacent roads, resulting in inaccurate road centerline extraction and generation of incorrect pipelines. As can be seen in Fig. 12 e, roads/pipelines were not closed properly or were missing because some small or secondary roads were filtered out during the road selection process. Based on the generated network, the design capacity of each pipeline could be further estimated to complete the design of the stormwater drainage system, see Fig. 13   for an example of the designed drainage for Case Study 2 under a 3-year event. More importantly, it should be noted that our methodology could be further used for system optimization purposes, such as comparing and validating the structure and layout of existing pipe networks, or assessing the suitability of existing or newly planned system capacity. As shown in the example in Fig. 13 , if the drainage system requires pipe expansion (e.g., a new return period of 10 years is adopted), the proposed algorithm can help identify and optimize where and to what extent the existing pipeline needs to be expanded by quickly estimating and displaying the changes in pipe diameter at different locations. The statistical summary and sample data of the changes in design capacity when the service level is upgraded from 3 to 10 years for both case studies are shown in Table 3  . In general, the average and maximum pipe diameters change with the planned service level, but not all pipelines need to be enlarged. In such a case, our model provides an efficient tool to study and optimize the detailed changes in each pipeline.  4 Conclusions The design and planning of drainage system has always been an important issue in urban flood management. The traditional drainage design is labor-intensive and error-prone, and the development of automatic generation method can effectively improve the efficiency of system design and planning. Meanwhile, the automatic method can better adapt to the rapid development and changes of urban construction, and improve the flexibility and sustainability of urban drainage system. To address these issues, this paper proposed an automated framework that integrates the whole set of urban drainage design processes, from urban land use detection, to catchment hydrological characterization, to drainage network topology generation, and finally to design capacity calculation. The main results obtained are summarized below.(1) The results showed that the proposed deep learning model could effectively detect and segment urban land uses, especially for water bodies, buildings and roads, with a detection accuracy of 90 %, 79 % and 78 %, respectively. Meanwhile, it was still necessary to supplement with the prior knowledge to further improve the detailed description of the shape and boundary of different land uses, so as to ensure the accuracy of subcatchment division and hydrological characterization.  (2) The accuracy of road network extraction could directly affect the performance of the generated drainage network topology. Meanwhile, the results demonstrated the importance of selecting and optimizing the algorithm parameters (i.e., connection angle and constraint length). In this study, the highest CSI index was achieved when the connection angle was between 50 and 60 degrees, with an unrestricted length of the main pipes.  (3) The automatic framework could greatly reduce the burden of field survey and manual processing of land use data, while efficiently generating the stormwater drainage system. The comparison of the generated network topology with the ground truth showed a high degree of agreement, confirming the effectiveness of the method. In the two case studies, only 8 % and 21 % of the pipelines did not match the ground truth, indicating that the proposed method can well reproduce the process and effect of expert design.  (4) Based on the automated processes and open source datasets employed in this study, the proposed framework can be easily applied to new study areas. In terms of semantic segmentation, the DeepLabv3+ model was trained with the ability to segment features of multiple land use types, which is applicable to most cities. The open source datasets (especially the remote sensing imagery, OSM and DEM data) are available in most urban areas. As long as the above data are fed into the algorithms, the network topology and pipe capacity can be obtained automatically. The two case studies also illustrated how the framework can be applied to new regions, demonstrating the transferability of the framework.    The developed method also had some limitations. For example, to generate a drainage network, the locations of the outlets need to be manually defined in advance. For roads with complex structures and loops, it is necessary to further improve the selection method of connection pipes. In addition, the drainage topology generation did not consider the effects of traffic flow, construction feasibility, economic cost and other related indicators, and future work will optimize the design of the drainage system based on these indicators. Despite its limitations, the framework provided a general, applicable and efficient tool for accurate and automated generation of stormwater drainage system based mainly on open source datasets. It is of great value and importance for the primary design and management of urban drainage, especially for areas with limited data, and can be further used to evaluate and optimize system performance and guide the direction of future mitigation or adaptation plans.
1 Introduction Drought and aridity are fundamentally different, although both of them are capable of characterizing environmental dryness (Djebou et al., 2015; Salvati et al., 2012 ). Contrary to long-term climate phenomenon, drought is a temporary phenomenon and caused by abnormal moisture deficiency of an area during a period (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). Based on the physical processes involved, drought is mainly classified into abnormal precipitation deficiency (meteorological drought), soil moisture deficiency (agriculture drought), shortage of streamflow (hydrological drought) (Mishra and Singh, 2010; Palmer, 1965a; Trenberth, 2018 ). While, aridity is a climate phenomenon, which is the long-term average climatic moisture conditions over a region (Agnew and Anderson, 1992; Maity et al., 2023 ). Based on the ratio of long-term average precipitation (P) to long-term average energy (potential evapotranspiration, PET) (Yin and Porporato, 2023 ), arid, semiarid, sub-humid and humid regions are divided (Zhang and He, 2016; Zhang et al., 2015 ). The concepts of drought and aridity are often indistinguishable, and it is widely accepted that aridity regions are prone to drought because they are more frequently to have below-average P and experience P with greater interannual variability (Smakhtin and Schipper, 2008 ). Actually, drought is mainly resulted from imbalance of water supply and demand. In other words, once the moisture supply of an area is abnormally lower than climatically expected appropriate moisture supply or actual water demand over a period, drought will occur regardless of which the climate region belongs to. Accordingly, droughts exist not only in arid and semi-arid regions, but also in sub-humid and humid regions, which highlights that understanding and addressing drought needs to be combined with climatic moisture condition. In addition to climatic water condition, social water scarcity stress is also crucial in affecting drought. In the absence of man-made influence of drought, meteorological conditions mainly dominate the drought occurrence and characteristics over a region (Furusho-Percot et al., 2019; Velluet et al., 2014 ). However, since the mid-nineteenth century, urbanization, along with agricultural irrigation expansion and industrial developments, has greatly increase water consumption and exacerbated water scarcity stress (AghaKouchak et al., 2021; Di Baldassarre et al., 2018; Etienne et al., 2016; Güneralp et al., 2015; Kreibich et al., 2019 ). Water scarcity stress, combined with rapid population growth, intensifies the overuse of water in humid regions and the existing water resource tensions in non-humid regions (Lian et al., 2021 ), thereby further increasing the exposure to droughts and amplifying the negative effects of droughts (Unfried et al., 2022 ). Undoubtedly, understanding and addressing drought in isolation from water scarcity stress will pose challenges to combat drought. Accordingly, although background climate moisture condition is emphasized in understanding and addressing drought, above suggests that water scarcity stress condition is also a vital factor affecting drought and need to be considered (Sivakumar and Wilhite, 2002; Trenberth, 2018 ). In addition to aforementioned climate moisture condition and water scarcity stress, the urgency and significance of mitigating drought impacts have also been widely and strongly recognized (Eslamian et al., 2017; Melesse et al., 2019; Unfried et al., 2022; Wang and Asefa, 2019 ), especially as drought has become the most widespread and costly natural disaster under global warming (Cook et al., 2020; Dai, 2013; Mishra and Singh, 2010; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Drought mitigation refers to methods or technical and practical means to mitigate the hazardous effects of drought on people, livelihoods and other environmental factor (Eludoyin et al., 2017 ). Studies indicated that drought mitigation includes three components: drought assessment and monitoring; prioritization of areas for drought management, and development and implementation of drought mitigation strategies (Green and Eslamian, 2014; He et al., 2014; Van Huijgevoort et al., 2012 ). However, there are three main problems in the current research of drought mitigation. First, with regard to the above three vital components of drought mitigation, most research has focused on drought assessment and monitoring, particularly in developing drought indices, such as Standardized Precipitation Index for meteorological drought (McKee et al., 1993 ), soil moisture percentiles for agricultural drought (Wang et al., 2011 ), Standardized Runoff Index for hydrological drought (Shukla and Wood, 2008; Wilhite and Glantz, 1985 ), and Socio-Economic Drought Index for socioeconomic drought (Liu et al., 2020 ). Although drought index can synthesize single or multiple hydroclimatic variables to quantify drought characteristics (Botterill and Hayes, 2012; Hayes et al., 2012; Trenberth, 2018 ), most drought indices fail to quantify the water deficit based on physical process, which impedes the preparation of extra water sources for mitigating drought (Wang and Asefa, 2019 ). Second, research on drought assessment/monitoring and drought mitigation strategies development/implementation is often carried out separately and not well integrated. This unintegration mainly due to the fact that drought assessment/monitoring fail to provide accurate information on water demand for drought recovery, and therefore cannot be used directly for government to make targeted drought mitigation decisions and policies (Maliva and Missimer, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Third, prioritization of areas for drought management is often neglected in previous research in contrast to drought assessment/monitoring and drought mitigation strategies development/implementation (Maliva and Missimer, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Actually, drought mitigation also needs to make a compromise option between maximizing mitigation effectiveness and minimizing mitigation costs. All in all, a systematic and efficient drought mitigation practices is premised on a good integration of assessment/monitoring, prioritization of areas for drought management, and mitigation strategies development/implementation. Given the urgency of reducing the drought risk and lessening economic losses during and after drought event, there is a strong need to have a comprehensive framework based on the above systematic and efficient drought mitigation practices, for efficiently and proactivity mitigating drought (Werick, 1993; Whipple Jr, 1994; Yevjevich et al., 1978 ). This framework should include: (1) the accurate drought assessment for timely monitoring (to help decision-maker to recognize drought alert); (2) the judgement of the resilience to drought disturbances (to determine mitigation necessity); (3) the quantification of water demand for drought mitigation based on drought monitoring (to identify mitigation difficulty); and (4) the statistics of regional social water scarcity conditions (to identify mitigation urgency and prioritization). To achieve this comprehensive framework, there are two key points need to be addressed. One is to link drought index with water deficit based on surface water balance to quantify specific water demand for drought mitigation under different drought severity (Maliva and Missimer, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023 ), which can bridge the gap between assessment/monitoring and drought mitigation strategies development/implementation. The other is to consider the prioritization of areas for drought management on the basis of the first point above for improving drought mitigation practices. Accordingly, focus on solving above two key points, this study intends to integrate drought index, drought resilience, drought recovery, water scarcity stress, and climatic moisture conditions to build a comprehensive drought mitigation framework. This study contributes to the decision and implementation of water resource reallocation for meeting water deficiency, and provides a benchmark for the decision-makers to generate water supply (water transfer) plan for reducing the vulnerability of natural and social systems to drought. Motivated by the urgent need to proactively mitigate drought, we proposed a comprehensive framework by integrating drought index-resiliency-recovery, water scarcity stress, and climatic moisture condition to give appropriate options of drought mitigation over different climate regions in China. Considering that hydrological drought is an indicator of water resource availability, which can easily lead to agricultural water shortage and socio-economic damage drought (Guo et al., 2020; Konapala and Mishra, 2020; Shukla and Wood, 2008; Van Loon and Van Lanen, 2011 ), this study intends to take hydrological drought as mitigation target. Therefore, the objectives of this study are: (1) to integrate drought assessment and mitigation by linking hydrological drought characteristics identified by the Standardized Water Availability Index (SWAI, taking water yield as surface water deficit/surplus metric) with specific water deficit; (2) to quantify the water demand for hydrological drought mitigation under various hydrological drought severity over different climate regions in China; (3) to proposed a comprehensive framework by integrating hydrological drought index-resiliency-recovery, climatic moisture condition, and water scarcity stress to determine the priority of hydrological drought mitigation over different climate regions in China. This study is expected to provide an optimal allocation of hydrological drought mitigation measures for stakeholders to make precise anti-drought measures and adapt appropriate drought-related water management.  2 Methods 2.1 Framework for hydrological drought mitigation We propose a comprehensive framework for hydrological drought mitigation based on surface water balance, hydrological drought index and water scarcity stress to give appropriate hydrological drought mitigation measures in different climate regions of China. The main components of this framework are summarized in Fig. 1  . 2.1.1 Water deficit/surplus estimation This study took the difference between P and ET as water deficit/surplus metric. Meanwhile, ET is the key for the assessment of P-ET. Here, we improved the PT-JPL model with vegetation dynamics (Fisher et al., 2008 ) to estimate the actual ET at grid scale with spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km. The PT-JPL model was developed from Priestley-Taylor method based on ecophysiological constraint function driven by relative humidity (RH), vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and vegetation indices. The PT-JPL model is described as:(1) LE = L E S  + L E c  + L E i      (2) LE = f wet   + 1 - f wet     f sm     α Δ Δ + γ   R ns   - G   + 1 - f wet     f g  f t  f m  α Δ Δ + γ   R nc   + f wet   α Δ Δ + γ   R nc       (3) G = R n  Γ c  + 1 - NDVI - N D V I min    NDV I max   - N D V I min       ( Γ s  - Γ c  )        (4) R ns   = R n  exp - k R n   LAI       (5) R nc   = R n  - R ns        In above equations, LE  represents the latent heat flux from the ET (W m−2 ) and can be converted into ET  (mm s−1 ). The LE  is divided into soil evaporation (LEs  ), canopy transpiration (LEc  ), and interception evaporation (LEi  ). G  is the soil heat flux (W m−2 ), Rns   is net radiation to the soil (W m−2 ), Rnc   is net radiation to the canopy (W m−2 ), Rn   is the net radiation (W m−2 ). Moreover, f wet     is the relative surface wetness (R H  4    ), f sm     is the soil moisture constraint (R H  VPD / β     ), f g    is the green canopy fraction (f APAR   / f IPAR     ), f t    is the plant temperature constraint (exp - T max   - T opt     / T opt      2      ), f m    is the plant moisture constraint (f APAR   / f APA R max       ), f APAR     is the fraction of the photosynthesis active radiation (PAR) absorbed by green vegetation cover (m 1  E V I + b 1    ), f IPAR     is the fraction of the PAR intercepted by total vegetation cover (m 2  N D V I + b 2    ), T opt     is the optimum plant growth temperature (T max     at max P A R f APAR   T max   / V P D     ), NDVI  is the normalized difference vegetation index, EVI  is the enhanced vegetation index, LAI is leaf area index (m2  m−2 ), RH  is the relative humidity (%), VPD  is the vapor pressure deficit (kPa), T max  is the maximum air temperature (°C). In the PT-JPL method (Fisher et al., 2008 ), parameters are set as: α   = 1.26 (PT coefficient), Δ   is the slope of the saturated vapor pressure curve (kPa °C−1 ), γ   = 0.066 kPa °C−1  (the psychrometric constant), β   = 1.0 kPa (a sensitivity index for the soil constraint on VPD), k Rn    = 0.6 (the extinction coefficient), Γ s    is the bare soil area parameter (i.e., 0.325), Γ c    is the better vegetation coverage parameter (i.e., 0.05), m 1  = 1.2 ×   1.136 (an empirical parameter in the fraction of PAR absorbed by green vegetation cover), m 2  = 1.0, b 1  = 1.2 ×  −0.04, b 2  = −0.05. The GIS-based PT-JPL model was improved by optimizing the PT-JPL model parameters according to in-situ  observed ET values of 12 land use types, and combining remote sensing data. Thus, the ET values can be estimated from site scale to the regional scale, and take vegetation dynamics into account. Parameters used in the PT-JPL model have been proved that m 1 , T opt    , and β   are the most sensitive to the model output (Tang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Meanwhile, average temperature has a well correlated with the optimized T opt     according to previous studies (Hu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Therefore, m 1  and β   in this study were optimized based on the observed ET values of 12 land use types, T opt     was estimated by the average temperature during the growing season. Compared with in-situ  observed ET, the two parameters were optimized when the results presented root-mean-minimum (RMSE) values. The optimized parameters were substituted into the model by annual MODIS land cover types of data (varied annually), so that vegetation dynamics could be incorporated in the modified PT‐JPL model. The optimized model combined with MODIS annual land cover type data to achieve taking vegetation dynamics into account in the evaluation of the ET.  2.1.2 Standardized water availability index (SWAI) Owing to the neglect of the role of ET in surface water-balance, most drought indices cannot provide specific information for water resources management. In addition, regional drought conditions really depend on actual available remaining water on surface land, that is the difference between P and ET (Li et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In water balance equation, the difference between P and ET is equal to Q ± ΔS (runoff + change in storage), which can better reflect regional hydrological drought state. Therefore, a reliable hydrological drought index that can accurately capture and quantify the surface water deficiency or surplus requires appropriate estimation of P-ET (Zhang and He, 2016; Zhang et al., 2015 ). A physical-based hydrological drought index driven by P-ET is urgently needed as an indicator to predict water demand for hydrological drought mitigation at a range of timescales on spatial. We then used the difference between P and ET as deviations, and converted it into a surface water availability anomaly index (S ). The obtained S  values were aggregated at different temporal scales, and further transformed into a standardized normal distribution to build a physics-based hydrological drought Index: Standardized Water Availability Index (SWAI). The S  values and its accumulation were formulated as:(6) S = C j  d    d = P - E T           (7) S i , j  k  = ∑ l = 13 - k + j  12  S i - 1 , l   + ∑ l = 1  j  S i , l    case  j < k    S i , j  k  = ∑ l = j - k + 1  j  S i , l    case  j ≥ k            where C j    is the climatic characteristic (stands for local significance of moisture departures) (Palmer, 1965b ), and d  (water deficit) can be obtained by P  minus ET. S i , j  k    is the corresponding accumulated S  by aggregating itself at different time scales (1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 9 months, 12 months, and 24 months). k  is the time scale, j  is the given month and i  is the given year, S i - 1 , l     is the monthly S  in the month l  of the year (i -1), and S i , l     is the month S  in the month l  of the year i . Finally, the accumulated S  at different time scales was transformed into the standardized normal distribution by using a three-parameter log-logistic distribution function and classical approximation of standardization (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ).  2.1.3 Validation of SWAI In this study, runoff depth (RD) and terrestrial water storage (TWS) were selected to verify whether SWAI can capture hydrological drought and land water storage variation. RD is calculated by recording runoff and is very sensitive to hydrological drought conditions (Zhang et al., 2015 ). TWS refers to water stored above and under earth surface (surface water, groundwater, soil moisture, canopy water and snow water), and is of significant implications for hydrologic extremes such as droughts and flooding (Andersen et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2010; Thomas et al., 2014 ). For testing the sensitivity of SWAI to runoff and water storage at different climate regions, the correlation between monthly RD with monthly SWAI and the correlation between monthly TWS with monthly SWAI were estimated and compared at different time scales (1-month, 3-months, 6-months, 9-months, and 12 months) in arid, semi-arid, sub-humid and humid regions. Results show that the median RSWAI-RD  (the Spearman correlation coefficients between SWAI and RD) over 1–12 month (months) timescales oscillated between 0.64 and 0.81, and the median RSWAI-TWS  (the Spearman correlation coefficients between SWAI and TWS) over 1–12 month (months) timescales oscillated between 0.42 and 0.73 (Fig. S1 ). The average RSWAI-RD  over 1–12 month (months) timescales oscillated between 0.64 and 0.79, and the average RSWAI-TWS  over 1–12 month (months) timescales oscillated between 0.44 and 0.70 (Fig. 2  d). In different climate regions, the RSWAI-RD  over 1–12 month (months) timescale were better in humid regions than non-humid regions, and the same applies to the RSWAI-TWS  over 1–12 month (months) timescale. The median RSWAI-RD  over 1–12 month (months) timescale got the best performance in humid regions (ranging from 0.78 to 0.89), followed by sub-humid regions (ranging from 0.75 to 0.82), semi-arid regions (ranging from 0.51 to 0.76) and arid regions (ranging from 0.35 to 0.58) (Fig. 2 b). The median RSWAI-TWS  over 1–12 month (months) timescale got the best performance in sub-humid regions (ranging from 0.46 to 0.81), followed by humid regions (ranging from 0.52 to 0.76), semi-arid regions (ranging from 0.34 to 0.73) and arid regions (ranging from 0.22 to 0.57) (Fig. 2 c). In general, SWAI can effectively capture the variability of runoff and water storage in drought monitoring (Fig. 2 d).  2.1.4 Drought identification and characterization The major drought events during 1982–2015 across river basins of China were characterized by SWAI. Drought events here were defined as a period in which the SWAI had been below −0.5 (Zhang et al., 2015 ) for at least 3 consecutive months. The first month in which the SWAI was negative and remains negative for 3 consecutive months, was used as the onset time here. Similarly, the first month in which the SWAI was positive and at least remains positive for 3 consecutive months, was used as the end time. The previous drought duration did not end, and the next one began; two adjacent drought durations were merged. In addition, the antidrought duration was less than 3 months, the two drought durations were combined into one drought duration. Accordingly, we identified all duration from 1982 to 2015 based on SWAI, and selected duration lasting six months or more as the major droughts. The severity of droughts can be categorized into extremely wet (SWAI≥2), severely wet (1.5 ≤ SWAI<2), moderately wet (1 ≤ SWAI<1.5), mild wet (0.5 ≤ SWAI<1), near normal (−0.5 < SWAI<0.5), mild drought (−1 < SWAI≤-0.5), moderate drought (−1.5 < SWAI≤-1), severe drought (−2 < SWAI≤-1.5), extreme drought (SWAI≤-2) (Zhang et al., 2015 ).   2.2 Water scarcity assessment The ratio of water withdrawal and water availability (Water Scarcity Index, WSI) over a period can be used to quantify regional water scarcity condition at a specific time (Sun et al., 2021 ). The greater the WSI value, the more serious the water scarcity situation in the region. In this study, we used annual water scarcity index to reflect the pattern of water scarcity at river basin and national scale. WSI assessment is described as:(8) WSI = WW  WA   = IR + I N R + U R W  WA       (9) I R 10 d a y   = max 0 , K c  × E T 0  - P         P = P 10     P 10  ⩽ 40    P = 40 + S F 1.25 P 10  - 40    0.82   - 2.94     10 9.55 × 10 - 4   × K c  × E T 0         P 10  > 40           (10) W A m  = Q m  - E F R m       EF R m  = 0.6 × M M F m     case     M M F m  ⩽ 0.4 × M A F    EF R m  = 0.3 × M M F m     case     M M F m  > 0.8 × M A F    EF R m  = 0.45 × M M F m     case    0.4  × M A F < M M F m  ⩽ 0.8 × M A F         where WW  is the annual water withdrawal, in this study it is divided into three parts: annual irrigation requirements (IR ), annual industry requirements (INR ), and annual urban and rural withdrawal (URW ).
