The net radiation data from 1982 to 2015 with spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° from Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) was downloaded from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5546316 . The dataset of surface albedo from 1982 to 2000 with spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° was from AVHRR (http://www.glass.umd.edu/Download.html ), the dataset of surface albedo from 2001 to 2015 with spatial resolution of 500 m × 500 m was from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) (http://www.glass.umd.edu/Download.html ). Annual CO2  data from 1982 to 2015 was downloaded from the NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) ESRL (Earth System Research Laboratory) (https://www.esrl.noaa.gov/gmd/ccgg/trends/gl_data.html ). The dataset of Leaf Area Index (LAI) from 1982 to 2000 with spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° was from AVHRR (http://www.glass.umd.edu/Download.html ), the dataset of LAI from 2001 to 2015 with spatial resolution of 500 m × 500 m was from MODIS (http://www.glass.umd.edu/Download.html ). The dataset of Monthly Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) from 1982 to 2000 with spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° was from MEaSUREs (https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/vip01v004/ ), the dataset of LAI from 2001 to 2015 with spatial resolution of 500 m × 500 m was from MODIS (https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/vip01v004/ ). The dataset of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from 1982 to 2000 with spatial resolution of 8 km × 8 km was from Global Inventory Modeling and Mapping Studies (GIMMS) (https://poles.tpdc.ac.cn/en/data/9775f2b4-7370-4e5e-a537-3482c9a83d88/?q=NDVI ), the dataset of NDVI from 2001 to 2015 with spatial resolution of 500 m × 500 m was from MODIS (https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/vip01v004/ ). All datasets above encompass over a range of data sets with varying spatial resolutions, we re-gridded them to a standard grid of 0.01° spatial resolution for the further calculation.  3.2 Data for validation The GIS-based PT-JPL model was validated by in-situ observed ET data (8 flux tower sites and 4 on-site field experiments) covered with 12 different land-cover types across the China (Lan et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2019 ). The performance of the GIS-based PT-JPL model basically captures the ET changes under different land cover types and is significantly better than the original version (with lower RMSE and bias compared to observations). The specific algorithms of the GIS-based PT-JPL model and its performance are described in Shao et al. (2019)  and Lan et al. (2021) . In this study, monthly RD of 261 gauging station control areas from 1982 to 2000 and monthly TWS of 261 gauging station control areas from 2004 to 2010 were used to detect the effectiveness and ability of the SWAI to capture variation in runoff and water storage (Fig. 2 a). Monthly RD values of 261 gauging station control areas from 1982 to 2000 were estimated by runoff records form the Hydrological Yearbook published by the Hydrological Bureau of the Ministry of Water Resources of China. The corresponding control areas of 261 gauging stations cover different climate regions, including arid, semi-arid, sub-humid and humid regions, as shown in Fig. 2 a. In addition, monthly TWS values of above 261 gauging station control areas from 2004 to 2010 were obtained from NASA/German Space Agency's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE).  3.3 WSI and population data Based on the population data density, the industrial and domestic water withdrawal data at the prefecture level were downscaled to obtain the industry demand and domestic water withdrawal data at the grid scale in 2020. The industry demand and domestic water withdrawal data at prefecture-level was estimated by disaggregating the National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBSC) water withdrawal data at provincial scale, and it can be obtained from (Zhou et al., 2020 ). Population data in 2020 at 1 km scale was obtained from the LandScan Global Population Data.   4 Results 4.1 Water scarcity conditions in river basins of China In this study, WSI was used to represent regional water stress at basin scale. Generally, the higher the WSI value, the more serious the water stress condition. The threshold value of WSI is set at 0.4 to define severe water stress (Vorosmarty et al., 2000 ). Moreover, area with a WSI greater than 1 needs to rely on non-renewable resources or water diversions because its water withdrawal exceeds its water available. As shown in Fig. 3  a, WSI at river basin scale varied significantly across China in terms of spatial distribution. In general, almost all severe water stress (WSI >0.4) were distributed in northern China, while almost no water stress occurred in the river basin of southern China. In addition, it can be found that WSI of river basins varied in different climate regions (Fig. 3 a & Fig. 3 c). River basins in semi-arid regions had the largest water stress (average WSIriver basin  = 1.09, median WSIriver basin  = 0.44), followed by the river basins in arid regions (average WSIriver basin  = 1.08, median WSIriver basin  = 0.41). However, although river basins in sub-humid and humid regions were densely populated (average total population of 6.85 million and 9.91 million, median total population of 5.83 million and 8.31 million, respectively), their water resources were not under great pressure due to abundant water availability (average WSIriver basin  of 0.33 and 0.22, median WSIriver basin  of 0.17 and 0.14, respectively) (Fig. 3 c). Overall, severe water stress mainly concentrated in river basins in arid and semi-arid regions, especially in semi-arid regions with extremely low water availability and relatively high population density. Considering the differences among WSI of river basins in different climate regions, we selected four typical large river basins (Fig. 3 b) to further analyze and confirm the differences of water stress in arid, semi-arid, sub-humid and humid regions. The selected typical large river basins are Heihe River Basin (mainly representing arid river basin), Yellow River Basin (mainly representing semi-arid river basin), Yangtze River Basin (mainly representing sub-humid and humid river basin), and Pearl River Basin (mainly representing humid river basin). The population of the selected four typical river basins accounts for more than half of the national population (about 53.82 %). Among them, the Yangtze River Basin had the largest population (accounting for 32.93 % of the national population), but the lowest WSI (average WSIriver basin  = 0.19, median WSIriver basin  = 0.12). However, the Yellow River Basin had the highest WSI (average WSIriver basin  = 1.52, median WSIriver basin  = 0.80), but its population (accounting for 12.23 % of the national population) was much lower than that of Yangtze River Basin and Pearl River Basin (Fig. 3 d). Overall, the water resource pressure in the Yellow River Basin and Heihe River Basins with relatively small populations is much higher than that in the Yangtze River Basin and Pearl River Basin. In other words, water stress was greater in arid and semi-humid regions than in humid and sub-humid regions, despite the high population density in humid and sub-humid regions.  4.2 Drought frequency in different reaches of river basin For revealing the frequency of drought in different reaches of river basins (especially on the lower of the river basins), this study evaluated the number of drought months at different drought severity in the upper-middle reaches and the lower reaches of the Heihe River Basin, Yellow River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Pearl River Basin (the 4 selected river basins) from 1982 to 2015 (408 months in total). Simultaneous drought (SD) means that drought occurs simultaneously in the middle-upper reaches and the lower reaches of river basin, and lower reaches drought (LRD) is defined as the drought that occurs in the lower reaches of river basin. And then, the number of SD months and the number of LRD months were counted and compared under different drought severity (Fig. 4  ). In general, the months of SD at mild severity was the highest (from 108 in Yangtze River Basin to 158 in Heihe River Basin) compared with other drought severity in the four selected river basins, followed by the months of SD at moderate severity (from 18 in Yangtze River Basin to 79 in Heihe River Basin). The frequency of SD at mild severity in Yellow River Basin, Heihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Pearl River Basin respectively accounted for 34 %, 39 %, 26 % and 29 %, and the frequency of SD at moderate severity in these river basins respectively accounted for 16 %, 19 %, 4 % and 11 %. Moreover, the frequency of SD at mild severity (moderate severity) in arid regions and semi-arid regions (Heihe River Basin and Yellow River Basin) was higher than that in sub-humid and humid regions (Yangtze River Basin and Pearl River Basin). The higher the frequency of SD, the more difficult for drought recovery on the river basin (no matter the whole river basin or the lower reaches of river basin). Above results indicate that drought recovery in a certain period in these basins is undoubtedly challenging, especially in arid and semi-arid regions. The comparison between SD months and LRD months at different drought severity in Yellow River Basin, Heihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin and Pearl River Basin were analyzed. The lower reaches of river basin are not only densely populated but also somewhat dependent on water resources from the upper and middle reaches. Once drought occurs in both the upper-middle reaches and lower reaches of the river, drought recovery in the lower reaches is more limited and uncertain. Accordingly, the higher the ratio of SD months to LRD months in river basin, the more difficult for the drought recovery in the lower reaches of this river basin. The results show that in the Heihe River Basin (the selected typical river basin in arid regions), its ratios of SD months to LRD months at different drought severity (except extreme severity) ranged from 82 % (mild severity) to 53 % (severe severity). The ratios of SD months to LRD months at different drought severity (except extreme severity) in Yellow River Basin (the selected typical river basin in semi-arid regions) also represented relatively high values and ranged from 77 % (mild severity) to 42 % (severe severity). Compared to the Heihe River Basin and the Yellow River Basin, the ratios of SD months to LRD months at different drought severity (except extreme severity) in the Yangtze River Basin and the Pearl River Basin were relatively smaller (the Yangtze River Basin: ranging from 53 % at mild severity to 17 % at severe severity; the Pearl River Basin: ranging from 66 % in mild severity to 30 % in severe severity) (Fig. 4 a & Fig. 4 b & Fig. 4 c). Extreme drought did not occur simultaneously in of upper and middle reaches of the Yellow River Basin and Yangtze River Basin (SD months at extreme is 0) (Fig. 4 d). However, all the lower reaches of these four selected river basins experienced extreme drought (Fig. 4 d). These findings show that drought recovery in the lower reaches is more limited and uncertain, especially in arid and semi-arid regions.  4.3 The resilience of river basins to drought disturbances Whether river basins can recover from drought or prolonged droughts is still a matter of debate. Recent observations exhibit that drought may have caused unexpectedly large reductions in river flows in Australia, the United States and China (Avanzi et al., 2020; Saft et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2018 ). The alternation of river runoff in the river basin after drought may provide conclusive evidence to reveal whether river basins can recover from drought. Accordingly, we investigated recovery from drought by statistically analyzing the annual runoff and P of the Yellow River Basin, Heihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Pearl River Basin. Fig. 5   mainly shows the annual precipitation P against annual runoff in the Yellow River Basin, Heihe River Basin, Yangtze River Basin, and Pearl River Basin before drought, during the drought, and after the drought. It indicates the conversion of annual P in river basin to runoff during or after the drought (drought and post-drought). The results show that runoff of the selected four river basins all reduced during the drought. However, it’s worth noting that only in the Pearl River Basin, the runoff could recover to the pre-drought state after the drought (Fig. 5 d). Significantly, runoff declined during and after the drought (even under P) and appeared not to have recovered to the pre-drought state in the Yellow River Basin, Heihe River Basin, and Yangtze River Basin. Runoff in the Heihe River Basin reduced during the drought, and after the drought the reduction had persisted, indicating that it could not recover from the drought (Fig. 5 b). Runoff in the Yellow River Basin reduced both during and after the drought and did not recover at post-drought (Fig. 5 a). Runoff in the Yangtze River Basin reduced during the drought and appeared to have recover after the drought, but did not recover to the state of pre-drought (Fig. 5 c). Overall, runoff of the river basins in humid regions trends to have ability to recover from drought. But river basins in arid, semi-arid and sub-humid regions were found to have reduced runoff after drought and had not recovered at post-drought time. The differences of annual runoff coefficient (RC) during and after drought (RC after drought minus RC during drought) of these four selected river basins were further investigated to reveal and illustrate the nonrecovery of river basin from drought (Fig. 6  ). Thereinto, the differences of annual RC during and after drought were evaluated at gauging station control area scale (36 gauging stations in Yellow River Basin, 2 gauging stations in Heihe River Basin, 76 gauging stations in Yangtze River Basin and 29 gauging stations in Pearl River Basin). In Yellow River Basin, RC decreased after drought in 16 out of the 36 gauging control areas (decreased by 0.02 ∼ 4.40), accounting for almost 68.2 % of the whole river basin area. RC after drought in Heihe River Basin decreased by 8.4 %. In Yangtze River Basin, RC decreased after drought in 43 out of the 76 gauging control areas (decreased by 0.01 ∼ 2.53). As for the Pearl River Basin, most of RC improved after drought (16 gauging control areas increased by 0.001 ∼ 2.26), accounting for more than 60 % of the whole river basin area. In general, drought recovery in river basins of river basins in arid, semi-arid and sub-humid regions is limited and uncertain. In addition, the runoff states of 261 gauging stations across China during and after drought were used to understand the drought recovery at larger scale (Fig. 7  ). The 261 gauging stations and their runoff states were divided into humid type and non-humid type. The number of non-humid gauging stations with low and very low runoff state (annual runoff ≤100 million m3 ) increased rapidly from water year 1985 and peaked at the end of the drought in 1992. Over the 7 years after the drought, there was no trend of increasing recovery, and by 1992, 58 % (47 % in 1985) of non-humid gauging stations remained within a low-runoff state. In addition, the number of non-humid gauging stations with normal and high runoff state (annual runoff ≥100 million m3 ) decreased from 1985 and bottomed out in 1992, and had not recovered in the next time. This persistence within a low state does not support the argument that drought recovery is controlled by the post-drought duration, especially in non-humid regions. However, in humid regions, the number of gauging stations with low (very low) runoff state (annual runoff ≤300 million m3 ) and the number of watersheds with normal (high) runoff state (annual runoff ≥300 million m3 ) both showed small amplitude fluctuation and maintained no significant change overall. For example, the number of humid gauging stations with low (very low) runoff state increased from drought year 1983 and peaked (n = 72) at the end of the drought in 1986. But after 5 years, it declined and almost returned to its original number (63 in 1991, 58 in 1986). For another example, the number of humid gauging stations with low (very low) runoff state peaked (n = 68) at the end of the second drought in 1992, and is rapidly declined to (even less than) its original number after 2 year (59 in 1994, 61 in 1991). To sum up, above results show that river basins resilience to drought is finite and suggest that the effects of hydrological droughts can persist prolong time, especially in non-humid regions.  4.4 Water demand for hydrological drought mitigation The water demand for drought mitigation (from initial drought severity to normal condition) was evaluated at basin scale. Here, 56 river basins across China over different climatic regions were selected. These 56 river basins cover the control areas of the above 261 gauging stations. Fig. 8   and Fig. S2  show the water demand for drought mitigation at different month in the 56 river basins. As illustration, four levels of drought severity were considered: mild drought, moderate drought, severe drought, and extreme drought. It should be noted that extreme droughts occur only in some river basins, and only in certain months (Fig. S2 ). Thereinto, more river basins in semi-arid regions experienced extreme drought, compared to river basins in arid, semi-humid and humid regions. The extreme drought in semi-arid river basins were mainly concentrated in Mar and Dec (with recovery water of 14.3 mm ∼ 42.68 mm in March, 14.33 mm ∼ 119.76 mm in December). Extreme drought in arid river basins was concentrated in August, and extreme drought in sub-humid and humid river basins was manly concentrated in February, November, and December (Fig. S2 ). Overall, regardless of the severity of drought (except extreme drought), the amount of water demand for drought mitigation was the lowest in arid basins and largest in humid basins (Fig. 8  & Fig. S2 ). For the mild drought severity, the water demand for drought mitigation: ranged from 2.72 mm (December) to 7.40 mm (July) in arid basins, 3.48 mm (December) to 25.06 mm (July) in semi-arid basins, 3.88 mm (December) to 36.45 mm (July) in sub-humid basins, and 15.27 mm (December) to 48.84 mm (June) in humid basins. For the moderate drought severity, the water demand for drought mitigation: ranged from 5.21 mm (January) to 13.51 mm (July) in arid basins, 6.37 mm (December) to 48.02 mm (July) in semi-arid basins, 6.78 mm (December) to 63.39 mm (August) in sub-humid basins, and 27.06 mm (December) to 93.06 mm (June) in humid basins. For the severe drought severity, the water demand for drought mitigation: ranged from 7.27 mm (December) to 20.51 mm (July) in arid basins, 9.85 mm (January) to 65.64 mm (August) in semi-arid basins, 11.41 mm (December) to 78.32 mm (August) in sub-humid basins, and 31.86 mm (January) to 118.80 mm (May) in humid basins. The differences between the water demand for drought mitigation at different month is also worth noting, because to some extent, it indicates the difficulty of drought mitigation (Fig. 8 ). Overall, regardless of the severity of drought (except for extreme drought), the maximum water demand for drought mitigation in semi-arid and semi-humid river basins both occurred in July and August. To some extent, this indicates that drought mitigation is more difficult in July and August for semi-arid and sub-humid river basins. In arid river basins, the maximum water demand for drought mitigation mainly occurred in June and July, which was one month earlier than that in the semi-arid and sub-humid river basins. With respect to humid river basins, the maximum water for mild and moderate drought mitigation mainly occurred in June and August, the maximum water demand for severe drought mitigation mainly occurred in May and July (one month earlier than that for mild and moderate drought recovery). In terms of the amount of water demand for drought mitigation and the month with the maximum water demand for drought mitigation appears, it is 13 the most difficult and complicated to realize drought mitigation in humid river basins through short time water transfer (as opposed to arid, semi-arid and sub-humid river basins).   5 Discussion This study proposed a comprehensive framework for hydrological drought mitigation by integrating water scarcity stress, drought index-resilience-recovery, and climatic moisture condition. This framework provides specific information on the amount of water demand for drought recovery, which is crucial for maintaining regional water supply safety under different hydrological drought severities. Comparing to the previous water demand assessment method for drought recovery (e.g., copula-based approach and the time series analysis based on the autocorrelations), this method not only quantifies the balance of water supply and demand, but also provides the minimum amount of water demand for drought mitigation at different initial drought severity. It should be noted that the water demand assessment for drought mitigation is derived by a physically-based multiscalar hydrological drought index (SWAI, driven by P-ET). According to surface water-balance equation, river basin P-ET is equal to Q ± ΔS (runoff + change in storage), which can reflect the condition of surface water deficiency or surplus. Based on P-ET and the SWAI index, an evaluation algorithm of water demand for drought mitigation was proposed, which could capture the difference between existed regional water availability and regional normal regional water availability condition. Currently, knowledge of drought recovery over river basins are limited and often disputed. Previous studies assumed that river basin may recover from drought after a wet period (Peterson et al., 2021 ). However, the arrival of this wet period is irregular and indefinite, which means that the recovery does not necessarily occur within a given time after a drought (Ault, 2020; Brodribb et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2021; Van Loon, 2015 ). For instance, Peterson et al. (2021)  investigated and analyzed the recovery of 161 river basins in Victoria State of Australia in response to the Australia Millennium Drought. Their founding shows that 37 % of the 161 river basins remained a low and very low runoff state even 7 years after the end of the Millennium Drought. Moreover, the results in our study also show that most arid, semi-arid and sub-humid river basins not recovered at post-drought time (their runoff represented a decreased trend after drought and not recovered to its pre-drought state). Our findings highlight that hydrological drought can lead to the unsteady of runoff, and make the drought recovery in river basins limited, especially in arid, semi-arid and sub-humid regions. For river basins that cannot recover from drought under natural means for a period, it is necessary to discuss the need for artificial water transfer and examine the anti-drought water storage. For instance, the Yellow River Basin (mainly located at semi-arid regions), its lower reaches have densely population (Fig. 3 ) and high drought frequency (Fig. 4 ), and it is heavily influenced by the inflow from its upper and middle reaches. In addition, the frequency of drought (including mild, moderate, and severe drought) occur simultaneously in its upper-middle and lower reaches are relatively high (Fig. 4 ). The observational data show that runoff in the Yellow River Basin reduced both during and after the drought (drought period: 1990–1992) and did not recover at post-drought (Fig. 5 ). Correspondingly, its annual runoff coefficient also decreased when drought ended and precipitation increased (Fig. 6 ). Clearly, above results shows that those river basins whose runoff did not return to normal or even decreased after the drought are unable to recovery from drought through natural means, let alone drought mitigation tasks. There is an urgent need for water resources managers, governments, and policymakers to consider the water requirements for the purposes of drought recovery by artificial water transfer. It is worth mentioning that the difficulty of getting enough water in the next few months to mitigate the drought (reaching the normal status) would vary by regions. We concluded that the priority of water transfer and drought mitigation should be given to the densely populated semi-arid regions. In one hand, the water demand to mitigate the drought in the following months may be difficult to obtain in the arid and humid regions (especially in the extremely dry initial conditions). Since arid regions are generally far away from water-rich regions, and water demand for mitigating drought are huge in humid regions. In another hand, we find that it is the semi-arid river basins with huge population size facing the highest water stress (Fig. 3 ). Moreover, the water demand for drought mitigation in semi-arid regions was obviously less than that in humid and semi-humid regions. Considering the low precipitation, high population density and relatively small water demand for drought mitigation, the densely populated semi-arid regions should be given priority for drought mitigation and water transfer. Although this study considered social water resource stress based on estimating WSI and provide water demand for drought mitigation based on physical processes and surface water-balance, this method does not couple social water system (human-dominated water resources, e.g., agricultural, and industrial water) into natural hydrological cycle. Since the mid-19th century, along with major industrial and agricultural developments, population growth has increased water consumption and exposure to drought (AghaKouchak et al., 2021 ). Natural climate variability and human activities have emerged as the main drivers of observed Anthropocene water availability variability, water stress and drought evolution. Accordingly, it is necessary to consider the two-way interactions of human activities with changing drought (AghaKouchak et al., 2021 ). Future work can further improve the effectiveness of drought resistance by incorporating the impacts of social water stress on drought and integrating natural and social water system. In addition, due to the limited access to long-term continuous observations of runoff and soil moisture, up-to-date drought recovery and mitigation conditions were not applied and shown in this study. Future work can also improve the assessment of the prioritization of areas in drought management by increasing the availability of observational data, such as runoff, to further enhance the effectiveness of the integrated drought mitigation framework.  6 Conclusions The disconnection between hydrological drought assessment and mitigation makes it difficult to implement effective hydrological drought mitigation measures. The key of linking hydrological drought assessment and mitigation is to quantify the amount of water demand for hydrological drought mitigation with hydrological drought index based on surface water balance. Accordingly, we developed a SWAI-based method to quantify the water demand for hydrological drought mitigation under various drought severity. Furthermore, a comprehensive framework was proposed by integrating water scarcity stress, drought index-resilience-recovery, and climatic moisture conditions, to investigate the priority of hydrological drought mitigation over different climate regions in China. Contrary to humid river basins, non-humid river basins have a higher simultaneous drought frequency and a more finite resilience to drought disturbances. Moreover, the WSI of non-humid river basins is significantly higher than that of humid river basins, especially in densely populated semi-arid river basins, such as the Yellow River Basin. Although the non-humid regions bear greater water scarcity stress and the lowest resilience to drought disturbances, the water demand for hydrological drought recovery (3 mm ∼ 7 mm in mild drought, 5 mm ∼ 14 mm in moderate drought, 7 mm ∼ 21 mm in severe drought) is significantly less than that of the humid regions (15 mm ∼ 49 mm in mild drought, 27 mm ∼ 93 mm in moderate drought, 32 mm ∼ 119 mm in severe drought). However, compare with non-humid river basins, humid river basins have higher resilience to drought, but greater water demand for drought recovery. Our findings therefore highlight that densely populated non-humid river basins should be prioritized or not ignored when developing and implementing drought mitigation measures, as they are more water scarcity stress, lower resilience to drought disturbances and less water demand for drought mitigation. This work highlights the complexity of the hydrological drought mitigation, since its optimal strategies was dominated by the coupling effects of water scarcity stress, drought characteristics, drought recovery and climatic moisture condition.
