1 Introduction Acid in–situ leaching (AISL) is considered a standard underground uranium mining method. Uranium resources are recovered from sandstone–hosted deposits by circulating lixiviants (sulphuric acid) via injection and pumping. With the application of this technique, high surface disturbance is avoided and is also appropriate for low–grade uranium ores (IAEA, 2018a, b; Ma et al., 2014a; Kidd, 2009 ). During this process, sulphuric acid extracts uranium from uranium–bearing minerals and alters gangue minerals, resulting in the migration and precipitation of ions in the groundwater aqueous environment. The water–rock reaction mechanism is a crucial factor affecting the variation in groundwater chemical components and contents. Hence, it has a major impact on the quality of groundwater. This process can be described as the reverse of the uranium mineralisation process. The previously reported works in the literature have concentrated on the geochemical properties of uranium (Ram et al., 2011; Han et al., 2021; Song et al., 2020 ) and the hydrochemistry characteristics of the aqueous environment (Malov, 2016; Lu et al., 2023; Escario et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the mineral characteristics (Su et al., 2020; Robin et al., 2020 ) and permeability (Zhao and Li, 2021; Zeng et al., 2021 ) have been also analysed. However, the relationship between the alterations in the hydrochemical characteristics of ions and the occurrence of water–rock reactions has not been extensively explored. The forms of uranium minerals and the physicochemical properties of groundwater have a significant impact on the recovery of uranium from ore–bearing aquifers (Langmuir, 1978; Shi, 1990; Su et al., 2020 ). Over the past few decades, research on the acid leaching of uranium has highlighted the migration and oxidation of uranium, along with the environmental implications of uranium transport (Morrison et al., 1995; Yue and Wang, 2011; Alam and Cheng, 2014; IAEA, 2016; Saunders et al., 2016; Smedley and Kinniburgh, 2023; Ma et al., 2014b ). These works considered various factors, such as the geochemical properties of minerals and the physicochemical parameters of groundwater, including pH, redox potential (Eh), ionic components, and seepage fields. Shi (1986)  applied thermodynamics to calculate the distribution of uranium species in natural water in a hypogene zone. Their findings demonstrated that UO2 CO3  was the dominant uranium species in weakly acidic water, whereas UO2 2+  was dominant in the acidic water of the sulphide oxidation zone. However, UO2 (SO4 )n 2–2n  was absolutely dominant when the SO4 2–  concentration exceeded 400 mg/L. Gao et al. (2003a, b)  revealed the migration characteristics of uranium using a column leaching experiment and concluded that uranium migration underwent multiple cycles of dissolution, precipitation, and redissolution; for instance, dissolved uranium precipitates when pH>4.6 and Eh < 420 mV. In contrast, U(Ⅵ) dissolves when 2.0 < pH<4.6 and 420 mV<Eh < 650 mV, whereas U(Ⅳ) dissolves when pH<2.0 and Eh > 650 mV. Based on this observation, the flow path of uranium migration can be divided into a completely leached zone, an effective leached zone, a uranium precipitation zone and a non–leached zone. Shi et al. (2004)  reported that pH=2.0 and Eh = 700 mV are critical conditions for uranium migration. Ram et al. (2011)  conducted dissolution experiments to investigate the relationship between Fe (FeIII , FeII ) and oxidation–reduction potential on the dissolution of synthetic uraninite. It was reported that the uraninite dissolution rate was highly dependent on Fe concentration at oxidation–reduction potentials of 460–565 mV but exhibited a low dependency at < 420 mV. Furthermore, Ram et al. (2013)  emphasised that excessive SO4 2–  leads to a reduction in the oxidation–reduction potential, thereby hindering the formation of Fe(III) complexes and the dissolution of uraninite. Based on the field AISL tests, Zhou et al. (2020)  discovered a strong positive correlation between the dissolution of uranium and the reduction of Fe(III) and Eh. However, the impact of introducing sulphuric acid on the chemical compositions of groundwater and the correlations of various chemical components have not been systematically investigated. Uranium recovery and reagent consumption are considerably affected by the mineralogical features of an ore (Lottering et al., 2008; Bowell et al., 2011; Sapsford et al., 2012 ), including its primary mineral composition, mineral crystallinity, and bulk composition. In addition, the mineralogy of the associated gangue and oxidised uranium may also affect uranium recovery (Charalambous et al., 2014 ). Lottering et al. (2008)  evaluated the uranium leaching response of low–grade ores in South Africa via uranium leaching tests. More specifically, they used residue analysis to determine that quartz, muscovite, pyrophyllite and albite are non–acid consumers, whereas chlorite is a critical acid consumer. Youlton and Kinnaird (2013)  investigated the gangue–sulphuric acid interactions during the acid leaching of uranium. It was discovered that smectite lowers the U concentration, whereas a high zeolite concentration increases acid consumption and causes gelling of the pregnant leach solution. Ben Simon et al. (2014)  constructed a reactive transport model to assess the impact of ore mineralogical composition on secondary minerals in AISL mining. The model illustrated that the dissolution of carbonate and iron oxide consumes acid and buffers the pH, whereas increasing its content can boost alunite precipitation. The existence of higher acidity leachate enables gypsum precipitation and lessens alunite precipitation. In addition, increasing the carbonate content is conducive to the precipitation of secondary minerals (alunite, gypsum and kaolinite). Simultaneously, the precipitation of kaolinite surges with silicate (feldspar and mica) content. However, the critical reaction processes and directions of gangue minerals under sulphuric acid leaching conditions are not fully understood, especially the relative dissolution and precipitation capacity of multiple minerals. During the AISL process, the erosion of sulphuric acid and the dissolution of gangue minerals are intertwined with the oxidation of uranium ore (Wang et al., 2022a; Bhargava et al., 2015; Dangelmayr et al., 2017 ). For this strategy, the primary hydrogeochemical action in aquifers systems can be only qualitatively assessed using the graphic and ion combination ratio methods, in conjunction with conducting multivariate statistical analysis (Cui et al., 2022; Chang and Wang, 2010; Lin et al., 2021 ). Quantitative modelling of hydrogeochemical evolution is rare. Inverse modelling has been frequently used to quantify and identify the underlying mechanisms of hydrogeochemical evolution (Han and Liu, 2004; Zhu et al., 2017 ). Particularly, the water–rock interactions in regional hydrogeochemistry have been examined, which explain the sources of the differences in aqueous solution components and the relative contribution rates of each source during the hydrogeochemical process (Wang et al., 2023 ). However, this phenomenon is rarely reported in AISL mining. Therefore, inverse modelling may determine the reaction of gangue minerals and the hydrogeochemical evolution mechanisms in natural uranium–bearing aquifers. Such an investigation is crucial to understanding the role of these processes in uranium recovery. In this research, different concentrations of sulphuric acid were employed to soak sandstone–type uranium ore in Inner Mongolia. The hydrochemical characteristics and inverse modelling were analysed based on soaking tests, and the water–rock reaction mechanism of the uranium leaching process was ascertained under varying sulphuric acid concentrations. The specific objectives of this work were to (i) identify the variations in the hydrochemical characteristics of leachate following AISL mining, (ii) quantitatively assess the reactant amounts and reaction directions involved in hydrochemical reactions during AISL mining, and (iii) clarify the correlations between the hydrochemical characteristics and water–rock reactions. This work’s findings yield novel insights into the hydrochemical evolution mechanisms of AISL mining in groundwater systems. Meanwhile, a deep understanding of hard–to–observe phenomena such as mineral dissolution was provided, lucidating the origins of pore plugging and acid consumption during uranium leaching in the AISL process.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The Bayan–Uul area in the north–central Erlian Basin of Inner Mongolia, China, hosts sandstone–type uranium deposits with apparent roll–front features. In the early stage of the Saihan formation, warm and humid reduction conditions were conducive to enriching pyrite and uranium mineralisation. After that, a dry and hot climate at the end of sedimentation facilitated uranium activation and migration, boosting uranium formation (Liu et al.,2023; Guo, 2014 ). The deposit is primarily controlled by the paleo–valley’s sand bodies in the Saihan formation’s upper portion. The creation of the ancient valley was affected by the existence of negative landforms generated by the basement structure. The basement strata include Lower Cambrian, Upper Carboniferous and Lower Permian. The Mesozoic–Cenozoic sedimentary caprocks were developed to varying degrees from the Jurassic to the Quaternary. Uranium ore bodies manifested in the paleo–valley sand bodies in the upper part of the Saihan formation during the Lower Cretaceous period. The latter was developed in the valley sand body under the control of the phreatic–interlayer oxidation zones. The groundwater types are bedrock fissure water, clastic rock pore water, and loose rock pore water. Clastic rock pore water is the central groundwater type, and the sedimentary environment regulates its abundance. The clastic rock pore water of the Saihan formation is regulated by the northeast–trending paleo–valley and is distributed in the middle of the stepwise alpine plain. Therefore, the aquifer spreads in a northeast–trending belt with a stable distribution. The lithology of the aquifer consists of a mixed layer of sandstone and sandy conglomerate with a thickness of about 30–80 m. There are two to four layers of mudstone and local argillaceous siltstone interlayers. The aquifer is rich in confined groundwater with a buried depth (10–45 m) and a high permeability coefficient (8.9 ∼ 13.2 m·d–1 ). The groundwater is a single hydrochemical type: anionic multicomponent–Na type water with a salinity of 1.99 g·L–1  (Guo, 2014; Qin, 2022; Wang et al., 2022a and 2023 ) (Fig. 1  ).  2.2 Samples 2.2.1 Sampling and preparation The uranium ore used for this work came from an interlayer oxidation zone–type deposit in Inner Mongolia (Erlian Basin, China). The ore materials were obtained from the drill core samples of ore–bearing aquifers at depths of 100–150 m in the uranium mining area. In total, 156 samples were collected from the cores of 24 evenly distributed boreholes. The sample collection information is listed in Table S1  of Supporting Information S1 . The sample was grey sandstone with a medium–fine gravel structure and massive texture comprising clastic components and matrix. The samples consisted of gravel with pores filled with sand particles and clay minerals. The samples were naturally dried, crushed and sieved to obtain four different particle sizes (<0.3 mm, 0.3–1.0 mm, 1.0–3.0 mm and > 3.0 mm) to enhance the reaction between the samples and sulphuric acid during the soaking test (Fig. 2  a). A composite sample was prepared by mixing equal masses (40 g) of the four different particle sizes, yielding a total of 160 g (Fig. 2 a). A composite sample representing the average grain size, mineralogy and uranium content of one of the deposits was assembled to yield homogeneous samples for all the soaking tests.  2.2.2 Sample analysis Imaging of the petrology and mineralogy of the ore materials was conducted at the State Key Laboratory of Nuclear Resources and Environment, East China University of Technology, using a JEOL J7600F back–scattered electron (BSE) microscope and JXA–8230 electron microprobe (EPMA). Meanwhile, a scanning electron microscope (Nova NanoSEM450, FEI, America) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (SEM–EDS; SDD Inca X–Max20, Oxford, England) was used to characterise the morphological features and elemental composition of the ore samples. In addition, the conventional X–ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of the phase composition of the ore samples was conducted using a DRON–8 diffractometer at a voltage of 40 kV, current of 40 mA, scanning angle of 0–140°, and scanning speed of 0.05°·s−1 . The phases were identified by decoding the XRD patterns using the International Centre for Diffraction Data (ICDD) diffraction database. The quantitative changes in the XRD patterns were assessed based on the height of the peak of the primary diffraction maximum of a mineral. Furthermore, a major element analysis was performed on the ore samples at ALS Laboratories, Guangzhou, China using the ALS fusion disk XRF analysis method ME–XRF26. Trace elements were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP–MS; ME–MS81). The SEM photographs of the samples can be found in Liao (2022), Chen (2022)  and Liu et al. (2023) . Fig. 2 b shows the EDS elemental analysis at selected spots, and Fig. 2 c depicts the XRD patterns and phase identification. Table 1   enlists the chemical composition of the samples. First, the SEM analysis shows that the occurrence of uranium largely comprises U–bearing minerals, uranium minerals and adsorption uranium (Chen, 2022 ). U–bearing minerals include U–bearing ilmenite, U–bearing anatase and U–bearing rare earth minerals, which are mostly scattered in fine particles in quartz, feldspar, and matrix. Uranium minerals include uraninite, uranium black, coffinite and wisaksonite. These uranium minerals are commonly associated with chlorite, calcite, quartz, rutile and feldspar, and are always intergrown with pyrite. Meanwhile, pyrite is an essential vehicle for uranium adsorption. Greater amounts of uranium are absorbed into clay minerals. The clastic components mostly included quartz, feldspar and detritus but also lesser amounts of mica, calcite and clay minerals (Liao, 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Liu, 2022a, b ). Feldspar minerals include K–feldspar, albite, anorthite and plagioclase. Plagioclase is a microcline with evident lattice twins (Chen, 2022 ). Ferric minerals consist of ferric sulphides (pyrite) and ferric oxides (FeO and Fe2 O3 ) (Chen, 2017; Guo, 2014 ). Pyrite is mostly produced as cement and minor clastics, which can suggest the activation, migration and enrichment of uranium (Le, 2021 ). Partial pyrite is oxidised to hematite (Liao, 2022 ). Clay minerals mainly comprise montmorillonite, kaolinite and illite, along with minor chlorite, which incompletely fills the pores with dispersed particles and adheres to the particle surface in a thin film (You et al., 2015 ). Second, the EDS analysis demonstrated that the ore samples predominantly consisted of Si and Al, with lesser contents of Na and K (Fig. 2 b). These outcomes are consistent with the XRF results presented in Table 1 . Third, the XRD analysis reveals that the ore samples mainly comprised quartz (37.30 %), K–feldspar (26.64 %), plagioclase (33.23 %) and kaolinite (2.83 %) (Fig. 2 c). Peaks of the remaining minerals could not be observed in the spectra; therefore, their contents are considered negligible. Finally, the XRF analysis demonstrated that the major elements predominately comprised SiO2  and Al2 O3 , with contents of 74.52–75.09 % (average: 74.81 %) and 11.31–11.49 % (average: 11.40 %), respectively (Table 1 ), indicating that the ores have a high clay content. The Na2 O, K2 O and Fe2 O3  contents generally range between 1 % and 5 %. The high contents of Al2 O3 , K2 O and Na2 O suggest that the ores have a high feldspar content, which is consistent with the XRD results (Fig. 2 c). In addition, the high content of Fe2 O3  indicates that the ore constitutes pyrite or ferric silicate. The MgO and CaO contents were generally < 1 %, with averages ​​of 0.35 % and 0.414 %, respectively, signifying that the ore has a low carbonate content. The CO2  content of < 0.2 % also reveals that the ore has a low carbonate content. The U content ranged from 59.3 ppm to 64.8 ppm (average 62.05 ppm) in the trace elements, showing that the ore has a minor uranium content.   2.3 Soaking tests Soaking tests were conducted at a liquid/solid ratio of 500 mL/120 g. The tests were performed in a 500 mL conical flask, combining 120 g of the composite sample and 500 mL of sulphuric acid (H2 SO4 ). The conical flask was closed and stirred in a shaker at a temperature of 25 °C and rotation speed of 120 r/min (Fig. 2 d). Four sets of tests were executed at H2 SO4  concentrations of 2 g/L, 5 g/L, 8 g/L, and 10 g/L, respectively, to compare the dissolution rates under different acidity conditions. Two parallel tests were also conducted in each set to reduce errors. Soaking tests were performed for 1–512 h (21.33 d). The pH and Eh values were measured at the end of each test. The leachates were filtered to 0.45 μm  for chemical analysis (chromatography and ICP–MS), such as U, K+ , Na+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , ΣFe, Si, Al3+  and SO4 2– . The concentrations of Fe3+  and Fe2+  were determined using EDTA titration. The test data were verified via the anion–cation balance using the following formula:(1) E = ∑ m c  - ∑ m a   ∑ m c  + ∑ m a        where E  represents the relative error (%) and m c  and m a  denote the milligram equivalent concentrations of cations and anions (meq/L), respectively. An E  value within ± 5 % confirms the reliability of the water quality analysis results. All the water sample test results fulfilled the analysis requirements following inspection.  2.4 Data analysis A statistical summary and visualisation of the test data were conducted in this work. The hydrochemical characteristics and water–rock reaction mechanism were analysed to reveal the reactions between minerals and sulphuric acid during the AISL process. The hydrochemical analysis focussed on the correlation between the different hydrochemical parameters. Pearson’s correlation coefficients and p –values were calculated for carrying out the correlation and significance analysis, respectively, with p –values < 0.05 considered significant for this work. Meanwhile, PHREEQC v3.6.2 was used to calculate the species distribution and saturation indices (SIs) of the mineral phases. This software package uses inversion simulations to analyse the water–rock reaction that occurs during the acid leaching of uranium (Fig. 3  ). 2.4.1 Speciation and saturation index calculations A speciation calculation distributes the total concentration of elements in the solution among aqueous species using an aqueous model, the results of which are the activities of the aqueous species. With these activities, the SI of minerals relative to water can be calculated (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ). The SI is the central parameter reflecting the dissolution and precipitation of minerals in an aqueous solution. PHREEQC software was used to calculate the species distribution and concentration in the leachate, with minteq.v5.dat as the database (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ). Simultaneously, the SI of each mineral was calculated to determine the saturation state of the mineral phases.  2.4.2 Inverse–modelling calculations 1) Modelling philosophy    Inversion simulation is based on the modelling of mass and charge conservation. It analyses the composition differences between the leaching agent and leachate. Its mathematical equations are expressed as follows (Plummer et al., 1980, 1983, 1990 ):(2) ∑ p = 1  p  α p  β p , k   = Δ m  T , k ( f i n a l )   - Δ m  T , k i n i t i a l      = Δ m  T , k | k = 1 , ⋯ , j       (3) ∑ p = 1  p  μ p  α p  = R S f i n a l   - R S i n i t i a l   = ∑ i = 1  I  v i  m i f i n a l      - ∑ i = 1  I  v i  m i i n i t i a l      = Δ R S     where the mass transfer coefficient ɑp   is the number of moles of the p th  mineral entering (positive) or leaving (negative) the solution. βp, k   stands for the stoichiometric coefficient of the k th  element in the p th  mineral. mT, k   represents the sum of the net moles of that element entering or leaving the solution via dissolution, precipitation, biological degradation or gas transfer of P  phases along the flow path. mi   denotes the molality of the i th  species in solution. vi   represents the valence of the i th  species in solution. There are j  equations of the form of (2), one for each element (excluding hydrogen and oxygen), which are required to define the composition of the P  phases (minerals) considered in the model. The chemical components of the leaching agent, leachate and potential reactants in the ore minerals (reaction minerals) must be clarified to establish the inverse model. Therefore, the leachate concentration at 512 h was selected as the final hydrochemical component and the sulphuric acid concentration as the initial hydrochemical component. The analysis of the mineral composition determined the potential reactants. The PHREEQC software was used to perform inversion calculations of the change in the solution components before and after the soaking test. The primary chemical reactions and their degree were then inferred (Fig. 4  ). The major advantage of inverse modelling with PHREEQC lies in its capability to involve uncertainties in the analytical data, producing more robust inverse models; that is, small changes in input data do not produce large differences in model–calculated mole transfers (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013; Parkhurst, 1977 ). This work assigned an uncertainty limit of 5 % to all chemical data for the leaching agent and leachate. This limit was selected because it is close to the smallest uncertainty limit needed to obtain a charge balance (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ).2) Potential reactants    Table 2   presents the potential reactants for the composite sample, which were determined from the sample analysis in Section 2.2.2 . The sulphate mineral content was low. Besides gypsum, mirabilite and alunite were selected based on the previously reported works in the literature (Ben Simon et al., 2014; Chen, 2022 ). Zhao and Li (2021)  discovered that sandstone pore plugging is mainly caused by Fe(OH)3  and gypsum precipitation. Hence, Fe(OH)3  should be substituted in the simulation calculation. Carbonate minerals react with sulphuric acid to produce carbon dioxide, expressed as CO2  (g) in the inversion simulation. Because some ions have ion exchange, four exchange species (NaX, KX, CaX2  and MgX2 ) were added to the inversion simulation (Zhu et al., 2017; Wickham, 1992 ). The U element in the leachate is of no concern here because its content was too low (generally < 1 %). It primarily originates from the dissolution of uraninite and schoepite and the desorption of adsorbed uranium (Zheng, 2017 ). Schoepite is considered the most common oxidation product of uraninite (Deditius et al., 2007 ). However, the minerals associated with the uranium ore are challenging to analyse due to their complicated types and contents. Therefore, inversion simulations mostly calculate the reactions of the associated minerals (i.e. potential reactants).3) Model optimal solution screening    An accurate determination of the reactants and their molarity of participation in the reaction adheres to the principles of mass and charge conservation. In this process, the simulation usually offers multiple solutions because the number of potential reactants used in the simulation is more than the actual reactants involved in water–rock reactions. For instance, the model outputs all feasible solutions that conform to the equilibrium equation and the thermodynamic law of the reaction. However, invalid solutions are also output that do not conform to the actual hydrogeological conditions. The application of reasonable constraints can filter out invalid results and retain the optimal solution. Although the inverse modelling calculations may be constrained to only make the potential water–rock reactants dissolve or precipitate, they cannot constrain the molarity of the dissolving or precipitating reactants. Therefore, the preliminary results were screened according to the dissolution or precipitation of reactants. Next, the results were screened according to the initial mineral content, thermodynamic properties and slag analysis. According to the capacity of the potential reactants to dissolve or precipitate in sulphuric acid and their SI presented in Section 3.1.3 , anorthite, albite, FeO, K–feldspar, calcite, pyrite, hematite, dolomite, and microcline were forced to dissolve (positive mole transfer) if they were used in an inverse model. Gypsum and quartz were only forced to precipitate (negative mole transfer). Due to the leachate being strongly acidic (pH<2.1), the CO2  generated by the reaction of carbonate minerals and sulphuric acid escaped as gas (negative mole transfer). Furthermore, NaX and KX were forced to dissolve in the Ca–Na and Mg–Na cation exchange systems, whereas the corresponding cation alternating adsorption products CaX2  and MgX2  were forced to precipitate (Zhu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023 ). An increase in the Mg content indicates the precipitation of illite. Similarly, an increase in the S content suggests the precipitation of gypsum, mirabilite, or alunite. Assuming that the composite samples were completely dissolved, the maximum concentrations of each ion were obtained using the calculations in Table 1 . Correspondingly, the dissolved amount of each reactant should be lower than the maximum concentration of its corresponding ion. These results are as follows: CCa–max  = 0.023 mol/L (e.g. dolomite, calcite, anorthite, Ca–Montmorillon), CFe–max  = 0.048 mol/L (e.g. FeO, pyrite, hematite, chlorite), CMg–max  = 0.028 mol/L (e.g. illite), CAl–max  = 0.715 mol/L (e.g. kaolinite, K–feldspar, muscovite, albite, microcline, alunite), CNa–max  = 0.231 mol/L, CK–max  = 0.236 mol/L and CSi–max  = 3.99 mol/L.    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Hydrochemical characteristics of leachate 3.1.1 Soaking test results Fig. 5   illustrates the temporal changes in the pH, Eh and leachate concentrations of U, SO4 2– , ∑Fe, Fe3+ , Fe2+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Al3+ , Na+ , K+ , and Si (Table S2  in Supporting Information S1 ). The acidification of an aquifer induces geochemical reactions between the sulphuric acid and minerals in the host rock (Lagneau et al., 2019 ). Oddo et al. (1981)  emphasised the significance of Eh–pH conditions in AISL. Appropriate batch tests were performed to illustrate this phenomenon (Fig. 2 d). All the leachates were acidic for the four soaking test groups. The pH values exhibited ranges of 1.43–2.03, 1.16–1.56, 0.98–1.31 and 0.91–1.24, which increased by 0.60, 0.40, 0.33 and 0.33, respectively. The Eh values had ranges of 280.50–245.00 mV, 494.50–405.50 mV, 499.50–415.50 mV and 507.50–418.50 mV, and decreased by 35.5 mV, 89.0 mV, 84.0 mV and 89.0 mV, respectively. The total dissolved solids (TDS) values of the leachates at 512 h were 4.54 g/L, 9.9 g/L, 13.02 g/L, and 14.31 g/L, respectively. Therefore, the pH values decreased, whereas the Eh and TDS values increased with sulphuric acid concentration. This outcome indicates that the water–rock interactions of the ore sample became more vigorous, and the leachate became more oxidising with the increase in the sulphuric acid concentration. In addition, the dissolution reactions of the minerals caused a rise in leachate TDS of over 1 g/L due to increases in ions such as SO4 2– , Ca2+ , and Mg2+  (among others) originating from the composition of the sulphuric acid and the accompanying host–rock dissolution. It is also worth noting that the Fe3+ /Fe2+  concentration ratios of the leachates at 512 h were 0.10, 0.22, 0.31, and 0.40 respectively, indicating that the Fe3+  concentration propagated more than the Fe2+  concentration and that leachate oxidation increased with sulphuric acid concentration. In the four groups of soaking tests, the U concentration of the leachate slowly increased with time because impurity minerals compete with uranium ore for sulphuric acid in the leaching process, resulting in the slower dissolution of uranium ore. A decreased impurity of the mineral dissolution increases uranium ore dissolution and leachate U concentration. For example, calcite, hematite and pyrite are more likely to react with sulphuric acid and slow down the dissolution of uranium ore (Wang, 2022b; Lu et al., 2023 ). Wang et al. (2001) reported on the ability of impurity minerals to compete with the uranium ore for sulphuric acid in the AISL process, which can be ranked from strong to weak as calcite, hematite and pyrite. However, the U concentration rapidly increased within the first 3 h because of the desorption of adsorbed uranium. Zhou et al. (2020)  attributed this result to an ion exchange process driving uranium desorption; for example, the complexation of UO2 SO4  weakens the absorbability of U, inducing the absorption of protons instead of UO2 2+ . In the four groups of soaking tests, the U concentration increased with sulphuric acid concentration, suggesting that an increasing concentration fosters the dissolution of uranium ore. The Fe3+  concentration rapidly increased within 3 h, and then fluctuated. During n this process, the Fe3+  concentration increased as ferric minerals dissolved to form Fe3+ , and then reduced as the redox reaction between Fe3+  and U(Ⅳ) generated Fe2+  and U(Ⅵ) (Lagneau et al., 2019; Collet et al., 2022; Laxen, 1971 ). The variations in Fe2+  and ΣFe concentrations were similar at sulphuric acid concentrations of 8 g/L and 10 g/L, indicating that an increase in sulphuric acid concentration above 8 g/L has a negligible impact on the Fe2+  and ΣFe concentrations. Consequently, the soluble ferric minerals in the ore are largely dissolved, whereas the insoluble minerals dissolve slowly or are insoluble. The concentrations of Ca2+ , Mg2+  and Al3+  were closely similar at sulphuric acid concentrations of 5 g/L, 8 g/L and 10 g/L, which were much higher than those at 2 g/L. These results indicate that soluble carbonate and feldspar are largely dissolved at sulphuric acid concentrations > 5 g/L. The changes in leachate Si concentration were similar, suggesting that the sulphuric acid concentration exerts no considerable impact on the dissolution of silicate minerals.  3.1.2 Hydrochemical types and chemical component correlations The major cations of the leachate were Ca2+  and Mg2+  at a sulphuric acid concentration of 2 g/L. The total cation concentrations (mmol/L) were ranked as Ca2+  > Mg2+  > Na+  > Al3+  > Fe2+  > K+  > Fe3+  with < 416 h of immersion. Next, Na+  dominated after 416 h. These results demonstrate that calcium and magnesium minerals dissolve faster than sodium minerals. However, sodium minerals dissolve more than calcium or magnesium because soaking time increases due to their limited content. Similarly, the major cations in leachate were Ca2+  and Al3+  at sulphuric acid concentrations of 5 g/L, 8 g/L and 10 g/L. The total cation concentrations (mmol/L) were ranked as follows: Ca2+  > Al3+  > Mg2+  > Fe2+  > Na+  > K+  > Fe3+ . The Al3+  concentration exceeded the Ca2+  concentration after 300 h of immersion. This finding shows that the dissolution of aluminium minerals accelerated with the increase in the sulphuric acid concentration, with more aluminium than calcium minerals dissolving as the soaking time increased. Overall, the total molar cation concentrations (meq/L) were ranked Ca2+  > Mg2+  > Na+  > K+  according to the Shukarev classification. The Ca+  and Mg2+  contribution ranges were 40–60 % and 25–40 % of the total cationic charge (TZ+  = Na+  + K+  + 2 Mg2+  + 2Ca2+  in meq/L), respectively. The major anion was SO4 2– , and the leachate was the Ca–Mg–SO4  type. A Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r ) analysis was performed to determine the relationships between pH and Eh, and the TDS and chemical components (including Al3+ , Ca2+ , Fe3+ , Fe2+ , ∑Fe, K+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , Si, U, SO4 2–  and Fe3+ /Fe2+ ) (Fig. 6  ; Tables S3 and S4  in Supporting Information S1 ). Fig. 6  clearly shows that each chemical component of the leachate was positively associated with TDS, with all correlations being statistically significant (p  < 0.05). Among these chemical components, TDS had the strongest positive correlation with SO4 2–  concentration (r  = 0.99) and the weakest positive correlation with Si (r  = 0.46). This outcome points out that the leachate TDS is critically dependent on the SO4 2–  concentration. Consequently, the TDS of groundwater is primarily determined by the SO4 2–  concentration in the AISL process. In addition, the Eh share the strongest positive correlation with Fe3+  concentration (r  = 0.79) and SO4 2–  concentration (r  = 0.74) and the strongest negative correlation with pH (r  = –0.88). This result indicates that the oxidation of leachate heavily depends on the sulphuric acid and Fe3+  concentrations (Escario et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2016 ). Furthermore, the pH had the strongest negative correlation with Fe3+  concentration (r  = –0.80) and the weakest negative correlation with Fe2+  concentration (r  = –0.16), suggesting that the Fe3+  produced by ferric mineral dissolution is closely related to the groundwater’s acidity. In contrast, Fe2+  may be affected by many factors, including acidity. It is also worth noting that the positive correlations between the U and Fe concentrations (r  = 0.46 for Fe3+  and r  = 0.67 for Fe2+ ) were weak. Ram et al. (2011)  also discovered that this correlation was weaker at Eh < 420 mV, whereas the dissolution of uranium shared a strong linear positive correlation with Fe concentration at Eh = 460–565 mV.  3.1.3 Solution species and mineral saturation analysis Fig. 7   illustrates the variation in the species distribution of the leachate with increases in pH (Table S5  in Supporting Information S1 ). The dominant U species in the leachate were UO2 SO4 , UO2 (SO4 )2 2–  and UO2 2+ , which constituted > 99.8 % of the total species (Fig. 7 a). The percentages of these three species against pH are shown in Fig. 7 a, revealing that most of the dissolved U was in the form of UO2 SO4  at a sulphuric acid concentration of 2 g/L. The increase in the sulphuric acid concentration from 2 g/L to 10 g/L led to a decrease in UO2 SO4  and UO2 2+  and an increase in UO2 (SO4 )2 2– . Meanwhile, the major U species in the leachate shifted from UO2 SO4  alone to the coexistence of UO2 SO4  and UO2 (SO4 )2 2– . Eventually, when pH became < 1, the content of UO2 (SO4 )2 2–  reached 56.9 %, that of UO2 SO4  fell to 36.2 % and that of UO2 2+  fell to 6.9 %. These results indicate that SO4 2–  becomes more strongly complex with uranyl ions with increasing acidity. Therefore, the uranium mobiles are primarily UO2 (SO4 )2 2–  and UO2 SO4  at acidic pH values (0.95–2.03). Furthermore, Fe2+  and FeSO4  were the dominant Fe(Ⅱ) species in the leachate. As the sulphuric acid concentration increased from 2 g/L to 10 g/L, the FeSO4  content decreased from 32.82 % to 16.0 %, whereas Fe2+  rose from 65.31 % to 72.4 % (Fig. 7 b). Meanwhile, FeSO4 +  and FeHSO4 2+  were the dominant Fe(Ⅲ) species in the leachate. As the sulphuric acid concentration increased from 2 g/L to 10 g/L, FeSO4 +  decreased from 75.35 % to 48.5 %, whereas FeHSO4 2+  proliferated from 3.76 % to 34.6 % (Fig. 7 b). These results are associated with changes in S species. As the sulphuric acid concentration increased from 2 g/L to 10 g/L, SO4 2–  decreased to 16.4 %. In contrast, HSO4 –  increased to 75.6 % (Fig. 7 c). The major S species in the leachate shifted from SO4 2–  to HSO4 – . Furthermore, the change in the Fe species indicates that Fe2+  has a low affinity for HSO4 – , whereas Fe3+  has a high affinity for HSO4 –  and SO4 2– . For other species, Ca2+  and CaSO4  were the dominant Ca species, Mg2+  was the dominant Mg species, and AlSO4 +  was the dominant Al species (Fig. 7 d). The distributions of these species were less affected by changes in sulphuric acid concentration. Fig. 8   illustrates the SI of the potential reactants with changes in pH (Table S6  in Supporting Information S1 ). The SI of minerals is crucial for determining mineral dissolution and precipitation (Zhu et al., 2017 ). The findings reveal that gypsum was close to saturation (SI=–1.05–0.05) (Fig. 8 a) and quartz was supersaturated (SI=0.63–2.13) (Fig. 8 c). Hematite was supersaturated (SI>0) at pH>1.47, and unsaturated (SI<0) at pH<1.46 (Fig. 8 d). Other minerals remained unsaturated. From this analysis, it can be argued that quartz and gypsum were saturated throughout the soaking process. The transition of hematite from saturated to unsaturated suggested that it can continue to dissolve with increasing sulphuric acid concentration. The change in uraninite saturation from –0.53 to –1.95 at a sulphuric acid concentration of 2 g/L became close to the saturated state. At sulphuric acid concentrations of ≥ 5 g/L, the saturation of uraninite was lower than –6, indicating that its solubility increases with sulphuric acid concentration. In addition, Fe(OH)3  was unsaturated (SI=–5.17 to –7.8), which can prevent Fe(OH)3  colloid precipitation from plugging sandstone pores (pH<2). However, the hydrolysis of Fe3+  in an acidic environment (pH=2.0–4.0) generates Fe(OH)3  precipitates of plug sandstone pores (Zhao and Li, 2021; Wen et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018 ). Therefore, controlling groundwater within a strongly acidic range (pH<2) can dissolve Fe(OH)3  colloids. Fig. 9   depicts a matrix heatmap of the correlations between the chemical components of the leachate and the SI of minerals (Table S7  in Supporting Information S1 ). The leachate concentrations of Ca2+ , SO4 2–  and TDS were significantly positively correlated with the SI of gypsum (r  = 0.82) and mirabilite (r  = 0.83), indicating that gypsum and mirabilite can continue to dissolve during the soaking process. Quartz was supersaturated, and its SI has no significant correlation with TDS because quartz weakly reacts with sulphuric acid and contributes little to TDS. Weak leaching of the remaining minerals, along with their small contributions to TDS, caused insignificant correlations between mineral SI and TDS. Otherwise, significant positive correlations between Si concentration and the SI of various silicate minerals revealed that changes in Si concentration are jointly affected by various silicate minerals. The concentrations of Na+ , K+ , Al3+  and Mg2+  had weak correlations with the SI of clay minerals and feldspar, possibly due to the precipitation of clay minerals and feldspar.   3.2 Characteristics of mineral chemical reactions 3.2.1 Slag analysis Fig. 10   presents the micro–morphological features of the slag and its EDS elemental composition at selected spots. Scattered granular minerals were bonded on the slag’s surface at the sulphuric acid concentration of 2 g/L (Fig. 10 a). Compared to the initial sample (Fig. 2 b), the granular minerals were reduced but their bonding was tight. At 5 g/L of sulphuric acid concentration, the slag surface featured more small pores (Fig. 10 b), suggesting a specific degree of dissolution at this concentration, with the original structure being destroyed because of the dissolution of easily soluble substances, such as calcite (Zhao et al., 2019 ). The slag particles became closely bonded at the sulphuric acid concentrations of 8 g/L and 10 g/L. Certain areas became smooth, with a tiny minority of granular minerals on the surface (Fig. 10 c and d) due to the deposition of secondary minerals on the surface or pores of the minerals (Ma et al., 2014a ). The EDS analysis demonstrated that Si and Al still dominate the slag. Compared with the EDS results of the initial sample before the soaking test (Fig. 2 b), the proportions of Na, U and Si decreased with sulphuric acid concentration. Meanwhile, those of Mg, S, K, Ca and Fe increased, and that of Al initially increased and then decreased. This outcome implies that the dissolution of primary minerals and the formation of secondary minerals under sulphuric acid soaking resulted in a notable change in the elemental composition of the ore sample. The precipitation of clay minerals could interpret the increase in the K, Mg, Ca and Al contents. The dissolution of uraninite led to a decrease in the U content. Moreover, the dissolution of albite or the precipitation of mirabilite caused a decrease in Na content. The reduction in Si content was affected by the dissolution or precipitation of feldspar and clay minerals. In addition, the Fe content of the slag was increased, which may be attributed to the precipitation of ferric–bearing materials, such as Fe(OH)3  colloids (Zhao and Li, 2021 ) or the massive dissolution of acid–consuming minerals (Wang et al., 2021 ). Although these results explain the variation in the elemental content of the ore sample, the changes in the leachate ion concentration were not considered. Therefore, inverse modelling calculations were conducted for further analysis.  3.2.2 Mineral dissolution and precipitation analysis Fig. 11   illustrates the mole transfer of reactants calculated by inverse modelling (Tables S8 and S9  in Supporting Information S1 ). Based on the positive or negative molar number of reactants transferred, the mineral reactions occurring in AISL mining were as follows: the dissolution of dolomite, calcite, FeO, hematite, K–feldspar, anorthite, chlorite and alunite, precipitation of kaolinite, illite, Ca–Montmorillonite and mirabilite, and generation of CO2  (g). Small amounts of pyrite dissolution appeared in the models. The ion exchange in the leachate was primarily Na–K and Na–Mg. In terms of changes in the primary chemical components of leachate, the increase in the Ca2+  concentration was attributed to the dissolution of anorthite, dolomite, calcite and chlorite, whereas the reduction was chiefly attributed to the precipitation of Ca–Montmorillonite. By increasing the sulphuric acid concentration, the contributions of anorthite to Ca2+  in the leachate were 5.21 mmol/L, 5.21 mmol/L, 3.16 mmol/L and 3.4 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of Ca–Montmorillonite to leachate Ca2+  were –0.311 mmol/L, –0.279 mmol/L, 0 mmol/L and 0 mmol/L, respectively. These results indicate that the impact of anorthite and Ca–Montmorillonite on the leachate Ca2+  concentration was weakened with increasing acidity. In addition, by increasing the sulphuric acid concentration, the contributions of dolomite to leachate Ca2+  were 5.36 mmol/L, 5.32 mmol/L, 13.5 mmol/L and 15.2 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of calcite to leachate Ca2+  were 6.42 mmol/L, 6.42 mmol/L, 10.26 mmol/L and 12.4 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of chlorite to leachate Ca2+  were 0.019 mmol/L, 0.019 mmol/L, 0.053 mmol/L and 0.061 mmol/L, respectively. These results indicate that dolomite, calcite, and chlorite significantly affected the leachate Ca2+  concentration with increasing acidity. In summary, the dissolution of dolomite and calcite was the dominant cause of the increase in the Ca2+  concentration in the leachate. Moreover, the rise in the Mg2+  concentration was mostly attributed to the dissolution of dolomite and chlorite, whereas illite precipitation decreased the Mg2+  concentration. By increasing the sulphuric acid concentration, the contributions of dolomite to leachate Mg2+  were 5.36 mmol/L, 5.32 mmol/L, 13.5 mmol/L and 15.2 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of chlorite to leachate Mg2+  were 5.12 mmol/L, 5.12 mmol/L, 14.281 mmol/L and 16.437 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of illite to leachate Mg2+  were 0 mmol/L, 0 mmol/L, –12.6 mmol/L and –16.57 mmol/L, respectively. These results suggest that dolomite, chlorite and illite have a significant impact on the leachate Mg2+  concentration with increasing acidity. In addition, the ion exchange between Na+  and Mg2+  also occurred during the acid leaching process, which contributed –3.15 mmol/L, –2.54 mmol/L, –4.62 mmol/L and –4.14 mmol/L, respectively, to the leachate Mg2+  concentration. Therefore, the dissolution of dolomite and calcite was the prominent cause of the increase in the leachate Mg2+  concentration. At the same time, the precipitation of illite and Na-Mg exchange were the dominant causes of the decrease in the leachate Mg2+  concentration. In summary, the dissolution of dolomite, calcite and illite and Na–Mg exchange contributed more to the leachate of chemical components or TDS. The increased in Fe (Fe2+  or Fe3+ ) concentrations were primarily attributed to the dissolution of FeO, pyrite, hematite and chlorite. With the increase in the sulphuric acid concentration, the contributions of FeO to leachate Fe were 1.75 mmol/L, 1.75 mmol/L, 9.83 mmol/L and 9.53 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of pyrite to leachate Fe were 0.05 mmol/L, 0.05 mmol/L, 0.66 mmol/L and 0.63 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of hematite to leachate Fe were 0.74 mmol/L, 0.74 mmol/L, 3.69 mmol/L and 3.86 mmol/L, respectively. The contributions of chlorite to leachate Fe were 3.329 mmol/L, 3.329 mmol/L, 9.285 mmol/L, and 10.686 mmol/L, respectively. These results indicate an increased dissolution of FeO, pyrite, hematite and chlorite with increasing acidity. In summary, the dissolution of FeO and chlorite considerably affected the increase in the leachate Fe concentration. Moreover, chlorite was mainly dissolved because the FeO content was usually low. For mineral precipitates, by increasing the sulphuric acid concentration, the precipitation amounts of kaolinite were 10.1 mmol/L, 10.41 mmol/L, 54.01 mmol/L and 60.47 mmol/L, respectively. The precipitation amounts of illite were 0 mmol/L, 0 mmol/L, 12.6 mmol/L and 16.57 mmol/L, respectively. The precipitation amounts of mirabilite were 13.25 mmol/L, 13.25 mmol/L, 29.23 mmol/L and 32.38 mmol/L, respectively. These results indicate that kaolinite, mirabilite and illite precipitation increased with acidity. Furthermore, the precipitation amounts of Ca–Montmorillon were 1.89 mmol/L, 1.69 mmol/L, 0 mmol/L, and 0 mmol/L, respectively, indicating the precipitation amounts of Ca–Montmorillon decreased with increasing acidity. Therefore, kaolinite and mirabilite were the main precipitates. The amounts of acid consumed from the 2 g/L, 5 g/L, 8 g/L and 10 g/L of sulphuric acid solutions during the soaking process were calculated as 90.657 mmol/L, 90.517 mmol/L, 318.373 mmol/L and 363.824 mmol/L, respectively (calculated as equivalent amounts of CaCO3 ). These results point out that the acid consumption of minerals is similar due to the low acidity and slow dissolution rate of minerals. The mineral dissolution rate accelerated, and acid consumption significantly increased with the rise in acidity. At sulphuric acid concentrations of 2 g/L, 5 g/L, 8 g/L and 10 g/L, the changes in the acid consumption ratio of each mineral were: dolomite (11.82 %→11.75 %→8.48 %→8.36 %), calcite (7.08 %→7.09 %→3.22 %→3.41 %), FeO (1.93 %→1.93 %→3.09 %→2.62 %), hematite (2.44 %→2.45 %→3.48 %→3.18 %), pyrite (0.06 %→0.06 %→0.21 %→0.17 %), K–feldspar (27.07 %→26.85 %→38.17 %→38.66 %), anorthite (17.24 %→17.27 %→2.98 %→2.8 %), chlorite (16.67 %→16.69 %→13.33 %→13.25 %) and alunite (15.69 %→15.91 %→27.04 %→27.55 %), respectively. This finding indicates that the primary acid–consuming minerals were K–feldspar, alunite, chlorite, anorthite and dolomite. The proportion of acid consumed by K–feldspar and alunite increased with sulphuric acid concentration, suggesting an increase in dissolution rates and quantities of K–feldspar and alunite. Moreover, dolomite, calcite, anorthite, and chlorite dissolve faster; however, due to their low mineral content they dissolve less, thus reducing their acid consumption. These methods can be used to evaluate acid consumption during AISL production.    4 Conclusion The theoretical foundation of the AISL process aims to elucidate the relevant hydrochemical characteristics and reaction mechanisms. A qualitative analysis of the chemical components of the leachate and the dissolution or precipitation of minerals is required due to the complex water–rock reactions. To this end, in this work, sulphuric acid soaking tests were applied to simulate the AISL process with a sandstone–type uranium ore from Inner Mongolia. The hydrochemical evolution of the recovered uranium was determined via the analysis of the leachate’s hydrochemical characteristics, the slag’s mineralogical characteristics, and inverse modelling. The findings suggest that water–rock interactions between the sulphuric acid and gangue minerals mainly affect the leachate’s chemical composition. The lixiviation and oxidation activities increase with sulphuric acid concentration. The leachate’s hydrochemical type was Ca–Mg–SO4. The U species in the leachate were primarily UO2 SO4 , UO2 (SO4 )2 2–  and UO2 2+ . In addition, TDS was significantly correlated with SO4 2–  concentration, indicating that the increase in groundwater TDS is mainly caused by sulphuric acid injection. The Eh values exhibited the strongest positive correlations with the concentrations of Fe3+  and SO4 2–  and the strongest negative correlation with pH, inferring that the oxidation of leachate significantly depends on the concentrations of sulphuric acid and Fe3+ . Moreover, pH had the strongest negative correlation with the Fe3+  concentration and the weakest negative correlation with the Fe2+  concentration, specifying that Fe3+  produced by ferric mineral dissolution is closely related to the acidity of groundwater. At the same time, Fe2+  may be affected by numerous factors, such as acidity. TDS was significantly positively correlated with the SI of mirabilite, suggesting that TDS increases are the major cause of mineral precipitation blockage. This result complements the correlation analysis of the hydrochemical components involved in the AISL process and determines the potential relationships between the ions. It also broadens the value of the limited data obtained during actual production, as it can be used to infer more potential information without information by relying on ionic correlations. Subsequently, the micro–morphological features of the slag suggested the occurrence of mineral dissolution and secondary mineral formation. The inverse–modelling results indicate that the dissolution of dolomite, calcite, FeO, hematite, pyrite, K–feldspar, anorthite, chlorite and alunite, and the precipitation of kaolinite, illite, Ca–Montmorillonite and mirabilite, accompanied by Na–K and Na–Mg exchanges, occur in the groundwater system during AISL mining. The dissolution of dolomite, calcite, illite and Na–Mg exchange greatly contributes to hydrochemical evolution and mainly affects the groundwater chemical composition. The newly formed precipitates were mostly kaolinite and mirabilite; the precipitation capacity of which increased with acidity. Chlorite dissolution was a major source of Fe in the leachate. Our work provides valuable insights into the water–rock interactions of sandstone–type uranium in AISL mining and explains the phenomena of mineral dissolution and precipitation in ore–bearing aquifers. A solid reference is thus provided for the mining degree of mineral resources in the actual production processes. Moreover, it was demonstrated that the primary acid–consuming minerals in the AISL process were K–feldspar, alunite, chlorite, anorthite and dolomite. These results can help evaluate acid consumption during AISL production. In summary, the hydrogeochemical analysis and inverse modelling of the soaking test for uranium minerals revealed the hydrochemical evolution and mineral corrosion characteristics of ore–bearing aquifers. However, other potential factors related to mineral heterogeneous distribution and hydrodynamic strength require different test conditions for reliable evaluation. Therefore, future research must integrate drilling core data, chemical compositions of lixivium in the monitoring well, and groundwater flow velocity to conduct the spatio–temporal analysis and prediction of the site.  5 Foundation item Project (42372295, 42062017, 42107093) supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China ; Project (20224BAB203038 ) supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Jiangxi Province, China.
1 Introduction Methane (CH4 ) is a powerful greenhouse gas (GHG) with a global warming potential 28 times greater than carbon dioxide (CO2 ) over a 100-year period, contributing to 16–25 % of atmospheric warming (Kirschke et al., 2013; Etminan et al., 2016; Rosentreter et al., 2021 ). It is estimated that atmospheric CH4  concentration has increased from 722 to 1859 ppb since the industrial revolution, leading to a rate of 7.3 ± 0.6 ppb yr−1  during the period of 2007–2019 (Schaefer et al., 2016; Dlugokencky, 2021 ). Global aquatic environments release 202.3–424.6 Tg CH4  yr−1 , representing roughly 53 % of global CH4  emissions (Rosentreter et al., 2021 ). This estimate of global aquatic CH4  emissions remains largely uncertain due mainly to the high variability of regional and global settings and emission pathways. Estuaries receiving substantial carbon and nitrogen from high human activities are essential environments for carbon cycling and outgassing (Wells et al., 2020 ), which have attracted attention in projecting global CH4  budgets (Zheng et al., 2022 ). Although global estuaries are projected to release 0.02–0.91 Tg CH4  yr−1  (Rosentreter et al., 2021; Rosentreter et al., 2023 ), increasing temperature and anthropogenic activities can cause hypoxia and eutrophication, which can collectedly enhance CH4  emissions from estuarine environments (Nisbet et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2020 ). In addition, estuaries are mostly vulnerable to tidal fluctuations, which can substantially alter the pathways and magnitudes of CH4  emissions (Wells et al., 2020 ). Estuary CH4  budget has attracted considerable attention, yet the patterns and pathways contribution of CH4  emissions remain constrained. CH4  fluxes decreased significantly from upper to lower sections due mainly to the decrease in external nutrients inputs along Pearl River Estuary (Chen et al., 2024 ). The hotspots of CH4  emissions were also associated with sewage inputs in Cochin Estuary (Hershey et al., 2023 ), further indicating that human activities are main contributors to the enhanced CH4  emissions. The underlying mechanisms of enhanced CH4  emissions could be that high nutrients inputs can cause hypoxia and eutrophication, which provide the favorable conditions and substances for methanogens (Wells et al., 2020; Downing et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022 ). In addition, as a temperature dependence process, CH4  production is more sensitive to temperature than CH4  consumption (Yvon-Durocher et al., 2014; Shelley et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2020 ), resulting in net increase in CH4  emissions with increasing temperature. CH4  production in water and sediments can be emitted through both diffusive and ebullitive pathways, showing different responses to temperature changes, in which high temperature is beneficial to ebullition while low temperature is favorable for diffusion (DelSontro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2021 ). Therefore, estuarine CH4  emissions are not only driven by temperature-induced production, but also affected by temperature-induced modification to emission pathways. In addition, CH4  emissions from global estuaries could be highly variable across different climates, which can make the projections of global estuary CH4  budget uncertain due to the lack of available measured data. It has been also reported that 166 estuaries along the Australian coastline experienced temperature increase at a rate of 0.2 °C yr−1 , which was an order of magnitude higher than the rate predicted by global ocean models (Scanes et al., 2020 ). More studies are therefore required regarding the temperature sensitivity of CH4  emissions in estuaries, which are of great significance to project CH4  budget under climate warming. Diffusive and ebullitive pathways contribute differently to total CH4  emissions across global aquatic ecosystems (Wu et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Bubble events only occurred in waters <3 m depth, and contributed to 18–22 % of total CH4  emissions over the whole lake (DelSontro et al., 2016 ). However, ebullition dominated over 90 % of total CH4  emission in aquaculture ponds (Yang et al., 2020 ) and urban rivers (Chen et al., 2021 ). Estuaries are generally characterized by tidal fluctuations, which can decrease water residence time for benthic CH4  production and increase water column CH4  oxidation (Rosentreter et al., 2018; Wells et al., 2020 ), ultimately decreasing CH4  emissions. Tidal fluctuations can also provide additional constraints on gas transfer velocity, affecting the quantification of CH4  flux (Ho et al., 2016; Rosentreter et al., 2017 ). tidal fluctuations alter CH4  emissions pathways by the fact that CH4  can be emitted by diffusion and lateral exports under flooding tides while ebullition under ebbing tides (Capooci et al., 2024 ). It is also expected that estuary CH4  fluxes may increase greatly under ebbing tides (Khan et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023 ) as CH4  can emit directly without oxidation in water column. Therefore, more studies are required regarding the magnitudes and pathways of CH4  emissions under tidal fluctuations in estuaries. Globally, estuaries are assumed to contribute <0.11 % of aquatic environments (Rosentreter et al., 2021 ), suggesting that estuaries may be not the main contributors to global CH4  budget. However, there is a synergistic interaction between the influence of increasing temperature and nutrient enrichments in many estuaries (Scanes et al., 2020 ), which can lead to a disproportional increase in CH4  emissions and further shift the estuaries from CH4  sinks to sources (Wells et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ). These inconsistent results highlight a comprehensive understanding of CH4  emissions in estuaries caused by human activities and climate warming on a regional scale, which is critical to achieve a more integrated understanding of estuary CH4  emissions. In light of the sparse knowledge about patterns, pathways and temperature influence of estuary CH4  emissions, we investigated diffusive and ebullitive CH4  emissions under tidal fluctuations and climate warming in a nutrient-rich subtropical estuary. The objectives of this study are: (1) to characterize the patterns of CH4  emissions in response to different human intensity and seasonal changes; (2) to verify the importance of tidal fluctuation and ebullition pathway to regulate CH4  emissions; (3) to identify what are the relevant roles of nutrients and temperature in affecting CH4  emissions. This study provides a robust insight into the temperature sensitivity and pathways of estuarine CH4  emissions, which have broader implications for projecting global CH4  emissions under human modifications and climate change.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Min River Estuary is located in subtropical zone of southeast China (25°55́–26°10́N, 119°09́–119°41́E), which is the largest estuary in Fujian Province (Fig. 1  a). The river length and drainage area are 562 km and 60,992 km2 , respectively. Annual runoff is approximately 561 × 108  m3 , of which 60 % occurs from March to September. Min River Estuary is situated in a subtropical humid monsoonal climate, with a mean annual temperature of 19.6℃ and mean annual precipitation of 1350 mm (Qi et al., 2023 ). Estuary banks of upper, middle and lower sections are plain, mountain and salt marsh, respectively. Estuary width and water area increases greatly along the estuary, and is dominated by tide in the lower estuary. This estuary is characterized by regular semi-daily fluctuations, with two high tides and two low tides every 6 h. The annual mean tide range is approximately 4 m, which can affect the upper boundary that distinguishes the North and South branches (Fig. 1 b). The upper estuary is mainly dominated by river water and the annual salinity of surface water is <0.5 ‰. Salinity in the middle (sites S5-S7) and lower (sites S8-S11) estuary were 1–5 ‰ and 5–14 ‰, respectively (Qi et al., 2023 ). This estuary is also highly affected by human activities as the land use types are highly different (Figs. 1  and S1 ). Urban area is responsible for 56.3–79.6 % of total land area in the upper estuary (Li et al., 2021 ). The upper estuary (sites S1-S4) flows through the Fuzhou urban (Fig. S1 ), which has the highest population density and receives a large amount of sewage discharged from urban river networks (Qi et al., 2023 ). The middle (sites S5-S7) and lower (sites S8-S11) estuary are classified as suburban and countryside sections, which are located in canyon and marsh, respectively.  2.2 Samples collection and measurements Four campaigns in April (spring), July (summer), September (autumn) and December (winter) of the 11 sampling sites along the Min River Estuary were conducted in 2021 to investigate spatial and seasonal variability of diffusive CH4  emissions (Fig. 1 b). During each sampling season, water and gas samples were carried out through the main channel under the duration of high tide within several days. Water at a depth of 20 cm were stored in a 100 mL gas-tight glass serum bottle vial injected with 100 µL HgCl2  solution for preservation, free of bubbles and headspace (Li et al., 2022 ). Gas was collected with a 50 mL syringe with air tightness (KDL, Shanghai) at a height of 1 m above the water surface, and then stored in a 50-mL airbag (Delin, Dalian, China) (Yang et al., 2020 ). In addition, a polyethylene bottle was used to collect 500 mL water at the 20 cm depth for the determination of water NO3 − , NO2 − , NH4 +  and dissolved organic carbon (DOC). These samples were stored in a cool box and immediately transported to the laboratory for analysis. During the sample collection, a digital anemometer (UT363, UNI-T, China) was used to measure wind speed and atmospheric pressure at a height of 1 m above water surface. Water temperature, DO and pH value were measured in situ  with a portable water quality instrument (SL1000, HACH, USA). Water salinity and turbidity were measured by a salinometer (salt6+, Eutech, USA) and portable turbidimeter (NTU, ZD-2A, China). These parameters were measured in three replicates at each sampling site. After the water was sampled, it was filtered by a 0.45 μm filter and stored in −20 °C condition until analysis. NO3 − , NO2 −  and NH4 +  were determined by a flow analyzer (SKALAR SAN++, SKALAR, Netherlands). The detection limits were 0.5 μM for NO3 −  and NH4 +  and 0.1 μM for NO2 − . DOC was determined by a total organic carbon analyzer (TOC-L CPH, Shimadzu, Japan). 400 mL water was filtered with 0.45 μm glass filter membrane, and the total suspended particulate (TSP) was weighted before and after the drying filter membrane. In addition, a floating chamber was used to collect the total CH4  flux including diffusive and ebullitive pathways (Yang et al., 2020 ) under the flooding and ebbing tides. The sampling site of floating chamber was near to the S9 (Fig. 1 b). Samplings were investigated on a sunny day at the beginning of each month over the 2021. The floating chamber was deployed on the water surface with a headspace volume of 50 L. Chamber was wrapped with aluminum foil to avoid the solar radiation effect of the headspace gas. One side of the pipe was attached to the top of the chamber and the other side was connected with a three-way valve. Gas samples were collected from the three-way valve during the 60 min at a 15 min interval at the middle time under the middle time period of high flooding and low ebbing tides. The first headspace gas collected with a 50 mL syringe was discarded and second sampling was stored in a 50-mL airbag (Delin, Dalian, China). Gas samples were collected at triplicate. The fitting relationship was acceptable if the linear correlation between gas concentrations and time was >0.95. During the sampling, air temperature in the floating chamber was also determined.  2.3 Diffusive, ebullitive and total CH4  fluxes 2.3.1 Diffusive CH4  emissions CH4  concentration in the vial was determined by the headspace balance (Johnson et al., 1990 ) combined with a gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) (GC-2014, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). 20 mL water in the serum bottle was replaced by the same volume of helium gas (99.999 %) to create a headspace. These serum bottles were shaken for 30 min to maintain the balance between the water and gas phases. Column and detector temperatures of the gas chromatograph were maintained at 60 °C and 200 °C, respectively. The gas chromatograph was calibrated with three CH4  standard gas mixtures (2.06, 8.05, and 98.6 ppm CH4 ), from which r2  > 0.99 for the linear relationship between CH4  concentration and peak area was acceptable. The Q 10  value typically represents the proportional change in temperature per 10 °C change in a process (DelSontro et al., 2016 ). In addition, the apparent activation energy (E a ) was used to assess the sensitivity of ebullition, diffusion and total CH4  emissions to temperature. The extreme values of CH4  fluxes were excluded from the linear relationship. We simulated three levels of increased nitrogen concentrations (1.5×, 2×, and 2.5× that of current levels) that are conservatively within the magnitude of increase by the end of 2050 and 2100 reported in Beaulieu et al. (2019) . We further simulated a future that nutrient managements were improved resulting in nitrogen concentration 0.75× that of current levels. Current levels of nitrogen concentrations were the average investigated value in the present study. In addition, we also stimulated the effects of global warming on CH4  emissions under 2 °C (SSP2-4.5) and 4 °C (SSP5-8.5) warming scenarios in Min Jiang River Estuary. We first established the relationship of water temperature with air temperature over the year 2021. Then the average monthly temperature of the last 30 years in Fuzhou city were used to predict the month water temperature under current, 2 °C and 4 °C warming scenarios (Table S2 ). The statistical models of water temperature and total CH4  fluxes over the year 2021 (Table S3 ) were performed to predict monthly CH4  emissions under the current, 2 °C and 4 °C warming scenarios.  2.6 Statistical analysis A natural logarithm of the response ratio (RR) as a metric of the effect size was used to determine the magnitudes of CH4  emissions responding to the increased nitrogen concentrations. The RR was calculated as the ratio of CH4  emissions in increased nitrogen (Xh  ¯    ) to the value of ambient nitrogen (Xc  ¯    ). The logarithm of RR was estimated to represent the effect size induced by the increased nitrogen as follows (Hedges et al., 1999 ):(11) ln R R = ln ( Xh  ¯   Xa  ¯    ) = I n Xh  ¯   - l n Xa  ¯       where the Xh  ¯     and Xa  ¯     are the values of CH4  emissions in increased and ambient nitrogen groups, respectively. Positive and negative values of lnRR showed positive and negative effects, respectively, and overlap zero presented no effect. The variation (V ) of lnRR was estimated according to the equation below:(12) V = S h  2  n h  X h  2    + S a  2  n a  X a  2        where the S h  and S a  are the standard deviations of the CH4  emissions in the increased and ambient nitrogen groups, respectively; n h  and n a  are the sample number of increased and ambient nitrogen groups, respectively. Statistical analysis was performed using the SPSS software version 22.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA) and Origin 2021 (OriginLab, Massachusetts, USA). CH4  emissions and environmental parameters across season changes and estuary sections were analyzed using two-way ANOVA. The correlations between CH4  emissions and environmental factors were analyzed by ggcor and ggplot2 package in R language. Random forest in R language was conducted to analyze the factors explaining the maximum variability of CH4  flux.   3 Results 3.1 Diffusive CH4  emissions and associated factors Water NO3 −  and NO2 −  concentrations were significantly higher in upper than lower estuary, and higher in cold than warm seasons (Fig. S2 ). Water DO and DOC concentrations were also higher in cold than warm seasons. Dissolved CH4  concentrations were in a range of 0.18–11.2 µmol L−1 , which were significantly higher in winter than in spring, summer and autumn (p  = 0.001) (Fig. 2  ). CH4  concentrations were 179 % higher in upper than in middle and lower estuary. Diffusive CH4  fluxes ranged from 3.08 to 375 μg m−2  h−1  along the estuary, and were higher in winter than in spring, summer and autumn. Diffusive CH4  fluxes were also significantly higher in upper than in middle and lower estuary (p  < 0.001), with 75 % more in upper than in middle and lower estuary. Diffusive CH4  fluxes were observed to positively relate to TSP, turbidity, NH4 +  and DOC/NO3 − , but were negatively correlated with air temperature (Fig. 3  a). Random forest model further showed that turbidity, TSP, NH4 + , NO3 − , DOC/NO3 −  and NO2 −  were the critical factors affecting CH4  fluxes, collectedly explaining 43 % of CH4  variance (Fig. 3 b). Based on the results, nitrogen was a critical factor affecting CH4  emissions. By integrating CH4  emissions from several estuaries, nitrogen concentrations showed a positive effect on CH4  emissions, likely reflecting that high water productivity increase CH4  emissions (Fig. 4  a). It is projected that further increased nitrogen concentrations will substantially increase diffusive CH4  emissions by 32–123 % under 1.5, 2, and 2.5× increase nitrogen scenarios (Fig. 4 b). On the contrary, assuming a 0.75× increase in nitrogen concentration, diffusive CH4  emissions could decrease by roughly 18 %.  3.2 CH4  emissions under tidal fluctuation Under flooding tide, the diffusive and ebullitive CH4  fluxes were in a range of 12.6–67 μg m−2  h−1  and 59–477 μg m−2  h−1 , respectively (Fig. 5  a and b). However, the diffusive and ebullitive CH4  fluxes under ebbing tide increased at the rates of 8.68–97 μg m−2  h−1  and 153–3290 μg m−2  h−1 , respectively. Total CH4  fluxes were also significantly higher under ebbing (166–3328 μg m−2  h−1 ) than under flooding tides (71–656 μg m−2  h−1 ) (p  < 0.001). The diurnal tide released 1.99–39.9 mg m−2  d−1  of CH4  at the annual scale. Ebullition pathway predominated the CH4  emissions, representing 82–90 % and 92–98 % of total fluxes under the flooding and ebbing tides, respectively. Tidal fluctuation aggravated the variability of CH4  fluxes, leading to one order magnitude difference and affecting the ebullition contribution to total emissions.  3.3 Temperature sensitivity of CH4  emissions During the monthly observations, diffusive and ebullitive CH4  fluxes were substantially higher in the warm than the cold months, reflecting that CH4  emission is highly temperature dependent. Diffusive and ebullitive CH4  fluxes were positively correlated with water temperature under flooding and ebbing tides (p  < 0.001). Based on the temperature dependence of CH4  emissions, the ecosystem level Q 10  and E a  for ebullition were 3.20 and 0.38 eV, respectively, whereas the Q 10  and E a  for diffusion were 2.40 and 0.28 eV, respectively, under the flooding tide (Fig. 5 c and Table 1  ). However, under the ebbing tide, E a  for ebullition and diffusion were 0.85 eV and 0.50 eV, respectively, and Q 10  for ebullition and diffusion were 13.8 and 4.80, respectively (Fig. 5 d and Table 1 ). The Q 10  and E a  were significantly higher under ebbing than flooding tides. The linear regression between temperature and CH4  emissions further supported the effects of warming on diffusive fluxes and especially on ebullitive fluxes, explaining 38–70 % and 41–83 % of the variance, respectively. We used the relationship of water and air temperature investigated, and multi-year monthly air temperature of Fuzhou City (Fig. 6   and S6 , Table S2 ) to stimulate the increase of CH4  fluxes in Min Jiang River Estuary under 2 °C and 4 °C warming scenarios by 2100. Currently, CH4  fluxes were in a range of 240–796 μg m−2  h−1  with the month changes, while increased at the rates of 252–1056 μg m−2  h−1  and 270–1384 μg m−2  h−1  under the 2 °C and 4 °C warming scenarios, respectively (Fig. 7  a). Cold months showed lower stimulation of CH4  emissions than warm months under the 2 and 4 °C warming scenarios. The increase in CH4  emissions by warming was lower under 2 °C than 4 °C warming scenarios, with the increase of 5.2 %–29 % and 12 %–70 %, respectively (Fig. 7 b). Warming in warm months would largely promote CH4  emissions, with a maximal stimulation occurring in July and August (∼70 %) under 4 °C warming scenario. Generally, annual CH4  fluxes would increase by 17 ± 9 % and 40 ± 22 % by 2100 under the 2 and 4 °C warming scenarios, respectively.   4 Discussion 4.1 Enhanced CH4  emission by high human activity Global estuaries are critically affected by human activities, resulting in a substantial variability of CH4  emissions and causing an uncertainty of the projected CH4  budget (Wells et al., 2020; Rosentreter et al., 2023 ). In this study, it was observed that diffusive CH4  fluxes decreased significantly from upper to low estuary, which were in line with previous studies that CH4  fluxes increased from minimally- to highly-impacted estuaries (Wells et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ). The increased CH4  emissions under high human activity could be attributed to the water and sediment eutrophication that can increase labile carbon availability, anoxia and microbial activity for methanogenesis (DelSontro et al., 2018; Wells et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ). Likewise, our findings broadly align with these expectations that high nutrients and low DO concentrations were observed in the upper estuary, in which large amounts of water with high nutrients and low DO were discharged from domestic sewage (Qi et al., 2023 ), promoting CH4  production in benthic sediments. In addition to the low nutrients and high DO concentrations, low CH4  emissions in the lower estuary as expected may be that high turbidity and the induced low light conditions inhibit biological growth (Wells and Eyre, 2019; Wells et al., 2020 ) and further decrease the carbon quality for the methanogenesis (Cory and Kling, 2018 ). By comparing the fluxes between estuaries, we found one order of magnitude increase of CH4  fluxes with the increasing human activity intensity (from 6.46 to134 μg m−2  h−1 , Wells et al., 2020 ; from 5.46 to 35.6 μg m−2  h−1 , Li et al., 2022 ). Therefore, human activities have shifted the estuaries from sink to source of CH4  emissions, and these switches would be further strengthened by the combined stressors of hypoxia and eutrophication in human modification estuaries. There was a seasonal variability of the diffusive CH4  emissions, with generally higher in cold than warm seasons. Such seasonal CH4  emissions shift was not expected given that temperature was lower, DO concentrations were higher, and microbial respiration was lower in the cold than in the warm seasons. The reason may be that low-temperature seasons could increase the inhibition of CH4  oxidation more than on the production (Wells et al., 2020 ), while warmer and less saline waters in warm seasons (high freshwater discharge) can stimulate the oxidation of CH4  (Dutta et al., 2015 ). In addition, lower freshwater inputs and correspondingly longer residence times in the cold seasons (termed as dry season) can provide favorable conditions for biogeochemical reactions (Rosentreter et al., 2018; Flury and Ulseth, 2019 ), as well as the increase in CH4  production and accompanying emissions. We also found that the CH4  fluxes were higher in temperate than subtropical and tropical estuaries globally, further suggesting that climate regimes can drive the continental variability of CH4  emissions and low-temperature environments have higher diffusive CH4  emissions. In addition, different CH4  emissions were accompanied by environmental factors showing seasonal and spatial changes (Fig. S4 ), reflecting that CH4  emissions are the results of multiple factors effects. Therefore, the changes in nutrients, DO and temperature induced by human modifications and seasonal changes collectedly mediate CH4  production and oxidation, leading to the high variability of CH4  emissions in estuaries.  4.2 Tidal fluctuations dominated the variability of CH4  emissions Ebullition and diffusion are assumed the two important pathways of CH4  emissions from aquatic environments (DelSontro et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020 ), but their contributions to CH4  emissions are highly variable across six types of inland waters. Globally, ebullition was responsible for 62–84 % of total CH4  emissions across six inland aquatic environments, while the data for estuaries have not yet been addressed (Zheng et al., 2022 ). By integrating the data of ebullitive and diffusive CH4  from global estuaries, we estimated that the ebullition pathway contributed to roughly 84 % of total CH4  emissions (Fig. 8  ). Previous studies have also documented 50–90 % of ebullition contribution in lakes and ponds (Houweling et al., 2020 ), 95–99 % in coastal ponds (Yang et al., 2020 ), and one-fold difference between lakes (42 %) and rivers (81 %) (Wang et al., 2021 ). In this study, we found that ebullition was yet the main pathway of CH4  emissions in the estuary, potentially accounting for 82–99 % of the total emissions. However, high difference in CH4  fluxes between flooding and ebbing tides was attributed to the ebullition fluxes that were 6 times higher under the flooding than ebbing tides (Fig. 5 ). Under the ebbing tide, more CH4  was directly emitted by ebullition as shallow water can largely limit the oxidation and dissolution of CH4 -rich bubbles releasing from benthic sediments (Wu et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2020 ). In addition, high ebullition fluxes under the ebbing tide were also linked to abundant exogenous and underground inputs of CH4  that are the important compositions of aquatic CH4  emissions (Wells et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2022 ). The fact that ebullition contributed more to CH4  emissions under ebbing than flooding tides further confirmed that shallow water is favorable to the ebullition release, leading to diurnal hotspot shifts of CH4  emissions. The monthly observation data over a year showed that ebullition contribution was higher in warm than cold months, suggesting the temperature dependence of ebullition. It has been also reported that warming strongly boosts CH4  emissions through a disproportional increase in ebullition (Aben et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2018 ). Seasonal and tidal changes will increase the variability of CH4  emissions by altering transfer pathways and water environments in which CH4  is produced and consumed, which should be highly underlined in further CH4  projections.
