Prior to the time-scale collection, we collected samples every half hour spanning 24 h at each month to reveal the temporal variation of CH4  emissions across tidal fluctuations. However, the capture of the high variability of CH4  emissions requires long-term, multi-frequency, high time resolution monitoring to reveal diurnal, monthly and annual variations of CH4  emissions in further study. Although the contribution of diffusion and ebullition emission pathways under tidal fluctuations was clarified, temporal variation characteristics of CH4  ebullition emissions is not adequately captured (e.g. before, during and after high tide), it is therefore recommended that subsequent study should cover multiple tidal cycles for CH4  emissions in estuaries.  4.3 Climate warming increases estuary CH4  emissions As temperature dependence of CH4  production (Yvon-Durocher et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2020 ), CH4  emissions are highly variable with varying temperatures (Aben et al., 2017; Praetzel et al., 2021 ). In this study, ebullitive CH4  flux was significantly correlated with water temperature, indicating that CH4  production responds quickly to water temperature changes. The temperature-ebullition exponential relationship indicates that climate warming will increase CH4  ebullition by 10.5 % per 1 °C warming, which was close to the value of urban rivers (12.5 %) (Chen et al., 2021 ) and was within the range of global freshwater ecosystems (6–20 %) (Aben et al., 2017 ). The high difference in CH4  increase responding to temperature changes across freshwater ecosystems could be attributed to the synergistic interaction between warming and eutrophication that can strongly enhance CH4  production (Aben et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2018; Beaulieu et al., 2019 ). We also found that the ecosystem-level Q 10  of ebullition was higher than that of diffusion, further suggesting the high-temperature dependence of ebullition CH4  emissions. Our Q 10  values were within the aquatic environments including pond, lake, river and paddy, and these Q 10  values were higher for ebullition than diffusion (Table S4 ). Given the high increase in ebullition emissions under the ebbing tide, the Q 10  value of ebullition was substantially higher under the ebbing than flooding tides as the ebullitive CH4  can emit directly from the shallow water when it is produced from benthic sediments. Global CH4  fluxes were higher in temperate than subtropical and tropical estuaries (Fig. 8 ), further suggesting that climate regimes can increase the variability of CH4  emissions globally. Higher CH4  emissions in subtropical estuaries could be attributed to that high temperature and rich nutrients can facilitate benthic CH4  production (Li et al., 2022; Wells et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the synergistic effects of increasing nutrients and temperature under global warming may facilitate the importance of subtropical estuaries to global estuary CH4  budget. In addition, apparent activation energy (E a ) is a reliable measure of the temperature sensitivity of CH4  emissions (Yvon-Durocher et al., 2014 ), which can reflect the variability of CH4  emissions in response to temperature changes. The E a  values for CH4  emissions under the flooding and ebbing tide were in a range of 0.28–0.85, with higher values in ebullition CH4  and in ebbing tide, indicating that ebullition CH4  emissions in shallow water have higher temperature sensitivity. By comparing the E a  between the estuary, pond, lake and river, we found that our E a  values were comparable with these ecosystems and eutrophication can amplify the E a  (Table S4 ), indicating that eutrophication shows a synergistic effect on temperature sensitivity of CH4  emissions. It was reported that the E a  for CH4  emission was 0.96 eV, corresponding to a 1.70-fold increase in CH4  emissions under the 4 °C warming scenario in ponds (Zhu et al., 2020 ). The seasonal observations demonstrated that E a  for the ebullition CH4  emission was 0.86 eV in urban rivers, which can lead to a 1.5-fold increase in ebullition CH4  emissions under the 4 °C warming scenario (12.5 % per 1 °C × 4 °C = 50 %) (Chen et al., 2021 ). Likewise, our projected annual CH4  emissions under the 4 °C warming scenario in the estuary was a 1.50-fold increase compared to ambient temperature, which further suggests that climate warming has a consistent influence on the increase in CH4  emissions across estuarine environments. It should be noted that warming can enhance primary productivity and eutrophication, providing more organic carbon substrate for methanogenesis (Davidson et al., 2018 ). In addition, hypoxia caused by warming and eutrophication could favor methanogenesis and decrease aerobic CH4  oxidation (Aben et al., 2017; Beaulieu et al., 2019 ), ultimately increasing CH4  emissions. Therefore, temperature sensitivity of CH4  production is highly enhanced and a disproportionate increase in CH4  emissions concomitantly occurs under the combined effects of warming, eutrophication and hypoxia, leading to the global estuaries as CH4  sources. In addition, our projected CH4  emissions under warming scenarios may be uncertain as the hypoxia and eutrophication under further climate warming have not yet been considered.  4.4 Implications for estuary CH4  emissions The bottom-up methane emission from global estuaries were 0.02–0.91 Tg CH4  per year (Rosentreter et al., 2021 ), while substantially higher rate of 5.96 Tg CH4  per year was projected using the averaged flux and total water body of global estuaries (Zheng et al., 2022 ). These inconsistent estimated CH4  emissions from global estuaries suggest that some gaps have not yet been considered in projecting CH4  emissions from global estuaries. Floating chambers can capture both ebullition and diffusion fluxes, while the boundary layer model quantifies only diffusion (Deemer et al., 2016; Sawakuchi et al., 2014 ). Previous observations on CH4  emissions from the estuary water body were the diffusion (Ho et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ), however, it has been identified that the diffusion pathway consists a minor contribution to the total emissions. The estimates of global estuary CH4  emissions were uneven, with heavy representation data on diffusion fluxes but a remarkable scarcity in ebullition (Rosentreter et al., 2021; Rosentreter et al., 2023 ). Therefore, CH4  emissions budgets from global estuaries were likely underestimated due to the lack of data on ebullition, which underlines more investigations on CH4  ebullition in estuaries. We used the floating chamber to conduct the continuous measurements of ebullition and diffusion CH4  over one year, demonstrating that ebullition contributed to 82–98 % of the total CH4  fluxes. In addition, ebullition CH4  fluxes were substantially higher under ebbing than flooding tides, highlighting the crucial role of ebullition CH4  in total emissions. This critical hotspot of CH4  emissions could be a factor causing an underestimation of the CH4  emissions from global estuaries when upscaling CH4  fluxes from diurnal to annual scales. In addition, given the inconsistent CH4  bubbles (Chen et al., 2021 ), seasonal water levels (Wells et al., 2020 ) and diurnal variation of tides in estuaries, more observations on the CH4  emission are further required under such changing environments. In this study, CH4  emissions as CO2  equivalent accounted for 74 % of global potential warming (CH4  + N2 O) (Fig. S6 ), indicating that CH4  may be more crucial to climate warming in human-impacted estuaries. In addition, our CO2 :CH4  ratios were decreased by increasing human activity intensity (Fig. S7 ), indicating that human alterations to estuarine carbon cycles are causing an increase in CH4  emissions and modifying the estuarine CH4  into ‘natural’ v. ‘anthropogenic’ sources (Wells et al., 2020 ). The CO2 :CH4  ratios were lower in most global rivers, especially in temperature change sensitivity zones (Table S5 ), suggesting that global aquatic carbon cycles and outgassing are increasingly strengthened by climate warming. Our projected CH4  emissions under the 2 °C and 4 °C scenarios also demonstrated that the increase of estuary CH4  emissions was more sensitive to high than low-temperature months. In addition, the fact that CO2 :CH4  ratios were significantly decreased under warming (Zhu et al., 2020 ) further suggests that warming will emit a disproportionate increase in CH4  emissions, likely posing a positive feedback global warming loop. The consistently ongoing warming and human modifications of estuaries (Scanes et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022 ) underline that these warming- and human activity-induced increases in estuary CH4  fluxes have wider implications for carbon budgets.   5 Conclusion High human activity and climate warming were observed to strongly increase CH4  emissions in estuaries. CH4 concentrations and fluxes in urban section increased by 179 % and 75 %, respectively, compared with suburban and rural sections. Tidal fluctuations shifted the magnitudes and pathways of CH4  emissions, with high CH4  fluxes and more ebullition contribution under the ebbing tide as benthic CH4  was directly emitted from sediments. Ebullition pathway represented higher temperature sensitivity, which would be further stimulated by climate warming. It is conservatively projected that CH4  emissions increase by 17 % and 40 % under the 2 °C and 4 °C warming scenarios by the end of 2100, respectively. The contribution of CH4  emissions from subtropical estuaries to the global estuary CH4  budget will be boosted by global warming and human activities. Therefore, our results shed light on climate warming, human activities and tidal fluctuations alter environmental factors for CH4  production, flux and pathways, collectively influencing CH4  dynamics, which will strengthen our understanding how estuaries affect global CH4  cycles.
1 Introduction Baseflow is the portion of streamflow that persists during periods of low precipitation, snowmelt, or ice melt. It is mainly fed by subsurface flow, including groundwater discharge and shallow unsaturated flow (Price, 2011 ). Baseflow dynamics determine water availability during periods of water stress. Therefore, understanding the sources and magnitude of baseflow is key to water supply sustainability for humans and ecosystems (Tetzlaff and Soulsby, 2008 ). Hydrologists and hydrogeologists use the term baseflow slightly differently (Staudinger et al., 2019 ), in the present study, baseflow is synonymous with groundwater contribution to streamflow. A variety of hydrological approaches can be used to characterize baseflow dynamics. The long-term ratio of baseflow to total streamflow is known as the baseflow index (BFI). The rate at which flow decreases after a precipitation event is expressed by the baseflow recession constant (Kb ). Both BFI and Kb  can be calculated from continuous streamflow records (Smakhtin, 2001 ). Sources of baseflow can be characterized using hydrologic tracers like major ions, stable water isotopes and d-excess (e.g., Singh et al., 2019; Campbell and Ryan, 2021; Lone et al., 2021; Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ). Relatedly, the amount of time that stream water has spent in the catchment (since falling as precipitation) can be expressed by the mean transit time (MTT) and young water fraction (Fyw ) (Kirchner, 2016 ). In general, rivers with a higher BFI, higher Kb , longer MTT and lower Fyw  provide more consistent streamflow during dry spells (McGuire et al., 2005; Hale and McDonnell, 2016 ). Baseflow characteristics vary widely between – and within – watersheds and are influenced by complex interactions between climate, geology, geomorphology, topography, and evapotranspiration (ET) rates (Price, 2011; Beck et al., 2013 ). Catchment geology and geomorphology influence baseflow generation because of more porous and permeable bedrock (Abebe and Foerch, 2006; Santhi et al., 2008; Capell et al., 2011 ), greater soil depth (Kosugi et al., 2006 ), and deeper active groundwater flow zones (Asano et al., 2002; Zimmer et al., 2012 ) increase baseflow contribution. Some studies have found a relationship between slope and baseflow dynamics (McGuire et al., 2005; Vivoni et al., 2007; Zimmer and Gannon, 2018 ) where, in general, steeper, headwater catchments tend to have quicker baseflow recession (low Kb ) but higher BFI (Beck et al., 2013 ). Contrary, such headwater catchments generally yield low Fyw  which is partially explained by longer groundwater flow paths, deep vertical infiltration, wherein snow dominated systems, persistence of snowpacks in mountain catchments result in low Fyw  (Gentile et al., 2023 ). Despite a large body of literature on baseflow processes, the dominant controls on baseflow magnitude and sources remain unclear in some settings (Price, 2011 ). Beck et al. (2013)  compiled a global dataset of BFI and Kb  estimated form hydrograph data. Their results in data-poor regions, including (semi-) arid and (sub-) arctic areas, exhibited high uncertainty due to the small number of data points in those regions. For example, of the 3394 catchments investigated by Beck et al. (2013) , the vast majority are in the US, Canada, various countries in Europe and Australia, while only one catchment was located in India. Furthermore, it remains difficult to disentangle the impacts of different surface and subsurface catchment characteristics under the influence of complex geology, topography and land use (Price, 2011; Richardson et al., 2020 ). Mountain regions possess several characteristics associated with low catchment storage (e.g., thin soils, exposed bedrock, steep slopes) and were once thought of as “Teflon basins” with limited capacity for delayed flows (Williams et al., 2015; Schmieder et al., 2019 ). However, recent research has shown that groundwater is a major contributor to streamflow in mountain watersheds (Hayashi, 2020; Somers and McKenzie, 2020  and references therein). Understanding where and when baseflow is generated in mountains is particularly important since mountains are disproportionately large contributors to global water supply (Viviroli et al., 2007, 2020 ). This is because mountains receive more precipitation, experience less evapotranspiration than lowlands, and store water as snow and ice. As the climate changes, mountain “water towers” are threatened by a rapid loss of snowpack and glacier mass (Immerzeel et al., 2020 ) while downstream, water demand is increasing (de Jong, 2015; Viviroli et al., 2020 ). Consistent groundwater discharge to mountain rivers as baseflow can sustain mountain water resources as the climate continues to warm and less snow and ice melt are available during dry periods (Tague and Grant, 2009; Somers et al., 2019 ). Existing studies of baseflow in mountains point to geology, geomorphology and topography as factors controlling baseflow generation (Tague and Grant, 2004; Katsuyama et al., 2005; Bloomfield et al., 2009; Somers et al., 2016; Segura et al., 2019 ) and MTT (McGuire et al., 2005; Hale and McDonnell, 2016; Pfister et al., 2017 ). Saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat ), the ability of the aquifer material to transmit water, is most often cited as the dominant factor controlling baseflow generation in mountains. However, most existing studies use rock type as a proxy for Ksat , rather than measuring it in the field, lending some uncertainty to previous results. Field characterization of this parameter is particularly difficult in mountains, due to limited accessibility, a lack of observation wells, and high natural variability in this parameter. Mountains also exhibit considerable geologic complexity which may influence baseflow generation mechanisms and magnitudes. In solid rock, Ksat  is enhanced by conduits, fracture networks and faults which can convey a variety of recharge sources to both headwater and higher-order streams (Bicalho et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019 ). Lithologic contacts and geologic structures may also be important for channelling groundwater flow (e.g., Gremaud et al., 2009 ) but their potential importance in baseflow generation has received little attention. Previous studies on mountain baseflow dynamics are concentrated in certain mountain ranges (Somers and McKenzie, 2020 ) and are not easily transferable to other mountain ranges/catchments as the physiographic characteristics vary considerably. The Himalayas have received less attention than other mountain ranges in mountain groundwater research (Jeelani, 2008; Shah et al., 2017; Jeelani et al., 2017; Somers and McKenzie, 2020; Lone et al., 2021 ) despite its critical role in supplying water for hundreds of millions of people downstream (Immerzeel et al., 2010 ). The Upper Indus Basin (UIB) was recently found to be the most critical mountain water tower on earth, meaning that it produces a large amount of dry-season runoff, and that water demand downstream is extremely high and dependent on this flow (Lutz et al., 2016; Immerzeel et al., 2020 ). Groundwater research progress in the Himalayas has been impeded by data scarcity, lack of resources and accessibility. As mountain glaciers retreat globally, there is a growing need to understand baseflow sources, dynamics, and their vulnerability to climate change, particularly in understudied mountain regions. In this study, we investigate the baseflow dynamics in space and time in a geologically complex watershed of the UIB in the western Himalayas. We hypothesize that the contribution of groundwater to baseflow in different areas of the catchment is primarily related to Ksat  of the underlying geology. Our study objectives are to:Measure and assess the spatial variability in Ksat  for the different geologic units in a high mountain watershed of the UIB.  Characterise baseflow sources and residence time in three nested sub-catchments using stable water isotope sampling, Fyw  and a Bayesian mixing model.  Compare spatial patterns in stream groundwater contribution to Ksat  and surface topography.    To achieve our objectives, we measure Ksat  using geophysical methods and slug tests across varied geologic units in our high-elevation study site in the UIB. We then sampled precipitation, glacier water, groundwater, and stream water for determination of ratios of stable water isotopes (δ18 O and δ2 H). We used two different approaches to characterize baseflow generation for three geologically distinct sub-catchments, including Fyw  and a Bayesian end member mixing model. Finally, Ksat , surface topography, Fyw , and mixing analysis results are compared to infer the controls on baseflow dynamics across the watershed.  2 Study area Our study watershed is located within the UIB in the western Himalayas (Fig. 1  a). The UIB has experienced a significant temperature increase over the last 30 years and the glacier area declined by 29 % between 1962 and 2013 (Marazi and Romshoo, 2018 ). Stream discharge shows a statistically significant declining trend over the last six decades, concurrent with glacier recession, despite increasing precipitation (Rashid et al., 2020 ). We focus on the Liddar watershed in the upper Jhelum catchment of the UIB between latitudes of 33° 40′ 0″ N to 34° 12′ 35″ N and longitudes of 75° 09′ 0″E to 75° 32′ 0″E. The total catchment area is 1243 km2  (Fig. 1 ) and the elevation ranges from 1579 to 5295 m above mean sea level (m asl). The Liddar River flows into the Jhelum River, one of five major tributaries to the Indus River. The Liddar River originates from the Kolahoi glacier (West branch) and Sheshnag Lake (East branch) (Marazi and Romshoo, 2018 ). The total glacier cover (as of 2018) in the watershed was 33.5 ± 2.0 km2  corresponding to 2.7 % of the total watershed area and occurring between an altitude range of ∼3600 to ∼5020 m asl with mainly northwest orientation (Marazi and Romshoo, 2018; Romshoo et al., 2023 ). The topography of the Liddar watershed is varied and rugged with snow, glaciers, and rock outcrops covering the upstream region (>3600 m asl). Alpine meadows and dense evergreen coniferous forest cover the midstream region (1600–3600 m asl). The downstream region is covered by alluvial plains (1580–2200 m asl (Rashid et al., 2020 ). The mean annual precipitation recorded at the Pahalgam weather station is 1240 mm (Fig. 2  ; Sarah et al., 2021 ). Snow is the dominant form of precipitation from November to March and widespread during January and February months, sourced from westerlies (Lone et al., 2021 ). Currently, snowfall constitutes 52 % of the overall annual precipitation, contributing approximately 55 % to the annual streamflow (Romshoo and Marazi, 2022 ). The annual mean discharge for the years 2017 to 2019, as recorded at Site-1, Site-2, and Site-3, was 14.25 m3 /s, 25.57 m3 /s, and 9.61 m3 /s, respectively (Fig. 2 ). The low mean discharge observed at Site-3 corresponds to the diversion of stream water through irrigation canals used for agricultural in the downstream area. The maximum mean monthly temperature of 19 °C occurs in July and the minimum mean temperature during winter is −1.7 °C and occurs in January (Rashid et al., 2020; Sarah et al., 2021; Sarah et al., 2024 ). The watershed is composed of heterogeneous geology, ranging from hard rock to alluvium, making it an ideal watershed to investigate baseflow dynamics across discrete geology. The hard rocks are composed of Panjal volcanics, agglomeratic slate, gneissose granite, Muth quartzites, fenestella shales, metamorphic schists, and Zewan and Syringothyris limestone varieties (Wadia, 1975; Singh, 1982 ). The lithology comprises Paleozoic rocks to recent alluvium, while Triassic limestones and Panjal volcanics are dominant (Middlemiss, 1910; Wadia, 1975 ). The Triassic limestones occur as isolated rock units surrounded by Palaeozoic sedimentary and volcanic rocks superimposed by Plio-Pleistocene lacustrine and fluvioglacial sediments called Karewa deposits (coarse to medium-grained sand, conglomerates, silt, marls, clay, lignite) and alluvium (Fig. 1 c; Singh, 1982; Wadia, 1975 ). The Karewa deposits comprise unconsolidated clays, sands, and conglomerates with lignite beds that have a thickness of ∼1300 m (Singh, 1982; Wadia, 1975 ). Four key aquifers in this region were identified by Jeelani (2008) , including the limestone aquifer, volcanic aquifer, alluvial aquifer, and the karewa aquifer. The Triassic limestones contain karst geomorphological features including solution cavities, conduits, shafts, caves, and large springs, which act as important groundwater reservoirs (Shah et al., 2017 ). High Ksat  values, around 1000 m/d, have been reported in the limestone aquifer facilitated by both conduits and fractures. The volcanic aquifer is also fractured and has a relatively high Ksat  of approximately 6 m/d (Jeelani, 2008 ). A lower Ksat  was observed in the alluvium (0.1–5 m/d) and Karewa sedimentary aquifer (1–10 m/d) consisting of fine sand, silt, and clay (Jeelani, 2008 ). Three sites within the watershed were chosen for baseflow estimation to capture the distinct topography and geology of the upstream (Site-1), midstream (Site-2), and downstream (Site-3) areas of the watershed. The upstream site (Site-1) has the steepest topographic gradient and the study section of the river is underlain by limestone. The midstream site (Site-2) has more moderate topographic gradient and is underlain by volcanic rock (hard rock). The downstream site (Site-3) has the lowest topographic slope and is underlain by alluvial deposits.  3 Methods 3.1 Geophysical methods to estimate hydraulic conductivity Geophysical methods offer an efficient and inexpensive way to characterize heterogeneous hydrogeological flow systems in places where few monitoring wells exist (Grobbe et al., 2021 ). Electrical resistivity geophysical methods use electrical resistivity of a geological material as an indirect measurement of its permeability (or Ksat ) and fracture network. We collected vertical electrical sounding (VES) measurements and applied an established relationship between resistivity and Ksat  (Archie, 1942; Lesmes and Friedman, 2005; Miller, 2012 ) to estimate the Ksat  of the main aquifer units in the Liddar River watershed. We conducted VES surveys at 17 sites distributed along the river network from high to low elevation (Fig. 1 c). Five to seven soundings were performed at each site. Multiple VES measurements were collected in three of the four main watershed lithologies: karstified limestone, hard rocks (volcanics) and alluvium. Ksat  estimates from VES surveys were then compared to slug test results performed at lower elevations (described in the next section). A ‘Deep Resistivity Meter-AIM-705-C2’ was used for VES measurements with Schlumberger settings. We used a Schlumberger array with current electrode spacing (AB/2) varying from 1 m to a maximum of 200 m. This technique has been successfully applied in varied lithological settings (Rosa et al., 2017 ) to investigate subsurface layers (Heigold et al., 1979; Díaz-Curiel et al., 2016 ) and derive aquifer parameters like Ksat , transmissivity, and porosity (Worthington and Barker, 1972; Chandra, et al., 2008; de Almeida et al., 2021 ). The apparent resistivity data was processed in IX1D®v2 (Interpex Limited), a commercial software for resistivity data inversion and interpretation. The processed and interpreted data were used to infer the true resistivity and depth of the geoelectric layers, aquifer thickness, and Dar Zarrouk parameters: longitudinal conductance (SL) and transverse resistance (T) for each aquifer (Supplementary Table S1 ). Dar Zarrouk parameters (Maillet, 1947; Niwas and Lima, 2003 ) are related to the aquifer properties as follows:(1) SL = h i  / ρ i      (2) T = h i  × ρ i      Where, hi  is the thickness of the ith  layer and ρi  is the resistivity of the ith  layer. We can then estimate Ksat  from the values of SL and T (Niwas and Singhal, 1981 ). To estimate Ksat  from geoelectrical measurements, we applied the relation provided by Chandra et al. (2008)  established in hard rock aquifers with the underlying assumption that the aquifer experiences steady-state flow in a homogeneous medium, where groundwater quality remains fairly constant:(3) K sat  = A σ  or  K sat  = A  1 / ρ     Where σ is the electrical conductivity, ρ is the resistivity, and A is a constant equal to 2.176E-03 determined by Chandra et al. (2008) . Eq.s 3 shows that Ksat  is inversely proportional to the aquifer resistivity (ρ), because low-resistive formations are usually highly fissured or porous water-saturated materials (Chandra et al., 2008 ). Similarly, the Ksat  in alluvium aquifers was derived from the relationship presented by Heigold et al. (1979) :(4) K sat  = 386.40 ρ - 0.93283       Where ρ is the resistivity. Ksat  calculated from VES has a number of sources of uncertainty, including the spatial resolution of data, instrument error and geologic heterogeneities. We minimized these errors through data quality control checks including data smoothing and filtering out the outliers and noise. Highly heterogeneous soil and rock properties, the presence of fractures and variations in groundwater flow can increase uncertainty in Ksat  from aquifer resistivity measurements (Rubin and Hubbard, 2006; Lu et al., 2021 ). Despite these sources of uncertainty, several studies have shown a good correlation between hydrogeological and geophysical parameters (Pfannkuch, 1972; Singhal et al., 1998; Niwas and de Lima, 2003; Chandra, 2006 ). For example, Kelly and Frohlich (1985)  confirmed a strong positive correlation between aquifer resistivity obtained from geoelectrical measurements and hydraulic conductivity obtained from pumping tests.  3.2 Slug tests to estimate hydraulic conductivity We carried out slug tests in the lower watershed in all three lithology types (limestone, hard rock and alluvium) to provide additional estimates of Ksat  and to ground-truth our VES measurements. A slug test is a relatively quick and inexpensive in-situ measurement of Ksat  that can be performed on an observation well. During the test, the hydraulic head in a well is changed suddenly, and the time taken for the subsequent recovery of the well water level is recorded (Fitts, 2012 ). We used the Hvorslev (1951)  equation to calculate horizontal hydraulic conductivity (Kh ):(5) K h  = r  2    log e  L p  R      2 L p  T L         where K h  is horizontal hydraulic conductivity (cm/sec), r  is the radius of the piezometer or well casing (cm), R  is the radius of the perforated or slotted screen interval (cm), L p  is the length of the perforated or slotted screen interval (cm), and T L  is the time lag for the water level to return to 37 % of the initial change in water level. The time lag (T L ) is determined by recording the water-level change through time following the sudden head change, and is normalized to the maximum water-level change (Fetter, 2001 ).  3.3 Terrain analysis Advanced Space-borne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) DEM data of 30 m resolution was retrieved from the USGS Earth Explorer portal (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/ ). The DEM data was used to delineate the stream network, stream order, and stream gradient (SG) for the catchment. SG in units of m/km were measured by delineating the stream profile of the main stream and then dividing the change in elevation (m) by the horizontal distance (km).  3.4 Stable water isotope sampling and analysis Several field campaigns were carried out between 2017 and 2019 to collect surface and groundwater samples in the Liddar watershed (Supplementary Table S3 ). Water samples were collected during the low-flow period in autumn and winter from precipitation (rain and snow), snowpack, snowmelt, glacier melt, stream water and groundwater across the watershed (Fig. 1 b). The stream water samples were collected along the main stem of the Liddar River to document the spatial variability. The precipitation samples were composite monthly samples collected at six selected sites across the catchment using precipitation collectors following the guidelines provided by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA, 1983 ). The precipitation samples were volume-weighted based on precipitation data at the Pahalgam weather station (elevation, 2214 m asl) located within the watershed. During winter, fresh snow taken as bulk samples from entire profile (snow depth range from 0.3 to 1 m during sampling period) were collected using PVC tube of two-inch diameter and transferred in 500 ml HDPE container, allowed to melt at ambient temperature. Besides this, limited bulk samples of snowpack from relatively old snow from high elevation sites were collected in 500 mL HDPE bottles, allowed to melt at room temperature and then immediately transferred to 10 mL HDPE vials sealed with a parafilm tape to avoid any fractionation. Glacier melt samples were collected during the autumn season (dominant ablation period) in the form of melt near the snout and some supra-glacier channels in 10 mL vials. Groundwater samples were collected along the stream from wells and springs during each field expedition in 10 mL vials. The sampling wells, located in the elevation range from 1600 to 2200 m asl, private tubewells, tubewells installed by the central groundwater board (CGWB) and Jal Shakti department J&K were pumped and purged for at least five minutes before collecting each sample. The sampling depth of wells ranges from 1-10 m from ground surface. All water samples collected for isotope analysis were sealed properly with a parafilm tape to avoid any isotopic fractionation before laboratory analysis. The samples were analysed for stable isotopes of oxygen (δ18 O) and hydrogen (δ2 H) at the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) – Geosciences Division and National Geophysical Research Institute of India (CSIR-NGRI). They were analysed for δ18 O and δ2 H using an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (IRMS, Delta V plus, Thermo Scientific). The isotope measurements were performed by equilibrating 300 μl of water sample with CO2  and H2  respectively for 16 h at 25 °C (Maurya et al., 2009 ). The results are denoted in the standard δ-notation expressed in units of per mil (‰) and defined relative to the Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW). The overall precision of the measurements was 0.1 ‰ for δ18 O and 1 ‰ for δ2 H based on analyses of multiple aliquots of the secondary laboratory standards in each batch. Deuterium excess (d-excess) is a metric which expresses the abundance of 2 H over 18 O calculated as:(6) δ  2  H = 8 ∗ δ  18  O     D-excess was calculated for each water sample and provides a measure of non-equilibrium isotopic fractionation (Dansgaard, 1964; Dütsch et al., 2017 ). Along with δ18 O, d-excess has been used widely as tracer for end member mixing analysis in mountain settings (eg. Singh et al., 2019; Lone et al., 2021 ). Since it has been found that d-excess measurements serve as a tracer for end-member mixing analyses in alpine catchments, where high-elevation snowmelt contribute to the catchment's streamflow (Sprenger et al., 2024 ). To gain insights into local evaporative processes, we compute the line-conditioned excess (lc-excess; Landwehr and Coplen, 2006 ), which is used to understand the deviation of a sample's isotopic composition from local meteoric water line (LMWL). Based on our LMWL, we calculated lc-excess as follows:(7) l c - e x c e s s = δ  2  H - α × δ  18  O - β     Where α    and β    are slope and intercept of LMWL, respectively.  3.5 Young water fraction We use the measured stable water isotope results to calculate the Fyw  in streamflow at three locations in the Liddar River watershed (Site-1, 2 and 3 in Fig. 1 c). Fyw  is the proportion of streamflow that fell as precipitation more recently than some threshold, usually 0.2 years. It is calculated based on the damping of the annual variation in stable water isotopic ratios in streamflow compared to precipitation. Kirchner (2016)  proposed Fyw  as an alternative to MTT because it is free from aggregation errors that arise given the heterogeneity of hydrologic systems. Fyw  is a useful metric to characterize baseflow source and has been used extensively in recent literature (e.g., Schmieder et al., 2019; Gallart et al., 2020 ). We calculated the Fyw  by iteratively fitting sinusoidal functions (Eqs. (8) and (9) ) to our time series δ18 O data from precipitation and streamflow (Kirchner, 2016 ; Fig. 5 ) following previous studies (e.g., McGuire and McDonnell, 2006; Kirchner, 2016; He et al., 2020 ):(8) C p  t    = a p  cos 2 π f t    + b p  sin 2 π f t    + k p      (9) C s  t    = a s  cos 2 π f t    + b s  sin 2 π f t    + k s      (10) A P  = a p   2  + b p   2    ,  A s  = a s   2  + b s   2        (11) φ P  = tan  - 1   ( b  p  / a p  ) ,  φ s  = tan  - 1   ( b  s  / a s  )      where, Cp (t) and Cs (t) are the δ18 O for precipitation and streamflow at time t, f is the frequency (yr−1 ), kp  and ks  represent the vertical shift of the sine wave, and ap , bp , as  and bs  are coefficients for determining the amplitude (i.e., AP  and AS ) and phase shift (i.e., φp  and φs ) of seasonal precipitation and streamflow isotopic cycles. Fyw  was then calculated as the amplitude ratio between stream water and precipitation (Kirchner, 2016 ):(12) F yw   = A S  A P       To minimize the impact of outliers, we employed an iterative re-weighted least squares (IRLS) R script for the fitting calculation using the script by von Freyberg et al. (2018) .  3.6 Bayesian isotope mixing model Next, we applied a Bayesian end-member mixing model (EMMA) to quantify the contribution of different source waters to streamflow during low-flow conditions at three locations (Site-1, Site-2 and Site-3 in Fig. 1 c). Mixing analysis has been used widely in hydrology to quantify sources of streamflow based on a variety of tracers, often stable water isotopes, electrical conductivity (EC), chloride (Cl− ) and silica (SiO2 ) (Gibson et al., 2000; Klaus and McDonnell, 2013; Throckmorton et al., 2016; Lone et al., 2021 ). One advantage of using stable water isotope tracers to quantify groundwater contribution to streamflow is that they are not affected by water–rock interactions as other tracers such as EC, SiO2  and other dissolved solutes (Klaus and McDonnell, 2013; Singh et al., 2019 ). The classic isotope mixing model approach (described in Hooper et al., 1990 ) requires that the number of streamflow sources (end members) can be one greater than the number of tracers used. There are few assumptions related with the mixing model that; i) each source has a unique and sufficiently distinct isotopic signature that can be differentiated from other sources; ii) Isotopes behave conservatively, meaning they mix without undergoing significant fractionation or transformation after leaving their source; iii) isotopic signatures of the sources remain relatively constant over the time and space scales of interest. When these requirements are not met, EMMA can lead to inconclusive results or poorly constrained uncertainty (Aravena et al., 1993; Carrera et al., 2004; Widory et al., 2013 ). Specifically, there can be substantial variability in end member signatures in space and time and it is difficult to transfer this uncertainty to the EMMA results, which can lead to misinterpretation of the quantitative estimation (Ji et al., 2017; He et al., 2020 ). A Bayesian mixing model approach uses a probability distribution to represent each end-member and carries the uncertainty through to the results to assist in interpretation (Soulsby et al., 2003; He et al., 2020 ). The Bayesian approach performs efficiently in spite of spatio-temporal variability of the stable isotope data and small sample size. Its sensitivity to the sampling uncertainties induced by meltwater fractions is also lesser as compared to a linear EMMA (Ward et al., 2010; Cable et al., 2011 ). It also allows more end members (sources) to be applied than the number of tracers plus one. Several open access codes are available to apply Bayesian mixing models, including MixSIR, SIAR, SIMMR and MixSIAR (Moore and Semmens, 2008; Parnell et al., 2010; Stock et al., 2018 ), which have been used to solve stable isotope mixing equations. We used SIMMR to determine the proportion of different streamflow sources at three estimation sites in the watershed with δ18 O and d-excess as our hydrologic tracers. SIMMR (version 0.4.6.9000; Parnell, 2019 ) is an open-source Bayesian model for R that employs a Gibbs sampler (JAGS) and permits the use of prior distributions. The Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method was used to calculate and estimate probability density functions during the analysis, as outlined in previous studies (Stock and Semmens, 2016; Stock et al., 2018 ). This approach preserves the chosen samples of the prior distribution over the posterior distribution to a degree that is comparable to the likelihood function. A correlation matrix of joint posterior probability distribution for contributions for stream sources is given in Supplementary Fig. 1 . The likelihood function is determined by the discrepancies between predictions and observations. We used an uninformative prior distribution where the total contribution of water from all sources equals one. The mixing equations are presented below (Parnell et al., 2010; Stock et al., 2018 ):(13) Z ij   = ∑ k = 1  k  P k  S jk   + b jk      + ε jk       (14) S jk    N μ jk   , ω jk  2         (15) b jk    N λ jk ,   τ jk  2         (16) ε ij    N 0 , σ j  2         Where, Z ij      is the isotopic value of tracer j  of sample i (i = 1,2,3,4,….,N) ; P k     is the proportion of source k (k = 1,2,3,4,…..,N)  following the Dirichlet distribution, which is estimated by the mixing model; S jk      is the source value k  of isotope j , which is normally distributed with a mean of μ jk      and standard deviation (SD) of ω jk  2     reflecting the spatiotemporal uncertainty of the sources; b jk      is the enrichment factor of isotope j  on source k , which is normally distributed with a mean of λ jk      and SD of τ jk  2    ; and ε jk      is the residual error for unquantified variation between individual mixtures, which is normally distributed with a mean of zero and SD of σ j  2    . At each of our three baseflow estimation sites, three end members were used: precipitation (rain and snow), meltwater (snow melt and glacier melt), and groundwater (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). The δ18 O and d-excess data were categorized by season for each site into winter (December-February), spring (March-May), summer (June-August), and autumn (September-November). We quantified the groundwater contribution to streams (i.e., baseflow contribution) during the low-flow period: September – February. We assumed that tracers exhibit conservative behaviour in the stream and open water fractionation is insignificant. The end member sources are crucial for maintaining streamflow. We used Bayesian mixing model at the sub-catchment scale in order to minimize the variability in the isotopic signatures. The groundwater end member signature for each site was based on samples within the target geological unit only (i.e., the Site-1 EMMA uses a groundwater signature based only on limestone groundwater samples). The mean and SD of each end-member was provided as an input to the SIMMR  to calculate the proportion of each source and associated uncertainty in the stream mixture. To ensure convergence of the Bayesian EMMA, the Gelman-Rubin test performed by SIMMR must yield a value between 1 and 1.1, ideally below 1.05 (Gelman et al., 2014; Stock and Semmens, 2016 ). More information is available in Supplementary Table S2 . Furthermore, the distribution of source (end member) contributions calculated by the Bayesian EMMA serves as a measure of both source contribution variability and uncertainty. A larger standard deviation in the calculated source contribution (Sjk ) captures both greater variability in the source contribution over time and uncertainty arising from overlapping end-member signatures. The calculation considers Gaussian uncertainties for the stable isotopic measurements from each source, assumed to be uncorrelated. The resulting mean values are reported with their 95 % confidence intervals, based on Gaussian parsimony, indicating that there is a 95 % likelihood that the true source contributions fall within the presented ranges. Each baseflow estimation site is associated with a different geologic unit and elevation range (Site-1 = limestone and upstream, Site-2 = volcanics/hard rock and midstream, Site-3 = alluvium and downstream). Stream discharge data from stream gauges located at these sites was obtained from the Department of Irrigation and Flood control, Jammu and Kashmir. The absolute proportion of baseflow in terms of discharge were accounted for each site.   4 Results 4.1 Hydraulic conductivity Resistivity measurements were conducted and interpreted at 17 VES sites (Fig. 1 ). The VES results indicate that geological resistivity varies considerably across the catchment and within each geological unit. Overall, resistivity increases with depth and the highest resistivity (∼3000 Ωm) were observed at a depth of ∼170 m below the ground surface. The resistivity in hard rocks (mostly volcanics) ranges from 200 to >3000 Ωm at different VES sites. The highest resistivity (∼3000 Ωm) was observed at hard rock sites VES-4 and VES-11. In limestone lithology, resistivity ranges from 30–800 Ωm, with the lowest resistivity values were observed at the VES-17 site and highest at the VES-1 site. In lowland alluvial lithology, the electrical resistivity of subsurface material varies from ∼10–200 Ωm with the lowest resistivity observed at the VES-14 site and highest at the VES-4 site. The Dar Zarrouk parameters (total longitudinal conductance, SL, and total transverse resistance, T) were calculated from the resistivity and are given in the Supplementary Table S1 . Ksat  was then calculated for each aquifer and results are shown in Table 1  . The fractured hard rock had some of the lower inferred Ksat  values of 0.63–41.21 m/d, while the limestone lithology values were higher from 13.62 – 55.29 m/d. Lowland alluvial plains of the watershed had highly variable Ksat , ranging from 0.04 m/d to as high as 84.31 m/d at sites where the lithology was dominated by gravel, sand, and contacts between different lithologies. The highest inferred Ksat  of 84.31 m/d was observed at VES-10 in alluvium. Slug tests were performed in unused private borewells/tubewells within the watershed and Ksat  values calculated using the Hvorslev equation are also shown in Table 1 . The Ksat  values estimated from the Dar Zarrouk formula overlap with the Ksat  calculated from the slug tests in most cases. However, the Ksat  of alluvium ranges widely in the VES measurements but falls on the lower end of the slug test results.  4.2 Characterization, distribution and variability in isotopic composition of water sources Samples were collected from several sources including precipitation (rain and snow), snowmelt, snowpack, glacier melt, streamflow, and groundwater (springs and existing borewells/tubewells). The isotope signature of these water components vary over space and time during the observation period (Fig. 3  ). 4.2.1 Stable water isotopes of precipitation (rain and snow) Rain δ18 O values range from −11.17 ‰ to −2.87 ‰ (SD of 2.82 ‰) with a mean value of −6.47 ‰. However, lower δ18 O (−13.19 ‰ to −10.95 ‰) was observed in snow precipitation of winter time. Therefore, snow being more depleted in the heavier isotopes than rain, allows samples of stream water, groundwater, glacier melt, snowpack, and snowmelt fall within the isotopic range between rain and snow (Fig. 4   ). Precipitation (rain and snow) isotopic values showed marked variations over the time during observation period. A pronounced seasonality was observed in the precipitation isotope data representing different seasons during the observation period (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). The mean δ18 O values of precipitation was highest during summer (−3.79 ‰), and tend to be lower during autumn (−4.88 ‰) and spring (−7.12 ‰), with the lowest values occurring during winter (−10.58 ‰). Such seasonal variations of isotopic values of precipitation are attributed to the seasonal change in the hydro-meteorological parameters and the moisture sources. As a result, precipitation formed in cold air masses exhibits greater heavy isotope depletion than precipitation formed in warmer air masses (Beria et al., 2018 ). Consequently, this explains the snow being more depleted in heavier isotopes than rainfall at a given location. The LMWL had a slope of 7.61 ± 0.21 and an intercept of 11.18 ± 1.8 (Fig. 4 ), representing the lesser slope and higher intercept as compared to the global meteoric water line (GMWL). The lower slope, comparative to the GMWL, indicates evaporation influence or a different regional moisture origin and the higher intercept represents the moisture recycling which reflects the interaction between the local atmospheric moisture and isotopic character of precipitation. These isotopic signatures are characteristic of the western Himalayan moisture sources, as evident from the studies by Kumar et al. (2018)  (δ2 H = 7.95 ∗ δ18 O + 11.51) and Jeelani et al. (2013)  (δ2 H = 7.59 ∗ δ18 O + 11.79). The precipitation samples show noticeable variation in isotopic composition with changing elevation of sampling sites. Precipitation samples of snow having δ18 O less than −11.0 ‰ represent the higher elevation sites (>2400 m), notably in winter, the precipitation is dominated by snow and is widespread above an altitude of 2300 m asl. Similarly, the samples of rain with δ18 O greater than −4.0 ‰ represent the low elevation sites (<1700 m; Fig. 5 ). δ18 O of precipitation inversely correlates with elevation, as the δ18 O values of precipitation and elevation yields a precipitation isotopic lapse rate of −0.33 ‰ per 100 m increase in elevation. Precipitation lapse rate is relatively high compared to other water sources (Fig. 5 ) because the isotopic composition of precipitation varies systematically with elevation, becoming generally more depleted in heavier isotopes as rain out increases with elevation (Beria et al., 2018 ). Similar findings are also reported on the isotopic lapse rates of precipitation from nearby catchments in the western Himalaya (Jeelani et al., 2017; Lone et al., 2021 ).  4.2.2 Stable water isotopes of snowpack, snow melt and glacier melt Snowpack and snowmelt δ18 O range between −11.38 to −9.56 ‰ and −11.02 ‰ to −8.69 with a mean value of −10.72 ‰ and −9.74 ‰ respectively. The snow pack samples show differential isotopic composition and range in between snow and snowmelt along the meteoric water line (Fig. 5 ). Snowmelt samples were relatively enriched in heavier isotopes than snowpack, suggesting the post-depositional processes taking place over space and time that effect the residual snowpack isotopic composition during transformation to snow melt water. The possible reasons on changing isotopic composition of snowpack include, snow sublimation, rain on snow, snowpack age, canopy effects on snowpack, phase transformation of snowpack, and snow redistribution due to winds, causing mixing of snowpack (Beria et al., 2018 ). Upon comparing the lc-excess of snowpack with that of rain, the mean lc-excess of snowpack exhibits a positive deviation from the lc-excess of rain (Fig. 3 c), this suggests a difference in the moisture sources between rain and snow precipitation. Consequently, in the western Himalayan region, the western disturbances (moisture sources originating over the Mediterranean Sea and adjoining areas) are intensive during winter season with snow being dominant precipitation and Indian summer monsoon active during summer and autumn season with rain being dominant form of precipitation (Lone et al., 2021 ). A significant (R2  = 0.63) altitudinal variation of δ18 O was observed in snowmelt, with the lapse rate of −0.22 ‰ of δ18 O per 100 m rise in the elevation (Fig. 5 ). However, we did not establish lapse rates for snowpack samples due to inconsistent sampling locations and dates. Glacier melt δ18 O varies between −5.98 to 9.47 ‰ with a mean value of −7.94 ‰. Mean δ18 O of glacier melt was higher than snowmelt but lower than rain samples. Glacier melt δ18 O also inversely correlates with elevation resulting in lapse rate of −0.21 ‰ per 100 m rise in the elevation (Fig. 5 ), which is similar to the lapse rate of snowmelt water. Samples from glacier site with δ18 O less than −11.0 ‰ (Fig. 4 ) correspond to the high elevation site (>4800 m) where mean annual temperature remains sub-zero.  4.2.3 Stable water isotopes of groundwater Groundwater δ18 O values vary spatially across the study area (Fig. 4 ) with higher δ18 O (isotopically enriched) in downstream samples (mean: −5.80 ‰) and lower δ18 O (isotopically depleted) in upstream samples (mean: −8.11 ‰). The δ18 O has negative relationship with elevation corresponding to the isotopic lapse rate of −0.14 ‰ per 100 m increase in elevation (Fig. 5 ). Groundwater samples show small correlation (R2  = 0.31) with elevation, the observed isotopic lapse rate of groundwater was less among all other water sources. Isotopic composition of groundwater (springs and wells) vary in space and time. For example, the δ18 O of groundwater springs (−8.82 ‰) in the upper catchment show relatively lower δ18 O signatures compared to the springs of the downstream catchment (−7.02 ‰). The lower isotopic values at the upstream suggest the groundwater recharge from high altitude precipitation, whereas higher values towards the downstream area are suggestive of the mixing of recharge sources (rain, melt from snow/glacier and stream). Besides this, higher δ18 O values of groundwater were observed in summer months and lower δ18 O values in winter months. As evident from Fig. 5 , few groundwater samples with δ18 O greater than −5.00 ‰ from shallow groundwater at lower elevation sites represent rain dominated recharge condition, collected during summer months. Further, higher δ18 O values also suggest the increased evaporative enrichment in shallow groundwater during the warmer summer months, which is also evidenced by the low d-excess and negative lc-excess of these groundwater samples (Fig. 3 c).  4.2.4 Stable water isotopes of stream water Stream water δ18 O values varied between −10.8 and −3.79 ‰ (SD = 0.99 ‰) with a mean of −7.09. Temporally, the stream water showed the marked variations between low flow (baseflow; mean: −6.23 ‰) and non-low flow (mean: −7.56 ‰) streamflow. The isotopic composition of stream water exhibited a more limited variation in contrast to precipitation and meltwater (Fig. 3 a). This suggests that the water derived from headwater streams is mixed, resulting in the formation of composite stream water having narrower range of isotopic composition. Spatially, the main river and tributary streamflow δ18 O was depleted at higher elevations (−6.17 ‰ to −8.99 ‰) and enriched at lower elevations (−3.62 ‰ to −7.96 ‰). Stream water δ18 O exhibit inverse relation with elevation (not a strong correlation, R2  = 0.28), the observed isotopic lapse rate of stream water is −0.27 ‰ per 100 m increase in elevation (Fig. 5 ) which is lower than precipitation but higher than groundwater, glacier melt and snowmelt. The lower isotopic values of streams at higher elevations is due to the influence of high altitude isotopically depleted precipitation, whereas higher isotopic values suggest the mixing of waters from different flow paths and elevations in the downstream catchment. Therefore, the stream water isotopic composition responds to the spatial variability of isotopic composition of the other catchment water sources.  4.2.5 Excess (d- and lc-) Rain d-excess values range from 5.18 ‰ to 22.7 ‰ with a mean value of 14.2 ‰ and snow d-excess values range from 17.15 ‰ to 21.8 ‰ with a mean value of 18.3 ‰. The spread of precipitation isotopes around the LMWL was also evident in d-excess and lc-excess values (Fig. 3 b, c). The mean d-excess of snow was relatively higher than rain as snow is the dominant form of precipitation during winter season, the ambient air temperature is relatively lower and results in more depleted heavier isotopes than rainfall. This can be further explained by the lc-excess values of snow, which exhibit a shift towards the positive lc-excess values compared to rain (Fig. 3 c), suggesting no significant influence of sublimation process observed in fresh snow, thus resulting in higher d-excess values. Mean stream baseflow d-excess was higher than that of rain but lower than that of groundwater, and considerably lower than the mean value of snow (Fig. 3 b). Similarly, groundwater samples show mean d-excess values close to that of rain, demonstrating an apparent bias towards the d-excess value of rain. Consequently, the lc‐excess values for groundwater are predominantly negative, indicating that the samples are below the LMWL and have undergone evaporation during infiltration. Therefore, d-excess can be seen as indicator of the amount of water that has evaporated after precipitation, however it is challenging to interpret in relation to specific local-scale processes (Michelon et al., 2023 ).   4.3 Young water fraction The δ18 O of precipitation, encompassing both rain and snow, followed an annual cycle with depleted values during winter and more enriched values during the spring and summer. Streamflow followed a similar annual pattern but the signal was damped compared to precipitation (Fig. 6  ). The amplitude of the annual isotopic variation in precipitation (AP ) was 7.28 ± 0.72 ‰ and the streamflow amplitude (AS ) was 4.64 ± 0.34 ‰ for the catchment as a whole. However, we calculated the amplitudes AS  and AP  at our three baseflow estimation sites and their corresponding results of Fyw  are given in Table 2  . Site-1 (limestone) and Site-2 (hard rock) had similar Fyw  (38 and 36 %, respectively). However, Site 3 (downstream, alluvium) had a higher Fyw  (0.55) than Site-1 and Site-2, indicating that unlike upstream sites a larger proportion of stream water at the downstream site is younger than the threshold age of 0.2 years. Streams with larger Fyw  contain more recent precipitation than baseflow (e.g. Kirchner, 2016; von Freyberg et al., 2018 ), which is also evident from the low baseflow contribution at Site-3. As we observe low Fyw  at upstream sites, it is generally found that Fyw  decreases at high elevations and has been attributed in some cases to the groundwater storage potential, persistence of winter snowpacks and limited liquid water input to the catchments during low flow period, which results in lower Fyw  (Gentile et al., 2023 ). However, in glacier dominated catchments, Fyw  at high elevations has been found several orders higher than snow dominated catchments and attributed to large free-draining of groundwater (Ceperley et al., 2020 ) and also glacier meltwater connectivity with groundwater in mountain proglacial areas (Muller, 2023 ) could influence the Fyw .  4.4 Bayesian mixing model The Bayesian mixing analysis was performed by using δ18 O and d-excess values of precipitation, meltwater (snow melt and glacier melt), and groundwater to identify the end member contribution to streamflow. The end member mixing plots reveal considerable variation in the isotopes of source water at the three estimation sites in the catchment. The stream water isotope values fall significantly within the domain of isospace defined by the end members (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). The Bayesian mixing model converged using our input data, producing a Gelman-Rubin value of 1, satisfying the convergence criteria of being between 1 and 1.05. The model results yielded estimates and uncertainty ranges for the contribution of each end member for each streamflow sample collected during the low flow period (September − February). The output results show a differential contribution from the end member sources to streamflow at different sites. The end member contribution to streamflow at each baseflow estimation site is shown in Table 3  . The groundwater contribution to streamflow (baseflow) during the low flow period is substantial and varied between baseflow estimation sites. The upstream site (Site-1, limestone) had the largest groundwater contribution to streamflow (72 %) with less uncertainty (SD = 11 %) at this site compared to the lower sites. The midstream site (Site-2, hard rock) had the next largest groundwater contribution to baseflow (56 %) and higher uncertainty (SD = 19 %). The downstream site (Site-3, alluvium) had the lowest contribution of groundwater to baseflow (43 %) and a similar uncertainty to Site-2 (SD = 18 %). However, Site-3 has large credible interval (Supplementary Table S2 ) approximately 7.7 % to 76 %, which suggests that baseflow proportions at Site-3 is more uncertain. Precipitation (rain and snow) is a minor contributor (11 ± 5 % and 11 ± 6 %, respectively) to streamflow at Sites-1 and 2 during this period but is substantially higher at Site-3 (28 ± 12 %). The meltwater (snow and glacier) contribution to streamflow is larger than the precipitation contribution at Sites-1 and 2 but similar to the precipitation contribution at Site-3. The meltwater contributions have a higher variability compared to the precipitation contributions. The relative baseflow proportions of 72 %, 56 % and 43 % translates into 2.45 m3 /s, 4.66 m3 /s and 3.90 m3 /s of baseflow at Site-1, Site-2 and Site-3 respectively (Table 3 ). However, after subtracting the baseflow contributions from upstream sites to the sites downstream, these flows become 2.45 m3 /s, 2.21 m3 /s and 1.69 m3 /s. Therefore, absolute baseflow proportions were consistent with the relative proportions of baseflow.  4.5 Combined results We combined the Ksat  measurements, terrain analysis, Fyw  and mixing model results to enhance our understanding of groundwater and baseflow dynamics in different areas of the Liddar watershed. In a conceptual Fig. 6  upstream site (Site-1, limestone) had a relatively high Ksat , the highest topographic slope (40 m/km) the largest groundwater contribution to baseflow (72 % ± 11), the lowest Fyw  (36 %). This area also has lower order (1st-2nd order), high stream gradient (Fig. 8 ). The midstream site (Site-2, hard rock) has the lowest Ksat , a medium slope (30 m/km), a similar Fyw  (38 %) to Site-1, and the next largest groundwater contribution to baseflow (56 % ± 19). The midstream area has 3rd-4th order streams while the downstream area includes 5th and 6th order streams. The downstream site (Site-3, alluvium) had a medium Ksat , the lowest topographic slope (12 m/km), the lowest contribution of groundwater to baseflow (43 % ± 18) and the highest Fyw  (55 %).   5 Discussion 5.1 Hydraulic conductivity of mountain aquifers Our reported Ksat  values are relatively high, 15 of 17 VES sites and all of our slug test sites indicated Ksat  values above 1 m/d. The limestone areas were associated with some of the highest Ksat  values, consistent with the karstified nature of these aquifers (Jeelani, 2008 ). In the hard rock aquifers, we infer that a highly fractured bedrock underlies unconsolidated sediments, like boulders and gravel. Although lower permeability than the limestone aquifers, the fractured nature of the hard rock lends this geological unit substantial permeability. There are also lithological contacts between quartzites/slates and volcanics present, which likely enhance the permeability and baseflow contribution of the hard rock unit in discrete areas. The observed Ksat  of alluvium was particularly variable, including both the highest and lowest Ksat  observations. This may be because of the spatial heterogeneity in grain size of the alluvial material which includes sands and gravels but also clay lenses. The occasional very high Ksat  values inferred from resistivity data at some alluvium sites may be related to the alluvial aquifer system overlying a more electrically conductive substratum (clays or shales). In this case, the electrical current flow in the aquifer is greatly influenced by the electric nature of its substratum, which controls the relationship between Ksat  and resistivity (Niwas and de Lima, 2003 ). These results demonstrate that both consolidated and unconsolidated mountain lithologies exhibit Ksat  values that are capable of transmitting substantial amounts of water and agree with previous studies that suggest that mountain bedrock should not be considered impermeable in mountain hydrological models (e.g., Frisbee et al., 2011 ). Where many previous studies of mountain groundwater use geology as a proxy for Ksat  (e.g., Paznekas and Hayashi, 2016 ), the present study compiles field measurements of Ksat  from geophysics and slug tests to characterize Ksat  of different mountain aquifers. A lack of data characterizing Ksat  and other geological characteristics in mountains remains a barrier to accurate physically-based hydrogeological modelling in mountains (Thornton et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the presented Ksat  observations may serve to guide future modelling applications and incorporate groundwater processes into our understanding of climate change impacts on mountain waters.  5.2 Baseflow generation in sub-catchments with distinct lithologies 5.2.1 Upstream, limestone catchment The upstream, high-slope catchment underlain by a limestone aquifer showed a high Ksat , a low Fyw  in streamflow and a high contribution of baseflow to dry season streamflow (Fig. 7   a). The observed high Ksat  and large groundwater contribution to baseflow is likely caused by the karstified nature of these aquifers, which allows them to transmit large volumes of water and feed baseflow from their shallow but substantial storage. Furthermore, the 1st and 2nd order streams in this area have relatively high stream gradient than higher order streams (Fig. 7 a) and the mean channel slope is higher than other areas of the Liddar watershed. These factors contribute to a steep hydraulic gradient which supports baseflow (Fig. 7 b). The relatively low Fyw  in streamflow here is a logical corollary to the large contribution of groundwater to baseflow. The dominance of snow over rain in the upper catchment may also increase the age of runoff (Campbell et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, Fyw  in karst aquifers can be altered by bidirectional fluid exchange between matrix/small fractures and conduits controlled by the hydraulic gradient, mixing older and younger waters and vice versa (Zhang et al., 2020 ).  5.2.2 Midstream, hard rock catchment The mid-elevation, medium-slope catchment underlain by hard rock had a lower mean Ksat  than the upstream site, accompanied by a medium baseflow contribution and a similar Fyw  to the upstream site, which is relatively low (Fig. 7 a). Although the mean Ksat  observed by geophysics was lower than the limestone, individual Ksat  measurements were highly variable, particularly from VES surveys. This variability is thought to be a result of local fracture networks and geological contacts between volcanics, quartzites and slates (Table S1 ). These fracture networks may play an important role in generating baseflow by creating local high permeable zones conducive for higher baseflow generation. The wide range of baseflow contributions observed at this site (38–66 %) supports the argument that local circulation zones induce spatial and temporal variability in the baseflow contribution in hard rocks. Furthermore, the midstream catchment had medium topographic slope driving medium hydraulic gradients between the aquifer and the stream (Fig. 6 b), paralleling the medium contribution of baseflow in this area.  5.2.3 Downstream, alluvial catchment The lower-elevation catchment underlain by alluvium was characterized by a lower topographic slope, variable Ksat , the highest Fyw  and lowest baseflow contribution compared to the mid- and high-elevation catchments. The larger Fyw  in the alluvial catchment suggests that quick, shallow lateral flow is the predominant flow path for streamflow generation. The water table in the alluvium is generally only 2–3 m below ground surface with low stream gradient (Fig. 7 ). Therefore, the low hydraulic gradient between the stream and these aquifers and insignificant water levels fluctuations (<1m) may also play a role in the magnitude of baseflow contribution in the lower catchment (Fig. 7 a). At a few sites in the alluvial downstream catchment, we observed medium sandy lithology overlain by clay lenses, giving rise to perched aquifer conditions. These clay lenses may inhibit connectivity between the alluvial aquifer and the river and may explain the reason for substantially lower groundwater contribution to baseflow observed in the lower alluvial catchment. Alluvial aquifers are considered to be important sources of streamflow and baseflow in many regions (Price, 2011; Tetzlaff and Soulsby, 2008 ) including mountainous regions (e.g., Szmigielski et al., 2018 ). Our study also shows a substantial baseflow contribution from alluvial lithology. However, we observed that the alluvial aquifer contributed a smaller proportion of baseflow compared to the hard rock and limestone upper areas of the watershed. This may be because of the clay lenses and low hydraulic gradient mentioned above which may not have been present in other watersheds mentioned previously carried out studies (Price, 2011; Tetzlaff and Soulsby, 2008 ).  5.2.4 Colluvium Colluvium and talus deposits were present in the headwaters of the Liddar watershed overlying bedrock. While these areas were not possible to isolate in our study, they may also be important for generating baseflow (Cowie et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2004 ). The colluvium material may facilitate more groundwater recharge to fractured bedrock, and act as a high-porosity groundwater storage reservoir which later feeds the streams as baseflow. Moreover, the high slope of the underlying bedrock surface may facilitate lateral groundwater flow over vertical percolation (Fig. 8 ; Clow et al., 2003; Pierson, 1982 ).   5.3 Controls on baseflow generation in a geologically heterogeneous high mountain watershed Our results indicate a wide range of groundwater contributions to baseflow within each sub-catchment (i.e., some high contributions were observed at lower elevations and some low contributions were observed at high elevations. The channel gradient (and elevation) shows a corollary relationship with groundwater contribution to streamflow. The headwater streams have high stream gradient (Fig. 7 ) and a higher hydraulic gradient between the aquifer and the stream, enhancing groundwater fluxes (McGuire, et al., 2005 ). The steeper mountain terrain in the upstream catchment also facilitates rapid percolation through fractures and deep groundwater flow paths bypassing the headwater streams (Jasechko et al., 2016; Kirchner, 2016 ). The high topographic gradient may also drive deeper groundwater circulation, which would contribute to the lower Fyw  in streams observed in the upstream and midstream sites. Conversely to our results, Williams et al. (2016)  and Cowie et al. (2017)  used end member mixing approaches in mountain hydrological systems and found that baseflow contribution to streamflow decreased with elevation in Himalayan (Bhutan) and Rocky Mountain (USA) study sites, respectively. In this study, hydraulic conductivity of the distinct lithologies in the different catchments shows a significant relationship to the baseflow contribution. The highest groundwater contribution to baseflow was observed in the highest permeability aquifer unit (karst limestone), while the hard rock and alluvial aquifers had comparatively lower Ksat  values and lower groundwater contributions to baseflow, indicating the key role of hydraulic conductivity in controlling baseflow generation. This agrees with previous findings in the Canadian Rocky Mountains which found higher winter flows in catchments underlain by more permeable bedrock while topographic influence was not discernible (Paznekas and Hayashi, 2016 ). We therefore argue that irrespective of altitude, the permeability of the geological material is a critical control on baseflow contribution. The baseflow contribution from aquifers in heterogeneous geology either located in headwaters or downstream depends on the permeability of the bedrock and overlying material as well as Ksat  and connectivity with the streams. In addition to catchment-scale river gradients, local reach or hillslope-scale stream gradients also play a significant role in baseflow contribution to streams and can be different from the larger-scale river gradients. However, the thickness of the deeper fractured zones facilitating delayed groundwater flows is smaller in these types of montane high-altitude catchments. Therefore, these highly fractured zones form a part of the local groundwater flow system, instead of regional gradients, discharging to lower order streams of the headwater as seen in this watershed (Toth, 1963 ). With this perspective, we consider the subsurface heterogeneity as the first order control to be incorporated in the hydrological models so as to capture heterogeneity in baseflow contribution in discrete lithology. The same can be used to better inform hydrological models to assess the climate change impacts on baseflow contribution in high-altitude montane catchments.  5.4 Uncertainty and limitations Given the remote, high-altitude study watershed, we lacked certain field data that would have expanded the scope of our study and decreased uncertainty in mixing estimations. Specifically, we lacked high-resolution meteorological data and soil cover data which restricted the use of these variables in understanding their influence on baseflow generation. A lack of boreholes in the headwater area of the catchment meant that our groundwater samples and slug tests were biased towards the middle and lower elevation areas of the catchment. An adequate model fit was achieved to the available data (R2  = 0.87 and 0.88 for precipitation and streamflow, respectively) but a longer time-series would allow us to capture inter-annual variability in Fyw  which Stockinger et al. (2019)  indicate can be substantial. While the present study examines baseflow generation in three nested sub-catchments in a high-mountain watershed, inclusion of more sub-catchments and/or other watersheds would improve our ability to define the relationships between baseflow generation and catchment characteristics like Ksat , topography etc. One challenge was the difficulty of collecting Ksat  data in mountains. Our future work seeks to expand data collection or compile existing studies to improve our statistical understanding of how mountain catchment characteristics influence baseflow generation. Traditional end member mixing models assume that the isotopic composition of all end members are fixed and distinct (Hooper et al., 1990 ). However, in practice, there may be variability and some overlap in the isotopic signatures of potential end members. In our study, there is some overlap in the isotopic signatures of precipitation and meltwater, creating competing source contributions in the stream mixture. However, the use of a Bayesian approach allowed us to incorporate the spread in source water signatures into the uncertainty of the posterior probability distributions, as demonstrated by the substantial uncertainty ranges (represented by the standard deviations) in the posterior probability distributions (up to ∼20 %). Moreover, the difference in baseflow proportion between Sites 1, 2 and 3 is greater than the uncertainty, that increases the confidence in our results. He et al. (2020)  compared EMMA and Bayesian mixing approaches in a glacierized basin in Kyrgyzstan and found that the Bayesian approach reduced the uncertainty associated with limited meltwater sampling.  5.5 Significance of results This study provides a rare detailed analysis of Himalayan groundwater and baseflow generation processes. As glaciers in this area retreat under continued climate change, groundwater may become an increasingly important part of streamflow generation (Tague and Grant, 2009; Somers et al., 2019 ). Therefore, a better understanding of the factors controlling groundwater discharge is required to inform water management policies and climate change mitigation plans for groundwater resources in highly vulnerable montane aquifers. It is often assumed that high-elevation montane watersheds have limited storage capacity. However, our results demonstrate high proportions of streamflow come from groundwater in the upstream portion of the watershed where the permeability of limestone and hard rock aquifers is enhanced by deep or well-connected bedrock fractures. Whereas previous studies use rock type as a proxy for Ksat , we provide a set of field observations which can be used in future hydrogeological modelling to understand climate change impacts. Our results demonstrate that winter low-flow in the headwaters is composed mostly of groundwater which flows predominantly through fractures in hard rock aquifers and solution cavities in limestone lithology. Because of these properties, baseflow contributions from aquifers with deeper groundwater reserves may be more resilient to hydroclimatic variability and extreme weather patterns. Meanwhile, contribution to baseflow from shallow water reserves as seen in alluvium aquifers may be more vulnerable to hydroclimatic variability forced by climate change. Future work is needed to link surface water processes to baseflow generation in the UIB including detailed monitoring of snow cover and depth, potential evapotranspiration, soil depth, topography, land cover variables, and catchment structure. An integrated understanding of baseflow generation mechanisms is needed to understand the impact of climate change on baseflow and to develop adaptation or mitigation strategies for vulnerable mountain water resources like the UIB.   6 Conclusions Groundwater is a substantial contributor to mountain streamflow and is expected to become even more important as mountain glaciers and snowpack rapidly recede. Our study investigates the spatial variability in hydraulic conductivity and baseflow dynamics in the Liddar watershed of the Upper Indus Basin (UIB), which encompasses a heterogeneous landscape and geology. Vertical Electrical Sounding (VES) measurements were combined with slug tests to characterize hydraulic conductivity (Ksat)  in limestone, hard rock and alluvial lithologies. Stable water isotopic sampling was conducted to characterize the young water fraction (Fyw ) and a Bayesian mixing model was used to determine the proportions of streamflow coming from different water sources during the low-flow season. We find that both Ksat  and topography (and resulting hydraulic gradient) control the complexity and magnitude of baseflow contribution to streams. However, Ksat  exerts a dominant control on baseflow contribution as observed in the watershed. The steep, upstream area underlain by limestone has a relatively high Ksat , a low Fyw  (38 %) and a high groundwater contribution to streamflow (72 % ± 11) during the low flow period. The midstream area underlain by hard rocks has a relatively low Ksat , a low Fyw  (36 %) and second highest groundwater contribution (56 % ± 19). The flatter, downstream area underlain by alluvium has a variable Ksat , a higher Fyw  (55 %) and the lowest groundwater contribution to streamflow (43 % ± 18). Both the consolidated and unconsolidated mountain aquifers investigated in this study have substantial permeability, and contribute large proportions of streamflow via groundwater discharge. Our results contribute to improved conceptual understanding and enable future numerical modelling of mountain groundwater flow systems and projection of climate change impacts on the critically important water resources of the Himalayas.
1 Introduction Methane (CH4 ) is the second largest contributor to the global warming after carbon dioxide (CO2 ) (Günther et al., 2020 ). In the last three decades, CH4  concentration in shallow aquifers has considerably increased, mostly resulting from upward migration of thermogenic gases from deeper aquifers (Wilson et al., 2021 ). These gases escape either through anthropogenically created conduits (e.g., improperly sealed active and leaking energy wells) or natural deformation features (e.g., faults and fractures) (Darrah et al., 2014 ). Excessive CH4  concentrations, although non-toxic at low levels, can worsen global warming, degrade water quality, and mobilize heavy metals such as benzene and xylene, by reducing metal oxides present in the aquifer (Vidic et al., 2013 ). Once CH4  reaches an unconfined aquifer, it either retains as free-phase mobile gas (i.e., mobile CH4 ) (Van De Ven and Mumford, 2020 ), leaks to the atmosphere (i.e., leaked CH4 ) (Cahill et al., 2017 ), dissolves into water (i.e., solubility trapping) (Pray et al., 1952 ), traps by groundwater in the form of ganglia or blobs (i.e., residual trapping) (Juanes et al., 2006 ), or accumulates below capillary barriers as a mobile phase (i.e., capillary pinning) (Saadatpoor et al., 2010; Ershadnia et al., 2021a ).
