Finally, establish a connection between the velocity field and coefficient tensor of hydrodynamic dispersion (Zheng et al., 2023b ):(17) ∂ ∂ t   ε p  c     + u g  + u e      · ∇ c = ∇ · D D  + D E     ∇ c         where D D     is the dispersion tensor, m2 /s; D E     is the effective diffusion, m2 /s; t  is time. The second part of the substitute equation is applicable to the coupling of ionic transport and the thermodynamic reaction adsorption equilibrium model. The former was solved based on COMSOL Multiphysics, while the latter was solved by the PHREEQC code. Interfaces between the two software have been developed using MATLAB. The coupling process mainly involves three steps (Guo et al., 2018 ): first, a geometric model based on the initial concentration of ions in the solution has been established, with boundary conditions setting, and mesh partitioning performing. Then, the concentrations of ions at each mesh node were calculated based on the time step, and the corresponding thermodynamic equilibrium model at each node has been solved. Finally, the obtained data were used as initial values to calculate the ion concentrations for the next time step until the calculation was completed.   2.3 Numerical model The numerical model was developed using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6. The model consists of 14,278 elements (Fig. S1 ), and the total simulation duration was 7 days. The initial conditions were set according to Section 2.1 . Inlet and outlet boundaries were set as flow boundaries, the outer wall and upper cover of the sandbox were set as waterproof boundaries. Electrode surfaces were set as conductive boundaries and insulated from water, the remaining parts were considered as insulated boundaries. On the boundaries of waterproofing and insulation the normal velocity component vanished. Compared to traditional hydrogeological conceptual models, the flow boundary of the model in this study can be precisely controlled, which is crucial for improving the accuracy of the model. At the same time, electrodes can influence the electrical potential within the model without directly interacting with the water flow, allowing for the study of electroosmotic and hydraulic migration phenomena separately by controlling variables. Other waterproof insulation boundaries are simplified to reduce computational complexity. The numerical model was based on the assumption of local chemical equilibrium (Rezaee et al., 2019 ), meaning that the rates of physical and chemical interactions between components in the system were much faster than the diffusion migration rate. Under this condition, kinetic processes occurred after each time step integration, which were not part of the finite element discretization. Therefore, thermodynamic interactions for each time step were considered to occur instantaneously compared to solute migration. A non-iterative sequential split operator approach was used to construct the numerical model. The accuracy of the model was quantified by four mathematical and statistical indicators: mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), deviation percentage (PBIAS), and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE).MAE = ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - S i       n      RMSE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - S i      2        PBIAS = ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - S i     × 100   ∑ i = 1  n  M i         NSE = ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - M i   ¯       2  - ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - S i      2   ∑ i = 1  n  M i  - M i   ¯       2        where Mi   is the ith measured value; Si   is the ith simulate value; M i   ¯      is the mean measured value; and n is the total number of data. Good fits are given by PBIAS      < 10, MAE and RMSE far smaller than the measured average values, and NSE close to 1.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Calibration and validation of parameters One of the primary factors influencing the evolution of uranium plume is the adsorption properties of the medium. In the model, calculations for this part were implemented through PHERRQC. The simulated results of surface complexation of the medium are presented in the form of adsorption percentages compared to experimental data (Fig. 2  ). The results indicate that the adsorption of U(VI) by the medium reached its peak at pH 4–5, with a maximum adsorption rate of approximately 94 %. At pH≤4, U(VI) oxide was the main form present, and the adsorption capacity of kaolinite was stronger than that of quartz. (KsOH)2 UO2 +  dominated in the surface complexes and reaching a maximum at pH ≈ 3.5, approximately 54.46 %. After pH>4, uranyl carbonate became the primary form of the surface complexation, and the adsorption on quartz surfaces gradually increased, jointly controlling the adsorption of U(VI). The maximum proportions of (KsOH)2 UO2 CO3 -  and (QOH)2 UO2 CO3  reached 34.71 % and 30.85 %, respectively. The dominant changes in mineral adsorption are consistent with previous studies (Spear et al., 1999; Morrison et al., 2001; Dong et al., 2012 ) but exhibit differences in numerical values due to the varying proportions of quartz and kaolinite in the medium (Da et al., 2022 ). Another factor influencing the evolution of plume is the medium permeability. The optimal values for the hydraulic conductivity and electroosmotic coefficient were determined by comparing the simulated and measured values of electrical and hydraulic gradients after 1 h of system operation (Fig. 3  ). The optimal diffusion coefficient was determined to be 0.72 m2 /d through the tracer experiments conducted on the control group. Biological and chemical clogging occurring during the remediation process led to changes of the medium permeability (Gao et al., 2023 ). The hydraulic conductivity in both the Control group and the EKR group showed little variation, and there was even a slight increase in the Section 1  of Control group (Fig. S2 ), which possibly due to the flushing effect of the water flow (Zheng et al., 2024 ). Chemical clogging mainly occurred in Section 2 and 3  of the EPR group, attributed to the reduction precipitation of U(VI) (Wang and Wu, 2019; Zheng et al., 2024 ). The hydraulic conductivity change in Section 2  was more severe, indicating that biological clogging occurred simultaneously. Due to the fixation of microorganisms in this part, microbial proliferation did not spread downstream. Compared to the beginning of the experiment, the decrease of hydraulic conductivity in EPR after 7 days was approximately 32 % to 42 %. The optimal electroosmotic conductivity showed better fitting results around 3.5 × 10-4  S/m. Based on these results, the optimal tortuosity factor fitted was approximately 0.31. Other parameters of the model are listed in Table S1 - S3 .  3.2 Evolution of uranium plume in EKR group Fig. 4   shows the pH variation along the x -axis under the influence of electrolysis. After the simulation begins, acidifier in cathode chamber and protons produced by anodic electrolysis permeated from the front end towards the middle of the sandbox. The simulation results show a good fit between experimental and calculated pH values (Fig. 4 a). Over time, the pH inside the sandbox displayed a decreasing trend, with the greatest fluctuation observed near the electrodes (15 to 17 cm on the x -axis). As time progresses, the magnitude of this fluctuation gradually diminished around 35 to 40 cm of the sandbox due to the delayed transmission, and ultimately stabilized around a pH value of 4.5 (Fig. 4 b). The model does not consider the dissolution of kaolinite caused by the system acidity. Previous studies have shown that at lower pH levels (1.5–3), the daily dissolution rate of kaolinite is about 1 %, while at higher pH levels (5.0), this effect can be almost negligible (Rezaee et al., 2019 ). Fig. 5   shows the evolution of uranium plume in the EKR over different time periods. The distribution of plume fitted well with the measured data. On the second day after the simulation begins, there was a sharp change in the uranium concentration gradient along the x -axis (Fig. 5 a), which is related to the permeability of the medium (Zheng et al., 2023b; Zheng et al., 2024 ). The slow migration speed and medium adsorption hinder the lateral development of the concentration gradient. However, as time progresses, most of the uranium gradually accumulated towards the cathode chamber, and the concentration gradient became more gradual as the concentration decreases (Fig. 5 b, c). After 7 days (Fig. 5 d), almost all of the U (VI) in the groundwater has been removed at the positions of 29 to 50 cm within the sandbox. The highest concentration in Section 2  was near the cathode, approximately 0.46 times (1.12 mg/L) the initial concentration.  3.3 Evolution of uranium plume in EPR group Unlike the static hydraulic in EKR, wastewater was inputted through the inlet in EPR to form a continuous groundwater flow field. The system pH was primarily controlled by the continuous input of external sources (including the addition of cathodic acidifier). The pH variations caused by electrolysis and chemical reactions have limited effects on the system, resulting in smoother changes (Fig. 6  ). During the first two days, the pH was around 5, closer to the quality of the wastewater. Additionally, due to the limited diffusion of the acidifier over a short period, there was a slight upward trend in pH along the x -axis. As time progressed, because the acidifying agent was added to the cathode chamber daily, the pH gradually decreased, and the distribution along the x -axis became more stable. After 7 days, the pH was approximately around 4.0, and after 30 days, the simulation results indicated stability around 3.5. Therefore, under the influence of external inputs, the pH variations resulting from internal reactions have minimal impact, and the pH of the system is primarily governed by the external environment. The evolution of plume shows that the installation of PRB has a significant effect on the removal of uranium from groundwater and exhibits a noticeable retardation effect on the uranium migration (Fig. 7   a, c-f). Additionally, due to the electric field, uranium shows significant enrichment near the cathode, which delayed the spread of the uranium plume. For the control group, the contamination plume front reaches the outlet (60, 10) at 7 days with a concentration of approximately 2.310 mg/L (Fig. S3 ). After 8 d, the uranium concentration at the outlet of the sandbox reached the same level as at the inlet, indicating that other environmental factors were unable to reduce uranium, and that all uranium reduction came from microorganisms. However, for the EPR group, the contamination plume broke through the entire sandbox in 30 days, with an outlet concentration of approximately 0.037 mg/L. After the contamination plume broke through the PRB, there was a noticeable increase in uranium concentration at the outlet in short term. This was due to the continuous accumulation of sulfate reduction products, which led to a decrease in microbial activity (Spear et al., 1999; Spear et al., 2000; Zheng et al., 2024 ). On a longer time scale (Fig. 7  b), the uranium concentration at the outlet increase slowly, this is because the decline in reducing capacity reduced the rate of sulfate reduction, and the inhibition of microbial activity by reduction products also weakened. At 600 days, the concentration at the outlet was approximately 1.342 mg/L. The above simulation results fitted well with the measured values and demonstrated high reliability in mathematical statistics (Figs. 5 and 7 ): the MAE value of EKR and EPR was 0.054 and 0.075, respectively; while the RMSE value was 0.083 and 0.096, respectively, which was in line with reasonable range. The NSE of EKR (0.81) was higher than at the EPR (0.72), while both were at a better reliability. Higher PBIAS values indicate that the measured values were generally slightly higher than the predicted values, but still within reasonable range (8.35 of EPR and 9.58 for EPR). This may be influenced by environmental factors, which results in the theoretical performance of the system being lower than actual. In addition, the evolution of sulfate contaminated plumes has also been simulated. Due to the larger kinetic constant of the sulfate reaction, the reduction is more thorough, and the reduction rate exceeds 99 % after 7 days, which fits well with the measured values (Fig. S4 ).  3.4 Optimization and evaluation of the composite remediation system To ensure the efficiency of uranium removal and assess the expected lifespan of the materials, the limiting factors affecting the system were further evaluated. In the composite remediation system, uranium migration is controlled by both the flow field and the electric field. First, the dominance of fields in the system was analyzed (Fig. S5 ). The dominance of the fields can be analyzed by separately calculating the driving forces of the flow field and electroosmosis. Since the dimensions of the two fields have been unified, the migration speed of U(VI) under the influence of a single field can be quantitatively calculated. The results show that within the PRB, the velocity field generated by water flow was approximately 6.03 × 10-6  m/s; while the velocity field generated by electroosmosis was approximately 1.71 × 10-6  m/s. Compared to electroosmosis, water flow remains the primary driving force for uranium migration. Under the water flow flushing, uranium was difficult to be stably and long-term adsorbed onto the electrode surface. This also determines the difference in removal mechanisms between EKR and EPR. EKR primarily relies on electrophoresis to concentrate uranium at the cathode for removal. In EPR, due to the influence of water flow, electroosmosis migration is reduced. At this time, the role of the electric field is mainly to slow down the migration speed of uranium, allowing them to stay longer in the PRB for more thorough reduction. Therefore, in real aquifers with flowing water, EKR is more suitable as an auxiliary means to reduce the migration rate of pollutants and increase the contact time between pollutants and PRB materials. The model was optimized according to the World Health Organization's drinking water uranium content standard (0.03 mg/L). Increasing the voltage is a possible solution, but it has lower efficiency and increases safety risks. The most prudent approach is to increase the width of the PRB (Fig. 8  ). As seen, with EKR assistance, when the width of the PRB increased to 60 cm (Fig. 8 a), the system can ensure no breakthrough within 360 days. Under the same conditions without EKR, the width of the PRB needed to increase to 80 cm (Fig. 8 b). It's worth noting that this optimization should be carried out without affecting the electrode positions. Increasing the distance between electrodes would increase resistance, leading to a decrease in current and current density, which could diminish or even nullify the electroosmotic driving force.   4 Conclusions By establishing a multi-physics coupled numerical model suitable for PRB and EKR, the evolution of uranium plume in a composite groundwater remediation system was demonstrated in detail. The model can not only simulate remediation results, evaluate system performance, and predict system lifespan, but also guide the establishment of groundwater uranium pollution remediation systems in real sites. The model has certain limitations in considering environmental factors. In real site, there may be more environmental change such as temperature and moisture content, which are important aspects to consider in subsequent coupled model research. Based on the experimental and simulation results, the following conclusions can be drawn:(1) The pH changes caused by electrode hydrolysis in a coupled field can significantly affect the adsorption of uranium by the medium, with maximum adsorption occurring at pH 4–5. The reduction process of uranium can lead to biological and chemical clogging, reducing the permeability of the medium.  (2) In the coupled field, the driving force of water flow on solutes is approximately 3.5 times that of the electric field. However, the application of an electric field can significantly slow the evolution of the uranium plume, which results in a higher remediation efficiency for the system. Therefore, in the composite remediation system, electrokinetic remediation is only suitable as an auxiliary remediation method.  (3) The residence time of uranium in the system is the fundamental factor limiting remediation efficiency. Setting the electric field opposite to the flow field effectively delays uranium migration. Increasing the width of the PRB is an effective way to improve remediation efficiency. With EKR assistance, setting the PRB thickness to 60 cm ensures the effective operation of the system for 360 days. With minor modifications in parameters, the model could be adapted to simulate similar systems, with other contaminants. The numerical model and the draft of the manuscript was completed by Fuxin Zheng; The experiment operation and manuscript structure were designed by Yuanzheng Zhai; The measurement and calibration of the data were performed by Weifeng Yue.
1 Introduction In catchments where land cover is dominated by agricultural areas, nitrate (NO3 − ) concentrations in groundwater and surface water can be very high, exceeding both drinking water limits and thresholds for good status of surface water ecosystems (Bechmann et al., 2014; Iital et al., 2014; Kalvāns et al., 2021; Maastik et al., 1993; Matiatos et al., 2021; Stalnacke et al., 2009; Van Camp et al., 2021; Wassenaar et al., 2006 ). Besides the well documented problems of water quality deterioration and eutrophication, questions remain about the origin of nutrients and their ability to leach from different subsurface reservoirs. Studies have proved that soil and the unsaturated zone could act as significant long-term reservoirs for NO3 − , supplying it to the water table for decades after agricultural activities have ceased (Ascott et al., 2017; Refsgaard et al., 1999; Sebilo et al., 2013; Sugita and Nakane, 2007; Wang et al., 2013 ). The problem is especially pronounced in catchments where natural remediation (e.g., denitrification) in the subsurface is limited. Denitrification could be hampered by the rapid transport of NO3 −  to the water table or due to the lack of electron donors such as reactive organic matter, pyrite and other Fe-bearing minerals in the aquifers that could drive the different denitrification processes (Green et al., 2008; Tesoriero et al., 2007; Turkeltaub et al., 2016 ). Leaching of nitrate to the water table is sensitive to the amount and timing of groundwater recharge (Böhlke, 2002; Suchy et al., 2018; Van Camp et al., 2021; Visser et al., 2021 ). While the general timing of fertilizer application in temperate climates is constrained to definite periods in a year depending on the growth-cycle of the crops (spring and early autumn), the timing and magnitude of groundwater recharge is more variable. In cold temperate and boreal climates the groundwater recharge has been shown to be seasonally biased towards spring snowmelt (Ala-aho et al., 2015; Clark, 2015; Jasechko et al., 2017, 2014; Nygren et al., 2020; Raidla et al., 2016; Schilling et al., 2021 ). Recharge is often inhibited during summer due to actual evapotranspiration exceeding the amount of precipitation, and during winter due to snow cover and frozen ground (DeWalle and Rango, 2008; Hyman-Rabeler and Loheide, 2023; Lundberg et al., 2016 ). Thus, melting of seasonal snowpack at the start of the spring season often makes up a signification portion of the annual groundwater recharge and controls the seasonal fluctuations of river discharge and groundwater levels (Earman et al., 2006; Earman and Dettinger, 2011; French and Binley, 2004; Jasechko et al., 2017; Nygren et al., 2020; Rodhe, 1998 ). The melting of the snowpack creates special conditions for infiltration and subsequent groundwater recharge that can also influence the fate of pollutants (Lundberg et al., 2016 ). For example, it has been shown that the infiltration of snowmelt can create a N flux from the soil to the shallow saturated zone due to enhanced mineralization of N from soil organic matter and fertilizer (Pellerin et al., 2012 ). Furthermore, the rise of the water table increases the hydraulic conductivity near the ground surface through a process termed “transmissivity feedback” which may lead to significant leaching of solutes stored in the unsaturated zone (Bishop, 1991; Laudon et al., 2004; Rodhe, 1998 ). Karst aquifers are especially vulnerable to agricultural pollution due to short residence times and a quick transfer of water from the recharge to the discharge areas (European Commission, 2003; Kalvāns et al., 2021; Musgrove et al., 2016; Padilla et al., 1994; Panno and Kelly, 2004 ). In addition, surface water bodies in karst areas usually have a high baseflow component, which leads to the deterioration of water quality of springs and related surface water bodies, when the baseflow contains high concentrations of nutrients and other pollutants (Briand et al., 2013; El Gaouzi et al., 2013; Panno et al., 2001; Stueber and Criss, 2005; Van Camp et al., 2021 ). Thus, it is critical to understand the functioning of groundwater systems that provide baseflow and nutrient loads to groundwater dependent ecosystems (GDEs) for designing measures to improve the status of water bodies as required by the Water Framework Directive by the European Commission (Kløve et al., 2011 ). The problem of high NO3 −  concentrations in rivers with a high baseflow component (≥50 %; Protasjeva and Eipre, 1972 ) is very acute in northern Estonia, where several surface and groundwater bodies are in bad status partly due to elevated concentrations of N-total (TN), NO3 −  and pesticides (Marandi et al., 2020 ). Here, catchments with high proportion of agricultural land (frequently >50%) overly carbonate rock aquifers with high groundwater vulnerability. For this reason, the Nitrate Vulnerable Zone (NVZ) has been established in north-eastern and central Estonia under the requirements of the Nitrates Directive (European Commission, 1991 ). Central to the NVZ is the Pandivere Upland, which is an important regional water divide and a groundwater recharge area in northern Estonia (Perens and Vallner, 1997 ). Despite the reduction from point-source pollution (wastewater) in Estonian rivers during the last 30 years, the positive changes in water quality are hindered by an increase in diffuse NO3 −  loading from agricultural lands (Nõges et al., 2022 ). Similarly to rivers, there has been an increase in NO3 −  concentrations in the shallow aquifers of the NVZ during the last 10–15 years (Leisk, 2022 ; Marja et al., 2017 ), although a number of measures have been implemented to improve the water quality in the region (Water Act, 2020 ). Rivers in the northern part of the NVZ transport the nutrients to the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea, where it is estimated that up to 21 % of TN and 32 % of P-total (TP) loads originate from diffuse losses from agricultural land (Helcom, 2022 ). Thus, it seems that the current measures are insufficient for improving the water quality in the NVZ and for reaching the goal of good status for surface and groundwater bodies in the area. Due to high baseflow component of the rivers in the region, any improvements to the existing measures rest on our ability to understand the nutrient transport and storage in local groundwater systems. Previous studies have established a clear link between fertilizer use and groundwater NO3 −  concentrations in the Pandivere Upland. Higher concentrations of NO3 −  correspond to larger nitrogen losses from agricultural land (Maastik et al., 1993; Metsur & Tamm, 1994 ). The same studies also show that the maximum NO3 −  concentrations coincide with spring floods pointing to importance of nitrate leaching during major groundwater recharge events. A strong relationship between river and groundwater NO3 −  concentrations in Pandivere Upland has also been shown with higher NO3 −  concentrations in rivers corresponding to higher NO3 −  concentrations in aquifers (Iital et al., 2022 ). However, the exact mechanisms behind the formation of groundwater quality and NO3 −  concentrations have not been studied in detail. In this contribution, we studied three springs with high NO3 −  concentrations related to a fractured carbonate aquifer in the Sõmeru River catchment. The catchment is located on the northern slope of the Pandivere Upland in north-eastern Estonia. Previous studies have shown that the river is in bad status partly due to high TN concentrations. A statistically strong and significant relationship (r2  = 0.75, p>0.001) exists between the TN concentrations in springs and the TN concentrations in the river (Iital et al., 2022 ). In this contribution, spring discharge, nutrient concentrations (N- and P-species), general water chemistry and stable isotopic composition (δ18 O, δ2 H) were monitored during a 2-year period. We compared spring data with modelled daily groundwater recharge and used multivariate statistical analysis to integrate different observations into generalized components that characterize the functioning of the springs. By the application of these different methods, we aim to 1) characterize the seasonal pattern of groundwater recharge; 2) describe the interrelationship between groundwater recharge and spring discharge, water quality and NO3 −  concentrations and 3) understand the factors influencing the spring water quality and seasonal changes in spring functioning.  2 Study area 2.1 General description Pandivere Upland (80–166 m. a.s.l; Fig. 1  ) is a carbonate rock plateau located in north-eastern Estonia. It is one of the largest karst areas in the region with a surface area of ∼ 2500 km2  (Kink, 1997a; Koit, 2018 ). The upland is an important groundwater recharge area. An area of approximately 1400 km2  at the top of the upland lacks a permanent river network and is rich in karst forms such as ponors, dolines, vertical joints, and karst lakes (Heinsalu, 1963; Maves, 2002 ). Besides surficial karst forms, buried karst cavities can also be found which usually lie 5–10 m from the surface but can be found at depths down to 75 m in larger tectonic fault zones (Maves, 2002 ). Groundwater recharge in the area can reach up to 40 % of the annual precipitation amount (Vallner and Porman, 2016 ). More than 200 springs are located at the foot of the upland (at absolute heights of 68–110 m. a.s.l; Fig. 1 ; Maastik et al., 1993 ) which serve as headwaters for rivers in the region. These rivers are characterized by high baseflow component up to 80 % (Iital et al., 2022; Maastik et al., 1993; Protasjeva and Eipre, 1972 ). The appearance of springs on the slopes of the upland is related to several geological features such as fault zones, buried bedrock valleys and outcrops of argillaceous limestone (Maves, 2002 ). The Sõmeru River catchment is located on the northern slope of the Pandivere Upland (Fig. 1 ). The elevation of the catchment ranges from 130 m a.s.l in its southern margin down to 59 m a.s.l at the river mouth (Fig. 1 ). Sõmeru River is a tributary of Selja River which flows into the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea (Fig. 1 ). The length of the Sõmeru River is 16.3 km and its catchment area is 86 km2  (Estonian Environment Agency, 2022 ). Based on measurements made in 2021–2023, the discharge of the river varies from 0.14 to 3 m3 /s. The baseflow component of the Sõmeru River has not been estimated, but for Selja River previous estimates of baseflow range from 47 % (Protasjeva and Eipre, 1972 ) to 70 % (Iital et al., 2022 ). Estonia belongs to the Dfb (warm-summer humid cold climate) climate zone according to Köpper-Geiger classification (Beck et al., 2018; Kottek et al., 2006 ). The average long-term (1991–2020) mean temperature and annual precipitation in and around the Pandivere Upland are 5.5 °C and 680 mm, respectively (Estonian Environment Agency, 2024 ). The monthly mean temperature ranges from −5.5 °C in February to +17.2 °C in July. Precipitation is distributed quite evenly throughout the year with monthly mean precipitation ranging from 34 mm in April to 90 mm in August. The average snow cover duration in the period of 1950–2016 was 110–120 days with a median snow depth of 28–34 cm (Viru and Jaagus, 2020 ). The snow cover usually forms in December and reaches its maximum depth by late February/early March after which it decreases rapidly until the final snowmelt by the beginning of April.  2.2 Geology and hydrogeology The bedrock of the catchment consists of fractured and karstic Upper Ordovician carbonate rocks (Fig. 2  ; Suuroja et al., 2015, 2006 ). These rocks are covered by a thin sedimentary cover deposited during the Quaternary (predominantly < 5 m; Heinsalu, 1963; Suuroja et al., 2015, 2006 ). Karst fractures are more common in the upper 30 m of bedrock, but near tectonic faults, these can reach down to 75 m below the ground surface (Maves, 2002 ). Karst phenomena on the Pandivere Upland are related to both recent and palaeo-karst features. The most frequently observed karstic land forms are springs, ponors and dolines (Heinsalu, 1963; Maves, 2002 ). Compared to other parts of the Pandivere Upland, the Sõmeru River catchment is rather scarcely populated with surficial karst features. The most prominent of these are Mõdriku Hiieallika, Vetiku and Mõdriku Vanamõisa spring groups. Other karst features in the catchment are dolines and ponors that fill with water during spring snowmelt and slowly dry up over summer (Maves, 2002 ). The sedimentary cover in the catchment consists mainly of Pleistocene sandy loam till that forms undulating till planes. Thicker deposits of Quaternary sediments can be found in buried valleys, eskers and kame fields. These landforms mainly contain sand and gravel of glaciofluvial origin with thicknesses reaching up to 25 m in the study area (Suuroja et al., 2015 ). Sõmeru catchment is bound by two large radial esker ridges (Fig. 3  ). Due to thin sedimentary cover, the vulnerability of groundwater in the bedrock aquifers is high, with about 30% of the catchment classified as unprotected groundwater area (Iital et al., 2022 ). Local studies have shown that in soil and sediment profiles, large carbonate rock cobbles are embedded inside the sandy loam till matrix and that with depth, their share increases to >50% (Krapiva, 1977 ; Perens et al., 1978 ; Estonian Land Board, 2022b ). Gradually, this mixed material turns into fractured limestone. This heavily weathered limestone mixed with Quaternary sediments is considered as the epikarst zone in this study (Bakalowicz, 2004; Williams, 1983 ). The carbonate sequence below the epikarst is characterized by alternating layers of micro- to small crystalline bioclastic/aphanitic limestone and dolomitized limestone (Pirgu, Nabala and Rakvere Formations) interlaid with clayey limestone and marl (by Vormsi, Oandu, Keila and Haljala Formations; Estonian Land Board, 2020; Suuroja et al., 2015, 2006 ). Aquifers in these carbonate rocks form the Silurian-Ordovician aquifer system, which can be separated into three main aquifers (Porkuni-Pirgu, Nabala-Rakvere, Keila-Kukruse) and two main semi-confining layers (Vormsi and Oandu-Keila; Fig. 2 ; Jõgar, 1977, 1983; Perens et al., 1978 ) in the study area. Hydraulic conductivity of the sandy-loam till overlying the carbonate bedrock is small varying from 0.001 to 1 m/d (Krapiva, 1977; Perens and Vallner, 1997 ). Hydraulic conductivity of the aquifers in carbonate bedrock is up to four magnitudes higher, but due to the karstification, their hydraulic conductivity decreases with depth (Perens and Vallner, 1997 ). This is a commonly observed global phenomenon in low-dip carbonate aquifers (Worthington, 2001 ). Generally, hydraulic conductivity in the upper 20 m of the carbonate sequence varies from 10 to 50 m/d and decreases to values from 5 to 8 m/d at depths of 20–50 m and from 1 to 2 m/d at depths of 50–100 m (Perens and Vallner, 1997 ). The bedrock aquifers are characterized by sporadic lateral zones (1–2 m thick) of high hydraulic conductivity. These zones are separated from each other by 5–10-m-thick layers with much lower hydraulic conductivity (10-5  to 10-2  m/d; Perens and Vallner, 1997; Jõgar, 1983 ). The water conducting zones make up only 3–15 % of the total thickness of a given aquifer and consist mainly of 1–30 mm wide wavy fractures, often located at the bedding planes in the carbonate rock (Perens et al., 1978 ). The karst aquifers discharge through a number of spring groups that appear on the slopes of the Pandivere Upland in specific elevations (Heinsalu, 1963; Maves, 2002 ). The studied springs (Mõdriku, Vetiku and Rägavere) in the Sõmeru catchment are located at the heights of 68–80 m a.s.l. on the northern slope of the upland (Fig. 2 ; Estonian Environment Agency, 2022 ; Jõgar, 1983; Maves, 2002 ). They coincide with the outcrop area of the Nabala-Rakvere aquifer (Fig. 3 ; Heinsalu, 1963 ). Mõdriku and Vetiku spring groups consisting mainly of confined springs, are located at higher elevation (78–80 m a.s.l.) in surface depressions which are related to vertical joints and fractures. Spring lakes have formed inside the depressions at both Mõdriku and Vetiku. Rägavere spring is part of a larger group of free-draining springs (so-called Mõdriku Vanaküla spring group) which is located downstream at a lower elevation (68 m a.s.l). Their appearance coincides with structural boundary between the outcrop of the Nabala-Rakvere aquifer, the underlying Oandu-Keila semi-confining layer and a buried bedrock valley. The maximum discharge of these spring groups can reach >1 m3 /s (Estonian Environment Agency, 2022 ; Maves, 2002 ). The Mõdriku Hiieallika spring group forms the headwaters of the Sõmeru River while the Mõdriku Vanaküla spring group is located about 3 km downstream on the river bank. The Vetiku spring group is located 2 km west of the Mõdriku Vanaküla spring group and is connected to the Sõmeru River via a small brook (Fig. 2 ). The previously estimated catchment areas for Mõdriku Vanaküla and Vetiku spring groups are ∼ 35 km2  and ∼ 60 km2 , respectively (Jõgar, 1983 ).  2.3 Land and soil cover According to the CORINE Land Cover database (Estonian Environment Agency, 2023a ), the agricultural land covers about 65 % of the catchment (Fig. 3 a). The main cultivated row crops include winter wheat, spring barley, rap, corn, winter barley and rye (ARIB, 2020 ). In grasslands, leguminous grasses and lucerne are grown together with other perennial grasses in different proportions. The importance of other land cover types is smaller with 20 % of the catchment covered by forests (mixed, broad-leaved and coniferous), 11 % by natural grassland and woodland-shrubs and 4 % by urban areas (Estonian Environment Agency, 2023a ). The majority of the soils (74 %) in the catchment have an intermediate texture (sandy loam, loam; Fig. 2 b, Kmoch et al., 2021 ). Sandy soils (sand, loamy sand) and clay soils (clay loam, clay) make up 12 % and 4 % of the soil cover, respectively. Soils are predominately moderately developed cambisols and little developed regosols (Kmoch et al., 2021 ).  2.4 Agriculture Sõmeru catchment belongs to the Estonian Nitrate Vulnerable Zone (NVZ, Fig. 1 ), but there is no data available on the exact fertilizer use on the catchment scale. However, by using results from previous studies, publicly available data and some general assumptions, it can be shown that the manure and mineral fertilizers are the most important inputs of N in the catchment (for more details see ESM-1, Tables S1 and S2 ). The total amount of N from manure and mineral fertilizer makes up 95.6 % (109 kgN/ha and 63 kgN/ha, respectively) of estimated N inputs, while the share of untreated wastewater is only 0.1 % (0.23 kgN/ha), which is even less than estimated wet deposition of N (4.2 %; 7.5 kgN/ha). It has been shown that the water quality changes  in the rivers and groundwater of Pandivere Upland generally follow the changes in fertilizer use which have themselves been related to major socio-economic changes in Estonia (Leisk, 2022 ; Nõges et al., 2022 ). Historically, the amount of nitrogen applied by fertilizers in Estonia fell at the start of the 1990s after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Estonian independence. This is illustrated by historical data on the use of mineral fertilizers that decreased from the maximum value of 110,000 tN in 1987 to 16,500 tN by 1996 (Fig. 4  b). An increase in fertilizer application occurred in 2006–2007 when Estonia had joined the European Union. The amount of applied mineral fertilizer increased to 35,000 t of N by 2008 followed by a decrease probably due to the 2007–2008 financial crisis (Fig. 4 b). In the last 10 years the amounts of nitrogen applied by mineral fertilizer have been relatively stable (Fig. 4 b; Statistics Estonia, 2020 ). The amount of mineral fertilizer applied per hectare (kgN/ha) has followed a similar pattern (Fig. 4 b). The corresponding changes in water quality are exemplified by the time-series of NO3 −  concentrations in the Rägavere spring from 1981 to 2021 located in the Sõmeru catchment (Fig. 4 a). The period from early 1980s to early 1990s is characterized by high yearly average NO3 −  concentrations up to 60 mg/L. The concentrations decrease markedly from early 1990s to 2007 with yearly average concentrations of ∼20 mg/L. This coincides with the Estonian independence and the collapse of the agricultural system of the Soviet Union. The third and final period is characterized by an increase in NO3 −  concentrations after 2007 which lasts until the present and coincides with the period during which Estonia has been a member of the European Union. During the final period the yearly average concentrations have risen to ∼40 mg/L but maximum values have frequently exceeded the drinking water limit of 50 mg/L.   3 Materials and methods The data used in this study has been collected mainly during the PUTJD920 project carried out by the Department of Geology at Tallinn University of Technology and the Laboratory for Applied Geology and Hydrogeology at the Ghent University. During the study period, the same sampling sites were also monitored in the framework of the LIFE IP CleanEst project by the Geological Survey of Estonia, Water and Environmental Engineering Research Group at the Tallinn University of Technology and the Estonian Environmental Research Centre. The hydrochemical and isotopic data collected during this project are presented in a report by Iital et al. (2022)  and are also used in this study. In total, 210 samples were taken from the springs and wells in the period from 2020 to 2022 (ESM-3, Table S5 ), of which 131 were collected during the PUTJD920 project and 79 are from the report by Iital et al., (2022) . Below we’ll discuss the methodology used in the PUTJD920 project. For details about the LIFE IP CleanEst project the reader is referred to the abovementioned report. 3.1 Monitoring network and field sampling The monitoring of springs in the Sõmeru catchment lasted for 26 months (August 2020 − October 2022). The water year used in the data analysis is from October to September. Automatic data loggers for measuring spring stage, electrical conductivity and temperature (hourly time-step) were installed in 3 studied spring outlets at the end of July 2020. For Mõdriku and Vetiku spring groups the spring group outlet discharging from the spring lake was monitored. A stage-discharge curve was constructed for all three springs to convert automatic water level measurements to spring discharge. Water samples for general hydrochemistry and isotopic composition were taken periodically from the springs. From Mõdriku and Rägavere springs, which were part of the LIFE IP CleanEst project monitoring network, a total of 55 samples were taken for NO3 −  and TN, 47 samples for Cl−  and SO4 2−  and 30 samples for other hydrochemical parameters (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , HCO3 − , NH4 + , F− , TP, δ18 O, δ2 H) during the monitoring period. The average sampling frequency was twice a month for NO3 − , Cl−  and SO4 2−  and once a month for other hydrochemical parameters. For Vetiku site which was not part of the LIFE project monitoring network, the average sampling frequency was the same from January 2021 to May 2022. Before and after this period, samples from Vetiku spring outlet were taken in quarterly intervals (March, May, August, November). The total number of samples from the Vetiku spring outlet was 37 for NO3 −  and TN and 28 for Cl− , SO4 2−  and other hydrochemical parameters. In addition to the spring group outlets, two individual springs located upstream form the spring lakes of Mõdriku and Vetiku were monitored for hydrochemistry and stable isotopic composition in quarterly intervals during the study period. Also, four wells in the vicinity of the springs in the Nabala-Rakvere bedrock aquifer were sampled 2–7 times during the study period, depending on the well (see Table 1  and ESM-2 for more details). In two wells (Mõdriku-1 and well no. 17498) water level, electrical conductivity (only in well Mõdriku-1) and temperature were monitored with automatic data loggers (hourly time-step) from July 2020 to October 2022 and from February 2021 to October 2022, respectively. The locations of the sampling points are shown on Fig. 2  and their general description is given in the electronic supplementary material  (ESM-2, Table S3 ). Field parameters (pH, EC, temperature and DO) were measured with the WTW MultiLine® Multi 3630 IDS Set F multimeter. All the water samples for hydrochemical and isotopic analysis were filtered with 0.45 μm filters. Alkalinity titration was carried out in the field using the Hach AL-DT Alkalinity Test Kit. During the period from January 2021 to May 2022 NO3 −  concentrations in the spring outlets were determined with LCK 339 test kit (based on ISO 7890–1) using the Hach DR-2800 field spectrophotometer (see ESM-2, Table S5 ).  3.2 Laboratory analysis Hydrochemical and isotopic data discussed in the paper has been measured in different laboratories at the Department of Geology at Tallinn University of Technology, Laboratory for Applied Geology and Hydrogeology at Ghent University, Institute of Ecology at Tallinn University and Centre of Geological Processes Research and Modelling at University of Latvia (see also ESM-2). For samples collected before November 2021, major and minor ion concentrations were measured in the Department of Geology at Tallinn University of Technology with the Thermo Dionex ICS-1100 ion chromatograph (for more details see ESM-2, Table S4 ). Fe2+  and Mn2+  concentrations were determined in the Laboratory for Applied Geology and Hydrogeology at Ghent University using atomic adsorption spectrometry with an analytical precision of ±0.005 mg/L. Isotope ratios of hydrogen and oxygen were measured at the Department of Geology at Tallinn University of Technology using a Picarro L2120-i Isotopic Water Analyzer. Reproducibility of the stable isotope measurements was ±0.1 ‰ for δ18 O and ±1 ‰ for δ2 H. Total nitrogen (TN) and DOC concentrations were determined in the laboratory of the Institute of Ecology at Tallinn University by Analytik Jena multi N/C 3100 TOC/TNb analyzer. The hydrochemical and isotopic composition of samples collected after November 2021 were measured at the Tallinn University and at University of Latvia, respectively. The samples for cations and anions were analyzed in the laboratory of the School of Natural Sciences and Health at Tallinn University by high-pressure liquid chromatography using the SHIMADZU® RID-10 A or CDD-10 A conductivity detectors and Shodex IC YS-50 and Shodex IC SI-50 4 E columns. The isotopic composition was measured at the Environmental Dating Laboratory at the Centre of Geological Processes Research and Modelling, University of Latvia using the Picarro L2130-i Isotopic Water Analyzer. More details about the laboratory methods can be found in ESM-2. Table S5  lists all data used in the study with references to respective laboratories where the results have been measured. The consistency of the database was evaluated using duplicate samples and the combination of different data sources was deemed to be acceptable for the purposes of this study (for more details see ESM-2).  3.3 Time-series analysis Autocorrelation and cross-correlation functions were utilized to measure the response times of spring discharge, electrical conductivity (EC), and NO3 −  concentrations to groundwater recharge. The shape and slope of the autocorrelation function (ACF) correlogram reveal the “memory effect” or system inertia, which can be quantified as the time lag (k) until the coefficient value (rk ) falls below 0.2 (Jeannin and Sauter, 1998; Mangin, 1984 ). In contrast, the cross-correlation function (CCF) is a bivariate method used to explain the linear dependency of two different time series, such as rainfall/recharge and spring discharge/EC. In other words, the cross-correlation analysis views the system as a filter that transforms the input time-series of precipitation or recharge to an output time-series of spring discharge or another parameter (Jeannin and Sauter, 1998 ). Precipitation record is not a suitable input for CCF calculations in cold temperate climates as large amounts of precipitation is stored for several months in snowpacks and released during a short snowmelt period (Koit et al., 2022 ). The accumulation of precipitation as snow in winter and subsequent snowmelt weeks or months later results in low correlation between spring discharge and precipitation. Furthermore, the most intense precipitation events in the study area usually occur in the summer when high evapotranspiration hinders groundwater recharge. We aim to overcome these issues by using the daily modelled groundwater recharge as an input signal for cross-correlation analysis that already considers the effects of snow deposition, snowmelt and evapotranspiration.  3.4 Modelling of daily groundwater recharge To calculate daily groundwater recharge, the potential evapotranspiration (PET) was estimated using the modified Penman-Monteith method (FAO-56) and the FAO calculator (Allen et al., 1998; Raes and Munoz, 2009 ). Daily PET was calculated with data from six meteorological stations (Fig. 1 ), using the daily minimum and maximum air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and sunlight hours obtained from the Estonian Environmental Agency. Groundwater recharge was then modeled using the PRMS-IV modeling system (Markstrom et al., 2015 ). The PRMS is a deterministic, distributed-parameter, physical-process-based model that computes recharge to the groundwater reservoir as a vertical flow from the soil zone. Soil infiltration is partitioned between capillary and preferential-flow reservoirs. The capillary reservoir represents the soil water content between the wilting point and field capacity, while the preferential-flow reservoir represents fast lateral interflow through large openings in the soil profile. The total groundwater recharge in the PRMS model is the sum of excess soil water, gravity drainage, and groundwater flow from cascade upslope reservoirs and seepage from surface-depression storage. The development and calibration of PRMS-IV requires a significant amount of data and parameters. The following were used in this study: Digital Elevation Map (Estonian Land Board, 2022a ), CORINE Land Cover Map (Estonian Environment Agency, 2023a ), Soil Map (Kmoch et al., 2021 ), Geological Base Map (Geological Survey of Estonia, 2022 ) and weather data provided on request by the Estonian Environment Agency. The PRMS-IV model was constructed for the Selja River catchment which is larger than the catchment of the Sõmeru River (Fig. 1 ) as no discharge time-series needed to calibrate the model is available from the latter. To calibrate and validate the model, daily discharge data of the Selja River measured in the Varangu hydrological station during the period from 2011 to 2022 was used. The discharge data was provided by the Estonian Environmental Agency. A detailed description of the model structure, parameters and calibration results can be found in Hunt (2021) . The recharge was modelled for four water years starting from October 2018 and ending in September 2022 to test the model in different hydrological and meteorological conditions. The precipitation and air temperature were interpolated by also considering the slope of the land surface using data from meteorological stations in and around the Pandivere Upland (Fig. 1 ) by multiple linear regression as described in Markstrom et al., (2015) . To provide an independent empirically based estimate as a comparison to the modelled groundwater recharge, annual recharge was also estimated using the chloride mass-balance (CMB) method (Eriksson and Khunakasem, 1969; Scanlon et al., 2002; Wood, 1999 ). CMB can be used to estimate groundwater recharge when the following boundary conditions are met (Wood, 1999 ): (1) chloride in groundwater originates solely from precipitation falling directly on the aquifer; (2) chloride is conservative in the studied system; (3) the chloride mass-flux does not change over time and (4) there is no recycling or concentration of chloride in the aquifer. When these conditions are met, the recharge flux can be calculated from a simple relationship:(1) R = P eff   ∙ Cl  Prec   Cl  GW        where R is recharge (mm), Peff  is effective precipitation (precipitation minus surface runoff, mm) and ClPrec  and ClGW  are Cl−  concentrations in precipitation and groundwater, respectively. Precipitation data is from Väike-Maarja meteorological station 7 km SW from the boundary of the PRMS model area. As there is no permanent surface water network in the central part of the Pandivere Upland (see Section 2.2 ), the precipitation measured in the Väike-Maarja station was taken to be equal to effective precipitation. As such, the recharge estimates based on CMB will be maximum estimates as any fraction of surface runoff would decrease the effective precipitation and together with it the amount of water available for infiltration. Cl−  concentrations in precipitation were estimated using data from 5 stations around the PRMS model area (Fig. 1 ) and their relative share to the model area was calculated using Theissen polygons delineated with the QGIS 3.10 A Coruna software. The details on groundwater data used for recharge estimates together with the assumptions used in selecting the data are discussed in ESM-2.  3.5 Multivariate statistical analysis Factor analysis (FA) was used to assess the multivariate variability of time-series of groundwater recharge, spring discharge, hydrochemistry and climatic parameters (temperature, local precipitation, PET, change in snow water equivalent or Δ SWE) during the period of August 2020-Septmeber 2022 (n = 791). Due to different sampling frequency of the parameters, the gaps in the time-series not measured with daily resolution (e.g., precipitation, snow water equivalent, spring discharge, spring electrical conductivity) were filled using linear interpolation prior to analysis. The resulting factor scores of FA were clustered using the Agglomerative Cluster Analysis (AHC) to delineate the periods in time-series that could be associated with different components in the flow system. The Ward’s method was used for agglomeration and Euclidean distance as the proximity measure in AHC. The data was standardized (n-1) prior to FA analysis. The FA and AHC analysis were run by using the XLSTAT 2023.1.3 software by Addinsoft. Multivariate statistical analysis was only carried out for the hydrodynamic and hydrochemical time-series from the outflow of the Mõdriku spring group. Mõdriku spring group is used as the model system in this study, to reveal the main processes that characterize the functioning of the springs in the catchment. Mõdriku and Vetiku springs are very similar to each other in terms of their geological setting and seasonal discharge dynamics (see also Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ). Both springs showed a clear seasonal trend in discharge, electrical conductivity and NO3 −  concentrations. The main reason for choosing Mõdriku springs over Vetiku was a more complete set of hydrochemical and isotopic data from the former site. Rägavere springs was not used as a model system due to the reason that it represents only one spring inside the larger Mõdriku Vanaküla spring group of >30 springs on the slopes of Sõmeru River (see Section 2.2 ). The total discharge of the spring group is very hard to estimate and it was not measured during this study. Rägavere spring is also located at a lower elevation from the Mõdriku springs and most of its catchment area coincides with that of Mõdriku springs. Thus, it was hypothesized that the main processes affecting Rägavere springs are already manifested in the time-series of the Mõdriku springs.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Groundwater recharge Groundwater recharge simulated with the PRMS-IV modelling system for the period 2018–2022 agrees reasonably well with estimates made using the CMB method and with previous recharge estimates in the study area (Fig. 5  ). The range of PRMS-modelled yearly recharge (105–200 mm) is close to historic estimates for groundwater recharge made using the baseflow estimations during minimum discharge of rivers in the studied section of the Pandivere Upland (90–240 mm; Eipre, 1981; Vallner and Metslang, 1971; Vallner and Porman, 2016 ). The estimated range of groundwater recharge made using PRMS and CMB methods overlap for all water years, but the mean CMB estimates are generally smaller. The difference between modelled recharge and the average CMB estimates is <15% for water years 2018/2019, 2019/2020 and 2021/2022. For 2020/2021, the average CMB estimates are 30% higher than the modelled recharge estimates. There are several reasons that could explain the observed differences between the two methods. Firstly, as the study area is underlain by fractured carbonate rocks with vertical fractures or joints, point recharge may occur besides diffuse recharge. It has been shown previously, that the CMB method will underestimate recharge in this case (Somaratne & Smettem, 2014 ). Secondly, despite the careful procedure of choosing appropriate groundwater samples for CMB calculations (see ESM-2), some samples could contain additional Cl−  from agricultural sources or road salt which would lead to underestimation of groundwater recharge with the CMB method. Daily recharge values estimated with the PRMS-IV modelling system are shown on Fig. 6  . Modelled recharge has a clear seasonal pattern with high groundwater recharge during late autumn and early spring and much smaller recharge during the period from late spring to early autumn. Thus, the recharge does not correlate with precipitation as the months with highest precipitation usually occur in summer and early autumn. This is because usually, PET exceeds cumulative precipitation from April to October. Thus, the main periods for groundwater recharge are late autumn (November-December) when PET is low and early spring (February-April) when water stored in seasonal snowpack is released. On average, the recharge during the snowmelt period from February to April makes up 45–75% of annual modelled recharge during the studied water years. Autumn recharge (from October to December) is smaller, comprising 20–40% of annual recharge. The modelled recharge in the remaining months is <20%, being as low as 5% in 2018/2019. This is in line with previous estimates from snowmelt dominated regions where snowmelt period has been shown to comprise >50% of annual groundwater recharge (Earman et al., 2006; French and Binley, 2004; Jasechko et al., 2017 ). The only exception is the water year 2019/2020, when no permanent snow-cover developed. During that year, 75% of annual recharge occurred through-out the winter and early spring period (i.e., from December 2019 to March 2020; Fig. 6 ). The highest modelled groundwater recharge was calculated for the water year 2019/2020, when the annual recharge was 198 mm. This water year had the highest annual precipitation amount in the studied period from 2018 to 2022 (732 mm). For water years 2020/2021 and 2021/2022 when spring functioning was studied (Section 4.3 ), the smaller annual recharge of 105 mm was calculated for the water year 2020/2021. However, the precipitation amount during that year (591 mm) was the second highest of the study period. The lower recharge could be related to smaller precipitation amount during the late autumn (103 mm; October-November) and low maximum SWE values (53 mm) compared to other water years when permanent snow cover developed (2018/2019, 2020/2021, 2021/2022). Recharge estimations for the period 2018-2022 show that the development of thick snow cover and high SWE values in winter generally result in higher annual groundwater recharge and prolong the period when groundwater recharge can occur. In the water years 2018/2019 and 2021/2022, when the maximum SWE was higher (77 and 89 mm, respectively), the modelled recharge for the month of April was 19 and 16 mm, respectively. On the contrary, recharge estimates for April in 2019/2020 and 2020/2021, when the winter snow cover was absent or much thinner (maximum SWE of 12 and 53 mm, respectively), was markedly smaller (3 and 10 mm, respectively). At the same time, PET exceeded precipitation in April during all water years. Thus, the snowpack can function as a water reservoir for groundwater recharge which allows the process to continue longer into the spring season (Earman and Dettinger, 2011; Meriö et al., 2019 ). It is important to note that although the amount of SWE and thickness of the snow cover are the most important factors in determining the amount of recharge from snowmelt, other factors (e.g., sublimation, mid-winter melt events followed by subsequent freeze back) may also have an effect (Hyman-Rabeler and Loheide, 2023 ).  4.2 General characterization of spring hydrochemistry and hydrodynamics The discharge of Mõdriku and Vetiku spring group was highly variable during the study period with values from ∼0.001 m3 /s to maximum values of 0.41 m3 /s and 0.93 m3 /s, respectively (ESM-3, Table S7 ). The spring outflows in Mõdriku and Vetiku became virtually dry in early autumn (late September-October). The electrical conductivity (EC) of the springs was rather similar with values of 588 ± 43 and 547 ± 116 μS/cm, respectively (Table S7 , ESM-3). The discharge of Rägavere spring was much smaller on average but more stable in time with values from 0.02 to 0.04 m3 /s (Table S7 , ESM-3). The EC of the Rägavere spring (699 ± 23 μS/cm) was also more stable but higher than in the Mõdriku and Vetiku springs. NO3 −  concentrations were the highest in the Vetiku spring group and in the Rägavere spring with values of 44 ± 20 and 48 ± 16 mg/L, respectively (ESM-3, Table S7 ). In the Mõdriku spring group, the NO3 −  concentrations were lower with values of 25 ± 14 mg/L. The environmental quality standard for NO3 −  of 50 mg/L was exceeded in 41% (n = 23) of samples in the Rägavere spring (maximum value of 80 mg/L), while in the Vetiku springs 57% (n = 21) samples exceeded this threshold (maximum value of 69 mg/L). No exceedances were measured in samples from Mõdriku springs, but the maximum values were very close to the environmental quality standard (47 mg/L). Maximum discharge in all studied springs occurred in April at the end of the snowmelt period. Minimum discharge was measured during the autumn months of October and November. The NO3 −  concentrations followed approximately the same pattern, but their maximum occurred slightly earlier at the start of the snowmelt period (February-March) whereas the minimum was observed together with minimum discharge. The highest values of EC were observed during the whole high-flow period from late autumn to early spring (period from November to March) that coincided with the main groundwater recharge events (Section 4.1 ). Minimum EC values were observed together with minimum discharge in the autumn. General hydrochemical and isotopic composition of spring water is typical for shallow groundwater in the area (ESM-3, Fig. S1 ). Groundwater discharging from the Mõdriku, Vetiku and Rägavere springs is characterized by oxic conditions and CaMg-HCO3  or Ca-HCO3  water type with average δ18 O values from − 11.2 to − 11.7 ‰ (Table 1  ; ESM-3). This shows that the springs are fed by shallow groundwater flow systems in the upper portion of the carbonate bedrock where the hydraulic conductivity is the highest (see Section 2.2 ). The hydrochemistry in the shallow part of the Nabala-Rakvere aquifer (down to 15 m, Täkusamba and Tahu wells; Table 1 ) differs from springs only slightly by higher EC values (620–730 μS/cm). This groundwater is still characterized by oxic conditions, CaMg-HCO3  water type and high NO3 −  concentrations (40–60 mg/L). Hydrochemical composition of the shallow bedrock aquifer is also very similar to the individual springs monitored in Mõdriku and Vetiku spring group that are located upstream from the main spring group outlets (Table 1 ). Shallow well no. 24420 (depth 15 m) located at the top of the esker between the Mõdriku and Rägavere springs (Fig. 2 ) is in the anoxic (Fe-reduction) zone and has a higher EC value (733 ± 13 μS/cm) compared to Mõdriku and Vetiku springs. This shows that under areas with thicker overburden, more hydrochemically evolved water can be found. The NO3 −  concentrations here are below detection limit. The Mõdriku-1 well that opens the deeper part of the Nabala-Rakvere bedrock aquifer (20–30 m b.g.s), lies in the NO3 − -reduced zone (ESM-3, Fig. S1 ). Generally, the groundwater in the deeper part of the Nabala-Rakvere aquifer has a similar hydrochemical composition to the shallow bedrock wells. However, its Mg/Ca ratio and SO4 2−  concentrations are higher and NO3 −  is below detection limit. The latter shows that the deeper portion of the aquifer lies below the redox front between oxic and anoxic conditions controlled probably by pyrite oxidation coupled to denitrification (Postma et al., 1991 ). Isotopic composition of anoxic groundwater is also slightly depleted compared to springs and shallow wells (δ18 O values from −11.9 to −12.0 ‰). Given the mineralogical composition of the bedrock, the two main processes controlling the hydrochemical composition of groundwater are carbonate mineral dissolution and pyrite oxidation. Brown et al. (2016) have proposed that the proportion of HCO3 −  and SO4 −  (the C-ratio; Table 1 ) in groundwater reflects the relative importance of carbonate reactions consuming protons derived from soil CO2  (C-ratio of 1) and carbonate reactions coupled to sulfide (pyrite) oxidation (C-ratio of 0.5). The C-ratios in springs and shallow part of the bedrock aquifer are very close to 1 (0.94–0.96; Table 1 ), showing that carbonate reactions related to CO2  dissolution are much more important compared to pyrite oxidation. The pyrite oxidation reaction plays a bigger role in the deeper part of the bedrock (Mõdriku-1 well) and occasionally also inside the overlying sediments of the Quaternary cover (C-ratios of 0.80–0.88; Table 1 ). The autocorrelation functions (ACFs) of the spring discharge showed long memory effects with the maximum value of 75 days for the Rägavere spring. The ACF values for Mõdriku springs and the 30 m deep bedrock well Mõdriku-1 located next to it also showed similarly long memory effects (71 and 72 days, respectively; Fig. 7  ). A slightly shorter memory effect of 66 days was found in Vetiku springs. These values are higher than those reported from some of the more developed binary karst systems in other parts of Estonia (Koit, 2022; Koit et al., 2022 ). This shows that although the Pandivere upland is the largest karst region in Estonia (Kink, 1997b; Koit, 2018 ), the karst here is of a more diffuse nature. Carbonate rocks in studied part of the upland are characterized by a homogeneous network of small joints and fissures (apertures from 2 to 30 mm) that have developed in conditions of diffuse autogenic recharge (Heinsalu, 1963; Maves, 2002; Perens et al., 1978 ). The cross-correlation functions (CCFs) were calculated to assess the response of spring discharge, EC and NO3 −  concentrations (output) to the modelled groundwater recharge (input; Section 4.1 ). These three parameters describe different properties of the karst system (Koit et al., 2022 ): 1) the pressure/energy transfer (discharge), 2) the general solute transport (EC) and 3) specific nutrient transport (NO3 − ). The CCF correlation coefficients for the recharge versus discharge in three studied springs were moderate as expressed by maximum cross-correlation co-efficient rxy (k ) of 0.26–0.28 (Fig. 8  ). This indicates a great degree of signal modulation and rather low transmissivity of the fractures in the studied system which agrees with the results of the auto-correlation analysis. The response times calculated from CCF lag to maximum rxy (k ) were similar to the ACF memory effects (53 to 72 days). The response time was the shortest in the Rägavere spring and the longest in the Mõdriku springs. This shows that although the Rägavere spring has the longest memory, it also has the shortest response time. The latter could be related to the location of the Rägavere spring in the groundwater flow field. The spring is located at lower elevation at the outcrop of the Nabala-Rakvere bedrock aquifer (Section 2.2 ). Thus, it probably responds the quickest to changes in hydraulic head in the aquifer (see also Section 4.4 ). The CCFs for recharge versus EC in the springs are similar to discharge (maximum rxy (k ) of 0.16–0.28). However, the CCF lags are much shorter varying from 3 to 6 days in Mõdriku and Vetiku springs and up to 28 days in the Rägavere spring (Fig. 8 b). The short lags show that the solute transport in groundwater systems connected to the springs is much faster than the water flow from the recharge areas to the spring. This suggest that the solute transport in aquifers connected to the springs is mainly controlled by the piston flow mechanism, where groundwater recharge causes a rise in water table which produces a pressure pulse. The pulse travels through the phreatic conduits much faster than the recharging water, pushing the water already present in the aquifer towards the springs (Ford and Williams, 2013 ). Thus, it is the pre-event water present in the subsurface that appears first in the spring outlets after the onset of groundwater recharge (Aquilina et al., 2006; Ford and Williams, 2013; Lakey and Krothe, 1996; Worthington, 2019 ). For Mõdriku and Rägavere springs the CCF lags for recharge versus NO3 −  concentrations (Fig. 8 c) are similar to those of EC with values of 11 days and 13 days, respectively (ESM-3). This suggests that the nutrients reaching the spring outlets at the start of the high flow period are also released from storage rather than leached directly from the overlying soil. In Vetiku springs, the CCF lag for NO3 −  is much longer (61 days), showing that the nutrients are transported to the spring through more regional groundwater flowpaths.  4.3 Climatic, hydrodynamic and hydrochemical factors describing spring functioning The general groundwater hydrochemistry together with auto- and cross-correlation analysis discussed above already describe some important aspects of spring functioning. However, further analysis is required to explain seasonal changes in water quality and the origin of NO3 −  in springs. The spring functioning was analysed in more detail by delineating specific periods of spring behavior during a water year using multi-variate statistical analysis and Mõdriku springs as the model system. The parameters used included hydrochemical parameters (Table 1 ), climatic variables (PET, precipitation amount, SWE) and hydrological parameters (spring discharge, modelled groundwater recharge). A multi-variate chemograph was constructed using factor analysis (FA) and agglomerative cluster analysis (AHC). The eigenvalues of the FA suggested that the first five components (eigenvalues ≥ 1) represented 63 % of the total variance in the dataset. As the eigenvalues of components F4 and F5 were < 1.5 and made up only 10 % of the cumulative variance, the first 3 components (representing 52 % of the total variance) were considered the most important for characterizing the spring functioning and are subject to further interpretation below (Table 2  ). The strength of the contribution of the factors was evaluated using the value of the squared cosines. F1 explained 25% of the variance and the parameters with the strongest positive contributions were recharge, EC, NO3 − , SO4 2− , Cl− , Na+ , Ca2+ , Mg2+  and pCO2 , while δ18 O had a strong inverse contribution. As shown previously in Section 2.2  and ESM-1, fertilizer use is the main source of NO3 −  in the area. For elevated Cl−  concentrations the possible sources are agriculture (both mineral fertilizer and manure) and road salt (Böhlke, 2002; Oberhelman and Peterson, 2020; Panno et al., 2006 ). Ca2+ , Mg2+  and SO4 2−  originate from the two main chemical processes in the studied aquifers − carbonate mineral dissolution and pyrite oxidation − as discussed in Section 4.2 . Baseline concentrations of Na+  and K+  are probably related to silicate mineral dissolution during recharge, but anthropogenic sources such as fertilizers and wastewater treatment plant effluents (for Na+ ) can also increase the concentrations of these ions (Stueber & Criss, 2005 ). Previous studies have shown that water in the Quaternary cover and underlying epikarst zone in the area is characterized by high TDS concentrations and high concentrations of Na+ , K+ , Ca2+ , SO4 2−  and Cl−  (Table 1 ). At the same time, high Ca2+ , Mg2+ , HCO3 −  and NO3 −  concentrations and high pCO2  values are characteristic to shallow bedrock aquifer (down to depths of 15 m; Table 1 ). Thus, we argue that the factor F1 represents the older (pre-event) water in the shallow bedrock aquifer and possibly also in the Quaternary cover/epikarst zone that is in storage prior to major groundwater recharge events. At the start of groundwater recharge in autumn and later at the start of snowmelt in early spring, this water is transported to the spring outlets by the pressure pulse mechanism (Aquilina et al., 2005, 2006; Fidelibus et al., 2017; Huebsch et al., 2014; Jukić and Denić-Jukić, 2009; Meeks and Hunkeler, 2015; Pinault et al., 2001; Williams, 1983 ). This hypothesis is further supported by strong positive contributions of modelled recharge and ΔSWE to this component and a strong negative contribution of PET (Table 2 ). The negative contribution of δ18 O is probably related to the fact that this stored water has a lighter isotopic composition compared to the yearly average isotopic composition of the springs due to the dominance of snowmelt recharge in the aquifers of the Pandivere Upland (Raidla et al., 2016 ). F2 explained 19% of the variance with the strongest positive contribution of spring discharge, PET, NO3 −   and Ca2+  while an inverse contribution can be observed for K+ , NH4 +  and TP (Table 2 ). The period with both high spring discharge and PET occurred during the latter stages of the snowmelt from April to May. The component F2 is interpreted as water reaching the springs from the overlying reservoirs of soil and sedimentary cover during the latter stages of the high-flow period. As the contribution of recharge to this component is low (Table 2 ), the factor F2 characterises a delayed arrival of water to the springs that infiltrated during the melting of the seasonal snowpack (new water or the event-water component). During the snowmelt period, the hydraulic connection between the soil zone and the spring could be enhanced by rising groundwater levels in the subsurface and the reduction of the unsaturated zone thickness. This leads to an increase in transmissivity and solute leaching through a process known as the “transmissivity feedback” (Bishop, 1991; Laudon et al., 2004; Rodhe, 1998 ). We have also considered factor F3 characterized by positive contributions of F−   and Mg/Ca ratio as a distinctive component for describing the seasonal water quality changes in the studied springs although it explains only 7% of the variance. All other ions and parameters most relevant to factors F1 and F2 show an inverse or weakly positive contributions to this component (Table 2 ). Strong contributions of F−  and Mg/Ca could be related to water stored in the bedrock aquifer (Celle-Jeanton et al., 2003; Ćuk Đurović et al., 2022 ). High F−  concentrations have been reported previously from aquifers in the Estonian Silurian and Ordovician carbonate rocks and from wells deeper than 30 m in the Sõmeru catchment (Iital et al., 2022; Karro and Uppin, 2013 ). However, F−  can also originate from the soil zone. It has been shown, that F−  can accumulate in the soil due to the use of phosphate fertilizers as well as through deposition of atmospheric fluoride, but usually majority of F−  is adsorbed to soil particles (Edmunds and Smeadly, 2005; Muthu Prabhu et al., 2023; Walna et al., 2013 ). Thus, F−  transport can be retarded with respect more conservative ions originating from the soil or the land surface (e.g., NO3 − , Cl− ) which can explain its late arrival in the spring. Thus, the F3 probably represents a mixed component of inputs which result from delayed inflow from the soil zone and the increased influence of baseflow from the bedrock aquifer after the snowmelt period. The influence of components F1-F3 on the spring water quality changes during the water year. Thus, the dominance of a given component in a specific period can refer to important aspects of the spring functioning. To study these patterns more thoroughly, the hydrograph of the Mõdriku spring group was divided into 4 phases by AHC clustering based on FA scores for different components (Fig. 9  ). Both studied water years (2020/2021 and 2021/2022) began with a phase we call the “autumn minimum ” (AHC cluster no. 1, Fig. 9 ). This period started in late August/early September and was characterized by the negative or very small positive influence of all three factors (e.g., spring discharge, EC, Ca2+ , SO4 2− , NO3 − , Mg/Ca and F− ). The dominance of negative factor scores has been interpreted as an indication of a general process of dilution occurring in a spring (Ćuk Đurović et al., 2022 ). However, this can also indicate that the factors described above do not represent the processes ongoing during this phase. Indeed, although concentrations for most of the hydrochemical constituents decrease during that period, an increase in TP and NH4 +  concentrations was observed. This can be explained by the influence of the wastewater treatment plant effluent of nearby Vinni village that discharges into the spring group and had TP values from 1.3 to 10 mgP/L in the period of 2019–2022 (Estonian Environmental Agency 2022; ESM-1). As spring discharge is very low during this phase, a smaller dilution of the effluent takes place compared to other times of the year. Most importantly, however, pCO2  values increased and δ18 O values became more enriched during this phase. At the same time, the DOC concentrations increased to >1 mgC/L. All these changes suggest that water in the spring during the low-flow minimum originated from the soil and the sedimentary cover and the inflow of groundwater from the bedrock aquifer was negligible. It is also worth noting that at the start of the phase, most of the individual spring outlets in the Mõdriku and Vetiku spring groups became dry, pointing at the loss of connection between the springs and the bedrock aquifers due to low groundwater levels. The water in the spring was probably also diluted by precipitation and influenced by evaporation as marked by the enrichment in isotopic composition. The second phase called the “autumn –winter recovery ” (AHC cluster no. 2, Fig. 9 ) started in December in both water years with an increase of factor score of F1 to positive values. This coincided with the time when the discharge from Mõdriku and Vetiku spring groups started to increase. It followed on from the period of 2–3 weeks of prior groundwater recharge. The influence of F1 was characterized by an increase in spring discharge, EC, Ca2+ , K+ , Na+ , NO3 − , SO4 2−  and Cl−  together with a decrease in TP, NH4 + , pCO2  and δ18 O (Table 2 , Fig. 9 ). The dominance of F1 indicates that these hydrochemical changes are caused by mobilization of stored water in the subsurface through the piston-flow mechanism. The pCO2  and δ18 O values are at their lowest (∼−2.5 and ∼ −11.8‰, respectively) at the start of the period, but evolved towards higher values as the phase progressed. The discharge and the chemical composition of spring water also stabilized in the second part of the phase (i.e., in January-February), when a permanent snow cover had developed and groundwater recharge was hindered. Final part of the phased coincided with the start of snowmelt in late February-early March when the EC, Cl− , SO4 2−  and NO3 −  reached their maximum concentrations. The third phase “spring maximum ” (AHC cluster no. 3, Fig. 9 ), began during highest spring discharge in both water years (March 2021 and April 2022, respectively). The phase coincided with the latter part of the snowmelt period. An increase in the contribution of F2 indicates the arrival of relatively younger water from the soil, sedimentary cover and/or the epikarst zone. At the same time, the influence of F1 started to decrease, but remained high during the first part of the phase. Thus, the transition from the dominance of the component F1 to the component F2 was gradual and the spring water was a mixture of these components during most of the phase. The influence of F2 became more pronounced as the phase progressed. Most of the parameters influencing F1 (e.g., EC, Cl− , modelled recharge, SWE) decreased gradually during the period, accompanied by a slight depletion in δ18 O values and the rise in pCO2  values (Fig. 9 ). It is worth noting that during both water years the phase ended in May when modelled groundwater recharge became very small. The final phase of the water year, “baseflow recession ” (AHC cluster no. 4, Fig. 9 ), was characterized by steady decrease in spring discharge and in concentrations of most ions. This period represents the recession flow phase, when the system is no longer influenced by groundwater recharge and a gradual emptying of storage takes place (Grasso and Jeannin, 2002 ). The period from May to September during both 2020/2021 and 2021/2022 was characterized by very low modelled groundwater recharge (4–15 mm; Section 4.1 ). At the start of the phase, the impact of F2 decreased but remained high and there was an increase in the influence of F3. This exemplifies the gradual change in water quality and mixing between different components during phase transitions. As the time progressed, a general decrease in dissolved constituents was observed, while the δ18 O values became similar to values found in the shallow bedrock aquifer (∼−11.5‰; Table 2 ).
