For example, many previous studies did not consider or only used simple representations of the effect of forest age when estimating NEE or NEP. Studies using flux observations (Besnard et al., 2018 ) have shown that, in addition to climate and soil properties, forest age is powerful in explaining spatial and temporal variations in NEP, and that reliable maps of forest age distributions are important in accurately predicting NEP both spatially and temporally. The limitation in representing some key processes also leads to the current uncertainties in forest carbon and water flux simulations. Despite the development of various stomatal conductance models, such as the empirical Ball-Berry model (Ball et al., 1987 ) and the Medlyn model (Medlyn et al., 2011 ) based on optimal carbon–water economics theory, the calibrated key parameters (e.g., the stomatal slope parameter g1 (Medlyn et al., 2011 )) may not be necessarily applicable across the globe and under extreme climatic conditions. As flux observations continue to accumulate, machine learning is increasingly regarded as a promising approach to mining the relationships between carbon and water fluxes and climatic and environmental variables (Jung et al., 2020; Reichstein et al., 2019 ). Such data-driven approaches offered an alternative to the process-based models and have shown considerable potential in recent years. For example, Random Forest (RF) has been widely utilized in constructing various carbon flux datasets (Jung et al., 2020; Tramontana et al., 2016; Zeng et al., 2020 ) by upscaling flux observations from the site to the regional scale. RFs were often considered superior for estimating carbon and water fluxes primarily due to their ability to handle complex nonlinear relationships between flux and climate and environmental predictors (which include the response of stomatal conductance to climatic and environmental changes). By integrating multiple decision trees, RFs also effectively reduce overfitting and enhance prediction performance. However, for both process-based modelling and machine learning, the coarse resolution of the forcing data may also cause considerable uncertainties in ET and NEP estimation and in investigating their relations to climate dynamics. This may lead to difficulties in dealing with surface heterogeneity when the model is applied. For example, the resolution of climate reanalysis data commonly used in NEE and ET estimation is usually at ∼ 10 km scale (Tramontana et al., 2016 ), which may make it difficult to accurately represent local meteorological conditions (Fig. 1  ) and environmental controls with high spatial heterogeneity. It represents only the average condition of predictors in each coarse grid point and can lead to scale mismatch. This makes the values of meteorological variables used to analyze the global variability of forest responses to climate change differ considerably from the local ‘real’ conditions at many forest locations. Such error appears to be greater when representing atmospheric moisture conditions than air temperature (Fig. 1 ), and the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) (Knoben et al., 2019) between reanalysis and observations was even lower than 0.5 at some stations. In addition, the scale of forest stands may sometimes be as small as 10–100 m (Shang et al., 2023 ), while the climate reanalysis data that drive forest NEP and ET products have a resolution of 10 km and higher (Jung et al., 2020 ) which is insufficient to characterize the spatial heterogeneity (e.g., sub-pixel forest stand heterogeneity). Inputting these ‘averages’ into the NEP and ET estimation models may yield results that are inconsistent with the averages obtained by inputting the ‘real’ heterogeneous surface conditions and local climate into models. A previous study (Jung et al., 2017 ) also suggested that the effects of water and temperature on terrestrial carbon dynamics may be different at different scales. Water-related effects may be more important than temperature-related effects at small scales because spatial heterogeneity in precipitation, soil moisture, water vapor, etc., may be higher than temperature, and coarse-scale data and large-scale analyses may offset heterogeneity and underestimate the impact of actual water-related factors (Jung et al., 2017 ). There is still a lack of a global site-scale (i.e., small-scale) analysis of the effects of water-related variables (e.g., VPD) (previous flux-station-based analyses can have insufficient spatial and temporal distributions and spans) to clarify whether the effects of water-related variables are underestimated at small scales. Therefore, utilizing site-scale data can potentially mitigate the negative impacts of coarse-resolution data and their associated uncertainties. Meteorological stations offer a wider and denser distribution in global forests compared to flux station networks. By integrating meteorological station-scale observations, soil moisture data, remote sensing data, and forest age information, machine learning approaches show promise in estimating ET and NEE at forest meteorological stations. This approach is particularly valuable for reducing errors caused by scale mismatch. This method enables us to obtain more reliable estimates and achieve more accurate insights into forests' responses to climate dynamics across the globe. Consequently, we employ the RF algorithm to estimate daily-scale ET and NEE data from forest meteorological stations worldwide. This allows us to investigate changes in ET, NEP, and EWUE, as well as their relationships with climate dynamics across various forest ages. The findings of this study provide a meteorological station-level understanding of carbon and water flux dynamics and their response to climate change. This knowledge is crucial for forest management strategies aimed at achieving carbon neutrality and enhancing climate adaptation. By offering insights at this scale, our research contributes valuable information to support more targeted and effective forest management practices in the face of ongoing climate challenges.  2 Methods 2.1 EWUE definition and general research framework EWUE can be represented by the ratio of NEP or GPP and ET (Tian et al., 2016 ). At the flux station, NEE and latent heat (LE) data are directly observed and can be converted to NEP and ET directly. By dividing the values of NEP and ET, we can obtain the value of EWUE. Although many studies have used GPP/ET to measure water use efficiency, the GPP data from the flux stations were partitioned from the observations of NEE (i.e., empirically partitioned into GPP and ecosystem respiration), and thus may introduce uncertainty. In addition, since the objectives of this study are more relevant to carbon neutrality, the net carbon flux is what we are more concerned about. Therefore, NEP/ET was used in this study to represent EWUE. In this study, the observations of ET and NEE at the flux stations were firstly utilized to develop site-scale ET and NEP prediction models and 5-fold cross-validation was performed (Fig. 2  ). Then, the two models were applied to forest weather stations separately to estimate the daily time-series data of NEP and ET and calculate EWUE for each meteorological station. Finally, the following analyses were performed based on the generated data, respectively:a) Temporal and spatial variation patterns of ET, NEP, and EWUE.  b) Analyze the differences in NEP and EWUE for forest age and different forest types.  c) Use linear correlation analysis and convergent cross-mapping (CCM) analysis to investigate the relationship between climate and ET, NEP, and EWUE.  d) Use linear correlation analysis to explore the effects and mechanisms of decadal-scale and seasonal-scale VPD changes on ET, NEP, and EWUE.    The details of each step are described in the following sections.  2.2 RF prediction models of NEP and ET Using the daily NEE and ET flux observations from 91 forest flux stations (Fig. 3  ) in FLUXNET2015 (Pastorello et al., 2020 ) and combining a variety of predictors, we trained daily-scale NEE and ET estimation RF models. Predictors from multiple sources of data were used (Table 1  ). Predictors for the ET estimation model included downward shortwave radiation (RSDN), temperature (Ta), temperature daily range (TArange), VPD, wind speed (WS), surface soil moisture (SSM), leaf area index (LAI), soil sand content proportion (sand_perc), root depth (root_depth). The NEE estimation model further included forest_age and soil organic carbon content (soc), but not WS (it was excluded in the NEE simulation). Using the Google Earth Engine platform, we extracted the values of various variables within a 500 m radius around the flux stations (as well as the meteorological stations). The RF models were constructed based on the 'RandomForestRegressor' function from the ‘scikit-learn’ package of Python, with the n_estimators parameter set to 500 (Table 2  ) and default values used for the other parameters. We set n_estimators to a larger value of 500 (the default value is 100) to increase the reliability of ensemble learning by including more trees and ensuring the diversity of the trees. The other parameters were set to default values without parameter optimization, which refers to the practice of a previous study on ET prediction (Wang et al., 2022 ). While parameter optimization can enhance accuracy in cross-validation of flux station data, its effectiveness may not necessarily translate when applied to meteorological stations. Random Forest (RF), being an ensemble learning method, inherently possesses the ability to largely avoid overfitting. Given this characteristic, we opted to use the default parameters provided in Python's 'scikit-learn' library for all parameters except 'n_estimators' (as shown in Table 2 ). However, future research could explore the use of advanced hyperparameter optimization tools such as Optuna and Hyperopt. These tools hold the potential to further improve prediction accuracy. By leveraging such sophisticated optimization techniques, we may be able to fine-tune our models to better capture the nuances of meteorological station data, potentially leading to more precise estimations of carbon and water fluxes. We evaluated model accuracy by 5-fold random cross-validation. The daily-scale ET model had an R-squared of 0.80 and mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.38 mm/d. The NEE model had a R-squared of 0.75 and MAE of 0.84 gC m−2  d-1 . Compared to previous data-driven daily NEE (Shi et al., 2022 ) and ET estimation studies, the model performance and accuracy of this study are relatively high. In the ranking of feature importance (IMP) of the two models, RSDN, TA, and LAI all ranked relatively high. Even as a steady-state variable (without temporal variation), forest_age showed high importance in the NEE model. Compared to the NEE model, sand_perc was ranked higher in the ET model, indicating that the hydraulic characteristics of soil are relatively important for ET.  2.3 Model application at meteorological stations After developing the Random Forest models for NEE and ET, we applied them to forest meteorological stations in the Global Daily Summary (GSOD) in-situ meteorological station record dataset. The forest extent and type classification data for these stations were derived from the 500 m resolution land cover data MCD12Q1 from MODIS imagery. The main forest types include evergreen needle-leaf forest (ENF), deciduous needleleaf forest (DNF), evergreen broadleaf forest (EBF), deciduous broadleaf forest (DBF) and mixed forest (MXF). Forest type and rooting depth at meteorological stations exhibit considerable variability. Additionally, forest age shows significant variation across these stations. In tropical regions, many meteorological stations are situated in forests older than 250 years, while in other areas, such as southern China, the forests are relatively young (Fig. 4  ). When calculating NEP, ET, and EWUE on an annual scale, we filtered out values for years with fewer than 270 days of site records. This ensured a robust dataset for our analysis. Subsequently, we analyzed the characteristics exhibited by the derived NEP, ET, and EWUE data under different forest age groups and rooting depths. We also examined how these variables were affected by climate factors such as VPD. This comprehensive analysis allows us to understand the complex interactions between forest characteristics, climate factors, and carbon and water fluxes across diverse forest ecosystems.  2.4 Correlation and convergent cross-mapping analysis To assess the impact of these climate factors on NEP, ET, and EWUE, Pearson’s linear correlation method was initially used to measure the magnitude of this influence. Further, considering the spatio-temporal and nonlinear nature of the Earth system, we employed CCM, a nonlinear state-space causal inference method (Sugihara et al., 2012 ), to evaluate the effects that Pearson’s correlation methods cannot detect. CCM reconstructs a nonlinear state-space according to Takens' theorem to reveal causal relationships. Specifically, if we can predict variable X from the reconstruction space of variable Y, then we consider X to have a causal effect on Y, with the causal magnitude measured by the correlation (ρ) between predicted X and actual X. CCM methods and their derivatives are now widely used in ecology and climate science (Gao et al., 2023; Sugihara et al., 2012 ). In our study, our X represents climate factors, while Y represents NEP, ET, or EWUE. The specific implementation of CCM relies on the Python package ‘pyEDM’. We used the ‘EmbedDimension’ function to determine the value of the important parameter ‘E’ in the CCM function, while providing larger values for ‘sample’ and ‘libsize’ to ensure convergence and improve the accuracy of results as much as possible. We analyzed the relationship between various climate factors and annual-scale ET, NEP, and EWUE by different forest types using correlation analysis and CCM methods. For the impact of elevated VPD, which has received much attention recently, we explored the relationship between decadal-scale VPD changes and ET, NEP and EWUE using correlation analysis. Meanwhile, considering that the mechanism of VPD rise may act differently in different seasons, we selected stations in the Northern Hemisphere and analyzed the effects of VPD rise in spring and summer, exploring the complex relationship between the amount of change in VPD, LAI, ET, NEP, and EWUE. This creates an integrated perspective on the effects caused by the recent Northern Hemisphere warming, early onset of the spring, greening, and VPD rise.   3 Results 3.1 ET, NEP and EWUE patterns Despite the wide global distribution of meteorological stations, the number of forest meteorological stations remains relatively limited. Only over 300 stations have estimated values of annual ET, NEP and EWUE (Fig. 5  ). For NEP, most stations exhibit positive values, indicating they are carbon sinks. However, from 2003 to 2010 to 2011–2019, NEP decreased at 129 of the 213 sites (approximately 60.6 %), while it increased at only 84 sites. This suggests that more stations have experienced a decline in net carbon sequestration capacity. For ET, most sites had daily average ET values higher than 1 mm, and from 2003 to 2010 to 2011–2019, ET increased at 129 of 202 sites (approximately 63.9 %). Regarding EWUE, most stations had values between 0 and 1. From 2003 to 2010 to 2011–2019, 119 of the 202 stations (approximately 58.9 %) showed a decrease in EWUE. For the effect of forest age, we found that there was considerable variability in NEP across forest age groups (Fig. 6  ). We found higher NEP in groups where forests were younger than 60 years old, with forests in the 21–30 years old group exhibiting the highest median NEP values (∼1.2 gC m−2  d-1  or 0.44 kgC m−2  yr−1 ). NEP decreased substantially when forests were older than 60 years and some of the sites became carbon sources. The median NEP increased slightly when the forest was older than 100 years. When the forest is older than 200 years, NEP decreases substantially, but the variability appears to be higher, possibly because more sensitive to disturbance (Luyssaert et al., 2008 ). In terms of EWUE, when the forest age is less than 60 years, there is little difference in EWUE across groups. When forest age is over 60 years, EWUE decreased, with sites in the 91–100 age group exhibiting the lowest median EWUE. Median EWUE appeared to increase slightly when forest age exceeded 100 years. Different forest types also exhibited different values of NEP and EWUE (Fig. 7  ). Median NEP was highest for EBF and lowest for DNF. EWUE was relatively high for EBF and ENF, followed by DBF and MXF. EWUE was the lowest for DNF. This is in general agreement with the ranking of water use efficiency of different forest types derived from a recent meta -analysis on this issue (Zhang et al., 2023 ).  3.2 Climate effects 3.2.1 Pearson’s correlation analysis At the annual scale, only the forest age shows a significant linear correlation with NEP, specifically, of EBF (Fig. 8  ). There is no significant correlation between forest age and NEP in other types of forests from Pearson’s linear correlation. Considering the distribution of meteorological stations in EBF forests, this indicates that the NEP of EBF forests with ages over 250 in South America and South Asia is lower than that of forests with ages less than 100 in South America and Southeast Australia. Environmental variables have a consistent impact on the annual scale ET of different types of forests. Annual scale ET is significantly positively correlated with several variables (e.g. TA, VPD, RSDN). ET and Arid Index (long-term precipitation divided by potential evaporation (Programme, 1997 )) showed negative correlations since a lower Aridity Index value represents a higher degree of aridity. It can be explained that the energy limitations in the high Aridity Index region (the more humid regions) correspond to a low ET.  3.2.2 CCM-based analysis In addition to correlation analysis, we used the CCM method and selected RSDN and VPD, which account for a high proportion of importance in the NEP model, to respectively represent the climatic and environmental conditions (e.g., moisture and heat) and detect the magnitude of their impacts on NEP and EWUE (Fig. 9  ) in the northern hemisphere. Except for DBF and ENF, the NEP and EWUE of other forest types are affected by RSDN and VPD detected through CCM (EWUE or NEP: Predictor). In DBF, the impact of RSDN and VPD on NEP cannot be detected by CCM. From the perspective of NEP, the ρ  of NEP: Predictor is larger than Predictor: NEP. This confirms that RSDN and VPD affect the NEP of EBF and MXF. Horizontally, the impact of VPD on NEP is less than that of RSDN. Vertically, in EBF, the impact of RSDN and VPD is greater than in MXF. From the perspective of EWUE, the ρ  of EWUE: Predictor is larger than Predictor: EWUE. This indicates that the impact of RSDN and VPD on EWUE has been detected in a nonlinear space. Horizontally, except for DBF, the impact of RSDN on EWUE of other forest types is much greater than that of VPD; vertically, the impact of RSDN on EWUE is: EBF>ENF>MXF>DBF, and the impact of VPD on EWUE is: EBF>DBF>MXF>ENF. It illustrated that the EWUE of ENF is mainly influenced by ecosystem productivity (controlled by RSDN), while that of DBF is mainly influenced by reduced stomatal conductance (controlled by VPD) in the northern hemisphere. This suggests that changes in EWUE in different forest types may be dominated by different mechanisms due to biophysical differences (Wang et al., 2018 ). CCM was initially developed as a causal inference method, suitable for moderate to weak degrees of one-way and two-way causal inference, with higher ρ  being the main factor. Subsequently, with the more widespread use of CCM and the development of derivative methods, the interpretation of CCM results has changed. Here, the smaller ρ  of predictor: NEP does not necessarily prove the existence of a reverse-direction causation. When there is a strong causation from X to Y, then even if there is no feedback causal influence from Y to X (Sugihara et al., 2012 ). For example, in MXF, the ρ  of RSDN: NEP has a larger convergent value, which can be explained as in MXF, RSDN controls NEP, thus the ρ  of RSDN: NEP reflects this strong influence.   3.3 Impacts of VPD increase Global VPD is projected to increase (He et al., 2022 ) and can influence forest hydrology and carbon uptake capacity considerably. Here we revisited its impacts at meteological stations. 3.3.1 Decadal scale effects Based on a decadal-scale analysis (Fig. 10  ) comparing 2003–2010 and 2011–2019, ΔVPD exhibited a significant positive correlation with ΔET only (R=0.156, p < 0.05). Linear correlations between ΔVPD and ΔNEP and ΔEWUE were not significant (p > 0.1). This suggests that as VPD rises, the ET of the forests may increase, but changes in NEP and EWUE may not be significant. This suggests that the effect of increased atmospheric moisture demand on ET in forests is significant, but not on NEP and EWUE. It can be related to the distribution of forest meteorological stations in this study. Multi-year average VPD was relatively low at most stations, with annual average VPD values below 0.5, especially at a large number of stations in the middle and high-latitude regions of the northern hemisphere. Under low VPD conditions, leaf stomatal conductance may increase as VPD rises (Soni et al., 2012; Woodruff et al., 2010 ). It can lead to an increase in photosynthetic rate under low VPD conditions (Sellin et al., 2017, 2013 ). It is consistent with the positive correlation relation found in previous studies (He et al., 2022 ) between VPD and satellite-based vegetation index (NIRv, near-infrared reflectance of vegetation) and contiguous solar-induced fluorescence (CSIF) measurements in the high latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Furthermore, in humid conditions, a positive correlation between VPD and ecosystem respiration may exist, as higher VPD often corresponds to higher temperatures. When these two effects are combined, the insignificant linear correlation between VPD and NEP can be explained. Thus, from a space-for-time perspective, future increases in VPD in the context of warming may lead to increased ET but may not necessarily result in significant decreases in NEP and EWUE, particularly in the mid- and high-latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere.  3.3.2 Seasonal scale effects With global warming and earlier spring phenology, the seasonal changes in spring and summer showed differences (Fig. 11  ). Significant positive correlations were found between spring ΔVPD and spring ΔET. Summer ΔVPD and spring ΔET also showed a significantly positive correlation. A significant negative correlation was found between summer ΔET and spring ΔLAI, but not with summer ΔLAI. This suggests that the advance of spring phenology in the Northern Hemisphere is accompanied by vegetation greening that increases ET, but at the same time may have led to higher spring water consumption and reduced water carryover from spring to summer (Lian et al., 2024 ). It can subsequently increase the risk of summer vegetation browning. Summer ΔNEP showed a significant positive correlation with spring and summer ΔVPD, but the correlation coefficients were low, suggesting that a slight increase in VPD may lead to an increase in summer NEP. It is consistent with findings in Sector 3.3.1 and can be explained by the rise in photosynthetically active radiation (promoted photosynthesis) and air temperature that often accompanies VPD increase. It was beneficial for vegetation growth, especially at high latitudes, which is energy-limited. ΔEWUE was significantly correlated with multiple factors. Summer ΔEWUE was significantly and positively correlated with ΔET in spring, which suggests the possibility that vegetation may choose a conservative stomatal strategy to increase EWUE in summer to adapt to a possible summer moisture deficit after excessive water consumption in spring. The findings suggested a different mechanism for the effects of VPD changes in spring and summer. Given the higher reliability of measured VPD from meteorological stations compared to reanalysis data, meteorological station VPD monitoring should be more frequently used in early warning of forest moisture deficits and possible browning and reduced carbon sequestration capacity.    4 Discussion 4.1 Implication To investigate how forests contribute to the global carbon cycle and how they might respond to changes in climate and environmental conditions or management practices, researchers have used various long-term modelling approaches such as machine learning. In previous machine learning-based models of forest carbon and water fluxes and EWUE, using coarse climate reanalysis as input can cause uncertainties (Li et al., 2023a; Tramontana et al., 2016; Zeng et al., 2020 ). In this study, we simulated forest NEP, and ET and calculated EWUE based on in-situ meteorological observations instead of using coarse climate reanalysis and applied the models to forest meteorological stations instead of coarse reanalysis grids. We found that forest age is of important influence on NEP and EWUE at the global scale. For future studies focusing on station scales, this study may be valuable because it enhances the available information volume on more accurate carbon and water fluxes at the station level (Fig. 12  ). This increase in data availability is especially significant at MXF, DBF, and EBF, which allows global site-scale studies of these types of sites to move from flux stations with only a few data to meteorological stations with several times the amount of data. It provided a meteorological station-level understanding of carbon and water flux dynamics and their response to climate change to the contribution of forest ecosystems to carbon neutrality and can support future station-level studies. Generally, the accuracy of this study’s NEP and ET simulations is relatively high. The R-squared in the daily-scale simulations reached 0.75 and 0.8, respectively. The accuracy is higher than most of the previous process-based models and also machine-learning-based NEE (Shi et al., 2022 ) and ET models using climate reanalysis inputs. It may be because this study used state-of-the-art datasets for forest age, rooting depth, etc. in the simulations. Although these estimates contain uncertainties, it is undeniable that they have incorporated much in-situ observational or inventory information. Meteorological station-level estimates can provide more reliable relationships between NEP and forest age due to the more accurate measuring of meteorological variables. Meteorological station observations such as VPD, which are more accurate compared to climate reanalysis data, are also important to more accurately constrain our understanding of the global variability of VPD impacts on forests. It also has greater utility for local forest managers and can be combined with more ground-based evidence and experiments.  4.2 Comparison with reanalysis data-based studies Compared to recent studies based on reanalysis, our results exhibit both consistencies and inconsistencies. For example, compared to recent remote sensing and reanalysis data-based estimates (Huang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023a ), our results are partially consistent in showing an increase in EWUE in Eastern Europe and a decrease in EWUE in Siberia, which may be related to the relatively high consistency of meteorological data in these regions (Fig. 1 ). However, our study found an inconsistent decline in EWUE in the forests of northwestern North America after 2000, whereas indicate an increase in EWUE in these areas. VPD data in reanalysis datasets for this region show significant discrepancies compared to observations (Fig. 1 ), which may lead to these inconsistencies. However, these inconsistencies could also be due to differences in study periods and the inclusion of ecosystem respiration in the calculation of EWUE in our study. The inclusion of ecosystem respiration may weaken the positive trend in EWUE compared to using GPP divided by ET to represent EWUE. Besides, independently derived NEP data based on top-down atmospheric inversion (Jiang et al., 2022 ) suggest that this region became a carbon source between 2010 and 2019, which aligns to some extent with our findings. Previous studies of VPD’s influence on carbon–water cycles at the flux tower level (Xu et al., 2023b ) are generally considered to be more reliable due to using station observations. However, many global-scale studies struggled to ensure the accuracy of coarse-scale VPD data. For instance, in the ERA5-land reanalysis data, the inconsistency between VPD data from 10 km grids and those from forest meteorological stations is higher than the inconsistency in air temperature data (Fig. 1 ). This suggests that previous coarse-scale studies may not have accurately captured the impact of VPD on forest carbon and water cycles (Li et al., 2023a ). Considering that 10 km scale soil moisture products from reanalysis, land surface models or satellite remote sensing are also not enough accurate, recent global-scale studies attempting to distinguish between the contributions of VPD and soil moisture to forest carbon and water cycles may be uncertain (Liu et al., 2020 ). Our study may have more accurately assessed the impact of global VPD changes on forest carbon and water fluxes at the meteorological station level. It suggests that EWUE in different forests is driven by various mechanisms. For instance, the EWUE of DBF sites is significantly driven by VPD, while that of ENF is more frequently influenced by RSDN. Furthermore, seasonal-scale analysis reveals distinct mechanisms for the effects of VPD changes in spring and summer. In the future, combining more in-situ soil moisture sttaion observations or higher precision soil moisture estimates at the site level has potential, as this would more accurately capture land–atmosphere interactions than previous studies using reanalysis and land surface model outputs. This will significantly enhance the understanding of carbon and water cycles in areas without flux towers.  4.3 Challenges, uncertainty, and future directions 4.3.1 Challenges and uncertainty Although in-situ station meteorological measurements reduce the uncertainty of meteorological inputs, land cover change and the impacts of other management histories and ecosystem disturbances (Jung et al., 2020 ) were not explicitly included in the assessment. Natural disturbances like wildfires, insect outbreaks, or human-induced deforestation can significantly impact NEP and EWUE. Their detailed impacts are still not negligible, and ecosystem disturbances within 500 m of the site may still significantly affect the ET, NEP and EWUE estimates and their relationships with predictors or environmental variables. In this study’s analyses of NEP and EWUE responses to climate factors, the impacts of extreme climate events (e.g., extreme droughts, and heat waves) remain uncertain (Frank et al., 2015; Reichstein et al., 2013 ). It is partially because machine learning tends to underestimate the impact of extreme values (underestimating extremely high values and overestimating extremely low values), thus representation of the response to the impact of extreme events can be inadequate. Fortunately, some machine learning methods that can adapt to extreme values have been proposed (Pickering et al., 2022 ). Increasing flux observations across the globe can record and capture more extreme climate impacts and increase the data availability on the studies of extreme conditions. It can thus improve model predictions of extreme climate events’ impacts, due to observation can also capture climate extremes better than reanalysis data at station scale. Forest microclimates (De Frenne et al., 2021; Zellweger et al., 2020 ) may also be important for forest ecosystems (e.g., differences in understory and above-canopy temperatures), which may drive the forests’ response to the warming climate. Current forest meteorological stations’ observations make it difficult to characterize changes in vertical microclimate variation (e.g., in temperature, VPD and WS) well. Forest microclimates often mitigate extreme temperatures, making conditions cooler in the summer and warmer in the winter compared to open areas (De Frenne et al., 2021 ). This buffering effect significantly alters transpiration rates and photosynthetic efficiency, thereby affecting ET and NEP measurements and estimation. The density and type of canopy cover influence microclimates by controlling the amount of light, heat, and moisture reaching the forest floor. Different tree species and canopy densities lead to variations in microclimate, affecting stomatal behaviour and thus ET. Additionally, horizontal and vertical variations within the forest create diverse microclimatic conditions, causing significant differences in local ET and NEP estimates. Seasonal changes further complicate the relationship between microclimates and ecosystem functions. For instance, the seasonal leaf phenology in deciduous forests can lead to drastic changes in microclimate throughout the year, influencing seasonal patterns of ET and NEP​. Understanding these microclimates and their drivers is crucial for accurately predicting the responses of forest ecosystems to climate change and improving the reliability of ecosystem models​. The combination of remote sensing data and microclimate modelling may be helpful to better characterize microclimate impacts. For example, LiDAR (Jarron et al., 2020 ) can provide information on the 3D structure of forest canopies as well as more accurate estimates of LAI, helping to understand the relationship between different canopy densities and microclimate. Microclimate modelling (Maclean, 2020 ) can also provide higher-resolution climate datasets and thus help to generate high-resolution carbon and water flux estimates in the future. The predictor variables used for model training are the following shortwave radiation, forest age, and soil moisture, which have uncertainties because they are estimates, and these uncertainties affect the ET, NEP, and EWUE estimates. For example, errors in forest age can affect NEP estimates because they determine the balance between photosynthesis and respiration. Underestimation of forest age may lead to overestimation of NEP, while overestimation of forest age may underestimate NEP. Uncertainty in SSM estimation affects measures of water stress, while deep-layer soil moisture may be a more important driver of forest ecosystem carbon and water flux estimation (Xu et al., 2023b ). However, current remote sensing-based methods have not yet been able to accurately estimate deep soil moisture distribution, making it difficult to accurately characterize deep root water uptake processes (Gao et al., 2014 ) and thus causing uncertainty.  4.3.2 Future directions To further improve model accuracy, more variables related to plant traits could be included. It can also deepen the understanding of ‘climate-plant trait-ecosystem function’ relationships (Rowland et al., 2021; Sakschewski et al., 2016 ). Therefore, we suggest that additional monitoring and observations of plant traits can be implemented around meteorological stations in the future given that current observations on plant traits are already linked to the FLUXNET2015 flux stations (Migliavacca et al., 2021 ). It is promising in combination with carbon and water flux prediction models based on the meteorological station scale. For example, leaf nitrogen content and canopy height could further deepen our understanding of the effects of variability in different forest ecosystems on ET, NEP and EWUE. In addition, we realized that we may have built accurate daily-scale estimation models of forest ET and NEP and produced daily-scale data that have relatively finer temporal resolution. This makes it possible to provide additional value in studies of problems that require high temporal resolution, such as the effects of changing phenological periods in the Northern Hemisphere on NEP, ET and other relevant issues (Gu et al., 2022; Keenan et al., 2014; Li et al., 2023b; Piao et al., 2008 ), which requires accurate daily-scale and station-level data. The use of monthly scale data to study these issues is not in-depth, and reliable daily scale data are thus needed, and the data at the meteological station level has the potential to serve as a complementary validation of such studies. The produced daily data is also crucial for studying the impact of extreme weather events on forest ecosystems. Events such as heavy precipitation, storms, and other climate extremes can occur within a few days, and using monthly data is insufficient to effectively capture these short-term impacts. Station data on ET and NEP can also be used to calibrate and validate remote sensing products and ecosystem models, enhancing their accuracy and reliability. Long-term continuous ET and NEP data of the meteorological stations can also help to reveal trends in forest ecosystem changes under climate change. In this study, the use of MODIS-derived variables limits the temporal span to post-2000. If not relying on MODIS data, it is possible to generate longer temporal series of carbon and water fluxes from meteorological station observation records for the last century (although the accuracy may decrease without remote sensing data). This longer time series is beneficial for assessing the long-term impacts of climate change on forest water and carbon cycles.    5 Conclusion Previous estimations and analyses of forest carbon and water fluxes have extensively relied on coarse-scale reanalysis climate data, which potentially introduce uncertainties in flux estimates and their attribution analysis. Discrepancies have arisen in attributing the dynamics of carbon and water fluxes across different scales, and the sparse global distribution of flux stations has impeded the development of a comprehensive global perspective on site-scale attribution. This study utilized in-situ meteorological data and machine learning at weather station scales to reassess the variations in global forest carbon and water fluxes and their responses to hydroclimatic changes. We provided a novel perspective for analyzing the climatic controls on carbon and water flux dynamics over broader regions and longer periods compared to flux station networks. We suggest that future research should focus more on the impact mechanisms of hydroclimatic dynamics on carbon and water fluxes and ecosystem functions at the weather station scale, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of the specific impacts of scale effects in attribution. Furthermore, machine learning methods have demonstrated higher prediction accuracies for NEP and ET and can potentially replace process-based models, whose global applicability of parameters needs enhancement. Future studies should consider employing various advanced machine learning methods to further explore the complex relationships between carbon and water fluxes and their predictors, thereby improving simulation accuracy. The detailed findings of this study are as follows:a) About 60.6 % of forest meteorological stations showed a decrease in NEP from 2003 to 2010 to 2011–2019. 63.9 % of the stations showed an increase in ET. 58.9 % of the stations showed a decrease in EWUE. NEP and EWUE significantly declined in forests older than 60 years. Younger forests exhibited higher NEP, with forests aged 21–30 years showing the highest median NEP values. Variability in NEP and EWUE was also evident across different forest types. EWUE in different forest types is driven by varying mechanisms, with DBF sites significantly influenced by VPD and ENF sites by RSDN.  b) In regions where site and reanalysis data VPDs are inconsistent, such as northwestern North America, our results show inconsistency with previous studies based on reanalysis data but are more consistent with top-down atmospheric inversion-based findings that are independent of meteorological data.  c) Slight summer VPD increases were associated with higher NEP, especially in high-latitude areas. Early spring phenology and increased spring VPD reduced available water carried over to summer, potentially causing summer water shortages.  d) Incorporating more site-specific observations, such as plant traits, could enhance the understanding of the relationships between climate, plant traits, and ecosystem functions. This study highlights the potential for meteorological station-level data to provide reliable estimates and improve the understanding of forest carbon and water flux dynamics, supporting forest management for carbon neutrality and climate adaptation.
1 Introduction Environmental models need to be evaluated against field observations for their fitness-for-purpose and their ability to model system dynamics (Beven, 2002; Hrachowitz et al., 2014; Beven, 2019; Parker, 2020; Beven and Chappell, 2021; Beven and Lane, 2022 ). Hydrological models utilize precipitation data and other meteorological inputs to simulate fluxes such as streamflows and states such as soil moisture as outputs. For a model to be considered good, simulated hydrological quantities should be consistent with corresponding available observations where consistency between observed and predicted quantities is measured using one or multiple objective functions depending upon the purpose of modeling. Model evaluation is complicated by the uncertainty due to the presence of errors in model input and observed output quantities (e.g., Renard et al, 2010; Le Coz et al., 2014; Beven, 2019, 2023; Bárdossy and Anwar, 2023 ). In what follows, the term ‘model’ will be used to refer to both model structures and any parameter set of a model structure. Often, a single parameter set of a model structure that optimizes a goodness-of-fit (GoF) measure is used as the optimal parameter set (e.g., Knoben et al., 2020; Kratzert et al., 2019; Mai, 2023 ). In some cases, several optimal parameter sets, referred to as pareto optimal, are identified based on multi-objective optimization (Harvey et al., 2023 ). However, the optimal parameter set is not well defined for hydrological models (Beven and Binley, 1992 ) because there often exist several parameter sets and model structures − referred to as equifinal models − that simulate the observed hydrological quantities with acceptable accuracy over the period of available data (Beven, 2006 ). A single optimal parameter set obtained by a global optimization routine (e.g., Duan et al., 1992; Tolson and Shoemaker, 2007 ) depends upon the objective function being considered and the calibration period (Beven, 2023 ), and hence is ill-defined given a finite calibration period and a small number of observed hydrological quantities – in most studies only observed streamflow data are used to evaluate a model. Even though equifinal models may yield appoximately equally acceptable streamflow estimates over the calibration period, their performance for other periods might be very different. A validation period is typically used for independent assessment of model performance, but different parameter sets may perform acceptably for a validation period also. Further, equifinal parameter sets may yield very different simulations of internal fluxes and states (Gallart et al., 2007; Khatami et al., 2019; Hughes and Farinosi, 2021 ). Equifinality may also exist in terms of pre-calibration model setup such as model discretization (Refsgaard et al., 2022 ). Many methods have been proposed within the hydrologic literature to evaluate models and quantify uncertainties (see Gupta and Govindaraju (2022)  for a recent review) including formal Bayesian methods (e.g., Kuczera et al., 2006; Vrugt et al., 2022 ), frequentist methods (Pande 2013a, 2013b ), information-theoretic methods (Gong et al., 2013; Weijs et al., 2010a; 2010b; 2013 ), and generalized likelihood uncertainty estimation method (GLUE; Beven and Binley, 1992, 2014 ). The formal statistical methods use a probabilistic likelihood function to quantify the information in hydrological data and are based on aleatoric assumptions about the uncertainties. Thus, these methods are not applicable in hydrological modeling without strong assumptions because uncertainties encountered in hydrology are dominantly epistemic (Beven, 2019 ). Epistemic uncertainties, by definition, have unknowable statistical properties for a given amount of data (Gupta and Govindaraju, 2022 ). The errors in hydrology may vary from event to event in an arbitrary but non-random manner and are nonstationary (Beven, 2016 ). Further, there may be observed events that do not satisfy mass balance or other physical constraints, referred to as disinformative periods (Beven and Westerberg, 2011 ; Frame et al., 2023 ). These disinformative periods may introduce biases during parameter estimation and affect the antecedent conditions for subsequent events (Beven and Smith, 2015 ). Therefore, it is very difficult to realistically define probabilities in the case of epistemic errors (Berger and Smith, 2019 ) even though probabilities have a sound epistemic underpinning (Jaynes, 2002; Montanari and Koutsoyiannis, 2012; Nearing et al., 2016 ). To some extent, the problem of wrong assumptions can be addressed by making inference in spectral space, but this method has limitations as well (Schaefli and Kavetski, 2017; Gupta and Govindaraju, 2022 ). Information-theory based GoF metrics do not account for such uncertainties and are often used for finding an optimal parameter set. Several attempts have been made to model rainfall, streamflow and structural errors separately and explicitly (e.g., Renard et al., 2010 ), however these studies show that the parameters of these error models cannot be identified without strong prior information on these errors; that is, structural and measurement uncertainties cannot be separated. The idea of multi-objective optimization has also been used in hydrological modeling (e.g., Yapo et al., 1998; Efstratiadis, & Koutsoyiannis, 2010; Shafii et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2023 ) where several models are obtained by optimizing multiple objectives simultaneously. These studies show that no single model is best for all the objective functions. Typically, a set of models, referred to as Pareto front, is obtained such that no model in the set is better or worse than other models in terms of all the objectives. While Pareto fronts address some of the problems with identifying a single model based on a single objective function, they do not address issues arising from uncertainty in the data and several good models within the limits of uncertainty might still be rejected (type-2 error) in the process. Along with streamflow, soil moisture and evapotranspiration data (e.g., Refsgaard et al., 2022; Mei et al., 2023 ), isotope data (Iorgulescu et al., 2007; Beria, 2020 ), groundwater levels (Gallart et al., 2007 ) etc. have been used in earlier studies to reduce equifinality. Typically, uncertainties in these data, including uncertainty due to scale mismatch between some data, are not considered while comparing observed quantities against their corresponding simulated values. In the GLUE framework, subjective likelihoods based on hydrological reasoning, also referred to as informal likelihoods, are used to evaluate the degree to which a model is consistent with the data. The informal likelihood may be any GoF metric such as Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE). The idea behind using informal measures is to reduce the over-conditioning of the parameter sets on data (e.g., Smith et al., 2008 ). The main limitation of the early application of informal likelihood measures was that the modeler had to decide the threshold value of NSE (or any other GoF metric) beyond which a model could be deemed behavioral. This is a subjective choice given the epistemic uncertainties in hydrological data. Also, GoF measures collapse all the information in hydrological data into a single number, and thus, may not be able to represent information in hydrological data well (Gupta et al., 2008 ). However, several such GoF measures emphasizing different parts of the hydrograph (or another response variable) may be used in combination to address this problem, as is done in multi-objective optimization, but the fundamental problem remains that these measures may be impacted by the uncertainties (Beven, 2024 ). The limits-of-acceptability (LoA) method has been proposed within the GLUE framework to address some of the limitations of early GLUE applications (Beven, 2006; Liu et al., 2009; Krueger et al., 2010; Coxon et al., 2014 ; Hollaway et al., 2018; Beven, 2019; Beven and Lane, 2022 ). LoAs are defined as the upper and lower bounds over streamflow (or any other relevant quantity) such that these bounds reflect the effects of errors in hydrological data (Beven et al., 2022; Gupta et al., 2023a ). Thus, a model that simulates streamflows within LoAs (while accounting for potential outliers) may be considered as being consistent with the data. The goal is to identify an adequate sample of models that simulate streamflow within LoAs. Note that this approach is different from identifying the good models based on comparing observed and simulated streamflow in that LoAs must be defined before any model calibration to reduce interactions between measurement and structural uncertainties. Further, since LoAs are defined for each time step, a model can be evaluated at the timestep level using the LoA framework, which is also useful in understanding why a model fails. The main advantage of the LoA method is that the conditions of model acceptability are defined before any model evaluation takes place. Once the LoAs are defined, a likelihood function can be based on the LoAs, which can also be used in Approximate Bayesian Computation framework (Nott et al., 2012; Sadegh and Vrugt, 2013; Vrugt and Sadegh, 2013 ; Vrugt and Beven, 2018 ). The traditional applications of formal Bayesian methods do not impose any limits on the spread of the error distribution, allowing a greater interaction between structural and measurement uncertainties. Indeed, the formal Bayesian methods assign a small probability to bad models but never reject them (Lindley, 2013 ), while GLUE and LoA methods allow rejection of models. Often, LoAs are defined based on streamflow uncertainty only (e.g., Coxon et al., 2014 ), and the effect of precipitation uncertainty is included by subjectively increasing the width of the LoA (e.g., Krueger et al., 2010 ). In some small catchment studies where inputs could be assumed well known and LoAs were based only on streamflow uncertainty (e.g., Hollaway et al., 2018 ), all the evaluated models were rejected. Beven (2019)  proposed a method to define LoAs based on variability of runoff ratios of rainfall-runoff events. This method accounts for both the precipitation and streamflow measurement uncertainties, but the method is applicable to flashy watersheds only and cannot account for timing errors without further assumption (Beven et al., 2022b ). Gupta et al. (2023a)  proposed a decision tree (DT) based method to define LoAs. This method accounts for the effects of both streamflow and precipitation uncertainty. One of the advantages of the DT method is that it can use data from donor watersheds  (watersheds other than the watershed where the model is to be evaluated) to define LoAs. Hence, DTs can be used to define LoAs for both gauged and ungauged catchments. Gupta et al. (2023a)  derived DT-based LoAs for four subbasins located within St. Joseph River Watershed (SJRW). This study builds on Gupta et al. (2023a)  by applying these LoAs to evaluate a hydrological model. One interesting application of DT-based LoA is that it can be used to evaluate a hydrological model even at ungauged locations. Prediction at ungauged basins (PUB) is one of the most important and challenging problems in hydrological science (Hrachowitz et al., 2013 ). To constrain the simulations in an ungauged basin, information is transferred from similar donor watersheds to the parent watershed by parameter regionalization or streamflow signature regionalization (Razavi and Coulibaly, 2013 ). Essentially, rainfall-runoff process in the ungauged watershed is inferred using the data from other similar gauged catchments. But the regionalization process has significant additional uncertainty which is also difficult to quantify (Wagener and Montanari, 2011 ). DT-based LoAs can be useful for addressing the PUB challenge by providing a simple metric to evaluate models at ungauged locations while accounting for data uncertainties. Also, DT-LoAs allow model evaluation at each time-step as opposed to signature-based constraints which are unaffected by the streamflow timing information. Therefore, this study also explores the suitability of ML-based LoAs in evaluating models at ungauged locations. If the uncertainties in data are large, several models might be consistent with the observed streamflow time series, but many of these models may not necessarily represent catchment dynamics satisfactorily (Hrachowitz et al., 2014; Wagener et al., 2021 ). To address this problem, the use of hydrological signatures has been proposed (Gupta et al., 2008; Euser et al., 2013; Hrachowitz et al., 2014; Fenicia et al., 2018; Kavetski et al., 2018 ). According to this methodology, a model can only be accepted as behavioral if it reproduces the observed signatures well, along with observed sequences of streamflow. An example of such a signature-based constraint is the long-term runoff coefficient (LRC) of a watershed (Kiraz et al., 2023 ); the simulated LRC should equal the observed LRC within the margin of errors. It is believed that the effect of errors in precipitation and streamflow will be reduced over a long timescale because of cancellation of errors (e.g., Kavetski et al., 2018 ). These constraints can be referred to as soft constraints. In this study, the role of signature-based soft constraints in identifying behavioral models will also be explored. The use of soft constraints can be particularly beneficial in ungauged catchments (e.g., Dal Molin et al., 2023 ). The objectives of the study were as follows:(1) To test the suitability of DT-based LoAs for evaluating a conceptual hydrological model,  (2) To understand the impact of model input and observed streamflow uncertainties on hydrological model evaluation,  (3) To evaluate the capability of streamflow-based signatures (soft constraints) in identifying nonbehavioral models,  (4) To explain why a model is rejected or accepted as a behavioral model.    The main novelty of this paper lies in using DTs to evaluate a hydrological model in the LoA framework. This method accounts for both model input (e.g., precipitation) and streamflow uncertainty; other LoA-based methods (except the runoff-ratio method) neglect precipitation uncertainty. A significant advantage of DTs is that they can be used for regionalization of streamflow to evaluate a hydrological model at ungauged locations at a time-step level, while accounting for uncertainties. Gupta et al. (2023a)  presented an empirical and theoretical analysis of the DTs for defining LoAs, but they did not test the method for a hydrological model. This study presents the modeling analysis using the LoAs thus defined. Also, some new results regarding the behavior of QRF defined LoAs are presented in this study. Further, a well-known spectral property of streamflow time series called long-term persistence (discussed below) has been used as streamflow-based signature – this signature can be applied at both gauged and ungauged locations. The long-term persistence of a time series translates to a Hurst exponent (H) of the time series between 0.5 and 1.0. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this paper provides the first attempt to test the utility of H as a signature for model evaluation at both gauged and ungauged locations (see Westerberg and McMillan, 2015; McMillan, 2021  for a review of signatures used in hydrology; also see Yadav et al., 2007; Shafii and Tolson, 2015 ). We note that other spectral properties such as the auto-correlation function etc. have been used in earlier studies to calibrate hydrological models (Winsemius et al., 2009; Castiglioni et al., 2010; De Vleeschouwer and Pauwels, 2013 ), but long-term persistence has not been used in this context. Typical hydrological modeling studies calibrate a model either in time domain or signature domain (e.g., Coxon et al., 2014 ). The ‘signature domain only’ calibration is done to avoid the biases introduced by systematic errors in hydrological data (Fenicia et al., 2018 ), but signatures may lose some of the information contained in streamflow time series especially the timing information. Thus, this study combines calibration in time domain and signature domain. It will be shows that using only LoAs over streamflows may result in acceptance of physically unrealistic simulations; signatures are used to identify these unrealistic simulations.  2 Hydrological model and data 2.1 Hydrological model The Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA; Burnash, 1995 ) model along with a snow model and a runoff routing model was used in this study. SAC-SMA has been used in several studies to simulate streamflow (Sorooshian et al., 1993; Vrugt et al., 2006; Kratzert et al., 2019 ). It is a conceptual model with several parameters requiring calibration. Two other models, a snow model and a runoff routing model, were used along with SAC-SMA to model snowmelt and quick runoff routing. The SAC-SMA model simulates infiltration, percolation, evapotranspiration, and surface runoff. The runoff routing model routes the runoff to a streamflow outlet. Evapotranspiration calculations were based on potential evapotranspiration calculated using the Hamon equation (Hamon, 1963 ). The snow model used was snow-17 (Anderson, 1976 ), and the routing model used was a unit hydrograph represented by a gamma distribution. The combined model has a total of 24 parameters that were varied within predefined ranges to simulate streamflow and other hydrological fluxes. A list of these parameters along with their ranges, as used in this study, is provided in Table 1  .  2.2 Study area Four subwatersheds in the St. Joseph River Watershed (SJRW) were used as test cases in this study (Fig. 1  ). SJRW drains a total area of approximately 3000 k m  2    , overlapping the states of Michigan, Indiana, and Ohio in eastern USA. Climate in this watershed is characterized by hot summers and cold winters, with precipitation falling throughout the year. Snowfall is an important component of the hydrological cycle in the SJRW with the contribution of snowfall to total precipitation in nearby gauges ranging between 5–7 % – the ratio was computed using the mean snow to liquid ratio of 12:1 (Baxter et al., 2005 ). The major land use types are cropland and forest (Mallya et al., 2020 ). The four SJRW stations are identified by their USGS (United States Geological Survey ) station numbers at the outlet where streamflows are measured. A list of these stations along with some of the characteristics of corresponding drainage areas are provided in Table 2  . Notably, the average lag between precipitation and streamflow at USGS-04178000 was approximately 1.5 days, much larger than that of the downstream station USGS-04180500 (0.886 days). The drainage area of USGS-04178000 also had a larger BFI and is underlaid by the Michindoh aquifer, which may be responsible for the larger delay between precipitation and streamflow peaks in this watershed.  2.3 Hydrological data Data from six NCDC (National Climate Data Center) precipitation gauges outside but near the SJRW were used to compute daily areal average precipitation using the Thiessen polygon method. Other meteorological data required for the SAC-SMA are average daily temperatures which were also available from the six NCDC stations. Mean daily streamflow data were available from the USGS website (USGS, 2016 accessed on Sep 02, 2018). Data from calendar years 2001–2016 were used in this study, with 2001–2010 data being used for identifying behavioral models and the remaining data being used for independent validation. For three of the gauges (04180500, 04180000, 04178000) the year 2001 was used as the warm-up period and the years 2002–2010 were used for model evaluation (or calibration). For the gauge 04179520, year 2002 was used as the warm-up period and the years 2003–2010 were used for model evaluation, because streamflow data for the year 2001 were not available for this station. In addition, data from 431 watersheds located in Ohio River Basin (ORB) were used to develop a machine learning (ML) model for the ungauged scenario as discussed below. Some details of these watersheds can be found in Gupta et al., (2023a) . Data from ORB were used to regionalize streamflow in the ungauged scenario and to augment the training data in the gauged scenario (explained below).  2.4 Computation of event runoff ratio To obtain some insights into precipitation and streamflow measurement uncertainty, event runoff ratios were computed for events in the available data (Beven and Smith, 2015; Beven, 2019 ). The rainfall-runoff events were separated and a master recession curve (MRC), determined for each catchment, was appended to each event. Subsequently, event runoff ratios of events were computed as the ratio of total observed streamflow volume (after appending the MRC) to total observed precipitation volume. The computed event runoff ratio can be highly uncertain for the events for which snowmelt is important; therefore, these events were excluded from the analysis. Snow affected events were identified as the ones that had average minimum temperature below 0 °  C   or were preceded by an event with average minimum temperature below 0 °  C   . The first condition removes the events with snowfall, and the second condition removes the events immediately after the snowfall event because melt from the preceding snowfall event may add to the runoff in the current event.   3 Model evaluation 3.1 Limits-of-Acceptability and likelihood function The details of LoA construction for SJRW and ORB using DTs can be found in Gupta et al. (2023a) . Briefly, a DT-based method called quantile random forest (QRF) was used to define LoA. QRF yields a distribution for the response variable for a given predictor vector. It divides the predictor space into several contiguous and non-overlapping sub-regions. This division is carried out using the calibration/training data; the algorithm for defining these sub-regions can be found in any ML textbook (e.g., Hastie et al., 2009 ). To determine the distribution of the response variable for any predictor vector, first the sub-region to which the predictor vector belongs is determined and then the training points falling in each sub-region are used to define the distribution. The process of division of predictor space into different sub-regions can be visualized as a tree (see Fig. 2 in Gupta et al., 2023a ). Division of predictor space is carried out iteratively which can be visualized as growth of the tree into different nodes. The nodes obtained after the final iteration are referred to as leaf nodes. To avoid overfitting, QRF develops several trees by bootstrapping the training data. In this study, QRF models were developed using the predictor variables listed in Table 3   and streamflow was the response variable. Therefore, QRF yielded a distribution of streamflow values for a given value of predictors at a timestep. This distribution represents the variability in recorded streamflow values for ‘similar’ hydrological conditions including the effects of errors in hydrological data. Note that the data in the relevant leaf nodes from different trees are collated together to define the streamflow distribution at a timestep. A similar argument to define LoAs was also made in Winsemius et al. (2009) ; these authors defined LoAs over a few streamflow signatures based on interannual variability of the signatures. Gupta et al. (2023a)  claimed that LoAs defined using QRF can account for both precipitation and streamflow uncertainty because QRF groups similar predictor variables (trainign points that are close to each other in predictor space) into leaf nodes and the large  difference between responses can be attributed to lack of relevant predictor variables, or inability of model to identify hydrologically similar timesteps, and/or errors in predictor variables (primarily precipitation and temperature in this study) and response variables (streamflow in this study). Note that some variability in leaf nodes would still exist even in the ideal case when all the relevant predictor variables were used for QRF development and the model inputs and observed output were error free. When constructing LoAs using QRF, one has to decide the lower and upper percentiles of a response variable in a leaf node to be used as the lower and upper LoAs. When defining the distribution of streamflow for a timestep, some streamflow values might be repeated across multiple trees. These values will get higher weight during the computations of percentiles. In what follows, the results corresponding to 1st percentile and 99.5th percentiles will be discussed in detail. The choice of these percentiles is somewhat arbitrary. These have been chosen so that as many as possible behaviors of rainfall-runoff response of the watershed, as suggested by the calibration data, are captured. The 97.5th percentiles were also used to define upper LoAs; some of these results are presented in Supplementary Information  (SI) and only sparingly discussed in the main text. In this study, three QRF models were used to test the applicability of LoA concept in three different scenarios:(1) Gauged-single scenario (LoAGS ): The QRF models were trained using data from only the watersheds where the LoAs were to be constructed. For example, to construct LoAs for the station 04180500, data from only this station were used. In this case, the meteorological data were used as inputs and streamflow as output.  (2) Gauged scenario (LoAG ): The QRF models were trained using data from multiple watersheds including data from the station where LoA were to be constructed. In this study, data from 431 watersheds in Ohio River Basin (ORB) along with the data from the four SJRW stations were used to develop this model (see Gupta et al., 2023a  for details).  (3) Ungauged scenario (LoAUG ): The QRF model was trained using data from only the ORB watersheds; data from the four SJRW stations were not used to train the model. This scenario represents the ungauged case when data are not available at the station where a hydrological model is to be evaluated.    The gauge-single scenario represents the case where we focus on data from a single watershed to develop a hydrological model. The gauged scenario represents the case where data from several watershed are available and are used here to test the utility of such a dataset in terms of model validation in a particular watershed – this has become a popular practice in ML application for streamflow prediction (e.g., Kratzert et al., 2019, 2024 ). To keep the manuscript concise, the results of gauged scenario are discussed in the SI only (Text S3; Figs. S9–S14 ). The ungauged scenario is used to test the usefulness of data available across multiple nearby watersheds in terms of model evaluation in a particular watershed where streamflow data are not available. The LoAs were constructed using data from the calibration period (2001–2010) and the remaining data (2011–2016) were kept as an independent validation period. In the ungauged scenario, the QRF model was trained using data from the 431 ORB watersheds and data from the SJRW stations were not used. Therefore, we expect that the transfer of information from gauged to ungauged location would incur additional uncertainty. Gupta et al. (2023a)  tested the developed QRF models in terms of their ability to simulate observed streamflow. The tests were carried out in the ungauged scenario as it is a more stringent test. The NSEs between observed and simulated streamflows obtained for the stations 04180500, 04180000, 04179520, and 04178000 were 0.57, 0.63, 0.60, and 0.36, respectively (See Gupta et al., 2023a  for more details). These NSEs seem good enough to define LoAs except for the station 04178000 (Gupta et al., 2023a ). Despite the low NSE of 0.36, LoAs developed for station 04178000 were nevertheless quite useful. Gupta et al. (2023a)  further showed that LoAs constructed for these four stations accounted for the effects of streamflow and precipitation measurement uncertainty. The effect of aleatoric streamflow uncertainty was approximated using the probabilistic rating curve analysis. Effects of potential epistemic uncertainties in peak streamflow values were also tested: it was shown that the LoAs obtained would envelop the true peak streamflow values even if the observed values underestimated the true values by up to 100 %. The typical errors in peak streamflow have been reported to be 20–40 % (Di Baldassarre and Montanari, 2009 ). The uncertainty in precipitation was estimated using the Monte-Carlo sampling of the rain-gauges without replacement. Further, the LoAs obtained using the QRF method were compared against those obtained by using the runoff-ratio method. Some other properties of the LoAs obtained using the QRF method are discussed below. Streamflow time series were simulated by the hydrologic model using a total of 10  6     parameter sets sampled uniformly from the parameter space (Table 1 ). While this is a small sample given the large number of free parameters, it is still useful to achieve the objectives of this study. A parameter set was considered behavioral if it satisfied the following four criteria:(1) At least 1 - α   100 %    of the simulated streamflows are enveloped by the LoA.  (2) At least 1 - α   100 %    of the simulated rising limb flows are enveloped by the LoA.  (3) At least 1 - α   100 %    of the simulated recession flow are enveloped by the LoA.  (4) At least 1 - α   100 %    of the simulated peak streamflow values that were greater than 90 percentile streamflow value, are enveloped by the LoA.    These criteria were used to ensure that all parts of the hydrograph are well simulated by a behavioral parameter set. Otherwise, it is possible that a parameter set simulates the high streamflow within LoAs but does not simulate the low flows well at several timesteps. These criteria could be varied depending upon the intended application of the model (Beven and Lane, 2022 ). Two values of α    were used: α = 0.05    (5 % outliers) and α = 0.00    (no outliers). The α = 0.05    is used to allow for outliers since LoAs are defined using only 10 years of data, leaving room to accommodate future surprises. When α = 0.00   , a parameter set was considered behavioral only if it simulated streamflow within LoA at all the time steps (no outliers). Note that the choice of outliers allowed for identifying models and the percentiles range used to define LoAs are two independent choices. The LoAs are defined using the observed  data while outliers refer to the timesteps at which a simulation  is allowed to violate the LoAs. Each behavioral model was assigned a likelihood value using the following procedure. First, each time-step in the calibration period was assigned a score using the equation (Hollaway et al., 2018 )(1) Scor e t  = ( y ^  t  - y t  )  / ( L U t  - y t  )  , ( y ^  t  - y t  )  ≥ 0    ( y ^  t  - y t  )  / ( y t  - L L t  )  , ( y ^  t  - y t  )  < 0             where Scor e t     denotes the score value at timestep t   ,  y ^  t     denotes simulated value at timestep t   , y t     denotes observed value at timestep t   , L U t     (99.5th or 97.5th) and L L t     (1st percentile) denote the upper and lower LoAs at timestep t   , respectively. A positive (negative) score value at a time step implies overprediction (underprediction). Second, each timestep was assigned a weight based on their score as follows:(2) W t  = 1 - S c o r e t  , 0 ≤ S c o r e t  ≤ 1    1 + S c o r e t     2  , - 1 ≤ S c o r e t  < 0        0 , o t h e w i s e              Finally, the likelihood L M       of a model M    was computed as follows:(3) L M    = C 1 T  ∑ t = 1  T  y t  - y ^  t     ( W  t  + δ )       - 1   ,    δ = min { W t  | t ∈ 1 , T    , W t  ≠ 0 } ,         where T    denotes the number of calibration timesteps and C    is the scaling factor so that likelihood values for different models sum up to one. Note that the likelihoods at different timesteps are summed rather than multiplied to avoid stretching of likelihood surface due to bad simulations at a few timesteps where bad simulations at these timesteps may be due to uncertainties in data. Underpredictions were penalized more heavily in the computations of weights (Eq. (2) ) because the QRF defined LoAs such that models with consistent underpredictions are more likely to be accepted than the ones with overpredictions as both observed and simulated streamflow are bounded below by zero and L L t     defined by QRF are close to zero; thus, LoAs are biased toward models underpredicting streamflow as behavioral. Further, this likelihood function was defined following the intuition that (1) the models that simulate streamflow with large deviations from the observed streamflow should get lower likelihood, and (2) the timesteps at which streamflow is simulated outside the defined LoAs should be penalized more heavily. Predictive uncertainty at a timestep was computed as the 99 % credible region defined using the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of simulated streamflows using behavioral parameter sets and for both calibration and validation periods. The percentile values were defined based on the cumulative distribution function (CDF) at each timestep using the weighted sum of the likelihood values as defined in Eq. (3) . The likelihoods were computed using the calibration period and the same likelihoods were used for the validation period. Note that the 99 % predictive uncertainty band will not necessarily envelop 99 % of observations even in the calibration period; this is because the band is formed by the simulated streamflow time series that are identified based on LoAs, not the measured streamflows. However, observations that are missed by the predictive uncertainty band would indicate either model structural errors and/or large epistemic errors in model inputs and/or observed outputs.  3.2 Streamflow-based signatures Five streamflow-based hydrological signatures were used to further constrain the acceptable model behaviors. These constraints include the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the streamflow time-series, the Hurst exponent (H) of the streamflow time series, the baseflow index (BFI), the flow duration curve (FDC), and the long-term runoff coefficient (LRC). The observed and simulated signatures were compared to check whether the simulated signatures reflect the expected watershed function. These signatures are summarized in Table 4  . For a model to be accepted as behavioral by the ACF constraint, the observed and simulated ACF for the lags 1–100 days should pass the nonparametric Wilcoxon paired rank sum test at 5 % significance level. For a model to be acceptable as behavioral by the FDC constraint, the observed and simulated streamflow time series should pass the nonparametric paired Kolmogorov-Smirnov D test at 5 % significance level. For a model to be accepted as behavioral by the LRC constraint, the simulated LRCs should be between 0.6 L R C o b s      and 1.4 L R C o b s     , where LRCobs  denotes observed LRC. Signature values may also be affected by data uncertainty (Westerberg and McMillan, 2015 ); therefore, the acceptance criteria on these signatures were set to wide margins to avoid false negative errors (rejecting a good model). For example, Westerberg and McMillan (2015)  reported ≈ 20 %    uncertainty in LRC with rain-gauge density of 1 135  k m  - 2      for the 135 k m  2     Brue catchment, accounting for both precipitation and streamflow uncertainties. To compute observed BFI, first baseflow was estimated using the method proposed by Collischonn and Fan (2013)  and then, BFI was computed as the ratio of total baseflow and total streamflow. Simulated baseflow was obtained directly from the SAC-SMA as one of the outputs. In this study, the method of Collischonn and Fan (2013)  was used to compute a range of BFI values instead of just one BFI value (Appendix A ). Basically, an Eckhardt filter (Eckhardt, 2005 ) was applied iteratively where each iteration produced a baseflow time-series. One of the parameters required by the filter is BF I m a x      which is an uncertain parameter; in each iteration BF I m a x      was fixed to the BFI value computed in the previous iteration. The iterative procedure was stopped when the BFI value converged. According to the BFI constraint, a model was accepted as behavioral only if it simulated BFI within this range (see Table 2  for the range of BFI values used for different test watersheds). Again, very relaxed limits are applied on the simulated BFI because of uncertainties involved in computing BFI from the observed streamflow data. The Hurst exponent of a simulated streamflow time series was estimated using the periodogram of the time series. Periodogram of a time series is very noisy irrespective of the amount of data available to estimate it (Priestley, 1982 ); therefore, a piecewise linear curve was fitted to the estimated periodogram (Kim et al., 2016 ). The streamflow periodogram can be approximated by ω    1 - 2 H      as ω    approaches zero (Beran, 1994 ), where H    denotes the Hurst exponent and ω    denotes the frequency in radians/day. Thus, H    was estimated by(4) H = - s 2  + 0.5 ,     where s    denotes the slope of the periodogram on log–log plot near ω = 0   . There are several methods to estimate H    (see Montanari et al., 1999 ) but these methods yield significantly different value of H   . A good method to estimate value of H    is to fit a stochastic FARIMA model to streamflow time series (Montanari et al., 1997; Gupta et al., 2023b ); but this method is computationally infeasible for this study as it takes significant computational resources for just one streamflow time series, making it practically impossible to implement for 10  6     simulated time series. Therefore, Equation (4)  was adopted in this study. It is known that the H    value for a typical streamflow time series lies between 0.5 and 1 (Montanari et al., 1997; Mudelsee, 2007 ) because of long-range memory. Indeed, Gupta et al. (2023b)  fitted FARIMA models to streamflow time series from more than 500 watersheds across the USA; all of the models were well fitted to the time series with H    value between 0.5 and 1. Therefore, H    value of a simulated streamflow time series should fall between 0.5 and 1 for a model to be accepted as behavioral according to this constraint.
