A relaxed limit has been used on H    because estimating H    values requires large amount of data that are not typically available and to avoid rejecting good models. It will be shown that even this relaxed limit on H    can be helpful in identifying non-behavioral simulations. Since the streamflow time series were not de-seasonalized before computing the H values, the computed H values will also reflect the effect of streamflow seasonality. The periodogram of a stationary stochastic time series is the sample estimate of power spectral density which, in turn, is the square of the absolute values of the Fourier coefficients of the corresponding autocorrelation function (Priestley, 1982 ). Therefore, signature ACF and H used in this study are closely related to each other. However, the ACF signature cannot be used in the ungauged scenario. But the Hurst exponent can be used in both gauged and ungauged scenarios, since we constrain H value of simulated streamflow between 0.5 and 1.0, irrespective of the H value of the observed streamflow series. Similarly, none of the other signatures (FDC, BFI, and LRC) can be used in the ungauged scenario unless the value of these signatures is estimated using the data from donor watersheds which themselves have significant uncertainties associated with them (e.g., Dal Molin et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, the simulations with extremely high or low values of BFI may still be rejected as non-behavioral in ungauged basins. In this study, simulations with BFI values of less than 0.10 or greater than 0.90 were considered non-behavioral in the ungauged scenario.  3.3 Other evaluation metrics To analyze the behavioral models, three other performance metrics were used: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE; Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ), relative peak bias, and peak timing errors. NSE is computed using the equation:(5) NSE = 1 - ∑ t  Q t  - Q ^  t     2   ∑ t  Q t  - Q  ¯      2        where Q t     and  Q ^  t     denote the observed and simulated streamflows at timestep t   , and  Q  ¯      denotes the average observed steamflow over the period of evaluation. Relative peak bias and peak timing errors were computed for the peak streamflow timesteps, with streamflow magnitude greater than 90 percentile streamflow value over the calibration period. Relative peak bias was calculated as:(6) R e l a t i v e  p e a k  b i a s = 1 T  p   ∑ i  Q i  - Q ^  i      Q  ¯    p       where T  p     denotes the number of peak timesteps used to compute the peak simulate error, Q i     and   Q ^  i     denote the observed simulated streamflow value at time i   , and  Q  ¯    p     denote the average of observed streamflow over the peak timesteps. Similarly, peak timing error was computed as:(7) P e a k  t i m i n g  e r r o r = ∑ i  t ^  i  - t  i      T  p       where t i     and  t ^  i     denote the observed and simulate time of peak. There were some peaks without corresponding simulated peak by a model; the delay was set to 6 days for these peaks. Similar to the relative peak bias, relative rising limb and recession limb biases were also computed for rising and recession limbs of the hydrograph, respectively.   4 Results 4.1 Limits-of-acceptability (LoAs) Fig. 2   shows the LoAs obtained by the QRF method in the gauged-single and ungauged scenarios along with observed streamflow and precipitation. Here, 99.5th percentiles were used to define upper LoAs. The LoAs obtained by using 97.5th percentile values are shown in Fig. S1  (SI). The two LoAs envelop the observations at most of the time-steps. This is also evident from Table 5   which lists the fractions of observations enveloped by the LoAs. The LoAs were the widest in the ungauged scenario which is desirable since we want to include as many rainfall-runoff behaviors as possible and we expect larger uncertainty in model simulations at ungauged basins. In the gauged-single scenario, the lower LoAs were close to zero at all the timesteps. Models consistently underpredicting observed streamflow are less likely to be rejected even if they are bad simulators of a watershed’s hydrological processes, thus needing to penalize underpredictions more heavily in the likelihood function (Eq. (2) ). Similarly, the LoAs allowed large overpredictions of the low flows. There were timing errors between observed peaks and LoA peaks (for example, at time step 2630); the timing errors were pronounced at gauge 04178000. These timing errors could be due to timing and magnitude errors in precipitation, and/or due to discretization of precipitation and streamflow to daily scale (Gupta et al., 2023a ). A notable feature is the presence of peaks in LoAs, especially in the ungauged scenario, at some time steps where the streamflow is in a recession phase; again likely due to potential epistemic uncertainty in precipitation. These features have been discussed in detail in Gupta et al. (2023a) . To get insights into the uncertainties in the model input precipitation and streamflow data, event runoff ratios were plotted against total precipitation and initial event streamflow (Fig. 3  ), where initial event streamflow was used as a proxy for antecedent moisture condition (Beven, 2019 ). A wide range of runoff ratios were observed for a given precipitation volume and initial event streamflow. There were some events with either very small runoff ratio for large precipitation volumes and very large runoff ratios for small precipitation volumes. Two events had runoff ratios significantly greater than 1; which are disinformative for model evaluation. But note that the event with runoff ratio ≈ 2.1    was preceded by a snowmelt event; therefore, runoff ratio computation is still uncertain for this event even though the snow affected events have been removed from the analysis. The other disinformative event occurred in summer. These results suggest large uncertainties in the model input precipitation and/or streamflow data. The QRF model is used to define LoAs at each timestep by identifying other timesteps that are deemed ‘similar’ in the sense defined by the QRF method (see Gupta et al., 2023a ), that is, based on similarity of predictor variables. To get insights into the LoAs defined by the QRF model in the gauge-single scenario, LoAs at three timesteps (referred to as t 1  , t 2  ,    and t 3    ) were analyzed in more detail. The areal average cumulative precipitation over previous 1–6 days were plotted against the streamflow corresponding to the time steps that were identified by the QRF model as similar to timesteps t 1  , t 2  ,    and t 3     (Figs. 4–6    ). The streamflows and the corresponding cumulative precipitations at t 1  , t 2  ,    and t 3     are marked by the red crosses in these plots. Each plot shows the lower LoA (1st percentile) and upper LoA (99.5th percentile). Some timesteps may be repeated in a group (due to repetition in leaf nodes across different trees) and, therefore, get higher weights during the computation of percentiles; therefore, it is possible that more than 1.5 % of the timesteps fall outside the LoA. Each Figure also lists the runoff ratio of the events to which these three timesteps belonged. The timestep shown in Fig. 4  (referred to as t 1    ) had the highest recorded streamflow in the calibration period. The QRF identified some timesteps that were similar to the timestep t 1     in terms of precipitation sequences during the past six days; but it also identified many timesteps that were dissimilar to the timestep t 1     in that sense. This is because QRF gives different importance to a predictor variable in different trees (Fig. S2  in SI); some timesteps that are dissimilar in terms of precipitation but similar in terms of temperature can be grouped together. Thus, the timesteps that are hydrologically dissimilar may be identified as similar by the QRF model. Notably many timesteps selected by the QRF, that were indeed similar to the timestep t 1     in terms of precipitation, had wide range of streamflow values: from ≈ 0    to ≈ 440 m  3  s  - 1     . Fig. 4  also shows that the streamflows were skewed to the low values which is partly because of small number of peak events and partly because of QRF grouping hydrologically dissimilar timesteps in the leaf nodes. This Figure, along with Fig. 3 , suggests that the low value of lower LoAs at peaks is due to errors in the model input precipitation and/or observed streamflow, due to skewness of the streamflow data toward the low values, and due to QRF model grouping hydrologically dissimilar timesteps in the leaf nodes. The timestep t 2     shown in Fig. 5  has very low runoff ratio of 0.08. This event was not affected by snow, and the observed streamflow did not respond to the rainfall pulse at all. The low runoff ratio is because of dry antecedent conditions and an overestimation of precipitation magnitude and/or spatial variability of precipitation. There were many timesteps with similar history of precipitation sequences with a wide range of streamflow values, resulting in wide LoAs. It also suggests that the antecedent moisture conditions are not well captured by the predictor variables supplied to the QRF model. Fig. 6  shows the timestep t 3     with a typical runoff ratio value. Again, the timesteps grouped as similar by QRF had very wide range of streamflows, but the LoA range determined by 1st and 99.5th percentiles were still narrow because several low flow timesteps got higher weights during the computation of percentiles. But note the LoAs were still wide relative to the observed streamflow. In summary, these results suggest large errors in streamflow measurements and the interpolated areal average precipitation, neglect of spatial variability of precipitation, skewness of the streamflow data toward low values, and identification of hydrologically dissimilar timesteps is the reason for wide LoAs at the extreme flow (both high and low flow) timesteps. Some suggestions to improve upon the QRF algorithm to obtain tighter LoAs have been made later in the paper.  4.2 Analysis of gauged-single scenario (LoAGS ) Table 6   lists the number of models accepted as behavioral for the gauged single and the ungauged scenarios, for the two cases: (i) when 5 % outliers were allowed and (ii) when no outliers were allowed. The number of behavioral models were very different when 99.5th percentiles were used as upper LoAs compared to when 97.5th percentiles were used as upper LoAs. The number of accepted behavioral models were significantly larger in the ungauged scenario which is expected given the wider LoAs in this scenario. Interestingly, when no outliers were allowed and 97.5th percentiles were used as the upper LoA, no behavioral models were identified in the gauged-single scenario for three watersheds. Fig. 7   shows the calibration and validation period compliance with LoAs of the behavioral models determined in the gauged-single scenario. The compliance of behavioral models during the validation period ranged from 50 % to 100 % (Fig. 7 ). Typically, a wide range of validation compliance values were obtained for a given calibration compliance. The validation compliance of the most models was smaller than the calibration compliance indicating non-stationarity in the data. In early GLUE applications and even in some recent studies, NSE has been used as the informal likelihood measure. But NSE may be significantly impacted by a few critical timesteps (e.g., Clark et al., 2021 ) making it unfit for model evaluation, especially if the critical timesteps are impacted by the uncertainties. Fig. 8   shows the scatter plot of likelihood values against NSEs for behavioral models when 5 % outliers were allowed, to understand the effect of errors in data on NSE. The models with low NSEs were always assigned low likelihood values. Models with high NSEs were assigned a range of likelihood values from the smallest to the largest. Thus, behavioral models with low NSE values will have very small contributions to predictive uncertainty computation. Importantly, several models with high NSE values will also have small contributions to predictive uncertainties because many of these models violated LoAs at several timesteps (but at less than 5 % timesteps) and these timesteps were penalized heavily during the likelihood computation. Note that several models with NSEs greater than 0.5 were not even accepted as behavioral. To further investigate the properties of the behavioral models, the observed streamflows were divided into seven ranges: 0–5 percentiles, 5–20 percentiles, 20–40 percentiles, 40–60 percentiles, 60–80 percentiles, 80–95 percentiles, and 95–100 percentiles. Fig. 9  a and b show the score values (Eq. (1) ) assigned to different behavioral simulations for the seven observed streamflow ranges at gauge 04180500. The width of the shaded part is proportional to the probability density of scores. The low flows were overestimated while the high flows were underestimated by most of the behavioral models. This general pattern was more pronounced when no outliers were allowed. This pattern has been observed in many other studies (e.g., Yilmaz et al., 2008; Kratzert et al., 2019 ), especially where some form of mean-squared-error is used as objective function. But such an optimization was not carried out in this study, suggesting other factors, such as aggregation of the precipitation and streamflow data to daily scale, might be partly responsible for this result. Fig. 9 a also shows that some behavioral models underpredicted low flows and overpredicted high flows, violating the LoAs. Fig. 9  shows that many models violated LoAs at the timesteps with 5–20 and 95–100 percentile flow ranges. That is, the outliers had to be allowed for the extremely high and low flows. Fig. 9 c shows that many behavioral models violated the upper LoA (overprediction) during the low flows. While the overpredictions of low flows could be justified to some extent because of overestimation of areal average precipitation in the preceding events and/or the current event, model structural deficiency also seems to be contributing to the large over predictions. This raises the question if the models violating the upper LoAs at the low flow timesteps could be rejected as unfit-for-purpose? This is discussed later. Fig. 10   shows 99 % credible regions (CR) for calibration and validation periods for the gauge 04180500, for the cases of 5 % outliers allowed (CR5) and no outliers allowed (CR0). As expected, the CR5 was wider than CR0 at all the timesteps. Most of the observations were enveloped by both the CRs. Some observations were not enveloped by CR0 but were enveloped by CR5; also, some observations were missed by both the CRs. At several peak flow timesteps, observations were very close to upper bounds of CR, especially in the case of CR0 because most of the behavioral models underpredicted the high flows as discussed above. The CR0 missed several peaks. At some peak flow timesteps, there was a timing error between observed and predicted streamflows which might be due to model deficiency, errors in precipitation timing, and/or aggregation of temporal variability to daily scale and aggregation of spatial variability to the watershed scale. For example, at timesteps 1525, 1571, 1628, 1640, 1656, and 1661 during the validation period (Fig. 10 b), observed streamflows peaked one day before the simulated streamflow peaks. Also, there was no lag between precipitation peaks and observed streamflow peaks at these timesteps, implying timing errors in the validation phase are likely due to model deficiencies or daily discretization. Such errors were fewer in the calibration period. However, there were many timesteps with one day lag between precipitation and observed streamflow in the calibration period. The credible regions obtained for the other three stations are shown in Figs. S3–S5  (in SI).  4.3 Usefulness of streamflow signatures for constraining the simulations in the gauged-single scenario Fig. 11   shows the percentage of behavioral models accepted after constraining the models by various streamflow-based signatures, for the gauged-single scenario. Clearly, all the signatures, except the FDC, identified some models as non-behavioral that were identified as behavioral by the LoA constraints alone. The signature BFI had the most discrimination power, as using both LoA and BFI as the constraints resulted in the least number of behavioral models. The signature H also had significant discrimination power. All except one simulation had H values greater than 0.5, and several simulations had H values greater than 1 which could be rejected as unfit-for-purpose. Fig. 12   compares the 99 % credible region over streamflows with LoA only constraint (CRL) and with all the constraints (CRLS), for the station 04180500. The CRLS were wider than the CRL at several timesteps especially at the peaks. CRLS enveloped the observations at most of the time steps. There were timing errors in CRLS between observed peaks and the simulated peaks. The results were similar for other stations (Figs. S6–S8 , SI). Some of the peak values were missed by the CRLS, suggesting that the SAC-SMA may be limited for peak flow simulations in the SJRW, or that areal average precipitation data have large errors, or that sub-daily scale variability and spatial variability of precipitation are really important in the SJRW.  4.4 Fitness-for-purpose of the evaluated models Fig. 13   shows characteristics of behavioral models obtained after applying different constraints: LoA with 5 % outliers (blue dots), LoA with no outliers (orange), and LoA with 5 % outliers and signature constraints (green dots). Note that only BFI and LRC were used to determine fitness-for-purpose among the indices shown in Fig. 13 ; other indices were used only to get better insights into the modeling. Most of the behavioral models obtained without allowing any outliers, were physically unrealistic with BFIs close to 1 and LRCs smaller than 0.25 (Fig. 13 a). Because these models had large evapotranspiration (indicated by small LRC) and simulated baseflow as the only source of water in river, these models had very large relative peak bias (Fig. 13 b). This explains why the peaks were missed when no outliers were allowed (Fig. 10 ). Moreover, all the models that did not violate the LoAs at any timestep had positive recession and rising limb biases (Fig. 13 c), implying that these models underpredicted the observed streamflows at most of the timesteps which is again because of the overestimation of ET by these models. Therefore, the models that satisfied the wide LoA without any outliers can be rejected as unfit-for-purpose. Among the behavioral models that were physically realistic according to the signature constraints, almost all violated the LoAs at some calibration period timesteps, implying that these models would also be unfit-for-purpose if the limits were applied strictly. But allowing for outliers resulted in some simulations that could be used for predictions. Among these models, several had large peak timing errors and large peak magnitude errors (Fig. 13 b). The large timing errors of these models was due to slow routing of quick runoff, suggesting that these models are not fit-for-purpose; these models were accepted as behavioral because of the wide LoAs and allowance of outliers. Several models selected based on LoA with 5 % outliers had a wide range of rising and recession limb biases. NSE values were used to assess the quality of fit of the simulated streamflow time series to the observed streamflow time series (Fig. 13 d). The NSE values ranged from < 0    to ≈ 0.70   . A wide range of validation NSEs were obtained for a given calibration NSE. Many models had a low calibration NSE but a higher validation NSE. In summary, none of the evaluated models simulated all aspects of streamflow time series satisfactorily, even given the wide LoAs defined by the QRF. While some outliers must be allowed since the LoAs are based on the limited calibration period data, we expect that the main difficulty should be in defining LoAs for the extremely low and high flows. Specifically, the lower LoAs during the low flows and the upper LoAs during the high flows may be too close to observations, potentially resulting in violation of these LoAs even by a good model. On the other hand, QRF allowed large underpredictions of the high flows and large overpredictions of the low flows: The model violating these LoAs indicate model structural deficiency. Therefore, the behavioral models obtained by allowing 5 % outliers were further constrained where a model was retained as behavioral only if it did not violate the upper LoAs during the bottom 20 % flows, lower LoAs during the top 10 % flows, and did not violate the LoAs during other timesteps. This stricter constraint reduced the number of behavioral models from 48,345 to 856 for the station USGS-04180500; most of these 856 models were again physically unrealistic (very high BFI and very high ET). Therefore, all the 1-million simulations evaluated in this study can be deemed unfit-for-purpose.  4.5 Qualitative analysis of some models to understand the impact of uncertainty To further understand the effects of various uncertainties on model simulations, Fig. 14   shows the streamflow time series simulated by three models (parameter sets of the SAC-SMA). These models had very different physical characteristics and fits to the observed time series. The model-1 with smallest calibration NSE (=0.14) also had the smallest peak bias. The low NSE of this model resulted from the model significantly overestimating streamflow during summer. Further the model-1 had large LRC of 0.49 indicating underestimation of evapotranspiration and/or overestimation of areal average precipitation in summer. The models 2 and 3 had calibration NSE of 0.54 and 0.69 with peak biases of 0.44 and 0.43, respectively. These two models had different BFIs: 0.35 and 1.00, respectively. The model-3 is clearly physically unrealistic with BFI of 1.00 event though it had the best fit to the data with NSE of 0.69: the large NSE of this model is likely due to compensation of the areal average precipitation overestimation by the overestimation of watershed’s water retention capacity during the summer months. The event around timestep 2800 that occurred during summer months had the event runoff ratio of 0.05 and had a significant amount of observed areal average precipitation (>60 mm precipitation within a day). All the three models significantly overestimated the streamflow for this event indicating that the overestimation of areal average precipitation, during this event and/or the preceding event, is dominating the structural errors. Effects of the precipitation overestimation can be seen on subsequent overestimation of the low flows. The event around timestep 2730 recorded an increase in observed streamflow with two peaks but a little precipitation was observed during this event; in fact, no precipitation was recorded within the preceding four days (including the peak day) of the second peak. This suggests that the areal average precipitation of this event is underestimated. The models-2 and 3 had peak timing and magnitude errors for the first two events. There were small observed streamflow peaks before these events but no precipitation indicating that precipitation was underestimated which resulted in drier simulated antecedent conditions compared to the true antecedent conditions. This contributed to delay and underestimation of these peaks. Fig. 14  illustrates how uncertainties in model input precipitation introduces errors in simulated streamflow in a complex manner which can be difficult to separate from model structural errors. This also suggests that increasing the number of simulations beyond the 1-million included in the analysis might not result in finding more acceptable and physically realistic simulations.  4.6 Analysis of ungauged scenario Fig. 15  a shows the percentage of behavioral models accepted by using different constraints in the ungauged scenario. A large number of models were accepted as behavioral when only LoA were used as constraints. The number of behavioral models reduced significantly when H or BFI were used as additional constraints. Note that very relaxed criterion for H and BFI were used in this case (Table 2 ). Fig. 15 b–e show calibration and validation NSEs of the behavioral models obtained after applying all the constraints. Even after applying all the constraints, a large number of models were accepted as behavioral, implying a larger uncertainty is associated with prediction in ungauged basins than in gauged basins. The NSE of the behavioral models ranged from negative to strong positive values. Fig. 16   shows the 99 % credible regions when model evaluation was done using LoA constraints only (CRL) and using both LoA and signature constraints (CRLS); similar plots for other stations are shown in SI (Figs. S15–S17 ). Both CRL and CRLS enveloped most of the observations. Interestingly, CRLS were wider than CRL at most of the timesteps even though CRLS were created using much smaller number of simulations. These results illustrate the challenge associated with prediction at ungauged basins.   5 Discussion Fig. 14  illustrates that a model may not be able to simulate some events because of uncertainties in data. The errors in streamflow simulation may be due to errors in areal average precipitation time series, uncertainty in true precipitation intensity due to discretization of input precipitation to daily scale which can result in both peak timing and magnitude errors, neglect of spatial variability of precipitation, and errors in extremely low and high streamflow estimation from the gauge height data. Timing error of 1-day may also occur for an event due to daily discretization if the most of the event precipitation occurred later in the day. Therefore, a model evaluation method must consider these uncertainties. This paper presented an application of QRF-based LoA in evaluating the hydrological model SAC-SMA, where the LoA were defined for streamflow time series. This allowed the evaluation of models (i.e., parameter sets of the model structure) individually for each time step. A total of 10  6     parameters sets were sampled from the prior parameter ranges. This is a small set given that the total number of free parameters was 24. However, useful insights could be obtained using this set. Further, five streamflow-based signatures were used along with LoA to reject the models that could simulate streamflow within the LoA but still could not reproduce specific aspects of streamflow dynamics. Two of the subjective choices associated with the QRF-based LoA method are: (1) What quantiles should be used to define the lower and upper LoA bounds, and (2) how many and how should the outliers be allowed. Allowance for outliers is required because of the finite amount of data used to define LoAs and the dominance of epistemic uncertainties in hydrological data (Beven and Lane, 2019; Gupta et al., 2023a ) along with aleatoric uncertainties (de Oliveira and Vrugt, 2022 ). It is possible that a model simulates low and medium flows well but provides consistently poor simulations of a few high flows observed in the calibration period. Thus, a poor model might be accepted if allowance for outliers is not made carefully. Similarly, a good model might be rejected because it violates the LoAs at a few time steps if no outliers are allowed. We selected outliers in a manner that a model is accepted as behavioral only if it simulates all parts of the streamflow time series (rising limb, recession limb, and peaks) consistent with the observations. There can be other ways of allowing for outliers, depending on the purpose of the modeling exercise and available information about the uncertainties in data. For example, Beven et al. (2022a, b)  accepted some models that satisfied LoAs at largest observed peak timesteps while allowing for outliers at other timesteps. The behavioral models produced calibration and validation NSE values ranging from less than 0 to ≈    0.70 (Figs. 13 and 15 ). The signature-based constraints in addition to LoA significantly reduced the number of behavioral models. Among the five signatures-based constraints used in this study, the baseflow index (BFI) and the Hurst exponent (H) were the most useful for the four watersheds used in this study, but the importance of a signature depends upon the watershed being considered (Coxon et al., 2014 ). The important point here is that several simulations accepted as behavioral by the LoA constraint alone produced unrealistic streamflow dynamics. In fact, the majority of the models that did not violate LoAs at any calibration timestep were physically unrealistic. One interpretation is that the uncertainties in hydrological data were so large that several models with poor NSE values could not be rejected. On the other hand, many models with high NSE values were rejected (not shown), implying that these models simulated streamflows outside the wide LoAs more than 5 % of the time. Similarly, Beven et al. (2022a, b)  rejected all the parameter sets of TOPMODEL after applying all the constraints, even though the NSE values of several rejected models were strong. Beven et al. (2022a, b)  defined LoA using the runoff ratio method that accounts for both precipitation and streamflow uncertainties and also allowed for timing errors. Thus, these results suggest a departure from using widely used GoF measures alone as model evaluation criterion, in line with previous studies (e.g., Beven, 2019; McMillan, 2021 ). Gupta et al. (2008)  also suggested a similar shift in model evaluation practice, specifically emphasizing the role of multiple hydrological signatures in model evaluation. Another interpretation is that the QRF defined LoAs were too wide beyond the uncertainties in data and did not allow a rigorous test for model evaluation where, following Kirchner et al. (1996) , a rigorous test should have small false positive error. This study provides insights into the LoAs defined by the QRF model. The QRF defined LoAs were wide at the high and low flow timesteps because of (1) uncertainty in model input and observed output data (Figs. 3–6 ), (2) grouping of hydrologically dissimilar timesteps in the leaf node, and (3) fewer high and low flow timesteps (Figs. 4–6 ). Note that the different trees give different importance to a predictor variable while grouping the training points in the leaf nodes. This is why QRF identifies some timesteps as ‘similar’ that are hydrologically dissimilar. The wide LoAs are one of the reasons why several physically unrealistic models were accepted as behavioral. This suggests that a better definition of LoAs is required for a more rigorous test. In a future study, different ways of identifying similar timesteps using ML will be evaluated. For example, the node split condition in the decision tree may be modified so that the samples with similarity in terms of all the predictors variables are more likely to be grouped together in a leaf node. Streamflows at the previous timesteps could be used as predictor variables to better identify the timesteps with similar antecedent conditions. Other machine learning algorithms such as Long Short-Term Memory Network, which has been shown to yield state-of-the-art performance in streamflow simulations (Kratzert et al., 2019 ), may be used to better identify hydrologically ‘similar’ timesteps. These results also illustrate the inadequacy of NSE in terms of evaluating fitness-for-purpose of a model. Several authors (e.g., Gupta et al., 2009 ; Knoben et al., 2019 ; Clark et al., 2021 ) have shown the problems with using NSE as an evaluation metric. The NSE produced by a model can be poor because of errors in model input and observed output data or because of an inadequate model structure. Note that the effects of model inputs may affect the model simulations for several timesteps. Fig. 10  suggests that a reason for the low NSEs of behavioral models was consistent underestimation of high flows, which could have been due to underprediction of areal average precipitation for these events (Bárdossy et al., 2022; Bárdossy and Anwar, 2023 ) given that only six gauges were available for the watersheds considered in this study (Fig. 1 ). Further, Fig. 14  suggests the overestimation of the areal average precipitation during some low flow events during summer months (resulting in overestimation of streamflow and lower NSE). Therefore, we conclude that NSE is not a suitable metric to decide fitness-for-purpose. Despite the wide LoAs, most of the models were still rejected and some outliers had to be allowed to retain physically realistic models. Fig. 9  showed that the outliers had to be allowed mainly for the low flows, implying that the low flows were critical in identifying behavioral and non-behavioral models. Since the QRF LoAs already allowed large overpredictions of the low flows, one interpretation of these results is that the SAC-SMA has structural deficiency in term of simulating low flows. Other interpretation is that the large overpredictions occur because of precipitation overestimation during the preceding events, affecting the simulated antecedent conditions. Given the current lack of knowledge of the errors in model inputs, it is still difficult to decide between the two interpretations. However, these large overpredictions do suggest important structural errors in the SAC-SMA. Large BFI of many behavioral models suggest that either the ET or the baseflow component of the models needs revision. The distribution of water between different storage elements might also be problematic which might also affect ET. Beven and Lane (2022)  proposed eight general principles for defining fitness-for-purpose. One of the principles was that the model should not contradict the secure evidence about the hydrological functioning of the watershed. Following this principle, we would want a model to produce all the possible hydrological signatures for physical consistency, but this may not be possible because hydrological models are necessarily simplified representations of hydrological processes. Therefore, a possible way to apply this principle is to rank the different constraints according to their relevance to the purpose of modeling. Subsequently, the different constraints can be applied progressively, thus, creating a ranking of behavioral simulations – the models identified as behavioral after all the constraints will be assigned the highest rank. The lower rank models can be used progressively to create predictive uncertainty bound that satisfy some decision criteria such as the coverage probability and width of uncertainty bound. Shafii et al. (2015)  demonstrated a similar Pareto rank-based approach to identify behavioral simulations, but they did not account for uncertainties in data (the fifth principle in Beven and Lane, 2022 ). One of the benefits of the DT-based LoAs is that they can be constructed even at ungauged locations by using data from donor watersheds – so called regionalization. Further, LoAs so constructed provide natural way of quantifying uncertainty in predictions. In this scenario, wider LoAs were obtained and, consequently, additional models were accepted as behavioral. The wider LoAs are desirable since we expect that the regionalization would incur additional uncertainty in modeling. Using the streamflow-based signatures H and BFI significantly reduced the number of behavioral models, but still resulted in some behavioral models that could be used to make predictions (Fig. 15 ). The LoAs on signatures were defined loosely in this study but tighter limits could be defined using regionalization methods (e.g., Yadav et al., 2007 ).  6 Summary and concluding remarks This study is the first attempt to use ML-constructed LoAs to evaluate the conceptual hydrological model SAC-SMA. Of note, the methodology proposed in this paper can be applied at both gauged (referred to as gauged-single) and ungauged locations. Therefore, LoAs were constructed for both the gauged and the ungauged scenarios in this study. LoAs were wider for the ungauged scenario as expected since transferring information from donor watersheds incurs additional uncertainty and, typically, the donor watersheds do not contain enough information to compensate for the absence of information from the parent watershed (Gupta, 2024 ). However, very wide LoAs were obtained even in the gauged-single scenario. It is suggested that this is partly due to large uncertainty in precipitation interpolation and streamflow uncertainty. Another reason is that QRF grouped several hydrologically dissimilar timesteps in the leaf nodes, suggesting the need to further explore the ML algorithms to define LoAs. This paper has made some suggestions to better define LoAs using ML. Allowing violations of LoAs at 5 % of the calibration timesteps yielded several models as behavioral, but many of these models could not simulate specific hydrograph features adequately. Using streamflow-based signatures can help with this limitation. The Hurst exponent (H) was used as one of the signatures with very relaxed acceptability criterion, but it still was useful in constraining behavioral parameter space. Among other signatures, the BFI (applied at both gauged and ungauged locations) also showed significant discriminating power. Since none of the tested models could simulate all aspects of streamflow hydrograph adequately even given the wide LoAs, all the 1-million models tested in this study were rejected as unfit-for-purpose. The errors in the model input precipitation affects the streamflow residuals in a complex manner that are difficult to model using a formal probabilistic approach. For example, peak timing errors in some the events were due to dry antecedent condition which, in turn, was due to underestimation of the pre-event precipitation. Similarly, precipitation overestimation in an event may affect the low flow simulations for several subsequent days. The LoA approach attempts to define the variability in response variable due to the effects of errors in data, before model simulations. This approach also allows to identify the timesteps where a parameter set and also the model structure is failing, thus, proving hints for model improvement. For example, low flow timesteps were critical for separating behavioral models from non-behavioral models in this study. Beven and Lane (2022)  suggest that a model should also be hydrologically consistent to qualify as fit-for-purpose, i.e., the model should give ‘right answer for right reasons’ (Kirchner, 2006 ). Since all the models will eventually be rejected as more constraints are applied, we suggest that different constraints should be ranked according to their relevance to the purpose of modeling where the models satisfying all the constraints can be given the highest rank (e.g., Beven et al., 2022b ). 1 Introduction Dam failures are among the most catastrophic events that can affect the territory, sometimes causing loss of human lives as well as considerable damage to the anthropic activities developed downstream of the dams and to natural heritage. The modelling of the catastrophic floods due to such events can be traced back to two main aspects, namely the generation of the outflow hydrograph and the downstream propagation. As regards the outflow hydrograph generation, it is necessary to distinguish between concrete dams and earthen dams. In the former case the definition of “dam-break” is usually adopted in the literature, and a sudden collapse of the dam is reasonably assumed, which leads to the generation of a hydrograph having the peak at the beginning of the phenomenon. In the case of earthen dams, the definition of “dam-breach” is instead adopted, and the modelling becomes more complex, since the failure of such dams, which can be triggered by piping or overtopping, consists in a progressive erosion of the dam body induced by a water flow through a breach that enlarges over time. Therefore, it can be guessed that the resulting hydrograph has a rising phase, unlike the one resulting from concrete dams’ failure. There is an extensive literature on dam-breach modelling, which cannot be recalled in the short space of this introduction. The reader can refer to a recent and extensive review proposed by Zhong et al. (2021) , which provides a broad overview valid for both conventional dams and landslide dams. Even more recently, Macchione et al. (2023)  highlighted the key factors of simplified physically based modelling. There are also articles that deal with empirical and semi-analytical formulas useful for estimating the peak flow rate (see for example Wang et al., 2018 ). Considerable importance is also linked to the study of the flood wave propagation, as this aspect allows for the flood hazard assessment and, thus, throws light on the consequences and damages on the territory. The propagation of a flood wave has been widely modelled through the Saint-Venant or Shallow Water Equations (SWEs), that are also applicable to dam-break or dam-breach flood waves. In recent times, more and more accurate computational models and increasingly powerful calculation tools for the resolution of the SWEs are available. For example, among the latest studies, Ferrari et al. (2023)  proposed a high-resolution procedure for improving hazard mapping related to dam failures. For the calibration/validation of these models, it is possible to carry out the reconstruction of historical cases of dam failure, such as the Big Bay earthen dam failure (e.g., Macchione et al., 2016a; Yochum et al., 2008 ) or the Malpasset concrete dam failure (e.g., Hervouet and Petitjean, 1999; Valiani et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2011 ). A recent review of historical dam-break events has been conducted by Aureli et al., 2021 . In situations where prompt action is required, it is preferable to refer to models that are simple and quick to apply. Various analytical solutions have been proposed for the downstream propagation of dam failure flood waves. For instance, some analytical solutions have been formulated for dam-break flow on frictionless channel (e.g., Zanuttigh and Lamberti, 2001; Chen et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020 ), some others are based on the hypothesis of kinematic flood wave (e.g., Hunt, 1984; Chen and Capart, 2020 ). However, the choice of a complete model is preferable, as neglecting terms such as friction or inertial terms can have significant consequences on the numerical results (Ferrari et al., 2023; Fread, 1982 ). A more recent study, carried out by Wang et al. (2023) , considers instead the hydraulic resistance as well as the inertial terms, assuming anyway a horizontal channel. However, the longitudinal slope should also be taken into account so that the proposed solution can be applied to a real case. From a theoretical point of view, the propagation of a flood wave can be studied by means of dimensionless formulations through which reducing the number of independent parameters that control the routing behaviour. This kind of studies are very significant since they allow for the discovery of the features of the flood wave routing such as their downstream attenuation. The dimensionless formulations can also be useful to produce graphical solutions, that are very suitable in emergency situations. For example, regarding the dam-break case, Sakkas and Strelkoff (1976)  proposed a dimensionless formulation of the SWEs characterized by a Froude number and two dimensionless parameters describing the cross-sectional shape. A further contribution in this scope can be attributed to Wetmore and Fread (1981) , who proposed dimensionless graphs in which the reference dimensionless parameters were a Froude number and a dimensionless characteristic value of the flow velocity. This method has been later reworked by other authors (Anonymous, 1982; Fread et al., 1991; French, 1994 ). As regards the dam-breach problem, the analytical and/or dimensionless formulation is somehow more complicated than the dam-break problem. Indeed, it is necessary to take into account a multiplicity of physical and geometrical factors and boundary conditions that influence the generation of the breach outflow hydrograph. Consequently, it is expected that a considerable number of numerical solutions or graphs is required in order to cover all the possible scenarios that can occur in the real-world. To the best of the authors' knowledge, very few articles have proposed dimensionless and/or analytical solutions for the problem of hydrograph propagation due to dam breaching. A reference study for this field has been proposed by Ponce et al. (2003) , who provided dimensionless attenuation graphs, demonstrating that with the same flood volume and downstream topography, different peak discharges attenuate to the same value at a certain distance downstream from the dam. However, the results of Ponce et al. (2003)  are limited to few postulated dam-breach scenarios and, thus, do not cover the whole real-world variability. Another interesting work is that of Capart (2013) . He proposed an analytical solution, however at the price of some simplifying hypotheses. In particular, as regards the generation of the hydrograph, he does not take into account the morphology of the reservoir (i.e., he assumes the surface of the lake constant with depth); the breach is assumed to have a rectangular shape and constant width. As regards the propagation, the basic hypothesis is that the water flow is kinematic. In a more recent, very interesting work, Chen and Capart (2020)  proposed analytical solutions of greater generality valid for both dam-break and dam-breach. Also in this latter work the kinematic hypothesis for wave propagation is assumed. In this work, a dimensionless formulation of the 1D full-momentum SWEs is proposed in order to study the downstream attenuation of dam-breach flood waves. In addition to not neglecting any term of the governing equations, dam-breach scenarios are analysed in such a way as to cover most of the real-world variability, overcoming in this way the limitations of the previous studies above illustrated. In the following section, the key factors in the dam-breach problem will be pointed out and the specific contribution of this study will be presented more in detail.  2 Key factors in the dam-breach flood wave generation and propagation As highlighted in the introduction, the dam-breach problem is somehow even more complicated than the dam-break problem. A synthetic but rather exhaustive overview of the factors that are involved in the numerical modelling of such an event is shown in Table 1  . It shows the parameters that influence both the generation phase and the propagation phase of the flood wave. To help the reader have a summary of the factors taken into account in this article, the same table shows the symbols of the parameters used in the following sections. As it can be seen, at least eleven factors come into play, which make it difficult to frame the phenomenology in a synthetic dimensionless formulation. The present study, which is related to earthen dam failure, provides a complete overview of the dam-breach wave propagation phenomenon, since it takes into account all the factors listed in Table 1 . An appropriate dimensionless formulation allowed for the achievement of two important results. Firstly, the dimensionless full-momentum SWEs have been characterized by means of two parameters: one of them has been shown to be predominant in controlling the downstream attenuation of the flood wave. Secondly, the dimensionless dam-breach hydrographs were discovered to be substantially similar for reservoirs having the same morphological characterization (which is expressed by the exponent of the level-volume curve). In this way, the downstream attenuation of the dimensionless peak discharge can be easily obtained. This study therefore contributes shedding light on the peculiarities of the dam-breach wave generation and propagation phenomena, gaining thus an intrinsic theoretical value. Finally, given the broad validity of the proposed method, it can also be helpful to carry out a quick assessment of the peak flow discharge attenuation at a target distance from a real dam. To validate the applicability of the proposed attenuation graphs, two kinds of comparison are carried out. Firstly, three cases of hypothetical failure of real earthen dams are considered and the results of the proposed method are compared to the results of 2D numerical simulations taken as a reference, to demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve results comparable to those of a complete hydraulic model without having the burden of implementing it. Secondly, the model is also applied to the reconstruction of the observed peak discharge attenuation from the Baige dam-breach flood, to verify that the method gives results consistent with observed data.  3 Dam-breach hydrograph generation 3.1 Numerical model background In a previous article (see Macchione et al., 2023 ) it was shown that the dam-breach phenomenon has some peculiarities that can be made evident through a dimensionless formulation which allows for the identification of a fundamental parameter, G   , which characterizes the dam-reservoir system. The numerical values assumed by this parameter characterize the peculiarities of the dam-breach in the full range of cases that can occur in the real-world. As already mentioned, this parameter is generated by the nondimensionalization of the simplified physically based model proposed by Macchione (2008)  (for details see Macchione, 2008; Macchione and Rino, 2008; Macchione et al., 2023 ). The model was developed for homogeneous or zoned earthen dams, without rigid impermeable cores or concrete facings, and assumes a simplified geometry for the breach cross-section: a triangular shape in a first phase, called formation stage, and then, when the lower vertex of the breach reaches the base of the dam body, a trapezoidal shape. During the entire erosion process, it is assumed that the breach sides maintain a constant inclination. Indicating with β    the angle between the breach sides and the zenithal direction, tan β    is the breach shape parameter of the model. The model indicates with Z    and Y    the levels of the water surface and of the breach bottom, respectively, above the natural ground, i.e., with respect to the base of the dam. Moreover, the occurrence of critical flow through the breach is assumed, and h c     is the water depth (precisely the critical depth) at the breach cross-section (see Fig. 1  ). The enlargement of the breach is related to the hydrodynamic characteristics of the outflow. The model is characterized by a single calibration parameter, called v e    , inserted in the equation that manages erosion velocity, which the model considers to vary over time as a function of the mean shear stress. For conventional earthen dams without rigid elements it is suggested to assume v e     = 0.07 m/s (see Macchione, 2008; Macchione et al., 2023 ). Another important feature of this model is the introduction of a reservoir level-volume curve of the power-law type to take into account the morphology of the reservoir in the computation of the outflow hydrograph, identifying with α 0     and W 0     the curve exponent and coefficient, respectively. Thus, if Z M     is the dam height, W M     = W 0  Z M   α 0      is the volume stored with the water level in the reservoir at the dam crest (as it happens in the case of overtopping). The suitability of this curve type to describe the morphology of reservoirs located in different regions of the world has been previously demonstrated (see Macchione et al., 2016b ). The parameter G   , which according to the Macchione (2008)  model plays a fundamental role in the dam-breach phenomenon (see Macchione and Rino, 2008; Macchione et al., 2023 ) has the following expression:(1) G = v e  W M  g   Z M  7 / 2         where g    is the acceleration due to gravity. As already mentioned, parameter G    characterizes the dam-reservoir system and, in most of the real cases, ranges from 10-1  to 103 . High values of G    indicate a high erosion velocity in comparison with draining velocity and, conversely, low values of G    indicate fast draining reservoirs (Macchione and Rino, 2008 ). Finally, it is mentioned that, for a quick calculation of the peak outflow discharge generated by this model, the formulas proposed by De Lorenzo and Macchione (2014)  can be used.  3.2 Analysed dam-breach scenarios In this section, we want to recall the plausible ranges of the parameters that influence the breach outflow hydrograph generation in the real-world. For a comprehensive framework the reader is referred to Macchione et al. (2023) . Using the simplified physically based dam-breach model illustrated in the previous section (Macchione, 2008 ), for a given dam-reservoir system, the hydrograph shape and the extent of the peak flow discharge depend on the value assumed for tan β    (see Macchione et al., 2023 ). Macchione and Rino (2008)  carried out an analysis of historical observations of this parameter and found a range of values from 0.2 to 2 in 90 % of cases. In the present work, the values 0.2 and 1 have been chosen to perform the analysis, since the greatest variations in peak discharge occur within this range (see Macchione et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, previous studies (Macchione and Rino, 2008; De Lorenzo and Macchione, 2010; Macchione et al., 2023 ) demonstrated that the influence of tan β    on the outflow hydrograph shape varies with the G    parameter. Since the values of G  cover several orders of magnitude, in this work a logarithmic progression, G    = 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000, was chosen as representative of most of real cases of dam-reservoir systems. Covering the whole range of variability of parameter G    has also the advantage to consider indirectly a possible variability of calibration parameter v e     according to Eq. (1) . Another parameter to be taken into account is the exponent α 0     of the level-volume curve which characterizes the morphology of the reservoir. Identifying with S M     the lake surface area corresponding to the dam crest level, Macchione et al. (2016b)  highlighted that α 0     “represents the ratio between the volume that the reservoir would have if it were a cylinder with a base equal to S M     and height equal to Z M     and the actual volume of the reservoir”. It can be seen that α 0     affects the extent of the peak discharge and the shape of the breach outflow hydrograph (Macchione and Rino, 2008; De Lorenzo and Macchione, 2014 ). In most cases, the value of α 0     varies between 1 and 4 and, in this study, the calculations were performed assuming three values: α 0     = 1.5, 2.5, 4. Further involved parameters, for which constant values have been considered, are the following: the average embankment slope, s    = 2.5 (horizontal:vertical), and the crest width, w c     = 0. Note that in the real-world the flood volume is also a very important variable in the flood hydrograph propagation, but in this study the dimensionless formulation that will be illustrated below makes the dimensionless hydrographs and the respective propagation independent of the volume. In this work, dam-breach scenarios induced by overtopping were considered, in which the initial water level in the reservoir coincides with the dam crest level (Z    = Z M    ). Furthermore, all the analysed scenarios assume the total emptying of the reservoir, therefore the flood volume precisely coincides with the reservoir volume up to the dam crest, W M    , which will be referred to below as the flood volume. Indeed, this is the most precautionary approach to consider in predictive applications, since it is based on the most severe scenario that could happen. Finally, by changing the three variable parameters among the chosen values (tan β    = 0.2, 1; G    = 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000; α 0     = 1.5, 2.5, 4), several dam-breach scenarios have been conceived in this study. Note that the combination of G    = 0.1 and tan β    = 1, regardless of the value of α 0    , does not lead to the total emptying of the reservoir (see Macchione et al., 2023 ), therefore these cases have been excluded from the analysis. In light of the above, a total of 27 dam-breach hydrographs have been computed to study their behaviour during downstream propagation. In order to have an idea of the huge variability of the shape and peak of these hydrographs in dimensional form, Fig. 2   shows all the conceived hydrographs calculated assuming, as an example, the flood volume equal to 10 million m3 . In Section 5.2  it will be shown that an appropriate way of making the hydrographs dimensionless gives rise to hydrographs that are very similar to each other, for a given value of α 0    .    4 Dam-breach flood wave propagation The target of this work is to study the dam-breach flood wave propagation in order to understand which parameters have the greatest influence on the downstream attenuation of the wave peak. The flood wave routing is governed by the Shallow Water Equations (SWEs), which will be described in the following Section 4.1 , together with the numerical scheme applied to solve the system of equations. Then, Section 4.2  will show a dimensional analysis of the dam-breach flood wave that will allow for the identification of the dimensionless parameters governing the flood wave propagation. 4.1 Theoretical background The one-dimensional (1D) SWEs, written in conservative form, constitute the following system (Cunge et al., 1980 ):(2) ∂ U  ∂ t   + ∂ F U     ∂ x   = S U        where:• U = A   Q            is the variables vector, being A    the cross-section flow area and Q    the flow discharge;  • F U    = Q   Q  2  A  + g I 1             is the flux vector, being I 1  = ∫ 0  h x      h x    - η    b x , η    d η   , η    the integration variable representing the vertical distance from the bottom of the cross-section, b    the cross-section width at height η   , h    the water depth above the cross-section thalweg and g    the acceleration due to gravity;  • S U    = 0   g A S 0  - S f     + g I 2             is the source terms vector, being I 2  = ∫ 0  h x      h x    - η    ∂ b  ∂ x      h = c o n s t   d η   , S 0     the longitudinal bed slope and S f     the friction slope, estimated by applying the Manning equation:   (3) u = 1 n  R  2 3   S f  1 2        in which u    is the flow velocity, n    is the Manning roughness coefficient, and R    is the hydraulic radius of the cross-section flow area. Macchione and Morelli (2003)  demonstrated that this scheme gives increasingly accurate results as the value of α    increases and can guarantee a level of accuracy comparable to that of second order schemes. For the simulations of dam-breach flood wave propagation carried out in this work, a value of 0.95 was assumed for the α    coefficient. Since it is an explicit numerical integration method, the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy stability condition must be fulfilled:(5) C r  = m a x u   + c    Δ t  Δ x   ≤ 1     where C r     is the Courant number, c = g A   / B      is the wave celerity, and B    is the top width of the cross-section flow area.  4.2 Dimensionless formulation In order to find the formulation of the dimensionless parameters that govern the propagation, the continuity and momentum equations should be written in dimensionless form. The dimensionless parameters that have been found through the nondimensionalization illustrated above are very useful for shedding light on the propagation behaviour of the dimensionless flood wave. Among them, the ψ    parameter is the most significant one. High values of the ψ    parameter are indicative of a kinematic behaviour of the flood wave. Given an upstream boundary condition (i.e., a given dam-breach hydrograph) and for the same value of Fr  p    , the higher the ψ    parameter is, the higher the dimensionless peak discharge values along the channel are. Note that ψ   , in addition to being one of the parameters that govern the propagation of a dimensionless flood wave, is also the ratio between the weights of the source term and the ∂ I 1   ∗   / ∂ x  ∗      term, respectively. For this reason, the attenuation of the dimensionless peak discharge depends almost only on the value of ψ   . This parameter can assume values that cover four orders of magnitude, from 10-1  to 103 . On the other hand, the value that ϕ    can assume is not completely independent of ψ   . To demonstrate this, consider for simplicity the case of a triangular cross-section (ε    = 1) with a gentle side slope S s    , such that S s   2     ≅ 0. In these cases, defining as m    the ratio between the side slope S s     of the triangular cross-section and the longitudinal bed slope S 0     of the channel, and considering for simplicity the Fr  p     parameter instead of ϕ   , the two dimensionless parameters are linked by a power-law (see Appendix A ):(23) Fr  p  = a ψ  17 46       where:(24) a = 128 m  5     1 / 46   Q p 0    11 / 23    g  1 / 2   n  12 / 23   W M   17 / 46         Thus, for a given upstream boundary condition (i.e., given Q p 0      and W M    ), the value of Fr  p     depends on the values of ψ    and m   . In other words, for a given value of ψ   , the Fr  p     parameter can vary within a range defined by two plausible extreme values for the m    ratio. However, as will be demonstrated in Section 5.1 , the variability of Fr  p    , and therefore of ϕ    too, does not significantly influence the attenuation of the dimensionless flood wave, that is governed by the ψ    parameter.   5 Dimensionless peak discharge attenuation This section shows the results of the numerical simulations carried out by numerical resolution of the dimensionless equations (16) and (17) . The dimensionless solution depends not only on the boundary condition, but also on the numerical values assumed for the parameters ϕ   , ψ    and ε   . All other parameters being equal, the solution depends on the shape of the cross-section, i.e., on the numerical value of ε   . In this work, the results obtained by setting ε    = 1, which corresponds to the triangular cross-section, are shown. In fact, this value provides the highest peak discharge values along the valley, therefore it can be considered the situation that envelops the curves having ε    < 1. Furthermore, this assumption has widely been proposed in the literature (e.g., Sakkas and Strelkoff, 1973; Zanuttigh and Lamberti, 2001; Macchione and Viggiani, 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). Although the calculations are limited to a single numerical value of the ε    parameter, the variability of the other two parameters (ϕ    and ψ   ) and of the dam-breach hydrograph, which in turn depends on G   , α 0     and tan β   , could lead to the mistaken belief that drawing a huge number of graphs is necessary to represent all the situations that can happen in the real-world. Instead, the considerations reported in the following sub-sections show a modest influence of the ϕ    parameter and a strong similarity of the dimensionless dam-breach hydrographs corresponding to the same value of α 0    , regardless of the numerical value of the other parameters. Therefore, it will be shown that just three graphs allow for a complete description of the phenomenon. 5.1 Quasi-independence from the ϕ    parameter In order to demonstrate the quasi-independence of the attenuation from the ϕ    parameter, Fig. 3   shows the dimensionless peak discharge attenuation curves obtained considering the same upstream boundary condition (the one given by G    = 0.1, tan β    = 0.2 and α 0     = 2.5) and assuming several values of ψ    in such a way to cover most of the real-world variability. For each value of ψ   , two values of ϕ   , corresponding to plausible extreme values for the m    ratio, have been assumed. Indeed, the ratio m    between the side slope S s     of the river cross-section and the longitudinal bed slope S 0     may change depending on the bed morphology. Therefore, with the aim of covering all the possible situations that can happen in the real-world, a minimum of about 1.5 and a maximum of about 500 were assumed for the ratio m    between S s     and S 0    , imposing anyway the upper constraint S s     ≤ 1. As it can be observed, the attenuation curves obtained for the same ψ    value and corresponding to the maximum and minimum values of the ϕ    parameter (the solid and dotted lines, respectively) are practically the same. Moreover, Fig. 3  shows that the attenuation gets lower and lower as the ψ    parameter increases, confirming what has been said above.  5.2 Influence of the dam-breach boundary condition on the attenuation As already mentioned, the results shown in Fig. 3  are related to the same upstream boundary condition. However, the effect of the dam-breach hydrograph variability on the peak discharge attenuation should be also investigated. In this regard, the method chosen to make the time and the discharge dimensionless allows the dimensionless hydrographs to be made independent of the flood volume. Indeed, with different flood volumes and the same values of G   , tan β    and α 0    , the corresponding dimensionless hydrographs coincide with each other (see Appendix B ). Fig. 4   shows the dimensionless outflow hydrographs corresponding to the analysed dam-breach scenarios outlined in Section 3.2  (see Fig. 2 ). The dimensionless hydrographs have been plotted assuming the time of peak as the reference instant. It can be seen that the hydrographs corresponding to different values of G    and tan β   , with the same α 0    , vary very little from each other, except in the very first part of the rising limb, characterized by flow discharges lower than 30 % of the peak, in which the curves differ more. The dimensionless outflow hydrograph corresponding to G    = 1 and tan β    = 1 is the only one that differs more from the others, as low values of G    correspond to dam-breach cases that are very sensitive to the assumed breach shape (see Macchione et al., 2023 ). The remaining hydrographs fall within a very narrow band, at least in the phase of the phenomenon in which Q  ∗      ≥ 0.3. Therefore, the proposed dimensionless formulation allows reducing the variability of the upstream boundary conditions to a limited number of hydrographs, since the shape of the dimensionless hydrograph depends almost only on the numerical value of the parameter α 0    .  5.3 Simulation results in graphical form All the dimensionless hydrographs illustrated in Fig. 4  have been propagated assuming different values of the ψ    parameter (0.25, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 25 and 250). The simulations have been carried out through a MATLAB code implemented for the numerical resolution of the 1D SWEs based on the Lax-Friedrichs scheme, as already mentioned in Section 4.1 . The corresponding attenuation curves are shown in Figs. 5-7    . Confirming what has been said, most of the curves corresponding to the same values of ψ    and α 0     fall within a very narrow band. The only exception is the dimensionless peak attenuation curve given by G    = 1 and tan β    = 1, due to the difference in dam-breach hydrograph already shown above. In particular, the latter curve differs more from the others in the case of α 0     = 1.5. All the figures confirm what has already been observed in Fig. 3 : the higher the ψ    value, the more accentuated the kinematic character of the flow and, therefore, the smaller the attenuation of the peak discharge along the valley. Furthermore, from Fig. 4  it can be noted that the lower the α 0     value, the steeper the rising limb of the discharge hydrograph at the dam site and, consequently, the greater the role of the inertial terms. Therefore, the bundles of curves drawn for the same ψ    are wider for the lowest value of α 0     and become narrower as α 0     increases. Overall, Figs. 5-7  allow us to obtain an estimate of the attenuation of the peak discharge of any dam-breach hydrograph. In particular, as will be shown in the next section, the graphs can be applied recursively even in non-prismatic and variable-slope riverbeds. Furthermore, it is worth highlighting that the proposed attenuation curves could be used even for cases other than total failure scenarios as long as the dimensionless breach outflow hydrograph has a shape similar to one of the three families shown in Fig. 4 . In this latter case, W M     has to be intended as the released water volume. Therefore, the graphs can be easily applied to real cases.   6 Quick assessment of the peak discharge attenuation The graphs presented in Figs. 5-7  can be used to carry out a quick assessment of the downstream attenuation of the peak discharge given by the hypothetical failure of a real earthen dam. The procedure required to apply the proposed method is described in the following sub-sections. 6.1 Method application procedure A quick assessment of the downstream attenuation of the peak discharge for a real earthen dam can be carried out by dividing the downstream river in reaches characterized by a roughly constant slope. In reference to the single river reach, having length L   , the dimensionless parameter ψ    can be estimated using an average longitudinal slope, S 0 , m     , and considering an average cross-section to compute the uniform flow area A p     and top width B p     corresponding to Q p 0     . Based on these latter variables, the flow depth h p     can be estimated considering the triangular cross-section having the same flow area and top width of the actual one. Thus, identifying the graph (among Figs. 5-7 ) corresponding to the closest value of α 0    , and calculating the dimensionless abscissa x  ∗      ≡ L  ∗      = L A p  / W M     through which entering the graph, the attenuated peak discharge Q p   ∗   L  ∗         at the end of the river reach can be estimated through the curves bundle corresponding to the given value of ψ   . If the value of ψ    falls between the values of two bundles, the attenuated peak discharge Q p   ∗   L  ∗         can be estimated through linear interpolation. The aforementioned procedure has to be applied reach by reach, from upstream to downstream, by assuming, from the second reach on, the attenuated peak discharge at the end of the previous reach as the initial peak discharge Q p 0     . Resuming, the proposed method allows for the quick estimation of the downstream attenuation of a dam-breach flood wave knowing the morphology of the upstream reservoir, the longitudinal slope and cross-section of the downstream river and, finally, the breach outflow hydrograph (flood volume and peak discharge). Since the application of the proposed method does not require a run of a calculation code, the speed of application depends on the operator's skills to process a DEM. Anyway, as illustrated above, only simple operations are needed for the method application (i.e., extracting a thalweg longitudinal profile and river cross-sections). Therefore, the proposed method certainly requires much less time than just setting up a hydrodynamic model, furthermore completely saving the operator from the burden of the computational times.  6.2 Roughness coefficient evaluation In the 2D numerical simulations, the irregularities of the main river, which cause additional flow resistance, are inherently taken into account through the DEM which is used to create the computational domain. The attenuation curves illustrated in Figs. 5-7 , instead, have been obtained through 1D numerical simulations on prismatic channels and, therefore, no channel irregularity was considered. In order to take into account the irregularities of the river reaches when calculating the values of A p     and B p     using the Manning formula, the roughness coefficient can be evaluated based on the approach proposed by Cowan (1956) , who provided the following formula:(25) n = n 0  + n 1  + n 2  + n 3  + n 4     f m      in which:• n 0     is the basic roughness value for a straight and uniform channel;  • n 1     is the additive value to account for channel irregularity, up to 0.020 s/m1/3  depending on the degree of irregularity;  • n 2     is the additive value to account for cross-section irregularity, up to 0.015 s/m1/3  depending on the character of variations in cross-section size and shape;  • n 3     is the additive value to account for obstructions, up to 0.060 s/m1/3  depending on the effect of obstruction;  • n 4     is the additive value to account for vegetation, up to 0.100 s/m1/3  depending on the type and density of vegetation;  • f m     is an adjustment factor to account for the degree of channel meandering, between 1 and 1.3 depending on the ratio between the meander length l m     ≡ L    and the straight length l s     of the river reach.    The values of the roughness factors listed above can be chosen based on the tables presented in many literature manuals (see for example Chow, 1959 ).   7 Applications to real earthen dams In this section, the validity of the graphs of Figs. 5-7  for predictive purposes will be tested. First, the results of the proposed method will be compared to the results of 2D numerical simulations taken as a reference. Secondly, the method will be applied to the Baige case study for the reconstruction of the observed peak discharge attenuation along the Jinsha River (China). 7.1 Comparison with the results of 2D numerical simulations for the hypothetical failure of three real earthen dams Three earthen dams located in the Calabria region (Italy) have been selected: the Nocelle, Castagnara and Menta Dams. Two of these dams have already been selected by Macchione et al. (2023) , and one of them by Macchione et al. (2022) , as examples to carry out a numerical application, in which indicative values were used for the geometric and topographical characteristics of these dams and the corresponding reservoirs. In this work, more accurate information about these dam-reservoir systems was considered. In the following sub-sections, the hypothetical failure of these dams will be simulated both in terms of outflow hydrograph generation and propagation of the consequent flood waves in the downstream areas. The results of the numerical simulations, carried out by means of a 2D full-momentum hydrodynamic code, will be taken as a reference solution. Thus, the applicability of the proposed method for predictive purposes will be tested by comparing the downstream attenuation curves constructed through consultation of the proposed graphs with the reference solution. 7.1.1 Description of the case studies The geometric and topographical characteristics of the selected dams and the corresponding reservoirs are shown in Table 2  , in which also the value of the dimensionless parameter G    is shown. Fig. 8   shows the topographic characteristics of the territories downstream of the dams. In particular, the 5 m resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) is illustrated in plan view for each case study, together with the thalweg line and the control cross-sections used to visualize the results of the numerical simulations, which will be better discussed below. Furthermore, Figs. 9–11     (a) illustrate the thalweg longitudinal profile for each case study, respectively, in which x    is the progressive distance from the dam location, measured along the development of the thalweg line, except for the valley sections in which the dam-breach flood is expected to occupy entirely the floodplain areas and, therefore, the thalweg line is no more representative. In these latter cases, the distance along the valley course has been considered. As it can be seen from Figs. 9–11  (a), the main river downstream of each dam has been divided in reaches having a roughly constant longitudinal slope, with an average value, S 0 , m     , calculated through the Taylor-Schwartz formula:(26) S 0 , m   = 1 L  ∑ k  S 0 , k   L k      in which L    is the length of the river reach, and S 0 , k      and L k     are, respectively, the slope and length of the river segments between two consecutive contour lines, which in this case had a difference in elevation of 10 m. From the control cross-sections (XS) illustrated in Fig. 8 , the flow depth-width curves have been extracted [see Figs. 9–11  (b)], being h    the flow depth and B    the top width, in order to evaluate an average B h       curve for each river reach. The latter was used to create an average synthetic cross-section, symmetric with respect to the vertical axis, that can be representative of each river reach [see Figs. 9–11  (c)]. The topographic and morphological information illustrated in Figs. 9–11  will be used hereinafter for the application of the proposed method, as will be shown in Section 7.1.4 .  7.1.2 Dam-breach scenarios The outflow hydrographs generated by the hypothetical failure of the selected dams have been computed by means of the Macchione (2008)  model. In particular, two breach shape scenarios have been considered for the Nocelle Dam, assuming the values 0.2 and 1 for the tan β    parameter. Instead, only the breach shape scenario given by tan β    = 0.2 was considered for the other case studies, since the scenario given by tan β    = 1 does not entail the full emptying of the reservoir in the cases of the Castagnara and Menta Dams, in light of the low value of the dimensionless parameter G    (see Table 2 ). Fig. 12   shows the dam-breach hydrographs computed according to these breach shape scenarios.  7.1.3 Numerical simulations The downstream propagation of the dam-breach hydrographs illustrated in Fig. 12  was simulated by using the TUFLOW 2D Explicit HPC (Heavily Parallelised Compute) Solver. This version uses a GPU hardware for high-speed execution and applies a second order solution accuracy in space and fourth order accuracy in time. As already mentioned above, the topographic information was derived by a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) having a resolution of 5 m, used as base to build the computational domain compound by structured cells of 10 m side. A constant value of 0.05 s/m1/3  has been used for the Manning roughness coefficient. This value falls within the range of 0.025–0.1 s/m1/3  that is typically used in the literature to model historical dam-break events (e.g., Valiani et al., 2002; Pilotti et al., 2011; Petaccia et al., 2016 ). The flood waves characteristics were extracted in terms of discharge and water surface elevation in correspondence of the control cross-sections illustrated in Fig. 8 . In particular, the peak discharge in each cross-section was considered in order to compare the flood wave attenuation to that predicted applying the proposed method.  7.1.4 Method application In this section, a quick assessment of the downstream attenuation of the peak discharge for the selected case studies will be carried out applying the procedure explained in Section 6 . The attenuation curves thus obtained will be then compared with those resulting from the 2D numerical simulations. For the application of the proposed method, the roughness coefficient has to be evaluated as explained in Section 6.2 .
