In this work, the basic roughness value is n 0     = 0.05 s/m1/3 , i.e., the value used in the 2D reference simulations. Furthermore, the obstructions and the vegetation have not been considered here, since they were not taken into account in the 2D numerical simulations. As regards the other factors, the values assumed for the river reaches of each analysed case study are illustrated in Table 3  , together with the adjusted n    values. Through application of the procedure explained in Section 6.1 , a quick assessment of the peak discharge attenuation at the end of each river reach has been carried out for the selected case studies. Table 4   shows the length L    of the river reaches, the distance x    of the downstream end of the river reaches from the dam, and the values of all the variables involved in the application of the proposed method, i.e.:• the peak discharge Q p 0      at the beginning of the considered river reach;  • the uniform flow area A p     and top width B p     corresponding to Q p 0     , estimated assuming the average slope S 0 , m      and attributing the Manning roughness coefficient n    of Table 3  to the average cross-section of the river reach (see Figs. 9-11 );  • the flow depth h p     corresponding to the triangular cross-section having the same flow area and top width of the actual one;  • the dimensionless parameter ψ    [Eq. (19) ], on which the attenuation strongly depends;  • the dimensionless length L  ∗      of the river reach, used as the abscissa x  ∗      to enter the attenuation graph corresponding to the α 0     value closest to the given one (Fig. 6  for all the case studies analysed here).    Furthermore, Table 4  shows the dimensionless peak discharge Q p   ∗   L  ∗         at the end of the river reach, estimated through consultation of the attenuation graph knowing L  ∗      and ψ   , and the corresponding attenuated peak discharge Q p  x       = Q p 0   Q p   ∗   L  ∗        . The performance of the method has been evaluated computing the error committed in the quick assessment of Q p  x       by taking as a reference the attenuated peak discharge Q p , 2 D   x       predicted by the 2D simulations. As it can be seen, the error is always low, being 4.3 % on average, with a maximum value of 10.7 %. Finally, Fig. 13   shows the graphical comparison between the peak discharge attenuation curves obtained through the 2D simulations and the attenuation predicted through the proposed method. As it can be seen, the proposed method, albeit quick and simplified, is able to obtain results very close to those predicted through 2D numerical simulations which, in the case of large calculation domains and in the absence of HPC tools, may require very long computation times.   7.2 Comparison with observed data from the Baige landslide dam-breach flood The case study examined for the validation of the method proposed in Section 6  is the Baige landslide dam (China). In November 2018 a landslide occurred close to Baige village, on the border between Tibet and Sichuan Province, clogging the Jinsha River. Reaching a maximum elevation of 2966 m a.s.l., the dam body was more than 100 m-high compared to the original riverbed, which had an elevation of 2861 m a.s.l. (Xue et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ). To reduce the potential damage due to the overtopping of such a high dam, with a maximum potential stored volume of 790 million m3 , a diversion channel with a bottom elevation of 2952.5 m a.s.l. was excavated in the dam body (Xue et al., 2021 ). In this way the maximum potential stored water volume was reduced by approximately 260 million m3 . Following the overtopping of the diversion channel, the progressive erosion of the dam body was triggered. From the discharge hydrograph observed at the Baige location (see Fig. 14  , taken from Zhang et al., 2023 ), a released water volume W M     of 549 million m3  has been estimated, with a peak discharge Q p 0      equal to 31000 m3 /s. During the dam-breach flood event, the discharge hydrographs have been measured in many cross-sections of the Jinsha River, up to 600 km downstream of the Baige landslide dam location. Therefore, this case study can be used for the validation of the proposed method through comparison with field data. The data required for the application of the method have been obtained from Zhang et al. (2023) , who provided a detailed database as supplementary material. Fig. 15   (a) illustrates the thalweg longitudinal profile of the Jinsha River, in which x    is the progressive distance from the Baige landslide dam location, as well as the river reaches that have been identified for the method application. Fig. 15  (b) shows the flow depth-width curves extracted from the Suwalong, Benzilan, Wujing and Shigu cross-sections (Zhang et al., 2023 ), which have been used to evaluate an average B h       curve. The latter was used to create an average synthetic cross-section, symmetric with respect to the vertical axis, that can be representative of all the analysed river reaches [see Fig. 15  (c)]. Table 5   shows the evaluation of the roughness coefficient according to the method illustrated in Section 6.2 . Given the quite homogeneous characteristics of Jinsha River, the same value has been used for river reaches 1–3, while the last river reach has been characterized separately given the presence of a hairpin along the river in proximity to the Shigu cross-section (see Zhang et al., 2023 ). In particular, the presence of the hairpin has been taken into account by adding a medium effect of obstruction, n 3     = 0.02 s/m1/3  (Chow, 1959 ), and increasing the meandering factor to 1.3. As regards the other roughness factors, the following values have been selected: a basic value n 0     = 0.05 s/m1/3  based on the value that Zhang et al. (2023)  assigned to the river bed; a value n 1     = 0.005 s/m1/3  to account for minor cross-section irregularities; a value n 2     = 0.005 s/m1/3  because large and small cross-sections are shown to alternate occasionally; and a value n 4     = 0.015 s/m1/3  to account for a medium effect of river vegetation. The parameters of the reservoir level-volume curve have been evaluated by power-law interpolation of the water level and lake volume data provided by Zhang et al. (2023) , assuming 2865 m a.s.l. as a reference elevation, and are equal to α 0     = 2.71 and W 0     = 2829 m3-α0 . Given the α 0     value, the graph of Fig. 6 , corresponding to α 0     = 2.5, must be used to carry out a quick assessment of the peak discharge attenuation for the Baige case study. Indeed, the upper part (i.e., Q  ∗      > 0.3) of the measured breach outflow hydrograph in dimensionless form shows quite good correspondence with the family of curves of Fig. 4  (b). Table 6   shows the river cross-sections in which the method has been applied, the distance x    of each cross-section from the dam, the average slope S 0 , m      and the length L    of the river reaches illustrated in Fig. 15  (a), and the values of all the variables involved in the application of the proposed method. The performance of the method has been evaluated computing the error committed in the quick assessment of Q p  x       by taking as a reference the measured peak discharge Q p , o b s   x      . Finally, Fig. 16   shows the graphical comparison between the observed peak discharge attenuation curve and the one predicted through the proposed method. As it can be seen, there is a very good agreement between the measured data and the results of the proposed method, which gives a maximum error of 10 % at almost 600 km from Baige.   8 Conclusions Studying the downstream propagation of a dam-breach flood wave in order to identify the most influent parameters on the wave peak attenuation was the target of this work. A dimensionless formulation of the conservative 1D Shallow Water Equations, written for a prismatic channel having power-law type cross-section, allowed for the identification of two dimensionless parameters: ϕ    and ψ   . It has been demonstrated that the former, which is related to the Froude number of the downstream channel when the maximum peak discharge flows, does not influence much the attenuation. On the other hand, the ψ    parameter, which depends on the flood volume, the downstream longitudinal slope, the cross-sectional flow area and depth, is crucial in determining the peak discharge attenuation. As regards the shape of the breach outflow hydrograph, thanks to the dimensionless formulation proposed in this work, it has been demonstrated that the most influent parameter is the exponent α 0     of the level-volume curve which characterizes the reservoir morphology. The discoveries of the similarity of the propagation behaviour with the same ψ    parameter, and of the similarity of the dam-breach hydrographs with the same exponent of the level-volume curve, led to an economy in the number of graphs to produce in order to cover much of the possible real-world variability in terms of peak discharge attenuation along the downstream river (see Figs. 5-7 ). Based on the results mentioned so far, a method was proposed to carry out a quick assessment of the peak discharge attenuation for a given case study using the attenuation graphs here provided. The application of the proposed method requires the subdivision of the main river downstream of the dam in river reaches having a roughly constant slope and to identify for each of them an average cross-section that could be representative of the morphology of the given river reach. The method has been validated through application to three hypothetical case studies, by comparing the peak discharge attenuation predicted by means of the proposed method to the attenuation curves obtained by means of 2D full-momentum hydrodynamic simulations, taken here as a reference. Furthermore, data from the Baige landslide dam-breach flood have been used for a further validation of the method. The performance of the proposed method has been evaluated by means of the error in the attenuated peak discharge at the end of each analysed river reach, obtaining very low errors. In conclusion, the results illustrated in this paper shed light on the peculiarities of the dam-breach wave propagation phenomenon, providing, for the first time, a framework that covers almost the entire extent in which real cases may fall, with reference to both the generation of the dam-breach hydrograph and its downstream propagation. Also, the results presented above are very useful to carry out a quick assessment of the peak discharge attenuation at a certain distance from a real earthen dam. To obtain the same assessment by means of a 2D simulation, a long time may be required for setting up the computational domain and for numerical running, above all in case a HPC tool is not available. In light of the above, the proposed method is very valuable in emergency situations, in which a rapid intervention is needed, providing quick and accurate results for the river reaches downstream of the dam until the cross-sections are clearly identifiable. Therefore, the proposed method allows the boundary condition to be transferred immediately upstream of the remaining part of the computational domain, where the flood risk evaluation is of interest and therefore there is the need to carry out a 2D hydrodynamic analysis.
1 Introduction Fluoride, as a trace mineral, is widely distributed in the air, water and soil (Rao et al., 2021 ). However, the fluoride enrichment in the environment, stemming from natural and anthropogenic sources, can lead to the fluoride contamination in groundwater that pose a great threat to the safety of drinking water, human health and ecosystems (Cao et al., 2023 ). High fluoride groundwater occurs in more than 25 countries such as the United States (Harkness and Jurgens, 2022 ), India (Rao et al., 2021 ), Pakistan (Rafique et al., 2015 ), Nigeria (Emenike et al., 2018 ), Ghana (Ganyaglo et al., 2019 ), Iran (Dehbandi et al., 2018 ), and China (Guo et al., 2012 ), which can affect approximately 200 million people worldwide. Among those, China is one of the most affected countries in the world that are being threatened by groundwater fluoride contamination (Cao et al., 2023 ). The human exposure to fluoride-polluted groundwater will cause grave dental fluorosis and other health problems (Olaka et al., 2016 ). According to WHO Guidelines for drinking water quality, the F−  content greater than 1.5 mg/L in drinking water is considered unsafe for humans (WHO, 2011 ), while China’s standard limit refers to 1 mg/L based on GB 5749–2022 (MEE, 2022 ). Accordingly, it is a necessity to undertake a comprehensive study on the genesis, hydrogeochemical evolution and driving factors of high F−  groundwater, which is of vital importance to ensure safe drinking water and public health. Many studies showed that fluoride contamination of groundwater can be induced by natural factors, including dissolution of fluoride-containing minerals (Su et al., 2019 ), water-soluble and exchangeable fluorine in soil (Brindha et al., 2016 ), evaporation (Wang et al., 2021a ), alternating cation adsorption (Jia et al., 2019 ), competitive adsorption (Chen et al., 2021 ), and alkaline environment (Cao et al., 2023 ). The hydrolysis of fluoride-containing minerals is assumed to be the main source of F−  elements in groundwater, and the high F−  groundwater is mainly derived from the dissolved minerals of fluorite, apatite, cryolite, biotite and tophus (Rao et al., 2020 ). The dissolving and precipitating process of minerals such as fluorite, gypsum, calcite and dolomite can strongly affect the F−  concentration in groundwater due to the hydrogeochemical process (Wang et al., 2024; Brindha et al., 2016 ). The decrease of Ca2+  content arising from calcite and dolomite precipitation can lead to the weathering and dissolution of fluoride-rich minerals and rocks under the water–rock interaction, resulting in an increase in the concentration of F−  in groundwater (Marghade et al., 2018 ). It is also found that competitive adsorption (such as F− –OH− , F− –HCO 3 −     exchange) and intense evaporation under arid climate are the dominant factors influencing F−  enrichment in the aquifer. Recent studies also suggested that high F−  groundwater can be induced by anthropogenic factors (Chen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022; Xu et al, 2022 ), including the utilization of agricultural fertilizers and pesticides, irrigation activities and LULC changes. Jia et al (2019)  found that the groundwater F−  pollution in the southern Chinese Loess Plateau was mainly caused by the use of chemical fertilizers such as superphosphate, nitrogen phosphate and potassium. Chen et al (2017)  demonstrated that the utilization of nitrogen fertilizer during agricultural cultivation led to elevated F−  concentration in groundwater in the Zhongning area of northwestern China. Yang et al (2022)  reported that agricultural irrigation increased shallow groundwater level and enhanced evaporation effect that cause an increase in the F−  concentration in aquifer. Moreover, irrigation activities led fluoride-containing minerals in soil to infiltrate into aquifer that increased groundwater F−  concentration. Li et al. (2021a)  also showed that the spatial variation of groundwater F−  and As concentrations in Shanxi Province was strongly influenced by LULC changes. However, the key drivers of the spatiotemporal variation of high fluoride groundwater under natural and anthropogenic influences remain to be further explored. Numerous methods have been developed and applied to study the spatiotemporal variation and hydrochemical composition of groundwater. Hydrogeochemistry is a viable tool to discover the formation and variation of chemical composition, and evaluate the migration, accumulation and transformation processes of various pollutants in the aquifer (Li et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022 ). Stable isotope technique is also an effective method to analyze the isotopic composition and hydrochemical characteristics of groundwater as the H and O stable isotopes can identify the source and fate of pollutants in groundwater system (Zhong et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, many studies also use the saturation index (SI) and chlor-alkali index (CAI) to identify the source and enrichment mechanism of high F−  groundwater by evaluating the dissolution of fluoride-containing minerals and the adsorption of cation alternation in aquifer system (Lu et al., 2023 ). But these conventional methods still suffer from various limitations for analyzing and interpreting the main factors influencing spatiotemporal variation of groundwater fluoride concentration. Hence, a novel hybrid approach that combines hydrogeochemistry, isotope analysis and LULC based on remote sensing data is adopted in this study to assess the spatiotemporal variations of high F−  groundwater driven by natural and anthropogenic processes. The Yinchuan basin is a populated and intensively cultivated agricultural area in the northwestern China. However, the basin is growingly dependent on groundwater due to the socioeconomic development, rapid population growth, and dramatic urbanization and industrialization. As a result, groundwater quality of the Yinchuan basin is becoming growingly vulnerable to environmental pollution driven by natural and anthropogenic factors (Yang et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021a; Zhong et al., 2022a; Zhu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ). Although the problems in groundwater contamination have been extensively investigated in recent studies (Wang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2018b ), such as arsenic pollution (Feng et al., 2022a ), nitrate pollution (He et al., 2022 ), and groundwater salinization (Zhang et al., 2023 ), the origin, evolution and drivers of high F−  groundwater surrounding the study area still remain to be studied. Herein, the present study attempts to fill this gap by adopting a novel hybrid approach to interpret the genesis and spatiotemporal variation of groundwater fluoride contamination in the Yinchuan basin under natural and anthropogenic influences. To solve the above issues, this paper mainly focuses on the following four aspects: I) investigate the spatiotemporal variation in the hydrochemical characteristics of high F−  groundwater in the Yinchuan basin, II) analyze the genesis and hydrogeochemical process of high F−  groundwater by applying hydrogeochemical and isotopic methods, III) interpret the enrichment mechanism of fluoride in groundwater under the influence of natural factors, and IV) elucidate the spatiotemporal variation of high F−  groundwater under the influence of anthropogenic activities by using hydrochemical analysis and LULC based on remote sensing data. The present research will ameliorate our understanding of the occurrence, hydrogeochemical evolution and driving factors of high F−  groundwater under the influence of natural and anthropogenic processes in arid and semi-arid regions.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Background of study area The Yinchuan basin (105°87′-106°88′ E, 37°76′-39°24′ N) is geographically located in the northern part of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous region, China (Fig. 1  ), with the Helan Mountains in the west and Ordos block in the east. The basin is one of the most important agricultural areas in the arid and semi-arid region of China, with thousands of years of history. The study area occupies a total area of about 7790 km2 , with nearly 165 km long from south to north, 10–60 km wide from east to west, and an altitude of 1100 m to 1200 m (Wang et al., 2021b ). The basin is characterized by a typical continental climate with the annual temperature of 9 °C. The annual rainfall reaches around 187 mm, and 68 % of annual total rainfall occur during June to September. The annual evaporation is about 1800 mm, approximately ten times higher than annual average precipitation (Zhong et al., 2022b ). The Yinchuan basin is a Cenozoic rift basin around the Ordos block in the North China Craton that is controlled by extensional fault systems. The unconsolidated Quaternary sediments are widely distributed in the Yinchuan basin with a maximum thickness of about 1700 m (Fig. 2  a), and the sediments become thinner from the center toward the edge of the basin (Li et al., 2022 ). As shown in Fig. 2 c, the sedimentary profile of the Yinchuan basin is characterized by three major geomorphic units from Helan Mountain in the west to Yellow river in the east (Wang et al., 2004; Li et al., 2021c ): 1) piedmont pluvial plain, which is mainly composed of coarse gravel sediments, 2) alluvial plain, which is mostly comprised of sand and gravel sediments, and 3) lacustrine plain, which mainly consists of fine sediments such as sand, silt and clay. A geologic cross-section map depicting the controls of major geomorphic units, including piedmont pluvial plain, alluvial plain, and lacustrine plain in the Yinchuan basin is illustrated in Fig. 2 b. According to the lithological and geological features, groundwater aquifers are mainly divided into gravel aquifers, sand and gravel aquifers, and sand aquifers in the Yinchuan basin (Guo et al., 2014 ). Due to the presence of clay layers, the aquifer system varies from a single-layer to a multi-layer aquifer structure as indicated in Fig. 2 c. The single-layer phreatic aquifer zone is mostly located in the western part along the Helan Mountain and the southern part of the basin, and the multi-layer aquifer zone is distributed in the most part of the Yinchuan basin. The thickness of the aquifer shows an uneven variation across the basin. In the central part of the Yinchuan basin, the burial depth of phreatic aquifer generally ranges between 1–3 m below ground surface, with a thickness of 10–50 m (Qian et al., 2014 ). The burial depth of the first confined aquifer is between 30–110 m, with a thickness of 50–100 m. The burial depth of the second confined aquifer is between 230–250 m, with a thickness of 50–100 m (Fig. 2 d). In the eastern edge of the Helan Mountain, the hydraulic gradient in the alluvial plain is relatively large with a range of 1.5 ‰-3.8 ‰ in the confined aquifer (Feng et al., 2022a ). In the Yinchuan basin, groundwater is mainly recharged by rainfall infiltration, irrigation infiltration, channel leakage and lateral recharge. In the agricultural cultivation area of the basin, the infiltration from irrigation water and Yellow River exceeds over 80 % of the total groundwater recharge (Yang et al., 2018a ). The phreatic water basically indicates a flow path from southwest to northeast (Feng et al., 2022b ). In the western part of the basin, the runoff conditions are good due to the high hydraulic gradient. In the central and eastern areas, the runoff conditions become poor because of the relatively low hydraulic gradient and the predominance of clay-sand mixtures in the sediments of study area. Groundwater flow conditions in confined aquifers are similar to those of phreatic aquifers. Groundwater discharge mainly occurs by evaporation and artificial exploitation (Ren et al., 2024 ). The main discharge mode of unconfined water is evaporation, accounting for over 45 % of the total groundwater discharge (Feng et al., 2022b ), while the main discharge mode of confined water is the artificial exploitation that is mostly used for agricultural irrigation in the basin.  2.2 Sample collection and analysis 721 water samples were collected from the research area (Fig. 1 ) in 2004 (n = 372) and 2014 (n = 349), including 346 samples from phreatic water and 26 from surface water in 2004, and 337 samples from phreatic water and 12 from surface water in 2014. Among those, 389 isotopic samples were from phreatic water (n = 351) and surface water (n = 38). Prior to sampling, the polyethylene bottles (0.5 L) and glass bottles (0.5 L) were prewashed and rinsed 3 times with deionized water for collecting water samples. Groundwater samples were extracted with submersible pump and filtered with a 0.45 μm pore size membrane. Surface water samples were taken at a depth of about 0.5 m below the water surface, and phreatic water samples were taken at a depth of 5 to 50 m below the ground. The sampling locations were all recorded on-site with a portable GPS. All samples were classified, categorized, and then conserved in a refrigerator with storage temperature of 4 °C. The chemical analysis of water samples was completed within one week after sampling. The concentrations of Na+ , K+ , Ca2+  and Mg2+  were measured by Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectrometer (Perkin Elmer 40 ICP AES, USA). The concentration of HCO 3 −     was determined by titration method. The concentrations of Cl− , SO 4 2−    , NO 3 −     and F−  were analyzed by Ion chromatography (Dionex ICS-600, USA). D and 18 O test samples were analyzed by the Xi 'an Geological Survey Center of China Geological Survey. The measurement accuracy of chemical analysis was checked through the charge balance error (CBE) by using the formula: CBE = ∑ c a t i o n s - ∑ a n i o n s  ∑ c a t i o n s + ∑ a n i o n s     × 100 %    for ensuring quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC). All the sampling procedures, conservation and transport, and analytical methods were carried out according to the technical specifications (HJ 164–2020) of China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE, 2020 ). The accuracy errors of chemical analysis for all the samples were below 10 %.  2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Hydrochemical diagrams Piper trilinear diagram is an effective graphic tool to analyze the hydrochemical composition of groundwater and evaluate the main hydrochemical types (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The diagram consists of two triangles and a diamond, represented by three common types of cations (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ +K+ ) and three common types of anions (Cl− , SO 4 2−    , HCO 3 −    +CO 3 2−    ) in milligram equivalents per liter. The three edges of the lower left triangle refer to the milligram equivalent percentage of the three cations, and the three edges of the lower right triangle stand for the milligram equivalent percentage of the three anions, respectively. The location of the water sample points in the diamond can reflect the hydrochemical facies of groundwater. Gibbs diagram (Gibbs, 1970 ) can illustrate the degree of natural evolution of groundwater and interpret the formation mechanism and hydrochemical process of groundwater. The Gibbs plot is a set of semi-logarithmic coordinates with the ration of bulk cation concentration Na+ /(Na+ +Ca2+ ) and the ratio of bulk anion concentration Cl− /(Cl− +HCO 3 −    ) as the horizontal axis and TDS (mg/L) as the vertical axis. The diagram can identify the influence of evaporation, precipitation and rock weathering on groundwater hydrochemistry. In this study, Piper and Gibbs diagrams were executed with MATLAB (Version R2021a).  2.3.2 Stable isotope technique Stable isotope analysis is a vital method to study the spatial and temporal variation patterns of surface water and groundwater by analyzing the isotopic composition. Stable H and O isotopes are often used as ideal tracers to identify the recharge source, controlling mechanism and hydrochemical process of the groundwater (Zhong et al., 2019 ). In particular, the integration of hydrochemistry and isotope analysis provides an effective way for analyzing the source, migration, mixing and hydrochemical evolution of groundwater under the influence of natural and anthropogenic factors (Zhu et al., 2023 ). In the arid regions being strongly affected by evaporation, it is often found that the slope of δ2 H-δ18 O of groundwater is below the global precipitation line 8, and has a larger total dissolved solids (TDS) value. In this study, D and 18 O isotopes (d-excess) are applied to assess the effect of precipitation and evaporation on F−  enrichment, and isotope analysis is combined with hydrochemistry to elucidate the hydrogeochemical evolution and controlling mechanism of F−  in the aquifer.  2.3.3 Hydrogeochemical modeling 2.3.3.1 Saturation index Saturation indices (SI) is the most commonly used tool to analyze the equilibrium state of the minerals in water and identify the dominant geochemical processes controlling groundwater chemistry (Garrels and Mackenzie, 1967 ). SI is expressed as the logarithmic ratio of the ion activity product (IAP) to the solubility product constant (Ksp), which can be obtained with the equation (Su et al., 2019 ).(1) SI = l g IAP  K sp         SI<0 indicates an unsaturated state of solution and the mineral elements will continue to dissolve. SI=0 indicates that the mineral component in the solution is in a saturation state, and SI>0 indicates a supersaturated state of solution.  2.3.3.2 Chlor-alkali index The chlor-alkali index (CAI) consisting of CAI-I and CAI-II is often employed to identify the cation exchange process and study the effect of alternating cation adsorption on fluoride enrichment in aquifer system (Cao et al., 2023 ). The CAI-I and CAI-II are obtained with the following equations (Wu et al., 2018 ):(2) CAI - I = Cl  -  - ( Na  +  + K  +  )   Cl  -       (3) CAI - I I = Cl  -  - ( Na  +  + K  +  )   HCO  3  -  + SO  4  2 -   + CO  3  2 -   + NO  3  -         The positive CAI values indicate a reverse ion exchange process, and the occurrence of Na+  and K+  exchange in the aquifer with Ca2+  and Mg2+  in rocks. The negative CAI values indicate that there exists a chloro-alkaline disequilibrium (Rao et al., 2024 ). The greater the absolute value is, the larger the cation exchange capacity is.   2.3.4 Land use and land cover Land use and land cover (LULC) that integrates remote sensing and geographic information system (GIS) is developed as a robust method for studying the influence of LULC changes on groundwater (Li et al., 2021c ). In this research, LULC data were obtained from the Geospatial data cloud (https://www.gscloud.cn ) of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The remote sensing image data from Landsat 7 SLC corrected by SLC-off model and Landsat 8 OLI at 30 m resolution were used to delineate the LULC variation of the Yinchuan basin in 2004 and 2014. Radiometric calibration, atmospheric correction, image mosaic and extraction of remote sensing dataset were implemented with ENVI 5.3 and ArcMap 10.8 (Usman et al., 2020 ). The LULC of the Yinchuan basin was classified and vectorized into six land use types: cropland, forest land, grassland, bare land, water bodies and urban land. Given the prominent role of LULC in studying the global environmental change (Yan et al., 2022 ), the LULC is used as a key indicator of anthropogenic activities to identify and interpret the influence of LULC changes on the spatiotemporal variation in groundwater F−  concentration.    3 Results 3.1 Hydrochemical characteristics of groundwater Groundwater hydrochemistry in 2004 and 2014 were analyzed. It is observed in Table S1  that in 2004, the average concentration of Na+  was 265.38 mg/L. The mean concentrations of SO 4 2−     and HCO 3 −     in anions were 403.53 mg/L and 412.33 mg/L, respectively. The lowest and highest contents of F−  in groundwater were 0.12 mg/L and 14.73 mg/L, respectively, with a mean of 1.04 mg/L. The mean concentrations of major cations displayed a descending order of Na+ >Ca2+ >Mg2+ >K+ , and the mean concentrations of major anions showed a trend of HCO 3 −    >SO 4 2−    >Cl− >CO 3 2−    >F− . In 2014, the mean concentration of Na+  was 249.22 mg/L, and the mean concentration of HCO 3 −     was 440.39 mg/L. The lowest and highest contents of F−  in groundwater were 0.10 mg/L and 16.06 mg/L, respectively, with a mean of 1.02 mg/L. While the mean content of the major cations was Na+ >Ca2+ >Mg2+ >K+ , the major anions was HCO 3 −    >SO 4 2−    >Cl− >F− >CO 3 2−    . Piper trilinear diagram (Fig. 3  ) reveals the hydrochemical facies of groundwater samples in 2004 and 2014 with F− <1 mg/L, F− =1–1.5 mg/L and F− >1.5 mg/L. The result shows that the samples with the same range of F−  concentration in 2004 and 2014 had same hydrochemical facies. The hydrochemical facies of groundwater with concentration of F− <1 mg/L in 2004 and 2014 were SO4 ·Cl-Ca·Mg, HCO3 -Ca·Mg and SO4 ·Cl-Na. However, the hydrochemical facies of groundwater with concentration of F− =1–1.5 mg/L were primarily SO4 ·Cl-Ca·Mg and SO4 ·Cl-Na. The hydrochemical type of high fluoride groundwater with F− >1.5 mg/L was mainly SO4 ·Cl-Na. Accordingly, it can be derived that the main hydrochemical types of groundwater with concentration of F− <1 mg/L were SO4 ·Cl-Ca·Mg, HCO3 -Ca·Mg and SO4 ·Cl-Na in 2004 and 2014, while the hydrochemical types of high fluoride groundwater with concentration of F− =1–1.5 mg/L were SO4 ·Cl-Ca·Mg and SO4 ·Cl-Na, and concentration of F− >1.5 mg/L was SO4 ·Cl-Na. The statistical results of major ions in surface water in 2004 and 2014 are shown in Table S2 . It is observed that the mean concentrations of major cations in surface water of 2004 displayed a descending order of Na+ >Mg2+ >Ca2+ >K+ , and the mean concentrations of major anions showed a basic trend of SO 4 2−    >HCO 3 −    >Cl− >CO 3 2−    >F− . Meanwhile, the mean content of the major cations in surface water of 2014 was Na+ >Ca2+ >Mg2+ >K+ , and the major anions was HCO 3 −    >SO 4 2−    >Cl− >CO 3 2−    >F− . Among those, the average concentration of F−  was 0.97 mg/L in 2004 and 0.57 mg/L in 2014 that did not exceed China’s standard limit of 1 mg/L. However, the highest F−  concentration in surface water was 2.50 mg/L in 2004 that greatly exceeded the standard limit. Meanwhile, the highest concentration of F−  in surface water was 0.90 mg/L in 2014, which are significantly reduced comparted to 2004. It is also observed in Fig. S1  that the main hydrochemical types of surface water in 2004 and 2014 were SO4 ·Cl-Na and SO4 ·Cl-Ca·Mg.  3.2 Isotopic characteristics of groundwater Stable isotope compositions of groundwater and surface water samples in 2004 and 2014 were analyzed. As illustrated in Fig. 4  , δ18 O and δ2 H of groundwater samples in 2004 ranged from −13.21 ‰ to −6.61 ‰ and −94.58 ‰ to −55.19 ‰ (Fig. 4 a), and groundwater samples in 2014 ranged from −13.95 ‰ to −6.86 ‰ and −95.58 ‰ to −51.79 ‰ (Fig. 4 b), respectively, indicating that the variations of isotope values in groundwater are almost similar. The δ18 O and δ2 H of surface water samples in 2004 ranged from −11.49 ‰ to −6.73 ‰ and −87.49 ‰ to −58.14 ‰, surface water samples in 2014 ranged from −10.89 ‰ to −0.15 ‰ and −79.63 ‰ to –23.74 ‰, respectively, displaying that the variation of isotope values in surface water in 2014 is larger than that in 2004 due to stronger evaporation. The groundwater evaporation line (GWEL: δ2 H=4.992δ18 O-24.254 in 2004 and δ2 H=4.733δ18 O-24.667 in 2014) and surface water evaporation line (SWEL: δ2 H=4.992δ18 O-24.254 in 2004 and δ2 H=4.846δ18 O-23.844 in 2014) were obtained with the isotope values of groundwater and surface water, respectively. In Fig. 4 , the slope (k = 7.21) of the LMWL lied below the GMWL (Craig, 1961 ), indicating that the Yinchuan basin has arid climatic conditions with low rainfall and intensive evaporation. The GWEL lies below the LMWL in both two periods, indicating that groundwater is recharged by precipitation and affected by evaporation. The SWEL also fall below the LMWL, suggesting that surface water was naturally recharged by rainfall and strongly influenced by evaporation.  3.3 Spatiotemporal variability of high fluoride groundwater Fig. 5   demonstrates the spatial distribution of F−  in groundwater with content greater than China’s standard limit of 1 mg/L. In 2004, 140 groundwater samples exceeded the standard limit, with an exceeding rate of 40.46 % and F−  content in a range of 0.12 mg/L to 14.73 mg/L. The mean F−  concentration of groundwater in 2004 (n = 346) reached 1.04 mg/L, slightly higher than 1.02 mg/L in 2014 (n = 337) as well as the standard limit of 1 mg/L. In 2014, 87 groundwater samples exceeded the standard limit, with an exceeding rate of 25.81 % and F−  content in a range of 0.1 mg/L to 16.06 mg/L. Hence, it can be derived that the exceeding rate of groundwater samples in 2014 is greatly smaller than that in 2004, and the mean F−  concentration in 2014 is slightly lower than that in 2004, indicating a decreasing trend of groundwater F−  pollution in the study area. Meanwhile, the annual rainfall rose from 185.65 mm in 2004 to 225.59 mm in 2014, accounting for an increase of 21.51 %. This provides strong evidence that the spatiotemporal variation in groundwater F−  concentration in 2004 and 2014 is greatly influenced by the change in precipitation due to the dilution effect in aquifer. The spatial distribution of high F−  groundwater exhibited a great variation in 2004 (Fig. 5 a) and 2014 (Fig. 5 b). In 2004, high F−  groundwater with the content of F− >1 mg/L was distributed across the Yinchuan basin, demonstrating severe F−  contamination in groundwater. The most polluted area with the content of F− >5 mg/L was mainly located near the northern part of Yinchuan and the eastern part of Wuzhong. In 2014, high F−  groundwater with the content of F− >1 mg/L was only distributed in a small area of the basin, indicating a great decrease of F−  contamination in groundwater. The most polluted area with the content of F− >5 mg/L was mainly located in the eastern part of Shizuishan and the eastern part of Wuzhong city. Accordingly, it is found that the polluted area with the content of F− >1 mg/L in 2014 is significantly reduced in both scope and scale compared with 2004, whereas the most polluted area with the content of F− >5 mg/L in 2014 is slightly enlarged in a small area of the southern and northern basin. It is notable that except a small area in the lower reach of the river, the polluted area with high fluoride concentration almost disappeared near both sides of the Yellow river.  3.4 Spatiotemporal variation of LULC The distribution of LULC in the Yinchuan basin shows that the land use type varied significantly between 2004 and 2014 (Fig. 6   and Table S3 ). In 2004, the area of six land use types was 5224.849 km2  (cropland), 0.034 km2  (forest land), 1543.194 km2  (grassland), 189.802 km2  (water bodies), 361.057 km2  (bare land) and 471.064 km2  (urban land), respectively. In 2014, the cropland area reached 5,248.565 km2 , with an increase of 0.45 %. The forest area was only 0.073 km2  despite an increase of 113.33 %. The grassland area reached 1292.145 km2  with a decrease of 16.27 %. The water bodies area reached 251.760 km2  with an increase of 32.64 %. The bare land area reached 163.641 km2  with a great decrease of 54.68 %. The urban land area reached 833.815 km2  with a significant increase of 77.01 %. The variation of the area in LULC displayed a descending order: forest land (+113.33 %) > urban land (+77.01 %) > water bodies (+32.64 %) > cropland (+0.45 %) > grassland (−16.27 %) > bare land (−54.68 %). Among those, the urban land (+362.751 km2 ), grassland (−251.049 km2 ) and bare land (−197.416 km2 ) were the land use types with the largest area change. Land use area transfer matrix of Yinchuan basin is visualized by Chordal diagram in Fig. 6 . It can be seen that during 2004–2014, the reduced cropland area (8.42 %) was mainly converted into urban land (3.82 %), grassland (3.05 %) and water bodies (1.52 %). The reduced grassland (36.7 %) was mainly converted into cropland (24.33 %) and urban land (8.48 %) during the same period. Meanwhile, the bare land area (63.30 %) was transferred into grassland (42.74 %) and urban land (11.13 %). The decrease of cropland and grassland area contributed greatly to the increase of urban land, and areas of water bodies and bare land were partly converted into urban land. As illustrated in Fig. 13 a and 13b, it is found that LULC of the Yinchuan basin exhibited a spatial variation during 2004–2014. In the central, northern and southern parts of the basin, the urban land of Yinchuan and Shizuishan significantly expanded during 2004–2014, while the urban land of Wuzhong increased moderately. In the eastern and northwestern parts of the basin, the bare land of Shizuishan was greatly reduced during the same period, which was mainly transferred into urban land in the western area, cropland and grassland in the eastern area, respectively. The LULC changes can influence the spatiotemporal distribution of high fluoride groundwater.   4 Discussion 4.1 Natural factors affecting groundwater fluoride concentration 4.1.1 Dissolution of fluoride-rich minerals The fluorite and apatite are the main fluoride-containing minerals in the Yinchuan basin as well as the major source of F−  in groundwater, which originate from the rocks including limestone, gravel, sandstone, mudstone, claystone (Li, 2020; Han et al., 2023 ). Previous studies show that fluoride content in limestone, gravel, sandstone, mudstone and claystone is 210 mg/kg, 640 mg/kg, 320 mg/kg, 520 mg/kg and 640 mg/kg, respectively (Li et al., 2021c; Jing et al., 2022 ), which greatly contribute to F−  enrichment in the aquifers. Lu et al (2023)  studied the origin of F−  in groundwater using the SI, and found that the precipitating process of calcite and dolomite can promote the F−  release of fluoride-bearing minerals and thus cause the elevated F−  content in groundwater. The precipitating process of calcite, gypsum and dolomite will reduce the Ca2+  content in groundwater, promote the dissolving process of fluoride-containing minerals, and thus increase the F−  content in groundwater (Guo et al., 2012 ). The chemical reaction processes are expressed by the following equations (Lu et al., 2023 ):(4) Ca F 2  + 2 HCO  3  -  → CaCO  3  ↓ + 2 F  -  + H 2  O + CO  2  ↑      (5) Ca F 2  → Ca  2 +   + 2 F  -      (6) Ca  2 +   + Mg  2 +   + OH  -  + 2 HCO  3  -  → C a M g ( CO  3  )  2  ↓ + 2  H 2  O      As illustrated in Fig. 7  a, the SI values of calcite and dolomite in samples of 2004 are all above zero, while the SI values of fluorite and gypsum in most samples are also greater than zero, indicating that F−  in groundwater reached supersaturation state, and fluoride-containing minerals such as fluorite can no longer dissolve in groundwater and will precipitate. As observed in Fig. 7 b, the SI values of calcite and dolomite in most samples of 2014 are above zero, displaying that the minerals of calcite and dolomite in groundwater reached supersaturation state that decrease the Ca2+  content and increase the dissolving of fluoride-containing minerals and groundwater fluoride concentration. The SI values of fluorite and gypsum in samples are all less than zero, implying that they are being dissolved in groundwater (Liu et al., 2021 ). The SO 4 2−     and Ca2+  in groundwater mostly originate from the dissolved gypsum that increase the concentration of SO 4 2−     in groundwater. The SI values of fluorite increases with the elevated F−  content, suggesting that the dissolved fluoride minerals are the major source of natural fluoride in groundwater. Spearman correlation coefficient can demonstrate the correlation between groundwater indices. As shown in Fig. 8  a and 8 b, Na+  is significantly correlated with Cl− , SO 4 2−     and TDS, accounting for 0.87, 0.80 and 0.88 in 2004, 0.91, 0.81 and 0.40 in 2014, indicating that the dissolved halite and gypsum may be the vital source of the chemical components in groundwater. Mg2+  shows a positive correlation with Cl− , SO 4 2−     and TDS, accounting for 0.51, 0.66 and 0.72 in 2004, 0.63, 0.72 and 0.33 in 2014, respectively. Cl−  is strongly positively correlated with SO 4 2−     and TDS, accounting for 0.71 and 0.84 in 2004, 0.81 and 0.43 in 2014, respectively. It is thus suggested that the main ions in groundwater may come from the dissolved sulfate, gypsum and halite. F−  shows a positive correlation with NO 3 −    , accounting for 0.34 in 2004 and 0.32 in 2014, respectively, indicating that except for anthropogenic sources, there are other sources of fluoride in groundwater (Qu et al., 2022; Su et al., 2023 ). F−  showed a weak positive correlation with Na+ , Cl−  and SO 4 2−     in 2004, while F−  exhibited a weak positive correlation with CO 3 2−     and a weak negative correlation with Ca2+  in 2014, with correlation coefficients of 0.17 and −0.27, suggesting that F−  enrichment is probably affected by competitive ion adsorption and mineral solution-precipitation.  4.1.2 Evaporation effect As displayed in Gibbs diagram (Fig. 9  ), a small part of groundwater samples with three levels of F−  concentration (F− <1.0 mg/L, F− =1–1.5 mg/L and F− >1.5 mg/L) were located in the evaporation dominance area with high TDS, indicating that evaporation effect is the factor influencing the F−  enrichment in groundwater. However, most of samples with concentrations of F− <1.0 mg/L, F− =1–1.5 mg/L and F− >1.5 mg/L were located in the rock weathering dominance area, with TDS of 300 to 2000 mg/L, while a moderate part of groundwater samples with concentration of F− <1.0 mg/L, F− =1–1.5 mg/L and F− >1.5 mg/L were located in the precipitation dominance area, with TDS value of 10–30 mg/L, suggesting that the F−  enrichment is strongly influenced by the water–rock interaction and the precipitation. It is notable that a number of samples with concentration of F− >1.5 mg/L were located outside the three dominant areas with high TDS, implying that groundwater fluoride pollution is influenced not only by natural factors, but also by anthropogenic factors. The deuterium excess (d) value is able to measure the process of water evaporation and condensation (Olaka et al., 2016 ). When the evaporation occurs, the d value falls, and TDS of the water will increase at the same time (Li et al., 2019 ). As illustrated in Fig. 10  ,  the d values of samples in 2004 and 2014 ranged from −4.53 ‰ to 22.63 ‰ with a dense distribution between −1‰-10 ‰. The TDS values varied between 400 mg/L and 4130 mg/L and the d value indicated a decrease with the increasing TDS, suggesting that evaporation process has effect on groundwater. The d value of atmospheric precipitation was defined as d = δ2 H-8δ18 O (GMWL) and d = δ2 H-7.21δ18 O (LMWL), displaying that the slope of GMWL (K=8) and LMWL (K=7.21) is higher than that of GWEL (K = 4.992) in 2004 and (K=4.733) in 2014, as indicated in Fig. 4 .  It implies that evaporation process can influence the hydrochemical evolution and fluoride enrichment in groundwater.  4.1.3 Competitive adsorption and alkaline environment The competitive adsorption of F−  and HCO 3 −     can strongly influence the F−  enrichment in groundwater (Zabala et al., 2016 ). As illustrated in Fig. 11  a, the F−  concentration varied between 0.10 mg/L and 16.06 mg/L in 2004 and 2014, while HCO 3 −     concentrations ranged from 100 mg/L to 1200 mg/L. When the F−  concentration in groundwater is below 1.5 mg/L, no obvious correlation between F−  and HCO 3 −     is observed, but when it is above 1.5 mg/L, a significant positive correlation between F−  and HCO 3 −     is observed, indicating that high HCO 3 −     concentration is favorable to dissolve carbonate and fluoride-containing minerals, and competitive adsorption of F−  and HCO 3 −     increases groundwater fluoride concentration in the study area. The results are in accord with the recent studies of Su et al (2019) . Alkaline environment and competitive adsorption of F−  with OH−  can contribute to the fluoride enrichment in groundwater. Due to the similarity of ionic radius between F−  and OH− , it is favorable to competitive adsorption of two ions in groundwater. Therefore, F−  can be released to groundwater by desorption or exchange with OH−  in alkaline environment. Hu et al found that when the pH is higher than the zero-point charge of the adsorbent, F−  is released from clay minerals because of competitive adsorption of OH−  (Hu et al., 2022 ). In Fig. 11 b, the pH values of most samples in 2004 and 2014 ranged from 6.93 to 8.5, displaying a weakly alkaline environment. Among those, the pH value of high fluoride groundwater with F− >1.5 mg/L mostly lied within the range of 7.2 to 8.5, suggesting that high pH is more favorable for the fluoride enrichment in groundwater due to competitive adsorption of F−  and OH−  under alkaline condition (Xu et al., 2022 ). The cation exchange process of Na+ , K+  with Ca2+ , Mg2+  affects the enrichment and adsorption mechanisms of F−  in groundwater. While the ratio of (Na+ -Cl− ) and (Ca2+ +Mg2+ -SO 4 2−    –HCO 3 −    ) can identify the mechanisms of cation exchange and adsorption, the CAI can then measure direct cation exchange or reverse cation exchange. The scatter diagram (Fig. 11 c) shows the correlation between (Ca2+ +Mg2+ -SO 4 2−    –HCO 3 −    ) and (Na+ -Cl− ) of groundwater samples in 2004 and 2014. It is observed that the slopes of the fitted lines for groundwater samples in both 2004 and 2014 were close to −1, and (Na+ -Cl− ) was significantly negative correlated with (Ca2+ +Mg2+ -SO 4 2−    –HCO 3 −    ), implying that the cation exchange and adsorption occurs in the aquifer. The results of CAI values for groundwater samples in 2004 and 2014 are demonstrated in Fig. 11 d. The values of both CAI-I and CAI-II in 22.58 % of samples in 2004 and 44.59 % of samples in 2014 are greater than zero, Na+  and K+  will replace Ca2+  and Mg2+  from the surface of minerals and increase the concentrations of Ca2+  and Mg2+  in groundwater, leading to the precipitating of fluoride-containing minerals and decrease of F−  concentration in the aquifer. On the contrary, the values of CAI-I and CAI-II in some samples are below zero, Ca2+  and Mg2+  will replace Na+  and K+  from the surface of minerals, elevate Na+  and K+  contents in groundwater and reduce Ca2+  and Mg2+  contents, which promote the hydrolysis of fluoride-containing minerals and increase the F−  concentration in groundwater.   4.2 Anthropogenic factors affecting groundwater fluoride concentration 4.2.1 Effect of fertilizers and pesticides The massive application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in agricultural production can considerably affect the fluoride concentration in groundwater. The fertilizers and pesticides that contain the F−  elements are the most important agricultural inputs for increasing crop yield, reducing crop loss and boosting agricultural productivity (Zeng et al., 2023 ). Meanwhile, the excessive use of agricultural fertilizers and pesticides can cause the F−  elements to infiltrate into aquifer under the leaching effect that greatly increase the F−  concentration in groundwater, particularly in intensive agricultural areas. Khyalia et al investigated the F−  pollution of groundwater in the rural areas of India, and found that farmers' excessive application of fertilizers and pesticides in crop fields is the main source of high fluoride in groundwater (Su et al., 2023; Khyalia et al., 2024 ). Qu et al studied F−  and NO 3 −     pollution in groundwater in the Ordos basin, China by using the hydrochemical method and source analysis, and found that high F−  and NO 3 −     groundwater has similar pollution source, and the intensive agricultural activities greatly influence F−  and NO 3 −     concentrations in groundwater because of the massive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides (Qu et al., 2022; Das et al., 2023 ). In Fig. 12  a, 56.1 % of samples in 2004 with the content of F− >1.5 mg/L and 76.5 % of samples with the F−  content of 1–1.5 mg/L lied below the trend of Evaporite dissolution with low nitrate content, while only 27.3 % of samples (F− >1.5 mg/L) and 18.8 % of samples (F− =1–1.5 mg/L) were located between Evaporite dissolution and Wastewater and fertilizers with high nitrate content, indicating that the evaporite dissolution is the dominant factor for increased F−  content in groundwater. In Fig. 12 b, 25.71 % of samples in 2014 with the content of F− >1.5 mg/L and 37.0 % of samples (F− =1–1.5 mg/L) were distributed below the trend of Evaporite dissolution with low nitrate content, while 57.4 % of samples (F− >1.5 mg/L) and 48.6 % of samples (F− =1–1.5 mg/L) lied inside the trend of Wastewater and fertilizers with high nitrate concentration, demonstrating that the wastewater and fertilizers have strong influence on the elevated F−  concentration in groundwater. However, the samples of high fluoride groundwater (F− >1 mg/L) in 2014 decreased significantly compared to 2004, reflecting a decreasing trend of groundwater fluoride concentration during the two periods. It is generally recognized that when nitrate concentrations in groundwater are high, the co-presence of high F−  and Cl−  content is probably influenced by the effluents from agricultural practices and human activities (Xu et al., 2022 ). During the period 2004–2014, the volume of fertilizers and pesticides used in the study area experienced a great change that can influence the F−  concentration in groundwater. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, the total volume of agricultural fertilizers including complex fertilizer (with the F−  element of 1161.21 mg/kg), nitrogen fertilizers (741.98 mg/kg), phosphorus and potassium fertilizers (106.90 mg/kg) increased from 0.2761 to 0.3967 million tons in Ningxia region during 2004–2014 (China NBS, 2016; Luo et al., 2017 ). However, the organic fertilizers with lower F−  content gradually replaced the inorganic fertilizers in agriculture for reducing the agricultural pollution in the region (Gao and Ma, 2006 ), and increased from 35.17 % in 2005 to 48.7 % in 2011, 59.2 % in 2012, 90 % in 2013, and 92.7 % in 2014 (Ma et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015 ), which can greatly mitigate the F−  contamination in groundwater and lead to a decrease of F−  concentration in the study area. Meanwhile, Liu et al (2019)  reported that acetamiprid, avermectin and lambda-cyhalothrin are the mostly used pesticides in the study area, which contain the F−  element of 51.87 mg/kg, 32.20 mg/kg and 30.92 mg/kg, respectively. According to statistics (China NBS, 2016 ), the volume of pesticides used in Ningxia region decreased from 1800 tons in 2004 to 1600 tons in 2005, and increased gradually to 2600 tons in 2014, which can affect groundwater F−  concentration in the Yinchuan basin. Accordingly, the intensive use of fertilizers and pesticides is the anthropogenic source of F−  in the aquifer that has strong influence on the spatiotemporal variation of F−  concentration in the study area.  4.2.2 Effect of irrigation activities Irrigation activities can strongly affect the groundwater F−  concentration. In agricultural region, the irrigation is the largest water use sector, and plays a critical role in crop cultivation and food security. However, many studies found that the contaminated irrigation water is the primary source of groundwater pollution in the agricultural regions due to irrigation return flow (Brindha et al., 2016; Qu et al, 2022 ). Yang et al (2022)  investigated the driving factors of groundwater F−  and NO 3 −     pollution in an intensive agricultural region of Shandong Province, China, and the results demonstrated that the irrigation activities caused the fluorine-containing substance in soil to infiltrate into aquifer, and increased fluoride and nitrate concentration in groundwater. Chen et al (2021)  also studied the hydrochemical characteristics of fluoride in groundwater in an agricultural irrigation area of the Yellow River Basin, and the results showed that the Wei River, the major source of irrigation water, can dilute and reduce fluoride concentration in groundwater through the infiltration of irrigation water. Thus, irrigation activities are the key factor influencing the variation in groundwater fluoride concentration. As exhibited in Fig. 5 a, high fluoride groundwater with the concentration greater than 1 mg/L was widely distributed across the Yinchuan basin, indicating severe fluoride contamination in groundwater. As a traditional agricultural area in the arid region, the Yinchuan basin suffers severe water scarcity, and agricultural activities rely heavily on groundwater as the major source of irrigation water across the basin. Meanwhile, the groundwater was seriously polluted with F−  due to the natural and anthropogenic factors. Thus, the long-term use of fluoride-polluted groundwater for agricultural irrigation caused the accumulation and enrichment of F−  in aquifer system, which worsened the situation of F−  pollution in groundwater in the Yinchuan basin. Because the F−  elements stemming from fluoride-contaminated soil through agricultural fertilizers and pesticides and fluoride-contaminated groundwater can be released, accumulated and enriched in the aquifer due to the infiltration of precipitation and irrigation water, eventually resulting in an elevated F−  concentration in the study area. However, the spatial distribution of high fluoride groundwater varied greatly in 2014. As illustrated in Fig. 5 a and b, groundwater fluoride pollution in the Yinchuan basin is reduced spatially and temporally on a large scale. The spatiotemporal variation in high fluoride groundwater is mainly caused by a switch of irrigation water from fluoride-polluted groundwater to Yellow river water during the period 2004–2014. Given the problems in water scarcity and groundwater pollution, the local governments reestablished the agricultural irrigation system consisting of a huge network of reservoirs, lakes, rivers, canals and drains across the Yinchuan basin, which are diverted from the Yellow river with improved water quality (Wang, 2007 ). This not only mitigates the agricultural water scarcity and reduces the dependence of agricultural cultivation on groundwater, but also enhances the groundwater pollution risk control and improves the agricultural water management (Chen, 2006 ). As a result, the use of irrigation water from the Yellow river in agriculture greatly decreased the groundwater F−  concentration due to the dilution effect in aquifer. Accordingly, the switch of irrigation water from fluoride-polluted groundwater to Yellow river water is the major factor influencing the spatiotemporal variability of high F−  groundwater.  4.2.3 Effect of LULC changes The LULC changes driven by human activities can significantly alter the regional hydrogeochemical processes, and affect the spatial and temporal variation of F−  concentration in groundwater. Li et al (2021b)  evaluated the distribution characteristics of F−  and As concentrations in the urban, suburban and industrial lands in Shanxi Province during the period of 2010–2015 and 2016–2018, and found that the spatial variations in F and As concentration in groundwater are strongly influenced by urban expansion and LULC changes. Pant et al (2021)  also assessed the influence of geogenic and anthropogenic processes on the F−  concentration in the Bundelkhand region of India, suggesting that groundwater in the densely populated agricultural or industrial areas is severely polluted with F−  due to the domestic sewage and industrial wastewater. Particularly, the infiltration of landfill leachate and chemical fertilizers in grassland and cropland increased the F−  concentration in groundwater. Thus, the LULC change is the main factor affecting spatiotemporal variation in groundwater F−  concentration. As displayed in Fig. 13   and Table S4 , high F−  groundwater with the content greater than 1 mg/L varied greatly along with the LULC changes. It is observed in Fig. 13 a that in 2004, 38.55 % of samples in cropland, 55.32 % of samples in grassland, 22.22 % of samples in water bodies, 46.15 % of samples in bare land, and 35.71 % of samples in urban land surpassed the standard limit of 1 mg/L. However, the spatial distribution of high F−  groundwater in 2014 changed greatly. As indicated in Fig. 13 b, 24.89 % of samples in cropland, 37.78 % of samples in grassland, 14.29 % of samples in water bodies, 37.50 % of samples in bare land, and 18.75 % of samples in urban land were greater than the standard limit, accounting for a percentage decrease of 13.66 % in cropland, 17.54 % in grassland, 7.93 % in water bodies, 8.65 % in bare land, 16.96 % in urban land while compared with 2004. Since the forest land only occupies a tiny percentage (0.01 %) of the total land area and no sampling point is located within the forest land, the percentage change of samples and F−  concentration in forest land is not calculated. Based on the above results, it is found that the spatiotemporal variability of high fluoride groundwater in 2004 and 2014 are strongly affected by LULC changes of the basin during the two periods. The remote sensing and GIS-based mapping demonstrated that the distribution of LULC in the Yinchuan basin changed greatly during 2004–2014. As shown in Table S3 , the urban land (+77.01 %), grassland (−16.72 %), cropland (+0.45 %) and bare land (−54.68 %) are the main contributors to the spatial variation in LULC. While the reduced grassland (−251.049 km2 ) was converted to cropland and urban land, the F−  concentration of samples with F− >1 mg/L from cropland (+23.716 km2 ) increased from 1.94 mg/L to 2.81 mg/L during 2004–2014, indicating a great variation of groundwater F−  concentration. When the urban land (+362.751 km2 ) greatly expanded in the central, southern and northern parts of the basin, the F−  concentration of samples with F− >1 mg/L from urban land increased from 1.47 mg/L to 1.75 mg/L, displaying a moderate variation in F−  concentration. The reduced bare land (−197.416 km2 ) was mainly transferred to grassland in the northeastern area and urban land in the northwestern area of the basin. Meanwhile, the F−  concentration of samples with F− >1 mg/L from bare land slightly decreased from 1.27 mg/L to 1.15 mg/L during 2004–2014, the grassland increased from 1.67 mg/L to 1.91 mg/L, exhibiting a moderate change in F−  concentration. Therefore, LULC changes are the major factor influencing the spatiotemporal variation of groundwater F−  concentration in the Yinchuan basin.    5 Conclusions In this study, the genesis and spatiotemporal variations of high fluoride groundwater in an intensive agricultural area were explored using a hybrid approach. The results showed that 40.46 % of samples in 2004 and 25.81 % of samples in 2014 exceeded the standard limits, indicating the occurrence of severe fluoride contamination in groundwater. The main hydrochemical type of high F−  groundwater with F− >1.5 mg/L was SO4 ·Cl-Na. The origin and spatiotemporal variations of high F−  groundwater in the Yinchuan basin were mainly driven by natural and anthropogenic processes. The hydrogeochemical and isotopic evidence suggested that the enrichment mechanisms of high F−  groundwater were strongly affected by natural factors. The dissolution of fluoride-containing minerals such as fluorite and apatite, precipitation, evaporation, cation exchange, competitive adsorption of HCO 3 −     and OH−  with F− , and alkaline environment were the major factors influencing the groundwater F−  concentration in the study area. It is also found that the spatiotemporal variation in groundwater fluoride concentration was strongly influenced by anthropogenic activities. Among those, the application of fertilizers and pesticides, irrigation practices and LULC changes were the main factors affecting the spatiotemporal variability of high F−  groundwater across the study area. The remote sensing and GIS-based mapping indicated that the spatial variations in urban land (+77.01 %), grassland (−16.27％) and bare land (−54.68 %) were the main drivers of the spatiotemporal variations of groundwater fluoride concentration in the Yinchuan basin. The findings from the present study provide a better understanding on the genesis and spatiotemporal variations of high F−  groundwater under the influence of natural and anthropogenic processes in arid and semi-arid agricultural regions, which can help enhance the pollution risk control and improve the groundwater resources management.
1 Introduction Globally, agricultural water use accounts for around 70 % of freshwater withdrawal (Ozdogan et al., 2010 ). For many regions in South Asia, irrigation water consumption exceeds 90 % of freshwater withdrawal (Meier et al., 2018 ). The intensity of water withdrawals for this purpose, combined with substantial temporal and spatial climatic variability in the region, has led to periodic water shortages, troubling groundwater trends, and conflicts over surface water resources (Asoka et al., 2017; Janakarajan, 2016; Rodell et al., 2009 ). Intensification of these trends and tensions can be tied to the dramatic expansion of irrigated areas in recent decades, associated with increased demand due to population growth and urbanization and to increased access to the equipment and energy required to extract irrigation water (Pingali, 2012 ). Indeed, the current state of water resources in the region and the social and political tensions associated with it constitute a regional freshwater crisis (Wirsing, 2011 ), and there is significant concern about how the crisis can be addressed now and in the future. In this context, the ability to obtain reliable estimates of irrigation water demand and to understand its influence on the hydrological cycle is of considerable importance for governments and decision-makers at multiple levels. While in situ monitoring is a key pillar for any effort to obtain such estimates, the physical scale of the issue has motivated satellite-informed estimates of water consumption (Zohaib & Choi, 2020 ) and water resource trends (Rodell et al., 2018; Rodell et al., 2009 ) across the region. These observations can be used as direct diagnostic tools, and they can also be combined with prognostic Earth system models (ESMs) to provide process-based and potentially predictive tools for water resource analysis (Nie et al., 2018; Ozdogan et al., 2010 ). The latter approach offers several advantages, including the value of merging data streams to enhance confidence in results, the ability of ESM to provide spatially and temporally continuous estimates of water use, and the inherent ability of models to forecast water use into the future, where diagnostic approaches are tied more tightly to the past observational record. However, large uncertainties exist in these ESM-based irrigation estimates owing to differences in parameters, irrigation estimation methods, meteorological forcings. In an ESM, estimates of irrigation impacts on water resources can be highly sensitive to remotely sensed and field-informed parameter inputs such as fractional irrigated area, crop type, soil texture, irrigation season and frequency of application, and source water partition (i.e., surface water vs. groundwater vs. unconventional water sources). In a modern gridded land surface model (LSM), the fractional irrigated area is often drawn from a satellite-derived product. These fractional irrigated area products have improved in resolution and reliability over the past several decades, but they are still a source of considerable uncertainty for irrigation modeling. For example, the estimates of the irrigated area in South Asia by Meier et al. (2018)  and arrive at an area that is 32 % greater than that reported by the Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA; Siebert et al., 2013) and 26 % greater than the Food and Agriculture Organizations (FAO) statistical estimate (FAOSTAT; FAO, 2016). Soil texture information can also be a great source of uncertainty as it influences simulation of water infiltration, soil water content, and evaporation in fields identified as actively irrigated (Niu et al., 2011 ). From the perspective of water resource analysis, another important irrigation-related parameter is the ratio used to determine which percentage of irrigation water is sourced from surface water vs. groundwater. Spatially gridded maps of this partitioning ratio are far less common than irrigation fraction (i.e., IF) maps because they require ground observations, and these observations are rare and might not capture current conditions. In part, for this reason, many studies have neglected the partitioning of irrigation source water or simply assumed surface water irrigation, which may be an acceptable assumption when groundwater is not a major source for irrigation or when the focus of the simulation is the irrigation impact on soil water and fluxes to the atmosphere (Evans & Zaitchik, 2008; Lawston et al., 2015; Yilmaz et al., 2014 ). However, this assumption severely limits the application of such models to water resource analysis in South Asia, where severe groundwater depletion has been observed by the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite system (Girotto et al., 2017; Loomis et al., 2019b; Rodell et al., 2018 ) and has been attributed primarily to irrigation. Therefore, including groundwater withdrawal information is crucial to capture the irrigation impact on groundwater sustainability. Another key consideration when simulating irrigation is the timing of the irrigation season. In ESM, effective growing seasons are often used as the periods when irrigation can be applied. Some models use predefined crop calendars to determine the growing seasons, but these calendars generally lack year-to-year variability (Wada et al., 2014 ). Other models determine growing seasons based on meteorological forcings, such as precipitation and temperature (Alcamo et al., 2003; Wisser et al., 2008 ), or satellite data products, such as greenness vegetation fraction (Ozdogan et al., 2010 ). Different growing season estimates can have a substantial impact on the simulation of the irrigation processes, adding to the uncertainty of the irrigation water demand estimates. In addition to these surface conditions and irrigation parameters, estimates of irrigation water use are sensitive to uncertainties in meteorology, especially precipitation. For simulation of irrigation with an offline LSM—i.e., a simulation in which the ESM does not simulate its own meteorology—the choice of the meteorological forcing dataset can be critical. Satellite-informed and hybrid satellite / in situ datasets are frequently employed for this purpose since in situ networks are too sparse to support high resolution, real-time distributed precipitation estimates in most regions. In South Asia, satellite-informed and modeled precipitation estimates exhibit large uncertainty, due to complex terrain (particularly in the mountains) and the sparsity of in situ observational networks to inform hybrid precipitation products (Song et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2014; Wang & Zeng, 2012; Yoon et al., 2019; You et al., 2015 ). This study is motivated by both the importance of producing reliable irrigation water use estimates in South Asia and the recognized challenges associated with obtaining reliable parameter maps, meteorological forcing, and irrigation simulations from satellite-informed LSMs. The goal of this study is to 1) generate long-term modeled spatially and temporally continuous irrigation water demand in South Asia and 2) examine the underlying model sensitivities to different input datasets and model parameters. We draw model inputs from multiple credible sources and perform a study of irrigation water withdrawal estimates using an advanced LSM that includes an irrigation model. Specifically, we examine the influence that different satellite-informed estimates of precipitation, irrigation fraction, soil texture, and groundwater irrigation ratio have on the model’s simulation of irrigation water use.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Noah-MP LSM and irrigation scheme All experiments in this study are conducted using a South Asia Hydrological Monitoring System developed within NASA’s Land Information System framework (Kumar et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2020 ) using the Noah-MultiParameterization (Noah-MP) land surface model, version 3.6. Noah-MP augments the Noah land surface model with enhanced options for simulating the surface energy balance, snow, frozen soil, groundwater, runoff, and leaf dynamics (Ek et al., 2003; Livneh et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2011 ). A benefit of using Noah-MP is that the model provides multiple parameterizations for a variety of physical processes that users can customize and adapt for targeted regions or simulation objectives. For instance, in this study subsurface hydrologic processes are represented using the TOPMODEL (Niu & Yang, 2007 ), which accounts for the water exchange between a soil column and an unconfined aquifer. Noah-MP has been shown to have the ability to represent the soil moisture, runoff, and snowfields relatively well in South Asia river basins (Xue et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2021 ). This study focuses on evaluating the uncertainty associated with input data for an irrigation scheme within Noah-MP. This irrigation scheme was first presented by Ozdogan et al. (2010)  for the Noah LSM and was implemented for Noah-MP and improved by Nie et al. (2018) , who added source water partitioning to the scheme. The irrigation algorithm works by determining 1) the location of actively irrigated lands, 2) the timing of irrigation applications, 3) the amount of irrigation water applied, and 4) the source of applied water (i.e., groundwater vs. surface water irrigation). The location of irrigation water is determined by an irrigation fraction map, with the percentage value representing the percent area within each grid that is available for irrigation, should water balance and vegetation conditions call for it. The timing of the irrigation is determined by satisfying the following conditions: 1) the current time is within the growing season of the year; 2) the soil moisture is below a certain threshold. The growing season or irrigation season in Noah-MP is defined as the months of a year when the greenness vegetation fraction (GVF) is larger than a certain threshold (GV F th   )    . This threshold is calculated as,(2.1) GV F th   = G V F min   + a × G V F range   ,     where GV F min      is the minimum GVF of the year, GV F range      is the range of GVF for the year, and a     is a calibration parameter. The second condition to be satisfied to trigger irrigation is that the soil moisture averaged within the rooting depth is lower than a specific soil moisture threshold (S M th     ), which is calculated as,(2.2) S M th   = S M wilt   + S M FC   - S M wilt      × b ,     where S M wilt      and S M FC      are the wilting point and the field capacity of the corresponding soil texture, and b  is a calibration parameter (Fig. 1  ). Both a    and b    are determined by calibrating simulated irrigation water demand to FAO water use reports. The rooting depth is calculated as,(2.3) h rt   = G V F  × d crop   ,     where GVF denotes the greenness fraction for the corresponding month and d crop      is the maximum rooting depth of the corresponding row crop. Fig. 1  shows an illustration of the irrigation process simulated by this irrigation scheme. Irrigation begins when observed GVF becomes the GVF threshold determined by equation (2.1). In this specific illustration, a dual-season irrigation schedule is indicated by the shaded period in Fig. 1 . Once irrigation is triggered, the amount of water for irrigation is calculated as the water amount that fills the root zone soil from the current soil moisture level to field capacity. Then the groundwater ratio map is applied to partition the estimated total irrigation amount into groundwater and surface water irrigation, with the groundwater part being extracted from the groundwater reservoir.  2.2 Experiment design 2.2.1 Retrospective simulation and irrigation simulation The research domain for all simulations is bounded by latitudes 5 °  N    and 40 °  N    and longitudes 58 °  E    and 100 °  E   , as shown in Fig. 2  . We first experiment to compare an irrigation simulation (IRRI) to a retrospective simulation (RETRO) using one combination of parameterizations. Both simulations are built upon the South Asia Hydrological monitoring system described in Zhou et al. (2021) . The IRRI and RETRO simulations use the same meteorological forcing and parameter combinations, except that the RETRO simulation does not have the irrigation scheme enabled. Both simulations are conducted at a spatial resolution of 10 km, a temporal resolution of 30 min, and an output resolution of 1 day. The results of both simulations are evaluated against other independent reference products to quantify the general accuracy of the irrigation simulation and its impact on the water and energy fluxes. Both simulations are driven by meteorological forcing fields drawn from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis v5 (ERA5), including precipitation, surface pressure, incoming shortwave, and longwave radiation, 2-m air temperature, 2-m specific humidity, and 10-m wind speed for the period of 2000–2015. In this set of simulations, the model is configured using the International Soil Reference and Information Centre (ISRIC) soil texture map (Hengl et al., 2017 ). For the IRRI simulation, the irrigation fraction map is generated by combining the Global Irrigated Area Map (GIAM) dataset and the irrigation map from Ambika et al. (2016) , which is generated by combining yearly Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) – Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data, Indian Remote Sensing Land Use and Land Cover data, and vegetation condition index data. The GIAM dataset is a static irrigation area that covers entire Asia but is only generated based on data from year 2000 while the irrigation map from Ambika et al. (2016)  covers only India but provides an irrigation map every year from 2000 to 2015. These two irrigation maps are then combined by using the yearly irrigation maps from Ambika et al. (2016)  for India and GIAM irrigation fraction for the remaining research domain. We refer to this combined dataset as our “hybrid” irrigation map. For the groundwater ratio map, the GIAM groundwater ratio map is used to provide the gridded categorical groundwater value (i.e., 100 %, 0, or mixed), and the grid cells where the categorical groundwater value is “mixed” are assigned with groundwater ratio values provided by Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA). Note that GMIA groundwater ratio values are only available at the county scale so this composite groundwater ratio map may not reflect details of groundwater irrigation spatial variability at a finer scale. In the IRRI simulation, the growing season is estimated using equation (2.1) based on the monthly time-varying greenness vegetation fraction (GVF) product calculated from the MODIS-NDVI and the MODIS-International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land cover data (Case et al., 2013; Nie et al., 2018 ). In equation (2.1), GV F min      and GV F range      are calculated independently for different years. This means that the potential irrigation timing window varies year by year as the effective growing seasons differ between years, as informed by the time-varying GVF. Representing the interannual variability of the vegetation conditions in this manner has been reported to improve the model simulation of irrigation demand variation in response to vegetation changes, especially under drought (Nie et al. 2018 ). As a baseline simulation for irrigation, IRRI simulation is calibrated against FAO national irrigation water demand (i.e., a    and b    in equation (2.1) and (2.2) calibrated).
