It should be noted that the quality of the calibration strongly depends on the quality of the reference dataset. Since the FAO dataset provides only one year’s irrigation water requirement data at the country level (e.g., Afghanistan in 2002, Bangladesh in 2008, Cambodia in 2006), we interpret our calibrated simulation only as a representative baseline to be used for a general assessment of the irrigation impact on water and energy fluxes across the region.  2.2.2 Influence of input parameters on the irrigation simulation To quantify the influence that different input parameter datasets and meteorological forcings have on simulated irrigation, eight sets of irrigation simulations are conducted in addition to the baseline IRRI simulation. These simulations cross the alternate inputs listed in Table 1  , which include the choice of precipitation forcing, soil texture datasets, GVF threshold approach, irrigation fraction, and groundwater irrigation ratio maps. In these simulations, the calibrated parameters (a    and b   ) remain the same as in IRRI. We note that this set of simulations is performed as a one-at-a-time test of input parameters (Saltelli & Annoni, 2010 ). As such, it should be interpreted as an examination of how a choice between commonly used datasets might influence simulation results, and not as a comprehensive sensitivity analysis that would account for interactions between multiple parameter datasets. Precipitation:  The alternative precipitation dataset is the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) Final Version 06B precipitation dataset (Huffman et al., 2015 ). In general, IMERG and ERA5 have similar spatial climatological patterns (Fig. 3  ), with precipitation concentrated on the west coasts of the Indian peninsula and Indochina peninsula, and the south side of the Himalaya Mountain range. Both datasets show a wetting trend in annual precipitation on the western part of the domain and a drying trend on the eastern side. However, the magnitude of the trends differs in the two datasets, with IMERG indicating larger magnitude trends in both directions. Soil texture:  The alternative soil texture dataset is the FAO global soil texture dataset, which has a two-layer, 16-category dataset at 5-minute spatial resolution (https://iridl.ldeo.columbia.edu/SOURCES/.NASA/.ISLSCP/.GDSLAM/.Hydrology-Soils/.soils/.dataset_documentation.html ). The FAO dataset is widely used in land surface models but the spatial pattern and the sources for data compilation differ significantly from the relatively new ISRIC datasets. GVF threshold approach:  In the IRRI simulation, GV F th      is calculated differently for each year using GV F min      and GV F range      calculated with data for a specific year. Here an alternative approach is tested to calculate GV F th     , in which a constant GV F th      is calculated by using the constant GV F min      and GV F range      calculated with data from all years from 2000 to 2015. Since irrigation is triggered when GVF    exceeds this threshold that depends on GVFmin   and GVFrange   (Eq. 2.1), replacing the annually varying values with constant values will tend to reduce the simulated irrigation season in dry years and increase it in wet years. Irrigation fraction maps:  Three alternative irrigation fraction maps, including the GIAM Asia, GMIA equipped irrigation, and Global rain-fed, irrigation, and paddy croplands (GRIPC) map (Salmon et al., 2015 ) are applied in the sensitivity simulations. The GIAM is an irrigation fraction map developed based on remote sensing data collected between the years 2000 and 2010 (Thenkabail et al., 2009 ). Note that the GIAM Asia is different from the global GIAM used to create the hybrid irrigation fraction in the baseline simulation. The GMIA datasets are mainly developed based on an irrigation census survey of 10,825 sub-nation units from FAO, World Bank, and other international organizations around the year 2005. We tested the irrigation fraction map generated based on areas equipped for irrigation (GMIA_EI) at 5 arc-minutes spatial resolution. Finally, the 1 km GRIPC irrigation fraction map provided by Salmon et al. (2015)  is estimated by a tree-based classification model with inputs from MODIS Land Cover Type Product, gridded climate datasets, and national to subnational surveys. These irrigation maps, along with the hybrid map used in IRRI show very different irrigation locations and percentages (Fig. 4  ), i.e., GIAM tends to have the largest irrigation intensity overall as compared to the other datasets and GRIPC shows less irrigation intensity in southern India and eastern India when compared to the GIAM. Furthermore, the hybrid and GMIA equipped irrigation fraction maps both show significantly less intensity than GIAM and GRIPC maps and the hybrid map shows less intensity in northern India and more intensity in eastern and western India. Groundwater ratio maps:  Two alternative groundwater ratio maps, namely GMIA and GIAM (Fig. 5  ), are applied. Even though the GIAM groundwater ratio map is categorical, the areas that have been assigned with 100 % irrigation are much less than that indicated in GAIM such as for the states of Rajasthan and Gujarat. For these areas, the combined groundwater ratio map may exhibit greater uncertainty as there might be cases that 1) grid cells with larger than zero irrigation ratio in GAIM may not be updated if they fall into the zero-irrigation category in GIAM; 2) groundwater ratio with mixed categories within a county in GIAM may be estimated using this method as the county-level data in GMIA represents the average. Nevertheless, the three groundwater ratio maps together provide a reasonable range of variability that may help represent the irrigation uncertainty propagating into groundwater storage change.   2.3 Evaluation products 2.3.1 ET products The ET products used to evaluate our simulation irrigation scheme include SSEBop, ALEXI, GLEAM_A, and GLEAM_B products. SSEBop:  The Operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop) model is a land surface temperature-based model used by the US Geological Survey (USGS) Famine Early Warning System Network (FEWS NET) to operationally produce actual evapotranspiration for drought monitoring and early warning (Senay et al., 2013; Senay et al., 2020 ). This model utilizes the MODIS Aqua satellite’s air temperature and global gridded weather dataset as inputs. This product has a 1-month time resolution and 1 km spatial resolution. ALEXI:  The Atmosphere-Land Exchange Inverse model (ALEXI) is developed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). The spatial resolution is 0.05 degree or 5 km. The data is from 2001 to 2020 with a temporal resolution of 1 day. The ALEXI model is built upon the two-source energy balance (TSEB) model, which estimates the soil and canopy energy balance separately. ALEXI improves ET estimation by adding a planetary boundary layer (PBL) thermal energy model which relates the rising air temperature during the morning PBL growth phase to the sensible heat flux. GLEAM : The Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) is a process-based ET model which separately estimates the different components of ET, such as transpiration, bare soil evaporation, rainfall interception loss, open-water evaporation, and sublimation (Martens et al., 2018 ). This study uses both GLEAM v3.5a and v3.5b for ET validation, both of which are global datasets with a spatial resolution of 2 . 5 °  × 2 . 5 °     and a temporal resolution of 1 day. GLEAM v3.5a spans from 1980 to 2020 and the input data includes satellite data and reanalysis data while GLEAM v3.5b spans from 2003 to 2020 and the input data only contains satellite data. These two GLEAM products are hereafter referred to as GLEAM_A and GLEAM_B.  2.3.2 ESA CCI soil moisture dataset ESACCI:  The ESACCI surface soil moisture product (Gruber et al., 2019 ) provides a comprehensive dataset of soil moisture observations derived from multi-source satellite-based microwave sensors. In this study, we utilize the combined active–passive soil moisture data set, which is based on four active and twelve passive microwave products and is integrated to a daily scale at a quarter degree spatial resolution. The product has been intensively evaluated with in situ observations and has been proven to be able to detect irrigation signal in some previous applications (Qiu et al., 2016; Zohaib & Choi, 2020 ) albeit with limitations that might lead to underestimates of the influence of irrigation on soil moisture. Groundwater dataset and terrestrial water storage (TWS) dataset. In this study, the influence of the irrigation scheme on simulated groundwater is evaluated by both GRACE Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) satellite observations and in-situ groundwater observations. The GRACE satellite measures the variation of Earth’s gravity field with a twin satellite system. The signal from the GRACE satellite system is used to estimate TWS anomalies, which comprises anomalies in surface water storage, soil moisture storage, ice and snow water storage, and groundwater storage. This study utilizes the monthly regularized mass concentration solution (mascons) provided by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) (Loomis et al., 2019a ). This product has been used to derive the TWS trend globally and in various regions (Loomis et al., 2019a; Loomis et al., 2021; Loomis et al., 2019b ). The monthly in-situ groundwater observations are from Loomis et al. (2019a; b) , but with an extended interpolation domain for the deep layer. The gridded groundwater storage anomalies were derived from historical depth-to-water (DTW) measurements at over 12,000 locations, separated into shallow (representing unconfined groundwater) and deep (representing confined groundwater) layers as a function of reported well type. Water level anomalies from individual locations were gridded to a 0.25°x0.25° spatial resolution using an ordinary kriging interpolation scheme and converted to storage anomalies using specific yield and storativity coefficients for the shallow and deep layers, respectively.    3 Results and discussion 3.1 RETRO vs. IRRI simulation The simulated evapotranspiration (ET) from RETRO and IRRI simulations are compared to four global gridded ET products: SSEBop, ALEXI, GLEAM_A, and GLEAM_B (see Section 2.2.1  for details). Both SSEBop and ALEXI are averaged to 10 km spatial resolution to calculate the RMSE against IRRI and RETRO. GLEAM_A, GLEAM_B, RETRO, and IRRI are all averaged to 50 km spatial resolution before being compared with each other. All comparisons are conducted over a common period from 2003 to 2014. By simulating irrigation, IRRI substantially reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) of simulated ET when compared to SSEBop and ALEXI products for heavily irrigated areas (Fig. 4  and Fig. 6  (a)(b)(c)(d)). For example, the IRRI reduces ET RMSE by 8 % and 19 % on average, respectively, when compared to SSEBop and ALEXI in grids that have more than 20 % irrigation fractions. IRRI increases the RMSE of ET when compared to GLEAM_A (Fig. 6 (e) and (f)) and GLEMA_B (not shown). The reason that GLEAM products show closer agreement with RETRO may due to the fact that GLEAM lacks representation of anthropogenic activities, including irrigation. Although GLEAM may capture some impact of irrigation due to its assimilation of satellite soil moisture products (Yin et al., 2020 ), previous studies have noted that the GLEAM soil moisture assimilation update is rather “conservative” for some regions due to discrepancies in the utilized soil moisture information (e.g., satellite products vs. GLDAS) (Martens et al., 2017 ). SSEBop and ALEXI, in contrast, are diagnostic satellite-based estimates that inherently include anthropogenic activities. To further examine the irrigation impact on the temporal variability and the comparisons amongst products, Fig. 7   shows the long-term averaged monthly climatological time series of ET averaged over the six selected areas (Fig. 1 ). SSEBop has the most distinctive seasonal pattern, with a higher peak occurring in spring or summer, which is different from other ET products in terms of both magnitude and phase. In addition, SSEBop also has the largest ET estimate amongst all the ET products. This is most notable in the Northern India area and the Upper Indus area, where the average monthly ET in SSEBop is 8–62 mm larger than other products. GLEAM_A and GLEAM_B agree well with RETRO for both seasonal variation and magnitude of ET, while ALEXI ET agrees better with IRRI, in particular in indicating a dual-peak seasonal pattern. For example, in the Upper Indus area, ALEXI and IRRI products have a smaller ET peak from March to April and a larger peak from August and September, but GLEAM products show a distinguishably smaller magnitude with no clear peak in springtime. SSEBop does not capture the dual-peak seasonal pattern for this region. The general agreement between GLEAM products with the RETRO simulation most likely results from similar ET algorithms in the models. Note that on one side, satellite-based ET estimates vary due to uncertainties arising from noises and errors in raw data as well as the underlying retrieval algorithms. On the other side, the representation of irrigation in prognostic models is often simplified, and it relies on a range of assumptions about water management and water use efficiency. Both factors present challenges in accurately quantifying and evaluating the impact of irrigation on ET. Irrigation impacts soil moisture both directly, through water infiltration, and indirectly through plant water uptake. Here we examined the irrigation impact on surface soil moisture (SSM) by comparing the simulations with the ESACCI surface soil moisture product (Gruber et al., 2019 ). The correlation between monthly surface soil moisture simulated in RETRO and ESACCI, along with its difference to correlation between IRRI and ESACCI are shown in Fig. 8  . The RETRO shows a high correlation with ESACCI SSM products across the research domain, indicating that RETRO generally captures the seasonality of surface soil moisture. In portions of Pakistan where surface water irrigation is intense and in Bangladesh where the predominant crop is rice, RETRO has a lower correlation with observations (Fig. 8 (a)). Including an irrigation scheme in the simulation (IRRI) increases soil moisture correlations in Pakistan, indicating that simulating irrigation shifted the seasonality of surface soil moisture in a manner that increases agreement with ESACCI SSM. Representing irrigation, however, does not provide improvement in Bangladesh (Fig. 8 (b)). One possible reason is that rice paddy cultivation may rely on a particular irrigation scheduling, which is not correctly represented by a generic irrigation rule in Noah-MP. Fig. 9   shows a comparison of ssm time series among the six focus regions. in the northern india region, both retro and irri overestimate ssm when compared to esacci. in other areas, both retro and irri capture the ssm variation in the pre-monsoon and monsoon seasons, which indicates the model generally captured the soil moisture response to precipitation as a dominant signal. the performance of retro and irri differ in the post-monsoon seasons. for instance, in the rajasthan region, esacci shows a peak ssm during the monsoon season and a second peak or “plateau” after the monsoon season (Fig. 9 (b)). Both RETRO and IRRI capture the first peak of SSM which indicates the first peak is caused by the increase in precipitation during the monsoon season. The RETRO, however, drops to minimum SSM right after the first peak and generally maintains this minimum SSM or reaches a second peak in much later months instead of maintaining a “plateau” pattern. Although IRRI correctly simulated the “plateau” pattern after the first peak, the magnitude of this pattern is overestimated. The difference in the ability to capture the second SSM peak between RETRO and IRRI indicates that this second peak is caused by the irrigation process. The overestimation of this second peak in IRRI is likely caused by a less robust calibration process of the irrigation parameters or the uncertainty in detecting irrigation signal in ESA CCI soil moisture due to its coarse spatial resolution. The IRRI might be further improved if more irrigation reference data are available or the irrigation parameters are directly calibrated against satellite-based soil moisture products at finer spatial resolution that are capable of detecting irrigation such as SMAP, which has a data record that mostly post-dates the period of our simulations. In the Uttar Pradesh region, mixed results are found in the post-monsoon season (Fig. 9 (e)). The mismatch between IRRI and ESACCI in the post-monsoon season generally results from an inaccurate irrigation (growing) season representation in the IRRI simulation. For example, IRRI matches better with ESACCI in the post-monsoon season for 2008–2009 while RETRO better agrees with ESACCI in the post-monsoon season from year 2002 to 2003 (Fig. 9 ). The performance of IRRI in 2008–2009 post-monsoon season implies that Uttar Pradesh is normally irrigated which is generally captured by the algorithm to determine irrigation season or growing season (equation (2.1)) in IRRI. The failure of IRRI and the success of RETRO in capturing SSM in the post-monsoon season from 2002 to 2003 implies that Uttar Pradesh was not irrigated in the post-monsoon season during the year 2002 to 2003. This abnormal irrigation condition can result from reduction in irrigation or farming area due to scarcity of water resource. These conditions are not well represented in the model’s irrigation scheme (Kumar et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2005 ). On the other hand, smaller irrigation signals might not be detected by ESACCI datasets considering their limited spatial resolution and uncertainty. An alternative simulation approach that better accounts for the management response to climate indirectly reflected by vegetation conditions will be discussed in the sensitivity analysis section. We also note that future work could integrate soil moisture observations along with observed vegetation fraction in order to improve the simulation of irrigation timing (Nie et al., 2022). The heavy dependency on groundwater sources for agricultural irrigation in South Asia has led to dramatic depletion in water storage, which has been captured by NASA’s Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) measurements. Fig. 10   shows a spatial comparison of the terrestrial water storage (TWS) trends estimated from RETRO, IRRI, observed by GRACE, and in-situ observation. RETRO and IRRI show a distinctive difference in TWS trend estimation, especially in Northwestern India (Fig. 10 (a) and (b)). TWS trends in RETRO are mostly positive in the western part of the domain in response to an increasing trend in precipitation (Fig. 3 ) while IRRI simulates a negative TWS trend due to groundwater irrigation. The location of this declining TWS trend in IRRI is consistent with GRACE observation and in-situ observation (Fig. 10 (c) and (e)). The in-situ observation also confirms that this declining trend is mainly from deep groundwater which is likely due to groundwater pumping for irrigation. The TWS declining signal in IRRI simulation, however, is restricted to a smaller extent of an area when compared to GRACE or in-situ observation (Fig. 10 ). This difference in groundwater depletion extent can be attributed in part to uncertainty in the irrigation groundwater ratio map and lack of lateral groundwater transportation module in NoahMP v3.6. When averaged over the Rajasthan region, IRRI simulation can replicate the declining trend relatively well (Fig. S1 ).  3.2 Irrigation sensitivity All results presented to this point have relied on a single set of model input parameters and meteorological fields. Here we consider the robustness of those results to changes in the input datasets. We are concerned both with the influence of inputs on estimates of the long-term water balance and the influence of parameters and forcing on interannual variability in water demand, which is a function of interactions between climate conditions and simulated irrigation water application decisions. As IRRI is calibrated to available national data on irrigation water applications, and as these data are at best rough estimates of total irrigation water use, we do not attempt to evaluate the impact of our alternative input datasets on the accuracy of simulation relative to “observed” water applications. Rather, we focus on the sensitivity of simulations to different input datasets, using IRRI as a reference dataset. In general, the simulated irrigation water amount is most sensitive to irrigation fraction. This sensitivity is consistent with expectation, given the essential role of the irrigation fraction map in determining where irrigation can be activated in the simulation. It is also consistent with Puy et al. (2021) , who showed that across multiple types of hydrological models, irrigation water withdrawals are largely conditioned by the irrigated areas and their uncertainty on a global scale. As shown in Fig. S2  and Fig. 11  , for the three simulations with alternative irrigation fraction maps, IF_GIAM, IF_GMIA, and IF_GRIPC estimates 22.4 %, 12.6 %, and 23.1 % more irrigation amount in the northern India region and 40.0 %, 11.3 % and 36.7 more irrigation amount in the Uttar Pradesh region. Differences vary largely when comparing the three datasets in the Rajasthan region, where IF_GIAM and IF_GRIPC lead to 12.0 % and 18.1 % more irrigation amount while IF_GMIA reduces it by 12.5 %. IF_GIAM and GRIPC greatly disagree with each other in southern India, with IF_GIAM resulting in more irrigation while IF_GRIPC shows the opposite when compared to IRRI (Fig. S2 ). In the Chhattisgarh region, IF_GIAM increases the irrigation amount by 34.5 % while IF_GMIA reduces the irrigation amount by 34.3 % (Fig. 11 (f)). Besides the long-term averaged irrigation amount, the use of different irrigation fraction sources also affects the interannual variability of irrigation demand, especially for Northern India, Gujarat, and Uttar Pradesh (Fig. 11 ). This is due to the nonlinear interaction between the irrigation fraction and the other factors at play in determining the irrigation amount. However, the interannual variability is less impacted for Rajasthan, Upper Indus, and Chhattisgarh, where the simulated differences from IRRI are more consistent across years. Choice of the soil texture dataset also has an important impact on simulated irrigation water (Fig. 11 ), with FAO generally leading to 36.6 %, 36.6 %, and 287.7 % more irrigation water demand in Rajasthan (Fig. 11 b), Upper Indus (Fig. 11 c), and Chhattisgarh (Fig. 11 f) regions when compared to ISRIC, and these differences are all statistically significant among all years. The impact due to the choice of soil texture dataset for these three regions is larger than for any other parameters tested in this study. The influence of the soil texture dataset on interannual variability in simulated irrigation water is not particularly evident in most of the focus regions, except for the Chhattisgarh region, where drought years are associated with particularly large differences and wet years exhibit smaller differences. This may be due to the amplified impact of drainage characteristics in years with very large irrigation water demand. Sensitivity to soil texture is a particular challenge and opportunity area for land surface modeling, as this parameter is not readily observed from remote sensing platforms. The fact that total simulated water use depends so strongly on this parameter for multiple regions emphasizes the importance of developing reliable field-based datasets of soil properties and implementing them in models used for water resource analysis. Differences in simulated irrigation water use due to choice of precipitation forcing are not as large as the differences brought by irrigation fraction or soil texture, reflecting the fact that the precipitation forcing datasets used in this study showed reasonably good agreement in irrigated portions of the study area. The greatest difference is found in the Northern India region, where IMERG produces wetter conditions, causing 9 % less irrigation water to be applied across the simulation period. In this region, the interannual variability in simulated irrigation water also shows notable differences due to disagreement between the two precipitation datasets. The alternative GVF threshold approach in general leads to increased irrigation amount as the use of long-term maximum and minimum GVF values tends to create a greater GVF range, leading to a correspondingly lower threshold value and longer simulated growing season. However, this tendency can be reversed quite dramatically under conditions of severe drought. During those dry conditions, when vegetation growth is significantly curtailed, the observed vegetation condition may be much lower than the long-term GVF range informed threshold. In consequence, the effective growing season could be very short, or even absent due to a cropping failure. For instance, in Rajasthan and Gujarat, this alternative GVF approach substantially reduces simulated irrigation demand by 56.2 % and 38.7 % in a drought year, 2002 (Fig. 11 (b) and (d)). On one hand, this sensitivity may indicate an advantage to the alternative approach of using long-term GVF statistics: adjusting the GVF range every year means that the model may simulate irrigation applications even when water shortages have led farmers to abandon their crops, simply because GVF will reach its annual maximum for that year at some point in the season. On the other hand, it is possible that using the long-term thresholds will lead to exaggerated reductions in irrigation in dry years because it does not adjust for the influence of natural vegetation variability that is included in the gridded satellite GVF signal. The sensitivity of this influence to dataset and model resolution, and approaches to realizing the advantages of both approaches, is a topic of ongoing research. Looking beyond irrigation water to simulated ET, which is a direct indicator of on-field consumptive water use in irrigation, we see some similarities in the relative impacts of alternate input datasets but also some interesting differences (Fig. 12  ). In general, simulated ET, like irrigation water, is most sensitive to irrigation fraction and soil texture datasets in the focus regions. Changing the soil texture dataset from ISRIC to FAO generally increases the simulated ET for all selected regions except for the Gujarat (e.g., −2.5 % in 2002) and the Uttar Pradesh regions (e.g., −5.6 % in 2000). Using the alternative GVF method generally decreases the simulated ET in dry years due to less irrigation and this decrease is most notable in the Rajasthan, the Upper Indus, and the Gujarat regions. The alternative GVF method also alters the long-term trend in most regions, in particular for the Upper Indus regions. This difference in trend is particularly relevant for water resource assessment, and it points to a possible advantage of the alternate approach of using long-term GVF statistics. This is due to intensification (e.g., infilling) of irrigation within a grid cell. This intensification might not be fully reflected in infrequently-updated percent irrigated area datasets. Lacking representation of this intensification can lead to trends in GVF minimum and maximum within irrigated grid cells over simulation period. Using annual GVF statistics may mask part of this trend by imposing a trend in the GVF threshold for the beginning of the irrigation season. Whether such a trend is appropriate depends on background vegetation conditions and local cropping practices. In the focus regions, the influence of the choice of precipitation is mostly observed in the Rajasthan and the Gujarat regions, with 2.7 % and 2.6 % change on average. Simulated ET does not show high sensitivity to the two precipitation datasets for the other regions, although precipitation is among the most important factors to determine ET in many natural environments. For example, the simulated ET shows a high difference in the Tibetan plateau due to the large difference in the two precipitation datasets (Fig. 3  and Fig. S3 ). It should be noted that the limited sample of precipitation choices in our study may not well represent the discrepancies among the existing precipitation products for South Asia reported in other studies (Song et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2014; Wang & Zeng, 2012; Yoon et al., 2019; You et al., 2015 ). For SSM, soil texture remains the most impactful factor, which shows high influence for most of the focus regions except for the Northern India (+0.3 %) and the Gujarat regions (+0.3 %) (Fig. 13  ). The selection of different soil texture datasets also has a meaningful influence on simulated SSM interannual variability in the the Uttar Pradesh, the Northern India, and the Chhattisgarh regions. Interestingly, simulated SSM tends to be more sensitive to different GVF methods (e.g., −20.3 % in the Rajasthan region in 2002, Fig. 13 (b)) than to different irrigation fraction methods, which differs from the sensitivity of simulated irrigation water and ET. The sensitivity of SSM to different precipitation data is similar to that of ET, implying a consistent response of surface soil moisture and ET to the precipitation signals (Fig. S4 ). The influence of different groundwater ratio maps is most impactful for long-term groundwater trends (Fig. S5 ). Specifically, the GMIA groundwater ratio map enlarges the simulated groundwater depletion trend significantly in the Northern India, Rajasthan, and the Upper Indus regions. In the Northern India and Gujarat regions, the GMIA dataset leads to closer agreement with GRACE TWS observations, while in Rajasthan and the Upper Indus the use of that dataset leads to a depletion trend larger than GRACE-derived estimates. The simulated groundwater with the GIAM groundwater ratio map remains similar to the simulated groundwater with the hybrid map except for a slightly decreased groundwater trend in the Gujarat regions.   4 Conclusion The purpose of this study was twofold. First, we implemented a prognostic irrigation model for simulations of the distributed water balance in Noah-MP applied to South Asia. We described and, to the extent possible, evaluated the behavior of this scheme in simulating hydrological states and fluxes in retrospective offline simulations. Second, we performed a simplified one-at-a-time sensitivity test to explore the uncertainties of irrigation simulations in response to single substitution of input datasets for irrigation fraction, irrigation groundwater ratio, soil texture, GVF approach, and precipitation forcings. The one-at-a-time approach is not a comprehensive evaluation of model sensitivity to these fields: we do not test for sensitivities that emerge from interactions between these input fields, and we also do not provide a comprehensive assessment of all parameters and meteorological fields that might have some influence on the model’s simulation of irrigation. Nevertheless, the simplified approach does help us to understand how a modeler’s choice between commonly used input datasets would be expected to affect model predictions. For the first aim, our results show that representing irrigation has a significant impact on the simulation of hydrological terms in this intensively managed region. Overall, RETRO agrees more closely with GLEAM_A and GLEAM_B ET while IRRI agrees better with ALEXI ET. Including irrigation was shown to reduce the RMSE of ET as compared to ALEXI and SSEBop for most of the area. Irrigation also alters the seasonality of ET, leading to closer agreement with ALEXI ET, especially for the Northern India, Upper Indus, and Uttar Pradesh regions. For surface soil moisture, RETRO, in general, captures the seasonal to the interannual variation observed in the ESACCI dataset. The impact of irrigation on surface soil moisture is mixed, leading to closer agreement with ESACCI in Pakistan while reducing agreement in Northwest India. These mixed results could stem both from potential uncertainties sourced from the model input parameters and uncertainty in the ESACCI dataset in detecting small-scale irrigation signals. Representing irrigation is critical for capturing the spatial pattern of the TWS trend observed by TWS. This has the largest impact in Rajasthan and surrounding areas, where there is a steady groundwater decline due to irrigation pumping from confined aquifer systems. Simulation of irrigation and its hydrological impacts is known to be sensitive to model parameterization and climate forcing input (Puy et al., 2021; Wisser et al., 2008 ). This is particularly true for data-limited or climatically and hydrologically complex environments. Our one-at-a-time sensitivity test compared against IRRI simulation indicated that of the factors considered, irrigation estimation changed the most in response to irrigation fraction and soil texture datasets, when data sources for each were swapped independently of the other fields. Large discrepancies exist among currently available soil texture and irrigation fraction datasets, highlighting the need for continued development of these types of products with the aid of new technologies and emerging datasets. The approach to calculating GVF triggers for irrigation also had meaningful impacts on the simulations. In particular, GVF in our modeling system plays a leading role in determining the start and end of the irrigation season, with an influence on the simulation of total irrigation water and year-to-year variability. Were the modeling system to be applied for forecast or projection, when observed GVF is unavailable, then the decision on how to represent vegetation (e.g., climatology vs. dynamic phenology model) may be important for predicting demand-driven irrigation water applications. The Influence of the precipitation dataset on irrigation in this study is primarily a function of the agreement or disagreement between IMERG and ERA-5 across irrigated portions of the study region. In Northwestern India, where there is a significant difference between these datasets, the resulting impact on irrigation amount in our one-at-a-time substitution analysis was as large as the impact from the choice of irrigation fraction map and included a significant impact on interannual variability. When looking at the propagation of all parameters, methodological, and meteorological sensitivities into ET and surface soil moisture, we find that the response of ET is similar to that of irrigation amount in one-at-a-time substitution simulations, while surface soil moisture is more sensitive to soil texture and GVF approach than to irrigation fraction. The choice of groundwater ratio map has a negligible impact on surface hydrological conditions in one-at-a-time substation simulations (the only potential influence is via impacts at the bottom of the soil column), but it has a significant direct impact on the simulation of groundwater trends. Besides the sensitivities to the explored factors, the land surface model itself also adds uncertainty to irrigation estimates, such as simplified soil hydrology representation, weakness in soil water and ET exchange, limited crop types and the associated rooting depth characterization. Given these results, future work will examine the potential of generating more consistent and reliable irrigation parameter datasets by incorporating local in-situ measurements such as crop distribution and their irrigation scheduling, soil properties, and groundwater pumping records. Such data with finer spatiotemporal resolution could also improve the robustness of calibrating irrigation related parameters. Meanwhile, utilizing reliable remote-sensing satellite observations capable of detecting irrigation signals may help constrain the irrigation uncertainty and reduce its dependency on parameters. For example, SMAP and Sentinel high-resolution soil moisture products have been reported to be able to detect irrigation signals for medium to large irrigation-equipped areas (Jalilvand et al., 2021; Lawston et al., 2017 ). Integrating this information into the model via data assimilation or other statistical methods may improve the overall representation of the water and energy budget for South Asia under human intervention.
1 Introduction Regional land subsidence caused by overexploitation of groundwater is a worldwide geological hazard (Herrera-García et al., 2021 ). Relation between changes in groundwater levels and aquifer compaction is explained by the principle of effective stress (Terzaghi, 1925 ). Long-term excessive exploitation of groundwater lowers the hydraulic head, which decreases the pore water pressure in the aquifer system. This increases the effective stress in both the pumping unit and adjacent formations, leading to compaction of the aquifer. The amount of compaction is primarily associated with the compressibility of the compacting layers. The resulting accumulated compaction of subsurface layers extends its effect to the land surface, which manifests itself as land subsidence. Land subsidence can easily cause damages to critical infrastructures, and leads to higher relative sea-level and increases flood risk in low-lying coastal areas (Gambolati and Teatini, 2021 ). In order to mitigate land subsidence, many areas around the world have implemented restrictions on groundwater pumping and even artificially recharged the aquifer system. In some instances, reductions in groundwater pumping have led to groundwater level recovery and, depending on the type of aquifer, triggers uplift of the land surface (Amelung et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2007; Lu and Danskin, 2001; Parker et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Aquifer compaction consists of an elastic component and inelastic component, in which elastic compaction can recover after groundwater replenishment, while inelastic compaction is a permanent component that is not recoverable (Gambolati and Teatini, 2021; Wilson and Gorelick, 1996 ). Both cases result in a change in ground surface elevation proportional to variations of groundwater level and to the thickness of the compacting layers. Elastic deformation generally occurs in clay and sand layers (aquitards and aquifers) when the hydraulic head is kept above the previous lowest level, i.e., the level of pre-consolidation stress (maximum past level of effective stress). When the pre-consolidation stress is exceeded, the aquitard may undergo significant, irreversible grain rearrangement that results in inelastic compaction in aquitards (more compressible than aquifers). The inelastic compaction reduces porosity and storage coefficient and thus threaten the groundwater storage and supply capacity of the aquifer system (Liu et al., 2022 ). Almost all permanent subsidence occurs in regions experiencing excessive groundwater withdrawal due to the irreversible compaction of aquitards during the typically slow process of aquitard drainage (Riley, 1969 ). Later controls on groundwater extraction and aquifer recharge can only result in a small amount of ground uplift (Chaussard et al., 2016 ). This phenomenon, commonly referred to as elastic rebound, is caused by the relaxation of elastically compressed aquifer materials when pore pressure is regained (Waltham, 2002 ), as demonstrated by an injection experiment that was conducted at the Wilmington oilfield in Long Beach, California, which had experienced severe subsidence due to oil reservoir compaction (Allen and Mayuga, 1969 ). Typical response of the ground surface to rapid artificial recharge during a short-term pumping test is represented by curve A in Fig. 1  , which reflects the immediate and direct correlation between changes in ground elevation and hydraulic head. On the contrary, surface elevation changes after termination of prolonged groundwater extraction are generally described by a transition of minor movements from subsidence to uplift (curve B in Fig. 1 ), as documented in Venice, Italy (Gatto and Carbognin, 1981 ). A more complicated pattern is shown when groundwater pumping is of larger spatial and temporal scales. The characteristics and mechanism of regional surface elevation change, especially the elastic rebound after experiencing a long-term groundwater level drawdown, are still unclear. Therefore, the long-term history of groundwater drawdown in Taiyuan city and its recovery in recent years, presents a great chance for improving our understanding of this post-pumping mechanism. Taiyuan is the capital and largest city of Shanxi Province, Northern China, with a total area of 6,988 km2  and a permanent population of over 5 million habitations. Due to its water shortages and population growth, Taiyuan, similar to other cities, has been forced to depend heavily on groundwater extraction for its water supply. The intense groundwater exploitation formed large regional cones of depression in the 1980s and 1990s, inducing several land subsidence centers with cumulated subsidence over 3 m by the year of 2000, which has been observed from continuous Global Positioning System (GPS) stations (Tang et al., 2018 ), repeated differential leveling (Ma et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2006 ), and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) (Liu et al., 2018a; Tang et al., 2018; Tang and Liao, 2014 ). This history of land subsidence in Taiyuan city is discussed in more detail in Section 2 . These declines in groundwater and the induced land subsidence, prompted the local authority to take actions to govern the use of groundwater resources. Back in the early 1990s, the government announced regulations to impose bans on groundwater abstraction and from 2000 onward, strict control of groundwater pumping became the norm across the whole province (Frank et al., 2016 ), making a dramatic reduction in groundwater pumping in the region. Most groundwater use in Taiyuan city was substituted for surface water imported from Yellow River by an inter-basin water transfer project operated in 2003. The groundwater level in Taiyuan city has gradually recovered since 2000, and the rate of land subsidence has therefore been substantially decreased and even turned into land uplift (Tang et al., 2022 ). The purpose of this paper is to examine the recent ground surface elevation change in response to the post-pumping groundwater recharge in more detail. Thanks to the documented leveling measurements and the available InSAR data from multiple SAR satellites over a long period of time, and the history of groundwater contour maps, we are able to examine the spatial–temporal evolution of land surface response to the groundwater drawdown and recovery in Taiyuan city. In this study, the historical subsidence data recorded by optical leveling survey from 1956 to 2000 and the InSAR data from multiple space-borne SAR sensors covering the period of 2003–2020 are utilized to examine the ground elevation change in response to groundwater level variation before and after the termination of groundwater pumping. Utilizing the groundwater level contours from the 1965–2019 period, high-resolution, multi-temporal mapping of the groundwater level variations were constructed and compared with the ground elevation change. A hydrogeological interpretation of the ground displacement measurements will be analyzed, illustrating that the land surface uplift is consistently following the spatial and temporal evolution of groundwater recovery. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2  describes the history of land subsidence and groundwater exploitation in the study area. Section 3  shows the datasets used in the present study and Section 4  describes the methods applied to the analysis of the InSAR data to retrieve the long-term maps of ground displacement. Section 5  demonstrates the results of ground elevation change obtained. Lastly, Section 6  presents the discussion and Section 7  presents the conclusions.  2 Study area 2.1 Description of the study area Taiyuan city is located in the middle of Shanxi Province, the northern end of Taiyuan basin, China (Fig. 2  a). Fenhe River, the second largest tributary of the Yellow River, flows through the city traversing about 100 km from north to south. The Lvliang Mountains form the western boundary of the city, while the Taihang Mountains form the eastern boundary. Topographically, the elevation is high in the north and low in the south, high on the east and west sides and low in the middle, descending in a step-like manner from the mountainous area to the basin. Due to the influence of the neotectonic movement, the terrain on the east and west sides of the basin has obvious asymmetry. The west mountain area is directly connected with the basin by faults, with wide elevation difference, large slope, and short alluvial fan of the side mountain. On the east side, the topography changes slowly, and there are loess hills and tableland with different widths between the mountain and the basin. The edge mountain alluvial fan extends into the center of the basin, forming a broad alluvial fan inclined plain (Ma et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2006 ). Taiyuan city is located in this broad, flat Fenhe River alluvial plain. The basin's unconsolidated sediments are composed of alternating layers of sands and clays, due to the alternating deposition of alluvial and lacustrine sediments. Sediments are coarse near the perimeter of the city and the tops of pluvial fan deposits, and become progressively finer towards the center of the basin (Fig. 3  ). The aquifer system in Taiyuan city can be divided into three layers: the upper (illustrated as Unit 1 in Fig. 3 c), middle (illustrated as Unit 2 in Fig. 3 c), and lower (illustrated as Unit 3 in Fig. 3 c) layers. Most of the groundwater in this city is pumped from the middle and lower aquifer layers. The unconfined to semi-confined aquifers in the basin have a depth of 5–25 m, and are composed of medium sand and medium coarse sand with gravel in the north, and fine to medium coarse sand with alternating layers of clay in the south. The thickness of the middle confined aquifer varies between 20 m and 40 m, which is greater than that of the upper one. In the Wujiabao region, the middle confined aquifer consists of silt, fine sand, and medium sand with interlayers of silty clay from the surface down to the bottom. The thickness of the lower confined aquifer varies from 90 to 105 m. Overall, from the northern part to the southern part of the city, sediments become finer and groundwater heads drop. Groundwater discharge in Taiyuan is mainly by the artificial groundwater extraction and natural evapotranspiration. Groundwater is recharged by atmospheric precipitation, seepage from rivers and lakes, irrigation losses, and lateral seepage from the surrounding mountains.  2.2 History of land subsidence and groundwater exploitation in Taiyuan city Over the past 60 years, a rapidly growing population and economy development in Taiyuan city led to an increase in groundwater pumping in the aquifer system, resulting in a notable subsidence of the land surface due to the compaction of unconsolidated sediments. The evolution of subsidence history can be divided into four stages: initial stage from 1956 to 1981, developing stage from 1981 to 1989, affected-area extension stage from 1989 to 2000, and deaccelerating stage after 2000 (Ma et al., 2006 ). By 2000, the area affected by land subsidence had reached 453.3 km2 , forming four subsidence centers in the city (Xizhang, Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao). After 2000, the subsidence rates in the city center were decreasing and the subsiding area was expanded to the suburb in the south of the city and formed a new subsidence center in Xiaodian district (see Fig. 7  in this paper), which has been observed from InSAR measurements (Liu et al., 2018a; Tang et al., 2018 ). The spatial extent of land subsidence centers is matched with the groundwater depression cones. In addition, the period of intense groundwater exploitation in 1981–1989 is also consistent with the period of the rapid development of land subsidence. This indicates that the land subsidence in Taiyuan was mainly caused by overexploitation of groundwater in the aquifer system. In order to control groundwater overuse, the local government in Taiyuan has implemented a water management program since 2000, reducing the amount of groundwater extraction through comprehensive measures such as water conservation, sewage utilization, wells closure and improving water use efficiency. At the same time, an inter-basin water transfer project, named Wanjiazhai Water Diversion Project (WWDP), has been built to import surface water from the Yellow River to the city of Taiyuan (Fig. 2 a). This project has a designed water transfer capacity of 6.4 × 108  m3  per year to the city of Taiyuan (Xie et al., 1999 ). Since the operation of this water diversion project in 2003, a total of 21.9 × 108  m3  of water has been diverted to Taiyuan by 2020 (the blue line in Fig. 4   b), which has been greatly alleviating the water shortage in this region. Under this background, the structure of water supply in Taiyuan has changed. As can be seen from Fig. 4 a, from 1996 to 2019, the ratio of surface water supply in Taiyuan has increased from a low of 16 % in 1999 to a high of 55 % in 2019, and the ratio of groundwater supply has decreased from a peak of 76 % to the lowest of 27 %. The amount of groundwater extraction in Taiyuan city decreased from a peak of 4.62 × 108  m3  in 2002 to the lowest of 2.29 × 108  m3  in 2019 (the red line in Fig. 4 b). From 1986 to 2009, the groundwater depth in Taiyuan city decreased by 31 m while it turned into a continuing rise after 2009 and recovered 26 m by 2021 (the green line in Fig. 4 c) as a result of the drastic reduction of groundwater extraction. The curve of the groundwater level in Fig. 4 c follows well with the curve of the aquifer water level in Fig. 1  (the blue line) with a rapid decline during massive pumping and recovery by natural recharge. With the recovery of groundwater level, the rates of land subsidence have been decreasing and even reversed to land uplift in some locations (Tang et al., 2022 ). As shown in Fig. 4 c, a leveling point located in the south of Taiyuan sank by 43 mm from 1990 to 2009 and it gradually stabilized after 2009. Data from a GPS station in Taiyuan urban area even show a progressive land uplift since 2014, with a cumulative uplift of nearly 70 mm by the end of 2021. These indicate that the rise of groundwater levels led to pore pressure recovery and elastic rebound in the aquifer system.   3 Datasets 3.1 Multi-sensor SAR data To investigate the long-term land surface deformation in Taiyuan city, we used a large archive of SAR images from multiple sensors onboard the ENVISAT (ENVI), COSMO-SkyMed (CSK), TerraSAR-X (TSX), and Sentinel-1 (S1) satellites. The ENVI dataset is spanning between August 2003 and September 2010 with 39 acquisitions. After a seven-month gap, the CSK dataset with 30 acquisitions span May 2011 to November 2013. With one-month overlap with the dataset from CSK, the TSX data were acquired from October 2013 to August 2017 with 67 acquisitions. Finally, 113 acquisitions from S1 satellite cover between March 2017 and November 2020, with five-month overlap with the TSX dataset. The list of acquisition dates for these SAR images can be seen in Tables S1–S4 in the Supplementary Material . The ENVI, CSK and TSX datasets were acquired in descending orbit, while the S1 dataset was acquired in ascending track. The parameters of the SAR datasets are listed in Table 1  . Fig. 2 a and c show the spatial and temporal coverage of the SAR datasets in the study area, respectively. The spatial extent for each SAR image swath is not uniform. The ENVI, CSK and TSX images acquired in conventional StripMap mode is limited to the north of the Taiyuan basin, which mainly covers our study area of Taiyuan city. Thanks to the extensive spatial extent of S1 images acquired in IW mode, it covers the whole Taiyuan basin. However, since a single frame image from S1 cannot cover our study area, we need two frames of data to be concatenated and cut into the study area during the processing (see Fig. 2 a). The ENVI, CSK and TSX datasets were imaged in the StripMap mode, which is the conventional acquisition mode for these sensors. The S1 dataset were acquired in Interferometric Wide swath (IW) mode scanned by the Terrain Observation with Progressive Scans SAR (TOPSAR) technique, which provides images with a large swath width and moderate resolution (De Zan and Monti Guarnieri, 2006 ).  3.2 Leveling records, groundwater level and continuous GPS data The leveling survey has been conducted in Taiyuan city since 1956 but with a sparse density of leveling points in space (up to several kilometers) and at low frequency of repeated measures in time (up to several years). Based on a network of 114 leveling benchmarks, accumulated land subsidence contour maps in Taiyuan city for several periods have been documented (Ma et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2005 ). We reconstructed the historical subsidence contour maps for the periods 1956–1981, 1956–1989 and 1956–2000 (Fig. 10 ) to study the ground elevation change response to groundwater drawdown. The elevation changes at leveling points located in the subsidence centers were concatenated with the 2003–2020 InSAR measurements to obtain a long-term continuous deformation for studying the ground elevation change before and after the termination of groundwater pumping. A long-term monitoring program of groundwater levels in wells and boreholes was carried out from 1965 through 2019 by the local hydrology department. The archives of groundwater level contour maps for the years: 1965, 1981, 1989, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2010, 2018, and 2019 were collected from Shanxi Hydrology and Water Resources Survey Bureau. These multi-temporal contours of groundwater level were re-vectorized in the ArcMap platform and interpolated into continuous maps using the kriging geostatistical method (see Fig. 6   ). Two additional maps of the spatial–temporal variation of the groundwater level (2003–2010 and 2010–2019) were also reconstructed (see Fig. 12 ). Ground displacement data from two continuously operating GPS stations are available for this study, which were used to validate the InSAR-derived ground surface displacements (Fig. 8  ). These two GPS stations are part of the Shanxi Continuously Operating Reference Stations (SXCORS), which was constructed by Shanxi Institute of Surveying, Mapping and Geoinformation. They are located in the built-up area in the central city of Taiyuan (A001 and A008, see locations in Fig. 2 b). The daily GPS coordinates time series were obtained by the GAMIT/GLOBK software and the detailed strategy of the GPS data analysis can be found in (Tang et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2012 ). The GPS measurements are in a daily frequency and in the comparison, they were resampled into a weekly frequency by a 7-day moving average. The time span of GPS measurements available in this study is from May 2009 to Jul 2020 at A001 and from Nov 2009 to Nov 2018 at A008.   4 Methods 4.1 Multi-temporal InSAR time series analysis While many InSAR time series analysis approaches have been developed in recent years, most of them share similar characteristics so that they can be categorized into two types of techniques: Persistent Scatterer InSAR (PSI) (Ferretti et al., 2001; Hooper, 2008 ) and Small Baseline Subset (SBAS) (Berardino et al., 2002 ). The PSI technique utilize the superior scattering stability of point-like scatterers to track high-quality displacement information (centimeter- to millimeter-scale) through time at point target locations. The point-like targets are often associated with stable man-made structures such as buildings, poles, and corners, so that the PSI technique is mainly used in urban areas. The SBAS techniques utilize distributed targets for deformation monitoring. Distributed targets occur in natural environments (meadows, fields, bare soil) where many similarly bright scatterers contribute to the information in a resolution cell, such that the SBAS works better in non-urban areas and facilitates densely sampled deformation maps. In this study, we chose SBAS method for analyzing the ENVI and CSK datasets, and used PSI method for analyzing TSX and S1 datasets. The PSI technique forms interferograms referenced to one reference image. For ENVI and CSK datasets, the quality of interferograms referenced to only one reference image are generally low due to the irregular acquisitions from these two satellites. Therefore, for these two datasets, we selected interferometric pairs by controlling the spatial and temporal baselines of interferograms to suppress decorrelated effects and exploited the distributed scatterers to increase the density of measurement points by the SBAS approach. The high resolution (3 m) of TSX images and the regular, frequent, short temporal baseline (12 days) acquisitions of S1 dataset make a generally high quality of interferograms. Therefore, we could detect a reasonably high density of point-like targets for those datasets using the PSI technique. We used StaMPS (Stanford Method for Persistent Scatterers) software package to implement both the PSI and SBAS analysis in this study. The PS selection in StaMPS is based on phase characteristics (Hooper et al., 2007 ), which was developed to work even in terrains devoid of man-made structures and/or undergoing non-steady deformation. The SBAS approach in StaMPS identifies distributed targets named as slowly decorrelating filtered phase (SDFP) pixels using phase analysis (Hooper, 2008 ). For interferograms generation, we applied DORIS software (Kampes and Usai, 1999 ) to generate interferograms for the StripMap mode datasets from ENVI, CSK and TSX satellites. S1 interferograms were generated using GMTSAR software (Xu et al., 2017 ) and the Enhanced Spectral Diversity method was used for the TOPS-mode data alignment to reach the azimuth alignment accuracy of 0.001 pixel so keeping the phase mismatch between the burst boundaries. For interferogram combinations, we set a 1500-day temporal threshold and a 1070-m perpendicular baseline threshold for both ENVI and CSK datasets, which constructs 193 interferograms for ENVI dataset and 185 interferograms for CSK dataset (Table 1 , Figs. S1 and S2  in the Supplementary Material ). The TSX dataset was referenced to image acquired on 12 April 2015 and 70 interferograms were formed (see Table 1  and Fig. S3 ), while the S1 dataset was referenced to image on 20 January 2019 and 112 interferograms were generated (see Table 1  and Fig. S4 ). The topographic phase component is computed using the 90 m SRTM DEM (Farr et al., 2007 ) and subtracted from the interferograms. Once the interferograms are generated and high-quality pixels are identified, the interferometric phase values (modulo 2π) of the identified pixels are unwrapped using the 3D phase unwrapping algorithm (Hooper and Zebker, 2007 ). The deformation time series and the annual velocity of deformation are resolved from the unwrapped phase values of the interferometric network using the least squares method. The estimated deformation can be biased by several errors, such as DEM error, orbital error, atmospheric error and noise. The DEM errors are related to the perpendicular baseline, which is calculated and removed by using the multi-baseline differential interferograms. The long-wavelength component of atmospheric delays and orbital error (phase ramp) are estimated by the best fitting plane of the unwrapped phase. The small-scale atmospheric delays are filtered in time and space assuming that the delays are temporally uncorrelated while the deformations are correlated in space and time.  4.2 Fusion of multi-sensor InSAR time series There are two factors that prevent us from obtaining long-term and homogeneous information about the dynamics of surface deformation from multiple SAR satellites in the study area. The first one is that the time span of each individual SAR dataset used in our study is limited to a few years. Second, each dataset is independently processed by SBAS/PSI methods as described in Section 4.1 , and the retrieved displacement time series are relative to the first acquisition date of each individual dataset, resulting in an offset between different displacement results (see examples in Fig. 7 ). Therefore, there is a need to merge the displacement time series from different SAR sensors, enabling us to investigate the long-term evolution of surface deformation in a common time 7nce. Here, we proposed to use the SVD (Singular Value Decomposition) method to concatenate the displacement time series derived from different SAR satellites.
