This problem can be solved by the SVD method to obtain the estimate of v  , and then the merged deformation time series is computed by multiplying the rate v   by the corresponding time interval. This proposed fusion method can also be used to merge time series of displacements from different observation techniques, such as measurements from spirit leveling, GPS and InSAR. Since the displacement results from different satellites are in different LOS direction, we first converted each LOS displacement into vertical direction by assuming a negligible component of deformation in horizontal direction. This assumption is reasonable because the ground surface deformation in Taiyuan city is mainly caused by the overexploitation of groundwater that the induced displacement field is predominantly one-dimensional, along the vertical direction. The assumption of the dominant vertical deformation in the study area is also validated in (Liu et al., 2018b ) by comparing the ascending and descending InSAR deformations results. Therefore, the vertical deformation can be simply obtained as:(7) d v  = d LOS   c o s θ       where d LOS     is the derived deformation in LOS direction of each individual SAR dataset, and θ   is the incidence angle of the radar signal.   5 Results 5.1 Groundwater recovery assessment Fig. 6  shows the temporal evolution of groundwater level in a long-term time frame for the period 1965–2019 derived from interpolating the historical groundwater-level contour maps using the kriging geostatistical method, as described in Section 3.2 . Before 1965, groundwater levels did not change significantly because there was no a lot of groundwater being used. The amount of groundwater extraction increased rapidly due to the rapid growth of population and economy in the 1980s and 1990s (Fig. 6 b–d), sending the groundwater levels down significantly and forming four large regional cones of depression by 2000 in the study area (Xizhang, Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao, Fig. 6 d). The contour lines of accumulated subsidence in different periods from leveling measurements were overlaid on the groundwater level maps in Fig. 6 b–d. The distribution of land subsidence centers and groundwater depression cones is spatially consistent, which indicates the well-known cause-effect relationship that groundwater extraction driving the aquifer-system compaction and the subsequent surface land subsidence. The groundwater depression cone in Wujiabao was formed in the 1960s and developed rapidly in the 1980s (Yan et al., 2006 ). Overexploitation of groundwater dropped the groundwater level in this area by 41.56 m during 1981–2000 with an average rate of 2.19 m/year. The depression cones in Wanbailin and Xiayuan were formed during the 1970s. From 1981 to 2000, the groundwater level in Wanbailin declined by 38.69 m with an average rate of 2.04 m/year, while in Xiayuan the groundwater level declined by 27.25 m with an average rate of 1.43 m/year. The Xizhang groundwater depression cone in the north of the city was formed in 1980s, the declining rate was 1.99 m/year during 1981–2000 and groundwater level declined by 37.83 m in that period. In the southeast of Taiyuan, the groundwater depression cone in Beiying was formed in 1981 and the groundwater level dropped by 72.16 m during 1981–2000. After 2000, the local authority adopted strict control on groundwater use and increased inter-basin surface water transfers, which slowed down the decline of groundwater levels and even resulted in groundwater recovery across most of the study area (Fig. 6 f–i).  5.2 Land surface deformation rates from multi-sensor InSAR data The land surface deformation rates over Taiyuan city from the four SAR datasets processed by SBAS/PSI methods described in Section 4.1  are shown in Fig. 7 . The rates have been converted into the vertical direction. The former land subsidence centers are marked in Fig. 7 a as the black polygons with their names labeled alongside. The time series extracted from the four datasets at points P1-P5 inside each subsidence center (red circles in Fig. 7 ) are shown in Fig. 8 , as a representative of temporal evolution of ground deformation at each subsidence center. By comparing the four maps of subsidence rate in Fig. 7 , the most prominent feature is the pattern change from land subsidence to land uplift in the central area of Taiyuan in the three former land subsidence centers (Wanbailin, Xiayuan and Wujiabao). The ground surface in these three subsidence centers show similar temporal evolution with a pattern of “subsidence to uplift”, which can be clearly observed in the deformation time series from the four datasets in different time periods (Fig. 8 ). The ground subsidence in Wanbailin had been arrested in the period of Aug 2003-Sep 2010 as observed from ENVI data that the subsiding rate is minimal (only 4.4 mm/year at the point P2) (Fig. 8 b). The subsidence switched to uplift as detected from CSK data (May 2011-Nov 2013, 8.2 mm/year at P2) and became relatively stable during the TSX period (Oct 2013-Aug 2017, 1.2 mm/year) and again continued to uplift during the S1 period (Mar 2017-Dec 2020, 5.8 mm/year). The two former subsidence centers (Xiayuan and Wujiabao) were still undergoing significant subsidence during the ENVI period with a subsiding rate of 28.2 mm/year at P3 in Xiayuan (Fig. 8 c) and 36.1 mm/year at P4 in Wujiabao (Fig. 8 d). They both reversed to a continuing land uplift afterwards. However, the uplifting rates at P4 in Wujiabao (16.3 mm/year, 3.7 mm/year and 10.1 mm/year for CSK, TSX and S1 dataset, respectively) are faster than that at P3 in Xiayuan (8.9 mm/year, 0.7 mm/year and 9.3 mm/year for CSK, TSX and S1 dataset, respectively). Actually, the transition from subsidence to uplift in Taiyuan first occurred in Xizhang, the northern suburb of the city, as we observed in the ENVI data (Figs. 7 a and 8 a). The point P1 located in this region exhibits an uplifting rate of 16.3 mm/year (Fig. 8 a) during the ENVI period and 2.4 mm/year during the CSK period. However, the ground surface changes into a slight land subsidence again during the TSX period with a rate of 8.4 mm/year and reduces to 5.9 mm/year during the S1 period. We anticipate that the prevailing land uplift in Taiyuan was induced by the elastic rebound of the aquifer system due to the recovery of the groundwater level, which will be discussed in Section 6 . The most significant subsidence was occurring in the southern part of Taiyuan city in Xiaodian district (Fig. 7 a–d). This is a new subsidence center which was formed between 2003 and 2010 as observed from the ENVI dataset (the green polygon in Fig. 7 a), because it was not found before the year of 2000 as observed in the contour map from leveling measurements. Land subsidence in this region developed with a decreasing rate from 61.2 mm/year during the ENVI period to 57.2 mm/year during the TSX period and to 51.9 mm/year during the S1 period at P5 (Fig. 8 e). However, the spatial extent of the subsidence area is expanding to the south in the Taiyuan basin and to the southeast in Jinzhong city.  5.3 Fusion results of multi-sensor InSAR time series and accuracy assessment In order to obtain the long-term continuous displacement time series derived from the four independent SAR datasets, we applied the fusion method described in Section 4.2  to merge the multiple InSAR displacement time series. Since the SVD method requires a time overlap between two datasets, the seven-month gap between ENVI and CSK datasets used in this study makes the connection between these two datasets challenging. To overcome this problem, a simple linear extrapolation of InSAR time series is applied to make their periods to overlap, which is reasonable because the time gap is short that we do not expect abrupt changes during this period. We assessed the accuracy of the InSAR displacements and to examine the consistency of the merged time series by comparing with independent observations from continuous GPS stations. This comparison was done at the two available GPS stations A001 and A008. The comparison between the concatenated InSAR time series (the black circles) and the vertical GPS displacements (the red triangles) is shown in Fig. 9  b and d. The results show that the InSAR displacement time series jointed together continuously between different datasets and the InSAR and GPS measurements are generally in good agreement. The RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) between InSAR and GPS displacements is 10.6 mm at A001 and 11.8 mm at A008. Both the InSAR and GPS displacement time series at these two GPS stations show positive rates of ground deformation, confirming the occurrence of land uplift in Taiyuan city. Given the close proximity of A001 and A008, the time series of ground displacements at the two sites are very similar. Fig. 9  shows the continuous displacement time series from Aug 2003 to Dec 2020 at the four representative locations P1-P4 merged from the four InSAR datasets (P5 is excluded in the fusion because it is not located in the common area of the different SAR datasets). These continuous time series help us to better investigate the dynamic evolution of ground deformation in a long-term time frame. From the continuous displacement time series, we can observe the time when subsidence stopped and the time when uplift started in the three former subsidence centers (Wanbailin, Xiayuan and Wujiabao) in Aug 2010. In Xizhang, the time of the transition from uplift to subsidence is in Jan 2013.  5.4 Sixty-five-year’s evolution of spatiotemporal surface deformation By comparing the historical subsidence data recorded by traditional optical leveling survey with the InSAR measurements, it helps us understand the long-term dynamic of land surface from the onset of subsidence to the cessation of subsidence and the transition to land uplift. The accumulated land subsidence contour maps for the periods 1956–1981 (Fig. 11   a), 1956–1989 (Fig. 11 b) and 1956–2000 (Fig. 11 c), were compiled from leveling measurements (Ma et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2006 ). The 2003–2010 accumulated deformation was derived from the ENVI dataset (Fig. 11 d), while the 2011–2013 deformation was derived from the CSK dataset (Fig. 11 e) and the 2013–2020 deformation was obtained by merging the TSX and S1 datasets (Fig. 11 f). According to the leveling measurements, no obvious land subsidence was observed before 1965. From 1965 to 1970, land subsidence developed slowly. During the 1970s and 1980s, due to the rapid economic growth, groundwater use increased and land subsidence expanded rapidly. The land subsidence center of Wujiabao was formed during 1970–1981, and developed rapidly from 1989 to 2000, with the maximum accumulated subsidence of 2797 mm in 2000. The subsidence centers in Wanbailin and Xiayuan are close in space and they were formed in the period 1981–1989. By 2000, the maximum accumulated subsidence was reaching 951 mm in Wanbailin and 1414 mm in Xiayuan. In the north, the land subsidence center in Xizhang was formed in the period 1981–1989 and the maximum subsidence reached to 697 mm by the year of 2000. After 2000, the subsidence expanded to the south and formed a new subsidence center in Xiaodian as observed from InSAR measurements (Fig. 11 d–f). This is consistent with the fact that the industrial development of Taiyuan has been moved to the south since 2001, and the formation of a new economic development zone in Xiaodian District has contributed to greater groundwater exploitation. In comparison with historical subsidence data, the recent InSAR measurements confirmed the deceleration of land subsidence and its transition to land uplift as a result of the dramatic reduction of groundwater withdrawal in Taiyuan. Given the spatial–temporal evolution of deformation in Fig. 11 , the deceleration of land subsidence or land uplift spreads from the north to the south of Taiyuan. With the historical records of leveling measurements (Table 2  ), we concatenated them with InSAR displacement time series in the four subsidence centers at points P1-P4 to show the land deformation in a 65-year time frame, as shown in Fig. 11 g. The logistic model (Coussy, 2010; Dong et al., 2023 ) fits the displacement time series very well, which can describe the full life cycle of land subsidence, that is, it starts slowly before 1980, increases rapidly during 1980–2000, and finally levels off after 2003 (red lines in Fig. 11 g). In summary, the subsidence rate in the Taiyuan city as a whole generally decreased from 2003 following the termination of groundwater pumping, and then the ground elevation gradually switched to slight uplift since about Aug 2003 in the north and Aug 2010 in the central region, and tends to be stable after Dec 2020. The temporal evolution of the entire cycle of elevation change generally follows the shape of curve B in Fig. 1 . We took displacements at these four representative points to illustrate the ratio of net uplift to total land subsidence in the former subsidence centers (Table 2 ). In Xizhang, the subsidence stopped in Aug 2003 with a net subsidence of 749 mm, and then the ground began to show uplift with a net uplift of 69 mm by the end of 2020. The amount of land surface rebound is ∼ 9.2 % of the net subsidence. Land subsidence in the central region continued until Aug 2010 with a net subsidence of 1127 mm in Wanbailin, 1817 mm in Xiayuan, 3343 mm in Wujiabao. After that, the ground in these regions show a continuing uplift. By the end of 2020, we observed a net uplift of 89 mm, 88 mm, and 120 mm in the previously subsiding areas of Wanbailin, Xiayuan and Wujiabao, accounting for 7.9 %, 4.8 % and 3.6 % of the total subsidence in each of these regions, respectively.   6 Discussion 6.1 Land surface response to groundwater drawdown and recovery The maps of groundwater level increments after the launch of the water transfer project for the periods of 2003–2010 and 2010–2019 are shown in Fig. 12  . Groundwater levels in the whole study area show a general rise after 2003, although the timing of rising groundwater levels varies spatially, which was spatially expanding from the north to the south (Fig. 12 a and c). As can be seen from Fig. 12 a, the north of Taiyuan in Xizhang is the first region to show groundwater recovery, following the interruption of groundwater pumping and the operation of the WWDP water diversion project in 2003. By 2010, groundwater levels have increased by up to 55 m in this region, almost returning to its original level as in 1965. With the rising groundwater levels, the land surface in the north switched from land subsidence to land uplift as seen in Fig. 12 b. Within the central and southern regions of Taiyuan city, the groundwater levels still showed a decrease between 2003 and 2010 (Fig. 12 a), despite the fact that surface water from Yellow River has been supplied to this city. In this period, the land in the Wanbailin, Xiayuan and Wujiabao subsidence areas was still subsiding (Fig. 12 b), but the rates of subsidence are much lower than they were before 2000, particularly in Wanbailin which is situated in the area between rising and falling groundwater levels. Groundwater level increment values for the 2010–2019 period (Fig. 12 c) highlight the groundwater level rise in the central Taiyuan, with values ranging from a low of 0.0–10 m to a peak of 52 m. Following the groundwater recovery, the ground subsidence in Wanbailin, Xiayuan and Wujiabao reversed to land uplift during this period (Fig. 12 d). In the south, despite the fact that groundwater levels have been rising over the past few years, subsidence in Xiaodian continued due to the delayed compaction of the aquifer system. The southeastern part of Taiyuan has seen only a slight recovery in groundwater levels, compared to other regions, due to its status as a new economic center, where it is still heavily dependent on groundwater for water supply in the past two decades. In the north, the water level tends to be stabilized in the 2010–2019 period as no significant change can be observed in Fig. 12 c, but the ground surface shows a slight subsidence possibly due to delayed compaction of aquitards following the groundwater decline during the 1980s. The observed correlations between rising groundwater level and land surface uplift can be attributed reasonably to the elastic rebound of the aquifer as a consequence of the unloading of effective stress due to the increase in pore pressure, which is associated with the recovery of groundwater levels following the cessation of groundwater pumping. This interpretation is referred to as the pore-elastic rebound of an aquifer and is caused by the release of elastically compressed aquifers when the pore-water pressure is regained. Specifically, in regard to this hydro-mechanical coupling effect, when the piezometric head rises, the areas of the aquifer that have been recharged will experience a decrease in compressive strain, resulting in a dilatation that causes an elastic rebound. Despite this, even when groundwater returns to its original level, only a small amount of the initial aquifer compaction can be recovered, as we discussed in Section 5.4  that the land surface uplift is less than 10 % of the previous subsidence in our study area.  6.2 Effect of geological conditions on land subsidence and uplift The groundwater level decline due to overexploitation is the main cause for land subsidence in Taiyuan city, yet the spatial extent and magnitude of land subsidence is not only dependent on the amount of groundwater withdrawal, but is also impacted by stratigraphic heterogeneity and characteristics of the geological formation. By comparing the long-term groundwater level changes, ground deformation and clay layer stratigraphy in the subsidence centers (Fig. 13  ), several interesting and important characteristics have been observed. The greatest land subsidence was happening in Wujiabao, with an amount of subsidence of 3343 mm from 1956 until it came to an end in Aug 2010 (also see Table 2 ). The main reason is that the cumulative thickness of the clay layers (low permeability) in Wujiabao is large and the formation is mostly interlayered with sand and the thickness of individual clay layer is small. When groundwater level drops, the water drainage in the thin clay layer is easier, and the aquitard compaction is fast and the compaction rate is high, leading to a more significant land subsidence (Ma et al., 2006 ). Though both Wanbailin and Xiayuan have a large thickness of cumulative clay layers, their land subsidence is not as pronounced as Wujiabao due to the thicker individual clay layer, which results in slower drainage and less compaction of the aquitard. The smallest cumulative thickness of clay layers in Xizhang results in the smallest land subsidence in comparison to other subsidence centers in Taiyuan (Fig. 13 ). The occurrence of land subsidence always lags behind the formation of groundwater depression cones. Clay has a poor conductivity and low permeability, which makes it difficult for the pore water to drain out when under pressure. This leads to a slow aquitard compaction, and a time lag and delay between land subsidence and the drawdown of groundwater level (Ma et al., 2006 ). When each individual clay layer in the aquifer system is thicker, the hysteresis effect is more evident. This is why we saw a minor land subsidence during 1965–1980 in Wanbailin and Xiayuan while the groundwater level experienced a dramatic drawdown (Fig. 13 ). The increase in the rate of land subsidence in these two areas after 1980 is mainly resulting from the rapid decline of groundwater before 1980 because of the lagging effects due to the presence of thick aquitards in the aquifer system. The clay layer which was thinner in Xizhang and Wujiabao caused a shorter time delay between the subsidence and the lowering of the groundwater level, that is the rapid land subsidence consistently followed the drawdown of groundwater level. Such observations confirms that ground subsidence is not just related to declining groundwater levels, but also dependent on stratigraphic properties (i.e., the thickness of clay layers, the number of interbedded layers, configurations of clay and coarse sand). The same is true to ground uplift in response to the rising groundwater level. Despite the fact that groundwater decline has stopped in 2002, land subsidence in Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao was still occurring until Aug 2010. This suggests the residual (time-delayed) compaction due to the presence of thick clay layers in the aquifer systems in these regions. The areas of aquifer and aquitard that have been depleted will continue to experience compaction due to time-dependent consolidation caused by the decrease in groundwater pressure in the previous pumping, until the groundwater level recovers to the level to compensate for the pore pressure deficits in these sections. If thick clay layers are present in the aquifer system, the water flows through them more slowly, then the recharge of groundwater and subsequent rise in groundwater level will be delayed. In such cases, the relaxation of elastically compressed aquifer materials will take a longer time to cause the elastic rebound. In Xizhang, the land uplift occurred as soon as the rising groundwater level in 2003. The reason for this is that the thin clay layers in Xizhang make a more rapid groundwater recharge and a fast pore-elastic rebound of the aquifer system. The ratio of ground rebound relative to the previous subsidence is also higher (see Table 2 ) when there are more interbedded layers in the aquifer system and when each individual layer is thin. Spatially, the InSAR displacement maps also reveal the intimate connection between groundwater withdrawal, faults and land subsidence/uplift. The southeastern boundary of the elongated subsiding zone in Xiaodian is aligned with the Tianzhuang fault, which is an NEE-WE-NNE buried normal fault in the southeast of Taiyuan (Fig. 12 ). Differential subsidence was observed between the two sides of the Tianzhuang fault that significant subsidence was found on the west side while little subsidence was detected in the east side of the fault. The maps suggest that the spatial distribution of ground deformation is controlled by Quaternary faults by acting as obstacles to lateral groundwater flow in the subsurface (Amelung et al., 1999 ), creating groundwater level differences across the fault (Fig. 12 a and c), and constraining the migration of land subsidence/uplift on the surface (Fig. 12 b and d).  6.3 Implications for groundwater management and hazard mitigation in the context of rising groundwater levels Groundwater pumping for human development has severely depleted the aquifer system in Taiyuan as well as other regions around the world. Over the past few decades, many regions have implemented strategies to reduce groundwater pumping to alleviate ground subsidence, such as bans on groundwater abstraction, closing wells, and even artificial water injection. Most groundwater use in Taiyuan was substituted for surface water imported by inter-basin water transfer project. These practices have dramatically reduced groundwater pumping and resulted in groundwater recovery. How does the groundwater recovery affect the spatiotemporal evolution of land subsidence? The answer to this question can improve our understanding of the sustainability and budget of groundwater resources in the aquifer system. This study has shown that land subsidence in Taiyuan has been contained through the inter-basin water transfer project and the careful management of the aquifer system. Our results show that the depleted aquifer exhibit an elastic rebound in the later stage of groundwater recharge after termination of groundwater pumping, although the rebound magnitude is less than 10 % of the former pumping-induced subsidence. To avoid negative effects of the rising groundwater level due to natural/artificial groundwater recharge, any changes to the groundwater system are required to be monitored. InSAR remote sensing is a promising source of spatially consistent, high-quality data that is relevant to groundwater system monitoring because it measures ground elevation change in response to the changing amount of groundwater at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions (Adams et al., 2022; Chaussard et al., 2016; Neely et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2022 ). Utilizing the high-spatial-resolution measurements of surface displacement, decisions can be made about where to place future monitoring, extraction and injection bores. Another concern is that the rising groundwater level would cause adverse impacts on the built environment and agricultural lands. In the urban area of Taiyuan, at the time when the groundwater levels were low due to artificial pumping, a lot of buildings and other sensitive structures were constructed and did not appear to be an issue. With regard to the engineering implications, the greatest risk to foundation integrity is the decrease in effective stress as the pore water pressure regains during the rising of the groundwater table, causing the swelling and heave of clays (Johnson and Wilkinson, 1994 ). Implications for underground structures are most likely to be water ingress into basements, tunnels, and parking garages, causing damages to building fabric (Allocca et al., 2022 ). With high groundwater levels, repair and maintenance of existing, and the construction of new, underground structures will be more difficult and costly. This is a great concern to many previous anthropogenic subsidence areas in China due to massive groundwater extraction and now experiencing groundwater level recovery with relation to the termination of groundwater pumping, like in Beijing (Dong et al., 2023 ), Shanghai (Zhang et al., 2015 ), Tianjin (Yu et al., 2023 ), Xi'an (Li et al., 2023 ), Su-Xi-Chang (Wang et al., 2020 ).   7 Conclusion In this paper, land subsidence and uplift response to groundwater drawdown and recovery in Taiyuan city, Northern China, was documented in detail by integrating use of leveling, InSAR displacement data and groundwater level maps. By means of leveling data from 1956 to 2000 and time series of InSAR displacement data covering the period of 2003–2020, the spatial and temporal evolution of ground deformation has been analyzed for the periods before and after the termination of groundwater pumping. Groundwater level maps from 1965 to 2019 show groundwater drawdown before 2000 and four large groundwater depression cones were formed (Xizhang, Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao) in Taiyuan city. The declining groundwater levels induced subsidence centers at each groundwater depression cones, with cumulated subsidence of 749 mm in Xizhang, 1127 mm in Wanbailin, 1817 mm in Xiayuan, and 3343 mm in Wujiabao, respectively. After 2000, following the strong reduction of groundwater extraction, the rise of groundwater level first occurred in the north of Taiyuan in Xizhang and stabilized in 2010, with a rise of up to 55 m, which almost returns to its original level as in 1965. Groundwater recovery expanded from the north to the central area of Taiyuan during 2010–2019, leading to the rising groundwater level in the previous groundwater depression cones in Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao with a maximum magnitude of 52 m in these regions. With the rising groundwater levels, the land subsidence centers have switched from subsidence to uplift. In Xizhang, the subsidence stopped in Aug 2003 and then the ground began to show uplift with a magnitude of 69 mm by the end of 2020, accounting for ∼ 9.2 % in magnitude comparing to the amount of previous subsidence. In Wanbailin, Xiayuan, and Wujiabao, land subsidence continued until Aug 2010 and then the ground surface shows a continuing uplift in these regions. By the end of 2020, we observed a ground uplift of 89 mm in Wanbailin, 88 mm in Xiayuan, and 120 mm in Wujiabao, accounting for 7.9 %, 4.8 % and 3.6 % of the previous subsidence in each of these subsidence center. These results show that, even when groundwater returns to its original level, only a slight amount of the initial aquifer compaction can be recovered during groundwater recharge, because aquitards have an inelastic compressibility that is several orders of magnitude larger than the elastic compressibility of aquitards and aquifers. The spatial extent and magnitude of land subsidence/uplift is not only dependent on the amount of groundwater level drawdown/rise, but is also impacted by stratigraphic characteristics in the aquifer and the distribution of buried faults. An analysis of the trends in groundwater level and ground deformation suggests that the land uplift is a result of a poro-elastic rebound mechanism in the porous aquifer system. This phenomenon was attributed to the rise of piezometric level as a consequence of the termination of groundwater pumping, related effective stress unload and ground displacement rebound when the aquifer is recharged. Our findings allow us to conclude that the groundwater management practices adopted in Taiyuan could produce positive effects on restoring the depleted aquifer system, which could be an exemplar city to serve as a model for aquifer-depleted regions elsewhere in the world.
1 Introduction The Northwest China (NWC) is situated within the heartland of the Eurasian continent, distant from maritime influences. The NWC is subject to the interplay of atmospheric circulation patterns, such as the summer monsoon, westerlies, and plateau monsoon (Guo et al., 2020 ). The geographical position, coupled with the topographical features and thermal effect of Tibetan Plateau, leads the most parts of the NWC experience arid climatic conditions, typified by limited water resources and scarcer precipitation. The combination of plateau, temperate continental, and temperate monsoonal climatic regimes further enriches climatic diversity. The intricate physical geography makes ecosystems that are notably fragile, include a diverse climatic classifications, spanning arid, semi-arid, semi-humid, and humid zones (Gao et al., 2018; Shi et al., 1994 ). The NWC is typical area of fragile ecological environment and high sensitivity to climate change, holding significant importance in the global climate system (Zhang et al., 2023b ). Hence, impacts of climate change in the NWC has consistently become as an important scientific issue. Precipitation serves as a crucial driver factor of the ecological environment and socio-economic development of the NWC. As the primary source of 'solid water reservoirs' and directly supplying water resources to the middle and lower reaches, precipitation plays a vital role in supporting industrial, agricultural, domestic, and ecological needs. Variations in precipitation have profound effects on the climate, ecology, and water resources. The different phases of precipitation significantly impact the absorption and reflection of solar radiation, consequently influencing mass and water cycle processes (Daloz et al., 2020; Dingman, 2015; Lynn et al., 2020 ). The shifting phases of precipitation also intricately affect runoff and snow melt processes (Li et al., 2020b ). Particularly noteworthy is the critical role of snowfall in regulating regional water resources, given the vulnerability to climatic aridity and ecological fragility in the NWC. Snow cover mitigates the impact of environmental factors on soil, while snow melt and glacier meltwater serve as essential water sources for rivers in mountainous (Clason et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2013 ). Understanding the phases of precipitation patterns holds profound scientific significance and practical utility for water resource management and planning initiatives in the NWC. In the early 2000 s, the climate in the drylands of the NWC shifted from “warming and drying” trend to “warming and wetting” trend (Shi et al., 2002; Shi et al., 2006 ). Different with other regions at similar latitudes globally, the NWC has experienced a continuous increase in precipitation, runoff, and glacier melt since the mid-1980 s. However, increase in precipitation may not fully compensate for the decreasing terrestrial water storage associated with the melt of solid water (glaciers, permafrost, snow cover, etc.), potentially linked to the precipitation phase. Global warming has gradually transitioned precipitation phases from rain to snow, affecting the melt rates of snow and glacier (Barnhart et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Twardosz et al., 2012 ), and altering the seasonal distribution of runoff (Berghuijs et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021a ). Studies have shown a decreasing trend in the Snowfall to Precipitation Ratio (SPR) in various regions, including Switzerland, New England, the western United States, Finland, and within China, such as the Tianshan Mountains, Tibetan Plateau, and NWC (Gillies et al., 2012; Guo & Li, 2015; Hou et al., 2023; Huntington et al., 2004; Irannezhad et al., 2017; Knowles et al., 2006; Serquet et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016 ). Despite numerous studies on historical changes in precipitation phases, there is considerable interest in future changes, especially with the use of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) data. CMIP6 contains the latest and advanced climate models, providing substantial simulated data for studying future climate changes in the NWC. The CMIP6 has been used to estimate future climate trends in the NWC (Qin et al., 2021; Wang & Zhai, 2022 ). The results indicate a significant increase in both temperature and precipitation under various emission scenarios. However, the severity of drought in the NWC is expected to worsen under high emission scenarios (Li et al., 2020a ). The investigation on future changes in snowfall and precipitation phases remains limited, and the performance of CMIP6 data in simulating precipitation phases in the NWC is not yet to be comprehensively understood. As a crucial region of “the Silk Road Economic Belt” initiative, the NWC serves as a frontier of open development and a commercial logistics hub connecting Eurasia. The fragile ecological environment and water scarcity significantly constrain sustainable socioeconomic development. Therefore, the study of future precipitation phase prediction in the NWC holds substantial social significance and practical value for facilitating the coordinated development of the regional economy and society. In this study, the latest CMIP6 climate models are used to investigate two key scientific questions concerning precipitation phase dynamics and future projections in the NWC: (1) Evaluation of CMIP6 models performance in simulating precipitation phase over the NWC, and (2) assessment of future changes in snowfall and SPR under three scenarios. The study is arranged as follows: Section 1  is Introduction. Section 2  provides an overview of the data sources and methodological approaches. In Section 3 , we evaluate the simulation performance of multiple CMIP6 models for snowfall and SPR in the NWC, selecting the top-performing models for future projections. Section 4  analyzes seasonal and sub-regional variations in snowfall and SPR under future scenarios, and explores potential mechanisms for biases in precipitation phase estimations by CMIP6 models. Finally, we conclude with a summary of findings. This research aims to contribute insights for future precipitation change predictions and enhancements in hydrological forecasting models, providing a scientific foundation for effective management of regional water resources and disaster response in the NWC.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Study area The Northwestern China (NWC), spanning from 70°E to 113°E and 28°N to 51°N, encompasses Xinjiang, Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, Shaanxi, and parts of Inner Mongolia (Fig. 1  ). Positioned in the Eurasian hinterland, the NWC is deeply inland and distant from maritime influences. High plateau and mountainous terrain impede moist airflow, resulting in scarce regional precipitation. Apart from the southeast, where average annual precipitation exceeds 400 mm, other regions experience precipitation below this threshold, showing a decreasing trend from east to west, making it the driest regions globally at similar latitudes (Gao et al., 2015 ). Annual snowfall averages below 25 mm, primarily concentrated in northern Xinjiang, where it exceeds 2.5 to 6 times that of other regions in the NWC (Hou et al., 2022 ). Under global warming, extreme weather events in the NWC are increasingly frequent (Wang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023a ). The NWC is divided into seven typical watersheds or mountainous areas to analyze changes of snowfall and SPR at the sub-regional scale (Fig. 1 ).  2.2 Observation data The observation data used in this study is the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD), which is a surface meteorological element driving dataset designed for China with high spatial–temporal resolution (Yang et al., 2019 ). The dataset is available in the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (http://data.tpdc.ac.cn/en/data/8028b944-daaa-4511–8769-965612652c49/). The CMFD is generated by assimilating conventional meteorological observations from the China Meteorological Administration into background fields derived from prominent international sources, including Princeton reanalysis data, GLDAS data, GEWEX-SRB radiation data, and TRMM precipitation data. With a horizontal resolution of 0.1°, the accuracy of CMFD is relatively high (He et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2010 ). The observational data selected for this study span daily near-surface air temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, and specific humidity within the NWC region, encompassing the period from 1979 to 2018. It is imperative to note that the CMFD dataset, as utilized in this study, does not inherently distinguish the phase of precipitation. Consequently, a dynamic threshold parameterization scheme is implemented to extract snowfall data from the total precipitation.  2.3 Model data This study incorporates data from 21 CMIP6 models during 2019–2100, encompassing near-surface air temperature, precipitation, and snowfall variables. The selected models encompass scenarios from three distinct emission pathways: SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5. Comprehensive descriptions of each model are provided in Table 1  . To assess the simulation performance of CMIP6 data, historical simulations spanning from 1979 to 2014 and future projections under SSP2-4.5 for the years 2015–2018 are combined to establish the historical period in this study, aligning with the timeline of CMFD data. It is essential to highlight that, prior to any analytical procedures in this study, the CMIP6 data undergo uniform resampling to a resolution of 0.1° × 0.1° grid by bilinear interpolation. This standardization ensures consistency in the spatial representation of the data and facilitates meaningful cross-model comparisons.  2.4 Precipitation phase separation scheme The CMFD dataset lacks distinction of precipitation phase. Therefore, it becomes imperative to extract snowfall data from precipitation records within the CMFD dataset before assessing CMIP6 model data. Previous studies in the NWC often rely on fixed threshold temperatures or probabilistic statistical methods for segregating precipitation phases. However, the transition between precipitation phases is influenced by various factors, exhibiting considerable regional and altitudinal disparities. Hence, a comprehensive parameterized rain-snow separation model is needed. This study adopts the parameterized precipitation phase identification scheme, which uses surface temperature, relative humidity, air pressure, and elevation, with wet bulb temperature serving as the decisive factor (Ding et al., 2014 ). The approach fully integrates regional daily meteorological conditions to discern precipitation types effectively. The model has demonstrated its efficacy in capturing variations in snowfall patterns over the NWC (Ding et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2023 ). NSE ranges from negative infinity to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating better model performance. The CMFD data illustrates that high snowfall regions are predominantly situated in high-altitude areas such as the Tibetan Plateau, Tianshan Mountains, and Altai Mountains. The average annual snowfall exceed 600 mm in southern Plateau of Qinghai, peaking at 800 mm. Conversely, the Tarim Basin desert area and the Hexi Corridor exhibit minimal snowfall, averaging less than 10 mm annually. The spatial distribution of average annual snowfall as simulated by CMIP6 MME is similar to that of CMFD, emphasizing larger snowfall amounts in high-altitude regions, notably the Karakoram Mountains registering a maximum average annual snowfall of 580 mm. However, notable numerical disparities exist between CMIP6 MME simulation and CMFD data (Fig. 2 c). Particularly in high-altitude areas like the Tianshan Mountains, Qilian Mountains, and the Source Region of the Three Rivers, results of CMIP6 MME simulation display a discernible underestimation for snowfall, with differences ranging from 100 to 400 mm. The Qilian Mountains region exhibits the most substantial difference, typically around 300 mm. In contrast, the Kunlun Mountains, Karakoram Mountains, and the outer edge of the Tarim Basin manifest a distinct overestimation, with discrepancies ranging from 100 to 300 mm. While CMIP6 MME tends to overestimate snowfall in low-altitude areas, the numerical discrepancies are comparatively minor. The trend of annual snowfall in the NWC from 1979 to 2018 is shown in Fig. 3  . In low-altitude areas, the variation of snowfall is relatively small, whereas high-altitude regions manifest a predominant increasing trend, notably evidenced by the peak value observed in the southern Karakoram Mountains, showcasing a maximum increase rate of 120 mm·10a-1 . The regions experiencing a decrease in snowfall are predominantly situated in the southeastern NWC, with the lowest value of −41.27 mm·10a-1  observed at the eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau. However, it is noteworthy that the snowfall trend in high-altitude areas simulated by CMIP6 MME is opposite to the observed data. Moreover, Fig. 3 c indicates that CMIP6 MME significantly underestimates snowfall trend in high-altitude areas, reaching as low as −60 mm·10a-1 . Conversely, there are regions in the southeastern NWC where CMIP6 MME overestimates the snowfall trend. At the sub-region scale, notable regional disparities exist in the average annual snowfall over the NWC from 1979 to 2018 (Table 2  ). The highest average annual snowfall is recorded in the Plateau of Qinghai with 296.12 mm, while the lowest is observed in the Hexi Inland River Basins, with a value of 43.26 mm. The CMIP6 MME effectively captures the spatial distribution and extreme snowfall regions compared to CMFD, numerical disparities persist between observed data and simulation results. Specifically, in the Plateau of Qinghai, Qilian Mountains, and Tianshan Mountains regions, results of CMIP6 MME simulation indicate an underestimation of snowfall, with the most significant underestimation occurring in the Qilian Mountains at −100.56 mm. In other regions, CMIP6 MME tends to overestimate snowfall. CMIP6 MME performs less effectively in simulating the snowfall trend compared to snowfall. The simulation results fail to reflect an increasing trend in snowfall in high-altitude areas, instead manifesting a conspicuous decreasing trend. Furthermore, underestimation of the snowfall trend is evident across all regions in CMIP6 MME, with the largest deviation observed in the Tianshan Mountains at –33.66 mm·10a-1  and the smallest in Eastern Part of Lanzhou at −3.36 mm·10a-1 .  3.2 The bias in the climatology of SPR The changes of precipitation phase has significantly attracted widely attention (Prein & Heymsfield, 2020; Wang et al., 2016 ). The Snowfall-Precipitation Ratio (SPR), as a widely adopted indicator of precipitation phase, is importance in water cycle (McCrystall et al., 2021; Tamang et al., 2020 ). A higher SPR indicates a greater proportion of snowfall in total precipitation. Fig. 4  a illustrates the spatial distribution of SPR over the NWC from 1979 to 2018. Similar to the distribution of the climatology of snowfall, high SPR values are also found in high-altitude areas, with most regions in Tibetan Plateau, Karakoram Mountains, Tianshan Mountains, and Altai Mountains showing an average 100 % of SPR. Low-altitude areas exhibit lower SPR values, with the average SPR in the Junggar Basin around 30 %, Tarim Basin and Hexi Corridor around 10 %, and the lowest SPR in the eastern NWC below 5 %. The CMIP6 MME similarly captures the general spatial distribution of SPR but exhibits significant numerical differences (Fig. 4 a, c). Specifically, CMIP6 performs well in reproducing the SPR in low-altitude areas but falls short in simulating high-altitude areas. The results indicate that the SPR in the Kunlun Mountains is simulated at 70 %-80 %, while the SPR in the Tianshan Mountains and the eastern Tibetan Plateau is simulated at 30 %-40 %, with these two areas showing the largest deviations (Fig. 4 c, deviation range 50 %-80 %). CMIP6 demonstrates a clear underestimation of SPR in high-altitude areas, simultaneously, an overestimation of SPR in low-altitude areas. For instance, the SPR deviation in the southern edge of the Tarim Basin is in the range of 30–40 %, and the overestimation deviation in the southern foothills of the Altai Mountains is around 20 %. In other regions, the SPR deviations are relatively smaller, with the eastern part of the NWC exhibiting the smallest absolute deviation. The variation in SPR in the high-altitude regions of the NWC is not particularly pronounced, because SPR in these areas approaches 100 % (Fig. 5  a). The Tarim Basin, Junggar Basin, and Hexi Corridor demonstrate a noticeable increasing trend in SPR, with the highest observed value at the southern edge of the Tarim Basin reaching 11.10 %·10a-1 . In contrast, the Qaidam Basin, Yellow River source region, and Tianshan Mountains experience a clear decreasing trend in SPR, with the lowest observed value in the Qaidam Basin at −0.92 %·10a-1 . Additionally, slight decreasing trends are observed in the northern part of the Altai Mountains and the eastern part of the NWC. While SPR remains relatively unchanged in the southern part of Qinghai, Qilian Mountains, and Kunlun Mountains. The CMIP6 MME simulations indicate an overall decreasing trend of SPR across the NWC, with the most significant downward trend in the north-central part of the Tibetan Plateau. Only a slight upward trend in SPR is observed in the eastern-central part of the Tarim Basin, with an increase rate of approximately 0.15 %·10a-1 . Comparing the biases of the two datasets, it becomes evident that CMIP6 MME generally underestimates the trend of SPR in the NWC. The most significant underestimation occurs in the Tarim Basin and Junggar Basin, while the Qaidam Basin and Yellow River Source show overestimation. The deviations of SPR in the eastern part of NWC, Tianshan Mountains, and the northern part of the Altai Mountains are relatively small. At the sub-region scale, the Plateau of Qinghai, Tianshan Mountains, and Qilian Mountains exhibit relatively high average SPR from 1979 to 2018, showing a decreasing trend in SPR, although some regions display insignificant downward trends (Table 3  ). Conversely, Eastern Part of Lanzhou records the lowest average SPR, with a slight decreasing trend. The Tarim River Basin, Altai Mountains, and Hexi Inland River Basins demonstrate an increasing trend in average SPR. While CMIP6 MME broadly captures the regional pattern of SPR, deviations are noticeable in simulating high-SPR areas. Particularly significant disparities between the two datasets are observed in the Qilian Mountains, Plateau of Qinghia, and Tianshan Mountains, where CMIP6 MME underestimates the SPR. The SPR tends to be overestimated in other regions, although the deviations are less pronounced. The SPR in all regions simulated by CMIP6 MME demonstrates a decreasing trend, with the Plateau of Qinghai exhibiting the most substantial decline, followed by the Qilian Mountains. In regions where SPR is decreasing, results of CMIP6 MME simulation are consistent with the spatial pattern of CMFD. However, CMIP6 MME fails to capture the increasing trend in SPR in the Altai Mountains, Hexi Inland River Basins, and Tarim River Basin. Moreover, the simulation deviations in SPR for these regions are considerable.  3.3 Evaluation of the simulated precipitation phase Through the analysis of CMIP6 models simulations of snowfall and SPR, it can be concluded that CMIP6 MME results still show deficiencies in reproducing the climatological and spatiotemporal variability of snowfall and SPR over the NWC. Consequently, a detailed examination of each model simulation performance is imperative. Firstly, the average biases of each model in simulating snowfall and SPR were calculated (Fig. 6  ). The results indicate that most models tend to overestimate annual snowfall over the NWC, with 13 models exhibiting overestimations exceeding 20 mm. ACCESS-ESM1-5 demonstrates the highest overestimation, reaching up to 86.98 mm. Conversely, four models show underestimation of annual snowfall over the NWC. Moreover, most of models underestimate annual SPR over the NWC, with discrepancies ranging from −1.45 % to −18.91 %. Significant differences are observed between models, with only IPSL-CM6A-LR and KIOST-ESM showing a trend of SPR overestimation. To evaluate the simulation performance of CMIP6 models, the normalized standard deviation ratio, correlation coefficient, and RMSE between each model data and CMFD were calculated, and the Taylor plot was generated based on the results (Fig. 7  ). The analysis revealed that EC-Earth3-Veg, INM-CM5-0, GFDL-CM4, EC-Earth3-Veg-LR, INM-CM4-8, and EC-Earth3 are closer to observational data, while CanESM5 and FGOALS-g3 exhibit considerable discrepancies, indicating sub-optimal simulation performance. Additionally, a comprehensive ranking of CMIP6 models was conducted using correlation coefficients, RMSE, and NSE between each model and CMFD data (Table 4  ). The top five models identified were INM-CM4-8, EC-Earth3, EC-Earth3-Veg, INM-CM5-0, and Earth3-Veg-LR, consistently exhibiting correlation coefficients exceeding 0.7 and NSE around 0.5, indicative of relatively superior simulation performance. For future changes of snowfall and SPR over the NWC, an ensemble mean utilizing these top five models is employed for estimation.  3.4 Projection of snowfall changes in the future Projections of snowfall are derived over the NWC by ensemble average of the five optimal models selected in Section 3.3 . The analysis reveals notable trends (k ) from 2019 to 2100 under different emission scenarios. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, the average annual snowfall over the NWC does not exhibit significant change. However, the declining trend are evidently under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, with rates of −1.04 mm·10a−1  and −2.94 mm·10a−1 , respectively, with statistical significance at the 99% level (Fig. 8  a). Further examination across near-term (2019–2040), mid-term (2041–2070), and long-term (2071–2100) reveals consistent reductions in snowfall across emission scenarios. In the near-term, little disparity is observed in snowfall changes among the three emission scenarios, with reductions of −6.95 mm, −7.87 mm, and −5.64 mm compared to the baseline period (1979–2014), with the most pronounced decrease noted under the SSP2-4.5 scenario and the least under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. In the mid-term, snowfall decreases by −7.34 mm, −7.93 mm, and −12.68 mm under the three scenarios, with a notably greater reduction observed under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, while alterations in snowfall under the SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios exhibit no significant deviation from the near-term. While the SSP1-2.6 scenario shows relatively stable reductions of −7.84 mm in the end of century, reductions intensify under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, reaching −12.57 mm and –22.68 mm, respectively. In three scenarios, the future snowfall over the NWC continues to exhibit a spatial distribution largely consistent with historical periods, with the trend of decrease as greenhouse gas emissions increase, although not particularly pronounced (Fig. 9  ). The reduction in snowfall over the Tibetan Plateau is most significant. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, areas with annual snowfall exceeding 300 mm are present in the Tibetan Plateau, but with increasing emissions, these areas gradually reduce. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, such areas with substantial snowfall are only found in the Karakoram Mountains. Moreover, regions in the southeastern part of the Hexi Corridor, where annual snowfall typically exceeds 50 mm, also experience a decrease with rising emissions. Quantitatively, the average annual snowfall over the NWC from 2019 to 2100 under the three scenarios is projected to be 99.48 mm, 97.42 mm, and 92.75 mm, respectively. In terms of the interannual trend of snowfall, a similar pattern of decreasing change rates with increasing emissions is observed. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, approximately 20.61 % of grids show an increasing trend in snowfall, primarily observed in regions such as the Qaidam Basin, Hexi Corridor, northern Altai Mountains, and eastern Tianshan Mountains, with rates of increase not deemed significant, all remaining below 1 mm·10a−1 . Significant declines in snowfall are observed in the Kunlun Mountains, southern Qinghai, and central-southern Shaanxi. Under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, the proportion of grids with increasing snowfall trends decreases to 12.77 %, mainly due to the shift from increasing (under SSP1-2.6) to decreasing trend in snowfall in the northern Altai Mountains, eastern Tianshan Mountains, and eastern periphery of the Tibetan Plateau. Meanwhile, areas displaying decreasing trend expand, primarily encompassing the southern NWC and northern Xinjiang regions, with the Tibetan Plateau witnessing an accelerated rate of decrease, reaching −5.5 mm·10a-1 . Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, only 4.35 % of grids show increasing snowfall trends, primarily concentrated in the eastern part of the Tarim Basin. Most regions experience a relatively swifter rate of decrease in snowfall, with certain parts of the Tibetan Plateau even reaching −13 mm·10a-1 . However, the snowfall in northern Altai Mountains exhibites a decreasing trend under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, which shows an increasing trend under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. The average annual snowfall over the NWC from 2019 to 2100 shows no significant disparity under the three scenarios (Fig. 9 a, c, e). To further investigate the trends, the forthcoming decades were segmented into three intervals: near-term (2019–2040), mid-term (2041–2070), and long-term (2071–2100), with discrepancies in annual snowfall scrutinized in relation to the baseline period (1979–2018) (Fig. 10  ). In the near-term, the snowfall exhibits a spatial pattern of increased under three scenarios in northern regions and decreased snowfall in southern regions of the NWC. The increase in snowfall is particularly pronounced in the Altai Mountains under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. The SSP5-8.5 scenario shows more widespread areas with increasing snowfall trends, likely due to moderate warming facilitating heightened atmospheric moisture retention, thus leading to increased snowfall. In the mid-term, high-altitude areas demonstrate a declining trend in snowfall amidst escalating emissions, with the Tibetan Plateau experiencing a particularly noticeable decline. In the long-term, disparities in snowfall among the scenarios become more conspicuous over the NWC, predominantly in high-altitude locales. Under the SSP1-2.6, the annual snowfall increases in the part of Altai Mountains, Tarim Basin, and Hexi Corridor in the near-term and long-term. Under the SSP2-4.5, the snowfall in Altai Mountains increases, which increased area of snowfall obviously enlarge in the Tarim Basin and Hexi Corridor in the mid-term and long-term. In most cases, snowfall in the Altai Mountains, Tarim Basin, and Hexi Corridor remains in an increasing state. Distinctions of annual snowfall in the Altai Mountains, Tarim Basin, and Hexi Corridor under the three scenarios are less discernible, suggesting a relatively lower sensitivity to temperature fluctuations.  3.5 Projection of SPR changes in the future Similar to snowfall, the average annual SPR decreases over the NWC in the future (Fig. 11  ). Reduction rates of −0.19 %·10a-1 , −0.64 %·10a-1 , and −1.50 %·10a-1  are projected under the three scenarios, respectively, all statistically significant at the 99 % confidence level. In the near-term, there are no significant discrepancies in SPR changes among the three scenarios, with reductions of −3.06 %, −2.83 %, and −3.38 %, respectively, compared to the baseline period. The decline in SPR amplifies in the mid-term across all scenarios, notably under the SSP5-8.5 which exhibits the most pronounced reduction. In the long-term, a slight decrease in SPR is observed under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, with a change of −3.82 % compared to the baseline period. However, SPR under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios experiences more substantial declines, with reductions of −6.44 % and −11.14 %, respectively. Increasing in amplitude of climate warming leads to more snowfall being converted into rainfall, resulting in a decrease in SPR. Fig. 12   illustrates the spatial distribution of the average annual SPR and its trends over the NWC from 2019 to 2100. In terms of average SPR over the NWC in the future, high-value areas remain concentrated in mountain areas such as the Altai Mountains and Kunlun Mountains, with little difference in average SPR among the three scenarios. Under the SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios, areas with SPR greater than 60 % exist only in the Kunlun Mountains and Karakoram Mountains. However, compared to the other two scenarios, there is a noticeable decrease in SPR in the eastern Tianshan Mountains under SSP5-8.5, and a decrease is also observed in the Qilian Mountains and Tibetan Plateau. The distribution of SPR trends shows a decreasing trend under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, particularly pronounced in high-altitude areas. Conversely, under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, the SPR trend in most areas of the NWC is not significant.And there is a relatively clear downward trend in SPR in the high-altitude areas of the southern NWC, but the rate of decrease does not exceed 1 %·10a-1 . Additionally, the eastern Tianshan Mountains and the western part of the Hexi Corridor show an indistinct upward trend in SPR, with an increase rate of about 0.2 %·10a-1 . In the near-term, most areas of the NWC exhibit a decreasing trend in SPR, with reductions generally within −10 %, and most low-elevation areas experiencing declines within −3% (Fig. 13  ). The most severely decrease in SPR occurs under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, while the downward trend in SPR is relatively weak under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, consistent with the distribution of snowfall discussed earlier. Areas experiencing increases in SPR include the northern part of the Hexi Corridor under SSP1-2.6, the Tarim Basin, and the Altai Mountains under SSP2-4.5. Across all scenarios, the SPR decline is more pronounced in parts of the Kunlun Mountains, western Qinghai, and northern Xinjiang compared to other regions. In the mid-term, SPR decreases in all regions compared to the baseline period, with a slightly higher rate of decrease compared to the near term. However, there is minimal variation in SPR in the western NWC during this period, with the SSP2-4.5 scenario showing the least decline in SPR. By the end of the 21st century, under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, a few areas east of the Tianshan Mountains experience a shift to increased SPR compared to the baseline period, with most areas showing a rebound in SPR compared to the medium term. However, SPR under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios shows a more severely downward trend.   4 Discussion 4.1 Projection of precipitation phase changes at the sub-region scale To better understand changes in snowfall and SPR over the NWC, the trends of typical mountainous areas and river basins in average annual snowfall and SPR were analyzed (Fig. 14  ). Overall, most regions exhibit a decreasing trend in annual snowfall over the NWC in the future, with the Plateau of Qinghai experiencing the most pronounced decline (Fig. 14 c). Specifically, the Plateau of Qinghai demonstrates decreasing trends in snowfall under three scenarios: −0.33 mm·10a-1 , −2.31 mm·10a-1 , and −7.59 mm·10a-1 , respectively. In the near-term, snowfall in low-altitude areas is expected to increase under the SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios, while decreasing under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, although not significantly. Snowfall in mountainous areas and the Plateau of Qinghai exhibits significant regional differences. Except for the Altai Mountains and Tianshan Mountains under the SSP2-4.5 scenario and the Plateau of Qinghai under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, which show an increasing trend in snowfall, other regions show a decreasing trend. Notably, the decrease in snowfall in the Altai Mountains under the SSP1-2.6 scenario is more pronounced than under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. In the mid-term, the snowfall decline in high-altitude regions moderate in comparison to the near-term, while it intensifies in low-altitude areas. Apart from the Altai Mountains, demonstrating a consistent decrease in snowfall across all scenarios, other regions illustrate divergent trends. Under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, most regions display an upward trend in snowfall, contrasting with a downward trend under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. However, the reduction in snowfall within the Qilian Mountains and Tarim River Basin is more pronounced under the SSP2-4.5 scenario compared to the SSP5-8.5 scenario. By the end of century, several regions exhibit a swifter decline in snowfall compared to the near-term and mid-term, with the Plateau of Qinghai under the SSP5-8.5 scenario projecting a trend of −10 mm·10a-1 . Conversely, snowfall in the Altai Mountains indicates a non-significant upward trend under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Additionally, the Qilian Mountains and Hexi Inland River Basin depict weak upward trends under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. In summary, while snowfall in high-altitude areas generally demonstrates a fluctuating downward trend, snowfall in low-altitude areas displays a more pronounced decline over time, with high-altitude regions experiencing a considerably faster reduction in snowfall compared to low-altitude areas. In the future, the distribution of SPR trends in various regions is similar to the snowfall trends. However, the increase of SPR are less frequent compared to snowfall. Because that as temperatures rise, the atmosphere moisture-holding capacity also increases (Li et al., 2018 ). However, even temperature increases during cold conditions can have negative effects on SPR (Wang et al., 2022 ). When warming occurs below the temperature threshold for snowfall, snow intensity tends to increase (Zhao et al., 2020 ). In all emission scenarios, the SPR across regions in the future shows consistent decline trend, with the rate of decline accelerating as increasing emission intensity (Fig. 15  ). The most significant decline in SPR is observed in the Plateau of Qinghai, with significant decline rate of −0.25 %·10a-1 , −0.89 %·10a-1 , and −1.87 %·10a-1  under the three emission scenarios, respectively. Following closely is the Tarim River Basin, while the Eastern Part of Lanzhou exhibits the slowest decline in SPR. In the near-term, low-altitude areas show an increasing trend in SPR, with the Altai Mountains and Tianshan Mountains also indicating an increase in SPR under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. By the mid-century, while the Altai Mountains, Hexi Inland River Basin, and Tianshan Mountains exhibit an insignificant increase in SPR under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, other regions experience a descending trend, with most regions under the SSP5-8.5 scenario with statistical significance at the 99% level. Towards the end of the century, almost all regions show a descending trend in SPR, with the Tarim River Basin experiencing a significant decline rate of −2.98 %·10a-1  under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. However, the SPR in the Plateau of Qinghai under the SSP1-2.6 scenario shows no significant changes. Although regional differences in SPR trends are smaller compared to snowfall distribution, the Hexi Inland River Basin, Tarim River Basin, and Tianshan Mountains exhibit larger fluctuations in SPR trends over time, with more pronounced differences under different emission scenarios. It is anticipated that high-altitude areas will experience a more pronounced rate of warming compared to low-altitude areas in the future (Lalande et al., 2021 ). Correspondingly, there will be a more significant decrease in snowfall and SPR. High-altitude areas typically have relatively low surface temperatures, and once the ambient wet-bulb temperature approaches the threshold for rain-snow conversion near freezing point, the ice particles will start to melt (Prein & Heymsfield, 2020; Wilson, 1941 ). This implies a shift from snow to rain, resulting in a rapid decline in snowfall and a sharp decrease in SPR (Deng et al., 2017; Krasting et al., 2013; Ye, 2008 ). Additionally, temperature is not the sole factor influencing snowfall trends in high-altitude areas. Atmospheric circulation will also significantly impact snowfall changes, such as the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and mid-latitude westerlies (Liu & Yin, 2001 ). Studies suggest that the weakening of the Indian monsoon has led to a decrease in snowfall on the Plateau (Wu, 2005 ). As the 'Asian water tower', the decline in solid water resources and the alteration of precipitation phases witnessed in high-altitude areas across the NWC will impact the replenishment dynamics of numerous rivers. Moreover, these changes will pose risks and challenges to downstream populations relying on such water sources for agriculture and live.  4.2 Future alterations in seasonal snowfall The annual snowfall decreases over the NWC in future projections. However, seasonal variations in snowfall exist, and the influence of warming across different temperature ranges on snowfall varies. Therefore, investigating changes in snowfall at the seasonal scale over the NWC is imperative. The snowfall for each season—spring (March to May), summer (June to August), autumn (September to November), and winter (December, January, and February of the following year) was calculated over the NWC. Interannual trends for each season from 2019 to 2100 were subsequently analyzed (Fig. 16  ). The findings reveal that spring and summer snowfall over the NWC are declining across all three emission scenarios (Fig. 16 a, b), with the most pronounced decrease observed in spring snowfall. Nevertheless, the trend in spring snowfall under the SSP1-2.6 scenario did not show statistical significance. Autumn snowfall exhibits a faint increasing trend under the SSP1-2.6 scenario but significant decreasing trends under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. In contrast, winter snowfall exhibits an increasing trend under all three scenarios. Specifically, spring snowfall is projected to exhibit an increasing trend in the near-term and mid-term under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, transitioning to a downward trend in the long-term, without statistical significance. This trend is characterized by a gradual deceleration in the rate of change over time. Conversely, spring snowfall shows a consistent decrease across all periods under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, with a slowdown in the rate of decline over time. A significant decline in spring snowfall is observed under SSP5-8.5 scenario, with a deceleration in the rate of change during the mid-term compared to the near-term, eventually reaching an extreme value of −2.49 mm·10a-1  by the end of century. A declining trend of summer snowfall is evident across all future periods. While no significant differences in snowfall trends emerge across the periods under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, the most substantial decrease is observed in the mid-term under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, with the near-term exhibiting the weakest decline. Similarly, a significant reduction in summer snowfall is noted across all periods under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, although with a trend of slowing change over time. Autumn snowfall displays a recent decrease followed by an increase in the middle and late stages under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, whereas the reverse trend is observed under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. The most noticeable change in autumn snowfall occurs in the mid-term under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. In contrast, winter snowfall exhibits a decreasing trend in the long term under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, while it tends to increase in other scenarios, although none of these trends are statistically significant. In general, the disparities in spring and autumn snowfall manifest more prominently across various scenarios and time periods, underscoring a heightened sensitivity to temperature fluctuations. This heightened sensitivity is likely attributed to the increased probability of frequent phase transitions between precipitation forms during these seasons in the NWC, influenced by rising temperatures, resulting in a greater proportion of snowfall transitioning to rainfall. There is less snowfall in summer, and its decline rate is relatively slow, but in most cases, it has passed the significance test.  4.3 Possible mechanism of precipitation phase bias in CMIP6 models CMIP6 provides a new perspective for investigating the climate change over the NWC. Nevertheless, significant uncertainties exist in simulation of snowfall and the SPR within the NWC domain. The estimations by CMIP6 models are influenced by parameters, resolution settings, and other contributing factors, engendering notable disparities in output among diverse models (Liang & Yan, 2016; Wang et al., 2017 ). Hence, it becomes imperative to understand the underlying mechanisms giving rise to simulation biases, which is important for enhancing the performance of model predictions. A multifaceted interplay of various factors encompassing relative humidity, surface temperature, air pressure, and elevation impact on snowfall (Ding et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015 ), with the alteration in precipitation phase indirectly influenced by a multitude of variables. Previous studies indicate that the accuracy of snow cover simulated by CMIP6 models is not good in major snowfall regions in China and even the Northern Hemisphere. Precipitation and temperature are the main sources of bias in simulating snow cover in CMIP6 models, and the interaction between precipitation bias and temperature bias is equally important (Zhang et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, discrepancies between CMIP6 simulated snowfall and SPR compare to observed data could potentially be ascribed to biases in regional thermal dynamics and dynamic precipitation processes (Wang et al., 2023 ). This section gives a brief discussion on the correlation between precipitation phase biases simulated by each CMIP6 model and biases in surface temperature and precipitation. Furthermore, partial correlation analysis was employed to eliminate auto-correlation between precipitation bias and temperature bias. Snowfall biases across all models exhibit a positive correlation with precipitation biases and a negative correlation with temperature biases by partial correlation analysis (Fig. 17  ). Notable disparities exist in the correlation coefficients between snowfall biases and precipitation biases among the models, ranging from 0.04 to 0.74. Conversely, the correlation coefficients between snowfall biases and temperature biases range from −0.40 to −0.13, with no discernible differences observed among the models. Additionally, the correlation between snowfall biases and temperature biases surpasses that with precipitation biases across 11 models. The SPR biases simulated by all models exhibit a negative correlation with temperature biases and precipitation biases, with correlation coefficients ranging from −0.75 to −0.25 and −0.61 to −0.07, respectively. Overall, SPR biases appear to be more influenced by temperature, with 14 models demonstrating a more pronounced impact of temperature on SPR. Consequently, the simulated temperature biases of CMIP6 models emerge as a pivotal factor contributing to precipitation phase biases in the NWC. Nevertheless, the significance of precipitation biases should not be neglected. The increase in surface temperature alters the vertical temperature gradient, impacting the melting level height and facilitating the transition of snowfall to rainfall (Prein & Heymsfield, 2020; Wang et al., 2022 ). Additionally, air humidity plays a role in the melting rate of snow droplets. As humidity increases, the vapor pressure difference between the surface of the snow droplets and the ambient air decreases, resulting in the evaporative cooling effect becomes smaller, thereby fostering the transition from snow to rain. Meanwhile, increased humidity may also reduce the heat transfer from the air to snow droplets, potentially slowing down the transition rate and leading to precipitation in the form of sleet (Ding et al., 2014 ). CMIP6 data exhibit temperature “warm bias” and precipitation “wet bias” in the NWC, particularly evident during the cold season (Yang et al., 2021b ). These biases affect the simulation of vertical temperature and humidity profiles by the models, consequently impacting the accuracy of snowfall and SPR reproduction. Furthermore, overestimation of total precipitation distort the proportion of snowfall in the total precipitation. Moreover, differences in altitude and topography also result in misjudgments of snowfall and precipitation phase. An anti-correlation between temperature bias and elevation in CMIP6 models is found, whereas snow cover correlates positively with the elevation. The higher the elevation, the greater the biases for temperature and snow cover, suggesting that the models is difficulty for representing physical processes in high-altitude areas (Lalande et al., 2021 ). In general, high-altitude areas typically have higher snowfall threshold temperatures. In the complex terrain of the NWC, low-resolution simulations may overestimate water vapor transportation and underestimate threshold temperatures, thereby compromising the simulation accuracy of snowfall and SPR.   5 Conclusions The performance of 21 CMIP6 models in simulating snowfall and precipitation phase over NWC is evaluated, identifying five models with better performance, which are used to estimate future changes in snowfall and precipitation phase. Additionally, analyses are conducted on future snowfall changes at both sub-regional and seasonal scales, followed by an exploration of potential mechanisms in the biases of CMIP6 simulations. Most of CMIP6 models exhibiting a tendency to overestimate snowfall while underestimating SPR over the NWC. The simulation performance of CMIP6 is poor in high-altitude mountainous areas and relatively better in low-altitude areas. This could be attributed to the lower resolution of the models, making it difficult to simulate the complex terrain of high-altitude regions. Following a comprehensive evaluation of 21 CMIP6 model simulations, superior performance of EC-Earth3-Veg, INM-CM5-0, GFDL-CM4, EC-Earth3-Veg-LR, INM-CM4-8, and EC-Earth3 are identified. During 2019–2100, the snowfall is not statistically significant change under the SSP1-2.6 scenario, which is projected to decline notably under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, particularly in high-altitude areas like the Tibetan Plateau and Tianshan regions. Significant variations of exist in high-altitude areas among different scenarios. The SPR over the NWC is expected to decrease across all emission scenarios, with rates of −0.19 %·10a-1 , −0.64 %·10a-1 , and −1.50 %·10a-1 , respectively. The pronounced reductions in SPR are observed in the Tibetan Plateau and northern Xinjiang. At the sub-region scale, the majority of areas demonstrate a declining trend in annual snowfall under all scenarios, with the most substantial decreases observed on the Plateau of Qinghai. Decreases in snowfall are more pronounced in high-altitude regions compared to low-altitude areas, although snowfall in low-altitude areas exhibit increasing in some cases. On the other hand, the SPR over the NWC exhibits a consistent decreasing trend, with the Plateau of qinghai experiencing the most pronounced decline. The reduction of SPR intensifies in most regions while the low-altitude areas display increasing trends in SPR in the near-term. Snowfall in winter shows an increasing trend, while spring and autumn snowfall exhibit overall decreases. The snowfall biases in all CMIP6 models exhibit a positive correlation with precipitation biases and a negative correlation with temperature biases. The simulation bias of surface temperature in CMIP6 models is identified as a key factor contributing to precipitation phase biases in NWC. As a complex process influenced by multiple factors, the simulation results of precipitation phase in CMIP6 still exhibit significant uncertainties. In the future, it is essential to integrate various climate factors and conduct in-depth analyses of the mechanisms in simulation errors of snowfall and precipitation phase.
1 Introduction Precipitation is an essential component of research on global climate and the water cycle (Sorooshian et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2012; Duan and Bastiaanssen, 2013; Ashouri et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Baez-Villanueva et al., 2020 ); thus, obtaining accurate precipitation information plays a critical role in monitoring and researching natural disasters, such as frequent floods and droughts (Mastrantonas et al., 2019; Amjad et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021b; Wei et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2022 ). Rain gauge stations can provide the most reliable measurements of precipitation at a specific point scale (Yin et al., 2021 ). However, these point-based measurements are inadequate for capturing the spatiotemporal variability of precipitation, particularly in oceanic and remote mountainous areas (Duan et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ). With remarkable developments in satellite remote sensing and spatial interpolation techniques, many different gridded precipitation products have been developed. These products provide complementary or alternative data sources for continuous precipitation estimates, particularly for poorly gauged or ungauged areas. Currently, remotely sensed and gauge-interpolated precipitation datasets are primary categories of the gridded precipitation products. They are freely available and can provide precipitation estimates with a near-global coverage at fine spatial and temporal resolution.
