Examples include the Soil Moisture to Rain (SM2RAIN) algorithm for precipitation estimation based on Advanced SCATterometer (SM2RAIN-ASCAT) (Brocca et al., 2019 ), the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) (IMERG) Early Run (IMERG-E) from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) (Huffman et al., 2019 ), and the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) global unified gauge-based analysis from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (Xie et al., 2007 ). The performance of SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC products have been evaluated in the GPM Era, and the results indicated that they present multiple types of precipitation errors, including low correlation, large bias, and false detection of precipitation (Chen et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022 ), which are related to their data sources and retrieval algorithms. Therefore, before using such products in hydrological studies, the quality of the precipitation estimates could be improved by combining multiple open-access precipitation products. In recent years, studies have performed collocation-based merging framework to minimize the error variance and maximize the correlation of merged product against the unknown truth. Regarding the minimized error variance, the error variance (in terms of RMSE) of each collocated product was obtained using triple collocation (TC) analysis with unknown truth series (Roebeling et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; Alemohammad et al., 2015; Massari et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Duan et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2022 ), and used to calculate their weights for data fusion based on the least-squares solution (Dong et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022 ). For example, Dong et al. (2020)  developed a TC-based merging framework to optimally merge three independent precipitation products (soil moisture inverted, model-based, and satellite products) over Europe; their results demonstrated that the TC-based merged product was significantly better than any of the parent precipitation products. Lyu et al. (2020)  implemented a TC formulation to merge two satellite-only and ERA-Interim/ERA5 precipitation products across mainland China; they also found that the merged result was better than the parent datasets and the TC merging method outperformed the dynamic Bayesian model averaging approach. Such merging scheme has been frequently applied to improve the estimation of other hydrological elements, including soil moisture (Yilmaz et al., 2012; Gruber et al., 2017 ), evapotranspiration (Park et al., 2023 ), snow depth (Xiao and Che, 2018 ), and terrestrial water storage (Yin and Park, 2021 ). In addition, the merging weights can be computed using the correlation coefficients of independent collocated members solved by the extended TC (McColl et al., 2014 ), and a good case study was presented by Beck et al. (2021)  for the merged soil moisture product. Recently, Wei et al. (2023b)  proposed an Extended Triple Collocation for maximized Correlation (ETCC) method with a definite correlation function to combine the SM2RAIN-ASCAT, ERA5, and IMERG-E precipitation products, and its merged product was evaluated by three reference precipitation datasets at a near global scale and compared with the TC merging. They proved that the ETCC-merged product was generally superior to any of the collocated measurements but also the TC-merged dataset, especially in the correlation. This result has confirmed that ETCC is a promising merging method that has great potential for precipitation fusion. Despite the improvements realized by collocation-based merging, merged products still present some biases in estimating the spatiotemporal variability of precipitation (as shown in Lyu et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022 ). These biases might primarily originate from reanalysis and satellite precipitation products, which have relatively poor accuracy (Chen et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021a ). Previous studies have used a bias-adjustment procedure to effectively correct the errors and biases in individual reanalysis and satellite precipitation products. The corrected precipitation products were then merged to improve their performance in hydrological simulations (Yin et al., 2021 ). Such merging scheme (correction + fusion) is unsuitable with the mutually independent assumption of the ETCC- and TC-based merging methods. A different scheme (fusion + correction) has been included in the existing merging studies (Beck et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2022 ). For instance, Yin et al. (2022)  established a combination of support vector machine (SVM) and quantile-based cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching and verified that SVM-CDF has the highest accuracy in hourly precipitation forecasts. This finding suggests that precipitation biases in data forecasting may be further reduced by the bias-adjustment method. The similar scheme could be applicable in the collocation-based fusion for the merged precipitation product. To address the concerns mentioned above, the aim of this study was to improve daily precipitation estimates over mainland China using a new merging framework. This framework was proposed to combine the ETCC merging and CDF matching (ETCCCDF). In principle, the ETCCCDF-merged product should be generally superior to any of the collocated measurements, which can prove the effectiveness of the proposed framework (Dong et al., 2020; Koster et al., 2021 ). We tested the ETCCCDF framework as following steps: first, the maximized correlation of the ETCC method was applied for data fusion using three independent precipitation products from SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC, and then bias correction was implemented at daily scale using CDF matching for the merged product. The ETCCCDF-merged and parent precipitation products were evaluated using a set of statistical metrics from 2007 to 2014. Data comparisons were also conducted between the ETCCCDF framework and other merging methods, including ETCC, TC, and combination of TC with CDF. The paper is organized as follows: the study area and all precipitation datasets are introduced in Section 2 ; the methods used, including the proposed framework and evaluation metrics, are described in Section 3 ; the results are presented in Section 4 ; important results and critical questions are discussed in Section 5 ; and the main conclusions are provided in Section 6 .  2 Study area and datasets 2.1 Study area The study area covered mainland China and ranged from 73 to 135°E longitude and 18-53°N latitude, as shown in Fig. 1  a. The elevation variation gradually decreased from west to east, with a three-step distribution. Chen et al. (2013)  classified mainland China into eight subregions based on critical information regarding elevation, mountain chains, and average annual precipitation. Three coastal subregions, including northern China (NC), the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River (CJ), and southeastern China (SE), were selected in this study to analyze the specific typhoon-induced rainfall events. Owing to the monsoon climate, different levels of typhoons frequently land and/or cross the three subregions and induce large-scale and heavy rainfall events, which are harmful to the development of the local economy (Jiang et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2022b ). Moreover, another two subregions in the western China, comprising Xinjiang (XJ) and Tibetan Plateau (TP), were also selected to prove the validity of this merging framework at complex terrain areas with sparse stations.  2.2 Ground precipitation observations The in situ daily precipitation dataset from 2304 meteorological stations across mainland China was obtained from the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) website (https://data.cma.cn/ ). The distribution of these stations is shown in Fig. 1 b, with most located over eastern China and relatively sparse networks located over western China (such as XJ and TP). After undergoing a series of rigorous quality controls, all station data with high accuracy and reliability (Shen et al., 2010 ) were selected in this study as the reference dataset to evaluate the performance of the merged precipitation products. Additionally, the observation reference was processed at the daily scale to ensure temporal consistency with the UTC time period of the daily satellite precipitation product (Wei et al., 2022 ).  2.3 Parent precipitation products The independent precipitation products SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC for the study period 2007–2014 were used in this study. Table 1   summarizes the basic information and relevant parameters of these precipitation products and indicates their sources. SM2RAIN-ASCAT is a global-land satellite precipitation product and produced based on the SM2RAIN algorithm, which uses the inversion of water balance equation and the input of soil moisture (Brocca et al., 2019 ). The soil moisture data is derived from the Advanced SCATterometer (ASCAT) satellite retrievals on board three Meteorological Operational satellites. The version 1.5 of the SM2RAIN-ASCAT product offers “bottom-up” daily precipitation estimates in the relatively short period of 2007 to present with a spatial resolution of 0.1° and was used here. IMERG-E is a new-generation and open-access multi-satellite precipitation product that was generated by NASA using the unified U.S. IMERG algorithm (Huffman et al., 2019; Huffman et al., 2020 ). The near real-time IMERG-E, which does not include gauge adjustments for the estimation bias of remote sensing, is one of three levels of the state-of-the-art IMERG suite and available using only forward propagation, with a latency of approximately 4 h (https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/directory ). Owing to the short latency, certain passive microwave (PMW) sensor estimates were not used to generate the IMERG-E product. At present, the version 06B is one of the GPM IMERG-E series, and it has a spatiotemporal resolution of 0.1°/0.5 h and quasi-global coverage of full 60°S/N latitude. The daily precipitation product IMERG-E V06B with the UTC day was used in this study. CPC is a global land unified gauge-based daily precipitation dataset produced by the NOAA Climate Prediction Center (Xie et al., 2007 ). An optimal interpolation algorithm with orographic consideration was used to create the CPC product based on more than 30,000 station historical reports and approximately 17,000 gauges in real time. These data sources include individual regional datasets over the contiguous United States (CONUS), Mexico, South America, Australia, and gauge networks elsewhere from the Global Telecommunication System (GTS). CPC has real-time operations and provides a 0.5° longitude-latitude and daily precipitation estimates from 1979 to the present. Overlapping stations were observed between the 2304 stations of CMA and CPC gauges. We checked the CPC used stations and made a comparison with CMA stations. Approximately 200 stations from mainland China were included in CPC (Shen and Xiong, 2016 ), and the majority of CMA stations (>91.3 %) were not included in the creation of CPC product. Therefore, this justified the independence of the stations used for the evaluation of CPC and our merged precipitation products.   3 Methodology 3.1 Proposed framework for enhanced precipitation estimation This study attempts to combine the ETCC merging with a correlation function and CDF matching with a bias adjustment to establish a new merging framework (called as ETCCCDF) for blending multi-source precipitation products. The objective of this merging framework is to obtain high-quality daily precipitation estimations by three steps (Fig. 2  ), namely, (1) preprocessing, (2) data fusion, and (3) post-processing, which are expressed as follows: Step (1): Preprocessing. Because of the mismatched spatial grid cell in the parent precipitation products, they need to be processed to consistent resolution before applying them for data fusion and post-processing. Both the 0.1° resolution daily satellite precipitation products SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E and the 0.5° resolution daily gauge-based precipitation analysis CPC were resampled using a bilinear interpolation approach for each 0.25° grid cell. This ensured fusion results within a 0.25° grid cell on a daily scale. Step (2): Data fusion. For maximizing the correlation of merged precipitation product against the unknown truth, a merging method, Extended Triple Collocation for maximized Correlation or ETCC (Wei et al., 2023b ), was applied for data fusion at given 0.25° grid cell. There are three processes of the ETCC method for the data fusion. Firstly, let x  , y , and z represent the precipitation series from SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC products, respectively, the correlations ρ xy    , ρ xz    , and ρ yz     of each possible pairing, i.e., (x , y ), (x , z), and (y , z), were computed by equations (1)  − (3) . Note that before using ρ xy    , ρ xz    , and ρ yz     values, they were enforced a minimum value of 0.01 when small and negative values (Koster et al., 2021 ). Secondly, based on the extend triple collocation framework (McColl et al., 2014 ), the correlations ρ Rx    , ρ Ry    , and ρ Rz     between each collocated measurement (x , y , z) and the unknown truth (R ) were calculated by using equations (4)  − (6) , ρ xy    , ρ xz    , and ρ yz     values. In terms of the TC theory, the ETCC method need to be satisfied for four assumptions: each triplet measurement linearly related to the true geophysical variable; the zero cross-correlation assumption based on mutually independent collocated products, including their independent errors; the zero error cross-correlation assumption based on the errors unrelated to the true value; and the zero error expectation assumption (Alemohammad et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018 ). Thirdly, a correlation function ρ RM   w x  , w y  , w z       , of merged precipitation product (M ) without the truth value, was established, as shown equation (7) . In the correlation function, only weights (w x   , w y   , w z   ) of collocated measurements were unknown, and accordingly, their optimal weights could be determined by an Exhaustive Attack method to search the maximized value of ρ RM   w x  , w y  , w z       . Note that the Exhaustive Attack is a brute-force method and it requires a long computing time (at least 3 h) for all cells of mainland China when merging three precipitation products. Based on the optimal weights, a weighted sum way was applied to merge a triplet grouping of the preprocessed SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC to generate one merged precipitation product (0.25°, daily). Regarding the inference of the correlation function ρ RM   w x  , w y  , w z       , further details are presented in the literature (Wei et al., 2023b ).(1) ρ xy   = C o r r ( x , y )      (2) ρ xz   = C o r r ( x , z )      (3) ρ yz   = C o r r ( y , z )      (4) ρ Rx   = ( ρ xy   ρ xz   / ρ yz   )  1 / 2       (5) ρ Ry   = ( ρ xy   ρ yz   / ρ xz   )  1 / 2       (6) ρ Rz   = ( ρ xz   ρ yz   / ρ xy   )  1 / 2       (7) ρ RM   = 1 C MM     w x  ρ Rx   C xx    + w y  ρ Ry   C yy    + w z  ρ Rz   C zz           where Corr (·) is the conceptive formula of correlation; C kk   , k ∈ M , x , y , z       is the variance of the subscript dataset. Step (3): Post-processing. Although the purpose of the ETCC method is to maximize the correlation of the merged precipitation product against the unknown truth, the bias of merged product has not been targeted and still exists as seen in Section 4.3 . A distribution mapping method, cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching, is performed in bias correction for the target product by considering a benchmark dataset by matching their cumulative distribution frequencies to provide more accurate results (Müller and Thompson, 2013; Rabiei and Haberlandt, 2015 ). Generally, the gamma distribution with shape and scale parameters is used to fit the two data series, estimate the quantile of the target, and find a transformation of the target against the benchmark dataset based on quantile mapping. The transformation procedure is represented as follows:(8) P cr   = c d f b - 1   cd f s  P s           where P cr     and P s    are the CDF-corrected and target series, respectively; cd f b - 1      represents the inverse cumulative distribution function of the benchmark dataset, and cd f s     denotes the cumulative distribution function estimated from the target data. The biases of the daily ETCC-merged product were continuously reduced by the CDF-matching method to correct the precipitation distributions for each 0.25° grid cell. Here, the CPC, which has relatively low error and bias values, was selected as the benchmark dataset and used for the bias correction of merged precipitation product, such as the gauge-adjustment satellite precipitation products (Tian et al., 2010; Mega et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2022 ). And then, it can obtain a final merged precipitation product with a spatiotemporal resolution of 0.25°/day. Finally, using the above-mentioned three steps, it could improve precipitation estimates by maximizing the correlation and reducing systematic bias, which will further heighten the accuracy of the fusion results. In addition, the TC merging method with a goal of minimizing the error variance and it combined with CDF matching as called TCCDF, were employed to merge the same triplet group. The specific calculation process of TC merging approach was presented in the literatures (Chen et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2023b ), and the implementation of TCCDF approach for merged product was similar with that of ETCCCDF framework. The ETCC, TC, and TCCDF merging approaches were used to demonstrate the robust performance of the ETCCCDF framework.  3.2 Evaluation metrics Seven statistical metrics were used to comprehensively evaluate and compare the parent precipitation products and fusion results at a daily scale. These performance metrics include the modified Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009 ), correlation coefficient (CC), relative bias (RB), root-mean-square error (RMSE), critical success index (CSI), probability of detection (POD), and false alarm ratio (FAR) (Wei et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2021a ). KGE is a comprehensive indicator for balancing the CC, bias, and variability terms. The CC, RB, and RMSE are used to quantitatively determine the correlation, systematic bias, and absolute difference between the precipitation products and CMA observations. CSI is a comprehensive detection metric, which includes the POD and FAR that show the ratio of correct detection and false detection events to total observed events, respectively. KGE, CC, RB, and RMSE range in (−∞, 1], [−1, 1], (−∞, +∞), and [0, +∞), and their perfect scores are 1, 1, 0, and 0, respectively. CSI, POD, and FAR range from 0 to 1, and their perfect scores are 1, 1, and 0, respectively. Five thresholds, namely, 1, 5, 10, 25, and 50 mm/day, were set to determine no-rain/rain, light, moderate, heavy, and extreme rainfall events, respectively. The equations for the above-mentioned performance metrics are given as follows (Wei et al., 2023a ):(9) KGE = 1 - ( C C - 1 )  2  + ( β - 1 )  2  + ( γ - 1 )  2    , β = S  ¯   G  ¯    , γ = C V S   C V G        (10) CC = ∑ i = 1  n  G i  - G  ¯      S i  - S  ¯        ∑ i = 1  n  G i  - G  ¯      2    ∑ i = 1  n  S i  - S  ¯      2          (11) RB = ∑ i = 1  n  ( S i  - G i  )   ∑ i = 1  n  G i    × 100 \%       (12) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  S i  - G i     2        (13) CSI = H H + M + F   = 1 1 / 1 - F A R    + 1 / P O D - 1       (14) POD = H H + M       (15) FAR = F H + F       where S i    (average value of S  ¯    ) and G i    (average value of G  ¯    ) are the evaluated target and reference dataset, respectively; C V S     and C V G     are the variation coefficients of the evaluated target and reference dataset, respectively; H=Hit is the number of rainfall events detected by the evaluated target and reference dataset simultaneously; M=Miss is the number of rainfall events observed by the reference dataset but not detected by the evaluated target; and F=False alarm is the number of rainfall events not observed by the reference dataset but detected by the evaluated target.   4 Results 4.1 General performance of parent precipitation products Fig. 3   shows the spatial patterns of the four performance metrics (CC, RB, POD, and FAR) for SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC in mainland China over the study period. The three precipitation products have obviously different characteristics of the CC metric in space, in which the CCs of SM2RAIN-ASCAT exhibited a relatively high value in the central region than that in other parts, CCs of IMERG-E exhibited degradation from SE to XJ, and CCs of CPC weakly decreased from east to west. It is clearly observed that the SM2RAIN-ASCAT is weakly correlated (an average CC of 0.458) with observations and evidently performs the worst, while the CPC is strongly correlated (an average CC of 0.725) with the CMA observations. In terms of RB, SM2RAIN-ASCAT presented significant spatial heterogeneity and severe overestimation of precipitation in XJ and the southwest with a large positive bias. IMERG-E overestimated the precipitation amount in most regions, while distinctly contrary in TP region. The RB for CPC is in a relatively stable state, with most values ranging from −10 % to 10 %. The PODs of CPC (an average value of 0.862) were considerably high for successfully captured rainfall events, and it was obviously better than those of two satellite precipitation products, especially in coastal areas. SM2RAIN-ASCAT performed well in hitting the rain events over the south of China. The advantageous performance of CPC was indicated by the lowest FAR values, whereas SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E were accompanied by comparatively high FAR values, and their spatial variations exhibited obvious differences in the detection of precipitation. Generally, CPC is capable of estimating precipitation amounts with high correlation and limited biases and detecting precipitation occurrence with high hit rates, while SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E exhibit poor reliability. This implies that the accuracy of satellite precipitation products must be improved.  4.2 Evaluation of ETCCCDF-merged precipitation product Fig. 4   shows the boxplots of seven performance metrics (KGE, CC, RB, RMSE, CSI, POD, and FAR) for the parent and ETCCCDF-merged precipitation products over mainland China. After the three parent precipitation products underwent data fusion and bias correction, the precipitation estimates showed significant improvement in terms of some metrics. This illustrates that the ETCCCDF-merged product displayed an overall better performance than the collocated products, particularly for the SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E. In detail, the KGE for ETCCCDF estimates was above 0.62 at the 50th percentile, which was higher than that for CPC at the 50th percentile and SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E at the 75th percentile. This finding is similar to that of the CC metric. Moreover, ETCCCDF estimates had a more high-level consistency with ground observations than any of parent precipitation products. Meanwhile, the ETCCCDF estimates exhibited smaller RB with most values varying from −10 % to 10 % and the lowest RMSE at the three percentiles compared to each collocated measurement. The high absolute difference of SM2RAIN-ASCAT and relatively large overestimations of IMERG-E did not contribute to the ETCCCDF-merged product, which was simultaneously maximized the correlation and reduced the bias of the precipitation estimates. Compared with satellite precipitation products, the ETCCCDF-merged product had a relatively high hit ratio, which was attributed to the good POD scores of CPC. ETCCCDF estimates also presented the concentrated ranges of the FAR index and the smaller values relative to the satellite precipitation products. The high POD and low FAR contributed to the high CSI value of ETCCCDF-merged product. Nonetheless, the ETCCCDF estimates presented a slightly worse performance in detecting the precipitation occurrence than CPC. The main reason for this is that SM2RAIN-ASCAT has a clearly poor capability for the detection of precipitation. To further validate the data fusion effects of the ETCCCDF framework, the performance of its merged product was compared with the parent precipitation products at different regions. Fig. 5   shows the China’s maps of four performance metrics (KGE, CC, RB, and RMSE) for the ETCCCDF-merged product and its boxplots in the coastal areas (NC, CJ, and SE) and western areas (XJ and TP). From the KGE metric, ETCCCDF-merged product performed better than satellite precipitation products in the two regions, and its improvement degree in the western areas was larger than that in the coastal areas relative to IMERG-E. Combined with spatial maps in Fig. 3 , the ETCCCDF-merged product exhibited a significantly high correlation and small bias relative to satellite precipitation products in whether the coastal areas or not the western areas. The CC and RB of SM2RAIN-ASCAT were obviously poor in the western areas, whereas the median CC and RB values for the merged product were closer to 0.7 and 0 %, respectively. Regarding the RMSE score, ETCCCDF-merged product obtained a better performance of precipitation estimates compared to satellite precipitation products over the costal and western areas. Compared with the CPC, ETCCCDF-merged product performed slightly better in the coastal areas and it had more concentrated numerical range for the four metrics over the western areas. All the above results demonstrate that ETCCCDF-derived data is a satisfactory merged precipitation product not only in the coastal areas but also the western areas.  4.3 Comparison of the ETCCCDF framework against the other collocation-based algorithms Fig. 6   shows the spatial variabilities of weight of each collocated measurement used in ETCC and TC methods for data fusion over mainland China. In whether the ETCC or TC merging methods, the CPC, that had a high reliability as shown in Fig. 3 , contributed the most for merged product in most regions, particularly in coastal areas with many values of weight more than 0.7. It is reasonable because the CPC product contains the point-scale ground gauges that provide closer values to the true precipitation. The weight of SM2RAIN-ASCAT was generally larger than that of IMERG-E at most grids and provided the most information in XJ and TP regions. These results are relatively consistent with the analysis of Brocca et al. (2019) . By comparison of same collocated measurement in the two collocation-based merging methods, there were two significant differences in space: the weight values were obvious discrepancy in same grid cell; due to the negative value of error variance from TC analysis, the weights of TC merging had a “nan” value in some grids, such as CJ, SE, XJ, and TP, whereas the weight value in ETCC method belonged to its normal numerical range of 0 − 1. It proves that the performance of ETCC method is more robust than that of TC merging for the optimal weight of each collocated measurement. This finding is consistent with the result as shown in the literature (Wei et al., 2023b ). Fig. 7   shows the empirical cumulative distribution frequency (ECDF) curves of seven performance metrics (KGE, CC, RB, RMSE, CSI, POD, and FAR) for the four merged precipitation products in mainland China. A descending order of usability is observed for the ECDF curves of KGE derived from the ETCCCDF-, TCCDF-, ETCC-, and TC-merged products. As for the CC and RMSE indices, the performance of the CDF-matching merged products displayed a few improvements based on the collocation fusions. Because the ETCC merging maximizes the correlation (CC) or TC merging minimizes the error variance of merged precipitation product, the bias has not been aimed singly and could still be improved. Additionally, the POD values did not improve from ETCC method (average value of 0.886) to ETCCCDF framework (average value of 0.831) and from TC merging (average value of 0.879) to TCCDF scheme (average value of 0.802). This may be the reason that the CPC had relatively low POD values compared to the ETCC- and TC-merged products and may explain the small hit rates of the CDF-matching merged products. In contrast, the FAR values of ETCCCDF- and TCCDF-merged products are much smaller than those of ETCC- and TC-merged products. In terms of the CSI indicator, ETCC-merged product has a better performance in capturing the precipitation occurrence than TC estimates, which explains that the ETCCCDF-merged product outperforms the TCCDF-merged product. In short, these findings suggest that ETCCCDF is a more effective framework for merged precipitation product; moreover, further improvements in some statistical metrics were observed after bias correction using the CDF-matching method. To further investigate the performance of the CDF-matching method, a comparison of the merged precipitation products was performed before and after bias adjustment. Fig. 8   shows the time series of the RB metric for ETCCCDF- versus ETCC-merged products and TCCDF- versus TC-merged products during the study period. It is clear to observe that both ETCC- and TC-merged products without bias correction show markedly positive RB values, especially during the dry season (October to April). This implies that precipitation fusion requires a more robust scheme. Thus, the quantile-mapping CDF-matching method is input into the ETCCCDF and TCCDF schemes to decrease the biases of the initial merged precipitation products again. It is noteworthy that the CDF-matching method effectively diminished the obvious overestimation of ETCC- and TC-merged products. In other words, ETCCCDF and TCCDF estimates exhibited small changes in the magnitude of systematic biases, with most RB values in the range of −30 % to 30 %. This indicates that the bias correction, which effectively reduces the biases and further improves the performance of the collocation-based merged products, is an important procedure in the precipitation fusion.  4.4 Typhoon-related precipitation analysis Accurately estimating heavy rainfall during typhoon events is important for early disaster warning. To determine how the ETCCCDF-merged product performed in capturing typhoon-associated rainfall events, this section evaluates and compares the accuracy of ETCCCDF-merged and other precipitation products in coastal areas within the subregions NC, CJ, and SE. Two typhoons were selected as examples for the assessment: Typhoon Morakot, which landed in Fujian province on August 9, 2009, with a maximum wind speed of 33 m/s; Typhoon Fitow, which is the 23th strong typhoon in 2013 and also landed in the Fujian province on October 7. Fig. 9   shows the spatial patterns of daily precipitation from the CMA observations and different precipitation products during the two typhoon events. Table 2   lists the quantitative statistical indicators for the corresponding Fig. 9 . For the Typhoon Morakot as shown in Fig. 9 a, the rainfall centers were located in eastern parts of CJ and SE, and the overall trend of rainfall volumes decreased from east to west. Except for the SM2RAIN-ASCAT, the precipitation products were generally consistent with the ground observations in terms of spatial variations, and they presented spatial correlation values greater than 0.73. Note that SM2RAIN-ASCAT had an obvious overestimation of no-rain events in the west of the coastal areas and serious underestimation of extreme rainfall in the area where the typhoon landed. IMERG-E had the larger error with a RMSE value of 18.60 mm/day and evidently overestimated the field of heavy rainfall with the highest FAR value of 0.236. Although CPC performed the best among the parent precipitation products, it still had large negative RB value during the typhoon. After the data fusion, the ETCCCDF-merged product provided greater details on rainfall based on the improved CC and RMSE metrics and exhibited a relatively high performance in capturing the heavy rainfall events compared with the parent precipitation products, with a CSI value of 0.642. Regarding the Typhoon Fitow as presented in Fig. 9 b, the spatial patterns of all precipitation products were basically similar to those of CMA observations, with the rainfall amounts in the east of the coastal areas decreasing from northeast to southwest and almost no-rain event in other areas. Similarly, SM2RAIN-ASCAT exhibited a significant underestimation of heavy rainfall, illustrating that the SM2RAIN algorithm tends to underestimate the extreme value of precipitation due to soil moisture saturation. In the manufacturing process of SM2RAIN-ASCAT product, producer pointed out that this product has the underestimation of peak rainfall events (Brocca et al., 2019 ). IMERG-E showed the best KGE (0.761) and RB (−4.52 %) metrics, but it had an obvious overestimation for the spatial coverage of moderate and heavy rainfall. CPC matched well with the ground observations (CC of 0.892), while it had a larger underestimation for the rainfall amount. The ETCCCDF-merged product had some improvements in estimating and catching the rainfall events relative to each collocated measurement, while it performed worse than IMERG-E in terms of KGE metric due to the extremely poor performance of individual triple-input dataset. As the two typhoon events mentioned above, ETCCCDF- and TCCDF-merged products were superior to ETCC- and TC-merged products in estimating rainfall spatial coverage and volumes, respectively, with a decrease in bias and an increase in KGE owing to the daily correction using the CDF matching method. In terms of many metrics, ETCCCDF-merged product exhibited a more satisfactory performance in reproducing the two typhoon-associated precipitation events, compared with the TCCDF-merged product. Not only that, ETCCCDF-merged product had a first-class detection capability for heavy rainfall events over the coastal areas from 2007 to 2014, as shown in Fig. 10  . For the precipitation level, ETCCCDF estimates outperformed the three collocated measurements and other merged products based on the precipitation maps and most metrics.   5 Discussion 5.1 The performance of ETCCCDF-merged product A merging framework that combines the ETCC merging and CDF matching methods was proposed and a 0.25° resolution merged precipitation product was generated at the daily timescale. The performance of the ETCCCDF-merged product was examined comprehensively, and the results showed that it provided high-precision precipitation estimates. ETCCCDF-merged product exhibited a better overall performance than any of the three independent global gridded precipitation products (SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC) (Fig. 4 ), similar to the results reported by Lyu et al. (2020)  and Chen et al. (2022) . Meanwhile, ETCCCDF-merged product also presented better robustness and reliability than each collocated product at different spatial ranges including the coastal areas (NC, CJ, and SE) and western areas (XJ and TP) (as observed in Fig. 5 ). Importantly, ETCCCDF-merged product showed a better performance in the Kling-Gupta efficiency, correlation, absolute difference, and detection of heavy rainfall events than CPC analysis at the daily scale. Therefore, the superiority of ETCCCDF-merged product compared with the three collocated measurements over mainland China was proven by capturing the spatiotemporal distribution of precipitation (as summarized in Table 3  ), including typhoon-related and heavy rainfall events (Fig. 9 , Fig. 10 , and Table 2 ). These illustrate that the proposed framework is effective in providing a better representation of daily precipitation. However, the ETCCCDF-merged product has some shortcomings. For example, ETCCCDF estimates performed slightly worse than CPC in the detection of precipitation occurrence over mainland China (Table 3 ). In addition, ETCCCDF-merged product presented a lower usability compared with the IMERG-E in terms of KGE metric during Typhoon Fitow (Table 2 ). These deficiencies are related to parent precipitation products. In the future, a more perfect merged precipitation product could be generated based on the better-performance contributors (Wei et al., 2023a ), such as using atmospheric reanalysis precipitation product ERA5 or ERA5-land (Xu et al., 2022 ) to replace the SM2RAIN-ASCAT data.  5.2 The robustness of ETCCCDF framework There are different purposes among the ETCC, ETCCCDF, and TC for the data fusion. ETCC merging purely maximizes the correlation of merged product against the unknown truth, but it does not aim the bias (Wei et al., 2023b ). In the ETCCCDF framework, that combines the ETCC merging and CDF matching, it optimizes the correlation and reduces the bias of merged product in sequence. TC merging does not optimize the correlation or bias separately, and it minimizes the error variance (RMSE) (Lyu et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022 ), which contains the correlation and bias components (Gupta et al., 2009 ). Therefore, the ETCCCDF framework could obtain a better performance relative to ETCC and TC merging methods in theory. To test the robust performance of the ETCCCDF framework, a cross-comparison with the ETCC, TCCDF, and TC merging approaches was carried out in Section 4.3  and Section 4.4 . The ETCCCDF framework was found to be more accurate than the ETCC, TC, and the combined scheme TCCDF in terms of many statistical metrics (Fig. 7 ). The positive RB values of ETCC- and TC-merged products were significantly reduced, which indicates that the bias adjustment of the empirical CDF matching method leads to improvements (Fig. 8 ). This emphasizes that bias correction should be performed after data fusion, which is similar to the combinations of Beck et al. (2019)  and Yin et al. (2022) . The CC or RMSE value after the bias adjustment showed a small improvement owing to the maximized correlation or minimized error variance in the collocation fusions. The POD values of both ETCCCDF- and TCCDF-merged products did not show any improvements in the daily statistics relative to the corresponding ETCC and TC estimates due to the relatively low POD of CPC used in the CDF-matching method (Table 3 ). For all that, ETCCCDF framework presented more improvements in catching the heavy rainfall events, compared to other merging approaches (Fig. 9  and Fig. 10 ). In general, from these statistical results, one can conclude that the ETCCCDF framework is more robust to obtain precipitation estimates with a high accuracy. The different-inputs collocation-based methods, including the single instrumental variable algorithm, double instrumental variable algorithm (IVD), TC, quadruple collocation (QC), and extended IVD, had been applied for the comprehensive assessment of evapotranspiration products (Li et al., 2022a ). Thus, to further test the robustness of our proposed framework, it should be compared with the IVD, QC, and other developed methods based on collocation theory in future research (Xu et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2022 ).  5.3 Limitation of the ETCCCDF framework Despite the superior merging framework in this study, two limitations should be noted. Firstly, the ETCCCDF framework also needs to meet the assumptions of TC analysis, which could limit its application scope for the hydrological and meteorological researches. In this study, the zero error expectation assumption had not been satisfied when executing the merging framework. Some studies suggested that the precipitation errors in the real world follow a skewed distribution, not Gaussian, which was shown in Xu et al. (2020)  and Wei et al. (2023b) . Additionally, we selected SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC precipitation products to satisfy the zero cross-correlation assumption (i.e., independent assumption), which is difficult to truly achieve. These would affect the accuracy of ETCCCDF estimates. Even so, this study proves that the ETCCCDF continues to be a viable framework for blending multiple precipitation products. Secondly, the ETCCCDF framework does not aim the rain classification to improve the detection capability of precipitation. For the objective, Lyu et al. (2020)  separated the rainfall and snowfall (RS) components of parent precipitation products to design a precipitation merging scheme, and demonstrated that the RS-based merging was superior to precipitation merging directly, particularly in winter. Dong et al. (2022)  used categorical TC merging algorithm to correct the no-rain/rain detection error of merged precipitation product, and proved that the final merged precipitation product had a satisfactory performance for no-rain/rain detection. Considering these works, a multi-objective merging framework concerning but not limited to the maximized correlation, reduced bias, and improved detection, should be established in the future to obtain more accurate merged precipitation product.   6 Conclusions High-quality precipitation data are of immense importance for the research of water-induced disasters. In this study, a combined data fusion and bias correction framework was developed to improve daily precipitation estimates. This framework (ETCCCDF) was to blend three mutually independent precipitation products (SM2RAIN-ASCAT, IMERG-E, and CPC) using an extended triple collocation (ETCC) merging method first, and then adjust the initial merged product using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching algorithm. A new daily precipitation dataset, ETCCCDF-merged product, was produced at a 0.25° grid cell and systematically validated at the point scale for the period 2007 to 2014 over mainland China. The primary findings are summarized as follows.(1) In terms of daily statistics, the ETCCCDF-merged product showed a significant improvement over the three collocated measurements in terms of correlation, bias, and absolute difference, as indicated by the increased comprehensive metric KGE of 0.634 relative to the SM2RAIN-ASCAT (0.196), IMERG-E (0.492), and CPC (0.619). Importantly, the ETCCCDF-merged product exhibited a more satisfactory reliability for the precipitation estimates at different spatial ranges.  (2) Regarding the robustness, the ETCCCDF framework was superior to the ETCC, TCCDF, and TC approaches for the precipitation fusion. ETCC method effectively improved the correlation and reduced the error of collocated members, particularly for the SM2RAIN-ASCAT and IMERG-E. However, ETCC-merged product overestimated the rainfall amounts especially during the dry season and failed to capture the rainfall events (FAR of 0.396). The CDF-matching method was effective in correcting the bias of ETCC-merged product and some metrics of ETCCCDF-merged product obtained superior estimation scores than ETCC estimates.  (3) During Typhoon Morakot in 2009 and Typhoon Fitow in 2013, ETCCCDF-merged product generally performed best in reproducing the spatial pattern and volumes of heavy rainfall events, with the higher KGE, lower RMSE, and highest CSI.    In general, the combination of ETCC merging and CDF matching has considerable potential for improving the accuracy of daily precipitation estimates, particularly in data-sparse areas. Moreover, ETCCCDF is a promising and simple merging framework that does not require the reference dataset, which is the opposite of machine learning and Bayesian model averaging. Consequently, this study suggests that the ETCCCDF framework will substantially benefit applications of multisource precipitation products in hydrological and meteorological fields.
1 Introduction Riverine floods are the most frequent, wide-spread and severely impacting natural hazards across the world affecting ∼ 21 million people annually and causing large-scale disruption to human wellbeing and the economy (Doocy et al., 2013; Dottori et al., 2023; Dubey and Singh, 2021; Garg and Mishra, 2019; Liu et al., 2023; Pandey et al., 2022; Quesada-Román et al., 2022; Rentschler et al., 2022; Serinaldi et al., 2018; Wing et al., 2022; Zheng and Huang, 2023 ). Moreover, changes in hydro-meteorological variables with rising temperatures and human interventions are likely to have significant influence on local and regional scale hydrology with a predicted 54 million people affected by flooding annually by 2030 (Gangopadhyay et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2015; Park et al., 2011; Tripathi et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2018 ). Seasonal flooding of the flood prone, Brahmaputra River catchment in North East India affects the socio-economic status of millions of people annually (Chembolu et al., 2019; Dubey and Singh, 2021; Kumar, 2017; Pandey et al., 2022 ). The region experiences devastating floods due to extreme rainfall events, the large-scale tributary network and their flashy nature, and the hydro-morpho-dynamic characteristics of the river. The frequency and severity of extreme floods in the catchment have led researchers and practitioners to put continuous efforts into development of comprehensive flood mitigation plans with advanced early warning systems, improved floodplain management, and sustainable land use practices (Bigger and Webber, 2021; Chembolu et al., 2019; Dubey et al., 2021; Hacking, 2019 ). These activities seek to develop long-term resilience in the face of growing concern due to changing hydrological patterns and climatic variability in the Brahmaputra River catchment (Ghabelnezam et al., 2023; Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021 ). Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly being recognised as viable options for addressing complex fluvio-societal challenges such as catastrophe risk reduction, especially in floodplain and coastal environments (Agaton and Guila, 2023; Gain et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2022; Opperman and Galloway, 2022 ). They span a wide range of conservation and sustainable management measures and address multidimensional social concerns while also improving human well-being and biodiversity (Cohen-Shacham et al., 2016, 2019; Mendes et al., 2020; Nesshöver et al., 2017 ). NbS include nature-inspired, nature-based and environmentally friendly structural or non-structural techniques that are useful in dealing with hydro-meteorological hazards, addressing the vulnerability and risk assessments, climate change adaptation and mitigation efforts in the catchment (Debele et al., 2023; Gonzalez-Flo et al., 2023; Sahani et al., 2019; Shah et al., 2020 ). Wetlands play an important role as nature-based solutions for flood reduction by storing and holding flood water and recharging aquifers to increase the ground water table (Acreman and Holden, 2013; Bullock and Acreman, 2003 ). They provide buffer storage to retain runoff during the storm events, attenuate peak flows and gradually release excess water downstream (Craft and Casey, 2000; Hattermann et al., 2008; Heimann and Krempa, 2011; Smith et al., 1995 ). There are many studies that have utilized hydrological and hydrodynamic model simulations to study the influence of the wetlands (Ameli and Creed, 2019; Hu et al., 2015; Sheng et al., 2012; Smolders et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2020b, 2020a; Temmerman et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2008 ) and lakes (Lai and Wang, 2017; Tang et al., 2020c; Vinten et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Yang and Liu, 2010 ) on the hydrological response of a catchment. These studies reported a reduction of 5 to 10 % in flood peaks and up to 90 % reduction in downstream flood inundated area in the smaller catchments (<1000 km2 ) and a significant reduction in upstream flooding as well due to reduced backwater effects. However, Their efficiency is restricted because of limited storage capacity, which may be filled relatively early during large rainfall events (Liu et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020a ). Wetland ecosystems have been rapidly degrading worldwide in past decades reducing storage capacity (Alongi, 2022; Assessment et al., 2005; Bridgewater and Kim, 2021; Fluet-Chouinard et al., 2023; Gardner and Finlayson, 2018; Nejadhashemi et al., 2012 ). Restoration or rejuvenation of these wetland capacities has always been a consideration, but very few studies have been conducted on the associated flood control benefits. Yang et al., (2008)  studied the effects of various wetland restoration scenarios in the Broughton Creek watershed, and found that 90 % restoration was the optimal scenario for flow reduction, whereas 50–80 % wetland restoration was more cost-effective. Wang et al., (2010)  examined the effects of wetland conservation and restoration and found that a loss of 10 to 20 % of the wetlands led to a significant increase in discharge. This demonstrates that the potential of wetlands in mitigating floods is reliant on available storage capacity, which may be restricted for natural wetlands depending on local meteorological and hydrologic conditions (Y. Tang et al., 2020b ). A few other studies have also examined wetland rejuvenation impacts by increasing the capacity up to 100 % from the existing wetland capacity and observed a significant reduction in streamflow (Goyette et al., 2023; Kersbergen et al., 2020; Pattison-Williams et al., 2018; Rousseau et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2010 ). Table S2  provides additional information on the scale of rejuvenation of these studies. Although wetland rejuvenation can increase wetland storage and reduce flood risk, the hydrologic response of wetlands is also influenced by precipitation characteristics such as magnitude, duration and its frequency (Hu et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013; Sheng et al., 2012; Smolders et al., 2015; Wamsley et al., 2009, 2010 ). In particular, studies have shown that wetland storage can be insufficient during the monsoon season with moderate to large rainfall events since they become ineffective once the storage is full (Ahmad et al., 2020; Leon et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020a, 2020b; Yang and Liu, 2010 ). Therefore, several recent studies (e.g. Smith et al., 2022; Opperman and Galloway, 2022; Johnson et al., 2022 ) emphasize the need of controlled wetland management for successful flood risk reduction. Bokhove et al., (2019)  proposed a NbS strategy to draw down large lakes and reservoirs prior to extreme rainfall events that resulted in mitigating the flood risk. This technique aims to increase the overall amount of accessible storage for flood control and similar approaches have been proposed for wetlands too (Chen et al., 2019; Leon and Alnahit, 2016; Leon et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020c; Tang et al., 2020a , see table S1 ). These studies demonstrate that for long duration or seasonal precipitation, the pre-release of water stored within large water bodies ahead of projected significant rainfall events that may result in downstream flooding is an effective strategy for increasing the effectiveness of lakes in catchment scale flood control. Such dynamic control systems can be remotely controlled using devices such as gates and syphons (Qin et al., 2019 ), tilted weirs (Yang et al., 2010 ) or water can be simply pumped to the nearby streams (GMDA, 2018 ). Similar approaches have been applied for reservoir management and operation optimization of dams and weirs for flood mitigation and low flow management, (Wang et al., 2013; Ahn et al., 2018; Ehsani et al., 2017 ); including approaches combining wetlands/lakes and catchment reservoir operation for reducing the floods and drought risk (Lai and Wang, 2017; Wu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019 ). These strategies overall have the potential to significantly increase the effectiveness of flood control operations that caters multiple water demands related to power generation and consumptive water uses. However, no study has yet assessed the catchment-scale influence of managing only natural and rejuvenated wetlands with ecological considerations for larger catchments like the Brahmaputra River catchment which have significant numbers of existing wetlands. Previous studies have investigated the use of unmanaged natural wetland systems for flood risk reduction. The current study presents a hydro-ecological wetland management approach that optimizes wetland release policy based on rainfall, evapotranspiration, and ecosystem water requirements of wetlands under different rejuvenation scenarios. The study aims to investigate, a) the influence of the proposed management approach under different wetland rejuvenation approaches on catchment and tributary scale streamflow reduction; b) the influence of wetland location (multiple active wetlands in upstream, mid-stream and downstream regions) on catchment-scale streamflow reduction; and c) the occurrence of flood threat levels (warning level, danger level and high flood level) under the proposed wetland management approach. The outcomes of the study are anticipated to amplify the flood control efficacy of natural wetlands in the catchment, providing socio-economic benefits.  2 Study area The Brahmaputra River, one of the largest river systems in the world, originates in the Himalayan Mountains and traverses through plain reaches of India and Bangladesh before flowing into the Bay of Bengal. The river drains a catchment area of 580, 000 km2  that includes parts of China (50 %), India (36 %), Bhutan (7 %) and Bangladesh (7 %). The present study focuses on the Indo-Bhutan part (∼1,90,000 km2 ) of the river catchment (Fig. 1  ) that covers majority of the catchment tributary network and has significant socio-hydrological impact on the region (Dubey et al., 2021 ). The average annual precipitation in this catchment is 2300 mm, of which 80 % occurs between June and October in the monsoon season and the other 20 % occurs during the pre-monsoon period (March to May). The average annual flow of the Brahmaputra River at Guwahati station is approximately 20,000 m3 /s with an average flow of 4,500 m3 /s in low flow season (non-monsoon) and 28,000 m3 /s during the flooding period (monsoon), indicating high variability in the river flow hydrograph. This region was historically covered by a large number of wetlands dispersed throughout the river catchment (900 km2 ), many of which disappeared in the last 20 years. Figure S1  shows the location of major wetlands present in the catchment. The river catchment is subject to severe flooding events and usually experiences recurrent floods with 6 to 9 flood waves during the monsoon period (Apurv et al., 2015 ). Fig. 1  shows the catchment network with sub catchments, reservoirs equivalent to wetland storage (REWs) and major cities along the riverbank. The 2022 Brahmaputra River floods inundated 28 districts of the state affecting approximately 2 million people, and at several locations the river was flowing above the danger level. In addition, the river morphology is extremely complex with a multi-thread nature due to high flow and sediment variability, severely erodible banks and significant sediment transport (Chembolu and Dutta, 2018, ASDMA 2020 ). Figure S2  shows the ongoing efforts by regional water resources departments to restore wetlands to their natural capacity, having historically silted up or shrunk due to encroachment. Severe flooding events, flat alluvial river corridor and dynamic morphological changes control the socio-economic status of the region. As the climate changes, the hydrological behavior of the catchment may have enhanced consequences on fluvial-hydro-sociological impact of the region.  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Basic description of the hydrological model and data used for the present study This study uses the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) which is a catchment-scale hydrological model developed by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA)-Agriculture Research Service (Arnold et al., 2012;Arnold et al., 1998 ). SWAT subdivides a catchment into multiple sub-catchments based on the terrain and stream network. Further, the sub-catchments are discretized to Hydrological Response Units (HRU) based on unique combinations of classes of soil/land-use/slope, which are fundamental units of simulations in SWAT. A detailed description of the model with governing equations is presented by Neitsch et al., (2011) . SWAT uses several geospatial datasets that define the catchment characteristics such as a digital elevation model (DEM), soil cover and land use maps for simulating the hydrologic processes. In the present study, the topography of the Brahmaputra River catchment was derived from SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) DEM at a 30 m grid resolution which is used for the delineation of the drainage network. The catchment was divided into 40 sub catchments with some of the outlets specified near major cities of the region i.e.,  Dibrugarh, Jorhat, Tezpur, Guwahati and Dhubri. A global land use / land cover map was used in this study, provided by the European Space Agency (ESA) for the year 2020 at 10 m grid resolution. The Brahmaputra River catchment consists majorly of evergreen forest (70.61 %), grassland (5.62), crop land (19.34 %), built up (0.42 %), water bodies (3.95 %) and wetland (0.06 %) based on the land use classification used in this study. The soil characteristics map was clipped from a digital soil map prepared by FAO (Food and Agricultural Organization, 1974) globally at 0.9 km grid resolution, which includes hydrological properties of the soil. The sub catchments were further divided into 1322 HRUs, with overlay of land use/soil features and terrain slope generated using DEM. Weather variables like precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, and relative humidity influence the hydrologic cycle, which in turn controls the water balance of a catchment. Thus, other than geospatial datasets, SWAT also requires several meteorological datasets. The IMD (Indian Meteorological Department) gridded daily precipitation and temperature minimum/maximum datasets were utilized in this study (1979–2020) at 0.25°×0.25° resolution. Other parameters including relative humidity, solar radiation and wind speed gridded globally on a daily time scale at a high resolution of 0.25°×0.25° were provided by Texas A&M University (1979–2014). These datasets were combined, and the input meteorological data were prepared for the Brahmaputra River catchment at 281 grid points. Other datasets such as river cross-sections, discharge and water levels were obtained from the Government Water Resources Department of India. Table 1   summarizes the details of the data sources used for SWAT modeling of the study area.  3.2 Hydrological modeling of the catchment with wetlands SWAT represents a simple conceptual module for wetlands. The catchment-scale wetlands are incorporated as i) a reservoir on the stream with controlled outflow and, ii) storage pond/ potholes away from the stream as isolated waterbodies. The model simulates only one wetland per sub-catchment, which has a specified area that receives the sub-catchment runoff. In the case of multiple wetlands in the sub-catchment, a “Reservoir Equivalent to Wetland Storage (REW)” is incorporated, which has the storage capacity equal to total storage of the wetlands in the sub-catchment. In SWAT, wetlands away from the stream carry no spatial location in the sub-catchment and wetland attributes such as area and volume are proportionally distributed among the HRUs (Rahman et al., 2016 ). These wetlands cannot be controlled at a daily scale and required minimum storage to sustain the wetland ecosystem cannot be achieved. However, the wetlands incorporated as a reservoir on the mainstream can receive, store and release water at any point in time and minimum storage as per the user requirements can be achieved. We represented wetlands as a reservoir for our simulations because the present study looks for wetland modules that can be controlled at a daily level during the monsoon season depending on the rainfall events. The step-by-step methodology for incorporation of wetlands in SWAT in text ST1.  3.3 Release policy of reservoir Equivalent wetland storage (REW) SWAT computes wetland/reservoir (REW) volume on a daily interval using the water balance equation, which includes initial volume, inflow, outflow, precipitation and losses due to evaporation and seepage. The general water balance equation governing hydrological processes in a wetland/reservoir is shown here.(1) V stored  t + 1   = V stored  t  + V inflow  t  - V outflow  t  + V pcp  t  - V evap  t  - V seep  t      Here, V stored     is the maximum volume for REWs at the start of the day, V inflow    , V outflow     are the volume of water entering the REW through the catchment and water flowing through the REW respectively, V pcp     is the volume of rainfall occurring over the REW area, V evap     is volume of water lost due to evaporation and V seep     is volume of water lost due to seepage. Wetlands naturally fill during the initial monsoon period and thus if left to drain slowly naturally would provide ineffective storage for subsequent peak rainfall events. Therefore, in this study, to make the wetlands efficient in flood risk reduction throughout the monsoon season, an approach is proposed to enable dynamic storage of wetlands (incorporated as REW) by draining the available water in REWs prior to rainfall events. Most of the wetlands have an ecosystem depending on the standing water such as aquatic biota, which cannot be risked by draining the wetland completely (Leon et al., 2018 ). The wetland bodies are subject to different water requirements (evapotranspiration, seepage, anthropogenic losses etc.), which highlights the criticality of incorporating both the hydrological and the ecosystem requirements to optimize wetland management. Among all losses, the evapotranspiration (ET) is mainly dominant during the monsoon period where the soil conditions reach saturation, and the ET requirements of wetlands varies seasonally and spatially in the catchment; for instance, higher ET requirements (∼35–40 mm/day) in the monsoon period and below 30 mm/day in pre monsoon period. The study therefore considers ET and environmental storage as standing water requirements to optimize the individual wetland (REW) release to sustainably manage the ecosystem of the wetlands. The release policy includes maintaining an optimal amount, Vrequired,  which is 10 % of the maximum REW storage (i.e. , Vmax ) in addition to the ecosystem requirement of the REW (i.e.,  ET requirement) throughout the simulations (Li et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2020a ). In the present study, wetlands were modelled as REW’s, which were controlled to provide buffer storage for accommodating rainfall-induced flood water. A release policy of the REW is thus designed depending on the rainfall hyetograph in the sub-catchment for the controlled flow scenarios from the REW. The rainfall distribution across the catchment was proportioned into sub-catchments with the grid points lying in each sub-catchment while relating to the REW’s of that sub-catchment. A threshold rainfall for each sub-catchment, which is 95th percentile rainfall was chosen to decide the release of the flow from REWs (Zhai et al., 2005 ). Fig. 2   provides a schematic representation of the release policy. The water budgeting of the wetland (REW) for a controlled release policy can be represented by the equation given below, such that for a precipitation event peaking on day i   and first exceeding the precipitation threshold n   days prior to the peak.(2) V r e q u i r e d   = 0.1 V m a x    + E T  R e q u i r e m e n t     (3) V outflow  = V inflow  t  + V pcp  t  - V evap  t  - V seep  t  + ( V stored  t - 1   - V required  t  )    t = i - n    V inflow  t  + V pcp  t  - V evap  t  - V seep  t    i - n < t < i    V inflow  t  + V pcp  t  - V evap  t  - V seep  t  - ( V stored  t - 1   - V required  t  )    t = i            (4) Q r e l e a s e  t  = V o u t f l o w  t  86400      Where, Q r e l e a s e    = average daily flow out of the wetland (m3 /s)   3.4 Hydrodynamic model In the present study a hydrodynamic model, HEC-RAS was setup for the Brahmaputra River to compute the water surface elevations at different locations along the river. HEC-RAS is a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model used to simulate hydraulic variables such as hydraulic depth and velocity for steady and unsteady flow conditions. The model set up was carried out for a river reach from upstream of Dibrugarh to downstream of Dhubri of 560 km with 60 cross-sections provided by the Brahmaputra Board at approximate intervals of 9 km in the streamwise direction. More details of the HEC-RAS model calibration and validation is discussed in the authors’ previous works (Chembolu, 2020; Chembolu et al., 2019; Dubey, 2016; Dubey et al., 2022 ). SWAT-simulated discharge data of the Brahmaputra River catchment with controlled wetlands was used to carry out the steady flow simulations (Fig. 3  ). The simulated water surface elevations at different cities along the river were compared with the in-situ records of threat levels i.e. , Danger Level (DL), Warning Level (WL) and High Flood Level (HFL) of the river at those gauging stations from CWC (https://cwc.gov.in/flood-forecasting-hydrological-observation ). This analysis provides the information on percentage reduction of monsoon-season river water levels due to reduced river discharge resulting from controlled wetlands of the catchment.  3.5 Scenarios simulated The Brahmaputra River catchment is composed of several wetlands in various sub-catchments that have historically shrunk by more than 25 % in the last two decades due to catchment erosion, anthropogenic encroachments, and agricultural activities. The mean depth of the Deeopor Beel (a major wetland near Guwahati City) was observed to reduce from 2 m to 1 m and the variability of maximum depth is between 5 m in monsoon season to 1 m in dry season (Ahmed et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2012 ). For other wetlands in the catchment, studies report siltation of up to 3 m (Das and Bhattacharjee, 2015 ). Table S3  includes more detailed information on the wetland statistics of the catchment. The present study analyses five rejuvenation scenarios based on the literature available. The scenarios include, EWS (Existing wetland scenario) and RS1 to RS4 rejuvenation scenarios with 20 %-30 % increase in present area along with 2–3 m average depth (Figure-4). The catchment is divided into three regions designated as upstream, midstream, and downstream to assess the impact of non-operational REWs on downstream flood impact. The wetlands (REWs) in these regions were modeled as REWs within the sub-catchments. In the upstream region, the total number of REWs is 4 and the total area of reservoirs is ∼ 30 km2 . The midstream region contains 3 REWs with a total area of ∼ 40 km2  and the downstream region contains 3 REWs with a total area of ∼ 30 km2 . The present study involved wetland rejuvenation by increasing both the surface area and the average depth of the wetlands. Fig. 4   depicts the scenarios that were simulated in this study. The study’s baseline scenario was simulated for existing wetland areas with 1 m of average depth for uncontrolled conditions. The uncontrolled wetlands however were not considered in this study, since preliminary testing showed much less impact even with maximum rejuvenation (RS-4).  3.6 Calibration and validation SWAT features an extended calibration tool SWAT Calibration and Uncertainty Programs (SWAT-CUP) for the calibration and validation procedure. Here, the SUFI-2 (Uncertainty in Sequential Uncertainty Fitting) approach in SWAT CUP was used to calibrate the model. Based on previous literature for the study area, 14 SWAT parameters were listed for the sensitivity analysis (Table S4 ), of which CN2 (curve number), CH_N2 (Manning’s roughness), GWQMN (Threshold depth of water) and GW DELAY (groundwater delay) were found to be more sensitive than others, indicated by lower P-values. The parameters having P-value less than 0.05 indicate a 95 % chance that the parameter has some effect (Table S4 ). The accuracy of the model has been assessed with standard goodness of fit metrics that are most commonly used standards for comparing simulations of hydrological models (Le and Pricope, 2017 ). Table 2   shows the range of these goodness of fit metrics and their acceptable values (Sao et al., 2020 ). The model was initially simulated for a period of 3 years (2005–2007) as a warm-up period. The model was then further calibrated for the period of 2008–2009 on a daily scale to attain a close resemblance of the observed discharge hydrograph at different gauging stations of the Brahmaputra River at Guwahati and Tezpur and at a tributary outlet of Subanshiri River. The parameters were adjusted within an acceptable range to calibrate the model. In total, 27,500 simulations in 11 iterations were performed to obtain satisfactory performance of the model. Using the same parameters, the model was validated for the year 2010 on a daily scale. The calibration and validation statistics are shown in the Figure S3 . The calibration period shows the average values of R2 , NSE, RSR and PBIAS as 0.80, 0.65, 0.47 and 17.9 respectively. For the validation period these values are 0.80, 0.65, 0.45 and 15.9 respectively (Table 2 ).   4 Results 4.1 Effect of wetland release on water availability in the wetland This section discusses the flow response of the managed wetlands (referred to as REWs in this study) to the hydro-ecological release during the peak rainfall event. The overflow from uncontrolled wetlands during the peak event reaching the nearby stream is similar to the inflow to the wetlands. Fig. 5  a shows the response of wetland overflow for a peak rainfall month. Period 1 shows that when rainfall is not predicted to exceed the threshold, the overflow from the wetland is the same as inflow with the wetland storage at full capacity. However, when the peak rainfall above the threshold is predicted (Period 2), the prior release of outflow (shown in red dot) was higher than the inflow in order to make more storage available in the wetland that can accommodate the flood volume of the forthcoming peak event. It was observed that the varying ecological requirements resulted in variation of prior releases. This heterogeneity in wetland release was further observed to influence the wetland storage on the threshold rainfall days where the flow coming out of the wetlands on the day of peak events is modified overflow (which is less than inflow) due to storing of excess flood water in available wetland storage. The maximum outflow from the wetlands was reduced by ∼ 300 m3 /s on the peak rainfall day during the event. Period 3 shows the tail of the high rainfall event, where after a certain storage for rainfall above threshold, the overflow and inflow are observed to be similar as in case 1. Furthermore, the average daily water depth requirement and available water depth in the wetland is shown in Fig. 5 b. There was no wetland release before the event however wetland storage was released prior to the peak rainfall event. It is observed that the wetland remains full before the peak event which is 700 to 800 mm more than the required water depth. The daily scale response of the wetland during the event shows minimum available water depth was equal to the water requirement of that day whereas the maximum release was observed to be equal to available wetland depth excluding the standing water requirement of wetland on that day. The average water depth required during the monsoon period is observed to be approximately 135 mm whereas the average available water was greater than 600 mm in the wetland, meeting the wetland ecosystem requirements.  4.2 Catchment-scale hydrological response to controlled wetlands The annual variability of two hydrological scenarios corresponding to the proposed wetland management approach is discussed here. First, the streamflow reduction in the main river with inclusion of the release policy in the catchment under existing and rejuvenated wetland (RS-4) scenarios and second, the same behavior at tributary level in one of the major sub-catchments. The discharge variability in the main river at Guwahati is ∼ 7500 to 37,000 m3 /s in the pre-monsoon season and ∼ 18,000 to 38,000 m3 /s in the monsoon season. At Guwahati, a maximum peak discharge reduction of 390 m3 /s in the pre-monsoon period and 440 m3 /s in the monsoon period is observed under controlled existing wetlands conditions (EWS). With the rejuvenation of these wetlands, the range of peak discharge reduction increased between 320–2300 m3 /s in pre-monsoon and 650–2400 m3 /s in monsoon periods. The discharge variability of the Kameng River (a tributary catchment) with the uncontrolled existing wetland is between 400–3200 m3 /s in the pre-monsoon period and 800–6250 m3 /s in the monsoon period. With the managed wetlands, the monthly peak discharge reduction of 0–5.9 % and 4–6.6 % in the existing scenario and, 0–27 % and 16–32 % in the rejuvenated scenario is observed in pre-monsoon and monsoon seasons respectively. The analysis of discharge data at the Brahmaputra River (Guwahati) and tributary river, the Kameng River, is carried out to understand the percentage contribution of the tributary catchment in peak flow reduction of the main river. It is observed that the controlled wetlands in the Kameng River catchment contribute to a maximum discharge reduction of 65 m3 /s and 255 m3 /s in existing and rejuvenated conditions during the peak flood event. The implementation of wetland release strategies substantially reduces the streamflow for the rejuvenated wetland scenario (Table 3  ), with the highest streamflow reduced by ∼ 6 % in the catchment and ∼ 28 % in the sub-catchment, while the maximum peak flow reduction for existing wetland scenarios reaches 1.5 % for the catchment and 7.5 % for the sub-catchment. Fig. 6   shows the seasonal variability of river flow and its reduction at Guwahati gauging station due to fluctuations in upstream and midstream wetlands (REWs) in both existing and rejuvenated conditions under the proposed approach. The recorded flow levels of warning, danger and high flood conditions are also displayed on the plot. This plot shows (a) the changes in cumulative wetland (REWs) volume due to different release scenarios of the wetlands at different rainfall thresholds of the sub- catchments; (b) the magnitude of reduction in streamflow of the main river due to controlled operation of wetlands (REWs); and (c) the frequency of days when the discharge is reduced below the warning, danger, and high flood conditions due to controlled wetlands (REWs). Fig. 6  shows the managed wetlands’ influence on flow reduction in pre-monsoon and monsoon periods and behaves independently as isolated wetlands under non-operating seasons. Further, these wetlands are observed to be more effective in flow reduction in rejuvenated scenarios. The analysis showed that the majority of streamflow reduction is < 400 m3 /s in the existing scenario (75 % of days show this reduction). In the rejuvenated scenario, 35 % of days show streamflow reduction of < 400 m3 /s, 30 % of days show reduction of 400–1000 m3 /s and 35 % of days show > 1000 m3 /s reduction. Further it is observed that the rejuvenated wetlands reduced the occurrence of discharge greater than warning condition by 50 %, danger condition by 50 % and high flood condition by 100 %. For the simulation year, it was observed that the wetland (REW) volume fluctuates more during the monsoon than it does during the pre-monsoon, indicating more days with rainfall over threshold as well as more days when controlled wetlands (REWs) are in operation.  4.3 Impact of wetland restoration scenarios on streamflow reduction under the proposed management approach The impact of the proposed management approach on streamflow reduction was assessed using a number of different wetland rejuvenation scenarios by varying surface area and depth of the wetlands (REWs). In different scenarios, the average depth of the wetlands (REWs) was increased to 2–3 m, respectively, and increasing the surface areas by 20 %-30 %. Fig. 7   shows the sub-catchment scale streamflow reduction (%) under different rejuvenation scenarios using a controlled wetlands approach. It was observed that the average streamflow reduction in the catchment varied between 0 for upstream sub-catchments with no wetlands (REWs) to a maximum of 22 % reduction in the downstream region influenced by the majority of wetlands (REWs). In the upstream region, the main cities like Dibrugarh and Jorhat showed the least amount of change in the maximum streamflow reduction, which was less than 5 % in all cases. Moving towards downstream cities i.e. , Tezpur, Guwahati, and Dhubri, the streamflow reduction was increased to nearly 5 % at Tezpur and 17.3 % reduction at Dhubri. The maximum streamflow reduction was observed for rejuvenation scenario RS-4 of 3 m wetland depth and 30 % increase of wetland area. For example, in this scenario, the streamflow reduction was nearly 4.8 % at Dibrugarh, 6 % in Jorhat, 4.5 % at Tezpur, 6.4 % at Guwahati and 17.3 % at Dhubri. The equivalent variability was 1.83 % at Dibrugarh and at 2.4 % Dhubri for the existing scenario (EWS). Further, the area contributing to a streamflow reduction of > 10 % in RS-4 is 35,000 km2  while the maximum reduction of > 5 % in existing wetland case (EWS) was contributed to by 2500 km2 . This shows that increase in capacity of the wetlands, number of contributing wetlands and a management approach for wetland storage regulation has a significant influence on streamflow reduction of the catchment.  4.4 Impact of wetland location on streamflow reduction under the proposed management approach The influence of wetland location and inactivity was examined at the catchment outlet (Dhubri). Fig. 8   shows different cases of response to inactive and active wetlands (REWs) under existing and rejuvenation scenarios. It is observed that the percentage streamflow reduction is increased with the extent of rejuvenation under all the cases of wetland location. The observations also suggest that upstream wetlands (case 1) cause more streamflow reduction than the midstream (case 2) and downstream wetlands (case 3) under independent scenarios. Contrastingly, in case 4 (active upstream and midstream wetlands) and case 5 (all wetlands active) the percentage streamflow reduction increased with increases in contributing number of wetlands (Fig. 8 ). The lowest limit of discharge reduction can be observed to be similar in all the cases of wetland influence. The plots also show that more peaks in clusters of streamflow reduction can be observed during the monsoon period while a single peak on the lower reduction side can be noticed in the pre-monsoon period. The falling limb of the streamflow reduction distribution is observed to be flattening with increase in number and area of wetlands (REWs). In cases 4 and 5, uniform variability of reduction during the season can be observed relative to other cases, due to multiple wetlands’ (REWs) contributions at different times. In terms of the impact of wetland restoration scenarios at the catchment level, the percentage of streamflow reduction in pre-monsoon season was greater than observed during the monsoon period.
