Situated at an elevation of approximately 850 m above sea level, the basin is distinguished by two tied lakes, Macro Prespa and Micro Prespa. These lakes are linked by a narrow artificial channel and separated by an alluvial isthmus in Greece (Kolaneci, 2004; Krstić, 2012 ). Small Prespa Lake, the focus of our study, encompasses a total area of 47.4 Km2 , with 43.5 Km2  within Greek territory and 3.9 Km2  in Albania (Fig. 1  ). The lake primarily receives water from diverse surface runoff and lateral subterranean flows that interact with aquifers, and, seasonally, from the Devoll River on the Albanian side (Fijani et al., 2019; Tziritis, 2014 ). The Prespa region experiences significant seasonal climate variations. The summer months are hot and dry, with an average temperature of 23.6 °C during the warmest periods and 0.8 °C during the coldest month in winter (Fijani et al., 2019 ). The area records an average annual air temperature of 14 °C and receives about 647 mm of rainfall annually (Hollis and Stevenson, 1997 ). The Prespa lakes host a variety of aquatic ecosystems and are recognized as a crucial wetland habitat for waterbirds. They harbor diverse phytoplankton, zooplankton, aquatic plants, and fish species, including several endemics. Several human settlements surround the lakes, and anthropogenic pressures have significantly impacted Small Prespa Lake in recent decades, notably due to intensified agricultural irrigation (Grazhdani, 2023 ). Additionally, elevated concentrations of Chl-a in the lake have raised concerns about potential eutrophication, further emphasizing the importance of monitoring WQ. The data pertaining to WQ utilized in this study was collected throughout the period spanning from June 1, 2012, to May 31, 2013, at regular intervals of 15 min. A multi-parameter sensor was established at a 1.5-meter depth along the northern expanse of the lake to measure various physicochemical parameters, encompassing DO, oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), Chl-a, water temperature (Temp), electrical conductivity (EC), and pH. Over the course of the annual monitoring period, the sensor recorded cumulative depth changes, reaching an approximate depth of 3 m, with slight variations discerned. Table 1   presents the statistical parameters of the measured WQVs in Prespa Lake, offering a comprehensive overview of the lake’s environmental status over the study period. The temperature shows significant variation, with a wide range between the minimum and maximum values, indicating seasonal influences. The pH values are generally stable, suggesting a consistent aquatic environment, although the low minimum value may indicate occasional acidic inputs. High kurtosis in pH and Chl-a suggests frequent extreme values, which could be due to episodic pollution events or algal blooms. The skewness in the ORP and Chl-a data indicates that these variables are not symmetrically distributed, likely influenced by varying environmental conditions and human activities. The data on DO and EC further support these interpretations, highlighting variability that is crucial for assessing ecological health and guiding management decisions. Despite the unavailability of more recent WQ data for Small Prespa Lake, our study focuses on harnessing existing data to develop a framework that improves the predictive capabilities of ML models. This framework is particularly geared towards forecasting WQVs, such as Chl-a, using multi-stage optimization applied to a time-series WQ dataset. Notably, recent studies by Tziritis (2014), Fijani et al. (2019) , Barzegar et al., (2020) and Zamani et al., (2023)  have also utilized contemporary WQ data. The principal aim of our study is to conduct a comparative analysis between those previous studies and our current work, assessing advancements and accuracy in WQ forecasting.  2.2 Data preprocessing We aimed to forecast WQVs six hours ahead (e.g., Chl-a(t+6)  and DO(t+6) ) using lag times of key easily measured WQ parameters such as pH, ORP, water temperature, and EC. The data preprocessing involved examining lag times from 6 to 24 hour, with a 24-hour lag ultimately proving optimal for these variables. This timeframe allowed us to incorporate recent historical data effectively, enhancing the model’s predictive accuracy. Additionally, we employed PCA to manage the high dimensionality of our dataset. PCA is a prevalent method for dimensionality reduction, effectively capturing the most significant variances within the data (Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016 ). By identifying and focusing on the principal components, PCA not only simplifies the data but also ensures that the critical patterns and dynamics are preserved, facilitating more efficient and precise modeling. This approach was chosen for its ability to distill the essential features that drive changes in WQ, laying a solid foundation for our forecasting model. PCA was selected over other dimensionality reduction techniques for several reasons. First, it is an unsupervised method, meaning it can analyze the inherent structure of the entire dataset without using the outcome variable (Geller, 2011 ). Second, PCA effectively reduces a large set of correlated variables to fewer representative features (Bae et al., 2010 ). Given the presence of many interrelated WQ measurements in the dataset, using PCA to consolidate related variables was deemed advantageous. Finally, by compressing the dataset to 5 principal components that accounted for 90 % of the total variance, PCA allowed the subsequent ML models to operate on the data more efficiently. The reduced feature space decreased computational requirements and complexity without sacrificing critical information contained in the original measurements. Then, the dataset was divided into training (70 %) and testing (30 %) subsets. These carefully executed data preprocessing steps laid the foundation for constructing ML models that would ultimately yield promising results in the subsequent stages of the analysis.  2.3 Modeling strategy In this study, we developed a diverse array of models, including tree-based (e.g., GBR, LGBM, XGB) and neural network (NN) architectures (e.g., MLP) tuned using the GWO. To further enhance the performance of forecasting model, we applied NSGA-II and GA for ensembling the individual ML models. This meta-ensemble modeling strategy leverages the strengths of different ML models, enhancing their performance across both training and testing datasets. The XGB, LightGBM, and GBR are all ensemble tree-based models that are effective at handling nonlinear associations and complex feature interactions within environmental data (Zheng et al., 2022 ). Tree-based algorithms build models in a stage-wise fashion and are robust against overfitting (Elith et al., 2008 ). They have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in various forecasting tasks, including WQ modeling, algal bloom forecasting, and other environmental applications (Fan et al., 2018; Manley et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022 ). For example, LightGBM has shown robust performance in forecasting algal bloom indicators, evidenced by its success in multi-step forecasting of Chl-a levels in lakes, where it achieved high accuracy (Yoon et al., 2023 ). Similarly, XGB has proven highly effective in WQ forecasting (Liu et al., 2020 ). In a pertinent study, XGB was applied to predict DO levels in streams, yielding superior performance compared to support vector regression (Yusri et al., 2022 ). Recognized as universal function approximators, MLPs excel at capturing complex nonlinear patterns and learning directly from raw data without assuming underlying relationships. Previous studies have validated their effectiveness in modeling nonlinear associations, particularly in representing variables such as nitrate and phosphorus concentrations (Bhattarai et al., 2021 ). Utilizing a diverse set of models (e.g., tree-based and NNs) provides complementarity and balances the individual limitations of each algorithm. For example, while NNs such as MLP may struggle with extrapolation, tree-based models handle this better (Ruaud et al., 2022 ). Models such as XGB, LightGBM, and MLP also facilitate faster training times on large datasets compared to other algorithms, an essential feature given the temporal resolution and volume of the time series data used (Elith et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Each of these models offers tunable hyperparameters to control complexity and prevent overfitting, enhancing their generalizability (He and Fan, 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Open-source and well-documented implementations of each model are readily available, making them easily accessible and reproducible. Optimization techniques have been widely applied in previous works to improve ML models for WQ modeling. Earlier studies have employed methods ranging from mathematical programming and metaheuristic algorithms to parametric tuning to optimize predictive performance (Boah and Twum, 2020; Haghiabi et al., 2018 ; Kalaivanan and Vellingiri, 2023; Shams et al., 2023; Uddin et al., 2023; Yang, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022 ). For example, Shams et al., (2023)  demonstrated that model optimization via grid search significantly improved various ML models for predicting WQ indicators, while Yang et al. (2023) introduced novel integrative methods to optimize DO forecasting accuracy. Such works highlight the advantages of optimizing ML models through techniques such as those applied in the current study. Notably, data preprocessing involving lag time feature engineering and dimensionality reduction using PCA, along with modeling and GWO optimization, was performed using Python (v2023.14.0) libraries, including scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, PyCaret, and matplotlib. For NSGA-II optimization, MATLAB (MATLAB R2022a) was employed. The next part delves more into the structure of each employed model. 2.3.1 Multi-layer Perceptron The Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP), a type of ANN, is composed of multiple layers of neurons that can learn complex nonlinear relationships between inputs and outputs. It is widely used for regression tasks and has shown significant success in various applications, including hydrological modeling (Meshram et al., 2022; Rahman et al., 2022 ). The primary advantage of MLPs over traditional models, such as empirical or physically-based models, is their ability to capture the nonlinear and dynamic behavior of hydrological processes without requiring numerous parameters and assumptions that are challenging to estimate or verify (Widiasari and Nugroho, 2017 ). An MLP typically consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. The input layer receives the input variables and transmits them to the hidden layers, where each hidden layer performs a nonlinear transformation using a weighted sum and an activation function, such as sigmoid , tanh , or ReLU . The output layer then produces the final output variables through another weighted sum and activation function, with the weights representing the parameters that need to be learned from the data (Ghorbani et al., 2018 ). The learning process of an MLP involves both forward propagation and backpropagation. During forward propagation, the network processes the input data to compute the outputs using the current weights and activation functions. These computed outputs are compared to the true targets using a loss function, such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) , which quantifies the model’s error. In backpropagation, the error is propagated backward through the network to adjust the weights in a direction that minimizes the loss. This adjustment is done by calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight using the chain rule and then updating the weights using a learning rate. This iterative process of forward and backward passes continues until the model’s error is minimized, effectively fitting the training data. Various learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent, can be employed to update the weights based on the gradients, enabling the MLP to optimize its performance (Ghorbani et al., 2018 ; Widiasari and Nugroho, 2017) . The mathematical equations for the MLP can be found in numerous foundational texts and research papers (Yilmaz and Kaynar, 2011 ; (McClelland and Rumelhart, 1988 )).  2.3.2 eXtreme gradient boosting eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) is an ensemble model consisting of multiple decision trees trained using a gradient boosting technique. In this model, decision trees split the input data space into distinct regions based on specific decision rules. The ensemble effect is achieved by aggregating the outputs of multiple trees, enabling the modeling of complex functions and interactions (Piraei et al., 2023 ). XGB enhances learning by progressively adding trees that specifically address the residual errors of preceding trees. It trains trees sequentially, and each new tree is tailored to fit the negative gradient of the loss function (Szczepanek, 2022 ). This gradient-boosting approach effectively minimizes the loss function across iterations . In constructing trees, XGB recursively splits the input space to reduce heterogeneity in the output values of the resultant regions. It uses criteria such as information gain  or the Gini index  to identify optimal splits. The splitting process stops when it reaches a predefined maximum depth or when further splits fail to substantially improve the selected criterion (Tao et al., 2022 ). Additionally, tree pruning is applied to remove certain branches or leaves based on regularization terms to avert overfitting. This pruning process aims to enhance generalization and reduce model complexity (Piraei et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2022 ). Readers can find the mathematical formulations of XGB in various foundational texts and research papers (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Friedman, 2001 ).  2.3.3 Gradient boosting regression Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR) is an ensemble model that consists of decision trees trained using gradient boosting, known for its strong performance in hydrological applications such as streamflow forecasting and WQ forecasting (Liu et al., 2017; Nesru, 2023 ). The model integrates multiple decision trees that divide the input space into regions with consistent outputs. GBR's learning process is iterative, with each tree built to correct the errors of its predecessors, thereby refining the model's accuracy over time. Each tree in the ensemble is trained on the negative gradient of a chosen loss function, aimed at minimizing the loss through successive iterations (Hastie et al., 2004 ). This strategic training method targets improvements in model performance and ensures a focused development approach. The trees are constructed by recursively splitting input variables to reduce output variability, enhancing the results' predictive strength and homogeneity (Friedman, 2001 ). The complexity of the trees is regulated by parameters such as maximum depth , minimum samples per leaf , and regularization  techniques. These controls are crucial for preventing overfitting and ensuring the model's generalizability across different datasets (Friedman et al., 2010 ). By utilizing simple trees within a complex ensemble framework, GBR effectively captures intricate data relationships, making it highly effective in environments with complex data structures where simpler models may fail (James et al., 2013 ). This ensemble approach not only boosts the robustness but also significantly improves the model's predictive accuracy.  2.3.4 Light Gradient-Boosting Machine The Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) is an advanced ensemble model that uses gradient-boosted decision trees to enhance predictive accuracy. LightGBM utilizes a leaf-wise tree growth strategy, significantly improving learning efficiency on large datasets (Lange and Sippel, 2020 ). This ensemble method constructs its model by summing outputs from multiple decision trees, each of which partitions inputs into regions with constant outputs. The decision trees are trained sequentially, fitting residual errors to minimize a specified loss function through gradient boosting (Ma et al., 2023 ). The tree construction process in LightGBM involves recursive splitting aimed at reducing output heterogeneity while pruning techniques are applied to enhance generalization. These techniques include setting limits on tree depth , defining minimum leaf samples , and applying regularization  methods. LightGBM’s leaf-wise split strategy offers distinct advantages over traditional level-wise growth, particularly in terms of computational and memory efficiency (Lange and Sippel, 2020 ). Moreover, LightGBM effectively leverages gradient boosting for efficient learning, and its innovative tree architecture is particularly well-suited for handling large datasets and complex hydrological modeling tasks (Kumar et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023 ). The combination of a leaf-wise split approach and an ensemble model structure ensures reliable performance, making LightGBM a robust choice for water forecasting problems. The core mathematical principles behind LightGBM can be found in the literature (Friedman, 2001; Ke et al., 2017 ).   2.4 Optimization techniques 2.4.1 Grey wolf Optimizer The Swarm Intelligence algorithm known as the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), developed by Mirjalili et al. (Mirjalili et al., 2014 ), has recently garnered significant interest (Altay and Varol Altay, 2023; Heramb et al., 2023 ; Hossain et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2020; Safari et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ). This algorithm is inspired by wolves' hunting strategies and social hierarchy (Ullah et al., 2023 ). In the GWO, wolves are categorized into distinct groups—Alpha , Beta , Delta , and Omega —each reflecting their roles and hierarchical status (Fig. 2  II) (Mirjalili et al., 2014; Wang and Li, 2019 ). The Alpha  wolf, representing the group leader, possesses the most critical information about the location of the prey. Following in rank and authority is the Beta  wolf, who commands other members and serves as the immediate successor should the Alpha  wolf perish. The Delta  wolf holds the third rank. All other wolves are designated as Omega  wolves, making up the lowest tier of the hierarchy (Wong et al., 2014 ). Within the context of the GWO, each member of the wolf pack follows specific algorithms to efficiently encircle and capture their targetprey (Mirjalili et al., 2014 ; Wong et al., 2014 ):(1) D →  = C →  . X →  δ  - X ←          It is essential to acknowledge that the primary rationale for employing the GWO in this study stems from its robust performance in scenarios involving large datasets and numerous features (Faris et al., 2018 ). While gradient-based training methods can efficiently manage small datasets with fewer features without incurring additional computational costs, the GWO is particularly effective for large datasets. This effectiveness arises from its ability to navigate the considerable number of local optima that make standard training algorithms largely ineffective (Mirjalili, 2015 ). Additionally, GWO requires the specification of relatively few algorithm parameters, and prior benchmarking has demonstrated its faster convergence and superior optimization performance compared to other metaheuristics (Mirjalili et al., 2014 ). Given the extensive, multidimensional dataset and the complex interactions of features involved in WQ modeling, GWO was chosen to efficiently optimize the hyperparameters of various models, including XGB, LightGBM, MLP, and GBR. Its stochastic search mechanism fosters diversity during optimization runs, and its low computational demand facilitates rapid tuning across multiple algorithms. The proven success of GWO in previous studies for machine learning hyperparameter tuning further supported its selection for this modeling task (Makhadmeh et al., 2023; Maroufpoor et al., 2019 ).  2.4.2 Grey wolf optimized Machine learning models The methodological framework for optimizing ML models with the GWO is depicted in Fig. 3  . The optimization process initiates with establishing a population of grey wolves, each representing a possible solution. This assembled population sets the foundation for upcoming steps (Hossain et al., 2022 ). Following this, GWO’s internal parameters are set, utilizing critical ML parameters identified from the literature. In formulating the hyperparameter tuning strategy, careful consideration was given to selecting key ML model parameters (see Table 2   in the Result section). Each parameter was chosen based on its critical role in shaping the behavior and performance of the respective models. Moreover, to ensure precision, the ranges or bounds for these parameters are meticulously defined based on previous research and expert knowledge (Altay and Varol Altay, 2023; Heramb et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2020; Mirjalili, 2015; Putatunda and Rama, 2018; Safari et al., 2023; Ullah et al., 2023 ). The fitness values serve as a metric, guiding the selection of the population’s three ideal individuals. Throughout this process, optimal solutions are chosen, and grey wolves’ locations are adjusted, all aimed at maximizing KGE. The optimization involves adjusting two fundamental parameters in GWO: population size  and iteration number . The optimization then transitions into an iterative method, initiated after selecting the top three wolves, α , β , and δ,  and establishing the baseline population (Altay and Varol Altay, 2023; Heramb et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2020; Safari et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Notably, other grey wolves have the potential to reach the status of ideal individuals. To achieve this, they adjust their positions based on advice derived from the current optimal solutions, bringing them closer to the target prey. Subsequently, a new population is generated, reflecting a fresh set of potential solutions. This stage experiences updates in the regulating factors, particularly in the vectors, specifically vectors a →    , A →    , and C →    . The fitness levels of the new population's individuals are computed, and the selection process identifies the top three components—α, β, and δ—based on their superior fitness values. The best solution is finalized during this phase, and the performance of the improved models is evaluated through testing (Heramb et al., 2023 ). Our optimization process began with defining the KGE as the fitness function for optimization. Traditionally, optimization algorithms, including GWO, aim to minimize the fitness function. To adapt GWO to maximize a metric, we transformed the maximization problem into a minimization problem by taking the negative of the objective function. For GWO optimization, a two-step strategy was employed to expedite the process, which is particularly beneficial for more time-efficient GBMs. In the first step, optimization was performed on a subsample comprising half of the training dataset to identify preliminary optimal parameters. This approach accelerated the parameter search while conserving computational resources. Then, the problem dictionary was defined to minimize the fitness function (negative KGE) within the hyperparameter ranges specified in Table 2 . These ranges were determined through iterative testing, balancing model performance against overfitting risks. While initial parameter ranges were informed by literature, adjustments were made based on our study’s specific requirements. Further customization of the parameter ranges can either restrict exploration (if too narrow) or introduce noise (if too wide). A comprehensive analysis was conducted to test various population sizes  and determine the optimal population size  for the GWO algorithm. The GWO optimizer was then initialized with a designated population size  and iteration  count. In the second step, the search was refined by transitioning to the full dataset once convergence was achieved with the subsample. The lower and upper bounds for the optimization parameters were judiciously determined by scaling the values from the initial optimization by factors of 0.7 and 1.3, respectively, providing a reasonable exploration range around the optimal solutions. The optimization process was concluded based on two termination conditions: reaching the maximum iteration count of 200 or having negative KGE stabilize for 50 consecutive iterations. This dual termination strategy ensured efficiency while allowing for a thorough exploration of the solution space. If termination conditions were not met, the process was reiterated from Step 2. Finally, each model (e.g., LightGBM, XGB, GBR, MLP) was trained using the best hyperparameters identified by GWO on the complete dataset, with appropriate adjustments to hyperparameter sets as detailed in Table 2 . This comprehensive methodology harmonizes optimization techniques, parameter tuning, and iterative processes, culminating in an optimal solution with consideration for computational efficiency. Throughout the process, convergence and validation set performance were closely monitored. Various population sizes  and bounds were experimented with for each model, and optimal results were achieved with specific population sizes  and iterations .  2.4.3 NSGA-II enhanced ensemble strategy for Chl-a forecasting To enhance the forecasting accuracy of Chl-a, a two-stage modeling approach was adopted, leveraging the distinct strengths of various ML models. This method leverages the diverse strengths inherent in various ML models, optimizing their performance across both training and testing datasets. The implementation of NSGA-II further refines this process, strategically maximizing KGE on both training and testing data, with the decision variables revolving around the assignment of weights to each of the four ML models within an ensemble framework (Deb et al., 2002 ). The rationale for adopting this two-stage modeling approach is multifaceted. Ensemble methods, which amalgamate multiple models, have consistently demonstrated enhanced predictive capabilities compared to individual models (Diouf and Seck, 2019; Shin et al., 2020 ). This integration allows for harnessing specific strengths from each constituent model while concurrently mitigating individual limitations. Moreover, the NSGA-II algorithm, known for its excellence in multi-objective optimization (MOO), effectively addresses non-linearities and complex interactions within the modeling framework (Deb et al., 2002; Verma et al., 2021 ). Specifically, its aptitude for simultaneously optimizing multiple objectives underscores its utility in this context. The two-stage approach ensures superior generalization and heightened forecasting accuracy by intricately optimizing model performance, safeguarding against overfitting, and ensuring robust performance on unseen data (Diouf and Seck, 2019 ). The NSGA-II, developed by Deb et al., (2002) , is a robust MOO algorithm that extends the principles of GA. It is particularly adept at addressing complex optimization challenges involving multiple conflicting objectives and is widely recognized for its ability to delineate a set of optimal solutions, known as the Pareto front. This front represents the trade-offs among conflicting objectives, offering a spectrum of viable solutions (Naserizade et al., 2021 ). In this study, we employed the NSGA-II MOO algorithm to optimize model performance across both training and testing datasets by maximizing KGE. Similar to GWO, this involved minimizing the negative KGE (−f(x)) to achieve the objective. The decision variables were the weights assigned to each of the four ML models in an ensemble approach. The fitness function calculated the objectives; constraints  were set such that the model weights summed to one, and a population size  of 300 was used over 400 generations . The NSGA-II optimization resulted in a Pareto front showing the trade-off between training and testing errors across diverse solutions. The Pareto optimal solution closest to the origin (0,0) coordinates indicates a model with the most balanced performance − nearly equal error on train and test datasets. This suggests the model does not overfit the training data but rather has found a generalizable relationship that transfers well to new unseen data. Specifically, the Euclidean distance from each Pareto solution to the origin (0,0) was calculated using Eq. (8) .(8) d = ( KGE  train   )   2  + KGE  test      2          The final Chl-a forecasting model was determined by selecting the Pareto optimal solution with the minimum Euclidean distance. This ensures a low and balanced forecasting error on both the training and held-out test data. In developing data-driven predictive models, a crucial objective is to balance the effective fitting of the training data with ensuring generalization to unseen data. To address this, we compared the efficacy of single-objective GA optimization with MOO, NSGA-II, for creating ensembles to forecast Chl-a levels. This approach emphasizes finding a Pareto solution with optimal generalized performance. Fig. 4   visually represents the two main stages of our methodology, each comprising a series of well-defined steps. This structured approach ensures the robustness and reliability of our predictive models, ultimately contributing to more accurate WQ forecasting.   2.5 Model evaluation criteria In order to conduct a statistical assessment of the functionality of the advanced models in comparison to the standalone models, three metrics—Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Percent Bias (PBIAS)—were used (Moriasi et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2009 ). NSE quantifies how well the plot of observed versus forecasted data fits the 1:1 line. Values closer to 1 indicate more accurate model forecasting. KGE assesses the correlation (r), variability ratio (α), and bias ratio (β) between observed and simulated data. A KGE value closer to 1 indicates that the model performs well across these three aspects. PBIAS measures the average tendency of the simulated estimates to be larger or smaller than their observed counterparts. A value of 0 indicates an unbiased model (Moriasi et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2023 ). The mathematical formulations are outlined below.(9) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y i  ^     2   ∑ i = 1  n  ( y i  - y  ¯   i  )   2       (10) K G E = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( α - 1 )  2  + ( β - 1 )  2        (11) PBIAS = 100 × ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - y i  ^   ∑ i = 1  n  y i  ^        where, y i     represents observed data values at each time step i   , while y i  ^     denotes the model’s forecasted data values at the same time steps. The mean of the observed data over the evaluation period, y  ¯   i    , serves as a baseline for calculating deviations in the NSE metric. The correlation coefficient r    measures the degree of linear correlation between the observed and forecasted data, providing insight into the model's predictive accuracy. The variability ratio α   , defined as the ratio of the standard deviation of the forecasted data to that of the observed data, assesses how well the model captures data variability. Lastly, the bias ratio β   , calculated as the ratio of the average forecasted values to the average observed values, evaluates the model’s tendency to overestimate or underestimate the magnitude of the observed data, indicating the presence of any systematic bias in the model outputs.   3 Results 3.1 Grey wolf optimization results This study aimed to design an enhanced ML modeling framework for forecasting two WQ parameters − Chl-a and DO − in Small Prespa Lake, Greece. Table 2  summarizes the default parameters, their respective lower and upper bounds, and the optimized values attained through GWO for four distinct models (e.g., GBR, XGB, LightGBM, and MLP). A thorough exploration of hyperparameter tuning within our research is initiated, delving into the nuanced adjustments crafted to enhance the performance of XGB, GBR, LightGBM, and MLP. Shifting focus to XGB, LR  assumes a crucial role in regulating convergence speed and training efficiency. MD  was tuned to balance the complexity of individual trees and their ability to capture intricate patterns. SS  was adjusted to enhance diversity within the ensemble, while CBT  controlled feature sampling to prevent overfitting. In GBR, NE  influenced ensemble diversity and robustness. MSL  and MSS  were adjusted to control decision tree granularity, impacting overall model complexity. For LightGBM, the LR  influenced convergence behavior and training efficiency. SS  and CBT  mirrored their roles in XGB, regulating data and feature sampling. NL  uniquely controlled the maximum number of leaves in a tree, influencing the model's overall complexity. In the case of MLP, HLS  were tuned to determine the architecture and capacity of the NN . Al  represented L2  regularization strength, striking a balance between fitting the data and avoiding overfitting. LR  influenced optimization convergence, and the SLV , designated as constant “Adam” based on experience, leveraged the known effectiveness of the Adam optimizer. The convergence curves of negative KGE as the objective function value of GWO-optimized models, depicted in Fig. 5   for Chl-a forecasting, reveal distinct patterns for each model. The LightGBM model exhibits a rapid decrease in negative KGE during the initial iterations, followed by smoother improvement, stabilizing around iteration  48. This quick convergence indicates efficient early exploration and swift identification of optimal solutions by the GWO. In contrast, the XGB model shows a gradual decrease in negative KGE with periods of stability, achieving convergence at iteration  49. This trend suggests consistent and steady improvement in solutions, indicative of a reliable optimization process. The GBR model shows a steady decrease in negative KGE up to around iteration  76, followed by stabilization, with an early sharp fall highlighting GWO’s ability to transition to superior solutions swiftly. The GBR model achieved optimal results with a population size  of 40. Lastly, the MLP model experiences an initial swift fall in negative KGE, followed by fluctuations, and eventually converges around iteration  24, achieving a solution with a less significant improvement in the final negative KGE compared to GBMs. For MLP, a larger population size  of 70 was necessary, indicating rapid initial optimization with further fine-tuning needed for stabilization. In forecasting DO, the optimized LightGBM model demonstrates a notable decrease in negative KGE within the initial 26 iterations , followed by a smooth convergence, stabilizing around iteration  50. This rapid improvement suggests that GWO efficiently identifies and adjusts hyperparameters, enhancing model performance swiftly with a population size  of 20. The smooth descent implies a favorable search space conducive to effective exploration. The consistently decreasing curve reflects optimization efficiency, highlighting GWO’s ability to rapidly discover promising solutions and incrementally refine them without encountering stagnation. This pattern underscores LightGBM’s consistent and efficient optimization process across different forecasting tasks, reaching optimal solutions quickly. The distinct optimization behaviors across models highlight the variability in how each model explores and converges to optimal solutions when combined with GWO. LightGBM consistently shows efficient early exploration and rapid convergence, making it a robust choice for both Chl-a and DO forecasting. In contrast, models such as XGB and GBR provide steady and reliable optimization processes suitable for scenarios requiring consistent improvement over iterations. The MLP model’s quick initial optimization, followed by fine-tuning, suggests its potential for scenarios where rapid near-optimal solutions are needed, with additional iterations for refinement. The GWO yielded notable improvements in predictive accuracy across individual ML models in forecasting Chl-a and DO, respectively (Table 3  ). For Chl-a, specifically, the LightGBM model experienced an increase of 0.22 in training KGE and 0.15 in test KGE after GWO optimization. The XGB model exhibited a substantial improvement, with a surge of 0.33 in training KGE and 0.23 in test KGE. Similarly, the GBR model achieved an advancement of 0.08 in training KGE and 0.11 in test KGE. Even the MLP model, while showing comparatively smaller improvements, saw an increase of 0.03 in training KGE and 0.07 in test KGE. In terms of achieving the greatest improvement after GWO optimization for Chl-a, the XGB model stands out. Post-GWO, the XGB demonstrated substantial model improvement across KGE and NSE metrics with 0.23 and 0.27 improvements in test sets, respectively. Conversely, the MLP model with 0.07 enhancement in the KGE test exhibited the lowest improvement in comparison to the other three models, suggesting that GWO had a comparatively smaller impact on improving the MLP model's predictive performance. This aligns with earlier observations in environmental data forecasting, where optimized GBMs demonstrated superiority over tuned DL models such as MLP. A study shows the superiority of LightGBM and XGB compared to MLP for predicting solar radiance (Soleymani and Mohammadzadeh, 2023 ). In another study, Schmitt demonstrated that GBM had higher prediction accuracy than DL (Schmitt, 2022 ). Addo et al. (2018)  proved that tree-based models were more stable than the models based on ANNs. In the financial subject, based on the observations of Gunnarsson et al. (2021) , XGB outperformed other introduced models, including MLP for credit scoring. Furthermore, in comparative analysis across diverse tabular dataset benchmarks, the consistently superior performance of gradient-boosting decision trees—specifically XGB, LightGBM, and CatBoost—over their NN counterparts was evident, with MLP among the optimized models (McElfresh et al., 2023 ). There are some other studies that have shown GBMs handle skewed or heavy-tailed feature distributions and other dataset irregularities more effectively than NNs (Borisov et al., 2024; Gorishniy et al., 2021; Grinsztajn et al., 2022; Shwartz-Ziv and Armon, 2021 ). Table 3  illustrates that optimizing the LightGBM model for forecasting DO using GWO has also proven effective, as evidenced by some improvements across multiple performance metrics. Notably, NSE and KGE increased by 0.08 and 0.05, respectively, in the training set and 0.03 and 0.07 in the test set. Additionally, PBIAS improved from −12.31 % to −4.76 % in the test set, reflecting satisfactory model performance. These results underscore the efficacy of GWO in fine-tuning model parameters and enhancing predictive performance. Our findings align with previous studies that have applied GWO in combination with gradient-boosting decision trees to improve performance and predictive capabilities. For example, a recent study employed GWO alongside other optimization algorithms to fine-tune ML models for fault early warning, concluding that LightGBM is more reliable than NN models such as LSTM-CNN (Delpla et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, in a separate instance involving carbon price forecasting across different carbon emission trading markets, integrating GWO optimization with XGB proved beneficial. The GWO-XGB model achieved superior forecasting accuracy compared to the standalone XGB (Li et al., 2024 ). Additionally, the efficacy of GWO for tuning model hyperparameters was validated by comparing its performance against grid search and random search. The percent improvement in KGE with GWO was higher relative to random search and grid search due to GWO’s exhaustive search approach. Specifically, GWO improved KGE by 6.15 %, 5.25 %, 3.6 %, and 3.75 % more than the best grid search hyperparameters for XGB, LightGBM, GBR, and MLP, respectively. Compared to random search, GWO achieved an even greater improvement in KGE, with increases of 7.6 %, 7.3 %, 6.65 %, and 5.25 % for the four models, respectively. The scatter plots in Fig. 6   provide valuable insights into the performance of various machine learning models in forecasting Chl-a and DO levels in Small Prespa Lake. The r  metric measures the strength of the linear regression between observed and forecasted values, with the strongest linear relationship occurring when r  equals 1. For DO forecasting, the LightGBM model exhibits excellent performance, achieving a correlation coefficient (r ) of 0.96, with very tight clustering around the regression line. For Chl-a forecasting, all models (GBR, MLP, LightGBM, and XGB) demonstrate a positive correlation between forecasted and actual values, with r  ranging from 0.85 to 0.91. LightGBM exhibits the strongest performance, indicated by the tightest clustering around its regression line (r  = 0.91), followed closely by GBR (r  = 0.89). Despite the overall strong performance, the scatter plots reveal a consistent pattern of slight underestimation at higher Chl-a values (>5 μg/L) and overestimation at low values (<2 μg/L) across all models, particularly noticeable in MLP. This issue likely arises from the complex and non-linear relationships between input features and high quantile values, which standard ML models might struggle to capture. Employing ensemble methods by combining multiple models can help better capture these complex relationships.  3.2 Ensemble models results The implementation of the NSGA-II ensemble model (NSGA-II-EM) involved setting parameters such as population size , generations , crossover , and mutation probabilities . The objective functions focused on maximizing KGE (minimizing negative KGE) on both training and testing data. Table S1  illustrates the ensemble configuration for MOO along with GA as a single optimization in this study. NSGA-II-EM simultaneously optimized training and testing errors as objectives to generate solutions across an optimal Pareto front (Fig. 7  I). The resulting ensemble from this front achieved a trade-off between training error and generalization error. Solutions at one extreme maximized the KGE train by overfitting the training data, while those at the other extreme exhibited better generalization but poorer training fit. This dual-objective and ensemble-based methodology empowered NSGA-II to uncover generalized solutions effectively. In contrast, employing single-objective GA optimization often led to overfitting issues. Optimizing solely for training error typically yielded an ensemble too closely tailored to the training data, while prioritizing testing error tended to produce an ensemble favoring test performance but lacking training fit. In essence, when the GA is solely optimized for training error (KGE train), convergence after 40 generations  leads to an ensemble that perfectly fits the training data (KGE train = 0.978). However, this overfitting resulted in poorer performance on the test set (KGE test = 0.892). Conversely, when optimization focused solely on test performance (KGE test), the GA solution achieved a maximum KGE test of 0.905 (Fig. 7 II). Nevertheless, despite its superior test metrics, this ensemble demonstrated a poorer training fit with a KGE train of 0.935 (Fig. 7 I and 7II). Essentially, the single-objective GA tended to prioritize one dataset over the other, often resulting in suboptimal performance overall. Table 4   provides detailed information on decision variables and objective function values for critical solutions depicted in Fig. 7 . Among these, Solutions 1 and 2 were suggested by the GA, while Solution 4 was ultimately chosen. The proposed approach involved determining the optimal solution based on its minimum Euclidean distance, effectively mitigating extremes and leading to a comprehensive and robust solution. The chosen solution achieved a KGE train of 0.948 and a KGE test of 0.905. For better comparison, previously utilized metrics were computed and presented in Table 3  (EM column), demonstrating competitiveness even against the best individually optimized ML models across key metrics. The ensemble model attained higher correlation on both training (0.97) and testing (0.90) datasets and better performance on the test set with NSE of 0.92 and KGE of 0.91, outperforming the top standalone model LightGBM, which had respective values of 0.82 and 0.84. Additionally, the ensemble model achieved a lower PBIAS of −5.88 % on the test data compared to −11.53 % for LightGBM, indicating improved model fit. This enhanced generalization capability underscores the benefits of the two-stage modeling approach, with GWO hyperparameter tuning followed by NSGA-II ensemble optimization. As shown in the radar plot (Fig. 8  ) comparing model metrics on the test set, the ensemble model attained improved performance across multiple indicators, including NSE, KGE, and PBIAS. The integrated optimization framework enhanced the KGE test performance by 7 % compared to the best-optimized model, LightGBM, and by up to 16 % compared to the optimized MLP.   4 Discussion The findings of this study reveal the significant impact of GWO on enhancing the performance of ML models for forecasting Chl-a and DO in Small Prespa Lake, Greece. By meticulously tuning hyperparameters specific to each model—GBR, XGB, LightGBM, and MLP—GWO significantly improved key performance metrics, including NSE and KGE, across both training and test datasets. The reasons for these improvements are multifaceted and warrant thorough examination. Firstly, GWO’s effectiveness in hyperparameter tuning stems from its nature-inspired optimization algorithm, which mimics the leadership hierarchy and hunting mechanism of grey wolves (Mirjalili et al., 2014 ). This approach allows GWO to efficiently explore and exploit the search space, avoiding local optima and finding the best possible hyperparameter configurations. In the case of LightGBM, the rapid and efficient optimization observed in the convergence curves indicates that GWO quickly identified optimal hyperparameters, enhancing the model’s predictive accuracy. This efficiency is crucial in environmental modeling, where the complexity and variability of data can hinder model performance if not properly optimized (Song et al., 2023 ). Secondly, the improved performance of GBR and XGB models post-optimization highlights GWO’s capability to handle the intricate balance between bias and variance. By fine-tuning parameters such as learning rate, maximum depth, and subsample ratios, GWO ensured that these models maintained high accuracy while avoiding overfitting (Qiu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022 ). The consistency in the performance of these gradient-boosting models across different datasets demonstrates their robustness, particularly in handling skewed or irregular data distributions common in environmental studies. The steady and reliable improvements in these models emphasize the importance of targeted hyperparameter optimization in achieving superior predictive performance (Gao et al., 2020 ). Lastly, while MLP required larger population sizes  for optimization, the substantial improvements observed post-optimization justify the computational expense. MLPs, being neural network-based models, inherently require extensive fine-tuning due to their complex architecture. GWO’s ability to adaptively adjust parameters such as hidden layer sizes , learning rates , and regularization  strengths enabled the MLP to achieve significant performance gains. This is particularly important in scenarios where rapid initial optimization followed by fine-tuning is crucial, as it ensures that the model can quickly adapt to the data’s underlying patterns and nuances (Dehghanbanadaki et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2021 ). The comparative analysis, conducted post-optimization, highlights the enhanced performance of GBMs compared to neural network-based models. Optimized iterations of LightGBM and XGB consistently surpassed the performance of the MLP model, corroborating existing research that underscores the effectiveness of GBMs with skewed or irregular datasets. Additionally, the incorporation of the NSGA-II ensemble model resulted in further improvements in predictive accuracy. This ensemble approach successfully balanced training and generalization errors by harnessing the strengths of various models, leading to increased robustness and generalization capabilities, as evidenced by improved metrics across multiple evaluations. Supporting this, several studies in the literature corroborate our findings, demonstrating that ensemble models excel beyond individual ML models. Our research, conducted at Small Prespa Lake, draws comparisons with findings from Zamani et al. (2023) , who found that their deep learning-based NSGA-II-EM outperformed the combined LSTM and CNN model by (Barzegar et al., 2020 ) in forecasting Chl-a concentrations. Notably, our study achieved superior outcomes relative to those reported by Zamani et al. (2023). Additionally, Gao et al. (2020)  showed that their designed ensemble models exceeded the performance of a hybrid model, demonstrating the advantages of integrating multiple methodologies. A similar advancement was reported by Jia et al. (2023) , who applied ensemble models to natural language processing (NLP) to capitalize on the strengths of diverse models, thereby enhancing predictive accuracy and generalization. Moreover, Mahmud et al. (2023)  concluded that among their three proposed models, the hybrid ARMA-GARCH model excelled over the standalone ARMA and PROPHET models, illustrating its superior predictive accuracy for drought forecasting. In a related study, Song et al. (2023)  combined LSTM with metaheuristic optimization techniques to boost DO forecasting, affirming the superior performance of ensemble models using GA and NSGA-II, which mirrors the findings of our current study.  5 Summary and conclusions This study aimed to develop an enhanced ML framework for forecasting Chl-a and DO concentrations in Small Prespa Lake, Greece. Using a high-resolution time series dataset of physicochemical measurements, four complementary ML algorithms − MLP, XGB, LightGBM, and GBR − were optimized using GWO at the first stage. For DO, the initial results from the base LightGBM model, fine-tuned with GWO optimization, were so promising that further multi-objective NSGA-II optimization was deemed unnecessary. For Chl-a, the models were optimized using GWO and further improved through multi-objective NSGA-II ensembling. The modeling process involved rigorous data preprocessing, including lag time feature engineering and PCA dimensionality reduction. Following hyperparameter tuning with GWO, the models demonstrated significant improvement in KGE, validating the optimization approach. The NSGA-II-EM achieved superior performance, increasing testing KGE by 7 % compared to the best individual optimized model for forecasting Chl-a. The MOO enabled the selection of solutions that balanced model fit and generalization capability, and the integrated framework attained high accuracy in Chl-a forecasting on the test set. This research showcases the efficacy of techniques such as advanced preprocessing, algorithm optimization, and multi-objective ensembling in advancing ML for WQ forecasting. Based on the promising results, future endeavors could explore hybrid ML approaches, combining tree-based models with other NNs such as LSTM or GRU and optimizing the hybrid architecture using multi-objective algorithms. Such an integration could enhance predictive capabilities. Moreover, exploring emerging swarm and evolutionary optimization algorithms, such as Salp Swarm Algorithm and Moth-Flame Optimization, for hyperparameter tuning and ensemble weighting could be a fruitful avenue for further research. The strength of this study lies in implementing a comprehensive ML approach not previously explored for this application. Accurately forecasting WQ parameters including Chl-a and DO levels is crucial for managing and protecting precious water resources. The results of our study hold considerable implications for planners, engineers, and modelers. For planners, these improved forecasting models can facilitate the development of more effective water management strategies, proactively monitor potential WQ issues, and prevent deterioration (Delpla et al., 2019; Wai et al., 2022 ). They can leverage these predictive models to design superior water treatment and distribution systems, ensuring safe and clean water supplies (Nasir et al., 2022 ). Engineers and modelers can optimize the operation of existing water infrastructure, reduce costs, and ensure that treatment processes are adjusted in real-time based on accurate forecasting of WQ parameters. These advanced techniques can help develop more precise and comprehensive models of water systems, leading to improved decision-making and policy development (Ejigu, 2021; Mosleh and Negahban-Azar, 2021 ). Our research could be highly beneficial for existing programs and initiatives related to WQ management and environmental monitoring in Greece and beyond. For example, the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research (HCMR), a leading marine research institution in Greece, could integrate our predictive models into their monitoring programs to enhance their ability to assess and manage WQ parameters in lakes and coastal areas. The methods and findings of this study have the potential to be generalized to other areas with similar characteristics. Key characteristics of such areas include the availability of comprehensive and high-resolution time series data for physico-chemical parameters, similar environmental conditions, and where noticing a parameter level in advance is crucial. However, customizing the ML framework to suit different regions' specific characteristics and requirements may be required for optimal performance. Moreover, ensuring the quality and consistency of input data is essential for model accuracy and reliability. Additionally, adapting models to account for temporal and spatial variability in environmental conditions is necessary for maintaining forecasting accuracy over time. Nevertheless, several sources of uncertainty must be acknowledged. First, data availability over extended periods could further enhance model learning and trend detection capabilities. Moreover, like other machine learning techniques, our models assume that the relationships between input variables and dependent WQVs are consistent over time. However, this assumption may not hold true in dynamic environmental systems, where factors influencing WQ can change. This temporal and spatial variability introduces uncertainty into the forecasting of the model. Furthermore, the selected machine learning models struggled to capture complex and non-linear relationships between input features and high quantile values. This limitation could affect the accuracy of forecasting during extreme events or unusual conditions. Additionally, there may be uncertainties related to data quality and measurement errors in the input variables. Inaccuracies in sensor data or inconsistencies in data collection protocols can propagate through the model, impacting its reliability. Employing ensemble methods that combine multiple models could better capture these intricate relationships and reduce uncertainty. Despite these challenges, the methodology and insights gained contribute significantly to strengthening predictive capabilities and proactive monitoring for improved water management. Future studies can shed light on developing models that can adapt to changing environmental conditions and incorporate temporal and spatial variability more effectively. Addressing these uncertainties will enhance the robustness and applicability of ML models in real-world WQ forecasting scenarios.
1 Introduction The Jingjiang Reach of the middle Yangtze River connects with Dongting Lake through three diversion branches (distributaries), the Songzi River, Hudu River, and Ouchi River. In recent decades, water and sediment within the mainstream of the Jingjiang Reach have usually flowed into Dongting Lake, even though water–sediment diversion through the three distributaries has been continuously declining (Yu et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2022, 2023 ). Nevertheless, two back-flow events occurred in 2015 and 2017 (Feng et al., 2019 ). On June 1st , 2015, a cruise ship named “Eastern Star” carrying 454 people sank during a storm in the Jianli segment of the Jingjiang Reach. Only 12 survived. As attempts were taking place to rescue people trapped in the upturned hull, the Changjiang Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters enforced emergency regulation of the TGD, which reduced the reservoir outflow from 17200 m3 /s to 7000 m3 /s and lowered the water level along the Jingjiang Reach. During this period, the total back-flow volume was 1.27 × 108  m3 . The second back-flow event occurred on July 1st , 2017, as the first flood of the year began to form in the middle and lower Yangtze River. For flood-control purposes, the TGD reduced its outflow from 27300 m3 /s to 8000 m3 /s, which effectively suppressed any further water-level rise in Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake. While the reservior operations took place, the total back-flow volume was 0.56 × 108  m3 . The foregoing two back-flow events are historically rare phenomena, which both occurred during the flood season of the Yangtze River, when the water level within Jingjiang Reach is usually high and hardly able to form the inverse water-surface slope required for back-flow between Jingjiang mainstream and Dongting Lake. During both historical events, TGD operation played the dominant role even though the flood season water discharge was huge from the tributary rivers, such as the Xiangjiang River, Zijiang River, Yuanjiang River and Lishui River (located in the southwest of Dongting Lake), producing a rapid rise in water level within the lake (Feng et al., 2019 ) that faciliated the back flow. This may be interpreted as follows. Other than the two severe events mentiond above, back-flow has not occurred in recent years even when the water discharge from the southwest four rivers and other tributaries was very large during the flood season, including 1954 when tributary water discharges were the largest on record (Yu et al., 2018 ). However, during the flood seasons of 2015 and 2017, the TGD outflow was substantially reduced because of reservoir operations, resulting in abnormally low water-level conditions within the Jingjiang Reach and subsequent inverse water-surface slopes for back-flows between the Jingjiang mainstream and Dongting Lake (Feng et al., 2019 ). Besides providing emergency regulation for special events, the TGD modulates the intra-year hydrologic process downstream. More precisely, the TGD attenuates the deluge peak during a flood event, stores water during the impoundment period, and augments the outflow during drought (Zhu et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023a ). Since 2010, the TGD has witnessed two important changes in its mode of operation. First, the start time of the impoundment was shifted from early October to mid-September to mitigate downstream drought during the flood recession period (Li et al., 2013 ). Second, regulation of small- and medium-sized flood was implemented to generate a compensation effect on flood control in the vicinity of Chenglingji and areas south of the Jingjiang Reach, to increase electricity production, and to quickly evacuate ships blocked between the TGD and the Gezhou Dam. This regulation measure has constrained the TGD outflow to be less than 45000 m3 /s through trapping incoming water discharges larger than 40000 m3 /s rather than the previous 55000 m3 /s (Cai, 2011 ). By bringing forward impoundment of the TGD, there is a corresponding early fall in water level within the Jingjiang Reach (Zheng et al., 2015 ). Meanwhile, the small- and medium-sized flood regulation of the TGD reduces its outflow during the flood season (Cai, 2011 ). Consequently, flow within the Jingjiang Reach mainly scours medium–low water channels but rarely submerges bars and beaches during TGD-impoundment and flood periods (Li et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023b ). This promotes sedimentation and augments flow resistance at the crests of bars and at beaches, and finally triggers a significant fall in low-water level and a slight change (even a slight rise) in flood-water level for the same discharge (Han et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, sediment interception by the TGD has brought about remarkable erosion in the Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake, causing the water-level to decline for the same discharge (Zhou et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023b ). Hence, the TGD operation inevitably affects the hydrodynamic inter-jacking between Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake and interferes with the occurrence frequency of a given back-flow event. It is obviously important to understand the mechanism of hydrodynamic inter-jacking and thus be able to track a given back-flow event during the post-TGD period. In fact, other major human activities that have occurred along the Yangtze mainstream, such as the lower Jingjiang Cutoff Projects and impoundment of the Gezhou Dam, have also impacted significantly on the hydrodynamic inter-jacking (Zhu et al., 2022, 2023 ). Here, the contribution ratios of the foregoing human interference and natural driving factor (i.e. precipitation) are identified only as a quantitative expression of the hydrodynamic inter-jacking has been put forward. Downscaling apllied on satellite data can only obtain precipitation and/or runoff results at large spatial scale (e.g. a catchment scale) when hydrologic models are simultaneously used (Zhang et al., 2019 ). To remedy this, we adopt hydrologic analysis based on measured flood processes at adjacent sites, accompanied by Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) survey data, to ascertain flood-encounter combinations within the intersection area between river mainstreams and tributaries when information is lakcing on reservoirs, barrage structures, and land use (Jiang et al., 2023 ). However, large numbers of photograph-control points are required by the UAV survey method. Previous investigations have also focused on the impacts of tributary influx on mainstream flow structure, including changes to core flow velocity, turbulent kinetic energy, recirculation vortices, helical flow, and secondary current (Lu et al., 2023; Song et al., 2022, 2023 ). The foregoing provides fundamental insight concerning the hydrodynamic behavior within the intersection area. Approches to quantify the interactions between mainstream rivers and their distributaries/tributaries usually include calculations of the variation in water storage capacity of a distributary/tributary lake (Kummu et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2014a; Dai et al., 2021 ), quantification of the water level difference between a mainstream river and a distributary/tributary lake (Lai et al., 2014b ), formulation of a (kinetic/potential) energy index for the mouth of a connection channel (Chen et al., 2018 ) or a hydrodynamic index for back-flow evaluation (Luo et al., 2022 ), construction of an integrated hydrodynamic model (e.g. flood-wave propagation model) for back-flow identification (Dias de Paiva et al., 2013 ), and establishment of empirical formulae for estimating flow discharge at the connection channel mouth (Li et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022 ). Of these approaches, the last is the most direct and convenient for estimating the flow discharge at the mouth. However, existing empirical formulae can only represent the discharge for one or the other of the normal-flow and back-flow events, not both. Such formulae are usually derived from simple correlation analyses and regression tests, rather than fundamental hydrodynamic theory. Moreover, it should be noted that the situation is more complicated for Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake. The three distributaries, i.e., the Songzi, Hudu, and Ouchi rivers, are each more than 100 km long and their back flow may occur in one or more of the following three ways: (1) water flows into Jingjiang Reach from connection-channel segments close to the near-mainstream mouths; (2) water flows into the connection channels from the core lake basin, and (3) water flows into Jingjiang Reach from the core lake basin through long-distance transport within the connection channels. To overcome the foregoing difficulties, we first quantify hydrodynamic inter-jacking between the Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake by establishing empirical flow-discharge formulae at the two ends of the three distributaries using the Saint-Venant Equation and the Fall Index Method, based on long-term water discharge-level series from 1955 to 2023 recorded at nearby hydrological stations. These formulae provide fair representation of both the normal-flow and back-flow discharges. Then, we plot hydraulic zoning charts to provide a method for rapidly identifying which of the three kinds of back-flow events is of interest. Finally, we explore the effects of human interference and precipitation on flow discharge at two ends of the three distributaries and estimate the occurrence frequency of back-flow events during the post-TGD period. Findings from this study should also be relevant in assessing engineering projects planned for the intersection area between Jingjiang Reach and Dongting Lake, and lead to better hydraulic control of the river–lake connection system, which is beneficial for policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders.  2 Geographical setting The Jingjiang Reach is situated in the middle Yangtze River, stretching 347 km from Zhicheng hydrological station to the outlet of Dongting Lake at Chenglingji (Fig. 1  a). Water discharge is regularly diverted from Jingjiang Reach into Dongting Lake through the mouths of three distributaries located at Songzikou, Taipingkou, and Ouchikou (Fig. 1 b). In detail, water from the middle Yangtze River enters the mouths of the distributaries and flows over long distances within the connection channels, finally entering the core lake basin (Fig. 1 b). The Jingjiang Reach is divided into upper and lower segments at Ouchikou (Fig. 1 b). The three connection channels (i.e., the Songzi, Hudu, and Ouchi rivers) are intricately configured and have main stems that stretch distances of 135 km, 138 km, and 106 km, respectively (Fig. 1 b). Additionally, there are another four major tributaries supplying water to Dongting Lake from the southwest, namely the Xiangjiang, Zijiang, Yuanjiang, and Lishui rivers (Fig. 1 b). After redistribution in the core lake basin, water flows back into Jingjiang Reach at Chenglingji (Fig. 1 b). Water discharge along the Jingjiang Reach is recorded at Zhicheng hydrological staion, that at Songzikou is evaluated as the sum of flow records obtained at Xinjiangkou and Shadaoguan hydrological stations, that at Taipingkou is acquired from Mituosi hydrological station, and that at Ouchikou is calculated as the sum of flow records obtained at Kangjiagang and Guanjiapu hydrological stations (Fig. 1 b). Water discharges at mouths located at the near-lake ends of the Songzi and Hudu rivers are respectively recorded at Anxiang and Dongjiadang hydrological stations, that at the near-lake mouth of the east branch of Ouchi River is measured at Nanxian hydrological station, and that at the near-lake mouth of the convergence segment of the middle and west branches of Ouchi River is estimated as the sum of flow records at Kangjiagang and Guanjiapu hydrological stations minus the record at Nanxian hydrological station, noting that Sanchahe hydrological station only documents the water level at the convergence segment (Fig. 1 b). Water levels at the two ends of the connection channels are also recorded at the foregoing hydrological stations. Daily water discharge and level time series at the hydrological stations over the past 68 years (1955–2023) were obtained from the Changjiang Water Resources Commission and the hydrology website (URL: yzt.hnswkcj.com :9090/#/) for Hunan Province, China.  3 Methods 3.1 Change mechanism for flow discharge at two ends of the connection channels Owing to hydrodynamic inter-jacking effects at the two ends of the connection channels, the correlation between water level and discharge is not single-valued, and so our calculations are based on the Saint-Venant momentum equation (Xu et al., 2012 ) given as:(1) i - ∂ h  ∂ s   + 1 g  ∂ v  ∂ t   + v g  ∂ v  ∂ s   + v v    R C 2    = 0     where i  is river bed slope, h  (in m) is water depth, v  (in m) is flow velocity, s  (in m) is flow distance, t  (in s) is time, R  (in m) is hydraulic radius, C  (in m1/2 /s) is Chézy coefficient, and g  (in m/s2 ) is acceleration due to gravity. According to the Fall Index Method (Dai, 2001 ), the inertia item in Eq. (1)  may be ignored, so that:(2) q = Q Δ z α    = f z       where Δz  (in m) is the water-level difference between reference and target stations, α  is the fall index and ranges from 0 to 1, Q  (in m3 /s) is the actual flow discharge, and q  is a correction factor for flow discharge, which is also called the single-valued flow discharge. In this study, target stations are located at the two ends of the connection channels, whereas reference stations are located at intervals within the channels. According to Eq. (2) , the flow discharges at the ends of the channels are directly related to water levels at the target stations and water-level difference Δz  values (between reference and target stations), as displayed in Figs. S1-S3 . However, we rather expect that this kind of correlation can be projected onto two other driving factors, namely, the water discharge from the Yangtze mainstream and the total discharge from the four southwest tributary rivers. This provides a more convenient way to predict flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels because the mainstream and tributary water discharges are single-valued and consecutively recorded at relevant hydrological stations. The foregoing projection can be achieved provided the target-station water levels and the target-reference-station Δz  values depend strongly on mainstream and tributary water discharges, given hydrodynamic inter-jacking at the two ends of the connection channels. Figs. S4-S7  show the dependences are as follows: (1) Water levels at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels are positively correlated with water discharge from Zhicheng station; and those at the near-lake ends of the connection channels (except for Nanxian station) are positively correlated with water discharges from Zhicheng station and the four southwest tributary rivers. The water level at Nanxian station only remains positively correlated with water discharge from Zhicheng station because Nanxian station is isolated from the west and south lake basins which receive water discharges from the four southwest tributary rivers. (2) When low water levels are recorded at corresponding target stations, the Δz  values appear uncorrelated with water discharges from Zhicheng station and the four southwest tributary rivers. For high water levels, the Δz  values become either positively or negatively correlated with the water discharges. In other words, water discharges from the Yangtze mainstream and the four southwest tributary rivers are strongly associated with water levels at target stations and Δz  values between reference and target stations, and therefore determine flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels. The impact of the Yangtze mainstream and the four southwest tributary rivers on flow discharge at the two ends of the connection channels at different times within a complete hydrological cycle is as follows (Lai et al., 2014a; Dai et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018 ): (1) During the dry season, water discharges are small in the Yangtze mainstream and four southwest tributary rivers, and so lakeward flow discharges and water levels are correspondingly low in the connection channels. (2) As the four southwest tributary rivers enter the flood season, their water discharges increase, causing the lakeward flow to experience jacking at the near-lake ends of the connection channels. As a result, water surface slopes within the connection channels decline, leading to decreases in Δz  values between the reference and target stations distributed along the connection channels and corresponding reductions in lakeward flow discharges at the ends. (3) As the Yangtze River enters the flood season, the water discharge at Zhicheng increases and water levels rapidly rise at target stations at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels, resulting in the Yangtze mainstream dominating the interaction with the four southwest tributary rivers, thus augmenting the Δz  values. Hence, lakeward flow discharges increase at the two ends of the connection channels. (4) Subsequently, water discharges from Zhicheng station and the four southwest tributary rivers gradually decrease, water levels along the connection channels drop, and lakeward flow discharges at the ends of the connection channels correspondingly reduce, indicating that the next dry season has arrived. During the above cycle, if the water level within the Yangtze mainstream is extremely low or the jacking effect of the four southwest tributary rivers is exceedingly strong, back flows may occur from the connection channels into the mainstream.  3.2 Derivation of empirical formulae for flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels Flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels are influenced by water discharges from Zhicheng station and the four southwest tributary rivers, and so are decomposed into two parts, expressed as:(3) Q = a 0  + a 1  Q z  + a 2  Q f      where Qz   (in m3 /s) represents the water discharge component related to the flow at Zhicheng station when the Yangtze mainstream dominates the interaction with the four southwest tributary rivers, Qf   (in m3 /s) is the component impacted by water discharges from the four southwest tributary rivers when the Yangtze mainstream plays an inferior role in the interaction, and a 0 , a 1  and a 2  are correction coefficients. When a back-flow event occurs, the flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels have negative values. To deal with this problem, a synthetic discharge, which is consistently positive, is introduced to characterize the flow discharge. Noting the dominance of the four southwest tributary rivers when interacting with the Yangtze mainstream during a back-flow event and the functional relationship among Q , z , and Δz  in Eq. (2) , the synthetic discharge can be expressed as:(4) Q  ¯   = a Q f  + 1 - a    Q f ′  = f z   Δ z α  = f z r  , z t         where Q  ¯     (in m3 /s) is synthetic discharge, Q f ′    (in m3 /s) is total water discharge from the four southwest tributary rivers, zr   (in m) and zt   (in m) are water levels at reference and target stations, and a  is a weighting coefficient in the range from 0 to 1. Given the high positive correlation between zr   and zt   (Fig. S8 ), Eq. (4)  may be further simplified to give:(5) Q  ¯   = a Q f  + 1 - a    Q f ′  = g z t         Rearranging Eq. (5) ,(6) Q f  = 1 a  g z t    - 1 - a  a  Q f ′       It can be seen from Eqs (5) and (6)  that linear relationships hold between the flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels and the total water discharge from the four southwest tributary rivers, and so we analogously infer that:(7) Q z  = a 3  Q z ′      where Q z ′    (in m3 /s) is the water discharge at Zhicheng station, and a 3  is an empirical coefficient. Substituting Eqs (6) and (7)  into Eq. (3) , we obtain:(8) Q = a 0  + a 2  1 a  g z t    - 1 - a  a  Q f ′     + a 4  Q z ′      where a 4  is the correction coefficient. Simplifying Eq. (8) , we obtain the final form of the empirical formula that governs flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels as follows:(9) Q = a 0  + a 5  z t α  + a 6  Q f ′  + a 4  Q z ′      where a 5  and a 6  are further empirical coefficients. The coefficients in Eq. (9)  are quantitatively determined using the following three-step procedure: (1) In Eq. (5) , we assume Qf   = Q , which is reasonable because the flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels are primarily influenced by the water discharges from the four southwest tributary rivers during back-flow events. (2) We adjust the value of a  in Eq. (5)  to obtain the highest correlation coefficient (R 2 ) for the linear or curve fitting between a Q f  + 1 - a    Q f ′     and zt  . The resulting equation gives an expression for g (zt  ). (3) We substitute expression of g (zt  ) into Eq. (8)  to obtain a preliminary form of Eq. (9) , and then execute multiple linear regression between the dependent variable Q  and the independent variables z t α   , Q f ′   , Q z ′    in Eq. (9)  to obtain its final form.  3.3 Identification of driving-factor contributions to flow discharges at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels Unlike the intense human interference along the Yangtze mainstream that has greatly impacted on the flow discharges at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels (Zhu et al., 2022, 2023 ), human activities implemented in the Dongting Lake basin (e.g., land-use changes and sand mining) (Xie et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018 ) and along the four southwest tributary rivers (e.g., reservoir construction) (Yu et al., 2018 ) have had rather little effect on the flow discharges at the near-lake ends of the connection channels, and are not considered herein. Major human activities along the Yangtze mainstream comprise the lower Jingjiang Cutoff Projects initiated in October 1966 (Fig. 1 b), impoundment of the Gezhou Dam started in January 1981 (Fig. 1 a and 1b), initial impoundment of the TGD begun in June 2003 (Fig. 1 a and 1b), and test impoundment of the TGD commenced in September 2008 (Zhu et al., 2022, 2023 ). Accordingly, we divide the 1955–2023 inclusive period into the following five stages: 1955–1966, 1967–1980, 1981–2002, 2003–2008 and 2009–2023. Contribution ratios of driving factors on flow discharges at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels during each of the five stages are identified using the variable control approach (Dai et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2019 ). Table 1   lists the final form of the empirical formulae for the flow discharges, which attain high values of R 2 . Growth in Q z ′    enlarges flow discharge, whereas increasing Q f ′    reduces flow discharge. However, the contribution weights of Q f ′    in all the formulae are far smaller than those of Q z ′   , given the much lower absolute values of coefficients before Q f ′    than those before Q z ′   . This implies that Q z ′    is the dominant factor in determining flow discharge. High values of Q z ′    and Q f ′    tend to cause normal-flow and back-flow events respectively, and so the difference between their contribution weighting reflects both commonly occurring normal-flow and rare back-flow events within the connection channels over the past decades.  4.2 Verification of empirical formulae Fig. 2   shows that there is good consistency between the calculated (using the empirical formulae in Table 1 ) and observed results for the flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels, with high R 2  values achieved.
