Fig. 3   further demonstrates high consistency between the calculated and observed daily time series of flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels obtained by substituting the observed daily time series of zt   (i.e. zsdg  , zmts   and zgjp  ), Q z ′   , and Q f ′    during 2017–2023 into the empirical formulae. As indicated in Table 2  , close agreement is obtained between the calculated negative estimate and observed value of discharge Q 1  at Taipingkou. Calculated negative discharge only occurred during 3rd  ∼ 8th  July 2017 at Ouchikou when the historical back-flow event actually happened, whereas positive values of discharge Q 1  occupied the remainder of the period at the two mouths (Fig. 3 c and 3e). To be more precise, there is good agreement between the calculated and observed values of maximum normal-flow/back-flow discharge and cumulative normal-flow/back-flow volume at Songzikou, Taipingkou, and Ouchikou over the duration of the back-flow event, for calculations based on hourly zt  , Q z ′   , and Q f ′    data (Table 2 ). Please note that the back-flow event in 2015 was primarily triggered by artificial guidance (Feng et al., 2019 ), and so is not considered herein. The foregoing results confirm that the empirical formulae in Table 1  provide robust simulations of the flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels. Noting that Q f ′    has hardly any impact on the flow discharges, we ignore it and re-establish the empirical formulae as listed in Table 3  . The new formulae provide sensible results with high R 2  values.  4.3 Hydraulic zoning charts for rapid identification of back-flow events By applying the formulae listed in Table 3 , the hydraulic zoning charts in Fig. 4   are obtained. In Fig. 4 , the red/blue/green shaded areas and horizontal lines represent functional relationships among flow discharges at the two ends of the connection channels, water levels at corresponding target stations, and the water discharge at Zhicheng station. Fig. 4  shows that the two ends of all three connection channels undergo considerable ranges in water level at the target stations and water discharge at Zhicheng station during normal-flow events, but limited ranges during back-flow events. If we focus on extreme back-flow events during which lake-basin water flows along the length of each connection channel into the Yangtze mainstream, such that the flow discharges at both ends of each connection channel are negative, then the value ranges of the two variables become further constrained as indicated by the magenta-shaded areas in Fig. 4 . In order to facilitate rapid identificaiton of back-flow events into the future, Table 4   -Table 6   summarize the value ranges depicted in Fig. 4 .  4.4 Contributions of driving factors on flow discharges at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels Table S1  lists empirical formulae for flow discharges at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels during the first four historical stages. Based on formulae in Table 3  and Table S1 , flow discharges are reconstructed assuming the presence (or absence) of a given dam. Tables S2-S4  list the results for the three distributaries. Table 7   lists the contribution ratios of driving factors deduced for the five stages, from which the following can be inferred: (1) From the first to the second stage, the contribution from riverbed adjustment due to the lower Jingjiang Cutoff Projects dominated the reductions in flow discharge at the three near-mainstream ends, whereas the contribution from precipitation was secondary. (2) Form the second to the third stage, operation of the Gezhou Dam exerted no impact on flow discharge reductions at the three near-mainstream ends, characteristic of the dam acting as a low-head power station with small storage (Zhu et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, riverbed adjustment and precipitation appear to have made comparable contributions. The remarkable contribution of riverbed adjustment is related to both the sustained fall in riverbed level after implementation of the lower Jingjiang Cutoff Projects and the sediment-trapping effect of the Gezhou Dam (Zhu et al., 2023 ). (3) From the third to the fourth stage, TGD operations contributed 3 %∼4% to the flow discharge reductions at the three near-mainstream ends, demonstrating the effect of water regulation of the TGD during its initial impoundment. By comparison, riverbed adjustment made a much higher contribution, suggesting a greater impact of TGD sediment-trapping on the downstream riverbed than from water regulation. However, the precipitation made the highest contribution. (4) From the fourth to the fifth stage, precipitation increased markedly, leading to corresponding Δ Q ′     increments at Songzikou and Ouchikou, with the predominant precipitation contribution occurring at these two near-mainstream ends. Although ΔQ 3  at Taipingkou was also noticeably positive, Δ Q 1 ′     was overwhelming, so causing Q 1 to  decrease. Absolute values of both P 1 ′    and P 2 ′    increased remarkably in Cases D and E compared with Case C, implying the greater significance of both the sediment-trapping effect and water regulation of the TGD during test impoundment than during initial impoundment.   5 Discussion 5.1 Future trends of back-flow events at the two ends of the connection channels Hydrological statistics show that only Taipingkou (i.e., Mituosi station), located at the junction between the Hudu River and the Yangtze mainstream (Fig. 1 b), has experienced back-flow events since 2018 and this occurrence frequency has increased considerably recently with 68 days for such events in the first nine months of 2023 (Fig. 5  ). Meanwhile, the other two near-mainstream ends at Songzikou and Ouchikou have witnessed sustained normal-flow events. We attribute the discrepant behavior at the near-mainstream ends to different contributions from the driving factors. During the fifth stage, riverbed adjustment within the Yangtze mainstream played the most important role in the flow discharge reduction at Taipingkou (Table 7 ) and erosion at Taipingkou was less than that at the other two near-mainstream ends at Songzikou and Ouchikou (Zhu et al., 2023 ). Together these led to weaker diversion ability and higher back-flow frequency of occurrence at Taipingkou. Precipitation in the upper Yangtze River is set to decline until at least the end of this century (Zeng et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015 ). Yearly water discharge within the Yangtze mainstream and yearly water diversion into the three connection channels will diminish. Even so, water-level differences (for specific Q z ′    values) between the mainstream and near-mainstream ends of the connection channels will hardly change, because the riverbeds of the mainstream and near-mainstream ends of the connection channels will continue to experience comparable rates of erosion (Zhu et al., 2023 ). Precipitation has become the major driving factor for flow discharge changes at Songzikou and Ouchikou (Case D in Table 7 ), but the future decline in precipitation is limited (Wang et al., 2015 ), and will not radically alter water-level differences between the mainstream and the two near-mainstream ends of the connection channels for normal-flow cases. Thus, back-flow is not likely to occur at the two near-mainstream ends at Songzikou and Ouchikou in forthcoming decades, noting that the two historical back-flow events in 2015 and 2017 occurred under extreme retrorse water-level differences due to large reductions in mainstream flood peaks (i.e., from 17200 m3 /s to 7000 m3 /s in 2015 and 27300 m3 /s to 8000 m3 /s in 2017) driven by TGD operations (Feng et al., 2019 ). Conversely, back flow will still occur at Taipingkou given the roughly stable water-level difference. Back-flow events have not been observed at the four hydrological stations (Anxiang, Dongjiadang, Sanchahe, and Nanxian) located at the near-lake ends of the connection channels. Presently, water levels in the west and south lake basins are falling, weakening the jacking effects on flow discharges at Anxiang, Dongjiadang, and Sanchahe stations, meanwhile the water level in the east lake basin is rising, strengthening the jacking effect on flow discharge at Nanxian station (Gao et al., 2020, Lai et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2023 ). Hence, back-flow events are only likely to occur at Nanxian station in the future. The foregoing qualitative prediction of back-flow events at the two ends of the connection channels is entirely based on their being subject to natural conditions. However, human interference, such as TGD operation and artificial guidance at the near-mainstream ends of the connection channels (Feng et al., 2019 ), could lead to back-flow events developing over a very short timeframe. Therefore, correct prediction of back-flow events at the two ends of the connection channels largely depends on judicious use of Fig. 4  and Tables 4-6 .  5.2 Potential impacts of back flow and countermeasures Moderate back-flow volumes can relieve flood-control pressure on Dongting Lake in the wet season. However, frequent back-flow events could break the interconnected network system within the lake, lead to unfavorable impacts on local ecosystems, water quality, and human acitivities. Since TGD began impoundment, the dry season for the whole Dongting Lake has been brought forward greatly, damaging certain aquatic organisms in the lake (Wu et al., 2017, 2020 ). Back-flow events during the wet season, when the storage lake loses water, may aggravate this problem. The back-flow discharge may also alter the pattern of vegetation distribution in the Jingjiang Reach, as demonstrated in other rivers with inflow tributaries (Song et al., 2022, 2023 ). In terms of water quality, lake water loss during a back-flow event weakens the self-purification ability of the water body, and as a consequence, pollutant concentration increases (Mosley, 2015; Geng, et al., 2023 ). Back flow can also carry sediment from the lake basin into the three connection channels, promoting deposition (Li et al., 2016 ), increasing the occurrence frequency of zero-flow events in the channels (Chen et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022 ) during the dry season, and finally degrading their water quality. As opposed to beneficial flood control in Dongting Lake, severe back flow afflux augments flood risk in the Jingjiang reach. This is of course counter to the original engineering intention that Dongting Lake should act as the flood storage area for the Jingjiang Reach (Nakayama T and Shankman D, 2013 ; Liu et al., 2024 ). Meanwhile, the back flow causes the transverse velocity to increase in the main navigation channel (Yang et al., 2024 ) as it enters the Jingjiang Reach and may lead to vessels deviating from their designated shipping route, leading to navigation accidents. Finally, just like tributary inputs, the back flow might alter the riverbed erosion–deposition pattern within the mainstream segment downstream of the confluence outlet (Song et al., 2022, 2023 ), in turn affecting both flood control and navigation in the Jingjiang River. Hence, proper operational regulation of cascade reservoirs (especially the TGD) in the upper Yangtze is needed to achieve sustainable benefits for both the mainstream and the lake through the connection channels. To resist an imminent back-flow event, the reservoir operators should be acutely aware of downstream weather forecasts and increase outflow appropriately before a storm arrives if back flow is predicted to occur at the ends of the connection channels. The predictions could be based in practice on the highly efficient empirical formulae and corresponding hydraulic zoning charts (tables) presented in this study. It is also recommended that ancillary works be constructed along the connection channels to store superfluous water entering the channels during the period of reservoir operation; this water can be released later to relieve zero-flow events in the channels during the dry season.   6 Conclusion We present empirical formulae (R 2  = 0.84 ∼ 0.98) for quantifying flow discharges at the two ends of the three distributaries of the Jingjiang Reach in the middle Yangtze River, China. High consistency is achieved between observed flow discharges and calculated results using these formulae. Hydraulic zoning charts have been devised based on two variables, water discharge at Zhicheng hydrological station and water levels at target stations, that provide rapid identification of normal-flow/back-flow events at the distributary ends, with corresponding value ranges of the two variables evaluated. Before TGD impoundment, riverbed adjustment caused by the lower Jingjiang Cutoff Projects and Gezhou Dam determined changes in flow discharge at the near-mainstream ends of the distributaries, with contribution ratios of 75 %∼93 % and 50 %∼59 %, respectively. After impoundment, precipitation became the dominant factor, with contribution ratios of 63 %∼82 % during the initial impoundment of the TGD and −180 %∼757 % during the test impoundment. Since 2018, only Taipingkou has witnessed back-flow events, but with an obvious increase in occurrence frequency. In the future, it is surmised that back-flow events might occur with increasing frequency at Mituosi (i.e., Taipingkou) and Nanxian hydrological stations. To address the challenges posed by such back-flow events, it is essential that optimal reservoir operation and water resource utilization are achieved in a timely fashion. The present study has provided a robust, straightforward method for quantifying both the normal-flow and back-flow discharges at two ends of long connection channels between a mainstream river and a distributary lake. This innovative method can readily be transferred to other mainstream-distributary/tributary intersection systems. In the future, it is expected that accurate back-flow prediction will be based on results from climate models, which would provide a more reliable incoming flow boundary, in combination with knowledge of the operational regulation of upstream cascade reservoirs. It is also recommended that recent technological advances in remote sensing and GIS be integrated into the monitoring and forecasting systems to reduce uncertainty in backflow identification.
1 Introduction River flow routing is of paramount importance for water resource management (Choudhury et al., 2002 ), climate change assessment (Dutta et al., 2017 ), hydroecological evaluation (Shin et al., 2020 ), and flood hazard and risk assessment (Dottori et al., 2016 ). The middle and lower reaches of large-scale alluvial rivers, such as the Yangtze River (Lu et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019 ), Amazon River (Neal et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2017 ) and Mekong River (Kummu et al., 2014; Ang et al., 2022 ), are normally connected to tributary river networks, fluvial lakes, and floodplains. Considering that the interactions between water systems in large-scale watersheds are strong and complex in terms of flow divergence and convergence, backwater effects, and floodplain storage (Meade et al., 1991; Lai et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2017 ), it is necessary to consider a complex river network as a whole system and to develop an integrated model at a large scale (Lai et al., 2013; Munar et al., 2018 ). For flow routing in large-scale watersheds, hydrological and hydrodynamic models are considered indispensable tools (Fleischmann et al., 2018 ). Over the past few decades, hydrological models have been developed based on the empirical relationship between the storage volume and outflow discharge within a river reach (Paiva et al., 2013 ), the Muskingum method and variations (Choudhury et al., 2002; Getirana et al., 2017 ), kinematic wave methods (Singh, 2001; Li et al., 2015; Chen and Capart, 2020 ), diffusion wave methods (Moussa and Bocquillon, 2009; Yamazaki et al., 2011 ), and sequences of linear reservoir methods (Lindström et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2018 ), which have the advantages of requiring limited computational effort and data and have been verified to be satisfactory in many practical applications. However, hydrological models may oversimplify the representation of physical processes, and phenomena such as looped stage-discharge relationships, backwater effects, and significant momentum transfer at river reach confluences cannot be fully considered (Paiva et al., 2013; Munar et al., 2018; Ming et al., 2020 ), thereby limiting the accuracy of flow routing (Zhao et al., 2017 ). Recent advances in hydrodynamic models based on the St. Venant equations have made it possible to accurately simulate flow processes in complex river networks and obtain detailed dynamic information (Ming et al., 2020; Possa et al., 2022 ). However, in large-scale watersheds, detailed topographic data for an entire region are commonly difficult to obtain. In particular, when the water system distribution is complex, the complexity of hydrodynamic modeling and the computational cost increase substantially. Therefore, to date, data requirements and computational constraints are still hindering the broad application of hydrodynamic models in large-scale flow simulation (Ming et al., 2020 ). Coupled hydrological-hydrodynamic models can overcome the limitations of the data constraints of individual hydrodynamic models and the rough simulation performance of individual hydrological models and are considered promising approaches for large-scale flow routing (Liu et al., 2018; Munar et al., 2018 ). Several studies have developed coupled hydrological-hydrodynamic flow routing models by applying different models to different subregions of large-scale watersheds (e.g., Kummu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019; Tokuda et al., 2021 ). For instance, Bravo et al. (2012)  used the distributed hydrological model MGB-IPH with the Muskingum-Cunge method for a basin and its tributaries, and it was coupled with a 1D hydrodynamic model for the main drainage network. Then, the coupled model was applied to the entire Upper Paraguay River Basin for flow routing. Siqueira et al. (2018)  developed a coupled hydrological and hydrodynamic model for South America, in which the floodplain in each of the discretized unit catchments was generalized to a simple storage model; flow routing was performed by using the linear reservoir method and the local inertial method for the floodplain and river channel within each unit, respectively. Nevertheless, the numerical instabilities of the coupled algorithm and the corresponding data requirements are still the main challenges limiting the practical application of coupled hydrological and hydrodynamic models (Bravo et al., 2012; Munar et al., 2018 ). In the recent literature, offline coupling algorithms have been commonly used to realize the coupling of hydrological rainfall-runoff models with hydrodynamic flow routing models, and the hydrographs obtained from hydrological models are generally used to establish the upstream boundary conditions for hydrodynamic models (Munar et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018 ). However, in the case of coupling hydrological flow routing models with hydrodynamic models in different study regions, which is the concern of this study, the offline coupling approach is not applicable because it occurs in one direction and cannot represent the interactions between different models, such as backwater effects (Lopes et al., 2018 ). In particular, the model integration and computation processes are more difficult if there are several connection points between the hydrological and hydrodynamic models. Recently, the internal coupling approach has been applied in several studies, in which information can be exchanged two-way at the common boundary and the feedbacks between hydrological and hydrodynamic modules can be represented (Liu et al., 2018; Siqueira et al., 2018; Fleischmann et al., 2018 ). However, hydrological and hydrodynamic modules are solved separately and explicitly in many internal coupling approaches; therefore, the time step is generally limited to ensure the stability and accuracy of the coupling algorithm, resulting in low computational efficiency. In addition, the full coupling approach, in which all the equations are solved simultaneously at each time step before advancing to the next time step (Morita and Yen, 2002 ), still needs to be further explored. As the most typical river-connected lake in China, Dongting Lake is located on the southern bank of the middle reach of the Yangtze River and plays an important role in flood control, water supply, and aquatic ecosystem protection in the middle reach of the Yangtze River Basin. The complex hydraulic interactions between the Yangtze River and Dongting Lake, such as strong backwater effects and flow divergence and confluence, result in an intricate river–lake relationship that affects and restricts each other (Yu et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2023 ). In recent decades, the river–lake relationship between the Yangtze River and Dongting Lake has been distinctly altered by ongoing climate change and intensive anthropogenic activities (Lai et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2015 ). Especially after the operation of the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) began in 2003, the downstream flow regime and topographic conditions have drastically changed, and the associated problems of aggravated drought (Huang et al., 2021 ), flooding activities deterioration (Hu et al., 2015 ), and wetland habitat degradation (Guo et al., 2023 ) have become increasingly serious, consequently receiving widespread attention. In this context, it is necessary to establish a mathematical model capable of effectively implementing flow routing to quantitatively evaluate the flow behavior of the Yangtze-Dongting system under changing hydrological and topographic conditions. Numerous studies have been carried out to construct full hydrodynamic models of the Yangtze-Dongting system. For instance, Chai et al. (2020)  developed a 1D hydrodynamic model for the middle reach of the Yangtze River to simulate flow processes, in which the diversion and confluence flows were all given based on observed data. Zhang et al. (2020)  established a 1D/2D coupled hydrodynamic model to predict the flow regime in the Yangtze-Dongting system, but the topographic data used were quite old. In practical applications, full hydrodynamic models are generally limited by many constraints. On the one hand, an individual mainstream model is incapable of accounting for the intricate interactions between the mainstream, lake, and distributaries. On the other hand, the riverbed of the Yangtze-Dongting system has been frequently altered in recent years, and topographic data are scarce for areas other than those of the mainstream channel; therefore, mismatches among topographic data in different subregions may result in inaccuracies in hydrodynamic flow routing. To fill the current research and practical gaps, the objective of this study is to develop a large-scale flow routing model with high computational efficiency and low data requirements by coupling a 1D hydrodynamic model of the Yangtze mainstream with an innovative hydrological model of Dongting Lake and a hydrological empirical model of diversion tributaries connecting the mainstream and lake. In the hydrological modeling modules, the empirical relationships derived from hydrological data during different periods are used to represent the impacts of topographic variations on the hydrological regime, thereby alleviating the contradiction between rapid topographic variations and the difficulty of obtaining topographic data for lake and distributary channels. In addition, we propose a fully coupled method by utilizing an implicit coupling algorithm, which significantly improves the computational efficiency and accuracy of large-scale flow routing.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The Yangtze River, with a total length of 6300 km and a catchment area of 1.8 million km2 , is known as China's golden waterway, providing a lifeline for sustainable socioeconomic development (Dai et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2021 ). The Yangtze River is usually divided into upper, middle, and lower reaches according to differences in the geographic environment and hydrological characteristics (Xia et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018 ). As a reach of the middle Yangtze River, the Jingjiang River extends from Zhicheng station to Chenglingji station, with a length of 347 km and a hydraulic slope of approximately 0.5‱. There are three diversion tributaries on the right side of the Jingjiang River, connecting the mainstream with Dongting Lake through the diversion outlets of Taiping, Songzi, and Ouchi, which are referred to as the Sankou outlets. As the second-largest freshwater lake in China and a typical floodplain lake, Dongting Lake is well known for its specific basin morphology and complex water network system (Nakayama and Watanabe, 2008; Huang et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2018 ). Currently, the water from the upper Yangtze River flows into the Jingjiang River through Zhicheng station and partly flows into Dongting Lake through the Sankou outlets. The lake is also fed by the Xiangjiang, Zishui, Yuanjiang, and Lishui Rivers in the Dongting Lake Basin, which are referred to as the Sishui rivers. Finally, the lake discharges into the Yangtze River from the only outlet, Chenglingji station, and then drains along the mainstream through Luoshan station, as depicted in Fig. 1  (b). During the flood season of the Dongting Lake Basin (May to August), the lake expands and covers a large water surface area, and the average water surface slope between Yangliutan and Chenglingji stations is approximately 0.22‱. During periods other than the flood season, the active flows are generally constrained to the main channels, the lake behaves like a river, and the average water surface slope between Yangliutan and Chenglingji stations is approximately 0.56‱. After the operation of TGR began in 2003, a large amount of sediment was deposited in the reservoir, resulting in significant erosion of the downstream riverbed, which primarily occurred in low-flow channels (Han et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2022 ). Recent studies have revealed that the erosion of the mainstream channel, Dongting Lake area and Sankou distributary channels has occurred at unequal rates (Li et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2016 ), which may impact the diversion capacity of the Sankou distributaries, the flood detention function of the lake, and the hydrological regime of the Yangtze-Dongting system (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Therefore, to explore the hydrological changes induced by topographic changes in the whole region after TGR operation, the river system investigated in this study included the mainstream Yangtze River from Zhicheng to Luoshan (approximately 380 km), the Sankou distributaries, and the Dongting Lake area downstream of the gauging stations of the Sishui rivers (Fig. 1 ).  2.2 Data Daily discharges along the Yangtze mainstream from Zhicheng to Luoshan obtained at four gauging stations (i.e., Zhicheng, Shashi, Jianli, and Luoshan) and daily water level data measured at five gauging stations (i.e., Zhicheng, Shashi, Xinchang, Jianli, and Luoshan) were used to calibrate and validate the mainstream hydrodynamic model and set the upstream and downstream boundaries of the coupled model. Based on the 1985 Yellow Sea Datum with Beijing 54 coordinates, the topographic data used in the mainstream hydrodynamic model referred to the 1D cross-sectional elevation data (1998 and 2016) from Zhicheng to Luoshan, and the number of cross-sections was 248, with a spatial interval of approximately 1.5 km. To develop the hydrological model of the Dongting Lake area, we collected daily water level data from the Chenglingji, Yangliutan, and Nanzui stations, which are located at the outlet and in the upper parts of Dongting Lake, respectively. Considering that the correlation between the water levels at Nanzui and Yangliutan is strong (Sun et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2017 ), as depicted in Fig. S1 , the water level at Yangliutan station was used as the representative water level in the upper part of Dongting Lake in this study. The daily inflow discharges to Dongting Lake were obtained from the four gauging stations of the Sishui rivers (i.e., Xiangtan, Taojiang, Taoyuan, and Shimen stations) and the five gauging stations of the Sankou outlets (i.e., the Xinjiangkou and Shadaoguan stations for the Songzi Outlet, the Mituosi station for the Taiping Outlet, and the Kangjiagang and Guanjiapu stations for the Ouchi Outlet). The daily discharge data obtained at the Sankou outlets were also used to develop the empirical hydrological model of the Sankou distributaries. The daily outflow discharge of Dongting Lake was obtained at Chenglingji station. All of these hydrological data were available from 1992 to 2020. Considering that the impoundment of the TGR began in 2003, the periods of 1992–2002 and 2003–2020 were defined as the pre-TGR and post-TGR periods, respectively. Moreover, the TGR started its regular operation in 2009, so the post-TGR period can be subdivided into the initial period (2003–2008) and the normal period (2009–2020) of TGR operation. All topographic and hydrological data were obtained from the Changjiang Water Resources Commission (CWRC), China (https://www.cjh.com.cn ). Below the gauging stations on the Sankou distributaries and Sishui rivers, the ungauged area accounts for approximately 20 % of the total Dongting Lake Basin area (Xie et al., 2019 ), and the annual runoff volume in the ungauged area is approximately 9 % of that of the Dongting Lake Basin (Chang et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2018 ). Due to the unavailability of ungauged inflow data, this study employed the scaling factor derived from the annual difference between the total inflow and outflow volumes of Dongting Lake to correct the daily inflow data (Zhang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020 ). Although the spatial and temporal characteristics of ungauged runoff cannot be fully accounted for in this approach, the water balance can be maintained on an annual scale. According to Yang et al. (2021)  and Habiyakare et al. (2021) , in the Dongting Lake Basin, the total water resources associated with evaporation and groundwater are negligible compared to the gauged flows coming into the modeling domain, so they were not considered in this study.   3 Methods 3.1 Module division and model description The study region was divided into three subregions based on the structure of the river–lake–tributaries system and the characteristics of flow divergence and confluence, that is, the Yangtze River mainstream from Zhicheng to Luoshan, the Sankou distributary channels, and the Dongting Lake area downstream of the gauging stations of the Sishui rivers and Sankou outlets. In this study, three modules were established for the three subregions, and different flow routing models were developed for each module. 3.1.1 Mainstream module Since the operation of the TGR began, intensive and frequent topographic surveys have been conducted along the Yangtze River mainstream; thus, topographic data for the mainstream channels are widely available and sufficient for hydrodynamic modeling. Considering the data requirements and computational costs, 1D hydrodynamic models are generally regarded as simpler and more effective tools than complex two- and three-dimensional hydrodynamic models for large-scale flow routing (Lian et al., 2007; Bravo et al., 2012 ). Therefore, a 1D unsteady hydrodynamic model was developed for the mainstream module in this study, and it can be described by the St. Venant equations and written as:(1)  ∂ Q  ∂ x   + ∂ A  ∂ t   = 0     (2) ∂ Q  ∂ t   + ∂ ∂ x   Q  2  A    + g A ∂ Z  ∂ x   + g n  2  | Q | Q  A R  4 / 3     = 0     where Q  is the discharge; A  is the cross-sectional area; x  is the distance in the flow direction; t  is time; h  is the flow depth; Z  is the water level; g  is the acceleration due to gravity; and n  is the Manning roughness coefficient. For the mainstream reach, according to the Preissmann four-point implicit finite-difference scheme, the St. Venant equations can be discretized as linear equations with respect to the section discharge and water level increments in time (i.e., Δ Q = Q  n  - Q  n - 1     , Δ Z = Z  n  - Z  n - 1     ) and can be solved based on the chasing method (Cunge, 1980; Lai et al., 2013 ). The corresponding recursive relations are as follows:(3) Δ Z j  = L j + 1   + M j + 1   Δ Z j + 1       (4) Δ Q  j + 1   = P j + 1   + R j + 1   Δ Z j + 1       where the superscript n  represents the current time step and is removed from Eqs. (3) and (4)  for simpler expression; the subscripts j  and j  + 1 represent the section sequence numbers; Δ Z    and Δ Q    are the increments of water level and discharge in a time step, respectively; and L , M , P,  and R  are recursive coefficients. To ensure that the chasing method can be implemented successfully from the upper boundary to the lower boundary, the governing equations of the cross sections at the diversion and confluence points should be expressed in a uniform form with Eqs. (3) and (4) . Each diversion point (i.e., the Songzi, Taiping, and Ouchi outlets) can be expanded into a virtual river section with a length equal to 0 and a section sequence numbered from j  to j  + 1. There should be(5) Z j  = Z j + 1       (6) Q j + 1   = Q j  + Q d      where Z j    and Z j + 1     denote the upstream and downstream stages of the virtual reach, respectively; Q j    and Q j + 1     denote the upstream and downstream discharges, respectively; and Q d    is the diverted discharge at the diversion point. By converting Eqs. (5) and (6)  into the form of Eqs. (3) and (4) , we can obtain(7a) L j + 1   = Z j + 1  n - 1   - Z j  n - 1       (7b) M j + 1   = 1     (7c) P j + 1   = P j  + Q j  n - 1   - Q j + 1  n - 1   + R j  Z j + 1  n - 1   - Z j  n - 1     - Q d      (7d) R j + 1   = R j      where the superscript n- 1 represents the last time step and all variables are known at that time step. For the confluence point (i.e., Chenglingji station), the same approach as that used for diversion points is applied, yielding recursive coefficients L , M , and R , consistent with Eq. (7), while the coefficient P  is as follows:(8)  P j + 1   = P j  + Q j  n - 1   - Q j + 1  n - 1   + R j  Z j + 1  n - 1   - Z j  n - 1     + Q c      where Qc   is the confluence discharge at Chenglingji station. All the recursive coefficients mentioned above and flow variables for each section can be calculated with the chasing method from the boundary conditions. For the mainstream module, the inflow process at Zhicheng and the stage-discharge relationship at Luoshan are considered as the upstream and downstream boundary conditions of the mainstream hydrodynamic model, respectively, with a time step of one day. The flow diversion processes at the Sankou outlets and the confluence process at Chenglingji are input into the model as the lateral boundaries. The Manning roughness coefficient n  is the only free parameter to be calibrated and validated in hydrodynamic modeling (Saleh et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2013 ). After the impoundment of the TGR, the mainstream channel of the Yangtze River experienced a significant adjustment. Especially after the normal operation of the TGR began in 2009, the Manning roughness coefficient of the mainstream channel changed obviously (Zhang et al., 2017; Chai et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, representative flood years for the pre-TGR period and the normal operation period were selected to calibrate the roughness coefficients. Considering that 1998 was the maximum flood year during the pre-TGR period and that the flood peak level at the Luoshan station nearly reached the maximum value in 2016 during the post-TGR period, 1998 and 2016 were selected as the representative flood years for the pre-TGR period and post-TGR period, respectively. In addition, 1999 and 2017 were selected for the validation of the roughness coefficients for the pre- and post-TGR periods, respectively. For each cross-section, the roughness coefficients usually vary with water depth (Lai et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2017 ), so we divided each section into subsections according to water levels and calibrated the roughness coefficient of each subsection separately. The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE ) and mean absolute error (MAE ) were used to evaluate the calibration and validation results.  3.1.2 Diversion module A simplified hydrological empirical model was developed to simulate flow diversion processes based on stage-discharge rating curves. Previous studies have demonstrated that the diversion flows of the Sankou distributaries and the stages of the Yangtze River mainstream are strongly correlated and that the rating curves of the diversion discharges with the water levels at the nearest mainstream stations are relatively stable, even when the mainstream riverbed is unstable (Li et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2019 ). Therefore, according to the location distribution of the mainstream hydrological stations and Sankou outlets, as shown in Fig. 1 (c), the diversion discharges at the Songzi, Taiping, and Ouchi outlets can be represented by the stages at the Zhicheng, Shashi and Xinchang stations, respectively. Then, the governing equations for the diversion module can be expressed as:(9) Q SZ   = f 1  Z ZC         (10) Q TP   = f 2  Z SS         (11)  Q OC   = f 3  Z XC         where QSZ  , QTP  , and QOC   are the daily mean diversion discharges at the Songzi, Taiping, and Ouchi outlets, respectively; and ZZC  , ZSS  , and ZXC   are the daily water levels at the Zhicheng, Shashi, and Xinchang stations, respectively. Generally, the empirical equations fi   (i  = 1,2,3) are in the form of high-order polynomials, which can be determined based on the least squares method and a trial-and-error procedure with observed data (Sun et al., 2019 ). The stability of the correlations in Eqs. (9) to (11)  depends mainly on the stability of the topography of the Sankou distributary channels. Therefore, different diversion rating curves obtained from the observed hydrological datasets in different periods can be used to reflect the influence of topographic changes in the Sankou distributary channels. In this study, the stage-discharge rating curves of the diversion module were established based on the available hydrological data from 1998 and 2016, and the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) was used to evaluate the accuracy of the fitted rating curves.  3.1.3 Lake area module As a traditional hydrological method of flow routing, the Muskingum method is based on the empirical relationship between the storage volume and weighted discharge as an empirical substitute for the momentum balance equation (Koussis, 2009 ). Hence, the Muskingum method is unable to account for backwater effects and is not suitable for flow routing in Dongting Lake. In recent years, the hydraulic performance graph (HPG), which summarizes the backwater profiles for all possible discharge levels in an open-channel reach (Yen and González-Castro, 2000; Schmidt and Yen, 2008 ), and the volume performance graph (VPG), which describes the channel storage characteristics for each HPG flow scenario (Hoy and Schmidt, 2006 ), have been utilized in several studies for unsteady flow routing in channels with strong backwater effects (Leon et al., 2013; Saharia et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021 ) and have been proven to be accurate and computationally efficient (Leon and Gifford-Miears, 2018 ). However, to date, HPGs and VPGs (PGs) must be pre-created with hydrodynamic models where topographic data are necessary and are often not appropriate for large-scale applications. According to the theory of the Muskingum routing method and PG routing method, we established the empirical relationships between the storage volume and the weighted discharge and downstream water level, and combined them with the water balance equation, thereby establishing an innovative routing method fully considering backwater effects. The lake area was generalized as a simple storage unit with runoff, and the complex hydrodynamic conditions within the lake were not considered in this study. Similar methods for simplifying floodplain lakes into simple storage units have been reported in previous studies (e.g., Cunge, 1975; Paiva et al., 2013; Kummu et al., 2014 ). The storage volume of the unit is influenced by three factors: the total inflow, the outflow, and the outlet stage. The flow routing scheme can be expressed as(12) I = Q SZ   + Q TP   + Q OC   + Q SR   + q     (13) S = F I , O , Z CLJ         (14) Δ S = I i  + I i + 1    2  - O i  + O i + 1    2    Δ t     where Q SR     is the total inflow of the Sishui rivers; q  is the ungauged interval inflow from the catchment; Z CLJ     is the water level at Chenglingji; I  and O  are the total inflow and the outflow of the lake area, respectively; S  is the volumetric water storage; Δt  is the time step; and ΔS  is the storage change from time step i  to i  + 1. Eqs. (12) to (14)  constitute the governing equations of the lake module, which can be used to obtain the outflow of Dongting Lake based on the inflow of the lake and the water level at Chenglingji station. Notably, the hydrological stations on the Sishui rivers and Sankou distributaries are located at a distance from the lake area, so the flood propagation time from each station to the lake area is considered. Specifically, the flood propagation time is 2 days for the Shimen station and 1 day for the Xiangtan, Taojiang, and Yuanjiang stations on the Sishui rivers (Wan et al., 2000 ). For the Sankou distributaries, the flood propagation time is 1 day for all five hydrological stations. As the flow motion equation in the hydrological flow simulation model, Eq. (13)  describes the relation among the inflow, outflow, outlet stage, and storage volume of the storage unit, and can be pre-established as a family of storage curves, with similar meaning as the VPG established by Hoy and Schmidt (2006) . In this section, Eq. (13)  is derived based on the St. Venant equations, and the procedure is described in detail as follows. For the momentum equation of flow in a wide-shallow channel of a lake, by neglecting the inertia terms in Eq. (2) , the equation can be written as(15) ∂ Z  ∂ x   = n  2  Q  2   A  2  h  4 / 3         where h  is the flow depth. The differential form of Eq. (15)  is(16) Z u  - Z d   Δ x   = n  2  Q  2   A  ¯    2  h  ¯    4 / 3         where Zu   and Zd   are the stages at the upper part and outlet of the storage unit, respectively; Δ x    is the distance between the two sections; A  ¯     and h  ¯     are the cross-sectional area and the flow depth at a specific cross section according to the mean value theorem, respectively; and the slope of this specific cross section is equal to the average water surface slope ( ( Z u  - Z d  )  / Δ x )   . Then, the water level in this section can be expressed as the weighted value of Zu   and Zd   (Z  ¯   = β Z u  + (1 - β ) Z d    ), and the flow depth can be expressed as h  ¯   = Z  ¯   - Z b   ¯     , where Z b   ¯     is a coefficient representing the riverbed elevation. In addition, with the experience of Muskingum routing method, the weighted discharge of inflow and outflow (Q ¯  = α I + (1 - α ) O  ) can be used to represent the flow pattern in the reach, namely, the representative discharge. Then, Eq. (16)  can be expressed as the relationship between the water stage and the representative discharge, that is,(17) Z  ¯   = n  2  Q  ¯    2  Δ x  ζ  4  ( Z u  - Z d  )       3 / 22   + Z b   ¯   = K (  Q  ¯    2  Z u  - Z d    )   b  + C     where α   and β   are the weighting coefficients within the range of 0 to 1; ζ = B  / H   is the fluvial facies coefficient; B  and H  represent the average channel width and the average water depth, respectively; and K , C , and b  are undetermined parameters. The linear relationship of Z  ∼ Q  2  / Z u  - Z d      b    in Eq. (17)  is an implicit function that describes the relationships among Zu  , Zd  , I , and O  by using the empirical coefficients α  , β  , and b , which can be determined by a trial-and-error algorithm with observed discharge and water level data. The specific process for determining Eq. (17)  is described in Text S1 and Fig. S2  in the Supporting Information . For the mass continuity equation, the integral form of Eq. (1)  can be expressed as(18) ∫ 0  Δ x   A   T 1   - A   T 0     d x = ∫ T 0   T 1   ( I - O )  d t     where T 0  and T 1  are the beginning and ending moments of the integration period, respectively. Suppose that the water level in the storage unit starts to rise from moment T 0  and that the storage volume at this moment is considered the dead storage capacity (S 0 ); then, the left side of Eq. (18)  can be expressed as(19) ∫ 0  Δ x   A   T 1   - A   T 0     d x = ∫ 0  Δ x   A   T 1   d x - ∫ 0  Δ x   A   T 0   d x = ∫ 0  Δ x   A   T 1   d x - S 0      According to the median integral theorem, there should be ∫ 0 Δ x   A  T 1   dx = A ( Z λ   T 1   )  Δ x  , where Z λ  = λ Z u  +(1- λ ) Z d    is the water level in a specific section, namely, the representative water level, and λ   is a weighting coefficient within the range of 0 to 1. In addition, the right side of Eq. (18)  represents the relative storage volume S   T 1     above S 0  at any moment T 1  after T 0 . Assuming that S 0  is approximately constant, Eq. (18)  can be expressed as(20) S   T 1   = f Z λ    T 1         Eq. (20)  indicates that the relative storage volume is a function of the representative water level. The left side of Eq. (20)  can be derived from daily data for I  and O , and the right side can be calculated based on daily data for Zu   and Zd  , for which the coefficient λ  needs to be determined by a trial-and-error algorithm. Then, Eq. (20)  can be obtained based on a fitting algorithm, and the relevant details are provided in Text S2 in the Supporting Information . By combining Eq. (17)  and Eq. (20) , we can obtain the storage relationships among the storage volume, inflow, outflow, and outlet stage, as expressed in Eq. (13) . In practical applications in Dongting Lake flow routing, Eq. (13)  needs to be pre-established based on hydrological data and then combined with the water balance equation (i.e., Eq. (14) ) to compute the lake outflow based on the inflow data and outlet stage data. Consequently, a lake module for performing flow routing was developed. In contrast to the Muskingum method, which establishes the relationship between the storage volume and representative discharge, the storage relationship established in this study accounts for the effect of the outlet stage and therefore can be used to reflect the backwater effect. Notably, the parameters in the above equations change when the topography of the lake area is adjusted, so the parameter values for different periods should be calibrated according to the corresponding hydrological data. In addition, to avoid cumulative errors caused by ungauged inflow over multiple years, the most representative flood years of the pre- (1998) and post-TGR (2016) periods were selected for establishing storage curves and performing flow routing for Dongting Lake. By comparing the simulated and observed outflow processes of Dongting Lake and calculating the values of NSE  and MAE , the performance of the hydrological lake model is validated.   3.2 Coupling of hydrological and hydrodynamic modules 3.2.1 Description of the full coupling approach For the coupled model, the inflow processes at the Zhicheng station on the Yangtze mainstream and the Xiangtan, Taojiang, Taoyuan, and Shimen stations on the Sishui rivers are used to establish the upstream boundary conditions, and the stage-discharge relationship at the Luoshan station is used to establish the downstream boundary condition. By repeatedly running the coupled model with the initial boundary conditions, the steady-state solution is recognized as the initial condition for setting up the coupled model. To ensure a water volume balance and the continuity of flow variables among the mainstream, diversion, and lake modules, an implicit fully coupled approach is developed in this section, which is generally more stable with larger time step size than the explicit approach, thus greatly improving the computational efficiency of the coupled model. In the coupling process, each module is run sequentially, and the governing equations of each module can be solved simultaneously at the same time step by using an iterative algorithm. The detailed coupling procedure is shown in Fig. 2   and is described as follows: (1) Calculate the recursive coefficients in Eqs. (3) and (4)  for each mainstream river section with the flow variables (i.e., water level and discharge) for the mainstream channel at the last time step, except for the virtual diversion and confluence reaches. (2) Determine the diversion flows of the Sankou distributaries from Eqs. (9) to (11)  and the confluence flow at Chenglingji station from Eqs. (12) to (14)  with the flow variables for the mainstream at the last time step and the inflow data for the Sishui rivers at the current time step. Then, calculate the coefficients in Eqs. (7) and (8) for the virtual diversion and confluence reaches. (3) Run the 1D hydrodynamic model of the mainstream module with the diversion and confluence flows obtained from step (2), and determine the flow variables of the mainstream for the current time step with the chasing method. (4) According to the mainstream flow variables obtained from step (3), recalculate the diversion and confluence flows with the iterative relaxation method, and update the coefficients in Eqs. (7) and (8). The iterative relaxation method is specified as follows:(21) Q  k + 1   = ω Q  k + 1   + 1 - ω   Q  k      where Q   is the discharge of the diversion and confluence flows, k  is the iteration number, and ω  = 0.25 is the relaxation parameter. (5) Repeat steps (2) to (4) until the error between the flow variables derived from two successive iterations is lower than the threshold value of ε  = 10-3 ; then, proceed to the next time step, and continue the calculation.  3.2.2 Performance evaluation of the coupled model Flow routing for the Yangtze-Dongting system was conducted for 1998 and 2016 to evaluate the performance of the coupled model, and the boundary conditions for each year are depicted in Fig. S3  in the Supporting Information . The simulated stage and discharge processes at each hydrological station for the mainstream, the Sankou distributaries, and the Dongting Lake outlet were compared with the observed data, and the NSE  and MAE  were used to assess the accuracy of the modeling results.   3.3 Application of the coupled model 3.3.1 Flood wave movement simulation with the coupled model Dongting Lake responds to the flood pulses of both the Yangtze River mainstream and the four rivers in the catchment, and the movement of flow in the river–lake system presents complex spatial patterns (Yu et al., 2018 ). The coupled model developed in this paper fully considers the hydraulic interactions among water systems and can be used as an effective tool to simulate flood wave propagation and attenuation, as well as to characterize flood wave travel times at a full scale. Since the actual flooding process typically includes multiple successive flood peaks, a flood simulation scenario is established based on hypothetical idealized single-peak inflow processes, which are used to effectively distinguish the sources of flood waves based on the actual hydrological year of the maximum flood event. In addition, considering that the impoundment of the TGR significantly changed the hydrological regime of the middle reach of the Yangtze River and that the TGR is currently in its normal operation phase, the maximum flood events should be selected based on recent observed data series. According to the observed discharge data at Zhicheng station on the Yangtze River and four gauging stations on the Sishui rivers, the actual hydrological years of maximum flooding for the Yangtze River and the Sishui rivers during the normal operation period of the TGR (2009–2020) are 2020 and 2017, respectively, as depicted in Fig. 3  (a) and 3(c). The hypothetical idealized single-peak discharge processes derived from the maximum actual flood processes of the Yangtze River and Sishui rivers are shown in Fig. 3 (b) and 3(d), respectively. Fig. 3  also shows that the flood seasons differ between the Sishui rivers and the mainstream of the Yangtze River. Specifically, the main flood season is from May to August for the Sishui rivers, while it is from July to September for the Yangtze mainstream. Additionally, due to differences in drainage area, the flood magnitude is greater in the Yangtze mainstream than in the Sishui rivers. The hypothetical maximum inflow processes for the Yangtze mainstream and Sishui were used to establish the inflow conditions, and the mean stage-discharge relationship at Luoshan station derived from observed data during the normal operation period of the TGR (2009–2020) was used to establish the downstream boundary condition for this hypothetical scenario. The mainstream topographic data from 2016 and the aforementioned roughness coefficients calibrated in 2016 were used in the mainstream module for this hypothetical scenario, and the aforementioned storage curves and stage-discharge rating curves established in 2016 were applied in the lake module and diversion module for this hypothetical scenario, respectively. The coupled model validated in Section 3.2.2  was used to perform flood wave simulations for the hypothetical scenario. The flood propagation processes in the river–lake–distributary system were analyzed by comparing the hydrograph for each gauging station, and the flood wave travel times were identified by calculating the difference in time to peak discharge among different gauging stations.  3.3.2 Assessing the impact of topographic changes on the hydrological regime In this section, to investigate the differences in hydrological regime arising from topographic changes in the Yangtze mainstream, Dongting Lake, and Sankou distributary channels, flow routing simulations were performed for a typical hydrological year under different topographic conditions with the same upstream and downstream boundary conditions. The mainstream topographic data from 1998 (2016), the roughness coefficients calibrated in 1998 (2016), the Sankou diversion rating curves for 1998 (2016), and the lake storage curves for 1998 (2016) were used to represent the topographic conditions of the mainstream distributary channels and lake area in 1998 (2016). We selected 2016 as a typical wet year, and the discharge processes of the Zhicheng and Sishui rivers in 2016 and the stage-discharge relationship at Luoshan station in 2016 were taken as the upstream and downstream conditions, respectively, for both the 1998 and 2016 topographic conditions. By performing flow routing simulations for 2016 based on these two sets of topographic conditions and comparing the simulated water levels and discharge hydrographs for the gauging stations, the impact of topographic changes on the hydrological regime from 1998 to 2016 was quantitatively assessed.    4 Results and discussion 4.1 Model calibration and validation 4.1.1 Hydrodynamic model of the mainstream module The calibration and validation results for the mainstream module at the main gauging stations are given in Figs. 4 and 5   , and the calculated values of NSE  and MAE  for discharge and stage at each gauging station are provided in Tables S1 and S2  in the Supporting Information . All of the NSE  values are above 0.980 for discharge and above 0.960 for stage, and the MAE  values are all below 800 m3 /s for discharge and mostly below 0.5 m for stage, suggesting that the hydrodynamic model of the mainstream module achieved satisfactory accuracy. In addition, the calibration results indicate that the roughness coefficients of the mainstream riverbed increased obviously after the operation of the TGR. Under topographic condition in the pre-TGR period, the calibrated roughness coefficients ranged from 0.016 to 0.025 for low discharge levels and from 0.018 to 0.023 for high discharge levels. Under topographic condition in the post-TGR period, the calibrated roughness coefficient ranged from 0.023 to 0.032 for low discharge levels and from 0.021 to 0.031 for high discharge levels.  4.1.2 Stage-discharge relationships for Sankou distributaries Based on the fitted polynomial functions, the stage-discharge relationships for the Sankou outlets and the corresponding three mainstream gauging stations in 1998 and 2016 were obtained, as shown in Fig. 6   and Table S3  in the Supporting Information . As shown in Fig. 6 , the coefficients of determination (R 2 ) of the rating curves fitted by high-order polynomial functions are all above 0.980, which suggests that the simulations of the Sankou diverted flows based on the stage-discharge relationships are highly reliable.  4.1.3 Storage curves for Dongting Lake The daily water levels at Yangliutan (ZYLT  ) and Chenglingji (ZCLJ  ) and the total inflow (I ) and outflow (O ) of Dongting Lake from 1992 to 2002 and from 2003 to 2020 were used to determine the empirical coefficients of Eq. (17)  for the pre-TGR period and post-TGR period, respectively. The results show that for the pre-TGR period and post-TGR period, the R 2  of Z ¯  ∼  Q ¯  2  / Z YLT  - Z CL J       b    reaches a maximum when the parameter combination (α , β , b ) is (0.29, 0.31, 0.32) and (0.34, 0.33, 0.22), with R 2  = 0.973 and R 2  = 0.934, respectively, as illustrated in Fig. S4  in the Supporting Information . In this context, Eq. (17)  for the pre-TGR period and post-TGR period can be expressed as(22) 0.31 Z YLT   + 0.69 Z CLJ   = 0.01 0.29 I + 0.71 O    2  Z YLT   - Z CLJ        0.32   + 22.02     (23) 0.33 Z YLT   + 0.67 Z CLJ   = 0.11 0.34 I + 0.66 O    2  Z YLT   - Z CLJ        0.22   + 20.41     The relationship curves between ZCLJ   and ZYLT   at each representative discharge level (Q  ¯    ) are shown in Fig. 7  . The relationship curves match well with the observed data points at different discharge levels. Compared to the HPG proposed by Yen and González-Castro (2000) , Fig. 7  displays the same function of representing the relationships among the inflow, outflow, and outlet stage of Dongting Lake, but the method proposed in this study to establish Fig. 7  requires only hydrological data and eliminates the dependence on topographic data. In the process of establishing the storage curves described in Section 3.1.3 , a relative lake storage volume above a certain water level is needed. Taking 1998 and 2016 as typical flood years in the pre- and post-TGR periods, respectively, the water level at Chenglingji station rose from 20 m and fell back to 20 m from February 18 to November 18 in 1998 and from March 9 to October 12 in 2016, indicating that Dongting Lake experienced complete storage and release processes during these two periods. Therefore, with ZCLJ  =20 m as the water level corresponding to the dead storage capacity (S 0 ), the daily hydrological data from the storage-release periods were used to calculate the storage processes according to Eq. (14) . According to the method for determining the value of λ  described in Section 3.1.3 , Eq. (20)  yielded the best fit with the weighting coefficient λ  of 0.6 in 1998 and 0.5 in 2016, and the R 2  values reached 0.986 and 0.980 in 1998 and 2016, respectively. More details are provided in Figs. S5 and S6  in the Supporting Information . The relationships between the storage volume and representative water level in 1998 and 2016 can be expressed as(24) S = 1.12 Z λ  2  - 35.18 Z λ  + 210.15     (25) S = 0.45 Z λ  2  + 5.37 Z λ  - 393.16     where Z λ  = 0.6 Z YLT   + 0.4 Z CLJ      in Eq. (24)  for 1998 and Z λ  = 0.5 Z YLT   + 0.5 Z CLJ      in Eq. (25)  for 2016. By combining Eq. (22)  with Eq. (24)  and Eq. (23)  with Eq. (25) , the sets of storage curves representing the lake storage-weighted discharge-outlet stage relationships in 1998 and 2016 were obtained, as shown in Fig. 8  . The storage curves depicted in Fig. 8  are very similar to the VPG developed by Hoy and Schmidt (2006)  but do not require to be constructed by hydrodynamic models and can be established using hydrological data only. To evaluate the performance of the storage curves in lake flow routing, Fig. 8  were used to simulate the outflow processes of Dongting Lake in 1998 and 2016. A comparison between the measured and simulated outflow processes in 1998 and 2016 is shown in Fig. 9  , with the NSE  reaching 0.921 and 0.968 and the MAE  reaching approximately 1,000 m3 /s and 850 m3 /s, respectively. This indicates that the storage curves developed in this study are highly effective for performing flow routing for Dongting Lake.   4.2 Coupled model performance evaluation To analyze the performance of the coupled model and its applicability, flow routing was conducted for 1998 and 2016 on a full scale. Comparisons of the observed and simulated processes of daily discharge and daily stage in 1998 and 2016 at the main gauging stations are shown in Figs. 10 and 11   , and the calculated values of the NSE  and MAE  for discharge and stage are listed in Table S4  in the Supporting Information . All of the NSE  values for the stage (discharge) are greater than 0.970 (0.960), and most of the MAE  values for the stage (discharge) are less than 0.4 m (1000 m3 /s), which indicates that the simulated results agree very well with the observations and that the performance of the coupled model is highly satisfactory for flow routing in the middle reach of the Yangtze River and Dongting Lake. It should be noted that although a large time step size (i.e., Δt  = 1d) was selected for computing the coupled model, the numerical stability of the computations was still guaranteed; thus, the implicit fully coupled approach proposed in this study ensures sufficient modeling accuracy while significantly improving computational efficiency.  4.3 Application of the coupled model 4.3.1 Simulation of flood wave propagation The simulation results for the hypothetical scenario are shown in Fig. 12  . The flood wave travel time from the Sishui rivers to the Dongting Lake outlet was approximately 7 days, and the flood wave travel time along the Yangtze mainstream from Zhicheng station to Jianli station was only approximately 2 days. Due to the flood detention function of Dongting Lake, the flood peaks of the Sishui rivers and the Yangtze mainstream were significantly reduced. Fig. 12 (a) shows that the inflow flood peak for the Sishui rivers was about 49,700 m3 /s, while the lake outflow flood peak was only about 39,000 m3 /s, with a reduction rate of 22 %. The flood peak at Zhicheng station was approximately 51,800 m3 /s, while the flood peak at Jianli station was only 38,500 m3 /s, with a reduction rate of 26 %. According to the water level hydrographs for the main gauging stations along the mainstream (Fig. 12 (b)), there are two obvious rise and fall processes at the Shashi and Jianli stations. Apparently, the first process is caused by the backwater effect of the Dongting Lake outflow on the mainstream, and the other process is caused by flood propagation from upstream of the Yangtze mainstream. This suggests that during a flood event, the backwater effect of Dongting Lake outflow on the mainstream flow process can propagate at least to the upstream Shashi station. Note that the Jingjiang River is a lowland river, so the backwater reach of the Dongting Lake outflow can extend hundreds of kilometers above the outlet (Nittrouer et al., 2012; Ganti et al., 2016 ). Therefore, even though the Shashi and Jianli stations are far from the outlet of Dongting Lake, with distances of 250 km and 87 km, respectively, they are still inside the backwater reach of the lake, which has been extensively reported in previous studies (e.g., Yang et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2021 ). Based on observation data and hydrodynamic modeling, several studies have investigated flood wave propagation in the Yangtze-Dongting system (Li et al., 2003 ), the flood peak reduction capacity of Dongting Lake (Chang et al., 2010 ), and the influence range of the backwater effect of the Dongting Lake outflow (Sun et al., 2021 ). The simulation results of the hypothetical scenarios explored in this section are very similar to those reported in previous studies conducted for the pre-TGR period. This indicates that since the operation of the TGR began, the flood detention function of Dongting Lake and the range of the lake outflow backwater effect have not significantly changed. Moreover, the coupled model developed in this study is capable of correctly describing the flow divergence and confluence processes, backwater effect, and flood storage characteristics of Dongting Lake and is effective for investigating flood wave propagation and attenuation processes on a full scale.  4.3.2 Assessment of the impacts of topographic changes on the hydrological regime The simulation results of the hydrological processes in 2016 for the main hydrological stations under topographic conditions in 1998 and 2016 are given in Fig. 13  . Although the upstream and downstream boundary conditions are identical, the hydrograph at each station is significantly different due to channel/lake bed adjustments and mainstream roughness variations. The water level along the Yangtze River mainstream significantly decreased from 1998 to 2016. Furthermore, the degree of decrease in the water level was greater upstream than downstream and was greater during the low-flow period (i.e., when the discharge at Zhicheng station was below 10,000 m3 /s) than during the high-flow period (i.e., when the discharge at Zhicheng station was above 30,000 m3 /s). For instance, the average decrease in the water level during the low-flow period was more than 2.2 m at Shashi station and 1.0 m at Jianli station, while the average decrease in the water level during the high-flow period was approximately 0.6 m at Shashi station and only 0.1 m at Jianli station. Due to the obvious decrease in the water level of the Yangtze mainstream, the discharge at the Sankou outlets also decreased, with a maximum degree of decrease of about 800 m3 /s, as depicted in Fig. 13 (e). However, the reduction in the Sankou diverted flow accounted for only about 4 % of the total inflow of the Sankou distributaries and the Sishui rivers, which was 19,000 m3 /s, and therefore did not result in a remarkable reduction in the Dongting Lake outflow, as shown in Fig. 13 (f). The maximum reduction in Dongting Lake outflow was approximately 1,500 m3 /s when the outflow discharge was approximately 16,000 m3 /s, and this reduction was considered relatively small. This was mainly because the lower boundary conditions are identical for both flow routing scenarios, and the storage capacity of Dongting Lake changed only slightly from 1998 to 2016, as shown in Fig. 8 ; therefore, the variation in the lake outflow processes was not obvious. The above results are qualitatively similar but quantitatively slightly different from those of previous studies, such as the analyses of Zhu et al. (2016)  and Chai et al. (2020) . This is mainly because previous studies generally focused only on the topographic changes in the mainstream channel and failed to adequately consider the impacts of topographic adjustment in the lake area and distributary channels on the hydrological regime of the whole river–lake system. In contrast, this study evaluates the impacts of the overall topographic changes in mainstream, lake, and distributary channels on the overall hydrological regime by using a large-scale hydrological and hydrodynamic coupled model, which provides accurate simulation results by fully considering the hydraulic interactions among water systems and does not require topographic data for lake and distributaries.    5 Conclusions To realize flow routing in large-scale interactive river–lake–distributary water systems, for which detailed topographic data for whole systems are difficult to obtain, this paper presents a new coupled hydrological-hydrodynamic model and applies it to the Yangtze-Dongting system. A 1D hydrodynamic model is used in the Yangtze River mainstream module, and hydrological methods are employed to establish the diversion relationships for the Sankou distributaries module and the storage curves for the Dongting Lake module. Additionally, a fully coupled approach is developed with an implicit coupling algorithm and an iterative relaxation method for coupling and solving the model, satisfying the accuracy and efficiency requirements for unsteady flow simulations. Despite the complex water system and the scarcity of topographic data in the lake area, the coupled model developed in this paper can be used to accurately and efficiently describe the complex relationship between divergence and confluence flows in the river–lake system, reflect the storage and release processes of the lake, and analyze the impact of the backwater effect on flood wave propagation. Note that the lake is generalized to a simple storage unit and the diversion module is developed based on empirical hydrological relationships, so the detailed hydrological information inside the lake and the distributaries cannot be described. In the coupled model established in this paper, only mainstream cross-sectional data are required as topographic data, and the diversion relationships and lake storage curves are obtained solely with hydrological data, i.e., without any topographic data. The hydrological empirical models calibrated from hydrological data in different periods can be used to reflect the influence of topographic changes in different periods. Therefore, the coupled model can be used to analyze the hydrological regime variations caused by topographic adjustments at a full scale, and the amount of data required is significantly reduced, thus effectively alleviating the contradiction between rapid topographic adjustments in alluvial rivers and lakes and the difficulty of obtaining detailed topographic data. Under the constantly shifting topographic conditions of the Yangtze-Dongting system, the model developed in this study can be used as a simple but effective tool for the quantitative evaluation of hydrological regimes and provides a technical basis for flood disaster prevention, water resource management, and aquatic ecosystem protection.
1 Introduction Evapotranspiration (ET) is a fundamental process consisting of three main components: soil evaporation, vegetation transpiration, and interception evaporation. At a global scale, land surface ET represents approximately half of the incoming solar radiation and releases more than 60 % of terrestrial precipitation back into the atmosphere, making it a critical aspect of the land water cycle, second only to precipitation (Brustaert, 1986; L’vovich et al., 1990; Korzoun, 1978 ). ET plays a vital function in both the water and energy balance (Yao et al., 2017 ), making it a significant factor in climate change. Additionally, the soil and vegetation processes involved in ET and soil moisture transfer can affect crop physiological activities and yield, ultimately affecting ecosystem productivity (Beer et al., 2009 ). Therefore, the precise estimation of ET is of paramount importance for climate change research, ecological monitoring, and agricultural water management. In-depth research on the processes and mechanisms of ET along with accurate estimation technique is of great theoretical and practical value for exploring the global water cycle, regional climate change, improving agricultural water resource utilization efficiency, and promoting sustainable development. Flux observation sites can provide valuable long-term site-scale evapotranspiration data. However, due to their limited coverage, they cannot meet the needs of large-scale research (Sun et al., 2019; Friedrich et al., 2000 ). Fortunately, with the advancement of remote sensing technology, ET estimation methods based on remote sensing data have emerged in recent years. Empirical models utilize regression relationships between measured station evapotranspiration and factors such as temperature, net radiation of the land surface, vegetation index, and diurnal temperature range (Wang and Liang, 2008; Wang et al., 2007; Jackson et al., 1977 ), to estimate regional evapotranspiration. The empirical model is concise and easy to use. However, since the coefficients of the model depend on ground-measured data, these coefficients are only suitable for small-scale research. Surface energy balance models, on the other hand, use the surface energy balance equation to estimate evapotranspiration, which can be classified into single-source energy balance models and dual-source energy balance models. The single-source model does not distinguish between soil and vegetation, such as the Surface Energy Balance Algorithm for Land (SEBAL) (Bastiaanssen et al., 1998b; Bastiaanssen et al., 1998a ) and Mapping Evapotranspiration at High Resolution with Internalized Calibration (METRIC) (Allen et al., 2007 ). Single-source models often require calibration and are designed for small regions (Allen et al., 2011, Bhattarai et al., 2017, Timmermans et al., 2007 ). In areas with homogeneous vegetation coverage, a single source method may be applicable (Timmermans et al., 2007 ). The dual-source model calculates soil evaporation and vegetation transpiration separately, such as the S-W model (Shuttleworth and Wallace, 1985 ) and the N95 model (Norman et al., 1995 ). For heterogeneous terrain, the modeling of the dual source model is more realistic, but many researchers have found that compared to the single source model, the computational complexity of the dual source model does not improve much (McShane et al., 2017; Timmermans et al., 2007 ). The Penman-Monteith (PM) (Monteith, 1965; Penman, 1948 ) formula-based remote sensing evapotranspiration model is another critical tool for estimating evapotranspiration. Cleugh (Cleugh et al., 2007 ) incorporated MODIS measurements of leaf area index to estimate surface conductance, which facilitated the estimation of surface conductance over extensive regions. Mu (Mu et al., 2011; Mu et al., 2007 ) then improved upon Cleugh’s model and estimated global evapotranspiration. The Penman-Monteith-Leuning (PML) model (Leuning et al., 2008 ) expanded upon this by introducing a straightforward biophysical model for surface conductance, enabling the calculation of daily average evaporation. Subsequent PML series models (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016 ) incorporated carbon–water coupling to calculate gross primary productivity. Despite its strong physical mechanism, the PM model’s reliance on numerous parameters makes it challenging to accurately calculate through remote sensing (Yao et al., 2013 ). The Priestley-Taylor formula (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ) is a widely used method for estimating potential evapotranspiration that is further developed based on the PM model. With the introduction of a physical correction factor or modification of the PT parameters, potential evapotranspiration can be converted into actual evapotranspiration (Miralles et al., 2011; Fisher et al., 2008 ). To facilitate the remote sensing acquisition of PT model parameters, Yao et al. (2013)  proposed the MS-PT model, which introduced the diurnal temperature range as a substitute for relative humidity and vapor pressure difference. The PT model contains certain physical processes, requires fewer model-driven parameters for estimating evapotranspiration. Nonetheless, most existing evapotranspiration estimation models are either limited to small-scale areas or applied globally, and they rarely consider the unique characteristics of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) (Chang et al., 2018 ). The QTP is the world’s largest alpine ecosystem (Li et al., 2019 ), more than 50 % of it is covered by alpine grasslands (including alpine meadows and alpine steppes). These grasslands exhibit distinct ecosystem and climatic features (Chang, 2019; Zhang et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014 ) that are not well represented by existing models. Several studies have assessed the accuracy of different models for estimating ET in alpine grassland (Zhu et al., 2014 ) and found that all of the models have some limitations. Chang (Chang, 2019 ) found that at the station scale, the Priestley-Taylor method was the best for estimating evapotranspiration from alpine grasslands. Therefore, it is of great significance to improve the existing models to better suit the plateau. In terms of spatiotemporal analysis on the QTP, Song et al. (2017)  conducted an analysis of the spatiotemporal changes in evapotranspiration between 2000 and 2010 and found a significant decreasing trend, while Han et al. (2021)  found a slight decrease in evapotranspiration from 2001 to 2018. Wang (Wang et al., 2013 ) analyzed station meteorological data to study the reference evapotranspiration (ET0 ) pattern of the QTP, and observed an increasing–decreasing-increasing trend during the period from 1961 to 2010. Furthermore, their predictions for the period from 2011 to 2100 indicated a continuous increase in ET0  throughout the 21st century. These studies highlight the importance of understanding evapotranspiration dynamics on the plateau and the need for more refined and accurate models. Motivated by the unique vegetation composition and heterogeneity of the QTP, this study introduces the PT-SIMI (Shortwave Infrared Soil Moisture Index) model. This novel framework builds upon the established MS-PT model, aiming to enhance evapotranspiration estimations specifically within the QTP. The PT-SIMI model incorporates two key innovations: (1) An alternative methodology for calculating the fraction of green vegetation that addresses inaccuracies stemming from the QTP's diverse vegetation types. (2) A novel approach that integrates SIMI into soil moisture constraint calculations. This integration aims to rectify underestimations observed in the QTP, where significant diurnal temperature variations occur. The PT-SIMI model was then utilized to estimate the evapotranspiration over QTP from 2011 to 2020 and conduct spatiotemporal analysis. The results demonstrate that the improved model enhances the accuracy of evapotranspiration estimation on the QTP and offers a scientific foundation for water resource governance and ecological environment conservation of the QTP. The subsequent sections are structured as follows: Section 2  presents an overview of the study area and data sources, while Section 3  outlines the method used to improve the existing models and introduces our PT-SIMI model. Section 4  compares the performance of the PT-SIMI model with that of two other models. In Section 5 , the PT-SIMI model is applied to estimate evapotranspiration over the QTP from 2011 to 2020, and spatiotemporal analysis is conducted.
