The limitations of this study, environmental factors of evapotranspiration, and future research directions are discussed in Section 6 , while Section 7  offers the final remarks and conclusions derived from this research.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, an inland plateau situated in Asia, holds the distinction of being the highest plateau globally. It is renowned as the “roof of the world” and often referred to as “the third pole.”. It spans from 25° to 40° N and 73° to 104° E, with a general altitude of 3000–5000 m and an average altitude exceeding 4000 m (Fig. 1  ). The QTP exhibits distinctive features of the tundra climate (Beck et al., 2023 ), with strong radiation, low temperatures, and a distinct dry and wet season (Li et al., 2020, Ren et al., 2023 ). The plateau serves as a crucial water source for major Asian rivers, and lakes like Namco and Qinghai Lake provide essential water resources for millions of people, as well as playing a crucial role in downstream ecosystems and economic development. Alpine grassland prevails as the primary land cover type on the QTP (Fig. 2  ), this classification uses MODIS Land Cover Type (MCD12Q1) products (Friedl and Sulla-Menashe, 2022 ). These grasslands exhibit a high sensitivity to climate change and have demonstrated greater vulnerability to drought compared to other ecosystem types (Li et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014 ). Therefore, it becomes crucial to acquire a comprehensive understanding of the evapotranspiration process, specifically in alpine grasslands. Such understanding can facilitate the development of effective measures to preserve the water resources and ecological balance of the QTP.  2.2 Data 2.2.1 Remote sensing data MOD09GA is one of the surface reflectance products of MODIS, providing daily global surface reflectance data at a spatial resolution of 500 m. Covering visible and infrared bands, it can be used for monitoring vegetation cover, vegetation growth state, land use change, fire monitoring and other applications on land surfaces. At the same time, the product also provides a variety of quality control parameters to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the data. MOD09GA products are important data sources for remote sensing data analysis, land use planning, climate change, and ecological environment research. In this study, surface reflectance data were used to retrieve albedo and calculate biophysical constraints. Specifically, near-infrared and red band surface reflectance were employed to generate different vegetation indexes via surface reflectance composites.  2.2.2 Meteorological data ECMWF Reanalysis v5 (ERA5) is the most recent version of ECMWF's atmospheric reanalysis, providing a comprehensive analysis of the global climate (Bell et al., 2021; Hersbach et al., 2020 ). It provides daily and hourly climate reanalysis parameters. The ERA5 dataset, with its wide coverage and long-term series data, can well meet the needs of model input. Although the spatial resolution of this dataset is relatively low, studies have shown that coarse-resolution meteorological data does not significantly affect model performance (Cleugh et al., 2007; Leuning et al., 2008; Mu et al., 2007 ). The meteorological data used in this experiment include two distinct time durations: 2002–2017, which corresponds with the flux tower data, and 2011–2020, for estimating the ten-year period ET. It mainly includes air temperature (dewpoint temperature, daily maximum, minimum and mean, unit: K). The data were then utilized to calculate the relative humidity (RH), vapor pressure difference (VPD), diurnal temperature range (DT) and biophysical constraints for the Priestley-Taylor model.  2.2.3 Ground observed data To verify the retrieval accuracy of the model, four plateau flux tower sites provided by FLUXNET or ChinaFlux dataset (Delwiche et al., 2021; Pastorello et al., 2020 ) and three sites provided by the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC) (Ma et al., 2020 ) were selected as validation.(See Table 1  ). The four stations obtained by FLUXNET or ChinaFlux are CN-Hgu: Hongyuan, CN-Dan: Dangxiong, CN-HaM: Haibei Alpine Tibet site and CN-Ha2: Haibei Shrubland. And the three stations obtained by TPDC are BJ, SETORS, and MAWORS. The locations of the seven sites on the QTP are shown in Fig. 1 . Among them, the grassland sites are all alpine grasslands. Despite its ability to provide a continuous dataset, the eddy covariance method may experience gaps due to unfavorable meteorological conditions or instrument failures. In the FLUXNET dataset, considering the correlation between flux and meteorological variables, marginal distribution sampling (MDS) (Reichstein et al., 2005 ) was employed for gap filling, and daily latent heat data (W·m−2 ) with high quality (QC>0.8) was used in this study. For the TPDC dataset, access is limited to half-hour or hour-scale data, requiring conversion of half-hour data to daily-scale for analysis on these sites.    3 Methodology The primary emphasis of this research revolves around the evaluation of the Priestley-Taylor model’s applicability on the QTP. This section introduces three models: the Priestley-Taylor Jet Propulsion Laboratory (PT-JPL) Algorithm, the Modified Satellite-Based Priestley-Taylor Algorithm (MS-PT) and our improved model, the Shortwave Infrared Soil Moisture Index (SIMI)-Based Priestley-Taylor Algorithm (PT-SIMI). 3.1 Priestley-Taylor equation Priestley and Taylor (1972)  proposed a method to calculate the potential evapotranspiration of the underlying surface, which is called the Priestley-Taylor (PT) equation:(1) LE = α Δ R n  - G     Δ + γ        where, LE    is latent heat flux (W/m2 ), R n     is net radiation (W/m2 ),G    is soil heat flux (W/m2 ), α    is the PT coefficient of 1.26 (dimensionless), Δ    is slope of saturation-to-vapor pressure curve (kPa °C−1 ),γ    is the psychrometric constant (∼0.066 kPa °C−1 ).  3.2 Priestley-Taylor Jet Propulsion Laboratory (PT-JPL) algorithm In order to apply the Priestley-Taylor equation to the unsaturated underlying surface and obtain the actual evapotranspiration, researchers have explored the PT coefficient α, by modifying its value or incorporating constraints. For instance, Fisher et al. (2008)  developed a bio-meteorological methodology known as the PT-JPL algorithm. This algorithm divides evapotranspiration into canopy transpiration, soil evaporation, and canopy interception evaporation, and considers biological and meteorological limiting factors of evapotranspiration, such as vegetation index, relative humidity, temperature, and water vapor pressure difference. Furthermore, it establishes a physical correction term to convert the estimated potential evapotranspiration by Priestley-Taylor into actual evapotranspiration. The PT-JPL algorithm can be depicted as:(2) LE = L E s  + L E c  + L E i      (3) L E c  = 1 - f w e t      f g  f T  f M  α Δ Δ + γ   R nc       (4) L E s  = f w e t   + f S M   ( 1 -  f w e t      ) α Δ Δ + γ   ( R  ns   - G )      (5) L E i  = f w e t   α Δ Δ + γ   R nc        where, LEs   is soil evaporation, LEc   is canopy transpiration, LEi   is interception evaporation, Rnc   = R n  - R ns      is net radiation to the vegetation, Rns   = R  n   e x p ( -  k  R  n     LAI )    is net radiation to the soil, G  is soil heat flux (if unavailable, assumed to be zero), fwet   = RH4   is relative surface wetness, fSM  =  RH  VPD  β     is soil moisture constraint, fg   = f APAR   f IPAR      is green canopy fraction, fT   = e x p ( - T max   - T opt    T opt       2  )   is plant temperature constraint, fM   = f APAR   f APARmax      is plant moisture constraint, fAPAR   is fraction of PAR absorbed by green vegetation cover, fIPAR   is fraction of PAR intercepted by total vegetation cover, VPD is the vapor pressure deficit (kPa), β  = 1 kPa, Tmax   and Topt   is maximum air temperature and optimum plant growth temperature (25 ℃), respectively.  3.3 Modified Satellite-Based Priestley-Taylor algorithm (MS–PT) Based on the PT-JPL algorithm, Yao et al. (2013)  proposed a modified satellite-based Priestley-Taylor algorithm (MS-PT), incorporating constraints from the NDVI. The fraction of green vegetation in the scene (fv  ) is defined as:(6) f v  = NDVI - N D V I  min   NDVI  max   - N D V I  min         where NDVImax   = 0.95 and NDVImin   = 0.05 (Zhang et al., 2009 ). They also introduced diurnal temperature range (DT) to calculate soil moisture constraints, which showed a higher correlation with ground measurements.(7) f sm   = ( 1 DT   )  DT  D T max           where DTmax   = 40℃ (Yao et al., 2013 ). Rnc  , Rns   and G  were calculated as follows: Rnc   =R n  f v    ; Rns   =R n  ( 1 - f  v  )    ; and G =0.18 R  n  ( 1 - f  v  )    . The MS-PT model solves the difficulties of the PT-JPL algorithm in satellite calculation of RH and VPD, making it more convenient for satellites to calculate evapotranspiration.  3.4 Shortwave infrared soil moisture index (SIMI) based Priestley-Taylor algorithm (PT-SIMI) Although the MS-PT model has a high correlation with the ground measured data and performs well in most global sites, we found that it considerably underestimates evapotranspiration in the QTP (as shown in Fig. 3  ). Therefore, we examined the performance of MS-PT model using four sites in QTP and four other sites (CN-Cha: Changbaishan, a mixed forest site located in Jilin; CN-Cng: Changling, a grasslands site located in Jilin; CN-Qia: Qianyanzhou, an evergreen needleleaf forest site located in Jiangxi; CN-Sw2, a grasslands site located in Inner Mongolia). As shown in Fig. 3 , blue scatter points are sites not located on the QTP, while red scatter points are sites located on the QTP. Notably, the MS-PT model's estimations for evapotranspiration at plateau stations deviate from the 1:1 line, indicating a systematic underestimation of latent heat flux (LE). This discrepancy may be attributed to the QTP's unique characteristics, including the prevalence of alpine meadows with moist soil as the dominant vegetation cover, high altitude, and significant diurnal temperature variations. Current methods for calculating soil moisture constraints within the MS-PT model, as exemplified by Eq. (7) , often yield underestimated values due to large diurnal temperature variations (DT). This underestimation, in turn, affects the accuracy of evapotranspiration estimations. To address this limitation, revising Eq. (7)  or adopting alternative calculation methods better suited for quantifying soil moisture constraints in the QTP is crucial. Such revisions would enable a more precise evaluation of both soil evaporation and overall evapotranspiration components. In this study, we introduce the Shortwave Infrared Soil Moisture Index (SIMI) as a refined approach to calculating soil moisture constraints, aiming to overcome the underestimation of evapotranspiration observed in the MS-PT model when applied to the QTP. The SIMI is a simple and practical index based on the sensitivity of MODIS shortwave infrared band 6 and band 7 to water content (Yao et al., 2011 ),(8) SIMI = 0.7071 ρ 6  2  + ρ 7  2         where ρ 6     and ρ 7     are MODIS shortwave infrared band 6 and band 7, respectively. A strong negative correlation exists between the SIMI and ground-measured 0–10 cm averaged soil moisture (Yao et al., 2011 ). In order to ensure that the constraint is positively correlated with soil moisture and limit its value to 0–1, in this study, the soil moisture constraint is defined as:(9) f sm   = SIM I max   - S I M I  SIMI  max   - S I M I  min         where SIMImax   = 1, SIMImin   = 0. Concurrently, it should be noted that the maximum value of NDVI in the QTP seldom exceeds 0.95. Additionally, during the dry season, there are dead alpine meadows present in the QTP, which can still intercept a portion of the Rn , ultimately affecting the Rn  obtained by the soil. The fv   calculated by the MS-PT formula has little difference across the entire QTP. Therefore, it is imperative to properly adjust and optimize the calculation method in the model. Hence, we replace fv  , NDVI - N D V I  min   NDVI  max   - N D V I  min       to 1.16 ∗ N D V I - 0.14  1.0 ∗ N D V I - 0.05      (García et al., 2013 ).(10) f v  = 1.16 ∗ N D V I - 0.14  1.0 ∗ N D V I - 0.05        Formula 10 is only related to the NDVI within the same pixel, and is less affected by vegetation types, as it does not need to consider the applicability of maximum and minimum NDVI values in different regions.   4 Results 4.1 Model performance assessment The above three models were applied to the QTP using the Google Earth Engine platform, and the output LE estimated values were compared with the measured daily-scale LE data (W/m2 ) from ground observed data. To assess the accuracy of the models, statistical metrics such as the coefficient of determination (R2), mean bias, and root mean square error (RMSE) were employed.  4.2 Site-scale performance evaluation of PT-JPL, MS-PT and PT-SIMI The satellite-based evapotranspiration values are compared with the daily-scale data values of the flux tower (Fig. 4  ). The CN-HaM site has a significant amount of missing remote sensing data, primarily caused by cloud cover and other factors, resulting in limited simulated data from the model. Therefore, data from three years is plotted for this site, while data from only one year is used for other sites to improve the visibility of the figure. Statistical metrics to evaluate the model’s performance are shown in Table 2  . Overall, the predicted values of the three models demonstrate a comparable trend to the observed values, as illustrated in Fig. 4 . However, there are notable variations in deviation and accuracy across different sites. It is evident that the MS-PT model significantly underestimates the latent heat flux at the four locations on the QTP, as indicated by the scatter deviating from the curve of the observed values. On the other hand, the PT-JPL model exhibits a slightly higher trend than the observed line, while the PT-SIMI model falls in between the two. Table 2  reveals that the MS-PT model shows negative bias, indicating an underestimation of evapotranspiration at all seven sites, with an RMSE ranging from 26.39 to 47.43 W/m2 , which is substantially larger than that of the PT-SIMI and PT-JPL models. The PT-JPL model, in contrast, exhibited overestimation on most sites. The R2  values among the three models do not show substantial disparities. The PT-SIMI model performs the best at the grassland sites on QTP, with the bias closest to 0 and the smallest RMSE. However, at the Ha2 site, while the PT-SIMI model excels in terms of R2 , it does not outperform the PT-JPL model on this site, despite being better than the MS-PT model. This discrepancy may be credited to differences in land cover types, as the Ha2 site is a wetland site, characterized by a more unique and complex ecosystem than grasslands. Ultimately, the PT-SIMI model proved to perform better at alpine grassland sites.  4.3 Ablation study To assess the influence of the two modified components of the PT-SIMI model on the estimated latent heat flux value, this section examines the gradual removal of these components and compares the changes in the model output. The objective is to identify the elements that most affect the model output, so as to achieve a better understanding of the model’s functionality and limitations. The primary difference between PT-SIMI and MS-PT is the change in fv   and fsm  . In this section, we will individually alter one component of the MS-PT model. The model with a modified fv   component will be labeled PT-SIMIv , while the modification of the fsm   component will be denoted PT-SIMIm . The change in both will be recorded as PT-SIMI as described above. Overall, compared with the models PT-SIMIv and PT-SIMIm, which only modified one component, the PT-SIMI model with both components modified, showed significantly less Bias and RMSE.(see Table 3  ). However, this model presented a disadvantage at the CN-HaM site, where it had the highest R2 , even though there was no marked contrast in R2  among all sites. Regarding the modified components of the model, it was observed that in most sites, the benefits obtained by modifying only fsm   were greater than those obtained by modifying only fv  . This observation indicates that the MS-PT model is not suitable for describing soil moisture constraint in the QTP.   5 Qinghai-Tibet Plateau’s evapotranspiration spatial pattern and trend 5.1 Spatial pattern 5.1.1 Annual average and interannual variation The PT-SIMI model was applied to estimate evapotranspiration for the QTP during the period of 2011–2020, and the average annual evapotranspiration distribution for the 10-year period is shown in Fig. 5  . Overall, the evapotranspiration in the QTP exhibits a gradual decrease from the southeast to the northwest, aligning with the vegetation distribution pattern. There are more forests and lower elevations in the southeast, where the evapotranspiration is higher, with the highest annual evapotranspiration value exceeding 1000 mm/year. Moving northwest, vegetation coverage decreases, elevation increases, and climate zones change, all resulting in decreased evapotranspiration. The lowest annual evapotranspiration value was less than 200 mm/year. In addition, the lakes on the plateau, such as Qinghai Lake, also significantly contribute to evapotranspiration. By subtracting the ten-year average from the annual average LE distribution predicted by the model for 2011–2020, a difference map as shown in Fig. 6   is obtained. The data reveals that the evapotranspiration in the majority of QTP in 2011 and 2012 was lower than the ten-year average (red part), while in 2019 it surpassed the ten-year average (green part). Considering the correspondence between precipitation and evapotranspiration (Berg and Sheffield, 2019; Chai et al., 2022 ), this is consistent with the China Climate Bulletin (China Meteorological Administration, 2011; 2012; 2019 ), which declared that the national average precipitation in 2011 reached its lowest point in the previous 60 years, resulting in a severe drought in the southwest region. In contrast, the national precipitation was high in 2019, with some areas, such as Tibet and Qinghai, experiencing higher precipitation levels than in the same periods of history.  5.1.2 Seasonal average LE The seasonal LE estimates for QTP from 2011 to 2020 are mapped in Fig. 7  . The spatial distribution of LE exhibits significant seasonal differences. Overall, the distribution of LE in the four seasons is similar to the annual average, with less in the northwest and more in the southeast. In winter, due to low temperatures, precipitation and vegetation dormancy, the seasonal mean LE was the lowest. Only a few forest areas along the southwestern border maintained a relatively high evapotranspiration value, while most of the plateau areas had an evapotranspiration value of less than 40 W/m2 . Conversely, in summer, the evapotranspiration value was the highest, which was related to the high temperature, abundant precipitation, and dense vegetation growth. In most areas, the seasonal mean LE in summer reached 80 W/m2 , and some areas in the southwest were even higher than 120 W/m2 . The evapotranspiration rate in spring and autumn was between that of summer and winter, with slightly higher values in spring than in autumn.  5.1.3 Monthly average LE The spatial distribution pattern of monthly average evapotranspiration over the QTP from 2011 to 2020 is shown in Fig. 8  . The figure clearly illustrates that the spatial distribution of twelve-month LE bears resemblance to the annual distribution, with a higher value in the southeast and lower in the northwest. Among them, evapotranspiration from January to June showed a gradually increasing trend, mainly due to the gradual increase in temperature and the onset of vegetation growth. On the contrary, it continuously decreased from July to December. In general, the evapotranspiration during the months of Jan. to Mar. and Oct. to Dec. was relatively lower, with most areas experiencing values below 40 W/m2 . Conversely, during the months of April to September, evapotranspiration was generally higher, with most areas experiencing values above 60 W/m2 .   5.2 Theil–Sen estimator and Mann-Kendall' test of multi-year time series ET data 5.2.1 Annual First, the ten-year ET line chart of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau from 2011 to 2020 was drawn. The trend line chart is shown in Fig. 9  . As depicted in Fig. 9 , the annual mean evapotranspiration values during the period of 2011–2020 varied between 450 to 530 mm/year, with a ten-year average of 478 mm/year. The minimum value was recorded in 2012, while the maximum value was observed in 2019. However, there was a sharp decline in 2020, which corresponded to the distribution maps in Fig. 6 . To investigate the trend of evapotranspiration over the QTP from 2011 to 2020, both Sen estimator and Mann-Kendall test were employed. The calculated results revealed a slope of 1.55, an intercept of 463.40, and a p-value of 0.72, indicating evapotranspiration over the past decade has been relatively stable. Furthermore, Theil-Sen estimator and Mann-Kendall test were conducted to analyze the spatial distribution of evapotranspiration over the QTP from 2011 to 2020. The trend change in evapotranspiration is illustrated in Fig. 10  , while its significance level is presented in Fig. 11  . As illustrated in Fig. 10 , there was an increasing trend in ET observed in the central region of the plateau, particularly in the central and western parts. Conversely, a declining trend in ET was observed in the southeast region, where more forests are distributed. This highlights notable spatial disparities in the trends of ET across the plateau region. Statistical analysis revealed that pixels with an upward trend account for 60.74 % of the entire plateau area. However, only 11.35 % of these pixels showed a significant upward trend (p < 0.05), while an even smaller percentage of 2.35 % of the pixels showing a downward trend exhibited a significant downward trend (p < 0.05). This suggests that although the plateau presents a general trend of water increase, there is significant spatial heterogeneity in this trend, with low statistical significance.  5.2.2 Seasonal Fig. 12   shows the monthly distribution of evapotranspiration over the QTP during 2011–2020. The evapotranspiration in July was the largest, at 87.19 W/m2 , while the evapotranspiration in December was the smallest, at only 10.16 W/m2 . Evapotranspiration over the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau was lowest in winter, gradually increased in spring, reached its peak in summer, and then gradually decreased with temperature, rainfall and vegetation. Figs. 13 and 14    illustrate the variation trend and significance level of seasonal evapotranspiration over the QTP during the period of 2011–2020. In spring, an overall increasing trend in evapotranspiration was observed. During the summer, the trend of increasing and decreasing evapotranspiration was evenly distributed; in the western part of the QTP, there was a decreasing trend in evapotranspiration that was opposite to the annual trend. The Theil-Sen estimator indicated relatively smaller slopes, suggesting that the decrease in ET was small. Additionally, the decreasing trend during the summer was only significant in a small portion of the region. In autumn, the central and western regions of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau exhibited an upward trend in evapotranspiration, whereas the southwest forests exhibited a declining trend, with some regions experiencing a significant decline. However, in winter, there was more missing data, and the trend of evapotranspiration showed an increase in the north and midwest and a decrease in the south. From 2011 to 2020, the variation trend of evapotranspiration in spring, autumn, and winter in the QTP aligns with the annual variation trend, but the annual seasonal variation trend in most regions is not significant.    6 Discussion 6.1 Principal innovations and discoveries This study proposed the PT-SIMI model by introducing the Shortwave Infrared Soil Moisture Index into the calculation of soil moisture constraint, and modifying the parameter of the fraction of green vegetation in the scene. Based on the PT-SIMI model, the evapotranspiration of the QTP from 2011 to 2020 was estimated, and a spatiotemporal analysis was conducted. The results showed that the estimations generated via the PT-SIMI model were in strong agreement with the measured data on the ground and outperformed those of the MS-PT model and the PT-JPL model, especially in alpine grassland. The advantages of the PT-SIMI model are: (1) improved the soil moisture constraint, making it more sensitive to soil moisture change, and (2) the improved fraction of green vegetation in the scene in PT-SIMI model is not prone to extreme values, and is less affected by the type of ground objects. As for the estimated evapotranspiration, the spatial distribution pattern of ET on the QTP exhibited a declining trend from southeast to northwest (Feng et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2007 ). Although the methods used are different, the magnitude and spatial pattern of evapotranspiration are basically in line with previous studies (Shang et al., 2023; Han et al., 2021 ). In general, the distribution of LE in the four seasons is similar to the annual distribution, with lower values in the northwest and higher values in the southeast. However, the spatial distribution of LE displays distinct seasonal variations, with peak values occurring during summer and reduced values during winter (Yao et al., 2013 ). Regarding the change trend of the evapotranspiration of the QTP from 2011 to 2020, it was found that the evapotranspiration of the QTP was relatively stable during this period, and there were obvious spatial differences in the evapotranspiration of the QTP, with the central and western regions revealing an increasing trend and some regions showing a significant increase. Conversely, the central and southern forest areas showed a decreasing trend; although the majority of these regions did not exhibit a significant decrease, the trend is similar to the previous analysis using GLASS data (Cai et al., 2022 ).  6.2 The impact of input remote sensing data on model uncertainty Since the estimation of evapotranspiration relies on the retrieval of model parameters from remote sensing data, the use of different remote sensing data as inputs introduces uncertainties that affect evapotranspiration modeling. These uncertainties are mainly caused by the mismatch between the resolution of remote sensing data and the scale of ground stations, as well as the uncertainty of the algorithm for producing remote sensing products (Bai et al., 2018 ). On the basis of using MODIS modeling as input, we further explored the impact of replacing the input data with higher resolution Landsat data, comparing it with ground-based measured data, as shown in Fig. 15  . Despite the higher resolution of Landsat images, the discrepancy in the width of regression line confidence intervals is not obvious at most sites: except for the BJ and MAWORS sites, the confidence intervals of the models using Landsat images are not always narrower than those using MODIS. It is worth noting that Landsat has a long return period and less data available in the corresponding time period, which may not be conducive to direct comparison with ground-measured data. Nevertheless, using Landsat as input data, there is not much difference in R2  across different sites and, at some sites, even performs better. This difference reflects the impact of different input remote sensing data on model uncertainty, indicating that the adopted model has a certain robustness to variations in the input data.  6.3 Correlation analysis between evapotranspiration and environmental factors Understanding the complex interplay between evapotranspiration and environmental factors is crucial for accurately estimating and spatiotemporally analyzing actual evapotranspiration over the QTP. To this end, this section investigates the correlations between NDVI, precipitation, soil moisture (represented by SIMI), air temperature (Ta ), and annual average evapotranspiration (LE) across different land cover types (Fig. 2 ). As shown in Fig. 16  , it can be seen that there is a close relationship between different land use types and different environmental factors. Specifically, (1) the evapotranspiration of the water body shows the highest positive correlation with air temperature, while its correlation with precipitation, NDVI, and soil moisture is relatively small. This is because water body evapotranspiration mainly depends on water evaporation, so its relationship with air temperature is very close. (2) In grasslands, air temperature, precipitation, NDVI, and soil moisture are all positively correlated with LE, and the correlation between air temperature, soil moisture, and LE is the highest because soil moisture is closely related to soil evaporation, while air temperature not only affects soil evaporation but also affects vegetation transpiration. (3) Forests are different from other types because they have higher vegetation coverage, so the impact of air temperature on vegetation transpiration is more pronounced. (4) The main factor for bareland is soil moisture, as bareland has almost no vegetation, and the main evapotranspiration contribution comes from soil evaporation. The outcomes of the correlation analysis provide critical details for further refining the PT-SIMI model by offering an in-depth understanding of how different environmental factors influence evapotranspiration across varying land cover types. For example, customizing the model for specific land cover categories, such as forests and grasslands, could potentially enhance the accuracy of evapotranspiration estimates in the QTP.  6.4 Limitations and future research Despite the PT-SIMI model performed well in this experiment, there are still limitations that should be taken into account in future experiments.(1) This study has advanced our understanding of evapotranspiration in alpine grasslands on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, but some contents were simplified during modeling. For example, alpine grasslands were treated as a homogeneous category, despite the existence of numerous types with varying transpiration characteristics. Additionally, the potential impacts of grazing activities on vegetation and subsequent evapotranspiration were not taken into account. Furthermore, this study did not fully consider the effects of glacier and snow melting, as well as soil composition and characteristics on evapotranspiration. Future research endeavors could focus on developing new index and parameter calculation methods by integrating multi-band remote sensing data. This would facilitate a more accurate evaluation of the contributions of different grassland types, grazing activities, glaciers, and soil factors to evapotranspiration processes.  (2) Surface reflectance data is severely missing, requiring high-quality data interpolation for reconstruction. Significant data gaps occur after cloud removal processing, rendering areas with missing data unable to estimate evapotranspiration. This not only poses challenges in assessing the accuracy of evapotranspiration models but also make it difficult to obtain mature evapotranspiration products.  (3) Flux observation data is insufficient, and more data is needed for ground validation. Currently, there are relatively few flux towers on the QTP, with even fewer publicly available data. Although this study used seven flux observation sites, they could not fully represent the entire region due to the extensive expanse of the QTP. Additionally, the land cover type of the sites used is mainly alpine grassland, while the QTP has a complex ecosystem. Therefore, the accuracy of the model with excellent performance in alpine grassland sites on other land cover types needs to be further verified by experiments.  (4) High-resolution evapotranspiration products are not achieved. Future research could consider applying downscaling or image fusion algorithms in combination with the PT-SIMI model to obtain high spatiotemporal resolution evapotranspiration products.      7 Conclusion Based on the unique characteristics of the QTP, this study has proposed the PT-SIMI model by improving the MS-PT model. The PT-SIMI model considers the soil moisture constraint and fraction of green vegetation in the scene, and has developed an evapotranspiration retrieval model that is more suitable for QTP, and provides high-precision estimation results. The verification results based on ground measured data show that the PT-SIMI model is better suited for the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau than the MS-PT model and PT-JPL model at most sites. The study found that the average evapotranspiration over the QTP from 2011 to 2020 was 478 mm/year, with a spatial distribution pattern that exhibited a decreasing trend from southeast to northwest. The evapotranspiration in 2019 was the highest, reaching nearly 530 mm/year, while it was relatively lower in 2011, 2012 and 2017. The central and western regions of the plateau showed an increasing trend in evapotranspiration, with some areas showing a significant increase. However, the central and southern parts of the forest area demonstrated a decreasing trend, although most of the decrease was not significant. These findings suggest that there are significant spatial differences in evapotranspiration values over the QTP. As for the correlation between evapotranspiration and environmental factors, the impact of air temperature on evapotranspiration is dominant in the water body, grassland and forest, while the effect of soil moisture is more significant in the bareland and grassland. Future research should consider adding flux tower data from different land cover types to verify the PT-SIMI model. Given the wide coverage of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the model's excellent performance in alpine grassland sites on other land cover types needs to be further verified through experiments. Additionally, future studies may consider the application of downscaling or image fusion algorithms, combined with the PT-SIMI model, to obtain evapotranspiration products with high spatiotemporal resolution. 1 Introduction Hydrological modeling has been instrumental in advancing flood forecasting, managing water resources, and comprehending climate change and ecosystem functions (Donnelly et al., 2022, 2024a; Singh, 2018 ). Uncertainty in hydrological modeling is a significant and inherent aspect that arises from various sources throughout the modeling process (Beven, 2016 ). Quantifying and reducing predictive uncertainty arising from data errors and model misspecification is an ongoing challenge in hydrology (Blöschl et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021a ). The most common approach to describe predictive uncertainty is to use residual error models that assume the difference between observation and simulation aggregates all sources of uncertainty (Li et al., 2021a; McInerney et al., 2017; Quilty et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2015; Tyralis & Papacharalampous 2023 ). It has long been known that autocorrelation, heteroscedasticity, and non-Gaussianity exist in hydrological residual errors (Bates & Campbell, 2001; Kuczera, 1983; McInerney et al., 2020; Papacharalampous et al., 2020; Sorooshian & Dracup, 1980 ). How to properly characterize these issues is the key to yielding reliable and accurate streamflow predictions (Smith et al., 2015 ). Autocorrelation is routinely captured by the p th order Autoregressive (AR(p )) models or more general Autoregressive Moving Average (ARMA) models (Bates & Campbell, 2001 ). Li et al. (2021a)  proposed a probabilistic Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) as a residual error model, and demonstrated that LSTM was able to reduce the autocorrelation of the remaining errors due to its intrinsic memory architecture, which can not be achieved by a more rigid Markov order 1 characterization. Heteroscedasticity can be roughly addressed by two strategies: (1) transformational strategy and (2) conditional strategy (McInerney et al., 2017 ). In the transformational strategy, function transformations such as logarithm, Box-Cox (Box & Cox, 1964 ), Log-sinh (Wang et al., 2012 ), wavelet transformation (Jiang et al., 2020 ), and others are used to stabilize the error variance after transforming the observation and simulation. In the conditional strategy, the error variance is commonly conditioned on streamflow magnitude and/or other related variables (e.g., rainfall). Linear regression is a commonly used method to model the relationship between the magnitudes of streamflow and their error variance. It has been criticized for leading to unstable error models with unreliable and inaccurate predictive performance (Evin et al., 2013; Schoups & Vrugt, 2010 ,). A Gaussian distribution, which is often assumed for random errors in residual error modeling, rarely holds in hydrology, although suitable transformations can help make errors more Gaussian-like (Beven et al., 2008; McInerney et al., 2017 ). To account for the assumption of non-Gaussian errors, a Student’s t  distribution (Marshall et al., 2006 ), a mixture of Gaussian (Li et al., 2016, McInerney et al., 2021; Schaefli et al. 2007 ) and a Skewed Exponential Power (SEP) distribution (Schoups & Vrugt, 2010 ) have been proposed to address skewness and/or kurtosis in errors. However, the predictive ability of residual error models may be limited by the assumed variances of the various distributions, which either remain constant or vary linearly with streamflow magnitude. Thus, integrating non-Gaussian errors with non-linearly varying variances is worth investigating, while still challenging in hydrological error modeling. Recently, deep learning gained widespread prominence in hydrology due to its advanced architecture and significant flexibility (Jahangir et al. 2023, Zou et al. 2023, Song 2022, Kao et al. 2020, Razavi 2021, Shen et al. 2023, Shen 2018, Kao et al. 2021 ). However, while most research has focused on providing deterministic predictions, few studies have embarked on quantifying uncertainty and offering probabilistic predictions in deep learning (Althoff et al., 2021; Donnelly et al., 2024b; Shen et al., 2021 ). Fang et al. (2020)  employed Monte Carlo dropout to account for the uncertainty of model weights for LSTM networks in soil moisture predictions. Li et al. (2021b)  suggested Monte Carlo dropout is not a suitable Bayesian approach to provide reliable posterior distributions. Therefore, they proposed variational Bayesian inference to model the uncertainty of LSTM weights in streamflow predictions. Klotz et al. (2022)  applied three Mixture Density Networks (MDNs; Bishop, 1994 ) with different kernel distributions and a Monte Carlo dropout technique to LSTM networks and compared their performances for uncertainty estimation in rain-runoff modeling. They directly applied these models in streamflow predictions and indicated that the MDN approach provided better uncertainty estimates than the Monte Carlo dropout. It is noted that MDN combining a neural network with a mixture density model can predict the conditional probability distribution of the response (Bishop, 1994 ). Besides, any continuous probability distribution can be approximated closely by a finite mixture of Gaussian according to the universal approximation theorem (McLachlan et al., 2019 ). Recent studies have directly examined the ability of MDN to improve uncertainty estimates for streamflow predictions (Klotz et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). However, a deep understanding of the specific properties of streamflow captured by MDN, extending beyond its predictive capabilities, remains empty. Besides, they often set a fixed number of mixture components (e.g., three) in MDN depending on the modelers’ experiences, which may harm the performance of the model. There is no common rule to choose the optimal number of mixture components as so many hyperparameters (e.g., number of layers, number of hidden units) exist in neural networks which complicates the problem. In this study, we introduce a novel residual error model that enhances the accuracy and reliability of streamflow predictions in distributed hydrological modeling by integrating a hydrological model with MDN networks. MDN is utilized to generate a conditional probability distribution that captures the heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussian nature of residual errors. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance of MDN characterizing the properties of hydrological residual errors. The proposed model was tested using synthetic data that mimic the properties (i.e., heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussian) of residual errors, and subsequently demonstrated in a real catchment. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2  presents descriptions of Mixture Density Networks and model selection criteria. Sections 3 and 4  describe the synthetic data and a real catchment, and implement the proposed model. Sections 5 and 6 present the discussion and conclusions of this study, respectively.  2 Methodology 2.1 Residual error models In a reduced form, a hydrological model to predict streamflow can be cast as(1) y t  = f θ ∼  , x ∼  t    + e t  ,  t = 1 , ⋯ , N       where y t    is the observed streamflow value at time step t  , f ( ∙ )    is the modeled streamflow value in a hydrological model with the input data vector x ∼  t    and the parameter vector θ ∼   , e t    is the residual error or the difference between observation and simulation, and N  is the length of observed data. The residual e t    is believed to contain all sources of errors (e.g., data errors, model structural errors, and model parameter errors) in hydrological residual error modeling (Evin et al., 2014; Schoups & Vrugt, 2010; Smith et al. 2015 ). Many studies have shown that the mean and variance of the residuals are conditioned on streamflow magnitudes and depend on their own previous values (Bates & Campbell 2001; Evin et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2019; Schoups & Vrugt, 2010 ). A non-zero mean, non-constant variance, and autocorrelation of the residual properties reflect the predictions of hydrological models are biased, heteroscedastic, and persistent, respectively. Let the selected predictors (e.g., streamflow magnitude, previous residuals) be X = [ x 1  , ⋯ , x N  ]  ∈ R  K × N      with K   predictors in a regression model. The conditional distribution of e t    given x t  ∈ R  K     is p ( e t  | x t  )   , which is often a non-Gaussian distribution (Li et al., 2016; Marshall et al., 2004; McInerney et al., 2021; Schoups & Vrugt, 2010 ). The goal of a residual error model is to approximate a conditional distribution p ( e t  | x t  )    that is a non-Gaussian distribution with non-linear time-varying statistical features (e.g., mean and variance) given input data x t   . In this study, we focus on modeling heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity of residual errors, and will show how to develop a residual error model using a mixture density network in the next section. Fig. 1   illustrates the structure of mixture density networks-based residual error models with three mixture components.  2.2 Mixture density networks Mixture density networks were developed by Bishop (1994) . It is a general framework for modeling conditional distributions, in which neural networks combine a mixture of distributions (e.g., Gaussian) (Bishop, 2006 ). Here, using an MDN model, the conditional density distribution of the residual e t    given the selected predictors x t    can be expressed as(2) p e t  | x t    = ∑ i = 1  M  w i , t   x t   ϕ e t  | θ i , t   x t           with:(3) ∑ i = 1  M  w i , t   x t   = 1 ,     0 ≤ w  i , t   x t   ≤ 1       where M   denotes the number of mixture components, w i , t   x t       is the mixing weight for the i  th     kernel ϕ ∙      at time step t  . The kernel function ϕ ∙      can be any type of parametric density distribution, and is governed by a vector of parameters θ i , t   ( x t  )  ∈ R  D     (e.g., mean and variance) with the number of parameters D  . In MDN, the parameters w i , t   , θ i , t       are time-varying values given x t    and are generated by the outputs of neural networks. In contrast, traditional mixture distribution models, such as Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA; Hoeting et al., 1999 ), typically assume that certain parameters (e.g., weights and variance) are constant values estimated using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm across all data (Raftery et al., 2005 ). In this study, a Gaussian distribution is used as the kernel function ϕ ∙      since it is a mathematically convenient and commonly used distribution with long use in nonparametric kernel density estimation techniques (Sharma et al., 1997 ). Then, θ i , t   x t     can be further expressed as μ i , t   , σ i , t  2      with the mean μ i , t   x t       and the variance σ i , t  2  x t       of Gaussian distributions. Thus, mixtures of Gaussians with time-varying parameters w i , t   , μ i , t   , σ i , t  2      given x t    are generated by MDN. However, the parameters cannot be directly outputted by the neural networks, so constraints should be taken. Therefore, the parameters w i , t   , μ i , t   , σ i , t  2      can be constrained by(4) w i , t   = exp z i , t , 1     ∑ i = 1  M  exp z i , t , 1        μ i , t   = z i , t , 2     σ i , t  2  = ln 1 + e x p z i , t , 3      + ∊        where the vector z t  = z i , t , j     1 ≤ i ≤ M , 1 ≤ j ≤ 3   ∈ R  M × 3      are the direct outputs of the neural networks at time step t  . A Softmax function and a Softplus function are used to constrain the values of w i , t     and σ i , t  2   , respectively. A minimum value ∊   (e.g., 10  - 6    ) is applied to the Softplus function for numerical stability (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2016 ). The Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) criterion used as a loss function for neural networks can be written as:(5) NLL = - ∑ t = 1  N  ln ∑ i = 1  M  w i , t   x t   g e t  | μ i , t   x t   , σ i , t  2  x t             where g ( ∙ )    represents a Gaussian distribution. The loss function NLL enables a conventional neural network to capture predictive uncertainty that cannot be achieved by common loss functions (e.g., Mean Square Error). Once the conditional density distribution p e t  |  x t       is obtained, we can further calculate some quantities of interest. The conditional mean and the conditional variance of p e t  |  x t       can be calculated as(6) E t  x t   = ∑ i = 1  M  w i , t   x t   μ i , j   x t         (7) s t 2  x t   = ∑ i = 1  M  w i , t   x t   σ i , t  2  x t   + ∑ i = 1  M  μ i , t   x t   - ∑ j = 1  M  w i , t   x t   μ i , t   x t     2           where E t  x t       and s t  2  x t       represent the conditional mean and the conditional variance of p e t  |  x t      , respectively; the index i   or j   denotes the i t h    or j   th mixture component.  2.3 Model selection The number of mixture components (as a hyperparameter) should be determined before training an MDN. However, the number heavily depends on the modelers’ experiences (Klotz et al., 2022; Peel & McLachlan 2000; Zhou et al. 2020 ). In this study, we use the control variable method to explore this problem, which means only the number of mixture components is not fixed. Then, to select the appropriate number, two popular model selection criteria, the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974 ) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978 ) were tested. AIC and BIC can be calculated by(8) AIC = 2 K - 2 In L ^   = 2 K + 2 N L L  ^        (9) BIC = K In N  - 2 In L ^   = K In N  + 2 N L L  ^        where K   is the total number of neural networks’ parameters, including weights and biases, in MDN; N   is the length of data, L ^    is the maximized value of the likelihood function, and 2 N L L  ^     is the minimized value of the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) function. Note that the structural difference between traditional neural networks and MDN is only the last fully connected layer. The number of parameters in the last fully connected layer for traditional neural networks is N hidden   + 1   , while it is 3 M ∙ N hidden   + 3 M    in MDN. When increasing one mixture component, K   will add 3 N hidden   + 3   . N hidden     is the number of hidden units in the neural networks. Both AIC and BIC penalize the number of parameters in the model and make a trade-off between model prediction and model complexity. The lowest value of the criterion is preferred.  2.4 Model assessment To assess the performance of probabilistic models, several popular metrics including Reliability, Sharpness, and NLL (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007 ) are considered in this study. Reliability refers to the proportion of observations covered by the predictive distribution in a specific prediction interval; Sharpness is a property of the predictive distribution and is the width of the predictive distribution in a specific prediction interval. Reliability and Sharpness are commonly used together. NLL is an overall metric of probabilistic predictions and is used in a negative orientation. It is calculated based on the predictive PDF (Probability Density Function). Detailed information about these metrics can be found in the previous literature (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007 ).  2.5 Model setup MDN is a flexible probabilistic framework that can be integrated into any neural network. Thus, based on MDN, a probabilistic model MDN-LSTM is built using a deep learning network LSTM. As a benchmark, a similar model MDN-ANN is also built using a traditional network ANN. The LSTM was manually set as a single LSTM layer with 50 hidden units and a fully connected layer; the ANN was set as a single layer with 100 hidden units. The calibration data was used to calibrate the MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM models, and the remaining data were used to validate their predictions. Two forms of regularization techniques, early stopping (Bishop, 2006 ), and dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014 ), were simultaneously applied to avoid overfitting of the neural networks. In light of implementing early stopping, the calibration data set was partitioned in a 70:30 ratio, with the former subset serving as the training data for the neural networks, and the latter subset being utilized to halt the training process. The dropout rate was set as 0.1, which is a common value in machine learning. A popular and improved gradient-based optimization algorithm Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014 ) was implemented to train the neural networks. We used the default hyperparameters of Adam in this study: ρ = 0.001   , β 1  = 0.9   , β 2  = 0.999   , ∊ = 10  - 8     . The maximum epochs of training were set as 1,000.  2.6 Case study Both synthetic data and real catchment data were used to evaluate the performance of two proposed models, MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM. We generated synthetic data in a stepwise manner embodying characteristics typical of residuals, including heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity, to deepen the understanding of the predictive capabilities of the MDN-based model. Then, we applied the real catchment data to further demonstrate the model’s capabilities. (1) Synthetic Data. The MDN-based residual error model is proposed to characterize the heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity of residual errors seamlessly in this paper. We generate three synthetic data sets that mimic the features of residual errors using three commonly used equations: LHO  (a L inear function with a HO moscedastic Gaussian distribution of errors); LHE  (a L inear function with a HE teroscedastic Gaussian distribution of errors); HEM  (a nonlinear function with a HE teroscedastic non-Gaussian distribution (i.e. M ultimodal distribution) of errors). The synthetic data sets of LHO, LHE, and HEM are separately generated by(10) y t  = 10 x t  + ε t  ,    ε t  ∼  N 0 , 1         (11) y t  = 5 x t  + ε t  ,    ε t  ∼  N 0 , x t          (12) y t  = ± x t 2  + ε t  ,    ε t   ∼ N 0 , x t           where x t    in Equations (10) and (11)  ranges from 0 to 10, and x t    in Equation (12)  uniformly ranges from −10 to 10. The predictor samples are uniformly generated from x t    by sorting the sampled data with a sample size N =    2,000. The response data generated in Equations (10)–(12)  has the features of Gaussianity/non-Gaussianity and homoscedasticity/heteroscedasticity. Therefore, these synthetic data can be used to evaluate the capabilities of the MDN-based model. (2) Real Catchment Data. MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM were applied to model distributed hydrological residual errors in the Source of the Yellow River (SYR), China. The hyperparameters of neural networks were configured to be the same as those utilized in the synthetic data application. The study explored and extended Li et al. (2021a)  to properly characterize the properties of the errors. In Li et al. (2021a) , a distributed, physical-based hydrological model MIKE SHE was used to simulate daily streamflow for the periods of warm-up (1992–1994), calibration (1995–2010), and validation (2011–2015) in the SYR catchment. As shown in Fig. 2  , the residual errors of MIKE SHE exhibited heavy autocorrelation, heteroscedasticity, and non-Gaussian attributes. Here, the proposed two probabilistic neural networks were employed to capture the complex properties of the residual errors, utilizing four predictors that consisted of 3-day antecedent precipitation and three simulated variables from MIKE SHE (namely, soil moisture, streamflow, and one-step lag residuals). These predictors were consistent with those used in the prior investigation.   3 Results 3.1 Application to synthetic data We tested the two proposed probabilistic models, MDN-LSTM and MDN-ANN in the synthetic data. The first 1,500 synthetic samples were used as the calibration data and the remaining samples were used as the validation data. The detailed model settings can be found in Section 2.5. Each model was calculated with four different numbers of mixture components: “0com ”: the model is neural networks (ANN or LSTM) with a zero mean and constant variance of Gaussian error, operating independently of an MDN framework; the neural networks are optimized using the Adam optimizer with an MSE loss function, and the error variance is estimated with a Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) method. “1com ”, “2com ” and “3com ”: the MDN models have one, two, and three mixture, respectively. Table 1   shows the number of parameters in MDN-LSTM and MDN-ANN. Neural networks in MDN-LSTM and MDN-ANN have different structures and complexities. For different sets of components, the number of parameters for MDN-LSTM ranges from 10,652 to 11,059, whereas for MDN-ANN, it ranges from 302 to 1,109, an order of magnitude smaller. The effects of neural networks within an MDN framework can be evaluated in the synthetic data. Intuitively, the 0com, 1com, and 2com models are expected to be the ideal model for the three synthetic data sets, LHO, LHE, and HEM, respectively. Next, we will verify our assumption through analyzing the results. Table 2   and Table 3   show the performance of MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM with different numbers of mixture components tested in the three synthetic data. Overall, only the AIC can select the “true” number of mixture components in all three synthetic data; the models including MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM with the “true” number of mixture components can provide the best performance measured by NLL in the validation period. Compared with AIC, BIC only works well for the data sets of LHO and LHE. For HEM, BIC chooses the model with 1 mixture component as optimal, which is evidently not correct considering the NLL values of the validation and the true underlying processes. Specifically, although the 1com models of MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM display minimum BIC values of 2,357 and 74,032, respectively, their NLL values of −242 and −185 are higher than those of the 2com mode, which are −427 and −357 during the validation period. This suggests a potential misidentification of the model. In addition, we can find that overly complex models worsen the model performance in terms of the NLL values in validation. For instance, for LHE, using a model with more than one mixture component is redundant and has a larger NLL value than a model with one mixture component; MDN-LSTM always has a worse performance with larger values of NLL than MDN-ANN. Fig. 3   shows the comparison of synthetic data and MDN-ANN’s predictive distribution. MDN-ANN with a suitable number of mixture components produces good coverage of the synthetic data. For HEM, 0com (i.e. a model with a constant variance of Gaussian error) cannot capture the heteroscedastic and bimodal distribution; 1com (i.e. a model with one mixture component) only captures heteroscedasticity and ignores the bimodal distribution; 2com and 3com can capture the heteroscedastic and bimodal distribution well. MDN-LSTM has a similar predictive distribution with MDN-ANN and thus is not plotted here.  3.2 Application to a real catchment Table 4   lists the performance of MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM with various numbers of mixture components in the SYR catchment. The AIC model selection criterion identified both neural networks with two mixture components as optimal, with values of −4,034 and 16,048, respectively. This aligns with the probabilistic metric NLL, which shows the best values of −1,354 and −1,389 during the validation period among the various sets of components, respectively. Compared with AIC, BIC yields divergent outcomes. Specifically, BIC identifies one mixture component as the optimal setting for MDN-ANN, with a value of 1,486, while two mixture components are deemed optimal for MDN-LSTM, with a value of 88,718. However, MDN-ANN with a single mixture component only achieves an NLL value of −1,123 during the validation period, which is not the best NLL value among the four sets of components. This suggests that BIC may lack stability and accuracy in identifying the appropriate number of mixture components. Similar conclusions are also illustrated in the synthetic data application. Thus, it can be demonstrated that AIC is more suitable for determining the number of components. When comparing the performance of MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM, it has been observed that the MDN-LSTM consistently yields lower values for the NLL metric. Fig. 4   shows probabilistic streamflow predictions with a 90 % prediction interval for MDN-LSTM in the validation period. We present hydrographs exclusively generated by the MDN-LSTM model with zero (0com) and two mixture components (2com), as the hydrographs produced by 1com and 3com are analogous visually to those generated by 2com. It can be found in Fig. 4  that the 0com model significantly overestimates low-flow (i.e., below the 10th percentile) uncertainty and underestimates high-low (i.e., above the 90th percentile) uncertainty while 2com can provide reasonable uncertainty bands, as demonstrated by the metrics of Sharpness and Reliability presented in Table 5  . For an optimal prediction, the Reliability value should be closer to 90 % with a smaller Sharpness value in a 90 % prediction interval. When comparing 0com and 2com, the 2com model’s intervals are, on average, approximately 20.98 % and 76.22 % narrower, providing more accurate or equal uncertainty coverage for all flows and low flows, respectively; for high flows, while the 2com model has larger uncertainty intervals (i.e., 326 m3 /s) than the 0com model (i.e., 143 m3 /s), its uncertainty coverage nears 90 %, signifying enhanced reliability. Thus, the 2com model offers flexibly wide uncertainty intervals for large flows and narrow uncertainty intervals for low flows. In the study by Li et al. (2021a) , they yielded a 117 m3 /s of uncertainty intervals with a 91.12 % of uncertainty coverage for all flows. We can find that the 2com model can produce narrower uncertainty intervals (i.e., 113 m3 /s) with similar uncertainty coverage. Checking residual error assumptions is an essential step in validating the plausibility of model predictions, as shown in Fig. 5  . Autocorrelation, heteroscedasticity, and non-Gaussianity for residual errors are detected with plots of the Sample Partial Autocorrelation Function (SPAF), scatterplots, and Quantile-quantile (QQ) plots, respectively. Overall, while all models exhibit comparable performance in terms of reducing autocorrelation, LSTM with an MDN framework demonstrates superior capability in capturing heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity compared to the 0com model that assumes Gaussian errors. Specifically, the scatters of the residuals tend to fan out and are covered well by changing predictive distributions generated by MDN-based models. The 0com model only provides static predictive distributions and cannot cover low and high flows. Besides, MDN-based models provide much straighter lines in the QQ plots than 0com. This means a conditional mixture of Gaussian distribution is more appropriate to describe the distribution of residual errors in MIKE SHE, as compared to a Gaussian distribution. To gain a deep understanding of the prediction behaviors, the weights of individual mixture components in MDN-LSTM are displayed in Fig. 6  . MDN with 5 mixture components (5com) and 10 mixture components (10com) are also computed to investigate weight changes arising from augmented model complexity. The weights show evident seasonality analogous to streamflow. Distinct weights exhibit differential activation patterns, with selecting masses engaged during periods of flow rising whilst others become operative during times of receding streamflow. This may imply that MDN-based models possess the ability to capture certain physical characteristics of hydrological processes.   4 Discussion Deep learning has gained widespread prominence in hydrology research and commonly uses the Mean Square Error (MSE) as a loss function for regression tasks. The premise underlying the utilization of such a loss function posits that the data remains stationary and adheres to a Gaussian distribution, as per the conventions of statistical analysis (Bishop, 2006; Liu et al., 2022 ). However, residual errors generated by streamflow modeling exhibit complex heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity, representing the presentence of nonlinear shifts in variance and shape over varying magnitudes of streamflow (Bates & Campbell, 2001; McInerney et al., 2021; Schoups & Vrugt, 2010 ). Thus, we proposed an MDN-based residual error model that can generate conditional mixture density to characterize the properties of residual errors. Two MDN-based residual error models, MDN-ANN and MDN-LSTM, were investigated in synthetic data and catchment data. Our results show that standard neural networks with an MSE loss function (i.e., 0com) cannot produce reasonable results when violating its inherent Gaussian assumptions. In comparison, MDN-based models effectively capture characteristics, including heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity in the residual errors, yielding better probabilistic streamflow predictions. When the MDN employs LSTM as its backbone, it can also eliminate autocorrelation in the residual errors due to LSTM's memory-dependent architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this approach, for the first time, guarantees uniform consideration of all characteristics in the hydrological residual errors. However, MDN-based models are not suitable when the residual errors are close to a Gaussian distribution. This observation highlights the importance for the modeler to thoroughly assess the presence of heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity within the data, prior to employing MDN techniques. Prior research, such as that by Evin et al. (2013)  and Schoups & Vrugt (2010) , primarily used linear regression models. In contrast, our model establishes a non-linear relationship between streamflow magnitudes and their error variance, providing increased flexibility across varied catchment scenarios. Compared with standard neural networks, MDN-based models by modifying loss function lead to extra tasks of selecting the appropriate number of mixture components. Prior studies have predominantly relied on expert experiences to directly ascertain it, without employing an automated approach (Klotz et al., 2022; Peel & McLachlan, 2000; Zhou et al., 2020 ). We initially tested two model selection criteria, AIC and BIC. The results show that AIC can always choose the model with the best model performance over the validation period while BIC lacks this capability. The reason could be that AIC imposes less penalty on the number of model parameters and is more sensitive than BIC. With the increasing number of mixture components, the redundant components tend to “switch off” with the corresponding small parameters (e.g., weights shown in Fig. 6 ). Note that hyperparameters such as numbers of hidden units, and layers, should be fixed when using AIC or BIC.  5 Conclusion In this study, we present novel residual error models that combine a neural network with a mixture density model to generate conditional mixture distributions. The proposed models were tested in synthetic data and catchment data and demonstrated their superiority in capturing heteroscedasticity and non-gaussianity of residual errors. The model selection criterion AIC is more effective in determining the optimal number of mixture components than BIC. Our study encourages applying mixture density networks for residual error modeling, integrating a hydrological model with probabilistic neural networks to enhance hydrological predictive performance. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to use the model for characterizing heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity. The proposed model, capable of generating time-varying mixture distributions, also holds potential for addressing non-stationary weather and water issues in a changing environment. Some limitations may exist in our study. Firstly, as only a single catchment is tested for the proposed model, a large number of catchments (e.g., hundreds) will be collected to enhance our conclusions. Secondly, instead of CPU, GPU can be expected to accelerate the training speed. Thirdly, the proposed model can be further enhanced by integrating with Variational Bayes (Blei et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021b, 2022 ) to account for the parameter uncertainty in the weights and biases of neural networks, which was not considered in our research. Lastly, the efficacy of BIC may be limited to a low number of mixture components, as determined in this study to be three or fewer. When the optimal number of mixture components is very high (e.g., ≥ 10   ), the usefulness of this conclusion remains uncertain and warrants further exploration.
1 Introduction Anthropogenic climate change (ACC) accelerates the global water cycle, leading to more frequent extreme climate events (Allan et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 2006 ) and compound extreme events (Mukherjee et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2023; Zscheischler and Lehner, 2022 ). Recently, the successive runoff-heat extremes (SRHE) events, i.e., the occurrence of an extreme runoff event followed by a heatwave event within 7 days (Chen et al., 2021 ), have attracted widespread research attention due to their serious impacts on human society and ecosystems (Gu et al., 2022; Liao et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ). For example, Japan suffered a successive flood-heat extreme event in 2018 caused by heavy rainfall from Japanese summer monsoon, which lasted for about one week and followed by rapid temperature rising and drying due to the Northwestern Pacific Subtropical High, resulting in 300 deaths and 10-billion U.S. dollar loss (Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Relative to the single extreme event, such compound extreme events have caused higher risks on human society due to the superposition of time urgency and extreme (Leonard et al., 2013; Ridder et al., 2020 ). Extreme runoff events destroy buildings and other structures, paralyzing the power grid, and the subsequent heatwaves may prevent vulnerable groups from using air conditioning and other facilities (Clark et al., 2019; Kayaga et al., 2020 ). The outbreak and spread of diseases also endanger the health of the vulnerable group (Baqir et al., 2012; Basagaña et al., 2011 ). The urgency of compound extremes makes it difficult for global countries to restore and adjust its infrastructure system within a short period of time, often resulting in the superimposed serious risks (AghaKouchak et al., 2018 ). Along with global warming, the SRHE events have occurred more frequently in many regions of the world (Gu et al., 2022; Liao et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Chen et al. (2021)  indicated that the probability of SRHE occurrence after 2000 in southern, northwestern, and northeastern China has increased about 5–10 times than that during 1961–1980. Khan et al. (2023)  also found the increasing probability of the compound extreme heat and precipitation events from 1950 to 2010 in the Upper Midwestern United States, especially in Iowa (+10.1 %), northern Illinois (+5.04 %), and Michigan (+5.04 %). The SRHE occurrence is related to the land-atmospheric feedback mechanisms, tropical cyclones/anticyclones, and atmospheric circulation (Chen et al., 2021; Chen and Zhai, 2017; Chiang and Sobel, 2002; Satoh et al., 2011 ). Anthropogenically intensified climate warming has increased surface temperature and water vapor and enhanced the convective available potential energy. Collectively these factors lead to the increasing extreme precipitation and heatwave occurrence, providing a favorable condition for SRHE occurrence (Ning et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2022; You and Wang, 2021; Zhang and Villarini, 2020 ). The alternation of tropical cyclones and anticyclones, and the rapid movement of wind and pressure bands, also increase the probability of extreme precipitation and high temperatures (Favre and Gershunov, 2006; Hobgood, 1986; Walker, 2012; Wang et al., 2019 ). The attribution of extreme events is important for disaster risk management and climate change adaptation (Otto et al., 2015 ). The commonly used climate change attribution methods include the optimal fingerprint method and the event attribution method (Zhai et al., 2018 ). The optimal fingerprint method uses the spatiotemporal modal response of simulated climate system to determine whether the signals match observations, and eliminates the noise interference from the internal variability by maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio and enhancing the signal characteristics of climate change (Allen and Stott, 2003; Hasselmann, 1993; Ribes et al., 2013 ). The event attribution method quantifies the probability or magnitude of the human (−induced) or natural factors in influencing event occurrence, usually by using the Fraction Attributable Risk (FAR) and Probability Ratio (PR) indices (Stott et al., 2016; Stott et al., 2004 ). Mounting evidences have shown that ACC has driven the occurrence of extreme temperature and precipitation, and increased the risk of water disasters (Chen and Sun, 2017; Engdaw et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2020; Pall et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2020 ). Some studies focused on quantifying the anthropogenic signals in the changing compound extreme event occurrence. Aihaiti et al. (2021)  analyzed the warm and wet events in CMIP6 future simulations by using PR, and found that the mean risk of the warm-wet events in China can respectively increase by 5.5 and 10.0 times under 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming. Zhang et al. (2022)  based on the PR method indicated that ACC has increased the risk of compound dry and hot events during 1951–2010 across the global land (especially in tropics) except for part of Eurasia and North America. Based on the results of historical single-forcing simulation, Chiang et al. (2022)  indicated that greenhouse gases alone have amplified the natural frequency of warm-dry events by 1.5–5 times and the warm-humid events by 2–9 times across tropical and extratropical regions. Wang et al. (2023)  evaluated the 2020 record-breaking SRHE event in China by the storyline attribution method, and found that the ACC exacerbated the extreme precipitation in the mid-lower reaches of the Yangtze River during June–July 2020 (∼6.5 %) and warmed the co-occurring seasonal extreme heat in South China (∼1°C). Recent advances have been made in SRHE projections based on CMIP5 and CMIP6 data (Gu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023 ), with the main findings that the global future risk of SRHE will intensify especially in the tropical, east Asia, and Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Gu et al., 2022; Liao et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Based on the ISIMIP (the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project) model simulation data, our recent study (Zhou et al., 2023 ) evaluated the projected changes and uncertainties in global SRHE characteristics and population exposure, and quantified the contributions of flood and heatwave frequency to SRHE frequency during the twenty-first century. Results show that ACC is expected to exacerbate the future SRHE risk, but with the significant uncertainty in model projections. However, little attention in previous studies has been paid to the attribution of historical SRHE occurrence and its changing characteristics during the past several decades of warming, which is fundamental to understand SRHE risks under climate change, reduce model projection uncertainty, and guide disaster mitigation of the SRHE events. Here, we evaluate globally the impact of ACC on the characteristics and probability of SRHE occurrence during 1950–2014 based on the “anthropogenic and natural both (ALL)” and “natural only (NAT)” experiments based on the simulation data of five GCMs in CMIP6. Attribution analyses of SRHE risk with different durations and different intervals between extreme runoff and heatwave (IRH) are conducted over the global land by using FAR. The objectives of this study are to (1) evaluate the change in the long-term mean SRHE characteristics (frequency, IRH, duration) caused by ACC; (2) evaluate the anthropogenic signals in the trends of SRHE characteristics; and (3) quantify the impact of ACC on the risk of SRHE occurrence with different durations and IRHs. In the following, Section 2  describes the CMIP6, the fifth-generation of European Center for Medium Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) reanalysis product (ERA5) and the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) data used in this study and introduces SRHE and the statistical methods used in this study. The results of the spatio-temporal change and trend estimation in SRHE characteristics caused by anthropogenic and natural forcings, as well as the attribution of SRHE with different characteristics, are presented in Section 3 . The discussion and conclusions are presented in Sections 4 and 5 , respectively.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Data In this study, the 1950–2014 global gridded daily near-surface (2 m) maximum temperature (Tmax  ), minimum temperature (Tmin  ), and total runoff data are obtained from five GCMs (see Table 1  ) participating in CMIP6 (https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/ ). The five GCMs are chosen because each of them has three available realizations [r(1, 2, 3/4)i1p1f1] of the daily Tmax  , Tmin   and runoff driven by both ALL and NAT simulations from 1950 to 2014 (Table 1 ). The [r(1, 2, 3/4)i1p1f1] refers to three realizations or ensemble members (r1, 2, 3/4) from NAT and ALL forcings of five CMIP6 models under the same conditions of initialization method (i1), physics (p1), and forcing (f1). The “ALL” simulation is forced by both anthropogenic (e.g., human emissions of greenhouse gases, aerosols and ozone, changes in land cover use) and natural (e.g., volcanic and solar activities) factors, while the “NAT” simulation is forced solely by natural factors. Comparisons of ALL and NAT simulations reflect the impact and sensitivity of ACC on SRHE occurrence and characteristics. In this study, all five GCM data are resampled to 1°×1° grids over global land using the linear interpolation method. In order to reduce the uncertainty in each GCM, we use the arithmetic mean of three realizations [r(1, 2, 3/4)i1p1f1] to extract the SRHE events globally at 1° grid land areas except the Greenland and Sahara regions (where only few extreme runoff events are identified throughout the year). The daily data of Tmax   and Tmin   from ERA5 (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ ) are used for validating daily Tmax   and Tmin   in the ALL simulations of the five selected CMIP6 GCMs. Since the ERA5 data started in 1950 and both ALL and NAT simulation data ended in 2014, the 1950–2014 is chosen as the study period. ERA5 is a global climate reanalysis dataset released by the ECMWF (Bell et al., 2021; Hersbach et al., 2020 ), which provides the global data of atmospheric, surface, and ocean variables. This dataset is selected in this study due to its high spatial (0.25°×0.25°) and temporal (1 h) resolution from 1950 to the present and its wide applications in meteorological and hydrologic studies (Dullaart et al., 2019; Gleixner et al., 2020; Yilmaz, 2023 ). The daily runoff data from GLDAS (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/ ) are used for validating daily runoff in the ALL simulations of CMIP6 GCMs. GLDAS is the NASA land modeling system to produce the optimal fields of land surface states and fluxes in near-real time using advanced land surface modeling and data assimilation techniques (Kumar et al., 2016; Rodell et al., 2004 ). In this study, the GLDAS daily runoff data from 1950 to 2014 driven by the Catchment-based Land Surface Model (CLSM) are chosen, since only CLSM directly outputs daily runoff data among the land surface models used. All the ERA5 and GLDAS data are resampled to 1°×1° grids over global land using the linear interpolation method to match the spatial resolution of GCM data.  2.2 SRHE event In this study, a SRHE event is defined as the occurrence of an extreme runoff event followed by a heatwave event within 7 days (Chen et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2021 ). The extreme runoff and heatwave events are extracted at the grid scale using the peak-over-threshold approach (Bezak et al., 2014; Caissie et al., 2019 ), which quantifies the occurrence of extreme events from the probabilistic perspective and takes into account climate differences between different regions (Dodangeh et al., 2019; Rahmani et al., 2016; Tramblay et al., 2019; Wasko et al., 2021 ). An extreme runoff event is considered when daily runoff depth (i.e., the daily cumulative depth of water caused by precipitation) exceeds the 99th percentile for each grid (Wrzesien and Pavelsky, 2020; Yin et al., 2018 ). A heatwave event is defined as the daily Tmax   or Tmin   exceeds the 95th percentile, which lasts for at least three consecutive days (Guerreiro et al., 2018 ). For comparison purpose, we use the same thresholds in ALL and NAT for extracting the extreme runoff and heatwave events, which are estimated from the NAT simulation during 1950–2014 (Fig. S1 ).
